Christianity is not dead people being taught to behave more respectably.
It is God giving life.
You do not need Jesus merely to improve your old life.
You need new life.
And the Holy Spirit is essential because regeneration—being born again—is the work of God, not the achievement of human determination.
Paul writes that God saved us “through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).
That destroys spiritual pride.
You cannot stand before God someday and say:
“I resurrected myself.”
“I purified my own heart.”
“I conquered sin sufficiently to earn salvation.”
“I made myself acceptable.”
No.
The Gospel removes boasting because salvation belongs to God.
The Father purposes salvation.
The Son accomplishes redemption through His death and resurrection.
The Spirit applies God's saving work, giving life, dwelling in believers, sanctifying them, and conforming them to Christ.
One God.
Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Not three gods.
Not one Person changing costumes.
The historic Christian confession recognizes the biblical revelation of one God in three distinct divine Persons.
And notice something else.
The Holy Spirit does not come to make Himself the center of a personality cult.
Jesus said of the Spirit:
“He will glorify me” (John 16:14).
That is one of the safest biblical tests for supposedly “spiritual” Christianity.
Does it glorify Jesus Christ?
Does it lead toward truth?
Does it produce repentance?
Does it make sin more comfortable—or expose it?
Does it make people obsessed with personalities, platforms, manifestations, and status—or does it make Christ increasingly precious?
The Spirit of God magnifies the Son of God.
This is why the Holy Spirit will never lead you into something contrary to the character and truth God has revealed in Scripture.
The Spirit who inspired the Word does not contradict the Word.
And sometimes His work in us hurts.
Because the Comforter is also holy.
We often want comfort without conviction.
Healing without confession.
Freedom without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without surrender.
But when God loves you, He does not merely soothe everything that is destroying you.
He confronts it.
Jesus said concerning the Spirit:
“When he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment” (John 16:8).
Conviction and condemnation are not identical.
Condemnation says there is no hope.
Gospel conviction exposes sin so that sinners may see their need and flee to Christ.
The Spirit does not expose your darkness because Jesus enjoys humiliating broken people.
He brings sin into the light because Christ came to save sinners.
There is a difference between being exposed for destruction and being exposed for surgery.
A surgeon opens a wound because healing requires reaching what is underneath.
Perhaps that explains why certain passages of Scripture have bothered you.
Why a sermon followed you home.
Why you could not enjoy the sin afterward the way you enjoyed it before.
Why something inside you kept whispering:
“This is not who Christ is calling you to be.”
Maybe you thought God had abandoned you because you were uncomfortable.
What if some of that discomfort was mercy?
David prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10).
That prayer came after scandal.
After lust.
After adultery.
After deception.
After devastating sin.
David did not need public-relations management.
He needed mercy.
He needed cleansing.
He needed God.
And perhaps somebody reading this has a scandal nobody knows about.
Not necessarily a scandal that would become tomorrow morning’s headline.
Maybe yours lives inside your browser history.
Your private messages.
Your marriage.
Your imagination.
Your bitterness.
Your pride.
Your hidden addiction.
Your jealousy.
Your secret compromise.
Your resentment toward God.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well spiritually.
But you know.
And God knows.
That realization can feel terrifying.
But this is where the Gospel becomes unbelievably beautiful.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had successfully cleaned itself.
He came because we could not.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).
Not the impressive.
Not the spotless.
Not those who finally got everything together.
The ungodly.
Christ bore sin on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose bodily from the grave.
And forgiveness is offered not because sin is insignificant but because the sacrifice of Christ is sufficient.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who paid what you could never pay.
This is our story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But grace does not mean Jesus leaves us unchanged.
The same grace that forgives begins transforming.
And again, the Holy Spirit is essential.
Paul writes:
The Greek verb translated “walk” is περιπατεῖτε — peripateite.
It carries the ordinary image of walking, and figuratively it describes the way a person conducts life.
Not visit the Spirit occasionally.
Walk.
Step after step.
Monday morning.
Tuesday afternoon.
Friday night when temptation becomes loud.
Sunday after church.
At work.
In traffic.
Behind the closed door.
When you are praised.
When you are rejected.
When nobody would discover what you are about to do.
Walk by the Spirit.
This does not mean Christians become instantly incapable of sin.
Galatians itself describes conflict between flesh and Spirit.
The Christian life includes warfare.
But hear this carefully:
Struggle is not permission to surrender.
You may be fighting something you thought you would have conquered years ago.
Do not make peace with it.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Seek appropriate help and accountability.
Keep returning to Christ.
Depend upon the Spirit.
There may be somebody reading these words with tears in their eyes because you are tired of promising Jesus that “this was the last time.”
Do not confuse your inability to conquer sin through sheer willpower with permission to continue sinning.
And do not confuse your struggle with proof that Christ has no power to transform you.
You need something stronger than shame.
You need the Holy Spirit.
Because biblical transformation is more than learning to suppress bad fruit.
God changes the tree.
Galatians calls the result “the fruit of the Spirit”:
“love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).
Notice Paul calls it fruit.
Fruit grows from life.
You can tape plastic apples onto a dead tree, but you have not made the tree alive.
And Christianity can become exactly like that when we try to manufacture holiness for appearances.
Plastic patience.
Plastic kindness.
Plastic church smiles.
Plastic “God is good” answers.
Plastic spirituality.
Meanwhile, behind the leaves, the tree is dying.
The Spirit produces something real.
He transforms people increasingly into the likeness of Christ.
Paul describes believers as being transformed “from one degree of glory to another,” adding, “this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).
Transformation is often slower than our impatience would prefer.
But God is not merely making you look religious.
He is forming Christlike character.
Sometimes that formation happens through suffering.
And that may be where this becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe your biggest question is not:
“Why can’t I stop sinning?”
Maybe it is:
“Where was God when my world collapsed?”
Where was God when the marriage broke?
When someone betrayed you?
When the person you prayed for still died?
When the door remained closed?
When your child walked away?
When depression-like darkness seemed to settle over your days?
When you begged for an answer and heaven seemed silent?
Romans 8 does not pretend believers never hurt.
It tells us creation groans.
Believers groan.
And astonishingly, the Spirit meets us in that groaning.
Paul writes:
The Greek verb translated “helps” is remarkable: συναντιλαμβάνεται — synantilambanetai.
It carries the idea of taking hold together with someone against a burden.
Picture that.
Your weakness does not automatically repel the Spirit.
In the believer’s weakness, He helps.
Paul continues:
“For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us…” (Romans 8:26).
Have you ever hurt so deeply that prayer became almost impossible?
You opened your mouth.
Nothing.
No beautiful sentence.
No theological vocabulary.
Just tears.
Maybe silence.
Maybe one broken word:
“Jesus…”
Romans 8 says your inability to construct an impressive prayer does not mean God has abandoned you.
The Spirit helps believers in weakness.
That means some of your holiest moments may not have sounded holy at all.
They may have sounded like crying.
And Romans 8 goes further.
Those who belong to Christ receive the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry:
“Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15).
Paul preserves the Aramaic word אַבָּא — ʾAbbā in Greek letters as Ἀββᾶ.

It is a deeply relational address for father, but it should not be reduced to the simplistic claim that it merely means “Daddy.” Its significance in the New Testament is profound: through Christ and by the Spirit, believers are brought into a genuine filial relationship with God.
You were not merely rescued from something.
In Christ, you were brought into something.
A family.
Adoption.
Belonging.
The Spirit “bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16).
Somebody needs that tonight.
Because your earthly father may have failed you.
Maybe “father” is not automatically a safe word in your memories.
Maybe the person who should have protected you wounded you.
Maybe abandonment taught you to expect everyone eventually to leave.
And without realizing it, you began projecting human failure onto God.
But the Father revealed by Jesus is not a larger version of the person who wounded you.
Through Christ, by the Spirit, believers are welcomed as God's children.
And when you fall?
The Spirit does not teach you to run away from Jesus and hide behind fig leaves.
He leads you toward the truth of the Gospel.
Confess.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Remember whose blood cleanses sinners.
Remember who your Advocate is.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that Jesus is still Jesus when you are ashamed of yourself.
This does not trivialize sin.
It makes grace astonishing.
The Holy Spirit is also essential because Christianity is not merely about surviving until heaven.
Christ sends His people into the world.
Before His ascension, Jesus told His disciples:
“You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses…” (Acts 1:8).
Then came Pentecost.
The frightened became witnesses.
The Gospel crossed boundaries.
Christ was proclaimed.
The church moved outward.
And this is important because the Spirit’s power was never given merely to make Christians feel powerful.
Power was connected to witness.
Jesus must be proclaimed.
People need the Gospel.
Your family needs the Gospel.
Your friends need the Gospel.
The coworker everybody avoids needs the Gospel.
The person silently falling apart while posting smiling photographs needs the Gospel.
The skeptic needs the Gospel.
The lukewarm churchgoer needs to hear Christ clearly.
The person convinced they are too dirty for God needs to hear about the cross.
The religious person convinced they are good enough without grace needs the Gospel too.
And perhaps this article is not supposed to end with you.
Maybe someone came into your mind while you were reading.
Someone struggling.
Someone hiding.
Someone grieving.
Someone drifting from Jesus.
Someone pretending everything is okay.
Do not automatically dismiss that person from your mind.
Send this privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, be honest.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer sees and realizes:
“I am not the only one fighting.”
Not because every sentence will feel equally urgent today.
There may be a morning when shame returns.
There may be a temptation when Galatians 5 needs to be opened again.
There may be a season when you need to remember that Christianity was never supposed to be powered by your flesh.
And please understand this clearly:
Following a page does not make anybody a disciple of Jesus.
Sharing a Christian article does not earn favor with God.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent of sin, endure suffering, and grow in biblical truth, supporting this work can be one practical way of helping Gospel-centered resources continue reaching others.
Not because you can purchase His blessing.
Not because clicking a button proves your faith.
But because faithful ministry requires people who care enough about spreading biblical truth to help carry it forward.
One share can travel somewhere you cannot.
One tag can reach someone you did not know was struggling.
One honest comment can give another believer courage to stop hiding.
One saved article can become a reminder on a difficult night.
And one person encountering the truth of Jesus is worth more than another piece of content disappearing silently into a feed.
But before you leave, there is one final question.
Not:
“Have you ever felt the Holy Spirit?”
Not:
“Can you explain every theological debate about spiritual gifts?”
Not:
“Have you ever had an extraordinary spiritual experience?”
The deeper question is:
Do you belong to Jesus Christ?
Paul says something uncompromising:
“Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).
That is why the Holy Spirit is essential for every Christian.
There is no biblical category called Christianity without the Spirit.
He gives life.
He indwells believers.
He points us to Christ.
He convicts concerning sin.
He sanctifies.
He produces fruit.
He strengthens.
He helps us in weakness.
He assures believers of adoption.
He equips Christ's people for service.
He empowers witness.
And through His work, Jesus is glorified.
Maybe you came into this article asking why you need the Holy Spirit.
Maybe the more uncomfortable question is whether you have been attempting to live Christianity without depending upon Him.
Trying to defeat flesh with flesh.
Trying to manufacture holiness.
Trying to heal yourself.
Trying to carry grief alone.
Trying to perform your way back into God's affection.
Trying to become strong enough that you no longer need grace.
You will never graduate from needing grace.
That is not failure.
That is Christianity.
Come back to Jesus.
If there is sin, confess it.
If there is rebellion, repent.
If there is pride, surrender it.
If there is shame, bring it into the light of the cross.
If you have never trusted Christ, do not hide behind religion.
Turn to Him.
The scandal of your sin does not have the authority to write the final chapter when the crucified and risen Christ becomes your Savior and Lord.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted His church.
The Corinthian believers had histories filled with sins Paul could name openly—yet after listing them, he wrote words that still sound like thunder against hopelessness:
“And such were some of you.”
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Were.
That little word carries a graveyard inside it.
There are things grace can turn into past tense.
Not because your past never happened.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because Christians become instantly flawless.
But because your worst chapter does not have to become your identity.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
Jesus Christ saves.
And the Holy Spirit takes people who could never manufacture spiritual life inside themselves and makes them alive in Christ.
So when the enemy points backward and whispers,
“Look what you were,”
the Gospel teaches the redeemed to look toward Christ and answer:
“Look what Jesus has done.”
Share that truth.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
And comment something honest—not something impressive.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Maybe your comment becomes confession.
Maybe somebody replies with prayer.
Maybe your share reaches a prodigal.
Maybe somebody scrolling alone at 2:00 in the morning discovers that the God they have been running from is still calling them toward repentance, mercy, and life in Jesus Christ.
Because this was never ultimately about making Gospel Warrior bigger.
It is about making Jesus known.
And if God has entrusted us with a screen, a voice, a platform, a resource, or an opportunity, may we use it faithfully for the glory of Christ.
The Spirit does not come merely to make you feel something for a moment; He makes alive those who belong to Christ so that Jesus can transform what sin tried to make the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE NEVER HEARD JESUS SPEAK?
paragraphs:
“MY SHEEP HEAR MY VOICE”—BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE NEVER HEARD JESUS SPEAK?
What John 10:27 Really Means, How Christ Leads His People, and Why Every Christian Must Learn the Difference Between the Shepherd’s Voice and the Voices Inside Their Own Head
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that has comforted millions of Christians.
It has also quietly terrified some of them.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27
Beautiful words.
Until you are sitting alone at two in the morning, Bible open, heart exhausted, asking a question you are almost ashamed to admit:
“Jesus… if I am really one of Your sheep, why can’t I hear You?”
Maybe you have watched other Christians say things with astonishing confidence.
“God told me.”
“The Lord spoke to me.”
“Jesus said this was the person I should marry.”
“God told me to quit.”
“God told me to move.”
“God gave me a word for you.”
And somewhere underneath your polite smile, another thought appeared.
What about me?
Why does God apparently speak so clearly to everyone else?
Maybe you prayed.
You waited.
You listened.
Nothing.
No audible voice.
No supernatural whisper.
No sentence suddenly appearing inside your mind.
Just silence.
And eventually the silence began accusing you.
Maybe my faith is weak.
Maybe God is disappointed in me.
Maybe I am spiritually deaf.
Maybe I am not actually one of His sheep.
But what if the problem is not that Jesus has abandoned you?
What if part of the problem is that Christians sometimes use the phrase “hearing God’s voice” in ways that are much broader than the way Jesus is using it in John 10?
Because when Jesus said,
“My sheep hear my voice,”
He was not handing Christians a technique for receiving secret messages.
He was revealing something infinitely deeper.
He was revealing the relationship between the Shepherd and the people He saves.
And when you understand what Jesus actually said, one of the most confusing phrases in modern Christianity becomes one of the most beautiful promises in the Gospel.
The Greek text of John 10:27 reads:
“Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.”
Transliterated:
Ta probata ta ema tēs phōnēs mou akouousin, kagō ginōskō auta, kai akolouthousin moi.
“My sheep hear/listen to My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me.”
Notice the movement.
My sheep.
My voice.
I know them.
They follow Me.
Jesus is describing belonging, recognition, relationship, and discipleship.
The Greek verb translated “hear” is ἀκούω — akouō.
It can mean to hear, listen to, or pay attention to what is spoken. Context determines the nuance.
And the context matters enormously.
Jesus had already painted the picture earlier in the chapter.
“The sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.” — John 10:3
Then:

“And when he putteth forth his own sheep, he goeth before them, and the sheep follow him: for they know his voice. And a stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers.” — John 10:4–5
Jesus is using shepherd imagery.
The sheep belong to the shepherd.
They recognize the shepherd.
They trust the shepherd.
They follow the shepherd.
And then Jesus takes the metaphor somewhere breathtaking.
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11
Suddenly the passage is no longer primarily about your ability to detect spiritual impressions.
It is about Jesus.
The Shepherd.
The One who knows His sheep.
The One whose sheep belong to Him.
The One whose sheep recognize and follow Him.
And ultimately…
the Shepherd who dies for them.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity does not begin with your ability to hear God.
Christianity begins with a God who came looking for sinners.
You were not wandering through the wilderness successfully tuning your spiritual frequency until you finally discovered Jesus.
Jesus came for the lost.
Jesus called sinners.
Jesus laid down His life.
Jesus rose again.
Jesus saves.
And His sheep respond to their Shepherd.
But there is another detail in John 10 that makes Christ’s statement even more powerful.
Immediately before verse 27, some of the Jewish leaders demand:
“If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly.” — John 10:24
Jesus responds:
“I told you, and ye believed not.” — John 10:25
Then He says:
“But ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep.” — John 10:26
And only then:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27
The immediate contrast is not between Christians who receive private revelations and Christians who do not.
The contrast is between unbelief and the people who recognize, receive, and follow Jesus.
They were standing physically close enough to hear Jesus’ audible voice.
Their ears worked perfectly.
Yet they did not believe.
That should stop us.
Because apparently a human being can hear the sound of Jesus’ physical voice…
and still fail to truly “hear” the Shepherd.
So whatever John 10:27 means, it cannot simply mean detecting audible sound.
There is a deeper hearing.
A hearing that receives Christ.
A hearing that recognizes Him for who He is.
A hearing that produces following.
Jesus says something similar elsewhere:
“He that is of God heareth God’s words.” — John 8:47
And again:
“Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice.” — John 18:37
This is why we must be careful with one popular Christian assumption.
“My sheep hear My voice” does not mean every Christian is promised a continuous stream of individualized, extra-biblical sentences from Jesus.
God certainly can communicate however He chooses.
Scripture records dreams.
Visions.
Angelic messages.
Prophetic revelation.
Audible speech.
Providential guidance.
The Holy Spirit directing particular servants.
We should never reduce Almighty God to a formula and announce what He is incapable of doing.
But neither should we promise believers something the text itself does not promise.
And that distinction can rescue somebody from years of unnecessary spiritual anxiety.
Because perhaps you have been waiting for Jesus to speak while ignoring the place where He has unquestionably spoken.
Scripture.
The Bible is not God’s old voice.
It is not the spiritual equivalent of yesterday’s newspaper while Christians search for something newer and more exciting.
Jesus Himself repeatedly treated Scripture as authoritative.
When Satan tempted Him in the wilderness, Jesus answered:
“It is written.”
Again:
“It is written.”
Again:
“It is written.”
The incarnate Son of God did not treat written revelation as spiritually inferior.
Neither should we.
Paul writes:
The Greek word in 2 Timothy 3:16 is extraordinary:
θεόπνευστος — theopneustos.
It means “God-breathed.”
Scripture is God-breathed.
Paul continues that Scripture is profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
Think about that.
Some Christians desperately ask God for a word while their Bible remains closed.
They want direction but avoid doctrine.
They want whispers but resist commands.
They want revelation without repentance.
They want God to tell them whom to marry while ignoring what He already said about holiness.
They want God to reveal their destiny while refusing to forgive the person they hate.
They want God to confirm their dreams while avoiding Christ’s call to deny themselves.
And sometimes what we call “I can’t hear God” actually means:
“I don’t like what He has already said.”
That sentence hurts.
Because I have done it too.
It is easier to search for a mysterious spiritual impression than to obey a clear biblical command.
A mysterious voice might tell me something exciting.
Scripture might tell me to repent.
A mysterious voice might tell me I am entering my breakthrough season.
Scripture might tell me to forgive my enemy.
A mysterious voice might flatter my plans.
Scripture might crucify my pride.
And suddenly the real question becomes uncomfortable.
Do I want God to speak…
or do I want God to agree with me?
Because those are not the same thing.
This is where spiritual discernment becomes desperately important.
Not every thought in your head is God.
Not every coincidence is a divine instruction.
Not every powerful emotion is the Holy Spirit.
Not every dream is prophetic.
Not every open door means “go.”
Not every closed door means “stop.”
Not every person who says “God told me” was actually told something by God.
Human beings have desires.
Fears.
Memories.
Trauma.
Biases.
Imaginations.
Expectations.
And Scripture warns us that deception is real.
This is why John tells believers:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.” — 1 John 4:1
Notice that biblical faith does not demand gullibility.
It demands discernment.
Paul similarly writes:
Test.
Examine.
Hold fast to what is good.
Christian maturity is not believing every spiritual-sounding impression.
Christian maturity is increasingly learning to submit everything to the truth God has revealed.
So how does Jesus actually speak to His people?
First and foundationally, Christ addresses us through the Scriptures that testify about Him.
Jesus said of the Scriptures:
“They are they which testify of me.” — John 5:39
After His resurrection, on the road to Emmaus, Jesus did something astonishing.
Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He interpreted the Scriptures concerning Himself.
The Bible is not a collection of inspirational quotations centered on you.
Its great storyline leads us to Christ.
Creation.
Fall.
Promise.
Covenant.
Sacrifice.
Kingdom.
Prophecy.
Incarnation.
Cross.
Resurrection.
Church.
New creation.
Jesus stands at the center.
And when the Holy Spirit opens our understanding of Scripture, He does not lead us away from Christ into spiritual fascination with ourselves.
He glorifies Christ.
Jesus Himself said of the Spirit:
“He shall glorify me.” — John 16:14
That is an enormously important test.
Because there is a kind of spirituality that constantly talks about “God” while strangely making the individual the center of everything.
My destiny.
My promotion.
My breakthrough.
My enemies.
My prophetic word.
My season.
My blessing.
My platform.
My success.
But the Holy Spirit’s ministry is profoundly Christ-centered.
He convicts.
He teaches.
He reminds Christ’s disciples of Jesus’ words.
He glorifies the Son.
He forms Christlike fruit in believers.
So when you wonder whether something is from God, ask whether it agrees with Scripture and leads toward the character, truth, holiness, love, humility, and lordship of Jesus Christ.
God will never “lead” you to commit adultery.
God will never “tell” you to abandon biblical truth.
God will never “reveal” that Jesus is unnecessary.
God will never contradict His own holy character.
The Holy Spirit does not compete with the Word He inspired.
But what about impressions?
Convictions?
A strong sense that you should call someone?
An unexpected burden to pray?
A persistent thought about serving somewhere?
A circumstance that seems providential?
Christians from different theological traditions understand these experiences differently, and we should acknowledge that rather than pretending every faithful believer explains them identically.
Some Christians believe particular gifts of revelation continue today.
Others believe certain revelatory gifts belonged uniquely to the apostolic era.
Faithful Christians have debated these questions for generations.
But believers across those differences can affirm something crucial:
No personal impression has the authority of Scripture.
And no impression should be treated as permission to contradict Scripture.
This means humility should become part of our vocabulary.
Instead of carelessly saying,
“God told me you need to marry that person,”
perhaps we should sometimes say,
“I have a strong impression about this, but I could be wrong. Please test it against Scripture and seek wisdom.”
That sentence contains something desperately missing from much modern spirituality.
Humility.
Because claiming divine authority for our personal thoughts is serious.
If I say, “I think…”
you can disagree with me.
But if I say, “God told me…”
I have placed enormous pressure on your conscience.
I have effectively put God’s name behind my opinion.
That should make every Christian careful.
Especially pastors.
Teachers.
Parents.
Spouses.
Leaders.
Influencers.
Anyone with spiritual authority.
Never use “God told me” to control someone.
Never use Jesus’ name to manipulate another person into doing what you want.
Never weaponize supposed revelation.
The Shepherd does not need your manipulation to lead His sheep.
And perhaps someone reading this has been wounded precisely there.
Someone told you God said you had to stay.
Someone told you God said you had to give them money.
Someone told you questioning them meant questioning God.
Someone used spiritual language to control your choices.
And because you loved Jesus, you were afraid to resist.
Hear this carefully:
Biblical submission to Christ is not blind submission to every human being who claims divine authority.
Test what you are told.
Search the Scriptures.
Seek godly wisdom.
Look at fruit.
And keep Jesus—not a personality—at the center.
Because sheep ultimately belong to the Shepherd.
This also means something beautiful for the believer who feels spiritually numb.
Your relationship with Christ is not measured by how dramatic your spiritual experiences are.
Some days Scripture may pierce your heart.
Other days you may read a chapter and feel almost nothing.
Some prayers may leave you overwhelmed by God’s presence.
Others may feel like words hitting the ceiling.
Some worship services may bring tears.
Others may not.
Your emotions fluctuate.
Christ does not.
Your concentration fluctuates.
Christ does not.
Your spiritual intensity fluctuates.
Christ does not.
And look at what comes immediately after “My sheep hear My voice.”
Jesus says:
“And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.” — John 10:28
Read that again.
The emphasis moves immediately toward Christ’s keeping power.
“I give…”
“They shall never perish…”
“No one will snatch them out of My hand.”
Then:
“My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand.” — John 10:29
You may have arrived at John 10 terrified because you wondered whether you were holding tightly enough to Jesus.
And Jesus turns the picture around.
The Shepherd is holding His sheep.
That does not make obedience irrelevant.
Jesus explicitly says His sheep follow Him.
But our hope is not finally located in the perfection of our grip.
It is located in the faithfulness of Christ.
And that is where this becomes deeply personal.
Because maybe you have followed strange voices.
Maybe the voice was money.
Maybe approval.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe lust.
Maybe success.
Maybe religion without Christ.
Maybe your own wounded heart.
Maybe somebody told you that you would finally be valuable if enough people admired you.
So you followed.
And followed.
And followed.
Until one day you looked around and realized you had wandered farther than you ever intended.
Sin always has a voice.
It promises before it destroys.
“Just once.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You deserve this.”
“You can repent afterward.”
“This will finally satisfy you.”
“You are too far gone anyway.”
Then after you fall, the voice changes.
“Look at you.”
“God could never want you now.”
“You knew better.”
“Hide.”
“Pretend.”
“Run.”
That is one of sin’s cruelest tricks.
Temptation says, “Come closer.”
Shame says, “Never go home.”
But the Gospel tells another story.
There is a Shepherd who came for sinners.
Jesus did not come for people who had successfully repaired themselves.
He came to seek and save the lost.
At the cross, the Good Shepherd became the Lamb who was slain.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Grace is God dealing with your sin through the blood of His Son.
Repentance, therefore, is not payment for grace.
It is the sinner turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Not because an algorithm happened to place another Christian article on your screen.
But because somewhere beneath your exhaustion, compromise, questions, disappointment, religious performance, or secret shame…
you still want Jesus.
Maybe faintly.
Maybe desperately.
Maybe you do not even know what you want anymore.
But something inside you knows that running has not healed you.
Hiding has not healed you.
Pretending has not healed you.
And perhaps the Shepherd’s words are confronting you again:
“Follow me.”
Not:
“Fix everything first.”
Not:
“Become impressive.”
Not:
“Make yourself worthy.”
Follow Me.
Bring the sin into the light.
Bring the questions.
Bring the wounds.
Bring the addiction you keep promising you will defeat alone.
Bring the resentment.
Bring the secret browser history.
Bring the pride.
Bring the church hurt.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
Jesus already knows His sheep.
“I know them.”
Those words can sound frightening until you realize who is speaking them.
The Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
He knows.
And still He calls.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that baptizes rebellion.
Grace that finds sinners where they are and refuses to leave them unchanged.
The Gospel does not say your sin is harmless.
It says Christ is mighty to save.
The Gospel does not tell you to celebrate your chains.
It announces that Jesus came to break the dominion of sin.
The Gospel does not tell you to manufacture a better identity.
It calls you to die and rise with Christ.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So tomorrow morning, when you wonder how to “hear God,” do not begin by trying to empty your mind until a mysterious sentence appears.
Open Scripture.
Read slowly.
Read in context.
Ask what the author actually meant.
Ask what the passage reveals about God.
Ask how it points toward Christ and fits within the whole counsel of Scripture.
Pray for the Holy Spirit to illuminate your understanding and transform your heart.
Then obey what is clear.
When Scripture commands forgiveness, forgive.
When Scripture exposes sexual immorality, flee it.
When Scripture commands love, love.
When Scripture calls you to repentance, repent.
When Scripture tells you to pray, pray.
When Scripture tells you to gather with believers, do not isolate yourself indefinitely.
When Scripture tells you Christ is sufficient, stop searching for another savior.
And when circumstances, impressions, advice, desires, dreams, opportunities, or internal thoughts seem to be leading you somewhere, test them.
Never make the Bible say what it does not say.
Never confuse your desires with God’s decrees.
Seek wisdom.
Pray.
Listen to mature believers.
Examine your motives.
Watch the fruit.
And where Scripture has given freedom, do not become paralyzed waiting for a supernatural sign God never promised to provide.
Sometimes wisdom looks remarkably ordinary.
Pray.
Think.
Seek counsel.
Make the wisest faithful decision you can.
Trust God.
Walk.
Because the Christian life is not primarily about decoding secret messages.
It is about knowing and following Jesus.
And perhaps this article exposed something you have never admitted.
Maybe you have been chasing voices while neglecting the Word.
Maybe you have been following a preacher more closely than Christ.
Maybe somebody’s “prophetic word” has controlled your life for years.
Maybe you have mistaken anxiety for God’s voice.
Maybe you have been terrified that God abandoned you because you do not experience Him the way somebody else claims to.
Or maybe you know exactly what Christ has already commanded…
and you have simply refused to follow.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Do not turn the comment section into a stage for pretending everybody is strong.
Let it become a place where people remember they are not the only ones fighting.
And somebody you know may desperately need this truth.
Maybe even share it for the person who does not yet believe, because the center of this message is not a technique for hearing supernatural voices.
It is Jesus Christ.
There will probably come another night when emotions become louder than truth.
Come back then.
Read John 10 again.
Remember the Shepherd.

Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, faithfully, and for God’s glory—not as a transaction for blessing, not as a way of purchasing God’s favor, and never as a substitute for belonging to and giving faithfully through your local church.
Jesus Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be earned.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9
Your greatest need is not membership in a platform.
Your greatest need is Christ.
So hear the Shepherd where He has truly spoken.
Trust what He has revealed.
Test every other voice.
Repent when His Word exposes you.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Jesus.
And when your feelings scream that you are abandoned, remember the words surrounding the verse that once frightened you:
“My sheep hear my voice…”
“I know them…”
“They follow me…”
“I give unto them eternal life…”
“They shall never perish…”
“No one will snatch them out of My hand.”
Maybe you thought Christianity depended on whether you could hear Jesus loudly enough.
But perhaps John 10 has been telling you something better all along.
The miracle is not merely that the sheep recognize the Shepherd.
The miracle is that the Shepherd knows their names, laid down His life for them, rose from the grave—and still calls wandering sheep home.
Share that truth.
Because somewhere tonight, another sheep is listening through a storm of voices…
and desperately needs to remember which Shepherd died to bring them home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RAHAB WAS A PROSTITUTE—SO WHY IS SHE CELEBRATED FOR FAITH?
paragraphs:
RAHAB WAS A PROSTITUTE—SO WHY IS SHE CELEBRATED FOR FAITH?
The Bible did not erase the scandal from her story. It did something far more shocking: it showed what happens when a sinner believes God—and discovers that yesterday’s shame does not have the authority to write tomorrow’s ending.
Joshua 2; Joshua 6:22–25; Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25
There is something uncomfortable about Rahab.
Maybe that is precisely why we need her story.
Because Scripture does not introduce her by telling us how much she prayed.
It does not tell us she came from a respectable family.
It does not introduce her as a religious woman, a moral example, or someone whose past had already been cleaned up enough to make church people comfortable.
Joshua introduces her with a word.
זוֹנָה — zônâ.
A prostitute.
And centuries later, when the New Testament remembers her, the Holy Spirit does not quietly edit that word out of her biography.
Hebrews calls her:
Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē.
“Rahab the prostitute.”
James does it too:
Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη.
Rahab the prostitute.
That should bother us just enough to make us pay attention.
Because this woman is not remembered in Scripture merely as someone who had once lived in sexual sin.
She appears in Hebrews 11.
The chapter filled with people remembered for faith.
Abel.
Enoch.
Noah.
Abraham.
Sarah.
Moses.
And then...
Rahab.
The prostitute.
How did she get there?
That question becomes even more piercing when we realize that James also uses Rahab as an example of living faith expressed through action.
And Matthew places a woman named Rahab in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
The Bible refuses to hide what she had been.
Yet the Bible also refuses to let what she had been become the final definition of what God was doing with her.
And maybe that is where this story stops being about an ancient woman behind the walls of Jericho...
and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because some of us know what it feels like to believe that one chapter of our lives has become our name.
Addict.
Adulterer.
Liar.
Abuser.
Cheater.
Drunk.
Porn addict.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Divorced.
Promiscuous.
Backslider.
Prisoner.
The person who destroyed the marriage.
The parent who failed the children.
The Christian who knew better and did it anyway.
The person who smiles in church while carrying memories nobody in the room knows about.
Sometimes people do not even have to call you by your past anymore.
You do it to yourself.
You can be forgiven and still wake up remembering.
You can worship and still remember.
You can read your Bible and still remember.
You can hear someone preaching about sexual purity, marriage, addiction, betrayal, or repentance...
and suddenly your mind walks back into a room God has already called you out of.
That is why Rahab matters.
Not because prostitution was insignificant.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because God shrugs at rebellion.
And certainly not because Scripture is teaching that faith gives us permission to remain unchanged.
Rahab matters because her story destroys two lies at the same time.
The first lie says:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
The second says:
“Your sin is all that matters.”
The Gospel agrees with neither.
Sin is serious enough that Jesus had to die.
Grace is powerful enough that Jesus willingly did.
And Rahab’s story begins inside a city that was about to face judgment.
Jericho.
Israel had crossed toward the land God had promised, and Joshua sent two men secretly to spy out the land.
Joshua 2:1 tells us that they entered the house of Rahab.
A prostitute.
Before long, the king of Jericho learned that Israelite men had entered the city, and Rahab was commanded to surrender them.
But she had hidden them.
Then something extraordinary came out of this Canaanite woman’s mouth.
She told the spies that the people of Jericho had heard what Israel’s God had done.
They had heard about the Red Sea.
They had heard about the defeat of the Amorite kings.
The city was afraid.
But Rahab did something with what she heard.
She believed.
Listen carefully to Joshua 2:11.
Rahab declares:
כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת
Ki YHWH Eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma'al ve'al-ha'aretz mittachat.
In context, the sense is:
“For YHWH your God—He is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.”
Do not rush past that.
Rahab lived in Canaan.
Jericho had its walls.
Its culture.
Its gods.
Its king.
Its security.
Its assumptions about reality.
But Rahab had heard what YHWH had done...
and she reached a conclusion that changed the trajectory of her life.
Your God is God.
Not merely Israel’s tribal deity.
Not one god among many.
God in heaven above and on earth beneath.
Something had happened inside her before Jericho’s walls ever fell.
Rahab had changed allegiance.
That is why Hebrews does not celebrate prostitution.
It celebrates faith.
Hebrews 11:31 says:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη οὐ συναπώλετο τοῖς ἀπειθήσασιν...
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē ou synapōleto tois apeithēsasin...
“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient...”
And then Hebrews tells us why:
she had received the spies in peace.
Notice the first word.
Πίστει — pistei.
“By faith.”
That is the point.
She was not celebrated because she had been a prostitute.
She was celebrated because she believed the God of Israel and acted on that belief.
There is an enormous difference.
Christianity does not turn sin into virtue.
Grace does something better.
It turns sinners toward God.
And this is exactly why James can use Rahab when explaining that genuine faith does not remain an invisible claim with no consequences.
James 2:25 asks:
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη... οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη...
“Likewise, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works...?”
James points specifically to what she did: she received the messengers and sent them out by another way.
Rahab did not merely say:
“I believe Israel’s God is real.”
Her belief moved her.
It changed what she risked.
It changed whom she sided with.
It changed what she did.
Her actions did not make prostitution righteous.
Her actions demonstrated the reality of the faith she professed.
This matters enormously.
Because biblical faith is not merely agreeing that God exists.
Biblical faith entrusts itself to God.
There are people who know Christian vocabulary but have never surrendered.
People who can sing worship songs and protect secret idols.
People who can post Bible verses and live two completely different lives.
People who believe facts about Jesus while resisting the authority of Jesus.
Rahab had less theological information than many of us have.
But when the truth reached her, she acted.
That should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the question is not:
“How much Scripture do I know?”
Perhaps the more frightening question is:
“What have I done with the truth God has already shown me?”
Rahab knew judgment was coming.
So she pleaded for mercy.
Not only for herself.
For her family.
Her father.
Her mother.
Her brothers.
Her sisters.
Those belonging to them.
The spies gave her instructions involving a scarlet cord.
Joshua 2:18 describes it as:
תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי — tiqvat chut hashani
the cord of scarlet thread.
It would mark the house where Rahab and her family were to gather.
Later, when Jericho fell, Joshua commanded that Rahab and those belonging to her be brought out.
Joshua 6:25 tells us that Rahab and her family were spared and that she lived among Israel.
There is a temptation here to preach beyond what Scripture actually says.
The scarlet cord has often been treated in Christian preaching as a picture of the blood of Christ.
That can be a beautiful theological association, especially when considered alongside the Bible’s broader themes of sacrifice and deliverance.
But we should be careful.
Joshua itself does not explicitly say:
“This scarlet cord represents the future blood of Jesus.”
We do not need to force that meaning into the passage to make Rahab’s story powerful.
The text is already breathtaking.
A woman living inside a condemned city heard about the true God.
She believed.
She changed allegiance.
She acted on that faith.
She sought mercy.
And when judgment came...
she was found on the side of the God she had trusted.
Then the story became even more astonishing.
Because Rahab did not simply survive Jericho.
She became part of the people of Israel.
And generations later, Matthew 1:5 records:
Σαλμὼν δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Βόες ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ...
“Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab...”
Boaz.
The man who would marry Ruth.
Their family line continued.
Eventually came David.
And generations after David...
Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A woman whose introduction included the word prostitute appears in the opening genealogy of the Gospel according to Matthew.
Her scandal was not removed from Scripture.
But neither was she removed from God’s redemptive story.
That does not mean Rahab earned salvation by being brave.
It does not mean sexual sin became irrelevant.
It means the grace of God is capable of bringing people with real histories into a future they could never manufacture for themselves.
And now we arrive at the place where Rahab’s story may hurt.
Because perhaps you believe Jesus forgives sinners...
in theory.
You believe He forgave Peter.
You believe He forgave Paul.
You believe He rescued Rahab.
You believe He showed mercy to the woman caught in adultery.
You believe the thief beside Christ could hear, “Today you will be with Me in Paradise.”
You believe grace for everybody in the Bible.
But when your own history enters the room...
suddenly you become a theologian of condemnation.
You say:
“God forgives, but you don't know what I did.”
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your children do not know.
Maybe the people sitting beside you in church do not know.
Maybe the person everyone calls “strong in faith” goes home and fights something they are terrified anyone will discover.
Maybe you have repented...
but you cannot forgive yourself.
Maybe you secretly think God tolerates you instead of loves you.
Maybe you imagine Jesus looking at you with crossed arms, permanently disappointed that you were not somebody else.
But listen.
The Gospel does not say your sin was small.
It says Christ is greater.
The Gospel does not save you by rewriting history and pretending you never sinned.
It announces that Jesus entered history to redeem sinners.
At the cross, grace did not call evil good.
Jesus bore sin.
First Peter 2:24 says Christ Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says the One who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Romans 5:8 does not say Christ died for us once we became respectable.
God demonstrates His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up so Jesus will finally tolerate you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy you desperately need.
The Greek New Testament often uses the word:
μετάνοια — metanoia
for repentance.
It carries the idea of a change of mind, a turning of understanding and orientation that Scripture presents as producing a changed direction of life.
Grace does not tell you:
“Stay in Jericho. Nothing matters.”
Grace calls you out.
Grace changes allegiance.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace forgives...
and grace transforms.
Rahab was not rescued because prostitution was acceptable.
Rahab was rescued by faith.
That distinction protects the Gospel from two distortions.
One distortion removes repentance and turns grace into permission.
The other removes grace and turns Christianity into a museum for people who can hide their stains.
Jesus destroys both.
The church is not supposed to be a showroom for people pretending they never needed mercy.
It is a people gathered around a crucified and risen Savior because every one of us desperately needed mercy.
Some sins become public.
Others remain private.
Some people carry scandals everyone knows.
Others carry scandals only God knows.
But at the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast.
And nobody gets to say:
“My darkness is stronger than His blood.”
That is why the name attached to Rahab matters.
Rahab the prostitute.
At first it sounds almost cruel.
Why keep mentioning it?
Why would Hebrews repeat it?
Why would James repeat it?
Perhaps because Scripture is not embarrassed by what grace has conquered.
The title does not glorify the prostitution.
It magnifies the distance grace traveled.
It reminds us who she had been...
so we can marvel at what faith in God did with her future.
The scandal remained part of the testimony.
But the scandal did not get the final word.
God did.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years trying to erase your story.
You wish you could delete the photographs.
Delete the messages.
Delete the relationship.
Delete that night.
Delete those years.
Delete the websites.
Delete the substances.
Delete the betrayal.
Delete the abortion.
Delete the affair.
Delete the prison record.
Delete the secret.
Delete the version of yourself you cannot stand remembering.
But Christianity offers something greater than deletion.
Redemption.
God can take a chapter you would never have written...
and refuse to let it become the ending.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Because Jesus is.
Not because sin deserves celebration.
Because mercy does.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Sometimes they do not.
Relationships can carry scars.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Restitution may be necessary.
Earthly consequences can remain.
Repentance can be painful.
But consequences are not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who are in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation.
Read that again slowly.
Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
Not condemnation waiting for the next time your past flashes through your mind.
No condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That does not belong to everyone merely because they feel spiritual.
It belongs to those who are in Christ.
And that brings this entire story to you.
Not your neighbor.
Not your ex.
Not the hypocrite you wish would read this.
You.
Where is your allegiance?
Do you merely know that Jesus exists?
Or have you entrusted yourself to Him?
Are you protecting the very sin He is calling you to confess?
Are you asking Jesus to save you from hell while refusing to let Him rule your life?
Are you performing Christianity publicly while Jericho still owns your heart privately?
Rahab heard.
Rahab believed.
Rahab acted.
And when everything around her eventually collapsed, she discovered that trusting the true God had been worth everything.
You do not need Rahab’s exact story.
You need Rahab’s God.
And the revelation given to us is greater now.
We know the name of the promised Savior.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who lived without sin.
The Lamb who gave Himself for sinners.
The King who was crucified.
The Savior who rose from the grave.
The Lord before whom every knee will bow.
Jesus does not invite you to cosmetically improve your old life.
He calls you to Himself.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop negotiating with the thing destroying you.
Stop hiding behind the excuse that you have gone too far.
Stop calling bondage your identity.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Your past may explain wounds in your life.
It may explain consequences.
It may explain why certain battles are difficult.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ...
your past does not own you.
Jesus does.
And maybe this is the sentence someone desperately needs tonight:
You are not being invited to pretend the scandal never happened. You are being invited to discover what Jesus can write after it.
Rahab could not change how Joshua 2 introduced her.
But Joshua 2 was not the last place her name would appear.
Her name appears again.
In Israel.
In a genealogy.
In Hebrews.
In James.
In the testimony of faith.
Think about that the next time Satan tries to convince you that your worst chapter must also be your final chapter.
The enemy loves periods.
Jesus writes sentences after them.
This is why you should never look at another broken human being and assume you know how their story ends.
That prostitute could become a woman remembered for faith.
That addict could become a faithful father.
That prisoner could become a disciple.
That broken marriage may encounter resurrection grace.
That lukewarm believer may wake up.
That prodigal may come home.
That person crying behind the bathroom door tonight may someday comfort thousands.
That person who thinks God could never use them may discover that God has never been intimidated by ruined material.
We do not know every earthly outcome.
We should never promise that every relationship will be restored, every consequence removed, every illness healed, or every circumstance repaired exactly as we desire.
But we can promise what Scripture promises:
Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
Maybe this article found you because somebody shared it.
Maybe they did not know what you have been fighting.
Maybe they had no idea what you did.
Maybe nobody does.
But God does.
And you are still reading.
So be honest.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your sin to strangers.
But you can stop pretending.
Let other believers know that behind the screen there is a real human being who needs prayer.
And if God has already carried you from a place of shame into grace, tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Your testimony may become the doorway through which another frightened sinner realizes there is still hope.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
Somebody may believe their sexual history disqualifies them.
Somebody may be drowning in shame.
Somebody may be sitting in church convinced that if everyone knew the truth, they would be abandoned.
Somebody may need Rahab tonight.
Send this privately to the family member who stopped going to church because shame convinced them they no longer belonged.
Share it with the believer who fell.
Share it with the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only for respectable people.
Share it with the person whose past keeps screaming louder than grace.
Because there may come a night when your own memories become loud again, and you need to remember:
Rahab's past was real.
Her sin was real.
God's judgment was real.
Her faith was real.
And God's mercy was real.

We want this community to be a place where biblical truth is not watered down, sin is not romanticized, broken people are not discarded, and everything keeps leading back to Jesus Christ—repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, discipleship, and transformation through the Gospel.

Scripture teaches that God is glorified by lives of faith, obedience, love, worship, generosity, and faithful service. But supporting Gospel work can certainly be one practical expression of that generosity when it is done freely, sincerely, and for the sake of helping truth reach people.
Not because sharing saves you.
Jesus saves.
Christ knows His own.
Do it because truth worth receiving can also be truth worth carrying to somebody else.
Perhaps glorifying God through your life today looks like repentance.
Perhaps it looks like forgiving someone.
Perhaps it looks like confessing hidden sin.
Perhaps it looks like finally asking for help.
Perhaps it looks like supporting Gospel work.
Perhaps it looks like sharing this article so the Rahab in somebody else's life discovers that Jesus Christ still receives sinners.
Whatever it is...
do not merely admire Rahab's faith.
Ask yourself whether yours moves.
Because one day the walls we trust will fall.
Reputation.
Money.
Beauty.
Success.
Followers.
Approval.
Secret identities.
Every Jericho eventually proves unable to save us.
Only Christ can.
Rahab's story does not whisper that sin does not matter.
It announces something infinitely better:
Sin does not have to have the final word when a sinner turns in faith toward the mercy of God.
She entered the biblical story carrying a label associated with shame.
She is remembered in Hebrews among people of faith.
She appears in James as an example of faith demonstrated through action.
And her name appears in Matthew's genealogy leading toward Jesus Christ.
That is not the celebration of prostitution.
That is the triumph of grace.
So when your past knocks on the door tonight...
when shame whispers your old name...
when the enemy drags out evidence from chapters you wish had never existed...
remember the woman behind the wall.
Remember Jericho.
Remember Rahab.
Then remember something infinitely greater than Rahab.
Remember Jesus.
Because your deepest hope is not that you can rewrite yourself.
Your deepest hope is that Christ redeems sinners.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about a life surrendered to Jesus is this:
The chapter you thought would make God throw the whole story away may become the very place where future generations discover just how astonishing His grace really is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY YOU CANNOT LIVE THE CHRISTIAN LIFE WITHOUT THE HOLY SPIRIT
paragraphs: WHY YOU CANNOT LIVE THE CHRISTIAN LIFE WITHOUT THE HOLY SPIRIT

You can know the verses, attend the church, sing the songs, fight the temptation, and promise God you will change—but Christianity was never meant to be lived by human strength. Jesus did not save you merely to make you try harder. He gave you Someone.
There is a kind of Christianity that looks alive from a distance.
The Bible is open.
The worship music is playing.
The person knows when to say “Amen.”
They know the language of faith. They know the right Christian answers. They may even know how to encourage everyone else.
But somewhere behind the smile is an exhausted soul whispering a question nobody hears:
“Why am I still struggling this much?”
You prayed.
You promised.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You walked away.
Then went back.
You told God, “This time I mean it.”
And perhaps you did mean it.
That is what makes the failure hurt so badly.
Maybe your struggle is not something scandalous enough to become public gossip. Maybe nobody knows about it at all.
Maybe it is anger.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Jealousy.
Fear.
A secret relationship.
The need for approval.
A mouth that worships Jesus on Sunday and destroys people on Monday.
A heart that knows how to look holy while quietly becoming cold.
Or maybe there is no dramatic hidden sin.
Maybe you are simply tired.
Spiritually tired.
Tired of trying to become the Christian you thought you would have become by now.
And somewhere along the way, you began confusing Christianity with an endless cycle of human effort:
Try harder.
Fail.
Feel guilty.
Promise more.
Try again.
Fail again.
Hide better.
But what if the problem is not that Jesus gave you too little?
What if you have been trying to accomplish through human strength what God intended to accomplish through His Spirit?
That question takes us directly into one of the most breathtaking truths in Scripture.
Before Jesus went to the cross, He prepared His disciples for something they could barely comprehend.
He was leaving.
Imagine hearing that.
They had walked beside Him.
Heard His voice without opening a Bible.
Watched blind eyes open.
Watched storms surrender.
Watched demons flee.
They had eaten with Him, traveled with Him, questioned Him, disappointed Him, and still been loved by Him.
And now Jesus tells them He is going away.
Yet in John 14:16, Jesus promises that the Father will give them “another Helper.”
The Greek expression is striking:
ἄλλον παράκλητον — allon paraklēton.
“Another Helper,” “Advocate,” or “Comforter,” depending on the translation and the aspect being emphasized.
The word ἄλλον — allon carries the idea of another, while παράκλητος — paraklētos describes one called alongside—an advocate, helper, or intercessory presence.
Jesus was not telling His disciples, “I am leaving, so become stronger.”
He was telling them that they would not be abandoned.
Then He identifies Him:
τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας — to Pneuma tēs alētheias
“the Spirit of truth.”
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from self-improvement.
Jesus did not die merely so guilty people could receive better rules.
He died and rose again so sinners could be reconciled to God, forgiven by grace, made new, and brought into a life in which God Himself dwells within His people by the Holy Spirit.
The Holy Spirit is not an optional upgrade for unusually spiritual Christians.
He is essential to Christian life.
Not because the Spirit replaces Jesus.
Because the Holy Spirit glorifies Jesus.
Jesus says in John 16:14:
ἐκεῖνος ἐμὲ δοξάσει — ekeinos eme doxasei.
“He will glorify Me.”
That one sentence protects us from two dangerous extremes.
Christianity without the Holy Spirit becomes dry human religion.
But talk about the Holy Spirit that continually draws attention away from Jesus also misses the biblical picture.
The Spirit glorifies Christ.
He points to Christ.
He opens our understanding to Christ.
He conforms believers to Christ.
He empowers believers to witness to Christ.
He does not come to make Jesus less central.
He makes the glory of Jesus impossible to ignore.
And perhaps that is exactly why the enemy would love for Christians to misunderstand Him.
Some believers are afraid of the Holy Spirit because they have seen emotional excesses committed in His name.
Others reduce Him to a theological concept.
Others treat Him almost like an impersonal spiritual electricity—something you “tap into” when you need power.
But Scripture speaks differently.
The Holy Spirit teaches.
He guides.
He speaks.
He can be grieved.
He distributes gifts according to His will.
He bears witness.
He intercedes.
He is not an “it.”
He is divine Person.
He is God.
When Peter confronted Ananias in Acts 5, he said that Ananias had lied to the Holy Spirit, and then described that sin as lying to God.
The biblical witness is unmistakably serious.
The Spirit is not a motivational feeling you experience during your favorite worship song.
And this did not suddenly appear out of nowhere in Acts.
Go all the way back to the opening lines of Scripture.
Genesis 1:2 speaks of:
רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים — ruach Elohim
the “Spirit of God.”
The Hebrew word רוּחַ — ruach can carry meanings associated with spirit, wind, or breath depending on context.
Before humanity builds its first city...
before Abraham...
before Moses...
before David...
before Bethlehem...
the Spirit of God is already there in the biblical story.
Then the prophets begin pointing toward something astonishing.
Ezekiel speaks of God giving His people a new heart and putting His Spirit within them.
Joel prophesies of God pouring out His Spirit.
And centuries later, after the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus, frightened disciples are gathered in Jerusalem.
Then Pentecost comes.
Acts 2 describes a sound like a mighty rushing wind and tongues as of fire. The disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit.
Peter—the man who had recently denied Jesus—stands and publicly proclaims Him.
Think about that transformation.
The same Peter who collapsed under the pressure of being associated with Jesus now publicly announces the risen Christ.
What changed?
The resurrection had happened.
Peter had encountered the risen Jesus.
And now, according to Christ's promise, the Holy Spirit had come upon the disciples with power for witness.
Jesus had told them plainly in Acts 1:8:
“You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses.”
The Greek word translated “power” is:
δύναμις — dynamis.
Power. Ability. Might.
But notice what the power is for.
Not spiritual celebrity.
Not religious performance.
Not proving that you are more anointed than somebody else.
Witness.
Jesus says, in effect, that the Spirit's power will send His followers outward bearing testimony about Him.
That means one of the clearest signs of the Spirit's work is not how impressive we appear.
It is how faithfully our lives point toward Jesus.
And here is where this becomes painfully personal.
Some of us have spent years asking God to make us stronger when God has been teaching us dependence.
We want enough strength that eventually we will not need to depend so desperately on Him.
But dependence is not Christianity's embarrassing beginner stage.
Dependence is the Christian life.
Paul writes in Romans 8 that those who belong to Christ have the Spirit of Christ.
He goes even further.
“If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.”
That is how essential the Holy Spirit is.
Not an accessory.
Not an advanced course.
Not something reserved for pastors, missionaries, Pentecostals, charismatics, or Christians who seem more emotional than you.
Every person who truly belongs to Christ belongs to a Spirit-indwelt people.
Paul tells believers in 1 Corinthians 6:19 that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit.
Stop there for a moment.
A temple.
You may look at yourself and see everything you regret.
God sees someone purchased at a price.
You see the history.
God sees redemption.
You remember what you did.
God knows what Christ has done.
You remember the bed.
The bottle.
The browser history.
The lie.
The betrayal.
The rage.
The abortion.
The affair.
The addiction.
The years you wasted.
The prayers you abandoned.
The people you hurt.
The nights you would erase if heaven allowed you to rewrite your history.
And the Gospel does not pretend sin does not matter.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God went to the cross.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
Truth matters.
But grace means your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when you come to Christ.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God calls evil good.
He does not.
Grace is scandalous because God takes genuinely guilty people, forgives them through Christ, cleanses them, adopts them, and begins transforming them by His Spirit.
Paul reminds the Corinthians of people whose lives had been characterized by serious sin, then says something astonishing:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes grace.
“You were washed.”
“You were sanctified.”
“You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Do you see it?
The Gospel does not merely say, “Behave better.”
The Gospel says Christ saves sinners.
The Spirit transforms those Christ saves.
This is why Galatians 5 does not tell believers merely to grit their teeth harder.
Paul says:
Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε — Pneumati peripateite.
“Walk by the Spirit.”
Walk.
That is ordinary language.
Step after step.
Tuesday morning.
Friday night.
When nobody is watching.
When temptation appears.
When anger rises.
When the phone is in your hand.
When the old memory returns.
When somebody wounds you.
When loneliness whispers that one compromise will not matter.
Walk by the Spirit.
Christian maturity is not one enormous spiritual leap.
It is thousands of surrendered steps.
And then Paul describes what the Spirit produces:
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
Self-control.
Notice the language.
The fruit of the Spirit.
Fruit is produced by life within.
You can tape plastic apples onto a dead tree, but that does not make the tree alive.
And Christians can do something similar.
We can tape Christian behavior onto an unchanged public image.
Smile.
Quote Scripture.
Say the right things.
Avoid getting caught.
Maintain the reputation.
But the Holy Spirit goes beneath appearances.
He confronts motives.
He exposes bitterness nobody else sees.
He challenges pride hidden beneath ministry.
He touches wounds we converted into excuses.
He convicts us where we learned to rationalize sin.
Jesus says in John 16 that the Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.
Conviction is uncomfortable.
But conviction can be mercy.
Imagine having an infection and losing the ability to feel pain.
Pain may hurt, but sometimes pain warns you that something is wrong.
In a similar way, when the Word of God pierces your heart and the Spirit exposes something you have been protecting, the answer is not always to run from the discomfort.
Sometimes the discomfort is an invitation:
Come into the light.
Stop hiding.
Confess it.
Repent.
Return.
Jesus is still calling you.
Maybe that is happening while you read this.
Maybe one particular sin has been sitting in your mind since the beginning of this article.
You know exactly what it is.
You have renamed it.
Excused it.
Managed it.
Compared it with somebody else's worse behavior.
But deep down, you know.
Do not silence conviction.
Run toward Christ.
First John 1:9 teaches believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not because confession earns forgiveness.
Because Christ is faithful, and His atoning work is sufficient.
This is where the Holy Spirit's ministry becomes incredibly tender.
He does not merely expose sin.
Romans 8 reveals that the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that believers are children of God.
The Spirit does not only confront you in rebellion.
He assures God's children of adoption.
There is a difference between conviction that leads you toward repentance and condemnation that tells you there is no hope.
Romans 8 begins with thunder:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation.
Not because your sin was imaginary.
Because Christ's sacrifice was real.
The cross did not minimize your guilt.
The cross dealt with it.
And the resurrection announces that the crucified Jesus lives.
So when the Holy Spirit exposes something, His purpose is not to whisper, “You are beyond redemption.”
He points you toward the Savior.
Jesus.
Again Jesus.
Always Jesus.
That is why the Spirit is essential when you are weak.
Romans 8:26 says:
τὸ Πνεῦμα συναντιλαμβάνεται τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ ἡμῶν
“The Spirit helps us in our weakness.”
There are nights when eloquent prayers disappear.
You sit on the edge of the bed and have nothing.
No beautiful Christian vocabulary.
No spiritual energy.
No impressive faith speech.
Just...
“God, help me.”
Maybe only tears.
Maybe silence.
Maybe you do not even understand what is happening inside you.
Romans 8 says the Spirit helps believers in their weakness and intercedes according to God's will.
You are not disqualified because you ran out of impressive words.
God was never impressed by vocabulary.
He desires truth in the inward being.
The Holy Spirit is also essential because Christianity requires transformation, not merely information.
You can memorize verses and remain proud.
Study theology and remain cruel.
Know Greek words and refuse to forgive your spouse.
Defend biblical morality online while secretly feeding private sin.
Win an argument about Jesus and represent Jesus terribly.
Knowledge matters enormously.
Truth matters.
Doctrine matters.
But biblical knowledge was never intended to stop at information.
Second Corinthians 3:18 describes believers being transformed into Christ's image “from one degree of glory to another,” and Paul says this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
Transformation.
That is what God wants.
Not merely better religious vocabulary.
Christlikeness.
And transformation can hurt.
Because sometimes the Spirit must put His finger on the very thing you keep asking God not to touch.
Your resentment.
Your ego.
Your secret.
Your relationship.
Your ambition.
Your addiction to applause.
Your unwillingness to forgive.
Your obsession with control.
We say, “Holy Spirit, change me.”
Then He exposes something.
And we say, “Not that.”
But surrender with exceptions is not complete surrender.
The question is not whether you can hide something from people.
You probably can.
The question is whether you are willing to bring it before God.
David prayed in Psalm 51 after devastating sin:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים — lev tahor bera-li Elohim
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Then he pleaded:
וְרוּחַ קָדְשְׁךָ אַל־תִּקַּח מִמֶּנִּי — veruach qodshekha al-tiqqach mimmeni
“and take not your Holy Spirit from me.”
We should read David in his covenantal setting rather than mechanically transferring every circumstance of Israel's king to the believer under the new covenant. Yet the cry remains haunting.
David had finally seen what sin had done.
He did not merely need reputation repair.
He needed cleansing.
That may be where somebody reading this is standing today.
You do not need better camouflage.
You need cleansing.
You do not need another excuse.
You need repentance.
You do not need to convince everybody that you are fine.
You need Jesus.
And the beautiful news is that Jesus receives repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who told His disciples about the Holy Spirit walked toward Golgotha knowing exactly what humanity was.
He knew Peter would deny Him.
He knew Judas would betray Him.
He knew the crowd would turn.
He knew the nails were coming.
Still He went.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
This is not motivational Christianity.
This is Gospel.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ saving.
And those who repent and believe in Him are not simply offered a second chance to perform better.
They are brought into new life.
The Spirit gives life.
Jesus tells Nicodemus in John 3 that one must be born of the Spirit.
The Greek language is vivid:
γεννηθῆναι ἐκ Πνεύματος — gennēthēnai ek Pneumatos
“to be born of the Spirit.”
Christianity is not fundamentally bad people becoming respectable.
It is spiritually dead sinners receiving life through God's saving work.
That is why behavior modification cannot replace regeneration.
You cannot discipline a corpse into life.
You need resurrection power.
And once God gives life, the Spirit does not become unnecessary.
He leads.
Romans 8:14 says those led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.
He produces fruit.
He empowers witness.
He gives gifts for the good of Christ's body.
He helps believers pray.
He strengthens God's people.
He illuminates the truth He inspired in Scripture, never contradicting the Word He gave.
And this point desperately matters today.
Not every strong feeling is the Holy Spirit.
Not every coincidence is a message from God.
Not every viral prophecy came from heaven.
Not every person who says “God told me” is speaking for God.
The Holy Spirit does not contradict Holy Scripture.
The Spirit who inspired the Word does not suddenly become the author of teachings opposed to it.
So test what you hear.
Open your Bible.
Read verses in context.
Do not build theology on emotional clips.
Do not surrender discernment because somebody speaks confidently.
The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth.
And truth has a name at the center of Christianity:
Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the better question is no longer simply, “Why is the Holy Spirit essential for every Christian?”
Perhaps the question has become:
Am I actually walking in dependence on Him?
Because you can believe correct doctrine about the Spirit while practically living as though everything depends on you.
You wake up without prayer.
Face temptation without Scripture.
Make decisions without seeking God's wisdom.
Carry wounds without surrender.
Attempt ministry through personality.
Attempt marriage through willpower.
Attempt holiness through shame.
Attempt Christianity through exhaustion.
And eventually you wonder why your soul feels empty.
A branch disconnected from the vine does not need motivational speeches.
It needs abiding.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
Nothing.
The Christian life begins with Christ.
Continues through Christ.
Depends upon Christ.
Ends in the glory of Christ.
And the Holy Spirit continually turns the believer's heart toward Christ.
So tonight, before another scroll...
before another distraction...
