before another promise that tomorrow you will finally fix yourself...
maybe the most honest prayer you can pray is painfully simple:
“Holy Spirit, expose what I keep hiding.
Lead me into truth.
Make me hate what dishonors Jesus.
Give me strength where I am weak.
Produce in me what I cannot manufacture.
Teach me to obey.
Make me more like Christ.
Glorify Jesus in my life.”
And then open Scripture.
Obey what God has already made clear.
Confess known sin.
Seek reconciliation where possible.
Forgive.
Turn away from temptation.
Ask mature believers for help when you need accountability.
Do not confuse dependence on the Spirit with passivity.
The Spirit-empowered Christian life is active obedience fueled by divine grace.
Perhaps you fell again yesterday.
Repent.
Perhaps you have been spiritually cold for months.
Return.
Perhaps you are ashamed even to pray.
Pray anyway.
Perhaps you have never truly surrendered yourself to Christ.
Then stop trying to renovate a life Jesus is calling you to surrender.
Come to Him.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
You are not being invited to become impressive.
You are being invited to belong to Jesus.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the conviction into another passing emotional moment.
Be honest.
Your comment may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed to see tonight.
And think of one person who needs this message.
Not your entire friends list.
One person.
The friend quietly drifting.
The believer drowning in shame.
The family member who knows Christianity intellectually but has never understood life in the Spirit.
The person who thinks failure has written the final chapter.
There may come a night when you are the person who needs to read it again.

We want this community to remain a place where Christ is greater than personalities, Scripture is greater than trends, repentance is never separated from grace, and broken people are continually pointed toward Jesus.
It does not.
You do not.
Christ alone is Savior, and the Gospel cannot be bought.
But Scripture does show believers freely supporting Gospel ministry and participating generously in work that advances the truth.
Pray.
Send it privately to somebody hurting.
Because the goal was never to build an audience that merely watches Christian content.
The goal is people encountering truth.
Sinners repenting.
Wounded believers returning.
Families opening Scripture.
Prodigals coming home.
Christians becoming disciples.
And Jesus being glorified.
You were never meant to manufacture the Christian life by yourself.
You need the Spirit who gives life.
The Spirit who leads.
The Spirit who convicts.
The Spirit who strengthens.
The Spirit who produces fruit.
The Spirit who helps in weakness.
The Spirit who glorifies Christ.
And when He puts His finger on the chapter you desperately wish you could erase, remember this:
The Holy Spirit does not expose your darkness so you can build a home inside your shame; He brings it into the light so you can run to the Savior who already carried your sin to the cross.
Your scandal does not have to write your final sentence.
Jesus still does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT DOES THE ENTIRE BIBLE REVEAL ABOUT GOD’S DESIGN FOR MARRIAGE?
paragraphs:
WHAT DOES THE ENTIRE BIBLE REVEAL ABOUT GOD’S DESIGN FOR MARRIAGE?
Before There Was a Wedding Dress, a Church Ceremony, or a Marriage License, There Was a Garden—and What God Did There Still Changes Everything

There is a sentence buried near the beginning of the Bible that has survived empires, wars, revolutions, broken homes, changing cultures, human rebellion, adultery, divorce, tears, funerals, and thousands of years of people trying to redefine love.
It is only a few words.
But Jesus Himself reached back to it when people questioned Him about marriage.
Paul reached back to it when explaining the mystery of Christ and His Church.
And perhaps we need to reach back to it now.
Because somewhere tonight, a husband and wife will lie inches apart in the same bed and feel miles away from each other.
Someone will stare at a wedding photograph and wonder where those two smiling people went.
Someone will discover a message that was never meant to be discovered.
Someone will whisper, “I don't love you anymore.”
Someone else will desperately pray, “God, please save my marriage.”
Someone who has never married will wonder whether biblical marriage is still worth believing in.
Someone divorced will read an article about marriage and immediately feel the sting of everything that went wrong.
Someone betrayed by a spouse may wonder whether God understands what covenant-breaking feels like.
And someone carrying sexual sin, regret, shame, or a shattered past may quietly assume that whatever beautiful design God intended was meant for better people.
People with cleaner histories.
People who didn't make their mistakes.
People whose stories never became scandals.
But that is exactly where we must begin.
Not with your marriage.
Not with your divorce.
Not with your loneliness.
Not with modern politics.
Not with Hollywood.
Not even with the Church's failures.
We have to go farther back.
Back before the scandal.
Back before the fall.
Back before shame.
Back before anyone had ever broken anyone else's heart.
Back to a garden.
“And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness...” (Genesis 1:26, KJV).
Then Scripture says:
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” (Genesis 1:27, KJV).
Notice something extraordinary.
Marriage does not begin with human beings inventing a social arrangement and asking God to bless it.
The biblical story presents humanity itself as God's creation.

Male and female are not introduced as competitors fighting for value. Both bear the dignity of being created by God. Both stand beneath His authority. Both belong to the Creator before they belong to one another.
Then Genesis takes us closer.
God forms the man, places him in the garden, and declares something startling.
“It is not good that the man should be alone...” (Genesis 2:18, KJV).
Until that moment, the repeated rhythm of creation had been good... good... good.
Then suddenly:
Not good.
The man is surrounded by creation and yet lacks a corresponding human companion.
God brings the woman to him.
And Adam erupts:
“This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh...” (Genesis 2:23, KJV).
Then comes the sentence that echoes through the rest of Scripture:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24, KJV).
The Hebrew is breathtaking.
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
ve-davaq be-ishto
The key verb, דָּבַק (dāvaq), carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, sticking closely.
Not casually visiting.
Not consuming someone until they cease satisfying you.
Not treating another human being as disposable.
Clinging.
Holding fast.
And then:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad
“They shall become one flesh.”
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.

That union certainly includes sexual union, but the biblical vision cannot be reduced to sex. Genesis describes a new human bond in which a man leaves his father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Marriage, according to Scripture, is therefore not merely two people saying, “You make me happy.”
It reaches deeper than happiness.
It says, in effect:
I am no longer approaching you merely as someone I consume for my fulfillment.
We are joined in a covenantal life beneath God.
And then...
Genesis 3 happens.
The serpent speaks.
God's word is questioned.
Desire reaches for what God forbade.
Sin enters.
Eyes open.
Nakedness becomes shame.
Blame replaces innocence.
The man who had celebrated the woman as “bone of my bones” begins distancing himself:
“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me...” (Genesis 3:12, KJV).
Can you hear the fracture?
The first marriage does not remain untouched by the first sin.
That matters enormously.
Because the Bible does not tell us that marriage is difficult merely because husbands and wives need better communication techniques.
The problem runs deeper.
Sin enters human relationships because sin entered human hearts.
Selfishness enters.
Lust enters.
Pride enters.
Manipulation enters.
Domination enters.
Bitterness enters.
Fear enters.
Hiding enters.
Blame enters.
And suddenly the person you were supposed to protect can become the person you wound.
This is why changing partners cannot, by itself, cure the deepest human problem.
You carry yourself into every relationship you enter.
And so does the other person.
Two sinners can stand beneath flowers, exchange rings, sign papers, smile for photographs, and sincerely mean every word they say...
and still desperately need grace.
Marriage does not eliminate the need for the Gospel.
Marriage exposes it.
Keep reading the Bible and you discover something else uncomfortable.
Scripture does not airbrush families.
Abraham's household contains painful relational complications.
Jacob's family becomes tangled in favoritism, rivalry, jealousy, and grief.
David's sexual sin with Bathsheba and his actions against Uriah become one of Scripture's darkest demonstrations of what happens when desire is severed from obedience to God.
Solomon, despite extraordinary wisdom, disobeys God's commands and allows his many wives to turn his heart toward other gods.
The Bible refuses to pretend that every marriage it records is a marriage God endorses.
This distinction matters:
Biblical description is not automatically biblical prescription.
Sometimes Scripture shows us human behavior precisely so we can see its devastation.
And through all of this, God's commands continue protecting the holiness of marriage.
“You shall not commit adultery.”
Adultery matters because covenant matters.
Faithfulness matters because people are not disposable.
Bodies matter because God created them.
Sex matters because Scripture refuses to treat it as spiritually meaningless recreation.
Marriage matters because God says it matters.
But then Jesus arrives.
And when religious leaders attempt to pull Him into a dispute concerning divorce, Jesus does something remarkable.
He takes them back.
Not merely to the customs of their day.
Back to creation.
Jesus asks whether they have read that the Creator made humanity male and female and then invokes Genesis 2:24.
The Greek wording preserves the ancient thunder:
ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Then Jesus says:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω
ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” (Matthew 19:6, KJV).
Look carefully at the subject.
God joins.
Marriage in Jesus' teaching is not treated merely as a private romantic contract between autonomous individuals.
God is not an ornamental guest standing politely in the corner of the ceremony.
The Creator stands over marriage.
This is why Christian marriage cannot finally be defined by whatever two people happen to feel today.
Feelings matter.
Affection matters.
Romance can be beautiful.
But feelings fluctuate.
Covenant says something deeper.
“I remain faithful because love is more than appetite.”
That does not mean Scripture commands someone to pretend evil is acceptable.
It does not mean abuse should be hidden.
It does not mean victims should be manipulated with Bible verses into protecting violence, coercion, criminal behavior, or unrepentant wickedness.
Biblical covenant faithfulness must never be weaponized to provide cover for sin.
Jesus Himself acknowledges the devastation of sexual immorality in His teaching about divorce, while other New Testament passages address abandonment and serious covenant rupture.
Christian communities should never use “God hates divorce” as a slogan to silence someone whose life or safety is in danger.
God's holiness is not permission for an abuser to continue abusing.
And God's design should never become camouflage for human evil.
But neither should the hardness of the human heart be allowed to redefine God's original intention.
Jesus explicitly says that Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart, “but from the beginning it was not so.” (Matthew 19:8, KJV).
There it is again.
The beginning.
Jesus keeps taking us back to the design.
But the Bible still isn't finished.
Because eventually Paul writes words so radical that Christian husbands could spend their entire lives learning how to live them:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (Ephesians 5:25, KJV).
Read it slowly.
Not:
Husbands, control your wives.
Not:
Husbands, demand service.
Not:
Husbands, remind everyone that you are important.
Love your wives...
as Christ loved the Church.
And what did Christ do?
He gave Himself.
The Greek verb behind “love” here is connected with ἀγαπάω (agapaō), and Paul's model is not sentimental romance but Christ's self-giving love.
So biblical headship can never legitimately become an excuse for cruelty, narcissism, intimidation, or selfish domination.
The measuring stick is Jesus.
The crucified Christ.
The One who gives Himself for His bride.
A man claiming biblical authority while terrorizing his wife has missed the Christ-shaped center of the passage.
A husband's calling is terrifyingly costly because the model standing before him is a Savior with wounds in His hands.
And Paul addresses wives within this same Christ-centered vision of covenant faithfulness, respect, and ordered devotion.
Yet then Paul does something astonishing.
He quotes Genesis again.
“For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.”
And immediately afterward:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.” (Ephesians 5:31–32, KJV).
There.
That changes everything.
Marriage was never merely about marriage.
From Eden onward, God was writing something into this covenant that would ultimately help illuminate something greater than itself.
Christ.
And His Church.
Paul calls it:
μυστήριον μέγα
mystērion mega
“A great mystery.”
Suddenly Genesis and Calvary seem to face one another across the pages of Scripture.
A bridegroom.
A bride.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Sacrificial love.
Union.
And a love willing to give itself for the beloved.
But do not misunderstand the picture.
Human marriage does not save us.
A good spouse cannot wash away your sins.
Marriage cannot reconcile you to God.
Jesus can.
Jesus does what no husband or wife could ever do.
He takes sinners who have broken covenant with God and offers reconciliation through His own blood.
That is why the Gospel speaks so powerfully into sexual failure, adultery, pornography, betrayal, divorce, promiscuity, lust, shame, regret, and every other place where people quietly think:
“God could forgive other people...
but surely not me.”
Listen.
The Bible's sexual ethic is serious because God's holiness is serious.
Repentance is not optional.
Sin cannot simply be renamed until guilt disappears.
Jesus did not die so we could become comfortable with the sins destroying us.
He died to save sinners.
And that means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you were cheated on.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out your intimacy.
Maybe resentment has become your nightly companion.
Maybe you have been divorced.
Maybe you caused the divorce.
Maybe you begged someone to stay and watched them leave anyway.
Maybe your marriage looks wonderful online and feels almost dead behind the front door.
Maybe you have been single so long that every article about marriage feels like someone pressing on a bruise.
Maybe your spouse died and the word “marriage” still opens a room in your heart you have been afraid to enter.
Maybe you are reading this while wondering whether God has forgotten you.
He has not.
And marriage is not the ultimate destination of the Christian life.
Jesus is.
Jesus Himself lived a perfectly complete human life without marrying.
The New Testament honors both marriage and faithful singleness.
Your worth is therefore not measured by whether someone puts a ring on your finger.
Your deepest identity is not “husband.”
Not “wife.”
Not “single.”
Not “divorced.”
Not “widowed.”
Not “betrayed.”
Not even “failure.”
For the Christian, the deepest identity is found in Christ.
And this is where God's design for marriage becomes even more beautiful.
Marriage is precious...
but it is temporary.
Jesus teaches that the resurrection life will not simply perpetuate earthly marriage as we know it.
Earthly marriage therefore points beyond itself.
The Bible begins with a marriage in a garden...
and moves toward another wedding image near its end.
Revelation announces:
“Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.” (Revelation 19:9, KJV).
Do you see the arc now?
Genesis.
A bride and bridegroom.
Rebellion.
Brokenness.
Covenants shattered.
Prophets calling God's people back.
Christ arriving.
The Bridegroom giving Himself.
The Church being prepared.
Revelation.
A wedding supper.
The Lamb.
The story of Scripture does not ultimately terminate in your wedding photograph.
It terminates in Christ's triumph.
Marriage points beyond itself toward a greater covenant reality.
That is why Christians should neither worship marriage nor trivialize it.
Marriage cannot bear the weight of being your god.
Your spouse cannot complete what only Christ can complete.
If you demand that another sinner become your savior, eventually you will punish them for failing to be Jesus.
Your husband cannot be Jesus.
Your wife cannot be Jesus.
But together, by grace, husband and wife can learn to point toward Jesus.
When a husband forgives instead of keeping ammunition for the next argument...
when a wife chooses truth instead of contempt...
when both confess rather than hide...
when repentance replaces defensiveness...
when tenderness returns after months of coldness...
when temptation is dragged into the light before it becomes destruction...
when “I'm sorry” finally comes without an excuse attached...
when prayer returns to a house that had forgotten how to pray...
when two wounded sinners stop demanding perfection from each other and begin kneeling before the One who is perfect...
something happens.
Not perfection.
Grace.
And perhaps that is the word some marriages desperately need tonight.
Grace.
Not cheap grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that refuses consequences.
Not grace that protects abuse.
Not grace without repentance.
Biblical grace.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then points trembling sinners toward a crucified and risen Savior.
Because the Gospel is not:
“Pretend nothing happened.”
The Gospel says:
Something terrible did happen.
Sin separated humanity from God.
And Jesus Christ entered our ruin.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now repentance and forgiveness are proclaimed in His name.
That is why there is hope for the husband ashamed of what he has done.
Hope for the wife who has hardened her heart.
Hope for the couple sitting silently in the counselor's office.
Hope for the person whose marriage cannot be restored because the other person refuses repentance.
Hope for the divorced believer wondering whether there is still a place at God's table.
Hope for the sexually broken.
Hope for the ashamed.
Hope for the abandoned.
Hope for the lonely.
Hope even for the person who created the scandal.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because Jesus does.
This is where Christianity refuses both despair and denial.
We don't have to say the wound wasn't deep.
We don't have to call betrayal harmless.
We don't have to rewrite God's commandments.
We don't have to pretend every broken marriage can necessarily be restored exactly as it was.
We don't have to pretend earthly consequences magically disappear.
We can look directly at the wreckage...
and then look directly at the cross.
The cross is where God's hatred of sin and God's love for sinners meet without either being compromised.
And resurrection tells us ruins do not intimidate Jesus.
Maybe your marriage needs counseling.
Get wise, biblically faithful help.
Maybe you need to confess something tonight.
Confess it.
Maybe you need to stop hiding pornography.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe you need to apologize without saying, “but you...”
Do it.
Maybe your spouse is unsafe and you need immediate protection and wise pastoral, professional, or legal help.
Seek it.
Maybe reconciliation is possible.
Pursue it truthfully.
Maybe circumstances have reached a point where simplistic slogans cannot responsibly answer what must happen next.
Seek mature biblical counsel rather than letting strangers on social media make life-altering decisions for you.
But whatever your situation, do not confuse hopelessness with holiness.
Jesus is still Jesus.
The cross is still enough.
Repentance is still possible.
Grace is still available.
Truth still matters.
And God is still capable of making saints out of people with histories they wish they could erase.
Maybe that is why this subject hits so hard.
Because almost nobody reaches the biblical vision of marriage without eventually seeing themselves exposed.
The selfish husband.
The resentful wife.
The secret lust.
The unforgiving heart.
The careless words.
The manipulation.
The fantasies.
The pride.
The cold silence.
The desire to win instead of reconcile.
The years we can never get back.
And suddenly we stop asking:
“What is wrong with marriage today?”
and begin asking something much more frightening:
“Lord... what is wrong in me?”
That question can become holy ground.
Because repentance begins when we stop editing the evidence.
Be real.
And if God has already restored something you once thought was impossible, tell someone what He did. Your testimony may become the reason another exhausted believer does not give up tonight.
Then send this to the person whose marriage nobody knows is hurting.
Not to shame them.
To sit beside them.
It is lived by sinners who desperately need a flawless Savior.
Because there may come a night when anger is louder than covenant.
A night when temptation looks easier than faithfulness.
A night when you need to remember what marriage was designed to point toward.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped bring you closer to Scripture, consider staying with this mission.

Following Gospel Warrior keeps biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment within reach—not only for married believers, but for families, seekers, struggling Christians, lukewarm hearts, and people who may still be trying to understand who Jesus really is.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing.
It cannot.
Not because God needs our money.
He does not.

We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, generosity, love, truth, worship, and service. Supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of that stewardship when it is done freely and sincerely—not under spiritual coercion.
If this ministry has spiritually fed you, consider helping us place that same truth in front of someone else.
Not merely to increase a number.
A wife crying where nobody can see her.
A young man learning about marriage from pornography instead of Scripture.
A young woman terrified that faithful love no longer exists.
A divorced believer who assumes God has discarded them.
A couple smiling publicly while privately collapsing.
Or an unbeliever who has never understood that the deepest love story in the Bible is not ultimately about finding the perfect spouse.
It is about the holy Bridegroom who came searching for sinners.
Jesus Christ.
The One who loved His people when they were not lovely.
The One who remained faithful when humanity had been faithless.
The One who did not merely send advice from heaven.
He came.
He entered our world.
He carried a cross.
He gave Himself.
He rose from the grave.
And He still calls sinners home.
So what does the entire Bible reveal about God's design for marriage?
It begins with God's creation, not ours.
It joins man and woman in a one-flesh covenant.
It calls for faithfulness rather than disposability.
It exposes what sin does to intimacy.
It demands holiness without pretending human beings are flawless.
It calls husbands toward Christ-shaped, sacrificial love.
It calls marriage into a life ordered beneath the lordship of Jesus.
It refuses to make marriage an idol.
It honors faithful singleness.
It offers grace to people whose sexual and marital histories are shattered.
And ultimately...
it points beyond every earthly wedding.
Toward Christ.
Toward His redeemed people.
Toward a covenant no human betrayal can overthrow.
Toward the Lamb.
Toward the day when every temporary sign gives way to the reality it was pointing toward.
Perhaps your story became something you never imagined.
Perhaps the photograph cracked.
Perhaps the promises were broken.
Perhaps you broke them.
Perhaps all you can see now is the scandal.
But if you are willing to bring the truth into the light, repent where repentance is yours to make, receive the grace Christ purchased, and place the ruins into the hands of Jesus...
do not assume the final sentence has already been written.
Because when human love reaches the chapter it cannot repair, Jesus is still holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEX, SINGLENESS, MARRIAGE, DESIRE, AND SELF-CONTROL: 1 CORINTHIANS 7 WITHOUT THE AWKWARD SILENCE
paragraphs:
SEX, SINGLENESS, MARRIAGE, DESIRE, AND SELF-CONTROL: 1 CORINTHIANS 7 WITHOUT THE AWKWARD SILENCE
The chapter Christians sometimes whisper about is the chapter many of us desperately need to hear—because Jesus is not ashamed to enter the places where desire, loneliness, temptation, marriage, disappointment, and holiness collide.
There are Bible chapters we underline in public.
And there are Bible chapters we quietly hope nobody asks us about.
First Corinthians 7 has a way of becoming the second kind.
Sex.
Marriage.
Singleness.
Sexual desire.
Abstinence.
Self-control.
A believing spouse married to an unbeliever.
People wondering whether they should marry at all.
People already married wondering what faithfulness now requires.
People burning with desire.
People capable of remaining single.
People trying to follow Christ while carrying bodies, hormones, histories, wounds, temptations, expectations, and loneliness.
And somewhere along the way, Christians learned to become strangely uncomfortable talking about some of the very things Scripture refuses to ignore.
So perhaps we should begin with the sentence somebody reading this has been afraid to say aloud:
“I love Jesus... but I still have sexual desires.”
Or:
“I’m single, and sometimes the loneliness is unbearable.”
Or:
“I’m married, and our intimacy is struggling.”
Or:
“I keep falling sexually, asking forgiveness, promising God it will never happen again, and then finding myself back in the same place.”
Or perhaps yours is harder:
“I’ve made sexual choices I deeply regret, and I wonder whether God still sees me as clean.”
If any of those sentences sound familiar, keep reading.
Not because this article will excuse sin.
It won't.
Not because Scripture lowers God's standard when obedience becomes difficult.
It doesn't.
Keep reading because the Gospel offers something infinitely better than pretending.
It offers redemption.
Paul begins this discussion with words that remind us that we are entering an ongoing conversation:
“Περὶ δὲ ὧν ἐγράψατε...”
Peri de hōn egrapsate...
“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote...” (1 Corinthians 7:1).
That opening matters.
Paul is answering questions.

We possess Paul's answer in Scripture; we do not possess the Corinthians' original letter. That means humility is necessary whenever we reconstruct exactly what they had asked or exactly how their statement about “not touching a woman” functioned in the conversation.
But what follows is unmistakably practical.
Paul refuses to discuss spirituality as though Christians suddenly stopped being embodied human beings when they were converted.
He speaks about sexual immorality.
He speaks about husbands.
He speaks about wives.
He speaks about mutual marital responsibility.
He speaks about temporary abstinence.
He speaks about temptation.
He speaks about self-control.
He speaks about singleness.
He speaks about marriage.
He speaks about divorce.
He speaks about widows.
He speaks about divided households.
He speaks about devotion to the Lord.
In other words, Paul walks straight into the room many churches would rather keep locked.
And perhaps that is because Christianity was never intended to save some invisible spiritual version of you while leaving the rest of you untouched.
Jesus claims all of you.
Your mind.
Your money.
Your ambitions.
Your relationships.
Your sexuality.
Your loneliness.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your desires.
Your body.
Your future.
Paul uses a striking word when addressing the sexual realities facing the Corinthians:
“πορνείας”
porneias.
It comes from porneia, a broad New Testament term associated with sexual immorality.
Paul does not pretend sexual sin is imaginary.
But notice something equally important.
He does not solve sexual brokenness by declaring the body evil.
Christianity is not salvation from having a body.
The body belongs to the Lord.

That is why the immediate context matters. Just before chapter 7, Paul had confronted sexual immorality in chapter 6 and reminded believers that their bodies are members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit.
Then comes one of Scripture's most radical discussions of marital intimacy.

Paul tells husbands and wives to fulfill their marital responsibility toward one another, and then says something astonishing in the ancient world: the husband's body is not simply his private possession over against his wife, and the wife's body is not simply hers over against her husband. The obligation is reciprocal.
Mutuality.
Not male entitlement.
Not female entitlement.
Not coercion disguised as Christianity.
Not “you owe me whatever I demand.”
Paul immediately speaks of abstaining only by mutual agreement for a limited period for prayer, followed by coming together again.
The Greek phrase is:
“ἐκ συμφώνου”
ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
Together.
Mutually.
Christian marital intimacy is therefore never permission for selfish domination.
The person beside you is not a product.
Not an outlet.
Not an object God provided to satisfy uncontrolled appetite.
Your spouse bears the image of God.
Marriage does not erase personhood.
And Paul's words become painfully relevant when he warns married couples against unnecessarily depriving one another, lest temptation exploit their lack of self-control.
The word appearing in 1 Corinthians 7:5 is:
“ἀκρασίαν”
akrasian.
Lack of self-control.
That word exposes something modern culture desperately tries to hide.
Desire is real.
But desire is not God.
Feeling something intensely does not automatically make obeying it righteous.
That principle reaches far beyond sexuality.
“I want it” is not the same sentence as “God approves it.”
“I feel it” is not the same sentence as “I must obey it.”
“My body wants this” is not the same sentence as “this owns me.”
That is where discipleship becomes painfully real.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that battle feels like.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You blocked the number.
Then unblocked it.
You ended the relationship.
Then loneliness brought you back.
You promised yourself you would stop watching.
Stop fantasizing.
Stop messaging.
Stop crossing that boundary.
Stop feeding the secret.
And perhaps afterward you sat alone with that familiar combination of temporary satisfaction and crushing shame.
You knew better.
You loved God.
And somehow you still fell.
So you started wondering whether the fact that temptation keeps returning means your Christianity must be fake.
Listen carefully.
Temptation and surrender are not identical.
Desire and obedience are not identical.
Being tempted does not require you to enthrone the temptation.
The Christian life is not the disappearance of every disordered desire the moment you believe.
It is learning, by the Spirit, that Jesus Christ has a greater claim upon you than your impulses do.
That is self-control.
Not pretending you have no desires.
Not hating your body.
Not becoming emotionally numb.
Self-control is desire placed beneath lordship.
And some battles will require far more than whispering, “I'll try harder tomorrow.”
You may need confession.
Accountability.
Distance from a compromising relationship.
A changed routine.
Filters and boundaries.
A pastor.
A mature Christian friend.
Professional counseling where wounds, compulsive patterns, or trauma are involved.
You may need to stop protecting the secrecy that keeps protecting the sin.
Because darkness survives on one sentence:
“Nobody can know.”
Grace answers:
“Bring it into the light.”
But Paul does not merely speak to married people.
He says something the modern church desperately needs to recover:
Singleness is not spiritual failure.
Paul himself can speak positively of remaining unmarried and wishes others could share his gift, while recognizing that different people receive different gifts from God.
That changes everything.
Because somewhere a single Christian has begun to believe that marriage is graduation and singleness is detention.
Everybody keeps asking:
“When are you getting married?”
Nobody asks:
“What is Christ forming in you right now?”
People announce engagements and thousands celebrate.
Someone quietly remains faithful to Jesus through another year of singleness, loneliness, temptation, service, prayer, generosity, ministry, and unseen obedience...
and almost nobody notices.
Heaven does.
Your relationship status does not determine your value before God.
Jesus was never married.
Paul was unmarried when he wrote these words.
Christian maturity therefore cannot possibly be measured by possession of a wedding ring.
Paul even sees advantages in singleness because an unmarried believer can possess a particular freedom for undivided devotion to the Lord.
That does not make marriage inferior.
And it certainly does not make sexual desire dirty.
Paul honors marriage while honoring singleness.
That balance matters.
Marriage is not a cure for lust.
And singleness is not automatically purity.
A lustful single person does not magically become holy during a wedding ceremony.
You carry yourself into marriage.
Your habits.
Your expectations.
Your wounds.
Your pornography addiction.
Your selfishness.
Your communication patterns.
Your understanding of intimacy.
Your capacity—or incapacity—to sacrifice.
Marriage may give sexual desire a covenantal home, but marriage was never designed to replace sanctification.
A spouse cannot do the work of the Holy Spirit for you.
And that is why Paul's famous words need to be heard without childish snickering:
If people are not exercising self-control, “it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9).
Paul is not saying:
“Grab the nearest Christian and marry them because you're horny.”
Marriage is covenant.
Marriage requires fidelity, sacrifice, patience, service, forgiveness, responsibility, and love.
His point is more serious.
God does not demand that every believer possess the same calling to celibate singleness.
For some, marriage is the fitting path.
For others, singleness provides extraordinary freedom for devotion to Christ.
Neither status makes you spiritually elite.
The question underneath the chapter is not:
“Which status makes me more important?”
The deeper question is:
“How can I belong faithfully to Christ where I am?”
That question becomes even harder when Paul addresses believers married to unbelievers.
Some Corinthians apparently found themselves in religiously divided marriages.
Paul does not casually command the Christian spouse to abandon the unbeliever.
If the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain, Paul says the believer should not divorce them.
Then comes hope:
“How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?” (1 Corinthians 7:16).
Paul is not teaching that one spouse personally becomes the Savior of the other.
Jesus saves.
The believing spouse cannot regenerate another human heart.
But God may work through faithful Christian presence.
That matters to the husband praying quietly for his wife.
The wife who comes to church alone.
The believer whose spouse does not understand why Jesus matters so much.
You cannot manipulate somebody into conversion.
You cannot nag somebody into regeneration.
You cannot argue somebody into loving Christ.
But you can remain faithful.
You can pray.
You can love.
You can live the Gospel before them.
You can speak truth with grace.
And you can entrust the outcome to God.
Then Paul introduces another principle that cuts directly against our age of perpetual dissatisfaction:
“Let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him” (see 1 Corinthians 7:17).
We spend enormous portions of our lives imagining that obedience will begin when circumstances change.
When I get married...
When my spouse changes...
When I stop feeling lonely...
When my sex drive becomes easier...
When somebody finally chooses me...
When my marriage heals...
When my past stops hurting...
Then I'll become serious about God.
Paul keeps pulling us back to faithfulness now.
You can obey Jesus now.
Single.
Married.
Widowed.
Longing.
Disappointed.
Tempted.
Healing.
Waiting.
You do not need another person's body to make your life meaningful.
You need Christ.
And perhaps that sentence hurts because you wanted this article to promise that God will eventually give you the relationship you want.
Scripture gives us no universal promise that every Christian will marry.
But it gives something better than a promise of romance.
It gives Christ Himself.
This is where 1 Corinthians 7 becomes more beautiful than a chapter about sex.
Paul's concern eventually rises above the question of whether somebody should marry.
He wants believers living with undivided devotion to the Lord.
That is the center.
Not sexual repression.
Not romantic obsession.
Not marriage worship.
Not singleness worship.
Jesus.
The single Christian belongs to Jesus.
The married Christian belongs to Jesus.
The sexually tempted Christian belongs to Jesus.
The husband belongs to Jesus.
The wife belongs to Jesus.
The widow belongs to Jesus.
The person with a sexual past belongs to Jesus.
And if you belong to Him, then even your sexuality must eventually kneel before Him.
This is where some readers may become uncomfortable.
Because grace is beautiful until grace tells us to repent.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make us feel less guilty while we continue worshiping what is destroying us.
The Gospel announces forgiveness—and transformation.
Repentance is not payment for grace.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has encountered grace.
Maybe your scandal is sexual.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe there was an affair.
Pornography.
A secret relationship.
Years of promiscuity.
Sex outside marriage.
A double life.
Emotional infidelity.
A pattern you keep rationalizing because admitting what it is would require surrender.
Perhaps your shame whispers:
“God can forgive other people. Not this.”
Look at the cross.
Jesus knew what He was purchasing when He died.
Your sin did not surprise Him.
Your darkest chapter was not discovered after Calvary.
Christ did not go to the cross for an imaginary, cleaned-up version of you.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives adulterers—and tells them to leave adultery.
Grace that forgives sexually immoral people—and calls them to holiness.
Grace that receives the ashamed—and teaches them to walk in light.
Grace that does not say sin doesn't matter.
Grace says sin mattered so much that the Son of God bled for sinners.
And if sexual sin has become your identity, remember what Paul had already told these same Corinthians.
After listing serious sins, including forms of sexual immorality, he says:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Some.
Of.
You.
Then:
“But you were washed... you were sanctified... you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11)
Do you see it?
Corinth was not a museum of spotless religious people.
It was a church filled with trophies of grace.
People had histories.
Jesus was writing new ones.
That is why shame cannot have the final sentence.
You may have done it.
But you are not required to remain what sin made you.
You may have slept in the wrong bed.
Loved the wrong person.
Broken the covenant.
Crossed the boundary.
Fed the addiction.
Hidden the messages.
Returned to the website.
Lied to your spouse.
Lied to your pastor.
Lied to yourself.
And there may still be earthly consequences that repentance does not magically erase.
Grace is not denial.
Forgiveness does not always remove consequences.
Reconciliation may require time.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Some relationships must end rather than be “repaired” because the relationship itself is sinful.
Some wounds require patient healing.
But hear this:
Your worst sexual sin does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Christ does.
So stop running from the only One who can actually make you clean.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Confess.
Receive mercy.
Walk differently.
And when you fall, do not turn repentance into theater.
Run back to Christ.
Not because sin is trivial.
Because Christ is sufficient.
Maybe your struggle is different.
Maybe you have remained sexually pure, but you are angry.
You obeyed.
You waited.
You watched other people marry.
You prayed.
Another birthday came.
Another wedding invitation arrived.
Another friend announced a pregnancy.
Another Sunday sermon accidentally made you feel as though “family” means husband, wife, and children—and you wondered where that leaves you.
There is grief in singleness that married people should not mock with clichés.
But there can also be extraordinary beauty.
Your life is not waiting to begin.
Your body is not wasted because nobody is sleeping beside you.
Your love is not meaningless because it is not romantic.
Your home can become a place of hospitality.
Your time can become ministry.
Your resources can become generosity.
Your loneliness can deepen compassion.
Your freedom can become mission.
Your longing can become prayer.
Your whole life can say:
“Jesus is enough to build a life around.”
And married Christians need that witness.
Because marriage itself can become an idol.
Some people expect a spouse to provide what only Christ can provide.
Perfect understanding.
Perfect security.
Perfect satisfaction.
Perfect companionship.
Perfect affirmation.
No human being survives beneath the weight of being somebody else's messiah.
Your husband cannot be Jesus.
Your wife cannot be Jesus.
Your future spouse cannot be Jesus.
And your sexual fulfillment cannot be Jesus.
Christ alone occupies that throne.
That is where self-control finally makes sense.
Christian self-control is not merely saying “no” to sex outside God's boundaries.
It is saying “yes” to something greater.
Yes to Christ.
Yes to holiness.
Yes to covenant.
Yes to faithfulness.
Yes to seeing another person's body as sacred rather than consumable.
Yes to believing obedience is better than temporary pleasure.
Yes to trusting that no orgasm, fantasy, affair, hookup, pornographic image, secret conversation, or forbidden relationship can satisfy the hunger for eternity God placed within the human soul.
Maybe you are reading this at the exact moment temptation is calling you back.
Put the phone down.
Delete the conversation.
Leave the room.
Call somebody.
Pray badly if you cannot pray beautifully.
Just tell Jesus the truth.
“Lord, I want this right now more than I want obedience.”
That is a terrifying prayer.
It may also be the beginning of freedom.
Because God can work with honesty.
Stop performing.
Stop pretending mature Christians never struggle.
Stop confusing secrecy with strength.
And married believers—stop assuming this chapter exists merely to tell single people what they cannot do.
Paul's words confront you too.
Are you tender toward your spouse?
Are you faithful when nobody is watching?
Have you turned intimacy into leverage?
Have resentment and silence replaced affection?
Have you allowed pornography to teach you what a spouse's body is “supposed” to be?
Have you become demanding instead of giving?
Have you confused headship with domination?
Have you forgotten that Christian marriage is supposed to display covenant faithfulness rather than selfish consumption?
The Gospel does not merely ask:
“Are you technically married?”
It asks what Christ is doing inside your marriage.
And single believers—do not spend your singleness rehearsing resentment.
You are not half a Christian.
You are not waiting for another human being to complete the image of God in you.
You are not spiritually defective because you experience desire.
And you are not permitted to use loneliness as permission for sexual compromise.
Both truths must remain together.
Desire deserves compassion.
Sin requires repentance.
Marriage deserves honor.
Singleness deserves honor.
Sex belongs inside God's design.
Self-control belongs to Christian discipleship.
And Jesus belongs at the center of all of it.
That is 1 Corinthians 7 without the awkward silence.
Not:
“Sex is disgusting.”
Not:
“Desire is evil.”
Not:
“Marriage fixes everything.”
Not:
“Single people are spiritually superior.”
Not:
“Married people are spiritually superior.”
Not:
“Do whatever feels authentic.”
The message is far more demanding and far more beautiful:
Whatever your relationship status, belong wholly to Christ.
Maybe that is what you needed somebody to tell you tonight.
Not another purity slogan.
Not another marriage cliché.
Not another lecture pretending human desire is simple.
You needed to remember that Jesus can enter the messy room.
The bedroom.
The lonely apartment.
The damaged marriage.
The secret browser history.
The unanswered prayer.
The engagement.
The divorce papers.
The widow's empty side of the bed.
The single person's Saturday night.
The married couple trying to find one another again.
The believer trembling after another failure.
He enters all of it as Lord.
And Savior.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't give strangers the details of something that should remain private—but don't run from conviction either.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not fighting alone.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't use this article as a weapon against them.
Send it as an invitation.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But one practical way you can help Gospel truth reach more people is by supporting the work that produces and distributes it.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
The greatest response to this article is not giving Gospel Warrior money.
It is giving Jesus your life.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Seek help where secrecy has imprisoned you.
Honor your spouse.
Honor your singleness.
Flee sexual immorality.
Practice self-control.
Receive grace.
Follow Jesus.
Then share the truth so someone else can find the road home.
Because perhaps the most shocking truth in a chapter filled with sex, marriage, desire, singleness, and self-control is that none of those things gets the final word.
Jesus does.
And when Jesus gets the final word, the sentence shame wrote over your life can be crossed out by grace.
Your scandal may explain where you have been, but only Jesus has the authority to declare what you are becoming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGES WE WOULD RATHER NOT TALK ABOUT
paragraphs:
THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGES WE WOULD RATHER NOT TALK ABOUT
They loved, betrayed, waited, manipulated, endured, failed, forgave, and sometimes shattered one another—and buried inside their complicated marriages is a warning modern Christians desperately need before we confuse what the Bible records with what God approves.
Somewhere tonight, a husband and wife will lie inches apart in the same bed and feel miles away from each other.
Someone will stare at a wedding photograph and wonder where those two smiling people went.
Someone will discover a message that was never supposed to be discovered.
Someone will whisper, “I forgive you,” while wondering whether trust can ever breathe again.

Someone else will remain in a relationship where the word “submission” has been weaponized against them, and they have been made to believe that enduring cruelty without seeking help is somehow holiness.
And somewhere, a single Christian will read another beautiful marriage testimony online and quietly ask God, “Why hasn’t that happened for me?”
Then we open the Old Testament.
And surprisingly, we do not find a collection of spotless marriages posing for religious photographs.
We find Adam blaming Eve.
Abraham and Sarah carrying promises from God while also carrying fear, impatience, cultural pressures, and the devastating consequences surrounding Hagar.
We find Isaac and Rebekah beginning with tenderness but eventually inhabiting a household fractured by favoritism and deception.
We find Jacob loving Rachel, Leah aching to be loved, two sisters trapped inside a family structure filled with rivalry, jealousy, children, servants, bargaining, and heartbreak.
We find David accumulating wives while his household slowly becomes a place of sexual sin, violence, rivalry, grief, and bloodshed.
We find Solomon—the king famous for wisdom—allowing his many marriages to become part of his spiritual downfall.
This is where some readers make a dangerous mistake.
They assume that because something happened in the Bible, God must have approved of it.
He did not.
The Bible is sometimes brutally honest precisely because God refuses to edit human sin out of the story.
Scripture is not embarrassed by broken people.
It exposes them.
And perhaps that is one reason these ancient marriages still feel disturbingly modern.
Because underneath the tents, livestock, royal palaces, arranged unions, inheritance customs, and ancient Near Eastern social structures were human hearts.
Hearts like ours.
Hearts that wanted to be chosen.
Hearts terrified of rejection.
Hearts capable of extraordinary faithfulness and astonishing selfishness.
Hearts that could love someone in the morning and wound them before nightfall.

And if we read these marriages carefully—not merely asking, “What did these people do?” but, “What does the whole counsel of Scripture reveal about what God intended?”—something extraordinary begins to emerge.
The first marriage appears before sin enters the human story.
Before adultery.
Before divorce.
Before jealousy.
Before polygamy.
Before domestic manipulation.
Before husbands and wives learned how to hide from each other.
Genesis takes us back to the beginning.
After God creates the woman and brings her to the man, Adam responds with words of recognition and belonging:
“Bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.”
Then Genesis 2:24 gives the foundational pattern:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew is worth slowing down for.
The verb דָּבַק — dabaq — carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, remaining closely joined.
And then comes:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Marriage in the biblical vision is not merely two people sharing an address, a surname, expenses, children, or physical intimacy.
It is covenantal union.
That does not mean spouses cease to be individual persons. It means marriage creates a profound relational union characterized by faithfulness, belonging, and covenant commitment.
And notice something important.
Genesis gives us this pattern before the Bible gives us the disasters.
That matters.

Because when later generations multiply wives, practice favoritism, commit adultery, exploit power, deceive one another, or fracture their households, those stories must be read against God’s creational design—not used to rewrite it.
Consider Abraham and Sarah.
Their story contains magnificent faith.
It also contains fear.
God had promised Abraham descendants, yet the waiting became unbearable.
Genesis 16 records Sarah giving Hagar to Abraham according to a practice understandable within their ancient cultural world.
But culturally understandable does not mean spiritually ideal.
Human beings have always been tempted to “help” God fulfill promises on our timetable.
That temptation did not die with Abraham.
Modern Christians do it too.
We pray.
We wait.
Nothing changes.
Then anxiety begins preaching.
“God is taking too long.”
“You need to fix this yourself.”
“You cannot trust Him with this.”
“Take control.”
And sometimes the greatest damage in a marriage does not begin with hatred.
It begins with fear.
Fear of never having children.
Fear of losing financial security.
Fear that our spouse will leave.
Fear that we married the wrong person.
Fear that God has forgotten us.
Fear makes terrible decisions look reasonable.
Abraham and Sarah teach us that a marriage can belong to people of genuine faith and still contain moments of catastrophic human weakness.
That should humble every Christian couple.
Being believers does not make us incapable of damaging each other.
We still need repentance.
We still need wisdom.
We still need accountability.
We still need grace.
Then there is Isaac and Rebekah.
Their early story contains one of Scripture’s tender descriptions: Isaac loved Rebekah.
But years later their family became divided.
Isaac favored Esau.
Rebekah favored Jacob.
Favoritism became fertile soil for secrecy.
Secrecy produced manipulation.
Manipulation deepened division.
Eventually a son fled from home.
How many modern families understand that pattern?
Not necessarily because one parent literally chooses one child over another, but because alliances begin forming inside the home.
Mom tells the daughter what she refuses to tell Dad.
Dad makes the son his emotional confidant against Mom.
One parent becomes “the good one.”
The other becomes “the problem.”
Children learn how to navigate the tension.
Soon the family is technically together while emotionally divided into teams.
The house still stands.
But covenant intimacy is bleeding behind the walls.
Then Jacob enters one of the saddest marriage stories in Genesis.
He loves Rachel.
But through Laban’s deception, he first receives Leah.
Eventually the household expands into a painful web involving Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, and Zilpah.
Read those chapters slowly and you will hear something deeper than ancient genealogy.
You will hear a woman desperate to be loved.
After Leah bears Reuben, Genesis 29:32 records her hope that perhaps now her husband will love her.
Then another son.
Then another.
There is something almost unbearable about watching a human being try to earn affection through performance.
Maybe now he will love me.
Maybe now she will respect me.
Maybe if I earn more.
Maybe if I lose weight.
Maybe if I become more agreeable.
Maybe if I never complain.
Maybe if I give him sex whenever he wants it.
Maybe if I become more spiritual.
Maybe if I serve harder.
Maybe if I stop needing anything.
Maybe then I will finally be enough.
But marriage was never designed to answer the deepest question of human worth.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Only Christ can.

That does not excuse emotional neglect. Husbands and wives are commanded to love faithfully. But if your entire identity depends upon another fallen human being constantly proving your worth, even a loving marriage will eventually collapse beneath expectations it was never created to bear.
And this is where the Gospel begins reaching into places marriage advice cannot reach.
Because Christianity does not ultimately say, “Find the perfect person who will finally make you whole.”
It says that reconciliation with God comes through Jesus Christ.
Before you are somebody’s husband or wife…
before you are single, divorced, widowed, rejected, betrayed, desired, unwanted, happily married, or barely holding your marriage together…
your deepest problem is sin, and your deepest need is Christ.
That changes how we read David.
David is one of Scripture’s most sobering warnings against romanticizing biblical heroes.
He was Israel’s celebrated king.
He was also capable of horrific sexual and moral failure.
Second Samuel 11 records his taking Bathsheba and arranging the death of her husband Uriah.
Whatever sentimental versions of the story modern culture sometimes creates, the biblical narrative is dark.
David possessed royal power.
Uriah died because David abused it.
Then Nathan confronted him.
“You are the man.”
David’s response in 2 Samuel 12:13 is painfully brief:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Psalm 51 opens a window into the repentance associated with David’s sin:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Notice what repentance does not sound like.
“I was lonely.”
“My marriage wasn’t meeting my needs.”
“She understood me.”
“He made me feel alive again.”
“We never meant for anyone to get hurt.”
“God knows my heart.”
Repentance stops editing the confession.
“I have sinned.”
That sentence can become the doorway through which grace enters a dying marriage.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
David was forgiven, but his actions still produced terrible consequences.
Biblical grace is not God pretending sin did not matter.
Grace is costly.
And nowhere do we see its cost more clearly than at the cross.
But before we arrive there, Solomon gives us another warning.
First Kings 11 says Solomon loved many foreign women and accumulated hundreds of wives and concubines. The text specifically explains that his wives turned his heart after other gods.
The central issue in the biblical warning is covenant unfaithfulness and idolatry.

This matters when Christians discuss Old Testament restrictions concerning intermarriage. The biblical concern cannot responsibly be reduced to modern racial categories. Scripture’s theological concern was Israel’s covenant loyalty to the LORD and the danger of being drawn into idolatry.
Solomon had wisdom.
But possessing wisdom is not the same as obeying wisdom.
That should frighten anyone who knows enough Bible to become proud.
You can know Hebrew words.
You can quote theology.
You can teach Sunday school.
You can preach.
You can post Scripture every morning.
You can have thousands of followers who believe you are spiritually mature.
And still neglect your spouse.
Still entertain secret conversations.
Still feed pornography.
Still manipulate.
Still flirt.
Still nurture resentment.
Still become spiritually cold.
Still construct a private life completely different from your public Christianity.
Knowledge cannot substitute for obedience.
And neither can religious reputation.
Then the Old Testament gives marriage language an even greater theological depth.
Malachi 2:14 describes the wife as:
אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ
eshet beritekha—
“the wife of your covenant.”
There is the word:
בְּרִית — berit.
Covenant.
That changes everything.
Biblical marriage is more than a prolonged romantic mood.
Feelings matter enormously.
Affection matters.
Desire matters.
Tenderness matters.
Friendship matters.
But covenant says, “My faithfulness is not supposed to disappear every time my emotions change.”
This does not mean Scripture commands someone to silently remain in immediate danger or conceal abuse.
It never gives an abuser divine permission to terrorize a spouse.
Christian teachings about headship, submission, forgiveness, reconciliation, or covenant must never be twisted into weapons for coercion, violence, sexual abuse, threats, or control.
If you are in immediate danger, getting to safety and seeking appropriate help is not rebellion against God.
And forgiveness does not automatically mean immediate restoration of trust.
Trust can be shattered in minutes and rebuilt over a long period through truth, repentance, accountability, changed behavior, wisdom, and time.
This distinction matters because some Christians have been told that preserving the appearance of a marriage matters more than confronting evil inside it.
Scripture never calls darkness light merely because the darkness lives under a Christian roof.
But there is another mistake modern Christians make.
We sometimes read every difficult marriage as disposable.
Our culture can train us to treat covenant with the logic of consumerism.
If the product stops satisfying me, replace it.
If someone more exciting appears, upgrade.
If marriage becomes difficult, assume difficulty itself proves we chose incorrectly.
The Bible offers something far deeper.
Not endless tolerance of evil.
Not romanticized suffering.
Not pretending betrayal does not hurt.
But covenant faithfulness rooted in the character of a faithful God.
And then Jesus does something decisive.
When questioned about marriage in Matthew 19, Christ reaches past generations of human brokenness and points back to Genesis.
He quotes the creation pattern.
Male and female.
Leaving.
Holding fast.
One flesh.
In other words, Jesus does not use the later dysfunctions of Old Testament marriages as the definition of marriage.
He returns to the beginning.
That is crucial for understanding everything we have just read.
Abraham is not the standard.
Jacob is not the standard.
David is not the standard.
Solomon is certainly not the standard.
God’s design is the standard.
And ultimately, for Christians, marriage finds an even greater horizon in Christ.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:25:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
But Paul does not stop there.
He gives the terrifying measure of that love:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“As Christ loved the church.”
And what did Christ’s love look like?
A cross.
Self-giving.
Sacrifice.
Holiness.
Grace.
Truth.
Jesus did not love His people because they had performed well enough to deserve Him.
Romans tells us that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That does not make sin irrelevant.
It makes grace astonishing.
This is where every Old Testament marriage eventually points us beyond itself.
Not because every marriage is a direct allegory of Jesus.
But because every broken human relationship exposes how desperately humanity needs redemption.
The Bible contains scandal after scandal.
Deception.
Jealousy.
Sexual sin.
Betrayal.
Manipulation.
Favoritism.
Idolatry.
Power abused.
Promises broken.
Families shattered.
And God did not hide any of it.
Why?
Because Scripture is not a public-relations campaign for human beings.
It is the story of a holy God dealing with sinful people and moving history toward redemption.
Then Jesus came.
Not as another flawed patriarch.
Not as another king corrupted by desire.
Not as another husband who failed his covenant.
Christ came as the faithful Bridegroom.
He loved His people unto death.
He carried sin to the cross.
He rose from the grave.
And now sinners who repent and believe are not merely given better relationship advice.
They are given new life.
That means there is hope for the husband who finally admits, “I have become cold.”
Hope for the wife who realizes bitterness has colonized her heart.
Hope for the couple who cannot remember how to speak without fighting.
Hope for the person who committed adultery and is finally willing to stop hiding.
Hope for the spouse devastated by betrayal who needs wisdom, safety, truth, and time.
Hope for the single Christian who has spent years believing marriage is the missing proof of God’s goodness.
Hope for the widow who still reaches toward the other side of the bed.
Hope for the divorced believer carrying shame into church every Sunday.
Hope even for the person reading this who knows that everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
But you know.
God knows.
There are things nobody else sees.
And perhaps the question is no longer, “How do I make my marriage look Christian?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What would happen if Jesus were actually allowed into the room I keep locked?”
Into the resentment.
Into the browser history.
Into the secret messages.
Into the financial deception.
Into the pride.
Into the emotional affair you insist is “just friendship.”
Into the fantasies.
Into the unforgiveness.
Into the silence.
Into the need to control.
Into the words you keep using as weapons.
Into the wounds you have refused to acknowledge.
Into the loneliness you are terrified to admit.
Marriage does not need better pretending.
It needs truth.
And sinners do not need better camouflage.
We need a Savior.
Maybe you have spent years blaming your spouse for everything.
Maybe your spouse has genuinely sinned against you.
Both things can sometimes be true: another person can be responsible for the evil they committed against you while God is simultaneously confronting something sinful inside your own heart.
Repentance is not accepting responsibility for someone else’s sin.
It is finally taking responsibility for yours.
That is one of the most liberating lessons buried inside these ancient marriages.
God works with real people.
Not Instagram marriages.
Not staged anniversary photographs.
Not couples who have learned how to smile through church.
Real people.
Abraham and Sarah had complications.
Isaac and Rebekah had dysfunction.
Jacob’s household was painfully fractured.
David created devastation.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom and still wandered.
Yet through this deeply imperfect history, God continued moving His redemptive promise forward until, in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
That is not permission to sin.
It is evidence that human sin cannot defeat God’s redemptive purposes.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody needs to hear tonight.
Your failure does not have to write the final sentence.
Your betrayal does not have to become your identity.
Your wounds do not have to become your god.
Your marital status does not determine your worth.
Your past does not possess authority greater than the blood of Jesus Christ.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus does not merely cover our scandal so we can continue producing more of it.
He calls us to repent.
To turn.
To confess.
To forgive.
To seek wisdom.
To make restitution where appropriate.
To pursue holiness.
To tell the truth.
To put sin to death.
To love sacrificially.
To become, by the power of the Spirit, different people.
That is the difference between cheap religious sentiment and the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say, “What you did doesn’t matter.”
The Gospel says sin mattered enough that Christ went to the cross.
And grace is powerful enough that sin does not have to own you anymore.
So perhaps tonight the most spiritual thing you can do is not post another Bible verse.
Maybe it is putting the phone down and telling your spouse:
“I was wrong.”
Maybe it is confessing something you have hidden.
Maybe it is seeking pastoral counsel and qualified professional help.
Maybe it is establishing boundaries where serious harm has occurred.
Maybe it is choosing faithfulness when nobody would ever know if you compromised.
Maybe it is finally admitting that you cannot heal your marriage through willpower.
Maybe your prayer tonight is only:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That prayer is not too small.
The tax collector in Jesus’ parable could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
And Jesus said that man went home justified.
This is Christianity.
Not impressive people proving themselves worthy of God.
Sinners coming empty-handed to Christ.
Be truthful. You can simply comment, “Jesus, change me.”
If your marriage is hurting and you do not know what comes next, comment, “Pray for us.”

And if you are single, widowed, divorced, or waiting, you are not a secondary Christian. Marriage is not the Gospel. Jesus is. Your completeness is not postponed until another human being chooses you.

Not because every sentence will apply today, but because covenant gets difficult, memories get selective, emotions become loud, and sometimes we need to return to truth when feelings are trying to rewrite it.
Not as an accusation toward your spouse. Not as a passive-aggressive message aimed at somebody.
And consider sending this privately to the person who would never publicly admit that they are struggling.
Salvation is by grace. The Gospel is not for sale.
Supporting Gospel work, however, can be one voluntary expression of Christian generosity and stewardship when done freely and joyfully.
Save what you may need again.
Follow so you can continue growing with us.
And above everything else, go back to Jesus.
Because the greatest lesson from the marriages of the Old Testament is not that good people always build perfect families.
They did not.
It is that humanity has always been desperately capable of turning covenant into chaos when the human heart wanders from God.
Yet across generations of flawed husbands, wounded wives, complicated families, terrible decisions, shattered trust, repentance, mercy, judgment, and astonishing grace, God kept writing.
He kept moving history toward Bethlehem.
Toward Calvary.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward Jesus.
And perhaps He is confronting your story now.
Not because every marriage will end the way we want.
Not because every broken relationship will necessarily be restored.
Not because repentance erases every earthly consequence.
But because nobody who comes to Jesus in repentance and faith has to remain the person sin made them.
The Bible never promised you a scandal-free human story.
It revealed something better:
a Savior powerful enough to redeem sinners inside one.
Your worst chapter may explain how you arrived here—but only Jesus has the authority to write who you become next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She loved him before the crown.
paragraphs: She loved him before the crown.
Before Jerusalem called him king. Before the throne. Before the royal palace. Before Israel sang about his victories until his name became impossible to ignore.
Michal loved David when he was still the young warrior standing beneath the dangerous shadow of her father.
And somehow, the woman Scripture explicitly tells us loved David would one day look through a window at the same man...
and despise him in her heart.
That should make us uncomfortable.
Because somewhere between “Michal loved David” and “Michal despised him,” something happened.
Actually, many things happened.
A murderous father.
A weaponized marriage.
A desperate escape.
Years of separation.
Another husband.
A forced reunion.
A kingdom.
Other wives.
Unspoken wounds.
And finally, one terrible conversation in which two people who once belonged to each other seemed incapable of reaching each other anymore.
This is not the tidy Bible romance many people expect.
It is a story about what can happen when love is dragged through fear, political ambition, separation, resentment, disappointment, and unresolved pain.
But more than that, it is a warning.
You can once love deeply and later become bitter.
You can once protect someone and later despise them.
You can survive the enemy outside your house while allowing something poisonous to grow inside your heart.
And perhaps the most frightening part is this:
You may not notice when love begins turning into contempt.
The first time Michal enters David's story by name, Scripture tells us something extraordinarily personal.
“Michal Saul’s daughter loved David.” (1 Samuel 18:20)
The Hebrew is striking:
וַתֶּאֱהַב מִיכַל בַּת־שָׁאוּל אֶת־דָּוִד
Vatte’ehav Mikhal bat-Sha’ul et-David.
“And Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved David.”
The verb comes from אָהַב — ’ahav — “to love.”
Scripture does not merely tell us that Michal married David.
It tells us she loved him.
But before we turn this into a romantic fairy tale, look at what happens immediately afterward.
Her father sees her love...
and recognizes an opportunity.

Saul had become jealous and afraid of David. David's victories were increasing. The people admired him. Saul understood that the LORD was with David, and the king who should have been shepherding Israel became increasingly obsessed with eliminating the man he perceived as a threat.
So when Saul learns that Michal loves David, he does not respond like a father protecting his daughter's heart.
He sees leverage.
“I will give him her, that she may be a snare to him.” (1 Samuel 18:21)
The Hebrew word translated “snare” is מוֹקֵשׁ — moqesh.
A trap.
Something designed to catch.
Something intended to destroy.
Think about the tragedy of that.
Michal's love became material for Saul's scheme.
Something beautiful in her heart was pulled into something ugly in his.

Saul demanded a dangerous bride-price from David involving the Philistines, apparently hoping David would die in the attempt. David survived and exceeded the requirement, and Michal became his wife (1 Samuel 18:25–27).
Even their wedding story had death hanging over it.
Then Saul tried to kill David.
And Michal did something that deserves to be remembered.
She saved her husband's life.
When Saul sent men to watch David's house and kill him, Michal warned him:
“If thou save not thy life to night, to morrow thou shalt be slain.” (1 Samuel 19:11)
Then she helped David escape through a window.
Do not rush past that scene.
Imagine the night.
Her father is king.
Her husband is hunted.
Soldiers are outside.
Michal has to choose.
And she chooses to help David live.
The woman who would later watch David through a window with contempt once used a window to save his life.
That detail is almost unbearably poetic.
One window witnessed love risking everything.
Another window would witness love collapsing into contempt.
David escaped.
But Michal remained behind.
And this is where romantic retellings can become dangerously simplistic.
David's life continued.
So did Michal's.
Saul eventually gave Michal, David's wife, to another man, Palti son of Laish (1 Samuel 25:44).
Years passed.
David acquired other wives.

Then, during the political negotiations surrounding David's growing kingdom, David demanded Michal's return, specifically identifying her as the wife he had obtained with the bride-price he had paid (2 Samuel 3:13–14).
The biblical narrator does not give us a private diary from Michal explaining what those years did to her.
So we should resist pretending Scripture tells us what it does not.
We do not know every emotion she carried.
We do not know whether she spent years longing for David, resenting David, grieving David, adapting to her new life, or moving through combinations of all of them.
But Scripture gives us one devastating image.
When Michal is taken away from Palti, he follows her.
Weeping.
“Her husband went with her along weeping behind her to Bahurim.” (2 Samuel 3:16)
Then Abner orders him to go back.
And he does.
That is one of those small biblical scenes that leaves a large ache.
No speech explains everything.
No narrator tells us precisely what Michal felt.
There is simply a woman being moved again through the political world of powerful men...
and a man walking behind her crying until he is commanded to turn around.
Then Michal is back with David.
But the David she receives is not the David she once helped through the window.
He is rising as king.
His household has changed.
His world has changed.
And Michal has changed too.
Then comes 2 Samuel 6.
The ark of the LORD is being brought toward Jerusalem.
David is celebrating before the LORD.
Scripture says:
“David danced before the LORD with all his might.” (2 Samuel 6:14)
The Hebrew uses the expression:
מְכַרְכֵּר בְּכָל־עֹז
mekharker bekhol-‘oz
David was vigorously whirling or dancing “with all his strength.”
This is not David performing at a royal banquet to impress dignitaries.
He is rejoicing before the LORD as the ark comes into the city.
The king is not ashamed to humble himself in celebration before his God.
And Michal sees him.
Through a window.
“When she saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD, she despised him in her heart.” (2 Samuel 6:16)
The Hebrew is even sharper:
וַתִּבֶז לוֹ בְּלִבָּהּ
vattivez lo belibbah.
“She despised him in her heart.”
The verb בָּזָה — bazah — carries the sense of regarding something as contemptible, insignificant, or unworthy.
Once:
She loved David.
Now:
She despised David.
Same woman.
Same man.
Different heart.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to look at someone you once loved and wonder:
What happened to us?
There was a time when you waited for their message.
Now their voice irritates you.
There was a time when you defended them.
Now you quietly collect evidence against them.
There was a time when their presence felt safe.
Now the room changes when they enter.
Maybe you are married.
Maybe divorced.
Maybe estranged from a parent.
Maybe wounded by a child.
Maybe betrayed by a friend.
Maybe disappointed by someone in church.
Maybe the person you resent is lying beside you every night and neither of you knows how to talk anymore.
Contempt rarely announces itself with trumpets.
It accumulates.
A disappointment here.
An unanswered wound there.
A conversation avoided.
An apology never offered.
A humiliation remembered.
A suspicion rehearsed.
A grievance fed in silence.
Until one day you are no longer merely hurt by someone.
You have begun looking down on them.
That is spiritually dangerous.
But we also have to be careful not to flatten Michal into the stereotype of “the bitter wife who hated worship.”
The biblical story is more complicated than that.
Michal had lived through her father's violent jealousy.
She had helped David escape an assassination attempt.
She had been separated from David.
Her father gave her to another man.
She was later taken from that man and returned to David.
Meanwhile, David's household included multiple wives.
None of that makes contempt righteous.
But biblical faithfulness requires us to acknowledge the whole story instead of turning a wounded human being into a cartoon villain.
Likewise, biblical faithfulness does not require pretending David was flawless.
David was God's anointed king, a man Scripture profoundly honors, and an ancestor in the royal line leading ultimately to Jesus Christ.
David was also a sinner.
The Bible does not sanitize him.
His later adultery with Bathsheba and orchestration of Uriah's death are condemned with terrifying clarity (2 Samuel 11–12). His household would experience devastating consequences.
Scripture's heroes are not our saviors.
Jesus is.
That distinction changes everything.
When Michal finally confronts David after the celebration, her words drip with sarcasm:
“How glorious was the king of Israel to day...” (2 Samuel 6:20)
She accuses him of exposing himself shamefully before the female servants.
