David responds that his celebration was “before the LORD,” who had chosen him rather than her father and Saul's house, and declares that he is willing to humble himself still further (2 Samuel 6:21–22).
This is not a gentle marital conversation.
You can almost hear years of history exploding underneath the words.
Michal attacks David's dignity.
David invokes God's rejection of her father's dynasty.
The argument is about what happened outside.
But it carries the weight of everything that happened before.
How many marriages do that?
You think you are arguing about dishes.
You are actually arguing about feeling unseen for seven years.
You think you are arguing about money.
You are actually arguing about trust.
You think you are arguing about a Facebook post.
You are actually bleeding from a wound nobody ever treated.
You think the problem started tonight.
But tonight merely opened the door to something that has been living in the house for years.
And Scripture ends Michal's story with one haunting sentence:
“Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death.” (2 Samuel 6:23)
We should say only what Scripture allows us to say.

The verse states that Michal remained childless until her death. The text does not explicitly explain every biological, relational, or theological mechanism behind that childlessness, so we should be cautious about confidently declaring details God did not reveal.
But literarily, the ending is devastating.
The woman introduced to us loving David disappears from the biblical narrative with barrenness and distance.
Love.
Separation.
Contempt.
Silence.
End.
And if that were the whole message, this would simply be one of Scripture's saddest marriage stories.
But Michal and David's fractured relationship exposes something much larger about the human condition.
We do not merely need better communication techniques.
We need redeemed hearts.
Because contempt is not only something that happens between husbands and wives.
We can despise people in our hearts while maintaining Christian appearances.
We can sing worship songs while resenting our spouse.
We can quote Scripture while secretly celebrating somebody's failure.
We can lift our hands on Sunday and refuse forgiveness on Monday.
We can post verses about grace while keeping a private courtroom inside our minds where the people who hurt us are retried every night.
Jesus goes straight for the heart.
“For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts...” (Matthew 15:19)
The Gospel does not merely renovate appearances.
Christ comes for the heart.
And this is where the story turns toward us.
Maybe you are Michal in this story.
You were hurt.
Moved around by circumstances you could not control.
Disappointed by people who should have protected you.
And somewhere along the way your pain hardened.
You stopped crying.
Then you stopped hoping.
Then you started despising.
Or maybe you are David.
You became so focused on the battle, the calling, the responsibility, the future, that you failed to notice what was dying close to home.
Maybe you can defend everything you did.
Maybe they can defend everything they felt.
And maybe your home is still bleeding.
The Gospel does not ask which biblical character you can use to justify yourself.
The Gospel asks whether you will bring your own heart to Jesus.
Because David cannot save Michal.
Michal cannot save David.
And neither can save you.
But the Son of David can.
Jesus Christ enters the story of humanity not as another flawed king trying to hold together a broken kingdom, but as the righteous King David could only foreshadow.
Where human kings fail, Jesus remains faithful.
Where human love becomes contaminated by selfishness, His love remains holy.
Where sin creates shame, Christ bears shame.
Where guilt demands judgment, Jesus carries judgment for sinners at the cross.
Where we deserve condemnation, grace opens a door through repentance and faith.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That does not mean every broken marriage will automatically be restored.
Scripture never gives us permission to make promises God has not made.

Reconciliation can require repentance, truth, wisdom, boundaries, accountability, safety, and time. Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil never happened, nor does it require remaining exposed to abuse or danger.
But no heart is beyond the reach of Christ.
The bitterness can be confessed.
The pride can be confessed.
The lust can be confessed.
The cruelty can be confessed.
The neglect can be confessed.
The secret messages can be confessed.
The emotional affair can be confessed.
The hatred can be confessed.
The coldness can be confessed.
The years of pretending can be confessed.
And at the cross, confession does not meet a Savior shocked by your scandal.
It meets the Savior who already knew.
Jesus knew what was hidden when He went to Calvary.
And He went anyway.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin so seriously that the Son of God bears its judgment, and loving sinners so deeply that forgiveness is offered through Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)
Maybe you have spent years looking through a window at somebody else's failures.
Jesus is asking you to look into your own heart.
Maybe you have memorized everything they did wrong.
What if tonight you finally asked:
“Lord, what is happening inside me?”
That prayer can be terrifying.
Because sometimes the person who wounded you really did sin against you.
And Jesus may still expose what bitterness has been doing to you afterward.
Their sin does not justify yours.
Your sin does not justify theirs.
At the cross, excuses die.
So does hopelessness.
This is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is mercy calling you home.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance, carrying the idea of a changed mind and turning that results in a changed direction.
Jesus does not call you to decorate the prison.
He calls you out.
Maybe your marriage still looks beautiful in photographs while dying privately.
Maybe nobody knows you have not really spoken in months.
Maybe intimacy disappeared.
Maybe trust was shattered.
Maybe you have started fantasizing about a life where the other person simply disappears.
Maybe your relationship ended years ago, but the bitterness followed you into every relationship afterward.
Maybe this is not about marriage at all.
Maybe when you read Michal's name, another face appeared in your mind.
Your father.
Your mother.
Your pastor.
Your former friend.
Your child.
Your ex.
The person who betrayed you.
The person you still cannot mention without feeling your body tense.
Do not confuse carrying bitterness with carrying justice.
God can handle justice.
You were never designed to drink poison every morning so you could remember who hurt you.
Bring the wound to Christ.
Bring the anger.
Bring the questions.
Bring the memories.
Bring the part of you that does not even want to forgive yet.
Tell Him the truth.
Christianity is not pretending.
The cross is where pretending ends.
Maybe your first honest prayer is only:
“Jesus, I don't know how to release this.”
Then start there.
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, forgive me. I have become cruel.”
Start there.
Maybe:
“Jesus, I still love them, but I don't know how to trust them.”
Start there.
Maybe:
“Jesus, I don't even know what I feel anymore.”
Start there.
He already knows.
The point is not to manufacture emotion.
The point is surrender.
Sit with it.
Pray.
Open 1 Samuel 18–19 and 25, then 2 Samuel 3 and 6 for yourself.
Read slowly.
Then ask God what your own heart has become.
You do not have to publish the details of your private pain. But sometimes three simple words are enough to stop hiding behind the illusion that everything is fine.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person walking through this kind of battle.
And if one particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider sending this to them.
Not as a weapon.
Not as a passive-aggressive accusation.
Not with, “See? This is you.”
Share it with the believer who has become cold.
Share it with the person who stopped going to church.
Share it with the seeker who thinks Christianity is about pretending Christians never fall apart.
And yes, share it with the unbeliever who needs to discover that the Bible does not hide human scandal—and that the Gospel is precisely about what God does with sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
There are truths you do not need only once.
There may come a night when an argument has just ended, the house is silent, your heart is furious, and you need to remember that contempt does not have to become your permanent address.
Supporting a Christian ministry does not purchase God's favor. It does not make someone more saved, more righteous, or more loved by God.
But freely supporting Gospel work that has genuinely strengthened your faith can be one practical expression of stewardship and partnership.
If this ministry has fed you spiritually, consider helping us feed someone else.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
But because somewhere in your circle may be a Michal looking through a window with a heart becoming harder every day.
Somewhere there may be a David who knows how to fight giants but has no idea what is happening inside his own home.
Somewhere there is a husband sleeping beside a wife who cries when he cannot hear her.
Somewhere there is a woman carrying ten years of resentment beneath a Sunday smile.
Somewhere there is a believer wondering whether Jesus still wants anything to do with them after what they have done.
They need to know.
The answer is not David.
The answer is not Michal.
The answer is Jesus.
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores what sin has corrupted in the heart.
Jesus gives new life.
Jesus does not promise that every earthly relationship will end exactly the way we want.
He promises something infinitely greater to everyone who truly belongs to Him:
He will not abandon the work of redemption He has begun.
So before you close this...
look through the window one more time.
Not Michal's window.
Your own.
Who have you begun to despise?
What wound have you allowed to become your identity?
What sin are you defending because somebody else sinned first?
What conversation have you avoided?
What confession have you postponed?
What part of your heart have you refused to place before Christ?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Do not waste the conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy in Michal's story is not merely that a marriage fell apart.
It is that Scripture lets us see how far the human heart can travel—from love to contempt.
But your story is still being written.
The cross stands in the middle of human scandal and declares that sin does not get the final word over everyone who turns to Christ.
Grace does.
So repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek wise help where restoration requires help.
Establish safety where danger exists.
Tell the truth.
Stop performing.
Stop hiding.
And run to Jesus.
The woman who once helped David escape through a window would eventually watch him through another window and despise the man she once loved.
Never underestimate what an untreated wound can become.
But never underestimate what Jesus can do with a heart finally surrendered to Him.
Your wound may explain part of your story.
Your sin may have scarred part of your story.
Your failure may have darkened part of your story.
But none of them deserves the final sentence.
Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BARRENNESS WAS PAINFUL IN SCRIPTURE—BUT IT WAS NEVER PROOF THAT GOD HAD ABANDONED YOU
paragraphs: BARRENNESS WAS PAINFUL IN SCRIPTURE—BUT IT WAS NEVER PROOF THAT GOD HAD ABANDONED YOU

Some of the women who carried the deepest ache in Scripture were not forgotten by God. And if you have ever mistaken an unanswered prayer for evidence that God has walked away from you, you need to stay with this until the end.
There is a kind of pain that becomes especially difficult to explain when everybody around you seems to be receiving the very thing you have begged God for.
You smile at their announcement.
Then cry when you get home.
You congratulate them.
Then stare at the ceiling at 2:17 in the morning wondering why heaven seems to have remembered everybody except you.
Another pregnancy.
Another birth.
Another family photograph.
Another prayer answered for somebody else.
And somewhere underneath the smile you have learned to wear is a question you may be afraid to say aloud:
“God… did You forget me?”
Maybe your barrenness is physical.
Maybe you have prayed for a child until you no longer know what words to use.
Maybe you have watched months become years.

Maybe you have experienced the grief of infertility, miscarriage, failed treatments, unanswered questions, or the unbearable awkwardness of people asking when you are going to have children as though they were asking what you planned to eat for dinner.
Or perhaps your barrenness has another name.
The marriage that never came.
The marriage that collapsed.
The ministry that never grew.
The business that died.
The reconciliation that has not happened.
The child who still has not returned to Christ.
The prayer you have prayed so many times that lately you have begun wondering whether God is tired of hearing it.
Whatever form it takes, barrenness can whisper a terrible theology into a wounded heart:
“If God loved you, this would have happened by now.”
But Scripture refuses to let that lie stand.
Because when you actually open the Bible, something astonishing happens.
You discover women whose empty wombs became places of profound anguish—but whose emptiness was never sufficient evidence that God had abandoned them.
Sarah knew barrenness.
Rebekah knew barrenness.
Rachel knew barrenness.
Hannah knew barrenness.
Elizabeth knew barrenness.
And these are not insignificant footnotes hiding in obscure corners of Scripture.
Their stories stand inside the unfolding history of redemption.
The Bible does not sanitize their pain.
It lets us hear it.
Rachel's anguish becomes almost unbearable in Genesis 30:1:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Those words are not polished religious language.
They sound like pain.
Rachel watched Leah bear children while she remained childless, and comparison turned suffering into something even sharper. Genesis tells us that Rachel envied her sister.
That detail matters.
Because the Bible is remarkably honest about what prolonged disappointment can do inside the human heart.
Pain can become envy.
Waiting can become anger.
Silence can become suspicion.
Somebody else's blessing can suddenly feel like evidence against you.
And perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
You love your friend.
You really do.
But when she tells you she is pregnant, something breaks inside you.
Then guilt arrives because you think a good Christian should only feel happiness.
So now you are carrying two wounds instead of one:
the grief itself…
and the shame of how grief has affected you.
Scripture does not hide Rachel's struggle.
It records it.
And yet Rachel's anguish was not proof that she had vanished from God's sight.
Genesis 30:22 eventually says something breathtaking:
“God remembered Rachel.”
The Hebrew language behind the idea of remembering is important. The verb is זָכַר — zākar — “to remember.”
But when Scripture says God “remembered” someone, it does not mean God had suffered a lapse of memory and suddenly thought, “Oh, Rachel! I forgot she existed.”
God does not misplace His children.
Biblical “remembering” often points toward God acting faithfully in accordance with His purposes and covenant.
The waiting woman had never disappeared from His sight.
And that distinction may be exactly what somebody reading this needs tonight:
God's delay is not proof of God's amnesia.
Then there is Hannah.
Few passages portray the emotional violence of infertility more honestly than 1 Samuel 1.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
And Hannah did not suffer privately in some protected corner where nobody could touch the wound.
Her rival provoked her.
Repeatedly.
Scripture says this happened “year by year.”
Think about those words.
Year.
By.
Year.
Not one difficult afternoon.
Not one disappointing month.
A recurring wound.
A repeated humiliation.
A pain that returned with the calendar.
And Hannah wept.
She could not eat.
Her heart was grieving.
Eventually she entered the presence of God carrying so much anguish that the priest Eli misunderstood what he was witnessing.
1 Samuel 1:10 says she was “in bitterness of soul” and “prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.”
There is a Hebrew expression behind this description of Hannah's condition: מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — marat nāfesh — conveying the idea of deep bitterness or anguish of soul.
This was not mild disappointment.
Hannah was devastated.
Yet watch what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Hannah's tears proved she had no faith.
It does not say her infertility proved God hated her.
It does not say childlessness made her less valuable than Peninnah.
And it certainly does not authorize Christians today to look at an infertile woman and assume that hidden sin, weak faith, insufficient prayer, or divine rejection must explain her suffering.
That conclusion is not ours to make.
The text does say that the LORD had closed Hannah's womb, which means we should not soften Scripture merely because the statement makes modern readers uncomfortable.
God is sovereign.
But divine sovereignty and divine abandonment are not the same thing.
That distinction is enormous.
A season you cannot understand is not automatically evidence that God has rejected you.
And the biblical story makes something else clear.
Hannah was still praying.
Still going to the house of the LORD.
Still pouring out her soul.
Still bringing the wound toward God rather than pretending it did not exist.
She did not come before Him with Instagram-ready faith.
She came crying.
Her prayer was messy enough to be misunderstood.
And God was not frightened by it.
Perhaps you have been trying to sound spiritual when what you actually need to do is tell God the truth.
“Lord, I am jealous.”
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I don't understand.”
“Lord, watching them receive what I prayed for hurts.”
“Lord, I know You are good, but right now I cannot understand what You are doing.”
That is not permission to accuse God of evil.
It is permission to stop pretending before the God who already knows your heart.
Biblical faith is not emotional dishonesty.
The Psalms prove that repeatedly.
Faith can weep.
Faith can lament.
Faith can ask how long.
Faith can tremble while still reaching toward God.
Then centuries later, another woman appears in the Gospel of Luke.
Elizabeth.
Luke 1:6 gives us a detail that should permanently destroy the cruel idea that infertility automatically reveals spiritual failure.
Elizabeth and Zechariah are described as righteous before God, walking faithfully in His commandments.
And the next verse tells us:
“But they had no child, because that Elisabeth was barren, and they both were now well stricken in years.”
Do not rush past the sequence.
Faithful.
And childless.
The Greek word used for “barren” is στεῖρα — steira.
Luke does not present Elizabeth's condition as proof that she was spiritually defective.
In fact, he has just told us something about the couple's faithfulness.
That should make us extraordinarily careful about the things Christians say to suffering people.
“Maybe you haven't prayed enough.”
“Maybe you need more faith.”
“Maybe there is some secret sin.”
“Maybe you haven't claimed the promise.”
Those words can crush people.
And unless Scripture gives us grounds to diagnose someone's suffering that way, we have no authority to manufacture explanations God has not revealed.

Jesus Himself dismantles simplistic equations between suffering and personal guilt elsewhere in Scripture. In John 9, when the disciples encountered a man blind from birth and immediately wanted to know whose sin had caused the condition, Jesus refused their simplistic diagnosis.
Not every wound is a secret code revealing that somebody has been rejected by God.
Not every empty place is divine punishment.
Not every delay means denial.
And not every prayer will be answered in the precise manner we desire.
That last sentence matters.
Because there is a dangerous way to preach Sarah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elizabeth.
We can turn their stories into a formula:
“They waited and eventually had babies, so if you believe enough, you will too.”
That sounds encouraging.
But Scripture never gives us permission to make that universal promise.
The Bible records miraculous conceptions.
It does not promise every infertile believer biological children in this present life.
We must never transform a description of what God did for one person into a guarantee God has made to everyone.
Otherwise we eventually place a crushing burden on the person whose prayer remains unanswered.
They begin thinking:
“Maybe my faith wasn't strong enough.”
No.
The Gospel gives you something deeper than a formula for obtaining the life you imagined.
It gives you Christ.
And this is where the story becomes bigger than fertility.
Because every human being eventually encounters a place where life does not unfold according to the script we wrote.
Some receive children.
Some do not.
Some marry.
Some remain single.
Some experience dramatic healing.
Some faithfully endure chronic suffering.
Some prayers receive answers that leave entire families celebrating.
Other prayers leave faithful Christians holding mysteries they will not understand on this side of eternity.
Christian hope cannot therefore rest on the promise that God will always give us the particular earthly outcome we desire.
It rests on something infinitely stronger.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He took flesh.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the rejected.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He carried sorrow.
And ultimately He walked toward a Roman cross.
There, something that looked like catastrophic defeat became the center of redemption.
The Messiah was mocked.
Stripped.
Wounded.
Crucified.
The disciples watched their hopes bleed.
Then came the tomb.
Sealed.
Silent.
Dark.
If appearances alone were trustworthy, Friday looked like abandonment.
But Sunday was coming.
The stone moved.
Christ rose.
Death did not get the final word.
Sin did not get the final word.
Shame did not get the final word.
The grave did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior message:
Not because Jesus promises to rewrite every earthly circumstance exactly the way we request.
But because everyone who belongs to Christ is being carried toward a redemption deeper than any temporary circumstance can destroy.
Your identity is not “the barren woman.”
Your identity is not “the man whose marriage failed.”
Not “the woman nobody chose.”
Not “the couple who couldn't conceive.”
Not “the parent whose child walked away.”
Not “the Christian whose prayer still hasn't been answered.”
If you are in Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Adopted into God's family.
Loved because of Christ, not because your life resembles somebody else's testimony.
And perhaps this is where the knife reaches the deepest place.
Because sometimes what we desperately want from God slowly becomes the thing we believe we need in order to know that God loves us.
A baby.
A spouse.
Healing.
Money.
Recognition.
A restored relationship.
A breakthrough.
And without realizing it, our prayer changes from:
“God, I deeply desire this…”
to:
“God, unless You give me this, I cannot believe You are good.”
That is where disappointment can become spiritual danger.
The gift begins competing with the Giver.
And Jesus loves us too deeply to tell us that our salvation depends upon receiving every earthly gift we desperately desire.
The cross has already settled the question of whether God moved toward undeserving sinners in love.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Look at Calvary when circumstances tempt you to ask whether God cares.
Look at the pierced hands of Christ.
You may not understand His providence.
You may not understand the timing.
You may never receive a complete explanation for some suffering in this life.
Christianity does not require us to pretend otherwise.
But the Gospel announces that God has acted decisively in Jesus Christ to save sinners.
And that means your greatest need is not finally fertility.
It is not marriage.
It is not success.
It is reconciliation with God.
Sin is the deepest barrenness of humanity.
We were not merely disappointed people needing improved circumstances.
We were sinners needing redemption.
We could not rescue ourselves.
Religion could not cleanse us.
Good works could not erase our guilt.
Then Jesus came.
The righteous One for the unrighteous.
The spotless Lamb for the guilty.
The Savior for sinners.
He carried our sins to the cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
Grace entered the scandal.
Mercy entered the failure.
Life entered the grave.
And now the invitation is not “be impressive enough for God to accept you.”
It is repent and believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Bring the sin.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the resentment.
Bring the secret anger.
Bring the sexual sin.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the years of pretending.
Bring the disappointment you were afraid to admit.
Bring the questions.
Bring the tears.
Bring the barren places.
But come to Jesus.
Maybe you have been angry with God for years.
Tell Him the truth and repent where that pain has turned into unbelief or sin.
Maybe you have compared your life with everyone else's until gratitude has almost disappeared.
Confess it.
Maybe you have quietly hated people whose blessings reminded you of your emptiness.
Confess it.
Maybe church became unbearable because everybody else's testimony sounded like an accusation against your life.
Come back to Christ.
Not to performance.
Not to pretending.
To Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished Christian response.
Three words.
That is enough.
Or comment, “I'm still fighting,” if your faith has been bruised but you refuse to walk away from Jesus.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer crying behind a smiling profile picture.
And if God has carried you through infertility, miscarriage, prolonged singleness, unanswered prayer, or another season of deep waiting, share whatever part of your testimony you can share wisely.
Not because everyone's story will end like yours.
But because somebody needs to hear how Christ sustained you when the answer had not arrived.
This is what Christian community can look like.
Not pretending.
Bearing burdens.
Weeping with those who weep.
Pointing wounded people toward Christ.
And please hear this carefully if you know someone struggling with infertility.
Do not turn their womb into a theological investigation.
Do not demand explanations.
Do not promise what God has not promised.
Do not tell them, “Your miracle is definitely coming,” as though you have access to God's hidden decree.
Do not use Hannah as a weapon.
Sit with them.
Pray with them.
Weep with them.
Remind them of what Scripture actually promises.
Christ will not abandon His people.
Nothing can separate those in Christ from the love of God revealed in Him.
There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
God is working toward the ultimate good of conforming His people to the image of His Son.
Christ will raise His people.
Christ will return.
Christ will make all things new.
Those promises are strong enough to carry grieving Christians without inventing promises Scripture never made.
And if your own body has become the place where your grief lives, hear this too:
Your worth is not measured by your reproductive capacity.
Motherhood is beautiful.
Fatherhood is beautiful.
Children are gifts from God.
But biological parenthood is not the entrance requirement for the kingdom of heaven.
Jesus Christ Himself never married and never fathered biological children.
The apostle Paul could speak positively about singleness.
The New Testament does not construct human worth around fertility.
Our final hope is not the continuation of our biological bloodline.
Our hope is resurrection.
That changes everything.
It means Christianity can honor the longing for children without turning children into gods.
It can grieve infertility without treating infertile people as incomplete human beings.
It can pray boldly for conception while refusing to manipulate grieving couples with false guarantees.
It can celebrate miraculous answers while standing faithfully beside those whose stories unfold differently.
That is mature hope.
Hope with tears in its eyes.
Hope that refuses counterfeit certainty.
Hope anchored not in an outcome…
but in a Person.
Jesus.
Perhaps you began reading this thinking about an empty womb.
But somewhere along the way another empty place came to mind.
The prayer.
The marriage.
The child.
The diagnosis.
The dream.
The silence.
And perhaps you have interpreted that emptiness as God's verdict on you.
Look again.
An empty place is not automatically an abandoned place.
Hannah wept in an empty place.
Rachel cried from an empty place.
Elizabeth lived faithfully through an empty place.
And at the very center of Christianity stands another empty place:
an empty tomb.
The emptiness that appeared to announce the end became evidence that death had been defeated.
That does not mean every empty place in your life will become the earthly miracle you desire.
It means emptiness does not have authority to tell you who God is.
Jesus does.
The cross does.
The resurrection does.
So cry if you need to cry.
Seek appropriate medical care if infertility is part of your story.
Receive wise pastoral care.
Talk with trusted believers.
Lament honestly.
Pray boldly.
And surrender the outcome to God without pretending surrender means the desire no longer hurts.
There is no shame in saying:
“Father, I still want this.”
There is also profound faith in eventually adding:
“But Jesus, even here, You are still my Lord.”
That sentence may cost you tears.
Say it anyway.
Because Christianity was never about forcing God to become the supporting character in the life story we planned.
It is about being reconciled to God through Christ and learning to say with our whole lives:
Jesus is enough to be Lord even when I do not understand what He has permitted me to carry.
Send it privately to the couple who may be hurting quietly.
Share it with the believer who thinks unanswered prayer means God has rejected them.
Not as pressure. Not as superstition. Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God—nothing we do purchases grace.
Share because truth is worth carrying to wounded people.
One share can place the Gospel in front of someone whose suffering you know nothing about.
There may come a night when you need these truths again.
We want it to help sustain a growing work of biblical nourishment, discipleship, spiritual sharpening, Gospel proclamation, and Christ-centered resources.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting your salvation.
Your share cannot forgive you.
Your comment cannot cleanse you.
Your generosity cannot purchase God's favor.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His righteousness can make sinners right with God.
Only His resurrection gives us living hope.
That is why everything must return to Him.
If you have never truly surrendered to Jesus Christ, perhaps the deepest question raised by this article is not whether God will give you the thing you have been asking for.
It is whether you belong to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding behind religion.
Stop bargaining.
Stop waiting until you become “good enough.”
You will never clean yourself enough to make the cross unnecessary.
Come to Jesus because the cross is necessary.
Come because grace is real.
Come because sinners can be forgiven.
Come because shame does not have to write your final chapter.
Come because the Savior who died for sinners rose from the grave.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become testimony.
Let somebody scrolling through darkness discover hundreds of human beings saying, in different ways:
“I hurt too.”
“I waited too.”
“I questioned too.”
“But Jesus met me there.”
Because maybe the sentence you need to carry away from this entire article is not complicated at all.

The place where nothing seems to be growing may still be a place where God has never stopped seeing you—and even when He does not give the ending you asked for, the scars of Jesus forbid us from calling His redeeming love indifferent.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: POLYGAMY IN THE BIBLE: Permission, Regulation, or a Record of Human Brokenness?
paragraphs: POLYGAMY IN THE BIBLE: Permission, Regulation, or a Record of Human Brokenness?

Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had two wives and two concubines. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why do Christians insist that biblical marriage points to one man and one woman? The answer is more uncomfortable—and far more beautiful—than either side of the argument usually admits.
There is a question hiding inside some of the most scandalous marriages in Scripture.
And if we are afraid to ask it, we may never understand what the Bible is actually doing.
If polygamy is wrong, why does the Bible contain so much of it?
Why doesn't God strike Abraham dead when Hagar enters his tent?
Why does Jacob become the father of the twelve tribes while living inside a painfully complicated household involving Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah?
Why does Scripture call David a man after God's own heart while refusing to erase the women accumulated around his throne?
Why does the Law of Moses contain instructions dealing with a man who has more than one wife?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
Does the Bible's regulation of polygamy mean God approved of it?
Stay with that question.

Because buried beneath the marriages, rivalries, pregnancies, tears, jealousies, kings, concubines, commandments, and broken households is something much bigger than an argument about ancient marriage.
It is the story of what God does when His perfect design collides with human brokenness.
And ultimately, it is the story of Jesus.
The Bible begins marriage in a garden.
Not in Abraham's tent.
Not in Jacob's household.
Not in David's palace.
Not in Solomon's enormous royal harem.
In Eden.

Before sin entered the world, before power corrupted kings, before lust distorted covenant, before women became bargaining pieces in political alliances, God established something astonishingly simple.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew is worth seeing:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzāḇ-’îš ’eṯ-’āḇîw wə’eṯ-’immōw, wəḏāḇaq bə’ištōw, wəhāyū ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
A man leaves.
He dābaq—clings, holds fast—to his wife.
And they become basar echad...
בָשָׂר אֶחָד
“One flesh.”
Notice where Scripture begins.
One man.
His wife.
One covenantal union.
One flesh.
That matters because when Jesus was later confronted with a controversy about marriage and divorce, He did something extraordinarily revealing.
He did not begin with Abraham.
He did not point to Jacob.
He did not cite David's household.
He certainly did not appeal to Solomon.
Jesus went backward.
Past Moses.
Past Israel's kings.
Past patriarchal customs.
Back to creation.
He said:

“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female... For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?”
Then Christ said:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh.”
The Greek of Matthew 19:5 contains the unmistakable phrase:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dýo eis sárka mían
“the two into one flesh.”
And then Jesus says:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω
What God has joined together, let man not separate.
Jesus' method matters enormously.
When human relationships had become tangled in centuries of sin, customs, concessions, arguments, and legal questions, Christ pointed His listeners back to the beginning.
Back to what God intended before humanity began rewriting the arrangement.
That gives us an essential principle for reading difficult biblical narratives:
Everything the Bible records is not necessarily everything the Bible recommends.
That distinction changes everything.
The Bible tells us Cain murdered Abel.
That does not mean Scripture approves murder.
The Bible tells us Noah became drunk.
That does not make drunkenness God's design.
The Bible tells us David committed adultery with Bathsheba and orchestrated Uriah's death.
Recording David's sin is not endorsing David's sin.
Scripture is brutally honest about its heroes because the Bible is not propaganda for human greatness.
It is revelation of God's holiness and man's desperate need for redemption.
And that is precisely why the polygamous households of Scripture deserve careful reading.
Consider Abraham.
God had promised him offspring.
Years passed.
The promise seemed impossible.
Sarai was barren.
Then Genesis 16 records the moment human impatience tried to accomplish God's promise through human engineering.
Sarai gave Hagar to Abram.
Hagar conceived.
And almost immediately the house fractured.
Genesis does not give us a romantic portrait of expanded marriage.
It gives us contempt.
Pain.
Jealousy.
Blame.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
Eventually, a woman and her son are sent into the wilderness.
You can read that story merely as ancient history.
Or you can hear its warning.
When human beings refuse to trust God's timing, they often create wounds that God's grace must later enter and redeem.
Then comes Jacob.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban's deception he first received Leah.
Then Rachel.
Then Bilhah.
Then Zilpah.
Children entered the household through multiple women, and the home became a battlefield of longing and comparison.
One woman desperate to be loved.
Another desperate for children.
Servants drawn into a competition they did not create.
Sons growing up inside the emotional fallout.
Genesis 30 even records Rachel crying to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
That does not sound like paradise.
It sounds painfully human.
The tragedy is not simply that several women shared one husband.
It is that human beings created in God's image were caught in a system of rivalry, favoritism, insecurity, bargaining, jealousy, and pain.
And Scripture refuses to airbrush any of it.
Leah knows what it feels like to lie beside a man whose heart belongs somewhere else.
Rachel knows what it feels like to watch another woman hold babies while her own arms remain empty.
Jacob's children learn what favoritism feels like.
Eventually one favored son receives a special garment, his brothers burn with resentment, and Joseph is sold.
Broken relationships have consequences.
Sin rarely stays inside the room where it began.
It leaks under the door.
It reaches children.
It shapes families.
It becomes inheritance.
And suddenly the question “Did biblical people practice polygamy?” feels much smaller than the question the narratives themselves force us to confront:
What happened to the people inside those households?
But then someone opens Exodus and says:
Wait.
God's Law actually regulates a situation involving another wife.
Correct.
And we should not hide it.
Exodus 21:10 contains this Hebrew:
אִם־אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח־לוֹ שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע
’Im-’aḥereṯ yiqqaḥ-lō...
“If he takes another...”
The command continues by protecting the first woman's food, clothing, and marital rights from being diminished.
That is significant.
But regulation is not necessarily celebration.
A law addressing a broken social reality does not automatically declare that reality to be the creational ideal.
Sometimes law restrains damage in a world where human beings are already doing damage.
And Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive key.
When discussing divorce in Matthew 19, His opponents appeal to Moses.
Jesus responds that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts.
Then comes one of the most important sentences for this entire discussion:
“but from the beginning it was not so.”
There it is.
A distinction between God's creational pattern and accommodations made within a fallen human world.
The Law can meet broken people inside broken structures while still pointing beyond those structures to something better.
That means we should be extremely careful about arguing:
“God regulated it, therefore God idealized it.”
Those are not identical claims.
Consider this.
If vulnerable women were already living within polygynous households in the ancient world, what would happen if God's Law simply ignored them?
Who would protect the woman displaced by another wife?
Who would protect her food?
Her clothing?
Her marital rights?
Regulation can function as restraint.
It can place boundaries around human behavior precisely because human beings cannot be trusted to use power without harming someone.
And then Deuteronomy gives us something even more direct.
Israel's future king is warned:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Wəlō yarbeh-lō nāšîm, wəlō yāsūr ləḇāḇō.
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Read those words again.
Do not multiply wives...
lest his heart turn away.
Then watch what happens to Solomon.
The king famous for wisdom becomes the living demonstration of the warning he should have obeyed.
First Kings records that Solomon had seven hundred wives of royal status and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
It is almost impossible to comprehend.
But Scripture does not conclude:
“Look how blessed Solomon was because he possessed so many women.”
It says his wives turned his heart away.
The king who built the temple allowed his heart to become a sanctuary for other gods.
The man with almost unimaginable romantic access could not remain faithful to the God who gave him everything.
And that should disturb us.
Because Solomon's story exposes something modern people still struggle to admit:
Having more does not mean being more satisfied.
More bodies cannot cure a divided heart.
More sexual access cannot heal spiritual emptiness.
More attention cannot manufacture faithfulness.
More relationships cannot replace communion with God.
You can possess what the world envies and still lose what your soul needs most.
Solomon had a kingdom.
Solomon had wealth.
Solomon had power.
Solomon had women.
Solomon had reputation.
Solomon had wisdom.
And still his heart wandered.
Maybe that is where this ancient discussion suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because you may never have seven hundred wives.
But you can still have a Solomon heart.
A heart that always needs another.
Another relationship.
Another flirtation.
Another secret conversation.
Another fantasy.
Another image.
Another person giving you attention.
Another notification.
Another escape.
Another hidden tab.
Another emotional affair.
Another excuse.
Another thing you tell yourself you deserve because nobody knows how lonely you have been.
Polygamy may feel like an ancient subject.
The divided heart is not.
That is the real danger.
We can debate Abraham while hiding Hagar in our own phones.
We can condemn Solomon while secretly multiplying substitutes for God.
We can defend biblical marriage publicly while betraying covenant privately.
We can know the Hebrew word for “one” and still live with two lives.
One at church.
Another in secret.
One your spouse sees.
Another your browser knows.
One your family knows.
Another God sees.
And perhaps that is why this question cannot remain academic.
Scripture is not merely asking what Abraham did.
It is asking what your heart is doing.
The scandal of the Bible is not that it contains broken people.
The scandal is how much those broken people resemble us.
We want a sanitized Bible filled with heroes who never failed because then we can keep Christianity safely at a distance.
But God gives us Abraham stumbling.
Jacob deceiving.
Judah failing.
David lusting.
Solomon wandering.
Peter denying.
Thomas doubting.
Paul remembering that he once persecuted Christ's church.
Why?
Because if Scripture were the story of flawless people reaching a flawless God, there would be no hope for people like us.
The Bible is something far more glorious.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing sinners.
It is the story of promises surviving human stupidity.
It is the story of grace entering households already damaged by sin.
It is the story of God refusing to abandon His redemptive purposes even when His people make a catastrophe of their lives.
And all those broken roads eventually lead somewhere.
To Jesus Christ.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit His bride.
The King whose heart cannot be seduced away from His Father.
The faithful One standing where unfaithful humanity failed.
And when the New Testament speaks of marriage at its deepest theological level, Paul takes us somewhere breathtaking.
Ephesians 5 quotes Genesis:
“For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.”
Then Paul says:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Suddenly marriage is bigger than romance.
Bigger than companionship.
Bigger than sex.
Bigger even than family.
Marriage becomes a living sign pointing toward Christ's covenant love for His people.
Jesus does not collect brides because one bride is no longer interesting enough.
He does not become bored with His church and search for something newer.
He does not abandon His covenant when His bride becomes difficult.
He loves.
He gives Himself.
He sanctifies.
He cleanses.
He remains faithful.
At the cross, Christ does not merely tell us what covenant faithfulness looks like.
He bleeds it.
That is the center.
Not Abraham.
Not Jacob.
Not David.
Not Solomon.
Jesus.
Christian ethics cannot be built by asking, “What is the worst behavior I can find a biblical character doing without immediately being struck dead?”
That is a disastrously low way to read Scripture.
The Christian question is:
What does creation reveal?
What does God's law reveal?
What do the consequences of human sin reveal?
What does Jesus teach?
What does the Gospel restore?
What does Christ call His redeemed people to become?
That is why the presence of polygamy in Scripture should not embarrass Christians.
If anything, the Bible's refusal to conceal these households should strengthen our confidence in its moral seriousness.
Scripture shows humanity as humanity actually is.
Beautiful.
Created in God's image.
Capable of covenant.
And catastrophically bent by sin.
The Bible does not need its heroes to be innocent because its ultimate Hero is Jesus.
And maybe you needed to hear that for reasons having nothing to do with polygamy.
Maybe your own story is complicated.
Maybe your marriage has scars.

Maybe your family tree contains adultery, divorce, abandonment, abuse, betrayal, children from different relationships, secret affairs, sexual sin, pornography, resentment, or years you desperately wish you could erase.
Maybe when Christians talk about “biblical families,” you quietly feel like yours could never qualify.
Listen carefully.
The Bible is full of families that would make many churches uncomfortable.
God does not redeem imaginary families.
He redeems real people.
People with histories.
People with consequences.
People who made terrible decisions.
People wounded by decisions they never made.
People carrying shame from bedrooms nobody else knows about.
People who cannot go backward and make everything clean.
And that is precisely where grace becomes more than a religious word.
Grace does not mean sin did not matter.
Grace means sin does not get the final word.
Repentance is not pretending the past was acceptable.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who already knows the entire truth.
Jesus did not die because our scandals were small.
He died because our sin was deadly.
And He rose because death itself would not have the last word over those who belong to Him.
So if you have been unfaithful...
repent.
If you have been living two lives...
bring the hidden one into the light.
If lust has been multiplying inside you...
stop feeding what is starving your soul.
If you have used another human being to medicate your loneliness...
come back to Christ.
If you have been wounded by someone else's betrayal...
do not mistake their sin for your worth.
If your family story is complicated...
do not assume it is beyond redemption.
Jesus specializes in walking into stories human beings thought were already ruined.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Hagar still wept.
Leah still knew rejection.
David's family still suffered devastating consequences.
Solomon's kingdom still fractured.
Grace is not a time machine.
Grace is something better.
Grace is God entering the wreckage and refusing to let wreckage have the final word.
That is the Gospel.
Not “your choices never mattered.”
Not “sin isn't serious.”
Not “God approves whatever makes us happy.”
The Gospel says something far more powerful:
You were more lost than you wanted to admit, and in Christ you are more loved than you dared to hope.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
The sinner does not save himself by rewriting the definition of sin.
God saves sinners through the blood of His Son.
And resurrection means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
This is why the theme of Gospel Warrior will always come back to the same breathtaking truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling the scandal righteous.
By redeeming the sinner.
Not by pretending brokenness is God's design.
By restoring broken people toward His design.
Not by erasing truth.
By joining truth and grace in the person of Jesus Christ.
So was polygamy in the Bible permission, regulation, or a record of human brokenness?
The most careful answer requires us to distinguish those categories.
Scripture undeniably records polygamy.
The Mosaic law regulates circumstances in which multiple wives existed and protects vulnerable people within those circumstances.
Deuteronomy explicitly restrains Israel's king from multiplying wives.
The narratives repeatedly expose rivalry, favoritism, jealousy, family fragmentation, and spiritual danger within prominent plural households.
Genesis presents the foundational one-flesh union.
And when Jesus explains marriage, He reaches behind fallen customs and legal controversies to that beginning: the two become one flesh.
That is why description must never automatically become prescription.
Regulation must never automatically become idealization.
And brokenness must never be confused with creation.
But do not finish this article thinking the point was merely to win an argument about polygamy.
The deeper question is sitting much closer to home.
What have you normalized simply because God has not destroyed you for it?
What have you mistaken for permission because grace gave you another morning?
What compromise have you defended because somebody in the Bible also failed?
What secret multiplication is dividing your heart?
What would happen if, instead of asking how close you can live to brokenness, you asked how completely you can surrender to Christ?
Be honest.
Tell the truth.

And if Christ has already brought you through sexual brokenness, betrayal, family chaos, or a season you once believed would destroy you, consider sharing your testimony without exposing details that belong in private. Somebody reading quietly may need to know that repentance is real, forgiveness is real, healing is possible, and Jesus is still restoring people.

Not because every sentence must be agreed with without opening your Bible, but because difficult questions deserve more than slogans. Return to Genesis 2. Read Genesis 16. Read Genesis 29–30. Read Exodus 21. Read Deuteronomy 17. Read 1 Kings 11. Read Matthew 19. Read Ephesians 5.
Test everything by Scripture.
Send it privately to someone who has been carrying shame and needs to hear that Jesus does not require a spotless past before He calls someone to repentance.
You do not prove your salvation by supporting a ministry.
Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be put behind a paywall.

But if this ministry is bearing genuine spiritual fruit in your life, supporting it voluntarily can help us keep producing and distributing Christ-centered resources so more people can encounter biblical truth. Sharing the article costs nothing, yet it may put the Gospel in front of someone who would never walk into a church.
Do it because you believe biblical truth should keep moving.
Do it because another exhausted believer needs encouragement.
Because another confused Christian needs Scripture.
Because another prodigal needs to hear that the Father's house is not closed.
Because another wounded marriage needs truth and grace.
Because another person scrolling at 2:00 in the morning may be one article away from finally whispering:
“Jesus... I need You.”
Open your Bible.
Turn from sin.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Seek help where wisdom requires help.
Bring darkness into the light.
Love your spouse faithfully.
Protect the vulnerable.
Stop using grace as permission to remain unchanged.
And run to Jesus.
Someone carrying sexual shame.
Someone who thinks their past disqualifies them.
Someone angry at the Bible because nobody ever explained passages like these honestly.
Someone wondering whether Jesus would still want them if He knew everything.
He already knows.
That is what makes grace so staggering.
The cross was never God's reward for people who successfully hid their scandals.
It was God's rescue mission for sinners who could never save themselves.
So comment.
Share.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because Abraham could not save you.
Jacob could not save you.
David could not save you.
Solomon—with all his wisdom—could not save you.
Only Christ can.
And perhaps the greatest miracle in all of Scripture is not that God managed to use people with complicated stories.
It is that He still does.
Your scandal may explain some of your scars, but it does not get to write the last sentence—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The “I AM” Statements of Jesus—and What John Wants You to See
paragraphs: The “I AM” Statements of Jesus—and What John Wants You to See

He did not merely tell hungry people where to find bread, frightened people where to find safety, grieving people how to cope with death, or lost people which road to take. Again and again, Jesus pointed to Himself—and said, “I AM.” John wants you to understand why.
There are moments in Scripture when two ordinary words suddenly become almost unbearably heavy.
“I am.”
We use them every day.
I am tired.
I am afraid.
I am struggling.
I am fine.
Sometimes that last one is the biggest lie we tell.
But when Jesus speaks those words in the Gospel of John, something happens. The words begin carrying the weight of eternity.
Jesus does not merely say, “I know where you can find bread.”
He says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς
Egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs.

“I am the bread of life.”
—John 6:35
He does not merely say, “I can show you some light.”
He says:
ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου
Egō eimi to phōs tou kosmou.

“I am the light of the world.”
—John 8:12
He does not merely offer directions to God.
He says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή
Egō eimi hē hodos kai hē alētheia kai hē zōē.

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
—John 14:6
And eventually John records something even more staggering.
Jesus says:
πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί
Prin Abraam genesthai, egō eimi.

“Before Abraham was, I am.”
—John 8:58
Not, “Before Abraham was, I was.”
“I am.”
And the people listening understood that Jesus had said something enormous, because John immediately tells us:

“So they picked up stones to throw at him.”
—John 8:59
Why?
Because John is not merely collecting memorable quotations from an inspirational teacher.
He is revealing Jesus Christ.

And if you really see what John wants you to see, you cannot comfortably reduce Jesus to a moral example, a religious philosopher, a miracle worker, a spiritual therapist, or somebody who exists merely to improve the life you already planned to live.
John opens his Gospel by taking us behind Bethlehem.
Before the manger.
Before Mary.
Before Abraham.
Before humanity.
Before creation itself.

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
—John 1:1
Then comes the astonishing announcement:

“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
—John 1:14
That is the Jesus speaking when we hear those words:
“I am.”
And perhaps that explains why His statements feel so personal.
Because Jesus does not introduce Himself through abstract theology alone.
He meets human beings precisely where human beings hurt.
Hungry?
I am the bread of life.
Lost in darkness?
I am the light of the world.
Searching desperately for somewhere safe?
I am the door.
Tired of being led by voices that use you, manipulate you, abandon you, or condemn you?
I am the good shepherd.
Standing beside a grave wondering whether death gets the final word?
I am the resurrection and the life.
Confused about which way leads to God?
I am the way, the truth, and the life.
Trying to produce spiritual fruit while your soul is drying out?
I am the true vine.
Do you see it?
Every statement confronts a human insufficiency.
And every statement points to the sufficiency of Christ.
That is what makes these words beautiful.
It is also what makes them dangerous to our pride.
Because Jesus does not say, “You already possess everything you need within yourself.”
He reveals that our deepest need is ultimately found outside ourselves—and fulfilled in Him.
We need bread because we hunger.
We need light because darkness is real.
We need a shepherd because sheep wander.
We need resurrection because we die.
We need a way because we are lost.
We need a vine because branches cannot sustain life independently.
And that is exactly where the Gospel begins offending the self-sufficient heart.
We would rather have Jesus as an accessory.
Jesus as encouragement.
Jesus as emergency assistance.
Jesus as the One we call after every other door has closed.
Jesus added to our ambitions, our relationships, our careers, our plans, our identities, our desires.
But John's Gospel will not allow us to make Jesus small enough to fit comfortably into the corner of our lives.
Listen again.

“I am the bread of life.”
—John 6:35
Jesus said this after feeding thousands.
Imagine being there.
Your stomach is empty.
Jesus multiplies bread.
You eat until you are satisfied.
Then you discover something remarkable:
There is more.
The next day, you go looking for Jesus.
Wouldn't you?
Free bread yesterday.
Maybe free bread today.
But Jesus sees beneath their appetite.
He tells them:

“You are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.”
—John 6:26
That sentence still reaches into churches today.
Because it is possible to want what Jesus gives without truly wanting Jesus.
God, fix my marriage.
God, heal my body.
God, give me the job.
God, restore my finances.
God, remove my anxiety.
God, protect my children.
God, open the door.
God, answer this prayer.
None of those prayers is automatically wrong.
But eventually Christ confronts us with a terrifyingly intimate question:
If I did not give you the thing you are asking for, would I still be enough?
Jesus does not merely multiply bread.
He declares Himself to be the bread.
And the Greek intensifies the statement:
ἐγώ εἰμι — egō eimi — “I am.”
Then:
ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς — ho artos tēs zōēs — “the bread of life.”
The One standing before them is not merely offering temporary satisfaction.
He is pointing to Himself as the answer to humanity's deepest spiritual hunger.
You can feed your body and starve your soul.
You can have money and starve.
You can have followers and starve.
You can have applause and starve.
You can have relationships and starve.
You can sit in church every Sunday and still be starving because Christianity was never supposed to be merely proximity to religious things.
It is communion with Christ.
And then Jesus says:

“I am the light of the world.”
—John 8:12
Light does something uncomfortable.
It reveals.
We love light when we are lost.
We sometimes hate it when we are hiding.
Jesus says in John 3 that people loved darkness rather than light because their works were evil.
That means encountering Christ does not merely make us feel better.
Sometimes He exposes us first.
The secret habit.
The bitterness you have justified for years.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair hidden behind deleted messages.
The envy disguised as criticism.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The unforgiveness you keep calling boundaries.
The religious performance covering a heart that has become cold.
The smiling profile picture.
The carefully edited testimony.
The Sunday worship.
The private darkness.
And suddenly Christ walks into the room.
Not carrying a flashlight to humiliate you.
Coming as Light to rescue you.
That distinction matters.
Conviction says, “Bring this into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Hide from God because He could never want you now.”
But the Gospel says something scandalously different.
The Light already knows what is hiding in the room.
And He came anyway.
That is grace.
Not pretending sin is harmless.
Not renaming darkness.
Not excusing rebellion.
Grace is God knowing the entire truth about sinners and still sending His Son to save those who repent and believe.
Maybe somebody reading this has become exhausted from hiding.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say “God is good.”
You know what worship song to post.
You know how to look strong.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know.
Something is wrong.
Something has been eating your soul.
And you are terrified that if people knew everything, they would look at you differently.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling you toward the light.
Not so you can remain unchanged.
So you can be forgiven, cleansed, restored, and transformed.
Be honest.
Not because typing three words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when someone finally stops pretending.
Then Jesus says:

“I am the door of the sheep.”
—John 10:7
The Greek is direct:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα
Egō eimi hē thyra.
“I am the door.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
“I am one door among many equally valid doors.”
Later, the same Gospel records:

“No one comes to the Father except through me.”
—John 14:6
That claim clashes violently with a culture that wants Jesus to be admirable without being exclusive.
People are often comfortable saying Jesus was loving.
Jesus was compassionate.
Jesus cared about the poor.
Jesus taught forgiveness.
Yes.
But John refuses to let us stop there.
The loving Jesus is also the Jesus who claims to be the way to the Father.
Grace does not mean every road reaches God.
Grace means God opened a road for people who could never rescue themselves.
And the road has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Then He says:

“I am the good shepherd.”
—John 10:11
In Greek:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
The adjective καλός — kalos carries the sense of good, noble, beautiful, excellent, worthy.
And what makes this Shepherd good?
Jesus immediately explains:
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
This is where Christianity separates itself from every attempt to climb toward God through human goodness.
The Shepherd does not stand at a distance shouting instructions to wounded sheep.
He comes for them.
He knows them.
He calls His own.
And ultimately...
He dies for them.
There is Calvary hidden inside the Shepherd statement.
The cross was not an accident that ruined Jesus' mission.
The cross was central to His saving mission.
The Shepherd knew the wolves were coming.
He stayed.
He knew betrayal was coming.
He stayed.
He knew the nails were coming.
He stayed.
He knew the scourging was coming.
He stayed.
He knew the mockery was coming.
He stayed.
He knew sinners would spit upon Him.
He stayed.
Why?
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
You have probably had people leave when loving you became inconvenient.
Maybe somebody promised forever and disappeared.
Maybe someone knew your weakness and weaponized it.
Maybe someone used your vulnerability against you.
Maybe the person who was supposed to protect you became the person you needed protection from.
Human shepherds fail.
Jesus does not.
And then John brings us to a cemetery.
Lazarus is dead.
Martha is grieving.
Jesus arrives seemingly too late.
If you have ever buried someone you loved, you understand something about this chapter that cannot be learned from vocabulary alone.
There is theology before the funeral.
And then there is theology while standing beside the coffin.
Martha tells Jesus:

“Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
—John 11:21
Can you hear the grief inside that sentence?
I believed You could have stopped this.
Where were You?
Some Christians are afraid to admit they have whispered something similar.
God, where were You?
Where were You when the diagnosis came?
Where were You when my marriage collapsed?
Where were You when my child walked away?
Where were You when they died?
Where were You when I begged You?
Jesus does not respond to Martha with a motivational slogan.
He gives her Himself.
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.

“I am the resurrection and the life.”
—John 11:25
Not merely:
“I perform resurrections.”
I am the resurrection.
Then Jesus goes to the tomb.
And He weeps.
That matters.
The One who knows resurrection is coming still weeps beside people who are hurting.
Christian hope is not emotional numbness.
Faith does not require pretending death doesn't hurt.
Jesus wept.
Then He called Lazarus out.
But Lazarus's resurrection was still only a sign pointing toward something greater.
Because Lazarus would eventually die again.
Jesus was moving toward another tomb.
His own.
The Shepherd would lay down His life.
The Bread would be broken.
The Light would enter the darkness.
The Son would be crucified.
And then...
the grave would lose.
This is where every “I AM” statement begins converging toward the cross and empty tomb.
Then comes one of the most controversial sentences Jesus ever spoke:

“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
—John 14:6
Look carefully.
Jesus does not merely say:
“I know the way.”
He says:
I am the way.
Not:
“I teach truth.”
I am the truth.
Not:
“I can improve your life.”
I am the life.
Christianity therefore rises or falls with Christ.
Not with your church attendance.
Not with your denomination.
Not with your pastor.
Not with Gospel Warrior.
Not with your parents' faith.
Not with how many Bible verses you know.
Jesus Christ Himself is the center.
And that means the most important question is not:
“Are you religious?”
It is:
Do you belong to Christ?
Have you repented?
Have you believed the Gospel?
Are you trusting Christ or merely Christianity as a cultural identity?
Because there will be people who know Christian language but never surrender to the Christ they talk about.
And perhaps that is why the final great metaphor is so devastating.

“I am the true vine.”
—John 15:1
Then:

“Abide in me, and I in you.”
—John 15:4
The Greek verb is:
μένω — menō
To remain.
To stay.
To abide.
To continue.
Christianity is not supposed to be one emotional altar call followed by decades of spiritual distance.
Abide.
Stay near Christ.
Remain in His Word.
Depend upon Him.
A branch disconnected from the vine cannot manufacture life by trying harder.
Jesus says:

“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
—John 15:5
That sentence destroys spiritual pride.
You need Him today.
Not only the day you were converted.
Today.
Tomorrow.
When you succeed.
When you fail.
When everyone applauds.
When nobody notices.
When prayer feels powerful.
When prayer feels dry.
When you feel spiritually strong.
When you can barely whisper His name.
Remain.
And now we have to return to perhaps the most explosive “I AM” in John's Gospel.
Jesus is arguing with religious opponents who appeal to Abraham.
Then He says:

“Before Abraham was, I am.”
—John 8:58
The wording is startling.
πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι
“Before Abraham came into being...”
ἐγὼ εἰμί
“I am.”
This language naturally recalls the Old Testament revelation of God, especially Exodus 3:14, where God reveals Himself to Moses.
The Hebrew reads:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
Ehyeh asher ehyeh.
Often translated:
“I AM WHO I AM”
or
“I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.”
The ancient Greek translation of Exodus, the Septuagint, renders the declaration:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ὤν
Egō eimi ho ōn.
“I am the One who is.”
We should handle the linguistic connection carefully rather than pretending every occurrence of the ordinary Greek phrase ἐγώ εἰμι automatically constitutes a quotation of Exodus 3:14.
Context matters.
But John's larger portrait is unmistakably exalted.
John begins by identifying the Word as God.
He presents Jesus doing works and making claims that provoke accusations of making Himself equal with God.
Thomas ultimately encounters the risen Christ and says:

“My Lord and my God!”
—John 20:28
And John tells us why he wrote the Gospel:

“These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.”
—John 20:31
That is what John wants you to see.
Not merely seven beautiful metaphors to put on coffee mugs.
He wants you to see Jesus.
The Bread.
The Light.
The Door.
The Shepherd.
The Resurrection.
The Way.
The Truth.
The Life.
The Vine.
The eternal Son who entered human history, took on flesh, walked among sinners, laid down His life, rose from the dead, and calls people to believe in Him.
And suddenly this stops being an article about ancient Greek words.
It becomes personal.
Because sooner or later, every one of us finishes the sentence:
I am what I did.
I am what happened to me.
I am unwanted.
I am damaged.
I am addicted.
I am divorced.
I am ashamed.
I am a failure.
I am the worst thing I have ever done.
I am too far gone.
I am beyond forgiveness.
But the Gospel interrupts our self-written identities with a greater declaration.
Jesus says:
I AM.
Your sin is real.
But Jesus is greater.
Your shame may be deep.
But His grace reaches deeper.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not possess authority to become your savior, your master, or your final identity.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend sin was insignificant.
He demonstrated how serious it truly is.
And He demonstrated the magnitude of divine love.
The sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the Gospel invitation is not:
Clean yourself up enough so God might tolerate you.
It is:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
The Bread is still offered to the hungry.
The Light still shines into darkness.
The Shepherd still calls wandering sheep.
The Resurrection still stands stronger than the grave.
The Way still leads to the Father.
The Vine still gives life to branches that remain in Him.
Maybe your story contains chapters you wish you could tear out.
Scandal.
Addiction.
Adultery.
Pride.
Religious hypocrisy.
Secret sin.
Failure.
Grief.
Abandonment.
Years wasted running from God.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what sin tried to destroy.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Grace is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace means the scandal does not get to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is why we keep saying:
Because Peter's denial was not his final chapter.
Thomas's doubt was not his final chapter.
The Samaritan woman's history was not her final chapter.
The cross itself looked like the final chapter.
Then Sunday morning came.
Jesus rewrites everything.
If something in this article exposed a place where you have been hiding from Christ, do not turn conviction into another passing emotion.
Bring it to Him.
Confess your sin.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask another mature believer to walk with you if you need help.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need to discover that grace is not merely theology on a page.
And please do not keep this message trapped on your screen.
Send it privately to someone who would never comment publicly.
Share it with the believer who feels spiritually empty.
Share it with the person who believes their past has disqualified them forever.
Even share it with the unbelieving friend willing to investigate who Jesus actually claimed to be.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
We are saved by grace, not by supporting a ministry.
If your desire is to glorify God, glorify Him first by trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, serving faithfully, and making the Gospel known.
But after all the Greek words...
after the theology...
after the comments...
after the sharing...
there is still one question John refuses to let you escape.
Who is Jesus to you?
Not to your pastor.
Not to your parents.
Not to your denomination.
Not to the person who sent you this article.
To you.
Because the Gospel of John was not written merely so that you could understand the “I AM” statements.
John tells you explicitly why he wrote.
So that you may believe.
And by believing...
have life in His name.
Maybe you came into this article thinking the “I AM” statements were descriptions of Jesus.
Perhaps now you see something deeper.
They are also confrontations.
When you are starving, Jesus says, I AM.
When you are wandering, I AM.
When darkness has swallowed the room, I AM.
When death stands beside you, I AM.
When every road has failed you, I AM.
When your strength is gone, I AM.
When your past screams your name louder than grace...
Jesus still stands over your story.
I AM.
And perhaps the sentence you most desperately need to remember tonight is this:
Your darkest chapter may explain why you came to the tomb—but the risen Jesus still has authority to write what happens after it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE COMPARE MARITAL LOVE TO INTOXICATION?
paragraphs:
WHY DOES SCRIPTURE COMPARE MARITAL LOVE TO INTOXICATION?
The Bible uses language so intense that it can make religious people uncomfortable—but behind those words is a breathtaking truth about marriage, desire, covenant, and the God who refuses to let sin have the final word.
There is a verse in the Bible that sounds almost dangerous when you first hear it.
Not because it celebrates sin.
Not because God momentarily lowers His standard of holiness.
But because God speaks about marital love with an intensity many Christians have never been taught to expect from Scripture.
“Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:19 in the King James Version.
Read those final words again.
“Be thou ravished always with her love.”
Some modern translations render the thought even more startlingly:
Be intoxicated with her love.
And suddenly we have a question.
Why?

Why would Scripture—a book that repeatedly warns against drunkenness, uncontrolled appetites, adultery, lust, and sexual immorality—borrow the language of intoxication to describe the love between a husband and his wife?
The answer takes us somewhere much deeper than romance.
It takes us into desire.
Into covenant.
Into temptation.
Into the human heart.
And eventually, inevitably, to Jesus Christ.
Because there are desires God does not merely command us to suppress.
There are desires He wants to redeem.
The Hebrew behind Proverbs 5:19 matters.
The final portion reads:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The word אַהֲבָה (ahavah) means “love.”
תָמִיד (tamid) carries the sense of “continually,” “always,” or “regularly.”
But the word that makes the verse unforgettable is תִּשְׁגֶּה (tishgeh), from the Hebrew root שׁגה (shagah).

Depending on context, the verb can carry ideas such as wandering, going astray, being captivated, or being overcome. That is why English translations vary. Some use language such as being “ravished,” others “intoxicated,” others “captivated.”
And context is everything.
Proverbs 5 is not telling a man to lose moral control.
It is warning him not to give his sexuality to another woman.

The chapter is a father’s urgent instruction concerning sexual faithfulness. The forbidden woman initially appears desirable, but the path of adultery leads toward bitterness, loss, regret, and destruction. Then, directly against the counterfeit, Scripture presents the covenant alternative:
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Then:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then comes the astonishing command:
Let her satisfy you.
Remain captivated by her.
Be overwhelmed with love for the woman to whom you have given your covenant.
That changes everything.
God is not comparing marital love to sinful drunkenness because drunkenness is good.
He is using vivid language to describe absorption, delight, fascination, and powerful affection within the boundaries of covenant.
In other words:
Don’t become intoxicated with what will destroy you.
Become deeply captivated by the person you promised to love.
That is a word our generation desperately needs.
Because we live in an age that has become extraordinarily skilled at separating desire from covenant.
Swipe.
Watch.
Hide.
Delete the history.
Close the browser.
Send the message.
Erase the message.
Tell yourself it means nothing.
Tell yourself your spouse would not understand.
Tell yourself everybody does it.
Tell yourself you deserve this because your marriage has been difficult.
And slowly, quietly, the heart that once delighted in what God gave begins craving what God has forbidden.
The scandal rarely begins in a hotel room.
Sometimes it begins with attention.
Someone noticed you.
Someone laughed at your joke.
Someone listened to what your spouse seemed too exhausted to hear.
Someone made you feel attractive again.
Someone made you feel important again.
And you told yourself:
We’re only talking.
That sentence has buried more boundaries than many people would ever admit.
Scripture understands the human heart better than we do.
That is why Proverbs does not merely say, “Do not commit adultery.”
It redirects desire.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
There is something profoundly beautiful here.
God is not embarrassed by covenant desire.
He created the body.
He created affection.
He created attraction.
He created marriage.
Before pornography corrupted desire…
before adultery weaponized desire…
before lust detached desire from love…
