before shame convinced people that physical intimacy itself must somehow be dirty…
God looked upon the man and woman He had created and declared His creation “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
Sin did not invent sexuality.
God did.
Sin distorted it.
And redemption does not require us to call God’s good creation evil.
Redemption teaches us to receive God’s gifts according to God’s design.
That is why the Song of Songs can speak about marital and romantic desire with language that is poetic, physical, tender, and intense.
Song of Songs 5:1 contains another extraordinary expression:
שְׁתוּ וְשִׁכְרוּ דּוֹדִים
shethu veshikhru dodim.
“Drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.”

Translations differ over exactly how to express the final wording and who is being addressed, but the imagery is unmistakably celebratory. The Hebrew verb שָׁכַר (shakar) is associated with becoming drunk or intoxicated, while the poetic context celebrates love rather than condemning drunken excess.
Again, Scripture takes the imagery of abundance and overwhelming delight and places it within a celebration of love.
Why?
Because biblical holiness is not emotional anesthesia.
God does not save human beings by turning them into creatures who feel nothing.
He teaches us what to love.
He teaches us how to love.
He teaches us where desire belongs.
That distinction matters.
The Bible condemns drunkenness precisely because intoxication can surrender the faculties that should remain under righteous control.
Ephesians 5:18 says:
“And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.”
The Greek begins:
καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ
kai mē methyskesthe oinō
“And do not become drunk with wine…”
Then Paul gives the contrast:
ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι
alla plērousthe en pneumati
“…but be filled with the Spirit.”
So Scripture is not confused.
It does not condemn drunkenness in one place and secretly endorse it somewhere else.
The Bible can use intoxication metaphorically because metaphors borrow a recognizable feature of something without endorsing every feature of the comparison.
When someone says, “I was drunk with happiness,” they are not necessarily saying they consumed alcohol.
They mean the happiness was overwhelming.
Likewise, the language of Proverbs communicates something powerful:
Let covenant love have your attention.
Treasure your spouse.
Return to her.
Return to him.
Cultivate delight instead of feeding fantasies about someone else.
And that may be where this becomes painful.
Because someone reading this remembers what marriage used to feel like.
You remember talking until two in the morning.
You remember waiting for their message.
You remember how your stomach felt when you saw their name appear on your phone.
You remember the wedding.
You remember the promises.
You remember believing nothing could separate you.
Then came bills.
Children.
Stress.
Work.
Exhaustion.
Disappointments.
Arguments that were never completely resolved.
Words that cannot be pulled back into the mouth once spoken.
Silences that lasted too long.
Beds where two bodies were inches apart while two hearts felt miles away.
Maybe nobody cheated.
But something disappeared.
And now you are reading a command to “rejoice with the wife of thy youth,” and instead of inspiration you feel grief.
Because you want to ask:
What if the delight is gone?
That is where shallow Christianity often gives shallow answers.
“Just pray harder.”
“Go on a date.”
“Be more romantic.”
Sometimes those things help.
Sometimes the wounds go deeper.
Betrayal can be real.
Neglect can be real.
Abuse can be real.
Trauma can be real.
Broken trust can be real.
And Scripture never requires someone to pretend evil is harmless in order to appear spiritual.
Forgiveness is not calling darkness light.
Grace is not pretending betrayal did not hurt.
Reconciliation, where possible, involves truth.
Repentance involves truth.
Healing involves truth.
The cross itself proves that God does not heal sin by pretending sin is insignificant.
Look at Calvary.
If sin were insignificant, there would have been no cross.
Jesus Christ did not bleed because our rebellion was trivial.
He bled because our rebellion was deadly.
And He loved us anyway.
That is the shocking center of Christianity.
Not that decent people occasionally make mistakes and God politely overlooks them.
The Gospel is that sinners who could never cleanse themselves were pursued by a holy God.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.”
Romans 5:6.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we finally deserved Him.
Christ died for the ungodly.
And suddenly the theme of covenant becomes even larger.
Marriage is precious, but marriage is not the Savior.
Your husband cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
Your wife cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
Romance cannot save your soul.
Sex cannot heal the deepest separation between humanity and God.
Being desired cannot give you eternal life.
Only Jesus can.
And sometimes our relationships begin collapsing under expectations no human being was created to carry.
We ask another sinner:
Make me whole.
Never disappoint me.
Always understand me.
Make me feel valuable.
Make me feel beautiful.
Make me feel wanted.
Never change.
Never fail.
Never leave me emotionally hungry.
Then another imperfect human being inevitably fails to become God for us.
And resentment grows.
Christian marriage becomes healthier when Christ returns to the center because both husband and wife can finally stop demanding salvation from each other.
Jesus is Savior.
Your spouse is your spouse.
And because Christ is Savior, you can begin learning how to love another imperfect person without pretending imperfection is righteousness.
This is where Proverbs 5 becomes far more profound than “have a passionate marriage.”
It is teaching covenant loyalty in a world of counterfeit pleasures.
The forbidden woman offers something.
The covenant wife represents something else.
One path says:
Take what feels good now.
The other says:
Cherish what you promised before God.
One whispers:
Nobody will know.
Covenant asks:
Who are you becoming?
One says:
You deserve this.
Wisdom asks:
Where does this road end?
That question could save someone reading this today.
Where does this road end?
Not:
How exciting does it feel tonight?
Not:
How much attention am I receiving?
Not:
Can I hide it?
Where does this road end?
Proverbs 5 forces us to look past the first taste toward the final consequence.
Because temptation loves editing.
It shows you the kiss but cuts out the confession.
It shows you the excitement but cuts out the devastated spouse.
It shows you the fantasy but cuts out the children asking why everything changed.
It shows you the secret message but cuts out the moment the phone is discovered.
It shows you pleasure without consequence.
Scripture restores the missing scenes.
And then Scripture does something even more beautiful.
It points you home.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Maybe somebody needs those words before doing something they will spend years wishing they could undo.
Go home.
Not merely to your address.
Go home in your heart.
Turn away from the fantasy.
Delete what needs to be deleted.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
End the conversation that has crossed boundaries.
Stop feeding the secret life.
Ask for help.
Seek wise pastoral counsel.
Seek qualified professional help when the situation requires it.
Do not keep walking toward the cliff because turning around feels embarrassing.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation’s sake.
Repentance is turning.
The New Testament word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), carrying the idea of a changed mind, a reorientation that produces a changed direction.
Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel terrible about where they have been.
He came to call sinners out of death and into life.
Maybe your scandal is adultery.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe emotional infidelity.
Maybe years of bitterness.
Maybe you stopped touching your spouse because resentment became safer than vulnerability.
Maybe you have been comparing the person beside you with carefully edited strangers on a screen.
Maybe your spouse does not know how lonely you have become.
Maybe your marriage looks beautiful on Facebook and feels empty behind the front door.
Maybe you are unmarried and this exposes the way you have been treating other people’s bodies as entertainment.
Maybe you are the betrayed spouse and reading about marital delight hurts because somebody else shattered what you guarded.
Or maybe your deepest scandal has nothing to do with marriage.
You simply know what it is like to want something God has said cannot give you life.
Then hear this carefully.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is not because consequences magically disappear.
It is because Jesus Christ specializes in resurrecting what sin declares finished.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
Again and again, Scripture introduces us to human beings whose stories contain things they would probably have preferred erased.
Jesus did not pretend sin was righteousness.
Neither did He reduce people to their sin.
Grace tells the truth and then opens a door.
Christ’s words to the woman caught in adultery capture both realities:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Grace.
And transformation.
Forgiveness.
And a new direction.
No condemnation from Christ for the repentant sinner does not mean sin suddenly becomes harmless.
It means sin no longer gets to be the sinner’s master.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal have the final word.
And perhaps now we can understand why Scripture dares to speak so intensely about marital love.
God is not ashamed of holy affection.
He is protecting it.
He knows counterfeit intimacy can destroy real intimacy.
He knows lust consumes people while covenant learns to cherish them.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume.
Adultery takes what covenant has not given.
Selfishness asks, “What can you do for me?”
Covenant asks, “How can I faithfully love you before God?”
And biblical marital intimacy belongs inside that larger reality of knowing, giving, faithfulness, tenderness, exclusivity, sacrifice, delight, and covenant.
This does not mean every Christian marriage will feel emotionally intoxicating every day.
Proverbs is wisdom literature, not a promise that spouses will permanently experience romantic euphoria.
There will be ordinary Tuesdays.
There will be sickness.
There will be aging.
There will be exhaustion.
There may be seasons when intimacy requires patience, communication, medical care, counseling, repentance, rebuilding trust, or simply learning to be tender again.
Biblical love is deeper than adrenaline.
The command to rejoice in your spouse does not mean manufacturing a permanent emotional high.
It means refusing to treat covenant love as disposable simply because novelty has faded.
Sometimes mature love looks less like fireworks and more like someone sitting beside a hospital bed at 3:17 in the morning.
Sometimes “intoxicated with her love” eventually looks like wrinkled hands still reaching for each other after fifty years.
Sometimes passion becomes patience.
Sometimes attraction becomes admiration.
Sometimes romance becomes endurance.
Sometimes love becomes the quiet sentence:
I am still here.
And perhaps that is more beautiful than the first rush ever was.
Because anyone can become fascinated by novelty.
Covenant learns to rediscover wonder in someone familiar.
That is difficult.
It is also sacred.
And there is an even greater love behind every faithful human covenant.
Jesus.
The Bridegroom who did not abandon His people when they became difficult to love.
The Savior who knew exactly what our sin would cost Him and walked toward the cross anyway.
The King who was betrayed, mocked, stripped, beaten, pierced, and crucified—and who rose again.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of humanity desperately climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming for sinners.
That is why the answer to corrupted desire cannot merely be “try harder.”
We need new hearts.
We need grace.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need Christ.
We need forgiveness when we fall and strength to walk differently when we rise.
And perhaps somebody has reached this sentence carrying a secret.
Nobody around you knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your church does not know.
Your family does not know.
But God knows.
And you expected that sentence to terrify you.
Maybe it should sober you.
But it should also give you hope.
Because the God who knows the chapter you hide is the same God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Stop running.
Come into the light.
Not because exposure is painless.
Because darkness cannot heal what it is allowed to keep.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Notice who is faithful.
He is.
When you have been faithless, He remains who He is.
When you have wandered, Christ still calls sinners to return.
When you have polluted something God intended to be beautiful, grace can begin the painful, holy work of restoration.

And when restoration of a particular human relationship is complicated or not possible, Christ Himself remains sufficient. The Gospel is larger than a marital status and larger than a relationship outcome.
So no, Scripture is not giving Christians permission to become drunk.
It is giving married people a picture of covenant delight so consuming that forbidden counterfeits should lose their throne.
Be captivated by faithful love.
Protect it.
Cultivate it.
Thank God for it.
And above everything else, be captured by the greater love to which every Christian marriage ultimately points:
the love of Christ.
Be honest.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable, but because there may come a night when temptation makes you forget what daylight taught you.
Someone may be sitting beside a spouse tonight while silently wondering whether their marriage is worth fighting for.
Someone may believe sexual sin has placed them beyond the reach of Christ.
Let this reach them.
And even send it to the person who does not believe in Jesus yet.
Because beneath this discussion about marriage is a much greater announcement:
There is a Savior for sinners.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior is a requirement for salvation.
It is not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by purchasing access to a ministry.
And not because anyone should be manipulated into giving by being told that God will love them more if they pay.
The Gospel allows no such bargain.
But if this ministry genuinely helps you grow in Christ, supporting it can be one practical, voluntary way of helping biblical content continue reaching people who need it.

Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing, and building resources intended to point people toward Jesus. Sharing this article costs nothing, yet it can carry the Gospel into a home we could never personally enter.
Jesus does not need another customer.
He calls disciples.
He calls sinners to repent.
He calls the weary to come.
He calls the hidden into the light.
He calls the forgiven into holiness.
He calls husbands to faithfulness.
He calls wives to faithfulness.
He calls the unmarried to purity.
He calls His people away from counterfeit intoxications and toward something infinitely greater:
Himself.
So go back to the question.
Why does Scripture compare marital love to intoxication?
Because God understands how powerfully the human heart can become captivated.
And instead of pretending desire does not exist, biblical wisdom asks where that desire will lead you.
Toward consumption or covenant?
Toward secrecy or truth?
Toward betrayal or faithfulness?
Toward a counterfeit that promises life and quietly steals it…
or toward the wisdom of the God who created love in the first place?
Maybe tonight the greatest miracle will not be that you suddenly feel something spectacular.
Maybe it will be simpler.
You put the phone down.
You close the secret conversation.
You confess.
You pray.
You reach across the bed.
You ask forgiveness.
You choose faithfulness again.
You ask Jesus to teach your heart how to love what is holy.
And somewhere between the scandal you cannot undo and the grace you could never earn, you discover the truth that has rescued sinners for two thousand years:
Jesus is still writing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DO UNTO OTHERS…” — THE GOLDEN RULE IS MORE RADICAL IN CONTEXT THAN IT SOUNDS
paragraphs: “DO UNTO OTHERS…” — THE GOLDEN RULE IS MORE RADICAL IN CONTEXT THAN IT SOUNDS

We turned one of Jesus’ most dangerous commands into a polite little slogan. Then we put it on classroom walls, greeting cards, and inspirational posters—while quietly ignoring what He actually meant.
“Treat people the way you want to be treated.”
You have probably heard it since childhood.
It sounds gentle.
Reasonable.
Almost obvious.
Be nice.
Be fair.
Don’t hurt people because you wouldn’t want them to hurt you.
And somewhere along the way, one of the most piercing statements Jesus ever spoke became something safe enough to print on a coffee mug.
But there is a word in the original Greek that should make us stop.
A tiny word.
Four letters in English transliteration.
Οὖν — oun.
“Therefore.”
And once you see why Jesus said therefore, the Golden Rule stops being merely a lesson about manners.
It becomes a mirror.
And some of us may not like what we see in it.
Matthew records Jesus saying:
Πάντα οὖν ὅσα ἐὰν θέλητε ἵνα ποιῶσιν ὑμῖν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, οὕτως καὶ ὑμεῖς ποιεῖτε αὐτοῖς· οὗτος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται.
Panta oun hosa ean thelēte hina poiōsin hymin hoi anthrōpoi, houtōs kai hymeis poieite autois; houtos gar estin ho nomos kai hoi prophētai.
In straightforward English:
“Therefore, whatever you want people to do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.”
Matthew 7:12.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not merely say, “Don’t do bad things to people.”
That would already require restraint.
Jesus went further.
Do.
The Greek verb is ποιεῖτε — poieite.
Do.
Act.
Practice.
This is not merely a command to keep your hands clean.
It is a command to get your hands involved.
There is an enormous difference between refusing to wound someone and actively seeking their good.
You can walk past a hungry person without insulting him.
You can ignore a lonely woman without mocking her.
You can refuse to gossip about someone without ever defending her.
You can watch a brother collapse under a burden without adding another ounce to it.
You technically “didn't hurt them.”
But Jesus did not merely command His followers to become harmless.
He calls us to love.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because perhaps you have spent years congratulating yourself for the evil you did not commit while Jesus has been looking at the good you continually refused to do.
You didn't betray him.
But did you forgive him?
You didn't insult her.
But did you notice her?
You didn't steal from them.
But when you had abundance and they were desperate, did their suffering ever interrupt your comfort?
You didn't destroy that struggling Christian.
But did you ever call him?
You didn't publicly shame the woman whose life was falling apart.
But did you sit beside her when everyone else disappeared?
You didn't become somebody's enemy.
But did you become their neighbor?
That hurts differently.
Because suddenly the Golden Rule isn't asking only:
“What evil have I avoided?”
It is asking:
“What love have I withheld?”
And then comes that little word again.
Οὖν.
Therefore.
Whenever you encounter a “therefore,” you should ask what it is there for.
Jesus is not dropping Matthew 7:12 into empty space.
This statement comes inside the Sermon on the Mount, where Christ has been dismantling our comfortable definitions of righteousness from the inside out.
He has spoken about anger.
Lust.
Divorce.
Truthfulness.
Retaliation.
Giving.
Prayer.
Fasting.
Money.
Anxiety.
Judgment.
Trusting the Father.
And earlier He said something so radical that we often hurry past it:
“Love your enemies.”
Not tolerate them.
Not simply avoid murdering them.
Love them.
Pray for those who persecute you.
Why?
Because Jesus is revealing something about the character of His Father.
God gives sunlight to people who worship Him and people who reject Him.
Rain falls upon fields belonging to the righteous and the unrighteous.
Then Christ asks the devastating question: if you love only the people who love you, what is remarkable about that?
That is the world’s version of love.
“I'll be good to you because you're good to me.”
“I'll respect you because you respect me.”
“I'll call you because you called me.”
“I'll forgive you once you apologize properly.”
“I'll support you if you support me.”
“I'll treat you well as long as you remain useful, loyal, agreeable, safe, and easy to love.”
That is reciprocity.
Jesus is calling His disciples beyond mere reciprocity.
That changes the Golden Rule completely.
Because “do unto others” is easy when the “others” adore you.
But what happens when “others” means the person who wounded you?
The relative who embarrassed you?
The friend who disappeared when you needed them?
The Christian who disappointed you?
The person who misunderstood your intentions?
The coworker who took credit for something you did?
The stranger whose worldview irritates you?
The person who cannot repay you?
The person whose apology never came?
Now imagine something painfully simple.
Your phone is in your hand.
A name appears on the screen.
Immediately your chest tightens.
You remember what they said.
You remember the betrayal.
You remember the night you cried while they apparently slept just fine.
And there is a part of you—perhaps a very wounded part—that wants them to experience what you experienced.
Not necessarily destruction.
Just enough pain to understand yours.
You want them to know what it felt like.
You want justice.
Maybe you even want God to “deal with them.”
Then Jesus walks directly into that private courtroom in your heart and asks a terrifying question:
If you were standing where they are standing, how would you desperately hope to be treated?
Not: “Did they earn mercy?”
Not: “Do they deserve kindness?”
Not: “Will they appreciate it?”
Not even: “Will they change?”
What would you desire if the roles were reversed?
Suddenly the Golden Rule is no longer hanging on a classroom wall.
It is standing in your living room.
It is sitting beside your marriage.
It is entering your comment section.
It is reading your private messages.
It is listening to the way you describe someone who isn't present.
It is standing beside you while you decide whether to forgive.
And it knows something we hate admitting.
We are extraordinarily creative when explaining why our failures deserve context...
and why their failures deserve judgment.
When we lose our temper, we were exhausted.
When they lose theirs, they have a character problem.
When we forget, we were overwhelmed.
When they forget, they don't care.
When we withdraw, we need space.
When they withdraw, they're selfish.
When we fail, we want people to remember our whole story.
When someone else fails, we sometimes reduce their entire story to their worst five minutes.
We want mercy with footnotes for ourselves...
and justice without context for everyone else.
Jesus destroys that double standard with one sentence.
Whatever you would want others to do for you, do that for them.
Not because they are always innocent.
They aren't.
Neither are you.
Not because boundaries are unbiblical.
They aren't. Love does not require enabling abuse, remaining in danger, pretending evil is good, or abandoning wisdom and justice.
Forgiveness is not the same thing as calling evil harmless.
Reconciliation and restored trust can involve repentance, truth, wisdom, safety, and time.
Jesus never commands us to rename darkness “light.”
But He does forbid hatred from becoming the lord of our hearts.
That distinction matters.
Because someone reading this has been deeply hurt.
Perhaps abused.
Betrayed.
Manipulated.
Humiliated.
And Christian language may even have been used against you.
“Just forgive.”
“Be nice.”
“Turn the other cheek.”
Maybe those words were used to pressure you into remaining silent while someone continued hurting you.
That is not what the Golden Rule means.
If you were being harmed, wouldn't you want someone to tell you the truth?
Wouldn't you want someone to protect you?
Wouldn't you want someone to help stop the evil?
Then doing unto others can sometimes mean telling the truth when silence is easier.
Protecting someone vulnerable.
Confronting sin with humility.
Establishing a necessary boundary.
Seeking lawful justice.
Refusing to help someone continue destroying themselves and others.
Love is not always soft.
But biblical love is never revenge wearing religious clothing.
And now the knife turns toward us.
Because the Golden Rule does not merely govern how we treat the people who wounded us.
It governs how we treat the invisible.
The waiter who made a mistake.
The cashier moving too slowly.
The elderly person trying to understand technology.
The employee who cannot do anything for your career.
The janitor nobody notices.
The person online whose face you cannot see while you type words you would never say across a dinner table.
The homeless man everyone learned to walk around.
The new believer who still smells like the life Jesus is rescuing him from.
The Christian who should “know better” but is still fighting battles you cannot see.
The unbeliever whose life makes you uncomfortable.
The child asking for your attention while your phone keeps vibrating.
Your spouse after the argument.
Your aging parents when patience becomes expensive.
Your enemy.
Your neighbor.
The person you wish Jesus had excluded.
He didn't.
οἱ ἄνθρωποι — hoi anthrōpoi.
People.
Human beings.
And perhaps that is why this teaching feels impossible when we finally hear it.
Because it is exposing something deeper than bad manners.
It exposes the self-centeredness of the human heart.
We instinctively place ourselves at the center.
My pain.
My schedule.
My reputation.
My comfort.
My money.
My inconvenience.
My wounds.
My rights.
My side of the story.
Then Jesus says, in effect:
Take the tenderness you naturally wish others would show you...
and start carrying it toward them.
That is not natural.
That is transformation.
And this is precisely why Christianity cannot ultimately be reduced to “be a good person.”
If the message of Jesus were merely “try harder to be nice,” we would not need a cross.
We would need motivational speakers.
We would need better habits.
We would need etiquette lessons.
But Christianity announces something far more devastating and far more beautiful:
We are sinners who need rescue.
The same heart capable of extraordinary tenderness can harbor envy, lust, bitterness, pride, greed, hypocrisy, cruelty, and self-righteousness.
We have not loved God perfectly.
We have not loved our neighbors perfectly.
We have not even lived up to the standards we demand from other people.
And if God treated us only according to what our sins deserved, none of us could stand before Him boasting.
That is where the Golden Rule leads somewhere far greater than itself.
It leads us toward Christ.
Because before Jesus commanded radical love...
He embodied it.
Think about the scandal of the Gospel.
Humanity did not treat God as humanity wanted to be treated.
We rebelled against our Creator.
Ignored Him.
Used His gifts while rejecting His authority.
Loved darkness.
Broke His commands.
Worshiped created things.
Then when the Son of God came among us, human beings mocked Him.
Spat upon Him.
Struck Him.
Rejected Him.
Humiliated Him.
Nailed Him to a Roman cross.
And hanging there, Jesus was not dying because humanity had finally become worthy of love.
“God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
While we were sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became useful.
Not after humanity apologized sufficiently.
Not after we earned another chance.
Christ moved toward sinners with saving grace.
This does not mean God ignored justice.
The cross proves the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required more than sentimental forgiveness.
At Calvary, mercy and justice meet.
Christ bears sin.
The innocent One suffers for the guilty.
The debt we could never pay is answered by the One we could never deserve.
And suddenly “Do unto others” becomes more than moral instruction.
It becomes the fruit of having encountered a Savior who loved us when we were spiritually bankrupt.
You forgive because you have been forgiven.
You show mercy because you live by mercy.
You become generous because everything you possess was first received.
You stop keeping score because at the foot of the cross your own record gave you nothing to boast about.
You stop asking, “Does this person deserve love?”
because somewhere inside you another question begins whispering:
“Did I deserve Calvary?”
And there it is.
The scandal.
The grace.
The place where Christianity breaks our pride.
You may have spent years trying to become the hero of your own story.
Maybe you hid the addiction.
The bitterness.
The affair.
The pornography.
The rage.
The jealousy.
The secret messages.
The unforgiveness.
The double life.
The spiritual numbness.
Maybe everyone thinks you're strong.
Maybe you know exactly when to say “Amen.”
Maybe your Bible is highlighted.
Maybe your worship playlist is full.
Maybe people come to you for prayer.
And still...
there are people you secretly hate.
People you would enjoy seeing humbled.
People whose suffering produces a satisfaction in you that you would never admit inside a church building.
Jesus sees it.
And remarkably, He has not brought you here merely to crush you.
He exposes wounds so they can be healed.
He exposes sin so it can be confessed.
He calls sinners into the light because grace has nothing to fear from honesty.
Repentance is not God screaming, “Stay away from Me.”
Repentance is the King saying:
Turn around. Come home.
Maybe the person you need to treat differently is your spouse.
Maybe your child.
Maybe your mother.
Maybe your father.
Maybe someone in your church.
Maybe someone who will never know you read this.
Maybe the first person who needs the mercy of Christ tonight is the person staring back at you from the mirror—not self-excusing mercy, but the mercy that finally stops hiding and confesses:
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
That prayer can change everything.
Not because the sentence is magical.
Because Christ saves sinners who come to Him.
The Golden Rule cannot save you.
Your kindness cannot wash away your guilt.
Your generosity cannot purchase forgiveness.
Your religious activity cannot resurrect a dead heart.
Only Jesus saves.
The One crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
The One who takes scandal and writes grace across it.
The One who takes shame and gives a new name.
The One who takes rebels and makes them sons and daughters.
The One who takes hearts trained to ask, “What can I get?” and teaches them to ask, “How can I love?”
This is why following Jesus eventually reaches your wallet too.
Not because money buys favor with God.
Never.
Grace cannot be purchased.
And Christian generosity should never be manufactured through guilt or coercion. Scripture teaches believers to give from a willing heart, not under compulsion.
But grace changes what we do with what God has entrusted to us.
Our time.
Our attention.
Our voices.
Our homes.
Our platforms.
Our possessions.
Our money.
Everything becomes something we can place in the service of love.

So if Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, confronted your sin, helped you understand Scripture, pointed you toward Jesus, or reached you during a night when you desperately needed truth, you can help this ministry continue and expand.
And certainly not because salvation can ever be purchased.
Support because you freely believe this work should continue.
Support because another exhausted believer may need tomorrow the truth that reached you today.
Support because someone scrolling at two in the morning may be one article away from opening a Bible again.
Support because Gospel-centered words can travel into rooms you and I may never enter.
And there is already an extraordinary amount available freely.
But money is not the only way to help.
Sometimes the most valuable thing you can give costs nothing.
Not merely because “sharing helps the algorithm.”
Someone may be quietly losing their faith.
Someone may believe Christianity is nothing more than moral performance because nobody has clearly shown them the grace of Jesus.
Someone may need to discover that Christ is not waiting for them to repair themselves before coming to Him.
One share can put the Gospel in front of someone who would never walk into a church.
Send this privately to the person who is tired of pretending everything is okay.
And when that moment comes, you may need to read these words again—not because this article is sacred, but because the words of Jesus are.
Invite your family.
Your friends.
The believer who is struggling.
The Christian who has grown cold.
The seeker asking questions.
Even the unbeliever who thinks Jesus has nothing to say to people like them.
And before you leave...
I want you to do something harder than sharing.
Be honest.
Who came into your mind while you were reading this?
You don't have to type their name.
Maybe you shouldn't.
But you know.
The person you struggle to forgive.
The person you avoid.
The person you quietly resent.
The person whose humanity became difficult for you to see after what they did.
Bring that person before Jesus.
Then bring your own heart before Him too.
Read the other comments too.
Pray for someone.
Encourage somebody.
You may discover that the person sitting beside you digitally has been fighting the same battle in silence.
Because perhaps this is how the Golden Rule begins to leave the page.
Someone sees pain...
Someone sees confession...
and doesn't condemn.
Someone sees loneliness...
and answers.
Someone receives mercy from Jesus...
and finally stops rationing mercy to everyone else.
Imagine what would happen if Christians became known not merely for quoting the Golden Rule but for living under the rule of the Golden King.
Homes would change.
Marriages would change.
Churches would change.
Enemies would encounter a kind of love they could not easily explain.
The lonely would be noticed.
The ashamed would hear about grace.
The wounded would encounter truth without cruelty.
The sinner would hear both the seriousness of repentance and the breathtaking news that there is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
And the watching world might begin to glimpse something no slogan could ever adequately communicate:
what a human being starts becoming when Jesus Christ rewrites the heart.
So when you hear those familiar words again—
“Do unto others...”
don't reduce them to politeness.
Remember οὖν.
Therefore.
Remember the Sermon.
Remember your enemy.
Remember your neighbor.
Remember your own sin.
Remember the mercy you needed.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that Christianity is not the story of good people proving how righteous they are.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a righteous Savior...
then transformed into people who begin giving away the mercy they themselves could never have purchased.
And perhaps the next great act of discipleship in your life will not happen beneath stained glass.
Perhaps it will happen when somebody hurts you...
and the old version of you reaches for revenge...
but the redeemed version remembers Jesus.
Perhaps it will happen when you notice the person everyone else ignores.
Perhaps it will happen when you tell the truth with love.
Perhaps it will happen when you forgive.
Perhaps it will happen when you give.
Perhaps it will happen when you stop asking whether somebody deserves your kindness and remember how much of your life depends upon grace.
Because in the end, the Golden Rule is not golden because it makes us nicer.
It is radical because Jesus is teaching redeemed people to look beyond themselves.
And no one has ever demonstrated that love more completely than Christ Himself.
He saw sinners.
He knew exactly what we had done.
He knew exactly what it would cost.
And He went to the cross.
If this message should keep reaching people, help carry it.
Pray for this ministry.
Because the question is no longer merely, “How do I want people to treat me?”
The deeper question is:
“After receiving this much mercy from Jesus... what kind of person is His grace teaching me to become?”
And when the world hands you another reason to harden your heart, remember this:
The hands you wanted to close in anger may become the very hands Jesus uses to prove that grace had the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE CELEBRATE DESIRE IN ONE PASSAGE—AND CONDEMN IT IN ANOTHER?
paragraphs: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE CELEBRATE DESIRE IN ONE PASSAGE—AND CONDEMN IT IN ANOTHER?
Maybe God Isn’t Trying to Kill Your Desires. Maybe He Is Trying to Rescue Them Before They Kill You.
There is a strange tension in the Bible that most of us have felt but few of us have known how to name.
In one place, Scripture seems to warn us about desire as though it were a loaded weapon.
In another, desire sounds almost holy.
David writes:
Then James writes:
So which is it?
Is desire something God gives…
or something that drags us into sin?
Should Christians distrust what they want?
Should we suppress desire?
Should we follow it?

And what do we do with those desires we have prayed about for years—the desire to be loved, to marry, to succeed, to be noticed, to build something meaningful, to escape loneliness, to experience intimacy, to provide for our families, to be healed, to be financially secure, to matter?
Here is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the question is not simply:
“What do you desire?”
Perhaps the more revealing question is:
“What has your desire taught you to worship?”
That question can expose an entire life.
And before this is over, you may discover that some desires you have been ashamed of were never inherently sinful…
while other desires you have been defending may have quietly been competing with Jesus for the throne of your heart.
That is the battlefield.
Not desire versus no desire.
But desire surrendered to Christ versus desire enthroned above Christ.
The original languages help us see something English can sometimes hide.
James describes temptation this way:
“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας…”
The crucial Greek word is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia.
It can refer to desire, longing, craving, or lust depending on context.
That matters.
Because a word associated with sinful craving in one passage does not mean that the mere capacity to desire is itself sinful.
The moral character of desire is revealed by its object, orientation, context, and relationship to God.
James is describing desire functioning rebelliously.
He continues with terrifying imagery:
“εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν…”
“Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin…”
James does not describe temptation as something harmless.
He pictures a conception.
Then a birth.
Then growth.
Then death.
Desire whispers.
Sin conceives.
Death eventually arrives.
That is why the temptation you keep calling “small” should never be treated casually.
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I have come to destroy you.”
It usually says:
“You deserve this.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You need this to be happy.”
“Just once.”
“You can repent afterward.”
“God understands.”
“This isn’t hurting anyone.”
And sometimes the most dangerous sentence of all:
“This is just who I am.”
But Jesus did not shed His blood merely to help us become comfortable with everything our fallen hearts demand.
He came to redeem us.
There is a difference between being loved in our brokenness and being left unchanged in our brokenness.
Grace does the first.
Grace refuses to do the second.
And this is where Scripture’s treatment of desire becomes breathtakingly beautiful.
Christianity is not fundamentally the story of God turning human beings into people who want nothing.
It is the story of God rescuing what we love.
The Gospel does not produce empty hearts.
It produces reordered hearts.
Before Christ, we can desire created things as though they were gods.
After Christ begins transforming us, we increasingly learn to receive created things as gifts without asking those gifts to become our Savior.
That difference changes everything.
You can desire marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can desire financial stability without worshiping money.
You can desire success without making achievement your identity.
You can desire intimacy without turning another person's body into an object for your consumption.
You can desire recognition without becoming enslaved to applause.
You can desire justice without becoming consumed by hatred.
You can desire rest without making comfort your god.
You can desire ministry growth without secretly needing numbers to prove your worth.
You can even desire something good so desperately that the good thing begins occupying a place in your heart that belongs only to God.
And that may be one of the most painful truths in this entire conversation:
A good desire can become a terrible master.
Abraham wanted a son.
That desire was not inherently evil.
Hannah wanted a child.
That longing was not inherently evil.
Paul desired the salvation and spiritual maturity of others.
That was not evil.
Jesus Himself expressed profound desire.
The existence of desire, therefore, cannot be the biblical definition of sin.
The question becomes what happens when desire meets the lordship of God.
Can you desire something deeply and still say:
“Jesus, if You say no, You are still enough”?
That is where idols begin trembling.
Because an idol is not always a golden statue sitting in a pagan temple.
Sometimes it is the future you cannot imagine living without.
Sometimes it is the person whose approval determines whether you feel valuable.
Sometimes it is the relationship you know dishonors God but cannot bring yourself to release.
Sometimes it is the money you say you need before you can finally feel safe.
Sometimes it is pornography behind a locked screen.
Sometimes it is attention.
Sometimes revenge.
Sometimes success.
Sometimes ministry itself.
Sometimes it is the version of your life you expected God to give you.
And when He does not…
you become angry with the Giver because you wanted the gift more than you wanted Him.
That hurts.
Because many of us have prayed prayers that sounded spiritual while quietly presenting God with terms.
“Lord, bless this relationship.”
But we never asked whether the relationship honored Him.
“Lord, make this business successful.”
But we never asked what success was doing to our character.
“Lord, give me more.”
But we never asked why “enough” kept moving farther away.
“Lord, open this door.”
But perhaps mercy was the hand keeping it closed.
We wanted God to sanctify our plans.
God wanted to sanctify us.
And those are not always the same thing.
Psalm 37:4 is frequently turned into something resembling a divine vending machine:
Delight in God, and He will hand you whatever your heart requests.
But read the movement of the passage.
“Delight thyself also in the LORD…”
The center is already shifting.
The heart is being directed toward Yahweh.
The Hebrew name represented by LORD is יהוה — YHWH, the covenant name of God.
And “desires” in Psalm 37:4 comes from the Hebrew מִשְׁאֲלוֹת — mish'alot, carrying the sense of requests, petitions, or desires.
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say:
“Delight yourself in your desires.”
It says:
“Delight thyself also in the LORD.”
God Himself is central.
This is not a technique for manipulating heaven.
It is relationship.
And when God becomes your delight, something extraordinary begins happening.
You still have desires.
You still cry.
You still hope.
You still ask.
You still dream.
But slowly…
sometimes painfully…
the Holy Spirit begins teaching your heart a new language.
“I want this, Lord…
but I want You more.”
That sentence is spiritual warfare.
“I love this person…
but I will not disobey You to keep them.”
“I want success…
but not if success costs me my soul.”
“I want to be seen…
but Your approval must become greater than their applause.”
“I want relief…
but I refuse to seek relief in something that crucified my Savior.”
“I want my prayer answered…
but even before the answer comes, Christ is still worthy.”
This is not desire dying.
This is desire being discipled.
And some of you reading this know exactly where the battle is.
You have deleted it before.
Then downloaded it again.
You promised God you were finished.
Then loneliness came.
Stress came.
Midnight came.
The memory came.
The message came.
The photograph appeared.
The old number called.
The craving woke up.
And suddenly the thing you swore you hated looked beautiful again.
That is why James uses the language of being drawn away and enticed.
Temptation rarely presents the hook first.
It presents the bait.
The affair does not initially show you the shattered spouse.
Pornography does not show you what repeated objectification may do to your mind, relationships, and expectations.
Greed does not show you the years sacrificed at the altar of “just a little more.”
Pride does not show you the loneliness waiting at the top.
Bitterness does not show you how the person who hurt you can continue occupying your mind without paying rent.
Sin advertises pleasure.
It hides the invoice.
And James tells us where the invoice eventually leads:
“…sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
That does not mean every temptation immediately produces every possible consequence.
James is describing sin’s trajectory.
And Scripture refuses to romanticize it.
But now hear the Gospel.
Because if this article ends with you staring at your desires and thinking, “Then I am disgusting,” you have missed Jesus.
The Gospel is not:
Fix your desires perfectly, and perhaps Christ will accept you.
The Gospel is that sinners who could not rescue themselves were loved by a Savior who came looking for them.
Jesus walked toward scandal.
Toward the sexually broken.
Toward the greedy.
Toward the proud.
Toward religious hypocrites.
Toward social outcasts.
Toward people with histories they wished they could erase.
He did not call darkness light.
He did something infinitely better.
He entered our darkness to bring us into His light.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely offer motivational advice to sinful humanity.
He bore sin.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
And resurrection morning announced that sin and death would not have the final word.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
The Greek New Testament commonly uses μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance, carrying the idea of a change of mind that involves a decisive turning.
Biblical repentance is deeper than feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas experienced devastating remorse.
Remorse alone is not redemption.
Repentance turns toward God.
It brings the secret into the light.
It stops negotiating with the sin.
It stops renaming bondage as personality.
It stops asking, “How close can I get without technically sinning?”
And begins asking:
“How close can I walk with Jesus?”
Maybe that is the question somebody needed tonight.
Not:
“How much can I get away with?”
But:
“What is this desire doing to my love for Christ?”
Does it make obedience seem burdensome?
Does it require secrecy?
Does it depend upon disobedience?
Does it make another human being an object rather than someone bearing God's image?
Does it demand that Scripture be reinterpreted simply so you never have to tell yourself no?
Does it dominate your imagination?
Does losing it feel more terrifying than losing intimacy with God?
If so, do not merely manage it.
Bring it to Jesus.
And do not wait until you “feel spiritual.”
Come trembling.
Come ashamed.
Come confused.
Come after failing again.
Come while part of you still wants the sin.
That may sound shocking, but honesty is better than pretending.
You can pray:
“Jesus, part of me still wants what is destroying me. I cannot heal my own heart. Change what I love.”
That is a frightening prayer.
It is also a beautiful one.
Because sometimes we keep asking God to change our circumstances while He is trying to change our appetites.
We ask Him to remove consequences.
He wants to remove chains.
We ask Him to make temptation disappear.
He teaches us dependence.
We ask Him to give us what we desire.
He begins transforming the person doing the desiring.
And eventually you may look back at something you once thought you could never live without and whisper:
“How did that ever own me?”
Grace.
That is how.
Not because you became stronger than everybody else.
Because Christ met you in the scandal and started rewriting the story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Even desire.
Especially desire.
Perhaps your greatest testimony will not be that God gave you everything you once wanted.
Perhaps your testimony will be that Jesus became more precious than some of the things you once believed you could never surrender.
Read that again.
There are things you once begged God to give you that you may someday thank Him for withholding.
There are doors whose closing felt like rejection that may someday look like rescue.
There are relationships whose ending felt like death that may have been mercy.
There are appetites you currently call “me” that Christ may one day make foreign to you.
There are wounds presently screaming for counterfeit comfort that Jesus can begin healing with something deeper than distraction.
And there are desires already inside you that God may not want to destroy at all.
He may want to purify them.
The desire to be loved?
There is something profoundly human there.
But no human being can bear the weight of becoming your Messiah.
The desire to matter?
You bear the image of God; your value does not need to be manufactured by applause.
The desire for intimacy?
God created human beings for relationship, but intimacy becomes destructive when detached from God's design and love of neighbor.
The desire to accomplish something meaningful?
Work can glorify God, but achievement makes a cruel savior.
The desire for justice?
Scripture repeatedly cares about justice, but vengeance belongs to God.
The desire for pleasure?
God created a world filled with good gifts, but gifts become chains when we worship them rather than the Giver.
Christian maturity does not mean becoming emotionally dead.
Jesus wept.
Jesus loved.
Jesus experienced compassion.
Jesus experienced anguish.
Jesus desired.
Jesus could say in Gethsemane, in the agony before the cross, that if possible the cup might pass—and yet surrendered Himself to the Father's will.
There is the pattern.
Real desire.
Real anguish.
Real surrender.
Not pretending you do not want something.
Not lying to God.
Not manufacturing religious numbness.
But bringing the full weight of your desire beneath the authority of the Father.
That is surrender.
“Father, this is what I want.
But You are God.
I am not.
And I trust You.”
Somebody reading this has spent years believing surrender means losing.
You imagine placing your desire into God's hands and watching Him crush it.
But the hands you are afraid to trust are scarred hands.
Jesus is not asking you to surrender to a stranger.
He is asking you to trust the One who was crucified for sinners.
Look at His hands.
Then decide whether He is worthy of your heart.
This is why the cross must remain at the center of every conversation about desire.
Without the cross, Christianity becomes behavior management.
Try harder.
Want less.
Behave better.
Hide your failures.
Smile at church.
Repeat.
But the Gospel exposes that exhausting cycle.
We do not need cosmetic modification.
We need resurrection.
We need new hearts.
We need forgiveness.
We need the Spirit of God.
We need desires increasingly reordered around the beauty and supremacy of Jesus Christ.
And when we fall?
We do not redefine sin so we can feel innocent.
Neither do we run from Christ because we feel filthy.
We confess.
We repent.
We receive grace.
We stand again.
We keep walking.
Maybe you failed last night.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your browser history knows.
Maybe your bank statement knows.
Maybe your spouse suspects.
Maybe the messages are still sitting on your phone.
Maybe your addiction is not sexual at all.
Maybe it is approval.
Control.
Food.
Status.
Shopping.
Money.
Anger.
Attention.
Work.
Envy.
Fantasy.
The desperate need to win every argument.
Maybe your idol wears respectable clothes.
Jesus still sees it.
And Jesus still calls sinners to come.
Not tomorrow after you have cleaned yourself up.
Now.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not grace that excuses the chain.
Grace that breaks it.
Not grace that says sin does not matter.
Grace that proves sin mattered enough for the Son of God to go to a cross.
Not grace that leaves you lying where you fell.
Grace that says:
“Rise. Follow Me.”
So why does Scripture celebrate desire in one passage and condemn it in another?
Because Scripture does not teach that all desire is automatically righteous or automatically sinful.
Desire has a direction.
Desire has an object.
Desire can become disordered.
Desire can entice.
Desire can be surrendered.
Desire can increasingly be shaped by God.
The Bible is not contradicting itself.
It is exposing us.
The same human capacity that can hunger after what destroys us can, by God's transforming grace, increasingly hunger after what is holy.
The issue is not merely:
“Do I desire?”
The issue is:
What do I desire, why do I desire it, what am I willing to do to obtain it, and is Jesus still Lord when He tells me no?
That last question may be the one you remember.
Is Jesus still Lord when He tells you no?
When the relationship ends?
When the opportunity disappears?
When obedience costs you?
When nobody applauds?
When you have to delete the number?
When you have to confess?
When you have to walk away?
When the prayer remains unanswered?
When following Christ means disappointing the appetite screaming inside you?
Is He still Lord?
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But you also do not have to keep pretending.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that chains really can break.
Do not make the comment section a courtroom.
Make it a place where broken people point broken people toward Jesus.
And if one person came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore that.
Or send this privately.
A share may seem small.
But you do not know who is awake at 2:00 a.m. asking God for a reason not to return to the thing destroying them.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what was obvious when we were spiritually clear.
Come back when the appetite gets loud.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating.
Come back when the old life begins looking beautiful again.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person asking difficult questions.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who knows there must be more.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who is willing to listen.
It does not. Grace cannot be bought.

But voluntary support can help Gospel Warrior continue creating, publishing, maintaining, and expanding Christ-centered content and resources so more people can encounter Scripture and hear the Gospel.
If you have been asking how you can help this ministry continue, this is one practical way.
Not from guilt.
Not because God will love you more.
But because when believers value Gospel work, they can freely choose to help sustain it.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help.
Pray.
Share.
Save the articles that strengthen you.
Invite others to follow.
Put biblical truth into somebody else's feed.
Because support is bigger than money, and the Gospel must never be treated like merchandise.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
And perhaps tonight the greatest thing you can place into His hands is not your money, your success, your reputation, or even your plans.
Perhaps it is the desire you have been terrified to surrender.
Open your hands.
Tell Him the truth.
“Jesus…
I want this.
Maybe more than I should.
Maybe more than I want You.
I cannot change my heart by pretending.
Forgive me.
Teach me to desire what is good.
Teach me to hate what destroys me.
Teach me to receive Your gifts without worshiping them.
Teach me to trust You when You give.
Teach me to trust You when You withhold.
And if I have made an idol out of something beautiful…
become more beautiful to me than the idol.
I surrender it to You.
You are Lord.
Rewrite me.”
And remember this when desire starts whispering again:
The desire you surrender to Jesus may feel like something you are losing today, until grace reveals that Christ was rescuing your heart from becoming owned by what it wanted.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM, JACOB, DAVID, SOLOMON: SCRIPTURE DOESN’T HIDE WHAT POLYGAMY PRODUCED
paragraphs:
ABRAHAM, JACOB, DAVID, SOLOMON: SCRIPTURE DOESN’T HIDE WHAT POLYGAMY PRODUCED
The Bible Recorded Their Multiple Wives—But Look Closely at the Tears, Rivalry, Violence, Idolatry, and Broken Homes That Followed
There is something almost frightening about the honesty of the Bible.
Scripture could have cleaned up its heroes.
It could have edited Abraham.
Protected Jacob’s reputation.
Softened David’s failures.
Hidden Solomon’s compromises.
It could have given us sanitized patriarchs, polished kings, uncomplicated families, and spiritual giants whose private lives matched the greatness of their public callings.
But God did not give us propaganda.
He gave us truth.
And sometimes the truth is painful enough to make you uncomfortable.
Abraham had Sarah…and Hagar entered the household.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel…and eventually Bilhah and Zilpah.
David accumulated wives and concubines.
Solomon multiplied wives on a scale almost impossible to comprehend.
And here is the question Christians sometimes avoid:
If these men belonged to God, why does Scripture record their polygamy?
Does that mean God approved of it?
Or have we confused something the Bible describes with something the Bible prescribes?
Keep reading, because the answer is not found merely by counting wives.
Look at what happened inside the homes.
Listen to the women.
Watch the children.
Follow the jealousy.
Follow the competition.
Follow the sexual disorder.
Follow the violence.
Follow the spiritual compromise.
Follow the tears.
Then go all the way back to Eden…and finally forward to Jesus Christ.
Because when Scripture tells the whole story, polygamy does not emerge as God's beautiful alternative to monogamy.
It emerges inside a fallen world God is patiently redeeming.
Before Abraham ever took Hagar…
before Jacob entered a house divided between sisters…
before David accumulated wives…
before Solomon filled his palace with them…
there was Eden.
And Eden matters.
Genesis 2:24 says in Hebrew:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzov-’ish ’et-’aviv wə’et-’immō, wədavaq bə’ishtō, wəhayu ləvasar ’eḥad.
The heart of it is breathtaking:
A man leaves father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad — “one flesh.”
Not merely two people occupying the same house.
Not a political arrangement.
Not a collection of partners surrounding one powerful man.
One-flesh covenant union.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something enormously important.
He went backward.
Past Solomon.
Past David.
Past Jacob.
Past Abraham.
Back to creation.

Jesus appealed to the Creator’s design and quoted Genesis: a man is joined to his wife, and the two become one flesh. Then Christ declared that what God has joined together, man must not separate (Matthew 19:4–6).
The Greek expression in Matthew 19:5 is:
“οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
hoi dýo eis sárka mían
“the two into one flesh.”
Notice the direction Jesus points us.
Not toward the complicated marital arrangements of fallen kings.
Toward creation.
Toward God’s intention.
Toward covenant.
Toward one flesh.
That distinction changes everything.

Because the existence of polygamy in biblical history does not automatically establish divine approval of polygamy any more than the existence of deception, drunkenness, murder, adultery, slavery, betrayal, or warfare in biblical narratives automatically means God celebrates everything Scripture records.
The Bible is brutally honest about human beings.
And thank God it is.
Because if Scripture only contained spotless people, most of us would eventually wonder whether there was room inside its pages for people like us.
Then Abraham enters the story.
God had promised him descendants.
But time passed.
Sarah remained barren.
The promise seemed increasingly impossible.
And Genesis 16 takes us into one of the most painfully human moments in the patriarch’s life.
Sarah had an Egyptian servant named Hagar.
Sarah told Abraham to go to Hagar so perhaps a family could be built through her.
Abraham agreed.
Hagar conceived.
And almost immediately, the household began bleeding.
Hagar’s pregnancy changed the relationship between the women. Sarah felt humiliated and blamed Abraham. Conflict intensified. Sarah dealt harshly with Hagar, and Hagar fled.
Think about that.
Before Ishmael was even born, the arrangement had already produced relational fracture.
This is not the picture of some peaceful biblical endorsement of one man surrounded by happily interchangeable wives.
There is pain here.
A barren woman hurting.
An enslaved Egyptian woman caught inside the decisions of people more powerful than herself.
A husband who agreed to the arrangement.
Jealousy.
Contempt.
Anger.
Flight.
And yet—this is where the Gospel-shaped beauty of Scripture begins appearing even in the wreckage—God saw Hagar.
The vulnerable woman running through the wilderness was not invisible to Him.
Human beings had made a mess.
God had not lost sight of the wounded person inside it.
Later, Sarah gave birth to Isaac, and the household tension did not simply evaporate. Genesis 21 records another painful separation as Hagar and Ishmael were sent away.
God cared for them.
God heard the boy.
God preserved them.
But do not miss the human tragedy.
Trying to manufacture the promise through human means did not make Abraham’s family simpler.
It made the family more complicated.
God remained faithful.
That does not mean every human decision involved was therefore wise.
That distinction matters enormously.
God’s ability to redeem our decisions should never be mistaken for His endorsement of everything we did before redemption arrived.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that means.
You made a decision years ago.
Maybe God has shown you mercy since then.
Maybe He even brought something beautiful out of the wreckage.
And because something beautiful eventually emerged, you have been tempted to rewrite the past and call the original compromise good.
Don't.
Grace does not require pretending sin never hurt anybody.
Grace is more magnificent than that.
Grace can look directly at the wound and still say:
God is not finished.
Then comes Jacob.
If anyone tries to romanticize biblical polygamy, Jacob’s household should make that exceedingly difficult.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Laban deceived Jacob and gave him Leah.
Jacob then married Rachel also.
Genesis 29:30 states the emotional imbalance plainly: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Imagine living inside that sentence.
Leah knew.
Rachel knew.
Jacob knew.
God knew.
One woman had the husband’s affection.
The other desperately wanted it.
Leah began bearing children, and even the names surrounding those births reveal something heartbreaking about her longing to be loved.
Then Rachel, unable to bear children, became jealous of her sister.
Genesis 30:1 gives us her agonizing cry:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
This is not domestic tranquility.
This is desperation.
Competition enters reproduction itself.
Bilhah enters the arrangement.
Then Zilpah.
Children are born into a household where motherhood, affection, status, fertility, and rivalry are tangled together.
And then Scripture gives us one of the strangest and saddest little scenes in the story.
Mandrakes.
Rachel wants the mandrakes belonging to Leah’s son.
Leah responds with the accusation that Rachel has taken her husband.
An agreement follows.
Jacob will sleep with Leah that night in exchange for the mandrakes.
Pause there.
A night with a husband has effectively become something negotiated between rival wives.
How did we get here?
A man loved one sister more.
Two sisters became wives of the same man.
Servants became additional sexual partners.
Fertility became competition.
Intimacy became bargaining.
And the children grew up inside the emotional architecture of that home.
Years later, favoritism continued into the next generation.
Joseph, Rachel’s son, became Jacob’s specially loved son.
His brothers hated him.
They eventually sold him.
God would magnificently redeem Joseph’s suffering and use him to preserve lives.
But once again:
God redeeming dysfunction is not God endorsing dysfunction.
Please remember that sentence.
Because some of the greatest misunderstandings of Scripture happen when we look at what God accomplished despite human sin and conclude that the human sin must have been part of His moral ideal.
No.
Joseph’s story does not glorify jealous brothers.
It glorifies a sovereign God who can take what human beings intended for evil and bend the story toward saving life.
Then comes David.
David loved God.
David wrote psalms that have carried grieving believers through dark nights for thousands of years.
David worshiped.
David fought Goliath.
David knew repentance.
David also failed terribly.
Both are in the Bible.
That should make us tremble.
Because spiritual usefulness does not make a person immune to sexual compromise.
Anointing does not make temptation harmless.
Past victories do not guarantee future obedience.
Second Samuel 5:13 tells us David took additional wives and concubines in Jerusalem.
Then comes Bathsheba.
David sees her.
Desires her.
Takes her.
She becomes pregnant.
Uriah is eventually killed after David attempts to conceal what happened.
Nathan confronts the king.
“You are the man.”
David had power.
David had women.
David had a kingdom.
David had victories.
And still he reached for another man’s wife.
That is what unchecked appetite does.
It teaches the heart that having much means you deserve more.
And God did not call David’s actions harmless because David was His chosen king.
Nathan exposed him.
David confessed.
God forgave him.
But forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence.
The sword entered David’s house.
And then David’s family descended into scenes almost unbearable to read.
Amnon violated Tamar.
Absalom killed Amnon.
Absalom rebelled against David.
And during that rebellion, David’s concubines became part of a public act of humiliation and sexual degradation.
We must be careful here.
Not every tragedy in David’s household can responsibly be reduced to a simplistic equation—“David had multiple wives, therefore every later disaster happened solely because of polygamy.”
Scripture deserves better than careless arguments.

But neither should we ignore the world the narrative shows us: accumulated wives and concubines existed alongside sexual entitlement, fractured relationships, competing sons, political succession struggles, abuse, revenge, rebellion, and devastating family disorder.
The Bible does not airbrush any of it.
And then Solomon walks onto the stage.
The wisest king.
The builder of the temple.
A ruler whose fame crossed borders.
A man blessed with extraordinary wisdom.
And yet Scripture had already warned Israel’s kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 said that the king was not to multiply wives for himself lest his heart turn away.
Read that again.
The warning came before Solomon’s collapse.
Do not multiply wives…
lest the heart turn away.
Then 1 Kings 11 arrives with devastating precision.
Solomon had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
And Scripture does not present the number as a trophy of spiritual maturity.
The text immediately tells us where this went.
His wives turned his heart away.
The man who possessed extraordinary wisdom did something wisdom had warned against.
That should terrify every believer who thinks knowing Scripture is the same thing as obeying Scripture.
You can know truth and still negotiate with temptation.
You can teach wisdom and still violate wisdom.
You can have spiritual history with God and still allow your heart to drift.

Solomon’s problem was also specifically tied to covenant unfaithfulness and idolatry. First Kings 11 emphasizes that many of these marriages connected him to women from nations whose gods would draw Israel away from the LORD. Solomon eventually followed other gods and built places associated with their worship.
So we should not oversimplify the text as though mere ethnicity were the issue.
The theological danger Scripture identifies is apostasy.
His heart turned away from the LORD.
And suddenly Deuteronomy’s warning sounds prophetic:
Do not multiply wives…
lest your heart turn away.
Solomon multiplied wives.
His heart turned away.
The kingdom would eventually be torn.
What looked like royal abundance became spiritual poverty.
What looked like power became bondage.
What looked like a palace filled with love became a heart divided from God.
And perhaps this is where the story stops being ancient history.
Because you may never have seven hundred wives.
You may never sit on David’s throne.
You may never live inside Jacob’s tents.
You may never make Abraham’s mistake.
But you know what it is to want something badly enough to rationalize it.
You know what it is to say:
“God understands.”
“Everybody does it.”
“It isn’t hurting anyone.”
“I can control this.”
“I still love Jesus.”
“I’ll stop eventually.”
“This one compromise won’t change me.”
Maybe your divided heart does not look like Solomon’s palace.
Maybe it looks like the browser history you keep deleting.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The flirtation you refuse to end.
The secret messages.
The emotional affair.
The pornography.
The bitterness.
The obsession.
The idol you renamed “success.”
The compromise you renamed “freedom.”
The disobedience you renamed “complicated.”
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you can continue functioning spiritually while your heart is slowly moving.
Solomon did not become foolish because he lacked information.
He became unfaithful while possessing extraordinary wisdom.
That is the warning.
Knowing where the cliff is does not save you if you keep walking toward it.
But this article is not ultimately about Abraham.
It is not ultimately about Jacob.
It is not ultimately about David.
It is not ultimately about Solomon.
It is about the One toward whom their entire broken history was moving.
Jesus Christ.
Because the Bible does something astonishing.
It does not hide the scandal in the family line through which the Messiah eventually comes.
Matthew opens the New Testament by giving us a genealogy.
Abraham is there.
Jacob is there.
David is there.
Solomon is there.
Read that slowly.
God did not need a spotless family tree to bring the spotless Savior into the world.
The genealogy of Jesus contains human failure, sexual scandal, outsiders, broken families, compromised kings, grief, judgment, mercy, and grace.
And then comes Jesus.
Not another compromised patriarch.
Not another king whose appetites conquered him.
Not another son of Adam needing redemption.
The sinless Son of God.
Jesus does not enter the scandal to excuse it.
He enters to save sinners from it.
That is the Gospel.
We have sinned.
Not merely “made mistakes.”
Sinned.
We have broken God’s commands outwardly and inwardly.
We have lusted.
Lied.
Manipulated.
Envied.
Used people.
Hidden things.
Made idols.
Broken promises.
Protected reputations while hearts decayed.
And no amount of religious performance can rewrite what we have done.
But Jesus Christ came.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And the Gospel does not say, “Clean your scandal until God can tolerate you.”
The Gospel calls you to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Bring the lust.
Bring the adultery.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the broken marriage.
Bring the secret relationship.
Bring the shame.
Bring the consequences you cannot reverse.
Bring the memories you wish you could erase.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the family wounds.
Bring the sin you committed.
Bring the wounds others caused you.
Bring the thing you are terrified Christians would discover.
Bring it to Christ.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the blood of Jesus does.
There is a difference between grace and permission.
Permission says, “Keep going. It doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Come home. Jesus paid dearly to rescue you from what is destroying you.”
Biblical grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Biblical grace makes repentance hopeful.
You can turn around because Someone is waiting at the end of your surrender.
Jesus.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying consequences that will not disappear tomorrow.

Christianity does not promise that repentance automatically repairs every marriage, restores every lost year, removes every earthly consequence, or makes every wounded person immediately trust you again.
But Jesus can make you new.
He can forgive.
He can cleanse.
He can teach you faithfulness.
He can rebuild integrity one surrendered decision at a time.
He can break patterns your family has repeated for generations.
He can teach a wandering heart to come home.
David discovered something astonishing after catastrophic sin.
When confronted, he did not ultimately find salvation in pretending he had never fallen.
He cried to God for mercy.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
That is still the prayer.
Not:
“God, make everybody believe I never failed.”
But:
“God, change me.”
Maybe that needs to become your prayer before you scroll any farther.
Jesus, change me.
Not my spouse first.
Not my ex first.
Not the person who exposed me.
Not the church that disappointed me.
Me.
Search me.
Expose what I keep defending.
Break what is killing my intimacy with You.
Teach me covenant faithfulness.
Teach me holiness.
Teach me how to love without using people.
Teach me to repent without making excuses.
Teach me to receive grace without turning grace into permission.
And Jesus…
rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But do not let conviction evaporate into another scroll.

And if Christ has already been restoring something you once thought was beyond redemption, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer finally believes there is still a road home.
Be honest.
Did this hit somewhere you were not expecting?
Then do not keep it trapped on your screen.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
But if this ministry is helping you hear biblical truth in a world overflowing with spiritual noise, you can help carry that truth farther.
Someone hiding an affair.
Someone addicted to pornography.
Someone furious with God.
Someone convinced his past has disqualified him forever.
Someone who has confused biblical description with biblical approval.
Someone who needs to discover that Scripture does not hide human scandal—and neither does Jesus run from repentant sinners caught inside it.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who thinks the Bible hides the failures of its heroes.
It doesn't.
That honesty is part of what makes its message so devastatingly beautiful.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way of helping biblical content reach people who may never walk into a church building before they encounter truth on a screen.
But before you leave, remember the four men we started with.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
The Bible did not erase their failures.
And God did not abandon His redemptive purpose.
That does not mean their failures were harmless.
It means God's grace is greater than human wreckage.
Abraham’s household knew conflict.
Jacob’s household knew rivalry.
David’s household knew devastating consequences.
Solomon’s multiplied marriages became entangled with a heart that turned toward other gods.
Yet across generations of fractured humanity, God continued moving history toward Christ.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem the person who lived it.
You cannot make sin innocent.
But Jesus can make the sinner clean.
You cannot undo every consequence.
But Jesus can change what kind of person walks through those consequences.
You cannot crawl backward into Eden.
But through Christ, you can be reconciled to the God who made Eden.
So stop using broken biblical men as permission to remain broken.
Their failures were never given to you as excuses.
Their stories are warnings.
And the mercy God showed them is an invitation.
Repent.
Come home.
Trust Christ.
Let the King who never betrayed His Bride teach you what covenant love looks like.
Let the Savior who never surrendered to temptation rescue you from the appetites that have been mastering you.
Let the One who already knows the chapter you are ashamed of become Lord of the chapters that remain.
And when somebody tells you your scandal means God could never use you again, remember the genealogy.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
Then Jesus.
Not because scandal became holy.
Because grace entered the scandal and refused to let sin write the ending.
Your scandal may explain some of your scars—but once you surrender the pen to Jesus, it does not get to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE DESCRIBE SEDUCTION SO VIVIDLY IF SEXUALITY IS TOO DIRTY TO DISCUSS?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE DESCRIBE SEDUCTION SO VIVIDLY IF SEXUALITY IS TOO DIRTY TO DISCUSS?

Maybe God was never embarrassed by sexuality. Maybe we were. And perhaps the silence that was supposed to keep Christians “pure” has left generations completely unprepared for the moment temptation whispers their name.
There is a scene in the Bible that would make some Christians uncomfortable if it were preached exactly as it was written.
Night is falling.
A young man is walking down a street he probably should not be walking down.
He passes near a particular corner.
