There is a woman there.
She has been waiting.
She approaches him.
She grabs him.
She kisses him.
Then she begins talking.
And Scripture does not hurriedly close the curtain.
It lets you hear her.
It lets you watch the temptation develop.
It records the atmosphere, the timing, the clothing, the touch, the words, the invitation, the rationalization—and eventually the catastrophe.
Why?
If sexuality is too dirty for Christians to discuss, why does the Bible discuss sexual temptation with such startling honesty?
Why does Proverbs describe seduction instead of merely saying, “Don’t commit adultery”?
Why does Scripture contain poetry celebrating marital desire?
Why does Paul speak openly about husbands and wives giving themselves to one another?
Why does the Bible talk about bodies, desire, temptation, adultery, prostitution, lust, nakedness, marriage and sexual union?
Perhaps we have confused holiness with silence.
And those are not the same thing.
The Bible is sexually moral.
But it is not sexually embarrassed.
That difference matters enormously.
Because while many believers grew up hearing almost nothing except “don’t do it,” temptation was busy giving them an education of its own.
Pornography taught them.
Movies taught them.
Music taught them.
Broken relationships taught them.
Secret browser histories taught them.
Abusive experiences taught some of them.
Loneliness taught them.
Fantasy taught them.
Culture spoke loudly while the Church sometimes whispered awkwardly.
And then we wondered why so many people knew how to hide sexual brokenness better than they knew how to bring it to Jesus.
Open Proverbs 7 and watch what happens.
A father is warning his son about destructive sexual temptation. But he does something fascinating.
He tells him a story.
He remembers looking through the lattice of his window and seeing an inexperienced young man walking toward danger.
The Hebrew describes him as lacking lev—לֵב—literally “heart,” but in biblical Hebrew the heart can represent the inner center of judgment, understanding and moral discernment.
The problem is not that the young man possesses a body.
The problem is that he is walking toward temptation without wisdom governing that body.
He moves toward her corner as darkness falls.
Then she appears.
Proverbs describes her speech as seductive. Earlier, Proverbs 5:3 says:
כִּי נֹפֶת תִּטֹּפְנָה שִׂפְתֵי זָרָה
Ki nofet tittofna siftei zarah.
Literally, the imagery is something like:
“For the lips of the forbidden woman drip honey.”
Honey.
Not poison.
That is precisely the warning.
Sin rarely introduces itself by announcing the funeral it intends to cause.
It introduces itself by advertising the pleasure it can provide.
Temptation usually shows you the honey before it shows you the grave.
Proverbs 7 makes that psychology painfully vivid.
The woman approaches the young man, seizes him, kisses him and speaks boldly. She tells him that her bed is prepared. She describes perfume and fragrance. She invites him into prolonged intimacy.
Scripture lets the reader feel the gravitational pull of the temptation.
Then comes one of the most haunting transitions in biblical wisdom literature.
The young man follows.
And suddenly the imagery changes.
He was imagining a bedroom.
Wisdom sees a slaughterhouse.
He was imagining pleasure.
Wisdom sees an arrow.
He was imagining one night.
Wisdom sees death.

Proverbs compares him to an ox going toward slaughter and a bird rushing into a snare without realizing that its life is at stake. The chapter ultimately warns that the path of destructive sexual temptation descends toward death. Proverbs 7 deliberately narrates the progression rather than pretending temptation is unattractive.
That may be one reason the Bible describes seduction so vividly.
God is teaching His children to recognize temptation before they are standing inside it.
A vague warning can be forgotten.
A picture stays with you.
And Scripture knows something we sometimes refuse to admit:
Sexual sin can feel attractive.
If it never felt attractive, nobody would need to resist it.
Calling temptation attractive is not approving it.
It is understanding why temptation works.
The Bible does not need to lie about the sweetness of the bait in order to tell the truth about the hook.
But there is another side to this that Christians desperately need to recover.
The Bible's sexual ethic is not built upon the idea that sex itself is filthy.
Go back before Proverbs.
Before David and Bathsheba.
Before Judah and Tamar.
Before Samson and Delilah.
Before Corinth.
Before human sexual sin entered the story at all.
Go back to Eden.
God creates humanity male and female.
God establishes marriage.
Genesis describes husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
And Genesis 2:25 gives us an extraordinary picture:
They were naked...
and they were not ashamed.
Read that again.
Naked.
Not ashamed.
Before sin corrupted human relationships, nakedness between husband and wife was not presented as inherently filthy.
Sexuality did not originate in pornography.
It did not originate in Hollywood.
It did not originate in a nightclub.
It did not originate with Satan.
Human sexuality exists inside God's created order.
Sin did not invent sexuality.
Sin distorts what God made.
That distinction changes everything.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the curtains can destroy the home.
The problem is not that fire exists.
The question is whether it remains where it belongs.
And Scripture does not merely tolerate marital intimacy.
At times, it celebrates it with language so vivid that modern readers can become uncomfortable.

Proverbs 5 tells a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth and describes marital delight without embarrassment. Verse 19 even uses language translated as being “intoxicated,” “captivated,” or “exhilarated” with her love.
That is in your Bible.
The same Bible that warns against adultery tells a husband to delight deeply in his wife.
That destroys the simplistic idea that Christianity teaches:
“Sexual desire is dirty.”
No.
Biblically, the issue is not merely whether desire exists.

The questions are what the desire seeks, whom it honors, whether it obeys God, whether it exploits another person, whether it violates covenant, and whether Christ rules the heart carrying that desire.
The New Testament continues this remarkable honesty.
Paul writes to Christians in Corinth—a city and congregation wrestling with serious questions concerning sexuality—and does not pretend bodies are spiritually irrelevant.
He writes:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The verb pheugete carries the straightforward force of fleeing.
Not negotiating.
Not seeing how close you can stand.
Not proving how spiritually mature you are by lingering beside the temptation.
Flee.

And porneia—πορνεία—is the Greek term commonly rendered “sexual immorality,” used in the New Testament for illicit sexual conduct. Paul repeatedly uses the term in warnings concerning Christian holiness.
But listen carefully to Paul's reasoning.
He does not say:
“Flee because bodies are disgusting.”
He says something almost opposite.
Your body matters to God.
First Corinthians 6 declares that the believer's body is for the Lord and culminates in this astonishing command:
Glorify God in your body.
The Christian answer to sexual brokenness is therefore not hatred of the body.
It is redemption of the whole person.
Your body matters.
What you do with it matters.
What you watch matters.
Who you use matters.
Who uses you matters.
What fantasies you continually feed matters.
What secret relationship you protect matters.
What messages you delete matters.
What you repeatedly return to at 1:17 in the morning matters.
Not because Jesus is standing over you disgusted that you possess sexuality.
But because He purchased you at tremendous cost.
First Corinthians 6 grounds bodily holiness in belonging to Christ: believers are “bought at a price” and therefore called to honor God with their bodies.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years confusing conviction with disgust.
You failed sexually.
Maybe yesterday.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe nobody knows.
You promised God it would never happen again.
Then it happened again.
You cleared the history.
Deleted the messages.
Blocked the person.
Unblocked the person.
Cried.
Prayed.
Went to church.
Raised your hands during worship while carrying a secret you were terrified anyone might discover.
You heard Christians talk about sexual purity and every sentence felt like another shovel of dirt landing on your coffin.
So eventually you stopped asking:
“How can I become free?”
And started asking:
“Would Jesus even want me if He knew everything?”
Listen carefully.
He already knows everything.
That is what makes grace so staggering.
The Gospel is not Jesus discovering the sanitized version of you.
The Gospel is Jesus knowing the truth and going to the cross for sinners anyway.
But grace does not tell you that the chains are harmless.
Grace opens the prison door.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could decorate our captivity with Christian vocabulary.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Restore.
Transform.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from both sexual shame and sexual permissiveness.
One voice says:
“Your desires define you. Follow them.”
Another says:
“Your desires make you disgusting. Hide them.”
Jesus calls us somewhere else entirely.
“Follow Me.”
That means your strongest desire is not necessarily your master.
Your worst failure is not necessarily your final chapter.
Your past does not possess authority greater than Christ's blood.
And your body does not belong to pornography, an affair, an ex-lover, a secret fantasy, an algorithm, your trauma, another person's exploitation, or the appetite that keeps demanding one more look.
For the Christian, Paul says:
“The body...is for the Lord.”
That sentence is revolutionary.
Because Christianity does not ultimately offer sexual repression.
It offers lordship.
Jesus becomes Lord even here.
Especially here.
The Bible therefore speaks about sexuality precisely because sexuality matters.
It can participate in covenant love.
It can create profound vulnerability.
It can become entangled with betrayal.
It can be used selfishly.
It can become addictive.
It can leave memories that follow someone for decades.
It can be weaponized.
It can be commercialized.
It can be separated from love and turned into consumption.
And within God's design for marriage, sexual intimacy can also express delight, exclusivity, tenderness and mutual belonging.

Paul even speaks with striking reciprocity when addressing married couples in 1 Corinthians 7. Husband and wife are both told to fulfill their marital responsibilities toward one another; neither spouse is presented as the only person whose embodied marital concerns matter. Paul also says periods of abstinence should be by mutual agreement.
And Hebrews says:
“Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure.”
Notice the balance.
Honor the marriage bed.
Keep the marriage bed pure.
Not:
Pretend the marriage bed does not exist.
Biblical purity is not pretending sexuality disappeared when you became a Christian.
Purity is bringing sexuality under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That is much harder than silence.
Silence can hide things.
Jesus transforms them.
And perhaps this explains why Proverbs 7 is so graphic in its warning.
God knows that the person who cannot identify temptation may become its easiest prey.
The young man in Proverbs keeps walking.
That detail should haunt us.
Because catastrophic failures often begin with ordinary steps.
One message.
One search.
One conversation.
One rationalization.
One hidden friendship.
One click.
One more drink.
One private meeting.
One thought:
“I can handle this.”
Then another:
“Nobody will know.”
Then the oldest lie:
“Just this once.”
And somewhere between the first compromise and the final collapse, the person asks:
“How did I get here?”
One step at a time.
That is why wisdom speaks before the bedroom.
It speaks at the corner.
Before the kiss.
Before the invitation.
Before desire overwhelms judgment.
Before secrecy becomes a lifestyle.
Before two families are crying.
Before a spouse discovers the messages.
Before a child wonders why Mom and Dad no longer live together.
Before the ministry collapses.
Before shame begins whispering that suicide, disappearance or permanent isolation would be easier than confession.
Wisdom stands at the beginning of the road and says:
Do not go that way.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because God sees farther down the road than you do.
This is one of the most loving dimensions of biblical commands that modern culture frequently misunderstands.
God's “no” is not always deprivation.
Sometimes God's “no” is a guardrail placed twenty feet before a cliff.
And if you have already gone over the cliff?
Then we need the rest of the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not merely the announcement:
“You sinned.”
If that were the whole message, none of us would have hope.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.
At the cross, sin is neither minimized nor declared harmless.
It is taken so seriously that the Son of God bears judgment for His people.
And grace is so astonishing that guilty people can be forgiven.
That includes sexual sinners.
The adulterer can repent.
The porn-addicted can seek freedom.
The person who sold their body is not beyond Christ.
The person who used someone else's body is not beyond repentance.
The sexually exploited are not contaminated beyond redemption.
The divorced and devastated are not abandoned.
The person carrying memories they wish they could erase is not invisible.
The virgin is not superior because of virginity.
The sexually broken person is not beneath the reach of mercy because of brokenness.
Everybody comes to Christ empty-handed.
Nobody walks into the kingdom boasting.
At the foot of the cross, our résumé burns.
There is only mercy for sinners who come to Jesus.
But mercy is not permission to remain enslaved.
When Jesus forgives, He also calls people into a new life.
Repentance is not paying God back for forgiveness.
You could never pay Him back.
Repentance is turning because grace has opened another road.
This is why Christians need to become capable of speaking about sexuality without becoming either vulgar or terrified.
Our children need more than:
“Don't have sex.”
They need a theology of the body.
Teenagers need to know why desire can become overwhelming.
Singles need something deeper than being treated as spiritually incomplete until marriage.
Married couples need permission to discuss intimacy honestly and respectfully.
People trapped in pornography need pathways toward confession, accountability, discipleship and practical boundaries.
Victims of sexual abuse need to hear clearly that another person's sin against them is not their moral stain.
Those struggling with temptation need brothers and sisters who know how to say both:
“This can destroy you.”
And:
“Come into the light. We are not abandoning you.”
Church should be one of the safest places on earth to confess sin.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Jesus is sufficient.
Imagine what would happen if Christians stopped confusing secrecy with holiness.
Imagine fathers speaking wisely to sons before pornography does.
Mothers speaking tenderly and truthfully to daughters.
Husbands and wives learning to communicate instead of silently accumulating rejection and resentment.
Pastors preaching passages like Proverbs 5 and 7 without embarrassment.
Believers confessing temptation before temptation becomes catastrophe.
Imagine somebody saying:
“I need help.”
And instead of hearing—
“How could you?”
They hear—
“Thank you for telling the truth. We're going to walk toward Jesus together.”
That is discipleship.
Truth without grace can crush a person.
Grace without truth can leave a person chained.
Jesus brings both.
And maybe that is why this article found you tonight.
Maybe you thought you were simply reading something about sexuality.
But somewhere along the way, a face appeared in your mind.
A memory.
A browser history.
A relationship.
A wound.
A secret.
A habit.
A compromise.
Something you have been negotiating with God about.
Something hidden behind the words:
“I'm okay.”
You don't have to tell Facebook everything.
Wisdom does not require public exposure of every private struggle.
But you do need honesty before God.
And serious bondage often requires bringing trustworthy, mature Christian help into the darkness too.
No more pretending that secrecy is protecting you when secrecy may actually be protecting the chain.
You do not have to explain the details.
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, write:
And if Jesus has already begun restoring an area of your life you once thought could never be healed, tell somebody beneath this article:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer desperately needed to read tonight.
And please—do not merely react to this and keep scrolling.
There may be a night when temptation sounds convincing again and you need to remember where the road ends.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Send it privately to the believer who has been disappearing lately.
Send it to the husband trying to rebuild trust.
The wife carrying silent heartbreak.
The young man being discipled by pornography.
The young woman convinced her past made her permanently dirty.
The Christian who thinks repeated failure means Jesus has finally run out of mercy.
Even send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity teaches that sexuality itself is filthy.
Let them encounter what Scripture actually says.
It is not a purchase of God's favor.
It does not replace belonging to and supporting a faithful local church.
And it should not be confused with a biblical requirement to tithe.
Scripture teaches generosity that is willing rather than coerced; Paul says giving should not be “reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary financial support can become a very practical act of partnership in Gospel work.
If this ministry has spiritually fed you and you want to help it continue and expand, you can become one of the people helping carry that work.
Not because God needs your money.
Not because we can sell grace.
Grace cannot be bought.
But Gospel ministry still requires people willing to pray, serve, give, create, share and send.
It is partnership.
It is helping keep Scripture moving.
Helping keep discipleship accessible.
Helping another article reach another screen...
which may reach another person...
who may finally whisper after years of running:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And whether you ever give financially or not, keep pursuing Jesus.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who doesn't believe yet.
And keep sharing the Gospel.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is standing at the same corner as the young man in Proverbs 7.
They can hear temptation calling.
They can see the honey.
They cannot yet see the slaughterhouse.
Maybe your share reaches them before they take another step.
Maybe your comment tells them they are not the only Christian fighting.
Maybe your testimony convinces them confession is possible.
Maybe your courage gives someone else permission to stop hiding.
But above everything else, remember this:
The answer to sexual brokenness is not pretending you never had a body.
It is surrendering your whole body, your whole history, your whole sexuality, your whole shame, your whole future—and your whole heart—to Jesus Christ.
He is not frightened by the chapter you wish had never been written.
He knows every page.
He knows every secret paragraph.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows what you chose.
He knows what you regret.
He knows where you are still struggling.
And the cross declares that scandal does not have to receive the final sentence.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive mercy.
Walk in truth.
Run when temptation calls.
And when you fall, do not run away from Christ as though your blood could clean what only His blood can cleanse.
Run to Him.
Because perhaps the most dangerous lie sexual shame ever told you was that Jesus would rewrite everybody's story...
except yours.
But the pen is still in the hands of the Redeemer.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Want Justice Until Grace Is Offered to Someone You Think Deserves Ruin.
paragraphs: You Want Justice Until Grace Is Offered to Someone You Think Deserves Ruin.
The Gospel becomes uncomfortable when the mercy that saved you is offered to someone whose sins make you angry.
There is a kind of grace everybody loves.
Grace for the exhausted mother.
Grace for the grieving father.
Grace for the teenager who made one terrible mistake.
Grace for the addict begging God for another chance.
Grace for the wounded believer crawling back to church after years away.
We hear those stories and something inside us whispers, “Yes. That is what Jesus does.”
But then another name appears.
Someone who did not merely stumble.
Someone who hurt people.
Someone whose choices left wounds in other people’s lives.
Someone whose past cannot be cleaned up with a sentimental testimony and soft music.
Someone you believe should pay.
And suddenly grace does not feel beautiful anymore.
It feels offensive.
Maybe even unjust.
Because it is easy to celebrate mercy when you identify with the person receiving it.
It becomes much harder when you identify with the person they wounded.
And harder still when you look at what they did and quietly think:
God, please tell me You are not going to forgive that.
That is where the Gospel begins exposing something in us.
Because almost everyone wants grace for sinners in theory.
The real test comes when grace has a face.
Especially a face you believe deserves ruin.

And before you continue, understand something important: Scripture never asks you to pretend evil is not evil. Christianity does not require victims to call abuse harmless, betrayal insignificant, violence acceptable, exploitation excusable, or injustice imaginary.
God is not morally confused.
The cross itself proves that sin is far more serious than our culture wants to believe.
But the cross also reveals something equally terrifying.
God's mercy can reach people we would have written off forever.
And if that bothers us, perhaps we need to meet the man writing 1 Timothy again.
His name was Paul.
But before churches quoted his letters...
before missionaries followed his example...
before Christians named their children after him...
there were believers who knew him by another reputation.
Persecutor.
Enemy.
Threat.
Paul does not sanitize it.
He does not rewrite his résumé so his testimony sounds respectable.
He reaches backward into the ugliest chapter of his own life and describes himself with three devastating Greek words:
“βλάσφημον καὶ διώκτην καὶ ὑβριστήν”
blasphēmon kai diōktēn kai hybristēn.
A blasphemer.
A persecutor.
An insolent, violent aggressor.
Then comes one of the most scandalous turns in his testimony:
“ἀλλὰ ἠλεήθην”
alla ēleēthēn.
“But I received mercy.”
Read that again.
Not:
“But I proved everybody misunderstood me.”
Not:
“But what I did really wasn't that serious.”
Not:
“But there were circumstances that made my behavior acceptable.”
Paul does not defend himself.
He confesses.
And then he says:
I received mercy.
That is scandalous grace.
Paul had persecuted the very people whose Savior would eventually commission him.
Acts records Saul ravaging the church and dragging men and women away to prison. The New Testament does not hide that history merely because Paul later became an apostle.
His conversion did not make yesterday imaginary.
Grace did not require history to lie.
And this matters enormously because Christians sometimes confuse forgiveness with minimizing evil.
They are not the same thing.
Biblical mercy does not say, “It didn't matter.”
Biblical mercy says, “It mattered so much that Christ had to die.”
At Calvary, God did not sweep human evil underneath a celestial rug.
Justice and mercy met at a cross.
Sin was condemned.
A price was paid.
And astonishingly, the One paying it was not the guilty sinner hanging beside Christ.
It was Christ Himself.
That is why Christianity can speak about radical forgiveness without pretending sin is trivial.
Jesus Christ did not come into the world because humanity needed encouragement.
He came because sinners needed rescue.
Paul says it with breathtaking simplicity:
“Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς ἦλθεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἁμαρτωλοὺς σῶσαι”
Christos Iēsous ēlthen eis ton kosmon hamartōlous sōsai.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.”
Then Paul adds:
“ὧν πρῶτός εἰμι ἐγώ”
hōn prōtos eimi egō.
“Of whom I am foremost.”
Notice the uncomfortable grammar.
Paul does not merely say, “I was the foremost.”
He says, “I am.”
He is not denying transformation. The persecutor really did become a servant of Christ.
But Paul apparently never reached the stage of Christian maturity where grace became something he thought other people desperately needed while he merely deserved.
He remembered the pit.
He remembered who found him there.
And perhaps that is one reason grace becomes smaller in our hearts when memory becomes selective.
We remember what people did to us with astonishing clarity.
But sometimes we remember what Christ forgave in us only vaguely.
Their sin remains high-definition.
Ours slowly becomes blurred.
Their rebellion was wicked.
Ours was complicated.
They deliberately sinned.
We were struggling.
They deserve consequences.
We needed understanding.
And without noticing it, we begin standing before the cross as though Jesus died for two completely different categories of people:
sinners...
and us.
But Scripture destroys that illusion.
“For all have sinned.”
All.
That does not mean every sin causes identical earthly damage.
It does not mean every crime deserves the same civil consequence.
It does not mean the betrayed spouse and the betrayer occupy identical positions in the harm that occurred.
It does not mean an abused person must immediately restore trust to an abuser.
It does not mean repentance eliminates accountability.
It does not mean forgiveness requires reconciliation without wisdom, safety, truth, or demonstrated change.
And it certainly does not mean Christians should protect perpetrators while pressuring wounded people into silence.
Grace is not complicity.
Mercy is not pretending.
Forgiveness is not permission.
The Gospel does not erase justice.
It tells us why justice matters so profoundly.
But here is the question that cuts deeper than almost any theological debate about mercy:
If the person who hurt you genuinely repented...
if there were no excuses...
if they stopped hiding...
if they confessed what they had done...
if they accepted rightful consequences...
if they turned to Jesus Christ broken over their sin...
would you actually want God to forgive them?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit inside that question.
Because sometimes we say we want repentance when what we really want is ruin.
Sometimes we say, “I just want justice,” while somewhere underneath those words another desire is breathing:
I want them to hurt.
I want them humiliated.
I want everyone to know.
I want their worst moment to become their permanent identity.
And then Jesus walks into the courtroom.
Not denying the evidence.
Not intimidating the wounded.
Not calling darkness light.
Not pretending consequences do not matter.
He simply asks a terrifying question:
What if My blood is enough for them too?
That is where scandalous grace begins.
Because the Gospel is not merely the announcement that people like you can be forgiven.
The Gospel announces that genuinely guilty people can be forgiven.
People with records.
People with victims.
People with shameful histories.
People whose names make others uncomfortable.
People whose repentance cannot undo the damage they caused.
People who may still face consequences tomorrow even though Christ has forgiven them today.
The cross does not promise that repentance removes every earthly consequence.
David was forgiven, yet consequences followed his sin.
The thief beside Jesus received paradise, but he still died on a Roman cross.
Paul received mercy, but he never pretended persecution had been harmless.
Grace changes our standing before God.
It does not rewrite history by pretending the wound never happened.
It rewrites the sinner.
And there is an enormous difference.
Paul says:
“ὑπερεπλεόνασεν δὲ ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν”
hyper-epleonasen de hē charis tou kyriou hēmōn.
The grace of our Lord overflowed exceedingly.
The verb is almost excessive by design.
Grace did not merely reach Paul.
It overflowed toward him.
It superabounded.
It went beyond the boundaries his past appeared to have constructed around his future.
That is why Paul's story is not fundamentally a celebration of Paul.
It is a revelation of Jesus.
Paul explains exactly why his mercy matters:
“ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο ἠλεήθην”
alla dia touto ēleēthēn.
“But for this reason I received mercy...”
Why?
So that in him, Jesus Christ might display:
“τὴν ἅπασαν μακροθυμίαν”
tēn hapasan makrothymian.
His extraordinary fullness of patience.
And Paul says his life became an “ὑποτύπωσιν” — hypotypōsin — a pattern, an example, for those who would later believe in Christ for eternal life.
In other words:
Paul's ugly past became evidence of Christ's astonishing patience.
Think about that.
The enemy of the church became evidence that Jesus can save enemies of the church.
The persecutor became proof that persecutors are not beyond repentance.
The man Christians once feared became the man God used to tell generations of frightened sinners:
There is mercy here.
That does not make Paul's persecution beautiful.
Jesus made redemption beautiful.
There is a difference.
God does not need to rename evil in order to redeem an evildoer.
He does not call the scandal righteous.
He brings grace into the scandal.
And maybe that is exactly where this becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years defining someone by the worst thing they ever did.
Or perhaps...
you are the person who did the terrible thing.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you carry a chapter of your life that makes you wonder whether Christians would still hug you if they knew everything.
Maybe you have sat in church listening to testimonies about grace while secretly wondering whether there is an invisible footnote beneath the Gospel:
Except people like you.
Listen carefully.
Paul wrote 1 Timothy 1 for people who would wonder exactly that.
He says Jesus displayed His patience in him as a pattern for people who would later believe.
Paul essentially stands before history with blood on the résumé and mercy over his life and says:
Look at what Jesus can do with a guilty man.
Not an innocent man falsely accused.
A guilty man.
That is the scandal.
And that is the hope.
Your sin is not stronger than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Your shame is not older than His mercy.
Your history is not more authoritative than His cross.
But grace does not merely invite you to feel better about yourself.
It calls you to repent.
Jesus does not save us so we can decorate our chains.
He saves us to break them.
Grace is not God saying, “Continue.”
Grace is God saying, “Come.”
Come out of hiding.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Turn.
Believe.
Surrender.
Follow Christ.
The same grace that pardons begins transforming.
Paul did not receive mercy so Saul could become a more comfortable persecutor.
Saul met Christ and his direction changed.
That is repentance.
Not perfection overnight.
Not pretending temptation disappears.
But a genuine turning of the heart toward Jesus that begins producing a changed life.
And perhaps the reason some people hate the doctrine of grace is because they mistake grace for God allowing guilty people to escape justice.
But Christianity says something far more shocking.
Justice was not escaped.
Justice fell upon Christ.
“He was wounded for our transgressions.”
At the cross, Jesus voluntarily stood in the place of sinners.
The innocent One bore judgment so guilty people who trust Him could receive mercy without God becoming unjust.
That means forgiveness is never cheap.
Every forgiven sin points toward scars.
Every Christian standing in heaven will be there because the Lamb was slain.
Nobody will swagger through the gates of the kingdom carrying a résumé.
Nobody will look across eternity at another redeemed sinner and say:
“I belonged here more than you.”
There will only be trophies of mercy.
Former liars.
Former adulterers.
Former idolaters.
Former haters.
Former addicts.
Former hypocrites.
Former rebels.
Former religious pretenders.
People whose sins were visible.
People whose sins were hidden behind respectable clothing.
All washed by the same Christ.
All rescued by the same Gospel.
All singing about the same Lamb.
And perhaps heaven will expose how strangely selective our earthly outrage sometimes was.
We wanted God to forgive our secret pride but punish their public scandal.
We wanted mercy for our lust but destruction for their betrayal.
We wanted patience with our bitterness but immediate judgment for their cruelty.
We wanted the cross to cover everything behind us while drawing a line immediately before them.
But there is only one Savior.
And sinners do not get to determine whose sin is too scandalous for His blood.
There is another side to this truth, however, and wounded people especially need to hear it.
If somebody harmed you, God's willingness to forgive a genuinely repentant sinner does not mean He is indifferent toward what happened to you.
Jesus sees victims too.
He cares about truth.
He cares about justice.
He cares about the oppressed.
He condemns exploitation and hypocrisy.
He does not require you to manufacture trust where trust has been destroyed.
You can forgive while maintaining boundaries.
You can release personal vengeance to God while cooperating with legitimate accountability.

You can desire someone's salvation while recognizing that restoration to a particular relationship, office, ministry, or position may require conditions that forgiveness alone does not automatically restore.
Grace does not make wisdom unnecessary.
And Christian communities should never use “forgive” as a weapon to keep wounded people quiet.
The God who offers mercy to the sinner is also the God who hears the cries of those sinned against.
That is why the Gospel's tension is so difficult.
God cares about the wounded.
And God can save the wounder.
We usually find one side easier to believe than the other.
But at the cross, neither disappears.
Justice matters.
Mercy matters.
Truth matters.
Repentance matters.
Victims matter.
The guilty can still be redeemed.
And Jesus remains at the center of all of it.
Maybe you came into this article thinking about somebody else.
Maybe their face appeared immediately when you read the title.
But what if the Holy Spirit has been slowly turning the mirror around?
What if the deepest question is not whether that person deserves grace?
What if the question is whether you ever did?
That changes everything.
Because grace, by definition, cannot be deserved.
If you deserve it, it is wages.
If God owes it to you, it is payment.
Grace begins precisely where deserving ends.
And the Christian's confession is not:
“I was slightly better than the people God condemned.”
It is:
“I needed Christ.”
Maybe your scandal never made the news.
Maybe your sin never destroyed a career.
Maybe nobody created a post exposing what you did.
Maybe your darkness was quiet.
Pride can be quiet.
Envy can be quiet.
Pornography can be quiet.
Hatred can be quiet.
Self-righteousness can be quiet.
Unbelief can be quiet.
A heart can rebel against God while maintaining an excellent public reputation.
And that respectable sinner needs the same Savior.
This is why self-righteousness cannot survive very long at the foot of the cross.
The closer you stand to Calvary, the harder it becomes to boast.
You begin realizing:
I am not the prosecutor here.
I am another sinner who needed an Advocate.
And suddenly Paul's words stop sounding ancient.
“ἀλλὰ ἠλεήθην.”
But I received mercy.
Maybe that needs to become your sentence.
I lied.
But I received mercy.
I betrayed.
But I received mercy.
I hated.
But I received mercy.
I hid.
But I received mercy.
I wandered.
But I received mercy.
I became religious and proud.
But I received mercy.
I knew better and still rebelled.
But I received mercy.
Not because sin stopped mattering.
Because Jesus mattered more.
And if Christ has shown you that kind of mercy, there will eventually come a moment when He asks you to stop clutching another person's debt as though their destruction could heal you.
That does not mean pretending.
It does not mean immediately trusting.
It does not mean abandoning lawful justice.
It means surrendering vengeance to the Judge who actually knows every fact.
Romans 12 does not tell believers that evil is imaginary. It tells us not to avenge ourselves, but to leave judgment to God.
That is freedom.
You do not have to become someone's judge, jury, and executioner to acknowledge that what they did was wrong.
God sees.
God knows.
God judges rightly.
And if that person never repents, God will not accidentally overlook evil.
But if that person does repent and runs to Christ...
then Christians must face the scandalous possibility that the blood which cleansed us can cleanse them.
That might hurt.
It might confuse you.
You might need time to process it.
But heaven does not become less just because another sinner gets saved.
Grace does not steal justice from you.
At Calvary, grace proves how costly justice really was.
Perhaps somebody reading this right now is standing on the other side of that sentence.
You are not struggling to forgive the guilty person.
You are the guilty person.
And you have wondered whether there could possibly be a future after what you did.
Paul would tell you:
Look at me.
Then he would immediately point beyond himself:
Look at Christ.
Do not hide behind grace while refusing repentance.
But do not hide from Christ because you think your sin is greater than His mercy.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Make restitution where restitution is appropriate and possible.
Accept consequences that truth requires.
Seek forgiveness without demanding that wounded people immediately trust you again.
Do not manipulate people with your conversion.
Do not use Jesus as public-relations management.
Repent because Jesus is Lord.
And then believe the Gospel.
Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
Guilty ones.
People like Paul.
People like us.
If this exposed something in you, do not rush past it.
Maybe you have been secretly wishing destruction on somebody.
Maybe you have been calling vengeance “discernment.”
Maybe you have forgotten how much Christ forgave you.
Or maybe shame has convinced you that Jesus would receive everyone except you.
Be honest before God.
And please do not merely react to this article and move on.
There may come a day when somebody's failure tests whether you really believe what you say about grace.
Send it privately to the believer who has almost given up.
Send it to the person convinced their past disqualified them forever.
Even send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only a religion for respectable people.
Let them encounter Paul.
Then let Paul point them toward Jesus.

Salvation cannot be purchased, and supporting a ministry does not make anyone more righteous before Christ. But those who believe this kind of Gospel-centered work should continue can voluntarily help support its reach so more people can encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the hope found in Jesus.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be earned.
Eternal life is not merchandise.
Christ is the Savior.
And perhaps that is the final scandal.
The people standing around the throne will not be people who successfully proved they never needed mercy.
They will be people who discovered they needed more mercy than they ever imagined...
and found more mercy in Jesus than they ever dreamed possible.
So the next time you look at someone and think,
They deserve ruin...
remember the persecutor who became an apostle.
Remember:
“ἀλλὰ ἠλεήθην.”
But I received mercy.
Then look toward the cross.
Because the question was never whether sinners deserved grace.
The wonder is that Jesus gives grace to sinners at all.
And one day you may discover that the person you believed was too ruined for redemption became another living demonstration of the patience of Jesus Christ.
Just like Paul.
Just like countless believers.
Maybe...
just like you.
Never make another person's worst chapter bigger than the blood of Christ—and never forget that Jesus once met you in a chapter you could not rewrite yourself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A CITY WAS STARVING SO BADLY THAT PEOPLE WERE PAYING FORTUNES FOR ALMOST NOTHING. THEN ELISHA MADE AN IMPOSSIBLE PREDICTION.
paragraphs: A CITY WAS STARVING SO BADLY THAT PEOPLE WERE PAYING FORTUNES FOR ALMOST NOTHING. THEN ELISHA MADE AN IMPOSSIBLE PREDICTION.

The Siege of Samaria became so horrific that a donkey’s head cost eighty pieces of silver and mothers were discussing the unthinkable. Then, while everyone could see only death, Elisha said that by this time tomorrow food would be abundant—and four dying outcasts were about to discover that God had already moved.
There are Bible stories we make safe because we have heard them too many times.
We know the ending.
We know God wins.
We know deliverance comes.
So we read quickly.
But imagine reading 2 Kings 6 without knowing chapter 7 exists.
Imagine being inside Samaria.
Not reading about the famine.
Smelling it.
Living it.
Watching another day begin while wondering what can possibly be sold because nearly everything worth eating has already disappeared.
This wasn't someone complaining that groceries had become expensive.
This was societal collapse.
Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had surrounded Samaria. The siege was doing exactly what ancient sieges were designed to do: isolate a population until hunger accomplished what weapons had not.
Nobody needed to storm the walls if starvation could break the people inside them.
And Scripture does not sanitize what happened.
The Hebrew says:
“וַיְהִי רָעָב גָּדוֹל בְּשֹׁמְרוֹן”
Vayehi ra'av gadol b'Shomron.
“There was a great famine in Samaria.”
Great famine.
Not inconvenience.
Not scarcity that could be solved by cutting expenses.
Famine.
Then the writer gives us prices.

A donkey's head was selling for eighty pieces of silver, while a quarter-kab of something the Hebrew text calls ḥiryônim—traditionally rendered “dove's dung,” though the precise identification has been debated—was selling for five pieces of silver.
Whatever precisely that second commodity was, the narrator's point is unmistakable.
Desperation had rewritten the economy.
Things nobody would normally value had become costly because people were starving.
And there is something frighteningly human about that.
When you become desperate enough, you can start paying enormous prices for things that cannot truly feed you.
Some people do it with money.
Some with relationships.
Some with pornography.
Some with attention.
Some with alcohol.
Some with applause.
Some with achievement.
Some with religious performance.
Some spend years purchasing tiny moments of validation with pieces of their soul.
A little affection.
A little escape.
A little pleasure.
A little numbness.
A little feeling that somebody finally sees them.
And the price keeps rising.
Your peace.
Your marriage.
Your integrity.
Your prayer life.
Your ability to look yourself in the mirror without remembering what you have been hiding.
That is one of sin's cruelest economies.
It makes almost nothing look priceless when the soul is starving.
But Samaria was about to descend somewhere darker still.
The king of Israel was walking along the city wall when a woman cried to him for help.
He asked what was wrong.
Her answer is one of those passages of Scripture you wish were not there.
But God allowed it to remain in His Word because the Bible does not pretend human brokenness is prettier than it really is.
The woman described an agreement with another mother.
They would eat her son first.
Then they would eat the other woman's son.
Her child was killed and eaten.
The next day, however, the second mother hid her own son.
Stop there.
Don't rush toward the miracle yet.
A child was dead.
A mother had participated in something almost impossible to comprehend.
Another mother was hiding her son.
A king was standing on a wall listening to the horror happening beneath his government.
This is what starvation had done.
And when the king heard it, he tore his clothes.
Underneath his royal garments, the people saw sackcloth.
He was grieving.
But grief is not necessarily repentance.
A person can hate the consequences of a broken world without surrendering the heart to God.
The king's next reaction exposes something terribly familiar.
He wanted Elisha dead.
The prophet became the target.
When people cannot control their circumstances, they often search for somebody to blame.
Sometimes even God.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
You prayed.
Nothing changed.
You waited.
Nothing moved.
You tried to obey.
The door remained closed.
You watched someone else receive the thing you begged God for.
Then a dangerous sentence quietly formed somewhere inside you:
“Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?”
That is essentially where the chapter leaves us.
And perhaps that sentence is closer to your heart than you want anyone to know.
Why should I keep praying?
Why keep believing?
Why remain faithful?
Why keep forgiving?
Why keep fighting temptation?
Why keep worshiping when heaven feels silent?
Why should I wait any longer?
Then Elisha speaks.
Not motivational optimism.
Not positive thinking.
Not a prediction based upon military intelligence.
The Hebrew begins:
“שִׁמְעוּ דְּבַר־יְהוָה”
Shim'u devar-YHWH.
“Hear the word of the LORD.”
Then comes the impossible announcement:
“כָּעֵת מָחָר”
Ka'et machar.
“About this time tomorrow…”
Tomorrow.
Elisha declares that fine flour will sell for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel at the gate of Samaria.
Think about the absurdity of that statement from inside the city.
Today people are paying fortunes for almost nothing.
Tomorrow flour will be affordable.
Today starvation.
Tomorrow abundance.
Today mothers are desperate.
Tomorrow food will flood the market.
And Elisha doesn't announce a five-year agricultural recovery program.
He says tomorrow.
One of the king's officers hears this and essentially responds:
Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could that happen?
You can almost understand his skepticism.
Almost.
Because everything visible contradicted the promise.
There was still an army outside.
Still famine inside.
Still no supply route.
Still no visible rescue force.
Still no logical mechanism connecting “today” with Elisha's “tomorrow.”
And this is where faith is often misunderstood.
Biblical faith is not pretending circumstances aren't real.
Samaria's famine was real.
The enemy was real.
The dead child was real.
The empty stomachs were real.
Biblical faith does not require you to call darkness light.
Faith takes God seriously even when you cannot yet see how His word could possibly be fulfilled.
The officer's tragedy wasn't that he understood the impossibility.
Everyone understood the impossibility.
His tragedy was treating God's power as though it were imprisoned inside the boundaries of what he could imagine.
Elisha answered that he would see the promised abundance with his own eyes...
but he would not eat from it.
Then the camera of Scripture moves.
Away from the palace.
Away from the king.
Away from Elisha.
Away from the powerful.
Toward four men sitting outside the gate.
Four men described by the text as מְצֹרָעִים — metzora'im, people afflicted with a serious skin condition that left them marginalized from ordinary community life.
They are trapped between two kinds of death.
Behind them is a starving city.
Ahead of them is an enemy army.
So they ask one of the most brutally logical questions in Scripture:
“מָה אֲנַחְנוּ יֹשְׁבִים פֹּה עַד־מָתְנוּ”
Mah anachnu yoshvim poh ad-matnu?
“Why are we sitting here until we die?”
Read that again.
Why are we sitting here until we die?
There are moments when those words stop being ancient history.
Why am I sitting in the same secret sin until something in me dies?
Why am I sitting in bitterness?
Why am I sitting in shame?
Why am I sitting behind excuses?
Why am I sitting inside a version of Christianity that knows church language but has lost hunger for Christ?
Why am I sitting here until I die?
The four men reasoned that remaining where they were meant death.
Returning to the city meant death.
Approaching the Arameans might mean death.
But there was at least the possibility of mercy.
So at twilight they got up.
No army marched with them.
No sword-bearing battalion followed.
Four desperate outcasts simply started walking.
And while they walked...
God was doing something they could not hear.
Scripture says the Lord caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots, horses and a great army.
The Syrians concluded that Israel had hired foreign kings against them.
Panic erupted.
They ran.
They abandoned tents.
Horses.
Donkeys.
Food.
Silver.
Gold.
Clothing.
Everything.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
The four men did not defeat the army.
Elisha did not defeat the army.
The king did not defeat the army.
Samaria's starving population did not defeat the army.
The Lord acted.
By the time the four men reached the enemy camp, the battle they feared was effectively already over.
They arrived expecting perhaps to beg for their lives.
Instead...
silence.
An abandoned camp.
Food waiting inside tents.
Can you imagine the first bite?
Men who had been waiting to die suddenly eating food left behind by the army they feared.
Then another bite.
Then drinking.
Then discovering silver.
Gold.
Clothing.
They ate.
They drank.
They carried valuables away and hid them.
Then they returned and gathered more.
You can hardly blame them.
People who have lived with scarcity often grab tightly when abundance finally arrives.
But eventually conscience interrupted appetite.
They looked at one another.
And what they said may be the spiritual heartbeat of the entire story:
“הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה יוֹם־בְּשֹׂרָה הוּא”
Hayom hazeh yom-besorah hu.
“This day is a day of good news.”
The Hebrew word besorah means good news, glad tidings.
And they realized something.
Good news this important could not remain hidden inside their private feast.
People were starving behind those walls.
Children were starving.
Families were starving.
The city didn't know what these four men knew.
The food already existed.
The enemy had already fled.
Deliverance had already happened outside the walls.
But inside Samaria people were still behaving as though nothing had changed because they had not yet heard the news.
That image reaches far beyond Samaria.

We should be careful not to flatten this Old Testament event into an allegory in which every character secretly represents something else. Second Kings 7 is first a real account of God's deliverance of Samaria and the fulfillment of His word through Elisha.
But when Christians read this story within the whole testimony of Scripture, we cannot miss the resonance.
There is good news that cannot rightly be hoarded.
The New Testament calls it the Gospel.
And unlike Samaria's temporary rescue from famine, the Gospel addresses humanity's deepest catastrophe: sin, guilt, judgment, alienation from God and death.
The Gospel is not:
“Become better and maybe God will love you.”
It is not:
“Fix yourself before approaching Jesus.”
It is not:
“Hide the scandalous chapters and present God with the respectable version of yourself.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Jesus Christ.
We sinned.
Christ came.
The Son of God took on flesh.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our circumstances.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
At the cross, grace did not pretend sin was inexpensive.
Grace revealed exactly how costly our redemption was.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
And now forgiveness is proclaimed to sinners who could never purchase it.
That is why grace is so scandalous.
Because the people receiving it cannot brag that they deserved it.
The four starving men didn't manufacture the feast.
They discovered it.
And sinners do not manufacture salvation.
Christ accomplished what we could not accomplish.
Salvation is received by grace through faith, and genuine faith turns us toward Christ in repentance, surrender and a transformed life.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needs.
You have spent years believing your worst chapter disqualified you from coming home.
You think Jesus would receive the cleaner version of you.
The sober version.
The sexually pure version.
The less angry version.
The version who finally has prayer figured out.
The version who stopped failing.
So you keep waiting to become worthy of grace before asking for grace.
But if you could make yourself worthy of the cross, you would not need the cross.
Jesus did not die for imaginary people with imaginary sins.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People who knew better and did it anyway.
People who promised God, “Never again,” and returned.
People whose shame has been whispering:
Stay outside.
Hide.
God is tired of you.
But Scripture's answer is not that sin doesn't matter.
It matters so much that Christ died.
And Scripture's answer is not that repentance doesn't matter.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe.
The answer is that your sin does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Christ.
You are not being invited to excuse your darkness.
You are being invited to bring it into the light.
Repentance says:
No more hiding.
No more renaming sin so I can keep it.
No more pretending I can save myself.
Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.
Forgive me.
Cleanse me.
Rule me.
Change me.
I am Yours.
And maybe right now you feel like one of those four men outside Samaria.
Too broken for one world.
Terrified of the next step.
Unsure what will happen if you move toward God.
Then hear their question again:
“Why are we sitting here until we die?”
You do not need to know every detail of tomorrow before taking the next obedient step today.
Come to Christ.
Not because tomorrow will necessarily bring money.
Not because Christianity guarantees that every sickness disappears overnight.
Not because following Jesus means your enemies will always vanish before breakfast.
Second Kings 7 is not a blank cheque promising every believer a twenty-four-hour reversal of every crisis.
That would misuse the text.
Come because Jesus Christ is worthy.
Come because sin cannot give you what it promises.
Come because forgiveness is real.
Come because there is mercy for the repentant sinner.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because the King who knows the worst thing about you still calls sinners to Himself.
And once you have tasted the good news...
don't hide it.
That is where those four men became more than survivors.
They became messengers.
“We are not doing right,” they realized.
“This day is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent.”
There are people on your Facebook friends list who may never tell you they are starving spiritually.
The smiling profile picture won't tell you.
The family photo won't tell you.
The jokes won't tell you.
The promotion announcement won't tell you.
Somebody can look successful and still go to bed asking whether life is worth continuing.
Someone can quote Scripture publicly while privately losing the battle against temptation.
Someone can sit in church every Sunday while quietly wondering whether God could ever forgive what nobody else knows.
Someone you know may be one Gospel conversation away from discovering that Jesus has not stopped calling them.
So if this article reminded you of somebody, don't merely think about them.
Send it privately if public tagging would embarrass them.
We cannot manipulate God with engagement.
But if you genuinely want your online presence to glorify God, one practical way to do that is to use the reach He has given you to make Christ known.
Let your profile carry something besides arguments, entertainment and photographs.
Let somebody encounter the Gospel there.
You don't know who is reading quietly.
You don't know who is starving behind a screen.
You don't know whose “Samaria” is collapsing tonight.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own heart, be honest.
And if Christ has already brought you through something you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony does not make you the hero.
Jesus is the Hero.
That is precisely why your testimony matters.
Because there may come a night when God's promises feel less believable than your circumstances, and you may need to remember Samaria.
At sunset, nothing looked different.
The walls still stood.
The famine still hurt.
The people still believed the enemy was outside.
Yet beyond their sight, God had already acted.
Again, this does not mean every unanswered prayer has a miracle scheduled for tomorrow.
It means visible circumstances are never the final measurement of God's sovereignty.
Elisha said, “Tomorrow.”
The officer laughed at the impossibility.
And tomorrow came.
The people eventually went out.
The abandoned camp was plundered.
Food flooded Samaria.
The prices fell exactly as the word of the LORD had declared.
And the officer who had mocked God's word saw the abundance...
but never ate it.
He was trampled at the gate.
It is a sobering ending.
Because it is possible to stand close to the evidence of God's work and remain personally untouched by its blessing.
It is possible to know Bible verses without trusting the God who spoke them.
To attend church without surrendering to Christ.
To admire Jesus without following Jesus.
To discuss grace without receiving grace.
To see bread and remain hungry.
Do not settle for proximity to Christianity.
Come to Christ Himself.
The goal isn't simply another follower.
The goal is another person repeatedly brought within reach of Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing and discipleship centered upon Jesus Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support earns favor with Christ.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture and developing resources intended to point people toward Jesus.
Not out of guilt.
Out of mission.
The four starving men eventually understood that abundance carried responsibility.
“This day is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent.”
Christians have infinitely greater news.
The Son of God came.
The cross happened.
The debt was paid.
The grave was opened.
Jesus Christ is risen.
Forgiveness is offered.
Sinners can come home.
Captives can be freed.
The ashamed can step into the light.
The spiritually starving can discover the Bread of Life.
So how could we feast on grace and never tell the hungry where the Bread is?
Maybe you entered this article feeling surrounded.
Maybe your finances look surrounded.
Your family.
Your marriage.
Your mind.
Your faith.
Maybe you have been sitting between two terrible options thinking there is no road forward.
Samaria reminds us that God does not need visible possibilities before He can act.
But the greater Gospel reminds us of something even better:
Our deepest hope is not that every earthly siege ends tomorrow.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus.
And when Jesus takes hold of a ruined story, He does not merely edit the embarrassing sentences.
He redeems the person inside them.
Peter had denial.
Paul had persecution and blood on his résumé.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace met sinners where human pride would have expected rejection.
That doesn't make sin beautiful.
It makes the Savior beautiful.
This is what we mean when we say:
From scandal...
to grace.
The scandal is real.
The wounds are real.
The consequences can be real.
Repentance is necessary.
But Jesus is greater than the chapter you thought would become your identity.
Your failure does not have to write the final sentence.
Your addiction does not have to write the final sentence.
Your shame does not have to write the final sentence.
Your past does not have to write the final sentence.
Your worst night does not have to write the final sentence.
Jesus Christ holds the pen of redemption.
So come out of hiding.
Tell the truth.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
And when you discover the good news...
don't bury it in the tent.
Tell somebody.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is still sitting outside the gate believing death is the only ending available.
And maybe God will use the good news you refused to keep to yourself to show them otherwise.
Never forget this: the starving men thought they were walking toward death, only to discover that God had already made a way where they could see none.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MAN PAUL HANDED OVER TO SATAN—AND THE TERRIFYING REASON IT MAY HAVE BEEN AN ACT OF LOVE
paragraphs:
THE MAN PAUL HANDED OVER TO SATAN—AND THE TERRIFYING REASON IT MAY HAVE BEEN AN ACT OF LOVE
There is a sentence in your Bible so severe that many Christians would rather rush past it. But buried inside those frightening words is something astonishing: Paul was not trying to destroy a sinner. He wanted a sinner saved.
There are Bible verses we underline because they comfort us.
There are verses we post because they inspire us.
And then there are verses that make us stop.
Read them again.
And quietly wonder...
“Did the Bible really just say that?”
This is one of them.
A scandal had erupted inside the church at Corinth.
Not outside the church.
Inside it.

A man identified with the Christian community was involved in sexual immorality of such a shocking kind that Paul said it was not even commonly tolerated among the surrounding Gentiles: a man “had” his father’s wife.
Yet perhaps the most disturbing part of the chapter is not merely what the man had done.
It is what the church had apparently become willing to tolerate.
Paul writes that instead of mourning, they had become arrogant.
Then comes the sentence that has disturbed readers for centuries.
In the original Greek of 1 Corinthians 5:5:
“παραδοῦναι τὸν τοιοῦτον τῷ Σατανᾷ εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκός, ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου.”
A careful, fairly literal rendering is:
“To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord.”
Read the final words again.
Because they change everything.
“So that the spirit might be saved.”
Paul's objective was not revenge.
It was not humiliation for entertainment.
It was not religious cruelty dressed up as holiness.
Something far more sobering was happening.
Paul was willing to let a man experience the terrible consequences of refusing repentance because something infinitely more valuable than the man's temporary comfort was at stake.
His soul.
And suddenly this ancient scandal begins getting uncomfortably close to home.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing that can happen to you is not that God allows your comfortable life to collapse.
Perhaps the most dangerous thing is being allowed to remain comfortable while sin quietly destroys you.
We have created a Christianity where many people think love means affirmation.
Jesus never taught that.
Biblical love does not celebrate what is killing the person it loves.
A doctor who discovers cancer and says nothing because the diagnosis might upset you is not compassionate.
A father watching his child walk toward traffic does not whisper, “I respect your journey.”
Love intervenes.
Love warns.
Love sometimes wounds before the wound becomes fatal.
And Corinth had forgotten this.
Paul had received a report of sexual immorality in the congregation, and instead of the church grieving over the spiritual destruction taking place, they had apparently become puffed up.
The Greek is striking.
Paul says:
“καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ”
“You have become puffed up.”
The verb carries the idea of becoming inflated with pride.
Imagine the tragedy.
A man's spiritual life is collapsing...
sexual sin has invaded the fellowship...
the holiness of Christ's church is being publicly contradicted...
and somehow people are still proud of themselves.
That may be one of the most frightening pictures of spiritual blindness in the New Testament.
Because you can become so sophisticated about grace that you stop grieving over sin.
You can become so afraid of sounding judgmental that you stop warning people headed toward destruction.
You can even use the vocabulary of love to protect the very bondage from which Jesus died to deliver us.
But grace never makes peace with the sin that nailed Christ to the cross.
Grace forgives sinners.
Grace cleanses sinners.
Grace restores sinners.
Grace transforms sinners.
Grace does not look at chains and rename them freedom.
Paul therefore commands the church to remove this persistently immoral man from their fellowship.
And this is where we need to understand the frightening phrase:
“παραδοῦναι...τῷ Σατανᾷ”
“To hand over...to Satan.”
Paul uses remarkably similar language elsewhere.
In 1 Timothy 1:20, speaking of Hymenaeus and Alexander, he writes:
“I handed [them] over to Satan so that they might be disciplined not to blaspheme.”
Notice something easily missed.
Again, the purpose is corrective.
“So that they might be disciplined.”
The Greek verb connected with that purpose, παιδεύω, belongs to the language of training, instruction, correction, or discipline.
Paul's goal was not simply, “Make them suffer.”
It was, in effect:
May discipline teach them what rebellion refused to teach them.
That changes how we should hear 1 Corinthians 5.
The Corinthian offender was to be removed from the protected fellowship of the gathered church and placed outside its recognized communion.
Paul later says plainly:
“Remove the evil person from among yourselves.”
This was church discipline at its most severe.
But even severe discipline had a redemptive horizon.
“...so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord.”
Do not miss the heart beating underneath the severity.
Paul wanted the man back.
Back from deception.
Back from sexual bondage.
Back from rebellion.
Back from spiritual numbness.
Back under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Back to repentance.
Back to life.
Sometimes grace comes running toward you with open arms.
Sometimes grace stands in your path and refuses to let you keep pretending.
Sometimes grace whispers.
Sometimes grace overturns tables.
Sometimes grace says, “Neither do I condemn you.”
And that same grace says, “Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Because Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make us comfortable while remaining enslaved.
He came to save us from our sins.
This is where the passage becomes personal.
Maybe nobody has removed you from a church.
Maybe nobody knows what you are doing.
Maybe your reputation is intact.
Your family thinks you're okay.
People still call you brother.
Sister.
Pastor.
Leader.
Believer.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You know the worship songs.
You know the Christian language.
But there is a room inside your life where Jesus has been knocking...
and you keep locking the door.
The affair nobody knows about.
The pornography deleted from your history but not your appetite.
The bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
The secret messages.
The money.
The addiction.
The hatred.
The manipulation.
The relationship you know dishonors Christ.
The pride that refuses correction.
The double life that has become so normal you barely feel conviction anymore.
And perhaps you have been interpreting God's patience as God's permission.
That is dangerous.
Romans 2 teaches that God's kindness is intended to lead us toward repentance.
His patience is mercy.
But mercy should never become an excuse for rebellion.
There comes a terrifying point when God may allow a person to taste the bitter fruit of what that person insists on choosing.
Not because sin suddenly became stronger than God.
But because consequences can sometimes awaken what comfort allowed to sleep.
Think of the prodigal son.
The father did not travel into the far country every evening to replenish the son's money so that rebellion could remain comfortable.
The son eventually found himself emptied.
Hungry.
Humiliated.
Looking at food meant for pigs.
And somewhere in that wreckage...
“He came to himself.”
Sometimes the pigpen reveals what the party concealed.
Sometimes losing what you worshipped reveals what you should have worshipped all along.
Sometimes the collapse you begged God to prevent becomes the place where you finally hear Him.
That does not mean every tragedy is God's punishment for a specific sin. Scripture does not permit us to make that reckless conclusion.
It does mean God loves His children too deeply to treat rebellion as harmless.
Hebrews tells us that the Lord disciplines those He loves.
Discipline and rejection are not identical.
Sometimes discipline is evidence that God refuses to abandon His children to destruction.
And this is where Paul's phrase becomes even more difficult:
“εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκός”
“For the destruction of the flesh.”
What exactly does that mean?
Christians should resist pretending the interpretive question is simpler than it is.

The Greek word σάρξ—sarx, “flesh”—can refer to the physical body, but Paul can also use “flesh” in ways connected to fallen human existence and sinful inclination. Because of this, interpreters have understood Paul's language differently. Some see possible physical suffering or even death; others understand the destruction as the breaking of sinful fleshly rebellion through severe discipline.
We should not claim more certainty than Scripture gives us.
But Paul's stated purpose is unmistakable:
“ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ”
“So that the spirit might be saved.”
Salvation—not annihilation—is where Paul's sentence is pointing.
And that means church discipline, properly practiced, is not supposed to be ecclesiastical revenge.
It is not permission for pastors to become tyrants.
It is not authorization for Christians to publicly humiliate people they dislike.
It is not spiritual abuse.
Biblical discipline should mourn.
Paul asked why the Corinthians had not mourned.
That one word exposes so much counterfeit holiness.
Because when another believer falls, the Christian response should never secretly enjoy the scandal.
We should not feast on someone's collapse.
We should not turn another person's worst moment into entertainment.
We should not become excited because somebody else's sin makes our righteousness look brighter.
We mourn.
Because this is a human being.
A soul.
Someone Christ calls to repentance.
Someone who could have been you.
Someone who, apart from grace, is you.
There is no room at the foot of the cross for proud executioners.
Only sinners who know where mercy found them.
And then something extraordinary appears later in Paul's correspondence with Corinth.
In 2 Corinthians 2, Paul speaks about an offender who had received punishment from the majority. Now Paul says something almost shocking after the severity we have just encountered.
The punishment is enough.
Forgive him.
Comfort him.
Reaffirm your love for him.
Why?
Because the man could become overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Stop there.
Christian discipline had reached its redemptive purpose, and Paul refused to allow discipline to become permanent condemnation.
This is crucial.

Some interpreters have connected the offender of 2 Corinthians 2 with the sexually immoral man of 1 Corinthians 5. That identification is possible and has a long history, but the text does not explicitly tell us they are the same man, so we should not present the connection as proven fact.
But whether or not these passages describe the same individual, the Gospel pattern could not be clearer.
Sin must be confronted.
Repentance must matter.
And the repentant must not be crushed beneath endless shame.
Paul tells them to forgive.
Comfort.
Reaffirm love.
And then he gives a reason that should make every unforgiving church tremble.
So that Satan does not outwit us.
Think about the irony.
In 1 Corinthians 5, a man is handed over to Satan with salvation as the stated goal.
In 2 Corinthians 2, the church is warned that Satan can gain an advantage when forgiveness and restoration are withheld.
The enemy does not care which ditch destroys you.
He will whisper while you sin:
“It doesn't matter.”
Then when conviction finally breaks you, he changes his sermon:
“You can never come back.”
Before repentance, Satan minimizes sin.
After repentance, he maximizes shame.
Before the fall:
“God will forgive you.”
After the fall:
“God could never forgive you.”
Same liar.
Different sentence.
And somebody reading this has been living under the second sentence for years.
You repented.
But you still hate yourself.
You confessed.
But you still replay it.
You believe Jesus forgives other people.
You preach grace to everybody except the person staring back from your mirror.
Your scandal happened five years ago.
Ten years ago.
Twenty.
But every time you try to worship, your memory drags the old evidence into the courtroom.
“Remember what you did?”
Yes.
You remember.
But perhaps hell is hoping you forget something infinitely greater.
What Jesus did.
The Gospel is not the announcement that your sin wasn't serious.
The cross proves it was deadly serious.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ took sin so seriously that He bore its judgment Himself for everyone who turns to Him in repentant faith.
Your forgiveness was not purchased cheaply.
It was purchased with blood.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The sinless Son of God carried the judgment sinners deserved.
And He rose from the grave.
That means Christianity does not offer sinners denial.
It offers something infinitely better.
A Savior.
You do not need to rename your sin.
You can confess it.
You do not need to defend your darkness.
You can bring it into the light.
You do not need to pretend the scandal never happened.
You can bring the scandal to the cross.
Because Jesus specializes in stories everybody else thinks are already over.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ turned him into an apostle.
The thief reached the end of his ruined life with nothing left to offer Jesus but faith...
and discovered that grace can reach a dying criminal on a cross.
This is the Gospel.
Not good people earning God's approval.
Guilty people receiving mercy through Jesus Christ and being transformed by the Holy Spirit.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But please hear this carefully.
Grace does not mean everybody automatically receives salvation regardless of repentance and faith.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
The cross is not God's permission slip for continuing comfortably in rebellion.
The cross is God's invitation to die to the old life and belong to Christ.
Maybe this article did not reach you because you needed an interesting explanation of an uncomfortable Bible verse.
Maybe you needed a mirror.
What are you protecting that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What sin have you been calling “a struggle” when deep inside you know you have stopped fighting it?
What relationship are you unwilling to place beneath Christ's authority?
What secret would terrify you if it appeared on a screen in front of everybody you love?
You do not have to tell the internet every detail.
But you need to stop lying to God.
And maybe, finally...
to yourself.
Come home.
Not after you fix yourself.
Not when you feel worthy.
Not when the consequences disappear.
Come to Jesus now.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask for help.
Bring another mature, trustworthy believer into the battle where appropriate.
Cut off what keeps pulling you backward.
Stop negotiating with the thing Christ died to free you from.
And when you fall, do not run away from the Savior.
Run toward Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Christ purchased forgiveness.
Confession stops pretending we do not need it.
And perhaps the church needs repentance too.
Because some churches have confused tolerance with grace.
Others have confused cruelty with holiness.
Jesus gives us permission for neither.
Truth without love becomes a weapon.
“Love” without truth becomes permission to die quietly.
But in Jesus Christ we encounter grace and truth.
The church should be one of the hardest places in the world to comfortably cherish unrepentant sin...
and one of the safest places in the world for a broken sinner genuinely seeking Christ to confess, repent, heal, and come home.
Imagine that church.
A church where holiness matters.
Where nobody celebrates sin.
Where leaders are accountable too.
Where discipline is never weaponized to protect powerful people.
Where repentance is real.
Where forgiveness is real.
Where broken people are not discarded.

Where restoration does not necessarily erase every earthly consequence or automatically restore every former position, but where repentant people are still treated as human beings for whom Christ's mercy is not exhausted.
That is the difference between biblical restoration and cheap grace.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened.
Restoration does not always mean returning someone immediately—or ever—to the same position of authority.
Trust may require time.
Victims must not be pressured into unsafe reconciliation.
Crimes should not be concealed beneath religious language.
Church discipline must never become a shield for abuse.
But neither should a genuinely repentant believer be sentenced by Christians to lifelong spiritual exile after Christ has extended mercy.
We are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Maybe now you understand why this disturbing chapter belongs inside the Gospel story.
The man Paul handed over to Satan was not being treated as though his soul were worthless.
The severity existed precisely because his soul mattered.
Sin mattered.
The church mattered.
The holiness of Christ mattered.
Eternity mattered.
And salvation mattered.
Which leaves us with a question far more frightening than:
“Why would Paul hand someone over to Satan?”
The deeper question may be:
What if God loves us enough to destroy the comfortable lies keeping us from repentance?
What if the closed door saved you?
What if being exposed saved you?
What if losing the relationship woke you up?
What if the consequence you hated finally made you confront the bondage you loved?
What if the night you thought God had abandoned you became the night you finally stopped running from Him?
We should never romanticize suffering or assume every painful event is divine discipline.
But Scripture gives us something better than a promise of uninterrupted comfort.
It gives us a God who works even through discipline for the good of His children.
A Father who loves.
