A Savior who bleeds.
A Spirit who convicts.
A Gospel that tells the truth about our sin without surrendering us to despair.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.

And if Christ has already brought you through your own season of rebellion, discipline, repentance, or restoration, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed believer realizes that coming home is still possible.
Not because every paragraph is comfortable.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks he has gone too far.
Send it to the sister who cannot forgive herself.
Send it to the person who needs somebody to love them enough to tell the truth.
Stay close to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Christ.

And if this ministry is helping you glorify God, consider supporting the work rather than merely consuming it. We support Christian ministry because we want Gospel-centered work to continue reaching people.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Do it, if you choose to do it, to point another human being toward Jesus.
Someone whose marriage is dying.
Someone hiding an addiction.
Someone convinced God no longer wants them.
Someone comfortable in sin.
Someone drowning in shame after repentance.
Someone who will never tell you how close they were to giving up.
You may never know which sentence reaches them.
You may never know which share interrupts someone's darkness.
You may never know which testimony sends a prodigal walking home.
But you can refuse to hide the light you have received.
And before you leave this article, remember the man in Corinth.
Remember the scandal.
Remember the terrifying sentence.
Remember its purpose.
“So that the spirit might be saved.”
The Gospel is severe about sin because Calvary reveals how deadly sin really is.
But Calvary also reveals something else.
There is mercy for sinners.
Real sinners.
Exposed sinners.
Disgraced sinners.
Church sinners.
Secret sinners.
People whose stories contain chapters they wish they could burn.
Jesus Christ did not come for imaginary people with sanitized histories.
He came to save sinners.
So repent.
Come into the light.
Receive His grace.
And let Him begin writing what shame told you could never be written.
Because sometimes the chapter that feels like the end of your story is only the place where grace finally takes the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMEN NOBODY ASKED
paragraphs:
THE WOMEN NOBODY ASKED
What Bilhah, Zilpah, Rizpah, and Hagar Reveal About Women With Less Power—and the God Who Still Saw Them
There are women in the Bible whose stories make us uncomfortable because Scripture refuses to clean the blood off the floor before inviting us into the room.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Rizpah.
Hagar.
Their names are easy to read past.
Their lives are not.

They lived in worlds where other people frequently possessed more social, economic, familial, or political power than they did. Decisions involving their bodies, children, homes, futures, and security could be made by people standing above them.
And here is what makes their stories especially disturbing:
Sometimes the people with greater power were themselves wounded people.
Rachel was suffering.
Leah was suffering.
Sarah was suffering.
David was carrying the responsibility of a kingdom suffering under famine.
Pain was everywhere.
But pain does not automatically make everything we do with power righteous.
Sometimes wounded people wound people with less power.
Sometimes somebody else's desperation becomes your captivity.
Sometimes you become the solution to a problem you never created.
And perhaps that sentence already feels too personal.
Because maybe you know what it is like to have somebody else's expectations placed on your shoulders.
Maybe you were the child who had to keep the family peaceful.
The wife expected to absorb everything quietly.
The employee who could not afford to say no.
The woman whose usefulness seemed more important than her heart.
The person everyone needed—but nobody really asked, “How are you?”
Maybe people discussed your future while you sat in the room.
Maybe they decided what was “best” for you without ever asking what happened inside you afterward.
If so, do not rush through these women.
Sit beside them.
Because the Bible does something extraordinary with people the powerful world might have treated as background characters.
It remembers their names.
And ultimately, their stories lead us toward Jesus Christ—the King who did not use His authority to consume the vulnerable, but gave Himself to save sinners.
Start with Bilhah.
Rachel is devastated by infertility. Genesis 30 opens with Rachel envying Leah and crying to Jacob for children.
Then she says something that can sound almost ordinary after centuries of familiarity with the story:
“Here is my maid Bilhah.”
The Hebrew is sharper when we allow ourselves to hear the social relationship being described:

הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה
hinneh ʾamati Bilhah
“Here is my female servant, Bilhah.”
Rachel continues:

בֹּא אֵלֶיהָ וְתֵלֵד עַל־בִּרְכַּי
bo ʾeleha wetēled ʿal-birkay
“Go in to her, and she shall bear upon my knees.”
Genesis then says Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob as a wife, and Bilhah conceived and bore him a son.
Stop there.

Do not import twenty-first-century assumptions carelessly into an ancient household. Surrogacy-like arrangements involving enslaved or servant women existed within the ancient world, and Scripture is describing a household vastly different from ours.
But neither should we make the opposite mistake.
Description is not endorsement.
The Bible can faithfully tell us what human beings did without declaring everything they did morally ideal.
And what is striking in Genesis 30 is whose voices dominate the naming of Bilhah's children.
Bilhah carries Dan.
Rachel names him.
Bilhah carries Naphtali.
Rachel names him.
Rachel interprets the pregnancies through Rachel's struggle with Leah.
Bilhah's womb becomes part of another woman's rivalry.
Read that again slowly.
A woman can be hurting deeply and still possess power over somebody more vulnerable than herself.
That is one of the uncomfortable truths these stories force Christians to confront.
Victimhood in one relationship does not guarantee righteousness in another.
Rachel knows the agony of infertility.
But Bilhah still occupies the weaker social position.
Then Leah enters the same pattern.
When Leah stops bearing children, Genesis says:

וַתִּקַּח אֶת־זִלְפָּה שִׁפְחָתָהּ
vattiqqaḥ ʾet-Zilpah shifḥatah
“She took Zilpah her female servant.”
Leah gives Zilpah to Jacob as a wife.
Zilpah bears Gad.
Then Asher.
Again, the children speak loudly in the story.
The mother barely speaks at all.
Rachel speaks.
Leah speaks.
Jacob appears.
Children are named.
The household grows.
Israel's tribal history advances.
And Bilhah and Zilpah almost disappear behind what their bodies produced.
Yet they did not disappear from God's story.
Dan mattered.
Naphtali mattered.
Gad mattered.
Asher mattered.
Four tribes of Israel came through women whose own recorded speech is strikingly absent from these birth narratives.
That should make us careful whenever we confuse silence with insignificance.

The Bible does not give us permission to invent Bilhah's or Zilpah's inner thoughts. We should not manufacture trauma Scripture does not explicitly describe, pretend we know every detail of their consent, or force modern psychological categories onto an ancient text.
But the text gives us enough to recognize an unequal social arrangement.
Their comparative lack of recorded voice does not mean they lacked personhood before God.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction.
Because perhaps people know what you produced but not what producing it cost you.
They remember the meal.
Not the exhaustion.
They remember the children you raised.
Not the nights you cried.
They remember the ministry you helped build.
Not the moment somebody used “God's will” to pressure you into silence.
They remember what you gave.
They never asked what was taken.
And somewhere inside you is a dangerous question you have been afraid to ask:
Did God see what nobody else noticed?
Hagar answers.
Hagar is perhaps one of Scripture's clearest portraits of a woman living beneath the power of others.
Sarah is barren.
The promise seems delayed.
Years pass.
Hope hurts.
So Sarah gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham.
Again, we should read the ancient account honestly.
Hagar is not introduced as a socially equal woman entering negotiations from an equal position.
She is Sarah's Egyptian servant.
Then she becomes pregnant.
Conflict erupts.
Sarah complains to Abraham.
Abraham tells Sarah that Hagar is in her hand.
Sarah treats her harshly.
The Hebrew verb describing Sarah's treatment is built from the root ענה, ʿ-n-h, associated here with affliction or harsh treatment.
And Hagar runs.
A pregnant foreign servant woman flees into the wilderness.
No powerful relatives are mentioned coming to retrieve her.
No wealth protects her.
No institution intervenes.
But Someone finds her.
The messenger of the LORD meets Hagar by a spring.
And then Scripture records words that should shake anyone who has ever believed God only notices important people:

כִּי־שָׁמַע יְהוָה אֶל־עָנְיֵךְ
ki-shama YHWH ʾel-ʿonyekh
“For the LORD has heard your affliction.”
Her son's name, Ishmael—יִשְׁמָעֵאל, Yishmaʿel—is tied to this declaration that God hears.
The woman who could be ordered around by human beings discovers that heaven has been listening.
Then Hagar does something extraordinary.
She speaks of the God who spoke to her as:

אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
ʾattah ʾEl Roʾi
“You are El-roi”—commonly understood along the lines of “God of seeing,” though the exact wording of the surrounding Hebrew is difficult and translations vary.
Do not miss the wonder.
Hagar had been looked at as a servant.
Looked at as a solution.
Looked at as a reproductive answer.
Looked at as a problem when household conflict erupted.
But in the wilderness she discovers what it means to be seen by God.
Not used.
Seen.
Not merely evaluated.
Seen.
Not reduced to what she can provide.
Seen.
And perhaps that is where this article found you.
You have spent years being useful.
Useful to your family.
Useful to your church.
Useful to your spouse.
Useful to your employer.
Useful to everyone.
And secretly you have wondered whether anybody would still love you if you stopped producing.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not announce that your value comes from your usefulness.
Your deepest problem is not merely that other people have failed to see you. Like every descendant of Adam, you are a sinner who needs reconciliation with a holy God.
And this is where Christianity offers something infinitely greater than self-esteem.
God sees you completely—including the parts you desperately hope nobody sees.
Your wounds.
Your resentment.
Your hidden sins.
Your bitterness.
Your compromises.
Your fear.
Your secret hunger to be loved.
Nothing is hidden.
And still the Gospel says Christ came for sinners.
That is grace.
Not God pretending your sin is harmless.
Not God calling evil good.
Grace is God confronting sin so completely that the Son of God goes to the cross to deal with it.
Hagar encounters the God who sees.
But centuries later, in Jesus Christ, we discover just how far the God who sees is willing to go to save.
Before we reach Calvary, however, there is another woman sitting on a rock.
Her name is Rizpah.
And her story may be one of the most agonizing scenes in the Old Testament.
Rizpah was a concubine of Saul.
Her social position was connected to royal power without giving her the power of the king.
Then comes 2 Samuel 21.

Israel is suffering famine. The narrative connects the crisis to Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites. David asks the Gibeonites what restitution they require. They request seven male descendants of Saul.
Among those handed over are Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth.
They die.
And then their mother does something almost unbearable to imagine.
וַתִּקַּח רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה אֶת־הַשַּׂק
“Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth.”
She spreads it for herself on a rock.
And she stays.
From the beginning of harvest until rain comes.
By day she keeps the birds away.
By night she keeps the wild animals away.
She cannot reverse what happened.
She cannot command an army.
She cannot issue a royal decree.
She cannot restore breath to her sons.
But she can stay.
So she stays.
Imagine the nights.
The smell.
The grief.
The exhaustion.
The sound of wings.
The movement in the darkness.
A grieving mother with almost no political power refuses to abandon the bodies of her children.
Then one of the most quietly explosive sentences in the narrative appears:

וַיֻּגַּד לְדָוִד
vayyuggad leDavid
“And it was told David…”
The king hears what Rizpah has done.
Her vigil reaches the throne.
David then acts to gather the bones of Saul and Jonathan, as well as those who had been executed, and provides burial.
Rizpah did not command the king.
Her faithfulness became impossible for the king to ignore.
There is something sacred in that.
Not because grief always changes earthly authorities.
It does not.
Not because every faithful protest receives justice before sunset.
It does not.
But because Scripture refuses to treat this grieving concubine as scenery.
It records her name.
Her sackcloth.
Her rock.
Her endurance.
Her defense of the dead.
Her action reaches David's ears.
And her story has survived thousands of years.
Somebody needs to hear this:
Powerlessness is not the same thing as worthlessness.
Bilhah had less power.
Zilpah had less power.
Hagar had less power.
Rizpah had less power.
But none of them was invisible to the biblical story.
And now we have to ask the uncomfortable question.
What do these women reveal about us?
Not merely about “society.”
Us.
Christians.
Families.
Churches.
Marriages.
Ministries.
Employers.
Parents.
Leaders.
Anyone who has power over somebody else.
Because almost everybody is Bilhah somewhere and Rachel somewhere else.
Almost everybody knows what it means to lack power in one room while possessing it in another.
You can be mistreated by your boss and harsh toward your children.
Ignored by your husband and cruel toward the waitress.
Disrespected by church leadership and controlling toward the volunteer beneath you.
Marginalized in one relationship and manipulative in another.
That is why these stories cannot merely become weapons we point outward.
The Gospel turns the mirror toward us.
How do you treat people who cannot advance your career?
How do you speak to people who cannot punish you?
How do you treat the person serving your food?
The cleaner?
The employee who needs the job?
The child who cannot leave?
The elderly parent who now depends on you?
The spouse who trusted you with vulnerabilities nobody else knows?
The church member nobody considers influential?
The struggling believer who has nothing impressive to offer your ministry?
Your theology of human dignity is revealed most clearly by how you treat people whose approval you do not need.
And then Jesus enters the picture.
Not merely as an inspirational example.
As Lord.
As Redeemer.
As the crucified and risen King.
Jesus possessed authority unlike anyone else.
Yet listen to how He described His mission in Mark 10:45:
Καὶ γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἦλθεν διακονηθῆναι, ἀλλὰ διακονῆσαι…
“For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve…”
And then:
καὶ δοῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν
“…and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
The Greek word λύτρον—lytron—means a ransom, the price associated with release.
Look at the difference.
Sinful human power says:
“What can you give me?”
Jesus says:
“I give My life.”
Sinful power consumes.
Jesus serves.
Sinful power sacrifices the vulnerable to preserve itself.
Jesus, though innocent, willingly gives Himself for guilty sinners.
Sinful power asks who is beneath me.
Jesus kneels.
Touches lepers.
Receives children.
Speaks with socially despised people.
Responds to beggars.
Honors women as disciples and witnesses.
Calls sinners to repentance.
And then walks toward a cross.
This is why Christianity cannot reduce the answer to vulnerable women—or vulnerable men—to vague empowerment slogans.
Our hope is deeper.
Our hope has nail scars.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
The One with all authority willingly humbled Himself.
The sinless One died for sinners.
The rejected Stone became the cornerstone.
The crucified Christ rose.
And in Him, people whom human societies separate by ethnicity, status, and sex stand equally dependent upon grace.
Paul writes:
οὐκ ἔνι Ἰουδαῖος οὐδὲ Ἕλλην, οὐκ ἔνι δοῦλος οὐδὲ ἐλεύθερος, οὐκ ἔνι ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ· πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς εἷς ἐστε ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”
Paul is not claiming earthly distinctions magically cease to exist.
He is declaring something glorious about standing in Christ.
Slave and free come to Christ needing the same grace.
Male and female come needing the same Savior.
Jew and Gentile enter the family of God through Christ.
No human being reaches the foot of the cross carrying a VIP pass.
And no repentant sinner kneeling there is second-class.
That means the Church must never baptize domination simply because domination happens to benefit the powerful.
Neither can we twist stories like Hagar's, Bilhah's, Zilpah's, or Rizpah's into claims Scripture itself never makes.
Faithfulness means refusing both errors.
We do not sanitize the text.
And we do not rewrite it.
We let Scripture disturb us where Scripture is disturbing.
We let it correct us where we have confused cultural power with God's character.
And then we look to Christ.
Maybe you came into this article thinking about women who had less power.
But perhaps somewhere along the way you realized the Holy Spirit was asking about what you do with yours.
That realization matters.
Because repentance begins when excuses stop.
Maybe you need to repent for using someone's dependence against them.
Maybe you have controlled with money.
Manipulated with Scripture.
Demanded silence in the name of “submission.”
Used your position in ministry to make questioning you feel like questioning God.
Perhaps you made somebody's vulnerability expensive.
Perhaps you treated another person's forgiveness as permission to keep hurting them.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
You are the one who was controlled.
And you have carried shame for years because somebody convinced you that what happened proved something was wrong with you.
Listen carefully.
Another person's sin against you does not become righteous because they possessed authority.
And being sinned against does not remove your own need for Christ either.
The Gospel gives us something more beautiful than competing claims of innocence.
At the cross, victims can bring wounds that God does not minimize.
Sinners can bring guilt God does not excuse.
The abused do not have to call evil good.
The guilty do not have to pretend they never sinned.
Both are summoned into the light.
There, justice matters.
Truth matters.
Repentance matters.
Forgiveness matters.
Grace matters.
And Jesus remains Lord.
Maybe your prayer tonight is not eloquent.
Maybe it is only:
“Jesus, You see me.”
That is enough to begin speaking honestly.
Or perhaps:
“Jesus, forgive me for how I have used power.”
Do not run from that conviction.
Run to Christ.
Repentance is not God destroying the repentant sinner.
It is grace dragging what was killing you into the light.
Christ did not die so we could become better at hiding.
He died and rose to make sinners new.
You can simply write, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you are exhausted from fighting quietly, comment, “Pray for me.”
If God has been healing places nobody else knows about, write, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if you have spent years pretending everything is fine when it isn't, perhaps today is the day to say, “No more hiding.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing one honest sentence into the light is how we stop rehearsing the lie that nobody else understands.
Someone reading beneath you may discover they are not alone.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list may need this truth more than you realize.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity, partnership, and a desire to help biblical teaching reach another person.
And beyond the products, there is something we care about far more.
Discipleship.
Not because every sentence is perfect, but because there may come a day when you forget again that human power and divine worth are not the same thing.
Share it with the woman who has spent her life feeling like Bilhah—needed but rarely heard.
Send it to the grieving mother who understands something of Rizpah's rock.
Send it to the leader who needs to remember that authority in the kingdom of Christ is never permission to consume people.
Send it to the man who wants to become more like Jesus in the way he treats women, children, employees, strangers, and everyone who possesses less power than he does.
But before you leave, remember the four women.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Hagar.
Rizpah.
One bore children while another woman spoke their names.
One bore children while another woman celebrated.
One ran into a wilderness and discovered that God had heard her affliction.
One sat beneath the dead until her grief reached the ears of a king.
Different women.
Different stories.
Different wounds.
But together they whisper a warning to anyone with power:
Be careful what you do with people who cannot easily say no to you.
And they whisper hope to anyone who feels powerless:
Human beings may overlook you without heaven losing sight of you.
But there is one final truth even greater than being seen.
The God who sees did not remain distant.
Jesus came.
Jesus served.
Jesus touched the rejected.
Jesus called sinners to repentance.
Jesus carried the cross.
Jesus gave His life as a ransom.
Jesus rose from the grave.
And Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
So bring Him the part of your story nobody wanted to hear.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him your own sins too.
Bring Him what people did to you.
Bring Him what you did to others.
Bring Him the wilderness.
Bring Him the rock.
Bring Him the years when you felt useful but unloved.
Bring Him the nights when nobody came.
Because grace does not mean the scandal never happened.
Grace means the scandal does not get the final word.

You may have been treated like a footnote in someone else's story, but beneath the eyes of Christ, you were never invisible—and at His cross, even the darkest chapter can become the place where grace begins writing again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JEZEBEL WANTED ONE MAN’S VINEYARD SO BADLY SHE HAD HIM KILLED FOR IT — THEN GOD SENT ELIJAH
paragraphs: JEZEBEL WANTED ONE MAN’S VINEYARD SO BADLY SHE HAD HIM KILLED FOR IT — THEN GOD SENT ELIJAH

Naboth thought he was simply protecting his family’s inheritance. He had no idea that saying “no” to a king would put a death sentence over his head. But when powerful people buried an innocent man beneath lies, God showed Israel—and us—that heaven sees what happens when nobody else is willing to speak.
There was a vineyard beside a palace.
That is where the scandal began.
Not on a battlefield.
Not before an invading army.
Not in some pagan temple filled with idols.
A vineyard.
A piece of land.
Something a king wanted.
Something another man would not surrender.
And before the story was finished, an innocent man would be publicly disgraced, falsely accused, executed, and robbed of the inheritance he had refused to sell.
The people responsible would apparently get away with it.
Apparently.
Because there was one detail Jezebel's carefully constructed plan could never eliminate.
God saw everything.
And if you have ever watched someone manipulate the truth and prosper from it...
If you have ever been punished for doing what was right...
If someone has ever lied about you, taken something from you, destroyed your reputation, or made you wonder whether integrity is worth the price...
Stay with this story.
Because Naboth's vineyard is not merely a story about a wicked queen.
It is a terrifying revelation about what happens when desire becomes entitlement, entitlement becomes manipulation, manipulation becomes injustice—and injustice assumes God is not watching.
It begins in 1 Kings 21.
King Ahab had a palace in Jezreel, and beside it was a vineyard belonging to a man named Naboth.
Ahab looked at the vineyard and wanted it.
At first, his request sounds almost reasonable.

He told Naboth to give him the vineyard so he could turn it into a vegetable garden because it was close to his palace. In exchange, Ahab offered him a better vineyard or, if Naboth preferred, its value in money.
This is important.
Naboth was not refusing because Ahab offered nothing.
He was not stubbornly rejecting an obviously profitable business transaction.
Something deeper was happening.
Naboth answered:
“The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.”
In Hebrew, the heart of his answer includes the words נַחֲלַת אֲבֹתַי — naḥalat avotai: “the inheritance of my fathers.”
That changes everything.
To Ahab, it was convenient real estate.
To Naboth, it was inheritance.
To Ahab, it was a vineyard beside the palace.
To Naboth, it represented something entrusted through generations.

Behind Naboth's refusal stood Israel's covenant understanding of the land. Leviticus 25:23 declares that ultimately the land belonged to God, while Numbers 36 reflects the importance of preserving tribal inheritance.
Naboth was not merely saying:
“I don't like your offer.”
He was effectively saying:
“There are things money does not give me the right to sell.”
And somebody reading this needs that sentence.
There are things you should never trade merely because someone offers you something attractive in return.
Your integrity.
Your obedience.
Your marriage vows.
Your conscience.
Your faithfulness to Christ.
Your convictions.
Your worship.
Your soul.
Jesus would later ask the question that exposes every bargain this world tries to make with us:
“What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
Naboth had something Ahab's money could not purchase.
Conviction.
And conviction becomes expensive when powerful people want what your obedience refuses to surrender.
Ahab returned home.
But instead of accepting Naboth's answer, Scripture gives us an almost embarrassing picture of the king.
He was “heavy and displeased.”
He lay down on his bed.
Turned his face away.
Refused to eat.
Imagine it.
A king with wealth, servants, authority, land, luxury, influence—and he is miserable because one man owns one vineyard he cannot have.
That is what unchecked desire does.
It convinces you that everything you already possess is worthless because of the one thing God has not given you.
Some people do not lose their peace because they have nothing.
They lose their peace because someone else has something.
That is the poison of covetousness.
Ahab did not need Naboth's vineyard.
He wanted it.
And eventually his desire became more important to him than the man who owned it.
Then Jezebel entered the room.
She asked why Ahab was so troubled and why he would not eat.
He told her what happened.
And Jezebel's response revealed something frightening about her understanding of power.
“Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel?”
In other words:
You're the king.
Why should anybody be allowed to tell you no?
Then she essentially told him to get up, eat, and be happy.
“I will give thee the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”
Notice what disappeared from the conversation.
God.
Covenant.
Justice.
Truth.
Naboth's rights.
Naboth's family.
Naboth himself.
When desire becomes an idol, people eventually become obstacles.
And obstacles are easier to destroy than neighbors are to love.
Jezebel wrote letters in Ahab's name.
She sealed them with his seal.
She sent them to the elders and nobles in Naboth's city.
The machinery of authority was now being used to manufacture a lie.
She commanded them to proclaim a fast and place Naboth prominently among the people.
Then they were to seat two worthless men opposite him and have them accuse Naboth of blaspheming God and the king.
The Hebrew text uses an especially striking expression:
בֵּרַכְתָּ אֱלֹהִים וָמֶלֶךְ — berakhta Elohim va-melekh.
Literally, the verb normally means “bless,” but in this context it functions euphemistically for “curse.” Naboth was to be accused of cursing God and the king.
The irony is almost unbearable.
Jezebel used the appearance of religious concern to murder a righteous man.
She weaponized morality.
She wrapped corruption in ceremony.
She ordered a fast while arranging a killing.
She invoked God's honor while violating God's commands.
That should disturb every religious person who reads this.
Because wickedness does not always walk into the room announcing itself as wickedness.
Sometimes it carries religious vocabulary.
Sometimes it knows the right words.
Sometimes it invokes God while crushing the people God commands us to love.
Not everyone who uses God's name represents God's heart.
Jesus warned about religious hypocrisy for precisely this reason.
And then the plan worked.
That may be one of the most painful sentences in this entire story.
The plan worked.
The elders and nobles did what Jezebel commanded.
The false witnesses testified.
Naboth was taken outside the city.
And they stoned him.
He died.
Pause there.
Because Scripture does not allow us to turn Naboth into a theological prop.
This was a man.
A human being.
Someone's family.
Someone who had walked through that vineyard.
Someone who had watched seasons come and go across that land.
Someone whose fathers had preserved an inheritance that eventually reached his hands.
He refused to betray it.
And they killed him for it.
There are moments when obedience does not appear to win.
That needs to be said in a Christianity that sometimes reduces faithfulness to formulas for immediate success.
Naboth obeyed.
Naboth still died.
The lie appeared stronger than the truth.
The powerful appeared stronger than the righteous.
Jezebel's letters appeared stronger than Naboth's integrity.
And heaven appeared silent.
Maybe that is where this story finds you.
You did what was right and still lost something.
You told the truth and someone believed the lie.
You stayed faithful and somebody betrayed you.
You refused to compromise and watched someone less honest get ahead.
You prayed for justice and nothing seemed to happen.
You wondered:
“God, did You see this?”
Naboth's vineyard gives an answer.
Yes.
He saw it.
Jezebel received the news:
“Naboth is stoned, and is dead.”
No grief.
No remorse.
No trembling.
Just an obstacle removed.
She told Ahab to arise and take possession of the vineyard.
And Ahab went.
That scene is chilling.
Naboth is dead.
Ahab is walking through the vineyard.
The king finally has what he wanted.
Perhaps the vines looked exactly the same.
Perhaps the soil felt ordinary beneath his feet.
Perhaps from a human perspective the case was closed.
Naboth could not appeal.
Jezebel controlled the narrative.
The witnesses had testified.
The local authorities had cooperated.
The victim was buried.
The king had the property.
Perfect crime.
Except for God.
Then Scripture says:
“And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite.”
Read that again.
The word of the LORD came.
Nobody had to send Elijah a secret copy of Jezebel's letters.
Nobody had to leak the conspiracy.
Nobody needed to persuade God to investigate.
He already knew.
The earthly court had failed.
Heaven had not.
And God sent a prophet directly into the vineyard.
Imagine Ahab seeing Elijah approaching.
Of all people.
Elijah.
The prophet who had stood against the prophets of Baal.
The prophet who had confronted Ahab before.
And now Elijah was walking toward him through the vineyard Ahab had obtained through an innocent man's blood.
Then came God's question.
In Hebrew:
הֲרָצַחְתָּ וְגַם־יָרָשְׁתָּ — haratzachta vegam-yarashta?
“Have you killed, and also taken possession?”
What a sentence.
Ahab might not have thrown the stones.
But God did not allow him to hide behind technicalities.
He accepted the benefit of the crime.
He walked into the vineyard.
He took possession.
And God held him accountable.
This is where Scripture dismantles one of humanity's favorite hiding places:
“I didn't personally do it.”
Ahab allowed wickedness to serve his desire.
And heaven saw through the excuse.
God told Elijah to pronounce judgment.
In the place where dogs had licked Naboth's blood, dogs would lick Ahab's blood.
Judgment was also pronounced upon Jezebel, whose violent end would later be recorded in 2 Kings 9.
The palace had power.
But not ultimate power.
The queen had influence.
But not ultimate authority.
The king had a seal.
But God had the final word.
And there is both comfort and terror in that.
Comfort for Naboth.
Terror for Ahab.
Comfort for the falsely accused.
Terror for the unrepentant oppressor.
Comfort for the person whose tears nobody noticed.
Terror for the person who believes secrecy means innocence.
There are no sealed rooms before an omniscient God.
No deleted conversation disappears from His knowledge.
No hidden motive escapes Him.
No carefully edited public image confuses Him.
No applause changes His verdict.
No crowd can vote truth into falsehood or falsehood into truth.
Hebrews 4:13 says that no creature is hidden from His sight.
That includes what they did to you.
And it includes what you have done to others.
That second sentence matters.
Because it is easy to read 1 Kings 21 and identify with Naboth.
It is much harder to ask whether there is any Ahab in us.
What vineyard are you staring at?
Whose life are you secretly envying?
What do you believe you deserve?
What “no” have you refused to accept?
What resentment have you been feeding because God allowed someone else to possess what you wanted?
Whom have you manipulated?
Whose reputation have you quietly damaged?
Have you ever allowed another person to do something sinful because the result benefited you?
Have you dressed selfishness in spiritual language?
Have you convinced yourself that because nobody confronted you, God must not care?
Be careful.
The road to Naboth's vineyard begins long before the stones.
It begins in the heart.
James describes the progression with frightening clarity: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin, when fully grown, brings forth death.
First Ahab saw.
Then Ahab wanted.
Then Ahab resented.
Then Jezebel manipulated.
Then men lied.
Then a crowd condemned.
Then stones flew.
Then Naboth died.
Then Ahab took possession.
Sin grows.
That is why Jesus does not merely come to improve our behavior.
He comes for the heart.
And this is where the story takes an unexpected turn.
When Ahab heard Elijah's judgment, Scripture says he tore his clothes, put sackcloth upon himself, fasted, lay in sackcloth, and went about subdued.
Then God spoke to Elijah again.
“Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me?”
Because Ahab humbled himself, God said the announced calamity upon his house would not come in his own days but in his son's days.
Do not misunderstand this.
Consequences remained.
Judgment was not erased as though Naboth's blood did not matter.
And Ahab's later life demonstrates that his spiritual condition was deeply troubled.
But even here, in one of Israel's darkest royal stories, God notices humility.
That is extraordinary.
The God who saw Naboth's blood also saw Ahab bow.
The God who sees injustice also sees repentance.
This is why biblical judgment is never permission for Christians to become self-righteous.
The story is supposed to make us tremble before God, not merely point at Jezebel.
Because if God judged every hidden sin immediately...
Who among us could stand?
That question leads us beyond Naboth's vineyard.
It leads us to another innocent Man.
Another conspiracy.
Another group of false witnesses.
Another miscarriage of justice.
Another innocent victim condemned while powerful people protected their interests.
Jesus Christ.
Naboth is not Jesus, and we should not force every detail of the narrative into an artificial allegory.
But Christians cannot read the broader biblical story of an innocent man destroyed through corrupt testimony without eventually remembering the perfectly innocent Son of God.
At Jesus' trial, false witnesses arose.
Religious and political interests collided.
Crowds were manipulated.
The innocent was condemned.
Christ was taken outside and crucified.
But unlike Naboth, Jesus knowingly walked toward His death as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
And here the Gospel exposes us.
We want to imagine ourselves standing beside Naboth.
But before the holiness of God, we discover that we have also been Ahab.
We have coveted.
We have lied.
We have manipulated.
We have remained silent when truth was inconvenient.
We have benefited from things we should have challenged.
We have wanted God's gifts more than God.
We have sinned.
And the Gospel is not that good people like Naboth are rescued from bad people like Ahab.
The Gospel goes deeper.
The Gospel says sinners can be reconciled to a holy God because Jesus Christ bore sin and conquered death.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
God does not pretend sin is harmless.
He deals with it.
Jesus bears the judgment sinners deserve, and all who repent and trust in Him receive forgiveness—not because their sin was small, but because His sacrifice is sufficient.
That is grace.
Not God saying the scandal did not matter.
God redeeming sinners without becoming unjust.
Not pretending the blood was never spilled.
But answering human sin through the blood of His Son.
This is why repentance is not humiliation to be avoided.
Repentance is mercy calling your name before judgment has the final word.
Maybe your vineyard has been hidden for years.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have become skilled at appearing fine.
Maybe your church friends know the polished version.
Maybe your family knows the edited version.
Maybe the secret is not murder or theft.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Pornography.
Adultery of the heart.
Envy.
Greed.
Pride.
Unforgiveness.
Dishonesty.
A secret relationship.
A double life.
A grudge you keep feeding.
A person you refuse to forgive.
A compromise you keep renaming so you do not have to call it sin.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to come.
Not to hide.
Not to perform.
Not to manufacture another religious image.
Come.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice those words in 1 John 1:9.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Christianity does not offer you better camouflage.
Jesus offers cleansing.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life protecting the vineyard where your sin is buried.
Bring it into the light.
The cross has already proved that God's grace is greater than the scandal of a genuinely repentant sinner.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because consequences never exist.
Not because victims do not matter.
Not because justice disappears.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus can take a human story marked by sin, shame, rebellion, failure, grief, and ruin and write redemption where we thought only an ending remained.
If Naboth's story made you angry, remember that God cares about justice more perfectly than you do.
If Ahab's story convicted you, remember that conviction is an invitation to repent rather than another excuse to hide.
If Jezebel's manipulation frightened you, examine whether power, influence, religion, or reputation have ever become tools for getting your own way.
And if the cross gave you hope...
Run to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Somebody reading this has been pretending for too long.
If that is you, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your life. But you can stop pretending before God.
Someone who thinks their story is beyond redemption may read your words tonight and discover that Christ still receives sinners.
Then think of one person who needs Naboth's vineyard.
Not somebody you want to attack with it.
Somebody you love.
Someone struggling with envy.
Someone recovering from betrayal.
Someone who was falsely accused.
Someone who thinks powerful people always get away with evil.
Someone hiding sin.
Someone drifting from Christ.
Someone who has almost stopped believing that God sees.
Save it too.

Because there may come a night when you are tempted to trade your inheritance for convenience, when somebody's apparent success makes compromise look attractive, or when injustice makes you wonder whether God has forgotten.
Come back to the vineyard.
God saw Naboth.
God saw Ahab.
God saw Jezebel.
And God sees you.

Jesus Christ alone is Savior. But if you genuinely want to help Gospel-centered truth travel farther, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
It helps support deeper discipleship content, biblical nourishment, encouragement, spiritual sharpening, and resources designed to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
Do not leave Jesus outside the vineyard.
Do not admire Naboth's conviction while protecting Ahab's desires inside your own heart.
Do not condemn Jezebel's manipulation while excusing your own secret compromises.
Do not celebrate Elijah's courage while remaining silent when truth becomes costly.
And above everything...
Do not read about judgment without running toward the Savior who bore judgment for sinners.
Naboth's blood cried out against injustice.
But there is another blood that Scripture says “speaketh better things.”
The blood of Jesus.
The blood that does not tell guilty sinners there was never a crime.
The blood that announces that the debt can be paid.
The blood that does not make repentance unnecessary.
The blood that makes forgiveness possible.
The blood that tells the ashamed they can come home.
The blood that tells the sinner there is mercy.
The blood that tells the broken that God is still writing.
So bring Him the part of your story you keep hiding.
Bring Him your vineyard.
Bring Him the envy.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the damage you cannot undo.
Bring Him the truth.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Christ.
Because the most dangerous thing in Naboth's vineyard was never the king who wanted more land.
It was the human heart believing it could have what it wanted without answering to God.
And the greatest hope in the story is that the God who walks into our hidden vineyards carrying truth is the same God who sent His Son carrying a cross.
And never forget:
You may be able to hide the vineyard from people—but you never have to hide your broken story from the Savior who went to the cross to redeem sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ATTRACTION, DESIRE, LUST, AND COVETING: DOES THE BIBLE REALLY TREAT THEM AS THE SAME THING?
paragraphs: ATTRACTION, DESIRE, LUST, AND COVETING: DOES THE BIBLE REALLY TREAT THEM AS THE SAME THING?

You noticed someone was beautiful. Your heart reacted. A thought entered your mind. And suddenly you wondered, “Did I just sin against God?” What Jesus actually said may convict you deeply—but it may also free you from a burden He never asked you to carry.
There is a moment almost nobody talks about honestly.
You see someone.
Something registers.
They are beautiful. Handsome. Attractive.
And before you have even finished processing what happened, another voice enters your mind.
Was that lust?
Then comes the guilt.
Maybe you are married, which makes the guilt worse.
Maybe you are single and desperately trying to honor Christ.
Maybe pornography has been part of your past, so now you distrust almost every physical reaction you experience.
Maybe you have been taught that simply finding another person physically attractive means you have already committed adultery in your heart.
So you begin policing every glance.
Every feeling.
Every physical reaction.
Every thought.
And somewhere between your desire to be holy and your fear of becoming impure, you start wondering whether holiness means becoming incapable of noticing beauty at all.
But what if we have collapsed several different experiences into one word?
Attraction.
Desire.
Temptation.
Lust.
Coveting.
Are they really identical?
Does Scripture condemn the involuntary recognition that another human being is attractive?
Does temptation itself make you guilty?
Does every desire equal lust?
And when Jesus said that a man who looks at a woman “to lust after her” has already committed adultery with her in his heart, was He saying that noticing beauty is adultery?
This matters more than we realize.
Because if we call something sin that Scripture does not call sin, we can crush tender consciences.
But if we rename sin so that it sounds harmless, we can soothe consciences that desperately need repentance.
The Gospel does neither.
Jesus does not excuse the darkness.
And Jesus does not condemn you for something He never called darkness.
He brings the light.
So come closer.
Because before this is finished, some people are going to realize they have been carrying guilt Jesus never placed on them.
Others are going to realize they have been calling something “attraction” that God has been asking them to surrender for years.
And some of us may discover both at the same time.
The first thing we need to understand is surprisingly simple:
The Bible does not treat every experience of attraction, desire, temptation, lust, and coveting as though they were automatically identical.
That becomes especially important when we look at the language of Scripture itself.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus takes His listeners beyond the external command against adultery and exposes what can happen inside the heart.
The Greek text says:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial expression is πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn.
The verb is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, related to ἐπιθυμία — epithymia, meaning desire, longing, or craving depending upon context.
And context matters enormously.
The word itself cannot simply be translated in every occurrence as “sexual lust,” because the same word-family can describe desires that are not sinful.
That fact alone should make us careful.
Desire is not automatically evil merely because desire exists.
The moral question is: What is being desired? In what way? Toward what end? And what is the heart doing with that desire?
Jesus is not giving humanity a command never to recognize physical beauty.
He is confronting a look connected with a heart that desires another person wrongly.
There is a profound difference between your eyes recognizing that someone is attractive and your heart beginning to possess them in imagination.
One notices.
The other takes.
One recognizes beauty.
The other begins inwardly consuming a person who does not belong to you.
And that difference becomes even clearer when we go backward into the Hebrew Scriptures.
The tenth commandment says:
לֹא תַחְמֹד — lo taḥmod
“You shall not covet.”
The verb חָמַד — ḥamad can involve desiring, taking pleasure in, or coveting something desirable. Again, context determines its moral character.
But look carefully at what the commandment names.
Your neighbor's house.
Your neighbor's wife.
Your neighbor's servants.
Your neighbor's animals.
Anything belonging to your neighbor.
The issue is not that the human mind is capable of recognizing value.
The issue is a heart reaching possessively toward what belongs to another.
Coveting whispers:
I want what is not mine.
I should have what they have.
I want that person.
I want that marriage.
I want that body.
I want that life.
And suddenly this subject becomes much larger than sex.
You can covet someone's spouse.
You can covet someone's income.
Someone's house.
Someone's body.
Someone's influence.
Someone's ministry.
Someone's career.
Someone's children.
Someone's opportunities.
Someone's popularity.
Someone's platform.
Someone's life.
Social media has given coveting an endless scrolling feed.
We can spend hours looking through windows into other people's lives until gratitude slowly dies inside us.
Their vacation.
Their marriage.
Their physique.
Their engagement.
Their promotion.
Their home.
Their success.
Their seemingly perfect family.
And somewhere inside you, almost silently, something begins saying:
Why don't I have that?
That is why this conversation cannot stop with sexuality.
Coveting is a heart problem.
And Jesus has always been after the heart.
But here is where many sincere Christians become unnecessarily terrified.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
James describes something moving through stages.
The Greek of James 1:14–15 says:
ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος
Then James continues:
εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν
The imagery is almost frightening.
A person is drawn.
Enticed.
Then desire “conceives.”
And what does it give birth to?
ἁμαρτίαν — hamartian.
Sin.
James deliberately describes progression.
Desire entices.
Desire conceives.
Sin is born.
Sin matures.
Death follows.
That should sober us.
But it should also prevent us from flattening the entire process into a single moment.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet remained without sin.
So temptation cannot automatically equal sin.
Otherwise we would have to say Christ sinned merely by being tempted, which Scripture emphatically denies.
That distinction may be the sentence someone reading this desperately needed tonight:
Being tempted is not the same thing as consenting to temptation.
The unwanted thought that suddenly enters your mind is not necessarily the same thing as the thought you invite to sit down, lock the door, and stay.
The first glance may encounter beauty.
The second can become a decision.
But even “first glance versus second glance” is only a practical illustration, not a mathematical biblical rule. The deeper question is what the heart is doing.
Are you recognizing?
Or are you consuming?
Are you encountering temptation?
Or are you feeding it?
Are you noticing someone?
Or have you begun mentally undressing them?
Are you appreciating beauty?
Or are you constructing a fantasy?
Are you resisting the thought?
Or secretly hoping it returns?
There is the battlefield.
Not simply in the existence of your eyes.
In the allegiance of your heart.
And this is where we need courageously honest language.
Sometimes Christians call lust “attraction” because attraction sounds innocent.
“I just think about her sometimes.”
“I just like looking at him.”
“We're only friends.”
“I would never actually do anything.”
But meanwhile the imagination has already built a secret room.
Conversations happen there.
Touches happen there.
Relationships happen there.
Bodies are possessed there.
A different marriage exists there.
Nobody else can see it.
But you keep visiting.
That is exactly why Jesus' words are so devastating.
Human beings tend to define righteousness by what nobody caught us doing.
Jesus walks through the locked door.
He goes deeper than behavior.
Into motive.
Into imagination.
Into desire.
Into the private theater where nobody sees what you replay except God.
You may never have touched them.
You may never have messaged them.
You may never have crossed the physical line.
And still Jesus asks:
What have you been doing with them in your heart?
That question hurts.
Because some scandals never become public.
Some affairs never leave the imagination.
Some pornography never appears on a screen because the screen is inside the mind.
Some coveting never becomes theft because the heart has learned how to steal without moving its hands.
And if that exposes something hidden in you, don't run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Because conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction says, “Bring this into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Hide from God because He could never want you now.”
One voice leads toward repentance.
The other drives you deeper into hiding.
And hiding is where lust grows strongest.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
You deleted the history.
You closed the tab.
You erased the conversation.
You promised God it was the last time.
Then came loneliness.
Stress.
Rejection.
A fight with your spouse.
A sleepless night.
A memory.
A photograph.
A name.
And suddenly you were standing at the same door again.
Maybe you have prayed:
“Jesus, why am I still fighting this?”
Listen carefully.
The fact that there is a battle does not mean Christ has abandoned you.
But grace does not mean making peace with the enemy.
Grace teaches us to come into the light.
To confess.
To repent.
To remove what feeds the sin.
To stop protecting the secret pathways that keep leading us back into captivity.
Because Jesus did not die merely to make sin less embarrassing.
He died to redeem sinners.
And redemption changes ownership.
Your eyes belong to Christ.
Your imagination belongs to Christ.
Your sexuality belongs to Christ.
Your singleness belongs to Christ.
Your marriage belongs to Christ.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your desires themselves must eventually kneel before Christ.
That does not mean becoming less human.
It means becoming human as God intended.
This is where another misconception must die.
Sexual desire itself is not an invention of Satan.
God created human beings male and female.
Marriage was God's idea before sin entered the world.
Sexual union within God's covenant design is not dirty.
The enemy did not create sexuality.
He corrupts what God created.
Sin repeatedly takes a good appetite and says:
You do not need God's boundaries.
Hunger says, “Food is good.”
Gluttony says, “I will not be governed.”
Rest says, “My body has limits.”
Sloth can say, “I refuse rightful responsibility.”
Stewardship says, “Resources can serve God's purposes.”
Greed says, “More will save me.”
Sexual desire says, “God created intimacy.”
Lust says, “I want gratification without submitting that desire to God's will and the dignity of the other person.”
And coveting says:
“I want what God has not given me.”
That is why the answer is not simply learning how to stop feeling.
The answer is learning how to desire under the lordship of Jesus Christ.

Even the Greek word epithymia forces us to think more carefully. The word can be used according to context for powerful desires, including sinful ones; therefore, no responsible reading can simply say, “Every desire is lust.”
The problem is not that you are capable of wanting.
The question is whether what you want agrees with the will of God—and whether desire has become your master.
And that brings us to something uncomfortable.
You can lust without touching.
You can covet without stealing.
You can commit idolatry without kneeling before a statue.
Because the heart is capable of turning almost anything into a throne.
A person can become your idol.
Romance can become your idol.
Marriage can become your idol.
Sex can become your idol.
Being desired can become your idol.
Even the desperate need to feel attractive can become an idol.
Some people are not primarily addicted to sex.
They are addicted to being wanted.
Read that again.
Sometimes the hunger underneath the behavior is:
Tell me I matter.
Tell me I'm beautiful.
Tell me somebody would choose me.
Tell me I am enough.
And lust offers counterfeit medicine for a wound it can never heal.
For a few moments, attention makes you feel valuable.
Then the moment disappears.
And the hunger returns.
So you need another message.
Another image.
Another flirtation.
Another fantasy.
Another person.
Another secret.
Another hit of being desired.
Until eventually you discover something terrifying:
You were drinking salt water to cure thirst.
And Jesus is standing beside the well saying that there is another kind of water.
Living water.
This is why Christianity cannot merely say, “Stop lusting.”
The Gospel goes deeper.
It asks why your soul keeps returning there.
What are you trying to medicate?
Loneliness?
Rejection?
Insecurity?
Bitterness?
A loveless marriage?
Past abuse?
Pride?
Curiosity?
Boredom?
The need for control?
The need to escape?
The desire to feel powerful?
The desire to feel wanted?
Sin must still be called sin.
But if we only cut leaves while leaving roots underground, we should not be surprised when the weeds return.
Jesus wants the roots too.
And maybe this is where grace finally becomes more than a religious word.
Because the person reading this who has failed sexually does not need a softer definition of sin.
You need a bigger Savior.
The adulterer needs Jesus.
The porn addict needs Jesus.
The person trapped in fantasy needs Jesus.
The jealous spouse needs Jesus.
The single Christian burning with desire needs Jesus.
The person secretly coveting somebody else's marriage needs Jesus.
The wounded person using sexual attention as anesthesia needs Jesus.
The self-righteous Christian who has never physically committed adultery but has privately consumed people in imagination needs Jesus.
And the person who has spent years drowning in false guilt because they thought merely recognizing another person's attractiveness made them filthy—
you need Jesus too.
Not because attraction itself automatically makes you guilty.
But because every part of you ultimately belongs under His loving lordship.
The cross leaves no room for boasting.
And the empty tomb leaves no room for despair.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not calling darkness light.
Not pretending consequences do not exist.
But neither is Christianity the announcement that your worst chapter gets the final sentence.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had blood connected to his former life.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
The Samaritan woman's relational history was known completely by Christ.
Again and again, Jesus encountered people whose stories contained things they wished they could rewrite.
Then Jesus entered the story.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not travel backward and make sin righteous.
Grace moves into the ruins and begins redemption.
So if you have been feeding lust, repent.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
If there is a conversation you know is becoming inappropriate, stop pretending.
If there is an account that repeatedly pulls you toward sin, remove it.
If there is pornography hidden on your device, bring the battle into the light.
If there is a person you are emotionally possessing in your imagination who belongs to someone else, surrender that fantasy to Christ.
If comparison has made you resent the life God has given you, confess the coveting.
If you have reduced human beings made in God's image into bodies for your consumption, repent.
But if you are condemning yourself merely because you noticed someone was attractive, stop inventing commandments God did not give you.
Holiness is not pretending beauty does not exist.
Holiness is learning to see people without consuming them.
Imagine that.
Looking at another human being and remembering:
That is not an object.
That is an image-bearer.
That person has fears.
A childhood.
A family.
A soul.
A story.
They are not pixels.
Not a fantasy.
Not a body assembled for your gratification.
Not something for your imagination to possess.
They belong first to God.
Suddenly the question changes.
Instead of asking only:
“How close can I get before this becomes sin?”
You begin asking:
“How can I look at this person in a way that honors Jesus?”
That is transformation.
Not merely avoiding adultery.
Learning purity.
Not merely resisting pornography.
Learning to see human beings again.
Not merely refusing coveting.
Learning contentment.
Not merely suppressing desire.
Learning to place desire at the feet of Christ.
And there will be days when you fail.
That sentence is not permission.
It is reality.
When you fail, do not turn failure into identity.
Confess it.
Repent.
Get up.
Return to Christ.
The enemy wants one fall to become a thousand because shame tells you:
“You already ruined everything. Why keep fighting?”
The Gospel says:
Come back.
Again.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Christ's blood is sufficient.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write your entire story publicly.
But you can take one small step out of darkness.
Sometimes four honest words are the first crack in a prison wall.
And please—do not keep this article only for yourself.
Someone on your Facebook friends list is silently drowning in shame.
Someone thinks temptation itself means God has rejected them.
Someone else has been feeding lust while calling it harmless attraction.
Someone's marriage is being invaded by a fantasy nobody knows exists.
Someone is seventeen years old and terrified because nobody ever explained the difference between temptation and consent.
Someone is fifty-seven and has carried secret shame for thirty years.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because a person might need the truth.
But hear this clearly:
Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity rather than giving under compulsion.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Tell another person about Jesus.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
And that brings us back to the person who began reading this article wondering:
Am I filthy because I felt attraction?
No—the biblical categories require more care than that.
Attraction is not automatically lust.
Desire is not automatically sinful.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
But desire can become disordered.
A look can become lustful.
Attraction can be deliberately cultivated into fantasy.
Desire can conceive sin.
And coveting can quietly teach your heart to reach for what God has not given you.
So do not become careless.
But do not become hopeless either.
Bring your eyes to Jesus.
Bring your imagination to Jesus.
Bring your sexuality to Jesus.
Bring your loneliness.
Bring your marriage.
Bring your singleness.
Bring the pornography history.
Bring the fantasies.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the comparison.
Bring the secret messages.
Bring the shame.
Bring the part of you that still wants what it should not have.
Bring the part of you that is terrified God is tired of forgiving you.
Bring all of it.
Because the goal of Christianity is not becoming a person who can boast:
“I was never tempted.”
The goal is becoming a person who can say:
“Even my desires belong to Jesus.”
And perhaps the greatest scandal is not that sinners have wanted what they should not want.
Perhaps the breathtaking scandal is that the holy Son of God knew exactly what was inside us—
and went to the cross anyway.
Not to approve our chains.
To break them.
Not to rename darkness.
To lead us into light.
Not to leave us ashamed beside the wreckage of yesterday.
To make us new.
So the next time temptation whispers, You will always be this person, remember the cross.
When shame whispers, God doesn't want you anymore, remember the empty tomb.
When lust whispers, You need this, remember Christ.
When coveting whispers, God has withheld something necessary from you, remember Christ.
When your heart says, I cannot change, remember Christ.
And when your past tries to introduce you by the name of your worst chapter, remember the One holding the pen.

Your temptation does not have to become your surrender, your failure does not have to become your identity, and your scandal does not have to become the final sentence—because the scarred hands of Jesus are still rewriting stories.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE PURE IN HEART SHALL SEE GOD” — BUT WHAT IF THE HEART YOU HIDE IS THE HEART JESUS WANTS?
paragraphs: “THE PURE IN HEART SHALL SEE GOD” — BUT WHAT IF THE HEART YOU HIDE IS THE HEART JESUS WANTS?
Jesus never said, “Blessed are those who look clean.” He went somewhere far more frightening—and far more beautiful. He went straight to the heart.
There is a version of you that people know.
And then there is the version of you that appears when the room is quiet, the phone is face down, the door is locked, the smile disappears, and there is nobody left to impress.
That person has thoughts nobody hears.
Memories nobody knows still hurt.
Temptations you would never post about.
Motives you do not always understand yourself.
Questions you are almost afraid to ask God.
Maybe resentment you buried beneath Christian vocabulary.
Maybe lust you keep promising will be the last time.
Maybe jealousy hidden behind congratulations.
Maybe pride disguised as discernment.
Maybe bitterness you renamed “boundaries” because admitting you still hate what happened feels too uncomfortable.
Maybe you serve, give, pray, worship, quote Scripture, encourage people, and say all the right things...
while privately wondering:
If people could actually see my heart, would they still believe I belong to Jesus?
And perhaps an even more frightening question:
If God already sees it, how could I ever be called pure?
That is why one sentence from Jesus can feel simultaneously like a promise and a sword.
“Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.” — Matthew 5:8
The Greek reads:
Μακάριοι οἱ καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ, ὅτι αὐτοὶ τὸν Θεὸν ὄψονται.
Makarioi hoi katharoi tē kardia, hoti autoi ton Theon opsontai.
Blessed are the pure in heart, because they shall see God.
Read it again.
Jesus did not say blessed are the people with spotless reputations.
He did not say blessed are those who have mastered religious appearances.
He did not say blessed are those who never struggle.
He said:
καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ — katharoi tē kardia.
Pure in heart.

The word καθαρός — katharos carries the idea of being clean or pure. And καρδία — kardia, “heart,” in biblical usage reaches far deeper than emotion alone. It points toward the inner person—the place of desires, intentions, affections, thoughts, loyalties, and motives.
Jesus is putting His finger on the place nobody else can fully inspect.
The inside.
That is terrifying if Christianity is merely about maintaining an image.
But it is breathtakingly good news if Christianity is about Jesus transforming sinners.
Because the Gospel is not God teaching dirty people how to pretend they are clean.
The Gospel is God doing for sinners what sinners cannot ultimately do for themselves.
David understood this.

After terrible moral collapse, after adultery, deception, abuse of power, and bloodshed had shattered the illusion that he could trust his own heart, David did not merely pray, “God, help me behave better.”
His prayer went deeper.
In Psalm 51:10, the Hebrew says:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Look carefully at those words.
לֵב — lev: heart.
טָהוֹר — tahor: clean, pure.
And David cries to God to create this heart within him.
That changes everything.
David had finally discovered something many religious people spend years avoiding:
You can modify behavior while the heart remains untouched.
You can stop one outward action while secretly continuing to love the sin that produced it.
You can become better at hiding without becoming holier.
You can clean the outside while protecting what is rotting inside.
And Jesus had very strong words for religion like that.
He confronted religious leaders who carefully maintained external appearances while corruption remained within. His concern was never that outward obedience does not matter. It matters enormously.
His concern was that outward religion can become camouflage.
You can raise your hands in worship while refusing to release hatred.
You can know theology while craving applause.
You can preach forgiveness while quietly hoping someone suffers.
You can post Bible verses while feeding a secret addiction.
You can talk about holiness while enjoying another person's downfall.
You can defend truth while secretly worshiping the feeling of being right.
You can even do things “for God” while desperately wanting people to notice that you did them.
That is what makes the words of Jesus so piercing.
“Blessed are the pure in heart.”
Not merely clean hands.
A clean heart.
Yet Scripture beautifully connects the two.
Psalm 24 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and stand in His holy place. The answer includes:
נְקִי כַפַּיִם וּבַר־לֵבָב
Neki khappayim uvar-levav.
Clean hands and a pure heart.
The biblical vision refuses to separate inward devotion from outward life.
Real heart transformation eventually touches the hands.
What you love changes what you do.
What you worship shapes how you live.
What rules the heart eventually leaves fingerprints on your choices.
But here is where people sometimes misunderstand Matthew 5:8.

A pure heart does not mean that a Christian has reached a state where he or she never experiences temptation, never battles sinful desires, never needs confession, and never again requires the mercy of God.
If that were what Jesus meant, who among us could stand?

The apostle John writes to believers that if we claim to have no sin, we deceive ourselves. Yet in that very context he gives extraordinary hope: as believers walk in the light, “the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.”
The Greek of 1 John 1:7 says:
τὸ αἷμα Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ καθαρίζει ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ πάσης ἁμαρτίας
The blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.
There it is again.
Cleansing.
But notice who provides it.
Jesus.
This is where purity stops being a trophy for impressive Christians and becomes a testimony to grace.
The pure heart is not the heart that never needed washing.
It is the heart that has been brought into the light of God.
The heart that stops negotiating with darkness.
The heart that no longer wants to protect the very thing Christ died to save us from.
The heart that can finally say:
“Jesus, there it is.
I hate admitting it.
I cannot excuse it anymore.
I cannot blame everybody else.
I cannot rename it.
I cannot hide behind church attendance.
I cannot bury it beneath ministry.
This is my sin.
Have mercy on me.”
That is not hypocrisy.
That is repentance.
Hypocrisy says, “I must make sure nobody discovers who I really am.”
Repentance says, “Jesus already knows who I really am, so I am coming into the light.”
Do you see the difference?
One hides because reputation is precious.
The other confesses because Christ is precious.
And perhaps that is where this article has found you.
Maybe you have spent years trying to look pure rather than asking Christ to purify you.
You became skilled at managing perception.
People think you are strong.
People come to you for prayer.
People ask you for advice.
People assume your marriage is fine.
People assume your faith is strong.
People assume the smile means peace.
But God sees the exhausted soul underneath all of it.
And maybe you are tired.
Tired of editing yourself.
Tired of deleting the browser history.
Tired of pretending the marriage does not hurt.
Tired of smiling at somebody you secretly resent.
Tired of promising God, “Never again,” only to crawl back into the same darkness.
Tired of performing Christianity while wondering whether you still know Christ.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the version of you that everybody sees.
Jesus came for the person hiding underneath it.
That person.
The ashamed person.
The angry person.
The addicted person.
The jealous person.
The wounded person.
The person who knows exactly how to say “God is good” while privately wondering why God allowed something to happen.
The person still carrying something from ten years ago.
The person reading this while thinking:
If only you knew.
Jesus knows.
And the scandal of grace is that He knew before the nails pierced His hands.
He knew before the whip tore His back.
He knew before the crown of thorns was driven against His head.
He knew before Calvary.
The cross was never God's response to discovering that humanity was better than expected.
The cross happened because our condition was worse than we wanted to admit—and God's mercy was greater than we dared imagine.
Jesus did not die for the carefully edited version of you.
Christ died for sinners.
That is the Gospel.
Not “clean yourself until God can tolerate you.”
Not “hide your worst parts until you become respectable.”
Not “perform enough Christianity to compensate for what you did.”
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we failed to live, died for sinners, and rose again in victory.
Our hope is not the purity of our résumé.
Our hope is Christ.
And Scripture makes the connection astonishingly explicit.
When Peter described God's work among Gentile believers in Acts 15:9, he said God was:
τῇ πίστει καθαρίσας τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν
tē pistei katharisas tas kardias autōn.
Having cleansed their hearts by faith.
Their hearts were cleansed through faith.
Not ethnicity.
Not religious pedigree.
Not ceremonial superiority.
Faith.
And biblical faith is not vague optimism.
It reaches outside ourselves and rests upon God and His saving work.
So when Jesus says, “Blessed are the pure in heart,” do not hear:
“Blessed are those impressive enough to deserve God.”
Hear the call of a King who refuses to settle for outward religion.
He wants your heart.
Not because your heart is naturally beautiful.
Because He intends to rule there.
This means purity of heart involves more than avoiding obviously scandalous sins.
It reaches our loyalties.
Our motives.
Our secret loves.
It asks uncomfortable questions.
Why did you really post that?
Why did their success hurt you?
Why does being overlooked make you angry?
Why do you need everybody to know you were right?
Why are you serving?
Why are you giving?
Why are you praying publicly?
Why are you refusing to forgive?
Why do you keep returning to that fantasy?
Why do you want that person's approval so badly?
Why are you afraid of losing something God never promised you?
Why does criticism devastate you more than sin does?
Why does human applause feel more immediate than God's pleasure?
Those questions are uncomfortable because impurity is not always obvious wickedness.
Sometimes it is divided allegiance.
Jesus said nobody can serve two masters.
A heart can become fractured by competing gods.
Christ and money.
Christ and approval.
Christ and sexual desire.
Christ and revenge.
Christ and status.
Christ and control.
Christ and comfort.
Christ and self.
We want Jesus as Savior while quietly reserving one locked room with a sign that says:
Mine.
And Christ loves us too much to pretend that locked room does not matter.
Purity of heart means increasingly wanting one supreme thing above every rival:
God.
David prayed elsewhere:
“Unite my heart to fear thy name.”
What a prayer.
Because sometimes the greatest problem is not that we have no desire for God.
It is that we desire God and refuse to release the idols competing with Him.
Part of us wants holiness.
Part wants the secret sin.
Part wants Jesus.
Part wants applause.
Part wants forgiveness.
Part wants revenge.
Part wants surrender.
Part wants control.
And somewhere in that war, Jesus says:
“Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
This promise is enormous.
They shall see God.
Christian hope ultimately reaches toward the day when God's redeemed people will dwell in His presence. Revelation 22:4 gives one of Scripture's most astonishing promises concerning God's servants:
“They shall see his face.”
Think about that.
The Bible begins with humanity hiding from God.
Adam sins.
Adam hears God.
Adam hides.
That has been our story ever since.
Sin says:
Hide.
Grace says:
Come.
Sin makes us cover ourselves.
Grace clothes us in what we could never provide for ourselves.
Sin makes us flee the light.
Christ brings us into it.
And the story ends not with God's redeemed children hiding behind trees...
but seeing His face.
Do you understand the magnitude of that?
The Gospel takes hiding sinners and brings them home.
From shame to sonship.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From darkness to light.
From rebellion to reconciliation.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the most powerful evidence that Christ is working in your heart is not that you never struggle anymore.
Perhaps it is that you can no longer make peace with the darkness you once protected.
You fall—and something inside cries for Christ.
You sin—and instead of building a permanent home there, you want to return.
You become aware of pride—and you hate what it does to your fellowship with God.
You notice envy—and instead of baptizing it with excuses, you bring it before Jesus.
You recognize lust—and you stop calling slavery freedom.
You discover bitterness—and you realize revenge cannot heal what wounded you.
You stop asking:
“How much can I get away with and still call myself Christian?”
And begin asking:
“How much of me can Jesus have?”
That is a different heart.
Not a heart boasting in perfection.
A heart being conquered by grace.
There may even be someone reading this who believes his or her past permanently disqualifies them.
You know what you did.
Maybe nobody else knows.
You remember the room.
The conversation.
The betrayal.
The abortion.
The affair.
The lie.
The theft.
The pornography.
The cruelty.
The years wasted.
The person you wounded.
The family you failed.
The promise you broke.
The season when you walked away from God and did things the current version of you can barely believe.
And every time you hear words like “pure” or “holy,” something inside whispers:
Not you.
But hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ does not specialize in polishing people who already look righteous.
He saves sinners.
The cross is not decoration for respectable people.
It is God's declaration that sin is deadly serious and His grace is astonishingly deep.
There is no cleansing apart from Christ.
There is no repentance without admitting that something needs to die.
There is no resurrection without a grave.
Bring the heart into the light.
Stop protecting what is destroying you.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what Christ calls sin.
Seek reconciliation where Scripture requires it and where it can rightly and safely be pursued.
Cut off the pathways that repeatedly carry you back into darkness.
Stop feeding what you keep asking God to kill.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray when you feel nothing.
Pray when you feel filthy.
Pray when you are ashamed.
Pray when your prayer is only:
“Jesus, help me.”
And remember this:
You are not cleansing yourself so Jesus will finally love you.
You come to Jesus because He alone is your hope.
The blood of Christ cleanses from sin.
God cleanses hearts through faith.
And the Spirit continues His sanctifying work in those who belong to Christ.
That destroys both pride and despair.
Pride cannot say, “Look how pure I made myself.”
Despair cannot say, “There is no cleansing available for someone like me.”
The Gospel answers both:
Look to Christ.
Maybe right now you need to stop reading for ten seconds.
Not to perform.
Not to manufacture emotion.
Just to tell God the truth.
What is sitting between you and wholehearted surrender?
What are you hiding?
What have you renamed because calling it sin would require repentance?
Whose approval have you been worshiping?
