What resentment are you feeding?
What private habit keeps pulling you away from the light?
What are you terrified Jesus might ask you to surrender?
Do not answer for the person beside you.
Do not think about the friend who “needs to read this.”
You.
Your heart.
Your Jesus.
Your surrender.
Because one day, likes will disappear.
Followers will disappear.
Money will remain behind.
Titles will remain behind.
Bodies will return to dust.
The opinions of people who once controlled your emotions will become irrelevant.
And nothing will matter more than belonging to Christ.
So do not settle for looking Christian.
Do not settle for Christian aesthetics.
Do not settle for Bible verses in a biography while Christ remains outside the locked rooms of your life.
Ask God for what David asked:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Ask Him to expose false motives.
Ask Him to break idols.
Ask Him to teach you to love what He loves.
Ask Him for courage to confess.
Ask Him for grace to forgive.
Ask Him to make Jesus more precious than the sin you keep returning to.
And when the Spirit exposes something ugly, do not mistake conviction for abandonment.
Run toward Christ.
The enemy wants exposure to become despair.
The Gospel turns exposure into an invitation to repentance and grace.
Peter failed publicly.
David fell catastrophically.
Paul once persecuted the church.
Their sins were not harmless.
Grace never requires us to pretend evil was insignificant.
Grace does something infinitely more powerful.
It tells the truth about sin while pointing sinners to a Savior greater than their sin.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create spectators who scroll through Christian content and momentarily feel inspired.
We want people in Scripture.
People praying again.
People repenting.
People returning to Jesus.
People learning sound biblical truth.
People discovering that Christianity is not merely content to consume but a life surrendered to Christ.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God does not owe spiritual blessing to anyone because they financially supported a ministry.
We support Gospel work because we love Christ and want biblical truth to reach people.
What is Jesus exposing in your heart?
Be honest.
Your comment does not have to tell strangers every detail.
God knows the details.
Sometimes three honest words are enough to stop pretending.
And somebody scrolling through those comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle behind a smile.
You may need it again on a night when shame tells you to hide from God.
Sharing Christian truth does not earn God's favor, but it can become a simple act of witness—placing the Gospel where another wounded, wandering, ashamed, or searching person may encounter it.
Not for numbers.
For people.
Because behind every screen is a soul.
Behind every polished profile may be a hidden battle.
Behind every hidden battle is a heart God already sees.
And there is still a Savior calling sinners out of darkness.
Maybe that is what “pure in heart” finally forces us to confront.
Not:
“Have I become impressive enough for God?”
But:
“Will I stop hiding long enough to let the light of Christ reach every room?”
Jesus already knows what is behind the door.
He knows what happened.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows what you keep replaying.
He knows the temptation.
He knows the resentment.
He knows the secret.
He knows the wound.
He knows the person beneath the Christian vocabulary.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Be washed.
Follow Christ.
The goal is not merely cleaner behavior.
The goal is God Himself.
“Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
One day faith will become sight.
One day the war with sin will be over.
One day shame will have no hiding place because shame itself will be gone.
One day those redeemed by Christ will see the One their souls were created for.
Until then, keep bringing the heart into His light.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Because the heart you are most ashamed to expose may be the very place where the grace of Jesus writes its most unforgettable testimony.
You spent years hiding the scandal, but Jesus was already preparing to write grace across the place you thought could never be redeemed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID RACHEL AND LEAH’S RIVALRY SHAPE ISRAEL?
paragraphs:
WHY DID RACHEL AND LEAH’S RIVALRY SHAPE ISRAEL?
Two sisters fought to be loved. One husband played favorites. Children became caught inside a competition they never created. And somehow, from this painfully fractured home, God built the family that would become Israel—and eventually brought Jesus Christ into the world.
There are Bible stories we sanitize because the truth makes us uncomfortable.
Rachel and Leah’s story is one of them.
We remember Jacob’s romance.
We remember the seven years that “seemed unto him but a few days” because of his love for Rachel.
We remember Laban’s deception.
We remember Leah’s children and Rachel’s barrenness.
But if we read Genesis slowly enough to feel what is actually happening inside that house, the story stops looking like a beautiful ancient romance.
It starts sounding painfully modern.
One woman feels unwanted.
Another woman has what her sister desperately wants.
A husband’s favoritism hangs over the household.
Children are born into emotional wounds that existed before they did.
Names become testimonies.
Pregnancy becomes competition.
Sex becomes negotiation.
Jealousy enters the bedroom.
Resentment enters motherhood.
And two sisters who should have been able to comfort each other begin measuring their worth against each other.
Then comes the part that should leave us stunned:
God does not call the dysfunction good.
But He refuses to let the dysfunction have the final word.
That distinction matters.
Because somebody reading this knows what it feels like to come from a family where love was unevenly distributed.
Somebody knows what it is like to watch a sibling receive the affection, approval, opportunity, beauty, attention, inheritance, or recognition you desperately wanted.
Somebody knows what it is like to quietly wonder:
“Why wasn’t I enough?”
And that question is sitting underneath much of Leah’s story.
Genesis 29:30 tells us Jacob “loved also Rachel more than Leah.”
Then comes one of the saddest verses in the story:

“When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.”
—Genesis 29:31, KJV
The Hebrew deserves careful attention.

The word translated “hated” is שְׂנוּאָה, senu’ah, from the Hebrew root שׂנא (s-n-ʾ), “to hate.” In biblical usage, however, this language can function comparatively in contexts of preference and rejection. Genesis itself has just told us that Jacob loved Rachel “more than Leah.” So the point is not something we should flatten into a simplistic psychological diagnosis of Jacob.
The text gives us something more concrete and devastating.
Leah was the less-loved wife.
She knew it.
Rachel knew it.
And God saw it.
That may be the first truth someone needs tonight:
God sees the person everyone else overlooks.
Leah conceives and gives birth to Reuben.
She names him רְאוּבֵן, Re’uven, and Genesis records her reasoning:
“Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me.”
Listen to that sentence.
Not merely:
“God gave me a son.”
But:
“Now my husband will love me.”
A baby has entered the world, and Leah is already hoping this child can repair the wound in her marriage.
Then Simeon is born.
“Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated, he hath therefore given me this son also.”
Then Levi.
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons.”
Do you hear the progression?
Maybe now he will love me.
Maybe now he will see me.
Maybe now he will stay close to me.
Maybe now I will finally be enough.
Three sons.
Three cries from a wounded heart.
And this is where the ancient story becomes a mirror.
How many things have you secretly turned into your own Reuben?
Maybe if I become successful, they will respect me.
Maybe if I lose the weight, somebody will want me.
Maybe if I earn more money, my family will finally be proud.
Maybe if my ministry grows, I will feel important.
Maybe if people praise me, share my posts, recognize my work, or finally apologize for what they did, the ache will disappear.
Maybe if I become useful enough…
beautiful enough…
spiritual enough…
successful enough…
someone will finally choose me.
But human achievement makes a terrible savior.
Then something remarkable happens.
Leah conceives again.
Judah is born.
And this time her words change.
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
Therefore, Genesis says, she called his name יְהוּדָה, Yehudah—Judah.
The name is connected in the narrative with the Hebrew verb ידה (y-d-h), “to praise” or “give thanks.”
Notice what is missing from Leah’s words.
Jacob.
For this moment, at least, her statement is no longer:
Maybe my husband will love me.
Maybe my husband will attach himself to me.
Maybe this will finally make me enough.
She says:
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
And from Judah comes a line that will eventually lead to David…
and generations later, according to the flesh, to Jesus Christ.
Do not rush past that.
The woman desperate to be chosen by Jacob becomes the mother of Judah.
Judah becomes the tribe associated with Israel’s royal line.
And the New Testament deliberately identifies Jesus as descended from Judah.
Revelation 5:5 calls Christ:
“the Lion of the tribe of Juda.”
God did not need Leah to win Jacob’s favoritism before He could give her life covenant significance.
That is not sentimental encouragement.
That is woven into the biblical storyline.
But Rachel is hurting too.
And Scripture refuses to make this a simplistic story where Leah is the wounded saint and Rachel is merely the villain.
Rachel is loved deeply by Jacob.
Yet Rachel cannot conceive.
Genesis 30:1 says:
“And when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister…”
The Hebrew verb is קנא (q-n-ʾ), a word associated with jealousy or zeal.
Then Rachel says something desperate:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
This is not the voice of a woman who feels victorious because her husband prefers her.
It is the voice of somebody discovering that being envied does not mean being whole.
Leah has children and wants Rachel’s love-position.
Rachel has Jacob’s affection and wants Leah’s fertility.
Each woman is staring at what the other possesses.
And comparison turns both blessings into pain.
That is what envy does.
It can make you incapable of enjoying what God has placed in your hands because you cannot stop staring at what He placed in someone else’s.
Rachel sees Leah’s children.
Leah sees Rachel’s affection.
Neither woman seems able simply to look at her own life without looking sideways.
And maybe neither can we.
We scroll.
We compare marriages.
Bodies.
Homes.
Children.
Ministries.
Careers.
Followers.
Vacations.
Testimonies.
We see someone else celebrating the very thing we have begged God for, and suddenly their blessing feels like evidence that God has forgotten us.
But another person’s blessing is not proof of your abandonment.
Rachel’s pain becomes so intense that she gives Jacob her servant Bilhah in accordance with an ancient reproductive arrangement, and Bilhah bears children for Rachel.
The names again expose the emotional battlefield.
When Bilhah bears Naphtali, Rachel says:
“With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed.”
The Hebrew is striking:
נַפְתּוּלֵי אֱלֹהִים נִפְתַּלְתִּי עִם־אֲחֹתִי
Naphtulei Elohim niftalti ‘im-achoti…
The precise force of naphtulei Elohim has been translated in different ways, including “mighty wrestlings” or “wrestlings of God,” but the context is unmistakable:
Rachel sees herself wrestling with her sister.
Think about how tragic that is.
These are not enemies from rival nations.
They are sisters.
But wounded hearts can turn people who should be companions into competitors.
Then Leah gives her servant Zilpah to Jacob.
More sons follow.
The household grows.
The rivalry deepens.
And then Scripture gives us one of the strangest scenes in the entire story.
Mandrakes.
Reuben finds mandrakes and brings them to Leah.
Rachel wants them.
Leah responds:
“Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son’s mandrakes also?”
There it is.
Years of pain inside one sentence.
Rachel answers by bargaining:
Jacob can sleep with Leah that night in exchange for the mandrakes.
When Jacob returns from the field, Leah goes out to meet him:
“Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son’s mandrakes.”
It is heartbreaking.
The man Leah once hoped would love her is now being negotiated between sisters.
This is not Scripture endorsing the arrangement.
The Bible is often brutally honest about human behavior without presenting every behavior it records as righteous.
That is essential for understanding Genesis.
Polygamy appears repeatedly in the Old Testament narrative, but its appearances are consistently accompanied by jealousy, rivalry, conflict, inheritance disputes, or family fracture.
Genesis began somewhere very different.
One man.
One woman.
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Human beings complicate what God designed.
And Genesis lets us watch the consequences unfold.
But God keeps working.
Not because deception is holy.
Not because favoritism is holy.
Not because rivalry is holy.
Not because envy is holy.
Not because sexual bargaining is holy.
God works because His faithfulness is greater than human failure.
Eventually Genesis says:
“And God remembered Rachel…”
This does not mean God had literally forgotten her and suddenly recalled that she existed.
In biblical language, when God “remembers,” the expression often signals His movement toward covenantal action.
Rachel conceives.
Joseph is born.
The woman who once cried, “Give me children, or else I die,” finally holds a son.
But the story refuses to become a fairy tale.
Rachel later conceives Benjamin.
The delivery is devastating.
Genesis 35 records that Rachel experiences severe labor.
As she is dying, she names the child בֶּן־אוֹנִי, Ben-Oni—commonly understood as “son of my sorrow” or “son of my affliction.”
Jacob renames him בִּנְיָמִין, Binyamin—Benjamin, conventionally understood as “son of the right hand.”
Rachel dies.
The woman Jacob loved so fiercely does not get the ending we might have written for her.
And Leah?
Scripture does not narrate Leah’s death in the same way.
But years later, when Jacob is preparing to die, he tells his sons where he wants to be buried.
The cave of Machpelah.
And then he says something easily overlooked:
“There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah.”
Leah.
The overlooked wife.
The woman who spent years longing for Jacob’s affection.
She rests in the ancestral burial place of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah.
And Jacob asks to be buried there too.
Rachel and Leah’s story shaped Israel because their rivalry became intertwined with the formation of Jacob’s household, from which the tribes of Israel emerged.
Through Leah came Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah.
Through Rachel came Joseph and Benjamin.
Through their servants Bilhah and Zilpah came Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
These sons and their descendants would become foundational to Israel’s tribal identity.
But Scripture does something even more astonishing later.
When Boaz marries Ruth, the elders of Bethlehem bless her with these words:
“The LORD make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel…”
Rachel and Leah.
Together.
Not Rachel against Leah.
Not Leah defeating Rachel.
Together.
The women who spent years comparing themselves are remembered generations later as the women who “built the house of Israel.”
God wrote a bigger sentence over their lives than rivalry.
And that is where their story reaches into ours.
Maybe you were Rachel.
Loved in one area.
Empty in another.
People assumed you had everything because they could see what you possessed, but nobody could see what you cried about when the room became quiet.
Maybe you were Leah.
Always standing beside somebody who seemed easier to love.
Always wondering whether you were the consolation prize.
Always trying to earn affection.
Always doing one more thing in hopes somebody would finally look at you and say:
“You are enough.”
Maybe you have been both.
Envied and insecure.
Blessed and broken.
Loved and lonely.
Smiling and comparing.
Serving God while quietly asking why He gave somebody else the thing you begged Him for.
Rachel and Leah reveal something uncomfortable:
You can receive something precious and still be miserable when comparison becomes the lens through which you see it.
But the Gospel takes us deeper than “stop comparing yourself.”
Because comparison is not merely a bad habit.
At its deepest level, it can expose what our hearts believe will justify us.
What would have to happen before you finally believed you mattered?
Who would have to choose you?
What would you have to achieve?
What would God have to give you?
What would somebody have to say about you?
And what if the answer you are looking for cannot ultimately be supplied by another human being?
Leah wanted Jacob to love her.
Rachel wanted a child.
Both desires were understandable.
The danger came when created gifts carried the unbearable weight of becoming ultimate.
Only God can carry that weight.
And this is where Judah matters.
Because Leah’s story eventually enters the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Matthew begins his Gospel by identifying Jesus as the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
And within that genealogy stands Judah.
Generations of human scandal follow.
Judah and Tamar.
Rahab.
David and Bathsheba’s shattered story.
Exile.
Broken kings.
Broken families.
Broken promises made by broken people.
Then Jesus.
The genealogy of Christ does not read like humanity successfully cleaning itself up until it becomes worthy of God.
It reads like grace entering history again and again until God Himself comes to rescue sinners.
Jesus does not arrive because humanity finally became respectable.
Jesus arrives because humanity needs redemption.
At the cross, Christ does what Jacob never could.
He does not merely choose the more attractive sister.
He does not love according to fertility, beauty, social position, performance, usefulness, popularity, or comparison.
He gives Himself for sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
You do not have to produce your own Reuben so Jesus will love you.
You do not have to outperform your Rachel.
You do not have to defeat your Leah.
You do not have to earn the cross.
You could not.
That is why it is grace.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly uses χάρις, charis—grace, favor, gift.
And grace destroys the scoreboard.
At the foot of the cross, the question is no longer:
“Am I more worthy than her?”
“Am I more successful than him?”
“Did God give them more?”
“Why does everybody choose them?”
The question becomes:
“What do I have that I did not receive?”
And then:
“How could Christ love a sinner like me enough to bleed for me?”
This is where rivalry can finally die.
Not through better self-esteem alone.
Not through pretending rejection does not hurt.
Not through convincing yourself you are superior after all.
But by discovering an identity deeper than human preference:
In Christ, the believer is reconciled to God by grace.
Forgiven.
Adopted.
Redeemed.
Not because somebody finally picked you first.
Because Jesus gave Himself for you.
And perhaps that is why this story hurts so beautifully.
Rachel and Leah spent so much of their lives trying to win something from each other.
Yet God was writing Israel through both of them.
The sister you envy may not be your enemy.
The brother you compete against may not be your enemy.
The person whose blessing triggers your insecurity may be revealing a wound Jesus wants to confront.
So be honest.
Who is your Rachel?
Who is your Leah?
Whose life have you been watching so closely that you have stopped thanking God for your own?
What blessing cannot make you happy because somebody else possesses the blessing you really wanted?
What rejection are you still trying to reverse through achievement?
What are you still trying to prove?
And how long are you going to make another human being responsible for giving you an identity only Christ can secure?
Repentance begins with truth.
Maybe yours begins tonight.
Your honesty may become permission for somebody else to stop hiding.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this—not because you want to accuse them, but because you know they have spent years feeling second-best—send this to them.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to earn God’s favor.
But if this biblical teaching has helped you, sharing it is one practical way to help put Scripture in front of someone who may never have searched for it themselves.
“When will I finally be loved?”
Someone may be living Rachel’s desperation:
“Why has God given this to everybody except me?”
Let the Gospel reach them.
Because comparison rarely dies in one encounter.
There may be a night when the old wound returns.
When someone else gets engaged.
When somebody announces the pregnancy.
When another ministry grows.
When the promotion goes elsewhere.
When somebody receives the applause you wanted.
Come back and remember:
God is not writing your life by somebody else’s timeline.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Jesus, follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. We want this community to remain a place where Scripture is opened seriously, sin is not disguised, grace is not cheapened, wounded people are pointed toward Christ, and the Gospel remains the center.
Scripture does not permit us to turn financial support into a spiritual transaction.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be a genuine act of generosity and partnership.
Come to Christ.
Because merchandise cannot redeem you.
A ministry cannot redeem you.
Your accomplishments cannot redeem you.
Your spouse cannot redeem you.
Your children cannot redeem you.
Being chosen by people cannot redeem you.
Jesus can.
Turn from sin.
Trust in Christ.
Receive the grace you could never earn.
And stop asking the world to give you the verdict that was settled for the believer at the cross.
Rachel was loved and still suffered.
Leah was overlooked and still mattered profoundly in God’s unfolding covenant story.
Both women carried wounds.
Both women became part of Israel’s story.
And neither woman could see, in the middle of those painful nights, how far beyond their rivalry God’s purposes would reach.
Centuries later, people would speak their names together:
“Rachel and Leah, which two did build the house of Israel.”
Together.
Imagine that.
After all the comparison.
After all the tears.
After all the pregnancies.
After all the bargaining.
After all the “she has what I want.”
God’s story became larger than their rivalry.
And from Leah’s Judah would eventually come the King before whom every human competition becomes embarrassingly small.
Jesus Christ.
The Lion of Judah.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One who takes stories scarred by sin, jealousy, rejection, manipulation, grief, and human failure and writes redemption where we expected only ruins.
So perhaps the question is no longer whether you were Rachel or Leah.
Perhaps the question is whether you are finally willing to give Jesus the wound that has kept you competing.
Because perhaps the most heartbreaking thing about Rachel and Leah was not that they lacked blessings.
It was how often pain convinced them that the other woman’s blessing determined their worth.
Do not spend another year fighting somebody Jesus never commanded you to defeat.
Bring the wound to Him.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the rejection.
Bring the desperate need to be chosen.
Bring the secret question you are embarrassed even to admit.
Christ already knows.
And grace is still calling your name.
You may have spent half your life begging to be somebody’s first choice, only to discover that the deepest healing begins when Jesus becomes yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DIVORCE, ADULTERY, AND GRACE: THE CONVERSATION CHRISTIANS OFTEN OVERSIMPLIFY
paragraphs:
DIVORCE, ADULTERY, AND GRACE: THE CONVERSATION CHRISTIANS OFTEN OVERSIMPLIFY
What if the person sitting quietly in church carrying the label “divorced” has a story nobody bothered to hear—and what if the person who shattered a marriage is not beyond the reach of the blood of Jesus?
There are some sins Christians know how to talk about.
And then there are the ones that make the room uncomfortable.
Divorce.
Adultery.
Remarriage.
Betrayal.
Abandonment.
The husband who walked away.
The wife who was unfaithful.
The spouse who begged the other person to stay.
The marriage that looked beautiful in Facebook photographs while quietly dying behind a locked bedroom door.
The Christian who made terrible choices, repented, and still wonders whether the church will ever see anything except the worst chapter of their life.

And somewhere between “God hates divorce,” “just forgive them,” “once an adulterer, always an adulterer,” and “God just wants you happy,” wounded human beings have sometimes been crushed beneath sentences that sounded biblical because they were short enough to fit on a graphic.
But Scripture is not careless with marriage.
And neither is Jesus.
Marriage matters enormously to God. So does covenant faithfulness. So does sexual purity. So does repentance.
But people matter to Him too.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because biblical truth refuses to flatter the adulterer.
And biblical grace refuses to throw away the repentant adulterer.
Biblical truth refuses to pretend divorce is insignificant.
And biblical compassion refuses to assume that every divorced person is equally responsible for the destruction of a marriage.
Jesus will not let us turn sin into something harmless.
But He will not let us turn sinners into something hopeless either.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that distinction before reading another sentence.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending of a story surrendered to Jesus Christ.
When religious leaders questioned Jesus about divorce, they asked Him whether a man could divorce his wife for various reasons.
Jesus did something remarkable.
He took them backward.
Past their arguments.
Past their loopholes.
Past their attempts to determine the minimum requirement.
Back to creation.
“Have ye not read,” Jesus asked, before pointing them to the creation of male and female and declaring that husband and wife become “one flesh” (Matthew 19:4–5).
Then comes the sentence Christians rightly take seriously:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6).
The Greek behind “joined together” is συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen, from a verb carrying the idea of joining or yoking together.
Jesus' vision of marriage was not disposable companionship.
It was covenantal union.
One flesh.
Faithfulness.
A joining intended to endure.

That matters because modern culture can treat marriage like an agreement that survives only while both people remain satisfied. Jesus takes us somewhere deeper. Marriage is not merely two consumers continuing a relationship while the relationship meets their expectations.
Something sacred has happened.
But the conversation does not end there.
The Pharisees immediately brought Moses into the argument: Why, then, did Moses permit a certificate of divorce?
Jesus answered:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8).
Do not rush past those words.
ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως — ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs.
“But from the beginning it has not been so.”
Jesus distinguishes God's creation ideal from accommodations made in a world damaged by human hardness.
That single distinction should make us more careful than many conversations about divorce have been.
Divorce exists in Scripture not because broken covenant is beautiful, but because sin is devastating.
Hardness exists.
Betrayal exists.
Sexual immorality exists.
Abandonment exists.
And sometimes Christians speak about divorce as though divorce itself suddenly appeared in an otherwise perfectly healthy marriage, without asking what happened before the papers were signed.
A certificate can be the visible ending of a marriage whose devastation began much earlier.
That does not make every divorce righteous.
It means wise Christians investigate rather than merely label.

Jesus continues in Matthew 19:9 with one of the most debated sentences in Christian discussions of divorce and remarriage. The crucial Greek word is πορνεία — porneia, a broad sexual-immorality term. Jesus does not therefore give us permission to treat marital faithfulness casually. Quite the opposite. He confronts the casual divorce culture around Him while recognizing sexual immorality as profoundly destructive to covenant.
That means adultery is serious.
Not “a mistake.”
Not “I followed my heart.”
Not “we fell in love.”
Not “God knows my intentions.”
Adultery destroys trust, wounds spouses, destabilizes families, and violates the covenant faithfulness marriage is supposed to embody.
Scripture does not romanticize betrayal.
And if you are currently maintaining an adulterous relationship while calling it God's blessing, grace is not permission to continue.
Repentance means turning.
Jesus did not die so we could rename darkness.
He died to rescue us from it.
But there is another error Christians can make.
We can become so determined to condemn adultery that we forget what Christianity actually says about adulterers who repent.
And that is where the Gospel becomes scandalous.
Not scandalous because God suddenly decides sin does not matter.
Scandalous because the blood of Christ is powerful enough to cleanse people whose sin mattered terribly.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She was not brought in for counseling.
She was brought in publicly.
Her humiliation became somebody else's theological demonstration.
“Caught in adultery.”
Imagine having your entire identity compressed into that phrase.
Not daughter.
Not neighbor.
Not image-bearer.
Adulteress.
Perhaps you understand that feeling.
Divorced.
Cheater.
Failure.
Homewrecker.
Abandoned.
Damaged.
Unwanted.
The religious crowd was ready to make her worst moment her final definition.
Jesus would not participate.
He confronted the accusers, and eventually they left.
Then He addressed the woman.
And notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say adultery was acceptable.
He also did not say she was beyond redemption.
His words held mercy and holiness together:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more” (John 8:11).
There is the Gospel tension many of us desperately need to recover.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
Grace.
“Sin no more.”
Truth.
Jesus neither crushed her with condemnation nor comforted her into continuing rebellion.
He rescued her from both.
Some churches have truth without tenderness.
Some have tenderness without truth.
Jesus has both perfectly.
And when either one disappears, wounded people receive a distorted picture of Christ.
This is why Christians must be cautious with another sentence often repeated around divorce: “God hates divorce.”

The underlying truth that God opposes covenant treachery should never be weakened. But Malachi 2:16 itself contains a genuine Hebrew translation difficulty, and responsible Christians should acknowledge it rather than pretending there is none.
The Hebrew includes:
כִּי־שָׂנֵא שַׁלַּח — kî-śānēʾ šallaḥ

The traditional English rendering became familiar as “I hate divorce.” Yet the Hebrew form translated “hates” can naturally be read in the third person, which helps explain why several contemporary translations render the passage along the lines of the man who hates and divorces his wife acting violently or faithlessly.
That linguistic discussion should not become an excuse for treating divorce casually.
Read the surrounding passage.
Malachi's burden is covenant treachery.
The woman being discarded is called “the wife of thy covenant” (Malachi 2:14).
God is confronting faithlessness.
That is the point we dare not lose.
And ironically, using Malachi as a weapon against every divorced person can obscure the very injustice Malachi is confronting.
Imagine a faithful spouse betrayed repeatedly and then abandoned.
Imagine that person walking into church carrying grief, humiliation, financial fear, confused children, sleepless nights, and the unbearable question, “Was I not enough?”
Then somebody who knows almost nothing about the circumstances casually says:
“God hates divorce.”
Perhaps what that broken person needed was not a slogan.
Perhaps they needed somebody to sit beside them and say:
“Tell me what happened.”
The church should defend marriage fiercely.
But defending marriage and defending the appearance of marriage are not always identical.
We must never use Scripture to pressure somebody to pretend evil is good.
Neither should Scripture be twisted into an automatic command for divorce whenever marriage becomes difficult.
There is an enormous difference between inconvenience and covenant devastation.
Marriage requires forgiveness because every marriage contains two sinners.
People become selfish.
People speak cruelly.
People disappoint one another.
People need repentance, patience, sanctification, counseling, accountability, prayer, humility, and sometimes years of rebuilding.
Christian marriage cannot survive on the philosophy, “You disappointed me, therefore God wants me to leave.”
But neither should Christians look at severe betrayal, abandonment, manipulation, or danger and offer nothing except “try harder.”
Paul adds another dimension in 1 Corinthians 7.
He strongly urges married believers toward reconciliation and faithfulness. Yet when discussing a believer married to an unbelieving spouse who chooses to leave, Paul writes:
χωριζέσθω — chōrizesthō
“Let [the unbelieving spouse] separate.”
He then says the brother or sister is “not under bondage” in such circumstances (1 Corinthians 7:15).
Christians disagree about some implications of these passages, particularly the precise conditions under which remarriage is permissible. Faithful interpreters have reached different conclusions.
We should be humble enough to say that.
But disagreement over difficult applications does not require confusion about the center.
God honors marriage.
God condemns adultery.
God opposes covenant treachery.
God calls sinners to repentance.
God commands forgiveness.
Reconciliation is beautiful where genuine repentance and restoration make reconciliation possible.
And grace is not reserved for people whose histories are tidy.
Maybe now this article has stopped being theological for you.
Maybe there is a name in your mind.
Maybe it is yours.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe they cheated.
Maybe you left.
Maybe they left.
Maybe you signed papers you never imagined signing when you stood before an altar.
Maybe everybody thinks you destroyed the marriage, while almost nobody knows what was happening behind the door.
Maybe you were the one who actually did destroy it.
And perhaps that is why you almost stopped reading.
Stay.
Because Christianity has something astonishing to say to guilty people.
Not innocent people pretending to be guilty.
Guilty people.
People who actually sinned.
David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged circumstances that resulted in Uriah's death.
Scripture does not sanitize it.
When Nathan confronted David, he did not offer an excuse.
“I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13).
And Psalm 51 lets us hear what repentance sounds like when excuses finally die:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים — lēv ṭāhôr berā-lî ʾĕlōhîm
“Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).
David did not ask God to improve his public image.
He asked for a clean heart.
That is repentance.
And if you committed adultery, your greatest need is not to convince everybody that there were complicated circumstances.
Your greatest need is Jesus.
Confess what was yours.
Stop blaming your spouse for the sin you chose.
End what must be ended.
Tell the truth.
Accept consequences.
Seek accountability.
Make restitution where possible.
Do not demand instant trust from people you wounded.
Do not weaponize forgiveness by telling your spouse, “If you were a real Christian, you would get over it.”
Repentance does not dictate the timetable of the wounded.
Repentance bows.
And then—listen carefully—receive grace.
Because there comes a moment when continually refusing Christ's forgiveness can masquerade as humility.
If you have genuinely repented and entrusted yourself to Christ, you do not honor Jesus by declaring that your sin is more powerful than His cross.
Paul wrote:
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Washed.
That word should make somebody cry.
Because some stains feel permanent.
Some memories return at 2:00 in the morning.
Some consequences remain even after forgiveness.
Grace does not always erase earthly consequences.
It does something greater.
It changes who owns your future.
This is why Romans 8:1 sounds almost impossible to the ashamed:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα — ouden ara nyn katakrima.
No condemnation.
Now.
Not because adultery became harmless.
Not because betrayal became imaginary.
Not because divorce stopped hurting.
Because Jesus Christ bore judgment for sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin was no big deal.”

The Gospel says your sin was so serious that the Son of God went to a cross—and His sacrifice was so sufficient that the repentant sinner does not have to remain chained to the identity of the condemned.
That is scandalous grace.
Perhaps you are on the other side.
You were faithful.
They weren't.
And everybody keeps talking to you about forgiveness as though forgiveness means pretending nothing happened.
It doesn't.
Christian forgiveness relinquishes personal vengeance to God. It does not require calling evil good.
Trust can be shattered in minutes and rebuilt over years.
Forgiveness and trust are related, but they are not identical.
Reconciliation requires more than one person's willingness when the other remains committed to deception or rebellion.
And you are allowed to grieve.
Jesus does not stand over your broken heart shouting, “Move on.”
He knows betrayal.
He knows rejection.
He knows what it is to be wounded by people He loved.
Bring Him your anger before it becomes bitterness.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the humiliation.
Bring Him the nights when you cannot understand how somebody who promised forever could become a stranger.
Bring Him even the parts you are embarrassed to pray.
Jesus is not frightened by an honest prayer.
Maybe the miracle you want is restoration of your marriage.
Pray for it.
Fight for what can biblically and safely be restored.
Seek wise pastoral care and qualified professional help where appropriate.
But do not make the restoration of another human relationship your savior.
Christ must remain Christ.
Because even a restored marriage cannot do what only Jesus can do.
And even a marriage that never returns can leave behind a person whom Jesus is still rebuilding.
That is what grace means.
Grace is not God pretending the wreckage never happened.
Grace is God entering the wreckage.
The cross itself proves it.
Jesus was betrayed.
Jesus was stripped.
Jesus was publicly humiliated.
Jesus was wounded.
Jesus was condemned.
Jesus died.
Then resurrection turned what looked like the ending into the doorway of redemption.
That does not mean every earthly relationship gets resurrected exactly as it was.
It means no surrendered life has to remain buried beneath its worst day.
Maybe your marriage survived adultery.
Tell somebody.
Some couple reading this believes there is no road home.
Your testimony might become the flashlight they desperately need.
Maybe your marriage did not survive.
Tell the truth about what Jesus did in you afterward.
Maybe you were the guilty one and Christ broke you, humbled you, cleansed you, and transformed you.
Do not glorify the sin.
Glorify the Savior who refused to leave you inside it.
And maybe you are currently standing dangerously close to adultery.
The messages have become personal.
The conversations are being deleted.
You tell yourself nothing physical has happened.
You look forward to hearing from that person more than your spouse.
You are feeding privately what you would be ashamed to reveal publicly.
Stop.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Bring it into the light.
Delete what needs deleting.
End what needs ending.
Tell somebody spiritually mature enough to hold you accountable.
Run toward Jesus before fantasy becomes devastation.
Sin always sends the invoice later.
Your spouse is worth protecting.
Your children are worth protecting.
Your conscience is worth protecting.
And Christ is infinitely more satisfying than stolen affection.
Let those words become a small public declaration that secrecy will not own you anymore.
There are moments when the strongest prayer a wounded Christian can offer is allowing another believer to know that prayer is needed.
Someone scrolling beneath you may need to discover that Christians are not a museum of people with flawless marriages.
We are a family of sinners who desperately need a flawless Savior.
Not because every sentence will answer every complicated marital situation, but because pain has a way of making us forget what we knew when we were thinking clearly.
Come back when shame whispers.
Come back when anger rises.
Come back when somebody you love calls at midnight and says, “My marriage is falling apart.”
Send this to that person who has silently carried the label “divorced” like a scarlet letter.
And when you share this, do not share it to win an argument.
Share it to open a door.
There are people who will never walk into a church this Sunday who may read something about Jesus because you were willing to place it in front of them.

If Gospel Warrior helps you keep Christ in front of your eyes in a world constantly pulling your attention elsewhere, follow us and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the person who does not yet believe—to follow too.

We want this community to be somewhere people encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ without pretending brokenness does not exist.
We will never tell you that purchasing something earns God's blessing.
But generosity can be an act of worship when it flows freely from love for God and love for people.
Come to Christ.
A church cannot erase guilt.
A new relationship cannot heal the deepest wound.
A motivational quote cannot resurrect a dead heart.
Jesus can save.
Jesus can forgive.
Jesus can transform.
Jesus can teach the betrayed person how to live without becoming consumed by bitterness.
Jesus can take the adulterer who genuinely repents and teach them faithfulness.
Jesus can humble the self-righteous Christian who knows everybody else's marriage story but has never examined their own heart.
Jesus can restore what human beings thought was impossible to restore.
And where particular earthly consequences cannot be undone, Jesus can still redeem the person walking through them.
That is why the Christian conversation about divorce can never merely be:
“Who broke the rule?”
It must eventually become:
“Where is Christ in the wreckage?”
He is calling the sinner to repentance.
He is calling the wounded toward healing.
He is calling the bitter toward forgiveness.
He is calling the self-righteous toward humility.
He is calling the church toward truth wrapped in compassion.
He is calling all of us away from the illusion that respectable people need less grace than scandalous ones.
At the foot of the cross, the betrayed and the betrayer both discover something unsettling.
Neither one is the Savior.
Jesus is.
So protect marriage.
Honor covenant.
Flee adultery.
Tell the truth about sin.
Take repentance seriously.
Do not weaponize Scripture against wounded people.
Do not weaponize grace to excuse rebellion.
Do not call darkness light.
And never tell a repentant sinner whom Christ has cleansed that their darkest chapter has become their permanent name.
The nails in Jesus' hands say otherwise.
The empty tomb says otherwise.
The Gospel says otherwise.
Maybe your story contains a wedding photograph you can hardly look at anymore.
Maybe it contains court papers.
Maybe screenshots.
Maybe confessions.
Maybe years of counseling.
Maybe reconciliation.
Maybe consequences that cannot be reversed.
Maybe a ring that came off.
Maybe a marriage that survived.
Maybe shame nobody knows about.
Whatever brought you here, bring the truth into the presence of Jesus.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
The truth.
Because Jesus does some of His most beautiful rewriting in chapters we were certain had ruined the entire book.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but once the pen is surrendered to Christ, your scandal does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE WHEN WE’RE AFRAID… BUT RARELY UNDERSTAND
paragraphs: “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE WHEN WE’RE AFRAID… BUT RARELY UNDERSTAND

Romans 8:31 does not promise that nobody will fight you. It promises something far more terrifying to your enemies, more comforting to the wounded, and more glorious than an easy life: if you belong to Jesus Christ, nothing that comes against you can overturn what God has determined to accomplish for you in Christ.
You have probably heard the verse when somebody was trying to encourage you.
Maybe you were afraid.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe everything you worked for was collapsing.
Maybe you were sitting alone after midnight, staring at a ceiling while your mind rehearsed every possible way your life could fall apart.
And somewhere in the middle of the fear, someone said:
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
It sounds powerful.
Almost invincible.
But there is a problem.
People can be against you.
Very much against you.
They can reject you.
Lie about you.
Abandon you.
Misunderstand you.
Mock your faith.
Break promises.
Close doors.
Damage your reputation.
Take advantage of your kindness.
And sometimes the person fighting against your peace is the person staring back at you in the mirror.
So what did Paul mean?
Was Romans 8:31 merely religious motivation?
Was he saying Christians become untouchable?
Was he promising that believers will always win the court case, get the promotion, defeat the sickness, escape suffering, silence their critics, and eventually watch every enemy regret opposing them?
No.
And somehow, the real meaning is even better.
Paul writes in Romans 8:31:
Ti oun eroumen pros tauta? Ei ho Theos hyper hēmōn, tis kath’ hēmōn?
A faithful rendering is:
“What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?”
Notice the question Paul does not ask.
He does not ask, “Who will ever oppose us?”
He asks, in effect, what opposition can ultimately prevail when God Himself is for His people?
That difference changes everything.
The Greek expression ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν — hyper hēmōn means “for us,” “on our behalf,” or “in our interest.”
And Paul does not leave “God is for us” floating in the air as a motivational slogan.
He proves it.
The very next verse says:
“ὅς γε τοῦ ἰδίου υἱοῦ οὐκ ἐφείσατο…”
“He who did not spare His own Son…”
There is the foundation.
Not your bank account.
Not your popularity.
Not your circumstances.
Not whether everybody likes you.
Not whether your plans succeeded this year.
Not whether the door opened.
Not whether your body feels strong.
Not whether your family finally understands you.
Paul points to a cross.
God being “for us” does not mean God gives us everything our frightened hearts demand.
It means God has already given the greatest gift He could give:
His Son.
And suddenly Romans 8:31 becomes much deeper than the inspirational quote printed on a coffee mug.
Because some of us have secretly interpreted “God is for me” to mean:
“God will make my life go the way I want.”
Paul means something infinitely greater:
God has acted decisively for sinners through Jesus Christ, and no created power can finally overthrow His saving purpose for those who are in Christ.
That matters because Romans 8 begins in a courtroom.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Think about that.
The chapter that eventually asks, “Who can be against us?” begins by dealing with the greatest thing that was against us.
Our guilt.
Our sin.
Our condemnation.
Before you worry about the person who betrayed you, there was a deeper problem.
Before the diagnosis.
Before the divorce papers.
Before the rejection.
Before the financial disaster.
Before the nights when anxiety would not let you sleep.
Humanity’s deepest problem was never merely that painful circumstances were against us.
Sin was against us.
The righteous judgment of God against sin was real.
And we could not rescue ourselves.
We did not need better self-esteem.
We needed reconciliation.
We did not merely need encouragement.
We needed redemption.
We did not merely need God to improve our circumstances.
We needed God to save us.
And this is where the scandal becomes grace.
God did not look at guilty sinners and pretend sin did not matter.
He did something unimaginably costly.
Romans 8:3 says God sent “His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin” and condemned sin in the flesh.
Jesus Christ stepped into our world.
The sinless One came for sinners.
The innocent One was rejected.
The righteous One suffered.
The beloved Son went to the cross.
Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine and needed inspiration.
He died because sin is devastatingly serious—and because the love of God is astonishingly deep.
At Calvary, grace was not God shrugging His shoulders at evil.
Grace was costly.
Christ bore what sinners could never repair by religious performance.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now the person trusting in Christ can hear Romans 8:31 differently.
“If God is for us…”
Not because we were impressive enough.
Not because we prayed perfectly.
Not because we never fell again.
Not because we finally became respectable enough for God to tolerate.
God is for His people because their hope rests in Christ.
Somebody needs to hear that slowly.
Because you may have spent years believing God loves the cleaned-up version of you.
The version who remembers to pray.
The version who never loses patience.
The version who does not struggle with temptation.
The version who does not wake up discouraged.
The version who has answers.
The version who smiles at church.
But you know the other version too.
The version nobody sees.
The thoughts you would never put on Facebook.
The private shame.
The recurring temptation.
The memory you wish you could erase.
The prayer you stopped praying because disappointment exhausted you.
The thing you promised God you would never do again.
And then you did it again.
You may have wondered:
“How could God possibly still want me?”
Romans 8 does not answer by telling you to stare harder at yourself.
It turns your eyes toward Christ.
Listen to Paul’s next question:
“Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?”
Then:
“It is God who justifies.”
And then:
“Who is to condemn?”
Paul answers by pointing directly to Jesus Christ—the One who died, was raised, is at the right hand of God, and intercedes for His people.
Do you see what Paul is doing?
He keeps asking courtroom questions.
Who can successfully prosecute those whom God justifies?
Who can deliver a final condemning verdict against the person whose hope is in the crucified and risen Christ?
Satan may accuse.
People may accuse.
Your memories may accuse.
Your own conscience may remind you of sins you genuinely committed.
Christianity does not require pretending those sins never happened.
The Gospel announces something better:
Jesus died for sinners.
Repentance does not mean calling darkness light.
It means bringing darkness into the light and running toward the mercy of Christ.
Grace is not permission to keep loving sin.
Grace is the undeserved mercy that receives the repentant sinner and begins transforming the person who could never transform himself.
This is why “God is for us” cannot biblically mean “nothing painful will happen.”
Look at what Paul says only a few sentences later.
He speaks about tribulation.
Distress.
Persecution.
Famine.
Nakedness.
Danger.
Sword.
Those words destroy the prosperity-gospel interpretation of Romans 8:31.
Paul does not say:
“If God is for you, there will be no tribulation.”
He essentially says:
Tribulation may come—and it still cannot separate you from Christ.
Distress may come—and it still cannot separate you from Christ.
Persecution may come—and it still cannot separate you from Christ.
Loss may come.
Tears may come.
Funerals may come.
Opposition may come.
And Christians are not promised exemption from every earthly tragedy.
Jesus Himself told His disciples that they would face trouble.
The apostles suffered.
Paul suffered.
Faithful believers throughout history have suffered.
So Romans 8:31 is not a divine promise that every battle ends the way you wanted.
It is the announcement that no battle can finally overthrow the saving purpose of God in Christ.
That is much stronger.
Because a faith built on “God will prevent anything painful from happening to me” collapses the moment pain arrives.
But a faith anchored in the crucified and risen Jesus can whisper through tears:
“This hurts…
but Christ has not abandoned me.”
That is Romans 8 faith.
It is possible for something to hurt you without ultimately defeating God’s purpose for you.
It is possible for someone to reject you without changing your standing in Christ.
It is possible to lose something precious without losing Jesus.
It is possible to walk through a season you never would have chosen and discover that the presence of God is not measured by the absence of suffering.
And there is another detail we often overlook.
Paul asks:
“What then shall we say to these things?”
What things?
Look backward.
Romans 8 has already spoken about suffering.
It says creation groans.
Believers groan.
We wait.
We hope.
We experience weakness.
Sometimes we do not even know what we ought to pray.
That may be one of the most human sentences in the Bible.
There are moments when pain becomes too complicated for polished prayers.
You sit there.
You try to speak.
Nothing comes.
Maybe only tears.
Maybe only:
“Jesus…”
And Romans 8 says the Spirit helps us in our weakness.
God’s faithfulness toward His children does not depend upon their ability to manufacture impressive spiritual emotions.
Then comes Romans 8:28, another verse frequently removed from its context:
“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to His purpose.”
Paul is not saying all things are good.
Betrayal is not good.
Abuse is not good.
Death is an enemy.
Sin is not secretly holy because God can redeem broken situations.
Evil remains evil.
But evil does not become sovereign.
That belongs to God.
The astonishing Christian hope is that God is so sovereign, wise, and faithful that even what He hates and what wounds us cannot finally frustrate His redemptive purpose.
And what is the “good” toward which Romans 8 is moving?
The next verse tells us.
Those God foreknew He also predestined “to be conformed to the image of His Son.”
There it is.
Sometimes we define “good” as comfortable.
God is making His people like Jesus.
We define “good” as getting what we wanted.
God is preparing a redeemed people for glory.
We define “God is for me” as God supporting every personal ambition.
Scripture defines God’s saving purpose around Christ.
That means there may be moments when God’s faithfulness does not look like the answer you requested.
Sometimes the door stays closed.
Sometimes the relationship ends.
Sometimes healing does not come in the timing we desperately wanted.
Sometimes obedience costs something.
Sometimes following Jesus means losing the approval of people whose approval once controlled you.
But if you are in Christ, your story is not ultimately being written by rejection.
Or shame.
Or failure.
Or suffering.
Or your worst chapter.
Jesus Christ has entered the story.
And Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
That is why Romans 8 eventually explodes into one of the greatest declarations of Christian assurance ever written:
“For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers…”
Paul keeps going.
Height.
Depth.
Anything else in all creation.
None of it “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Read those last words again.
In Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is the center.
Romans 8:31 is not ultimately a celebration of how unstoppable you are.
It is a celebration of how sufficient Christ is.
Christian confidence is not:
“Nobody can touch me.”
It is:
“Nothing can separate me from Jesus.”
Not:
“I will never lose.”
But:
“Christ has already conquered sin and death, and my ultimate hope is secured in Him.”
Not:
“My enemies will eventually watch me become successful.”
But:
“My identity is no longer determined by the verdict of my enemies.”
Maybe that is the freedom you actually needed.
Because some of us have been living as defendants in a courtroom God already dismissed.
Still trying to prove ourselves.
Still arguing with voices from ten years ago.
Still checking whether the people who rejected us finally recognize our worth.
Still hoping success will make somebody regret how they treated us.
Still fantasizing about the day we can say:
“Look at me now.”
But what if grace is calling you somewhere better?
What if healing is not finally making them regret losing you?
What if healing is reaching the point where Jesus is enough even if they never apologize?
What if freedom is no longer needing your enemies to lose before you can believe God loves you?
That changes the verse.
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
People can be against you.
But they cannot become God.
Your past can testify against you.
But your past cannot crucify Jesus twice and reverse His finished work.
Suffering can shake you.
But suffering cannot dethrone Christ.
Death itself can take a believer’s earthly breath.
But death cannot separate the believer from the love of God in Christ.
That is the audacity of Romans 8.
The Christian is not promised an opponent-free life.
The Christian is promised a Christ-secured hope.
And maybe you are reading this while fighting something nobody knows about.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
You have learned how to answer, “I’m okay.”
You know how to post the photograph.
You know how to laugh at the right moment.
You know how to worship while your heart feels exhausted.
But somewhere beneath all of it is a question you have been afraid to ask:
“God… are You still for me?”
If you belong to Jesus, do not measure the answer by today’s circumstances.
Look toward Calvary.
“He who did not spare His own Son…”
The cross is not evidence that Christians never suffer.
The cross itself proves otherwise.
The cross is evidence that God’s saving love goes deeper than suffering.
And the empty tomb announces that suffering and death do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Perhaps you have never actually surrendered to Him.
You know verses.
You know Christian language.
Maybe you even share Christian posts.
But Christianity is not ultimately sharing religious content.
You can own a Bible and never surrender.
You can attend church while secretly building your identity around everything except Christ.
Romans 8:31 is not permission to assume God endorses us regardless of our relationship to His Son.
The magnificent assurance of Romans 8 belongs within the Gospel reality Paul repeatedly describes as being “in Christ.”
So do not merely admire the promise.
Come to the Savior at the center of it.
Repent.
Stop defending the sin Jesus died to save you from.
Bring Him the secret.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The sexual sin.
The resentment.
The double life.
The religious performance.
The thing you keep hiding because you are terrified of what happens when the light reaches it.
Bring it to Jesus.
There is grace for sinners.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a new life that does not begin with pretending you were never broken but with confessing that you desperately need a Savior.
Not because a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing a confession into the light begins with refusing to hide behind another polished Christian response.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer walking through a battle.
Let the body of Christ behave like the body of Christ.
Pray for one another.
Carry one another.
Remind one another where hope actually lives.
And then think of one person who needs Romans 8 tonight.
Not the person who will merely “like” it.
The person whose faith is hanging by a thread.
The person going through a divorce.
The father terrified about his family.
The mother crying where her children cannot see her.
The believer ashamed of falling again.
The friend who thinks suffering means God abandoned them.
The skeptic who believes Christianity is nothing more than motivational religion.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not. Salvation cannot be purchased, and the glory of God cannot be reduced to an engagement metric.

If this ministry is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent more deeply, heal biblically, and stand stronger in the Gospel, one practical way you can help us glorify God together is by helping that truth travel farther than it could travel without you.
Your share may enter a home we could never enter.
Your tag may reach someone we could never identify.
Your comment may encourage someone who thought they were struggling alone.
Your support can help Gospel-centered resources continue reaching believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, wounded Christians, and even unbelievers who desperately need to hear about Jesus.
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus cannot be bought.

But it can be a practical way of supporting a ministry that is committed to spreading Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, conviction, discipleship, healing, repentance, and the message of redemption through Jesus Christ.
And there is something bigger than merchandise behind the invitation.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Invite the person who thinks Jesus could never forgive what they have done.
Invite even the unbeliever who has questions nobody has taken seriously.
Because eventually you may have a day when Romans 8:31 feels harder to believe than it does right now.
On that day, come back.
Read the context again.
Remember:
Paul never promised that nobody would stand against you.
He promised something better.
They cannot overturn the verdict of the God who justifies.
They cannot separate you from the Christ who died and rose.
They cannot transform suffering into sovereign power over your eternity.
They cannot erase the cross.
They cannot seal the tomb again.
They cannot dethrone Jesus.
And if Christ has you, even death itself cannot carry you somewhere His love cannot reach.
Leave looking at Jesus.
Because the greatest news in Romans 8 is not that you finally became strong enough to defeat everything against you.
The greatest news is that when you had no hope of saving yourself, God gave His Son.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ intercedes.
Christ holds His people.
And Christ will have the final word.
So when tomorrow comes against you…
when fear comes against you…
when accusation comes against you…
when temptation comes against you…
when disappointment comes against you…
when grief comes against you…
when your own trembling heart begins whispering that perhaps God has forgotten your name…
do not answer by pointing to how strong you are.
Point to the cross.
Point to the empty tomb.
Point to Jesus.
And whisper the truth the enemy desperately wants suffering to make you forget:
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
Not because nobody will try.
But because nobody can finally defeat the saving purpose of the God who gave His Son for His people.
Your darkest chapter may still bear the scars of what happened—but scars are not proof that Jesus abandoned the story; sometimes they are the very place where grace leaves its signature.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SPIRITUAL CHEATING: WANTING GOD’S BLESSINGS WHILE GIVING YOUR HEART TO ANOTHER MASTER
paragraphs: SPIRITUAL CHEATING: WANTING GOD’S BLESSINGS WHILE GIVING YOUR HEART TO ANOTHER MASTER

You can sing to Jesus with your mouth, ask Him to bless your future, and still quietly give your deepest loyalty to something else. And perhaps the most frightening part is how long a divided heart can look religious before it finally gets exposed.
There is a kind of betrayal nobody around you may ever see.
No secret hotel room.
No suspicious messages.
No photograph that can expose you.
No human lover waiting somewhere in the darkness.
You can be sitting in church when it happens.
Bible open.
Hands raised.
Worship music playing.
You can whisper, “Jesus, I love You,” and genuinely feel something while saying it.
And yet another master may already have your heart.
Money.
Approval.
Sex.
Success.
Comfort.
A relationship.
Status.
Pornography.
Career.
Control.
Politics.
Possessions.
Your appearance.
Your reputation.
Your plans.
Even ministry.
Anything can become spiritually dangerous when something created begins occupying the place in your heart that belongs to the Creator.
And that is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because many of us do not actually want to abandon God.
We want something far more subtle.
We want God and the idol.
We want Jesus to save us while another master satisfies us.
We want God to protect our families while ambition owns our attention.
We want God to heal our marriages while lust keeps a hidden room in our minds.
We want God to bless our finances while money determines our worth.
We want God to give us peace while control remains our functional savior.
We want Christ when eternity is discussed, but something else when Monday morning arrives.
We want His promises.
His protection.
His forgiveness.
His heaven.
His blessings.
But sometimes, if the truth were dragged into the light, we would discover that we have been asking Jesus to finance a life in which He is not actually Lord.
And Scripture has a devastating name for this.
Adultery.
James writes:
Moichalides, ouk oidate hoti hē philia tou kosmou echthra tou theou estin?
A close rendering is:
“Adulteresses, do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?”
James 4:4.
That first Greek word is brutal.
μοιχαλίδες — moichalides.
Adulteresses.

James is using the language of covenant betrayal. His point is not that every ordinary enjoyment of creation makes someone an enemy of God. Scripture itself teaches that God gives good gifts. The issue is a heart that embraces the rebellious value system of the world in opposition to its Creator.
This language did not appear from nowhere.
Throughout the Old Testament, God described His covenant people’s idolatry with the imagery of marital unfaithfulness. They belonged to Him, yet repeatedly chased other gods.
So when James reaches for the language of adultery, he is exposing something we desperately prefer to rename.
We call it “priorities.”
God calls us back to fidelity.
We call it “just trying to get ahead.”
Jesus asks who our master is.
We call it “something I need.”
God asks why we cannot surrender it.
We call it “just one weakness.”
The Holy Spirit keeps touching the locked door.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Because somewhere beneath your public Christianity, there may be a name you already know.
Something you desperately want God to bless...
but desperately do not want Him to touch.
Read that again.
Because your idol is not always the thing you openly worship.
Sometimes your idol is simply the thing you cannot imagine surrendering if Jesus asked for it.
Jesus said something that leaves remarkably little room for negotiation:
“Οὐδεὶς δύναται δυσὶ κυρίοις δουλεύειν.”
Oudeis dynatai dysi kyriois douleuein.
“No one is able to serve two masters.”
Then He makes the confrontation unmistakable:
“You cannot serve God and mammon.”
Matthew 6:24.
The Greek word translated “serve” is δουλεύειν — douleuein, from language associated with serving as a slave.
Jesus is not describing a casual hobby.
He is talking about mastery.
Ownership.
Allegiance.
The question is therefore deeper than:
“Do you believe in God?”
The demons believe that God exists.
The harder question is:
What actually masters you?
What controls your decisions?
What determines whether you feel valuable?
What are you terrified of losing?
Where does your mind run when nobody is watching?
Whose approval can make your day?
Whose rejection can destroy it?
What compromise are you willing to defend because obedience would cost too much?
What do you keep telling God He cannot have?
That is where this article stops being about “people out there.”
Now it is about us.
Because spiritual cheating rarely begins with someone consciously saying, “I reject Jesus.”
It often begins with a whisper.
“I need this too.”
A little admiration.
A little secret pleasure.
A little more money.
A little more attention.
A little compromise.
A little bitterness we refuse to release.
A little relationship we know is pulling us away from Christ.
A little habit we promise to quit later.
A little success so people will finally know our name.
Then slowly, almost invisibly, the gift becomes the goal.
The desire becomes the demand.
The preference becomes the master.
And eventually we are praying to God for enough blessing to keep feeding the very thing competing with Him.
That is the scandal.
A person can want the gifts of God without wanting the government of God.
We can ask Him for provision while worshiping wealth.
Ask Him for a spouse while worshiping romance.
Ask Him for influence while worshiping recognition.
Ask Him for ministry growth while worshiping numbers.
Ask Him for healing while worshiping comfort.
Ask Him for children while turning those children into the center of our identity.
Ask Him for success while secretly needing success to tell us we matter.
Even a blessing can become an idol when we love the blessing more than the One who gave it.
Jesus had already located the battlefield.
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Matthew 6:21.
The Greek word for heart is καρδία — kardia.
In biblical thought, the heart is far more than sentimental emotion. It concerns the inner person—the center from which desires, intentions, loyalties, and decisions emerge.
Jesus is going after the throne room.
Your heart.
And here is where many religious people become very skilled at hiding.
We learn Christian vocabulary.
We know when to say “God is good.”
We know which worship songs make us emotional.
We know how to post a Bible verse.
We know how to look peaceful in church.
We know how to say, “I’m praying about it.”
We know how to explain away the compromise.
We know how to make bondage sound complicated enough that nobody confronts it.
But you can fool a congregation.
You can fool your spouse.
You can fool your followers.
You can even fool yourself for a terrifyingly long time.
You cannot fool Christ.
He sees what happens after the worship music stops.
He sees the browser history.
The deleted conversation.
The obsession with money.
The resentment.
The envy when somebody else succeeds.
The hunger to be admired.
The relationship you know is dragging your soul backward.
The secret fantasy.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The greed disguised as ambition.
The cowardice disguised as wisdom.
The addiction disguised as stress relief.
The self-righteousness disguised as holiness.
And before shame tells you to stop reading, understand something absolutely essential.
Jesus exposes idols not because He delights in humiliating sinners, but because He came to save sinners.
The Gospel is not God discovering that you are worse than He expected.
The cross proves He already knew the cost.
Jesus did not walk toward Calvary because humanity had finally become impressive enough to deserve Him.
He came for sinners.
He ate with scandalous people.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called wanderers home.
He carried a cross.
He was crucified.
He died for sins.
And He rose again.
Grace does not say your spiritual adultery does not matter.
Grace says it mattered enough for Christ to bleed—and that His mercy is greater than the sin you finally bring into the light.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God standing over a filthy person shouting, “Clean yourself before you come near Me.”
The Gospel announces that Christ came for people who could not rescue themselves.
Repentance is the turning of the sinner toward God.
It is the collapse of our negotiations.
No more excuses.
No more editing the confession.
No more calling chains jewelry.
No more asking Jesus to become one important relationship among many competing gods.
You come home.
Maybe you have spent years thinking repentance means God wants to take everything enjoyable away from you.
But what if the thing He is trying to take is the chain around your neck?
What if you keep calling it freedom because you have forgotten what breathing feels like?
The pornography promises pleasure and eventually demands secrecy.
Money promises security and eventually demands your life.
Approval promises belonging and eventually makes everyone your judge.
Success promises significance and moves the finish line every time you approach it.
Lust promises intimacy without covenant and leaves you hungrier.
Control promises safety and gives you anxiety because the universe refuses to obey you.
Bitterness promises justice while slowly poisoning the person carrying it.
An idol always makes promises it cannot ultimately keep.
Jesus does something radically different.
He tells you the cost.
“Follow Me.”
Die to self.
Take up your cross.
Lose your life for His sake.
And then you discover the great paradox of discipleship:
the Master who asks for everything is the only Master who gave everything for you.
Mammon never died for you.
Pornography never loved you.
Applause was never crucified for you.
Success never carried your sin.
Your career cannot resurrect you.
Your relationship cannot cleanse your conscience.
Your followers cannot defeat death.
Your possessions cannot stand beside your grave and command you to rise.
But Jesus can.
This is why Christianity is not merely adding Jesus to an already crowded heart.
Christ does not come as another decoration for the shelf.
He comes as Lord.
And perhaps the deepest question in this entire article is not whether you have ever said that Jesus is Lord.
It is whether there is anything in your life to which you are quietly saying:
“You can have everything, Jesus...
except this.”
That “except” may be revealing your master.
And if something inside you just became uncomfortable, do not run from that discomfort.
Bring it into the light.
David prayed after devastating moral failure:
“לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים”
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
Psalm 51:10.
The Hebrew verb בְּרָא — bera, from ברא — bara, carries the sense of creating. David does not merely ask God to make him look more respectable.
He asks for heart-level work.
That is what some of us need.
Not better camouflage.
Not a cleaner Christian image.
Not another inspirational quote over the same secret chains.
A clean heart.
Maybe you have been asking God to change your circumstances while God has been confronting your allegiance.
Maybe you have been praying, “Lord, why haven't You given me what I want?”
And somewhere beneath that prayer is another question:
“If God never gives me this, will He still be enough?”
That question can expose a throne.
If the answer is no, pay attention.
If losing something would make you believe life is no longer worth living, pay attention.
If obedience to Jesus feels unacceptable whenever it threatens a particular desire, pay attention.
Not because every strong desire is automatically idolatry.
But because strong desires become dangerous when they become ultimate demands.
There is a difference between saying:
“Lord, I deeply desire this.”
and saying:
“Lord, I must have this in order to be whole.”
Jesus is not competing to become one ingredient in your wholeness.
“In Him” is where the New Testament repeatedly locates the believer's life.
And this is where the emotional rollercoaster turns.
Because maybe you recognize yourself.
Maybe badly.
Maybe you have been spiritually cheating for years.
Maybe your lips kept saying Jesus while your life kept crawling back toward another master.
Maybe you promised Him after the last relapse.
Then failed.
Promised again.
Failed again.
Cried.
Repented.
Went back.
And now shame whispers:
“Don't bother coming home this time.”
Listen carefully.
That voice is not the Gospel.
The Gospel never says sin is harmless.
But neither does the Gospel say Christ is powerless.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
The Christian hope is not that faithful believers never stumble.
The hope is Christ.
His blood.
His righteousness.
His resurrection.
His intercession.
His grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
His Spirit who transforms His people.
And when you fall, the answer is not to make peace with the mud.
Come back to Jesus.
Again.
Not casually.
Not pretending repentance is permission to schedule the next rebellion.
Come honestly.
Bring the idol by name.
“Jesus, I love money more than I want to admit.”
“Jesus, I need people to admire me.”
“Jesus, I keep returning to lust.”
“Jesus, I have made this relationship more important than obedience.”
“Jesus, I am terrified of surrendering control.”
“Jesus, I have wanted Your blessings more than I have wanted You.”
There is something terrifying and liberating about finally telling God the truth He already knows.
You do not confess to inform Him.
You confess because you are finished hiding.
And this is where scandal begins turning into grace.
