But what if tonight Jesus is lovingly putting His finger on the sentence itself?
What if the question is not whether you have always been this way?
What if the question is whether Jesus has permission to change what you have always been?
Read that again.
What if the question is not whether you have always been this way, but whether Jesus has permission to change what you have always been?
Because the cross means your past can explain you without owning you.
Your failures can humble you without naming you.
Your wounds can affect you without becoming your master.
Your personality can describe tendencies without becoming an excuse for disobedience.
And your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Peter could deny Jesus and still be restored.
Paul could carry the shameful history of persecuting Christians and still become an apostle of grace.
The Gospel does not hide the scandal.
It does something infinitely better.
Jesus enters it.
He redeems.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross shows how serious sin is.
And then it shows how astonishing God's mercy is.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, the sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith does not have to build a permanent home inside yesterday.
Maybe your prayer tonight should be brutally simple:
“Jesus, show me what I keep calling personality that You call something I need to surrender.”
That prayer might hurt.
Pray it anyway.
Ask Him about your anger.
Ask Him about your words.
Ask Him about your pride.
Ask Him about how you treat your spouse when nobody else is watching.
Ask Him about the way you respond when corrected.
Ask Him about the resentment you keep feeding.
Ask Him about the secret habit you keep excusing.
Ask Him about the apology you refuse to give.
Ask Him about the person you refuse to forgive.
Ask Him about the version of yourself you keep defending.
Then remember:
Conviction is not an invitation to run away from Jesus.
It is an invitation to run toward Him.
The answer to discovering sin in yourself is not self-hatred.
It is repentance and faith.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Receive mercy.
Ask the Spirit for power.
Make the apology.
Seek reconciliation where appropriate.
Ask mature believers to walk with you.
Open the Bible again tomorrow.
And when you fail, do not transform grace into permission to quit.
Come back to Christ.
Again.
The beautiful scandal of Christianity is that Jesus already knew exactly whom He was saving.
You did not surprise Him.
The cross was not built for impressive people who had finally mastered themselves.
It was built because sinners needed a Savior.
And the empty tomb announces that sin, shame, death, and your former life do not get the last word.
Jesus does.
So perhaps it is time to retire one sentence.
“That’s just how I am.”
And replace it with something more Christian.
“That's something Jesus is still changing in me.”
Can you feel the difference?
One closes the door.
The other opens it.
One protects the pattern.
The other brings it before Christ.
One says, “Accept my chains.”
The other says, “Jesus, make me free.”
Be honest.
Someone else reading your words may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
Better yet, read it first for yourself.
Not because you need another saved post collecting digital dust, but because the next time you hear yourself say, “That's just how I am,” you may need to come back and remember:
In Christ, who you have been is not the limit of who He is making you.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, confronting what needs confronting, encouraging you when you are exhausted, and continually pointing you toward Jesus Christ, consider staying close to this work.

Following Gospel Warrior helps you remain connected to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever you have been praying for to follow too.
It does not.
Not because giving money makes someone more spiritual.
It does not.
And certainly not because God needs our money.
He does not.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one practical expression of that surrender can be generously supporting Gospel-centered work we believe is bearing good fruit.
And there is something else we want believers to know.

If this ministry strengthens you, helps you open Scripture again, calls you toward repentance, reminds you of grace, or gives you something worth sending to a struggling person at midnight, your support helps that work continue.
Not as religious advertising.
As mission.
A wounded wife who has mistaken emotional walls for strength.
A father who has never apologized.
A daughter carrying bitterness.
A believer secretly convinced they can never change.
A Christian who loves Jesus but has spent years protecting the one room in their heart they refuse to let Him renovate.
Maybe they won't.
Maybe tonight they will stop.
Maybe the Holy Spirit will use one ordinary sentence to expose an extraordinary lie.
Maybe somebody will whisper:
“Jesus… I don't want to stay this way.”
And that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus does not merely expose what needs changing and abandon us beside the wreckage.
He forgives.
He restores.
He teaches.
He disciplines those He loves.
He gives His Spirit.
He forms His character in His people.
He picks fallen disciples back up.
He writes resurrection into places we thought were finished.
So bring Him the temper.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the defensiveness.
Bring Him the coldness.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the habits.
Bring Him the excuses.
Bring Him the sentence you have repeated for twenty years.
Bring Him the person you thought you could never become.
Then place all of it before the One who makes sinners new.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing you can say about a chain is:
“That's just who I am.”
And perhaps one of the most beautiful things a redeemed sinner can say is:
“That may be who I was, and it may still be where I struggle—but Jesus Christ is not finished with me.”
Because your personality may explain the battlefield.
But it does not get to overrule the King who is transforming you on it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FACE YOU CALLED THE ENEMY
paragraphs: THE FACE YOU CALLED THE ENEMY
What “Our Struggle Is Not Against Flesh and Blood” Changes About How You See the Person Who Hurt You
What if one of Satan’s most effective victories is not simply getting people to hurt each other…
…but convincing Christians that the person who hurt them is the enemy?
Read that again.
Because somewhere in your life, there may be a face you have attached to the word enemy.
The person who betrayed you.
The spouse who broke your trust.
The relative who keeps reopening wounds you thought had healed.
The church member who embarrassed you.
The pastor who disappointed you.
The friend who disappeared when you needed them.
The coworker who seems determined to make your life miserable.
The person whose political opinions make your blood boil.
The stranger online whose comment made something dark rise inside you.
You see their face.
You remember what they said.
You replay what they did.
And something inside you whispers:
That person is my enemy.
Then Paul walks into that battlefield with one sentence that changes the entire way a Christian is supposed to see human conflict:
“For we wrestle not against flesh and blood…”
Ephesians 6:12.
The Greek is even more arresting:
ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα
Hoti ouk estin hēmin hē palē pros haima kai sarka.
The heart of the statement is unmistakable.
Our struggle—ἡ πάλη, hē palē—is not ultimately against αἷμα καὶ σάρκα, haima kai sarka: “blood and flesh,” the ordinary biblical way of referring to human beings in their mortal humanity.
Paul does not say there is no struggle.
That matters.
Christianity is not pretending everything is peaceful when it is not.
Paul uses the language of struggle, conflict, wrestling.
There really is a battle.
There really are wounds.
There really is evil.
There really are lies worth confronting.
There really are people who manipulate, deceive, betray, exploit, abuse, persecute, slander, and destroy.
But Paul reaches into our instinctive interpretation of conflict and says:
You are looking at the battlefield incorrectly.
Because the person standing in front of you is not the deepest enemy behind the war.
Paul continues:
“…but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.”
This is not permission to become superstitious.
It is not permission to blame a demon every time somebody disagrees with you.
It is not permission to stop thinking carefully about psychology, trauma, consequences, justice, responsibility, or human choices.
And it certainly does not mean people are innocent of everything they do.
Scripture repeatedly holds human beings responsible for sin.
Judas betrayed Jesus.
Herod acted wickedly.
Pilate made decisions.
Religious leaders conspired.
People lied.
People murdered.
People persecuted.
Human responsibility does not disappear simply because spiritual evil exists.
But Ephesians 6 exposes something deeper.
Behind the visible conflicts of this fallen world stands an invisible kingdom of darkness that delights whenever hatred multiplies.
That means Satan does not necessarily need you to abandon Christianity publicly.
Sometimes he only needs you to hate someone privately.
He does not always need to make you deny Jesus.
Sometimes he only needs to make you despise someone Jesus told you to love.
And that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because it is easy to read Ephesians 6:12 while imagining demons somewhere in the distance.
It is harder to read it while remembering the person you cannot forgive.
The person whose name changes your mood.
The person whose failure secretly makes you happy.
The person you hope gets exposed.
The person you have mentally sentenced a thousand times.
The person you have reduced to the worst thing they ever did.
Suddenly Paul’s words become uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the battle is not only happening around you.
Perhaps part of the battlefield is happening inside you.
You were wounded.
Then anger came.
Anger became resentment.
Resentment became rehearsed conversations.
Rehearsed conversations became assumptions.
Assumptions became contempt.
And eventually you stopped seeing a human being.
You saw an enemy.
That is exactly where the Gospel interrupts us.
Because Jesus Christ did something almost impossible for the human heart to understand.
He loved His enemies.
Not theoretically.
While nails were being driven through Him.
While people mocked Him.
While soldiers gambled for His clothing.
While religious leaders celebrated His suffering.
While the crowd watched.
Jesus prayed:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
Luke 23:34.
That does not make crucifixion less evil.
It reveals how astonishing Christ is.
Jesus never confused forgiveness with pretending evil was good.
He called sin what it was.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He exposed corruption.
He warned of judgment.
He overturned tables.
He rebuked religious leaders.
And still…
He loved sinners enough to die for them.
This is where Christianity becomes more than inspirational language.
Because Jesus does not merely ask you to admire His mercy.
He commands His disciples to imitate it.
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you…”
Matthew 5:44.
That command feels beautiful until your enemy has a name.
Then Christianity becomes costly.
Love your enemies.
That one too, Lord?
Pray for those who persecute you.
After what they did?
Forgive.
But they never apologized.
Bless.
But they tried to destroy me.
And perhaps your heart answers:
Jesus, You don't understand.
Except He does.
He understands betrayal.
Judas kissed Him.
He understands abandonment.
His disciples ran.
He understands false accusations.
Witnesses lied.
He understands humiliation.
Soldiers mocked Him.
He understands physical suffering.
They scourged Him.
He understands public shame.
They stripped Him.
He understands injustice.
An innocent Man was condemned.
He understands rejection.
His own people cried for His crucifixion.
And from the cross, Jesus showed us something terrifyingly beautiful:
You can recognize evil without becoming consumed by hatred for the person committing it.
That is spiritual warfare.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks less like shouting at darkness and more like refusing to let darkness reproduce itself inside you.
Read that slowly.
Sometimes the enemy hurts you through someone else…
and then tries to recruit you through the wound.
Someone sins against you.
Now bitterness wants you.
Someone humiliates you.
Now vengeance wants you.
Someone lies about you.
Now hatred wants you.
Someone abandons you.
Now hardness wants you.
The first wound may have been inflicted by another person.
But the next battle happens inside your heart.
And this is why Paul does not merely tell Christians who the enemy is.
He tells them what to wear.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The readiness of the Gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
Notice what is missing.
Hatred.
There is no belt of hatred.
No breastplate of revenge.
No helmet of superiority.
No shield of contempt.
No sword of humiliation.
No armor piece called “winning the argument.”
The armor of God looks remarkably unlike the weapons we instinctively reach for.
Because the kingdom of Jesus does not defeat darkness by becoming darker.
It overcomes evil with good.
That is exactly what Romans 12:21 says:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.”
There are two ways evil can defeat you.
It can destroy you from outside.
Or it can convince you to become like it from inside.
The second victory may be far more dangerous.
Because you can survive somebody’s cruelty and still allow bitterness to reshape your soul.
You can leave the abusive relationship and carry the abuser inside your thoughts for twenty years.
You can block the number while still replaying the conversation every night.
You can move churches while resentment moves with you.
You can win the court case and lose your peace.
You can prove that you were right and slowly become someone you no longer recognize.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending none of it happened.
And this must be said carefully.
If someone is abusing you, Ephesians 6:12 does not command you to remain available for abuse.
If someone is dangerous, loving them does not require giving them unrestricted access to you.
If a crime has been committed, forgiveness does not mean preventing legitimate authorities from pursuing justice.
Romans 13 recognizes the proper role of governing authority.
Jesus Himself sometimes withdrew from people who intended Him harm.
Paul escaped dangerous situations.
Biblical forgiveness and biblical wisdom are not enemies.
You can forgive and establish boundaries.
You can love someone and refuse to enable them.
You can pray for someone and still testify truthfully about what they did.
You can desire somebody’s salvation while also recognizing that reconciliation requires more than pretending trust was never shattered.
Forgiveness releases personal vengeance into God's hands.
Reconciliation ordinarily requires truth, repentance, and restored trust.
And trust may take time.
Sometimes wisdom means distance.
But distance does not require hatred.
That distinction could set someone free tonight.
Because perhaps you thought forgiveness meant saying:
It didn't matter.
No.
The cross proves sin matters enormously.
Forgiveness says:
It mattered so much that I cannot heal it by pretending it was nothing. But I refuse to become the permanent prisoner of what you did to me. I surrender vengeance to God.
That is different.
And maybe this article found you while you are carrying somebody.
Not physically.
Inside you.
Their voice.
Their betrayal.
Their accusation.
Their rejection.
Their affair.
Their abandonment.
Their cruelty.
Their hypocrisy.
Their failure.
Their name has been living rent-free in your nervous system.
You wake up and remember.
You lie down and replay it.
You imagine conversations that never happen.
You imagine apologies they may never give.
You imagine finally saying the sentence that will make them understand how badly they hurt you.
And underneath everything is a quiet question:
How could they do this to me?
But perhaps Jesus is asking another question tonight.
What is this doing to you?
Because the enemy would gladly use another person's sin to build a prison inside your soul.
And every time you rehearse hatred, another brick goes up.
Every fantasy of revenge adds another.
Every moment of contempt adds another.
Until eventually the person who wounded you may have moved on…
but you are still living inside the cell.
Jesus came to open prison doors.
Not merely the obvious ones.
The invisible ones too.
This is why the Gospel changes how Christians see people.
Every human being you meet bears the dignity of being made in the image of God.
Every human being is fallen.
Every human being desperately needs grace.
And every human being—including the one writing this and the one reading it—is capable of becoming the villain in someone else's story.
That should humble us.
Because before the Gospel tells you to forgive your enemies, it tells you something even more devastating:
You were once God's enemy.
Romans 5 says:
“For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son…”
When we were enemies.
Not when we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not when we had finally become lovable.
Not when we had earned another chance.
Enemies.
And Christ died for us.
That changes everything.
Christian forgiveness does not begin with how deserving the other person is.
It begins with remembering how undeserving we were.
The cross destroys our ability to stand beneath Jesus receiving mercy while simultaneously standing over everyone else demanding payment.
We owed a debt we could never repay.
Jesus paid it.
We stood guilty.
Jesus showed mercy.
We wandered.
Jesus pursued.
We rebelled.
Jesus loved.
We sinned.
Jesus bled.
And now the forgiven become forgivers.
Not because evil suddenly becomes acceptable.
Because grace has become unforgettable.
This is the scandal of grace.
The murderer can repent.
The adulterer can repent.
The addict can repent.
The liar can repent.
The hypocrite can repent.
The religious fraud can repent.
The prodigal can come home.
The bitter Christian can repent too.
Nobody is beyond the reach of Christ while there is breath and opportunity to turn to Him.
That does not erase earthly consequences.
Grace is not the cancellation of truth.
Grace is God meeting guilty people in truth and offering them what they could never purchase for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new life.
This is why you cannot look at people exactly the same after understanding Ephesians 6:12.
The atheist arguing with you online is not your ultimate enemy.
The unbelieving relative mocking your faith is not your ultimate enemy.
The Christian who disappointed you is not your ultimate enemy.
The person trapped in sexual sin is not your ultimate enemy.
The addict is not your ultimate enemy.
The political opponent is not your ultimate enemy.
The angry teenager is not your ultimate enemy.
The confused skeptic is not your ultimate enemy.
The prodigal child is not your ultimate enemy.
They may oppose you.
They may sin against you.
They may believe destructive things.
They may need correction.
They may require boundaries.
They may even require legal accountability.
But they are still people for whom Christ's Gospel must be proclaimed.
And once you understand that, evangelism changes.
You stop trying merely to win arguments.
You start longing to win people.
You stop treating unbelievers as interruptions to Christian culture.
You begin seeing them as souls.
You stop celebrating when opponents collapse.
You start wondering whether brokenness might become the doorway through which they finally cry out to Jesus.
Imagine if the Church remembered this.
Imagine Christians who could confront lies without hating liars.
Expose darkness without becoming cruel.
Defend truth without losing tenderness.
Practice discernment without developing contempt.
Stand against evil without forgetting the humanity of those trapped inside it.
Imagine believers who actually believed that conversion is possible.
Because Saul once breathed threats against Christians.
Then Jesus met him.
And the persecutor became Paul.
Think about that.
If the early Christians had only seen Saul according to what he had done, they would have seen a monster.
Jesus saw what grace could make him.
That does not mean Christians should naively place themselves in danger.
Acts itself records the understandable fear believers initially had toward Saul.
But grace wrote another chapter.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Maybe that is why you should hesitate before declaring that somebody will “never change.”
You do not know what Jesus may do with the next chapter.
And perhaps the person most urgently needing another chapter is not the person who hurt you.
Perhaps it is you.
Maybe bitterness has exhausted you.
Maybe hatred has become strangely comforting because it feels safer than grief.
Maybe anger has protected you from admitting how deeply you were wounded.
Maybe you have told everybody you are “over it,” but one mention of their name proves otherwise.
You do not have to pretend tonight.
Jesus already knows.
Bring Him the ugly prayer.
Lord, I don't want to forgive them.
Bring Him the honest prayer.
Lord, part of me still wants them to hurt.
Bring Him the exhausted prayer.
Lord, I cannot carry this anymore.
Bring Him the frightened prayer.
Lord, if I release this anger, I don't know what will be left.
You do not impress Christ by hiding wounds from the One who bears scars.
Bring Him everything.
Then remember:
Forgiveness is not pretending justice does not matter.
It is refusing to make yourself God.
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Romans 12:19.
You can put the gavel down.
God has not surrendered His throne.
He sees what happened.
He knows what was said.
He knows what was stolen.
He knows what was hidden.
He knows what nobody believed.
He knows what you cannot prove.
And because He is Judge, you do not have to become one in your heart every morning.
Release them to Him.
Again tomorrow if necessary.
And again the day after that.
Sometimes forgiveness is a decisive act followed by a long healing process.
But every surrender declares something to hell:
You will not turn their sin into mine.
That is warfare.
When hatred says, “Destroy them,” and the Spirit leads you to pray for them…
warfare.
When bitterness says, “Replay it,” and you surrender the memory to Christ…
warfare.
When pride says, “You would never do what they did,” and the cross reminds you that you live by mercy too…
warfare.
When Satan says, “That person is beyond redemption,” and you remember Saul of Tarsus…
warfare.
When shame says, “You are beyond redemption,” and you remember the blood of Jesus…
warfare.
Because Ephesians 6 was never given so Christians could become fascinated with darkness.
It was given so Christians could stand in Christ.
And perhaps this is where the story turns.
You thought this article was about the person who hurt you.
Maybe Jesus has been talking about your heart the whole time.
Not condemning you.
Calling you out of captivity.
You cannot change what they did.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot force repentance.
You cannot manufacture reconciliation.
You cannot make someone understand your pain.
But through Christ, yesterday does not have to own tomorrow.
That is what Jesus does.
He walks into scandals and writes grace.
He walks into graves and writes resurrection.
He walks into shame and writes redemption.
He walks into bondage and writes freedom.
He walks into ruined people and begins making them new.
And He can walk into this wound too.
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, don't rush past it.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that healing is possible.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not twenty.
One.
Maybe they have been consumed by family conflict.
Maybe betrayal is eating them alive.
Maybe politics has taught them to hate strangers.
Maybe church hurt has pushed them toward abandoning Jesus.
Maybe they are fighting a person when the deeper battle is for their own heart.
Send this article privately if their wound is too personal for a public tag.
Because forgiveness is rarely a lesson we need only once.
Tomorrow the memory may return.
When it does, come back and remember:
Flesh and blood are not the ultimate enemy.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, healing, repentance, and the truth of Jesus Christ, you can also help this ministry keep putting Gospel-centered resources in front of people who need them.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, caring for your family, or serving people around you.
Your support helps us keep pointing wounded people toward Jesus.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Jesus could never want someone like them.
Live it.
Because somewhere soon, somebody is going to offend you.
Somebody will misunderstand you.
Somebody may wound you.
And when their face appears in your mind, remember Paul's words:
“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.”
See the sin clearly.
Tell the truth.
Set boundaries when necessary.
Seek justice where appropriate.
Protect the vulnerable.
Refuse manipulation.
Do not call darkness light.
But never surrender your heart to hatred.
Look at people through the shadow of a cross where the Son of God died for His enemies.
And remember that once…
you needed that mercy too.
Maybe the greatest evidence that Christ has won the battle is not that your enemy finally falls.
Maybe it is that after everything they did to you, Jesus refused to let hatred have the final word in you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY PAUL SHOOK THE SNAKE INTO THE FIRE
paragraphs:
WHY PAUL SHOOK THE SNAKE INTO THE FIRE
The serpent expected Paul to die. The people expected judgment. But God was writing a completely different ending—and what Paul did next may expose the venom you have been carrying far too long.
There are moments when life does not even give you time to recover before something else bites you.
Paul had just survived a shipwreck.
Think about that.
The storm had already been violent enough.
The ship was gone.
The cargo was gone.
The soldiers had considered killing the prisoners.
The sea had nearly swallowed everyone alive.
Paul finally crawled onto the shore of Malta soaked, exhausted, cold, and probably carrying the physical consequences of fourteen terrifying days at sea.
And then, while he was simply trying to help build a fire…
a snake fastened itself to his hand.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Not literally.
But spiritually.
Emotionally.
You survived one thing only to be bitten by another.
You survived the betrayal, then came the financial problem.
You survived the funeral, then came the family conflict.
You survived the addiction, then temptation returned.
You survived the breakup, but bitterness followed you onto the shore.
You survived the season that almost destroyed your faith, and just when you thought you could finally warm yourself beside the fire…
something came out of the wood.
That is where Acts 28 becomes painfully personal.
Luke writes:
Acts 28:3
The Greek is even more vivid.
The creature is called an ἔχιδνα—echidna—a viper or venomous snake.
And Luke says it καθῆψε τῆς χειρὸς αὐτοῦ—kathēpse tēs cheiros autou.
It fastened onto his hand.
It did not merely appear near Paul.
It attached itself to him.
And sometimes that is the difference between a problem and a wound.
Some things happen around you.
Other things fasten themselves to you.
A betrayal happens…
then distrust fastens itself to you.
Abuse happens…
then shame fastens itself to you.
Failure happens…
then the sentence “I will never be enough” fastens itself to you.
Someone abandons you…
then fear of abandonment starts following you into every relationship.
You commit a sin you deeply regret…
Christ offers forgiveness, yet condemnation still hangs from your hand years later.
The event may have lasted minutes.
The venom can remain in your thinking for decades.
And here is what makes the scene even more brutal.
People were watching.
Acts tells us that when the islanders saw the creature hanging from Paul’s hand, they immediately began interpreting his suffering.
They said:
“No doubt this man is a murderer. Though he has escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”
Acts 28:4
Paul had not even collapsed…
and people had already written his obituary.
They saw the snake and assumed they understood the man.
They saw suffering and called it guilt.
They saw circumstances and constructed a theology around them.

The word translated “Justice” is Δίκη—Dikē—which in the Greco-Roman world could refer to divine justice and was also personified as a goddess. The islanders were interpreting Paul’s circumstances through their own worldview.
The sea did not kill him?
Then surely divine justice sent the snake.
Case closed.
Except they were completely wrong.
And that should humble every Christian who has ever looked at another person’s suffering and quietly decided,
“I know why God allowed this.”
Sometimes you do not.
Job’s friends made that mistake.
They looked at suffering and assumed hidden wickedness.
Jesus confronted similar thinking when His disciples encountered the man born blind and asked:
“Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered:
“It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him.”
John 9:2–3
Be careful when you interpret somebody else’s storm.
Be careful when you interpret somebody else’s snake.
And be especially careful when you interpret your own suffering as proof that God has abandoned you.
Paul was bitten.
But Paul was not abandoned.
That distinction could save someone’s faith tonight.
The presence of pain is not proof of the absence of God.
Paul was exactly where God’s providence had brought him, yet there was still a storm.
There was still a shipwreck.
There was still cold.
There was still a snake.
Biblical Christianity never promises that obedience makes Christians untouchable.
Jesus Himself said:
“In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
John 16:33
Christian faith is not the promise that nothing painful will ever fasten itself to your hand.
It is the confidence that nothing can ultimately separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God.
And then Paul does something astonishing.
Acts 28:5 says:
“He, however, shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm.”
The Greek expression is beautifully forceful:
ὁ μὲν οὖν ἀποτινάξας τὸ θηρίον εἰς τὸ πῦρ…
ho men oun apotinaxas to thērion eis to pyr…
He shook the creature off…
into the fire.
The verb ἀποτινάσσω—apotinassō—carries the idea of shaking something off.
Paul did not negotiate with the snake.
He did not study the snake.
He did not carry the snake around as evidence of how difficult his journey had been.
He did not make the snake his identity.
He shook it off.
Now hear this carefully, because Acts 28 should not be turned into a motivational slogan that ignores what the passage actually says.
Luke is describing a historical event.

This passage is not permission for Christians to handle venomous snakes, deliberately expose themselves to danger, refuse appropriate medical care, or presume that God must miraculously protect them from physical harm.
Paul did not pick up the snake to prove his faith.
The snake unexpectedly attacked him.
The miracle was God’s sovereign protection, not Paul performing a religious stunt.
But there is still a powerful truth in the way Paul responded.
What attached itself to Paul did not become Paul.
And what happened to you does not have to become your identity either.
Read that again.
What attached itself to Paul did not become Paul.
You may have been betrayed.
You are not betrayal.
You may have failed.
You are not your failure.
You may have sinned terribly.
Your sin is serious—but if you have come to Jesus Christ in genuine repentance and faith, your sin does not have the authority to write the final chapter of your life.
You may have been abused.
What somebody did to you does not define your worth.
You may have gone through divorce.
You may have gone through bankruptcy.
You may have gone through addiction.
You may have buried somebody you thought would grow old beside you.
You may have disappointed people.
You may have disappointed yourself.
You may even be reading this while secretly carrying something nobody on Facebook knows.
But the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Jesus Christ is greater than the worst chapter of your story.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean trauma becomes imaginary.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means your past does not possess greater authority than the cross.
This is where Christianity separates itself from cheap inspiration.
The Gospel does not tell sinful people,
“You were perfect all along.”
Scripture says something infinitely more powerful.
We have sinned.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Our guilt before a holy God is real.
And therefore our greatest problem is deeper than bad circumstances, difficult people, trauma, disappointment, or snakes emerging from fires.
We need reconciliation with God.
And this is where Jesus enters the story.
Not merely as an inspirational teacher.
Not merely as an example.
Not merely as someone who helps good people become slightly better.
Christ came for sinners.
Paul himself would write:
Romans 5:8
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
The Gospel is God demonstrating how much sin mattered by giving His Son—and demonstrating how enormous His grace is by offering forgiveness to people who could never purchase it themselves.
That is scandalous grace.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can be cleansed.
The rebel can come home.
The addict can repent.
The sexually broken can be restored.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can bow.
The religious hypocrite can finally stop pretending.
The person everybody gave up on can become evidence that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the snake hanging from your hand right now is not something somebody did to you.
Perhaps it is something you did.
That is harder to admit.
Maybe you have been blaming your childhood for something God has been telling you to repent of.
Maybe pornography has fastened itself to your private life.
Maybe resentment has become so normal that you call it discernment.
Maybe pride has learned Christian vocabulary.
Maybe jealousy hides behind criticism.
Maybe you worship God publicly while feeding something privately that is slowly poisoning your marriage, your mind, your integrity, or your relationship with Christ.
Maybe everybody sees the fire…
but only you know about the snake.
Do not merely manage what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Shake it off.
Not through willpower alone.
Not through positive thinking.
Not by pretending temptation does not exist.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Repent.
Seek accountability.
Remove access to what repeatedly leads you into sin.
Ask mature believers for help.
And run to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9
Notice where Paul threw the snake.
Into the fire.
There are things you should not keep souvenirs from.
Some doors need to stay closed.
Some numbers need to remain deleted.
Some conversations need to end.
Some secret accounts need to disappear.
Some environments need to be abandoned.
Some relationships require biblical boundaries.
Some habits need more than another emotional promise that “this was the last time.”
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened.
The New Testament word μετάνοια—metanoia—speaks of repentance, a genuine turning of mind and direction toward God.
Grace does not teach us to cuddle the snake.
Grace teaches us to leave the old master and belong to Christ.
But there is another detail in Acts 28 that many people rush past.
The people were waiting for Paul to die.
Acts 28:6 says they expected him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead.
Imagine the silence.
Everyone staring.
Waiting.
Watching.
Perhaps you know that feeling too.
Some people remember the old you so clearly that they cannot imagine anything else.
They remember your addiction.
Your divorce.
Your scandal.
Your prison sentence.
Your breakdown.
Your affair.
Your bankruptcy.
Your anger.
Your rebellion.
Your years away from God.
Your worst decision.
And sometimes you can almost feel people waiting for you to become that person again.
Paul simply kept standing.
Eventually, the observers changed their minds dramatically and wrongly concluded that he was a god.
First murderer.
Then god.
Same Paul.
Different public opinion.
That should teach you something.
If you build your identity from what people say about you, you will spend your entire life being emotionally dragged between condemnation and worship.
One crowd will call you worthless.
Another will call you extraordinary.
Neither crowd gets the final word.
God does.
Paul knew who he belonged to.
Earlier, during the storm, he had said:
“the God to whom I belong and whom I worship.”
Acts 27:23
That was Paul’s anchor.
Not public opinion.
Not the snake.
Not the storm.
Not Rome.
Not Malta.
Not his chains.
“I belong to God.”
There is somebody reading these words who desperately needs to recover that sentence.
If you are in Christ…
you belong to Him.
Your scandal does not own you.
Your shame does not own you.
Your addiction does not own you.
Your critics do not own you.
Your trauma does not own you.
Your achievements do not own you.
Jesus Christ purchased His people at immeasurable cost.
And perhaps that is why the enemy of your soul has worked so relentlessly to convince you that your worst moment is your permanent name.
Because shame whispers,
“Hide.”
Jesus says,
“Come.”
Shame says,
“You are too dirty.”
Jesus cleanses sinners.
Shame says,
“If people knew everything, nobody could love you.”
The cross says God already knows the depth of human sin—and Christ still came.
Shame says,
“Your story ended there.”
The resurrection says death itself does not get the final word.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
And something remarkable happens after Paul survives the snake.
The story keeps moving.

Paul later ministers on Malta. Publius receives him. Publius’s father is sick with fever and dysentery. Paul prays, lays his hands on him, and the man is healed. Others on the island who were sick also come and receive healing.
The hand that had just carried a snake becomes a hand laid upon a suffering man in prayer.
Do not miss that.
The wounded hand became a serving hand.
The hand everybody expected to become swollen and useless was soon being used in ministry.
God can do something beautiful with the places where you thought your story was finished.
Again, we must be biblically careful: Acts 28 does not promise that every believer will experience miraculous physical healing or supernatural protection in exactly the same manner as Paul.
But it unmistakably shows the sovereignty of God working through circumstances that looked catastrophic.
The shipwreck did not stop the mission.
The snake did not stop the mission.
The opinions of the crowd did not stop the mission.
And eventually Paul continued toward Rome.
What looked like interruption was still inside providence.
Maybe you have spent years asking,
“God, why did You allow this?”
Some questions may not receive complete answers in this life.
Christianity does not require us to pretend otherwise.
But Scripture repeatedly reveals a God who can accomplish His purposes even through suffering without calling evil good.
Joseph could look backward at the cruelty committed against him and say:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
Genesis 50:20
Not that evil secretly became good.
It was evil.
But evil did not outrank God.
The cross itself is the ultimate demonstration.
Human beings committed the greatest injustice in history against the sinless Son of God.
Yet through that very cross, according to God’s sovereign purpose, redemption came.
Then the tomb was opened.
That means Christians do not need to pretend their scars never happened.
We point to the scars and say:
“Jesus met me there.”
You survived the sea.
Then came the snake.
But perhaps you are still here because the story is not finished.
Perhaps your testimony will not be,
“Nothing painful ever happened to me.”
Perhaps it will be,
“It happened. It hurt. I cried. I stumbled. I needed help. There were nights I questioned everything. But Jesus Christ did not abandon me.”
That testimony has weight.
Because somebody else is still floating in the wreckage you once escaped.
Somebody else is staring at the same addiction.
Somebody else is hiding the same shame.
Somebody else is sitting inside a parked car crying before walking into the house because nobody there knows how exhausted they really are.
Somebody else opened Facebook tonight because silence felt unbearable.
And somehow…
they found this.
Maybe you did too.
What is still hanging from my hand that Jesus is calling me to stop carrying?
Bitterness?
Pornography?
Unforgiveness?
Pride?
Secret sin?
Condemnation?
Fear?
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ?
A version of yourself God has been calling you to bury?
You do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But you do need to stop hiding from God.
He already knows.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the forgiveness purchased by Christ rather than trying to manufacture your own righteousness.
And if you already belong to Him but you have wandered…
come home.
There is still grace.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because an algorithm can advance the Kingdom of God by itself.
But because somebody in your circle may be quietly drowning while looking perfectly fine in photographs.
If Christ has used these words to strengthen you, sharing Gospel-centered truth is one practical way you can help place that truth in front of someone who might never search for it themselves.
Because there may come a night when the snake returns to your memory and you need to remember:
what fastened itself to you does not have to define you.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped attending church.
Invite the believer who is tired.
Invite the person who has questions.
Invite the person everybody else has written off.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
Because Christianity begins with the astonishing announcement that Christ came precisely because humanity is broken by sin—and sinners can be reconciled to God through Him.
But supporting Gospel work can be a practical expression of generosity and partnership when done freely, prayerfully, and with the right heart.
Leave changed.
Because Paul shaking a snake into a fire is fascinating.
But the greater story is not about Paul being powerful.
It is about God being faithful.
Paul was not the hero of Christianity.
Jesus is.
Paul eventually died.
Every miracle in Acts points beyond the messenger toward the God who reigns over life and death.
And the greatest victory promised to Christians is not that every snake will fail to bite.
It is not that every storm will disappear.
It is not that every sickness will be healed before death.
It is not that everybody who misunderstood you will eventually apologize.
Our hope is greater.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him has a hope no storm, accusation, failure, grave, devil, or serpent can ultimately destroy.
So perhaps tonight is your fire.
Perhaps tonight is where you finally stop carrying what should have been surrendered years ago.
Let the bitterness fall.
Let the secret life come into the light.
Let the shame lose its throne.
Let repentance become more than a word.
Let grace become more than a doctrine you quote for other people.
Come to Christ yourself.
The snake may explain part of what happened to you.
It does not get to write the ending.
The storm may explain why you are tired.
It does not get to name you.
Your scandal may explain yesterday.
It does not possess tomorrow.

Because when Jesus Christ takes hold of a surrendered life, even the chapter you thought would permanently disqualify you can become the place where somebody else discovers what grace actually looks like.
And maybe the most powerful thing you will ever do with the thing that tried to poison your future…
is finally stop carrying it.
Shake it into the fire.
Then keep walking with Jesus.
The venom may have touched your story—but it does not get to hold the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET YOUR FOUNTAIN BE BLESSED”: What Proverbs Really Means About Marriage, Desire, and the Sexuality God Refuses to Be Ashamed Of
paragraphs: “LET YOUR FOUNTAIN BE BLESSED”: What Proverbs Really Means About Marriage, Desire, and the Sexuality God Refuses to Be Ashamed Of

Proverbs 5:18 is not an embarrassed whisper about sex. It is a startling invitation to discover why God created marital desire, why lust can never satisfy what it promises, and why even a sexually broken past does not have to write the final chapter of your story.
There are Bible verses people read quickly because reading them slowly would make them uncomfortable.
Proverbs 5:18 is one of them.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
We can read those words in church.
We can underline them.
We can quote them at a wedding.
But sit with them long enough and something becomes impossible to ignore:
God is talking about sexuality.
Not Satan.
Not Hollywood.
Not pornography.
Not modern culture.
God.
And He is not speaking as though marital desire were a dirty secret He reluctantly tolerates.
He speaks of blessing.
He speaks of rejoicing.
He speaks of a husband delighting in his wife.
And when you understand the verses surrounding Proverbs 5:18, the passage becomes even more striking.
Because this is not merely a romantic proverb.
It is a warning delivered while a man is standing dangerously close to destroying his own life.
Maybe that is why somebody reading this right now needs to keep reading.
Because perhaps nobody knows what you have been looking at.
Nobody knows about the messages.
Nobody knows about the fantasy you keep returning to.
Nobody knows how lonely your marriage has become.
Nobody knows what happened to you before marriage.
Nobody knows what you did after marriage.
Nobody knows why you delete the history.
Nobody knows why certain memories still make you feel dirty.
Nobody knows why you can worship Jesus on Sunday and still feel ashamed of what happens inside your mind on Monday night.
But God knows.
And remarkably, Proverbs 5 does not begin by telling sexually tempted people that desire itself is the enemy.
It teaches us that desire needs a holy home.
Listen to the Hebrew of Proverbs 5:18:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yəhî-məqōrəkhā bārūkh, ūśəmaḥ mēʾēšet nəʿūrekhā.
A careful rendering is:
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
That word translated “fountain” is מָקוֹר — māqôr.
A fountain.
A spring.
A source from which something flows.

Within the imagery of Proverbs 5, water language becomes intimate language. The chapter speaks of drinking water from your own cistern, of springs, fountains, and streams. Then comes the command to rejoice in the wife of your youth.
The imagery is poetic, but the message is not vague.
God is calling a husband away from sexual unfaithfulness and toward joyful, exclusive, covenant faithfulness with his wife.
And notice something beautiful.
The text does not merely say:
“Do not commit adultery.”
It says:
Rejoice.
That changes the conversation.
Biblical holiness is not simply the absence of forbidden pleasure.
It is learning to receive good pleasure in the place God designed it to flourish.
That means Christianity does not teach that sex is inherently filthy.
Sin corrupts sexuality.
Lust distorts sexuality.
Adultery betrays sexuality.
Pornography can train sexuality away from covenant love and toward consumption.
Exploitation weaponizes sexuality.
But God created humanity male and female before Genesis ever recorded the fall.
Marriage did not crawl out of humanity's rebellion.
It existed in Eden.
Genesis describes husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
Then Scripture says something our shame-saturated culture—and sometimes our shame-saturated churches—can struggle to say without embarrassment:
They were naked and were not ashamed.
Think about that.
Before sin introduced hiding, there was nakedness without shame.
Then sin came.
And almost immediately, people began covering and hiding.
That pattern has never really stopped.
We hide bodies.
We hide wounds.
We hide browsing histories.
We hide affairs.
We hide fantasies.
We hide sexual trauma.
We hide dissatisfaction.
We hide addictions.
We hide the fact that sometimes husband and wife can sleep inches apart while emotionally living miles away.
We hide because shame whispers:
If anybody really knew you, they would never look at you the same way again.
And eventually shame tries to make us believe God feels the same way.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
Jesus already knows.
That is simultaneously terrifying...
and unbelievably beautiful.
Because the One who knows the whole story is the One who walked toward the cross.
Proverbs 5 itself is painfully realistic about temptation.

The chapter begins with a warning about forbidden sexual attraction. What initially tastes sweet eventually becomes bitter. What looks like freedom can become bondage. What promises intimacy can leave devastation behind.
That pattern is ancient.
Only the technology changed.
The human heart did not.
The forbidden woman of Proverbs did not have Instagram.
She did not have encrypted messaging.
She did not appear through a glowing screen at 1:17 in the morning.
There were no dating apps sitting secretly inside a married person's phone.
There were no private browser tabs delivering thousands of sexually explicit images within seconds.
But Proverbs understood something about human desire long before smartphones existed:
Forbidden pleasure becomes powerful when we stare only at the invitation and refuse to imagine the destination.
That is why wisdom makes us look beyond the moment.
Sin says:
Just tonight.
Wisdom asks:
And then what?
Lust says:
Nobody will know.
Wisdom asks:
What is this doing to your heart?
Temptation says:
You deserve this.
Wisdom asks:
What will this cost the people who trusted you?
Sin shows you the entrance.
God loves you enough to show you where the road leads.
And then, in the middle of the warning, Proverbs does something magnificent.
It turns the man's eyes homeward.
Drink from your own cistern.
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Be captivated by covenant love.
In other words:
Stop searching in forbidden places for what God designed to flourish through faithful love.
There is something deeply countercultural here.
Our culture frequently treats sexual freedom as having access to as many choices as possible.
Biblical wisdom describes freedom differently.
Freedom is not being enslaved to every appetite demanding satisfaction.
Freedom is being able to say:
My desire does not own me. Christ does.
That does not make marital sexuality cold, mechanical, or merely dutiful.
Read Proverbs 5:18–19 carefully.
The language is affectionate.
Physical.
Joyful.
Passionate.
The Bible is not embarrassed by marital desire.
And neither should Christians be.
But we must also understand what the passage is not saying.
It is not permission for a husband to treat his wife as an object created for his gratification.
A covenant is not consumption.
Biblical marriage is not “I possess your body, therefore you owe me whatever I want.”
The New Testament destroys that selfish reading.

When Paul discusses marital intimacy in 1 Corinthians 7, he speaks in astonishingly reciprocal language. Husband and wife owe marital affection to one another, and Paul applies bodily responsibility mutually—not merely to the woman.
And Ephesians 5 goes deeper still.
A Christian husband is commanded to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.
That is cruciform love.
Sacrificial love.
A love that does not ask first:
“What can I take from you?”
It asks:
“How can I lay myself down for your good?”
That changes sexuality.
Because Christ-centered marital intimacy cannot be separated from Christ-centered love.
Tenderness matters.
Trust matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Patience matters.
Safety matters.
Mutual care matters.
Listening matters.
The person beside you is not pornography with a pulse.
Your spouse bears the image of God.
And perhaps that sentence exposes one of the great lies of lust.
Lust teaches us to look at a human being and see a body.
Jesus teaches us to look at a body and remember there is a human being.
A soul.
A history.
A person God sees.
A person Christ considered worth dying for.
Pornography says, “Consume.”
Covenant says, “Cherish.”
Adultery says, “Take.”
Covenant says, “Remain faithful.”
Lust asks, “What can this person give me?”
Love asks, “How can I seek this person's good?”
And perhaps now Proverbs 5:18 sounds different.
“Let your fountain be blessed.”
Not poisoned.
Not scattered everywhere.
Not secretly divided among strangers.
Blessed.
Then:
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
There is another word here worth noticing.
שָׂמַח — śāmaḥ.
Rejoice.
Be glad.
Take joy.
God is not merely protecting marriage from something.
He is protecting something for marriage.
Joy.
Trust.
Exclusivity.
Intimacy.
A shared history that becomes increasingly precious precisely because it was not disposable.
And yet...
this is where somebody's heart sinks.
Because maybe you already crossed the line.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe yesterday.
Maybe before you came to Christ.
Maybe after.
Maybe your story does not sound like Proverbs 5:18.
Maybe it sounds like Proverbs 5's warning.
And now you are wondering whether an article about sexual holiness has anything left to say to someone who was not holy.
It does.
Because Proverbs tells us what wisdom looks like.
But the Gospel tells us what God does with sinners who have failed to live wisely.
And this is where Jesus becomes more than a moral teacher.
He becomes our only hope.
There was a woman in John 4 whose relationship history was complicated enough that Jesus could have reduced her to it.
He did not.
He told the truth about her life.
He did not pretend sin did not matter.
But He also did not treat her as disposable.
He offered living water.
There was another woman in John 8 publicly exposed in sexual sin.
Her accusers wanted a spectacle.
Jesus would not join their cruelty.
Neither did He rename sin as righteousness.
Grace and truth stood together.
“No condemnation” was not permission to continue unchanged.
Mercy opened the door to a different life.
That is the Jesus sinners still meet.
He does not save us by pretending darkness is light.
He saves us by entering our darkness and bringing us into His light.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not God saying:
“What you did doesn't matter.”
Grace is God saying:
“What you did matters so much that My Son went to a cross—and My mercy is so great that your sin does not have to own you anymore.”
This is why the cross is scandalous.
Jesus Christ, the sinless One, bears judgment for sinners.
The innocent dies for the guilty.
The Holy One receives what rebels deserve.
And those who repent and trust in Christ receive what they could never earn.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Reconciliation.
A new identity.
A new heart.
A new direction.
Not because sexual sin is insignificant.
Because the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
Maybe you have committed adultery.
Repentance is possible.
Maybe pornography has had you chained for years.
Freedom is worth fighting for.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.

Restoration may require confession, patience, counseling, accountability, forgiveness, rebuilt trust, and a long road rather than one emotional night—but broken does not automatically mean beyond redemption.
Maybe you are single.

Proverbs 5 does not mean you are incomplete because you do not have a spouse. Jesus Himself lived without marriage, and the New Testament honors singleness as a legitimate calling. Sexual holiness for the unmarried is not meaningless deprivation; it is fidelity to Christ with the body entrusted to you.
Maybe you are widowed.
Maybe divorced.
Maybe betrayed.
Maybe your spouse abandoned the covenant while you desperately wanted to save it.
This passage is not a weapon God gave people so they could crush those already bleeding.
And if sexual abuse is part of your story, hear this clearly:
Someone else's violence against you is not your sexual sin.
Biblical teaching about marriage must never be twisted into a command to tolerate coercion, violence, exploitation, or abuse.
God's design for sexuality is not the protection of predators.
It is holiness expressed through covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, truth, dignity, and care.
And perhaps the hardest person for you to think about right now is yourself.
You believe Jesus forgives other people.
You just cannot imagine Him forgiving that.
You know the verse.
You know the theology.
You can explain grace to somebody else.
But when the room becomes quiet, you still remember.
And shame sits beside you.
Listen carefully.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, your darkest chapter does not outrank His cross.
The Gospel does not say you never sinned.
It says your sin does not get the final word.
The Gospel does not erase repentance.
It creates repentance.
It does not make holiness unnecessary.
It makes holiness possible.
It does not tell you to celebrate the chains Jesus died to break.
It tells you that the prison door is open.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek accountability where needed.
Ask forgiveness where appropriate.
Get serious about removing access to what repeatedly drags you into sin.
Fight for your marriage.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your conversations.
Guard the little compromises that nobody else notices yet.
Because almost nobody wakes up one morning and randomly destroys twenty years of marriage.
There are usually smaller funerals first.
A boundary dies.
Then honesty.
Then secrecy becomes normal.
Then somebody else's attention starts feeling intoxicating.
Then rationalization arrives.
“We're just friends.”
“My spouse doesn't understand me.”
“Nothing physical happened.”
“I deserve to feel wanted.”
“It's only online.”
And eventually people discover that a thousand tiny permissions can build a road toward something they once swore they would never do.
So guard the fountain.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because God understands its power.
Not because marriage makes temptation disappear.
Because covenant gives desire somewhere holy to belong.
Not because your spouse will always satisfy every emotional longing.
No human being can carry the weight that belongs to Christ alone.
Your spouse is not your Savior.
Your husband cannot be Jesus for you.
Your wife cannot be Jesus for you.
Marriage is precious.
Christ is ultimate.
And this is perhaps the deepest truth underneath Proverbs 5.
Every earthly fountain eventually reveals its limits.
Beauty ages.
Bodies change.
Hormones change.
Health changes.
Marriage goes through seasons.
Romance rises and falls.
But Christ remains.
You can have a passionate marriage and still desperately need Jesus.
You can be single and profoundly whole in Jesus.
You can have a sexually broken past and become holy through Jesus.
You can be betrayed and still be held by Jesus.
You can repent after catastrophic failure and discover that Jesus does not specialize in cosmetic improvement.
He raises dead things.
That is Christianity.
Not behavior modification wearing church clothes.
Resurrection.
Maybe this article found you before you crossed a line.
Then hear it as mercy.
Run before you have to crawl home wounded.
Maybe it found you while you are crossing the line.
Then stop calling bondage freedom.
Come into the light.
Maybe it found you after everything exploded.
Then do not confuse consequences with abandonment.
Repentance does not always remove earthly consequences, and rebuilding trust may take time.
But Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Maybe it found you while you were quietly starving inside your marriage.
Then have the conversation you keep postponing.
Not with accusation.
Not with comparison.
Not with fantasy.
With truth.
Ask what has been hurting.
Listen.
Pray.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help where needed.
Learn each other again.
Remember why covenant matters when feelings fluctuate.
And if you are the person hiding something...
perhaps today is the day hiding begins to die.
Not because public humiliation saves anybody.
It does not.
Jesus saves.
But secrecy gives sin oxygen.
Bring darkness into wise, appropriate light.
There may be tears.
There may be difficult conversations.
There may be consequences.
But there can also be grace.
Because your story does not have to end where your sin wanted to take it.
That is not permission to romanticize scandal.
It is a celebration of the Savior who can redeem sinners from it.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling adultery faithfulness.
Not by calling lust love.
Not by calling bondage freedom.
He rewrites us by forgiving what we confess, transforming what sin distorted, and teaching redeemed people how to walk differently.
Be honest.
If your marriage needs prayer, simply write:

And if Christ has already brought you through sexual brokenness, betrayal, addiction, shame, or a season when you thought restoration was impossible, consider leaving a testimony—not graphic details, not another person's private story, but enough to remind somebody drowning in shame that Jesus still restores people.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to know they are not the only person fighting.
Somebody may be sitting beside a sleeping spouse while talking privately to someone they should not be talking to.
Somebody may be drowning in pornography and convinced no serious Christian struggles like they do.
Somebody may believe sexual failure permanently disqualified them from coming home to God.
Put truth where darkness can find it.
Send it privately to the friend who does not need another lecture but desperately needs to remember Jesus.
Temptation has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made obvious today.
Come back when you need the reminder:
The forbidden fountain cannot give you what it promised.
But hear this carefully, because Scripture matters more than marketing:
Nor should anyone be pressured into giving.
Paul's words about Christian generosity are explicit:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each person according to what he has determined in his heart... not under compulsion.
God loves willing generosity, not spiritual manipulation.
So support your local church faithfully and practice generosity as Scripture and Christian conscience direct you.
Your sharing helps truth travel farther.
Your prayers matter.
Your comments help create a community where struggling people realize they are not fighting alone.
whether you share publicly or send this quietly to one person...
do not miss the greater invitation.
Come home to Christ.
Because eventually this is not primarily about sex.
It is about worship.
It is about what gets your eyes.
What gets your imagination.
What gets your secret affection.
What gets your body.
What gets your loyalty.
What gets your heart.
And Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make you slightly more respectable while your secret chains remained untouched.
He came to redeem you.
All of you.
Even the rooms you keep locked.
Even the memories you wish you could erase.
Even the desires you are afraid to confess.
Even the marriage you fear cannot be repaired.
Even the shame you have carried so long that it feels like your name.
The fountain can be guarded.
The covenant can be honored.
The wandering heart can repent.
The wounded can seek healing.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come into the light.
And the sinner can discover that Jesus Christ is still better than everything sin promised.
So rejoice in what God calls good.
Run from what destroys.
Love instead of consuming.
Cherish instead of using.
Repent instead of hiding.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek restoration where restoration is possible.
And when shame tries to introduce you by the worst thing you have ever done, remember the name Jesus speaks over everyone who belongs to Him:
Redeemed.
Maybe your fountain has been polluted.
Maybe your covenant has been wounded.
Maybe your history has pages you would burn if you could.
But the cross stands precisely where sinners run out of ways to rewrite themselves.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the cross—but grace decides who walks away from it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Being Nice the Same as Being Christlike?
paragraphs:
Is Being Nice the Same as Being Christlike?
The Comfortable Lie That Could Be Keeping You From Becoming Like Jesus
You can be nice and still be nowhere near Jesus.
That sentence may bother you.
Maybe it should.
Because somewhere along the way, many of us quietly replaced Christlikeness with niceness.
We learned to smile.
We learned not to offend anyone.
We learned how to say, “God bless you.”
We learned how to appear patient when people were watching.
We learned how to avoid uncomfortable conversations.
We learned how to keep the peace, protect our reputation, and make sure everyone walked away thinking we were good people.
And eventually, without realizing it, we began measuring spiritual maturity by how pleasant we appeared.
But then you open the Gospels.
And Jesus ruins that definition.
Jesus was compassionate beyond anything this world had ever seen, but He was not controlled by people's approval.
He touched lepers others avoided.
He welcomed children others considered interruptions.
He defended the vulnerable.
He wept with grieving people.
He fed the hungry.
He forgave sinners.
He washed the feet of men who should have been washing His.
Yet this same Jesus looked religious hypocrites in the eyes and called them what they were.
He overturned tables.
He confronted exploitation.
He exposed hidden motives.
He told comfortable people uncomfortable truth.
He loved a rich young ruler enough to put His finger directly on the idol that owned his heart.
He told a woman caught in sin neither, “You are disgusting,” nor, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
He gave her mercy...
and then called her away from sin.
Jesus was infinitely loving.
But biblical love is not the same thing as being agreeable.
And that distinction might expose something in us.
Because sometimes what we call “being nice” is actually fear.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of confrontation.
Fear of losing friends.
Fear of being misunderstood.
Fear that someone will unfollow us.
Fear that our family will think we've become “too serious about God.”
Fear that obedience might cost us the comfortable version of Christianity we have built around ourselves.
So we remain silent when love should speak.
We laugh at what grieves God because we don't want the room to become awkward.
We watch someone we love destroy themselves and convince ourselves that saying nothing is “kind.”
We soften repentance until repentance means nothing.
We speak endlessly about God's acceptance while becoming strangely embarrassed by His holiness.
We want Jesus as Savior...
but sometimes we edit Him as Lord.
That isn't Christlikeness.
It is approval-seeking wearing Christian clothes.
There is a Greek word in the New Testament that helps us see the difference.
In Ephesians 4:15, Paul speaks about:
“ἀληθεύοντες δὲ ἐν ἀγάπῃ”
alētheuontes de en agapē
The thought is commonly expressed as “speaking the truth in love.”
Notice what Christianity refuses to separate.
Truth.
And love.
Not truth without love.
Not love emptied of truth.
Truth in love.
That changes everything.
Truth without love can become cruelty.
Love without truth can become sentimental permission for destruction.
But when truth and love meet under the lordship of Jesus Christ, something beautiful happens.
Grace does not pretend the wound isn't there.
Grace enters the wound to heal it.
Think about a doctor discovering something dangerous in your body.
Imagine the doctor looking at the scan, seeing the disease, smiling politely, and saying:
“Everything looks wonderful. I didn't want to upset you.”
Would you call that kindness?
Of course not.
You would call it betrayal.
Why?
Because love tells the truth when the truth can save someone.
Yet many Christians have somehow accepted a definition of love that would make a truthful doctor seem cruel and a dishonest doctor compassionate.
Jesus never loved that way.
Look at the woman at the well in John 4.
Her story was complicated.
Five husbands.
The man she was currently with was not her husband.
A history carrying enough brokenness for generations of sermons to speculate about her.
And there she was...
at a well...
talking to Jesus.
Watch Him carefully.
Jesus did not humiliate her.
He did not reduce her to her sexual history.
He did not treat her as contaminated.
He did not make her earn the privilege of speaking with Him.
But neither did He pretend her life was whole.
He brought the hidden places into the light.
And remarkably, she ran back toward the very community from which she seemed socially separated and said:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?”
Think about that.
She had been exposed...
but somehow she did not feel discarded.
That is what happens when truth comes through Jesus.
The truth exposes you without abandoning you.
Convicts you without crushing you.
Calls your sin what it is without declaring that your sin must be the final chapter of your life.
That is the Gospel.
And that is where being merely “nice” falls painfully short.
Niceness often says:
“I don't want you to feel uncomfortable.”
Christlike love says:
“I care too much about you to watch you walk toward destruction without reaching for you.”
Niceness asks:
“What will make this interaction easiest?”
Christlikeness asks:
“What would love require of me?”
Sometimes the answer is gentleness.
Sometimes silence.
Sometimes patience.
Sometimes listening for an hour without trying to fix someone.
Sometimes giving money without announcing it.
Sometimes forgiving someone who never deserved another ounce of mercy from you.
And sometimes...
love has to tell the truth.
Not arrogantly.
Not with a Bible used like a hammer.
Not with the smug satisfaction of someone who enjoys being right.
But trembling.
Prayerfully.
Humbly.
With tears if necessary.
Because Christians should never speak about another person's sin as though we have forgotten the Cross that was required for ours.
Before you expose someone's darkness, remember yours.
Before you condemn someone's failure, remember Peter.
Peter promised loyalty.
Peter sounded brave.
Peter believed he was ready to die beside Jesus.
Then the pressure came.
A servant girl asked a question.
And the courageous disciple collapsed.
Three times.
“I don't know Him.”
Imagine that moment.
Jesus had called him.
Jesus had taught him.
Peter had watched miracles with his own eyes.
He had walked on water toward Christ.
He had seen the transfiguration.
And when loyalty became expensive...
Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
If Christianity were merely a religion of good behavior, Peter's story should have ended beside that fire.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Disqualified.
Finished.
But Jesus rewrites everything.
After the resurrection, John 21 takes us to another charcoal fire.
That detail matters.
Peter's shame had a smell.
Smoke.
Fire.
Memory.
Failure.
And Jesus walked directly into the place Peter probably wanted desperately to forget.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
Again.
“Lovest thou me?”
Again.
“Lovest thou me?”
Three denials.
Three questions.
And restoration.
Jesus did not restore Peter by pretending the denial never happened.
He restored him by confronting the heart beneath it and calling him forward again.
“Feed my sheep.”
This is grace.
Grace isn't God looking at sin and shrugging.
Grace is God looking directly at sinners and offering what sinners could never manufacture for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Restoration.
A new beginning.
A new heart.
A new direction.
A new Master.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people can become slightly nicer.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because the sinless Son of God took their judgment upon Himself.
At the Cross, Jesus was not demonstrating mere niceness.
He was demonstrating holy, sacrificial love.
Our sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
God's love was great enough that Christ willingly came.
That is why the Gospel can never honestly say, “You're fine exactly as you are; nothing needs to change.”
But neither does the Gospel say, “Clean yourself up and perhaps Jesus will finally want you.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
Come to Christ.
Come guilty.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with the addiction you keep hiding.
Come with the bitterness you have justified for years.
Come with the browser history nobody knows about.
Come with the affair.
Come with the pride.
Come with the jealousy.
Come with the secret messages.
Come with the religious performance.
Come with the resentment.
Come with the prayerlessness.
Come with the hypocrisy.
Come with the thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
But come ready to surrender it.
Because Jesus does not merely improve sinners.
He saves them.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō — carrying the idea of a changed mind, a turning of one's thinking and direction.
Biblical repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns toward God.
It stops negotiating with sin.
It stops asking how close to darkness we can stand while still calling ourselves Christians.
It says:
“Jesus, You are right. I am wrong. Have mercy on me. Change me.”
And He is merciful.
This is where some of us need to stop reading for everyone else.
Don't think about the person you wish would see this article.
Don't think about your spouse.
Your ex.
Your pastor.
Your rebellious child.
Your judgmental relative.
Your lukewarm Christian friend.
For a moment...
just you.
Are you actually becoming like Jesus?
Or have you simply become good at looking nice?
Because they are not the same.
You can smile and harbor hatred.
You can avoid arguments and still refuse to forgive.
You can give compliments and secretly envy the person receiving them.
You can attend church and crave human approval more than God's approval.
You can share Bible verses and never obey the ones that confront you.
You can say, “I'll pray for you,” because you don't know what else to say...
and never pray.
You can look gentle while being spiritually indifferent.
You can be considered a wonderful person by almost everyone who knows you...
and still keep Jesus outside locked rooms in your heart.
Jesus addressed something painfully similar when He spoke about religious people who looked clean outwardly while corruption remained within.
Christ is not interested in polishing the mask.
He wants the heart.
The Greek word used repeatedly in the New Testament for hypocrite is ὑποκριτής — hypokritēs.
It came to carry the sense of a pretender, one playing a part.
An actor.
And perhaps that is what makes this question so uncomfortable.
How much of our Christianity has become performance?
The church voice.
The Christian caption.
The worship song playing in the car.
The inspirational post.
The carefully selected verse.
Meanwhile...
God knows what happens when the screen goes dark.
God knows what we replay in our minds.
God knows whom we refuse to forgive.
God knows what we delete.
God knows what we secretly desire.
God knows where our money goes.
God knows what our public kindness is hiding.
God knows whether we want holiness...
or merely a holy reputation.
And somehow, astonishingly, He still calls us to come.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that baptizes rebellion.
Grace that brings sinners out of hiding.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογέω — homologeō.
At its heart is the idea of acknowledging, agreeing, confessing.
We stop rewriting the charges.
We stop defending ourselves.
We stop saying, “Everyone does it.”
We stop saying, “That's just how I am.”
We stop saying, “At least I'm better than them.”
We agree with God.
Sin is sin.
And mercy is mercy.
Then something extraordinary happens.
The person who comes into the light discovers that Jesus was already there.
Maybe you have spent years trying to be “nice” because deep inside you are terrified that if people saw the real you, they would leave.
So you became useful.
Agreeable.
Funny.
Generous.
Easygoing.
Always available.
Never angry.
Never needy.
Never honest.
You learned to say “I'm fine” while breaking internally.
Maybe niceness became your armor.
If everyone likes me...
maybe nobody will leave me.
If I never disappoint anyone...
maybe I will finally feel worthy.
If I keep everyone happy...
maybe I'll be safe.
But Jesus did not die so you could spend your entire life auditioning for human approval.
Your identity is not secured by everyone liking you.
And becoming Christlike will sometimes mean disappointing people who preferred the version of you they could control.
Jesus Himself said in John 15:18 that the world hated Him.
So the goal of Christian maturity cannot possibly be universal approval.
But be careful here.
Being disliked does not automatically mean you are being persecuted for righteousness.
Sometimes people dislike Christians because Christians are behaving badly.
Cruelty is not courage.
Arrogance is not boldness.
Insulting people is not evangelism.
Winning an argument is not the same as winning a soul.
