Being obnoxious is not evidence that you are carrying a cross.
Scripture gives us a far more demanding picture.
Galatians 5 describes the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, and temperance.
Christlike people should therefore become profoundly kind.
Patient.
Gentle.
Merciful.
But those qualities grow from the Holy Spirit, not from an addiction to approval.
That distinction is enormous.
People-pleasing niceness says:
“I will be kind so you will accept me.”
Christlike kindness says:
“Because Christ has loved me, I can love you even when you reject me.”
People-pleasing says:
“I cannot tell you the truth because I might lose you.”
Christlike love says:
“I will tell you the truth gently because losing your approval is less frightening than watching you destroy yourself.”
People-pleasing says:
“I need everyone to think I am good.”
The Gospel says:
“There is none righteous, no, not one.”
And then points us toward the only truly Righteous One.
Jesus.
That is freedom.
You no longer have to manufacture a spotless image.
Jesus already knows the scandal.
He knows everything.
And the Gospel is the announcement that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Ask Peter.
Ask the woman at the well.
Ask Zacchaeus.
Ask the thief dying beside Christ.
Ask Saul of Tarsus, who went from persecuting Christians to proclaiming the Christ he once opposed.
The Bible is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
But grace interrupted.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal wasn't real.
By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
Maybe that's why you're still reading.
Maybe beneath all the theological language and religious vocabulary, one question has been following you through every paragraph:
Does Jesus still want me?
After what I've done?
After how long I've pretended?
After promising God I would stop and going back again?
After becoming someone I barely recognize?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin is insignificant.
It tells you that Christ is sufficient.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not reserved for people who have managed to become impressive enough for God.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
Then verse 10 reminds us that the saved life becomes a life created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us where it found us.
It transforms us.
So no...
being nice is not the same as being Christlike.
Christlikeness is deeper.
Costlier.
Holier.
More courageous.
More tender.
It means loving people who cannot repay you.
Forgiving when revenge would feel better.
Speaking truth when silence would protect your reputation.
Remaining silent when your ego desperately wants the last word.
Serving when nobody applauds.
Repenting when you are wrong.
Giving without needing recognition.
Refusing to compromise just because compromise would make people comfortable.
Showing mercy because you remember how desperately you needed mercy.
Standing for truth without becoming hateful toward the people you hope that truth will rescue.
And above everything else...
following Jesus when following Him costs something.
So ask yourself one question tonight.
Not, “Am I nice?”
Ask:
“Am I becoming like Christ?”
And don't rush your answer.
Sit with it.
Let God search the places behind your public Christianity.
The Psalmist prayed:
“חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי”
Chaqreni El, veda levavi.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
That prayer from Psalm 139 is dangerous in the best possible way.
Because once you invite God into the rooms you have been protecting, you may discover things that need surrendering.
But you will also discover that the One searching you is the One who can transform you.
So pray it.
Search me, God.
Show me where kindness has become cowardice.
Show me where conviction has become cruelty.
Show me where I want applause more than obedience.
Show me where I am pretending.
Show me whom I need to forgive.
Show me whom I need to ask forgiveness from.
Show me what I need to confess.
Show me where I have been merely nice...
when You called me to become like Jesus.
And then give Him permission to rewrite the story.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished Christian response.
Be honest.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop suffering alone.
And when you see someone else write those words, don't judge them.
Pray for them.
That is what Christian community should look like.
If one person came to your mind while reading this, don't use this article as a weapon against them.
They may never tell you.
Share it anyway.
Come back when you feel the pressure to choose popularity over obedience, harshness over gentleness, performance over repentance, or approval over Christ.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well.
The Gospel was never meant to terminate with us.
What God places in our hands can become something we place in someone else's.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money purchases spiritual blessing.
It doesn't.
They don't.
Jesus purchased our redemption with His blood; it cannot be bought with ours.
But Christians can glorify God by freely using their resources, voices, opportunities, generosity, and influence in ways that advance what is true and good.
And there is something larger behind the articles you see.
The goal is not merely more content.
It is deeper discipleship.
More Scripture opened.
More truth understood.
More wounded believers encouraged.
More wandering hearts pointed home.
More Christians equipped to follow Jesus when nobody is applauding.
Your hope is Jesus.
Your salvation is Jesus.
Your righteousness is Jesus.
Your forgiveness is found in Jesus.
Your transformation comes through Jesus.
Your story is ultimately about Jesus.
So share the Gospel.
Share truth.
Save what you need to remember.
Follow so you can keep growing with us.
But above all...
follow Christ.
Because at the end of your life, the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that some people didn't think you were nice.
It would be spending your life convincing everyone you were good while never surrendering the hidden heart to the only One who could make you new.
Jesus did not come to make your mask more convincing.
He came to call you out of the grave.
And maybe the part of your story you are most ashamed of is exactly where grace is about to write words you never thought could belong there:
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Restored.
His.
Your scandal may explain yesterday, but once Jesus takes the pen, it does not get to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PARABLE OF THE TEN VIRGINS IS MORE SOBERING THAN YOU REMEMBER
paragraphs: THE PARABLE OF THE TEN VIRGINS IS MORE SOBERING THAN YOU REMEMBER
The most frightening part of Matthew 25 is not that five women fell asleep. All ten did. The terrifying difference was revealed when somebody shouted in the darkness: “The bridegroom is coming.”
There is a sentence Jesus told His disciples that should make every person who calls himself or herself a Christian examine what is happening beneath the surface of their faith.
Not because Jesus wanted His followers terrified that He was unwilling to save them.
Not because salvation is earned by religious performance.
Not because one mistake can somehow overpower the blood of Christ.
But because it is possible to look ready for Jesus while living completely unprepared to meet Him.
That distinction is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Jesus said:
“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom.”
Ten virgins.
Ten lamps.
Ten people waiting for the same bridegroom.
Ten people who apparently expected him to come.
From a distance, there was almost nothing separating them.
And perhaps that is exactly why this parable is so disturbing.
Because Jesus did not describe five obvious enemies standing beside five faithful disciples.
He described ten people waiting.
Ten people carrying lamps.
Ten people who knew a bridegroom was coming.
Ten people who became tired.
Ten people who slept.
Ten people who eventually heard the announcement.
Yet only five entered the wedding feast.

If you have ever assumed that knowing Christian language, attending church, carrying a Bible, posting Scripture, listening to worship music, serving in ministry, growing up in a Christian family, or calling Jesus “Lord” automatically means your heart belongs to Him, do not rush past this parable.
Stay here.
Because before the story ends, a door closes.
And somebody standing outside that door is still saying,
“Lord, lord…”

Jesus tells this parable in Matthew 25:1–13, immediately following His teaching about His return and the necessity of watchfulness in Matthew 24. The context matters. This is not primarily a motivational story about being organized. It is an eschatological warning—a warning concerning readiness for the coming of the Son of Man.
The Greek opening is striking:
“Τότε ὁμοιωθήσεται ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν…”
“Then the kingdom of heaven will be compared to…”
Jesus places us inside a wedding scene.
The ten young women take their lamps and go out to meet the bridegroom. Five are described as wise and five as foolish.
The words are:
“πέντε δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἦσαν μωραὶ καὶ πέντε φρόνιμοι.”
Five were μωραί—mōrai, foolish.
Five were φρόνιμοι—phronimoi, prudent, sensible, wise.
And immediately Jesus tells us what separated them.
The foolish took their lamps.
But they did not take oil with them.
The wise took oil in containers along with their lamps.
That sounds like such a small difference.
Until midnight.
That is often how spiritual neglect works.
It looks small before the crisis.
A prayer life slowly disappearing.
Secret sin quietly being protected.
Conviction repeatedly postponed.
Forgiveness continually resisted.
Repentance always scheduled for later.
Jesus publicly confessed but privately ignored.
A heart becoming colder while the Christian vocabulary remains intact.
Nobody necessarily notices.
The lamp is still there.
The appearance is still there.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You still know the songs.
You can still quote verses.
You may even know exactly how to look spiritually alive.
But Jesus is not merely interested in whether you know how to carry a lamp.
He knows whether you belong to Him.
Then something happens in the parable that many people overlook.
The bridegroom delays.
Matthew writes:
“But while the bridegroom was delaying…”
And because he did not arrive when they expected, all ten became drowsy.
All ten slept.
Read that again.
The foolish slept.
But the wise slept too.
That matters because this parable is sometimes preached as though the wise virgins stayed awake all night while the foolish ones fell asleep.
That is not what Jesus said.
“ἐνύσταξαν πᾶσαι καὶ ἐκάθευδον.”
They all became drowsy and slept.
The decisive difference was not that one group possessed limitless physical stamina.
The difference was preparation.
The wise were ready for a delay.
Their readiness survived waiting.
And that speaks directly into a generation that has learned how to become excited about God but often struggles to endure with God.
It is one thing to cry during worship.
It is another thing to remain faithful when the emotion disappears.
It is one thing to promise Jesus everything after surviving a crisis.
It is another thing to walk with Him six months later when life feels ordinary again.
It is one thing to post, “God is good,” when the prayer is answered.
It is another thing to whisper, “Though He slay me, yet will I trust Him,” when heaven feels silent.
What happens to your faith when the Bridegroom seems delayed?
When you prayed and nothing changed?
When you obeyed and still suffered?
When somebody you loved died?
When the marriage did not heal the way you begged God to heal it?
When temptation came back?
When the excitement faded?
When you discovered that following Christ involves crosses as well as miracles?
That is where borrowed excitement stops being enough.
Midnight eventually comes.
And suddenly the silence is shattered.
“Ἰδοὺ ὁ νυμφίος, ἐξέρχεσθε εἰς ἀπάντησιν.”
“Behold, the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!”
Imagine that moment.
Eyes opening.
Feet hitting the ground.
Hands reaching for lamps.
Wicks being trimmed.
Hearts racing.
The waiting is over.
The bridegroom is here.
And suddenly something that had been invisible becomes painfully visible.
The foolish virgins realize their lamps are going out.
So they turn to the wise:
“Give us some of your oil.”
There is tragedy hidden inside that request.
Because there are things another Christian can share with you.
Someone can share Scripture with you.
Someone can preach to you.
Someone can pray for you.
Someone can disciple you.
Someone can encourage you.
Someone can tell you about Jesus.
Someone can sit beside your hospital bed and remind you of eternity.
Your grandmother can pray for you for thirty years.
Your pastor can preach Christ until his voice gives out.
Your spouse can plead with you to come home to God.
Your mother can put your name on every prayer list she can find.
Your friend can send you this article tonight.
But nobody can repent for you.
Nobody can believe in Christ for you.
Nobody can surrender your heart for you.
Nobody can have your relationship with Jesus on your behalf.
Christian parents cannot transfer salvation genetically.
A church cannot place Christ into an unrepentant heart through proximity.
And one believer's faithfulness cannot substitute for another person's unbelief.
There comes a point when borrowed Christianity is exposed.
This does not mean Christians should refuse to help others. Scripture repeatedly commands love, generosity, intercession, discipleship, correction, encouragement, and the proclamation of the Gospel.
The point is different.
There are realities of personal allegiance to Christ that cannot be transferred at the final moment.
And we should be careful here with the oil.

Throughout Christian history, interpreters have suggested various meanings for the oil. Some associate it with the Holy Spirit, others with genuine faith, persevering obedience, spiritual readiness, or the inward reality accompanying outward profession.
But Jesus does not explicitly stop the parable and say, “The oil represents this one specific thing.”
So we should not pretend He did.
The unmistakable emphasis is readiness.
Five were prepared for the bridegroom.
Five were not.
And when the bridegroom finally arrived, there was no longer time to manufacture yesterday's preparation.
While the foolish virgins went away to obtain oil, the bridegroom came.
Then Scripture says:
“καὶ αἱ ἕτοιμοι εἰσῆλθον μετ’ αὐτοῦ εἰς τοὺς γάμους…”
“And those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast.”
Those who were ready entered.
And then come five Greek words carrying enormous weight:
“καὶ ἐκλείσθη ἡ θύρα.”
“And the door was shut.”
The door.
Was.
Shut.
There are moments in Scripture when a short sentence feels heavier than an entire chapter.
This is one of them.
Because the Bible's message of grace is gloriously open.
Christ receives sinners.
Jesus ate with people respectable religion despised.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the broken.
He forgave the guilty.
He restored failures.
He told weary sinners to come.
The Gospel invitation goes into the world.
“Come.”
“Believe.”
“Repent.”
“Receive.”
Christ's mercy is greater than the scandal of your past.
But the Bible never teaches that the opportunity to repent should therefore be treated casually forever.
Grace is not permission to postpone Christ.
Grace is the reason to run to Him now.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 6:2:
There is an urgency to the Gospel precisely because eternity is real.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been postponing Jesus for years.
“Later.”
When I am older.
When I finish enjoying myself.
When I fix my life.
When I stop this addiction.
When I get married.
When the children grow up.
When business slows down.
When I have fewer problems.
When I finally feel spiritual.
Later.
Later.
Later.
But you were never promised later.
You were given today.
And Christianity is not ultimately about cleaning yourself enough to approach Jesus.
If you could save yourself, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
The Gospel says something far more astonishing.
You cannot make yourself righteous before God, so the righteous Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus lived the obedience we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
Your hope is not that you can accumulate enough religious oil to purchase heaven.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not the achievement of human boasting.
But saving grace does not leave a person permanently indifferent to the Savior.
Grace transforms.
Faith bears fruit.
The forgiven begin learning obedience.
The redeemed begin longing for the Redeemer.
Not perfectly.
Not without stumbling.
Not without battles.
But genuinely.
That is why this parable should not drive a sincere struggling Christian into obsessive terror every time they fail.
Peter failed spectacularly.
He denied Jesus three times.
And Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met him.
The disciples fled.
Christ gathered them again.
The Christian Gospel is not “Never stumble or Jesus will stop loving you.”
The Gospel is that sinners are saved by the grace of God through Christ—and those who belong to Christ are called to abide in Him, trust Him, follow Him, repent when they sin, and persevere in faith.
There is a difference between struggling with sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and deciding you no longer want to get up.
There is a difference between weakness that cries, “Jesus, help me,” and rebellion that says, “Jesus, leave me alone.”
Maybe you are tired.
Maybe your prayer life is barely a whisper.
Maybe you have been fighting the same temptation so long that you are embarrassed to tell anyone.
Maybe you opened this article feeling like a hypocrite.
Maybe nobody knows what happened last night.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is fine.
Maybe your children think your faith is strong.
Maybe your church friends see the smile but never see you crying in the car before walking through the doors.
Maybe your Bible has stayed closed longer than you want to admit.
Maybe you love Jesus, but your spirit feels exhausted.
Then hear this carefully:
The answer is not pretending harder.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Return to Christ.

First John 1:9 does not tell believers to hide their sin until they become impressive enough for God. It says that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
There is cleansing for the person willing to stop hiding.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is forgiveness for sinners.
There is a cross standing between your guilt and God's judgment.
And there is an empty tomb declaring that sin and death do not get the final word over those who are in Christ.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter's scandal did not become the final chapter.
The cross was not the end of the story.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority to write your ending when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But then Jesus brings the parable back to its terrifying conclusion.
The foolish virgins return.
The door has already closed.
And they cry:
“Κύριε κύριε, ἄνοιξον ἡμῖν.”
“Lord, lord, open to us.”
Notice what they call Him.
Lord.
That should sober every churchgoing person reading this.
Religious vocabulary alone is not saving faith.
Knowing what to call Jesus is not the same as belonging to Jesus.

The language also echoes another terrifying warning from Christ in Matthew 7:21–23, where people say, “Lord, Lord,” while Jesus exposes the absence of a genuine relationship expressed in obedience to the Father's will.
Then comes the answer nobody wants to imagine hearing:
“Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς.”
“Truly I say to you, I do not know you.”
Not:
“You did not collect enough achievements.”
Not:
“You were not famous enough.”
Not:
“You did not have enough followers.”
Not:
“You weren't successful enough.”
“I do not know you.”
Christianity reaches its center here.
Jesus.
Not merely information about Jesus.
Not Christian aesthetics.
Not denominational identity.
Not inherited religion.
Not public performance.
Jesus Christ Himself.
This is why eternal life is described relationally in John 17:3: knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent.
And this is why the question underneath the parable is far more personal than:
“Do you believe the Second Coming is real?”
The deeper question is:
Do you know the Bridegroom?
And does He know you as His own?
Then Jesus gives the command that should follow us long after we finish reading:
“Γρηγορεῖτε οὖν…”
Grēgoreite oun.
“Therefore, keep watch.”
“For you know neither the day nor the hour.”
Watch.
Not by staring nervously at the sky every morning.
Not by setting dates Jesus told us we do not know.
Not by turning every headline into speculative prophecy.
Watch by belonging faithfully to Christ.
Watch by refusing to make peace with hidden sin.
Watch by forgiving.
Watch by praying.
Watch by remaining in His Word.
Watch by loving your neighbor.
Watch by carrying the Gospel.
Watch by remembering that your possessions will stay here.
Your trophies will stay here.
Your titles will stay here.
Your house will belong to somebody else.
Your phone will eventually stop ringing.
Your social-media account will eventually become silent.
And one day somebody may speak about you in the past tense.
But Christ will still be King.
So what are you waiting for?
If you need to repent, repent now.
If you need to forgive, begin now.
If you need to confess something hidden, bring it into the light.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, stop treating eternity like an appointment you are guaranteed the opportunity to reschedule.
Come to Christ.
Not because you have become worthy.
Come because He is merciful.
Come because the cross is enough.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because the Bridegroom is worth knowing.
And if your heart is saying, “But you don't know what I've done…”
No.
I may not.
Jesus does.
The woman caught in sin had a scandal.
The thief beside Christ had a scandal.
Peter had a scandal.
Paul carried memories of persecuting the church.
The Bible is filled with people whose histories would have destroyed their reputations.
Then grace entered the story.
Grace did not rename evil as good.
Grace confronted sin, forgave sinners who came to God through faith, and created new lives.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not scandal to excuses.
Not scandal to religious camouflage.
Scandal to repentance.
Scandal to the cross.
Scandal to forgiveness.
Scandal to transformation.
Scandal to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe somebody came to your mind while you were reading.
Send it to them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not as a weapon.
Send it because you love them enough to want them at the wedding feast.
You do not know where this message will land.
So share it as mission, not marketing.
If your spirit has been exhausted lately, comment, “pray for me.”
If you have been fighting to remain faithful, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If Christ is exposing something you have been hiding, comment, “no more hiding.”
If you know God is still restoring your life, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if this brought you face-to-face with your need for mercy, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not because typing words into a comment box saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around ourselves.
And read the other comments.
Pray for somebody.
Encourage somebody.
Remind somebody that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is where the sinner stops running from the One who can save.
There may come a night when you need to read Matthew 25 again.
There may come a season when your lamp feels dim and waiting feels unbearably long.
Return to Jesus' words.
The Bridegroom may seem delayed.
But the Bridegroom has not forgotten His promise.
It does not purchase salvation, blessing, answered prayer, or a better standing before Christ. The Gospel cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel work can be an act of Christian generosity when it is done freely, joyfully, and for the glory of God.
But the greatest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is Jesus.

If this ministry continually turns your attention toward Christ, strengthens you in Scripture, challenges hidden compromise, encourages you when faith becomes difficult, and equips you to help another person find the Gospel, then consider becoming part of what keeps that work moving.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help carry the Gospel farther.
Pray for the people reading beside you.
And above everything else, follow Jesus.
Because eventually every lamp, every reputation, every religious appearance, every excuse, and every hidden chamber of the heart will encounter the same announcement:
The Bridegroom has come.
And when that moment arrives, you will not care how many people thought you looked Christian.
You will care about one thing.
Jesus.
So do not merely admire the lamp.
Know the Bridegroom.
Do not merely prepare your public image.
Bring Him your heart.
Do not wait until the door closes to become serious about the One standing on the other side.
Come while mercy is calling.
Come while grace is being offered.
Come with the addiction.
Come with the shame.
Come with the questions.
Come with the secret.
Come with the years you wasted.
Come with the failure you cannot undo.
Come with empty hands.
Come to the cross.
And discover that the Savior who warns us so seriously about the closed door is the same Savior who stretched His arms open on a cross to bring sinners home.
Perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying with you tonight:
Do not wait until midnight to discover that you spent your whole life carrying the lamp while never truly knowing the Bridegroom.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU CAN GO TO CHURCH EVERY SUNDAY AND STILL NOT KNOW JESUS
paragraphs: YOU CAN GO TO CHURCH EVERY SUNDAY AND STILL NOT KNOW JESUS

The most terrifying possibility is not that someone rejected Christianity. It is that they spent years around Christianity, learned its language, sat in its pews, sang its songs—and never truly knew Christ.
There is a seat in the church that remembers the shape of your body.
You have sat there so many Sundays that nobody questions whether you belong.
You know when to stand.
You know when to sit.
You know when the worship team is about to repeat the chorus.
You know when the preacher is getting ready to close.
You know how to bow your head when someone prays.
You know how to say, “God is good.”
You may own several Bibles.
You may have Christian songs saved on your phone.
You may post Scripture.
You may serve.
You may give.
You may have been baptized years ago.
People may even come to you when they need prayer.
And yet there is a question so serious that most of us would rather spend another decade being religious than sit alone long enough to answer it.
Do you actually know Jesus?
Not—
Do you know about Him?
Not—
Do you believe Christianity is true?
Not—
Does your family go to church?
Not—
Did you once walk down an aisle, raise a hand, repeat a prayer, or have an emotional experience?
But do you know Him?
Because according to Jesus Himself, it is possible to be astonishingly close to religious activity while remaining frighteningly far from Him.
And that should disturb every comfortable heart.
Jesus gave one of the most sobering warnings in the New Testament:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.”
Then He continued:
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?”
And then come words nobody who claims the name of Christ should read casually:
“And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Matthew 7:21–23.
Read that again carefully.
These were not people claiming atheism.
They called Him “Lord.”
The Greek intensifies the moment:
Κύριε, Κύριε — Kyrie, Kyrie — “Lord, Lord.”
There is urgency in it.
Recognition.
Religious vocabulary.
They even pointed toward works performed in His name.
But Jesus did not say, “I knew you once, but eventually I forgot you.”
The Greek text says:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς — oudepote egnōn hymas
“I never knew you.”
Never.
That word should stop us.
Because apparently a person can know the vocabulary without knowing the Voice.
A person can participate in Christian culture without belonging to Christ.
A person can become familiar with church without being transformed by the Gospel.
You can know the songs and still hide the sin.
You can carry a Bible and still refuse its authority.
You can lift your hands during worship while refusing to surrender what those hands keep reaching for Monday through Saturday.
You can know how Christians are supposed to sound while your private life tells another story.
And none of this means church attendance is bad.
Quite the opposite.

Scripture teaches believers not to forsake assembling together (Hebrews 10:25). The early church devoted itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42). Christians need the gathered church.
The danger is not going to church.
The danger is believing that going to church can substitute for knowing Christ.
A hospital is a wonderful place for a sick person to receive care.
But sleeping in the hospital parking lot does not make you a doctor.
Standing inside a church building does not make you spiritually alive.
Jesus confronted people who knew Scripture extraordinarily well and still missed the One to whom Scripture pointed.
He told them:
“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.”
Imagine that tragedy.
Studying words about eternal life...
while refusing to come to the One who gives it.
Knowing prophecy...
without knowing Christ.
Knowing doctrine...
without loving Christ.
Defending biblical truth publicly...
while resisting biblical truth privately.
Talking about grace...
without ever falling helplessly into it.
That is why this article is not an attack on churchgoers.
It is a mirror for every one of us.
For me.
For you.
For the preacher.
For the worship leader.
For the person in the back row.
For the person who has attended church for forty years.
For the person who started last Sunday.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about becoming better at appearing Christian.
It is about reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the hardest people to convince that they need rescuing are those who have learned how to look rescued.
Nicodemus knew something about that.
He was not the neighborhood scandal.
He was respectable.
Religious.
Educated.
A Pharisee.
A ruler among the Jews.
And when he came to Jesus, Christ did not congratulate him for having accumulated enough religion.
Jesus shattered his confidence with words that still confront religious hearts:
“Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.”
John 3:3.
The Greek phrase translated “born again” is:
γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν — gennēthē anōthen
The word ἄνωθεν — anōthen can carry the sense of “again” and “from above.”
Nicodemus needed something religion could not manufacture.
Life from above.
Not behavior modification.
Not reputation management.
Not a cleaner religious résumé.
New life.
This is where Christianity becomes deeply uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve the version of you that everybody sees.
He came because the deepest problem is something you cannot repair yourself.
Sin.
Not merely mistakes.
Not merely imperfections.
Sin.
The Hebrew Scriptures use the word חָטָא — chata, with the basic idea of sinning or missing what is right.
The New Testament frequently uses ἁμαρτία — hamartia, “sin.”
But biblical sin is more than occasionally doing something regrettable.
It is rebellion against the holy God who created us.
It reaches into desire, allegiance, worship, thought, motive, and action.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
All.
The hypocrite.
The addict.
The respectable church member.
The skeptic.
The pastor.
The person reading this with tears forming.
The person reading this defensively.
All.
That means your greatest problem is not that you need to become more religious.
Your greatest problem is that sin separates humanity from the holy God—and no amount of religious performance can erase guilt.
That is terrible news.
Until you see the cross.
Because Christianity does not announce that good people can climb high enough to reach God.
The Gospel announces that God came down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, entered human history.
He lived without sin.
He touched people religion avoided.
He ate with sinners.
He confronted hypocrites.
He welcomed the broken.
He called people to repentance.
He exposed darkness not because He delighted in humiliation, but because grace does not heal what pride insists on hiding.
Then the sinless Christ went to a Roman cross.
And something infinitely greater than another public execution was happening there.
Peter writes:
1 Peter 2:24.
Paul writes:
2 Corinthians 5:21.
Isaiah had written centuries earlier:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities...”
Isaiah 53:5.
The cross was not Jesus helping decent people become slightly better.
It was Christ giving Himself for sinners.
Your secret.
Your shame.
Your lust.
Your pride.
Your bitterness.
Your deception.
Your self-righteousness.
Your hidden addiction.
Your religious performance.
Your years of pretending.
Your attempts to bargain with God.
Your Sunday Christianity followed by Monday rebellion.
Bring all of it into the light.
Because there is something more powerful than your scandal.
Grace.
But biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Look at the cross and you will see exactly how seriously God takes sin.
Grace is costly.
Christ bore what sinners deserved so that those who trust in Him could receive what they could never earn.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Righteousness in Christ.
Adoption.
New life.
And the invitation of Jesus is not “Pretend harder.”
It is:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Mark 1:15.
The Greek word translated “repent” is:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite
It speaks of repentance—a changed mind that involves turning from sin toward God.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself sufficiently so Jesus will finally accept you.
You cannot.
It is the sinner dropping the weapons.
No more excuses.
No more hiding.
No more defending the darkness because admitting it feels too humiliating.
You come to Christ.
And this is where someone reading this may feel exposed.
You know how to look faithful.
But you know what happens when nobody is watching.
You know the browser history.
You know the conversations.
You know the bitterness you keep feeding.
You know the compromise you renamed “struggle” because calling it sin would require you to confront it.
You know how many times conviction came and you buried it beneath another worship song.
You know how easy it has become to say “Amen” without surrendering.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are spiritually strong.
But privately you are exhausted from maintaining the image.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
There is nothing hiding behind your smile that escaped His sight.
And still the Gospel is being proclaimed to you.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is great.
John writes:
1 John 1:9.
The Greek word for confess is related to ὁμολογέω — homologeō, carrying the idea of acknowledging or confessing.
Stop negotiating with what God has named.
Bring it into the light.
This may be the moment somebody finally whispers:
“Jesus, I have known church...
but I don't know whether I have known You.”
That sentence may hurt.
Say it anyway if it is true.
Christ is not threatened by your honesty.
The Gospel is for sinners.
Remember the criminal crucified beside Jesus.
No years of church attendance remained for him.
No opportunity to build a Christian reputation.
No decades available to impress anyone.
He could not climb down from his cross and spend the next thirty years proving he deserved salvation.
He had nothing to offer Christ except a guilty man’s desperate appeal:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.”
Luke 23:42.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
Luke 23:43.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not permission to continue loving sin.
Grace purchased by Christ.
Grace received by someone who had no religious résumé left to present.
Grace reaching a condemned man while nails held him to wood.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But notice something else.
The criminal did not merely add Jesus to an otherwise comfortable life.
He had reached the end of himself.
And perhaps that is where some of us need to arrive.
At the end of pretending.
At the end of “I’m fine.”
At the end of comparing ourselves with worse sinners so we can feel righteous.
At the end of believing that sitting beneath sermons automatically means we have surrendered to the Savior those sermons proclaim.
You can fool a congregation.
You can fool your Christian friends.
You can fool your family.
You can eventually become frighteningly good at fooling yourself.
But you cannot fool Jesus.
And strangely...
that is wonderful news.
Because the Jesus who sees everything is the same Jesus who receives repentant sinners.
You do not have to manufacture a cleaned-up version of yourself before coming.
Come honestly.
Come guilty.
Come tired.
Come ashamed.
Come with questions.
Come with your ruined reputation.
Come with your religious reputation.
Come with the part of your story you swore nobody would ever hear.
But come to Christ.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
John 6:37.
Do not confuse that grace with permission to remain unchanged.
When Christ saves, He becomes Lord.
Grace forgives us and begins transforming us.
Jesus said:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.”
John 14:15.
Obedience does not purchase salvation.
It is fruit, not the price.
Ephesians makes the order beautifully clear:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Then immediately:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works...”
Ephesians 2:8–10.
Saved by grace.
Not by works.
Saved for a transformed life in Christ.
That distinction matters.
Otherwise we turn Christianity into one of two distortions.
Either we say, “Perform enough and perhaps God will love you.”
That is not the Gospel.
Or we say, “Claim Jesus, continue embracing sin without repentance, and nothing needs to change.”
That is not the Gospel either.
Biblical Christianity says you cannot save yourself.
Christ saves sinners by grace.
And the Christ who saves also calls us to follow Him.
This is why the question is deeper than, “Did you attend church this week?”
The question is:
Who is Jesus to you?
A tradition?
An accessory?
A Sunday appointment?
A name you use when life collapses?
A theological subject?
A childhood memory?
Or your Savior and Lord?
Paul gave the Corinthians this sobering instruction:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.”
2 Corinthians 13:5.
Not examine everybody else.
Yourself.
So forget the person you were about to send this article to for thirty seconds.
Forget your spouse.
Forget your rebellious child.
Forget the hypocrite you know.
Forget that church member whose life frustrates you.
Stand alone before the question.
Do I know Jesus?
Has there been repentance?
Am I trusting Christ, or am I trusting my religious history?
When I sin, do I justify darkness or bring it into His light?
Do I want Jesus Himself—or merely the comfort, community, blessings, identity, and appearance associated with Christianity?
Do I love the Savior, or have I simply become accustomed to His name?
You do not need to answer publicly to impress anyone.
But answer before God.
And if something inside you is breaking right now, do not run from that conviction.
Run to Christ.
You can pray, but understand this carefully: there is no magical arrangement of words that purchases salvation.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ.
Speak honestly to Him.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Place your trust in the crucified and risen Jesus.
Ask Him for mercy.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose from the dead.
Christianity stands upon a living Christ.
And because He lives, your story does not have to end where your sin left it.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated past.
Zacchaeus had exploited people.
The thief was dying under criminal judgment.
Their stories were different.
Christ remained the center.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to these words:
Not because Jesus makes our past imaginary.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because Christians become flawless overnight.

Jesus rewrites everything because in Him condemnation gives way to justification, alienation to reconciliation, slavery to freedom, spiritual death to life, and hopelessness to an inheritance that sinners could never purchase.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe only you and God know it.
Maybe your scandal is not the kind people gossip about.
Maybe yours is religion without relationship.
Years of appearing close to Jesus while keeping your heart at a carefully controlled distance.
If so, you are not reading this by accident in the sense that these words have now placed a real question before you.
What will you do with Christ?
Do not mistake being moved for being changed.
Take this seriously.
Open the Scriptures.
Read the Gospel of John slowly.
Pray honestly.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek mature, biblically faithful believers who will walk with you.
Become rooted in a church that faithfully teaches Scripture and centers its life on Christ.
And if you realize you have been pretending, tell someone trustworthy.
Darkness grows comfortably in secrecy.
Bring it into the light.
Not as a formula.
Not as a performance.
Not so strangers will think you are spiritual.
Let it be an honest confession that says, “I am done pretending.”
And if Christ has already begun restoring places in your life you thought were beyond redemption, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to know they are not the only person fighting that battle.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It does not.
Christ alone saves.
But if Gospel-centered truth has helped you, sharing it and supporting the work are practical ways you can help put that truth in front of another person who may never walk voluntarily into a church.
One share can become someone else's midnight encounter with Scripture.
One tag can reach the friend who has been quietly falling apart.
One saved article can be waiting for you on the night temptation returns.
So save this.
Talk about it.
Bring it into conversations beyond a comment section.
Support should never be confused with purchasing God's blessing.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot buy God's love.
But Christians have always been able to use their resources voluntarily to help Gospel ministry and biblical teaching reach others.
Deeper discipleship.
Biblical nourishment.
Accountability.
Spiritual sharpening.
Resources that keep directing attention away from ourselves and back toward Jesus Christ.
Do not leave this article merely knowing more about Jesus.
Know Him.
Do not settle for being recognized at church while remaining a stranger to surrender.
Do not let another Sunday convince you that proximity to Christianity is the same thing as belonging to Christ.
The doors may open every week.
The songs may continue.
The sermons may continue.
Your familiar seat may still be waiting.
But eternity is too serious for pretending.
Jesus is too glorious for half-hearted religion.
Sin is too deadly to decorate with Christian vocabulary.
And grace is too astonishing to leave unopened while you spend your life trying to look saved.
Come to Christ.
Not to an image.
Not to a performance.
Not merely to a denomination, tradition, ministry, page, preacher, or Christian brand.
To Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The Christ who calls sinners to repent.
The Christ who forgives.
The Christ who transforms.
The Christ who knows His sheep.
The Christ who can take the chapter you wish you could tear from your story and make even your scars testify that mercy had the final word.
So the next time you walk through those church doors, remember:
The greatest question is not whether the people inside know your name.
It is whether you know His.
And perhaps the most haunting tragedy would be to spend your whole life sitting near the things of Jesus while never surrendering your life to Jesus Himself.
Don't spend a lifetime sitting in His house while keeping the door of your heart closed to its King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO CHANGE YOUR LIFE—BUT ROMANS 12:2 SAYS THE BATTLE MAY BE HAPPENING INSIDE YOUR MIND
paragraphs:
YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO CHANGE YOUR LIFE—BUT ROMANS 12:2 SAYS THE BATTLE MAY BE HAPPENING INSIDE YOUR MIND
What the “Renewing of Your Mind” Really Requires—and Why Following Jesus Means More Than Thinking Positive Thoughts
There is a frightening possibility that many Christians know Romans 12:2 by heart...
and still have never allowed Romans 12:2 to happen to them.
We quote it.
We highlight it.
We put it on wallpapers, journals, coffee mugs, captions, and church graphics.
“Be transformed by the renewing of your mind.”
Beautiful words.
But what if Paul was describing something far more disruptive than becoming more optimistic?
What if renewing your mind means allowing Jesus Christ to confront the patterns of thought you have protected for years?
The resentment you keep rehearsing.
The lust you keep rationalizing.
The comparison you keep feeding.
The fear you have started calling wisdom.
The bitterness you call discernment.
The pride you call confidence.
The compromise you call freedom.
The obsession with approval you disguise as kindness.
The secret habit nobody at church knows about.
The voice inside your head that keeps telling you that because of what you did, what happened to you, or how badly you failed, God could never make something holy out of your life.
And suddenly Romans 12:2 stops being a decorative Bible verse.
It becomes an invasion.
Because Christianity is not Jesus helping the old you become slightly more comfortable.
The Gospel announces something far more radical:
Christ died for sinners and rose again, and those who belong to Him are being made new.
That transformation reaches even the place nobody else can see.
Your mind.
Romans 12:2 reads in the King James Version:
“And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.”
But Romans was originally written in Greek, and when we look at Paul’s language, the force of his words becomes difficult to escape.
The Greek text includes:
“καὶ μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός...”
In straightforward English:
Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of the mind.
Notice something important.
Paul does not merely say, “Think happier thoughts.”
He presents two competing patterns.
Conformity.
Transformation.
Something is always trying to shape you.
That is where this gets personal.
Because you can love Jesus sincerely and still discover patterns in your thinking that have been shaped more deeply by the surrounding age than by the truth of God.
The Greek word translated “be conformed” is συσχηματίζεσθε—syschēmatizesthe.
The idea is conformity to a pattern or form.
And Paul identifies the pattern:
“τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ”—tō aiōni toutō.
This age.
Many English translations traditionally render aiōn here as “world,” and that communicates an important truth, but “age” brings us closer to the word Paul actually uses.
Paul is warning believers not to allow the values and patterns of the present age to become the mold determining how they live.
And that should make every Christian uncomfortable for at least a moment.
Because conformity rarely announces itself.
Nobody wakes up and says:
“Today I would like the surrounding culture to slowly disciple me away from Christ.”
It happens quietly.
One video.
One compromise.
One fantasy.
One resentment.
One repeated message.
One unquestioned assumption.
One appetite continually fed.
One lie entertained long enough that eventually it stops feeling like a lie.
The age says:
Protect yourself at all costs.
Jesus says forgive.
The age says:
Your desires define you.
Jesus calls you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him.
The age says:
Destroy the person who wounded you.
Jesus tells His people to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them.
The age says:
Your worth depends on being admired.
The Gospel says your deepest identity is not something you manufacture for an audience; salvation is received by grace in Christ.
The age says:
Hide your sin so people will continue respecting you.
The Gospel brings sinners into the light, where confession meets the mercy of God.
And somewhere between Sunday worship and Monday morning...
between opening your Bible and opening your phone...
between singing “I surrender all” and secretly clinging to the one thing you refuse to surrender...
there is a war over what will shape your mind.
But then Paul gives us the glorious opposite of conformity:
“ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε.”
Alla metamorphousthe.
“But be transformed.”
The word is μεταμορφοῦσθε—metamorphousthe.
Transformation.
A profound change.

The same Greek verb is used in the New Testament when Jesus is transfigured before His disciples in Matthew 17:2 and Mark 9:2, though the contexts are obviously different. Paul also uses this language in 2 Corinthians 3:18 when describing believers being transformed into Christ’s image.
Romans 12:2 therefore does not invite us merely to perform cosmetic Christianity.
God is interested in more than polishing your religious appearance.
You can change your vocabulary without changing your heart.
You can stop posting certain things and remain enslaved internally.
You can learn when to say “Amen.”
You can carry the right Bible.
Know the right worship songs.
Follow Christian pages.
Argue theology online.
Attend church every week.

And still allow jealousy, pornography, greed, rage, unforgiveness, vanity, self-righteousness, fear, or the hunger for human approval to occupy rooms inside your mind that you have never surrendered to Christ.
Jesus did not go to the cross merely to improve your public image.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
And those whom God saves, He does not abandon to the tyranny of the old life.
This is why the surrounding context matters enormously.
Romans 12 does not begin with verse 2.
It begins with mercy.
Paul writes in Romans 12:1, “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God...”
That “therefore” carries the enormous theological weight of everything Paul has been explaining about sin, justification, grace, Christ, faith, the Spirit, and God’s mercy throughout Romans.
Christian transformation does not begin with:
“Make yourself good enough so God will finally accept you.”
It begins with mercy.
Read that again.
Mercy comes before the command.
Grace comes before transformation.
The Gospel comes before Christian obedience.
You do not renew your mind so Jesus will finally decide you are worth dying for.
Christ died for sinners.
You do not transform yourself into somebody impressive enough to earn the cross.
You come to the cross empty-handed.
Repentant.
Needy.
Unable to boast.
And there you discover that the Savior you needed was already willing to bleed for sinners.
That changes everything about Romans 12:2.
Because renewing your mind is not self-salvation.
It is the response of a life that has encountered the mercy of God.
Paul describes believers presenting their bodies as a living sacrifice.
Then comes:
Do not be conformed.
Be transformed.
And how does Paul say this transformation takes place?
“τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός.”
Tē anakainōsei tou noos.
“By the renewing of the mind.”
The noun ἀνακαίνωσις—anakainōsis—carries the sense of renewal, a making new.
And νοῦς—nous—refers to the mind, understanding, or faculty of thought and moral judgment.
This is where shallow interpretations of the verse begin falling apart.
Biblical mind renewal is not manifestation.
It is not pretending negative circumstances do not exist.
It is not staring into a mirror repeating flattering statements until the universe gives you what you want.
It is not merely replacing “I can't” with “I can.”
Sometimes biblical renewal means replacing “I can” with:
“I cannot do this apart from Christ.”
Sometimes renewing your mind means discovering that the thought making you feel strongest is actually pride.
Sometimes it means discovering that what feels like freedom is slavery.
Sometimes it means realizing that the person you have blamed for everything is not responsible for your refusal to forgive.
Sometimes it means admitting that you were wrong.
And that hurts.
Because everybody loves transformation until transformation touches something they wanted to keep.
There are thoughts you have rehearsed so often they now sound like your own voice.
“I will never forgive them.”
“I need this sin.”
“I deserve revenge.”
“Nobody could love me if they knew.”
“I've gone too far.”
“God could use somebody else, but not me.”
“My value depends on what people think about me.”
“If I lose this relationship, I am nothing.”
“If God really loved me, my life wouldn't hurt like this.”
And the tragedy is that a lie repeated for years can begin feeling more believable than truth heard for five minutes.
That is why renewal matters.
Your feelings are real, but they are not infallible.
Your thoughts are yours, but they are not automatically true.
Your culture is powerful, but it is not your Lord.
Your past affected you, but it does not possess final authority over who you become in Christ.
Jesus does.
And renewal requires truth.
Jesus prayed to the Father in John 17:17:
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.”
This is why a Christian cannot seriously pursue the renewing of the mind while continually starving himself or herself of Scripture.

You cannot endlessly consume voices discipling you toward lust, envy, outrage, materialism, vanity, unbelief, and self-worship and then wonder why fifteen distracted minutes with an open Bible seem unable to quiet the noise.
This is not a call to hide from the world.
Jesus prayed not that His disciples would simply be removed from the world, but that they would be kept from evil.
The question is not merely:
“What am I watching?”
It is:
“What is what I'm watching teaching me to love?”
Not merely:
“What am I listening to?”
But:
“What is it teaching me to believe?”
Not merely:
“Who am I following?”
But:
“Who is discipling my desires?”
Your mind has a diet.
And eventually, what continually feeds your mind begins influencing what feels normal.
This is why renewing your mind requires more than occasionally adding Scripture to an otherwise uninterrupted flood of worldly formation.
There are moments when obedience means turning something off.
Unfollowing.
Walking away.
Closing the tab.
Ending the fantasy before it becomes an action.
Refusing to replay the offense.
Opening Scripture when your flesh wants stimulation.
Praying when anxiety wants another hour of rumination.
Confessing when shame tells you to hide.
Seeking wise Christian fellowship when isolation tells you nobody would understand.
Forgiving when every emotion in you wants revenge.

And no—this does not mean serious anxiety, trauma, depression, or other mental-health struggles can always be reduced to “you didn't read your Bible enough.” Human beings are embodied creatures, and wise pastoral care, Christian community, and appropriate professional help can all have legitimate places.
But whatever our circumstances, Scripture still calls Christians to bring their thinking beneath the truth and lordship of Jesus Christ.
Renewal also requires repentance.
That word makes modern ears uncomfortable.
But repentance is not an embarrassing side room of Christianity.
Jesus preached repentance.
The apostles preached repentance.
The Gospel does not merely comfort us in what destroys us.
Christ calls us out of darkness.
Repentance means that when God's truth exposes sin, we stop negotiating with it.
We stop renaming it.
We stop building theological excuses around it.
We bring it into the light.
Maybe that is why this article found you.
Not because you needed another inspirational quote.
Maybe there is something you already know.
Something the Holy Spirit has been pressing upon your conscience.
A relationship.
A browser history.
A private conversation.
A bitterness.
An obsession.
A dishonest business practice.
A secret addiction.
A hidden pride.
A grudge you have nurtured so carefully that you no longer know who you would be without it.
And maybe you keep asking God for peace while protecting the very thing disturbing your obedience.
Do not run from conviction.
Conviction that leads you toward Christ is mercy.
The cross proves that God is not waiting for cleaned-up people to impress Him.
At Calvary, the ugliness of human sin and the astonishing grace of God meet.
Jesus was crucified.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose again.
And forgiveness is not purchased by your ability to repair yourself.
Our hope rests in Christ.
So when Scripture exposes what is broken inside you, you do not have to hide.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can return.
You can say:
“Jesus, I have believed lies.”
“Jesus, I have protected sin.”
“Jesus, I have allowed this age to shape places in me that belong to You.”
“Have mercy on me.”
“Change me.”
And then comes another part of Romans 12:2 that is frequently neglected.
Paul connects renewal with discernment:
“εἰς τὸ δοκιμάζειν ὑμᾶς τί τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ...”
The verb δοκιμάζειν—dokimazein—can carry the idea of testing, examining, discerning, or approving what proves genuine.
Paul is describing people whose transformed minds increasingly discern and approve what God wills—what is good, pleasing, and perfect.
In other words, renewal changes more than what you think about.
It changes how you evaluate life.
Before renewal:
“How close can I get to sin without technically sinning?”
After renewal:
“Does this please Christ?”
Before:
“Everybody does it.”
After:
“What has God said?”
Before:
“What will make people admire me?”
After:
“What will glorify God?”
Before:
“What do I feel like doing?”
After:
“Lord, what would faithfulness look like here?”
That does not happen overnight.
Christian maturity is not microwave spirituality.
There may be battles you must fight repeatedly.
There may be lies you must answer with truth again tomorrow.
There may be mornings when you wake up and the old thought is already waiting beside the bed.
There may be days when temptation feels louder than Scripture.
There may be setbacks that humiliate you.
But do not confuse a continuing battle with permission to surrender.
Run back to Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Christ does.

The Christian life is not sinless perfection achieved through mental discipline. Our sanctification rests upon the work of God and calls us into active obedience. Philippians 2 holds those truths together beautifully: believers are commanded to work out their salvation while recognizing that God is at work in them.
You fight because grace has found you.
You resist because another King now has your allegiance.
You open the Word because you need truth more than another dopamine hit.
You pray because dependence is not weakness in the kingdom of God.
You confess because darkness grows in secrecy.
You gather with believers because Christianity was never designed as solitary self-improvement.
You remember the Gospel because shame will keep trying to convince you that your worst chapter gets the final sentence.
But shame does not hold the pen.
Jesus does.
Peter had a chapter of denial.
Paul had a chapter of persecuting Christians.
The woman caught in adultery had a chapter everybody wanted to turn into her entire identity.
The thief beside Jesus had a life that appeared almost finished before grace met him at a cross.
Scripture never teaches that sin is trivial.
It teaches something better:
Grace is greater than anything sinners can earn.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by removing repentance from Christianity so nobody becomes uncomfortable.

Jesus rewrites everything by meeting guilty, wounded, rebellious, exhausted human beings with truth and grace, bringing sinners to repentance and faith, forgiving those who come to Him, and beginning a transformation that reaches all the way into how we think, love, choose, forgive, suffer, hope, and live.
Maybe your greatest need today is not a different life.
Maybe it is a renewed mind inside the life you already have.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to change your circumstances while He has been exposing what must change within you.
Maybe the prayer is no longer:
“God, make everybody else different.”
Maybe tonight it becomes:
“Lord, begin with me.”
Search me.
Correct me.
Expose every lie I have made comfortable.
Teach me to recognize the pattern of this age before I mistake it for wisdom.
Teach me Your Word until truth becomes more precious to me than the approval of people.
Teach me to hate what destroys intimacy with You.
Teach me to love what Christ loves.
Renew my mind.
Transform my life.
Make me more like Jesus.
Be real.
If you are exhausted from fighting thoughts nobody else knows about, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
If God has been restoring you and you know He is not finished with your story, comment, “Christ is still changing me.”
Not because typing words earns grace.
It doesn't.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And somebody reading your comment may finally realize:
Not because saving a post changes you, but because tomorrow the old voices may return, and you may need to remember what Scripture actually says.
Send this to the believer who looks strong publicly but has privately admitted, “My mind is exhausted.”
Not as a superstition.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace, not social-media engagement.
But supporting faithful Christian work can be one practical way believers help useful teaching and Gospel resources continue reaching others.

Invite your family. Invite your friends. Invite the Christian who has grown cold. Invite the believer who is barely hanging on. Invite the seeker with difficult questions. Invite even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely religion for people pretending to have perfect lives.
Jesus is calling you deeper than a page.
Deeper than content.
Deeper than inspiration.
Deeper than religious appearance.
Romans 12:2 is not asking whether you can quote the verse.
It is asking what is shaping you.
What has your attention?
What feeds your imagination?
What defines success for you?
What thought keeps ruling you?
What secret keeps controlling you?
Whose approval are you terrified to lose?
What lie have you repeated so long that you now call it truth?
And what would happen if you finally placed that thought beneath the authority of Jesus Christ?
Maybe the transformation you have been praying for begins with surrendering the sentence you keep repeating inside your head.
The world wants a mold.
Your flesh wants control.
The enemy traffics in lies.
But Jesus speaks truth.
And when Christ takes hold of a life, the old story no longer gets unquestioned authority over the ending.
So come back to the Word.
Come back to prayer.
Come back to repentance.
Come back to fellowship.
Come back to truth.
Most of all...
come back to Jesus.
Bring Him the thoughts you are ashamed of.
Bring Him the memories that still sting.
Bring Him the appetite you have been feeding.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the scandal.
Because the mind surrendered to Christ does not have to remain imprisoned by every pattern that once shaped it.
And perhaps years from now, when you look back at the person you were becoming before Jesus interrupted the pattern, you will realize something breathtaking:
God did not merely change what you were thinking.
By His grace, He was changing who you were becoming.
The lie may have lived in your mind for years—but it still does not get the final word when Jesus is Lord.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Does Revelation Use So Much Symbolism? Because Heaven Is Showing You What Your Eyes Cannot See
paragraphs: Why Does Revelation Use So Much Symbolism? Because Heaven Is Showing You What Your Eyes Cannot See

The beasts, the dragon, the Lamb, Babylon, strange numbers, terrifying visions, a woman clothed with the sun, and a city descending from heaven—Revelation was never written to make Jesus impossible to find. Its symbols were written to make Him impossible to forget.
Maybe you have done it too.
You opened the book of Revelation because you wanted to understand the end.
Then you met a dragon.
A beast rising from the sea.
Another beast.
Seven heads.
Ten horns.
Four horsemen.
A woman clothed with the sun.
A prostitute called Babylon.
A Lamb who looks as though He has been slain.
A scroll no one can open.
Stars falling.
Trumpets sounding.
Bowls being poured out.
A city descending from heaven.
And somewhere between Revelation 1 and Revelation 22, you quietly wondered:
“Why couldn’t God just say what He meant?”
That question is more important than it sounds.
Because if we misunderstand why Revelation speaks in symbols, we can spend our lives obsessing over the symbols while missing the Person standing at the center of them.
And Revelation tells us His name almost immediately.
Jesus Christ.
The opening words are:
“Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ”
Apokalypsis Iēsou Christou.
“The revelation of Jesus Christ” (Revelation 1:1).
That Greek word ἀποκάλυψις (apokalypsis) means an unveiling, disclosure, or revelation.
Think about that.
The final book of Scripture does not introduce itself as “The Concealment of Jesus Christ.”
It is an unveiling.
Revelation is not God hiding Christ behind a mountain of impossible riddles.
It is God pulling back the curtain.
And once you understand that, the symbolism begins to look very different.

Revelation uses symbolism because there are realities ordinary description cannot communicate with the same force, because its imagery is deeply rooted in the Old Testament and the world of its first readers, because symbols can reveal the spiritual character of earthly powers, and because John is being shown history from heaven’s perspective.
That last part matters.
You already know what a throne looks like from earth.
Revelation wants you to see what earthly thrones look like from heaven.
You know what empires call themselves.
Civilized.
Powerful.
Permanent.
Necessary.
Glorious.
Heaven sometimes calls them beasts.
You know what temptation looks like when it enters your life.
Attractive.
Profitable.
Pleasurable.
Harmless.
Heaven shows you a dragon behind the rebellion.
You know what Jesus looked like when Rome crucified Him.
Defeated.
Humiliated.
Bleeding.
Dead.
But heaven looks at the crucified Christ and declares:
Lion.
Lamb.
King.
Conqueror.
Worthy.
Do you see what Revelation is doing?
The symbols are not making reality less clear.
They are exposing a deeper reality.
That is why Revelation cannot be responsibly interpreted by treating every image as though John invented it in isolation.
Its symbolic world is saturated with earlier Scripture.
Daniel saw beasts representing kingdoms.
John sees beasts.
Daniel saw “one like a son of man.”
John sees “one like a son of man.”
Ezekiel saw extraordinary heavenly creatures and the glory of God.
John sees heavenly creatures surrounding God's throne.
Exodus gives us plagues.
Revelation echoes plagues.
Genesis gives us the serpent.
Revelation identifies “the ancient serpent” with the devil and Satan.
Babylon oppressed God's people in Israel's history.
Revelation transforms Babylon into a symbolic picture of the arrogant, seductive, persecuting world-city opposed to God.
The tree of life appears near the beginning of the biblical story.
It appears again at the end.
The Bible has been moving somewhere all along.
That is why ripping Revelation away from Genesis, Exodus, the Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Zechariah, and the rest of Scripture almost guarantees confusion.
Revelation is not a biblical appendix detached from everything before it.
It is more like a breathtaking symphonic finale in which themes you have heard throughout Scripture suddenly return together.
Creation.
Exodus.
Temple.
Sacrifice.
Kingdom.
Exile.
Babylon.
Messiah.
Judgment.
New creation.
The symbols are carrying biblical memory.
And sometimes one image carries an entire theology.
Consider the Lamb.
Revelation 5 creates one of the most extraordinary reversals in Scripture.
John hears that “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” has conquered.
You expect him to turn and see a lion.
He turns.
And sees a Lamb.
Not merely a Lamb.
A Lamb standing as though slain.
The Greek word used is ἀρνίον (arnion), “lamb.”
That image is staggering.
Power looks different in the kingdom of God.
The Messiah conquers through sacrificial victory.
The One who was slaughtered stands.
The wound did not get the final word.
Death did not get the final word.
Rome did not get the final word.
The grave did not get the final word.
Jesus does.
This is one reason Revelation's symbolism is so unforgettable.
You could write a paragraph saying Christ triumphed through His sacrificial death and resurrection.
That would be true.
But John shows you a slaughtered Lamb standing beside the throne.
Now try forgetting it.
That is what powerful biblical symbolism does.
It does not merely enter your mind.
It occupies your imagination.
And Revelation desperately needed to reshape the imagination of its original hearers.
Remember who first received this book.
Revelation addresses seven churches in Asia—Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.
These were real Christian congregations living within the Roman world.
Some faced suffering.
Some faced compromise.
Some faced deceptive teaching.
Some were spiritually asleep.
Some were enduring faithfully.
Some had become comfortable.
Some believed they were spiritually wealthy while Christ exposed their poverty.
Revelation was not originally handed to comfortable modern readers with prophecy charts spread across a table.
It was sent to churches that needed to know how to remain faithful to Jesus.
That changes the question.
Instead of only asking, “What future event does this symbol predict?”
We also need to ask:
“What would this vision have demanded from the Christians who first heard it?”
Faithfulness.
Endurance.
Worship.
Discernment.
Resistance to idolatry.
Refusal to compromise with evil.
Confidence that Christ reigns.
Hope that suffering will not last forever.
That is why one of the most dangerous ways to read Revelation is to turn it into a codebook for satisfying curiosity while ignoring its repeated calls to holiness.
You can argue about the identity of the beast and still live like one.
You can calculate numbers and neglect your first love.
You can debate Babylon while secretly loving everything Babylon sells.
You can study Armageddon while refusing to forgive your brother.
You can talk endlessly about the Antichrist while barely talking about Christ.
And suddenly the book intended to unveil Jesus becomes a hiding place from Jesus.
That should disturb us.
Because Revelation was not given merely so Christians could know things.
It was given so Christians could overcome.
“Here is a call for the endurance and faith of the saints,” Revelation says (Revelation 13:10).
There is another Greek word worth remembering:
ὑπομονή — hypomonē.
Endurance.
Steadfastness.
Patient perseverance under pressure.
Revelation does not merely ask, “Can you identify the symbols?”
It asks:
Will you remain faithful when following the Lamb costs you something?
That question reaches straight through the centuries.
Because our idols may wear different clothing, but the human heart has not changed nearly as much as we imagine.
We still worship power.
We still compromise for comfort.
We still sell convictions for acceptance.
We still confuse wealth with blessing.
We still want Christianity without a cross.
We still want Jesus as Savior while quietly negotiating whether He really gets to be Lord.
Revelation tears away that illusion.
There are only two ultimate allegiances running through its visions.
The Lamb and the dragon.
The kingdom of God and rebellious worldly power.
The worship of the Creator and the worship of created things.
The New Jerusalem and Babylon.
Faithfulness and compromise.
Life and judgment.
And suddenly Revelation stops being strange.
It becomes painfully personal.
Because Babylon is no longer merely something you are trying to identify on a map.
Babylon becomes the seductive voice whispering:
“You can have everything you want. Just bend your knee a little.”
The beast becomes more than a puzzle.
It becomes a terrifying picture of human power when power becomes idolatrous, blasphemous, coercive, and hostile to God.
The dragon becomes more than a frightening creature.
Revelation itself identifies him:
“that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9).
John does not leave that particular symbol to our imagination.
And then there is 666.
Perhaps no biblical number has produced more speculation.
Revelation 13:18 says:
“Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.”

Ancient Greek and Hebrew letters could carry numerical values, which made forms of numerical wordplay possible. One historically influential interpretation connects 666 with “Nero Caesar” when the name is rendered in Hebrew letters, and the textual variant 616 found in some ancient manuscripts is often discussed because a Latinized form of Nero's name can produce that value.
That historical connection deserves serious consideration.

But Revelation's theological message cannot safely be reduced to an endless hunt for whichever contemporary politician, celebrity, technology, barcode, organization, computer system, or world event happens to frighten us this decade.
Generations of Christians have watched people confidently identify the beast.
And generations have watched those identifications collapse.
Revelation calls for wisdom, not panic.
Its symbolism should produce discernment, not superstition.
And perhaps that is where some of us need to repent.
Because fear can become addictive.
There is a strange excitement in believing every headline might secretly be Revelation unfolding before your eyes.
Another war begins.
Someone says, “Revelation.”
A new technology appears.
“Revelation.”
A disease spreads.
“Revelation.”
A political leader rises.
“Revelation.”
A strange event happens in the sky.
“Revelation.”
But Jesus did not give His church Revelation so every generation could live addicted to sensationalism.
He gave His church a vision large enough to survive suffering.
Look at the throne.
That is where Revelation repeatedly pulls our eyes.
Before the beast.
Before Babylon falls.
Before the judgments reach their climax.
There is a throne.
And Someone is sitting on it.
That changes everything.
The world can look chaotic from underneath.
Revelation shows you history from above.
Earth says, “Everything is falling apart.”
Heaven says, “God has not abandoned His throne.”
Earth says, “The empire is unstoppable.”
Heaven says, “Its time is limited.”
Earth says, “The martyrs lost.”
Heaven shows them before God.
Earth says, “Jesus was slaughtered.”
Heaven says, “Worthy is the Lamb.”
Earth says, “Death wins eventually.”
Then Revelation gives us one of Scripture's most beautiful promises:
“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:4).
Every tear.
Read that again slowly.
Every tear.
Not some.
Not only the respectable tears.
Not only the tears you cried in church.
The tears nobody saw.
The tears you swallowed because your children were watching.
The tears you wiped away before walking into work.
The tears you cried after someone betrayed you.
The tears from the funeral.
The tears from the diagnosis.
The tears after you failed God again and wondered whether there was any road home.
The tears of Christians persecuted for the name of Jesus.
The tears of people who died praying for deliverance they did not live long enough to see.
Revelation says history is moving toward a world where God Himself wipes them away.
This is why Revelation is not fundamentally a horror story for Christians.
It is hope written in the language of apocalypse.
Yes, judgment is real.
Sin is serious.
Satan is real.
Hell is not a metaphor we are free to dismiss because it makes modern people uncomfortable.
God's holiness is not negotiable.
Christ will judge evil.
But the center of Christian hope is not our ability to decode tomorrow.
It is Jesus Christ.
The One who says:
“Fear not.”
The One who says:
“I am the first and the last.”
The One who says:
“I died, and behold I am alive forevermore.”
The One who holds “the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:17–18).
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say death does not exist.
He says He holds the keys.
Maybe that is the word somebody reading this needed tonight.
The thing frightening you is not sovereign.
Cancer is not sovereign.
Your past is not sovereign.
Your shame is not sovereign.
Your addiction is not sovereign.
The person who abandoned you is not sovereign.
The government is not sovereign.
The economy is not sovereign.
Satan is not sovereign.
Death is not sovereign.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And the symbolism of Revelation keeps hammering that truth into our imagination until we finally begin to see the world differently.
This is also why Revelation contains such severe warnings against compromise.
Jesus loves His church too much to flatter it.
