He tells Ephesus that it has abandoned its first love.
He tells Sardis that it has a reputation for being alive but is dead.
Imagine that.
Everybody thinks the church is alive.
The programs are running.
The music is playing.
People know the name.
The social media page looks healthy.
The calendar is full.
But Jesus walks into the room and says:
Dead.
That possibility should terrify every Christian organization, ministry, church, preacher, writer, and content creator—including us.
Because it is possible to build a reputation around Jesus while slowly losing intimacy with Jesus.
It is possible to post Scripture without obeying Scripture.
It is possible to defend biblical truth publicly while hiding private sin.
It is possible to tell everyone else to repent while protecting the room in our own heart where we refuse to let Christ enter.
And Revelation will not allow us to hide there.
Jesus says:
“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent” (Revelation 3:19).
Repent.
The Greek verb is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It carries the idea of changing one's mind, turning, reconsidering, repenting.
Biblical repentance is not performing sadness for God.
It is turning.
Coming out of agreement with sin.
Returning to Christ.
And here the message of Revelation becomes the message of the Gospel itself.
The scandal is that sinners like us rebelled against a holy God.
The scandal is that humanity crowned its Creator with thorns.
The scandal is that the innocent Son of God was nailed to a Roman cross.
But grace entered the scandal.
The Lamb was slain.
His blood purchases people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” for God (Revelation 5:9).
The condemned can be forgiven.
The filthy can be washed.
The rebellious can become worshipers.
The spiritually dead can live.
The compromised can repent.
The runaway can come home.
The story can be rewritten.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because Jesus paid for sinners with His blood.
That is grace.
Grace is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is Jesus entering the scandal, bearing sin, defeating death, and writing redemption where judgment should have been the final sentence.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe now you understand why Revelation needs symbols.
How do you paint the horror of satanic rebellion?
A dragon.
How do you paint political power corrupted into idolatry?
A beast.
How do you paint a civilization intoxicated with luxury, exploitation, immorality, and spiritual adultery?
Babylon.
How do you paint Christ's paradoxical victory through sacrifice?
A slaughtered Lamb standing.
How do you paint God's final dwelling with redeemed humanity?
A radiant city coming down from heaven.
How do you paint restored creation?
A river of the water of life.
The tree of life.
No curse.
No night.
No death.
The face of God.
The Bible begins with humanity driven away from God's presence.
It ends with redeemed humanity seeing His face.
That is not random symbolism.
That is the Gospel story reaching cosmic completion.
And maybe you came here wanting to understand dragons.
But God wanted to talk to you about your heart.
Maybe you wanted to identify Babylon.
Jesus wanted to expose what you refuse to surrender.
Maybe you wanted a timeline.
Jesus wanted your allegiance.
Maybe you wanted information about the end.
Jesus wanted to ask whether you belong to Him now.
Because Revelation eventually leaves every reader standing before an invitation.
“The Spirit and the Bride say, ‘Come.’”
And:
“Let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (Revelation 22:17).
Come.
After beasts and battles.
Come.
After trumpets and bowls.
Come.
After judgment.
Come.
After Babylon falls.
Come.
The Bible ends with grace still calling thirsty people.
So if you have been running from Christ, come.
If secret sin has hollowed you out, repent and come.
If religion has replaced relationship with Jesus, come.
If you have compromised so long that you barely recognize yourself anymore, come.
If you are ashamed of what you have become, come.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
The Lamb who exposes sin is also the Lamb who was slain for sinners.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are terrified anyone might discover.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Be honest before God.

And if you have experienced the mercy of Jesus after believing your story was too damaged to redeem, tell somebody what Christ did. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to interrupt another person's despair.
Not because every paragraph needs to be remembered, but because there will probably come a day when the world looks more powerful than the Lamb.
Read it again then.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. Grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased. We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in worship, obedience, love, generosity, service, and faithful witness.

But if this ministry is bearing good spiritual fruit in your life, you can freely choose to help sustain and spread that work. Share because somebody in your circle may be thirsty for the Gospel and afraid to admit it. Follow because staying close to biblical truth in a noisy world matters.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not merely become fascinated with Revelation.
Become fascinated with Jesus.
The beast is not the hero of Revelation.
The dragon is not the hero.
Babylon is not the hero.
666 is not the hero.
The Antichrist is not the hero.
The end times are not the hero.
Jesus Christ is.
The Lamb who was slain.
The King who lives.
The Lord who sees His suffering church.
The Judge before whom evil cannot hide forever.
The Bridegroom who is coming.
The Savior who still says, “Come.”
The One who takes humanity's darkest scandal and writes grace across the pages with scars still visible in His victory.
And perhaps that is the image Revelation wants burned into your heart when you finally close the book:
The dragon does not get the last word.
The beast does not get the last word.
Babylon does not get the last word.
Your suffering does not get the last word.
Your sin does not have to get the last word.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your grave will not get the last word.
Jesus does.
And when the Lamb writes the final sentence, every counterfeit kingdom falls silent.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LIE WITH”: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE DESCRIBE SEX SO DIRECTLY IN SOME PASSAGES—AND SO DELICATELY IN OTHERS?
paragraphs: “LIE WITH”: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE DESCRIBE SEX SO DIRECTLY IN SOME PASSAGES—AND SO DELICATELY IN OTHERS?

Sometimes the Bible says “lie with.” Sometimes it says “know.” Sometimes it speaks of becoming “one flesh.” That difference is not embarrassment, contradiction, or primitive language. Look closely enough, and the words themselves begin exposing something our culture desperately wants us to forget: the Bible never treats the human body as meaningless.
There is a sentence in Genesis that lands almost violently because of how little it tries to soften itself.
Potiphar’s wife looks at Joseph.
She desires him.
And then she says it.
In Hebrew:
שִׁכְבָה עִמִּי — shikhvah ‘immi.
Literally:
“Lie with me.”
Genesis 39:7.
No poetry.
No candlelight.
No romantic speech.
No elaborate euphemism.
Just desire stripped down to its demand.
Lie with me.
And Joseph runs.
But elsewhere Scripture can sound almost startlingly different.
Genesis 4:1 says:
וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ
Veha’adam yada et-Chavvah ishto.
“And the man knew Eve his wife…”
The Hebrew verb is יָדַע — yada, “to know.”
Yet the next words tell us Eve conceived and gave birth to Cain.
So the reader knows what happened.
Sexual union occurred.
But Genesis does not say, “Adam lay with Eve.”
It says Adam knew her.
Why?
Why can the same Bible describe sexual activity with the blunt physical language of “lie with” in one place and the deeply relational language of “know” in another?
Why does Scripture sometimes pull back the curtain…
and other times leave it almost closed?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What if the difference is trying to tell us something about sex itself?
Because once you see the pattern, you may never read these passages—or perhaps even your own history—the same way again.

The Hebrew expression in Genesis 39 is real and direct. The imperative שִׁכְבָה — shikhvah comes from the Hebrew root שׁכב — shakhav, “to lie down.” With עִמִּי — ‘immi, “with me,” Potiphar’s wife is issuing a sexual proposition: “Lie with me.” The Hebrew text itself preserves precisely that directness.
That matters.
Scripture is not afraid of human sexuality.
The Bible is sometimes more direct about the body than religious people are comfortable being.
Yet Scripture is not pornographic.
That distinction matters enormously.
Pornography exposes the body in order to stimulate consumption.
Scripture can speak plainly about the body in order to expose truth.
One tries to awaken lust.
The other can awaken conscience.
And those are not remotely the same thing.

When Scripture tells the story of Joseph, the direct wording fits the moral pressure of the scene. Joseph is not participating in a tender description of marital intimacy. He is being propositioned by his master's wife.
The sentence feels abrupt because the temptation is abrupt.
“Lie with me.”
And Joseph’s response reveals something our generation desperately needs to recover.
He does not first ask:
Can I get away with this?
He does not calculate whether anybody will discover it.
He does not say, “We have chemistry.”
He does not rename temptation “authenticity.”
He does not call forbidden desire “my truth.”
Joseph sees beyond the bedroom.
Beyond the woman.
Beyond the opportunity.
Beyond secrecy.
Beyond immediate pleasure.
He sees God.
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” he asks in Genesis 39:9.
That is the center of biblical sexual ethics.
Not merely:
“What am I allowed to do?”
But:
“Whose am I?”
And suddenly this ancient bedroom in Egypt becomes painfully modern.
Because some of us know exactly what “Lie with me” sounds like today.
It may not arrive in Hebrew.
It may arrive through Messenger at 1:17 in the morning.
“Are you awake?”
It may arrive through an old relationship suddenly resurfacing.
“I miss you.”
It may arrive through a private browser window.
A disappearing message.
A hotel room.
A flirtation nobody knows about.
A marriage that feels empty.
A loneliness nobody at church knows exists.
A screen glowing against your face while the rest of the house sleeps.
Sometimes temptation does not deliver a theological argument.
Sometimes temptation only whispers:
Nobody will know.
But Joseph knew Someone already did.
And then Scripture gives us another word.
Not shakhav.
But yada.
“To know.”
Genesis 4:1 places יָדַע — yada immediately before Eve's conception. In context, “Adam knew Eve his wife” is clearly describing marital sexual union, while using the ordinary Hebrew verb for knowing.
That does not mean every occurrence of yada is sexual. Far from it. Its normal semantic world is knowledge.
Context determines meaning.
And that is exactly what makes Genesis 4:1 so striking.
The Bible could describe the physical event.
Instead, here it describes the union through the language of knowing.
Perhaps we should allow that to disturb the shallow categories our culture has handed us.
Because sex, biblically understood, was never designed to be merely something bodies do while persons remain untouched.
Bodies belong to persons.
Sex joins bodies.
And therefore sexual union reaches into territory involving vulnerability, covenant, trust, knowledge, belonging, consequences, memory, and sometimes new life.
The Bible's vocabulary can move accordingly.
Sometimes Scripture needs to tell you what happened.
Sometimes it wants you to feel something of what the union means.
Sometimes “lie with” is exactly the language a narrative requires.
Sometimes “know” carries the intimacy the writer wishes to communicate.
Sometimes Scripture uses still other expressions.
This variety is not evidence that the Bible cannot decide how to talk about sex.
It is evidence that biblical language is richer than a single English expression.
Even the New Testament preserves something similar.
Matthew 1:25, speaking of Joseph and Mary before Jesus' birth, contains the Greek:
οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν αὐτὴν
ouk eginōsken autēn
Literally, “he was not knowing her.”
The verb comes from γινώσκω — ginōskō, “to know,” yet the context gives it the sexual sense traditionally expressed in English as Joseph not “knowing” Mary sexually before the birth of Jesus.
The language of knowing crossed from the world of the Hebrew Scriptures into the biblical Greek tradition.
But the New Testament can also speak with extraordinary directness when necessary.
Paul writes:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate.
Not stare at it long enough to decide whether you can handle it.
Not keep it nearby as long as you promise yourself you remain spiritually stronger than it.
Flee.

The Greek text of 1 Corinthians 6:18 really is that forceful: φεύγετε, “flee,” followed by τὴν πορνείαν, sexual immorality. Paul then grounds his appeal in the believer's body, describing it as belonging to God and concluding with the command to glorify God in the body.
Do you see what Christianity does?
It refuses two opposite lies.
One lie says:
Sex is dirty.
The other says:
Sex is meaningless.
Scripture accepts neither.
If sex were inherently dirty, Scripture would not place marital union inside God's good creation.
If sex were meaningless, Scripture would not surround sexual behavior with such serious moral boundaries.
The biblical vision is more beautiful and more demanding:
Your body matters because you matter.
And your sexuality matters because God refuses to treat you as disposable flesh.
That is why the Bible can be direct without being obscene.
It can be modest without pretending sex does not exist.
It can celebrate marital intimacy while condemning sexual immorality.
It can say “lie with.”
It can say “know.”
It can say “one flesh.”
Different expressions.
Different contexts.
One profoundly embodied theology.

Even Paul's teaching to married Christians refuses to treat marital sexuality as something exclusively controlled by the stronger spouse. In 1 Corinthians 7:3, the Greek text tells the husband to render what is due to his wife and immediately says the wife likewise toward her husband:
τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί.
The reciprocity matters.
Husband toward wife.
Likewise wife toward husband.
Paul's language places mutuality into a world where readers might have expected only male privilege.
And suddenly the Bible's sexual vocabulary is doing more than describing anatomy.
It is revealing theology.
Bodies are not toys.
People are not products.
Desire is not automatically lord.
Marriage is not permission for selfishness.
And sex is not salvation.
That last sentence may be the one somebody reading this desperately needs.
Sex is not salvation.
Neither is romance.
Neither is being wanted.
Neither is being touched.
Neither is being desired by someone you thought would never notice you.
And perhaps that is where this article stops being about Hebrew vocabulary and starts becoming about you.
Because maybe you clicked because the title sounded controversial.
But now memories are appearing.
A face.
A room.
A relationship.
A mistake.
Something you did.
Something done to you.
Something you keep repeating.
Something you promised God you would never do again.
Something nobody in your church knows.
Maybe your sexual history feels less like theology and more like wreckage.
Maybe you have wondered whether purity belongs only to people who never made your mistakes.
Maybe you have learned to sing worship songs while carrying a secret you are terrified would change how everybody sees you.
Maybe you have whispered:
God, You can forgive almost anything.
Then quietly added:
But surely not this.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to keep themselves clean enough for Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners needed a Savior…
and the Savior came.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross because humanity needed better public relations.
He went because sin is real.
Our guilt is real.
Our rebellion is real.
Our shame is real.
And God's mercy is more astonishing than we imagined.
Biblical grace does not look at sin and say:
“It wasn't really wrong.”
Grace looks directly at sin and says:
Christ's blood is sufficient for repentant sinners.
That is infinitely better.
Because if salvation depended upon pretending our sins were harmless, some of us would have no hope.
But salvation rests upon Jesus.
The crucified One.
The risen One.
The One who receives sinners.
The One who calls us to repent.
The One who forgives.
The One who cleanses.
The One who does not merely improve our image but begins transforming our lives.
That means repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Him.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can truly cleanse you.
There is a difference between conviction and hopeless condemnation.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Condemnation whispers:
Hide forever.
Conviction says:
This must change.
Despair says:
You can never change.
The Gospel says:
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Maybe the most important “knowing” in your life is not who has known your body.
Maybe it is realizing that God knows you.
Not the edited you.
Not Sunday-morning you.
Not the Facebook version.
You.
The history.
The temptation.
The pornography.
The affair.
The fantasy.
The compromise.
The loneliness.
The regret.
The wounds.
The things you chose.
And, importantly, the things that were forced upon you and therefore were not your sin to confess as though you had chosen them.
He knows.
And still the Gospel calls you toward Christ.
That is why Christian holiness cannot be reduced to sexual reputation.
Some people have spotless reputations and desperately unrepentant hearts.
Others carry shattered histories and have fallen weeping at the feet of Jesus.
The question is not whether your biography contains scandal.
The question is what happens when your scandal encounters grace.
Because grace does not merely erase a headline.
Grace begins rewriting a life.
Maybe you fell.
Repent and come home.
Maybe you are currently compromising.
Come into the light.
Maybe pornography has quietly become your secret master.
Stop protecting what is destroying you. Seek Christ, bring the struggle into trustworthy Christian accountability, and flee what repeatedly feeds it.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Do not rename it.
Do not romanticize it.
Do not blame everybody except yourself.
Repent.
Seek wise pastoral help.
Accept that repentance may involve painful truth and consequences.
But do not conclude that your sin is greater than Christ.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from being told that holiness means you are somehow less human.
You are not less human because you refuse to surrender your body to every desire.
Jesus Himself demonstrates that sexual activity is not what makes a human life complete.
Maybe you are married and intimacy has become wounded, complicated, distant, painful, or weaponized.
Do not turn isolated verses into instruments of coercion.
Biblical marital intimacy belongs inside the larger Christian commands of love, faithfulness, mutual concern, holiness, and self-giving—not domination.
And maybe somebody violated you.
Please hear this without ambiguity:
Another person's sexual sin against you does not make you morally dirty before God.
What someone did to your body is not automatically something your conscience must confess as though you consented to it.
Jesus is not standing over the wounded asking why they were wounded.
He is near to the brokenhearted.
This is why language matters.
Because eventually our words reveal our theology.
“Lie with me” can describe an act.
“Know” can communicate relational intimacy.
“One flesh” speaks of union.
“Flee” speaks of danger.
And “grace” tells sinners where hope is found.
The Bible does not need to blush when speaking about sex because God created the body.
But Scripture also refuses to worship sex because the body was created for God.
That changes everything.
Your body is not your god.
Your desires are not your god.
Your sexual past is not your god.
Your virginity is not your god.
Your marriage is not your god.
Your singleness is not your god.
Your shame is not your god.
Your appetite is not your god.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And this is where the story becomes beautiful.
Joseph ran from the invitation to sin.
Centuries later, another Joseph guarded the woman entrusted to him, and Matthew deliberately tells us that he did not “know” Mary sexually before Jesus' birth.
Then Jesus came.
The Son of God entered our world not to exploit human weakness but to rescue human beings enslaved by sin.
He touched people society considered untouchable.
He received repentant sinners.
He exposed hypocrisy.
He called people out of darkness.
And eventually…
He allowed His own body to be nailed to wood.
Hands pierced.
Feet pierced.
Blood poured out.
Not because bodies do not matter.
Because redemption cost something.
The Christian answer to sexual brokenness is therefore not:
“Pretend it never happened.”
It is:
Bring it to the cross.
Bring the secret.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the regret.
Bring the wounds.
Bring the memories.
Bring the relationship you know God has been telling you to leave.
Bring the browser history.
Bring the double life.
Bring the shame you have carried for twenty years.
Bring all of it into the light of Christ.
Not because exposure itself saves you.
Jesus saves.
And the same Christ who says, “Follow Me,” is not asking you to crawl toward Him after you have repaired yourself.
You come because you cannot repair yourself.
You repent because He is Lord.
You believe because He is Savior.
You surrender because grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
So run.
Not merely from sexual sin.
Run to Jesus.
That is the part we sometimes forget.
Joseph did not resist temptation merely because sex was dangerous.
He resisted because God was precious.
Christian holiness cannot survive forever if it is built only upon fear of consequences.
Eventually you need something more beautiful than your temptation.
You need Christ.
Be real.
Sometimes the first crack in secrecy is simply admitting:
I need Jesus.

And if somebody came to your mind while reading this—someone fighting pornography, carrying sexual shame, recovering from betrayal, wrestling with temptation, questioning whether Christ could possibly forgive them—send this to them privately.
It is the recognition that the body matters to God.
You may need it on a night when temptation becomes louder than conviction.
You may need these words when shame tries to convince you that running away from God is safer than running toward Him.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the friend who does not yet believe.
Invite even the person who thinks Christianity has nothing intelligent or compassionate to say about sexuality.

We want this ministry to remain a place where difficult questions are not avoided, Scripture is not manipulated, sin is not celebrated, wounded people are not discarded, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anybody should pressure you into giving.
Scripture says:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ … μὴ … ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each person should give as purposed in the heart, not under compulsion.
God loves willing generosity.
Pray for the ministry.
Send biblical truth to somebody who needs it.
There are many ways to participate in Gospel work.
Because ultimately Gospel Warrior is not the Gospel.
A ministry is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ is the center of the Gospel.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
And He is still taking stories that look irredeemable and writing endings nobody thought possible.
So now perhaps we understand why Scripture can say:
“Lie with me.”
And elsewhere:
“Adam knew Eve.”
The Bible is not confused about sex.
We are.
We turned covenant into consumption.
We turned bodies into products.
We turned desire into identity.
We turned intimacy into entertainment.
We turned private sin into public normality and then wondered why so many people feel privately empty.
But Scripture keeps calling us back.
Your body matters.
Your choices matter.
Your wounds matter.
Your repentance matters.
Your marriage matters.
Your singleness matters.
Your holiness matters.
But none of those things is your Savior.
Jesus is.
So when temptation whispers,
“Lie with me…”
remember the man who ran.
When shame whispers,
“Hide from God…”
remember the Savior who came looking for sinners.
When your past whispers,
“This is who you will always be…”
look at the cross.
Because the final word over a repentant sinner does not belong to lust.
It does not belong to pornography.
It does not belong to adultery.
It does not belong to abuse.
It does not belong to your worst night.
It does not belong to the person who used you.
It does not belong to the secret you have carried.
It does not even belong to scandal.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
And maybe that is the sentence you need to save tonight:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story, but when your life is surrendered to Christ, it does not get to write the ending.
Because somewhere tonight, another screen is glowing in another dark room…
another person is hiding…
another believer thinks they have gone too far…
another wounded soul believes their story has already been ruined.
And perhaps the next truth they encounter will remind them:
Jesus still receives sinners.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still heals the wounded.
Jesus still forgives the repentant.
Jesus still makes all things new.
And the scandal you thought would become the last sentence of your life may become the very place where the world sees just how astonishing His grace really is.
The wound may remember what happened—but grace remembers who has the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THIS TOO SHALL PASS” — IS IT ACTUALLY IN THE BIBLE?
paragraphs:
“THIS TOO SHALL PASS” — IS IT ACTUALLY IN THE BIBLE?
The Four Words Christians Keep Quoting as Scripture… That Scripture Never Actually Says
“This too shall pass.”
Maybe someone whispered those words to you beside a hospital bed.
Maybe you repeated them after a relationship collapsed.
Maybe you typed them beneath someone’s post when you didn’t know what else to say.
Maybe you told yourself those four words while staring at a ceiling at 2:17 in the morning, wondering how much longer you could carry what nobody else knew you were carrying.
“This too shall pass.”
It sounds biblical.
It feels biblical.
It has been repeated so often in Christian conversations that many people assume there must be a verse somewhere that says exactly that.
There isn’t.
You can search the Psalms.
You can search Proverbs.
You can search the prophets.
You can search the words of Jesus.
You can search the letters of Paul.
You will find extraordinary promises about suffering, endurance, eternity, restoration, and the temporary nature of this present world.
But you will not find a Bible verse that simply says:
“This too shall pass.”
And strangely enough, discovering that does not make the Christian hope weaker.
It makes it stronger.
Because Christianity does not offer you a sentimental slogan promising that every painful circumstance will disappear exactly when you want it to.
Christianity gives you something infinitely greater.
It gives you Jesus Christ.
And there is an enormous difference between believing, “Eventually my circumstances will change,” and believing, “Even if my circumstances do not change today, Christ will not abandon me.”
Maybe that distinction is exactly what somebody reading this needs right now.
Because perhaps you have been waiting for “this” to pass.
The grief.
The loneliness.
The financial pressure.
The unanswered prayer.
The betrayal.
The consequences of your own mistakes.
The shame you cannot seem to silence.
The temptation that keeps returning.
The season where everybody thinks you are strong because they cannot hear what happens inside your head when the room gets quiet.
You keep saying:
“This too shall pass.”
But somewhere underneath those words is another question.
“When?”
And underneath that question may be another one.
“God… where are You?”
That is where a slogan reaches its limit.
And where Scripture begins speaking with far greater power.

Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 4:17–18 about suffering with language far more astonishing than “this too shall pass.” He called the believer’s present affliction temporary when measured against an eternal glory beyond comparison, and then directed our eyes beyond what can presently be seen.
The Greek makes the contrast especially vivid.
τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν… αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης
to gar parautika elaphron tēs thlipseōs hēmōn… aiōnion baros doxēs
Paul contrasts present θλῖψις — thlipsis, affliction, pressure, distress, with an αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης — aiōnion baros doxēs, an eternal weight of glory.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not pretend suffering does not hurt.
He does not tell grieving Christians to smile harder.
He does not reduce agony to a motivational quote.
He changes the scale.
Your suffering may feel enormous when measured against Tuesday.
It may feel unbearable when measured against this month.
It may feel endless when measured against the last three years.
But Paul measures present suffering against eternity.
And suddenly the equation changes.
Not because the suffering becomes imaginary.
Because eternity becomes enormous.
This is one of Christianity’s most radical claims:
The Christian does not ultimately overcome suffering because every earthly problem receives an earthly solution.
The Christian overcomes because suffering does not receive the final word.
Jesus does.
That matters, because some things do not simply “pass” in the neat way inspirational sayings imply.
Some people pray for healing and continue living with illness.
Some marriages are not restored.
Some prodigal children take years to return.
Some never return in this lifetime.
Some believers carry scars until death.
Some funerals leave an empty chair that remains empty.
Some consequences cannot be reversed.
Some apologies arrive too late.
Some doors never reopen.
Some questions remain unanswered on this side of eternity.
So biblical Christianity cannot merely promise:
“Hold on. Everything will eventually become comfortable again.”
Jesus never promised His disciples that.
In fact, He told them plainly:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation.”
But He did not stop there.
“...but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
That is John 16:33.
And the Greek word translated “tribulation” is again related to θλῖψις — thlipsis.
Pressure.
Affliction.
Distress.
Jesus did not say, “You might experience pressure if something goes wrong.”
He prepared His followers for it.
And then He grounded their courage not in the disappearance of trouble but in Himself:
ἐγὼ νενίκηκα τὸν κόσμον
egō nenikēka ton kosmon
“I have overcome the world.”
That is stronger than “this too shall pass.”
Because sometimes God removes the storm.
Sometimes God carries you through the storm.
And sometimes the storm continues long enough that you discover something about Christ you never would have learned standing beneath a cloudless sky.
There are people reading this who know exactly what that means.
You asked God to remove something.
Instead, He began changing you inside it.
You prayed for escape.
He started teaching endurance.
You begged Him to change another person.
He exposed something in your own heart.
You wanted relief.
He began producing repentance.
You wanted answers.
He gave you His presence.
You wanted the chapter erased.
Jesus began rewriting what the chapter meant.
That is the strange mathematics of grace.

God can take something Satan intended for destruction, something another person intended for harm, something the fallen world produced through suffering, or even something you created through your own sinful choices—and without ever calling evil good, God can redeem what seemed irredeemable.
Joseph understood something like this after being betrayed and sold by his own brothers.
Genesis 50:20 records his words:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
The Hebrew contains an extraordinary contrast.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
attem chashavtem alai ra‘ah; Elohim chashavah letovah
The same Hebrew root, חשב — chashav, appears in the contrast: what they intended or planned for evil, God intended for good.
God did not need Joseph’s brothers to have pure motives in order to accomplish His purposes.
Their evil remained evil.
Their guilt remained real.
Yet their sin was not sovereign.
God was.
Somebody needs to hear that distinction.
What happened to you may have been wrong.
What they did may actually have been evil.
What you did may actually require repentance.
Christianity does not require us to rename darkness as light.
Grace does something more astonishing.
It declares that darkness does not possess enough authority to prevent God from accomplishing His purposes.
And perhaps that is why Romans 8:28 has comforted suffering Christians for centuries.
“And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.”
That verse does not say all things are good.
Cancer is not good.
Abuse is not good.
Betrayal is not good.
Sin is not good.
Death is an enemy.
Paul’s claim is that God is capable of working through “all things” toward His redemptive purposes for His people.
And Romans 8 does not climax with Christians receiving easier circumstances.
It climbs toward something far greater.
Conformity to the image of Christ.
Then Paul moves through suffering, persecution, danger, and death before declaring that nothing in all creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is biblical hope.
Not:
“Nothing painful will happen.”
But:
“Nothing can separate me from Christ.”
Not:
“I will never cry again.”
But:
“My tears are not the final chapter.”
Not:
“I understand everything God is doing.”
But:
“I know the One holding me when I understand nothing.”
And this reaches all the way back into the Psalms.
Psalm 23 does not say:
“Because God is my shepherd, there will be no valley.”
David says:
“Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil…”
Why?
Not because valleys are imaginary.
Not because believers never suffer.
Not because every problem disappears overnight.
The center of David’s confidence is painfully simple:
“for thou art with me.”
כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי
ki attah immadi
“For You are with me.”
That may be one of the most important corrections to the popular phrase “this too shall pass.”
The deepest Christian comfort is not that “this” will pass.
It is that He is with you while you pass through it.
Read that again.
Because there is a difference.
A tremendous difference.
If your hope depends entirely upon circumstances changing, every delayed answer can feel like abandonment.
But when your hope is anchored in Christ, you can grieve and still worship.
You can hurt and still believe.
You can tremble and still pray.
You can say, “I don’t understand You, God,” without saying, “Therefore I will leave You.”
Faith is not pretending the valley is beautiful.
Faith is discovering that the Shepherd entered it with you.
And nowhere is that truth clearer than at the cross.
Christianity does not worship a distant God shouting encouragement toward suffering humanity from the safety of heaven.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
Jesus entered our broken world.
He experienced rejection.
Betrayal.
Injustice.
Mockery.
Physical agony.
And death.
At Calvary, the disciples could have looked at everything happening and concluded:
This is the end.
Their Messiah was crucified.
Their expectations shattered.
Their courage collapsed.
The One they believed would redeem Israel lay dead.
Saturday must have felt like proof that hope had failed.
But Saturday did not know Sunday was coming.
The stone was not the final punctuation mark.
The resurrection changed everything.
And here is where “this too shall pass” becomes almost embarrassingly small compared with the Gospel.
The Gospel does not merely announce that bad seasons eventually end.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ entered death itself and came out victorious.
Paul therefore taunts death in 1 Corinthians 15:
“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
The Greek word for victory is νῖκος — nikos.
Victory.
Triumph.
Conquest.
Death—the thing human beings cannot outrun, negotiate with, purchase their way out of, or permanently defeat—has met Someone stronger.
Jesus Christ.
So yes.
This world is passing.
Scripture actually says that.
First John 2:17 says:
“And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.”
Paul similarly writes in 1 Corinthians 7:31 that “the fashion of this world passeth away.”
Revelation eventually gives us the breathtaking destination toward which biblical hope moves: God dwelling with His people, death defeated, mourning ended, tears wiped away.
Revelation 21:4 declares:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying…”
So there is a profoundly biblical sense in which we can say that the present order of suffering will not last forever.
But Scripture gives that confidence a foundation.
Not fate.
Not positive thinking.
Not “the universe.”
Not karma.
Not time.
Christ.
This is why Christians should be careful with phrases that sound biblical.
A statement can contain a measure of truth without being Scripture.
And when we attach “the Bible says” to something the Bible never actually says, even accidentally, we blur the difference between human wisdom and the Word of God.
You do not need to make the Bible say something it never said in order to comfort somebody.
What Scripture actually says is better.
When you are shattered:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart…” — Psalm 34:18.
When you are afraid:
“What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.” — Psalm 56:3.
When you are exhausted:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28.
When you feel abandoned:
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” — Hebrews 13:5.
When suffering feels meaningless:
God is working toward purposes larger than what you presently see.
When death feels final:
Jesus says, “I am the resurrection, and the life…” — John 11:25.
Those promises do not need improvement.
But perhaps there is another reason this phrase matters.
Sometimes “this too shall pass” becomes our way of waiting for pain to disappear while avoiding what God wants to do in us through it.
We want the season to pass.
God wants the old person to pass away.
We want circumstances transformed.
God wants hearts transformed.
We want God to fix what hurts.
Sometimes God first confronts what is sinful.
Because not every difficult season is merely something to survive.
Some seasons expose us.
The argument exposed your pride.
The temptation exposed your divided heart.
The financial collapse exposed what you worshipped.
The loneliness exposed how desperately you needed human approval.
The scandal exposed what secrecy had protected.
The consequences exposed what compromise had been quietly building.
And suddenly the prayer changes.
It is no longer merely:
“God, make this pass.”
It becomes:
“Jesus, do not let me pass through this unchanged.”
That is a dangerous prayer.
Because Christ loves us too much merely to make us comfortable while leaving our idols untouched.
Maybe what needs to “pass” is not merely your suffering.
Maybe the hiding needs to pass.
The pornography needs to pass.
The bitterness needs to pass.
The secret messages need to pass.
The affair needs to pass.
The drunkenness needs to pass.
The hatred needs to pass.
The religious performance needs to pass.
The obsession with approval needs to pass.
The version of Christianity where Jesus is Savior but never Lord needs to pass.
Maybe you have spent months asking God to change your circumstances while the Holy Spirit has been putting His finger on your heart.
And you know it.
This is where the Gospel becomes uncomfortable before it becomes beautiful.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult seasons easier.
He came to save sinners.
He calls us to repentance.
He calls us away from sin and toward Himself.
And repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up sufficiently to earn mercy.
You cannot do that either.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience, died for sinners, and rose again victorious.
Forgiveness is not purchased by your tears.
Grace is not wages for good behavior.
Salvation is the gift of God received through faith in Christ.
And when Christ saves someone, He does not simply cover yesterday.
He begins transforming tomorrow.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes, not merely opportunities.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose stories appear permanently stained.
Then Jesus enters the story.
Scandal meets grace.
Shame meets mercy.
Sin meets the cross.
Death meets resurrection.
And suddenly what looked like the final chapter becomes the place where redemption begins writing.
That is our heartbeat:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because the past becomes good.
Not because Christians pretend scars never happened.
Because Jesus is capable of giving sinners something the world cannot manufacture:
forgiveness.
A new identity.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A new direction.
And ultimately resurrection life.
So if you are reading this while waiting for “this” to pass, perhaps your first prayer should not be:
“Lord, when will this end?”
Perhaps it should be:
“Lord Jesus, who are You calling me to become while I am here?”
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have sinned, repent.
If shame has convinced you that Jesus could never receive you, look again at the cross.
If you have fallen repeatedly, stop using grace as permission to remain down and start trusting grace as the power that calls you back to Christ.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, do not mistake familiarity with Christianity for reconciliation with God.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still need Christ.
You can attend church and still need Christ.
You can post Bible verses and still need Christ.
You can encourage everybody else and still desperately need Christ.
Come to Him.
Not after you repair yourself.
Now.
Bring the wreckage.
Bring the guilt.
Bring the questions.
Bring the secret nobody knows.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the failure you cannot undo.
Bring the heart you cannot heal.
Jesus is not intimidated by ruins.
He specializes in resurrection.
And perhaps that is what you really needed instead of four comforting words.
Not:
“This too shall pass.”
But:
Jesus Christ will remain.
Hebrews 13:8 says:
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.”
Your season changes.
Jesus remains.
People change.
Jesus remains.
Your strength changes.
Jesus remains.
Your emotions change.
Jesus remains.
Your circumstances change.
Jesus remains.
This world itself will pass away.
Jesus remains.
And if you belong to Him, your ultimate future is not determined by the chapter currently making you cry.
It is determined by the risen Christ.
If this exposed something you have been carrying quietly, do not turn the moment into another scroll and forget.
Be honest.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light is the first honest step after months of pretending.
And somewhere on your Facebook friends list is probably someone whose smile is hiding a war.
Not merely because you enjoyed it.
Send it privately to the friend who stopped talking about God.
Send it to the believer who is tired.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing more substantial to offer than religious slogans.
If this ministry is helping you grow closer to Christ, there is also a practical way to stand behind the work.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
God's favor cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So support Christian work because you want Christ proclaimed—not because you think giving money earns another ounce of God's love.
And tonight, when the room becomes quiet again…
when the problem is still there…
when the diagnosis has not changed…
when the person has not returned…
when the prayer still seems unanswered…
when you are tempted to whisper, “This too shall pass” just to survive another hour…
remember something stronger.
Maybe it will pass tomorrow.
Maybe it will take years.
Maybe some scars will remain until Jesus calls you home.
But if you are in Christ, the valley cannot keep you forever.
Sin will not have the final word.
Shame will not have the final word.
Your scandal will not have the final word.
Your suffering will not have the final word.
The grave will not have the final word.
Jesus will.
And when everything temporary has finally passed away, the One who carried you through every trembling chapter will still be standing.
Your pain may belong to this chapter—but Jesus has already secured the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Didn’t Stop Believing in God. You Just Slowly Built a Life That Barely Needs Him.
paragraphs: You Didn’t Stop Believing in God. You Just Slowly Built a Life That Barely Needs Him.
The most dangerous distance from Jesus may not begin when you deny Him. It may begin when your life becomes comfortable enough that you no longer notice how little you depend on Him.
There was no dramatic goodbye.
No angry prayer.
No Bible thrown across the room.
No announcement that you had stopped believing.
You still believed in God.
You still called yourself a Christian.
You still knew the songs.
You still knew when to say “Amen.”
You still had verses stored somewhere in your memory from years of sermons, Sunday school lessons, devotionals, conferences, and conversations.
You could still tell someone that Jesus died for their sins.
You could still pray when somebody became sick.
You could still post something about God when life became painful.
And if someone asked you directly, “Do you believe in Jesus?”
You would probably answer immediately.
“Of course.”

But somewhere between surviving, succeeding, paying bills, raising children, chasing deadlines, solving problems, building a career, scrolling through your phone, planning tomorrow, and trying to make life comfortable...
something happened.
Not rebellion.
Not necessarily apostasy.
Something quieter.
You became good at living without consciously depending on the One you still claimed to believe in.
And that may be one of the most frightening spiritual conditions imaginable.
Because obvious rebellion can alarm the conscience.
Pain can drive someone to their knees.
Failure can expose pride.
Sin can become so ugly that eventually you cry out for mercy.
But comfort?
Comfort can let you sleep while your heart slowly forgets its hunger for God.
That is why the words of Jesus to the church in Laodicea remain so unsettling.
“I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.”
Then Jesus exposes what was underneath their lukewarmness:
“For you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing…”
Revelation 3:15–17.
There it is.
The sentence that should make comfortable Christians uncomfortable.
“I need nothing.”
The Greek expression is devastatingly simple:
οὐδὲν χρείαν ἔχω — ouden chreian echō
“I have need of nothing.”
That was Laodicea’s illusion.
Notice what Jesus did not accuse them of saying.
They did not say, “There is no God.”
They did not say, “Jesus is false.”
They did not say, “We reject Christianity.”
Their problem was exposed in something far more subtle.
They had reached a condition in which they perceived themselves as having no need.
And Jesus looked beneath everything they possessed and said:
“…not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.”
Revelation 3:17.
They thought they were rich.
Jesus said they were poor.
They thought they could see.
Jesus said they were blind.
They thought they were clothed.
Jesus said they were naked.
Their greatest poverty was hidden beneath their prosperity.
And perhaps that is why this passage feels so painfully modern.
Because some of us have not abandoned Jesus.
We have simply arranged our lives so efficiently that we rarely need to consciously depend on Him.
The alarm wakes us.
The calendar directs us.
The salary sustains us.
The refrigerator feeds us.
The doctor treats us.
The GPS guides us.
The internet answers us.
Entertainment distracts us.
The credit card rescues us.
Our experience advises us.
Our routines stabilize us.
Our competence reassures us.
And none of those things is inherently sinful.
Work is not the enemy.
Planning is not the enemy.
Medicine is not the enemy.
Technology is not the enemy.
Financial stability is not the enemy.
Having a comfortable home is not automatically evidence of spiritual compromise.
The danger begins when gifts quietly replace dependence upon the Giver.
When provision makes us forget the Provider.
When competence becomes self-sufficiency.
When routine replaces communion.
When knowing about God becomes a substitute for walking with God.
When we stop asking, “Jesus, what do You want?” because we already know what we want and simply hope He will bless it.
You can become so competent at managing your life that prayer starts feeling optional.
You can become so familiar with Scripture that reading it stops feeling urgent.
You can become so accustomed to church that worship stops producing wonder.
You can know Christian vocabulary while your private life becomes increasingly prayerless.
You can defend biblical truth online while barely opening your Bible when nobody is watching.
You can sing about surrender while carefully protecting the areas you refuse to surrender.
You can say, “Jesus is Lord,” while constructing your schedule as though every hour belongs exclusively to you.
And perhaps the most terrifying part is this:
You may not notice.
Spiritual drift rarely announces itself.
It usually whispers.
Not tonight.
You’re tired.
Pray tomorrow.
Read Scripture later.
You already know that passage.
Skip church this week.
You’ve been busy.
Everybody struggles with that sin.
Don’t make such a big deal about it.
You’re doing better than most people.
God understands.
And little by little, what once troubled your conscience becomes normal.
What once drove you to prayer barely crosses your mind.
What once broke your heart becomes entertainment.
What once made you tremble before God becomes another theological discussion.
You still believe.
But you no longer burn.
And eventually you can become more disturbed by losing your Wi-Fi connection than by realizing you have barely spoken to Jesus all day.
That sentence hurts because some of us know exactly what it means.
There was once a season when you prayed differently.
Remember?
Maybe you were younger.
Maybe you were broken.
Maybe you had nothing.
Maybe your marriage was collapsing.
Maybe you were unemployed.
Maybe someone you loved was sick.
Maybe addiction had dragged you into places you never thought you would go.
Maybe shame had finally crushed the image you were trying to maintain.
Maybe you had reached the end of yourself.
And you prayed because prayer was not religious decoration.
It was oxygen.
“Jesus, please.”
“Jesus, help me.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
You opened Scripture because you were desperate for a word from God.
You worshiped differently because grace felt unbelievable.
You cried when you thought about the cross because you knew what Christ had rescued you from.
Then things improved.
The prayer was answered.
The job came.
The bills became manageable.
The relationship healed.
The crisis passed.
The children grew.
The house became quieter.
Your confidence returned.
Life became stable.
And somewhere along the way...
“Jesus, I need You” became “Jesus, I’ll talk to You when I have time.”
This is one of prosperity’s ancient temptations.
Long before Laodicea, Moses warned Israel about precisely this danger.

As Israel prepared to enter a land of abundance, Moses warned them that after they had eaten and become satisfied, built good houses, multiplied their possessions, and experienced prosperity, their hearts could become proud.
Then came the warning:
“…then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God…”
Deuteronomy 8:14.
Notice the sequence.
Blessing.
Satisfaction.
Increase.
Pride.
Forgetfulness.
Not necessarily intellectual atheism.
Functional forgetfulness.
Living as though the God who gave everything is no longer necessary.
Later Moses warns them against saying:
“My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.”
Deuteronomy 8:17.
Human nature has not changed much.
We pray desperately for the opportunity.
Then eventually congratulate ourselves for what we built with it.
We pray for the job.
Then the job becomes too important for prayer.
We pray for children.
Then family responsibilities become the reason we have no time for God.
We pray for financial stability.
Then money becomes the source of our security.
We pray for healing.
Then after healing, we forget the desperation that once brought us near.
We ask God to rescue us from the wilderness...
and then sometimes the Promised Land becomes the place where we forget Him.
Maybe that is where you are.
Not scandalously rebellious.
Just spiritually comfortable.
Not denying Christ.
Just rarely desperate for Him.
Not running from church.
Just attending without hunger.
Not throwing away your Bible.
Just leaving it unopened.
Not saying prayer is useless.
Just living like it can wait.
Not renouncing Jesus.
Just slowly building a life that barely needs Him.
And before shame tells you to stop reading, you need to see something beautiful in Revelation 3.
Because Jesus does not expose Laodicea merely to humiliate them.
He exposes them because He loves them.
Listen to His words:
“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent.”
Revelation 3:19.
The Greek word translated “repent” is:
μετανόησον — metanoēson
It is an imperative.
Repent.
Turn.
Change your mind and direction.
Come back.
Jesus does not flatter lukewarmness.
He calls it what it is.
But neither does He abandon the lukewarm church without invitation.
And then comes one of Scripture’s most famous images:
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.”
Revelation 3:20.
Read that in context.
Jesus is addressing a church.
People who presumably carried His name.
People who had religious identity.
People who believed themselves prosperous.
Yet Christ pictures Himself at the door, knocking.
That should shake us.
Because it is possible to maintain Christian activity while resisting intimate fellowship with Christ.
Possible to talk about Jesus while keeping certain doors closed to Jesus.
Possible to sing His name publicly while ignoring His knock privately.
And still...
He knocks.
That is grace.
The risen Christ could have walked away.
He could have left them with their wealth and illusion.
Instead, He confronted them.
He called them to repentance.
He offered fellowship.
“If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.”
This is not a picture of a desperate Savior begging human beings to make Him relevant.
This is the sovereign, risen Christ mercifully calling complacent people back into fellowship with Himself.
The knock is mercy.
The rebuke is mercy.
The conviction you feel while reading this may itself be mercy.
Because the frightening condition is not merely being lukewarm.
It is becoming so comfortable in lukewarmness that you no longer care.
So if something inside you is uncomfortable right now...
if you are remembering what your prayer life used to be...
if you know worship has become mechanical...
if you have been hiding a compromise...
if you have been calling spiritual numbness “being busy”...
if you have been surviving on yesterday’s encounters with God...
do not waste the conviction.
Do not turn this into another article you emotionally react to and spiritually forget ten minutes later.
Come home.
Not to religion.
To Christ.
Christianity is not primarily about becoming more disciplined so God will finally accept you.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never save themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Your greatest problem was never poor time management.
It was sin.
And your deepest solution is not a better morning routine.
It is Christ crucified and risen.
Jesus did not die because you needed motivational improvement.
He died for sinners.
He carried sin to the cross.
He shed His blood.
He bore judgment.
He rose from the grave.
And forgiveness is offered through Him.
That means repentance is not paying an entrance fee back into God's affection.
It is turning away from sin and self-rule toward the Savior whose grace is greater than your failure.
You may have drifted.
Christ remains worthy.
You may have become distracted.
Christ remains glorious.
You may have become self-sufficient.
Christ remains your true source of life.
You may have neglected prayer.
The throne of grace has not disappeared.
You may have hidden sin.
There is still cleansing in Christ.
You may feel ashamed that you allowed your heart to become cold.
But shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
This is what Gospel Warrior means when we keep returning to these words:
Your scandal may never become public.
There may never be headlines.
Nobody may discover what happened inside your soul.
Your scandal may simply be that the Savior who gave everything for you became an accessory to the life He gave you.
But grace can rewrite even that story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is costly precisely because sin matters.
The cross proves both.
At Calvary, we see how serious our rebellion is...
and how staggering God's mercy is.
So maybe tonight you need to stop performing.
Put the phone down.
Close the other tabs.
Turn off the noise.
Sit somewhere alone.
And tell Jesus the truth.
“Lord, I still believe in You.
But I have been living like I barely need You.
I have depended on my money.
My intelligence.
My routines.
My relationships.
My experience.
My plans.
My comfort.
My own strength.
Forgive me.
I don't want to know You only as theology.
I want communion with You.
Expose what I have protected.
Break what needs breaking.
Restore what has grown cold.
Teach me again to depend on You.”
Maybe tears come.
Maybe they don't.
Repentance is not measured by emotional volume.
Come honestly.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Make restitution where Scripture requires it.
Seek accountability where secrecy has been feeding sin.
Open the Bible again—not to complete a religious streak, but to hear the Word of the God you love.
Pray again—not because your prayer earns God's favor, but because through Christ you have access to your Father.
Worship again.
Serve again.
Forgive again.
Obey again.
And when you fail, do not build a house in shame.
Run again to Christ.
Because mature Christianity is not finally the story of becoming so strong that you need Jesus less.
It is discovering more deeply how completely you need Him.
Jesus said:
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
John 15:5.
Not less.
Not “you can accomplish a few spiritual things.”
Nothing.
The Christian life begins with dependence, continues through dependence, and ends with dependence.
The goal is never independence from Christ.
The goal is abiding in Christ.
So ask yourself the question you may have avoided for months:
If everything comfortable in my life remained exactly the same, but the conscious presence of Christ disappeared from my daily life...
how long would it take me to notice?
Do not answer quickly.
Let it hurt where it needs to hurt.
Would your schedule change?
Would your spending change?
Would your entertainment change?
Would your conversations change?
Would your marriage notice?
Would your children notice?
Would your browser history notice?
Would your ambitions notice?
Would your private thoughts notice?
Would you notice?
This is not written so you can identify another lukewarm Christian.
This is written so we can stop pointing across the room long enough to let Revelation 3 examine us.
Maybe you have been following Jesus for thirty years.
Maybe three months.
Maybe you are reading this while secretly wondering whether you even believe anymore.
Maybe you are the pastor who knows how to preach while privately running on fumes.
Maybe you are the mother who serves everybody while her own soul is exhausted.
Maybe you are the businessman who thanks God publicly but privately trusts the numbers more than the Lord.
Maybe you are the young believer who once burned with passion but discovered that endless scrolling can anesthetize spiritual hunger.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus knows.
“I know your works.”
And remarkably...
He is still knocking.
That is the scandal of grace.
The One we neglect continues calling us.
The One we sin against offers forgiveness.
The One we pushed toward the margins calls us back to the center.
The Savior does not say, “Clean yourself completely, become impressive again, and perhaps I will consider fellowship with you.”
He calls you to repent and open the door.
So open it.
Today.
Not when another tragedy forces you to need God.
Not when the money disappears.
Not when the diagnosis comes.
Not when the marriage cracks.
Not when somebody dies.
Not when your strength finally fails.
You do not have to wait for God to remove every earthly support before admitting that He was your true need all along.
Come while the refrigerator is full.
Come while the job is secure.
Come while the body is healthy.
Come while life is comfortable.
Come while you still have plans for tomorrow.
Come because Jesus is worthy when you are desperate...
and Jesus is worthy when everything is going well.
Not as a magic phrase.
Not as public performance.
Let it simply be your confession that self-sufficiency has gone far enough.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only believer fighting their way out of spiritual numbness.
Your honesty may give another person permission to become honest before God.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because somebody you love may be drifting quietly.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your mind while reading.
Send it to your family.
Send it to the longtime Christian who knows all the answers but may need to hear the question again.
Send it even to the person who does not yet believe, because beneath all our attempts at self-sufficiency is the same human need for reconciliation with our Creator.
There may come a day when comfort starts making you sleepy again.
Come back and remember.

We want this community to remain a place where believers, struggling Christians, seekers, and even unbelievers can encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.

Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for supporting your local church, caring for your family, giving generously to people in need, or obeying whatever stewardship God has entrusted to you. Salvation cannot be purchased. Grace cannot be bought.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the One you need.

Do not confuse supporting a Christian ministry with supporting Christ Himself. Christ needs nothing from us as though He were deficient. We are the needy ones. Everything we possess already belongs to God, and every act of Christian generosity should flow from grace, gratitude, love, and willing obedience—not guilt, coercion, or an attempt to purchase blessing.
So if you want to glorify God, begin where Scripture begins:
Give yourself to Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Obey Christ.
Love people.
Serve faithfully.
Give freely.

And when you choose to support faithful Gospel ministry—whether through your local church, missionaries, ministries, generosity toward the poor, sharing biblical truth, or voluntarily supporting Gospel Warrior—do it because Christ has already given you infinitely more than you could ever repay.
Follow because none of us outgrows our need to be reminded of Scripture.
choose Christ.
Because perhaps you never stopped believing in God.
Perhaps you simply became so capable, so busy, so distracted, and so comfortable that you forgot what your soul once knew:
You were never meant to become good at living without Jesus.
And maybe the sound you thought was condemnation...
was actually the Savior knocking.
The tragedy is not that you needed Jesus when everything fell apart; the tragedy would be finally getting everything you wanted and forgetting that Jesus was always the treasure.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID BIBLICAL PATRIARCHS TAKE CONCUBINES—AND WHY DID GOD ALLOW IT?
paragraphs:
WHY DID BIBLICAL PATRIARCHS TAKE CONCUBINES—AND WHY DID GOD ALLOW IT?
The Bible Never Hides the Scandal of Its Heroes. It Shows Us What Happens When Broken People Try to Accomplish God’s Promise Their Own Way—and Why Every Shattered Story Ultimately Makes Us Desperate for Jesus.
There is a question many Christians quietly carry but are sometimes afraid to ask.
If Abraham was a man of faith… why Hagar?
If Jacob was chosen by God… why Bilhah and Zilpah?

If these men were patriarchs—men whose names appear in the sacred history of redemption—why do their households sometimes look less like pictures of marital peace and more like families collapsing beneath jealousy, rivalry, wounded women, competing children, favoritism, and grief?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
Why did God allow it?
Because when you actually read the Bible instead of merely reading sanitized Bible-story versions of it, something startling happens.
The halos disappear.
Abraham struggles.
Sarah becomes desperate.
Jacob plays favorites.
Rachel burns with jealousy.
Leah aches to be loved.
Hagar runs into the wilderness.
Children inherit conflicts their parents helped create.
The Bible does not airbrush any of it.
And that may be one of the strongest evidences that we have misunderstood what Scripture is trying to show us.
The Bible is not primarily a museum displaying flawless religious heroes.
It is the story of a holy God working through profoundly flawed human beings until history arrives at the One Man who does not need His sins covered, explained, excused, or forgiven.
Jesus Christ.
So before we answer why patriarchs had concubines, we have to establish something absolutely essential:
Biblical description is not automatically biblical prescription.
The fact that Scripture tells us something happened does not mean Scripture tells us to imitate it.
Cain murdered Abel.
Abraham lied about Sarah.
Jacob deceived Isaac.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Judas betrayed Him.
Scripture records all of these things without endorsing them.
And concubinage must be read with the same care.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ—pilegesh.

In the social world reflected in the Old Testament, a concubine occupied a recognized but generally subordinate domestic position compared with a primary wife. The exact legal and social circumstances were not identical in every biblical account, so we should resist pretending that one simple modern definition explains every occurrence.
But Scripture clearly distinguishes concubines in passages such as Genesis 25:6, where Abraham’s offspring through them are distinguished from Isaac in matters of inheritance.
And here is where the Bible becomes painfully human.
In the ancient world, children meant far more than sentiment.
Children meant descendants.
Inheritance.
Household survival.
Labor.
Security.
Family continuity.
And for Abraham and Sarah, the question of descendants carried something infinitely greater:
the promise of God.
God had promised Abraham offspring.
But Sarah remained barren.
Year followed year.
Promise remained promise.
Her womb remained empty.
Imagine that pain before judging the desperation that followed it.
Every month another reminder.
Every year another disappointment.
Every promise from God apparently colliding with what her body seemed incapable of producing.
Then Sarah looked at Hagar.
And desperation whispered something that desperation still whispers today:
Maybe God needs my help.
Genesis 16 tells us that Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham so that a family might be established through her.
The Hebrew behind Sarah’s hope contains a heartbreaking wordplay around being “built up” through Hagar.
Sarah wanted a house.
A future.
A child.
Something tangible she could finally hold.
And instead of continuing to wait for the God who had promised, Abraham and Sarah attempted to produce through human strategy what God had promised through divine faithfulness.
That is where this ancient story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because maybe you have never taken a concubine.
But perhaps you have tried to manufacture what God told you to trust Him for.
Maybe God seemed slow, so you forced the relationship.
Maybe loneliness became unbearable, so you compromised.
Maybe money became frightening, so integrity became negotiable.
Maybe you prayed for years and eventually decided obedience was costing too much.
Maybe you knew what Scripture said—but another voice whispered:
“There has to be another way.”
That is Genesis 16.
Not merely a strange ancient sexual arrangement.
A mirror.
Human beings trying to accomplish God's purposes without waiting for God's way.
And notice what happens next.
Hagar conceives.
For one brief moment, the plan appears to work.
That may be the most dangerous part.
Disobedience sometimes produces immediate results.
The wrong relationship can temporarily soothe loneliness.
The dishonest decision can temporarily solve the financial problem.
The compromise can temporarily open the door.
The shortcut can temporarily look like an answered prayer.
Hagar became pregnant.
Problem solved?
No.
Problem multiplied.
Contempt entered the household.
Sarah became angry.
Abraham became passive.
Hagar was mistreated.
Hagar fled.
The house that was supposed to be “built” began breaking apart.
This is one of Scripture’s recurring warnings:
Just because something works does not mean God authored it.
And just because God brings redemption out of a decision does not mean He approved the decision.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because somebody reading this has been confusing God’s mercy after your compromise with God’s approval of your compromise.
They are not the same thing.
God can rescue you from a road He never told you to take.
He can forgive a sin He never commanded.
He can redeem consequences without calling the choices that created them righteous.
That is grace.
And Hagar’s story contains an astonishing picture of it.
She runs.
Pregnant.
Mistreated.
Vulnerable.
A foreign Egyptian servant caught inside someone else’s attempt to solve a spiritual problem through human means.
And God sees her.
This matters.
The narrative does not treat Hagar merely as reproductive equipment.
God meets the woman in the wilderness.
The forgotten woman is not forgotten by heaven.
The person pushed toward the margins of Abraham’s household is still visible to Abraham’s God.
Hagar responds to the God who encountered her with words associated with the astonishing confession:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro'i.
“You are a God who sees me.”
Think about that.
Sarah saw a solution.
Abraham saw an opportunity for an heir.
Ancient society could see a servant.
God saw Hagar.
Maybe that is why you needed this article today.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to become collateral damage in somebody else’s choices.
Someone used you.
Someone promised something and disappeared.
Someone else's selfishness changed your life.
Someone made a decision, and somehow you were the one left carrying the consequences.
People may know what happened.
God knows what it did to you.
He sees you.
Not the polished Facebook version of you.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the “I’m fine” version.
You.
And this is where the subject of concubines becomes much bigger than ancient marriage customs.
It becomes the story of what God does inside human wreckage.
Jacob’s household reinforces the lesson.
Rachel could not bear children and cried to Jacob in anguish.
Eventually her servant Bilhah entered the struggle.
Leah later gave Jacob Zilpah.
Children were born, but so were rivalry, comparison, competition, favoritism, and enormous emotional complexity.
Read those narratives slowly and you will not walk away thinking, “What a beautiful model for Christian marriage.”
You will feel the ache.
That is part of the point.
Scripture does not need to interrupt every paragraph with the sentence, “This arrangement is painful.”
The narrative shows you.
Look at the jealousy.
Look at the rivalry.
Look at the bargaining.
Look at children becoming entangled in adult wounds.
Look at women desperate to be loved.
Look at men failing to lead their households faithfully.
Look at what happens when human desire, cultural customs, reproductive desperation, power, favoritism, and sin collide.
Then go farther back.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before kings accumulated wives and concubines.
Before humanity learned how efficiently we could complicate what God created.
Return to Genesis.
God creates a man and a woman.
The man leaves father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Not one man collecting women according to wealth, power, fertility, politics, or desire.
One covenant union.
Jesus Himself reaches back to creation when teaching about marriage.
That matters enormously.
When human beings asked Jesus about difficult marital arrangements, Christ pointed beyond generations of broken human practice toward what God intended “from the beginning.”
That is how Christians should read the patriarchs.
Not by asking, “Abraham did it, so why can't I?”
But by asking:
“What was God's design before human sin distorted it?”
The patriarchs were not the standard.
God was.
And ultimately Christ is.
This also helps explain why Old Testament law can regulate broken social realities without presenting those realities as creation ideals.
God dealt with real people inside real cultures already scarred by sin.
Regulation is not necessarily celebration.
Restriction is not necessarily endorsement.
Tolerance within a fallen social order is not identical to declaring something morally ideal.
Jesus makes a similar distinction when discussing divorce. Moses permitted certain arrangements because of human hardness, Christ explained, but “from the beginning” it was not so.
That principle should make us very careful about building morality merely from the existence of an Old Testament practice.
God meets humanity in the wreckage.
Then He moves His people toward His holiness.
But there is another uncomfortable truth.
Concubinage was connected not merely to fertility but sometimes to wealth, status, dynasty, household expansion, and royal power.
And power has always been dangerous in the hands of sinful people.
Eventually Scripture gives us kings with multiple wives and concubines.
Solomon becomes the terrifying monument to where accumulation can lead.
The man renowned for wisdom still possessed a heart capable of wandering.
That should humble every believer.
Knowledge does not make you immune to temptation.
Ministry does not make you immune.
Bible knowledge does not make you immune.
A platform does not make you immune.
Being used by God does not make you immune.
If Abraham could stumble…
if Jacob could create terrible family dysfunction…
if David could fall…
if Solomon could wander…
then perhaps the appropriate response to biblical scandal is not arrogant judgment.
It is trembling dependence upon grace.
Because there is something frighteningly familiar about these men.
We just hide our concubines under different names.
Approval.
Pornography.
Secret messages.
Emotional affairs.
Money.
Status.
Ministry platforms.
Addictions.
Relationships we know God never told us to enter.
Private compromises we pray nobody discovers.
We create little substitutes for trust.
Things we run toward when waiting on God hurts too much.
And eventually those substitutes begin demanding payment.
That is why this article is not really about Abraham's bedroom.
It is about your heart.
And mine.
What have you brought into your life because you became tired of waiting for God?
What have you called “necessary” that Scripture calls compromise?
What have you defended simply because culture normalized it?
What have you kept because letting it go would hurt?
What is living inside your spiritual house today that God never asked you to bring inside?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because the greatest danger is not that we read Genesis and condemn Abraham.
The greatest danger is that we recognize Abraham’s impatience in ourselves and still refuse to repent.
Yet this is precisely where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
God did not abandon Abraham.
That does not mean Abraham’s failures did not matter.
It means Abraham's failures were not stronger than God's covenant faithfulness.
God continued His redemptive purpose.
Isaac came.
Jacob came.
Israel came.
Kings rose and fell.
Prophets cried out.
Generations sinned, repented, wandered, returned, failed, and waited.
Until eventually another Son appeared in the story.
Not Abraham's attempt to manufacture the promise.
Not Jacob manipulating circumstances.
Not David collapsing beneath desire.
Not Solomon drowning beneath abundance.
Jesus.
The faithful Son.
The promised Seed.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit His bride but gives Himself for her.
The King who does not use His power to collect women for His pleasure but lays His life down to redeem sinners.
The Savior who encounters disgraced women without using them.
The Lord who sees the Hagar in the wilderness.
The Christ who speaks with the Samaritan woman despite her complicated relational history.
The One who receives sinners, exposes darkness, commands repentance, grants forgiveness, and creates something new.
Suddenly you understand why Scripture refuses to sanitize its heroes.
If Abraham were perfect, we might worship Abraham.
If David were spotless, we might make David our savior.
