But if you genuinely believe this ministry is bearing good fruit, supporting it voluntarily can help that work continue.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not because clicking “share” somehow earns heaven.
They need to know that Jesus has not abandoned them.
They need to know grief is not the end of discipleship.
They need to know remembrance and healing can coexist.
They need to know that remarriage after widowhood is biblically permitted when it is in the Lord.
They need to know that remaining single can also be a faithful path.
They need to know that yesterday can be honored without sacrificing tomorrow.
Because somebody you know is grieving quietly.
Somebody is carrying flowers to a grave while secretly wondering whether God has any chapters left for them.
Somebody has begun loving again and hates themselves for it.
Somebody remarried years ago but still cries when an old photograph appears.
Somebody is terrified that moving forward means leaving their beloved behind.
Tell them the truth.
Death can close a chapter without making the chapter meaningless.
A new chapter does not have to burn the pages that came before it.
And Jesus Christ is Lord over the whole story.
The love was real.
The loss was real.
The grief is real.
But so is grace.
So is resurrection.
So is redemption.
And so is the possibility that the God who carried you through the chapter you thought would kill you is not finished writing yet.
You do not honor the dead by burying the rest of your life beside them; honor the love that was, surrender the life that remains to Christ, and trust the Redeemer with every page still unwritten.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JEZEBEL WAS WICKED—BUT NOT FOR HALF THE REASONS SOCIAL MEDIA CLAIMS
paragraphs:
JEZEBEL WAS WICKED—BUT NOT FOR HALF THE REASONS SOCIAL MEDIA CLAIMS
We turned one of Scripture’s most terrifying women into a stereotype about makeup, confidence, and “difficult women.” The Bible tells a darker story—and if we actually listen to it, we may discover that the spirit we keep accusing others of can hide much closer to home.
Her name has become an insult.
Jezebel.
Say it in certain Christian circles and everybody thinks they know exactly what it means.
A seductive woman.
A woman who wears too much makeup.
A woman who dresses provocatively.
A controlling wife.
A strong woman who intimidates men.
A woman with influence.
A woman who questions leadership.
A woman somebody simply does not like.
Sometimes the accusation becomes even more dramatic: “She has a Jezebel spirit.”

And just like that, a biblical name attached to bloodshed, idolatry, persecution, deception, abuse of royal authority, and unrepentant rebellion against God gets reduced to a convenient religious label we can throw at somebody who makes us uncomfortable.
But there is a problem.
Some of the things Christians routinely say about Jezebel are not what Scripture actually says.
And that matters.
Because when we exaggerate someone’s sins beyond the biblical text, we do not become more biblical.
We become less biblical.
Jezebel was wicked enough without our inventions.
Terrifyingly wicked.
But if we want to understand why, we have to stop listening to social-media mythology long enough to hear the Bible.
The first major introduction to Jezebel comes in 1 Kings 16:31. Ahab, king of Israel, married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and then went and served Baal.
That sentence is not merely telling us about a troubled marriage.
Something catastrophic was entering Israel’s royal house.
Ahab erected an altar for Baal in Samaria. Baal worship was promoted while Israel belonged covenantally to YHWH.
Jezebel was not merely an unpleasant queen.
She became a powerful enemy of the worshipers of the living God.
And Scripture eventually gives us one of the most chilling descriptions of her actions.
When Obadiah secretly protected the prophets of the LORD, 1 Kings 18:4 explains what was happening:
“Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD.”
The Hebrew is brutally direct:
בְּהַכְרִית אִיזֶבֶל אֵת נְבִיאֵי יְהוָה
behaḵrît ʾÎzeḇel ʾet neḇîʾê YHWH
The idea is that Jezebel was cutting off—destroying—the prophets belonging to YHWH.
People were hiding in caves because this woman was persecuting God’s servants.
Let that correct the caricature immediately.
Jezebel's defining evil was not that she knew how to apply eyeliner.
People were hiding from her because prophets were dying.

And somehow we have taken that terrifying biblical reality and turned “Jezebel” into an accusation we sometimes throw at women because of clothing, personality, beauty, influence, confidence, disagreement, or cosmetics.
That should trouble us.
Because there actually is a makeup scene in Jezebel’s story.
It happens shortly before her death.
Second Kings 9:30 says that when Jezebel heard Jehu had arrived, she painted her eyes, arranged her hair, and looked from a window.
And from that one scene, enormous assumptions have sometimes been constructed.
But read carefully.
The text tells you what she did.
It does not say that God condemned her because she painted her eyes.
It does not say cosmetics constituted “the Jezebel spirit.”
It does not say women who wear makeup resemble Jezebel.
It does not establish eyeliner as the theological explanation for her judgment.
Her judgment had already been pronounced before that scene.
Long before she looked out that window, Scripture had documented what she had done.
She promoted idolatry.
She persecuted the prophets of YHWH.
She threatened Elijah.
She participated in a royal system that led Israel deeper into rebellion.
And then came Naboth.
That story should make every person with power uncomfortable.
Naboth owned a vineyard near Ahab’s palace.
Ahab wanted it.
Naboth refused.
Not merely because he was stubborn.
He told the king, “The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.”
So the king went home angry, lay on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat.
Then Jezebel entered.
She discovered why her husband was sulking and essentially told him to get up because she would obtain the vineyard for him.
And this is where the story becomes horrifying.
Jezebel wrote letters using Ahab’s name.
She sealed them with his seal.
She contacted the elders and nobles of Naboth’s city.
She ordered a public fast.
She arranged for Naboth to be placed prominently before the people.
Then she commanded that two worthless men accuse him falsely of blaspheming God and the king.
The accusation worked.
Naboth was taken outside the city.
And stoned.
Dead.
Then a message returned to Jezebel.
Naboth was dead.
Her response was essentially: Go take the vineyard.
Read that slowly.
A man had property the powerful wanted.
He would not surrender it.
So authority was weaponized.
Religion was weaponized.
Witnesses were weaponized.
Public reputation was weaponized.
Legal process was weaponized.
And an innocent man died so powerful people could possess what belonged to him.
That is Jezebel.
Not a woman who simply had a strong personality.
Not a woman who refused to be quiet.
Not a woman wearing lipstick.
This was corruption powerful enough to manufacture guilt and destroy an innocent person.
And here is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because Jezebel becomes very easy to condemn when she remains thousands of years away.
But Scripture was never given merely so that we could stare at someone else’s darkness.
It also shines light into ours.
Maybe you have never murdered anyone.
But have you ever destroyed someone's reputation because you wanted control?
Have you ever repeated something you never verified because believing it benefited you?
Have you ever used spiritual language to punish somebody who would not give you what you wanted?
Have you ever called manipulation “discernment”?
Have you ever called jealousy “concern”?
Have you ever recruited other people into your offense so that somebody else would appear guilty?
Have you ever told only the part of the story that made you look innocent?
Have you ever used the name of God to strengthen an accusation God never told you to make?
Suddenly Naboth's vineyard does not feel so ancient.
Sometimes vineyards look like reputations.
Sometimes they look like ministries.
Sometimes they look like relationships.
Sometimes they look like careers.
Sometimes they look like somebody's dignity.
Sometimes we cannot possess what another person has, so instead of surrendering our envy, we begin building a case against them.
And the frightening thing about Jezebel's scheme was that it looked religious.
She proclaimed a fast.
Think about that.
A fast.
Something associated with humility before God became part of the machinery used to murder an innocent man.
You can use religious language and still be operating in rebellion against God.
You can quote Scripture while destroying someone.
You can say “the Lord showed me” when the Lord said nothing.
You can pray publicly while plotting privately.
You can call something discernment when it is actually suspicion.
You can make another believer the villain of your testimony because acknowledging your own sin would cost too much.
And this is precisely why casually labeling people “Jezebel” can become spiritually dangerous.
The very accusation supposedly meant to expose manipulation can itself become manipulative.
Imagine being a woman in a church who disagrees with somebody in authority and suddenly hearing, “Jezebel.”
Imagine being outspoken.
“Jezebel.”
Beautiful.
“Jezebel.”
Confident.
“Jezebel.”
Wearing makeup.
“Jezebel.”
Setting boundaries.
“Jezebel.”
None of those things, by themselves, establishes the biblical pattern associated with Jezebel.
If we are going to invoke Scripture, Scripture deserves the right to define its own terms.
And yet there is another passage people cannot ignore.
Second Kings 9:22 contains Jehu’s accusation concerning Jezebel. The Hebrew reads:
עַד־זְנוּנֵי אִיזֶבֶל אִמְּךָ וּכְשָׁפֶיהָ הָרַבִּים
ʿad-zenûnê ʾÎzeḇel ʾimməḵā ûḵəšāpehā hārabbîm
It speaks of Jezebel's “whoredoms” and her “many sorceries/witchcrafts.”
That language should not be erased.
But neither should we make it say whatever we want.

In the prophetic world of the Old Testament, sexual-infidelity language can carry both literal and covenantal/idolatrous dimensions depending upon context. Jezebel's story is unquestionably saturated with idolatry and opposition to YHWH. The Hebrew keshaphim language in 2 Kings 9:22 also explicitly associates her with sorceries.
So yes—the Bible gives us very serious categories.
We do not need fabricated ones.
And centuries later, the name appears again.
Jesus addresses the church at Thyatira in Revelation 2.
The Greek text says:
ἀλλὰ ἔχω κατὰ σοῦ ὅτι ἀφεῖς τὴν γυναῖκα Ἰεζάβελ...
alla echō kata sou hoti apheis tēn gynaika Iezabel...
“But I have this against you: you tolerate that woman Jezebel...”
The passage describes her as calling herself a prophetess and teaching and misleading Christ's servants into sexual immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols.
The Greek uses the verbs:
διδάσκει — didaskei — “she teaches”
and
πλανᾷ — plana — “she leads astray,” “deceives,” or “misleads.”
That is crucial.
The New Testament use of the name focuses again on corrupt spiritual influence—teaching that leads Christ's servants away from faithfulness into immorality and idolatrous compromise.
And Revelation says something astonishing immediately afterward.
Christ says He gave her time to repent.
Do not miss that.
Even there.
Even in a passage of terrifying judgment.
Repentance is still mentioned.
That changes the temperature of this entire conversation.
Because Christianity is not ultimately a religion of finding Jezebel in everybody else.
The Gospel asks a far more dangerous question.
What needs to repent in me?
That is where Jesus enters this story.
Because without Jesus, an article about Jezebel becomes another opportunity to feel righteous by studying someone else's depravity.
“She was terrible.”
Yes.
But what are we going to do with ours?
Her idolatry may have been visible in temples dedicated to Baal.
Ours can be hidden behind respectable lives.
Her idol had a name.
Ours might be money.
Approval.
Sex.
Status.
Control.
Influence.
Politics.
A relationship.
A ministry.
Our image.
Our followers.
Even our own theology can become an idol when winning arguments becomes more precious to us than resembling Christ.
Jezebel manipulated a legal process to get Naboth's vineyard.
We manipulate conversations.
She used false witnesses.
We use screenshots without context.
She weaponized accusation.
We weaponize posts.
She wanted control.
So do we.
She could not tolerate the prophetic word opposing her.
Sometimes neither can we.
And suddenly this article is no longer about an evil queen.
It is about the human heart.
Your heart.
Mine.
The heart that knows how to hide rebellion behind explanations.
The heart that knows how to justify bitterness.
The heart that knows how to make its own desires sound holy.
The heart that wants God—provided God does not touch the throne we secretly occupy.
And then comes Jesus Christ.
Not another influencer diagnosing everybody's “spirit.”
Jesus.
The One who knows exactly what is hidden.
The One before whom manipulation cannot hide behind charm.
The One before whom lust cannot hide behind privacy.
The One before whom pride cannot hide behind ministry.
The One before whom greed cannot hide behind ambition.
The One before whom bitterness cannot hide behind “discernment.”
The One who sees every Naboth we have wounded.
Every truth we twisted.
Every person we secretly hated.
Every compromise we protected.
Every idol we fed.
Every room of the heart we hoped He would never enter.
And instead of telling sinners to clean themselves up enough to deserve Him, Christ went to the cross.
This is the scandal.
The Holy One died for the unholy.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The King allowed Himself to be falsely accused.
Think about that after reading Naboth's story.
Naboth was falsely accused and condemned.
Centuries later Jesus Christ would also stand before false testimony.
But Jesus was not merely another innocent victim.
He willingly went toward the cross as the Lamb of God, bearing sin, fulfilling the Father's redemptive purpose.
At Calvary, God did not pretend evil was harmless.
He demonstrated how deadly sin truly is.
And at the same cross, He demonstrated how immeasurable His grace is.
That means the message is not:
“Find the Jezebel.”
The message is:
Repent.
Come home.
Stop hiding.
Bring the idol into the light.
Bring the manipulation into the light.
Bring the sexual sin into the light.
Bring the bitterness into the light.
Bring the false accusation into the light.
Bring the secret addiction into the light.
Bring the religious pride into the light.
Bring the need for control into the light.
And come to Jesus.
Because Christianity does not teach that sinners transform themselves into saints through embarrassment.
We are saved by grace through faith, and the Christ who forgives also transforms.
Grace is not God pretending your sin did not matter.
Grace is God providing in Christ what you could never provide for yourself.
And repentance is not God humiliating you for returning.
It is the sinner finally dropping the weapon, abandoning the idol, and coming home to the Father.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you expected an article exposing Jezebel.
And somewhere along the way Scripture started exposing you.
It exposed me too.
That is what the Word does.
It refuses to remain a telescope pointed at somebody else's sin.
Eventually it becomes a mirror.
So before you ever call another human being “Jezebel” again, remember what the biblical record actually emphasizes.
Idolatry.
Persecution of God's prophets.
Abuse of power.
False accusation.
Bloodshed.
Manipulation.
Opposition to the word of God.
Sorcery.
And, in Revelation's Jezebel imagery, deceptive teaching associated with sexual immorality and idolatrous compromise.
Those are serious things.
Serious enough that we should never cheapen them into Christian slang.
And there is another truth we need to recover.
Strong women are not automatically Jezebels.
Scripture contains courageous women whom God honored.
Deborah exercised leadership.
Esther risked her life before a king.
Abigail confronted David's destructive anger with extraordinary wisdom.
Priscilla helped instruct Apollos more accurately in the way of God.
Mary Magdalene became a witness to the risen Christ.
Strength is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Female influence is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Beauty is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Makeup is not Jezebel's defining sin.
Her rebellion against God is.
And men should not read this article with smug relief either.
Ahab is standing right there.
Scripture does not permit him to disappear behind his wife's wickedness.
First Kings 21 says Ahab “sold himself to do wickedness” and that Jezebel urged him on.
Ahab wanted the vineyard.
Ahab accepted the fruit of the injustice.
Ahab went down to possess what a murdered man had owned.
God confronted him too.
So the Jezebel story cannot honestly become an excuse for blaming women for male sin.
Ahab answered to God for Ahab.
Jezebel answered to God for Jezebel.
And you will answer to God for you.
I will answer to God for me.
That may be the sentence somebody needed today.
Stop spending your entire spiritual life diagnosing everybody else.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your pastor.
Your former church.
Your ex.
Your mother.
Your father.
Your political enemy.
The person who hurt you.
The Christian who disagreed with you.
There may indeed be real sin in their lives, and Scripture never requires us to pretend evil is good.
But while examining everyone else, do not neglect the person standing before your mirror.
David prayed:
“Search me, O God.”
Not:
“Search everybody who annoys me.”
Search me.
Know me.
Try me.
See whether there is any grievous way in me.
That is where revival begins.
Not when we discover a new label for somebody else.
When we finally become honest about ourselves before God.
But you also do not have to hide.
Maybe your battle is different.
Maybe you have been falsely labeled, spiritually manipulated, or crushed beneath accusations that Scripture itself never made against you.
Then hear this carefully:
Human labels do not outrank the verdict of Jesus Christ.
Run to Him.
Let Scripture—not somebody's anger—define sin.
Let Scripture—not social-media theology—shape your conscience.
And let Christ—not your accusers—be the center of your identity.
There is no glory in pretending we never needed grace.
The glory is that Jesus saves people who desperately do.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this—not somebody you want to attack, but somebody who has been wounded by careless biblical accusations—send this to them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Christ alone saves.
Supporting sound Christian content can help that content reach the exhausted believer scrolling alone at midnight.
The woman who has spent years believing God hates her.
The man hiding an addiction behind Sunday clothes.
The believer who has almost walked away.
The skeptic who still cannot stop thinking about Jesus.
The person who needs someone to open Scripture without turning it into a weapon.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet but cannot stop wondering whether Jesus might actually be who Christians say He is.
And please do not leave this merely thinking about Jezebel.
Leave thinking about Jesus.
Jezebel reminds us that evil is real.
Naboth reminds us that innocent people can suffer beneath corrupt power.
Ahab reminds us that allowing and benefiting from evil does not erase personal responsibility.
Revelation reminds us that churches can tolerate destructive teaching.
But Jesus reminds us that judgment is not God's only word to sinners.
“Repent.”
There is still time.
That word is mercy.
The same Christ who exposed sin at Thyatira offered time to repent.
The same Lord who sees through every disguise still calls sinners to Himself.
And the Gospel declares something Jezebel's story could never accomplish by itself:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is mighty to save.
Maybe your story has scandal in it.
Real scandal.
Not gossip.
Not rumors.
Your own choices.
Your own rebellion.
Things you would erase if you could.
Things you pray nobody ever discovers.
Things you have never forgiven yourself for.
Listen.
The Gospel was never designed for people with spotless histories.
It is good news for guilty people.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
Jesus Christ calls people to repent and believe.
Jesus Christ forgives.
Jesus Christ restores.
Jesus Christ transforms.
Jesus Christ can take the chapter you thought disqualified you and make it the place where grace becomes undeniable.
So do not spend another night hiding behind somebody else's sin.
Come into the light.
Drop the label.
Drop the mask.
Drop the idol.
Drop the excuse.
Come to Christ.
And remember this when the screen goes dark and you are alone again:
The Gospel is not the story of how well you hid your scandal. It is the story of what Jesus can do when you finally bring it into His light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES BEING A GOOD PERSON GET YOU INTO HEAVEN?
paragraphs: DOES BEING A GOOD PERSON GET YOU INTO HEAVEN?
The answer may destroy the lie you’ve trusted your whole life—but it could also introduce you to the grace you never knew you desperately needed.
Imagine this.
Your life is over.
The noise is gone.

The deadlines. The bills. The arguments. The accomplishments. The reputation you spent years protecting. The mistakes you prayed nobody would discover. The compliments. The criticisms. The money. The house. The followers. The people who loved you and the people who misunderstood you.
All of it is suddenly behind you.
And now you stand before God.
What would you say?
Maybe something like this:
“I tried to be a good person.”
“I never murdered anyone.”
“I loved my family.”
“I helped people.”
“I gave when I could.”
“I wasn’t perfect, but nobody is.”
“I think I did more good than bad.”
For millions of people, somewhere beneath all the religious language and cultural Christianity, that is the hope.
That somehow, when everything is finally weighed, the good side of the scale will be heavier.
But there is a terrifying question most of us avoid asking:
What if heaven never operated on a scale?
What if the question was never whether you were better than the person standing next to you?
And what if being “good” cannot save you—not because good works are meaningless, but because the standard you must meet is infinitely greater than human comparison?
Stay with me.
Because this is not an article about telling you that you are worthless.
It is about discovering why Jesus went to a cross for people who could never rescue themselves.
And somewhere between your goodness and your guilt, between everything you have done right and everything you desperately wish you could undo, there is a scandal called grace.
Jesus once encountered a wealthy man who apparently had many things going for him.
He was serious enough about eternal life to run to Jesus. He knelt before Him. He asked one of the greatest questions a human being could ask:
“Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?” — Mark 10:17, KJV
Notice the question.
What shall I do?
That question still lives inside us.
What can I do?
How much goodness is enough?
How religious must I become?
How many sins can I commit before I cross the line?
How many prayers compensate for the things I regret?
How many charitable acts erase what I did when nobody was looking?
Jesus immediately challenged the man's understanding of goodness:
“Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God.” — Mark 10:18, KJV
The Greek expression is striking:
οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς ὁ Θεός
oudeis agathos ei mē heis ho Theos
Literally, in natural English:
“No one is good except One—God.”
Jesus was not teaching that kindness is worthless or that every human action is equally evil.
He was exposing the standard.
We normally define goodness horizontally.
God defines it vertically.
We look at the neighbor who cheated on his wife and say, “At least I didn't do that.”
We look at the criminal on television and think, “I would never.”
We remember the money we donated.
The elderly person we helped.
The children we provided for.
The friend we forgave.
The church services we attended.
And those things can genuinely be good.
But then we quietly compare our brightest moments with somebody else's darkest ones and call the difference righteousness.
Scripture does something far more uncomfortable.
It compares us with God.
And suddenly the measuring stick changes.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
The Greek contains three words that dismantle human boasting:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον
pantes gar hēmarton
“For all have sinned.”
Not some.
Not merely criminals.
Not merely atheists.
Not merely adulterers, addicts, hypocrites, corrupt leaders, abusers, thieves, and people whose sins became public scandals.
All.
The respectable father.
The faithful churchgoer.
The generous businesswoman.
The pastor.
The missionary.
The person reading this article.
The person writing it.
All.
This is where Christianity becomes offensive to human pride.
Because the Gospel does not divide humanity into good people who deserve heaven and bad people who deserve hell.
It announces something far more humbling:
We are all sinners who need a Savior.
Think about a glass of crystal-clear water.
Drop one tiny amount of poison into it.
Would you drink it because most of the glass was still water?
Of course not.
Or imagine standing before a judge after committing a serious crime and saying:
“Yes, Your Honor, I committed that crime. But yesterday I helped an old woman carry her groceries.”
The judge may recognize the good deed.
But the good deed does not erase the crime.
That is the problem with treating morality like spiritual mathematics.
We imagine:
Ten good deeds minus three sins equals seven points of righteousness.
But guilt does not disappear because goodness happened somewhere else.
And deep inside, most of us already know this.
There are things you have done that you cannot undo.
Words you cannot pull back into your mouth.
People you cannot unhurt.
Years you cannot relive.
Thoughts you would never project onto a screen.
Moments when you knew what was right and deliberately chose something else.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your scandal never reached Facebook.
Maybe your scandal lives only inside your memory.
But you know.
And God knows.
Now comes the part that changes everything.
Christianity does not say:
“Try harder until God finally loves you.”
It says something astonishing.
God came for sinners.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6, KJV
Without strength.
Not spiritually impressive.
Not finally cleaned up.
Not deserving.
Christ died for the ungodly.
That means the cross is not God's reward for good people.
The cross is God's rescue for guilty people.
And that distinction changes everything.
Ephesians 2:8–9 puts the matter with almost brutal clarity:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Listen to the Greek:
τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
tē gar chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
That word χάριτι — chariti, from χάρις — charis, means grace, favor, gracious kindness.
Then comes:
οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων
ouk ex ergōn
“not from works.”
There goes the scale.
There goes the résumé.
There goes the spiritual trophy cabinet.
There goes the argument that says, “God owes me heaven because I behaved better than somebody else.”
Salvation is not wages God pays to impressive people.
It is a gift God gives through Christ.
And a gift you have earned is no longer a gift.
This is why Jesus had to die.
If human beings could become acceptable to God simply by becoming sufficiently moral, Calvary becomes incomprehensible.
Why the nails?
Why the blood?
Why the crown of thorns?
Why Gethsemane?
Why the cry from the cross?
Why would the sinless Son of God willingly walk toward crucifixion if humanity merely needed better behavior?
The cross declares something devastating about our condition and something breathtaking about God's love:
Our sin was serious enough that Christ had to die—and God's love was great enough that Christ willingly did.
That is the scandal.
The innocent One stood where the guilty should have stood.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people nicer.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
Peter writes that Christ “once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
The just.
For the unjust.
To bring us to God.
That is the Gospel compressed into one breathtaking movement.
You cannot purchase it.
You cannot outperform your past until you deserve it.
You cannot donate enough money to acquire it.
You cannot buy forgiveness.
You cannot earn heaven by supporting Gospel Warrior, a church, a pastor, a charity, or any Christian organization.
Please hear that clearly.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Salvation was purchased by Christ, not by you.
And the price was His blood.
That is why one of the most unforgettable pictures of grace appears beside Jesus at Calvary.
A criminal is dying next to Him.
This man has no remaining lifetime in which to construct an impressive religious résumé.
No decades of charitable service.
No opportunity to become a respected member of society.
No years of church attendance.
No missionary journeys.
No chance to climb down from his cross and prove that his conversion is sincere through thirty years of good behavior.
He is dying.
And he turns toward Jesus.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.”
Jesus answers:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:42–43, KJV
Think about that.
The dying criminal had nothing left to offer Christ except himself.
Empty hands.
A guilty history.
A death sentence.
And faith directed toward a King dying beside him.
He could not repair his entire past.
But Jesus could rewrite his eternity.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that phrase means more to you than you expected.
Because perhaps you have spent years trying to become the kind of person whose goodness finally makes the shame disappear.
You smile.
You work.
You provide.
You help.
You post encouraging things.
People call you a good person.
But at night there is another version of you that nobody sees.
The regret comes back.
The pornography.
The affair.
The abortion.
The rage.
The addiction.
The dishonesty.
The secret messages.
The bitterness.
The years away from God.
The marriage you damaged.
The child you wounded with words.
The person you never forgave.
The faith you abandoned.
The double life.
Or perhaps your hidden sin is quieter.
Pride.
Self-righteousness.
Jealousy.
Greed.
A cold heart.
Religious hypocrisy.
The secret pleasure of feeling morally superior to people whose sins happen to look different from yours.
And you keep trying to compensate.
Maybe if I become better...
Maybe if I serve more...
Maybe if I pray longer...
Maybe if I give more...
Maybe God will finally accept me.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not God standing at the top of a staircase shouting, “Climb harder.”
The Gospel is Christ coming down to rescue people who could never climb high enough.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6, KJV
Not morality as the way.
Not philanthropy as the way.
Not church membership as the way.
Not religious heritage as the way.
Jesus.
This is why Christianity is fundamentally Christ-centered.
Our hope is not that God will eventually discover that we were pretty decent people.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ is a perfect Savior.
But now someone may ask the obvious question:
“If good works don't get me into heaven, why bother being good?”
Because grace does not merely forgive.
Grace transforms.
Keep reading Ephesians.
Immediately after Paul says salvation is “not of works,” he writes:
Do you see the order?
This matters enormously.
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Good works are not the root of salvation.
They are its fruit.
We do not obey so that Jesus will finally decide to save us.
We obey because the Jesus who saves also changes us.
Real faith does not say, “Since grace exists, sin doesn't matter.”
Real grace teaches us that sin mattered enough to put Christ on a cross.
The person who has truly encountered grace cannot look casually at the wounds of Jesus and say, “Wonderful. Now I can sin without caring.”
Grace produces gratitude.
Repentance.
Love.
Obedience.
A changed direction.
Not sinless perfection overnight—but a new relationship with sin, Christ, and holiness.
This is where another beautiful Greek word matters.
When the New Testament speaks of repentance, it uses μετάνοια — metanoia, related to μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It speaks of a change of mind, a turning, a profound reorientation that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed because you got caught.
It is more than crying because sin produced consequences.
It is turning toward God.
And perhaps that is exactly where you are right now.
Maybe you opened this because you wanted an answer to a theological question:
“Does being a good person get you into heaven?”
But somewhere along the way, the question became personal.
Am I right with God?
That is a much more important question.
And you do not need to hide behind your goodness anymore.
You also do not need to hide behind your badness.
Some people think they are too good to need grace.
Others think they are too broken to receive it.
Both misunderstand the cross.
The self-righteous person says, “I don't need that much forgiveness.”
The ashamed person says, “There couldn't possibly be enough forgiveness.”
Calvary answers both.
Your goodness cannot replace Jesus.
Your scandal cannot overpower Jesus.
There is no moral résumé impressive enough to make the cross unnecessary.
And there is no repentant sinner so filthy that Christ's grace becomes insufficient.
The Apostle Paul knew something about scandal.
Before he became the great missionary whose letters fill much of the New Testament, he persecuted Christians.
His past was not imaginary.
He could not pretend it never happened.
Yet he wrote:
“This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners...” — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
Christ came to save sinners.
That means Christianity is not fundamentally the story of good people finding a reward.
It is the story of guilty people finding a Redeemer.
The Gospel does not say your past never happened.
Grace says your past does not have to have the final word.
Your sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have to write the ending.
Jesus does that.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So what do you do?
Stop negotiating with God.
Stop presenting your goodness as currency.
Stop pretending.
Come to Christ.
Confess the truth.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the crucified and risen Jesus Christ rather than your ability to save yourself.
Tell Him the truth you have been afraid to admit.
“Lord, I have sinned.”
No performance.
No religious theater.
No carefully edited version.
Just truth.
And faith.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Maybe your prayer begins with only a few broken words.
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That is a better place to stand than a mountain of self-righteousness.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, don't rush away from the conviction.
Bring it into the light.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
It doesn't.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting our need for Him becomes a small act of honesty after years of hiding.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Someone else may need to see living evidence that grace still changes people.
And please don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
Not because an algorithm can save a soul.
They may never walk into a church this week.
They may never search for a sermon.
The friend who walked away from church.
The brother who thinks Christianity is only about rules.
The sister drowning beneath shame.
The person who believes they are too good to need Jesus.
The person who believes they are too broken for Jesus to want them.
Let sharing become mission rather than mere engagement.
Because there will probably come another day when the enemy drags your past into the courtroom of your mind and tries to convince you that Jesus could forgive everyone except you.
Come back and remember:
Your confidence was never supposed to rest in how impressive you became.
Your confidence rests in Christ.
But hear this carefully because we never want financial support confused with the Gospel:
It cannot purchase salvation. It cannot replace repentance, faith, obedience, generosity to those in need, or faithful participation in the life and mission of Christ's church.
Scripture says giving should not be done “grudgingly, or of necessity,” because “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Christian generosity is a response to grace—not the price of grace.
For some supporters, that recurring gift may be part of their personal offering to Gospel ministry. Give prayerfully, freely, responsibly, and with Christ—not pressure—at the center.
And the purpose goes deeper than merchandise.
We want Scripture opened.
Truth shared.
Wounded believers strengthened.
Lukewarm hearts awakened.
Seekers pointed toward Jesus.
Families discipled.
The ashamed reminded that forgiveness exists.
And people trapped in the exhausting religion of “trying to be good enough” introduced to the Savior who did what they could never do for themselves.
Invite the friend who is struggling silently.
Invite the believer who needs daily Scripture and encouragement.
Invite the skeptic willing to listen.
Invite even the person who says they don't believe.
Let them encounter biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, spiritual nourishment—and above everything else, Jesus Christ.
Because someday every achievement we applauded will be behind us.
Every possession will belong to someone else.
Every title will disappear.
Every carefully maintained reputation will become history.
And the question will not be whether you managed to look better than the worst person you knew.
The question underneath the Gospel is infinitely more personal:
What have you done with Jesus Christ?
Maybe you have spent your entire life trying to become good enough for heaven.
Today you can finally stop trying to be your own savior.
Good works matter.
Holiness matters.
Obedience matters.
Love matters.
Generosity matters.
A transformed life matters.
But none of those things can climb onto the cross and take the place of Jesus.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works—and the people Christ saves are then recreated for good works.
That is the order.
Grace first.
Then transformation.
Christ first.
Then the life that follows Him.
The criminal beside Jesus had no impressive résumé left to present.
Only a guilty past.
Empty hands.
And faith turned toward a crucified King.
And somehow...
that was exactly where grace found him.
So if your hands feel empty today, perhaps you are finally ready to stop showing God your résumé and start reaching for Christ.
Because perhaps the most beautiful thing about arriving before Jesus with empty hands is discovering that empty hands are finally ready to receive a gift.
You were never going to impress your way into heaven—but Jesus loved sinners enough to open the way home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EVERY TIME GENESIS ADDS ANOTHER WIFE, THE FAMILY DRAMA GETS WORSE
paragraphs: EVERY TIME GENESIS ADDS ANOTHER WIFE, THE FAMILY DRAMA GETS WORSE

Genesis never has to preach a sermon saying, “Look how beautifully this arrangement is working.” It simply opens the bedroom doors, lets us hear the crying from the tents, introduces us to the jealous sisters, abandoned women, wounded sons, rival mothers, and divided brothers—and allows the wreckage to speak.
There is something almost uncomfortable about reading Genesis slowly.
Because once you notice it, you cannot unsee it.
Another wife enters the story.
Then tension enters with her.
Another woman is brought into an already complicated household.
Then somebody becomes jealous.
Somebody feels unwanted.
Somebody starts competing.
Somebody gets used.
Somebody gets angry.
And eventually...
children inherit a war they did not start.
Genesis does not read like sanitized religious propaganda. It reads disturbingly like a family history nobody had time to clean up before publication.
And that may be one of the strongest evidences of what Scripture is actually doing.
The Bible is not pretending its heroes were better than they were.
It is showing us something far greater:
God remained faithful even when the people carrying His promises were catastrophically human.
That distinction matters.
Because the Bible recording something does not mean the Bible is recommending it.
Genesis tells us what people did.
It does not automatically tell us to imitate everything they did.
And when you follow the marriages through Genesis, an unsettling pattern begins emerging.
God's original picture is strikingly simple.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before Israel.
Before kings accumulated wives.
Before humanity learned how spectacularly complicated it could make relationships...
there was Eden.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression translated “one flesh” is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people occupying the same property.
Not a political alliance.
Not a reproductive arrangement.
Not one man collecting women as symbols of wealth, power, fertility, or status.
One flesh.
And centuries later, when religious leaders questioned Jesus about marriage, Christ did something enormously important.
He went backward.
Not merely to Moses.
Back to creation.
Jesus quoted Genesis and said:
“the two shall become one flesh.”
The Greek wording preserved in Matthew 19:5 is:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
“The two [shall become] one flesh.”
Then Jesus said:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
That means when Christians try to understand God's design for marriage, the controlling picture is not Abraham's household dysfunction.
It is not Jacob's wives and concubines.
It is not Solomon's palace.
It is creation as interpreted by Jesus Christ.
And that changes how you read Genesis.
Because Genesis does not hide polygamy.
It shows you what happens inside it.
The first explicit polygamist mentioned in Scripture is not exactly introduced as the patron saint of healthy families.
His name is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 says:
“And Lamech took two wives.”
The Hebrew is brutally uncomplicated:
וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים
Vayyiqqach-lo Lemekh shtei nashim.
“Lamech took for himself two wives.”
And soon this same Lamech is boasting about violence.
That does not prove that having two wives caused his violence. Scripture does not make that causal claim, and we should not manufacture one.
But literarily, something has shifted.
Genesis 2 gave us one man and one woman becoming one flesh.
Genesis 4 gives us Lamech taking two wives.
The Bible doesn't stop and flash a warning sign.
It doesn't have to.
Keep reading.
Because eventually we reach Abraham.
And here the story becomes painfully human.
God promised Abraham descendants.
But the promise seemed delayed.
Sarah was barren.
Time passed.
Bodies aged.
Hope became harder to hold.
And eventually Sarah did what frightened human beings have been doing ever since Eden:
she tried to help God accomplish what God had promised.
Hagar enters the story.
And almost immediately, peace leaves the room.
Sarah gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham.
Hagar conceives.
Then Genesis 16:4 tells us that when Hagar realized she was pregnant, Sarah became diminished in her eyes.
The woundedness escalates.
Sarah blames Abraham.
Abraham tells Sarah that Hagar is in her power.
Sarah treats Hagar harshly.
Hagar runs away.
Read that again without religious distance.
A pregnant woman runs into the wilderness.
This is not romantic.
This is not harmonious.
This is not a glowing advertisement for multiplying wives.
This is a household collapsing under jealousy, power imbalance, fear, impatience, and human attempts to manufacture God's promise.
And yet...
God sees Hagar.
That may be one of the most beautiful turns in Genesis.
The woman who appears expendable to everyone else is not invisible to God.
Hagar encounters the LORD and says:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro'i.
Commonly rendered, “God who sees me.”
Think about that.
Abraham's household had become complicated enough that Hagar could be used, mistreated, and driven into the wilderness.
But heaven knew exactly where she was.
Maybe that is where this story suddenly stops being about ancient marriage customs and starts becoming about you.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to be the Hagar in somebody else's story.
Useful when they needed you.
Disposable when you became inconvenient.
Perhaps somebody else's decisions created wounds you are still carrying.
Perhaps you have wondered whether God noticed what happened behind the closed door.
He did.
The God who found Hagar still sees people nobody else bothers to look for.
But Abraham's family crisis does not end there.
Isaac is born.
And eventually Ishmael and Hagar are sent away.
Two sons of Abraham now stand on opposite sides of a fractured household.
The promise of God survives.
The family does not emerge without scars.
Then comes Isaac.
And something interesting happens.
Compared with the patriarchal households around him, Isaac's recorded marriage story is remarkably different.
One wife.
Rebekah.
That marriage certainly has problems.
Favoritism eventually tears through the family.
Isaac favors Esau.
Rebekah favors Jacob.
Deception enters.
Jacob steals the blessing.
Esau wants Jacob dead.
So Genesis is not claiming monogamy magically makes sinful people healthy.
It doesn't.
One husband and one wife can still lie.
Manipulate.
Play favorites.
Withhold affection.
Destroy trust.
Marriage structure cannot replace holiness.
And that is important because the ultimate problem in Genesis is deeper than polygamy.
The ultimate problem is sin.
Then Jacob enters the story.
And Genesis turns the family-drama dial until it nearly breaks off.
Jacob loves Rachel.
He works seven years for her.
Genesis says those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her.
It sounds beautiful.
Until the wedding night.
Jacob wakes up.
And it is Leah.
The deceiver has been deceived.
Jacob confronts Laban.
Then he receives Rachel too, with another seven years of labor attached.
Now two sisters are married to the same man.
And Genesis does not make us wait long before showing the emotional consequences.
Genesis 29:30 tells us Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Then comes one of the saddest lines in the patriarchal narratives:
“When the LORD saw that Leah was hated...”
The Hebrew verb is:
שְׂנוּאָה
senu'ah.
It can carry the sense of being hated or unloved in comparison.
Whatever English nuance we choose, Leah knows she is not the woman Jacob wanted.
Imagine waking every morning knowing your husband would have preferred your sister.
Imagine sitting across from her.
Eating beside her.
Raising children beside her.
Watching his eyes change when she enters the tent.
Leah begins bearing sons.
And listen to the names.
Reuben.
Because, she says, the LORD has looked upon her affliction, and perhaps now her husband will love her.
Then Simeon.
Because the LORD has heard that she is unloved.
Then Levi.
“Now this time my husband will be attached to me.”
Do you hear her?
This is not genealogy anymore.
This is a woman trying to earn love by producing children.
Maybe another baby will make him love me.
Maybe another accomplishment.
Maybe another sacrifice.
Maybe if I become useful enough.
Beautiful enough.
Successful enough.
Spiritual enough.
Quiet enough.
Available enough.
Maybe then somebody will finally choose me.
Thousands of years have passed since Leah named those boys, and human beings are still doing exactly the same thing.
We just changed the currency.
Some people chase love through sex.
Some through achievement.
Some through money.
Some through ministry.
Some through appearance.
Some through social media.
Some become whatever everybody around them needs because somewhere inside them is still a Leah whispering:
“Maybe now I will be loved.”
Then something changes.
Leah gives birth again.
This time she names him Judah.
Genesis 29:35 records her saying:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
יְהוּדָה
Yehudah.
Judah.
Praise.
For a moment, her eyes move.
From Jacob...
to Yahweh.
And you need to remember that name.
Judah.
Because Genesis is quietly building toward something Leah could never have imagined.
Rachel, meanwhile, has Jacob's love but cannot conceive.
So now we encounter one of the cruelest paradoxes in the family.
Leah has children and desperately wants Jacob's affection.
Rachel has Jacob's affection and desperately wants Leah's fertility.
Each woman possesses what the other aches for.
And neither is content.
Rachel cries to Jacob:
“Give me children, or I shall die!”
Jacob becomes angry.
Then Rachel gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob.
Bilhah bears children.
Leah stops bearing for a time and responds by giving her servant Zilpah to Jacob.
Now stop.
Look at this household.
Jacob.
Leah.
Rachel.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Children arriving through four women.
Two sisters competing.
Servants pulled into reproductive rivalry.
Mandrakes being negotiated.
Affection being bargained over.
Sexual access to Jacob becoming part of the sisters' competition.
This is not a peaceful household.
It is heartbreak with tents.
And children are growing up inside it.
That part matters.
Because adults sometimes convince themselves that their relational chaos belongs only to them.
It rarely does.
Children breathe the atmosphere their parents create.
They learn who is favored.
They learn who is rejected.
They learn which mother has influence.
They notice whose children receive attention.
They inherit rivalries long before they understand their origin.
And eventually Jacob's sons demonstrate exactly how fractured this family has become.
Joseph is Rachel's son.
Rachel was the woman Jacob loved.
And Joseph becomes Jacob's favorite.
Genesis 37 says Israel loved Joseph more than his other sons.
Then comes the special robe.
The brothers see the favoritism.
They hate Joseph.
The hatred intensifies.
Then one day they see him approaching.
And brothers begin discussing the murder of their brother.
Let that sink in.
The relational fractures that once existed among mothers are now bleeding through their sons.
Joseph is stripped.
Thrown into a pit.
Sold.
His robe is dipped in blood.
And Jacob—the father who once deceived his own father using clothing—is deceived by his sons using clothing.
Sin has a strange way of echoing through families.
Different generation.
Same darkness.
Different room.
Same wound.
Different names.
Same poison.
Maybe that is why Genesis can feel frighteningly modern.
Because perhaps your family also has stories nobody likes discussing.
The affair.
The divorce.
The secret child.
The addiction.
The favoritism.
The parent who left.
The father who loved one sibling differently.
The mother who manipulated everybody.
The inheritance fight.
The betrayal.
The thing your relatives carefully avoid mentioning whenever outsiders are around.
You can love Jesus and still come from a deeply complicated family.
The Bible is filled with them.
But here is where Christianity becomes breathtaking.
God does not merely observe broken families from heaven.
He enters human history through one.
Remember Leah's son?
Judah.
The child born when the unwanted woman said:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Judah's own story becomes scandalous.
Genesis 38 records the painful story involving Tamar.
Failure.
Sexual sin.
Deception.
Hypocrisy.
Public shame.
Judah initially condemns Tamar until the evidence exposes him.
Then he admits:
“She is more righteous than I.”
And from that scandalous history comes Perez.
Generations pass.
Perez's line leads eventually to David.
And Matthew begins the Gospel of Jesus Christ by opening the family records.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Perez.
And eventually...
Jesus.
Do you see what God did?
He did not erase the scandal before writing the genealogy.
He put grace right through the middle of it.
Matthew 1 even deliberately mentions women whose stories remind us how surprising and messy the messianic line is.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
“the wife of Uriah.”
Then Mary.
And finally:
Jesus, who is called Christ.
The Gospel does not say your sin doesn't matter.
It says something infinitely more powerful.
Your sin matters so much that the Son of God had to die.
And His grace is so powerful that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the family wasn't broken.
Not pretending Abraham always trusted perfectly.
Not pretending Jacob's household was healthy.
Not pretending Judah was innocent.
Not pretending David's history was clean.
God tells the truth about the scandal...
and then sends Jesus into it.
That is why the cross matters.
Jesus did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to save sinners.
At Calvary, Christ carried guilt He did not commit.
He bore judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The answer to the chaos in Genesis is not merely:
“Make better relationship choices.”
Yes, obedience matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Sexual holiness matters.
Marriage matters.
Repentance matters.
But behavioral improvement alone cannot resurrect a sinful heart.
We need Christ.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need new hearts.
Maybe your family's story has already become something you wish you could rewrite.
Maybe you cannot undo the adultery.
Maybe you cannot restore the childhood your children should have had.
Maybe you cannot unsay what was screamed.
Maybe you cannot go backward and become faithful sooner.
Maybe you cannot erase the years you wasted.
Maybe you were the wounded person.
Maybe you were the person doing the wounding.
Maybe...
you were both.
Then hear the Gospel carefully.
Repentance does not mean pretending the damage never happened.
Grace does not call evil good.
Forgiveness does not turn sin into righteousness.
The cross does something far more astonishing.
Jesus meets guilty people in the truth...
forgives those who turn to Him...
and begins making them new.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Abraham's choices still had consequences.
Jacob's family still carried scars.
David would later discover the same painful truth.
Forgiveness is real.
Consequences can also be real.
But consequences do not get to become your god.
Shame does not get to become your identity.
Your father's failure does not have to become your destiny.
Your mother's wound does not have to become your personality.
Your family's pattern does not have to become your children's inheritance.
In Christ, generational repetition can meet genuine repentance.
The liar can begin telling truth.
The adulterer can become faithful.
The bitter can forgive.
The absent parent can repent and become present.
The wounded can stop using their wounds as permission to wound others.
The sexually broken can pursue holiness.
The proud can confess.
The hidden can finally step into the light.
Not because human beings are strong enough to rewrite themselves.
Because Jesus Christ is alive.
This is why the recurring household chaos in Genesis should not make us look down on those people.
It should make us recognize ourselves.
We are not standing above Jacob's family shaking our heads.
Without grace, we belong in the photograph.
Our costumes changed.
Our technology changed.
Our houses changed.
Human hearts did not.
We still envy.
We still manipulate.
We still lust.
We still compete.
We still play favorites.
We still use people to fill places only God can fill.
We still try to manufacture blessings instead of trusting God.
And God is still calling sinners to repentance.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
“Why did these biblical families have so much drama?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What pattern am I carrying that Jesus is asking me to surrender?”
That question is harder.
Because now Genesis has stopped being ancient history.
Now it is standing in your living room.
Be honest.
Who are you becoming?
What are your children learning from the way you love?
What secret compromise have you renamed “complicated”?
What bitterness have you protected because somebody genuinely hurt you?
Whose approval are you still chasing?
What did your parents hand you that you are now handing to somebody else?
And what needs to end with you?
Not through self-righteousness.
Through surrender.
Through repentance.
Through Christ.
There are truths you understand differently after midnight.
They need to know that Scripture does not hide broken families.
And Jesus is not frightened by broken people.
Salvation cannot be bought. God's favor cannot be purchased. We support because grace has already been freely given in Christ, not because financial support purchases grace.
But never confuse the library with the treasure.
The treasure is Christ.
Never confuse Christian merchandise with the mission.
The mission is Christ.
The goal is Christ.
The books will eventually wear out.
The shirts will fade.
The mugs will break.
The social-media algorithms will change.
Our names will eventually disappear from people's feeds.
But Jesus Christ remains.
And perhaps that is the final lesson hidden beneath all those tents, marriages, rivalries, births, betrayals, tears, and graves in Genesis.
Human beings kept making the story messier.
God kept moving His promise forward.
Abraham failed.
God remained faithful.
Sarah stumbled.
God remained faithful.
Hagar ran into the wilderness.
God saw her.
Isaac's household fractured.
God remained faithful.
Jacob deceived and was deceived.
God remained faithful.
Leah was unwanted.
God saw her.
Rachel wept.
God heard.
Joseph entered a pit.
God was with him.
Judah fell into scandal.
God was not finished.
And generations later, from that impossibly complicated family tree...
came Jesus Christ.
So when you look at the branches of your own family and see things you wish had never happened, do not make either of two mistakes.
Do not call the darkness light.
And do not assume the darkness is stronger than Christ.
Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where it is wise, truthful, and possible.
Protect those who need protection.
Tell the truth.
Break with sin.
Run toward Jesus.
Because the greatest miracle in the biblical family tree is not that human beings finally stopped making a mess.
It is that God brought the Savior through the mess.
And He is still doing what grace has always done:
meeting sinners in stories that look ruined...
and writing redemption where everyone else expected an ending.
Your family may have handed you the scandal—but in Christ, you do not have to hand the scandal to the next generation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LIFE AND DEATH ARE IN THE POWER OF THE TONGUE” — DOES PROVERBS 18:21 REALLY TEACH MANIFESTATION?
paragraphs: “LIFE AND DEATH ARE IN THE POWER OF THE TONGUE” — DOES PROVERBS 18:21 REALLY TEACH MANIFESTATION?
What if one of the most quoted Bible verses about the power of your words has been made to say something it was never actually saying?
“Speak it into existence.”
“Declare your future.”
“Your words create your reality.”
“Never say anything negative, because the universe is listening.”
And somewhere in the middle of those statements, Proverbs 18:21 is often brought forward as the biblical proof:
“Death and life are in the power of the tongue.”
It sounds convincing.
Almost biblical.
Almost.
But there is a massive difference between believing that words matter and believing that human words possess a God-like creative force capable of manufacturing whatever reality we desire.
And that difference matters because one view puts our speech under the lordship of God.
The other can quietly put us in His place.
So before you make another declaration over your bank account, your body, your relationship, your career, your future, or your dreams and call it biblical faith, we need to return to the text.
Not the slogan.
Not the viral clip.
Not the motivational preacher.
The text.
Because Proverbs 18:21 is far more powerful than manifestation theology makes it.
The Hebrew reads:
מָוֶת וְחַיִּים בְּיַד־לָשׁוֹן וְאֹהֲבֶיהָ יֹאכַל פִּרְיָהּ
Māweth weḥayyîm beyad-lāshôn, we’ohăveyhā yō’khal piryāh.
A straightforward rendering is:
“Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit.”
Notice something immediately.
The Hebrew expression is בְּיַד־לָשׁוֹן — beyad-lāshôn.
Literally, “in the hand of the tongue.”
The word יָד, yad, means “hand,” but “hand” can function as an image of power, agency, or capacity. That is why English translations naturally render the expression as “in the power of the tongue.”
But Proverbs is not presenting the tongue as a magic wand.
It is describing the extraordinary capacity of human speech to produce consequences.
And the second half of the verse makes that unmistakably practical:
“…those who love it will eat its fruit.”
Fruit.
Consequences.
What comes out of your mouth eventually produces something that you may have to live with.
That is wisdom literature.
And the verse immediately before it says:
“From the fruit of a man’s mouth his stomach is satisfied; he is satisfied by the yield of his lips.”
Proverbs 18:20.
The context is not teaching that you can verbally summon houses, promotions, spouses, wealth, healing, or success into existence.
It is teaching that words bear fruit.
Words can destroy reputations.
Words can reconcile families.
Words can provoke violence.
Words can stop violence.
Words can humiliate a child so deeply that the sentence follows him into adulthood.
Words can tell a frightened daughter, “You are loved. I’m here. We will walk through this together.”
Words can spread lies.
Words can confess truth.
Words can seduce.
Words can encourage.
Words can deceive a congregation.
Words can preach Christ to someone who thought God had forgotten him.
Death and life.
Sometimes they really do travel through the mouth.
You already know this, even if you have never studied Hebrew.
You remember things people said to you.
Some sentences disappeared within minutes.
Others stayed for twenty years.
Maybe someone you trusted looked at you and said, “You’ll never become anything.”
Maybe a parent compared you to someone else until you began believing you were permanently inadequate.
Maybe a spouse used your deepest insecurity as ammunition during an argument.
Maybe somebody publicly embarrassed you and called it a joke.
Maybe you were the one who said something.
That may be the harder possibility.
Maybe the sentence you wish you could erase came from your mouth.
You were angry.
Wounded.
Jealous.
Exhausted.
Afraid.
And for five seconds you allowed your tongue to carry what your heart had been hiding.
Then you saw their face change.
Too late.
The words were already out.
This is why Proverbs 18:21 does not need manifestation theology to make it powerful.
Reality is devastating enough.
A tongue does not need supernatural creative sovereignty to destroy a marriage.
A lie can do it.
A tongue does not need mystical energy to destroy someone's reputation.
Gossip can do it.
A tongue does not need to “manifest” death to crush another person's spirit.
Cruelty can do it.
And a tongue does not need magical power to become an instrument of life.
Truth can do it.
Grace can do it.
Encouragement can do it.
An apology can do it.
The Gospel proclaimed through ordinary human lips can point a dying sinner to the living Christ.
This distinction is crucial.
The Bible absolutely teaches that words are powerful.
But Scripture does not therefore teach that our words are sovereign.
God's words are sovereign.
That distinction belongs to God.
Genesis does not begin with humanity speaking its preferred reality into existence.
It begins with God.
“And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.”
Genesis 1:3.
God speaks creation into existence because God is Creator.
Psalm 33:9 says:
“For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.”
That is not a technique Scripture gives us to imitate so that we can become miniature creators of reality.
That is a declaration of God's incomparable authority.
Isaiah 46:9–10 presents God as the One who declares the end from the beginning and whose purpose will stand.
Human beings speak.
God speaks.
But those two facts do not mean human speech possesses God's sovereign authority.
We are image-bearers.
We are not God.
This is where some modern teaching becomes spiritually dangerous.
Biblical faith can slowly be transformed from “God, Your will be done” into “My will must happen because I declared it.”
Prayer becomes technique.
Faith becomes force.
God becomes the mechanism through which I obtain the life I have scripted.
And disappointment becomes terrifying because now, when suffering comes, people may wonder:
“Did I say the wrong thing?”
“Did I confess something negative?”
“Did my words attract this?”
“Was my faith too weak?”
Think about how cruel that theology can become in a hospital room.
A faithful Christian receives a devastating diagnosis.
Someone tells her, “Don't speak that diagnosis. Don't give it power.”
But acknowledging reality is not unbelief.
Paul acknowledged suffering.
David acknowledged fear.
Jeremiah acknowledged grief.
Job acknowledged agony.
Jesus Himself said in Gethsemane:
“My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.”
Matthew 26:38.
That was not a failed confession.
That was truth spoken in anguish.
Biblical faith does not require pretending that pain does not exist.
Biblical faith looks directly at pain and still trusts God.
There is an enormous difference.
Jesus prayed:
“My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”
Matthew 26:39.
There is biblical faith in its purest form.
Not denial.
Not manifestation.
Not controlling reality through vocabulary.
Trust.
“Not as I will, but as You will.”
That sentence destroys the illusion that mature faith means forcing God to agree with our preferred outcome.
Sometimes faith says, “Lord, heal me.”
Sometimes faith says, “Lord, provide.”
Sometimes faith says, “Lord, open this door.”
Sometimes faith says, “Lord, please restore this marriage.”
But biblical faith can also say:
“Even if Your answer is different from what I desperately want, You are still God, and I am still Yours.”
That is not weak faith.
That is surrendered faith.
And surrender is something manifestation culture often struggles to understand because manifestation places enormous emphasis on what I desire, what I envision, what I declare, and what I attract.
The Gospel does something radically different.
The Gospel brings us to Jesus Christ and teaches us to say:
“Not my will.”
That hurts.
Because sometimes what we want is not sinful.
You can desperately want your mother to survive.
You can desperately want the pregnancy to continue.
You can desperately want the marriage restored.
You can desperately want the job.
You can desperately want the prodigal child to come home tonight.
You can pray with tears.
You can ask boldly.
You can gather believers around you.
You can trust God's power completely.
And still refuse to pretend that your words control God's providence.
God is not waiting for us to discover the correct verbal formula.
He is our Father.
This is also why James speaks so severely about the tongue.
James does not describe it as a manifestation instrument.
He compares it to a fire.
“The tongue is a fire…”
James 3:6.
Then comes one of Scripture's most uncomfortable pictures of human inconsistency:
“With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.”
James 3:9.
Read that slowly.
We worship God with the same mouth we use to wound people made in His image.
Sunday:
“Praise You, Jesus.”
Monday:
“You're useless.”
Sunday:
“Lord, have mercy.”
Tuesday:
“I will never forgive you.”
Sunday:
“Holy, holy, holy.”
Wednesday:
Gossip.
Slander.
Mockery.
Lies.
Manipulation.
James does not let us hide behind religious vocabulary.
“From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.”
James 3:10.
Maybe Proverbs 18:21 was never meant to make you obsessed with declaring a luxury future.
Maybe it was meant to make you terrified of casually destroying people with your mouth.
That hits differently.
Because it is much easier to declare, “I am blessed and highly favored,” than to apologize to someone you humiliated.
It is easier to speak prosperity over yourself than to stop speaking poison about your enemy.
It is easier to make declarations in a mirror than to confess:
“I lied.”
“I gossiped.”
“I manipulated you.”
“I used Scripture to win an argument.”
“I spoke to my children in a way that did not reflect Christ.”
“I weaponized something you told me in confidence.”
“I said I forgave you, but I have been quietly destroying your reputation.”
Now we are getting closer to the biblical power of the tongue.
Jesus takes us deeper still.
“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”
Matthew 12:34.
There it is.
The tongue is not merely a speech problem.
It is a heart revealer.
Eventually, the heart leaks.
You can manage your public vocabulary for a while.
You can learn Christian phrases.
You can know when to say “God bless you.”
You can post verses.
You can sound spiritual.
But eventually pressure squeezes the heart, and something comes out.
That angry sentence.
That cruel joke.
That jealous whisper.
That sexually suggestive message.
That dishonest explanation.
That secret gossip.
That arrogant response.
The mouth exposes what image management tries to conceal.
And Jesus continues:
“I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak.”
Matthew 12:36.
That is infinitely more serious than, “Be careful what you say because you might manifest something negative.”
Jesus says our words matter because they reveal us before God and affect people who bear His image.
So what happens when you realize your tongue has been an instrument of death?
This is where the article could end with guilt.
But Christianity does not end at exposure.
It leads us to a cross.
Maybe you have spoken words you cannot retrieve.
Maybe your child still remembers them.
Maybe your former spouse still remembers them.
Maybe your parents died before you apologized.
Maybe the person you slandered never discovered that you were the source.
Maybe your mouth has praised Jesus publicly while privately tearing people apart.
Maybe you are reading this and thinking:
I have done damage I cannot undo.
You may not be able to unsay what you said.
But your story does not have to end where your sin exposed you.
Because Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not polished sinners.
Not sinners with good branding.
Sinners.
People with filthy mouths and filthy hearts.
People with secrets.
People with shame.
People who have injured others.
People who need forgiveness rather than self-improvement.
At the cross, Christ did not merely offer you better vocabulary.
He offered Himself.
The sinless Son of God bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness that they could never manufacture for themselves.
This is scandal becoming grace.
This is why our message will always come back to the same truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because He pretends your sin never mattered.
Grace is not God calling darkness light.
Grace is Christ paying for guilty people and transforming those who belong to Him.
And when Christ changes a person, He also begins changing how that person speaks.
Paul writes:
Ephesians 4:29.
Notice again what Scripture emphasizes.
Not “Use your words to create whatever reality you desire.”
Build people up.
Give grace.
Speak truth.
Put away falsehood.
Forgive.
Encourage.
Confess Christ.
Let the redeemed tongue become an instrument in the Redeemer's hands.
And yes, Scripture contains powerful language about confession.
Romans 10:9 says:
“If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.”
But even here, the power is not in magical syllables.
The object of faith is Jesus Christ.
The mouth confesses Him.
The heart believes in Him.
The Savior saves.
Your confession does not make Jesus Lord.
You confess Jesus because He is Lord.
That distinction changes everything.
Christianity is not manifestation with Bible verses attached.
It is surrender to the crucified and risen King.
So yes.
Life and death really are in the power of the tongue.
Just not in the way social-media spirituality often tells you.
Your words matter enormously.
Speak truth when lying would be easier.
Speak grace when cruelty would be satisfying.
Speak repentance when pride wants excuses.
Speak forgiveness when bitterness wants revenge.
Speak encouragement when someone is barely surviving.
Speak the Gospel when someone needs to hear that Christ receives repentant sinners.
And sometimes the holiest thing your tongue can do is stop.
Do not send the message.
Do not repeat the rumor.
Do not expose the secret.
Do not make the cruel joke.
Do not use someone's weakness to make yourself look stronger.
Do not call gossip “discernment.”
Do not call manipulation “prophecy.”
Do not use “God told me” as a weapon to control somebody when God has not spoken what you are claiming.
And do not confuse confidence in your own declarations with faith in Jesus Christ.
Real faith does not require you to become sovereign.
Real faith rests because God already is.
Perhaps this exposed something.
Not somebody else.
You.
Maybe you remembered a name while reading.
A conversation.
A text message.
A child.
A spouse.
A parent.
A church member.
Someone you wounded.
Do not rush past that conviction.
If repentance is needed, repent.
If an apology is needed, make it without excuses.
If restitution is possible, pursue it.
If gossip has been spread, correct what you can.
And if shame is telling you that Jesus could never forgive what came out of your mouth, remember Peter.
Peter swore that he would never abandon Jesus.
Then, under pressure, his mouth betrayed what fear had done to his courage.
“I do not know the man.”
Again.
And again.
Then the rooster crowed.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Imagine carrying those words.
The last hours before the crucifixion, and Peter's mouth had denied the Man he loved.
But Peter's failure was not the final sentence of Peter's story.
The risen Jesus came for him.
Restored him.
Commissioned him.
And the mouth that once said, “I do not know Him,” would later publicly proclaim Christ.
That is grace.
Jesus did not rewrite Peter's story by pretending the denial never happened.
He rewrote it through forgiveness, restoration, and transformation.
Maybe that is why you needed to read this today.
Your tongue may have written chapters you are ashamed of.
Jesus Christ is still greater than your worst chapter.
Repentance does not mean your story is over.
It may mean you are finally handing the pen back to the rightful King.
If this exposed something hidden in you, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not as a formula.
Not as a magical phrase.
Let it be the beginning of an honest prayer.
If you have been fighting to surrender your words, anger, gossip, bitterness, or secret wounds to Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you are exhausted and need other believers to pray for you, comment, “pray for me.”

And if Christ has already begun changing the person you used to be, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to encourage someone who thought transformation was impossible.
Not because saving a post changes your life, but because there may be a day when anger is rising, your fingers are hovering over “send,” and you need to remember that the tongue bears fruit.

We never want to manipulate your conscience or pretend otherwise. But one practical way you can choose to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you is to help sound biblical teaching reach more people.
And there is much more available for those who want to keep growing.
But before you leave, remember what Proverbs actually placed before us.
מָוֶת וְחַיִּים בְּיַד־לָשׁוֹן
“Death and life are in the hand of the tongue.”
Your tongue is powerful.
But it is not God.
Your words matter.
But they are not sovereign.
You do not need to manifest your destiny.
You need Christ.
You need His truth when your mind is confused.
His grace when your sin is exposed.
His forgiveness when your words have wounded someone.
His Spirit to transform your heart.
His wisdom to govern your tongue.
His cross when guilt accuses you.
His resurrection when your story looks finished.
And His lordship when you are tempted to make yourself the author of a future that belongs to Him.
So before you speak tomorrow, remember this:
The greatest miracle is not getting your tongue to create the life you want.
It is Jesus taking the heart behind that tongue—the angry heart, frightened heart, proud heart, wounded heart, sinful heart—and making it new.
And when He does…
the mouth begins telling a different story.
A story where confession replaces pretending.
Where grace replaces condemnation.
Where truth replaces deception.
Where blessing replaces cursing.
Where repentance replaces excuses.
Where Christ replaces self at the center.
Maybe your mouth has spoken death.
Bring it to Jesus.
Maybe your words created a scandal you wish you could erase.
Bring that too.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of flawless people learning how to say the right things until they obtain the right life.
It is the story of guilty people meeting a perfect Savior.
And sometimes the words you most regret become the place where grace teaches you to speak differently for the rest of your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU FOLLOWED THEM FOR THEIR CONTENT. BUT WHAT IF JESUS ASKED WHY?
paragraphs:
YOU FOLLOWED THEM FOR THEIR CONTENT. BUT WHAT IF JESUS ASKED WHY?
Is Following Adult Creators on Social Media a Form of Compromise—or Can a Christian Really Say, “I’m Just Looking”?
There is a kind of compromise that does not feel like compromise anymore.
It does not begin in a motel room.
