It does not begin with an affair.
Sometimes it begins with a blue button that says Follow.
One tap.
That’s all.
Nobody at church knows.
Your spouse may never notice.
Your parents cannot see it.
Your Christian friends probably will not ask.
And because you have not physically touched anyone, messaged anyone, or perhaps even purchased anything, you tell yourself the easiest sentence in the world to believe:
“I’m only following them.”
But there is another question.
One that reaches much deeper than whether you technically committed a physical sexual act.
Why are you following them?
That question changes everything.
Because Jesus has always been interested in the place beneath the behavior.
The heart.
And if you stay with me until the end, we are going somewhere uncomfortable—but not toward condemnation.
Toward a cross.
Toward grace.
Toward the possibility that the thing you are afraid Jesus will expose may be the very thing He wants to free you from.
Maybe you follow an adult creator because you find that person attractive.
Maybe you tell yourself it is harmless because the content on your feed is not technically explicit.
Maybe you follow models, influencers, actors, adult entertainers, thirst-trap accounts, or creators whose entire online presence is deliberately sexualized.
Maybe you never comment.
Never message.
You just watch.
Scroll.
Return.
Watch again.
And somewhere along the way, your conscience became quieter.
Not necessarily because the behavior became holier.
Maybe because it became familiar.
That distinction matters.
The Bible does not contain a verse saying, “Thou shalt not follow an adult creator on social media.”
So we must be careful.
We should never manufacture commandments God did not give.
But neither should we use technological novelty to escape moral principles God made unmistakably clear.
The real biblical question is not simply:
“Is following this account forbidden?”
The deeper question is:
“What am I deliberately placing before my eyes, what am I inviting into my desires, and where is it leading my heart?”
Thousands of years before smartphones, Job said something astonishing:
בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי
Berit karati le'enai.
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
That is the force of Job 31:1.
The Hebrew בְּרִית — berit means covenant.
Job was describing intentionality.
Not accidental sight.
Not the involuntary recognition that another human being is attractive.
Not merely existing in a world where sexuality is visible.
He was talking about governing what he allowed his eyes to become attached to.
That matters enormously because Christianity does not teach that noticing beauty is sin.
Being sexually attracted is not automatically sin.
Temptation itself is not identical to sin; Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin.

And seeing provocative content unexpectedly while scrolling is not morally identical to deliberately searching for it, following it, revisiting it, lingering over it, or using another person's body as fuel for lust.
That distinction may rescue someone reading this from unnecessary shame.
But it may also remove somebody else's favorite excuse.
Because there is a difference between something appearing before your eyes...
and arranging your digital life so that it keeps coming back.
A follow is not merely observation.
In ordinary social-media use, following usually communicates something like:
Show me more of this.
Put this person in my feed.
Bring this content back tomorrow.
Keep the connection available.
And if the reason you want that recurring access is sexual stimulation, fantasy, lust, or the enjoyment of someone else's sexualized body, then the issue is no longer merely technological.
It has become spiritual.
Jesus went directly there.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text reads in part:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn...
The crucial idea is not merely that someone happened to see a woman.
Jesus speaks of looking πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—looking with the purpose or movement toward lustful desire.
He concludes that such a person has already committed adultery with her ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ—“in his heart.”
Read that carefully.
Jesus did not condemn eyesight.
He confronted intentional lust.
That means the Christian question cannot stop at:
“Did I touch anyone?”
Jesus takes us deeper:
“What was I doing with them in my heart?”
And suddenly that harmless follow button becomes harder to hide behind.
Because if you follow someone specifically because their body sexually excites you...
if you wait for provocative posts...
if you revisit their profile when you are lonely...
if their pictures become material for fantasy...
if you would immediately become uncomfortable if Jesus physically sat beside you while you scrolled...
then perhaps the question is no longer whether this is “technically pornography.”
Perhaps the question is whether you are feeding something Christ told you not to feed.
And before anyone weaponizes this article against somebody else, hear this clearly.
This applies to men and women.
It applies to married people and single people.
It applies to pastors and teenagers, ministry workers and new believers.
It applies whether the person being lusted after is female or male.
And this article is not permission to degrade adult creators themselves.
They are not objects.
They are human beings.
Image-bearers.
People with histories, wounds, choices, families, fears, sins, hopes, and souls.
Christians must never fight objectification by dehumanizing the person being objectified.
Jesus died for sinners.
That includes sexual sinners.
That includes consumers.
That includes creators.
That includes you.
That includes me.
The Gospel gives nobody permission to stand at the foot of the cross and boast.
But grace also does not require us to rename compromise as freedom.
Paul wrote:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:18.
Notice the verb.
Φεύγετε — pheugete.
Flee.
Paul does not say negotiate with it.
Study how close you can stand to it.
Follow it but promise yourself not to go further.
Keep it available because you have “self-control.”
Ask how much sexual stimulation you can consume before God technically calls it sin.
Flee.
Sometimes spiritual maturity looks surprisingly unimpressive.
Sometimes it looks like an unfollow.
A block.
A deleted bookmark.
A conversation with your spouse.
A confession to someone trustworthy.
A phone left outside the bedroom.
A filter installed when nobody forced you to install it.
Sometimes holiness looks like losing access to something your flesh desperately wanted to keep.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading this are not really asking whether following adult creators is compromise.
You already know why you follow them.
You are actually asking:
“How much can I keep without feeling like I have walked away from Jesus?”
That is a different question.
And it is the question compromise loves.
Compromise rarely walks through the front door announcing:
“I am here to destroy your intimacy with Christ.”
It whispers:
It isn't that serious.
Everyone does it.
At least you're not sleeping with anybody.
You're still going to church.
You're still praying.
You're still married.
You aren't buying the explicit stuff.
You're just looking.
Just looking.
Those two words have protected a lot of hidden rooms.
Then nighttime comes.
The house becomes quiet.
Your thumb moves almost automatically.
One profile.
Another.
Another.
You feel the rush.
Then afterward...
silence.
Maybe shame.
Maybe numbness.
Maybe nothing anymore.
And that “nothing” can be more frightening than the shame.
Because at least shame sometimes tells you your conscience is still fighting.
There are people who once felt convicted after five minutes and now can scroll sexualized content for an hour without feeling much at all.
Not every feeling of guilt comes from God, and Christians must never confuse obsessive shame with holiness.
But neither should we celebrate a conscience simply because it has learned to stop protesting.

Paul gives believers another filter in Philippians 4:8: whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and worthy of praise—these are the things upon which the Christian mind is called to dwell.
That does not mean Christians must live terrified of every beautiful person or every swimsuit photograph.
It means discipleship reaches the imagination.
Your attention matters.
Your mental diet matters.
What you repeatedly rehearse matters.
What you deliberately place before your eyes matters.
And here is a question worth sitting with:
Is this account helping me see this person as someone made in God's image—or training me to consume that person's body?
Do not answer quickly.
Especially if you are married.
Because there may be another human being sleeping beside you who cannot compete with a digitally curated parade of bodies.
They were never supposed to.
Your spouse has morning breath.
Bad days.
Wrinkles eventually.
Stress.
Ordinary clothes.
Illness.
Exhaustion.
A real body that changes.
A real personality that sometimes irritates you.
A real soul requiring patience and sacrifice.
The screen asks almost nothing from you.
It presents selected images, controlled lighting, flattering angles, editing, fantasy, novelty.
And then you may unknowingly bring that artificial marketplace of attention into a covenant where another human being is trying to be loved.
That can become devastating.
Not because your spouse must be the only attractive person you ever notice.
Scripture never commands pretending attractive people cease to exist after marriage.
But covenant love teaches the heart not to turn every attraction into consumption.
There is a difference.
A profound one.
Maybe you are single.
Then hear this too.
Purity is not something you practice merely so that one day you can give a future spouse an impressive résumé.
Purity belongs first to Christ.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your mind belongs to Christ.
Your sexuality belongs under the lordship of Christ.

Paul's argument immediately surrounding his command to flee sexual immorality is breathtaking: the believer's body is for the Lord, united to Christ, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, bought with a price, and therefore called to glorify God.
That means biblical sexual ethics are not ultimately:
“God hates sex.”
Quite the opposite.
God created sexuality.
The Christian story does not call the body dirty.
It calls the body significant.
So significant that Paul says:
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
And there is the deeper issue.
Not merely:
“Can I follow this creator?”
But:
“Can I glorify Christ in why I am following this creator?”
That question reaches places legalism cannot.

Suppose you follow an adult creator because that individual also discusses business, fitness, culture, or another legitimate subject, and you have no sexual motive, do not consume explicit material, and are not being drawn toward lust.
Scripture does not give us grounds to declare the mere digital act of following that person intrinsically sinful in every conceivable circumstance.
We should be biblically precise.
The identity or occupation of the account owner does not magically make every click sinful.

But if following that account repeatedly draws you into lust, sexual fantasy, explicit material, temptation, secrecy, masturbation fueled by that person's content, dishonesty toward your spouse, or a pattern you know weakens your obedience to Christ, then arguing over whether the follow itself is technically sinful may be missing the entire point.
Paul writes elsewhere that not everything permissible is beneficial and that he will not be mastered by anything.
There are things you may be capable of touching without technically violating a command that nevertheless begin to master you.
And Christians were not redeemed merely to ask:
“What can I get away with?”
We were redeemed to ask:
“How can Christ be glorified in me?”
There is another uncomfortable dimension.
Your follow is attention.
Attention has value.
Online, attention can become reach, influence, social proof, and sometimes money.
That does not mean every follow makes you morally responsible for everything another person does, nor can we simplistically claim that clicking “follow” equals directly financing pornography.
That would overstate the case.
But Christians should still ask whether their attention is helping sustain a digital ecosystem they privately believe is destructive.
You cannot control the internet.
You can decide what you intentionally reward with your eyes.
Yet this is where I refuse to leave you drowning in guilt.
Because perhaps you have already gone much further than following.
Maybe you have watched pornography for years.
Maybe you have paid creators.
Maybe you have hidden transactions.
Maybe you have lied to your husband.
Maybe you have lied to your wife.
Maybe you are the creator.
Maybe sexual attention became the way you learned to feel valuable.
Maybe pornography became anesthesia for loneliness.
Maybe fantasy became the place you went whenever real life hurt.
Maybe you have promised God fifty times:
“This is the last time.”
And then came fifty-one.
And now you are reading an article about social media when underneath the question is something much more desperate:
“Would Jesus still want me if He knew everything?”
He knows.
Everything.
And the Gospel is still the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had successfully hidden their scandal.
He came for sinners.
The cross is not God's reward for people who cleaned themselves before arriving.
The cross is where guilty people discover what grace actually costs.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ calls sinners to repentance and faith.
And repentance is not God saying:
“Become clean enough so I can finally love you.”
Repentance is the turning of a sinner who has finally realized that the thing he was clutching cannot save him—and Christ can.
Grace does not whisper:
Keep the chains.
Grace unlocks them.
Grace does not say:
Your sin doesn't matter.
Grace says:
Your sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed, and His mercy is greater than the thing you thought could never be forgiven.
This is why Christian conviction and Christian condemnation must never be confused.
Conviction brings the hidden thing toward Christ.
Condemnation tells you to hide from Him.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Condemnation says:
“If anyone knew, you would be finished.”
The Gospel says:
Jesus already knows—and He is calling you out of darkness.
Maybe tonight your repentance begins with something almost laughably small.
Unfollow.
Unfollow.
Unfollow.
Delete.
Block.
Cancel.
Then stop pretending the battle ends there.
Bring somebody trustworthy into the fight.
If you are trapped in a compulsive pattern, seek mature pastoral accountability and, where appropriate, qualified professional help.
If you betrayed your spouse, do not use “grace” as another hiding place.
Walk toward truth, wisdom, repentance, and restoration.
If you stumble again, do not turn a fall into an identity.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Get up.
Fight again.
Sanctification is not pretending temptation disappeared.
It is learning where to run when temptation appears.
Maybe Job's ancient words need to become painfully modern for us:
בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
Maybe your covenant with your eyes begins with your screen.
Not because your phone is evil.
Because your heart is valuable.
Because the people on that screen are human beings, not products for your fantasies.
Because your spouse, present or future, deserves covenant faithfulness rather than comparison with an endless feed.
Because your children may someday learn digital holiness by watching you.
Because secret habits eventually shape public character.
Because Christ deserves more than whatever remains of your attention after your appetites have eaten first.
So...
Is following adult creators on social media a form of compromise?

It can be—and when you deliberately follow them in order to feed lust, cultivate sexual fantasy, repeatedly consume sexualized material, or keep yourself near temptation that you know is mastering you, calling it “just following” does not make the underlying desire spiritually neutral.
But do not turn that conclusion into a weapon for policing everybody else's follower list.
Start with your own heart.
Ask yourself before God:
Why am I following?
What am I hoping to see?
What happens inside me when I see it?
Does this lead me toward Christ or repeatedly awaken desires I know I should flee?
Would I defend this behavior because it is genuinely pure—or because I desperately do not want to surrender it?
And perhaps the hardest one:
If Jesus asked for this account tonight, would I give it to Him?
No dramatic music.
No audience.
Just you.
Your phone.
Your history.
Your Savior.
What happens next?
Be honest.

And if Christ has already been freeing you from pornography, lust, sexual compromise, or secret digital habits, tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that freedom is possible.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Not to announce that you are better than anyone.
Not to shame adult creators.
Not to embarrass struggling Christians.

If you genuinely want your online life to glorify God, then let your digital choices become part of your discipleship. Supporting and sharing Christ-centered resources can be one practical way to help truth reach people beyond your own screen—but it should flow from love for Christ, never from guilt, pressure, or an attempt to purchase God's favor.
And do not keep the blessing to yourself.
Invite your family.
Your friends.
The believer who has become lukewarm.
The Christian secretly struggling with lust.
The seeker asking whether Jesus could really forgive them.
Even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely a collection of rules.
But please remember this.
Sharing this article cannot purchase blessing.
Commenting cannot earn forgiveness.
Unfollowing every provocative account on earth cannot wash away one sin.
Jesus does that.
We support Gospel work because we have been loved—not so that we can buy His love.
We share truth because grace found us—not so that sharing can earn grace.
We pursue holiness because Christ saved us—not so holiness can become our Savior.
And maybe that is what somebody needed to hear most.
You are not standing outside Christ's door trying to scrub your search history clean enough to knock.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Bring Him the phone.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the loneliness underneath it.
Bring Him the marriage you wounded.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot seem to control.
Bring Him the version of yourself nobody online knows exists.
Bring Him the scandal.
Because the hands that were pierced for sinners are still powerful enough to rewrite what sin tried to make permanent.
And perhaps one day you will look at the account you once thought you could never unfollow...
the habit you thought you could never break...
the shame you thought would follow you into the grave...
and realize Jesus was never trying to take life away from you.
He was calling you back to it.
The screen remembers what you followed—but the cross declares that your past does not get the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IT FELT LIKE GOD… BUT WAS IT?
paragraphs:
IT FELT LIKE GOD… BUT WAS IT?
What “Test the Spirits” Really Means Before You Trust That Voice, Follow That Sign, or Call That Feeling God
There is a frightening sentence a Christian can say with absolute sincerity:
“I just feel like God told me.”
Maybe you have said it.
Maybe you were sitting alone when an overwhelming thought entered your mind.
Maybe somebody spoke a “prophetic word” over you and somehow knew exactly what you had been struggling with.
Maybe a door suddenly opened after months of prayer.
Maybe you dreamed something so vivid that you woke up trembling.
Maybe you saw the same phrase three times in one day.
Maybe you felt an unusual peace about a relationship.
Maybe a video appeared on your feed at exactly the moment you were asking God for an answer.
And something inside you whispered...
This cannot be a coincidence.
This has to be God.
But Scripture gives us a warning that can be uncomfortable precisely because it destroys one of our favorite assumptions:
Something can feel spiritual without being from God.
Something can feel powerful without being true.
Something can arrive at the perfect moment and still require testing.
Something can even use Christian language and still deserve examination.
That is why the apostle John did not tell believers to believe everything spiritual.
He told them almost the opposite.
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God...” — 1 John 4:1, KJV
Look closely at the Greek:
“Ἀγαπητοί, μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα εἰ ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστιν...”
Agapētoi, mē panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou Theou estin...
In plain sense:
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to determine whether they are from God.”
That word deserves your attention:
δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete.
Test.
Examine.
Put to proof.
John does not teach spiritual gullibility.
But neither does he teach cynical unbelief.
He teaches discernment.
And notice something beautiful before we go any further.
John begins with:
Ἀγαπητοί — Agapētoi.
Beloved.
This warning comes wrapped in love.
God does not teach His children discernment because He wants them frightened of everything spiritual.
He teaches discernment because He loves them too much to leave them vulnerable to deception.
That changes everything.
Testing something is not necessarily evidence that your faith is weak.
Sometimes testing it is exactly what biblical faithfulness requires.
You are not dishonoring God by asking whether something truly came from Him.
God Himself commanded His people not to believe every spiritual claim automatically.
And somebody reading this desperately needs that freedom.
Because perhaps you have been afraid to question something.
Someone told you, “God said...”
And because they sounded confident, you became afraid that questioning them meant questioning God.
Or maybe nobody else said anything.
Maybe the voice was inside your own heart.
And that can be even harder.
Because feelings are persuasive.
Especially wounded feelings.
Lonely feelings.
Desperate feelings.
Hopeful feelings.
When you desperately want something to be God's will, almost anything can begin looking like confirmation.
That relationship you cannot release.
That opportunity you desperately need.
That person you cannot stop thinking about.
That decision you already want to make.
That dream.
That coincidence.
That unexplained peace.
Suddenly every song sounds prophetic.
Every sermon sounds personal.
Every random post becomes confirmation.
Every open door feels divinely arranged.
And somewhere between desire and interpretation, we can accidentally rename what we want...
“God's will.”
That is why biblical discernment matters.
Because your emotions are real, but they are not Scripture.
Your intuition may be useful, but it is not infallible.
Your circumstances matter, but circumstances alone do not define truth.
An open door is not automatically God's door.
A closed door is not automatically God's rejection.
Peace is precious, but subjective peace by itself is not sufficient proof that God has spoken.
A dream can deeply affect you without becoming divine revelation.
A coincidence can make you stop and think without becoming a command from heaven.
And somebody's confidence when saying “God told me” does not give their words the authority of Scripture.
John tells us why caution is necessary:
“...because many false prophets have gone out into the world.”
Not one.
Many.
And John immediately brings the test toward Jesus Christ.
“Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God...” — 1 John 4:2, KJV
The Greek centers the confession on:
Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα
Iēsoun Christon en sarki elēlythota.
Jesus Christ having come in the flesh.
This matters enormously.

John was confronting false teaching about Christ. His test was not a mystical technique for detecting invisible beings by sensations. The immediate context concerns truth and error expressed through teachers and spiritual claims, especially what they confess concerning Jesus Christ.
In other words, biblical discernment is profoundly Christ-centered.
The question is not merely:
“How did this make me feel?”
The deeper question is:
“What does this say about Jesus?”
Does it agree with the Jesus revealed in Scripture?
Does it confess the true Christ rather than reinventing Him?
Does it lead toward obedience to Christ or away from Him?
Does it glorify Christ or subtly enthrone me?
Does it agree with what God has already revealed?
Because God does not need to contradict yesterday's Scripture to give you today's guidance.
The Holy Spirit does not wage war against the Word He inspired.
Jesus prayed to the Father:
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.” — John 17:17
So if a voice tells you adultery is acceptable because “this person understands me better than my spouse”...
You do not need another sign.
If an impression tells you revenge is justified because somebody deserves to suffer...
You do not need a prophetic confirmation.
If somebody tells you God commanded you to do something Scripture identifies as sin...
You do not need to wonder whether you are resisting the Holy Spirit.
You already have revelation sufficient to reject the claim.
God will never require you to disobey God in order to obey God.
Read that again.
God will never require you to disobey God in order to obey God.
But deception is rarely effective when it arrives looking obviously evil.
That is what makes discernment difficult.
Temptation sometimes arrives looking like relief.
Pride can dress itself as calling.
Control can call itself leadership.
Obsession can call itself love.
Fear can call itself wisdom.
Cowardice can call itself peace.
Impulsiveness can call itself faith.
Selfish ambition can call itself purpose.
Bitterness can disguise itself as discernment.
And sometimes what we call “God closing the door” is simply us refusing to walk through a difficult one.
Sometimes what we call “God giving me peace” is actually the relief we feel after choosing what we wanted all along.
This is why the Christian life cannot safely be built on vibes.
And there is another danger.
Not every misleading spiritual impression must be blamed directly on a demon.
Sometimes the problem is us.
Our desires.
Our assumptions.
Our fears.
Our incomplete understanding.
Our emotional wounds.
Our eagerness to interpret ordinary circumstances as extraordinary messages.
Scripture says:
“The heart is deceitful above all things...” — Jeremiah 17:9, KJV
That does not mean every emotion is evil.
It means our internal world is not an infallible authority.
Even sincere Christians can sincerely misunderstand something.
Peter loved Jesus.
Peter was sincere.
Yet when Jesus began explaining that He would suffer and be killed, Peter rebuked Him.
Think about that.
Peter's instincts probably felt protective.
Loving.
Reasonable.
Surely suffering could not be God's plan for the Messiah.
Then Jesus answered Peter with words that should sober every believer who assumes sincerity guarantees discernment:
“Get thee behind me, Satan...” — Matthew 16:23, KJV
Peter was not necessarily consciously trying to serve Satan.
He was thinking wrongly about God's plan.
His feelings about what Jesus should do were colliding with what the Father actually intended.
That means sincerity alone cannot be our test.
Intensity cannot be our test.
Timing cannot be our test.
Popularity cannot be our test.
Miraculous appearance cannot be our test.
Even supernatural phenomena, by themselves, cannot be the final test.
Jesus warned that false christs and false prophets would show “great signs and wonders” in an attempt to deceive. Paul likewise warned about deception associated with signs and lying wonders.
Scripture therefore never gives us permission to say:
“It was supernatural, therefore it was God.”
The biblical question remains:
Is it true?
Does it agree with God's revealed Word?
Does it confess and honor the biblical Christ?
What fruit does it produce?
Does it move you toward holiness, truth, love, humility, repentance and obedience?
Or does it make you increasingly fascinated with yourself?
There is a kind of spirituality where Jesus becomes little more than a supporting character in someone's personal destiny story.
Everything becomes:
My breakthrough.
My season.
My blessing.
My enemies.
My promotion.
My prophetic word.
My financial miracle.
My relationship.
My platform.
My calling.
My destiny.
And Jesus quietly disappears behind the enormous shadow of the self.
That should concern us.
Because the Holy Spirit's ministry is not to make Christ smaller so we can become enormous.
Jesus said concerning the Spirit:
“He shall glorify me...” — John 16:14, KJV
There is the center.
Jesus.
Jesus.
Jesus.
Not spiritual entertainment.
Not mystical addiction.
Not chasing signs.
Not obsessively decoding numbers.
Not needing another prophetic video every morning before you can make ordinary decisions.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
Savior.
King.
The Spirit of God does not lead us away from Christ into endless fascination with ourselves.
He magnifies Christ.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do when something “feels like God” is wait.
You do not have to panic.
You do not have to manufacture certainty.
You do not have to announce it immediately.
You do not have to build your future around one dream tonight.
You do not have to marry someone because somebody prophesied that person was “the one.”
You do not have to quit your job tomorrow because a video appeared on your feed.
You do not have to send money because somebody claims God revealed that your miracle depends upon your offering.
You can test.
You can pray.
You can search Scripture.
You can seek counsel from mature believers.
You can examine the fruit.
You can ask whether your own desires are distorting your judgment.
And you can wait.
God is not intimidated by careful biblical discernment.
Truth survives examination.
But there is something deeper here.
Something more personal.
Maybe the voice you have struggled most to discern is not somebody else's.
Maybe it is the one inside you saying:
“You've sinned too badly for Jesus to want you.”
Test that spirit.
“You failed again. God must be finished with you.”
Test it.
“You are disgusting.”
Test it.
“You should hide from God until you become better.”
Test it.
“You have ruined everything beyond redemption.”
Test it.
Because conviction and condemnation do not produce the same destination.
The Holy Spirit exposes sin, yes.
Christianity does not minimize sin.
The cross itself proves how serious sin is.
But the Spirit's conviction drives sinners toward Christ.
Condemnation whispers that you should run away from Him.
The Gospel says something radically different.
You sinned.
But Christ came for sinners.
You fell.
But grace is still calling.
You hid.
But Jesus already knows where you are.
You are guilty.
But at Calvary, the sinless Son of God carried the judgment sinners deserved.
You cannot cleanse yourself.
But His blood cleanses.
You cannot rewrite your past.
But Jesus can redeem what your past means for your future.
And suddenly “test the spirits” becomes more than a warning about false prophets somewhere on the internet.
It becomes intensely personal.
What voice has been shaping your understanding of God?
The voice of your trauma?
The voice of your shame?
The voice of religious manipulation?
The voice of your desires?
The voice of culture?
The voice of an influencer?
The voice of a preacher who made himself indispensable?
The voice of your fear?
Or the truth revealed in Jesus Christ?
Some of us have called anxiety “discernment” for years.
Some have called suspicion “wisdom.”
Some have called bitterness “righteous anger.”
Some have called emotional dependency “God's will.”
Some have called compromise “grace.”
Some have called legalism “holiness.”
Some have called spiritual abuse “submission.”
Some have called celebrity Christianity “anointing.”
And perhaps the most painful question is this:
What if the thing you desperately wanted to be from God...
wasn't?
That hurts.
Because discernment sometimes costs us something.
A relationship.
A dream.
A teacher we admired.
A belief we inherited.
A ministry personality we trusted.
A decision we wanted God to approve.
An identity we built around a spiritual experience.
But losing an illusion is not losing God.
Sometimes losing the thing falsely labeled “God” is how we rediscover the God who was there all along.
Jesus is not threatened when counterfeit certainty collapses.
He remains.
When the sign disappears...
Jesus remains.
When the prophecy fails...
Jesus remains.
When your feelings change...
Jesus remains.
When the relationship ends...
Jesus remains.
When the door closes...
Jesus remains.
When you realize you misunderstood something...
Jesus remains.
When your theology is corrected...
Jesus remains.
When your emotions scream one thing and Scripture tells you another...
Jesus remains.
And perhaps this is where grace becomes scandalous.
Because even when you were wrong...
Jesus can still redeem you.
Even when you confused your desire with His voice.
Even when you followed something you should have tested.
Even when you ignored warnings.
Even when you believed somebody who manipulated your hunger for God.
Even when you made the wrong decision.
Even when you said, “God told me,” only to discover later that perhaps He had not...
Grace is not standing at the end of the road laughing at you.
Christ calls people to repent.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is turning.
Coming home.
Returning to truth.
You can say:
“Lord, I was wrong.”
There is freedom in those words.
“Lord, I wanted it so badly that I called my desire Your voice.”
“Lord, I followed feelings instead of truth.”
“Lord, I trusted someone simply because they sounded spiritual.”
“Lord, I ignored Scripture because I preferred the answer I wanted.”
“Lord Jesus, forgive me.”
And the Gospel answers your confession not with a slammed door...
but with a cross.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins...” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice where John ultimately takes his readers after warning them about deception.
Not into paranoia.
Not into fear of demons hiding behind every circumstance.
Not into obsession with detecting invisible enemies.
He reminds believers:
“Ye are of God, little children, and have overcome them: because greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world.” — 1 John 4:4, KJV
Greater.
Not equal.
Not barely surviving.
Greater.
Biblical discernment therefore does not produce terrified Christians suspicious of everything.
It produces believers anchored so deeply in Christ that counterfeits become easier to recognize because they increasingly know the real thing.
Know Jesus.
Know His Word.
Know His Gospel.
Know His character as revealed in Scripture.
Stay close to healthy Christian community.
Receive correction.
Practice humility.
Pray for wisdom.
And when something feels like it came from God...
do not worship the feeling.
Bring it into the light.
Test it.
Does it contradict Scripture?
Reject it.
Does it diminish the biblical Jesus?
Reject it.
Does it excuse sin?
Reject it.
Does it make a human teacher functionally unquestionable?
Be extremely careful.
Does it depend primarily on emotional intensity rather than truth?
Slow down.
Does it flatter your pride while avoiding repentance?
Examine it.
Does it make you afraid to test it?
That itself should make you cautious.
But if something agrees with Scripture, magnifies the true Christ, encourages faithful obedience, bears godly fruit, survives wise examination, and remains consistent with the Gospel...
then walk humbly.
Not arrogantly declaring that every impression you experience carries divine authority.
Humbly.
Because mature discernment does not need theatrics.
And maybe tonight you need to stop asking only:
“Did I feel something?”
And start asking:
“Is it true?”
Maybe you need to stop saying:
“I know it was God because I had peace.”
And start saying:
“Lord, whatever I feel, make me obedient to what You have actually revealed.”
Maybe you need to release something you have been forcing God to endorse.
Maybe you need to repent.
Maybe you need to forgive.
Maybe you need to admit you were deceived.
Maybe you need to stop hiding.
Or maybe you simply need Jesus again.
Not another sign.
Not another algorithmically delivered “prophetic word.”
Not another coincidence.
Not another emotional high.
Jesus.
Somebody reading silently may need to know that returning to truth is possible.
And if someone you love is making a major decision because something merely “feels like God,” do not use this article as a weapon against them. Send it with love.
Because one day the feeling may become overwhelming.
The opportunity may look perfect.
The person may sound convincing.
The coincidence may seem impossible.
And on that day you may need to remember three words:
Test the spirits.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, see Jesus more clearly, repent more deeply, or stand stronger in your faith, help us keep that work moving. One practical way to glorify God is to steward what He has given you for the spread of His truth. Salvation and God's grace cannot be bought.
If this truth matters, carry it farther.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it flows from love for Christ rather than pressure, guilt, or an attempt to earn His favor.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Jesus can.
A ministry cannot reconcile you to God.
Jesus can.
An article cannot transform a dead heart.
Christ can.
So above everything else written here...
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Open His Word.
Test what you hear.
Test what you feel.
Test what people confidently claim.
And cling to Christ so tightly that when counterfeit voices whisper His name, you recognize that something is wrong because you have learned the voice of truth through His Word.
Maybe the most dangerous spiritual lie is not the one that sounds evil.
Maybe it is the one that sounds almost like God...
while quietly leading you away from Jesus.
And maybe the grace you need tonight is realizing that even if you followed the wrong voice yesterday, Jesus is still calling you back to truth today.
The feeling may have fooled you. The voice may have confused you. The sign may have failed you. But Jesus Christ has not changed—and grace still knows the road home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TALK ABOUT BREASTS, KISSING, DESIRE, AND BODIES SO OPENLY?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TALK ABOUT BREASTS, KISSING, DESIRE, AND BODIES SO OPENLY?
The passages some Christians quietly skip may reveal something beautiful about creation, desire, marriage, shame, holiness—and the God who refuses to abandon our bodies to either lust or disgrace.
There are verses in the Bible that almost nobody volunteers to read aloud in church.
You know the ones.
The verses where lovers kiss.
Where a husband delights in his wife.
Where breasts are mentioned without embarrassment.
Where beauty is noticed.
Where longing is spoken instead of hidden.
Where a man and woman desire one another so intensely that modern Christians sometimes read the passage, look around the room, clear their throats, and quietly move on.
And somewhere along the way, many believers absorbed a strange message:
God is comfortable talking about blood, war, betrayal, murder, crucifixion, demons, judgment, adultery, and death...
but surely He becomes embarrassed when the Bible talks about the human body.
Except He doesn't.
And that should make us ask a question much deeper than whether certain Bible verses make us uncomfortable.
Why did God allow Scripture to speak about kissing, breasts, physical attraction, sexual desire, nakedness, marriage, and bodies so openly?
Maybe because God is not ashamed of what He created.
Maybe because sin did not invent the human body.
Maybe because Satan does not own sexuality.
Maybe because biblical holiness was never supposed to mean pretending desire doesn't exist.
And maybe some of us have spent years trying to make God ashamed of something He originally called good.
Go back before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before exploitation.
Before lust became an industry.
Before human beings learned to use bodies as merchandise.
Before anyone knew what sexual shame felt like.
Genesis says:
"וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ"
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha'adam betsalmo.
"And God created the human in His image."
Then comes something extraordinary.
Humanity is created male and female, and Genesis 1:31 says God looked upon what He had made and declared it:
"טוֹב מְאֹד"
Tov me'od.
"Very good."
Not barely acceptable.
Not spiritually unfortunate.
Not something God tolerated until human beings could become sufficiently religious to stop having bodies.
Very good.
Then Genesis 2 gives us one of Scripture's most vulnerable descriptions of human existence:
"וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים"
Vayyihyu sheneihem arummim.
"The two of them were naked."
The man and his wife were naked...
and they were not ashamed.
Do not miss that.
Nakedness appears before shame.
The body appears before lust.
Sexual difference appears before sin.
Marriage appears before the Fall.
Human sexuality did not crawl out of humanity's rebellion against God.
It existed within God's good creation.
Then sin entered.
And almost immediately, something happened to the human relationship with the body.
They hid.
That is one of the saddest transitions in the Bible.
Genesis 2 ends with nakedness without shame.
Genesis 3 gives us hiding.
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
We hide our bodies.
We worship our bodies.
We compare our bodies.
We sell bodies.
We exploit bodies.
We obsess over bodies.
We starve bodies.
We abuse bodies.
We use other people's bodies.
We hate our own bodies.
And sometimes religious culture responds to the world's distortion of sexuality by acting as though sexuality itself must have been the problem.
But Scripture refuses that shortcut.
The Bible neither worships sex nor pretends sex does not exist.
It puts desire underneath the lordship of God.
That is why one of the most startling books in Scripture begins with a woman saying:
"יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ"
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
"Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth."
That is Song of Songs 1:2.
It is in the Bible.
Not hidden in an appendix.
Not smuggled into Scripture by somebody who hoped God wouldn't notice.
There it is.
Desire.
Affection.
Longing.
A kiss.

And Song of Songs becomes even more physically expressive as the poetry unfolds. The lovers admire one another's appearance. They long for one another's presence. They speak of fragrance, touch, beauty, lips, arms, hair, eyes, mouths, and breasts.
Song of Songs 7 even contains the Hebrew:
"שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ"
Shenei shadayikh.
"Your two breasts."
There is no need to make that phrase dirtier than Scripture makes it.
But there is also no need to pretend it says something else.
The poetry is sensual.
The question is why sensual poetry belongs in Holy Scripture.
And part of the answer may expose two opposite lies our culture keeps telling us.
The first lie says:
"If something is sexual, it must be dirty."
The second says:
"If something is sexual, you should be free to do whatever you desire."
The Bible teaches neither.
Scripture can celebrate marital desire while commanding sexual holiness.
It can acknowledge beauty without turning a person into an object.
It can speak about breasts without becoming pornography.
It can celebrate sexual intimacy without separating intimacy from covenant, faithfulness, responsibility, and love.
That difference matters enormously.
Pornography says, "Take."
Covenant love says, "I give myself faithfully to you."
Pornography separates a body from the dignity of the person inhabiting it.
Biblical love refuses to do that.
Lust asks what another person's body can do for me.
Love asks how I can honor the person God has entrusted to my care.

That is why Proverbs can say to a married man, in remarkably physical language, that he should rejoice in the wife of his youth and be continually delighted by her love. Proverbs 5:19 even speaks openly of her breasts.
Again...
the Bible isn't embarrassed.
But notice the context.
Proverbs 5 is not granting unlimited permission to chase sexual stimulation.
It is doing almost exactly the opposite.
The chapter warns a man against adultery and directs his sexual delight toward his own wife.
Desire is not being erased.
It is being ordered toward faithfulness.
That distinction changes everything.
Christianity does not teach that holiness means becoming less human.
It teaches that everything human—including desire—must be brought under the reign of Jesus Christ.
And Jesus takes desire seriously enough to go beneath behavior and address the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, when Jesus speaks about looking at a woman with lustful intent, the Greek uses a form of:
ἐπιθυμέω
epithymeō.
The word can refer to strong desire or longing; context determines whether that desire is righteous or sinful. Desire itself is therefore not automatically identical with sexual sin.
What Jesus confronts is desire directed toward someone in a way that violates faithfulness in the heart.
He refuses to let us reduce purity to:
"Well, technically, I didn't touch anybody."
Jesus goes after the heart.
The secret stare.
The cultivated fantasy.
The inward possession of another person.
The place nobody sees except you...
and God.
And suddenly this becomes uncomfortable for reasons that have nothing to do with Song of Songs.
Because it is possible to be embarrassed by biblical sexuality while secretly consuming distorted sexuality.
It is possible to blush at the word "breasts" in Scripture and then stare at someone's body online.
It is possible to demand modesty from everybody else while refusing to discipline your own eyes.
It is possible to look sexually respectable in church while carrying an entire hidden world inside your phone.
Maybe that sentence landed somewhere you didn't want it to.
Stay with me.
Because the Gospel is not coming to humiliate you.
It is coming to bring you into the light.
There are people reading this who learned sexuality through pornography before anyone taught them theology.
Some learned it through abuse.
Some through jokes.
Some through shame.
Some through movies.
Some through secret searches at midnight.
Some were told that their body was disgusting.
Some were taught that virtually every sexual feeling was sinful.
Some were never taught anything at all.
And some have spent years trying to figure out whether God is disgusted with them because desire exists inside them.
Listen carefully.
Scripture does not teach that the existence of sexual desire makes you filthy.
It teaches that our desires, like every other dimension of fallen human life, need redemption, wisdom, boundaries, self-control, and surrender to God.
There is a difference between experiencing temptation and choosing to cultivate sin.
There is a difference between noticing beauty and consuming a person with your imagination.
There is a difference between marital delight and exploitation.
There is a difference between intimacy and using someone.
And Christianity's answer to sexual brokenness is not merely:
"Stop wanting."
The Gospel goes deeper.
"Become Christ's."
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:19:
And then:
"You are not your own."
Those words are devastating to both sexual shame and sexual entitlement.
To shame, they say:
Your body is not worthless.
To lust, they say:
Neither is anybody else's.
Your body belongs to Christ.
The body you are tempted to hate belongs to Christ.
The body you are tempted to misuse belongs to Christ.
And the person you are tempted to reduce to a body bears a dignity you do not have permission to erase.
Paul's conclusion is magnificent:
"Glorify God in your body."
Not apart from your body.
Not after escaping your body.
In your body.
Christian redemption is astonishingly physical.
Jesus did not merely send us an idea.
ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Ho Logos sarx egeneto.
"The Word became flesh."
John 1:14.
Flesh.
The eternal Son entered embodied human existence.
He hungered.
He thirsted.
He became tired.
He touched lepers.
He ate meals.
He wept.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died bodily.
And then Christianity makes an even more outrageous claim:
His body did not remain in the grave.
Jesus Christ rose.
Christian hope is not the permanent abandonment of embodiment.
It includes resurrection.
That means the biblical story of the body is bigger than sex.
Creation.
Fall.
Shame.
Incarnation.
Cross.
Resurrection.
Redemption.
Glory.
Your body sits inside that enormous story.

And perhaps that is why Satan has worked so successfully to convince generations of people that their bodies are either gods to worship, products to advertise, weapons to manipulate others, objects to compare, instruments for pleasure, or sources of shame.
Jesus offers another identity.
Redeemed.
Belonging to Him.
This does not make every desire holy.
It means every desire must meet the Holy One.
And some desires must die.
Some habits must be confessed.
Some relationships must change.
Some browser histories need to stop being repeated.
Some secret messages need to end.
Some fantasies need to be starved instead of fed.
Some marriages need tenderness restored.
Some wounded people need time, safety, wise pastoral care, and sometimes professional help because someone else sinned against their body.
Some Christians need to repent of sexual sin.
And some Christians need to repent of making people feel dirty for possessing the ordinary humanity God created them with.
Both errors wound people.
Jesus calls us somewhere better.
Truth without shame.
Grace without compromise.
Holiness without pretending.
Love without exploitation.
Desire without idolatry.
Bodies without worshiping bodies.
Marriage without embarrassment over the intimacy God permits within it.
Singleness without treating unmarried believers as incomplete human beings.
And repentance without believing your scandal gets the final word.
Because maybe this is where the article stops being about "those strange verses in the Bible."
Maybe now it is about you.
About what you watched last night.
About what happened to you years ago.
About the marriage that has become cold.
About the desire you have been hiding.
About the shame you never named.
About the person you keep imagining.
About the addiction everybody thinks you defeated.
About the secret relationship.
About the memory that still makes you feel contaminated.
About the part of your story you are terrified Jesus will uncover.
What if He already knows?
And what if He is still calling you?
The woman caught in adultery had a scandal.
The woman at the well had a complicated relational history.
David had sexual sin in his story.
Corinth contained believers coming out of profoundly broken sexual backgrounds.
The Gospel did not pretend those things were harmless.
Grace never needs to rename darkness as light in order to rescue someone from it.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He forgives sinners.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He calls people out of darkness.
He teaches them another way to live.
The Christian message is not:
"Your desires determine who you are."
It is:
Jesus Christ can redeem the person your desires could never save.
And perhaps somebody needs that tonight.
You are sitting alone with a screen in your hand.
Nobody knows what you have been fighting.
Nobody knows how many times you promised God it was the last time.
Nobody knows the shame that hits immediately afterward.
Nobody knows how desperately you want to be clean.
You pray.
You fail.
You cry.
You promise.
You relapse.
You hide.
Then Sunday arrives and you know exactly how to smile.
But Jesus knows the person underneath the smile.
He knows what is behind the deleted history.
He knows what happened in that relationship.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows what you willingly chose and what was done to you against your will—and those are not morally the same thing.
He knows where responsibility belongs.
He knows where repentance is needed.
He knows where healing is needed.
And He knows exactly where you are.
The answer is not to run farther into darkness.
Come into the light.
"If we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That is 1 John 1:9.
Notice the word cleanse.
Not merely expose.
Cleanse.
This is why the cross matters.
Christianity is not fundamentally a campaign to make sexually broken people behave better.
Christianity announces that the Son of God came for sinners.
At Calvary, Jesus carried sin's judgment.
And when a sinner turns to Christ in repentance and faith, forgiveness is not purchased by performing enough purity afterward.
Christ paid.
Grace is not God's permission to continue living enslaved to sin.
Grace breaks sin's claim to be your master.
Maybe your story contains sexual scandal.
Jesus is not intimidated by scandal.
Maybe your story contains wounds you didn't choose.
Jesus is not frightened by wounds.
Maybe you have spent years believing you are beyond restoration.
Look at the cross again.
There is blood there for sinners.
There is mercy there for the ashamed.
There is a Savior there who knows the entire truth about you and still commands you to come.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because He came precisely because it does.
This is why Scripture can speak honestly about bodies.
God intends to redeem whole people.
Your Christianity was never supposed to exist only from the neck upward.
Your eyes belong to Jesus.
Your imagination belongs to Jesus.
Your sexuality belongs to Jesus.
Your singleness belongs to Jesus.
Your marriage belongs to Jesus.
Your wounds belong before Jesus.
Your desires must bow before Jesus.
Your body belongs to Jesus.
And when everything belongs to Him, holiness stops being merely a list of things you aren't allowed to touch.
Holiness becomes freedom to belong completely to the One who died and rose for you.
So yes.
The Bible talks about kissing.
It talks about breasts.
It talks about desire.
It talks about nakedness.
It talks about sex.
It talks about adultery.
It talks about lust.
It talks about marriage.
It talks about bodies.
And it does so because the God of Scripture is not afraid of the truth about being human.
He created what sin distorted.
He confronts what lust corrupts.
He protects what exploitation cheapens.
He forgives what repentance brings into the light.
And through Jesus Christ, He is restoring what the Fall shattered.
Be honest.

And if your story is too personal to explain publicly, you don't owe strangers your private details. Even a simple "no more hiding" can become your reminder that darkness does not get to own the rest of your story.
Not because clicking "Share" earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Salvation is grace.
Someone's marriage may be hurting.
Someone may think pornography has permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may have confused holiness with hatred of their own body.
Someone may desperately need to discover that repentance is not the doorway to rejection.
It is the road home to grace.
Share it with the husband or wife who needs encouragement.
Send it to the believer who has been fighting silently.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Give freely, prayerfully, and without compulsion.
Surrender to Jesus.
If there is sin, repent.
If there is shame, bring it into His light.
If you have fallen, stop running away from the only Savior capable of raising you.
If you have been wounded, know that what someone did to you does not make you morally dirty.
If you are married, honor your covenant.
If you are single, do not believe the lie that sexual experience is required for a meaningful human life. Jesus Himself lived a fully human life without marriage or sexual intercourse.
If desire is raging, don't worship it and don't pretend it isn't there.
Bring it under Christ.
Because Christianity does not end with a frightened sinner hiding behind leaves.
It ends with redeemed people belonging completely to God.
That is the journey.
From nakedness without shame...
to sin and hiding...
to bodies distorted by lust and wounded by exploitation...
to the Word becoming flesh...
to a Savior's body broken on a cross...
to an empty tomb...
to resurrection...
to redemption...
to glory.
So the next time someone asks:
"Why does the Bible talk about breasts, kissing, desire, and bodies so openly?"
Tell them:
Because God is not embarrassed by His creation.
Because He tells the truth about our corruption of it.
Because holiness does not require pretending we have no bodies.
Because desire needs redemption, not worship.
Because sex is not God.
Because shame is not God either.
Because our bodies were never meant to belong to lust, pornography, exploitation, culture, comparison, or ourselves.
They were meant to glorify the One who created them.

And because when sin turned nakedness into hiding, God began unfolding a redemption story that would eventually lead to Jesus Christ—the Savior who entered human flesh, carried human sin, died a human death, walked bodily out of a grave, and now calls ashamed sinners out from behind whatever they have been hiding behind.
Maybe that is why this subject makes us uncomfortable.
It gets too close.
Too close to our browser histories.
Too close to our marriages.
Too close to our wounds.
Too close to our fantasies.
Too close to our shame.
Too close to the places where we desperately want Jesus...
but still haven't completely opened the door.
Open it.
He already knows what is behind it.
And grace is standing closer than your shame wants you to believe.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story, but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Marriage Is Sacred—which Is Exactly Why Betrayal Hurts So Deeply
paragraphs:
Marriage Is Sacred—which Is Exactly Why Betrayal Hurts So Deeply
The wound is not proof that marriage meant too little. Sometimes it hurts this badly because, before God, it was supposed to mean so much.
There is a particular kind of silence that enters a room after betrayal is discovered.
The furniture hasn't moved.
The photographs are still hanging where they were yesterday.
The coffee cups are still in the cupboard. The children may still need breakfast. Work still expects you to show up. People still send ordinary messages about ordinary things.
But nothing feels ordinary anymore.
Because somewhere between what you believed and what you just discovered, an entire world collapsed.
Maybe it was a message you were never supposed to see.
A confession that came too late.
A name that suddenly explained months of distance.
A relationship that was called “just friendship” until the truth could no longer survive beneath that description.
Maybe there was physical adultery.
Maybe there was pornography hidden behind passwords and deleted histories.
Maybe it was an emotional attachment secretly receiving the tenderness, attention, vulnerability, or desire that belonged within the marriage.
Or maybe you are reading this from the other side.
You were the one who betrayed.
You are the one carrying the secret.
You know what your spouse does not know.
You know what happened.
You know what almost happened.
And somewhere underneath the excuses, the rationalizations, the loneliness, the anger, the unmet needs, and all the sentences beginning with “but,” you know something sacred has been wounded.
That is what makes betrayal so devastating.
Marriage is not merely an arrangement between two adults who enjoy each other's company.
In Scripture, covenant is involved.
And covenant makes betrayal heavier because love was entrusted there.
The Bible does not romanticize marriage as though two sinners standing at an altar suddenly become incapable of selfishness. Scripture is far more realistic about the human heart than that.
But neither does Scripture treat marriage casually.
Hebrews 13:4 begins with striking words:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν…”
Timios ho gamos en pasin…
“Let marriage be held in honor among all…”
That word τίμιος — timios carries the sense of something honored, valuable, precious.
Marriage is not disposable simply because our culture has learned to treat promises as temporary whenever feelings change.
And the verse continues:
“καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…”
kai hē koitē amiantos…
“…and let the marriage bed be undefiled.”
The word ἀμίαντος — amiantos means undefiled, unstained.
Then Scripture gives the warning modern ears often wish Christianity would soften:
God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
Hebrews 13:4 does not say this because God hates human intimacy.
It says it because God takes covenant faithfulness seriously.
Sexual faithfulness matters precisely because marriage matters.
And suddenly the tears of the betrayed spouse begin making terrible sense.
You weren't grieving merely because someone “broke a rule.”
You were grieving because something precious was treated as common.
Something entrusted was mishandled.
Something promised was violated.
The person who once looked into your eyes and said, in one form or another, “I choose you,” made choices that caused you to wonder whether any of those words were real.
That can fracture something inside a person.
You begin interrogating memories.
Was that trip real?
Was that anniversary real?
When you said you loved me, did you mean it?
Were you thinking about someone else while lying beside me?
How long was I living inside a story whose missing pages everybody seemed to know except me?
Betrayal doesn't only injure the present.
It can make you suspicious of your own past.
And sometimes the most painful question is not:
“Why did you choose them?”
It is:
“Why wasn't I worth protecting?”
Please hear this carefully.
Another person's sin is not a reliable measurement of your worth.
The betrayed husband is not automatically inadequate because his wife was unfaithful.
The betrayed wife is not automatically undesirable because her husband pursued someone else.
Someone else's disobedience cannot rewrite what God says about the value of a human being made in His image.
That does not make betrayal hurt less.
But it matters when shame begins whispering that you caused another person's sin merely by failing to be perfect.
Marriage never required perfection.
It required faithfulness.
And there is an important difference.
This is also why Christians should never use Scripture as a weapon against the wounded.
“Just forgive.”
“Submit.”
“Don't destroy your family.”
“God hates divorce.”
“Stop bringing up the past.”
Bible verses can become instruments of cruelty when ripped from their context and placed into the hands of people more interested in protecting appearances than confronting sin.
Biblical forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
Reconciliation can be real.
Restoration can be breathtakingly real.
But biblical grace does not require calling darkness light.
Jesus never had to minimize sin in order to forgive sinners.
He went to the cross precisely because sin is serious.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace is God dealing with evil at immeasurable cost.
That changes everything.
Because if you are the betrayed spouse, Christianity does not demand that you pretend you were not wounded.
You may grieve.
You may tell the truth.
You may seek wise pastoral and professional help.
You may establish appropriate boundaries.
You may refuse manipulation.
You may insist that repentance become more than tears produced by being caught.

And if abuse, coercion, threats, stalking, or violence are involved, protecting immediate safety is not a betrayal of biblical marriage. Seek appropriate local help and trusted support rather than remaining isolated because someone has convinced you that suffering silently is holiness.
Jesus does not need lies to defend marriage.
Truth honors what God made sacred.
But now we have to turn toward the person who betrayed.
Because perhaps that person is you.
And maybe you've almost stopped reading.
Don't.
Not yet.
Because condemnation is not the final sentence I want you to hear.
But neither am I going to give you counterfeit grace.

If you are hiding adultery, pornography, sexual immorality, an emotional affair, secret messages, or another relationship that you know violates your marriage covenant, repentance cannot begin while you are still negotiating with the darkness.
You cannot ask Jesus to heal what you are determined to keep hiding.
You cannot rebuild trust while protecting the secret that destroyed it.
You cannot call something “a mistake” when you are still making arrangements to repeat it.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling terrible about consequences.
It is turning.
It is bringing darkness into light.
It is refusing to keep feeding what is killing you.
It is accepting that forgiveness does not automatically erase earthly consequences.
It is understanding that the person you wounded may need time.
A lot of time.
You may be forgiven before you are trusted again.
Those are not contradictions.
Trust is not demanded.
Trust is rebuilt.
Slowly.
Truthfully.
Consistently.
Sometimes painfully.
And if you are thinking, “But my marriage was already broken,” that may explain the environment in which temptation grew.
It does not make betrayal righteous.
Loneliness matters.
Neglect matters.
Sexual rejection can hurt.
Emotional abandonment can hurt.
Cruelty can devastate a marriage.
Those wounds deserve honest attention.
But someone else's sin does not transform our sin into holiness.
Jesus calls us beyond blame-shifting because He loves us too much to leave us hiding behind excuses.
And here is where the Gospel becomes far more beautiful than cheap religious advice.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν…”
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas, kathōs kai ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian…
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church…”
And then comes the part that destroys every selfish definition of love:
“καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς”
kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
“…and gave Himself up for her.”
Look carefully at the direction of Christ's love.
He gave Himself.
That is the opposite of betrayal.
Betrayal asks:
“What can I secretly take while keeping everything else?”
Christlike love asks:
“What can I faithfully give?”
Betrayal protects self at another person's expense.
Jesus gave Himself for His bride.
Betrayal says, “My appetite deserves this.”
Christlike love says, “Love is worth sacrifice.”
That is why the Christian vision of marriage can never be reduced to staying technically married while emotionally destroying one another.
A marriage can remain legally intact while tenderness dies behind closed doors.
People can sit beside one another in church while resentment has been sleeping between them for years.
They can upload anniversary photographs while privately wondering whether the relationship is already gone.
God is not impressed by appearances.
He desires truth in the inward being.
But perhaps this is where your story becomes complicated.
Because you still love the person who betrayed you.
And you hate that you still love them.
One hour you want restoration.
The next hour you cannot stand hearing their voice.
You remember the person you married, then remember what they did.
You want to forgive.
Then another detail surfaces and you feel as though discovery day happened all over again.
Healing after betrayal rarely moves in a straight line.
A song can trigger it.
A location.
A date.
A notification sound.
A late arrival home.
A phone turned face-down on a table.
Something completely harmless can suddenly awaken everything.
That does not necessarily mean healing has failed.
Wounds remember.
And deep wounds require patient truth.
But there is something even betrayal does not get to own forever.
Your future.
The Gospel makes an audacious claim:
Sin can be judged truthfully without being allowed the final word over everyone who comes to Christ.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not grace that excuses betrayal.
Grace that confronts it.
Not grace that protects lies.
Grace that drags them into light.
Not grace that tells the wounded to stop hurting.
Grace that sits beside shattered people.
Not grace that lets the betrayer continue unchanged.
Grace that calls sinners to repentance and then begins making different people out of them.
The cross proves both realities simultaneously.
Our sin is worse than our excuses admit.
God's mercy is greater than our shame imagines.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
Christ bore sin.
And the risen Jesus is still in the business of taking stories that look irredeemable and writing chapters human beings could never manufacture.
That does not mean every betrayed marriage will be restored.
Scripture itself recognizes sexual immorality as a grave covenant violation, and Christians should be careful not to promise an outcome God has not promised.
Some marriages do survive betrayal.
Some become astonishing testimonies of repentance, forgiveness, accountability, patience, counseling, rebuilt trust, and transformed love.
Others do not.
The Gospel is not a formula guaranteeing that every marriage will return to what it was.
Sometimes what existed before betrayal should not simply be recreated anyway.
Perhaps there was silence where communication should have been.
Pride where humility should have lived.
Secret resentment.
Spiritual neglect.
Unaddressed wounds.
Patterns everybody learned to tolerate.
If reconciliation occurs, the goal cannot merely be to rebuild the same house with the same cracks and hope the next storm behaves differently.
Christ calls people into truth.
And truth may require confession.
Accountability.
Transparency.
Pastoral wisdom.
Qualified counseling.
Changed routines.
Broken contact with an affair partner.
Patience with questions.
Sexual integrity.
Financial transparency where relevant.
Digital transparency where appropriate and mutually agreed.
And above all, genuine repentance that survives after the emotional crisis has passed.
Because anyone can cry when consequences arrive.
Transformation is revealed by what happens when nobody is applauding anymore.
That is the uncomfortable beauty of repentance.
It keeps walking after the dramatic moment is over.
Maybe you betrayed your spouse years ago and have genuinely repented, but shame still introduces you by your worst chapter.
Adulterer.
Unfaithful.
Dirty.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Listen carefully to the Gospel.
Repentance does not mean pretending you never committed the sin.
Redemption means the sin no longer possesses the authority to define who you ultimately are in Christ.
Paul reminded the Corinthians of people whose histories included sexual immorality and adultery, and then wrote words that still sound almost impossible:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then he speaks of washing, sanctification, and justification in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Were.
That little word is a doorway.
The Gospel does not say your past never happened.
The Gospel says Jesus Christ can make your past cease being your master.
There are scars grace does not erase from history.
But scars are not the same thing as chains.
And maybe you are not the betrayer.
Maybe you're the one still staring at pieces of a life you did not break.
Then hear this too:
You are more than the person somebody cheated on.
More than the spouse somebody lied to.
More than the one who wasn't chosen in a moment when covenant demanded choosing you.
Your identity was never supposed to rest entirely inside another human being's ability to love you perfectly.
No spouse can carry the weight of being your savior.
There is One who can.
Jesus.
The Bridegroom who does not betray His bride.
The Savior who knows every hidden room and still calls sinners into light.
The Shepherd who does not abandon His sheep when they become inconvenient.
The Christ who was Himself betrayed with a kiss.
Think about that.
Jesus knows betrayal.
Judas did not arrive wearing the face of an enemy.
He arrived as someone who had walked beside Him.
Someone who had eaten with Him.
Someone close enough to kiss Him.
Jesus understands what it means for treachery to come through familiar hands.
And yet betrayal did not stop the mission of Christ.
The cross looked like scandal.
God turned it toward redemption.
The tomb looked final.
Jesus walked out.
So maybe the sentence you need tonight is this:
What happened to you may become part of your story, but through Christ it does not have to become the ending of your story.
And if you are the one who caused the devastation, your sentence is different but equally urgent:
Stop hiding.
Come home to truth.
Not merely home to your spouse.
Home to Christ.
Repent because Jesus is worthy, even before you know whether the marriage will survive.
Confess because truth belongs to Him.
Cut off what is feeding the sin.
Seek mature biblical accountability.
Stop demanding immediate trust.
Stop making your spouse comfort you for the pain your choices created.
Learn how to sit inside the consequences without running back toward the very darkness that produced them.
Let repentance cost you something.
Then keep walking.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make guilty people feel temporarily sorry.
He died and rose to make people new.
And for the wounded spouse…
You do not have to manufacture healing tonight.
You don't have to solve the rest of your life before morning.
You don't have to pretend you're stronger than you are.
Bring the rage.
Bring the questions.
Bring the humiliation.
Bring the memories.
Bring the fear that nobody will ever love you faithfully.
Bring the part of you that still wants the marriage.
Bring the part that wants to run.
Bring the part that cannot imagine trusting anyone again.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
The Psalms prove that God is not frightened by anguished prayers.
He would rather meet you in truth than watch you perform strength from a distance.
Maybe your first act of honesty is simply writing:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because a comment saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes putting truth into words is the moment someone stops pretending.
And somebody reading beneath you may discover they are not the only Christian whose marriage has bled.
That matters.
Because churches are filled with people carrying stories nobody sees.
The husband singing worship songs while wondering whether his wife still loves him.
The wife lifting her hands while fighting flashbacks from what she discovered.
The repentant spouse terrified that God will never use them again.
The couple sitting together who nearly didn't make it.
The divorced believer wondering whether everyone sees a failure whenever they look at them.
The single Christian afraid marriage is no longer worth believing in.
They need more than slogans.
They need Jesus.
They need truth strong enough to confront sin and grace deep enough to reach sinners.
So if someone came into your mind while reading this, send this to them.
Not as gossip.
Not as a weapon.
Not as a passive-aggressive message to shame your spouse publicly.
Send it because somebody may be drowning quietly.
Save it too.
Because pain has a strange way of making us forget what we knew yesterday.
You may need these words again.
We want them here.
Not merely to increase a number.
We want people close enough to biblical truth to encounter Christ.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical resources into the hands of people who need them.
God's grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased. But believers can choose to support ministry as an act of generosity and stewardship.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone more spiritual.
But because your timeline reaches people this page may never reach.
Someone you know may be smiling publicly and bleeding privately.
Someone may have betrayed their spouse last night and be desperately looking for permission to keep hiding.
Someone may have discovered an affair this morning.
Someone may be considering walking away from Jesus because Christians gave them clichés when what they needed was truth and compassion.
Someone may believe their worst decision permanently disqualified them from grace.
Put the Gospel where they might find it.
And remember this before you leave:
Marriage is sacred—which is exactly why betrayal hurts so deeply.
But betrayal is not more powerful than the blood of Christ.
Adultery is serious.
So is grace.
Covenant matters.
So does repentance.
Consequences are real.
So is redemption.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.

He rewrites everything by entering the wreckage with truth, bearing sin at the cross, calling sinners to repentance, meeting the wounded with mercy, and proving through an empty tomb that what looked like the end does not always get to remain the end.
So bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the confession you have been terrified to speak.
Bring Him the pieces you cannot put back together.
And whether Christ restores the relationship, rebuilds your life through a road you never expected, or begins first by rebuilding the person staring back at you in the mirror…
give Him the pen.
Because the wound may explain why you are bleeding today—but Jesus Christ still has authority over what your story becomes tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID GOD EVER CELEBRATE POLYGAMY?
paragraphs:
DID GOD EVER CELEBRATE POLYGAMY?
The Bible records men with multiple wives—but recording a broken story is not the same thing as calling the brokenness good. And when we follow the story all the way back to Eden and all the way forward to Jesus, something becomes painfully clear.
There is a question many Christians quietly hope nobody asks.
If God designed marriage...
If marriage was supposed to mean something sacred...
If Jesus spoke about a man and a woman becoming “one flesh”...
Then why does the Bible contain so many men with multiple wives?
Abraham had Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob married Leah and Rachel and fathered children through Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon famously accumulated hundreds.
And Scripture does not erase their names.
It does not airbrush their families.
It does not rewrite their histories so the heroes look cleaner than they really were.
So the uncomfortable question remains:
Did God ever celebrate polygamy?
Stay with that question.
Because the answer exposes something much larger than ancient marriage customs.
It reveals how easily we can confuse what God patiently permits in a fallen world with what God actually desires.
And if we make that mistake while reading their stories...
we may be making the same mistake while interpreting our own.
The first thing we need to understand is simple but enormously important:
The Bible describing something does not automatically mean the Bible is prescribing it.
Scripture records murder.
That does not make murder holy.
Scripture records adultery.
