That does not make adultery God's design.
Scripture records deception, drunkenness, slavery, incest, betrayal, idolatry, political corruption, sexual exploitation, cowardice, revenge, and war.
Sometimes Scripture reports human behavior with surprisingly little immediate commentary because the narrative itself—and ultimately the larger biblical story—reveals the consequences.
Polygamy must be read with that same literary and theological care.
And before Abraham ever entered the story...
before Jacob ever met Rachel...
before David ever became king...
before Solomon ever constructed his enormous household...
Genesis gives us something earlier.
A beginning.
A pattern.
A design.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression translated “one flesh” is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
“one flesh.”
Not merely two people occupying the same household.
Not merely a legal contract.
Not merely reproduction.
There is union here.
Covenantal joining.
Two lives becoming bound together in a unique relationship.
And notice what is striking about the creation account.
God could have begun humanity with Adam and several women.
He did not.
The narrative presents one man and one woman brought together by God.
That becomes even more significant because Jesus Himself later reaches backward past centuries of distorted human practice and returns His listeners to this beginning.
When questioned about divorce, Jesus says in Matthew 19:4–6:

“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female... For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?... What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Jesus quotes Genesis.
But listen carefully to what He does.
He does not begin with Abraham.
He does not say, “Look at Jacob.”
He does not appeal to David.
He does not point toward Solomon.
He goes farther back.
“From the beginning...”
That matters.
Because when fallen human history becomes confusing, Jesus points us toward creation to recover God's intention.
The Greek text of Matthew contains the expression:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν — hoi dyo eis sarka mian
“the two [shall become] one flesh.”
The two.
Jesus' appeal is to the creation pattern.
And that should immediately change how we read every polygamous household appearing afterward.
Because the Bible's first explicit appearance of a man taking two wives does not occur in Eden.
It occurs after the Fall.
And the man is not presented as a model of covenant faithfulness.
His name is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 tells us:
“And Lamech took unto him two wives.”
That sentence can look almost harmless when isolated.
But context changes everything.
Lamech comes from Cain's line.
Soon afterward he boasts to his wives about killing a man and magnifies vengeance beyond even Cain.
Polygamy enters the biblical narrative not inside the perfection of Eden but within humanity's expanding brokenness east of Eden.
That does not by itself settle every theological question surrounding every later plural marriage.
But it should stop us from casually claiming that Scripture introduces polygamy as an ideal worthy of celebration.
Then Abraham enters the story.
God promises Abraham descendants.
Years pass.
Sarah remains barren.
The promise feels impossible.
And human beings do what frightened human beings have done throughout history.
They try to accomplish God's promise through human control.
Genesis 16 tells us that Sarai gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abram.
A child comes.
But so does pain.
Hagar conceives.
Tension explodes.
Sarah becomes bitter.
Hagar suffers.
Eventually a mother and child are driven into the wilderness.
Yet even there, God sees Hagar.
That detail matters enormously.
Because biblical interpretation becomes cruel when we turn real human beings into mere props for theological arguments.
Hagar was seen by God.
Her suffering mattered to Him.
Her son mattered.
God's compassion toward people inside a broken arrangement does not necessarily mean He is endorsing every human decision that created that arrangement.
That distinction reaches far beyond polygamy.
God's mercy toward us in our mess is not proof that our mess was His original intention.
Read that again.
Because some of us have built entire defenses around the fact that God has still blessed us.
“He hasn't abandoned me.”
True.
“He still provides for me.”
Perhaps.
“I still feel His mercy.”
Thank God.
But none of those statements automatically mean every decision we made was righteous.
Sometimes grace meets us precisely where obedience would never have taken us.
That is what makes grace grace.
Then comes Jacob.
He loves Rachel.
He receives Leah through Laban's deception.
Then he marries Rachel.
Then Bilhah and Zilpah enter the reproductive rivalry.
And what follows?
Competition.
Jealousy.
Bargaining.
Heartache.
A woman desperate to be loved.
Another desperate for children.
Servants drawn into a struggle larger than themselves.
Children born into complicated rivalries.
Eventually brothers become so consumed by jealousy that Joseph is sold.
Again, Scripture does not need to insert a sentence after every episode saying:
“By the way, this family arrangement is painful.”
The story shows you.
You can hear the heartbreak.
Leah's naming of her sons reveals a woman aching to be seen and loved by her husband.
Genesis does not romanticize this household.
God works through it.
But that is different.
Very different.
God's ability to redeem dysfunctional families should never be confused with God's endorsement of their dysfunction.
And that brings us to David.
This is where the discussion becomes harder because David is not merely another ancient figure.
He is Israel's celebrated king.
A man after God's own heart.
A central figure in the messianic story.
And David had multiple wives.
So did God celebrate it?
We need to read carefully.
Deuteronomy 17:17 had already warned Israel's future king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away...”
The Hebrew verb often rendered “multiply” comes from רבה — ravah, carrying the idea of becoming or making many, increasing, multiplying.
The warning is unmistakable.
Israel's king was not supposed to use royal power to accumulate wives.
Yet David did.
And his household became a place of devastating sexual and relational disorder.
Then Solomon takes royal accumulation to an almost grotesque extreme.
First Kings 11:3 says:
“And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines...”
And then Scripture tells us exactly what happened:
“and his wives turned away his heart.”
This is almost an echo of the warning in Deuteronomy.
Do not multiply wives...
lest the king's heart turn away.
Solomon multiplies wives...
and his heart turns away.
That is not celebration.
That is tragedy.
The man famous for wisdom ignored wisdom and discovered that intelligence cannot protect a heart committed to disobedience.
But someone may raise another difficult passage.
In 2 Samuel 12:8, while confronting David over Bathsheba and Uriah, God says through Nathan that He had given David his master's house and his master's wives.
Doesn't that mean God approved of David's polygamy?
This passage deserves careful treatment rather than a convenient answer.
Nathan is confronting David's outrageous ingratitude and abuse of power. David already possessed enormous royal privilege, yet he took Uriah's wife and arranged Uriah's death.

The language of “giving” occurs in the context of the transfer of Saul's royal house and status to David. Ancient royal succession could be described through possession of the former king's household. The passage's purpose is not to establish polygamy as God's creation ideal. Its purpose is to expose David's covetousness:
You had abundance, yet you took what was not yours.

Whatever interpretive questions remain around the precise historical implications of “your master's wives,” that verse cannot simply erase Genesis 2, Deuteronomy 17, the destructive narrative patterns surrounding plural marriages, Jesus' appeal to creation, and the New Testament's marital vision.
We must allow clearer biblical patterns and immediate literary context to govern our conclusions rather than building an entire theology from one difficult sentence.
There is another category we need to understand.
Regulation is not necessarily celebration.
The Law of Moses contains provisions addressing situations involving plural marriages.
Exodus 21:10 protects the food, clothing, and marital rights of a woman when another wife is taken.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives and favors one over another.
Why regulate something if it is not ideal?
Because fallen societies create real victims.
Law sometimes restrains human sin and protects vulnerable people within social realities without declaring those realities to be the creation ideal.
Jesus gives us a powerful interpretive principle when discussing divorce in Matthew 19.
Moses permitted certain provisions because of the hardness of human hearts.
Then Jesus says:
“but from the beginning it was not so.”
Those words are thunder.
From the beginning it was not so.
There are things God regulates because humanity is broken.
There are things God tolerates temporarily because human hearts are hard.
There are situations in which divine law limits damage.
But accommodation to human hardness should never automatically be transformed into God's eternal ideal.
Jesus keeps taking us back to the beginning.
And then the New Testament moves marriage toward something even deeper.
Marriage becomes an earthly sign pointing beyond itself.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:31–32:
There it is again.
Genesis.
One flesh.
But now Paul pulls back the curtain.
Marriage points toward Christ and His Church.
The Greek word Paul uses for “mystery” is:
μυστήριον — mystērion
a mystery—something once hidden and now disclosed within God's redemptive purpose.
Christian marriage is not ultimately about romantic fulfillment.
It is supposed to become a living picture of covenant faithfulness.
Christ loves His bride.
Christ gives Himself for His bride.
Christ sanctifies His bride.
Christ does not exploit His bride.
Christ does not discard His bride when she becomes inconvenient.
Christ lays down His life.
And suddenly the question “Did God celebrate polygamy?” becomes part of a much larger question:
What kind of love tells the truth about Jesus?
This is where Scripture stops being an ancient argument and walks into our homes.
Because most of us reading this probably are not deciding whether to acquire another spouse.
But we are constantly tempted to do spiritually what these broken biblical characters did relationally.
We divide our hearts.
We want Jesus...
and something else.
Jesus and secret lust.
Jesus and money.
Jesus and applause.
Jesus and bitterness.
Jesus and pornography.
Jesus and the relationship we know is pulling us away from Him.
Jesus and the hidden messages.
Jesus and the image we maintain online.
Jesus and the private life nobody sees.
Jesus and control.
Jesus and revenge.
Jesus and ourselves.
We want a Savior without surrender.
A kingdom without a King.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Grace without transformation.
And maybe that is why this ancient question cuts deeper than we expected.
Because the scandal is not merely that biblical men had divided households.
The scandal is that we still have divided hearts.
And Jesus wants the whole heart.
Not because He is insecure.
Because He is Lord.
The Gospel does not announce that morally impressive people successfully climbed their way toward God.
The Gospel announces that sinners could not save themselves...
so God came for them.
Jesus Christ entered our fallen history.
He carried our sin.
He bore judgment at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now repentance is not God demanding that filthy people clean themselves before approaching Him.
Repentance is the sinner finally stopping the flight from the One who can make him clean.
The Greek New Testament uses the word:
μετάνοια — metanoia
repentance.
A profound turning.
A changed mind that results in a changed direction.
Grace does not whisper:
“Keep hiding.”
Grace says:
“Come into the light.”
Grace does not tell the adulterer that adultery does not matter.
Grace offers forgiveness and commands a new life.
Grace does not tell the sexually broken person that holiness is impossible.
Grace introduces us to the Holy One.
Grace does not rewrite God's standards to protect us from conviction.
Grace rewrites us.
That may be the most important sentence in this entire article.
God's grace is not God's declaration that our rebellion was secretly righteousness all along.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves through Jesus Christ.
That is why the Bible's scandals are so strangely comforting.
Abraham's family was messy.
Jacob's family was messy.
David's house became catastrophic.
Solomon's wisdom did not prevent his wandering.
Yet God's redemptive purpose continued.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because God's mercy was greater than human failure.
And eventually the promised Son arrived.
Not Abraham.
Not Jacob.
Not David.
Not Solomon.
Jesus.
The faithful Son.
The righteous King.
The Bridegroom who does not betray His bride.
The Savior who does not abandon His people.
The Lamb who takes away sin.
And perhaps you came into this article curious about polygamy...
but somewhere along the way another question started bothering you.
What have I been calling acceptable simply because God has been patient with me?
That is the question worth sitting with.
Not what your culture celebrates.
Not what your friends normalize.
Not what social media applauds.
Not what another Christian managed to rationalize.
What has Jesus said?
What does Scripture reveal?
Where have you confused God's patience with God's approval?
Where have you mistaken mercy for permission?
Where are you asking God to bless something He is asking you to surrender?
Do not run from that conviction.
Bring it to Christ.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
Real forgiveness.
Not cosmetic religion.
Not pretending.
Not performing Christianity while secretly bleeding.
Confess.
Repent.
Come home.
Maybe your marriage has already been shattered.
Maybe adultery entered your story.
Maybe divorce did.
Maybe sexual sin did.
Maybe you made choices years ago that cannot simply be reversed without creating additional suffering.
Maybe your family history is so complicated that articles about “biblical marriage” normally make you feel condemned before you reach the third paragraph.
Hear this carefully:
Jesus is not intimidated by complicated histories.
The Bible itself is filled with them.
The Gospel is not about traveling backward through time until every terrible decision disappears.
It is about what happens when sinful human beings meet the crucified and risen Christ now.
Repentance may require difficult obedience.
Forgiveness may require confession.
Restoration may require time.
Consequences may remain.
Some situations may require wise pastoral and professional counsel because simplistic solutions can harm innocent people.
But nobody is beyond the reach of Christ merely because their history is scandalous.
That is precisely where our theme becomes more than a slogan.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by calling sin holiness.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking guilty people and making forgiveness possible through His blood...
taking wandering people and calling them home...
taking divided hearts and teaching them faithfulness...
taking shame and replacing its final word...
taking sinners and making them sons and daughters of God.
So did God ever celebrate polygamy?

When the whole biblical storyline is allowed to speak, Scripture records polygamy, regulates situations created by it, and shows God mercifully working through families practicing it—but it does not present polygamy as the creation ideal Jesus calls humanity back to.
The creation pattern is one man and one woman becoming one flesh.
The narratives repeatedly expose the anguish associated with divided marriages and households.
Israel's kings are warned against multiplying wives.
Solomon becomes a devastating example of that warning fulfilled.
Jesus explicitly returns marriage ethics to “the beginning.”
Paul again quotes the one-flesh creation text and connects marriage with Christ and the Church.
God's redemption of polygamous people is therefore not the same as God's celebration of polygamy.
And that distinction matters.
Because if God could work through Abraham's failures, Jacob's chaos, David's household, and Solomon's disastrous compromises without declaring their every decision righteous...
then maybe you finally understand something about your own life.
God working through you does not mean God approves of everything in you.
Sometimes His greatest work begins when we finally stop defending the thing He has been trying to heal.
So be honest.
Did this expose something deeper than the question you originally came here to answer?
And if Christ has already taken part of your scandal and turned it into testimony, tell us what He has done. Someone reading your comment may be convinced that their story is not over either.

There are conversations coming when someone will say, “But people in the Bible had multiple wives,” and you will want to remember the difference between biblical description, legal regulation, divine patience, redemption, and God's revealed creation pattern.

Salvation and God's grace cannot be bought—but because freely choosing to support Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people with Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement, and the message of Jesus Christ.
Jesus already paid the price you could never pay.
Your money cannot purchase grace.
Your shares cannot purchase forgiveness.
Your comments cannot purchase heaven.
The Gospel is infinitely better than that.
Christ died for sinners. Christ rose victorious. Christ calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, and be transformed by His grace.
And maybe that is why Scripture never needed perfect human heroes.
It had something better.
A perfect Savior.
The Bible did not hide the scandal because God already knew grace would have the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS EXPLAINED THE BRONZE SERPENT TO NICODEMUS—AND MANY CHRISTIANS READ RIGHT PAST IT
paragraphs:
JESUS EXPLAINED THE BRONZE SERPENT TO NICODEMUS—AND MANY CHRISTIANS READ RIGHT PAST IT
The strange Old Testament story Jesus deliberately brought into a midnight conversation about salvation—and why understanding it may change the way you see the Cross forever.
There was poison in their blood.
People were dying.
And God told Moses to make a serpent.
If that sentence sounds strange, it should.

Because thousands of years later, during one of the most important conversations ever recorded, Jesus reached back into that disturbing scene in the wilderness and told Nicodemus that what happened there was pointing toward Him.
Not merely toward healing.
Not merely toward faith.
Toward the Cross.
And once you understand why Jesus chose this particular story, John 3:16—the verse almost everybody knows—begins to burn with a depth many people have never noticed.
But first, you have to walk into the wilderness.
You have to hear the cries.
You have to see what sin had done.
And perhaps hardest of all...
you have to admit that the dying people in that wilderness may look more like us than we want to believe.
Numbers 21 records Israel becoming impatient during the journey. They spoke against God and against Moses:
“Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness?”
They despised the provision God had given them.
Then came judgment.
Numbers 21:6 says:
וַיְשַׁלַּח יְהוָה בָּעָם אֵת הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים
Vayeshallaḥ YHWH ba'am et-hanneḥashim hasśerafim.
The LORD sent among the people the “fiery serpents.”
The Hebrew expression הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים (hanneḥashim hasśerafim) combines the word for serpents with a term related to burning. The text does not invite us to romanticize what happened.
People were bitten.
People died.
Then something changed.
The people came to Moses and finally said the words rebellion hates to say:
“We have sinned.”
Not...
“We made mistakes.”
Not...
“We were misunderstood.”
Not...
“Everybody has issues.”
“We have sinned.”
That confession matters.
Because grace becomes cheap whenever sin becomes imaginary.
The people asked Moses to intercede, and God gave him an astonishing command:
“Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.”
So Moses made a bronze serpent and lifted it up.
Imagine being bitten.
The venom is already inside you.
Your strength is disappearing.
You cannot negotiate with the poison.
You cannot outrun it.
You cannot become moral enough to reverse it.
You cannot promise the venom that tomorrow you will do better.
You are dying.
Then comes the word:
Look.
That is all.
Look at what God has provided.
And live.
The Hebrew of Numbers 21:9 says that when a bitten person looked toward the bronze serpent,
וָחָי
vāḥāy.
“And he lived.”
Do not rush past that.
He lived.
Not because bronze possesses healing power.
Not because staring at an object is magic.
Not because Moses invented a religious technique.
God attached His promise to the provision He commanded.
The dying person had nothing with which to boast.
He could only trust the word of God enough to look.
Centuries passed.
The bronze serpent itself eventually became a trap. Israel began burning incense to it, and King Hezekiah destroyed it. Second Kings 18:4 even records the contemptuous name given to it:
נְחֻשְׁתָּן
Nehushtan.
Essentially, a piece of bronze.
Think about the irony.
Something God once used became something people later idolized.
Human beings are remarkably capable of worshiping the instrument while forgetting the God who gave it.
We can do it with traditions.
Buildings.
Leaders.
Platforms.
Denominations.
Religious objects.
Even ministries.
Nothing that points toward Jesus should ever be allowed to replace Jesus.
Then, centuries after Moses raised that serpent in the wilderness, a Pharisee walked through the darkness to speak privately with Christ.
His name was Nicodemus.
John tells us he came to Jesus “by night.”
Nicodemus was not spiritually uneducated.
He was a Pharisee.
A ruler of the Jews.
Jesus later called him “the teacher of Israel.”
This was not an ignorant pagan asking Christianity 101 questions.
This was a religious man.
A knowledgeable man.
A respected man.
And Jesus told him:
“You must be born again.”
Imagine what that must have done to him.
Nicodemus had pedigree.
Jesus spoke of birth.
Nicodemus had religious achievement.
Jesus spoke of something only God could ultimately produce.
Nicodemus had knowledge.
Jesus exposed his need.
The Greek phrase translated “born again” is:
γεννηθῆναι ἄνωθεν
gennēthēnai anōthen.
The word ἄνωθεν (anōthen) can carry the sense of “again” and “from above,” and John appears to exploit that richness. Nicodemus hears Jesus in terms of another physical birth.
Jesus is speaking about the radical life of the Spirit that comes from above.
Nicodemus knew religion.
But religion could not resurrect him.
And that is where some of us need to stop pretending.
You can know worship songs and still need Christ.
You can quote Scripture and still need Christ.
You can attend church and still need Christ.
You can have Christian parents, Christian friends, Christian books, Christian tattoos, Christian posts, Christian vocabulary and a carefully maintained Christian reputation...
and still desperately need Christ.
Jesus did not tell Nicodemus to polish the old man.
He told him he needed new birth.
Then Jesus reached into Israel's Scriptures and chose the story of poisoned people staring at a bronze serpent.
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”
The Greek is startling:
καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, οὕτως ὑψωθῆναι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
Kai kathōs Mōysēs hypsōsen ton ophin en tē erēmō, houtōs hypsōthēnai dei ton huion tou anthrōpou.
“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”
There is one little Greek word here that should stop us:
δεῖ
dei.
“Must.”
The Son of Man must be lifted up.
The Cross was not an unfortunate interruption in Jesus' mission.
The Cross was central to His mission.
Jesus had come to save sinners.

Later in John, the language of Jesus being “lifted up” clearly points toward His death. John 12:32–33 records Jesus saying that when He is lifted up from the earth He will draw people to Himself, and John immediately explains that He said this to indicate the kind of death He would die.
Jesus was going to be lifted up.
Not upon a throne of earthly conquest.
Upon a Roman cross.
But there is a question here that can make the whole passage uncomfortable:
Why compare Himself with the serpent?

The bronze serpent was not evil magic and it was not a portrait suggesting Christ Himself was sinful. Scripture is emphatic that Jesus “knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21), “did no sin” (1 Peter 2:22), and was “without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
Yet Paul gives us language that helps illuminate the scandal of the Cross:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
And Galatians 3:13 declares:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.”
The sinless One stood where the guilty should have stood.
He bore what belonged to us.
Isaiah had already spoken of the Servant who would be “wounded for our transgressions” and “bruised for our iniquities.”
The serpent lifted in the wilderness represented before the dying Israelites the very judgment associated with their condition, while God's appointed provision brought life to those who looked.
At Calvary, something infinitely greater happened.
Jesus did not merely stand near sinners.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree.
The Holy One entered the place of condemnation without becoming sinful Himself.
The Judge stepped into the judgment.
The innocent Son bore the penalty of the guilty.
And suddenly the wilderness does not feel ancient anymore.
Because there is poison in us too.
We just give it respectable names.
Pride becomes “knowing my worth.”
Greed becomes “ambition.”
Lust becomes “just being human.”
Bitterness becomes “protecting my peace.”
Gossip becomes “telling the truth.”
Unforgiveness becomes “having boundaries.”
Self-righteousness becomes “discernment.”
Secret compromise becomes “nobody's perfect.”
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, we learn how to decorate what Jesus came to crucify.
That may be the serpent bite we keep reading past.
The Israelites could see the wounds on their bodies.
Our wounds can hide behind church clothes.
Behind ministry.
Behind Bible verses.
Behind smiles.
But God sees beneath the profile picture.
He knows what happened last night.
He knows the thought you keep feeding.
He knows the person you still hate.
He knows the browser history.
He knows the jealousy.
He knows the secret messages.
He knows the prayerlessness.
He knows the addiction nobody knows exists.
He knows the tears you wipe away before anybody enters the room.
And He knows something else too.
He knows exactly how helpless you are to save yourself.
That is why the Gospel is such offensive news to human pride...
and such beautiful news to exhausted sinners.
The dying Israelite did not heal himself before looking.
He looked because he could not heal himself.
And Christianity does not begin with becoming good enough for Jesus.
It begins with admitting you never could be.
The Gospel does not say:
Fix yourself and perhaps God will love you.
It says that God acted for sinners who could not rescue themselves.
And immediately after Jesus speaks about the serpent being lifted up, John gives us words known around the world:
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son...”
Do you see the connection now?
John 3:16 was not dropped randomly onto a greeting card.
It comes immediately after Jesus speaks about dying people in the wilderness and the Son of Man being lifted up.
“For God so loved the world...”
This is love standing in the shadow of a cross.
Not sentimental love.
Not indulgent love.
Holy love.
Costly love.
Saving love.
A love that does not pretend the poison is harmless.
A love that provides the remedy at unimaginable cost.
The Greek verb John repeatedly uses for believing is πιστεύω (pisteuō).
Biblical faith is not merely admitting that Jesus existed.
The demons know who He is.
Saving faith looks away from self and rests in Christ.
The Israelites did not stare at their wounds until the wounds healed.
They looked toward God's provision.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years staring at the wound.
“I ruined my marriage.”
“I betrayed somebody.”
“I had the abortion.”
“I cheated.”
“I became addicted.”
“I walked away from God.”
“I wasted years.”
“I knew better.”
“I failed my children.”
“I preached things I wasn't living.”
“I don't even recognize myself anymore.”
You keep staring at the bite.
Jesus says:
Look to Me.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
Because Christ bore judgment for everyone who belongs to Him.
Not because repentance does not matter.
True faith turns toward Christ, and Christ does not merely forgive us so that we can comfortably return to the chains He died to break.
Grace is not permission to keep petting the serpent.
Grace calls sinners out of darkness.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
It is the turning of a heart that has stopped defending its rebellion and comes to Christ empty-handed.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
We prefer complicated salvation because complicated salvation leaves room for pride.
Give us ten religious achievements.
Give us fifty prayers.
Give us a mountain to climb.
Give us something impressive enough that when we finally reach heaven, we can quietly believe we helped save ourselves.
But God puts a dying man in the desert and says:
Look.
Then He puts His crucified Son before the world and says:
Believe.
There is no trophy for the poisoned man.
There is only mercy.
And maybe you have been trying to earn what Jesus purchased.
Maybe you have been punishing yourself because accepting forgiveness feels too easy.
But look again at Calvary and tell me grace was easy.
It was free to you.
It was not cheap to Him.
There were nails.
There was blood.
There was shame.
There was rejection.
There was a crown of thorns.
There was darkness.
And there was the sinless Son of God willingly laying down His life.
Then came the tomb.
Then came Sunday.
And the One who was lifted up on the Cross walked out of the grave alive.
Christian hope does not end with a dying Savior.
We proclaim a risen King.
The serpent story therefore forces a question far more personal than theological curiosity:
Where are you looking?
At yourself?
Your morality?
Your church attendance?
Your accomplishments?
Your suffering?
Your failures?
Your religious reputation?
Your pastor?
Your denomination?
Your past?
Or Christ?
Because the bronze serpent itself eventually became an idol.
And Christians can still turn things that should point toward Christ into substitutes for Christ.
Even Gospel Warrior must never become that.
This ministry is not your Savior.
No pastor is your Savior.
No Christian book is your Savior.
No amount of sharing religious content saves your soul.
Jesus Christ saves.
That distinction matters deeply to us.
If this article exposed something you have hidden behind religion, don't manufacture a polished response. Be honest before God.
And believers who see those words...
pray.
Don't perform.
Don't condemn.
Pray.
Because there are real human beings behind those comments.
Somebody may be fighting for their marriage.
Somebody may be trying not to return to an addiction.
Somebody may be sitting alone wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
Somebody may have walked into church smiling this morning and cried in the car afterward.
Somebody needs to discover that Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners.
This is where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted His church.
Jesus transformed Paul into an apostle.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to construct an impressive religious résumé.
He had only a dying plea:
“Lord, remember me.”
And Jesus gave him paradise.
That is scandalous grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that is powerful enough to rescue evil people and begin making them new.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
God still knows it.
Maybe your scandal happened entirely inside your heart.
God knows that too.
Maybe everybody applauds the version of you they see while you are terrified of the version only God sees.
Christ already knows.
And still the Cross stands.
Look.
The blood has not lost its power because your story became ugly.
The resurrection did not become less true because you fell again.
But do not confuse grace with permission to remain where grace found you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Seek accountability where needed.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Run from what keeps dragging you toward darkness.
And keep looking to Christ.
Not once as a religious moment you remember from childhood.
Day after day.
When shame says, “Hide”...
look to Christ.
When pride says, “You don't need mercy”...
look to Christ.
When temptation says, “One more time”...
look to Christ.
When Satan whispers, “After what you did, God could never want you”...
look to Christ.
When self-righteousness whispers, “At least you're better than them”...
look to Christ.
The Cross destroys both despair and boasting.
Nobody standing beneath Calvary can truthfully say, “My sin wasn't serious.”
And nobody trusting the crucified and risen Christ needs to say, “My sin is stronger than His grace.”
This is why this message needs to travel beyond the people who already agree with it.
Not as superstition.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Not because sharing a post proves that you are a faithful Christian.
Religious.
Respected.
Confused.
Searching in the dark.
And perhaps this is the conversation that finally makes him look toward Jesus.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only a collection of religious rules.
Let them encounter Christ.

It is not an act that earns God's favor, and we will never pretend that it is. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him; supporting Gospel work can be one voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in making biblical truth available to others.
You need Jesus.
Not our merchandise.
Not our page.
Not our name.
Jesus.
The same Christ who spoke to Nicodemus in the darkness still calls people out of darkness today.
And perhaps that is the detail we have been reading past.
The story of the bronze serpent was never ultimately about becoming fascinated with a serpent.
It was about learning where a dying person must look.
Nicodemus came to Jesus at night.
Years later, after Jesus had been lifted up and crucified, John tells us that Nicodemus came with Joseph of Arimathea to care for His body.
The man who once approached Jesus beneath the cover of darkness was there when the lifted-up Savior was taken down from the Cross.
Imagine what he must have remembered.
“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness...”
Now he had seen it.
Not bronze.
Not a wilderness pole.
Jesus.
Lifted up.
The words from that nighttime conversation were no longer abstract theology.
There was blood on the body Nicodemus helped carry.
And maybe that is where this article needs to leave you.
Not staring at Nicodemus.
Not staring at Moses.
Not staring at the serpent.
Not staring at Gospel Warrior.
Not even staring endlessly at your own sin.
Look higher.
There is a Cross.
There is an empty tomb.
There is a Savior.
There is mercy for the guilty.
There is cleansing for the stained.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is life for the dying.
There is grace for the scandal.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Talk to God.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Trust the One who was lifted up.
And if Christ has already rescued you, carry this Gospel toward somebody who is still dying from the poison.
Because somewhere tonight, another Nicodemus is still walking through the darkness.
And somewhere tonight, another wounded soul is still staring at the poison...
when God is calling them to look toward the Savior.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the Cross—but grace decides who you can become after you look to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DOGS CAME FOR AHAB’S BLOOD—AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART WAS THAT GOD HAD WARNED HIM
paragraphs: THE DOGS CAME FOR AHAB’S BLOOD—AND THE MOST TERRIFYING PART WAS THAT GOD HAD WARNED HIM

Elijah spoke the warning. Ahab heard it. Judgment did not fall immediately. Then one ordinary evening, servants washed a dead king’s chariot—and dogs began licking the blood away. But buried inside this terrifying story is something even more astonishing: before judgment came, God had given Ahab an opportunity to humble himself.
There was blood in the chariot.
Not the blood of a nameless soldier.
Not the blood of a servant.
Not Naboth’s blood this time.
The king’s.
Ahab—the man who once had power, property, soldiers, servants, influence, wealth, and a palace decorated with ivory—was dead.
And somewhere near the pool of Samaria, someone had to clean up what remained.
Imagine that scene.
The battle was over. The shouting had stopped. The royal armor could no longer protect the man who wore it. The chariot that had carried a king now carried the evidence of his mortality.
Water struck wood.
Blood ran down.
And then the dogs came.
Scripture records the moment with almost frightening simplicity:
“And one washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood… according unto the word of the LORD which he spake.”
—1 Kings 22:38, KJV
The Hebrew makes the image just as stark:
וַיָּלֹקּוּ הַכְּלָבִים אֶת־דָּמוֹ
wayyālōqqû hakkəlāḇîm ʾet-dāmô
“And the dogs licked up his blood.”
The verb behind “licked” comes from לָקַק (lāqaq)—to lick or lap.
הַכְּלָבִים (hakkəlāḇîm) means “the dogs.”
דָּמוֹ (dāmô) means “his blood.”
There is nothing metaphorical about what the narrator wants us to see.
A king had bled.
Dogs were licking it.
And Scripture immediately tells us why this horrifying detail matters:
כִּדְבַר יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר דִּבֵּר
kiḏḇar YHWH ʾăšer dibbēr
“according to the word of YHWH which He had spoken.”
That is the sentence that should make us tremble.
Because the dogs were not the beginning of Ahab’s story.
They were the end of a warning.
Long before servants washed that bloodstained chariot, there was another man’s blood crying from the ground.
His name was Naboth.
And Naboth had something Ahab wanted.
A vineyard.
That was all.

Ahab was king of Israel. He possessed enormous resources. He had authority most people could never imagine. Yet he looked at one ordinary man’s inheritance and decided that what he already possessed was not enough.
That is one of sin’s oldest lies.
You will finally be satisfied when you get just one more thing.
One more relationship.
One more possession.
One more experience.
One more promotion.
One more secret pleasure.
One more compromise.
One more thing God has not given you.
Naboth’s vineyard was close to Ahab’s palace, and Ahab wanted it for a vegetable garden. He offered Naboth another vineyard or money in exchange.
But Naboth refused.
Not merely because he was stubborn.
Israel’s land inheritance was bound up with covenant responsibility. Naboth answered:
“The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.”
—1 Kings 21:3, KJV
So Ahab went home.
And sulked.
The king of Israel lay on his bed, turned his face away, and refused to eat because another man would not surrender what belonged to his family.
Then Jezebel entered the story.
When she discovered why Ahab was miserable, she effectively asked what kind of king allows someone to tell him no.
Then she arranged the unthinkable.
Letters were written in Ahab’s name.
His seal was used.
False witnesses were produced.
Naboth was accused of blaspheming God and the king.
And an innocent man was taken outside and stoned to death.
Think about the horror of that.
A man died because someone powerful wanted what belonged to him.
False testimony.
Manipulation.
Abuse of authority.
Murder.
And when Naboth was dead, Jezebel told Ahab:
“Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth… for Naboth is not alive, but dead.”
—1 Kings 21:15, KJV
Ahab went down to take possession.
Perhaps he thought the problem was over.
Naboth was dead.
The paperwork was handled.
The vineyard was available.
Nobody powerful enough seemed able to stop him.
But there was one detail Ahab had forgotten.
God had seen everything.
Every letter.
Every lie.
Every false witness.
Every stone.
Every drop of innocent blood.
Every step Ahab took toward the vineyard he should never have possessed.
And this is where the story suddenly becomes uncomfortable for people like us.
Because most of us will never steal a vineyard.
Most of us will never arrange a judicial murder.
Most of us will never sit on a throne.
So it is tempting to keep Ahab at a safe distance and say, “What a wicked man.”
But Scripture does not give us stories of sinful people merely so we can feel morally superior to them.
It gives us mirrors.
Maybe your vineyard has another name.
Maybe nobody knows about it.
Maybe there is a conversation you keep deleting.
Maybe resentment has lived inside you so long that you no longer recognize it as resentment.
Maybe you know how to worship publicly while feeding something privately that Christ has told you to kill.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary without Christian surrender.
Maybe you can post Scripture and still refuse to forgive.
Maybe you sing about holiness while negotiating with temptation.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are spiritually healthy because they cannot see the room inside your heart where you keep telling Jesus,
“Everything but this.”
That room matters.
Because hidden sin is never hidden from God.
Ahab entered Naboth’s vineyard believing he was arriving to claim property.
Instead, Elijah was waiting for him.
Imagine the moment.
The vineyard Ahab thought would satisfy him became the place where the Word of God confronted him.
Ahab saw Elijah and said:
“Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?”
—1 Kings 21:20, KJV
What a revealing sentence.
Elijah was not Ahab’s real enemy.
Ahab’s sin was.
But when we become determined to protect our sin, the person telling us the truth can start feeling like the enemy.
The preacher becomes “judgmental.”
The friend becomes “negative.”
The spouse becomes “controlling.”
The Scripture becomes “too extreme.”
Conviction becomes something we try to silence instead of mercy we should receive.
Elijah answered him:
“I have found thee: because thou hast sold thyself to work evil in the sight of the LORD.”
—1 Kings 21:20, KJV
Then came the warning that would echo all the way to that bloody chariot:
“In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.”
—1 Kings 21:19, KJV
The Hebrew is devastatingly personal.
בִּמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר לָקְקוּ הַכְּלָבִים אֶת־דַּם נָבוֹת יָלֹקּוּ הַכְּלָבִים אֶת־דָּמְךָ גַּם־אָתָּה
The force of the final words is essentially:
“your blood—yes, yours.”
Not somebody else’s.
Yours.
Ahab had treated Naboth’s blood as the cost of obtaining what he wanted.
God had not forgotten it.
But now we need to be careful with the biblical text.
There is a detail often lost when this story is retold.

First Kings 21:19 connects Elijah’s warning with the place where Naboth’s blood had been licked. First Kings 22:38 later says Ahab’s blood was licked by dogs when his chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria.

Those locations create an interpretive question, and faithful Bible reading should not pretend the question does not exist. Some interpreters understand Elijah’s language as fulfilled principally in the corresponding humiliation—the dogs licking Ahab’s blood—rather than requiring the identical geographical point. The biblical narrator himself gives us the interpretive key: the dogs licked Ahab’s blood “according unto the word of the LORD which he spake.”
In other words, Scripture itself wants us to connect the warning with the fulfillment.
But before the dogs…
before the battle…
before the arrow…
before the bloodstained chariot…
something happened that reveals the heart of God in a way many people overlook.
Ahab humbled himself.
Yes.
Ahab.
After Elijah announced judgment, Scripture says:
“And it came to pass, when Ahab heard those words, that he rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his flesh, and fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and went softly.”
—1 Kings 21:27, KJV
Then God spoke to Elijah:
“Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me?”
—1 Kings 21:29, KJV
Read that again.
God noticed.
The God who saw Naboth murdered also saw Ahab humble himself.
The God who saw the wickedness also saw the sackcloth.
And because Ahab humbled himself, God postponed the announced disaster upon his house.
Do not misunderstand this.
The passage does not turn Ahab into a righteous hero, nor does the rest of his story demonstrate the enduring transformed life we associate with genuine covenant faithfulness.
But it reveals something magnificent about God.
God is not eager to miss repentance.
He notices humility.
Even in Ahab.
And if God noticed Ahab humbling himself…
what makes you think He will ignore you when you truly come to Him broken?
Maybe you have done things you cannot undo.
Maybe someone was hurt because of you.
Maybe your marriage carries scars from choices you made.
Maybe your children remember a version of you that makes you ashamed.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out part of your soul.
Maybe pride has poisoned relationships.
Maybe money became your god.
Maybe bitterness became your shelter.
Maybe you knew better.
That may be the sentence hurting you most.
I knew better.
Ahab knew the God of Israel existed.
Ahab heard prophets.
Ahab witnessed divine intervention.
Ahab received warnings.
Yet knowledge without surrender did not save him.
And religious familiarity will not save us either.
You can know Bible verses and still need repentance.
You can attend church and still need repentance.
You can lead people and still need repentance.
You can have thousands of followers and still need repentance.
You can call Jesus “Lord” with your mouth while resisting His lordship in the place nobody sees.
The terrifying lesson of Ahab is not simply that God judges wicked kings.
It is that warnings are mercy.
Conviction is mercy.
The uncomfortable sermon is mercy.
The Scripture that ruins your excuses is mercy.
The friend who lovingly tells you the truth is mercy.
The sleepless night when your conscience refuses to leave you alone may be mercy.
Because there is something far more frightening than being convicted of sin.
It is becoming comfortable with it.
Ahab continued.
Then came the battle at Ramoth-gilead.
Before going, he received another warning.
The prophet Micaiah foretold disaster.
Ahab did not like what Micaiah said.
That is another frightening pattern in his life: when truth contradicted what Ahab wanted, Ahab treated the messenger as the problem.
So he went to battle anyway.
And Ahab disguised himself.
Read that slowly.
The king entered battle disguised.
There is something almost haunting about that image.
A man can disguise himself from soldiers.
He cannot disguise himself from God.
Ahab changed his appearance.
He did not change the Word God had spoken.
Then Scripture gives us one of the most chillingly understated sentences in the Old Testament:
“And a certain man drew a bow at a venture…”
—1 Kings 22:34, KJV
The archer apparently did not know he was firing toward the king of Israel.
He simply drew.
Released.
The arrow flew.
And it struck Ahab between the joints of his armor.
Think about the irony.
Ahab had disguised his identity.
Armor covered his body.
He had gone into battle attempting to avoid becoming an obvious target.
Yet one arrow found the opening.
Not because Scripture is teaching fatalistic superstition.
But because human strategies cannot nullify the Word of God.
Ahab remained propped in his chariot while blood poured from his wound.
By evening, he was dead.
The king who wanted Naboth’s vineyard could no longer hold anything.
Not his palace.
Not his ivory.
Not his land.
Not his crown.
Not even the blood inside his own body.
They carried him back to Samaria.
Then somebody washed the chariot.
Water.
Blood.
Dogs.
And suddenly Elijah’s warning was no longer merely a sermon from yesterday.
It was history.
“And the dogs licked up his blood… according unto the word of the LORD which he spake.”
That sentence should sober every person who has been postponing obedience.
Because delayed judgment can masquerade as permission.
You sinned…
and nothing happened.
So you did it again.
You compromised…
and your life did not collapse.
So you assumed perhaps God was not concerned.
You ignored conviction…
and still woke up the next morning.
You crossed another boundary…
and nobody discovered it.
You kept the relationship.
Kept the bitterness.
Kept the secret.
Kept the hidden account.
Kept the habit.
Kept saying, “Eventually.”
And because judgment did not arrive immediately, you quietly began interpreting God’s patience as approval.
Please hear this:
God’s patience is not permission.
It is mercy giving you room to repent.
The New Testament asks:
“Despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?”
—Romans 2:4, KJV
God’s patience has a destination.
Repentance.
And here is where Ahab’s bloody chariot points us beyond Ahab.
Because if the Bible ended by telling sinners only that judgment is coming, none of us would have hope.
Ahab is not the only king whose blood was shed.
There was another King.
Another public humiliation.
Another day when blood flowed.
But this King had stolen no vineyard.
He had murdered no Naboth.
He had worshiped no idol.
He had exploited no innocent person.
He had committed no sin.
Jesus Christ, the Son of God, stood where guilty people deserved to stand.
Ahab’s blood testified that judgment against sin is real.
Christ’s blood announces that mercy for sinners is real.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because His own sin finally caught Him.
He had none.
He died for ours.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
—Isaiah 53:5, KJV
The scandal of the Gospel is not that God decided sin did not matter.
The scandal is that sin mattered so much that redemption required the blood of the spotless Lamb of God—and love ran so deep that the Son willingly gave Himself for sinners.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
The cross does not tell us, “You were never really guilty.”
The cross says something infinitely better:
Your guilt can be forgiven.
Your record can be cleansed.
Your chains can be broken.
Your heart can be made new.
Your past does not have to become your eternal identity.
Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
It is laying down the vineyard.
Opening the locked room.
Confessing what you have protected.
Stopping the excuses.
Coming into the light.
Turning from sin and toward Christ.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Not because dogs licking the blood of an ancient king fascinated you.
Maybe somewhere between Ahab’s vineyard and Ahab’s chariot, God put His finger on something in you.
Something you have defended.
Something you have delayed dealing with.
Something you hoped time would make less serious.
Do not wait for consequences to teach you what conviction is already telling you.
Run to Christ now.
Not after you become cleaner.
Not after you repair yourself.
Not after you feel worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
That is why it is grace.
Come honestly.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
No performance.
No religious costume.
No disguise.
No blaming Jezebel.
No blaming your childhood.
No blaming your spouse.
No blaming culture.
No pretending the vineyard somehow became yours legitimately.
Just truth.
And mercy.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to confess private details publicly. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Or if you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation and you refuse to surrender your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not condemn them.
Pray for them.
Because behind some profile picture tonight is a human being trying desperately to find the courage to come home.

Not because every article deserves saving, but because there may come a night when compromise begins sounding reasonable again and you need to remember a vineyard, an arrow, a bloodstained chariot, and the God whose warnings should never be treated casually.
Supporting Gospel work does not earn favor with God.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one voluntary expression of generosity—and sharing biblical truth can help place the message in front of someone who desperately needs it.
Come to Jesus.
Because one day every possession will leave your hands.
Every title will disappear.
Every applause will stop.
Every carefully maintained image will become irrelevant.
Ahab once had an ivory palace.
In the end, a servant was washing his blood from a chariot.
What mattered then was not what Ahab owned.
It was whether Ahab belonged to God.
And that question reaches across thousands of years and sits quietly in front of us now.
What are you protecting that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What warning have you been calling an inconvenience?
What sin have you renamed so you can continue living with it?
What would happen if tonight—without pretending, bargaining, or hiding—you finally opened your hands?
Be honest.
Because the deepest lesson of Ahab’s story is not merely that dogs eventually licked a wicked king’s blood.
It is that God warned him first.
Again and again, God spoke.
And even when Ahab humbled himself, God noticed.
That means the warning you are hearing today is not evidence that God delights in destroying sinners.
It may be evidence that, in His mercy, He is still calling you before it is too late.
And unlike Ahab, you are reading this side of Calvary.
You know the name of the King who took the sinner’s place.
Jesus.
The One who does not merely expose your darkness.
He can forgive it.
The One who does not merely reveal your chains.
He can break them.
The One who does not merely confront your past.
He can redeem it.
The One who takes people whose stories should have ended in judgment and writes grace where nobody expected grace to appear.
So remember this when temptation whispers that God will never deal with your sin.
Remember it when shame whispers that God could never forgive your sin.
Both voices lie.
God is holy enough to judge sin.
And in Jesus Christ, He is merciful enough to forgive the sinner who comes to Him.
The blood on Ahab’s chariot tells you not to play with sin; the blood on Christ’s cross tells you that you do not have to die hiding in it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOW DO YOU KNOW WHETHER YOU TRULY REPENTED—OR JUST FELT GUILTY?
paragraphs: HOW DO YOU KNOW WHETHER YOU TRULY REPENTED—OR JUST FELT GUILTY?
Because feeling terrible about what you did is not always the same as turning away from it—and one of the most dangerous places to live is between conviction and surrender.
There is a kind of crying that changes nothing.
That sentence may bother you.
Maybe it should.
Because some of us have cried over the same sin we later returned to.
We hated the consequences.
Hated the shame.
Hated looking ourselves in the mirror.
Hated imagining somebody finding out.
We promised God we would never do it again.
And in that moment, we meant it.
Or at least we thought we did.
Then the temptation came back.
The secret browser opened again.
The message was sent again.
The lie slipped out again.
The bitterness was fed again.
The relationship we knew was dragging us away from Christ pulled us back again.
The bottle opened.
The gossip returned.
The pride resurfaced.
The hidden compromise found another hiding place.
And suddenly we were back on our knees saying words that sounded painfully familiar:
“God, I’m sorry.”
But somewhere beneath those words was a terrifying question.
Am I actually repenting... or am I only feeling guilty?
That question matters because Scripture makes a distinction many Christians overlook.
Paul writes:
—2 Corinthians 7:10
The Greek is striking.
ἡ γὰρ κατὰ θεὸν λύπη μετάνοιαν εἰς σωτηρίαν... κατεργάζεται
Hē gar kata Theon lypē metanoian eis sōtērian... katergazetai.
In context, Paul is not teaching that tears earn salvation. He is describing sorrow that operates according to God and produces μετάνοια — metanoia, repentance.
The word carries the idea of a changed mind, a reorientation, a turning of one's thinking and disposition.
But notice something painfully important.
Paul distinguishes λύπη — lypē, sorrow or grief, from μετάνοια — metanoia, repentance.
In other words:
Feeling sorrow is not automatically repentance.
You can feel terrible and still refuse to turn.
You can hate what sin did to your life without yet hating what sin does to your fellowship with God.
You can regret getting caught without grieving that you rebelled against the One who loved you.
You can miss your marriage without surrendering the adultery.
You can hate your hangover without surrendering drunkenness.
You can hate your anxiety after pornography without surrendering lust.
You can hate losing people's trust without surrendering deception.
You can hate the consequences of your anger while still believing you had the right to explode.
And perhaps most frightening of all...
You can become emotionally exhausted by your sin while still secretly negotiating with it.
That is why guilt and repentance must never be confused.
Guilt can say,
“I cannot believe I did that.”
Repentance begins saying,
“I cannot continue making peace with what Christ died to save me from.”
Guilt often looks backward.
Repentance turns toward God.
Guilt asks,
“How do I stop feeling horrible?”
Repentance asks,
“How do I return to the Lord?”
And Scripture has a beautiful Hebrew word for that turning.
שׁוּב — shuv.
It means to turn, return, or come back.
God says through the prophet Joel:
שֻׁבוּ עָדַי בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם
Shuvu ʿadai b'khol-levavkhem.
“Return to Me with all your heart.”
—Joel 2:12
Keep reading and something extraordinary happens.
God does not merely command sinners to return.
He reveals what kind of God they are returning to.
“Rend your hearts and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God, for He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love...”
—Joel 2:13
Do you see it?
Biblical repentance is not a terrified sinner crawling toward a God who reluctantly tolerates him.
It is a sinner turning from rebellion toward the God who is gracious and merciful.
Repentance is not payment for grace.
Repentance runs toward grace.
And that changes everything.
Because some people reading this have confused self-hatred with holiness.
You think punishing yourself proves you are sorry.
So you replay what you did.
You call yourself disgusting.
You mentally prosecute yourself every night.
You assume God must be tired of you.
You pray, but you keep your emotional distance.
You read Scripture but feel like an intruder.
Someone mentions forgiveness and immediately a voice inside whispers:
“Not after what you did.”
Listen carefully.
That voice is not giving you the Gospel.
The Gospel never minimizes sin.
The cross makes minimizing sin impossible.
Something so catastrophic had happened between humanity and God that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
But the same cross that exposes the horror of sin announces the astonishing magnitude of grace.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel guiltier.
He came to save sinners.
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
—Luke 19:10
That means repentance is not sitting indefinitely in the ashes proving how miserable you are.
It is coming home.
Think about Judas.
He betrayed Jesus.
Then Matthew tells us that when Judas saw Jesus condemned, he regretted what he had done. He returned the thirty pieces of silver and confessed:
“I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.”
—Matthew 27:4
Those words sound remarkably close to repentance.
He admitted wrongdoing.
He experienced anguish.
He returned the money.
He confessed Jesus' innocence.
And yet Judas' sorrow ended in death.
Then look at Peter.
Peter had insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Hours later, standing in a courtyard, Peter denied even knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke records one of the most devastating moments in the Gospels:
“The Lord turned and looked at Peter.”
—Luke 22:61
Imagine that look.
The face Peter had watched heal lepers.
The eyes that had looked upon crowds with compassion.
The Teacher Peter had called the Christ.
Now looking directly at him after his denial.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
Peter cried.
Judas regretted.
Both failed catastrophically.
Both experienced sorrow.
But their stories did not end in the same place.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
Not to pretend Peter's denial never happened.
Not to call betrayal insignificant.
Jesus brought Peter directly to the wound.
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?”
Three denials.
Three questions.
And then:
“Follow Me.”
—John 21:19
That is the scandal of grace.
Peter's worst night did not get the final sentence over his life.
Jesus did.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But we need to be careful here.
Grace did not mean Peter could shrug and say, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
Jesus restored him—and called him again to follow.
That is one of the clearest signs of genuine repentance.
You begin moving toward Christ instead of merely trying to escape the emotional consequences of sin.
This does not mean genuine Christians never struggle with recurring sin.
If repeated temptation automatically proved repentance was false, many sincere believers would collapse into despair.
Sanctification can involve warfare.
Habits may need to be dismantled.
Temptations may return.
Old wounds may still ache.
You may stumble and need to confess again.
Scripture does not teach sinless perfection as the evidence that repentance happened.
But it does teach something very different from comfortable coexistence with sin.
John the Baptist said:
“Bear fruit in keeping with repentance.”
—Matthew 3:8
Fruit.
Not theatrical remorse.
Not religious vocabulary.
Not one emotional altar call followed by intentional compromise.
Fruit.
Repentance begins becoming visible.
Maybe you confess the lie instead of merely asking God privately to make the guilt disappear.
Maybe you finally delete the secret access point.
Maybe you end the adulterous relationship instead of asking God to “give you strength” while keeping the number.
Maybe you return what you stole.
Maybe you ask forgiveness without adding, “But you also hurt me.”
Maybe you stop blaming your childhood, your spouse, your stress, your loneliness, your hormones, your coworkers, or your circumstances for choices you need to own.
Those factors can profoundly affect us.
Some wounds require patient healing.
Some patterns require wise pastoral counsel, accountability, and professional help.
But repentance stops using explanations as permission.
It says:
“This may explain part of my struggle, but I will no longer use it to rename sin.”
David understood something about this.
After his adultery with Bathsheba and his role in Uriah's death, Psalm 51 records his cry of repentance.
In Hebrew he pleads:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
—Psalm 51:10
David did not merely ask God to make the scandal disappear.
He wanted God to change him.
That is different.
And perhaps that is the question you need tonight.
If God offered to remove every earthly consequence of your sin—but asked you to surrender the sin itself—would you still want freedom?
If nobody ever discovered it...
Would you still want to stop?
If your reputation could remain untouched...
Would holiness still matter?
If there were no embarrassment...
Would grieving God be enough reason to turn?
That question reaches places religious performance cannot reach.
Because worldly sorrow is often devastated by what sin costs me.
Godly sorrow begins seeing what sin is before God.
David prayed:
“Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight.”
—Psalm 51:4
David obviously sinned against human beings too. His words are not denying that. He is recognizing the ultimate Godward character of sin.
Sin is more than breaking a rule.
It is rebellion against a Person.
Against the God who gave you breath.
Against the Savior who loved sinners all the way to a cross.
Against the One who knows the thing nobody else knows and still calls you to come into the light.
And this is where guilt can become either a doorway or a dungeon.
Guilt that drives you away from Christ becomes destructive.
Conviction that drives you toward Christ can become mercy.
Because there is a difference between the Spirit exposing your sin and condemnation telling you there is no way home.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
That does not mean sin no longer matters.
It means condemnation does not own the believer anymore.
Christ does.
So when the Holy Spirit exposes something, the answer is not:
“I need to hate myself harder.”
The answer is:
“I need to stop hiding.”
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō, carrying the sense of acknowledging or confessing.
Stop editing the confession.
Stop calling lust “a weakness.”
Stop calling greed “ambition.”
Stop calling gossip “concern.”
Stop calling unforgiveness “boundaries” when what you actually mean is cherished hatred.
Stop calling pride “knowing my worth.”
Stop calling manipulation “love.”
Stop calling deliberate compromise “a season.”
Bring it into the light.
Name it before God.
And then look toward Christ.
Because repentance without Jesus becomes another form of self-salvation.
You cannot scrub your soul clean enough to deserve Him.
You cannot cry enough tears to purchase forgiveness.
You cannot punish yourself enough to supplement Calvary.
You cannot perform enough good deeds to reverse yesterday.
The blood of Jesus is not the down payment while your remorse pays the remaining balance.
Christ said:
“It is finished.”
The Greek of John 19:30 is breathtakingly concise:
Τετέλεσται — Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
The saving work accomplished at the cross does not need your self-condemnation added to make it effective.
You repent because Christ is worthy.
You come because grace has opened the door.
You surrender because Jesus is Lord.
You trust because the crucified and risen Christ is sufficient.
And then your life begins changing—not to purchase His love, but because you have encountered it.
That is why genuine repentance can hurt deeply while simultaneously producing hope.
You can weep and still know where you are going.
Home.
You can confess something ugly and still know who is waiting.
Jesus.
You can finally admit, “I did it. I chose it. It was sin. I have no excuse.”
And instead of discovering that Christ has disappeared...
you discover the Savior who already knew.
He knew before you confessed.
He knew before you clicked.
Before you drank.
Before you lied.
Before you cheated.
Before you exploded.
Before you went back.
Before everybody else discovered who you could become at your worst...
Jesus knew.
And the cross still happened.
Please do not misunderstand that.
Foreknown sin is not permitted sin.
Grace is never permission to remain in rebellion.
Paul anticipated that distortion:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!”
—Romans 6:1–2
Grace does something infinitely better than giving you permission to stay chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
So how do you know whether you truly repented or merely felt guilty?
Do not measure it only by how hard you cried.
Ask where the sorrow is taking you.
Is it taking you toward confession?
Toward Christ?
Toward surrender?
Toward making wrongs right where possible?
Toward cutting off deliberate provision for sin?
Toward accountability?
Toward obedience?
Toward a growing hatred of what separates your heart from God?
Toward new fruit—even imperfect, trembling, slowly growing fruit?
Or are you simply waiting for the uncomfortable feeling to disappear so life can return to normal?
Because if all you want is relief from guilt while keeping the sin...
you do not actually want repentance yet.
But even now, there is grace in discovering that.
Because you can repent of your refusal to repent.
You can tell Jesus the truth.
“Lord, part of me still wants this sin.”
That prayer may sound ugly.
It may also be the most honest prayer you have prayed in years.
“Jesus, I know this is wrong, but I still love it.”
“Jesus, I want You, but part of me does not want to surrender this.”
“Jesus, I am tired of making promises I break.”
“Jesus, change what I cannot seem to change.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Now you are no longer performing.
Now the mask is coming off.
And Christ has always done extraordinary things with people who finally stop pretending.
The Gospel is filled with scandalous people.
Tax collectors.
Prostitutes.
Religious hypocrites.
Thieves.
Persecutors.
Cowards.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Broken people with histories they could not erase.
Jesus did not rewrite their stories by pretending the earlier chapters never existed.
He rewrote them by redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
Peter's denial remained part of his testimony.
Paul never needed to pretend he had not persecuted the church.
Their past became evidence not of their greatness...
but of the breathtaking mercy of God.
Maybe yours can too.
Maybe someday the very thing you are terrified someone will discover will become part of the testimony you use to tell another trembling sinner:
“I thought Jesus was finished with me too.”
Maybe your deepest shame will become the place from which you point most passionately toward grace.
Not because the sin was beautiful.
Because the Savior is.
That is Gospel Warrior.
We do not glorify scandals.
We glorify the Christ who redeems sinners.
We do not preach shame without a Savior.
We preach repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
We do not tell broken people to decorate their chains.
We point toward the One who breaks them.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, do not rush past that moment.
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove your spirituality.
But because sometimes confession begins when somebody finally has enough courage to stop pretending everything is fine.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
But if this message glorifies Christ and you believe someone in your circle needs to hear it, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.
There may be someone scrolling tonight who thinks guilt means God no longer wants them.
Someone hiding pornography.
Someone drowning in an affair.
Someone imprisoned by bitterness.
Someone secretly drinking again.
Someone who betrayed people they love.
Someone sitting in church every Sunday while privately wondering whether Jesus could possibly receive them again.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's conviction feel distant tomorrow.
Come back when guilt starts whispering that hiding is easier than confession.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to earn spiritual status.
Not because God needs your money before He can work.
But because Gospel ministry has real costs, and believers can freely choose to support work that helps spread biblical truth.
Pray.
Give away one of the free resources.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.
It is measured by a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly where this entire article needed to end.
Not with your guilt.
Not with your failure.
Not even with your tears.
But with Jesus.
Peter failed.
Jesus restored.
David sinned.
God showed mercy to the repentant king, though consequences remained.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The cross itself looked like humanity's darkest scandal.
Yet through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ came the announcement sinners desperately needed:
There is forgiveness.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is cleansing.
There is a way home.
So tonight, do not merely ask:
“Do I feel guilty?”
Ask:
“Where is my guilt taking me?”
If it drives you into hiding, bring it into the light.
If it makes you punish yourself, look at the cross.
If it makes you despair, look at the empty tomb.
If it exposes a sin you still cherish, stop negotiating.
If restitution is possible and appropriate, begin making things right.
If you need accountability, ask for it.
If you need pastoral help, seek it.
If the struggle has become deeply entrenched or destructive, reach for wise professional help alongside mature Christian support rather than fighting alone.
And if you have truly fallen...
turn.
שׁוּב — shuv.
Return.
If your heart is broken...
turn.
If your reputation is shattered...
turn.
If this is the hundredth time you have needed mercy...
turn.
Not toward excuses.
Not toward self-hatred.
Not toward another empty promise.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Repentance does not mean you were never the person who did those things.
It means, by the grace of God, that sin no longer gets unquestioned ownership of the person you are becoming.
The Gospel does not say your scandal was imaginary.
It says your scandal does not have to write your final chapter.
And maybe that is the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades:
Your tears may reveal that your heart is hurting—but only turning to Jesus reveals where your heart is going.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN TECHNOLOGY BE USED TO STRENGTHEN HOLINESS?
paragraphs: CAN TECHNOLOGY BE USED TO STRENGTHEN HOLINESS?
The screen that has helped distract a generation from God may also become one of the places where a surrendered generation learns to seek Him again.
There is something strangely revealing about the glow of a phone in a dark room.
Nobody else is watching.
Nobody knows what you searched.
Nobody sees what you deleted.
Nobody hears what you listened to through your headphones.
Nobody knows whether you opened Scripture or pornography, worship or gossip, prayer or another hour of mindless scrolling.
Nobody knows.
Except God.
And perhaps that is where this conversation about technology and holiness really needs to begin.
Not with artificial intelligence.
Not with smartphones.
Not with algorithms.
Not with whether Christians should delete social media, install another Bible app, throw away their televisions, or retreat from the digital world entirely.
It begins with the heart.
Because technology has accomplished something remarkable: it has placed enormous power within inches of the human soul.
With the same device, you can read the Gospel of John or feed an addiction.
You can encourage somebody contemplating giving up or publicly humiliate someone you have never met.
You can listen to Scripture while driving to work or spend the journey poisoning your heart with envy.
You can send money to a missionary.
You can betray your marriage.
You can learn theology.
You can spread a lie.
You can pray with someone thousands of miles away.
You can secretly become somebody you would be ashamed for your family to meet.
Same screen.
Same hands.
Different master.
And that is why asking, “Is technology good or evil?” may be the wrong question.
A more uncomfortable question is:
What is technology revealing about who is ruling me?
Jesus said something centuries before smartphones that sounds terrifyingly contemporary:
“The lamp of the body is the eye.”
Matthew 6:22.
What enters through your eyes matters.
What repeatedly receives your attention matters.
What you rehearse in secret matters.
And Scripture’s call to holiness was never merely about looking respectable when other Christians were watching.
The apostle Peter writes:
1 Peter 1:15–16, KJV.
Behind Peter’s words stands an ancient command from Leviticus. In Hebrew:
קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי
Qedoshim tihyu, ki qadosh ani.
“You shall be holy, for I am holy.”
Holiness is not Christian cosmetic surgery.
It is not learning how to appear religious.
The Hebrew idea of קָדוֹשׁ — qadosh carries the sense of being holy, set apart, belonging to God.
And when the New Testament speaks of holiness, it uses words from the same spiritual world of consecration. Peter says:
ἅγιοι γενήθητε
hagioi genēthēte—
“become holy.”
That changes the question completely.
The question is no longer simply, “Can I use this?”
The question becomes:
“Can I use this while belonging completely to Jesus?”
Because holiness reaches your browser history.
Holiness reaches your private messages.
Holiness reaches the videos you watch after everyone goes to sleep.
Holiness reaches the comment you are about to type while angry.
Holiness reaches the photographs you keep returning to.
Holiness reaches your playlists.
Holiness reaches your search history.
Holiness reaches what you laugh at.
Holiness reaches what you secretly wish would appear next.
And suddenly the most dangerous thing about your phone may not be what technology can do.
It may be what technology can expose about you.
Paul wrote:
“All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient… I will not be brought under the power of any.”
1 Corinthians 6:12, KJV.
Read that last sentence again.
“I will not be brought under the power of any.”
That sounds almost prophetic in an age engineered around attention.
One more notification.
One more reel.
One more video.
One more refresh.
One more argument.
One more image.
One more purchase.
One more scroll before prayer.
Then prayer never happens.
You told yourself you were checking something for five minutes.
Forty-seven minutes disappeared.
The Bible remained unopened.
The person beside you remained unnoticed.
