His love becomes better than being desired by somebody who is pulling you away from Him.
And slowly, painfully, genuinely, grace teaches your heart to want differently.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
But truly.
This is why fighting temptation cannot be separated from abiding in Christ.
You do not defeat sin by becoming impressed with your own discipline.
You fight from dependence.
Jesus said:

“without me ye can do nothing.”
—John 15:5, KJV
The person who says, “I would never do that,” may be in more danger than the person who says, “Lord, keep me.”
Peter once sounded certain too.
He insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Hours later, a servant girl frightened him into denying that he even knew Christ.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine Peter’s stomach dropping.
Imagine remembering Jesus’ words.
Imagine realizing that the version of yourself you thought existed had just collapsed in a courtyard.
Luke records one devastating detail:

“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.”
—Luke 22:61, KJV
Jesus looked at him.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Not Peter’s exact circumstances.
But the collapse.
The moment after temptation wins.
The screen goes dark.
The conversation ends.
The anger cools.
The person leaves.
The lie has already been told.
The secret has already been opened.
And suddenly the pleasure that screamed so loudly five minutes earlier becomes strangely quiet.
Then shame begins talking.
Look at you.
Again.
You call yourself a Christian?
God must be sick of you.
Don’t pray now. You’re a hypocrite.
Hide.
That voice sounds spiritual because it talks about your sin.
But notice where it wants to take you.
Away from Jesus.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Condemnation says:
Stay in the dark.
Conviction exposes the wound so it can be treated.
Condemnation tells you the wound has become your identity.
And the Gospel says something scandalously beautiful to the genuinely repentant sinner:
Your worst failure does not have to write your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Jesus restored Peter.
Not because Peter’s denial was insignificant.
Not because Jesus pretended it never happened.
But because grace is greater than the sinner it rescues.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
There was another charcoal fire.
There were questions.
“Lovest thou me?”
And there was restoration.
“Feed my sheep.”
The man who had publicly denied Christ would later publicly proclaim Christ.
The coward became a witness.
The failure became a shepherd.
The scandal became testimony.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal was righteous.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by telling sinners to love themselves exactly as they are and remain unchanged.
Jesus rewrites everything through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, restoration, and transformation.
That is grace.
And maybe your story currently feels stuck somewhere between the courtyard and the restoration.
Maybe you love Jesus.
But you keep falling.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you are spiritually strong.
Maybe you worship publicly while fighting privately.
Maybe you lead people while wondering whether your own secret battle disqualifies you from being loved.
Hear this carefully:
Do not use grace as permission to remain in chains.
But do not let shame convince you that chains are stronger than Christ.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it to God.
Where appropriate, confess to a trustworthy mature believer who can pray with you and hold you accountable.
Remove access.
Stop protecting the pathway that keeps taking you back to the same pit.
If the app keeps becoming a doorway, delete it.
If the conversation keeps becoming seductive, end it.
If being alone with that person keeps awakening what should not be awakened, stop arranging opportunities to be alone.
If late-night isolation repeatedly becomes the battlefield, change your routine.
If your phone becomes a trap behind a locked bedroom door, stop treating unrestricted privacy like a sacred human right.
If pride keeps making you hide, tell somebody trustworthy.
You cannot repent of what you insist on protecting.
And please understand this:
Running is not weakness when God told you to flee.
Joseph ran.
Paul told Timothy to run.
Scripture repeatedly tells believers to flee particular forms of evil.
Sometimes the most courageous spiritual decision you will make is not standing there proving you can handle temptation.
It is admitting:
“I know what this does to me, and I love Jesus too much to keep negotiating with it.”
That is not cowardice.
That is wisdom.
And Paul adds something else that many people miss:
“…with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”
With them.
You were never supposed to fight alone.
Isolation gives temptation oxygen.
The enemy loves private Christianity because private Christianity can become unaccountable Christianity.
You need believers who know more than your Sunday face.
People who can ask the uncomfortable question.
People who can pray when you are exhausted.
People who love you enough not to applaud what Jesus wants to remove.
People who will remind you of the Gospel when shame makes you forget it.
People you can call before the fall instead of only after it.
Maybe today is the day you stop hiding.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more failure.
Today.
Maybe the first act of fleeing is closing something.
Maybe it is deleting something.
Maybe it is confessing something.
Maybe it is ending something.
Maybe it is walking away from someone.
Maybe it is finally saying aloud:
“This has more control over me than I have admitted.”
There is no trophy in pretending.
There is grace in coming into the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly.
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not judge them.
Pray for them.
You do not know what it cost them to type it.
Maybe that comment is somebody’s first tiny movement out of darkness.
And if this article made you think of somebody, do not merely think about them.
Or send this privately.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity, financial support, purchases, or religious performance.
But if Christ has given you something worth hearing, there is beauty in refusing to keep it to yourself.
Somebody scrolling your profile tonight may be losing a battle you know nothing about.
Someone may have prayed this morning:
“God, please help me.”
And perhaps one way you can serve them is simply by putting truth where they might encounter it.
Not because you expect to fail.
Because temptation has a way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made painfully obvious today.
Come back when the whisper starts again.
Remember Joseph’s coat.
Remember Peter’s tears.
Remember Timothy’s command.
Remember Christ’s cross.
Do not negotiate with what Jesus is calling you to flee.
It does not make you more righteous. Supporting a ministry is not the measure of whether you glorify God.
But generosity, sharing biblical truth, encouraging believers, and helping Gospel-centered resources reach people can genuinely be ways we steward what God has entrusted to us.
More importantly, staying connected means staying near a stream of biblical encouragement meant to keep pointing you back to Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who is quietly questioning everything.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely a religion for people who have their lives together.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally became good enough for God.
It is the announcement that sinners who could never rescue themselves have been offered a Savior.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling people to repent and believe.
Offering forgiveness that cannot be purchased.
Grace that cannot be earned.
A new life we could never manufacture.
And power to fight sins we once thought would own us forever.
So when temptation returns—and it may—remember this moment.
You do not owe temptation a conversation.
You do not owe lust one more look.
You do not owe pride the last word.
You do not owe bitterness another night.
You do not owe secret sin another password.
You do not owe your old chains loyalty.
You belong to Christ.
Run from what is killing you.
Run toward righteousness.
Run toward faith.
Run toward love.
Run toward peace.
Run with believers who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.
And when you stumble, do not run away from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Stand again.
Then keep running.
Because the Christian life is not the story of people who were never tempted.
It is the story of people learning that Jesus is better than what temptation promised them.
What are you choosing today—“No more hiding,” “I’m still fighting,” or “Pray for me”?
You do not have to publish the details.
Just refuse to let darkness convince you that you must fight alone.
Because somewhere between temptation’s whisper and tomorrow’s regret, there is still a door.
And sometimes grace looks like Jesus showing you the door while there is still time to run.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID ALREADY HAD WOMEN—AND STILL TOOK URIAH’S WIFE
paragraphs: DAVID ALREADY HAD WOMEN—AND STILL TOOK URIAH’S WIFE
The terrifying truth about David and Bathsheba is not that David had nothing. It is that he had much—and sin still whispered, “You need one more.”
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every comfortable Christian uncomfortable:
David already had wives.
He already had a throne.
He already had victories.
He already had wealth.
He already had honor.
He already had the testimony of a man whom God had raised from obscurity.
And still...
he looked across a rooftop and wanted what belonged to another man.
That changes the way we read the scandal.
Because suddenly this is no longer merely an ancient story about a king, a woman, adultery, and murder.
It becomes a mirror.
And mirrors are frightening when we stop using them to examine everybody else.
Second Samuel 11 opens with kings going out to battle while David remains in Jerusalem. One evening he rises from his bed and walks on the roof of the palace. From there he sees a woman bathing.
The text tells us she was very beautiful.
David asks who she is.
And the answer should have ended everything.
“Is this not Bathsheba... the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
Wife.
That word was the boundary.
That word should have been enough.
She belonged in a covenant David had no right to invade.
But sin has a frightening ability to turn a boundary into an inconvenience when desire has already begun negotiating with conscience.
David sent messengers.
David took her.
The Hebrew narrative is painfully direct.
וַיִּשְׁלַח דָּוִד מַלְאָכִים וַיִּקָּחֶהָ
Vayyishlach David mal’akhim vayyiqqacheha.
In plain sense: David sent messengers, and he took her.
That verb matters.
לָקַח — laqach.
To take.
The story does not invite us to romanticize David’s actions as some beautiful forbidden love story.
The king saw.
The king inquired.
The king sent.
The king took.
And Bathsheba later sent David a message containing words capable of collapsing an entire kingdom into three syllables of terror:
הָרָה אָנֹכִי
Harah anokhi.
“I am pregnant.”
Now David has a problem.
Or at least that is how unrepentant sin thinks.
Not, “I have sinned.”
Not, “I have violated another household.”
Not, “I have offended the God who gave me everything.”
The immediate problem becomes:
How do I keep anyone from finding out?
And this is where David’s fall becomes terrifyingly relatable.
Because sometimes the second sin is committed to protect the first.
Then the third protects the second.
Then the lie needs another lie.
The hidden message needs another hidden message.
The browser history gets erased.
The conversation gets deleted.
The money gets moved.
The explanation gets rehearsed.
The smile gets practiced.
Church clothes go on.
Worship music plays.
Hands rise.
Everybody thinks everything is fine.
But somewhere underneath the worship...
Uriah is carrying a letter.
David summoned Bathsheba’s husband home from the battlefield and tried to maneuver him into sleeping with his wife so that the pregnancy might appear to be his.
But Uriah refused the comforts of home while his fellow soldiers remained in battle.
Think about the irony.
The foreign-born Hittite soldier displayed loyalty while Israel’s anointed king practiced betrayal.
David even got Uriah drunk.
Still, Uriah would not cooperate with David’s cover-up.
So David crossed another line.
He wrote instructions to Joab ordering that Uriah be placed where the fighting was fiercest and then abandoned so that he would be struck down.
And then David did something almost unbearable to contemplate.
He put Uriah’s death sentence into Uriah’s own hands.
The faithful soldier carried the letter that would arrange his own death.
Uriah did not know what was written.
David did.
Uriah went back to battle.
The plan worked.
Uriah died.
David eventually brought Bathsheba into his house.
To observers, perhaps the scandal looked contained.
The king had survived.
The evidence had been absorbed into a respectable-looking arrangement.
But Scripture closes the chapter with the verdict no palace wall could silence:
What David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD.
God saw it.
That is the sentence every secret sin eventually encounters.
God saw it.
The deleted messages?
God saw them.
The private compromise?
God saw it.
The thing nobody in your church knows?
God knows.
The resentment hidden beneath politeness?
The pornography behind the locked screen?
The emotional affair you keep calling friendship?
The money nobody knows you took?
The bitterness you have justified for years?
The secret relationship?
The pride underneath your ministry?
The addiction you have learned to disguise?
The version of yourself you carefully present while another version lives behind closed doors?
God sees.
And here is what makes David’s scandal even more sobering.
David was not a starving man stealing bread.
He was a king who had been given abundance.

When Nathan finally confronted him, God reminded David of what had already been placed in his hands. In 2 Samuel 12:8 the LORD speaks of having given David his master’s house and his master’s wives into his arms, along with Israel and Judah, adding that if this had been too little, He would have given him still more.
Then comes the devastating question of verse 9.
מַדּוּעַ בָּזִיתָ אֶת־דְּבַר יְהוָה
Maddua bazita et-devar YHWH?
“Why have you despised the word of the LORD?”
Notice what God does not say.
“David, you simply fell in love with the wrong person.”
No.
David’s sin is exposed as contempt for God’s word expressed through evil action.
God explicitly names Uriah.
God explicitly names Uriah’s wife.
God explicitly holds David responsible for Uriah’s death, even though an Ammonite sword physically killed him.
David arranged it.
David abused his authority.
David tried to conceal it.
David was responsible.
This matters especially because careless retellings can turn Bathsheba into the convenient villain of David’s story.
Scripture does not give us permission to do that.

Second Samuel 11 concentrates its moral agency overwhelmingly on David’s actions. David saw. David inquired. David sent. David took. David attempted the cover-up. David manipulated Uriah. David wrote the order. David arranged the battlefield betrayal.
And when Nathan arrived with God’s indictment, Nathan did not point his finger toward Bathsheba.
He pointed it at the king.
אַתָּה הָאִישׁ
Attah ha’ish.
“You are the man.”
Imagine the silence.
David had listened as Nathan told him about a rich man with many sheep who stole the single beloved lamb of a poor man.
David became furious.
The rich man deserved judgment.
How easy it is to recognize ugliness when somebody else is wearing it.
How easy to condemn another person’s adultery while protecting our lust.
To condemn somebody’s dishonesty while exaggerating our own story.
To rage about corruption while cheating quietly when it benefits us.
To expose another Christian’s hypocrisy while maintaining a private room in our own soul where Jesus is not welcome.
David pronounced judgment on the man in Nathan’s story.
Then Nathan shattered the illusion:
You are the man.
Not your enemy.
Not the culture.
Not the politician you hate.
Not your former spouse.
Not the hypocrite who wounded you.
You.
And me.
Before grace becomes breathtaking, sin must become personal.
That is one reason this story refuses to die.
We keep thinking satisfaction will arrive after the next thing.
One more purchase.
One more promotion.
One more relationship.
One more sexual experience.
One more compliment.
One more follower.
One more victory.
One more secret indulgence.
Then we will finally feel full.
But David already had “more.”
And still he took Uriah’s wife.
Because the deepest problem was never the size of David’s collection.
It was the condition of David’s heart.
Sin does not merely say, “I want something.”
At its deepest level it says, “God, what You have given me is not enough. Your boundary is standing between me and what I believe will satisfy me. Therefore I will decide what is good for myself.”
That ancient rebellion still speaks fluently today.
James later describes temptation as desire drawing a person away and enticing him. Desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin when fully grown brings forth death.
Look at David’s progression.
A look.
An inquiry.
A summons.
A taking.
A pregnancy.
A cover-up.
Manipulation.
A death order.
A funeral.
A secret.
Sin promised David a moment.
It handed him a chain.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you are still respected.
Maybe people quote your posts.
Maybe your children think you are strong.
Maybe your spouse trusts you.
Maybe your pastor shakes your hand every Sunday.
Maybe you know exactly when to say “Amen.”
But your soul is tired.
Tired of passwords.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of deleting.
Tired of explaining.
Tired of remembering which version of the story you told.
Tired of promising God, “This is the last time.”
Tired of being terrified that somebody will discover what God already knows.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not telling you to become better at hiding.
Jesus Christ did not come to make sinners more respectable.
He came to save sinners.
David’s story does not end on the rooftop.
It does not end with Uriah’s grave.
It does not even end when Nathan points at David and says, “You are the man.”
Something astonishing happens next.
David says:
חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה
Chatati laYHWH.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
No elaborate defense.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No blaming loneliness.
No blaming royal pressure.
No blaming Uriah.
No public-relations strategy.
“I have sinned.”
And Nathan responds that the LORD has put away David’s sin.
Do not misunderstand that grace.
Forgiveness did not mean David’s actions suddenly had no earthly consequences.
Second Samuel 12 makes painfully clear that consequences remained.
Biblical grace is not God pretending evil was harmless.
Grace is costly precisely because sin is truly evil.
David could be forgiven without Uriah becoming less dead.
That should sober us.
Forgiveness does not always reverse every consequence we created.
Repentance may save a soul while leaving scars that must still be faced with humility.
A marriage may be forgiven and still require years of rebuilding trust.
Money may be forgiven and still need to be repaid.
A lie may be forgiven while its damage requires confession and repair.
Grace is not permission to sin cheaply.
Grace is the miracle that guilty people can come home at all.
And David’s repentance eventually bleeds into one of Scripture’s most famous prayers.
Psalm 51.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
The Hebrew is unforgettable:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“A clean heart create for me, O God.”
The verb בָּרָא — bara, “create” — is striking.
David did not merely need improved behavior.
He needed God to do something deep within him.
And so do we.
Christianity is not behavior modification wrapped in religious vocabulary.
The Gospel goes deeper.
We need hearts reconciled to God.
We need guilt answered.
We need sin forgiven.
We need desires reordered.
We need new life.
We need Christ.
And this is where David’s scandal becomes part of an even greater story.
Centuries later, Matthew begins the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Names pass by like generations marching toward Bethlehem.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Boaz.
Jesse.
David.
And Matthew does something startling.
When he reaches Solomon, he deliberately recalls the scandal by identifying Solomon’s mother in relation to Uriah.
Uriah’s name survives in the genealogy leading to Christ.
The Bible does not airbrush the family history of the Messiah.
It remembers the wound.
It remembers the dead soldier.
It remembers the scandal.
And still...
Jesus comes.
Not because the scandal was acceptable.
Because grace is greater than the scandal.
Jesus did not descend into a spotless human genealogy because spotless humanity did not need rescuing.
He entered our broken history as the sinless Savior.
David took another man’s wife and arranged another man’s death.
Jesus Christ, the Son of David, came not to take life but to lay down His own life for sinners.
David used power to protect himself.
Jesus used His authority in perfect obedience to the Father and willingly humbled Himself.
David sent Uriah carrying a sentence of death.
Jesus carried the cross toward His own death.
David tried to hide guilt.
At Calvary, Christ dealt with guilt.
David deserved judgment.
So do we.
Yet at the center of Christianity stands a cross where the holy Son of God bears sin and where mercy is offered to repentant sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
That does not make sin small.
It shows us how costly redemption is.
Maybe that is why you have read this far.
Perhaps this article stopped being about David several paragraphs ago.
Perhaps there is a Bathsheba-sized boundary you have been approaching.
Perhaps there is a Uriah-sized casualty you keep refusing to acknowledge.
Perhaps there is a Nathan-sized truth God has been sending toward your conscience.
Maybe you have not committed David’s particular sins.
But you recognize the machinery.
Wanting.
Rationalizing.
Taking.
Hiding.
Defending.
Repeating.
Pretending.
And somewhere beneath all of it...
God is calling your name.
Not so you can manufacture a cleaner image.
So you can repent.
Come into the light.
Confess what God already knows.
First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
The answer is not self-hatred.
The answer is not religious performance.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
Repentance means turning from sin toward God, trusting not in your ability to erase your record but in the crucified and risen Savior.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem what you surrender to Him.
You may have consequences to face.
Face them with Him.
You may owe someone the truth.
Tell it with humility.
You may need to end the secret relationship.
End it.
You may need accountability.
Seek it.
You may need to stop calling bondage “just a struggle” and finally drag it into the light.
Do it.
Not because confession purchases grace.
Because grace gives sinners somewhere to run.
David’s story should frighten anyone who thinks past victories make future compromise impossible.
The man who killed Goliath was still capable of falling to lust.
Yesterday’s faithfulness does not give us permission to stop guarding our hearts today.
A giant in front of you may be less dangerous than an unchecked desire inside you.
Read that again.
David knew how to fight giants.
His greatest disaster began when he stopped fighting himself.
And perhaps somebody you know is standing on that rooftop right now.
They have not sent the message yet.
They have not crossed the boundary yet.
They have not destroyed the marriage yet.
They have not made the secret irreversible yet.
Send this privately to the believer who has become spiritually tired.
Come back and remember the rooftop.
Remember Uriah.
Remember Nathan.
Remember David’s tears.
Remember the cross.
And please, do not turn the comments into a courtroom where everybody prosecutes David while hiding themselves.
Make them a place of honesty.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your sin. Protect appropriate privacy, especially where other people could be harmed.
But you can still say:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Or simply:
“Pray for me.”
And if you have personally experienced the mercy of Jesus after failure, leave a testimony—not to glorify the scandal, but to glorify the Savior who met you in it.
Someone reading underneath you may desperately need evidence that repentance is not the end of the story.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build an audience around outrage.
Not to turn biblical scandals into entertainment.
Not to make merchandise out of somebody else’s failure.
We want to keep placing Scripture, repentance, grace, discipleship, healing, accountability, and Jesus Christ in front of people who are hungry for truth.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing or salvation.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption; we never could.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with your resources, Scripture calls believers to steward what God has entrusted to them for His purposes. Supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of that stewardship.
another prodigal...
another wounded marriage...
another secret sinner...
another skeptic...
another person standing on a rooftop of temptation who desperately needs to hear the voice of God before one decision becomes ten years of regret.
If you want to support that mission and go deeper with us:
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody in your circle may be hiding behind a smile tonight.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person struggling with secret sin.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for people with clean histories.
Because Scripture contains David’s scandal for a reason.
God could have hidden it.
He did not.
God could have preserved only David’s victories.
He did not.
We received Goliath...
and Bathsheba.
The worshipper...
and the adulterer.
The king...
and the conspirator.
The man exposed by Nathan...
and the broken sinner crying for a clean heart.
Then God gives us Jesus.
That is where our hope must finally rest.
Not in David.
Not in Christian celebrities.
Not in pastors.
Not in ministries.
Not in Gospel Warrior.
Jesus.
Only Jesus is the spotless King.
Only Jesus can bear the sinner’s guilt.
Only Jesus can reconcile us to God.
Only Jesus can give the repentant sinner a future that is no longer defined solely by the worst chapter of the past.
David already had women—and still took Uriah’s wife.
That is the warning.
David was exposed, confessed his sin, and received mercy he could never deserve.
That is grace.
But Jesus Christ is greater than David.
That is the Gospel.
So before you close this article, ask yourself the question Nathan forced David to face:
Where am I still trying to make somebody else “the man” because I am afraid to admit that God is speaking to me?
Then stop running.
Stop editing the evidence.
Stop negotiating with the boundary.
Stop protecting what Jesus is calling you to surrender.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
And when Christ begins rewriting the story, never confuse His grace with approval of the chapter He rescued you from.
Because the most astonishing thing about grace is not that God pretends the scandal never happened.
It is that Jesus can meet a repentant sinner in the wreckage—and the wreckage does not get the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHERE WAS DAVID WHEN TAMAR NEEDED JUSTICE?
paragraphs:
WHERE WAS DAVID WHEN TAMAR NEEDED JUSTICE?
He killed a giant when Israel was afraid. He wrote songs we still sing when our hearts are broken. But when his own daughter walked away violated, crying, and desolate, Scripture records something terrifying: David became angry. And then the story moves on.
There are screams in the Bible that seem to keep echoing long after the page has been turned.
Tamar's is one of them.
She walked away with ashes on her head.
Her royal robe was torn.
Her hand was on her head.
And she was crying aloud as she went.
The Hebrew refuses to make the scene comfortable:
"וַתֵּלֶךְ הָלוֹךְ וְזָעָקָה"
Vattēlekh halokh vezā‘āqāh.
She went on...
crying out.
The final word comes from זָעַק (za‘aq)—to cry out, to call out in distress.
Tamar did not disappear quietly.
She made noise.
She grieved publicly.
Something terrible had happened to a daughter of the king, and she walked through the aftermath carrying evidence of devastation on her body.
And somewhere in the kingdom was David.
David.
The shepherd who had once run toward Goliath.
The warrior who had faced lions and bears.
The king who knew what it was to be hunted.
The poet who could find language for grief when other people could barely breathe.
The man who wrote of a God who hears the cries of the afflicted.
Tamar needed that man.
But more importantly, she needed her father.
She needed her king.
And the question hanging over 2 Samuel 13 is painfully difficult to escape:
Where was David when Tamar needed justice?

This story needs to be handled carefully because Tamar is not a sermon illustration. She is not a prop for a clever Christian message. Scripture presents her as a woman with a voice, moral clarity, dignity, and devastating grief.
Amnon wanted her.
But Scripture exposes immediately that what he called desire was not covenant love.
Tamar was his half-sister. Amnon was David's son. Tamar was David's daughter.
Then Amnon's cousin Jonadab helped devise the trap.
Amnon pretended to be ill.
David unknowingly became part of the mechanism that placed Tamar within Amnon's reach when he sent her to prepare food for him.
Then Amnon ordered everyone else out.
The door closed.
And Tamar realized what he intended.
What follows is one of the most heartbreaking speeches in the historical books.
She resisted him.
She reasoned with him.
She named the evil.
"אַל־אָחִי אַל־תְּעַנֵּנִי"
'Al, 'achi, 'al-te‘annēni.
"No, my brother, do not violate me."
Then:
"כִּי לֹא־יֵעָשֶׂה כֵן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל"
Ki lo-ye‘aseh khen beYisra'el.
Such a thing must not be done in Israel.
Listen to Tamar.
She understood something Amnon's appetite had made him forget.
Being part of God's covenant people was supposed to mean something.
Israel was not supposed to imitate the wickedness surrounding it while continuing to wear the name of God.
Tamar appealed to morality.
To community.
To consequences.
To shame.
She even tried to find a way out of the room by telling him to speak to the king.
She was fighting with the only weapons she had left—truth, reason, words.
But Scripture says:
"וְלֹא אָבָה לִשְׁמֹעַ בְּקוֹלָהּ"
Velo avah lishmoa‘ beqolah.
He was unwilling to listen to her voice.
That sentence should disturb us.
Because before Amnon violated Tamar's body, he rejected Tamar's voice.
He heard her.
He simply decided her "no" did not matter.
He was stronger physically, and he used that strength against her.
The biblical narrator does not romanticize it.
This was not forbidden romance.
This was not uncontrollable passion.
This was not two people making a mistake.
Tamar resisted.
Amnon overpowered her.
The Hebrew text describes what he did with the verb עִנָּה (‘innah), language carrying the sense of afflicting, humiliating, or violating her in this context.
And immediately afterward, the "love" Amnon claimed to have felt turned into hatred.
That exposes what his desire had been all along.
Love does not consume another human being and throw them away.
Lust says, "I want you because of what you can give me."
Love seeks the good of the beloved.
Amnon wanted possession.
When possession was achieved, his obsession became contempt.
He ordered her out.
Tamar protested again because throwing her away compounded the evil.
Again, he would not listen.
Then comes one of the coldest moments in the chapter.
Amnon does not even call Tamar by her name.
He tells his servant to put "this" out and bolt the door behind her.
A princess entered that room.
Amnon treated her as disposable when she left it.
But heaven did not forget her name.
Tamar.
Scripture keeps calling her Tamar.
Remember that if someone has ever reduced you to what happened to you.
God's Word does not call her "the damaged woman."
It does not rename her by Amnon's sin.
Her violator's behavior does not become her identity.
Her name remains Tamar.
She tears the distinctive robe associated with the king's virgin daughters.
She puts ashes on her head.
She walks away crying.
Then Absalom sees her.
He apparently understands almost immediately.
And his response contains another painful silence.
He tells his sister, in effect, to be quiet for the present because Amnon is her brother.
Then Scripture gives us one Hebrew word that feels almost unbearable:
"וַתֵּשֶׁב תָּמָר וְשֹׁמֵמָה"
Vattēshev Tamar veshomemah.
Tamar remained...
שֹׁמֵמָה — shomemah.
Desolate.
Devastated.
Laid waste.
In her brother Absalom's house.
And now David finally enters the aftermath.
"וְהַמֶּלֶךְ דָּוִד שָׁמַע אֵת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה וַיִּחַר לוֹ מְאֹד"
Vehammelekh David shama‘ et kol-haddevarim ha'elleh, vayichar lo me'od.
King David heard about all these things, and he became very angry.
David heard.
David became angry.
And in the Masoretic Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 13, no punishment of Amnon by David is then recorded.
That distinction matters.
We should not claim Scripture explicitly says, "David did absolutely nothing," because the text does not give us a comprehensive diary of every action David took.
But we can say what Scripture actually gives us.
It records his anger.
It does not record David bringing Amnon to justice in this chapter.
It does not record him publicly defending Tamar.
It does not record him removing Amnon from privilege.
It does not record him comforting his daughter.
It does not record him rebuking Amnon in the Masoretic wording of verse 21.
And there is an ancient textual detail worth knowing.

The Greek Septuagint tradition preserves an additional statement at this point saying, in substance, that David did not grieve or rebuke Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn. That longer reading is a textual variant, so it should not simply be presented as though every Hebrew manuscript contains it. Yet its existence is striking, particularly because another episode later says of David's son Adonijah that his father had never challenged him by asking why he behaved as he did.
Whatever conclusions we draw about the precise textual history, the narrative before us is devastatingly clear about the result.
Tamar is desolate.
Amnon remains alive and within the royal family.
David is angry.
Absalom is furious.
Justice does not arrive through the king.
And eventually Absalom decides to manufacture his own.
For two years, he waits.
Then Amnon dies at Absalom's command.
That does not make Absalom righteous.
Vengeance is not biblical justice merely because injustice preceded it.
But the story shows what can grow when evil is allowed to fester inside a family.
Silence does not necessarily kill sin.
Sometimes silence gives sin somewhere to breed.
That is where this ancient royal scandal becomes frighteningly modern.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like when everybody is angry about what happened...
but nobody does anything.
Someone says, "That's terrible."
Someone cries with you.
Someone says they will pray.
Someone tells you not to destroy the family.
Someone reminds you that the offender is still your father, mother, brother, sister, pastor, leader, spouse, relative, or friend.
Someone worries about the church's reputation.
Someone worries about the ministry.
Someone worries about the family name.
Someone worries about scandal.
And the wounded person quietly wonders:
Does anybody worry about me?
There are families where protecting appearances became more important than protecting the wounded.
There are churches where forgiveness was preached to victims before repentance was demanded from offenders.
There are communities where "grace" became another word for avoiding consequences.
That is not biblical grace.
Grace does not call evil good.
Forgiveness does not require pretending nothing happened.
Repentance is not public-relations management.
And protecting a powerful person's reputation at the expense of the wounded does not glorify Jesus Christ.
Jesus never needed darkness to protect His reputation.
He is the Light.
This is also where we must resist an easy interpretation of David.
David was not merely "the bad father in Tamar's story."
David was a complicated man standing underneath consequences of his own sin.
Only one chapter earlier, David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and orchestrated Uriah's death. Nathan confronted him, and David confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD."
God forgave David.
But forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence.
Nathan had announced that calamity would arise from David's own house.
Then 2 Samuel begins showing the house unraveling.
This does not mean Tamar's violation was her punishment for David's sin.
Absolutely not.
Tamar was not guilty of David's adultery.
Tamar was not responsible for Amnon's violence.
We must never turn a victim into collateral blame in someone else's theology.
But the narrative does force us to confront something about David.
How difficult must it have been for a father compromised by his own sexual sin to discipline a son guilty of sexual wickedness?
Scripture does not explicitly tell us David's inner psychology, so we should not pretend that it does.
But the question is legitimate.
Sometimes yesterday's tolerated sin becomes today's compromised authority.
Sometimes we become hesitant to confront in others what we have excused in ourselves.
We whisper, "Who am I to judge?"
But there is a difference between hypocritical condemnation and righteous accountability.
Repentance does not disqualify you from calling evil evil.
Repentance should make you more serious about it.
David knew grace.
What Tamar needed was a father transformed enough by grace to stand for what was right.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being about David.
Because now it is looking at us.
Where are you when Tamar needs justice?
Where are you when someone tells you what happened?
Where are you when believing them might cost you a friendship?
Where are you when truth threatens the reputation of someone you admire?
Where are you when the offender is talented?
Popular?
Generous?
Powerful?
Family?
Where are you when confronting darkness might create a scandal?
Maybe the question is even closer.
Where were you when somebody needed you?
That question hurts.
Maybe you stayed silent.
Maybe you protected someone you should have confronted.
Maybe you were more frightened of embarrassment than injustice.
Maybe you called avoidance "peace."
Maybe you called cowardice "wisdom."
Maybe you encouraged someone to forgive because you did not want to deal with what repentance and accountability would actually require.
If conviction is rising in you, do not run from it.
Run to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people never fail.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be confronted, forgiven, redeemed, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
David's story itself proves that Scripture does not sanitize its heroes.
The Bible could have hidden this chapter.
It didn't.
It could have protected David's legacy.
It didn't.
It could have reduced Tamar to a footnote.
It didn't.
Why?
Because God's truth does not need human heroes to look flawless.
There is only one flawless King.
And His name is Jesus.
David could defeat Goliath but could not save his own household from its corruption.
Jesus is the greater Son of David.
David's kingdom fractured under human sin.
Christ's kingdom is founded upon perfect righteousness.
David heard and became angry.
Jesus sees.
Jesus knows.
Jesus acts.
And at the cross, we discover that God does not solve evil by pretending evil is insignificant.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the blood of the Son of God.
Grace is not God shrugging at wickedness.
Grace is unimaginably costly.
At Calvary, justice and mercy meet.

Jesus bears the judgment sinners deserve so that everyone who repents and believes in Him can be forgiven—not excused, not declared innocent because sin never mattered, but cleansed because Christ paid the debt.
That means the Gospel has a word for the violated.
And it has a word for the violator.
To the wounded:
What happened to you does not have authority to rename you.
Your shame belongs neither on your forehead nor in your identity.
Jesus sees what people ignored.
He hears what others tried to silence.
He is near to the brokenhearted.
Healing may be long. Trauma may leave deep wounds. Seeking safety, wise pastoral care, professional help, lawful justice, and appropriate accountability is not a failure of faith.
And forgiveness, biblically understood, does not mean calling evil acceptable or placing yourself back into danger.
To the sinner:
Do not use grace as camouflage.
Repent.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Stop blaming your childhood, your loneliness, your marriage, temptation, alcohol, pornography, stress, anger, hormones, or the person you wounded.
Call sin what God calls it.
Turn from it.
Come to Christ.
There is forgiveness even for horrifying sinners who truly repent and believe.
That truth should not cheapen justice.
It should magnify the blood of Jesus.
The cross tells us simultaneously:
Your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
And Christ's mercy is greater than your sin can comprehend.
That is scandal becoming grace.
Not because God rewrites history by pretending the evil never happened.
Jesus rewrites everything because He can take what sin intended for destruction and refuse to allow darkness the final word.
He can redeem the sinner.
He can restore the broken.
He can heal what others abandoned.
He can expose what families buried.
He can create testimony where shame demanded silence.
He can take ashes and eventually bring beauty.
And maybe somebody reading this has been Tamar for years.
You kept functioning.
You smiled in photographs.
You went to church.
You served.
You raised children.
You worked.
You laughed when everybody else laughed.
But there is still a locked room somewhere inside your memory.
A door.
A voice.
A betrayal.
And a younger version of yourself asking why nobody came.
Jesus knows that room exists.
You do not have to pretend it never happened in order to prove you have faith.
Bring your wounds to Him.
Not because every memory disappears overnight.
Not because every consequence suddenly vanishes.
But because the Savior who carried scars after the resurrection is not ashamed of wounded people.
And perhaps somebody else reading this is David.
You heard.
You became angry.
But you stayed passive.
There is still time to repent.
There is still time to speak.
There is still time to stop protecting what should have been confronted.
There is still time to apologize without defending yourself.
There is still time to become the person who believes the wounded, pursues truth, protects the vulnerable, demands biblical accountability, and refuses to confuse silence with peace.
And maybe somebody reading this is closer to Amnon than you want to admit.
Your sin may not look like his.
But you have used people.
Manipulated affection.
Consumed bodies through pornography.
Crossed boundaries.
Hidden secret messages.
Turned human beings made in God's image into objects for your appetite.
Stop before your heart becomes harder.
Jesus is calling you into the light.
Repentance will cost your pride.
Unrepentant sin can cost far more.
This is why stories like Tamar's must not disappear beneath comfortable Christianity.
Someone needs to share this.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.

But if Christ has given you truth that could wake someone up, encourage a wounded believer, confront hidden sin, or lead someone toward repentance, then using what you have to spread that truth can become an act of Christian service.
So if this article made you think of somebody, send it to them.
If you have been carrying something silently, you don't have to tell strangers details that should remain private. Simply comment, "Christ is still healing me."
If conviction exposed something you need to bring before God, comment, "Jesus, have mercy on me."
If you have spent too long pretending everything is fine, comment, "No more hiding."
And if you are standing beside somebody whose voice was ignored, comment, "I will not look away."
Sometimes somebody reading the comments needs to discover they are not the only person fighting their way toward the light.
Because there may come a day when anger tempts you toward vengeance, shame tempts you toward hiding, or failure tempts you toward believing God is finished with you.
Come back and remember:
David failed.
Tamar was devastated.
Amnon sinned grievously.
Absalom chose vengeance.
A royal family fractured.
Yet none of them is the Savior of this story.
Jesus is.
Scripture will not allow us to manipulate people that way.
But if these resources genuinely serve you, financially supporting their continued production can be one practical way you choose to participate in spreading biblical truth.
Not to make our name greater.
To help make Christ known.
And before you leave Tamar standing in the pages of 2 Samuel, hear the question one final time.
Where was David when Tamar needed justice?
Then allow the Holy Spirit to turn the question around.
Where will you be when the wounded person God places in your path needs someone courageous enough to listen?
Because perhaps one of the most haunting tragedies in Tamar's story is not merely that an evil man hurt her.
It is that the people who knew something terrible had happened could not give her back what had been taken.
But Jesus enters stories human beings cannot repair.
He does not erase the truth.
He redeems people inside it.
He does not call darkness light.
He brings light into darkness.
He does not tell the shattered that their wounds never mattered.
He shows them His own scars.
And He does not offer sinners permission to remain what they were.
He says:
Follow Me.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Become new.
The scream people failed to answer was never too distant for God to hear.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF GOD WASN’T ASHAMED TO PUT BREASTS, KISSING, SEMEN, MENSTRUATION, DESIRE, AND MARITAL PLEASURE IN SCRIPTURE—WHY ARE WE ASHAMED TO READ IT?
paragraphs: IF GOD WASN’T ASHAMED TO PUT BREASTS, KISSING, SEMEN, MENSTRUATION, DESIRE, AND MARITAL PLEASURE IN SCRIPTURE—WHY ARE WE ASHAMED TO READ IT?

Maybe the problem was never that the Bible talks about the human body too openly. Maybe the problem is that we have spent so long letting pornography, shame, abuse, lust, and religious embarrassment define these words that we have forgotten God spoke about the body first.
There are verses some Christians read loudly.
And there are verses we suddenly read very, very quietly.
We proclaim John 3:16 without hesitation.
We underline Romans 8.
We quote Psalm 23 at funerals.
We put Philippians 4:13 on shirts, coffee mugs, journals, and Facebook posts.
But then we arrive at the Song of Songs.
And suddenly everybody starts clearing their throat.
We meet a woman speaking about kisses.
A husband praising his wife's breasts.
A wife delighting in being desired.
We turn to Leviticus and find Scripture discussing semen and menstruation with an almost startling matter-of-factness.
We find Proverbs telling a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth and delight in her love.
And some of us instinctively want to close the Bible.
Not because God became inappropriate.
Because somewhere along the way, we became uncomfortable with something God was never embarrassed to acknowledge.
Read that again.
The God who thundered from Sinai is not embarrassed by the human body.
The God who inspired Scripture did not need us to censor Him.

And maybe some of the shame Christians carry today exists precisely because we have allowed the world to talk endlessly about sexuality while the Church has sometimes responded with little more than silence, awkwardness, warnings, or whispers.
So pornography discipled people.
Movies discipled people.
Hookup culture discipled people.
Trauma discipled people.
Locker rooms discipled people.
Social media discipled people.
Secret browser histories discipled people.
And then many Christians walked into marriage carrying desires they did not understand, wounds they never named, expectations shaped by fantasy, and shame they mistakenly thought came from God.
But what if we went back?
Not back to culture.
Back to Scripture.
Back before pornography stole desire.
Back before lust distorted intimacy.
Back before abuse weaponized vulnerability.
Back before shame convinced people that their bodies were inherently filthy.
Back to the God who created humanity male and female and looked upon His creation and called it “very good” (Genesis 1:27, 31).
Because the Bible does not begin with embarrassed bodies.
It begins with naked people who had no shame.
Genesis 2:25 says the man and his wife were both naked, “and were not ashamed.”
Then sin entered.
And what appeared almost immediately?
Hiding.
Covering.
Fear.
“I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10).
Do you see the tragedy?
God created the body.
Sin introduced shame.
And ever since Eden, humanity has been confusing the two.
Some people worship the body.
Others despise it.
Some exploit it.
Others pretend it barely exists.
The Gospel does neither.
Christianity does not teach that matter is evil and spirituality means escaping physical existence. At the center of Christianity stands one of the most astonishing declarations imaginable:
The Word became flesh.
Jesus Christ did not rescue humanity by refusing embodiment.
He entered it.
He was conceived.
Born.
Held.
Hungry.
Thirsty.
Tired.
Touched.
Wounded.
Crucified in a real human body.
Raised bodily from the dead.
The Christian story is not God saying the body does not matter.
It is God entering His creation to redeem fallen human beings completely.
Which makes our embarrassment about some biblical language worth examining.
Open Song of Songs 1:2 and the Hebrew does not blush:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
Literally, the woman longs for the kisses of her beloved's mouth.
The Hebrew verb is not secretly describing a committee meeting.
It means kissing.
The text itself speaks openly of kisses and love.
And notice something Christians sometimes miss.
The woman speaks.
She desires.
She expresses affection.
She is not presented merely as an object being desired by a man.
Her voice fills the poem.
Later she says:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.”
That word תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah carries the idea of desire or longing.
She knows she is desired.
And within the poetry of Song of Songs, that knowledge is not presented as inherently dirty.
Then there are the breasts.
Yes.
Breasts.
Not a modern addition.
Not something inserted by a corrupt translator.
The Hebrew word שַׁד — shad, with the dual form שָׁדַיִם — shadayim, means breasts. It appears repeatedly in Scripture, including several times in Song of Songs.
Song of Songs speaks poetically and appreciatively about the beloved's body.
Why?
Because biblical holiness is not the denial that bodies exist.
Holiness is the ordering of the whole person under God.
That distinction changes everything.
Pornography says, “Consume this body.”
Lust says, “Use this person in your imagination.”
Abuse says, “Your boundaries do not matter.”
Promiscuity says, “Covenant does not matter.”
Shame says, “Your body itself is disgusting.”
But biblical marital love says something profoundly different:
“You are not a product.
You are not pornography.
You are not an object.
You are a person bearing God's image, worthy of dignity, fidelity, tenderness, honor, and covenant love.”
Scripture can celebrate marital affection without endorsing lust because desire and lust are not identical things.
Sin did not invent attraction.
Sin corrupts God's gifts.
Food is good; gluttony corrupts appetite.
Money can serve good purposes; greed corrupts stewardship.
Authority can protect; domination corrupts authority.
Sexuality belongs to God's created order; sexual sin distorts it.
And perhaps that is why Satan gains so much ground whenever Christians decide the answer to sexual corruption is simply never to speak honestly about sexuality.
Silence does not create innocence.
Sometimes silence simply leaves someone else holding the microphone.
Then we reach Leviticus.
Surely, we imagine, the Bible will become vague there.
It does not.
Leviticus 15:16 contains the Hebrew expression:
שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע — shikhvat-zera
The verse refers directly to an emission of semen. The Hebrew זֶרַע — zera means “seed,” and in this bodily context the phrase refers to semen.
Later in the same chapter, Scripture addresses a woman's menstrual discharge. The Hebrew text uses נִדָּה — niddah in this ritual-purity context.
God put these realities into Israel's law.
Without pornography.
Without crude entertainment.
Without giggling.
Without pretending biology does not exist.
That distinction matters enormously.
Leviticus 15 is not an erotic passage. It concerns ritual purity under the Mosaic covenant.
And “unclean” in these passages must not carelessly be turned into “morally sinful.”
Those categories are not automatically identical.
That matters because generations of people—especially women—have sometimes absorbed the idea that ordinary bodily processes make them personally disgusting before God.
The text does not give us permission to make that leap.
The chapter addresses ritual states and purification within Israel's covenantal worship system.
Men are addressed.
Women are addressed.
Bodily discharges are addressed.
Human biology is treated seriously.
There is no need to sanitize the passage, and there is certainly no need to weaponize it against someone's dignity.
Then consider Proverbs 5.
The chapter warns a man intensely against adultery.
And what is God's answer to forbidden sexual desire?
It is not, “Become incapable of desire.”
It redirects desire toward covenant faithfulness.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth” (Proverbs 5:18).
Then Scripture describes marital delight in language so intimate that many believers have probably raced through the verses hoping nobody asks them to explain them.
But perhaps we should stop racing.
Because God is teaching something.
Faithfulness is not merely avoiding somebody else's bed.
Marriage is supposed to contain delight.
Tenderness.
Exclusive affection.
Joy.
Desire that has learned covenant instead of consumption.
This is important because there are Christians who know exactly what God says “no” to but have never discovered the beauty behind God's “yes.”
No adultery.
No pornography.
No fornication.
No exploitation.
No lustful consumption of another person.
Yes.
Those boundaries matter.
Jesus Himself takes sexual sin so seriously that He confronts lust at the level of the heart in Matthew 5:27–28.
But if our theology stops with prohibition, we have not told the whole biblical story.
God does not merely redeem people from something.
He redeems us for something.
For holiness.
For faithfulness.
For love.
For self-control.
For covenant.
For the ability to see another human being as an image-bearer rather than an object for consumption.
And this is where some people reading this may feel something painful rising.
Because not everybody hears the word “sexuality” and thinks of marriage.
Some remember what happened to them.
Something stolen.
Something watched.
Something done.
Something they did.
Something they cannot erase from their memory.
A bedroom.
A screen.
A relationship.
An abortion.
An affair.
A secret.
An addiction.
A violation.
A betrayal.
A night you desperately wish you could remove from history.
Maybe you have spent years believing that if Christians really knew everything about you, they would never look at you the same way again.
Maybe you believe Jesus looks at you that way too.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say sin is imaginary.
It says grace is greater.
Jesus never needed to rename darkness “light” in order to forgive sinners.
At the cross, sin is taken so seriously that Christ dies.
And sinners are loved so deeply that Christ dies for them.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Not humiliation.
Redemption.
Remember the woman in John 8 who was dragged into public shame after being caught in adultery.
People stood around her carrying stones.
Jesus did not call adultery holy.
Neither did He surrender the woman to her accusers.
After the accusers departed, His words held grace and transformation together:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Grace did not say, “Nothing happened.”
Grace said, in effect, “What happened will not have the final word.”
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Maybe your story contains a chapter you would never voluntarily read aloud.
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter.
Maybe your sexuality has been distorted by pornography.
Jesus can redeem what lust discipled.
Maybe adultery shattered your marriage.
Repentance cannot make betrayal nonexistent, but Christ can create something beyond the ruins that sin produced.
Maybe somebody violated you.
Their sin does not determine your worth.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you knew were wrong and now conviction is crushing you.
Do not confuse conviction with a sentence of hopelessness.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Hide forever.”
The Gospel says:
Come.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Walk differently.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
That verse is for sexual sin too.
The blood of Jesus does not mysteriously lose its power when the sin becomes embarrassing.
Think about that.
We sing that His blood washes sin.
Then someone confesses pornography and we act as though we discovered an exception.
Someone confesses adultery and we wonder whether grace has enough oxygen to reach that far.
Someone admits years of secret sexual sin and believes their testimony is permanently destroyed.
But Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
David's history contained devastating sexual sin and bloodshed.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The Corinthian church included people rescued from serious sexual immorality, and Paul told them:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Do not miss the miracle hidden inside that grammar.
Your past can be true without being your master.
Your sin can be real without becoming your identity.
Your wounds can be real without becoming your destiny.
Your body can have memories while your soul learns freedom.
You can repent without pretending.
You can heal without rewriting history.
Because Jesus does something infinitely better than pretending the scandal never happened.
He writes grace into the story after it.
This is why Christians must recover the courage to talk biblically about bodies.
Our children need something better than embarrassment.
Teenagers need something stronger than “don't.”
Singles need theology that honors holiness without treating unmarried people as incomplete human beings.
Married couples need permission to understand that covenant affection is not spiritually inferior to prayer, worship, service, or Bible reading simply because it involves the body.
People trapped in pornography need more than shame.
People wounded by sexual abuse need compassion without blame.
People living in sexual sin need truth without hatred.
And everybody needs Jesus.
Because sexual brokenness is not solved merely by becoming more sexually informed.
We need regenerated hearts.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need repentance.
We need grace.
We need a Savior.
Christian sexual ethics are not ultimately about pretending desire does not exist.
They are about surrendering desire to Christ.
Jesus does not merely ask for your church attendance.
He claims your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your browser history.
Your relationships.
Your private messages.
Your fantasies.
Your body.
Your future marriage.
Your present singleness.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your secrets.
All of you.
Paul writes:
There it is.
Not despise your body.
Not worship your body.
Not sell your body.
Not use somebody else's body.
Glorify God in your body.
The Gospel is neither prudish nor pornographic.
It is holy.
And holiness is far more beautiful than either extreme.
So perhaps the question is not:
“Why does the Bible talk about breasts, kisses, semen, menstruation, desire, and marital pleasure?”
Perhaps the more revealing question is:
Why did we ever think God needed our embarrassment to protect His holiness?
God does not need censorship.
He requires faithful interpretation.
Song of Songs is poetry, so read it as poetry.
Leviticus is covenantal law, so read it in its covenantal and ritual context.
Proverbs is wisdom literature, so hear its wisdom.
Jesus' teaching exposes the heart, so let it expose yours.
Paul's teaching on the body calls Christians toward holiness, so surrender your body to Christ.
Context protects us from turning Scripture into either pornography or prudishness.
And Christ stands at the center of the whole Christian story.
Creation tells us the body is God's workmanship.
The Fall explains why desire becomes distorted and shame enters human experience.
The Law demonstrates that God speaks seriously about embodied human life.
Wisdom celebrates faithful covenant love.
The prophets expose spiritual and physical unfaithfulness.
Jesus enters human flesh.
The cross purchases sinners.
The resurrection declares that embodied existence matters.
The Holy Spirit makes believers temples.
And the promised resurrection tells Christians that God is not ultimately throwing His creation away.
He is making all things new.
Maybe this article made you uncomfortable.
Good questions sometimes begin there.
Not because discomfort proves something is true.
But because discomfort can reveal assumptions we have never examined.
So examine them with Scripture open.
If this exposed shame you have been carrying, you do not have to describe your private history publicly.

And if you have already watched Christ redeem an area of your life you once thought could never be restored, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because an algorithm is sacred.
Because somebody you know may be silently drowning in shame while appearing perfectly fine at church.
Send this privately to the person you know is fighting pornography.
Send it to the Christian who has confused holiness with embarrassment.
Send it to the wounded person who needs to hear that what was done to them does not erase their God-given dignity.
Because sooner or later somebody will tell you Christianity teaches that the human body is inherently dirty, and you may need to return to the Scriptures and remember what they actually say.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It cannot.
It doesn't.
Scripture does not give us authority to make those claims.

What Scripture does teach is that Gospel ministry may legitimately receive material support. Paul writes that “the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).
Scripture also guards the giver from spiritual manipulation:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart… not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7)
The Greek is striking:
μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs—
not from grief or reluctance, and not from ἀνάγκη — anankē, necessity, constraint, or compulsion.
That means biblical generosity should never need spiritual blackmail.
And sometimes support costs nothing at all.
One share may place the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
One tag may find somebody on the night they were preparing to give up.
One comment may tell another struggling Christian, “You are not fighting alone.”
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be mission.
Give freely.
Share intentionally.
Tag personally.
Save what strengthens you.
Follow so you can keep growing with us.
But above everything else—
Follow Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church cannot bleed for you.
A Christian product cannot cleanse your conscience.
Only Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
Only Jesus rose from the grave.
Only Jesus can take the parts of your story you are terrified to uncover and bring them beneath the authority of His truth and the mercy of His cross.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear tonight.
God already knows about the body.
He already knows about the desire.
He already knows about the addiction.
He already knows what happened behind that door.
He already knows what appeared on that screen.
He already knows what somebody did to you.
He already knows what you did.
He already knows what you regret.
He already knows what you have been hiding.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Come into the light.
Repent where you have sinned.
Receive grace where you have been forgiven.
Seek healing where you have been wounded.
Learn holiness where desire has been distorted.
Stop calling God's creation dirty.
Stop calling sin harmless.
Stop calling shame repentance.
And stop believing your darkest chapter is powerful enough to steal the pen from Jesus.
The scandal may explain how you arrived here—but grace can determine where your story goes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Church Growth Is Not the Same Thing as Disciple Growth
paragraphs: Church Growth Is Not the Same Thing as Disciple Growth

What if the numbers are rising, the rooms are filling, the posts are spreading, the programs are multiplying—and Jesus is still asking a question our statistics cannot answer: “Are they becoming My disciples?”
There is a kind of success that looks beautiful from the platform.
More people.
More views.
More followers.
More campuses. More programs. More volunteers. More registrations. More hands raised. More people walking through the doors.
And none of those things are necessarily bad.

A crowded church can be a gift from God. A growing ministry can become an instrument through which thousands hear the Gospel. Technology can carry Scripture into homes a preacher may never physically enter. Programs can serve families, strengthen marriages, teach children, feed the hungry, equip believers, and introduce searching people to Jesus Christ.
Numbers matter because numbers represent people.
The book of Acts itself sometimes tells us how many people responded to the Gospel. After Peter preached Christ at Pentecost, approximately three thousand people were added.
But Scripture does something fascinating after mentioning the number.
It tells us what those people became devoted to.
“They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.”
Acts 2:42.
The miracle was not merely that approximately three thousand people appeared on a ministry report.
They began following Jesus together.
That distinction may be one of the most uncomfortable conversations the modern Church needs to have.
Because church growth is not automatically disciple growth.
You can gather a crowd without forming disciples.
You can increase attendance without increasing obedience.
You can build visibility without building spiritual maturity.
You can create excitement without creating endurance.
You can have people who know the worship songs but barely know the Scriptures.
People who know when to raise their hands but do not know how to carry their cross.
People who can quote their favorite preacher but cannot forgive the person who wounded them.
People who want the promises of Jesus while quietly resisting the commands of Jesus.
People who love Christian content but are not actually becoming more like Christ.
And before pastors point at congregations, before congregations point at pastors, perhaps every one of us should allow this question to come closer.
Much closer.
Because this article is not ultimately about “those churches.”
It is about us.
It is about you.
It is about me.
If every statistic disappeared tonight, what evidence would remain that we are actually following Jesus?
That question reaches places attendance numbers cannot.
Jesus gave His Church a commission in Matthew 28:18–20 that should still define Christian success.
After His resurrection, He came to His disciples and declared that all authority in heaven and on earth had been given to Him. Then came the command Christians have repeated for centuries.
The Greek text contains words worth slowing down long enough to hear:
“πορευθέντες οὖν μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη”
Poreuthentes oun mathēteusate panta ta ethnē.
In context: “Therefore, as you go, make disciples of all nations.”
The crucial command is μαθητεύσατε—mathēteusate—from μαθητεύω, mathēteuō.
Make disciples.
Not merely attract spectators.
Not merely accumulate admirers.
Not merely produce religious consumers.
Make disciples.
Jesus continues:
“βαπτίζοντες αὐτοὺς…”
Baptizontes autous…
“Baptizing them…”
And then:
“διδάσκοντες αὐτοὺς τηρεῖν πάντα ὅσα ἐνετειλάμην ὑμῖν”
Didaskontes autous tērein panta hosa eneteilamēn hymin.
“Teaching them to observe everything I have commanded you.”
That word τηρεῖν—tērein—carries the sense of keeping, observing, holding to.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
Teach them merely to know what I commanded.
Teach them merely to agree with what I commanded.
Teach them merely to post what I commanded.
Teach them merely to listen to sermons about what I commanded.
He commissioned His followers to make disciples who are taught to observe what He commanded.
Truth is meant to enter the life.
The Gospel does not merely produce informed listeners.
The Gospel creates transformed followers.
And suddenly our measurements become more uncomfortable.
Because attendance is relatively easy to count.
Obedience is harder.
You can count how many people entered a building.
How do you measure the husband who finally repented to his wife because Christ convicted him of his pride?
You can count video views.
How do you count the woman who closed the door, fell beside her bed, and finally surrendered the secret sin she had protected for years?
You can count followers.
How do you count the teenager who refuses to compromise when nobody from church is watching?
You can count baptisms—and Scripture gives us every reason to celebrate baptism.
But discipleship does not stop when someone comes out of the water.
The Great Commission includes teaching baptized believers to live under the commands of Jesus.
That means Christianity was never intended to become a weekly religious event surrounded by an otherwise self-governed life.
Jesus did not die and rise again merely to improve our Sundays.
He claims us.
Our relationships.
Our money.
Our sexuality.
Our ambitions.
Our grudges.
Our private habits.
Our screens.
Our mouths.
Our schedules.
Our hidden rooms.
Our reputations.
Our dreams.
Our wounds.
Our future.
Everything.
This is where disciple growth begins to hurt.
Crowds can celebrate Jesus while discipleship confronts us with Jesus.
Crowds ask, “What can I receive?”
Disciples eventually learn to ask, “Lord, what must change in me?”
And Scripture never romanticizes the difference.
In John 6, Jesus had an enormous crowd around Him after feeding the multitude. Yet when His teaching became difficult, many who had been following Him turned away.
John records one of the saddest sentences in the Gospel:
“After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.”
Then Jesus turned to the Twelve and asked whether they wanted to leave too.
Peter answered:
“Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
There it is.
The difference between attraction and allegiance.
Some stayed while the bread was multiplying.
Peter stayed because he had begun to understand who Jesus was.
That is discipleship.
Not “Jesus is useful to me.”
But “Where else would I go?”
Not “I follow Him while following Him improves my life.”
But “Even when I do not understand everything, He is Lord.”
That kind of Christianity cannot be manufactured by marketing.
It cannot be produced by better lighting.
It cannot be sustained by emotional music.
It cannot be substituted with branding.
None of those things are automatically sinful. Excellence can honor God. Communication matters. Hospitality matters. Creativity matters. Stewardship matters.
But none of them can do what only the Holy Spirit working through the Word of God and the Gospel of Jesus Christ can do.
Paul understood this.
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”
1 Corinthians 3:6.
God gives the growth.
That truth should humble both the discouraged small church and the celebrated large church.
The small congregation should not automatically assume small numbers mean failure.
The large congregation should not automatically assume large numbers mean faithfulness.
The question is not simply, “Are we growing?”
The deeper question is, “What are we growing into?”
Because a ministry can become larger without becoming deeper.
A Christian can become busier without becoming holier.
A person can consume sermons for twenty years while remaining spiritually immature in the same areas nobody is permitted to confront.
And perhaps that person is reading this right now.
Maybe you know Christian language.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know the verses.
You know the worship playlists.
You know how to look strong around believers.
But somewhere underneath the Christian appearance, you know there are doors Jesus has been knocking on that you have kept locked.
A relationship you refuse to surrender.
Bitterness you continue feeding.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Pride disguised as discernment.
Gossip disguised as concern.
Greed disguised as ambition.
Prayerlessness hidden beneath busyness.
A hunger for recognition disguised as ministry.
A public Christianity that has become stronger than your private communion with Christ.
And maybe the hardest sentence in this entire article is this:
You can be surrounded by Christian activity and still resist Christian discipleship.
That should not drive us into hopelessness.
It should drive us to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of impressive people successfully proving their devotion to God.
It is the story of sinners rescued by grace.
Peter himself is proof.
The man who said, “Lord, to whom shall we go?” would later deny that he even knew Jesus.
Three times.
Peter collapsed under pressure.
His courage disappeared.
His promises failed.
The disciple became the scandal.
And yet Jesus was not finished with him.
After the resurrection, Christ restored Peter.
Not by pretending the failure never happened.
Not by redefining denial as faithfulness.
Not by calling sin harmless.
Jesus brought Peter face-to-face with love, calling, and restoration.
Grace did not tell Peter his failure did not matter.
Grace refused to let his failure have the final word.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not save us because our discipleship record is impressive.
He saves sinners through His finished work—through His death for our sins and His victorious resurrection—and then calls those He saves to follow Him.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace brings us into a new life under a new King.
This is why genuine discipleship contains repentance.
Repentance is not a humiliating entrance fee Christians pay before God finally decides to love them.
It is the turning of a heart that has encountered the truth and mercy of God.
Jesus receives sinners.
Then He changes sinners.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He teaches.
He disciplines.
He transforms.
He takes people with histories that should have buried them and gives them testimonies that point beyond themselves.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe this is why the Church cannot afford to confuse audiences with disciples.
An audience watches.
A disciple follows.
An audience can disappear when the message becomes uncomfortable.
A disciple may stumble, wrestle, question, cry, fail, repent, get back up—and continue following Christ.
An audience wants inspiration.
A disciple needs transformation.
An audience may ask whether the sermon was good.
A disciple eventually asks whether the Word is changing the way he or she lives.
And churches need more than impressive weekends.
We need men who know how to repent.
Women who know who they are in Christ.
Fathers who pray with their children.
Mothers who know Scripture.
Young people who can withstand temptation when culture calls holiness foolish.
Older believers who pour decades of wisdom into younger believers.
Christians who forgive.
Christians who confess.
Christians who serve when nobody applauds.
Christians who give without needing recognition.
Christians who can suffer without abandoning Christ.
Christians who can open Scripture for themselves and faithfully handle what it says.
Christians who know the Gospel well enough to share it.
Christians who make disciples who make disciples.
Paul described this kind of multiplication when he told Timothy:
“What you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.”
2 Timothy 2:2.
Look at the movement.
Paul.
Timothy.
Faithful people.
Others also.
The Gospel keeps moving through people whose lives become channels through which truth reaches another generation.
That is growth heaven understands even when social media never notices it.
The grandmother teaching her grandson to pray.
The pastor faithfully shepherding eighty people without ever becoming famous.
The young believer opening Scripture with a struggling friend.
The former addict telling another broken person where mercy found him.
The businessman refusing dishonest profit because Jesus is Lord.
The woman forgiving someone she once swore she would hate forever.
The believer deleting what keeps dragging him toward sin.
The exhausted Christian whispering, “Jesus, help me,” and choosing obedience one more time.
No spotlight.
No viral clip.
