A damaged kingdom around him.
Idols throughout the land.
A crown far too heavy for a child.
His ancestry gave him every excuse to continue the pattern.
But eventually...
the boy sought God.
The idols fell.
The neglected Word was opened.
The king humbled himself.
The covenant was remembered.
And worship returned.
Yet even Josiah's remarkable faithfulness could not permanently heal Judah or erase its sin.
The world still needed a better King.
So God sent One.
Jesus.
The King who did not inherit our corruption but stepped into our broken world.
The King who never sinned.
The King crowned with thorns.
The King whose throne of suffering became a cross.
The King who carried the judgment His people deserved.
The King who entered death and walked out alive.
The King who does more than renovate ruined temples.
He raises the dead.
So when the enemy points at your history and says, “This is where you came from,” point to the cross and remember whose you can become.
When shame tells you your worst chapter is your identity, remember Jesus.
When family history whispers that nothing will ever change, remember Josiah—and then look beyond Josiah to Christ.
When God's Word exposes you, do not run from the wound of conviction.
Run toward the Savior.
Tear down the idols.
Stop protecting the secret.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
Because the most important thing about Josiah was never that an eight-year-old boy wore a crown.
It was that the God of grace could write a different story through a life surrounded by the wreckage of sin.
And the greatest news of the Gospel is that the same God still calls sinners out of darkness through Jesus Christ.
Your family history may explain some of your scars.
Your sin may explain some of your ruins.
Your past may explain why certain battles are so difficult.
But none of those things has the authority to be your savior, your master, or your final identity.
Jesus Christ does not merely edit the ending.
He makes sinners new.
So perhaps the question is no longer...
“What did I inherit?”
Perhaps the question is...
“What will I surrender to the King?”
Because sometimes the most powerful evidence that grace has entered a family is that the pattern everybody expected to continue...
ends with someone who finally bows to Jesus.
You may have inherited the ruins—but in Christ, you do not have to hand the ruins to the next generation.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HATE THE SIN, LOVE THE SINNER” — DID JESUS ACTUALLY SAY THIS?
paragraphs:
“HATE THE SIN, LOVE THE SINNER” — DID JESUS ACTUALLY SAY THIS?
Jesus never spoke those exact words. What He actually said is far more uncomfortable to the self-righteous, far more merciful to the broken, and far more powerful than the slogan we keep repeating.
There is a sentence Christians have repeated so often that many people assume it came straight from the mouth of Jesus:
“Hate the sin, love the sinner.”
It sounds biblical.
It sounds balanced.
It sounds like something Jesus could have said.
But He didn’t.
Not in Matthew.
Not in Mark.
Not in Luke.
Not in John.
You can search the recorded words of Christ and you will not find Jesus saying, “Hate the sin, love the sinner.”
And before someone panics, this does not mean Christians are supposed to stop calling sin sin.
Jesus never softened sin into something harmless.
He spoke about repentance.
He spoke about judgment.
He spoke about hell.
He spoke about adultery, hypocrisy, greed, lust, unbelief, unforgiveness, pride, and the corruption that comes from the human heart.
Jesus was not afraid of offending people with truth.
But here is where things become uncomfortable.
Jesus was also not afraid of offending religious people with grace.
And perhaps that is why this question matters more than we realize.
Because sometimes a sentence can contain an element of truth and still become a shield behind which we hide a heart that does not resemble Christ.
We say, “I hate the sin but love the sinner.”
Jesus says:
“Love your enemies.”
That is harder.
Much harder.
In Matthew 5:44, the Greek text records:
“ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν”
agapate tous echthrous hymōn
“Love your enemies.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
“Tolerate them.”
“Love them only after they change.”
“Make sure they know how disgusted you are first.”
“Love the respectable sinners but despise the really bad ones.”
No.
“Love your enemies.”
And suddenly Christianity stops being a slogan and becomes a cross.
Because anybody can love someone whose failures are socially acceptable to them.
Anybody can show mercy toward the sins they personally understand.
Anybody can be compassionate toward someone whose brokenness resembles their own.
But what happens when you encounter the person whose sin disgusts you?
What happens when their choices make you angry?
What happens when they have wounded people?
What happens when they represent everything you oppose?
What happens when the sinner is not somebody “out there” but your son?
Your daughter?
Your husband?
Your wife?
Your parent?
Your friend?
What happens when the sinner...
is you?
That is where the slogan begins to crack open.
Because Christianity was never the story of righteous people standing safely at a distance from sinners.
Christianity is the story of a holy God coming near to them.
And if you are wondering how near...
He came close enough to be crucified.
There is something we must establish clearly.
Sin is real.
Sin destroys.
Sin separates humanity from God.
Sin is not merely trauma, imperfection, personal preference, or an unfortunate mistake.
The New Testament commonly uses the Greek word ἁμαρτία — hamartia — for sin.
Scripture's diagnosis of humanity is devastatingly universal:
“πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον”
pantes gar hēmarton
“For all have sinned.”
Romans 3:23.
All.
Not “those people.”
Not just atheists.
Not just addicts.
Not just adulterers.
Not just criminals.
Not just sexually immoral people.
Not just corrupt politicians.
Not just hypocritical churchgoers.
Not just whoever happens to be the target of Christian outrage this week.
All.
That means before I point across the street...
I have to look into the mirror.
Before I speak about “the sinner,” I have to remember something Christianity will never allow me to forget:
I am talking about a category that includes me.
And so are you.

That does not erase meaningful distinctions between sins, consequences, victims, responsibilities, or earthly justice. Scripture does not teach that every sinful act produces identical earthly consequences.
But before the holiness of God, none of us gets to build our home on the moral high ground.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
And then comes the part we often forget.
Romans does not stop at verse 23.
The thought continues into Romans 3:24:
“δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι”
dikaioumenoi dōrean tē autou chariti
“being justified freely by His grace.”
Read those words again.
Freely.
By His grace.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not pretending everybody is fine.
Not changing God's commandments whenever culture changes.
But guilty people being justified by grace because Someone else paid what they could never pay.
This is where Jesus destroys both cheap tolerance and loveless religion.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
The cross says sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
But the cross also says the sinner mattered enough for Christ to come.
That distinction changes everything.
Think about Jesus at a dinner table.
Religious people noticed something scandalous about Him.
He kept eating with the wrong people.
Tax collectors.
People with terrible reputations.
People respectable religious society preferred to keep at arm's length.
Matthew 9 tells us that tax collectors and sinners were reclining at the table with Jesus and His disciples.
The Pharisees noticed.
Of course they noticed.
“Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
There is an entire theology of superiority hidden inside that question.
Why is He so close to them?
Why does He sit with them?
Why doesn't He keep His distance?
Doesn't He know what kind of people they are?
Jesus heard them.
And His response should still shake churches.
“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”
Then He tells them to learn what this means:
“I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.”
And then:
“For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Do not misunderstand Him.
Jesus is not saying sin is healthy.
His physician metaphor says precisely the opposite.
Something is desperately wrong.
People need healing.
People need rescue.
People need repentance.
People need salvation.
But doctors do not heal sick people by standing outside the hospital shouting about how disgusting disease is.
They come close.
Jesus came close.
And His closeness was not approval.
It was rescue.
That distinction desperately needs to return to Christian witness.
You can love someone without approving everything they do.
You can tell someone the truth without humiliating them.
You can disagree without dehumanizing.
You can call sin what God calls sin without treating the person trapped in it as though they are beyond redemption.
You can have biblical convictions without developing a Pharisee's heart.
Because the Gospel does not ask us to choose between truth and love.
Jesus embodied both.
John 1:14 describes Him as:
“πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας”
plērēs charitos kai alētheias
“full of grace and truth.”
Not fifty percent grace and fifty percent truth.
Full of grace.
Full of truth.
We often separate what Jesus perfectly held together.
Some want grace without truth.
That eventually becomes permission.
Others want truth without grace.
That eventually becomes cruelty.
Jesus gives neither.
He looks at sin with perfect holiness and at sinners with astonishing mercy.
And nobody demonstrates this more powerfully than Jesus Himself.
Consider Zacchaeus.
A tax collector.
Not merely unpopular.
A man participating in a system notorious for exploitation.
Jesus sees him in a tree.
And instead of shouting:
“Zacchaeus! Fix your life and maybe I'll speak to you afterward!”
Jesus says He must stay at his house.
Again...
scandal.
People grumbled.
“He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.”
There it is again.
The scandal of grace.
But watch what happens when grace enters the house.
Zacchaeus changes.
He promises radical restitution.
He gives.
He makes wrongs right.
And Jesus declares that salvation has come to the house.
Then Jesus gives us one of the clearest descriptions of His mission:
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
Luke 19:10.
Not merely identify the lost.
Not mock the lost.
Not build an audience by raging at the lost.
Seek them.
Save them.
There is an enormous difference.
And Christians should ask ourselves a painful question:
When sinners encounter us, do they feel the holiness of Christ calling them out of darkness...
or merely our disgust telling them they are unwanted?
Because disgust cannot save anybody.
Outrage cannot regenerate a heart.
Shame cannot resurrect the spiritually dead.
Only Christ can.
And the Gospel is not “become respectable enough that God will finally love you.”
The Gospel is that God acted toward us in Christ while we were still sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν”
eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn
“while we were still sinners...”
Christ died for us.
Still sinners.
Not cleaned-up sinners.
Not church-ready sinners.
Not sinners who finally had their theology perfectly organized.
Still sinners.
That should destroy spiritual arrogance.
Because if Christ waited until you deserved His love...
He would still be waiting.
And so would I.
This is where “hate the sin, love the sinner” can become dangerous if we use it carelessly.

The problem is not necessarily the desire behind the phrase. Christians rightly understand that love does not require approving evil. Scripture itself commands believers to abhor evil and cling to what is good. Romans 12:9 says:
“ἀποστυγοῦντες τὸ πονηρόν, κολλώμενοι τῷ ἀγαθῷ”
apostygountes to ponēron, kollōmenoi tō agathō
“Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good.”
So yes.
Christians must reject evil.
We cannot rename darkness “light” simply to avoid offending someone.
We cannot celebrate what God calls sin and call that compassion.
Love tells the truth.
But notice the same biblical context.
Romans 12 is overflowing with commands about genuine love, honoring others, patience, generosity, blessing persecutors, refusing vengeance, feeding enemies, overcoming evil with good.
Biblical hatred of evil was never permission to hate people.
And Jesus pushes this even further.
He commands love not merely for difficult people...
but enemies.
Why?
Because that is what the Father is like.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Maybe the person you have been calling “a sinner” is somebody Jesus is asking you to love.
Maybe you have technically defended biblical truth while quietly enjoying someone's humiliation.
Maybe you have reposted their scandal.
Mocked their collapse.
Smiled when somebody you disliked finally got exposed.
Maybe you called it discernment.
Maybe God called it pride.
Maybe you know exactly which verses condemn somebody else's behavior...
but somehow keep skipping the verses confronting your bitterness.
That is the frightening thing about religious pride.
It can memorize Scripture while avoiding repentance.
It can defend holiness while secretly feeding hatred.
It can speak accurately about someone else's sin while remaining completely blind to its own.
Jesus told a story about that too.
A Pharisee and a tax collector entered the temple to pray.
The Pharisee essentially thanked God that he was not like other people.
The tax collector could barely lift his eyes.
His prayer was simple:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
The Greek is piercing:
“ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ”
ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
And Jesus says the tax collector went home justified.
The broken man knew something the religious man had forgotten.
He needed mercy.
Maybe that is what some of us have forgotten.
We became Christians long enough ago that we forgot what it felt like to need rescue.
We learned Christian vocabulary.
We learned worship songs.
We learned theology.
We learned what Christians should condemn.
And somewhere along the road...
we forgot the pit Christ pulled us from.
But grace remembered.
Grace found you.
Grace found me.
Grace entered scandals.
Grace sat at tables.
Grace touched lepers.
Grace welcomed the rejected.
Grace confronted hypocrites.
Grace called sinners to repentance.
Grace carried a cross.
And grace did not stay dead.
This is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But please understand what “rewrites” means.
Jesus does not rewrite God's definition of sin to make us comfortable.
He rewrites the sinner's story through redemption.
He does not tell darkness that it was light all along.
He brings us out of darkness.
He does not tell the guilty that guilt is imaginary.
He provides forgiveness.
He does not tell captives that their chains are beautiful.
He breaks them.
He does not merely improve sinners.
He makes people new.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
That is 2 Corinthians 5:17.
In Christ.
That is the center.
Not moral improvement.
Not Christian branding.
Not political identity.
Not respectability.
Not winning arguments on Facebook.
Christ.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And that means there is something even more important than asking:
“Did Jesus say, ‘Hate the sin, love the sinner’?”
The better question is:
How did Jesus actually love sinners?
He came near without becoming corrupted by their sin.
He told truth without surrendering compassion.
He offered mercy without pretending repentance was unnecessary.
He forgave.
He restored.
He confronted.
He called.
He sought.
He sacrificed Himself.
He died.
And He rose.
That is the pattern.
So maybe instead of spending our lives repeating a sentence Jesus never said, we should spend our lives obeying the sentences He actually did say.
“Love your enemies.”
“Judge not, that you be not judged.”
“Whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them.”
“Forgive.”
“Follow Me.”
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
And yes...
“Go, and sin no more.”
Truth and grace.
Again.
Always.
Jesus does not save us so we can comfortably remain enslaved to what destroys us.
Grace is not God's permission slip for sin.
Grace is God's rescue of sinners.
Titus 2 says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness.
Real grace transforms.
Real grace teaches.
Real grace sometimes wounds our pride before healing our hearts.
And perhaps this article is doing that to somebody right now.
Maybe you opened this expecting ammunition against somebody else's sin.
And somehow Jesus turned the mirror toward you.
Maybe the sin you need to hate today is not theirs.
Maybe it is your pride.
Your secret pornography.
Your adultery.
Your gossip.
Your greed.
Your unforgiveness.
Your envy.
Your self-righteousness.
Your hatred.
Your hidden double life.
Your addiction.
Your dishonesty.
Your cruelty.
Your religious performance.
Your refusal to forgive the person who wounded you.
Maybe you have spent years pointing at the darkness in everyone else because looking at your own became unbearable.
But listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
The thing you are hiding?
He knows.
The thing nobody at church knows?
He knows.
The browser history.
The private messages.
The resentment.
The secret relationship.
The relapse.
The lie.
The thoughts you would be terrified for anybody else to hear.
He knows.
And He is still calling you.
Not deeper into hiding.
Out.
Into the light.
This is where conviction becomes beautiful.
Because the hand exposing the wound is the hand pierced to heal you.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because you were almost good enough.
He went because you could never save yourself.
At the cross, God's hatred of sin and God's love toward sinners are not cheap slogans.
They become blood and wood and nails and mercy.
The sinless Son bears judgment.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
Justice is not dismissed.
Grace is not sentimentalized.
And the sinner who comes to Christ empty-handed discovers something astonishing:
There is mercy here.
There is forgiveness here.
There is a new beginning here.
There is no scandal too filthy for the blood of Jesus to cleanse when a sinner truly turns to Him.
No past so permanent that Christ cannot redeem it.
No chain stronger than His power.
No grave deeper than His resurrection.
That does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean victims should be forced into unsafe situations.
It does not mean justice becomes unnecessary.
It does not mean repentance is merely saying sorry.
Biblical grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Grace is God doing what we could never do for ourselves and transforming those who belong to Christ.
So if you are reading this while carrying a secret...
stop running.
If you have wandered from Jesus...
come home.
If religion made you proud...
repent.
If shame convinced you God could never receive you...
look at the cross.
If you have been using truth as a weapon instead of carrying it with tears...
repent.
If you have been calling evil good because you feared rejection...
repent.
Every road eventually arrives at the same place.
Jesus.
Not “those sinners.”
Us.
You.
Me.
All of us standing before the cross with empty hands.
And maybe the most Christlike way to say “hate the sin, love the sinner” is not to say it at all.
Maybe it is to live something deeper:
Abhor evil.
Cling to good.
Tell the truth.
Love your enemy.
Seek the lost.
Call sinners to repentance.
Forgive as you have been forgiven.
And never forget that you stand by grace.
If this exposed something you have been hiding behind religion, do not perform for anybody.
Just be honest.
Sometimes the beginning of freedom is finally refusing to hide.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
There may come a day when somebody you love confesses something that shocks you, and before you react, you may need to remember how Jesus dealt with sinners...
and how Jesus dealt with you.
It does not. The Gospel cannot be bought, salvation cannot be purchased, and God's grace is not for sale.
If you have received something spiritually valuable here, help put it in front of somebody who may never search for it themselves.
Invite someone to follow.
Do you know Jesus?
Have you repented?
Are you trusting Him rather than your own goodness?
Because one day you will not stand before God holding a Christian slogan.
You will stand before Him needing a Savior.
And there is only One.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
King forever.
The question was, “Hate the sin, love the sinner—did Jesus actually say this?”
No.
He said something harder.
He showed something greater.
And then He stretched out His arms on a cross and demonstrated just how far holy love was willing to go to rescue sinners like us.
You were never the scandal Jesus was afraid to touch—you were the sinner He was willing to bleed to redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Masturbation Become a False Comfort?
paragraphs:
Can Masturbation Become a False Comfort?
When the Thing That Soothes You Starts Quietly Owning You
There are nights when nobody knows.
The room is quiet.
The phone is close.
The loneliness is louder than usual.
Maybe you are not even thinking about sex at first.
Maybe you are thinking about rejection.
Stress.
A marriage that feels cold.
A relationship that ended.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
The pressure you carried all day.
The memories you wish you could erase.
Or simply that strange emptiness that settles over the soul when everyone else has gone to sleep.
And you want relief.
Not necessarily rebellion.
Not necessarily some dramatic declaration that you are walking away from God.
Just relief.
Something that will make the ache disappear for a few minutes.
And that is where this conversation becomes deeper than masturbation.
Because sometimes the most spiritually dangerous question is not merely:
“Is this sexual act sinful?”
Sometimes the deeper question is:
“What am I asking this behavior to do for my soul that I should be bringing to God?”
Stay with that question.
Because it may uncover something you have been fighting for years without understanding why you keep returning to it.
The Bible does not contain a verse that explicitly says, “You shall not masturbate.”
That needs to be stated clearly.
Christians should never pretend Scripture says something it does not say.

Genesis 38 is sometimes used as though Onan’s sin were simply masturbation, but the passage describes something different: Onan deliberately refused his covenantal responsibility to provide offspring for his deceased brother while exploiting the sexual relationship for himself. We should not force that passage to say more than it actually says.
But saying that Scripture never explicitly names masturbation does not mean Scripture has nothing meaningful to say about it.
The Bible speaks profoundly about sexual desire.
About lust.
About the imagination.
About self-control.
About enslavement.
About the body.
About secrecy.
About worship.
About comfort.
And ultimately about what happens when a human heart repeatedly runs somewhere other than God for salvation from its pain.
That is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
Can masturbation become a false comfort?
Yes.
Not because an orgasm possesses some mystical power that automatically separates a person from God.
But because almost anything can become spiritually disordered when we repeatedly ask it to give us what only God can ultimately provide.
Food can become comfort.
Alcohol can become comfort.
Work can become comfort.
Shopping can become comfort.
Entertainment can become comfort.
Attention can become comfort.
Pornography can become comfort.
Sex can become comfort.
And masturbation can become comfort too.
The issue is not merely what your hands are doing.
The issue may be where your heart is running.
Jesus repeatedly went beneath visible behavior and exposed the hidden movements of the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The Greek expression translated “to lust after her” contains the verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire, long for, or covet. Desire itself is not automatically sinful; context determines its moral character. Here Christ is confronting sexual desire that deliberately turns another person into the object of covetous consumption.
Jesus takes holiness into places nobody else can see.
The imagination.
The intention.
The private gaze.
The secret appetite.

That matters enormously when discussing masturbation because, for many people, masturbation is intertwined with pornography, sexual fantasy, remembered images, imagined bodies, or the deliberate cultivation of lust.
At that point the Christian cannot honestly reduce the question to:
“Where does the Bible specifically mention masturbation?”
The more revealing question becomes:
“What am I feeding in my heart while I do it?”
And perhaps an even deeper one:
“Why do I need this right now?”
That question can hurt.
Because sometimes the answer is not:
“I am overwhelmed with sexual desire.”
Sometimes the answer is:
“I feel unwanted.”
“I feel anxious.”
“I am lonely.”
“I am angry.”
“I cannot sleep.”
“I hate myself tonight.”
“I had a terrible day.”
“My spouse rejected me.”
“I miss someone.”
“I feel numb.”
“I need something to make me feel good.”
“I don't want to think anymore.”
Suddenly the struggle looks different.
You thought you were fighting a sexual habit.
You may also have been trying to medicate a wounded heart.
And if that is true, shame alone will never heal you.
You can hate the behavior and still return to it because you have never addressed the wound underneath it.
This is one reason Paul's words in 1 Corinthians are so penetrating.
He writes:
The Greek phrase behind “I will not be dominated” uses ἐξουσιασθήσομαι — exousiasthēsomai, carrying the sense of being brought under another's authority or mastery.
That gives us an extraordinarily useful biblical question.
Not merely:
“Can I technically do this?”
But:
“Is this mastering me?”
Can you say no?
Can you experience loneliness without immediately needing sexual release?
Can you experience anxiety without reaching automatically for pornography or fantasy?
Can you lie awake uncomfortable without needing the familiar escape?
Can you feel rejection without soothing yourself sexually?
Can you go without it without becoming restless, irritable, preoccupied, or consumed?
Can you bring the urge before Christ rather than obeying it immediately?
Because there is a difference between experiencing desire and being ruled by desire.
Paul tells believers in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and concludes:
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
Think about the dignity contained in that sentence.
Your body is not garbage.
Your sexuality is not garbage.
Your sexual desire does not make you disgusting.
Christian holiness is not hatred of the human body.
Christianity makes the astonishing claim that the body matters so much that Christ redeemed the whole person and promises bodily resurrection.
Your body belongs to the Lord.
Which means the Christian question is not simply:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
It becomes:
“How can this body glorify the One who purchased me with His blood?”
That changes everything.
Because now sexuality is no longer merely about release.
It becomes discipleship.
And discipleship includes learning that not every desire must immediately become an action.
Paul names ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia, self-control, among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23.
Self-control is not pretending desire does not exist.
It is not becoming emotionally numb.
It is not despising sexuality.
It is the Spirit-produced freedom to experience a desire without becoming its servant.
There is tremendous freedom in realizing:
An urge is not a command.
You can feel something without obeying it.
You can experience temptation without surrendering to it.
You can experience loneliness without anesthetizing it.
You can experience sexual tension without believing you will collapse unless you release it immediately.
And sometimes the moment between desire and action becomes holy ground.
Because that is where you discover what actually owns you.
Maybe you have promised God a hundred times:
“Never again.”
Then three days later you fell.
Maybe three hours later.
Maybe twenty minutes later.
Then came the familiar disgust.
“How could I pray after doing that?”
“How could God still want me?”
“I promised Him.”
“I knew better.”
“I am filthy.”
“I am fake.”
“I should hide.”
And this is where another enemy enters the room.
Not merely lust.
Shame.
Shame tells you that because you fell, you should run away from the only Person who can restore you.
But watch what happens after humanity's first sin.
Adam tells God in Genesis 3:
“I was afraid... and I hid myself.”
Sin has been teaching human beings to hide ever since.
Hide the browser history.
Hide the fantasies.
Hide the habit.
Hide from your spouse.
Hide from your pastor.
Hide from your Christian friends.
And eventually...
hide from God.
But hiding does not heal what grace is inviting into the light.
The apostle John writes:
The Gospel does not say:
“Clean yourself thoroughly enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you again.”
The Gospel says something far more scandalous.
Christ came for sinners.
Real ones.
Secret ones.
Repeat offenders.
People whose browser histories would humiliate them.
People whose imaginations would horrify them if projected onto a church screen.
People who love Jesus and still find themselves fighting desires they wish had disappeared years ago.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Romans 5:8 says:
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you became impressive.
Not after thirty flawless days.
Not after your sexuality became perfectly ordered.
While we were still sinners.
Jesus walked knowingly toward the cross.
The nails entered His hands.
His blood was poured out.
The innocent Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserved.
And He rose from the grave.
That means your darkest sexual failure does not get the final sentence over your life.
Jesus does.
This is where repentance must be rescued from misunderstanding.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia refers to repentance, a turning associated with a changed mind and direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling disgusting after orgasm.
Regret is not necessarily repentance.
Self-hatred is not repentance.
Crying is not automatically repentance.
Repentance turns.
It brings darkness into light.
It stops defending what God is exposing.
It asks what feeds the pattern.
It removes what repeatedly leads toward sin.
It seeks accountability where needed.
It learns to flee instead of negotiate.
It receives forgiveness while pursuing transformation.
Paul's instruction in 2 Timothy 2:22 is remarkably practical:
“Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace.”
Notice both movements.
Flee.
And...
pursue.
Christian freedom is not achieved merely by spending your entire life saying:
“Don't masturbate. Don't masturbate. Don't masturbate.”
Because a soul obsessed with avoiding darkness may still have no idea how to live in the light.
You need something greater to pursue.
Christ.
Prayer.
Friendship.
Service.
Scripture.
Meaningful work.
Healthy exercise.
Rest.
Community.
Marriage honored faithfully where applicable.
Honest conversations.
Serving hurting people.
Learning to sit before God without entertainment constantly drowning out your interior life.
You do not merely remove false comfort.
You discover a better Comforter.
Jesus said in Matthew 11:28:
“Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
Read those words again.
Come to Me.
That invitation reaches far beyond sexual temptation.
Come to Me when you are lonely.
Come to Me when rejection burns.
Come to Me when the memories return.
Come to Me when your body is screaming for release.
Come to Me when pornography is one tap away.
Come to Me when you have already failed.
Come to Me when you hate yourself.
Come to Me when you are tired of promising that this time will be different.
Come to Me.
Not because masturbation is somehow the greatest sin imaginable.
It isn't.
But because Christ refuses to settle for merely modifying your behavior when He intends to transform your heart.
Perhaps masturbation has become your false comfort.
Then the goal is not simply to take your comfort away.
God may be revealing the deeper hunger beneath it.
Maybe you need to grieve.
Maybe you need friendship.
Maybe you need reconciliation.
Maybe you need professional help for trauma or compulsive behavior.
Maybe you need to confess pornography use to someone trustworthy.
Maybe you need practical boundaries around your phone.
Maybe you need to stop carrying your devices into bed.
Maybe you need to recognize the emotional triggers that precede the behavior.
Maybe you need to learn that temptation often arrives when you are exhausted, isolated, angry, stressed, rejected, or bored.
And maybe you need to stop treating every relapse as proof that Christ has abandoned you.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin.
A struggling Christian may fall.
A struggling Christian may weep.
A struggling Christian may need help repeatedly.
But there remains something inside saying:
“Jesus, I don't want anything to own the part of me that belongs to You.”
That struggle matters.
Proverbs says the righteous person falls seven times and rises again.
Your story does not have to end on the floor.
Get up.
Not because the fall was meaningless.
Not because holiness does not matter.
Get up because Christ is still worthy.
Get up because grace is not permission to remain chained; grace is God's power calling slaves into freedom.
Get up because Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
And notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say there are no consequences.
He does not say there is no discipline.
He does not say Christians never struggle.
He says there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ.
The Judge became the Savior.
The debt was answered at the cross.
So when conviction comes, run toward Christ.
When condemnation whispers, “Hide from Him,” recognize the lie.
Conviction says:
“This cannot continue. Come home.”
Condemnation says:
“You are disgusting. Stay away.”
Jesus calls sinners home.
Maybe somebody reading this has never admitted the struggle to another human being.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
You post Scripture.
You worship.
You serve.
You encourage other people.
And then night comes.
You know exactly what happens next.
This article is not asking you to perform public humiliation.
But it is asking you to stop pretending before God.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows.
Tell Him what happens before the urge.
Tell Him who appears in your fantasies.
Tell Him what loneliness feels like.
Tell Him about the pornography.
Tell Him about the memories.
Tell Him about the shame afterward.
Tell Him you are tired.
Tell Him you want freedom even if part of you still wants the sin.
That last prayer may be one of the most honest prayers you ever pray:
“Jesus, part of me still wants this. But I want to want You more.”
He can work with honesty.
He already sees through performance.
And if masturbation itself is not consistently accompanied by pornography or explicit fantasy in your situation, you still have worthwhile questions to bring before God.
Does it strengthen self-control or weaken it?
Does it become compulsive?
Does it affect intimacy with your spouse?
Does it encourage fantasies about people who are not your spouse?
Does it become an escape from emotional pain?
Can you abstain freely?
Does your conscience remain troubled?
Can you sincerely bring the behavior before God and say:
“Lord Jesus, be glorified in my body”?
Romans 14 gives Christians an important principle concerning disputed matters: “Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.”

That verse should not be ripped from context and turned into a simplistic masturbation proof-text. Paul is addressing conscience and disputable matters. But the principle remains sobering: the Christian should not deliberately bulldoze a conscience that is sincerely trying to obey God.
If you continually need to silence conviction before doing something, investigate that honestly.
And remember something else.
Not every uncomfortable feeling is automatically the Holy Spirit.
Some Christians have been taught to experience crushing shame simply for possessing sexual desire.
Sexual desire itself is not evidence that you are spiritually defective.
God created human beings as embodied, sexual creatures.
The goal is not to become incapable of desire.
The goal is for desire to come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That is the center of this entire conversation.
Not masturbation.
Lordship.
Who gets the throne?
Who decides what your body is for?
Who defines freedom?
Who comforts you?
Who receives your imagination?
Who teaches you what love is?
Who gets your wounds?
Who gets your loneliness?
Who gets you when nobody is watching?
Jesus did not die merely to become one more coping mechanism beside all the others.
He is Lord.
And because He is Lord, He can enter even the rooms inside you that you have kept locked for years.
That is the scandal of grace.
Christ already knows what is behind the door...
and He still knocks.
Not to humiliate you.
To redeem you.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture shame.
Not to create Christians who merely look clean online.
But to keep pointing wounded, tempted, exhausted, compromised, recovering, hungry people back toward Jesus Christ, biblical truth, repentance, forgiveness, healing, discipleship, and transformation.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But perhaps you need to stop fighting completely alone.
And when you see someone else write those words, don't condemn them.
Pray for them.
There is a real human being behind that comment.
Someone's son.
Someone's daughter.
Someone's husband.
Someone's wife.
Someone who may have spent years believing nobody else understands.
Let the comments become a place where grace is louder than humiliation.
Send it privately to the friend who has trusted you with their struggle.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot merchandise your way into forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price you could never pay.
And perhaps tonight, when the familiar urge comes again, something will be different.
Maybe you will recognize what is underneath it.
Maybe it isn't only lust.
Maybe you are lonely.
Maybe you are hurting.
Maybe you are scared.
Maybe you are exhausted.
And instead of immediately reaching for the comfort that disappears minutes later, perhaps you will whisper:
“Jesus... I need You more than I need escape.”
Perhaps your hands will tremble.
Perhaps the temptation will not disappear instantly.
Perhaps holiness will feel less like a dramatic victory and more like surviving the next ten minutes with Christ.
Then another ten.
Then another.
And if you fall?
Do not build a house where you fell.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Learn what led you there.
Reach for trustworthy help.
And rise again.
Because the Christian story was never about sinners becoming impressive enough to deserve Jesus.
It is about Jesus being powerful enough to redeem sinners.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted Him.
Paul persecuted His people.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly disgraced.
The thief beside Him was dying under judgment for his crimes.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose worst chapters looked final.
Then grace entered the story.
And that may be the truth your shame desperately does not want you to believe:
The chapter you are most ashamed of may become the place where you finally discover just how far the mercy of Jesus Christ was willing to come looking for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGE LAWS THAT MAKE CHRISTIANS UNCOMFORTABLE—AND THE JESUS-CENTERED TRUTH WE MISS WHEN WE READ THEM WRONG
paragraphs: THE OLD TESTAMENT MARRIAGE LAWS THAT MAKE CHRISTIANS UNCOMFORTABLE—AND THE JESUS-CENTERED TRUTH WE MISS WHEN WE READ THEM WRONG
Divorce. Captive women. Multiple wives. Broken homes. Laws that sound disturbing to modern ears. Did God approve of all of it—or is something far deeper happening in the pages we are tempted to skip?
There are passages in the Bible that almost nobody puts on a coffee mug.
Nobody decorates the nursery with them.
Nobody chooses them for the wedding invitation.
And sometimes, if we are painfully honest, we read them and quietly wonder...
God, why is this in Your Word?
A man gives his wife a certificate of divorce.
A soldier desires a woman captured in war.
A household contains more than one wife.
A vulnerable woman finds herself inside an ancient legal arrangement that feels painfully foreign to everything we know.
Then somebody who already doubts Christianity opens the Bible, points at one of those passages, and asks the question you were hoping they would never ask:
“So your God approves of this?”
And suddenly you feel trapped.
Defend the passage too quickly, and you may make God sound cruel.
Reject the passage because it makes you uncomfortable, and you place your feelings above Scripture.
Ignore it, and the question remains.
But there is another way.
The way Jesus Himself taught us to read.

And once you see it, some of the strangest marriage laws in the Old Testament begin telling a much larger story—not about God delighting in human brokenness, but about a holy God entering a brutally broken human world, restraining evil, protecting people within fallen circumstances, revealing His purposes progressively, and ultimately leading us toward the One who would bear human sin upon a cross.
Jesus Christ.
Before we go any further, remember this:
Not everything the Bible regulates is something the Bible celebrates.
That distinction changes everything.
The Bible records murder without endorsing murder.
It records adultery without blessing adultery.
It records polygamy without presenting polygamy as Eden's design.
It records slavery, warfare, betrayal, divorce, exploitation, family dysfunction, and terrible human decisions because Scripture does not airbrush humanity.
The Bible is brutally honest about us.
And that honesty begins almost immediately.
Before there were divorce certificates...
before Israel...
before Moses...
before kings accumulated wives...
before war fractured families...
there was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 describes the foundational pattern:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
One man.
One woman.
One covenant union.
One flesh.
Jesus later reaches backward through centuries of Israel's complicated marital history and deliberately brings His hearers back there.
Not first to Moses.
To creation.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, Jesus answered by quoting Genesis and then declared:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
But they pushed Him.
Why, then, did Moses permit divorce?
And Jesus gave an answer that unlocks much of the tension Christians experience when reading Old Testament marriage legislation:
“Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.”
Read those words again.
From the beginning it was not so.
Jesus distinguishes between God's creational design and a concession operating within human hardness.
That matters enormously.
The Greek expression translated “hardness of heart” is σκληροκαρδία — sklērokardia.
A hard heart.
A stubborn heart.
A heart resistant to God's intention.
Jesus does not say divorce existed because God's ideal marriage needed improvement.
He points to human sin.
That means some Old Testament laws must be understood not as photographs of Eden restored, but as God's legislation addressing people living east of Eden.
There is a difference between God creating an ideal and God regulating damage after humans abandon that ideal.
Imagine an emergency room.
A surgeon treating a gunshot wound is not endorsing gunshot wounds.
The treatment exists because something has gone terribly wrong.
In a similar way, biblical law sometimes meets human beings inside circumstances already twisted by sin and places boundaries around what fallen people are doing.
Consider Deuteronomy 24.
The Hebrew text speaks of a סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת — sefer keritut, literally a written document or “certificate of cutting off,” a certificate of divorce.
Modern readers sometimes approach the passage as though God is enthusiastically introducing divorce.
But Jesus refuses that reading.
The legislation addresses a situation in which divorce is already occurring and establishes legal boundaries around what follows.
And notice something easy to miss.
The woman is not merely an object endlessly transferable between men.
Once divorced and subsequently married to another man, the first husband cannot simply reclaim her later after that second marriage ends.
A boundary has been drawn.
The law restrains the former husband.
The woman cannot simply be treated as property that can be passed out, reclaimed, and recycled according to male convenience.
Does that mean Deuteronomy 24 represents the fullness of God's vision for marriage?
Jesus says no.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
But does that mean the law is meaningless or morally embarrassing?
Again, no.
It reveals God governing a fallen society while still pointing beyond that society toward His original intention.
And then we arrive at one of the passages that can make modern Christians deeply uncomfortable.
Deuteronomy 21:10–14.
A woman has been taken captive in warfare.
A victorious Israelite soldier finds her attractive.
At first glance, the power imbalance is horrifying.
She has lost.
Her world has collapsed.
Perhaps her family is gone.
Perhaps everything familiar has disappeared.
She is vulnerable.
So what does God's law do?
It does not allow the soldier simply to seize her sexually in the heat of conquest.
There is a process.
She enters the household.
She receives time to mourn her father and mother.
A full month.
Her grief is acknowledged.
If the relationship later ends, the man is forbidden to sell her.
He cannot turn her into merchandise.
He must release her.
The text explicitly forbids treating her as something to be sold after what has happened.
Does that erase every moral difficulty modern readers feel when encountering an ancient warfare text?
No.
We should not pretend that it does.
Faithfulness to Scripture does not require pretending difficult passages are easy.
But neither should we commit the opposite mistake: reading an ancient law as though its purpose were to create the broken situation it is actually regulating.
The law enters a world where defeated women could be extraordinarily vulnerable and places restrictions on the victorious man.
His power is not absolute.
His desire is not absolute.
Her humanity cannot simply disappear because he won a battle.
That pattern appears elsewhere.
Exodus 21:7–11 addresses another ancient arrangement involving an economically vulnerable woman. Again, modern readers understandably recoil at the social institution surrounding the text.
But look carefully at what the law requires.
If the man takes another wife, he may not deprive the first woman of food, clothing, or marital provision.
And if he refuses those obligations?
She goes free.
Without paying him.
In other words, the law places obligations upon the socially powerful and provides consequences when those obligations are violated.
That does not mean Christians should resurrect Israel's ancient civil arrangements.
It means we must learn to ask the right interpretive question.
Not merely:
“Why does this situation exist in the Bible?”
But:
“What is God's law doing inside this already-existing fallen situation?”
That question changes the landscape.
And then there is polygamy.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
Men associated with enormous moments in redemptive history had multiple wives.
So did God design marriage that way?
Look at the stories.
Really look.
The Bible rarely needs to interrupt the narrative and scream, “THIS IS GOING BADLY.”
The consequences tell you.
Sarah and Hagar.
Pain.
Jealousy.
Abraham caught between households.
Jacob, Leah, and Rachel.
Competition.
Tears.
Favoritism.
Children growing up inside rivalry.
Then David.
Then Solomon, whose many wives ultimately helped turn his heart toward other gods.
Scripture does not hide the wreckage.
Sometimes the Bible condemns sin through direct command.
Sometimes it lets you stand inside the burning house long enough to smell the smoke.
The existence of polygamous men in Scripture is no more proof that polygamy represents God's ideal than David's adultery proves adultery represents God's ideal.
The heroes of Scripture are not the Hero of Scripture.
That distinction may save someone's faith.
Abraham is not Jesus.
Moses is not Jesus.
David is not Jesus.
Solomon is not Jesus.
They are sinners standing inside the same story of redemption that eventually reaches us.
And this is where everything begins moving toward the cross.
Because biblical marriage is ultimately bigger than marriage.
The prophets describe covenant faithfulness between God and His people.
Malachi calls a wife אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ — eshet beritekha, “the wife of your covenant.”
Marriage is not merely possession.
Not merely sexuality.
Not merely social convenience.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Loyalty.
Love that keeps its word.
Then the New Testament opens something breathtaking.
Paul writes:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25.
Notice the command.
ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate.
Love.
And what defines that love?
Christ.
Not domination.
Not selfish entitlement.
Not “I am the man, therefore I get whatever I want.”
Christ.
And what did Christ do?
ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν — heauton paredōken.
“He gave Himself up.”
Suddenly biblical authority in marriage cannot honestly be interpreted through selfish male privilege.
The Husband-pattern is a crucified Savior.
The model is Jesus giving Himself.
Bleeding.
Serving.
Sacrificing.
Seeking the holiness and good of His bride.
The cross turns worldly power upside down.
The world says:
“If you have power, make people sacrifice for you.”
Jesus says:
“If you love, give yourself.”
And perhaps this is where the Old Testament marriage laws stop being merely an intellectual problem and become painfully personal.
Because it is easy to analyze ancient Israel.
Harder to analyze our own hearts.
You may never hand someone a Hebrew sefer keritut.
But have you emotionally abandoned the person you promised to love?
You may never have multiple wives like Solomon.
But have you allowed another person, fantasy, addiction, ambition, secret conversation, pornography, resentment, or hidden desire to occupy a place in your heart that belongs inside your covenant?
You may never live under ancient Israelite household legislation.
But have you ever used power selfishly?
Manipulated somebody who trusted you?
Demanded submission while refusing sacrifice?
Quoted Scripture to win an argument while refusing to resemble Jesus?
Suddenly the ancient text is no longer sitting safely three thousand years away.
It has walked into the room.
And now it is looking at us.
Somebody reading this has been wounded by marriage.
Somebody was abandoned.
Somebody was betrayed.
Somebody stayed awake while their spouse slept beside them, wondering how two people sharing one mattress could somehow feel thousands of miles apart.
Somebody begged God to restore a marriage that still collapsed.
Somebody carries shame because they were the one who destroyed it.
Somebody committed adultery.
Somebody lied.
Somebody left.
Somebody became cold.
Somebody is divorced and still feels as though the word has been tattooed across their forehead.
Somebody thinks their past permanently disqualifies them from being deeply loved by God.
And this is where Christianity becomes more than an argument about ancient law.
Because Jesus did not come merely to explain Moses.
Jesus came to save sinners.
The same Jesus who reaffirmed the seriousness of marriage also sat near a well speaking with a woman whose relational history was shattered.
Five husbands.
And the man she currently had was not her husband.
Jesus knew.
Every chapter.
Every relationship.
Every regret.
Every whispered accusation.
Every failure.
He knew.
And He stayed.
He spoke truth without pretending her life was whole.
But He did not reduce her to her scandal.
He offered living water.
That is Jesus.
Truth without cruelty.
Grace without pretending sin does not matter.
Holiness without hopelessness.
Conviction without abandonment.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that Christ died.
But the resurrection says your sin does not have to write the final sentence.
Maybe your marriage story is beautiful.
Thank God.
Protect it.
Maybe your marriage is wounded.
Seek Christ, wisdom, prayer, biblical counsel, repentance, safety where necessary, forgiveness where appropriate, and help from mature believers.
Maybe your marriage ended.
Do not rewrite Scripture to make sin harmless.
But do not rewrite the Gospel to make grace powerless either.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Jesus sees you.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Repent.
Not performative regret.
Not excuses.
Not “I made mistakes.”
Repentance.
Bring the ugliness into the light.
Christ's blood is not reserved for respectable sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is why Christians should never read Old Testament marriage laws merely asking, “Which ancient regulations do I copy?”
We read them within the whole biblical story.
Creation tells us the design.
The fall tells us why relationships fracture.
The law shows God confronting and restraining sin among a covenant people in an ancient world.
The prophets deepen the language of covenant faithfulness.
Jesus takes us back to creation and exposes hardness of heart.
The apostles show marriage illuminated by Christ and His Church.
And the Gospel tells sinners where shattered covenant-breakers can finally find mercy.
At the cross.
The Bible begins with a marriage in a garden.
And near its end, Revelation gives us the marriage supper of the Lamb.
Do you see the thread?
Marriage was never merely about us.
Human marriage is temporary.
Christ and His redeemed people are forever.
Every faithful Christian marriage is meant to whisper something about that greater covenant.
Every broken marriage reminds us how desperately humanity needs redemption.
Every repentant sinner restored by Christ becomes evidence that failure does not have sovereign authority over the future.
Jesus does.
This is why we must stop weaponizing difficult Old Testament passages.
And we must stop being ashamed of them too.
Read them carefully.
Read historically.
Read grammatically.
Read covenantally.
Read canonically.
Read them through what Jesus Himself reveals about God's intention.
Do not flatten every biblical law into the same category.
Do not confuse description with prescription.
Do not confuse regulation with celebration.
Do not isolate Moses from Genesis.
Do not isolate Genesis from Jesus.
And never isolate any difficult biblical passage from the great redemptive story reaching its climax in Christ crucified and risen.
Because when Scripture exposes human hardness, the answer is not pretending humanity was never hard.
The answer is a Savior who can give us new hearts.
Maybe that is the part we resist.
We want God to explain everyone else's brokenness.
God wants to confront ours.
We want to discuss ancient husbands.
Jesus asks what kind of husband you are.
We want to discuss ancient wives.
Jesus asks whether you have been faithful.
We want to debate Moses.
Jesus asks whether our hearts are hard.
And suddenly this article isn't about “those strange Old Testament marriage laws” anymore.
It is about you.
Me.
Our excuses.
Our wounds.
Our lust.
Our selfishness.
Our marriages.
Our divorces.
Our secrets.
Our covenant-breaking hearts.
And a crucified King standing before sinners with scarred hands.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write your whole story publicly.
But maybe you need to stop pretending.

And if you once thought these Old Testament passages proved God did not care about vulnerable people, but now you want to study Scripture more carefully, say so. Honest questions are better than borrowed answers.
Someone on your Facebook friends list is quietly wrestling with these exact passages.
Someone thinks Christianity cannot answer them.
Someone has been wounded by a church leader who used biblical marriage language to justify selfishness, control, or abuse.
Someone divorced years ago and still wonders whether Jesus wants them anywhere near Him.
Difficult passages rarely become easy after one reading, and someday someone may ask you the question this article just helped you face.

If you genuinely want your resources to glorify God, then steward them prayerfully. Support faithful Gospel work where the Lord leads you. Share biblical truth instead of merely consuming it. Help put Scripture in front of people who may never walk voluntarily into a church.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the exhausted Christian.
Invite the lukewarm believer who knows something has gone cold.
Invite the skeptic who still has questions.
Invite the person recovering from divorce.
Invite the husband who needs to rediscover sacrificial love.
Invite the wife who feels unseen.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks the Bible has nothing meaningful to say to a modern world.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's approval.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase your sins.
You cannot purchase redemption.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Christianity's invitation has never ultimately been:
“Become impressive.”
It is:
“Come to Christ.”
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Him.
And let the One who carried your sin begin rewriting everything your sin tried to destroy.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing about the Bible's broken marriages is not that God allowed their ugly stories to remain on the page.
Perhaps the most shocking thing is that He kept pursuing broken people through them...
until the story reached a cross...
an empty tomb...
and a Bridegroom who gave Himself to redeem a bride who could never rescue herself.
So when you encounter those uncomfortable Old Testament marriage laws again, do not run from the page.
Look closer.
Behind the divorce certificates, fractured households, human hardness, compromised men, vulnerable women, covenant failures, tears, and consequences is a story moving relentlessly toward Jesus.
And maybe your own story feels scandalous right now.
Maybe there are chapters you wish could be ripped out.
Maybe your family knows.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
Your scandal may explain where you have been.
It does not possess the authority to decide who Christ can make you become.
The pages you are most ashamed of may become the very pages where future generations discover how fiercely Jesus saves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES JESUS POINT BACK TO GENESIS?
paragraphs: WHY DOES JESUS POINT BACK TO GENESIS?

When people tried to pull Jesus into the arguments of His day, He did something startling: He reached past the controversy, past human tradition, and back to the beginning. And what He showed us there still confronts every heart that would rather ask, “What can I get away with?” than, “What did God intend?”
There is a kind of question we ask God when we already know what we want Him to say.
We do not always come looking for truth.
Sometimes we come looking for permission.
Permission to leave.
Permission to compromise.
Permission to rename what God has already spoken about.
Permission to protect our pride.
Permission to keep the bitterness.
Permission to keep the secret.
Permission to make Scripture bend around the life we have already decided to live.
And perhaps that is why one moment in the ministry of Jesus feels so painfully modern.
Some Pharisees approached Him with a question about divorce.
Matthew records it this way:
“Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?”
Matthew 19:3.
It sounds like a theological question.
But Matthew tells us they were testing Him.
This was not merely a wounded person quietly asking Jesus what to do with a shattered marriage. It was a confrontation.
A trap.
A controversy.
And Jesus could have entered their debate on their terms.
He could have started with their arguments.
He could have begun by cataloguing the competing interpretations surrounding divorce.
Instead, Jesus did something profound.
He went backward.
Past their controversy.
Past their preferred interpretations.
Past their attempts to find the boundary line of what was permissible.
Back to creation.
Back to Genesis.
Back to the moment before sin fractured the human story.
Jesus answered:
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female...?”
Matthew 19:4.
Those words “from the beginning” matter.
The Greek is:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς — ap’ archēs
“From the beginning.”
Then Jesus draws directly from Genesis 1:27 and Genesis 2:24.
He does not treat Genesis as disposable religious scenery.
He appeals to creation as authoritative for understanding God’s design.
That should make us stop.
Because when Jesus was confronted with a question about what humans may do, He pointed His hearers toward what God had done.
When they wanted to discuss permission, Jesus discussed purpose.
When they wanted to know how far something could be broken, Jesus showed them what it looked like before it was broken.
And perhaps that is one reason Genesis matters so much.
Genesis does not merely tell us where humanity came from.
It begins revealing what humanity was made for.
Genesis 1:1 opens:
בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים
Bereshit bara Elohim.
“In the beginning, God created...”
The first subject of Scripture is not you.
Not me.
Not humanity.
God.
Before your pain, God.
Before your questions, God.
Before human governments, cultures, philosophies, algorithms, movements, denominations, arguments, and scandals—
God.
And that changes everything.
Because if God is Creator, then reality does not begin with what I desire reality to be.
It begins with Him.
We are creatures before we are commentators.
We receive life before we define life.
We inherit a creation we did not speak into existence.
And Genesis says something breathtaking about the human beings God placed within that creation:
וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha’adam betsalmo...
“So God created man in his own image...”
Genesis 1:27.
Human dignity begins there.
Not in usefulness.
Not in wealth.
Not in beauty.
Not in intelligence.
Not in sexuality.
Not in popularity.
Not in whether somebody wanted you.
Not in whether somebody abandoned you.
Not in whether your father was proud of you.
Not in whether your mother understood you.
Not in the number beside your name on a social-media profile.
Human worth is rooted in something far deeper.
We are creatures made by God, and humanity was uniquely made in His image.
That means the person you despise bears a dignity you did not give them.

It means the unborn, the elderly, the disabled, the poor, the powerful, the forgotten, the stranger, and the person whose life seems completely unlike yours cannot have their fundamental human worth measured merely by convenience or social status.
And it means something else.
Your worst chapter is not the author of your value.
But Genesis does not remain in Eden.
The story darkens.
The serpent speaks.
Human beings distrust the goodness of God.
The forbidden fruit is taken.
Sin enters the human story.
Shame follows.
Then hiding.
Listen to the heartbreaking words of Adam:
“I was afraid... and I hid myself.”
Genesis 3:10.
There it is.
One of humanity’s oldest spiritual reflexes.
Hiding.
We are still doing it.
We have simply become better at decorating the hiding places.
Some hide behind success.
Some behind ministry.
Some behind theology.
Some behind humor.
Some behind anger.
Some behind relationships.
Some behind pornography.
Some behind endless scrolling.
Some behind religious performance.
Some know exactly how to lift their hands during worship while desperately hoping nobody discovers what those same hands were doing in secret.
Some preach grace to everyone except themselves.
Some post Bible verses while their marriage is bleeding behind a locked door.
Some say, “God is good,” because admitting, “I am barely holding on,” feels too dangerous.
We learned to hide a long time ago.
But God came looking.
“Where are you?”
Genesis 3:9.
God was not lacking geographical information.
The question exposed Adam.
Where are you?
That question still travels through Scripture.
And eventually, it reaches us.
Where are you?
Not where does everybody think you are spiritually?
Where are you?
Where are you?
Not what did you tell your pastor?
Where are you?
Not how many Christian books have you read?
Where are you?
Maybe you are angry with God.
Maybe you are quietly addicted.
Maybe your marriage is hanging by a thread.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary without actually surrendering to Christ.
Maybe everybody calls you strong because nobody has seen you cry in the car before walking into the house.
Maybe there is something on your phone you would panic if your spouse saw.
Maybe you have not prayed sincerely in months.
Maybe you love Jesus, but you are exhausted.
Maybe you failed again last night.
And the instinct inherited from Eden whispers:
Hide.
Jesus came to destroy the lie that hiding can save you.
This is where understanding why Jesus points back to Genesis becomes bigger than a debate about origins or marriage.
The Bible’s story runs from creation to fall, from promise to fulfillment, from rebellion to redemption, and ultimately toward new creation.
Jesus does not merely remind us what humanity was supposed to be.
He comes to rescue sinners who have become what we were never supposed to become.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from self-improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to help reasonably good people become slightly better versions of themselves.
He came for sinners.
Mark records His words:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Mark 2:17.
That means your scandal does not surprise Christ.
But neither does His grace give you permission to remain enslaved to it.
Grace is not Jesus standing at a distance saying, “Your sin does not matter.”
Grace cost blood.
The cross tells us simultaneously that sin is more serious than we wanted to admit and that God's love toward sinners is more astonishing than we dared to hope.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ bears judgment for sinners.
The innocent One suffers.
The Son gives Himself.
The Lamb is slain.
And Peter describes what happened with staggering clarity:
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.”
1 Peter 2:24.
Notice both sides.
He bore our sins.
Grace.
That we might die to sin.
Transformation.
Biblical grace does not say, “Stay hidden.”
It says, “Come into the light.”
It does not say, “Pretend there was never a wound.”
It says, “Bring the wound to the Physician.”
It does not say, “Your choices do not matter.”
It says there is forgiveness so deep that sinners can repent, be cleansed, and learn to walk differently.
And this makes Jesus’ return to Genesis even more beautiful.
When Christ points us toward the beginning, He is not inviting us into nostalgia.
He is revealing God's design in a world distorted by sin.
In Matthew 19, after Jesus points to creation, the Pharisees raise Moses and divorce.
Jesus responds:
“Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
There it is again.
“From the beginning.”
Jesus distinguishes between accommodation to human hardness in a fallen world and God's creational intention.
That principle reaches deeper than marriage.
Sin makes us ask:
“What am I allowed to do?”
Love asks:
“What glorifies God?”
Sin searches for loopholes.
Surrender searches for the will of the Father.
The hardened heart asks:
“How close can I stand to the edge without falling?”
The transformed heart asks:
“How close can I walk with Jesus?”
That is a completely different way to live.
And no, this does not mean Christians should weaponize Genesis against wounded people.
Jesus did not commission His followers to become experts at throwing Scripture like stones.
Truth without love becomes cruelty.
But what our culture calls love can also become cruelty when it requires us to hide truth.
Jesus gives us something better.
“Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”
John 1:17.
Grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Christ.
This matters especially when talking about marriage, sexuality, identity, human dignity, family, and creation, because these subjects are attached to real people.
Real wounds.
Real temptations.
Real divorces.
Real betrayals.
Real confusion.
Real children.
Real regret.
Real loneliness.
Real stories.
Somebody reading this has been divorced.
Somebody was abandoned.
Somebody stayed and was betrayed anyway.
Somebody carries guilt because they know they were the one who shattered trust.
Somebody grew up watching their parents destroy each other and secretly wonders whether lifelong love is even real.
Somebody is wrestling with desires they never asked to experience.
Somebody is trying to understand what obedience to Jesus will cost them.
Christian truth must never require us to stop seeing the person standing in front of us.
Jesus could look directly at sinners without pretending sin was righteousness.
And sinners could approach Him without discovering that holiness had disappeared.
That combination is breathtaking.
Consider the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Jesus does not join the mob in destroying her.
Neither does He rename adultery as holiness.
He tells her:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
Mercy.
And repentance.
Grace.
And transformation.
Jesus refuses our favorite false choice.
We often think we must either condemn people without mercy or affirm everything without discernment.
Jesus does neither.
He loves sinners enough to receive them.
He loves sinners enough to call them out of sin.
And He loves sinners enough to die for them.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace makes hiding unnecessary.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite

The word carries the idea of changing one’s mind, turning from the former orientation toward a new one. In the biblical call to repentance, this is not merely feeling guilty. It is a genuine turning toward God.
Jesus begins His public proclamation in Mark with:
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Mark 1:15.
Repent.
Believe.
Not:
Fix yourself until God tolerates you.
Not:
Hide until you become presentable.
Not:
Build an impressive religious résumé.
Come to Christ.
Turn.
Believe.
That is why your story can change.
Not because motivational language is powerful enough.
Not because positive thinking can resurrect a dead heart.
Not because your past suddenly becomes good.
But because Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Paul tells the Corinthians:
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
2 Corinthians 5:17.
Did you hear that?
Creation language returns.
Genesis begins with creation.
The Gospel produces new creation in those united to Christ.
And Scripture ends not with God surrendering creation to darkness, but with the promise of renewal.
“Behold, I am making all things new.”
Revelation 21:5.
Genesis begins in a garden.
Human rebellion brings exile and death.
Christ enters our ruined world.
The cross appears like defeat.
The tomb is sealed.
Then Sunday morning arrives.
The stone cannot keep the Author of life inside.
Jesus rises.
Death does not get the final word.
Sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Satan does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
This is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because He edits history and pretends your sin never happened.
Not because Christianity offers spiritual amnesia.
Jesus rewrites everything because redemption can give a sinner a future their rebellion could never produce.
Ask Peter.
He denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
“I do not know the man.”
Then the rooster.
Then the eyes of Jesus.
Then Peter goes outside and weeps bitterly.
If Peter's failure had been the final chapter, his story would have ended in disgrace.
But resurrection morning came.
And later, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus restored the disciple who had denied Him.
“Do you love me?”
John 21.
Peter's scandal was real.
So was Christ's grace.
Peter was not restored so that denial could become acceptable.
He was restored so that a fallen disciple could follow Jesus again.
Maybe that is what somebody needs to hear tonight.
You fell.
Get up and run toward Christ.
You sinned.
Confess it.
You wandered.
Come home.
You destroyed trust.
Stop defending yourself and begin walking in truth.
You have been hiding.
Come into the light.
You are ashamed.
Look at the cross.
You think God could never want someone who has done what you have done.
Remember who Jesus welcomed.
Tax collectors.
Sexually broken people.
Religious hypocrites who finally humbled themselves.
Doubters.
Cowards.
Outcasts.
Failures.
Sinners.
People like us.
But do not confuse His welcome with permission to drag your chains into eternity and call them freedom.
Jesus saves us from sin, not merely from embarrassment about sin.
There may be consequences you still have to face.
Forgiveness does not always erase earthly consequences.
Relationships may need years of rebuilding.
Trust may need to be earned.
Restitution may need to happen.
A confession may cost you something.
Following Christ may dismantle a life you spent years constructing.
But there is a freedom deeper than protecting an image.
There is the freedom of having nothing left to hide from the One who already knows everything.
So why does Jesus point back to Genesis?
Because beginnings reveal design.
Because creation tells us that God—not human appetite—is Creator.
Because Genesis exposes the dignity of humanity and the catastrophe of rebellion.
Because the fracture we experience now makes sense only when we understand that something has gone terribly wrong.
And because the Gospel announces that God has not abandoned His creation to sin and death.
The Bible does not begin with human self-definition.
It begins:
“In the beginning, God...”
And your redemption does not begin with you either.
It begins with God.
His holiness.
His mercy.
His Son.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His invitation.
Maybe you clicked this article expecting theology.
And maybe somewhere between Genesis and Calvary, theology found you.
So here is the question you cannot outsource:
Where are you?
Still hiding?
Still negotiating?
Still asking how much of your old life Jesus will allow you to keep?
Still wanting a Savior who forgives you but never a Lord who commands you?
Still performing Christianity while secretly starving for Christ?
You do not need another hiding place.
You need Jesus.
Come honestly.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
The Gospel does not promise that repentance will make every earthly consequence disappear.
It promises something infinitely greater:
Christ Himself.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
New life.
A new allegiance.
A new hope.
And finally, resurrection.
Or simply:
“Pray for me.”

And if Christ has already carried you from a chapter of scandal into a story of grace, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needs to read tonight.
Send it privately to the person who is ashamed to walk into church.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, consider following and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. The goal is not merely more religious content. It is daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
But hear this clearly:
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot glorify God by clicking a button while refusing Him your heart.

Yet Scripture does teach believers to use their resources, voices, generosity, and opportunities for God's glory. So if this ministry genuinely helps you grow in Christ, supporting and sharing it can be one practical expression of stewardship and partnership in spreading biblical truth.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody in your circle may need the Gospel.
If God has given you a voice, use it for His glory.
If He has given you resources, steward them for His glory.
If He has given you a testimony, stop burying it.
If He has given you truth, do not hoard it.
And above everything, if He has given you Christ—
treasure Him.
Because eventually every argument ends.
Every trend expires.
Every platform disappears.
Every human opinion becomes dust.
But the Word of our God stands forever.
And when the world keeps asking us to reinvent what it means to be human, Jesus still has the courage to take us back to the beginning.
Perhaps the most haunting question is not whether we have read Genesis.
It is whether we will follow Jesus when He tells us what it means.
The God who found humanity hiding among the trees of Eden is still calling sinners out of hiding—and this time, the road home passes beneath a blood-stained cross and out through an empty tomb.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “ONCE SAVED, ALWAYS SAVED?” — THE TERRIFYING HOPE HIDDEN IN JESUS’ WORDS: “HE WHO ENDURES TO THE END”
paragraphs:
“ONCE SAVED, ALWAYS SAVED?” — THE TERRIFYING HOPE HIDDEN IN JESUS’ WORDS: “HE WHO ENDURES TO THE END”
What if the question isn’t whether you once prayed a prayer…but whether the Jesus you once confessed is still the Jesus you are following?
There is a kind of Christianity that knows exactly when it “got saved.”
It remembers the date.
The church.
The altar.
The raised hand.
The tears.
The prayer.
Maybe you remember yours.
