Bring Him the desires you are embarrassed to admit exist.
But do not place them on the throne.
Place them at the feet of Jesus.
And pray something dangerous:
“Lord, if what I want contradicts what You want, change me.”
That prayer may change your relationships.
It may change your habits.
It may change your entertainment.
It may change your ambitions.
It may change what you do when nobody is watching.
It may expose excuses you have protected for years.
But what if the thing you are afraid to surrender is the very thing keeping you from experiencing the freedom of obedience?
What if God saying “no” is not cruelty?
What if it is rescue?
A child may become furious when a father pulls him away from traffic.
The child feels restricted.
The father sees the truck.
We see moments.
God sees roads.
We see desire.
God sees destination.
“There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.”
Maybe God brought these words across your screen because there is still time to turn around.
Do not merely ask whether something feels right.
Ask whether it agrees with Scripture.
Ask whether it glorifies Christ.
Ask whether it requires you to redefine something God has already called sin.
Ask whether you have been seeking godly counsel or merely searching for someone who will agree with you.
Ask whether you are following Jesus or asking Jesus to follow your desires.
And then be brutally honest before God.
Not before the internet.
Not before religious people.
Before Him.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.”
— Psalm 139:23–24, KJV
That is not the prayer of somebody who trusts every feeling.
That is the prayer of somebody who trusts God enough to let Him expose what the heart cannot see clearly by itself.
Talk to Jesus.
Right now.
You do not need polished religious language.
“Jesus, forgive me” is enough to begin an honest confession.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light begins with finally refusing to pretend.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle nobody can see.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because there may come a night when your emotions become louder than your convictions and you need to remember:
A feeling can be sincere without being sovereign.
Someone you know may currently be standing at the entrance of a road that seems completely right.
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
You may never know that they read it.
But sharing biblical truth can place a warning, an invitation to repentance, and the hope of Christ in front of someone at exactly the moment they need it.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God's blessing cannot be purchased.
Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in helping biblical content reach more people.
But please remember this after you leave this page.
Do not share merely because a sentence made you emotional.
Do not comment merely because everyone else did.
Respond first to Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A Christian book cannot save you.
A church cannot save you.
A pastor cannot save you.
Your feelings cannot save you.
Your good intentions cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
So when your heart says, “Follow me,” but Christ says, “Follow Me”...
you already know which voice deserves the throne.

And someday, looking back over roads God prevented you from taking, prayers He refused to answer the way you demanded, relationships He removed, sins He exposed, desires He crucified, and tears you once thought meant He had abandoned you...
you may finally understand:
The road that felt like God was taking something from you may have been the road where Jesus was saving you from losing yourself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM, SARAH, AND HAGAR: FAITH, SEX, POWER, AND THE DISASTER OF HUMAN SHORTCUTS
paragraphs:
ABRAHAM, SARAH, AND HAGAR: FAITH, SEX, POWER, AND THE DISASTER OF HUMAN SHORTCUTS
God made a promise. They grew tired of waiting. A bedroom became their solution—and generations felt the consequences. But buried inside one of Genesis’ most uncomfortable family scandals is a warning for anyone who has ever tried to “help God” fulfill what only God could accomplish.
There are sins that begin with rebellion.
And then there are sins that begin with impatience.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes the most dangerous moment in your spiritual life is not when you stop believing God.
It is when you still believe Him…
but decide He is taking too long.
Abraham knew what God had said.
Sarah knew what God had promised.
There would be offspring. There would be a future. God had called Abram out beneath the night sky and told him to look upward.
Count the stars—if you can.
“So shall your offspring be.”
Then Genesis records one of the foundational statements of biblical faith:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה
Vehe’emin baYHWH.
“And he believed in the LORD.”
And God counted that faith as righteousness.
Genesis 15:6.
The promise was magnificent.
The problem was the calendar.
Days became months.
Months became years.
Sarah remained barren.
Abraham became older.
And eventually the distance between what God had promised and what their eyes could see became almost unbearable.
Have you ever lived there?
God said something.
You believed Him.
You prayed.
You waited.
Nothing happened.
So you prayed harder.
Still nothing.
Eventually, a frightening thought slipped quietly into your mind:
Maybe I need to make this happen myself.
That sentence has destroyed more than we realize.
Genesis 16 opens without thunder, demons, pagan altars, or armies.
Just disappointment.
“Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children.”
The sentence is devastating precisely because of what God had already promised.
There was a promise…
but no baby.
A word from God…
but no visible fulfillment.
And then Sarah looked at Hagar.
Hagar was Egyptian.
A servant.
A woman living inside Abraham and Sarah’s household without the social power possessed by either of them.
And Sarah developed a plan.
She told Abraham to sleep with Hagar so perhaps she could obtain children through her.
We should not sanitize the scene because Sunday-school familiarity has made it comfortable.
This involved faith.
Sex.
Marriage.
Infertility.
Social hierarchy.
Female vulnerability.
Male passivity.
Power.
Pain.
And a desperate attempt to manufacture by human strategy what God had promised to provide by divine faithfulness.
Genesis says Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
And Abraham agreed.
That may be one of the most terrifying parts of the chapter.
The man who had believed God beneath the stars now walked into a bedroom arranged by unbelieving impatience.
Not because he had necessarily stopped believing the promise.
Perhaps something more relatable happened.
He began believing that human intervention was necessary to accomplish it.
And that is where this story finds us.
Because we do the same thing.
God tells us to trust Him, but we manipulate.
God tells us to wait, but we force doors open.
God tells us to remain faithful, but loneliness begins rewriting our standards.
God tells us not to compromise, but the opportunity looks too perfect to lose.
God tells us that obedience matters, but we convince ourselves that the destination is righteous enough to justify a questionable road.
We pray…
then manipulate.
We surrender…
then secretly take control again.
We say, “Your will be done,” while constructing backup plans in case His will takes too long.
And sometimes the shortcut works.
That is what makes shortcuts so dangerous.
Hagar became pregnant.
Think about that.
The plan produced exactly what human wisdom expected it to produce.
There was conception.
There would be a child.
If results alone proved God’s approval, Abraham and Sarah could have called the strategy successful.
But visible success is not always evidence of divine approval.
Sometimes disobedience produces results.
Sometimes compromise opens doors.
Sometimes manipulation gets you what you wanted.
Sometimes the relationship you should never have entered makes you temporarily happy.
Sometimes the dishonest decision increases your income.
Sometimes the shortcut actually works.
And that is precisely why Christians must never confuse effectiveness with obedience.
Hagar conceived.
And immediately the household began collapsing.
Genesis tells us that when Hagar realized she was pregnant, her mistress became diminished in her eyes.
The Hebrew describes Sarah as becoming “light” or diminished in Hagar’s estimation.
Suddenly the social arrangement had shifted.
The barren mistress.
The pregnant servant.
The promise.
The womb.
The household.
The jealousy.
The humiliation.
Everything became combustible.
Sarah blamed Abraham.
Abraham responded by putting Hagar back under Sarah’s authority.
Then comes an uncomfortable Hebrew word.
Genesis 16:6 says Sarah dealt harshly with Hagar.
The Hebrew verb is:
וַתְּעַנֶּהָ
vatte‘anneha.
It comes from the root ענה (‘anah), a word that can carry the sense of afflicting, humbling, oppressing, or treating harshly.
Hagar fled.
Do not rush past that.
She fled.
A pregnant woman ran into the wilderness because remaining where she was had become unbearable.
And here Scripture does something extraordinary.
God sees the woman everyone else has been using.
Abraham saw a possible route toward a son.
Sarah saw a possible solution to barrenness and later a painful rival.
But God saw Hagar.
The angel of the LORD found her near a spring in the wilderness.
Found her.
That word matters when you feel forgotten.
God did not approve of everything that had happened.
He did not pretend the household was healthy.
He did not rename sin as wisdom.
But He found the wounded woman in the wilderness.
Then Hagar gave God one of Scripture’s most beautiful names:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro’i.
“The God who sees me.”
Imagine that.
The servant.
The outsider.
The pregnant fugitive.
The woman caught inside somebody else’s attempt to force God’s promise…
became the person in this chapter who declared:
God sees me.
Maybe somebody reading this needs those words more than anything else.
God sees you.
He sees what happened behind the closed door.
He sees the humiliation nobody knows about.
He sees the marriage that looks peaceful online and feels unbearably lonely at home.
He sees the child crying after everyone else has gone to sleep.
He sees the believer secretly exhausted from pretending faith never hurts.
He sees the consequences of decisions you regret.
He sees the wounds caused by decisions that were not even yours.
And He sees the wilderness where you ended up after somebody else used power selfishly.
You are not invisible to God.
But the story does not end at Genesis 16.
Ishmael was born.
Years passed.
God returned to Abraham.
And the Lord made something unmistakably clear.
The covenant promise would not ultimately be accomplished through Abraham and Sarah’s shortcut.
Sarah herself would bear the promised son.
Abraham laughed.
Sarah would later laugh too.
Human impossibility was staring directly at divine promise.
And God did what human strength could never manufacture.
Isaac was born.
His Hebrew name, יִצְחָק (Yitzḥaq), is connected with laughter.
The laughter of disbelief was transformed into the laughter of astonishment.
God had waited until human strength could not take the credit.
That is often where grace becomes unmistakable.
God sometimes allows our strength to reach its end because we are addicted to signing our names beneath miracles.
We want testimonies that secretly say:
“Look what God and I accomplished.”
But Scripture keeps confronting us with a God who delights in accomplishing what human beings cannot.
Then Genesis 21 becomes painful again.
Sarah saw Ishmael and demanded that Hagar and her son be sent away.
Whatever interpretive questions surround the precise nature of Ishmael’s behavior in that scene, the family fracture was now undeniable.
Abraham was deeply distressed because Ishmael was his son.
That sentence deserves to remain painful.
Ishmael was not an abstract theological mistake.
He was Abraham’s child.
Hagar was not a literary prop.
She was a human being.
This is what sin does.
We often imagine shortcuts as moments.
God sees their consequences spreading through people.
Your decisions have names attached to them.
Faces.
Families.
Memories.
Sometimes children.
Sometimes spouses.
Sometimes friendships.
Sometimes churches.
Sometimes people who never chose the situation but nevertheless carry wounds from it.
That is why repentance cannot merely mean feeling embarrassed about being caught.
Repentance means agreeing with God about sin and turning toward Him.
It means refusing to romanticize the shortcut simply because it once seemed necessary.
But notice something equally important.
God did not abandon Ishmael.
God heard the boy.
God met Hagar again.
God provided water.
God preserved them.
God had purposes for Ishmael even though Ishmael was not the covenant son through whom the promised line leading ultimately toward Christ would proceed.
That distinction matters.
The biblical story is not saying, “Isaac mattered and Ishmael did not.”
It is saying that God sovereignly chose the covenant line through Isaac while still seeing, hearing, preserving, and caring for Hagar and Ishmael.
Grace refuses our simplistic categories.
Human beings create disasters.
God still sees people inside them.
Then centuries later, the apostle Paul reached back into this family history when writing to the Galatians.
He described the two sons using a striking contrast.
Ishmael was born:
κατὰ σάρκα
kata sarka—
“according to the flesh.”
Isaac came:
διὰ τῆς ἐπαγγελίας
dia tēs epangelias—
“through the promise.”
Paul then explicitly says:
ἅτινά ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα
hatina estin allēgoroumena—
these things are being treated allegorically.
He uses Hagar and Sarah in his argument concerning slavery and freedom, human effort and divine promise, Sinai and the freedom belonging to the children of promise.
We should be careful here.
Paul is not giving Christians permission to turn every detail of Genesis into whatever symbolism we invent.
He tells us what theological use he is making of this history.
And his argument eventually explodes into one of Christianity’s great declarations:
“For freedom Christ has set us free.”
Galatians 5:1.
There is the Gospel hiding behind Abraham’s family scandal.
Human flesh tries to accomplish what only divine promise can accomplish.
And ultimately, salvation itself works exactly that way.
You cannot manufacture your own righteousness.
You cannot negotiate yourself into heaven.
You cannot compensate for your sins with enough religious activity.
You cannot erase yesterday by behaving better tomorrow.
You cannot make yourself spiritually alive.
You cannot save yourself.
Religion says:
Try harder.
Grace says:
Christ has done what you could never do.
The flesh says:
Produce something God will accept.
The Gospel says:
Receive what God has provided in His Son.
Abraham’s greatest problem was not simply that he slept with Hagar.
Sarah’s deepest problem was not merely jealousy.
Hagar’s deepest need was not merely escape from Sarah.
Their story sits inside humanity’s greater catastrophe:
We keep trying to control what belongs to God.
And that rebellion reaches all the way back to Eden.
We want God’s blessings while keeping our hands on the steering wheel.
We want His promises on our timetable.
His kingdom according to our strategy.
His gifts without His waiting room.
His will without surrender.
His salvation with something of ourselves left to boast about.
Then Jesus arrives.
Not as humanity’s shortcut to God…
but as God’s promised Savior for humanity.
The New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the climactic promised offspring in Abraham’s covenant story.
Paul writes in Galatians 3:16 that the promises ultimately point toward Christ.
And suddenly the stars Abraham once stared at become part of something unimaginably larger.
Abraham could not see Bethlehem.
He could not see a virgin carrying the Messiah.
He could not see Jesus walking dusty roads through Galilee.
He could not see nails.
A cross.
A sealed tomb.
An empty grave.
But God could.
Before Abraham ever touched Hagar…
God knew Christ was coming.
Before Sarah laughed…
God knew Christ was coming.
Before Hagar ran into the wilderness…
God knew Christ was coming.
Before Ishmael cried…
before Isaac was born…
before Jacob…
before Judah…
before David…
before exile…
before Bethlehem…
God knew exactly where His promise was going.
Jesus.
This is why the Gospel is stronger than your worst shortcut.
Read that again.
The Gospel is stronger than your worst shortcut.
Your sin may create consequences.
Repentance does not magically erase every earthly result of our choices.
Forgiveness does not mean every broken relationship instantly repairs itself.
Grace does not mean history never happened.
Abraham could not go backward and make Genesis 16 disappear.
But God could move redemption forward.
That may be the word somebody desperately needs today.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
Jesus can redeem what yesterday tried to destroy.
Maybe your “Hagar” was not a person.
Maybe it was a decision.
A relationship you forced.
A marriage entered for the wrong reasons.
A dishonest business arrangement.
A sexual compromise.
A ministry ambition.
A financial shortcut.
A secret addiction.
A manipulation disguised as prayer.
A door God never opened that you kicked down because you were tired of waiting.
And now you are living with something you created while trying to escape uncertainty.
You keep asking:
“Have I ruined everything?”
Look at Abraham.
The Bible does not hide his scandal.
It records it.
Then continues telling the story of grace.
That is Christianity.
Not God pretending righteous people never failed.
God redeeming sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Abraham would later become celebrated as a man of faith.
Not because Genesis 16 never happened.
But because failure did not have the authority to write the final chapter of his life.
Peter denied Jesus.
David committed terrible sin.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a shattered relational history.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes.
Yet again and again Scripture announces the same scandalous truth:
Grace gets the final word for those who come to God through Christ.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that excuses sin.
Grace that exposes sin, forgives the repentant sinner, and begins transforming the person who comes to Jesus.
This is why the cross is so offensive to human pride.
At Calvary, you cannot brag.
You arrive guilty.
Christ arrives righteous.
You bring sin.
Christ brings blood.
You bring debt.
Christ brings payment.
You bring death.
Christ brings resurrection.
You bring nothing capable of saving yourself.
And Jesus becomes everything you need.
So maybe the most important question in Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar’s story is not:
“How could they do that?”
Maybe the question is:
“Where am I doing the same thing?”
Where are you forcing what God told you to trust Him with?
What are you manipulating because prayer feels too slow?
What compromise have you renamed “wisdom”?
What relationship are you refusing to surrender?
What secret sin are you protecting because you believe losing it would hurt more than disobeying God?
What did you manufacture in the flesh that you are now asking God to bless?
Be honest.
This story hits harder when we stop treating Abraham like an ancient stranger.
There is a little Genesis 16 in all of us.
We hate waiting.
We fear uncertainty.
We crave control.
And sometimes we would rather create an Ishmael today than wait for an Isaac tomorrow.
But faith says:
God does not need my sin to accomplish His will.
God does not need my manipulation to fulfill His promise.
God does not need my compromise to secure my future.
God does not need me to become sovereign.
He asks me to trust Him.
And when I fail?
Run toward Christ.
Not away.
Repent.
Confess.
Stop defending the shortcut.
Stop blaming everybody around you.
Stop pretending consequences mean grace has disappeared.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Because the same God who found Hagar in the wilderness still sees wounded people.
The same God who remained faithful to Abraham despite Abraham’s failure still keeps His promises.
And the same God who brought Isaac from an impossible womb brought Jesus from the grave.
That is our hope.
Not Abraham’s perfection.
Not Sarah’s perfection.
Certainly not ours.
Christ.
Jesus Christ crucified for sinners and risen from the dead.
Your comment might become the sentence another wounded believer reads tonight and realizes:
I am not the only one fighting this.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. Nothing we do can purchase His grace.
Someone is about to make a permanent decision because they are tired of waiting.
Someone is considering adultery because their marriage feels empty.
Someone is about to compromise because obedience seems unproductive.
Someone is hiding beneath shame because they believe their worst decision disqualified them forever.
Someone needs to discover that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
And when it does, come back and remember Abraham.
Remember Sarah.
Remember Hagar.
Remember the wilderness.
Remember the consequences.
Remember the promise.
And above everything else…
remember Christ.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession becomes the first crack through which light finally enters.
Tell us what God is confronting in you.
Tell us where you need prayer.
Tell us how Christ has restored you after a shortcut you thought had ruined your story.
Because Abraham’s family teaches us something terrifying and beautiful:
Human shortcuts can create consequences that last far beyond the moment…
but they cannot overthrow the sovereign grace of God.
Maybe you made the wrong turn.
Maybe you forced the wrong door.
Maybe you slept in the wrong bed.
Maybe you trusted the wrong person.
Maybe you manipulated something that should have been surrendered.
Maybe there are consequences you cannot undo.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend none of it happened.
It asks you to bring all of it to Jesus.
The scandal.
The shame.
The consequences.
The wilderness.
The regret.
Bring it to the cross.
Because the blood of Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending your sin was never sinful.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He forgives sinners.
He reconciles rebels to God.
He gives new life.
He transforms hearts.
He turns condemnation into justification for those who trust Him.
He takes people whose stories should have ended in shame…
and makes them trophies of grace.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you after everything else fades:
Your shortcut may explain how you reached the wilderness, but it does not get to decide whether Jesus can lead you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT “DELIGHT YOURSELF IN THE LORD” ACTUALLY MEANS
paragraphs: WHAT “DELIGHT YOURSELF IN THE LORD” ACTUALLY MEANS

Psalm 37:4 may be one of the most loved promises in Scripture—and one of the easiest to misunderstand. God never promised to become the delivery system for everything your heart wants. He offers something infinitely better: a heart so captivated by Him that even your desires begin to change.
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.”
You have probably read those words when you wanted something badly.
A relationship.
A breakthrough.
A job.
A restored marriage.
A child.
Healing.
Financial relief.
An answered prayer you have whispered so many times that you almost feel embarrassed saying it again.
Maybe you held Psalm 37:4 close and thought, If I love God enough, perhaps He will finally give me this.
And then He didn’t.
The relationship ended.
The door stayed closed.
The diagnosis remained.
The person never came back.
The opportunity went to somebody else.
The prayer seemed to disappear into heaven without an answer.
And somewhere beneath your worship songs, church attendance, Bible verses, and carefully constructed Christian smile, a dangerous question began growing:
God, You said You would give me the desires of my heart. So why didn’t You?
That question deserves more than a Christian cliché.
Because Psalm 37:4 is not a blank check from heaven.
It is something far more beautiful.
And far more dangerous to the old version of you.
The original Hebrew reads:
וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל־יְהוָה וְיִתֶּן־לְךָ מִשְׁאֲלֹת לִבֶּךָ
Ve-hit‘annag ‘al-YHWH, ve-yitten-lekha mish’alot libbekha.
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.”
The word translated “delight” comes from the Hebrew root עָנַג, ‘anag, carrying the sense of taking exquisite delight, finding pleasure, enjoying something deeply.
But notice where the delight is directed.
Not toward what God can give.
Toward God Himself.
That changes everything.
David does not say, “Delight yourself in the blessings of the LORD.”
He does not say, “Delight yourself in the gifts of the LORD.”
He does not say, “Delight yourself in the life you hope the LORD will eventually give you.”
He says:
Delight yourself in the LORD.
God is not merely the road to the treasure.
God is the Treasure.
And sometimes the reason Psalm 37:4 hurts us is because we quietly reverse it.
We want to delight ourselves in what we hope God will give us, while using God as the pathway to get there.
We want Jesus—and the relationship.
Jesus—and the money.
Jesus—and the healing.
Jesus—and the promotion.
Jesus—and the marriage.
Jesus—and the recognition.
Jesus—and the dream.
Then life strips something away, and suddenly we discover which side of the “and” our heart was really worshiping.
That discovery can feel like a scandal.
But sometimes exposure is the beginning of grace.
Because Jesus does not expose our idols merely to humiliate us.
He exposes them to free us.
Psalm 37 was written in a world where righteous people could look around and see wicked people apparently prospering.
That matters.
The psalm begins:
“Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.” — Psalm 37:1
David is speaking to people tempted to compare.
People watching others prosper.
People wondering why obedience seems costly while compromise seems profitable.
People who could look at somebody else’s life and whisper:
Why do they have what I prayed for?
That sounds painfully modern.
You open Facebook and see someone celebrating the marriage you wanted.
Someone bought the house.
Someone got promoted.
Someone’s ministry exploded.
Someone is traveling.
Someone announces a pregnancy while you are still praying through tears.
Someone seems healthy while your body is exhausted.
Someone who does not appear to care about God seems to be thriving, while you are trying desperately to obey Him and barely holding yourself together.
And comparison begins preaching its own gospel.
God forgot you.
You are behind.
You should have more by now.
Maybe obedience isn't worth it.
But David answers that anxiety with a sequence that changes the meaning of verse four.
“Trust in the LORD, and do good…”
“Delight thyself also in the LORD…”
“Commit thy way unto the LORD…”
“Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him…”
Psalm 37:3–7.
Trust.
Delight.
Commit.
Rest.
Wait.
That is the atmosphere surrounding “He shall give thee the desires of thine heart.”
This is not a formula for controlling God.
It is an invitation to surrender to Him.
And that may be exactly where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because what if the deepest miracle of Psalm 37:4 is not merely God giving your heart what it presently desires?
What if part of His grace is teaching your heart what is actually worth desiring?
There are things you once begged God for that you now thank Him for withholding.
Think about that.
There may have been a person you thought you could never live without.
A door you were furious God closed.
An opportunity you believed would define your future.
A dream you thought had to happen for you to be happy.
At the time, “no” felt cruel.
Years later, you could finally see mercy hiding inside it.
You thought God was taking something from you.
He may have been rescuing you from something you could not yet see.
And sometimes we never receive that explanation in this life.
Biblical faith does not require pretending every disappointment eventually becomes understandable.
Sometimes we trust God without getting the missing chapter.
That is why delight is so much deeper than positive thinking.
Delighting in God means God Himself becomes increasingly precious to you.
His character.
His presence.
His Word.
His holiness.
His mercy.
His promises.
His kingdom.
His Son.
You begin wanting what pleases Him because you are beginning to love Him more than the life you once demanded from Him.
This does not mean every ordinary desire disappears.
Scripture does not teach that Christians stop wanting marriage, children, provision, meaningful work, friendship, healing, justice, safety, or relief from suffering.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane with terrifying honesty.
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me…”
Then came surrender:
“…nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39
There is mature faith in those words.
Jesus did not pretend suffering felt pleasant.
Biblical surrender is not pretending you do not want something.
It is wanting God more.
It is being able to say:

“Father, You know what I want. I have cried over it. I have prayed about it. I have imagined receiving it. But I refuse to make this desire my god. If You give it, I will worship You. If You withhold it, hold me close enough that I will still worship You. If You change my desire, change it. If You make me wait, teach me how to wait without becoming bitter. I want Your will more than I want control.”
That kind of prayer terrifies the flesh.
Because the flesh wants God to sign our plans.
Jesus asks us to follow His.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading these words needs to become painfully honest.
What happens to your relationship with God when He does not give you what you want?
Do you still want Him?
If the relationship never comes…
is Jesus enough?
If the promotion goes to somebody else…
is Jesus enough?
If people never applaud your obedience…
is Jesus enough?
If the prayer takes years…
is Jesus enough?
If following Christ costs you something you desperately wanted to keep…
is Jesus still Lord?
Those are not easy questions.
Do not answer them quickly.
Because there is a difference between saying Jesus is enough while everything is going well and discovering that He is enough when something you love is lying shattered at your feet.
Peter knew something about that kind of collapse.
He had promised Jesus:
“Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.” — Matthew 26:33
Then fear arrived.
Pressure arrived.
And Peter denied even knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering your own voice saying, “I do not know the man.”
Imagine watching Jesus go toward the cross carrying not only humanity’s sin but the sin of the disciple who had just abandoned Him.
Peter's failure was public.
Ugly.
Humiliating.
A scandal.
But the resurrected Christ did not leave Peter inside the worst chapter of his story.
Jesus restored him.
Jesus recommissioned him.
Jesus still had work for him to do.
That is the Gospel.
Not good people earning good things from God.
Not religious people learning the secret formula for getting their desires fulfilled.
The Gospel is that sinners who could never rescue themselves are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Grace came looking for guilty people.
And when Jesus saves a person, He does not merely improve the circumstances surrounding that person's heart.
He begins transforming the heart itself.
The desires begin changing.
The appetite begins changing.
Things that once tasted irresistible begin tasting empty.
Things you once ignored begin becoming precious.
Scripture becomes more than inspirational quotations.
Prayer becomes more than asking for things.
Repentance becomes more than feeling guilty.
Holiness becomes more than religious restriction.
Jesus becomes more than someone you call when your plans are falling apart.
He becomes Lord.
This is why Psalm 37:4 cannot faithfully be reduced to:
“Love God and He will give you everything you want.”
Imagine telling that to Paul.
Paul pleaded with the Lord concerning his “thorn in the flesh.”
He asked repeatedly for it to depart.
God's answer was not the removal Paul requested.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9
Paul wanted relief.
God gave sustaining grace.
Was the promise broken?
No.
Paul was learning something deeper than getting his preferred circumstance.
He was discovering the sufficiency of Christ inside a circumstance he would not have chosen.
Sometimes God changes the situation.
Sometimes God changes you inside the situation.
Sometimes He does both.
And sometimes He asks you to trust Him while neither seems to be happening yet.
That word “yet” matters.
Because waiting exposes what comfort can hide.
Waiting reveals whether we want God's hand more than God's heart.
And perhaps you have been waiting so long that you are exhausted.
You still believe.
But barely.
You still pray.
But your prayers are shorter now.
You still worship.
But sometimes the lyrics catch in your throat.
You see people testify about answered prayers, and you are happy for them…
mostly.
Then you go somewhere private and wonder when your testimony is coming.
Please hear this carefully:
Your waiting is not proof that God has abandoned you.
The cross forever destroys the idea that God's love can be measured simply by how comfortable the present moment feels.
Look at Jesus.
If someone had looked at Calvary on Friday afternoon and judged God's plan solely by appearances, everything would have looked lost.
The Messiah was bleeding.
The disciples were scattered.
Hope appeared buried.
The stone rolled shut.
But God was not finished.
Sunday was coming.
The cross looked like scandal.
Resurrection revealed victory.

And that does not mean every painful earthly story receives the ending we personally choose. Christianity does not promise that every grave will open before our funeral or that every loss will be reversed according to our timetable.
It promises something greater.
Christ has risen.
Sin can be forgiven.
Death has been defeated.
Those who belong to Christ have a living hope.
And one day God will make all things right.
So delighting yourself in the Lord is not spiritual bargaining.
It is not:
“God, I will worship You so You will give me what I really want.”
It becomes:
“God, teach my heart to recognize that You are what I need most.”
And strangely, beautifully, painfully, when God becomes your treasure, your desires stop owning you the way they once did.
You can desire marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can desire provision without worshiping money.
You can desire healing without making physical comfort your god.
You can desire success without needing applause to know who you are.
You can desire restoration while refusing to make another human being your savior.
You can ask boldly while surrendering completely.
You can cry and still trust.
You can grieve and still worship.
You can hurt and still believe.
You can say, “Lord, I desperately want this,” without saying, “Lord, I cannot love You unless You give it to me.”
That is freedom.
Maybe that is what God is doing in you right now.
Maybe you came asking God to change your circumstances, and somewhere along the journey He started changing you.
Maybe the closed door exposed an idol.
Maybe the heartbreak exposed your dependency.
Maybe success exposed your pride.
Maybe failure exposed your fear.
Maybe waiting exposed your unbelief.
Maybe loneliness exposed how desperately you need communion with Christ.
Maybe your scandal became the place where grace finally became more than a Christian word.
And if something hidden in you has been exposed while reading this, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Repentance is not God standing over you waiting to destroy you.
In Christ, repentance is turning from sin and returning to the One who saves sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
You do not have to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Jesus did not go to the cross for an imaginary, polished version of you.
He knows the envy.
The lust.
The pride.
The bitterness.
The secret resentment toward God.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The compromise nobody knows about.
The religious performance.
The hidden addiction.
The jealousy you disguise as criticism.
The anger underneath your smile.
The desire you have placed above obedience.
He knows.
And still the Gospel says:
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
The blood of Christ is sufficient for sinners who stop defending their sin and come to Him in faith.
Perhaps your prayer tonight does not need to be, “Lord, give me the desires of my heart.”
Maybe it needs to become:
“Lord, take my heart.
Search what I desire.
Expose what has become an idol.
Forgive what has become sinful.
Heal what has become wounded.
Correct what has become distorted.
And teach me to delight in You.”
You do not need to tell strangers every private detail. Simply comment, “Jesus, change my heart.”
And if you have been exhausted by waiting but refuse to walk away from Christ, comment, “I’m still trusting.”
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only believer struggling to hold onto faith.
That matters.
We were never meant to pretend our way through discipleship.
And if you know someone who has been angry with God because a prayer was not answered the way they expected, send this article to them.
Your share might place biblical truth in front of them at exactly the moment they need it.
Because eventually all of us will face the question:
Do I delight in God—or only in what I hope God will give me?
Let them encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered not on personalities, but on Jesus Christ.
Supporting a Christian ministry does not purchase God's favor.
Sharing a post cannot save your soul.
Buying Christian merchandise cannot substitute for repentance, faith, obedience, generosity to your local church, or actual discipleship.
Jesus saves.
Grace is not for sale.

If your desire is to glorify God, do it first by trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, pursuing holiness, serving faithfully, giving generously as God leads you, and making His Gospel known.
If you have been receiving from this ministry and believe in what Gospel Warrior is doing, you can support the mission here:
Delight yourself in the Lord.
Not merely in what He can place inside your hands.
In Him.
Because eventually your hands will lose everything they are holding.
Money changes.
Bodies weaken.
People leave.
Careers end.
Possessions break.
Applause fades.
Beauty changes.
Plans collapse.
Earthly life itself ends.
But Christ remains.
And perhaps that is why the deepest fulfillment of the human heart cannot finally be found in receiving everything we once wanted.
It is found in discovering Someone infinitely better.
Jesus Christ.
The One who took our sin.
The One who bore our judgment.
The One who entered our shame.
The One who was crucified.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who forgives repentant sinners.
The One who restores ruined people.
The One who can take the chapter you thought disqualified you and make it part of a testimony of grace.
So bring Him the desire you are afraid to surrender.
Bring Him the prayer that still hurts.
Bring Him the disappointment you have been hiding behind worship songs.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the unanswered question.
Bring Him the broken dream.
Bring Him the secret sin.
Bring Him the heart that wants the gift more than the Giver.
And say:
“Jesus, I wanted You to give me the desires of my heart.
But now I am asking You for something deeper.
Give my heart new desires.
Teach me to want what You want.
Teach me to hate what destroys me.
Teach me to love what pleases You.
And if everything I thought I needed must be shaken before I discover that You are my treasure…
then hold me while You teach me to delight in You.”
That prayer may not instantly change your circumstances.
But surrendering your heart to Christ changes the place from which you face them.
Because the greatest answer to Psalm 37:4 is not finally having everything you wanted sitting around you.
It is waking up one day and realizing that somewhere between your disappointment, your surrender, your repentance, and His relentless grace…
Jesus became the One your heart wanted most.
And when Christ becomes your Treasure, even the things you never received can no longer prove that you were unloved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why Sin Pays Wages Even When It Looks Harmless
paragraphs: THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why Sin Pays Wages Even When It Looks Harmless

Romans 6:23 contains one of the most terrifying words in Scripture—and one of the most beautiful. What if the sin you keep calling harmless has already put you on a payroll… and what if Jesus came to tear up the contract?
There are things that do not look dangerous when they begin.
A private message.
A hidden browser tab.
A little bitterness you keep feeding because, after what they did, anger feels justified.
A lie that makes life easier.
A relationship you know is pulling your heart away from God, but losing it feels more painful than disobeying Him.
A secret habit nobody knows about.
A compromise at work.
An appetite you keep promising yourself you can control.
A grudge you have carried so long that you no longer call it hatred. You call it boundaries.
Pride disguised as confidence.
Greed renamed ambition.
Lust renamed chemistry.
Gossip renamed concern.
Drunkenness renamed unwinding.
Envy renamed motivation.
Revenge renamed closure.
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, something happens.
What once disturbed your conscience becomes familiar.
What once made you pray becomes something you defend.
What once made you ashamed becomes something you joke about.
What once felt like a chain begins to feel like part of your personality.
That is one of sin's most frightening abilities.
It rarely introduces itself by showing you the funeral.
It shows you the pleasure.
It shows you the attention.
It shows you the money.
It shows you the fantasy.
It shows you the relief.
It shows you the person you desperately want.
It shows you the temporary escape.
It shows you what you think you are gaining.
Then it quietly sends the bill.
And Paul wrote one sentence that exposes the entire transaction:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Romans 6:23.
Read it again, because there is a word hiding inside that verse that changes everything.
In Greek, the opening phrase reads:
τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος
ta gar opsōnia tēs hamartias thanatos
“For the wages of sin [is] death.”
That word translated “wages” is ὀψώνια — opsōnia.
Paul did not merely describe an unfortunate consequence.
He used the language of compensation.
Pay.
Wages.
What is received for service rendered.
And suddenly Romans 6 becomes painfully personal.
Sin has a payday.
You may enjoy the work before you receive the wages.
You may convince yourself nothing serious is happening.
You may look around and see other people doing the same thing.
You may even appear successful while something inside you is dying.
But sin never becomes harmless simply because its consequences have not arrived yet.
That is the deception.
A paycheck does not necessarily arrive the moment the work is performed.
Neither do all the visible consequences of sin.
Some wages arrive quickly.
Some take years.
Some appear in relationships.
Some appear in character.
Some appear in the conscience.
Some consequences ripple through families.
And Scripture ultimately points beyond every temporal consequence to the deepest catastrophe of sin: death and alienation from the God who is the source of life.
That is why Romans 6:23 cannot be understood properly as an isolated religious slogan.
Paul has been building an argument.
Earlier he asks:
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?”
His answer is forceful:
“God forbid.”
Romans 6:1–2.
Grace is not God's permission slip for rebellion.
Grace is God's rescue from rebellion.

Paul's argument throughout Romans 6 is that those united with Christ must no longer treat sin as their rightful master. He speaks of slavery, obedience, righteousness, sanctification, death, and life because sin is far more than an occasional mistake.
Sin wants dominion.
This is why one of the greatest lies a person can believe is:
“It isn't hurting anybody.”
Maybe you have said it.
Maybe you are saying it now.
But Scripture forces us to ask a harder question.
What is it doing to you?
What is it teaching your heart to love?
What is it teaching you to hide?
What are you becoming while repeatedly surrendering to it?
Jesus said:
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
Matthew 6:21.
Your repeated choices are not spiritually neutral.
They reveal loves, allegiances, desires, fears, and masters.
And sometimes the most dangerous sin in your life is not the one everyone can see.
It is the one you have successfully explained away.
David knew something about that.
Before the adultery.
Before the pregnancy.
Before the manipulation.
Before Uriah's death.
Before Nathan stood in front of a king and exposed him.
There was a look.
Then desire.
Then taking.
Then concealment.
Then another sin to protect the first one.
That is how darkness often grows.
One compromise needs another compromise to keep it alive.
One lie requires another lie.
One secret demands another locked door.
And eventually you are no longer merely hiding the sin.
You are protecting the version of yourself that needs the sin to remain hidden.
Then Nathan tells David a story.
David becomes furious at the guilty man in Nathan's story.
And Nathan says:
“Thou art the man.”
2 Samuel 12:7.
Imagine that silence.
David could recognize wickedness when it belonged to somebody else.
He struggled to see it when it lived in his own house.
So do we.
We condemn somebody else's affair while feeding our own lust.
We condemn somebody else's dishonesty while manipulating the truth ourselves.
We condemn somebody else's arrogance while secretly believing we are spiritually superior.
We condemn addiction while being unable to put down the thing controlling us.
We condemn idols made of wood and stone while organizing our lives around money, approval, sex, success, comfort, influence, romance, appearance, or ourselves.
And God, in His mercy, sometimes sends a Nathan into our lives.
A sermon.
A verse.
A friend.
A consequence.
A sleepless night.
A moment when the noise disappears and the excuses stop working.
Maybe this article is becoming one of those moments for you.
Not because I know your secret.
I don't.
But God does.
And perhaps there is something you have been calling harmless that your conscience has been calling something else.
You know the sentence you keep using.
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“Everybody does it.”
“At least I'm not as bad as…”
“God knows my heart.”
“We love each other.”
“It's just entertainment.”
“It's only online.”
“Nobody will ever know.”
“I deserve this.”
“I'll repent later.”
That last one may be the most frightening.
Because repentance is not a coupon we keep in our pocket while deliberately purchasing another night of rebellion.
The Greek word commonly translated “sin” in Romans 6:23 is ἁμαρτία — hamartia.

But we must be careful with simplistic word studies. Biblical sin is not adequately explained by the popular phrase “missing the mark” alone. In Paul's argument, sin is portrayed almost like a ruling power, a master seeking obedience.
Romans 6:12 says:
“Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof.”
Notice the language.
Reign.
Obey.
Sin does not merely want visitation rights.
Sin wants a throne.
That is why harmless-looking compromises matter.
You think you are making an exception.
Sin is attempting to establish a kingdom.
You think you are feeding an appetite.
The appetite may be learning how to command you.
You think you are keeping a secret.
The secret may be keeping you.
You think you possess the habit.
One day you discover the habit possesses you.
Jesus described the seriousness of slavery to sin plainly:
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
John 8:34.
Yet this is exactly where many Christian messages become distorted.
Some stop at condemnation.
They expose the wound and leave the sinner bleeding.
Romans 6:23 does not.
The verse has another half.
And the second half changes eternity.
τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος
to de charisma tou theou zōē aiōnios
“But the gift of God [is] eternal life…”
Do you see the contrast?
Wages.
Then gift.
The wages are earned.
The gift is given.
Sin pays.
God gives.
Death is what rebellion earns.
Eternal life is not a salary God owes good people for behaving well enough.
It is grace.
The Greek word Paul uses is χάρισμα — charisma, a gracious gift.
That distinction destroys both pride and despair.
Pride says, “I can make myself good enough for God.”
The Gospel says you need a gift you cannot earn.
Despair says, “I have become too filthy for God.”
The Gospel says the gift was never purchased by your moral perfection in the first place.
It was purchased at terrible cost by Another.
Paul finishes:
“…through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
There He is.
Jesus.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious performance.
Not motivational optimism.
Not “manifesting” a better future.
Not pretending your sin does not matter.
Not cleaning yourself up sufficiently to deserve God's attention.
Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not say sin is harmless.
The Gospel says sin is so deadly that the Son of God went to the cross.
And the Gospel does not say sinners are hopeless.
It says the Son of God went to the cross.
Both truths meet at Calvary.
Your sin is worse than your excuses say.
God's grace is greater than your shame says.
At the cross, we discover that God does not save us by pretending evil is good.
Justice is not discarded.
Sin is taken with deadly seriousness.
Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree,” as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
Paul writes that Christ “died for our sins according to the scriptures” in 1 Corinthians 15:3.
And Romans 5:8 gives us words that should break the heart of anyone who thinks they must become lovable before approaching God:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after the shame faded.
Not after we learned Christian vocabulary.
Not after our reputation recovered.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is not self-hatred.
It is not performing sadness so God will finally agree to love you.
Biblical repentance involves turning to God from sin, abandoning the illusion that rebellion can give us the life only God can give.
And grace does not merely forgive the old master while leaving us chained to him.
Romans 6 points toward liberation.
Paul says:
“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.”
Romans 6:14.
Maybe you need to hear that differently today.
Sin may have wounded you.
Sin may have embarrassed you.
Sin may have cost you years.
Sin may have damaged relationships you wish you could repair.
You may still be living with consequences that forgiveness does not magically erase.
But if you belong to Christ, sin does not own the final sentence of your story.
Jesus does.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
Imagine living with that memory.
“I know not the man.”
Then the rooster.
Then the eyes of Jesus.
Then Peter went out and wept bitterly.
It looked like scandal.
Failure.
Cowardice.
The collapse of everything Peter thought he was.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ restores him.
“Lovest thou me?”
Then:
“Feed my sheep.”
John 21.
Peter's failure was real.
Peter's grief was real.
But so was Christ's restoration.
That is grace.
Grace does not edit the past until sin becomes imaginary.
Grace takes guilty people and gives them a future they could never manufacture for themselves.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
Maybe only three people know.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have spent years constructing an image that makes everyone believe you are okay.
You smile.
You work.
You serve.
You post Scriptures.
You attend church.
You tell people, “God is good.”
And He is.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know there is a locked door inside you that you are terrified to open.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the version of you that everybody sees.
He came to save sinners.
That means you can stop negotiating with darkness.
You can stop defending what is destroying you.
You can stop confusing secrecy with safety.
You can bring your sin into the light before God.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are not words for people who never failed.
They are words desperately needed by people who have.
Perhaps you are reading this while fighting the same temptation you promised God you would never touch again.
Perhaps you fell last night.
Perhaps you are sitting beside somebody who has no idea what is happening inside you.
Perhaps you have become exhausted from being two people—the person everybody knows and the person nobody sees.
Do not turn Romans 6:23 into another weapon for self-destruction.
Let it become a warning sign pointing you toward the Savior.
The wages of sin is death.
Yes.
Do not soften it.
Do not rename it.
Do not romanticize it.
Do not play with what crucified Christ.
But do not stop reading halfway.
The gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
There is still a gift.
There is still a Savior.
There is still mercy.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still a way home.
And maybe today your most spiritual sentence is not something impressive.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
The tax collector in Jesus' parable would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He cried:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
Luke 18:13.
Jesus said that man went home justified.
Not the man boasting about his religious accomplishments.
The broken man who knew he needed mercy.
So stop auditioning for grace.
You cannot earn a gift.
Come to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Where appropriate and safe, seek godly accountability instead of building another hiding place.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Cut off the access that continually feeds temptation.
Open your Bible when your feelings tell you to run from God.
Pray when shame tells you He does not want to hear your voice.
Find mature believers who will love you enough to tell you the truth and stay beside you while you learn to walk in it.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the ground.
Look again to Christ.
Christian freedom is not the freedom to make sin comfortable.
It is freedom from sin's claim to be your rightful master.
This is why the “harmless” sin matters.
Not because God is trying to steal your joy.
Because the thing promising you freedom may actually be charging you with your life.
Sin says, “Take.”
Jesus says, “Receive.”
Sin says, “Hide.”
Jesus calls us into the light.
Sin says, “You need this.”
Jesus says, “Come unto me.”
Sin promises life and pays death.
Christ entered death and rose again so sinners could receive life.
That is the Gospel.
And if something inside you has been exposed while reading this, do not rush away from that conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Be honest.
Did this hit somewhere you were not expecting?
Do not let conviction become another emotion you forget tomorrow.
Come back to Romans 6:23 when temptation begins advertising the pleasure but hiding the paycheck.
And think of one person right now.
Not fifty people.
One.
The friend whose smile has not looked the same lately.
The husband quietly struggling.
The wife carrying shame.
The son drifting.
The daughter hiding pain.
The believer who has become numb.
The person who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to be good.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves.
That matters.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person who has not prayed in years.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the skeptic who thinks grace is too good to be true.
Even invite the unbeliever who does not yet understand why Christians keep talking about a cross.
Deal honestly with Jesus.
Because eventually the screen goes dark.
The comments stop.
The notifications disappear.
The public image means nothing.
And you are left with the question Romans 6 has been asking all along:
Who is your master?
If sin has been paying you wages you never wanted, stop pretending the paycheck is harmless.
Run to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one final indulgence.
Not when you feel cleaner.
Come as the sinner who needs mercy.
Come as the prodigal who finally understands that the far country cannot become home.
Come with the secret.
Come with the shame.
Come with the addiction.
Come with the bitterness.
Come with the consequences.
Come with the pieces.
Jesus Christ did not shed His blood so you could become better at hiding your chains.
He came to set captives free.
And when the Accuser points toward everything you have done, the Christian does not ultimately answer, “Look how good I became.”
The Christian points toward a cross.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward a risen King.
Toward Jesus.
The wages were death.
But God offered a gift.
And the gift has a name.
Jesus Christ our Lord.
And if Jesus has rewritten a chapter of your life that once looked impossible to redeem, tell somebody about it.
Because somebody else is still sitting in the chapter you survived.

Sin will always hide the paycheck until after the pleasure—but Jesus can meet you even in the wreckage, break the chains, forgive the sinner, and write grace where you thought only shame could remain.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Tamar. Rahab. Ruth. Bathsheba. Why Are These Women Named Before Jesus Is Born?
paragraphs: Tamar. Rahab. Ruth. Bathsheba. Why Are These Women Named Before Jesus Is Born?

Before Matthew tells us about the virgin, the manger, the wise men, or the Child called Jesus, he makes us walk through a family history filled with sexual scandal, outsiders, grief, shattered reputations, abuse of power, and astonishing grace. And he does it for a reason.
Most people hurry through genealogies.
Abraham begot Isaac. Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah.
Names.
More names.
More names.
We want Bethlehem. We want angels. We want the star. We want Mary holding the newborn Christ.
But Matthew will not let us get to the manger that quickly.
Before he shows us Jesus, he opens the family records.
And hidden among generations of fathers and sons, four references suddenly interrupt the rhythm.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
And “the wife of Uriah”—Bathsheba.
Then comes Mary.
If you have ever wondered whether the parts of your story that embarrass you have permanently disqualified you from being used by God, do not rush past these women.
Stay here.
Because before Matthew announces the birth of the Savior, he deliberately reminds us what kind of world the Savior came to save.
Matthew begins:
“Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ…”
Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou.
“The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ…” — Matthew 1:1.
Then the rhythm begins.
Father.
Son.
Father.
Son.
Generation after generation.
Until Matthew writes that Judah fathered Perez and Zerah “ἐκ τῆς Θάμαρ”—ek tēs Thamar, “by Tamar.”
Later: Boaz “ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ”—by Rahab.
Then Obed “ἐκ τῆς Ῥούθ”—by Ruth.
Then Solomon “ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου”—literally, by “the [woman] of Uriah.”
Matthew does not even call Bathsheba by name there.
He calls attention to Uriah.
And suddenly this genealogy is not merely a list.
It is a testimony.
Not because these women were the only sinners in Jesus’ genealogy. Far from it. The men surrounding them were sinners too, sometimes spectacularly so.
And not because Matthew is teaching that women themselves were somehow scandalous intrusions into an otherwise respectable family line.
No.
The shock is much deeper.
God did not sanitize the human history into which His Son entered.
Jesus stepped directly into it.
Tamar’s story is uncomfortable enough that many Christians have probably never heard a sermon about it.
Genesis 38 introduces us to a family collapsing under sin.

Tamar married Judah’s son Er. Er died under divine judgment. According to the family obligation described in the narrative, Judah’s next son, Onan, was expected to preserve his dead brother’s line through Tamar. Instead, he exploited the situation while deliberately refusing the responsibility attached to it. He also died under judgment.
Judah then promised Tamar his younger son Shelah when the boy grew older.
But Judah did not keep his word.
Tamar waited.
And waited.
And eventually realized she had been abandoned in a vulnerable position.
What happened next is disturbing and complicated. Tamar disguised herself, Judah mistook her for a prostitute, and Judah slept with his own daughter-in-law without realizing who she was.
She became pregnant.
When Judah later heard that Tamar was pregnant, his response was terrifyingly hypocritical.
He wanted her punished.
Until Tamar produced the evidence showing who the father was.
And Judah finally confessed:
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי”
Tzadeqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Not “Tamar never sinned.”
Not “everything Tamar did should be imitated.”
Judah is acknowledging that, in the situation narrated, Tamar had been more in the right than he was because he had failed to give her Shelah as promised.
The scandal exposed something Judah would rather have kept hidden.
His own failure.
And from that broken chapter came Perez.
And through Perez eventually came David.
And through David eventually came Jesus.
Matthew refuses to erase Tamar from the record.
Her name remains.
Maybe that matters to someone reading this who has spent years believing that the worst chapter of your life became the title of your entire story.
Maybe people remember you by what happened.
Maybe they know the divorce.
The addiction.
The pregnancy.
The affair.
The betrayal.
The arrest.
The collapse.
The years you ran from God.
Maybe your own memory keeps dragging you back into rooms Jesus has already called you to leave.
Hear this carefully: grace does not mean sin never mattered.
The cross proves sin mattered so much that Christ had to die.
Grace means sin does not get the final word over everyone who comes to Christ.
Then Matthew writes another name.
Rahab.
If this is the Rahab of Joshua—as the longstanding Christian identification understands her—her résumé does not begin in a synagogue.
It begins in Jericho.
And Scripture identifies Rahab as a prostitute.
Not metaphorically.
Not because Christians later tried to make her past sound dramatic.
Hebrews still calls her that when celebrating her faith, and James likewise points to her actions in receiving and protecting the messengers.
Think about that.
God did not need Scripture to lie about Rahab’s past in order to honor what His grace produced in her.
That should free somebody.
We often think redemption requires pretending.
Pretending the addiction never happened.
Pretending the marriage was never broken.
Pretending we were never sexually immoral.
Pretending we never doubted.
Pretending we never became cold toward God.
Pretending our family was healthier than it really was.
The Bible does something much more powerful.
It tells the truth.
And then it shows what God can do with people whose truth is ugly.
Rahab had heard what Israel’s God had done.
And somewhere inside a woman surrounded by a condemned city, faith awakened.
She told the Israelite spies that the LORD their God was God in heaven above and on earth beneath.
Then she acted on what she believed.
Hebrews later summarizes it with two astonishing words:
“Πίστει Ῥαὰβ…”
Pistei Rhaab.
“By faith Rahab…”
By faith.
The prostitute became a woman remembered for faith.
Do not miss that.
Scripture remembers where she came from without imprisoning her there.
Her past remains part of her testimony.
It does not remain the master of her identity.
That is what Jesus does.
The Gospel is not God pretending you were always clean.
The Gospel is God cleansing people who cannot cleanse themselves.
It is not God announcing that rebellion was harmless.
It is God announcing that the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
There is a difference.
Maybe you have been trying to become worthy enough to come home.
You keep telling yourself, “After I fix this…”
“After I stop struggling…”
“After I become consistent…”
“After I get myself together…”
Then I will come back to God.
But if sinners could repair themselves before approaching God, we would not need a Savior.
Christ did not come as a trophy for people who successfully rescued themselves.
He came to seek and save the lost.
Rahab did not climb out of Jericho and eventually become worthy of mercy.
Mercy found her while Jericho was still Jericho.
Then comes Ruth.
Her story feels gentler, but underneath its tenderness is enormous pain.
Ruth is a widow.
Naomi is a widow.
The future looks empty.
And Ruth is a Moabite woman entering Israel.
Yet Ruth makes one of Scripture’s most breathtaking declarations of loyalty.
The Hebrew includes:
“עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי”
‘Amekh ‘ammi, ve’Elohayikh Elohai.
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
Those are not merely romantic words about human loyalty.
Ruth is binding her future to Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God.
She walks toward Bethlehem with a grieving woman who believes she has come home empty.
Think about the irony.
Naomi says she came home empty.
But walking beside her is Ruth.
And inside Ruth’s future is Obed.
Inside Obed’s future is Jesse.
Inside Jesse’s future is David.
And inside David’s royal line, according to the promise of God, is the coming Messiah.
Naomi thought she was looking at emptiness.
God was writing genealogy.
Maybe that is where this article finds you.
You have been calling this season empty.
Empty bank account.
Empty bedroom.
Empty chair.
Empty marriage.
Empty prayers.
Empty plans.
Empty heart.
You prayed and nothing happened the way you expected.
You lost someone.
Someone left.
Something died that you were sure God would preserve.
And now you are standing in the ruins trying to understand how a good God could possibly write anything beautiful from this.
Ruth whispers across the centuries:
You cannot always tell what God is doing by looking at what you have lost.
Sometimes providence looks like an ordinary road back to Bethlehem.
Sometimes redemption enters wearing work clothes and gleaning grain from the edges of somebody else’s field.
Sometimes the chapter that feels like an ending is carrying a beginning you cannot yet see.
Then comes the most haunting reference of all.
Matthew does not say “Bathsheba.”
He writes of “the wife of Uriah.”
That wording makes the reader remember.
Uriah.
The faithful soldier.
The husband David betrayed.

Second Samuel does not soften David’s actions. David saw Bathsheba, inquired about her, sent messengers, and had her brought to him. After she became pregnant, David attempted to conceal what he had done. Eventually he arranged for Uriah to be placed where he would be killed in battle.
Then David took Bathsheba as his wife.
For a moment, the king may have believed the story had been buried.
But God sent Nathan.
That matters.
Because biblical grace is never permission to protect powerful people from truth.
The Bible does not rewrite David’s evil into romance.
It exposes it.
And Matthew, generations later, refuses to let the royal genealogy become propaganda.
“The wife of Uriah.”
Four words that keep the wound visible.
Four words reminding every king that God remembers the person power would prefer to erase.
And yet…
Solomon came through Bathsheba.
The royal line continued.
Not because David’s sin was acceptable.
Not because Uriah’s death was insignificant.
Not because consequences disappeared.
But because human evil could not cancel God’s redemptive purpose.
That is one of the hardest truths of grace.
God can redeem what He never approved.
Read that again.
God can redeem what He never approved.
He can bring beauty out of a situation without calling the evil beautiful.
He can forgive sin without redefining sin.
He can restore sinners without pretending nobody was wounded.
He can write redemption after devastation without asking us to call devastation good.
That is why Christianity is not positive thinking.
It is resurrection.
Positive thinking tells the tomb to look less dark.
Jesus walks into death and comes out alive.
And now we begin to understand why these women appear before the birth of Christ.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
The wife of Uriah.
Different women.
Different wounds.
Different circumstances.
Different moral complexities.
We should not flatten their stories into one category.
Tamar was not Rahab.
Ruth was not Bathsheba.
Bathsheba should not be blamed for David’s abuse of royal power.
Ruth’s loyalty should not be treated as scandal merely because she was a Moabite.
Their stories deserve to be heard as Scripture actually tells them.
But Matthew places their memories into the genealogy leading toward Jesus.
And then comes another woman.
Mary.
And suddenly the pattern reaches its climax.
Matthew has been saying “begot… begot… begot…”
Until Jesus.
The wording changes.
Joseph is identified as the husband of Mary, “of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.”
Jesus is not presented as Joseph’s biological son.
Matthew is preparing us for the virgin conception he immediately explains.
The genealogy reaches Jesus Christ, but Jesus enters the story uniquely.
The Savior comes into the human family while remaining the promised Christ.
He inherits a real human history.
A history containing kings and prostitutes, patriarchs and outsiders, faithful people and catastrophic sinners.
He does not stand at a safe distance from our wreckage.
He enters the human story.
And eventually He carries human sin to a Roman cross.
This is where genealogy becomes Gospel.
Because maybe Tamar is not the person in this story you recognize.
Maybe Judah is.
Maybe you were the hypocrite.
Maybe Rahab is not the person you recognize.
Maybe you are the person who lived for years in rebellion while knowing somewhere inside that God was real.
Maybe Ruth is you.
Still faithful.
Still walking.
Still grieving.
Still wondering why obedience has become so expensive.
Maybe you recognize David.
And that terrifies you.
Because you did something that wounded somebody.
You covered it.
You justified it.
You blamed circumstances.
You hoped time would bury it.
But the Holy Spirit keeps bringing you back to the truth.
Then do not run from conviction.
Run with it to Christ.
Repentance is not God destroying your hope.
Repentance is God refusing to let the thing destroying you remain hidden.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Blood-bought forgiveness.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because humanity needed motivational advice.
He died because we needed atonement.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed mercy.
We needed a righteousness we could never manufacture for ourselves.
The genealogy points toward a Child.
The Child grows toward a cross.
And the cross opens an empty tomb.
That is the Gospel.
Your sin is more serious than the world tells you.
And the grace of Jesus Christ is more powerful than your shame tells you.
You cannot save yourself.
But Christ actually saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People who have been wounded.
People who have wounded others.
People whose families are complicated.
People who wish they could tear pages out of their own biographies.
Jesus does not ask you to edit your history before coming to Him.
He asks you to repent and believe.
Bring Him the truth.
The real truth.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The sexual sin.
The pride.
The secret messages.
The resentment.
The hypocrisy.
The unbelief.
The hidden browser history.
The anger toward God.
The years you wasted.
The thing nobody knows.
Bring it into the light.
Not because confession earns salvation.
Jesus earns salvation.
But the person who comes to Christ no longer has to build a home inside the darkness.
There is a dangerous version of Christianity that teaches people how to look redeemed without actually surrendering.
Smile.
Post a verse.
Attend church.
Say “God is good.”
Keep the secret locked downstairs.
Jesus wants deeper than your image.
He wants you.
And maybe that is why this genealogy feels so strangely comforting.
The Bible is not embarrassed by broken people.
It simply refuses to leave brokenness unchallenged and unredeemed.
God's grace does not airbrush Scripture's families.
It invades them.
Tamar’s chapter was not deleted.
Rahab’s former life was not rewritten.
Ruth’s foreignness was not concealed.
Uriah’s name was not erased to protect David’s reputation.
And still…
Jesus came.
That may be the three-word sermon somebody desperately needs tonight.
Jesus still came.
After Abraham’s failures.
After Jacob’s deception.
After Judah’s hypocrisy.
After Tamar.
After Rahab.
After Ruth’s grief.
After David and Bathsheba.
After murder.
After idolatry.
After divided kingdoms.
After exile.
After generations of waiting.
Jesus still came.
And if you think your family is too dysfunctional for God to touch, look at His genealogy.
If you think your history is too dirty for grace, look toward His cross.
If you think you wandered too far, look at Rahab.
If grief convinced you nothing remains, remember Ruth walking into Bethlehem.
If hidden sin is eating you alive, remember David standing before Nathan.
If somebody else’s sin has become part of your story, remember that Scripture can tell the truth about the wound without making the wound your final identity.
And if shame keeps whispering, “People like you do not belong near Jesus,” open Matthew 1.
Read the names again.
Then keep reading until you reach the name above every name.
Jesus.
Ἰησοῦς.
The name Matthew connects with the announcement that He will save His people from their sins.
Not merely inspire them.
Not merely improve their reputation.
Save them.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
But understand what that means.
Grace does not mean scandal becomes sacred.
Grace means Jesus is greater than the scandal.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace turns people from darkness toward the Light.
Grace does not tell sinners to remain exactly as they are.
Grace meets us where we are, forgives us through Christ, and begins transforming us into people who increasingly look like Him.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess honestly.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy purchased at the cross.
You do not have to publish the details.
God already knows them.
Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed person finally believes there is still a road home.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page either.
Not as a performance.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with heaven.
There may come a night when shame tries to rename you.
Come back and read the genealogy again.
Because the first chapter of Matthew destroys that illusion.
Christianity is for sinners because Christ came to save sinners.
Come to Jesus.
A ministry cannot cleanse you.
A book cannot justify you.
A shirt cannot redeem you.
A church cannot die in your place.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Support ministry if the Lord leads you.
Share truth because you love people.
Give because you love God.
But never confuse supporting the messenger with receiving the Message.
The Gospel is Jesus Christ crucified for sinners and risen from the dead.

And the same Savior whose genealogy carried memories of Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah is still gathering people with histories nobody would have chosen and writing testimonies nobody could have imagined.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“How could God ever use someone with a story like mine?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What might Jesus write next if I finally surrender the pen?”
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
Bathsheba.
And then…
Jesus.
The genealogy was never telling you that sin does not matter.
It was preparing you to meet the One powerful enough to redeem sinners.
And remember this when shame comes knocking again:
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you wish had never been written; He went to the cross so it would not have to be the final chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO CHANGE YOUR LIFE—BUT WHAT IF HE WANTS TO CHANGE YOUR MIND FIRST?
paragraphs:
YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO CHANGE YOUR LIFE—BUT WHAT IF HE WANTS TO CHANGE YOUR MIND FIRST?
What Scripture Really Means When It Says, “We Have the Mind of Christ”—and Why It May Confront the Version of Christianity You Have Become Comfortable With
There is a frightening possibility that many Christians know how to speak about Jesus while still thinking nothing like Him.
We know the vocabulary.
We know when to say, “God is good.”
We know how to post the verse.
We know how to worship when the music rises.
We know how to smile when someone asks how we are doing.

We know how to say, “I’m praying about it,” even when underneath those words we are furious, jealous, terrified, bitter, exhausted, secretly compromising, desperately comparing ourselves with everyone around us, and wondering why following Jesus has not silenced the war inside our heads.
And then Paul writes one sentence that refuses to leave us comfortable:
“ἡμεῖς δὲ νοῦν Χριστοῦ ἔχομεν.”
Hēmeis de noun Christou echomen.
“But we have the mind of Christ.”
—1 Corinthians 2:16
Read that again.
Not merely information about Christ.
Not merely admiration for Christ.
Not merely religious feelings toward Christ.
“The mind of Christ.”
And perhaps the reason those words have become familiar without becoming devastating is that we have sometimes made them mean something Scripture never intended.
Having the mind of Christ does not mean Christians become omniscient.
It does not mean every thought that enters a believer’s head came from God.
