That means Christians should never fear sincere investigation.
Ask questions.
Examine the claims.
Read the Gospels.
Study the apostolic testimony.
Look at what Christianity actually claims rather than what somebody on social media says it claims.
But do not dismiss Jesus merely because resurrection sounds impossible.
Of course resurrection sounds impossible if death has the final authority.
That is precisely the point.
The Christian claim is not that dead people naturally get back up.
The claim is that God raised Jesus.
And Acts 17 tells us that after the mocking, something quieter happened.
Paul walked away.
No dramatic record of the entire city converting.
No description of thousands rushing forward.
Just names.
Dionysius.
Damaris.
And others.
They believed.
I love that Scripture remembers their names.
The crowd mocked.
But heaven was not measuring the success of Paul's sermon by the volume of the laughter.
Somebody believed.
Never forget that when you share Jesus.
You may post truth and receive almost nothing.
Someone may laugh.
Someone may scroll.
Someone may argue.
Someone may mock you privately.
But somewhere there may be a Damaris reading silently.
Somewhere there may be a Dionysius whose heart is cracking open.
Someone may never comment, but tonight they might pray for the first time in years.
You do not know what God may do with one faithful witness.
So do not be ashamed of Christ.
And do not confuse being mocked with being defeated.
Athens laughed at resurrection.
The resurrection did not become less true because someone laughed.
Truth does not require applause to remain truth.
And perhaps that is the word somebody desperately needs today.
You have been allowing the crowd to determine how loudly you love Jesus.
You have been measuring obedience by reactions.
You have been hiding convictions because you fear losing approval.
Remember Paul standing among the philosophers.
He did not need to prove he was the smartest man in Athens.
He needed to faithfully proclaim Christ.
Neither do you need to win every argument.
You need to belong to Jesus.
And before you think about the unbeliever who needs this article, allow Scripture to turn its light toward you.
What altar have you built?
What has your heart begun worshiping?
What sin are you protecting?
What obedience are you postponing?
What would Jesus ask you to surrender that makes you instinctively reach for an excuse?
Be honest.
Maybe the real scandal is not that Athens had idols.
Maybe the scandal is how easily Christians can have them too.
Maybe your idol is approval.
Maybe comfort.
Maybe money.
Maybe lust.
Maybe control.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe yourself.
And Jesus does not expose idols because He delights in humiliating you.
He exposes what is killing you because He calls you away from false gods and back to the living God.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not sentimental grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives and transforms.
Grace that does not merely cover yesterday but begins rewriting tomorrow.
Grace that can take a persecutor named Saul and turn him into a preacher named Paul.
Grace that can enter your scandal and refuse to leave you there.
So if something inside you has been exposed while reading this, don't hide.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from it.
Trust in Jesus Christ.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to make Christ willing to receive repentant sinners.
You need Christ because you cannot save yourself.
Maybe your prayer tonight is nothing impressive.
Maybe it sounds like:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Say it sincerely.
Maybe tears come.
Maybe they don't.
Salvation is not measured by emotional intensity.
Look to Christ.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Not as a magic formula.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing our struggle into the light is the first public crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And when you see somebody else write those words, don't treat their vulnerability like content.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Christ.
Let the comment section become more than reactions.
Let it become a place where wounded people discover they are not the only ones fighting to keep their eyes on Jesus.
Then think of one person.
Just one.
The friend who has been drifting.
The brother who laughs whenever Christianity comes up.
The daughter who stopped going to church.
The coworker asking questions.
The Christian who looks strong but is quietly unraveling.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
But if this message faithfully points people toward Christ, sharing it can be one practical way of helping another person encounter the truth you believe matters eternally.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is continuing to be challenged, encouraged, corrected, strengthened, and pointed back to Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Even invite the person who doesn't believe any of this yet.
They are welcome to hear.
They are welcome to investigate.
They are welcome to ask.
But before you leave, return one last time to Athens.
See Paul standing there.
Hear the philosophers.
Watch the faces.
Then hear those words:
Resurrection of the dead.
Someone laughs.
Someone hesitates.
Someone believes.
The Gospel has reached the point where every listener must wrestle with Jesus.
And somewhere in that crowd are Dionysius and Damaris.
They could have laughed too.
They could have walked away.
They could have said, “Perhaps someday.”
But Acts remembers them among those who believed.
Thousands of years later, we still know their names.
Not because they were the loudest people in Athens.
But because when Christ was proclaimed, their response changed.
So what will your response be?
Not your parents' response.
Not your pastor's.
Not the response your Christian friends expect.
Yours.
Because one day the laughter of every crowd will disappear.
Your followers will not matter.
Your possessions will not matter.
Your reputation will not matter.
The applause will fade.
The arguments will end.
And the question you kept postponing will remain:
What did you do with Jesus Christ?
Athens thought Paul had brought them another strange idea.
Paul had brought them news.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ calling sinners to repentance.
Christ offering mercy.
Christ coming again.
And that same Gospel has somehow crossed empires, oceans, languages, persecutions, centuries, and generations until tonight it arrived on the screen in front of you.
Maybe you thought you were simply reading another article.
Maybe God is using it to make you stop running.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
And whatever you do after closing this page...
Do not laugh your way past the empty tomb.
Because the crowd may remember your scandal, but the risen Christ can still rewrite your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “YOUR TWO BREASTS ARE LIKE TWO FAWNS”: Why Would God Put THAT in the Bible?
paragraphs: “YOUR TWO BREASTS ARE LIKE TWO FAWNS”: Why Would God Put THAT in the Bible?
The verse some Christians rush past may expose something far deeper than sexuality—and reveal what sin distorted, what shame buried, and what Jesus came to redeem.
There are verses Christians underline.
There are verses Christians memorize.
There are verses we print on coffee mugs, hang above fireplaces, whisper beside hospital beds, and post beneath sunsets.
And then there are verses we hope nobody asks us about.
Song of Songs 4:5 is one of them.
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
Not hidden in some obscure manuscript.
Not inserted by a modern translator trying to be provocative.
There it is.
And the original Hebrew does not rescue embarrassed readers by making the language less direct.
שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים תְּאוֹמֵי צְבִיָּה הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים
Transliterated approximately:
Shenei shadayikh kishnei ‘ofarim, te’omei tseviyyah, haro‘im bashoshanim.
Literally, the opening words mean:
“Your two breasts are like two fawns…”
The Hebrew noun שָׁדַיִךְ (shadayikh) really does refer to “your breasts.”
So we cannot explain the verse away.
We have to understand it.
And perhaps the reason this verse makes some Christians uncomfortable is not because Scripture has become inappropriate.
Perhaps it is because sin has taught us to see something God created through eyes distorted by shame, exploitation, pornography, lust, insecurity, comparison, abuse, and fear.
That changes the question completely.
The question is no longer merely, “Why would God allow breasts to be mentioned in Scripture?”
The deeper question becomes:
What happened to us that we can read about murder, betrayal, warfare, crucifixion, greed, demons, judgment, adultery, and human depravity without blinking…
but when Scripture describes the beauty of the human body within the poetry of covenant love, suddenly we become uncomfortable?
Stay with that question.
Because this is not really an article about breasts.
It is about what happened to beauty after Eden.
It is about what happened to intimacy after sin.
It is about the difference between desire and exploitation.
It is about the difference between seeing someone and consuming someone.
And ultimately, it is about a Savior who does not merely forgive sinners.
Jesus begins restoring what sin shattered.
Go back to the beginning.
Before shame entered the human story, Genesis gives us an astonishing sentence:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25.
Read it slowly.
Naked.
And unashamed.
Those two realities once existed together.
There was a time in human history when the body was not merchandise.
There was no pornography.
No sexual trafficking.
No adultery.
No predatory gaze.
No insecurity generated by comparison.
No person staring into a mirror wondering whether their body was worthy of being loved.
No man secretly training his eyes to consume women.
No woman believing her value depended upon whether men desired her.
No wounded spouse wondering why she was no longer enough.
No child growing up carrying shame because someone violated what should have been protected.
There was nakedness…
without shame.
Then came sin.
And almost immediately, something changed.
Genesis 3 says their eyes were opened, they realized they were naked, and they covered themselves.
The body had not suddenly become evil.
Humanity had fallen.
That distinction matters.
Christianity does not teach that the physical body is inherently dirty.
God created human beings embodied.
Male and female.
Physical.
Emotional.
Relational.
And God looked upon His creation and declared it “very good.”
The tragedy is not that humanity possesses bodies.
The tragedy is what fallen humanity has learned to do with them.
We objectify.
We compare.
We fantasize.
We exploit.
We commodify.
We abuse.
We worship beauty.
We despise ourselves when we believe we do not possess enough of it.
We take something designed to participate in covenant intimacy and turn it into entertainment.
Then, after generations of sexual brokenness, we sometimes open Song of Songs and act surprised that God is willing to speak about embodied love.
But Scripture refuses to surrender human sexuality to pornography.
It refuses to let lust have the final definition of desire.
It refuses to let exploitation have the final word about the body.
And that is part of why Song of Songs matters.
The book is love poetry.
It contains longing, admiration, beauty, desire, separation, pursuit, delight, and commitment expressed through the imagery of the ancient world.
When the beloved is compared to fawns, lilies, doves, gardens, towers, spices, fruit, and fountains, we are entering poetry—not an anatomy textbook.
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle…”
Why fawns?
Think tenderness.
Delicacy.
Beauty.
Symmetry—the text specifically calls them twins.
Youthful grace.
Something admired rather than seized.
Something contemplated poetically rather than described crudely.
The imagery belongs to a world of gardens, animals, fragrance, vineyards, lilies, springtime, and flourishing life.
That matters.
Because biblical poetry communicates through pictures.
When Song of Songs 4:4 compares the woman’s neck to “the tower of David,” nobody imagines that her neck was literally made from masonry.
When her teeth are compared to a flock of sheep, nobody imagines wool growing from her mouth.
When her lips are compared with scarlet thread, nobody imagines sewing material attached to her face.
These are poetic images.
So when the poem describes her breasts as twin fawns grazing among lilies, the writer is not offering crude anatomical commentary.
He is communicating beauty through the language of tenderness, harmony, delicacy, and delight.
And notice something else.
The woman is not merely a body in Song of Songs.
She speaks.
She desires.
She chooses.
She searches.
She longs.
She praises.
She is praised.
There is mutuality throughout the poetry.
That is profoundly different from pornography.
Pornography asks, “How can this body satisfy me?”
Covenant love asks, “How can I cherish this person?”
Pornography separates the body from personhood.
Biblical love refuses to do that.
Pornography trains people to consume.
Love learns to behold without dehumanizing.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why that distinction hurts.
Maybe pornography has been your secret for years.
Nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your church does not know.
Your children certainly do not know.
Sunday morning, you worship.
Monday night, you hide.
You know how to delete the history.
You know how to close the browser.
You know how to promise God, “Never again.”
Then the loneliness returns.
The temptation returns.
The screen lights up.
And the cycle begins again.
Desire.
Click.
Pleasure.
Silence.
Shame.
Repentance.
Resolve.
Then another fall.
And somewhere along the way you began wondering whether God was disgusted with you.
Listen carefully.
Your sin matters.
Jesus does not call lust harmless.
Christ's standard goes deeper than outward adultery. In Matthew 5:28, He exposes lust in the heart itself.
So grace does not mean pretending your bondage is innocent.
Grace means your bondage does not have to become your identity.
There is a difference.
Repentance does not say, “It doesn't matter.”
Repentance says, “It matters so much that I am bringing it into the light.”
Maybe pornography is not your story.
Maybe shame is.
Maybe you have spent years hating your body.
You compare yourself with edited photographs.
You notice every scar.
Every wrinkle.
Every kilogram.
Every sign of aging.
You have stood in front of a mirror and silently insulted someone made in the image of God.
You.
Perhaps somebody once mocked your body.
Perhaps someone you loved compared you with another person.
Perhaps your spouse rejected you.
Perhaps someone touched you in a way they never had the right to.
And now even beautiful biblical language about the body makes something inside you tense.
God sees that wound too.
Song of Songs does not teach that physical beauty determines human worth.
It does show us something our wounded culture desperately needs to recover:
embodied human love does not have to be dirty.
Beauty does not have to become an idol.
Desire does not have to become exploitation.
Sexuality does not have to become pornography.
The body does not have to become merchandise.
And marriage does not have to become emotionally lifeless simply because Christians are frightened of acknowledging attraction.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept pure.
Purity, biblically understood, is not the annihilation of marital desire.
It is desire rightly ordered.
That is radically different.
Sin says, “Take.”
Covenant says, “Give.”
Lust says, “Use.”
Love says, “Cherish.”
Pornography says, “Consume.”
Covenant says, “Know me—and remain faithful.”
Sin separates pleasure from holiness.
God calls His people toward a holiness capable of governing desire rather than pretending desire does not exist.
And here is where we must be careful.

Song of Songs is first and directly a collection of human love poetry. Christians through the centuries have also found echoes in its language that remind them of God's covenant love and, by theological extension, Christ's love for His people.
But we do not need to erase the human love poem to make the book spiritual.
God is not embarrassed by what He inspired.
And neither should we be.
Yet every beautiful thing in Scripture eventually confronts us with the tragedy of the Fall.
Because we know love is not always like this.
Marriages fracture.
Desire wanders.
People betray vows.
Bodies age.
Beauty fades.
Affection cools.
Pornography invades bedrooms.
Adultery destroys families.
Abuse turns places that should have been safe into places of terror.
Some people reading these words have discovered messages on a spouse's phone that changed their lives forever.
Some have heard the sentence:
“I don't love you anymore.”
Some have watched the person who promised “until death do us part” walk away.
Some carry sins they committed.
Others carry wounds somebody committed against them.
Some carry both.
And suddenly Song of Songs does not feel romantic anymore.
It feels like evidence from another world.
A world where love has not yet broken.
And that is exactly where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus entered our broken world.
Not as an idea.
Not as an inspirational slogan.
The Word became flesh.
John 1:14.
Think about that.
The God who created human bodies did not rescue humanity by despising embodiment.
The Son took on human flesh.
He became tired.
He became hungry.
He wept.
He bled.
He was touched.
He suffered.
His body was beaten.
His hands and feet were pierced.
He died.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
Christian redemption is not God saying matter never mattered.
The resurrection announces that God's answer to human brokenness is bigger than escaping creation.
He is making all things new.
That includes the sinner who thinks sexual sin has permanently disqualified him.
The woman who believes shame has permanently named her.
The husband who has been hiding.
The wife who has been wounded.
The unmarried believer fighting loneliness.
The person who has confused attention with love.
The believer whose private browser history contradicts his public worship.
Jesus already knows.
That may terrify you.
But it can also become the beginning of freedom.
Because the Christ who knows the entire truth about you is the Christ who went to the cross for sinners.
You do not have to clean yourself enough to become eligible for mercy.
You come into the light.
You confess.
You repent.
You turn.
You trust Christ.
And grace meets you there.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that baptizes bondage and calls it freedom.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives and then teaches us how to walk differently.
Grace that says your worst chapter does not get naming rights over the rest of your story.
Peter knew scandal.
David knew scandal.
The woman caught in adultery knew public shame.
The Samaritan woman knew relational brokenness.
Paul knew what it meant to have a past he could never undo.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose histories should have destroyed them.
Then grace interrupts.
That is the Gospel.
Not good people becoming slightly better.
Dead people receiving life.
Guilty people receiving mercy.
Captives finding freedom.
Prodigals coming home.
Enemies being reconciled.
Sinners being washed.
And perhaps that is why this strange, beautiful, uncomfortable verse belongs in your Bible.
Because God refuses to surrender any territory of human existence to the enemy.
Not your body.
Not your sexuality.
Not your marriage.
Not your desires.
Not your wounds.
Not your memories.
Not even your shame.
Christ lays claim to all of you.
The parts you show at church.
And the parts you hide when everyone goes home.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“Why does the Bible mention breasts?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What has sin taught me to see that Jesus wants to teach me to see differently?”
That question reaches far beyond Song of Songs.
How do you see women?
How do you see men?
How do you see your spouse?
How do you see your own body?
How do you see sex?
How do you see singleness?
How do you see beauty?
How do you see people whose bodies attract you?
As images?
As opportunities?
As comparisons?
As objects?
Or as human beings carrying the image of their Creator?
And what are you feeding your eyes when nobody is watching?
Do not rush past that.
Because there are moments when the most spiritual thing you can do is stop pretending.
Maybe this is yours.
Maybe tonight needs to become the night the secret ends.
Not because somebody manipulated you.
Because Christ is worthy of the room you have kept locked.
Tell Him the truth He already knows.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, my eyes have wandered.”
“Jesus, I have used people in my imagination.”
“Jesus, I have hated the body You gave me.”
“Jesus, I have carried shame for something somebody did to me.”
“Jesus, I have confused lust with love.”
“Jesus, I need mercy.”
And then remember why there is a cross.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
The scandal is real.
But scandal does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write your private details publicly. But if you want to mark this moment, comment, “No more hiding.”
If you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your heart has been wounded and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if you have already watched Jesus begin restoring something you thought could never be restored, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting.
That comment might become somebody else's courage to come into the light.
Not because every Christian needs another post on a timeline.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
We want to go where the text goes.
Not beyond it.
Not around it.
Through it.
Always toward Jesus.
Scripture gives a real basis for believers voluntarily supporting Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living through Gospel work in 1 Corinthians 9:14.
But Scripture also protects the heart of giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says giving must not be reluctant or compelled.
So hear this clearly:
It does not replace obedience.
It does not purchase God's favor.
It does not buy salvation.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is a gift.
Your support helps keep the message moving.
More teaching.
More discipleship.
More resources.
More opportunities for one wounded person scrolling alone at midnight to encounter Scripture when they were about to surrender to despair.
Send it to the person God brought to your mind while you were reading.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is hiding.
Somebody is ashamed.
Somebody thinks their secret has made them unreachable.
Somebody thinks their marriage is too broken.
Somebody believes pornography owns them.
Somebody despises their own reflection.
Somebody has confused being desired with being loved.
Somebody is wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
And the answer of the cross is not that sin does not matter.
The answer is that Jesus went far enough to save sinners from it.
The body sin taught you to objectify was created by God.
The sexuality culture taught you to worship belongs under the lordship of Christ.
The shame that told you to hide can be dragged into the light.
The sin that whispers, “This is who you are,” does not have authority to rewrite what Jesus has redeemed.
Song of Songs 4:5 is not an embarrassing mistake God forgot to edit out of Scripture.
It belongs inside a Bible that tells the truth about being human.
A Bible containing gardens and graves.
Weddings and betrayals.
Desire and discipline.
Nakedness and shame.
Adultery and forgiveness.
Bodies and resurrection.
Sin and blood.
Scandal and grace.
And standing at the center of that entire story is not human sexuality.
It is Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling hidden people into light.
Calling guilty people toward repentance.
Calling wounded people toward healing.
Calling the ashamed toward grace.
Calling the redeemed toward holiness.
Maybe you opened this because a verse about “two breasts” caught your attention.
Maybe God used the uncomfortable verse to bring you somewhere far more uncomfortable:
your own heart.
Do not run now.
The Savior already knows what is there.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the body you hate.
Bring Him the memories you cannot erase.
Bring Him the chapter you wish had never been written.
Because the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is not that Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
It is that He can take a life marked by scandal and write grace across pages you thought were ruined forever.
Your shame may remember the old chapter—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still writing the next one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS CHRISTIANITY JUST ANOTHER RELIGION?
paragraphs:
IS CHRISTIANITY JUST ANOTHER RELIGION?
The question sounds harmless—until you realize Christianity makes a claim so radical that, if it is true, you cannot walk away from Jesus unchanged.
Maybe you have heard it before.
“Christianity is just another religion.”
Different buildings. Different books. Different prayers. Different traditions. Different names for God.

People are born, struggle, search for meaning, try to become better human beings, grow old, and eventually die. Religion, some say, is simply humanity trying to make sense of the space between the cradle and the grave.
And maybe part of you has wondered whether they are right.
Maybe Christianity really is just one spiritual road among many.
Maybe Jesus is simply Christianity’s contribution to humanity’s long collection of religious teachers.
Maybe the cross is merely Christianity’s symbol.
Maybe grace is simply Christianity’s vocabulary.
Maybe heaven is Christianity’s version of the same hope human beings have carried for thousands of years.
But there is a problem.
A massive one.
Christianity, at its biblical center, does not begin with humanity climbing toward God.
It begins with God coming down for humanity.
And once you understand that difference, the entire picture changes.
Religion can become a story about human beings searching for God.
The Gospel is the announcement that God came searching for sinners.
Religion can become, “Look what I have done for God.”
The Gospel announces, “Look what God has done for us in Christ.”
Religion asks, “What must I accomplish to become worthy?”
The Gospel confronts us with something simultaneously humiliating and beautiful:
You could never make yourself worthy.
So Christ came for the unworthy.
That is where the scandal begins.
And perhaps that word makes you uncomfortable.
Good.
Because the cross was never meant to flatter human pride.
Imagine standing before God carrying everything you have ever used to convince yourself that you are a good person.
Your kindness.
Your church attendance.
Your charitable giving.
Your theology.
Your baptism.
Your Christian family.
Your Bible knowledge.
The times you helped someone.
The sins you avoided.
The reputation you carefully protected.
The prayers nobody heard.
The sacrifices nobody noticed.
You place all of it before God and whisper,
“Surely this counts for something.”
Then Scripture says something devastating.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
Paul wrote it in Greek:
“Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως…”
Tē gar chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs…
“For by grace you have been saved through faith…”
Then comes the sentence human pride desperately wants to edit:
“οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων…”
ouk ex ergōn.
“Not from works.”
Not because you accumulated enough religious points.
Not because you managed to look cleaner than the person sitting beside you.
Not because God examined your résumé and discovered that heaven would be fortunate to have you.
Salvation is described as God’s gift, not humanity’s achievement.
And immediately afterward, Ephesians 2:10 makes something equally important clear: grace does not leave us unchanged. Those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
That order matters.
We do not perform good works so Christ will save us.
Christ saves us, and His grace begins transforming the way we live.
That is not cheap grace.
That is transforming grace.
Christianity therefore cannot faithfully be reduced to “be good and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel is far more disturbing than that.
It says something is wrong with us that morality alone cannot repair.
Sin.
There is a word modern people sometimes want removed from the conversation.
Sin sounds judgmental.
Ancient.
Heavy.
But remove sin from Christianity and eventually the cross becomes incomprehensible.
Why would the Son of God enter human history, suffer rejection, endure crucifixion, and rise from the dead if humanity merely needed better advice?
You do not need a crucified Savior if your deepest problem is insufficient inspiration.
You need a motivational speaker.
You do not need resurrection if humanity merely requires moral improvement.
You need education.
But Scripture diagnoses something deeper.
We have rebelled against the God who created us.
We have loved things more than Him.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Hated.
Envied.
Manipulated.
Worshiped ourselves.
Hidden behind respectable appearances.
Sometimes we even use religion to hide from God.
That may be the most frightening possibility of all.
You can know Christian songs without knowing Christ.
You can quote Scripture while secretly protecting the very sin Scripture is confronting.
You can sit in church while your heart lives somewhere else.
You can post verses publicly and compromise privately.
You can know when to raise your hands.
When to say amen.
When to look spiritual.
When to tell everybody, “God is good.”
And still carry a locked room inside your soul where you desperately hope Jesus will never enter.
But He already knows what is inside.
The pornography.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The jealousy.
The addiction.
The secret messages.
The dishonest money.
The hatred toward someone who wounded you.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The unforgiveness disguised as boundaries.
The obsession with appearing holy.
The exhaustion of pretending.
The secret thought you would never say aloud:
“If these people actually knew me, would they still love me?”
And beneath that question is an even deeper one.
“If God actually knows me…how could He?”
This is where Christianity stops being merely an interesting religious discussion.
Because He does know you.
Completely.
And the astonishing announcement of the Gospel is not that your sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
The astonishing announcement is that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Jesus does.
This is why the Gospel is scandalous.
God does not save sinners by pretending they were never sinners.
He saves sinners through Jesus Christ.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters the darkness and brings people into the light.
Grace does not tell the guilty, “Nothing happened.”
Grace announces that Christ has done something about what happened.
The cross simultaneously destroys our boasting and destroys our despair.
You cannot boast because you did not save yourself.
You do not have to despair because Christ saves sinners.
Think about the people Jesus welcomed.
Tax collectors.
Moral failures.
Social outsiders.
People carrying histories they could not erase.
People religious society knew how to label.
And Jesus did not merely give them affirmation.
He called people to repentance, faith, forgiveness, restoration, obedience, and new life.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing at a distance saying, “Become respectable and then come to Me.”
The Gospel is Christ entering the wreckage and calling sinners to Himself.
That is why one of the earliest summaries of Jesus’ preaching contains two urgent words: repent and believe.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that finally stops defending its rebellion.
It is the moment the excuses begin dying.
“Yes, Lord. That is sin.”
“Yes, Lord. I have been hiding.”
“Yes, Lord. I cannot save myself.”
“Yes, Lord. I need mercy.”
And faith reaches toward Christ with empty hands.
Not a résumé.
Not a trophy.
Not an argument.
Empty hands.
That is why Christianity is so offensive to pride.
The moral person needs grace.
The immoral person needs grace.
The religious person needs grace.
The atheist needs grace.
The pastor needs grace.
The prisoner needs grace.
The person reading this article needs grace.
And so does the person who wrote it.
Nobody enters the kingdom by presenting God with an impressive spiritual résumé.
We come through Christ.
Jesus said something astonishing in John 14:6. The Greek text preserves the force of His claim:
“Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή…”
Egō eimi hē hodos kai hē alētheia kai hē zōē.
“I am the way and the truth and the life.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
“I will show you an interesting way.”
“I know one possible truth.”
“I have discovered a useful spiritual technique.”
He pointed to Himself.
“I am…”
The center of Christianity is therefore not ultimately a philosophy.
It is a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And He continued:
“οὐδεὶς ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸν πατέρα εἰ μὴ δι’ ἐμοῦ.”
“No one comes to the Father except through Me.”
That is an enormous claim.
We should not soften it simply because modern ears may find exclusivity uncomfortable.
But neither should Christians wield it arrogantly.
Because the man who said those words would soon walk toward a cross.
Christian exclusivity is not supposed to produce Christian superiority.
How could it?
If salvation is grace, Christians have nothing to boast about except Christ.
A drowning man does not brag because someone rescued him.
He points toward his rescuer.
That is what Christianity is supposed to be.
Not Christians standing over the world shouting,
“Look how good we are.”
But forgiven sinners telling other sinners,
“Look how good Christ is.”
And this is where some Christians need repentance too.
Because Christianity has sometimes been represented by arrogance, hypocrisy, cruelty, manipulation, greed, scandal, and people who carried the name of Jesus while behaving nothing like Him.
If someone wounded you while wearing Christianity as a label, pretending it never happened would not honor Christ.
Human hypocrisy does not become holy because someone places a Bible beside it.
Sin inside a church is still sin.
Abuse does not become righteous because someone quotes Scripture.
Manipulation does not become discipleship because a religious leader does it.
Jesus Himself repeatedly confronted religious hypocrisy.
So perhaps you did not reject Jesus.
Perhaps you rejected a distorted picture of Him.
Then look again.
Not merely at Christians.
Look at Christ.
See Him touching the untouchable.
See Him receiving the rejected.
See Him confronting the proud.
See Him weeping.
See Him washing His disciples’ feet.
See Him betrayed.
See Him arrested.
See Him crucified.
Then listen to the words spoken from the cross:
“Father, forgive them.”
Christianity stands or falls with Jesus.
And especially with what Christians have proclaimed from the beginning:
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
If Jesus remained dead, Christianity collapses into another human religious movement centered around a deceased teacher.
The apostle Paul was startlingly direct about this: if Christ has not been raised, Christian faith is futile.
Christianity therefore does not ask you merely to admire an ethical system.
It makes historical claims about Jesus.
And then it makes a personal demand.
What will you do with Him?
That question is harder than asking whether Christianity is “a religion.”
Because labels allow distance.
Jesus does not.
Perhaps you have spent years studying Christianity while carefully avoiding Christ.
Perhaps you grew up around Him.
Your grandmother prayed.
Your mother took you to church.
You know Christmas.
You know Easter.
You know John 3:16.
You know the songs.
You know the language.
But knowing Christian culture is not the same thing as knowing Christ.
You can live beside a well and still die thirsty.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Something underneath the arguments has become personal.
Because beneath “Is Christianity just another religion?” may be another question you are almost afraid to ask:
“Could Jesus still want someone like me?”
Now we have reached the heart of it.
Because perhaps your real obstacle was never comparative religion.
Perhaps it was shame.
You know what you did.
You remember the night.
The decision.
The betrayal.
The abortion.
The affair.
The relapse.
The lie.
The person you hurt.
The promise you broke.
The years you wasted.
The prayer you stopped praying because you felt hypocritical even saying God's name.
Maybe everyone thinks you are fine.
You became skilled at smiling.
But some nights the past climbs into bed beside you.
And when the room becomes quiet, you hear accusations nobody else can hear.
“You ruined everything.”
“You crossed the line.”
“God might forgive people…but not you.”
Listen carefully.
That voice does not get the final word.
The cross does.
This is precisely why Jesus came.
Christianity is not the story of good people receiving medals.
It is the story of sinners receiving mercy because of Christ.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The thief dying beside Jesus had no lifetime remaining in which to construct an impressive religious record.
He had only a guilty past, a dying body, and a desperate appeal to Christ.
And grace met him there.
That does not make sin small.
It makes Jesus enormous.
This is the heartbeat behind everything Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing justice.
But by taking guilty, shattered, rebellious human beings and doing what human beings cannot do for themselves.
Forgiving.
Redeeming.
Restoring.
Transforming.
Making alive.
Maybe you thought Christianity was primarily about turning bad people into respectable people.
The Gospel goes deeper.
Christ makes spiritually dead people alive.
Maybe you thought Christianity meant cleaning yourself before approaching God.
Jesus calls you to come to Him.
Maybe you thought you needed to fix everything first.
You cannot perform spiritual surgery on your own heart.
Come to Christ.
Come with the addiction.
Come with the questions.
Come with the shame.
Come with the pride.
Come with the doubt.
Come with the past.
Come honestly.
But understand this:
Jesus loves you too much merely to decorate your chains.
He came to set captives free.
Grace welcomes us where we are, but grace does not make peace with the sin destroying us.
Christ calls us to follow Him.
There will be things to surrender.
There will be habits that must die.
There may be relationships that must change.
There may be apologies you need to make.
There may be restitution.
There will be days when following Jesus costs you something.
But none of that purchases salvation.
It is the fruit of belonging to the One who saved you.
And maybe today your first act of honesty is painfully simple.
“Jesus, I need You.”
No performance.
No religious theater.
No pretending.
Just surrender.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you do not have to keep pretending spiritually either.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person fighting.
That is what Christian community should look like.
Not a museum filled with people pretending they were never broken.
A family of redeemed people pointing one another toward Christ.
And if one person came to mind while you were reading this, do not ignore that.
Maybe they stopped attending church.
Maybe they still believe but have become cold.
Maybe they were wounded by Christians.
Maybe they think they have sinned too much.
Maybe they do not believe at all.
Maybe they would never open a Bible, but they would read something you shared because they trust you.
Send this to them.
Is Christianity just another religion?
Let them encounter the Gospel.
Because someday the person who needs to reread it may be you.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who thinks Jesus could never want them.
Even invite the unbeliever who disagrees with us.
They are welcome to read.
They are welcome to ask.
They are welcome to examine the claims of Christ.
Not to purchase God's favor.
Not to prove that you love Jesus.
Not because grace can be bought.
It cannot.
Sharing costs nothing, and it matters enormously.
If Gospel Warrior has fed you spiritually, consider helping us put that same biblical nourishment in front of somebody who has never seen it.
Not because clicking “share” saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
Christ purchased redemption; we cannot.
But because when the Gospel has been entrusted to us, love does not want to keep good news locked inside a private room.
There is a world filled with people trying desperately to climb toward God.
Some are climbing through morality.
Some through achievement.
Some through religion.
Some through spirituality.
Some through self-improvement.
Some have stopped climbing entirely because they are exhausted.
And Christianity announces something astonishing into all that exhaustion.
God came down.
The Word became flesh.
Jesus entered our suffering.
Christ bore sin.
The Savior died.
The tomb was occupied.
Then the tomb became empty.
Grace walked out alive.
And the invitation still stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Maybe Christianity looked like another religion from far away.
But come closer.
At the center you will not merely find rules.
You will find a cross.
You will not merely find human beings searching for God.
You will find the Shepherd seeking the lost.
You will not merely find instructions for becoming worthy.
You will find grace for people who finally admit they are not.
And you will find an empty tomb declaring that your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
Not, “Are my parents Christian?”
Not, “Do I attend church?”
Not, “Am I better than most people?”
Not even merely, “Do I believe Christianity exists?”
The question is:
What have I done with Jesus Christ?
Because someday every distraction becomes silent.
Every achievement remains behind.
Every title disappears.
Every follower count becomes meaningless.
Every carefully constructed image collapses.
And you stand before the God who knew every chapter all along.
If you belong to Christ, the wonder of the Gospel is that your story is no longer ultimately defined by the chapter you are most ashamed of.
It is defined by the Savior who took sinners from condemnation toward forgiveness, from rebellion toward reconciliation, from death toward life.
So share the Gospel.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because somebody needs to see believers becoming honest again.
“Jesus rewrote my story.”
Maybe you are not ready to say that yet.
Then perhaps your comment is simply:
Because the chapter that made you think your story was over may become the very place where future generations see what the grace of Jesus Christ can do.
Your scandal may explain where you have been. Only Jesus gets to decide what grace can make of what comes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MARRIAGE IS HOLY—BUT SCRIPTURE NEVER SAYS EVERY CHRISTIAN MUST MARRY
paragraphs: MARRIAGE IS HOLY—BUT SCRIPTURE NEVER SAYS EVERY CHRISTIAN MUST MARRY
What If the Life You Keep Calling “Incomplete” Is the Very Life Christ Intends to Use for His Kingdom?
There is a particular kind of pain that rarely gets mentioned from the pulpit.
It happens when everyone else seems to be moving forward.
Another engagement.
Another wedding.
Another pregnancy announcement.
Another smiling photograph with a caption about “God’s perfect timing.”
And you are happy for them.
You really are.
But somewhere beneath the congratulations, beneath the heart emojis, beneath the smile you have learned to wear so well, a question whispers from somewhere you don't like admitting exists:
“What is wrong with me?”
Maybe you are 27.
Maybe 37.
Maybe 57.
Maybe you have never married.
Maybe you thought you would be married by now.
Maybe you were married once and buried the person you thought would grow old beside you.
Maybe betrayal destroyed what you believed would last forever.
Maybe divorce left scars you still don't know how to explain.
Maybe you desire marriage deeply, but the right person has never appeared.
Or maybe—and this can feel almost forbidden to say in some Christian circles—you genuinely do not believe God is calling you to marriage.
And somewhere along the way, Christian culture may have accidentally taught you something Scripture never did:
That marriage is graduation and singleness is the waiting room.
That the married Christian has “arrived,” while the unmarried Christian is still waiting for God to finish writing the story.
But what if Jesus never said that?
What if Paul never said that?
What if the Bible honors marriage magnificently without ever turning marriage into a requirement for every disciple?
And what if some of the shame you have been carrying was never placed on your shoulders by Jesus at all?
Read that again.
Because somebody has spent years asking God to remove a stigma that God never gave them.
Marriage is holy.
Marriage is beautiful.
Marriage was designed by God.
Marriage must not be mocked, cheapened, casually discarded, sexually corrupted, or treated as merely a social contract.
Scripture reaches all the way back to creation and declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” — Genesis 2:24
Jesus Himself reaches back to that creation account when teaching about marriage in Matthew 19:4–6.
Christianity is not anti-marriage.
Far from it.
Hebrews 13:4 says in Greek:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…”
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled…”
The word τίμιος—timios—carries the sense of something precious, honored, valuable.
Marriage is not disposable.
It is not merely a ceremony, a tax status, a romantic accessory, or two people agreeing to stay together until happiness becomes inconvenient.
Biblically, marriage carries covenantal weight.
And yet here is where Christians must be careful.
Saying marriage is holy is not the same as saying marriage is mandatory.
Calling marriage good does not require calling singleness defective.
Honoring husbands and wives does not require treating unmarried believers as unfinished human beings.
Because when Jesus Christ walked this earth in perfect humanity, He never married.
Think about what that means.

If marriage were necessary for a human life to be spiritually complete, emotionally meaningful, or fully pleasing to God, we would be forced into an impossible conclusion about the sinless Son of God.
Jesus was not half a man because He had no wife.
He was not waiting for His “real life” to begin.
He was not incomplete.
He was not behind.
He was not less mature.
He was not less human.
His identity was not constructed around a wedding ring.
His life was completely surrendered to the Father.
And then Jesus said something astonishing.
While discussing marriage, divorce, and the disciples' reaction to His teaching, Christ acknowledged that not everyone would live the same marital story.
Matthew 19:12 preserves His words in Greek:
“εἰσὶν… εὐνοῦχοι… οἵτινες εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν.”
There are those who have embraced such a life “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”
Then Jesus says:
“ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν χωρείτω.”
Ho dynamenos chōrein chōreitō.
In essence: the one able to receive this, let that person receive it.
Jesus did not command every disciple to remain unmarried.
But neither did He command every disciple to marry.
That matters.
Then Paul walks directly into the conversation.
And if anyone still believes every faithful Christian must eventually marry, 1 Corinthians 7 becomes extraordinarily difficult to explain away.
Paul writes:
“To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them if they remain as I am.” — 1 Corinthians 7:8
Notice the word.
Good.
Not shameful.
Not tragic.
Not second-class.
Not “good temporarily until God finally sends somebody.”
Good.

Paul then makes clear that marriage is also good and appropriate. He explicitly says that if people marry, they have not sinned. His concern in the chapter is not to manufacture a hierarchy of human worth but to teach believers how to live faithfully before Christ in the circumstances and callings in which they find themselves.
Later he explains one of the potential advantages of unmarried life:
“But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord.” — 1 Corinthians 7:32
That does not mean married Christians cannot be passionately devoted to Jesus.
Christian history is filled with husbands and wives who have served Christ beautifully.
A godly marriage can preach the Gospel without a microphone.
A husband laying down selfishness to love his wife sacrificially can reflect Christ's covenant love.
A wife faithfully loving her husband can display extraordinary grace.
A Christian home can become a refuge.
Children can be discipled.
Strangers can be welcomed.
Meals can become ministry.
Hospitality can become worship.
Forgiveness inside marriage can become a living testimony that Jesus still resurrects things human beings thought were dead.
Marriage can be breathtakingly holy.
But singleness can be holy too.
That is the truth we sometimes seem afraid to say.
The unmarried believer is not a Christian in the lobby waiting to be admitted into adulthood.
She can disciple.
He can preach.
She can evangelize.
He can serve.
She can travel where God sends her.
He can pour himself into ministry.
She can nurture spiritual sons and daughters.
He can become a faithful uncle, brother, mentor, missionary, pastor, servant, friend, giver, teacher, intercessor, caregiver, or witness.
The Kingdom of God does not inspect your left hand before deciding whether your life can matter.
And perhaps someone needs that sentence tonight.
Because you have been measuring your worth with somebody else's wedding photographs.
Stop.
Not because marriage doesn't matter.
Because Christ matters more.
Marriage is a gift.
It is not a god.
And when a good gift becomes the condition upon which you permit yourself to believe your life is meaningful, that gift has quietly begun occupying a throne it was never meant to have.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Some people do not merely desire marriage.
They believe marriage will save them.
“If I can just find somebody, I won't feel lonely anymore.”
“If somebody finally chooses me, I'll know I'm valuable.”
“If I get married, I'll stop struggling sexually.”
“If I get married, I'll finally be happy.”
“If I get married, then my life can begin.”
But marriage cannot bear the weight of being your messiah.
Your husband cannot save your soul.
Your wife cannot heal every wound.
Romance cannot cleanse guilt.
Sex cannot provide eternal identity.
A wedding cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus can do that.
And some married people know this more painfully than anybody.
You can sleep beside someone and still feel lonely.
You can wear a ring and still battle insecurity.
You can have beautiful wedding photographs and a bleeding marriage.
You can sit beside your spouse in church while privately wondering how two people living under one roof became strangers.
Marriage is holy.
Marriage is also inhabited by sinners.
That means marriage needs the Gospel just as desperately as singleness does.
The single person needs Jesus.
The married person needs Jesus.
The divorced person needs Jesus.
The widow needs Jesus.
The person desperate to marry needs Jesus.
The person called to remain single needs Jesus.
The person whose marriage is thriving needs Jesus.
The person whose marriage is hanging by a thread needs Jesus.
The ultimate dividing line in eternity will never be married versus unmarried.
It will be whether you belong to Christ.
That is why your deepest question cannot merely be:
“Will I ever get married?”
There is a more important question.
“Does Jesus have all of me?”
Because you can find a spouse and lose yourself spiritually.
You can obtain the relationship you prayed for while gradually abandoning the God you once prayed to.
You can become so obsessed with finding “the one” that you forget there is already One before whom every knee will bow.
Jesus Christ is not the consolation prize for people who could not find a spouse.
He is the treasure.
He is the Bridegroom of His redeemed people.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
He is the Lamb who was slain.
He is the King who is coming again.
Your relationship status does not determine your access to Him.
And maybe this is where the tears come.
Because perhaps nobody ever told you that you were allowed to stop apologizing for being unmarried.
Maybe family gatherings have become interrogations.
“When are you getting married?”
“Why are you still single?”
“You're too picky.”
“Your biological clock is ticking.”
“Don't worry, God has someone for you.”
Maybe they mean well.
But notice what that final sentence assumes.
Does Scripture promise every Christian a spouse?
No.
God may indeed lead you into marriage.
Pray about it.
Desire it without shame.
Prepare yourself for covenant rather than fantasy.
Seek wisdom.
Develop character.
Refuse desperation.
Do not lower biblical convictions simply because loneliness has become loud.
But never turn a personal desire into a divine promise God never made.
God promised something infinitely greater than universal marriage.
He promised Himself.
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.” — Hebrews 13:5
That promise belongs to the believer whether there is another person sleeping beside you or not.
And if God does lead you into marriage, enter it knowing your spouse is not your Savior.
If God calls you to a season of singleness, do not waste that season treating it as meaningless.
If He grants you lifelong singleness for concentrated Kingdom service, do not allow people to make you ashamed of an offering Christ Himself dignified.
And if you desperately want marriage while God has not yet provided it, you do not have to pretend the waiting doesn't hurt.
Christian maturity is not pretending.
You can tell Jesus you are lonely.
You can cry.
You can grieve dreams that haven't happened.
You can admit that another wedding invitation sometimes hurts.
You can rejoice with someone and then go home and weep.
Faith is not emotional anesthesia.
Jesus is not frightened by your honesty.
Bring Him the ache.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the sexual temptation.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the nights when you wonder whether anybody will ever choose you.
Then remember the cross.
Before you were impressive enough.
Before you fixed yourself.
Before you had anything worthy to offer Him.
Christ moved toward sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Become desirable enough and perhaps God will choose you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
He carried sin.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Your greatest scandal was never that you were single.
Your greatest scandal was sin.
And your greatest need was never a wedding.
It was redemption.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
This is where Jesus rewrites everything.
The world tells you your worth depends upon being wanted by another human being.
Jesus points toward a bloodstained cross and shows you what your redemption cost.
Culture asks whether somebody put a ring on your finger.
The Gospel asks whether Christ has made your heart new.
Culture says, “Find someone who completes you.”
Jesus says, in effect, “Come to Me.”
And when Christ becomes the center, something beautiful happens.
Marriage can stop being an idol and become a gift.
Singleness can stop being a verdict and become a place of faithfulness.
Widowhood does not become easy, but it does not become meaningless.
Divorce does not have to become your permanent identity.
Past sexual sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Failure does not have to have the last word.
Shame does not get authorship rights over a life purchased by Jesus.
Maybe your story contains things you wish you could erase.
Maybe you compromised because you were terrified of being alone.
Maybe you stayed with someone you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you crossed sexual boundaries and have been carrying secret shame ever since.
Maybe you broke somebody's heart.
Maybe somebody broke yours.
Maybe you have lived with pornography, lust, emotional dependency, adultery, bitterness, or regret.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Grace does not call sin harmless.
Grace calls sinners home.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God turning you away from what is killing you and toward the One who gives life.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by bringing sinners through repentance into forgiveness, cleansing, restoration, obedience, and a new life centered upon Him.
So whether you are married or single, stop asking your relationship status to tell you who you are.
Ask Christ.
If you belong to Jesus, your first identity is not single.
Not married.
Not divorced.
Not widowed.
Not rejected.
Not unwanted.
Not somebody's ex.
Not somebody's future spouse.
You are Christ's.
And that changes the question.
Instead of only asking, “God, when will You send me somebody?”
Perhaps tonight you need to ask:
“Jesus, what do You want to do with the life I already have?”
That question can change everything.
There are prayers you can pray now.
People you can disciple now.
Neighbors you can love now.
Scripture you can study now.
Habits you can surrender now.
People you can forgive now.
Ministry you can support now.
The Gospel you can share now.
Holiness you can pursue now.
You do not need a wedding certificate before obedience becomes possible.
Your calling to follow Jesus has already begun.

And if this exposed something hidden in you—an idol, a fear, shame over being single, resentment toward God, desperation for marriage, or the belief that another human being must complete what only Christ can redeem—don't hide behind another religious smile.
Be honest.
Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need proof that God is still faithful when life does not follow the timeline we imagined.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not fifty.
One.
The unmarried friend who laughs at the jokes but cries afterward.
The Christian woman wondering whether she is somehow less valuable because nobody has proposed.
The man who is considering marrying someone who pulls him away from Jesus simply because he is tired of being alone.
The divorced believer convinced his usefulness to God ended with his marriage.
The widow who feels invisible.
The married couple who needs to remember that their spouse was never meant to replace Christ.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. Sometimes one Gospel-centered article arrives in a person's life at precisely the moment their heart has become willing to listen.
It doesn't.
Only Jesus saves.
Not because God needs your money.
He doesn't.

But because Gospel ministry in this world requires believers who do more than consume what strengthens them. Scripture repeatedly celebrates willing, generous partnership in Gospel work. If this ministry is bearing biblical fruit in your life, supporting it is one practical way you can help Gospel-centered teaching keep reaching people who are hurting, searching, doubting, repenting, rebuilding, and discovering Jesus.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Encourage someone.

Because glorifying God is bigger than supporting any single ministry. We glorify Him by trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, proclaiming His Gospel, serving faithfully, giving freely rather than under compulsion, and using whatever He has placed in our hands for His Kingdom.
Married?
Make your marriage about Jesus.
Single?
Make your singleness about Jesus.
Waiting?
Wait with Jesus.
Heartbroken?
Run toward Jesus.
Widowed?
Hold onto Jesus.
Divorced and repentant over your own failures?
Come to Jesus.
Ashamed of your past?
Come to Jesus.
Afraid nobody will ever choose you?
Look again at the cross.
Because your life does not become valuable when somebody finally says, “I do.”
Your life finds its deepest meaning when you can look at the crucified and risen Christ and say:
“I am Yours.”
And perhaps the chapter you thought God forgot to finish is not unfinished at all.
Perhaps Jesus is already writing something you could not recognize because you were waiting for the story to look like everybody else's.
Marriage is holy.
But marriage is not your Savior.
Singleness may be difficult.
But singleness is not your shame.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And whether He leads you toward a wedding altar or gives you grace to walk a different road, the highest calling of your life remains exactly the same:
Follow Him.
Because one day, when every earthly title disappears and every human story reaches its final page, the question will not be whether you managed to become somebody's husband or wife.
The question that echoes into eternity is whether you belonged to Jesus.
So don't spend your entire life waiting for another human being to begin a story Christ has already called you to live.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TEMPTATION YOU KEEP LOSING TO MAY NOT BE STRONGER THAN YOU—YOU MAY BE FIGHTING IT WITHOUT THE HOLY SPIRIT
paragraphs:
THE TEMPTATION YOU KEEP LOSING TO MAY NOT BE STRONGER THAN YOU—YOU MAY BE FIGHTING IT WITHOUT THE HOLY SPIRIT
How the Spirit of God meets you in the seconds nobody sees, exposes the lie beneath the craving, points you toward the escape God has already provided, and teaches you to choose Jesus when everything inside you wants to surrender
There is a moment before almost every fall.
A small moment.
Quiet enough that nobody else notices it.
Your hand has not done it yet.
Your mouth has not said it yet.
The message has not been sent.
The website has not been opened.
The lie has not been spoken.
The bottle has not been reached for.
The angry words are still behind your teeth.
The secret conversation has not crossed the line.
The bitterness has not yet become revenge.
The temptation is there...
but the sin has not happened yet.
And sometimes the most important spiritual battle of your entire day happens inside that tiny space.
You know what makes that moment terrifying?
You can love Jesus and still feel temptation.
You can worship on Sunday and be tempted on Monday night.
You can know Scripture and still hear another voice whispering, Just once.
You can have experienced God's grace and still discover desires inside yourself that embarrass you.
You can sincerely want holiness and still find yourself staring at the same door you promised God you would never walk through again.
And perhaps you have wondered something you were afraid to say aloud:
If the Holy Spirit really lives in me, why am I still tempted?
Maybe an even more painful question has followed it:
If God is really changing me, why does part of me still want things that could destroy me?
Listen carefully.
The presence of temptation is not proof that the Holy Spirit has abandoned you.
Jesus Himself was tempted—yet without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 says that Christ was “tempted like as we are, yet without sin.”
That changes the conversation immediately.
Temptation and sin are not identical.
Being tempted does not make you guilty of committing the temptation.
Jesus experienced genuine temptation without surrendering to sin.
So the question is not simply whether temptation will come.
It will.
The deeper question is:
What happens when it comes?
Because Scripture does not tell Christians merely to become tougher versions of themselves.
It gives us something infinitely better.
Someone.
Paul writes in Galatians 5:16:
The Greek is striking:
Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε — Pneumati peripateite.
Literally, the language carries the sense of walking, conducting one's life, by the Spirit.
And then Paul speaks about ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς — epithymian sarkos—the desire or craving of the flesh.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say the Christian will never experience conflicting desires again.
In fact, the verses immediately following describe conflict between flesh and Spirit.
Christianity is not God turning you into a person who can no longer be tempted.
Christianity is Christ redeeming you, placing His Spirit within you, and teaching you that temptation no longer has to become your master.
There is a difference between hearing temptation...
and obeying it.
Between feeling an impulse...
and enthroning it.
Between experiencing desire...
and surrendering your body to it.
And that distinction may change the way you fight.
Because many believers begin losing before temptation becomes intense.
They lose when they believe the first lie:
Because I feel it, I have to obey it.
No.
You do not.
The Holy Spirit creates a new possibility inside the life surrendered to Christ.
Not effortless perfection.
Not sinless independence.
Dependence.
Paul says something even stronger in Romans 8:13: it is “through the Spirit” that believers “mortify the deeds of the body.”
The Greek expression behind “by the Spirit” is πνεύματι — pneumati.
That matters.
Biblical warfare against sin is not:
Me versus temptation.
It is:
Me, dependent upon the Spirit of God, responding to the grace of God, putting sin to death because I now belong to Jesus Christ.
There is an enormous difference.
Willpower says:
I am strong enough.
The Gospel says:
Christ is enough, so I don't have to pretend I am.
And maybe this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because you know the cycle.
Temptation.
Negotiation.
Compromise.
Sin.
Silence.
Shame.
Promises.
Then temptation again.
You told God, “Never again.”
And you meant it.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You blocked the number.
Then unblocked it.
You walked away.
Then returned.
You confessed your anger and exploded again.
You promised to stop gossiping, but the conversation felt too delicious to leave.
You said you forgave them, yet you keep replaying imaginary arguments where you finally make them hurt the way they hurt you.
You promised God you would stop feeding the secret addiction.
Then midnight came.
Loneliness came.
Stress came.
Rejection came.
And suddenly the thing you hated yesterday looked comforting tonight.
That is something temptation does remarkably well.
It rarely introduces itself as destruction.
It introduces itself as relief.
Pornography may whisper, comfort.
Gossip may whisper, connection.
Greed may whisper, security.
Pride may whisper, significance.
Revenge may whisper, justice.
Drunkenness may whisper, escape.
Sexual compromise may whisper, love.
Envy may whisper, you deserve what they have.
Bitterness may whisper, you are only protecting yourself.
Temptation often advertises the immediate sensation while hiding the eventual cost.
And this is one of the places where the Holy Spirit helps us.
He leads us into truth.
Jesus called the Holy Spirit “the Spirit of truth” in John 16:13.
Temptation survives on distorted vision.
The Spirit leads us toward reality.
Temptation says:
You need this.
Truth says:
God is enough.
Temptation says:
Nobody will know.
Truth says:
Nothing is hidden from God.
Temptation says:
You can repent later.
Truth says:
Do not presume upon grace.
Temptation says:
This will heal the ache.
Truth asks:
Then why did it leave you emptier last time?
Temptation says:
You have already gone too far.
The Gospel says:
Run to Christ.
And there is something important here.
The Holy Spirit does not merely help you feel bad after sin.
He helps you recognize the lie before surrender.
Sometimes His work feels dramatic.
Often it doesn't.
Sometimes it is simply Scripture returning to your mind.
A sudden conviction.
A holy discomfort.
A remembered consequence.
An urge to leave the room.
A realization that you need to call someone.
A thought that says, Don't send that.
A reminder:
You belong to Jesus.
Do not despise those moments because they seem ordinary.
The escape God provides does not always arrive looking supernatural.
Sometimes the “way of escape” looks like closing the laptop.
Walking outside.
Calling a mature Christian.
Confessing what you are hiding.
Going to sleep.
Leaving the party.
Ending the conversation.
Blocking access.
Handing someone your password.
Opening your Bible.
Praying when you do not feel spiritual.
Running physically from a place where you know you become spiritually weak.
First Corinthians 10:13 gives one of Scripture's clearest promises concerning temptation:
“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful...”
Then comes the promise that God will, with the temptation, provide “a way to escape” so that it can be endured.
The Greek word translated temptation is πειρασμός — peirasmos.
Depending on context, the word can carry the idea of testing or temptation.
And the “way out” is expressed with ἔκβασις — ekbasis—an outlet, an exit, a way through.
But notice the center of Paul's promise.
It is not your faithfulness.
God is faithful.
That may be the sentence somebody desperately needed tonight.
Because you have been measuring the possibility of victory by the history of your failures.
God tells you to look somewhere else.
At His faithfulness.
You failed yesterday?
God remains faithful.
You feel weak tonight?
God remains faithful.
The temptation feels familiar?
God remains faithful.
Your flesh is screaming?
God remains faithful.
The enemy is accusing?
God remains faithful.
And when temptation comes, the Spirit helps you see something the flesh desperately wants you to overlook:
the exit.
But an exit must be taken.
This is where Christians sometimes become confused.
Depending upon the Holy Spirit does not mean becoming passive.
Grace does not mean sitting inside temptation while demanding God remove every desire.
Scripture gives astonishingly active commands.
Flee sexual immorality.
Flee idolatry.
Resist the devil.
Put sin to death.
Make no provision for the flesh.
Take thoughts captive.
Watch.
Pray.
Submit yourself to God.
The Holy Spirit does not replace obedience.
He empowers it.
Think about Joseph.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly pursued him.
Joseph did not stand there trying to prove how spiritually mature he was.
Genesis 39:12 says he “fled, and got him out.”
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is run.
Not negotiate.
Not analyze.
Not see how close you can get.
Run.
There are doors you do not need enough strength to stand beside.
You need enough humility to walk away from them.
And maybe your repeated defeat has less to do with temptation being irresistible and more to do with the fact that you keep leaving the door unlocked.
You pray:
“Lord, deliver me.”
But keep the number.
“Lord, protect my mind.”
But keep feeding it images that inflame lust.
“Lord, help me stop drinking.”
But keep alcohol within reach.
“Lord, protect my marriage.”
But continue the emotionally intimate conversation you would hide from your spouse.
“Lord, remove my envy.”
But spend hours studying everyone else's highlight reel.
“Lord, free me from anger.”
But replay the offense every night.
The Holy Spirit's help is not permission to maintain provision for the flesh.
Romans 13:14 says:
“Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.”
Some victories begin when prayer becomes practical.
Delete it.
Leave.
Confess.
Block it.
Tell somebody.
Stop visiting the place.
Change the routine.
Move the device.
End the secret.
Bring darkness into light.
Not because those actions save you.
Jesus saves.
But because genuine dependence upon Jesus produces obedient movement.
And then comes one of the most beautiful dimensions of the Spirit's ministry.
He does not merely say no to destructive desire.
He reshapes what you love.
Galatians 5 does not end with “try harder.”
It describes the fruit of the Spirit:
love,
joy,
peace,
longsuffering,
gentleness,
goodness,
faith,
meekness,
temperance.
That last word in the KJV, temperance, speaks of self-control.
The Spirit is forming something in you.
Slowly sometimes.
Painfully sometimes.
But really.
You begin discovering that sanctification is not merely God restraining your hands while your heart remains permanently chained to Egypt.
He begins changing the heart.
Things that once controlled you start losing their throne.
Not always overnight.
Sometimes freedom looks dramatic.
Sometimes freedom looks like choosing Jesus again...
and again...
and again...
until one day you realize the temptation that once shouted now only whispers.
But perhaps you are reading this after you already failed.
Maybe the temptation is no longer theoretical.
You crossed the line.
Again.
And now shame is speaking.
Look at you.
Fake Christian.
You prayed and still did it.
God must be finished with you.
Don't even bother praying.
And this is where you must distinguish the conviction of the Holy Spirit from hopeless condemnation.
The Spirit exposes sin to lead you toward Christ.
Condemnation wants exposure to drive you away from Him.
Conviction says:
This is sin. Bring it into the light.
Condemnation says:
You are disgusting. Hide.
Conviction leads toward repentance.
Condemnation leads toward despair.
And the Gospel says something scandalously beautiful to the believer who has fallen.
Run toward Jesus.
Not away.
Hebrews tells us that Jesus is not a High Priest incapable of sympathizing with human weakness.
He was tempted.
Yet without sin.
And because of Him, Hebrews 4:16 calls us to come boldly to the throne of grace to obtain mercy and find grace for help in time of need.
Read that again.
The throne you expected to find only judgment at is called a throne of grace.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Your sin is not small.
The cross proves that.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But God's grace is not small either.
The cross proves that too.
Jesus did not die because you were almost good enough.
He died because sinners needed a Savior.
He was crucified.
He bore sin.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not found by convincing God you will perform better next time.
Forgiveness is found in Christ.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling horrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Turning from sin.
Turning toward God.
And the Spirit continually turns our eyes toward Christ.
This is why your deepest strategy against temptation cannot merely be:
Stop wanting bad things.
You need a greater treasure.
Jesus.
You cannot permanently defeat worship with willpower.
You defeat lesser gods by seeing the glory of the true King.
Sin says:
Choose me.
Jesus says:
Follow Me.
Sin says:
I will satisfy you.
Jesus says:
“Come unto me.”
Sin says:
Hide.
Jesus calls you into light.
Sin promises life and produces death.
Jesus walked into death and came out alive.
And now His Spirit lives in His people.
That means when temptation comes tomorrow—and it may—you do not have to panic because the feeling appeared.
Recognize it.
Bring it into the light immediately.
Ask what lie it is selling.
Remember what Scripture says.
Call upon Christ.
Ask the Holy Spirit for strength.
Look for the exit.
And take it.
Not five minutes later.
Now.
Because temptation grows while you negotiate with it.
Some conversations should last one sentence:
No. I belong to Jesus.
Then move.
Run if necessary.
Pray while running.
Call somebody while running.
Cry while running.
But run toward Christ.
And if you fall?
Do not build a house in the mud.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive God's forgiveness in Christ.
Learn where the door was left open.
Seek accountability.
Get back up.
Follow Jesus again.
This is not permission to treat sin casually.
It is precisely because grace is so costly that we refuse to make peace with what nailed our Savior to a cross.
Maybe somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
Nobody knows.
Your church sees one version of you.
Your family sees another.
Your phone knows another.
Your browser history knows another.
Your thoughts know another.
And God knows all of them.
Yet you are still reading.
Perhaps this is the moment the hiding ends.
Not because somebody publicly humiliated you.
Because Jesus is calling you into light.
You don't need another secret promise made at 2:00 a.m.
You need surrender.
You need Christ.
You need the Spirit's strength.
You need brothers or sisters in Christ who can walk with you.
You may need to say the humiliating sentence:
“I need help.”
And that sentence may become the doorway to freedom.
Not because public comments magically defeat sin.
They don't.
Jesus does what no comment section ever could.
But sometimes a small act of honesty becomes the first crack in the wall we have spent years constructing.
And when you see somebody else write those words, don't become their judge.
Pray for them.
You don't know what battle they fought just to type that sentence.
This is what the Church should look like.
Not sinners pretending they were never wounded.
Redeemed people carrying one another toward Jesus.
And please—share this.
Not because Gospel Warrior needs another statistic.
The person laughing at memes this afternoon may be crying behind a locked door tonight.
The married couple everyone admires may be quietly drifting apart.
The teenager who never talks about faith may be fighting pornography.
The church member who always smiles may be drowning in shame.
Put truth where wounded people can find it.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend struggling silently.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet.
Let them encounter Scripture.
Let them encounter conviction.
Let them encounter grace.
Most of all, let them encounter Jesus.
We don't want to manipulate your conscience.
We want Christ to rule it.
And there is more.
Supporting the ministry helps us keep putting biblical resources into people's hands.
Jesus is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Jesus Christ.
We are only pointing toward Him.
