And perhaps tonight the Spirit of God is pointing at one specific door in your life.
You know the one.
The conversation you need to end.
The secret you need to confess.
The app you need to remove.
The relationship boundary you need to restore.
The bitterness you need to surrender.
The temptation you keep feeding while praying for God to starve it.
Don't wait until the desire becomes louder.
The exit may already be standing open.
Take it.
And when your flesh whispers, You need this, remember the wounded hands of the Savior who already gave Himself for you.
When shame whispers, Hide, remember the empty tomb.
When Satan whispers, You will always belong to this, remember whose Spirit lives in those who belong to Christ.
When you feel weak, don't pretend to be strong.
Run to the One who is.
Because the Holy Spirit's answer to temptation is not merely a louder version of your willpower.
He leads you into truth.
He brings God's Word to bear upon the lie.
He strengthens obedient resistance.
He produces new fruit.
He points you toward Christ.
And by the Spirit, the Christian keeps putting sin to death.
One surrendered choice at a time.
One opened exit at a time.
One confession at a time.
One act of obedience at a time.
One return to Jesus at a time.
So when temptation knocks again, remember:
You do not have to give every desire that enters your heart permission to become your master. The door may be shaking—but Jesus still owns the house.
Because someday you may discover that the moment you thought was only another temptation...
was actually the moment God was teaching you how to walk free.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Religious Leader Asked Jesus, “Who Is My Neighbor?” Jesus Answered With a Story That Made the Wrong Person the Hero.
paragraphs: A Religious Leader Asked Jesus, “Who Is My Neighbor?” Jesus Answered With a Story That Made the Wrong Person the Hero.

The Good Samaritan is not merely a lesson about being nice to strangers. It is a confrontation with the human heart—a story about the people we excuse ourselves from loving, the mercy we cannot earn, and the Savior who refuses to let religion become a hiding place.
There is something dangerous about asking Jesus a question when you have already decided what answer you want.
Because Jesus has a way of answering the question beneath the question.

And sometimes His answer dismantles the little courtroom we have built inside ourselves—the courtroom where we are always innocent, our enemies are always guilty, our compassion always has reasonable limits, and God conveniently agrees with us.
That is what happened on a road in Luke 10.
A man stood up.
Not an atheist.
Not a pagan.
Not someone ignorant of Scripture.
Luke calls him a νομικός — nomikos, a lawyer, meaning an expert in the Law of Moses.
He knew the commandments.
He knew the theological vocabulary.
He knew how religious discussions worked.
And he asked Jesus one of the greatest questions a human being could possibly ask:

“Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
—Luke 10:25
But Luke tells us something important about the question.
The man stood up ἐκπειράζων αὐτόν — ekpeirazōn auton.
He was “testing Him.”
This was not simply a desperate sinner crying, “How can I be saved?”
There was a test inside the question.
Jesus responded by directing the expert back to the very Law he claimed to understand.

“What is written in the law? how readest thou?”
—Luke 10:26, KJV
The man answered beautifully.
Love God completely.
Love your neighbor as yourself.
He was drawing from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18.
And Jesus said:

“Thou hast answered right: this do, and thou shalt live.”
—Luke 10:28, KJV
That should have ended the conversation.
It didn’t.
Because knowing the commandment and surrendering to the commandment are two very different things.
Luke then gives us one devastating sentence:

“But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour?”
—Luke 10:29, KJV
There it is.
Willing to justify himself.
The Greek is even more revealing:
ὁ δὲ θέλων δικαιῶσαι ἑαυτόν — ho de thelōn dikaiōsai heauton
Literally, he was wanting to justify himself.
That sentence is the doorway into the entire parable.
The man did not merely need information about neighbors.
He needed a boundary.
He needed to know where his obligation ended.
How far does love have to go?
Who qualifies?
Who doesn’t?
Who can I walk past without violating the commandment?
Who is close enough to deserve my compassion?
And, perhaps more uncomfortably:
Who am I biblically permitted not to love?
We still ask that question.
We just dress it differently.
“Lord, surely You don't mean him.”
“Surely You don't expect me to forgive her.”
“You know what they did.”
“You know what they said about me.”
“You know how many times I helped them.”
“You know what kind of people they are.”
“They chose this.”
“They hurt me first.”
“They believe differently.”
“They vote differently.”
“They worship differently.”
“They betrayed me.”
“They embarrassed me.”
“They never apologized.”
“Surely, Jesus… there has to be a line.”
And Jesus begins telling a story.
“A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho…”
No name.
No résumé.
No ethnicity explicitly identified.
No explanation of whether he deserved help.
Just a man.
Traveling.
And then everything collapsed.
He fell among robbers.
They stripped him.
Beat him.
Took what he had.
And left him.
Luke's description is chilling:
ἡμιθανῆ — hēmithanē
“Half-dead.”
Try not to read that too quickly.
Picture him.
Dust sticking to blood.
Clothing torn away.
Possessions gone.
Body broken.
Breathing, perhaps, but barely.
Unable to rescue himself.
Unable to negotiate.
Unable to prove that he was worthy of assistance.
Unable to offer repayment.
All he could do was lie there.
And then footsteps came.
A priest.
Of all people.
If anyone should understand mercy, surely the priest should.
Jesus says:

“And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side.”
—Luke 10:31, KJV
He saw him.
That matters.
This was not ignorance.
The wounded man was not invisible.
He was seen.
And passed.
Then another man approached.
A Levite.
Another person associated with Israel's religious life.
Perhaps this time.
Perhaps he will stop.
Luke says he came to the place.
He saw the man.
And he also passed by on the other side.
Two religious men.
Two sets of eyes.
Two opportunities for mercy.
Two decisions to keep moving.
Jesus does not tell us their motives.
That matters too.
We should resist inventing excuses the text itself does not give them.
Maybe they were afraid.
Maybe they were hurried.
Maybe they suspected danger.
Maybe they had explanations that sounded perfectly reasonable inside their own minds.
Jesus does not tell us.
He tells us what they did.
They saw suffering.
And they passed by.
That should disturb every Christian who has ever learned how to explain why somebody else's pain is not our responsibility.
Because you can know Scripture and still cross the road.
You can attend worship and still cross the road.
You can post Bible verses and still cross the road.
You can defend Christian doctrine online and still cross the road.
You can sing about the love of God while carefully avoiding the person whose suffering would inconvenience your schedule.
You can be religiously correct and mercifully absent.
Then Jesus introduces the third traveler.
And this is where the story becomes scandalous.
“But a certain Samaritan…”
Stop there.
A Samaritan.
Jesus did not choose the hero His audience might naturally expect.

The Gospels themselves preserve evidence of the social and religious hostility between Jews and Samaritans. In John 4:9, the Samaritan woman is astonished that Jesus, a Jew, asks her for a drink, and the text explicitly notes the strained relations between Jews and Samaritans. In Luke 9:52–53, a Samaritan village refuses to receive Jesus because He is traveling toward Jerusalem.
So when Jesus said:
Σαμαρίτης δέ τις — Samaritēs de tis
“But a certain Samaritan…”
the story had crossed an uncomfortable line.
The person expected to be outside the moral circle was walking into the center of the story.
The outsider was about to do what the religious insiders had failed to do.
And then comes one of the most beautiful words in the passage.
The Samaritan saw the wounded man and:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη — esplagchnisthē
“He was moved with compassion.”
This is not detached sympathy.
The verb describes deep, inward compassion—a visceral movement of mercy.
He saw him…
and something moved inside him.
Then compassion became action.
He approached.
He bound the wounds.
He poured on oil and wine.
He lifted the wounded man onto his own animal.
He brought him to an inn.
He cared for him.
The next day, he gave the innkeeper two denarii and promised to cover additional legitimate expense when he returned.
Notice what mercy cost him.
Time.
Resources.
Comfort.
Convenience.
Money.
Attention.
Risk.
Interruption.
Mercy was not something he felt while continuing down the road.
Mercy changed his itinerary.
And suddenly the question asked at the beginning of the story starts collapsing.
“Who is my neighbor?”
The lawyer wanted Jesus to identify the proper recipient of neighbor-love.
Jesus instead told him about a man who became a neighbor through mercy.
Then Jesus turned the question around:

“Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?”
—Luke 10:36, KJV
Look carefully at what Jesus did.
The original question was essentially:
Who qualifies as my neighbor?
Jesus' closing question becomes:
Which man acted as a neighbor?
The lawyer answered:

“He that shewed mercy on him.”
—Luke 10:37, KJV
Even that response is striking.
He does not say, “The Samaritan.”
He says:
“The one who showed mercy.”
And Jesus answered:
“Go, and do thou likewise.”
That is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because Jesus does not allow us to admire the Samaritan from a safe distance.
He sends us toward the road.
Toward wounded people.
Toward inconvenient people.
Toward people who cannot repay us.
And sometimes toward people we would never have chosen.
The parable exposes something ugly in us.
We love asking who deserves mercy because that allows us to remain the judge.
Jesus asks whether we are willing to become merciful.
We ask:
“Who is worthy of my love?”
Jesus moves us toward another question:
“Will you love the person God has placed in front of you?”
And this reaches far beyond giving money to someone in need.
Maybe the person lying beside your emotional road is your spouse.
Maybe you have been living in the same house while walking past each other's wounds.
Maybe it is your child.
Your father.
Your mother.
Your brother.
Your sister.
Someone at church.
Someone who disappointed you.
Someone everybody else quietly abandoned.
Maybe it is the person whose name makes your chest tighten.
The person you blocked.
The person you avoid.
The person you privately decided no longer deserves kindness.
This does not mean Scripture commands you to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Biblical love does not require pretending evil is good, eliminating wise boundaries, enabling sin, or refusing appropriate protection and justice.
Mercy is not the denial of truth.
Jesus is full of grace and truth.
But neither can “boundaries” become a holy-sounding word we use to baptize hatred.
There is a difference between protecting yourself from ongoing harm and feeding bitterness until another person's suffering no longer matters to you.
Jesus knows the difference.
And so does the heart when the Holy Spirit begins searching it.
Maybe the most frightening possibility is this:
You can spend years trying not to become the wounded man…
and slowly become the person who walks past him.
You survive your own pain.
You build walls.
You become careful.
Suspicious.
Harder.
You tell yourself that nobody helped you, so why should you help them?
And without realizing it, yesterday's wounded traveler becomes tomorrow's passerby.
But Jesus interrupts that cycle.
Because the Gospel does something human resentment cannot do.
The Gospel reminds us that before we start congratulating ourselves for being the Samaritan, we should remember how desperately we needed mercy.
We were not saved because we had accumulated enough moral points.
We did not negotiate our way into grace.
We could not cleanse our own guilt.
Sin was not a shallow scratch requiring motivational advice.
Scripture says:

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
And:

“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
That changes everything.
The deepest Christian motivation for mercy is not:
“Be nicer so God will finally love you.”
It is:
In Christ, look at the mercy God has shown sinners who could never purchase it.
Jesus Christ went to the cross.
Our sin was real.
God's holiness was real.
Judgment was real.
And the Son of God willingly gave Himself.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ, not because sin does not matter, but because Jesus dealt with sin at a cost we could never pay.
The Gospel does not merely tell wounded sinners to crawl harder.
It announces a Savior.
And when grace reaches a human heart, it begins changing how that heart sees everybody else.
You cannot earn salvation by becoming a Good Samaritan.
That would reverse the Gospel.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith, not the product of our works or moral heroism (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But do not stop reading at verse 9.
Ephesians 2:10 says believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
Grace saves us.
Then grace transforms us.
We do not show mercy in order to purchase Christ.
We show mercy because Christ has taken hold of us.
That distinction matters.
Christian compassion is not the admission price into heaven.
It is one of the fruits that should increasingly appear in a life being transformed by the King of heaven.
So perhaps the Good Samaritan is asking you something tonight.
Not merely:
“Do you understand this parable?”
But:
Who have you been walking past?
Whose pain did you notice but decide was too inconvenient?
Whose name have you turned into a category instead of remembering they are a human being made in God's image?
Who became “those people” to you?
Who have you reduced to their worst moment?
And what if the person Jesus is commanding you to treat as a neighbor is the person you hoped He would exclude?
Be honest.
This may hit harder than you expected.
Maybe there is another side too.
Maybe right now you are not identifying with the priest.
Or the Levite.
Or even the Samaritan.
Maybe you feel like the man in the dirt.
Half-alive.
Stripped by betrayal.
Beaten down by consequences.
Robbed by addiction.
Crushed by grief.
Exhausted from fighting battles nobody knows exist.
People have looked at you and kept walking.
Even religious people.
Perhaps especially religious people.
And somewhere inside you, you began wondering whether God would walk past too.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Jesus is not ashamed of ruined people who come to Him.
He touched lepers.
He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He received the rejected.
He restored failures.
He forgave the repentant.
He welcomed the broken.
He went to a cross between criminals.
Peter denied Him—and Peter's story was not over.
A thief dying beside Him turned toward Him—and his story was not over.
Saul persecuted the church—and his story was not over.
Scandal did not get the final sentence.
Grace did.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives and then says, “Follow Me.”
Grace that finds sinners but refuses to leave them unchanged.
Grace that produces repentance.
Grace that destroys our excuses.
Grace that teaches enemies to become neighbors.
Grace that turns wounded people into people who bind wounds.
Grace that takes a heart filled with hatred and teaches it to kneel before Jesus.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe today your next act of obedience is not dramatic.
Maybe it is a phone call.
An apology.
A meal.
A hospital visit.
A private gift.
A prayer.
A conversation.
A decision to stop humiliating somebody whose sin became public.
A decision to forgive while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
A decision to see a human being where you previously saw only an enemy.
Maybe your Jericho road is not somewhere far away.
Maybe it is your Facebook feed.
Your workplace.
Your church.
Your dining table.
Your family group chat.
Your neighborhood.
Maybe someone is bleeding where everybody can see them…
and everybody keeps scrolling.
Do not merely “like” a story about mercy.
Become a neighbor.
And if this article exposed someone you have been walking past, do not rush away from that conviction.
Take it to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask Him to remove bitterness.
Ask Him for wisdom where reconciliation is complicated.
Ask Him for courage where mercy will cost something.
Ask Him to make your life look increasingly like a life that has actually encountered grace.
Then make the comment section more than an algorithm.
Make it an altar of honesty.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your story.
But sometimes three honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer:
I am not the only one still fighting.

Not because saving a post is spiritual obedience by itself, but because there may come a day when resentment feels justified again, when somebody wounds you again, when compassion becomes expensive again, and you need to remember the road between Jerusalem and Jericho.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Send it privately to the friend whose faith is exhausted.
Send it to the Christian who has become discouraged by hypocrisy.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about religious people proving they are better than everyone else.
Let them encounter Jesus instead.
And if Gospel Warrior is helping you encounter Scripture, conviction, grace, healing, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ more deeply, stay close.
We will never place a price tag on grace.
But generosity can be an act through which believers intentionally help Gospel-centered work reach farther.

Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, encouraging wounded believers, confronting comfortable religion, calling sinners toward repentance, and pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
The Samaritan's road is still in front of us.
People are still wounded.
Religion can still become an excuse.
Enemies can still become neighbors.
And Jesus is still asking what we will do with the mercy we ourselves have received.
One day nobody will remember how polished our Christian image looked.
But heaven sees the cup of cold water.
The unseen generosity.
The forgiveness that cost us tears.
The wounded person we refused to abandon.
The enemy we stopped dehumanizing.
The stranger we finally saw.
The sinner we loved enough to tell the truth to.
The broken believer we helped carry when they could no longer carry themselves.
And above all, the Savior whose mercy made any of our mercy possible.
So go back to the road.
Look again.
The person you were prepared to walk past may be the very place where Christ is exposing what your religion has done to your heart.
And perhaps the greatest scandal in the story was never that the Samaritan became the hero.
Perhaps the scandal is that sinners like us received mercy from God—and then somehow imagined we could afford to become stingy with it.
Never forget this: the road where somebody else's wounds interrupt your plans may become the road where Jesus reveals what grace has actually done to your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Cain Asked, “Am I My Brother’s Keeper?”—Jesus Gave Humanity a Different Answer
paragraphs: Cain Asked, “Am I My Brother’s Keeper?”—Jesus Gave Humanity a Different Answer
The first murderer tried to escape responsibility for his brother. Thousands of years later, Jesus Christ stepped into a murderous world and showed us what it actually means to love one another.
There is blood in the ground.
And God hears it.

Before humanity built its first great cities, before kings raised armies, before nations drew borders, before anyone learned how to disguise hatred beneath respectable language, two brothers walked into a field.
Only one walked out.
Cain had already been warned.
Sin was crouching at the door.
Jealousy was eating him alive.
His brother Abel had done nothing deserving death, yet something inside Cain could not tolerate seeing another person accepted when he felt rejected.
So Cain rose against his brother.
And killed him.
Then came the question.
Not Cain’s question.
God’s.
“Where is Abel thy brother?”
Cain answered:
“I know not: Am I my brother’s keeper?”
Genesis 4:9.
In Hebrew, the question carries the sting even more directly:
הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי
Ha-shomer achi anokhi?
Literally, the thought is:
“Am I the keeper of my brother?”
The Hebrew word שֹׁמֵר — shomer comes from שָׁמַר — shamar, a verb carrying the sense of keeping, watching, guarding, preserving, or attending carefully to something entrusted to you.
Cain had murdered his brother.
Then he spoke as though his brother’s welfare had never been his concern.
That may be one of the darkest sentences ever spoken by a human being.
Not merely because Cain lied.
But because Cain’s question exposed something that still lives inside the fallen human heart.
“Why should his suffering concern me?”
“Why should her loneliness become my problem?”
“Why should I forgive?”
“Why should I notice?”
“Why should I help?”
“Why should I care what happens to someone else?”
“Am I really responsible for anybody but myself?”
Cain asked that question beside blood-soaked ground.
We ask it in cleaner places.
Behind locked doors.
Behind glowing screens.
Inside churches.
Inside marriages.
Inside families that have stopped speaking.
Inside friendships we quietly abandoned.
Inside communities where everybody sees the wounded person but assumes somebody else will stop.
We may never lift a weapon against our brother, yet we can become remarkably skilled at walking past his pain.
We change the subject.
We say, “I’ll pray for you,” and sometimes forget before the conversation is over.
We know somebody is unraveling, but reaching out feels inconvenient.
We know someone needs forgiveness, but resentment feels safer.
We know someone is wandering from Christ, but we are afraid the conversation might become uncomfortable.
We see the lonely.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The grieving.
The doubting.
The exhausted mother.
The silent father.
The teenager pretending everything is fine.
The believer who has not prayed honestly in months.
The person sitting three seats away in church whose smile has become a survival mechanism.
And somewhere deep inside the old nature, Cain’s question still whispers:
“Am I my brother’s keeper?”
Then Jesus enters the story.
And humanity receives a radically different answer.
Not merely through something Christ said.
Through what Christ did.
The apostle John deliberately brings Cain and Jesus into the same conversation.
He writes that we should not be “as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother” (1 John 3:12).
Then, only a few verses later, John shows us the opposite of Cain:
“Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.”
1 John 3:16.
The Greek is breathtaking:
ἐν τούτῳ ἐγνώκαμεν τὴν ἀγάπην, ὅτι ἐκεῖνος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἔθηκεν
En toutō egnōkamen tēn agapēn, hoti ekeinos hyper hēmōn tēn psychēn autou ethēken.
In essence:
“By this we have come to know love: He laid down His life for us.”
Do you see the reversal?
Cain took his brother’s life.
Christ laid down His own life.
Cain asked why he should keep his brother.
Jesus came to seek and save the lost.
Cain spilled innocent blood because of his hatred.
Jesus shed His innocent blood because of His love.
Cain stood over his dead brother and distanced himself from responsibility.
Jesus looked upon guilty sinners and willingly entered their suffering.
Cain essentially said:
“His life is not my responsibility.”
Christ said:
“I lay down my life for the sheep.”
That is the Gospel.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to condemn Cain when there is blood on his hands.
It is harder to recognize Cain when his attitude appears inside ours.
Scripture does not allow Christians to congratulate themselves simply because they have never committed murder.
John continues:
“But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?”
Then:
“My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
That hurts.
Because sometimes our Christianity sounds more compassionate than it actually is.
We know Christian vocabulary.
We know when to say “God bless you.”
We know how to post the verse.
We know how to lift our hands during worship.
We know how to tell somebody we will pray.
But Jesus does not merely call us to perform compassion.
He transforms people so deeply that love begins taking flesh.
Hands.
Time.
Money.
Forgiveness.
Presence.
Patience.
Sacrifice.
Truth.
Mercy.
A phone call nobody sees.
A meal nobody posts.
A conversation with the person everyone else avoids.
A prayer whispered beside someone who has finally admitted, “I don’t think I can keep doing this.”
A brother refusing to let another brother disappear quietly into darkness.
A sister sitting beside another sister while her carefully constructed world falls apart.
Not because these things earn salvation.
They cannot.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no human being can boast (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the very next verse says that believers are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace does not purchase our indifference.
Grace transforms us.
Jesus did not save us because we loved perfectly.
Jesus saves sinners who could never rescue themselves—and then begins teaching rescued sinners how to love.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not:
“Love people enough and perhaps God will save you.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better:
Christ saves sinners by grace, and the grace that saves us begins changing what we love.
That is why Jesus could say:
“A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you.”
John 13:34.
Listen to the Greek phrase at the heart of it:
καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς
kathōs ēgapēsa hymas
“As I have loved you.”
That changes everything.
Jesus did not merely say, “Be nicer.”
He gave Himself as the pattern.
Love one another…
as I loved you.
And how did He love us?
When convenient?
No.
When deserved?
No.
When we had cleaned ourselves up?
No.
Romans 5:8 destroys that illusion:
“While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Jesus loved at tremendous cost.
He touched people society avoided.
He welcomed children others considered interruptions.
He ate with people respectable religion despised.
He wept with the grieving.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He spoke truth to sinners without surrendering sinners to despair.
He washed feet.
Even feet that would soon run away from Him.
And eventually those feet carried Him toward Golgotha.
There the question hanging over humanity since Genesis received its greatest answer.
“Am I my brother’s keeper?”
Look at the cross.
The Son of God did something greater than merely “keep” guilty people at a safe distance.
He entered our ruin.
He bore our sins.
He took upon Himself what we could never remove from ourselves.
Isaiah had prophesied that the LORD would lay upon Him “the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).
Peter would later write that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Paul declared that Christ died for our sins and rose again (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The Gospel is not sentimental advice about humans becoming nicer to one another.
It is news.
Holy God.
Sinful humanity.
Real guilt.
Real judgment.
A real Savior.
A real cross.
A real grave.
A risen Christ.
And forgiveness offered through Him.
Jesus did not come merely to improve Cain’s descendants.
He came to redeem sinners.
That includes people with beautiful testimonies.
And people with scandalous ones.
People whose failures are public.
And people whose sins have remained hidden behind locked doors, deleted histories, polished reputations, religious language, and Sunday clothes.
Maybe that is where this article finds you.
Not standing over Abel.
But standing over something you damaged.
A marriage.
A friendship.
Your children’s trust.
Your integrity.
Your prayer life.
Your purity.
Your testimony.
Your relationship with God.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun one chapter of your life.
And whenever you remember it, you hear the accusation:
“This is who you are.”
But Scripture tells another story.
Cain’s story reminds us what sin does.
The cross reveals what grace has done.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not receive the final word over everyone who belongs to Jesus Christ.
This is why our message remains:
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin should be romanticized.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
Grace is not God pretending sin did not happen.
Grace cost blood.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
Grace looks directly at the ugliness of our rebellion and announces that Christ’s sacrifice is sufficient for everyone who turns to Him in repentant faith.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history as though the sin never occurred.
He rewrites the sinner.
He forgives.
Cleanses.
Reconciles.
Restores.
Transforms.
Makes alive.
And sends redeemed people back into a wounded world carrying a completely different question.
Not:
“Why should I care?”
But:
“Jesus, who can I love because You first loved me?”
Not:
“Is that person my responsibility?”
But:
“How can I refuse compassion after receiving so much mercy?”
Not:
“What will helping them cost me?”
But:
“What did rescuing me cost Christ?”
That is dangerous Christianity.
Dangerous to selfishness.
Dangerous to bitterness.
Dangerous to comfortable religion.
Dangerous to the walls we build around ourselves.
Paul writes:
ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βαστάζετε
Allēlōn ta barē bastazete.
“Bear ye one another’s burdens.”
Galatians 6:2.
And then:
“so fulfil the law of Christ.”
There are burdens around you right now.
Somebody you know is carrying one.
Maybe they have not told you.
Maybe they tried.
Maybe you were distracted.
Maybe God brought their face into your mind while you were reading this.
Do not automatically silence that thought.
Send the message.
Make the call.
Pray with them.
Forgive where Scripture calls you to forgive.
Tell the truth where love requires truth.
Sit beside the grieving.
Encourage the exhausted.
Feed someone hungry.
Help the believer who stumbled toward restoration with gentleness, as Galatians 6:1 teaches.
Point the ashamed toward Christ rather than making yourself their savior.
You cannot carry everybody.
You are not omnipotent.
You are not the Messiah.
You cannot rescue every wounded person you encounter.
And Christian love does not mean enabling abuse, tolerating evil, abandoning wise boundaries, or pretending justice does not matter.
Jesus is the Savior.
You are not.
But “I cannot save everyone” must never become an excuse for “therefore I will love no one.”
There is probably an Abel closer than you think.
A brother.
A sister.
A spouse.
A child.
A parent.
A coworker.
A stranger.
A believer slipping quietly toward isolation.
A person who desperately needs to discover that Christians do not merely preach about a Savior who loves wounded people.
They have been loved by that Savior so deeply that His love has begun changing the way they see wounded people.
And perhaps the person bleeding quietly is you.
Maybe you have spent years being everybody else’s keeper while secretly falling apart.
You answer every message.
Carry every burden.
Encourage everyone.
Smile.
Serve.
Post Scripture.
Show up.
Then lie awake at night wondering whether anyone would recognize your exhaustion if you finally stopped pretending.
Hear this carefully:
You need more than people.
You need Christ.
Human beings can sit beside your wounds.
Only Jesus can deal with your deepest problem—sin—and reconcile you to God.
Only His blood can cleanse the guilty conscience.
Only the risen Christ can give eternal life.
And you do not have to make yourself presentable before coming to Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come empty-handed.
Confess your sin.
Stop defending what God calls sin.
Stop bargaining.
Stop hiding.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
There is mercy in Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Maybe your prayer tonight is not impressive.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Pray it sincerely.
Maybe:
“Lord, I have become cold.”
Tell Him.
“Lord, I hate somebody.”
Confess it.
“Lord, I am jealous.”
Bring it into the light.
“Lord, I keep pretending.”
Stop pretending.
“Lord, I need forgiveness.”
Come to Christ.
The same Bible that tells us about Cain also tells us about a Savior whose blood speaks a better word.
Hebrews 12:24 speaks of Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, and “the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.”
Think about that.
Abel’s blood cried from the ground.
The blood of Jesus announces the astonishing mercy of the new covenant.
The murderer asks:
“Am I my brother’s keeper?”
The Savior stretches His hands upon a cross.
And Christianity has never been the same.
So when you see your brother hurting, remember Jesus.
When resentment whispers that somebody deserves abandonment, remember how much mercy you received.
When another believer falls, remember Galatians 6:1 and restore with gentleness rather than secretly enjoying their humiliation.
When somebody confesses their struggle, do not become another reason they regret telling the truth.
And when you fail at loving people—and you will—do not turn Christian compassion into another system of self-salvation.
Return to the Gospel.
Repent.
Receive grace.
Get up.
Love again.
Because the Christian life is not humanity climbing toward God by becoming morally impressive.
It is redeemed people learning to walk in the footsteps of the One who came down to rescue them.
And maybe this is why you needed to read this today.
Maybe somebody’s name has been haunting you through these paragraphs.
Do something with that conviction.
If reconciliation is biblically appropriate, take the first humble step.
If someone needs encouragement, contact them.
If somebody is suffering, stop assuming somebody else will notice.
If you have become Cain-like in your indifference, confess it.
If you are the wounded one, stop hiding from Christ.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only person fighting that battle.
There may come a night when Cain’s question begins whispering again.
A night when loving someone becomes expensive.
A night when forgiving becomes difficult.
A night when you become the wounded person.
Come back and remember:
Cain took his brother’s life. Jesus gave His life for His enemies and turned enemies into family.
That is the difference grace makes.

When believers voluntarily support Gospel work, they help make more Gospel-centered resources available to people who may be one article, one testimony, one Scripture, or one compassionate conversation away from seriously confronting the claims of Jesus Christ.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Kingdom itself.
God is not impressed by clicks.
Nobody purchases salvation.
Nobody buys grace.
Nobody earns forgiveness by sharing Christian content.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient lives, and one way believers may freely choose to steward their resources is by supporting faithful Gospel work.
Follow if you want to stay close to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
Share because someone you know may desperately need the message.
And comment because your testimony, confession, or simple “pray for me” may become the doorway through which another struggling believer finally finds the courage to stop hiding.
Then take the message beyond Facebook.
Look around.
Someone is carrying something.
Someone is bleeding where nobody can see.
Someone is wondering whether anybody notices.
Someone has convinced themselves they are too ruined to return to God.
Someone believes their scandal has become their identity.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them about the cross.
Tell them repentance is real.
Tell them grace is real.
Tell them forgiveness is real.
Tell them the tomb is empty.
Tell them sinners can be redeemed.
Tell them failure does not have to write the final sentence when a sinner comes to Christ.
Because thousands of years ago, Cain looked toward the brother he had failed to love and asked:
“Am I my brother’s keeper?”
And then, in the fullness of time, another Brother came.
Jesus Christ.
He did not murder His brothers.
His brothers murdered Him.
He did not spill their blood.
He gave His own.
He did not ask whether sinners were worth the inconvenience.
He went to the cross.
He rose from the grave.
And now everyone who belongs to Him is being taught a new way to live.
Not the way of Cain.
The way of Christ.
So when the world asks you why another person’s suffering should matter to you, remember the nails.
When bitterness asks why you should forgive, remember the mercy you received.
When selfishness asks why you should carry somebody else’s burden, remember the Savior who carried yours.
And when shame tells you your own story is already ruined beyond redemption, look again toward the empty tomb.
The blood in Cain’s field cried out because a brother had been killed; the blood at Calvary speaks because the Savior willingly died—and the empty tomb declares that death did not get the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THERE IS NOW NO CONDEMNATION”—BUT JESUS NEVER SAID THERE IS NOW NO NEED FOR REPENTANCE
paragraphs: “THERE IS NOW NO CONDEMNATION”—BUT JESUS NEVER SAID THERE IS NOW NO NEED FOR REPENTANCE

Romans 8:1 may be one of the most comforting sentences ever written to a guilty human heart. It may also be one of the most dangerously misunderstood. Grace does not give sin permission to stay. Grace gives sinners a Savior powerful enough to bring them home.
There is a sentence in the Bible that people reach for when shame becomes unbearable.
When the memories come back.
When the temptation won again.
When you promised God, “Never again,” and somehow found yourself standing in the wreckage of another again.
When everybody at church thinks you are doing well, but you know what happened when nobody was watching.
When your Bible is open but your conscience is screaming.
When you wonder whether God is tired of forgiving you.
Then you remember the words:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
And suddenly you can breathe.
But then another danger appears.
Because the same verse that can rescue a repentant sinner from crushing despair can be twisted into an excuse for an unrepentant sinner to remain comfortable in rebellion.
No condemnation.
Does that mean no consequences?
No repentance?
No war against sin?
No obedience?
Can I knowingly continue embracing what Christ died to save me from and simply whisper, “Grace”?
Paul’s answer is devastatingly clear.
No.
And understanding why may completely change the way you hear Romans 8:1.
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
Ouden ara nyn katakrima tois en Christō Iēsou.
A straightforward rendering is:
“Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say there is now no condemnation for sin.
He does not announce that evil has become harmless.
He does not declare repentance obsolete.
He does not say holiness no longer matters.
The breathtaking promise belongs to those who are ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — en Christō Iēsou — “in Christ Jesus.”
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of sinners discovering a theological loophole.
It is the story of condemned sinners being united to a crucified and risen Savior.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years confusing two completely different voices.
One voice says:
“You sinned. Run away from God. Hide. You are filthy. There is no hope for someone like you.”
The other says:
“You sinned. Come into the light. Confess it. Turn from it. Run to Christ. His mercy is greater than your failure.”
Those voices are not the same.
Condemnation drives you toward hopelessness.
Godly conviction drives you toward repentance.
One whispers, “There is no way home.”
The Gospel announces, “The way home has a name.”
Jesus Christ.
Romans 8:1 does not float by itself in the Bible.
There is a “therefore” at the beginning because Paul has already taken us somewhere.
He has taken us through the courtroom.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23.
He has taken us to the horrifying wages of rebellion.
“For the wages of sin is death…” — Romans 6:23.
He has taken us into the strange battlefield of the human heart where someone can recognize what is right and still experience the terrible power of indwelling sin.
Then near the end of Romans 7 comes the cry:
“O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?”
Listen carefully to the question.
Paul does not ask:
What rule will save me?
What excuse will save me?
What religious performance will save me?
He asks:
Who?
And the answer comes immediately:
“I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Then Romans 8 explodes into view.
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
Why?
Not because sin stopped being serious.
Because Jesus became the sinner’s substitute.
The Gospel does not say God looked at our rebellion and decided it did not matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin mattered enough that redemption required the blood of Christ.
God did not save us by pretending justice did not exist.
At the cross, mercy and justice meet in Jesus Christ.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the suffering Servant:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ
Vehu mecholal mipsha‘einu.
“He was wounded for our transgressions…” — Isaiah 53:5.
The Hebrew מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ — mipsha‘einu points to our transgressions, our rebellions.
Ours.
That is the scandal.
The innocent Christ suffers for guilty people.
The righteous One receives what rebels deserve so rebels united to Him can receive what they could never earn.
That is grace.
But grace becomes grotesquely distorted when we turn the wounds of Jesus into permission to keep loving the sins for which He was wounded.
Paul anticipated that distortion long before any of us made it.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” — Romans 6:1.
His response in Greek is wonderfully forceful:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
It carries the force of:
Absolutely not. May it never be.
Then Paul asks:
“How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?” — Romans 6:2.
That does not mean genuine Christians instantly become incapable of sin.
The New Testament would make little sense if it did.
Believers still stumble.
Believers still need confession.
Believers still need correction.
Believers still fight desires they wish would disappear overnight.
First John tells Christians:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9.
So the question is not whether a Christian ever falls.
The deeper question is:
What do you do when you fall?
Do you defend the darkness?
Or drag it into the light?
Do you rename sin so you can keep it?
Or confess sin because you want Christ more than you want your chains?
Do you use grace to silence conviction?
Or does grace make you want to run back into the arms of the One you have grieved?
There is an enormous difference between a believer struggling against sin and a person making peace with sin.
A struggling Christian may fall repeatedly and hate the fall.
A hardened heart eventually begins furnishing the prison cell.
It puts pictures on the walls.
Makes excuses comfortable.
Changes the vocabulary.
Calls bondage “freedom.”
Calls compromise “being authentic.”
Calls biblical correction “judgment.”
And eventually may use the blood of Jesus as theological camouflage for refusing the lordship of Jesus.
That is not what “no condemnation” means.
Grace is not God saying:
“Your sin does not matter.”
Grace is God saying:
“Your sin was so serious that My Son went to the cross—and My love is so astonishing that I gave Him for sinners like you.”
Keep reading Romans 8.
Paul says:
“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.” — Romans 8:2.
Free.
But free from what?
Not free to sin without concern.
Free from the dominion that once held us.
Later Paul writes:
That is not permission.
That is warfare.
And maybe that is what somebody needed to hear today.
You have mistaken struggling for hypocrisy.
You have assumed that because temptation still knocks, Christ must have abandoned the house.
You have hated yourself because the battle is still happening.
But the existence of battle is not necessarily evidence that God has left you.
Sometimes the battle exists precisely because surrender to sin is no longer acceptable to you.
Before Christ, darkness can feel like home.
When Christ begins transforming us, darkness increasingly feels like a prison.
You may still stumble into what once enslaved you.
But now something inside cries:
I don't want to live here anymore.
That cry matters.
Not because it earns salvation.
Jesus alone saves.
But because the Holy Spirit does not merely comfort God's children in sin. He transforms God's children toward the likeness of Christ.
So hear this carefully if you failed last night.
If you returned to pornography.
If anger controlled you again.
If pride poisoned another relationship.
If greed has quietly become your master.
If jealousy is eating you alive.
If you lied.
If you betrayed somebody.
If alcohol, lust, bitterness, gossip, dishonesty, envy, or secret compromise has become the room nobody is allowed to enter.
Do not hear Romans 8:1 saying:
Stay there.
Hear it saying:
Because of Christ, you can come out of hiding.
There is a world of difference.
Satan would love to push you toward either of two cliffs.
On one side:
Despair.
“You have sinned too badly. Jesus doesn't want you anymore.”
On the other:
Presumption.
“Sin all you want. Jesus doesn't care.”
The Gospel destroys both lies.
To despair, the Gospel says:
Look at the cross. His grace is greater than your record.
To presumption, the Gospel says:
Look at the cross. Your sin is more serious than you imagined.
And to both, Jesus says:
Come to Me.
The cross is where our excuses die without our hope dying with them.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not purchasing God's forgiveness with enough tears.
It is not self-punishment.
It is not trying to make yourself miserable enough that God finally decides you have suffered sufficiently.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō, carrying the idea of changing one's mind or turning in response to truth.
Biblical repentance involves a real turning toward God.
We stop defending what He calls sin.
We agree with Him.
We bring it into the light.
We turn toward Christ.
And even repentance itself does not become a medal we hold up before God and say, “See? Now I deserve You.”
No.
Empty hands.
That is how sinners come.
Empty hands.
Nothing to boast about.
Nothing to negotiate with.
Nothing but need.
And Christ.
Perhaps your greatest problem today is not that you think too little of grace.
Perhaps you have never realized how radical grace actually is.
Cheap grace says:
Jesus forgives me, therefore I don't have to change.
Biblical grace says:
Jesus has forgiven and claimed me, therefore I no longer want sin to remain my master.
Cheap grace asks:
How close can I get to sin without losing heaven?
Love asks:
How close can I get to Jesus?
That question exposes us.
Because sometimes we don't really want freedom from sin.
We want freedom from consequences.
We want Jesus to remove hell while leaving our idols untouched.
We want a Savior who forgives but never interrupts.
A King who never commands.
A Shepherd who never redirects.
A Physician who diagnoses nothing.
A cross without dying to self.
A resurrection without a grave.
But the Jesus of Scripture does not merely offer us improved circumstances.
He gives us Himself.
And when Christ takes hold of a human life, He does not simply rewrite its destination.
He begins rewriting the person.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Maybe your story contains chapters you desperately wish could be deleted.
Sexual sin.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Abortion.
Infidelity.
Years of unbelief.
Religious hypocrisy.
A ruined friendship.
A wounded child.
A wounded parent.
A secret habit.
Something you did.
Something you became.
Something you still cannot say aloud.
You cannot travel backward and prevent those pages from being written.
But Jesus Christ specializes in stories human beings would have thrown away.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted His people.
The woman of Samaria carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Christ reached the end of his life with nothing left to offer.
The Gospel is filled with people whose histories should have disqualified them from boasting.
And that is precisely the point.
Grace leaves no room for boasting.
Your scandal does not become beautiful because the sin was beautiful.
Sin destroys.
The beauty is that Jesus can enter what sin destroyed and write redemption where we expected only an ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal have the final word.
Maybe you need to stop running today.
Not tomorrow.
Today.
Stop rehearsing your defense.
Stop blaming everybody else.
Stop calling bondage personality.
Stop waiting until you “feel spiritual enough” to return.
Come filthy if you are filthy.
Come ashamed if you are ashamed.
Come trembling.
Come exhausted.
Come with the confession you have been terrified to speak.
But come to Jesus.
“If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” — 1 John 1:7.
Did you see it?
Walking in the light does not mean pretending you never needed cleansing.
It means you stop hiding from the One whose blood cleanses.
Somebody reading this has been punishing themselves for something Christ is calling them to confess and surrender.
You think hating yourself proves that you understand the seriousness of your sin.
But self-hatred cannot atone for you.
Shame cannot crucify itself for you.
Regret cannot rise from the dead.
Jesus already went to the cross.
Jesus already entered the grave.
Jesus already rose.
And if your faith is in Him, your hope is not that you have finally become good enough to escape condemnation.
Your hope is Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
Now.
What a word.
Not after you have spent twenty years compensating for your past.
Not after everybody you disappointed finally approves of you again.
Not after you have punished yourself adequately.
Now.
For those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is justification.
The believer's right standing before God rests on Christ, not on a flawless record of personal performance.
But the Christ who justifies also transforms.
Sanctification does not purchase justification, but justification is never meant to become an excuse for despising sanctification.
We are not saved because we became holy enough.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ, and the God who saves His people begins making them holy.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
But do not stop before Paul's next sentence:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…” — Ephesians 2:8–10.
Grace saves.
Grace changes.
Grace forgives.
Grace disciplines.
Grace receives prodigals.
Grace teaches prodigals that the pigpen was never home.
So when temptation whispers tonight:
“No condemnation. Go ahead.”
Answer it with the rest of Scripture.
No condemnation does not mean sin has become my friend.
It means sin no longer gets to condemn the one whose condemnation Christ bore.
And because Jesus purchased me at such a cost, I do not want to turn His wounds into permission to return willingly to the chains from which He is freeing me.
And when you fail—and believers sometimes grievously fail—do not let the enemy rewrite Romans 8:1 in the opposite direction.
Do not hear:
“There is now condemnation because you stumbled.”
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help when needed.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Put boundaries around recurring temptation.
Ask mature believers to walk with you.
Get back into Scripture.
Pray even when prayer feels embarrassing.
And run toward Jesus instead of away from Him.
The same Peter who denied Christ three times was restored by Christ.
Failure did not get the final sentence.
Jesus did.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Maybe there is something between you and God that has remained unnamed for too long.
You know what it is.
I don't.
The person sitting beside you may not.
But you know.
And God knows.
So be honest.
Has “grace” become the word you use when you do not want to surrender something?
Or has “condemnation” become the prison you remain inside because you cannot believe Christ could truly forgive somebody with your history?
Whichever side you are standing on, the road leads to the same Person.
Jesus.
Repent and come.
Believe and come.
Broken, come.
Ashamed, come.
Tired of fighting, come.
Tired of pretending, come.
There is no salvation hidden inside your performance.
There is no salvation hidden inside your rebellion either.
Salvation is in Christ.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who keeps smiling while falling apart.
The Christian who thinks another failure means God could never receive them again.
The person using grace to justify chains that are quietly destroying them.
The son.
The daughter.
The husband.
The wife.
The old friend you haven't spoken to in months.
Send this to them privately if that would be wiser.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when Romans 8:1 is no longer theology you are discussing.
It will be oxygen you need.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as a way to purchase God's favor.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness is not merchandise.
Jesus Christ paid the price sinners could never pay.
Because someday the sentence that matters most will not be the sentence shame wrote about you.
Not the sentence your past wrote.
Not the sentence people wrote after seeing your worst moment.
Not even the sentence you have repeated to yourself for years.
For everyone who is truly in Christ, another verdict has already thundered from the Gospel:
No condemnation.
Not permission to return to the grave.
Permission to stop living as though the grave still owns you.
So repent without running from Him.
Fight sin without believing your fighting earns His love.
Confess without pretending.
Obey without boasting.
Get up when you fall.
Walk in the light.
And when shame reaches for the pen again, remember who holds the final page.
Your worst chapter may explain why you came to Jesus—but it does not get to decide how Jesus finishes your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES JESUS STILL PURSUE PEOPLE TRAPPED IN LUST?
paragraphs: WHY DOES JESUS STILL PURSUE PEOPLE TRAPPED IN LUST?

Because the Savior who sees what you delete, what you hide, what you replay, what you fantasize about, and what you swear will never happen again… is still standing at the door of your shame—not to help you manage your chains, but to break them.
There is a particular kind of silence that comes after lust.
Before it, there is anticipation.
During it, there is escape.
After it…
silence.
The screen goes dark.
The browser closes.
The message gets deleted.
The fantasy ends.
The body settles down.
And suddenly you are left alone with the person you were trying not to think about.
You.
Maybe you have whispered, “God, forgive me,” so many times that the words almost embarrass you now.
Maybe you meant it every time.
Maybe you cried.
Maybe you deleted the app.
Maybe you blocked the person.
Maybe you promised Jesus, “Never again.”
Then three days later…
again.
Or three hours later.
Again.
And eventually the question changes.
At first you asked, “How do I stop?”
Then you started asking something darker:
“Why would Jesus still want me?”
That question is where this story begins.
Because lust does something beyond tempting the body. When repeatedly welcomed and fed, it begins teaching the soul a theology of shame.
It tells you that because you keep returning to the same darkness, Jesus must eventually stop returning for you.
It whispers that grace probably has a limit.
That Christ forgives ordinary sinners, but not people who knew better.
Not people who prayed afterward and still went back.
Not pastors.
Not husbands.
Not wives.
Not teenagers raised in church.
Not the person secretly consuming pornography while publicly posting Bible verses.
Not the believer carrying sexual memories nobody knows about.
Not the person whose imagination has become a room they would be terrified to let anyone enter.
Lust says, “If people really knew you, they would leave.”
Then shame adds:
“And if Jesus really knew you, He would too.”
There is just one devastating problem with that lie.
Jesus already knows.
He knows everything.
And He is still calling you out of the darkness.
Jesus never treated lust casually. In fact, some of His strongest words confront it directly.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text reads:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
Jesus says, in context, that the one who looks at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

The verb connected to this statement comes from ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire, long for, or covet. Desire itself is not automatically sinful in every biblical use of the word; context matters. But here Jesus is confronting desire deliberately turned toward sexual possession in the heart.
That means Jesus refuses the comfortable excuse:
“But I never actually touched anyone.”
Christ goes deeper.
Into the imagination.
Into intention.
Into what the eyes are being used to feed.
Into what you secretly rehearse.
Into the place nobody else can inspect.
Jesus takes sexual sin seriously precisely because He takes the human heart seriously.
He does not merely want your public behavior.
He wants you.
And that is why His pursuit of people trapped in lust should not be mistaken for approval of their lust.
Jesus does not pursue you because lust does not matter.
He pursues you because you matter too much to Him to leave you enslaved to it.
There is an enormous difference.
Modern culture often tells us that freedom means being able to satisfy desire.
Jesus offers something far more radical:
freedom from being ruled by desire.
The Gospel does not say, “Follow every appetite until you discover yourself.”
The Gospel says there is a King greater than your appetites.
There is a Savior greater than your urges.
There is a holiness greater than your fantasies.
And there is a joy deeper than the few minutes of counterfeit intimacy sin keeps selling you.
Think about how lust works.
It promises closeness while training you for isolation.
It promises satisfaction while increasing appetite.
It promises freedom while creating rituals you begin to feel powerless to resist.
It can reduce another human being—someone made in the image of God—to a body, an image, a fantasy, a source of stimulation.
Then, when it has taken what it wanted from you, shame walks through the door.
That pattern resembles what James describes:
“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος…”
James 1:14 teaches that each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his or her own desire.
Then James describes the progression.
Desire conceives.
Sin is born.
Sin matures.
Death follows.
Notice how brutally honest Scripture is.
The Bible does not romanticize temptation.
It shows you where the road goes.
But Scripture also refuses to tell the repentant sinner that the road back to God has been permanently closed.
And maybe that is the part you have forgotten.
Your sin has a story.
But so does the blood of Jesus.
Your temptation has a voice.
But so does your Shepherd.
Your past has evidence against you.
But the cross has something greater.
A verdict purchased by Christ.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about sins that included profound sexual brokenness. He did not pretend their former lives had been clean.
Then came three of the most beautiful words ever spoken over ruined people:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε”
kai tauta tines ēte
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because Corinth had somehow produced morally flawless Christians.
Not because temptation disappeared overnight.
Not because everybody suddenly acquired a spotless history.
Paul continues:
“ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε…”
“But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified…”
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is 1 Corinthians 6:11.
Read it again if shame has been preaching louder than Scripture.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
The Gospel is not God pretending your filth was clean.
The Gospel is Christ cleansing sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “try harder.”
If willpower alone could resurrect dead hearts, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
Jesus did not come merely to give sexually broken people better habits.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He came to forgive.
He came to cleanse.
He came to transform.
He came to make captives free.
And sometimes freedom begins with the most humiliating sentence a person can say:
“I need help.”
Maybe that sentence frightens you.
Because lust thrives in secrecy.
Pornography thrives there.
Affairs thrive there.
Emotional affairs thrive there.
Compulsive fantasy thrives there.
Secret messages thrive there.
The hidden folder thrives there.
The second account thrives there.
The relationship you keep calling “complicated” thrives there.
Sin loves rooms without windows.
Jesus keeps turning on the light.
Not because He enjoys humiliating you.
Because surgeons cannot remove what patients insist on hiding.
There is a moment in John 4 when Jesus meets a Samaritan woman beside a well.
The scene is already loaded with social tension. Jesus is a Jewish man speaking publicly with a Samaritan woman.
Then He touches the part of her history that could not remain hidden.
“Go, call your husband.”
She answers:
“I have no husband.”
Jesus tells her that she has had five husbands, and the man she currently has is not her husband.
Notice something remarkable.
Jesus knew this before He started the conversation.
He did not discover her history halfway through and suddenly reconsider whether she deserved His attention.
He approached the well already knowing.
He spoke to her already knowing.
He offered living water already knowing.
Truth did not cancel compassion.
Compassion did not cancel truth.
That is Jesus.
Some churches have failed people by giving them truth without tenderness.
Some corners of modern Christianity have failed people in the opposite direction by offering tenderness without repentance.
Jesus does neither.
He tells the truth that exposes us and offers the grace that can remake us.
The biblical word often translated “repent” is connected with the Greek μετάνοια — metanoia, repentance, a changed mind and turning that produces a changed direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling disgusting after sin.
You can hate how sin makes you feel and still love the sin itself.
You can cry after pornography and still protect access to it.
You can feel guilty about an affair and still keep the phone number.
You can ask God for deliverance while deliberately keeping the door unlocked for your next temptation.
Repentance gets practical.
Sometimes repentance looks like deleting something.
Sometimes it looks like ending contact.
Sometimes it looks like admitting the truth to your spouse.
Sometimes it means confessing to a mature, trustworthy Christian who can walk with you in accountability.
Sometimes it means putting serious boundaries around technology.
Sometimes it means refusing to take your phone into the room where you repeatedly fall.
Sometimes it means professional counseling when trauma, compulsive sexual behavior, relational wounds, or other deeper issues are involved.
Sometimes repentance means running.
Paul does not tell believers to negotiate with sexual immorality.
He writes:
pheugete tēn porneian
“Flee sexual immorality.”
1 Corinthians 6:18.
Flee.
There are battles Scripture tells you to stand and fight.
There are temptations Scripture tells you to run from.
You do not prove spiritual maturity by standing two inches from the fire and announcing how strong your faith is.
Sometimes holiness looks like running until the fire is behind you.
Joseph ran.
Paul says flee.
Jesus taught radical seriousness toward sin.
Yet here is what makes Christianity astonishing.
The command to flee sin is not a command to flee from Jesus.
Run from the pornography.
Run from the affair.
Run from the fantasy you deliberately cultivate.
Run from the messages.
Run from the secret account.
Run from the seductive situation.
Run from whatever repeatedly becomes your doorway back into slavery.
But while you are running from sin…
run toward Christ.
Some of you have been doing the opposite.
When you succeed spiritually, you pray.
When you fall, you disappear.
You skip Scripture.
You avoid worship.
You stop praying because you feel hypocritical.
You tell yourself you will return to Jesus after you have been “good” for a few days.
Do you realize what has happened?
You have accidentally turned your behavior into the price of admission to the presence of Christ.
But you do not clean yourself before coming to the One who cleanses you.
Hebrews tells us that Jesus is not a High Priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. He was tempted, yet without sin.
Then Scripture gives frightened sinners an astonishing invitation:
Approach the throne of grace with confidence so that you may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
Not the throne of humiliation.
Not the throne of “I told you so.”
The throne of grace.
That does not make sin less serious.
It makes grace more astonishing.
And someone reading this needs to understand the difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says:
“This is destroying you. Bring it into the light. Come back.”
Condemnation says:
“You are disgusting. Hide from God.”
One leads toward repentance.
The other drives you deeper into isolation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα…”
Ouden ara nyn katakrima…
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
for those who are in Christ Jesus.
No condemnation does not mean no correction.
No condemnation does not mean sin no longer matters.
It means those who belong to Christ do not live beneath the final judicial sentence their sins deserved, because Christ bore judgment for them.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the old pages never happened.
He rewrites everything by bringing redemption into a story sin appeared to have ruined.
This is the Gospel.
You sinned.
I sinned.
We have all fallen short of the glory of God.
Sin separates humanity from the holy God who created us.
And no amount of religious performance can erase our guilt.
So God did what we could never do.
Jesus Christ came.
The sinless Son of God entered our broken world.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
He remained pure where we became corrupted.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is not offered because sinners deserve another chance.
Forgiveness is offered because Jesus paid for it.
Grace is free to us.
It was unimaginably costly to Him.
So if you are trapped in lust, hear this carefully:
Jesus is not asking you to make peace with your chains.
He is calling you out of them.
He is not saying, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
He is saying, in effect, “Follow Me. Your sin will not be your master.”
You may stumble in the battle.
Sanctification can involve warfare.
Patterns built over years may require serious discipleship, accountability, confession, boundaries, renewed thinking, and repeated dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
But never confuse a battle with permission to surrender.
A Christian may experience temptation.
A Christian may struggle.
A Christian may fall and need repentance.
But the direction of discipleship is not making sin comfortable.
It is following Christ.
Maybe you fell last night.
Maybe five minutes ago.
Maybe this article found you immediately after you closed something you should never have opened.
Then do not waste the conviction.
Put the phone down.
Speak honestly to God.
No performance.
No religious speech.
Tell Him what happened.
Call sin what God calls it.
Ask forgiveness.
Turn.
Remove access where you can.
Seek trustworthy accountability.
And get back up.
Not because you are strong.
Because Christ is merciful.
There is something shame desperately does not want you to discover:
The moment you stop hiding is often the moment your chains begin losing their power.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your struggle. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
“Jesus, help me walk in purity.”

If Christ has already brought you through sexual bondage, pornography, an affair, destructive relationships, or years of secret shame, and it is appropriate for you to share, leave a testimony that points people to Jesus.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need proof that repentance is possible and that grace does not merely forgive—it transforms.
And please hear this before shame twists even that invitation:
You do not owe strangers the intimate details of your past.
Wisdom matters.
Privacy matters.
Other people's dignity matters.
But you do not have to keep pretending you have never needed grace.
Neither have I.
Neither has any Christian.
We meet at the foot of the same cross.
Maybe you know somebody who needs this article.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Somebody you love.
Send it privately to someone who needs hope.
Come back and remember:
Christ is greater than the appetite.
Christ is greater than the memory.
Christ is greater than the algorithm.
Christ is greater than the image.
Christ is greater than the secret.
Christ is greater than the relapse.
Christ is greater than the shame.
Christ is greater.
If you want to help this work reach more people, sharing this article publicly is one meaningful way to do it.
Jesus Christ alone is Savior, and our allegiance belongs to Him.

But if this ministry genuinely strengthens your walk with Christ, financially supporting and sharing Gospel-centered work can be a practical way of helping that work continue reaching people who are hiding behind screens, smiles, church attendance, addictions, broken marriages, private battles, and unbearable shame.
This is bigger than merchandise.
Bigger than an algorithm.
Bigger than a page.
Bigger than numbers.
The goal is people encountering biblical truth and being pointed toward Jesus Christ.
So share the article.
Tag wisely.
Invite someone who has been drifting.
But before you leave, there is one last person we need to talk about.
The person you were when you began reading.
The one who wondered:
“Why does Jesus still pursue people trapped in lust?”
Now you know.
Not because lust is harmless.
Not because holiness is optional.
Not because Jesus has lowered His standard.
Not because grace gives us permission to remain chained.
Jesus pursues sinners because saving sinners is exactly why He came.
He exposes because He loves.
He corrects because He loves.
He calls us to repentance because He loves.
He forgives because His blood is sufficient.
He transforms because resurrection power does not merely improve graves.
It empties them.
So when temptation comes again—and it may—remember who is calling you.
When shame tells you to hide…
remember Adam hid.
Christ came looking for sinners.
When lust tells you, “Just one more time”…
remember what it told you last time.
When condemnation whispers, “Jesus must be finished with you”…
look toward the cross.
The cross is what sin cost.
The empty tomb is what Christ conquered.
You are not being invited to become comfortable with darkness.
You are being summoned into light.
Repent.
Believe.
Confess.
Flee sexual immorality.
Seek accountability.
Cut off what keeps feeding the fire.
Fill your mind with what is true.
Walk by the Spirit.
Keep returning to Scripture.
Keep looking to Christ.
And when you fall, do not build a house on the ground.
Get up.
Come back.
Because the final word over the repentant sinner does not belong to pornography.
It does not belong to adultery.
It does not belong to your browser history.
It does not belong to the person who used you.
It does not belong to the person you used.
It does not belong to the worst night of your life.
It does not belong to shame.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you tonight is this:
Jesus did not walk into your darkness to decorate your chains—He came to lead you out of the prison.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Genesis 38 Is a Story About Sex—but It’s Also About Injustice, Hypocrisy, and Transformation
paragraphs:
Genesis 38 Is a Story About Sex—but It’s Also About Injustice, Hypocrisy, and Transformation
The chapter people are embarrassed to read may be one of the chapters God refuses to let us skip—because buried beneath the scandal of Judah and Tamar is a devastating confrontation with injustice, sexual hypocrisy, hidden sin, repentance, and the kind of grace that eventually leads us all the way to Jesus Christ.
There are chapters in the Bible we underline.
There are chapters we frame.
There are chapters we quote when someone is hurting.
And then there is Genesis 38.
The chapter people sometimes wish they could quietly turn past.
Sex.
Death.
Deception.
A widow dressed as a prostitute.
A respected man sleeping with the woman he thinks is one.
A pregnancy outside marriage.
A public accusation.
A threat of death.
Then, in one breathtaking moment, the accuser realizes that the evidence condemning the woman in front of him is actually pointing directly back at himself.
It sounds less like the genealogy of the Messiah and more like the kind of family scandal everyone hopes never becomes public.
But God did not remove it from Scripture.
And perhaps that is because Genesis 38 is not merely exposing what Tamar did.
It is exposing what Judah became.
And somewhere inside Judah's story, it may expose us too.
Because the most frightening person in Genesis 38 may not be the woman hiding her identity beside the road.
It may be the man who could recognize another person's apparent sexual sin immediately while remaining astonishingly slow to recognize his own injustice.
That is where this story stops being ancient.
That is where it gets painfully close.
Genesis 38 begins with Judah separating himself from his brothers and establishing a family in Canaan. His firstborn son, Er, marries a woman named Tamar.
Then Scripture gives us a chillingly brief statement:
“But Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; and the LORD slew him.”
The text does not tell us what Er's wickedness was.
That matters.
We should not invent sins Scripture does not reveal.
What Scripture does reveal is what happens afterward.

According to the family obligation reflected in the ancient practice later formally addressed in Israel's law, Judah tells his second son, Onan, to fulfill his responsibility toward his deceased brother's widow so that offspring might be raised for his brother.
Onan understands something important.
If Tamar bears a child through him under this arrangement, the child will preserve his dead brother's line.
And Onan does not want that.
Genesis says:
“And Onan knew that the seed should not be his…”
So when he has relations with Tamar, he deliberately prevents conception.
The Hebrew text makes the motive unmistakably important.
וְיָדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע
Vayyeda Onan ki lo-lo yihyeh hazzara.
“And Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
His sin cannot responsibly be reduced to one isolated sexual act detached from the story.
Look at the woman standing on the other side of his decision.
Tamar.
Widowed.
Dependent upon a family structure in which descendants, inheritance, household protection, and social survival carried enormous significance.
Onan takes the sexual privilege while deliberately refusing the familial responsibility attached to it.
He uses Tamar's body while frustrating the obligation intended to secure her future and preserve his brother's line.
This is sexual sin tangled together with selfishness, exploitation, and injustice.
And God sees it.
Onan dies.
Now Judah has another son, Shelah.
Judah tells Tamar to remain a widow in her father's house until Shelah grows up.
She waits.
Shelah grows.
But Judah does not give him to Tamar.
And suddenly the scandal becomes more complicated.
Because Tamar has been told to wait for something Judah is apparently unwilling to provide.
She is trapped by another person's promise.
Some people reading this know what that feels like.
You did what you were told.
You waited.
You trusted someone's word.
You believed the person with greater power would eventually do what was right.
And then you discovered that your obedience did not guarantee their integrity.
Tamar watches the years move.
Shelah is grown.
Nothing happens.
Then Tamar learns that Judah is traveling to Timnah.
She removes her widow's garments, covers herself with a veil, and sits where Judah will pass.
Judah sees her.
He assumes she is a prostitute.
And the man who has failed to secure justice for the widow within his household now approaches a woman he believes he can purchase for sex.
Do not rush through that irony.
Judah does not recognize Tamar.
But the reader is beginning to recognize Judah.
He negotiates the encounter.
He promises a young goat.
Tamar asks for a pledge until payment arrives.
“What pledge shall I give thee?”
She asks for his signet, cord, and staff.
Personal identifiers.
The ancient equivalent, in a sense, of leaving evidence with your name written all over it.
Judah agrees.
