Later he attempts to send payment and recover the pledge, but the woman cannot be found.
He eventually lets the matter disappear.
Or so he thinks.
Three months later, word reaches Judah.
Tamar is pregnant.
And Judah's reaction is ferocious.
“Bring her forth, and let her be burnt.”
Read that again.
The man who willingly participated in illicit sex is ready to pronounce catastrophic judgment upon the woman whose pregnancy exposes sexual wrongdoing.
He does not yet know that he is the father.
But that is precisely what makes the scene so terrifying.
Judah knows enough about sexual sin to condemn it when he thinks it belongs to someone else.
He simply has not learned to recognize himself inside the indictment.
And that is one of the oldest forms of hypocrisy on earth.
We can become furious about sins in other people that we have learned to rename in ourselves.
Their lust is disgusting.
Ours is weakness.
Their deception is wicked.
Ours was necessary.
Their cruelty is unforgivable.
Ours happened because we were hurt.
Their compromise proves their character.
Ours deserves context.
Their failure should be exposed.
Ours should remain private.
Genesis 38 reaches across thousands of years, grabs us by the conscience, and asks a brutal question:
What happens when the evidence finally has your name on it?
Tamar does not publicly scream Judah's name.
She sends the objects to him.
“By the man, whose these are, am I with child…”
Then comes the question.
“Discern, I pray thee, whose are these, the signet, and bracelets, and staff.”
The Hebrew verb used here is devastatingly significant:
הַכֶּר־נָא
Hakker-na.
“Please recognize.”
“Please identify.”
Those words echo an earlier moment in Judah's life.
Years before, Judah and his brothers sold Joseph and deceived their father Jacob. They dipped Joseph's garment in blood and brought it to their father.
Then they said:
הַכֶּר־נָא
Hakker-na.
“Please recognize whether it be thy son's coat or no.”
Judah once participated in presenting evidence to his father and asking him to recognize it.
Now Tamar presents evidence to Judah.
Hakker-na.
Recognize this.
Look carefully.
Whose signet?
Whose cord?
Whose staff?
Whose sin?
It is as though the words Judah helped use to break his father's heart have traveled through the years and returned carrying a mirror.
That is one reason Genesis 38 belongs exactly where it is.
This is not random scandal interrupting Joseph's story.
It is part of Judah's story.
And Judah needs to see Judah.
So do we.
There are moments when God's mercy does not feel like comfort at first.
It feels like recognition.
A conversation exposes you.
A verse will not leave you alone.
Your spouse says something you cannot dismiss.
Your child imitates the anger you thought you controlled.
Someone confronts you.
The consequences arrive.
The secret becomes harder to protect.
The Holy Spirit presses upon something you have spent years explaining away.
And suddenly the question is sitting in front of you.
Hakker-na.
Recognize this.
Not your neighbor's sin.
Not your pastor's failure.
Not your spouse's weakness.
Not what your parents did.
Not what the culture celebrates.
Not what someone else posted online.
Yours.
This is where Judah does something remarkable.
He could have used his authority to silence Tamar.
He could have lied.
He could have destroyed the evidence.
He could have doubled down.
He could have protected his reputation at the expense of the woman he had already wronged.
Instead, Judah says:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tsadqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
And Judah explains why:
“because that I gave her not to Shelah my son.”
This does not mean everything Tamar did becomes a universal model for Christian conduct.
Genesis often describes complicated human actions without commanding believers to imitate every detail.
Nor does Judah's confession mean Tamar was sinlessly righteous in every possible sense.
His statement is comparative and contextual.
Judah finally recognizes that his own failure toward Tamar lies at the heart of the crisis.
The finger he had pointed outward turns inward.
And something changes.
Genesis tells us Judah “knew her again no more.”
The man who began the chapter acting selfishly does not leave it exactly the same man.
And when Judah later reappears prominently in Joseph's story, something extraordinary happens.
Years earlier, Judah had helped send one brother into slavery while allowing his father to collapse into grief.
But in Genesis 44, when Benjamin faces enslavement, Judah offers himself instead.
“Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord…”
Do you see the transformation?
The Judah who once sacrificed a brother to preserve himself becomes the Judah willing to sacrifice himself for a brother.
Something has happened to this man.
Genesis does not give us a neat modern testimony explaining every stage of his inner transformation.
We should not pretend it does.

But the narrative gives us a Judah who has been confronted with his wrongdoing, publicly acknowledged that another was more righteous than he was, and later demonstrates a profoundly different posture of self-sacrifice.
That is transformation worth noticing.
And then the story becomes even more astonishing.
Tamar gives birth to twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez becomes an ancestor of David.
And Matthew begins his Gospel by tracing the genealogy that leads to Jesus Christ.
There, among Abraham and Isaac…
among Jacob and Judah…
among kings and generations…
Matthew deliberately writes:
Tamar is there.
Her story is there.
The scandal is there.
The failure is there.
And eventually…
Jesus is there.
Not because Jesus approves of sin.
Not because injustice does not matter.
Not because sexual brokenness becomes holy simply because God can redeem broken people.
But because human sin is not powerful enough to sabotage the redemptive purpose of God.
Jesus did not descend from a carefully edited family history.
The genealogy of Christ contains people whose stories include sexual failure, violence, deception, outsiders, broken families, compromised decisions, and devastating consequences.
Yet the holiness of Christ is not contaminated by the brokenness of the people through whom His human genealogy runs.
Instead, His arrival reveals something breathtaking about grace.
God enters the human story we actually have.
Not the sanitized one we pretend to have.
And maybe that is why Genesis 38 makes some of us uncomfortable.
We would rather tell God the version that makes us look better.
We edit the testimony.
We soften the motive.
We remove certain names.
We say, “I made mistakes,” when what we mean is, “I sinned.”
We say, “Things happened,” when we know there were choices.
We speak fluently about grace while desperately protecting ourselves from confession.
But the Gospel does not require you to convince Jesus that you were never scandalous.
The Gospel requires you to recognize that you need a Savior.
Scripture says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Judah.
Tamar.
You.
Me.
The person preaching.
The person hiding.
The person exposed.
The person doing the exposing.
And that is why Christianity cannot end with “Be better.”
If moral improvement alone could rescue humanity, we would not need a crucified and risen Christ.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need a righteousness we cannot manufacture.
We need Jesus.
At the cross, Christ does something Judah could never do for himself.
He bears judgment for sinners.
The sinless One stands in the place of the guilty.
“He hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
This is not cheap grace.
The cross is the ultimate declaration that sin is so serious it required the death of the Son of God—and that God's love is so astonishing that the Son willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
Repentance therefore is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Repentance is bringing the truth into the light and turning toward God.
Grace does not say your sin was insignificant.
Grace says Jesus is greater.
Forgiveness does not rewrite evil into goodness.
Jesus rewrites what happens next.
That distinction matters.
You may not be able to change what you did.
You may not be able to recover every year you wasted.
You may not be able to erase the message you sent, undo the betrayal, reclaim your innocence, repair every consequence, or force every person you wounded to trust you again.
Biblical grace does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
But through Jesus Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are fine.
Maybe you still know exactly when to raise your hands during worship.
Maybe your Bible has highlights everywhere.
Maybe you can explain theology.
Maybe your family believes you are strong.
But there is something you hope nobody ever asks about.
Something buried.
Pornography.
An affair.
Bitterness.
Dishonesty.
Sexual compromise.
A secret relationship.
Abuse of authority.
Years of hypocrisy.
A person you used.
Someone you abandoned.
Someone you still refuse to forgive.
Something you did when nobody was watching.
Something done to you that left wounds you have carried for years—and perhaps choices you later made from those wounds that you now regret.
Hear this carefully.
Jesus Christ does not need the edited version of you.
He already knows the truth.
The question is whether you are finally willing to recognize it.
Hakker-na.
Look again.
Whose is this?
Maybe the evidence is pointing toward you.
If so, do not run from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction exposes sin so that we will turn toward God.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not sanitized sinners.
Real ones.
People with names.
Histories.
Bodies.
Consequences.
Memories.
Failures.
Scandals.
That is who grace is for.
And if you have spent years pointing at everybody else's failures because looking at your own feels unbearable, perhaps Genesis 38 is your hakker-na moment.
Recognize it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Bring it to Jesus.
And discover that being exposed before God does not have to be the end of your story.
For the repentant sinner, exposure can become the doorway to restoration.
Maybe you need to pray something far less impressive and far more truthful tonight:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing one honest sentence into the light becomes a small public refusal to keep pretending.
Someone reading beside you may need to discover that Christians are not people who never struggle.
We are people who keep returning to Christ.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become testimony.
Confession.
Encouragement.
People reminding people that Jesus still receives sinners.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.
But if this message has helped you see Scripture more clearly, sharing it can place biblical truth in front of someone who may never have searched for it themselves.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who has been drifting.
Invite the seeker with difficult questions.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only for people who have managed to keep their lives clean.
Show them Genesis 38.
Then show them Jesus.
It is not a shortcut to spiritual maturity.
It is a practical way of supporting the work so more Scripture-centered content and discipleship resources can continue reaching people who need them.
Carry the Gospel.
Share truth.
Speak about Christ.
Pray.
Encourage someone.
Open Scripture with somebody.
Tell another sinner where you found mercy.
Because somewhere tonight there is a Judah who has not recognized himself yet.
Somewhere there is a Tamar who has been failed by people who possessed more power than she did.
Somewhere there is someone convinced that the most scandalous chapter of their life disqualifies them from ever coming home.
And somewhere there is a person who needs to hear what Genesis 38 has been whispering for thousands of years:
God is not frightened by the chapter you wish had never been written.
He tells the truth about sin.
He cares about injustice.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He calls sinners to repentance.
And through the blood of Jesus Christ, He offers something scandalous sinners could never manufacture for themselves.
Grace.
So when the evidence comes back…
when the mirror becomes impossible to avoid…
when the words hakker-na seem to land on your own heart…
recognize what is yours.
Then look beyond yourself.
Look to the cross.
Because your hope was never that there would be nothing in your past worth exposing.
Your hope is that there is a Savior whose mercy is greater than everything you finally stopped hiding.
The evidence may tell the truth about who you were—but the wounds in the hands of Jesus tell you who has the authority to write what comes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES GOD’S WORD CELEBRATE A HUSBAND DELIGHTING IN HIS WIFE’S BODY?
paragraphs: WHY DOES GOD’S WORD CELEBRATE A HUSBAND DELIGHTING IN HIS WIFE’S BODY?
The Verse Some Christians Almost Whisper—And the Beautiful, Holy Truth About Marriage, Desire, Faithfulness, and Grace That We Were Never Supposed to Be Ashamed Of
There is a verse in the Bible that can make even lifelong Christians suddenly lower their voices.
Not because it is sinful.
Because it is startlingly honest.
It does not come from pornography.
It does not come from a modern romance novel.
It does not come from a culture trying to erase sexual boundaries.
It comes from Scripture.
And once you understand why God allowed these words into His Word, you may never look at biblical marriage—or your own body—the same way again.
Proverbs 5 speaks to a husband about his wife:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Scripture becomes remarkably physical:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read the Hebrew and the language becomes even more striking:
דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Daddeha yeravvukha bekhol-et; be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The thought is essentially this:
May her breasts satisfy you at all times; may you continually be captivated—lost, exhilarated, even intoxicated—with her love.
That is in the Bible.
Not despite God's holiness.
Because God is holy.
And perhaps this is where some of us need healing.
Some Christians were taught how to condemn sexual immorality but were never taught how Scripture celebrates marital intimacy.
We learned what sex must not become.
We did not always learn what God designed it to be.
So shame quietly entered places where shame was never invited by God.
A husband can begin feeling guilty for desiring his wife.
A wife can begin believing that spirituality requires becoming disconnected from her own body.

Married couples can love Jesus deeply and still struggle to talk honestly about intimacy because somewhere along the way they absorbed the idea that holiness means pretending physical desire does not exist.
But God does not pretend.
God created human beings embodied.
Before pornography corrupted desire…
before adultery betrayed covenant…
before lust turned people into objects…
before humanity learned to exploit what God created…
there was a man.
There was a woman.
There was covenant.
There was nakedness.
And there was no shame.
Genesis 2:24–25 tells us that the man and woman become “one flesh,” and that they were naked and unashamed.
The Hebrew expression for one flesh is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not two souls pretending bodies do not matter.
Not two roommates sharing religious responsibilities.
One flesh.
God created marriage with spiritual, emotional, covenantal and bodily dimensions.
Then sin entered the world.
And suddenly the human body became complicated.
What God created for covenant became vulnerable to exploitation.
Desire could become lust.
Attraction could become adultery.
Sex could become manipulation.
Bodies could become commodities.
Pleasure could become an idol.
People could become objects.
And that distinction is crucial, because Proverbs 5 is not giving men permission to objectify women.
It is doing almost the opposite.
Look at the context.
The father is warning his son about sexual unfaithfulness.
Do not pour what belongs to covenant into the streets.
Do not surrender yourself to forbidden embraces.
Do not destroy your home chasing what does not belong to you.
Instead:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Do you see it?
God's answer to adulterous desire is not hatred of desire itself.
It is redeemed desire.
Directed desire.
Faithful desire.
Covenantal desire.
The passage does not say, “Stop being capable of attraction.”
It teaches the man where that delight belongs.
With his wife.
The woman to whom he has pledged himself.
The woman whose heart should be safe with him.
The woman whose body must never become merely an instrument for his gratification.
The woman he is called to cherish as a person created in God's image.
And Scripture dares to tell that husband:
Delight in her.
Notice her.
Desire her.
Remain captivated by her.
Do not spend your eyes, imagination, affection and sexuality everywhere else and bring your wife whatever happens to remain.
There is something painfully relevant about that command now.
A man can carry access to millions of sexualized images in his pocket.
A married person can secretly give strangers attention that covenant should have guarded.
Then Proverbs enters that world and says:
Come home.
Not merely to a house.
Come home with your eyes.
Come home with your imagination.
Come home with your affection.
Come home with your body.
Come home with your loyalty.
Rejoice in your wife.
That changes the verse completely.
“Let her breasts satisfy thee” is not biblical permission for male entitlement.
It is a rebuke to wandering desire.
The command is not, “Every woman exists for your pleasure.”
It is effectively saying:
Why are you wandering toward another woman when God has called you to faithful delight within your marriage?
The following verse makes the contrast unmistakable.
“Why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman?”
The same chapter that celebrates attraction establishes its boundary.
Covenant.
This is why biblical sexuality cannot faithfully be reduced either to “sex is dirty” or “anything consensual is therefore holy.”
Scripture gives us something richer.
Desire under discipleship.
Pleasure under covenant.
Bodies treated with dignity.
Faithfulness under the eyes of God.
And love that refuses to turn another person into merchandise.
The New Testament does not erase that bodily dimension.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7 that husband and wife owe marital care to one another, then makes an astonishingly countercultural statement of reciprocity.
The husband's body is not simply his to wield selfishly.
And neither is the wife's.
Paul's language is deliberately mutual.
The Greek of verse 3 begins:
Τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω
The husband is to render to his wife what is due within the marriage—and Paul immediately says the wife likewise toward her husband.
Then he tells couples not to deprive one another except by mutual agreement for a time.
Mutual.
That matters.
Biblical intimacy is not a weapon.
It is not coercion.
It is not domination dressed in Bible verses.
It is not a husband announcing, “Your body belongs to me,” while conveniently ignoring Paul's next words that his body also belongs to his wife.
The passage destroys selfish ownership by making the obligation reciprocal.
Christian marriage should therefore never use Scripture to excuse sexual cruelty.
Love does not rejoice in another person's fear.
Love does not manipulate.
Love does not humiliate.
Love does not demand that a wounded spouse pretend nothing hurts.
Jesus does not sanctify selfishness simply because selfishness happens inside a marriage certificate.
This is covenant intimacy.
Giving.
Receiving.
Trusting.
Listening.
Cherishing.
Serving.
Knowing and being known.
And this is where the subject becomes more painful than merely discussing one provocative verse.
Because some people reading this no longer feel desirable.
Maybe childbirth changed your body.
Maybe age changed it.
Maybe surgery changed it.
Maybe sickness changed it.
Maybe depression changed the way you see yourself.
Maybe years happened.
Maybe the mirror became cruel.
Maybe somebody compared you to another person.
Maybe pornography entered your marriage and made you feel as though you were competing against an endless digital parade of impossible bodies.
Maybe rejection from the person you love created a wound nobody sees when you walk into church.
You smile.
You worship.
You say, “God is good.”
But somewhere beneath your Sunday clothes is a question you are almost embarrassed to admit:
Am I still worth desiring?
Hear something deeper than cultural beauty standards.
Your worth was never created by somebody else's appetite.
Your dignity comes from your Creator.
You bear God's image.
Your body is not an accident God tolerates while waiting for your “spiritual” part to become important.
Christianity does not teach that bodies are worthless.
The Christian hope itself includes resurrection.
And Jesus Christ did not save His people by remaining distant from human flesh.
“The Word was made flesh.”
God the Son entered our humanity.
He walked.
He hungered.
He became tired.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
The Gospel is not God's abandonment of embodied humanity.
It is God's redemption of fallen humanity.
And that changes how Christians understand sexuality.
Our culture frequently tells us to worship desire.
Religious shame sometimes tells us to fear desire.
Scripture teaches us to surrender desire to God.
There is an enormous difference.
Jesus does not merely ask, “What do you want?”
He asks who rules your wanting.
Because desire makes a terrible god.
But surrendered desire can become part of a holy life.
That means the husband reading Proverbs 5 cannot point at verse 19 while ignoring verse 21:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.”
God sees.
The browser history.
The private messages.
The flirtation called harmless.
The comparison nobody hears.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The emotional affair rationalized as friendship.
The fantasies repeatedly fed.
The resentment carried into bed.
The selfishness.
The coldness.
The secrets.
God sees.
But here is where Christianity becomes something infinitely greater than moral surveillance.
The God who sees sinners is also the God who came looking for sinners.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity had successfully controlled every appetite.
He went because we had not.
The Gospel begins where pretending ends.
Maybe your marriage has been wounded by sexual sin.
Maybe you were the one who betrayed trust.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe pornography became a hidden room inside your life.
Maybe you have spent years consuming bodies on a screen and calling it harmless because nobody physically touched anyone.
Maybe you have been using your spouse instead of cherishing your spouse.
Maybe intimacy became transactional.
Maybe bitterness built a wall between two people who once could not imagine sleeping inches apart and feeling miles away.
Maybe there are wounds here that cannot be repaired by one emotional article.
Some wounds require confession.
Some require patient rebuilding.
Some require pastoral wisdom.
Some require professional counseling.
Some situations involving abuse require safety, accountability and serious intervention—not pressure to remain silent in the name of preserving appearances.
But whatever the story is, do not confuse conviction with a declaration that redemption is impossible.
Peter failed.
David's sexual sin brought devastating consequences.
The woman at the well carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
Again and again Scripture refuses two opposite lies.
Sin does not matter.
And sinners cannot be redeemed.
Both are false.
Jesus tells the truth about sin while opening the door to grace.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace walks into darkness and brings people out.
This is why the Christian message concerning sexuality is ultimately not:
“Try harder to stop wanting things.”
It is:
Bring your whole self under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your marriage.
Your loneliness.
Your attractions.
Your wounds.
Your failures.
Your body.
Your sexuality.
Your shame.
Your history.
Your secret tabs.
Your secret messages.
Your secret grief.
Everything.
Because Jesus is not interested in becoming Lord of the carefully edited version of you.
He came for you.
The real you.
And repentance means we stop defending what is killing us and turn toward the One who gives life.
Maybe the most beautiful thing about Proverbs 5 is not that God allows a husband to delight in his wife's body.
Maybe it is that God refuses to surrender human desire to the devil.
Think about that.
Satan did not invent marriage.
Pornography did not invent the human body.
Hollywood did not invent attraction.
Sin did not invent sexuality.
God created humanity male and female.
God created covenant.
God created the possibility of one-flesh union.
Sin corrupts.
God creates.
And redemption does not require us to call God's creation evil.
It teaches us to receive God's gifts according to God's wisdom.
Hebrews 13:4 captures the balance with extraordinary simplicity. The Greek says:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος
Marriage is honorable, precious, worthy of respect—and the marriage bed is to be undefiled.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say the marriage bed is inherently filthy.
It says it must remain undefiled.
There is a difference.
Something can be corrupted precisely because something good existed to corrupt.
So perhaps a husband needs to hear this:
It is not ungodly to find your wife beautiful.
Tell her.
Not only when you want intimacy.
Tell her when she is exhausted.
Tell her when age has changed what youth once looked like.
Tell her when she does not believe you.
Look at the woman who has walked through life beside you and remember that covenant love is supposed to become deeper than novelty.
And perhaps a wife needs to hear this:
Your body is not spiritually embarrassing.
You do not have to resemble an advertisement to possess dignity.
You do not have to compete with edited images.
Your value is not measured by measurements.
Your deepest identity is not “desirable woman,” “undesirable woman,” “young woman,” “aging woman,” “married woman” or “single woman.”
If you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
And perhaps unmarried Christians need to hear something equally important.
Proverbs 5 is not permission to imitate marital intimacy without marital covenant.
The beauty of the passage depends upon its boundaries.
A fireplace is beautiful partly because the fire has somewhere to belong.
Remove every boundary and the same flame that warmed the home can burn the home down.
God's commands are not evidence that He hates human joy.
Often they are evidence that He knows what human beings do to themselves when desire becomes master.
And maybe that is the question beneath the question.
Why would God's Word celebrate a husband delighting in his wife's body?
Because biblical holiness is not disembodied.
Because marital faithfulness is not merely refusing adultery; it includes cultivating covenant delight.
Because God does not want husbands scattering their desire everywhere.
Because wives are not objects, but neither must married love pretend bodies do not matter.
Because faithful marital intimacy can express tenderness, belonging, vulnerability and mutual delight.
Because the God who created covenant also created the bodies entering that covenant.
And because sin does not get the final word over what God created good.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat of everything we proclaim at Gospel Warrior.
From scandal…
to grace.
From hiding…
to confession.
From bondage…
to freedom.
From betrayal…
to restoration.
From shame…
to the cross.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
But by taking guilty, wounded, complicated human beings and doing what only grace can do.
Forgiving.
Cleansing.
Restoring.
Transforming.
Making dead hearts live again.
Did this touch something you normally do not talk about?
Did it expose shame?
Did it confront wandering eyes?
Did it make you think about your spouse differently?
Did it remind you that God is not finished restoring what sin damaged?
Then do not turn conviction into another moment you forget tomorrow.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him.
If you have sinned against your spouse, begin walking toward truth and repentance.
If your marriage is wounded, stop pretending that silence is healing it.
If your heart has wandered, come home.
If you have been carrying sexual shame from a past Christ has forgiven, stop treating the chains Jesus broke as though you are required to keep wearing them.
Sometimes one honest sentence is where hiding begins to lose its power.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.
There may be a husband who needs to come home with his eyes.
A wife who needs to know her dignity was never determined by comparison.
A marriage quietly drowning behind smiling photographs.
A believer trapped in pornography who has convinced himself there is no road back.
A Christian carrying years of sexual shame who desperately needs to understand the difference between God's conviction and hopeless condemnation.
It does not.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never could.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But Scripture does teach God's people to give willingly, generously and cheerfully to support Gospel work. If you have been asking how you can help Gospel Warrior continue creating Christ-centered articles, discipleship materials, books and resources—and help us reach more wounded, searching and spiritually hungry people—monthly support is one practical way to participate.
If this ministry genuinely helps you glorify God, you can glorify Him through generosity by freely choosing to support work that proclaims His Word.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Because somebody you know may be hiding behind a smile tonight.
Somebody's marriage may be bleeding quietly.
Somebody may believe sexual failure has disqualified them forever.
Somebody may desperately need to discover that biblical holiness is more beautiful than religious shame and more demanding than cultural permissiveness.
And perhaps God will use something as simple as your share to place truth in front of them at exactly the moment they were preparing to surrender to darkness.
Stay close to the Word.
Stay close to truth.
And above everything else, stay close to Jesus.
Because the final answer to corrupted desire is not shame.
It is not indulgence either.
It is redemption.
It is desire surrendered to Christ.
It is grace strong enough to forgive what you thought could never be forgiven.
It is truth strong enough to confront what you hoped would remain hidden.
It is a Savior strong enough to take the chapters you are ashamed to reread and refuse to let them become the final chapter of your life.
The world may remember your scandal.
The enemy may whisper your scandal.
You may still wake up remembering your scandal.
But scars surrendered to Jesus do not have to remain monuments to your shame; they can become reminders that grace reached you there too.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE CAPTIVE WOMAN LAW: WHY DID MOSES REGULATE MARRIAGE AFTER WAR?
paragraphs:
THE CAPTIVE WOMAN LAW: WHY DID MOSES REGULATE MARRIAGE AFTER WAR?
She had just lost everything. Then an Israelite soldier desired her. What God commanded next reveals something disturbing about the human heart—and something breathtaking about the God who refuses to leave human power without boundaries.
There are passages in the Bible people love to underline.
This usually isn’t one of them.
Deuteronomy 21:10–14 takes us somewhere uncomfortable.
Not beside still waters.
Not into a worship service.
Not to Bethlehem beneath a quiet star.
It takes us onto the aftermath of a battlefield.
Imagine the smoke.
The silence after screaming.
Homes emptied.
Families shattered.
Men dead or missing.
Women staring into a future they never chose.
And somewhere among the captives stands a woman whose name Scripture never gives us.
A soldier sees her.
He finds her beautiful.
He desires her.
And suddenly the Bible says something that can make a modern reader recoil:
"וְרָאִיתָ בַּשִּׁבְיָה אֵשֶׁת יְפַת־תֹּאַר וְחָשַׁקְתָּ בָהּ"
Ve-ra’ita bashivyah eshet yefat-to’ar, ve-chashaqta bah.
“And you see among the captives a woman beautiful in appearance, and you desire her…”
Then comes the possibility of taking her as a wife.
Stop there.
Because if we rush through those words trying to rescue the Bible from our discomfort, we may actually miss what the law is doing.
This woman is not standing there choosing between suitors.
She is a captive.
The power imbalance could hardly be greater.
Her nation has lost.
Her former life has been torn apart.
The man looking at her belongs to the victorious army.
Whatever else we say about this passage, we must not turn her captivity into a romantic love story.
It isn't.
And the Bible does not ask us to pretend that war is beautiful simply because Israel appears in the story.
The question is harder:
Why would God's law address this situation at all?
Why did Moses regulate what happened when an Israelite warrior desired a captive woman?
Because human beings do terrifying things when power is unchecked.
And one of the recurring movements of biblical law is the placing of boundaries around human power.

In the ancient world, defeated women could become part of the spoils of war. The Hebrew Bible itself knows this brutal reality. Deuteronomy therefore speaks into a world where conquest could leave a woman profoundly vulnerable.
And watch what happens.
The soldier's desire does not give him immediate sexual access to her.
Desire is interrupted.
Power is restrained.
Time is imposed.
The woman is brought into the house, and the text says:
"וְגִלְּחָה אֶת־רֹאשָׁהּ וְעָשְׂתָה אֶת־צִפָּרְנֶיהָ"
She is to shave her head and attend to her nails.
She removes the clothing of her captivity.
And then comes one of the most easily overlooked details in the entire law:
"וּבָכְתָה אֶת־אָבִיהָ וְאֶת־אִמָּהּ יֶרַח יָמִים"
U-vakh'tah et-avihah ve-et-immah yerach yamim.
She is to mourn her father and her mother for a full month.
A month.
Before the soldier can consummate the marriage, there is waiting.
Before his desire can proceed, her grief is given space.
Before she becomes someone's wife, the law recognizes that she is someone who has lost a world.
Think about that.
She is captive, but she is allowed to mourn.
She is vulnerable, but the soldier cannot simply treat the moment of victory as permission for immediate gratification.
Her tears interrupt his appetite.
Her grief interrupts his power.
Her humanity interrupts his desire.

Scholars disagree over some details of the passage and over precisely how its Hebrew conditional clauses should be parsed. One significant reading understands the command to take her as a wife as restricting the soldier from simply using a captive woman sexually; other interpreters understand the law more specifically as regulating the treatment of the captive whom the soldier has already determined to marry.
That distinction matters.
We should not claim more than the Hebrew itself allows us to prove.
But something unmistakable happens in the text: the man's power is restricted. He cannot simply see, desire, consume, discard, sell, and profit from the woman however he wishes.
Marriage brings obligations.
And if afterward he no longer wants her?
Listen carefully.
Ve-shillachtah le-nafshah.
He must let her go.
The expression carries the sense of sending her away for herself—to freedom.
Then God closes another door:
"וּמָכֹר לֹא־תִמְכְּרֶנָּה בַּכָּסֶף"
He absolutely must not sell her for money.
And another:
"לֹא־תִתְעַמֵּר בָּהּ"
He must not exploit her, deal tyrannically with her, or treat her as merchandise.
Why?
The final Hebrew words are painful:
"תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר עִנִּיתָהּ"
Because he has ‘innitah her.

The verb comes from ענה, ‘anah, a word associated with affliction, humiliation, or mistreatment. Translators render the phrase in different ways—“humiliated her,” “dishonored her,” or similar language.
Notice what Scripture does not do.
It does not allow the powerful man to tell himself that because everything happened within a legally regulated arrangement, therefore nothing painful happened to her.
The text remembers her humiliation.
That should trouble us.
It is supposed to.
Biblical faithfulness does not require pretending every social condition regulated in the Old Testament represents God's final picture of human flourishing.

Jesus Himself teaches us to distinguish between God's creational intention and concessions made within human hardness. When questioned about divorce, Christ reaches behind Mosaic regulation to God's intention “from the beginning” in creation.
That principle matters.
Regulation is not necessarily celebration.
Restriction is not necessarily endorsement of everything being restricted.
A law can confront an ugly reality without calling the reality beautiful.
If a government establishes rules protecting prisoners of war, it does not mean the government is celebrating captivity.
If a hospital establishes procedures for treating overdose victims, it is not endorsing drug abuse.

And when Torah places restraints around what victorious men may do with vulnerable women in an ancient war culture, we should not automatically read every surrounding social reality as God's timeless ideal.
But neither should we congratulate ourselves too quickly.
Because there is another danger here.
We can compare this law with the brutality of the ancient world and say, “See? It was more humane.”
There is truth in recognizing its restrictions.
But if that becomes our entire answer, we may stop listening to the woman.
She is still captive.
She still lost her former life.
She still exists within an ancient patriarchal world radically different from ours.
And Scripture does not require Christians to pretend otherwise.
The Bible is strong enough for difficult questions.
Our faith does not collapse when we admit that a passage makes us uncomfortable.
Sometimes discomfort is where serious reading begins.
And maybe that is where this ancient law suddenly gets frighteningly personal.
Because most of us will never stand on an ancient battlefield.
But almost every one of us will eventually possess some kind of power.
A husband has power that can be used to cherish or intimidate.
A parent has power.
A pastor has power.
A ministry leader has power.
A boss has power.
A wealthy person has power.
A popular person has power.
Someone holding another person's secret has power.
Someone being trusted by a wounded person has power.
Someone desired by another person has power.
And the question underneath Deuteronomy 21 is still alive:
What will you do when you possess something another person cannot easily resist?
That is where character is exposed.
Not when everybody is watching.
When you could take advantage.
When you could manipulate.
When you could use someone's loneliness.
When you could exploit someone's dependence.
When you could make another human being pay for your appetite.
When you could get away with it.
Power whispers:
“You can.”
God asks:
“But should you?”
Maybe your battlefield is a phone screen at 1:17 in the morning.
Maybe nobody knows about the messages.
Maybe somebody else's spouse has been giving you attention.
Maybe pornography has trained you to look at human beings as bodies existing for consumption.
Maybe someone emotionally vulnerable has become attached to you, and part of you enjoys having that control.
Maybe you call manipulation “love.”
Maybe you call lust “connection.”
Maybe you call possession “protection.”
Maybe you call domination “leadership.”
Maybe you have become very good at giving holy names to unholy appetites.
Then this strange ancient passage walks into the room.
And suddenly the unnamed captive woman is staring back at us.
Not asking whether we understand every ancient custom.
Asking whether we understand our own hearts.
Because sin has always been skilled at turning people into objects.
Lust says, “What can I get from you?”
Pride says, “How can you make me look?”
Greed says, “What are you worth to me?”
Bitterness says, “How can I hurt you?”
Power says, “What can I make you do?”
But love asks something entirely different:
“How can I seek your good even when it costs me?”
And this is where we have to be careful with Jesus.
We should not force Deuteronomy 21 into a cheap allegory and pretend the captive woman is secretly a coded prediction of Christ.
That would not honor the passage.
Jesus is not hidden inside every Hebrew noun.
But the whole biblical story does move toward Him.
The Law exposes sin.
The prophets cry for justice and faithfulness.
Human beings repeatedly demonstrate what happens when power and desire become corrupted.
And then Jesus comes.
Not as another man looking for vulnerable people to exploit.
But as the King who gives Himself for people who have nothing with which to purchase Him.
The New Testament describes Christ's love with the Greek word ἀγάπη—agapē—and its related verb ἀγαπάω, language repeatedly associated with self-giving love.
The Gospel turns the world's instinct upside down.
Human sin says:
“You are weaker than I am, so I can use you.”
Jesus says:
“I am Lord, therefore I will stoop to serve.”
Human sin grabs.
Jesus gives.
Human sin exploits weakness.
Jesus moves toward the broken.
Human sin asks what another person can provide.
Christ gives Himself.
And nowhere is that clearer than the cross.
Jesus Christ possessed authority beyond anything an ancient warrior could imagine.
Yet He did not use divine authority for selfish exploitation.
Philippians 2 tells us that Christ humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
That is power under holiness.
That is strength without exploitation.
That is kingship wearing a servant's towel.
And ultimately, a crown of thorns.
Here is where the story becomes yours.
Because perhaps you are not identifying with the soldier.
Perhaps you identify with the captive.
Perhaps somebody used power against you.
Maybe somebody called it love.
Maybe somebody quoted Scripture while controlling you.
Maybe a person who should have protected you instead exploited your vulnerability.
Maybe your body became somebody else's object.
Maybe your trust became somebody else's opportunity.
Maybe the person who wounded you was respected by everyone else.
And you have carried a question into church that you have been afraid to say aloud:
“Did God see what happened to me?”
Look again at the text.
Thousands of years ago, in a world of warriors and captives, God placed the grief of a nameless foreign woman inside His written Word.
Her mourning mattered enough to be mentioned.
Her treatment mattered enough to be regulated.
Her freedom mattered enough that the man was forbidden to sell her after rejecting her.
She does not disappear from God's sight simply because history forgot her name.
Neither do you.
The Gospel does not tell you that evil becomes good because you eventually survived it.
It does not require you to call abuse a blessing.
It does not demand that you pretend betrayal didn't hurt.
Jesus Christ enters a world where people humiliate other people—and He bears humiliation Himself.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And then the grave discovers something no empire, soldier, abuser, demon, or sinner can overturn:
Jesus gets the final word.
That is why grace is not sentimental.
Grace cost blood.
Forgiveness is not pretending sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves precisely how much sin matters.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for pleasure.
It is the mercy of God exposing what is killing you so that you can stop hiding and come home.
Maybe the hardest person for you to see in this passage is yourself.
Maybe you have used people.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe you manipulated affection.
Maybe you took what wasn't yours.
Maybe your private sexual life would horrify the people who admire your public Christianity.
Maybe you know exactly what it means to see something, desire it, and begin inventing excuses for taking it.
Do not run from Christ.
Run to Him.
Repentance does not mean explaining your sin until it sounds understandable.
It means bringing it into the light.
Calling it what God calls it.
Turning from it.
And trusting the crucified and risen Jesus Christ to forgive what you cannot erase.
The scandal of Christianity is not that Christians are people who never became filthy.
The scandal is that Christ washes sinners.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted His church.
The thief beside Him had nothing left to offer.
And still grace kept rewriting stories.
That does not remove earthly consequences.
It does not make restitution unnecessary.
It does not mean victims owe immediate trust to those who harmed them.
Grace is not permission to escape accountability.
Grace changes the sinner so radically that hiding stops being worth protecting.
So perhaps your prayer tonight is not complicated.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Perhaps you have spent years defending something God has been asking you to surrender.
Or maybe you are reading with tears because you were the one somebody else wounded.
Not because typing words earns healing.
Not because a comment saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing our struggle into the light is how isolation begins to lose its grip.
And somebody reading beneath you may realize for the first time that they are not the only believer still carrying scars.
That is what community can become when Christians stop performing perfection.
Not because Christianity needs dishonest defenders.
Because people need to discover that we do not have to amputate uncomfortable verses from the Bible to trust the God revealed through its whole redemptive story.
Because someday somebody will throw Deuteronomy 21 at you and say, “Explain this.”
And instead of panicking, perhaps you will remember:
Context matters.
Hebrew matters.
Ancient history matters.
Genre matters.
The difference between regulation and moral ideal matters.
The vulnerable person in the text matters.
And above everything, the whole counsel of Scripture matters.
Gospel Warrior exists because believers deserve more than inspirational fragments detached from context.
We need Scripture.
We need repentance.
We need theology strong enough for hard questions.
We need grace deep enough for ugly histories.

We need Jesus Christ—not a sanitized Jesus manufactured to keep everybody comfortable, but the crucified and risen Lord who confronts sin, receives repentant sinners, binds the brokenhearted, and transforms those who belong to Him.

If this ministry helps you grow deeper in Christ, following Gospel Warrior keeps that biblical teaching near you. Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too—not merely to grow a page, but because one encounter with biblical truth can begin a conversation that eternity makes worth having.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in worship, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and service.
And there is something even bigger behind what you see in the daily posts.
If you have been reading from a distance, perhaps this is the moment to come closer—not to a brand, but to a community determined to keep opening Scripture and pointing one another toward Christ.
Not as payment to God.
Not because sharing a post makes anyone more righteous.
A man secretly enslaved to lust.
A skeptic convinced Christians are afraid of difficult Bible passages.
A believer quietly losing faith.
A survivor wondering whether God noticed.
A sinner wondering whether forgiveness could possibly include them.
You may never know which person stops scrolling.
You may never know who reads until the end.
You may never know whose midnight prayer begins because you pressed “Share.”
But the Gospel has always traveled through ordinary people refusing to keep extraordinary news to themselves.
The captive woman of Deuteronomy 21 disappears from the biblical narrative without a name.
We do not know what became of her.
And perhaps that is one reason she remains unforgettable.
Because Scripture forces us to notice someone history could easily have reduced to spoil.
A woman grieving.
A woman vulnerable to another person's appetite.
A woman whose treatment God chose to address.
And thousands of years later, her story still whispers a warning into every human heart entrusted with power:
Having the power to take something does not give you the moral right to take it.
Then the Gospel takes us farther.
To a hill outside Jerusalem.
To the One who could have summoned legions of angels but instead stretched out His hands.
To the King who conquered not by exploiting the helpless, but by giving Himself for sinners.
To the Savior who takes scandal, shame, lust, wounds, guilt, captivity, grief, and histories we wish could be rewritten—and begins making all things new.
So be honest.
Did this passage hit harder than you expected?
Because perhaps the question hidden inside this disturbing ancient law was never only, “What was a soldier permitted to do with a captive woman?”
Perhaps another question has been waiting there all along:
What does your heart become when you finally have enough power to get what you want?
And when the answer exposes something ugly, do not hide.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still repentance.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still grace.
There is still Jesus.
And if Christ gets hold of your story, even the chapter you thought would define you forever does not have to write the ending.
Your worst chapter may explain your scars—but only Jesus has the authority to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE PERFECT AS YOUR HEAVENLY FATHER IS PERFECT” — IS JESUS REALLY DEMANDING SINLESS PERFECTION?
paragraphs:
“BE PERFECT AS YOUR HEAVENLY FATHER IS PERFECT” — IS JESUS REALLY DEMANDING SINLESS PERFECTION?
The verse that has terrified sincere Christians for centuries becomes breathtaking when you hear what Jesus was actually saying in context.
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”
— Matthew 5:48, KJV
Read that slowly.
Perfect.
Not better.
Not improving.
Not trying harder.
Perfect.
For some Christians, that single word has quietly become a whip.
You sinned again.
You lost your temper again.
You entertained that thought again.
You fell back into the habit you promised God you would never touch again.
You knew better…and still did it.
Then somewhere in the back of your mind comes the voice:
“Didn’t Jesus say you must be perfect?”
And suddenly Matthew 5:48 no longer sounds like good news.
It sounds impossible.
Maybe you have even wondered something you were afraid to say aloud:
“If Jesus commands perfection…and I am obviously not perfect…what hope is there for someone like me?”
But what if we have been hearing that verse without hearing the conversation surrounding it?
What if Jesus’ command is even more searching than “never make another mistake”—yet, at the same time, far more beautiful than the crushing interpretation many wounded believers have carried?
Because Jesus really did say it.
The Greek text reads:
Ἔσεσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι ὡς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος τέλειός ἐστιν.
Esesthe oun hymeis teleioi hōs ho patēr hymōn ho ouranios teleios estin.
“You therefore shall be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”
The word demanding our attention is τέλειοι — teleioi, the plural form of τέλειος — teleios.
It can carry the sense of being complete, mature, fully developed, or having reached the intended goal. Depending on context, “perfect” can indeed be an appropriate translation.
But here is where careless interpretation can hurt people.
We cannot simply take one possible dictionary meaning of teleios, choose whichever meaning comforts us most, and announce that Jesus merely meant, “Try to become spiritually mature.”
Context must decide what Jesus is saying.
And the context is devastatingly beautiful.
Jesus has just said:
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’”
Then He overturns the boundaries fallen human love prefers to draw:
“But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you…”
Why?
“…so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.”
Then Jesus points toward something we see every day but rarely stop to consider.
Sunlight.
Rain.
“For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust.”
That is the road leading directly to Matthew 5:48.
Jesus is talking about love.
Not sentimental love.
Not Facebook-post love.
Not loving people who already agree with you, affirm you, appreciate you, apologize to you, vote like you, worship like you, or treat you well.
Enemy love.
And suddenly “Be perfect” becomes frightening in an entirely different way.
Because Jesus is exposing one of humanity’s favorite counterfeits:
Selective love.
“If you love those who love you, what reward do you have?”
That question reaches through two thousand years and puts its hand directly on the modern heart.
It is easy to love the person who comments something kind under your post.
What about the person who humiliates you?
It is easy to pray for your children.
What about someone who wounded them?
It is easy to ask God to bless the friend who stood beside you.
What about the person who betrayed you?
It is easy to talk about grace until grace has the face of someone you believe does not deserve it.
And maybe that is exactly where this passage has found you.
Because there is probably a name you did not want appearing in your mind while reading this.
A father.
A mother.
An ex.
A spouse.
A pastor.
A friend.
A church member.
Someone who lied about you.
Someone who abandoned you.
Someone who never apologized.
Someone who left damage behind and continued living as though nothing happened.
And Jesus says:
Love your enemies.
Pray for those who persecute you.
Then:
Be teleioi as your heavenly Father is teleios.
In the parallel teaching recorded in Luke, Jesus says:
“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.”
— Luke 6:36
That parallel matters enormously.
Matthew emphasizes the completeness of the Father-like love to which disciples are called; Luke emphasizes the mercy that characterizes that love.
Jesus is calling His disciples beyond the incomplete love that says:
“I love people who deserve my love.”
The Father’s generosity is not confined to those who love Him.
The sun still rises over the field of the atheist.
Rain still falls upon the roof of the rebel.
God gives temporal kindness even to people who curse His name.
And Jesus looks at His followers and essentially asks:
Does your love resemble your Father?
That does not mean evil no longer matters.
It does not mean abuse should be tolerated.
It does not mean justice disappears.
It does not mean reconciliation can occur without truth.
It does not mean Christians must remain in dangerous situations.
Biblical love is not pretending wickedness is righteousness.
Jesus Himself confronted sin with extraordinary clarity.
But Christian love refuses to become evil simply because evil was done to us.
That distinction matters.
You can establish a boundary without hatred.
You can pursue justice without revenge.
You can tell the truth without delighting in another person’s destruction.
You can forgive while recognizing that trust may need to be rebuilt.
And sometimes you can pray for someone from a very safe distance.
Enemy love does not call darkness light.
It refuses to let darkness reproduce itself inside you.
But another question remains.
Does Matthew 5:48 mean Christians become sinlessly perfect in this present life?
If that is what Jesus means—absolute freedom from every sin from this moment onward—then the rest of the New Testament creates serious problems for that interpretation.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray:
“Forgive us our debts…”
— Matthew 6:12
Notice where that appears.
The very next chapter.
The same Sermon on the Mount.
Jesus does not teach His disciples, “Once you become Mine, you will never need forgiveness again.”
He teaches them to keep coming to their Father.
The apostle John is even more explicit:
“If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
Then comes one of the most precious promises ever given to guilty believers:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And shortly afterward:
“My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
— 1 John 2:1
Do you see the tension?
“Do not sin.”
Yet:
“If anyone does sin…”
Christianity does not lower God’s holiness to make sinners comfortable.
Neither does Christianity pretend redeemed people no longer need grace.
The Gospel does something infinitely greater.
It gives guilty people a righteous Advocate.
Jesus Christ.
This is where Matthew 5:48 must never be separated from the Gospel.
Because if your entire relationship with God depends upon establishing your own flawless record, you are already ruined.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot unsay the words.
You cannot unthink the thoughts.
You cannot go backward and become the person you should have been.
You cannot scrub your conscience clean enough to make yourself righteous before a holy God.
And that is exactly why Jesus did not merely come to become our motivational speaker.
He came to save sinners.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:21
Jesus lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He went willingly toward the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The Christian message is not:
“Become perfect enough so Jesus will finally accept you.”
It is:
Repent and come to Christ because you never could save yourself.
Grace is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin matters so much that redemption cost blood.
Yet grace also means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter when Christ becomes Lord of your story.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message remains:
Not because Jesus edits sin into something respectable.
He does something far more radical.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He teaches enemies of God to become children who increasingly resemble their Father.
This is where another use of teleios becomes illuminating.
Paul writes:
— Philippians 3:12
Then he continues:
“…but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own.”
Read that again.
Paul does not say:
“I have arrived.”
He says:
“I press on.”
Why?
Because Christ has made him His own.
That order changes everything.
Christ does not wait at the finish line saying:
“Become flawless and perhaps I will claim you.”
Paul says, in effect:
I keep running because Christ has already taken hold of me.
That is grace-fueled transformation.
The Gospel does not say holiness is unnecessary.
It makes holiness possible without making holiness the purchase price of salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, “not a result of works,” and yet Ephesians immediately says we were created in Christ Jesus “for good works.”
Grace saves.
Grace transforms.
And grace trains.
Titus says the grace of God trains believers “to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.”
Real grace never whispers:
“Your sin does not matter. Stay exactly as you are.”
Real grace says:
“Jesus paid for this. Now get up. Follow Him.”
Maybe you needed to hear that because you have confused two very different voices.
Conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says:
“This is sin. Bring it into the light. Confess it. Turn from it. Come back to Christ.”
Condemnation says:
“You are filthy. Hide. God is tired of you. There is no point returning.”
One pulls you toward repentance.
The other drives you toward despair.
And Scripture says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
— Romans 8:1
That verse does not say there is no correction.
No discipline.
No warfare.
No painful sanctification.
It says there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Maybe you failed this week.
Maybe last night.
Maybe five minutes before opening this article.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are strong, but privately you are exhausted from fighting something nobody knows exists.
Maybe you are terrified that your repeated weakness means Jesus has finally had enough.
Do not use grace as permission to keep feeding the sin that is destroying you.
But do not use your failure as an excuse to run away from the only Savior who can cleanse you.
Bring it into the light.
Name it before God.
Repent.
Seek help where help is needed.
Cut off whatever continually leads you toward destruction.
And run toward Christ.
Again.
The scandal of grace is not that sinners become acceptable because sin becomes acceptable.
The scandal is that the Holy One welcomes repentant sinners because Christ has paid what sinners could never pay.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame.
He had promised:
“Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.”
Hours later, he was denying that he even knew Him.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
That could have been the end of his story.
Failure.
Hypocrisy.
Cowardice.
Scandal.
But resurrection morning was coming.
And the risen Jesus did not pretend Peter had never failed.
He restored him.
“Do you love me?”
“Feed my sheep.”
Jesus rewrote the story without rewriting the truth.
Peter really failed.
Grace really restored him.
And Christ really transformed him.
That is what some of you reading this desperately need to understand.
You do not honor Jesus by pretending you never struggle.
You honor Him by bringing your struggle under His lordship.
You do not glorify Christ by hiding the wound.
You glorify Christ when the scar eventually points toward the Physician.
You do not magnify grace by minimizing sin.
You magnify grace by admitting how desperately you needed it.
And then comes the harder part.
The grace you receive begins changing the grace you give.
Because the same Jesus who forgives you commands:
Love your enemies.
Pray for your persecutors.
Become like your Father.
Not to become His child by earning enough points.
But because children increasingly bear the family resemblance.
Perhaps that is the part of Matthew 5:48 you were trying not to hear.
You were worried Jesus was demanding that you never stumble again.
Meanwhile, He was confronting the hatred you still feel justified carrying.
You want forgiveness for yourself and judgment for them.
Mercy for your failures and punishment for theirs.
Context for your mistakes and a permanent label for theirs.
Grace when you fall and fire when they do.
Jesus will not allow His disciples to build their lives there.
The cross destroys our illusion of moral superiority because every redeemed person stands beneath it as someone who needed mercy.
You and the person who hurt you may not share the same guilt.
Their offense may genuinely have been far greater.
Biblical forgiveness does not require pretending otherwise.
But at Calvary, nobody gets to boast that they saved themselves.
We all need Jesus.
So no, Matthew 5:48 should not be turned into a theological whip telling genuine believers that one remaining imperfection means Christ has rejected them.
But neither should we weaken it into:
“Just do your best. Nobody is perfect.”
Jesus' command is far too magnificent for that.
He calls His people toward the wholeness of a love patterned after the Father Himself.
A love that crosses enemy lines.
A mercy that refuses to mirror hatred.
A holiness that reaches deeper than appearances and begins transforming the heart.
And the God who commands transformation is also the God who works within His people.
“For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.”
— Philippians 2:13
That means your unfinished story is not permission for complacency.
It is an invitation to dependence.
You are not called to make peace with your chains.
You are called to follow Jesus out of them.
Sometimes that transformation feels spectacular.
Sometimes it looks painfully ordinary.
Apologizing.
Deleting the number.
Closing the browser.
Walking away from gossip.
Opening your Bible when you feel spiritually numb.
Praying for someone you still struggle to forgive.
Confessing what you wanted to hide.
Asking another believer for help.
Getting up after another failure.
Whispering:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And discovering He is still the Savior of sinners.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn this moment into another scroll.
Turn it into prayer.
Or simply:
“Pray for me.”
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your battle.
But there is something powerful about refusing to keep pretending that Christians never struggle.
Someone else reading the comments may discover they are not the only believer fighting their way back toward the light.

And if one particular person came to your mind while reading this—someone crushed by perfectionism, ashamed of repeated failure, or convinced God could never want them again—send this article to them.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
We support Gospel work because we have received grace, not because we are trying to purchase it.
If you want your resources to glorify God, prayerfully consider using some of what He has entrusted to you to support work that proclaims His Word.
Not as a spiritual performance.
As an invitation.
Someone may be quietly questioning whether God could forgive them.
Someone may be one secret failure away from walking away from the faith entirely.
Someone may have spent twenty years believing Christianity means pretending to be perfect.
Let them encounter the Gospel instead.
And comment.
Not for an algorithm alone.
For the person silently reading beneath you.
Because perhaps somebody needs to see that Christians are not people who never needed rescue.
We are people who discovered where Rescue has a name.
Jesus.
So when the enemy drags your failures into the courtroom of your mind and says:
“Look at you. Perfect? You?”
Do not answer by pretending you have never sinned.
Point toward Christ.
Yes, you have failed.
Yes, you still need sanctification.
Yes, Jesus commands a holiness and love deeper than anything the natural heart can manufacture.
And yes…
there is still grace.
The goal is not a Christianity that shrugs at sin.
The goal is Christlikeness.
Wholehearted love.
Mature faith.
Mercy resembling the Father.
A life progressively surrendered to Jesus until the One who began His good work brings it to completion.
So hear Matthew 5:48 again.
Not as permission to become casual about holiness.
Not as a whip telling repentant believers to despair.
Hear it as the voice of Jesus calling His redeemed people into the beautiful, impossible-without-God life of the kingdom:
Become what grace is remaking you to be.
Love beyond reciprocity.
Pray beyond resentment.
Forgive because you were forgiven.
Pursue holiness because Christ is worthy.
Repent when you fall.
Return when you wander.
Keep following when you feel unfinished.
And never confuse being unfinished with being abandoned.
Because the hands shaping you are scarred hands.
Your failure may explain a chapter of your story, but when you surrender the pen to Jesus, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID GOD EVER CALL POLYGAMY GOOD?
paragraphs:
DID GOD EVER CALL POLYGAMY GOOD?
Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had two wives and two concubines. David had several wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why would anyone say biblical marriage was meant to be one man and one woman? The answer becomes uncomfortable when we finally stop asking what biblical men did—and start asking what God actually called good.
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible.
You can read what happened and quietly assume God approved of it.
You can see Abraham doing something and assume Abraham's behavior must therefore represent God's ideal.
You can watch Jacob build a household around multiple women and conclude that because God continued working through Jacob, God must have endorsed everything Jacob did.
You can watch David collect wives, watch Solomon multiply them almost beyond comprehension, and eventually ask the question many Christians are afraid to answer plainly:
Did God ever actually call polygamy good?
Not, “Did polygamy occur in the Bible?”
Of course it did.
Not, “Did God continue working through people whose marriages were complicated, sinful, fractured, or far removed from Eden?”
Of course He did.
The question is much sharper.
Where does God call polygamy His design?
Where does He pronounce it good?
Where does Scripture hold up the multiplication of wives as the beautiful pattern humanity should imitate?
And once you begin looking for that verse instead of merely looking for polygamous men...
the silence becomes thunderous.
Because the Bible does something far more honest than sanitizing its heroes.
It lets you see them bleed.
It lets you watch their compromises produce consequences.

It lets you enter homes where jealousy sits at the dinner table, rivalry sleeps under the same roof, children inherit the tensions of their fathers, women ache to be loved, and powerful men discover that having more does not mean loving better.
And perhaps that is where this article becomes about more than polygamy.
Because some of us have made the same mistake with our own lives.
“If God hasn't stopped me, maybe He's okay with it.”
“If God is still blessing me, maybe this isn't really sin.”
“If God used that biblical person despite what he did, perhaps what he did wasn't wrong.”
But God's patience should never be confused with God's approval.
Grace is not God changing His definition of holiness so that we can remain comfortable.
Grace is God meeting sinners in the wreckage and refusing to abandon His redemptive purpose.
And to understand marriage, Jesus tells us where to look.
Not first to Abraham.
Not first to Jacob.
Not first to David.
Not first to Solomon.
Back further.
Before kings.
Before patriarchal customs.
Before broken households.
Before jealousy.
Before betrayal.
Before sin had distorted anything.
Jesus takes us back to Eden.
Genesis 2:24 gives us the foundational words:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew is worth slowing down for:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘al-kēn ya‘ăzāḇ-’îš ’eṯ-’āḇîw wə’eṯ-’immô wəḏāḇaq bə’ištô wəhāyû ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
A man leaves father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become “one flesh”—בָּשָׂר אֶחָד, basar echad.
One flesh.
Not merely one sexual encounter.
A new union.
A new kinship.
A covenantal joining so profound that Jesus would later appeal directly to this creation account when answering questions about marriage.
And notice something.
God did not begin the biblical story by giving Adam a collection of wives.
He gave the man the woman.
Genesis does not introduce marriage through a king's palace filled with wives and concubines.
It introduces marriage in a garden.
One man.
One woman.
One flesh.
Then sin enters.
And not long after Eden, something changes.
Genesis 4:19 introduces Lamech:
“And Lamech took unto him two wives.”
That sentence matters.
This is the Bible's first explicit description of a man taking two wives.
But look at where it appears.
Not in Genesis 2, where God's created order is unveiled.
Genesis 4.
After the fall.
In Cain's line.
And Lamech is not presented as a gentle model of covenant faithfulness. His speech later in the chapter boasts of violence.
Scripture does not stop to say, “And God approved of Lamech taking two wives.”
It simply tells us what happened.
That distinction—between description and prescription—changes how we read the entire Bible.
Scripture records murder.
It does not endorse murder.
Scripture records adultery.
It does not endorse adultery.
Scripture records deception, drunkenness, incest, betrayal, exploitation, idolatry, cowardice, vengeance, and catastrophic failures by people God nevertheless continued pursuing.
The Bible's willingness to tell the truth about human beings is not evidence that God approves of everything human beings do.
It is evidence that the Bible refuses to manufacture flawless heroes.
Then Abraham enters the story.
God promised Abraham offspring.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
The waiting became painful.
Then Genesis 16 happened.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
Abraham went in to Hagar.
Hagar conceived.
And immediately the household fractured.
The text tells us that when Hagar realized she had conceived, Sarah became diminished in her eyes. Sarah responded bitterly. Hagar was treated harshly. Hagar fled.
Stop there.
A woman ran into the wilderness.
This is what happens when biblical stories cease being stained-glass windows and become human again.
Hagar was not an argument.
She was a person.
Sarah was not merely a theological illustration.
She was a hurting woman who had waited years for something she desperately wanted.
Abraham was not an untouchable spiritual celebrity.
He was a man of faith who could also make disastrous choices.
And God?
God found Hagar.
That is grace.
God seeing the wounded does not mean God endorsed every decision that produced the wound.
God rescuing people from our broken arrangements does not mean He designed those arrangements.
That distinction may be exactly what somebody reading this needs tonight.
Perhaps God has been merciful to you inside something you should never have entered.
Don't mistake His mercy for permission.
His mercy may be the very thing calling you home.
Then comes Jacob.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban's deception, he married Leah first and Rachel afterward. The household eventually expanded through their servants Bilhah and Zilpah.
Read the story slowly and the romance disappears.
Leah desperately wants to be loved.
Rachel desperately wants children.
The sisters compete.
Children become entangled in the rivalry.
Genesis 30 opens with Rachel envying Leah and crying to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
That does not sound like Eden.
It sounds like heartbreak.
Leah names sons while hoping that perhaps now her husband will become attached to her.
Rachel battles infertility and jealousy.
Servants become involved in the struggle for offspring.
The household grows.
So does the pain.
Yes, God works through this family.
Yes, the twelve tribes of Israel emerge from Jacob's sons.
But God's ability to bring covenant history through human dysfunction should never be turned into an endorsement of the dysfunction.
That is one of the great themes of Scripture.
God can write straight through lines we made crooked.
That does not make crookedness straight.
Then there is David.
A man after God's own heart.
A worshiper.
A warrior.
A king.
And a man with multiple wives.
Does David's place in God's redemptive story prove that polygamy was God's ideal?
Look carefully at what God told Israel's kings before Israel even had a monarchy.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of the king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.”
That warning becomes haunting when Solomon walks onto the stage.
Solomon possessed wisdom, wealth, power, international influence...
and women.
First Kings 11 describes seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.
Then comes the sentence that should destroy the fantasy that multiplying wives represents some biblical pinnacle of masculine blessing:
“and his wives turned away his heart.”
The warning of Deuteronomy becomes flesh inside Solomon's palace.
The man famous for wisdom ignored God's warning and discovered that intelligence does not make disobedience safe.
You can be brilliant and spiritually compromised.
You can be powerful and internally divided.
You can possess what other people envy and still be losing your heart.
Solomon's household is not Scripture saying, “Look how wonderfully God designed polygamy.”
It becomes part of the tragic account of a king whose loves pulled his heart away from undivided devotion to God.
But someone may object:
“If God opposed polygamy, why did Old Testament law sometimes regulate situations involving multiple wives?”
That is a serious question and deserves a serious answer.
Biblical law sometimes addresses realities already present in a fallen society without presenting those realities as the creation ideal.
Regulation and endorsement are not identical.

For example, Exodus 21:10 protects a woman from being deprived of food, clothing, and marital rights if another wife is taken. Deuteronomy 21:15–17 protects the inheritance rights of the son of an unloved wife in a household containing two wives.
Those laws matter precisely because real women and children could be harmed by male power.
God's law placed obligations on men within social realities that existed.
But a law telling someone how he must treat vulnerable people within a broken arrangement does not automatically mean the arrangement itself is God's highest design.
Jesus gives us an interpretive clue when discussing another damaged marital reality: divorce.
In Matthew 19, religious leaders ask Him about divorce.
Jesus does something remarkable.
He does not begin with Moses.
He goes behind Moses.
Back to creation.
He says:
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female?”
Then He quotes Genesis:
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh.”
The Greek expression is striking:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
“The two into one flesh.”
Two.
Jesus then concludes:
“So then, they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
And when His questioners appeal to Moses' provision concerning divorce, Jesus explains that Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart.
Then Jesus says words that should govern how Christians think about God's intention for marriage:
“from the beginning it was not so.”
There it is.
Jesus distinguishes between what exists amid human hardness and what God established “from the beginning.”
