Maybe someone who has not prayed in ten years reads this tonight.
Maybe someone discovers that Christianity is not the story of perfect people impressing God.
It is the story of sinners rescued by Jesus.
And perhaps that is why Job’s daughters still matter thousands of years later.
Their names appear near the closing lines of a story that once looked finished in ashes.
They stand there like quiet witnesses that Job's darkest chapter was not his last chapter.
Jemimah.
Keziah.
Keren-Happuch.
Three names.
An inheritance among their brothers.
A father who once thought everything was over.
And a God who was still writing.
So when you look at the ashes of your own life, remember this:
You cannot always tell what God is doing by staring at the chapter that hurts.
Job could not see chapter 42 from the ash heap.
The disciples could not see Easter Sunday from Friday afternoon.
And you cannot see everything Jesus is doing from where you are standing tonight.
But you can see the cross.
You can see the empty tomb.
And because Christ is risen, the Christian's ultimate future is not determined by the ashes behind us.
It is secured by the Savior ahead of us.
The ashes may explain where you have been, but they do not have authority to write where Jesus is taking His redeemed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU PRAY WITH THE WRONG MOTIVE?
paragraphs:
CAN YOU PRAY WITH THE WRONG MOTIVE?
The Terrifying Possibility That God Hears Every Word of Your Prayer—While Seeing the Desire You Never Said Out Loud
What if the most dangerous thing about your prayer is not what you said…
but what you secretly wanted?
You closed your eyes.
You bowed your head.
You said, “Lord, please…”
Maybe you even cried.
And everybody listening would have called it a beautiful prayer.
But there was another prayer underneath the prayer.
A prayer without words.
“Make them regret what they did to me.”
“Give me this so people will finally respect me.”
“Bless me so I can prove them wrong.”
“Fix my marriage, but don’t ask me to forgive.”
“Change my spouse, but leave my pride untouched.”
“Give me success so I can finally feel important.”
“Let my ministry grow so people will know my name.”
“Give me what I want, Lord…
and please don’t examine why I want it.”
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because Scripture reveals something frightening and strangely merciful:
God does not merely hear the words coming from your mouth.
He sees the heart producing them.
And sometimes the greatest answer God can give to a prayer spoken from the wrong motive…
is no.
There is a sentence in the Bible that dismantles the comfortable assumption that simply asking God for something automatically makes the desire righteous.
James writes:
James 4:3
The Greek is even sharper.
“αἰτεῖτε καὶ οὐ λαμβάνετε, διότι κακῶς αἰτεῖσθε, ἵνα ἐν ταῖς ἡδοναῖς ὑμῶν δαπανήσητε.”
Aiteite kai ou lambanete, dioti kakōs aiteisthe, hina en tais hēdonais hymōn dapanēsēte.
The word translated “wrongly” is κακῶς — kakōs.
It carries the sense of asking badly, wrongly, improperly, with an evil or defective orientation.
And James does not leave us wondering what he means.
He exposes the motive.
“ἵνα ἐν ταῖς ἡδοναῖς ὑμῶν δαπανήσητε…”
“…so that you may spend it on your pleasures.”
The issue was not merely that these people prayed incorrectly.
The issue was that something inside them wanted to use God as the means to satisfy desires that had become their masters.
Read that again.
Because this can happen to religious people.
It can happen to churchgoing people.
It can happen to pastors.
It can happen to ministry leaders.
It can happen to people who know Scripture.
It can happen to you.
It can happen to me.
We can take something deeply selfish, dress it in Christian vocabulary, place “Lord” in front of it and “in Jesus’ name” behind it…
and still be asking with the wrong motive.
That should sober us.
But it should not drive us away from God.
It should drive us deeper into His presence.
Because Jesus did not teach us to stop praying when our hearts are messy.
He taught us what surrendered prayer looks like.
And perhaps nowhere is that more painfully beautiful than Gethsemane.
Jesus knew what was coming.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Beating.
Humiliation.
Nails.
A cross.
The sinless Son of God carrying the judgment our sin deserved.
And Jesus prayed:
“Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.”
Mark 14:36
Mark preserves the Aramaic word:
Ἀββᾶ — Abba.
The New Testament then gives the Greek:
ὁ πατήρ — ho patēr
“Father.”
And then comes the surrender that exposes so much of what passes for prayer in us:
ἀλλ’ οὐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω ἀλλὰ τί σύ
all’ ou ti egō thelō alla ti sy
“Yet not what I will, but what You [will].”
Jesus was not pretending the suffering was pleasant.
He was not emotionally numb.
He was not performing spirituality.
He brought the agony honestly before His Father…
and submitted His desire to the Father’s will.
That is one of the great differences between biblical prayer and using prayer as a religious form of self-worship.
Biblical prayer does not mean you cannot tell God what you want.
You can.
Tell Him.
Tell Him you want the marriage restored.
Tell Him you want the job.
Tell Him you desperately want healing.
Tell Him you want the opportunity.
Tell Him you are lonely.
Tell Him you want a spouse.
Tell Him you want the ministry to grow.
Tell Him you are tired of struggling financially.
Tell Him you want your child to come home.
Tell Him you want justice.
Tell Him what hurts.
God is not intimidated by your honesty.
But somewhere in mature prayer, another sentence begins appearing:
“Father, I want this…
but I want You more.”
That changes everything.
Because sometimes what we call unanswered prayer is actually a collision between what we desire and what God knows.
You see the opportunity.
God sees where it leads.
You see the relationship.
God sees what it is doing to your soul.
You see the money.
God sees what the money might awaken inside you.
You see the promotion.
God sees the pride you have not conquered.
You see the platform.
God sees whether your character could survive the applause.
You see the person you desperately want God to bring back.
God sees what you cannot see.
And because He sees what you cannot see, His “no” is not evidence that He stopped loving you.
Sometimes His refusal is mercy wearing clothes you do not recognize yet.
This is where motive becomes painfully important.
Imagine someone praying:
“Lord, make me successful.”
Nothing inherently sinful about that.
But underneath it might be:
“…because I need everyone who laughed at me to see that I won.”
Now success has quietly become revenge.
Another person prays:
“Lord, grow my ministry.”
Beautiful prayer.
But beneath it could be:
“…because I need to feel important.”
Now ministry has become medication for insecurity.
Another prays:
“God, deal with my husband.”
Maybe God needs to.
But underneath it could be:
“…because I refuse to examine myself.”
Another prays:
“Lord, expose what they did.”
Perhaps justice genuinely needs to come.
But underneath it could be:
“…because I want to watch them suffer.”
Do you see it?
The same sentence can rise from radically different hearts.
That is why prayer is not merely about vocabulary.
It is about worship.
Who sits on the throne of the request?
God?
Or you?
Jesus confronted this same heart problem when He spoke about people who practiced spirituality to be seen.
In Matthew 6:5, He warned against praying like hypocrites who loved praying publicly so they could be noticed by others.
The problem was not public prayer itself. Jesus prayed where others could hear Him.
The problem was the audience of the heart.
They appeared to be talking to God…
while secretly performing for people.
That is terrifying.
You can say God’s name while craving human applause.
You can preach Jesus while secretly building yourself.
You can serve people while needing their admiration.
You can give while wanting recognition.
You can pray while wanting someone nearby to notice how spiritual you sound.
And God sees all of it.
Jesus said:
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
Matthew 6:6
What a phrase.
Your Father sees.
He sees the prayer.
He sees the pain.
He sees the tears.
He sees the desire.
He sees the mixture.
He sees the part of you that genuinely wants His glory…
and the part still hungry for your own.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because if God only accepted people with perfectly purified motives, who among us could stand?
Even our best actions can carry traces of pride.
Even generosity can become self-congratulation.
Even service can become identity.
Even ministry can become ambition.
Even prayer can become manipulation.
We do not merely need better prayer techniques.
We need redemption.
We need Jesus.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally learned how to pray correctly.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never make themselves righteous have been offered reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Christ lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is offered to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That means discovering an ugly motive inside yourself does not have to end in despair.
It can become an invitation to repentance.
Maybe that is what God is doing in you right now.
Maybe He is not merely examining your prayer.
Maybe He is exposing the wound underneath it.
The insecurity.
The jealousy.
The bitterness.
The need to control.
The hunger to be noticed.
The fear of being forgotten.
The resentment you baptized as “justice.”
The ambition you renamed “calling.”
The obsession you renamed “faith.”
The demand you renamed “expectation.”
And suddenly your prayer becomes much shorter.
“Jesus…
I think I wanted the gift more than I wanted You.”
That prayer can change a person.
David understood something about this kind of exposure.
Near the end of Psalm 139, after declaring that God knows him completely, he prayed:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!”
The Hebrew begins:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
ḥoqrēnî ʾEl wədaʿ ləvāvî
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
Think about the courage of that prayer.
Not:
“Search my enemies.”
Not:
“Show me what is wrong with everybody else.”
Not:
“Vindicate me first.”
Search…
me.
That may be one of the hardest prayers you will ever sincerely pray.
“God, show me why I really want this.”
“Show me whether jealousy is hiding inside this request.”
“Show me whether I want Your glory or my recognition.”
“Show me whether I am asking for justice or secretly craving revenge.”
“Show me whether I want this relationship because it is good—or because I am terrified of being alone.”
“Show me whether I want money to become generous—or because possessions make me feel significant.”
“Show me whether I want influence to point people toward Jesus—or because being invisible terrifies me.”
“Search me.”
Be careful praying that.
God loves you too much to cooperate with every illusion you have about yourself.
Sometimes He answers that prayer by exposing something you hoped was not there.
And when He does…
do not run.
Repent.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of what is destroying you.

The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a change of mind and turning. Biblical repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed that you were exposed. It is a reorientation toward God.
And grace does not say:
“Your motives do not matter.”
Grace says:
“Bring even your corrupted motives to Jesus.”
Bring the envy.
Bring the pride.
Bring the lust for recognition.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the obsession.
Bring the need to control everything.
Bring the prayers you now realize were selfish.
Bring the prayers that were half faith and half fear.
Bring the ugly parts.
Christ already knows.
You are not informing Him.
You are surrendering.
And perhaps the prayer you have been begging God to answer needs to become another prayer entirely.
Instead of:
“God, give me this.”
Maybe:
“God, if this will draw me closer to Christ, give it according to Your wisdom. If it will become an idol, protect me from it.”
Instead of:
“God, make them pay.”
Maybe:
“God, bring justice according to Your righteousness, protect those who are being harmed, and keep bitterness from owning my heart.”
Instead of:
“God, make everybody see me.”
Maybe:
“Jesus, make Your name great, even if obedience means I remain unseen.”
Instead of:
“God, make my plans work.”
Maybe:
“Father, establish what honors You, redirect what does not, and give me enough faith to trust You when Your answer contradicts mine.”
That kind of prayer is frightening because surrender means giving God permission to contradict you.
We often want divine assistance.
Jesus calls us into divine lordship.
We want God to bless the blueprint.
He wants the blueprint placed on the altar.
We want Him to improve our kingdom.
Jesus tells us:
“Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness…”
Matthew 6:33
There is the great rearrangement.
His Kingdom first.
His righteousness first.
His glory first.
His will first.
And strangely…
that does not make prayer colder.
It makes prayer freer.
Because now you do not have to manipulate God.
You do not have to manufacture enough emotion to convince Him.
You do not have to believe that if you repeat the perfect formula, heaven becomes obligated to obey you.
You come as a child to a Father.
Jesus taught His disciples to begin:
“Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done…”
Matthew 6:9–10
Before daily bread…
His name.
Before our needs…
His Kingdom.
Before our plans…
His will.
And then we ask.
Daily bread.
Forgiveness.
Deliverance.
Everything necessary.
Christian prayer is not desirelessness.
It is reordered desire.
It is the human heart learning to say:
“God, here is what I want.
But You are God.
I am not.
You know what I cannot know.
You see tomorrow.
I do not.
You understand my heart better than I understand myself.
So I am asking boldly…
but I am surrendering completely.”
Maybe you have been angry because God has not answered something.
Maybe you stopped praying.
Maybe you secretly decided He did not care.
Maybe you watched somebody else receive what you begged Him for and whispered:
“Why them?”
And perhaps today God is not giving you the entire explanation.
Perhaps He is simply asking you to trust His character.
Not every unanswered prayer means your motives were wrong.
Please understand that.
Scripture does not permit us to look at every suffering believer and accuse them of defective faith or selfish motives simply because their prayer has not been answered the way they hoped.
Paul pleaded concerning his “thorn in the flesh,” yet God did not remove it. Instead, the Lord told him:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”
2 Corinthians 12:9
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane and still went to the cross.
So unanswered prayer is not automatic proof of sinful motives.
Sometimes the motive needs purification.
Sometimes the timing is different.
Sometimes God has purposes we cannot yet understand.
Sometimes the answer is no.
Sometimes the answer is wait.
Sometimes God gives something different from what we imagined.
And sometimes we may never receive a complete explanation in this life.
Faith is not pretending those realities do not hurt.
Faith is trusting God inside the mystery.
But James 4:3 still refuses to let us avoid the question:
Why am I asking?
That question might expose you.
Let it.
Because exposure in the hands of Jesus can become the beginning of healing.
Maybe your greatest prayer tonight should not be:
“God, give me what I have been asking for.”
Maybe it should be:
“God, give me a heart that wants what You want.”
And if you cannot honestly pray that yet?
Start even smaller.
“Jesus, make me willing to become willing.”
There is no need to perform here.
God already sees you.
And perhaps someone reading this right now knows exactly what has been exposed.
You have been asking God to change everyone around you while resisting His attempt to change you.
You have been praying for an open door because your identity has become attached to what is behind it.
You have been asking for vindication because bitterness has quietly become your companion.
You have been praying for blessing when what your soul desperately needs is surrender.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Not because typing a phrase earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because commenting saves you. Only Christ saves.
Let it simply become your public confession that you no longer want to hide your motives from the One who already sees them.
Let other believers see you.
Let somebody pray with you.
We were never meant to pretend our way through discipleship.
Not ten.
One.
The friend who has been angry at God.
The believer struggling with unanswered prayer.
The person confusing ambition with calling.
The person quietly wondering whether God still hears them.
If Christ has given us light, we should not be ashamed to let that light point beyond ourselves.
Because someday you may desperately want something again.
You may become convinced that one particular answer is the only answer you can survive.
Come back here.
Read James 4.
Read Matthew 6.
Read Mark 14.
Read Psalm 139.
Then ask again:
“Jesus, why do I want what I want?”
We want this community to remain a place where Scripture confronts us, grace restores us, and Jesus—not personalities, platforms, possessions, or applause—remains at the center.
We give and serve freely because grace has already been freely given to us in Christ.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and continue deeper with us:
He wants you.
Your heart.
Your sin.
Your ambitions.
Your wounds.
Your secret motives.
Your unanswered questions.
Your plans.
Your future.
Your surrender.
Because Christianity was never about persuading God to become a servant of our desires.
It is about sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ and gradually transformed until even our desires begin bowing before Him.
So tonight…
pray.
Ask boldly.
Cry if you need to.
Tell God exactly what you want.
There is no virtue in pretending you do not care.
But after you have said everything…
leave enough silence for the prayer beneath your prayer to be exposed.
Then whisper the words that frightened Gethsemane and opened the road toward Calvary:
“Not what I will…
but what You will.”
And remember this when heaven seems silent:
Sometimes the prayer God refuses to give you is the prayer He uses to reveal you—and what He reveals, Jesus is still able to redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH FEAR AND TREMBLING” — DOES THIS MEAN WE EARN SALVATION?
paragraphs: “WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH FEAR AND TREMBLING” — DOES THIS MEAN WE EARN SALVATION?
The frightening verse that sounds like salvation depends on you—until you read the next sentence and discover Who has been working inside you all along.
There are Bible verses that comfort you immediately.
And then there are Bible verses that seem to stare straight through you.
“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.”
Philippians 2:12.
Read quickly, and those words can sound terrifying.
Work out my salvation?
Does that mean I have to earn it?
Does that mean Jesus started something at the cross, but now the rest depends on me?
What if I haven't prayed enough?
What if I keep struggling with the same temptation?
What if my obedience has been inconsistent?
What if I love Jesus, but there are days when my faith feels weak?
What if I die before I finally become the Christian I know I should be?
Maybe you know that fear.
You believe in grace...
but somewhere beneath the worship songs, church attendance, Bible verses, Christian posts, and carefully composed answers, you are quietly keeping score.
Good week: maybe God is pleased with me.
Bad week: maybe He is pulling away.
Victory over temptation: maybe I'm really saved.
Fall again: maybe I'm not.
And without realizing it, you can begin treating Jesus like He made the down payment on your salvation while you spend the rest of your life trying desperately to finish paying the balance.
But that is not what Paul said.
And the words immediately following “fear and trembling” change everything.
Paul writes:
meta phobou kai tromou tēn heautōn sōtērian katergazesthe; theos gar estin ho energōn en hymin…
“…work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure.”
Philippians 2:12–13.
Do not stop reading after verse 12.
The word “for” matters.
The command is followed by its astonishing foundation:
God is working in you.
Paul does not say:
Work hard enough so God will finally save you.
He does not say:
Work for your salvation because Christ's work was insufficient.
He does not say:
Jesus handled the cross; now you handle the rest.
Paul tells believers to work out what God Himself is at work within them to accomplish.
That distinction is enormous.
The Greek verb translated “work out” is κατεργάζεσθε — katergazesthe, from katergazomai. It carries the sense of bringing about, producing, accomplishing, or carrying something through in practice.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not tell them to manufacture salvation.
He tells them to live out the implications of the salvation that belongs to them as people in whom God is already working.
And we know this because Philippians did not begin in chapter 2.
Earlier Paul had already written:
“πεποιθὼς αὐτὸ τοῦτο, ὅτι ὁ ἐναρξάμενος ἐν ὑμῖν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐπιτελέσει…”
pepoithōs auto touto, hoti ho enarxamenos en hymin ergon agathon epitelesei…
“He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.”
Philippians 1:6.
Who began the work?
God.
Who continues working within His people?
God.
Who brings His work toward completion?
God.
So where does obedience belong?
Right where Scripture puts it.
Not as the price paid to purchase God's grace...
but as the lived response of people who have received grace and in whom God is actively working.
That matters because Christianity is neither salvation by human achievement nor a grace that leaves us unchanged.
The New Testament refuses both distortions.
Paul could hardly be clearer about the basis of salvation when he writes:
Ephesians 2:8–9.
If salvation were earned by sufficiently impressive obedience, someone could eventually stand before God and say:
I did it.
I prayed enough.
I resisted enough.
I served enough.
I gave enough.
I suffered enough.
I became righteous enough.
I earned my place here.
But heaven will never echo with redeemed sinners congratulating themselves for saving themselves.
The song of eternity is about the Lamb who was slain.
Jesus Christ receives the glory because Jesus Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that bad people can become sufficiently good to deserve God.
The scandal is that the Holy One came looking for people who could never make themselves holy enough.
The Son of God entered our ruin.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called the wandering home.
And ultimately, He carried our sin to a Roman cross.
There, Jesus did not announce:
“I have made salvation possible if you can finish the job.”
He said:
“Τετέλεσται.”
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
John 19:30.
One word.
A universe of grace.
The cross destroys our fantasy of self-salvation because if human beings could become acceptable to God through sufficient moral effort, the cross would not be our only hope.
But Scripture says:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we finally conquered every secret struggle.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
This is where some people become nervous.
“If you emphasize grace that strongly, won't people think obedience doesn't matter?”
Paul anticipated that kind of reasoning.
Grace does not make sin harmless.
Grace makes holiness possible without making holiness the purchase price of salvation.
The same Paul who says salvation is “not a result of works” immediately continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.”
Ephesians 2:10.
Not saved by good works.
Saved for good works.
Those two little words—by and for—separate the Gospel from both legalism and lawlessness.
Works are a terrible savior.
But they belong in the life of someone following the Savior.
That brings us back to Philippians.
Paul is writing to Christians.
And there is another detail easily missed when English-speaking readers encounter the phrase “work out your own salvation.”
The commands in this passage are addressed to the Philippian believers corporately. The Greek forms are plural.
Paul is speaking to a church.
That matters because the surrounding passage is deeply concerned with their shared life—humility, unity, obedience, selflessness, and living faithfully together under the lordship of Christ.
Immediately before these verses stands one of the most breathtaking descriptions of Jesus in the New Testament.
Christ Jesus,
“though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped,”
but humbled Himself,
took the form of a servant,
became obedient unto death,
“even death on a cross.”
Philippians 2:6–8.
Then God highly exalted Him.
Paul's command to work out salvation therefore does not appear in a vacuum.
It stands beneath the shadow of the cross.
The One commanding Christian obedience is the apostle who has just pointed believers toward the obedience and humiliation of Jesus Christ.
Our obedience does not compete with Christ's work.
It flows beneath it.
So what about the frightening words?
“Fear and trembling.”
Are Christians supposed to spend every morning terrified that God might revoke salvation because they made a mistake yesterday?
Again, context matters.

“Fear and trembling” is a biblical expression of profound seriousness, reverence, humility, and awe before God. Paul uses related language elsewhere, including when describing the Corinthians' reception of Titus in 2 Corinthians 7:15 and servants' conduct toward earthly masters in Ephesians 6:5.
The phrase should not be emptied of seriousness.
God is holy.
Sin is serious.
Following Christ is not a game.
Grace is not permission to make peace with rebellion.
But neither should “fear and trembling” be twisted into a picture of a redeemed child frantically attempting to earn enough points to persuade an unwilling Father to love them.
Christian reverence is not casual.
But Christian reverence also stands before the God who has revealed Himself in Jesus Christ.
There is a difference between trembling because you believe salvation depends upon your flawless performance...
and trembling because you have finally begun to understand the holiness of the God who saved you at such immeasurable cost.
One says:
I must perform so He will accept me.
The Gospel says:
In Christ I have received grace I could never deserve—how could I treat that grace casually?
Maybe this is where the verse becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps your deepest problem is not theological confusion.
Perhaps you are exhausted.
You have been trying to prove yourself to God.
Nobody knows.
You smile at church.
You post the verse.
You say, “God is good.”
You know the correct Christian vocabulary.
But secretly...
you are tired.
Tired of wondering whether you prayed correctly.
Tired of wondering whether God still wants you after what happened.
Tired of promising, “Lord, I'll never do it again,” only to find yourself fighting the same battle.
Tired of comparing your spiritual life with somebody else's highlight reel.
Tired of carrying shame from a chapter of your story you wish you could tear out.
And perhaps you have mistaken your exhaustion for evidence that Jesus has abandoned you.
Listen carefully.
Philippians 2:13 does not say:
“God worked in you until you disappointed Him.”
It says:
“θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν…”
“For it is God who works in you.”
Even your desire for holiness is not something about which you can boast.
God works “both to will and to work for his good pleasure.”
That does not make you passive.
It makes you dependent.
You repent.
You obey.
You pray.
You open Scripture.
You resist temptation.
You confess sin.
You forgive.
You reconcile.
You serve.
You pursue holiness.
You flee what is destroying you.
You put sinful patterns to death.
You keep walking when obedience hurts.
But you do these things neither to purchase the blood of Christ nor to convince God that the cross should apply to you.
You do them as someone desperately dependent upon the God who works within His people.
This is why genuine grace does something legalism never can.
Legalism may change behavior temporarily through fear of rejection.
Grace reaches the heart.
Legalism says:
Obey, and perhaps you will finally be loved.
The Gospel says:
Look at Christ. You have encountered a love you could never purchase. Now follow Him.
And when you fall?
You do not call sin righteousness.
You do not excuse it.
You do not baptize rebellion with the word “grace.”
You repent.
You confess.
You return.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this desperately needed to hear.
Return.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel worthy.
Not after you manufacture enough shame to punish yourself.
Return to Jesus.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
Think about that.
Peter had walked beside Jesus.
He had heard His voice.
Seen miracles.
Watched storms obey Him.
Declared Him to be the Christ.
And when pressure came, Peter denied that he even knew Him.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster.
Imagine remembering Jesus' words.
Luke tells us Peter went out and wept bitterly.
If Peter's story ended there, it would be a story of scandal.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, beside a charcoal fire, Jesus confronted and restored Peter.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
The man who denied Jesus three times was given three opportunities to confess his love.
Then Jesus told him:
“Follow me.”
John 21:19.
That is grace.
Not pretending Peter never failed.
Not calling denial acceptable.
Not saying repentance does not matter.
Jesus brings Peter face-to-face with what happened...
and then refuses to let Peter's worst moment become the final sentence of his life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal has never appeared in public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe yours lives in browser history.
An affair.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
A lie.
An addiction.
A secret relationship.
Religious hypocrisy.
Years wasted running from God.
Words you cannot take back.
A marriage you damaged.
A child you wounded.
A person you still cannot forgive.
A version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
The Gospel does not tell you that those things do not matter.
It tells you something infinitely more powerful.
They do not have to be the final word.
Jesus does.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
Repentance is turning from the grave because Christ is calling you toward life.
And biblical faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is entrusting yourself to Christ.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance,” carries the idea of a changed mind that expresses itself in a changed direction.
Grace does not merely comfort us while leaving us chained to the same master.
Jesus saves sinners and begins transforming them.
Slowly sometimes.
Painfully sometimes.
Through battles nobody else sees sometimes.
But genuinely.
That is why “work out your salvation” is not permission for spiritual laziness.
There is effort in Christianity.
There is warfare.
There are habits to break.
There are temptations to flee.
There are crosses to carry.
There are apologies to make.
There are relationships requiring forgiveness.
There are nights when obedience will cost you.
There are moments when following Jesus means saying no to something every nerve in your body wants to say yes to.
But effort is not earning.
A rescued drowning man may have to learn how to walk again after being pulled from the water.
His walking did not perform the rescue.
It demonstrates that the rescued life is now being lived.
And perhaps that is the sentence you should remember whenever Philippians 2:12 frightens you:
Work out what God is working in.
Read verse 12.
Then refuse to separate it from verse 13.
“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling…”
Why?
“…for it is God who works in you…”
There is responsibility.
And there is divine empowerment.
There is reverence.
And there is grace.
There is obedience.
And beneath that obedience stands the finished work of Christ.
The Christian life is not:
“Jesus, watch me save myself.”
It is:
“Jesus, apart from You I have nothing. Keep changing me.”
So examine yourself.
Not because introspection can save you.
But because grace invites honesty.
Are you using grace as an excuse for a sin you have no intention of surrendering?
Repent.
Are you trying to earn through religious performance what Christ offers by grace?
Repent.
Are you hiding something because you are terrified Jesus will reject you if you finally bring it into the light?
Bring it to Him.
Are you spiritually exhausted because Christianity has quietly become a performance review?
Look again at the cross.
The nails were not driven through your hands.
The crown of thorns was not placed upon your head.
You were not scourged for your redemption.
You did not carry the sin of the world.
Jesus did.
And He rose.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of humanity climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners.
Jesus entered our darkness.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus conquered death.
Jesus rose.
Jesus calls sinners to repent and believe.
Jesus transforms those who belong to Him.
Jesus receives the glory.
So yes...
work out your salvation with fear and trembling.
Take holiness seriously.
Take repentance seriously.
Take obedience seriously.
Take sin seriously.
But take Jesus even more seriously.
Because the verse does not end with trembling.
It leads you straight to the God who is working within His people.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding behind religious performance, do not hide again.
Be honest before God.
Maybe somebody else scrolling through the comments needs to discover that they are not the only Christian still fighting.
And if Christ has already been restoring pieces of your life you thought were permanently destroyed, tell somebody what He has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to interrupt another person's despair.
Not because every sentence needs remembering, but because there may come a night when accusation returns and you need Philippians 2:12–13 in front of your eyes again.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to prove that you love God.
Christ alone saves.
But if this truth helped you, sharing it is one practical way you can help place the Gospel in front of someone who may never walk into a church.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior is a requirement for glorifying God. Scripture never teaches that, and we will never pretend that it does.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But voluntary generosity and sharing can be genuine ways of participating in Gospel ministry.
Because somewhere tonight there is a Peter hearing the rooster.
Somewhere there is a prodigal rehearsing an apology but afraid to come home.
Somewhere there is a Christian convinced that yesterday's failure canceled Calvary.
Somewhere there is someone whispering:
After everything I've done, could Jesus possibly still want me?
And perhaps God will use something as ordinary as your share to put the answer in front of them.
Yes, repentance matters.
Yes, obedience matters.
Yes, holiness matters.
But none of them replaces the Savior.
We do not obey so that someday Jesus might finally become enough.
We obey because Jesus is enough—and the God who saved us has not stopped working in us.
So when shame tells you your worst chapter has already determined your ending, remember the fisherman beside the charcoal fire.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember tetelestai.
Remember Philippians 2:13.
And remember this:
Your failure may explain a chapter of your story, but when a repentant sinner falls into the hands of Jesus, failure does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY FOR CENTURIES?
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY FOR CENTURIES?
The Bible records Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon having multiple wives. So was God approving it—or was Scripture showing us something far more devastating about the human heart?
There is a question many Christians quietly hope nobody asks.
Because once someone asks it, the easy answers begin falling apart.
“If marriage is supposed to be between one man and one woman, why did God allow men in the Bible to have multiple wives?”
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
These are not obscure villains hidden in forgotten genealogies.
They are some of the most recognizable names in Scripture.
And some of them had more than one wife.
So what are we supposed to do with that?
Pretend those passages are not there?
Explain them away?
Say, “Well, that was the Old Testament,” and quickly change the subject?
No.
The Bible does not need us to protect it from difficult questions.
It needs us to read it carefully enough to hear what it is actually saying.
Because one of the greatest mistakes we can make when reading Scripture is assuming that everything the Bible describes is something God prescribes.
The Bible records murder.
It does not endorse murder.
It records adultery.
It does not endorse adultery.
It records deception, incest, betrayal, drunkenness, idolatry, slavery, violence, political corruption, family dysfunction, and catastrophic moral failure.
Why?
Because the Bible is not propaganda for humanity.
It is the story of God entering humanity's wreckage to redeem it.
And that changes the question.
Maybe we should not merely ask:
“Why did God allow polygamy?”
Maybe we should also ask:
“What happened when human beings departed from God's original design?”
Because the first marriage in Scripture does not begin with a king surrounded by wives.
It begins in a garden.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Moses.
Before Israel.
Before sin had shattered human relationships.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 says in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzov-’ish ’et-’aviv ve’et-’immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
The words matter.
וְדָבַק — vedavaq.
He clings. He cleaves. He holds fast.
And then:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
Not merely a contract.
Not merely sexual access.
Not merely reproduction.
A covenantal union in which two lives become joined.
This is where the biblical story of marriage begins.
And centuries later, when religious leaders tried to drag Jesus into an argument about what Moses permitted, Jesus did something extraordinary.
He went backward.
Past Moses.
Past Israel's legislation.
Past centuries of broken human history.
Back to creation.
Jesus pointed to God's intention “from the beginning.”
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Scripture sometimes shows God dealing with human beings not as humanity ought to be, but as fallen humanity actually is.
Jesus gives us one of the clearest examples when discussing divorce.
The Greek of Matthew 19:8 reads:
λέγει αὐτοῖς ὅτι Μωϋσῆς πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ἐπέτρεψεν ὑμῖν ἀπολῦσαι τὰς γυναῖκας ὑμῶν, ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως.
The crucial word is:
σκληροκαρδίαν — sklērokardian.
Hardness of heart.
Jesus says Moses permitted divorce because of their hardness of heart, then immediately says:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs.
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
Notice what Jesus is doing.
Permission within a fallen society is not automatically identical to God's original ideal.
That verse is specifically about divorce, not polygamy, so we should not put words into Jesus' mouth and claim He was directly explaining every Old Testament plural marriage.
But the principle He reveals is extremely important.
God can regulate human brokenness without declaring that brokenness beautiful.
And suddenly, much of the Old Testament begins to make more sense.
When polygamy first explicitly appears in the biblical narrative, it does not appear in Eden.
It appears in Genesis 4.
And the man associated with it is Lamech.
“And Lamech took unto him two wives.”
That sentence is more significant than it first appears.
Lamech belongs to Cain's line, and the narrative soon presents him boasting about violence and vengeance.
The Bible does not introduce polygamy by saying, “And God commanded Lamech to take another wife.”
It simply tells us what Lamech did.
Humanity has left Eden.
Sin is spreading.
Violence is escalating.
Relationships are fracturing.
And now the marriage pattern of Genesis 2 has also been disrupted.
Then the pattern continues through history.
Abraham has Sarah and Hagar, and what follows?
Pain.
Jealousy.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
A woman fleeing into the wilderness.
A household torn apart.
Jacob ends up with Leah and Rachel.
What follows?
Rivalry.
Tears.
Competition.
A woman desperately longing to be loved.
Sisters measuring their worth against one another through children.
Read those chapters slowly enough and they stop feeling like ancient genealogy.
They begin feeling like a wounded family sitting around your dinner table.
Leah knows what it feels like to lie beside someone whose heart belongs somewhere else.
Rachel knows what it feels like to look at another woman's children while carrying an ache she cannot fix.
Jacob's household becomes a battlefield of longing, favoritism, jealousy, fertility, rejection, and competition.
The Bible never has to insert a sentence saying, “Polygamy causes complications.”
It shows you the complications.
That is one of Scripture's most powerful teaching methods.
Sometimes God gives you a command.
Sometimes He gives you a consequence.
David's household becomes even darker.
His multiplication of wives exists alongside a royal family increasingly marked by sexual sin, rivalry, betrayal, violence, and bloodshed.
Then comes Solomon.
The king who had almost everything.
Wisdom.
Wealth.
Power.
Prestige.
Influence.
And women.
Many women.
But centuries before Solomon was born, Deuteronomy had already warned Israel's future king not to multiply wives for himself lest his heart turn away.
The warning was there.
The boundary was there.
And Solomon crossed it spectacularly.
His marriages became entangled with the turning of his heart toward other gods.
So the Bible is not hiding the wreckage.
It is displaying it.
That matters because people sometimes reason like this:
“David had multiple wives, therefore God approved of multiple wives.”
But that logic would force us to approve everything else David did simply because Scripture records him doing it.
David committed adultery.
David arranged Uriah's death.
Scripture records those acts with brutal honesty precisely because biblical heroes are not the Savior.
That title belongs to Someone else.
The Bible is filled with deeply flawed men because the Bible is not ultimately about the greatness of men.
It is about the faithfulness of God.
Abraham cannot carry the story.
Jacob cannot carry it.
Moses cannot carry it.
David cannot carry it.
Solomon cannot carry it.
Every human hero eventually develops cracks.
And through those cracks Scripture keeps whispering:
You need Someone better.
This is where the question becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have never practiced polygamy.
But you know what it means to ask God to tolerate something He never called good.
We all know how to do that.
“God understands.”
“Everybody does it.”
“It isn't hurting anyone.”
“This is just how life works now.”
“Surely God won't mind.”
We become remarkably sophisticated theologians when we are defending the thing we do not want to surrender.
And this is where the ancient question about polygamy stops being an argument about ancient Near Eastern households and becomes a mirror.
Because the deeper story is about the terrifying patience of God with sinners.
Why didn't God destroy Jacob the moment his family became dysfunctional?
Why didn't He abandon David?
Why didn't He erase Israel every time they wandered?
Why did He continue working through people whose lives were painfully inconsistent with His holiness?
Because patience is not approval.
Mercy is not endorsement.
And God's willingness to work through broken people does not mean He celebrates their brokenness.
If it did, none of us would have hope.
Think about that.
If God only worked through people whose lives already perfectly reflected His design, Scripture would be very short.
And your story and mine would never make it past the first page.
God meets people in the wreckage.
But He does not call the wreckage Eden.
That distinction is everything.
The Old Testament law itself sometimes regulates situations it does not present as creation's ideal.
There are laws dealing with households where a man has two wives. Those laws protect rights and restrict injustice within realities already present in Israelite society.
Regulation is not necessarily celebration.
A guardrail beside a dangerous road is not an advertisement for driving off the cliff.
It exists because the danger is real.
And God repeatedly acts in Scripture to restrain the damage human sin does to other human beings.
This is why Deuteronomy 17:17 becomes so important.
Israel's king was warned not to “multiply wives” for himself so that his heart would not turn away.
God was not giving kings an unlimited divine endorsement of royal harems.
The Torah itself placed a warning directly against their multiplication.
And the biblical history eventually shows exactly why.
Solomon becomes the living cautionary tale.
But there is another witness people often overlook.
Malachi describes the wife as a covenant companion and confronts men for faithlessness toward “the wife of your youth.”
Marriage is not treated casually.
It is covenant.
And when Jesus arrives, He does not announce a revolutionary definition invented in first-century Galilee.
He reaches back to Genesis.
The beginning.
The garden.
The one-flesh union.
Then the New Testament continues with language such as Paul's requirement that an overseer be:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, an expression meaning a “one-woman man,” traditionally rendered “the husband of one wife.”
Christ does not move God's people farther from covenant faithfulness.
He calls them deeper into it.
But even that is not the deepest point.
Because Christian marriage ultimately points beyond marriage.
Paul says in Ephesians 5 that the mystery points to Christ and the Church.
And now everything changes.
Jesus does not collect disposable brides.
He has a Bride.
He does not exploit her.
He gives Himself for her.
He does not use covenant for His convenience.
He sheds His blood to establish covenant.
He does not abandon His Bride when she becomes difficult to love.
He sanctifies her.
Cleanses her.
Keeps her.
Loves her.
The ultimate answer to humanity's distorted love is not merely better marriage legislation.
It is Jesus Christ.
Because sin always takes what God made beautiful and bends it inward toward ourselves.
Love becomes possession.
Leadership becomes domination.
Sex becomes consumption.
Marriage becomes convenience.
Power becomes entitlement.
And religion itself can become camouflage.
But then Jesus walks into the wreckage.
Not to pretend the wreckage is beautiful.
To redeem the people trapped inside it.
That is the Gospel.
Christ does not stand at the edge of our scandals shouting instructions about how to climb out.
He enters our world.
He touches lepers.
He eats with sinners.
He speaks with the sexually broken.
He confronts hypocrites.
He welcomes repentant people.
He carries a cross.
And on that cross, the sinless Bridegroom dies for an unfaithful people.
That is why grace must never be confused with permission.
Grace is not God saying:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace is God saying:
“Your sin mattered enough that My Son bled for it—and I love you enough not to leave you enslaved to it.”
Maybe that is the sentence someone reading this needed.
Because perhaps your scandal has nothing to do with multiple wives.
Maybe it is pornography nobody knows about.
Maybe it is adultery you have carefully hidden.
Maybe it is emotional infidelity you keep calling “just friendship.”
Maybe it is bitterness toward your spouse.
Maybe your marriage is collapsing quietly while your Facebook photographs still look perfect.
Maybe you have been betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you are divorced and carrying shame you cannot seem to put down.
Maybe you grew up inside a home where “marriage” meant screaming, fear, manipulation, abandonment, or violence.
Maybe the word “family” does not make you feel safe.
Maybe it makes your chest tighten.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that brokenness was never broken.
The Gospel is the announcement that brokenness does not have to have the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why our message will always be:
Not from scandal to denial.
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to religious pretending.
From scandal...
to repentance.
From scandal...
to forgiveness.
From scandal...
to restoration.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite history by pretending it never happened.
He rewrites what history gets to become in the hands of a redeemed person.
Peter still denied Him.
But denial did not write Peter's final chapter.
Paul still persecuted Christians.
But persecution did not write Paul's final chapter.
The woman caught in adultery really had a scandal.
The Samaritan woman's relational history was real.
The thief really was dying beside Jesus for crimes he had committed.
The Gospel does not require fake backstories.
It creates redeemed endings.
And perhaps that is why the uncomfortable marriages of the Old Testament were never edited out.
We need to see them.
We need to see Abraham's household hurting.
We need to hear Leah crying.
We need to watch David's family fracture.
We need to see Solomon surrounded by abundance while his heart wanders.
Because Scripture is showing us again and again:
Having more does not heal the heart.
More women could not satisfy Solomon.
More power could not satisfy David.
More children could not make Leah feel fully loved by Jacob.
More human affection cannot fill the place designed for God.
And thousands of years later, we are still doing the same thing.
More followers.
More money.
More attention.
More relationships.
More sexual experiences.
More purchases.
More achievements.
More validation.
More.
More.
More.
And still...
the heart aches.
Perhaps the real scandal is not simply that ancient men accumulated wives.
Perhaps the scandal is that humanity keeps trying to multiply created things until they become enough to replace the Creator.
They never do.
Only Christ is enough.
So why did God allow polygamy to continue for centuries?
Scripture does not give us one isolated verse saying, “Here is the complete philosophical explanation for why I tolerated every plural marriage in biblical history.”
We should be humble enough to admit that.
But Scripture gives us enough to see the pattern.
God's creation establishes the one-flesh marriage union.
Human sin distorts what God made.
Biblical narrative honestly records that distortion.
The law restrains injustice within a fallen society and specifically warns kings against multiplying wives.
The narratives repeatedly expose the suffering surrounding plural marriages.
The prophets call God's people toward covenant faithfulness.
Jesus points back to what was true “from the beginning.”
And the New Testament ultimately reveals marriage as a sign pointing toward Christ and His Bride.
The Bible's trajectory is not from monogamy toward increasingly celebrated polygamy.
It points back toward covenant fidelity.
Back toward the beginning.
And ultimately forward toward the Bridegroom.
Jesus.
Maybe you started reading because you wanted an answer about polygamy.
But perhaps the Holy Spirit has brought you somewhere more uncomfortable.
Your own heart.
Because it is easy to put Solomon on trial.
Harder to ask what we have multiplied until it began stealing our hearts from God.
It is easy to analyze Jacob's dysfunctional home.
Harder to confront what we keep tolerating in ours.
It is easy to debate David's failures.
Harder to confess our own.
So don't leave this article merely knowing more.
Ask the question that matters:
“Jesus, what have I been asking You to tolerate that You are asking me to surrender?”
Stay there for a moment.
No performance.
No church language.
No pretending.
Just you and Christ.
If something came to mind...
don't run from it.
Run to Him.
Repentance is not the doorway into humiliation.
For the person who comes to Christ, repentance is the doorway home.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Not “some unrighteousness.”
Not “everything except the thing you're ashamed to name.”
All.
The blood of Jesus is stronger than the chapter you wish you could erase.
So if this exposed something hidden in you, you do not need to explain the details publicly. But you can make a simple declaration of surrender.
Let other believers know they are not the only ones fighting.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach people who desperately need it.

Invite your family. Invite the friend who has drifted. Invite the believer who is barely holding on. Invite the skeptic with hard questions. Even invite the person who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to them.
There is only one Savior.
There is only one cross.
There is only one blood sufficient to cleanse sin.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful answer hidden inside this uncomfortable question.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its people because God was never building His story around flawless human beings.
He was leading us toward a flawless Savior.
Abraham failed.
Jacob failed.
David failed.
Solomon failed.
Israel failed.
We fail.
But Jesus Christ remained faithful.
And when our sin multiplied, grace did not become permission to remain unchanged.
Grace came looking for us...
to forgive us,
to transform us,
and to bring us home.
God may meet you in the ruins, but He loves you too much to let the ruins become the name of your final chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A KING WAS SO HUMILIATED BY A WOMAN THAT HE ASKED HIS SERVANT TO KILL HIM
paragraphs: A KING WAS SO HUMILIATED BY A WOMAN THAT HE ASKED HIS SERVANT TO KILL HIM
He murdered his brothers to seize power. He burned people alive to keep it. But in the end, one unnamed woman standing above him shattered the reputation he was desperately trying to save.
There are deaths in the Bible that make you grieve.
There are deaths that make you tremble.
And then there are deaths that read like warnings carved into stone.
Abimelech’s was one of them.
He had spent his life reaching upward.
Up toward power.
Up toward recognition.
Up toward a throne he was never meant to possess through bloodshed.
But when his story finally ended, he was not standing above a kingdom.
He was lying beneath a tower.
Bleeding.
Broken.
His skull crushed by something dropped from the hands of a woman whose name Scripture does not even tell us.
And even then…
even with death closing in…
even after violence had brought him to the ground…
Abimelech was still worried about what people would say about him.
That may be the most frightening part of the story.
Because some people would rather control the story told about their death than surrender the life they still have to God.
Judges 9:53–54 records the moment:
“וַתַּשְׁלֵךְ אִשָּׁה אַחַת פֶּלַח רֶכֶב עַל־רֹאשׁ אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וַתָּרִץ אֶת־גֻּלְגָּלְתּוֹ”
The Hebrew describes a woman throwing an upper millstone upon Abimelech’s head and crushing his skull.
Then comes the detail that exposes what was still alive inside him even as his body was dying.
He urgently called the young man carrying his weapons and told him, in essence:
“Draw your sword and kill me, so they cannot say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’”
And his armor-bearer thrust him through.
Abimelech died.
But before we rush past that scene, we need to understand how he got underneath that tower.
Because nobody suddenly becomes Abimelech in Judges 9:54.
The man beneath the millstone had been forming for years.

Abimelech was a son of Gideon, also called Jerubbaal. After Gideon died, Abimelech went to his mother’s relatives in Shechem and appealed to blood loyalty. He essentially asked them whether they would rather be ruled by Gideon’s many sons or by one man who was their own flesh and blood.
The men of Shechem listened.
Money was taken from the temple of Baal-berith.
Abimelech used it to hire reckless men.
Then came the horror.
Judges 9 tells us that Abimelech went to his father’s house at Ophrah and killed his brothers—seventy sons of Jerubbaal—“on one stone.”
One survived.
Jotham.
Imagine the silence after that slaughter.
Brothers who had grown up together.
Men with names.
Memories.
Mothers.
Stories.
Futures.
Gone.
And what was Abimelech reaching for through all that blood?
Power.
He wanted to be king.
There is something terrifying about ambition when it becomes more precious than obedience.
There is something deadly about the human heart when it begins saying:
“I deserve this.”
“I need this.”
“I cannot let anyone stand in my way.”
“I have come too far to turn back now.”
That voice does not always begin with murder.
Sometimes it begins much smaller.
A lie you refuse to confess.
A relationship you know dishonors Christ but will not surrender.
A secret addiction protected behind passwords and deleted histories.
A bitterness you keep feeding because forgiveness feels too much like losing.
A ministry that slowly becomes more about being seen than seeing Jesus glorified.
A reputation you polish publicly while your private life collapses.
A hunger to win every argument.
A desperate need to prove people wrong.
A refusal to apologize because admitting guilt would wound your pride.
That is why Abimelech’s story should not merely make us stare at him.
It should make us examine ourselves.
Because sin rarely walks into your life announcing where it intends to take you.
It whispers.
Just this once.
Nobody needs to know.
You deserve it.
Protect yourself.
Protect your image.
Protect your position.
Do whatever it takes.
Then one compromise becomes another.
And another.
Until one day you discover that the thing you thought you controlled has been controlling you.
Abimelech reached the throne.
But getting what you desperately wanted is not always evidence that God approved the way you got it.
That sentence may hurt somebody reading this.
Because we live in a world that loves visible success.
Numbers.
Money.
Influence.
Titles.
Platforms.
Applause.
People assume that if something grew, God must have blessed it.
If somebody became powerful, God must have favored him.
If the door opened, God must have opened it.
Scripture is far less naive.
Abimelech became king.
And Abimelech was still under judgment.

Jotham had already spoken a prophetic warning against Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem. In his parable, the trees sought a king, and eventually the bramble accepted the position, declaring that if the trees truly wanted it to reign, they should take refuge beneath its shadow—but otherwise fire would come from the bramble.
The warning was devastating.
And eventually the alliance built around Abimelech began consuming itself.
Judges 9:23 says God sent an evil spirit—or a harmful spirit—between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and their relationship fractured.
The conspiracy that helped establish him became part of the environment that destroyed him.
The violence he used to climb upward eventually came back downward.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable in its symmetry.
Abimelech had killed his brothers on a stone.
Abimelech would eventually be struck down by a stone.
He had used violence to establish his name.
Now he was dying while desperately trying to protect that name.
He had climbed over bodies for power.
Now his own body was collapsing beneath a tower.
Judges does not leave the meaning of his death for us to invent.
It tells us.
“Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.”
That is Judges 9:56.
This was judgment.
Not random bad luck.
Not merely battlefield misfortune.
Not simply an embarrassing military accident.
Scripture interprets the event morally.
God was bringing Abimelech’s evil back upon him.
But there is another detail that should stop us cold.
When the millstone struck him, Abimelech apparently understood that he was dying.
He had only moments.
Maybe seconds.
And what mattered to him?
His reputation.
“Lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’”
Think about that.
His skull was crushed.
Death was approaching.
His kingdom could not save him.
His power could not save him.
His soldiers could not save him.
His reputation could not save him.
Yet reputation was still what occupied his mind.
He wanted control over the final sentence.
He could not control death anymore.
So he tried to control the obituary.
And thousands of years later, the irony is devastating.
His plan failed.
Because Scripture still tells us exactly what he did not want people saying.
A woman brought him down.
In fact, generations later, when David sent Uriah into danger, Joab anticipated David’s anger over soldiers approaching too close to a wall. He told the messenger to remind David of Abimelech:
“Who struck Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone upon him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez?”
That is recorded in 2 Samuel 11:21.
The reputation Abimelech tried to erase became the reputation history remembered.
Pride promised him control.
Pride could not even control one sentence after his death.
And maybe that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
How much of your life is being spent trying to control what people think about you?
How many things have you refused to confess because somebody might look at you differently?
How many tears have you swallowed because you need everyone to believe you are strong?
How many times have you said, “I’m okay,” when your soul was screaming?
How much sin survives because exposure feels more frightening than bondage?
Some people are not afraid of sin anymore.
They are afraid of being caught.
There is a difference.
Some are not heartbroken that they betrayed God.
They are heartbroken that somebody discovered it.
Some do not want repentance.
They want reputation management.
And the Gospel will not merely renovate your reputation.
Jesus came to resurrect dead hearts.
That is where Abimelech’s story forces us toward a question far bigger than Abimelech.
What do you do when the truth about you is ugly?
What do you do when you cannot rewrite your own past?
What do you do with the scandal?
The affair.
The addiction.
The rage.
The years wasted.
The secret messages.
The hypocrisy.
The selfishness.
The pride.
The betrayal.
The things nobody knows.
The things everybody knows.
The thing you would give anything to undo.
You can spend the rest of your life protecting your image.
Or you can bring the truth into the light of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Christianity does not teach that you save yourself by becoming better at hiding your scandal.
Christianity announces that the sinless Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus did not need reputation management.
He needed no cover story.
He committed no sin.
Yet He willingly entered our shame.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Stripped.
Crucified.
And unlike Abimelech, Jesus did not use another man’s weapon to escape humiliation.
He endured the cross.
Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus endured the cross, “despising the shame,” and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
The King of kings willingly endured public shame to rescue people drowning in private shame.
Do you see the contrast?
Abimelech was willing to die differently so people would speak differently about him.
Jesus was willing to die publicly so sinners could become different through Him.
Abimelech clung to reputation.
Jesus embraced the cross.
Abimelech spilled the blood of his brothers to gain a kingdom.
Jesus shed His own blood to redeem brothers and sisters for His Kingdom.
Abimelech destroyed others to exalt himself.
Christ humbled Himself to save others.
One king shows us what pride does when given power.
The true King shows us what holy love does with power.
Jesus Christ is not merely another character in the story of humanity.
He is the Savior toward whom our desperate need points.
And perhaps you are reading this while carrying something you have tried desperately to hide.
You know exactly what it is.
Nobody had to name it.
Your mind went there before your eyes reached this sentence.
You have become skilled at changing the subject inside your own soul.
You worship.
You smile.
You post Scripture.
You encourage other people.
You say “God is good.”
And He is.
But somewhere behind all of that is a locked room you keep hoping Jesus will not ask you to open.
He already knows what is inside.
And He is still calling you.
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
Abimelech’s story should destroy that illusion.
But because the Gospel announces something Abimelech never understood:
You do not have to protect a false version of yourself when grace offers you a new life.
Repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

The Greek word commonly translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν—homologōmen—from the idea of acknowledging or agreeing. Biblical confession is not negotiating with God about whether our sin was really sin.
It is coming into agreement with the truth.
“Yes, Lord.”
“It was sin.”
“I did it.”
“I cannot cleanse myself.”
“I need mercy.”
“I need Christ.”
That is radically different from Abimelech.
His dying concern was essentially:
Do not let them remember me this way.
Grace invites you to say:
Jesus, You already know me completely. Save me anyway.
And He does not save repentant sinners because they deserve another chance.
He saves because Christ is sufficient.
The cross is sufficient.
His blood is sufficient.
His resurrection is sufficient.
His grace is sufficient.
There is no sinless person reading this article.
Romans 3:23 says all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
But the story does not end at Romans 3:23.
Romans 6:23 tells us that although the wages of sin is death, the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That means your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Your failure does not become your savior, and neither does your success.
Jesus does.
This does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
Forgiveness does not make evil harmless.
Grace does not turn repentance into an excuse.
Sometimes wounds must be repaired.
Sometimes trust must be rebuilt.
Sometimes consequences remain.
But in Christ, condemnation does not get the final word over the redeemed.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
That is 2 Corinthians 5:17.
The Gospel does not say:
Hide better.
It says:
Come into the light.
The Gospel does not say:
Save your reputation.
It says:
Lose your life for Christ and find it.
The Gospel does not say:
Rewrite your own story until people admire you.
It says:
Surrender your story to the One who raises the dead.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have been living like Abimelech in one quiet way.
Not murdering brothers.
Not conquering cities.
But protecting the image.
Terrified of being known.
Terrified of confession.
Terrified that if people saw the real battle behind the profile picture, the church clothes, the family photos, the ministry position, the laughter, they would leave.
Listen carefully.
Do not confuse hiding with healing.
They are not the same thing.
A wound hidden beneath clothing is still a wound.
A chain covered by religious language is still a chain.
A secret sin decorated with excuses is still sin.
And Jesus loves you too much to call darkness light.
He calls you out because He calls you home.
Repent.
Turn.
Confess.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Stop trying to write an ending where everyone thinks you were stronger than you really were.
You were never meant to be your own savior.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “no more hiding.”
Not because strangers need your private details.
They do not.
You do not need to publicly disclose sensitive sins to prove repentance.
But perhaps those three words can become a line in the sand between pretending and surrender.
No more hiding.
If your spirit is exhausted and you need believers to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ has already been restoring parts of your life you once thought were beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not become their prosecutor.
Pray for them.
We have enough spectators.
The Church needs brothers and sisters willing to carry one another toward Jesus.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow.
Not as a superstition.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Send it to the believer who has drifted.
The person ashamed to return to church.
The friend who thinks God could never forgive what they have done.
The family member who needs Jesus.
Even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely about pretending to be good.
Let them discover that the Gospel is actually for people who finally admit they are not.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, and keep your eyes on Jesus Christ, follow and stay close.
Do it as support for Gospel work, not as a transaction with God.
You cannot purchase God’s blessing.
You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot earn heaven by supporting a ministry.
But if this work genuinely glorifies Christ and serves people with biblical truth, voluntarily supporting it is one practical way you can help that work continue and reach others.
Come to Jesus.
Not to us.
Not to a platform.
Not to merchandise.
Not to a religious image.
Jesus.
Because one day, every reputation we spent years constructing will become irrelevant.
The applause will stop.
The followers will move on.
The titles will belong to somebody else.
Our carefully managed public identities will disappear.
And what will matter is not whether we successfully convinced the world that we were good.
What will matter is whether we belonged to Christ.
Abimelech spent his final breath trying to protect his name.
Do not spend your life doing the same.
Let them know you needed mercy.
Let them know you were a sinner rescued by grace.
Let them know there were chapters you are ashamed of but a Savior you are not ashamed of.
Let them know Jesus found you in the wreckage.
Let them know repentance was painful but freedom was worth it.
Let them know your scars did not disappear overnight, but Christ taught you they no longer had to define you.
Let them know you stopped hiding.
And when people ask how someone with your past can still have hope…
tell them about the cross.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them about the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Tell them that grace is not permission to remain who you were.
Grace is the miracle that means, through Christ, you do not have to.
Abimelech desperately wanted history to remember a different sentence about his death.
You still have time to surrender the sentence being written by your life.
Do not die protecting the version of yourself Jesus came to crucify and make new.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEX WITH YOUR SPOUSE COULD MAKE BOTH OF YOU “UNCLEAN” UNTIL EVENING—SO WHY DID GOD SAY THAT?
paragraphs: SEX WITH YOUR SPOUSE COULD MAKE BOTH OF YOU “UNCLEAN” UNTIL EVENING—SO WHY DID GOD SAY THAT?

Leviticus 15 contains one of the Bible’s most misunderstood statements about sex—and when you finally understand what “unclean” meant, the passage stops sounding shameful and begins revealing something breathtaking about holiness, the human body, and why we desperately need Jesus.
There is a verse in Leviticus most Christians have probably never heard preached from a pulpit.
Maybe because it feels awkward.
Maybe because it raises questions we would rather not ask in church.
Maybe because the moment we read the word “unclean,” our modern minds immediately hear another word:
Dirty.
And that is where the misunderstanding begins.

Leviticus 15:18 speaks with startling directness about a man and woman having sexual intercourse involving semen and says that afterward both were to wash themselves with water and remain “unclean until evening.”
Read the Hebrew slowly:
“וְאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אִישׁ אֹתָהּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע וְרָחֲצוּ בַמַּיִם וְטָמְאוּ עַד־הָעָרֶב”
Ve’ishshah asher yishkav ish otah shikhvat-zara, verachatsu vammayim, vetam’u ad-ha‘arev.
In context, the meaning is essentially:
When a man lies with a woman in an intercourse involving semen, they are to bathe in water, and they will be ritually unclean until evening.
There it is.
No euphemistic escape.
No pretending the Bible does not talk about bodies.
No pretending God becomes embarrassed when the subject turns to sex.
But here is the question that changes everything:
If sexual intimacy between husband and wife was part of God’s good design, why could it make them “unclean”?
Was God calling marital sex sinful?
Was He saying intercourse contaminated a husband and wife?
Was sexual pleasure somehow shameful?
Was the marriage bed dirty?
No.
And confusing ritual uncleanness with moral wickedness can badly distort what Leviticus is actually teaching.
The Hebrew word appearing here comes from טָמֵא—ṭāmēʾ.
It refers in this context to ritual impurity.
That is not automatically the same thing as committing a moral sin.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because only two verses earlier, Leviticus says something similar about a man having an emission of semen.
He washes.
He remains ritually unclean until evening.
The text does not say he committed adultery.
It does not say he lusted.
It does not say he rebelled against God.
It describes a bodily condition that temporarily affected ritual status within Israel’s covenant worship system.
Move through Leviticus 15 and the pattern becomes impossible to ignore.
Discharges.
Semen.
Menstruation.
Blood.
Sexual intercourse involving semen.
Bodies doing what bodies do.
Some conditions were abnormal and required more extensive purification. Others were ordinary bodily events accompanied by temporary ritual impurity.
This is why one of the most important things you can remember when reading Leviticus is this:
“Unclean” does not automatically mean “sinful.”
A person could become ritually unclean without having committed a moral transgression.
And suddenly the scandal begins to change shape.
Because perhaps the shocking part of Leviticus 15 is not that God hated human bodies.
Perhaps it is that God cared enough about His people to teach them that approaching His holy presence was not casual.
Israel was learning to live with the presence of the Holy One in their midst.
Everything surrounding the sanctuary preached a sermon.
Clean.
Unclean.
Holy.
Common.
Approach.
Wait.
Wash.
Separate.
Return.
Again and again, Israel was being taught that God is not merely an accessory to ordinary life.
He is holy.
Human beings do not stroll casually into divine holiness on their own terms.
And yet notice something beautiful.
Leviticus 15:18 does not command a sacrifice for ordinary marital intercourse.
There is no condemnation of husband and wife for having sex simply because the temporary ritual impurity followed.
They wash.
They wait until evening.
Life continues.
That should immediately warn us against turning this passage into a declaration that marital sexuality is inherently dirty.
The rest of Scripture will not allow that interpretation anyway.
The Bible begins with God creating humanity male and female.
Before sin enters the world, God tells them to “be fruitful and multiply” in Genesis 1:28.
Genesis 2 presents husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
Before the serpent.
Before the fall.
Before shame entered Eden.
Marriage and sexual union did not originate in a brothel.
They originated in the creative purpose of God.
Sin corrupted human sexuality.
Sin did not create sexuality.
That distinction matters.
Hebrews 13:4 later speaks of marriage as honorable and the marriage bed as undefiled, while simultaneously condemning sexual immorality and adultery.
So Scripture refuses both extremes.
It refuses the lie that sex itself is dirty.
And it refuses the lie that whatever we desire sexually must therefore be holy.
God created sexuality.
Therefore God—not culture, pornography, Hollywood, lust, trauma, loneliness, TikTok, our hormones, or our private fantasies—has the authority to define its boundaries.
That may be where this ancient verse suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because our generation does not suffer from a lack of information about sex.
We are drowning in it.
Images.
Videos.
Jokes.
Secret messages.
Affairs hidden behind passwords.
Pornography watched after everyone falls asleep.
Bodies compared with edited bodies.
Marriages quietly bleeding because one spouse feels unwanted.
Singles carrying memories they wish they could erase.
Believers worshiping on Sunday while fighting fantasies on Monday.
People who have confused being desired with being loved.
People who gave their bodies hoping somebody would finally stay.
People who were used.
People who used others.
People who crossed boundaries.
People who were sinned against.
People carrying shame for things they chose.
People carrying shame for things they never chose.
And somewhere beneath all that noise is a human heart whispering:
Am I dirty now?
Can God still want me?
