Can Jesus really cleanse this?
That is where Leviticus becomes more than an ancient book about washing.
Because all those washings create a hunger.
Water could wash the body.
But what washes the conscience?
Waiting until evening could restore ritual status.
But what happens when the stain is inside us?
What happens when the problem is not merely something that happened to the body but something coming from the heart?
Jesus eventually put His finger directly on that wound.
In Mark 7, Christ teaches that genuine moral defilement comes from within—from the human heart—and He names things such as sexual immorality, adultery, greed, deceit, pride, and other evils.
Jesus moves the spotlight somewhere terrifying.
Inside.
That means the deepest human problem cannot be solved with soap.
You can wash your hands and still hate someone.
You can shower and still commit adultery in your imagination.
You can put on church clothes while hiding pornography on your phone.
You can sing worship songs while secretly manipulating someone sexually.
You can appear clean to everybody watching you and still know there is a locked room inside your soul that you desperately hope nobody opens.
Religion can teach you how to look clean.
Jesus came to make sinners new.
And that is where the story stops being merely about Leviticus 15.
It becomes about you.
About me.
About every person who has ever whispered:
“If people knew everything about me, would they still love me?”
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody caught you.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents never discovered it.
Maybe the browser history disappeared.
Maybe the messages were deleted.
Maybe years have passed.
Maybe everyone thinks you are the strong Christian.
But you remember.
And sometimes the enemy knows exactly which memory to replay.
That night.
That person.
That photograph.
That affair.
That addiction.
That decision.
That season.
That violation.
That secret.
And shame says:
Look at you.
Dirty.
Ruined.
Disqualified.
Unwanted.
Beyond restoration.
But shame does something the Gospel does not do.
Shame gives you an identity based upon your worst chapter.
Jesus confronts sin, but He does not need to leave the repentant sinner imprisoned inside it.
This is why the Gospel is so much bigger than behavior modification.
Jesus did not come merely to make dirty people behave more respectably.
He came to redeem sinners.
The cross is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross is the terrifying proof that sin matters more than we wanted to admit—and the breathtaking proof that God’s mercy reaches farther than we imagined.
Jesus Christ bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The One who had no sin entered our death so sinners could receive His life.
This is where all those ancient categories begin pointing beyond themselves.
Human beings need cleansing deeper than water.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation.
We need new hearts.
We need grace.
We need Christ.
The letter to the Hebrews repeatedly contrasts the old covenant’s external regulations and ceremonial washings with the deeper cleansing accomplished through Christ.
Hebrews 9 asks how much more the blood of Christ can cleanse our conscience so that we may serve the living God.
Think about those words.
Cleanse the conscience.
Because perhaps that is where you have been bleeding.
Nobody else sees it.
But you do.
Your conscience remembers what everybody else forgot.
And perhaps you have spent years trying to wash yourself.
More church attendance.
More promises.
More resolutions.
More religious activity.
“I will never do it again.”
“This is the last time.”
“God, forgive me, and I promise…”
Then you fell again.
And eventually you stopped believing you could ever really change.
Listen carefully.
Repentance is not pretending your sin was small.
Grace is not pretending your sin was harmless.
Forgiveness is not God lowering His holiness until your behavior becomes acceptable.
The Gospel is better.
Christ took sin seriously enough to die for sinners.
And grace is powerful enough to transform the people it forgives.
Maybe you need to stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Maybe you need to stop protecting the very secret that is poisoning you.
Maybe you need to confess.
Maybe you need accountability.
Maybe you need to tell your spouse the truth.
Maybe you need to delete what keeps pulling you backward.
Maybe you need to flee rather than negotiate with temptation.
Maybe you need mature pastoral help.

Maybe wounds from sexual abuse require compassionate, trauma-informed care—and if someone sinned against you, their evil is not transformed into your moral guilt simply because you were the one wounded by it.
And maybe, beneath everything else, you need to come home to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Now.
Because nobody gets clean enough to qualify for grace.
Grace is for people who finally realize they cannot save themselves.
This is why Leviticus 15:18 should never be weaponized to make faithful husbands and wives ashamed of marital intimacy.
The passage belongs to Israel’s ritual purity system.
It describes temporary ritual impurity following intercourse involving semen; it does not pronounce marital intercourse itself a moral transgression.
But neither should we swing to the opposite extreme and pretend the Bible has nothing serious to say about sex.
Scripture celebrates sexuality within God’s design while relentlessly confronting sexual sin.
God cares what we do with our bodies because our bodies matter.
Marriage matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Covenant matters.
Purity matters.
The person you desire is not an object.
The body on your screen belongs to a human being made in the image of God.
Your spouse is not merchandise for your appetite.
Your singleness is not permission for secret sexual slavery.
And your past is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
That last sentence may be the one somebody needs tonight.
Your past is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Maybe somebody told you that what happened to you made you permanently dirty.
Maybe religious people knew how to expose your scandal but never showed you the road home.
Maybe you became convinced that Christianity was simply God standing over you with folded arms saying:
“Disgusting.”
But look at Jesus.
Watch how He deals with sinners who come to Him.
He tells the truth about sin.
He never needs to rename darkness as light.
Yet He receives the broken.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
He gives people futures their histories said they did not deserve.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing justice.
He rewrites the sinner’s future through redemption.
There is an enormous difference.
The Gospel does not say:
“You never sinned.”
The Gospel says there is forgiveness in Christ.
The Gospel does not say:
“Your wounds never mattered.”
The Gospel says Jesus can meet you inside them.
The Gospel does not say:
“Stay exactly as you are.”
Jesus says, in effect:
Follow Me.
Come out of darkness.
Bring Me what you have been hiding.
Stop running.
Repent.
Believe.
Walk with Me.
Become new.
And perhaps that is why the words “until evening” feel unexpectedly beautiful when we read Leviticus 15 today.
The uncleanness was not forever.
Evening came.
The waiting ended.
There was a way back.
And while we should not flatten Israel’s ritual purity laws into simplistic Christian metaphors, the biblical storyline ultimately gives us something far greater than an evening sunset.
It gives us a cross.
It gives us an empty tomb.
It gives us a Savior.
There are stains water cannot touch.
But there is no repentant sinner beyond the mercy of Jesus Christ.
So if this article exposed something you have kept hidden, do not turn this moment into another five minutes of religious emotion before returning to the same chains.
Respond.
Pray.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help.
Return to Christ.
Not because commenting magically defeats temptation.
It does not.
But sometimes refusing to hide is the first crack in the wall.
If what you need most right now is prayer, simply write:
And if Jesus has already brought you through sexual brokenness, addiction, betrayal, shame, or a season you thought would destroy you, your testimony may become somebody else’s reason not to give up.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Then tell as much of your testimony as wisdom allows.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescue.
We are people whose only hope is a Rescuer.
Not merely because sharing helps a page grow.
Someone may be married and ashamed to ask this question.
Someone may have misunderstood Leviticus and concluded that God considers marital intimacy dirty.
Someone may be trapped in pornography.
Someone may believe sexual failure has permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may have been sexually wounded and still believes another person's sin made them worthless.
Put truth where shame can find it.
And if tagging someone regarding sexual struggles would embarrass or expose them, do not do that publicly. Send the article privately instead.
Love protects people even while truth confronts darkness.
Because someday someone may ask you:
“Why did Leviticus say sex made people unclean?”
And now you know the answer is far richer than:
“Because sex was dirty.”
It wasn't that simple.
Ritual impurity was not identical to moral guilt.
Marital intimacy was not thereby condemned.
The holiness laws taught Israel to distinguish categories of clean and unclean as they lived around God's sanctuary and covenant presence.
And across the unfolding biblical story, our attention is ultimately driven toward humanity's deeper problem:
Not merely bodies needing water…
but sinners needing redemption.
It cannot.
Not because sending money earns forgiveness.
It never will.
It does not.
And we will not tell you that supporting Gospel Warrior is a biblical requirement for glorifying God.
God is glorified through a life surrendered to Christ.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, discipling, and placing Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door before encountering it on a screen.
Every sincere share can carry biblical truth into a home we could never personally enter.
Every thoughtful comment can help another believer realize they are not fighting alone.
Every save keeps truth within reach.
Every follow keeps you connected to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite Christians who have grown cold.
Invite seekers.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Let them encounter Jesus for themselves.
If you believe work like this should continue…
If you want difficult passages explained instead of avoided…
If you want Scripture without sugarcoating, grace without compromise, conviction without hopelessness, and discipleship centered on Jesus Christ…
But whether you ever give one cent or not, hear this clearly:
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8).
The greatest response you could ever make to this article is not financial.
It is surrender.
Give Christ your sin.
Give Him your secret.
Give Him your sexuality.
Give Him your marriage.
Give Him your singleness.
Give Him the memories you cannot erase.
Give Him the desires you cannot control alone.
Give Him the room in your heart you keep locking whenever He gets too close.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where shame has been lying to you.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Offer forgiveness where Christ is calling you to release vengeance.
Seek wise help where wounds run deeper than an article can reach.
Then get up and follow Jesus.
Because perhaps the most astonishing thing hidden beneath this strange verse in Leviticus is not that two married people could become ritually unclean until evening.
It is that the God whose holiness taught Israel to wash is the same God who entered our broken world in Jesus Christ to accomplish the cleansing no basin of water could ever provide.
Your scandal may explain a chapter.
It does not have to write the ending.
Jesus still does His greatest work in lives everyone else thought were already ruined.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH FEAR AND TREMBLING”—THE VERSE THAT SOUNDS TERRIFYING UNTIL YOU READ THE NEXT SENTENCE
paragraphs: “WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH FEAR AND TREMBLING”—THE VERSE THAT SOUNDS TERRIFYING UNTIL YOU READ THE NEXT SENTENCE

Philippians 2:12 has frightened sincere Christians for generations. But Paul was not telling you to earn what Jesus purchased. He was telling you what happens when grace gets so deeply inside a human life that it can no longer remain hidden.
There is a particular kind of fear that only a sincere Christian understands.
It usually comes quietly.
Not during worship when your hands are raised.
Not when you are posting the Bible verse.
Not when everyone around you thinks your faith is strong.
It comes at 1:17 in the morning when the room is dark, the phone is finally silent, and there is nobody left to impress.
You remember the sin you promised God you would never commit again.
You remember how angry you became.
What you watched.
What you said.
What you secretly wanted.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The Bible that stayed closed.
The compromise nobody knows about.
And somewhere beneath all the Christian vocabulary, a frightening question begins whispering:
What if I’m not really saved?
Then you remember something Paul wrote:
“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.”
And suddenly the whisper becomes louder.
Work it out?
Does that mean salvation depends on me?
Does God forgive me and then wait to see whether I perform well enough to stay forgiven?
Should Christians spend their lives terrified that one terrible failure might erase the cross?
If you have ever read Philippians 2:12 and felt your stomach tighten, you need to keep reading.
Because one of the most frightening-sounding commands in the New Testament is followed immediately by one of its most comforting truths.
Paul writes:
Philippians 2:12–13
And the Greek brings the relationship between those two statements into beautiful focus:
“μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου τὴν ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίαν κατεργάζεσθε, θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν…”
meta phobou kai tromou tēn heautōn sōtērian katergazesthe, theos gar estin ho energōn en hymin…
In a close, wooden rendering:
“With fear and trembling, work out your own salvation, for God is the One working in you…”
Do not miss the word for.
Paul does not say:
“Work out your salvation because God has stopped working and everything depends on you.”
He says essentially the opposite.
Work it out…
because God is working in.
That changes everything.
The Greek verb translated “work out” is κατεργάζεσθε — katergazesthe.

Paul is not commanding the Philippians to manufacture a salvation they do not possess. The language points toward bringing something about, carrying it through, producing its consequences—working something into its appropriate expression.
There is an enormous difference between working for salvation and working out salvation.
You cannot work out what has never first been worked in.
Think of it this way.
An apple tree does not produce apples so that someday it might become an apple tree.
It produces apples because that is what it already is.
Fruit does not purchase identity.
Fruit reveals life.
That is why biblical Christianity can say without contradiction that salvation is entirely dependent upon the grace of God and yet that grace produces a transformed life.
Paul himself writes elsewhere that we are saved by grace through faith, not as the result of works, and then immediately says believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace excludes works as the basis of salvation while establishing good works as part of salvation’s resulting life.
You are not obeying so that Jesus might finally decide to save you.
You obey because the Jesus who saves sinners does not leave them untouched.
And this becomes even clearer when you notice what comes immediately before Philippians 2:12.
Paul has just taken us to Jesus.
Not merely to Christian discipline.
Not merely to moral improvement.
To Christ.
Philippians 2 describes the One who existed in the form of God, humbled Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
Then God highly exalted Him.
Every knee will bow.
Every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
And then Paul says:
Therefore…
Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.
That “therefore” matters.
The command stands beneath the shadow of the cross and before the throne of the exalted Christ.
This is not Paul handing frightened sinners a ladder and saying, “Climb high enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
The ladder could never reach heaven.
So Christ came down.
Jesus humbled Himself.
Jesus obeyed.
Jesus went to the cross.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Jesus is Lord.
And because salvation belongs to Him, those who belong to Him are called to live like His salvation is real.
That is where the “fear and trembling” belongs.
The Greek is φόβου καὶ τρόμου — phobou kai tromou.
Fear and trembling.
We should not sanitize those words until they mean nothing more than polite admiration. There is genuine gravity here.
But neither should we distort them into the picture of a redeemed child cowering before an unpredictable Father, wondering whether God is waiting for an excuse to throw him away.
In this context, the fear is bound up with the overwhelming seriousness of standing before God, belonging to Christ, and recognizing that the holy God Himself is at work within His people.
There is awe here.
Reverence.
Sobriety.
Holy seriousness.
The realization:
God is here.
God is working in me.
My life belongs to Jesus.
Sin is not a toy.
Grace is not cheap.
The cross is not trivial.
Eternity is real.
And perhaps this is where the verse becomes uncomfortable again—but uncomfortable in the way we actually need.
Because some of us have spent years wanting reassurance without repentance.
We want Jesus to silence the consequences while leaving our idols untouched.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
Grace without holiness.
A Savior who rescues us from hell but never interferes with our habits.
We say, “Nobody is perfect,” when sometimes what we really mean is, “Please stop asking me to fight this.”
We say, “God knows my heart,” forgetting that this should make us tremble before it makes us comfortable.
Yes.
He knows your heart.
Every room in it.
Every locked door.
Every hidden browser tab.
Every private conversation.
Every resentment you rehearse.
Every person you secretly envy.
Every compromise you have renamed “struggle” because calling it sin would require you to confront it.
Every tear you never showed anybody.
Every prayer you were ashamed to pray.
Every relapse.
Every wound.
Every excuse.
Every genuine attempt to crawl back toward Him.
He knows.
And still…
Jesus went to the cross for sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel says your sin was so serious that the Son of God shed His blood—and His grace is so astonishing that His blood is sufficient for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
That means “work out your salvation” is not permission to become casual about sin.
But neither is “fear and trembling” permission to become obsessed with earning God's love.
Both errors take your eyes off Christ.
Legalism says:
Look at your performance.
Carelessness says:
Your performance doesn't matter.
The Gospel says:
Look at Jesus—and because He is Lord, follow Him.
The legalist obeys hoping to become accepted.
The Christian obeys because in Christ he has received grace.
The careless person uses grace as permission to remain unchanged.
The transformed believer discovers that grace does something far more powerful.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace changes what we love.
Grace makes the forgiven sinner want to become like the Savior who forgave him.
And transformation can hurt.
Ask Peter.
He once looked Jesus in the face and essentially declared that even if everybody else abandoned Him, Peter would remain.
Hours later, beside a fire, Peter denied that he even knew Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine that moment.
The sound slicing through the night.
The memory of Jesus' words.
Peter realizing that the man he thought he was had just collapsed in public.
Scripture tells us Peter went out and wept bitterly.
That was fear and trembling of another kind.
The death of self-confidence.
But Peter's scandal was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus came looking for him.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Jesus confronted Peter.
Restored Peter.
Commissioned Peter.
And the mouth that once said, “I do not know Him,” would become a mouth proclaiming Christ.
That is Gospel territory.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not calling darkness light.
Not explaining away sin.
But meeting disgraced sinners with a crucified and risen Savior who can write something after the sentence they thought was the end.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your greatest spiritual battle is happening behind a smile.
You attend church.
You know when to say amen.
You know the songs.
You know the language.
But you also know what happens when nobody is watching.
Paul's words reach into that room.
“Not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence…”
In other words:
Who are you when the spiritual authority figure leaves?
Who are you when the pastor cannot see?
When your spouse cannot see?
When your parents cannot see?
When your Christian friends cannot see?
When nobody would ever know?
That is precisely where lived-out salvation becomes visible.
Christianity performed for an audience is easy.
Obedience in secret is different.
Paul wanted believers whose faith did not depend upon Paul standing in the room.
Because ultimately Paul was never the One working inside them.
God was.
And then comes verse 13.
The sentence exhausted Christians desperately need.
“For it is God who works in you…”
The Greek expression is breathtaking:
θεὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν
theos gar estin ho energōn en hymin
“for God is the One working in you.”

The word translated “working” is connected to ἐνεργέω — energeō, from which English eventually receives language such as “energy,” though we should allow the Greek word to carry its own meaning rather than reading modern English backward into it.
Paul's point is greater anyway.
The Christian life is not merely you trying harder for God.
God Himself is at work in His people.
And Paul becomes extraordinarily specific.
God works in you…
“both to will and to work for his good pleasure.”
Even the willing.
Even the desire.
Have you ever hated the fact that part of you still wanted sin?
Have you ever prayed something like:
“Jesus, I don't even know how to want You the way I should. Please change what I want.”
That prayer may be closer to Philippians 2:13 than you realize.
God works not merely upon behavior but upon desire.
He changes the “want.”
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes through discipline.
Sometimes through tears.
Sometimes through Scripture exposing the thing we desperately wanted to justify.
This does not make us passive.
Paul does not say:
“God works in you, therefore do nothing.”
He says:
God works in you…
therefore work it out.
Divine action does not eliminate Christian obedience.
It empowers it.
You repent.
God is working.
You resist temptation.
God is working.
You open Scripture when your flesh would rather scroll endlessly.
God is working.
You confess what pride wanted hidden.
God is working.
You forgive when bitterness wants revenge.
God is working.
You fall and return to Christ instead of running deeper into darkness.
God is working.
You begin wanting holiness more than the sin that once controlled you.
God is working.
Not because every effort earns another percentage point of salvation.
But because salvation is alive.
This is why genuine grace cannot be reduced to a transaction that leaves a person permanently indifferent to Christ.
The New Testament does not know a Christianity in which Jesus is merely an insurance policy for the afterlife while somebody else remains lord of the present.
Jesus saves us as Lord.
And His salvation reaches into actual life.
Your relationships.
Your sexuality.
Your money.
Your speech.
Your pride.
Your bitterness.
Your secret life.
Your ambitions.
Your entertainment.
Your wounds.
Your habits.
Your treatment of people who cannot benefit you.
Everything eventually comes beneath the question:
Does Jesus get this too?
And that may be the question somebody reading this has been avoiding.
You gave Jesus Sunday.
But not the relationship.
You gave Him the worship songs.
But not the addiction.
You gave Him the Christian posts.
But not the private messages.
You gave Him your public testimony.
But there is one locked room inside you where the sign still says:
Mine.
And Christ does not expose that room because He delights in humiliating you.
He exposes darkness because He loves you too much to call your chains freedom.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation says:
“There is no way home.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Jesus.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because you finally understand that the thing you were embracing is killing you and the Christ you were avoiding is your only hope.
And when you come?
You do not come boasting about your record.
You come with empty hands.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ receives those who come to Him.
Christ forgives.
Christ cleanses.
Christ changes people.
Then, for the rest of our lives, what He has placed within begins appearing without.
Sometimes beautifully.
Sometimes awkwardly.
Sometimes through victories that make us weep with gratitude.
Sometimes through battles that reveal how desperately dependent we still are upon grace.
That is why mature Christianity becomes less impressed with itself, not more.
The closer you get to the holiness of God, the less interested you become in pretending your righteousness originated with you.
You begin to understand why Paul could speak about exertion and grace in the same breath.
Christian obedience is real.
Christian effort is real.
Spiritual discipline is real.
Putting sin to death is real.
Perseverance is real.
But underneath every genuine movement toward Christ stands a deeper confession:
God is at work in me.
That keeps holiness from becoming pride.
And grace from becoming laziness.
So if you are reading Philippians 2:12 because you are terrified that one imperfect day means you must somehow re-earn the blood of Jesus, read verse 13.
If you are reading verse 13 as an excuse to remain comfortable in deliberate sin, read verse 12.
Keep them together.
Always.
Work out…
because God works in.
Fear and trembling…
because the living God is involved.
Obedience…
because Jesus is Lord.
Grace…
because you could never save yourself.
Transformation…
because the Savior who justifies sinners also refuses to abandon His people to the darkness from which He rescued them.
Maybe you failed yesterday.
Repent.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Come into the light.
Maybe your spiritual life feels numb.
Cry out to Christ.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity while privately drifting from Jesus.
Stop performing.
Come home.
Maybe you have been trying so hard to prove yourself worthy that Christianity has become one long panic attack.
Look again at the cross.
You will never improve upon Jesus' sacrifice.
You cannot add one ounce of saving merit to His blood.
Your confidence is not that you performed flawlessly.
Your confidence is Christ.
And precisely because Christ is worthy, grace teaches us not to treat sin casually.
This is the holy tension.
No boasting.
No pretending.
No cheap grace.
No self-salvation.
Just sinners being transformed by the God who saves them.
So tonight, when nobody else is watching, perhaps the most spiritual thing you can do is stop pretending.
Put the phone down.
Sit quietly before God.
Tell Him the truth.
Name the sin.
Name the fear.
Name the bitterness.
Name the exhaustion.
Name the thing you keep protecting.
And pray:

“Jesus, I cannot save myself. I cannot change myself apart from Your grace. Forgive me. Change what I desire. Teach me to obey You. Let what You are doing inside me become visible in the way I live. I belong to You.”
Then get up tomorrow and walk.
Not to purchase salvation.
Because Christ purchased sinners with His blood.
Not to impress God.
Because your hope rests in Christ.
Walk because grace has called you out of darkness.
Walk because Jesus is Lord.
Walk with reverence because God is holy.
Walk with confidence because God is working.
Walk with humility because even your strength to walk is grace.
And when you stumble, do not make peace with the mud.
Return to Jesus.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until one day faith becomes sight.

It is a practical way for those who are able and willing to support this Gospel-centered work so that more people can encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the message of Jesus Christ.
Invite your family. Invite the friend who is struggling. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the seeker with difficult questions. Even invite the person who does not yet believe.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot earn the cross.
You cannot impress your way into resurrection life.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
So work out what God is working in.
Tremble—not because Christ's cross is weak, but because the God who saved you is holy.
Obey—not to make Jesus love you, but because the Jesus who loved sinners unto death is worthy of everything.
Repent when you fall.
Receive His mercy.
Rise again.
Follow Him.
And never confuse the unfinished chapters of your transformation with the absence of the Author.
Your failure may explain yesterday, but when Jesus takes hold of the story, your failure does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS CHRISTIANITY ABOUT FOLLOWING RULES?
paragraphs:
IS CHRISTIANITY ABOUT FOLLOWING RULES?
If Christianity is just “be good, obey the rules, and try harder,” then why did Jesus have to die?
There is a version of Christianity that can make you exhausted without ever making you free.
Do this.
Don’t do that.
Read more.
Pray harder.
Stop failing.
Be better.
Try again.
And somewhere between another promise to God and another private failure, you begin wondering whether Christianity is really just an impossible list of rules with Jesus’ name written across the top.
You love God.
Or at least you want to.
But there are things about yourself you don’t want anybody to see.
The thoughts.
The habits.
The anger.
The secret compromises.
The nights when temptation won.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The Bible collecting dust while your phone gets hours of your attention.
The guilt you carry into church beneath clean clothes and a practiced smile.
And perhaps the most painful part is that you already know many of the rules.
Knowing them did not save you.
That is exactly where we need to understand Christianity correctly.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that bad people can save themselves by becoming better rule-followers.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners who could never rescue themselves have been pursued by a holy God through Jesus Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
The Bible does contain commands. Many of them.
Jesus did not abolish holiness. He did not turn obedience into something optional. He never preached a sentimental gospel where sin no longer mattered.
Jesus said:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
— John 14:15
So Christianity is certainly not anti-obedience.
But notice the order.
“If you love me…”
Then obedience.
That is radically different from saying, “Obey enough so that maybe I will love you.”
One produces desperate religious performance.
The other produces obedience flowing from relationship with Christ.
And perhaps this is where some of us have misunderstood God for years.
We have been trying to use obedience as currency.
We think:
Maybe if I pray enough, God will accept me.
Maybe if I stop this sin, He will finally want me.
Maybe if I attend church consistently, give money, serve people, read Scripture, clean myself up, and become respectable enough, I can finally stand before Him without shame.
But the Gospel destroys that entire system of spiritual bargaining.
Paul writes:
— Ephesians 2:8–9
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Favor given, not wages earned.
And that matters because Christianity begins with something human pride hates admitting:
You cannot save yourself.
Not because obedience is bad.
Because your problem runs deeper than behavior.
Scripture calls it sin.
The biblical picture is not merely that humanity occasionally breaks some divine regulations. Sin alienates us from God and leaves us unable to manufacture our own righteousness before Him.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23
All.
The respectable religious person.
The addict.
The pastor.
The prisoner.
The woman carrying a secret she has never told anyone.
The man everybody thinks has his life together.
The teenager hiding behind humor.
The church member who knows every worship song but has quietly become cold toward Christ.
You.
Me.
All.
And if Christianity were merely about following rules, the Gospel would not be good news.
It would be a scoreboard.
And every one of us would eventually discover that we lost.
This is why one of the most haunting Hebrew words in Scripture matters.
תּוֹרָה — Torah.
It is commonly translated “law,” but its semantic range includes instruction or teaching. God’s law reveals His holy character and teaches His people how they are to live.
The problem was never that God’s commands were evil.
Paul says plainly:
“So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.”
— Romans 7:12
The problem is us.
A mirror can reveal dirt on your face.
It cannot wash your face.
In a similar way, God’s righteous standard exposes what sin has done to us, but the law is not a ladder by which sinners climb into justification.
Paul writes:
— Romans 3:20
Read that again.
The law exposes.
Jesus saves.
And suddenly the cross begins making sense.
If human beings could become righteous before God simply by trying harder, Calvary would be unnecessary.
If morality could save us, Jesus would not have needed nails.
If religious achievement could reconcile sinners to God, there would have been no reason for the Son of God to bear the cross.
But Christianity does not point to a ladder reaching from earth to heaven.
It points to Christ coming down for us.
John’s Gospel says:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
— John 1:14
God did not shout instructions from a safe distance.
The eternal Son entered human history.
Jesus touched lepers.
He ate with people society despised.
He confronted hypocritical religion.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He wept.
He suffered.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was crucified.
And He rose again.
This is not the story of humanity successfully reaching God through religious performance.
It is the story of God acting to redeem sinners through His Son.
And there is a scene in Jesus’ ministry that makes this almost painfully clear.
A Pharisee named Simon invited Jesus to eat with him.
Then a woman entered.
Luke describes her simply as “a woman of the city, who was a sinner.”
She knew what people thought of her.
Imagine walking into a room where your reputation arrives before you do.
Imagine every eye knowing something about your past.
Imagine whispers that do not even need words.
She came to Jesus carrying an alabaster flask of ointment.
Then she stood behind Him weeping.
Her tears fell onto His feet.
She wiped them with her hair.
She kissed His feet.
She anointed them.
And Simon watched.
But he did not see repentance.
He saw scandal.
He thought:
“If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him…”
— Luke 7:39
There it is.
Religion looking at a broken person and seeing only a category.
Sinner.
Dirty.
Unworthy.
Disqualified.
But Jesus knew exactly who was touching Him.
That was the point.
She was not exposing information Jesus did not know.
She was bringing her brokenness to Someone who already knew.
Jesus told Simon a story about two debtors whose debts were canceled, then exposed the difference between Simon’s cold reception and the woman’s overflowing response.
And then Jesus said words she may have desperately needed to hear:
“Your sins are forgiven.”
— Luke 7:48
Not hidden.
Forgiven.
Not excused.
Forgiven.
Not renamed.
Forgiven.
That is grace.
Grace does not look at evil and call it good.
Grace looks at guilty people who come to Christ and offers what they could never purchase for themselves.
Forgiveness.
This is why the Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance,” matters so much.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It involves a genuine turning—a changed mind and orientation toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our self-esteem while leaving us enslaved to the very sins destroying us.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Mark records Jesus proclaiming:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.”
— Mark 1:15
Grace is free.
Grace is not cheap.
There is a difference.
You cannot purchase salvation.
Christ purchased redemption at a cost we could never pay.
Peter writes that believers were ransomed not with silver or gold,
“but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot.”
— 1 Peter 1:19
So what happens to obedience?
It finally gets put in its proper place.
We do not obey Christ in order to force Him to save us.
Those who belong to Christ are called to obey because He has saved them, because they love Him, because His Spirit is at work in them, because grace does not merely pardon—it transforms.
That is why stopping at Ephesians 2:9 gives an incomplete picture.
Immediately after saying salvation is not the result of works, Paul continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.”
— Ephesians 2:10
Do you see it?
Not saved by good works.
Saved for good works.
Works are not the root of our salvation.
They become fruit.
Jesus gives a similar picture:
“I am the vine; you are the branches.”
— John 15:5
A branch does not grit its teeth and manufacture life.
It abides.
Life flows from the vine.
Then fruit appears.
This is why Christianity without transformation is also a distortion of the Gospel.
Grace is not permission to make peace with sin.
Paul anticipated exactly that misunderstanding:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!”
— Romans 6:1–2
The Gospel rescues us from two cliffs.
On one side is legalism:
“I obey, therefore God must accept me.”
On the other is lawlessness:
“God accepts me, therefore obedience does not matter.”
The Gospel says something far more beautiful:
In Christ, salvation is God’s gift received through faith, and the grace that forgives begins transforming the person who has been forgiven.
You are not being invited merely to become religious.
You are being called to Christ.
And maybe this is where the article stops being theology on a screen and becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading this have been performing Christianity.
You know how to look saved.
You know when to say amen.
You know the songs.
You know the vocabulary.
You know which sins Christians condemn publicly.
But you also know what happens when nobody is watching.
Maybe you have spent years polishing the outside while something inside you has been dying.
Jesus spoke directly to religious leaders who mastered appearances while neglecting inward reality.
He said:
“For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence.”
— Matthew 23:25
That warning should frighten every person who knows how to perform religion.
Because Jesus is not looking for a better costume.
He wants the heart.
And somebody reading this may have the opposite problem.
You are not pretending to be righteous.
You feel too ruined to come home.
You think your scandal is bigger than His grace.
You have crossed lines.
Broken vows.
Hurt people.
Returned to sins you swore you would never touch again.
Maybe you have whispered:
“God must be finished with me.”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin is insignificant.
It tells you that Christ is a greater Savior than you imagined.
Paul wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners…”
— 1 Timothy 1:15
Jesus did not come looking for people who could prove they never needed saving.
He came to save sinners.
That does not mean everybody is automatically reconciled to God regardless of their response to Christ.
The New Testament repeatedly calls people to repentance and faith.
But it means your past does not possess greater saving power than Jesus possesses redeeming power.
Look at Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then denied Jesus three times.
Imagine hearing the rooster.
Imagine remembering Christ’s prediction.
Imagine realizing that, at the moment courage mattered, you failed.
Luke says Peter “went out and wept bitterly.”
But Peter’s failure did not become the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
“Do you love me?”
Jesus asked.
And then:
“Feed my sheep.”
See the movement.
Failure.
Grief.
Restoration.
Calling.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending Peter never denied Him.
Jesus rewrote Peter’s story by meeting the fallen disciple with restoring grace and calling him forward in faithful obedience.
That distinction matters.
Jesus does not redeem our stories by editing sin out of history.
He redeems us by refusing to let sin have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is Christianity.
Not “follow enough rules and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
Not “do whatever you want because grace means nothing matters.”
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Grace that forgives.
Truth that exposes.
Repentance that turns.
Faith that receives.
The Holy Spirit transforming.
A new life learning obedience from love.
And maybe now you understand why you have been so tired.
You have been trying to carry a Christianity Jesus never asked you to carry.
You have been trying to be your own savior.
Every failure becomes a verdict.
Every command becomes another weight.
Every Christian who appears stronger becomes another person to compare yourself against.
Every spiritual discipline becomes another opportunity to prove yourself.
But the Gospel says:
Stop bringing God your résumé as though Christ needs your qualifications.
Bring Him your sin.
Bring Him your shame.
Bring Him the thing you keep deleting from your history but cannot erase from your memory.
Bring Him the addiction.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The lust.
The hypocrisy.
The unbelief.
The secret life.
Bring the real you to the real Jesus.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Because repentance becomes possible when you stop hiding.
The cross already tells the truth about your sin.
It was serious enough that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And the cross tells the truth about grace.
God loved sinners enough to give His Son.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”
— John 3:16
Christianity is therefore not fundamentally a self-improvement program.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ that creates a new way of living.
Paul captures the heart of it:
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
— 2 Corinthians 5:17
Not merely a more disciplined old creation.
New.
That does not mean Christians become instantly flawless.
The New Testament itself was written to churches full of people still needing correction, repentance, growth, endurance, and sanctification.
But the direction has changed.
The allegiance has changed.
The center has changed.
Jesus is no longer an accessory to life.
He becomes Lord.
And obedience becomes something astonishing:
Not payment.
Worship.
You forgive because you have been forgiven.
You pursue purity because your body belongs to Christ.
You tell the truth because you belong to the One who is truth.
You love your enemies because your King loved His enemies.
You serve because your Lord washed feet.
You resist temptation not because resisting earns salvation, but because sin is no longer your rightful master.
You open Scripture not to accumulate spiritual points, but because you want to know the God who has spoken.
You pray not to impress heaven, but because through Christ you have access to the Father.
You obey because grace has changed what obedience means.
And when you fall?
You do not call darkness light.
You confess.
You repent.
You get up.
You run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needed tonight.
You do not have to hide.
You do not need another mask.
You need Jesus.
Not because typing words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops protecting the image.
And if you know someone who believes Christianity is nothing more than rules, share this with them.
Not to win an argument.
Send it privately to the person who thinks their past disqualifies them forever.
Because there may come another night when failure whispers that you must earn your way back to God, and you will need to remember again:
Christ is not asking you to purchase what His blood has already secured for those who trust in Him.
Salvation cannot be bought. God’s approval cannot be purchased.
Is Christianity about following rules?
Christianity includes commands, and genuine discipleship includes obedience.
But Christianity is not salvation by rule-keeping.
At its center stands a Person.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who came for sinners.
The Savior who carried the cross.
The Lamb whose blood was shed.
The risen Lord who conquered death.
The King who calls us to repent, believe, follow, abide, obey, and become His.
Rules can tell you where you went wrong.
Only Jesus can forgive you.
Rules can expose your guilt.
Only Jesus can reconcile you to God.
Rules can describe righteous living.
Only the grace of God can save sinners and begin making them new.
So stop trying to impress the One who already knows everything.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Christ.
And then obey Him—not like a terrified prisoner attempting to earn release, but as someone whose chains have been broken and whose life now belongs to the One who set him free.
Because perhaps the greatest scandal of grace is not that God lowered His standard so sinners could enter.
He did something infinitely more costly.
Christ met the demands sinners could never satisfy, bore sin in our place, rose victorious, and now offers salvation as a gift to those who trust in Him.
Your sin does not become beautiful.
Your shame does not become your identity.
Your failure does not need to become your final sentence.
Jesus takes sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith and begins writing something grace alone could write.
So when the old voice whispers, “You failed the rules again…”
Look toward the cross.
And remember:
The Gospel was never the story of how well you could save yourself. It is the story of how completely you needed Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PROVERBS 5 DOESN’T MERELY SAY “AVOID ADULTERY”—IT SAYS “ENJOY YOUR WIFE”
paragraphs: PROVERBS 5 DOESN’T MERELY SAY “AVOID ADULTERY”—IT SAYS “ENJOY YOUR WIFE”
God’s answer to forbidden desire is not merely a locked door. He points a husband back toward the woman he vowed to love—and says, “Rejoice.”
There is a devastating moment in Proverbs 5 that many people rush past.
Maybe because we already think we know what the chapter says.
Don’t commit adultery.
Don’t sleep with someone else’s wife.
Stay away from sexual temptation.
Be faithful.
All true.
But if that is all you hear when you read Proverbs 5, you have stopped reading before reaching one of the most startlingly beautiful things God says about marriage.
Because Scripture does not merely tell a husband what woman he must avoid.
It tells him what woman he should enjoy.
And that changes the entire conversation.

The father speaking to his son begins with a warning. Forbidden desire looks sweet before it becomes bitter. The temptation sounds smooth before the consequences begin screaming. What promises pleasure can eventually demand your honor, your years, your strength, your peace, your reputation, and your home.
Sin rarely introduces itself by showing you the funeral.
It shows you the flowers.
It doesn't show you the wife crying in the bedroom.
It shows you the message that made you feel wanted.
It doesn't show you the children wondering why Dad no longer lives at home.
It shows you the thrill.
It doesn't show you years of rebuilding trust.
It shows you ten minutes of secrecy.
It doesn't show you standing before God with everything exposed.
It whispers:
“No one will know.”
And then Proverbs says something terrifying:
God already does.
“For a man’s ways are before the eyes of the LORD.”
Nothing is hidden.
Not the hotel room.
Not the deleted conversation.
Not the second account.
Not the flirtation you keep calling harmless.
Not the emotional relationship you insist “isn't technically cheating.”
Not the pornography nobody knows you watch.
Not the comparison silently poisoning the way you look at your spouse.
Not the fantasy you continue feeding while physically remaining faithful.
God sees the road long before everybody else sees the wreckage.
But Proverbs 5 is not merely God standing beside the highway shouting, “DON'T GO THERE!”
There is another road.
And this is where the chapter becomes breathtaking.
“Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.”
Then comes Proverbs 5:18:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorkha barukh, uśemaḥ me'eshet ne'urekha.
A faithful sense of the Hebrew is:
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Look carefully at that word:
וּשְׂמַח — uśemaḥ.
Rejoice.
Be glad.
Take joy.
God could have stopped at prohibition.
He didn't.
He could simply have said, “Do not touch another woman.”
Instead, He turns the husband's eyes homeward.
Look at your wife.
The woman whose face you have seen tired.
The woman who has seen you without the polished version everyone else gets.
The woman who knows your strange habits, your weaknesses, your unfinished sentences, your fears, your failures.
The woman beside whom ordinary life happened.
Bills.
Children.
Laundry.
Arguments.
Sickness.
Work.
Disappointment.
Birthdays.
Funerals.
Morning breath.
Unanswered prayers.
Unexpected laughter.
Years.
And Scripture says:
Rejoice in her.
That matters because biblical faithfulness is much richer than merely avoiding another person's bed.
A marriage can contain no physical adultery and still become painfully empty.
You can remain legally married while becoming emotionally absent.
You can share an address while living separate lives.
You can sleep six inches apart and somehow feel six thousand miles away.
You can become experts at schedules, bills, children, responsibilities, groceries, church attendance, and getting through another week...
while forgetting how to delight in each other.
And perhaps one of the saddest sentences a spouse can silently carry is:
“I know you haven't left me.
But I don't know if you still want me.”
Proverbs 5 speaks directly into that distance.
The chapter's answer to adultery is not merely restraint.
It is redirected delight.
The text continues with startlingly physical language about the husband's wife, telling him to find satisfaction in her and remain captivated by her love.
God is not embarrassed by marital intimacy.
We often are.
God isn't.
We sometimes talk as though holiness means pretending married people aren't sexual creatures.
Scripture doesn't.
Sexual desire is not inherently dirty.
God created the covenant in which sexual intimacy belongs.

Genesis presents husband and wife becoming “one flesh.” Proverbs celebrates marital delight. Song of Songs speaks unabashedly of desire between lovers. The New Testament continues treating marriage as honorable and marital faithfulness as sacred.
The biblical answer to sexual chaos is therefore not hatred of sexuality.
It is holiness.
There is a difference.
Holiness doesn't say the fire is evil.
Holiness puts the fire in the fireplace so it warms the house instead of burning the house down.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that because perhaps you were taught only to fear desire.
Maybe sex was spoken about so shamefully that even after marriage you carried the shame into the marriage bed.
Maybe nobody taught you that tenderness between husband and wife could actually be received with gratitude before God.
Or perhaps your story is completely different.
Perhaps you crossed the line.
Maybe Proverbs 5 isn't theoretical for you.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you had the affair.
Maybe you became addicted to pornography.
Maybe you betrayed somebody who trusted you.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret that would change the atmosphere of your home if it were exposed.
Then don't misuse this article as an excuse to hide longer.
Sin grows remarkably well in darkness.
Jesus calls sinners into the light.
And this is where we must move from Proverbs to the heart of the Gospel.
Because Christianity's message is not:
Good people never fall.
Christianity's message is that sinners need a Savior.
David knew what sexual sin could destroy.
He took Bathsheba and arranged circumstances that resulted in Uriah's death. When Nathan confronted him, David could no longer hide behind royal power.
His response became one of Scripture's most painful prayers:
“Have mercy upon me, O God.”
That is where restoration begins.
Not with excuses.
Not with blaming your spouse.
Not with “I was lonely.”
Not with “She wasn't meeting my needs.”
Not with “He stopped paying attention to me.”
Not with “It was only online.”
Not with “Nothing physical happened.”
Repentance stops negotiating with the truth.
It confesses.
And then grace does something scandalous.
It meets the guilty person there.

This does not mean consequences disappear. Forgiveness does not make betrayal imaginary. Trust may require a long rebuilding process. Deep wounds do not close because someone says “sorry” once. In situations involving betrayal, abuse, coercion, or danger, simplistic advice about intimacy can cause further harm; wisdom, safety, truthful accountability, and qualified pastoral or professional help may be necessary.
But the Gospel announces something even our worst chapter cannot erase:
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
The ashamed.
The sexually broken.
The adulterer who repents.
The pornography addict who finally stops pretending.
The betrayed spouse trying to understand how to breathe again.
The husband realizing he spent years starving his marriage of affection.
The wife wondering whether she is still beautiful in her husband's eyes.
The single believer fighting desires nobody knows about.
The person whose past makes them wonder whether God could ever call them clean.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the edited version of us.
He died for sinners.
And resurrection means sin does not get the final sentence.
That is why our Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Not because Jesus calls evil good.
He doesn't.
Jesus rewrites everything because He confronts sin, bears judgment for sinners, offers forgiveness to those who come to Him, and begins transforming people who could never transform themselves.
Grace doesn't rename adultery.
Grace redeems adulterers.
Grace doesn't pretend betrayal didn't hurt.
Grace enters the wound.
Grace doesn't say repentance is unnecessary.
Grace makes genuine repentance possible.
And if you are married, perhaps Proverbs 5 is asking you a question more uncomfortable than, “Have you committed adultery?”
Perhaps it is asking:
Are you rejoicing in the spouse God has given you?
When was the last time you looked at your wife without comparing her to somebody filtered through a screen?
When was the last time you pursued her without wanting something in return?
When was the last time you touched her affectionately without every touch becoming a demand?
When was the last time you told her she was beautiful—and made her believe you meant it?
When did you last ask what she is afraid of?
What she dreams about?
What has been hurting?
What she needs prayer for?
When was the last time the two of you laughed until something inside the marriage felt young again?
Some men will spend enormous energy resisting temptation while spending almost no energy cultivating tenderness.
Proverbs points toward something better.
Don't merely run away from the strange woman.
Run home.
Don't merely delete the number.
Recover the conversation you stopped having with your wife.
Don't merely close the browser.
Open your heart.
Don't merely stop feeding fantasy.
Start feeding covenant love.
Don't merely ask God to make another woman less attractive.
Ask Him to teach you again how to cherish the woman beside you.
And wives should not hear this passage as though they carry responsibility for preventing their husbands' sin.
They don't.
A husband's adultery is not automatically evidence that his wife failed him. Scripture places moral responsibility on the person choosing sin.
Nor does Proverbs 5 teach that a wife exists merely for a husband's gratification.
Biblical marriage is covenantal, personal, loving, faithful, and ultimately shaped by the self-giving love revealed in Christ.
The New Testament makes the standard even more demanding.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Think about that.
Christ's model for husbands is not consumption.
It is sacrifice.
Not:
“What can she give me?”
But:
“How can I love her?”
Not entitlement.
Self-giving.
Not domination.
Service.
Not treating your wife's body as something owed to you.
Cherishing the whole person who entrusted her life to you.
This means Proverbs 5:19 cannot honestly be turned into biblical permission for selfishness or coercion.
Marital delight separated from marital love becomes another form of taking.
But Christ teaches husbands to give themselves.
And perhaps that is where somebody's marriage begins changing.
Not tonight in the bedroom.
But this afternoon in the kitchen.
With dishes.
With an apology.
With a phone being put down.
With eye contact.
With listening.
With forgiveness.
With:
“I haven't loved you the way Christ calls me to love you.”
Maybe romance begins again with repentance.
Maybe intimacy begins again with safety.
Maybe desire begins growing where tenderness has been replanted.
Maybe the miracle you keep asking God to perform in your marriage begins with something painfully ordinary:
You turn toward each other again.
Because the grass is not greener wherever temptation points.
Grass becomes greener where somebody faithfully waters it.
And Proverbs has been talking about water all along.
Your cistern.
Your well.
Your fountain.
Your covenant.
Your wife.
Your husband.
Your home.
Your marriage.
Water what God has entrusted to you.
The world will constantly offer alternatives.
A younger face.
A more attentive coworker.
An old flame who suddenly messages.
A stranger who laughs at your jokes.
A fantasy requiring none of the patience real marriage demands.
A screen offering bodies without covenant, pleasure without responsibility, and stimulation without sacrifice.
But fantasies never have to wake up with sick children.
Pornography never asks you to practice forgiveness.
An affair doesn't show you the mundane years that would eventually arrive there too.
Forbidden desire sells you a highlight reel while hiding the invoice.
Proverbs shows you the invoice.
Honor.
Years.
Strength.
Peace.
And ultimately the cords of sin itself.
But then wisdom points toward something temptation cannot manufacture:
Covenant.
To know someone...
and still choose them.
To age together.
To forgive.
To rediscover.
To endure seasons when feelings fluctuate.
To watch youthful attraction mature into something temptation cannot imitate because temptation has no history with you.
There is holiness in that.
There is beauty in wrinkles that arrived while two people kept choosing one another.
There is something profoundly sacred about hands that no longer look twenty-five holding each other after decades of storms.
“The wife of your youth” eventually becomes the wife of your old age.
And if God grants you those years, may you still look across the room and know:
There she is.
The woman I chose.
The woman I hurt sometimes.
The woman who forgave me.
The woman I forgave.
The woman with whom I built ordinary Tuesdays and unforgettable years.
My friend.
My covenant companion.
My beloved.
Rejoice.
Not because marriage is always easy.
Not because your spouse is perfect.
Not because attraction never requires cultivation.
Rejoice because covenant love is worth protecting.
And if your marriage is hurting right now, don't turn this article into another weapon.
Don't send it to your spouse with:
“SEE? YOU'RE THE PROBLEM.”
Read it first as a mirror.
Ask:
“Lord, what needs to change in me?”
Because transformation almost always becomes harder when we are obsessed with somebody else's repentance.
And for the person who isn't married, Proverbs 5 still speaks.
It tells you something about desire.
You do not become free by obeying every appetite.
Some desires must be denied because God loves you too much to call destruction freedom.
Jesus went even deeper than external adultery when He addressed lust arising in the heart.
So purity is not merely keeping bodies apart.
It reaches the imagination.
The eyes.
The heart.
The secret life.
That is why we need more than rules.
We need Christ.
We need new hearts.
We need the Holy Spirit producing what willpower alone cannot sustain.
We need grace when we fail and strength to walk differently afterward.
Maybe you have been hiding.
This could be the moment hiding ends.
Not because thousands of strangers on Facebook need your private details.
They don't.
But because Jesus is calling you out of darkness.
Talk to God truthfully.
Seek trustworthy, mature Christian accountability.
Where serious marital wounds exist, seek wise pastoral care and appropriate professional counseling.
Bring sin into the light instead of feeding it privately.
If necessary, take concrete steps that make obedience costly but possible.
And remember:
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward Christ today.
Be honest.
Sometimes the hardest person to stop deceiving is ourselves.
And if you know a husband who needs to remember that faithfulness is more than avoiding adultery, tag him—not to shame him, but because marriages are worth strengthening.
If you know a couple quietly fighting for their covenant, send this to them privately.
Not as a badge announcing that your marriage is perfect.
One share may put Scripture in front of someone before temptation gets the final word.

That is one simple way you can help spread biblical truth and glorify God—but supporting Gospel work should flow from willing worship and conviction, never guilt or the idea that God's favor can be purchased.
Invite your husband. Invite your wife. Invite your family. Invite the friend struggling secretly. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the seeker who isn't sure what they believe yet.
But after all the Hebrew, all the warnings, all the discussion about marriage, sexuality, temptation, repentance, and restoration, don't miss the heart of this chapter.
God does not merely want you standing far away from adultery congratulating yourself because you never crossed the line.
He wants your heart.
He wants holiness reaching into your desires.
He wants covenant protected.
He wants husbands learning to cherish rather than consume.
He wants wives loved as people rather than treated as objects.
He wants wounded marriages brought into truth.
He wants secret sin dragged into light.
He wants sinners running toward Christ instead of hiding behind religious appearances.
And He wants us to discover that His commands are not arbitrary fences around human happiness.
Sometimes the fence is there because there is a cliff on the other side.
Proverbs 5 shows us both.
The cliff...
and the fountain.
One path says:
Take what isn't yours.
The other says:
Rejoice in what God has entrusted to you.
One promises sweetness and ends in bitterness.
The other requires covenant faithfulness and can deepen into a kind of love lust could never manufacture.
So husband...
go home.
Look at your wife.
Not through the eyes of pornography.
Not through the eyes of comparison.
Not through the resentment of your latest argument.
Ask God to help you see her again.
Remember the girl you once prayed would say yes.
Remember the vows.
Remember the years.
Remember the mercy God has shown both of you.
And then love the woman standing in front of you now.
Not merely the memory of who she was.
Her.
Now.
And if your story already contains scandal...
remember this:
Peter's failure wasn't his final chapter.
David's sin wasn't the final sentence over his life.
The woman caught in adultery encountered Someone greater than the crowd holding stones.
The cross itself looked like history's darkest scandal until the empty tomb revealed that God was writing redemption through it.
Your sin is serious.
Your wounds are real.
Your consequences may be painful.
But Jesus Christ is still Jesus Christ.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive grace.
Walk differently.
Love faithfully.
And when temptation whispers that forbidden water will finally satisfy your thirst, remember the fountain God told you to bless.
Because sometimes the marriage Satan wants you to abandon is the very place where Christ is teaching you how covenant love survives the fire.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Don’t Have to Call Your Father a Good Man to Refuse to Become a Bitter One
paragraphs: You Don’t Have to Call Your Father a Good Man to Refuse to Become a Bitter One

You can tell the truth about what your father did, grieve what he never became, and still refuse to let his failures become your character—because Jesus did not save you merely from what was done to you; He came to save you from what the wound is trying to turn you into.
Some people hear the word father and think of safety.
You hear it and your body remembers something else.
A slammed door.
An empty chair.
A promise that never survived the weekend.
A voice that made you afraid to make mistakes.
A man who provided money but never tenderness.
A man everybody at church respected, while the people inside his house knew another version of him.
Or maybe there wasn't shouting.
That almost makes your story harder to explain.
He simply wasn't there.
Not emotionally.
Not spiritually.
Maybe not physically.
And years later, you still carry conversations you never got to have.
Dad, why wasn't I worth staying for?
Why couldn't you tell me you were proud of me?
Why did strangers receive the kindness we begged you to bring home?
Why did I have to become an adult while I was still a child?
Perhaps you've spent years trying to be a “good Christian” about it.
So you learned the religious answers.
“Honor your father.”
“Forgive.”
“Move on.”
And because you love Jesus, part of you wondered whether healing required rewriting history.
Maybe honoring your father meant calling him a good man when he wasn't one.
Maybe forgiveness meant saying the abuse wasn't really abuse.
Maybe grace required pretending the abandonment didn't leave scars.
Maybe being spiritual meant never admitting:
My father hurt me.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to lie in order to forgive.
You do not have to rename evil in order to overcome it.
You do not have to manufacture childhood memories you never had.
And you do not have to call your father a good man to refuse to become a bitter one.
That distinction may change something inside you.
Because Scripture does not command you to defeat evil by pretending evil was good.
It says something far more powerful.
Romans 12:21 reads in Greek:
“μὴ νικῶ ὑπὸ τοῦ κακοῦ, ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακόν.”
Μὴ νικῶ ὑπὸ τοῦ κακοῦ—do not be conquered by evil.
Ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακόν—but conquer evil with good.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say evil wasn't evil.
He calls it κακόν—evil.
Then he tells the Christian not to allow that evil to win.
That matters enormously when the evil came through someone whose blood runs through your veins.
Because sometimes evil wins twice.
First, when someone wounds you.
Then again, years later, when the wound begins deciding who you will become.
Your father exploded in anger...
and now anger lives in you.
Your father abandoned people...
and now you leave before anyone can leave you.
Your father never apologized...
and now “I'm sorry” gets stuck behind your teeth.
Your father controlled everybody...
and now control feels safer than trust.
Your father withheld affection...
and now tenderness makes you uncomfortable.
Your father humiliated you...
and now you hear his voice coming out of your mouth when your own child makes a mistake.
That moment can be terrifying.
You promised yourself:
I will never become him.
Then one day you hear yourself say something exactly the way he said it.
The room goes quiet.
Your child looks at you.
And for one horrible second, you see the past trying to become the future.
This is where Romans 12:21 becomes more than a verse for a wall.
Do not be conquered by evil.
The deepest victory over your father's sin is not getting an apology he may never give.
It is not finally winning an argument he may never understand.
It is not making him feel everything he made you feel.
The victory is that what wounded you does not get permission to reproduce itself through you.
Maybe he gave you anger.
It stops here.
Maybe he gave you abandonment.
It stops here.
Maybe he gave you manipulation.
It stops here.
Maybe he taught you that men don't cry, fathers don't apologize, affection is weakness, vulnerability is dangerous, and domination is strength.
By the grace of Jesus Christ...
it stops here.
Not because you are stronger than your father.
Not because positive thinking healed you.
Not because you buried the memories deeply enough.
Because Jesus Christ can redeem what sin tried to reproduce.
And perhaps that is what some wounded sons and daughters desperately need to hear:
Forgiveness does not require historical dishonesty.
You can forgive someone while telling the truth about what happened.
You can release personal vengeance without declaring the offender trustworthy.
You can pray for someone without pretending they are safe.
You can refuse hatred without denying consequences.
And where serious abuse or danger exists, forgiveness does not mean voluntarily placing yourself or your children back into harm's way.
Biblical forgiveness and automatic restoration of trust are not identical things.
Trust can be profoundly damaged.
Reconciliation involves realities forgiveness alone cannot manufacture in another person's heart.
You cannot repent for your father.
You cannot confess his sin for him.
You cannot force him to become safe.
You cannot make him tell the truth.
You cannot drag an apology out of a heart determined to remain proud.
But you can bring your own wounded heart to Christ.
That is where the story begins changing.
Because bitterness makes a seductive promise:
Keep the wound alive and you will remain protected.
But bitterness doesn't merely remember what happened.
It can begin building your identity around what happened.
Soon you're no longer simply a person whose father failed you.
You're interpreting friendships through him.
Marriage through him.
Authority through him.
Fatherhood through him.
Even God through him.
And that last one can become devastating.
Because an earthly father can distort the word father so badly that when Scripture speaks about God as Father, your heart instinctively attaches a human face to a divine name.
But God is not the magnified version of the man who wounded you.
Your earthly father's character does not define your heavenly Father's character.
You do not measure God by your father.
Your father must be measured by God.
Maybe your father disappeared.
God did not.
Maybe your father broke promises.
God does not.
Maybe your father treated your weakness with contempt.
Jesus moved toward broken people with compassion.
Maybe your father made love feel conditional.
At the cross, Christ loved sinners at unimaginable cost to Himself.
And this is where Christianity becomes far more than advice about managing resentment.
You don't merely need techniques for becoming less bitter.
You need a Savior.
Because if we're willing to tell the whole truth, eventually we discover something uncomfortable.
Your father was a sinner who needed grace.
And so are you.
His sins against you may have been horrific. Acknowledging your own sin does not minimize his. Christianity does not require that false equivalence.
But standing beneath the cross eventually destroys the fantasy that only other people need mercy.
Your father's sin wounded you.
Your own sin separates you from a holy God.
And Jesus Christ stepped into the scandal of human rebellion carrying a cross.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Betrayed.
Abandoned.
Struck.
Falsely accused.
Crucified.
Yet the Son of God did not become evil because evil was done to Him.
He overcame evil.
And at Calvary, He did something none of us could do for ourselves.
He bore sin.
He paid the debt.
He opened the way for guilty people to be reconciled to God through repentance and faith.
This is why the Gospel is not merely, “Try harder not to become your father.”
The Gospel says there is another identity available to you.
In Christ.
Maybe biology explains where you came from.
It does not have the final word over who you become.
Your father's temper does not have to become your inheritance.
His addictions do not have to become your destiny.
His emotional absence does not have to become the atmosphere of your home.
His refusal to apologize does not have to become your vocabulary.
His failures do not get authorship over the rest of your life.
Jesus does.
And that means one of the holiest sentences you may ever speak is not:
“My father was actually a good man.”
Maybe he wasn't.
Maybe he was complicated.
Maybe he loved you in some ways and devastated you in others.
Maybe he eventually changed.
Maybe he never did.
Maybe he's already dead, and the apology you've waited decades to hear is now an earthly impossibility.
The holy sentence may simply be:
“What he did was wrong, but by the grace of Jesus Christ, what he did will not decide what I become.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because somebody has been waiting years to say it without feeling guilty.
You are allowed to grieve the father you needed.
Grieve the conversations.
Grieve the birthdays.
Grieve the empty seat.
Grieve the hug you needed at eight years old.
Grieve the “I'm proud of you” that never came.
Grieve the apology.
Grieve the protection.
Grieve the version of childhood you watched other people have.
Grief tells the truth that something precious was missing.
But then bring that grief to Jesus.
Not because the past suddenly becomes acceptable.
Because you cannot afford to give yesterday permanent ownership of tomorrow.

Paul's command is surrounded by language about refusing repayment of evil for evil, pursuing peace as far as it depends on us, relinquishing personal vengeance, and answering an enemy's need with good.
Then comes the final blow:
Do not let evil conquer you. Conquer evil with good.
Your revenge is not becoming crueler than the man who wounded you.
Your victory is becoming freer than the wound expected.
Imagine the enemy watching generations of dysfunction and assuming he already knows the ending.
Grandfather wounded father.
Father wounded son.
Son wounds grandson.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Until Jesus enters the story.
And suddenly someone repents.
Someone gets honest.
Someone asks for help.
Someone learns how to apologize.
Someone stops screaming.
Someone puts down the bottle.
Someone tells their children, “I love you.”
Someone admits, “Daddy was wrong.”
Someone chooses gentleness when rage would have been easier.
Someone opens the Bible instead of reopening the family war.
Someone kneels beside a bed and prays over children who will never have to wonder whether their father wanted them.
And hell discovers that the wound did not become the inheritance.
Grace did.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not airbrushing dysfunctional families until everyone looks holy.
Not calling darkness light.
Grace walks straight into the ugliest chapter and declares that because of Jesus Christ, this chapter does not have to be the ending.
Maybe you're reading this with tears you didn't expect.
Maybe your father is the person you've spent your whole life trying not to become.
Maybe you're angry because he died before making things right.
Maybe you're grieving because he's alive but emotionally unreachable.
Maybe everyone tells you how wonderful he is, and you're carrying memories nobody else knows.
Or maybe the hardest truth is different.
Maybe you are the father somebody is recovering from.
Maybe your son barely calls.
Maybe your daughter keeps conversations short.
Maybe you've explained your behavior for years.
I worked hard.
I provided.
That's how my father raised me.
They were too sensitive.
Maybe.
But perhaps underneath those explanations is a relationship that needs repentance more than defense.
If your child tells you that you wounded them, your first calling is not to protect your reputation.
Listen.
Examine yourself before God.
Where you sinned, confess it without inserting excuses into the apology.
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“Will you forgive me?”
Those words will not erase history.
But humility can interrupt history.
You may not be able to rewrite their childhood.
But through Christ, you can repent in the chapter you're standing in now.
And if you're the wounded child, hear this too:
You do not have to wait for your father to change before surrendering your bitterness to Jesus.
Do not hand another human being that much authority over your soul.
If he repents, praise God.
If genuine reconciliation becomes possible, praise God.
If trust can slowly and wisely be rebuilt, praise God.
But if he refuses?
Jesus is still Lord.
