God had shown Peter that he should call no person common or unclean.
The vision was not merely about Peter's lunch.
God was preparing a Jewish apostle to cross a boundary he had resisted and carry the Gospel into a Gentile household.
Look at the beauty of that.
The animals come down.
But God is going after people.
Cornelius.
His household.
The nations.
People once standing outside.
People Peter might never have entered a house to meet.
People Christ had come to save.
The Gospel was moving outward.
Jerusalem.
Judea.
Samaria.
The nations.
And no ethnicity possessed a monopoly on the grace of Jesus Christ.
Then Acts 15 gives us another crucial moment.
Gentiles were turning to God.
The early church had to confront an enormous question: Must Gentile converts effectively become Jews and bear the Mosaic covenant requirements in order to belong to God's people?

The apostolic council did not impose Israel's entire dietary code upon Gentile believers. James said they should not make it unnecessarily difficult for Gentiles turning to God, while giving specific instructions concerning idolatrous pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood.
Paul likewise tells believers in Colossians not to allow others to pass judgment on them regarding food or drink, festivals, new moons, or Sabbaths.
That matters.
A Christian should therefore be extremely careful about turning Leviticus 11 into a weapon for condemning another believer.
A Christian may personally choose not to eat pork.
Someone may abstain for health reasons.
Someone may abstain because of conscience.
Someone may abstain because of culture.
Someone studying the Torah may develop a personal conviction about diet.
But abstaining from pork does not purchase justification before God.
And eating pork does not place a believer beyond the cleansing power of Christ.
Our righteousness is not sitting on a dinner plate.
Our righteousness is Christ.
And here is where this entire discussion becomes intensely personal.
You and I have something far worse than pork to worry about.
Sin.
Real sin.
Not ceremonial impurity.
Not an animal.
Not bacon.
Sin.
The thing inside us that whispers, Nobody knows.
The pride that knows how to disguise itself as spirituality.
The lust deleted from the history but not surrendered from the heart.
The bitterness we renamed “discernment.”
The greed we renamed “being blessed.”
The gossip we called “concern.”
The unforgiveness we justified because they really did hurt us.
The secret compromise we promised God we would quit after “one last time.”
That is where Jesus takes the conversation.
To the heart.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you are ashamed to admit, hear this carefully:
Jesus did not come merely to make dirty people behave cleaner.
He came to save sinners.
That distinction is everything.
Christianity is not humanity climbing toward God with increasingly impressive religious performance.
The Gospel announces that God came toward sinners in Jesus Christ.
The Holy One walked among the unholy.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
Christ bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And the scandal of grace is that people with histories they cannot erase can receive a future they could never earn.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to these words:
Not because Jesus pretends your scandal never happened.
Because He can redeem what sin tried to destroy.
Peter knew something about that.
Before he became the apostle walking into Cornelius's house, he had his own scandal.
He had sworn loyalty to Jesus.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The pressure.
And three denials.
“I don't know Him.”
Imagine carrying that memory.
Imagine remembering the face of the One you denied.
Imagine hearing the rooster again in your mind.
Peter could not rewrite that night.
But Jesus could rewrite Peter's future.
The failure was real.
The restoration was real too.
And perhaps that is why somebody reading this needs to stop pretending.
Maybe your deepest problem is not theological confusion about Leviticus.
Maybe you clicked because the title interested you...
but God has been pressing on something else the entire time.
Something hidden.
Something exhausting you.
Something you keep defending publicly and regretting privately.
You know what it is.
And perhaps nobody else does.
Jesus does.
And He is not asking you to clean yourself enough to become worthy of approaching Him.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Confess.
Stop negotiating with the thing Christ died to free you from.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the sinner finally agreeing with God that the prison is a prison and running toward the One holding the door open.
That is the Gospel.
Not “try harder until God likes you.”
Not “follow enough food regulations and maybe heaven will accept you.”
Not “hide your scandal so Christians think you're holy.”
Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Merciful.
Holy.
Enough.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a religious response.
Be honest.
There is no shame in admitting you need grace.
That is where every Christian begins.
Somebody may need to discover that the Bible is not a collection of disconnected religious restrictions.
It is a story moving toward Jesus.
Because sooner or later this question will come up again, and when it does, you should remember the distinction Scripture itself gives us.
Israel really was forbidden to eat pork.
The command really mattered.
It belonged within Israel's covenant life and its distinctions between clean and unclean.
We should not reduce God's stated concern for holiness to an unsupported claim that the prohibition was merely primitive health advice.
And Christians should read those commands through the unfolding biblical story that reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ and the apostolic mission to the nations.
The point is not that holiness disappeared.
Absolutely not.
In Christ, God's people are still called to holiness.
But holiness cannot be reduced to refusing one particular animal while tolerating the sins Jesus said proceed from the human heart.
The table changed.
The call to belong completely to God did not.
And perhaps that is the truth we needed all along.
The pig was never the hero of Leviticus 11.
God was.
The central issue was never the superiority of one dinner over another.
It was a holy God teaching a redeemed people:
You belong to Me.
And through Jesus Christ, the question eventually becomes even more piercing:
Does He have all of you?
Not just your church attendance.
Not just your Christian posts.
Not just the worship music playing in your car.
Your heart.
Your sexuality.
Your relationships.
Your money.
Your anger.
Your ambitions.
Your private habits.
Your wounds.
Your secrets.
Your future.
Your scandal.
All of you.
That is discipleship.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.

We want to keep creating Scripture-centered content that does more than generate religious noise. We want to help people open difficult passages, understand them in context, encounter Jesus Christ, repent where repentance is needed, receive grace where shame has taken root, and grow into mature disciples who can handle the Word of God faithfully.
Let your feed become one more place where Scripture, conviction, hope, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel can reach someone who may never voluntarily walk through a church door.
Grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased.
But voluntary financial support of Gospel ministry is deeply meaningful.

If you want to glorify God through generosity, begin with obedience to Him—not pressure from us. Then, if you believe supporting Gospel Warrior is one of the ways you should steward what He has entrusted to you, stand with us.
The goal is not to create consumers of Christian content.
The goal is disciples.
People who know Scripture.
People who recognize error.
People who repent quickly.
People who forgive deeply.
People who pray when nobody is watching.
People who carry the Gospel into homes, workplaces, friendships, comment sections, hospital rooms, broken marriages, lonely nights, and ordinary Tuesday mornings.
People who know that Jesus Christ is not an accessory to life.
He is Lord.
Pray.
Save it so you can return to it.
Invite another person to follow.
One share can carry Scripture into a home we could never enter ourselves.
One tag can reach someone who has been silently questioning God.
One honest comment can make another struggling believer realize they are not the only person fighting.
One saved article can become tomorrow's conversation.
And one surrendered life can influence generations.
So perhaps the final question is no longer:
“Why couldn't the Israelites eat pork?”
Now you know.

God had established clean and unclean distinctions for Israel, and the pig did not meet the requirements for permitted land animals. Those commands existed within Israel's covenant identity and God's call for His redeemed people to be holy.
But after reading all of this, another question remains.
What have you allowed into your heart that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
Pride?
Lust?
Bitterness?
Secret sin?
Religious performance?
Fear?
Unforgiveness?
Shame?
You don't need to tell strangers every detail.
But don't lie to God.
He already knows.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become someone else's reason not to give up tonight.
Because maybe you have spent years staring at the scandal.
Jesus is looking at what grace can make of the surrendered ruins.
Maybe you remember every failure.
Jesus remembers the cross.
Maybe you see the chapter you wish had never been written.
Jesus is still holding the pen.
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter when the Author of redemption is still writing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PROVERBS 7: THE SEDUCTION SCENE PARENTS RARELY TEACH THEIR CHILDREN
paragraphs: PROVERBS 7: THE SEDUCTION SCENE PARENTS RARELY TEACH THEIR CHILDREN
The Bible describes the bedroom before the bedroom ever happens—because God knows that destruction usually begins long before the door closes.
There is a chapter in Proverbs that many parents teach as a warning against sexual immorality.
But I wonder how many actually sit down with their sons and daughters and walk them through the scene.
Not merely the command.
The scene.
The darkness.
The loneliness.
The conversation.
The compliments.
The rationalizations.
The calculated touch.
The carefully chosen words.
The young man's silence.
The moment desire becomes stronger than discernment.
And the devastating sentence that comes afterward:
“He does not know that it will cost him his life.”
That is Proverbs 7.

And if you are a parent, grandparent, teenager, young adult, husband, wife—or simply someone who has ever discovered how quickly temptation can make something dangerous feel beautiful—you need to stay with this chapter.
Because Proverbs 7 is not merely an ancient warning about one seductive woman.
It is a window into how temptation works.
And somewhere inside this story, many of us will recognize ourselves.
The chapter begins with a father pleading with his son:
“My son, keep my words, and treasure up my commandments with you. Keep my commandments and live.”
The Hebrew expression behind “keep my commandments” uses שְׁמֹר מִצְוֹתַי — shemor mitzvotai.
שָׁמַר — shamar — carries the sense of keeping, guarding, watching over, preserving.
This father is not merely saying, “Memorize some religious rules.”
He is telling his son:
Guard this.
Protect this.
Hold onto this as though your life depends upon it.
Because eventually, it might.
He continues:
“Bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.”
That is where biblical parenting becomes uncomfortable.
Because eventually our children will walk into places where we cannot follow them.
There will be a night when Dad is not standing beside them.
There will be a conversation Mom cannot hear.
There will be a phone screen nobody else sees.
There will be a relationship developing privately.
There will be an invitation.
A compliment.
A message sent after midnight.
A secret account.
A deleted conversation.
A person who makes compromise sound reasonable.
And in that moment, parental surveillance cannot save them.
Something has to already be written on the heart.
That is why Proverbs 7 does not begin with sex.
It begins with Scripture.
Before Solomon shows us temptation outside the young man's heart, he shows us what should have been planted inside it.
Then the scene changes.
The father says:
“For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice, and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense.”
The Hebrew is devastating.
The young man is described as חֲסַר־לֵב — ḥasar-lev.
Literally, he is “lacking heart.”
In biblical Hebrew, lev—heart—can include the inner person, mind, will, understanding, and moral judgment.
The problem is not simply that this young man has hormones.
His deeper vulnerability is that desire is operating without wisdom.
And then comes one of the most important details parents sometimes rush past.
He is walking toward the wrong place before he commits the wrong act.
“He passes along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house, in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.”
Notice the progression.
Street.
Corner.
Road.
House.
Twilight.
Evening.
Night.
Darkness.
Sin often has an address before it has an action.
The young man is not suddenly transported into temptation.
He walks toward it.
Step after step.
That matters enormously in an age when “her corner” can fit inside a pocket.
Pornography does not require walking through a dangerous neighborhood anymore.
Neither does emotional adultery.
Neither does secret flirtation.
Neither does sexual compromise.
Neither does the carefully cultivated fantasy nobody knows about.
Sometimes the road to “her house” begins with unlocking a phone.
One search.
One image.
One follow.
One DM.
One conversation you know you should end.
One relationship you keep calling harmless.
One little compromise that whispers:
Nothing has happened yet.
But Proverbs 7 asks a more penetrating question:
Where are you walking?
Parents, this is why merely telling children, “Don’t have sex before marriage,” is not enough.
We must teach them how temptation develops.
Teach them to recognize the road before they reach the room.
Teach them that boundaries are not proof that God wants to steal their happiness.
Sometimes boundaries are evidence that God knows where roads lead.
Then she appears.
“And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart.”
The Hebrew description includes נְצֻרַת לֵב — netzurat lev, a difficult expression rendered variously by translators with ideas such as crafty, guarded, or secretive of heart.
The point of the scene becomes unmistakable through what follows.
She knows what she is doing.
She takes hold of him.
She kisses him.
She speaks boldly.
And then something particularly disturbing happens.
She brings religion into the seduction.
“I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows.”
Think about that.
She is essentially telling him:
I have been religious.
I fulfilled my obligation.
Everything is fine.
Now come with me.
This is one of the oldest spiritual deceptions in the world:
using outward religion to silence inward conviction.
I went to church.
I prayed.
I posted a Bible verse.
I gave money.
I worshiped.
I serve in ministry.
God knows my heart.
And therefore this compromise cannot really be that serious.
But religious activity never turns rebellion into holiness.
A worship song playing in the background cannot sanctify what God calls sin.
A Bible in your biography cannot make secret disobedience harmless.
Knowing Christian vocabulary cannot replace knowing Christ.
Then she makes him feel chosen.
“So now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.”
You.
That word can become intoxicating.
I wanted you.
I noticed you.
Nobody understands me like you.
My marriage has been dead for years, but you make me feel alive.
You are different.
You deserve this.
Nobody needs to know.
And suddenly temptation is no longer presenting itself as destruction.
It feels like validation.
That is why some people fall into sin while desperately trying to heal an unmet emotional hunger.
They are not merely seeking pleasure.
They want to feel wanted.
Seen.
Desired.
Important.
Chosen.
And temptation learns how to speak directly into that wound.
Then Proverbs becomes astonishingly cinematic.
She describes her bed.
“I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen; I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.”
Everything appeals to the senses.
Texture.
Color.
Fragrance.
Touch.
Atmosphere.
Anticipation.
Sin rarely advertises its funeral.
It sells the perfume.
It does not show you the spouse sobbing afterward.
It shows you excitement.
It does not show you the child discovering the messages.
It shows you secrecy.
It does not show you addiction.
It shows you pleasure.
It does not show you shame the next morning.
It shows you tonight.
It does not show you years of consequences.
It shows you minutes of gratification.
Then comes the invitation:
“Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love.”
Even the vocabulary is softened.
She does not call it betrayal.
She calls it love.
That is another lesson our children desperately need.
Not everything called “love” is love.
Biblically, love cannot be separated from truth, holiness, covenant faithfulness, and the good of the other person.
Lust says:
I want you because of what I can experience through you.
Love asks:
How can I honor God while seeking your true good?
Those are not the same thing.
Then she removes what appears to be the final obstacle.
“For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey.”
In other words:
We won't get caught.
And there it is.
One of temptation's favorite arguments.
Nobody will know.
Delete the history.
Erase the conversation.
Use another account.
Close the door.
Clear the browser.
Hide the receipt.
Rename the contact.
Tell your spouse you were somewhere else.
Tell your parents you are going somewhere else.
Nobody will know.
But Christian holiness has never been based merely on whether another human being is watching.
Joseph understood that centuries before the words of Proverbs 7 were written.
When Potiphar's wife tried to seduce him, Joseph did not merely say, “What if my master finds out?”
He said:
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
That changes everything.
Because when the room is empty, God is still God.
When the browser history is deleted, God is still God.
When your spouse never discovers it, God is still God.
When your parents never hear about it, God is still God.
When nobody screenshots the conversation, God is still God.
Holiness begins when God's presence becomes more real to us than the possibility of being caught.
Then Proverbs 7 delivers the line every parent should make their children understand:
“With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him.”
Words.
That is what finally moves him.
Not chains.
Not physical force.
Words.
Temptation has a vocabulary.
You deserve this.
Everyone does it.
Your marriage is already over emotionally.
You can repent afterward.
God will forgive you.
It isn't technically sex.
We're just talking.
I'm just looking.
I can stop whenever I want.
Nobody is being hurt.
This is who I really am.
God wants me happy.
Just once.
Just tonight.
Just one more time.
Then comes one of Scripture's most haunting images:
“All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter…”
Read that slowly.
He thinks he is walking toward pleasure.
Wisdom sees an animal walking toward slaughter.
Two interpretations of the same footsteps.
That is what sin does to perception.
It makes death look like life.
Bondage look like freedom.
Self-destruction look like self-expression.
Poison look like medicine.
And temporary pleasure look worth permanent damage.
Then Scripture says:
“He does not know that it will cost him his life.”
That sentence should haunt us in the right way.
Because sin always sends the bill later.
And sometimes the person who entered the room is not the same person who comes out.
Something has changed.
Trust.
Tenderness.
Integrity.
A marriage.
A conscience.
A ministry.
A family.
A friendship.
A child's perception of a parent.
Sometimes consequences ripple outward for years.
But this is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Because Christianity does not end with an ox walking toward slaughter.
It ends with a Lamb walking willingly toward a cross.
And that changes the story.
Jesus Christ did not come only for people who successfully avoided Proverbs 7.
He came for people who lived it.
For adulterers.
For sexually broken people.
For pornography addicts.
For people carrying secret histories.
For people who crossed lines they swore they never would cross.
For the betrayed.
For the betrayer who truly repents.
For the ashamed.
For the person who feels filthy when nobody else knows why.
For the son who ignored wisdom.
For the daughter who believed a lie.
For the husband hiding something.
For the wife carrying something.
For the person reading this who suddenly feels as though God has opened a locked room inside the heart.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not permission to keep walking toward destruction.
Grace is not God saying sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's mercy is.
Jesus came preaching repentance and faith.
At the cross, He bore sin.
He rose from the dead.
And Scripture declares that “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The answer to Proverbs 7 is not merely stronger willpower.
Ultimately, we need Christ.
We need new hearts.
We need truth stronger than seductive lies.
We need the Holy Spirit producing fruit in us that raw desire cannot manufacture.
We need brothers and sisters who know our battles.
We need confession instead of concealment.
Repentance instead of rationalization.
Grace instead of pretending.
And sometimes obedience looks dramatically unspiritual.
Block the number.
Delete the account.
Leave the room.
End the relationship.
Install accountability.
Tell your spouse the truth.
Tell a mature Christian you trust.
Get pastoral help.
Run.
Joseph ran.
Sometimes running is not cowardice.
Sometimes running is worship.
Parents, teach your children this before temptation teaches them something else.
Do not merely teach daughters how to avoid becoming the woman in Proverbs 7.
Teach sons not to become the undiscerning young man.
And do not reduce this chapter to blaming women.

Proverbs uses the scene of an adulterous woman instructively within its larger father-to-son wisdom setting, while Scripture condemns sexual immorality and adultery regardless of whether the sinner is male or female.
Teach your children dignity.
Teach them covenant.
Teach them the beauty of marital faithfulness.
Teach them why God's boundaries exist.
Teach them that sexuality is powerful precisely because it matters.
Teach them how pornography trains desire apart from covenant love.
Teach them how loneliness can weaken judgment.
Teach them how flattery works.
Teach them that secrecy feeds temptation.
Teach them to identify manipulative words.
Teach them that chemistry is not character.
Teach them that attention is not love.
Teach them that desire is not destiny.
Teach them that saying “no” can be an act of worship.
Teach them that if they fall, hiding from God is never the answer.
And above everything else, teach them Jesus.
Because eventually your children will leave your house.
Your rules cannot follow them everywhere.
But the Word hidden in their hearts can.
And the Christ you taught them to know is not confined to your living room.
Maybe, though, you are not thinking about your children anymore.
Maybe you are thinking about yourself.
Maybe you already walked down that street.
Maybe you entered the house.
Maybe you crossed the line.
Maybe your greatest fear is not temptation.
It is exposure.
And perhaps you have spent years believing that if people knew the whole story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Jesus already knows the whole story.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the church version.
Not the respectable version.
The whole story.
And He still calls sinners to repent and come to Him.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is restoration in Christ.
There is no need to rename darkness as light in order to receive mercy.
Bring the darkness into His light.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is turning from the road that is killing you toward the Savior who gives life.
That is why our message will always return here:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Grace is.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Christ redeems.
Not because sin was insignificant.
The cross says otherwise.
But because Jesus Christ has made forgiveness possible for sinners who could never rewrite their own histories.
Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not turn this moment into another emotional experience you forget tomorrow.
Be honest.
You do not have to publish intimate details of your sin. Wisdom still matters. But refusing secrecy in your heart can become the beginning of something different.
Not because every sentence must become a lecture tonight, but because one day you may need to sit beside your son or daughter and open Proverbs 7 together.
Send it privately to someone who needs grace more than embarrassment.

If you want your online life to glorify God, one meaningful way to do that is to use what God has placed in your hands—your voice, your reach, your sharing, your encouragement, and, where you freely choose, your financial support—to help sound biblical truth travel farther.
Come to Christ.
Because merchandise cannot save you.
A Christian page cannot forgive your sins.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones.
Only His grace can meet the repentant sinner at the place where the story seemed ruined beyond repair.
Proverbs 7 shows us a young man walking into darkness because he could not see where the road ended.
The Gospel shows us Jesus entering our darkness knowing exactly where His road would end.
At a cross.
For sinners.
For the guilty.
For the ashamed.
For people with browser histories they wish they could erase.
For people with memories they cannot erase.
For people whose greatest scandal is known only to God.
And for everyone who discovers that deleting evidence is not the same thing as receiving forgiveness.
So teach Proverbs 7 to your children.
Teach it before the culture teaches them desire without wisdom.
Teach it before pornography teaches them intimacy without covenant.
Teach it before social media teaches them that being desired means being valuable.
Teach them the street.
The corner.
The darkness.
The flattering words.
The perfumed bed.
The hidden slaughter.
But please…
do not stop there.
Teach them the cross.
Teach them that when temptation whispers, there is a better King to obey.
And if they ever fall, teach them not to run farther into darkness.
Teach them to run toward Jesus in repentance and faith.
Because perhaps the most important lesson a child can learn is not merely how to avoid becoming the broken person in Proverbs 7.
It is knowing where to go if one day they realize they already have.
Remember this when the enemy tells you your worst chapter deserves to become your final chapter:
The road into darkness may explain your scandal, but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still writing the story of grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Thought Faith Would Make the Storm Stop. Jesus May Be Teaching You Who He Is While It Still Rages.
paragraphs: You Thought Faith Would Make the Storm Stop. Jesus May Be Teaching You Who He Is While It Still Rages.
Maybe the greatest miracle in your storm will not be how quickly Jesus changes what is happening around you—but how deeply you discover who He is while everything around you is still shaking.
There is a kind of disappointment Christians rarely admit out loud.
You prayed.
You believed.
You tried to obey God.

You stopped running from Him. You opened your Bible again. You started praying when nobody was watching. You surrendered things you once defended. You whispered the name of Jesus through tears because sometimes His name was the only prayer you had enough strength to pray.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps without realizing it, you began expecting the weather to change.
Surely following Jesus would make this easier.
Surely obedience would prevent this kind of pain.

Surely faith would mean the diagnosis changed, the marriage healed, the child came home, the bills were paid, the anxiety disappeared, the betrayal was repaired, the grief became manageable, the door finally opened.
Surely Jesus would stop the storm.
But the wind kept blowing.
And now you are carrying a question you may be almost ashamed to ask:
“Jesus… if You are really with me, why is this still happening?”
That question is older than your suffering.
And one night on the Sea of Galilee, terrified disciples essentially asked it too.
Mark tells us that after Jesus had been teaching, He said to His disciples:
“Let us go across to the other side.”
They took Him in the boat.
Then everything changed.
Mark 4:37 describes a “great windstorm.”
The Greek is startling:
λαῖλαψ μεγάλη ἀνέμου — lailaps megalē anemou
A great, violent windstorm.
This was not an inconvenient drizzle interrupting a pleasant evening.
The waves were crashing into the boat so aggressively that the vessel was already filling with water.
And Jesus?
He was asleep.
That detail hurts differently when you have suffered.
Because sometimes the most painful part of the storm is not the storm.
It is what feels like the silence of God inside it.
You can survive people misunderstanding you.
You can survive someone walking away.
You can survive financial uncertainty, sleepless nights, bad news, rejection, disappointment and seasons when nothing seems to make sense.
But when heaven seems silent while your boat is filling with water?
That can shake something much deeper.
The disciples woke Jesus and cried:
Διδάσκαλε, οὐ μέλει σοι ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα;
Didaskale, ou melei soi hoti apollymetha?
“Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?”
Notice what fear did.
The storm outside them became an accusation inside them.
The question was no longer merely, “Will we survive?”
It became:
“Do You care?”
And perhaps that is where this story suddenly becomes yours.
Because suffering has a way of putting God on trial in the courtroom of our frightened hearts.
“Lord, do You care?”
“If You cared, why did You allow this?”
“If You loved me, why did You not prevent it?”
“If You heard my prayers, why has nothing changed?”
“If I really belonged to You, why am I still hurting?”
There are believers reading these words who do not need somebody to tell them to “just have more faith.”
You have faith.
You are simply tired.
There is a difference.
You still believe Jesus is Lord, but your hands are trembling.
You still know Scripture, but tonight the verses feel harder to hold.
You still worship, but sometimes your worship sounds more like weeping.
You have not abandoned Christ.
You are trying to find Him through the rain.
And Mark 4 contains something desperately important for people like you:
The presence of a storm is not proof of the absence of Christ.
Jesus was in the boat.
And the storm still came.
Do not miss that.
The disciples were not in that storm because they had disobeyed Jesus.
They were there after following His instruction.
Jesus Himself had said:
“Let us go across to the other side.”
Sometimes obedience leads you directly into circumstances you would never have chosen for yourself.
That destroys a dangerous version of Christianity which quietly teaches that enough faith should produce a sufficiently comfortable life.
Scripture never promises that.
Jesus Himself told His disciples, “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33).
Paul endured beatings, imprisonment, rejection, hunger, shipwreck and suffering while faithfully serving Christ.
Peter wrote to believers experiencing fiery trials.
James told Christians not if but when they encountered various trials.
And our Savior did not walk toward earthly comfort.
He walked toward a cross.
Christian faith is not a contract promising that nothing terrible will happen to you.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ and the astonishing promise that whatever comes, you ultimately belong to Him.
That changes the meaning of the storm.
Not necessarily its immediate intensity.
But its ultimate authority.
The disciples shook Jesus awake.
Then Mark says:
“He arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still.”
The Greek preserves the force of His command:
Σιώπα, πεφίμωσο — Siōpa, pephimōso.
“Be silent. Be still.”
The One who appeared to be doing nothing was never powerless.
The One who seemed unaware was never unaware.
Jesus stood before something the disciples could not control and spoke as its Lord.
The wind ceased.
There was a great calm.
But strangely, Jesus did not immediately congratulate His disciples.
He asked them:
“Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?”
This does not mean mature Christians never experience fear.
Scripture repeatedly shows faithful people frightened, grieving, confused and overwhelmed.
The deeper issue is what fear convinces us to believe about God.
The disciples had interpreted Jesus’ apparent inactivity as indifference.
“Do You not care?”
But Jesus cared before He stood up.
He cared while He slept.
He cared while the waves were crashing.
He cared while the boat was filling.
His care did not begin when the circumstances changed.
And somebody desperately needs that truth today.
Jesus does not begin loving you when your storm ends.
He is not waiting for your situation to improve before becoming faithful.
Your unanswered prayer is not proof that He has abandoned you.
Your tears are not evidence that Christianity failed.
Your suffering is not necessarily evidence that you somehow missed God.
Sometimes faith looks less like standing triumphantly on top of the waves and more like whispering from the bottom of the boat:
“Jesus, I am terrified… but I am still here.”
Maybe you expected faith to make you fearless.
But biblical faith is often trusting God while fear is still screaming.
Maybe you thought strong Christians never cried.
Jesus wept.
Maybe you thought faithful Christians never questioned.
The Psalms contain anguished questions addressed directly to God.
Maybe you believed following Jesus meant eventually reaching a place where life could no longer break your heart.
Then you discovered that Christians still bury people they love.
Christians still receive devastating diagnoses.
Christians still experience betrayal.
Christians still lose jobs.
Christians still experience depression, loneliness, persecution, disappointment and grief.
We are not immune to a fallen world.
We have a Savior who entered it.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not God shouting instructions toward drowning humanity from the safety of heaven.
The Gospel is God coming to us.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
Jesus experienced hunger.
Exhaustion.
Rejection.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Violence.
Grief.
And ultimately crucifixion.
The cross demolishes the accusation that God cannot understand suffering.
Jesus Christ entered suffering more deeply than we can comprehend.
At Calvary, the One who commanded the Sea of Galilee did something even more astonishing.
He did not command the nails to disappear.
He did not call angels to destroy His enemies.
He did not descend from the cross to prove His identity to the mockers.
He stayed.
Not because He lacked power.
Because He was accomplishing redemption.
The sinless Son of God bore sin, giving Himself for sinners so that everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can be forgiven, reconciled to God and given eternal life.
Then came the silence of the tomb.
Imagine being one of His disciples that Saturday.
Everything would have looked finished.
The Messiah dead.
The dream buried.
Hope sealed behind stone.
If Christianity ended on Saturday, despair would have had the final word.
But Sunday came.
Jesus rose.
And resurrection forever changed what Christians mean when we say God is faithful.
It means even death does not get the last sentence.
Because Scripture is filled with situations that looked final until God revealed they were not.
Peter’s denial looked like failure.
Grace rewrote him into a restored shepherd.
Paul’s persecution of Christians looked like an unforgivable scandal.
Grace transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer—no lifetime of religious accomplishments, no opportunity to repair his reputation, no years remaining to prove himself.
Only a dying confession of faith.
And Jesus gave him hope beyond the grave.
That is grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not calling darkness light.
Not redefining sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Grace tells the truth about our sin and then points us toward a Savior whose mercy is greater than our ruin.
Maybe your storm has exposed things in you that calm seasons successfully concealed.
Fear.
Control.
Anger.
Bitterness.
Secret unbelief.
Hidden sin.
The desperate need to control tomorrow.
Perhaps you thought your greatest problem was the storm.
Then the storm exposed your heart.
That happened to the disciples.
After Jesus calmed the sea, Mark gives us an extraordinary reversal.
The storm stops…
but their fear increases.
Mark says:
ἐφοβήθησαν φόβον μέγαν — ephobēthēsan phobon megan.
Literally, they “feared a great fear.”
Why?
Because suddenly the storm was no longer the most frightening reality in the boat.
Jesus was.
They looked at one another and asked:
“Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
There it is.
The question beneath the entire story.
Not:
“How can I avoid storms?”
Not:
“How can I guarantee that every prayer gets the answer I want?”
Not even primarily:
“How do I become less afraid?”
But:
Who is this?
That is what the storm uncovered.
The disciples already knew Jesus as Teacher.
The storm forced them to confront something infinitely larger.
Who speaks to creation and creation obeys?
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly portray the LORD as sovereign over the raging sea. Psalm 107 describes sailors overwhelmed by storm, crying to the LORD in distress, and God stilling the storm.
So when Jesus stands in a boat and commands the wind and sea, Mark is not merely presenting an inspirational story about staying calm under pressure.
He is revealing something about Jesus.
The storm becomes a theater for Christ’s identity.
And perhaps your storm is confronting you with the same question.
Who is Jesus when the prayer has not been answered yet?
Who is Jesus when the medical report still says what it said yesterday?
Who is Jesus when the person you love still has not returned?
Who is Jesus when your finances remain frightening?
Who is Jesus when grief wakes up beside you every morning?
Who is Jesus when you have obeyed and still cannot see the other shore?
If Jesus is only valuable when He gives you the life you wanted, eventually suffering will dismantle your faith.
But if Jesus Himself is the treasure…
the storm can take much from you without taking everything.
Paul learned something like this through his own suffering.
He pleaded with the Lord three times for his “thorn” to depart.
God did not give Paul the answer Paul initially requested.
Instead came the promise:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
That is not a verse for pretending pain does not hurt.
It is a declaration that sometimes Christ demonstrates His sufficiency not by immediately removing weakness but by sustaining His people inside it.
There are miracles of deliverance.
Praise God for them.
Pray boldly for them.
Ask God to heal.
Ask Him to restore.
Ask Him to provide.
Ask Him to open impossible doors.
The Jesus of Scripture truly heals, rescues, provides and delivers according to His sovereign will.
But never turn a miracle into something God owes us.
Because sometimes He parts the sea.
Sometimes He calms the sea.
And sometimes He gives His child enough grace to endure the sea until they reach home.
Faith trusts Christ in all three.
Perhaps that is where you are right now.
Still waiting.
Still hurting.
Still praying.
Still confused.
Then hear this carefully:
You do not have to manufacture a victorious smile to prove you trust Jesus.
Bring Him your actual heart.
The frightened one.
The disappointed one.
The exhausted one.
The heart that sometimes asks, “Do You care?”
Bring that heart to Christ.
But do not merely ask Jesus to change your circumstances.
Ask Him to reveal Himself.
“Lord, show me who You are here.”
“Teach me to trust You here.”
“Expose whatever this storm is revealing in me.”
“Forgive my unbelief.”
“Keep me near You.”
“If You remove this cup, I will praise You.”
“If You ask me to walk through it longer, hold me.”
“And whatever happens, do not let suffering steal my eyes from Christ.”
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years trying to become good enough for God while secretly drowning beneath guilt.
Your greatest storm may not be financial, relational or physical.
It may be the knowledge of what you have done.
The affair.
The addiction.
The abortion.
The lies.
The years wasted.
The secret nobody knows.
The faith you abandoned.
The family you wounded.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
You may think Christianity is for people whose boats are clean.
It is not.
Jesus came for sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Repair yourself and perhaps God will accept you.”
It announces that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
You cannot rewrite your past.
But Jesus can redeem a life surrendered to Him.
Your scandal does not become righteousness merely because you regret it.
Your sin needs forgiveness.
And forgiveness is precisely why the cross matters.
Bring the truth into His light.
Repent.
Stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Come to Him.
There is grace.
Real grace.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace strong enough to forgive you and holy enough to transform you.
Maybe the storm outside you will stop tomorrow.
I pray it does.
Maybe the phone will ring.
Maybe the doctor will call with unexpectedly good news.
Maybe restoration will begin.
Maybe the door will finally open.
We should never become so cynical about suffering that we stop asking God for deliverance.
But perhaps tomorrow the wind will still be blowing.
If it is, Christ will not suddenly become less Lord.
That may be the sentence you need to save and return to when another dark night comes:
The continuation of the storm does not mean the suspension of the sovereignty of Jesus.
Your circumstances can still be frightening while Christ remains faithful.
You can still have questions while Christ remains Lord.
You can still cry while Christ remains good.
You can still be waiting while Christ remains present.
And one day, whether through deliverance in this life or resurrection into the life to come, every believer in Christ will discover that no storm had authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
So if this article found you while your own boat feels like it is filling with water, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest.
And if the storm has exposed sin, fear, bitterness or something you have kept hidden from God and everyone else, perhaps your response is simply:
“No more hiding.”
Not because typing words earns grace.
It does not.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending.
And look around.
Somebody you know is currently smiling on Facebook while privately trying not to drown.
You may never know what sharing this article could interrupt.
A night of despair.
A crisis of faith.
A believer quietly wondering whether God has abandoned them.
A grieving mother.
An exhausted father.
A young Christian discovering that following Jesus does not make life painless.
A prodigal wondering whether there is still a road home.
It cannot.
Not because supporting a ministry earns salvation.
It never will.
And not because Christians must pay money in order to glorify God.
The Gospel forbids us from turning grace into a transaction.
But if you genuinely want to glorify God by helping Gospel-centered truth reach more people, supporting and sharing faithful Christian ministry can be one practical expression of stewardship.
Send it privately to someone whose storm has lasted longer than they expected.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is asking the same question those frightened disciples asked:
“Jesus… do You care?”
The cross answers.
The empty tomb answers.
And the Christ who remains Lord when the waves rise answers.
Yes.
But His love does not always reveal itself by preventing every storm.
Sometimes His love carries us through one.
Sometimes His power silences the wind.
Sometimes His grace sustains trembling disciples until morning.
And sometimes the storm you begged Jesus to remove becomes the place where you finally discover that what you needed most was not a life without waves—
but a Savior whom the waves must obey.
The storm may still be writing across the sky, but it never gets to write the final sentence of a life held by Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID GOD CREATE SEXUAL PLEASURE—or Is Pleasure Merely a Side Effect of Reproduction?
paragraphs: DID GOD CREATE SEXUAL PLEASURE—or Is Pleasure Merely a Side Effect of Reproduction?
What if one of the things Christians have been embarrassed to talk about was something God was never embarrassed to create?
There is a question many Christians would rather whisper than ask aloud.
Did God actually create sexual pleasure?
Not merely sex.
Not merely reproductive organs.
Not merely the biological machinery necessary to produce children.
Pleasure.
Desire.
Longing.
The breathtaking vulnerability of being wanted by the person who has covenanted to love you.
The warmth of a husband and wife reaching for each other when no child is being conceived, no pregnancy is possible, and no reproductive purpose seems immediately present.
Was that pleasure deliberately woven into God's design?
Or did God simply create reproduction...and pleasure happened to come along for the ride?
That question may sound dangerously close to territory Christians should avoid.
But perhaps that discomfort reveals something.
Because the Bible itself is considerably less embarrassed about married sexuality than many believers are.
And what Scripture actually says may surprise the person who grew up believing that holiness meant pretending the body did not exist.
Before we go any further, one boundary must be immovable.
The biblical celebration of sexual pleasure is not a license for sexual autonomy.
Scripture does not teach that because desire is powerful, whatever we desire must therefore be good.
It does not baptize adultery, pornography, exploitation, lust, coercion, fornication, or the use of another person's body for selfish gratification.
Jesus Himself takes sexual holiness seriously enough to address lust at the level of the heart.
So this is not an article arguing that pleasure is god.
It is almost the opposite.
It is an argument that pleasure has a God.
And when the gift is separated from the Giver, something beautiful can become destructive.
But when the gift remains under the wisdom of the One who designed it...
the story changes.
Go back before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before shame.
Before broken marriages.
Before sexual exploitation.
Before anyone ever used another human being as an object.
Go back before the Fall.
There is a man.
There is a woman.
There is God.
And there is no shame.
Genesis says:
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
vehayu levasar echad.
“They shall become one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24.
The Hebrew is strikingly physical.
Basar means flesh.
Echad means one.
The man “clings” or “cleaves” to his wife—דָבַק, davaq—and they become “one flesh.” The Hebrew text presents leaving, cleaving, and becoming one flesh as the movement of the marriage union.
Then Genesis adds something almost startling in its innocence.
The man and his wife were naked...
and they were not ashamed.
Think about that.
The Bible's first picture of marital nakedness is not pornography.
It is not exploitation.
It is not embarrassment.
It is covenantal innocence.

And immediately before this, God had already established humanity as male and female. Genesis 1:27 uses the Hebrew words זָכָר (zakar, male) and נְקֵבָה (neqevah, female), and God blesses them with the command to “be fruitful and multiply.” After surveying His creation, God calls what He has made “very good.”
So reproduction unquestionably belongs to God's purpose for human sexuality.
We should not erase that because modern culture dislikes boundaries.
Children are not an embarrassing biological consequence of sex in the biblical story.
Fruitfulness is presented as blessing.
But here is where the question becomes fascinating.
Does Scripture therefore teach that reproduction is the only meaningful purpose of marital sexual union—and that pleasure is merely an accidental biological side effect?
That conclusion becomes very difficult to maintain when you keep reading.
Because eventually you reach a passage that sounds almost scandalous to ears accustomed to treating holiness as discomfort with the body.
Proverbs 5.
The chapter warns a man against sexual unfaithfulness.
God could have answered adultery simply by saying:
“Do not desire.”
He does not.
Instead, biblical wisdom redirects desire toward covenant faithfulness.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then comes verse 19:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is the King James rendering.
The Hebrew is even worth slowing down for.
The text includes:
“בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד”
be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The sense is of being continually captivated, exhilarated, or intoxicated in her love.

Modern translations variously render the idea as being “captivated,” “enraptured,” or “intoxicated” by her love. The surrounding Hebrew language is deliberately affectionate and sensual, and the command appears precisely in a warning against seeking sexual satisfaction outside marriage.
Do not miss what just happened.
Scripture did not solve sinful sexuality by declaring pleasure sinful.
It confronted sinful sexuality by directing sexual delight toward faithfulness.
That distinction changes everything.
The problem was not that the man could experience desire.
The problem was where that desire might take him.
God's wisdom does not merely say, “Stay away from the adulteress.”
It effectively says:
Find your delight at home.
Rejoice in your wife.
Remain captivated by her love.
That is not embarrassed language.
That is not reluctant permission.
That is celebration within covenant.
And then there is the Song of Songs.
If you have ever wondered whether some Christians are more uncomfortable with married desire than the Bible is, read this book slowly.
Not crudely.
Not voyeuristically.
Reverently.
The poetry celebrates beauty, longing, fragrance, touch, admiration, exclusivity, desire, and mutual belonging.
At one point the beloved says:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
Song of Songs 7:10.
The Hebrew word behind “desire” is תְּשׁוּקָה—teshuqah.
Desire.
Longing.
The Song also speaks openly of “delights,” with translations reflecting the unmistakably pleasurable character of the poetry.
This is in the Bible.
God did not need to inspire an entire collection of romantic poetry in order to explain reproduction.
A biological command could have accomplished that.
“Be fruitful and multiply” was already sufficient.
Yet Scripture also gives us poetry celebrating the experience of lovers delighting in one another.
That matters.
It does not prove that every imaginable sexual desire is holy.
It proves something more careful and beautiful:
Biblical sexuality cannot adequately be described as reproduction with pleasure accidentally attached.
Pleasure, delight, desire, intimacy, mutual belonging, and covenant faithfulness are woven into the Bible's positive portrayal of marital union.
Then the New Testament does something equally important.
Paul writes to married Christians in Corinth:

In 1 Corinthians 7:3, the husband is told to fulfill his marital responsibility toward his wife, “and likewise” the wife toward her husband. The symmetry matters. Paul is not describing the wife as a reproductive instrument existing for the husband's use. He speaks reciprocally.
Then Paul says:
“μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους”
mē apostereite allēlous.
“Do not deprive one another.”
And if husband and wife temporarily abstain, Paul specifies mutual agreement—ἐκ συμφώνου, ek symphōnou—for a time devoted to prayer, followed by coming together again.
Notice what is absent.
Paul does not say:
“Come together again only when attempting conception.”
His pastoral concern includes marital intimacy itself.
That does not erase procreation.
It simply demonstrates that the New Testament recognizes a marital sexual relationship extending beyond an isolated reproductive event.
And perhaps now the deeper question begins to surface.
Why would God make covenant intimacy pleasurable?
Scripture does not give us a verse saying, “Here are the biochemical reasons I created orgasm.”
We should be honest about that.
The Bible is theological revelation, not a modern physiology textbook.
So Christians should resist pretending Scripture explicitly answers scientific questions it never directly addresses.
But Scripture gives enough revelation to reject two opposite errors.
One error says:
“If it feels good, God must approve.”
False.
Sin can feel good temporarily.
The other error says:
“If it feels good, God probably disapproves.”
Also false.

God created human beings capable of receiving good gifts with thanksgiving. Paul explicitly pushes back against an ascetic suspicion of God's creation, warning about those who forbid marriage and declaring that what God created is good when received rightly and thankfully.
Christian holiness is not hatred of creation.
It is creation restored to its proper relationship with the Creator.
Food is good.
Gluttony is not.
Rest is good.
Sloth is not.
Money can serve good purposes.
Greed does not.
Sexual pleasure within God's design can be good.
Sexual sin is not.
The existence of counterfeit pleasure does not prove authentic pleasure is evil.
Counterfeits exist because something valuable can be imitated.
And this may be where someone reading this suddenly stops thinking academically.
Because perhaps this isn't merely theology for you.
Maybe sex has never felt innocent.
Maybe someone introduced you to pornography before you understood what it was doing to your imagination.
Maybe you have slept with people whose names still carry memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe boundaries were crossed against you.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Maybe your spouse feels rejected.
Maybe you feel unwanted.
Maybe desire has become tangled with shame.
Maybe you keep promising Jesus that you will stop going back to that screen...
that conversation...
that fantasy...
that person...
and then midnight comes.
And you fall again.
Then Sunday morning comes.
You sing.
You smile.
You shake hands.
Nobody knows.
But you know.
And God knows.
So perhaps the real question underneath “Did God create sexual pleasure?” is something far more personal.
“After what I've done with sexuality...
does God still want me?”
Now we have reached the heart of the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of sexually clean people congratulating themselves while sexually broken people stand outside.
It is the story of sinners meeting a Savior.
Jesus did not die because our scandals were small.
He died because our sin was real.
And the cross does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves how much it matters.
Grace is not God pretending darkness is light.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do for themselves.
Jesus Christ bears sin.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus gives new life.
Jesus teaches us to stop asking, “How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
Grace teaches another question:
“How completely can I belong to Christ?”
That changes sexuality.
Because your body is no longer merely an appetite demanding satisfaction.
Your spouse is no longer an object existing to meet your needs.
Another person's body is not content.
Pornography is not harmless entertainment simply because nobody appears to be standing in your room.
Desire is not your master.
Jesus is Lord.
And if you are married, biblical sexual intimacy becomes something profoundly different from consumption.
It becomes giving.
Receiving.
Trust.
Tenderness.
Faithfulness.
Patience.
Mutuality.
Vulnerability.
Delight without exploitation.
Pleasure without idolatry.
Passion without betrayal.
Two people who can be naked without needing to perform for the imaginary audience pornography trained them to expect.
Two people learning each other rather than consuming each other.
Two imperfect sinners saying with their lives:
I am not shopping for someone else.
I am here.
I choose you.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Perhaps that is one reason the enemy has worked so relentlessly to separate sexuality from covenant.
Because sex detached from covenant can become consumption.
Bodies become products.
People become experiences.
Desire becomes entitlement.
Pleasure becomes master.
And when pleasure becomes master, it eventually becomes cruel.
It promises freedom while quietly demanding increasingly more.
But Christ does not merely tell us to suppress everything human.
He redeems human beings.
Paul takes Genesis 2:24—the language of one flesh—and in Ephesians 5 says something astonishing.
The “one flesh” mystery ultimately points beyond husband and wife.
“This mystery is great,” Paul says, and then speaks of Christ and the church. The Greek text explicitly connects the one-flesh quotation with Χριστόν—Christ—and ἐκκλησίαν—the church.
Marriage is not the Gospel.
Sex is not salvation.
But Christian marriage can point beyond itself.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Self-giving love.
Belonging.
A bridegroom who does not abandon His bride.
And suddenly sexuality becomes far too sacred to worship...
and far too sacred to trivialize.
So did God create sexual pleasure?
The most biblically careful answer is this:

God created humanity male and female, instituted the one-flesh marriage union, commanded fruitfulness, called His creation very good, and gave Scripture that positively celebrates marital desire, delight, satisfaction, and mutual sexual intimacy.

Therefore, while Scripture never gives a modern scientific explanation of why the human sexual response produces pleasure, the biblical witness gives us strong reason to understand marital sexual pleasure as belonging to God's good design rather than treating it as an embarrassing accident attached to reproduction.
But pleasure is not the purpose of life.
Jesus is greater than pleasure.
Marriage is not necessary for human worth.
Sex is not necessary for a meaningful life.
Jesus Himself lived without marriage and without sexual intercourse, yet He embodied perfect humanity.
That matters enormously.
Because our culture tells single people they are incomplete without sex.
Scripture does not.
Our culture tells married people they deserve constant sexual fulfillment.
Scripture does not.
Our culture says desire establishes identity and morality.
Scripture does not.
The Christian does not say, “I desire, therefore I must.”
The Christian learns to say:
“I belong to Christ, therefore even my desires must bow before Him.”
And that surrender is not the destruction of humanity.
It is freedom from being ruled by appetite.
Maybe you have been ashamed of your body.
Maybe you have worshiped your body.
Maybe you have used someone else's body.
Maybe someone used yours.
Maybe your sexual history reads like a collection of chapters you desperately wish could be torn from the book.
Listen carefully.
You cannot travel backward and become the person who never sinned.
But Jesus can write what happens next.
That is grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Redeeming the sinner caught inside it.
Peter could not undo his denial.
Paul could not un-persecute the church.
The woman caught in adultery could not rewrite yesterday.
But an encounter with Jesus meant yesterday did not have to own tomorrow.
The Gospel is not “Your past wasn't that bad.”
The Gospel is:
Your Savior is that good.
Repentance means bringing what you have hidden into the light.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Secret messages.
Fantasy.
Bitterness.
Sexual selfishness.
Shame.
The wounds you have never told anyone about.
The habits you keep renaming so you do not have to confront them.
Bring them to Christ.
Not because confession earns His blood.
Because His blood is sufficient for sinners who have nothing left to hide behind.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is Romans 8:1.
No condemnation does not mean no transformation.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us to follow.
Grace does not merely remove the sentence.
Grace begins rewriting the person.
Be honest.
If you need prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
If conviction has reached somewhere you have kept locked for years, comment, “no more hiding.”
And if Christ has already begun restoring what sin shattered, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only believer fighting a battle behind a Sunday smile.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Send it privately to the friend who would never admit publicly that this is their battle.
And if someone you love has walked so far from God that you wonder whether they would even read something Christian anymore...
send it anyway.
Sometimes God uses one uncomfortable question to open a door the person had kept locked for years.

If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider following closely and supporting this ministry so this kind of Christ-centered biblical teaching can continue reaching people who are searching, ashamed, wounded, skeptical, curious, or quietly desperate for truth.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone should manipulate you into giving money “for God.”
Scripture says giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion.
But voluntary generosity can genuinely become an act of worship when it flows from gratitude to God and a sincere desire to advance Gospel work.
One share can enter a home we have never visited.
One tag can reach someone whose private battle you know nothing about.
One saved article can be reopened during a night of temptation.
One honest comment can make another wounded Christian realize, “I'm not fighting alone.”
And Gospel Warrior is about more than a single article.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the lukewarm believer.
Invite the person asking difficult questions.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about the deepest parts of human existence.
Because we are not here to convince people that Christians have spotless histories.
We are here because Jesus Christ saves sinners.
And maybe that is what you needed to hear most.
Not merely that God created sexuality.
Not merely that marital pleasure can be good.
Not merely that reproduction matters.
But that even in one of the most intimate, wounded, confused, exploited, idolized, and shame-covered areas of human life...
Jesus is still Lord.
And Jesus is still Redeemer.
Your desires do not have to rule you.
Your failures do not have to name you.
Your wounds do not have to become your identity.
Your pornography history does not get the final sentence.
Your adultery does not get the final sentence.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Your loneliness does not get the final sentence.
Your past does not hold the pen.
Christ does.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive grace.
Walk in truth.
Learn holiness without shame and intimacy without idolatry.
And remember this when the accusations return:
The scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID COLLECTED WIVES LONG BEFORE BATHSHEBA ENTERED THE STORY
paragraphs: DAVID COLLECTED WIVES LONG BEFORE BATHSHEBA ENTERED THE STORY

Bathsheba was not the beginning of David’s compromise. Long before the rooftop, the secret summons, the pregnancy, and the bloodshed, Scripture had already been leaving warning signs in David’s story—and perhaps the most frightening part is how ordinary those warning signs looked.
Everybody remembers the rooftop.
A king walking when he should have been at war.
A woman bathing.
A lingering look.
A summons.
A pregnancy.
A desperate cover-up.
A loyal soldier deliberately abandoned to die.
Then a prophet standing before a throne and saying words that shattered the king’s illusion:
“You are the man.”
That is how many people remember David’s great scandal.
Bathsheba.
But what if the tragedy did not actually begin with Bathsheba?
What if 2 Samuel 11 was an explosion whose fuse had been burning for years?
Because long before David saw Bathsheba, David had already been collecting wives.
And Scripture noticed.
That detail matters because some of the most destructive sins in our lives do not begin on the night everything collapses.
They begin years earlier.
Quietly.
Respectably.
Incrementally.
One tolerated compromise.
One appetite we refuse to confront.
One boundary moved.
Then moved again.
One thing we know is spiritually dangerous, but because lightning does not immediately fall from heaven, we begin convincing ourselves that perhaps God does not care as much as we thought.
And eventually something that once troubled our conscience becomes normal.
That may be one of the most terrifying sentences you will read today:
You can become comfortable with something that is slowly preparing you for catastrophe.
David did not wake up one morning as a murderer.
He did not begin his story as the king who took another man’s wife.
He was the shepherd boy who trusted God when grown warriors trembled.
He was the young man who looked at Goliath and saw something everybody else had forgotten: the giant was enormous, but God was greater.
He wrote songs in caves.
He spared Saul when killing Saul could have accelerated his own promotion.
He wept.
He worshiped.
He prayed.
He loved God.
Scripture would remember him as a man after God’s own heart.
And that is precisely why his story should make believers uncomfortable.
Because spiritual history does not make anyone immune to spiritual compromise.
Yesterday’s obedience cannot substitute for today’s surrender.
You can have killed giants and still need to kill the appetite growing quietly inside you.
Before Bathsheba ever appears in David’s story, Scripture has already introduced us to multiple wives.
Michal was Saul’s daughter and David’s wife (1 Samuel 18:27).

Later, while David was living in the wilderness, we encounter Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, formerly the wife of Nabal. First Samuel 25:42–43 tells us that Abigail became David’s wife and then immediately says:
“David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel, and they both were his wives.”
The story continues.
Second Samuel 3:2–5 records sons born to David in Hebron through Ahinoam, Abigail, Maacah, Haggith, Abital, and Eglah.
Then comes a verse that is easy to read quickly because it does not immediately contain adultery, murder, confrontation, or judgment.
But slow down.
Second Samuel 5:13 says:
“After he left Hebron, David took more concubines and wives in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.”
More.
David already had wives.
Then David took more.
And all of this appears before the Bathsheba account of 2 Samuel 11.
The Bible is not hiding the trajectory.
But we must be careful here, because faithfully reading Scripture means refusing to confuse biblical description with biblical approval.
The fact that Scripture records something does not mean Scripture endorses it.
The Bible records polygamous households with devastating honesty, but the creation pattern reaches further back.
Genesis 2:24 describes the foundational marriage union: a man is joined to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad
“One flesh.”
Jesus Himself returns to this creation text when teaching about marriage.
In Matthew 19:5–6, the Greek preserves the same astonishing idea:
σάρκα μίαν
sarka mian
“One flesh.”
Jesus then declares that they are no longer two, but one flesh, and what God has joined together must not be separated.
One man.
One woman.
One covenantal union.
One flesh.
And there was another command David, as Israel’s king, should have known.
Long before David wore the crown, Deuteronomy had warned Israel about what a king must not do.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
velo yarbeh-lo nashim
Literally, in context:
“And he shall not multiply wives for himself…”
Then comes the reason:
“…lest his heart turn away.”
Do not rush past that.
God connected multiplied wives with the danger of a diverted heart.
The warning was not merely about royal administration.
It was about affection.
Desire.
Loyalty.
The heart.
And David multiplied wives.

This does not mean every detail of David’s later sin with Bathsheba can be reduced to one cause. Scripture does not say, “David committed adultery with Bathsheba because he had multiple wives,” so neither should we.
But Scripture absolutely allows us to see a pattern of accumulating women before the catastrophic events of 2 Samuel 11.
That distinction matters.
Bathsheba was not David’s first departure from the creation pattern for marriage.
And suddenly the rooftop looks different.
David’s fall remains shocking.
But it no longer looks completely isolated.
This is where David’s ancient story begins walking uncomfortably close to ours.
Because perhaps you do not have a rooftop.
Perhaps you have a phone.
Perhaps nobody is being summoned to a palace.
Perhaps it is a private message.
A hidden conversation.
A browser history.
An emotional attachment your spouse knows nothing about.
A flirtation you keep calling harmless.
A habit you keep deleting and reinstalling.
A fantasy you keep feeding.
A resentment you have rehearsed so many times that bitterness now feels justified.
A hunger for attention.
Money.
Power.
Pornography.
Approval.
Control.
Recognition.
Comfort.
Maybe there has been no catastrophic scandal.
Yet.
And that tiny word matters.
Yet.
We often want God to rescue us from the dramatic sin while protecting the smaller compromises that trained our hearts to tolerate it.
We pray, “Lord, don’t let me fall.”
God may answer:
“Then stop walking toward the edge.”
David’s story warns us that the scandal everyone eventually sees may have roots in compromises almost nobody noticed.
That should not make us obsessed with predicting everybody else’s downfall.
It should make us examine our own hearts.
What have you normalized that once bothered you?
What are you defending today that five years ago you would have called dangerous?
What appetite keeps asking for “more”?
Because that word follows David before Bathsheba.
More.
More wives.
More concubines.
More.
And appetites rarely announce when they have had enough.
Sin has a frightening vocabulary.
Just one more.
Just this once.
Nobody will know.
I deserve this.
I can handle it.
I’ll stop later.
David had power.
David had wives.
David had a palace.
David had military victories.
David had fame.
David had authority.
And when he saw another man’s wife, what he possessed did not silence what he wanted.
That is the deception of uncontrolled desire.
It keeps promising satisfaction while enlarging its own capacity to hunger.
Then Bathsheba entered the story.
Second Samuel 11 tells us David saw her from the roof.
He asked about her.
And someone answered with information that should have functioned like a wall:
“Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
Wife.
That should have ended the matter.
She belonged within another covenant.
But David sent messengers and took her.
She became pregnant.
David attempted concealment.
When Uriah refused to cooperate unknowingly with David’s cover-up, David escalated.
This is another horrifying feature of unrepented sin.
Sin rarely remains satisfied with being one sin.
Lust needed concealment.
Concealment needed manipulation.
Manipulation failed.
So manipulation gave way to murder.
David sent Uriah back to the battlefield carrying instructions that would arrange his own death.
Think about that.
Uriah carried the letter.
David carried the guilt.
And for a while, David appeared to have gotten away with it.
That may be one of the most dangerous moments in anyone’s spiritual life:
when disobedience appears successful.
No immediate thunder.
No visible judgment.
No prophet standing at the door.
The secret seems buried.
Life moves forward.
But 2 Samuel 11 closes with a sentence more terrifying than public exposure:
“The thing David had done displeased the LORD.”
People did not have to know.
God knew.
The palace could remain quiet.
Heaven was not confused.
Then God sent Nathan.
Nathan told David about a rich man with many sheep who stole the single beloved lamb of a poor man.
David became furious.
The king who could not clearly see his own sin could see somebody else’s sin immediately.
How painfully human.
We can become experts at recognizing in others what we have learned to excuse in ourselves.
David pronounced judgment.
Then Nathan spoke:
“You are the man!”
No committee.
No spin.
No royal public-relations strategy.
No hiding behind past victories.
No reminding Nathan about Goliath.
No pointing toward all the psalms David had written.
“You are the man.”
And here is where the Gospel begins shining through the wreckage.
David finally says:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Nathan replies:
“The LORD has taken away your sin. You are not going to die.”
Do not sentimentalize this moment.
David’s forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence of his actions. Second Samuel records terrible consequences within his house.
Grace is not God pretending sin did not matter.
Grace is astonishing precisely because sin mattered so much.
David deserved judgment.
Yet God showed mercy.
And David’s brokenness later erupts in the prayer preserved in Psalm 51:
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your unfailing love…”
The Hebrew opening cries:
חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים
chonneni Elohim
“Be gracious to me, O God.”
David does not negotiate.
He does not say, “Remember Goliath.”
He does not say, “But Saul was worse.”
He does not say, “Look at everything good I have done.”
He begs for mercy.
That is repentance.
Not reputation management.
Not getting caught and becoming embarrassed.
Not crying because consequences hurt.
Repentance stops defending the darkness and turns toward God.
“Against you, you only, have I sinned…”
“Create in me a pure heart, O God…”
David finally understood something every sinner eventually has to understand.
Our deepest problem cannot be solved by becoming better at hiding.
We need a new heart.
And David could not create one himself.
Neither can we.
This is where David’s story must ultimately take us beyond David.
To Jesus.
David was Israel’s celebrated king, but David needed a greater King.
David defeated Goliath but could not ultimately defeat the sin within David.
Jesus Christ came from David’s royal line, yet where David failed, Christ remained faithful.
David took what was not his.
Jesus surrendered what was rightfully His.
David used power to serve his desire.
Jesus used His authority in perfect obedience to the Father and gave Himself for sinners.
David arranged for an innocent man to die to conceal his guilt.
Jesus, the truly innocent Man, willingly died to cover the guilt of people like David.
And people like us.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at human sin.
Christ bore it.
The cross tells us simultaneously that our sin is worse than our excuses admit and God’s grace is greater than our shame can imagine.
That is why the Gospel is not:
“Try harder so God might tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
You do not need to wait until your private compromise becomes a public catastrophe.
You do not need a Bathsheba-sized scandal before you become serious about the thing quietly pulling your heart away from God.
Maybe this article found you before the rooftop.
Before the message.
Before the affair.
Before the divorce.
Before the addiction becomes public.
Before the resentment destroys the relationship.
Before the secret becomes a headline in your family.
Before the thing you keep controlling begins controlling you.
Then perhaps mercy is warning you early.
Listen.
There is still time to close the door.
There is still time to confess.
There is still time to tell somebody trustworthy.
There is still time to repent.
There is still time to bring the hidden thing into the light.
And if you are reading this after everything has already collapsed, David’s story has something to say to you too.
Scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
David sinned grievously.
David suffered consequences.
David needed mercy.
But God did not abandon His redemptive purpose.
And generations later, another name would appear in David’s line.
Jesus.
Matthew opens the genealogy of Christ by calling Him “the son of David.”
Think about the grace contained in those words.
David’s ugliest chapter could not cancel God’s promise.
This does not minimize what David did.
It magnifies the God who redeems sinners.
And perhaps that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
Your sin must be confronted.
Your excuses must die.
Repentance is necessary.
But your scandal does not possess more saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Your shame is not stronger than His grace.
Your past is not lord.
Jesus is Lord.
Maybe you have been hiding because you think exposure would make you unlovable.
Maybe you have spent years maintaining a Christian appearance while privately starving.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
Maybe you serve.
Teach.
Sing.
Preach.
Lead.
Post Bible verses.
Encourage everybody else.
And then you go home carrying something you hope nobody ever discovers.
David teaches us that spiritual usefulness is never permission to stop guarding the heart.
But David also teaches us that when God exposes sin, His purpose is not merely humiliation.
He calls sinners to repentance.
And the Gospel tells us where repentant sinners must ultimately run.
Not deeper into hiding.
To Christ.
