Two sets of wounds sit at one table.
Two personalities share one bedroom.
Two imperfect people discover that marriage has an uncomfortable way of exposing things singleness sometimes allowed them to hide.
Pride.
Selfishness.
Fear.
Control.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Impatience.
Childhood wounds nobody else could see.
Marriage can be beautiful.
Marriage can also be a mirror.
And sometimes the person you promised to love becomes the person standing closest when everything you have spent years hiding finally comes to the surface.
That is when “one flesh” stops sounding romantic.
Because becoming one is costly.
You can share a mattress and still live emotionally separated.
You can have sex and still refuse vulnerability.
You can share a surname and secretly maintain two kingdoms.
You can post anniversary pictures while barely speaking when the phone is put away.
You can sit beside each other in church while resentment sleeps between you at home.
You can know someone’s body...
and stop knowing their heart.
That is the tragedy.
We can perform the outward signs of togetherness while slowly becoming strangers.
Maybe someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You still say, “I love you.”
But something has changed.
Conversations became logistics.
Touch became rare.
Prayer disappeared.
Little disappointments became private resentments.
Private resentments became emotional walls.
And neither of you remembers exactly when the wall became taller than the marriage.
Maybe your story is worse.
Maybe there was betrayal.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Deception.
Words that cannot be unheard.
A secret discovered.
A trust shattered.
Maybe you were the one who caused the wound.
And you have wondered whether the sentence you destroyed can ever be rewritten.
Listen carefully.
Genesis 2:24 is not permission to romanticize brokenness.

And Christianity does not teach that saying “one flesh” magically removes consequences, makes abuse acceptable, eliminates the need for repentance, or means serious danger should simply be endured in silence.
But Genesis does reveal something enormous about God's intention for marriage.
Marriage was designed for a depth of union that cannot be reduced to sexual chemistry.
And Jesus confirms the seriousness of it.

When questioned about marriage and divorce, Christ reaches behind the arguments of His day and returns His hearers to creation. He cites the Genesis pattern and says that the two become one flesh. Then He adds the staggering conclusion:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
The marriage union, in Jesus' teaching, is not merely two people saying, “We like each other.”
He speaks of what God has joined together.
Think about that.
The Creator is brought into the sentence.
Marriage is therefore bigger than attraction.
Bigger than sexual compatibility.
Bigger than a wedding photograph.
Bigger than the butterflies that brought two people together.
Feelings change.
Bodies age.
Money disappears.
Beauty changes.
Pregnancies change bodies.
Illness enters houses.
Parents die.
Careers collapse.
Children grow up.
Desire can rise and fall.
Some mornings marriage feels like poetry.
Other mornings it feels like choosing faithfulness while standing in a kitchen full of dirty dishes with two exhausted people who barely slept.
That does not make the covenant meaningless.
Sometimes that is where covenant becomes visible.
Because biblical love is not merely something that happens to you.
Love also acts.
Love sacrifices.
Love tells the truth.
Love repents.
Love forgives.
Love seeks the good of another.
Love refuses to call selfishness “authenticity” simply because selfishness feels easier.
And suddenly “one flesh” begins to sound less like a wedding-night slogan and more like a lifetime of two people learning that covenant says:
Your life matters to me now.
Your holiness matters to me.
Your wounds matter to me.
Your future matters to me.
Your relationship with God matters to me.
I will not treat your body like an object while ignoring your soul.
I will not demand intimacy while refusing tenderness.
I will not call possession love.
I will not call control headship.
I will not call silence peace when bitterness is eating us alive.
I will not demand forgiveness while refusing repentance.
Because covenant love does not ask only:
“What can I receive from you?”
It asks:
“How can I faithfully love you before God?”
And then the Bible does something astonishing.
It takes us beyond Adam and Eve.
Beyond husband and wife.
Beyond the bedroom.
Beyond Eden.
All the way to Christ.
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 again in Ephesians 5.
He speaks of the two becoming one flesh.
Then he writes:
τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν
to mystērion touto mega estin
“This mystery is great.”
And then:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Paul is not saying that human marriage is Christ and the Church.
He is revealing that marriage mysteriously points beyond itself.
The Greek text explicitly connects this “great mystery”—μυστήριον...μέγα—with Christ and the Church.
And now Genesis explodes with Gospel significance.
The first Adam receives his bride.
The New Testament reveals Christ as the Bridegroom who loves His people.
And how does Christ love His Bride?
Not by using her.
Not by exploiting her.
Not by abandoning her when loving becomes costly.
Christ loves sacrificially.
He gives Himself.
That is the pattern Paul places before Christian marriage.
And this is where the Gospel becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not wait until His Bride was impressive.
He did not die for people who had finally cleaned themselves up enough to deserve Him.
He came for sinners.
For rebels.
For adulterers at heart.
For liars.
For the sexually broken.
For the ashamed.
For the religious hypocrite.
For the person who looks holy on Sunday and battles darkness on Monday night.
For people like us.
The scandal of grace is not that sin does not matter.
The scandal is that sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross...
and grace is so astonishing that He went willingly.
The cross never says your sin was small.
The cross says your sin was deadly.
And then it says something even more shocking:
His mercy is greater.
Maybe that is what someone needed to hear before reading another sentence.
Your sexual past does not have the authority to become your permanent identity.
Your pornography addiction does not get the final word.
Your adultery does not become righteous because grace exists—but neither does genuine repentance have to end in permanent exile from the mercy of Christ.
Your failed relationship is not your Savior.
Your successful marriage is not your Savior either.
Your virginity cannot save you.
Your wedding ring cannot save you.
Your spouse cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
That is why this teaching matters even if you are single.
“One flesh” is not a declaration that unmarried Christians are incomplete human beings.
Jesus Christ was never married, yet He was the perfect man.
Marriage is precious.
But marriage is not God.
And when we ask another human being to satisfy the deepest hunger that only Christ can satisfy, we crush that person beneath expectations no husband or wife was created to carry.
Your spouse was never meant to be your Messiah.
Your husband cannot bear the weight of being your god.
Your wife cannot bear the weight of being your savior.
Marriage flourishes most beautifully not when two people worship each other, but when two sinners learn to worship Christ together.
And maybe that is where healing begins.
Not with pretending.
Not with another filtered photograph.
Not with “We're fine.”
But with truth.
“I hurt you.”
“I have been selfish.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I have been hiding.”
“I need help.”
“I sinned.”
“Please forgive me.”
“Jesus, change me.”
There are marriages that do not need another romantic quote tonight.
They need repentance.
There are husbands who do not need another sermon about their wives submitting.
They need to look again at the crucified Christ and learn what sacrificial love actually costs.
There are wives carrying resentment that has hardened into contempt.
There are couples trying to repair intimacy without repairing trust.
There are people using sex to cover emotional distance.
There are others withholding affection as punishment.
There are secret phones.
Secret conversations.
Secret browser histories.
Secret fantasies.
Secret tears.
And Christ sees what nobody else sees.
But His exposure is not an invitation to run farther into darkness.
It is an invitation into light.
Repentance does not mean, “I got caught.”
Repentance means turning.
No more hiding.
No more renaming sin.
No more protecting the thing that is destroying you.
No more demanding that God bless what God has told you to surrender.
Come into the light.
Because the same Jesus who exposes sin is the Jesus who carried sin to Calvary.

And if you have been wounded by someone else's sin, forgiveness does not require pretending evil was good, denying consequences, abandoning wise boundaries, or instantly restoring trust that must be rebuilt truthfully.
Grace is not denial.
Grace tells the truth.
The cross proves it.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin did not matter.
He dealt with it.
That is why Christian restoration can never be built upon pretending nothing happened.
It must be built upon truth, repentance, grace, wisdom, and Christ.
Perhaps this is why the words “one flesh” are far more frightening—and far more beautiful—than we imagined.
God was never merely describing bodies touching.
He was establishing the pattern of a marital union in which two lives are joined so profoundly that Scripture can describe them as one flesh.
Sex expresses that union bodily.
Covenant gives it its marital home.
Faithfulness protects it.
Sacrificial love nourishes it.
Truth keeps it from becoming counterfeit.
Repentance repairs what sin tears.
Grace meets sinners inside it.
And Christ stands above it all.
Then Paul takes the mystery and points toward something greater still:
Christ and His Church.
That means every Christian marriage is living beneath a story bigger than itself.
A husband's love can whisper something about Christ's sacrificial love.
A marriage's faithfulness can testify that covenant means something.
Repentance after failure can demonstrate that grace is not theoretical.
Forgiveness can show a watching world that the Gospel reaches places human pride cannot repair.
And even when a marriage story has become scandalous...
Jesus is still the Redeemer.
That does not guarantee every earthly relationship will be restored exactly as we wish.
Scripture never gives us permission to make promises God Himself has not made.
But it does mean no repentant sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
No past is too filthy for His blood.
No shame is too old for His grace.
No hidden room in your heart is beyond His authority.
Jesus does not merely improve sinners.
He makes people new.
That is the Gospel.
And maybe the deepest question tonight is not simply:
“Do I understand one flesh?”
Maybe it is:
“Have I surrendered my whole life to Jesus Christ?”
Because you can understand Hebrew and still have a hardened heart.
You can parse Greek and still refuse repentance.
You can win arguments about marriage while losing your marriage.
You can defend biblical sexuality while secretly feeding lust.
You can know every verse...
and still not know the Savior those verses reveal.
So do not leave this article merely informed.
Let the Word examine you.
If something hidden was exposed while you were reading this, bring it to Jesus.
If you need to confess sin, confess it.
If you need wise pastoral help, seek it.
If you need professional help because your marriage is in serious crisis or danger, seek appropriate help.
If you need to apologize, stop rehearsing excuses.
If you have never trusted Christ, hear the heart of the Gospel: Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again. Turn from sin and trust Him.
Grace is not permission to remain who you were.
Grace is the mercy that meets you there and calls you to follow Jesus out.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And somewhere underneath this article may be another believer who reads your words and realizes:
“I am not the only one fighting.”
There are truths you do not need only once.
There may come a night when the emotions are gone, the argument is fresh, temptation is loud, or shame starts whispering again.
Come back.
Remember what covenant means.
Remember what repentance means.
Remember what grace cost.
Remember Jesus.
It does not.
It is not.
Scripture teaches generosity from the heart rather than giving under compulsion: “μὴ...ἐξ ἀνάγκης” — not from necessity or compulsion.
But voluntary generosity really can support Gospel work.

If you are looking for a place to direct additional voluntary support beyond the giving commitments you have prayerfully made before God, you can choose to make Gospel Warrior part of that generosity. Give freely, prayerfully, and without pressure.
Your sharing helps the message travel.
Your comments help create a place where people stop pretending.
Your tags may place truth in front of the exact person who needs it tonight.
Your prayers matter most of all.
Because perhaps Genesis 2:24 was never meant to leave us merely fascinated by the mystery of two becoming one.
Perhaps it was meant to make us look upward.
Toward the Bridegroom who did not abandon His Bride when loving her became costly.
Toward the Savior who stepped into our shame.
Toward the Christ who carried our scandal onto a cross.
Toward the risen King who still takes ruined stories, repentant hearts, shattered people, broken marriages, wounded souls, and sinners with nowhere left to hide...
and writes grace where everyone else expected the story to end.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU’RE PROBABLY NOT AS GOOD AS YOU THINK—AND THAT MAY BE THE BEST NEWS YOU HEAR TODAY
paragraphs: YOU’RE PROBABLY NOT AS GOOD AS YOU THINK—AND THAT MAY BE THE BEST NEWS YOU HEAR TODAY

What “All Have Sinned and Fall Short” Really Says About Human Goodness—and why Romans 3 was never written merely to make bad people feel worse, but to bring every kind of person to the same place: empty-handed before Jesus Christ.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can offend a decent person faster than it can offend a criminal.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
We know the verse.
We quote it.
We put it on evangelism cards.
But sometimes we hear it as though Paul were simply saying, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
That is not nearly strong enough.
The Greek reads:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou theou
“For all sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
And if we allow those words to do what Paul intended them to do, they dismantle one of humanity’s favorite hiding places:
“But I’m a good person.”
Maybe you are kind.
Maybe you work hard.
Maybe you love your children.
Maybe you have never cheated on your spouse.
Maybe you give money when somebody is hurting.
Maybe you return what does not belong to you.
Maybe you have spent years helping people who could never repay you.
Those things matter.
Scripture does not require Christians to pretend that every human action is equally wicked or that unbelievers are incapable of doing things that genuinely benefit other people.

Jesus Himself spoke of sinful human beings knowing how to give good gifts to their children (Matthew 7:11). Paul wrote of Gentiles who did not possess the Mosaic Law yet sometimes did things the Law required (Romans 2:14–15).
So Christianity does not teach the ridiculous idea that every person is as cruel as he could possibly become.
Romans 3 teaches something far more unsettling.
Human goodness cannot make sinful humanity righteous before a holy God.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because our favorite comparison is horizontal.
God’s standard is not.
We look sideways.
God looks perfectly.
We compare ourselves with the alcoholic.
The adulterer.
The corrupt politician.
The abusive father.
The hypocritical church leader.
The person whose scandal became public while ours remained conveniently hidden.
“I would never do what they did.”
Perhaps you wouldn't.
But Romans 3 will not permit you to make that person your measuring stick.
The standard is “the glory of God.”
τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ — tēs doxēs tou theou.
God's glory.
Not your neighbor's morality.
Not your pastor's reputation.
Not your parents' expectations.
Not society's constantly changing definition of decency.
God.
And suddenly the courtroom becomes very quiet.
Because you can outrun another sinner and still fall infinitely short of God's holiness.
Imagine two people trying to reach the stars by jumping.
One barely leaves the ground.
The other is an extraordinary athlete and leaps several feet into the air.
There is a genuine difference between their jumps.
But neither person reaches the stars.
That imperfect illustration gets us closer to Paul's devastating point.
There are meaningful moral differences between human beings. Some people live more disciplined, generous, peaceful, or outwardly honorable lives than others.
But nobody can stand before the blazing holiness of God, point to his moral résumé, and say:
“This is enough. You owe me acceptance.”
Nobody.
And that is where this verse becomes personal.
Because perhaps your greatest spiritual danger was never believing that you were evil.
Perhaps it was believing that you were good enough.
You didn't murder anyone.
But what happened inside you when someone humiliated you?
You never committed adultery.
But what have your eyes repeatedly consumed in secret?
You never robbed a bank.
But have you ever worshiped money while telling yourself you were simply being responsible?
You never abandoned your family.
But were you physically present while emotionally starving the people who needed your love?
You never publicly denied Christ.
But how many times did your silence quietly whisper, “I don't want these people to know I belong to Him”?
You worship on Sunday.
What owns your imagination on Monday?
You say, “God comes first.”
What does your calendar say?
What does your bank account say?
What does your browser history say?
What does the conversation you hope nobody ever hears say?
And deeper still...
What would happen if God exposed not merely everything you have done, but every motive underneath it?
That is where our self-defense begins to collapse.
Because sin is more than spectacular public scandal.
The Greek verb translated “sinned” is ἥμαρτον — hēmarton, from ἁμαρτάνω — hamartanō.
In Romans 3, Paul is not handing humanity a diagnosis of occasional imperfection.
He has spent the preceding chapters closing every escape route.
The openly rebellious cannot boast.
The moralist cannot boast.
The religious person cannot boast.
The Jew cannot boast in possessing the Law.
The Gentile cannot boast in ignorance of it.
Paul reaches his conclusion shortly before verse 23:
“There is none righteous, no, not one.” — Romans 3:10, KJV
Then:
“Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight.” — Romans 3:20, KJV
Then comes the sentence we so often isolate:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
But please do not stop reading there.
Because stopping at Romans 3:23 can leave a sinner staring at the wound while missing the Physician standing beside him.
The sentence continues into one of the most magnificent announcements in Scripture:
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 3:24, KJV
Look at the movement.
All have sinned.
Then...
justified freely by His grace.
The Greek word translated “freely” is δωρεάν — dōrean.
Freely.
As a gift.
Without you purchasing your justification with a pile of religious accomplishments.
And “grace” is χάριτι — chariti, from χάρις — charis.
Grace.
This is where Christianity separates itself from every attempt to build a ladder into heaven out of human goodness.
The Gospel does not tell bad people to accumulate enough good deeds until God finally becomes impressed.
The Gospel announces that sinners who cannot justify themselves may be justified by God's grace through the redemption found in Jesus Christ.
That means the answer to your sin is not becoming slightly better than somebody else.
The answer is Christ.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because Romans 3:23 humiliates our pride...
but Romans 3:24 destroys our despair.
You are worse than your carefully edited public version suggests.
Yet in Christ there is more grace than your shame told you could possibly exist.
Read that again.
Your respectable image cannot save you.
But neither does your ugliest chapter automatically place you beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
The religious person and the prostitute ultimately approach God through the same door.
The pastor and the prisoner.
The virgin and the adulterer.
The lifelong church member and the man who spent decades mocking Christianity.
The person whose sins became headlines and the person whose sins never escaped the bedroom.
Nobody enters God's kingdom carrying a certificate that says:
GOOD ENOUGH.
Those who are saved enter because of Jesus.
This is why Christianity can simultaneously destroy pride and create extraordinary hope.
At the cross, nobody gets to brag.
And nobody who comes to Christ in repentant faith gets to say His grace is insufficient.
Your goodness cannot make the cross unnecessary.
Your wickedness cannot make Christ's sufficient sacrifice inadequate.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not die merely to help basically good people become slightly nicer.
Christ died for sinners.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6, KJV
And again:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we conquered every addiction.
Not after we cleaned up our vocabulary.
Not after we restored our reputation.
Not after we became respectable enough for church people to stop whispering.
Christ died for sinners.
This does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means repentance is not a payment we hand God for salvation.
Jesus began His public proclamation with the call to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15). Genuine grace does not teach us to make peace with the sin that nailed our Savior to the cross.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your past will no longer be your master.”
That is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Not from scandal to pretending the scandal never happened.
Not from scandal to self-esteem.
Not from scandal to religious reputation management.
Not from scandal to “living your truth.”
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history and calling evil good.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He enters the sinner's real history with real mercy, pays for real guilt through His blood, gives real forgiveness to those who come to Him, and begins producing real transformation.
The cross does not minimize your sin.
The cross reveals how serious your sin actually is.
And then it reveals how astonishing God's grace actually is.
If sin were a minor personality defect, Calvary would be incomprehensible.
If human goodness could reconcile us to God, Christ's death would be unnecessary.
But Scripture says:
“Without shedding of blood is no remission.” — Hebrews 9:22, KJV
And Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold,
“But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” — 1 Peter 1:19, KJV
This is why boasting dies at the foot of the cross.
You cannot stand beside the crucified Son of God and congratulate yourself for being nicer than your neighbor.
Look at Him.
The crown.
The wounds.
The blood.
The rejection.
The cross.
Then try telling yourself your moral résumé was enough.
Calvary says otherwise.
But look again.
Because the cross is not merely God's indictment of human sin.
It is also God's breathtaking announcement of mercy.
The Savior knew what you were.
And He came.
He knew what humanity had become.
And He came.
He knew the betrayal.
He knew Peter would deny Him.
He knew the disciples would run.
He knew the mockery waiting at Golgotha.
He knew every generation that would use His name casually, ignore His commandments, exploit His grace, hide behind religion, and choose darkness.
And still...
He came.
This is why Romans 3:23 should never be weaponized merely to crush somebody.
Paul's argument crushes self-righteousness so grace can become visible.
And perhaps that is what God is doing in you right now.
Maybe you clicked this because you wanted theology.
And somewhere along the way, theology started reading you.
Maybe there is something you have been defending for years.
Something you renamed so you would not have to call it sin.
Pride became “standards.”
Greed became “ambition.”
Lust became “just looking.”
Bitterness became “boundaries.”
Gossip became “concern.”
Cowardice became “keeping the peace.”
Spiritual laziness became “being busy.”
Unforgiveness became “protecting myself.”
And slowly, almost invisibly, you learned how to stand near Christian language without letting Christ confront the locked rooms of your heart.
But He already knows what is behind the door.
You do not have to impress Him.
You cannot.
You do not have to deceive Him.
You cannot.
You do not have to outrun your past.
You cannot save yourself by running faster.
You need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
Maybe people ask you for prayer.
Maybe you post Scripture while privately wondering whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
Maybe the same temptation keeps returning.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again,” and then found yourself crying over the same failure.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Romans 3:23 is true about you.
But Romans 3:24 is there too.
Do not turn grace into permission to remain enslaved.
And do not turn your failures into evidence that Christ could never receive a repentant sinner like you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Run toward Christ instead of constructing another version of yourself for everyone else to admire.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice where your confidence rests.
Not in your ability to become impressive overnight.
He is faithful.
He is just.
Your hope is ultimately located outside yourself.
In Him.
That is freedom.
You can finally stop auditioning for a salvation you could never earn.
You can stop pretending another person's scandal somehow proves your innocence.
You can stop comparing stains.
You can stop hiding.
The ground beneath the cross is level.
And maybe that bothers the respectable part of us.
We want grades.
Rankings.
At least let God acknowledge that we were better than that person.
Then Jesus tells a story about a Pharisee and a tax collector.
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other people.
The tax collector could barely lift his eyes.
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13, KJV
Jesus said the second man went home justified.
That should haunt every religious heart that has learned to use somebody else's sin as a pedestal.
The question is not whether you can find someone worse than you.
You can.
The question is whether you are righteous enough to stand before God without Christ.
Romans answers that question.
No.
And then the Gospel answers the question you should ask next:
Can Christ save sinners who cannot save themselves?
Yes.
Completely.
That is why “all have sinned and fall short” is not ultimately a message about how worthless human beings are.
Human beings possess profound dignity because we were created in God's image (Genesis 1:26–27).
Sin does not erase the fact that humanity bears God's image.
It corrupts our relationship with our Creator, disorders our loves, enslaves us, brings guilt, and leaves us unable to establish our own righteousness before God.
So Christianity gives you two truths the modern world often struggles to hold together.
You possess enormous God-given dignity.
And...
you desperately need a Savior.
You matter enormously.
And you are not your own messiah.
You were worth creating.
But your goodness cannot redeem you.
You bear God's image.
But only Christ can reconcile you to God.
That is not hatred of humanity.
That is the diagnosis that makes the cure intelligible.
A doctor who lies about the disease does not love the patient.
And a preacher who tells sinners they are already spiritually healthy when Scripture says otherwise has offered comfort at the cost of truth.
But neither should we scream the diagnosis and hide the medicine.
So hear both.
All have sinned.
And...
redemption is in Christ Jesus.
There is your scandal.
There is your grace.
There is your story.
There is mine.
And if Jesus has confronted something hidden while you have been reading this, don't perform for us.
Be honest.
You do not have to explain the entire battle publicly.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “Please stand with me.”
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter when Jesus enters the story.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who believes being “a decent person” is enough.
The believer drowning in shame.
The churchgoer who knows all the language but has never surrendered.
The son who stopped believing.
The daughter who thinks she has gone too far.
The spouse who quietly carries guilt.
The friend whose scandal has convinced them Christians will never look at them the same way again.
Or send this privately.

Sharing the Gospel is one meaningful way we can glorify God by making Christ known. Supporting Gospel-centered work can also be an act of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, faithfully, and with the right heart. Grace cannot be purchased, and giving is never a substitute for repentance, faith, obedience, prayer, love, or faithful life in Christ.
Your support helps this ministry continue the work.
They are helping carry the message farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite even the friend who does not yet believe.
Both voices are lying.
You are not saved because you were better than everybody else.
And you are not beyond salvation because your chapter became uglier than theirs.
Jesus Christ is the difference.
So when Romans says, “All have sinned,” don't rush past the mirror.
Stand there.
Let pride die.
Let excuses die.
Let comparison die.
Then keep reading.

Because immediately beyond the devastating truth that you have fallen short stands the breathtaking announcement that justification comes freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
The verse that removes your last excuse also prepares you to understand your greatest hope.
Your goodness was never strong enough to become your savior.
Your scandal was never stronger than the Savior.
And when every mask finally falls, there is still a blood-stained cross, an empty tomb, and a risen Christ calling sinners out of darkness and into life.
You spent years trying to prove you were good enough; Jesus came to give repentant sinners something infinitely better than a polished reputation—grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Keep Asking God for Peace While Feeding Your Mind Everything That Steals It.
paragraphs: You Keep Asking God for Peace While Feeding Your Mind Everything That Steals It.
You prayed for God to quiet your mind last night. But what if some of the noise you are begging Him to remove is the same noise you keep inviting back in?
There is a strange kind of exhaustion that happens when your body is lying in bed but your mind refuses to come home.
The room is dark.
The house is quiet.
Everyone thinks you are resting.
But inside your head, a thousand conversations are still happening.
Things people said.
Things you wish you had said.
Bills.
Bad news.
What-ifs.
Someone else’s apparently perfect life.
Another frightening headline.
Another argument.
Another video.
Another comment section.
Another glimpse into somebody’s success that somehow makes your own life feel smaller.
You put your phone down.
Then pick it back up.
You tell yourself, “Just one more.”
One more reel.
One more headline.
One more notification.
One more search about the thing you are already terrified might happen.
And somewhere between midnight and exhaustion, you whisper:
“God, please give me peace.”
And He hears you.
He really does.
But perhaps there is a question we are afraid to ask.
What if we are praying for peace while repeatedly feeding our minds things that make peace harder to experience?
What if some of us are asking God to guard a door that we keep reopening?
That question hurts because it is easier to blame the world for our anxiety than to examine what we repeatedly permit into our thoughts.
And no, this is not an accusation against every anxious person.

Scripture does not teach that every experience of anxiety, distress, trauma, grief, depression, or mental suffering is simply the result of watching the wrong things. Human suffering is far more complicated than that. Faithful Christians can experience profound psychological distress. Elijah collapsed beneath despair. David wrote from places of anguish. Paul described pressures so severe that he and his companions “despaired even of life” in 2 Corinthians 1:8.
So this is not a message saying, “If you were spiritual enough, you would never feel anxious.”
That would be cruel.
And it would not be faithful to Scripture.
This is about something different.
This is about stewardship.

Because while you cannot control every thought that enters your mind, every tragedy that reaches your life, every wound somebody inflicts, or every physiological response your body experiences, Scripture does teach that what we deliberately dwell upon matters.
What we repeatedly watch matters.
What we continually rehearse matters.
What we voluntarily consume matters.
What we allow to occupy our attention matters.
And sometimes the uncomfortable truth is that we are asking Jesus to give us peace while building habits that continually agitate our souls.
Paul writes from imprisonment in Philippians 4:6–7:

“Μηδὲν μεριμνᾶτε, ἀλλ’ ἐν παντὶ τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ δεήσει μετὰ εὐχαριστίας τὰ αἰτήματα ὑμῶν γνωριζέσθω πρὸς τὸν Θεόν· καὶ ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡ ὑπερέχουσα πάντα νοῦν φρουρήσει τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν καὶ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.”
In context, the sense is:

Do not remain consumed by anxiety about anything; instead, in everything, bring your requests before God through prayer and petition with thanksgiving—and the peace of God, surpassing all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
Notice where Paul ends.
“ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.”
In Christ Jesus.
Biblical peace is not merely a breathing technique.
It is not pretending nothing hurts.
It is not positive thinking dressed in Christian vocabulary.
It is not the absence of every troubling circumstance.
Christian peace is rooted in a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And there is something beautiful buried inside Paul’s language.
The Greek verb translated “will guard” is φρουρήσει — phrourēsei.
It carries the sense of guarding, protecting, keeping watch.
Paul is describing the peace of God standing guard over the believer’s heart and thoughts in Christ.
Think about that.
Paul was writing about peace while living under conditions that were anything but peaceful.
His circumstances were not necessarily changing.
His God had not changed.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes we tell ourselves:
“I’ll have peace when this problem disappears.”
“I’ll have peace when I have more money.”
“I’ll have peace when they apologize.”
“I’ll have peace when the diagnosis changes.”
“I’ll have peace when my children straighten out.”
“I’ll have peace when I know what happens next.”
“I’ll have peace when God finally answers me.”
But Paul describes something far more supernatural.
Peace while you are still waiting.
Peace while the answer is still unclear.
Peace while the prison door is still closed.
Peace while tomorrow remains unknown.
Not because the situation is harmless.
Because Christ is still Lord.
But Paul does not stop at prayer.
And this is where the passage becomes painfully relevant to the modern Christian carrying a Bible in one hand and an endlessly scrolling phone in the other.
Immediately after speaking about prayer and God’s peace, Paul writes in Philippians 4:8:
Whatever is true.
Whatever is honorable.
Whatever is just.
Whatever is pure.
Whatever is lovely.
Whatever is commendable.
If there is excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise—
think about these things.
The word Paul uses is λογίζεσθε — logizesthe.
It is not describing a mind floating passively through whatever happens to appear before it.
It carries the idea of considering, reckoning, taking something into account, deliberately dwelling upon it.
Paul connects prayer with the direction of thought.
That is important.
We often want Philippians 4:6–7 without Philippians 4:8.
We want:
“God, guard my mind.”
But we resist:
“Child, pay attention to what you continually give your mind.”
We want divine peace without intentional stewardship.
We pray against fear and then spend hours consuming material engineered to keep us alarmed.
We ask God to free us from comparison and then repeatedly watch carefully curated versions of everybody else’s life.
We ask Jesus to purify our thoughts and then entertain ourselves with things that normalize what He calls us to flee.
We pray for freedom from anger while mentally replaying the offense for the hundredth time.
We pray for contentment and then scroll until somebody else’s house, body, marriage, vacation, ministry, career, children, possessions, or success convinces us that our own life is inadequate.
Then we wonder why our souls feel crowded.
Maybe you know exactly what this feels like.
You wake up and reach for your phone before speaking to God.
Before your feet touch the floor, strangers have already entered your mind.
Someone is furious.
Someone is dying.
Someone is fighting.
Someone is richer than you.
Someone is prettier than you.
Someone is mocking what you believe.
Someone says the world is collapsing.
Someone tells you that unless you are terrified, you are not paying attention.
Someone else tells you that unless your life looks like theirs, you are failing.
Ten minutes after waking up, your body is still underneath the blanket…
but your mind has already traveled through envy, outrage, lust, fear, comparison, gossip, tragedy, consumerism, political fury, and somebody else’s manufactured perfection.
Then we say:
“Why do I have no peace?”
Perhaps sometimes the answer is uncomfortable.
Because your attention has become a battlefield, and you have been leaving the gate open.

Jesus said in Matthew 6:22–23 that the eye is the lamp of the body. His teaching there is broader than modern media consumption, but the principle should still make us examine what captures our vision and allegiance.
What repeatedly enters us can shape us.
And modern technology has become extraordinarily skilled at capturing attention.
Your soul was not created to carry every tragedy on earth before breakfast.
You were not designed to know everybody’s opinion about everything.
You do not need to attend every digital argument.
You do not need to investigate every rumor.
You do not need to answer every insult.
You do not need to consume every disaster repeatedly to prove that you care.
You do not need to compare your ordinary Tuesday with somebody else’s edited highlight reel.
And you certainly do not need to surrender the first and last moments of every day to an algorithm.
Some of us desperately need permission to close the app.
Turn off the video.
Mute the account.
Leave the argument.
Stop rereading the message.
Stop searching for another frightening prediction.
Put the phone somewhere else.
Open Scripture.
Sit in silence before God.
Pray.
Give thanks.
Remember what is true.
Because there is a difference between being informed and being consumed.
There is a difference between awareness and obsession.
There is a difference between carrying legitimate concern before God and rehearsing catastrophe until fear becomes the loudest voice in the room.
Maybe your greatest battle tonight is not somewhere outside you.
Maybe it is the sentence you have repeated inside yourself all day:
“I’m going to lose everything.”
“I’ll never recover.”
“Nobody really loves me.”
“God has forgotten me.”
“I ruined my life.”
“My children will never come back.”
“I’ll always be this way.”
“There is no hope for someone like me.”
Stop there.
Not because your pain is imaginary.
Because despair does not get the authority to rewrite what God has said.
If you belong to Christ, your worst moment is not your final identity.
Your sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have the authority to write the ending.
Your failure may be real.
Grace is also real.
Your consequences may hurt.
Mercy is still real.
Your past may be scandalous.
The cross is greater.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by telling us to think positively until guilt disappears.
Jesus deals with sin by going directly to the cross.
There the spotless Son of God bears judgment for sinners.
There mercy does not ignore justice.
There grace is not cheap sentimentality.
Christ dies.
Christ is buried.
Christ rises.
And sinners who repent and trust Him are not merely taught how to manage their thoughts better.
They are reconciled to God.
That changes everything.
Because the deepest peace Christianity offers is not “nothing bad will happen to you.”
It is peace with God through Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:1 declares that having been justified by faith, “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Before peace becomes an emotion you chase, understand the reconciliation Christ purchased.
The Gospel reaches deeper than your nervous system.
Deeper than your circumstances.
Deeper than your reputation.
Deeper than your shame.
You can clean your feed and still need a Savior.
You can delete every social-media app and still have a sinful heart.
You can practice excellent mental discipline and still remain separated from God.
The answer is not digital minimalism as a substitute for Jesus.
The answer is Jesus.
And because we belong to Jesus, even our attention comes under His lordship.
That means repentance may sometimes look surprisingly ordinary.
Maybe repentance tonight looks like closing something you know has been feeding lust.
Maybe it looks like unfollowing the account that keeps feeding envy.
Maybe it means refusing another hour of rage-filled content.
Maybe it means admitting that you have turned fear into a ritual.
Maybe it means stopping the imaginary arguments you keep winning inside your head.
Maybe it means putting Scripture where your phone used to be at bedtime.
Maybe it means saying:
“Jesus, I have asked You for peace while continually filling my mind with things that steal my attention from You. Forgive me. Teach me to think on what is true.”
And perhaps you need to hear this too:
Do not turn Philippians 4 into another weapon against yourself.
When anxious thoughts come back tomorrow, that does not automatically mean you failed.
Bring them back to God.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Prayer is not a performance.
You are not trying to impress the Father with your emotional stability.
You are coming to Him because you need Him.
“ἐν παντὶ…”
In everything.
Bring it to Him.
The unpaid bill.
Bring it.
The child you cannot control.
Bring them.
The medical appointment frightening you.
Bring it.
The marriage that feels fragile.
Bring it.
The memory that still hurts.
Bring it.
The temptation you are ashamed to admit.
Bring it.
The future you cannot see.
Bring it.
The sin you have been hiding.
Especially that.
Bring it into the light.
You do not need to sanitize yourself before approaching Jesus.
You need to come truthfully.
The same Christ who exposed Peter’s weakness restored Peter.
The same Lord who confronted Saul transformed him into Paul.
The same Jesus who received sinners still receives repentant sinners.
Christianity is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Cowards.
Persecutors.
Outcasts.
Failures.
People with histories they could not erase.
Then grace entered the story.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappeared.
It means sin no longer had the final word.
Jesus did.
And He still does.
So tonight, before you ask God for peace again, perhaps ask another question:
“Lord, what have I been feeding my mind?”
Do not answer defensively.
Sit with it.
What receives your first attention in the morning?
What receives your final attention at night?
What repeatedly makes you afraid?
What continually makes you angry?
What feeds your envy?
What awakens lust?
What keeps reopening wounds?
What voice have you allowed to become louder than Scripture?
And what would change if you intentionally began feeding your mind what Paul calls true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and praiseworthy?
Not for one dramatic evening.
As a way of life.
Paul continues in Philippians 4:9 by telling believers to practice what they had learned, received, heard, and seen in him.
Then comes another promise:
“καὶ ὁ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ἔσται μεθ’ ὑμῶν.”
And the God of peace will be with you.
Did you catch the progression?
Not merely peace.
The God of peace.
That is what your soul ultimately needs.
Not simply a quieter feed.
Not merely fewer notifications.
Not just another productivity system.
God Himself.
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because somewhere underneath the endless scrolling, endless worrying, endless checking, endless comparing, endless consuming…
you were hungry.
You just kept feeding the hunger things that could never satisfy it.
And Jesus is still calling.
Come back.
Not when you become peaceful enough.
Now.
Come back while your thoughts are messy.
Come back while your hands are trembling.
Come back while your faith feels small.
Come back with the shame.
Come back with the compulsions.
Come back with the hidden tabs.
Come back with the resentment.
Come back with the questions.
Come back with the exhaustion.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek wise help where help is needed.
And remember that seeking appropriate medical or mental-health care is not a betrayal of faith. God’s providence is not threatened by receiving responsible care.
But whatever else you need to do, do not neglect the invitation standing at the center of the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Maybe someone you love is living exactly where these words landed.
They pray for peace but spend every night feeding fear.
They love Jesus but are exhausted.
They have been drowning quietly behind a smiling profile picture.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
But if Christ has used this message to confront, comfort, or awaken you, sharing truth can become one simple way of placing that truth where another hurting person might encounter it.
The friend who cannot sleep.
The mother carrying too much.
The father silently breaking beneath responsibility.
The young believer being discipled more aggressively by an algorithm than by Scripture.
The Christian who loves God but has been mentally exhausted for months.
Even the person who does not believe yet.
Sometimes one shared article becomes a doorway to a conversation you never knew somebody desperately needed.
And if this exposed something in you, do not hide behind silence.
There is no prize for pretending.
There are other believers fighting battles too.
Your honesty may give somebody else permission to stop pretending.
Because tonight’s conviction can become tomorrow morning’s forgotten intention.
Return to Philippians 4:6–9 when the noise starts again.
Read it slowly.
Pray it.
Practice it.
Let Scripture challenge what gets access to your attention.
But hear this clearly:
Share because the Gospel is worth carrying beyond yourself.
Never do either because you think God can be bought.
He cannot.
The blood of Jesus is not merchandise.
Grace is not a transaction.
Your share does not purchase His approval.
Christ already accomplished what no payment, platform, algorithm, good deed, or religious performance ever could.
Not as spiritual advertising.
As witness.
Maybe they need somebody to remind them:
You cannot always choose what knocks on the door of your mind.
But you do not have to give everything a room.
Pray.
Give thanks.
Think on what is true.
Guard what you consume.
Repent where necessary.
Receive grace where you have failed.
And keep returning to Jesus.
Because peace is not ultimately found when you finally control every circumstance.
Peace is found in the God who remains God when you cannot.
And maybe tonight the most important notification you receive will not come from your phone at all.
Maybe it will be the quiet conviction of the Holy Spirit reminding you that you have consumed enough noise.
Come back to the Word.
Come back to prayer.
Come back to truth.
Come back to the cross.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the mind you keep filling with fear is still a mind Christ is able to renew.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE MODERN-DAY PROPHETS BIBLICAL?
paragraphs:
ARE MODERN-DAY PROPHETS BIBLICAL?
Before You Say “God Told Me,” Read This—Because Not Every Voice That Sounds Spiritual Came From God
There are few sentences more powerful in Christian circles than these:
“God told me.”
Four words.
And suddenly the conversation changes.
Because how do you argue with God?
Someone says, “God told me you should marry me.”
“God told me to start this ministry.”
“God told me you need to give.”
“God showed me what is going to happen.”
“The Lord told me what you need to do.”
And sometimes the person speaking may sincerely believe it.
Sometimes they may even be right about something.
But sincerity is not Scripture.
Accuracy alone is not proof of divine authority.
Charisma is not confirmation.
A large following is not confirmation.
A title is not confirmation.
And saying “Thus says the Lord” does not automatically mean the Lord said anything.
That is precisely why this question matters.
Are modern-day prophets biblical?

The answer requires more care than a quick “yes” or “no,” because faithful Christians who affirm the full authority of Scripture have reached different conclusions about whether the New Testament gift of prophecy continues today.
But there is something Christians on every side of that debate desperately need to remember:
God never commands His people to surrender discernment.
He commands us to use it.
Paul wrote:
“Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:20–21
The Greek is striking.
“Prophecies” is προφητείας (prophēteias).
And “test” comes from δοκιμάζω (dokimazō)—to examine, test, prove, or determine genuineness.
In other words, biblical faith is not gullibility dressed in Christian vocabulary.
The church is not commanded to believe every supernatural claim.
We are commanded to test.
And that becomes uncomfortable when the person claiming divine revelation is someone we admire.
Someone with a microphone.
Someone with millions of views.
Someone who seems unusually spiritual.
Someone whose conference fills stadiums.
Someone whose predictions occasionally appear astonishing.
Or perhaps someone sitting across from you at church saying quietly:
“God gave me a word for you.”
The moment somebody claims to speak for God, the stakes become enormous.
Because throughout Scripture, God takes His words seriously.
Very seriously.
Jeremiah lived among people who claimed divine revelation while speaking from their own imagination.
God said:
“I have heard what the prophets have said who prophesy lies in my name, saying, ‘I have dreamed, I have dreamed!’”
—Jeremiah 23:25
Then comes a chilling description:
“Let the prophet who has a dream tell the dream, but let him who has my word speak my word faithfully.”
—Jeremiah 23:28
That distinction still matters.
There is an enormous difference between:
“I think God may be leading me…”
and:
“God said.”
One leaves room for human fallibility.
The other invokes divine authority.
And we should tremble before casually putting words into the mouth of the Almighty.
The Old Testament Hebrew word commonly translated “prophet” is נָבִיא (nāḇîʾ).
Biblical prophets were not simply motivational speakers with spiritual intuition.
They were commissioned messengers.
Again and again Scripture introduces prophetic revelation with words equivalent to:
“Thus says the LORD.”
כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה
Ko amar YHWH.
“Thus says the LORD.”
That is not branding.
That is authority.
And Scripture gives severe warnings about falsely claiming that authority.
Deuteronomy 18 warns Israel about the prophet who presumptuously speaks a word God has not commanded.
Jeremiah condemns prophets who speak “visions of their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.”
Ezekiel speaks against those who “follow their own spirit, and have seen nothing.”
That should make every Christian slow down before saying:
“God told me.”
But now we come to the New Testament.
Because something extraordinary happens.
At Pentecost, Peter explains the outpouring of the Holy Spirit by quoting the prophet Joel:
“And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh…”
Then:
“your sons and your daughters shall prophesy…”
—Acts 2:17
Later, Acts describes prophets in the early church.
Agabus is specifically named.
Acts 13 mentions “prophets and teachers” at Antioch.
Acts 21 tells us that Philip the evangelist had four unmarried daughters “who prophesied.”
Paul discusses prophecy extensively in 1 Corinthians 12–14.
So Christians cannot honestly pretend prophecy disappears the moment we turn the page from Malachi to Matthew.
It is clearly present in the New Testament church.

But neither may we simply assume that every person today calling himself or herself “Prophet” possesses the same authority as Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Peter, Paul, or the foundational witnesses through whom God gave Scripture.
That is where discernment becomes essential.
Paul writes that the church was:
—Ephesians 2:20
Notice the imagery.
Foundation.
A foundation is laid.
Jesus Christ remains the cornerstone.
The apostles occupied a unique, foundational role in redemptive history.
And whatever position Christians take concerning contemporary prophecy, nobody today gets to write another Gospel of Matthew.
Nobody gets to add another chapter to Romans.
Nobody gets to stand beside Scripture and announce:
“My revelation carries equal authority.”
The canon is not waiting for your favorite preacher's sequel.
Scripture remains the measuring line.
This is why Isaiah's ancient words remain so relevant:
“To the teaching and to the testimony!”
—Isaiah 8:20
And why Paul could tell Timothy that the sacred writings are able to make him “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus,” before declaring:
“All Scripture is breathed out by God…”
—2 Timothy 3:16
The Greek word translated “breathed out by God” is θεόπνευστος (theopneustos).
God-breathed.
That is an extraordinary category.
Your impressions are not theopneustos.
My feelings are not theopneustos.
A preacher's dream is not automatically theopneustos.
A viral prophecy is not theopneustos.
Scripture is.
And this distinction could save someone from enormous spiritual damage.
Because perhaps you have been wounded by someone who weaponized the phrase:
“God told me.”
Maybe somebody manipulated you with prophecy.
Maybe someone predicted something that never happened, then quietly changed the explanation afterward.
Maybe someone used spiritual authority to control your relationship.
Your money.
Your decisions.
Your conscience.
Maybe you were afraid to question them because you thought questioning them meant questioning God.
Listen carefully.
Testing a claimed revelation is not rebellion against God.
God Himself tells you to test.
The apostle John writes:
—1 John 4:1
Why?
“For many false prophets have gone out into the world.”
John did not say:
Believe everything supernatural.
He said:
Test it.
And his immediate test is profoundly Christ-centered.
What does this message say about Jesus Christ?
Because biblical prophecy never exists to make the prophet the star.
The Spirit glorifies Christ.
Jesus said concerning the Holy Spirit:
“He will glorify me.”
—John 16:14
That single truth exposes much of what passes for spirituality.
If someone's “prophetic ministry” constantly makes you obsessed with the prophet instead of Christ…
Be careful.
If you need their next livestream more desperately than you need Scripture…
Be careful.
If questioning their words is treated as questioning God…
Be careful.
If every revelation somehow ends with money flowing toward them…
Be careful.
If Jesus becomes background scenery while the personality on the stage becomes indispensable…
Something has gone terribly wrong.
The Holy Spirit does not come to build celebrity kingdoms.
He glorifies Jesus.
And here we must deal fairly with an important disagreement among Bible-believing Christians.

Some Christians are cessationists. Broadly speaking, they believe certain revelatory or sign gifts associated with the apostolic era no longer function in the church in the same way after the foundational apostolic period.

Other Christians are continuationists. They believe gifts such as prophecy continue, while insisting that contemporary prophetic impressions must be tested and cannot rival, correct, supplement, or override Scripture.
There are thoughtful, Christ-loving Christians on both sides.
So this article will not pretend a centuries-old theological discussion can be solved with a slogan.
But whichever position you hold, Scripture gives boundaries that cannot safely be ignored.
No modern revelation outranks Scripture.
No prophecy may contradict the Gospel.
No prophet becomes spiritually untouchable.
No supernatural manifestation proves by itself that God authorized the messenger.
No Christian should surrender conscience and biblical discernment to someone merely because that person claims divine revelation.
And Jesus Himself gave us an even more frightening warning.
“False christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders…”
—Matthew 24:24
Think about that.
Jesus did not say deception would always look ridiculous.
Sometimes deception looks supernatural.
That means “something incredible happened” is not enough.
Signs are not the ultimate test.
Jesus is.
Truth is.
Scripture is.
The Gospel is.
Character matters too.
Jesus said:
“You will recognize them by their fruits.”
—Matthew 7:16
Not merely by their predictions.
Not by their followers.
Not by their stage presence.
Fruit.
And what does the Spirit produce?
“Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.”
—Galatians 5:22–23
So perhaps the question should not merely be:
“Can this prophet tell me something about my future?”
Perhaps we should also ask:
Does this ministry make much of Christ?
Does it honor Scripture?
Does it produce repentance?
Does it display humility?
Is there accountability?
Can the leader be questioned?
Are failed claims acknowledged honestly?
Is money handled transparently?
Does the teaching lead people toward Jesus—or dependence upon the prophet?
Because there is something more important than knowing what will happen next Tuesday.
Knowing Christ.
We sometimes become so desperate for a word about tomorrow that we neglect the Word God has already given us today.
We want God to tell us who we will marry.
Meanwhile Scripture tells us how to love.
We want God to reveal our next career move.
Meanwhile Scripture tells us to work faithfully and honestly.
We want a prophecy about financial breakthrough.
Meanwhile Jesus warns us about greed.
We want someone to reveal our destiny.
Meanwhile Jesus says:
“Follow me.”
Maybe the most neglected revelation in some Christian lives is the Bible sitting unopened beside the bed.
And perhaps that hurts because we would rather receive a mysterious secret than obey a clear command.
“Forgive.”
We want another word.
“Repent.”
Another prophecy.
“Love your enemies.”
Something deeper, Lord.
“Take up your cross and follow me.”
And suddenly the problem is not that God has been silent.
The problem is that what He has already said costs us something.
That is where this conversation stops being about famous prophets on the internet.
Now it becomes about us.
Because there is another danger hiding underneath our obsession with prophetic voices.
Sometimes we want certainty more than we want God.
We are terrified of making the wrong decision.
Terrified of tomorrow.
Terrified of losing someone.
Terrified of suffering.
So when someone appears and says, “God showed me your future,” something inside us desperately wants to believe.
Not necessarily because we love truth.
Because we hate uncertainty.
And that fear can make us vulnerable.
But Christianity was never an invitation to control tomorrow.
It was an invitation to trust Jesus with tomorrow.
Faith does not mean knowing everything that is coming.
Faith means knowing the One who will still be there when it comes.
Maybe nobody has a prophetic word about your next five years.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you do not know whether the door will open.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe your prayer has not been answered the way you hoped.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe the diagnosis frightened you.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe someone you trusted failed you.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe a preacher disappointed you.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe somebody once spoke “God's will” over your life and those words became chains around your soul.
Jesus is still Lord.
And Jesus did not die so that another human being could become the mediator you cannot live without.
“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
—1 Timothy 2:5
One mediator.
Jesus Christ.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because Scripture is filled with people whose lives looked finished.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Scandal.
Then the risen Christ restored him.
Grace.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Scandal.
Then Jesus confronted him, saved him, and transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
Grace.
The Samaritan woman's history was complicated and exposed.
Scandal.
Then she encountered Jesus and ran toward the very people she might once have avoided.
Grace.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Scandal.
Then he turned toward the crucified King and heard words of paradise.
Grace.
That is the Gospel.
Not humanity climbing high enough to become impressive to God.
God coming down in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The greatest message Christianity has for you is not:
“A prophet knows your future.”
It is:
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
That is the announcement that shattered history.
That is the message demons hate.
That is the hope death cannot swallow.
That is the Word your shame cannot cancel.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ returning.
And if you have spent years chasing spiritual experiences while quietly running from Jesus, come home.
If your Bible has gathered dust while prophetic videos filled your history, come home.
If you have made an idol out of a minister, come home.
If someone manipulated you in God's name and you became afraid of Christianity itself, look beyond the person who wounded you and look again at Christ.
If you have claimed “God told me” when, deep inside, you knew it was your own desire speaking…
Repent.
There is grace even here.
Because repentance is not God's invitation to humiliation without hope.
It is His call out of darkness.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance—the language of a changed mind and turning that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Jesus does not expose sin merely to crush sinners.
He exposes darkness so we can stop hiding in it.
And maybe this article has exposed something.
Maybe you have followed voices more closely than you have followed Jesus.
Maybe you trusted personalities because reading Scripture for yourself felt harder.
Maybe someone told you what you desperately wanted to hear.
Maybe you have secretly been afraid that without a “prophetic word,” God will forget you.
He has not forgotten you.
You do not need spiritual theatrics to convince Jesus that you exist.
He knows your name.
He knows the sin you hide.
He knows the wound nobody sees.
He knows why you keep smiling when your soul feels exhausted.
He knows the questions you are afraid to say aloud.
And He still calls sinners to Himself.
Not to a personality.
Not to a platform.
Not to a prophetic celebrity.
To Himself.
Jesus said:
“Come to me…”
—Matthew 11:28
That invitation still stands.
Come to Christ.
Bring your questions.
Bring your disappointment.
Bring your skepticism.
Bring your wounds from church.
Bring your hidden sin.
Bring the parts of your story you wish could be deleted.
Bring the scandal.
Because Jesus specializes in rewriting stories that looked finished.
Not by pretending sin never mattered.
By paying for sin with His own blood.
At the cross, grace was not cheap.
It cost Christ everything.
And the resurrection announces that sin, Satan, shame, and death do not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So are modern-day prophets biblical?

Scripture unquestionably records prophecy as a genuine work of God and a gift present in the New Testament church. Faithful Christians disagree about whether and in what sense that gift continues today.
But Scripture leaves us no permission to be undiscerning.
Test every claim.
Hold tightly to Scripture.
Reject anything contradicting God's revealed Word and the apostolic Gospel.
Look at fruit.
Beware spiritual manipulation.
Never elevate a human messenger above Jesus.
And never let someone's claim of private revelation steal the authority belonging to God's written Word.
Perhaps the safest sentence some Christians could learn again is not:
“God told me.”
But:
“Scripture says.”
Then open the Bible.
Read it in context.
Handle it faithfully.
And point people toward Christ.
If this exposed something you have been afraid to admit, do not hide behind religious language.
And if you have ever been manipulated by someone claiming to speak for God, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your wound. But you can simply say, “Jesus, lead me into truth.”
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not alone.
Not because every sentence here deserves unquestioned acceptance—it does not.
Send it privately to the person who has quietly wondered, “Am I allowed to question this?”
Yes.
Open the Bible together.
Test everything.
Keep Christ at the center.
We want this community to be a place of daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment—not personality worship.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Jesus is not for sale.
Grace is not merchandise.
Salvation is not a membership benefit.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”
—Ephesians 2:8
Your greatest need is not access to another prophet.
Your greatest need is Christ.
So open your Bible.
Test the voices.
Refuse manipulation.
Repent when you are wrong.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Hold fast to what is good.
And follow Jesus even when nobody can tell you exactly what tomorrow holds.
Because you do not need to know every detail of tomorrow when you belong to the One who already stands there.
And when every other voice eventually falls silent, there is still one voice your soul cannot afford to miss:
The voice of the Shepherd calling you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHATEVER YOU ASK IN MY NAME” — THE PROMISE WE KEEP QUOTING BUT MAY HAVE NEVER UNDERSTOOD
paragraphs: “WHATEVER YOU ASK IN MY NAME” — THE PROMISE WE KEEP QUOTING BUT MAY HAVE NEVER UNDERSTOOD
What if the most important words in your prayer are not the words “in Jesus’ name” at the end…but the surrender of your life to the Jesus whose name you just spoke?
You prayed.
You believed.
You waited.
And nothing happened.
At least, nothing you could see.
You prayed for the relationship to survive.
It ended.
You prayed for the door to open.
It slammed shut.
You prayed for the money to come.
The bills kept arriving.
You prayed for the person you loved.
The answer you desperately wanted never came.
And somewhere between your last “Amen” and another night staring into the darkness, a frightening question slipped into your heart:
Did Jesus really mean what He said?
Because His words sound almost impossible to misunderstand:
“Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”
John 14:13.
And then Jesus says it again:
“If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it.”
John 14:14.
Those words can sound like a blank check from heaven.
Ask.
Use the Name.
Receive.
So we pray for the job.
The healing.
The marriage.
The breakthrough.
The money.
The opportunity.
The child.
The restoration.
The miracle.
And then we finish the prayer with the words we have heard Christians say thousands of times:
“In Jesus’ name, Amen.”
But what happens when the thing we asked for never comes?
Was our faith too small?
Did we pronounce the formula incorrectly?
Did somebody secretly have more faith than us?
Did Jesus break His promise?
Or...
have we sometimes turned one of the most beautiful invitations Jesus ever gave His disciples into something He never intended it to be?
Because there is a difference between using Jesus’ name and praying in Jesus’ name.
And that difference may change the way you pray for the rest of your life.
Listen carefully to the Greek words preserved for us in John 14:13:
“καὶ ὅ τι ἂν αἰτήσητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου, τοῦτο ποιήσω, ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ.”
Kai ho ti an aitēsēte en tō onomati mou, touto poiēsō, hina doxasthē ho patēr en tō huiō.
The phrase sitting at the center of everything is:
“ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου”
en tō onomati mou.
“In My name.”

The word onoma means “name,” but in biblical usage a name can carry far more than the sound used to identify someone. A name can represent the person, character, reputation, authority, and identity associated with the one who bears it.
That matters enormously.
Because Jesus was not handing His disciples a magical verbal password.
He was giving them access bound up with Himself.
Imagine an ambassador walking into another country carrying the authority of a king.
The ambassador does not arrive and say:
“I am here in the king’s name, therefore I may do whatever I personally desire.”
No.
Precisely the opposite.
To act in the king’s name means the ambassador no longer acts merely on his own agenda.
He represents the king.
His authority is real precisely because his mission is not ultimately his own.
Now bring that back into your prayer closet.
Praying in Jesus’ name is not dragging Jesus behind your desires.
It is bringing your desires underneath Jesus.
That changes everything.
“In Jesus’ name” is not spiritual punctuation.
It is surrender.
It is saying:
Jesus, I belong to You.
Jesus, Your character governs this request.
Jesus, Your purposes matter more than my preferences.
Jesus, if what I am asking would pull me away from You, I do not ultimately want it.
Jesus, if this desire contradicts Your Word, change my desire.
Jesus, if this door would destroy what You are forming inside me, keep it closed.
Jesus, if Your answer is different from mine, teach me to trust You.
Suddenly “in Jesus’ name” becomes one of the most dangerous things your flesh could ever sincerely pray.
Because sometimes we want Jesus to endorse the life we have already decided to live.
But Jesus did not die merely to become the signature beneath our plans.
He died and rose again to become Lord.
And there is something sitting inside John 14:13 that we cannot afford to ignore.
Jesus Himself tells us why He answers prayer:
“that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”
There it is.
The heartbeat of the promise.
The glory of God.
Not the worship of our comfort.
Not the enthronement of our ambitions.
Not the guarantee that every earthly circumstance will bend toward our preferred outcome.
The Father glorified in the Son.
This means the promise cannot honestly be separated from the purpose stated in the same sentence.
What you ask.
In whose name you ask.
And whose glory you seek.
They belong together.
This is why other passages about prayer matter so much.
Jesus later tells His disciples that if they abide in Him and His words abide in them, they may ask and receive according to that abiding relationship.
John 15 does not describe prayer as independence from Christ.
It describes prayer flowing from union with Christ.
And 1 John gives us another breathtaking clarification:
“This is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.”
According to His will.
Not because God is reluctant to bless His children.
Not because Christians should be terrified of asking boldly.
Scripture actually invites bold prayer.
Ask.
Seek.
Knock.
Bring your anxiety to Him.
Cast your cares upon Him.
Approach the throne of grace.
Cry out.
Persist.
Believe.
But biblical confidence is not confidence that God must obey us.
Biblical confidence is confidence that we may entrust ourselves completely to God.
There is an enormous difference.
Sometimes the greatest evidence of faith is not saying,
“God must give me this.”
Sometimes it is trembling while saying,
“Father, I desperately want this...but I still want You more.”
Jesus Himself showed us this kind of prayer.
Gethsemane.
Darkness.
Agony.
The cross approaching.
Jesus prayed concerning the cup before Him.
Yet His prayer moved toward surrender to the Father’s will.
Think about that.
The sinless Son of God did not teach us that authentic prayer means forcing our preferred outcome upon heaven.
He showed us perfect trust.
Desire expressed honestly.
Suffering acknowledged completely.
And obedience surrendered absolutely.
That is not weak prayer.
That is holy prayer.
Somebody reading this has been carrying disappointment with God for years because you thought an unanswered prayer meant He abandoned you.
Maybe you prayed until you had no words left.
Maybe people told you that you simply needed more faith.
Maybe somebody made you feel guilty because the miracle did not happen.
And now you barely pray anymore.
You still believe enough to feel guilty about your distance from God, but somewhere deep inside you are afraid to hope again.
Please hear this.
The Gospel does not promise that following Jesus means receiving every earthly outcome we request.
The Gospel promises something infinitely greater.
God gives us Christ.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Adoption.
Grace.
Eternal life.
A Savior who entered suffering rather than watching it from a safe distance.
A crucified King who knows what anguish feels like.
A risen Lord whom death could not hold.
Christianity is not the story of human beings discovering the correct phrase that makes God give them whatever they want.
Christianity is the scandalous story of rebels being reconciled to God through the blood of His Son.
We were not standing outside heaven because we had failed to discover the correct prayer formula.
We were sinners in need of mercy.
And Jesus came for us.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
The innocent for the guilty.
Christ bearing sin.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
And now we come to the Father not because our vocabulary is impressive, but because our confidence rests in Jesus Christ.
That is why His name matters.
His name is not an incantation.
His name is our refuge because He is our refuge.
His name is precious because the Person who bears it is precious.
His name carries authority because He possesses authority.
His name gives us confidence because our standing before God rests in Him rather than in ourselves.
So yes...
Pray in Jesus’ name.
Say the words.
There is nothing wrong with ending your prayers, “In Jesus’ name, Amen.”
Say them boldly.
Say them reverently.
But never imagine the syllables themselves are the power.
You can say “in Jesus’ name” while praying completely contrary to Jesus.
And you can sometimes forget to say the phrase aloud while your entire prayer is surrendered to His character, His authority, His Word, His mission, and His glory.
God is not fooled by religious vocabulary.
He sees the heart.
Maybe that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes what we call faith is actually baptized self-will.
We already know what we want.
Then we ask Jesus to approve it.
We choose the relationship and ask Him to bless it.
We choose the ambition and ask Him to accelerate it.
We choose the revenge and ask Him for justice.
We choose the lifestyle and ask Him for peace.
We choose our kingdom...
then sign His name underneath it.
But what if prayer was never meant to make Jesus more aligned with us?
What if prayer is one of the places where God makes us more aligned with Jesus?
Then unanswered prayer is not automatically meaningless.
Sometimes God says yes.
Sometimes His providence closes a door.
Sometimes He makes us wait.
Sometimes we do not understand what He is doing at all.
And sometimes we may carry questions all the way through this life.
We should be careful about pretending we know the secret reason behind every disappointment. Scripture does not give us permission to explain every tragedy with a neat sentence.
Job’s friends tried that.
They talked a lot.
They were very confident.
And they were wrong.
Faith does not require pretending pain does not hurt.
You can trust God and cry.
You can believe and grieve.
You can worship with questions.
You can say, “Lord, I do not understand,” without abandoning the Lord.
Biblical faith is not emotional dishonesty.
Sometimes faith looks like Job worshiping in devastation.
Sometimes it looks like David soaking his bed with tears.
Sometimes it looks like Paul pleading for the thorn to leave and hearing that Christ’s grace is sufficient.
Sometimes it looks like Jesus sweating in Gethsemane.
And sometimes it looks like you...
sitting on the edge of your bed at 2:17 in the morning...
whispering,
“Jesus, I don’t understand what You’re doing.
But I’m still here.”
Maybe that is your prayer tonight.
Not eloquent.
Not impressive.
Just honest.
“I’m still here.”
And maybe heaven values that prayer more than you realize.
Because the deepest transformation in prayer happens when you stop treating God merely as the means to something else.
When Jesus Himself becomes the treasure.
You wanted the blessing.
