Then somewhere along the road, you discovered the Blesser.
You wanted the door.
You discovered the Shepherd.
You wanted the answer.
You discovered Christ.
And eventually something inside you begins to change.
Your prayer moves from:
“Jesus, give me what I want.”
to:
“Jesus, teach me what You want.”
Then deeper:
“Jesus, change what I want.”
And deeper still:
“Jesus, I want You.”
That is where prayer stops being merely transactional and becomes relational.
And no, that does not mean you stop asking for specific things.
Ask boldly.
Ask for healing.
Ask for provision.
Ask for reconciliation.
Ask for wisdom.
Ask God to save your children.
Ask Him to restore broken marriages.
Ask Him to open doors for the Gospel.
Ask Him to provide employment.
Ask Him to deliver people from bondage.
Ask for miracles.
Ask big.
We serve a God for whom nothing is impossible.
But hold every request with open hands before the King.
Because sometimes we ask God for something good while He sees something we cannot see.
And faith says:
“Father, this is what I want.
But You are God.
I am not.
So I trust You with what happens next.”
That sentence can cost tears.
Real surrender usually does.
There may be somebody reading this right now who knows exactly what prayer you have been trying to force God to answer.
You have replayed it hundreds of times.
Maybe the issue is not that you need to pray louder.
Maybe tonight you need to open your hands.
Not because the desire itself is necessarily sinful.
But because even good desires can become gods when we decide we cannot trust God without them.
The relationship.
The marriage.
The healing.
The career.
The child.
The ministry.
The recognition.
The money.
The breakthrough.
Even good things become dangerous when our heart quietly says:
“God, I will trust You only if You give me this.”
Jesus offers something better than a contract.
He offers Himself.
And that brings us back to those words:
“ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου.”
En tō onomati mou.
In My name.
Perhaps you have spoken those words ten thousand times.
But tonight, hear them differently.
In His name means I am not coming because I am worthy.
I come because Christ is worthy.
I am not coming because I have performed perfectly.
I come through the One who obeyed perfectly.
I am not coming because my hands are clean enough.
I come because Jesus cleanses sinners.
I am not coming to manipulate God.
I am coming as His child.
I am not demanding that Jesus serve my kingdom.
I am asking Him to make my life useful for His.
That is freedom.
Because if your confidence depends upon your ability to pray perfectly, you will eventually despair.
But if your confidence rests in Christ...
you can come trembling.
You can come exhausted.
You can come ashamed.
You can come after failure.
You can come when your prayer sounds like nothing more than:
“Jesus...help me.”
The power is not in the sophistication of the person praying.
The hope is in the Savior to whom we belong.
And perhaps the greatest prayer you can pray tonight has nothing to do with money, healing, success, relationships, or opportunity.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus Christ, I have been trying to use Your name without surrendering my life to Your lordship.
Forgive me.
I have wanted Your blessings more than I wanted You.
I have asked You to build my kingdom while calling You King.
Have mercy on me.
Change my heart.
Change my desires.
Teach me to pray.
Teach me to obey.
Teach me to trust You when You say yes.
Teach me to trust You when You say no.
Teach me to trust You when You say wait.
And when I cannot understand Your hand...
help me trust Your heart.
Not my name.
Not my glory.
Not my kingdom.
Yours.
In Jesus’ name.
Amen.”
And perhaps for the first time in a long time...
you actually meant the ending.
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind silence.
There is no shame in admitting that your spirit is tired.
Someone scrolling beneath this article may desperately need the evidence of God’s faithfulness that your scars can give them.
Not because you need another post sitting in a folder somewhere, but because there will probably come another night when heaven seems quiet and you need to remember:
God is not a vending machine.
Jesus’ name is not a password.
Prayer is not manipulation.
Christ is Lord.
And His grace is still enough.
Not to purchase God’s favor.
Never.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God does not owe spiritual blessings to people who financially support a ministry.
If you want your resources to glorify God, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful expression of stewardship—but it must always flow freely from love, never guilt or spiritual pressure.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody behind a screen may be one unanswered prayer away from walking away from God—and the truth you share may reach them on the night they were ready to quit.
We cannot save anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But we can point.
We can testify.
We can share.
We can tell wounded people that unanswered prayer does not mean an absent Savior.
We can tell sinners that there is forgiveness at the cross.
We can tell prodigals there is a road home.
We can tell the ashamed that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
We can tell the exhausted believer:
You do not need a magical formula.
You need Christ.
And perhaps that is the truth hidden beneath the promise all along.
“Whatever you ask in My name...”
Not magic words.
Not a blank check.
Not permission to turn God into the servant of our desires.
A name.
A Person.
A Savior.
A King.
Jesus Christ.
The One who takes sinners carrying ruined stories and writes grace across pages we thought were already finished.
So when you pray tonight, ask boldly.
Cry honestly.
Believe deeply.
Repent quickly.
Surrender completely.
And say His name with reverence.
Because the greatest miracle of praying “in Jesus’ name” is not that Jesus becomes committed to everything you want.
It is that, by grace, you increasingly become committed to Him.
And when Christ becomes more precious than the answer you were begging Him to give, you begin to understand what prayer was always meant to do.
Sometimes the prayer that seems unanswered is the very place where Jesus begins rewriting the person who prayed it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHERE YOUR TREASURE IS, THERE YOUR HEART WILL BE ALSO” — NOTICE WHICH ONE JESUS SAYS MOVES THE OTHER
paragraphs: “WHERE YOUR TREASURE IS, THERE YOUR HEART WILL BE ALSO” — NOTICE WHICH ONE JESUS SAYS MOVES THE OTHER

You may have spent years waiting for your heart to love God more before changing what you do with your money, time, attention, and possessions. But Jesus said something far more unsettling: sometimes you don’t wait for your heart to move. You move your treasure—and discover your heart has been following it all along.
There is a sentence from Jesus that many Christians can quote without realizing how dangerous it is to everything competing for their devotion.
We put it on wall art.
We underline it in our Bibles.
We hear it during sermons about money.
And because it sounds familiar, we can miss the blade hidden inside it.
Jesus said:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” — Matthew 6:21
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because Jesus did not say:
“Where your heart is, there your treasure will be.”
He said:
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
That order matters.
The Greek text preserves the force beautifully:
ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου.
Hopou gar estin ho thēsauros sou, ekei estai kai hē kardia sou.
A straightforward translation is:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Look carefully at two words.
θησαυρός — thēsauros.
Treasure. A store. Something laid up. Something considered valuable.
And then:
καρδία — kardia.
Heart.
Not merely emotion in our modern sentimental sense, but the inner person—the center of desire, thought, intention, affection, and moral life.
But perhaps the most haunting word in the sentence is the ordinary-looking verb:
ἔσται — estai.
“Will be.”
Jesus places the treasure there...
and then speaks of where the heart will be.
That does not mean every act of spending mechanically manufactures love, nor that Jesus is giving us a simplistic psychological equation.
It means something deeper.
Your treasure and your heart refuse to remain strangers.
What you continually prize, protect, pursue, accumulate, sacrifice for, invest in, and refuse to surrender becomes entangled with your inner life.
And Jesus does not merely tell His disciples to inspect their treasure.
He tells them to move it.
“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth... but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.”
Then:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Maybe that explains something you have been unable to explain about yourself.
Maybe you have prayed:
“Jesus, why don’t I desire You like I used to?”
And perhaps part of the answer is hiding in places we rarely examine during prayer.
Your calendar.
Your browser history.
Your bank statement.
Your shopping cart.
Your ambitions.
Your conversations.
Your screen time.
Your dreams for the future.
The things you panic about losing.
The things you cannot imagine surrendering.
The things receiving the first and best of you.
Because treasure is bigger than money.
Money simply has an uncomfortable ability to expose treasure.
You can sing, “Jesus is everything to me,” on Sunday...
and then spend Monday through Saturday arranging an entire life around everything except Jesus.
You can say eternity matters most...
while almost every waking hour is invested in what expires.
You can say your children need Christ...
yet spend more energy preparing them to succeed financially than preparing them to stand faithfully before God.
You can pray for the lost...
and never inconvenience yourself for one.
You can say Scripture is precious...
while your phone receives hours and the Word receives leftovers.
You can tell Jesus, “You have my heart”...
while guarding your possessions as though they were your savior.
And then Christ speaks.
Not cruelly.
Not because He needs your wallet.
Because He wants you.
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Suddenly the question is no longer merely:
Where is my money going?
It becomes:
Where am I going?
Because every treasure has a destination attached to it.
And your heart keeps learning the road.
This is why the surrounding words of Jesus matter so much.
Immediately after speaking about treasure and heart, Jesus speaks about the eye and whether the body is filled with light or darkness.
Then He reaches the confrontation:
“No one can serve two masters.”
And finally:
“You cannot serve God and money.”
Notice what Jesus calls money in that sentence.
A potential master.
Money makes a wonderful servant.
It feeds children.
Builds homes.
Supports families.
Prints Bibles.
Sends missionaries.
Helps widows.
Feeds hungry people.
Creates jobs.
Supports churches.
Funds ministries.
Produces resources that can carry the Gospel into places you may never personally enter.
But money becomes terrifying when the servant climbs onto the throne.
Because money does not have to ask you to renounce Christianity.
It only has to whisper:
Trust me instead.
A little more and you will finally feel secure.
A little more and people will respect you.
A little more and you can stop worrying.
A little more and then you can become generous.
A little more...
A little more...
A little more.
Until one day you possess many things—
and discover those things have been possessing you.
Jesus does not condemn responsible provision. Scripture does not teach that possessing material things is inherently sinful. Nor does Christianity teach that every believer must own nothing.
The danger is deeper.
The danger is when the gift replaces the Giver.
When provision becomes identity.
When money becomes refuge.
When comfort becomes lord.
When accumulation becomes the quiet answer to the question:
What do I really trust to keep me safe?
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings giving treasure to God.
It is the story of God giving His treasure for human beings.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son...” — John 3:16
Before you ever surrendered anything to Jesus...
God gave.
Before you ever sacrificed...
Christ came.
Before you ever became generous...
He emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death.
Before you could purchase forgiveness—
forgiveness was purchased for you.
Not with silver.
Not with gold.
Not with religious performance.
But through the precious blood of Christ.
The cross destroys every attempt to turn Christianity into a transaction.
You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot donate enough money to erase one sin.
You cannot purchase God's affection.
You cannot finance your redemption.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Christian generosity is not:
“Give so God will love you.”
It is:
“God has loved you in Christ—so what still owns you?”
Grace changes the question.
The Gospel reaches into the clenched fist and says:
You can open your hand now.
Your Father is still God.
Your possessions were never your savior.
Your bank balance cannot forgive you.
Your house cannot resurrect you.
Your career cannot stand beside your grave and command you to rise.
Your reputation cannot wash away sin.
Your possessions cannot carry themselves through eternity.
But Jesus can save.
Jesus can forgive.
Jesus can restore.
Jesus can take the person who spent years chasing temporary treasure and rewrite the entire story.
That is what grace does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal is not the kind people gossip about.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your scandal is simply that you have called Jesus “Lord” while quietly allowing something else to function as lord.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe status.
Maybe your business.
Maybe approval.
Maybe your appearance.
Maybe entertainment.
Maybe the future you constructed in your imagination.
Maybe even ministry itself.
Anything can become treasure.
Anything can become an altar.
Anything can become the place where the heart begins building a home.
And sometimes the clearest evidence is not what makes you happy.
It is what you are terrified of losing.
Imagine Jesus sitting across from you tonight.
No crowd.
No church music.
No preacher.
No social media.
Just you and Christ.
And imagine Him asking:
“Show Me your treasure.”
What would you reach for?
Your Bible?
Your phone?
Your savings?
Your children?
Your achievements?
Your possessions?
Your audience?
Your plans?
And what if He asked something even harder?
“If I am truly your treasure, what in your life proves that I am?”
That question hurts.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Jesus exposes idols because idols eventually devour the people worshiping them.
He does not point toward heavenly treasure because heaven needs your money.
He points toward heavenly treasure because your heart matters to Him.
He wants your heart free.
Free from worshiping what rust can eat.
Free from being controlled by what thieves can steal.
Free from finding identity in what markets can erase.
Free from living terrified that tomorrow might remove what today gave you.
And notice what happens shortly afterward in Matthew 6.
Jesus begins talking about anxiety.
Food.
Drink.
Clothing.
Tomorrow.
Then He says:
“Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness...”
Do you see the movement?
Treasure.
Heart.
Master.
Anxiety.
Kingdom.
These are not disconnected spiritual sayings.
What you treasure touches what you serve.
What you serve touches what you fear.
And Christ calls you away from slavery to temporary things and toward trust in the Father.
That is why generosity can become an act of spiritual warfare.
Not because every donation is automatically holy.
Not because giving money guarantees blessing.
Not because God can be manipulated by an offering.
But because sometimes opening your hand is how you tell an idol:
You are not my master anymore.
Sometimes giving to someone in need says:
“My comfort is not my god.”
Sometimes supporting Gospel work says:
“My resources belong to Christ.”
Sometimes buying a Bible for another person says:
“The Word of God matters more than another unnecessary thing for me.”
Sometimes funding discipleship says:
“I want my earthly resources participating in eternal work.”
Sometimes quietly helping a struggling family says:
“My Father sees what nobody else needs to see.”
And sometimes generosity does something inside the giver that cannot be measured on a receipt.
Your treasure moves.
And slowly...
your heart notices where it went.

This is why Paul told wealthy believers not to put their hope “on the uncertainty of riches, but on God,” and called them to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share, thereby storing treasure for the future.
Not buying salvation.
Not purchasing miracles.
Not bribing heaven.
Learning where to place hope.
There is a world of difference.
And Gospel Warrior must live under that same truth.
If this ministry ever asks you to support something while directing your heart away from Christ, do not follow that direction.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the reason.
But if these articles have brought you back to Scripture...
if something you read here stopped you during a dark night...
if these words have helped you repent, pray again, forgive again, open your Bible again, or remember that Christ has not abandoned His people...
then consider whether you want to help keep that Gospel-centered work moving.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior proves you are a better Christian.
It does not.
And not because you should ever give money needed for essential responsibilities merely because someone pressured you spiritually.
You should not.
Support should come freely, prayerfully, honestly, and as an act of stewardship before God.
But glorifying God is not merely something Christians do with songs.
Scripture calls believers to glorify God with their whole lives.

So if you genuinely believe this ministry helps point people toward Jesus Christ, one practical way you can participate is by supporting it, sharing its biblical content, and helping put Christ-centered truth in front of another person who may desperately need it.
But hear this clearly:
The discount is not the treasure.
The merchandise is not the treasure.
Gospel Warrior is not the treasure.
Christ is.
The purpose of everything should be to keep pointing beyond itself toward Him.
Not as religious decoration.
Not to appear spiritual.
Jesus explicitly warned in this same chapter against practicing righteousness merely to be seen by people.
Somebody scrolling tonight may have everything money can buy and still feel completely empty.
Somebody may have walked away from church.
Somebody may be angry with God.
Somebody may be drowning in debt and shame.
Somebody may have made money their identity.
Somebody may be successful in public and spiritually starving in private.
Somebody may need one sentence to interrupt the direction of their life:
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Put that sentence in their path.
Because there may come a day when you need to read it again—not when you are poor, but when you are prospering.
Sometimes abundance tests the heart in ways suffering never could.
Not polished.
Not religious.
Honest.
There is no shame in admitting that your heart has wandered.
Peter wandered.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples failed.
The prodigal left home.
The thief on the cross arrived at the end of his life with nothing to offer Christ except desperate faith.
Grace still found them.
Maybe grace is finding you in this paragraph.
Maybe you realize your treasure has been traveling in the wrong direction.
Then you do not need to pretend.
Repent.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about yesterday.
It is turning.
Turn your eyes toward Christ.
Turn your trust toward Christ.
Turn your ambitions toward Christ.
Turn your resources toward purposes that honor Christ.
Turn your future toward Christ.
And when you stumble tomorrow, return to Christ again.
Your salvation rests not in the perfection of your surrender but in the perfection of your Savior.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the Christian who is tired.
Invite the seeker who still has questions.
Invite the person who says they no longer believe.
Even invite the friend who might roll their eyes at you.
You never know which seed God may use.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical resources into people's hands.
Help someone move from endless scrolling toward Scripture.
But before you click anything...
before you buy anything...
before you share anything...
before you comment anything...
do something more important.
Ask Jesus:
“Lord, where is my treasure?”
Then become quiet enough to let the question hurt.
Look at your life.
Look at your attention.
Look at your habits.
Look at your spending.
Look at your anxieties.
Look at your dreams.
Look at what receives your first thoughts in the morning and your final thoughts at night.
And if you discover that your treasure has wandered...
do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
The One speaking about treasure in Matthew 6 is the One who would eventually walk toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward mockery.
Toward nails.
Toward a cross.
Toward a borrowed tomb.
And then out of it.
The Gospel is not God standing at a distance demanding treasure from sinners.
The Gospel is God coming near in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners who treasured everything except Him.
We were the scandal.
Christ brought grace.
We brought sin.
He brought righteousness.
We brought debt we could never repay.
He brought a cross and declared the work finished.
And now the risen Christ does not merely want a percentage of your possessions.
He calls for you.
Your heart.
Your allegiance.
Your trust.
Your life.
Not because your surrender purchases His grace...
but because His grace has purchased you.
So perhaps the question tonight is not:
“How much should I give?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
“What has my treasure been teaching my heart to worship?”
Because someday everything you own will leave your hands.
Every house.
Every account.
Every possession.
Every title.
Every award.
Every carefully protected thing.
Your hands entered this world empty.
One day they will leave it empty.
But if your treasure is Christ...
you will discover that death cannot steal your Treasure.
The moth cannot touch Him.
Rust cannot corrupt Him.
Markets cannot devalue Him.
Thieves cannot take Him.
Time cannot weaken Him.
The grave could not hold Him.
And eternity will never exhaust Him.
So move your treasure toward what lasts.
Give when Christ calls you to give.
Share when truth deserves to travel.
Serve when nobody applauds.
Help people who cannot repay you.
Invest in Gospel work you have prayerfully judged faithful.
Feed someone.
Encourage someone.
Open your home.
Open your Bible.
Open your hands.
And above everything else...
cling to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most frightening tragedy would not be reaching the end of life and discovering you did not accumulate enough.
It would be discovering that you accumulated everything you wanted...
and trained your heart to live somewhere Christ was never your treasure.
So bring the heart home.
Bring the treasure home.
Bring the hidden idol into the light.
There is still grace.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still a cross for sinners.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still a Savior who receives repentant people.
And there is still time to change where you are laying up treasure.
Not for an algorithm.
Not for appearances.
Let it be a confession.
A small public line marking a private surrender:
Jesus, be my treasure.
Because wherever your treasure goes...
your heart will never remain far behind.
And maybe tonight, grace is asking you to move the treasure so your wandering heart can begin finding its way home.
When Christ becomes your Treasure, losing what cannot last no longer means losing everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE NEVER SAYS LEAH WAS UGLY
paragraphs:
THE BIBLE NEVER SAYS LEAH WAS UGLY
We turned one mysterious Hebrew word into a verdict on a woman’s worth—and somehow missed the breathtaking story God was actually writing through her.
There is a sentence about Leah that millions of people have heard without ever actually reading it in the Hebrew.
And once you see what the text really says, you may never read her story—or perhaps your own—the same way again.
Because somewhere along the way, Leah became “the ugly sister.”
Rachel was beautiful.
Therefore Leah must have been ugly.
Rachel was wanted.
Therefore Leah must have been undesirable.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Therefore there must have been something wrong with Leah.
It sounds logical.
It has been preached, illustrated, dramatized, painted, retold, and quietly absorbed into the Christian imagination.
There is only one problem.
The Bible never actually says Leah was ugly.
Read Genesis 29:17 carefully.
The Hebrew says:
וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת וְרָחֵל הָיְתָה יְפַת־תֹּאַר וִיפַת מַרְאֶה
Ve'einei Le'ah rakkot; veRachel hayetah yefat-to'ar vifat mar'eh.
Literally, the sentence describes Leah’s eyes as רַכּוֹת — rakkot, while Rachel is יְפַת־תֹּאַר — yefat-to'ar, beautiful of form, and וִיפַת מַרְאֶה — vifat mar'eh, beautiful of appearance.
The crucial word is rakkot.

It can carry the sense of tender, delicate, soft, or weak. English translations therefore differ. Some say Leah's eyes were “weak.” Others say “tender.” Others “delicate.” The meaning is sufficiently uncertain that responsible translations do not all render it the same way.
But notice what the Hebrew does not say.
It does not say Leah was ugly.
It does not describe her face as repulsive.
It does not call her body unattractive.
It does not pronounce her physically undesirable.
Rachel receives an explicit description of striking physical beauty. Leah receives a description specifically concerning her eyes.
Those are not the same statement.
Even the ancient Greek Septuagint renders Leah's eyes:
οἱ δὲ ὀφθαλμοὶ Λείας ἀσθενεῖς
Her eyes were astheneis—weak.
Not ugly.

The Hebrew wording and the ancient Greek translation preserve something that our retellings sometimes erase: Scripture gives us a contrast, but we should be careful not to manufacture an insult God never spoke.
And maybe that matters more than we realize.
Because human beings are extraordinarily good at turning comparison into condemnation.
If somebody else is beautiful, we assume we must be ugly.
If somebody else gets married first, we assume we are unwanted.
If somebody else's ministry grows, ours must be insignificant.
If somebody else has the body, family, career, platform, marriage, money, opportunity, confidence, or recognition we desperately wanted, something inside us whispers:
Then what does that make me?
That is where Leah's story becomes painfully modern.
You don't need to live in ancient Mesopotamia to understand what it feels like to stand beside somebody everybody seems to choose.
You only need a phone.
Scroll long enough and eventually you will find your Rachel.
Someone prettier.
Someone younger.
Someone more successful.
Someone whose marriage looks happier.
Someone whose children seem more accomplished.
Someone whose ministry gets noticed.
Someone whose photographs gather thousands of reactions while yours disappear almost unnoticed.
And suddenly you aren't simply looking at another person's blessing.
You are using their blessing as evidence against yourself.
Rachel is beautiful.
Therefore I must be ugly.
Rachel is loved.
Therefore I must be unlovable.
Rachel was chosen.
Therefore I must be the mistake.
But that second sentence did not come from God.
And that is where this story starts cutting deeper.
Because Leah's greatest wound was not that Scripture called her ugly.
Scripture never did.
Her wound was that she knew what it was like to be unloved.
Genesis 29 becomes almost unbearable when you stop treating these people like characters in a children's Bible and remember that they were human beings.
Jacob loved Rachel.
He agreed to serve Laban seven years for her.
Seven years.
And Scripture says those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her.
Then came the wedding.
The celebration.
The darkness.
And Laban deceived Jacob, giving him Leah instead.
Morning came.
Jacob discovered Leah.
And one of Scripture's most painful sentences followed:
“Behold, it was Leah.”
Imagine being the woman inside that sentence.
Imagine discovering that your wedding night was another man's deception.
Imagine knowing the man beside you had worked seven years—but not for you.
Imagine becoming someone's wife while knowing his heart was reaching for your sister.
Imagine living in the same household with the woman he actually wanted.
Imagine hearing their conversations.
Watching his eyes.
Noticing the difference.
Feeling comparison enter every room before you did.
This is not a romantic story.
It is a wounded family created partly through deception, favoritism, longing, rivalry, and human sin.
And Leah is caught inside it.
Then Genesis 29:31 says something astonishing.
The LORD saw.
That changes everything.
Before Leah receives what she longs for from Jacob, she is seen by God.
Before her circumstances are repaired, heaven notices her suffering.
Before anybody gives her the affection she aches for, the LORD sees the woman everyone else has reduced to a comparison.
That is one of the great movements of Scripture.
People look.
God sees.
People compare.
God knows.
People assign value according to desirability, usefulness, beauty, influence, status, productivity, or popularity.
God sees the person beneath all of it.
And perhaps you need to hear that tonight.
God sees you.
Not the edited version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the smiling Facebook photograph.
Not the version who says, “I'm blessed,” because explaining what is really happening would take too long.
He sees the part of you that wonders why somebody didn't choose you.
He sees the rejection you pretend stopped hurting years ago.
He sees the marriage where you feel invisible.
He sees the loneliness behind your jokes.
He sees you comparing your body to another person's body.
He sees the believer who worships publicly and cries privately.
He sees the person who keeps asking:
What was wrong with me?
And Leah's story whispers something important.
Another person's inability to love you properly is not God's definition of your worth.
But Leah's story becomes even more revealing when she begins having children.
She names her first son Reuben.
Her reasoning exposes her wound: the LORD has seen her affliction, and she hopes that now her husband will love her.
There it is.
The ache underneath everything.
Maybe now.
Maybe if I accomplish something.
Maybe if I give enough.
Maybe if I become useful enough.
Maybe if I lose the weight.
Maybe if I make more money.
Maybe if I stop being difficult.
Maybe if I become indispensable.
Maybe if my ministry succeeds.
Maybe if I become the person they wanted me to be...
then they will love me.
Have you ever lived inside that sentence?
Leah has another son.
Simeon.
Then another.
Levi.
And again her longing surfaces. Perhaps now her husband will become attached to her.
Read those names slowly and you can almost hear a wounded woman negotiating with rejection.
See me.
Hear me.
Stay with me.
Choose me.
Some people spend their entire lives doing exactly this.
They just stopped naming babies after the pain.
Now they name careers after it.
Relationships after it.
Achievements after it.
Bodies after it.
Bank accounts after it.
Ministries after it.
They become successful because somewhere deep inside is a terrified person still whispering:
Maybe now I'll finally be enough.
Then something happens when Leah's fourth son arrives.
Something subtle.
Something enormous.
Something that changes the direction of the story.
She names him Judah.
And this time her words change.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Not:
This time Jacob will love me.
Not:
This time Rachel will envy me.
Not:
This time everyone will finally recognize my worth.
This time I will praise the LORD.
Do you see it?
Her circumstances have not magically become painless.
But for one breathtaking moment, Leah's eyes move away from Jacob.
Away from Rachel.
Away from comparison.
Away from begging another human being to provide the verdict she desperately wants.
And upward.
This time I will praise the LORD.
And the son born at that moment is Judah.
Let that name sink in.
Judah.
Because the biblical story keeps moving.
Generations pass.
Kingdoms rise.
Kingdoms fall.
There is David.
There is exile.
There are centuries of waiting.
And eventually the opening chapter of Matthew begins tracing a genealogy toward a carpenter named Joseph and a young woman named Mary...
and toward Jesus Christ.
And there in the genealogy is Judah.
Leah's son.

The woman who spent so much time wondering whether she would finally be loved became the mother of Judah, and through Judah's line Scripture traces the royal and messianic genealogy that leads to Jesus Christ.
The rejected woman's story became woven into the earthly ancestry of the Redeemer.
Think about that.
Leah wanted Jacob to see her.
God was writing something she could not yet see.
Leah was thinking about whether one man would love her.
God's redemptive story was moving toward the One through whom God's love would be proclaimed to the world.
Leah could see the tent.
God could see generations.
Leah could see Rachel.
God could see Judah.
Leah could see rejection.
God could see redemption.
Leah could see what she lacked.
God knew what He was weaving through a broken family toward Christ.
That does not make Laban's deception good.
It does not make Jacob's favoritism good.
It does not mean suffering secretly becomes righteous simply because God can redeem what human sin has damaged.
Christianity does not require us to call evil good.
It declares something far greater:
evil does not get the final word when God is writing the story.
And this is where Leah's story reaches beyond Leah.
Because maybe you have been reading your entire life from one painful verse.
Rejected.
Divorced.
Betrayed.
Abandoned.
Overlooked.
Unwanted.
Childless.
Unemployed.
Addicted.
Ashamed.
Used.
Forgotten.
You took something that happened to you and quietly turned it into your identity.
They left me, therefore I am unlovable.
I failed, therefore I am a failure.
I sinned, therefore I am beyond redemption.
They chose somebody else, therefore I have no value.
But the Gospel interrupts that equation.
Your sin is real.
Your wounds are real.
Your failures may be real.
The consequences may be real.
Repentance may be necessary.
Forgiveness may be costly.
Healing may take time.
But Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the labels attached to broken people.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He took judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
The Gospel does not tell you that you were secretly perfect all along.
It tells you something infinitely better.
You can be redeemed.
Grace does not pretend there was never a scandal.
Grace takes sinners with real scandals, real shame, real rebellion, real wounds, real histories—and brings those who repent and believe into a story only Christ could write.
That is why we keep saying:
Not because Jesus edits history until nothing painful happened.
Not because Christianity is positive thinking with Bible verses.
Not because every earthly relationship will eventually give you the ending you wanted.
Jesus rewrites everything because the person who comes to Him in repentance and faith is no longer defined by condemnation.
There is forgiveness.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is new life.
There is a new identity centered not in human approval but in Christ.
And there is something almost unbearably beautiful near the end of Genesis.
Years later, Jacob gives instructions concerning his burial.
He speaks of the cave of Machpelah, the ancestral burial place.
Abraham and Sarah were buried there.
Isaac and Rebekah were buried there.
And then Jacob says:
“There I buried Leah.”
Leah.
Not merely “the other sister.”
Not merely the woman from the morning after Laban's deception.
Not merely the woman who spent years longing to be loved.
Leah became part of Israel's family story.
Her body rested in the ancestral burial place where Jacob himself asked to be buried.
Rachel's story matters profoundly too. This is not a contest between two wounded sisters, and Scripture gives us no permission to heal Leah by diminishing Rachel.
That would only repeat the disease of comparison.
Both women suffered.
Both women mattered.
Both became mothers within the family from which Israel's tribes emerged.
The point is not that Leah secretly “won.”
The point is that human beings are terrible at recognizing the full story while they are standing inside one chapter.
And maybe you are standing inside one of those chapters now.
Maybe someone left.
Maybe the diagnosis came.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe your child wandered away from God.
Maybe your prayers seem unanswered.
Maybe your secret sin has finally exhausted you.
Maybe everyone thinks you're strong, and you are barely holding yourself together.
Maybe you are Leah in the morning, staring at somebody else's disappointment and wondering whether your life will always feel like being the person no one wanted.
Please hear this carefully.
Do not turn your pain into a prophecy.
Do not turn rejection into identity.
Do not turn another person's beauty into evidence of your ugliness.
Do not turn somebody else's blessing into proof of God's abandonment.
And above everything else, do not make human acceptance the savior that only Jesus can be.
Jacob's love could never have healed everything inside Leah.
Neither can your spouse.
Neither can your followers.
Neither can your appearance.
Neither can your career.
Neither can applause.
Neither can money.
Neither can a ministry platform.
You were created for something human approval cannot provide.
Reconciliation with God.
And that is why every road in this story eventually has to lead beyond Leah.
Beyond Jacob.
Beyond Rachel.
Beyond Judah.
To Christ.
Maybe you have spent years saying:
Maybe now they will love me.
Jesus is calling you toward something deeper:
This time I will praise the LORD.
Maybe you have spent years hiding because you believed your scandal disqualified you.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Stop trying to make yourself clean enough to approach the One whose blood cleanses sinners.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is the undeserved mercy that receives us and begins transforming us.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needed today:
The chapter where you were rejected does not have authority to write the ending of the story God is redeeming.
If this exposed something you have been carrying quietly, don't hide behind another reaction button.
Be honest.
You don't need to explain everything.
Sometimes two or three honest words are enough to stop pretending.
And read the comments too.
Someone else may discover that the struggle they thought made them uniquely broken is being fought by another brother or sister in Christ.
Because it probably will.

Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't. Salvation is by grace, not social-media engagement. But if this biblical truth helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone you may never realize is quietly asking, “Why wasn't I enough?”
Share the article.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is having truth repeatedly placed in front of us in a world discipling us every hour in another direction.
It is Scripture.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Repentance.
Healing.
Accountability.
Spiritual sharpening.
And continually being pointed back toward Jesus Christ.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot share enough posts to erase one sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support Christian work because you love Christ and want His truth carried farther—not because you think God can be bought.
And before you leave this story, remember the woman with the tender eyes.
Remember how easily generations turned a description into an insult.
Remember the woman longing to hear, Now I love you.
Remember Reuben.
Simeon.
Levi.
Then remember Judah.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Remember that through Judah's line came David.
And ultimately...
Jesus.
The Lion of the tribe of Judah.

The Savior who entered a family history full of deception, rivalry, sexual scandal, broken relationships, outsiders, failures, and sinners—and was not contaminated by their sin, but came to redeem sinners from ours.
That is the Gospel.
Not spotless people presenting impressive résumés to God.
Sinners rescued by a spotless Savior.
So the next time somebody tells you Leah was simply “the ugly sister,” open the Bible.
Read the Hebrew carefully.
And then keep reading.
Because Leah's deepest story was never really about whether she could compete with Rachel's beauty.
It was about a God who saw an unloved woman...
and a redemptive story that eventually carried her family line toward Christ.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so beautifully.
We keep staring at the people who didn't choose us.
While grace keeps pointing us toward the Christ who calls sinners to Himself.
Because perhaps the most dangerous lie Leah's story exposes is not that people called her ugly.
It is the lie we still believe today:
that being unwanted by someone means being unusable by God.
It doesn't.
Come to Jesus.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Stop worshiping human approval.
Stop measuring your life against somebody else's beauty.
And let the Gospel have the final word.

Because the people who only saw Leah standing beside Rachel could never have imagined that somewhere beyond Leah's tears stood Judah... and beyond Judah's generations stood a cross, an empty tomb, and Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHERE WAS JESUS BETWEEN HIS DEATH AND RESURRECTION?
paragraphs:
WHERE WAS JESUS BETWEEN HIS DEATH AND RESURRECTION?
The Forgotten Hours Between “It Is Finished” and “He Is Risen” — And What Scripture Actually Says Happened After the Tomb Was Sealed
There is a silence in the Gospel story that almost feels unbearable.
Jesus is hanging on a cross.
His back has been torn open.
His hands and feet have been pierced.
The crowds have mocked Him.
His disciples have scattered.
His mother has watched what no mother should ever have to watch.
Then Christ speaks words that have echoed across two thousand years:
“It is finished.”
His head falls.
His breathing stops.
And Jesus dies.
Joseph of Arimathea eventually takes the body. Nicodemus comes with burial spices. They wrap Him and place Him inside a tomb.
A stone is rolled across the entrance.
Darkness.
Silence.
Friday becomes Saturday.
And somewhere between the agony of Calvary and the earthquake of resurrection morning comes one of Christianity’s most haunting questions:
Where was Jesus?
Was He simply dead in the tomb?
Was He in Paradise?
Did He descend into Hades?
What does Peter mean when he says Christ proclaimed something to “spirits in prison”?
Did Jesus go to hell and suffer after the cross?
Did He preach the Gospel to dead people so they could receive another opportunity to repent?
And what exactly happened before the stone rolled away?
These questions matter because careless answers can distort the Gospel itself.
So we cannot build our answer from paintings, medieval legends, dramatic sermons, internet clips, or ideas we heard somewhere years ago.
We have to go back to Scripture.
And when we do, something extraordinary emerges.
But first, we need to understand something that changes the entire question.
Jesus did not merely appear to die.
He actually died.
Christianity does not teach that Jesus fainted, entered a coma, secretly survived crucifixion, or somehow escaped the tomb.
His human body truly died.
The Gospel of John records that when the soldiers came to Jesus, they discovered He was already dead. Instead of breaking His legs, one soldier pierced His side.
Then His body was buried.
But physical death did not mean that the Son of God ceased to exist.
That distinction matters.
Jesus is one divine Person who possesses a truly divine nature and, through the incarnation, a truly human nature. His death was real human death; it was not the annihilation of the eternal Son.
And one sentence Jesus spoke from the cross gives us an enormous clue about what followed.
A criminal was dying beside Him.
This man could not repair his life.
He could not climb down from his cross.
He could not repay everyone he had wronged.
He could not build a religious résumé.
He could not perform years of good works.
He was running out of breath.
And yet something happened inside him.
While others mocked Jesus, this dying criminal turned toward Him and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.”
Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
Luke 23:42–43, KJV.
Do not rush past those words.
“Today.”
“With Me.”
“In Paradise.”
The Greek word translated “Paradise” is παράδεισος — paradeisos.
Jesus did not tell the repentant criminal, “Maybe.”
He did not say, “After you have suffered enough.”
He did not say, “When you have compensated for everything you have done.”
The dying sinner had nothing left to offer except faith directed toward a dying King.
And Jesus gave him a promise.
Today.
With Me.
Paradise.
That should sound painfully familiar to anyone who has ever believed they were too dirty to come home to God.
Maybe you have spent years believing you must clean yourself before Christ will receive you.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you hope nobody ever reads.
Maybe people know the edited version of you.
God knows the unedited one.
The private addiction.
The resentment.
The betrayal.
The secret messages.
The pornography.
The pride.
The abortion nobody knows about.
The affair.
The years you wasted.
The person you hurt.
The faith you abandoned.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The version of yourself you can barely stand remembering.
And perhaps you have quietly assumed:
Jesus could forgive other people.
Just not me.
Then look again at the man beside Him.
His final earthly location was a criminal’s cross.
His future was secured not because his past suddenly became respectable, but because the Savior beside him was sufficient.
That is scandalous grace.
But another biblical word must be understood.
When Peter preaches about the resurrection in Acts 2, he quotes Psalm 16:
“Because thou wilt not leave my soul in hell, neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.”
Acts 2:27, KJV.
The Greek word translated “hell” there is ᾅδης — Hades.
This is important because English readers can easily hear the word “hell” and immediately assume the final lake of fire or the place of final punishment described elsewhere in Scripture.
But Hades is the Greek term associated with the realm of the dead.
Peter's point is not that Jesus continued suffering there because Calvary somehow failed.
His argument moves toward resurrection.
Christ was not abandoned to Hades.
His body did not remain in corruption.
Death could not keep Him.
Acts 2:24 says God raised Jesus up, “having loosed the pains of death: because it was not possible that he should be holden of it.”
Not difficult.
Not unlikely.
Impossible.
Death had taken Someone it could not imprison.
And this connects with an ancient Hebrew word behind Peter’s quotation.
Psalm 16:10 reads:
“For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.”
The Hebrew term traditionally translated “hell” in that verse is שְׁאוֹל — Sheol.
Sheol in the Old Testament refers broadly to the realm of the dead or the grave, depending on context.
So when Scripture speaks about Christ, death, Hades, and resurrection, we must resist importing centuries of imagery into individual words without examining their biblical context.
And then we arrive at perhaps the most mysterious passage in this entire discussion.
First Peter 3.
Peter writes:
Stop there.
Because before Peter tells us anything mysterious, he tells us something unmistakable.
Why did Christ suffer?
For sins.
How many times?
Once.
Who suffered?
The Just.
For whom?
The unjust.
Why?
“That he might bring us to God.”
That is the Gospel sitting right in the middle of the mystery.
The Greek text contains the breathtaking expression:
δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων
dikaios hyper adikōn.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
Jesus was not dying because Rome accidentally defeated Him.
He was not dying merely as a political martyr.
He was not dying merely to give humanity an inspirational example of sacrifice.
The Righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
People like us.
Peter continues by describing Christ as:
θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκὶ ζωοποιηθεὶς δὲ πνεύματι
Thanatōtheis men sarki, zōopoiētheis de pneumati.
Put to death in flesh, but made alive in spirit.
Then comes the line that has generated centuries of theological discussion:
ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασιν πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξεν
“…he went and preached unto the spirits in prison.”
First Peter 3:19, KJV.
The phrase τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασιν means “the spirits in prison.”
And the verb ἐκήρυξεν — ekēryxen — means that He proclaimed or heralded.
What exactly does Peter mean?
Faithful Christians have proposed several major interpretations.

Some understand Peter to mean that after His death Christ went to the realm of the dead and proclaimed His triumph to imprisoned spiritual beings associated with the rebellion surrounding Noah’s generation.
Others understand the passage through the lens of Christ preaching by the Spirit through Noah to people who were alive in Noah’s day but were, by Peter’s time, “spirits in prison.”
Historic Christian traditions have also connected this passage with Christ’s descent to the dead.
The text is difficult enough that humility is necessary.
We should not pretend Scripture gives us a minute-by-minute itinerary of everything Christ did between His burial and resurrection.
It does not.
And we should be equally careful about another popular claim.
The Bible does not teach that Jesus spent those days being tortured by Satan in hell because His suffering on the cross was somehow incomplete.
That idea strikes at the sufficiency of Calvary.
Before Jesus died, He cried:
“It is finished.”
John 19:30.
The Greek word is:
Τετέλεσται.
Tetelestai.
It is finished.
Completed.
Accomplished.
The cross was not a down payment that required additional punishment from demons.
Jesus was not Satan’s helpless prisoner.
Satan did not become Christ’s torturer after Calvary.
The New Testament presents Christ’s death as victory.
Hebrews says that through death Christ would destroy the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil.
Colossians describes Christ disarming rulers and authorities and triumphing over them.
So whatever conclusions we reach concerning the difficult passages about Christ’s descent, they must remain consistent with the clear passages.
Jesus was victorious.
The sacrifice was sufficient.
The debt of sin was not waiting for Satan to finish collecting it.
Christ had accomplished what the Father sent Him to accomplish.
There is another passage often brought into this discussion.
Ephesians 4 says:
“Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth?”
Ephesians 4:9, KJV.
The Greek expression is:
τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς
ta katōtera merē tēs gēs.
Literally, “the lower parts of the earth.”
Again, interpreters disagree over the precise meaning.
Some understand this as Christ’s descent to the realm of the dead.
Others understand “the lower parts, namely the earth” as referring to His incarnation — His descent from heaven to earth.
Still others connect it specifically with His burial.
What we should not do is turn an interpretive possibility into a biblical certainty and then build elaborate stories Scripture never tells.
There is mystery here.
But mystery does not mean we know nothing.
We know Christ truly died.
We know His body was buried.
We know He promised the repentant criminal that he would be with Him in Paradise that day.
We know Peter speaks of Hades while declaring that Christ was not abandoned there.
We know Peter describes Christ proclaiming to “spirits in prison,” though sincere Christians differ about the precise timing and identity involved.
We know the New Testament presents His death not as defeat but as the decisive work by which sin is dealt with and death is ultimately conquered.
And we know something else.
Sunday came.
Imagine the tomb before sunrise.
Cold stone.
Roman authority outside.
A sealed entrance.
The disciples shattered.
Peter carrying the memory of denying Jesus three times.
Thomas drowning in confusion.
Mary grieving.
The religious establishment assuming the problem had finally been buried.
Rome believing another crucified man had disappeared into history.
And inside that tomb lies the body of Jesus Christ.
Friday had looked like scandal.
Saturday had felt like silence.
But God was not finished writing.
Then Sunday.
The stone moves.
The tomb opens.
And Jesus Christ rises bodily from the dead.
Not as a metaphor.
Not as an inspirational memory inside His disciples.
Not merely as “the spirit of Jesus living on.”
The crucified Jesus lives.
The grave is empty.
The King has risen.
And suddenly the silence between Friday and Sunday becomes personal.
Because some of you reading this are living in Saturday.
Something has died.
A marriage.
A dream.
A friendship.
Your reputation.
Your confidence.
Your ministry.
Your sense that God is near.
You prayed Friday.
Nothing changed Saturday.
You cried Friday.
Heaven seemed silent Saturday.
You believed God would intervene.
The stone still has not moved.
And you have begun confusing God's silence with God's absence.
But the tomb teaches us something devastatingly beautiful:
God can be accomplishing something enormous while everyone around you believes the story is over.
The disciples saw burial.
God knew resurrection was coming.
Peter saw failure.
Jesus already knew restoration was coming.
The criminal saw his final breaths.
Jesus saw Paradise.
The world saw a condemned Nazarene.
Heaven saw the Lamb of God completing the work of redemption.
Maybe that is why you needed to read this today.
Not merely to settle a theological curiosity about where Jesus was between death and resurrection.
Maybe the deeper question is:
Where are you right now?
Are you hiding?
Are you pretending?
Are you religious on Facebook and empty when the screen turns off?
Do you share Bible verses while secretly wondering whether God still wants you?
Do you know Christian vocabulary but no longer remember the last time you surrendered anything to Christ?
Maybe everyone thinks you are okay.
You know you are not.
And Jesus knows too.
But Christianity is not the announcement that good people can improve themselves.
It is the announcement that the Righteous One came for the unrighteous.
δίκαιος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
He came for sinners.
He came for the guilty.
He came for the ashamed.
He came for rebels who finally stop defending their rebellion.
He came for people who have destroyed things they cannot rebuild.
He came for Peters who swore they would never abandon Him and then did.
He came for thieves who have nothing left to offer except a desperate plea:
Remember me.
This is where grace becomes scandalous.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending sin never mattered.
Sin mattered enough for Calvary.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace cost blood.
Forgiveness cost the crucifixion of the Son of God.
That is why repentance matters.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our chains with Christian language.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
You cannot save yourself.
Your church attendance cannot erase your guilt.
Your generosity cannot purchase righteousness.
Your religious posts cannot substitute for surrender.
Your family’s Christianity cannot become yours by inheritance.
Christ is not asking you to become impressive.
He commands you to repent and believe the Gospel.
Come out of hiding.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the unbelief.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him your carefully managed public image.
Bring Him the thing you hope nobody discovers.
Not because sin is small.
Because Jesus is greater.
Maybe your story is different.
Maybe you love Christ, but you are exhausted.
You have been fighting quietly for months.
Nobody sees the war happening behind your smile.
Let another believer know they are not the only Christian who sometimes has to crawl toward Jesus.
And if you need prayer, there is no shame in saying:
“Pray for me.”
Someone reading the same words may stop and pray for a stranger they will never meet this side of eternity.
That is what the body of Christ can look like even through a screen.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” proves your salvation. It cannot.
Someone may have been told Jesus suffered under Satan after Calvary.
Someone may think their past has disqualified them from grace.
Someone may be living through the unbearable silence of their own Saturday.
Someone you know may never open a Bible study today.
But they might open something you shared.
Send this privately to the person whose faith is barely hanging on.
Save it too, because someday the silence between crucifixion and resurrection may mean something completely different to you than it means today.
We want it to become a place where people encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, healing, biblical truth, and above everything else, Jesus Christ.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and go deeper with us:
But before you leave, return one last time to that sealed tomb.
The disciples did not know what Sunday would look like.
They only knew Jesus had died.
Maybe that is where you are.
You cannot see what God will do next.
You cannot understand why He allowed this chapter.
You cannot imagine how anything beautiful could emerge from what has happened.
Christian hope does not promise that every earthly tragedy will reverse itself three days later.
It promises something infinitely greater.
Because Jesus Christ rose from the dead, death itself will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The Christian hope is resurrection.
The Christian message is Christ.
The Christian scandal is that guilty people can be reconciled to a holy God because the Righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
And the Christian invitation is still open:
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Friday says your sin is more serious than you imagined.
The cross says God's love is more costly than you imagined.
Saturday says silence does not mean God has surrendered the story.
Sunday says death does not get the last sentence.
Jesus does.
So where was Jesus between His death and resurrection?

Scripture gives us glimpses rather than the exhaustive itinerary our curiosity wants. His body truly lay in the tomb. He promised Paradise. Scripture speaks of Hades and of a proclamation to spirits in prison. Christians have disagreed about some details of those mysterious texts, and we should be humble where Scripture has not given us exhaustive clarity.
But Scripture refuses to leave the most important question unanswered.
Where is Jesus now?
Alive.
Risen.
Victorious.
And the Savior who walked out of His grave is still calling sinners out of theirs.
Because the stone they thought ended His story became the doorway through which resurrection announced that death had chosen the wrong King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A PROPHET WAS KILLED BY A LION BECAUSE HE DISOBEYED ONE COMMAND FROM GOD
paragraphs:
A PROPHET WAS KILLED BY A LION BECAUSE HE DISOBEYED ONE COMMAND FROM GOD
He survived confronting a king. He resisted money. He walked away obedient. Then one believable lie made him turn back—and what happened next should terrify every Christian who thinks yesterday’s obedience can replace hearing God today.
There was a dead man lying in the road.
Beside him stood a lion.
And beside the lion stood a donkey.
But the lion was not eating the body.
It was not attacking the donkey.
It simply stood there.
Almost like a guard beside the consequences of one terrible decision.
The story is found in 1 Kings 13, and Scripture never even gives us the dead man’s name. It repeatedly calls him אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים — ’ish ha’Elohim — “the man of God.”
That is what makes this story so unsettling.
This was not presented as the downfall of some openly pagan rebel who hated God.
This was a man God had used.
A man entrusted with a word from the LORD.
A man courageous enough to stand before a king.
A man through whom God had already demonstrated supernatural power.
And yet before the day was over, his body would be lying beneath the open sky because he abandoned a command God had personally given him.
If you have ever thought, “God has used me, so I must be okay,” keep reading.
If you have ever confused spiritual experience with spiritual safety, keep reading.
If you have ever allowed another person’s voice to overrule something Scripture had already made clear, keep reading.
Because the lion is not the most frightening thing in this story.
The most frightening thing is how believable the deception sounded.

Israel was spiritually fractured. Jeroboam had become king over the northern tribes and, fearing that continued worship in Jerusalem might eventually turn the people’s loyalty back toward the house of David, established alternative centers of worship.
Golden calves appeared.
An altar stood at Bethel.
Political convenience began dressing itself in religious clothing.
Then God sent an unnamed man of God from Judah to Bethel.
Imagine the scene.
King Jeroboam is standing beside the altar.
Incense is being burned.
The religious machinery of the kingdom is functioning.
Then an outsider walks into the middle of it carrying a word nobody in power wants to hear.
He cries against the altar by the word of the LORD and announces that a future descendant of David named Josiah will desecrate it.
Then he gives a sign.
The altar will split apart.
Its ashes will spill out.
Jeroboam does not repent.
He reaches out his hand and orders:
“Seize him!”
Then the king’s hand dries up.
He cannot pull it back.
And the altar splits.
The ashes pour out.
Suddenly the man whom the king wanted arrested is the man the king needs.
Jeroboam asks him to plead with God for the restoration of his hand.
The man of God does.
God restores it.
Think about how spiritually dangerous this moment could have become.
The man has confronted political power and survived.
A miracle has confirmed his message.
A king has experienced judgment and healing in front of him.
Now Jeroboam offers hospitality and a reward.
But the man of God refuses.
He explains why.
“For so was it charged me by the word of the LORD, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.”
—1 Kings 13:9, KJV
The Hebrew expression behind “word of the LORD” is דְּבַר־יְהוָה — devar-YHWH.
This was not a preference.
Not intuition.
Not merely a feeling.
God had spoken.
Do not eat there.
Do not drink there.
Do not return by the same road.
And initially, the man obeyed.
He refused the king’s table.
He refused the king’s reward.
He walked away.
If the story ended there, we would remember him as an extraordinary example of courage and obedience.
But it did not end there.
Because sometimes the temptation that cannot make you fall while you are standing before an enemy will return wearing the face of someone who sounds spiritual.
An old prophet living in Bethel heard what had happened.
His sons told him about the man of God.
The old prophet saddled a donkey, pursued him and eventually found him sitting beneath an oak.
“Art thou the man of God that camest from Judah?”
“I am.”
Then came the invitation.
“Come home with me, and eat bread.”
The man of God gave the correct answer.
He repeated God's command.
He knew what God had told him.
Then the old prophet said something devastating:
“I am a prophet also as thou art.”
And then he claimed that an angel had spoken to him “by the word of the LORD,” instructing him to bring the man of God home so he could eat and drink.
Then Scripture gives us five chilling words in the King James Version:
“But he lied unto him.”
—1 Kings 13:18
Read that again.
He lied.
The invitation sounded spiritual.
The messenger had religious credentials.
An angel was invoked.
God's name was attached to the claim.
Hospitality seemed harmless.
But it contradicted what God had already said.
And the man of God went back.
That is where this ancient story suddenly walks into our lives.
Because deception does not always arrive looking evil.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it knows Christian vocabulary.
Sometimes it says, “God told me.”
Sometimes it comes from someone older.
Someone respected.
Someone experienced.
Someone with a ministry.
Someone who sounds more confident about God's will for your life than you are.
But no human being receives authority to make God's revealed truth false.
The New Testament later gives Christians an indispensable principle:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.”
—1 John 4:1, KJV
The Greek verb translated “try” or “test” is δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete.
Test.
Examine.
Discern.
Do not surrender discernment merely because somebody uses spiritual language.
Paul goes even further in Galatians 1:8. Even if “an angel from heaven” preached a gospel contrary to the apostolic Gospel, believers were not to receive it.
That does not mean 1 Kings 13 and Galatians 1 are describing identical situations. They are not.
But the principle should sober us.
A supernatural claim does not outrank God's truth.
A charismatic personality does not outrank God's truth.
A title does not outrank God's truth.
A viral preacher does not outrank God's truth.
A dream does not outrank God's truth.
A feeling does not outrank God's truth.
And neither does Gospel Warrior.
Test what you read here against Scripture.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
His Word does not need our manipulation to remain true.
The tragedy in 1 Kings 13 is that the man of God already knew what God had commanded.
His problem was not lack of revelation.
His problem was abandoning the revelation he had received because another voice offered a contradiction wrapped in spiritual credibility.
So he went back.
He sat at the table.
He ate bread.
He drank water.
And then something extraordinary happened.
The same old prophet who had lied to bring him back suddenly received a genuine word from the LORD.
Imagine the silence at that table.
The meal is still there.
The man of God has already crossed the boundary.
Then judgment is announced.
“Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the LORD, and hast not kept the commandment which the LORD thy God commanded thee…”
—1 Kings 13:21, KJV
The Hebrew narrative uses the language of rebelling against the “mouth” of the LORD—פִּי יְהוָה, pi YHWH.
That image is painfully personal.
God had spoken.
The man had heard.
The man had obeyed…
until he did not.
After eating and drinking, he leaves.
Then the lion finds him.
Scripture says:
“And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him: and his carcase was cast in the way, and the ass stood by it, the lion also stood by the carcase.”
—1 Kings 13:24, KJV
The scene is deliberately strange.
Normally a lion that kills prey eats.
Normally a donkey standing beside a lion does not calmly remain there.
Yet the text emphasizes the lion, the donkey and the body standing together.

Later, when the old prophet hears about it, he says that this was the man of God who had disobeyed the word of the LORD, and that the LORD had delivered him to the lion according to the word spoken to him.
We should be careful here.
This passage does not teach that every tragedy is God's punishment for a particular act of disobedience.

Jesus Himself rejected simplistic assumptions that suffering automatically identifies someone as a worse sinner than everybody else. Scripture gives us Job. Scripture gives us martyrs. Scripture gives us faithful believers who suffer terribly.
So do not use this passage as a weapon against grieving people.
That would abuse the text.
But we should not soften what this particular text actually says either.
Within the narrative of 1 Kings 13, the man's death is explicitly connected to his disobedience.
And perhaps one of the most uncomfortable details is this:
The liar lived.
The deceived man died.
That bothers us.
It is supposed to bother us.
Why wasn't the old prophet killed?
Why did the man of God bear such severe consequences after being deceived?
The passage does not answer every question our emotions want answered.
And we should not invent explanations God did not give.
But it does destroy one excuse we desperately want to keep:
“Someone else misled me, therefore my obedience no longer matters.”
The old prophet was responsible for lying.
The man of God was responsible for abandoning the command he had received.
Both realities can exist at once.
Someone can genuinely wound you, manipulate you, pressure you or deceive you—and you can still need to bring your own response before God.
That is difficult.
But it is also liberating.
Because repentance begins when we stop handing everyone else ownership of our soul.
Maybe nobody has invited you back to Bethel.
Maybe your “one command” looked different.
You knew that relationship was pulling you away from Christ.
But somebody said, “God wants you happy.”
You knew dishonesty was wrong.
But everybody at work said, “That's just how business is done.”
You knew bitterness was poisoning you.
But someone said, “After what they did, you deserve to hate them.”
You knew sexual sin was destroying your conscience.
But culture renamed conviction “shame” and told you that holiness was repression.
You knew you needed to forgive.
You knew you needed to confess.
You knew you needed to stop pretending.
You knew Scripture said one thing.
But another voice made disobedience sound reasonable.
And somewhere along the road…
you turned back.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some of us are not reading about an unnamed man from Judah anymore.
We are remembering ourselves.
The moment we compromised.
The secret we protected.
The warning we ignored.
The conviction we kept postponing.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The Bible gathering dust while every other voice became louder.
And perhaps underneath all of it is a terrifying question:
Have I gone too far?
This is where we must be careful not to turn 1 Kings 13 into something it was never meant to be.
The Christian Gospel is not:
“Obey perfectly or God will send a lion after you.”
The Gospel is that none of us has obeyed perfectly.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
Every one of us has turned aside.
Every one of us needs mercy.
And God did not send Jesus Christ merely to make bad people behave better.
He sent His Son to save sinners.
Jesus obeyed where we failed.
Christ went all the way to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Lion we should ultimately behold is not the lion beside the road in 1 Kings 13.
It is the One Revelation calls “the Lion of the tribe of Juda.”
Jesus Christ.
And here is the breathtaking difference.
When our disobedience deserved judgment, Christ stepped into the place of sinners.
Not so that sin could become harmless.
Not so repentance could become optional.
But so guilty people could actually be forgiven, reconciled to God and transformed.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance: a turning, a change of mind that bears itself out in a changed direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about where you are.
It is turning toward God.
That means if this article is exposing something you have hidden, your next step is not despair.
It is Jesus.
If you compromised, turn to Jesus.
If you have been spiritually numb, turn to Jesus.
If another person's voice became louder than Scripture, turn to Jesus.
If you have been living two lives, turn to Jesus.
If you have been performing Christianity publicly while starving privately, turn to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
There is grace for sinners who come to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
That is why our message is not “From Scandal to Better Behavior.”
It is From Scandal to Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes Peter after denial and makes him a shepherd.
He takes persecuting Saul and makes him Paul, a servant of Christ.
He takes shame and gives forgiveness.
He takes rebellion and calls us to repentance.
He takes dead hearts and gives life.
He does not rewrite the past by pretending the sin never happened.
He rewrites what sin gets to do with the rest of your story.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your greatest spiritual battle happens after everybody thinks you have gone to sleep.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending you are stronger than you are.
Then stop pretending before Jesus.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes two honest words are enough to tell another believer, “I need somebody standing with me.”
And if Christ has already brought you through a season of compromise, deception, addiction, bitterness, shame or spiritual wandering, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Not because saving a Facebook post makes anyone spiritual, but because there are warnings we need to read twice.
Send it to the believer who has been hearing too many voices and opening Scripture too little.
But do it with love.
Not accusation.
Do not share this saying, “I know who needs this.”
Share it saying:
“Lord, keep all of us faithful.”
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, think more deeply about Christ, repent more honestly, or keep fighting when your faith felt exhausted, follow and stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet but is willing to listen.

We want this community filled with daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship and spiritual nourishment that ultimately points beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves your faith.
It does not.
Not because anyone can purchase blessing, salvation or spiritual status.
They cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But Christians can freely choose to support ministry work they believe is faithfully serving others.
If you are ready to support the mission and go deeper with us:
But before you leave this page, remember the unnamed man lying beside the road.
He had courage.
He had gifting.
He had experienced God's power.
He had spoken truth to a king.
And none of yesterday's obedience gave him permission to ignore God's word today.
That may be the warning somebody reading this needs.
Do not build your confidence on the fact that God used you yesterday.
Stay close to Christ today.
Do not assume every spiritual-sounding voice came from God.
Test it.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Listen.
Obey.
And when you fail—and every Christian still desperately needs grace—do not run away from the Savior because you are ashamed of needing a Savior.
Run toward Him.
The road back to Jesus is called repentance.
And the arms waiting there are scarred by the price He paid to redeem sinners.
The man of God turned back toward Bethel and found judgment on the road.
But if you have wandered from God, you are being called in another direction today.
Back to Christ.
Back to truth.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or simply:
“No more hiding.”
Then share this with somebody whose soul matters more to you than your comfort.
Because perhaps the most dangerous turn in your life will not look like rebellion when you make it.
It may look reasonable.
It may sound spiritual.
It may even come from someone you trust.
But when every other voice has finished speaking, there is still only one King worthy of your life.
Jesus Christ.
And if you remember only one sentence after you close this article, remember this:
The voice that persuaded you to turn away from God does not get the final word over the life that turns back to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “COUNT IT ALL JOY?” — THE VERSE THAT SOUNDS IMPOSSIBLE UNTIL YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT JAMES ACTUALLY SAID
paragraphs:
“COUNT IT ALL JOY?” — THE VERSE THAT SOUNDS IMPOSSIBLE UNTIL YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT JAMES ACTUALLY SAID
James 1:2 does not command you to enjoy your suffering. It calls you to see your suffering through the eyes of faith—and that changes everything.
There are Bible verses that sound beautiful when your life is beautiful.
Then there are Bible verses that almost hurt to read when everything is falling apart.
James 1:2 is one of them.
“Count it all joy…”
Easy to say when the bills are paid.
Easy to post when the marriage is healthy.
Easy to quote when the medical report came back clean, your children are doing well, your prayers appear to be answered, and you can still recognize the life you are living.
But what happens when you cannot?
What happens when you prayed…and the person still died?
When you begged God to save the marriage…and the papers still came?
When you tried to obey Him…and obedience seemed to cost you almost everything?
When the person who wounded you appears to be sleeping peacefully while you are still trying to heal from what they did?
When you have been asking God for an answer for so long that you are beginning to wonder whether heaven has gone silent?
Then somebody walks into your pain, quotes James 1:2, and says:
“Count it all joy.”
And somewhere inside you, something wants to scream.
Joy?
You want me to call this joy?
Maybe that is exactly where we have misunderstood James.
Because Scripture is not asking you to look at evil and call it good.
It is not asking a grieving mother to enjoy the funeral.
It is not asking a betrayed husband or wife to pretend betrayal does not hurt.
It is not telling the abused to celebrate abuse.
It is not commanding Christians to smile while their hearts are breaking.
And it certainly is not teaching that tears are evidence of weak faith.
Jesus Himself wept.
The sinless Son of God stood outside Lazarus’ tomb and cried.
So biblical joy cannot mean emotional denial.
James is saying something far deeper.
Something harder.
And, strangely enough, something far more beautiful.
The New Testament was written in Greek, and James 1:2 begins:
