Never trade the freedom Christ purchased for you just because the road of following Him became longer than you expected.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE CHURCH CANNOT PREACH GRACE BY PRETENDING REPENTANCE IS UNNECESSARY
paragraphs: THE CHURCH CANNOT PREACH GRACE BY PRETENDING REPENTANCE IS UNNECESSARY
When “come as you are” quietly becomes “stay as you are,” we have not made the Gospel more compassionate. We have forgotten what Jesus came to save us from.
There is a version of grace that almost everyone can applaud.
It comforts but never confronts.
It forgives but never calls anything sin.
It welcomes the wounded but never asks the rebellious to surrender.
It speaks endlessly about the love of Jesus while becoming strangely uncomfortable with the words Jesus Himself preached:
“Repent.”
And perhaps that is why this conversation matters so much.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is asking God to bless the very thing that is destroying them.
Someone is calling bondage “freedom.”
Someone is repeatedly returning to pornography and telling himself grace means he does not need to fight anymore.
Someone is carrying bitterness into another year because forgiveness feels too costly.
Someone is sleeping beside a person who is not their spouse while convincing themselves that a loving God would never interfere with their happiness.
Someone is hiding dishonesty behind ministry language.
Someone sings worship songs on Sunday while feeding an addiction in secret on Monday.
Someone has learned enough Christian vocabulary to explain grace while using that grace as permission never to change.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that such people have never entered a church.
Perhaps they have.
Perhaps we taught them how to feel accepted without teaching them what Jesus meant when He said:
“Follow Me.”
Grace is not God standing at a distance from our destruction saying, “It doesn’t matter.”
Grace is God entering our destruction in the Person of Jesus Christ, bearing our judgment on a cross, rising from the grave, and calling us out of the tomb with Him.
That difference is everything.
When Jesus began His public proclamation according to Mark 1:15, His message included these words:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek is breathtakingly direct:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
“Repair yourself until God accepts you.”
He did not say, “Become morally impressive, then come back.”
He did not say, “Pay for yesterday with enough good behavior tomorrow.”
The Gospel is not self-salvation.
Jesus announced good news.
Yet the same Jesus who proclaimed good news commanded repentance.

The Greek verb μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite carries the idea of changing one’s mind, but biblical repentance cannot be reduced to merely adopting a different opinion. In Scripture, the changed mind turns the person toward God. Sin is no longer defended as master. The sinner turns toward the One who saves.
That does not mean Christians become instantly flawless.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples misunderstood Jesus repeatedly.
The New Testament never presents Christian maturity as immediate sinlessness.
But there is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin.
One says:
“Jesus, I hate that I keep falling here. Have mercy on me. Help me fight.”
The other says:
“Jesus, I have decided this is no longer something You are permitted to confront.”
Those are not the same posture.
And some of us know exactly which one we have been living.
That is where this article becomes uncomfortable.
Because the easiest person to deceive spiritually is sometimes the person who already knows all the Christian answers.
You know Jesus died for sinners.
You know salvation is by grace.
You know Romans.
You know Ephesians.
You know how to say, “Nobody is perfect.”
All of those truths can be spoken correctly.
And then one terrifying little question remains:
Have you turned toward Christ, or have you merely learned enough about grace to become comfortable hiding from Him?
The Hebrew Scriptures give us another powerful picture.
In Ezekiel 18:30, God calls His people:
שׁוּבוּ וְהָשִׁיבוּ מִכָּל־פִּשְׁעֵיכֶם
shuvu vehashivu mikol-pish'eikhem
The language comes from the Hebrew root שׁוּב — shuv, meaning “turn” or “return.”
That image matters.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Returning.
Coming home.
Sin says, “Keep walking away.”
Shame says, “You have walked too far away to return.”
Grace says:
“Turn around.”
That is why biblical repentance and biblical grace are not enemies.
They meet in the arms of Jesus.
Repentance does not mean cleaning yourself before approaching Christ.
It means abandoning the fantasy that anything other than Christ can save you.
This is why Acts 2 is so striking.
Peter preaches Christ crucified and risen. The people are “pricked in their heart” and ask what they should do.
Peter answers:
Μετανοήσατε
Metanoēsate.
“Repent.”
Then comes the promise of forgiveness and the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Peter did not soften the Gospel by removing repentance.
He preached repentance because forgiveness was actually available.
Think about that.
A doctor who discovers cancer does not demonstrate compassion by hiding the diagnosis.
A firefighter does not love a sleeping family by whispering politely while their house burns.
And the Church does not love sinners by becoming embarrassed to tell them what Jesus came to rescue them from.
We can scream about judgment without love and distort the heart of God.
But we can also whisper about love while refusing to mention judgment, holiness, repentance, or surrender—and distort the Gospel just as surely.
Jesus gives us something infinitely better than either distortion.
Truth full of grace.
Grace full of truth.
A cross where sin is shown to be so serious that the Son of God dies—and sinners are shown to be so deeply loved that the Son of God willingly dies for them.
Look at the cross long enough and two lies become impossible to maintain.
You cannot honestly say:
“My sin does not matter.”
And you cannot honestly say:
“There is no hope left for someone like me.”
Calvary destroys both lies.
Your sin mattered enough for blood to be shed.
And you mattered enough for Christ to willingly shed His.
But we must be precise here.
You are not saved because your repentance is impressive enough.
You are not justified because you cried hard enough.
You are not forgiven because you accumulated enough remorse.
Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9 that salvation is by grace through faith, “not of works.”
Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He bore sin upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
Salvation rests upon Christ.
Even repentance is not a bargaining chip we place on God's counter and exchange for forgiveness.
We come empty-handed.
That is grace.
But empty hands cannot simultaneously cling to the throne of the sin from which Christ is calling us.
That is repentance.
And maybe this is where your heart started beating differently.
Because perhaps there is something you have been defending.
Not struggling with.
Defending.
There is a difference.
Maybe nobody knows.
The deleted messages.
The browser history.
The resentment.
The secret relationship.
The money.
The lies.
The substance you swear you can control.
The jealousy disguised as discernment.
The pride disguised as standards.
The cruelty disguised as “speaking truth.”
The unforgiveness you have rehearsed so many times that bitterness now feels like part of your personality.
You keep asking God for peace while protecting the thing disturbing your peace.
You keep asking Him for freedom while keeping a spare key to the prison.
And Jesus still calls:
“Come.”
Not because the sin is harmless.
Because His mercy is greater.
That is the scandal of grace.
Consider the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Jesus refused to participate in the mob’s self-righteous condemnation.
But He also did not rename adultery as righteousness.
After her accusers departed, Jesus told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Mercy.
Then transformation.
No condemnation from Christ toward the woman standing before Him.
But also no permission to return comfortably to what was destroying her.
This is where modern Christianity sometimes wants to cut Jesus’ sentence in half.
We love:
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
We become nervous around:
“Go, and sin no more.”
But Jesus said both.
Because perfect love does both.
Grace does not merely rescue you from the penalty of sin and then abandon you beneath its domination.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God that brings salvation also teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.
Read that carefully.
Grace teaches us to say no.
The very grace some use as an excuse not to change is described by Scripture as training believers toward godliness.
Real grace has teeth.
Not teeth that devour the repentant sinner.
Teeth that begin breaking the chains around that sinner.
And yes, sometimes transformation is painfully slow.
Sometimes sanctification looks like victory followed by tears, followed by confession, followed by getting up again.
A Christian may stumble terribly.
David did.
Peter did.
The Corinthian church was full of people requiring serious correction.
First John was written to believers and acknowledges the reality of sin while directing them toward confession and Christ our Advocate.
So this is not a message saying:
“Real Christians never fall.”
It is saying:
Real grace does not teach us to call falling freedom.
There is a difference between falling into the mud and building your house there.
There is a difference between needing mercy and demanding permission.
There is a difference between saying, “Father, forgive me,” and saying, “Father, redefine holiness so I never have to surrender.”
Jesus loves us too deeply for the second.
Remember Zacchaeus.
Jesus entered the home of a man despised as a tax collector.
Grace walked through his door before respectable society thought he deserved it.
But after encountering Jesus, Zacchaeus began talking about restitution.
Something changed.
Jesus did not merely become another decoration inside Zacchaeus’s old life.
Christ disrupted it.
That is what grace does.
Not because good works purchase salvation.
They do not.
But because encounters with Jesus produce fruit.
John the Baptist put it sharply in Matthew 3:8:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
Fruit does not create the tree.
Fruit reveals something about the tree.
And that distinction protects us from two cliffs.
Legalism says:
“Change enough and maybe God will love you.”
Cheap grace says:
“God loves you, therefore change is irrelevant.”
The Gospel says:
God loved sinners so profoundly that Christ died for us while we were sinners, and the Christ who saves us now calls us to follow Him.
Come filthy.
Come ashamed.
Come addicted.
Come angry.
Come confused.
Come after another failure.
Come when you have nothing impressive to offer.
But come to Jesus.
Do not come asking Jesus merely to become the chaplain of a life you refuse to surrender.
He is Savior.
He is Lord.
And there is astonishing tenderness in His lordship.
Some people hear “repent” and imagine God screaming, “Get away from Me.”
Biblical repentance announces almost the opposite:
The door home is open. Turn around.
The prodigal son rehearsed his shame while walking home.
He knew he had sinned.
He did not return declaring his rebellion healthy.
He returned confessing it.
And while he was still far away, the father ran.
Do you understand what that means for the person reading this with tears beginning to gather?
You can turn around.
Today.
Not after becoming impressive.
Not after fixing every consequence.
Not after proving yourself worthy.
You were never going to make yourself worthy.
That is why Jesus came.
The cross already tells the truth about your sin.
The empty tomb already tells the truth about His victory.
Stop hiding.
Come home.
Maybe you have spent years believing repentance means God wants to humiliate you.
But repentance is often the moment humiliation ends because pretending ends.
No more double life.
No more defending darkness.
No more exhausting performance.
No more smiling for church while secretly bleeding inside.
You finally say:
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“This is what I became.”
“This is what I keep returning to.”
“I cannot rescue myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
And the Christian Gospel does not answer that confession with:
“Try harder until God tolerates you.”
It points to Christ.
First John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Why “just”?
Because Christian forgiveness is not God pretending evil never happened.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Christ bore sin.
The debt was not waved away as meaningless.
The Savior paid at immeasurable cost.
This is why Romans 2:4 says that God's kindness leads toward repentance.
Not away from it.
Toward it.
Grace is not the cancellation of repentance.
Grace makes repentance possible without despair.
You can confess because there is mercy.
You can surrender because there is a Savior.
You can stop pretending because Jesus already knows.
You can come out of hiding because the One waiting for you bears scars.
So perhaps the question is no longer whether churches should preach repentance.
Perhaps the question is:
How could we preach the cross faithfully without it?
What exactly did Jesus die to save us from if sin is something we must never confront?
Why speak about forgiveness if there is nothing requiring forgiveness?
Why celebrate redemption if captivity is merely another lifestyle?
Why proclaim resurrection if nobody needs to come out of a grave?
The Gospel is glorious precisely because our condition was desperate and Christ was sufficient.
We were not slightly inconvenienced.
We needed salvation.
And Jesus saves.
This message must therefore never become ammunition for self-righteous Christians who enjoy identifying everybody else’s sins.
Before pointing across the room, look at your own heart.
Repentance begins here.
With me.
With you.
The proud need repentance.
The gossip needs repentance.
The pastor needs repentance.
The person addicted to pornography needs repentance.
The religious hypocrite needs repentance.
The greedy need repentance.
The sexually immoral need repentance.
The unforgiving need repentance.
The self-righteous person condemning everyone else needs repentance.
The person writing Christian articles needs repentance.
Nobody stands at the foot of the cross as the impressive one.
We stand there as people whose only boast is Jesus Christ.
So when the Church preaches repentance, it should never sound like superior people yelling at inferior people.
It should sound like rescued people shouting toward people still trapped in the fire:
“There is a way out. His name is Jesus.”
Be honest.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Somebody reading your words may discover they are not the only believer fighting that battle.
And somebody else may pray for you tonight.
If this message made you think of one person immediately, do not merely think about them.
It may be where hope begins.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday’s convictions feel distant tomorrow.
Return to it when you are tempted to rename what God is asking you to surrender.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the exhausted believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Not because Gospel Warrior can save anybody.
We cannot.
Jesus Christ saves.
This ministry exists to keep pointing toward Him.
It does not make you more spiritual, more forgiven, or more loved by God. Salvation cannot be bought, and supporting a Christian ministry should never be confused with supporting the Gospel itself.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with your resources, one practical expression of Christian stewardship can be voluntarily supporting work that helps spread His Word. Sharing this article publicly is another.
Do not leave this article merely supporting a ministry while refusing to surrender your heart to Christ.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
The merchandise cannot save you.
The library cannot save you.
Religion cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your tears cannot save you.
Your promises to “do better” cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Believe the Gospel.
And when you fall, do not run away from the One whose blood purchased forgiveness.
Run toward Him.
The Church does not need less grace.
We need grace in all its breathtaking biblical fullness.
Grace that welcomes the prodigal.
Grace that forgives the adulterer.
Grace that restores the failure.
Grace that confronts the hypocrite.
Grace that humbles the proud.
Grace that cleanses the guilty.
Grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace that finds sinners exactly where they are—
but loves them far too much to pretend captivity is freedom.
That is the scandal.
Holy God.
Guilty sinners.
A crucified Savior.
An empty grave.
Mercy offered to people who could never earn it.
And a voice still calling through the centuries:
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Me.
Maybe you came into this article afraid that repentance meant Jesus was finished with you.
Perhaps you can finally see the opposite.
He is calling you to turn because He is not finished with you yet.
Then close the screen for a moment.
Forget the comments.
Forget the shares.
Forget the algorithm.
Forget Gospel Warrior.
And answer the question that matters when nobody else can hear you:
What is Jesus asking you to stop defending and finally surrender?
Because the most dangerous prison may not be the sin you keep falling into.
It may be the sin you have finally stopped wanting freedom from.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JEROBOAM SENT HIS WIFE TO A PROPHET IN DISGUISE—But the Blind Prophet Knew Who She Was
paragraphs: JEROBOAM SENT HIS WIFE TO A PROPHET IN DISGUISE—But the Blind Prophet Knew Who She Was
He Changed Her Clothes So the Prophet Wouldn’t Recognize Her. But Jeroboam Forgot Something Terrifying: You Can Disguise Yourself Before People—You Cannot Disguise Yourself Before God.
She probably changed everything she could.
Her clothes.
Her appearance.
Perhaps the way she carried herself.
Anything that might whisper royalty.
Anything that might expose the palace.
Anything that might make an old prophet realize that the frightened woman standing at his door was actually the wife of King Jeroboam.
Her son was dying.
Her husband wanted answers.
But strangely, the king who wanted a word from God did not want the prophet to know who was asking.
Think about that.
Jeroboam still believed the prophet could hear from God.
He still believed Ahijah could tell him what would happen to his child.
He still wanted supernatural truth.
He simply did not want to approach that truth honestly.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story stops being merely Jeroboam’s story...
and quietly becomes ours.
Because there are moments when we want God to answer us without examining us.
We want His comfort without His correction.
His intervention without His authority.
His promises without His commands.
His healing without surrender.
His heaven while protecting the very idols He is asking us to abandon.
Jeroboam sent his wife toward Shiloh wearing a disguise.
But before her feet ever crossed the prophet’s doorway...
God had already told Ahijah who was coming.
That should make every hiding heart tremble.
And strangely...
it should also give every repentant heart hope.
Because the God who sees through the disguise is also the God before whom disguises are no longer necessary.
The story begins painfully.
Jeroboam’s son Abijah becomes sick.

This was not some political inconvenience. This was a child. A family was hurting. Behind the crown, the national crisis, the idolatry, and the judgment was a father and mother facing something parents have feared throughout human history:
What is going to happen to our child?
Jeroboam knew exactly where to seek an answer.
Ahijah.
The prophet of Shiloh.
And that detail matters enormously.
Ahijah was not a random religious figure Jeroboam suddenly discovered during a crisis.
Years earlier, Ahijah had been the prophet through whom God announced Jeroboam’s astonishing rise.

Ahijah had taken a new garment, torn it into twelve pieces, and told Jeroboam to take ten. God was tearing much of the kingdom from Solomon’s house and giving Jeroboam rule over ten tribes. Jeroboam’s throne had not begun merely with political ambition. He had received an extraordinary opportunity under the sovereign purposes of God.
Yet power exposed something inside him.
Fear.
Once Jeroboam possessed the kingdom, he became terrified of losing it.
He reasoned that if the people continued traveling to Jerusalem to worship, their loyalty might return to the house of David.
So Jeroboam constructed an alternative religious system.
Golden calves appeared at Bethel and Dan.
Unauthorized worship centers were established.
Priestly arrangements were altered.
A festival was instituted according to the king’s own design.
The tragedy is breathtaking.
Jeroboam received a kingdom from God...
then behaved as though he had to disobey God to keep what God had given him.
Scripture explicitly presents these innovations as sin.
And how many of us have done a smaller version of the same thing?
God gives us something...
then fear convinces us that sin is necessary to preserve it.
A relationship.
A career.
A reputation.
Money.
Influence.
Security.
Someone begins compromising because, “I cannot afford to lose this.”
Someone lies because the truth might cost too much.
Someone manipulates because surrender feels dangerous.
Someone knows what Scripture says but quietly constructs a more convenient Christianity—one that permits what Jesus is asking them to surrender.
And gradually the blessing becomes an idol because we become more afraid of losing the gift than grieving the Giver.
Then crisis arrives.
Jeroboam’s son becomes sick.
Suddenly the king who had built competing worship centers remembers the prophet of the LORD.
Isn’t that painfully human?
We can spend months avoiding God...
until the phone rings.
Until the doctor walks into the room.
Until the marriage starts collapsing.
Until the child is struggling.
Until the bank account empties.
Until the secret gets dangerously close to exposure.
Until the night becomes too quiet and all the things we used to drown out conviction stop working.
Then suddenly...
“Where is God?”
Jeroboam tells his wife to go to Ahijah.
But he adds one remarkable instruction:
Disguise yourself.
The Hebrew text describes her as מִתְנַכֵּרָה — mitnakkērāh, conveying the idea of making oneself unrecognizable, presenting oneself as another or disguising one’s identity.
Jeroboam believed human recognition could be manipulated.
There was just one problem.
Ahijah’s information was not ultimately coming from Ahijah’s eyes.
In fact, Scripture almost seems to underline the irony.
The prophet could not see.
His eyes had failed because of age.
The woman walking toward his house may have thought that made the deception easier.
An old man.
Failing eyesight.
A disguised queen.
What could possibly go wrong?
Everything.
Because while Ahijah could not see her...
God could.
Before she arrived, the LORD told Ahijah that Jeroboam’s wife was coming concerning her sick son and that she would be disguised.
Then comes one of the most cinematic moments in Kings.
Imagine it.
A frightened mother approaches the house.
Perhaps she has rehearsed what she will say.
Perhaps she believes the disguise has worked.
She reaches the entrance.
The blind prophet hears footsteps.
And before she can successfully become whoever she planned to pretend to be...
Ahijah speaks.
He identifies her as Jeroboam’s wife.
Then he asks, in essence:
Why are you pretending to be someone else?
The disguise survived the journey.
It did not survive the presence of truth.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
You have a disguise too.
Maybe nobody calls it that.
Maybe yours looks respectable.
You smile at church.
You repost Scripture.
You say, “God is good.”
You know when to raise your hands.
You know Christian language.
People think you are strong.
Your family thinks you are okay.
Your friends see the edited version.
Social media sees another version.
Church sees another.
Work sees another.
But somewhere beneath all those versions is a room inside your heart you desperately hope nobody opens.
The addiction.
The resentment.
The pornography.
The bitterness.
The affair nobody knows about.
The secret messages.
The envy.
The pride.
The private compromise.
The unforgiveness.
The double life.
The exhaustion.
The doubt you are afraid to admit.
Or perhaps your hidden thing is not scandalous at all.
Maybe you are simply hurting.
You tell everyone, “I’m fine,” because explaining the pain feels harder than carrying it.
You have become so skilled at appearing strong that nobody realizes how tired your soul has become.
Hear this carefully.
The lesson of 1 Kings 14 is not that Christians should become suspicious people constantly trying to expose everyone else.
The finger must first turn inward.
The terrifying question is not, “What is everyone else hiding?”
It is:
What am I still trying to disguise before God?
Hebrews later expresses the same reality with devastating clarity: no creature is hidden from God’s sight; everything lies exposed before the One to whom humanity must give account.
Not your browser history.
Not your thoughts.
Not your motives.
Not the conversation you deleted.
Not what happened when nobody was watching.
Not the wound you buried.
Not the jealousy you renamed “discernment.”
Not the hatred you renamed “boundaries.”
Not the greed you renamed “ambition.”
Not the fear you renamed “wisdom.”
God sees.
But here is where this message must not become cheap religious terror.
Because if all we say is, “God sees your sin,” we have not yet reached the fullness of the Gospel.
Yes.
God sees.
But Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had successfully hidden its darkness.
He came because we could not save ourselves from it.
John’s Gospel says that Light came into the world, while people loved darkness rather than light because their works were evil. Yet the same passage speaks of coming into the light.
That is the invitation.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
Jeroboam’s tragedy was deeper than simply having sin in his history.
David had grievous sin in his history too.

The biblical contrast in 1 Kings 14 concerns the direction of the heart. God indicts Jeroboam because he had not followed the LORD wholeheartedly as David had, but instead multiplied idolatry and turned away. The text is not teaching that David was sinlessly perfect—the wider biblical record makes that impossible—but it does contrast covenant allegiance and repentance with Jeroboam’s entrenched rebellion.
Jeroboam wanted information from God without reconciliation with God.
That is a dangerous form of religion.
“Tell me what happens next.”
But not...
“Lord, change me.”
“Protect my child.”
But not...
“Destroy my idols.”
“Give me an answer.”
But not...
“Take my throne.”
“Show me Your will.”
But not...
“Your will be done.”
We can even approach Jesus that way.
We can want Jesus as emergency assistance rather than Lord.
Jesus, fix my finances.
Jesus, restore my relationship.
Jesus, heal my body.
Jesus, protect my family.
Jesus, give me peace.
Jesus, open the door.
And Christ certainly invites suffering people to come to Him.
But He is more than an emergency service for collapsing circumstances.
He is Lord.
Savior.
King.
The crucified and risen Christ does not merely improve the disguise.
He calls the person underneath it into the light.
And that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity does not announce that good people successfully climbed their way to God.
The Gospel announces that sinners could not rescue themselves, so God acted in Christ.
Jesus did not die for your carefully managed Christian image.
He died for sinners.
He already knows what repentance will uncover.
The cross was never God discovering how terrible humanity could become.
The cross was God’s redemptive answer to human sin.
Christ was crucified.
Christ bore sin.
Christ rose.
And everyone who truly comes to Him in repentant faith does not have to construct a false identity before God.
You can finally tell the truth.
“Jesus...
this is me.”
Not the profile picture.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the person everybody thinks you are.
Me.
The angry me.
The addicted me.
The frightened me.
The ashamed me.
The wounded me.
The lustful me.
The proud me.
The exhausted me.
The confused me.
The me who promised You I would stop and did it again.
The me who knows Scripture but sometimes lives like I have never read it.
The me who has been hiding.
“Lord Jesus Christ...
have mercy on me.”
And suddenly the exposure you feared becomes the doorway through which repentance walks.
That does not mean repentance is painless.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Look again at 1 Kings 14.
Judgment is real.

Ahijah announces devastating consequences upon Jeroboam’s house. The child would die. Jeroboam’s dynasty would fall. The kingdom itself would eventually experience judgment because of persistent idolatry. When Jeroboam’s wife returned to Tirzah and crossed the threshold, the child died, just as the prophetic word had declared.
The Bible does not soften that scene for our comfort.
Neither should we.
Sin is not cute.
Idolatry is not harmless.
Rebellion against God is not spiritual self-expression.
There are consequences.
And yet even within this terrifying judgment appears a strange, heartbreaking detail.
The child Abijah is the one member of Jeroboam’s household in whom the LORD says something good was found, and he alone receives the honor of burial and national mourning.
Even judgment is not portrayed as divine blindness.
God sees distinctions humans may miss.
He sees what is hidden.
Good and evil.
Truth and deception.
Faith and performance.
Which brings us back to that doorway.
The disguised woman.
The blind prophet.
The God who sees everything.
Maybe you have been standing at that doorway for years.
You know something must change.
You feel conviction occasionally.
You promise yourself:
“Tomorrow.”
“After this relationship.”
“After this season.”
“After I make enough money.”
“When life settles down.”
“When I’m ready.”
But tomorrow keeps becoming another yesterday.
And the disguise becomes heavier.
Listen carefully.
You do not need another disguise.
You need Jesus.
Not religious cosmetics.
Not better Christian branding.
Not another motivational quote covering an untreated wound.
Jesus.
Repentance is not polishing your mask.
Repentance is bringing your real face into the light and turning from sin toward the Savior.
There is a profound difference between being exposed by shame and being exposed by grace.
Shame whispers:
“If they knew you, nobody could love you.”
The Gospel declares something far more astonishing:
God knew sinners completely, and Christ still came to save.
That does not excuse sin.
It destroys our excuse for hiding it.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Your sin is serious enough that Christ's sacrifice was necessary.
God's grace is magnificent enough that sinners who come to Christ need not remain what sin made them.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one theme:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by renaming rebellion.
Jesus rewrites lives through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation.
Peter denied Him...
and grace restored him.
Paul persecuted believers...
and Christ transformed him into a servant of the Gospel.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to manufacture a respectable religious résumé...
yet he turned toward the crucified King.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to make human failure the final sentence when sinners turn to God.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to become your final chapter when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Grace does not say:
“Keep the disguise.”
Grace says:
“You can take it off now.”
You are already seen.
Come home.
Maybe this article found you while you are fighting something nobody knows about.
Then stop pretending for one moment.
Not publicly, necessarily.
Not recklessly.
But before God.
Be truthful.
If conviction is burning in you right now, do not scroll quickly enough to silence it.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Seek wise pastoral or Christian help where you need accountability.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Bring darkness into the light.
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging, “I need Christ to change me,” becomes a small first refusal to keep pretending.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer still fighting.
And please...
do not keep this message trapped on your screen.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who looks completely fine and is quietly collapsing underneath a disguise.
Not because sharing an article earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by God's grace, not by social-media activity, financial support, merchandise purchases, or religious performance.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your mind while reading.
You cannot heal what you insist on hiding from the light.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who has learned how to look alive spiritually while dying inside.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely about pretending to be good.
Let them discover something radically different:
Christianity begins when pretending ends.
We do not come to Christ because our disguise fooled Him.
We come because it never did.
Ahijah was blind...
but God was not.
Jeroboam's wife changed her appearance...
but heaven knew her name.
Jeroboam attempted to obtain God's answer while concealing himself behind another person...
but God addressed the real issue.
Thousands of years later, the question still walks toward our own doorway:
Why are you pretending to be someone else?
Maybe the person you have been fooling is your family.
Maybe your church.
Maybe your spouse.
Maybe your friends.
Maybe yourself.
But never God.
He saw the first compromise.
He saw the tears afterward.
He saw you swear it would never happen again.
He saw you return.
He saw the shame.
He saw the nights.
He saw the wound that helped shape the behavior but can never justify the sin.
He sees the whole story.
And the breathtaking news of the Gospel is that the One who sees the whole story is the very One calling sinners to repentance and offering forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
So take off the disguise.
You were never hidden anyway.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive grace.
Walk in the light.
And when Jesus begins rewriting what shame told you could never change, do not hide that testimony either.
Tell somebody.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Jeroboam's story was never that God could see through a disguise.
Perhaps the most frightening thing was that Jeroboam knew where the prophet was...
knew God could speak...
wanted God's answer...
and still did not truly surrender.
Don't repeat his tragedy.
Do not merely ask God what is going to happen to your life.
Give your life to Christ.
The disguise may have carried you this far.
But grace is waiting for the person underneath it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: TAMAR WAS PASSED BETWEEN MEN WHILE HER FUTURE WAS BEING DECIDED FOR HER
paragraphs:
TAMAR WAS PASSED BETWEEN MEN WHILE HER FUTURE WAS BEING DECIDED FOR HER
She buried one husband. Then another man used what should have protected her for his own advantage. Then the man who promised her a future quietly left her waiting for one he never intended to give. But God was watching the woman everyone else had placed on hold.
There is a kind of pain that comes from losing someone.
And then there is another kind.
The pain of realizing that while you were grieving, other people were making decisions about your life as though your heart were not even in the room.
Tamar knew something about that pain.
Her story in Genesis 38 is uncomfortable.
Not uncomfortable because Scripture is careless with morality, but because Scripture refuses to sanitize what human sin actually does to people.
Tamar enters the biblical narrative almost without introduction.
No childhood.
No long description.
No recorded conversation about what she wanted.
Just one sentence:
“Judah got a wife for Er his first-born; her name was Tamar.”
In Hebrew:
וּשְׁמָהּ תָּמָר
U-shemah Tamar.
“Her name was Tamar.”
Her name.
Remember that.
Because before this chapter is finished, men will make decisions affecting her marriage, her widowhood, her motherhood, her security, and potentially her survival.
But God never forgets her name.
Judah chooses Tamar as a wife for his firstborn son, Er.
Then Scripture gives a terrifyingly brief judgment on Er: he was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.
We are not told here exactly what Er did.
That matters.
We should never accuse a biblical character of sins the Bible itself does not identify.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
Tamar became a widow.
Imagine the silence after that.
Whatever expectations she carried into that marriage disappeared.
Whatever future she imagined was buried.
And in the social world surrounding the text, widowhood could mean far more than loneliness. Marriage, offspring, household belonging, inheritance, and economic security were deeply connected.
Tamar had lost more than a husband.
Her future had become uncertain.
Then Judah spoke to his second son, Onan.
The Hebrew of Genesis 38:8 is striking:
בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ
Bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehakem zera le-achikha.
In sense:
Go to your brother’s wife, perform your brother-in-law duty toward her, and raise up offspring for your brother.
The verb behind this duty is connected with yibbum, the brother-in-law obligation later formally addressed in Deuteronomy 25:5–10.
The purpose was not simply sexual access.
It concerned family continuity.
Name.
Offspring.
Responsibility.
Protection within the covenant community.
But Onan knew something.
The text says:
וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע
Vayyeda Onan ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
And suddenly the ugliness becomes clearer.
Onan wanted something from the arrangement without accepting the responsibility attached to it.
Genesis says that when he went in to Tamar, he deliberately prevented conception because he did not want to provide offspring for his brother.
Do not rush past that.
Tamar had already buried one husband.
Now another man repeatedly entered the relationship while intentionally denying the very outcome his obligation was supposed to provide.
The biblical issue is larger than the simplistic way this passage is sometimes discussed.
The text itself emphasizes his refusal to provide offspring for his brother.
He accepted intimacy while sabotaging responsibility.
He participated physically while withholding covenant duty.
And God saw it.
Genesis says what Onan did was evil in the sight of the LORD.
The LORD put him to death also.
And Tamar became a widow again.
Two husbands.
Two funerals.
No child.
No secure future.
Then Judah spoke.
Perhaps these words initially sounded like hope:
“Stay as a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.”
Wait.
Just wait.
There is another son.
There is still a future.
There is still a possibility.
But the narrator lets us hear what Tamar could not hear.
Judah was afraid.
He thought Shelah might die like his brothers.
And so Tamar was sent away.
Genesis says:
שְׁבִי אַלְמָנָה בֵית־אָבִיךְ
Shevi almanah beit-avikh.
“Remain a widow in your father’s house.”
And she did.
That sentence hurts differently when you have ever been told to wait by someone who had no intention of keeping their promise.
Wait until things improve.
Wait until I am ready.
Wait until the timing is right.
Wait until they change.
Wait until someone finally chooses you.
Tamar waited.
Shelah grew.
And still Tamar was not given to him.
That detail changes everything.
She was not simply impatient.
Genesis explicitly tells us that Tamar saw Shelah had grown up and that she had not been given to him.
The promised future had arrived.
The promise had not.
There are people reading this who know that particular wound.
Not Tamar’s exact circumstances.
But the feeling.
Someone else controlled the decision.
Someone else held the authority.
Someone else made the promise.
And you were left living inside the consequences.
Maybe someone abandoned you and continued living as though nothing happened.
Maybe somebody used your vulnerability while calling it love.
Maybe a person kept you close enough to benefit from you but never close enough to honor you.
Maybe you were told to wait.
And wait.
And wait.
Until one day you realized you were not waiting for circumstances to change.
You were waiting for someone to become honest.
Tamar eventually stopped waiting.
What happens next is one of the Bible’s most morally complicated family scandals.
After Judah’s wife died and his period of mourning passed, Tamar learned that Judah was traveling toward Timnah for the sheep shearing.
She removed her widow’s garments.
She covered herself with a veil.
She positioned herself along his route.
Judah saw her and assumed she was a prostitute.
He did not recognize his own daughter-in-law.
He propositioned her.
Tamar asked what he would give her.
Judah promised a young goat.
But Tamar wanted collateral.
“What pledge will you give me?”
His seal.
His cord.
His staff.
In that world, these were not meaningless trinkets.
They were identifying objects.
Tamar did not merely obtain payment.
She obtained evidence.
Judah slept with her.
She conceived.
Then she left, removed the veil, and put the garments of her widowhood back on.
And approximately three months later, the scandal exploded.
Judah was told that Tamar had become pregnant through sexual immorality.
His response was horrifyingly swift.
“Bring her out.”
Judgment came quickly from a man who had been remarkably slow to examine himself.
Then Tamar did something extraordinary.
She did not scream.
She did not deliver a long accusation.
She sent the evidence.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
And essentially said:
Identify these.
Whose are they?
There is an almost poetic justice here.
The man prepared to expose Tamar publicly was forced to recognize himself privately.
Judah looked.
He knew.
And then Genesis records one of the most important confessions in the entire story:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tzadqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Or, in context, “She is more in the right than I.”
Then Judah explains why:
Because he had not given Tamar to Shelah.
There it is.
The truth finally spoken aloud.
Judah acknowledges his failure.
This does not mean Scripture is declaring every action Tamar took an ideal model for Christian ethics.
Genesis is narrating an ancient and deeply broken situation, not issuing Christians a command to imitate every decision within it.
But neither does Scripture allow us to turn Judah into an innocent observer.
His own confession identifies the injustice.
“I did not give her to my son Shelah.”
Tamar had been waiting inside a future Judah had promised but withheld.
And now the man prepared to condemn her discovered that his own failure was sitting in her hands.
Maybe that is where this story becomes dangerous to religious people.
Because we are often very good at seeing the visible scandal.
God sees the hidden chain of decisions that preceded it.
We see the pregnancy.
God saw the waiting.
We see Tamar by the road.
God saw Tamar sent home.
We see the disguise.
God saw the broken promise.
We see the moment everybody whispers about.
God sees the years nobody asks about.
That does not make sin righteous.
It means righteous judgment requires truth.
And this is where Genesis 38 begins reaching beyond Tamar.
Because some of us have become experts at judging the chapter of somebody’s life we happened to walk into while knowing nothing about the chapters that came before it.
We see the breakdown but not the betrayal.
The anger but not the wound.
The addiction but not the emptiness.
The divorce but not the years behind closed doors.
The coldness but not the abandonment.
The church absence but not what happened inside the church.
The scandal but not the suffering.
Again, pain does not make every response right.
Victimhood does not transform sin into holiness.
The Gospel never requires us to rename darkness as light.
But neither does Jesus teach us to become self-righteous spectators who throw stones while refusing to examine our own hearts.
Because eventually every one of us comes to the same terrifying place Judah reached.
The evidence points back at us.
Not Tamar’s evidence.
Ours.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our deception.
Our selfishness.
Our secret compromises.
Our carefully edited Christianity.
Our private browser histories.
Our resentment.
Our unforgiveness.
Our hunger to appear righteous instead of becoming holy.
Our tendency to condemn publicly what we secretly excuse privately.
And before the holiness of God, none of us survives by saying, “At least I am better than Tamar.”
We survive only by grace.
That is where this scandal begins moving toward something astonishing.
Tamar conceived twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez became part of the line of Judah.
Generations passed.
Names became genealogies.
Families became nations.
Kings came.
And then Matthew opened his Gospel with a genealogy that ancient public-relations consultants probably would have edited.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
And then—
Tamar.
Matthew 1:3 deliberately remembers her:
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar.”
Her name survived the scandal.
More than that.
Her story became part of the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
Think about what that means carefully.
The Gospel is not saying the Messiah needed sin.
God is never the author of evil.
The Gospel is showing something far more glorious:
Human sin cannot derail God’s redemptive purpose.
God does not need a spotless human family tree to send a spotless Savior.
Jesus entered a genealogy filled with broken people because He came to save broken people.
Tamar appears there.
Rahab appears there.
Ruth appears there.
David appears there, with Matthew deliberately reminding us of “the wife of Uriah.”
The genealogy refuses cosmetic surgery.
Then comes Jesus.
Not another compromised man.
Not another sinner requiring redemption.
The Redeemer Himself.
The sinless Son of God.
The One who would eventually stand before another condemned woman while religious men prepared to weaponize her shame.
The One who touched people respectable society avoided.
The One who ate with sinners.
The One who exposed hypocrites.
The One who welcomed repentant outcasts.
The One who carried our shame to a Roman cross.
The One who was stripped so sinners could be clothed in righteousness.
The One who was condemned though innocent so guilty people could be forgiven.
This is Christianity.
Not pretending your family tree has no Tamar.
Not pretending your hands contain no evidence.
Not pretending your past never happened.
Christianity begins when sinners stop defending themselves and come to Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years thinking the ugliest thing that happened to you disqualified you.
Maybe what somebody did to you still whispers that you are damaged goods.
Maybe what you did still follows you into worship.
Maybe you have become Judah, suddenly recognizing evidence of your own hypocrisy.
Maybe you have been Tamar, waiting while people with more power determined what happened next.
Maybe, if you are painfully honest, you have been both wounded and wounder.
Most of us have.
That is why we need more than inspiration.
We need a Savior.
Jesus does not merely improve scandalous people.
He raises spiritually dead people to life.
He does not merely teach us to manage shame.
At the cross, He deals with guilt.
He does not tell us repentance is unnecessary because our pain explains everything.
He calls us to repentance because His grace is powerful enough to forgive everything we genuinely bring to Him.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who already paid what you could never pay.
The cross says your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
And the cross simultaneously says His grace is greater than your shame can imagine.
That is why nobody reading this should use Tamar’s story to justify sin.
And nobody should use Tamar’s story to imprison a repentant sinner forever inside a past Jesus has forgiven.
The Gospel does neither.
It tells the truth.
Then grace enters the truth.
Perhaps you have been hiding.
Stop hiding.
Jesus already knows.
Perhaps you have been blaming everybody else.
Come into the light.
Jesus already knows.
Perhaps somebody’s betrayal convinced you God abandoned you.
Look again at Tamar.
Human beings were making decisions.
God was still writing history.
People saw a widow waiting in her father’s house.
God saw generations.
People saw scandal.
God saw a lineage through which, according to the flesh, the Messiah would eventually come.
People saw a woman whose future seemed suspended.
God had not lost the thread.
And if you belong to Christ, He has not lost yours.
That does not mean every earthly wound will receive the ending you wanted.
It does not mean every marriage will be restored, every betrayer will apologize, every stolen year will return, or every consequence will disappear.
Biblical hope is stronger than fantasy.
Our ultimate hope is Jesus Himself.
Forgiveness in Him.
Reconciliation with God through Him.
A new identity in Him.
Resurrection because of Him.
Eternal life with Him.
And transformation through His Spirit beginning now.
So be honest.
Did this story expose something?
Did you recognize Tamar’s waiting?
Judah’s hypocrisy?
Onan’s selfishness?
Or perhaps something in yourself you have been trying not to name?
Respond to God.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need forgiveness, ask Christ for mercy.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, come to Him.
He died for sinners and rose again.
You do not clean yourself enough to approach Him.
You come because you cannot save yourself.
And if you have spent too long pretending everything is fine, maybe today your confession is simply:
“No more hiding.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that you need prayer is the first crack in a wall you have spent years constructing.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not merely because you enjoyed it.
Someone may need to discover that the Bible does not hide broken families.
Someone may need to hear that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Someone may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from coming home.
There may come a night when shame starts speaking again, and you need to remember that Tamar’s name did not disappear in Genesis 38.
It appeared again in Matthew 1.
Stay close to daily Scripture, biblical conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and truth centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing.
It cannot.
We should never manipulate people by suggesting that God is more pleased with paying supporters than with those who cannot afford to give.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, truth, and service.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of that generosity.
Christ cannot be purchased.
Salvation is the gift of God received through faith in Jesus Christ.
So pray.
Repent.
Forgive.
Seek Christ.
Open your Bible.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Share truth.
Carry somebody else’s burden.
And remember Tamar.
The woman sent away to wait.
The woman whose future appeared to rest in the hands of men.
The woman standing inside one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable scandals.
Her name survived.
Her story continued.
And generations later, when Matthew began telling the world about Jesus Christ, there she was.
Tamar.
Because God is not embarrassed by the places where His grace demonstrates just how desperately humanity needs redemption.
Maybe people have already written the final sentence over your life.
Maybe you wrote it yourself.
Failure.
Ruined.
Unwanted.
Unclean.
Too late.
Too complicated.
Too far gone.
But if you are still breathing, you do not get to call the story finished while Jesus Christ is still calling sinners to Himself.
Come into the light.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the sin.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
And surrender all of it to the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Tamar is not simply that she survived a scandal.
It is that the scandal could not prevent God from carrying His redemptive promise forward until history reached Jesus.
What people treated like the end of Tamar’s story, God placed inside the genealogy of the Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Being a “Good Person” Won’t Save You—and That Offends People
paragraphs: Being a “Good Person” Won’t Save You—and That Offends People
The Gospel does not say you need to become a slightly better version of yourself. It says something far more offensive—and infinitely more beautiful: you need a Savior.
There is a sentence people love to say because it makes death feel less frightening.
“He was a good person.”
She helped people.
He loved his family.
She never hurt anybody.
He gave to charity.
He worked hard.
He wasn’t perfect, of course, but who is?
And beneath those words is often an assumption so deeply embedded in us that we rarely stop to examine it:
Surely good people go to heaven.
It sounds reasonable.
It sounds compassionate.
It even sounds fair.
There is only one problem.
That is not the Gospel Jesus Christ came to proclaim.
And before you get angry, keep reading—because what initially sounds like terrible news may become the most liberating news you have ever heard.
The Bible does not teach that heaven is populated by people who were good enough.
It teaches that heaven is populated by sinners who were rescued by grace.
That difference changes everything.
Paul writes in Romans 3:23:
Pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou Theou.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Notice the first word.
πάντες — pantes.
All.
Not merely murderers.
Not merely adulterers.
Not merely criminals whose sins became public enough to make the evening news.
All.
The religious.
The generous.
The polite.
The churchgoing.
The neighbor everybody loves.
The mother who sacrificed everything for her children.
The businessman who gives to charity.
The pastor behind the pulpit.
The person writing these words.
The person reading them.
All.
And that is where the Gospel begins offending human pride.
Because most of us do not measure ourselves against the holiness of God.
We measure ourselves against somebody worse.
“I may have lied, but I never cheated on my wife.”
“I may have cheated, but I never abandoned my children.”
“I may not go to church, but at least I’m not a hypocrite.”
“I have made mistakes, but deep down I’m a good person.”
Do you see what we are doing?
We keep moving the measuring stick until we can stand on the acceptable side of it.
We search the room for someone worse than us and quietly use that person as evidence that we must be okay.
But imagine standing before a judge after breaking the law and saying:
“Yes, Your Honor, I am guilty—but have you seen what the man in the next courtroom did?”
His guilt does not erase yours.
And neither does another person's sin make us righteous before God.
This is precisely why the Gospel can feel insulting before it feels beautiful.
The Gospel strips away comparison.
It does not allow the respectable sinner to stand above the scandalous sinner.
It puts us all at the foot of the same cross.
And perhaps that bothers us because we desperately want to contribute something to our rescue.
We want Jesus...
plus our morality.
Jesus...
plus our church attendance.
Jesus...
plus the fact that we raised decent children.
Jesus...
plus the money we gave.
Jesus...
plus the people we helped.
Jesus...
plus the list of terrible things we never did.
But Scripture will not let us turn salvation into a résumé.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says salvation is by grace through faith, “not of works,” so that no one can boast.
That destroys the spiritual scoreboard.
You cannot stand before God holding your good deeds like admission tickets to heaven.
Why?
Because Christianity does not teach that human beings merely need moral improvement.
It teaches that sinners need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need mercy.
We need new life.
We need Christ.
And suddenly the words of Jesus become much more uncomfortable.
A rich man once approached Him and addressed Him as “Good Teacher.”
Jesus answered:
“Why do you call Me good? No one is good but One, that is, God.”
Jesus was forcing the conversation toward the standard everyone conveniently forgets.
God.
Not your neighbor.
Not your pastor.
Not your ex.
Not the criminal on television.
God.
Absolute holiness.
Perfect righteousness.
Perfect love.
Perfect truth.
And when God becomes the standard, our favorite sentence begins collapsing:
“But I’m a good person.”
Good compared with whom?
That is the question.
Because if you compare a dirty shirt with something covered in mud, the shirt may look clean.
Put that same shirt beneath brilliant white light and suddenly every stain becomes visible.
God's holiness is that light.
And perhaps some of us avoid that light because we have spent years constructing a version of ourselves we can tolerate.
We remember the kindness and conveniently forget the cruelty.
We remember what we gave and forget whom we used.
We remember the prayers and forget the pride.
We remember the people we forgave and forget the grudges we still feed when nobody is watching.
We remember that we never physically committed adultery and conveniently ignore what Jesus said about lust.
We remember that we never murdered anyone and forget His warning about hatred and anger.
We polish the outside.
God sees the heart.
And that is terrifying...
until you understand why Jesus came.
Because Christianity does not end with:
“You are a sinner.”
If it did, despair would be the only logical response.
The Gospel says:
You are a sinner...
and Christ came for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Read those words carefully.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after we conquered every addiction.
Not after we fixed the marriage.
Not after we learned Christian vocabulary.
Not after we finally became worthy.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
There is the scandal.
The Holy One came for the unholy.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
Jesus did not come merely to make good people better.
He came to save sinners.
The cross makes absolutely no sense if goodness could save you.
If morality could reconcile humanity to God, Calvary was unnecessary.
If charity could remove guilt, Jesus did not need nails through His hands.
If religious activity could make us righteous, there was no reason for the Son of God to bear our sin.
If heaven could be earned by accumulating enough good deeds, Jesus could simply have handed humanity a checklist.
Instead...
He gave Himself.
Romans 6:23 captures the contrast with devastating clarity: the wages of sin is death, but God's gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Wages are earned.
A gift is received.
That distinction is the heartbeat of grace.
Sin pays wages.
God gives a gift.
And maybe this is where somebody reading needs to stop pretending.
Because you have been trying to negotiate with God.
You promised Him you would become better.
You said you would stop.
Then you returned to it.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You cried at the altar.
Then went home carrying the same secret.
You know how to smile when somebody asks how you're doing.
You know when to lift your hands during worship.
You know enough Christian language to convince everybody around you that your soul is healthy.
But late at night...
when the room becomes quiet...
you know.
Something is wrong.
Maybe nobody knows what you have done.
Maybe everyone knows.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe yours lives behind a locked screen.
Maybe you destroyed something precious.
Maybe somebody destroyed something inside you and bitterness became the way you survived.
Maybe you became addicted.
Maybe you became proud.
Maybe you became religious.
Maybe you became so good at appearing good that you eventually stopped noticing how far your heart had wandered from God.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not waiting for a better version of you before He will receive the repentant sinner who comes to Him.
You do not take a shower before taking a shower because you are too dirty.
You come because you are dirty.
And you do not become righteous enough to deserve Christ.
You come to Christ because you are not righteous enough to save yourself.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is infinitely more costly than that.
At the cross, sin mattered so much that Christ died.
And sinners mattered so much that Christ willingly came to save them.
Christian grace is not God shrugging at evil.
It is God providing, in His Son, what sinners could never provide for themselves.
That means the prostitute cannot boast.
The preacher cannot boast.
The recovering addict cannot boast.
The lifelong church member cannot boast.
The prisoner cannot boast.
The missionary cannot boast.
The person with the horrifying testimony cannot boast.
The person whose testimony sounds boring cannot boast.
Nobody reaches heaven saying:
“Look what I accomplished.”
The redeemed sing another song.
Look what Jesus did.
And that is why the Gospel simultaneously humiliates human pride and restores human dignity.
It tells the moral person:
You are not good enough to save yourself.
Then it tells the broken person:
You are not too ruined for Christ to save.
Do you understand how beautiful that is?
The same Gospel that closes the door on self-righteousness opens the door to the desperate.
You cannot be good enough to make the cross unnecessary.
And you cannot be broken enough to make the blood of Christ insufficient for the repentant sinner who comes to Him in faith.
The ground beneath the cross is level.
Maybe your whole life has been respectable.
You paid your taxes.
Loved your children.
Stayed faithful to your spouse.
Helped neighbors.
Gave money away.
Those things matter.
Good works matter.
Love matters.
Obedience matters.
Scripture absolutely calls Christians to lives of holiness, generosity, justice, mercy, self-control and sacrificial love.
But here is the order we cannot reverse:
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are the fruit of a life transformed by grace.
A tree does not become alive because somebody tapes fruit onto its branches.
A living tree bears fruit because life is already flowing through it.
In the same way, Christianity is not about taping religious behavior onto a spiritually dead heart.
It is about being made alive in Christ—and then beginning to live differently because Christ is changing you.
This is why grace is not permission to keep embracing sin.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
Grace does not say:
“Your sin does not matter.”
Grace says:
“Your sin does not get the final word.”
Repentance is not purchasing God's mercy.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy we desperately need.
Faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is entrusting yourself to Him.
Christ is not an accessory added to an otherwise self-sufficient life.
He is Lord.
And perhaps that is the deeper offense.
We do not merely want to be considered good.
We want to remain in control.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
A Savior without a Lord.
Resurrection without a cross.
But Jesus never marketed Himself as a spiritual enhancement package.
He called people to follow Him.
And following Jesus means eventually confronting the funeral of the person you thought you had to keep defending.
Your pride.
Your secret kingdom.
Your excuses.
Your carefully maintained reputation.
Your insistence that because somebody else sinned worse, your sin somehow does not count.
Then something extraordinary happens.
When you finally stop trying to prove that you are good enough...
you become free to admit that you need grace.
That is where the mask falls.
That is where confession begins.
That is where the tax collector in Jesus' parable becomes one of the most important men in the room.
He does not deliver God a résumé.
He cannot even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He simply cries for mercy:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
And Jesus says that man went home justified.
Not the man congratulating himself.
The man begging for mercy.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to be the other man.
Religious enough.
Respectable enough.
Useful enough.
Successful enough.
Nice enough.
And perhaps beneath all that effort is fear.
“What if God actually saw everything?”
He does.
That is frightening.
But here is what grace whispers from Calvary:
He knew—and Christ came anyway.
He knew humanity's rebellion before Bethlehem.
He knew the cross before the manger.
He knew Peter would deny Him.
He knew His disciples would scatter.
He knew sinners would mock Him.
He knew nails were coming.
Still...
He came.
That does not make sin small.
It makes His love astonishing.
So stop asking the question that human pride loves:
“Am I basically a good person?”
Ask the question eternity demands:
“Am I reconciled to God through Jesus Christ?”
Those are not the same question.
Your funeral may someday be filled with people saying wonderful things about you.
They may remember your generosity.
Your humor.
Your loyalty.
Your sacrifices.
Your accomplishments.
They may stand beside your coffin and say:
“He was such a good person.”
But human applause cannot justify a soul before a holy God.
You do not need a favorable character reference from humanity.
You need Christ.
And if that sounds offensive...
perhaps it is because grace leaves your ego with nothing to boast about.
But it leaves your soul with everything to hope for.
You do not have to spend another decade pretending.
You do not have to hide behind comparison.
You do not have to manufacture a spotless spiritual résumé.
You can come to Christ honestly.
Sinner.
Broken.
Ashamed.
Confused.
Addicted.
Religious.
Proud.
Exhausted.
Empty.
Come.
Not because your goodness deserves Him.
Because His grace is your only hope.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Romans 10 teaches that confession of Jesus as Lord and heartfelt faith in His resurrection belong to the response of salvation.
And when Christ saves you, do not misunderstand what happens next.
Grace does not leave you where it found you.
Jesus rewrites people.
The liar learns truth.
The proud learn humility.
The sexually broken learn purity.
The bitter learn forgiveness.
The greedy learn generosity.
The self-righteous learn mercy.
The hopeless discover hope.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without battles.
Not without stumbling and discipline and tears.
But genuinely.
Because salvation is more than behavior modification.
It is the beginning of a transformed life in Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
That has always been the story.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to build an impressive religious résumé.
He had nothing left to offer.
No decades of charity.
No missionary career.
No opportunity to repair his public reputation.
He had a dying body, a guilty history, and faith turned toward a crucified King.
And beside him hung Jesus.
That is the Gospel.
Not good people climbing high enough to reach God.
God coming down in Christ to rescue sinners who could never climb high enough.
So if this article offended you at first, ask yourself why.
Was it because Scripture called something evil that you want to keep?
Was it because you have built your confidence on being better than somebody else?
Was it because admitting you need salvation feels humiliating?
Or perhaps...
somewhere along the way...
the offense turned into relief.
Because if salvation depended upon being good enough, you could never know whether you had finally done enough.
Enough prayers?
Enough generosity?
Enough obedience?
Enough remorse?
Enough good years to outweigh the bad ones?
The Gospel removes that impossible ladder.
Christ is not asking you to climb your way to Him.
He calls you to repent, believe, and follow.
And perhaps today your prayer does not need to sound impressive.
Perhaps it needs to sound honest.
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”

If something hidden was exposed while you read this, do not hide behind religious language. Bring it into the light before God. Somebody scrolling beneath this article may need to discover that Jesus still restores real people with real histories.
And do not keep this message trapped on your screen.
Send it privately to the person whose faith is barely breathing.
Christ alone saves.
And when you share it, remember why.
Not so people will think you are good.
Not so God will owe you something.
Not because clicking “share” earns one centimeter of heaven.
when what they desperately need is empty hands stretched toward Jesus.

Because at the end of all our striving, all our image management, all our comparisons, all our secret shame and public respectability, the question is not whether we managed to convince the world that we were good people.
The question is what we did with Jesus Christ.
Your goodness cannot erase your sin.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter either.
At the cross, pride loses its argument...
and the repentant sinner discovers hope.
The moment you stop trying to prove that you are good enough may be the moment you finally understand why Jesus was good enough for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN SOMEONE WANTS ACCESS TO YOUR BODY BUT NOT RESPONSIBILITY FOR YOUR LIFE
paragraphs: WHEN SOMEONE WANTS ACCESS TO YOUR BODY BUT NOT RESPONSIBILITY FOR YOUR LIFE

They may call it love. They may say, “Why do we need a label?” They may want your touch, your loyalty, your vulnerability, your late-night conversations—and still refuse the covenant, responsibility, holiness, and sacrifice that biblical love requires. Before you give someone what God calls sacred, ask yourself one painful question: Do they actually want to love me… or do they only want access to me?
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that does not begin when someone leaves.
It begins while they are still there.
Still texting.
Still calling.
Still saying they miss you.
Still wanting to come over.
Still reaching for your body.
Still expecting your emotional availability.
Still becoming jealous when someone else gets your attention.
Still wanting privileges that feel suspiciously like commitment...
while carefully avoiding the responsibility of actually committing.
And perhaps that is why this hurts so much.
Because sometimes the person who is using you does not look cruel.
Sometimes they are affectionate.
Sometimes they are wounded too.
Sometimes they know exactly what to say when you begin pulling away.
“I care about you.”
“I’m just not ready.”
“Why do we have to complicate this?”
“Can’t we just enjoy what we have?”
Maybe you have heard those words.
Maybe you have said them.
Maybe you are living inside them right now.
And somewhere beneath all the chemistry, loneliness, hope, excuses, physical desire, and spiritual conviction, there is a question you have been afraid to ask:
If this person wants access to my body but refuses responsibility for my life, is this actually love?
Scripture gives us a far deeper vision of intimacy than our culture does.
Go all the way back to Genesis.
Before dating apps.
Before hookup culture.
Before pornography became available through a screen.
Before situationships had a name.
Before human beings learned a thousand sophisticated ways to separate sexual intimacy from covenantal responsibility, Scripture said:
“עַל־כֵּן֙ יַֽעֲזָב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד׃”
Genesis 2:24.
A careful translation is:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Notice the movement.
Leave.
Hold fast.
Become one flesh.
The Hebrew verb וְדָבַק — wəḏāḇaq, from dāḇaq — carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, remaining closely joined.
That matters.
Because the biblical vision does not begin with:
Take what you want.
Enjoy the body.
Avoid responsibility.
Keep your options open.
Disappear when things become inconvenient.
God's design places “one flesh” inside a relationship marked by a profound joining of lives.
Jesus Himself later reaches back to this very passage when teaching about marriage.
That means your body is not spiritually meaningless.
Sex is not merely recreation performed by consenting bodies.
Biblically, sexual union possesses a seriousness our culture desperately tries to make casual.
And casual sex often discovers too late that the body participated in something the heart cannot casually forget.
Paul understood that.
Writing to Corinth—a world hardly unfamiliar with sexual disorder—he did not treat the body as disposable packaging around the “real” spiritual person.
He wrote:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not keep it around until you become spiritually stronger.
Not see how close you can get without crossing whatever line you have drawn.
Flee.
Then Paul says something astonishing.
“τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς... ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν”
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
And then:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς”
“You were bought with a price.”
Therefore:
“δοξάσατε... τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι”
Glorify God in your body.
That changes the question completely.
The question is no longer merely:
“Do I want this person?”
Or:
“Does this person want me?”
The deeper question becomes:
“Does what we are doing glorify the Christ who purchased me?”
Because Christian sexual ethics are not fundamentally about God hating pleasure.
They are about belonging.
You belong to Christ.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your sexuality belongs under the lordship of Christ.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Christ.
Your loneliness belongs under the lordship of Christ.
Even that aching part of you that desperately wants someone to choose you belongs to Jesus.
And perhaps this is where the truth gets uncomfortable.
Sometimes we do not surrender our bodies because we are overwhelmed by lust.
Sometimes we surrender them because we are terrified of being abandoned.
Sometimes what looks like sexual temptation is actually loneliness wearing different clothes.
You were afraid that saying no would make them leave.
You were afraid boundaries would make you seem difficult.
Old-fashioned.
Religious.
Boring.
Unlovable.
So you compromised a little.
Then another little.
Then another.
And every compromise came with a promise whispered somewhere inside:
Maybe now they will choose me.
Maybe now they will stay.
Maybe now I will finally be enough.
But they kept taking pieces of intimacy while withholding the security your heart was begging for.
And slowly you began negotiating against yourself.
You called anxiety “butterflies.”
You called inconsistency “complicated.”
You called secrecy “privacy.”
You called sexual pressure “passion.”
You called crumbs “love” because you were starving.
Please hear this carefully.
This article is not telling you that every person who struggles sexually is an evil predator.
Christians must be more truthful and more compassionate than that.
Two people can genuinely care about each other and still participate together in something sinful.
Two wounded people can exploit one another without initially understanding the depth of what they are doing.
A boyfriend or girlfriend can feel genuine affection and still pressure the other sexually.
A person can sincerely believe they love you while behaving in ways that are selfish, immature, manipulative, or unholy.
And sometimes...
you may be the one demanding access.
You may be the person pushing boundaries.
You may be the one saying, “If you really loved me...”
You may be the one keeping somebody emotionally attached because you enjoy what they provide while secretly knowing you have no intention of offering faithful commitment.
The Gospel does not permit us to read articles like this only looking for somebody else's sin.
The Word is a mirror.
So before you send this to the person who hurt you, allow God to search you too.
Paul's words to the Thessalonians become especially piercing here:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν”
“This is the will of God: your sanctification.”
He continues by commanding believers to abstain from porneia—sexual immorality—and to live in holiness and honor.
Then, in the same discussion, Paul warns against transgressing against and exploiting another person in this matter.
Do you see how radical that is?
Biblical sexual holiness is not simply:
“Don't have sex.”
It asks what you are doing with another human being who bears God's image.
Are you honoring them?
Are you exploiting them?
Are you awakening intimacy while refusing responsibility?
Are you manipulating their fear of losing you?
Are you encouraging them toward Christ—or teaching them that keeping you requires compromising Him?
That question can expose an entire relationship.
Because someone who genuinely loves you should not require your disobedience to God as proof of your devotion to them.
Read that again.
Someone who genuinely loves you should not require your disobedience to God as proof of your devotion to them.
“I need this.”
“Everybody does it.”
“We're going to get married eventually.”
“God knows we love each other.”
“You're being too religious.”
“If you trusted me, you would.”
No.
Love does not need to drag you away from Jesus to prove that it exists.
Love should want your holiness more than it wants immediate gratification.
That does not mean a godly relationship will be free from temptation.
Quite the opposite.
Two people can deeply love Christ and still experience powerful sexual desire for each other.
Attraction is not automatically sin.
Temptation is not automatically defeat.
