Support the work because you believe the Gospel should travel.
Share because somebody else may need the truth.
But glorify God first and ultimately by belonging to Christ, obeying His Word, loving Him, loving others, and making His Gospel known.
Because one day every carefully closed tent will open.
Every reputation will become irrelevant.
Every secret will stand before the God who already knows.
And when that reality finally reaches your heart, there is only one safe place to run.
Not deeper into hiding.
Not toward another excuse.
Not toward another bottle.
Not toward another screen.
Not toward another carefully constructed version of yourself.
Run to Jesus.
The One who was stripped so sinners could be clothed in righteousness.
The One who bore shame without deserving it.
The One who carried sin without committing it.
The One who entered death and walked out alive.
The One who still receives repentant sinners.
Noah's story reminds us that even after the storm passes, the human heart still needs rescue.
The cross tells us where that rescue is found.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one question that may follow you long after these words disappear from your screen:
What is still lying uncovered inside your tent that you have never truly surrendered to Jesus?
Don't answer me if you don't want to.
Answer Him.
Then repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Confess where confession is needed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
And walk toward Christ instead of away from Him.
Because your most shameful chapter may explain where you have been...
but if you belong to Jesus, it does not get to decide where your story ends.
The tent may remember your shame, but the empty tomb declares that Jesus still writes endings sin never saw coming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES THE BIBLE NEED AN UPDATE? OR DOES THE MODERN WORLD NEED WHAT IT HAS BEEN TRYING TO REWRITE?
paragraphs:
DOES THE BIBLE NEED AN UPDATE? OR DOES THE MODERN WORLD NEED WHAT IT HAS BEEN TRYING TO REWRITE?
We update our phones, our laws, our language, our technology, and even our definitions of right and wrong. So here is the uncomfortable question: If the Bible was written thousands of years ago, why should anyone still allow it to speak with authority today?
Maybe you have heard it before.
“The Bible is outdated.”
“It was written for another culture.”
“People knew less back then.”
“Society has evolved.”
“Christianity needs to catch up.”
Perhaps you have even quietly wondered whether they have a point.
Because the world described in Scripture did not have smartphones buzzing beside beds at 2:00 in the morning.
Moses never had Instagram.
David never had to delete his search history.
Paul never received a notification telling him how many people liked his latest post.
Peter never sat beneath fluorescent lights while a doctor explained the results of a scan.
The woman at the well never had dating apps.
The prodigal son never had a credit score.
No biblical writer ever heard the words “artificial intelligence,” “social media algorithm,” or “virtual reality.”
So maybe the question sounds reasonable:
How can an ancient book possibly understand modern people?
But that question hides another question underneath it.
And the second question cuts much deeper.
Have human beings actually changed as much as our technology has?
Look around.
Our screens changed.
Our hearts didn't.
We still lie.
We still lust.
We still envy.
We still betray people we promised to love.
We still chase money believing one more number will finally make us feel secure.
We still crave approval.
We still fear rejection.
We still bury shame beneath achievement.
We still destroy relationships because pride refuses to say, “I was wrong.”
We still lie awake in expensive bedrooms wondering why success did not heal the emptiness.
We still smile for photographs while privately falling apart.
We still want to be known...
and simultaneously fear what would happen if somebody actually knew us.
Humanity has upgraded almost everything except the human heart.
And perhaps that is why Scripture can feel so disturbingly current.
Open the Bible expecting an ancient museum piece and something strange happens.
Eventually...
it starts reading you.
It finds the jealousy you renamed ambition.
The lust you renamed freedom.
The greed you renamed success.
The bitterness you renamed boundaries.
The pride you renamed self-respect.
The compromise you renamed being realistic.
The disobedience you renamed personal truth.
And suddenly the question changes.
Instead of asking,
“Does Scripture need updating?”
you begin wondering,
“What if Scripture keeps exposing the things every generation tries to rename?”
There is a line in Isaiah written centuries before Jesus walked the roads of Galilee:
יָבֵשׁ חָצִיר נָבֵל צִיץ וּדְבַר־אֱלֹהֵינוּ יָקוּם לְעוֹלָם
Yavesh chatsir, navel tsits; u-devar Eloheinu yaqum le'olam.
“The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God stands forever.”
—Isaiah 40:8
Notice the contrast.
Human things fade.
God's word stands.
Cultures rise.
Cultures fall.
Empires appear.
Empires disappear.
Philosophies become fashionable and then embarrassing.
Ideas celebrated by one generation are condemned by another.
Things society once called progress eventually become warnings in history books.
Yet Isaiah does not describe God's word desperately trying to survive cultural change.
He says it stands.
יָקוּם — yaqum.
It stands.

That does not mean every command in Scripture can be ripped from its covenant, literary, historical, and redemptive context and mechanically imposed on Christians today. The Bible itself contains different genres, covenants, historical situations, ceremonial laws, civil regulations for ancient Israel, wisdom literature, prophecy, poetry, apostolic instruction, and the unfolding story that reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Reading Scripture faithfully therefore requires interpretation.
Context matters.
Genre matters.
History matters.
Language matters.
The old covenant and new covenant matter.
And above everything, Christ matters.
Jesus Himself said:
“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets...”
He came not to abolish them, but to fulfill them.
—Matthew 5:17
That distinction matters enormously.
Christians are not called to pretend that every verse was written directly to twenty-first-century readers.
But neither are Christians permitted to pretend that a passage stops being true simply because twenty-first-century readers find it uncomfortable.
There is an enormous difference between correctly interpreting an ancient text...
and correcting God.
One asks,
“What did God mean?”
The other quietly asks,
“How can we make God mean what we already believe?”
And that temptation is not modern.
Jesus confronted it.

Religious people in His own day had traditions and interpretations that allowed them to maneuver around what God had commanded. Christ's response was devastating: they were effectively making the word of God void through the tradition they had handed down.
In other words, people were already trying to make revelation submit to human preference.
Different century.
Same heart.
And this is where the conversation becomes personal.
Because sometimes when we say,
“The Bible needs updating,”
what we really mean is,
“I found something in the Bible I don't want to surrender to.”

That is not always the reason someone struggles with Scripture. There are sincere intellectual questions about manuscripts, interpretation, difficult Old Testament passages, science, history, sexuality, suffering, judgment, slavery, women, violence, and apparent tensions within biblical texts. Christians should not mock those questions or hide from them.
Truth does not become stronger when believers are afraid of questions.
But intellectual questions and moral resistance are not always the same thing.
Sometimes we are investigating Scripture.
Sometimes Scripture is investigating us.
And we know the difference.
There are verses we do not merely misunderstand.
We understand them enough to know they are coming for something we love.
That relationship.
That habit.
That resentment.
That secret browser tab.
That dishonest business practice.
That unforgiveness.
That pride.
That identity we built without God.
That version of Christianity where Jesus can save us but never contradict us.
Then suddenly “interpretation” becomes very attractive.
Not because we discovered something new in Greek.
But because obedience became expensive.
Paul wrote something remarkable to Timothy:
πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος...
Pasa graphē theopneustos kai ōphelimos...
“Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable...”
—2 Timothy 3:16
One word should stop us.
θεόπνευστος — theopneustos.
God-breathed.
Paul continues by describing Scripture as profitable for teaching, correction, reproof, and training in righteousness.
Correction.
There is the word modern humanity struggles with.
Because correction assumes something about us that our culture often dislikes admitting:
We can be wrong.
Not merely uninformed.
Wrong.
I can sincerely believe something and still be wrong.
I can feel something intensely and still be wrong.
Millions of people can celebrate something and still be wrong.
A church tradition can become popular and still be wrong.
A preacher can become famous and still be wrong.
A Christian influencer can accumulate millions of followers and still be wrong.
And yes...
you and I can open Scripture already determined to make God agree with us.
That is why the Bible does not merely comfort.
It corrects.
And strangely enough...
that is mercy.
Imagine visiting a physician because something inside your body is killing you.
The doctor discovers the disease.
But instead of telling you, she smiles.
“You're perfect exactly as you are.”
You leave feeling affirmed.
Six months later you are dying.
Was that kindness?
Of course not.
Love tells the truth when the truth can save someone.
And Scripture's diagnosis of humanity is brutally consistent.
Our deepest problem is not insufficient technology.
It is sin.
We have rebelled against the God who made us.
And no software update can repair that.
No political revolution can remove it.
No educational degree can erase it.
No amount of money can purchase our innocence.
No self-help philosophy can resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
And Christianity's answer is not:
“Try harder.”
Christianity's answer has a name.
Jesus.
This is where the Bible becomes something infinitely greater than a collection of ancient moral instructions.
The Scriptures tell one enormous redemptive story.
Creation.
Rebellion.
Promise.
Covenant.
Sacrifice.
Prophecy.
A manger.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A returning King.
Humanity ran from God...
and God came looking for humanity.
Jesus Christ did not enter history merely to give civilization improved ethics.
He came for sinners.
He touched people respectable society avoided.
He ate with people religious society condemned.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He exposed sin.
He forgave the repentant.
He welcomed the broken.
And then He walked toward a Roman cross carrying something none of us could carry ourselves.
Our guilt.
The scandal of Christianity is not merely that Scripture calls sin “sin.”
The greater scandal is that the holy God offers mercy to sinners.
Think about that.
The liar can be forgiven.
The adulterer can be forgiven.
The addict can be forgiven.
The pornographer can be forgiven.
The proud can be forgiven.
The hypocrite can be forgiven.
The religious fraud can be forgiven.
The person who wasted decades can be forgiven.
The person reading this while carrying something nobody knows about can be forgiven.
Not because sin suddenly stopped mattering.
Because it mattered so much that Christ went to the cross.
Grace does not mean God updated His holiness.
Grace means Jesus paid for sinners.
That is why changing Scripture to make sin disappear would not make Christianity more compassionate.
It would make the cross increasingly unnecessary.
If humanity's fundamental problem can simply be redefined away, why Calvary?
Why blood?
Why sacrifice?
Why repentance?
Why forgiveness?
Why did Christ die?
But if Scripture is telling the truth...
the cross suddenly makes terrifying and beautiful sense.
We were worse than we wanted to admit.
And we were loved more than we dared imagine.
That is the Gospel.
Not God saying,
“You were right all along.”
God saying,
“You were lost. Come home.”
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe this stopped being an argument about whether an ancient book needs modernization several paragraphs ago.
Maybe something came to mind.
Something you have been defending.
Something you have been hiding.
Something you keep asking God to approve instead of asking Him to remove.
Maybe everybody around you says it is fine.
But when the noise disappears...
you know.
Because there is another way to “update” Scripture.
We don't need printing presses or committees.
We do it personally.
We skip the verses that confront us.
We quote promises without commands.
We want Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We want grace without repentance.
Heaven without holiness.
Forgiveness without confession.
Christianity without a cross.
We quietly create a customized Bible where God agrees with everything we already wanted.
But that god cannot save us.
Because we created him.
The living God is different.
He loves us enough to contradict us.
Paul wrote:
“Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind...”
—Romans 12:2
Read that direction carefully.
Scripture does not say:
Transform God's truth through the renewing of the culture.
It calls us to be transformed through the renewing of our minds.
That is the confrontation at the center of Christianity.
The Gospel does not arrive asking permission from every generation.
It arrives announcing a King.
Jesus Christ.
And every generation eventually faces the same question:
Will Jesus be reshaped into our image...
or will we surrender to His?
That does not mean Christians should refuse to learn.
Far from it.
Our understanding can need correction.
Our theology can need refinement.
Our translations can improve as scholarship examines manuscripts and languages.
Our cultural assumptions can distort interpretation.
Church traditions can become confused with biblical commands.
Christians have sometimes defended practices, prejudices, and systems by misusing Scripture.
We should be humble enough to admit it.
Jesus Himself condemned people who allowed human traditions to override God's command.
So yes...
our interpretations may need updating.
Our applications may need reconsideration.
Our traditions may need examination.
Our assumptions may need dismantling.
Our translations may need refinement.
Our hearts certainly need transformation.
But God's truth does not become false because another century arrived.
A compass does not become outdated because travelers prefer another direction.
And a lighthouse does not become hateful because sailors want the rocks to move.
The Bible does not need to know what TikTok is to understand pride.
It does not need Instagram to understand envy.
It does not need pornography websites to understand lust.
It does not need dating apps to understand sexual temptation.
It does not need cryptocurrency to understand greed.
It does not need artificial intelligence to understand humanity's desire to become like gods.
It does not need modern psychology vocabulary to understand shame, grief, fear, despair, guilt, temptation, reconciliation, hope, love, and forgiveness.
The technology changes.
The costume changes.
The vocabulary changes.
The human heart keeps showing up.
And Jesus keeps meeting it there.
So perhaps Scripture's age is not its weakness.

Perhaps its ability to survive empire after empire, culture after culture, criticism after criticism, while continuing to expose the same human heart is part of what makes the question so uncomfortable.
We keep announcing that humanity has outgrown the Bible...
while continuing to commit the sins it warned us about.
Wars remain.
Abuse remains.
Greed remains.
Exploitation remains.
Adultery remains.
Hatred remains.
Pride remains.
Loneliness remains.
Death remains.
And beneath our glowing screens, the ancient question still whispers:
What will a person gain by acquiring the world and losing his soul?
There are moments when Scripture feels old because it comes from another world.
And there are moments when Scripture feels frighteningly new because it describes the person staring at the page.
Maybe you.
Maybe me.
And this is where we must be careful.
The answer is not becoming a smug Christian who waves a Bible at everybody else's sins.
Jesus had some of His strongest words for religious hypocrisy.
Before Scripture becomes the sword we point across the room, it must become the mirror we are willing to stand before.
So ask yourself something harder than whether society needs Scripture.
Ask:
Where have I been trying to update God?
Where have I demanded permission where Christ asks surrender?
Where have I used “times have changed” to protect something I don't want Jesus touching?
Where have I confused grace with permission?
Where have I quoted Scripture publicly while ignoring it privately?
And if something inside you is answering...
don't run.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The Gospel invitation is still open.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave.
You do not need to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
You come because you cannot clean yourself.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the unbelief.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are exhausted from pretending to be.
But come honestly.
Jesus does not merely rewrite reputations.
He resurrects people.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness light.
Not by rewriting God's holiness.
He rewrites the sinner.
That difference is everything.
If this exposed something you have been wrestling with, don't manufacture a religious answer.
Be honest.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance is not the end of a person's story.
And if this made you uncomfortable...
maybe don't run from that discomfort yet.
Come back when the emotions settle.
Read the passages yourself.
Open your Bible.
Check the context.
Test what has been written here against Scripture.
Christian faith should never depend upon blindly believing a Facebook article.
Go to the Word.
And if someone you love has been saying, “The Bible is outdated,” don't send this to them as a weapon.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, think more deeply about Christ, repent, heal, or grow in faith, following and supporting this ministry helps us keep putting biblical truth in front of people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something on their screen.
Salvation cannot be purchased. God's grace is not for sale.
Share because someone else needs the Gospel.
Support because biblical discipleship requires people willing to carry it forward.
But before you leave, remember the question we started with.
Does Scripture need an update for the modern world?
Perhaps we have been asking the wrong question.
Because the Bible never promised to become fashionable enough for every generation to approve it.
It claims something far more unsettling.
That generations fade.
That human glory fades.
That cultures change.
That we change.
But God's Word stands.

And the Word ultimately points beyond itself to Jesus Christ—the crucified and risen Savior who still calls sinners to repent, still receives the broken, still forgives the guilty, still transforms lives, and still turns stories of shame into testimonies of grace.
So maybe the ancient book sitting unopened on the shelf is not waiting for modern humanity to correct it.
Maybe it has been waiting for us to become quiet enough to hear it.
And maybe the sentence we wanted God to rewrite...
was the very sentence He intended to use to rewrite us.
The world keeps asking God to update His Word. Jesus keeps offering to transform our hearts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Stephen Wasn’t One of the Twelve. Heaven Still Knew His Name.
paragraphs: Stephen Wasn’t One of the Twelve. Heaven Still Knew His Name.

He had no place among the Twelve, no Gospel bearing his name, and no earthly throne. He was chosen for an overlooked ministry need. Then Scripture describes him with words many Christians spend their entire lives longing to embody: full of faith, full of the Holy Spirit, full of grace, and full of power.
There is something almost unsettling about Stephen.
Because Stephen destroys one of the quiet lies many of us have believed about serving God.
The lie says you have to be important before God can use you.
You need the title.
The platform.
The microphone.
The following.
The position.
The recognition.
You need somebody important to notice you before your life can become important to the Kingdom.
Then Stephen walks into Acts.
Not as Peter.
Not as John.
Not as one of the Twelve.
Not as someone Scripture introduces with an impressive résumé.
Stephen appears in the middle of a church problem.
People were being overlooked.
Widows needed care.

The rapidly growing church in Jerusalem had encountered tension because the Hellenistic Jewish believers complained that their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. The Twelve called the disciples together and said that men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and wisdom, should be selected for this responsibility (Acts 6:1–4).
And among those selected was a man named Stephen.
Read Luke's description carefully.
Acts 6:5 describes him in Greek as:
Στέφανον, ἄνδρα πλήρη πίστεως καὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου
Stephanon, andra plērē pisteōs kai pneumatos hagiou.
Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit.
Not famous.
Full.
That difference may expose something in us.
We spend enormous amounts of energy trying to become visible.
God keeps looking for people willing to become full.
Full of faith when nobody applauds.
Full of the Holy Spirit when nobody knows your name.
Faithful when the assignment looks ordinary.
Faithful when your obedience does not photograph well.
Faithful when what God has put in front of you feels smaller than what you imagined for yourself.
And then Acts says something even more astonishing.

“Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people” in the wording familiar to readers of the King James tradition. In a number of modern translations following their underlying Greek textual tradition, Acts 6:8 reads “full of grace and power.”
The Greek wording represented there is:
Στέφανος δὲ πλήρης χάριτος καὶ δυνάμεως
Stephanos de plērēs charitos kai dynameōs.
Stephen was full of grace and power.
Charis.
Grace.
Dynamis.
Power.
Grace and power living in the same man.
That matters.
Because Christians sometimes imagine spiritual power as loudness.
Aggression.
Dominance.
A personality that overwhelms everyone else in the room.
But Stephen's power was surrounded by grace.
And his grace was not weakness.
This was a man so surrendered to Christ that when opposition came, he did not suddenly need a different character.
What was inside him simply came out.
Maybe that is the question we are afraid to ask.
What comes out of you when life starts throwing stones?
Not literal stones, perhaps.
A betrayal.
A diagnosis.
A rejection.
A marriage unraveling behind closed doors.
A child walking away from God.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
A ministry wound nobody knows about.
A temptation you thought you had defeated.
A financial collapse.
A church disappointment.
A private addiction.
A season where you still worship on Sunday while quietly wondering on Monday whether God has forgotten where you live.
What comes out when you are hit?
Because pressure does not merely hurt.
Pressure reveals.
Stephen had something inside him before the stones ever came.
And eventually everyone would see it.
Opposition arose against him. Men disputed with him, but Acts says they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking (Acts 6:9–10).
So the conflict escalated.
Accusations came.
Witnesses were brought forward.
Stephen was dragged before the council.
And there he stood.
A servant who had been selected in connection with caring for an overlooked need in the church was suddenly standing before powerful religious authorities.
No escape route.
No political influence.
No army.
No prestigious title capable of rescuing him.
But he had something his enemies could not manufacture.
The presence of God.
Acts 6:15 says those sitting in the council looked at Stephen and saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
Think about that.
His circumstances were becoming darker.
His face was reflecting something brighter.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what it feels like for life to become darker.
You have prayed.
You have waited.
You have tried to remain faithful.
But somewhere underneath the worship songs, Bible verses, church attendance, Christian posts, and “I'm okay” responses is a tired soul whispering:
“Jesus... where are You?”
Stephen's story does not insult that question with a cheap answer.
Because God did not keep Stephen from the courtroom.
God did not stop every accusation.
God did not make every enemy disappear.
And ultimately, God did not prevent the stones from being thrown.
Christianity does not promise that following Jesus will make you untouchable.
It promises something infinitely deeper.
You can belong completely to Christ even when obedience costs you everything.
Stephen began speaking.
And what followed in Acts 7 was not a speech about Stephen.
That may be one of the most beautiful things about him.
He was the one on trial...
but he talked about God.

He walked his hearers through Israel's history—Abraham, Joseph, Moses, the wilderness, the tabernacle, the temple—and confronted the pattern of resisting God's messengers and ultimately rejecting the Righteous One.
Stephen understood something modern Christianity desperately needs to remember.
The Gospel is not ultimately about making us the hero of our story.
Jesus is the Hero.
We are not saved because we discovered hidden greatness inside ourselves.
We are saved because the holy Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus lived without sin.
Jesus went willingly to the cross.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
Jesus reigns.
And sinners who repent and trust in Him receive what they could never purchase with morality, religion, influence, money, achievement, or reputation:
forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Mercy.
New life.
Grace.
That is why Stephen's story is so much bigger than courage.
Stephen was not merely a brave man facing death.
He was a redeemed man beholding Christ.
When his hearers became enraged, Acts gives us another description.
ὑπάρχων πλήρης πνεύματος ἁγίου
hyparchōn plērēs pneumatos hagiou.
Being full of the Holy Spirit.
There it is again.
Full.
Acts 7:55 says Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
Then Stephen said he could see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God's right hand.
They rushed him.
Dragged him outside the city.
And began throwing stones.
Stop there for a moment.
Do not sanitize this because you already know the ending.
Stones are heavy.
Stones tear skin.
Stones break bone.
Stephen was not reading Acts 7 from a comfortable chair.
He was living it.
One stone.
Then another.
Then another.
The voices.
The rage.
The pain.
The ground beneath him.
And somewhere nearby stood a young man named Saul.
Acts tells us that the witnesses laid their garments at Saul's feet, and Acts 8:1 says Saul approved of Stephen's death.
Imagine freezing that scene.
Stephen is dying.
Saul is watching.
If you knew nothing beyond that moment, who would you think was winning?
The killers?
The persecutor?
The mob?
Death?
This is where the Gospel rewrites everything.
Because Stephen looked beyond the stones.
And he prayed:
Κύριε Ἰησοῦ, δέξαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου.
Kyrie Iēsou, dexai to pneuma mou.
“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
And then...
something happened that should break the heart of every Christian who has ever fantasized about revenge.
Stephen fell to his knees.
His enemies were killing him.
And his final recorded concern was not vengeance.
He cried out:
Κύριε, μὴ στήσῃς αὐτοῖς ταύτην τὴν ἁμαρτίαν.
Kyrie, mē stēsēs autois tautēn tēn hamartian.
“Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”
Then he died.
Does that prayer sound familiar?
It should.
At the cross, Jesus prayed concerning His executioners, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34).
Stephen had spent so much of himself belonging to Jesus that, when death squeezed him, something resembling Jesus came out.
That may be one of the most frighteningly beautiful tests of discipleship.
Not, “How Christian do I look when everything is going well?”
But:
“When I am wounded, do I still look like Jesus?”
When they misunderstand you...
Jesus.
When they betray you...
Jesus.
When someone says the thing you will never forget...
Jesus.
When anger feels justified...
Jesus.
When revenge would taste satisfying...
Jesus.
Not because abuse should be excused.
Not because justice is evil.
Not because boundaries are unspiritual.
Not because wrongdoing should be hidden.
But because the Gospel can free a human heart from allowing another person's sin to become its master.
Stephen's enemies could crush his body.
They could not make hatred own his soul.
And perhaps there is someone you have been carrying for years.
Not physically.
Inside you.
Their voice.
Their betrayal.
Their face.
What they did.
What they took.
What they never apologized for.
Maybe you have replayed imaginary conversations a thousand times.
Maybe they moved on while you remained emotionally trapped at the scene of the wound.
Stephen's story does not tell you the wound was insignificant.
The stones were real.
It tells you Jesus can become greater than the stones.
Forgiveness does not call evil good.
Forgiveness places judgment where it ultimately belongs—with God—and refuses to let hatred become the permanent landlord of the heart.
And here is where Stephen's story becomes even more astonishing.
The man dying on the ground could not see everything God would do after his death.

Acts 8 says severe persecution broke out and believers were scattered through Judea and Samaria. Yet those scattered believers went about proclaiming the word. Later, Acts 11 specifically looks back to the persecution connected with Stephen and tells us that scattered believers traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, where the Gospel continued spreading and people turned to the Lord.
The enemy scattered Christians.
God scattered witnesses.
What looked like destruction became dispersion.
What looked like an ending became movement.
And Saul?
The young man standing there approving Stephen's death would not remain Saul the persecutor forever.
Jesus Christ would confront him.
The persecutor would become a preacher of the Christ he had opposed.
The man associated with chains would one day wear chains for Jesus.
The man who participated in persecuting believers would suffer for the name he once tried to silence.
Grace rewrote his story too.
Do not go beyond what Scripture actually says here. The Bible does not tell us that Stephen's prayer directly caused Saul's conversion. We do not need to invent what God chose not to reveal.
The truth Scripture does give us is powerful enough.
Saul was there.
Stephen prayed for his killers.
Stephen died confessing Jesus.
And the same book of Acts later shows Jesus stopping Saul on the road to Damascus and completely redirecting his life.
That is scandalous grace.
The kind of grace that makes heaven's mathematics incomprehensible to human pride.
The murderer can repent.
The religious hypocrite can repent.
The addict can repent.
The sexually broken can repent.
The bitter Christian can repent.
The prodigal can come home.
The person who has spent years pretending can finally stop pretending.
And you can repent too.
Maybe the most dangerous way to read Stephen's story is to admire Stephen without surrendering to Stephen's Lord.
You can say, “What incredible faith.”
You can share a quote.
You can feel goosebumps.
And remain unchanged.
But Stephen did not die so Christians centuries later could admire his courage.
His testimony points beyond himself.
To Jesus.
The risen Christ.
The reigning Christ.
The Christ Stephen saw at God's right hand.
The Christ to whom Stephen entrusted his spirit.
The Christ whose mercy Stephen reflected toward the people killing him.
So perhaps the question is no longer whether Stephen was one of the Twelve.
He wasn't.
The question is whether we have accidentally convinced ourselves that only “important” Christians can live lives that shake eternity.
Stephen had no apostolic seat among the Twelve.
Yet Scripture says he was full of faith and the Holy Spirit.
Full of grace and power.
Full of the Holy Spirit as death approached.
Maybe you will never preach to thousands.
Maybe your name will never appear on a conference banner.
Maybe no one will recognize the sacrifices you make.
Maybe your greatest ministry will happen around a kitchen table.
Beside a hospital bed.
Inside a struggling marriage.
During a midnight conversation with a suicidal friend.
While raising children who may not understand your prayers until decades later.
While caring for someone everybody else forgot.
While opening Scripture with one broken person.
While quietly refusing the sin everybody around you has normalized.
Maybe heaven's definition of significance has always been different from ours.
Stephen reminds us that you do not need to be famous to be full.
You do not need a title to be surrendered.
You do not need applause to be faithful.
You do not need millions of followers to follow Jesus well.
And you do not need a spotless past before grace can begin rewriting your future.
That is Gospel Warrior's heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes shame and writes redemption.
He takes rebellion and writes repentance.
He takes wounds and begins writing healing.
He takes sinners and writes “forgiven” over those who come to Him in faith.
He takes persecutors like Saul and makes them proclaimers.
He takes ordinary servants like Stephen and gives their faithfulness a witness that still speaks almost two thousand years later.
And maybe...
right now...
He is rewriting you.
Talk to Jesus.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary required.
Confess the sin.
Name the bitterness.
Admit the exhaustion.
Tell Him where you compromised.
Tell Him who you still hate.
Tell Him what you cannot fix.
Tell Him you need mercy.
Repent and turn toward Christ.
Grace is not permission to remain who we were.
Grace brings us to the Savior who forgives and transforms.
Or tell your testimony.
Someone reading the same comments may need to discover that they are not the only person Jesus is rebuilding.
And think of one person who needs Stephen's story tonight.
Not fifty people.
One.
The person whose faith feels insignificant.
The friend who thinks God cannot use them because they have no title.
The believer crushed by betrayal.
The prodigal who thinks they have gone too far.
The person carrying bitterness like a stone inside their chest.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty, but because someone in your circle may desperately need the truth you almost scrolled past.
Sharing the Gospel costs only a moment, but God can use a moment far beyond what you can see.
There may come a night when you become the one under pressure.
When you need to remember:
Stephen did not become full of the Spirit when the stones started falling.
He had been walking with God before the crisis arrived.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, confronting your complacency, helping you return to Scripture, or putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who desperately need it, consider helping this ministry continue and expand.
Not from guilt.
It does not.
Not because anyone can buy a blessing.
They cannot.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces generosity to your local church, care for your family, mercy toward the needy, or whatever faithful stewardship God has placed before you.
It does not.
Scripture says giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So let this be voluntary worship, never spiritual pressure.
Pray.
Those acts matter too.
Because support is not merely about funding content.
It is about helping truth travel.

Acts shows believers scattered after Stephen's death going everywhere proclaiming the word. The persecution associated with Stephen eventually sent believers as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, where people heard about the Lord Jesus and believed.
They were scattered.
But the Gospel was not silenced.
Stephen was buried.
But his witness was not buried with him.
The stones stopped falling.
But his testimony kept moving.
Nearly two thousand years later...
you just heard it.
And now you have a decision about what happens to it next.
Keep it.
Or carry it.
But above everything else...
follow Christ.
Because someday the titles disappear.
The follower counts disappear.
The applause disappears.
The money stays behind.
The platforms vanish.
And what will matter is not whether earth knew our name...
but whether we belonged to Jesus.
Stephen wasn't one of the Twelve.
He did not need to be.
He was full.
Full of faith.
Full of grace.
Full of power.
Full of the Holy Spirit.
And when the world emptied its hatred onto him, his dying lips were still full of Jesus.
When the stones revealed what Stephen was full of, they found Christ there. What will pressure reveal in us?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIANS REALLY EAT ANYTHING—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT FOOD?
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS REALLY EAT ANYTHING—OR HAVE WE MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS ABOUT FOOD?

Jesus spoke about what defiles a person. Peter saw a sheet descend from heaven. Paul said nothing is unclean in itself. Yet Leviticus still sits in our Bible, calling some animals clean and others unclean. So what actually changed—and what didn't?
There is a strange kind of tension that can happen at a Christian dinner table.
Someone bows his head and thanks God for the meal.
Someone else looks at what is on the plate and quietly wonders...
Can a Christian actually eat that?
Then come the questions.
Didn't God forbid certain animals?
Didn't Jesus say all foods were clean?
Didn't Peter refuse to eat unclean animals even after Christ's resurrection?
What about pork?
Shellfish?
Blood?
Food sacrificed to idols?
Were the food laws abolished, fulfilled, transformed, or simply ignored by modern Christians?
And beneath all those questions is a much deeper one.
When I open my Bible, am I willing to let Scripture correct me—even when it corrects something I have believed for years?
Because this isn't really an argument about bacon.
It is an argument about how we read the Bible.
And somewhere between Leviticus and the dinner table, Christians have sometimes made two opposite mistakes.
One side can turn dietary observance into a measuring stick for righteousness.
The other can speak as though the Old Testament was God's embarrassing first draft.
Both miss something beautiful.
Because Jesus did not come to rescue us from a defective God.
The God who spoke through Moses is the God revealed perfectly in Christ.
So we have to begin where Scripture begins.
God really did give Israel food laws.
Not imaginary laws.
Not suggestions.
Not merely ancient nutrition advice.
Actual covenant commands.
Leviticus 11 distinguishes between animals Israel could eat and animals Israel could not eat. Near the chapter's conclusion, the Hebrew says:
לְהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הַטָּמֵא וּבֵין הַטָּהֹר
lehavdil bein hattame uvein hattahor
"...to distinguish between the unclean and the clean..."
The two important Hebrew ideas are טָמֵא — tame, "unclean," and טָהוֹר — tahor, "clean."
Leviticus 11:47 goes on to distinguish "between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten."
We should not erase that.
God gave those distinctions to Israel within the Mosaic covenant.
They were real.
They mattered.
They taught God's covenant people that holiness reached into ordinary life.
Their worship mattered.
Their bodies mattered.
Their tables mattered.
What they touched mattered.
What they ate mattered.
God was teaching a people rescued from slavery that belonging to Him was not something confined to a religious ceremony.
Holiness followed them home.
It entered their kitchens.
It sat beside them at dinner.
And maybe that is the first conviction modern Christians need to recover.
We can become so eager to defend Christian liberty that we forget liberty was never permission to stop caring about holiness.
But then Jesus comes.
And something enormous happens.
In Mark 7, Jesus is confronting controversy surrounding ritual defilement. His focus is not a casual debate over someone's favorite meal. He drives the discussion toward the human heart.
The surviving Greek text contains this striking phrase:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
katharizōn panta ta brōmata
Literally, the wording carries the sense of "cleansing all foods."

That is why many modern translations render Mark 7:19 along the lines of Jesus declaring all foods clean. The immediate context is Jesus explaining that what enters a person from outside does not penetrate the heart and therefore is not what morally defiles the person.
Then Jesus turns the knife toward the place we would rather avoid.
The heart.
Because what comes from within?
Sexual immorality.
Theft.
Murder.
Adultery.
Greed.
Wickedness.
Deceit.
Sensuality.
Envy.
Slander.
Pride.
Foolishness.
Suddenly the person obsessing over another believer's plate has nowhere to hide.
You can inspect every ingredient...
and still have a filthy heart.
You can refuse pork while consuming pornography.
You can inspect food labels while feeding hatred.
You can meticulously avoid shellfish while devouring another person's reputation through gossip.
You can have a religiously impressive kitchen and an unrepentant soul.
And Jesus keeps dragging the conversation back to the place religious people often desperately try to escape.
The heart.
That does not mean God's earlier commands were evil.
It means those commands belonged within a covenantal story that was moving toward Christ.
And then we arrive at Peter.
Acts 10.
Peter is hungry.
He falls into a trance.
Something resembling a great sheet descends containing various animals.
A voice tells him to rise, kill, and eat.
Peter recoils.
He says he has never eaten anything common or unclean.
That detail matters.
This is after Jesus' resurrection.
Peter's instincts had not simply disappeared overnight.
But then comes the voice:
Ἃ ὁ θεὸς ἐκαθάρισεν σὺ μὴ κοίνου.
Ha ho Theos ekatharisen, sy mē koinou.
"What God has cleansed, you must not call common."
But here we need to be careful.
Acts itself tells us that Peter's vision is profoundly about people, particularly the inclusion of Gentiles.
Peter later explains the lesson: God showed him that he should not call any person common or unclean.
So it would be careless to reduce Acts 10 to: "Peter learned he could finally eat pork."
The vision is much bigger than Peter's lunch.
Cornelius is coming.
The Gentiles are coming.
People once regarded as outside are being brought near through Christ.
God is dismantling the barriers that would prevent Jewish believers from receiving Gentile believers as members of God's redeemed people.
The sheet is not merely about a menu.
It is about a mission.
It is about the Gospel crossing boundaries.
It is about grace walking through a Gentile doorway.
And that becomes even clearer in Acts 15.
A crisis erupts in the early Church.
Gentiles are believing in Jesus.
So the explosive question becomes:
Must these Gentile believers effectively come under the Mosaic covenant in order to belong to God's people?
The apostles gather.
They debate.
They listen.
They search what God is doing.
And the resulting apostolic letter does something incredibly important.
It does not impose the whole Mosaic law upon Gentile converts.

Acts 15:28–29 says that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and the apostles not to place a greater burden upon them beyond several requirements: abstaining from things sacrificed to idols, blood, what had been strangled, and sexual immorality.
Whatever debates Christians may have about every detail of those instructions, one fact is difficult to escape:
The apostles had the perfect opportunity to tell Gentile believers, "You must now observe the complete Levitical dietary code."
They did not do that.
And then Paul becomes even more explicit.
Romans 14 deals with believers whose consciences differed over food and sacred days.
And listen carefully to Paul's Greek:
οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ ὅτι οὐδὲν κοινὸν δι’ ἑαυτοῦ
Oida kai pepeismai en Kyriō Iēsou hoti ouden koinon di' heautou.
"I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself..."
Paul does not say this hesitantly.
He anchors his conviction "in the Lord Jesus."
Yet he immediately protects the conscience of the believer who considers something unclean.
That changes the atmosphere completely.
Christian freedom is real.
But Christian freedom is not selfish.
Paul will not allow the strict believer to condemn the free believer.
And he will not allow the free believer to despise the strict believer.
Read that again.
Because churches have been wounded over things smaller than dinner.
One Christian says, "I don't eat pork because I believe abstaining honors God."
Another says, "I receive it with thanksgiving because I believe I am free in Christ."
Paul's instinct is not:
"Excellent. Destroy each other."
It is almost the opposite.
Stop despising one another.
Stop passing judgment over disputable matters.
Walk in love.
Do not destroy your brother over food.
Because the kingdom of God is bigger than your plate.
This is where Christian maturity becomes painfully practical.
You may possess freedom...
and still choose restraint because you love someone.
You may possess a conviction...
and still refuse to turn that conviction into a throne from which you judge everyone else.
That is Gospel maturity.
And Paul does not stop there.
Writing to Timothy, he warns about people who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods God created to be received with thanksgiving.
Then comes another remarkable Greek statement:
ὅτι πᾶν κτίσμα θεοῦ καλόν, καὶ οὐδὲν ἀπόβλητον μετὰ εὐχαριστίας λαμβανόμενον
hoti pan ktisma Theou kalon, kai ouden apoblēton meta eucharistias lambanomenon
"For every creation of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when received with thanksgiving."
And now the biblical trajectory becomes difficult to miss.
Leviticus genuinely distinguishes clean and unclean animals for Israel.
Jesus redirects the question of defilement toward the heart and Mark records the striking language concerning the cleansing of foods.
Peter's vision uses clean/unclean categories while God prepares him to welcome Gentiles.
The Jerusalem Council refuses to place the full Mosaic yoke upon Gentile converts.
Paul says nothing is unclean in itself.
Paul tells Timothy that God's creation may be received with thanksgiving.
And Colossians tells believers not to allow others to sit in judgment over them regarding food, drink, festivals, new moons, or Sabbaths.
So...
Can Christians eat anything?

In terms of the Levitical clean-versus-unclean animal classifications as covenant obligations, the New Testament does not place Gentile Christians under Israel's complete dietary code as a requirement for belonging to God.
But that does not mean the Christian position is simply:
"Eat anything. Nothing matters."
Because Paul gives us a far more demanding principle.
"Whether you eat or drink...do all to the glory of God."
Do you see what happened?
The question changed.
Not merely:
"Am I technically allowed to eat this?"
But:
"Can I glorify Jesus in this?"
That is harder.
Because legalism loves minimum requirements.
Love asks deeper questions.
Is this wise for my body?
Am I enslaved by appetite?
Am I eating with gratitude?
Am I knowingly participating in idolatry?
Am I violating my conscience?
Am I wounding someone else's conscience merely to prove that I am free?
Is food controlling me?
Am I turning my personal conviction into a righteousness test God never commanded for the Church?
Am I judging someone Christ has received?
Those questions reach far beyond pork.
They reach into gluttony.
Addiction.
Vanity.
Self-control.
Hospitality.
Poverty.
Gratitude.
Fellowship.
Conscience.
Love.
And worship.
Because Christianity was never supposed to create people who obsess over religious boundaries while ignoring the condition of their souls.
Imagine standing before Jesus saying:
"Lord, I never ate the wrong animal."
But you never forgave your brother.
You hated your neighbor.
You secretly fed lust.
You worshiped money.
You crushed weaker believers with your pride.
You knew biblical terminology but never surrendered your heart.
That is precisely why Jesus' words in Mark 7 cut so deeply.
The most dangerous thing on your table may not be what is on your plate.
It may be what is sitting inside your heart.
And maybe this debate has become personal for you.
Maybe you grew up being told that eating certain foods could separate you from God.
Maybe you were taught that Christians who eat pork are disobedient.
Maybe you came from the opposite direction and were taught to mock believers who still abstain.
Maybe you've spent years frightened that one mistake could make you spiritually unclean.
Hear the Gospel.
Your justification before God does not come from your menu.
It comes through Jesus Christ.
You cannot diet your way into forgiveness.
You cannot cleanse your conscience by avoiding enough ingredients.
You cannot earn the cross.
Jesus did not bleed because your dietary discipline was almost sufficient.
He bled because it never could be.
Sin goes deeper than the stomach.
It reaches the heart.
And therefore salvation had to go deeper too.
Jesus carried sin.
Jesus bore judgment.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Jesus welcomes sinners who repent and trust Him.
And when He saves us, He does not merely hand us permission slips.
He gives us Himself.
That means Christian liberty should never make us arrogant.
And personal conviction should never make us self-righteous.
If you abstain from certain foods as a personal act of conscience before God, you do not need to be mocked.
Honor Christ.
Give thanks.
Remain humble.
If you eat foods another Christian abstains from, you do not need to feel spiritually inferior merely because another believer's conscience differs.
Honor Christ.
Give thanks.
Remain humble.
But neither person gets to replace Jesus with a plate.
The stricter Christian is not saved by abstinence.
The freer Christian is not spiritually mature merely because he exercises liberty.
Christ is the center.
And perhaps that is what this entire controversy has been trying to expose.
We humans desperately want something measurable.
Something visible.
Something we can point toward and say:
"See? I am one of the faithful ones."
But Jesus keeps pointing toward the heart.
Pride is harder to photograph than pork.
Bitterness has no nutrition label.
Lust doesn't appear on an ingredient list.
Greed isn't printed beside the calories.
Unforgiveness has no warning sticker.
Self-righteousness can sit at a perfectly biblical-looking table.
And still be starving for grace.
That is the scandal.
The person eating the "right" food can still desperately need Jesus.
The person eating the "wrong" food can still desperately need Jesus.
The religious person needs Jesus.
The rebellious person needs Jesus.
The disciplined need Jesus.
The addicted need Jesus.
The person who has memorized Leviticus needs Jesus.
The person who has never opened Leviticus needs Jesus.
All roads eventually lead us to the same humiliating and beautiful confession:
I cannot save myself.
And that is where scandal becomes grace.
Because Jesus does not merely rewrite your menu.
Jesus rewrites you.
He takes people obsessed with external purity and teaches them purity of heart.
He takes people abusing freedom and teaches them love.
He takes frightened consciences and teaches them grace.
He takes proud consciences and teaches them humility.
He takes divided tables and creates a family.
So before your next argument about food...
look across the table.
That believer belongs to Someone.
If Christ received them, be very careful before making food the test by which you reject them.
Be honest before Jesus.
Not to start another war. Tell us what Scripture taught you, what you once believed, what changed, or where you are still struggling.
Someone reading your testimony may realize they are not alone.
Come back to it with your Bible open.
Read Leviticus 11.
Read Mark 7.
Read Acts 10.
Read Acts 15.
Read Romans 14.
Read 1 Corinthians 8–10.
Read Colossians 2.
Read 1 Timothy 4.
Don't build your theology from a meme.
Don't build it from one isolated verse.
And don't build it from this article alone.
Go back to the Word.

One share may put biblical truth in front of a frightened believer, a confused seeker, a legalistic Christian, a person wounded by religion, or even someone who has never understood what Jesus actually came to do.
That share costs you almost nothing.
But God may use truth placed in someone's path in ways you will never see.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow deeper in Jesus Christ, consider doing something more than reading and leaving.
Stay with us. Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen—to follow too.

We want this ministry to keep producing Scripture-centered teaching, conviction, encouragement, Gospel truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment that continually points people away from religious performance and toward Jesus Christ.
Supporting Gospel ministry financially can be a genuine act of generosity and stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and for God's glory.
But if you have been praying about where part of your voluntary giving and ministry support can help spread biblical teaching, you can choose to stand with Gospel Warrior.
It is the mission.
More Scripture.
More Gospel.
More discipleship.
More wounded people reminded that Christ still receives repentant sinners.
More confused believers driven back into their Bibles.
More people discovering that Christianity is not about decorating an old life with religion.
It is about being made new in Jesus Christ.
And whether you support financially or cannot give anything at all, you can still help.
Pray.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Because ministry was never supposed to terminate with the person who received the truth.
Truth travels.
Grace travels.
Testimony travels.
The Gospel travels.
And maybe tonight the question you thought was about food has uncovered something far more important.
You came asking:
"What am I allowed to eat?"
But Jesus may be asking:
"What has been eating your heart?"
Pride?
Fear?
Legalism?
Shame?
Religious superiority?
Secret sin?
A desperate attempt to make yourself clean enough for God?
Bring it to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive grace.
Then get up and walk with Him.
Because the greatest miracle at the Christian table is not that certain foods can be eaten.
It is that sinners who had no right to sit at the King's table have been invited near through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And when grace finally reaches the heart, you discover that the most important thing Jesus wanted to cleanse was never your plate—it was you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE DID EVERYTHING “RIGHT”—AND STILL WALKED AWAY FROM JESUS
paragraphs: HE DID EVERYTHING “RIGHT”—AND STILL WALKED AWAY FROM JESUS
Understanding the Rich Young Ruler — Why Being a “Good Person” Wasn’t Enough, and Why His Most Dangerous Possession Wasn’t the Money in His Hands but the Throne in His Heart
Imagine meeting the kind of man most parents would have wanted their daughter to marry.
Young.
Successful.
Respected.
Religious.
Morally disciplined.
Financially secure.
And apparently serious about God.
He wasn't stumbling toward Jesus drunk.
He wasn't being dragged out of some scandal.
He wasn't publicly exposed as an adulterer, thief, murderer, or fraud.
He came looking for eternal life.
And according to Mark's account, he came running.
Then he knelt.
Think about that.
A man with status lowered himself publicly before a wandering Galilean teacher and asked the question underneath every human life:
“Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
It sounds like the beginning of a beautiful conversion story.
But it becomes one of the most haunting encounters in the Gospels.
Because this man came running to Jesus...
and eventually walked away from Him.
Not because Jesus rejected him.
Not because his past was too dirty.
Not because grace was unavailable.
He walked away because Jesus touched the one thing he did not want Jesus to touch.
And before you decide this story is about somebody with a larger bank account than yours, stay with it.
Because the rich young ruler may be much closer to your mirror than you think.

Matthew 19, Mark 10, and Luke 18 preserve this encounter from complementary perspectives. Matthew identifies the man as young. Luke calls him a ruler. All three accounts tell us he possessed great wealth.
But Mark gives us a detail that makes the entire scene almost unbearable.
After the man speaks about his obedience, Mark 10:21 says:
“Jesus, looking at him, loved him.”
The Greek is devastatingly beautiful:
ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν
emblepsas autō ho Iēsous ēgapēsen auton.
Jesus looked intently at him...
and loved him.
Do not miss that.
What Jesus says next is not cruelty.
It comes from love.
The command that wounds him comes from the Christ who loves him.
Jesus is not trying to humiliate the man.
He is trying to liberate him.
And sometimes the love of Jesus feels like surgery before it feels like healing.
The man had called Him “Good Teacher.”
Jesus immediately pressed the word “good.”
“Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.”
Jesus was not confessing sinfulness. The question forces the man to think more deeply about goodness—and about the identity of the One standing before him.
You are asking about eternal life.
You are calling Me good.
Do you understand what goodness actually is?
Do you understand whom you are speaking to?
The ruler's question contains the assumption that has haunted religious humanity for centuries:
What must I do?
There it is.
Give me the requirement.
Show me the standard.
Tell me the achievement.
Let me accomplish whatever remains.
Because that is how successful people often understand life.
Do enough.
Work enough.
Achieve enough.
Behave enough.
And eventually you earn the thing you want.
But eternal life is not another trophy for the shelf.
It cannot be purchased by morality.
It cannot be negotiated through religious achievement.
It cannot be earned by accumulating enough “good person” points.
Jesus points him toward the commandments.
Do not murder.
Do not commit adultery.
Do not steal.
Do not bear false witness.
Honor your father and mother.
Matthew also records Jesus saying, “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
And the young man essentially answers:
I have done that.
In Mark's wording:
“Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.”
Maybe you recognize something of yourself here.
“I don't cheat on my spouse.”
“I don't steal.”
“I try to help people.”
“I provide for my family.”
“I go to church.”
“I pray.”
“I believe in God.”
“I've never done anything that terrible.”
“I am basically a good person.”
And perhaps compared with another human being, you are.
That is precisely the problem with human comparison.
We keep finding someone worse than ourselves and using that person as evidence that we must be okay.
But your neighbor is not the standard of God's holiness.
Neither is the criminal on television.
Neither is the hypocrite at church.
Neither is your abusive ex.
Neither is the corrupt politician.
Neither is the person whose secret became public while yours remained hidden.
Scripture says, “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
The scandal of the Gospel begins here:
You do not merely need improvement.
You need rescue.
You do not merely need better habits.
You need reconciliation with God.
You do not simply need inspiration.
You need a Savior.
And the Savior was standing directly in front of this man.
Then Jesus placed His finger on the hidden throne.
“One thing you lack.”
Luke records the same terrifying diagnosis.
In Greek:
Ἔτι ἕν σοι λείπει
Eti hen soi leipei.
“One thing is still lacking for you.”
One thing.
Imagine hearing Jesus say that about your life.
Not your pastor.
Not your spouse.
Not the person criticizing you online.
Jesus.
You have built the reputation.
Protected the image.
Practiced morality.
Maintained respectability.
Maybe even learned Christian vocabulary.
But Christ sees underneath all of it.
And He knows exactly what you cannot imagine surrendering.
Jesus tells the ruler to sell what he possesses, give to the poor, have treasure in heaven, and then:
δεῦρο ἀκολούθει μοι
deuro akolouthei moi.
“Come, follow Me.”
That is the center of the encounter.
Not merely:
Sell.
Not merely:
Give.
But:
Follow Me.

Jesus was not presenting poverty as a universal purchase price for salvation, as though heaven could be bought by emptying a bank account. Scripture does not teach salvation by charitable liquidation. Zacchaeus, only a chapter later in Luke, responds to Jesus with radical generosity, but the details are not identical. The early church includes believers who still had homes in which Christians gathered. The Gospel consistently destroys the idea that eternal life can be earned through another human achievement.
The issue is deeper.
Jesus exposed the ruler's god.
The man believed he possessed great wealth.
The encounter revealed that, in another sense, his wealth possessed him.
He could imagine obeying commandments.
He could imagine respecting Jesus.
He could imagine discussing eternal life.
He could even kneel before Christ.
But when Jesus demanded the throne...
the man discovered where his worship really lived.
That is why this story cannot safely remain a story about rich people.
Your idol may not have a dollar sign attached to it.
What is the thing you would obey instead of Jesus?
Your relationship?
Your career?
Your reputation?
Your sexuality?
Your comfort?
Your ambition?
Your political identity?
Your secret habit?
Your bitterness?
Your children?
Your ministry?
Your dream?
Your need for approval?
Your carefully constructed image of being the Christian who has everything together?
What makes you quietly say:
“Jesus, You can have everything except that”?
That “except” may be revealing the throne.
An idol is not merely a statue sitting in a pagan temple.
An idol can be something good that has become ultimate.
Something you love more than obedience.
Something you trust more than Christ.
Something you fear losing more than you fear walking away from Jesus.
Something you cannot surrender even when the Savior says:
“Follow Me.”
And here is the sentence in the story that should break us.
The man became sorrowful and went away.
Matthew says he went away grieving.
Mark describes him as shocked or dismayed by the word and grieving.
Luke says he became deeply sad.
Why?
Because he had great possessions.
He wanted eternal life.
But he wanted something else too.
And when forced to choose, he walked away from Jesus holding the thing that could never save him.
Imagine the silence.
The footsteps getting farther away.
Jesus standing there.
The disciples watching.
The man's wealth still intact.
His reputation still intact.
His morality still intact.
His social position still intact.
And yet he is walking in the wrong direction.
There are losses that look like victories.
You can keep the relationship and lose obedience.
Keep the applause and lose intimacy with God.
Keep the secret sin and lose your tenderness toward Christ.
Keep the money and lose the treasure.
Keep the image and lose the truth.
Keep everything you were afraid to surrender...
and discover that what you protected was never capable of saving you.
This is why “I'm a good person” is such a dangerous place to hide.
Because good compared with whom?
Jesus had already redirected the man's attention toward God as the true measure of goodness.
Scripture's diagnosis is much deeper than “some people behave badly.”
“There is none righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10).
Isaiah describes even our righteous deeds, considered as grounds for standing before the Holy One, as polluted garments (Isaiah 64:6).
The Gospel does not divide humanity into good people who deserve heaven and terrible people who need Jesus.
The Gospel announces something far more humbling—and far more hopeful:
Sinners need Jesus.
Religious sinners need Jesus.
Irreligious sinners need Jesus.
Poor sinners need Jesus.
Rich sinners need Jesus.
Respectable sinners need Jesus.
Scandalous sinners need Jesus.
The addict needs Jesus.
The church member needs Jesus.
The prisoner needs Jesus.
The preacher needs Jesus.
The person whose sin became tomorrow's gossip needs Jesus.
And the person whose sin has remained hidden behind a polished smile needs Jesus.
That is why the disciples' reaction matters so much.
After Jesus speaks of the terrible spiritual danger surrounding wealth and uses the shocking image of a camel passing through the eye of a needle, they ask:
“Then who can be saved?”
Do not soften the image.
Jesus is describing impossibility.
And His answer is the doorway into the Gospel:
παρὰ ἀνθρώποις τοῦτο ἀδύνατόν ἐστιν, παρὰ δὲ θεῷ πάντα δυνατά
para anthrōpois touto adynaton estin, para de theō panta dynata.
“With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
There.
That is hope.
The story is not ultimately teaching you to save yourself by trying harder than the rich young ruler.
The disciples understood enough to ask the right question:
Who, then, can be saved?
Jesus' answer is not:
“The people who work hard enough.”
It is:
What is impossible with man is possible with God.
Salvation is God's work.
Grace is not God's reward for impressive people.
Grace is God's mercy toward people who cannot rescue themselves.
And this is where the road leads to the cross.
The rich young ruler could not let go of his treasure to follow Jesus.
But Jesus would soon continue toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward mockery.
Toward scourging.
Toward nails.
Toward a cross.
The One who told the ruler to surrender everything was Himself moving toward the place where He would give Himself for sinners.
Paul later writes of Christ:
Jesus did not die because we were already good enough.
He died because we weren't.
He did not rise from the grave to make morally respectable people slightly nicer.
He rose as the victorious Lord who saves sinners, defeats death, reconciles us to God, and calls us into a new life under His lordship.
Christianity is not:
“Look how good I became.”
Christianity is:
“Look how merciful Christ has been to me.”
That changes the way you read this entire story.
Perhaps you have been the rich young ruler.
Not financially.
Spiritually.
You have been close enough to Jesus to ask questions but unwilling to let Him rule.
You have known Bible verses while protecting secret compromises.
You have sung worship songs while negotiating obedience.
You have called Him Lord while reserving veto power over certain rooms in your heart.
You have mistaken conviction for condemnation and therefore run from the very Christ who was exposing your chains because He loved you.
Remember Mark's sentence:
Jesus looked at him...
and loved him.
Christ's exposure of an idol is not evidence that He delights in destroying you.
Sometimes He puts His finger on what hurts because He knows what is killing you.
The surgeon's knife and the murderer's knife may both cut skin, but only one cuts in order to heal.
Maybe Jesus has been touching something in you for months.
Forgive them.
“No.”
Confess it.
“No.”
End the affair.
“No.”
Tell the truth.
“No.”
Stop returning to that pornography.
“No.”
Release your bitterness.
“No.”
Stop worshiping money.
“No.”
Stop building your identity around people's approval.
“No.”
Make restitution.
“No.”
Come out of hiding.
“No.”
Follow Me.
And suddenly the rich young ruler does not feel ancient anymore.
He feels painfully familiar.
This is where repentance enters.
Biblical repentance is not emotional self-hatred.
It is not purchasing forgiveness through tears.
It is not cleaning yourself up sufficiently so Jesus will finally accept your application.
Repentance turns from sin toward God.
Faith rests in Christ.
You stop defending the throne you were never meant to occupy.
You stop presenting your moral résumé as though God owes you eternal life.
You come empty-handed to the crucified and risen Savior.
And you trust Him.
The scandal becomes grace.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The proud can be humbled.
The greedy can become generous.
The sexually broken can become pure.
The liar can become truthful.
The bitter can forgive.
The hypocrite can finally stop pretending.
The ashamed can come into the light.
Not because sin suddenly becomes unimportant.
Precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that Christ went to the cross.
And grace is so astonishing that Christ went willingly for sinners.
This is why Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not merely edit the embarrassing paragraphs of your story.
He gives you a new identity in Him.
The Gospel does not say your scandal was imaginary.
It says your scandal does not have to have the final word.
The cross tells the truth about your sin while simultaneously announcing the staggering depth of God's mercy.
And perhaps the saddest thing about the rich young ruler is that the Gospel account leaves us watching him walk away.
We are not told in these passages that he returned.
So don't invent an ending Scripture does not give us.
Instead, allow the unresolved ending to confront your ending.
What will you do when Jesus touches your “one thing”?
Will you walk away sorrowful?
Or will you finally open your hands?
Because one day every possession you protected will belong to someone else.
Every title will disappear.
Every follower count will become irrelevant.
Every trophy will gather dust.
Someone else will sleep in your room.
Someone else may drive your car.
Your name will eventually disappear from conversations you once dominated.
And you will stand before God with none of the earthly things you spent your life using to prove your worth.
Then the question will not be whether people thought you were a good person.
The question is whether you belong to Christ.
Do you understand why this matters?
You can admire Jesus and still walk away from Jesus.
You can kneel before Him and still refuse Him.
You can be moral and still need mercy.
You can be religious and still need regeneration.
You can know commandments and still resist the King.
You can possess everything the world envies...
and lack the one Treasure your soul was created for.
Jesus Christ.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already broken an idol that once controlled your life, tell someone what His grace did. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another struggling person realize they are not alone.
Not because every sentence deserves remembering, but because the question does:
What is the one thing I would rather keep than follow Jesus?
Come back to that question when success starts seducing you again.
Not to win an argument.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
If sharing biblical truth helps another person see Christ more clearly, glorify God with that opportunity.
The Gospel cannot be bought, and supporting a ministry does not save anyone.
Christ saves.
Invite your family. Invite the friend who is struggling. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the person who is searching. Even invite the unbeliever who has questions about Jesus.
But before you leave this article, return one last time to that road.
See the young man.
His hands are still full.
His heart is breaking.
Jesus is behind him.
His possessions are still his.
And he is walking away with everything...
except the One he actually needed.
Don't let that be your story.
Whatever Christ is exposing, bring it into the light.
Whatever sin you have been defending, repent.
Whatever idol you have been protecting, surrender it.
Whatever shame tells you that you have gone too far, look again at the cross.
The Savior who exposes sin is also the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The hands asking you to surrender are nail-scarred hands.
And the Jesus who says, “Follow Me,” is infinitely more valuable than everything you are terrified of leaving behind.
The tragedy was never that the young ruler had too little—it was that he walked away from Jesus believing what he held was worth more than the One who loved him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEMEN IN THE BIBLE: Why Did Leviticus Have a Law About Male Emissions?
paragraphs: SEMEN IN THE BIBLE: Why Did Leviticus Have a Law About Male Emissions?
The verse most Christians quietly skip may reveal something astonishing about holiness, shame, the human body—and why Jesus came all the way into the mess of being human to make sinners clean.
There are Bible verses people underline.
There are verses people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses preached from pulpits, printed on coffee mugs, memorized by children, whispered beside hospital beds, and quoted when life falls apart.
And then there is Leviticus 15:16.
A verse about semen.
Yes. Semen.
The kind of verse that can make a Bible study suddenly become very quiet.
The kind teenagers discover and laugh about.
The kind many adults read quickly and move past because nobody ever explained why the holy Word of God would speak so directly about something so private.
But maybe the discomfort is exactly why we should not skip it.
Because buried inside this strange ancient law is a truth many people desperately need to hear:
God is not embarrassed by the human body.
God is not frightened by the parts of your humanity you do not discuss in church.
And the Bible is far more honest about being human than many religious people are.
Listen to the Hebrew itself:
"וְאִישׁ כִּי־תֵצֵא מִמֶּנּוּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע וְרָחַץ בַּמַּיִם אֶת־כָּל־בְּשָׂרוֹ וְטָמֵא עַד־הָעָרֶב׃"
Ve’ish ki-tetze mimennu shikhvat-zara, verachatz bammayim et-kol-besaro, vetame ad-ha’arev.
“When a man has an emission of semen, he shall bathe his whole body in water and remain impure until evening.”
—Leviticus 15:16
The key expression is שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע — shikhvat zera.
Zera means “seed” or offspring-producing seed. In this context, the expression refers to semen.
There is no attempt to sanitize it.
No euphemistic escape hatch.
A man has a seminal emission.
He washes.
He remains tame—טָמֵא, ritually impure—until evening.

His clothing or leather on which the semen falls is washed and remains ritually impure until evening. Then the text goes even further: when the emission occurs through sexual intercourse between a man and woman, both wash and remain ritually impure until evening.
And that last detail destroys one of the easiest misunderstandings of the passage.
Because if you read the English word “unclean” and immediately hear “sinful,” you are going to misunderstand Leviticus.
Ritual impurity was not automatically moral guilt.
Read that again.
Ritual impurity was not automatically moral guilt.

Leviticus 15:18 explicitly includes ordinary sexual intercourse in this temporary impurity. The passage does not say that marital intercourse itself was sinful. It describes a bodily condition that temporarily affected a person's ritual status.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Hebrew Bible has vocabulary for sin, transgression, wickedness, guilt, and rebellion.
But here the central category is tum’ah—ritual impurity.
And Leviticus 15 does not isolate semen as though male sexuality were uniquely disgusting.
Look at the chapter.
It addresses abnormal male discharges.
Then seminal emission.
Then sexual intercourse involving semen.
Then menstruation.
Then abnormal female bleeding.
Male bodies.
Female bodies.
Blood.
Semen.
Sex.
Discharge.
Things modern Christians sometimes struggle even to say aloud are sitting there in Scripture because God gave Israel laws that reached into embodied human life.
This was not pornography.
It was holiness entering ordinary biology.
And there is another detail worth noticing.
The normal seminal emission of verses 16–18 receives a remarkably simple response.
Wash.
Wait until evening.

That is substantially different from the extended procedure described for an abnormal male discharge earlier in the chapter, which could involve a period of waiting and eventually sacrifices. Scholarly treatments of the chapter likewise distinguish the short-term impurity associated with semen from the more extensive process associated with an abnormal discharge.
In other words, Leviticus itself makes distinctions.
Not every discharge is treated identically.
Not every impurity means somebody committed sexual immorality.
Not every reference to bodily fluids is a secret medical prophecy.
And not every uncomfortable Bible verse needs a sensational explanation to become meaningful.
Sometimes the truth is already powerful enough.
But why would semen make someone ritually impure at all?
This is where we need humility.

The text gives the regulation very clearly, but it does not stop and provide modern readers with a paragraph explaining every symbolic reason behind it. Christians therefore should be careful about announcing theories as though Moses explicitly wrote them.

Some interpreters connect Israel's purity system with boundaries involving life, death, bodily wholeness, and access to sacred space. Others emphasize the ordered separation between ordinary embodied life and Israel's sanctuary holiness.
Whatever additional symbolism we explore, Leviticus itself eventually tells us why these purity distinctions mattered so seriously.
Verse 31 says Israel must be guarded concerning impurity so that they would not defile God's Tabernacle dwelling among them.
There it is.
The issue reaches toward the presence of God.
The God of Israel had chosen to dwell among His people.
And His presence was not treated casually.
Holiness mattered.
Approach mattered.
Purity mattered.
The sacred was sacred.
Maybe that feels strange because we live in a culture that has managed to make sexuality simultaneously public and deeply shameful.
Sex is everywhere...
yet genuine conversations about sexual brokenness are painfully difficult.
Bodies are displayed everywhere...
yet people quietly hate their own bodies.
Pornography is consumed behind locked screens.
Lust gets hidden behind deleted histories.
Marriages suffer in silence.
Young believers wonder whether normal bodily functions mean something is spiritually wrong with them.
