If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't perform for anyone.
But don't run from God either.
Somebody reading underneath you may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores broken people.
Then send this to someone.
Not because an algorithm needs another share.
Because a person might.
Send it privately to the person who feels rejected.
Send it to the Christian who has confused biblical conviction with permission to hate.
Send it to the believer who has been trying to manufacture what God asked them to trust Him for.
Because there may come a night when the wilderness feels louder than the promise, and you will need to remember again:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — God hears.
And you may need to remember:
יִצְחָק — God can bring laughter out of impossibility.
And above both names, remember the Name toward whom the biblical story ultimately directs us:
Ἰησοῦς Χριστός — Iēsous Christos — Jesus Christ.
Not because money purchases God's blessing.
It doesn't.
It never could.
That would contradict the Gospel of grace.
Paul's principle for Christian giving is that it should not be extracted through reluctance or compulsion. Christian generosity is meant to come willingly from the heart.
It helps us reach farther.
It helps us keep putting Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement, and the Gospel in front of people who might otherwise never encounter it.
And one of the simplest ways to support the mission costs nothing at all:
That share matters.
You may never know that your share was the reason they stopped scrolling.
The reason they opened a Bible.
The reason they prayed again.
The reason they finally told somebody, “I need help.”
The reason they remembered Jesus.
Stay close to Scripture.
Stay close to truth.
Stay close to the Gospel.
Jesus already paid the price you could never pay.
That is why we give.
That is why we serve.
That is why we share.
Not to buy grace.
Because we received grace.

And perhaps that is where Isaac and Ishmael finally leave us—not staring endlessly at two brothers and asking which human bloodline gives us permission to despise another, but staring at Jesus and realizing that the deepest war was never merely between families, tribes, or nations.
The rebellion was inside us.
And the reconciliation we needed most was reconciliation with God.
Two brothers once stood beside their father's grave.
One day every one of us will stand at the edge of eternity.
On that day, our ancestry will not save us.
Our religious vocabulary will not save us.
Our family reputation will not save us.
Our church attendance will not save us.
Our political tribe will not save us.
Our good intentions will not save us.
We need Jesus Christ.
So while there is still breath in your lungs, come home.
Repent.
Believe.
Forgive.
Lay down the hatred.
Lay down the secret sin.
Lay down the exhausting attempt to manufacture what only God can give.
And trust the Savior who specializes in walking into stories wrecked by human sin and writing endings nobody thought possible.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable truth hidden inside the story of Isaac and Ishmael is this:
You do not have to spend the rest of your life becoming the wound you inherited. Jesus can make you the place where the wound finally stops.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOSEPH NAMED HIS FIRST SON “GOD HAS MADE ME FORGET”—WHAT WAS HE TRYING TO LEAVE BEHIND?
paragraphs: JOSEPH NAMED HIS FIRST SON “GOD HAS MADE ME FORGET”—WHAT WAS HE TRYING TO LEAVE BEHIND?
His brothers sold him. His master’s wife accused him. His friends forgot him. Then Joseph gave his firstborn a name that revealed what success could never erase.
There are some things you survive…
but somehow, they keep surviving inside you.
You leave the house where it happened.
You stop talking to the person who hurt you.
Years pass.
Your circumstances change.
You learn how to smile again.
People look at you and think you are doing fine.
Maybe you even become successful.
But sometimes all it takes is a name.
A place.
A smell.
A familiar voice.
A certain date on the calendar.
And suddenly the person you thought you had buried inside yesterday starts breathing again.
Joseph knew something about that.
Before he wore fine linen in Egypt, he wore the clothes of a prisoner.
Before Pharaoh placed a gold chain around his neck, iron had known his body.
Before people bowed before him, people had thrown him away.
Before Joseph became powerful enough to command a nation, he had been powerless enough to hear his own brothers discussing what to do with him.
And when Joseph finally had a son, he did something extraordinary.
He turned his child’s name into a testimony.
Genesis 41:50–52 tells us:
“Unto Joseph were born two sons before the years of famine came…”
Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיִּקְרָא יוֹסֵף אֶת־שֵׁם הַבְּכוֹר מְנַשֶּׁה כִּי־נַשַּׁנִי אֱלֹהִים אֶת־כָּל־עֲמָלִי וְאֵת כָּל־בֵּית אָבִי
Vayyiqra Yosef et-shem habbekhor Menashsheh, ki-nashshani Elohim et-kol-amali ve'et kol-beit avi.
The sense is:
Joseph called his firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s house.”
Then he named his second son Ephraim, because, as Joseph declared:
כִּי־הִפְרַנִי אֱלֹהִים בְּאֶרֶץ עָנְיִי
Ki-hifrani Elohim be'eretz onyi.
“For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
Do not rush past those names.
Manasseh.
God has made me forget.
Ephraim.
God has made me fruitful.
Forget.
Then fruitful.
Pain.
Then purpose.
Affliction.
Then abundance.
But what exactly was Joseph trying to forget?
Because Joseph had not forgotten the facts.
We know that.
Years later, when his brothers appeared before him, Joseph recognized them.
He remembered.
He remembered his father.
He remembered his younger brother Benjamin.
He remembered the dreams of his youth.
Genesis 42:9 explicitly says:
“And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them.”
So when Joseph said God had caused him to “forget,” Scripture cannot reasonably mean that God erased Joseph’s memory like deleting a file.
Joseph remembered.
What changed was the power those memories possessed over his present life.
And maybe that is exactly where this story finds you.
Because perhaps you have been asking God to make you forget something He intends to redeem.
You have prayed:
“Lord, just take the memory away.”
But it remains.
You still remember what they said.
You remember who walked away.
You remember the betrayal.
You remember the funeral.
You remember the message you discovered.
You remember the humiliation.
You remember the night everything changed.
You remember who you were before the addiction.
Before the divorce.
Before the betrayal.
Before the failure.
Before your family fractured.
Before your faith became complicated.
Before you learned that people you trusted could wound you.
And because you still remember, perhaps you have wondered whether God has actually healed you.
Joseph’s story whispers something different.
Healing is not always the absence of memory. Sometimes healing is when the memory remains, but it no longer owns you.
Joseph was not pretending the pit never happened.
He was declaring that the pit would no longer determine who he became.
Think about what was behind him.
His brothers hated him.
Genesis 37 tells us they could not speak peaceably to him.
They stripped away the special garment his father had given him.
They threw him into a pit.
Then they sat down to eat.
That detail hurts.
Joseph was in the pit while his brothers were having a meal.
Eventually they sold him.
A human being.
Their own brother.
Twenty pieces of silver.
Then Joseph was carried into Egypt.
Imagine the journey.
Every mile taking him farther from home.
Every step reinforcing the same terrible reality:
Nobody is coming.
His father did not know where he was.
His brothers were responsible for his disappearance.
His old life was gone.
Then Joseph served in Potiphar’s house.
He acted faithfully.
God was with him.
Things began improving.
And then another betrayal came.
Potiphar’s wife repeatedly tried to seduce Joseph.
Joseph refused.
His reasoning was not merely social.
It was theological.
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” he said in Genesis 39:9.
Joseph ran from sexual sin.
And what did righteousness get him?
Prison.
She falsely accused him.
The innocent man was punished.
Joseph had done the right thing…
and still suffered.
Someone reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
You obeyed God and still lost something.
You told the truth and people believed the lie.
You remained faithful and somebody betrayed you.
You tried to honor Christ and watched someone who compromised appear to prosper.
There are seasons when obedience does not immediately look like victory.
Joseph teaches us that the absence of immediate vindication is not the absence of God.
Genesis 39 repeatedly emphasizes that the LORD was with Joseph.
In the house.
In the injustice.
In the prison.
God was there.
That changes the way we understand suffering.
Joseph was not abandoned in the pit.
He was not abandoned in slavery.
He was not abandoned when falsely accused.
He was not abandoned behind prison walls.
And neither the pit nor the palace was ultimately the center of Joseph’s story.
God was.
Then came another wound.
Joseph interpreted the cupbearer’s dream and asked him to remember him before Pharaoh.
Genesis 40:23 delivers one of Scripture’s painfully understated sentences:
“Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.”
Forgotten.
Again.
First rejected by his brothers.
Then falsely accused.
Then forgotten by someone he had helped.
Two more years passed.
Imagine those years.
No Genesis 41 yet.
No Pharaoh calling.
No chariot.
No promotion.
Just prison walls and a promise that seemed increasingly difficult to understand.
But then Pharaoh dreamed.
And suddenly the man forgotten in prison became the man Egypt desperately needed.
Joseph was brought before Pharaoh.
God gave him wisdom.
Joseph interpreted the dreams.
Pharaoh recognized extraordinary wisdom in him and elevated Joseph over Egypt.
In one breathtaking reversal, the prisoner became governor.
But then Joseph had a child.
And suddenly we discover that underneath the Egyptian clothing, underneath the authority, underneath the success…
there was still a man remembering where he came from.
So he named the boy Manasseh.
“God has made me forget…”
Perhaps Joseph was saying:
God has carried me beyond the season that once defined my entire world.
God has loosened suffering’s grip on me.
God has given me a life beyond the life I thought had been destroyed.
God has shown me that what happened to me does not have to become what rules me.
But there is another detail that makes this even more powerful.
Joseph did not stop with Manasseh.
His second son was Ephraim.
“God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
Not after the land of affliction.
In it.
That changes everything.
Joseph did not need to return to Canaan before he could become fruitful.
God produced fruit in Egypt.
The place associated with Joseph’s displacement became the place where God demonstrated His provision.
Maybe you keep telling yourself:
“When this season ends, I can live again.”
“When the pain disappears, I can serve God again.”
“When my family changes, I can have peace.”
“When someone apologizes, I can heal.”
“When God explains everything, I will trust Him.”
Joseph’s life confronts that thinking.
God can make you fruitful in the land of your affliction.
The place you would never have chosen may become the place where you discover dimensions of God you would never have known otherwise.
That does not make evil good.
The Bible never requires us to rename betrayal as goodness.
Joseph’s brothers sinned.
The false accusation was wrong.
The injustice was real.
The suffering mattered.
Biblical forgiveness is not pretending evil was acceptable.
And Joseph’s later words prove it.
Years after naming Manasseh, Joseph stood before the same brothers who sold him.
Now Joseph had power.
They did not.
He could finally make them feel what he had felt.
This was the moment revenge had been waiting for.
But grace had rewritten the man.
Joseph wept.
Eventually he revealed himself.
“I am Joseph.”
Imagine what those words did to that room.
The brother they discarded was alive.
The slave had become ruler.
The victim now possessed enormous power over the people who victimized him.
And yet Joseph could see something larger than revenge.
Genesis 50:20 records his famous words:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
Notice carefully what Joseph did not say.
He did not say:
“What you did was good.”
He said:
You meant evil.
Joseph called evil what it was.
But then he declared that human evil did not possess the final word.
God meant it unto good.
That is biblical redemption.
Not pretending the wound never happened.
Not calling darkness light.
Not denying injustice.
But discovering that sinful people cannot outmaneuver a sovereign God.
They may write a terrible chapter.
They do not get to write the ending.
And this is where Joseph’s story begins pointing beyond Joseph.
Because there would come another beloved Son.
Jesus Christ.
Rejected by His own.
Betrayed for silver.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Condemned though innocent.
And crucified.
At Calvary, human wickedness appeared to have reached its triumph.
The Messiah hung on a cross.
His body was broken.
His blood was shed.
He died.
He was buried.
For a moment, it looked as though darkness had written the final sentence.
Then came Sunday.
The stone was rolled away.
Christ rose from the dead.
And the cross—the instrument meant for shame and death—became the place where God displayed redemption.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We are not merely wounded people needing emotional improvement.
We are sinners needing reconciliation with a holy God.
Our greatest problem is deeper than what people have done to us.
It is the sin within us that separates us from God.
And Jesus did not come merely to make our lives easier.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He died.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
Grace does not tell you that your sin does not matter.
Grace tells you that your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is greater than the guilt you bring to Him.
Maybe the hardest thing you need to leave behind is not what somebody did to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
The secret.
The compromise.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The years you wasted.
The person you hurt.
The faith you abandoned.
The prayer life you neglected.
The version of yourself you are ashamed to remember.
You cannot save yourself by forgetting it.
You cannot heal yourself by hiding it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Repentance does not mean pretending yesterday never happened.
It means turning from sin and turning toward Christ.
And the Gospel announces something breathtaking:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
Peter denied Him and was restored.
Paul persecuted the church and became a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer—no years of ministry, no opportunity to repair his reputation, no lifetime of religious accomplishments.
He had only a dying prayer:
“Lord, remember me…”
And Jesus gave him paradise.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never existed.
By overwhelming it with grace.
Maybe that is why Manasseh matters so much.
Joseph could hold his son and realize:
“I have a future.”
The pit told him his story was over.
Manasseh said otherwise.
The chains said his identity was prisoner.
Manasseh said otherwise.
The accusation said his reputation was destroyed.
Manasseh said otherwise.
The forgotten years said nothing was changing.
Manasseh said otherwise.
Then Joseph could hold Ephraim and say:
“I am not merely surviving anymore.
God is producing fruit here.”
Maybe today you need your own Manasseh moment.
Not amnesia.
Surrender.
You need to stop visiting an old wound every morning and asking it who you are.
You need to stop allowing the person who rejected you to continue controlling your identity years after they walked away.
You need to stop rehearsing the accusation Christ has already answered with His blood.
You need to stop building a permanent home inside a chapter God intended you to walk through.
And perhaps you need an Ephraim moment too.
You need to believe that God can still produce something beautiful in a life that has been painfully interrupted.
Listen carefully:
You are not required to forget the facts in order to be free from their mastery.
Joseph remembered.
But he was no longer living in the pit.
And there is something else Joseph’s story teaches us.
Years later, the very brothers connected to his pain would stand before him needing bread.
Joseph’s suffering had somehow placed him where he could preserve lives.
That does not justify what they did.
It reveals what God can do despite it.
Your scars may someday speak to somebody still bleeding.
Your testimony may become somebody else’s reason not to give up.
The season you begged God to erase may eventually become the story through which another wounded person discovers Jesus.
So do not waste your pain.
Give it to Christ.
Let Him redeem what you cannot rewrite yourself.
And if this exposed something you have kept buried, do not hide behind religious language today.
Be honest.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes two or three honest words are enough to say, “I am still fighting. I still believe God is not finished with me.”
And read the other comments.
You may discover that the person beside you in this digital room has been carrying a wound that looks remarkably like yours.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Christ.
That is what the body of Christ should do.
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
They may look completely fine.
But perhaps the message God places before them through your simple share will remind them to look toward Jesus again.
There are truths you understand differently when the wound starts speaking again.
Come back when yesterday feels louder than grace.
Come back and remember Joseph.
Manasseh.
Ephraim.
The pit.
The prison.
The palace.
And above all…
the God who was present through all of it.
Scripture says giving should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That matters to us.
We do not want fear to make your decision.
We do not want guilt to make your decision.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Your support helps us keep going.
Your sharing helps us reach farther.
Your prayers matter.
Your participation matters.
And when believers freely use what God has entrusted to them to support Gospel-centered work, that generosity can become an act of worship offered to God.
And comment.
Tell us what God is doing.
Tell us what you are fighting.
Tell us what you are surrendering.
Tell us what Christ has already brought you through.
Because someone else may read your testimony and realize they are not alone.
Joseph called his first son Manasseh.
“God has made me forget.”
Then came Ephraim.
“God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
Maybe your Manasseh is not God erasing your memory.
Maybe it is God breaking your memory’s authority over you.
Maybe your Ephraim is not escaping every painful circumstance.
Maybe it is discovering that Christ can produce fruit even there.
And maybe one day you will look back at the chapter you thought would destroy you and realize something that Joseph eventually understood:
People wounded you.
Sin scarred you.
Life changed you.
But none of them possessed the pen.
Jesus Christ still does.
So bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the memory you cannot erase.
Bring Him your sin in repentance.
Bring Him your wounded heart in faith.
And let the Savior who walked out of His own grave show you what He can do with things everyone else thought were finished.
Because perhaps the miracle is not that one day you will remember nothing.
Perhaps the miracle is that one day you will remember everything…
and discover that the wound no longer gets to tell you who you are.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I CAN DO ALL THINGS THROUGH CHRIST” DOES NOT MEAN WHAT MOST PEOPLE THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs:
“I CAN DO ALL THINGS THROUGH CHRIST” DOES NOT MEAN WHAT MOST PEOPLE THINK IT MEANS
You may have been quoting Philippians 4:13 as a promise that Jesus will help you win. Paul wrote it as the testimony of a man who had learned how to lose everything without losing Christ.
There are Bible verses we read.
There are Bible verses we memorize.
And then there are Bible verses we quietly turn into something they were never meant to say.
Philippians 4:13 may be one of them.
You have probably seen it printed beneath the photograph of an athlete.
Written across a graduation card.
Posted before a job interview.
Quoted before an impossible examination.
Printed on shirts, mugs, gym walls, journals, posters, and social-media graphics.
“I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.”
It sounds unstoppable.
And it is powerful.
But perhaps not in the way many of us were taught to hear it.
Because Paul was not standing on a platform holding a trophy when these words came from his heart.
He was not telling Christians that faith guarantees the accomplishment of every dream.

He was not promising that if you believe strongly enough, every business will succeed, every illness will disappear, every relationship will survive, every door will open, every prayer will receive the answer you wanted, or every battle will end the way you imagined.
Paul was talking about something far more difficult.
He was talking about remaining faithful when the trophy never comes.
Read the sentences immediately surrounding the famous verse and the atmosphere changes.
Paul says that he has learned contentment whatever his circumstances. He knows what it means to have little. He knows what it means to have abundance. He knows fullness.
And hunger.
Plenty.
And need.
Then comes the sentence we love to quote.
“I can do all this through him who gives me strength.”
That surrounding context matters enormously.
The Greek of Philippians 4:13 reads:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.
A careful sense of the words is:
“In all things I have strength through the One who strengthens me.”
And suddenly the verse sounds different.
The word πάντα — panta — “all things” does not give us permission to detach the sentence from everything Paul has just described.
What are the “all things” Paul has been talking about?
Having plenty.
Having almost nothing.
Being satisfied.
Being hungry.
Living in abundance.
Living in need.
Paul is essentially saying:
“I can face this.”
Not merely success.
This.
Not merely victory.
This.
Not merely abundance.
This.
Whatever obedience to Christ requires of me here.
That is breathtakingly different from the motivational slogan we sometimes make this verse become.
Philippians 4:13 is not primarily the declaration of a man saying, “Christ will make me successful.”
It is the confession of a man saying:
“Whether I have much or almost nothing, Christ will be enough to keep me faithful.”
And maybe that is exactly why some of us need this verse more than we realized.
Because perhaps you believed Jesus would strengthen you by removing the thing that was crushing you.
But instead...
you are still carrying it.
Perhaps you prayed for the marriage.
And it still collapsed.
You prayed for the opportunity.
Someone else got it.
You prayed for the money.
The bills kept coming.
You prayed for healing.
The doctor still gave you news you never wanted to hear.
You prayed for your child.
And tonight you still do not know where that child is spiritually.
You prayed for the ministry.
It never became what you imagined.
You prayed for the business.
It failed.
You prayed for the door.
It stayed closed.
And somewhere in the silence you began wondering...
Did I not have enough faith?
Maybe you even whispered Philippians 4:13 while trying to convince yourself that Christians were supposed to win.
But what happens when you don't?
What happens when faithful Christians suffer?
What happens when obedient Christians become hungry?
What happens when the answer is no?
What happens when the miracle you were expecting never arrives in the form you expected?
Does Philippians 4:13 stop being true?
No.
That may be when you finally discover what it means.
Paul said something just before verse 13 that we rush past far too quickly:
He had learned contentment.
Learned.
Meaning Paul apparently did not wake up one morning automatically possessing supernatural emotional invincibility.
Contentment was learned.
Through experience.
Through deprivation.
Through provision.
Through disappointment.
Through hunger.
Through abundance.
Through suffering.
Through repeatedly discovering that circumstances could change without Christ changing.
The Greek word translated “content” in Philippians 4:11 is αὐτάρκης — autarkēs.
In the surrounding Greco-Roman world, the term could carry the idea of being sufficient or independent of external circumstances.
But Paul does something profoundly Christian with the idea.
His confidence is not:
“I am enough.”
His conclusion is:
Christ strengthens me.
Christian contentment is not self-sufficiency.
It is Christ-sufficiency.
That difference changes everything.
The world tells you:
“You have everything inside yourself.”
The Gospel tells you something simultaneously more humbling and more beautiful:
You are not your own savior.
Jesus is.
You do not have to manufacture infinite strength.
You have a Savior.
And sometimes the strength Christ gives does not look like mountains exploding out of your path.
Sometimes His strength looks like waking up tomorrow morning and still trusting Him.
Sometimes it looks like worshiping while confused.
Forgiving while wounded.
Obeying while afraid.
Remaining sexually pure when temptation is screaming.
Refusing bitterness when someone deserves your anger.
Praying again after yesterday's prayer seemed unanswered.
Opening Scripture when your emotions feel numb.
Getting out of bed when grief has made the room feel heavier than concrete.
Saying, “Jesus, I don't understand You right now... but I will not leave You.”
That is strength too.
Perhaps some of the greatest demonstrations of Philippians 4:13 happen where nobody applauds.
A widow sitting alone at a kitchen table whispering the name of Jesus.
A father wondering how he will provide but refusing to abandon his family.
A recovering addict trembling in a bathroom, staring at the temptation that once controlled him, whispering, “Jesus, help me.”
A betrayed spouse refusing to let another person's sin turn pain into hatred.
A young believer deleting what keeps dragging them back into darkness.
A Christian receiving terrible news and discovering through tears that Christ is still Christ.
Nobody makes posters of those moments.
Heaven sees them.
This is where prosperity-shaped Christianity becomes painfully inadequate.
If Philippians 4:13 means that Christians can accomplish whatever they set their minds to, then what do we say about Paul himself?
Paul suffered.
Paul was opposed.
Paul experienced deprivation.
Paul knew hunger.
Paul knew weakness.
Paul knew imprisonment.
And ultimately, Paul did not escape death.
Yet he belonged completely to Jesus.
The Gospel never promised that following Christ would make us untouchable.
Jesus Himself said His disciples would have trouble in this world.
Christianity is not the announcement that suffering has disappeared.
Christianity is the announcement that suffering no longer gets the final word.
Because Jesus entered suffering Himself.
Look at the cross.
If worldly success were the ultimate evidence of God's favor, Good Friday would look like God's greatest failure.
The Messiah was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Stripped.
Nailed to wood.
His enemies watched.
His followers scattered.
And the Son of God died.
From the perspective of ordinary human ambition, the cross looked like catastrophic defeat.
But heaven was writing something humanity could not yet see.
Redemption.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Grace.
Victory through apparent defeat.
And then came Sunday.
The stone moved.
The grave surrendered its prisoner.
Jesus Christ rose.
That is why Christians cannot measure God's faithfulness merely by whether today's circumstances feel victorious.
Sometimes Friday looks like the end while God already knows Sunday is coming.
Sometimes the story looks ruined because we are reading the middle.
And this is where Philippians 4:13 becomes dangerous in the best possible way.
It does not promise:
“You can have everything you want.”
It declares something better:
Whatever obedience to Christ requires, Christ Himself will supply strength to remain His.
You can follow Jesus with money.
You can follow Jesus without much money.
You can follow Jesus when people celebrate you.
You can follow Jesus when people misunderstand you.
You can follow Jesus when your body feels strong.
You can follow Jesus while your body is failing.
You can follow Jesus when prayers are answered exactly as hoped.
You can follow Jesus when all you have is enough grace for another twenty-four hours.
That does not mean suffering should be romanticized.
It does not mean Christians should refuse medicine, assistance, justice, wise counsel, financial help, or deliverance from abusive circumstances.
It does not mean pain does not hurt.
Paul himself gratefully received practical support from the Philippians.
In fact, immediately after the famous declaration, he tells them they had done well by sharing in his trouble.
That detail is beautiful.
Paul could say, “Christ strengthens me,” while simultaneously receiving help from other believers.
Those truths are not enemies.
Depending on Christ does not mean pretending you need nobody.
Sometimes Christ strengthens you through His people.
Through the meal someone brought.
Through the friend who answered at midnight.
Through the believer who prayed when you could barely form words.
Through the church that carried your burden.
Through generosity.
Through encouragement.
Through someone deciding that your suffering would not be yours to carry alone.
Maybe somebody reading this right now has been ashamed because you are tired.
You thought strong Christians never become exhausted.
You thought faith meant never crying.
Never questioning.
Never feeling afraid.
Never needing anyone.
But biblical strength is not emotional numbness.
Sometimes faith is trembling hands still reaching toward Jesus.
Remember the apostle who wrote Philippians 4:13.
He did not say:
“I was born knowing contentment.”
He said:
I learned.
Maybe Christ is teaching you too.
And lessons taught in valleys rarely feel like lessons while we are inside them.
They feel like loss.
Like waiting.
Like silence.
Like unanswered questions.
Like nights when everybody else is sleeping and you are staring into darkness asking God whether He still sees you.
He does.
And perhaps the scandal of grace is that Jesus does not wait until you become impressive before He comes near.
He meets sinners.
Failures.
The exhausted.
The ashamed.
The spiritually bankrupt.
The people whose carefully managed lives finally fell apart.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping good people become slightly better.
It is the Son of God rescuing people who could never rescue themselves.
We have sinned.
We have loved ourselves above God.
We have chased idols dressed as success.
Sometimes we have even used Scripture to baptize our ambitions.
We wanted Jesus to strengthen our plans when Jesus was calling us to surrender them.
That is uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the question Philippians 4:13 asks is not:
“What incredible thing can I accomplish?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“If Jesus doesn't give me what I want, will Jesus Himself still be enough?”
Sit with that.
If the promotion never comes...
is Christ enough?
If the relationship does not return...
is Christ enough?
If your name never becomes famous...
is Christ enough?
If nobody applauds your obedience...
is Christ enough?
If following Jesus costs you something you desperately wanted...
is Christ enough?
If God gives abundance, can you worship without making abundance your god?
And if abundance disappears, can you still say:
Jesus is Lord?
That is the battlefield.
Paul had discovered a secret many of us spend our entire lives trying to avoid.
Peace is not found by finally controlling every circumstance.
Peace is found when your circumstances lose the authority to determine whether Christ is worthy.
That kind of faith terrifies hell.
Because how do you defeat someone whose treasure is Christ?
Give them abundance?
They thank Jesus.
Take abundance away?
They cling to Jesus.
Praise them?
They glorify Jesus.
Reject them?
They run toward Jesus.
Let them live?
They live for Christ.
Let death come?
They awaken in the presence of Christ.
That is why the Gospel produces a kind of freedom money cannot manufacture.
And maybe right now you do not need another motivational speech telling you that you are unstoppable.
Maybe you need permission to admit:
“I am weak.”
Because Christianity has never depended upon pretending weakness does not exist.
Jesus meets us there.
Paul understood that elsewhere when he wrote about Christ's power resting upon him in weakness.
Grace does not always remove weakness.
Sometimes grace makes weakness the place where Christ becomes unmistakable.
So stop treating Philippians 4:13 like a blank check for ambition.
It is something infinitely more precious.
It is a lifeline for suffering saints.
It belongs to the person whose pantry is full...
and the person wondering how groceries will last until payday.
To the believer celebrating an answered prayer...
and the believer crying after the funeral.
To the Christian beginning something beautiful...
and the Christian watching something beloved end.
To the person standing on the mountain...
and the person who cannot remember what sunlight feels like from the valley.
Christ is not merely Lord of your victories.
He is Lord in the hospital room.
Lord in unemployment.
Lord in grief.
Lord when the bank account frightens you.
Lord when your children wander.
Lord when your plans collapse.
Lord when temptation comes.
Lord when you repent after falling again.
Lord when your heart feels alive.
Lord when worship feels difficult.
Lord when you understand.
Lord when you don't.
Jesus Christ is still Lord.
And if you have turned Christianity into a method of obtaining the life you wanted, perhaps today is the day to come back to the Gospel.
Not:
“Jesus, make my dreams happen.”
But:
“Jesus, You are my life.”
Not:
“Jesus, prove Yourself by giving me everything.”
But:
“Jesus, forgive me for loving Your gifts more than the Giver.”
Repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is turning around because Someone merciful is calling you home.
The Christ who exposes our idols is the same Christ who carried our sins.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for the polished version of you that finally gets everything together.
He died for sinners.
And He rose again.
Grace means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your failure does not have to own your identity.
Your shame does not get to name you forever.
Your suffering does not mean Christ abandoned you.
Your weakness does not surprise Him.
Bring it into the light.
Bring the ambition.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the secret sin.
Bring the resentment.
Bring the exhausted faith.
Bring the questions you were afraid Christians were not allowed to ask.
Bring the shattered expectations.
Bring yourself.
And surrender.
Maybe the miracle you need today is not the power to accomplish everything you imagined.
Maybe the miracle is discovering that when everything you imagined begins falling apart...
Jesus does not.
Pray.
There is a human soul behind that comment.
Someone may be holding together a marriage.
Someone may be fighting addiction.
Someone may be grieving.
Someone may be inches from giving up.
Let the body of Christ behave like the body of Christ.
And please don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, helping that truth reach someone else can become an ordinary act of Christian generosity.
But generous partnership can genuinely be one way believers choose to glorify God by helping sound biblical content continue reaching people.
whether you have plenty or little...
whether today feels victorious or devastating...
do not miss the message Paul was actually giving us.
“I can do all things through Christ” was never permission to make Jesus the servant of our ambitions.
It was the testimony of a surrendered man who discovered that neither abundance nor deprivation could separate him from the sufficiency of Christ.
Maybe you will get the promotion.
Maybe you won't.
Maybe the door will open.
Maybe it won't.
Maybe God will change the circumstance.
Maybe before He changes the circumstance, He will change you inside it.
But if you belong to Jesus, you are not walking into tomorrow alone.
The One who saved you is the One who strengthens you.
The One who forgives you is the One who keeps you.
The One who met you in your scandal is still writing grace into places you thought were beyond redemption.
So when life strips away the version of Christianity that depended upon everything going right...
you may finally discover the treasure Paul found:
Christ when you are full.
Christ when you are hungry.
Christ when you have plenty.
Christ when you are in need.
Christ when you understand.
Christ when you don't.
Christ when you stand.
Christ when you crawl.
Christ when the answer arrives.
Christ in the silence.
Christ.
Still Christ.
Always Christ.
And sometimes the greatest evidence that Christ strengthened you is not that you conquered the circumstance—but that the circumstance could not conquer your faith in Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS MENTION PROSTITUTES WHILE CONFRONTING RELIGIOUS LEADERS?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS MENTION PROSTITUTES WHILE CONFRONTING RELIGIOUS LEADERS?
The sentence must have stunned the temple courts: people carrying the kind of past respectable society whispered about were entering God’s Kingdom ahead of men who knew the Scriptures. Jesus was not celebrating their sin. He was exposing something far more terrifying—the kind of heart that can look religious while refusing to repent.
Imagine standing there when Jesus said it.
Not in a nightclub.
Not in a brothel.
Not in some notorious district where everyone expected sinners to be found.
In the temple.
The place associated with worship. Prayer. Sacrifice. Scripture. Religious authority.
And standing before Jesus were chief priests and elders—men whose lives, at least outwardly, appeared to belong to God.
Then Jesus said something that must have landed like a thunderclap:
“Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.”
Matthew 21:31, KJV.
Read it again.
The tax collectors.
The prostitutes.
Ahead of you.
There is something almost scandalous about those words until you understand what Jesus was actually saying.
He was not saying prostitution was righteous.
He was not calling sexual immorality harmless.
He was not teaching that a sinful lifestyle somehow gives someone preferential access to God.
Jesus was confronting a far more subtle danger:
the possibility of being surrounded by religion while remaining resistant to God.
And perhaps that is why this passage can still make religious people uncomfortable.
Because it is easier to identify somebody else's visible scandal than our own invisible rebellion.
Matthew records Jesus' words in Greek:
“οἱ τελῶναι καὶ αἱ πόρναι προάγουσιν ὑμᾶς εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.”
Hoi telōnai kai hai pornai proagousin hymas eis tēn basileian tou theou.
In straightforward English:
“The tax collectors and the prostitutes are going ahead of you into the kingdom of God.”
Notice the word Matthew uses for prostitutes:
πόρναι — pornai.
There is no attempt to sanitize what Jesus said.
But there is another word worth noticing:
προάγουσιν — proagousin.
They are “going ahead,” “going before.”
Jesus was not merely announcing that notoriously sinful people could someday be admitted after the respectable people had secured the best seats.
He turned the expected order upside down.
They were going ahead.
Why?
Jesus explains it immediately.
“For John came unto you in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him…”
Matthew 21:32.
There it is.
The scandal was not that prostitutes had somehow become righteous because they were prostitutes.
The scandal was that sinners heard God's call and believed while religious authorities heard God's call and refused.
That changes everything.
And Jesus had already prepared the trap.
He told them about a father with two sons.
The father told the first son to work in his vineyard.
The son essentially said:
No.
But afterward he changed his mind and went.
Then the father approached the second son.
That son sounded wonderful.
“Yes, sir.”
Respectful.
Correct.
Compliant.
Religious-sounding.
Except he never went.
Then Jesus asked the question that forced His opponents to pronounce judgment upon themselves:
Which son did the father's will?
They answered:
The first.
Exactly.
The son whose beginning was rebellion but whose story changed.
The son whose first word was “no” but whose final direction became obedience.
Then came the blow:
Tax collectors and prostitutes are going into God's Kingdom ahead of you.
Suddenly the parable was no longer about two imaginary sons.
It was about the people standing in front of Jesus.
And it is about us.
One son had rebellion in his mouth but eventually obedience in his feet.
The other had obedience in his mouth but rebellion in his life.
And Jesus was asking:
Which one actually belonged to the Father's will?
That question reaches frighteningly close to home.
Because some of us learned how to say the right things a long time ago.
“Praise God.”
“God is good.”
“I'll pray for you.”
“I surrender all.”
We know when to stand.
We know when to sit.
We know the songs.
We know the verses.
We know how Christians are supposed to sound.
We may know enough theology to correct somebody else's doctrine.
Enough Scripture to win an argument.
Enough Christian vocabulary to convince everyone around us that everything between us and God is fine.
And still...
God may be pointing toward something in our life and saying, “Give Me that.”
That relationship.
That secret.
That bitterness.
That pride.
That hidden sexual sin.
That dishonesty.
That unforgiveness.
That addiction nobody knows about.
That hunger for people's approval.
That private compromise hidden beneath a public Christian identity.
And our lips keep saying,
“Yes, Lord.”
While our lives quietly answer,
“No.”
That is the danger Jesus exposed.
Not imperfect Christianity.
Hypocritical resistance.
Not struggling sinners crawling toward God.
People convinced they do not need to crawl.
There is an enormous difference.
The Gospel has room for the broken person crying, “God, have mercy on me.”
What it does not offer is a comfortable hiding place for self-righteousness.
Jesus repeatedly confronted people who believed their outward respectability placed them safely above “those people.”
And perhaps “those people” is one of the most dangerous phrases religion can produce.
Those addicts.
Those adulterers.
Those prostitutes.
Those prisoners.
Those drunks.
Those people with ruined marriages.
Those people who wrecked their families.
Those people with histories everyone knows.
Those people who don't look like us.
Those people who don't know what we know.
Those people.
Then Jesus walks directly into our carefully constructed hierarchy of respectable sinners and scandalous sinners...
and tears up the seating chart.
Because at the foot of the cross there is no VIP section for people whose sins were easier to hide.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
All.
The prostitute needs Christ.
The preacher needs Christ.
The addict needs Christ.
The elder needs Christ.
The prisoner needs Christ.
The person holding a Bible every Sunday needs Christ.
Different histories.
Different temptations.
Different consequences.
Same desperate need for a Savior.
And that is where this passage becomes beautiful instead of merely terrifying.
Because Jesus' statement means that your past does not possess veto power over God's grace.
Think about that.
Your worst chapter does not get the final sentence.
Your shame does not own the publishing rights to your story.
Your sexual past does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your addiction is not stronger than the Savior.
Your divorce does not make you untouchable.
Your prison record does not make you unreachable.
Your abortion does not place you beyond forgiveness.
Your betrayal does not make repentance meaningless.
Your years of rebellion do not force Jesus to stop at the door.
The question is not:
“Have you ever said no to God?”
The first son did.
The question is:
When God calls you now, will you turn?
That is where the Greek language in this passage becomes painfully beautiful.
Matthew says that afterward the first son, “μεταμεληθεὶς”—metamelētheis—went.
The word carries the idea of experiencing a change of mind accompanied by regret.
He looked at his refusal differently.
Something shifted.
And then he went.
Jesus uses the related wording again when confronting the religious leaders:
“οὐδὲ μετεμελήθητε ὕστερον”
“you did not afterward change your minds” or “feel regret” so as to believe.
They saw other sinners responding.
They saw lives changing.
They saw people they probably considered morally beneath them believing John's message.
And still they would not yield.
That was the catastrophe.
Not simply that they had sinned.
Everyone standing there needed mercy.
Their danger was that they could witness repentance and remain unrepentant.
Imagine being so certain that you are close to God that you cannot hear God telling you to come closer.
Imagine knowing Scripture and missing the One Scripture was pointing toward.
Imagine being able to recognize everybody else's sin except the pride keeping you from grace.
That is why the prostitute in Jesus' statement is not the punchline.
The unrepentant religious heart is.
And if we read this passage merely thinking, “Those Pharisees and religious leaders were terrible,” we may repeat the very mistake the passage exposes.
Because the safest response is not:
“Thank God I'm not like them.”
It is:
“Jesus... search me.”
Search the parts of me that learned Christian language without Christian surrender.
Search the part that judges someone else's visible wounds while hiding my own infection.
Search my motives.
Search my secret browser history.
Search my resentment.
Search what I do with money.
Search what happens when nobody is watching.
Search the things I excuse because they are socially acceptable among Christians.
Search my pride when somebody with a darker past than mine begins burning brighter for Jesus than I do.
Search me.
Because there is another heartbreaking possibility hidden inside this passage.
Some people who feel least worthy of God's Kingdom may be closer to repentance than people who assume they already belong there.
The prostitute knows something is broken.
The tax collector knows everybody despises him.
The addict knows the chains exist.
But religious pride can anesthetize the conscience.
You can mistake familiarity with Christianity for surrender to Christ.
You can mistake church attendance for regeneration.
You can mistake biblical knowledge for obedience.
You can mistake ministry activity for intimacy with Jesus.
You can even become skilled at discussing repentance without repenting.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave that illusion untouched.
That is why His words can wound.
The Great Physician sometimes exposes the infection because He intends to heal the patient.
Conviction is not Christ standing over you saying, “You are disgusting. Stay away.”
The Gospel invitation says something astonishingly different:
Come into the light.
Stop hiding.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Me.
Jesus did not come to tell sinners how impressive they could become at hiding their stains.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ did not die for an imaginary, cleaned-up version of you.
He knew.
Every secret.
Every failure.
Every lustful thought.
Every compromise.
Every betrayal.
Every moment you knew better and did it anyway.
Every promise to God you broke.
Every “yes, Lord” followed by a practical “no.”
And still the Son of God went to Calvary.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because sin matters so much that redemption required the blood of Christ.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
Isaiah 53:5.
Grace is not God pretending your sin was harmless.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty people could never provide for themselves.
Jesus bore judgment.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
And now forgiveness is not offered because you managed to become respectable enough to deserve it.
It is offered through Christ.
That means the Gospel destroys despair and pride at the same time.
Despair says:
“I have done too much for Jesus to want me.”
The cross answers:
Look at how far He went to save sinners.
Pride says:
“I am not as bad as those people.”
The cross answers:
Then why did the Son of God have to die for you?
Nobody boasts at Calvary.
Nobody.
The former prostitute cannot boast.
The lifelong church member cannot boast.
The recovering addict cannot boast.
The theologian cannot boast.
The pastor cannot boast.
The person reading this article cannot boast.
We come empty-handed.
And we leave clothed in mercy.
That is why Jesus' words about prostitutes are not an insult against prostitutes.
They are an announcement of astonishing grace.
People society had reduced to their sin were responding to God.
People whose reputations had become their identities were discovering that God could write another chapter.
People others whispered about could enter God's Kingdom.
Scandal was meeting grace.
And grace was having the final word.
Maybe that is exactly why you found this today.
Maybe everybody thinks you're fine.
But you're tired.
Tired of maintaining the Christian version of yourself everyone expects.
Tired of saying “yes” publicly while living “no” privately.
Or maybe your story is different.
Maybe you carry the kind of past religious people remember even after God forgives you.
Maybe you have wondered whether Jesus truly wants people like you.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But Jesus is a greater Savior.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is not cleaning yourself sufficiently before approaching Christ.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the One who can save you from it.
Do not confuse grace with permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who receives sinners also calls sinners to follow Him.
Grace does not merely forgive the old road.
Grace teaches us to walk a new one.
Jesus does not say, “Your chains don't matter.”
He breaks chains.
He does not say, “Stay exactly where sin left you.”
He says, “Follow Me.”
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal renamed as righteousness.
Not sin celebrated.
Not holiness abandoned.
Scandal redeemed.
Guilt forgiven.
Shame confronted by mercy.
Rebellion interrupted by repentance.
Dead hearts made alive through Christ.
Stories everyone else thought were finished placed into the scarred hands of Jesus.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your first answer to God was no.
Maybe you spent ten years saying no.
Thirty years.
Maybe last night was another no.
The first son's story tells you something:
Your first answer does not have to become your final answer.
You can turn.
Today.
Not when you feel more spiritual.
Not after you repair your reputation.
Not after everyone forgets what you did.
Today.
“Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change me. I believe You died and rose again. I surrender what I have been hiding. Make my life Yours.”
Those are not magic words.
Christ is not looking for a formula.
He is calling people to repentance and faith.
And perhaps the most dangerous response to this article would be admiration without surrender.
“That was powerful.”
Then scroll.
“That convicted me.”
Then change nothing.
Remember the second son.
He said the beautiful thing.
Then never went.
So don't merely agree with Jesus today.
Respond to Him.
If something hidden has been exposed while you were reading, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not as theater.
Not to impress anyone.
Let it be your public acknowledgment that you are done pretending sin is harmless.
If you are spiritually exhausted and need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
If grace has been rebuilding something you thought was permanently destroyed, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if you are exhausted from maintaining appearances while something inside you is collapsing, comment, “no more hiding.”
Sometimes another wounded person needs to discover that he or she is not the only Christian still fighting.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support proves that you glorify God.
Scripture never permits us to sell righteousness or turn generosity into a spiritual entrance fee.
We glorify God through Christ-centered faith, obedience, love, generosity, worship, and lives surrendered to Him.
But one practical way you can freely choose to support Gospel-centered work is by helping us continue creating and sharing biblical content and discipleship resources.
A donation cannot cleanse you.
A Christian T-shirt cannot redeem you.
A ministry cannot forgive your sins.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
That is the entire point.
The prostitute does not enter because she paid.
The religious leader does not enter because he performed.
The sinner comes empty-handed to mercy.
And Christ receives those who come to Him.
So share the Gospel because somebody needs it.
Support faithful Gospel work because you want the truth to travel farther.
Give because grace has taught your heart generosity—not because anyone sold you God's approval.
And above everything else...
come to Jesus.
Because someday the titles disappear.
Pastor.
Leader.
Donor.
Church member.
Influencer.
Successful.
Respectable.
Broken.
Addict.
Adulterer.
Prostitute.
Scandal.
And one question remains infinitely more important than the labels people attached to us:
What did we do with Jesus Christ?
Perhaps that is why Jesus mentioned prostitutes while confronting religious leaders.
He was destroying the illusion that respectable appearances can substitute for repentance.
He was announcing that the Kingdom doors were open even to people society had written off.
And He was warning religious people that proximity to holy things is not the same as surrender to the Holy One.
The first son said no...
then turned.
The second son said yes...
then stayed where he was.
So perhaps the question Jesus leaves ringing through the centuries is not:
“What did you say?”
It is:
“Will you come?”
The frightening thing is not that your story contains scandal.
The frightening thing would be refusing the grace that could give your scandal a different ending.
Come home.
The Father is still calling.
Jesus is still saving.
Grace is still greater than the chapter you thought destroyed everything.
And the cross still stands as God's declaration that sinners do not have to remain what sin made them.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ, it does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY HID IN THE VINEYARDS UNTIL THE WOMEN BEGAN TO DANCE
paragraphs: THEY HID IN THE VINEYARDS UNTIL THE WOMEN BEGAN TO DANCE

Israel told the surviving men of Benjamin to wait among the vines of Shiloh. Then the young women came out dancing. What happened next is one of the Bible’s most disturbing scenes—and the final words of Judges tell us exactly why we should be horrified.
There are Bible stories we teach children.
There are Bible stories we embroider on pillows.
There are stories about lions whose mouths were shut, seas that opened, giants that fell, prison doors that broke apart in the night.
And then there is Judges 21.
Men hiding in vineyards.
Young women dancing.
A signal.
A sudden rush from the vines.
Women seized and carried away.
And behind it all, an entire nation desperately trying to repair a catastrophe that its own sin had helped create.
If you have never heard this story preached, there may be a reason.
It is uncomfortable.
Actually, uncomfortable is too gentle a word.
It is horrifying.
And perhaps the most dangerous way to read it is to open the Bible, see that Israel did it, and automatically assume that God approved it.
He did not command this scheme.
The text never says He did.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Judges 21 is not a beautiful picture of biblical courtship.
It is a funeral portrait of what human beings become when everyone decides that whatever seems right to them must therefore be right.
And before this story ends, Scripture leaves us with a sentence that sounds frighteningly modern:
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
Judges 21:25, KJV
But to understand why men were crouching among the vineyards of Shiloh waiting for dancing women, we have to walk backward through the wreckage.
And the road is soaked in tears.
The catastrophe begins before chapter 21.

Judges 19 records one of the darkest episodes in the Old Testament. A Levite and his concubine arrive in Gibeah, a Benjaminite city. During the night, wicked men surround the house where they are staying. What follows is sexual violence, brutality, abandonment, and death.
The woman dies.
Her body is divided and sent throughout Israel.
The nation is horrified.
Israel gathers against Gibeah and demands that Benjamin surrender the guilty men.
Benjamin refuses.
War follows.

Israel fights Benjamin, and the conflict becomes devastating. Thousands die. Benjamin is nearly annihilated. Judges 20:47 says only six hundred Benjaminite men escape into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon.
Six hundred men.
Almost an entire tribe has disappeared.
Then Israel looks at what has happened.
And weeps.
Judges 21:2–3 records them coming before God, lifting their voices, and crying bitterly:
“O LORD God of Israel, why is this come to pass in Israel, that there should be to day one tribe lacking in Israel?”
There is something painfully human about that question.
They are grieving a catastrophe after participating in the chain of decisions that produced it.
How often do we do the same thing?
We ignore compromise while it is small.
Excuse anger while it is growing.
Protect pride while it is hardening.
Tolerate lust while it is hiding.
Feed resentment while nobody can see it.
Then one day we stand in the wreckage asking:
“God… how did everything get here?”
That is one of the terrible lessons of Judges.
Sin rarely tells you where it is taking you.
It simply asks for the next step.
Then another.
Then another.
Until eventually you turn around and cannot recognize the landscape behind you.
Israel now faced another problem.
Earlier, the Israelites had sworn an oath:
“There shall not any of us give his daughter unto Benjamin to wife.”
Judges 21:1, KJV
Their anger had produced a vow.
Their war had nearly erased Benjamin.
Now their vow threatened to finish what the war had begun.
So instead of humbly recognizing the moral disaster surrounding them, they began looking for loopholes.
That is where the story becomes even darker.
Israel discovered that the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead had not joined the assembly.
An army was sent against the city.
The text records another slaughter, after which four hundred young virgin women were spared and brought to the surviving Benjaminites.
But there were six hundred surviving men.
Four hundred women were not enough.
Two hundred men remained without wives.
And Israel still had its oath.
They could not, according to their vow, “give” their daughters to Benjamin.
So someone devised a solution.
Not a command from God.
Not a prophetic revelation.
Not a beautiful act of providence presented for imitation.
A human scheme.
Judges 21:19–21 explains that there was a yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh. The Benjaminites were instructed to hide among the vineyards and watch.
When the daughters of Shiloh came out to dance, the men were told to emerge from hiding and take wives for themselves.
The Hebrew makes the force of the scene difficult to soften.
Judges 21:21 contains the verb:
וַחֲטַפְתֶּם
waḥăṭaptem
From the Hebrew root חטף (ḥ-ṭ-p), carrying the sense of snatching, seizing, or taking suddenly.
The instruction is essentially:
When the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance, come out from the vineyards and seize for yourselves, each man, his wife.
The women are described as coming:
לָחוּל בַּמְּחֹלוֹת
lāḥûl bammeḥōlôt
—to dance in the dances.
Picture the scene.
A festival.
Music.
Movement.
Young women celebrating.
Vineyards nearby.
And hidden among those vines are men waiting for the appointed moment.
The women do not appear to know the plan.
The narrative does not record their consent.
Then the signal comes.
The men emerge.
And two hundred women are taken.
It is supposed to make you uncomfortable.
More than uncomfortable.
The Book of Judges has been showing us, chapter after chapter, what happens when covenant faithfulness collapses.
This is not Scripture saying, “Look how people should behave.”
This is Scripture saying, “Look how far people can fall.”
That difference matters whenever we read violent or morally disturbing biblical narratives.
The Bible faithfully recording an event does not automatically mean God morally endorses every action inside that event.
Scripture sometimes shows human beings at their best.
And sometimes Scripture refuses to look away when human beings are at their worst.
Judges is filled with precisely that downward movement.
The book does not end with Israel flourishing.
It ends with Israel morally disintegrating.
And then comes the final verdict:
בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Bayyāmîm hāhēm ʾên melekh bəyiśrāʾēl; ʾîš hayyāšār bəʿênāw yaʿăśeh.
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
That sentence is not merely political information.
Within Judges, it functions as a devastating description of Israel’s moral condition.
Notice the tragedy.
The people knew religious language.
They assembled.
They made vows.
They offered sacrifices.
They spoke about preserving a tribe of Israel.
They even found a way to keep the technical wording of their oath.
“We cannot give our daughters to Benjamin.”
So what did they do?
They created circumstances in which Benjamin could take somebody else’s daughters.
Do you see how terrifying self-righteousness can become?
Human beings can become so committed to proving that they have technically kept one rule that they become blind to the people being crushed by their solution.
And suddenly Judges 21 stops feeling ancient.
Because we still know how to do this.
We know how to rename compromise.
We know how to search for loopholes.
We know how to protect appearances.
We know how to sound religious while avoiding repentance.
We know how to say, “Technically, I didn’t lie,” when we deliberately deceived someone.
“Technically, I didn’t cheat,” while feeding emotional intimacy we know belongs somewhere else.
“Technically, I forgave them,” while secretly enjoying their suffering.
“Technically, nobody knows,” while deleting messages before someone sees them.
“Technically, it isn’t adultery.”
“Technically, it isn’t stealing.”
“Technically, I never said those exact words.”
And slowly…
almost imperceptibly…
we begin doing what is right in our own eyes.
That is why this story is not merely about Benjamin.
It is about us.
The most frightening vineyard in Judges 21 may not be the vineyard at Shiloh.
It may be the hidden vineyard inside the human heart.
The place where motives crouch.
The place nobody sees.
The private browser.
The deleted conversation.
The secret resentment.
The addiction disguised as stress relief.
The bitterness disguised as discernment.
The pride disguised as standards.
The manipulation disguised as love.
The greed disguised as ambition.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The lust disguised as loneliness.
The disobedience disguised as “following my heart.”
We are remarkably talented at giving respectable names to things we do not want to surrender.
And that is why we need more than behavior modification.
We need a King.
Not merely an earthly ruler.
We need the King toward whom the whole biblical story ultimately points.
Jesus Christ.
Judges ends with:
“There was no king in Israel.”
The Gospel announces:
The King has come.
And what kind of King is He?
Not a king hiding in the vineyard waiting to take.
A King who enters the garden knowing He will be taken.
Do not miss that contrast.
In Judges, broken humanity keeps sacrificing other people to preserve itself.
In the Gospel, Jesus gives Himself to rescue sinners.
On the night He was betrayed, Christ entered Gethsemane.
Another dark place.
Another place surrounded by human sin.
But Jesus was not there hunting victims.
He was preparing to become the willing sacrifice.
When armed men arrived, Christ did not need to be overpowered because He had already chosen obedience to the Father.
The innocent One would stand in the place of the guilty.
The King would wear thorns.
The Judge would be judged.
The Creator would be mocked by creatures whose lungs were breathing because He sustained them.
Hands He formed would strike Him.
Voices He gave would condemn Him.
Men would drive nails through the hands that had healed the sick, touched lepers, blessed children, and broken bread for the hungry.
And from the cross would come words that still destroy the illusion that any sinner is beyond mercy:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
Luke 23:34, KJV
This is where scandal collides with grace.
Grace does not say the scandal was acceptable.
Grace does not rename evil.
Grace does not tell the wounded that their suffering did not matter.
Grace tells the truth about sin so completely that the Son of God had to die to deal with it.
And then grace tells sinners something almost impossible to believe:
You may come home.
Not because your sin was small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
The Gospel is not God pretending you never sinned.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin at the cross and offering forgiveness to everyone who turns to Christ in repentance and faith.
That includes the respectable sinner.
The secret sinner.
The religious sinner.
The sexually broken sinner.
The angry sinner.
The addicted sinner.
The hypocrite.
The person who has spent years hiding in emotional vineyards hoping nobody discovers what is really there.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to come.
That is why repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is connected with μετάνοια (metanoia)—a turning of mind and life toward God.
Jesus did not preach, “Hide better.”
He proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Mark 1:15, KJV
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this has been avoiding.
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret weekend.
Not after you delete the evidence.
Not after you make yourself respectable enough to pray again.
Come into the light.
Because the Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself sufficiently, and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
Christ receives repentant sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9, KJV
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those words are for people with histories.
People with regrets.
People who wish they could go backward.
People who have lain awake at 2:17 in the morning replaying something they said five years ago.
People terrified that if everyone knew the whole story, nobody would look at them the same way again.
Listen carefully.
Christianity does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears when you repent.
Some wounds require restitution.
Some relationships require difficult truth.
Some crimes require justice.
Some consequences remain.
Repentance is not an escape hatch from accountability.
But your past does not have greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 8:1, KJV
In Christ.
That is the difference.
Judges shows humanity desperately trying to repair human disaster with more human schemes.
The Gospel shows God accomplishing what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Redemption.
Not through another loophole.
Through a cross.
Not through pretending evil never happened.
Through Christ bearing sin.
Not through declaring sinners innocent because their actions were harmless.
Through justification by grace because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
And then comes resurrection.
The stone moves.
The grave empties.
Death loses its final word.
The King lives.
Suddenly the last sentence of Judges is not the last sentence of the Bible.
“There was no king…”
is not where the story ends.
There is a King.
His name is Jesus.
And perhaps that is why this strange, painful, horrifying chapter deserves to be read instead of hidden.
Because Judges 21 exposes what happens when human beings become their own moral authority.
It shows the danger of vows made in anger.
The consequences of collective violence.
The moral blindness created by self-justification.
The vulnerability of innocent people when powerful people become obsessed with solving problems they themselves helped create.
And it leaves us aching for something better.
Someone better.
A righteous King.
Jesus.
Ask God to search you.
Where are you doing what is right in your own eyes?
Where have you built a theological loophole around something Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What have you renamed because calling it by its biblical name would require repentance?
Who has been hurt while you were protecting your reputation?
What secret are you exhausted from carrying?
What vineyard are you hiding in?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If something hidden was exposed while reading this, you do not have to describe your sin publicly. But if you want others to know they are not fighting alone, comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If your faith has been exhausted lately but you refuse to walk away from Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Somebody reading quietly tonight may need evidence that Jesus still restores broken lives.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
Someone hiding.
Someone ashamed.
Someone who believes Christianity is only for people with clean histories.
Someone quietly destroying himself.
Someone who has been wounded by the sins of others.
Someone who has confused the terrible actions recorded in Scripture with the commands of God.
Or send this privately.
Save it too.
There are truths you understand differently when the night becomes difficult.

We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him. And one practical way believers may choose to participate in Gospel work is by supporting faithful teaching and helping biblical truth reach other people.
And there is more waiting for believers who are hungry to grow.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is not merchandise.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
Ephesians 2:8, KJV
The Gospel Warrior exists to point toward the King—not replace Him.
And maybe tonight, after all these centuries, those vineyards outside Shiloh still have something to say.
Human beings hide.
Human beings rationalize.
Human beings hurt one another.
Human beings create disasters and then create new disasters trying to repair them without surrendering to God.
But Jesus walks directly into our darkness.
He calls sin what it is.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He restores what shame said could never be restored.
He takes people whose stories look permanently stained and begins writing something grace alone could write.
So come out of the vineyard.
Stop hiding.
Stop negotiating.
Stop telling God why your particular compromise needs an exception.
Bring Him the real story.
The ugly chapter.
The secret chapter.
The chapter you wish nobody had ever written.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because the most unforgettable truth in this entire disturbing story is not that broken men once hid among vineyards waiting for women to dance.
It is that thousands of years later, broken people are still hiding—
and the King is still calling them into the light.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story, but when you surrender the pen to Christ, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SHOULD YOUR SPRINGS BE SCATTERED ABROAD?” THE SEXUAL METAPHOR HIDDEN IN PROVERBS 5
paragraphs: “SHOULD YOUR SPRINGS BE SCATTERED ABROAD?” THE SEXUAL METAPHOR HIDDEN IN PROVERBS 5
The Bible Says Something About Sexual Desire That Many Christians Were Never Taught—and It May Change the Way You Understand Temptation, Marriage, Shame, and Grace
There is a sentence in Proverbs that sounds almost innocent in English.
Until you understand what Solomon is talking about.
“Should your springs be dispersed outside, your streams of water in the wide plazas?” — Proverbs 5:16
Springs.
Water.
Streets.
At first glance, it sounds like irrigation.
It isn’t.
And when you read the words surrounding it, the meaning becomes impossible to ignore.

This is Scripture speaking with startling honesty about sexual desire, marital faithfulness, temptation, pleasure, consequences, and the devastating human tendency to pour something sacred into places where it was never meant to go.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 5:16 reads:
יָפוּצוּ מַעְיְנֹתֶיךָ חוּצָה בָּרְחֹבוֹת פַּלְגֵי־מָיִם
Yāfūtsū maʿyenōteykhā ḥūtsāh, bārəḥōvōt palgê-māyim.
Literally, the picture is of “your springs” being dispersed outside and streams of water flowing in the public squares.

The verb יָפוּצוּ, yāfūtsū, carries the idea of being scattered or dispersed. מַעְיְנֹתֶיךָ, maʿyenōteykhā, means “your springs” or “your fountains.” חוּצָה, ḥūtsāh, points outward—outside. Then comes בָּרְחֹבוֹת, bārəḥōvōt: in the broad places, streets, or public squares.
But Proverbs does not leave the metaphor floating without context.
The verse immediately before it says:
שְׁתֵה־מַיִם מִבּוֹרֶךָ וְנֹזְלִים מִתּוֹךְ בְּאֵרֶךָ
“Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well.” — Proverbs 5:15
Then comes the question about scattering your springs abroad.
Then:
“Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.” — Proverbs 5:17
And then the imagery becomes unmistakably marital:

“May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife you married in your youth—a loving doe, a graceful deer; may her breasts satisfy you at all times, may you be captivated by her love always.” — Proverbs 5:18–19
The water is not really the point.
Faithfulness is.
Desire is.
Sexual intimacy is.
Covenant is.
And the question beneath the question is devastating:
Why would you take what belongs inside covenant and scatter it outside?

The NET Bible notes that the “springs” being dispersed form part of an extended metaphor contrasting exclusive marital intimacy with sexual activity outside marriage. Scholarly interpreters broadly recognize Proverbs 5:15–20 as erotic imagery urging marital faithfulness, although they differ over precisely how narrowly each water image should be identified. Some interpreters understand the springs and streams in verses 16–17 specifically as imagery for male sexual potency or semen; others treat the imagery more broadly as the husband’s sexuality and sexual expression. Either way, the central message does not depend upon choosing the narrowest interpretation: sexual desire is not condemned, but it is directed toward covenant faithfulness.
That distinction matters.
Because some Christians grew up believing that holiness meant pretending sexuality barely existed.
Don’t talk about it.
Don’t admit temptation.
Don’t admit desire.
Don’t ask questions.
And if you failed sexually, hide it quickly enough that nobody discovers what happened.
But Proverbs 5 does something radically different.
God does not whisper awkwardly about sexuality.
He speaks directly into it.
The same chapter that warns about adultery also tells a husband to delight in his wife.
The same chapter that warns against forbidden sexual pleasure celebrates covenant sexual pleasure.
That means the biblical message is not:
Desire is dirty.
The message is:
Desire is powerful.
And powerful things must be guarded.
Fire inside a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire unleashed through the house can destroy it.
Water directed into the right place gives life.
Water scattered where it does not belong is wasted.
And sexual desire—one of the strongest appetites many human beings will ever experience—is capable of bonding, delight, tenderness, vulnerability, procreation, companionship, and covenant intimacy.
But separated from faithfulness, that same appetite can leave wreckage behind.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that wreckage feels like.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been watching after everyone goes to sleep.
Maybe nobody knows about the messages you deleted.
The second account.
The private conversation.
The emotional attachment you keep calling “just friendship.”
The pornography history you clear.
The flirtation you justify because “nothing physical happened.”
The fantasy you keep feeding.
The person you know you should stop contacting.
The marriage you have emotionally abandoned while still sleeping in the same house.
Or maybe you are not the person who wandered.
Maybe you are the person who was wounded by somebody else’s wandering.
You discovered the messages.
You saw the browser history.
You heard the confession.
You found out there was another person.
And suddenly a sentence from Proverbs written thousands of years ago does not feel ancient at all.
“Should your springs be scattered abroad?”

That question reaches through history and sits beside us in the age of smartphones, disappearing messages, private browsing, dating apps, pornography, secret accounts, emotional affairs, and endless digital access to bodies that do not belong to us.
The technology changed.
The human heart did not.
We are still tempted to scatter what God calls us to steward.
And notice something uncomfortable about Proverbs 5.
The chapter does not merely say, “Adultery is against the rules.”
It shows where the road goes.
Earlier in the chapter, temptation is described as sweet at first and bitter afterward.
That is how sin often works.
