Acts 15:37–38 tells us that Barnabas was determined to take Mark, but Paul did not consider it wise to take someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not continued with them in the work.
You can almost feel both sides.
Barnabas looks at Mark and seems to see a man worth another opportunity.
Paul looks at what happened in Pamphylia and sees a man who had already abandoned the mission once.
Barnabas is thinking about restoration.
Paul is thinking about reliability.
Barnabas sees what Mark might become.
Paul remembers what Mark had done.
And Scripture does something remarkably honest next.
It does not airbrush the apostles into stained-glass superheroes.
Acts 15:39 says:
“ἐγένετο δὲ παροξυσμός”
egeneto de paroxysmos.
There arose a sharp disagreement.
The word Luke uses is παροξυσμός — paroxysmos.
It carries the sense of a sharp provocation, irritation, or intense disagreement. It is the word from which English gets “paroxysm.”
This was not two men smiling politely and saying, “We simply have different leadership philosophies.”
Something hurt.
Something became sharp.
The disagreement became serious enough that Paul and Barnabas separated.
Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus.
Paul chose Silas and went another direction.
Sit with that for a moment.
Paul.
Barnabas.
Separated.
These were not immature strangers who had accomplished nothing together.
Barnabas had played an enormous role in Paul's own story.
After Saul's conversion, many disciples were understandably afraid of him. Acts 9:27 tells us that Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, explaining what had happened to him.
When others remembered Saul as dangerous...
Barnabas saw what grace was doing.
Think about the painful irony.
Barnabas once stood beside a man whose past made other believers suspicious.
That man was Paul.
Years later, Barnabas stood beside another man whose past failure made Paul unwilling to take him.
That man was Mark.
The same Barnabas who once believed that Paul's past did not have to determine Paul's future now refused to believe that Mark's failure had to determine Mark's future.
That does not automatically make Paul wicked.
And it does not mean Barnabas was incapable of error.
The Bible does not explicitly tell us, “Barnabas was completely right and Paul was completely wrong,” or the reverse.
We should not force Scripture to declare a winner where Scripture itself does not.
Paul's concern was understandable.
Missionary work in the first century was not a comfortable ministry conference.
There were dangerous journeys, persecution, physical suffering, uncertainty, opposition, and enormous responsibility. Paul knew firsthand what the mission could cost.
Perhaps from Paul's perspective, the question was not whether Mark could ever be forgiven.
The question was whether Mark was ready to be trusted again with this particular assignment.
Those are not always the same question.
Forgiveness can be given freely.
Trust can require rebuilding.
Reconciliation can be real while wisdom still recognizes consequences.
Grace does not require pretending that failure never happened.
And Barnabas apparently saw something else.
Mark was more than his failure.

Colossians 4:10 later identifies Mark as Barnabas's cousin. There was a family relationship between them, but Scripture gives us no permission to dismiss Barnabas's decision as mere nepotism. What we actually see is Barnabas taking Mark with him when Paul would not.
Barnabas did what his name had come to represent.
Acts 4:36 tells us that the apostles called Joseph “Barnabas,” meaning “son of encouragement.”
And sometimes encouragement is not telling somebody that what they did was okay.
Sometimes encouragement is looking at somebody who failed and saying:
“What you did matters.
But it does not have to be the final thing you do.”
Maybe somebody reading this needs exactly that distinction.
Your sin matters.
Your choices matter.
The people you hurt matter.
Repentance matters.
Consequences matter.
But because of Jesus Christ, your worst chapter does not have sovereign authority over the rest of your story.
Jesus does.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin never happened.
The Gospel is infinitely more costly than that.
Christ entered history, lived without sin, went willingly to the cross, bore sin's judgment, died, and rose again. Forgiveness is not cheap optimism. Grace was purchased at the cross.
That means Christianity gives us something the world struggles to understand.
We do not have to minimize failure in order to believe in restoration.
We can tell the truth about both.
Mark left.
Paul did not trust him for the next journey.
Barnabas took him anyway.
And then the years moved forward.
This is where the story becomes breathtaking.
Because Mark does not remain frozen in Acts 13.
He grows.
Something changes.
We are not given every conversation.
We are not shown every prayer.
We do not know how many nights Mark remembered turning back.
We do not know what Barnabas said to him on the ship to Cyprus.
We do not know how many times Mark had to prove himself when nobody was applauding.
We do not know whether Paul and Mark eventually sat across from one another and talked through what happened.
Scripture does not give us those scenes.
So we should not pretend it does.
But Scripture gives us something even better than speculation.
It gives us the later evidence.
In Philemon 24, Paul includes Mark among his fellow workers.
Read that again.
His fellow worker.
The man Paul once refused to take on the journey was later named among Paul's συνεργοί—his co-workers.
Then in Colossians 4:10, Mark appears again in Paul's circle, and Paul gives instructions concerning his reception.
The relationship was not permanently shattered.
The failed worker had become a fellow worker.
But there is one more verse.
And once you understand the history behind it, it hits differently.
Paul is nearing the end of his life.
Second Timothy carries the atmosphere of finality. Paul speaks of having fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith.
The missionary who once said, in effect, “I don't want Mark coming with us” now has very little road left.
And in 2 Timothy 4:11 he tells Timothy:
“Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.”
The Greek is beautiful:
“ἔστιν γάρ μοι εὔχρηστος εἰς διακονίαν”
estin gar moi euchrēstos eis diakonian.
“For he is useful to me for ministry/service.”
Εὔχρηστος — euchrēstos.
Useful.
Serviceable.
Beneficial.
Profitable for the work.
Do you see it?
Paul did not merely tolerate Mark.
He wanted him.
The man once considered unsuitable for the journey became useful to Paul in ministry.
That is restoration.
Not pretending Pamphylia never happened.
Not rewriting history.
Not calling abandonment faithfulness.
Not lowering the standard until failure no longer means anything.
Transformation.
Mark became someone Paul wanted beside him.
There is a Gospel-shaped lesson here that reaches far beyond one disagreement between missionaries.
Some of us are still living emotionally in our own Pamphylia.
The place where we turned around.
The marriage we damaged.
The promise we broke.
The ministry we abandoned.
The temptation we returned to.
The season when fear won.
The opportunity we wasted.
The person we disappointed.
The faith we pretended to have while secretly becoming cold inside.
And years later, even after repentance, a voice keeps whispering:
“You left once.
You failed once.
Everybody knows what you did.
Why would God use you now?”
But the Gospel does not tell you to answer that accusation by saying, “My failure wasn't serious.”
The Gospel teaches you to answer differently.
“My failure was serious enough that Christ had to die for sinners like me.
And His grace is powerful enough that my failure does not have to own me anymore.”
There is a dangerous counterfeit grace that says nothing needs to change.
Biblical grace says Christ receives sinners and then transforms them.
John Mark's story is powerful precisely because he does not remain the man who walked away.
Grace did not merely comfort him in failure.
Grace carried him beyond it.
And perhaps this is why the disagreement between Paul and Barnabas speaks so powerfully to relationships inside the Church.
Sometimes you will be Paul.
Someone has failed you, and you are struggling to trust them again.
Do not confuse forgiveness with pretending wisdom does not matter.
You can forgive someone without immediately returning every responsibility they once carried.
Restoration and accountability are not enemies.
Sometimes you will be Barnabas.
Everyone else sees what somebody did.
You see what Christ might still do with them.
You refuse to call evil good, but you also refuse to bury a repentant person underneath the rubble of yesterday.
You walk beside them while character is rebuilt.
And sometimes...
you are Mark.
That may be the hardest place of all.
You know you failed.
You know the criticism is not completely imaginary.
You cannot blame everybody else.
There really was a moment when you turned back.
There really was a responsibility you dropped.
There really was damage.
And now you have a decision.
Will shame become your identity?
Or will failure become the place where repentance begins?
Maybe you cannot return to exactly what you had.
Maybe some consequences remain.
Maybe some people will need time before they trust you.
Maybe certain doors will never reopen.
But Jesus Christ is not limited to reopening old doors.
He can make you faithful in places you never expected to stand.
This is where the theme of Scripture becomes painfully personal:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by lying about the scandal.
By redeeming the sinner.
Peter denied Christ and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians and became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
Mark abandoned a missionary journey and later became useful to the very apostle who once refused to take him.
Different stories.
Different circumstances.
The same Savior at the center.
And this is important: redemption does not mean every broken human relationship will end exactly like Paul and Mark's relationship did.
Some relationships remain distant.
Some wounds require boundaries.
Some consequences last.
Some people never reconcile this side of eternity.
Our hope is not in manufacturing a perfect ending to every earthly conflict.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
He is the One who saves.
He is the One who forgives.
He is the One who sanctifies.
He is the One who can take a life scarred by sin, failure, fear, and regret and make it useful for His glory.
So maybe the question is no longer:
“Did you fail?”
Maybe the question is:
“What are you going to do with the grace Christ is offering you now?”
Repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Make restitution where restitution is possible and appropriate.
Stop defending what God is asking you to surrender.
Receive forgiveness through Christ rather than trying to punish yourself into purity.
Then get up.
Walk faithfully.
Quietly, if necessary.
Slowly, if necessary.
One obedient day at a time.
You do not need to convince everyone overnight.
Mark's transformation was not recorded in one dramatic paragraph.
We see it across years.
Faithfulness has a way of writing sentences that apologies alone cannot write.
And maybe somebody in your life is a Mark right now.
Do not enable them.
Do not excuse destructive behavior.
But do not assume you know the final chapter either.
You may be staring at someone's Acts 13 while God is still writing their 2 Timothy 4.
That sentence deserves to stay with you.
You may be staring at someone's Acts 13 while God is still writing their 2 Timothy 4.
Maybe that someone is your child.
Your spouse.
Your friend.
A former ministry leader.
A believer who fell badly.
Maybe it is the person looking back at you in the mirror.
Jesus Christ specializes in stories that would be hopeless if the final chapter belonged to human failure.
The cross itself looked like catastrophe on Friday.
The tomb looked final.
Then Sunday came.
That is the heartbeat of Christianity.
Death does not get the last word.
Sin does not get the last word.
Shame does not get the last word.
Failure does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
Be honest.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes an honest sentence is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around ourselves.
Not as a superstition.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Scripture would never allow us to turn financial support or social engagement into a test of genuine faith.
We glorify God through Christ-centered faith, obedience, love, holiness, generosity, witness, and lives surrendered to Him.

But if this ministry is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent of sin, endure suffering, and grow in faith, supporting and sharing the work can be one practical expression of stewardship. It helps put biblical truth in front of people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read a story that reaches the wound they have been hiding.
Because one day you may become Mark again.
One day an old failure may start speaking louder than God's grace.
Come back and remember:
“Take Mark... for he is useful to me for ministry.”
And please do something that costs nothing.
There is a Mark somewhere who thinks leaving once means he can never come home.
There is a Barnabas wondering whether encouraging that broken person is worth the trouble.
There is a Paul learning that someone he once could not trust may not remain the person he remembers.
And there is somebody silently scrolling tonight who has already sentenced themselves to a future Jesus never pronounced over them.
Send this story into their darkness.
But above everything else...
come to Christ.
Because Barnabas cannot save Mark.
Paul cannot save Mark.
A ministry cannot save Mark.
A second chance by itself cannot save Mark.
Only Jesus can save sinners.
And the deepest miracle in this story is not simply that a man who once abandoned a mission eventually became useful again.

It is that the Gospel creates a world where failure can be confessed without becoming identity, where forgiveness does not require dishonesty, where consequences do not cancel grace, where broken people can become faithful people, and where yesterday's disappointment does not possess the authority to write tomorrow's ending.
Maybe you have been calling yourself by the name of your worst chapter.
Jesus is still writing.
The place where everyone thought your story ended may become the place from which grace writes the sentence nobody saw coming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Wanting Sex a Sin?
paragraphs:
Is Wanting Sex a Sin?
The desire you’re ashamed to admit may not be the sin you think it is—but what you do with that desire can either pull you toward God’s design or quietly teach your heart to live without Him.
There are questions Christians ask out loud.
And then there are questions we type into a search bar at 1:17 in the morning.
Questions we delete from our history.
Questions we would never ask during Bible study because everyone there seems so holy, so disciplined, so untouched by the struggle happening inside us.
This is one of those questions.
Is wanting sex a sin?
Maybe you’re single and the desire feels overwhelming.
Maybe you love Jesus, genuinely love Him, but your body still wants intimacy.
Maybe you’ve prayed, fasted, distracted yourself, worked longer hours, gone to the gym, opened your Bible, closed your Bible, opened your phone instead—and immediately wished you hadn’t.
Maybe you’re married, yet somehow lonelier beside your spouse than you ever imagined marriage could feel.
Maybe sexual desire has become tangled with pornography, fantasy, masturbation, memories, rejection, betrayal, loneliness, or shame.
Or maybe nothing dramatic happened at all.
Maybe you simply want sex.

And because nobody taught you how to distinguish desire from lust, temptation from consent, sexuality from sexual sin, you began wondering whether something was spiritually wrong with you simply because your body could still feel.
So hear this carefully:
Sexual desire itself is not inherently sinful.
Scripture does not teach that God created human beings as sexual creatures and then condemned them for possessing sexual desire.
Quite the opposite.
Before there was sexual immorality, before pornography, adultery, prostitution, exploitation, secret browser histories, broken marriages, or human shame, there was Eden.
And there was a marriage.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
ʿAl-kēn yaʿăzāḇ-ʾîš ʾeṯ-ʾāḇîw wəʾeṯ-ʾimmô, wəḏāḇaq bəʾištô, wəhāyû ləḇāśār ʾeḥāḏ.
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
That expression—בָּשָׂר אֶחָד, basar echad, “one flesh”—is not embarrassed by physical union.
God designed covenantal sexual union.
And notice something Christians sometimes forget:
Genesis 2 happens before Genesis 3.
Sex was not invented after humanity sinned.
Sexual union belongs to God’s good creation.
The Fall did not create sexuality.
The Fall distorted it.
That distinction changes everything.

Because Christianity does not teach that your body is disgusting and your spirit must somehow escape it. Scripture teaches that God created embodied human beings, male and female, and pronounced His creation “very good” in Genesis 1:31.
The problem, therefore, is not simply that human beings experience desire.
The deeper question is:
What is your desire asking you to do—and who has authority over it?
This is where Jesus takes us somewhere uncomfortable.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus says:
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
The crucial Greek expression includes:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
The verb ἐπιθυμέω—epithymeō means to desire, long for, or covet depending upon its context.
That matters enormously.
Because desire itself cannot automatically mean sinful lust in every biblical context.
The related noun ἐπιθυμία—epithymia can even describe a desire that is not evil. Jesus uses the related verb in Luke 22:15 when He speaks of His earnest desire to eat the Passover with His disciples.
So Matthew 5 cannot responsibly be reduced to:
“If you notice someone is attractive, you have committed adultery.”
Jesus is confronting something deeper.

He is exposing the deliberate cultivation of sexual desire toward someone in a way that violates covenant faithfulness—the inward movement that turns another human being into the object of possessive sexual consumption.
There is a difference between experiencing attraction and choosing to feed lust.
There is a difference between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside, feeding it dinner, turning off the lights, and asking it to stay the night.
You may not control every thought that flashes through your mind.
You are responsible for what you deliberately entertain.
That is why someone can experience sexual temptation without the temptation itself proving that he or she has already sinned.
Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus was “tempted as we are, yet without sin.”
Temptation and sin therefore cannot be identical.
James explains the progression:
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin…”
Notice the movement.
Desire.
Enticement.
Conception.
Sin.
Death.
James does not give us permission to play with temptation. He gives us a terrifying picture of what happens when disordered desire is embraced and allowed to conceive.
And maybe that is where this article stops being theological and becomes personal.
Because perhaps your real question was never:
“Is wanting sex sinful?”
Maybe your real question is:
“What do I do when I want something God has not given me permission to have right now?”
That question hurts more.
Because sometimes obedience means carrying a legitimate desire without fulfilling it illegitimately.
You can want companionship and still be single.
You can want marriage and still be waiting.
You can want sexual intimacy and still choose chastity.
You can be married and experience seasons when intimacy becomes difficult because of illness, distance, conflict, exhaustion, pregnancy, trauma, grief, or circumstances neither spouse expected.
Christian maturity does not mean reaching a place where you never experience desires that cannot immediately be satisfied.
Sometimes maturity means learning to bring those desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that can feel like dying.
Because sometimes it is.
Jesus said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
Christianity never promised that every desire inside us would receive permission merely because the desire feels powerful.
But neither does Jesus stand over the struggling person saying:
“Disgusting.”
Look at how He dealt with sexually broken people.
John 4 gives us a Samaritan woman whose relational history had become complicated and painful.
Jesus knew.
Before she explained herself, He knew.
Five husbands.
And the man she was currently with was not her husband.
Yet Jesus did not begin by humiliating her.
He asked for water.
He spoke with her.
He exposed the truth without treating her as disposable.
He offered living water.
That is Jesus.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
Grace walks directly into the scandal and offers redemption.
And this is where some of us need to stop hiding.
Because sexual shame grows beautifully in darkness.
Pornography loves darkness.
Adultery loves darkness.
Secret messages love darkness.
Fantasy loves darkness.
Double lives love darkness.
And shame whispers:
“If anybody knew what you were thinking about, they would never look at you the same way again.”
So you hide from Christians.
Then you hide from your spouse.
Then you hide from accountability.
Eventually you begin trying to hide from God.
But Adam already tried that.
It did not work.
And perhaps somebody reading this has pornography hidden behind a password right now.
Perhaps there is a conversation on your phone your husband or wife cannot see.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that fantasy is harmless because “nothing physical happened.”
Perhaps you keep returning to someone’s profile because you know exactly what looking at that person does inside you.
Perhaps loneliness has become your justification.
Perhaps you tell yourself:
“God understands.”
Yes.
God understands more completely than anyone.
And precisely because He understands, He loves you too much to call bondage freedom.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Φεύγετε—pheugete—“flee.”
Not negotiate.
Not see how close you can get.
Not keep the app and promise yourself you will be stronger tomorrow.
Flee.
And Paul’s reason is profoundly Christ-centered.
Just a few verses later:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
That destroys two opposite lies at once.
The first lie says:
“My body is evil.”
No.
Your body belongs to Christ and is destined for resurrection.
The second says:
“My body is mine, therefore whatever I desire sexually is automatically legitimate.”
Again, no.
“You are not your own.”
Christian sexual ethics cannot ultimately be reduced to “What am I allowed to get away with?”
The Christian asks something far more beautiful:
How can I glorify Christ with this body He purchased with His blood?
That means sexuality is not merely about avoiding pregnancy, disease, embarrassment, or getting caught.
It is about worship.
Your browser history can become an arena of worship.
Your dating life can become an arena of worship.
Your marriage bed can become an arena of worship.
Your loneliness can become an arena of worship.
Even your unfulfilled sexual desire can become an offering placed before Jesus.
Not because desire itself is necessarily dirty.
But because Jesus is worthy of lordship over everything—including what you desperately want.
And marriage does not turn selfish sexuality holy simply because two people possess a marriage certificate.
Scripture describes marital intimacy with tenderness and mutuality.
First Corinthians 7 speaks strikingly of reciprocal authority between husband and wife. Neither spouse is presented as merely existing for the sexual gratification of the other.
Biblical marriage never gives permission for coercion, manipulation, degradation, or abuse.
Sexual intimacy within marriage is meant to express covenantal union, mutual giving, faithfulness, tenderness, and love—not entitlement.
Song of Songs goes even further and reminds embarrassed Christians of something remarkable:
The Bible can speak positively about romantic and erotic desire within its proper context.
God is not frightened by marital passion.
He invented bodies.
He invented touch.
He invented marriage.
He invented covenant intimacy.
Satan did not invent sex.
He specializes in taking what God created and separating the gift from the Giver, pleasure from covenant, desire from holiness, bodies from dignity, and intimacy from love.
That is why pornography is such a counterfeit.
It promises intimacy without vulnerability.
Pleasure without covenant.
Bodies without souls.
Consumption without responsibility.
And afterward?
The screen goes dark.
And you are still lonely.
Sometimes lonelier.
Because what your soul was begging for could never actually be downloaded.
You wanted to be known.
You wanted to be wanted.
You wanted closeness.
You wanted comfort.
You wanted escape.
You wanted someone to choose you.
And pornography handed you pixels.
Jesus offers something radically different.
He does not merely say:
“Stop.”
He says:
“Come.”
Come thirsty.
Come ashamed.
Come tempted.
Come after the relapse.
Come after the secret.
Come after the relationship you knew crossed boundaries.
Come after the adultery.
Come after years of promiscuity.
Come after sexual decisions you wish you could erase.
Come after the night you promised would be the last time.
Come.
Not because repentance does not matter.
But because repentance is exactly where grace is taking you.
The New Testament word often translated “repentance” is μετάνοια—metanoia, carrying the idea of a changed mind, a turning of one’s orientation.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling horrible afterward.
You can hate consequences without hating sin.
You can cry and still refuse to surrender.
Repentance turns.
Repentance brings darkness into light.
Repentance deletes what needs deleting.
Repentance ends conversations that need ending.
Repentance seeks accountability.
Repentance stops blaming loneliness for choices.
Repentance confesses.
Repentance may fall again, but it stops making peace with the thing crucifying it.
And here is the Gospel:
Jesus did not die only for respectable sins.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
Sexual sin too.
The pornography.
The adultery.
The fornication.
The lust.
The secret.
The shame.
The years.
The things nobody knows.
The things you wish even you could forget.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
The cross means sexual sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
And grace is powerful enough that sexual sin does not have to define the rest of your life.
That is why the Gospel is neither:
“Sex doesn’t matter.”
Nor:
“You are permanently filthy because of what you did sexually.”
Both are lies.
The Gospel says:
Sin matters enormously—and Jesus saves sinners completely.
First Corinthians 6 contains one of the most astonishing sentences ever written to sexually broken people.
After naming several forms of unrighteousness, Paul says:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their past had magically vanished from history.
But because their past no longer possessed the authority to name them.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Maybe you need to read those words again because shame has been calling you by another name for years.
Washed.
Your worst sexual mistake does not have greater cleansing power than the blood of Jesus.
Your virginity is not your Savior.
Your sexual history is not your identity.
Your relationship status is not your righteousness.
Your self-control cannot justify you.
Christ does.
And if you belong to Him, your story does not have to end where the scandal happened.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we say at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never occurred.
He rewrites the story by entering it with nail-scarred hands.
So, is wanting sex a sin?
No—not simply because sexual desire exists.
God created human sexuality and designed sexual union for the covenant of marriage.
But sexual desire is not sovereign.
Jesus is.

When desire becomes lustful possession, when we deliberately cultivate sexual fantasies outside God’s design, when desire leads us into sexual immorality, adultery, pornography, exploitation, or other forms of disobedience, Scripture calls us not to rationalize it but to repent.
And when temptation comes?
Run toward Christ before you run toward the counterfeit.
Sometimes what feels like unbearable sexual hunger is carrying another hunger underneath it.
A hunger to be loved.
To be held.
To matter.
To stop feeling alone.
Sex can be beautiful.
But sex cannot bear the weight of being your god.
A spouse cannot bear it either.
Only Jesus can occupy the throne of a human heart without eventually destroying the person sitting beneath it.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Maybe you came looking for permission.
Maybe you found conviction instead.
Or perhaps you came expecting condemnation and discovered grace.
Whatever brought you here, do not waste this moment by merely scrolling onward.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Not the church version.
Not the cleaned-up version.
The truth.
“Lord, this is what I want.”
“Lord, this is what I keep watching.”
“Lord, this is who I keep fantasizing about.”
“Lord, my marriage is hurting.”
“Lord, I’m lonely.”
“Lord, I crossed the line.”
“Lord, I keep going back.”
“Lord, I need You.”
He already knows.
Confession does not inform God.
It stops us from pretending before Him.
Not because a Facebook comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing one honest sentence into the light is how we stop protecting the darkness.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that freedom is possible.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget everything we believed confidently in daylight.
Somebody is hiding.
Somebody thinks sexual failure disqualified them forever.
Somebody is one lonely night away from returning to chains Jesus has been helping them break.
If this truth glorifies God, helping biblical truth reach that person is worth more than protecting an algorithmically comfortable silence.
But financially supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help Scripture-centered discipleship continue reaching people who need it.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience around us.
It is about pointing an audience toward Him.
Jesus Christ.
The One who met the ashamed.
The One who touched the rejected.
The One who exposed sin without delighting in humiliation.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who carried our guilt to Calvary.
The One who walked out of the tomb.
The One who still breaks chains.
So tonight, when desire speaks loudly, remember something louder.
You are not merely a body trying to satisfy an appetite.
If you are in Christ, you are someone purchased at immeasurable cost.
Loved.
Called.
Being sanctified.
And when you stumble, do not make your bed in the dirt.
Run back to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Stand again.
Because perhaps the most dangerous lie sexual shame ever told you was that after everything you had done, Jesus would no longer want you near Him.
But the cross says otherwise.

Your desire does not have to become your master, your failure does not have to become your identity, and your scandal does not have to become your final chapter—because the hands rewriting your story still bear the scars that paid for it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “YOUR LOVE IS BETTER THAN WINE”: Why Does Scripture Compare Romantic Love to Intoxication?
paragraphs: “YOUR LOVE IS BETTER THAN WINE”: Why Does Scripture Compare Romantic Love to Intoxication?

Song of Songs 1:2 contains one of the Bible’s most startling descriptions of desire—and hidden inside it is a truth about love, longing, intimacy, and the human heart that many Christians were never taught how to talk about.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
That is in your Bible.
Not hidden in an obscure manuscript.
Not whispered by some embarrassed lover outside the boundaries of Scripture.
Right there.
In holy Scripture.
Then comes the line that makes the verse even more startling:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Ki-tovim dodekha mi-yayin.
“For your love is better than wine.”
Song of Songs 1:2.
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because perhaps somewhere along the way, some of us learned a version of Christianity that knew how to talk about temptation but became strangely uncomfortable talking about desire.
We learned how to say, “Don’t.”
Don’t lust.
Don’t fornicate.
Don’t commit adultery.
Don’t cross the boundary.
And those warnings matter.
Jesus takes sexual holiness so seriously that He reaches beyond outward behavior into the desires of the heart.
But if all we ever hear is what sexuality can become when corrupted by sin, we can accidentally forget something Scripture never forgot:
God created love before humanity corrupted it.
Desire was not invented in a nightclub.
Romance was not invented by Hollywood.
The human body was not designed by pornography.
Marriage was not humanity’s attempt to domesticate lust.
Before there was adultery, there was covenant.
Before there was pornography, there was nakedness without shame.
Before lust twisted desire into consumption, God created man and woman and declared His creation “very good.”
And somewhere inside the canon of Scripture sits an entire book in which lovers notice each other.
Long for each other.
Praise each other.
Search for each other.
Delight in each other.
And speak with a startling emotional and physical intensity.
The Song of Songs refuses to pretend that holy love must be emotionally cold.
That matters.
Because there are people reading this who have spent years believing that holiness means becoming less human.
It does not.
Jesus did not come to make you less human.
He came to redeem what sin has disfigured.
And that brings us back to those ancient Hebrew words:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן

The word דֹּדֶיךָ — dodekha comes from dod, a word associated here with love, affection, or expressions of romantic love. The JPS rendering captures the thought as, “your love is more delightful than wine.”
Then comes מִיָּיִן — mi-yayin.
“Than wine.”
Why wine?
Why would inspired Scripture put romantic love beside something capable of producing exhilaration?
Because comparison is not necessarily endorsement of everything associated with the thing being compared.
Song of Songs 1:2 does not say, “Become drunk.”
It says, in effect:
Your love surpasses wine.

Wine belonged to the sensory world of the ancient biblical writers. It could signify celebration, abundance, festivity, pleasure, and gladness, while Scripture elsewhere also gives unmistakable warnings about drunkenness and loss of self-control.
So this is not a biblical excuse for intoxication.
It is poetry.
And poetry reaches for something you can feel in order to describe something difficult to measure.
Think about what happens when someone you deeply love walks into a room.
Suddenly you notice everything.
Their voice.
Their laugh.
The way they look at you.
The smallest touch becomes enormous.
A message from them can change your afternoon.
Their absence can make a crowded room feel empty.
Their presence can make an ordinary Tuesday feel like somebody secretly turned the lights brighter.
Love does something to perception.
That is part of the force of the image.
The woman in the Song is not clinically describing affection.
She is overwhelmed by it.
His love is not merely acceptable.
Not merely appropriate.
Not merely useful.
It is better than wine.

And maybe that bothers us because we have become comfortable with a Christianity that can discuss doctrine without trembling, marriage without romance, purity without beauty, and obedience without delight.
But the Bible is not embarrassed by delight.
Sin is not defeated by pretending pleasure does not exist.
Sin is defeated when pleasure is returned to its rightful place beneath the lordship of God.
That distinction changes everything.
Because lust says:
I want your body for me.
Love says:
I want your good, even when it costs me.
Lust consumes.
Love gives.
Lust separates pleasure from covenant and responsibility.
Love willingly binds pleasure to faithfulness.
Lust asks, “How much can I take?”
Covenant asks, “How faithfully can I give?”
And suddenly Song of Songs begins exposing something deeper than romance.
It exposes our counterfeit versions of love.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that means.
You thought obsession was love because it kept you awake at night.
You thought jealousy was love because somebody was terrified of losing control over you.
You thought sexual attention meant you were valuable.
You thought being wanted meant being cherished.
You thought chemistry meant covenant.
You thought because someone could make your heart race, they deserved access to your heart.
Maybe you gave pieces of yourself away because you were desperate to hear someone say:
“I choose you.”
Maybe somebody said it.
Then left.
Maybe the person who once made you feel intoxicated eventually became the person whose name you could barely say without feeling something break inside you.
And now this verse sounds different.
“Your love is better than wine.”
Because wine wears off.
Infatuation can wear off.
Adrenaline wears off.
Beauty changes.
Bodies age.
Feelings fluctuate.
The late-night conversations eventually meet morning responsibilities.

The wedding photographs eventually become mortgage payments, dirty dishes, sick children, misunderstandings, exhaustion, forgiveness, and the thousand ordinary decisions through which covenant either deepens or dies.
Biblical love was never supposed to survive merely because two people remained intoxicated with each other.
The feeling may begin the song.
Faithfulness must learn to carry it.
That is why the Song is so beautiful.
It celebrates desire without making desire God.
And Christianity does something even more radical.
It points beyond every human love toward the One for whom the human heart was ultimately made.
We should be careful here.

Song of Songs is genuinely love poetry. We do not need to erase the man and woman from the poem in order to make the book spiritual. Jewish and Christian interpreters have also historically seen theological dimensions in the Song, but its celebration of human love should not simply be dissolved into allegory.
Yet within the whole biblical story, even the greatest human love cannot carry the weight of being our Savior.
Your husband cannot be Jesus for you.
Your wife cannot be Jesus for you.
Your boyfriend cannot save you.
Your girlfriend cannot heal every wound inside you.
Marriage cannot bear the weight of worship.
Romance cannot forgive your sins.
Sex cannot reconcile you to God.
Another human being cannot become the answer to the deepest ache of your soul.
And many of our heartbreaks begin when we ask human love to accomplish what only divine grace can do.
We ask someone:
“Make me enough.”
“Make me secure.”
“Tell me I matter.”
“Never disappoint me.”
“Never leave me emotionally hungry.”
“Fill every empty room inside me.”
Then two sinners stand before each other carrying expectations that belong to God.
Eventually somebody collapses under the weight.
Maybe both do.
This is where the Gospel enters the love story.
Not to destroy romance.
To rescue it from becoming an idol.
Because Jesus does not merely teach you how to find love.
Jesus shows you what love ultimately looks like.
A cross.
Not sentimentality.
Not butterflies.
Not attraction without sacrifice.
A blood-stained cross outside Jerusalem where the Son of God gave Himself for sinners who could never repay Him.
Romans 5 does not say Christ died for us after we became attractive enough.
He loved us while we were sinners.
That is scandalous love.
We cheated on God with our idols.
We wanted His gifts without His presence.
We chased pleasure while ignoring the Giver.
We worshiped bodies, money, approval, attention, status, romance, ourselves.
We wanted creation without Creator.
And instead of abandoning rebels to the consequences of rebellion, God sent His Son.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now forgiveness is offered not to people who successfully hide their scandal, but to people who bring their scandal into the light and trust the Savior.
That is why grace is so shocking.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace calls sinners home.
Maybe your romantic history is messy.
Maybe there are names you regret.
Beds you regret.
Messages you wish you had never sent.
Promises you broke.
Pictures you wish had never existed.
A marriage you damaged.
An affair nobody knows about.
A secret addiction behind an immaculate Christian profile.
Maybe you have learned how to lift your hands in worship while carrying shame you refuse to name.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ is not waiting for a cleaner version of you before He invites you to repent.
Bring the real story.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the church version.
Not the version where you conveniently become the victim in every chapter.
Bring the chapter where you were wrong.
Bring the desire.
Bring the lust.
Bring the adultery.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the loneliness.
Bring the relationship you know you have placed above God.
Bring the wounds other people inflicted upon you.
Bring the wounds you inflicted upon others.
Bring the thing you keep deleting from your browser but cannot delete from your conscience.
Bring it into His light.
Repentance is not Jesus humiliating you.
It is Jesus calling you out of the tomb you decorated because you were afraid to admit it was killing you.
And grace is not permission to return to chains.
Grace teaches us to belong to Christ.
Maybe that is what someone needs to hear tonight.
You do not need another counterfeit intoxication.
You need truth.
You need grace.
You need the Christ who knows exactly what happened and still calls sinners to Himself.
There is a reason counterfeit intimacy leaves people thirsty.
It promises transcendence but cannot sustain it.
It whispers, “One more person.”
“One more fantasy.”
“One more affair.”
“One more night.”
“One more message.”
“One more secret.”
“One more swipe.”
“One more body.”
And after “one more” comes another one.
Because lust is a terrible god.
It always wants another sacrifice.
Jesus is different.
At the cross, He became the sacrifice.
That is the Gospel.
And when Christ becomes Lord of our desires, He does not teach us to hate love.
He teaches us how to love without worshiping love.
He teaches husbands that love is sacrificial.
He teaches wives and husbands covenant faithfulness.
He teaches singles that their worth is not suspended until somebody chooses them.
He teaches the sexually broken that shame does not have to write the final chapter.
He teaches the lonely that loneliness is painful without making loneliness their identity.
He teaches the married that covenant is deeper than chemistry.
He teaches all of us that desire makes a terrible master but can become a beautiful servant when surrendered to God.
Then Song of Songs 1:2 can be heard without embarrassment.
“Let him kiss me…”
There is tenderness here.
Desire.
Delight.
And:
“Your love is better than wine.”
Not because losing control is holy.
But because faithful love can produce a delight that the poet reaches toward wine to describe—and then says love is better.
Better.
There is a word worth carrying home.
Some of us have settled for things that temporarily numb us because we have forgotten there are things worth loving that actually awaken us.
We settle for pornography instead of intimacy.
Attention instead of covenant.
Being desired instead of being known.
Fantasy instead of faithfulness.
Temporary intoxication instead of enduring love.
And sometimes we even settle for romantic love itself when Christ is standing at the center of history saying that no created person was ever designed to become our ultimate treasure.
Human love can be beautiful.
Marriage can be breathtaking.
A kiss can be holy within its proper covenantal home.
Desire can be received as part of God's created goodness.
But only Jesus can redeem the sinner.
Only Jesus can cleanse the conscience.
Only Jesus conquered death.
Only Jesus can take the scandal you thought would define you forever and write grace across the final page.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners from it.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain the details publicly.
But perhaps you need to stop pretending.
There is no shame in admitting you need prayer.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly drowning in a relationship they call love.
Somebody may think their sexual past has disqualified them from grace.
Somebody may be married and wondering where the tenderness went.
Somebody may be single and secretly wondering whether being unwanted romantically means being unwanted by God.
Somebody may love Jesus publicly while fighting sexual sin privately.
Put truth where they might find it.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what we knew clearly yesterday.
Come back when feelings become louder than truth.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow with you. Our desire is to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ into places where hurting people can encounter it.

Scripture gives a real basis for materially supporting Gospel ministry. Paul writes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from Gospel ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14). But Scripture also protects the heart of the giver: “not reluctantly or under compulsion”—God loves willing, cheerful generosity (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Those claims would go beyond what Scripture says.
Instead, if you prayerfully choose to support Gospel Warrior, let it be an offering freely given to help Gospel-centered teaching reach farther.
Give yourself to Christ.
Money cannot purchase grace.
An offering cannot erase sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Your deepest need is not membership in a ministry.
Your deepest need is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
So repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him your desires.
Bring Him your relationships.
Bring Him your sexuality.
Bring Him your marriage.
Bring Him your singleness.
Bring Him your loneliness.
Bring Him your shame.
Bring Him the love story that collapsed.
Bring Him the secret chapter.
Bring Him the person you still cannot forgive.
Bring Him the part of your heart that keeps reaching for another cup because the last one could not satisfy you.
Maybe you finally understand why that ancient line still burns after thousands of years:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Ki-tovim dodekha mi-yayin.
“Your love is better than wine.”
Human love can be intoxicating in the poetic sense—exhilarating, consuming, deeply delightful.
But even the sweetest human love is still a signpost.
It cannot become the destination of the soul.
Because eventually every earthly cup runs empty.
Every beautiful face grows older.
Every human heart reveals its limitations.
Every romance discovers that feelings alone cannot carry eternity.
And when every lesser cup finally reaches its bottom, Christ remains.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit.
The Savior who does not abandon repentant sinners.
The King who does not love you because you were spotless, but who gave Himself to cleanse and redeem His people.
The One whose grace reaches into bedrooms, broken marriages, secret addictions, lonely apartments, shattered engagements, guilty consciences, and stories we thought could never become testimonies.
So perhaps the question underneath Song of Songs 1:2 was never merely:
Why does Scripture compare romantic love to wine?
Perhaps it also forces us to ask:
What have I been drinking from because I am desperately thirsty to be loved?
And once that question reaches the heart, another follows.
What if the thing I keep asking another human being to give me can only finally be found in Jesus Christ?
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is reaching for another counterfeit cup.
Maybe your share will reach them first.
Maybe the resources you help sustain will put the words of Scripture in front of someone moments before they make a decision they cannot easily undo.
But ultimately, Gospel Warrior cannot save them.
You cannot save them.
I cannot save them.
Jesus can.
And perhaps that is the line worth remembering when everything else fades:
The world will keep offering you cups that make you forget your emptiness for a night; Jesus offers grace that can rewrite the story you thought you would carry forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID ISRAEL CARRY TWELVE STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN?
paragraphs:
WHY DID ISRAEL CARRY TWELVE STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN?
They Were Carrying More Than Stones. They Were Carrying Evidence That the God Who Brought Them Through Must Never Be Forgotten.
Imagine being the man who had to carry one.
The river is behind you now.
Your clothes carry the smell of the Jordan. Your feet have touched ground that should have been underwater. Your heart is still trying to understand what your eyes have just witnessed.
And there is a stone on your shoulder.
Heavy.
Awkward.
Pulled from the middle of a river where, moments before, nobody should have been able to stand.
You might have wondered why God wanted you to carry it.
After everything He had just done, why a stone?
Why twelve of them?
Why make twelve men go back toward the place everyone else was leaving?
The answer reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
Because God knew something about the human heart.
We forget.
We forget prayers that were answered once the crisis passes.
We forget doors God opened after we become comfortable inside the room.

We forget how desperately we cried when our marriage was breaking, when the diagnosis frightened us, when money disappeared, when temptation had us by the throat, when grief made getting out of bed feel like an act of war.
We remember the pain.
Then God carries us through it...
and eventually we can even forget the Deliverer.
That is why the stones matter.

Joshua 4 opens immediately after Israel crosses the Jordan. God commands Joshua to choose twelve men, one from each tribe, and have each man take a stone from the middle of the river, from the place where the priests bearing the ark had stood firmly. They were to carry those stones to the place where Israel camped.
Not eleven.
Not thirteen.
Twelve.
One corresponding to each tribe of Israel.
This was not merely one man's testimony.
God was marking what He had done for His covenant people.
And then Scripture tells us why.
The stones were to become a sign.
The Hebrew of Joshua 4:6 contains the words:
“לְאוֹת בְּקִרְבְּכֶם”
le’ot beqirbekhem
In context: “for a sign among you.”
Then comes the question God expected future children to ask:
“מָה הָאֲבָנִים הָאֵלֶּה לָכֶם”
Mah ha’avanim ha’elleh lakhem?
“What do these stones mean to you?”
That last idea matters.
Not merely, “What are those rocks?”
What do they mean to you?
There was supposed to be a story attached to them.
A child would see the stones.
Curiosity would become a question.
The question would become testimony.
The testimony would point to the LORD.
And another generation would hear that the God their fathers worshiped was not an imaginary God their ancestors invented to survive difficult times.
He had acted.
He had delivered.
He had made a way where there was no way.
The Hebrew word used in Joshua 4:7 is especially beautiful:
“לְזִכָּרוֹן”
lezikkaron
“For a memorial.”
The noun zikkaron carries the idea of remembrance or memorial. These stones were not magical. Israel was not commanded to worship them. They possessed no spiritual power in themselves.
They pointed beyond themselves.
That distinction matters.
The stones were evidence designed to provoke remembrance.
Look at them...
and remember Him.
Remember where you were.
Remember what stood in front of you.
Remember what God did.
Remember who brought you through.
Because the greatest danger after crossing the river may not always be the enemy waiting ahead.
Sometimes it is forgetting the God who brought you across.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
There was a season when you prayed differently.
You weren't casual then.
You weren't checking your phone every thirty seconds.
You weren't trying to sound spiritual.
You were desperate.
“Jesus, please.”
That was almost the entire prayer.
You promised God that if He brought you through, you would never forget.
Then somehow...
life became normal again.
The tears dried.
The emergency ended.
The relationship survived—or perhaps God gave you strength when it didn't.
The bill got paid.
The temptation loosened its grip.
The funeral passed.
The depression lifted enough for light to enter the room again.
The door opened.
You survived what you once thought would destroy you.
And somewhere between deliverance and comfort, your memory became shorter.
Maybe that is why you needed to encounter twelve stones today.
Because some of us are asking God for another miracle while standing beside forgotten evidence of His faithfulness.
Israel's Jordan crossing itself was deliberate covenant history.
Joshua later tells the people that the LORD dried up the Jordan just as He had dried up the sea before the previous generation.
The God of the Exodus was still the God of Israel.
The generation had changed.
God's faithfulness had not.
That is breathtaking.
The fathers had a sea.
Their children had a river.
Different obstacle.
Same faithful God.
Your testimony does not have to look like somebody else's testimony for Jesus Christ to be the same Lord.
Someone else's Red Sea does not invalidate your Jordan.
Someone may have been delivered instantly while your healing has taken years.
Someone may testify about a marriage restored while your testimony is that Christ held you together after the marriage ended.
Someone may tell how God spared a loved one's life while you still visit a grave.
Biblical faith does not require us to pretend every story ends the way we wanted.
Sometimes the miracle is deliverance from the fire.
Sometimes the testimony is that Christ remained faithful while we walked through it.
The stones were never saying, “God will make your life painless.”
They were saying:
Do not forget who brought you here.
And notice where the stones came from.
The middle.
Not the riverbank.
Not somewhere safe nearby.
God told them to take stones from the place where the priests' feet had stood in the Jordan.
They carried evidence out of the place they had passed through.
There is something painfully familiar about that.
Sometimes what you carry after suffering feels heavy because it came from the deepest part of the crossing.
A scar.
A memory.
A testimony you never wanted.
A tenderness you did not have before grief.
A compassion born from your own failure.
A humility produced when your secret sin finally broke you.
A dependence on Christ that comfortable Christianity never taught you.
Be careful here: Scripture does not teach that every wound is itself good or that every tragedy was secretly something pleasant.
But Scripture repeatedly shows us a God powerful enough to redeem what evil, suffering, sin, and death meant to destroy.
And nowhere is that clearer than at the cross.
Because eventually the biblical story brings us to something far more scandalous than twelve stones beside the Jordan.
It brings us to a cross outside Jerusalem.
Christianity does not center on humanity climbing its way toward God.
It centers on God coming to sinners in Jesus Christ.
Christ crucified.
The sinless One bearing sin.
The righteous One suffering for the unrighteous.
The Son of God entering death...
and rising again.
The cross looked like defeat.
God turned it into the proclamation of redemption.
The tomb looked final.
On the third day, it became empty.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that you can rewrite yourself.
Jesus saves sinners.
Jesus forgives the repentant.
Jesus receives the broken.
Jesus transforms those who come to Him in faith.
Jesus does not merely improve the old story.
He gives new life.
Maybe your past contains things you desperately wish you could erase.
Sexual sin.
Addiction.
Pride.
Adultery.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
A destroyed relationship.
Religious hypocrisy.
Years of pretending.
A secret nobody at church knows.
Words you cannot take back.
People you wounded.
Promises you broke.
Perhaps you have learned how to smile while carrying stones nobody else can see.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
Grace is greater precisely because sin is serious.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity needed motivational encouragement.
We needed reconciliation with God.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed rescue.
We needed a Savior.
And at Calvary, Christ paid a price we could never pay for ourselves.
So repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Him.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can cleanse you.
Maybe your deepest shame does not have to become the final sentence over your life.
Maybe the thing Satan keeps using to whisper, “Look what you did,” can eventually become the place from which you answer, “Look what Christ has done.”
Not because sin becomes beautiful.
Because grace is.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not editing the ugly chapters.
Not calling darkness light.
It is looking directly at the truth of human sin and then looking higher at the cross of Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Joshua's stones also reveal something desperately needed in our homes.
God expected children to ask questions.
Think about that.
The memorial was built with the next generation in mind.
“When your children ask...”
Tell them.
God's mighty works were not supposed to die inside the memories of those who experienced them.
Parents were expected to speak.
Children were expected to hear.
Faithfulness was supposed to become testimony.
And maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
What will your children know about what God has done in your life?
Do they know what Jesus rescued you from?
Do they know why you worship?
Do they know about the prayer God answered when nobody else knew you were praying?
Do they know there were nights you nearly gave up?
Do they know why certain Bible verses make your voice shake?
Do they know the person you were before Christ began changing you?
Or will they inherit your possessions without inheriting your testimony?
We carefully preserve photographs.
Documents.
Graduation certificates.
Jewelry.
Property.
Passwords.
Bank accounts.
Family recipes.
But sometimes we fail to preserve the stories of God's faithfulness.
Tell them.
Tell your children.
Tell your grandchildren.
Tell the young believer who assumes you have always been strong.
Tell the person who thinks their failure has disqualified them forever.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them you were not always okay.
Tell them about the river.
Tell them about the nights.
Tell them about the tears.
Tell them about the sin Christ confronted.
Tell them about repentance.
Tell them about mercy.
Tell them about the prayers that seemed unanswered and how God remained worthy anyway.
Tell them about the moment you discovered Christianity was not about performing religious goodness but about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Build memorials with your words.
Because somebody else's faith may be strengthened by remembering what God did when you thought your story was over.
And Joshua 4 goes even further.
The memorial was not only about Israel remembering.
Joshua says God acted so that “all the peoples of the earth” would know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, and so Israel would fear the LORD continually.
The miracle had a missionary horizon.
God's greatness was meant to be known.
That changes how we think about testimony.
Your testimony is not ultimately about making you impressive.
It is about making Christ known.
If God rescued you from addiction, Christ is the hero.
If He restored you after failure, Christ is the hero.
If He carried you through grief, Christ is the hero.
If He convicted you of hidden sin, Christ is the hero.
If He gave you strength to confess, repent, forgive, reconcile, endure, or begin again...
Christ is the hero.
The stones did not say, “Look how courageous Israel was.”
They said, in effect:
Look what the LORD did.
And perhaps that is why some testimonies never reach the people who desperately need them.
We are afraid of what people will think if they discover where our stones came from.
We want resurrection without admitting there was a tomb.
We want grace without admitting there was guilt.
We want testimony without vulnerability.
We want people to know we crossed the Jordan without letting them know how impossible the river once looked.
But somebody is still standing where you once stood.
Someone scrolling Facebook tonight thinks God could never forgive them.
Someone is fighting pornography secretly.
Someone's marriage is collapsing quietly.
Someone goes to church every Sunday while wondering whether anybody would still love them if the truth came out.
Someone has been away from Jesus so long that returning feels embarrassing.
Someone believes their failure is stronger than Christ's mercy.
They do not need you pretending you have never needed grace.
They need the truth.
You were a sinner too.
You still need grace every day.
And Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
So maybe your “stone” needs to speak.
Maybe your testimony needs to leave the private riverbank.
Maybe someone needs to hear:
“I almost gave up too.”
“I wandered too.”
“I failed too.”
“I hid too.”
“I cried too.”
“But Jesus met me there.”
That does not make you the Savior.
It points people toward the One who is.
This is why sharing Gospel-centered truth matters when it comes from the right motive.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Christ—not a commercial transaction.
But when Christ has given us truth worth remembering, love can move us to help put that truth in front of somebody else.
So if this article made you remember your own Jordan, don't let it disappear into your feed.
Not as a religious performance.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
If you are carrying something heavy and need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ is still working in parts of your life nobody else sees, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God and from yourself, comment, “no more hiding.”
If you have crossed a Jordan you thought would destroy you, tell us what Jesus has done.
Your comment may become somebody else's reason to keep seeking Christ tonight.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider staying close.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and voluntary generosity can be one expression of that worship.
Not because an algorithm is worthy of your obedience.
Because someone in your circle may need to remember that there is still a God who brings people through impossible places.
And after everything else in Joshua 4, perhaps this is the detail that should stay with us.
The river started flowing again.
Joshua 4:18 says that after the priests carrying the ark came up from the Jordan and their feet reached dry ground, the waters returned to their place and overflowed their banks as before.
Think about that.
The path disappeared.
Someone arriving later could look at that raging river and say:
“There was never a road there.”
And Israel could point toward twelve stones.
Yes.
There was.
We walked through it.
God made the way.
That is what testimony does.
Years later, people may look at you and never understand what Jesus brought you through.
They will see you worship but not know the night you almost walked away.
They will see the marriage but not know the war it survived.
They will see the smile but not know the grief behind it.
They will see the ministry but not know the repentance.
They will see the faith but not know how many times you cried, “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.”
They will see dry clothes.
You will remember the river.
So keep the stones.
Not to worship your past.
Not to glorify your pain.
Not to romanticize your sin.
Keep them in memory so that when the enemy tells you God has abandoned you, you can remember His faithfulness.
Keep them so your children can ask.
Keep them so your grandchildren can hear.
Keep them so strangers can discover that the hand of the LORD is mighty.
Keep them until every scar becomes an opportunity to point beyond yourself.
And when someone eventually looks at your life and asks...
“What do these stones mean?”
Tell them.
Tell them about the river.
Tell them about your failure.
Tell them about your fear.
Tell them about the night you thought everything was finished.
But do not stop there.
Tell them about the cross.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them about repentance.
Tell them about forgiveness.
Tell them about mercy you did not deserve.
Tell them about Jesus Christ.
Because the most unforgettable memorial is not the stone you carried out of the river.
It is the Savior who carried you through it.
The river may have covered the road again—but the stones still remember where God made a way.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD” — IS JAMES CONTRADICTING PAUL ABOUT SALVATION?
paragraphs:
“FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD” — IS JAMES CONTRADICTING PAUL ABOUT SALVATION?
Paul says we are justified by faith apart from works. James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. One Bible. Two apostles. One word—“justified.” It sounds like a contradiction… until you discover what each man was actually fighting.
Imagine standing before God with nothing left to hide behind.
No church attendance.
No Christian reputation.
No ministry title.
No baptism certificate in your hand.
No list of people you helped.
No money you gave.
No prayers you prayed.
No theological vocabulary.
No “But Lord, I tried to be a good person.”
Nothing.
Just you.
Your sin.
And a holy God.
What could possibly save you?
Paul’s answer is breathtaking.
Grace.
Received through faith.
Not your works.
Not your religious performance.
Not your ability to make yourself worthy.
Christ.
But then James walks into the conversation and says something so sharp that Christians have wrestled with it for centuries:
“Faith without works is dead.”
And then he goes even further:
“Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.”
Wait.
Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works.
James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
Did two inspired apostles just collide head-on?
No.
And understanding why may expose one of the most dangerous counterfeit versions of Christianity hiding in plain sight.
Because Paul and James are not enemies standing on opposite sides of the Gospel.
They are guards standing at opposite doors.
Paul is stopping the person who thinks, “I can earn my way into God’s acceptance.”
James is confronting the person who thinks, “I can claim faith in Christ while my life remains completely untouched by Him.”
Paul destroys self-righteousness.
James destroys empty profession.
And both leave us at the feet of Jesus.
Paul writes in Romans 3:28:
The Greek carries the force clearly:
λογιζόμεθα γὰρ δικαιοῦσθαι πίστει ἄνθρωπον χωρὶς ἔργων νόμου.
The crucial words are πίστει, pistei—“by faith”—and χωρὶς ἔργων νόμου, chōris ergōn nomou—“apart from works of law.”
Paul is demolishing the idea that sinners can establish their righteousness before God through what they accomplish.
We cannot.
That is the scandal of grace.
You don't bring God a résumé impressive enough to persuade Him to save you.
You bring Him your need.
The sinner does not climb a ladder of good works until he finally reaches Christ.
Christ came down for sinners who could never climb high enough.
Paul makes this devastatingly clear elsewhere:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
But never stop reading at Ephesians 2:9.
Because verse 10 changes the entire atmosphere:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works…”
There it is.
Not saved by good works.
Saved for good works.
Not works as the root of salvation.
Works as fruit flowing from a life recreated in Christ.
Grace does not merely forgive the old life and then leave it untouched.
Grace begins making something new.
That is exactly where James enters.
James asks:
“What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him?”
Notice the phrase that is easy to rush past.
“Though a man say he hath faith…”
James is examining a profession.
A claim.
Someone says he possesses faith.
Then James puts that claim under examination.
Suppose a brother or sister lacks clothing and daily food. You see the need. You offer spiritual-sounding words.
“Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled.”
And then you do nothing.
James essentially asks: What good was your speech?
Then comes the sentence that has disturbed comfortable Christianity for centuries:
“Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.”
In Greek:
οὕτως καὶ ἡ πίστις, ἐὰν μὴ ἔχῃ ἔργα, νεκρά ἐστιν καθ’ ἑαυτήν.
Hē pistis—the faith.
Erga—works, deeds, actions.
Nekra estin—is dead.
James is not telling spiritually dead sinners to manufacture enough good deeds until God owes them eternal life.
He is asking whether a faith that never lives, never moves, never acts, never produces anything, is living faith at all.
And then James says:
“Show me thy faith without thy works, and I will show thee my faith by my works.”
That word matters.
Show.
Faith itself is invisible.
I cannot open your chest and inspect whether you truly trust Christ.
Neither can you inspect mine.
But living faith becomes visible through what it produces.
Then James delivers one of Scripture’s most unsettling warnings:
“Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.”
That should shake anyone whose entire assurance rests merely on agreeing with Christian facts.
Demons possess theology.
They know God exists.
They recognize realities about Christ.
They tremble.
But intellectual acknowledgment is not the same thing as saving trust in Jesus Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still refuse Christ.
You can sing worship songs and still cherish secret sin.
You can post Bible verses while treating people cruelly when nobody online can see you.
You can say “Jesus is Lord” casually while arranging your actual life as though you are lord.
You can know about the cross without surrendering yourself to the Crucified One.
That is the terrifying possibility James forces into the light.
Not imperfect faith.
Not struggling faith.
Not the believer crying, “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
James is confronting dead profession.
There is a difference between a Christian who falls while fighting sin and a person who has made peace with sin while using Christianity as camouflage.
There is a difference between weakness and hypocrisy.
Between stumbling and settling.
Between needing grace and using “grace” as permission never to repent.
Real Christians still struggle.
Real Christians still fail.
Peter denied Christ.
David committed horrifying sins.
The Corinthian church needed severe correction.
The New Testament never teaches sinless perfection as the proof that someone belongs to Jesus.
But neither does Scripture present salvation as a lifeless verbal transaction that leaves a person permanently indifferent to Christ.
Jesus saves sinners as sinners.
And the Jesus who justifies also begins transforming those He has saved.
Slowly sometimes.
Painfully sometimes.
With battles, tears, setbacks, confession and discipline sometimes.
But He does not call darkness light simply because we have learned Christian language.
This is where Abraham becomes crucial.
Paul uses Abraham too.
That is not an accident.
Romans 4 points back to Genesis 15:6:
“Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.”
James quotes the same Scripture.
But James then points to Abraham offering Isaac.
Why?
Because Abraham's later obedience demonstrated the reality of the faith Scripture had already attributed to him.
James says:
“Seest thou how faith wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?”
Faith and works are not presented as rival saviors competing for credit.
The works reveal faith in action.
Abraham did not purchase God's grace with Isaac.
His obedience demonstrated the reality of his trust in God.
Then James brings in Rahab.
And what a choice.
Rahab.
A woman whose past carried scandal.
A Gentile.
A prostitute.
Someone many religious people might have considered the wrong person to use in a lesson about righteousness.
Yet she believed enough to act.
She received the messengers and sent them another way.
Her faith did not remain an abstract opinion sitting safely inside her mind.
It moved.
It risked.
It acted.
It changed allegiance.
Rahab's story whispers something beautiful into every life stained by yesterday:
Your scandal does not have to write your final chapter.
Grace can.
That is Gospel Warrior territory.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
This is why Paul and James must never be forced into a theological boxing ring.
Paul is answering something like:
“How can guilty sinners be made right with God?”
Not by earning it.
Not through boasting.
Not through works of the law.
By grace through faith in Christ.
James is confronting another question:
“What kind of faith is this person claiming if absolutely nothing comes from it?”
A dead one.
Paul attacks works offered as the cause or ground of justification.
James attacks a “faith” exposed as barren because it has no corresponding life.
And Scripture refuses to let us mutilate either truth.
Take Paul without James and someone may twist grace into permission for spiritual apathy.
Take James without Paul and someone may twist obedience into a ladder for earning God's acceptance.
Keep them together and the Gospel shines.
We are saved by grace.
Through faith.
Because of Christ.
Not because our works made us worthy.
Yet the faith through which we receive Christ is not intended to remain barren.
Even Paul says in Galatians 5:6 that what counts is “faith which worketh by love.”
This means your good works cannot save you.
But that does not make obedience meaningless.
Your generosity cannot purchase heaven.
Your baptism cannot make Christ indebted to you.
Your ministry cannot erase your guilt.
Your donations cannot wash away sin.
Your Christian merchandise cannot make you righteous.
Your Bible reading cannot become currency with which you buy God's mercy.
Only Christ saves.
His blood.
His righteousness.
His death.
His resurrection.
His grace received through faith.
Jesus did not cry from the cross, “It is almost finished—now complete the payment with enough good deeds.”
He said:
“It is finished.”
The debt of redemption is not waiting for your contribution.
But when grace truly grips a human heart, something begins happening.
The forgiven begin learning forgiveness.
The loved begin learning love.
The selfish begin learning generosity.
The proud begin learning humility.
The dishonest begin confessing truth.
The sexually broken begin bringing hidden darkness into the light.
The bitter begin fighting toward forgiveness.
The comfortable begin noticing the wounded.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
Not identically.
But really.
And maybe this is where this stops being a theological debate and becomes painfully personal.
What has your faith produced?
Not what have you posted.
Not what denomination do you belong to.
Not whether your parents were Christians.
Not whether you once walked an aisle.
Not whether you own six Bibles.
Not whether you can explain predestination.
Not whether you know worship lyrics.
What evidence is there that Jesus has become more than information to you?
When nobody sees the browser history…
When nobody hears the private conversation…
When the church service ends…
When your reputation cannot reward you…
When obedience costs something…
Who are you becoming?
That question is not meant to send every tenderhearted believer into terrified self-salvation.
Look first to Christ, not to your performance.
The ground of your hope is Jesus.
Your weakest day does not make His cross weaker.
Your tears do not strengthen His blood.
Your failures do not require a second Calvary.
When you sin, run toward Christ in repentance instead of hiding from Him in shame.
The Gospel is not “clean yourself up so Jesus might love you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
And that grace becomes the beginning of transformation rather than an excuse to avoid it.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to earn what Jesus offers by grace.
Stop boasting.
Come empty-handed.
Perhaps you have spent years claiming a faith that costs you nothing, changes nothing, confronts nothing, gives nothing, forgives nothing and surrenders nothing.
Stop hiding.
Come empty-handed too.
Both roads lead to the same cross.
The self-righteous need Jesus.
The rebellious need Jesus.
The religious need Jesus.
The addicted need Jesus.
The preacher needs Jesus.
The prostitute needs Jesus.
The theologian needs Jesus.
The person secretly falling apart behind a smiling profile picture needs Jesus.
We do not graduate from grace.
And maybe somebody reading this has been terrified because your life is messy.
You love Christ, yet you still struggle.
You repent, fall, grieve, confess, get up, fight again…and sometimes wonder whether God has finally become tired of you.
Listen carefully.
James does not say that faith without perfect works is dead.
He says faith without works is dead.
Fruit can be immature and still be fruit.
