Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive as one who has been forgiven.
Make the phone call.
Have the conversation.
Confess the truth.
Open the Bible again.
Come back to Christ.
Because the sweetest thing in 1 Samuel 14 was never really the honey.
It was mercy having the final word over a sentence of death.
And thousands of years later, at a cross outside Jerusalem, mercy would speak louder still.
When pride says, “Someone must pay,” look again at the cross—Jesus already did.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PORNOGRAPHY, OBJECTIFICATION, AND JESUS’ TERRIFYING WARNING ABOUT THE EYES
paragraphs: PORNOGRAPHY, OBJECTIFICATION, AND JESUS’ TERRIFYING WARNING ABOUT THE EYES

The screen goes dark. The history gets deleted. Nobody in the house knows. But Jesus said the real battle was never merely on the screen—it was happening somewhere no browser can hide: inside the heart.
There is a moment after pornography that almost nobody talks about.
The screen goes dark.
The room becomes quiet again.
Whatever excitement existed seconds earlier begins collapsing into something heavier.
You close the tab.
Delete the history.
Maybe clear the search bar.
Maybe put the phone facedown beside you.
And for a few seconds, you just lie there.
Alone.
Maybe ashamed.
Maybe numb.
Maybe promising God for the hundredth time that this really was the last time.
“Lord, forgive me.”
You mean it.
At least you think you mean it.
Then tomorrow comes.
Or three days.
Or two weeks.
And somehow your hand finds the phone again.
Your eyes begin wandering again.
The private negotiation begins again.
Just one look.
I won't go further.
Nobody knows.
I'm not actually touching anyone.
I'm not cheating physically.
It's only a screen.
Then the words of Jesus enter the room.
And suddenly all the excuses become very quiet.

“You have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.” — Matthew 5:27–28, KJV
Read the words beneath the English.
The Greek of Matthew 5:28 says:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
The force of the sentence matters.

Jesus is not teaching that noticing an attractive person is identical to adultery. He is not declaring that involuntary temptation itself is the completed sin. He is describing the gaze directed toward lust—the looking that welcomes desire, cultivates it, feeds it, and turns another human being into material for inward sexual possession.
That distinction matters because some tender consciences have been crushed by the idea that simply noticing beauty means they have already committed adultery.
That is not what Jesus is teaching.
But the other distortion is just as dangerous.
Some people use that distinction to excuse the second look.
And the third.
And the search.
And the fantasy.
And the saved video.
And the secret account.
And the midnight scrolling.
Jesus refuses both errors.
He does not condemn you merely for having eyes.
He confronts what your heart decides to do with what your eyes see.
And pornography is almost perfectly engineered around the very thing Jesus exposes.
The prolonged gaze.
The intentionally cultivated desire.
The consumption of another person's body for personal gratification.
Pornography whispers, “Look longer.”
Jesus asks what the looking is doing to your heart.
Pornography says, “They're only bodies.”
Jesus reveals people as human beings made by God, never commodities created for our consumption.
Pornography trains the imagination to ask, “What can this body give me?”
Christ teaches us to ask, “How can I love my neighbor?”
That is why objectification is not a small side effect of pornography.
It is woven into its logic.
A person becomes an image.
An image becomes stimulation.
Stimulation becomes consumption.
Consumption demands novelty.
And somewhere along that road, the human being on the screen becomes easier to forget.
She has a name.
He has a name.
They have histories.
Parents.
Wounds.
Fears.
Souls.
They bear the dignity belonging to human creatures made in God's image.
Yet lust can train the heart to stop seeing a person and start seeing parts.
And Jesus takes that seriously enough to say something terrifying immediately after His warning about lust.
“If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee…”
Matthew 5:29.
The Greek is startling:
“εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ὁ δεξιὸς σκανδαλίζει σε…”
ei de ho ophthalmos sou ho dexios skandalizei se…
“If your right eye causes you to stumble…”
Then:
“ἔξελε αὐτὸν καὶ βάλε ἀπὸ σοῦ…”
Take it away.
Cast it from you.
Jesus continues with the right hand.
Cut it off.
Throw it away.
This is deliberately shocking language.

But Jesus is not commanding His followers to mutilate their bodies. Removing an eye cannot remove lust from the heart. A blind person can still fantasize. Removing a hand cannot amputate sinful desire from the soul.
Jesus has already located the battlefield.
“ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
En tē kardia autou.
“In his heart.”
That is where the war is.
The eye may become a doorway.
The hand may become an instrument.
The phone may become an access point.
The browser may become a hiding place.
But the heart is where sin must ultimately be confronted.
Jesus' violent imagery communicates something modern Christianity can become dangerously reluctant to say:
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Some things should not be managed.
They should be removed.
Some doors should not merely be resisted.
They should be locked.
Some accounts should not merely be visited less frequently.
They should be deleted.
Some apps should disappear.
Some private browsing habits need to end.
Some phones need restrictions.
Some passwords need to belong to an accountability partner.
Some late-night routines need to change.
Some friendships need enough honesty for you finally to say:
“I need help.”
Because there comes a point when saying, “I'm praying about it,” while protecting unrestricted access to the very thing feeding the sin becomes spiritual contradiction.
Prayer is not supposed to become camouflage for refusing obedience.
Imagine someone standing inside a burning house praying for God to save him while refusing to walk through the open door.
Sometimes God's answer to your prayer for freedom looks painfully practical.
Delete it.
Block it.
Confess it.
Leave the room.
Call someone.
Stop carrying your phone into bed.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Run.
Paul's instruction concerning sexual immorality was not, “Study how close you can stand to it.”
“Flee fornication.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18, KJV
Flee.
There is movement in that word.
Joseph understood this long before smartphones existed.
Potiphar's wife offered secrecy, access, opportunity, and sexual temptation.
Joseph did not remain in the room to demonstrate how spiritually mature he was.
He ran.
He left his garment behind.
Sometimes victory looks less impressive than we imagined.
Sometimes victory is simply getting out of the room.
But pornography has another lie.
It tells you that because you have returned so many times, you are probably beyond restoration.
That lie has buried people almost as deeply as lust itself.
Because after repeated failure, shame begins preaching.
“You're disgusting.”
“You aren't a real Christian.”
“God must be tired of you.”
“Don't tell anybody.”
“Hide.”
And hiding is exactly where bondage grows best.
Remember the first human response after sin entered the world.
Adam and Eve hid.
Sin produced shame.
Shame produced hiding.
And God came looking.
“Where art thou?” — Genesis 3:9.
Not because God lacked information.
The question exposed the distance sin had created.
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
We hide behind humor.
Behind ministry.
Behind marriages.
Behind church attendance.
Behind deleted histories.
Behind Bible verses.
Behind worship playlists.
Behind the phrase, “I'm doing okay.”
And sometimes the person singing loudest on Sunday night is fighting a war nobody knows about by midnight.
Maybe that's you.
Maybe nobody knows how tired you are.
Maybe you've confessed the same sin to God so many times that even the words feel worn out.
Maybe you have wondered whether repentance still counts when you have failed again.
Hear this carefully.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the announcement that chains do not have to remain your master.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become comfortable with the darkness.
He shed His blood to redeem sinners from it.
The Gospel does not say sexual sin is insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required the death of the Son of God.
But grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly came.
Jesus knew what humanity had done.
He knew what humanity would do.
He knew every hidden browser.
Every affair.
Every fantasy.
Every secret addiction.
Every objectifying gaze.
Every relapse.
Every lie told to cover another lie.
And Christ still went toward Calvary.
Not because sin was harmless.
Because love was costly.
There the sinless Christ bore judgment for sinners.
There mercy and justice met.
There forgiveness was purchased not by our promises to improve but by His finished work.
And there is something pornography can never give you that Jesus freely offers.
To be completely known...
and still invited home.
Pornography offers exposure without intimacy.
Christ offers intimacy without exploitation.
Pornography says, “Consume.”
Jesus says, “Love.”
Pornography says, “Use.”
Jesus says, “Serve.”
Pornography says, “Take.”
Jesus gave Himself.
Pornography teaches you to detach someone's body from covenant, responsibility, sacrifice, and personhood.
The Gospel reveals a Savior whose love is demonstrated precisely through sacrifice.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Look at the contrast.
Lust asks:
What can I take from you?
Christlike love asks:
What can I give for you?
That is why freedom from pornography is not merely about becoming better at saying no.
It is about learning to see again.
Seeing women as image-bearers rather than images.
Seeing men as image-bearers rather than bodies.
Seeing sexuality as God's gift rather than our god.
Seeing marriage as covenant rather than consumption.
Seeing singleness as a life capable of holiness and fullness rather than a waiting room for sexual fulfillment.
Seeing your own body not as an appetite demanding obedience but as belonging to the Lord.
Paul writes:
Bought with a price.
That changes the question.
The Christian no longer asks only:
“Can I get away with this?”
We begin asking:
“Does this belong in a life purchased by Jesus Christ?”
And perhaps that question hurts.
Good.
Not because God delights in humiliating you.
Because conviction can be mercy.
The surgeon's warning sounds frightening when the disease is serious.
Jesus speaks fiercely because eternity matters.
He loves us too much to call slavery freedom.
And His warning in Matthew 5 does not stop with the eye.
Jesus speaks of Gehenna.
Judgment.
The stakes are eternal.
That truth should sober every one of us.
Christianity is not behavior modification with inspirational music.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance, faith, and a transformed life.
Yet we must never reverse the Gospel.
You do not defeat pornography so that Jesus will finally love you.
You come to Jesus because sinners cannot rescue themselves.
You do not cleanse yourself sufficiently and then approach Christ.
You approach Christ for cleansing.
You do not earn the cross.
You collapse beneath it.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV.
Notice the Gospel does not tell us to pretend.
Confess.
The Greek word commonly translated “confess” in that verse is homologeō—to acknowledge, to say the same thing, to agree.
Stop renaming what God has named.
Stop calling bondage “just a habit.”
Stop calling lust “appreciating beauty.”
Stop calling secrecy “privacy” when secrecy exists specifically to protect sin.
Stop promising tomorrow what obedience requires today.
Bring it into the light.
And if you fall?
Do not turn failure into permission to surrender.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Get up.
Remove access.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Fight again.
Not because repeated sin does not matter.
Because Jesus is still worthy of the fight.
Some people reading this have been fighting pornography for years.
Others clicked something for the first time recently and already feel the hook.
Some are husbands hiding it from wives.
Some are wives hiding it from husbands.
Some are teenagers terrified that their parents will discover their history.
Some are pastors.
Some are worship leaders.
Some are people who have never told another human being.
And some are reading this while carrying wounds connected to being objectified themselves.
If that is you, understand this:
Jesus does not look at you the way pornography does.
He does not reduce you to your body.
He does not measure your worth by desirability.
He does not consume you.
He knows you.
Your body is not merchandise.
Your dignity is not determined by somebody else's lust.
Your value is not established by whether somebody wants your body.
You were made by God.
And for those who have spent years objectifying others, repentance includes learning to recognize that dignity again.
The person on the screen is not pixels.
The woman walking past you is not a fantasy.
The man at the gym is not material for your imagination.
Look differently.
Not fearfully.
Not awkwardly.
Not with contempt for human beauty.
With holiness.
With love.
With honor.
Because purity is not learning to hate bodies.
God created bodies.
Christian purity is learning to refuse the lie that another person's body exists for your unauthorized consumption.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that pornography shocks you anymore.
Perhaps it is that it doesn't.
Things that once disturbed you can slowly become normal.
What once required searching becomes scrolling.
What once produced immediate conviction begins producing excuses.
What once made you weep before God becomes something you casually promise to deal with later.
That is why Jesus' words must remain sharp.
Not because Christ wants wounded sinners terrified to approach Him.
Because He refuses to let comfortable sinners sleep peacefully while walking toward destruction.
Wake up.
There is still grace.
There is still a cross.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still repentance.
There is still resurrection power.
There is still a Savior who receives sinners.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus and became a preacher of Christ.
The Corinthian church included people rescued from profound sexual sin, and Paul could write:
Were.
That word is beautiful.
Your sin may explain part of your history.
It does not have to dictate your destiny.
This is the scandal of grace.
Christ does not merely improve respectable people.
He resurrects sinners.
He enters stories we would rather delete and begins writing redemption across pages covered in shame.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So tonight, before you reach for the phone, remember whose eyes you have.
Before you search, remember whose body you belong to.
Before you hide, remember that Christ already knows.
Before shame convinces you to run away from Jesus, run toward Him.
And if something keeps dragging you back into darkness, take His warning seriously enough to become radical.
Not self-mutilation.
Surrender.
Remove access.
Destroy secrecy.
Confess the sin.
Seek trustworthy Christian accountability.
If necessary, seek qualified professional help alongside pastoral care, especially where compulsive behavior, trauma, or severe relational damage is involved.
Do whatever righteous wisdom requires to stop feeding what is trying to master you.
Your eye is not your master.
Your appetite is not your master.
Pornography is not your master.
If you belong to Christ, Jesus is Lord.
Maybe this article exposed something you have hidden for years.
Be honest.
If secrecy has been poisoning you and today you are choosing the light, comment, “No more hiding.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
And if Jesus has already begun restoring what sexual sin damaged, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading your three words may realize they are not the only person fighting.
That matters.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money purchases blessing. It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be bought.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it. If you want to glorify God through what He has entrusted to you, one legitimate expression of stewardship is helping faithful Gospel resources continue to be created, distributed, shared, and placed before people who might otherwise never encounter them.
Send it privately to the person God just brought to your mind.
Because perhaps somewhere tonight...
another room is dark.
Another phone is glowing.
Another person is seconds away from surrendering again.
And perhaps your share will place one sentence in front of them before temptation does.
Maybe they will stop.
Maybe they will pray.
Maybe they will confess.
Maybe they will finally ask for help.
Maybe they will discover that Jesus is not standing at the end of repentance with crossed arms.
He is the reason repentance can lead home.
And maybe years from now, they will barely remember the image they almost clicked...
but they will remember the night Christ interrupted them.
The screen can be turned off in a second—but only Jesus can teach the heart to see a human being again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID NEVER RETURNED TO THE TEN CONCUBINES ABSALOM HAD TAKEN—THEY LIVED LIKE WIDOWS
paragraphs: DAVID NEVER RETURNED TO THE TEN CONCUBINES ABSALOM HAD TAKEN—THEY LIVED LIKE WIDOWS

He came back to Jerusalem. He reclaimed his palace. He survived his son’s rebellion. But behind the restored doors of David’s kingdom were ten women whose lives would never return to what they had been—and one haunting Hebrew phrase exposes just how devastating the consequences of sin can become.
There is a sentence buried in 2 Samuel that is easy to read too quickly.
It comes after rebellion.
After betrayal.
After a father has been driven from Jerusalem by his own son.
After Absalom has died.
After David has wept one of the most agonizing cries recorded in Scripture:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!”
Eventually David returns to Jerusalem.
The throne is still his.
The palace is still standing.
The rebellion has failed.
The king has come home.
You might expect the story to begin settling down.
Instead, almost immediately, Scripture takes us behind the palace walls and makes us look at ten women.
Not soldiers.
Not generals.
Not politicians.
Ten women.
Women David had left behind.
Women Absalom had taken.
Women who would spend the rest of their lives in a condition Scripture describes with words so painfully strange that they should stop us in our tracks:
“living in widowhood.”
Except their husband was still alive.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 20:3 ends with the striking expression:
אַלְמְנוּת חַיּוּת — ’almenut ḥayyut

Literally, the language conveys the condition of living in widowhood. The Hebrew text describes them as shut away until the day of their death, and translations capture the expression as “living in widowhood,” “living as widows,” or “living as if in widowhood.”
Read that again.
Their husband had returned.
Their husband was alive.
Their husband was king.
Their material needs were provided for.
Yet they lived like widows.
And suddenly this obscure verse becomes unbearably human.
Because some consequences do not disappear when the crisis ends.
Some wounds remain after everybody else has gone home.
Some people survive another person’s sin only to discover that survival and restoration are not always the same thing.
And if you have ever wondered whether Scripture understands what it feels like to live with consequences you did not personally create, stay with these ten women for a moment.
Their story did not begin in 2 Samuel 20.

When Absalom’s rebellion forced David to flee Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 15:16 tells us that David left ten concubines behind “to keep the house”—to care for the palace. The Hebrew identifies them as עֶשֶׂר נָשִׁים פִּלַגְשִׁים — ‘eser nashim pilagshim, ten women, concubines.
David fled.
They remained.
Then Absalom entered Jerusalem.
And what happened next was not merely sexual behavior. It was a calculated political act of humiliation and royal usurpation.
Ahithophel advised Absalom to go in to his father’s concubines. A tent was then pitched on the roof, and 2 Samuel 16:22 says Absalom went in to them “in the sight of all Israel.”
Do not rush past that roof.
Because another terrible memory hangs over David’s rooftop.
Years earlier, David had walked on the roof of his palace and seen Bathsheba.
What followed was adultery, abuse of royal power, deception, the arranged death of Uriah, and an attempt to hide what had happened.
David thought the darkness could cover it.
God sent Nathan.

And Nathan told him that what David had done secretly would bring consequences into the open. In 2 Samuel 12:11–12, the judgment announced against David’s house included the shocking declaration that another would take his wives openly, “in the sight of all Israel.”
Then, chapters later, there is Absalom.
There is the roof.
There are the women.
There is all Israel watching.
The biblical narrator is forcing us to remember.
Sin travels farther than the sinner imagines.
David was forgiven when he confessed his sin. That is crucial. When David said, “I have sinned against the LORD,” Nathan answered, “The LORD also hath put away thy sin” (2 Samuel 12:13).
Grace was real.
Forgiveness was real.
But forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence.
That distinction matters enormously.
Some Christians secretly believe that if repentance is genuine, every consequence should immediately disappear.
The Bible never promises that.
You can be forgiven and still have relationships to repair.
Forgiven and still have scars.
Forgiven and still need to confess what you did to another person.
Forgiven and still have children affected by choices you regret.
Forgiven and still need accountability.
Forgiven and still reap consequences from seeds you wish you had never planted.
Forgiveness means your sin no longer condemns you before God when you are in Christ.
It does not mean sin was harmless.
Look at David.
Then look at the ten women.
When David finally returned to Jerusalem, Scripture says:

“And David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in ward, and fed them, but went not in unto them. So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood.”
—2 Samuel 20:3, KJV
That ending hurts.
“But went not in unto them.”
He provided for them.
But he never resumed sexual relations with them.
They remained confined until their deaths.
And here we must be careful.
Scripture does not tell us that these women seduced Absalom.
It does not tell us they invited what happened.
It does not give us access to their private thoughts, choices, fears, or degree of agency in the event.
Therefore we should not invent guilt where God’s Word does not assign it.

Some older commentators speculated about the women’s responsibility, while others understood their confinement as arising from the conventions surrounding the royal harem after Absalom had appropriated them. But the biblical text itself simply tells us what Absalom did and what David subsequently did; it does not narrate the women’s consent or motives.
That distinction matters.
Especially to the wounded.
Especially to the person who has carried shame for something someone else did to them.
Especially to someone who has confused what happened to them with what defines them.
Human beings are very good at handing shame to the wounded.
Jesus is not.
And perhaps that is where this ancient palace suddenly becomes frighteningly modern.
Because you may know what it feels like to be one of the people left behind after somebody else’s disaster.
Maybe your father’s addiction changed your childhood.
Maybe your spouse’s betrayal changed how easily you trust.
Maybe someone abused power over you and walked away while you carried the memories.
Maybe somebody made one selfish decision that altered your family for twenty years.
Maybe you are living inside consequences you never voted for.
Maybe everybody remembers the name of the person who caused the scandal…
but almost nobody remembers yours.
People remember David.
People remember Absalom.
People remember Bathsheba.
People remember Nathan.
People remember Ahithophel.
But ask most believers to name the ten women of 2 Samuel 20:3.
They cannot.
Scripture does not even give us their names here.
Yet God saw them.
That may be the sentence someone reading this desperately needed.
God saw them.
The biblical narrative did not allow them to disappear completely.
One verse preserved their tragedy for thousands of years.
Kings fought.
Armies marched.
Rebellions rose and collapsed.
Men competed for thrones.
And the Holy Spirit inspired Scripture that stopped long enough to tell us that ten women spent the remainder of their lives living like widows.
Heaven notices people history overlooks.
And maybe heaven has noticed you too.
But there is another truth here that we cannot soften.
David's household did not become this fractured overnight.
Long before Absalom’s rebellion, God had already given Israel’s kings a warning. Deuteronomy 17:17 commanded that the king was not to multiply wives for himself.
David was a man after God’s own heart, but “man after God’s own heart” never meant “man without grievous sin.”
The Bible refuses to airbrush its heroes.
That is one reason Scripture is so devastatingly believable.
David can kill Goliath in faith…
and later abuse his royal power terribly.
He can write psalms that have comforted broken hearts for three thousand years…
and still leave devastation inside his own family.
He can worship passionately…
and fail catastrophically.
He can genuinely repent…
and still live long enough to watch consequences unfold.
The Bible does not need David to be spotless.
Because David is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And that changes everything.
If you read the Old Testament searching for flawless human heroes, eventually every human throne disappoints you.
David points beyond himself.
We need a better King.
A King who does not exploit the vulnerable.
A King who does not take what belongs to another.
A King whose private life does not contradict His public righteousness.
A King who does not abandon His people when rebellion comes.
A King who does not merely provide bread from a distance but comes personally to the broken.
A King who touches lepers.
Receives outcasts.
Defends the condemned.
Calls sinners to repentance.
Forgives the guilty.
Restores the ruined.
And willingly gives Himself for people who rebelled against Him.
Jesus Christ is that King.
David returned to Jerusalem and entered his palace.
Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing He was going to a cross.
David's kingdom was shaken by his son's rebellion.
Jesus came into a world already in rebellion against God.
David survived while Absalom died.
Jesus, the sinless Son, willingly died so rebels could live.
Do you see the reversal?
At Calvary, the innocent King bears the judgment of the guilty.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
This is where scandal collides with grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that pretends consequences do not matter.
Grace with nail wounds.
Grace that tells the truth about sin because sin was serious enough to require the cross.
Grace that looks at repentant sinners and says their worst chapter does not have authority to write their final chapter.
David sinned.
David was exposed.
David repented.
David was forgiven.
David suffered consequences.
And still…
God's redemptive plan continued.
Eventually, through David's royal line, according to the flesh, came Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
God did not call David's evil good.
God did not erase the seriousness of his sin.
God did not pretend innocent people had not been affected.
Yet human failure could not derail God's redemptive purpose.
That is the difference between covering scandal and redeeming sinners.
The Gospel does not say:
“It never happened.”
The Gospel says:
“It will not have the final word.”
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Perhaps there is a chapter you keep trying to tear out of your story.
Something you did.
Something done to you.
A marriage that collapsed.
A secret nobody knows.
An addiction you keep feeding while telling everyone you are fine.
A betrayal you cannot undo.
A childhood wound that still follows you into adult rooms.
A private compromise beneath a public Christian image.
You know how to smile at church.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which verse to post.
But when everything becomes quiet, you still hear the chains moving inside rooms nobody else can see.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come to improve your disguise.
He came to save you.
There is an enormous difference.
Repentance is not learning how to hide the evidence more successfully.
Repentance is bringing the truth into God's light.
David learned painfully that hidden sin does not remain safely hidden.
You can bury something from people.
You cannot bury it from God.
Yet the terrifying holiness of God is not the end of the Gospel story.
The God who sees everything is also the God who sent His Son.
That means you do not need to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You confess.
You repent.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop calling chains “freedom.”
You stop calling compromise “complicated.”
You stop negotiating with the thing crucifying your soul.
And you run to Jesus.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
Because condemnation does not belong to those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because your past suddenly becomes beautiful.
Because Christ can take a story scarred by sin and make even the scars testify that mercy came.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal to denial.
Not scandal to religious reputation management.
Not scandal to pretending.
Scandal…
to confession.
Confession…
to repentance.
Repentance…
to mercy.
Mercy…
to restoration.
And restoration…
to a life that begins telling other broken people:
There is still a Savior.
Maybe you identify with David today.
Then repent.
Stop hiding.
There is mercy in Christ.
Maybe you identify more with those ten unnamed women.
Then hear this carefully:
What someone did to you is not the measure of your worth before God.
You are not merely somebody's aftermath.
You are not merely somebody's scandal.

And although this passage does not give us the rest of those women's inner stories, the whole counsel of Scripture reveals a God who repeatedly sees the afflicted, hears the brokenhearted, and draws near to those who cry to Him.
Maybe you are Absalom in this story—angry, ambitious, wounded, and using your pain as permission to wound others.
Stop before another person becomes collateral damage in your rebellion.
Pain does not become righteousness simply because it has a reason.
Bring it to Christ.
Maybe you are standing on a rooftop spiritually right now, one decision away from creating consequences you cannot predict.
Walk away.
Close the conversation.
Delete the secret account.
Confess the affair.
Tell someone about the addiction.
Return what is not yours.
Ask forgiveness.
Get accountable.
Run from temptation.
Do not wait until tomorrow's consequences explain today's warning.
Sin always promises control.
Then sends invoices.
Jesus offers something radically different.
Surrender.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new Master.
A new direction.
Life.
Be honest.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person still fighting.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, do not simply think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach down at them.

Sharing biblical truth is not a substitute for obedience, prayer, generosity, local-church faithfulness, or personally proclaiming Christ. But it can be one simple act of placing the Gospel where another wounded person may encounter it.
Because one day you may need to remember:
forgiveness does not mean sin was harmless, consequences do not mean grace has failed, and scars do not mean Jesus has finished writing.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromises, strengthening your walk with Christ, or helping you place biblical truth in front of people who desperately need it, consider staying close and supporting this ministry.
More importantly, the purpose is deeper discipleship.
Biblical nourishment.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Accountability.
Spiritual sharpening.
A community continually being pointed away from itself and back to Jesus Christ.
But before you leave this story, go back one last time.
Back through the palace doors.
Back past David.
Back past Absalom.
Back past the throne.
Back to ten unnamed women living out their days in a condition Scripture calls widowhood.
We do not know their private thoughts.
We do not know the conversations they had behind those guarded doors.
We do not know whether they cried at night.
We do not know whether they ever imagined their story would still be read thousands of years later.
So we will not invent what God chose not to reveal.
But we know this:
Their pain became part of a biblical warning that still speaks.
Sin reaches farther than we think.
Power can wound people who never asked to become part of the scandal.
Forgiveness is real.
Consequences are real.
Grace is real.
And David, for all his greatness, was never enough.
We needed another King.
We needed Jesus.
The King who entered our scandal without participating in our sin.
The King who carried our shame without deserving it.
The King who received wounds so wounded sinners could be reconciled to God.
The King who walked into death and walked back out.
So whatever room you believe your past has locked you inside…
do not mistake the room for the ending.
Bring your guilt to Christ.
Bring your wounds to Christ.
Bring your anger.
Your secrets.
Your regrets.
Your shame.
Your shattered family.
Your consequences.
Your unanswered questions.
Bring the pieces.
Because the Gospel has never been about pretending the pieces were never broken.
It is about what happens when the broken pieces finally reach the hands of the Redeemer.
Your scandal may explain some of your scars—but only Jesus gets to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE”: Biblical Passion That Money Cannot Buy
paragraphs: “MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE”: Biblical Passion That Money Cannot Buy
You can drown almost anything if the water rises high enough. But Scripture says there is a kind of love that can go under the flood—and come back burning.
There are some things money can buy.
A beautiful house.
A carefully chosen gift.
A plane ticket across the world.
Flowers delivered to a doorstep.
A wedding that leaves everyone speechless.
A comfortable bed.
A table overflowing with food.
Even the appearance of a perfect life.
But there is something money has never been able to purchase.
Love.
Not the kind that poses for photographs.
Not the kind that survives only while everything feels good.
Not attraction dressed up as covenant.
Not obsession mistaken for devotion.
Not affection that remains only until suffering arrives.
Real love.
The kind that walks through fire.
The kind that gets wounded and refuses to become counterfeit.
The kind that cannot be auctioned to the highest bidder.
The kind that remains when the gifts disappear, the applause stops, beauty changes, money runs low, and life becomes painfully different from what you imagined.
Thousands of years ago, Scripture described that love with an image so violent and beautiful that it still reaches into the human heart:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it…”
Song of Songs 8:7.
But the Hebrew carries something worth slowing down long enough to hear.
מַיִם רַבִּים לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְכַבּוֹת אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה
Mayim rabbim lo yukhelu lekhabbot et-ha’ahavah.
“Many waters are not able to extinguish love.”
Then:
וּנְהָרוֹת לֹא יִשְׁטְפוּהָ
Uneharot lo yishtefuha.
“Nor can rivers sweep it away.”
And then comes the line that destroys one of humanity’s oldest illusions:
אִם־יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶת־כָּל־הוֹן בֵּיתוֹ בָּאַהֲבָה בּוֹז יָבוּזוּ לוֹ
Even if a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly despised.
Read that again.
All the wealth of his house.
Everything.
And still he cannot buy love.
That is the scandal.
And perhaps somewhere inside that sentence is your story.
Because maybe you have spent years trying to purchase with performance what can only be received through love.
Maybe you learned early that affection came when you behaved.
Approval came when you succeeded.
Attention came when you looked attractive.
Praise came when you accomplished something.
Acceptance came when you were useful.
So you became useful.
Very useful.
You learned how to smile while exhausted.
How to serve while empty.
How to say, “I’m okay,” while something inside you was quietly collapsing.
You learned how to give people what they wanted because somewhere deep inside, you were terrified that if you stopped performing, they might stop loving you.
And eventually that way of thinking entered your relationship with God.
You may never have said it aloud.
But you started bargaining.
“God, if I become better…”
“If I pray more…”
“If I serve harder…”
“If I stop struggling…”
“If I become the Christian everyone thinks I should be…”
“Maybe then You will really love me.”
And that is where the Gospel walks into the room and overturns the table.
Because the Gospel does not announce that sinful people finally became lovable enough for God.
It announces something infinitely more astonishing.
God loved us while we were still sinners.
Romans 5:8 does not say Christ waited for humanity to become impressive.
It says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after every secret was confessed.
Not after every relationship was repaired.
Not after the shame stopped screaming.
Not after we became religious enough to deserve Him.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not make sin insignificant.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Yet God’s grace is so astonishing that the price was not placed into our hands.
Christ bore it.
This is where we must understand Song of Songs carefully.

Song of Songs is first and directly poetry celebrating human love, desire, covenant affection, longing, and marital devotion. We should not erase that meaning by pretending every romantic line is secretly an allegory with no concern for human marriage.
But neither should Christians read Scripture with Christ absent from the horizon.
The love celebrated in marriage points us toward something larger because throughout the New Testament marriage itself becomes a profound picture of Christ and His people.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:25:
There it is again.
Love gives.
But notice the difference between giving because you love and giving to purchase love.
That difference changes everything.
Song of Songs says wealth cannot purchase love.
The Gospel says Christ loved—and therefore gave Himself.
Christian generosity works the same way.
We do not give so God will love us.
We give because in Christ we have encountered a love we could never purchase.
We do not obey to make Jesus die for us.
He already died.
We do not repent so we can become valuable enough for the Savior.
We repent because the Savior is worthy, sin is deadly, and grace has opened the way home.
We do not surrender because surrender purchases salvation.
Salvation is the gift that finally teaches us why surrender is worth it.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needs to hear tonight.
You cannot buy what Jesus offers freely.
You cannot out-donate your guilt.
You cannot out-serve your shame.
You cannot perform your way into adoption.
You cannot impress the Father into calling you His child.
You cannot make the blood of Christ more effective by adding your achievements to it.
You come empty-handed.
That is humiliating to pride.
And breathtaking to the exhausted.
Because empty hands are exactly the hands capable of receiving a gift.
Maybe your life has been one long attempt to prove you are worth loving.
Jesus is not asking you to audition.
He is calling you to repent, believe, and come home.
And some of us desperately need to distinguish biblical love from the counterfeit version our culture often sells.
Biblical love is not merely intensity.
Intensity can disappear tomorrow.
Biblical love is not possession.
Jealous control can call itself love while slowly suffocating another human being.
Biblical love is not lust.
Lust asks, “What can I take from you?”
Love asks, “How can I seek your genuine good?”
Biblical love is not tolerating everything another person does.
Sometimes love confronts.
Sometimes love tells the truth.
Sometimes love establishes boundaries.
Sometimes love refuses to participate in destruction.
Sometimes love says the painful thing precisely because silence would be easier.

And love is not proved by remaining in danger. Song of Songs should never be weaponized to tell an abused person that “many waters cannot quench love,” therefore they must silently endure violence or coercion. Biblical love does not require pretending evil is good.
Love rejoices in truth.
And real love survives truth.
That may be why some relationships collapse the moment honesty enters the room.
They were being held together by performance.
Not love.
But imagine being completely known and still genuinely loved.
That is one of the deepest longings inside the human heart.
We hide because we fear that if people knew everything, they would leave.
We edit ourselves.
Crop the photograph.
Delete the history.
Hide the messages.
Cover the scars.
Change the subject.
Raise our hands during worship while secretly wondering whether God is disgusted with the person underneath them.
Then the Gospel does something terrifying.
It turns on the light.
And something beautiful happens.
Jesus does not expose darkness merely to humiliate sinners.
He brings darkness into the light so sinners can be forgiven, cleansed, restored, and transformed.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Grace is God dealing with sin at the cross so completely that the sinner who trusts in Christ can stop hiding behind excuses and finally confess the truth.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is one of grace’s beautiful consequences.
You stop defending the prison once you realize the door has been opened.
You stop decorating the chains.
You stop renaming bondage.
You finally say:
“Jesus, this is me.”
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the Sunday version.
Me.
The angry me.
The jealous me.
The lustful me.
The frightened me.
The addicted me.
The bitter me.
The hypocritical me.
The wounded me.
The one who knew better and still did it.
The one who promised You, “Never again,” and somehow ended up there again.
And Christianity makes an outrageous announcement to that person:
There is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Cross-shaped grace.
Resurrection-confirmed grace.
Grace that forgives you and then refuses to leave you enslaved to what was destroying you.
Because Jesus does not merely rewrite reputations.
He transforms people.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Think about Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then fear entered the room.
Three times he denied knowing Jesus.
Imagine carrying that memory.
The sound of your own voice denying the One you claimed you would die for.
Then the rooster.
Then the realization.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
What do you do when the person who betrayed Jesus is you?
John 21 gives us one of Scripture’s most tender scenes.
The resurrected Christ meets Peter again.
There is breakfast.
There is conversation.
There is restoration.
Jesus does not pretend Peter never failed.
But neither does Peter’s failure receive authority to write the final chapter of Peter’s life.
That authority belongs to Jesus.
Peter’s scandal was real.
Grace was more powerful.
Maybe yours is real too.
Maybe you have destroyed trust.
Maybe you have been carrying something you hope nobody ever discovers.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out something inside you.
Maybe resentment has lived in your heart so long that you no longer remember who you were before it moved in.
Maybe you walked away from God.
Maybe church hurt became the doorway through which you quietly abandoned prayer.
Maybe you still attend church physically, but spiritually you have been gone for years.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong because nobody knows how tired you actually are.
Listen.
The answer is not pretending harder.
Come to Christ.
Not merely to religious activity.
Christ.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who ate with people respectable society despised.
The One who confronted self-righteousness.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who carried a cross.
The One who died.
The One who was buried.
The One who rose.
The One who still saves.
And when the waters rise—and they will—remember the image Scripture gave us.
Many waters cannot quench love.
There will be waters.
Marriage discovers this.
Friendship discovers this.
Parenthood discovers this.
Discipleship discovers this.
There are hospital waters.
Funeral waters.
Betrayal waters.
Financial waters.
Temptation waters.
Depression and grief.
Long nights.
Unanswered questions.
Prodigal children.
Broken promises.
Aging bodies.
Empty chairs.
Prayers whose answers did not arrive in the form you expected.
Faith is not the promise that Christians will never enter deep water.
Sometimes faith sounds like Isaiah 43:2:
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee.”
Not if.
When.
And Christianity ultimately anchors hope not in the strength of our emotional passion for God, but in God’s faithfulness and the finished work of Christ.
Your emotions fluctuate.
His character does not.
Your grip sometimes weakens.
His promises do not become untrue because your hands are trembling.
This is why Christian love cannot finally be reduced to butterflies, goosebumps, worship music, romantic feelings, or inspirational moments.
Love becomes visible in faithfulness.
In forgiveness.
In truth.
In sacrifice.
In repentance.
In staying when staying is righteous.
In leaving sin when sin has become familiar.
In confessing when hiding would preserve your reputation.
In giving without trying to purchase applause.
In serving when nobody knows your name.
In choosing Christ when compromise would be easier.
And that brings us back to money.
“If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.”
Love cannot be bought.
And that truth must govern Christian ministry too.
It does not.
A donation is not forgiveness.
Buying a Christian book does not make someone righteous.
Supporting a ministry does not force God to bless you.
And no faithful Christian ministry should manipulate you into believing otherwise.
Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Your place in the family of God cannot be purchased.
But there is another biblical truth.
Grace produces generosity.
The New Testament repeatedly shows believers voluntarily supporting Gospel work, caring for those in need, and sharing material resources so ministry can continue.
Paul describes Christian giving in 2 Corinthians 9:7 with extraordinary clarity:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
That matters.

So if Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, brought Scripture into a dark season, helped you return to Jesus, encouraged you when you wanted to quit, or given you something worth sending to another struggling soul, you can help this work continue.
Not because giving money earns heaven.
But because voluntary generosity can put resources behind work you believe is worth continuing.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you want to help.
Never because you think God is selling His affection.
He is not.
And there is another way to help that may cost you nothing.
One share can put the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
You do not know who is awake at 2:13 in the morning scrolling through Facebook because their marriage is collapsing.
You do not know who is sitting alone wondering whether God could forgive what they have done.
You do not know which old friend is silently losing a battle nobody knows exists.
You do not know which unbelieving relative has rejected church but might still read an article you shared because they trust you.
Not for numbers.
For people.
And if you have watched Jesus patiently restore pieces of your life you thought were permanently ruined, tell somebody what He has done.
Your testimony might become another person’s reason to believe that their story is not finished.
Because eventually the waters rise.
And when they do, you may need to come back and remember:
Love is not proved by how much money someone spends.
Love is not proved by how impressive someone looks.
Love is not proved by emotion alone.
Love has weight.
Love has truth.
Love has faithfulness.
And at the center of the Christian story stands a cross where love was not purchased by us but demonstrated toward us.
Jesus did not come because humanity finally became worthy.
He came because sinners needed a Savior.
He did not die because sin was trivial.
He died because sin was deadly.
He did not rise merely to make bad people slightly nicer.
He rose victorious, and everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith receives a new identity, a new hope, and ultimately the promise of resurrection life.
That is why the Gospel is bigger than inspiration.
It is rescue.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person drifting from God.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Let them encounter the Word.
Use them.
Share them.
Study.
Test what you read against Scripture.
Grow.
And wherever truth confronts you, do not merely admire it.
Respond to it.
Because someday all the things we thought made us valuable will fall from our hands.
The money.
The accomplishments.
The titles.
The followers.
The possessions.
The carefully maintained image.
None of it can purchase the thing our souls need most.
But Jesus has already done what money could never do.
The question is not whether you can afford Him.
You cannot buy Him.
The question is whether you will stop trying to save yourself and receive the mercy you could never earn.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come into the light.
Let Christ begin transforming what shame told you must remain hidden forever.
Because the goal was never merely to build an audience.
The goal is to point human beings toward Jesus.
There are still people drowning beneath waters nobody else can see.
And they need to know there is a love money cannot purchase, suffering cannot cheaply imitate, and death itself could not hold in the grave.
When every counterfeit love has named its price, the scarred hands of Jesus will still be telling you that grace was never for sale.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU WERE SEALED: The Terrifyingly Beautiful Reason the Holy Spirit Is Called the Seal of Salvation
paragraphs: YOU WERE SEALED: The Terrifyingly Beautiful Reason the Holy Spirit Is Called the Seal of Salvation

If you belong to Jesus Christ, heaven did not merely hear your prayer, forgive your past, and leave you wondering whether anything really happened. God placed His own Spirit within you—and Scripture calls Him the seal, the guarantee, and the living witness that you belong to Christ.
There is a kind of fear Christians rarely admit out loud.
It usually comes at night.
After the worship music has stopped.
After the Bible has been closed.
After everyone who thinks you are “strong in the Lord” has gone home.
You remember something you did.
Something you said.
Something you thought you had conquered.
Maybe it was years ago.
Maybe it was this morning.
And suddenly a question crawls into the silence:
What if God is finished with me?
You know the verses about grace.
You know Jesus died for sinners.
You may have told other people that God forgives.
But when the person needing mercy is you, theology can suddenly feel much harder to believe.
You look at your failures and wonder whether a real Christian could have struggled this badly.
You look at your weakness and wonder whether God regrets receiving you.
You remember how passionate you once were, compare it with how exhausted you feel now, and somewhere beneath all the Christian vocabulary is a frightened soul asking:
Do I still belong to Him?
And into that fear, Paul writes something astonishing.
Not sentimental.
Not motivational.
Something infinitely stronger.
He says that when people hear the gospel of salvation and believe in Christ, something happens that human eyes cannot see.
Paul writes in Ephesians 1:13–14:
The crucial word is:
ἐσφραγίσθητε — esphragisthēte.
“You were sealed.”
Not because you finally became impressive.
Not because you accumulated enough church attendance.
Not because you learned Christian vocabulary.
Not because you stopped needing grace.
Paul’s sequence is breathtakingly Christ-centered: you heard “the word of truth,” the gospel of your salvation; you believed in Christ; and you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
Then Paul says something even more extraordinary.
The Holy Spirit is:
ἀρραβὼν — arrabōn
of our inheritance.
A pledge.
A deposit.
A guarantee pointing toward what God has promised to bring to completion.
In other words, Christianity is not merely God handing forgiven sinners a receipt and telling them to come back at the resurrection.
God gives Himself.
The Holy Spirit is not merely an emotion you experience during worship.
He is not spiritual electricity.
He is not goosebumps.
He is not a mystical accessory for unusually spiritual Christians.
He is God the Holy Spirit.
And Scripture says He dwells in those who belong to Christ.
That changes everything.
Because when Paul calls the Holy Spirit a “seal,” he is using language his original audience could understand.
A seal could identify ownership.
A seal could authenticate.
A seal carried the authority of the one whose mark it bore.
So when Scripture says the believer is sealed with the Holy Spirit, the picture is staggering:
God has marked His people as His own.
Think about that before you keep reading.
You may have spent years defining yourself by labels God never gave you.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Addicted.
Abandoned.
Failure.
Dirty.
Unwanted.
Hypocrite.
Damaged.
Too far gone.
You may still remember what people called you.
You may remember what you called yourself.
But the Gospel announces something scandalous.
Jesus Christ receives sinners who bring Him nothing but their need.
At the cross, He bore sin.
He suffered in the sinner’s place.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose bodily from the grave.
And everyone who truly turns to Christ in repentance and faith is not merely given another opportunity to become worthy.
They are received by grace.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Made new.
And indwelt by the Holy Spirit.
This is why the seal cannot be separated from Jesus.
The Holy Spirit does not exist to make much of you.
He glorifies Christ.
He does not whisper, “Look how extraordinary you are.”
He continually turns the sinner’s eyes toward the extraordinary Savior.
Your salvation rests ultimately not upon your ability to impress God but upon the finished work of Jesus Christ received through faith.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because some people have quietly turned Christianity into spiritual probation.
Jesus forgives you…
then apparently stands at a distance waiting to see whether you can keep yourself worthy of being forgiven.
But that is not Paul’s picture.

Paul says God Himself establishes believers in Christ, and in 2 Corinthians 1:21–22 he describes God as the One who places His seal upon His people and gives the Spirit in their hearts as a guarantee.
God is not merely waiting at the finish line.
God is involved in bringing His people home.
And perhaps you need to hear this because you have confused your changing emotional condition with God’s unchanging character.
Monday morning you feel close to God.
Tuesday you feel nothing.
Wednesday you worship and cry.
Thursday temptation knocks you flat.
Friday you wonder whether Wednesday was fake.
Saturday you promise God you will do better.
Sunday you lift your hands while secretly wondering whether everyone around you is more genuinely Christian than you are.
Then Monday comes again.
And you are exhausted.
But listen carefully:
The seal is not your emotional intensity. The seal is the Holy Spirit.
Your emotions matter, but they are terrible gods.
Your feelings fluctuate.
Christ does not.
Your spiritual temperature fluctuates.
Christ does not.
Your perception of God’s nearness fluctuates.
His covenant faithfulness does not.
This does not mean sin is harmless.
It means grace is greater than you imagined.
Paul—the very apostle who says believers are sealed—also gives one of the most sobering commands in the New Testament:
“Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30).
Read that again.
The Holy Spirit can be grieved.
Sin matters.
Bitterness matters.
Corrupt speech matters.
Sexual immorality matters.
Pride matters.
Dishonesty matters.
Unforgiveness matters.
Secret compromise matters.
The seal of salvation is never biblical permission to make peace with rebellion.
If anything, the presence of the Spirit makes our sin more grievous because sin is no longer merely breaking a rule written outside us.
We are grieving the One who dwells within us.
That is why genuine grace does not teach us to say:
“I am sealed, therefore it does not matter how I live.”
Genuine grace brings us to our knees saying:
“I belong to Christ. How could I keep embracing what nailed my Savior to the cross?”
There is a universe of difference between struggling against sin and surrendering yourself to sin.
One cries, “Lord, rescue me.”
The other says, “Lord, leave me alone.”
One falls and reaches for Christ.
The other builds a home in rebellion and demands that Christ bless it.
The Gospel never teaches sinless perfection in this present life.
But neither does it make peace with deliberate, cherished rebellion.
The Spirit who seals is also the Spirit who sanctifies.
The Spirit who assures us that we are children of God is also the Spirit by whom believers put sinful deeds to death.
Romans 8 brings those realities together beautifully.
Paul says that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Christ.
Then he says those led by the Spirit of God are God’s children.
Then comes one of the most intimate moments in Scripture.
The believer cries:
“Abba, Father.”
Abba is Aramaic.
Not a magic word.
Not a mystical formula.
A deeply relational address to the Father.
And Romans 8:16 says:
“The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.”
Do you see what Christianity is?
Not merely escaping hell.
Not merely joining a church.
Not merely adopting conservative morals.
Not merely becoming “religious.”
Through Christ, rebels become family.
The guilty are justified.
Enemies are reconciled.
Spiritual orphans cry, “Father.”
And God places His Spirit within them.
That is scandalous grace.
You arrived carrying evidence against yourself.
Jesus answered with wounds.
You arrived with shame.
Jesus answered with righteousness.
You arrived guilty.
Jesus answered with His blood.
You arrived spiritually dead.
God answered with life.
You arrived wondering whether someone like you could ever belong in the Father’s house.
And through Christ, God did more than leave the door unlocked.
He adopted you.
Then He placed His Spirit within you.
That is why the second Greek word matters so much:
ἀρραβών — arrabōn.
The Spirit is the pledge of the inheritance still to come.
There is a “now” and a “not yet” to Christian salvation.
You can be genuinely redeemed while still waiting for the full redemption of your body.
You can belong to Christ while still groaning in a broken world.
You can have the Spirit while still waiting for resurrection glory.
You can have genuine assurance while still fighting temptation.
You can be deeply loved by God while being painfully aware of how much transformation remains.
God has not completed everything He intends to do with you yet.
And that may be one of the most important sentences you read today.
Because perhaps you have been looking at unfinished construction and calling it abandonment.
You saw the scaffolding and assumed the Architect left.
You saw the mess and concluded there was no plan.
You saw another battle with temptation and decided nothing had changed.
But what if the very grief you feel over sin is evidence that you can no longer comfortably live where you once lived?
What if the war inside you exists because something inside you is now alive?
Before Christ, sin may have been home.
Now it feels like captivity.
Before Christ, you could justify it.
Now something within you cries for holiness.
Before Christ, you wanted God to leave your idols alone.
Now even when you stumble toward them, something in you whispers:
This isn't where you belong anymore.
That does not mean every feeling of guilt proves someone is saved.
Scripture calls us to examine ourselves, repent, believe the Gospel, and bear fruit consistent with repentance.
Assurance must never be manufactured by repeating, “I prayed a prayer once.”
Our confidence is Christ.
The biblical question is not merely, “Did I have an emotional religious experience?”
It is:
Am I trusting Jesus Christ?
Because salvation is found in Him.
And when you truly belong to Christ, the Holy Spirit is not merely beside you cheering you toward heaven.
He dwells within you.
The Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead is at work in God’s people.
Which means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is why you needed this article.
Because somewhere beneath your smile is a question you have been afraid to ask.
Can Jesus still want me after everything?
Look at the cross.
The cross was never God pretending sin was small.
Calvary proves sin is more terrible than we like to admit.
But Calvary simultaneously proves grace is more magnificent than we dared imagine.
Christ did not bleed because you were almost good enough.
He bled because sinners could never rescue themselves.
And resurrection morning announced that sin and death would not have the final word.
So repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel spiritual again.
Not after you clean yourself up enough to approach God.
Come to Christ now.
Bring the secret.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the affair.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the pride.
Bring the anger.
Bring the double life.
Bring the religious performance.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the thing you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
It is dropping the weapons with which you have been fighting the King who came to save you.
Confess your sin.
Trust Christ.
Stop asking darkness to give you what only Jesus can give.
And if you already belong to Christ but have wandered, do not turn the doctrine of sealing into an excuse to stay in the far country.
Come home.
The same Gospel that saved you is still the Gospel you need.
There may be consequences for what you have done.
There may be relationships requiring confession.
There may be habits that need to die.
There may be people you need to forgive.
There may be accountability you need to stop avoiding.
There may be a phone number you need to delete.
There may be an apology you need to make.
There may be a secret you need to drag into the light.
Grace does not always make repentance painless.
Grace makes repentance possible.
And this is where “sealed for the day of redemption” becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
There is a day coming.
A day when faith becomes sight.
A day when the war with sin ends.
A day when the believer will never again whisper, “God, why am I still like this?”
A day when death itself will surrender.
A day when Christ’s redeemed people will stand before Him not because they managed to save themselves, but because the Lamb was sufficient.
The Holy Spirit dwelling in believers now is God’s pledge pointing toward that promised future.
You are not home yet.
But if you are in Christ, God has not abandoned you on the road.
So when Satan points toward your past, point toward the cross.
When shame says, “Look what you did,” answer, “Look what Christ has done.”
When pride says, “Look how far you've come,” answer, “Look how much grace I have received.”
When despair says, “God cannot finish this,” remember the Spirit’s presence is itself a pledge of the inheritance to come.
And when temptation whispers, “You can go back,” remember whose you are.
Not because Christians become incapable of falling.
But because Christians no longer belong to the kingdom they were rescued from.
You have been bought at a price.
You belong to Christ.
So live like someone whose life has a new Owner.
And maybe right now you cannot write a theological paragraph about any of this.
Maybe all you can manage is three words:
Pray for me.
Then say them.

And if Jesus has already carried you through a season you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to stop another exhausted believer from giving up tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not as superstition.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns salvation or makes God owe you anything.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
Send it to the believer who thinks one terrible chapter erased the entire story.
Send it to the prodigal.
Send it to the skeptic.
Send it to the church kid who knows Christian language but does not know Christ.
Send it to the person drowning in shame.
Because there may come another night when your feelings become louder than your theology, and you need to remember again:
The seal is not the strength of your emotions. The seal is the Holy Spirit whom God gives to those who belong to Christ.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture, fight sin, heal through biblical truth, and keep your eyes on Jesus, stay close.
Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's favor.
Follow.
Pray.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.

Because glorifying God is bigger than supporting any ministry. We glorify Him by trusting His Son, obeying His Word, loving His people, proclaiming His Gospel, walking by His Spirit, and making much of Jesus Christ.
Maybe they will read about the cross.
Maybe conviction will begin.
Maybe they will finally confess what they have hidden for years.
Maybe they will call upon Christ.
Maybe a prodigal will remember the Father.
Maybe an exhausted Christian will realize the war is not proof that God has abandoned them.
Maybe somebody will discover what you are discovering right now:
The Gospel is not the story of respectable people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of spiritually dead sinners receiving life through a crucified and risen King.
It is scandal becoming grace.
Shame meeting mercy.
Rebellion meeting a cross.
Death meeting resurrection.
Orphans crying, “Abba, Father.”
And redeemed sinners discovering that God did not merely erase something from their record.
He gave them His Spirit.
So tonight, when your past tries to introduce you again, do not let it have the final word.
Remember whose mark you bear.
Remember whose Spirit dwells in you.
Remember whose blood purchased redemption.
Remember whose resurrection defeated the grave.
Remember whose promise stretches all the way to the day of redemption.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the old story.
He came to give sinners a new one.
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you—but His grace gets the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE VIRGINS OF JABESH-GILEAD: The Disturbing Aftermath of Benjamin’s Civil War
paragraphs:
THE VIRGINS OF JABESH-GILEAD: The Disturbing Aftermath of Benjamin’s Civil War
Israel thought the war was over. Then six hundred surviving men needed wives—and what happened next exposes just how far God’s people can fall when everyone begins doing what is right in their own eyes.
There are Bible stories we teach children.
David and Goliath.
Daniel in the lions’ den.
Noah and the ark.
And then there are passages we almost whisper about.
Passages that make you close the Bible for a moment and stare at the wall.
Judges 21 is one of them.
Because by the time you reach its final chapter, there are no shining heroes left.
There is only a devastated nation.
Dead brothers.
Burned cities.
Broken families.
An entire tribe standing on the edge of extinction.
And women who had absolutely nothing to do with the original crime suddenly paying for the sins of men.
This is where the story of the virgins of Jabesh-gilead begins.
But if you read only Judges 21, you will misunderstand it.
You have to walk backward through the smoke.
Back to a nameless woman.
Back to a doorway.
Back to Gibeah.
Back to one of the darkest nights recorded in Scripture.

Judges 19 tells us about a Levite traveling with his concubine. They enter Gibeah, a Benjaminite city, where certain men surround the house in which they are staying and demand that the Levite be handed over for sexual abuse.
The narrative deliberately echoes Sodom in Genesis 19.
What follows is horrifying.
The woman is handed outside.
She is abused throughout the night.
At dawn, she collapses at the doorway.
She dies.
Then the Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel.
Scripture does not ask us to admire this.
It wants us to be horrified.
Israel itself reacts with horror.
Judges 19:30 records:
“Consider it, take counsel, and speak.”
Something had happened that Israel understood could not simply be ignored.
The tribes gathered.
Benjamin was confronted.
But Benjamin refused to surrender the guilty men of Gibeah.
And outrage became war.
Israel fought Benjamin.
Benjamin fought Israel.
Thousands died.
Eventually the Israelite army devastated Benjamin so severely that only six hundred Benjaminite men escaped to the rock of Rimmon.
Six hundred.
An entire tribe of Israel had almost disappeared.
Then the anger cooled.
And Israel looked at what it had done.
Judges 21:2–3 describes the people coming before God, weeping bitterly:
“O LORD God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe missing in Israel?”
Read that slowly.
They are grieving a catastrophe in which their own decisions played a part.
They had sworn an oath at Mizpah:
“None of us shall give his daughter to Benjamin as a wife.”
Now Benjamin desperately needed wives if the tribe was going to survive.
But Israel had trapped itself with its own oath.
And instead of stopping to ask whether their entire way of thinking had become corrupted...
they searched for a loophole.
That is where Jabesh-gilead enters the story.
Someone asked who had failed to assemble before the LORD at Mizpah.
The answer was Jabesh-gilead.
And Israel decided that this absence deserved terrible punishment.

Judges 21:10–11 says the congregation sent twelve thousand warriors with instructions to strike Jabesh-gilead and kill its inhabitants, including women and children, while preserving young women who had not sexually known a man.
When the killing ended, four hundred young women remained.
Four hundred women whose homes had been destroyed.
Four hundred women whose families had been killed.
Four hundred women who had not started Benjamin’s rebellion.
Four hundred women who had not committed the atrocity at Gibeah.
Four hundred women who had not made Israel’s oath.
Yet now their lives were being used to repair the consequences of decisions made by others.
They were taken to the surviving Benjaminites.
But there was another problem.
There were six hundred Benjaminite survivors.
Only four hundred women had been found.
Two hundred men still had no wives.
So another plan was created.
During a festival of the LORD at Shiloh, the remaining Benjaminites were told to hide in the vineyards.
When the young women of Shiloh came out to dance, the men were instructed to seize wives for themselves and return to Benjamin.
This is in the Bible.
But that does not mean the Bible is saying, “Do this.”
That distinction matters enormously.
The book of Judges frequently describes human behavior without endorsing it.
In fact, the entire closing movement of Judges is structured to show Israel’s moral and spiritual disintegration.
The final sentence of the book gives us the interpretive key:
“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
In Hebrew:
בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Bayyamim hahem ein melekh beYisra’el; ish hayyashar be‘einav ya‘aseh.
Literally, the devastating idea is:
“In those days there was no king in Israel; each man would do what was right in his own eyes.”
Notice the frightening word.
יָשָׁר — yashar.
“Right.”
They were not necessarily walking around saying, “We choose evil.”
They were doing what seemed right to them.
That may be one of the most frightening descriptions of fallen humanity anywhere in Scripture.
Because sin does not always introduce itself by saying:
“I am evil.”
Sometimes sin says:
“This makes sense.”
“You deserve this.”
“There is no other option.”
“Everybody does it.”
“God will understand.”
“We're fixing the problem.”
And suddenly human beings can commit another wrong while convincing themselves that they are correcting the first one.
That is exactly what makes Judges 21 so disturbing.
Look at the progression.
A woman is violated.
That produces outrage.
Outrage produces war.
War produces slaughter.
Slaughter produces the possibility of tribal extinction.
Their oath produces another crisis.
That crisis produces the destruction of Jabesh-gilead.
That destruction provides four hundred women.
The shortage of women produces another scheme.
That scheme results in women from Shiloh being seized.
One sin.
Then another.
Then another.
Everybody solving the consequences of yesterday’s disobedience with tomorrow’s compromise.
And somewhere in the middle of all of it...
women without names are carrying the consequences.
That is not merely ancient history.
That is frighteningly human.
How many families know this pattern?
One lie required another lie.
One hidden affair required another deception.
One addiction required another excuse.
One uncontrolled temper created wounds that demanded apologies that were never made.
One financial compromise produced another.
One secret became ten secrets.
One moment of bitterness hardened into years of estrangement.
One person sinned...
and eventually everybody in the house was bleeding.
Maybe that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
Because somewhere between Gibeah and Jabesh-gilead, we recognize ourselves.
Not necessarily in the specific atrocities.
But in the pattern.
We break something.
Then instead of surrendering completely to God, we try to repair it our own way.
And sometimes our repair causes another wound.
Then we repair that wound.
Then another.
Until eventually we cannot even remember where the original compromise began.
This is what happens when human beings become their own moral authority.
And Judges repeatedly tells us that Israel had a deeper problem.
They needed righteous rule.
They needed a king.
Yet even Israel's later kings would fail.
Saul would fail.
David would sin grievously.
Solomon would turn aside.
The kingdom would fracture.
Kings could sit on Jerusalem's throne...
but no merely human king could cure the throne inside the human heart.
The Bible therefore keeps moving.
Past Judges.
Past Samuel.
Past Kings.
Past exile.
Past ruined Jerusalem.
Until eventually another King appears.
Not carrying a sword against sinners.
But walking toward a cross for them.
Jesus.
And suddenly the horror of Judges becomes part of a much larger biblical cry:
Who can save humanity from humanity?
Who can rescue sinners from what happens when everyone becomes their own king?
Who can cleanse guilt instead of merely relocating its consequences?
Who can stop the cycle?
The Gospel answers:
Jesus Christ.
The announcement surrounding His birth was:
“You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins.”
Matthew 1:21.
The Greek word translated “save” is:
σώσει — sōsei.
He will save.
Not merely inspire.
Not merely advise.
Not merely improve.
Save.
Because humanity did not merely need better circumstances.
We needed rescue from sin.
And this is where Judges 21 becomes painfully personal.
You may never have stood on an ancient battlefield.
You may never have seen Gibeah.
You may never have walked through Jabesh-gilead.
But you know what it feels like to wish you could reverse something.
Maybe there is a sentence you would give anything to pull back into your mouth.
A relationship you damaged.
A season you wasted.
A person you hurt.
A secret you buried.
A temptation you kept feeding.
A compromise you called harmless until it wasn't harmless anymore.
Maybe other people do not know.
Maybe they see the Sunday version of you.
The smiling photograph.
The Bible verse on your profile.
The “God is good” caption.
But you know.
And God knows.
That is where shame whispers:
“You have gone too far.”
“You ruined everything.”
“God could forgive somebody else, but not this.”
“Hide.”
And the Gospel walks directly into that darkness and says something shame never wants you to hear.
Jesus already knows.
And He still calls sinners to come.
Not to pretend.
Not to excuse.
Not to rename sin.
To repent.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance, carrying the idea of a changed mind and turning, a reorientation toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Christian repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns toward God.
It stops defending darkness.
It brings sin into the light.
It says:
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
And Scripture says:
