Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or faithfulness to Christ.

But glorifying God includes using what He has entrusted to us for His purposes. If these articles are genuinely helping people encounter biblical truth, sharing them and voluntarily supporting the work are practical ways you can help that truth reach another exhausted believer, another searching heart, another person who has been hiding, another soul that desperately needs to hear that Jesus Christ still saves.
But before you leave, look at your hands.
Really look at them.
Perhaps they are different from the hands you had thirty years ago.
They have carried children.
Signed documents.
Prepared meals.
Wiped tears.
Held hospital rails.
Opened Bibles.
Buried people you loved.
Made mistakes.
Asked forgiveness.
Worked.
Served.
Failed.
Prayed.
And if you belong to Jesus, those aging hands are not evidence that God is finished with you.
They are evidence that you are traveling toward a Kingdom where your hope was never youth in the first place.
So when the mirror tells you that you are fading, remember what Scripture tells you:
There is an outer story.
And there is an inner story.
There is what time is taking.
And there is what Christ is renewing.
There is what can be seen.
And there is what is eternal.
One day everything you used to prove that you mattered will fall from your hands—and if those hands are holding Christ, you will discover you were never losing your identity at all.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Say You Trust God—Until You Cannot Control the Outcome
paragraphs:
You Say You Trust God—Until You Cannot Control the Outcome
It is easy to call it faith when God is taking you where you wanted to go. The terrifying question is whether you will still trust Him when obedience cannot guarantee the ending you desperately want.
There is a version of trust that almost everyone can live with.
Trust God when the biopsy comes back clean.
Trust God when the person you love comes home.
Trust God when the application gets approved.
Trust God when the business survives.
Trust God when the prayer is answered exactly the way you prayed it.
Trust God when the door finally opens.
Trust God when the marriage is restored.
Trust God when the child returns.
Trust God when the money arrives before the deadline.
Trust God when there is still enough evidence to convince yourself that everything is going to be okay.
But there is another kind of trust.
The kind that begins when you have prayed until you have run out of eloquent words…and nothing has changed.
When you obeyed God and the situation still became harder.
When you did what Scripture said and did not receive the outcome you thought obedience would produce.
When you cannot see around the corner.
When heaven has not handed you an explanation.
When the person you desperately want God to change is still unchanged.
When the door remains closed.
When the doctor cannot promise you what happens next.
When somebody you love is slipping farther away and you cannot rescue them.
When your future feels like it is sitting behind a locked door and God has not given you the key.
That is where the question changes.
It is no longer:
“Do I believe in God?”
It becomes:
“Do I trust God when I cannot control what God allows next?”
And suddenly Proverbs 3:5–6 stops looking like something beautiful to print on a coffee mug.
It becomes surgery.
The Hebrew reads:

בְּטַח אֶל־יְהוָה בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ וְאֶל־בִּינָתְךָ אַל־תִּשָּׁעֵן׃
בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ׃
Bəṭaḥ el-YHWH bəḵol-libbekha, wə’el-binaṯəḵa ’al-tišša‘en. Bəḵol-dərāḵeḵa da‘ehu, wəhu yəyaššer ’orḥoṯeḵa.
“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make straight your paths.”
Notice what God does not say.
He does not say, “Trust Me, and I will give you the outcome you imagined.”
He does not say, “Acknowledge Me, and nobody you love will ever leave.”
He does not say, “Obey Me, and you will never lose anything.”
He does not say, “Follow Me, and your children will make every decision you prayed they would make.”
He does not say, “Believe hard enough, and suffering will become optional.”
The command is to trust Him.
That difference can expose an entire hidden theology inside us.
Because sometimes what we call trusting God is actually trusting God to produce the result we already selected.
We say, “Lord, Your will be done,” while quietly handing Him the script.
This person.
This job.
This healing.
This amount of money.
This timeline.
This answer.
This ending.
And somewhere inside the prayer is a condition we would never dare say aloud:
“God, I trust You…as long as You do this.”
Then life removes our ability to control the outcome, and suddenly we discover what our faith was leaning against.
That is why the Hebrew image in Proverbs is so piercing.
The verb translated “trust” is bāṭaḥ—בָּטַח—carrying the sense of trusting, relying upon, placing confidence in.
Then comes the warning:
אַל־תִּשָּׁעֵן — ’al-tišša‘en
“Do not lean.”
Do not support the full weight of your soul upon your own understanding.
Picture someone leaning against a wall because he believes the wall can hold him.
God is asking:
What are you leaning on?
Your calculations?
Your backup plan?
Your ability to predict people?
Your bank balance?
Your diagnosis?
Your connections?
Your intelligence?
Your ability to keep everybody happy?
Your ability to anticipate every possible disaster before it happens?
Control can feel like wisdom because control makes us feel safe.
Sometimes planning really is wisdom. Scripture commends prudence, diligence, counsel, and counting the cost. Biblical trust is not irresponsibility. Faith does not mean refusing to plan.
But planning becomes something darker when we demand from it what only God can give.
Security.
Sovereignty.
Certainty.
Control over tomorrow.
You can make plans.
You cannot become Providence.
And some of us are exhausted because we have been secretly trying.
Maybe that is why uncertainty hurts you so much.
You keep replaying the conversation because perhaps there is one sentence you could have said differently.
You keep checking your phone because perhaps the next notification will finally settle your heart.
You keep calculating the money.
Checking the symptoms.
Reading the messages again.
Watching the numbers.
Studying somebody's behavior.
Imagining every possible outcome.
Preparing for conversations that have not happened.
Fighting disasters that currently exist only in your mind.
And you call it “being prepared.”
But somewhere underneath all that preparation may be a frightened human heart whispering:
“If I can understand everything, maybe nothing can hurt me.”
Proverbs confronts that illusion gently and relentlessly:
“Do not lean on your own understanding.”
Not because understanding is evil.
Because your understanding is finite.
You do not know everything happening in the room you are standing in, much less everything God is doing throughout your life.
You see today.
God sees what today touches.
You see the closed door.
God sees what was behind it.
You see the delay.
God sees what the delay may accomplish.
You see what you lost.
God sees the entire story.
This does not mean every tragedy will become understandable in this lifetime.
Scripture never gives us permission to look at a grieving person and casually explain their pain as though we have been invited into God's secret counsel.
Some wounds remain mysterious.
Some prayers receive answers we would never have chosen.
Some faithful believers die without seeing the earthly resolution they longed for.
Hebrews 11 deliberately destroys the fantasy that faith always guarantees the preferred earthly ending.
Some conquered kingdoms, escaped the sword, received promises, and saw extraordinary deliverance.
Others suffered.
Others were imprisoned.
Others were killed.
And Scripture places them in the same chapter of faith.
That should shake us.
Because biblical faith is not confidence that God must give me the ending I want.
Biblical faith is confidence in God when I cannot guarantee the ending at all.
Ask Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Standing before Nebuchadnezzar and the furnace, they declared that their God was able to deliver them.
Then came three words that separate faith from manipulation:
“But if not…”
Daniel 3:18.
Their obedience was not dependent upon rescue.
God could deliver them.
They believed He could.
But they would not make God's faithfulness dependent upon whether He did what they desperately wanted Him to do.
That is trust.
“God, You can heal me.
But if the road becomes harder, You are still God.”
“Jesus, You can restore this relationship.
But I will not abandon You to keep someone who demands that I abandon You.”
“Father, You can open this door.
But if it stays closed, I will not call You unfaithful.”
“Lord, You can change my circumstances tonight.
But even if tomorrow looks frighteningly similar to today, I still belong to You.”
That kind of surrender sounds beautiful until it becomes your life.
Because surrender has a cost.
Control says, “Give me the map.”
Trust says, “Give me Your hand.”
Control says, “Tell me exactly how this ends.”
Trust says, “Stay with me while I walk.”
Control says, “Explain Yourself.”
Trust says, “Even when I cannot explain this, I will remember who You have revealed Yourself to be.”
And Christians are not asked to trust an unknown deity whose character is hidden behind the clouds.
We look at Jesus Christ.
At the cross, God did not remain distant from human suffering.
Christ entered it.
Betrayal.
Rejection.
Injustice.
Humiliation.
Pain.
Death.
Jesus knows what agony feels like from inside human flesh.
And in Gethsemane, we hear something breathtaking.
Jesus prayed:
“Father, if You are willing, remove this cup from Me. Nevertheless, not My will, but Yours, be done.”
Luke 22:42.
Christian surrender is not pretending you do not have a desired outcome.
Jesus expressed His desire.
You can too.
You can pray desperately for healing.
You can ask God to save the marriage.
You can plead for your child.
You can ask Him for provision.
You can beg Him to open the door.
You can cry until the prayer is barely recognizable as language.
Trust does not mean becoming emotionally numb.
Trust means your desire does not become your god.
“Father, this is what I want…
nevertheless.”
There may be no more frightening word in surrender.
And perhaps no more freeing one.
Nevertheless, You are God.
Nevertheless, Jesus is Lord.
Nevertheless, Your grace is sufficient.
Nevertheless, I will obey.
Nevertheless, I will not return to the sin You rescued me from simply because obedience became painful.
Nevertheless, I will not manufacture an Ishmael because waiting for Isaac terrifies me.
Nevertheless, I will not manipulate people to create an answer You have not given.
Nevertheless, I will not call darkness light because darkness offered me immediate relief.
Nevertheless.
Maybe somebody reading this is living inside that word right now.
You have done everything you know to do.
You prayed.
You waited.
You sought counsel.
You tried again.
You apologized.
You forgave.
You worked.
You fasted.
You cried.
You opened Scripture looking for something—anything—that would tell you how this story ends.
And God has not told you.
Maybe the deepest invitation in this season is not to discover the ending.
Maybe it is to discover whether Jesus Himself is enough while the ending remains hidden.
Peter once faced a moment when many disciples were walking away from Christ.
Jesus asked the Twelve whether they wanted to leave too.
Peter answered:
“Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
John 6:68.
Notice what Peter did not say.
“I understand everything.”
He didn't.
“I like everything You just said.”
Clearly, many people did not.
“I know what happens next.”
He certainly didn't.
His answer was essentially:
Where else would I go?
That is what mature trust eventually sounds like.
Not always triumphant.
Sometimes trembling.
Sometimes tear-soaked.
Sometimes whispered from the floor at two in the morning.
But still:
“Jesus…where else would I go?”
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than religious vocabulary.
Because our greatest problem was never merely that life was unpredictable.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We did not merely need circumstances repaired.
We needed reconciliation with God.
And we could not control that outcome either.
We could not perform enough righteousness to erase our guilt.
We could not rewrite our past.
We could not climb high enough to reach God.
So God came down to us.

Jesus lived the righteousness we could not produce, went willingly to the cross, bore sin, died, and rose again. Forgiveness is not something we purchase by controlling ourselves into perfection. Salvation is received by grace through faith in Christ.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven.
The scandal is that rebels can become sons and daughters.
The scandal is that Peter could deny Jesus and still be restored.
The scandal is that Paul could persecute the church and become a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The scandal is that your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
That is grace.
And grace ruins our obsession with control because grace begins where self-salvation ends.
Maybe your greatest surrender tonight is not your circumstances.
Maybe it is you.
Maybe you have spent years trying to manage your image while hiding your heart.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say “God is good.”
You know what to post.
You know what to tell people at church.
But privately, you are terrified.
Angry.
Exhausted.
Secretly bargaining with God.
Secretly resentful that obedience did not purchase the outcome you expected.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
God is not threatened by your honesty.
The Psalms are filled with people bringing confusion, grief, fear, questions, and anguish before Him.
But honesty before God is not permission to remain in rebellion.
Grace invites us out of hiding.
Repentance says:
“Lord, I have been trying to occupy a throne that belongs to You.”
“I have worshiped certainty.”
“I have trusted my plans more than Your character.”
“I have demanded explanations before obedience.”
“I have treated You like a means to my preferred ending.”
“Forgive me.”
If those words expose something hidden inside you, you do not need to perform for anyone.
But you can stop hiding.
There is no shame in admitting that surrender is a battle.
Sometimes one of the most courageous things a believer can say is:
“I want to trust Him, but I am struggling.”
And perhaps another believer reading your comment needs to know they are not the only one.
Then send this article to the person whose life currently contains a giant question mark.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Not because clicking “share” proves your faith. It doesn't.
We are saved by grace, not by social-media activity.
The mother still praying for her child.
The believer whose plans collapsed.
The person facing medical uncertainty.
The husband or wife fighting for a marriage.
The exhausted Christian who has begun interpreting God's silence as God's absence.
Let sharing become service.
Let your profile carry something deeper than another passing distraction.
Because today you may agree with these words.
Tomorrow you may need them.
There will come a moment when control slips through your fingers again.
When that moment arrives, return to Proverbs 3.
בְּטַח אֶל־יְהוָה בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ
Trust in the LORD with all your heart.
Not the portion that understands.
Not the portion that got its preferred answer.
Not only the portion standing in sunlight.
All.
Your frightened heart.
Your disappointed heart.
Your grieving heart.
Your confused heart.
Your hopeful heart.
Your exhausted heart.
Bring all of it.
Then comes Proverbs 3:6:
בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ
“In all your ways acknowledge Him.”
The Hebrew verb behind “acknowledge” is related to יָדַע — yāda‘, “to know.”
This is more intimate than occasionally remembering that God exists.
The invitation is to recognize Him, know Him, and live consciously before Him throughout your ways.
Then:
וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ
“He will make straight your paths.”
A straight path does not necessarily mean an easy path.
Calvary was not easy.
Paul's calling was not easy.
Peter's discipleship was not easy.
The road of obedience can pass through valleys.
Psalm 23 never says the shepherd prevents every valley.
It says the Shepherd is with us through it.
That changes everything.
Perhaps you have been asking God:
“Will this work out?”
And perhaps Scripture is inviting you into a deeper question:
“Whatever happens, will I walk with Christ?”
You may not control whether someone stays.
You can choose whether you stay faithful to Jesus.
You may not control tomorrow's diagnosis.
You can entrust tomorrow to the One who will already be there.
You may not control whether a door opens.
You can refuse to compromise your soul trying to kick it down.
You may not control what other people think about you.
You can live before the God who knows you completely.
You may not control when the answer comes.
You can decide where your heart will lean while you wait.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to give Christians shallow slogans for deep wounds, but to keep bringing hearts back to Scripture, repentance, grace, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and ultimately Jesus Christ.

If you genuinely want to glorify God, glorify Him first through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, holiness, mercy, and making His Gospel known. And if Gospel Warrior is one of the ministries helping you do that, supporting and sharing this work is one practical way you can help us place biblical encouragement in front of people who desperately need it.
Somebody who is currently standing where you once stood may need to hear that Jesus remained faithful even when the road hurt.
Because perhaps faith was never proven by your ability to predict what God would do next.
Perhaps faith is revealed when the future disappears behind the fog…
your hands finally open…
your carefully written ending falls to the floor…
and with tears in your eyes you can still whisper:
“Jesus, I do not know what happens next.
But I know who You are.
And I am still Yours.”
You do not have to know how the story ends when you know the One holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY IS NOT YOUR PROPERTY: WHAT 1 CORINTHIANS 7 ACTUALLY SAYS ABOUT SEXUAL AUTHORITY
paragraphs:
YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY IS NOT YOUR PROPERTY: WHAT 1 CORINTHIANS 7 ACTUALLY SAYS ABOUT SEXUAL AUTHORITY
One of the Bible’s most intimate passages has been used to demand sex, excuse rejection, shame wounded spouses, and defend selfishness. But when you actually read Paul’s words carefully, something breathtaking appears: Christian marriage was never supposed to be a battle over who gets control. It was supposed to become a place where two people learn what Christlike self-giving love costs.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can sound terrifying in the hands of the wrong person.
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband…”
Stop there, and someone can build a weapon out of Scripture.
But Paul did not stop there.
“…and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
That second sentence changes everything.
Because whatever interpretation you give the first half must survive the second.

Paul does not hand the husband a throne while placing the wife beneath it. He does something astonishingly reciprocal. He takes the language of authority and places husband and wife beneath the same obligation of self-giving.
And perhaps some marriages desperately need to hear that.
Because somewhere tonight, one spouse feels rejected.
Another feels pressured.
Someone is lying inches away from the person they married while emotionally feeling a thousand miles apart.
Someone has been told, “The Bible says you have to.”
Someone else has weaponized exhaustion, resentment, silence, or sexual withdrawal.
Someone desperately wants affection but is ashamed to admit it.
Someone dreads being touched because intimacy stopped feeling like tenderness and started feeling like an obligation they were never allowed to discuss.
And somewhere, two Christians love Jesus deeply but have never learned how to talk honestly about sex without embarrassment, defensiveness, guilt, accusation, or fear.
Then 1 Corinthians 7 enters the room.
Not to humiliate them.
Not to hand one spouse ammunition against the other.
Not to transform the marriage bed into a courtroom.
But to confront selfishness on both sides.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 7:3–5, KJV
The Greek underneath these words makes the reciprocity difficult to escape.
Paul writes concerning the wife:
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει
hē gynē tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei
And then concerning the husband:
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει
homoios de kai ho anēr tou idiou sōmatos ouk exousiazei
The crucial verb is ἐξουσιάζει—exousiazei—from ἐξουσιάζω, carrying the idea of exercising authority or having authority over something.
And Paul deliberately applies it both ways.
The wife does not possess unilateral sexual authority within marriage.
Neither does the husband.
Read that again.
Neither does the husband.
That is why this passage cannot honestly be reduced to, “My spouse owes me sex whenever I demand it.”
The very structure of Paul’s argument destroys unilateralism.
The person quoting verse 4 to establish his or her authority over a spouse must confront the fact that Paul simultaneously limits that person's independent authority too.
Marriage is not:
“Your body belongs to me, therefore I control you.”
It is much closer to:
“I entered a covenant in which my sexuality is no longer something I approach as though only my desires, preferences, frustrations, vulnerabilities, and needs matter.”
That difference is enormous.
And it gets deeper.
Verse 3 says:
“Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.”
The Greek contains the language:
τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω
tēn opheilēn apodidotō
The noun opheilē carries the idea of something owed or due, while apodidōmi means to give, render, or pay what is due.
Paul therefore does teach genuine marital obligation.
We should not soften Scripture until it says nothing uncomfortable.
Marriage involves sexual responsibility toward one's spouse.
But neither should we harden Scripture into something Paul did not say.
The responsibility is mutual.
The authority is mutual.
The consideration is mutual.
And when Paul addresses temporary abstinence, the decision is mutual.
“Except it be with consent…”
The Greek word is:
συμφώνου
symp​​hōnou
It comes from the idea of agreement or harmony. It is related to the word from which English gets “symphony.”
Two voices coming into agreement.
Not one spouse announcing.
Not one spouse demanding.
Not one spouse threatening.
Not one spouse quoting Scripture until the other submits from fear.
Agreement.
That matters enormously.
Paul envisions even temporary sexual abstinence for prayer as something husband and wife agree upon together.
So there are two opposite distortions we must refuse.
The first says, “My body is mine, my sexuality concerns only me, and marriage places no meaningful sexual responsibility upon me.”
Paul challenges that.
But the second says, “Your body belongs to me, therefore I may demand access regardless of your fear, pain, trauma, exhaustion, illness, emotional condition, or willingness.”
Paul's reciprocal language does not establish that either.
Biblical mutual authority is not permission for coercion.
Sexual coercion is not transformed into holiness because somebody attached a Bible verse to it.
If your spouse is frightened of you, something is wrong.
If your spouse has learned that saying “not tonight” will produce rage, intimidation, humiliation, threats, punishment, or spiritual condemnation, something is wrong.
If Scripture is being used to silence pain instead of shepherding the hurting person toward safety, truth, healing, and Christ, something is wrong.
And if you have experienced sexual coercion or abuse, this passage should never be used to tell you that abuse was God's design for marriage.
It was not.
Yet there is another person reading this who needs conviction from the opposite direction.
Maybe nobody is coercing you.
Maybe your spouse is gentle.
Maybe your marriage is physically safe.
But resentment became punishment.
You discovered that withholding affection could hurt your spouse, so eventually intimacy became leverage.
Perhaps sex became currency.
Reward.
Punishment.
Control.
“If you make me happy, maybe.”
“If you disappoint me, never.”
Months pass.
Then years.
Nobody talks about it anymore.
The bedroom becomes a graveyard where both people pretend nothing died.
Paul challenges that too.
“Defraud ye not one the other…”
Other translations render the thought as not depriving one another.
And notice again:
one another.
This passage keeps refusing to let either spouse become the center.
That is because Christian marriage is supposed to be shaped by something larger than sexual appetite.
The Gospel.
Jesus said:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
—Mark 10:45, KJV
There is the heartbeat.
Christ did not love by asking only:
“What am I entitled to receive?”
He gave Himself.
And Christian marriage slowly crucifies the selfish instinct that constantly asks:
“What about me?”
But be careful.
That truth cuts both ways.
Sometimes selflessness means lovingly giving yourself to your spouse when laziness would rather withdraw.
Sometimes selflessness means hearing your spouse say, “I am hurting,” and caring more about that person than about immediate gratification.
Sometimes love initiates.
Sometimes love waits.
Sometimes love gives.
Sometimes love listens.
Sometimes love repents.
Sometimes love asks, “Have I made you feel unwanted?”
And sometimes love has enough courage to ask an even more painful question:
“Have I made you feel unsafe?”
That conversation may reveal wounds nobody expected.
Childbirth can change things.
Illness can change things.
Medication can affect things.
Hormonal changes can affect things.
Stress can affect things.
Grief can affect things.
Betrayal can devastate intimacy.
Pornography can poison expectations.
Past sexual trauma can follow someone into a marriage bed long after the event itself ended.
Emotional abandonment can make physical intimacy extraordinarily difficult.
And unresolved bitterness can turn two bodies that once reached for each other instinctively into strangers.
This is where simplistic Christian slogans can do terrible damage.
“Just submit.”
“Just give him what he wants.”
“Just satisfy her.”
No.
Sometimes the most biblical thing a couple can do is finally tell the truth.
Because biblical intimacy is not merely bodies occupying the same bed.
It involves covenant faithfulness, tenderness, honesty, repentance, patience, sacrifice, and love.
Paul had already written only a few verses earlier:
“Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ?”
—1 Corinthians 6:15, KJV
Your body ultimately belongs to Christ.
Your spouse's body ultimately belongs to Christ.
That should put holy fear into every discussion of sexual authority.
Because you are not handling property.
You are loving someone for whom Christ died.
Someone made in God's image.
Someone whose tears God sees.
Someone whose vulnerabilities you were trusted to protect.
And perhaps this is where the passage becomes unbearably personal.
What if the biggest problem in your marriage is not frequency?
What if it is selfishness?
What if the argument about sex is only revealing something underneath it?
“I don't feel loved.”
“I don't feel desired.”
“I don't feel heard.”
“I don't feel safe.”
“I don't feel beautiful anymore.”
“I feel like you only touch me when you want something.”
“I feel rejected every time I reach for you.”
“I am exhausted.”
“I am ashamed of my body.”
“I don't know how to tell you what happened to me.”
“I still haven't forgiven you.”
“I am scared that if I tell you the truth, you won't understand.”
Suddenly this is not merely a theological debate.
There are human beings underneath the doctrine.
There is a husband wondering why his wife no longer reaches for him.
There is a wife quietly wondering whether her husband still finds her beautiful.

There is the couple whose baby finally fell asleep, whose bills are overdue, whose bodies are exhausted, whose patience is disappearing, and who cannot remember the last time they looked at one another without discussing chores.
There is the marriage damaged by pornography.
The marriage recovering from infidelity.
The marriage carrying trauma.
The marriage enduring chronic illness.
The marriage where rejection has accumulated for so long that neither person knows how to initiate without fear.
And Jesus walks into those places too.
Not merely the Sunday sanctuary.
The bedroom.
The argument.
The silence afterward.
The tears nobody else sees.
The shame.
The resentment.
The memories.
The loneliness.
The cross reaches there.
This is why Christian sexual ethics cannot ultimately be reduced to “Who has rights?”
At the center of Christianity stands a Savior who laid down His life.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Gave Himself.
That is radically different from using Scripture to demand that another person serve your appetite.
And wives are not called to manipulate, humiliate, punish, or casually neglect their husbands either.
Christian marriage confronts selfishness wherever it hides.
His selfishness.
Her selfishness.
Sexual selfishness.
Emotional selfishness.
Relational selfishness.
Because sin loves to turn gifts into weapons.
Sex is God's gift.
But lust can corrupt it.
Marriage is God's gift.
But selfishness can corrupt it.
Authority can serve.
But domination corrupts it.
Desire can draw spouses together.
But entitlement can poison desire until intimacy begins to feel like extraction rather than communion.
Maybe the question your marriage needs tonight is not:
“How often are we supposed to have sex?”
Maybe it is:
“How can I love you better?”
That question sounds less dramatic.
But it can save something.
Imagine a husband saying:
“I don't want you afraid to tell me when you're hurting.”
Imagine a wife saying:
“I didn't realize how deeply my constant rejection was affecting you.”
Imagine either spouse saying:
“I have been selfish.”
“I have used intimacy as leverage.”
“I have pressured you.”
“I have withdrawn from you.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I let pornography reshape what I expected from you.”
“I made you feel undesirable.”
“I made you feel used.”
“I need forgiveness.”
Now we are getting somewhere.
Because Christianity does not begin with pretending we have no sin.
It begins with bringing sin into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Maybe your marriage cannot be repaired by another argument over 1 Corinthians 7.
Maybe it begins with repentance.
Real repentance.
No excuses.
No “I'm sorry you felt that way.”
No Bible verses thrown like grenades.
Just truth.
“I sinned against you.”
And then grace.
Because this is what Jesus does.
He takes sinners whose desires became disordered, whose marriages became wounded, whose histories became complicated, whose choices became shameful…
and He does not merely expose them.
He redeems them.
The Gospel does not say your worst chapter must become your final chapter.
Peter denied Christ.
Thomas doubted.
The Samaritan woman's relational history was exposed in conversation with Jesus.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly disgraced.
Paul himself had persecuted Christians.
Yet Christ kept rewriting stories.
Not by pretending sin was harmless.
By confronting sin and pouring grace upon repentant sinners.
That is the difference between cheap affirmation and Gospel grace.
Grace does not say:
“Nothing needs to change.”
Grace says:
“You do not have to remain what sin has made you.”
So if you have pressured your spouse, repent.
If you have intentionally weaponized rejection, repent.
If pornography has entered your marriage, bring it into the light and seek help.
If adultery shattered trust, stop demanding instant restoration and begin walking the long road of truthful repentance.
If trauma is affecting intimacy, there is no shame in seeking wise, trauma-informed pastoral and professional help.
If physical pain is involved, appropriate medical care may matter.
If abuse or coercion is occurring, safety matters. Seeking outside help is not spiritual failure.
And if you and your spouse simply became distant somewhere between careers, children, dishes, bills, disappointments, and exhaustion…
reach for each other again.
Not merely sexually.
Humanly.
Sit together.
Talk.
Pray.
Listen.
Ask questions without preparing your defense while the other person answers.
Tell the truth without using truth as a weapon.
Forgive where genuine repentance is occurring.
Rebuild trust where trust was damaged.
Rediscover tenderness.
Because the goal of Christian marriage was never merely sexual access.
It is covenant love shaped increasingly by Christ.
And suddenly Paul's seemingly shocking statement begins to look different.
“The wife hath not power of her own body…”
Yes.
But keep reading.
“…and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body…”
There is no isolated sovereign ego in Christian marriage saying:
“Only my needs matter.”
Two people entered covenant.
And both belong first to Jesus.
That changes the entire conversation.
So tonight, before quoting 1 Corinthians 7 at your spouse, perhaps place yourself underneath it first.
Ask what it requires of you.
Not merely what it requires of them.
That is where Scripture becomes a mirror instead of a weapon.
And perhaps you felt something while reading this that you were not expecting.
Conviction.
Grief.
Relief.
Anger.
Hope.
Maybe memories surfaced.
Maybe you recognized yourself.
Maybe you recognized your marriage.
Don't run from that moment.
Take it to Jesus.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need forgiveness, ask.
If you need healing, begin seeking it.
If you need help, reach for trustworthy help.
If you need to have a conversation with your spouse, perhaps tonight is the night you stop pretending everything is fine.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, comment, “Jesus, change my heart.”
If your marriage needs prayer, comment, “Pray for us.”
If Christ is restoring something you thought was dead, comment, “Jesus is still healing us.”
You never know who will read your words and realize they are not the only Christian struggling behind a smiling family photograph.

Not because every sentence will be easy to accept, but because there may come a night when resentment returns and you need to remember that marriage was never supposed to become a contest over whose desires matter more.
Send this privately to the couple nobody knows is struggling.

Someone scrolling silently tonight may desperately need permission to stop weaponizing Scripture, stop hiding pain, repent of selfishness, seek healing, and bring Jesus back into the places they stopped talking about.
Christ purchased our redemption.
We support Gospel ministry because grace has already been given to us, not because financial support earns grace from God.
If you want to support the work and go deeper:
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the greater invitation.
Come back to Christ.
No article can forgive your sins.
No ministry can become your Savior.
Jesus can.
The One who exposed our sin carried that sin to Calvary.
The One who calls us to repentance also welcomes repentant sinners.
The One who commands husbands and wives to abandon selfishness demonstrated self-giving love with nails through His hands.
And maybe that is the sentence your marriage needs more than any other tonight:
Before asking how much of your spouse belongs to you, remember how completely both of you belong to Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD SAID HE’LL GIVE YOU THE DESIRES OF YOUR HEART… BUT PSALM 37:4 DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY PEOPLE THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs: GOD SAID HE’LL GIVE YOU THE DESIRES OF YOUR HEART… BUT PSALM 37:4 DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY PEOPLE THINK IT MEANS
What if the greatest gift God gives you isn’t everything your heart wants—but a heart that finally wants what He wants?
There is a Bible verse people love to quote when they are waiting for something.
A relationship.
A marriage.
A promotion.
A business breakthrough.
A house.
A healing.
A financial miracle.
A door to finally open.
A prayer they have whispered so many times that disappointment has begun creeping into their faith.
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.”
Psalm 37:4.
It sounds almost like a blank check from heaven.
Love God enough, and eventually He gives you what you want.
Serve Him.
Pray.
Believe.
Wait.
And perhaps one day the thing you have been dreaming about will finally appear.
But what happens when it doesn’t?
What happens when you delighted yourself in God…and the relationship still ended?
What happens when you prayed faithfully…and someone else got the opportunity?
What happens when you tried to obey God…and your life became harder instead of easier?
What happens when the desire was sincere, the prayer was passionate, the waiting was long…
…and God still said no?
That is where some believers quietly begin to wonder:
“Did God break His promise?”
Maybe you have wondered that yourself.
And if you have, Psalm 37:4 may be far more beautiful than you were ever told.
Because David was not teaching us how to convince God to finance our dreams.
He was teaching us what happens when God becomes our greatest treasure.
The Hebrew reads:
וְהִתְעַנַּג עַל־יְהוָה וְיִתֶּן־לְךָ מִשְׁאֲלֹת לִבֶּךָ
Ve-hit‘annag ‘al-YHWH, ve-yitten-lekha mish’alot libbekha.
A natural rendering is:
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.”
The word translated “delight” comes from the Hebrew עָנַג — ‘anag, carrying the sense of taking exquisite delight or finding pleasure.
Notice where the delight is directed.
Not toward the gift.
Toward YHWH.
That changes everything.
The verse does not say:
“Delight yourself in what God can give you.”
It says:
“Delight yourself in the LORD.”
God Himself is the center.
And that matters because Psalm 37 was never written as an isolated promise for acquiring whatever a person happens to desire.
Read the surrounding Psalm.
David begins:
“Do not fret because of evildoers.”
Why?
Because righteous people were watching wicked people prosper.
That feeling is painfully modern.
You try to live faithfully while someone dishonest seems to succeed.
You refuse to compromise while someone who compromises gets promoted.
You pray for a godly marriage while people who seemingly want nothing to do with God appear happily married.
You struggle financially while people living recklessly seem surrounded by abundance.
You are trying to follow Jesus…
and sometimes it looks like everyone running away from Him is getting ahead.
David understood that frustration.
And his answer was not:
“Don’t worry. God will eventually make you richer than them.”
His answer was deeper.
“Trust in the LORD.”
“Do good.”
“Dwell in the land.”
“Befriend faithfulness.”
“Delight yourself in the LORD.”
“Commit your way to the LORD.”
“Trust in Him.”
“Be still before the LORD.”
“Wait patiently for Him.”
Do you see it?
Psalm 37 is not primarily about acquiring things.
It is about learning to trust God when circumstances tempt you to believe that obedience is pointless.
And suddenly Psalm 37:4 becomes less like a vending machine…
and more like heart surgery.
Because there is something uncomfortable we need to admit.
Not every desire in our hearts should be fulfilled.
Scripture never teaches that every human desire is automatically good simply because it feels sincere.
Jeremiah warned that the human heart can deceive us.
James wrote that people can ask and not receive because they ask with wrong motives, intending to spend what they receive on their passions.
Jesus Himself taught us to pray:
“Your will be done.”
Not:
“My desires be done.”
That distinction can hurt.
Because sometimes what we call a “promise from God” is actually something we desperately want God to approve.
We want that person.
That opportunity.
That recognition.
That money.
That outcome.
That future.
And because we want it deeply enough, we begin assuming God must want it too.
Then we attach Psalm 37:4 to it.
“God promised.”
But perhaps God never promised you that particular thing.
Perhaps He promised you something better:
Himself.
This is where the Gospel begins exposing us.
Because underneath some of our prayers is a frightening question:
“If God never gives me the thing I want most…will God Himself still be enough?”
Read that again slowly.
If the marriage never comes…
is Jesus enough?
If the promotion never comes…
is Jesus enough?
If people never recognize your sacrifices…
is Jesus enough?
If the business does not become what you imagined…
is Jesus enough?
If the door remains closed…
is Jesus enough?
If your life looks completely different from the life you pictured ten years ago…
is Jesus enough?
That question reaches places inside us that inspirational Christianity rarely touches.
Because it exposes the difference between loving God…
and loving what we hope God will give us.
And I know that can sting.
Maybe you have spent years asking God for something.
Maybe you have watched other people receive what you begged Him for.
Maybe you have congratulated them publicly…
then cried privately.
Maybe you smiled when they announced the engagement.
Then went home wondering when it would finally be your turn.
Maybe someone announced a pregnancy while you were still praying through infertility.
Maybe someone celebrated a promotion while you were wondering how you would pay your bills.
Maybe someone testified about miraculous healing while your family was preparing for a funeral.
Those moments can make Psalm 37:4 feel cruel if we interpret it as a guarantee that sufficiently devoted Christians eventually receive whatever they want.
But David gives us something stronger than that.
He gives us a God worth trusting even when we cannot understand His timetable.
And Scripture shows us again and again that God’s love cannot be measured by whether He gives people every outcome they request.
Paul pleaded repeatedly for his “thorn” to be removed.
God did not remove it.
Instead, the Lord answered:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Paul asked for relief.
God gave sustaining grace.
And then there is Jesus.
In Gethsemane, hours before the cross, Christ prayed in agony.
He did not pretend suffering was pleasant.
He did not spiritualize His anguish.
He prayed:
“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
There is mature faith.
Not pretending you have no desires.
Not pretending disappointment does not hurt.
Not pretending unanswered prayer does not make you cry.
But bringing the desire completely before the Father and saying:
“Father, this is what I want…
but I want You more.”
That is surrender.
And surrender is where Psalm 37:4 begins becoming breathtaking.
Because delighting in God does something to the human heart.
The closer you walk with Christ, the more your desires begin changing.
Things that once controlled you begin losing their grip.
Things you once desperately needed for validation become less important.
Success begins looking different.
Relationships begin looking different.
Money begins looking different.
Recognition begins looking different.
Even suffering begins looking different.
You stop asking only:
“God, how can I get what I want?”
And slowly you begin asking:
“Jesus, what do You want to make of me?”
That is transformation.
God does not merely give gifts to the heart.
He transforms the heart that desires them.
And sometimes the miracle is not that God finally gives you what you wanted.
Sometimes the miracle is realizing…
you don’t want it anymore.
You prayed desperately for someone God eventually removed.
At first, you thought losing them would destroy you.
Years later, you realize His “no” protected you.
You begged for a door to open.
It stayed shut.
You were devastated.
Later you discovered what was behind that door.
You asked God for success.
Instead, He allowed obscurity.
And somewhere in that hidden season He broke an addiction to applause you did not even know you had.
You wanted God to change your circumstances.
God wanted to change you.
That is why unanswered prayer cannot automatically be interpreted as divine rejection.
Sometimes God says yes.
Sometimes God says wait.
Sometimes God redirects.
Sometimes God closes something we would have walked into enthusiastically.
And sometimes we will not understand His providence in this lifetime.
Biblical faith does not require us to pretend every tragedy has an explanation we can presently identify.
It asks us to trust the character of God when explanations fail.
And we can trust His character most clearly because of Jesus Christ.
The cross is the ultimate proof that God can bring redemption through circumstances that initially look like absolute defeat.
Think about the scandal of Calvary.
Jesus betrayed.
Jesus falsely accused.
Jesus mocked.
Jesus beaten.
Jesus stripped.
Jesus crucified.
To the disciples watching from the shadows, everything must have looked ruined.
Their Messiah was dead.
Their expectations collapsed.
Their imagined future buried behind a stone.
If they had judged God's faithfulness solely by Friday afternoon, they might have concluded that everything had gone wrong.
But Sunday was coming.
The tomb opened.
Christ rose.
Death lost its final word.
Sin's debt was answered.
Hope walked out of a grave.
And the greatest apparent catastrophe in human history became the centerpiece of redemption.
That does not mean every disappointment will receive a neat explanation three days later.
It means Christians have reason to believe that what looks unfinished to us is never outside the sovereignty of God.
The Gospel is the story of God taking what looked irredeemable and writing grace into it.
Our sin was scandalous.
His grace was greater.
Our rebellion deserved judgment.
Christ bore judgment for sinners.
We wandered.
He came seeking.
We sinned.
He offered forgiveness.
We were guilty.
Christ offered His righteousness.
We were spiritually dead.
He gives life.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is what you need to hear today.
You have been staring at one unanswered prayer so long that you have begun overlooking the Savior standing beside you.
You keep asking:
“Jesus, when are You going to give me what I want?”
And perhaps He is whispering through His Word:
“When did what you wanted become more precious than Me?”
That question hurts.
But sometimes grace hurts before it heals.
Because God loves us too much to allow our idols to masquerade forever as prayer requests.
Anything can become an idol.
Even something good.
Marriage can become an idol.
Ministry can become an idol.
Financial security can become an idol.
Family can become an idol.
Success can become an idol.
Even the dream of being “used by God” can become an idol if being seen becomes more precious than knowing Christ.
Psalm 37:4 calls us back.
Delight yourself in the LORD.
Not merely His blessings.
Not merely His answers.
Not merely His miracles.
Him.
And something remarkable happens when Jesus becomes the treasure of your heart.
You discover that the deepest desire underneath all your smaller desires was never ultimately money, romance, recognition, comfort, or success.
You were created for God.
Augustine famously expressed the truth that our hearts remain restless until they find their rest in Him.
The human heart keeps trying to make temporary things carry eternal weight.
No relationship can do that.
No bank account can do that.
No career can do that.
No number of followers can do that.
No house can do that.
No applause can do that.
Eventually every earthly treasure whispers the same confession:
“I cannot be your God.”
But Jesus can carry the weight of your soul.
And maybe this is why you are reading this now.
Perhaps you came expecting an explanation of Psalm 37:4.
But somewhere along the way…
Psalm 37:4 began explaining you.
Your disappointment.
Your obsession.
Your waiting.
Your hidden resentment.
Your exhausted prayers.
Your jealousy when someone else receives what you wanted.
Your fear that God has forgotten you.
Your temptation to compromise because obedience appears too slow.
God sees all of it.
And He is not calling you to pretend.
He is calling you to surrender.
Bring Him the real desire.
Not the religious version.
Tell Him what you actually want.
Tell Him what hurts.
Tell Him what you are afraid to lose.
Tell Him why you are angry.
Tell Him why waiting has exhausted you.
Then open your hands.
“Jesus, if this desire is good, purify it.
If it is premature, teach me to wait.
If it is dangerous, remove it.
If it has become an idol, dethrone it.
If You choose to give it, help me worship You instead of the gift.
And if You choose not to give it…
teach my heart to believe that Christ is still enough.”
That prayer may be harder than asking for the miracle.
But it may also be the beginning of one.
Because perhaps the greatest fulfillment of the desires of your heart is not God becoming obedient to your desires.
It is your desires becoming surrendered to God.
And when the heart increasingly delights in Him, it increasingly begins wanting what honors Him.
That does not mean Christians stop having ordinary desires.
You can desire marriage.
You can pray for children.
You can pursue a career.
You can build a business.
You can ask for healing.
You can pray for provision.
You can dream.
You can create.
You can ask boldly.
The Bible does not command emotional numbness.
But every desire eventually belongs at the feet of Jesus.
Open-handed.
Surrendered.
“Nevertheless, not my will, but Yours.”
And there is freedom there.
Because now your joy no longer depends entirely upon receiving one particular outcome.
You can rejoice when God says yes.
You can trust when He says wait.
You can follow when He redirects.
You can grieve when life hurts.
And through all of it, you can still say:
“My treasure has not changed.
His name is Jesus.”
If this exposed something hidden in your heart, don’t rush away from that conviction.
Be honest before God.
Maybe somebody else reading the comments has been ashamed of struggling with the same thing.
Your honesty may remind them they are not alone.
Not because you understand everything.
Not because you know exactly what God will do.
But because your hope is learning to rest in Christ rather than in one desired outcome.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
But because perhaps they have been silently wondering why God has not answered the prayer they never talk about anymore.
Someone scrolling tonight may be one disappointment away from walking away from God because nobody ever explained Psalm 37:4 to them in context.
Let them discover that Christianity is not the promise that God will give us every earthly thing our hearts demand.
It is the astonishing announcement that God has given sinners something infinitely greater:
Jesus Christ.
Because there may come a night when something you desperately wanted falls apart, and you will need to remember again:
A closed door does not mean Christ stopped being good.
Truth is worth sharing.
Supporting Gospel Warrior should never be treated as buying God's favor.
We support Gospel work because grace has already been freely given to us in Christ.
Jesus is calling for more than your support.
He wants your heart.
Not the polished heart you show people.
The real one.
The disappointed one.
The jealous one.
The wounded one.
The ambitious one.
The frightened one.
The heart still holding that one prayer and whispering:
“But God…I really wanted this.”
Bring Him that heart.
Repent where desire has become idolatry.
Receive grace where disappointment has turned into bitterness.
Trust Him where you cannot understand.
And remember that Christianity does not rest on God granting every wish we carry.
It rests on a crucified and risen Savior who gave Himself to rescue sinners.
Psalm 37:4 is not permission to make God the servant of our dreams.
It is an invitation for God Himself to become our delight.
And when Christ becomes the treasure…
even our desires begin learning how to kneel.
So share this with the person whose unanswered prayer has become a private crisis of faith.
Because maybe the answer you have been waiting for is not God finally placing your dream into your hands.
Maybe grace is opening your clenched hands…
and showing you that Jesus was the treasure all along.
You thought you were waiting for God to give your heart what it wanted; perhaps all this time, God was teaching your heart to want Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “UNCOVER NAKEDNESS”: The Disturbing Phrase in Leviticus 18 We Were Never Supposed to Read Casually
paragraphs: “UNCOVER NAKEDNESS”: The Disturbing Phrase in Leviticus 18 We Were Never Supposed to Read Casually
Why does God repeatedly use this strange expression for forbidden sexual relations—and what does an ancient Hebrew phrase reveal about sex, boundaries, shame, holiness, and the grace of Jesus Christ?
There are phrases in the Bible we read too quickly because slowing down would make us uncomfortable.
This is one of them.
“Uncover nakedness.”
Again.
And again.
And again.
Leviticus 18 repeats the expression so often that eventually you have to stop and ask:
Why?
Why not simply say, “Do not have sex with this person”?
Why speak of nakedness?
Why describe sexual violation as something being uncovered?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What if this ancient expression is exposing something about us too?
Not merely about bodies.
Not merely about sexuality.
But about what human beings do when desire stops listening to God.
Because buried inside Leviticus 18 is a truth our generation desperately needs to recover:
Not everything you desire belongs to you.
Not every intimacy you can pursue is yours to take.
Not every boundary that frustrates you exists to imprison you.
And sometimes what the world calls liberation, God recognizes as destruction.
Listen to the Hebrew.
Leviticus 18:6 says:
אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה אֲנִי יְהוָה
Ish ish el-kol she’er besaro lo tiqrevu legalot ‘ervah, ani YHWH.
In a fairly literal rendering:
“No one shall approach any close relative of his flesh to uncover nakedness. I am YHWH.”
The crucial Hebrew expression is:
לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה — legalot ‘ervah
“To uncover nakedness.”
The verb comes from גלה — galah, carrying the basic idea of uncovering, revealing, exposing, or making something no longer concealed.
The noun עֶרְוָה — ‘ervah refers to nakedness, especially exposed sexual nakedness or the private parts, with nuances depending on context.
Put them together in Leviticus 18 and we encounter a Hebrew sexual expression whose meaning becomes unmistakable from the laws surrounding it.
This is not merely a prohibition against accidentally seeing somebody without clothing.
The chapter is establishing boundaries around sexual access.
That becomes particularly clear because Leviticus itself changes its vocabulary when necessary.

For example, after repeatedly saying “uncover nakedness,” verse 20 addresses adultery using different and more explicit sexual language. Verses 22 and 23 likewise use other expressions for prohibited sexual acts. The chapter therefore does not depend upon one euphemism alone. Its surrounding language establishes that the subject is prohibited sexual relations.
And that matters.
Because if we reduce “uncover nakedness” to simply “seeing someone naked,” we miss the force of the passage.

One scholarly explanation describes the expression as a euphemistic way of speaking about sexual intercourse, although interpreters debate some of the phrase's precise lexical and relational nuances in individual verses.
So we should be careful.
We should not pretend every linguistic question surrounding עֶרְוָה has been solved.
But neither should uncertainty about some details erase what the chapter plainly does.
Leviticus 18 draws sexual boundaries.
And God takes those boundaries seriously.
Why?
Because biblical sexuality is never merely about bodies touching.
It involves covenant.
Kinship.
Faithfulness.
Vulnerability.
Trust.
Consequences.
Another person's dignity.
And ultimately, obedience to the God who created the body in the first place.
That is where this strange phrase becomes hauntingly beautiful.
“Uncover nakedness.”
Because nakedness is vulnerability.
When someone becomes naked before another person, something normally concealed becomes exposed.
Defenses disappear.
Privacy disappears.
Something guarded becomes accessible.
Sexual intimacy therefore reaches into territory far deeper than appetite.
Scripture begins its story of human sexuality not with shame, but with astonishing innocence:
“The man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25.
Think about that.
Naked.
Yet unashamed.
Known.
Yet safe.
Exposed.
Yet not exploited.
Vulnerable.
Yet not violated.
That was the garden.
Then sin entered.
And one of the first things humanity noticed was nakedness.
The man and woman covered themselves.
They hid.
And when God called, Adam answered that he was afraid because he was naked.
Something had changed.
The human body had not suddenly become evil.
Sexuality had not suddenly become evil.
Marriage had not suddenly become evil.
But sin had entered the human experience, and what had once existed without shame was now surrounded by fear, hiding, domination, blame, lust, exploitation, and broken trust.
That makes Leviticus 18 far more than an ancient list of people Israelites were forbidden to sleep with.
God is teaching His people that sexuality requires boundaries because human desire, after the Fall, cannot safely appoint itself as its own god.
Read the chapter carefully.
God repeatedly says:
אֲנִי יְהוָה — Ani YHWH.
“I am the LORD.”
That is the heartbeat beneath the prohibitions.
God does not merely say, “Don't.”
He reminds Israel:
“I am your God.”
Leviticus 18 opens by warning Israel not to pattern itself after Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going. Instead, God's people were to walk according to His statutes.
In other words:
Your culture does not get the final word about your body.
Your appetite does not get the final word.
Your trauma does not get the final word.
Your loneliness does not get the final word.
Your hormones do not get the final word.
Pornography does not get the final word.
Your secret messages do not get the final word.
The person telling you, “If it feels right, it must be right,” does not get the final word.
Ani YHWH.
“I am the LORD.”
And suddenly Leviticus 18 stops feeling ancient.
Because we live in a world obsessed with uncovering.
We uncover bodies for entertainment.
We uncover ourselves for validation.
We consume other people's nakedness through screens.
We reduce people bearing the image of God to pixels.
We call lust private because nobody else is physically standing in the room.
We maintain secret conversations we would panic to see projected onto the church wall.
We flirt with people who belong to someone else.
We rationalize emotional affairs because “nothing physical happened.”
We cross boundaries slowly enough that we can pretend we never crossed them.
And sometimes we do something even more dangerous.
We use grace to excuse what Jesus died to free us from.
Maybe that sentence hurt.
Stay with it.
Because this article was never written merely to explain Hebrew.
It was written for the person reading this with something hidden.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your family doesn't know.
Your friends at church would never suspect it.
You know exactly how to worship.
Exactly when to raise your hands.
Exactly what Christian words to use.
Exactly what Bible verse to post.
But there is another version of you that appears when the door closes.
Another browser history.
Another conversation.
Another appetite.
Another relationship.
Another fantasy.
Another compromise.
Another secret.
And somewhere along the way, you became exhausted from protecting the image of a person you know you are not consistently living as.
This is where people often misunderstand holiness.
We imagine God standing outside the bedroom because He hates pleasure.
Scripture presents something far richer.
The God who established sexual boundaries is the same God who created male and female.
The same God who established marriage.
The same God whose Scriptures can celebrate marital desire.
The same God who invented the human capacity for intimacy before humanity invented pornography, adultery, exploitation, abuse, or sexual shame.
God is not anti-sex.
He is against what destroys His good purposes for it.
Boundaries are not evidence that something has no value.
Often boundaries exist precisely because something has enormous value.
We put fences around dangerous cliffs.
We place priceless things behind protection.
We make covenants around promises too important to treat casually.
And God surrounds sexual intimacy with moral boundaries because bodies are not disposable.
People are not products.
Vulnerability is not merchandise.
And another person's nakedness is not simply something your desire has the right to possess.
But now comes the question that can terrify anyone who has already crossed the boundary:
What about me?
What about what I already did?
What about the affair?
What about the pornography?
What about the relationship?
What about the years of compromise?
What about the sexual choices I cannot undo?
What about what somebody did to me?
Here we must make a distinction that Christians sometimes tragically fail to make.
Being sexually sinned against is not the same as committing sexual sin.
If someone violated, abused, assaulted, manipulated, coerced, groomed, or exploited you, their sin is not transferred onto you as moral guilt.
Your wounds may be real.
Your confusion may be real.
Your grief may be real.
Your healing may take time.
But another person's evil does not make you spiritually filthy beyond the reach of Christ.
Jesus is not disgusted by the wounded person coming to Him for mercy.
And for the person who has sinned sexually, Scripture does not tell you to pretend it was nothing.
Grace does something much more powerful.
Grace allows you to call darkness darkness without believing darkness gets the last word.
That is repentance.
Not self-hatred.
Not religious theater.
Not posting enough Bible verses to drown out conviction.
Repentance is agreeing with God strongly enough to turn.
And Christianity makes an outrageous announcement to guilty people:
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth after listing patterns of serious sin, including sexual sin, and then said something staggering:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they became morally perfect overnight.
Not because consequences magically disappeared.
Not because sin suddenly stopped mattering.
But because something happened to them.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the story of clean people avoiding dirty people.
It is the story of a holy Christ rescuing sinners.
Jesus does not rewrite our scandal by pretending it never happened.
He rewrites it by entering the story with a cross.
The cross tells the truth about sin more brutally than our excuses ever will.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But the cross also tells the truth about grace more beautifully than our shame ever could.
God's mercy is so astonishing that Christ willingly went there for sinners.
At the cross, holiness and mercy do not cancel each other.
They meet.
Justice is not shrugged away.
Grace is not sentimentalized.
Christ bears sin.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
The ashamed are invited out of hiding.
The enslaved can begin walking toward freedom.
And the person whispering, “If everyone knew what I had done, nobody could love me,” encounters a Savior who already knows.
Completely.
And still calls sinners to come.
But come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without bargaining.
Come without editing the story.
Come without renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Jesus said:
“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”
Then He said:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Mark 2:17.
The Great Physician cannot heal the version of you that you keep insisting is not sick.
Bring Him the real wound.
Bring Him the real addiction.
Bring Him the real relationship.
Bring Him the real browser history.
Bring Him the real memories.
Bring Him the secret you keep trying to bury beneath Christian appearances.
Bring Him what you are ashamed to name.
Christ already knows what is underneath the covering.
And He still calls you toward the light.
Maybe this is why the language of Leviticus feels so piercing.
Human beings have spent thousands of years uncovering what God told us not to uncover...
while desperately covering what God is calling us to confess.
We expose bodies.
Then hide souls.
We reveal skin.
Then conceal sin.
We crave intimacy.
Then fear being truly known.
And Jesus walks directly into that contradiction.
Not carrying a camera to humiliate you.
Not carrying gossip to destroy you.
Carrying scars.
The hands reaching toward repentant sinners are wounded hands.
The Savior calling you out of darkness is the Savior who was stripped, mocked, wounded, publicly humiliated, and crucified.
He knows shame.
Yet He had no sin of His own to confess.
He bore ours.
And because He rose from the grave, shame does not get resurrection power over those who belong to Him.
Your past can explain some of your scars.
It does not have the authority to become your god.
Your temptation can describe a battle.
It does not have the authority to define your identity.
Your failure can become part of your testimony.
It does not have to become your destiny.
So perhaps the question after reading Leviticus 18 is no longer merely:
“What does ‘uncover nakedness’ mean?”
Perhaps another question has quietly appeared.
What have I been uncovering that God told me to guard—and what have I been hiding that Jesus is asking me to bring into His light?
Do not answer that publicly unless wisdom says you should.
But answer God.
Honestly.
Tonight.

If necessary, seek mature pastoral accountability. If there is addiction, pursue serious help. If there is an adulterous relationship, stop romanticizing what repentance requires. If pornography owns part of your private life, stop negotiating with it. If your marriage is wounded, pursue truth, wisdom, repentance, counseling, and restoration where restoration is safely possible.
And if you have been abused or exploited, please hear this carefully:
You do not need to repent for another person's crime against you.
Seek safety.
Seek wise support.
Tell someone trustworthy.
Healing is not betrayal of your faith.
Truth is not shameful.
What happened to you does not make you untouchable to Christ.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for wounded people.
There is also room there for repentant guilty people.
That is what makes grace scandalous.
Nobody gets to boast.
We come needing Christ.
If this exposed something hidden in your life, you don't have to tell strangers the details.
If Christ has already been restoring areas of your life you once thought were beyond redemption, tell someone else there is hope.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed to read tonight.
And please don't let this message die on your screen.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone may be drowning in pornography.
Someone may be considering adultery.
Someone may carry years of sexual shame.
Someone may believe Jesus could forgive everybody except them.
Someone may have been violated and still wrongly believes the shame belongs to them.
Leviticus 18 is not the kind of passage most Christians understand after one hurried reading.
It doesn't.
It can't.
And not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces the giving, generosity, service, and stewardship God may call you to practice through your local church and toward people in need.
It doesn't.
Scripture says Christian giving should be purposeful and voluntary—“not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That means support should come from worship, not spiritual pressure.
Your support helps the work continue.
Your sharing helps the message travel.
Your prayers matter.
And your participation can help put biblical truth in front of another human being at exactly the moment they need it.
Leviticus 18 teaches us that holiness has boundaries.
The cross teaches us that boundary-breakers can be forgiven.
And the resurrection teaches us that forgiven people do not have to remain what they were.
Maybe your story contains scandal.
Maybe it contains sexual failure.
Maybe betrayal.
Maybe addiction.
Maybe abuse.
Maybe years of hiding.
Maybe consequences you cannot reverse.
The Gospel never promises that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something greater:

Jesus Christ can take a sinner who finally stops hiding, wash what guilt has stained, begin transforming what sin has distorted, and write grace into places shame insisted could never become holy again.
So bring Him the chapter you wish you could tear out.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the desire.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him you.
Because perhaps the most dangerous nakedness was never an uncovered body.
Perhaps it is a soul standing completely exposed before a holy God with nowhere left to hide.
And perhaps the greatest miracle is discovering that the sinner who runs to Jesus in repentance does not find a Savior waiting to exploit that exposure...
but a Savior who already bore the shame of the cross to cover the repentant sinner in a righteousness that could never be earned.
You may remember the moment your scandal was exposed—but eternity will remember the Savior who refused to let your scandal have the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Song of Solomon Is Far More Sensual Than Many Christians Were Told
paragraphs:
Song of Solomon Is Far More Sensual Than Many Christians Were Told
The Bible did not blush when it spoke about married desire. We did. And somewhere between shame, silence, pornography, purity, longing, and grace, many Christians stopped hearing what this astonishing book was actually saying.
There is a book in your Bible that some Christians almost seem embarrassed to read out loud.
Not because it describes war.
Not because somebody gets murdered.
Not because a prophet announces judgment.
Because a woman says she wants the man she loves to kiss her.
Because a man looks at the woman he loves and notices her body.
Because she notices his.
Because they desire one another.
Because Scripture sometimes speaks about human sexuality without sounding ashamed that God created human beings with bodies.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
God allowed those words to remain in His Word.
“The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s. Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
That is essentially how the book begins.
Not with an apology.
Not with embarrassment.
With longing.
The Hebrew is striking:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
She speaks first.
Sit with that.

The woman is not merely the passive object of male attraction. She possesses a voice. Longing. Affection. Agency. She knows whom she loves, and she is not portrayed as morally contaminated merely because she desires him.
For Christians who were raised believing holiness requires pretending sexual desire does not exist, Song of Songs can feel almost scandalous.
But the scandal may not be what Scripture says.
The scandal may be how thoroughly sin has distorted something God created good.
There is an enormous difference between biblical desire and lustful consumption.
Pornography says, “Your body exists for my appetite.”
Biblical love says, “I delight in you.”
Pornography separates bodies from covenant, dignity, faithfulness, sacrifice, and personhood.
Song of Songs refuses to do that.
Its lovers do not speak like consumers browsing bodies.
They speak like people captivated by someone.
That difference matters.
Because Christianity is not a religion teaching that bodies are inherently dirty.
Christianity proclaims something far more astonishing:
“The Word became flesh.”
Jesus Christ did not save humanity by teaching us to escape embodiment. The eternal Son took on a genuine human body. He suffered bodily. He bled bodily. He died bodily. He rose bodily.
And Scripture ultimately promises resurrection.
So when Christians accidentally communicate that physical existence itself is shameful, we are not becoming more biblical.
We are becoming less biblical.
And Song of Songs confronts us with that fact in language many believers never expected to find between Genesis and Revelation.
Listen to Song 4:5 in Hebrew:
שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים תְּאוֹמֵי צְבִיָּה הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים
Shenei shadayikh kishnei ‘ofarim, te’omei tseviyyah, haro‘im bashoshanim.
A straightforward translation is:
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.”
Yes.
That is actually there.
The Hebrew noun שָׁדַיִךְ — shadayikh — means “your breasts.”
We do Scripture no favors by pretending otherwise.

Later, the poetry becomes even more intensely sensual. The woman’s body is compared with a palm tree and her breasts with clusters. The lover speaks of climbing the palm and taking hold of its branches.
Ancient love poetry communicates through metaphor, fragrance, gardens, fruit, wine, spices, animals, landscape, touch, sight, taste, and longing.
This is poetry.
Beautiful poetry.
Sensual poetry.
And yet there is something profoundly different about its sensuality from the sexual imagery saturating modern culture.
The Song can be explicit without becoming cheap.
Intimate without becoming pornographic.
Sensual without reducing either lover to an object.
There is admiration here.
Mutuality.
Longing.
Exclusivity.
Delight.
The woman can say:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve‘alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
Notice that word:
תְּשׁוּקָה
teshuqah.
Desire.
Scripture is not frightened by the word.
But Scripture refuses to let desire become god.
And that may be exactly where some of us need conviction.
Because there are two ways Christians can badly misunderstand sexuality.
One is worshiping it.
The other is despising it.
Our culture frequently does the first.
Church culture has sometimes reacted by drifting toward the second.
Neither is biblical.
Sex is a terrible god.
But God's creation is not therefore evil.
Desire can become corrupted, selfish, adulterous, exploitative, obsessive, abusive, pornographic, or idolatrous.
That is why repentance matters.
But corruption does not prove that the original gift was corrupt.
It proves something beautiful has been vandalized.
Genesis tells us that before human shame entered the story, the man and woman were naked and unashamed.
Then sin came.
And suddenly humanity hid.
We have been hiding ever since.
Behind pornography.
Behind promiscuity.
Behind jokes.
Behind shame.
Behind religious performance.
Behind secret browser histories.
Behind marriages where husband and wife have stopped talking honestly.
Behind loneliness.
Behind wounds nobody knows exist.
Some people reading this learned about sex from pornography before anyone trustworthy taught them about God's design.
Some were abused.
Some were betrayed.
Some were taught that sexual desire itself made them filthy.
Some carried questions into adulthood because nobody in church seemed safe enough to ask.
Some entered marriage expecting a wedding ring to instantly erase years of fear and shame.
It didn't.
Some discovered that wounds travel with us.
And some are reading this while carrying secret sin.
You love Jesus.
But there is something you keep returning to when nobody is watching.
A screen.
A fantasy.
A conversation.
A relationship.
A memory.
A hidden appetite.
And afterward comes the familiar collapse.
Delete.
Hide.
Promise.
Cry.
Pray.
Repeat.
Maybe Song of Songs makes you uncomfortable not because Scripture is impure…
but because sin taught us to see sexuality through broken eyes.
Jesus does not call us to pretend desire doesn't exist.
He calls us to holiness.
There is a difference.
Christ does not merely put religious curtains over our darkness.
He brings darkness into the light.

Jesus taught that lust reaches into the heart. He treated adultery seriously. He upheld God's design for marriage. He showed extraordinary mercy toward sexually broken people without ever redefining sin as righteousness.
That combination matters.
Truth without grace crushes wounded people.
Grace without truth leaves wounded people enslaved.
Jesus brings both.
Grace that tells the truth.
Truth that opens the door to grace.

And suddenly Song of Songs begins to feel less like the embarrassing book Christians need to explain away and more like part of God's answer to a world that has forgotten how to distinguish intimacy from consumption.
The Song says beauty can be noticed without becoming merchandise.
Desire can exist without becoming domination.
A woman's longing does not make her dirty.
A man's attraction does not automatically make him predatory.
Bodies are not gods.
Bodies are not garbage.
They are creatures of God.
And sexuality belongs beneath His lordship like everything else.
That means Song of Songs should never become an excuse for lust.
Quite the opposite.
It exposes how counterfeit lust really is.
Pornography promises intimacy while training people for isolation.
It promises satisfaction while cultivating appetite.
It promises connection while turning persons into images.
The Song keeps giving us persons.
“My beloved.”
“My love.”
“My dove.”
Not a category.
Not content.
Not a body detached from a soul.
Beloved.
And there is another important truth Christians should handle carefully.

For centuries, Jewish and Christian readers have also read the Song allegorically. Jewish interpreters have often seen echoes of God's covenant relationship with Israel; Christian interpreters have often heard echoes of Christ's love for His Church. The wider Christian canon certainly gives us a genuine bridegroom-and-bride pattern: Ephesians 5 connects Christian marriage with Christ and the Church.
That theological resonance is beautiful.
