We can learn how Christians talk before we ever learn what surrender feels like.
We can become familiar with Jesus without actually belonging to Jesus.
And that is why some of the most sobering words in the entire New Testament were not originally spoken to atheists mocking Christ.
Jesus said:
“Οὐ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι· Κύριε κύριε...”
Ou pas ho legōn moi, Kyrie Kyrie...
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord’...”
Notice those words.
Κύριε κύριε — Kyrie, Kyrie.
“Lord, Lord.”
These are people using the right title.
They know His name.
They address Jesus as Lord.
They are not standing there saying, “Jesus never existed.”
They are not laughing at Christianity.
They are appealing to Christ using language that sounds deeply religious.
And Jesus continues by describing people who point to extraordinary things they claim to have done in His name.
They effectively say:
Didn’t we prophesy in Your name?
Didn’t we cast out demons in Your name?
Didn’t we perform mighty works in Your name?
Listen carefully to what they are doing.
They are presenting their résumé.
Their defense is built around what they did.
We prophesied.
We cast out.
We performed.
We accomplished.
We had experiences.
We had ministry.
We had spiritual activity.
We had a reputation.
Surely that means we belonged to You.
Then comes the sentence that should make every person who casually wears the name “Christian” examine his or her heart.
Jesus says:
“οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
Not merely:
“You weren't impressive enough.”
Not:
“You didn't accomplish enough.”
Not:
“You had too many failures.”
The terrifying center of the statement is relational.
I never knew you.
And that distinction matters enormously, because this passage must never be twisted into the idea that salvation belongs to Christians who perform well enough.
That would contradict the Gospel itself.
We are not saved because our spiritual résumé impresses God.
We are saved by grace through faith. Salvation is God’s gift, not something we can boast about earning through works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
The same passage immediately continues by saying that those who are created in Christ Jesus are created for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace saves.
And saving grace changes people.
Not into flawless people overnight.
Not into people who never struggle.
Not into people who never stumble.
But into people whose relationship to Christ, sin, repentance, obedience, and grace is being transformed.
That is why Matthew 7 should not drive a sincere, struggling believer into endless panic every time he falls.
Peter failed catastrophically.
He denied Jesus.
Three times.
Yet Peter’s failure was not the final chapter of Peter’s story.
Jesus restored him.
David sinned terribly.
The thief beside Christ reached the final hours of a ruined life with nothing resembling an impressive religious résumé.
Yet he turned toward Jesus, and Christ gave him hope beyond the grave.
The Gospel has never been the announcement that respectable people can save themselves.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
So Matthew 7 is not telling broken people, “Become perfect enough and maybe Jesus will accept you.”
It is confronting something far more deceptive.
A person can possess Christian familiarity without possessing Christ.
That is the danger.
You can know worship songs and not know the One being worshiped.
You can own several Bibles while rarely allowing Scripture to confront you.
You can defend Christianity online while refusing Christ access to the hidden rooms of your life.
You can know theology.
You can serve.
You can give.
You can preach.
You can build a following.
You can have “Christian” written across your biography.
And still there remains a question nobody else can answer for you:
Do you actually know Jesus Christ?
Not merely:
Do people think you are a Christian?
Not:
Were you baptized once?
Not:
Did your parents raise you in church?
Not:
Can you explain salvation?
Not:
Did you once repeat a prayer?
Not:
Do you have Christian friends?
Not:
But:
Have you entrusted yourself to Christ?
Have you come to Him as a sinner who cannot rescue himself?
Have you stopped negotiating with the sins you secretly intend to keep?
When you fall, do you run away from Christ to protect your darkness, or do you come back into His light in repentance?
Is Jesus merely part of your identity...
or is He your Lord?
Because there is a difference between struggling against sin and peacefully making a home inside it.
There is a difference between stumbling and surrendering to rebellion.
There is a difference between weakness that drives you toward Christ and lawlessness that continually tells Christ, in practice, “You may have my religious language, but You will not have my life.”
Matthew uses the Greek word ἀνομία — anomia in verse 23.
It carries the sense of lawlessness.
Jesus describes these people as workers of lawlessness.
Again, the contrast is not between “people who have never sinned” and “people who have sinned.”
If sinless performance were the requirement, none of us could stand.
The contrast forces us toward a deeper question:
Who actually rules the heart?
And suddenly the funeral feels closer.
Not because you are supposed to live terrified that you might die tonight.
Not because manufactured fear produces genuine conversion.
But because mortality strips away our illusions.
One day, your phone will stop receiving your messages.
Someone else will eventually clean out your drawers.
Your social-media account will become strangely quiet.
Pictures of you will remain after you are gone.
People may scroll backward through years of your life.
Someone will discover an old voice message and cry because hearing your voice suddenly hurts.
Your clothes will still exist.
Your chair may still sit where you left it.
Your Bible may still be on the shelf.
But you will have stepped beyond reputation.
And no amount of applause from this side of eternity will rewrite reality on the other.
That is why this is not really an article about funerals.
It is about today.
Because today you can still respond.
Today grace is still being proclaimed.
Today Christ is still calling sinners to Himself.
Today you can stop hiding behind the version of yourself everyone else knows.
Maybe nobody knows what happened last night.
Maybe nobody knows what you keep deleting from your phone.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your children do not know.
Your followers certainly do not know.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing wonderfully.
And inside, something is dying.
Maybe you have become skilled at looking spiritually alive.
You raise your hands during worship while carrying a secret you refuse to surrender.
You share sermons you are no longer living.
You encourage everyone else while privately wondering when you became so numb.
You know exactly how to sound strong.
“God is good.”
“I'm blessed.”
“Keep praying.”
“Trust His timing.”
Beautiful truths.
But when the room becomes quiet...
when nobody is watching...
when there is nothing left to perform...
you know there is distance between the person people applaud and the person God sees.
If that is you, please understand something.
Jesus did not expose hypocrisy so hypocrites would have no hope. He exposes darkness because He calls people into the light.
The One warning us in Matthew 7 is the same Jesus who goes toward the cross.
The hands that warn sinners will soon be pierced for sinners.
The voice saying that religious performance cannot save you belongs to the Savior who came precisely because you cannot save yourself.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not:
“Build a reputation impressive enough for heaven.”
It is:
Christ came to rescue sinners.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
Your darkest chapter does not need to become the title of your eternity.
Your scandal does not have to be the last sentence.
Your pornography does not have to own you.
Your adultery does not have to define your final identity.
Your bitterness does not have to become your permanent home.
Your pride does not have to have the last word.
Your secret addiction does not outrank the mercy of Christ.
Your religious hypocrisy is not beyond His power to expose, forgive, cleanse, and transform.
But grace is not permission to keep hugging the chains Jesus died to break.
Grace calls you out.
Grace calls you home.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace does not merely change where forgiven sinners are going.
Grace begins changing the forgiven sinner.
This is where the theme of our lives becomes more than a slogan:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by telling you sin does not matter.

Jesus rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth and mercy, paying the price we could never pay, forgiving those who come to Him, and beginning a work of transformation that reaches deeper than reputation ever could.
Maybe your scandal isn't public.
Maybe your scandal lives entirely inside you.
Nobody knows.
But Jesus knows.
And somehow that is both terrifying and beautiful.
Because the Person who knows the worst thing about you is the very One inviting you to stop hiding.
You do not need to impress Him.
You cannot manipulate Him.
You cannot edit the footage.
You cannot delete the history.
You cannot hand Jesus the carefully curated version of yourself you hand everybody else.
He already knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become more respectable.
Not after you fix yourself.
Come as the sinner who finally admits:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Maybe you have called Him “Lord” for twenty years.
Then ask yourself something deeper tonight.
Does my life reveal that I want Jesus Himself, or merely the benefits associated with His name?
Do I love Christ?
Do I trust Christ?
When Scripture confronts me, am I willing to be corrected?
When I sin, do I excuse it indefinitely, or does the Spirit draw me toward confession and repentance?
Do I want Jesus to save me only from hell, or do I also want Him to save me from the sin destroying me?
And please do not turn those questions into another performance checklist.
The answer is not to stare endlessly at yourself until you manufacture assurance.
Look to Christ.
The Christian's confidence ultimately rests not in the perfection of his grip upon Jesus but in the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Trust Him.
Remain in Him.
Follow Him.
When you fall, confess.
When you wander, return.
When sin whispers that hiding would be easier, drag the darkness into the light.
When shame tells you that Jesus is finished with you, remember the cross.
When pride tells you that you don't need mercy, remember the cross again.
At the cross, both despair and arrogance lose their arguments.
You are more sinful than your reputation admits.
And Christ is more merciful than your shame wants you to believe.
Imagine your funeral again.
People are standing there.
They tell wonderful stories.
They speak your name with affection.
Perhaps they say you were successful.
Generous.
Funny.
Faithful.
Strong.
Perhaps hundreds of people comment beneath your final photograph.
But imagine something better than being remembered well.
Imagine actually belonging to Christ.
Imagine your deepest confidence at the end of life not being:
“People thought I was good.”
But:
“My hope is Jesus Christ.”
Not my résumé.
Not my reputation.
Not my ministry.
Not my followers.
Not my charitable acts.
Not my denomination.
Not my family history.
Not my public image.
Christ.
Only Christ.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose.
The One who receives those who come to Him.
The One whose grace can take the chapters we thought had ruined everything and begin writing redemption where we expected only shame.
And maybe that is why you needed to read this before your funeral instead of having someone read something beautiful about you at it.
You still have breath.
There is still time to be honest.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers every private detail. But you can stop pretending before God.
If you need words, let them be simple:
“Jesus, have mercy on me. I have hidden behind appearances long enough. I cannot save myself. Forgive me. Cleanse me. I trust You. Teach me to follow You—not merely with my mouth, but with my life.”
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Then think of one person you love.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to condemn.
Someone you genuinely love.
Someone who knows Christianity but may not truly know Christ.
Someone who has been running.
Someone who thinks being respectable is enough.
Someone whose wounds have driven them away from church.
Someone who believes their scandal has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Or send this privately.
Read Matthew 7 again when the noise disappears.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront what needs confronting, heal where Christ is healing you, and grow deeper in Jesus, follow and stay connected.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's favor, prove that you love Him, or earn salvation. We never want to manipulate something as sacred as glorifying God into a financial transaction.
But one genuine way believers may choose to glorify God is by willingly using their resources, reach, and influence to help sound Gospel teaching reach others.
Come to Jesus.
Because someday the room may be filled with people saying wonderful things about you.
Let them.
Love them well enough that they have wonderful things to remember.
Live humbly.
Serve generously.
Repent quickly.
Forgive freely.
Love deeply.
But never confuse their applause with Christ's salvation.
Your obituary cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot know Jesus for you.
Your pastor cannot surrender for you.
Your parents' faith cannot substitute for yours.
Your ministry cannot become your mediator.
There is one Mediator between God and humanity: Jesus Christ.
So before people gather someday to talk about how well they knew you, settle the infinitely greater question:
Do you belong to the Christ whose name you know?
And if that question unsettles you tonight, don't bury it beneath another distraction.
Open the Gospel.
Pray.
Seek Christ.
Talk with a mature, biblically faithful believer.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
There may come a day when people speak your name for the final time.
But the greatest story of your life will never be what people said about you after you died.
It will be what Jesus Christ did with a sinner who finally stopped hiding and came home.
Your funeral may remember the person everyone thought you were. Grace is rewriting the person Jesus already knows.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HANNAH PROMISED HER UNBORN SON TO GOD BEFORE SHE EVER CONCEIVED HIM
paragraphs:
HANNAH PROMISED HER UNBORN SON TO GOD BEFORE SHE EVER CONCEIVED HIM
Before Samuel had a heartbeat, Hannah had already opened her hands. And what happened next exposes one of the hardest questions of faith: Do you still want the blessing if God remains its rightful Lord?
There is something almost unbearable about Hannah’s prayer.
Not because it was eloquent.
It wasn’t.
Not because she stood before God sounding strong, composed, and spiritually impressive.
She didn’t.
She was shattered.
Her lips moved, but almost nothing came out.

And before the son she desperately wanted had lungs to breathe, fingers to wrap around hers, or a voice capable of calling her “mother,” Hannah made a promise that would eventually cost her something far deeper than the pain of waiting.
She promised the child back to God.
Read that slowly.
She surrendered Samuel before Samuel existed.
And maybe that is why her story still reaches into the places we protect from everybody else.
Because most of us know how to ask God for something.
Far fewer of us know how to place what we asked for back into His hands.
Hannah’s story begins in pain.
First Samuel tells us that Elkanah had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children. Hannah did not.
That difference became a wound.
Worse, it became ammunition.

Scripture says Hannah’s rival provoked her severely because of her barrenness. This was not a single insensitive remark that Hannah could forget by morning. The text describes recurring anguish. Year after year, when the family went to worship the LORD, the wound was reopened.
Imagine having your deepest unanswered prayer repeatedly placed beside somebody else’s answered one.
She has what you prayed for.
He received what you are still waiting for.
Their announcement appears while you are still grieving.
Their door opens while yours remains closed.
And you are trying to love God without pretending that it does not hurt.
That was Hannah.
Elkanah loved her, but even sincere human love could not repair what was happening inside her.
At one point he asked why she was weeping and why she would not eat.
But there are wounds another human being cannot love out of you.
There are rooms in the soul where even the people who genuinely love you cannot follow.
So Hannah went somewhere else.
She went before the LORD.
Scripture says she was in “bitterness of soul” and “wept sore.”
Then came the vow.
In Hebrew, 1 Samuel 1:11 begins:
וַתִּדֹּר נֶדֶר
Vattiddor neder.
Literally, the wording carries the force of “she vowed a vow.”
This was not a passing emotional thought.
Hannah was making a solemn promise before God.
Then she addressed Him:
יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת
YHWH Tseva’ot.
“The LORD of Hosts.”
The LORD of armies.
The God whose power Hannah could not manufacture, manipulate, or replace.
And then the broken woman began asking the Almighty to see her.
She pleaded that He would look upon her affliction, remember her, and not forget His servant.
Then came the sentence that changes the entire story.
If God gave her a son, she would give that son to the LORD “all the days of his life.”
Before conception...
surrender.
Before pregnancy...
consecration.
Before she heard a newborn cry...
open hands.
Hannah was asking God for something she had already determined must ultimately belong to Him.
That does not mean Christians should imitate Hannah by bargaining with God.
Her vow is a description of what Hannah did in this particular biblical moment, not a formula guaranteeing that God will grant whatever we promise to surrender.
God cannot be purchased with promises.
Prayer is not spiritual leverage.
Faith is not saying, “God, if I give You enough, You owe me what I want.”
The Gospel destroys that idea.
God owes sinners nothing, yet in Christ He gives grace we could never earn.
Hannah’s prayer is powerful for another reason.
It reveals surrender.
She wanted a son desperately, but she was willing to acknowledge that even the child she longed for would never cease to belong ultimately to God.
And there is a question hiding inside her prayer that eventually finds every believer:
What happens when the blessing arrives?
We talk often about trusting God while waiting.
But sometimes receiving is its own test.
Because it is possible to pray desperately for something and then, after receiving it, allow the gift to occupy the throne that belongs to the Giver.
We pray for the marriage...
then make the marriage our identity.
We pray for children...
then live as though they belong absolutely to us.
We pray for a business...
then let success consume the life God gave us.
We pray for influence...
then become addicted to being noticed.
We pray for provision...
then begin trusting money more than Providence.
We pray for healing...
then slowly forget the Healer.
Sometimes the most dangerous moment is not when your hands are empty.
Sometimes it is when they finally become full.
Hannah did not yet know whether those hands would ever hold a child.
She simply poured herself before God.
So intensely, in fact, that Eli the priest watched her mouth and assumed she was drunk.
Imagine that humiliation.
You finally bring your deepest pain into the presence of God...
and someone misunderstands your brokenness.
Hannah answered him:
“I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit.”
She explained that she had not been drinking.
She had been pouring out her soul before the LORD.
That sentence deserves to be remembered by anyone who has ever believed they needed polished words before approaching God.
Hannah did not perform.
She poured.
There is a difference.
Some prayers are beautifully spoken.
Others are barely spoken at all.
Some prayers sound like confidence.
Others are wet with tears.
Some prayers fill rooms.
Others are nothing more than trembling lips while the heart screams where nobody else can hear it.
God is not intimidated by the prayer you cannot make beautiful.
He does not require you to edit your grief before bringing it into His presence.

And this is where Hannah’s story becomes deeply Christ-centered—not because every detail is secretly about Jesus, but because the God to whom Hannah cried is the God whose saving purpose ultimately reaches its fullness in Christ.
Hannah needed mercy.
So do we.
Hannah could not create the answer she desired.
Neither can we create our own salvation.
And the Gospel announces something even greater than Hannah receiving Samuel.
God gave His Son.
Not because humanity negotiated successfully.
Not because sinners deserved Him.
Not because we offered God something impressive enough in exchange.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is Romans 5:8.
Hannah surrendered a beloved son into the service of God.
But we must not confuse her sacrifice with the saving work of Christ.
Samuel could serve Israel.
Samuel could speak God’s word.
Samuel could become a prophet and judge.
Samuel could anoint kings.
But Samuel could not carry away the sins of the world.
Only Jesus could do that.
At Calvary, Christ did not merely demonstrate surrender.
He accomplished redemption.
The sinless Son bore sin.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
The rejected Savior opened the way for guilty people to be reconciled to God.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings making heroic sacrifices for God.
It is the story of God’s grace toward sinners through Jesus Christ.
And grace changes what surrender means.
We do not surrender ourselves to make God love us.
We surrender because in Christ we discover how profoundly He already has.
We do not obey to purchase forgiveness.
We obey because forgiveness was purchased by Another.
We do not give ourselves to Christ hoping our sacrifice will become sufficient.
We give ourselves to Christ because His sacrifice already is.
And Hannah’s story keeps moving.
Scripture says she eventually left, ate, and her countenance was no longer sad.
Notice the timing.
Samuel had not been conceived yet.
Nothing visible had changed.
The answer had not arrived.
But something had happened between Hannah and God.
Then Scripture gives us one of the tenderest statements in the chapter:
“The LORD remembered her.”
Biblically, this does not mean God had previously forgotten Hannah and suddenly recovered the memory.
When Scripture speaks this way of God “remembering,” it points toward God turning His covenant attention toward someone and acting according to His purpose.
In due time, Hannah conceived.
A son was born.
She named him Samuel.
The woman who once cried because her arms were empty now held the child she had begged God to give her.
Imagine the first night.
The tiny breathing.
The warmth against her chest.
The fingers.
The cries.
The sleepy eyes.
Imagine nursing the answer to the prayer that had once made you weep until you could barely speak.
And then imagine remembering your vow.
Because Hannah remembered.
That may be the part of the story we rush past too quickly.
It is easy to make promises while desperate.
Keeping them after receiving what we wanted is different.
Hannah could have rationalized.
Surely God understands.
Surely I did not mean it quite so literally.
Surely I can modify the arrangement now.
Surely this child needs me more than the sanctuary needs him.
But after Samuel was weaned, Hannah took him to Shiloh.
She returned to the place connected with her tears carrying the evidence that God had heard her.
And standing before Eli, she essentially identified herself:
I am the woman who stood here praying.
Then came the words generations of believers have remembered:
“For this child I prayed.”
But do not stop reading there.
The next movement is what makes the story so costly.
God had granted her petition, and Hannah therefore gave Samuel to the LORD.
The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 1:28 contains a beautiful wordplay built around the root שׁאל (sha’al), “to ask.”
Hannah had asked.
God had granted what was asked.
And now the child was being given over to the LORD.
The answer became an offering.
The gift did not replace the Giver.
That is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because perhaps there is something you have been clutching.
A relationship.
A child.
A dream.
A career.
A platform.
A possession.
A future you have already scripted.
Maybe you have prayed, “Lord, give this to me.”
But you have never prayed the harder prayer:
“Lord, if You give it... it is still Yours.”
And maybe the thing you need to surrender is not something beautiful.
Maybe it is the scandal.
The secret.
The compromise.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The bitterness you have fed for years.
The shame you keep dragging behind you.
The private sin you keep renaming so you do not have to repent of it.
Maybe you have become skilled at looking spiritually alive while something inside you is starving.
Hannah poured out her soul.
Perhaps it is time you stopped hiding yours.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the version of you that everybody sees.
He came to save sinners.
Real sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Compromised sinners.
Religious sinners.
Broken sinners.
People whose stories contain chapters they wish could be burned.
And that is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Your scandal does not have to become the final sentence.
Your failure does not have to become your identity.
Your sin must not be excused—but it can be forgiven.
Your past cannot be rewritten in the sense that it never happened—but Jesus can redeem what your past means for your future.
Repentance does not mean pretending the darkness was harmless.
It means turning from sin toward the Savior who entered our darkness to rescue us.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace announces that Christ is mighty enough to forgive the guilty and transform the repentant.
This is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you are reading this while waiting for your own “Samuel.”
Maybe you have prayed until you are tired of hearing yourself pray.
Maybe another person’s blessing has become painful to watch.
Maybe you are genuinely happy for them and quietly devastated for yourself at the same time.
Maybe you keep wondering whether God sees you.

Hannah’s story does not give us permission to promise that every barren womb will conceive, every disease will disappear, every relationship will be restored, every financial crisis will end the way we desire, or every prayer will receive the answer we imagined.
The Bible does not teach that.
What it does show us is that unanswered prayer does not make pouring out your soul to God meaningless.
God is still God in the waiting.
Christ is still sufficient when the answer is delayed.
Grace is still grace when life hurts.
And your ultimate hope cannot rest in receiving your Samuel.
It must rest in Jesus.
Because even the greatest earthly answer is temporary.
Children grow.
Careers end.
Bodies age.
Money disappears.
Applause fades.
People leave.
Earthly blessings are real, beautiful, and worthy of thanksgiving—but none of them can carry the weight of being your savior.
Jesus can.
So perhaps the deepest question in Hannah’s story is not:
“What are you asking God to give you?”
Perhaps it is:
“If God gives it, will you still worship God more than the gift?”
And there is another question.
If He does not give you exactly what you asked for...
is Jesus still enough?
That question reaches somewhere sermons sometimes cannot.
Because surrender sounds beautiful until surrender has a name.
Until it has a face.
Until it is the thing you waited years to receive.
Hannah eventually stood with Samuel at Shiloh and did what she had promised before she ever knew his face.
She opened her hands.
And what looked like an ending became part of something much larger.
Samuel would grow in the presence of the LORD.
He would hear God calling his name.
He would become one of the pivotal prophetic figures in Israel’s history.
He would minister during a crucial transition in the nation.
He would anoint Saul.
Later, he would anoint David.
And through David’s royal line, according to God’s covenant purposes, history would eventually move toward Jesus Christ, the Son of David and the true King.
Hannah could not have seen all of that when she was crying.
She only knew the pain in front of her.
That should humble us.
You do not know everything God is doing.
You do not know how far obedience may travel beyond your lifetime.
You do not know what God may do through something surrendered to Him.
But do not turn that into another prosperity formula.
Surrender does not guarantee earthly greatness.
Faithfulness does not obligate God to make your story famous.
Sometimes obedience will be known only to God.
That is enough.
Because the goal of Christianity is not becoming impressive.
It is Christ.
So bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the waiting.
Bring Him the blessing.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the child.
Bring Him the future.
Bring Him the part of yourself you keep refusing to place on the altar.
Not because surrender purchases His grace.
But because grace has finally shown you that Jesus is worth trusting with everything.
And if this exposed something you have been holding too tightly, do not hide behind a polished response.
Let somebody pray with you.
Let somebody know they are not the only Christian who has cried while trying to keep believing.
But before you leave, remember Hannah.
Remember the woman whose lips moved while nobody heard her voice.
Remember the mother who asked.
Remember the mother who received.
And remember the mother who opened her hands.
Then look toward Christ.
Because Hannah gave back the son she had prayed to receive...
but at the heart of the Gospel stands the Father who gave the Son we never could have deserved.
And Jesus willingly gave Himself for sinners.
So when your hands are empty, trust Him.
When your hands are full, worship Him.
When your heart is breaking, pour it out before Him.
When sin has stained your story, repent and run to Him.
When grace finds you, do not make an idol of the blessing.
Open your hands.
Christ is better.
And perhaps the prayer you need tonight is no longer merely, “Lord, give me what I desperately want.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord Jesus, whether You give, withhold, restore, redirect, or ask me to release what I love, keep my heart Yours.”
Because sometimes the greatest evidence that grace has changed us is not that God finally placed something in our hands...
but that Jesus became precious enough for us to open them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE NEVER SAYS MARY MAGDALENE WAS A PROSTITUTE
paragraphs:
THE BIBLE NEVER SAYS MARY MAGDALENE WAS A PROSTITUTE
For centuries, millions have remembered her for a sexual past the Bible never gives her. But when you remove the legend and actually read the Gospel, something far more powerful appears: a woman Jesus delivered, a disciple who stayed near the cross, a mourner who refused to leave the tomb—and one of the first people entrusted with the news that changed human history.
There is something unsettling about discovering that a story you have heard your entire life is not actually written in the Bible.
Mary Magdalene.
Say her name and many people immediately imagine the same woman.
A prostitute.
A sexually immoral woman.
A notorious sinner who somehow wandered into the presence of Jesus, collapsed in repentance, and eventually became one of His followers.
Paintings have portrayed her that way.
Films have portrayed her that way.
Sermons have sometimes portrayed her that way.
Popular Christian imagination has repeated the picture so often that many believers assume there must be a verse somewhere that says it.
There isn't.
Read Matthew.
Read Mark.
Read Luke.
Read John.
Search every canonical Gospel passage in which Mary Magdalene appears.
You will discover something remarkable.
The Bible never calls Mary Magdalene a prostitute.
Not once.
And perhaps the most disturbing part of her story is not simply that history attached a label to Mary that Scripture never explicitly gave her.
It is how easily human beings can remember someone's supposed scandal longer than we remember what Jesus actually did in their life.
Maybe that is why this story matters far beyond Mary Magdalene.
Because somebody has probably done that to you.
Maybe they still remember the version of you that existed before Jesus began changing you.
The addict.
The adulterer.
The alcoholic.
The angry one.
The divorced one.
The prisoner.
The failure.
The hypocrite.
The woman who made that mistake.
The man who destroyed that relationship.
The Christian who fell.
The person everybody whispered about.
Sometimes people can remember the worst chapter of your life so clearly that they forget God kept writing after it.
But Jesus does not read your life the way gossip does.
And Mary Magdalene's story forces us to confront a breathtaking truth:
Human beings are often obsessed with labels.
Jesus is interested in resurrection.
Luke gives us one of the clearest biblical introductions to Mary.

After describing Jesus traveling through towns and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, Luke tells us that the Twelve accompanied Him, along with women who had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses.
Then comes her name.
“Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.”
Luke 8:2.
The Greek is striking:
“Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει.”
Maria hē kaloumenē Magdalēnē...
Mary, the one called Magdalene.
And what does Luke tell us about her past?
Seven demons had gone out from her.
That is what Scripture says.
It does not say seven lovers.
It does not say seven sexual sins.
It does not say prostitution.
It says demons.
We should be extremely careful not to make Scripture say what Scripture does not say.

In the biblical world, demonic affliction is not presented as another word for prostitution. The Gospels describe demonic oppression in connection with terrible suffering and bondage, but they do not give us permission to transform Mary's deliverance from seven demons into a sexual biography.
Whatever the complete nature of her suffering was, the text does not tell us.
So we should have the humility to stop where Scripture stops.
But Scripture tells us something else.
Jesus set her free.
Think about that.
Before Mary ever stood outside an empty tomb, she had already experienced another kind of liberation.
Before she announced that Christ was alive, Christ had changed her life.
Before she became associated with the greatest announcement in history, she knew what it was to need deliverance.
Something had held her.
Jesus was stronger.
Something had tormented her.
Jesus was stronger.
Something had occupied territory in her life.
Jesus was stronger.
And maybe somebody reading this understands that sentence more personally than anyone around you realizes.
You know what it feels like to smile while something inside you is collapsing.
You know what it means to carry a battle nobody else can see.
You know what it feels like to wonder whether freedom is possible anymore.
Mary's story whispers across two thousand years:
Jesus is stronger.
But here is where the biblical picture becomes even more beautiful.
Mary was not merely delivered from something.
She began following Someone.
Luke continues by naming Joanna, Susanna, “and many others,” explaining that these women helped provide for Jesus and His companions from their resources.
Mary Magdalene therefore appears not as a disposable background character but among women participating materially in Jesus' ministry.
She received grace.
Then her life became involved in the mission of the One who had given her grace.
That is discipleship.
Grace does not merely pull you out of the grave.
Grace teaches you whom to follow after you get out.
And this is where the prostitute tradition needs careful handling.

Immediately before Luke introduces Mary Magdalene in Luke 8, Luke 7 describes an unnamed woman known in the city as a sinner who approaches Jesus while He is eating in a Pharisee's house. She weeps at His feet, wets them with her tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them.
It is one of the most beautiful scenes of repentance, forgiveness and love in the Gospels.
But Luke does not name that woman Mary Magdalene.
Then, shortly afterward, Luke introduces “Mary, called Magdalene.”

Centuries later, especially in Western Christian tradition, different Gospel women became conflated. A highly influential homily by Gregory the Great in A.D. 591 treated the unnamed sinful woman, Mary associated with Bethany, and Mary Magdalene as the same figure.
The identification became enormously influential.
But influence is not inspiration.
Tradition can help us understand Scripture.
Tradition must never be allowed to quietly rewrite Scripture.
And there is another detail we must not miss.
Even Luke's unnamed “sinful woman” is not explicitly called a prostitute in the Gospel text.
She is called a sinner.
We should therefore resist the temptation to invent sexual details for her too.
There is a strange human instinct hiding underneath all of this.
We often sexualize a woman's shame before the text itself does.
We want the scandal.
Jesus keeps directing us toward grace.
We want the dirt.
Jesus keeps showing us what forgiveness does to a human heart.
We want to know exactly what somebody did.
Jesus asks whether we understand how much they have been forgiven.
That should make every Christian examine the way we speak about people.
Because perhaps you have never falsely called Mary Magdalene a prostitute.
But maybe you have frozen someone else inside a chapter Jesus has already forgiven.
Maybe God knows them as redeemed while you still know them by their rumor.
Maybe heaven is celebrating their repentance while your conversation is still recycling their failure.
Maybe Jesus has already rolled away the stone, and you are still introducing them by the grave.
That is not a small issue.
The Gospel changes how we see people.
Because nobody who belongs to Christ should forever be reduced to the worst thing they have done.
And Mary Magdalene's biblical story keeps moving.
Toward Jerusalem.
Toward darkness.
Toward a hill.
Toward a cross.
Imagine the scene.
The Teacher she followed is bleeding.
The One who delivered her is being mocked.
The hands through which healing came are pierced.
The voice that spoke freedom is growing weak beneath crucifixion.
The One who gave broken people dignity is stripped and humiliated before a crowd.
And Mary is there.
The Gospels place Mary Magdalene among the women connected with the crucifixion and burial scenes.
Then Sabbath passes.
Morning approaches.
And John takes us into one of the most emotionally devastating scenes in Scripture.
Mary goes to the tomb.
The stone has been moved.
She runs.
Peter and the other disciple come.
They eventually leave.
Mary stays.
That detail can break your heart if you have ever stood beside a grave.
John 20:11 says Mary remained outside the tomb weeping.
Sometimes faith does not look triumphant.
Sometimes faith looks like somebody crying outside a tomb because they do not understand what God is doing.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
You followed Jesus.
You prayed.
You believed.
And somehow you still ended up standing in front of something that looks dead.
A marriage.
A dream.
A ministry.
A friendship.
A child who walked away.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
A version of your life you thought God would preserve.
You are not necessarily faithless because you are crying.
Mary was crying within footsteps of the greatest miracle in human history.
Read that again.
She was weeping while resurrection was closer than she realized.
She thought the story had ended.
God had already changed the ending.
Then she turns and sees Jesus.
But she does not recognize Him.
She assumes He is the gardener.
Jesus asks why she is weeping and whom she is seeking.
Mary thinks perhaps this man has moved the body.
Then everything changes with one word.
Her name.
“Μαριάμ.”
Mary.
No theological lecture.
No dramatic introduction.
Her name.
And suddenly the supposed gardener is her risen Lord.
Mary responds:
“Ῥαββουνί.”
Rabbouni.
John himself explains the term as meaning “Teacher.”
Can you imagine her voice?
The shock.
The recognition.
The grief colliding with impossible joy.
The Person she watched die is standing in front of her.
Alive.
This is Christianity.
Not merely advice for becoming nicer people.
Not merely religious inspiration.
Not merely a moral philosophy.
At the center of the Christian proclamation stands Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Death did not keep Him.
The tomb did not defeat Him.
And the risen Jesus gives Mary a mission.
“Go to my brothers...”
Go.
Tell them.
Mary Magdalene goes to the disciples carrying a sentence that still echoes through history:
“I have seen the Lord.”
In Greek:
“Ἑώρακα τὸν κύριον.”
Heōraka ton kyrion.
“I have seen the Lord.”
Consider the transformation.
The woman introduced in Luke as someone from whom seven demons had gone out is now standing in John as a witness announcing the risen Christ.
Whatever darkness once marked her suffering does not receive the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why the theme of Mary Magdalene should never merely be, “She wasn't a prostitute.”
That correction matters.
But there is something infinitely greater here.
Mary Magdalene is not important because we can prove she was respectable.
She is important because Jesus Christ is merciful.
Christianity is not about proving that redeemed people were secretly good all along.
We were sinners in need of grace.
Every one of us.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The scandal of the Gospel is not that some people need redemption more than others.
The scandal is that the holy Son of God came for sinners at all.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose to make sinners new.
So do not misunderstand this article.
Correcting the historical portrayal of Mary Magdalene does not mean minimizing sexual sin, demonic bondage, repentance or humanity's need for salvation.
It means refusing to invent sins Scripture does not attribute to someone.
Truth matters precisely because Jesus matters.
And grace becomes even more beautiful when we do not have to exaggerate somebody's darkness to make Christ's light impressive.
Jesus does not need a fabricated scandal to be a magnificent Savior.
The cross is enough.
The empty tomb is enough.
Grace is enough.
Maybe Mary Magdalene's story is confronting another wound in you right now.
Perhaps people remember something about you that is true.
Not a misunderstanding.
Not a rumor.
Something you really did.
Then hear this carefully.
The Gospel is still for you.
Your defense before God is not, “People misunderstood me.”
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Maybe the accusation against you is true.
Grace can still be greater.
Peter really denied Jesus.
Paul really persecuted Christians.
The thief really was guilty.
Human sin does not become imaginary when grace arrives.
Grace is astonishing because Christ saves real sinners.
There is a difference between denying our sin and refusing to let forgiven sin become our permanent identity.
Repentance says, “I sinned.”
Grace says, “Jesus paid.”
Faith says, “I belong to Him now.”
Transformation says, “By His grace, I will not return willingly to the chains from which He freed me.”
And the resurrection says:
Your grave does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Jesus does.
Not your ex.
Not your critics.
Not the person who remembers your worst moment.
Not the voice inside your head replaying everything you wish you could undo.
Jesus Christ has the final word over everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
So perhaps we owe Mary Magdalene something very simple.
We should remember her the way Scripture presents her.
Delivered.
Following.
Giving.
Present.
Grieving.
Seeking.
Seeing.
Sent.
Not because she became the hero of Christianity.
She didn't.
Jesus is the Hero.
That is precisely the beauty of her story.
Mary points beyond Mary.
Toward Christ.
The Christ who delivers.
The Christ who receives sinners.
The Christ who goes to the cross.
The Christ who rises.
The Christ who calls people by name.
The Christ who turns mourners into witnesses.
The Christ who takes lives that look finished and writes another sentence.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Whose old identity are you still holding against them?
Who have you reduced to their failure?
And perhaps even harder:
What old identity are you still holding against yourself?
If you have repented and entrusted yourself to Christ, stop building your home inside a grave Jesus called you out of.
You are not glorifying God by pretending sin does not matter.
But neither do you glorify God by acting as though Christ's blood cannot cleanse what you have truly brought to Him.
Maybe somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
Church face on Sunday.
Private chains on Monday.
Smiling in photographs.
Dying quietly.
You do not need a better disguise.
You need Jesus.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Return to Christ.
There is mercy at the cross for sinners who stop running.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “no more hiding.”
If your spirit is exhausted and you need other believers to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ has been rebuilding a life you once thought was beyond repair, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Somebody scrolling silently may need to discover that Jesus is still transforming real people.
Not merely because an article needs reach.
Someone in your family may still believe their past disqualifies them from approaching Jesus.
Someone who would never walk into a church may read something you shared at two in the morning and encounter the Gospel when they least expected it.
Come back when accusation gets loud, or when you are tempted to define another believer by something Christ has forgiven.

Supporting Gospel-centered work is not a substitute for giving faithfully, serving your local church, caring for the poor, or obeying Christ in everyday life. But supporting and sharing faithful Christian teaching can be one practical way to help truth reach another person.
Follow Jesus.
The goal is not to build an audience around Mary Magdalene.
The goal is not even to build an audience around Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people toward the crucified and risen Christ.
Mary walked toward a tomb believing she was going to mourn a dead Jesus.
She walked away announcing a living Lord.
And perhaps that is why her real story is infinitely better than the legend attached to her.
People gave her a scandal Scripture never gave her.
Jesus gave her something greater than any label.
A testimony.
“I have seen the Lord.”

And maybe one day, when every false label has fallen away, when every forgiven sin has lost its accusing voice, and when every redeemed sinner stands only because of the mercy of Jesus Christ, we will finally understand:
The most important thing about your story was never what people called you.
It was who called your name.
Some people will remember your grave long after Jesus has called you out of it. Don't crawl back inside just to make their version of your story comfortable.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN GOD CALLS IDOLATRY ADULTERY
paragraphs: WHEN GOD CALLS IDOLATRY ADULTERY
The sin we learned to call “distraction” may be far more intimate than we ever wanted to admit—and the God whose heart we betrayed is still calling us home.
There are sins we confess quickly.
And then there are sins we rename.
We call greed “ambition.”
We call compromise “being realistic.”
We call obsession “passion.”
We call spiritual coldness “being busy.”
We call prayerlessness “a difficult season.”
And sometimes we call idolatry…
a distraction.
But God uses a much more disturbing word.
Adultery.
That word changes the temperature of the room.
Because distraction sounds accidental.
Adultery sounds relational.
Distraction says, “Something got my attention.”
Adultery says, “Someone who deserved my faithfulness was betrayed.”
And perhaps that is why Scripture’s language about idolatry can feel almost unbearable when we finally stop rushing past it.
God does not describe His people merely as people who violated a religious regulation.
He describes them as people who broke covenant.
People who were loved.
People who belonged to Him.
People who knew His goodness…
and then gave their hearts to another.
Listen to the ache behind Jeremiah 3:20:
“Surely, as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD.”
That is not the vocabulary of a distant deity irritated because somebody broke a technical rule.
That is covenant language.
Betrayal language.
Heartbreak language.
And suddenly idolatry becomes terrifyingly personal.

The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly use the language of marital unfaithfulness to expose Israel’s spiritual betrayal. One important Hebrew verb is זָנָה (zanah), commonly carrying the sense of committing fornication, playing the harlot, or acting unfaithfully. The prophets use this shocking imagery because Israel’s idolatry was not merely an intellectual mistake about theology.
It was covenant treachery.
God had redeemed them.
God had carried them.
God had provided for them.
God had revealed Himself to them.
And still they wandered.
Hosea turns this truth into one of the most painful living pictures in Scripture.

God commands the prophet into a marriage that will become a prophetic sign of Israel’s unfaithfulness. Hosea experiences something that allows the nation to see its spiritual condition in human terms.
The message becomes almost impossible to escape:
This is what your idolatry looks like from the side of the One who loves you.
And maybe that is where this becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because most of us do not have a carved Baal sitting in the living room.
We do not wake up and burn incense before Asherah.
We may never have bowed physically before a golden statue.
So we read the prophets and quietly exempt ourselves.
“Those people were idolaters.”
But idols learned how to survive without statues.
An idol can fit inside your pocket.
An idol can appear on your bank statement.
An idol can sleep beside you.
An idol can be your reputation.
Your body.
Your career.
Your children.
Your relationship.
Your politics.
Your comfort.
Your ministry.
Your audience.
Your wounded pride.
Your dream of finally becoming important.
Even something good can become spiritually destructive when it occupies the place that belongs to God alone.
That is why the first commandment reaches far deeper than ancient pagan religion:
“Thou shalt have no other gods before me.”
Exodus 20:3.
The Hebrew expression translated “before me” contains the phrase עַל־פָּנָי (ʿal-panai), literally carrying the sense of “before My face” or “in My presence.”
Think about that.
There is nowhere to hide another god from God.
Every rival lives before His face.
Every secret allegiance.
Every dependency.
Every affection we refuse to surrender.
Every thing we believe we cannot live without.
And here is the question that may expose more than we expected:
What devastates you when you lose it?
Not merely disappoints you.
Devastates you.
What determines whether you believe your life still has meaning?
Whose approval can control your entire day?
What do you repeatedly disobey God to keep?
What do you run toward when your soul hurts?
What occupies your imagination when nobody is demanding your attention?
What are you terrified God might ask you to surrender?
There may be an altar hiding inside those answers.
And sometimes the idol is not something obviously wicked.
Sometimes it is the thing you begged God to give you.
That relationship.
That opportunity.
That business.
That ministry.
That success.
That answered prayer.
We can receive a gift from God…
and slowly begin worshiping the gift instead of the Giver.
That is how subtle idolatry can become.
You can sing worship songs while worshiping human approval.
You can carry a Bible while worshiping money.
You can preach Jesus while worshiping influence.
You can build a ministry while worshiping your ministry.
You can pray for your family while making your family the ultimate source of your identity.
You can publicly say, “Jesus is Lord,” while privately living as though losing one created thing would make life no longer worth living.
Then James walks into the New Testament and refuses to soften the language.
“Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God?”
James 4:4.
The Greek text begins with one devastating word:
μοιχαλίδες — moichalides.
“Adulteresses.”

James is drawing upon the covenant imagery familiar from the prophets. His point is not that every friendship with an unbeliever or every enjoyment of created things is sinful. Scripture itself would contradict such an interpretation.
The issue is allegiance.
James is confronting a heart that wants intimacy with God while embracing a world-order opposed to God.
We want Christ…
and the throne.
Jesus…
and our idols.
Forgiveness…
without surrender.
Heaven…
without holiness.
Grace…
without repentance.
A Savior…
without a Lord.
But Jesus does not negotiate shared ownership of the human heart.
“No man can serve two masters.”
Matthew 6:24.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say serving two masters will be difficult.
He says you cannot do it.
Eventually one will command the allegiance the other was supposed to receive.
And this is where idolatry becomes adultery.
God is not merely asking, “Did you break My rule?”
He is exposing the deeper question:
“Has something else taken the love, trust, obedience, dependence, and devotion that belong to Me?”
That question hurts.
Especially when you know the answer.
Maybe your idol has a name.
Maybe you have been checking their profile again.
Maybe you know the relationship keeps pulling you away from Christ, but loneliness frightens you more than disobedience does.
Maybe your idol has a number attached to it.
Your salary.
Your follower count.
Your bank balance.
Your weight.
Your sales.
Your likes.
Your views.
And when the number goes down, your peace disappears with it.
Maybe your idol is success.
You told yourself you wanted to accomplish great things for God.
But somewhere along the way, “for God” became the religious language covering your desperate need to prove that you mattered.
Maybe your idol is control.
You pray, but only feel peaceful when God does what you planned.
You say you trust Him while quietly demanding that He explain Himself.
Maybe your idol is pain.
That sounds strange until you realize that even an old wound can become an identity.
You have carried what happened to you for so long that you no longer know who you would be without the anger.
And Jesus is standing at the locked room in your heart saying,
“Give Me this too.”
Maybe your idol is yourself.
Your preferences.
Your desires.
Your truth.
Your plans.
Your image.
Your comfort.
Your right to decide what obedience should cost.
That may be the oldest idol of all.
The serpent’s temptation in Eden was not merely about fruit.
It was the seduction of autonomy.
“Ye shall be as gods.”
Genesis 3:5.
Humanity reached for the throne.
And we have been reaching ever since.
But here is where this story takes the turn the Gospel always takes.
Because if all Scripture told us was that we had committed spiritual adultery, we would be exposed without hope.
Guilty.
Unfaithful.
Caught.
Without an excuse.
But the Bible does not end with the faithlessness of the bride.
It reveals the faithfulness of the Bridegroom.
Jesus Christ came for people whose hearts had wandered.
He came for idolaters.
He came for adulterers.
He came for the greedy.
The proud.
The religious hypocrite.
The sexually broken.
The self-righteous.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The person who promised God, “Never again,” and somehow ended up there again.
He did not come because we had remained faithful enough to deserve Him.
He came because He is faithful.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely offer motivational advice to spiritually distracted people.
He bore sin.
Our real guilt.
Our rebellion.
Our idolatry.
Our treachery.
Isaiah had already prophesied:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Isaiah 53:6.
There it is.
We wandered.
He was wounded.
We rebelled.
He bore judgment.
We chased other gods.
The Son of God stretched His hands upon a cross.
That is grace.
Not God pretending adultery does not matter.
Not God lowering holiness until sin becomes harmless.
Grace is infinitely more costly than that.
Grace is God dealing with sin so seriously that redemption required the blood of Christ.
The Greek New Testament uses the word χάρις — charis — for grace.
Grace is not permission to keep our idols.
Grace is the undeserved favor of God that meets sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
And when grace truly grips a human heart, repentance follows.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — speaks of repentance, a changed mind that expresses itself in a changed direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible because you were exposed.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns toward God.
It stops defending the idol.
Stops renaming it.
Stops negotiating with it.
Stops asking how close to the edge we can live while still calling ourselves Christian.
Repentance brings the hidden thing into the light and says,
“Jesus, this has occupied a place that belongs to You.”
Maybe you need to say that right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you finish scrolling.
Now.
“Jesus, I have loved something more than You.”
“Jesus, I have trusted something more than You.”
“Jesus, I have feared losing something more than I feared grieving You.”
“Jesus, I have called it harmless because I did not want to surrender it.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And hear this carefully:
The answer to idolatry is not merely trying harder to stop loving idols.
The deepest answer is seeing Christ as infinitely more worthy.
You do not simply need an emptier altar.
You need a greater Treasure.
Jesus.
The One who loved sinners while never approving sin.
The One who touched lepers.
Welcomed outcasts.
Confronted hypocrites.
Forgave repentant sinners.
Carried the cross.
Died beneath judgment.
Rose from the grave.
And now calls people who once belonged to darkness into His marvelous light.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of humans successfully climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming to rescue sinners who could never climb high enough.
This is why Romans 5:8 still destroys our excuses and our despair at the same time:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were sinners.
Not after we cleaned the house.
Not after we smashed every idol.
Not after we became impressive Christians.
Christ died for sinners.
But the Christ who receives you in grace does not leave you chained to the idols that were destroying you.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
The Gospel says your sin mattered so much that Christ died—and His mercy is so great that sinners who turn to Him can be forgiven, reconciled, cleansed, and made new.
That is the movement from scandal to grace.
Your scandal may be real.
Your secret may be ugly.
Your history may embarrass you.
Your spiritual adultery may have lasted years.
But your sin does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Your darkest chapter does not get final editorial control over the story Christ redeems.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old pages never existed.
But by redeeming people who could never rewrite themselves.
So tear down the altar.
Not because destroying an idol earns salvation.
Jesus alone saves.
Tear it down because the One who saved you deserves the throne.
Delete what repeatedly drags you into sin.
End the compromise you keep asking God to bless.
Confess what secrecy has protected.
Seek godly accountability.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship with believers.
Return to obedience.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the mud.
Run to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Notice who is faithful.
He is.
That is astonishing when you remember where we started.
We were talking about spiritual adultery.
Human unfaithfulness.
Broken covenant loyalty.
Wandering hearts.
Yet Scripture points us toward the faithfulness of God.
This is why conviction is not the same thing as condemnation for the person who is in Christ.
Conviction says, “Bring this into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Hide from God.”
Conviction exposes the idol so it can be forsaken.
Despair tells you there is no point returning.
But the Gospel says:
Come home.
Not because rebellion was small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
Maybe someone reading this has been hiding for years.
You still attend church.
Still smile.
Still post Bible verses.
Still say, “God is good.”
But there is a locked room in your soul.
You know what is inside.
And perhaps nobody else knows.
Jesus does.
And somehow He brought you all the way to this sentence.
Do not waste the conviction.
Put the phone down for a moment.
Forget who might see you.
Forget how religious you appear.
Forget your reputation.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not as a magic phrase.
Not because a Facebook comment saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing our struggle into the light is the first crack in a wall we have spent years constructing.
If you are still fighting to surrender something that keeps trying to reclaim your heart, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Somebody quietly reading may desperately need evidence that chains really can break.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page either.
Not for an algorithm.
For a soul.
One person may read because you shared.
One wandering believer may repent.
One exhausted Christian may come home.
One person who thought Jesus wanted nothing more to do with them may finally understand grace.
Because idols rarely knock once.
There may come another night when the old thing calls your name.
Come back and remember:
You already know where that altar leads.
And you know who is better.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and generous support can be one practical way believers choose to help Gospel-centered work reach more people.
Leave with Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy would be reading an article about idolatry…
feeling convicted…
sharing it…
commenting on it…
even supporting the ministry that published it…
while still refusing to surrender the idol Jesus exposed.
He does not ultimately want your engagement.
He wants you.
Your heart.
Your allegiance.
Your worship.
Your trust.
And perhaps tonight the question is no longer whether you have an idol.
Perhaps you already know.
The question is whether you will keep protecting what has been stealing from the God who gave Himself to save you.
The idol promises life and eventually demands everything.
Jesus asks for everything and gives us something no idol ever could:
Himself.
So come home.
Bring the shame.
Bring the compromise.
Bring the divided heart.
Bring the thing you cannot seem to release.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the secret.
Bring the scandal.
And lay it before the crucified and risen Christ.
Because when God calls idolatry adultery, He is showing us how serious our betrayal really is.
But when Jesus stretches out scarred hands toward repentant sinners, He shows us something even greater:
how far grace was willing to go to bring the unfaithful home.
You may have given your heart to an idol—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still reaching for the heart that wandered.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EZEKIEL 23 CONTAINS SOME OF THE MOST GRAPHIC SEXUAL METAPHORS IN THE BIBLE—WHY?
paragraphs: EZEKIEL 23 CONTAINS SOME OF THE MOST GRAPHIC SEXUAL METAPHORS IN THE BIBLE—WHY?
The Chapter Most People Want to Skip May Be the Chapter That Exposes What We Have Been Hiding From God
There are passages in the Bible people underline.
There are passages they frame.
There are passages they quote when life is falling apart.
And then there is Ezekiel 23.
A chapter so disturbing that many Christians read a few verses, feel uncomfortable, close the Bible, and quietly move somewhere safer.
But maybe that discomfort is part of the point.
Because Ezekiel 23 was never written to entertain sexual curiosity.
It was written to destroy spiritual denial.
And if you can stay with this chapter long enough—without sanitizing it, sensationalizing it, or pretending its words are not there—you may discover something terrifying about sin...
and something breathtaking about the God who refuses to leave His people trapped inside it.
Ezekiel does not whisper.
He does not soften the imagery.
He gives us two symbolic sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, and then immediately tells us who they represent:
Samaria and Jerusalem.
This is crucial.
The chapter is not primarily a story about two literal sexually promiscuous women.
God identifies the women with covenant communities.
“Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 23:4).
In Hebrew, the verse reads in part:
“שֹׁמְרוֹן אָהֳלָה וִירוּשָׁלִַם אָהֳלִיבָה”
Shomron Oholah, vi-Yerushalayim Oholivah.
Samaria is Oholah.
Jerusalem is Oholibah.

Even their names carry theological weight. Oholah is commonly understood in connection with “her tent,” while Oholibah carries the sense “my tent is in her.” The imagery points toward worship and sanctuary: Samaria had established its own rival religious system, while Jerusalem possessed the LORD’s sanctuary.
And suddenly the scandal becomes deeper.
This is not merely about sexual behavior.
It is about worship.
It is about covenant betrayal.
It is about people who belonged to God reaching toward idols, nations, political powers, military strength, and foreign alliances as though those things could give them what only God could give.
Ezekiel takes invisible apostasy...
and gives it a body.
That is why the imagery becomes so uncomfortable.
Because idolatry rarely feels as disgusting to us as it should.
We hear the word “idol” and imagine a little statue sitting on an ancient shelf.
God saw something far more intimate.
Betrayal.
His people had been rescued, claimed, loved, sustained, warned, and called to belong to Him—and yet their hearts repeatedly ran toward other gods and other powers.
So Ezekiel refuses to let apostasy remain an abstract theological word.
He makes betrayal feel like betrayal.
He makes unfaithfulness look like unfaithfulness.
He makes spiritual adultery impossible to perfume.
And then comes the verse almost everyone remembers once they encounter this chapter.
Ezekiel 23:20.
The Hebrew itself is deliberately graphic:
“אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׂר־חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם וְזִרְמַת סוּסִים זִרְמָתָם”

The wording compares the sexual anatomy of the desired lovers to donkeys and their emission to stallions. That is not an exaggeration invented by a provocative modern translation. The underlying Hebrew itself contains the animal comparison and the explicit reference.
Why would Scripture contain something like that?
Because God is not trying to arouse the reader.
He is exposing degradation.
The language is grotesque because the idolatry being portrayed is grotesque.
What Jerusalem regarded with fascination, Ezekiel portrays in humiliating, animalistic terms.
What looked impressive from a distance was spiritually degrading up close.
What appeared powerful...
was enslaving them.
And there is something painfully modern about that.
Sin still advertises itself better than it delivers.
It photographs beautifully.
It whispers, “You deserve this.”
It says, “Nobody needs to know.”
It says, “Just once.”
It says, “You can stop whenever you want.”
It says, “God is withholding something from you.”
And somehow what once disgusted you can eventually become what you defend.
What you once resisted can become what you secretly revisit.
What you once confessed with tears can become something you rename so you no longer have to call it sin.
That is why Ezekiel 23 can feel so invasive.
The chapter does not merely ask, “What have you done?”
It asks something more frightening:
What has your heart learned to desire instead of God?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still go to church.
Maybe you know when to raise your hands.
Maybe your Bible app still sends you a verse every morning.
Maybe people call you strong in the faith.
And maybe there is still a locked room inside your heart where Jesus is welcome to stand outside...
but not enter.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Pornography you keep promising to quit.
Bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
Money that stopped being a tool and became your security.
Attention you need so badly that silence feels like death.
A secret conversation.
A hidden addiction.
A hunger for admiration.
A career you would compromise almost anything to protect.
A political identity that stirs more passion in you than the kingdom of Christ.
A religious image you carefully maintain because admitting weakness feels more frightening than remaining enslaved.
An idol does not need a carved face.
Sometimes an idol is simply anything we ask to give us what we should ultimately seek in God.
Security.
Identity.
Worth.
Deliverance.
Meaning.
Power.
Love.
And this is where Ezekiel 23 becomes almost unbearable.
Because Jerusalem had evidence.
She had watched Samaria fall.
She knew where the road led.
And she followed it anyway.
That is one of the darkest mysteries of sin.
Sometimes we know.
We know the relationship is destroying us.
We know the habit is hollowing us out.
We know the secret is poisoning our prayer life.
We know that every time we return to it, something inside us becomes quieter.
We have watched other people wreck themselves on the same rocks.
And still...
we swim toward them.
Ezekiel describes Oholibah remembering Egypt and returning in desire to the patterns associated with her earlier unfaithfulness.
Memory became temptation.
The past became romanticized.
Bondage started looking beautiful again.
Have you ever noticed how sin edits your memories?
It shows you the pleasure...
and deletes the aftermath.
It reminds you of the intoxication...
and hides the shame.
It shows you Egypt’s food...
and somehow makes you forget Egypt’s chains.

That is why one of the most haunting lines in this chapter comes in Ezekiel 23:27, where God declares that He will put an end to this corruption so that His people will no longer look longingly toward Egypt or remember it in the same way.
The Hebrew contains the words:
“וְהִשְׁבַּתִּי זִמָּתֵךְ מִמֵּךְ”
Vehishbatti zimmatekh mimekh...
“I will cause your depravity/lewdness to cease from you...”
Do not rush past that.
God is not indifferent to what destroys His people.
His holiness is not passive.

His judgment in Ezekiel 23 is severe, and we should not dilute that severity. The chapter ends not with God shrugging at idolatry, but with accountability: they will bear the consequences of their idolatry and “know that I am the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 23:49).
Grace never means God discovers that sin was harmless after all.
The Bible’s grace is infinitely more costly than that.
Sin is so serious that forgiveness does not come through God pretending evil does not matter.
And this is where we must read Ezekiel carefully.

Ezekiel 23 itself is overwhelmingly a chapter of accusation and judgment. We should not force the cross into every metaphor as though Ezekiel’s original audience could see every detail we see after Christ.
But Ezekiel’s book does not end in chapter 23.
Keep reading.
The God who exposes corruption will later speak of cleansing.
“I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25).
The God confronting hardened hearts will promise:
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And then:
“I will put my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27).
That movement matters.
Exposure.
Judgment.
Cleansing.
A new heart.
A new spirit.
Restoration.
And when Christians reach the New Testament, the Gospel announces how staggering the cost of reconciliation truly is.
Jesus does not arrive telling sinners to clean themselves sufficiently so He can finally love them.
Christ comes for sinners.
He calls them to repent and believe.
He touches the unclean.
He receives the broken.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He forgives the repentant.
And ultimately...
He goes to the cross.
Paul writes:
Not when we finally became impressive.
Not when the browser history became clean enough.
Not when the addiction disappeared.
Not when the marriage was repaired.
Not when every theological question was answered.
Not when we became worthy.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
Jesus begins His public proclamation with the call to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
Repentance is not performing enough sadness to convince God you deserve another chance.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια—metanoia—a turning of mind and life toward God, a change of direction that bears fruit.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly where your chains have you.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ.”
And Christ does not merely offer better chains.
He offers Himself.
Maybe that is why this chapter bothers us so much.
Ezekiel 23 strips away the flattering names we give our idols.
It asks what happens when the thing you call “freedom” is actually mastering you.
When “I deserve to be happy” becomes permission to disobey God.
When “this is just how I am” becomes a fortress against repentance.
When “nobody is getting hurt” ignores what sin is doing to your soul.
When “God understands” quietly becomes “God will never confront me.”
He does understand.
Far more deeply than we do.
And precisely because He is holy and loving, He confronts what destroys.
Somebody reading this has been asking God for freedom while protecting the very thing from which you want freedom.
You pray about it.
Then reopen it.
You cry about it.
Then contact them again.
You delete it.
Then reinstall it.
You confess enough to reduce the guilt...
but not enough to kill the secrecy.
And perhaps your deepest fear is not that God knows.
Your deepest fear is that if you finally surrender, He will take away the thing you cannot imagine living without.
But what if the thing you cannot imagine living without...
is the thing keeping you from learning how to truly live?
There is a reason Jesus could say that whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for Christ and the Gospel will save it (Mark 8:35).
The Gospel does not offer cosmetic improvement.
Jesus did not die so we could decorate our prison cells with Bible verses.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
So stop negotiating with the idol.
Stop giving respectable names to what God has already exposed.
Stop waiting until you “feel spiritual enough” to come home.
Bring Him the ugly thing.
Bring Him the history.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the appetite for approval.
Bring Him the shame you are terrified somebody will discover.
Bring Him the version of you that you have spent years making sure nobody sees.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
The scandal of Christianity is not that God calls evil good.
He never does.
The scandal is that the Holy One makes a way for guilty people to be forgiven without calling their guilt innocence.
At the cross, grace is not cheap.
It is blood-bought.
Peter says Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Bring us to God.
That is the destination.
Not merely a better mood.
Not merely a cleaner reputation.
Not merely becoming religious.
God.
And maybe you have spent years thinking your story is too dirty for that.
Read Ezekiel 23 again.
Look at how ugly covenant betrayal is allowed to appear on the page.
Scripture does not need your life to be sanitized before it can tell the truth about you.
And then look at Jesus.
The woman publicly known as sinful could weep at His feet.
The tax collector could come down from the tree.
The thief dying beside Him could cry for mercy.
Peter could deny Him and later be restored.
Saul could persecute the church and become a servant of the Gospel.
The cross stands in the middle of human wreckage and announces that your sin is worse than your excuses admit...
and Christ’s mercy is greater than your shame wants you to believe.
That is the emotional violence of grace.
It destroys boasting and despair at the same time.
You cannot say, “I am good enough.”
The cross says you needed a Savior.
But you also cannot say, “I am too far gone.”
The cross says, “Look at the Savior.”
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing sin out of your history.
Not by calling darkness light.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking sinners who deserved judgment, washing them, forgiving them, reconciling them to God, and beginning the transforming work of making them new.
That is why your testimony does not have to be:
“Look how perfect I became.”
It can be:
“Look how merciful Christ has been.”
And if something in this article exposed a room inside you that you have kept locked for too long, do not perform spirituality right now.
Be honest.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
But sometimes bringing what has lived in darkness into honest confession is the first visible sign that you are finished pretending.
And if you see someone else comment that they are struggling, do not crush them.
Pray for them.
