Encourage them toward Christ.
Remind them that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is the collapse of the lie that we can save ourselves.
There may be a night when Egypt starts looking beautiful again.
There may be a night when the old addiction starts rewriting your memories.
There may be a night when the person God delivered you from suddenly seems irresistible again.
Come back and remember:
Chains can become nostalgic when you forget what captivity cost you.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because an algorithm can measure faithfulness. It cannot.

If you want to glorify God through Gospel-centered digital ministry, one practical way you can help is by supporting and sharing work that keeps pointing people back to Scripture and Jesus Christ. But it can materially support the continued creation and distribution of biblical content so that more people encounter the Gospel.
Not to prove you love Jesus.
Follow because discipleship requires more than occasional inspiration.
And comment because somebody reading beneath you may need to know they are not the only person fighting to come back to Christ.
Then pray.
Actually pray.
Turn toward Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek trustworthy pastoral help and Christian accountability where you need it.
Make restitution where repentance requires it.
Cut off access where temptation repeatedly enters.
And do not confuse reading an emotional article with surrendering your life to Jesus.
The article cannot save you.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A comment cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your tears cannot save you.
Your promises to “do better this time” cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And perhaps that is ultimately why Ezekiel 23 is still in our Bible.
Because before grace feels amazing, sometimes we need to remember what grace is rescuing us from.
The chapter is ugly because sin is ugly.
The judgment is terrifying because holiness is real.
And the Gospel is breathtaking because the God against whom we have sinned has made reconciliation possible through His Son.
So when the old Egypt calls your name again...
remember the chains.
When your idol promises life again...
remember what it took from you.
When shame whispers that you are too filthy to return...
look to Christ.
When pride whispers that you do not need to return...
look to the cross.
And when you finally bring the hidden thing into the light, you may discover that Jesus was never waiting for a prettier version of your confession.
He was calling you to come.
The thing you are most afraid to surrender may be standing between you and the freedom you keep asking Jesus to give you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: AGABUS TOOK PAUL’S BELT AND BOUND HIS OWN HANDS AND FEET WITH IT
paragraphs:
AGABUS TOOK PAUL’S BELT AND BOUND HIS OWN HANDS AND FEET WITH IT
The Warning Was Real. The Chains Were Coming. And Paul Still Walked Toward Jerusalem—Because Following Jesus Does Not Always Mean Escaping What Hurts.
Imagine watching a man take something that belongs to you...
then wrap it around his own wrists.
Around his ankles.
Tighter.
Until his hands and feet are bound.
The room goes quiet.
Nobody is laughing now.
Nobody is checking the time.
Nobody is wondering what is for dinner.
Because the prophet standing in front of you is wearing your future.
And then he speaks.
Not casually.
Not speculatively.
Not with the vague language of someone trying to impress a religious crowd.
He says:
“Τάδε λέγει τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ Ἅγιον...”
Táde légei tò Pneûma tò Hágion...
“Thus says the Holy Spirit...”
And suddenly you realize...
the belt in his hands is yours.
This happened.

Acts 21 tells us that Paul was staying in Caesarea when a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. This was not the first time Luke had introduced him. Years earlier, Agabus had foretold through the Spirit that a severe famine was coming, and Luke tells us that it occurred during the reign of Claudius.
Now Agabus appears again.
But this time there is no famine in his prophetic picture.
There is a belt.
There are bound hands.
There are bound feet.
And there is Paul.
The Greek of Acts 21:11 gives us the scene with startling simplicity:
“ἄρας τὴν ζώνην τοῦ Παύλου, δήσας ἑαυτοῦ τοὺς πόδας καὶ τὰς χεῖρας...”
He took Paul’s zōnēn—his belt or girdle—and having bound his own feet and hands, Agabus declared what the Holy Spirit was revealing.
The owner of that belt would be bound in Jerusalem and handed over to Gentile hands.
Picture Paul watching him.
The leather or cloth that had been wrapped around Paul's own body was now wrapped around the prophet.
His future had become visible.
His suffering had been acted out in front of him.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us want God to show us the future...
provided the future looks comfortable.
We pray, “Lord, show me Your will.”
But somewhere underneath that prayer may be another one:
“Lord, please make Your will painless.”
We ask God to open doors.
We rarely ask what faithfulness looks like when obedience leads through a door we would rather see remain closed.
We ask Him for protection.
For breakthrough.
For deliverance.
For restoration.
And Scripture gives us abundant reason to ask our Father for help.
But what happens when following Christ does not immediately remove the hardship?
What happens when the warning is not God's promise to prevent the fire...
but His preparation of His servant to walk through it?
That is what makes Agabus and Paul so uncomfortable for modern Christianity.
Agabus did not tell Paul that everything would become easy.
He did not announce that faithful Christians never suffer.
He did not say that sufficient faith would cancel the chains.
He told him the chains were coming.
And Paul did not run.
But we need to be careful here.
We should not turn this passage into reckless spirituality.

Paul was not chasing pain because pain was holy. Christianity does not teach us to manufacture suffering, ignore legitimate danger, reject wise counsel, or prove our devotion by making foolish decisions.
Something deeper was happening.

Before Agabus ever touched Paul's belt, Paul had already said that he was going to Jerusalem, compelled by the Spirit, while knowing that the Holy Spirit was testifying that imprisonment and afflictions awaited him.
Paul was not walking blindly into Jerusalem.
He knew suffering waited somewhere down that road.
Agabus made the warning terrifyingly visible.
And notice something important.
Agabus announced what would happen to Paul.
The people surrounding Paul responded by begging him not to go.
Those are not exactly the same thing.
The prophecy described the coming suffering.
The believers interpreted the warning as a reason Paul should avoid Jerusalem.
Their reaction was understandable.
They loved him.
Luke even includes himself among those pleading with Paul.
Imagine hearing people you love crying because of a decision you believe obedience requires.
Imagine watching their faces.
Imagine knowing that turning around could stop their tears.
Then hear Paul's answer.
“Τί ποιεῖτε κλαίοντες καὶ συνθρύπτοντές μου τὴν καρδίαν;”
Why are you weeping...
and breaking my heart?
Do not rush past that.
Paul had a heart that could break.
Sometimes we read the apostles as though holiness turned them into stone.
It didn't.
Paul was not emotionless.
Their tears hurt him.
Their pleading affected him.
This was not some invincible religious superhero marching toward suffering without feeling anything.
This was a man whose heart was being crushed by people who loved him.
And still he said, in substance:
I am ready.
Not only for chains.
Even for death.
For the name of the Lord Jesus.
That changes everything.
Because suddenly this story is not really about a belt.
It is about ownership.
Who owns Paul?
Rome?
The crowd?
Fear?
His friends?
His instinct for self-preservation?
Or Jesus Christ?
Paul had already answered that question with his life.
And maybe that is the question this ancient belt is laying across our lives now.
Who owns you?
It is easy to say “Jesus is Lord” when His lordship seems to agree with our plans.
It becomes much more revealing when obedience costs something.
When forgiveness costs your pride.
When repentance costs your secret sin.
When truth costs your popularity.
When purity costs the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
When integrity costs money.
When reconciliation requires humility.
When serving Christ means being misunderstood.
When saying yes to Jesus means saying no to something your flesh desperately wants.
That is when lordship stops being vocabulary.
It becomes surrender.
And some of us are asking Jesus to rescue us from the very surrender through which He intends to make us more like Himself.
We have quietly confused comfort with blessing.
Ease with favor.
Open doors with God's approval.
Pain with God's absence.
Yet look at Jesus.
The entire Christian faith stands beneath the shadow of a cross.
Christ did not save us by avoiding suffering.
He willingly went toward Jerusalem.
He knew betrayal was coming.
He knew rejection was coming.
He knew the cross was coming.
And in Gethsemane, Jesus did not pretend suffering was pleasant.
He prayed in agony.
Yet His surrender remained:
the Father's will.
That does not mean Paul's suffering was identical to Christ's saving work. It was not.
Jesus alone bore sin as the spotless Savior.
Jesus alone died as the sufficient sacrifice for sinners.
Paul could not redeem himself by suffering.
Neither can you.
Your pain does not purchase forgiveness.
Your tears cannot wash away your guilt.
Your religious sacrifice cannot make you righteous before God.
That is why this story must ultimately take us beyond Paul.
It must take us to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of brave human beings climbing toward God through suffering.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
The scandal of the Gospel is that guilty people can be forgiven.
Rebels can become children.
The sexually broken can be cleansed.
The addicted can find freedom.
The proud can bow.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The person who wasted years can still be redeemed.
The person whose past would make religious people whisper can be clothed in the righteousness of Christ.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the blood of Jesus does.
That is grace.
Not God pretending your rebellion was harmless.
God dealing with sin at the cross and offering mercy to those who turn to Christ.
And Paul knew something about scandalous grace.
Before people knew him as the apostle willing to be chained for Jesus...
they knew him as Saul.
The persecutor.
The enemy of the church.
The man associated with violence against believers.
He had approved of Stephen's death.
He had pursued Christians.
His reputation had preceded him.
Then Jesus met him.
Think about the breathtaking reversal.
The man who once helped put followers of Jesus in chains eventually became the man willing to wear chains for Jesus.
That is not self-improvement.
That is redemption.
That is what Christ does.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal looks different.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe people at church know the polished version of you.
They know the smile.
The Bible verse.
The Christian posts.
The “God bless you.”
But they do not know what happens when the room gets dark and the phone is in your hand.
They do not know the bitterness.
The pornography.
The affair.
The addiction.
The envy.
The secret messages.
The private compromise.
The anger you keep feeding.
The unforgiveness you have renamed “boundaries” because admitting hatred would hurt too much.
The pride hiding underneath religious language.
The prayerlessness.
The numbness.
The fact that you can sing about Jesus and still feel impossibly far from Him.
And perhaps your chains are invisible.
That does not make them less real.
Some chains are forged by other people.
Some are forged by circumstances.
And some are chains we keep fastening around ourselves.
Sin promises freedom and eventually starts tightening.
One compromise.
Then another.
Then another.
Until the thing you once chose begins feeling like something you cannot stop choosing.
That is why the Gospel does not merely say, “Try harder.”
It says there is a Savior.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
The answer to your deepest bondage is not pretending the chains are not there.
It is bringing the truth into the light and coming to Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One whose mercy is greater than the darkness you finally stopped defending.
Grace does not tell you to keep the chains.
Grace brings you to Jesus.
And Jesus does not merely offer you a cleaner reputation.
He calls you into a new life.
This is why Paul's response to Agabus is so powerful.
Paul had already been captured by something stronger than fear.
The love of Christ.
Once you understand what Jesus has rescued you from, surrender begins to look different.
You stop asking only:
“What will this cost me?”
And begin asking:
“After everything Christ has done for me, what belongs to Him?”
Your time belongs to Him.
Your body belongs to Him.
Your future belongs to Him.
Your money belongs to Him.
Your gifts belong to Him.
Your reputation belongs to Him.
Your platform belongs to Him.
Your comfortable plans belong to Him.
Not because giving those things purchases salvation.
Never.
We are not saved because we sacrifice enough.
We surrender because Christ has saved us by grace.
There is a universe of difference.
And eventually the believers surrounding Paul understood that they could not persuade him.
So the room that had been filled with pleading arrived at one of the hardest prayers human lips can speak:
“Τοῦ Κυρίου τὸ θέλημα γινέσθω.”
Let the will of the Lord be done.
That prayer sounds beautiful embroidered on a wall.
It sounds different when somebody you love may suffer.
It sounds different beside a hospital bed.
It sounds different after a funeral.
It sounds different when the answer you begged for does not come the way you hoped.
It sounds different when obedience costs you.
“The Lord's will be done.”
Those words are not fatalism.
They are surrender to a Lord who sees what we cannot see.
And what happened after Agabus bound himself?
Paul went to Jerusalem.
He was seized.
He was taken into Roman custody.
The road became dangerous exactly as the Holy Spirit had warned.
But Paul's chains did not silence the Gospel.
His captivity became part of the road on which he testified about Christ.
That is one of the stunning reversals running through Acts.
Men could bind the messenger.
They could not bind the message.
And perhaps somebody reading this feels bound right now.
Not metaphorically poetic.
Actually exhausted.
Actually ashamed.
Actually frightened.
You have prayed for God to remove something, and it is still there.
You have wondered whether hardship means God abandoned you.
Do not use Paul's story to assume every hardship is automatically God's specific assignment.
Scripture does not give us permission to call every painful circumstance divine guidance.
But it does give us something stronger:
suffering cannot automatically be interpreted as Christ's absence.
Sometimes faithfulness and hardship occupy the same road.
The cross proves that suffering is not, by itself, evidence that God has lost control.
And the resurrection proves that suffering does not get the final word.
That is where the Gospel catches us.
Not with the promise that Christians never cry.
Paul's friends cried.
Paul's heart broke.
Jesus Himself wept.
The promise is deeper.
Christ is Lord even in the tears.
And there is resurrection on the other side of the cross.
So maybe the question is not:
“How do I make sure nothing painful ever happens to me?”
Maybe tonight the question is:
“Jesus, will I still belong to You when obedience hurts?”
Because there may come a moment when your Christianity is reduced to that.
No applause.
No emotional worship music.
No crowd celebrating you.
No instant breakthrough.
Just you...
Christ...
and a decision.
Will you follow Him?
Not to earn His love.
Because at the cross, He has already shown the immeasurable depth of His love.
If you have been hiding from God, stop running.
If you have been protecting a secret sin, bring it into the light.
If you have reduced Christianity to inspirational content while refusing Christ's lordship over your private life, repent.
If you have fallen again, do not turn your failure into an excuse to remain on the ground.
Come back to Jesus.
Confess the truth.
Ask for mercy.
Seek biblical accountability where you need it.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray again.
Walk again.
Not because you are strong.
Because Christ is merciful.
Maybe you have spent years believing your worst chapter permanently disqualified you.
Remember Paul.
The persecutor became the preacher.
The man associated with imprisoning Christians became the prisoner proclaiming Christ.
His past was real.
Grace did not rewrite history by pretending his sin never happened.
Jesus rewrote Paul's future by refusing to let his sin have the final word.
And He is still saving sinners.
Still forgiving.
Still restoring.
Still transforming.
Still calling prodigals home.
Still breaking chains nobody else can see.
Still turning scandals into testimonies of grace.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already carried you through a season you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needs tonight.
Then send this article to one person.
Not fifty strangers.
One person whose name came into your mind while you were reading.
The Gospel cannot be purchased. God's grace is not for sale.

Supporting Gospel ministry can, however, be one practical way to use what God has entrusted to you so that Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources can continue reaching others. If you want to glorify God through your resources, prayerfully consider supporting faithful Gospel work—including this ministry—while also giving generously through your local church and wherever God leads you.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer quietly struggling.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Even invite the person who does not believe yet.
Because somewhere tonight there is another Saul who has no idea Jesus can rewrite his story.
Somewhere there is another exhausted believer staring at chains and thinking the chains mean the story is over.
They don't.
Agabus held Paul's belt.
Paul saw the chains coming.
The believers cried.
Paul's heart broke.
And still the Gospel kept moving.
Years later, we are still reading about the prisoner.
We are still preaching the Christ he refused to deny.
We are still discovering that Rome could restrain a man's wrists without restraining the Word of God.
So when the belt tightens...
when obedience costs...
when your heart breaks...
when following Jesus leads somewhere you would never have chosen for yourself...
remember who owns the belt.
Remember who owns your life.
And above everything else...

remember the Savior who willingly stretched out His own hands for sinners, entered death, shattered its claim, rose from the grave, and now offers forgiveness and eternal life to everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
The chains may become part of your chapter.
But they never get to become the Author.
Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “GIVE ME CHILDREN, OR I’LL DIE”: THE DESPERATE DECISION RACHEL THOUGHT WOULD HEAL HER HEART
paragraphs: “GIVE ME CHILDREN, OR I’LL DIE”: THE DESPERATE DECISION RACHEL THOUGHT WOULD HEAL HER HEART

Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob so she could have children through her servant—but Genesis 30 is not merely an ancient story about infertility, rivalry, and a complicated family. It is a mirror held painfully close to the human heart, exposing what can happen when a wounded soul becomes so desperate for what it wants that it tries to manufacture what only God can give.
There are sentences in the Bible that sound almost too raw to belong in Scripture.
No polished religious language.
No carefully composed prayer.
No attempt to make the speaker look spiritually mature.
Just pain.
Rachel looked at Jacob and said:
“Give me children, or I shall die.”
Genesis 30:1.
Imagine the room after those words.
Imagine Jacob’s face.
Imagine Rachel’s breathing.
Imagine the years of watching another woman receive what she desperately wanted.
And then imagine Bilhah standing somewhere inside this household while decisions were being made that would permanently change her life too.
This is not a neat Bible story.
It is jealousy.
Infertility.
Marriage.
Competition.
Power.
Sex.
Motherhood.
Desperation.
Human beings trying to survive desires so intense that those desires begin making decisions for them.
And perhaps that is exactly why Genesis does not hide it.
Because God is not frightened by the chapters of your life that would never make it into your testimony video.
He sees the envy you never admitted.
The prayer that became an obsession.
The blessing somebody else received that made you wonder whether God had forgotten your address.
The moment you smiled for someone while something inside you whispered, “Why them, Lord?”
And Genesis 30 takes us directly there.
Rachel had been deeply loved by Jacob. Genesis 29 tells us that Jacob loved Rachel and served years for her. But being loved by a man could not silence the ache of an empty womb.
Leah, meanwhile, had children.
Rachel did not.
And suddenly the woman who possessed something Leah desperately wanted—Jacob’s affection—became consumed by something Leah possessed.
Children.
That is one of the cruelest traps of comparison.
Comparison rarely reminds you of what you have.
It hypnotizes you with what you do not have.
You can be standing inside an answered prayer and still become miserable because somebody else received a different answer.
You can have a marriage and envy someone’s career.
Have the career and envy someone’s family.
Have children and envy someone’s freedom.
Have influence and envy someone’s peace.
Have money and envy someone’s marriage.
Have a ministry and envy someone else’s platform.
Comparison can make abundance feel like poverty.
Genesis says:
וַתְּקַנֵּא רָחֵל בַּאֲחֹתָהּ
Vatteqanne Rachel ba’achotah.
Rachel became jealous—or envious—of her sister.
Then the wound found a voice:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, ve’im-ayin, metah anokhi.
“Give me children, or else I die.”
That is not merely a request.
That is desperation talking.
Rachel had reached the dangerous place where one blessing had become emotionally equivalent to life itself.
“If I cannot have this, I cannot live.”
And many of us know that sentence.
We simply change the noun.
Give me this relationship.
Give me this healing.
Give me this baby.
Give me this promotion.
Give me this breakthrough.
Give me this ministry.
Give me this person back.
Give me this financial miracle.
Give me this answer.
Or I cannot be okay.
Sometimes the thing we desperately want is not sinful at all.
Children were not a sinful desire.
Marriage is not necessarily a sinful desire.
Healing is not sinful.
Provision is not sinful.
Success is not automatically sinful.
The danger begins when a gift becomes the functional god of our hearts.
When “Lord, I desire this” quietly becomes “Lord, I cannot trust You unless You give me this.”
Jacob’s response was sharp:
“Am I in the place of God?”
He understood something Rachel’s grief was struggling to accept.
Jacob could love Rachel.
Jacob could sleep beside Rachel.
Jacob could listen to Rachel.
But Jacob could not command conception.
There are places human beings cannot stand.
There are doors human beings cannot force open.
There are things no spouse, pastor, doctor, parent, friend, bank account, platform, or relationship can ultimately become for you.
Jacob was not God.
Neither is the person you are demanding save you.
Neither is the opportunity.
Neither is the relationship.
Neither is the thing you believe must happen before your soul can finally rest.
Then Rachel made her move.
Genesis 30:3 records:
הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה בֹּא אֵלֶיהָ וְתֵלֵד עַל־בִּרְכַּי וְאִבָּנֶה גַם־אָנֹכִי מִמֶּנָּה
Hinneh amati Bilhah, bo eleha, veteled al-birkai, ve’ibbaneh gam-anokhi mimmennah.
“Here is my servant Bilhah. Go in to her, that she may bear upon my knees, and I too may be built up through her.”
That last expression is striking.
וְאִבָּנֶה
ve’ibbaneh.
“I may be built up.”
The Hebrew comes from the verbal root בנה, banah—to build.
Some English translations naturally express the idea as Rachel “having children” or “building a family” through Bilhah. But the Hebrew imagery lets us feel something deeper in Rachel’s words:
I want to be built.
Something inside me feels unfinished.
Something inside me feels empty.
Maybe this will build what feels broken.
And there it is.
The ancient sentence that still lives inside modern hearts.
Maybe this will fix me.
Maybe if I finally get married, I will feel whole.
Maybe if I finally have a child, I will feel whole.
Maybe if the ministry grows, I will feel significant.
Maybe if I become successful, I will stop feeling small.
Maybe if enough people admire me, I will stop hating myself.
Maybe if I can obtain what somebody else has, the ache will finally disappear.
Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob.
The text says Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel named him Dan.
Her explanation contains another remarkable Hebrew word:
דָּנַנִּי אֱלֹהִים
Dananni Elohim.
“God has judged/vindicated me.”
The wordplay connects directly with the name דָּן, Dan.
Then Bilhah conceived again.
Another son.
Rachel named him Naphtali, saying:
נַפְתּוּלֵי אֱלֹהִים נִפְתַּלְתִּי עִם־אֲחֹתִי גַּם־יָכֹלְתִּי
The language is difficult to reproduce perfectly in English, but it communicates an intense wrestling or struggle associated with Rachel’s rivalry with her sister.
And that detail matters.
Because even after a son had arrived through Bilhah…
Rachel was still talking about Leah.
Think about that.
The child arrived.
The comparison survived.
That should terrify us a little.
Because sometimes we tell ourselves, “Once God gives me this, I’ll finally have peace.”
But if comparison is the disease, another possession cannot cure it.
If identity is the wound, another achievement cannot heal it.
If your heart is starving for God, another human being cannot become enough food.
You can win the competition and discover you are still competing.
You can reach the number and immediately need a bigger number.
You can get the applause and become terrified of losing it.
You can finally receive what you begged for and discover that the thing you worshiped cannot carry the weight of being your god.
Genesis 30 is descriptive before it is prescriptive.
The Bible faithfully records what these people did; that does not mean every recorded action is presented as God’s ideal.
Scripture is astonishingly honest about its families.
Abraham’s household was complicated.
Isaac’s household experienced favoritism and deception.
Jacob’s household contained rivalry, favoritism, jealousy, sexual complexity, manipulation, and deep wounds.
And yet…
God kept moving His redemptive purpose forward.
That does not make the dysfunction righteous.
It makes grace astonishing.
The Bible does not need perfect people to prove that God is faithful.
In fact, Scripture repeatedly gives us deeply flawed human beings so that when redemption arrives, nobody can pretend humanity saved itself.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that sentence more than anything else tonight.
Your family history does not shock God.
Your worst decision did not make Jesus drop the pen.
Your shame is not stronger than His grace.
Your past may explain some of your wounds, but through Christ it does not have to dictate your future.
Rachel’s story eventually takes another turn.
Genesis 30:22 says something profoundly important:
“Then God remembered Rachel…”
Those words do not mean God had literally forgotten she existed and suddenly remembered her name.
Biblically, this language signals God turning His covenant attention toward someone and acting on their behalf.
Then Scripture says God listened to her and opened her womb.
Rachel conceived.
And Joseph was born.
Do you see the painful irony?
Rachel spent part of Genesis 30 trying to construct an answer.
But ultimately God remained God.
This does not mean believers should never act, seek medical care, make plans, pursue opportunities, or use legitimate means available to them. Scripture does not teach passive fatalism.
It means something far more searching:
Our methods must never replace our trust.
We are called to obedience, not manipulation.
Faith does not mean doing nothing.
Faith means refusing to make an idol out of the outcome.
And now Genesis 30 begins pointing beyond Rachel.
Beyond Jacob.
Beyond Bilhah.
Beyond Leah.
Beyond Dan.
Beyond Naphtali.
Beyond Joseph.
Because the story of Genesis is moving somewhere.
Through this spectacularly imperfect family, God was forming Israel.
And through Israel’s story would eventually come the Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
That is the scandal of grace.
God works His redemptive purposes through family trees filled with sinners.
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ would ultimately bear its judgment.
But human failure cannot outmaneuver divine redemption.
Jesus did not come from a Bible filled with airbrushed people.
He entered the story of humanity precisely because humanity needed saving.
And the Gospel does not say, “Fix yourself enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that sinners who cannot save themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the answer to the deepest emptiness in us is not another Bilhah.
Not another strategy.
Not another achievement.
Not another relationship.
Not another attempt to build ourselves out of whatever we can reach.
It is Christ.
Maybe your version of Rachel’s cry has never been spoken aloud.
But God has heard it.
“Give me someone to love me or I’ll die.”
“Give me my marriage back or I’ll die.”
“Give me success or I’ll die.”
“Give me healing or I’ll die.”
“Give me money or I’ll die.”
“Give me a child or I’ll die.”
“Give me recognition or I’ll die.”
“Give me what they have or I’ll die.”
And Jesus confronts the lie beneath all of them.
Because what your soul ultimately needs is not merely a changed circumstance.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need forgiveness.
You need grace.
You need a new heart.
You need the One who died and rose again.
There are wounds God may heal by changing circumstances.
There are others He heals by changing us while the circumstances remain painful.
And sometimes the miracle begins when our prayer changes from:
“God, give me this so I can finally live…”
to:
“Jesus, even here, teach me that my life belongs to You.”
That is surrender.
Not pretending the desire no longer hurts.
Not pretending infertility does not hurt.
Not pretending loneliness does not hurt.
Not pretending betrayal does not hurt.
Not pretending unanswered prayer does not hurt.
Christian faith does not require emotional dishonesty.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Psalms cry.
Job grieved.
Paul knew weakness.
Biblical faith is not pretending pain is painless.
It is bringing pain under the lordship of Christ.
Maybe that is why this story found you.
Maybe you have been trying to manufacture something God never told you to manufacture.
Maybe comparison has been eating you alive.
Maybe somebody else’s blessing has quietly become your bitterness.
Maybe you are angry with God.
Maybe you have been asking another human being to occupy a throne that belongs only to Jesus.
Maybe you got what you wanted and still feel strangely empty.
Or maybe you are still waiting.
Still praying.
Still watching other people announce the very blessing you have begged God for.
And you are tired.
If that is you, do not turn this article into another moment of religious pretending.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may need to discover that Christians struggle too—and that struggling people can still cling to Christ.
Then send this to the person whose smile has been hiding a war.
“Give me this…or I’ll die.”
They may need somebody to remind them that Jesus Christ is still Lord in the waiting.
Because comparison has a way of returning.
Desperation has a way of returning.
And there may come a night when you need to read these words again and remember:
You do not have to manufacture your identity.
You do not have to earn your worth.
You do not have to become somebody else to be seen by God.
And you do not have to hide your sin from Christ.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the manipulation.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the thing you have never told anybody.
The Gospel is not Christ standing at a distance waiting for cleaned-up people.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness and new life to those who come to Him in faith.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace meets sinners truthfully and transforms them.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want to keep placing Scripture, biblical teaching, conviction, encouragement, Gospel truth, discipleship, and Christ-centered resources in front of people who are hungry to know Jesus more deeply.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially has biblical precedent. Paul spoke appreciatively of believers who partnered with him in giving and receiving (Philippians 4:14–18), and Scripture teaches believers to give willingly rather than under coercion: “for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It does not.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot pay God into blessing you.
Jesus Christ purchased redemption at a price none of us could pay.
Biblical giving should never be manipulated through guilt.

But if Gospel Warrior is a ministry you genuinely believe is glorifying Christ, spreading His Word, helping wounded people encounter biblical truth, and equipping believers to grow, your voluntary monthly support can become a practical offering of partnership that helps that work continue and expand.
If you have been asking, “How can I help?”
This is one way.
Pray.
Tag people who need them.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling Christians.
Invite seekers.
Invite the friend who walked away from church.
Invite the lukewarm believer who needs awakening.
Invite even the unbeliever who keeps asking questions about Jesus.
But please remember what matters most.
The merchandise is not the mission.
The discount is not the Gospel.
Jesus is the center.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
That costs nothing.
One share can cross into a life we could never personally reach.
One tag can find someone at exactly the wrong—or perhaps providentially right—moment.
One honest comment can give another hurting believer permission to stop pretending.
One saved article can become tomorrow night’s reminder that God has not disappeared.
And before you leave, go back to Rachel.
See her again.
A woman hurting so badly that she believed obtaining one thing might finally build what felt broken inside her.
Then look at yourself.
What have you been asking to build you?
A person?
A child?
Success?
Money?
Approval?
A ministry?
Attention?
Marriage?
Vindication?
What is the thing you secretly believe must happen before you can finally be whole?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Then bring it to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing about an idol is not that it is always something evil.
Sometimes it is something beautiful that we asked to do what only God can do.
Rachel wanted children.
You may want something equally understandable.
But beneath every legitimate longing lives an even deeper need.
To know God.
To be forgiven.
To be reconciled.
To belong to Christ.
To discover that your identity does not rise and fall with another person’s blessing.
To learn that waiting does not mean God has abandoned you.
To believe that your ugliest chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
And to discover that when sin, shame, rivalry, failure, grief, and human desperation have written what looks like the final sentence…
Jesus can still pick up the pen.
You may not be able to rewrite what happened—but in the hands of Jesus, what happened does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT DOES THE BIBLE REALLY SAY ABOUT REMARRIAGE?
paragraphs:
WHAT DOES THE BIBLE REALLY SAY ABOUT REMARRIAGE?
Before You Call Someone’s Second Marriage “Adultery,” Before You Tell a Divorced Christian They Can Never Love Again, and Before You Use Grace as Permission to Ignore Jesus—Read What Scripture Actually Says
There is a wedding ring sitting in a drawer somewhere tonight.
Not because someone stopped believing in marriage.
Not because they woke up one morning and decided covenant did not matter.
But because something they once believed would last until death… died while both people were still breathing.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you did the betraying.
Maybe you begged someone to stay.
Maybe you were the one who left.
Maybe there was adultery.
Maybe abandonment.
Maybe years of decisions you wish you could undo.
Maybe you have since remarried, and every time somebody quotes one of Jesus’ warnings about divorce, something cold moves through your chest:
Am I living in adultery right now?
Does God recognize my marriage?
Do I have to leave my present spouse to obey Jesus?
Can a divorced Christian ever marry again?
Or perhaps you are single after divorce, wondering whether wanting companionship again means you are rebelling against God.
These questions cannot be answered responsibly with a meme.
And they should never be answered by ripping one sentence from the Bible, weaponizing it against wounded people, and calling that faithfulness.
But neither can we answer them by saying, “God wants you happy,” as though happiness were the highest commandment in Scripture.
Jesus deserves something better from us.
Truth.
All of it.
Because the Bible’s teaching on remarriage is simultaneously more serious than modern culture often wants it to be…and more saturated with grace than religious shame sometimes allows it to be.
And before we talk about remarriage, we have to understand why divorce hurts so deeply in Scripture.
Jesus takes us backward.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, He did not begin with loopholes.
He went back to creation.

“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female… Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
—Matthew 19:4–6
That last idea becomes even sharper in Greek:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω
ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō
In straightforward sense:
“Therefore, what God joined together, let a human being not separate.”
That word συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen carries the idea of joining or yoking together.
Jesus therefore refuses to reduce marriage to paperwork, romance, sexual attraction, financial partnership, or social convenience.
Marriage is covenantal.
Two become one flesh.
That is why biblical Christianity cannot treat divorce casually.
Jesus does not.
And neither should we.
But notice what happens next.
The Pharisees bring up Moses.
Why, then, did Moses permit a certificate of divorce?
Jesus responds that Moses permitted it because of the hardness of human hearts, “but from the beginning it was not so.”
There is something devastatingly honest there.
Divorce exists in Scripture not because broken covenant is beautiful, but because human beings are broken.
Hardness.
Sin.
Betrayal.
Rebellion.
Human hearts capable of destroying what God intended to flourish.
Then Jesus speaks the sentence that has frightened countless divorced Christians:
“Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery…”
—Matthew 19:9
The crucial Greek expression is:
μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ — mē epi porneia
“except/on account of porneia.”
The word πορνεία — porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality, though interpreters have debated the precise scope intended in Matthew’s context.
And this matters.
Jesus is demolishing the idea that someone may discard a spouse for trivial reasons and then simply replace that spouse as though covenant meant nothing.
He is defending the sacredness of marriage.
He is exposing the sinfulness of covenant-breaking.
And Matthew records an exception involving porneia.

Christians have disagreed for centuries about exactly how that exception relates to remarriage. One longstanding interpretation understands Jesus as permitting divorce and subsequent remarriage for the innocent spouse after sexual immorality. Other Christians understand the exception more narrowly or believe that even where divorce is permissible, remarriage while the former spouse lives remains prohibited.
We should be humble enough to say that disagreement exists.
But we must not be dishonest about what the text says.
Jesus gives marriage enormous moral weight.
He condemns covenant-breaking divorce.
He identifies sexual immorality as an exceptional circumstance in Matthew’s account.
And He refuses to let human beings turn marriage into something disposable.
Then Paul takes us into another painful situation.
What happens when somebody does not commit adultery but simply abandons the marriage?
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul tells believers not to divorce an unbelieving spouse merely because that spouse does not share the faith.
If the unbelieving husband or wife is willing to remain, the Christian should not throw the marriage away.
Then comes verse 15:
“But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases…”
The Greek contains an important expression:
οὐ δεδούλωται — ou dedoulōtai
Literally, the brother or sister “has not been enslaved” or “is not bound as a slave” in such circumstances.
Paul then says:
ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ κέκληκεν ὑμᾶς ὁ θεός
“God has called you to peace.”
Here again, Christians who take Scripture seriously disagree about the implications.
Some understand “not bound” to mean that when an unbelieving spouse abandons the marriage, the deserted believer is released from the marriage and may eventually remarry.

Others understand Paul as permitting the separation while not necessarily granting permission for remarriage, pointing especially to his earlier instruction that a separated spouse should remain unmarried or be reconciled.
That disagreement should not be hidden.
If someone tells you that every detail of 1 Corinthians 7:15 has always been universally interpreted the same way, that overstates the evidence.
But Scripture gives us something that is not disputed.
A believer is not commanded to force an abandoning unbeliever to remain.
“Let him depart.”
God has called His people to peace.
Then there is one circumstance where Scripture is unmistakably explicit about freedom to remarry:
death.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 7:39
The Greek is beautifully direct:
ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι, μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ
eleuthera estin hō thelei gamēthēnai, monon en Kyriō
“She is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”
Death ends the marriage covenant.
Remarriage after widowhood is therefore clearly permitted.
But perhaps that is not why you clicked this article.
Perhaps your history is messier.
You did not lose your spouse to death.
You lost your marriage to sin.
Maybe even your own sin.
And this is where theological discussion becomes painfully personal.
Because there is another question hiding underneath “Can I remarry?”
It is:
“What does Jesus do with someone who has already ruined everything?”
Now we have reached the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the announcement that morally successful people get to keep their spotless records.
Christianity announces that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
That includes sexual sinners.
Adulterers.
The sexually immoral.
The selfish.
The deceptive.
The proud.
The people who destroyed things they should have protected.
Paul gives a terrifying list in 1 Corinthians 6 and says that the sexually immoral and adulterers will not inherit the kingdom of God.
But he does not stop there.
“And such were some of you…”
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε — kai tauta tines ēte
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes grace:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus…”
That is Christianity.
Not pretending sin never happened.
Not renaming adultery “finding yourself.”
Not baptizing selfishness with therapeutic vocabulary.
Not calling evil good.
But neither is Christianity telling the repentant sinner:
“You did something terrible, therefore terrible is what you will always be.”
Jesus Christ does something human beings cannot do.
He forgives guilty people without pretending they were innocent.
At the cross, grace does not deny the scandal.
Grace answers it.
Maybe you destroyed your first marriage.
Then repent.
Not performatively.
Not, “I made mistakes.”
Call sin what God calls it.
Confess it.
Where restitution or reconciliation is biblically possible and appropriate, pursue what obedience requires.
Ask forgiveness where you have sinned against people.
Stop blaming everybody else.
Bring the ugly truth into the light.
Because repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the grave.
The Greek word so often associated with repentance is μετάνοια — metanoia: a turning, a change of mind that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying people.
Grace transforms.
But what if you have already remarried?
What if children now call both of you Mom and Dad?
What if years have passed?
Should you divorce your current spouse to somehow undo the first divorce?
Scripture nowhere establishes a general command for Christians in an existing remarriage to dissolve that marriage as an act of repentance.
That would attempt to repair one broken covenant by breaking another.

Whatever sins may have surrounded the road into a present marriage should be confessed before God. But repentance now means faithfulness to Christ in the life actually before you—not pretending you possess a time machine.
If you are married now, honor your covenant now.
Love sacrificially now.
Become trustworthy now.
Be sexually faithful now.
Forgive now.
Pray together now.
Put Christ at the center now.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what yesterday did to you.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
David was forgiven, yet consequences remained.
Peter was restored, yet he still remembered the courtyard.
Grace does not mean history becomes imaginary.
Grace means history no longer gets the final word.
And that is why remarriage cannot be discussed faithfully without talking about redemption.
Some people reading this need permission to stop treating marriage casually.
Others need permission to stop treating themselves as permanently contaminated.
Some need conviction.
Some need comfort.
Some need to fight for the marriage they still have instead of fantasizing about another one.
Some need to repent of adultery.
Some need to forgive someone who abandoned them.
Some need wise pastoral counsel before entering another marriage.
Some need to stop allowing loneliness to make theological decisions for them.
And some remarried believers need to stop waking up every morning wondering whether Jesus secretly despises their family.
Listen carefully.
Your marital history is not your Savior.
Your perfect record would not have saved you.
Your broken record cannot save you.
Jesus saves sinners.
This is why Romans 8:1 remains breathtaking:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
“Therefore, now, no condemnation…”
Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
Not condemnation waiting behind the church door whenever someone discovers your history.
For those who are genuinely in Christ, there is no condemnation before God because Christ bore judgment for His people.
That grace should never make us casual about marriage.
It should make us more serious about marriage.
The person forgiven of covenant-breaking should understand covenant differently.
The adulterer who has truly encountered Christ should become fiercely faithful.
The liar should become truthful.
The selfish spouse should learn sacrifice.
The wounded spouse should discover that forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
The divorced believer should discover that “divorced” is a description of something that happened, not the name Jesus carved over their soul.
And anyone considering remarriage should slow down long enough to ask questions much deeper than:
“Do I deserve another chance?”
Ask:
“Will this marriage glorify Jesus Christ?”
“Have I genuinely repented of my contribution to the destruction of my previous marriage?”
“Am I entering this relationship from spiritual health or simply terror of being alone?”
“Have I sought mature biblical counsel?”
“Is this person truly following Christ?”
“Are there unresolved covenant obligations I am trying to escape?”
“Am I willing to make this marriage a testimony of Christlike faithfulness rather than another attempt to medicate my loneliness?”
Because biblical remarriage is not about getting another wedding.
It is about covenant.
And sometimes the most Christlike answer is not rushing toward another relationship.
Sometimes God needs to heal things in you that another person cannot heal.
Sometimes loneliness reveals idols.
Sometimes silence reveals wounds.
Sometimes singleness becomes the room where Jesus teaches you that being wanted romantically and being loved eternally are not the same thing.
Do not ask another human being to become your resurrection.
They cannot carry that weight.
Christ can.
And please hear this too:

If you are currently trapped in violence, coercion, credible threats, or serious abuse, do not interpret a discussion about the sanctity of marriage as a command to remain physically exposed to danger. Seek immediate safety, appropriate authorities where necessary, mature pastoral care, and qualified professional help. Christians differ on how abuse relates specifically to biblical grounds for divorce and remarriage, but protecting someone from immediate harm is not the same thing as treating marriage casually.
The church must be capable of saying two things at once:
Marriage is sacred.
And:
Broken people are not disposable.
We can defend covenant without crushing survivors.
We can preach repentance without withholding grace.
We can tell adulterers to repent without pretending adulterers are beyond redemption.
We can tell abandoned people that God sees them without automatically answering every complicated remarriage case with a slogan.
We can honor Jesus enough to refuse both extremes.
Because Jesus did not come to make sin irrelevant.
He came because sin was so deadly that nothing less than His blood could rescue us.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needs tonight.
Your divorce may be part of your story.
Your adultery may be part of your story.
Your abandonment may be part of your story.
Your courtroom may be part of your story.
Your shattered wedding vows may be part of your story.
Your lonely apartment may be part of your story.
Your second marriage may be part of your story.
But none of those things deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
From scandal…
to grace.
Not because the scandal was insignificant.
Because the Savior is greater.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need forgiveness, ask.
If you owe someone an apology, stop rehearsing excuses.
If your marriage is barely breathing, seek godly help before pride signs the death certificate.
If you are divorced and ashamed, stop assuming the whispers of religious people carry more authority than the Gospel.
If you are remarried, do not spend the rest of your marriage staring backward when Christ is calling you to faithfulness today.
And if you are wondering whether grace could possibly reach the particular wreckage carrying your name…
Look at the cross.
That is where Christianity answers scandal.
Not with denial.
With blood.
Not with excuses.
With atonement.
Not with “you were never guilty.”
With something infinitely better:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.”
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Not because every difficult question can be settled by one article, but because shame has a way of making us forget what grace taught us yesterday.
You need Jesus.
Not merely another marriage.
Not merely a restored reputation.
Not merely another chance at romance.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Christ.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who tells the truth about our sin and then bears the judgment sinners could never bear themselves.
The One who can take a chapter you wish had never been written and refuse to let it become the ending.
Because perhaps the greatest question is not:
“Can I marry again?”
Perhaps the question beneath it is:
“Can Jesus still make something holy out of a life that has been broken?”
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at Peter after denial.
Look at Paul after persecution.
Look at the countless sinners Scripture refuses to airbrush.
Then remember:
The Gospel has never been the story of flawless people presenting God with flawless histories.
It is the story of a flawless Savior rescuing people who desperately need grace.
And maybe your wedding ring is still sitting in that drawer.
Maybe another one is already on your hand.
Maybe there will never be another ring.
But your deepest hope was never supposed to fit around your finger.
Your deepest hope has nail scars in His hands.
Your past may explain the scars—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CHRISTIAN PURITY IS MORE THAN “DON’T HAVE SEX BEFORE MARRIAGE”
paragraphs: CHRISTIAN PURITY IS MORE THAN “DON’T HAVE SEX BEFORE MARRIAGE”

You can save your body for marriage and still give your heart to lust. You can wear a purity ring and secretly live impure. And you can have a sexual past you deeply regret—and still discover that Jesus Christ has not finished writing your story.
There is a version of Christian purity that is easy to measure.
Did you have sex before marriage?
Yes or no.
Virgin or not.
Pure or impure.
Good Christian or failure.
And somewhere along the way, many believers were handed an idea of purity that could almost fit on a bumper sticker:
“Don’t have sex until you’re married.”
That sentence contains an important biblical boundary.
But it is nowhere near the whole biblical vision.
Because Jesus did something uncomfortable with purity.
He moved the conversation from the bedroom...
to the heart.
And suddenly, people who thought they had never crossed the line discovered that the line ran directly through them.
Jesus said:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Matthew 5:28, KJV.
Read that slowly.

Jesus was not saying that temptation itself is identical to committing physical adultery. He was exposing something deeper: righteousness cannot be reduced to outward restraint while inward desire deliberately turns another human being into an object of lust.
You can keep your clothes on...
and still undress somebody in your imagination.
You can never touch their body...
and still consume them in your mind.
You can tell everybody, “I’m waiting for marriage”...
while secretly feeding desires you would be ashamed to place before Christ.
That is why biblical purity is so much bigger than virginity.
And this is where the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe you did wait.
Maybe you are waiting now.
Maybe nobody can accuse you of sleeping around.
But what happens when the door closes?
What happens when everybody goes to sleep?
What happens when the phone is in your hand and nobody is watching?
What happens when the person you keep fantasizing about appears on your screen?
What happens inside your imagination?
What happens in the private messages?
What happens with the emotional affair you keep calling “just friendship”?
What happens when you flirt with someone you have no intention of honoring?
What happens when loneliness becomes your excuse for consuming another person's body through a screen?
What happens when you become so obsessed with avoiding intercourse that you keep asking, “How far can we go without technically sinning?”
That question itself can reveal something.
Because love asks:
“How can I honor Christ and this person?”
Lust keeps asking:
“How close can I get to the boundary without crossing it?”
There is a difference.
And Scripture gives that difference a name.
When Paul wrote to the Thessalonian believers, he did not merely say, “Don’t have premarital sex.”
His words were much bigger:
“τουτο γαρ εστιν θελημα του θεου ο αγιασμος υμων απεχεσθαι υμας απο της πορνειας”
That is the Greek text of 1 Thessalonians 4:3.
One English rendering says:
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
1 Thessalonians 4:3.
Look at the word behind “sanctification”:
ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos.
Holiness.
Sanctification.
A life increasingly set apart to God.
And then Paul speaks about abstaining from πορνεία — porneia, a Greek term referring broadly to sexual immorality.

Paul's vision therefore cannot honestly be reduced to one slogan about reaching your wedding night without intercourse. The surrounding verses speak about holiness, honor, mastery of one's body, lustful passion, treatment of other people, and ultimately God's calling to holiness.
Purity is not merely something you refuse to do.
Purity is something God is forming you to become.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally a program for producing technically compliant virgins.
Jesus is making holy people.
People whose bodies belong to Him.
Whose eyes belong to Him.
Whose imaginations belong to Him.
Whose sexuality belongs to Him.
Whose relationships belong to Him.
Whose hidden browser history belongs to Him.
Whose dating life belongs to Him.
Whose marriage belongs to Him.
Whose loneliness belongs to Him.
Whose wounds belong to Him.
Whose desires are progressively being brought beneath His lordship.
And maybe that makes you uncomfortable.
Good.
But please keep reading.
Because what comes next matters even more.
If the Christian message about purity ends with “be clean,” then some of you will leave this article absolutely crushed.
Because you weren't.
You crossed the line.
Maybe willingly.
Maybe repeatedly.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe last night.
Maybe there are memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe somebody convinced you that because you gave away your virginity, you gave away your value.
Maybe you have heard Christian conversations about “purity” that made you feel like a damaged product.
Used.
Secondhand.
Less desirable.
Less spiritual.
Less worthy of a godly marriage.
And perhaps you learned how to smile in church while carrying a secret sentence inside your chest:
God forgives me, but I will never really be clean again.
Listen carefully.
That is not the Gospel.
Virginity and purity are not identical things.
Virginity describes whether a person has experienced sexual intercourse.
Biblical purity concerns holiness before God.
One is a state of sexual experience.
The other belongs to the transforming work of sanctification.
That distinction matters enormously because virginity, once physically lost, cannot simply be recreated as though history never happened.
But holiness?
Holiness is precisely where Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The Gospel does not require you to travel backward in time.
It calls you to Christ.
Your past may be irreversible.
Your redemption is not impossible.
That is the scandal of grace.
You may have consequences from yesterday that remain tomorrow.
Grace does not pretend sin never mattered.
The cross proves that sin matters more seriously than our culture wants to admit.
But the cross also proves that God's mercy runs deeper than your worst chapter.
Jesus did not bleed for an imaginary, polished version of you.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with appetites.
People with secrets.
People who crossed boundaries.
People who knew better.
People who promised God, “Never again,” and somehow found themselves crying over the same failure.
People like us.
And this is where purity culture can become dangerous when it loses the Gospel.
When virginity becomes the ultimate badge, people who kept it can become proud...
and people who lost it can become hopeless.
Jesus destroys both illusions.
The outwardly disciplined person still needs grace.
The sexually broken person can still receive grace.
Nobody gets to stand beneath the cross and boast.
Nobody who comes to Christ in repentance needs to stand beneath the cross believing redemption is reserved for cleaner people.
That is Christianity.
Not:
“Clean yourself so Jesus will want you.”
But:
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe.
Bring the darkness into His light.
And let the One who saved you begin transforming you.
This doesn't make sexual sin trivial.
It makes grace astonishing.
There is another side of purity we rarely discuss.
How you see people.
A woman is not a collection of body parts created for your consumption.
A man is not an emotional or sexual instrument created to make you feel wanted.
The person you are dating is not your private laboratory for discovering how much physical gratification you can extract while preserving the technical label “Christian.”
That person bears dignity before God.
That changes dating.
That changes flirting.
That changes pornography.
That changes fantasy.
That changes sexting.
That changes what you watch.

That changes how you dress—not because the human body is dirty, but because followers of Christ learn to think about themselves and others through love, dignity, wisdom, and holiness rather than exhibition, consumption, manipulation, or lust.
And it changes marriage too.
Because marriage is not graduation from purity.
Please hear that.
You do not practice purity until the wedding and then retire from holiness.
A wedding ring does not make selfish sexuality holy.
Marriage does not give someone permission to treat a spouse as an object.
Pornography does not become harmless because you're married.
Lust for somebody who isn't your spouse does not become acceptable because you waited until your wedding night.
Manipulation does not become love because vows were exchanged.
Purity follows you into marriage because holiness follows you into marriage.
Paul's words continue:
“that each of you should learn to control your own body in a way that is holy and honorable.”
Then:
“not in passionate lust.”
1 Thessalonians 4:4–5.
Holy.
Honorable.
Those words are beautiful.
Christian sexuality isn't merely about what is prohibited.
It is about learning to honor God with something powerful He created.
Your body isn't evil.
Sex isn't evil.
Desire itself isn't proof that something is wrong with you.
Scripture does not solve sexual sin by declaring human embodiment filthy.
The Christian answer is not hatred of the body.
It is holiness of the whole person.
And that means sometimes saying no—not because God hates pleasure, but because God refuses to let pleasure become your god.
Some desires must be denied.
Some relationships must end.
Some numbers need to be deleted.
Some conversations need boundaries.
Some applications may need to disappear from your phone.
Some secret habits need to be confessed to mature, trustworthy believers who can walk with you in truth and accountability.
Some couples need to stop asking whether they technically “went all the way” and start asking whether they are genuinely helping each other follow Jesus.

Some married people need to admit that the secret pornography habit followed them into marriage exactly because marriage was never going to cure what only truth, repentance, spiritual formation, wise accountability, and the grace of Christ could confront.
And some of you need to stop trying to defeat lust merely by hating yourself harder.
Shame can scream.
But screaming isn't sanctification.
Self-disgust can make dramatic promises.
But self-disgust cannot crucify Christ again for you.
You need Jesus.
You need His Spirit.
You need truth.
You need repentance that does more than feel terrible after sin and actually turns toward God.
You need grace strong enough to teach you to say no.
And sometimes you need another mature Christian who knows what is really happening.
Not the sanitized testimony.
Not the church answer.
The truth.
“I am struggling.”
“I keep going back.”
“I need help.”
“I don't want to hide anymore.”
There is enormous spiritual power in bringing what flourishes in secrecy into the light.
Not broadcasting intimate details to the internet.
Not turning confession into exhibition.
But refusing to maintain the double life.
Maybe your battle is pornography.
Maybe it is fantasy.
Maybe it is masturbation bound up with pornography or lust.
Maybe it is an affair.
Maybe it is sex outside marriage.
Maybe it is same-sex or opposite-sex lust that you know you are feeding rather than surrendering.
Maybe it is an emotional attachment to somebody else's spouse.
Maybe you keep sending messages you would immediately delete if your husband or wife walked into the room.
Maybe your issue isn't what you have done with your body at all.
Maybe it is what you have permitted your heart to worship.
Whatever it is...
Jesus already knows.
You are not informing Him when you confess.
You are finally agreeing with Him.
And perhaps the most dangerous prayer you could pray tonight is also one of the most beautiful:
“Jesus, I don't only want You to change what I do. Change what I love.”
Because purity isn't ultimately about becoming impressive.
It is about becoming Christ's.
There will be battles.
There may be setbacks.
Sanctification should never become an excuse for comfortable, deliberate sin, but neither should the existence of a battle convince a repentant believer that Christ has abandoned them.
Get up.
Confess.
Run toward Jesus instead of hiding from Him.
Remember Peter.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Remember the sexually disordered world into which the apostles preached Christ.
Remember the kinds of lives represented in the Corinthian church—and then remember Paul's astonishing words after listing patterns of serious sin:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then he speaks of washing, sanctification, and justification in the name of Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is 1 Corinthians 6:11.
The Gospel contains a were.
Your sin can describe where you have been without receiving permission to define whose you are forever.
Maybe that is why this article found you.
Not so you can send it to “that one person who really needs it” while protecting yourself from its blade.
Maybe you need it.
Maybe I need it.
Maybe all of us need to stop reducing holiness to the sins we can publicly prove we haven't committed.
Christian purity is more than:
“I didn't have sex.”
It is:
“Jesus, have my eyes.”
“Have my mind.”
“Have my body.”
“Have my dating life.”
“Have my marriage.”
“Have my singleness.”
“Have my desires.”
“Have my phone.”
“Have my wounds.”
“Have my sexuality.”
“Have my secret life.”
“Have all of me.”
And if something inside you is whispering, But you don't understand what I've done...
No.
Maybe I don't.
But the cross was not built for people with nothing to forgive.
Christ's blood is not intimidated by your history.
Repentance does not mean pretending yesterday never happened.
It means turning from sin toward the Savior who already knows yesterday and still calls sinners to Himself.
This is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting evil into good.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
He rewrites everything by taking sinners who were dead in sin and making them alive in Him.
By turning rebels into sons and daughters.
By turning shame into testimony.
By turning secrecy into confession.
By turning bondage into a battlefield where grace teaches us to fight.
By turning “this is just who I am” into “I belong to Jesus now.”
So perhaps your next act of purity isn't making another dramatic promise.
Perhaps it is telling the truth.
You don't have to tell strangers the intimate details.
Just let those three words become your declaration that secrecy will no longer have the final word.
Someone reading those comments may realize they are not the only Christian fighting for holiness.
Someone may find enough courage to confess.
Someone may come back to Jesus.
That matters.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't merely think about them.
Send it privately to the believer who has been quietly losing the war.
Share it with the teenager who thinks purity means nothing except virginity.
Share it with the married couple who discovered that a wedding ceremony did not automatically heal years of secret lust.
Share it with the Christian drowning in shame because they believe their sexual past permanently disqualified them.
Share it with the person who doesn't follow Jesus yet but needs to discover that Christianity isn't ultimately about polishing yourself until God tolerates you.
It is about sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made painfully clear today.
Come back when you need the reminder.
It doesn't.
Not because God needs your money.
He doesn't.
It doesn't.

We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one practical way believers may freely choose to support Gospel ministry is by helping sound biblical resources continue reaching people who need them.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, encouraging wounded believers, confronting comfortable Christianity, and pointing people back to Jesus.
Your heart.
Your repentance.
Your obedience.
Your secret places.
Your future.
Your sexuality.
Your shame.
Your wounds.
Your entire life.
Because the goal of Christian purity was never merely to arrive at a wedding altar sexually untouched.
The greater destination is to belong increasingly, joyfully, completely to Jesus.
And maybe your story contains chapters you would burn if you could.
Maybe your purity was shattered.
Maybe your innocence disappeared.
Maybe you became the person you once swore you would never become.
Maybe your private life would shock everyone who admires your public Christianity.
But if you can still hear the voice of Christ calling you out of darkness...
your story is not over.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in holiness.
And when shame points backward and whispers, “Look what you did,” lift your eyes toward the cross and remember what Jesus did.
Your worst chapter may explain your scars, but it does not get to write the final sentence when the pen belongs to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS ENTRUST MARY TO JOHN?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS ENTRUST MARY TO JOHN?
The Last Family Jesus Formed Before He Died—and the Heartbreaking Detail at the Cross Most People Read Too Quickly
There are words Jesus spoke from the cross that Christians have repeated for centuries.
“Father, forgive them.”
“I thirst.”
“It is finished.”
But hidden between the nails and the darkness is a moment so quiet that it is easy to read past it.
A dying Son looks down.
His mother is standing there.
And beside her stands a disciple.
Jesus looks at Mary.
Then at the disciple.
And with only a few words, He rearranges a family.
Why?
Why would Jesus, while enduring crucifixion, use some of His rapidly disappearing strength to make sure His mother would be cared for?
And perhaps the more difficult question…
Why John?
Jesus had brothers.

The Gospel of John itself tells us that Jesus had brothers, and earlier in His ministry they did not believe in Him. John 7:5 states plainly that “even his own brothers did not believe in him.” Yet after the resurrection, something changed. Acts 1:14 later places Mary and Jesus’ brothers among the believers gathered in prayer.
So we must be careful.
Scripture does not explicitly say, “Jesus chose John instead of His brothers because…”
Any explanation pretending the Bible gives us that sentence goes beyond what is written.
But Scripture does show us something.
Something beautiful.
Something almost unbearably human.
And once you see it, this tiny scene beneath the cross becomes much larger than a question about ancient family arrangements.
Because this is not merely a story about where Mary would live after Jesus died.
This is a story about what Jesus was doing even while He was dying.
Look again.
Mary is standing near the cross.
Try not to sanitize that sentence.
She is not looking at a polished cross hanging inside a church.
She is watching her Son die on one.
The child she once carried is now carrying the sin of the world.
The hands she once held are wounded.
The forehead she may once have kissed is crowned with thorns.
The voice that once called her “mother” is fighting through the agony of crucifixion.
She had known from the beginning that this Child belonged to God in a way no other child ever had.
The angel had come.
The promises had been spoken.
The shepherds had arrived.
Simeon had prophesied.
And Simeon had also warned her that a sword would pierce her own soul.
Now she is standing beneath that sword.
And Jesus sees her.
Do not move past that too quickly.
Jesus sees her.
While carrying the judgment our sin deserved…
He sees His mother.
While experiencing physical agony beyond what most of us can imagine…
He sees His mother.
While accomplishing the redemption of sinners…
He sees His mother.
While the machinery of Roman execution is killing Him…
He sees His mother.
The salvation of the world is unfolding, and Jesus is still attentive to the person standing in front of Him.
John records the moment:
“Woman, behold, your son!”
Then to the disciple:
“Behold, your mother!”
And John immediately adds that from that hour the disciple received her into his own household.
The Greek makes the scene even more striking:
“Γύναι, ἴδε ὁ υἱός σου.”
Gynai, ide ho huios sou.
“Woman, behold your son.”
Then:
“Ἴδε ἡ μήτηρ σου.”
Ide hē mētēr sou.
“Behold your mother.”
And then comes this:
“καὶ ἀπ’ ἐκείνης τῆς ὥρας ἔλαβεν ὁ μαθητὴς αὐτὴν εἰς τὰ ἴδια.”
Literally, the disciple received her “into his own”—an expression naturally referring to his own home or household.
John did not merely nod.
He received responsibility.
Jesus spoke.
John obeyed.
That matters.
Because biblical love is rarely satisfied with emotion alone.
Love moves.
Love receives.
Love carries.
Love makes room.
Love changes the household.
And perhaps someone reading this already knows why those words hurt.
Because you know what it feels like to need someone to make room for you.
You know what abandonment feels like.
You know what it means to wonder whether anybody notices what you are carrying.
Maybe your family is fractured.
Maybe the people who were supposed to protect you became the people who wounded you.
Maybe your mother is gone.
Maybe your father was never really there.
Maybe your children barely call anymore.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe grief changed the sound of your house.
Maybe you have hundreds of Facebook friends and still feel strangely alone when the phone goes quiet at night.
And then you come to Calvary…
and discover that the Savior bleeding for humanity still notices one grieving woman standing beneath His cross.
That is Jesus.
He is never so occupied with the multitude that He becomes indifferent to the individual.
He can carry the sins of the world and still see Mary's tears.
He can accomplish cosmic redemption and still address a human relationship.
The King of heaven is not emotionally careless.
But we must go deeper.
Why John?

John identifies the man at the cross as “the disciple whom Jesus loved.” Christian tradition has long identified this disciple with John, and that remains the conventional understanding behind the question we are considering.
What Scripture unquestionably emphasizes, however, is not merely his name.
It emphasizes his relationship to Jesus.
The beloved disciple was there.
At the cross.
When association with Jesus was no longer impressive.
When miracles seemed far away.
When the crowds had changed.
When following Jesus could be dangerous.
He was there.
There is something sobering about that.
Everybody loves resurrection Christianity when the tomb is already empty.
But Calvary reveals who will stand near Jesus when following Him hurts.
The disciple is not presented as flawless. None of Christ's disciples were.
But here, at this terrible hour, he is present.
And Jesus entrusts Mary to him.

We should not invent motives Scripture never states. We cannot prove that Jesus bypassed His brothers simply because they had previously been unbelieving. In fact, Acts later shows Jesus’ brothers among the praying believers, so their story did not end in unbelief.
That transformation itself is grace.
People who once did not believe would later be found among the believers.
Do not miss that either.
Someone's unbelief today does not tell you what Christ may do with that person tomorrow.
The skeptical brother can become the praying brother.
The resistant heart can surrender.
The person who laughed at your faith may someday kneel beside you.
Jesus rewrites stories.
But at the cross, in that particular hour, Jesus gives Mary into the care of the beloved disciple who is standing there.
And John receives her.
There is a profound lesson in that without forcing the passage to say more than it says.
Faithfulness is often revealed by presence.
Sometimes the holiest thing you can do is stay.
Stay when somebody is grieving.
Stay when there is nothing impressive to watch.
Stay when you cannot fix the situation.
Stay when you have no clever words.
Stay when everybody else has found a reason to leave.
Some people do not need your explanation.
They need your presence.
Mary could not stop the crucifixion.
John could not remove the nails.
Neither could change what was happening.
But they could stand near Jesus.
Maybe that is where some of you are right now.
You cannot fix what happened.
You cannot resurrect the marriage yourself.
You cannot force your child home.
You cannot undo the diagnosis.
You cannot rewind the funeral.
You cannot make the betrayal unhappen.
You cannot erase those years.
And you keep asking God, “What am I supposed to do?”
Sometimes faith begins with refusing to run away from the cross.
Stand there.
Weep there.
Pray there.
Wait there.
Because Friday is not the end of the Gospel.
And this scene also exposes something Christianity can easily forget.
Jesus does not merely save isolated individuals and then send them away alone.
The Gospel creates a people.
A household.
