“וּפִילַגְשׁוֹ אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁכֶם, יָלְדָה־לּוֹ גַם־הִיא בֵּן; וַיָּשֶׂם אֶת־שְׁמוֹ, אֲבִימֶלֶךְ”
“Ufilagsho asher bi-Shekhem… vayasem et-shemo Avimelekh.”
His concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he gave him the name Abimelech.
The Hebrew word פִּילֶגֶשׁ—pilegesh—means a concubine, a woman in a recognized but lower-status marital or domestic relationship than a primary wife in that ancient social setting.
And Scripture does not interrupt the story to say, “Gideon did this, therefore God approves of this.”
That is not how biblical narrative works.
The Bible often tells us what people did without telling us to imitate what they did.
That distinction matters.
Description is not automatically prescription.
The Bible records Abraham's failures without commanding them.
It records David's adultery without approving it.
It records Solomon's many wives while explicitly showing the spiritual catastrophe associated with them.
And Judges records Gideon honestly.
No public-relations department.
No polished biography.
No attempt to protect the reputation of one of Israel's celebrated deliverers.
That should tell you something beautiful about Scripture.
The Bible is not a museum filled with statues of flawless people.
It is the testimony of a holy God working among desperately flawed human beings.
And that means there may be hope for you.
Because Gideon's story did not begin with a fearless warrior.
It began with a frightened man.
When the angel of the LORD encountered Gideon in Judges 6, Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, trying to keep it hidden from Midian.
Imagine the scene.
Dust in the air.
Shoulders tense.
Eyes constantly checking the horizon.
Israel had been crushed so severely that people made hiding places in mountains and caves.
Then heaven addresses this frightened man with words that must have sounded almost absurd:
“The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour.”
God was speaking to something Gideon could not yet see in himself.
And some of you understand that.
You know what it is to love God while still being afraid.
To pray while questioning.
To worship while wondering why God has allowed something painful.
To believe and still whisper, “Lord, are You really here?”
Gideon knew that tension.
He asked questions.
He requested signs.
He put out the fleece.
And God patiently dealt with him.
Eventually, Gideon marched into battle with an army God intentionally reduced.
Thousands became hundreds.
Because God was going to make one thing unmistakable:
Israel's salvation would not come from human strength.
The victory belonged to the LORD.
Three hundred men.
Trumpets.
Jars.
Torches.
And God shattered Midian's power.
It is magnificent.
It is cinematic.
It is the part we preach.
But Judges does not end Gideon's biography at the victory celebration.
And neither should we.
Because winning a battle does not mean you have finished guarding your heart.
In fact, success can expose things suffering kept buried.
When you have nothing, dependence on God can feel natural.
When you have influence, money, admiration, authority, options, and people applauding your name...
something changes.
After Gideon's victory, Israel approached him with an extraordinary offer.
They wanted Gideon to rule over them.
Not merely Gideon.
His son.
And his son's son.
A dynasty.
Gideon answered magnificently:
“I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you.”
Judges 8:23.
Beautiful words.
But then the story becomes complicated.
Gideon requested gold from the spoil.
The people willingly gave it.
He made an ephod.
And Judges 8:27 says that Israel went astray after it and that it became “a snare unto Gideon, and to his house.”
Read those final words again.
“To Gideon, and to his house.”
The Midianites could not destroy Gideon's house.
But a snare could enter after the victory.
Then comes the wealth.
Then the many wives.
Then seventy sons.
Then the concubine in Shechem.
Then Abimelech.
And there is an irony in that name that is difficult to ignore.
Avimelekh is built from Hebrew words associated with “father” and “king,” commonly understood as “my father is king” or “father is king.”
Yet Gideon had said:
“I will not rule over you.”
He verbally rejected kingship.
But the world surrounding his later life begins to look remarkably royal.
Many wives.
An enormous household.
Great wealth.
Prestige.
Seventy sons.
And a son named Abimelech.
We should be careful not to claim more than Scripture explicitly tells us about Gideon's motives. The text does not open his mind and tell us precisely why he chose that name.
But the narrative tension is there.
And then Gideon dies.
The great warrior is buried.
The crowds disappear.
The stories remain.
And the consequences keep walking.
Abimelech goes to Shechem.
He appeals to his mother's relatives.
He asks them, essentially, whether they would rather be ruled by Gideon's seventy sons or by one man who is their own flesh and blood.
Money is given to him from the temple of Baal-Berith.
Abimelech hires reckless men.
Then he travels to Ophrah.
To his father's house.
To the place connected with Gideon's legacy.
And there, Judges 9 records one of the darkest scenes in the book.
Abimelech murders his brothers.
On one stone.
The sons of Gideon.
His own brothers.
One after another.
Only Jotham, the youngest, escapes.
Think about that.
The family of the man who defeated Midian was devastated from inside itself.
Gideon defeated an army with 300 men.
Yet after his death, his household became the scene of horrifying violence.
That should shake us.
Because you can win publicly and still neglect something privately.
You can be used by God and still need to guard your heart.
You can have yesterday's testimony and still need today's obedience.
You can destroy an altar to Baal in Judges 6 and later make something that becomes a spiritual snare in Judges 8.
Yesterday's obedience does not give us permission to coast today.
Yesterday's anointing is not a substitute for today's surrender.
And maybe this is where Gideon's story stops being ancient history and starts reading your mail.
Because perhaps your Midian has already fallen.
Maybe God answered the prayer.
Maybe you got the job.
Maybe the business grew.
Maybe people finally noticed you.
Maybe the relationship happened.
Maybe your ministry expanded.
Maybe your page gained followers.
Maybe people started listening when you spoke.
Maybe you survived the season you thought would kill you.
And strangely...
you prayed more when you were desperate.
You searched Scripture more when you were hurting.
You cried before God more when there was nothing in your bank account.
You depended upon Him when every door was closed.
Then the doors opened.
And somewhere between survival and success, something changed.
Not dramatically.
Quietly.
Prayer became shorter.
Conviction became negotiable.
Compromise became explainable.
What once disturbed you became normal.
You still knew Christian language.
You still remembered the testimonies.
You could still tell everyone what God had done.
But the heart that once trembled before Him had started getting comfortable.
That may be the frightening lesson buried inside Gideon's ending.
You do not only need God in the winepress.
You need Him after Midian falls.
You need Jesus when you are poor.
You need Jesus when you prosper.
You need Jesus when nobody knows your name.
You need Jesus when thousands recognize it.
You need Jesus when you are afraid.
You need Jesus when you finally feel powerful.
Especially then.
Because the Gospel is not merely God's method for getting weak people through difficult seasons.
Jesus Christ is our life.
Our righteousness.
Our King.
Our hope.
Our forgiveness.
Our rescue.
Gideon could save Israel temporarily from Midian.
But Gideon could not save Gideon from Gideon.
And neither can you save yourself from yourself.
That is why we need a better Deliverer.
Not merely another judge.
Not another warrior.
Not another inspirational leader.
We need Jesus Christ.
Gideon entered battle with 300 men and emerged victorious.
Jesus walked toward Calvary while His disciples scattered.
Gideon shattered jars and enemies fled.
Jesus allowed His own body to be wounded.
Gideon returned from battle carrying the prestige of victory.
Jesus was mocked, stripped, beaten, crowned with thorns, and nailed to a Roman cross.
Gideon's later household became marked by rivalry and bloodshed.
Jesus shed His own blood to create a redeemed family from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation.
Gideon said the LORD should rule Israel.
Jesus Christ is the King whose reign never ends.
And unlike every human hero in Scripture, Jesus does not need His biography edited.
There is no secret chapter where Christ becomes corrupted by success.
No hidden scandal.
No moral collapse.
No private contradiction waiting to destroy His public righteousness.
He was tempted, yet without sin.
He obeyed the Father perfectly.
He went to the cross willingly.
And there He carried the judgment sinners deserve.
This is where the story turns toward you.
Because perhaps you have your own Judges 8.
Something you do not put in the testimony.
Something after the victory.
Something behind the Christian vocabulary.
Maybe nobody knows.
The private messages.
The addiction.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The secret relationship.
The money.
The pride.
The resentment.
The compromise you keep renaming because calling it sin would require repentance.
Maybe you have become very good at remembering what God did through you while avoiding what God is confronting within you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not die only for the version of you everyone admires.
He died for sinners.
Real sinners.
People with chapters they wish could be ripped from the book.
People who have failed after victories.
People who knew better.
People who compromised.
People who wandered.
People who discovered that defeating an external enemy is sometimes easier than confronting the rebellion inside their own hearts.
And the answer is not hiding.
The answer is repentance.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Not “I'll fix myself first and then come back.”
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Turn.
Bring the darkness into His light.
The cross is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace that calls evil good.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then announces that the blood of Jesus is sufficient to cleanse the sinner who comes to Him.
That is the Gospel.
Your worst chapter does not become righteous because you explain it.
Your sin does not become harmless because other Christians have done worse.
But your sin does not have to write the final sentence either.
Jesus can.
Maybe that is exactly why you found this article.
Not because you needed another shocking Bible fact about Gideon's wives.
Maybe God is putting His finger on your Judges 8.
The thing after your testimony.
The compromise after your victory.
The idol made from something that once looked like blessing.
The hidden relationship.
The quiet pride.
The secret appetite.
The place where you have been saying, “The LORD shall rule,” while living as though something else already does.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected, didn't it?
If God exposed something while you were reading this, do not run from Him.
Run to Christ.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting their way back toward the light.
Not as an algorithm trick.
Somebody you love may be smiling publicly while losing a war privately.
Somebody may be one honest encounter with Scripture away from repentance.
Send this to your family.
Send it to the struggling Christian.
Send it to the person who stopped attending church.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks the Bible sanitizes its heroes, because one extraordinary mark of Scripture is how relentlessly honest it is about human failure.
You may need it again when success starts whispering that you no longer need the dependence that carried you through suffering.
Biblical generosity comes from a willing heart responding to God's grace.
But ministry does require real resources.
Research takes time.
Writing takes time.
Books and discipleship materials take resources.
Reaching more people requires support.
Think of it as voluntary ministry support—an offering of generosity, not a transaction with God and not a replacement for obedience to however Scripture and your conscience direct your giving.
And there is another way to support the mission that costs absolutely nothing:
Share.
One share can enter a home we cannot enter.
One share can reach an old friend at 2:00 in the morning.
One share can land before somebody sitting alone wondering whether God could possibly forgive what they have done.
You may never know what God does with it.
But you can put truth within reach.
We want Scripture opened.
We want Christ proclaimed.
We want wounded believers strengthened.
We want wandering hearts called home.
We want people who have spent years hiding to discover that repentance is not the doorway into humiliation—it is the doorway back into the light.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Jesus is calling sinners home.
That invitation costs you nothing because it cost Him everything.
Gideon's story warns us not to confuse being used by God with being beyond the need for God.
Not every hero finishes every chapter heroically.
Not every victory guarantees faithfulness tomorrow.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment in your spiritual life will not be when you are trembling in the winepress.
Perhaps it will be when the battle is over...
the applause is loud...
the gold is accumulating...
the doors are opening...
and you slowly forget Who gave you the victory.
So guard your heart.
Stay near the cross.
Stay humble.
Stay repentant.
Stay in Scripture.
Do not build an idol out of yesterday's blessing.
Do not let yesterday's testimony become today's excuse.
And if you have already wandered...
come home.
If your story contains things you are ashamed to admit...
come home.
If you have been living two lives...
come home.
If you won battles publicly and lost yourself privately...
come home.
Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
His blood is still sufficient.
His grace is still greater than your shame.
His resurrection still announces that death does not get the final word.
And your scandal does not have to write your ending.
The stone in Judges 9 became a place where brothers died.
But centuries later, another stone would be rolled away from another place of death.
And the empty tomb would announce to every broken Gideon, every wandering believer, every ashamed sinner, every exhausted soul, and every person convinced their story is already ruined:
Jesus Christ is alive.
Grace still rewrites stories.
What is happening in my heart after the victory?
Then give Jesus the honest answer.
Because the chapter you're most ashamed of may become the very place where you finally discover how astonishing His grace really is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “ADULTERY IN THE HEART”: Can Sexual Sin Happen Without Physical Contact?
paragraphs: “ADULTERY IN THE HEART”: Can Sexual Sin Happen Without Physical Contact?
Jesus said adultery can happen where nobody else can see it. But what exactly did He mean—and have we misunderstood one of His most uncomfortable warnings?
Nobody touched anybody.
No hotel room.
No secret meeting.
No physical affair.
No incriminating photograph.
Maybe nobody else on earth even knows.
And yet Jesus speaks words so penetrating that they leave nowhere for the human heart to hide.
“Adultery.”
That word usually makes us imagine bodies crossing a forbidden boundary.
Jesus takes us somewhere earlier.
Into the place before the bedroom.
Before the message.
Before the meeting.
Before the physical betrayal.
Into the heart.
And perhaps that is what makes Matthew 5:27–28 so uncomfortable.
Because you can hide a browser history.
You can delete a conversation.
You can close an app.
You can maintain a respectable reputation.
You can sit in church with your Bible open.
But you cannot delete anything from the eyes of Christ.
He sees the heart.
And what He says next is devastating.
Matthew records Jesus saying:
“Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις.”
Ēkousate hoti errethē: Ou moicheuseis.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’”
Then Jesus continues:
“ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman toward desiring her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28.
Read those words again slowly.
Not because Jesus is trying to make ordinary human existence impossible.
Not because noticing that another human being is physically attractive automatically makes someone an adulterer.
Not because temptation itself is identical to surrender.
The wording matters.
Jesus speaks of the one who is “looking”—βλέπων, blepōn—and then gives the direction or purpose of that look:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν.
Pros to epithymēsai autēn.
Toward desiring her.
The verb ἐπιθυμέω, epithymeō, can describe desire, longing, or coveting depending on context. Here the context is adultery.
Jesus is exposing the deliberate cultivation of sexual desire toward someone who is not rightfully yours.
That distinction matters.
There is a difference between seeing and staring.
Between noticing and nourishing.
Between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside.
Between an unwanted thought flashing through the mind and choosing to replay the fantasy because you enjoy what it gives you.
You may not control every temptation that appears.
But what do you do with it when it arrives?
That is where this passage becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes sexual sin does not begin when two bodies touch.
Sometimes it begins when the heart whispers:
Stay.
Look again.
Imagine more.
Nobody will know.
And instead of fleeing, we feed it.
That second look becomes a third.
That image becomes another.
That profile becomes a ritual.
That conversation becomes increasingly suggestive.
That private fantasy becomes somewhere we repeatedly visit.
Nothing physical has happened.
Yet something is happening.
Jesus refuses to let outward respectability become camouflage for inward rebellion.
That is the scandal of His words.
A person can appear faithful while privately feeding unfaithfulness.
A husband can technically never touch another woman while repeatedly undressing women in his imagination.
A wife can never physically enter another man's bed while secretly nurturing erotic or romantic fantasies about someone else.
A single believer can say, “But I'm not married, so technically I can't cheat on anyone,” while still training the heart to consume people sexually rather than honor them as image-bearers of God.
Pornography can make this deception especially easy.
Nobody touched you.
You touched nobody.
So the conscience tries to negotiate.
“At least I didn't actually do anything.”
But Jesus destroys the loophole.
The Kingdom of God is not merely concerned with where your body has been.
Christ cares about what your heart is becoming.
That is why this teaching is so much bigger than a prohibition against adultery.
Jesus is revealing something about holiness itself.
God does not merely want restrained hands.
He wants transformed hearts.
And suddenly the question changes.
It is no longer only:
“Did I sleep with someone?”
It becomes:
“What am I teaching my heart to desire?”
What do you repeatedly watch when nobody is around?
Whose body have you turned into material for private fantasy?
Which conversations do you keep returning to because they give you an emotional or sexual thrill you know you should not be feeding?
What would embarrass you if your spouse saw it?
What would you immediately close if Jesus physically walked into the room?
And perhaps the most piercing question of all:
Why are we imagining that He wasn't already there?
There is a strange insanity to secret sin.
We hide from people...
while sinning before the God from whom nothing is hidden.
We delete evidence...
while standing before the One who searches hearts.
We become terrified that a husband, wife, parent, pastor, friend, or church member might discover what God already sees perfectly.
Yet this is where this article could become crushing if we stopped too soon.
Because Matthew 5 was never given so that respectable sinners could point fingers at less respectable sinners.
Jesus takes the commandment and drives it through our carefully constructed categories until every self-righteous person has a problem.
Maybe you never committed physical adultery.
But have you ever deliberately cherished lust?
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus knows.
And if that makes you uncomfortable...
good.
But don't run from Him.
Because the One exposing the darkness is also the One who came to rescue sinners from it.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not the announcement that sexually spotless people may approach Jesus.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The sexually broken.
The porn-addicted.
The adulterer.
The fantasizer.
The ashamed.
The person who promised God, “Never again,” and then fell again.
The person whose marriage has been wounded.
The person carrying memories they desperately wish they could erase.
The person who has learned how to worship publicly while collapsing privately.
Jesus did not come because humanity was clean.
He came because we weren't.
And grace does not mean Jesus suddenly calls darkness light.
Grace means our darkness does not have the final word when we come to Christ in repentance and faith.
This is where many people misunderstand the Gospel.
They imagine only two possibilities.
Either minimize the sin so they don't have to feel ashamed...
or admit the sin and believe they are permanently ruined.
Jesus offers neither.
He does not minimize sin.
And He does not tell the repentant sinner that redemption is impossible.
He exposes.
He calls us to repentance.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
He teaches us to fight what once enslaved us.
That is why biblical conviction and condemnation are not identical experiences.
Conviction brings the darkness into the light so that we can turn toward Christ.
Hopeless shame whispers:
“Hide from God.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Sin says:
“Keep pretending.”
Jesus says:
“Follow Me.”
Your sexual history may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to write the final chapter of your life.
Your worst night is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Your secret browser history is not stronger than the cross.
Your affair is not stronger than the cross.
Your fantasies are not stronger than the cross.
Your shame is not stronger than the cross.
But grace is not permission to keep feeding what nailed Christ to that cross.
Grace teaches us to come out of hiding.
And Jesus' next words in Matthew 5 show just how seriously He wants His disciples to treat sin.
He speaks of tearing out the right eye and cutting off the right hand if they cause someone to stumble.
Jesus is using deliberately shocking language to communicate the radical seriousness with which sin must be confronted.
He is not giving Christians permission to mutilate their bodies.
Removing an eye would not remove lust from the heart anyway.
The problem Jesus has just identified is deeper.
The heart needs transformation.
But sometimes genuine repentance requires ruthless practical changes.
Delete the account.
Block the website.
End the flirtation.
Stop privately messaging the person.
Move the phone out of the bedroom.
Stop calling pornography “stress relief.”
Stop calling emotional infidelity “just friendship.”
Stop deliberately placing yourself where you know your resistance repeatedly collapses.
Tell a mature, trustworthy believer that you need accountability.
If your marriage has been wounded, pursue truth, repentance, wise pastoral care, and where appropriate professional counseling.
Stop protecting the darkness that is destroying you.
Because you cannot simultaneously starve a sin and keep feeding it.
And please hear this carefully:
The goal is not merely behavior modification.
You can install every filter available and still have a heart desperately searching for another idol.
The deepest question is not merely, “How do I stop looking?”
It is:
“What am I looking for when I look?”
Comfort?
Escape?
Power?
Validation?
Novelty?
Control?
Intimacy?
A momentary anesthesia for loneliness?
Sexual sin often promises something much larger than sex.
It whispers that it can soothe pain.
Make you feel wanted.
Make you forget.
Give you control.
Help you escape.
Then it takes far more than it promised to cost.
It offers pleasure without covenant.
Intimacy without vulnerability.
Bodies without souls.
Desire without responsibility.
Escape without healing.
And afterward?
The screen goes dark.
The fantasy ends.
The conversation stops.
And somehow the emptiness remains.
Because pornography cannot love you.
Fantasy cannot know you.
Lust cannot heal you.
And another human body cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Only Jesus can meet the deepest hunger of the human soul.
That does not mean sexual desire itself is evil.
God created human sexuality.
Within His design it is not dirty, embarrassing, or inherently sinful.
The problem is not that human beings can experience desire.
The problem is what sin does with desire.
It takes a gift and detaches it from God's boundaries.
It takes a person made in God's image and turns that person into an object for consumption.
Lust asks:
“What can this person's body give me?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor this person before God?”
Lust consumes.
Love seeks another's good.
Lust reduces.
Love recognizes dignity.
Lust wants the body while ignoring the soul.
Christ calls us to see the whole person.
And that is why victory cannot simply mean becoming better at looking away.
Christ wants to teach us how to see differently.
To see women as daughters, sisters, neighbors, and image-bearers—not objects.
To see men as sons, brothers, neighbors, and image-bearers—not fantasies.
To see our spouses not as possessions but as people entrusted to our faithful love.
To see our own bodies not as instruments for endless appetite but as belonging to God.
Maybe this article found you after another failure.
Maybe five minutes ago you were looking at something you shouldn't.
Maybe nobody knows about the conversations.
Maybe you have carried a secret for years.
Maybe you're reading this while lying beside someone who believes your heart belongs completely to them.
And something inside you is breaking.
Do not waste that moment.
Don't turn conviction into another promise you make emotionally tonight and forget tomorrow morning.
Bring the truth into the light.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible.
It is turning.
It is agreeing with God about the sin and turning toward Christ.
You may need to confess.
You may need accountability.
You may need to make changes that feel drastic.
You may need to surrender access to something you have protected for years.
But do not confuse losing access to your chains with losing freedom.
The chain was never freedom.
Jesus is.
And if you have already fallen sexually, hear the Gospel before shame distorts everything you just read.
Jesus did not die only for the sins you consider respectable.
The cross was built for guilty people.
First John 1:9 says that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
First Corinthians 6 describes people whose former lives included serious sexual sin, then gives one of the most beautiful turns in Scripture:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they became their own saviors.
They were washed.
Sanctified.
Justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewriting what the scandal thought would be the ending.
Maybe that is your word today.
Were.
You were enslaved.
You were hiding.
You were living two lives.
You were feeding something that was slowly consuming you.
But Jesus Christ is still saving sinners.
And sanctification means your present struggle does not have to become your permanent identity.
You may have to fight repeatedly.
Fight.
You may need someone beside you.
Tell them.
You may stumble and need to repent again.
Run back to Christ.
Do not turn repeated temptation into permission for surrender.
And do not turn a fall into an excuse to stay on the ground.
Get up.
Come into the light.
Follow Jesus again.
Somebody reading this has spent years believing, “If people knew what goes through my mind, they would never look at me the same way.”
Perhaps.
People are imperfect.
But Jesus already knows.
Every thought.
Every search.
Every fantasy.
Every failure.
Every rationalization.
Every relapse.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come.
Not because the sin doesn't matter.
Because the Savior is greater.
No graphic confession.
No performance.
Just honesty.
Someone reading the comments may realize for the first time that they are not the only Christian fighting a war nobody else can see.
And perhaps your honesty will help another person choose the light tonight.
Not because saving a post changes a heart.
Only God can do that.
Come back when the screen starts whispering.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating.
Come back when your mind tells you, “Just once.”
Then remember:
Jesus wants more for you than momentary escape.
You do not have to know who they are.
You probably won't.
That is the point.
Some of the fiercest spiritual battles happen behind completely ordinary profile pictures.
Send it privately to a struggling believer.
Share it with a married couple rebuilding trust.
Send it to the friend who keeps returning to pornography and believes change is impossible.
Let truth travel farther than shame.
Stay close to the Word.
Stay close to believers who will tell you the truth.
Stay close to Christ.
Christian giving must not be manipulated.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving is to come from what a person has purposed in the heart—not reluctantly or under compulsion.
He will not.
You cannot.
The favor we desperately need is found in Jesus Christ, not in a transaction.
If you want to support that mission voluntarily and help us reach farther:
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help.
Because somewhere tonight there is a person hiding behind a locked screen.
A spouse wondering why secrecy has entered the marriage.
A teenager learning desire from pornography before learning covenant from Scripture.
A believer convinced that because the sin happened only in the imagination, God does not care.
Another believer convinced that because God does care, God could never want them again.
Both need the truth.
Jesus takes hidden sin more seriously than we sometimes want Him to.
And Jesus receives repentant sinners more graciously than shame wants us to believe.
That is the tension of the Gospel.
Sin is worse than our excuses say.
Grace is greater than our despair says.
The answer to “Can sexual sin happen without physical contact?” is therefore yes: Jesus explicitly teaches that adultery can be committed in the heart when lust is deliberately cultivated.
But His teaching is not an invitation to obsessive terror over every involuntary thought or every moment of noticing another person's attractiveness.
It is a summons to stop making peace with cherished lust.
Stop feeding it.
Stop protecting it.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off what feeds it.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in the light.
And begin learning to see human beings again—not as bodies to consume, but as souls bearing the image of God.
Maybe nobody else knows your scandal.
Jesus does.
And strangely...
that may be the best news you have heard all day.
Because the One who knows the whole story is the very One who went to the cross to save sinners.
The secret you are terrified of bringing into Christ's light may be the very place where grace begins rewriting your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DAVID’S KINDNESS STARTED A WAR
paragraphs:
WHY DAVID’S KINDNESS STARTED A WAR
He Sent Comfort. They Saw a Conspiracy. And What Happened Next Reveals Something Terrifying About the Way We Can Respond to Grace.
Sometimes a war does not begin with hatred.
Sometimes it begins with kindness offered to someone who has become too suspicious to receive it.
A king had died.
His son was grieving.
David heard the news and decided to do something remarkably human.
He would send comfort.
No invasion.
No threat.
No ultimatum.
No army marching toward the border.
Just men carrying condolences to a grieving son.
And before the story was over, those men would be publicly humiliated, armies would mobilize, thousands of soldiers would enter the conflict, and what began as an act of kindness would become war.
But here is the part that should make us uncomfortable.
The kindness was not the problem.
The interpretation of the kindness was.
And somewhere inside this ancient story may be a frightening picture of something we still do today.
We become wounded enough to distrust love.
Proud enough to reject correction.
Suspicious enough to question mercy.
Ashamed enough to attack the hand reaching toward us.
And sometimes we become so accustomed to expecting betrayal that when grace finally arrives at our door...
we treat it like an enemy.
That is where the story begins.
Second Samuel 10 tells us that the king of the Ammonites died and his son Hanun became king in his place.
David remembered Hanun's father, Nahash.
So David said:
“אֶעֱשֶׂה־חֶסֶד”
’e‘eseh-chesed.
“I will show kindness.”
That Hebrew word matters.
חֶסֶד — chesed.
It is one of the richest words in the Old Testament. Depending upon its context, it carries ideas of kindness, loyalty, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, mercy, or faithful devotion.
David was not announcing war.
He was expressing chesed.
Second Samuel 10:2 records his intention:
“אֶעֱשֶׂה־חֶסֶד עִם־חָנוּן בֶּן־נָחָשׁ כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה אָבִיו עִמָּדִי חֶסֶד”
In context:
“I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me.”
So David sent servants to comfort Hanun concerning the death of his father.
Picture the scene.
Hanun has inherited a throne while burying a father.
Grief and power have arrived almost simultaneously.
Then representatives from Israel appear.
They have come because David remembers kindness and intends to answer kindness with kindness.
But before Hanun can simply receive the gesture, voices gather around him.
His officials begin whispering.
Do you really believe David sent these men because he honors your father?
Do you really believe they came to comfort you?
Maybe they are spies.
Maybe they are studying the city.
Maybe David intends to overthrow you.
The biblical text records their suspicion plainly.
The men carrying consolation are reinterpreted as men carrying conspiracy.
Nothing in the passage tells us that David secretly sent them as spies.
The stated intention is chesed and consolation.
Yet Hanun listens to suspicious counsel.
And this is where an ancient political disaster suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us know exactly what suspicion can do to a human heart.
Someone loves you...
and you search for the hidden motive.
Someone apologizes...
and you assume manipulation.
Someone tries to correct you...
and you hear condemnation.
Someone reaches toward you...
and every wound from your past screams, “Don't trust them.”
Sometimes those instincts exist because people really have betrayed us. Scripture never requires gullibility, and biblical wisdom does not mean pretending evil does not exist.
But discernment and cynicism are not the same thing.
Discernment seeks truth.
Cynicism has often already decided what the truth must be.
Hanun had David's messengers standing in front of him.
But he allowed other men's suspicions to tell him what those messengers supposedly meant.
Then suspicion became humiliation.
Hanun seized David's servants.
He shaved off half their beards.
He cut their garments so severely that they were exposed.
Then he sent them away.
Read that slowly.
They arrived carrying sympathy.
They left carrying shame.
They came to comfort a grieving king.
They returned humiliated by him.
The text says the men were:
“נִכְלָמִים מְאֹד”
nikhlamim me’od.
Deeply, exceedingly humiliated.
And David's response to his humiliated servants is one of the quietest beautiful moments in the chapter.
He did not immediately parade their shame before everyone.
He sent people to meet them.
Then he told them to remain in Jericho until their beards had grown back.
Then they could return.
There is tenderness hidden inside that command.
David gave humiliated men somewhere to recover.
He did not demand that they walk immediately back into public view while carrying visible evidence of what had been done to them.
He gave dignity time to heal.
Someone reading this needs that sentence.
Dignity sometimes needs time to heal.
Maybe somebody humiliated you.
Maybe something was exposed.
Maybe people laughed at the chapter of your life that nearly destroyed you.
Maybe your marriage collapsed publicly.
Maybe your addiction became known.
Maybe your failure became somebody else's conversation.
Maybe you made the mistake yourself and now you cannot escape the memory of who you were.
There are wounds that bleed privately and wounds that make you afraid to show your face again.
David looked at humiliated men and effectively told them:
Stay here until you are ready to return.
And centuries later, the Gospel reveals a King infinitely greater than David who receives ashamed people without delighting in their humiliation.
Jesus does not deny our sin.
He deals with it more seriously than we do.
But He does not save sinners by pretending they were never guilty.
He saves sinners by bearing what their guilt deserves.
That is why the cross is simultaneously horrifying and beautiful.
At Calvary, God's holiness is not discarded so mercy can survive.
Justice and mercy meet.
Sin is exposed as deadly.
Grace is revealed as astonishing.
And the innocent Son of God willingly bears the shame of sinners.
Jesus was mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Publicly humiliated.
Crucified.
The One who had no sin entered the place of shame for people drowning in it.
Hebrews tells us that Jesus endured the cross, “despising the shame.”
The King entered our disgrace so redeemed sinners could someday stand before God clothed not in their own righteousness, but in His.
That is why Christianity is not self-improvement with religious vocabulary.
It is rescue.
But return to Hanun for a moment.
Because his tragedy becomes worse.
After humiliating David's servants, the Ammonites realize they have made themselves offensive to David.
And here was the moment when everything might have changed.
Imagine if Hanun had stopped.
Imagine if he had admitted:
I listened to the wrong voices.
I misjudged David.
I humiliated innocent men.
I was wrong.
Scripture does not record him doing that.
Instead, the Ammonites hire military forces.
Their fear of consequences drives them deeper into conflict.
This is one of sin's oldest patterns.
We do wrong.
Then instead of confession, we defend it.
Instead of repentance, we recruit excuses.
Instead of surrender, we build armies around our pride.
One lie requires another.
One hidden message requires another hidden message.
One compromise needs another compromise to protect it.
One secret browser history becomes a carefully guarded life.
One affair becomes layers of deception.
One bitterness becomes an entire theology explaining why forgiveness is impossible.
One wounded ego begins collecting people who will agree that we were justified.
And eventually we are no longer merely protecting ourselves from other people.
We are protecting our sin from the truth.
That is when grace begins to feel threatening.
Not because grace is cruel.
Because grace asks us to stop pretending.
This is where Hanun's story becomes more than history.
It becomes a mirror.
How many wars inside us began because we refused to say three words?
“I was wrong.”
How many relationships died because pride considered apology more painful than separation?
How many years have people spent running from God because they assumed His call to repentance was an attempt to destroy their lives?
The enemy has been repeating variations of the same lie since Eden:
God cannot really be trusted.
His command is keeping something good from you.
His boundaries are oppression.
His truth is hostility.
His authority threatens your freedom.
And when that lie enters the human heart, we begin treating the God who gives life as though He were the enemy of life.
That is the tragedy of sin.
Sin does not merely make us guilty.
It distorts what we love, what we trust, and sometimes even how we interpret the goodness of God.
We begin calling chains freedom and freedom chains.
We hide from the only One who can cover our shame.
We run from the Physician because admitting sickness feels unbearable.
We reject the Savior because accepting salvation requires admitting we cannot save ourselves.
And still...
God comes near.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God looks at rebellion and calls it harmless.
He doesn't.
Not that repentance is optional.
It isn't.
Not that judgment is imaginary.
It isn't.
The scandal is that the holy God against whom we have sinned made the way for sinners to be reconciled to Himself through His Son.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son...”
Jesus did not come merely to make decent people slightly nicer.
He came seeking the lost.
He called sinners to repentance.
He touched the unclean.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He forgave.
He restored.
And then He walked deliberately toward Jerusalem knowing what waited there.
The cross.
Our culture can make the cross decorative because we have seen it on walls, necklaces, buildings, books, and screens.
But crucifixion was scandalous.
Humiliating.
Violent.
Public.
The Roman cross was not originally jewelry.
It was an instrument of execution.
And Christianity makes the staggering proclamation that the sinless Messiah willingly went there.
Paul writes in Greek:
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8 places that declaration inside something breathtaking: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we erased the history.
While sinners.
That is grace.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
The Gospel announces forgiveness and creates a new allegiance.
Repentance is not paying God back for mercy.
You could never pay Him back.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has finally stopped defending the very thing from which Christ came to rescue it.
And perhaps that is why this story hurts.
David's servants came carrying kindness.
Hanun received them as threats.
What are you doing with the grace God is putting in front of you?
Do not answer quickly.
What if the conviction you have been trying to silence is mercy?
What if the Scripture that disturbed you was not God pushing you away, but God exposing the thing destroying you?
What if the Christian who lovingly confronted you was not necessarily your enemy?
What if your exhaustion comes partly from maintaining defenses God never asked you to build?
What if you have spent years fighting a war against surrender?
You know the secret.
You know the bitterness.
You know the habit.
You know the relationship.
You know the pride.
You know what you keep deleting.
You know what happens when nobody is watching.
You know the version of yourself presented at church and the version that appears behind a locked door.
And perhaps you have become extremely good at explaining it.
But explanations cannot wash away sin.
Jesus can.
This is where the story can change.
Hanun's chapter shows what happens when suspicious pride keeps escalating.
Your chapter does not have to end there.
Because you can repent.
Right here.
No performance.
No religious theater.
No carefully polished Christian vocabulary.
Just truth.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
There are few sentences pride hates more.
And few sentences grace makes safer to say.
First John teaches that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide until you become worthy enough to return.
It tells you that Christ is the only sufficient Savior.
Come into the light.
Turn from sin.
Trust Christ.
Stop building armies around what Jesus died to free you from.
And if you have wandered far from God, do not confuse the distance you have traveled with the distance His grace is capable of reaching.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left in which to manufacture an impressive religious résumé.
Scripture is crowded with people whose stories would have looked hopeless if God had stopped writing where human failure put the period.
That is why we keep saying:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history as though your sin never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by changing God's standard.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's future through redemption.
Guilt can become forgiveness.
Rebellion can become repentance.
Bondage can become freedom.
The runaway can come home.
The ashamed can be restored.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The enemy can become family.
The scandal does not have to be the final sentence.
Grace can write what sin never could.
And maybe this article did not find you simply so you could press “like,” feel something for thirty seconds, and continue scrolling.
Maybe somebody you know is living like Hanun.
Suspicious of God.
Wounded.
Defensive.
Building armies around a heart that is secretly terrified.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list is one sleepless night away from giving up.
Maybe they would never walk into a church today.
But they might read something you shared.

If you want your life to glorify God, one practical way is to use what He has entrusted to you, including your voice and your reach, to point people toward Christ. You cannot know whose screen this might reach at exactly the moment they are finally ready to stop running.
Love them. Pray for them. Let the tag mean, “I thought of you, and I want you to know there is still grace.”
There are truths you understand differently when the night gets darker.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind silence.
You do not owe strangers the details of wounds that should remain private. But there is something powerful about believers refusing to pretend that discipleship means never struggling.
We need communities where repentance is not entertainment, broken people are not gossip material, and testimony is not reserved for people whose scars are already neat enough for a stage.
It does not.
Not because financial support earns salvation.
It never could.
Jesus purchased redemption. We don't.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase God's approval.
Not because clicking “share” makes anyone righteous.
Someone is misreading God's conviction as rejection.
Someone thinks they have sinned too badly to return.
Someone is exhausted from protecting a secret.
Someone is surrounded by voices telling them not to trust the King.
Someone is shaving the messengers, so to speak, because receiving grace feels more frightening than continuing the war.
And maybe God can use your ordinary act of sharing biblical truth to place one message in front of them:
You can stop fighting.
You can repent.
You can come home.
Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
The cross is sufficient.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And grace is still calling.
David sent kindness and Hanun heard conspiracy.
God sent His Son, and humanity crucified Him.
Yet even the cross we made into an instrument of rejection became, according to God's saving purpose, the place where redemption was accomplished.
Think about that.
Human beings gave Jesus a cross.
God raised Him from the dead.
Sin wrote scandal.
Grace answered with an empty tomb.
So perhaps the most dangerous question is not whether you have ever failed.
You have.
So have I.
The question is what you will do when grace stands at the gate.
Will you keep listening to the voices telling you to run?
Will you keep defending what is destroying you?
Will you keep hiding behind religion, success, humor, anger, lust, achievement, relationships, money, ministry, or pride?
Or will you finally surrender?
Because the war does not have to continue.
The King you have been running from is the only One who can save you.
And perhaps the grace you have spent years fearing is the very grace that has been pursuing you home.
Do not spend your life fighting the hands that were pierced to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES GOD EXPECT YOU TO BE PERFECT?
paragraphs:
DOES GOD EXPECT YOU TO BE PERFECT?
The Verse That Has Terrified Christians—and the Grace We Keep Missing
“Be perfect.”
Two words.
And depending on what you believe God means by them, they can either pull you toward your Father...
or make you terrified to come near Him.
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you are from trying to be the Christian you think God expects.
You pray, but sometimes your mind wanders.
You worship, but Monday arrives and anxiety comes back.
You promised God you would never return to that sin... and then you returned.
You told yourself you had forgiven them, until their name appeared on your screen and something ugly rose inside your chest.
You know the verses.
You know the worship songs.
You know how to smile when someone at church asks, “How are you?”
“Blessed.”
But there are nights when the performance ends.
The room becomes quiet.
And the question you would never say in front of everybody else crawls out of the darkness:
God... how disappointed are You in me?
Because Jesus really did say something frighteningly serious:
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.” — Matthew 5:48
There it is.
Not a motivational speaker.
Not an overzealous preacher.
Jesus.
And if we rip that sentence away from everything surrounding it, we can turn Christianity into an impossible treadmill:
Try harder.
Fail.
Feel ashamed.
Promise more.
Try harder.
Fail again.
Hide.
Repeat.
But what if the command of Jesus is far deeper—and far more beautiful—than the perfectionism that has been strangling you?
The Greek text reads:
“Ἔσεσθε οὖν ὑμεῖς τέλειοι ὡς ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος τέλειός ἐστιν.”
The word translated “perfect” is τέλειοι — teleioi, from τέλειος — teleios.
It can carry the sense of being complete, mature, brought toward its intended goal.
That does not mean Jesus is saying sin does not matter.
It does not mean holiness is optional.
And it certainly does not mean, “Relax. God doesn't care how you live.”
Jesus never lowered God's holiness to make sinners comfortable.
He did something infinitely greater.
He came to save sinners who could never reach God's holiness by themselves.
And the context of Matthew 5:48 matters enormously.
Immediately before this statement, Jesus says:
“Love your enemies.”
“Bless them that curse you.”
“Do good to them that hate you.”
“Pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.”
Then Jesus points toward the Father, who sends sunlight and rain without limiting His common kindness only to people we think deserve it.
Then comes:
“Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.”
Do you see it?
Jesus is not handing His disciples a checklist for neurotic religious flawlessness.
He is calling them into a mature, whole, Father-reflecting love that refuses to love only the lovable.
And suddenly the verse becomes even more confronting.
Because some of us would rather be religiously impressive than love our enemies.
We would rather count how many chapters we read than forgive the person who wounded us.
We would rather post a Bible verse than pray sincerely for someone who betrayed us.
We would rather appear holy than allow Jesus to invade the bitter room in our hearts where we have kept someone's name locked away for years.
God does care about holiness.
Deeply.
But biblical holiness is not cosmetic Christianity.
It reaches the hidden places.
The grudges.
The fantasies.
The envy.
The secret messages.
The pride nobody corrects because we learned to disguise it as spiritual confidence.
The resentment we justify because “they deserve it.”
The addiction we keep renaming a struggle because repentance sounds too final.
The double life.
The carefully maintained image.
The private compromise beneath the public worship.
And this is where perfectionism becomes dangerous.
Because perfectionism whispers:
Hide until you're better.
The Gospel says:
Come into the light because you cannot heal yourself.
Perfectionism says:
Make yourself acceptable, then approach God.
The Gospel says:
Christ came precisely because sinners could never make themselves acceptable before a holy God.
Perfectionism makes failure the end of your story.
Jesus makes repentance the doorway into another chapter.
This distinction matters because Scripture refuses to pretend Christians instantly become incapable of sin.
John writes to believers:
Then comes breathtaking hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:8–9
Notice what Christianity does not say.
It does not say sin is imaginary.
It does not say guilt is always unhealthy.
It does not say repentance is unnecessary.
It says something far more powerful:
Your sin is real, but the blood of Jesus is greater.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction drags the hidden wound into the light so Christ can deal with it.
Condemnation tells you there is no point coming home.
Conviction says, “This must die.”
Condemnation says, “You might as well die with it.”
Conviction points at your sin.
Condemnation tries to turn your sin into your identity.
But the Gospel announces that for the one who belongs to Jesus Christ:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
Not because your sin became harmless.
Because Christ bore judgment.
That is why the cross is so offensive to human pride.
We desperately want to contribute something to our rescue.
Surely my church attendance counts.
Surely my giving counts.
Surely my Bible reading counts.
Surely being better than that person counts.
But stand beneath the cross long enough and every spiritual résumé begins falling apart.
You don't see Jesus dying beside your accomplishments.
You see Jesus dying in the place of sinners.
The nails announce something your pride hates admitting:
You could not save yourself.
But those same nails announce something your shame desperately needs to hear:
Jesus did not wait for you to become worth saving before He came to save you.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6
Without strength.
Ungodly.
That was the condition.
Grace did not arrive after the cleanup.
Grace entered the crime scene.
This is why Christianity is not the story of good people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of spiritually dead sinners receiving life through Jesus Christ.
It is scandal becoming grace.
It is rebels being reconciled.
It is guilty people being justified.
It is slaves being redeemed.
It is prodigals coming home.
It is graves opening.
It is Jesus rewriting everything.
And perhaps the most astonishing tension appears in Hebrews.
The Greek of Hebrews 10:14 says:
“μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζομένους.”
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.”
Look closely at the tension.
τετελείωκεν — teteleiōken
“He has perfected.”
And:
ἁγιαζομένους — hagiazomenous
Those being sanctified.
Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
And His people are still being sanctified.
Finished accomplishment.
Ongoing transformation.
That is Christianity.
You are not accepted because you finally became impressive enough for God.
Those who are in Christ stand on Christ's finished work.
And the same grace that saves does not leave us comfortably chained to the sins from which Jesus came to deliver us.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Grace welcomes the filthy prodigal home.
And grace does not tell him to move the pigpen into the Father's house.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needs tonight.
Because there are two lies destroying people in opposite directions.
One says:
“I keep failing, therefore God could never want me.”
The other says:
“God forgives me, therefore I don't need to change.”
Neither is the Gospel.
Jesus receives sinners.
Jesus also says, “Follow me.”
Grace is free to us because its cost was paid by Christ.
And the grace that pardons us begins reshaping us.
Paul understood this tension intimately.
Listen to his startling confession:
“Οὐχ ὅτι ἤδη ἔλαβον ἢ ἤδη τετελείωμαι...”
“Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect...”
That is Philippians 3:12.
The apostle Paul essentially says:
I haven't arrived.
Think about that.
Paul.
Missionary.
Apostle.
Sufferer for Christ.
Writer of New Testament letters.
And he refuses to pretend he has reached final perfection.
But he does not use imperfection as permission to stop pursuing Christ.
He continues:
“I press on...”
That may be the word you needed.
Press on.
You fell?
Press on.
Repent.
You discovered pride in yourself again?
Press on.
Bring it to Jesus.
Your prayer life has become cold?
Press on.
Your marriage is hurting?
Press on toward Christ.
You've been secretly fighting something you are ashamed to name?
Stop protecting the darkness.
Bring it into the light.
Seek trustworthy biblical help.
Confess where confession is needed.
Cut off what feeds the sin.
And press on toward Jesus.
Christian maturity is not pretending you never stumble.
It is becoming increasingly unwilling to make peace with what nailed your Savior to a cross.
There is a massive difference between struggling against sin and settling into sin.
The believer may fall.
The believer may weep.
The believer may sometimes crawl.
But the Spirit keeps calling us toward Christ.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Three times.
Imagine hearing yourself say:
“I don't know Him.”
Imagine seeing Jesus afterward.
Imagine remembering every boast you made about your loyalty.
Peter had every reason to believe his greatest failure would become the title over the rest of his life.
THE MAN WHO DENIED JESUS.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, beside a charcoal fire, Jesus restored the disciple who had denied Him.
“Lovest thou me?”
And again.
“Lovest thou me?”
And again.
Three denials did not get the final word.
Grace did.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
His restoration was real.
And Jesus entrusted work to a man with scars in his testimony.
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not editing the ugly chapters out of your biography.
But discovering that when Jesus becomes Lord of the story, even the chapter you thought destroyed everything can become the place where grace shines brightest.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe only you and God know.
Maybe it happened years ago and you still punish yourself every morning for something Christ is calling you to bring fully beneath His mercy.
Maybe your “scandal” isn't sexual sin or addiction.
Maybe it is pride.
Bitterness.
Neglect.
Greed.
Religious hypocrisy.
A destroyed relationship.
A secret habit.
An abortion.
An affair.
A lie that grew larger than you intended.
Years wasted running from God.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying the terrifying thought:
If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.
Jesus already knows.
Not the cleaned-up testimony.
Not the edited version.
Everything.
And the Gospel invitation is not:
“Pretend it didn't happen.”
It is:
Repent and come to Christ.
Confession is not informing God.
He already knows.
Confession is when you stop defending what He came to forgive and transform.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
Faith is not confidence in your ability to maintain a flawless record.
It is resting your hope in Jesus Christ—crucified and risen—and entrusting yourself to Him.
So...
Does God expect you to be perfect?
If by “perfect” you mean, “Does God demand holiness, wholehearted allegiance, mature love, and transformation toward Christlikeness?”
Yes.
Jesus does not call us to comfortable compromise.
“Be ye holy; for I am holy.” — 1 Peter 1:16
But if by “perfect” you mean, “Must I achieve sinless personal perfection through my own performance before God will receive me?”
No.
That is precisely why you need a Savior.
If you could produce the righteousness necessary to rescue yourself, Calvary would be unnecessary.
The Gospel is not God lowering His standard until you can jump over it.
The Gospel is Jesus fulfilling what you could not, bearing sin at the cross, rising from the dead, and becoming the hope of everyone who turns to Him in repentant faith.
And then something extraordinary begins.
He changes you.
Sometimes dramatically.
Sometimes painfully slowly.
Often both.
The person who used to enjoy sin begins grieving it.
The person who never forgave begins learning forgiveness.
The person enslaved to approval begins discovering identity in Christ.
The liar begins loving truth.
The proud begin learning humility.
The bitter begin releasing vengeance.
The sexually broken begin learning purity.
The selfish begin learning generosity.
Not perfectly overnight.
But genuinely.
Because Christianity is not behavior modification with Jesus stickers attached.
It is new life.
And maybe this explains why you're so tired.
You have been trying to produce with willpower what can only grow through abiding in Christ.
Jesus said:
“Without me ye can do nothing.” — John 15:5
Not less.
Nothing.
You need Him when you fail.
You need Him when you succeed.
You need Him when temptation screams.
You need Him when worship feels effortless.
You need Him when the Bible seems alive.
You need Him when you read three paragraphs and feel nothing.
You need Jesus on your best Christian day every bit as truly as on your worst.
Because Jesus isn't merely the emergency room you visit after sin.
He is your life.
So stop asking only:
“How close am I to perfection?”
Ask:
“Am I becoming more like Jesus?”
Am I quicker to repent?
Quicker to forgive?
Slower to judge?
More honest about sin?
More compassionate toward wounded people?
More serious about holiness?
More dependent upon grace?
More willing to obey when obedience costs something?
More willing to love someone who cannot repay me?
More captivated by Christ than I was before?
That is a much harder mirror.
But it is also a far healthier one.
Because maturity does not make you increasingly impressed with yourself.
The closer you walk with Jesus, the less attractive self-glory becomes.
You begin realizing:
Every victory is grace.
Every breath is mercy.
Every answered prayer is kindness.
Every step toward holiness is evidence that God has not abandoned His work.
And when you stumble, you stop running away from the only One who can restore you.
You run toward Him.
Maybe you've spent years hiding because you believed God was waiting for the perfected version of you.
There is no perfected version of you waiting somewhere outside Christ.
There is only the sinner you are...
and the Savior who calls you.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without excuses.
Come without pretending.
Come without your religious résumé.
Come with the mess.
Come with the shame.
Come with the questions.
Come with the sin you're finally ready to stop defending.
Come to Jesus.
He is not asking you to become your own savior.
He is commanding you to follow the Savior you desperately need.
Talk to God.
And if you've experienced the patience of Christ while He continues changing you, tell somebody beneath this article:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer needed to discover they are not the only Christian fighting a battle behind a smile.
And think of one person who desperately needs this truth.
Not twenty.
One.
The friend who thinks God has given up on them.
The son who stopped attending church because shame became unbearable.
The daughter silently questioning whether she can ever come home.
The believer trapped between addiction and self-hatred.
The religious person who looks spotless publicly but is collapsing privately.
Send this directly to them if the conversation needs to remain private.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of loving obedience.

And if this ministry is helping you follow Jesus, stay close. Invite your family. Invite your friends. Invite struggling believers. Invite seekers. Invite the lukewarm. Even invite the unbeliever who has questions nobody has taken seriously.
But before you leave, remember the question that brought you here:
Does God expect you to be perfect?
He calls you toward the perfection, maturity, holiness, and wholehearted love revealed in Christ.
But He never told you to save yourself.
The Christian life is not a flawless person presenting God with an impressive record.
It is a redeemed sinner clinging to a flawless Savior while the Holy Spirit continues the transforming work of sanctification.
So when you fail...
Don't make peace with the sin.
And don't surrender to despair.
Repent.
Confess.
Get back up.
Return to Jesus.
Press on.
Because your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
The hands that were pierced for your sin are still holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE’S MOST SENSUAL BOOK: Why Is Song of Solomon in Scripture?
paragraphs:
THE BIBLE’S MOST SENSUAL BOOK: Why Is Song of Solomon in Scripture?
The book that talks about kisses, bodies, desire, longing, marriage, and love without apologizing—and the reason God refused to leave it out of His Word.
There is a book in your Bible that begins with a kiss.
Not a battle.
Not a miracle.
Not a commandment.
Not a sermon about judgment.
A kiss.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
And suddenly, some Christians become uncomfortable.
Because this does not sound like the language we expect to hear in church.
It sounds intimate.
It sounds passionate.
It sounds almost too human.

And as the poetry continues, it becomes even more startling. A man admires the beauty of a woman. A woman longs for the man she loves. They speak of fragrance, lips, embraces, breasts, gardens, desire, separation, longing, belonging, and consummated love.
And God allowed all of it into Scripture.
That raises a question far more important than whether the Song of Solomon makes modern Christians uncomfortable.
Why is it there?
Why would the Holy Spirit preserve such intensely romantic poetry in the Bible?
And perhaps the question underneath that question is even more personal:
What if our discomfort with Song of Solomon reveals something we have misunderstood about God?
The Hebrew title is breathtaking in its simplicity:
שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים
Shir ha-Shirim.
Literally, “Song of Songs.”
It is a Hebrew superlative—the song above songs, the supreme song.
And then, almost immediately:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu, ki-tovim dodekha miyyayin.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your love is better than wine.”
Song of Songs 1:2.
That is essentially what the Hebrew says. There is no need to sanitize it.
The Bible does not.
The poem is sensual because embodied human love is part of the world God created.

That does not mean every form of sexual desire is therefore holy. Scripture places sexual union within a larger biblical theology of covenant, faithfulness, holiness, self-giving love, and marriage. Jesus Himself reaches back to creation when speaking about marriage: “the two shall become one flesh” (Matthew 19:4–6; cf. Genesis 2:24).
But Christianity has never needed to pretend the body itself is evil.
The body is God's creation.
Marriage is God's creation.
Human sexuality is God's creation.
And sin did not create desire.
Sin distorted what God created.
That distinction changes everything.
Some people have been taught, explicitly or implicitly, that holiness means becoming embarrassed by embodiment.
Song of Songs refuses to cooperate.
The lovers notice each other.
They desire each other.
They miss each other.
They delight in one another.
The woman has a voice, longing, agency, and desire of her own. She is not merely an object being observed. Again and again she speaks.
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.”
Song of Songs 2:16.
Later comes one of the most famous declarations in the entire book:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְדוֹדִי לִי
Ani le-dodi ve-dodi li.
“I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine.”
Song of Songs 6:3.
Notice the mutuality.
Belonging meets belonging.
Love answers love.
This is not the language of exploitation.
It is the language of reciprocal delight.
And that matters enormously in a world that has repeatedly confused lust with love.
Lust asks:
“What can I take from you?”
Covenant love asks:
“How can I faithfully give myself to you?”
Pornography consumes bodies.
Biblical love recognizes persons.
Exploitation reduces someone to an appetite.
Covenant says, “You are my beloved.”
That may be one reason this ancient book feels strangely revolutionary in the modern world.
Our culture is simultaneously saturated with sexuality and starving for intimacy.
Bodies are everywhere.
Covenant is harder to find.
People can expose almost everything about themselves and still remain terrified of actually being known.
We swipe.
We scroll.
We compare.
We fantasize.
We consume.
We perform.
We hide.
And somewhere beneath all of it is an ancient human cry:
Does anybody see me and still want me?
Does anybody know me and remain?
Can I belong to someone without being consumed by them?
Can love survive when beauty changes?
Can desire become something more than appetite?
Song of Songs answers with poetry rather than a lecture.
And then, near its climax, the book says something astonishing:
“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm…”
Then comes the line generations have remembered:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-azzah khamavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death.”
Song of Songs 8:6.
Read that again.
Love is strong as death.
Not cheap.
Not disposable.
Not merely hormonal.
Not merely recreational.
Love lays claim upon the whole person.
And the poem continues with imagery of blazing fire before declaring that many waters cannot extinguish love and floods cannot sweep it away (Song of Songs 8:6–7).
Then comes an extraordinary statement about money:
If someone attempted to buy love with all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.
Love cannot finally be purchased.
That sounds painfully relevant now.
You can purchase attention.
You can purchase an image.
You can purchase an experience.
You can purchase access.
You can purchase artificial intimacy.
But you cannot purchase covenant love.
Real love must be given.
And here the Song begins opening a door into something even larger.
Christians should be careful at this point.
Song of Songs is genuine love poetry. We do not honor Scripture by pretending its human lovers and embodied imagery are not really there.
But neither should Christians read any biblical book as though it existed in isolation from the rest of Scripture.

Throughout the Bible, marriage becomes one of the great images used to describe God's covenant relationship with His people. The prophets use marital imagery concerning the LORD and Israel. In the New Testament, Christ is presented as the Bridegroom, and the church as His bride. Paul explicitly uses marriage to speak about Christ and the church in Ephesians 5:25–32. Revelation culminates in the marriage supper of the Lamb and the appearance of the Bride.
So Christians do not need to claim that every breast, kiss, garden, fragrance, or embrace in Song of Songs is a secret code about Jesus.
That can flatten the poem rather than honor it.
Something more beautiful is happening.
The human love celebrated in the Song exists inside a Bible whose ultimate story is about the covenant-making God pursuing, redeeming, cleansing, and finally dwelling with His people.
Human covenant love can therefore become a signpost.
Not the Savior.
A signpost.
Marriage cannot save you.
Romance cannot save you.
Sex cannot save you.
Finding “the one” cannot save you.
Another human being cannot carry the weight of being your god.
Eventually every earthly romance encounters weakness, misunderstanding, aging, disappointment, sickness, limitation, and death.
Even the most faithful marriage ends, in this age, when death separates husband and wife.
And suddenly the words become haunting:
“Love is strong as death.”
But the Gospel announces something Song of Songs by itself does not yet reveal in fullness.
Jesus Christ went into death.
And came back.
That is where Christian hope moves beyond romantic sentiment.
At the cross, we do not merely encounter an emotion called love.
We encounter love acting.
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
There is the scandal.
He knew what we were.
And He came anyway.
He knew the secret history.
The private compromises.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair.
The fantasy.
The bitterness.
The marriage barely surviving behind smiling photographs.
The loneliness hidden beneath jokes.
The shame attached to what happened to you.
The shame attached to what you did.
The years you cannot recover.
The promises you broke.
The person you used.
The person who used you.
The nights when you begged to be loved and settled for being wanted.
Jesus knew.
And the cross still happened.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at an unimaginable cost to Himself.
Christ does not redeem us because we finally become attractive enough for Him.
He loves sinners and gives Himself to rescue them.
This is why the Gospel is infinitely deeper than the modern command to “love yourself.”
Christianity does not ultimately say, “Look inside yourself until you discover that you were enough all along.”
It says something far more startling:
You were a sinner who could not rescue yourself, and yet you were loved by a Savior who willingly gave Himself for you.
You do not need to pretend the stain is imaginary.
Jesus washes sinners.
You do not need to rename darkness as light.
Jesus brings people out of darkness.
You do not need to rewrite your history to make yourself innocent.
Jesus can redeem a guilty history.
Repentance is not the enemy of love.
Repentance is what happens when grace finally makes hiding unnecessary.
Maybe that is where this article stopped being about an unusual Old Testament book and started becoming about you.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to want love so desperately that you accepted something counterfeit.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe somebody violated your trust and left you carrying shame that never belonged on your shoulders.
Maybe your marriage is cold.
Maybe your bed is empty.
Maybe your spouse is beside you, but somehow you have never felt farther apart.
Maybe you are single and tired of Christians treating marriage like the reward God gives people who finally become spiritual enough.
Maybe you are married and discovered that another human being cannot heal the deepest fracture in your soul.
Maybe you have confused being desired with being loved.
Maybe you have used another person because, for a few minutes, being wanted made the loneliness quieter.
Then morning came.
The screen went dark.
The door closed.
The conversation ended.
The secret remained.
And you were still hungry.
Listen carefully.
Your deepest hunger cannot be healed by pretending you do not have a body.
But neither can it be healed by worshiping your body.
You were made for God.
That is why every created pleasure becomes cruel when we demand that it become our Savior.
The Song celebrates created love.
The Gospel reveals redeeming Love.
And when those truths are kept in their proper places, something beautiful happens.
You can enjoy God's gifts without turning them into gods.
You can celebrate marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can acknowledge sexual desire without becoming its slave.
You can honor singleness without treating it as spiritual failure.
You can repent of sexual sin without believing sexual sin places you beyond Christ's mercy.
You can carry wounds without making those wounds your identity.
You can be honest.
Because Jesus already knows.
That may be the sentence somebody reading this needed tonight.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling sinners to come.
Not to remain unchanged.
To come and be changed.
The Jesus who said, “Come to Me,” is also the Jesus who says, “Follow Me.”
Grace does not merely comfort us inside our chains.
Grace begins breaking them.
Christ forgives.
Christ cleanses.
Christ restores.
Christ teaches us to love differently.
And perhaps this is where Song of Songs becomes unexpectedly confrontational.
Because the book asks whether we still believe love should be precious.
Whether another person's body should be treated as sacred rather than consumable.
Whether faithfulness still matters.
Whether waiting can sometimes be wisdom.
Three times the Song contains a recurring warning not to awaken or arouse love before its proper time (Song of Songs 2:7; 3:5; 8:4).
There is wisdom there.
Desire is powerful.
Fire is beautiful in a fireplace.
The same fire unleashed can burn a house to the ground.
The Christian response to desire is therefore neither worship nor disgust.
It is discipleship.
Bring your desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Bring your relationships there.
Bring your sexuality there.
Bring your marriage there.
Bring your singleness there.
Bring your memories there.
Bring your temptations there.
Bring your wounds there.
Bring the parts you keep editing out of your testimony.
Especially those.
Because Jesus has always been remarkably willing to enter stories respectable people would rather avoid.
A Samaritan woman with a complicated relational history.
A woman caught in adultery.
A prostitute weeping at His feet.
Tax collectors.
Outcasts.
The publicly disgraced.
The privately guilty.
And then the cross itself—the most scandalous place imaginable.
Public humiliation.
Nakedness.
Mockery.
Blood.
Condemnation.
Death.
And God turned the place of apparent defeat into the place from which forgiveness would be proclaimed to the nations.
That is the pattern of the Gospel.
Scandal does not get the final word.
Sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
