By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
So why is the Bible's most sensual book in Scripture?
Because God is not embarrassed by what He created.
Because covenant love matters.
Because bodies matter.
Because fidelity matters.
Because desire needs wisdom.
Because intimacy is more than consumption.
Because human love is beautiful but incapable of being God.
Because Scripture is honest enough to speak to the whole human person rather than merely the polished religious version we present on Sunday.

And because, when read within the whole sweep of Scripture, even the beauty of faithful human love can make the Christian heart ache for something greater—the final communion between Christ and His redeemed people.
The Bible begins with a marriage in a garden.
And near the end of Revelation, Scripture gives us another wedding.
“The marriage of the Lamb has come, and His wife has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).
Then Scripture ends with God dwelling with His people.
No more death.
No more mourning.
No more crying.
No more pain.
The separation ends.
The longing ends.
The exile ends.
The Bridegroom has His Bride.
And suddenly an ancient book filled with longing does not seem so strange inside the Bible after all.
We are creatures who long.
We long to know.
To be known.
To belong.
To be loved without being consumed.
To be seen without being abandoned.
Every human romance whispers about that hunger, but none can completely satisfy it.
Only Christ can finally bring the sinner home to God.
So perhaps the question is no longer, “Why would God put Song of Solomon in the Bible?”
Perhaps the question is:
What have you been asking to satisfy a hunger that was always leading you toward Him?
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Do not let this article disappear into another endless scroll.
Come back when desire becomes confusing, when shame begins speaking again, or when somebody tells you Christianity is embarrassed by human sexuality.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ. But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one voluntary expression of stewardship when you genuinely believe that work is bearing good fruit.
It is to Christ.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are hiding, come into the light.
If you have fallen, call upon Jesus.
If you have been wounded, bring the wound to Him.
If your desires have become your master, surrender them to the One who purchased you with His blood.
If you thought your scandal disqualified you from grace, look again at the cross.
Because the Gospel was never the story of impressive people making themselves worthy enough for God.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing sinners through the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is why one of Scripture's strangest, most sensual, most beautiful books belongs exactly where God placed it.
It reminds us that we were created to love.
The rest of Scripture teaches us how deeply that love has been wounded by sin.
And Jesus shows us what redeeming love ultimately costs.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A Savior who still receives sinners.
So when shame whispers, “After everything you've done, who could possibly want you?”
Do not answer with your feelings.
Answer with Calvary.
The deepest love story in Scripture is not that you finally found someone worth loving—it is that, in Jesus Christ, holy Love came looking for sinners who could never save themselves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL ASKED WHY CHRISTIANS WERE JOINING THEIR BODIES TO PROSTITUTES
paragraphs: PAUL ASKED WHY CHRISTIANS WERE JOINING THEIR BODIES TO PROSTITUTES
What Paul said next in 1 Corinthians 6 was not merely a warning about sex. It was a devastating reminder that Jesus did not redeem your soul while leaving your body behind.
There are Bible passages we like to frame.
There are Bible passages we like to underline.
And then there are Bible passages that seem to reach through the page, put a hand on the secret part of our lives, and ask a question we desperately hoped nobody would ever ask.
First Corinthians 6 is one of those passages.
Paul is writing to Christians.
Not pagans outside the church.
Not people who had never heard the Gospel.
Christians.
People who confessed Jesus.
People who had been washed.
People who had been sanctified.
People Paul could remind, only a few sentences earlier, that their former lives did not have to define them anymore:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε” — kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That little word carries an ocean of grace.

Paul does not pretend Corinth has a spotless past. He openly names sexual sin, idolatry, adultery, greed, drunkenness, abusive speech and exploitation. Then he turns toward people whose histories were anything but clean and essentially says:
That was you.
But something happened.
You were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is the atmosphere in which we must read what comes next. Paul is not throwing stones at sexually broken people from a safe religious distance.
He is speaking to redeemed people who are in danger of forgetting what redemption means.
And then he asks a question so uncomfortable that almost two thousand years later, Christians still feel its force.
“οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν μέλη Χριστοῦ ἐστιν;”
Ouk oidate hoti ta sōmata hymōn melē Christou estin?
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
Then comes the shock.
“ἄρας οὖν τὰ μέλη τοῦ Χριστοῦ ποιήσω πόρνης μέλη;”
Should I take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?
Paul answers:
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
May it never be.

The Greek text is unmistakably physical. Paul uses sōmata—bodies. He uses melē—members, parts belonging to a larger whole. He uses pornēs, from pornē—a prostitute. His argument is not that the human body is dirty.
It is almost exactly the opposite.
Your body matters so much that Paul connects what you do with it to your union with Christ.
And suddenly this ancient letter becomes painfully modern.
Because we have become experts at dividing ourselves.
Sunday belongs to Jesus.
Monday belongs to ambition.
The prayer life belongs to Jesus.
The browser history belongs to us.
The worship belongs to Jesus.
The private messages belong to us.
The Bible app belongs to Jesus.
The hidden folder belongs to us.
The public Christian identity belongs to Jesus.
The secret appetite...
well...
we tell ourselves that is nobody else's business.
Paul destroys that illusion.
Your body is not a spiritual side issue.
Your sexuality is not disconnected from your discipleship.
What happens behind a locked door does not become spiritually meaningless simply because nobody from church can see it.
And what happens on a screen can still train the desires of a real human heart.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe the people who read your Christian posts would never imagine it.
Maybe you have become so skilled at deleting the evidence that even you have started pretending there is nothing left to confess.
But there is Someone in the room.
Christ.
That is what makes Paul's argument so piercing.
He does not merely ask, “Why are you doing something immoral?”
He asks something deeper:
Have you forgotten whose you are?
Paul continues:
“ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν.”
The one joined to a prostitute is one body with her.
Then Paul reaches all the way back to Genesis:
“The two will become one flesh.”
And immediately he places beside that another reality:
“ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν.”
Ho de kollōmenos tō Kyriō hen pneuma estin.
The one joined to the Lord is one spirit with Him.
Notice the repeated word behind “joined”: kollaō.
To join.
To attach.
To cling.
Paul wants the Corinthians to understand that sex cannot simply be reduced to appetite.
The culture may say, “It is only physical.”
Paul says your physical life belongs inside a much larger spiritual reality.
The culture says, “It is my body.”
Paul is about to answer:
Not ultimately.
The culture says, “Nobody got hurt.”
Paul asks whether we have considered what sin does to the person committing it.
The culture says, “Follow the desire.”
Paul says:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not keep it close enough to enjoy but far enough away to maintain plausible deniability.
Not see how near you can stand before falling.
Flee.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is close the tab.
Delete the number.
End the secret conversation.
Walk out of the room.
Cancel the rendezvous.
Put the phone somewhere else.
Confess to a mature believer who will actually hold you accountable.
Stop calling bondage “a struggle” when you have quietly arranged your life so the temptation always has an unlocked door.
There are temptations Scripture tells us to resist.
Here, Paul tells us to run.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why.
You have promised God before.
“Never again.”
Then again happened.
You cried.
You repented.
You felt clean for three days.
Seven days.
Maybe three months.
Then loneliness came.
Or anger.
Or rejection.
Or boredom.
Or opportunity.
The screen lit up.
The old person messaged.
The memory returned.
The fantasy began.
And somewhere between temptation and surrender, you heard that terrible whisper:
You have already failed before.
What difference does one more time make?
A tremendous difference.
Not because one more failure makes you unreachable.
But because the voice telling you to surrender is lying about who owns you.
Listen to Paul.
“καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν.”
Kai ouk este heautōn.
“You are not your own.”
Then:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.”
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“You were bought with a price.”
And therefore:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
The Gospel underneath the command.
You were bought.
Paul does not say, “Clean yourself up so Jesus might consider purchasing you.”
Bought.
The transaction precedes the command.
Grace precedes obedience.
Redemption becomes the foundation of holiness.

Christ's claim upon the Christian is not the claim of an abusive master purchasing disposable property. It is the claim of the Redeemer who gave Himself to rescue sinners and now calls those redeemed people to live as people who belong to Him.
You were bought with a price.
What price?
Paul does not spell it out in this particular verse, but the center of his Gospel leaves no mystery about the direction of his thought.
Jesus Christ gave Himself.
The Son of God went to the cross.
The sinless One bore judgment for sinners.
The blood was real.
The nails were real.
The suffering was real.
The death was real.
And the resurrection was real.

In fact, resurrection is already part of Paul's argument in this very passage: God raised the Lord and will also raise believers by His power. That means Christianity does not treat your body as temporary garbage while God cares only about an invisible soul.
God intends resurrection.
Your body matters to Him.
And that changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“How much can I get away with and still call myself Christian?”
The question becomes:
“How can this body, purchased by Christ, glorify the One who purchased me?”
Your eyes can glorify God.
Your hands can glorify God.
Your sexuality can glorify God.
Your singleness can glorify God.
Your marriage can glorify God.
Your phone can be handled in a way that glorifies God.
Your bedroom can glorify God.
Your private decisions can glorify God.
Your refusal can glorify God.
Your repentance can glorify God.
Even the body in which you once sinned can become the body through which you now obey.
That is grace.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of this chapter is hidden just before all of these warnings.
Paul had already told them:
“And such were some of you.”
Some of you were sexually immoral.
Some of you were adulterers.
Some of you were greedy.
Some of you were drunkards.
Some of you exploited people.
But—
you were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified.
Paul can confront their sin fiercely because he believes Christ can transform sinners completely.
Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people should congratulate themselves for being cleaner than everyone else.
It is the announcement that guilty people can be washed.
The prostitute needs Jesus.
The person visiting the prostitute needs Jesus.
The pornography addict needs Jesus.
The adulterer needs Jesus.
The virgin needs Jesus.
The married person needs Jesus.
The sexually disciplined person needs Jesus.
The person who fell last night needs Jesus.
The person who has been walking faithfully for twenty years still needs Jesus.
Nobody reaches the cross with clean hands.
We come because we need mercy.
And there is something especially dangerous about Christians discussing sexual sin as though the only people who need repentance are “those people out there.”
Paul was writing to the church.
That should humble us.
The church can sing while hiding.
Preach while hiding.
Serve while hiding.
Lead while hiding.
Smile for photographs while hiding.
Post Scripture while hiding.
And hiding can become so normal that exposure begins to feel more frightening than bondage.
But Jesus did not die so that you could become better at hiding.
He died to bring sinners into the light.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“You are filthy. Run away from God.”
Biblical conviction says:
“This is sin. Run toward Christ.”
Condemnation tells you your failure is your identity.
The Gospel tells repentant believers that sin must be confessed and forsaken precisely because Christ has given them a new identity.
That is why the words immediately preceding this passage matter so much:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Maybe that word needs to become personal tonight.
Pornography does not have to write the final chapter.
Adultery does not have to write the final chapter.
Promiscuity does not have to write the final chapter.
Sexual compromise does not have to write the final chapter.
Your worst night does not have to become the title over the rest of your life.
The cross is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that tells sin it does not matter.
Grace powerful enough to call sin what God calls it and still open the door for the sinner to come home.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that cleanses.
Grace that teaches us to say no.
Grace that gets into the places we thought would always remain chained.
Grace that does not merely improve the scandal.
Grace rewrites the story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have been asking God to remove the consequences when what He wants first is your surrender.
Maybe you have been asking Him to make temptation disappear while protecting the very access points through which temptation keeps entering.
Maybe you want freedom without confession.
Restoration without repentance.
Victory without fleeing.
Jesus loves you too much to cooperate with the version of Christianity that lets you keep your chains as souvenirs.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Christ purchased redemption.
But genuine repentance stops defending the darkness and turns toward God.
Tell Jesus the truth.
He already knows.

If another person has been sinned against, biblical repentance may also require truth, responsibility, wisdom, restitution where appropriate, and a willingness to face consequences rather than using “grace” as an escape hatch.

And if your sexual history includes coercion, abuse, exploitation, or something done to you against your will, do not twist Paul's words into an accusation against yourself. Someone else's sin against your body is not your moral guilt. Seek wise pastoral and professional help where needed. Christ's compassion is not reserved for people whose wounds are simple.
But if this passage is exposing something you chose...
do not scroll quickly because you feel ashamed.
Stay here.
Not with me.
With Christ.
You are not being invited merely to feel terrible.
You are being invited to repent.
Those are not the same thing.
Judas regretted.
Peter wept and returned.
The Gospel does not merely produce people who hate what they have done.
It produces people who turn toward the Savior.
So turn.
Even if your voice shakes.
Even if you have prayed this prayer before.
Even if you are ashamed that you are still fighting something you thought you would have conquered years ago.
Turn again.
Jesus Christ is still the Savior of sinners.
And if you belong to Him, your battle for holiness is not an attempt to persuade Him to love you.
It is the response of someone who has been bought with a price.
Maybe tonight your prayer is only:

“Jesus, I have been treating as mine what You purchased. Forgive me. Clean me. Teach me to flee what dishonors You. Take my eyes, my thoughts, my desires, my relationships, my sexuality, my habits, my phone, my loneliness, my body. I belong to You.”
If this exposed something hidden, you do not have to describe your sin publicly. But you do not have to pretend either.
Let somebody know there is a real human being behind the screen who still wants Jesus more than the chains.
And if Christ has already brought you out of sexual bondage, shame, adultery, pornography, or another hidden prison, perhaps your comment should be:
Your testimony might become the reason somebody else realizes failure does not have to be final.
Not because an article can save you.
Only Christ saves.
Come back to Paul's words:
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
Glorify God in your body.
Not as a performance of spirituality. Not as a way of earning favor with God. Share it because somebody in your circle may be fighting a battle nobody knows exists.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.
Share it with the person who thinks sexual failure has permanently disqualified them from grace.
And yes, send it to the person who does not yet believe, because Christianity's message is not “good people save themselves.”
It is that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
But voluntary support can help Christian teaching and discipleship resources continue reaching people who might otherwise never encounter them.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has gone cold.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christians only know how to condemn broken people.
Let them encounter the scandalous message at the center of Christianity:
Sin is more serious than we wanted to admit.
Grace is greater than we dared to believe.
And Jesus is better than the chains we keep running back to.
Paul's words remain uncomfortable because they refuse to let us reduce Christianity to something that happens inside our thoughts.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your private life matters.
Your choices matter.
Holiness matters.
But underneath every command stands something even more breathtaking.
A price was paid.
Christ did not look at ruined sinners and walk away.
He came for them.
He died for them.
He rose again.
And those who belong to Him are no longer required to live as prisoners of the person they used to be.
“And such were some of you.”
Maybe one day somebody will describe the sin currently tormenting you...
and by the grace of Jesus Christ, you will be able to whisper:
That was me.
That was who I was.
But Jesus found me there.
Jesus forgave me there.
Jesus began changing me there.
I thought my scandal had already written the ending.
Then grace picked up the pen.
The sin you thought would become your final chapter may become the very place where future generations see just how completely Jesus Christ can rewrite a human life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN YOUR PASTOR QUIETLY BECOMES YOUR GOD
paragraphs:
WHEN YOUR PASTOR QUIETLY BECOMES YOUR GOD
You may still call him “Pastor.” You may still call Jesus “Lord.” But if one man’s voice can no longer be questioned, tested, or disobeyed without making you feel as though you have betrayed God Himself… something sacred may have been stolen from the throne.
There is a kind of idolatry that never bows before a statue.
It carries a Bible.
It sings worship songs.
It sits in the front row.
It says, “Amen, Pastor.”
It serves faithfully, gives generously, defends the ministry, attends every gathering, reposts every sermon, and tells everyone how “anointed” the man of God is.
And sometimes…
without realizing when it happened…
it becomes more afraid of disappointing the pastor than grieving Jesus Christ.
That sentence may make some people angry.
But perhaps an even more frightening question is this:
If your pastor were wrong about something, would you still be able to recognize it?
Or has his voice become so intertwined with the voice of God in your heart that questioning him feels like questioning God?
Read that again.
Because this article is not an attack on pastors.

Faithful pastors are gifts to Christ’s church. Scripture commands believers to respect those who labor among them, esteem faithful leaders, obey godly leadership, and honor elders who lead well. Christianity does not teach rebellion disguised as “discernment.” It does not give bitter people permission to slander shepherds, despise authority, or turn every disagreement into accusations of spiritual abuse.
But neither does Scripture give any pastor the throne that belongs to Jesus.
And that is where the danger begins.
Not when you love your pastor.
Not when you honor your pastor.
Not when you receive correction from your pastor.
Not when you thank God for your pastor.
The danger begins when the servant becomes functionally indispensable and Christ becomes strangely secondary.
Paul confronted something disturbingly similar in Corinth.
Christians were beginning to build identities around their preferred spiritual leaders.
“I follow Paul.”
“I follow Apollos.”
“I follow Cephas.”
Paul’s response was devastatingly simple:
“Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?”
That question still cuts through celebrity Christianity two thousand years later.
Was your pastor crucified for you?
Did your pastor bear the wrath your sins deserved?
Did nails enter your pastor’s hands for your redemption?
Did your pastor rise from the grave?
Will your pastor sit upon the throne of judgment?
Can your pastor forgive sins by his own authority?
Can your pastor give eternal life?
Then why would any human shepherd occupy the place in your soul reserved for the Shepherd who purchased you with His blood?
Paul later describes himself and Apollos using a wonderfully humbling Greek word:
διάκονοι — diakonoi.
Servants.
Ministers.
Paul asks:
“Τί οὖν ἐστιν Ἀπολλῶς; τί δέ ἐστιν Παῦλος; διάκονοι δι’ ὧν ἐπιστεύσατε…”
In context, the thought is essentially:
“What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed…”
Notice what Paul refuses to become.
The destination.
Paul understood something every pastor, preacher, prophet, teacher, evangelist, Christian creator, ministry founder, and spiritual mentor must remember:
A servant of Christ is supposed to help you see Jesus more clearly—not make himself impossible to see around.
The faithful shepherd does not need your worship.
He wants your maturity.
He does not need you emotionally dependent upon his personality.
He wants you dependent upon Christ.
He does not panic when you open your Bible and examine what he preached.
He should rejoice.
That is exactly what happened in Berea.
Paul was an apostle.
Think about that.
If anyone could have walked into town demanding unquestioning acceptance, surely an apostle of Jesus Christ could have tried.
Yet Acts 17:11 praises the Bereans because they received the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
They listened.
Then they checked.
They respected the messenger.
But Scripture remained the measuring line.
This destroys one of the most dangerous ideas ever allowed to grow inside Christian culture:
“If you question the pastor, you are questioning God.”
No.
Not automatically.
You can dishonor a pastor through arrogance, gossip, rebellion, false accusation, or contempt.
But carefully testing teaching against Scripture is not rebellion.
It is biblical discernment.
The Bereans examined even apostolic preaching.
So ask yourself something uncomfortable.
When your pastor teaches something you cannot reconcile with Scripture, what happens inside you first?
Do you think, “I need to search the Word”?
Or…
“He must be right.”
There is a difference.
A frightening difference.
Because the moment a human being becomes incapable of being wrong in your mind, that person has begun occupying territory no human being was meant to possess.
Maybe you have said it yourself:
“Pastor said it, so that settles it.”
But Christian faith does not ultimately rest upon Pastor said.
It rests upon God has spoken.
Your pastor may explain Scripture.
He does not own Scripture.
He may preach the truth.
He does not manufacture truth.
He may shepherd Christ’s sheep.
He does not own Christ’s sheep.
And perhaps this is where the article becomes painfully personal.
Maybe someone warned you once.
Maybe your spouse said, “I think something about this church is becoming unhealthy.”
And instead of listening, you immediately defended the pastor.
Maybe your child expressed discomfort.
You dismissed it.
Maybe another believer raised a legitimate biblical concern.
You called them rebellious.
Maybe someone left the congregation, and before hearing their story, you assumed they had abandoned God because they had left your pastor.
That should trouble us.
Leaving a particular church is not necessarily leaving Christ.
Disagreeing with a pastor is not necessarily rejecting biblical authority.
And loyalty to an institution is not automatically loyalty to Jesus.
Sometimes Christians become so emotionally fused with a ministry that criticism of the ministry feels like persecution of Christ Himself.
That is dangerous.
Because Jesus does not need a public-relations department willing to silence truth to protect His reputation.
He is the Truth.
If something is true, Christians should not fear bringing it into the light.
Here is another warning sign.
You need your pastor’s approval before you can feel that God approves of you.
His praise makes you feel spiritually alive.
His disappointment destroys you.
Being noticed by him feels like being noticed by heaven.
Being overlooked by him feels like God has forgotten you.
Now pastoral encouragement can be beautiful.
We all need brothers, sisters, mentors, teachers, and shepherds.
But no pastor was designed to carry the crushing weight of becoming your functional mediator before God.
There is already a Mediator.
Jesus Christ.
You do not need your pastor standing between your soul and the Father as though access to God runs through the pastor’s personality.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Through Christ, redeemed sinners are brought near to God.
Your confidence before God rests in Jesus—not in whether a respected preacher remembers your name.
And there is another sign that is even easier to miss.
You know your pastor’s sermons better than you know your Bible.
You can quote his catchphrases.
You know his stories.
You recognize his theology.
You have watched hundreds of clips.
But remove his voice from your life for thirty days…
and suddenly you do not know how to feed yourself spiritually.
That is not spiritual maturity.
A good pastor feeds sheep.
A great pastor also teaches sheep to keep feeding upon the Word when he is no longer standing in front of them.
Because pastors die.
Pastors move.
Pastors retire.
Pastors sometimes fail.
Pastors can become sick.
Pastors can change.
And yes…
pastors can sin.
Only Christ remains the same yesterday, today, and forever.
Your faith cannot be built upon a man surviving every scandal.
It must be built upon Jesus Christ surviving the grave.
Perhaps that is why some people completely lose their faith when a famous Christian leader falls.
They thought Jesus was the foundation.
Then the pastor fell…
and somehow their entire spiritual house collapsed with him.
That collapse reveals something.
Maybe the pastor had quietly become one of the load-bearing walls.
Please understand the difference.
When a pastor falls into serious sin, grieving is normal.
Anger may be appropriate.
Confusion is understandable.
Betrayal can hurt deeply.
But the sin of a shepherd does not make the Gospel false.
Jesus did not become less holy because Judas betrayed Him.
Christ does not become less trustworthy because one of His servants proved untrustworthy.
And your salvation was never secured by your pastor’s ability to remain impressive.
It was secured by the finished work of Jesus Christ.
There is another sign your pastor may be becoming too large in your spiritual world:
You defend him faster than you defend Scripture.
Someone misrepresents your favorite preacher and you immediately become furious.
But someone twists Scripture?
Silence.
Someone mocks your pastor?
You are ready for battle.
Someone casually blasphemes Christ?
Something is upside down.
Love your shepherd.
Pray for him.
Protect him from false accusations.
Refuse gossip.
Give him grace.
Remember that pastors are human beings carrying burdens most congregations never see.
But never confuse defending a man's reputation with defending the Gospel.
The church belongs to Jesus.
The pulpit belongs to Jesus.
The ministry belongs to Jesus.
The sheep belong to Jesus.
The glory belongs to Jesus.
The pastor belongs to Jesus.
Everything belongs to Jesus.
This is why Scripture’s most foundational confession leaves no room for rival gods.
Deuteronomy 6:4 begins:
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל — Shema Yisrael
“Hear, O Israel…”
and declares the LORD our God, the LORD alone/one.
The heartbeat of biblical faith has always been radical allegiance to God.
Not God plus a personality.
Not Christ plus a denomination.
Not Jesus plus your favorite preacher.
Not Scripture plus whatever the pastor says Scripture must mean.
God alone deserves worship.
And sometimes idolatry does not mean consciously thinking your pastor is divine.
Functional idolatry can be subtler.
It happens when a created person begins receiving the fear, dependence, unquestioning allegiance, identity, or ultimate devotion that belongs to the Creator.
You may never sing worship songs about your pastor.
You may never bow before him.
You may never call him divine.
But if losing his approval terrifies you more than disobeying Christ…
something needs examination.
If his interpretation can never be tested…
something needs examination.
If every person who disagrees with him automatically becomes your enemy…
something needs examination.
If exposing genuine sin inside the ministry feels worse to you than allowing the sin to continue…
something needs examination.
If you believe leaving his church means leaving God…
something needs examination.
If you cannot imagine following Jesus without following that particular man…
something needs examination.
But now comes the part that must not be missed.
This article is not asking you to replace pastor-idolatry with pastor-hatred.
That would simply exchange one sin for another.
Do not read this and begin hunting for flaws.
Do not become suspicious of every spiritual leader.
Do not weaponize these words against faithful pastors because you dislike correction.
Sometimes the pastor is not controlling.
Sometimes we simply do not like being told the truth.
Sometimes what we call “spiritual abuse” is actually biblical correction delivered by someone courageous enough to confront our sin.
Discernment cuts both ways.
Scripture commands Christians to respect faithful leaders. Elders who lead well are worthy of honor. Shepherds carry real responsibility before God for the souls entrusted to their care.
So honor your pastor.
Just do not enthrone him.
Listen to your pastor.
Just keep your Bible open.
Learn from your pastor.
Just remember who the Teacher ultimately points toward.
Receive correction.
But test teaching by Scripture.
Pray for your pastor.
But pray to God.
Thank your pastor.
But worship Jesus.
Follow godly examples insofar as they follow Christ.
But when a human leader and the revealed Word of God finally stand on opposite sides…
you already know where your allegiance belongs.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
And faithful pastors will ultimately want it that way.
Because a shepherd who genuinely loves Christ does not secretly dream of becoming the sheep’s destination.
He points beyond himself.
“Look at Christ.”
When praised:
“Look at Christ.”
When the ministry grows:
“Look at Christ.”
When people admire his preaching:
“Look at Christ.”
When people depend too heavily upon him:
“No. Look at Christ.”
Because faithful ministry understands what John the Baptist understood:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
Imagine a generation of pastors who lived that sentence.
Imagine churches where pastors were deeply loved but Jesus was infinitely more treasured.
Imagine believers who could honor authority without surrendering discernment.
Imagine Christians who could receive correction without becoming cultishly loyal.
Imagine shepherds secure enough to say:
“Check what I preach against Scripture.”
Imagine Christians mature enough to answer:
“I love you, Pastor. I thank God for you. But you did not die for me.
Jesus did.”
That is freedom.
And maybe this article uncovered something you did not expect.
Perhaps you realized your identity has become tangled around a church personality.
Perhaps you have been afraid to ask questions.
Perhaps you have defended things you should have examined.
Perhaps you have confused loyalty to a leader with loyalty to Christ.
Or perhaps you are a pastor reading this and realizing that somewhere along the road, the applause became intoxicating.
People began needing you.
And if you are painfully honest…
part of you enjoyed being needed.
There is grace for that too.
Come down from the throne.
You were never designed to survive there.
Neither was I.
Neither was any Christian leader.
There is only One whose shoulders can carry the worship of humanity without being corrupted by it.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where scandal meets grace.
Because the Gospel is not merely the announcement that idolaters are guilty.
It is the announcement that idolaters can be forgiven.
We have all placed created things where God belongs.
Pastors.
Relationships.
Money.
Children.
Politics.
Careers.
Ministries.
Influence.
Approval.
Even ourselves.
Yet Christ came for sinners exactly like us.
At Calvary, Jesus did what no pastor could ever do.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
The answer to pastor-idolatry is not merely “think less of your pastor.”
The deeper answer is:
See more of Jesus.
See Him until every celebrity shrinks.
See Him until human applause sounds small.
See Him until your fear of people loses its grip.
See Him until you can thank God for gifted leaders without needing them to be gods.
See Him crucified.
See Him risen.
See Him reigning.
See Him coming again.
Then look at every preacher you have ever admired.
Servants.
Useful servants, perhaps.
Gifted servants.
Beloved servants.
Faithful servants.
But servants nonetheless.
And if this article exposed something uncomfortable inside you, do not hide from it.
Bring it to Christ.
Repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is turning from the counterfeit because you have finally seen the beauty of the real King.
No performance.
No pretending.
Just honesty before God.
And if you know someone who has become so attached to a spiritual leader that questioning the leader now feels like questioning Jesus, do not send this article as a weapon.
Send it as a mirror.
There may come a day when admiration for a human voice begins growing larger than you realize, and you will need the reminder again:
The shepherd is never the Savior.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront hidden idols, heal through biblical truth, and walk more seriously with Jesus Christ, stay close by following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelievers—to follow as well.
It does not.
Not because giving money makes you more spiritual.
It does not.
He does not.
But one practical way believers can glorify God is by voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work so biblical resources can continue reaching people who need them.
Follow Jesus.
Test what you hear by Scripture.
Honor faithful shepherds.
Pray for them.
Love them.
Encourage them.
And never ask them to carry a glory that would eventually crush them.
Because the safest pastor is not the pastor who convinces you that you cannot live without him.
It is the pastor who spends his life preparing you to keep following Jesus when his own voice is gone.
And perhaps that is the question worth carrying with you long after you close this article:
If every preacher you admired disappeared tomorrow, would Jesus still be enough?
May the answer become the deepest confession of your life:
Yes.
Jesus is enough.
Never turn the finger pointing toward Christ into the god you worship instead of Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BEFORE JERUSALEM, THERE WAS SHILOH—AND WHAT HAPPENED THERE SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS GOD’S PRESENCE CAN BE TAKEN FOR GRANTED
paragraphs:
BEFORE JERUSALEM, THERE WAS SHILOH—AND WHAT HAPPENED THERE SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS GOD’S PRESENCE CAN BE TAKEN FOR GRANTED
Before David brought the ark to Jerusalem and before Solomon built the Temple, Israel gathered around another sacred place. Its story begins with promise, passes through tears and scandal, and ends with a warning so severe that centuries later God pointed back to Shiloh and said, in effect: Remember what happened there.
There was a time when an Israelite could hear the name “Jerusalem” and not think first of the Temple.
No magnificent house of cedar and stone crowned Mount Moriah.
No worshiper stood in Solomon’s courts.
No pilgrim sang the Songs of Ascents while climbing toward the city that would become inseparable from Israel’s worship.
Before Jerusalem became that place, there was Shiloh.
And if you have ever wondered why Shiloh mattered so much before Jerusalem, the answer is far bigger than geography.

Shiloh became a place where Israel assembled before the LORD. It was associated with the tent of meeting, the distribution of the Promised Land, the ministry of priests, the prayers of a brokenhearted woman named Hannah, the childhood of Samuel, the ark of the covenant—and eventually one of the most sobering demonstrations in Scripture that religious privilege is no substitute for faithfulness to God.
Shiloh’s story is beautiful.
Then uncomfortable.
Then heartbreaking.
And finally, it points beyond itself toward something infinitely greater.
Because Shiloh teaches us that sacred places cannot save sinful hearts.
Religious history cannot substitute for repentance.
Possessing symbols associated with God does not mean that we possess God.
And even Jerusalem itself would eventually discover the same terrifying truth.
But first, we need to return to the beginning.
After Israel entered Canaan, Joshua 18:1 records:
“And the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there. And the land was subdued before them.”
The Hebrew text calls the sanctuary the אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד—’ohel mo‘ed—the “tent of meeting.”
That wording matters.
This was not merely Israel’s national headquarters.
It was associated with meeting before the LORD.
Shiloh stood within the land God had promised Israel, and there the tribes gathered while the remaining territorial inheritances were apportioned.
Imagine the emotional weight of that moment.
Generations earlier, Abraham had lived as a stranger in the land.
Israel had endured slavery in Egypt.
They had witnessed judgment and deliverance.
They had crossed the sea.
They had wandered through the wilderness.
An entire generation had died before entering Canaan.
And now, at Shiloh, Israel stood inside the promise.
The tent was raised.
The tribes assembled.
The land was being distributed.
Shiloh therefore represented more than a location on a map.
It represented arrival.
Promise.
Inheritance.
Worship.
The presence and covenant faithfulness of the God who had brought His people out of bondage.
Long before Jerusalem became the great center of Israelite worship under the monarchy, Shiloh occupied an extraordinary place in Israel’s life.
But Scripture refuses to romanticize sacred history.
And that is where Shiloh becomes painfully relevant to us.
Years pass.
Joshua’s generation fades.
By the opening chapters of 1 Samuel, Shiloh is still associated with worship before the LORD.
Every year, Elkanah travels there with his family “to worship and to sacrifice unto the LORD of hosts in Shiloh” (1 Samuel 1:3).
And walking into this sacred setting comes one of the Bible’s most painfully relatable women.
Hannah.
She is loved, but she is hurting.
She is married, but something inside her feels unbearably empty.
She has endured provocation from her rival.
She weeps.
She cannot eat.
And eventually her anguish becomes prayer.
At Shiloh, Hannah does not arrive pretending she is fine.
She breaks.
First Samuel 1:10 says:
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.”
The Hebrew expression behind “bitterness of soul” is מָרַת נָפֶשׁ—marat nephesh.
Her pain was not superficial.
This was anguish reaching into the nephesh—the living self, the person, the inner life.
And perhaps this is where Shiloh stops being ancient history.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it means to enter worship carrying something nobody else can see.
You smiled this week.
You answered messages.
You went to work.
You took care of your children.
You posted photographs.
You said, “I’m okay.”
But God heard the prayer underneath the sentence.
Hannah stood before Him with tears instead of performance.
She moved her lips while her voice could not be heard.
And Eli, the priest, misunderstood her.
He thought she was drunk.
Think about that.
A woman is pouring out her soul before God—and the religious authority watching her initially misreads her brokenness.
Some wounds hurt twice.
First because of what happened.
Then because someone misunderstood how badly it hurt.
But Hannah kept bringing her heart before God.
And God remembered her.
Samuel was born.
The child she had prayed for was eventually brought to Shiloh and dedicated to the LORD.
The place that had witnessed Hannah’s tears would now witness Samuel’s growth.
First Samuel 3:1 tells us:
“And the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli.”
Then comes one of Scripture’s unforgettable nighttime scenes.
Samuel is lying down.
Eli’s eyesight has grown dim.
“The lamp of God” has not yet gone out.
And Samuel hears his name.
“Samuel.”
He assumes Eli called him.
He runs to the old priest.
“I called not,” Eli essentially tells him. “Lie down again.”
It happens again.
Then again.
Finally Eli understands.
This is the LORD.
Samuel returns and waits.
Then:
“Samuel, Samuel.”
And Samuel answers:
“Speak; for thy servant heareth.”
At Shiloh, a new prophetic voice was being raised.
Yet in the same place where Samuel was learning to recognize the voice of God, other men were treating holy things with contempt.
Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests.
But Scripture does not protect their reputations simply because they held religious office.
First Samuel 2:12 says:
“Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.”
That should stop every religious person in their tracks.
They were around sacred things.
They participated in a sacred system.
They carried sacred titles.
And Scripture says they did not know the LORD.
They abused their priestly position in connection with the sacrifices, and 1 Samuel also condemns their sexual immorality involving women serving at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
The scandal was not outside Shiloh.
It was inside.
And this is one of the recurring warnings of Scripture:
You can stand near holy things while your heart remains far from God.
You can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
You can own a Bible and resist the God who speaks through it.
You can sing about surrender while protecting the one sin you refuse to surrender.
You can build an audience around Jesus while secretly building a throne for yourself.
You can inherit religious tradition without inheriting living faith.
Shiloh proves that proximity to sacred things is not the same as intimacy with God.
And then the story becomes darker.
Israel goes to war against the Philistines and suffers defeat.
Instead of first responding with humble repentance and seeking the LORD rightly, Israel decides to bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh.
Their words in 1 Samuel 4:3 reveal the dangerous reasoning:
“Let us fetch the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of Shiloh unto us, that, when it cometh among us, it may save us out of the hand of our enemies.”
Notice the shift.
The ark was associated with the covenant and presence of the LORD.
But Israel began treating it as though possessing the sacred object could guarantee victory.
They wanted the symbol of God’s presence without submitting to the God whose presence the symbol represented.
That temptation did not die in the ancient world.
People still do it.
A cross around the neck.
A Bible on the nightstand.
A Christian verse in the bio.
Church attendance.
Baptism remembered from years ago.
A ministry position.
A famous preacher followed online.
A worship playlist.
None of those things is evil.
Some are beautiful expressions of faith.
But none can replace repentance and living trust in God.
You cannot use Christianity as a lucky charm.
You cannot carry the language of Jesus while refusing the lordship of Jesus and assume everything is fine.
Israel brought the ark into camp.
The people shouted so loudly that the earth rang again.
For a moment, it must have felt like revival.
Noise everywhere.
Religious excitement everywhere.
The enemy was frightened.
Surely victory was coming.
Then Israel was defeated.
Hophni and Phinehas died.
The ark was captured.
When Eli heard what had happened to the ark, he fell backward, broke his neck, and died.
Then Phinehas’s pregnant wife went into labor.
As she was dying, she named her child אִי־כָבוֹד—Ichabod.
First Samuel 4:21 explains:
“And she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God was taken…”
What a devastating ending to a chapter that began generations earlier with a nation gathering around the tent of meeting in the Promised Land.
Promise had become presumption.
Privilege had become complacency.
Priesthood had become scandal.
And people had confused the sign associated with God’s presence with obedience to God Himself.
Shiloh never became Jerusalem.

The ark did not simply return to Shiloh and restore the old order. After its return from Philistine territory, it remained for a long period at Kiriath-jearim, while the biblical story moved toward David, Jerusalem, and eventually Solomon’s Temple.
David later brought the ark to Jerusalem.
Solomon built the Temple.
Jerusalem became the great center of Israel’s worship.
But here is the part many people miss.
God did not allow Jerusalem to become a new religious lucky charm either.
Centuries later, the prophet Jeremiah stood in the gate of the LORD’s house and confronted people who were trusting in the Temple while persisting in sin.
They were effectively saying:
“The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD…”
They thought the existence of the sanctuary guaranteed security.
Then God told them to remember Shiloh.
Jeremiah 7:12 records:
“But go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel.”
That is why Shiloh matters so much.
Shiloh became a warning Jerusalem was commanded to remember.
The message was unmistakable:
Do not presume upon Me because you have My house.
Do not confuse religious privilege with covenant faithfulness.
Do not believe sacred architecture can shelter unrepentant rebellion.
Look at Shiloh.
Psalm 78 similarly looks backward and says that God “forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh” and then traces the story toward Judah and Zion.
Shiloh mattered before Jerusalem partly because its history became a theological warning to Jerusalem.
And Jerusalem eventually fell too.
The Babylonian armies destroyed Solomon’s Temple in 586 BC.
A building could not save a rebellious nation.
But even that is not the end of the story.
Because if the Bible ended with destroyed sanctuaries and sinful people, Shiloh would merely be a tragedy.
Instead, Scripture moves us toward Jesus Christ.
And Jesus does something astonishing.
When confronted over the Temple, He says:
“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
John immediately explains:
“But he spake of the temple of his body.”
The Greek word used there is ναός—naos, referring to the sanctuary or temple.
Jesus was pointing beyond stone.
Beyond architecture.
Beyond every earthly sanctuary that could be damaged, corrupted, invaded, or destroyed.
He was pointing to Himself.
Then at the cross, the One who never sinned bore the judgment sinners deserved.
The true scandal of the Gospel is not merely that humanity could become so sinful.
It is that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The innocent condemned.
The guilty offered mercy.
The righteous One bearing sins.
The King wearing thorns.
The Creator mocked by creatures.
The hands through whom all things were made pierced by nails.
And the mouth that could have pronounced judgment instead praying:
“Father, forgive them…”
Then He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
This is where every road in this story must finally lead.
Not Shiloh.
Not Jerusalem.
Jesus.
Christianity is not ultimately about finding the correct sacred location.
It is about reconciliation with the holy God through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide behind religious symbols.
It calls you to Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you to polish your reputation until God accepts you.
It tells you that sinners must repent and trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
The Gospel does not say your scandal is stronger than His grace.
It says there is forgiveness and redemption in Christ.
Maybe your own life feels like Shiloh.
There was once a season when you felt close to God.
You prayed.
You worshiped.
You meant what you sang.
Then something happened.
Maybe disappointment hardened you.
Maybe secret sin slowly became normal.
Maybe someone in the church wounded you.
Maybe you became very good at looking spiritually alive while privately becoming exhausted.
Maybe your Bible remained open while your heart slowly closed.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well.
But you know.
And God knows.
Here is what Shiloh whispers across thousands of years:
Do not confuse yesterday’s encounter with today’s surrender.
And here is what the cross declares louder:
Come home.
Not because your sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to die.
Not because God simply overlooks rebellion.
He calls you to repentance.
But because Jesus Christ really does receive sinners who come to Him.
There is grace for the ashamed.
Forgiveness for the repentant.
Mercy for the broken.
Restoration for the wandering.
There is no scandal in your history that gives you permission to declare yourself beyond the reach of the Savior.
Peter denied Him.
A thief was crucified beside Him.
Paul had persecuted His people.
Yet grace wrote chapters none of them could have written for themselves.
That does not make sin small.
It makes Christ glorious.
This is why our words, “From Scandal to Grace,” are not merely a slogan.
They describe the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus rewrites everything—not by pretending the old story never happened, but by redeeming people who could never redeem themselves.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not perform for the comments.
But do not keep performing before God either.
Let other believers know where they can stand with you.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed to read tonight.
Not because Shiloh is merely interesting biblical trivia, but because there may come a day when you are tempted to substitute religious familiarity for a living relationship with Christ.
Remember Shiloh then.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to earn a blessing.
Not because clicking “share” makes you righteous.
Somebody may be hiding behind religion.
Somebody may be Hannah, silently weeping where nobody understands.
Somebody may be Samuel, hearing God calling them back.
Somebody may feel like Ichabod has been written over their entire life—as though the glory is gone and nothing beautiful can ever come again.
They need to know that the story does not end at Shiloh.
It does not even end at Jerusalem.
It ends with our eyes fixed upon Jesus Christ—the crucified Savior, the risen Lord, the only One who can reconcile sinners to God.
Shiloh mattered because God met His people there.
Shiloh mattered because Israel’s inheritance unfolded there.
Shiloh mattered because Hannah wept there.
Samuel listened there.
Priests sinned there.
Judgment came there.
And generations later, Jerusalem was told to look backward and remember.
But Jesus matters infinitely more because every sanctuary before Him was temporary, while He is the risen Lord.
So when everything sacred in your life seems ruined…
when your reputation collapses…
when yesterday’s faith feels painfully distant…
when the consequences finally arrive…
when you discover that religious appearances cannot rescue you…
do not run toward another performance.
Run to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive the mercy you could never manufacture.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because the most haunting lesson of Shiloh is not simply that sacred places can fall.
It is that we can stand frighteningly close to the things of God while our hearts remain far from God—and still, through Jesus Christ, the repentant sinner can come home.
Your Shiloh may explain how everything fell apart, but Jesus Christ can still determine how your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS” — NOTICE JESUS DIDN’T SAY “PEACEKEEPERS”
paragraphs: “BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS” — NOTICE JESUS DIDN’T SAY “PEACEKEEPERS”

Some of the “peace” you have protected may actually be the silence that is slowly destroying you. Jesus did not bless pretending. He blessed people willing to enter what is broken with His truth, His mercy, and His love—and make peace.
There is a kind of silence that looks holy from across the room.
Nobody is shouting.
Nobody is confronting anybody.
Nobody is asking the uncomfortable question.
Nobody is talking about what happened.

The family still gathers for dinner. The marriage still has photographs online. The church still sings on Sunday. The friendship still exchanges polite messages. Everybody smiles when someone pulls out a camera.
“Everything is fine.”
Except it isn’t.
Something is bleeding underneath the table.
Someone is crying behind a locked bathroom door.
Someone is carrying resentment that has been fermenting for years.
Someone knows an apology should have happened a long time ago.
Someone is terrified that if the truth is finally spoken, the fragile little world everybody has worked so hard to preserve will collapse.
So everybody stays quiet.
Because quiet feels like peace.
Until Jesus walks into the room.
And says something that changes the definition.
“Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.”
Matthew 5:9.
Read it again slowly.
Not merely the people who prefer peace.
Not merely those who dislike arguments.
Not merely those who remain neutral whenever relationships fracture.
Not merely those who become experts at smiling while resentment grows beneath the surface.
“Blessed are the peacemakers.”
Matthew records Jesus’ words in Greek:
μακάριοι οἱ εἰρηνοποιοί, ὅτι αὐτοὶ υἱοὶ θεοῦ κληθήσονται.
Makarioi hoi eirēnopoioi, hoti autoi huioi Theou klēthēsontai.
“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.”
That word matters:
εἰρηνοποιοί — eirēnopoioi.
Peacemakers.
Those associated with the making of peace.
Jesus is describing something active.
Something costly.
Something that moves toward brokenness rather than merely arranging furniture around it.

And we need to be careful here, because Scripture does not give us a theological category called “peacekeepers” and then condemn everyone who fits it. “Peacekeeper” is a useful modern contrast, not another word Jesus used in this verse.
But the distinction can expose something uncomfortable in us.
Sometimes what we call “keeping the peace” is actually keeping everyone comfortable enough that nobody has to confront what is destroying the relationship.
We avoid the conversation.
We swallow the wound.
We pretend forgiveness happened when nobody repented.
We call fear “wisdom.”
We call avoidance “grace.”
We call enabling “love.”
We call silence “peace.”
And sometimes...
it isn’t peace at all.
Because biblical peace is deeper than the absence of noise.

James describes wisdom from above as first pure and then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruit. Then he writes that a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
Notice the order.
Pure.
Then peaceable.
Truth and peace are not enemies in the kingdom of God.
Righteousness and peace do not need to divorce each other so everybody can feel comfortable.
God does not ask you to purchase superficial harmony with counterfeit holiness.
And perhaps that is exactly where this becomes personal.
Because some of us learned very young that survival meant becoming the quiet one.
Maybe you grew up in a house where one wrong sentence could ignite the room.
So you became careful.
You learned facial expressions.
You learned footsteps.
You learned tones of voice.
You could tell something was wrong before anyone said a word.
You became the mediator.
The apologizer.
The one who changed the subject.
The one who absorbed tension.
The one who said, “It’s okay,” when it absolutely was not okay.
And eventually people started calling you peaceful.
But sometimes you weren’t peaceful.
You were afraid.
Afraid of rejection.
Afraid of confrontation.
Afraid somebody would leave.
Afraid somebody would become angry.
Afraid that telling the truth would cost you the relationship.
So you kept swallowing words until your silence became a prison.
Maybe you are doing it right now.
There is someone you need to forgive.
Someone you need to confront lovingly.
Someone you need to apologize to.
Something you need to confess.
A relationship where you have confused reconciliation with pretending nothing happened.
A wound you keep covering because exposing it feels dangerous.
And somewhere inside you is a sentence you have repeated for years:
“I just want peace.”
But Jesus may be asking you a harder question.
Do you want peace...
or do you simply want the tension to disappear?
Those are not always the same thing.
Because peacemaking can initially feel incredibly unpeaceful.
Sometimes peacemaking begins with trembling hands and the words:
“We need to talk.”
Sometimes it begins:
“I was wrong.”
Sometimes:
“I forgive you.”
Sometimes:
“What you did hurt me.”
Sometimes:
“I love you, but I cannot keep participating in this.”
Sometimes:
“I have been pretending.”
Sometimes:
“I need help.”
Sometimes:
“Please forgive me.”
And sometimes the most Christlike sentence you can say is one that costs your pride everything.
That is why peacemaking requires something peacekeeping-by-avoidance never will:
the cross.
Because before Jesus called His followers to become peacemakers, God Himself was already revealing what true peace would ultimately cost.
Us.
We were the rebels.
We were the sinners.
We were the guilty ones.
We were not standing on neutral ground waiting for God and humanity to negotiate reasonable terms.
Sin had separated us from God.
And God did not look at humanity's rebellion and say:
“Let’s pretend this never happened.”
He did not redefine evil so nobody would feel uncomfortable.
He did not sweep sin beneath the carpet of heaven.
He dealt with it.
At a cross.
Jesus Christ stepped directly into the hostility between sinful humanity and a holy God.
Not because our sin was insignificant.
Because His love was immeasurable.
The cross is where we discover that God’s peace is not cheap.
Jesus made peace through His blood.
That is why biblical peacemaking can never mean simply being “nice.”
Jesus was perfectly loving, yet He confronted hypocrisy.
He showed mercy to sinners, yet He called sinners to repentance.
He forgave, yet never pretended sin was righteousness.
He welcomed the broken, yet loved them too deeply to tell them that brokenness was their final identity.
Grace never required Jesus to lie.
And truth never required Jesus to stop loving.
Look at the cross.
There hangs perfect truth...
and perfect grace.
Perfect justice...
and astonishing mercy.
Sin exposed...
and sinners invited home.
That is peace.
Not pretending there was never a war.
But reconciliation purchased by Someone willing to bear the cost.
And perhaps now Matthew 5:9 becomes even more beautiful.
“Blessed are the peacemakers...”
Why?
“...for they shall be called the children of God.”
Peacemakers resemble their Father.
They carry the family likeness.
Not because making peace earns adoption into God’s family, but because those transformed by God increasingly begin to reflect the God who reconciles.
We do not become children of God by accumulating enough successful reconciliations.
Salvation is grace.
Christ saves.
But the life touched by Christ begins to carry the fingerprints of Christ.
Mercy starts appearing where revenge once lived.
Humility appears where pride once ruled.
Confession replaces excuses.
Forgiveness begins loosening chains.
Truth gets spoken without hatred.
Love develops courage.
And suddenly the person who once needed to win every argument begins asking:
“How can Christ be glorified here?”
That changes everything.
Because a peacemaker is not obsessed with winning.
A peacemaker is concerned with reconciliation under truth.
There are arguments you can win while losing your brother.
There are comments you can post that are technically correct while your heart is completely wrong.
There are Bible verses you can weaponize.
There are facts you can deliver with contempt.
There are apologies you can demand while refusing to examine yourself.
You can speak truth without love.
You can also speak about love while hiding from truth.
Jesus calls us somewhere harder.
Somewhere holier.
Truth with grace.
Conviction with compassion.
Courage without cruelty.
Mercy without compromise.
And this is where peacemaking becomes painfully practical.
Maybe the first person God wants to confront is not the person you are angry with.
Maybe it is you.
That possibility hurts, doesn’t it?
Because sometimes we read articles about reconciliation thinking of everyone who needs to apologize to us.
Their face appears immediately.
Their words.
Their betrayal.
Their hypocrisy.
Their failure.
But what if the Holy Spirit is bringing your face into the story too?
What if there was something you said?
Something you exaggerated?
Something you refused to admit?
Something you posted?
Something you repeated about somebody else?
Something you should have apologized for months ago?
What if the reason the relationship remains fractured is not entirely on the other side of the table?
Be honest.
You do not need to confess anything publicly that should remain private.
But before God...
no hiding.
No editing the story so you always remain the victim.
No rewriting the conversation so your cruelty becomes “discernment.”
No baptizing pride and calling it boundaries.
No disguising bitterness as wisdom.
No pretending indifference means you have forgiven.
Jesus already knows the whole story.
And still...
He calls you toward grace.
This is the scandal of the Gospel.
Jesus knows the version of you nobody else knows.
The jealous thought.
The secret resentment.
The private addiction.
The ugly reaction.
The words you wish you could retrieve.
The person you still struggle to forgive.
The nights when your Christianity felt stronger in public than it did alone.
He knows.
And the Gospel does not say, “Hide better.”
The Gospel says:
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Be transformed.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve the reputation of sinners.
He came to save them.
That means peacemaking begins vertically before it spreads horizontally.
We need peace with God.
Then, as people reconciled to God through Christ, we become people who carry His reconciling character into a fractured world.
This does not mean every broken relationship will be restored.
That needs to be said.
Some people will refuse peace.
Some will reject an apology.
Some will continue manipulating.
Some relationships require wise boundaries.
Some situations require distance and outside help.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
Reconciliation cannot be forced upon an unrepentant person as though one person can manufacture mutual trust alone.
Scripture itself recognizes limits.
Paul writes:
Those words matter.
εἰ δυνατόν τὸ ἐξ ὑμῶν...
“If possible... as far as it depends on you...”
God does not command you to control another person’s response.
He commands faithfulness with yours.
You cannot make someone repent.
You cannot make someone forgive.
You cannot force somebody to become trustworthy.
You cannot single-handedly create reconciliation between two unwilling hearts.
But you can refuse revenge.
You can reject bitterness.
You can tell the truth without becoming cruel.
You can repent where you sinned.
You can forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
You can pray for your enemy.
You can stop feeding the fire.
You can refuse to return evil for evil.
You can place justice in God's hands rather than allowing vengeance to consume yours.
You can become a peacemaker.
And perhaps somebody reading this right now has been waiting for permission to stop pretending.
Here it is.
Peace is not pretending.
You are allowed to tell the truth.
You are allowed to say you were hurt.
You are allowed to seek wise help.
You are allowed to establish appropriate boundaries.
You are allowed to refuse participation in sin.
You are allowed to pursue reconciliation without surrendering truth.
But there is another side.
You are not allowed to worship your wound.
You are not allowed to make bitterness your identity.
You are not allowed to use somebody else's sin as permanent permission for your own.
The cross will not let either of us remain comfortably self-righteous.
At Calvary, everyone comes empty-handed.
Victim.
Offender.
Prodigal.
Pharisee.
The ashamed.
The angry.
The religious.
The rebellious.
Every one of us needs Jesus.
And that is why the Gospel can do what human pride cannot.
It can bring enemies to the same cross.
It can turn persecutors into apostles.
Prodigals into sons.
The ashamed into witnesses.
The broken into restorers.
The scandal into testimony.
The grave into an empty tomb.
This is what Jesus does.
He rewrites stories we thought had already reached their final sentence.
Maybe yours feels finished.
It isn't.
Maybe your family feels too fractured.
Maybe your marriage has accumulated years of wounds.
Maybe your relationship with your child is hanging by a thread.
Maybe church hurt convinced you never to trust Christians again.
Maybe you became cynical because reconciliation sounded beautiful in sermons but impossible in real life.
Maybe the person you cannot forgive is yourself.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly relationship will end exactly as you hope.
It promises something greater.
Jesus Christ is still Lord over ruined things.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority over the Author.
Your sin is not greater than His blood.
Your shame is not stronger than His grace.
Your past is not more powerful than His resurrection.
So take the first faithful step.
Not twenty steps.
One.
Pray.
Repent.
Call.
Write.
Forgive.
Ask forgiveness.
Seek counsel.
Tell the truth.
Stop rehearsing revenge.
Stop waiting for the other person to become perfect before you obey Jesus.
And if the other person refuses peace?
You keep belonging to the Prince of Peace.
If they misunderstand you?
Stay faithful.
If they never apologize?
Keep surrendering vengeance to God.
If reconciliation requires time?
Walk patiently.
If trust must be rebuilt slowly?
Let truth and wisdom guide it.
Peacemaking is not weakness.
Sometimes it is one of the bravest things a Christian will ever do.
Because anyone can throw another stone.
Anyone can type another insult.
Anyone can gather people onto their side.
Anyone can replay an offense until hatred feels righteous.
But it takes someone crucified with Christ to say:
“I will not let what you did turn me into someone Jesus never called me to become.”
That is different.
That smells like Calvary.
That sounds like freedom.
And maybe this article did not reach you because you needed another inspirational paragraph.
Maybe there is a name sitting in your heart right now.
You know the name.
You felt it before you finished this sentence.
Maybe God is not asking you to fix everything tonight.
Maybe He is asking you to stop running from the first act of obedience.
Pray for that person.
Or repent to that person.
Or forgive that person.
Or finally ask mature, godly people for help navigating what happened.
But do not confuse avoidance with peace anymore.
Jesus said:
“Blessed are the peacemakers.”
Somebody reading beneath this article may desperately need evidence that grace still walks into broken rooms.
Then think of one person.
Not your entire friends list.
One person who has been carrying resentment, family conflict, church hurt, marital pain, unforgiveness, shame, or a relationship that feels beyond repair.
Or send this privately.
Because sometimes forgiveness is not a sentence we speak once.
Sometimes surrender is a battle we bring back to Jesus again and again.
And there is something bigger than merchandise.
Share if somebody else needs the message.

And comment—because your honest “pray for me,” your testimony, your confession, or your simple “Jesus, make me a peacemaker” may become the sentence another wounded believer reads at exactly the moment they are thinking about giving up.
But whatever you do after reading this, remember what matters most.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a product.
Not an algorithm.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
The One who did not merely tell enemies to stop fighting.
The One who came to reconcile sinners to God.
The One who carried our guilt.
The One who absorbed the judgment our sin deserved.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who still enters locked rooms.
The One who still breaks chains.
The One who still forgives sinners.
The One who still heals wounded hearts.
The One who still turns enemies into family.
The One who still makes peace.
And perhaps the relationship you thought was only a battlefield is about to become the place where somebody finally sees what the Gospel looks like when it puts on flesh.
Because sometimes the loudest evidence that Jesus has changed a human heart is not how fiercely that person can fight...
but how much it costs them to make peace anyway.
The world knows how to preserve grudges. The cross teaches wounded people how to become peacemakers.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DON’T MARRY SOMEONE JUST TO MAKE SOMEONE ELSE JEALOUS, ANGRY, OR IMPRESSED
paragraphs: DON’T MARRY SOMEONE JUST TO MAKE SOMEONE ELSE JEALOUS, ANGRY, OR IMPRESSED
Because the person standing beside you at the altar should never become collateral damage in a war they didn’t start.
There is something heartbreaking about saying “I do” while secretly hoping somebody else hears about it.
Read that again.
Because sometimes a wedding is not really about love.
Sometimes it is revenge wearing white.
Sometimes it is insecurity carrying flowers.
Sometimes it is loneliness dressed beautifully enough that nobody notices it is still loneliness.
Sometimes it is a wounded person quietly saying, “Look at me now.”
And sometimes the person smiling beside them has absolutely no idea that they have just been recruited into somebody else’s unfinished emotional war.
You wanted your ex to regret losing you.
You wanted the person who rejected you to finally see your worth.
You wanted your parents to stop questioning you.
You wanted your friends to believe you were happy.
You wanted people online to see the photographs, the ring, the celebration, the honeymoon, the captions.
Anything.
Jealousy.
Regret.
Pain.
Loss.
And somewhere underneath all of it was a wounded voice whispering:
“Now they’ll know what they lost.”
But what happens when the person you married eventually realizes they were never the destination?
They were the message.
That is where this gets serious.
Because marriage is far too sacred to turn another human being into your evidence that you have moved on.
Jesus said something about marriage that should make us tremble before treating it casually:
“Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”
Matthew 19:6
The Greek behind “joined together” is συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen, from a verb carrying the sense of joining or yoking together.
Jesus was not describing marriage as an Instagram announcement.
He was speaking about a union.
A covenantal joining.
Two lives being bound together before God.

And if you are thinking about marriage because you need somebody else to become jealous, angry, impressed, or sorry, you need to hear this before rings are purchased, invitations are mailed, and promises are spoken:
Another person’s heart is not a weapon.
Their future is not your revenge.
Their affection is not medicine for your wounded ego.
And marriage is not a stage where you prove to your past that you won.
Because eventually the wedding ends.
The photographs stop trending.
The congratulations slow down.
The flowers die.
The dress gets stored away.
Everybody goes home.
And then there are two people standing inside ordinary life together.
Bills.
Fatigue.
Misunderstandings.
Family problems.
Sickness.
Temptation.
Disappointment.
Sex.
Forgiveness.
Laundry.
Prayer.
Children, perhaps.
Loss.
Growing older.
Monday mornings when nobody is applauding.
That is marriage too.
And the person you marry deserves someone who chose them when there was no audience watching.
They deserve to know:
“I would still choose you if my ex never found out.”
“I would still choose you if nobody envied us.”
“I would still choose you if our wedding received five likes instead of five thousand.”
“I would still choose you if nobody was impressed.”
“I would still choose you because I am not using you to communicate with somebody from my past.”
That kind of honesty matters because Scripture does not define love by the reaction it produces in spectators.
It describes love by what it gives to the beloved.
Paul writes:
1 Corinthians 13:4
The Greek word translated “love” is ἀγάπη — agapē.
And then comes a devastating contrast for anyone using romance to provoke jealousy:
οὐ ζηλοῖ — ou zēloi
Love “does not envy” or is not consumed by jealousy.
Then:
οὐ περπερεύεται — ou perpereuetai
Love does not boast.
Think about that.
If the driving energy behind your relationship is, “Wait until they see us,” Scripture is asking you to examine what is actually happening inside your heart.
Not because posting wedding photographs is wrong.
Not because celebrating your spouse publicly is wrong.
Not because being happy after heartbreak is wrong.
But because there is an enormous difference between celebrating someone you love and using someone you claim to love as a billboard aimed at somebody else.
One says:
“I am grateful for you.”
The other secretly says:
“I hope they see you.”
Those are not the same heart.
And God sees the difference even when Facebook does not.
Maybe that hurts.
Maybe while reading this, somebody immediately came into your mind.
Maybe you are already dating someone good, but if you were brutally honest before God, part of what attracted you to the relationship was how it would make someone else feel.
Maybe you keep imagining your ex seeing the engagement announcement.
Maybe you are moving faster than wisdom allows because being married feels like proof that you were desirable after all.
Maybe somebody humiliated you.
Cheated on you.
Abandoned you.
Replaced you.
Ghosted you.
Told you nobody would ever want you.
Maybe they married someone else.
And now there is a part of you that desperately wants your own spectacular ending.
That wound is real.
But please hear this:
You do not have to destroy another person's future to prove that somebody else failed to recognize your value.
You do not need a spouse to become evidence that you were worth loving.
Your deepest worth was never supposed to come from whether another wounded human being chose you.
For the Christian, identity reaches somewhere much deeper.
It reaches the cross.
“But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8
Before your wedding.
Before your relationship status.
Before somebody finally recognized your beauty.
Before anybody regretted losing you.
Before you managed to make your life look impressive.
Christ loved sinners.
That changes the question.
Instead of asking:
“How can I prove they were wrong about me?”
The Gospel asks:
“What if I no longer need their regret to become free?”
That is a completely different kind of healing.
Because revenge keeps you emotionally connected to the person you claim you have moved beyond.
You are still arranging your life around their eyes.
Still wondering what they think.
Still measuring whether they noticed.
Still hoping they hurt.
Still waiting for their reaction.
They may not even know they still occupy that much space inside you.
But Jesus does.
And He does not expose wounds merely to shame wounded people.
He calls sinners into the light because grace does its deepest work where pretending finally ends.
Maybe the most spiritual thing you can do before marrying someone is not choose flowers.
Not choose a venue.
Not choose a photographer.
Maybe it is getting alone with God and asking:
“Jesus, why do I really want this?”
And then staying quiet long enough to hear an answer you might not like.
Scripture says:
“Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts.”
Psalm 139:23
The Hebrew begins:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
ḥoqreni El, veda levavi.
“Search me, God, and know my heart.”
That is a dangerous prayer when you have become skilled at explaining your motives to yourself.
Search me.
Not my ex.
Not the person who hurt me.
Not my parents.
Not everybody judging my relationship.
Me.
Lord, search me.
Show me whether I am choosing covenant or chasing validation.
