Show me whether I love this person or merely love what being with this person says about me.
Show me whether I am preparing for marriage or staging a comeback.
Show me whether I want a spouse or an audience.
Show me whether I am healed enough to love someone without secretly asking them to pay a debt somebody else created.
That prayer can save years of pain.
Because marriage magnifies what dating can sometimes hide.
Unhealed comparison eventually appears.
Unresolved attachment eventually speaks.
Resentment leaks.
Pride leaks.
Fear leaks.
And eventually the innocent person beside you begins asking the question nobody should have to ask inside a marriage:
“Are you actually here with me?”
Imagine hearing that from your husband.
Imagine hearing it from your wife.
Imagine discovering that every romantic photograph had a ghost standing just outside the frame.
Someone from the past.
Someone your spouse was still trying to impress.
Someone they were still trying to punish.
Someone whose opinion somehow remained more powerful than your presence.
That is why this is not merely relationship advice.
This is about loving your neighbor truthfully.
It is about refusing to use another image-bearer of God as emotional ammunition.
It is about repentance.
And repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō, carrying the idea of changing one’s mind or turning in response to truth.
Jesus begins His public proclamation with:
“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.”
Matthew 4:17
Repentance says:
“I cannot keep walking this direction just because my wound explains why I started walking it.”
Your pain may explain your temptation.
It does not have to become your master.
And perhaps that is exactly where somebody reading this is standing.
You have not married them yet.
Good.
There is still time to become honest.
Do not panic.
Do not immediately destroy a healthy relationship simply because you recognize mixed motives inside yourself.
Human motives can be complicated.
Bring them into the light.
Slow down if necessary.
Seek wise, biblically grounded counsel.
Talk honestly with mature believers who are not impressed by appearances.
And if the relationship is moving toward marriage, premarital counseling with a trustworthy pastor or qualified Christian counselor can uncover things romantic chemistry often cannot.
But whatever you do, stop asking another human being to heal something only Christ can ultimately reach.
Your future husband cannot become your Savior.
Your future wife cannot become your Savior.
Marriage cannot become your resurrection.
Being desired cannot become your justification.
A wedding cannot wash away shame.
A ring cannot crucify your past.
Jesus can meet you there.
Jesus can forgive.
Jesus can restore.
Jesus can teach wounded people how to love without turning love into retaliation.
This is why the Gospel is so much bigger than “find the right person.”
The Gospel tells us that our deepest problem is not singleness.
It is sin.
And our deepest answer is not marriage.
It is Christ.
Paul writes:
Ephesians 1:7
The word translated “redemption” is ἀπολύτρωσις — apolytrōsis.
Redemption.
Release purchased at a cost.
That is what Jesus offers.
Not cosmetic healing.
Not a carefully curated life designed to make the people who rejected you jealous.
Freedom.
You can become so free in Christ that you no longer need the person who hurt you to suffer before you can have peace.
So free that you can stop checking whether they viewed your story.
So free that you do not need to manufacture happiness where they can see it.
So free that your future marriage does not have to become a courtroom where you finally prove your worth.
So free that when you eventually stand beside somebody and say, “I do,” you can actually mean:
“I am here with you.”
Not them.
You.
And if you already married for some of the wrong reasons?
Then perhaps this article became uncomfortable several paragraphs ago.
Maybe you recognized yourself and felt your stomach tighten.
Do not use conviction as permission to abandon covenant casually.
The same Christ who exposes sin also calls us toward confession, forgiveness, faithfulness, truth, and transformation.
Your beginning may have been messy.
Your motives may have been mixed.
Your marriage may carry scars from decisions you now regret.
But the Gospel Warrior message exists for precisely this kind of human story:
Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
Not because Jesus pretends the earlier chapters never happened.
He redeems people inside stories that really happened.
Peter really denied Him.
Paul really persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman really had a complicated relational history.
The thief really hung on a cross because he was guilty.
Christian grace is not God announcing that sin never mattered.
Grace is astonishing precisely because sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
And resurrection tells us failure does not have to write the final sentence.
Maybe your marriage began partly out of jealousy.
Then repent of jealousy.
Maybe it began from pride.
Repent of pride.
Maybe you used your spouse.
Confess where wisdom permits and seek help in repairing what your selfishness damaged.
Then start learning how to choose them now.
Love them now.
Honor them now.
Pray for them now.
Become faithful now.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But surrendered to Christ, you do not have to keep repeating yesterday tomorrow.
And if you are single right now, please do not become so desperate to prove that you are lovable that you accept a covenant you are not ready to honor.
Being unmarried is not humiliation.
Being rejected is not proof that God rejected you.
Watching somebody else get married first does not mean heaven forgot your address.
And somebody else's relationship is not God's deadline for yours.
Wait with wisdom.
Heal honestly.
Grow in Christ.
Learn contentment that does not depend upon romantic attention.
Become the kind of person capable of loving another person rather than consuming them.
Then, if God leads you into marriage, enter it understanding that biblical marriage is not primarily a trophy for two attractive people who finally found happiness.
Paul ultimately points Christian marriage toward something astonishing:
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25
Look at the direction of that love.
Christ gave Himself.
Marriage shaped by Christ therefore moves away from:
“What can this person prove about me?”
toward:
“How can I faithfully love this person before God?”
That is where jealousy begins losing oxygen.
That is where pride starts dying.
That is where performance becomes covenant.
That is where the ex finally disappears from the room.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody desperately needed tonight:
The ex needs to disappear from the room.
Not physically.
Emotionally.
Stop letting someone who left become an invisible third person inside the relationship God may be asking you to steward faithfully.
Stop dressing for their reaction.
Stop posting for their reaction.
Stop dating for their reaction.
Stop marrying for their reaction.
Stop building your future around somebody who belongs to your past.
Bring the wound to Jesus.
Tell Him the ugly truth.
“Lord, I wanted them jealous.”
“Lord, I wanted them sorry.”
“Lord, I wanted everybody impressed.”
“Lord, I wanted to prove something.”
“Lord, I am still angry.”
“Lord, I am not as healed as I pretend.”
That prayer may not look impressive enough for social media.
But heaven has never required your performance.
Christ calls you into truth.
And maybe tonight truth sounds like tears.
Maybe truth sounds like repentance.
Maybe truth sounds like finally admitting that you have been calling revenge “moving on.”
If this exposed something hidden, do not hide behind embarrassment.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing what has lived silently in darkness into honest Christian community is where pretending begins to lose its grip.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting this battle.

Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow, but because there may come a night when loneliness starts negotiating with your convictions and you need to remember why marriage should never become revenge.
But before you leave this page, remember the person whose face appeared in your mind when you first read the title.
Maybe it was your ex.
Maybe it was the person you are dating.
Maybe it was yourself.
Now imagine standing at an altar someday.
Someone is looking into your eyes.
They are trusting you with years they can never get back.
They are trusting you with mornings and midnight conversations, weakness and aging, intimacy and disappointment, sickness and celebration.
They are trusting you with a heart God never gave you permission to use as ammunition.
When you look back into their eyes, may there be nobody else in the room you are secretly trying to impress.
No ghost.
No rival.
No revenge.
No audience.
Just truth.
Just covenant.
Just two imperfect people desperately dependent upon a perfect Savior.
Because the greatest victory after somebody breaks your heart is not making them jealous.
It is becoming so surrendered to Jesus that you no longer need them to be jealous at all.
Do not use somebody's heart to send a message to your past—place your wounded heart in the hands of Christ, and let Him write a future that no longer needs revenge to feel redeemed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LION DOESN’T NEED YOU TO DENY JESUS—HE JUST NEEDS YOU TO FALL ASLEEP
paragraphs:
THE LION DOESN’T NEED YOU TO DENY JESUS—HE JUST NEEDS YOU TO FALL ASLEEP
What “Be Sober-Minded and Watchful” Really Means When the War for Your Soul Gets Quiet
Some spiritual battles don't look like battles.
There is no dramatic moment.
No obvious temptation.
No crisis that sends you running to your knees.

Sometimes you are simply lying in bed at 1:47 in the morning, scrolling through things you never intended to see, feeding thoughts you would never say aloud, carrying wounds you refuse to surrender, and slowly becoming comfortable with a version of yourself that once would have terrified you.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still know the verses.
You might still attend church.
You might even encourage other people.
But something inside you has become sleepy.
Prayer feels optional.
Sin doesn't shock you like it used to.
Conviction gets dismissed more quickly.
Bitterness has been living in your heart so long that you've started calling it discernment.
Compromise has become “just being human.”
And somewhere between exhaustion, disappointment, distraction, temptation, entertainment, anxiety, secret wounds, and ordinary life...
you stopped watching the door.
That is why Peter's warning feels almost frighteningly modern.
He wrote:
“νήψατε, γρηγορήσατε.”
Nēpsate. Grēgorēsate.
Be sober-minded.
Be watchful.
Then comes the reason.
“ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν διάβολος…”
Your adversary, the devil.
Peter describes him moving about like a roaring lion, looking for someone to devour.
Notice what Peter does not say.
He does not tell frightened Christians to become obsessed with demons.
He does not tell believers to interpret every inconvenience as satanic activity.
He does not teach them to live terrified of Satan.
He tells them to stay awake.
That distinction matters.
The Greek word νήψατε — nēpsate carries the idea of sobriety, self-control, clear-headedness, freedom from the kind of intoxication that clouds judgment.
And spiritual intoxication can happen without alcohol ever touching your lips.
You can become drunk on attention.
Drunk on anger.
Drunk on lust.
Drunk on approval.
Drunk on success.
Drunk on outrage.
Drunk on entertainment.
Drunk on your own pain.
Drunk on the endless stimulation of a screen until silence becomes unbearable because silence might force you to hear what is happening inside your own soul.
Peter says:
Wake up.
Think clearly.
Do not let anything possess so much of your attention that you can no longer recognize what is happening spiritually.
Then comes γρηγορήσατε — grēgorēsate.
Watch.
Stay awake.
Remain alert.
Jesus used this same family of language when warning His disciples to watch and pray.
And perhaps one of the saddest pictures of spiritual warfare in the Gospels happened in a garden.
Gethsemane.
Jesus was approaching the cross.
The weight of what was coming pressed upon Him.
His disciples were nearby.
And He told them to watch and pray so that they would not enter into temptation.
But they slept.
Think about that.
One of history's most consequential spiritual moments was unfolding only a short distance away...
and they were sleeping.
Not rebelling.
Not renouncing Christ.
Sleeping.
That should disturb us.
Because sometimes the enemy does not need to convince you that Jesus is false.
He only needs to keep you spiritually drowsy long enough that temptation reaches the door before prayer does.
Sometimes he doesn't need you to hate Scripture.
He just needs everything else to become more interesting.
He doesn't need you to publicly renounce Christ.
He just needs you to postpone obedience.
Tomorrow I'll pray.
Tomorrow I'll forgive.
Tomorrow I'll confess it.
Tomorrow I'll stop.
Tomorrow I'll return to church.
Tomorrow I'll open my Bible.
Tomorrow I'll apologize.
Tomorrow I'll surrender this relationship.
Tomorrow I'll deal with what I'm hiding.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
And suddenly the sin you thought was visiting has its own bedroom.
This is where Peter's imagery becomes painfully serious.
The devil is described as an ἀντίδικος — antidikos.
An adversary.
An opponent.
Someone positioned against you.
Scripture does not present Satan as an equal opposite of God. Christianity is not a cosmic story about two equal gods fighting for control of the universe.
There is one sovereign God.
Satan is a creature.
Defeated, limited, rebellious, judged, and destined for final destruction.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
The cross was not Satan defeating Jesus.

The cross was the place where the Son of God bore our sins, satisfied divine justice for those who belong to Him, conquered the powers of darkness, and opened the way for guilty sinners to be reconciled to God.
So Peter is not trying to make Christians terrified of the lion.
He is teaching Christians not to behave like there is no lion.
There is a difference.
And maybe that is exactly where someone reading this has been living.
You didn't abandon Jesus.
You just stopped guarding your heart.
You kept feeding something you knew was weakening you.
One conversation became an emotional attachment.
One glance became a habit.
One wound became resentment.
One disappointment with church became isolation.
One season of exhaustion became prayerlessness.
One success became pride.
One compromise became another.
Nobody noticed.
Maybe even you didn't notice.
But slowly...
quietly...
your appetite changed.
You began craving what once convicted you and avoiding what once strengthened you.
And the frightening thing about spiritual drift is that it rarely feels like movement.
When you're drifting with the current, everything can feel strangely still.
Until you finally look toward the shore.
And realize how far you've gone.
But hear the Gospel before shame starts speaking louder than Jesus.
Peter does not say the believer's answer is to become strong enough to defeat Satan through sheer willpower.
The next verse says:
“ᾧ ἀντίστητε στερεοὶ τῇ πίστει…”
Resist him.
Firm in the faith.
Not firm in your personality.
Not firm in your emotions.
Not firm because you watched enough motivational videos.
Not firm because you promised yourself that this time would be different.
Firm in the faith.
Your defense against darkness is not confidence in yourself.
It is dependence upon Christ.
This changes spiritual warfare completely.
Spiritual warfare is not mainly shouting louder at the devil.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks remarkably ordinary.
Opening Scripture when your emotions are begging you to feed the lie.
Praying when you would rather scroll.
Walking away from the conversation you secretly enjoy but know dishonors Christ.
Confessing the pornography instead of protecting your reputation.
Deleting the number.
Forgiving the person.
Refusing to rehearse hatred.
Turning off the screen.
Calling a mature believer and saying, “I'm not doing well.”
Choosing truth when anxiety is manufacturing a thousand imaginary futures.
Worshiping when God feels distant.
Remaining faithful when obedience feels unrewarded.
Repenting quickly instead of defending yourself cleverly.
Sometimes the fiercest act of spiritual warfare is simply saying:
“Jesus, this belongs to You now.”
And meaning it.
There is something else we cannot miss.
Immediately before Peter says, “Be sober-minded and watchful,” he tells believers to cast their anxieties upon God because He cares for them.
That placement is beautiful.
Peter does not tell anxious Christians:
“Stop feeling things.”
He points them toward the God who cares.
Then he tells them to remain alert.
Why?
Because fear can distort perception.
Anxiety can make lies sound prophetic.
Pain can make temptation sound medicinal.
Loneliness can make destructive relationships look like rescue.
Exhaustion can make compromise feel reasonable.
Rejection can make applause feel necessary.
That is why spiritual sobriety includes learning where to put your anxiety.
You were never designed to carry tomorrow as though you were God.
Give it to Him.
The thing keeping you awake.
The child you're worried about.
The marriage that feels fragile.
The diagnosis you fear.
The bills.
The betrayal.
The future.
The unanswered prayer.
The shameful thing nobody knows.
The possibility that terrifies you.
Cast it upon Him.
Not because it doesn't matter.
Because you matter to Him.
And this is where spiritual warfare becomes deeply personal.
The enemy wants you isolated with your interpretation of your pain.
Jesus calls you into truth.
The enemy whispers:
“God abandoned you.”
The Gospel answers:
Look at the cross.
The enemy says:
“You've sinned too badly.”
The Gospel answers:
Look at the cross.
The enemy says:
“You will always be what you were.”
The Gospel answers:
Look at the empty tomb.
The enemy says:
“Hide.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
The enemy says:
“Pretend.”
Jesus says:
“Confess.”
The enemy says:
“Clean yourself up first.”
Jesus says:
Come to Me.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Biblical grace never says your sin doesn't matter.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so great that repentant sinners can be washed, forgiven, reconciled, restored, and transformed.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear.
Because perhaps your greatest spiritual battle right now isn't something happening around you.
It is the voice inside you telling you to hide from God until you're worthy of returning.
Listen carefully.
If you had to become worthy before coming to Jesus, nobody would ever come.
The Christian life begins with grace.
Continues by grace.
And ends in glory because of grace.
Peter knows this.
That is why this terrifying warning about a prowling lion does not end with the lion.
Keep reading.
Peter turns our eyes toward “the God of all grace.”
What a title.
Not the God of barely enough grace.
Not the God of grace for respectable sinners.
Not the God of grace until your third failure.
The God of all grace.
Peter says that after His people have suffered, God Himself will restore, establish, strengthen, and settle them.
God Himself.
Maybe those are the two words your exhausted heart needed today.
God Himself.
You thought your failure had written the ending.
God Himself.
You thought the addiction owned the final chapter.
God Himself.
You thought the divorce defined you.
God Himself.
You thought what happened to you destroyed everything.
God Himself.
You thought what you did disqualified you forever.
God Himself.
You thought the years you wasted could never be redeemed.
God Himself.
This is why the Gospel is greater than your scandal.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing consequences with sentimental Christianity.
He rewrites the sinner.
Peter himself is proof.
Think about the man writing these words.
Peter knew what it meant to be spiritually overconfident.
He once told Jesus, in effect, that even if everyone else fell away, he wouldn't.
Then came the courtyard.
Questions.
Pressure.
Fear.
And Peter denied even knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
The bold disciple collapsed.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine that sound.
Imagine realizing that the warning Jesus gave you hours earlier had just become your biography.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Scandal.
Failure.
Cowardice.
Shame.
If the Gospel were merely a religion for people with impressive records, Peter's story should have ended there.
But resurrection morning came.
Jesus rose.
And the risen Christ did not discard His broken disciple.
Jesus restored Peter.
The man who once fell asleep when Jesus told him to watch would eventually write to suffering Christians:
Be sober-minded.
Be watchful.
Do you see it now?
Those words weren't written by someone who had never fallen.
They were written by someone who knew exactly what happens when confidence replaces dependence.
Peter wasn't writing theory.
He had scars.
And maybe that's why this verse should not merely frighten you.
Maybe it should give you hope.
Because failure does not have to be your final identity.
You can wake up.
Today.
Not after you repair your reputation.
Not after you feel spiritual again.
Not when the temptation disappears.
Today.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning house.
Turn around.
Come home.
Bring the secret.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the pride.
Bring the doubt.
Bring the sexual sin.
Bring the anger.
Bring the numbness.
Bring the hypocrisy.
Bring the wound you've turned into an identity.
Bring the part of your story you pray nobody discovers.
Bring it into the light before darkness convinces you that hiding is safer.
Jesus already knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Christ.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is a new life available that cannot be manufactured by self-improvement.
The goal of spiritual warfare isn't to become fascinated with Satan.
It is to remain faithful to Jesus.
Eyes open.
Mind clear.
Heart guarded.
Bible open.
Knees bent.
Sin confessed.
Faith anchored.
Hands surrendered.
And when you fall?
Don't run from Christ.
Run toward Him.
When temptation screams?
Remember Christ.
When accusations come?
Remember Christ.
When suffering makes you question everything?
Remember Christ.
When your past comes knocking like it still owns the house?
Remember who bought the house.
You were purchased at a price.
The blood of Jesus speaks a better word over repentant sinners than shame ever could.
So perhaps today you need to stop blaming every struggle on spiritual warfare and ask a more uncomfortable question:
Where have I stopped watching?
Where have I become spiritually numb?
What am I tolerating today that once drove me to repentance?
What voice has become louder than Scripture?
What am I consuming that is quietly consuming me?
What relationship is pulling my heart away from Christ?
What secret have I protected longer than I've pursued freedom?
Where have I confused God's patience with God's permission?
Don't answer for anybody else.
This is between you and Jesus.
And if something came immediately to mind...
That may be the very place where repentance needs to begin.
Be honest.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that grace still reaches broken people.
Don't turn vulnerability into performance.
Turn it into testimony.
And please don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who is smiling publicly and losing a war privately.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Send it privately to the person who has disappeared from church.
Share it with the believer who is exhausted.
Share it with the person who thinks they've gone too far.
Share it with the skeptic who believes Christianity is only for polished people.
Let them discover what Peter discovered:
Jesus does extraordinary things with people who have fallen.
There may come a night when temptation feels stronger than it does right now.
A night when your thinking isn't clear.
A night when loneliness starts negotiating with your convictions.
A night when the lion roars.
Come back and remember:
νήψατε. γρηγορήσατε.
Stay sober-minded.
Stay awake.
Stay near Jesus.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you stay close to Scripture, don't simply consume truth and disappear.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not make God love you more.
But generosity can be an act of worship when it flows freely from love for Christ and a desire to help Gospel truth reach people.
And there is more.
Use them.
Share them.
Give them to new believers.
Send them to someone struggling.
Read something that strengthens your theology instead of merely feeding your algorithm.
Because your soul is being discipled by something every day.
The question is whether you are paying attention.
And maybe that is the sentence we should leave ringing in the room.
The enemy does not always need to destroy your Bible.
Sometimes he only needs to keep you too distracted to open it.
He does not always need to make you hate prayer.
Sometimes he only needs to convince you that you'll pray later.
He does not always need to convince you that Jesus isn't Lord.
Sometimes he only needs you to live tomorrow as though He isn't.
So wake up, beloved.
Not into paranoia.
Into Christ.
Not into fear.
Into faith.
Not into obsession with darkness.
Into deeper communion with the Light of the world.
The lion may roar.
But the lion does not sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
The accuser does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
Your temptation does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
Your trauma does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
Your worst night does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
Your scandal does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
And the Savior who restored a disciple who denied Him still restores broken people today.
So be sober-minded.
Be watchful.
Resist the enemy.
Stand firm in the faith.
Cast your anxiety upon God.
Stay close to Jesus.
And when shame tells you that your story is already over, remember this:
The rooster may announce your failure—but resurrection morning can still rewrite your future.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Do Some People Flirt Without Wanting a Relationship?
paragraphs:
Why Do Some People Flirt Without Wanting a Relationship?
When Someone Makes You Feel Chosen but Never Actually Chooses You
There is a particular kind of heartbreak nobody warns you about.
You were never officially together.
There was no anniversary.
No relationship status.
Maybe there was never even a kiss.
And yet somehow…
you still had something to grieve.
Because they looked at you differently.
They remembered little things about you. They found reasons to message you. They teased you. Complimented you. Stayed up talking to you. They made ordinary conversations feel strangely intimate.
Sometimes they acted jealous.
Sometimes they made you feel beautiful.
Wanted.
Seen.
And just when you started wondering whether this might actually become something…
they pulled away.
So you tried to convince yourself you imagined it.
Then they came close again.
Another message.
Another compliment.
Another late-night conversation.
Another little spark of hope.
Close enough to awaken your heart.
Never close enough to take responsibility for it.
And eventually you found yourself asking the question that can quietly torment someone for months:
Why would somebody flirt with me if they never wanted a relationship with me?
The answer is more complicated than, “They were playing you.”
Sometimes they were.
Sometimes they weren't.

People flirt for many reasons. Attraction does not automatically equal readiness for commitment. Some enjoy playful social connection. Some are lonely. Some crave affirmation. Some are genuinely attracted but emotionally unavailable. Some are uncertain about what they want. Some like the excitement of being desired. Some fear rejection and keep everything ambiguous. Others enjoy receiving relationship-level emotional intimacy without accepting relationship-level responsibility.
And sometimes two people simply interpreted the same interaction very differently.
That distinction matters.
Because not every person who flirts without pursuing a relationship is deliberately manipulative.
But neither does the absence of malicious intent erase the pain caused by prolonged ambiguity.
There is a difference between enjoying someone's company and continually feeding expectations you have no intention of fulfilling.
And this is where the issue becomes deeper than dating.
Because beneath the flirting is often something painfully human:
the desire to be wanted without the vulnerability required to truly be known.
We want attention.
We want affirmation.
We want someone to notice when we enter the room.
We want the message waiting on our phone.
We want proof that somebody could choose us.
And sometimes we want all of that while being terrified of what choosing someone back might require.
Commitment makes demands that flirting does not.
Flirting can remain fantasy.
Commitment eventually encounters reality.
Flirting can present the polished version of ourselves.
Relationship exposes impatience, insecurity, selfishness, wounds, habits, fears, expectations, differences, boundaries, sacrifice and responsibility.
It is easy to enjoy someone's admiration.
It is much harder to love another human being truthfully.
Perhaps that is why one small sentence in Scripture carries such enormous weight:
“Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No.’”
Matthew 5:37.
In the Greek text, the expression is strikingly direct:
ἔστω δὲ ὁ λόγος ὑμῶν ναὶ ναί, οὒ οὔ
Estō de ho logos hymōn nai nai, ou ou.
In context, Jesus is teaching about truthful speech rather than giving dating advice. We should not pretend otherwise.
But the principle reveals something beautiful about the character Christ forms in His people:
truth should not require manipulation to survive.
Our words should increasingly become trustworthy.
Our intentions should become cleaner.
Our lives should not depend upon calculated ambiguity.
Jesus is forming people whose yes can mean yes.
Whose no can mean no.
People who do not need to keep another person's heart suspended between hope and rejection simply because being desired feels good.
That can be uncomfortable to read.
Especially if you suddenly realize…
you haven't only been the person confused by mixed signals.
You may have given them.
Maybe there is somebody whose messages you answer whenever you feel lonely.
Somebody you keep emotionally nearby even though you already know you do not want a future with them.
You enjoy their compliments.
You like knowing they care.
You notice when they stop paying attention.
And the moment they begin moving on…
you suddenly become interested again.
Not necessarily because you want them.
But because you don't want to lose the feeling of being wanted by them.
That is where this stops being an article about “those people.”
Now it is about us.
The human heart can turn another person's affection into medicine for its own insecurity.
And Scripture is remarkably serious about the heart.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.”
The Hebrew begins:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
Mi-kol mishmar netzor libbekha.
The language carries the idea of guarding or watching over the heart carefully.
Not building a wall around it so nobody can ever enter.
Not becoming cynical.
Not assuming everyone has terrible motives.
Guarding it.
There is a difference.
Guarding your heart means you stop handing the deepest parts of yourself to ambiguity and then calling the anxiety “chemistry.”
Read that again.
Sometimes what feels intoxicating is not intimacy.
It is uncertainty.
One day they are close.
The next day they disappear.
Then they return.
Your emotions rise and fall according to their attention.
You begin examining punctuation.
Response times.
Emojis.
Views.
Likes.
Who reacted to whose story.
Why they were warm yesterday and distant today.
You can spend hours trying to decode behavior that one honest conversation could clarify.
And somewhere inside all that uncertainty, imagination begins writing a relationship that reality has never actually promised you.
That is dangerous territory for the heart.
Because you can become deeply attached not only to a person…
but to the person you hope they will eventually become.
You aren't mourning what happened.
You're mourning what almost happened.
What could have happened.
What you prayed might happen.
The future you quietly constructed from fragments.
And sometimes “almost” hurts more than goodbye because goodbye at least gives grief a name.
Ambiguity keeps grief alive.
But hear this carefully:
Someone's inability or unwillingness to choose you does not determine your value.
Your worth was never supposed to be measured by somebody's romantic attention.
This is where Jesus changes the entire conversation.
The Gospel does not tell you to become desirable enough that nobody will ever reject you.
The Gospel tells you that your deepest identity cannot safely rest in whether another human being desires you at all.
You were created for something far greater than becoming somebody's favorite notification.
And this is where many of us need to repent—not merely heal.
Because sometimes the problem is not that we loved someone too much.
Sometimes we made their attention too important.
We checked the phone before we prayed.
Their message changed our mood more quickly than God's promises changed our perspective.
Their silence could ruin our day.
Their compliment could resurrect it.
Slowly, almost invisibly, another human being gained authority over places in our hearts that belonged to God.
That is not romantic love at its healthiest.
That can become idolatry wearing perfume.
And Jesus loves us too much to merely help us manage our idols.
He calls us back.
Back to truth.
Back to Himself.
Back to a love that does not need mixed signals to keep us interested.
Look at Christ.
The One who knows everything about you does not love an imaginary version of you.
He knows the secret thoughts.
The insecurity.
The vanity.
The sexual temptation.
The desperate need for approval.
The relationships you replay in your head.
The messages you wish you had never sent.
The attention you secretly enjoyed receiving from someone you knew you shouldn't encourage.
The person you still check on.
The boundary you keep pretending isn't necessary.
He sees it.
All of it.
And the scandal of grace is that Jesus did not wait for sinners to become impressive before coming to rescue them.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
The Greek word translated “sinners” is:
ἁμαρτωλῶν — hamartōlōn.
Sinners.
Not people who finally got themselves together.
Not people with spotless relationship histories.
Not people who never confused attention with love.
Sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
That means Christianity is not primarily the story of wounded people learning better dating techniques.
It is the story of guilty and wounded people being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
And that changes how we love.
Grace does not say, “Your behavior doesn't matter.”
Grace says your sin mattered enough for Christ to die—and His mercy is powerful enough to transform you.
Maybe you have been using people for validation.
Repent.
Maybe you have knowingly kept someone emotionally attached because their attention comforts your loneliness.
Repent.
Maybe you are maintaining flirtatious intimacy with someone else's spouse or partner and hiding behind the excuse that “nothing technically happened.”
Repent.
Maybe lust has been disguising itself as connection.
Repent.
Maybe you have been obsessing over someone who has already made it clear they do not want a relationship.
Release them.
Maybe you keep returning to somebody who gives just enough affection to stop you from leaving but never enough honesty to build something real.
You are allowed to stop participating in confusion.
Repentance is not humiliation.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning of life toward God.
It is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Jesus does not expose our hearts so He can leave us bleeding beneath the light.
He exposes what is killing us so grace can reach what we have been hiding.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps the person reading this who most needs compassion is the person who flirts because silence terrifies them.
Maybe when nobody wants you, old wounds start talking.
“You're unattractive.”
“You're forgettable.”
“Nobody will choose you.”
“You're getting older.”
“You'll end up alone.”
So attention becomes anesthesia.
A compliment quiets the insecurity.
A flirtatious conversation makes you feel alive.
Another person becomes proof that you still matter.
But the relief never lasts.
So you need another message.
Another reaction.
Another person interested in you.
Another little emotional hit.
And eventually you can have ten people wanting your attention while still feeling completely unwanted inside.
Because human admiration cannot permanently heal an identity wound.
Only God can tell you who you ultimately are.
And if you belong to Christ, the question that rules your life can no longer be:
“Who wants me?”
The deeper question becomes:
“Whose am I?”
You belong to the One who purchased His people at immeasurable cost.
Jesus Christ was betrayed.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God flirting with humanity.
It is covenant love demonstrated at a cross.
Sacrificial.
Costly.
Holy.
Faithful.
Real.
So if you are wondering whether somebody wants you, perhaps you need to stop trying to extract a commitment from clues.
Ask.
Listen.
Watch their actions.
Respect their answer.
And when their actions continually contradict the fantasy you have built, have enough courage to believe reality.
You do not need to hate them.
You do not need to publicly expose them.
You do not need to post cryptic quotes hoping they feel guilty.
You do not need revenge.
You can forgive.
You can establish boundaries.
You can grieve.
You can pray for them.
And you can walk away without turning them into a villain.
Forgiveness does not require continued emotional access.
Neither does Christian love require romantic availability.
Sometimes love says:
I forgive you, but I cannot keep living inside this confusion.
Sometimes integrity says:
I care about you, so I will stop feeding feelings I cannot honestly reciprocate.
Sometimes maturity says:
I wanted this to become something, but you don't—and I will respect both your answer and my heart enough to stop pretending otherwise.
And sometimes repentance sounds like:
God, I have been using people's attention to fill something only You can heal.
That prayer may hurt.
Pray it anyway.
Because there are people walking around with hearts full of screenshots, unfinished conversations and imagined futures, wondering why they cannot move forward.
Maybe your freedom begins when you stop asking God to make somebody choose you…
and start asking Him to make you more like Jesus.
Imagine how different our relationships would become if Christians became known not merely for what we refused sexually, but for how carefully we handled human hearts.
No manipulation.
No breadcrumbing.
No collecting admirers.
No exploiting loneliness.
No pretending friendship while secretly cultivating sexual attention.
No using spiritual language to manufacture intimacy.
No keeping people as emotional backups.
Just truth seasoned with grace.
Clarity accompanied by kindness.
Attraction submitted to holiness.
Desire submitted to wisdom.
Relationships submitted to Christ.
That will not guarantee nobody ever gets hurt.
We are human.
Feelings develop.
Timing differs.
Attraction is sometimes one-sided.
Relationships sometimes end.
But there is an enormous difference between unavoidable heartbreak and avoidable deception.
Christian maturity should make us increasingly careful with that difference.
And if this article is exposing something hidden in you, don't rush past the discomfort.
Stay there for a moment.
Not in shame.
At the feet of Jesus.
Maybe you were hurt.
Maybe you did the hurting.
Maybe both are true.
Grace has room for that confession.
You do not need to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes two honest words are enough to say, “I need my brothers and sisters in Christ beside me.”
Not as a passive-aggressive weapon.
Not to embarrass them.
Send it privately to the believer who keeps returning to mixed signals.
If Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, there is also a practical way to help this ministry continue reaching people.
It does not.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and financial support does not make anyone more righteous before God.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one way believers may freely choose to participate in Gospel ministry is through generous support and sharing truth with others.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is helping biblical content travel farther than the darkness competing for people's attention.
And it is helping Gospel-centered messages reach the person scrolling alone at 2:00 in the morning who desperately needs to discover that their worst chapter does not have to be their final chapter.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm believer.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending they have perfect lives.
Let them encounter Jesus.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy is not that somebody flirted with you and never chose you.
Perhaps the greater tragedy would be spending your entire life begging human beings to validate a heart that was created to find its deepest identity in Christ.
People may send mixed signals.
People may change their minds.
People may desire you today and disappear tomorrow.
People may promise things they cannot carry.
But Jesus Christ is not another ambiguous almost-relationship.
At Calvary, love did not merely speak.
Love bled.
And when Christ rose from the grave, grace had the final word.
So stop building your worth around who texts back.
Stop measuring your beauty by who notices.
Stop confusing chemistry with character.
Stop calling uncertainty destiny.
Stop begging someone to become the answer to a question only God can ultimately answer.
Bring your loneliness to Jesus.
Bring your rejection.
Bring your need for validation.
Bring the person you cannot release.
Bring the person you misled.
Bring the conversations nobody knows about.
Bring the shame.
Bring the desire.
Bring all of it.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Set boundaries where wisdom requires them.
Make restitution where appropriate.
And receive the grace Christ purchased for sinners at the cross.
Because maybe the question was never only:
“Why do some people flirt without wanting a relationship?”
Maybe beneath it was another question:
“Why does being wanted matter so much to me?”
And deeper still:
“Can Jesus really heal the part of me that keeps searching for my worth in another person's eyes?”
Yes.
Not always instantly.
Not without surrender.
Not without truth.
But yes.
He can take the heart that was manipulated.
The heart that manipulated others.
The rejected heart.
The lonely heart.
The lustful heart.
The attention-starved heart.
The heart still waiting for somebody to choose it.
And He can rewrite its story.
Because sometimes the person you kept begging to choose you was never meant to become your salvation—and the Savior you actually needed had already chosen the cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is It a Sin to Have a Celebrity Crush?
paragraphs: Is It a Sin to Have a Celebrity Crush?
You can admire someone’s beauty, talent, personality, or presence without worshiping them. But there is a line—and sometimes your heart crosses it long before your behavior does.
It starts so innocently that calling it “sin” can sound almost ridiculous.
You see an actor in a movie.
A singer appears on your screen.
An athlete smiles during an interview.
Someone is attractive. Charismatic. Talented. Funny. Confident.
And something inside you says, Wow.
Nothing scandalous happened.
You did not abandon your faith.
You did not bow before a statue.
You just have a celebrity crush.
So why even talk about it?
Because Jesus has always cared about what happens in places nobody else can see.
And before you feel condemned for finding another human being attractive, hear this clearly:
Noticing beauty is not automatically lust.
Admiration is not automatically idolatry.
Finding someone attractive is not automatically adultery.
The question is not simply, “Did I notice them?”
The deeper question is:
“What did my heart do after I noticed them?”
That question changes everything.
Because Scripture does not portray temptation itself as identical to sin. Jesus Himself was “tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
So the first involuntary moment of attraction is not necessarily your moral failure.
You saw someone.
Your brain registered beauty.
Your emotions responded.
But what happens next?
Do you release the thought?
Or rehearse it?
Do you acknowledge attraction?
Or begin feeding fantasy?
Do you admire something about the person?
Or create an imaginary relationship with a person you do not actually know?
Do you appreciate beauty?
Or repeatedly return to their pictures because you enjoy what those images awaken inside you?
There is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we call something a “crush” because the word sounds harmless enough to protect us from examining what we are actually cultivating.
Jesus said:
“Everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
That is Matthew 5:28.
The Greek becomes especially important here.
The phrase translated “to lust after her” contains the verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō.
It can describe desire, longing, or craving. The word itself is not inherently sexual or sinful in every biblical context. Context determines its moral character.
And that matters.
Jesus was not teaching that merely seeing an attractive person is adultery.
The construction in Matthew 5:28 points toward looking with the purpose of desiring—a gaze that does not merely recognize attractiveness but entertains and cultivates wrongful desire.
That distinction can expose us.
Because there is a difference between:
“That person is attractive.”
…and:
“Let me keep looking because I want to enjoy imagining what it would be like to have them.”
One can be recognition.
The other can become cultivation.
And cultivation matters because Christianity is not merely concerned with what your body has done.
Jesus goes after the heart.
The hidden room.
The imagination.
The place where nobody sees what you replay.
Nobody sees the saved pictures.
Nobody hears the fantasy.
Nobody knows why you keep watching the same interview.
Nobody knows why you search their name at midnight.
Nobody knows why seeing them with someone else somehow makes you jealous even though they do not know you exist.
Nobody knows.
Except God.
And here is where many Christians immediately expect shame.
But watch what Jesus does throughout the Gospel.
He exposes hearts not because He enjoys humiliating sinners, but because hidden bondage cannot be surrendered while we keep pretending it is harmless.
Conviction is not Christ standing over you saying,
“Look how disgusting you are.”
Conviction brings you into the light so grace can reach the thing you stopped calling by its real name.
Maybe your celebrity crush really is nothing more than lighthearted admiration.
Fine.
You do not need to manufacture guilt where Scripture does not.
But maybe it has become something else.
Maybe this person occupies your imagination constantly.
Maybe you compare your spouse to them.
Maybe your real husband suddenly seems less handsome because you spend hours consuming edited images of men professionally styled, lit, trained, filtered, and presented for a camera.
Maybe your wife begins to feel ordinary because your feed continuously delivers carefully curated images of women whose appearance has become part of a commercial industry.
Maybe you are single, lonely, exhausted, and craving intimacy—and this imaginary attachment has become emotionally safer than risking real vulnerability with real people.
Maybe the celebrity is not really the deepest issue.
Maybe loneliness is.
Maybe disappointment is.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to turn human beings into experiences for your imagination.
Maybe rejection made fantasy feel safer than relationship.
Maybe you have been emotionally neglected so long that pretending someone desirable would choose you gives you ten minutes of relief from feeling invisible.
Suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Is having a celebrity crush a sin?”
It becomes:
“Jesus, what is my heart actually hungry for?”
That is the question worth asking.
Because idols often begin as good things asked to carry a weight they were never created to bear.
Beauty is good.
Talent can be good.
Art can be good.
Admiration can be good.
Human attraction belongs to God's created world.
But Scripture gives God a place in the human heart that belongs to Him alone.
The first commandment says:
“You shall have no other gods before Me.”
In Hebrew:
לֹא יִהְיֶה־לְךָ אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים עַל־פָּנָיַ
Lo yihyeh-lekha elohim acherim al-panai.
Exodus 20:3.
Idolatry is bigger than carved statues.
Anything created can become spiritually disordered when it begins receiving the devotion, identity, hope, dependence, or ultimate affection that belongs to the Creator.
And celebrity culture can make this especially subtle.
Because celebrities are not usually presented to us as ordinary human beings.
We consume fragments.
Performances.
Photographs.
Characters.
Interviews.
Highlights.
Public personas.
Carefully selected moments.
And then the imagination fills in everything we do not know.
You may know their favorite food.
Their birthday.
Their movies.
Their songs.
Their interviews.
Their clothes.
Their relationship history.
But you do not necessarily know them.
You know information about them.
That is not the same thing.
And this is where a celebrity crush can become emotionally deceptive.
You can fall in love with a person your imagination helped create.
You supply the missing personality.
You imagine how they would treat you.
You imagine conversations that never happened.

You imagine chemistry that has never been tested by disagreement, exhaustion, responsibility, morning breath, bills, sickness, disappointment, sacrifice, ordinary Tuesday afternoons, or the thousand unglamorous realities that make actual love costly.
Fantasy requires almost nothing from its object.
Real love does.
Real love serves.
Real love forgives.
Real love remains when someone is inconvenient.
Real love sees imperfections.
Real love is not sustained by camera angles.
And perhaps that is why fantasy can become so addictive.
The imaginary person never interrupts you.
Never misunderstands you.
Never disappoints you unless the news reports something you dislike.
Never asks you to wash dishes.
Never needs patience.
Never sees your weaknesses.
Never requires covenant.
You control the entire relationship because the relationship exists primarily inside your mind.
That can feel safe.
But Jesus did not die to imprison you inside relationships that exist only in your imagination.
He came to bring you into truth.
And truth may require asking painful questions.
Can I stop looking at this person whenever I choose?
Does thinking about them repeatedly produce sexual fantasies?
Am I emotionally escaping into an imaginary relationship?
Do I compare real people to a manufactured image?
Would I be comfortable allowing Jesus into the thoughts I deliberately cultivate about them?
Has admiration become obsession?
Does this person stir gratitude toward God—or discontentment with the life God has given me?
If you are married, there is another question that deserves courage:
Would you feel comfortable if your spouse knew exactly how you think about this celebrity?
Not merely that you think they are attractive.
Exactly how you think about them.
Because covenant changes the conversation.
Your spouse cannot compete with fantasy.
No human being can.
Fantasy can be edited endlessly.
Your spouse is real.
Real skin.
Real flaws.
Real moods.
Real wounds.
Real needs.
Real aging.
Real humanity.
And real covenant love is infinitely more meaningful than imaginary perfection because real love requires the death of selfishness.
If your celebrity crush has started making your spouse feel inadequate, comparison is already extracting a price.
But perhaps you are not married.
Perhaps this hits differently.
You are single.
You pray for someone.
Nothing happens.
You watch other people marry.
Nothing happens.
Another wedding invitation.
Another pregnancy announcement.
Another lonely night.
And somewhere along the way, the celebrity crush became a small emotional shelter.
Someone beautiful to imagine choosing you.
Someone exciting to daydream about.
Someone who cannot reject you because you never actually have to approach them.
And maybe God is not angrily ripping that shelter away.
Maybe He is gently showing you that your heart deserves something more real than an imaginary person temporarily anesthetizing a real ache.
Psalm 139:23–24 gives us one of Scripture's most courageous prayers:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart…”
The Hebrew word for heart there is לֵבָב — levav.
The biblical heart is not merely the place of romantic feelings. It is deeply connected with the inner person—thought, desire, intention, will.
“Search me.”
Not:
“God, tell me everybody else's problem.”
Search me.
That prayer is terrifying when prayed sincerely.
Because God may reveal that what you called harmless has become hunger.
What you called admiration has become escape.
What you called attraction has become lust.
What you called fandom has become obsession.
What you called entertainment has become comparison.
But He may also reveal something else.
You may discover that you have been tormenting yourself with guilt over simply noticing that another human being is attractive.
And in that case, you need truth too.
Christian holiness is not pretending beauty does not exist.
It is learning to see creation without demanding possession of it.
You can acknowledge:
“That person is beautiful.”
And then continue walking with Jesus.
You do not have to panic.
You do not have to interrogate every involuntary thought.
You do not have to become afraid of attraction.
The Christian life is not emotional amputation.
It is ordered affection.
That is why Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
Everything.
Even what you watch.
Even who you follow.
Even what you fantasize about.
Even what you admire.
Even what you secretly want.
And perhaps that gives us a better question than simply asking whether celebrity crushes belong in a universal category called sinful or harmless.
Ask:
Can I carry this attraction under the lordship of Jesus Christ?
Can you thank God for someone's beauty without coveting them?
Can you appreciate talent without worshiping the talented?
Can you enjoy entertainment without emotionally surrendering yourself to the entertainer?
Can you recognize attraction without feeding lust?
Can you admire a human being while remembering they are dust and breath just like you?
If yes, admiration does not need to become shame.
But if the answer is no…
Do not hide.
Please.
This is where the Gospel becomes beautiful.
Because Christianity is not the story of morally flawless people trying desperately to keep Jesus from discovering what they think about at night.
He already knows.
He knew before the cross.
And He went to the cross anyway.
Romans 5:8 says:
“God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned the search history.
Not after we conquered every fantasy.
Not after we became respectable.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Grace does not say:
“Keep the idol.”
Grace says:
“You don't need it anymore.”
Grace does not say:
“Lust doesn't matter.”
Grace says:
“Bring Me your lust. I can teach your eyes to see people differently.”
Grace does not say:
“Your loneliness is imaginary.”
Grace says:
“I see exactly where it hurts. Don't medicate your soul with fantasies that cannot love you back.”
Maybe you crossed the line.
Maybe you sexualized someone repeatedly.
Maybe your thoughts became explicit.
Maybe you hid it from your spouse.
Maybe obsession swallowed hours.
Maybe you know, without needing another paragraph, that something became spiritually unhealthy.
Then repent.
Not performatively.
Not dramatically for other people.
Repent before Christ.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia carries the sense of repentance, a turning or change of mind that expresses itself in a changed direction.
Turn.
Bring the imagination back.
Bring the desire back.
Bring the lonely heart back.
Bring the secret room back.
Jesus is not intimidated by what you find there.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
That is not permission to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to stop hiding it.
Delete what needs deleting.
Unfollow what repeatedly drags you into deliberate lust.
Stop watching the clips you know you are not watching innocently.
Talk honestly with your spouse if your secrecy has damaged your marriage.
Seek wise pastoral or Christian counseling help when obsession, compulsive sexual behavior, or deep loneliness is bigger than a social-media habit.
But do not confuse removing temptation with earning forgiveness.
Jesus is not waiting for your perfect streak before He welcomes the repentant.
Your obedience is the fruit of grace, not the purchase price of it.
And there is one more thing.
The celebrity you are crushing on needs Jesus too.
Think about that.
Strip away the fame.
The followers.
The money.
The face.
The body.
The awards.
The cameras.
The headlines.
The blue check.
The person on your screen is a human soul.
They will age.
They will suffer.
They will experience loss.
They will eventually die.
And before God, fame cannot purchase righteousness.
What if instead of merely fantasizing about famous people, Christians began praying for them?
What if the person you have been reducing to a body became someone whose soul you remembered?
What if attraction became intercession?

“Lord, protect them. Bring faithful Christians into their life. Lead them to truth. If they don't know Christ, let them encounter the Gospel. If they do know Christ, strengthen them to walk faithfully.”
Suddenly the person becomes human again.
Not an object.
Not an escape.
Not your imaginary soulmate.
A human being made in God's image who needs grace exactly as you do.
That is what Jesus does.
He takes the scandal hiding underneath our polished religious language and rewrites it with grace.
Not cheap grace.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that cleanses.
Grace that teaches us to look differently.
Grace that teaches us to love differently.
Grace that refuses to leave us chained to whatever once controlled our imagination.
So…
Is it a sin to have a celebrity crush?
Simply recognizing that a celebrity is attractive, enjoying someone's work, or experiencing an involuntary attraction is not automatically sin.

But deliberately cultivating lust, coveting someone, nurturing fantasies that violate faithfulness, allowing obsession to master you, or giving a created person the devotion that belongs to God crosses into territory Scripture directly warns us about.
The line is not fame.
The line is the heart.
And only you and God know what has been happening there.
So do not merely ask:
“How much can I get away with before this becomes sin?”
Ask something more beautiful:
“Jesus, how much of my heart can I give back to You?”
Maybe this article exposed something nobody knows.
If so, you do not need to publish the details of your struggle. But don't disappear back into hiding.
Someone reading the comments may need to know they are not the only person fighting for a clean heart.
We want your support to come freely, sincerely, and with Christ—not pressure—at the center.
But whatever you do after reading this, remember what matters most:
Do not trade a real Savior for an imaginary relationship.
Do not let a beautiful face become a hiding place for a wounded heart.
Do not mistake fantasy for love.
And when Jesus puts His finger on something you would rather keep hidden, do not run from Him.
Run toward Him.
Because the hands exposing the wound are the same hands that were pierced to redeem you.
Your secret desire does not have to become your secret master; Jesus can rewrite even the rooms of your heart nobody else has ever entered.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD TOLERATE POLYGAMY IF GENESIS PRESENTS ONE MAN AND ONE WOMAN?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD TOLERATE POLYGAMY IF GENESIS PRESENTS ONE MAN AND ONE WOMAN?
The Bible Records Men With Multiple Wives—So Why Did God Allow Something That Was Never His Original Design?
There is a question hiding in the pages of the Old Testament that many Christians have wondered about but are sometimes afraid to ask.
If God's design for marriage was one man and one woman...
why did Abraham have more than one woman in his household?
Why did Jacob marry Leah and Rachel?
Why did David have multiple wives?
Why did Solomon have hundreds?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
Why didn't God immediately stop them?
Read that question carefully.
Because there is an enormous difference between asking, “Does the Bible contain polygamy?” and asking, “Does the Bible present polygamy as God's ideal?”
Those are not the same question.
And confusing them can make Scripture appear to contradict itself when, in reality, something much deeper is happening.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not erase their dysfunctional families.
It does not hide their compromises so that religious people can feel more comfortable.
Scripture will tell you that a man trusted God...
and then tell you where that same man failed.
It will show you David worshiping...
and David sinning.
Solomon asking God for wisdom...
and Solomon later behaving foolishly.
Jacob receiving God's promises...
while living inside a household fractured by rivalry.
Why?
Because the Bible isn't primarily the story of good people becoming impressive.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing sinful people who desperately need redemption.
And that distinction changes everything.
Before Abraham...
before Jacob...
before David...
before Solomon...
before Israel had kings...
before Moses gave Israel civil regulations for life in a fallen society...
there was Eden.
And Eden matters.
Because when Jesus was questioned about marriage centuries later, He did something extraordinary.
He went backward.
Back beyond Moses.
Back beyond Israel.
Back beyond the patriarchs.
Back to the beginning.
Genesis 2:24 says in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן֙ יַֽעֲזָב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד׃
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew is beautiful.
וְדָבַק — wəḏāḇaq — carries the idea of clinging, holding fast, being joined.
בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — bə’ištô — “to his wife.”
And then:
לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
“One flesh.”
One covenant union.
The text does not introduce Adam and a collection of wives.

God forms the woman and brings her to the man, and Genesis describes the resulting covenant pattern as the man holding fast to “his wife” and the two becoming one flesh. The Hebrew text itself preserves that movement toward covenantal unity.
And Jesus deliberately returns to that beginning.
That is crucial.
When discussing marriage in Matthew 19, Jesus appeals to creation and says that the Creator made them male and female, then quotes Genesis 2:24 and speaks of the two becoming one flesh.
In other words, Jesus does not look at every marital arrangement recorded in Israel's history and say, “Whatever happened historically must therefore be the ideal.”
He goes back to creation.
That gives us a vital principle for reading the entire Bible:
Description is not automatically prescription.
The Bible describing something does not necessarily mean God is endorsing it.
Cain murders Abel.
Scripture records it.
It does not endorse murder.
Abraham lies.
Scripture records it.
It does not endorse lying.
David commits adultery.
Scripture records it.
It does not endorse adultery.
Solomon accumulates wives.
Scripture records it.
That does not automatically turn Solomon's household into God's blueprint for marriage.
This is where the question becomes more interesting.
Because someone may respond:
“But God didn't merely record polygamy. The Law actually contains regulations dealing with households involving more than one wife.”
Correct.
And that is precisely where we must distinguish regulation from approval.

Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses a situation involving two wives and protects the inheritance rights of the firstborn son when one woman is preferred over another. Whatever interpretive questions surround the precise household situation, the command's concern is unmistakable: personal favoritism must not be allowed to rob the rightful firstborn of his inheritance.
Exodus 21:10 likewise regulates obligations toward a woman when another wife is taken, insisting that her provision and marital rights not simply be discarded.
God is dealing with real people in a real fallen society.
And sometimes biblical law restrains the damage caused by human sin without presenting the damaged situation itself as the creation ideal.
Think about that.
A law regulating the consequences of something is not necessarily a celebration of that thing.

There is an enormous difference between God saying, “This is My beautiful design,” and God saying, in effect, “Since you are living in this broken reality, you may not use that reality as permission to exploit another human being.”
Jesus gives us an interpretive category for this when discussing divorce.
His words in Matthew 19:8 are devastating:
πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn
“because of your hardness of heart.”
Then Jesus says:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως.
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
There it is.
The distinction between what God permits within human brokenness and what God established “from the beginning.”
Jesus was speaking specifically about Mosaic permission concerning divorce, so we should not carelessly pretend that this verse directly says, “Moses permitted polygamy because of hardness of heart.”
It doesn't.
Biblical faithfulness requires us to say exactly what the text says.
But Jesus gives us an important theological category: some Mosaic provisions address fallen human realities without redefining the Creator's original design.
And when you look at the Old Testament's actual portrayal of polygamous households...
the supposed glamour disappears very quickly.
Look at Abraham's household.
Sarah cannot conceive.
Hagar enters the situation.
A child is conceived.
And almost immediately the house fills with contempt, jealousy, bitterness and pain.
Hagar suffers.
Sarah suffers.
Abraham is caught in the middle.
Ishmael eventually leaves with his mother.
Whatever someone thinks polygamy promises, Genesis does not paint this household like a romantic advertisement.
Then comes Jacob.
Jacob loves Rachel.
Laban deceives him into marrying Leah.
Jacob later marries Rachel as well.
And what follows?
Competition.
Comparison.
Jealousy.
Children becoming entangled in their mothers' desperation for affection.
One woman crying through fertility.
Another crying through infertility.
Leah longs to be loved.
Rachel longs for children.
Even the naming of children becomes part of the emotional battlefield.
Read Genesis 29 and 30 slowly sometime.
Don't rush through the names.
Listen to the women.
There are human hearts behind those verses.
The household may contain God's covenant promises...
but it also contains tears.
Then David.
More wives.
More children.
More household complexity.
And eventually a royal family marked by horrifying sexual sin, rivalry, murder and rebellion.
We should not claim that every tragedy in David's household was mechanically caused by polygamy; Scripture itself identifies multiple sins and responsible actors.
But neither should we romanticize the structure surrounding that fractured family.
Then Solomon.
The man famous for wisdom becomes perhaps Scripture's loudest warning against confusing divine patience with divine approval.
Long before Solomon lived, Deuteronomy 17:17 warned Israel's future king:
וְלֹ֤א יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ֙ נָשִׁ֔ים
wəlōʾ yarbeh-lô nāšîm
“He shall not multiply wives for himself.”
And why?
So that his heart would not turn away.
The warning could hardly be clearer.
Then Solomon multiplied wives.
And his heart turned.
The tragedy is almost unbearable.
God had already warned Israel's kings about the danger.
Solomon's story therefore cannot honestly be used as proof that God celebrated polygamy.
It functions much more naturally as a warning.
But now we arrive at something even deeper.
Because perhaps this question isn't really just about polygamy.
Maybe underneath it is another question:
“Why does God tolerate anything He hates?”
Why did God tolerate Abraham's fear?
Jacob's deception?
David's lust?
Peter's denial?
The disciples' pride?
Your compromise?
Mine?
Suddenly this stops being an ancient theological debate.
Now it is standing in our living room.
Because it is easy to look backward at Solomon and ask:
“How could he know God's Word and still live that way?”
Until the Holy Spirit turns the mirror around.
How can we know what Jesus taught about forgiveness...
and still carry bitterness?
How can we know what Scripture teaches about purity...
and secretly feed lust?
How can we know what Christ teaches about money...
and still worship possessions?
How can we sing about surrender on Sunday...
then spend Monday negotiating which parts of our lives Jesus is actually allowed to touch?
Be careful when you ask why God tolerated sinful people in Scripture.
Because eventually you may find yourself asking why He has been so patient with you.
And that is where this story becomes breathtaking.
God's patience is not proof that sin does not matter.
God's patience is often the space in which repentance is being offered.
Tolerance is not endorsement.
Patience is not approval.
Mercy is not moral indifference.
Sometimes the terrifying thing about grace is how long God keeps calling someone who keeps running.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
You knew better.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you went back.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You apologized.
Then repeated it.
You raised your hands in worship while carrying something inside that nobody in the room knew about.
And somewhere in the darkness you began wondering:
“Why hasn't God given up on me?”
Listen carefully.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is great.
The Gospel does not say God looked at human rebellion and decided holiness no longer mattered.
The Gospel says holiness mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross.
Jesus does not rescue us by pretending sin is harmless.
He rescues us by bearing sin's judgment and calling sinners into a new life.
That is why the Bible's messy marriages, shattered families and scandalous failures ultimately point beyond themselves.
Humanity needed more than better rules.
We needed redemption.
And then Christ came.
The New Testament takes marriage and places it inside an astonishing Christ-centered picture.
Paul points back to Genesis' “one flesh” language in Ephesians 5 and connects marriage to Christ and the Church.
Suddenly Eden's marriage imagery reaches toward something larger.
Christ...
and His Bride.
Not a Savior exploiting His Bride.
Not a Savior abandoning His Bride when she becomes difficult.
Christ loves.
Christ gives Himself.
Christ sanctifies.
Christ remains faithful.
And this is where the Gospel becomes painfully beautiful.
Jesus is the faithful Bridegroom for an often-unfaithful people.
We wandered.
He pursued.
We sinned.
He bore the cross.
We hid.
He called us into the light.
We brought scandal.
He brought grace.
We brought guilt.
He brought forgiveness.
We brought a ruined record.
He brought His righteousness.
This is why Christianity cannot merely be reduced to “be a better person.”
The Bible contains too many broken people for that.
The message is not:
“Look how wonderful all these biblical heroes were.”
The message is:
“Look how faithful God remained in the middle of human failure.”
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
Peter needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Even the New Testament's language concerning church leadership points toward marital faithfulness. In 1 Timothy 3:2 Paul uses the expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra
literally, “a man/husband of one woman/wife.”

Interpreters have discussed the exact scope of that expression, so it should not be forced to carry more weight than its context permits. But at minimum, it belongs to Paul's picture of an overseer whose domestic and sexual life must be above reproach, faithful and ordered rather than characterized by uncontrolled appetite.
So why did God tolerate polygamy?
The most careful biblical answer is not, “Because God changed His mind about marriage.”
Nor should we claim more than Scripture explicitly says.
The biblical storyline is more nuanced and more powerful.

Genesis establishes the creation pattern of a man holding fast to his wife and the two becoming one flesh. Fallen humanity departs from God's good order in countless ways. The Old Testament honestly records those departures and sometimes regulates broken situations to restrain injustice and protect vulnerable people. Israel's kings are explicitly warned against multiplying wives. Jesus later points people back to what God established “from the beginning.” And the New Testament ultimately places marriage inside the magnificent picture of Christ's covenant love for His Church.
God's patience with broken human arrangements should never be mistaken for God's abandonment of His holy design.
And maybe...
just maybe...
that is the part somebody reading this desperately needed to hear.
Because you may have made choices outside God's design too.
Maybe your family story is messy.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe sexual sin has followed you for years.
Maybe your children know a version of you that you wish you could erase.
Maybe your past contains chapters you would never post on Facebook.
And perhaps when Christians talk about God's design, all you hear is condemnation because you already know how far your life has fallen from it.
Then hear the rest of the Gospel.
Jesus does not only reveal God's standard.
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
The cross stands precisely where holiness and mercy meet.
Repentance does not mean pretending your sin never happened.
Grace means your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Bring Him the wreckage.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the relationship you destroyed.
Bring Him the shame you have polished until everyone thinks you are fine.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the scandal.
Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
David was forgiven, yet consequences remained.
Choices can leave scars.
Relationships can require years of rebuilding.
Some losses cannot simply be reversed.
But scars are not the same thing as abandonment.
Consequences are not proof that grace has failed.
And your worst chapter does not possess more authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is why our theme at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because scandal doesn't matter.
Because Jesus does.
Maybe this article exposed something deeper than an argument about Old Testament marriage.
Maybe somewhere between Adam, Jacob, David and Solomon...
you saw yourself.
If you did, don't hide.
And if your faith has been exhausted lately and you don't have impressive words left, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Sometimes honesty is where healing begins.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument.
Jesus already paid the price salvation required.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you understand Scripture, encounter Christ, repent honestly and grow deeper in biblical truth, supporting and sharing this ministry is one practical way you can help put Gospel-centered teaching in front of another person who may desperately need it.
Hard questions have a way of returning.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who has questions Christians sometimes seem afraid to answer.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks the Bible is simply a collection of perfect people pretending never to fail.
They may be surprised to discover something very different.
A book filled with deeply broken human beings...
and an astonishingly faithful God.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not leave merely knowing the answer to a theological question.
Know the Savior.
Because one day the question will not be whether Abraham had Hagar, whether Jacob married two sisters, whether David accumulated wives, or how Solomon wandered so far.
The question standing closest to eternity will be much more personal.
What did you do with Jesus?
The same Bible courageous enough to expose the scandals of its heroes is courageous enough to expose ours.
But thank God...
it does not end with scandal.
It leads us to a cross.
An empty tomb.
A risen King.
A faithful Bridegroom.
A Savior who still receives repentant sinners.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful answer of all.
God's patience with broken people was never proof that brokenness was His design; it was evidence that, even in the wreckage, He was still moving history toward the Redeemer.
And if you remember only one sentence after closing this article, remember this:
Your scandal may explain some of your scars—but it does not get to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GIDEON’S CONCUBINE GAVE BIRTH TO ABIMELECH—Who Later Murdered Nearly All His Brothers
