paragraphs: GIDEON’S CONCUBINE GAVE BIRTH TO ABIMELECH—Who Later Murdered Nearly All His Brothers
Gideon defeated an enemy army with 300 men. But the enemy growing inside his own house would become one of the darkest consequences recorded in Judges.
There is something terrifying about surviving the battlefield… only to discover that the greater tragedy was growing quietly inside your own home.
Gideon had watched God reduce an army to three hundred men.
He had heard the trumpets.
Seen the torches.
Watched Midian collapse.
He had experienced the kind of supernatural victory most believers can only imagine.
And yet Judges does not end Gideon’s story with the victory.
It takes us home with him.
That is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to a victorious believer is not the enemy he just defeated.
Sometimes it is what he allows after the victory.
Judges 8 tells us that Israel wanted Gideon to establish what amounted to a hereditary dynasty. Gideon answered with words that sounded wonderfully faithful:
“I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you.”
That was the right answer.
But what happened afterward complicates the picture.

Gideon accumulated enormous wealth. He possessed many wives. He fathered seventy sons. He made an ephod from the gold Israel had given him, and that ephod became a spiritual snare to Gideon and his household.
Then Scripture quietly introduces another woman.
And one child.
One verse.
Almost easy to overlook.
But that verse opens the door to one of the bloodiest family tragedies in the book of Judges.
“And his concubine that was in Shechem, she also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech.”
—Judges 8:31
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
וּפִילַגְשׁוֹ אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁכֶם יָלְדָה־לּוֹ גַם־הִיא בֵּן וַיָּשֶׂם אֶת־שְׁמוֹ אֲבִימֶלֶךְ
Ufilagsho asher biShekhem yaldah-lo gam-hi ben, vayasem et-shemo Avimelekh.
His פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh, commonly translated “concubine,” who lived in Shechem bore him a son.
His name was אֲבִימֶלֶךְ — Avimelekh.
And the name itself is haunting.
Avi — “my father.”
Melekh — “king.”
“My father is king.”
Perhaps the name reflected status, aspiration, or something else—we should not pretend Scripture tells us Gideon’s motive when it does not.
But the irony is impossible to miss.
Gideon had publicly declared:
“The LORD shall rule over you.”
Yet from Gideon’s own household emerged a son whose story would become consumed with making himself king.
Read that slowly.
A father can say the right words publicly while still leaving contradictions privately.
A person can win battles for God and still leave doors unlocked in his own soul.
You can know how to fight Midian and still fail to recognize what pride, compromise, appetite, influence, money, or unchecked ambition is doing inside your house.
That should frighten every one of us enough to examine ourselves.
Because your greatest spiritual danger may not always arrive looking like an enemy.
Sometimes it grows from something you tolerated.
Sometimes it begins as a compromise nobody confronted.
Sometimes it hides behind success.
And sometimes the consequences do not fully appear until years later.
Gideon eventually died.
Israel again turned toward the Baals.
And then Abimelech moved.
He went to Shechem—to his mother’s relatives—and made his argument.
Why should seventy sons of Gideon rule when Shechem could have one man?
Me.
And then came the line every manipulator knows how to exploit:
Remember…
I am your flesh and blood.
Abimelech appealed to tribal loyalty.
Family loyalty.
Identity.
Self-interest.
He did not need to prove that he was righteous.
He only needed to convince people that he was one of them.
And it worked.
The leaders of Shechem gave him seventy pieces of silver.
But notice where the money came from.
The house of Baal-berith.
Money associated with an idolatrous sanctuary financed Abimelech’s rise.
Then Abimelech used that money to hire what Scripture describes as reckless and worthless men.
And they followed him.
Now imagine the road to Ophrah.
Imagine the footsteps.
Imagine Gideon’s sons seeing their half-brother coming.
Perhaps some recognized him.
Perhaps somebody smiled.
Perhaps somebody thought family had arrived.
They had no idea death was walking toward them.
Judges 9:5 says:
וַיַּהֲרֹג אֶת־אֶחָיו בְּנֵי־יְרֻבַּעַל שִׁבְעִים אִישׁ עַל־אֶבֶן אֶחָת
Vayahărog et-echav benei-Yerubbaal, shiv'im ish, al-even achat.
He killed his brothers—the sons of Jerubbaal—
“seventy men…”
עַל־אֶבֶן אֶחָת — al-even achat.
“Upon one stone.”
One stone.
Again.
And again.
And again.
The text gives us no sentimental description.
No dramatic speeches from the victims.
No attempt to soften what happened.
Just the brutal image:
brothers slaughtered upon one stone.

There is a numerical detail worth handling carefully. Judges describes Gideon as having seventy sons, speaks of Abimelech killing the seventy, and then immediately tells us that Jotham, the youngest, survived because he hid. The narrative therefore presents Jotham as the surviving brother from that group; the “seventy” functions as the stated family total while the text itself makes the exception explicit.
Jotham escaped.
Think about that.
While Abimelech was building a throne…
Jotham was hiding to stay alive.
One brother wanted everybody to see him.
The other survived because nobody could find him.
One was being celebrated.
The other was probably terrified.
And if you have ever watched somebody who hurt you appear to prosper while you were barely surviving what they did…
you understand something of the emotional tension here.
Sometimes evil looks successful before judgment arrives.
Sometimes the person who betrayed you appears to move forward while you are still collecting the broken pieces.
Sometimes manipulation gets applause.
Sometimes arrogance gets a platform.
Sometimes wickedness gets money, influence, followers, connections, and power.
And you wonder:
“God… did You see this?”
Judges 9 answers:
Yes.
God saw everything.
But Jotham did something extraordinary before disappearing.
He climbed Mount Gerizim and cried out to the people of Shechem.
Then he told them a story.
The trees wanted a king.
They approached the olive tree.
The olive refused.
They approached the fig tree.
The fig refused.
They approached the vine.
The vine refused.
Finally they approached the thornbush.
And the thornbush accepted.
That image is devastating.
The fruitful trees were already occupied producing something valuable.
But the bramble wanted the throne.
There is a warning here that reaches far beyond ancient Shechem.
Never confuse someone’s hunger for authority with God’s qualification for authority.
Not everyone desperate to lead is called to lead.
Not everyone demanding recognition carries fruit.
Not everybody who says, “Follow me,” has been sent by God.
Jesus later gave His disciples an entirely different vision of greatness.
The rulers of the Gentiles “lord it over” others, He said, but among His followers greatness would be expressed through service.
That is why Abimelech’s kingdom feels so different from the kingdom of Christ.
Abimelech climbed upward by killing his brothers.
Jesus descended in humility to save His brothers and sisters.
Abimelech spilled other people’s blood to obtain a throne.
Jesus spilled His own blood to rescue sinners.
Abimelech sacrificed others for himself.
Christ gave Himself for others.
Abimelech said, in effect:
“Let them die so I can reign.”
Jesus came declaring through His actions:
“I will die so they can live.”
Do you see the Gospel hiding against the darkness?
This is why the ugliest stories in Scripture still matter.
They show us what human beings become when sin rules without repentance.
Abimelech got his kingdom.
For a while.
Three years passed.
Three years can feel like forever when you are waiting for justice.
But Scripture says God sent division between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem.
The alliance built on selfish ambition began devouring itself.
That is the nature of sin.
Sin promises partnership and eventually produces slavery.
It promises pleasure and eventually demands payment.
It promises control and eventually controls you.
It promises secrecy and eventually exposes you.
It whispers:
“Nobody will ever know.”
Then one day you discover that the thing you thought you controlled has become your master.
Maybe your battlefield is not Abimelech’s battlefield.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe it is pornography.
An affair.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Gambling.
Secret messages.
Jealousy.
Greed.
A hidden relationship.
A second life online.
Hatred toward somebody who hurt you.
A religious image protecting an unrepentant heart.
You still post Bible verses.
Still say “God bless.”
Still worship.
Still smile.
But somewhere inside you there is an Abimelech demanding a throne that belongs to Jesus.
And that is where this ancient story suddenly stops being ancient.
Because Abimelech is not merely a monster for us to stare at from a safe distance.
His story forces us to confront the terrifying potential of the human heart when ambition, idolatry, pride, violence, and self-rule are allowed to reign.
You may never murder seventy brothers.
But have you destroyed someone with words because they stood between you and what you wanted?
Have you secretly enjoyed someone else’s failure?
Have you manipulated people?
Have you used relationships to advance yourself?
Have you demanded recognition?
Have you protected your reputation more fiercely than your holiness?
Have you wanted the throne?
Be honest.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully beautiful.
Christianity does not teach that we are basically good people who occasionally make unfortunate mistakes.
Scripture goes deeper.
Our problem reaches the heart.
We need more than inspiration.
We need reconciliation.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new King.
We need Jesus.
Abimelech kept going.
Violence escalated.
Shechem eventually burned.
About a thousand men and women died in the tower of Shechem.
Then Abimelech marched against Thebez.
There was another tower.
People fled inside.
Abimelech approached its entrance, apparently intending to burn it as he had done before.
He had done this before.
It had worked before.
Perhaps he assumed it would work again.
But somewhere above him stood an unnamed woman.
Not a warrior whose biography Scripture celebrates.
Not a king.
Not a famous judge.
The Bible does not even give us her name.
She had an upper millstone.
And she dropped it.
The stone struck Abimelech’s head.
His skull was crushed.
The man who had slaughtered his brothers upon one stone was brought down beneath a stone.
And even while dying, Abimelech remained obsessed with his reputation.
He ordered his armor-bearer to kill him because he did not want people saying:
“A woman killed him.”
Imagine it.
His skull was shattered.
His kingdom was collapsing.
Death was seconds away.
And he was still worried about what people would say about him.
That may be one of the saddest portraits of pride anywhere in Scripture.
He was dying…
and still managing his image.
And suddenly the story asks us another uncomfortable question:
How much of your life is being spent trying to control what people think about you?
How much energy goes into appearing strong?
Appearing successful?
Appearing spiritual?
Appearing happy?
Appearing healed?
Appearing holy?
Maybe you are exhausted because you have been protecting an image Jesus never asked you to maintain.
Maybe repentance begins when you finally stop saying,
“What will people think?”
and start asking,
“What does God see?”
Because God already knows.
The secret.
The addiction.
The anger.
The compromise.
The night nobody knows about.
The message you deleted.
The tears you hid.
The resentment you buried.
The prayer life that disappeared.
The faith that feels weaker than everyone thinks it is.
He knows.
And somehow the Gospel still says:
Come.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
The final verses of Judges 9 make the theological meaning unmistakable.
God brought Abimelech’s evil back upon him, and the wickedness of Shechem returned upon its people.
Jotham’s warning had not vanished into the wind.
God had heard.
God had seen.
Justice had not been asleep.
But if all we learn from Abimelech is “bad people eventually get punished,” we have stopped too early.
Because you and I need more than justice against people worse than ourselves.
We need mercy for ourselves.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Jesus does not excuse sin.
He bears judgment against sin.
He does not tell sinners to hide more successfully.
He calls sinners into the light.
He does not merely improve people.
He saves.
The Gospel says that the throne belongs to Someone entirely unlike Abimelech.
A King who wore thorns instead of becoming one.
A King who did not murder His brothers to protect His throne.
A King whose enemies mocked Him while He prayed for forgiveness.
A King who carried a cross.
A King who entered death.
A King who rose again.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs right now.
Not another religious performance.
Not another promise that you will “do better.”
Not another week pretending everything is fine.
Repent.
Come home.
Tell Jesus the truth you think He does not already know.
Bring Him the hidden thing.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the part of you that keeps reaching for the throne.
The Gospel is not God saying your sin never mattered.
The Gospel is God showing just how much it mattered—
and then showing the immeasurable price Christ willingly paid to redeem sinners.
Grace is not permission to remain Abimelech.
Grace is Christ rescuing us from the kingdom of self and bringing us under His righteous reign.
Maybe this article exposed something.
There are moments when three words can become the first crack in a wall you have spent years building.
Not because every paragraph will be comfortable to reread.
God sees what is hidden.
Sin never makes a trustworthy king.
Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
And grace can rewrite what shame convinced you was already finished.
Not merely to increase numbers.
There may be an Abimelech slowly surrendering to ambition, bitterness, lust, pride, or secret sin.
There may be a Jotham hiding somewhere, wondering whether God saw what happened.
There may be someone smiling in photographs tonight while privately asking God whether life is still worth fighting for.
You may never know whose screen this reaches because you pressed Share.
Send it privately to the believer who has gone quiet.
Send it to the person who stopped attending church.
Send it to the person who thinks his scandal has disqualified him forever.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is about pretending Christians never fail.
The Bible does not hide the scandal.
It reveals what sin does—
and then points us toward the grace we desperately need.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially should never be presented as purchasing God’s favor, buying salvation, or replacing obedience to Christ. Scripture teaches willing, cheerful generosity—not giving under compulsion.
And there is another reason to stay connected.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace is not merchandise.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Your support simply helps put that message in front of another human being.
Gideon once stood before Israel after an astonishing victory and declared that the LORD should rule over them.
Yet within a generation, his own son reached for a throne.
Abimelech murdered for it.
Manipulated for it.
Destroyed people for it.
Killed brothers for it.
Burned cities for it.
And when death finally found him, he was still protecting his reputation.
Do not wait until everything collapses before surrendering your throne.
There is only one King who can carry the weight of your life.
His name is Jesus.
Give Him the secret.
Give Him the reputation.
Give Him the ambition.
Give Him the wound.
Give Him the past.
Give Him the future.
Give Him the throne.
Because the most frightening part of Abimelech’s story is not that a wicked man once wanted to become king.
It is realizing how desperately the human heart still wants to become its own king.
And the most beautiful part of the Gospel is that Jesus does not merely expose the rebel hiding inside us.
He died for rebels.
He forgives rebels who repent.
He transforms rebels who surrender.
And He makes sons and daughters out of people whose stories looked beyond redemption.
So before you leave this page, ask yourself one question you cannot answer casually:
Who is really sitting on the throne of my life?
If the answer exposes you, do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Because sometimes the stone that shatters your illusion is the mercy that finally drives you back to the King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABSALOM WAITED TWO YEARS Before Taking Revenge for What Happened to Tamar
paragraphs: ABSALOM WAITED TWO YEARS Before Taking Revenge for What Happened to Tamar

He barely spoke about it. He did not explode that day. He waited. And for two years, something deadly was growing behind the silence. But the most heartbreaking person in 2 Samuel 13 may not be the man who took revenge—or even the man he killed. It is the woman whose cries everyone else eventually learned to live around.
There are Bible stories that comfort you.
And then there are Bible stories that corner you.
They make you uncomfortable because there is no polished hero standing in the middle of the chapter. No quick resolution. No beautiful ending before the page turns.
Just sin.
Silence.
A wounded woman.
An angry brother.
A father who hears what happened.
And two years later...
blood.
This is 2 Samuel 13.
And if you read it too quickly, you may think this is simply the story of Amnon, Tamar, and Absalom.
It isn't.

It is also a terrifying picture of what can happen when lust is disguised as love, when wounded people are left carrying devastation, when anger is allowed to become hatred, and when human beings decide that because justice has not arrived quickly enough, they will become justice themselves.
And somewhere inside this story...
you may recognize yourself.
Maybe not in Amnon's crime.
Maybe not in Absalom's murder.
But perhaps in the waiting.
The resentment.
The memory you keep replaying.
The wound you say you have forgiven but still secretly rehearse.
The person whose name can change your breathing.
The injustice nobody seemed to take seriously enough.
The prayer you prayed while wondering why God did not fix everything immediately.
Before we talk about Absalom's revenge, however, we need to remember something Scripture refuses to let us forget.
This story begins with Tamar.
Not Absalom.
Tamar.
She was a daughter of David and the sister of Absalom. Amnon, another son of David, became consumed with desire for her.
The Hebrew text initially uses the language:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ — vayye'ehaveha
"He loved her."
But what follows exposes the horrifying difference between biblical love and selfish desire wearing love's clothing.
Real love does not manipulate someone into isolation.
Real love does not ignore "no."
Real love does not overpower.
Real love does not use another person's body to satisfy itself.
Amnon called what he felt love.
His actions revealed something else.
Tamar pleaded with him.
She reasoned with him.
She resisted him.
Scripture does not portray her as consenting to what happened.
Yet Amnon refused to listen.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 13:14 says:
וְלֹא אָבָה לִשְׁמֹעַ בְּקוֹלָהּ
"He was unwilling to listen to her voice."
Then Scripture records that he overpowered and violated her.
There is something unbearably important in those words.
He would not listen to her voice.
Because sin has a way of making another person's humanity inconvenient.
Lust says, "What I want matters more than what this costs you."
Pride says, "What I feel matters more than what God commands."
Bitterness says, "What they deserve matters more than what hatred is doing to me."
Sin keeps turning down every other voice until only desire remains.
Then something chilling happened.
After Amnon violated Tamar, the "love" he claimed to have for her became intense hatred.
The woman he supposedly could not live without became the woman he wanted removed from his presence.
Because she had never been loved properly in the first place.
She had been desired.
There is a difference.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that distinction.
You are not loving someone when you use them.
You are not loving someone when you manipulate them.
You are not loving someone when your affection requires them to violate God's commands.
You are not loving someone when their boundaries make you angry.
Biblical love does not consume another human being.
Biblical love seeks their good.
Tamar was thrown out.
The door was shut behind her.
And Scripture gives us one of the most haunting images in the chapter.
She put ashes on her head.
She tore the special garment she wore.
She placed her hand upon her head.
And she walked away crying aloud.
Not quietly.
Not invisibly.
Crying.
The Hebrew says:
הָלוֹךְ וְזָעָקָה — halokh weza'aqah
She went away crying out.
Do not rush past her cry just because you already know what Absalom eventually does.
Sit there for a moment.
A woman walked out of that house carrying something she never asked for.
Something had been done to her.
Her grief was not evidence that she was dirty.
Her devastation did not make her guilty of Amnon's sin.
The shame belonged to the one who violated her.
And perhaps this is where this ancient chapter suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because there are still Tamars.
People carrying wounds created by somebody else's sin.
People smiling in photographs while privately trying to understand what happened to them.
People sitting in churches while fighting memories nobody around them knows exist.
People who have spent years wondering whether God sees the room nobody else saw.
He does.
God does not confuse the wounded with the one who wounded them.
He does not need darkness to become light before He can see what happened there.
Then Tamar encountered Absalom.
He realized what had happened.
And Tamar remained in his house.
The Hebrew describes her with a devastating word:
שֹׁמֵמָה — shomemah
It carries the sense of being devastated, desolate, ruined, or left appalled.
The chapter does not give us some sentimental sentence saying everything quickly became normal again.
It simply leaves Tamar there.
Desolate.
And then David heard.
Scripture says King David became extremely angry.
But the chapter records no immediate punishment of Amnon by David.

We should be careful here. The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 13:21 explicitly tells us David was very angry; some ancient textual witnesses add an explanation for why David did not rebuke Amnon, but that additional wording is not present in the standard Hebrew Masoretic text. So we should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it actually does.
What the narrative undeniably shows is that Absalom's hatred began burning.
Second Samuel 13:22 says Absalom would not speak to Amnon either good or bad.
Then Scripture tells us why.
He hated Amnon because Amnon had violated Tamar.
Absalom's anger did not arise from an imaginary offense.
Something genuinely evil had happened.
That distinction matters.
The Bible does not require us to call evil good in order to forgive.
Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened.
Forgiveness is not calling abuse acceptable.
Forgiveness does not mean protecting an offender from appropriate consequences.
And forgiveness certainly does not mean telling wounded people that justice does not matter.
God cares about justice.
But there is a dangerous place where righteous anger can mutate into something else.
And Absalom went there.
Then comes one of the coldest transitions in the chapter.
וַיְהִי לִשְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים
"After two full years..."
Two years.
Let that settle.
Approximately 730 days.
Seasons changed.
Meals were eaten.
Conversations happened.
Life apparently moved forward.
But hatred was still alive.
Absalom did not kill Amnon the next morning in an uncontrollable explosion.
He waited.
He planned.
He arranged a sheep-shearing celebration.
He invited the king's sons.
He specifically pressed for Amnon to attend.
And he instructed his servants to watch until Amnon's heart was merry with wine.
Then came the command.
Strike him.
Kill him.
Two years of silence ended in seconds of violence.
And here is where this story reaches through thousands of years and grabs us.
Because not every revenge story ends with literal blood.
Sometimes revenge looks like refusing to speak to someone for years.
Sometimes it looks like destroying their reputation.
Sometimes it looks like secretly celebrating their failure.
Sometimes it looks like making sure everyone knows what they did.
Sometimes it looks like repeatedly reopening the case in your mind, prosecuting them again, sentencing them again, punishing them again.
Sometimes nobody around you knows you are angry anymore.
You go to work.
You raise your children.
You worship.
You post Scripture.
You say, "I'm okay."
But somewhere inside your soul...
it is still day one.
Absalom waited two years.
And time alone did not heal him.
That should destroy one of our favorite clichés.
Time does not automatically heal every wound.
Sometimes time simply gives bitterness deeper roots.
Healing requires something more than passing days.
Some wounds need grief.
Some need truth.
Some need appropriate justice.
Some need wise counsel.
Some need boundaries.
Some need patient restoration.
But every human heart ultimately needs God.
Because you can move thousands of miles away and still carry someone inside your anger.
You can block their number while keeping their memory permanently unblocked in your mind.
You can stop talking about what happened and still allow what happened to determine who you are becoming.
And that is where Absalom's story becomes frightening.
The original injustice against Tamar was real.
But Absalom's response created another evil.
Amnon's sin did not make Absalom's murder righteous.
One person's wickedness does not give another person permission to become wicked in response.
Scripture later gives the principle plainly:
"Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19).
That does not mean earthly authorities should ignore crime or that victims should remain in danger. Romans 13 immediately speaks about governing authority bearing responsibility against wrongdoing.
It means personal vengeance belongs in hands far more righteous than ours.
God can judge without becoming corrupted by hatred.
We cannot.
And maybe that is why this chapter hurts so badly.
Everybody seems to be losing something.
Tamar loses the life she knew.
Amnon is consumed by corrupt desire and later killed.
Absalom allows hatred to mature into murder and eventually enters a much larger rebellion that will tear David's household and kingdom apart.
David's family is fracturing before his eyes.
Sin never keeps its promises.
It always charges more than the advertisement said.
And this is exactly why we need more than moral improvement.
We need a Savior.
Because somewhere inside humanity's long history of lust, violence, shame, betrayal, silence, revenge, and broken families...
Jesus Christ entered.
Not as another wounded sinner looking for someone to punish.
Not as another powerful man exploiting vulnerable people.
But as the sinless Son of God.
Jesus does not minimize evil.
The cross itself proves how seriously God takes sin.
Grace is not God shrugging His shoulders at wickedness.
Grace is unimaginably costly.
At Calvary, Jesus bore sin's judgment so guilty people could be reconciled to God through faith in Him.
And that means the Gospel speaks to every person standing somewhere inside 2 Samuel 13.
To the wounded:
Jesus sees you.
To the ashamed:
what someone did to you does not put their guilt upon your soul.
To the bitter:
Jesus is not asking you to pretend the wound was imaginary. He is calling you to surrender vengeance before vengeance reshapes you.
To the person who has committed terrible sin:
repentance is still possible.
Do not hide behind excuses.
Do not rename lust "love."
Do not rename hatred "justice."
Do not rename pride "strength."
Bring the truth into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Run to Christ.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that sin doesn't matter.
The scandal is that Christ's grace can reach sinners who finally stop defending their darkness and come to Him empty-handed.
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23).
And yet sinners can be "justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (Romans 3:24).
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that refuses to leave you where it found you.
Maybe your two years have actually been twenty.
Maybe someone betrayed you and never apologized.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother wounded you.
Maybe somebody abused your trust.
Maybe the person who damaged you appears to be living happily while you are still collecting pieces.
You do not need to pretend that doesn't hurt.
But please hear this:
Do not give the person who wounded you permission to keep shaping the person you are becoming.
Bring the wound to Jesus.
Again, if necessary.
And again.
Forgiveness can involve a real process of surrender. Reconciliation and restored trust are separate questions and can require repentance, wisdom, safety, and changed behavior.
But vengeance?
Give it to God.
Because hatred promises power while quietly building a prison.
Absalom thought killing Amnon would settle something.
But 2 Samuel does not end at chapter 13.
More grief was coming.
More separation.
More rebellion.
More death.
Unhealed sin keeps writing sequels.
But Jesus writes another kind of story.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed Paul into a servant of the Gospel.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward Christ and received mercy.
This is what Jesus does.
He enters stories human beings would throw away.
He confronts sin without denying grace.
He gives mercy without calling evil good.
He receives repentant sinners without pretending repentance is unnecessary.
He takes people whose stories seem permanently defined by scandal...
and begins writing grace.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you thought this article would only be about Absalom waiting two years.
But perhaps God has put His finger on something you have been carrying much longer.
A name.
A memory.
A secret.
A hatred.
A shame.
A sin you keep defending.
A wound you keep hiding.
Be honest before God.
What has been growing inside you while everybody thought you were fine?
You don't have to tell the whole internet your private story.
But do not lie to Jesus about it.
He already knows.
And He is still calling you.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only one fighting.
Someone may pray because you were brave enough to ask.
Someone may see your testimony and realize that Jesus still restores people.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and salvation is God's gift of grace—not something bought by supporting a ministry.
But if this message helped you see Scripture more clearly, sharing it can place biblical truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
Send it to the believer who has become bitter.
Send it to someone who needs to know that what happened to them does not have to become the final sentence of their life.
It is practical support for the work of creating and distributing Gospel-centered resources.
God does not need our money.
We need His mercy.
The greatest response you can make to this message is not clicking a button.
It is surrendering your heart.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to release vengeance.
Seek help where you have been wounded.
Speak truth where silence has protected darkness.
Give appropriate justice to the authorities God has appointed.
And bring the parts nobody else sees to Jesus.
Because Tamar's cry reminds us that wounds are real.
Amnon's sin reminds us that desire without holiness can become destructive.
David's grief reminds us that anger alone does not repair what evil has broken.
Absalom's two-year wait reminds us that silence is not always healing.
And the Gospel reminds us that our worst chapter does not have to become our final chapter.
Jesus Christ walked toward a cross carrying sins He never committed.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And because the grave could not keep Him, sin does not get unquestioned ownership of the ending either.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one question:
What have I been carrying for two years—or twenty—that Jesus is asking me to finally place into His hands?
Do not wait until bitterness writes another chapter.
Do not wait until secret sin becomes public destruction.
Do not wait until shame convinces you that grace has forgotten your address.
Come to Christ.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is grace for the guilty.
There is refuge for the wounded.
There is freedom from vengeance.
There is a new life for those who belong to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Absalom's story was not simply that he waited two years.
It was that during those two years, the wound was still writing him—and Jesus is calling you to stop letting your wound hold the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABSALOM STOLE A NATION’S HEART—AND NEVER NOTICED WHAT WAS HAPPENING TO HIS OWN
paragraphs:
ABSALOM STOLE A NATION’S HEART—AND NEVER NOTICED WHAT WAS HAPPENING TO HIS OWN
He was handsome, wounded, charismatic, politically brilliant, and loved by the crowd. Then admiration became ambition, pain became rebellion, and the son of David discovered too late that winning people’s hearts is not the same thing as having a heart surrendered to God.
There is something terrifying about Absalom’s story.
Not because he looked dangerous.
Because he didn’t.
He looked like the kind of man people wanted to follow.
Scripture introduces him with an almost uncomfortable emphasis on his appearance:
“Now in all Israel there was no one who was praised as much as Absalom for his good looks. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.”
—2 Samuel 14:25
Think about that.
No blemish.
Admired throughout Israel.
Royal blood.
A commanding presence.
A prince with charisma, influence, access, and the kind of appearance people noticed when he entered a room.
And yet the tragedy of Absalom is not ultimately the story of a beautiful man.
It is the story of what can happen when an untreated wound learns how to become an identity.
Because before Absalom became a rebel, he was a brother whose sister had been violated.
Before he tried to steal a kingdom, something inside his own family had already shattered.
His sister Tamar had been sexually violated by their half-brother Amnon, another son of David. When David heard what had happened, Scripture says he became very angry.
But the biblical narrative records no adequate justice from David against Amnon.
And Absalom?
He went quiet.
Dangerously quiet.
Second Samuel tells us:
“But Absalom spoke to his brother Amnon neither good nor bad. For Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.”
—2 Samuel 13:22
Two years passed.
Two years.
Imagine what can grow inside a human heart for two years when grief is never properly surrendered, injustice seems unanswered, and anger is fed in silence.
Then Absalom arranged Amnon’s murder.
Amnon died.
Absalom fled.
The family fractured further.
Eventually Absalom returned to Jerusalem, but reconciliation with David remained painfully incomplete. For two years he lived in Jerusalem without seeing the king’s face.
The son was home.
But he was not restored to his father.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes proximity disguises estrangement.
You can live in the same house and be emotionally miles apart.
You can sit in church and be spiritually distant from God.
You can sing worship songs while privately nursing resentment.
You can smile for photographs while carrying a war nobody else can see.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still have rooms inside your heart where Jesus has not been allowed to touch the wound.
And wounds do not automatically make us wicked.
But wounds we refuse to surrender can become places where sin builds a throne.
Eventually David and Absalom were reunited.
Second Samuel 14:33 says Absalom bowed before the king, and David kissed him.
It sounds beautiful.
But something was still wrong.
Because reconciliation on the outside had apparently not healed what was happening inside Absalom.
Soon afterward, Scripture says:
“After this Absalom provided himself with chariots and horses, and fifty men to run before him.”
—2 Samuel 15:1
Read those words slowly.
“After this.”
After restoration.
After being allowed before his father.
After receiving the king’s kiss.
Absalom started building an image.
Chariots.
Horses.
Fifty men running before him.
Visibility.
Status.
Spectacle.
He did not announce the rebellion immediately.
That would have been too obvious.
Instead, Absalom understood something about human nature that manipulators have understood for thousands of years:
If you want someone’s allegiance, first convince them that you understand their disappointment.
So Absalom positioned himself beside the gate.
That was strategic.
The gate was where important civic and judicial business took place. People came there with disputes and grievances.
And Absalom was waiting.
He would rise early.
He would meet people.
He would ask where they were from.
He would listen to their cases.
Then he would say, essentially:
Your case is good.
Your complaint is legitimate.
The problem is that nobody appointed by the king is really listening to you.
And then came the poison wrapped in empathy:
“Oh, that I were made judge in the land, and everyone who has any suit or cause would come to me; then I would give him justice.”
—2 Samuel 15:4
Do you see it?
Absalom did not begin by saying:
“My father is terrible. Follow me.”
He began by saying:
“I understand you.”
“I see you.”
“You deserve better.”
“If only I were in charge…”
That sentence has destroyed more than kingdoms.
If only I had their position.
If only people recognized my gift.
If only I had their platform.
If only I were leading this ministry.
If only people listened to me instead.
If only I had what they have.
Be careful when disappointment begins rehearsing imaginary coronations.
Absalom was not merely collecting supporters.
He was cultivating emotional dependence.
When people approached and bowed before the prince, Absalom would reach out, take hold of them, and kiss them.
Personal.
Warm.
Accessible.
Charismatic.
The Bible then delivers one of the coldest descriptions of political manipulation ever written:
“So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.”
—2 Samuel 15:6
The Hebrew is devastating.
וַיְגַנֵּב אַבְשָׁלוֹם אֶת־לֵב אַנְשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vaygannēv Avshalom et-lev anshei Yisra’el.
Literally, the central image is that Absalom stole the heart of the people of Israel.
The verb comes from the Hebrew root גנב — g-n-b, associated with stealing.
Scripture does not merely say he persuaded them.
It says he stole their hearts.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because not everyone who captures your attention deserves your allegiance.
Not everyone who understands your pain should become your authority.
Not everyone who makes you feel seen is leading you toward God.
Not everyone with charisma has character.
Not everyone with followers is following Christ.
Not everyone who speaks about justice has surrendered to the Judge of all the earth.
And not everyone who appears wounded is therefore incapable of becoming dangerous.
Absalom had legitimate pain.
Tamar truly had been violated.
Amnon truly had committed evil.
David truly had failed grievously within his family.
None of that makes Absalom’s rebellion righteous.
That distinction is crucial.
Your wound can explain something about your behavior without making your sin holy.
Read that again.
Your wound can explain something about your behavior without making your sin holy.
Some of us have spent years calling bitterness “discernment.”
Calling revenge “justice.”
Calling jealousy “calling.”
Calling pride “confidence.”
Calling rebellion “freedom.”
Calling manipulation “leadership.”
Calling emotional control “love.”
Calling disobedience “following my heart.”
But Jesus does not merely rename our darkness.
He brings us into the light.
Absalom eventually declared himself king.
The conspiracy grew strong.
Messengers spread throughout Israel.
People defected.
Even Ahithophel, one of David’s counselors, joined Absalom.
Suddenly David—the giant-killer, warrior, king, and father—was fleeing Jerusalem.
Imagine that scene.
David had once run toward Goliath.
Now he was running from his own son.
There are battles where defeating the enemy feels glorious.
There are other battles where winning still feels like losing because the person on the other side is someone you love.
David crossed the Kidron Valley.
He climbed the Mount of Olives.
And Scripture says:
“So David went up by the Ascent of the Mount of Olives, and wept as he went up; and he had his head covered and went barefoot.”
—2 Samuel 15:30
The king was crying.
Barefoot.
Humiliated.
Rejected.
Betrayed.
Ascending the Mount of Olives.
And centuries later, another King would enter the darkness around Jerusalem.
Another Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
He too would cross the Kidron.
He too would go toward the Mount of Olives.
He too would experience betrayal.
But here the comparison must be handled carefully.
David was a deeply flawed king who suffered partly amid consequences connected to his own sin and failures.
Jesus was the sinless King.
David fled because his throne was being taken.
Jesus willingly walked toward the cross because He had come to give Himself.
David's son rebelled against his father.
Jesus, the eternal Son, perfectly obeyed His Father.
And that is why Absalom’s story does not ultimately leave us staring at Absalom.
It makes us long for a better King.
A King whose beauty is holiness.
A King whose charisma is never manipulation.
A King who does not steal hearts but transforms them.
A King who does not exploit wounded people but heals them.
A King who does not seize a throne through rebellion but receives the Kingdom in perfect obedience to the Father.
Jesus.
Absalom wanted a crown badly enough to betray his father.
Jesus already possessed divine glory and humbled Himself for sinners.
Philippians tells us that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.
Absalom said, in effect, “I should be king.”
Jesus knelt and washed feet.
Absalom collected followers to elevate himself.
Jesus called disciples to deny themselves.
Absalom manipulated grievances.
Jesus confronted sin while welcoming sinners.
Absalom wanted people to die for his kingdom.
Jesus died for His people.
That is the difference between human ambition and the Gospel.
And eventually, Absalom’s revolution collided with reality.
The battle turned against him.
Then came one of Scripture’s strangest and most haunting scenes.
Absalom was riding a mule when he encountered the thick branches of a great terebinth. Second Samuel 18:9 says his head became caught in the tree, while the mule beneath him continued onward.
The man who wanted to rise above his father was left suspended between heaven and earth.
The man who gathered people around himself was suddenly alone.
The prince celebrated for his appearance was helpless.
The movement kept moving.
The mule kept going.
But Absalom could not.
Joab and his men killed him despite David having commanded his commanders to deal gently with Absalom for his sake.
And when the news reached David, there was no celebration.
No triumphant speech.
No satisfaction that the rebellion had finally been crushed.
The king broke.
Scripture records his cry:
“O my son Absalom—my son, my son Absalom—if only I had died in your place! O Absalom my son, my son!”
—2 Samuel 18:33
That is not merely the cry of a victorious king.
That is the scream of a father.
“My son.”
Again.
“My son.”
Again.
“My son.”
And perhaps this is where the story becomes unbearable.
Because Absalom spent years trying to take something from his father…
while his father still loved him.
He wanted David’s throne.
But David wanted his son.
And now listen carefully, because the Gospel is about to turn the knife into a doorway of grace.
David cried:
“If only I had died in your place.”
But David could not ultimately redeem Absalom by dying for him.
Yet centuries later, the greater Son of David came.
And Jesus did die in the place of sinners.
Not merely as an emotional wish.
Actually.
Historically.
Voluntarily.
Sacrificially.
On the cross.
The Gospel is not God standing over rebels saying, “Try harder and perhaps I will tolerate you.”
The Gospel is that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
We were not innocent victims approaching a reluctant God.
We were sinners in need of reconciliation.
Romans 5:10 even speaks of us as enemies who were reconciled to God through the death of His Son.
We were rebels.
And the King came for rebels.
This is where Absalom’s story reaches through the centuries and grabs us.
Because maybe you never stole a literal kingdom.
But perhaps you have tried to sit on the throne of your own life.
Maybe God said forgive, and you said no.
God said confess, and you hid.
God said surrender, and you negotiated.
God said wait, and you manipulated.
God said flee temptation, and you kept the secret door unlocked.
God said love your enemy, and you rehearsed their destruction in your imagination.
God said trust Me, and you crowned your fear.
That is rebellion too.
Sin does not need an army.
Sometimes all it needs is one heart whispering:
“I will be my own king.”
And that is precisely why Jesus came.
Not merely to improve rebels.
To save them.
Not merely to make bad people behave better.
To make spiritually dead people alive.
Not merely to decorate our old throne room with Christian language.
To remove us from the throne and become Lord.
Maybe the hardest thing you need to admit today is that there is a little Absalom living inside the human heart.
We want the kingdom.
We want control.
We want recognition.
We want vindication.
We want to decide good and evil for ourselves.
And still—
Christ calls.
Still Christ receives repentant sinners.
Still His blood cleanses.
Still grace reaches people who have destroyed things they cannot rebuild.
Still the cross stands.
Still the tomb is empty.
Still Jesus saves.
This is why repentance is not humiliation designed to destroy you.
Repentance is coming home to reality.
It is laying down the stolen crown.
It is admitting:
“Jesus, You are King. I am not.”
Maybe nobody knows what you have been carrying.
Maybe you look like Absalom looked from the outside.
Beautiful life.
Good photographs.
Respectable reputation.
Strong personality.
People laughing around you.
People admiring you.
But underneath it all, something is bleeding.
Anger.
Pornography.
Envy.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Secret compromise.
An affair nobody knows about.
A resentment you have fed for years.
A hunger to be noticed.
A wound from your father.
A wound from your mother.
A wound from church.
A wound from someone who should have protected you.
Please hear this clearly:
What happened to you matters.
But what happened to you does not have to become what rules you.
Bring the wound to Christ before the wound becomes a throne.
Bring the anger to Christ before anger begins interpreting everything you see.
Bring the bitterness to Christ before bitterness starts calling itself wisdom.
Bring your ambition to Christ before applause becomes your oxygen.
Bring your secret sin into the light before you build an entire public identity around protecting what is hidden.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling you.
This is scandal becoming grace.
This is rebellion meeting mercy.
This is a stolen heart being reclaimed by its rightful King.
This is the Gospel.
Be honest.
You do not owe strangers the details of your private pain. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack through which light enters a carefully guarded room.

Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow, but because there may come a night when resentment starts preaching to you again, when ambition starts whispering again, when temptation tells you that you deserve the throne again.
Come back.
Read David’s tears.
Read Absalom’s ending.
Then look at the cross.
And remember who the King is.
But if this message points people toward Christ, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.
Someone may be drifting from Jesus.
Someone may be hiding.
Someone may be exhausted from pretending.
Someone may desperately need to remember that rebellion does not have to be the final chapter.
But the greatest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is opening Scripture again tomorrow.
It is being reminded of truth when the world becomes loud.
It is continuing to grow in repentance, grace, biblical understanding, healing, accountability, and spiritual maturity centered on Jesus Christ.
But before you leave, remember Absalom.
The hair.
The beauty.
The charisma.
The crowds.
The chariots.
The fifty men.
The stolen hearts.
The conspiracy.
The crown he wanted.
The tree.
The silence.
And a father crying,
“My son… my son…”
Then remember Jesus.
The rejected King.
The crown of thorns.
The wounded hands.
The cross.
The blood.
The empty tomb.
The risen Christ.
Absalom wanted his father’s throne and lost everything trying to take it.
Jesus surrendered Himself to His Father’s will and gave everything to bring rebels home.
So lay down the crown.
Stop running.
Stop hiding.
Stop pretending the wound is not becoming something dangerous.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the forgiveness you cannot purchase, the grace you cannot deserve, and the new life you cannot manufacture.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
The throne you keep fighting God for is nothing compared with the grace waiting for you when you finally kneel before the King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Empty Chair at Dinner Can Preach a Sermon About Eternity No Comfortable Sunday Ever Could
paragraphs: The Empty Chair at Dinner Can Preach a Sermon About Eternity No Comfortable Sunday Ever Could

There are moments when grief tears through every comfortable answer we have ever given about death—and in that unbearable silence, the resurrection of Jesus Christ becomes either everything or nothing.
There is an empty chair at the table.
Nobody moved it.
Maybe nobody has had the courage.

It still sits where it always sat, almost as though the person who belonged there might walk through the door again, apologize for being late, pull it backward across the floor, and sit down like nothing happened.
But something happened.
And everyone at the table knows it.
Maybe it was your father’s chair.
Your mother’s.
Your husband’s.
Your wife’s.
Your brother’s.
Your sister’s.
Your child’s.
Your best friend’s.
Maybe the loss happened years ago, and you thought you were finally learning how to carry it.
Then somebody cooked their favorite meal.
A familiar song started playing.
You found an old photograph while looking for something completely unrelated.
Someone laughed exactly the way they used to laugh.
Or you walked into the dining room and looked at that chair.
And suddenly...
you were back at the funeral.
That is one of grief’s cruelties.
It does not always knock before entering.
You can survive anniversaries you thought would destroy you, then fall apart on an ordinary Tuesday because you found their coffee cup behind another mug in the cabinet.
You can worship on Sunday and cry in the grocery store on Monday because you reached automatically for something they loved.
You can sincerely believe in Jesus Christ and still have nights when you would give almost anything just to hear that voice one more time.
And Christianity does not require you to pretend otherwise.
We sometimes speak about death so gently that we almost make the Bible sound embarrassed by grief.
We say, “They’re in a better place.”
We say, “Everything happens for a reason.”
We say, “Be strong.”
Sometimes those words are offered with genuine love.
But there are moments when the grieving heart does not need a slogan.
It needs something stronger than sentiment.
Because death is not sentimental.
Death separates.
Death interrupts.
Death leaves clothes hanging in closets and unfinished conversations trapped inside living hearts.
Death can turn a telephone number you once called without thinking into something you cannot bring yourself to delete.
Death can leave one side of a bed untouched.
Death can leave a birthday on the calendar belonging to someone who will not grow another year older in this present age.
And Scripture does something astonishing.
It does not ask us to call death beautiful.
Paul calls death an enemy.
That matters.
Christian hope is not built upon pretending death does not hurt.
Christian hope begins by looking death directly in the face...
and then looking beyond death to a risen Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:20:
“But now Christ has been raised from the dead...”
Those opening words are thunder.
Νυνὶ δὲ — Nyni de — “But now.”
Everything changes there.

Paul has spent the surrounding argument explaining how catastrophic it would be if Christ had not risen. If there is no resurrection, Christian proclamation collapses. Faith becomes futile. Sin retains its verdict. Those who have died in Christ are lost.
Then comes the earthquake:
But now.
Christ has been raised.
Not merely remembered.
Not merely admired.
Not merely preserved through the teachings of His followers.
Raised.
The Greek expression Χριστὸς ἐγήγερται — Christos egēgertai declares that Christ has been raised from among the dead.
Christianity does not ultimately offer grieving people a philosophy about death.
It announces an event.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ died.
Jesus Christ was buried.
And Jesus Christ rose.
That distinction is everything when you are staring at an empty chair.
Because if Jesus merely taught beautiful ideas and then remained inside Joseph’s tomb, grief eventually gets the final word.
If Jesus remained dead, every cemetery is telling us the ultimate truth about humanity.
If Jesus remained dead, the empty chair wins.
The coffin wins.
The grave wins.
Death wins.
But Paul refuses to leave us there.
“Νυνὶ δὲ Χριστὸς ἐγήγερται ἐκ νεκρῶν, ἀπαρχὴ τῶν κεκοιμημένων.”
Christ has been raised from the dead, “ἀπαρχὴ — aparchē”, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
Firstfruits.
That word carries enormous hope.
In the biblical world, the firstfruits were not merely an isolated piece of produce. They belonged to the beginning of a harvest.
Paul is saying something breathtaking.
The resurrection of Jesus is not merely an extraordinary miracle that happened to one Man long ago.
For those who belong to Christ, His resurrection is the beginning of the harvest.
The empty tomb is a promise that the cemetery does not receive the final chapter.
Paul continues:
“ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνῄσκουσιν, οὕτως καὶ ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ πάντες ζῳοποιηθήσονται.”
As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
Notice how brutally honest Scripture is.
In Adam all die.
The Bible does not hide the human catastrophe.
Death entered the human story through sin. Humanity is not merely suffering from unfortunate biological inconvenience. Something has gone profoundly wrong between creation and Creator.
And eventually every empty chair points toward the same terrifying reality.
We are mortal.
You are going to die.
I am going to die.
The people we love will die unless Christ returns first.
Money cannot negotiate with the grave.
Beauty cannot charm it.
Success cannot outrun it.
Followers cannot cancel it.
Possessions cannot bribe it.
There will eventually be a final meal, a final conversation, a final photograph, a final heartbeat.
Most of us simply do not know when.
And perhaps that is why an empty chair can preach a sermon no comfortable Sunday ever could.
Because that chair asks questions we spend much of our lives avoiding.
What happens when my chair is empty?
What happens when people are talking about me in the past tense?
What happens when my possessions belong to somebody else?
What happens when the accomplishments that consumed my attention cannot accompany me into eternity?
Most importantly...
Am I in Christ?
Not merely, “Do I believe there is a God?”
Not, “Was I raised Christian?”
Not, “Do I sometimes attend church?”
Not, “Am I basically a decent person?”
Paul's hope is explicitly centered “ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ — en tō Christō” — in Christ.
This is where grief becomes more than grief.
It becomes a confrontation with eternity.
The Gospel tells us something our pride desperately resists hearing: our deepest problem is not simply that someday we will die.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Paul eventually brings us directly there:
“τὸ δὲ κέντρον τοῦ θανάτου ἡ ἁμαρτία...”
“The sting of death is sin.”
Sin is not merely a collection of embarrassing mistakes.
Sin is rebellion against the holy God who gave us life.
Every secret compromise.
Every carefully hidden appetite.
Every bitterness we have nurtured.
Every lie.
Every act of lust.
Every moment of pride.
Every idol.
Every time we wanted God’s gifts while resisting God Himself.
We have sinned.
And the Gospel does not rescue us by lowering God's holiness until our rebellion looks harmless.
God does something infinitely more costly.
He sends His Son.
Jesus enters the human story.
The sinless One walks among sinners.
The Holy One touches the unclean.
The rejected find Him.
The ashamed find Him.
The religiously impressive discover that they need Him just as desperately as everyone else.
Then Christ goes to the cross.
There, the scandal becomes almost unbearable.
The innocent One is condemned.
The righteous One is mocked.
The Creator is surrounded by His creatures.
Nails.
Blood.
Darkness.
A crown designed as mockery.
A cross designed as humiliation.
And Jesus dies.
Christianity never asks grieving people to worship a God unfamiliar with graves.
Jesus stood before the tomb of Lazarus and wept.
Jesus knows what human tears feel like.
And then Jesus Himself entered death.
But death encountered Someone it could not keep.
The tomb was sealed.
Then came the third day.
And the story changed forever.
This is why Paul's words later in 1 Corinthians 15 sound almost defiant:
“Κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος.”
“Death has been swallowed up in victory.”
Not ignored.
Not renamed.
Not romanticized.
Swallowed up.
Then Paul speaks directly to death:
“ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ νῖκος; ποῦ σου, θάνατε, τὸ κέντρον;”
“Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?”
Imagine saying those words beside a grave.
Not because graves do not hurt.
Not because Christians do not cry.
Not because separation suddenly becomes painless.
But because Jesus walked into death and came out alive.
The Christian does not stand beside a grave saying, “Death isn't real.”
The Christian stands there saying:
Death is real—but Jesus Christ is greater.
That is resurrection hope.
And it is radically different from vague spirituality.
Our hope is not merely that “people live on in our memories.”
Memories are precious.
But memories cannot resurrect anybody.
Our hope is not merely that someone is “watching over us.”
Our hope rests on something far more solid.
Jesus Christ has risen.
And those who belong to Him will be raised.
Paul says:
“τῷ δὲ θεῷ χάρις τῷ διδόντι ἡμῖν τὸ νῖκος διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.”
“Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Notice where victory comes from.
Not through positive thinking.
Not through human goodness.
Not through religious achievement.
Through our Lord Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel.
We do not climb our way toward God.
Christ came down for us.
We do not erase our own guilt.
Christ bore sin at the cross.
We do not defeat death.
Christ defeated it.
We do not earn resurrection.
Christ becomes our hope.
Grace does what we could never do for ourselves.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been avoiding Jesus because you think you have gone too far.
You know what you have done.
Other people may not.
God does.
You remember the night.
The betrayal.
The addiction.
The secret.
The person you hurt.
The years you wasted.
The prayers you stopped praying.
Maybe grief itself changed you.
You became angry with God.
You stopped going to church.
You could not understand why He allowed someone you loved to die.
Maybe you sat at the funeral surrounded by Christians singing about God's goodness while something inside you screamed:
Then why did He let this happen?
God is not frightened by that question.
The Bible contains grieving saints asking agonizing questions.
Faith does not mean pretending pain is painless.
But grief can become dangerous when pain persuades us to run from the only One who can ultimately redeem what death has stolen.
Jesus never promised His followers immunity from funerals.
He promised something greater.
Resurrection.
And resurrection means death does not get the last word over those who are Christ's.
Your tears matter.
Your grief matters.
That empty chair matters.
The person you lost mattered.
But hear this carefully:
Christian hope does not mean we can confidently declare the eternal destiny of every person simply because we loved them.
Scripture does not give us permission to manufacture assurance where God has not spoken.
Our hope is Christ.
And therefore grief also whispers an urgent question to the living:
What will you do with Jesus?
You are still breathing.
Your chair is occupied today.
Your heart is still beating.
Grace is being proclaimed to you right now.
Do not spend your entire life preparing for everything except eternity.
You can prepare for retirement and remain unprepared to meet God.
You can insure your house, insure your vehicle, protect your accounts, schedule medical examinations, build an inheritance, organize your funeral...
and never reconcile with the God before whom you will stand.
Jesus Christ calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
It is surrender.
It is finally admitting:
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
And perhaps the empty chair has made you realize something you were too busy to see.
Life is short.
Eternity is not.
Maybe there is someone you need to forgive.
Someone you need to call.
Someone who needs to hear, “I love you.”
Maybe there is a sin you need to stop protecting.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity while privately starving.
Maybe everyone around you thinks your faith is strong, but God knows you have been slowly drifting.
Come home.
Not to religion.
To Christ.
Come with the questions.
Come with the anger.
Come with the grief.
Come with the shame.
Come with trembling hands if necessary.
But come.
The cross tells you sin is more serious than you imagined.
The resurrection tells you Jesus is more powerful than you imagined.
And grace tells you your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is the heartbeat of everything we proclaim at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites sinners into sons and daughters.
He rewrites condemnation through forgiveness.
He rewrites rebellion through repentance.
He rewrites shame through grace.
And ultimately, for everyone who belongs to Him, He will rewrite even the grave through resurrection.
Maybe tonight your family will gather around a table with an empty chair.
Maybe Christmas hurts now.
Maybe birthdays hurt.
Maybe Sunday lunch feels different.
Maybe there are recipes you cannot cook without crying.
Let yourself miss them.
Love leaves an ache when someone is gone.
You do not dishonor Christ by grieving.
But do not let grief convince you that death is sovereign.
It isn't.
Jesus is.
One day Christ will demonstrate completely what Easter morning announced decisively.
Death's reign has been broken.
So cry.
Remember.
Grieve.
Tell the stories.
Hold the photographs.
Thank God for every mercy you were given.
But when the empty chair starts preaching despair, preach the resurrection back to it.
Christ has risen.
When the cemetery tells you death is undefeated:
Christ has risen.
When grief whispers that everything beautiful eventually disappears:
Christ has risen.
When your own mortality frightens you:
Christ has risen.
When Satan reminds you of forgiven sins:
Christ has risen.
When the darkness feels final:
Christ has risen.
And because Christ has risen, everyone who truly belongs to Him possesses a hope stronger than the grave.
Sometimes the most courageous sentence a grieving believer can write is simply:
Let other believers pray with you.
Your testimony may become the sentence another grieving person desperately needed tonight.
And if this confronted you about your own eternity, do not hide behind religious language.
“Jesus, I need You.”
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting our need is the first crack in years of hiding.
Not fifty.
One.
The widow whose house became painfully quiet.
The father who buried a child.
The daughter who still reaches for her phone to call her mother.
The friend who stopped attending church after the funeral.
The believer smiling publicly while privately wondering whether God still sees them.
Not merely because an article deserves reach.
Your share may place resurrection hope in front of them at exactly the moment grief comes knocking.
Grief has seasons.
There may come another birthday, another anniversary, another ordinary Tuesday when you need to remember:
the grave is not greater than Jesus.
Supporting Gospel-centered work is not a substitute for supporting your local church, caring for your family, serving people in need, or giving as God leads you. Grace cannot be bought.
Share because somebody is grieving.
Tag because somebody is drifting.
Save because grief sometimes returns without warning.
And support the mission if God has genuinely placed that desire on your heart.
Because somewhere tonight there is an empty chair.
Someone will look at it.
Someone will remember.
Someone will cry after everyone else goes to sleep.
And someone desperately needs to know that Christianity does not answer that chair with a cliché.
It answers with an empty tomb.
The chair may remain empty in this present life.
The photographs may grow older while the face inside them never does.
The ache may remain in ways nobody else completely understands.
But for those who are in Jesus Christ, death does not possess the authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
And perhaps that is the sentence you need to carry with you tonight:
The chair may be empty, but because the tomb of Jesus is empty, death will never have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE GOSPEL DOES NOT DIVIDE HUMANITY INTO “CLEAN PEOPLE” AND “DIRTY PEOPLE”
paragraphs: THE GOSPEL DOES NOT DIVIDE HUMANITY INTO “CLEAN PEOPLE” AND “DIRTY PEOPLE”
Jesus did not come to congratulate the respectable and dispose of the ruined. He came because every one of us needs a Savior—and at the cross, the ground beneath our feet is terrifyingly level.
There is a kind of Christianity that knows how to stay clean without knowing how to love.
It knows which people to avoid.
Which scandals to whisper about.
Which sins are acceptable enough to mention in testimony and which ones make everybody uncomfortable.
It knows how to look at the addict and quietly think, At least I’m not like that.
It knows how to hear about the adulterer and say, How could someone do that?

It knows how to see the prisoner, the prostitute, the drunk, the sexually broken, the angry, the doubter, the backslider, the tattooed stranger, the pregnant unmarried woman, the divorced father, the ashamed teenager, the person walking into church after destroying almost everything in their life...
...and unconsciously divide the room.
Clean people over here.
Dirty people over there.
But there is a devastating problem.
That is not the Gospel.
And Jesus once told a story aimed directly at people who thought it was.
Luke tells us that Jesus addressed certain people who “trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others” (Luke 18:9).
That sentence should make religious people uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not describe atheists.
He described people confident in their own righteousness.
Then Jesus placed two men in the temple.
One was a Pharisee.
One was a tax collector.

To modern ears, “Pharisee” almost automatically sounds like the villain. That can make us miss the force of the story. In Jesus’ setting, the Pharisee represented visible religious seriousness, while tax collectors could be associated with exploitation and collaboration with Roman power.
In other words, if you had been standing nearby, you might have assumed you already knew which man God approved.
The Pharisee prayed:
“God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are...” (Luke 18:11, KJV).
Listen carefully.
He thanked God...
and then used another human being as the background against which he could admire himself.
That is one of the most frightening forms of pride because it can sound like worship.
You can mention God while worshiping your own goodness.
You can thank God while despising the person beside you.
You can know Scripture and still use someone else’s failure to make yourself feel holy.
You can condemn sins Jesus condemns while secretly committing another sin Jesus condemns—self-righteousness.
Then Jesus turns our attention toward the other man.
The tax collector does not perform.
He does not negotiate.
He does not produce a résumé.
Jesus says he stood “afar off.”
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beat his chest.
And then came one of the most desperate prayers in Scripture:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” (Luke 18:13, KJV)
The Greek is striking:
Ὁ Θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
The man has stopped comparing himself with everybody else.
He has nowhere to hide.
No one else to blame.
No religious costume strong enough to cover what he knows about himself.
Just...
God.
Mercy.
Me.
The sinner.
And Jesus says something that would have shattered the expectations of His listeners:
“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other...” (Luke 18:14, KJV).
The broken man asking for mercy went home justified.
The religious man admiring himself did not.
That is scandalous grace.
And before we turn the Pharisee into another “dirty person” so that we can congratulate ourselves for not being like him, we need to notice the trap.
The moment you say, Thank God I’m not self-righteous like that Pharisee, you may have climbed into his seat.
That is how deep our problem goes.
The Gospel does not divide humanity into good people who deserve Jesus and bad people who need Jesus.
Scripture draws the line somewhere much more devastating.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23, KJV)
The Greek word translated “all” is πάντες — pantes.
All.
Not merely the visibly ruined.
Not merely people with criminal records.
Not merely people whose sins became public.
All.
The gossip and the adulterer.
The proud and the promiscuous.
The greedy and the addicted.
The church member and the church avoider.
The preacher and the prisoner.
The person ashamed of what happened last night and the person secretly proud of forty years of respectable living.
All have sinned.
But this does not mean Scripture pretends that sin is harmless or that every action has identical earthly consequences.
Jesus never needed to redefine evil in order to love sinners.
Biblical grace is not God looking at sin and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace is infinitely more costly than that.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
This is where Christianity becomes unlike mere moral self-improvement.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself until God can tolerate you.”
It says Christ came for sinners.
Paul writes:
While we were still sinners.
Not after the rehabilitation.
Not after everybody respected us again.
Not after we finally conquered every temptation.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Christ died for sinners.
There is an ancient Hebrew word that helps us understand the heart of this mercy.
חֶסֶד — ḥesed.
The word carries a rich range of meaning in the Old Testament involving steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, mercy, and loyal love. No single English word captures every use perfectly.
David knew something about needing that mercy.
After adultery, deception, abuse of power, and the arranged death of Uriah, David did not come before God pretending that reputation management could rescue him.
Psalm 51 opens:
“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness...” (Psalm 51:1, KJV)
The Hebrew includes:
חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים כְּחַסְדֶּךָ
ḥonnēni Elohim keḥasdeka...
David's hope was not, “God, look how good I actually am.”
His hope was God's mercy.
And David did not call evil good.
He confessed.
“For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.” (Psalm 51:3, KJV)
This is where modern people sometimes misunderstand grace.
Grace does not eliminate repentance.
Grace makes repentance possible without despair.
Because repentance is not paying Jesus back.
It is turning from sin toward the One who alone can save you.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia refers to repentance, a turning or change of mind with moral and spiritual significance.
Jesus did not walk through the world telling broken people, “Remain exactly as you are because transformation would be judgmental.”
Neither did He say, “Transform yourself first, then perhaps I will receive you.”
He called sinners to Himself.
He forgave.
He restored.
He commanded repentance.
He transformed lives.
That balance matters.
Look at the woman dragged before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers reduced her to her worst known act.
She became a case.
A scandal.
A weapon.
A public spectacle.
They said she had been caught in adultery.
They wanted judgment.
Jesus exposed something they desperately wanted hidden: the moral superiority of the accusers was not as secure as they imagined.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” (John 8:7, KJV)
One after another, they left.
Then Jesus spoke to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Do not separate those words.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
Grace.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Transformation.
Jesus neither joined the mob nor celebrated the sin.
That is the Gospel-shaped tension our generation desperately needs.
Truth without grace can become a stone in a religious hand.
Grace without truth can become permission to remain enslaved.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
Maybe this is becoming uncomfortable because you know what it feels like to be the person everyone remembers for the worst chapter.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Maybe pornography has been eating away at your soul while everybody thinks you are fine.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you betrayed somebody who trusted you.
Maybe alcohol has become the thing you reach for when nobody is watching.
Maybe you abandoned your faith and now feel too ashamed to return.
Maybe you had an abortion and have carried grief or guilt you have never told anyone about.
Maybe you have been sexually broken in ways you cannot explain without crying.
Maybe you have screamed at God.
Maybe you have sat in church singing about freedom while privately wondering whether Jesus could possibly want somebody who has done what you have done.
Or perhaps your darkness looks more respectable.
Maybe your addiction is approval.
Maybe your drug is being admired.
Maybe you secretly enjoy hearing that someone failed because their collapse makes your life look better.
Maybe you forgive only when people suffer enough first.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary without developing Christlike mercy.
Maybe nobody would call your sin scandalous.
Maybe that is precisely why you have never confessed it.
Listen.
The cross destroys both kinds of boasting.
The openly broken person cannot say, “My sin does not matter.”
The outwardly respectable person cannot say, “I do not need mercy.”
At Calvary, both mouths are silenced.
And then...
both are invited.
This is why Paul could write:
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα...
Ouden ara nyn katakrima...
“Therefore now no condemnation...”
Do not confuse that with “no conviction.”
The Holy Spirit convicts.
God disciplines His children.
Scripture confronts sin.
But condemnation and conviction do not perform the same work.
Condemnation says, “There is no hope for someone like you.”
The Gospel says, “Run to Christ.”
Condemnation says, “Hide.”
Grace brings you into the light.
Condemnation chains your identity permanently to what you did.
The Gospel joins the repentant believer to Christ.
That does not erase consequences.
It does not magically repair every relationship.
It does not require victims to pretend they were never wounded.
Forgiveness is not permission for abuse to continue, and Christian mercy does not mean abandoning wisdom, justice, accountability, or appropriate boundaries.
But the Gospel declares something astonishing:
Your sin does not have greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Paul knew this personally.
Before he became the apostle who proclaimed Christ across the Roman world, he persecuted Christians.
He later described himself as a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man.
Then he wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (1 Timothy 1:15, KJV)
Paul's past was not rewritten by pretending it never happened.
Jesus rewrote what his past would ultimately mean.
Persecutor became preacher.
Enemy became servant.
Shame became testimony.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely improve reputations.
He raises the spiritually dead.
And perhaps the most dangerous person reading this is not the person crying because they know they have sinned.
It may be the person who still believes this article is mainly about somebody else.
Someone came into your mind when you read the title, didn't they?
The relative who embarrassed the family.
The Christian who fell publicly.
The person whose sexual sin disgusts you.
The addict who relapsed again.
The hypocrite.
The criminal.
The person whose theology irritates you.
The person whose life makes you uncomfortable.
Now comes the question we would rather avoid:
When you look at them, do you see a category...
or a soul?
Because Jesus ate with people respectable religion despised.
