In Mark 2, scribes questioned why He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
Jesus answered:
“They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick...” (Mark 2:17, KJV)
Then:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” (Mark 2:17, KJV)
A hospital that despises sick people has forgotten why it exists.
And a church that has room only for people who already look healed has forgotten the Gospel.
This does not mean the church should tolerate unrepentant abuse, exploitation, deception, predatory behavior, or destructive sin.
It means accountability should aim toward truth, repentance, protection, restoration where possible, and holiness—not self-righteous entertainment at another person's collapse.
Galatians 6:1 tells spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in transgression “in the spirit of meekness,” while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
Restore.
Gently.
Watch yourself.
The Gospel leaves very little room for swagger.
Imagine what would happen if our churches actually believed this.
The alcoholic could say, “I need help,” before losing everything.
The pornography-addicted husband could confess before the secret devoured his marriage.
The exhausted pastor could admit he is struggling before becoming another headline.
The teenager wrestling with shame could approach a mature believer without wondering whether confession would become gossip.
The woman carrying decades of regret could finally discover that the blood of Jesus is stronger than the voice accusing her at three in the morning.
And religious people could stop pretending that polished appearances are the same thing as holiness.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you have spent years believing there are two kinds of people:
people God could love...
and people like you.
Hear the Gospel.
Jesus knew what He was purchasing at the cross.
He was not deceived about you.
He did not discover your history after Calvary.
He does not need you to edit your testimony before approaching Him.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Let Him begin rebuilding what sin shattered.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9, KJV)
Notice who does the cleansing.
He does.
Christianity is not dirty people scrubbing themselves hard enough to become worthy of Jesus.
It is sinners being washed, justified, sanctified, and transformed through the saving work of Christ.
Paul reminded the Corinthian believers of lives marked by serious sin and then said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified...” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
Ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε...
Alla apelousasthe...
“But you were washed...”
Those words contain an entire resurrection.
Were.
Not because sin became acceptable.
Because Jesus changes people.
This is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not “From Scandal to Respectability.”
It is not “From Bad Reputation to Good Reputation.”
It is not “From Dirty People to People Who Can Now Look Down on Dirty People.”
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The Gospel does not give the redeemed permission to become the new Pharisees.
If Jesus pulled you from the pit, your testimony should make you more compassionate toward people still screaming from the bottom.
If Christ forgave you, forgiveness should astonish you.
If Christ washed you, you should never forget Who supplied the water.
If Christ carried your cross, you have no grounds for boasting except in Him.
So perhaps today you need to stop running.
Or perhaps you need to put down your stone.
Maybe you are the tax collector whispering, “God, have mercy on me.”
Maybe you are the Pharisee who suddenly realizes pride has been wearing religious clothing.
Maybe you are the woman surrounded by accusers.
Maybe you are one of the accusers.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for repentance.
That is the miracle.
Not affirmation of everything we have done.
Not denial of holiness.
Not cheap grace.
A crucified Savior.
An empty tomb.
Mercy purchased at immeasurable cost.
Forgiveness offered to sinners.
A new life that begins not when we finally become impressive enough for God...
but when we stop pretending we can save ourselves.
If something in this exposed what you have been hiding, do not turn this into another article you read, felt, and forgot.
Talk to Jesus.
And be honest.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter when a sinner turns to Jesus.
Not because an article can save you.
It cannot.
Give them the chance to hear about Jesus.
Christ alone saves.

Following Gospel Warrior can help you stay connected to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family. Invite your friends. Share it with the seeker. Send it even to the person who does not yet believe.
Not because Gospel Warrior is the destination.
Jesus is.
And remember this when your past whispers your old name:
Jesus does not need to pretend your scandal never happened to prove that His grace can write a greater ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER—AND THEN GOD GAVE THEIR CHILDREN NAMES NO PARENT WOULD EVER WANT TO CALL ACROSS THE HOUSE
paragraphs: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER—AND THEN GOD GAVE THEIR CHILDREN NAMES NO PARENT WOULD EVER WANT TO CALL ACROSS THE HOUSE

Jezreel. Lo-Ruhamah. Lo-Ammi. Three children. Three devastating names. But buried inside those names of judgment was a promise that reaches all the way to Jesus Christ—and perhaps straight into the part of your life you thought God could never redeem.
Imagine holding your newborn child for the first time.
Tiny fingers.
A heartbeat against your chest.
A face that has never seen betrayal, war, shame, rejection, or grief.
Then God tells you what to name the child.
Not a name meaning “beloved.”
Not “blessing.”
Not “peace.”
A name carrying judgment.
Then another child comes.
Another terrible name.
Then another.
And by the third child, the name itself sounds almost unbearable:
לֹא עַמִּי — Lo-Ammi.
“Not My People.”
This is where the book of Hosea begins.
Not with a comfortable sermon.
Not with religious sentiment.
With a marriage.
With children.
With scandal.
With judgment.
And, astonishingly, with grace already moving beneath the wreckage.
Because if you stop reading Hosea when the judgment falls, you will misunderstand Hosea.
And if you stop reading the story of your own life at your worst chapter, you may misunderstand what the grace of God can do too.

Hosea ministered during the eighth century before Christ, during the reigns named in the opening verse of the book. Israel could still look prosperous from the outside, but spiritually something was rotting underneath.
God's covenant people were running after other gods.
They had learned the terrifying art of appearing religious while giving their hearts elsewhere.
And before we point at ancient Israel, perhaps we should recognize how modern that sounds.
You can sing worship songs and still worship approval.
You can carry a Bible and secretly bow to money.
You can post Scripture and be consumed by lust.
You can speak about Jesus while being addicted to applause.
You can sit in church while resentment eats through your heart.
You can know Christian vocabulary without living in surrender to Christ.
Israel's deepest problem was not simply that they had broken religious regulations.
They had betrayed covenant love.
So God gave Hosea a calling that would make the prophet's own home into a living message.
The Hebrew of Hosea 1:2 is deliberately disturbing:
לֵךְ קַח־לְךָ אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים
Lekh qach-lekha eshet zenunim.
“Go, take for yourself a wife of whoredom/promiscuity.”
Translations differ in how they render the difficult expression אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים — eshet zenunim, but the theological explanation immediately follows:
כִּי־זָנֹה תִזְנֶה הָאָרֶץ מֵאַחֲרֵי יְהוָה
“For the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD.”
That is the point.
Hosea's marriage becomes a prophetic sign of something much larger.
Israel has been unfaithful to the God who loved her.
And Hosea obeys.
“So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim.”
Her name was Gomer.
And we should be careful here.

People sometimes tell Gomer's story with details Scripture itself never gives us. Hosea does not provide a modern biography explaining every stage of her life, every motive, or every circumstance surrounding the marriage. Even interpreters have debated precisely how Hosea 1 should be understood.
So we should not pretend to know what God chose not to tell us.
What Scripture makes unmistakable is the prophetic meaning:
Gomer and Hosea's household became a living picture of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness and God's response to it.
Then a child was born.
God said:
קְרָא שְׁמוֹ יִזְרְעֶאל
Qera shemo Yizre'el.
“Call his name Jezreel.”
Jezreel.
יִזְרְעֶאל — Yizre'el.
The name is connected with the Hebrew idea of God sowing or scattering seed.
But at this moment in Hosea, Jezreel carried blood-soaked historical associations.
God declares judgment concerning the bloodshed of Jezreel and announces that the kingdom of Israel will be brought to an end.
Imagine Hosea calling the boy home.
“Jezreel!”
People hear it.
They know the name.
They know the history.
The child himself has become a sermon walking through the neighborhood.
Judgment is coming.
Sin has consequences.
God's patience must never be confused with moral indifference.
That truth makes many modern ears uncomfortable because we prefer a God who comforts but never confronts.
But biblical grace cannot be understood apart from biblical holiness.
The God who forgives sin is the same God who calls sin what it is.
The cross itself proves this.
If sin were merely an insignificant mistake, Calvary would make no sense.
Jesus did not die because sin was trivial.
He died because sin was deadly.
Then Gomer conceived again.
A daughter.
And God gave her an even more painful name:
לֹא רֻחָמָה — Lo-Ruhamah.
The Hebrew word רָחַם — racham carries the idea of compassion, mercy, or tender pity.
Put לֹא — lo, meaning “not,” before it and the name becomes devastating:
“No Mercy.”
“Not Pitied.”
“Not Shown Compassion.”
Different English translations express the nuance differently, but the blow is unmistakable.
Imagine being that little girl.
Imagine hearing your name spoken every morning.
Lo-Ruhamah.
At the table.
Lo-Ruhamah.
Across the courtyard.
Lo-Ruhamah.
Every time someone called her, Israel was hearing a warning.
There comes a point when persistent rebellion encounters judgment.
This was not because God had suddenly become cruel.
The tragedy of Hosea is precisely the opposite.
Israel was rejecting the God whose covenant love had sustained her.
Sin was not liberation.
It was self-destruction dressed as freedom.
And maybe somebody reading this understands that more personally than you want to admit.
You thought the affair would make you feel alive.
It left wreckage.
You thought pornography would remain private.
It started rewriting the way you saw people.
You thought bitterness was protecting you.
It became a prison.
You thought money would quiet the insecurity.
You simply became afraid of losing more.
You thought walking away from God would finally make you free.
But at 2:17 in the morning, when nobody is watching and the noise is gone, something inside you still knows:
You were created for more than this.
There are sins we choose.
Then there are chains we discover afterward.
And God loves us too deeply to call chains freedom.
Then another son was born.
This time the name cuts even deeper:
לֹא עַמִּי — Lo-Ammi.
לֹא — not.
עַמִּי — my people.
“Not My People.”
The covenant relationship itself is now being invoked.
“For you are not My people…”
It is difficult to imagine a heavier name.
Jezreel spoke judgment.
Lo-Ruhamah spoke withdrawn compassion in the face of persistent rebellion.
Lo-Ammi struck at covenant identity.
Not My People.
And this is where someone carrying shame may begin to hear the wrong sermon.
Because shame whispers:
“That is your name too.”
Not wanted.
Not loved.
Not worthy.
Not recoverable.
Not Christian enough.
Not clean enough.
Not welcome anymore.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Maybe your family thinks you're fine.
Your church friends think you're fine.
But you know.
You remember the browser history.
The conversation you deleted.
The lie you never corrected.
The person you wounded.
The secret addiction.
The money.
The anger.
The compromise.
The years you wasted.
And somewhere along the way, you stopped merely saying, “I did something shameful.”
You started saying:
“I am shameful.”
That is one of Satan's favorite distortions.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Hide because there is no way home.”
But Hosea refuses to end where shame expects it to end.
Because immediately after the terrifying words “Not My People,” something happens.
God starts talking about restoration.
The same chapter that announces judgment suddenly declares that Israel's number will again be immeasurable and that in the very place where it had been said,
“You are not My people,”
they would be called:
בְּנֵי אֵל־חָי — benei El-chai
“sons of the living God.”
Do you see it?
The location of rejection becomes the location where restoration is announced.
The place associated with judgment becomes the place where grace speaks another word.
And Hosea is only beginning.
Later God says:
וְרִחַמְתִּי אֶת־לֹא רֻחָמָה
“I will have mercy on Lo-Ruhamah.”
Then:
וְאָמַרְתִּי לְלֹא־עַמִּי עַמִּי־אַתָּה
“I will say to Lo-Ammi, ‘You are My people.’”
And the response:
אֱלֹהָי
“My God.”
Read that again slowly.
The one called “No Mercy” receives mercy.
The one called “Not My People” hears:
“You are My people.”
This does not mean judgment was imaginary.
It means judgment was not the final word in God's redemptive purpose.
That distinction matters.
Biblical grace never says sin did not matter.
Biblical grace says sin mattered so much that redemption cost blood.
And centuries after Hosea carried this painful prophetic message, another Son would enter the story of Israel.
Jesus Christ.
He would not merely act out a prophetic sign.
He would fulfill God's saving purpose.
He would touch the unclean.
Eat with sinners.
Receive the rejected.
Call the wandering home.
Expose religious hypocrisy.
Tell sinners to repent.
Forgive the guilty.
And then He would walk toward a cross.
There the scandal becomes almost incomprehensible.
The sinless One bears the sins of sinners.
The innocent One is condemned.
The Shepherd is struck.
The Son of God gives Himself for people who have not loved God faithfully.
The New Testament describes it with breathtaking clarity:
Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“Christ died for us.”
Romans 5 places this death in the context of God's love toward sinners.
Not people who had finally made themselves respectable.
Sinners.
That is Christianity.
Not bad people becoming impressive enough for God.
Not broken people repairing themselves until heaven approves the workmanship.
Not religious people accumulating enough spiritual points.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
Christ forgives.
Christ reconciles.
Christ transforms.
And this is why Hosea's painful names cannot be reduced to an inspirational message about “believing in yourself.”
Hosea is not telling you that you were secretly wonderful all along.
The Gospel tells something far better.
You were more lost than self-help can repair…
and more deeply loved in Christ than shame wants you to believe.
Grace does not rename evil “good.”
Grace takes guilty people who come to Christ and gives them something they could never earn.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Adoption.
A new identity.
A new heart.
A new direction.
Life.
The apostle Peter later reaches directly into Hosea's language when speaking about God's people:
“Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.”
That is Hosea's language echoing inside the Gospel age.
Not because everybody automatically belongs to God regardless of repentance and faith.
But because God's mercy creates a people who belong to Him.
And that means your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Your adultery does not have to write the last sentence.
Your addiction does not have to write the last sentence.
Your pride does not have to write the last sentence.
Your secret life does not have to write the last sentence.
Your church hurt does not have to write the last sentence.
Your failure as a parent does not have to write the last sentence.
Your wasted years do not have to write the last sentence.
Your shame does not get editorial control over eternity.
Jesus does.
But hear this carefully.
Grace is not permission to remain where grace found you.
Jesus does not merely forgive us so that we can decorate our chains with Christian language.
He calls us to repent.
Repentance is not paying God back for mercy.
You cannot.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has finally stopped defending the thing that is destroying it.
Maybe that is what God is doing with you right now.
Maybe the reason this article feels uncomfortable is not because God hates you.
Maybe His Word is putting its finger on something you have spent months protecting.
Stop hiding.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel cleaner.
Not after you fix yourself.
Now.
The blood of Jesus is not reserved for people with respectable testimonies.
The Gospel is for sinners.
And Christians never graduate from needing grace.
Some of us simply become better at hiding how badly we need it.
So be honest.
If you need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply write:
And if Christ has already carried you through a season that should have destroyed you, don't hide the testimony either.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Someone scrolling through those comments may need to discover that Christians are not a museum of flawless people.
We are people who desperately need a Savior.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Christ alone saves.
But if God's truth has helped you, sharing it can put that truth in front of someone you may never know is struggling.
Someone's smiling profile picture may be hiding a collapsing marriage.
Someone posting jokes may be fighting despair.
Someone who has not entered a church for fifteen years may still stop long enough to read about Hosea.
Someone convinced that God could never want them again may discover that the Bible contains a story where “Not My People” is followed by the astonishing promise:
“You are My people.”
More importantly, we want this community to become something deeper than content people consume for a moment and forget.
A place for Scripture.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Biblical truth.
Healing.
Discipleship.
Spiritual nourishment.
And continual reminders that everything eventually has to lead back to Jesus Christ.
Because there may come a night when you need these three names again.
Jezreel.
Lo-Ruhamah.
Lo-Ammi.
You may need to remember that Scripture does not sentimentalize rebellion.
Judgment is real.
Sin destroys.
God is holy.
But you may also need to remember what happened afterward.
“No Mercy” encountered mercy.
“Not My People” was answered with “You are My people.”
And the story eventually leads us toward the One whose wounds tell guilty sinners that grace is not imaginary.
Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the friend quietly fighting addiction.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for respectable people.
Invite the skeptic willing to listen.
Invite the prodigal who still remembers the sound of worship songs from childhood.
And yes, invite the person whose life looks like a scandal right now.
Especially that person.
Because Christianity began spreading through a world full of people with complicated histories.
Liars.
Immoral people.
Religious hypocrites.
Thieves.
Persecutors.
The ashamed.
The rejected.
The self-righteous.
The desperate.
People like us.
And Christ is still saving people like us.
Hosea carried children whose names announced judgment through the streets of Israel.
But God did not allow those names to be the end of the story.
That is the breathtaking tension of Hosea.
Holy judgment.
Relentless covenant love.
Sin exposed.
Mercy promised.
The unfaithful confronted.
The broken pursued.
And eventually, for everyone who belongs to Christ, shame loses the right to introduce you by the name of the person you used to be.
Maybe people remember your scandal.
Jesus knows your whole story.
Maybe people know what you did.
Jesus knows what His blood can do.
Maybe someone has permanently attached a label to your name.
Jesus Christ is not intimidated by labels.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confession.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
Seek forgiveness where you wounded someone.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop asking darkness to give you what only Christ can give.
And come home.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Hosea's children is not simply that they received names of judgment.
It is that God deliberately returned to those very names and spoke restoration over them.
The wound became the location where mercy was announced.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this was meant to carry into tonight:
The name your failure gave you does not have to be the name grace leaves you with.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody still believes their scandal is the end of their story.
Maybe your share is how they encounter the message that it isn't.
Maybe your testimony is how they discover they are not alone.
Maybe the truth you almost scrolled past becomes the truth God uses to turn somebody's eyes back toward Jesus.
And long after they forget who shared the article, may they remember the Savior it pointed them toward.
Judgment may expose the name sin gave us—but at the cross, grace shows us what it cost for Jesus to call His people home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR SPOUSE IS NOT A SEXUAL OBJECT
paragraphs:
YOUR SPOUSE IS NOT A SEXUAL OBJECT
Reading 1 Corinthians 7 Without Weaponizing It — Because a Bible Verse Was Never Meant to Become a Weapon in the Bedroom
There is a particular kind of pain that happens when the person who promised to love you reaches for Scripture…and you realize they are not reaching for it to become more like Jesus.
They are reaching for it to win.
Maybe you have heard the verse.
Maybe you have quoted it.
Maybe someone quoted it while you were exhausted, grieving, sick, emotionally wounded, frightened, disconnected, or simply struggling.
“The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband…”
And suddenly the Bible was no longer being opened like bread.
It was being held like a weapon.
But keep reading.
Please.
Because the sentence does not stop where some people have conveniently stopped it.
Paul continues:
“…and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.”
That changes everything.

And if we are going to talk about sex, marriage, desire, obligation, rejection, intimacy, selfishness, manipulation, tenderness, and what husbands and wives owe one another, then we need enough courage to let Paul finish his sentence.
Because 1 Corinthians 7 does not hand one spouse ownership papers over the other.
Paul does something much more radical.
He dismantles selfishness on both sides.
The New Testament was written primarily in Koine Greek, so 1 Corinthians 7 is not a passage where Hebrew or Aramaic gives us the original wording. Greek does.
And the Greek matters.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7:3:
In straightforward English:
Let the husband give to the wife what is due to her, and likewise the wife to the husband.
Notice the movement.
Husband toward wife.
Wife toward husband.
Not domination.
Reciprocity.
Not “What can I demand?”
But “What should I give?”
Paul then says something astonishing:
“ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει…”
The wife does not exercise authority over her own body…
Someone determined to control a woman could stop reading right there.
But Paul does not.
“…ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει, ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.”
But the husband does; and likewise the husband does not exercise authority over his own body, but the wife does.
There it is again.
ὁμοίως — homoíōs.
Likewise.
Similarly.
In the same manner.
Paul refuses to give one spouse a principle he does not immediately apply reciprocally to the other.
That little word destroys a great deal of selfish theology.

If a husband reads verse 4 and hears, “Her body belongs to me, therefore I can demand whatever I want,” he has somehow managed to read the first half of Paul's argument while ignoring the second half that places his own body under the same reciprocal marital obligation.
And if either spouse reads the passage merely as ammunition for getting what he or she wants, something deeper has already gone wrong.
Because the controlling question of Christian marriage cannot simply be:
“What am I entitled to receive?”
Jesus keeps turning that question around:
“How can I love?”
“How can I serve?”
“How can I lay myself down?”
“How can I seek the good of the person God entrusted to my care?”
This is why 1 Corinthians 7 cannot be isolated from the rest of the New Testament.
The same apostolic witness that speaks about marital intimacy tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25
Christ does not give husbands a model of predatory entitlement.
He gives them a cross.
Christ loved His bride by giving Himself.
Sacrificially.
Tenderly.
At terrible cost to Himself.
Peter likewise commands husbands to live with their wives “according to knowledge,” giving honor to them as fellow heirs of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7).
And Paul describes love in words that should haunt every Christian who has ever used Scripture selfishly:
Love “seeketh not her own.” — 1 Corinthians 13:5
Read that again before demanding anything from your spouse.
Love does not insist upon its own way.
Christian marriage therefore cannot be reduced to two people standing across the bedroom keeping score.
“I did this for you.”
“You owe me that.”
“You rejected me yesterday.”
“You have to because we are married.”
“That is your duty.”
No.
Something sacred dies when intimacy becomes a debt-collection agency.
And something equally dangerous happens when affection and intimacy are deliberately weaponized as punishment, manipulation, revenge, or control.
Paul confronts that too.
He writes:
Do not deprive one another.
But once again, keep reading.
Paul immediately speaks about a temporary period of abstinence:
“εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν…”
except perhaps by agreement for a time.
That phrase matters enormously:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
By mutual accord.

The English word “consent” is often used in modern discussions, and we should be careful not to pretend Paul was writing a twenty-first-century legal or psychological definition of sexual consent. He was not.
But we should be equally careful not to erase what Paul actually did write.
When he discusses a temporary abstention from marital relations, he explicitly describes it as something undertaken together — by agreement.
Neither spouse is pictured as a disposable object.
Neither spouse is given permission to cultivate selfishness.
Neither spouse is told, “Your desires are the only desires that matter.”
The passage assumes a marriage in which husband and wife have obligations toward one another, and it expresses those obligations with striking reciprocity.
That is radically different from turning the passage into:
“You owe me your body whenever I demand it.”
A covenant is not a license for cruelty.
Marriage does not erase personhood.
And sexual intimacy is not biblical simply because it happens between married people.
The character of Christ still matters in the bedroom.
Love still matters.
Gentleness still matters.
Patience still matters.
Honor still matters.
Self-control still matters.
Sacrificial care still matters.
The fruit of the Spirit does not disappear when the bedroom door closes.
And perhaps someone reading this feels an uncomfortable knot forming in the stomach right now.
Because this is no longer theoretical.
Maybe you have been the spouse who pressured.
Maybe you have used sulking, anger, guilt, Scripture, silence, threats, spiritual language, or emotional withdrawal to get your way.
Maybe you never physically forced anything, so you convinced yourself everything was fine.
But somewhere inside, you know.
You were not asking:
“How can I love you?”
You were asking:
“How can I make you give me what I want?”
If that is you, do not defend yourself.
Repent.
Not because sexual desire within marriage is dirty.
It isn't.

Scripture can speak beautifully and positively about marital desire and delight. Proverbs 5:18–19 celebrates marital affection. Song of Songs does not blush at the joy of husband and wife desiring one another. Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage and the marriage bed.
Sex is not the villain.
Selfishness is.
Lust that reduces another person to something consumed is.
Pride is.
Control is.
Manipulation is.
Using God's Word to sanctify our selfishness is.
And repentance does not begin with explaining why your spouse made you behave that way.
Repentance begins when excuses finally die.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
Four words.
No footnotes.
No blame shifting.
No “but she…”
No “but he…”
No “you don't understand how long…”
Just truth.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
And perhaps you are reading from the other side.
You were the one pressured.
The one who learned to freeze.
The one who dreaded bedtime.
The one who felt guilty for having emotions, exhaustion, physical pain, fear, trauma, or limitations.
Maybe someone repeatedly quoted 1 Corinthians 7 until you began associating the voice of God with coercion.
Hear this carefully:
Jesus is not the person who weaponized His Word against you.
Do not confuse the misuse of Scripture with the character of its Author.
Christ is not cruel.
Christ does not need manipulation to establish His authority.
He is “meek and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29).
He sees people others overlook.
He receives the wounded.
He confronts sin without exploiting sinners.
He tells the truth without becoming abusive.
And at the cross, Jesus demonstrates what holy authority actually looks like.
He possesses all authority…
and gives Himself.
That is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
The King bleeds.
The Holy One bears shame.
The innocent Christ receives the judgment sinners deserve.
Jesus does not merely tell broken humanity to become better.
He comes for us.
He carries our sin.
He dies.
He rises.
He calls us to repent and believe.
And then grace begins rewriting people who thought their worst chapters had already determined their ending.
That includes marriages.
Maybe yours is cold right now.
Maybe resentment has accumulated so quietly that you no longer remember when tenderness disappeared.
Maybe sex has become mechanical.
Maybe rejection has created bitterness.
Maybe pornography has poisoned expectations.
Maybe betrayal shattered trust.
Maybe childbirth changed everything.
Maybe illness changed everything.
Maybe age changed everything.
Maybe trauma followed one of you into marriage.
Maybe one spouse feels constantly unwanted while the other feels constantly pressured.
Those wounds will not be healed by ripping one sentence out of 1 Corinthians 7 and throwing it across the bed.
You need truth.
You need difficult conversations.
You may need wise pastoral care.
In serious situations, you may need qualified professional help.

And where coercion, threats, violence, or abuse are present, the answer is not to tell the harmed spouse to endure danger silently because “marriage is sacred.” Seeking safety and appropriate help is not the same thing as despising marriage.
Marriage is sacred.
That is precisely why evil inside marriage should not be baptized with Christian vocabulary.
The goal is not merely more sex.
The goal is a marriage increasingly submitted to Jesus Christ.
Because you can share a bed and still be miles apart.
You can touch someone's body without knowing their heart.
You can technically fulfill a marital obligation while starving your marriage of tenderness.
And you can win an argument about 1 Corinthians 7 while losing the person lying beside you.
Your spouse is not pornography with a wedding ring.
Your spouse is not a mechanism God provided to regulate your sexual appetite.
Your spouse is not a reward for good Christian behavior.
Your spouse is not property.
Your spouse is a person bearing the image of God.
A soul.
A story.
A human being with fears you may not completely understand.
A person with wounds you may not see.
A person who may sometimes need affection that does not become a demand for sex.
A person who may need to know that your kindness is still real when the answer is not what you hoped for.
And yes, your spouse may also be someone quietly aching because rejection has become chronic and unexplained.
Someone wondering whether they are still desirable.
Someone embarrassed to admit how deeply repeated rejection hurts.
Someone who has stopped initiating because another “no” feels unbearable.
That pain matters too.
1 Corinthians 7 should not be weaponized in either direction.
Paul does not provide permission for coercive entitlement.
Neither does he celebrate selfish withholding.
He calls husband and wife away from isolated self-rule and toward reciprocal marital faithfulness.
That means mature Christian couples must learn something far more difficult than quoting verses at one another.
They must learn to talk.
To listen.
To confess.
To forgive.
To understand.
To wait.
To initiate without demanding.
To decline without humiliating.
To express desire without turning desire into entitlement.
To hear pain without immediately becoming defensive.
To address persistent sexual disconnection rather than pretending it does not matter.
To pursue healing where wounds have made intimacy frightening.
To refuse pornography's counterfeit education in sexuality.
To remember that the person beside them is someone Christ commands them to love.
And perhaps the most important question tonight is not:
“Am I getting enough?”
Maybe it is:
“Does my spouse experience the character of Jesus in the way I love them?”
That question is harder.
Because it reaches beyond the bedroom.
How do you speak when you are angry?
What happens when you do not get what you want?
Do you punish?
Withdraw?
Manipulate?
Shame?
Threaten?
Mock?
Compare?
Keep score?
Or can your spouse disagree with you and remain emotionally safe in your presence?
Can they tell you something painful without immediately paying a price for their honesty?
Can you repent without defending your reputation?
Can you forgive without storing ammunition for the next argument?
Can you love when love costs something?
Because Christian marriage is not ultimately about proving who has authority over whose body.
It is about two redeemed sinners learning that they both belong to Christ.
Paul has already established that larger reality earlier in the letter:
“Ye are not your own… For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body.” — 1 Corinthians 6:19–20
Before your body is a bargaining chip in marriage, your entire life belongs to Jesus.
That changes sexuality.
That changes marriage.
That changes the question.
Not:
“How much can I demand?”
But:
“Jesus, how can my sexuality glorify You?”
Not:
“How can I use this verse against my spouse?”
But:
“Lord, what is this verse exposing in me?”
Maybe what it exposes is entitlement.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe fear.
Maybe sexual selfishness.
Maybe deliberate withholding.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe years of unresolved hurt.
Maybe pride.
Maybe shame.
Maybe the inability to say, “I was wrong.”
Whatever Jesus exposes, bring it into the light.
Grace does not mean pretending sin is harmless.
Grace means sinners can finally stop hiding because Christ has made forgiveness possible.
At Calvary, Jesus carried real guilt.
Not imaginary guilt.
Real sin.
Our sin.
And the resurrection announces that sin does not get the final word over those who belong to Him.
So if you have sinned sexually against your spouse, repentance is possible.
If selfishness has corrupted intimacy, repentance is possible.
If bitterness has hardened you, repentance is possible.
If pornography has distorted your understanding of bodies and desire, repentance is possible.
If you have been living behind excuses, repentance is possible.
And if someone else's sin wounded you, their sin does not get to become your identity.
There is grace.
There is truth.
There is a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop hiding.
Not because every Christian marriage is secretly broken.
Because one day, after an argument, when emotions are louder than wisdom, you may need to read it again and remember:
Your spouse is not the enemy.
Your spouse is not an object.
And Scripture is not your weapon.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase one sin.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood atones.
Only His righteousness can cover the guilty.
We support Gospel work because we have been loved by Christ, not because supporting Gospel work makes Christ love us.
So tonight, before reaching for another verse to prove what your spouse owes you, perhaps put the weapon down.
Look at the person beside you.
Really look.
That is not an object.
That is not an entitlement.
That is not a body placed on earth merely to satisfy you.
That is a human soul.
And if you belong to Jesus, you have been called to love that soul in a way that increasingly resembles the Savior who loved you when you had nothing to offer Him.
Maybe your marriage has chapters you wish had never been written.
Maybe there has been selfishness.
Rejection.
Pressure.
Silence.
Shame.
Sin.
Tears nobody saw.
Nights you cannot get back.
Words you desperately wish you could pull out of the past.
But the Gospel was made for people with chapters they cannot rewrite themselves.
Bring the truth into the light.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek forgiveness where you have wounded.
Seek help where there is danger or deep brokenness.
Learn to listen.
Learn to honor.
Learn to serve.
Learn to love.
And let Jesus begin writing something neither of you could manufacture alone.
Because perhaps the most intimate thing you can give your spouse is not your body.
Perhaps it is a heart so surrendered to Christ that they no longer have to fear what you will do when you do not get your way.
Remember this:
The hands that should hold your spouse most tenderly are the hands that have finally surrendered their weapons at the feet of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Does “Alpha and Omega” Really Mean? The Name That Changes How You See Your Entire Story
paragraphs: What Does “Alpha and Omega” Really Mean? The Name That Changes How You See Your Entire Story

You have probably heard Jesus called “the Alpha and the Omega.” But when you understand what those words meant in Revelation—and what stands between the first letter and the last—you may never hear them the same way again.
There are moments when your life feels less like a testimony and more like evidence against you.
You remember what you did.
What you became.
The prayer you stopped praying.
The temptation you promised God you would never return to.
The relationship you damaged.
The secret nobody at church knows.
The night you cried and wondered whether you had wandered too far.
Maybe your story contains chapters you would tear out if heaven allowed editing.
And then, near the end of Scripture, Jesus speaks words that confront the deepest fear hiding underneath all of that shame:
“I am the Alpha and the Omega.”
We quote those words beautifully.
We put them on shirts, paintings, church walls, bookmarks, jewelry, and social-media graphics.
But what do they actually mean?
Because Jesus was not giving John a clever Christian slogan.
He was revealing who He is.
And once you understand that, something extraordinary happens: you begin to realize that the darkest chapter of your story does not have authority to write its ending.
The book of Revelation was written in Greek, and in Revelation 22:13 we read:
Ἐγὼ τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, ἡ ἀρχὴ καὶ τὸ τέλος.
Egō to Alpha kai to Ō, ho prōtos kai ho eschatos, hē archē kai to telos.
A careful translation is:
“I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.”
Alpha—Ἄλφα—is the first letter of the Greek alphabet.
Omega—Ὦ—is the last.
In English, we might instinctively hear something like “A to Z.”
But Revelation does something far greater than merely saying that Christ knows everything between two letters.
Jesus immediately explains the expression through two parallel declarations:
“the first and the last”
and
“the beginning and the end.”
He is not merely somewhere inside history.
He stands sovereign over its beginning and its consummation.
Before your first heartbeat, He was.
After the kingdoms of this world have vanished, He will be.
Before anybody knew your name, Christ was Lord.
When every monument erected to human greatness has become dust, Christ will still be Lord.
Your generation did not create Him.
Culture cannot redefine Him.
Governments cannot dethrone Him.
Sin cannot defeat Him.
Death could not hold Him.
Time cannot age Him.
And eternity will never exhaust Him.
This language becomes even more staggering when we recognize its biblical background.
Centuries before Revelation was written, the LORD declared through Isaiah:
אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן וַאֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן
Ani rishon va’ani acharon.
“I am the first and I am the last.”
Isaiah 44:6 continues by declaring that besides the LORD there is no God.
Isaiah 48:12 likewise records:
“I am he; I am the first, and I am the last.”
Now return to Revelation.
In Revelation 1:17–18, the speaker declares:
“I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore.”
Read that slowly.
I died.
Who died?
Jesus Christ.
And yet the One who died identifies Himself with the breathtaking biblical title “the first and the last.”
This is one reason Revelation gives such a towering vision of Jesus.
Christianity does not present Christ merely as an inspirational teacher pointing humanity toward God.
The New Testament presents Him as the eternal Son, worthy of worship, sharing in divine glory, victorious over death, reigning over history, and coming again.
John had already written concerning the Word:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος
En archē ēn ho Logos.
“In the beginning was the Word.”
Not “in the beginning the Word came into existence.”
The Word was.
John continues:
“and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
Then comes the scandalous wonder at the heart of Christianity:
ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“The Word became flesh.”
The One through whom all things were made entered the world He made.
The eternal stepped into time.
The Creator entered His creation.
The Holy One walked among sinners.
The Alpha became an embryo.
The King became a servant.
The One whom heaven worships allowed human hands to nail Him to wood.
And this is where “Alpha and Omega” stops being merely an interesting Bible study and begins reaching into the places you have been trying to hide.
Because the Alpha and Omega entered human history for sinners.
For people with scandals.
For people with addictions.
For religious hypocrites.
For adulterers.
For liars.
For the proud.
For the sexually broken.
For the bitter.
For people who have prayed beautiful prayers on Sunday and surrendered to ugly temptations by Tuesday.
For the person reading this who quietly wonders:
Would Jesus still want me if everyone knew everything?
That question has kept countless people hiding.
We become experts at selective Christianity.
We show people the worship-song version of ourselves while hiding the chapter that still smells like smoke.
We know how to say, “God is good,” while secretly wondering whether God could possibly forgive what we have done.
But the Gospel does not begin with you cleaning your story.
It begins with Christ entering it.
Scripture does not minimize sin. It calls us to repentance.
Jesus did not go to the cross because sin was insignificant.
He went because sin was deadly.
Romans tells us that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The same Gospel that exposes our guilt announces something we could never accomplish for ourselves:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we conquered every temptation.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
Grace is not God pretending your rebellion never mattered.
Grace is God dealing decisively with sin through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
The tomb did not get the final sentence.
Death discovered something terrifying:
It had swallowed the Author of life.
And it could not keep Him.
That is why Revelation 1:18 matters so much:
“I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.”
The Alpha and Omega carries keys.
Your grave does not.
Your shame does not.
Your addiction does not.
Your past does not.
Satan does not.
Jesus does.
And perhaps you need that truth because you have allowed one terrible chapter to become the title of your entire life.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Rejected.
Abused.
Unfaithful.
Failure.
Lukewarm.
Dirty.
Unwanted.
Hypocrite.
Too far gone.
But those words are not names Christ is required to write over the person who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
The Gospel gives sinners a new identity in Christ.
Paul writes:
Not a cosmetically improved old creation.
New creation.

The Gospel does not promise that earthly consequences magically disappear. Forgiveness does not make every broken relationship instantly whole, erase every painful memory, or remove the need to confess, make restitution where appropriate, seek help, or walk through a long process of healing and sanctification.
But your past no longer possesses the authority to determine your standing before God when you belong to Christ.
That authority belongs to Jesus.
And Jesus is not merely the Alpha of your redemption.
He is Omega.
Some people can believe that Jesus saved them years ago but struggle to believe He can finish what He began.
You remember when you first surrendered.
You remember the tears.
The hunger.
The Bible suddenly felt alive.
Prayer felt less like obligation and more like breathing.
Then life happened.
You stumbled.
You got distracted.
You became wounded.
Maybe church hurt you.
Maybe disappointment hardened you.
Maybe secret sin slowly hollowed you out.
Maybe you are still attending church while spiritually running on fumes.
And somewhere inside you is a frightened question:
Did I ruin everything?
Listen to Paul:
“He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ.”
Christ does not merely specialize in beginnings.
He brings His redemptive purposes to completion.
Alpha.
Omega.
Beginning.
End.
First.
Last.
That does not give Christians permission to become passive about sin. The Christ who saves also calls us to follow Him.
Grace does not say, “Remain exactly where sin left you.”
Grace says, “Come out of the grave.”
Repentance is not paying Jesus back for mercy.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One who is merciful.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance,” carrying the idea of a changed mind and turning reflected in a changed direction.
Real grace transforms.
Jesus does not merely forgive the adulterer and celebrate adultery.
He forgives and calls sinners into holiness.
He does not rescue us so we can proudly decorate our chains.
He breaks chains so we can walk with Him.
That is why this message should make us uncomfortable before it makes us comfortable.
Because perhaps the greatest question raised by “Alpha and Omega” is not whether Jesus is Lord of history.
He is.
The question is whether you are living as though He is Lord of you.
There are people who want Jesus as Alpha but resist Him as Omega.
They want Him to start salvation but not determine where their lives should go.
They want forgiveness without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A Savior who rescues them but never contradicts them.
But the Jesus of Revelation refuses to be reduced into a spiritual accessory.
He is King.
He does not merely want one hour of Sunday.
He wants your heart.
Your sexuality.
Your finances.
Your ambitions.
Your relationships.
Your private browser history.
Your resentment.
Your secret habits.
Your future.
Your wounds.
Your gifts.
Your plans.
Your entire life.
Maybe that is where this article found you.
Not at the beginning.
Not yet at the end.
Somewhere in the painful middle.
And the middle is where faith often becomes hardest.
We love beginnings because beginnings carry excitement.
We love endings because endings provide resolution.
But most discipleship happens between Alpha and Omega.
In the waiting.
In unanswered prayers.
In ordinary Tuesdays.
In hospital rooms.
In temptation.
In grief.
In loneliness.
In choosing forgiveness when your emotions still scream for revenge.
In opening Scripture when you feel spiritually numb.
In praying when heaven seems silent.
In resisting the temptation nobody would discover.
In trusting Jesus when you cannot understand what He is doing.
That middle can feel chaotic.
But it is not outside His sovereignty.
The Alpha has not lost you on the way to Omega.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody needs to save and reread tonight:
The Alpha has not lost you on the way to Omega.
Your story may currently contain a page you do not understand.
God has not surrendered His throne.
Christ is still Christ.
The resurrection is still true.
Grace is still available.
Repentance is still possible.
Forgiveness is still offered through Jesus.
And your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we say at Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Grace is.
Not because sin should be romanticized.
Christ should be glorified.
Not because everybody automatically receives a happy earthly ending.
But because the Gospel announces that guilty sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church had a past so morally chaotic that Paul could list devastating sins—and then write three astonishing words:
Were.
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is what grace does.
It does not pretend the scandal never existed.
It demonstrates that the scandal does not have to get the final word.
Jesus does.
Alpha.
Omega.
Maybe your repentance begins tonight.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become worthy.
You will never become worthy enough to make the cross unnecessary.
Come to Christ because you need mercy.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows it.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
Stop negotiating with the thing destroying you.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop hiding behind Christian vocabulary while your heart quietly runs from Jesus.
Come home.
And if you already belong to Christ but you have been spiritually exhausted, come back to the feet of your Savior.
You do not need a more impressive mask.
You need Jesus.
Sometimes confession begins with three trembling words typed beneath an article.
And sometimes somebody else who thought they were suffering alone reads those words and realizes they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
That is why sharing matters too.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God. We are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
But if this message glorifies Jesus and you believe someone else needs to encounter this truth, sharing becomes a simple opportunity to carry the message beyond yourself.
Send it to the believer who thinks their worst failure disqualified them forever.
Send it to your son.
Your daughter.
Your spouse.
Your brother.
Your sister.
The friend who stopped attending church.
The Christian who is exhausted.
Even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely religious people pretending to have perfect lives.
Let them discover what Christianity is actually about:
Not perfect people climbing their way toward God.
A holy God coming down to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
Because one night you may become the person who needs to read it again.

Invite your family, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. We want this community to become a place where people do not merely consume inspirational words but are continually pointed toward Scripture, repentance, grace, and Christ.
Because somewhere on somebody's Facebook feed is a person smiling in photographs while privately falling apart.
Someone ashamed of what they did last night.
Someone contemplating walking away from the faith.
Someone convinced Jesus could forgive everybody except them.
Someone who believes their scandal became their identity.
Let this reach them.
Tell them about the Alpha and Omega.
Tell them about the Christ who existed before their failure.
Tell them about the Savior who entered history.
Tell them about the cross where sin was judged and mercy was displayed.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them repentance is still possible.
Tell them grace is still real.
Tell them Jesus Christ still saves.
And then remember something for yourself.
Revelation does not end with humanity rescuing itself.
It ends with Christ reigning.
History is not wandering toward an accidental conclusion.
Jesus is coming.
The One who identifies Himself as Alpha and Omega will have the final word.
And for everyone who belongs to Him, that changes how we endure the middle.
Your tears are in the middle.
Your unanswered questions are in the middle.
Your sanctification is in the middle.
Your battles are in the middle.
Your healing may still be in the middle.
But Jesus is not merely standing at the beginning waiting to see whether you somehow survive until the end.
He is Lord.
First and Last.
Beginning and End.
Alpha and Omega.
So when your past whispers, “This is how your story ends,” remember who actually possesses the final word.
When shame says, “You will always be what you did,” look toward the cross.
When death says, “Everything eventually belongs to me,” look toward the empty tomb.
And when the middle of your story becomes so dark that you cannot imagine what God could possibly do with the pages ahead, remember the One who declared:
Ἐγὼ τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ.
“I am the Alpha and the Omega.”
He was there before your scandal.
He met sinners with grace at the cross.
He is Lord in the middle.
And He will still be King when every temporary thing has disappeared.
So repent.
Believe.
Come to Jesus.
Keep following Him.
And never give your worst chapter permission to impersonate your final page.
Because when Jesus holds the final word, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS WATER BAPTISM REQUIRED FOR SALVATION?
paragraphs:
IS WATER BAPTISM REQUIRED FOR SALVATION?
The question sounds like it is about water. But underneath it is a far more dangerous question: What—or Who—actually saves a sinner?
Imagine this.
A man hears the Gospel tonight.
For the first time in his life, he understands.
Jesus Christ is not merely a religious teacher. He is the crucified and risen Son of God. The man's sin is real. Judgment is real. Grace is real. The cross is real.
Something breaks inside him.
He repents.
He believes.
Through tears, he calls upon Christ for mercy.
He wants to be baptized. He intends to obey Jesus publicly. A baptism is arranged for tomorrow morning.
But tomorrow morning never comes.
He dies during the night.
Now answer carefully.
Was the blood of Jesus enough?
Or was that man one ceremony short of salvation?
That question has divided Christians, churches, families, denominations, theologians, and sincere Bible readers for generations.
Some will immediately say, “Of course baptism is required. Acts 2:38 says repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins.”
Others will answer, “No. Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.”
Then someone will quote Peter:
“Baptism…now saves you.”
And suddenly the discussion becomes louder.
Verses begin flying.
People defend traditions.
Denominations enter the room.
But perhaps before asking which theological camp wins, we should do something much more uncomfortable.
We should put down our denominational weapons, open the Scriptures, look carefully at what the apostles actually wrote, and allow Jesus Christ to remain where the Gospel places Him:
at the center.
Because water baptism matters enormously.
Jesus commanded it.
The apostles practiced it.
The earliest believers received it.
A Christian who knowingly refuses Christ's command to be baptized should not casually shrug and say, “It doesn't matter.”
It matters.
But there is another question.
Does water possess the saving power?
Or does Jesus?
Those are not identical questions.
And understanding the difference may rescue us from two opposite errors: making baptism meaningless on one side, or quietly making baptism another savior on the other.
Listen first to Paul.
Ephesians 2:8 begins in Greek:
“Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως…”
Tē gar chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs…
“For by grace you have been saved through faith…”
Then Paul continues:
“οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν, Θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον”
ouk ex hymōn, Theou to dōron
“not from yourselves; it is the gift of God.”
And then:
“οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων”
ouk ex ergōn
“not from works.”
Paul's language is devastating to human pride.
Grace.
Gift.
Not from yourselves.
Not from works.
Why?
“so that no one may boast.”

The Greek expression este sesōsmenoi carries the sense of having been saved with an abiding result. Paul places the source of salvation in God's grace and its reception through faith, not in something the sinner can present before God as an achievement.
That means nobody enters heaven carrying a receipt saying:
“I completed enough religious requirements.”
Nobody stands before God and says:
“My baptism earned this.”
Nobody points toward a church, pastor, denomination, sacrament, ministry, morality, family heritage, or religious résumé and says:
“That is why You owe me eternal life.”
The redeemed have only one boast.
Jesus Christ.
His righteousness.
His blood.
His death.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
His grace.
But someone immediately objects:
“What about Acts 2:38?”
Good.
We should not run from difficult verses.
Peter has just preached Christ crucified and risen. His hearers are cut to the heart and ask what they should do.
Peter tells them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins.
That verse must not be erased simply because it makes one theological system uncomfortable.
Repentance and baptism belong naturally together in apostolic Christianity.
In the New Testament, conversion was not designed to become the modern spectacle of someone saying, “I accepted Jesus twenty years ago, but I never felt any need to obey Him.”
Faith moved.
Repentance moved.
People confessed Christ.
People were baptized.
The normal New Testament pattern was not “believe now and perhaps consider baptism someday when it becomes convenient.”
Baptism was the public, embodied identification of a believer with Jesus Christ.
The Greek word baptizō carries the basic idea of dipping, immersing, or baptizing.
The water preached something.
I belonged to the old life.
Now I belong to Christ.
I was under another kingdom.
Now Jesus is Lord.
The old identity goes down.
A new identity rises.
This is why Romans 6 can speak so powerfully about baptism into Christ's death and walking in newness of life.
Baptism is not an embarrassing theological accessory Christians should hide because they are afraid someone might misunderstand grace.
Jesus commanded baptism.
We should honor what Jesus commanded.
But then we arrive at one of the strongest verses used to argue that water baptism itself is necessary for salvation.
First Peter 3:21.
And Peter says something astonishing.
The Greek text reads in part:
“ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σῴζει βάπτισμα…”
ho kai hymas antitypon nyn sōzei baptisma…
Baptism, corresponding to this, “now saves you.”
There it is.
We cannot pretend Peter did not write it.
But neither can we stop reading precisely where a slogan becomes convenient.
Peter immediately explains what he means:
“οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου…”
ou sarkos apothesis rhypou…
“not the removal of dirt from the flesh…”
Then:
“ἀλλὰ συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς Θεόν…”
alla syneidēseōs agathēs eperōtēma eis Theon…
but an appeal, pledge, or response involving a good conscience toward God.
And how does Peter finish the thought?
“δι’ ἀναστάσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ”
di’ anastaseōs Iēsou Christou
“through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”
Do not miss Peter's center.
Jesus.
The resurrection.
Peter does not describe Christian baptism as magical water that mechanically removes sin.

He explicitly distinguishes it from an outward washing of the body. The precise nuance of the rare Greek word eperōtēma has been debated and is variously translated as “appeal,” “pledge,” “answer,” or similar expressions. But Peter unmistakably connects baptism's saving significance to Christ's resurrection rather than to ordinary physical cleansing.
The water has meaning because of Jesus.
The baptism points to Jesus.
The conscience appeals to God because of Jesus.
The resurrection makes the proclamation meaningful because of Jesus.
Remove Christ and baptism becomes a bath.
Remove the resurrection and the water cannot resurrect anyone.
That distinction matters.
Because Christianity is not salvation through sacred plumbing.
Christianity is salvation through Jesus Christ.
And then something remarkable happens in Acts 10.
Peter is preaching Jesus to Cornelius and his household.
He has not finished arranging a baptismal ceremony.
While Peter is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls upon those hearing the message.
The Jewish believers are astonished.
Why?
Because Gentiles have received the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Peter then commands that they be baptized.
Notice the order.
They hear the Gospel.
They believe.
God gives them the Holy Spirit.
Then they are baptized.
Peter does not conclude, “Since they received the Spirit, baptism is unnecessary.”
Quite the opposite.
He commands baptism.
That protects us from both errors.
Their reception of God's Spirit before water baptism makes it very difficult to argue that God could not accept them until the instant water touched them.
Yet Peter's command to baptize them makes it equally difficult to argue that baptism does not matter.
Grace does not abolish obedience.
Grace creates obedient people.
Then there is Paul.

In 1 Corinthians, Paul confronts believers who are forming factions around Christian leaders. In that context he says that he is thankful he personally baptized only a limited number of them, lest people claim baptism into his name. Then he writes:
ou gar apesteilen me Christos baptizein alla euangelizesthai…
“For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel…”
And Paul immediately turns attention toward:
“ὁ σταυρὸς τοῦ Χριστοῦ”
ho stauros tou Christou
“the cross of Christ.”
Be careful here too.
Paul is not attacking baptism.
He baptized people.
He assumes Christians are baptized elsewhere in his writings.
His immediate concern is factionalism and the primacy of Gospel proclamation.

But his distinction between baptizing and preaching the Gospel is significant. At minimum, we should hesitate before speaking as though the physical act of baptism and the Gospel itself were simply interchangeable concepts.
Then look toward another scene.
Not a river.
Not a baptismal pool.
A cross.
Three dying men.
Jesus in the center.
Beside Him hangs a criminal who has nothing left to offer.
No ministry.
No restitution plan.
No years of righteous living.
No opportunity to climb down and be baptized.
He cannot repair his reputation.
He cannot undo his crimes.
He cannot impress God with his future.
His hands are literally nailed into helplessness.
And somehow, in the wreckage of his final hours, he looks toward the crucified Jesus and asks to be remembered when Christ comes into His kingdom.
Jesus does not answer:
“Unfortunately, you missed the water.”
He gives him a promise of Paradise.

Some Christians rightly caution that the thief lived at a unique moment in redemptive history before the death and resurrection of Christ were completed, so the episode should not be forced into answering every later question about Christian baptism.
Fair enough.
But the scene still reveals something breathtaking about the Savior.
Jesus can save the helpless.
Completely.
The criminal could bring Christ nothing except himself.
And perhaps that is exactly why this debate sometimes becomes uncomfortable.
Human beings like measurable things.
We like ceremonies we can document.
Dates we can remember.
Boxes we can check.
But grace leaves the sinner empty-handed.
The Gospel tells you that your salvation required something so costly that you could never purchase it…
and was given so freely that you could never earn it.
The Son of God had to bleed.
Jesus had to carry sin.
Jesus had to die.
Jesus had to rise.
And when you finally understand that, baptism becomes more beautiful, not less.
Because now you are not entering the water trying to make Jesus save you.
You enter because you have nowhere else you want your allegiance to belong.
Baptism becomes confession with your whole body.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
My old master no longer owns me.
My shame does not name me.
My past does not get the final word.
Jesus Christ does.
So, is water baptism required for salvation?
Christians have historically answered the precise sacramental question differently, and we should be honest about that rather than pretending every tradition reads every baptism passage identically.

Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, Churches of Christ, Restorationist, Reformed, Baptist, evangelical, and other traditions do not all explain baptism's relationship to regeneration, justification, covenant membership, faith, and salvation in exactly the same way.
But several biblical truths should remain firmly in view.
Salvation originates in God's grace.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
His death and resurrection are the foundation of salvation.
Salvation cannot be earned by human achievement.
Repentance and genuine faith cannot be reduced to empty words.
Jesus commanded His disciples to baptize.
The apostles baptized believers and treated baptism seriously.
Therefore baptism should never be mocked, postponed casually, or dismissed as meaningless.
At the same time, Scripture gives us substantial reason not to treat water as though water itself possessed saving power independent of Christ.
Perhaps the better question is not merely:
“Can I get into heaven without being baptized?”
That question can reveal something troubling.
Sometimes what we are really asking is:
“What is the minimum amount of obedience I can give Jesus and still be safe?”
But love does not speak that way.
Imagine someone saying:
“How much can I ignore my spouse before technically ceasing to love them?”
The question itself exposes the problem.
If Jesus commands you to be baptized and you are able to obey Him, why would someone who loves Christ spend his energy searching for permission to refuse?
Get baptized.
Not because Jesus' blood needs your water.
Get baptized because the One whose blood saved sinners deserves your obedience.
Not to purchase salvation.
Not to impress heaven.
Not because a pastor owns your soul.
Not because a denomination needs another statistic.
Get baptized because Jesus is Lord.
And if you have already been baptized, there is another danger.
Do not trust your baptism certificate instead of Christ.
You can go beneath water dry and come out wet while remaining spiritually untouched.
Water cannot substitute for repentance.
A ceremony cannot substitute for faith.
Religious vocabulary cannot substitute for regeneration.
Church attendance cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
And this may be where the question stops being theological and becomes painfully personal.
You remember your baptism.
But do you know Jesus?
You remember the church.
But have you surrendered?
You remember what the pastor said.
But have you repented?
Maybe everybody around you thinks you are fine.
Christian posts.
Christian vocabulary.
Christian family.
Christian music.
Christian friends.
Maybe even ministry.
But somewhere beneath all of it is a room inside your heart whose door you keep locked.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness you have baptized with religious excuses.
A relationship you know dishonors God.
Pride.
Secret messages.
Envy.
Greed.
Hatred.
An addiction you keep promising to surrender “next week.”
A version of Christianity that wants Jesus as Savior but becomes uncomfortable when He speaks as Lord.
And suddenly the real question is no longer whether enough water touched your body.
The question is whether Christ has your heart.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous.
Jesus does not renovate respectable sinners.
He raises dead ones.

He takes adulterers, liars, addicts, hypocrites, religious frauds, broken fathers, wounded mothers, rebellious sons, ashamed daughters, secret sinners, exhausted believers, and people who believe they have wandered too far…
and He calls them to repentance.
Then grace does what shame could never do.
Grace does not tell sin that it was acceptable.
Grace tells the sinner that Jesus paid what sin demanded.
The cross does not say your sin was small.
The cross says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His love was so extraordinary that He willingly came for sinners.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
Maybe you have spent years trying to become clean enough to approach Jesus.
You have it backward.
Come to Jesus because you cannot make yourself clean.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Stop pretending.
Bring Christ the thing you keep hiding.
And if you have trusted Christ but have never obeyed Him in baptism, do not turn grace into an excuse for disobedience.
Speak with faithful church leaders.
Study the Scriptures carefully.
Be baptized in obedience to Christ.
Let your life publicly say:
I belong to Jesus.
And if you were baptized years ago but your heart has wandered far from Him, do not imagine another religious performance can replace repentance.
Come home.
Christ is still the center.
Christ is still enough.
Christ is still calling sinners.
Christ is still forgiving the repentant.
Christ is still restoring the fallen.
Christ is still rewriting stories everybody else thought were finished.
This is what “From Scandal to Grace” means.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when the pen belongs to Jesus.
And if this article exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind theology.
Be honest.
Someone reading silently may desperately need the testimony God has already written into your life.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but you know is searching.
Jesus alone deserves that place.
You cannot buy Jesus.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Salvation is God's gift to undeserving sinners through Jesus Christ.
Invite your family. Invite your friends. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the seeker with uncomfortable questions. Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somewhere behind another screen may be a human being wondering whether there is still enough grace for them.
There is.
His name is Jesus.
The water is important.
The obedience is important.
The confession is important.
But never mistake the sign for the Savior.

Because when the water settles, when the church doors close, when the arguments end, when your religious achievements are stripped away and you stand before eternity with nothing in your hands, your hope will never be that you performed Christianity perfectly.
Your hope will be that Jesus Christ died for sinners…
and rose again.
The water can testify that you belong to Jesus—but only Jesus can turn a sinner's final chapter into the beginning of eternal life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY COULDN’T THE WAGES OF PROSTITUTION BE BROUGHT INTO GOD’S HOUSE?
paragraphs: WHY COULDN’T THE WAGES OF PROSTITUTION BE BROUGHT INTO GOD’S HOUSE?
The money could reach the sanctuary door. The scandalous person could reach the heart of God. And that difference changes everything.
There is a sentence buried in Deuteronomy that almost sounds too uncomfortable to preach.
It involves prostitution.
Money.
Worship.
And a God who apparently says, “Do not bring that into My house.”
At first glance, it can sound merciless.
Maybe even cruel.
Because what happens when the person holding that money is ashamed of how it was earned?
What if she wants to come back?
What if he is tired of living in darkness?
What if someone has finally reached the point where they hate what sin has done to them and desperately wants to give something to God?
Would God really look at a broken sinner trying to come home and say, “I don't want anything from you”?
No.
And that is exactly why we need to read the passage carefully.

Because buried inside this disturbing command is a distinction that exposes counterfeit worship, confronts our attempts to sanitize sin, and—when read through the larger biblical story—helps us understand something breathtaking about grace.
God refused the wages.
But God has never been afraid of rescuing the sinner.
Read the actual Hebrew:
“לֹא־תָבִיא אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה וּמְחִיר כֶּלֶב בֵּית יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ לְכָל־נֶדֶר כִּי תוֹעֲבַת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ גַּם־שְׁנֵיהֶם”
Lo-tavi etnan zonah u-mechir kelev beit YHWH Elohekha lekhol-neder, ki to'avat YHWH Elohekha gam-sheneihem.
In straightforward English:
“You shall not bring the fee of a prostitute or the price of a dog into the house of the LORD your God for any vow, for both are an abomination to the LORD your God.”
—Deuteronomy 23:18 in most English numbering; 23:19 in the Hebrew verse numbering.
Slow down over one expression:
אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה
’etnan zonah.
The payment—or hire—of a prostitute.
The command is not merely saying, “God dislikes certain coins.”
Coins do not commit sexual immorality.
Money has no conscience.
The issue is what that payment represented.

It was the proceeds of an act God forbade, and Israel was not permitted to take the fruit of sexual wrongdoing and ceremonially present it to God as though religious devotion could make its origin irrelevant.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because human beings have always been tempted to do something frighteningly similar.
We sin...
then try to give God something so we can feel clean without actually surrendering.
We compromise...
then worship loudly.
We exploit someone...
then donate publicly.
We nourish a secret addiction...
then lift our hands on Sunday.
We destroy someone privately...
then speak about God publicly.
We keep the idol...
and give God a percentage.
And somewhere beneath all that religious activity is the dangerous hope that perhaps sacrifice can substitute for repentance.
But God cannot be bribed into calling darkness light.
That is what makes this passage uncomfortable.
The Hebrew word translated “abomination” is תּוֹעֵבָה—to'evah—a word used in the Old Testament for things regarded as detestable or abhorrent before God.
Israel was being taught that worship could not be separated from holiness.
You could not drag rebellion to the altar, put religious wrapping around it, and suddenly rename it devotion.
And the preceding verse makes the setting even more striking:
“לֹא־תִהְיֶה קְדֵשָׁה מִבְּנוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא־יִהְיֶה קָדֵשׁ מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל”
Lo-tihyeh qedeshah mibbenot Yisrael, velo-yihyeh qadesh mibbeney Yisrael.

The precise historical sense of qedeshah and qadesh has been debated, and translations differ. They have often been understood in connection with prostitution, sometimes specifically cultic or ritual prostitution, while some scholarship is more cautious about that identification.
We should not pretend certainty where the language itself has generated serious discussion.
But the next command is unmistakably concerned with the ’etnan zonah—the prostitute's fee—and forbids bringing it into God's house as fulfillment of a vow.
Then comes another strange expression:
וּמְחִיר כֶּלֶב
u-mechir kelev.
“The price of a dog.”

There are different interpretations of precisely what this denotes. Some have understood “dog” literally and the expression as the proceeds or exchange value of a dog; others have connected it to the preceding sexual context.
Again, responsible interpretation requires humility.
But the central command does not require us to solve every disputed detail before hearing its thunder:
God would not allow His sanctuary to become a laundering operation for rebellion.
And maybe that sentence just found you.
Because perhaps you have spent years trying to give God everything except the one thing He has actually been confronting.
Your surrender.
You gave Him songs.
You gave Him church attendance.
You gave Him religious posts.
You gave Him money.
You gave Him Christian language.
You even gave Him tears.
But behind the worship was a locked room.
And every time Jesus approached that door, you whispered:
“Anything but this.”
The affair.
The pornography.
The bitterness.
The dishonest business.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The money nobody knows how you acquired.
The unforgiveness you have protected for years.
The image of yourself you carefully maintain while your private life collapses.
You wanted God to bless the offering without touching the source.
But the God of Scripture loves us too much to participate in that lie.
This is where Deuteronomy 23 becomes more than an ancient regulation.
It becomes a mirror.
Because one of humanity's oldest religious instincts is attempting to compensate for rebellion instead of abandoning it.
Saul learned this painfully.
When he disobeyed God's command and then appealed to sacrifice, Samuel answered:
“To obey is better than sacrifice.”
—1 Samuel 15:22.
Isaiah later thundered against worship divorced from righteous living.
Amos condemned religious assemblies offered alongside injustice.

David, after the catastrophe of his own sexual sin and the killing of Uriah, finally understood that religious performance could not manufacture a clean heart. His cry in Psalm 51 was not essentially, “Look what I can give You.”
It was:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
