That is repentance.
Not purchasing God's tolerance.
Not negotiating with holiness.
Not saying, “God, I'll give You this if You let me keep that.”
Repentance comes empty-handed and tells the truth.
“I sinned.”
No editing.
No public-relations strategy.
No spiritual cosmetics.
No blaming childhood, loneliness, temptation, another person, or circumstances as though explanation were absolution.
“I sinned.”
And then something astonishing happens in the biblical story.
Because if Deuteronomy were the end of Scripture, a terrified sinner might leave believing, “God rejects dirty things, therefore God must reject me.”
But keep reading.
Keep reading until you encounter Rahab.
A woman Scripture identifies with prostitution becomes part of Israel's story through faith and courageous allegiance to Israel's God.
Keep reading until you reach the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1 and find Rahab's name there.
Read that again.
Rahab.
In the genealogy leading to the Messiah.
The Gospel does not erase the scandal from the record as though Jesus needs a sanitized family history.
Grace walks directly into histories human beings would rather conceal.
And then keep reading until Jesus enters the story in flesh.
Watch Him sit with people respectable religion despised.
Watch Him receive sinners.
Watch Him confront sin without becoming contaminated by sinners.
Watch Him defend the broken without redefining evil as good.
Watch Him offer mercy without pretending repentance is unnecessary.
Watch Him approach the people everybody else had reduced to labels.
Tax collector.
Adulterer.
Sinner.
Unclean.
Outcast.
And then watch what grace does.
Jesus does not merely make sinful proceeds respectable.
He transforms sinful people.
That is infinitely greater.
God's answer to human defilement is not cosmetic rehabilitation.
It is redemption.
And redemption has a name.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the road leads to the cross.
At Calvary, Christ did not announce that sin had never mattered.
The cross announces precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that forgiveness is unimaginably costly.
Yet God's love is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved.
Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
—1 Peter 3:18.
Paul says:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8.
Do you see it now?

The holy God who would not accept the wages of prostitution as a sacred offering is the same God whose redemptive story reaches prostitutes, adulterers, thieves, liars, religious hypocrites, the sexually broken, the greedy, the ashamed, and people whose histories seem impossible to repair.
God does not call evil good.
He does something better.
He forgives sinners and begins making them new.
That is why grace is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings sinners home and teaches us to leave the old chains behind.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could decorate our cages.
He came to set captives free.
Maybe your scandal has a different name.
Maybe nobody knows it.
Maybe you have mastered smiling while carrying something that makes you terrified someone will eventually discover who you have been.
Perhaps you believe that if people knew everything, they would never look at you the same way again.
Maybe you're right about some people.
But you have confused their knowledge with God's.
God already knows.
Before your confession, He knew.
Before somebody discovered it, He knew.
Before you deleted the messages, He knew.
Before you learned how to hide it, He knew.
Before you started pretending you were okay, He knew.
And the Gospel invitation is still being announced.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Not because your past is insignificant.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because your sin was imaginary.
Because His cross was real.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
Because Jesus can give you what your religious performance never could:
a new heart, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a new direction.
There is a dangerous misunderstanding we must avoid here.

Deuteronomy 23 should never be weaponized to tell people with sexually sinful histories that they are permanently dirty, that their lives can never become useful to God, or that they are somehow a lower class of Christian after repentance.
That conclusion collides with the Gospel.
Paul reminded the Corinthian believers of lives marked by various forms of sexual immorality, idolatry, greed, drunkenness and other sins—and then wrote some of the most beautiful words imaginable:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the mud was clean.
Being washed.
Not renaming slavery freedom.
Being delivered.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace rewriting what happens next.
And please understand another important distinction.

Deuteronomy 23:18 is an instruction within Israel's covenant worship concerning what could be brought into the house of YHWH for a vow. We should not lazily turn it into a simplistic modern formula claiming that every dollar once connected with a sinful past remains permanently contaminated forever, even after repentance and changed circumstances.
The text does not authorize us to invent rules it does not state.
Its holiness principle, however, remains piercing:
Do not use worship to legitimize rebellion.
Do not imagine that giving something to God purchases permission to keep disobeying Him.
Do not use religious generosity as camouflage for unrepentant sin.
And that warning applies far beyond prostitution.
A businessman cannot knowingly exploit people Monday through Saturday and imagine a Sunday donation makes exploitation holy.
A preacher cannot knowingly manipulate people for money and then call the proceeds “blessing.”
A husband cannot abuse his family privately and imagine public ministry cancels it.
A Christian cannot deliberately live two lives and use worship as anesthesia.
God is not looking for spiritual hush money.
He wants truth in the inward being.
And that means this passage eventually turns its finger toward every one of us.
Because perhaps you have never sold your body.
But have you sold your integrity?
Perhaps nobody has ever paid you for sex.
But have you exchanged obedience for acceptance?
Have you traded conviction for applause?
Have you compromised truth to protect income?
Have you hidden sin because exposing it might damage your reputation?
Have you tried to offer God a polished Christian image while protecting a private rebellion?
Suddenly Deuteronomy 23 is not about “those people.”
It is about us.
That is what Scripture does.
We arrive expecting a window through which we can examine someone else's scandal.
God turns it into a mirror.
And then—mercifully—the mirror points us toward a Savior.
Because Christianity is not the story of clean people congratulating themselves for never becoming dirty.
It is the story of a holy Christ rescuing sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
Some scandals are public.
Some are hidden.
Some become headlines.
Some die inside locked bedrooms and erased browser histories.
But every sinner ultimately needs the same Savior.
Jesus.
So if this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't merely feel bad.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from it.
Where appropriate and safe, seek mature biblical accountability and make restitution where wrongdoing requires it.
And trust Christ rather than your ability to punish yourself.
Self-hatred is not the same thing as repentance.
Shame can stare endlessly at what you did.
Faith looks at what Christ has done and begins walking in a new direction.
Maybe somebody reading this believes they have crossed a line from which God could never bring them back.
Listen carefully.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
David committed adultery and arranged Uriah's death.
Rahab carried the label of prostitute.
Their stories do not make sin small.
They make mercy astonishing.
Your worst chapter does not give you permission to keep sinning.
But neither does it possess greater authority than Jesus Christ to determine what your final chapter must be.
That is why we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by changing God's definition of holiness.
Jesus rewrites everything by forgiving the repentant sinner, breaking chains, restoring what sin destroyed according to His wisdom, and creating a life that can now testify:
“I am not who I was.”
Maybe that is what somebody on your Facebook friends list desperately needs to hear tonight.
Not another argument.
Not another polished Christian cliché.
Hope.
Send it privately to someone who would never comment publicly.
Your comment may become the sentence another ashamed person reads and realizes:
“I am not the only one fighting this.”
That is what Christian community should do.
Not celebrate sin.
Not crush sinners.
Point sinners to Jesus.
Not because anyone can purchase God's favor.
And not because God needs our money.
We glorify God through faith, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and lives surrendered to Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of generosity when it is given freely and sincerely.
Follow so we can keep walking through difficult Scriptures together instead of surviving on shallow Christianity.
Because somewhere tonight there is a person convinced their scandal has become their identity.
Someone believes what they did is now who they are.
Someone is trying to pay God back.
Someone is hiding behind religious activity.
Someone is standing emotionally outside the house of God thinking:
“After what I've done, He could never want me.”
And perhaps Deuteronomy 23 has been misunderstood precisely at that point.
God's refusal of a sinful wage was never proof that repentant sinners were beyond redemption.
The Bible's story moves toward something infinitely greater than an acceptable offering brought by a sinner.
It moves toward the perfect offering given for sinners.
Jesus Christ.
The Lamb without blemish.
The righteous One for the unrighteous.
The Savior who did what our money, promises, vows, tears, religious performance, and self-punishment could never accomplish.
He reconciles sinners to God.
So stop trying to pay for what Jesus died to forgive.
Stop asking religious performance to accomplish what only the cross can accomplish.
Bring God your confession.
Bring Him your brokenness.
Bring Him the truth.
Turn from the darkness.
Trust the Son.
And then walk forward in the new life grace gives.
Because the most unforgettable thing about your scandal may not ultimately be what you did.
It may be what Jesus did with the life you finally surrendered to Him.
The altar could reject the wages of the old life while grace was already preparing to redeem the person who walked away from it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Gossip Sounded Almost Holy Because You Introduced It With “We Need to Pray for Them.”
paragraphs: The Gossip Sounded Almost Holy Because You Introduced It With “We Need to Pray for Them.”

Sometimes the most dangerous gossip in the church does not sound cruel. It sounds concerned. It mentions prayer. It lowers its voice. It may even quote Scripture. And somewhere between “I’m worried about them” and “please don’t tell anyone else,” another person’s private pain becomes public information.
“We need to pray for them.”
It sounded harmless.
Actually, it sounded spiritual.
There was concern in your voice. Maybe even genuine concern.
You weren't laughing.
You weren't mocking them.
You certainly wouldn't have called what happened next gossip.
You were simply explaining why everyone needed to pray.
So you told them about the marriage.
The relapse.
The financial disaster.
The child who walked away.
The private confession.
The ministry failure.
The rumor you had heard from someone who heard it from someone close to the situation.
You gave just enough detail for everybody to understand exactly what had happened.
Then someone asked another question.
You answered it.
Someone else said, “I knew something wasn't right.”
Another person remembered something strange the person had done six months earlier.
Someone connected another dot.
Twenty minutes later, the person you were supposedly praying for had been spiritually dissected in a room they never entered.
And maybe the most uncomfortable part is this:
Everybody eventually prayed.
That is what makes religious gossip so difficult to recognize.
It doesn't always arrive wearing the clothes of cruelty.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it sits in a prayer meeting.
Sometimes it begins with, “I'm only telling you this so you can pray.”
Sometimes it ends with “God help them.”
But between those two sentences, someone's dignity has been passed around the room.
Paul wrote something to the Ephesian believers that should make every Christian reconsider not only what we say, but why we say it.
Ephesians 4:29 reads in the Greek:
“πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω, ἀλλὰ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας, ἵνα δῷ χάριν τοῖς ἀκούουσιν.”
A careful sense of Paul's command is:
Let no corrupt or rotten word proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for building up according to the need, so that it may give grace to those who hear.
There is a word hiding in that sentence that deserves our attention:
σαπρός — sapros.
Rotten.
Bad.
Unfit.
Worthless.
The word can describe something spoiled or rotten. Here Paul applies it to speech.
That changes the question.
Because Christians often ask:
“Was what I said true?”
Paul forces us to ask something deeper.
“What did my words produce in the people who heard them?”
Truth matters enormously. Scripture never gives us permission to lie in order to protect someone.
But factual accuracy alone does not make every disclosure righteous.
Something can be true...
and still be unnecessary to repeat.
Something can be accurate...
and still violate a confidence.
Something can be technically correct...
and still be spoken from pride, resentment, curiosity, jealousy, self-importance, or the secret pleasure of possessing information other people do not have.
And perhaps that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because gossip has a strange emotional currency.
Knowing something makes us feel important.
Being the person who tells it makes us temporarily powerful.
We possess information.
People lean closer.
People listen.
Suddenly the room belongs to us.
And when religious language is wrapped around that feeling, we can experience the pleasure of gossip while preserving the appearance of righteousness.
“We really need to pray.”
But did they need the details to pray?
Did they need the name?
Did they need the history?
Did they need to know what happened behind that closed door?
Did they need the screenshots?
Did they need to hear what the husband supposedly said?
Did they need to know what the pastor confessed?
Did they need to know why she stopped attending church?
Did they need to know what his child did?
Did they need to know what happened in somebody else's marriage?
Or did part of us simply enjoy being the person who knew?
That question hurts.
Let it.
Conviction is not the enemy of grace.
Sometimes conviction is grace knocking before consequences kick the door down.
And Scripture is remarkably consistent about the stewardship of another person's story.
Proverbs 11:13 warns that the person who goes around revealing secrets is contrasted with the trustworthy person who keeps a matter covered.
Proverbs 17:9 goes even further: the person who covers an offense seeks love, while the person who keeps repeating the matter can separate close friends.

That does not mean Christians should conceal abuse, crimes, threats, exploitation, predatory behavior, or situations where someone is in danger. Biblical discretion must never become a religious excuse for protecting an abuser or silencing a victim. Appropriate authorities, safeguarding leaders, parents or guardians where appropriate, pastors, counselors, medical professionals, or law enforcement may genuinely need information.
Neither does “covering” sin mean pretending sin does not matter.
Jesus taught direct confrontation.
In Matthew 18:15, when a brother sins, the first movement is strikingly personal:
Go to him.
Between you and him.
The goal is not circulation.
The goal is restoration.
That is profoundly different from gossip.
Gossip moves outward.
Love moves toward.
Gossip asks, “Who else knows?”
Love asks, “How can this person be restored?”
Gossip collects details.
Love carries burdens.
Gossip enjoys the shock.
Love feels the weight.
Gossip turns somebody's failure into content.
Love remembers there is a human being underneath the scandal.
And that human being bears the image of God.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be that human being.
Maybe once...
the prayer request was about you.
You walked into church and noticed something different.
Two people became unusually quiet.
Someone who normally hugged you gave you that strange, sympathetic smile.
Another person approached you and said:
“I'm praying for you.”
You hadn't told them anything.
Your stomach dropped.
“How did you know?”
They hesitated.
And suddenly you understood.
Your private pain had traveled.
Maybe you told one person because you were drowning.
You thought they were safe.
You needed someone to sit beside you in the wreckage.
Instead, your confession developed legs.
Your weakest moment became somebody else's conversation.
Your marriage became a prayer request.
Your child became a discussion.
Your addiction became “something we should all be praying about.”
Your failure arrived in rooms before you did.
And perhaps nobody technically lied.
That almost made it worse.
Because every detail was true.
It simply wasn't theirs to distribute.
If that happened to you, Jesus sees the wound.
But now comes the harder question.
Have you ever done it to somebody else?
Maybe not maliciously.
Maybe you really were worried.
Maybe your intentions were mixed rather than evil.
Maybe you began with compassion and somewhere along the way curiosity took over.
Maybe you said:
“Don't tell anybody I told you.”
Think about that sentence.
If the information should not travel beyond the person you're speaking to...
why did it need to travel from you?

There are exceptions, of course. Serious danger, abuse, safeguarding concerns, necessary pastoral accountability, or seeking wise counsel can require carefully sharing information with the right person.
But “the right person” and “every interested person” are not the same thing.
There is a difference between seeking help and spreading a story.
There is a difference between accountability and entertainment.
There is a difference between warning someone who genuinely needs protection and making sure everybody knows what somebody did.
There is a difference between carrying someone's burden...
and carrying their business.
Paul gives us a beautiful alternative in Ephesians 4:29.
Our speech should be πρὸς οἰκοδομήν — pros oikodomēn.
Toward building up.
The picture behind oikodomē is construction, edification, building.
Then Paul tells us what speech should ultimately deliver:
χάριν — charin.
Grace.
Imagine that.
The Christian mouth is meant to become an instrument through which grace reaches another human being.
Not merely information.
Not merely opinions.
Not merely accurate observations.
Grace.
That does not mean every Christian sentence must be soft.
Jesus spoke hard truth.
The apostles rebuked sin.
Biblical love can confront, warn, correct, expose evil where necessary, and call people to repentance.
Grace is not pretending darkness is light.
But biblical correction seeks redemption rather than humiliation.
That distinction changes everything.
Ask yourself what would happen if the person you are discussing suddenly walked into the room.
Would your tone change?
Would you stop mid-sentence?
Would everyone become uncomfortable?
Would you suddenly realize that something supposedly said for their spiritual good could not comfortably be said in their presence?
That may tell you something.
There is another test.
Before telling someone's story, imagine Jesus sitting in the empty chair beside you.
Not imaginary Jesus who approves everything Christians do.
Jesus Christ.
The One who said people will give account for careless words.
The One who knows what happened.
The One who knows what actually happened.
The One who knows the details you got wrong.
The One who knows the context you never heard.
The One who knows their motives.
And yours.
Would you still say it?
Would you still give the name?
Would you still provide the details?
Would you still lean closer and whisper?
Because Jesus hears conversations that the subject never hears.
That should sober us.
But it should not drive us into hopelessness.
Because this article is not ultimately about becoming a person who never makes another mistake with their tongue.
It is about becoming a person whose tongue has been surrendered to Jesus.
Maybe while reading this, someone's face appeared in your mind.
Maybe several.
Maybe you remember exactly what you said.
Maybe you remember who you told.
Maybe you even remember the tiny rush you felt when they leaned closer.
Do not defend it.
Bring it into the light.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
There is no need for theatrics.
No performance.
No religious excuse.
Just repentance.
Lord, I talked about someone I should have prayed for.
I exposed what I should have protected.
I enjoyed information that should have broken my heart.
I called it concern when part of it was curiosity.
I called it discernment when part of it was judgment.
I called it a prayer request when I knew I was telling more than anyone needed to know.
Forgive me.
That prayer is not the end.
It may be the beginning.
Repentance sometimes requires repairing what our words damaged.
Maybe you need to stop a rumor instead of feeding it.
Maybe you need to tell the person you originally spoke to, “I shouldn't have shared that. Please don't repeat it.”
Maybe you owe someone an apology.
Maybe you need to become the person who changes the atmosphere when gossip begins.
Imagine this happening next Sunday.
Someone leans toward you.
“Did you hear what happened to—”
And instead of leaning closer...
you gently stop them.
“If they haven't given us permission to talk about this, maybe we shouldn't.”
The room becomes quiet.
Someone changes the subject.
The story dies there.
Nobody applauds.
Nobody knows what you prevented.
But heaven knows.
A reputation was protected.
A confidence remained intact.
A wounded person was not wounded again.
That is what spiritual maturity sometimes looks like.
Not saying the impressive thing.
Not possessing the secret thing.
Not becoming the person everybody calls when they want the latest church information.
Sometimes maturity sounds like silence.
And sometimes the holiest sentence in the room is:
“I don't think that's ours to share.”
There is something deeply Christlike about refusing to turn someone's lowest chapter into their permanent identity.
Because if anybody had the right to expose us completely, it was Jesus.
He knows everything.
Every thought.
Every hidden sin.
Every contradiction.
Every private failure.
Every moment that would destroy our carefully constructed reputation if it appeared on a screen behind us Sunday morning.
He knows.
And still...
the Gospel tells us that Christ came for sinners.
He did not minimize our sin.
He carried its judgment.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend humanity was innocent.
He demonstrated just how serious sin really is.
Yet the scandal of Christianity is that the Holy One willingly stood in the place of the guilty.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something gossip can never give:
redemption.
That means the worst true thing anyone could ever discover about you does not have to become the final word over you.
Jesus gets the final word.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Jesus transformed Paul into a herald of the Gospel.
The woman caught in adultery stood surrounded by accusation, yet Jesus neither celebrated her sin nor abandoned her to condemnation. He extended mercy and called her away from sin.
This is the rhythm of the Gospel.
Truth without denial.
Sin without excuses.
Repentance without pretending.
Grace without cheapening holiness.
Transformation without pretending the past never happened.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if Christ has treated us with such astonishing mercy, how can we casually make merchandise of another believer's shame?
Church should be one of the safest places on earth to confess that you are struggling.
Not because sin is ignored there.
Because grace lives there.
Imagine a church where a struggling believer could say, “I'm not okay,” without wondering how many phones would carry the story home.
Imagine men who could confess temptation and receive accountability rather than become tomorrow's rumor.
Imagine women who could admit their marriages were hurting without discovering later that half the church knew.
Imagine pastors who could seek legitimate accountability without every weakness becoming spectacle.
Imagine young believers discovering that Christianity is not a community of people pretending to have no scars...
but a family of redeemed sinners learning to carry one another toward Jesus.
That kind of church begins with ordinary Christians making extraordinary decisions with ordinary conversations.
It begins with you.
It begins with me.
It begins the next time someone says:
“Don't tell anybody, but...”
And perhaps the Spirit reminds us:
Their story is not our currency.
Their weakness is not our entertainment.
Their confession is not our content.
Their scandal is not our opportunity to feel righteous.
If they are drowning, help pull them toward Christ.
If they are sinning and you are biblically responsible to address it, speak truth to them.
If someone is endangered, get appropriate help.
If accountability is necessary, involve the people who actually need to be involved.
If wisdom is needed, seek it without unnecessarily exposing identities or details.
But if all we are doing is passing along another person's private failure because the information is interesting...
we should stop calling it prayer.
And repent.
Maybe this exposed something you have never wanted to call gossip because your version of gossip sounded spiritual.
If so, don't run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
You do not owe strangers your details.
You don't need to tell your whole story.
Sometimes two words are enough for believers to know there is a real person behind the screen who needs prayer.
And maybe you know someone who needs this message—not so you can weaponize it against them, but because you want both of you to grow.
Not “Who is the gossip?”
But:
“Jesus, what needs to change in me?”
It will arrive in a conversation.
A group chat.
A phone call.
After church.
Over coffee.
Someone will lower their voice.
And you will have seconds to decide whether their story stops with you.
But believers can freely and cheerfully support Gospel work and resources they believe are bearing good fruit.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Somewhere there may be another believer who has never realized that religious language can make sinful speech feel righteous.
And somewhere there may be someone preparing to repeat a story tomorrow who needs to remember one sentence tonight:
Just because you know somebody's scandal does not mean God appointed you to become its messenger.
Before you speak, remember the cross.
Remember how much Jesus knows about you.
Remember how much grace He has shown you.
Then ask whether the words leaving your mouth will carry corruption...
or grace.
Because one day you may discover that the person whose reputation you protected never even knew you protected it.
But Jesus knew.
And maybe that is enough.
The next time someone hands you another person's shame, you will reveal something about your own heart by what you do with it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PSALM 91 DOES NOT PROMISE CHRISTIANS A TROUBLE-FREE LIFE
paragraphs:
PSALM 91 DOES NOT PROMISE CHRISTIANS A TROUBLE-FREE LIFE
If You Think “No Evil Shall Befall You” Means Nothing Painful Can Touch a Christian, You Need to Read What Happened to Jesus
There is a version of Psalm 91 that sounds beautiful...
until you are standing beside a hospital bed.
Until the diagnosis comes back.
Until someone you prayed for still dies.
Until the marriage you begged God to restore falls apart.
Until the child you raised to love Jesus walks away.
Until the job disappears.
Until depression makes getting out of bed feel like warfare.
Until you prayed Psalm 91 over your family...
and trouble still found your address.
Then something frightening can begin happening inside your heart.
You start wondering whether God failed you.
Or worse...
whether you failed God.
Maybe you did not pray hard enough.
Maybe you did not believe strongly enough.
Maybe there was some secret sin.
Maybe Psalm 91 works for stronger Christians but somehow did not work for you.
And while everybody else is posting, “A thousand may fall at your side, but it will not come near you,” you are quietly asking a question you are almost ashamed to say aloud:
“Then why did it come near me?”
Please keep reading.
Because misunderstanding Psalm 91 can turn one of Scripture’s greatest songs of confidence into a source of unnecessary guilt.
Psalm 91 does not promise that Christians will never suffer.
It promises something far deeper:
When suffering enters the story, suffering does not get the final word.
God does.
The Psalm begins:
“He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.”
The Hebrew begins:

יֹשֵׁב בְּסֵתֶר עֶלְיוֹן
בְּצֵל שַׁדַּי יִתְלוֹנָן
“Yoshev b’seter Elyon, b’tsel Shaddai yitlonan.”
The imagery is intimate.
Dwelling.
Shelter.
Shadow.
Presence.
Notice what the Psalmist does not say.
He does not say, “Whoever belongs to God will never enter a frightening place.”
He speaks about where the believer dwells while living in a world where frightening places are real.
That difference matters.
Psalm 91 itself mentions terror.
Arrows.
Pestilence.
Destruction.
Danger.
Enemies.
Lions.
Serpents.
Trouble.
This is not a Psalm written for people pretending darkness does not exist.
It is a Psalm for people who have discovered where to hide when darkness comes.
And perhaps no verse reveals the heart of the Psalm more clearly than God’s own words near its conclusion:
“I will be with him in trouble.”
The Hebrew of Psalm 91:15 says:
עִמּוֹ־אָנֹכִי בְצָרָה
“Immo anokhi b’tzarah.”
“I am with him in trouble.”
Read that again.
Not merely:
“I will prevent all trouble.”
But:
“I will be with him in trouble.”
That changes everything.
Because sometimes we want a God who keeps us from the furnace...
while Scripture repeatedly reveals a God who also meets His people inside it.
Ask Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
God did not prevent them from being thrown into the fire.
He met them there.
Ask Daniel.
God did not prevent Daniel from entering the lions’ den.
He preserved Daniel through it.
Ask Joseph.
God did not prevent the pit.
Or slavery.
Or false accusation.
Or prison.
Yet Genesis repeatedly tells us that the LORD was with Joseph.
Ask Paul.
He loved Christ.
He preached Christ.
He suffered for Christ.
And his faithfulness did not produce a comfortable life.
He was beaten.
Imprisoned.
Rejected.
Shipwrecked.
Persecuted.
Hungry.
Exhausted.
Paul was not proof that God’s promises had failed.
Paul was proof that the presence and faithfulness of God can sustain a human being through circumstances that should have destroyed him.
And then...
look at Jesus.
Because this is where careless interpretations of Psalm 91 collapse.
Satan knew Psalm 91.
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, the devil brought Him to the pinnacle of the temple and quoted the Psalm back to Him:
“He shall give his angels charge concerning thee...”
Think about that.
Scripture was being quoted.
But Scripture was being abused.
The devil essentially told Jesus:
If the promise is true, prove it.
Jump.
Force God to protect You.
Turn divine protection into a spectacle.
Jesus refused.
He answered:
“Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.”
In Greek:
Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου.
“Ouk ekpeiraseis Kyrion ton Theon sou.”
“You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”
That moment should permanently change the way we read Psalm 91.
Because a biblical promise can be quoted accurately...
and still be interpreted wickedly.
Satan did not need to invent a fake verse.
He only needed to twist the purpose of a real one.
And people still do this.
“Nothing can happen to you if you really believe.”
“Real Christians should never be afraid.”
“If you have enough faith, disease cannot touch you.”
“If tragedy happened, somebody must not have trusted God enough.”
No.
That is not the Gospel.
And it is certainly not the life of Jesus Christ.
Jesus trusted His Father perfectly.
Jesus obeyed perfectly.
Jesus never sinned.
And Jesus suffered.
He was betrayed by someone close enough to kiss Him.
Abandoned by friends who swore they would stay.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Struck.
Scourged.
Humiliated.
Nailed to a cross.
And killed.
If Psalm 91 meant, “Anyone who trusts God will never experience physical suffering,” then the sinless Son of God would appear to contradict Psalm 91.
He does not.
He reveals how shallow that interpretation was.
The Father did not abandon Christ.
The cross was not evidence that God had lost control.
What looked like the greatest scandal in human history became the place where redemption was accomplished.
The innocent One condemned.
The Holy One numbered with transgressors.
The King wearing thorns.
The Creator pierced by creatures He created.
Jesus dying between criminals.
Scandal.
And yet...
grace was being written through every wound.
The cross looked like defeat on Friday.
The tomb looked final on Saturday.
Then Sunday came.
This is why Christians must never reduce biblical protection to temporary physical comfort.
Our hope is bigger than avoiding pain.
Our hope is resurrection.
Jesus Himself said:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
Notice that He did not say:
“You might have tribulation if your faith becomes weak.”
He said:
“You shall have tribulation.”
And in the same breath:
“I have overcome the world.”
Christian confidence is not pretending the storm does not exist.
It is knowing the storm is not sovereign.
Cancer is not sovereign.
Death is not sovereign.
Your persecutor is not sovereign.
Your past is not sovereign.
Your trauma is not sovereign.
Your failure is not sovereign.
Your worst night is not sovereign.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
This is why Romans 8 can declare that nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Paul includes tribulation.
Distress.
Persecution.
Famine.
Nakedness.
Danger.
Sword.
He does not say believers avoid all these things.
He says these things cannot separate believers from Christ.
That is stronger.
Imagine a father walking through a violent storm holding the hand of his frightened child.
The child feels the rain.
The child hears the thunder.
The child sees the lightning.
The storm is real.
But so is the father's hand.
Biblical faith does not require the child to pretend it is not raining.
Biblical faith says:
“My Father still has me.”
Maybe that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
Because perhaps you have been secretly angry with God.
You prayed.
You believed.
You fasted.
You quoted Scripture.
You asked other believers to pray.
And the thing you begged God not to allow...
happened anyway.
Now you smile at church while carrying questions you are terrified to admit.
Where were You, God?
Why didn't You stop it?
Did You hear me?
Do You still love me?
Those questions do not frighten God.
Scripture contains people crying, grieving, lamenting, questioning and asking how long.
Even Jesus cried from the cross:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
He was invoking the language of Psalm 22 while accomplishing the redemption toward which Scripture had been pointing.
Christian faith is not emotional dishonesty.
Sometimes faith sounds like worship.
Sometimes faith sounds like weeping.
Sometimes faith is singing loudly.
Sometimes faith is barely whispering...
“Jesus, I still trust You.”
And perhaps that whisper costs more than the song ever did.
Psalm 91 is not permission to become reckless either.
Jesus proved that in the wilderness.
Trusting God does not mean refusing wisdom, medical care, safety, responsibility, or ordinary precautions and then demanding that God miraculously rescue us.
Faith does not manipulate God.
Faith trusts God.
There is a difference between saying:
“God is able to protect me,”
and saying:
“God is obligated to fulfill my personal interpretation of protection.”
God can rescue miraculously.
And He does.
We should pray for healing.
Pray for deliverance.
Pray for protection.
Pray boldly.
Ask God to intervene.
There is nothing spiritual about expecting tragedy.
But our faith must remain anchored to God even when His answer does not resemble the ending we begged Him to write.
Because Christianity's ultimate promise is not:
“You will never die.”
It is:
Because Christ lives, death will not keep those who belong to Him.
That is infinitely greater.
Lazarus was raised...
and eventually Lazarus died again.
Every person Jesus healed during His earthly ministry eventually faced physical death.
But Christ's resurrection announces something far greater than temporary escape.
Death itself has been defeated.
This is why Paul can cry:
“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
The Gospel does not merely promise better circumstances.
The Gospel gives us a crucified and risen Savior.
And maybe your deepest problem today is not the trouble surrounding you.
Maybe it is the sin hiding within you.
Because Psalm 91 can become another place where we search for God's protection while avoiding God's authority.
We want shelter...
without surrender.
Deliverance...
without repentance.
Promises...
without obedience.
Heaven...
without the King.
We want Jesus to protect our plans while refusing to let Jesus become Lord over them.
But Christ did not die merely to make your present life safer.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
Every one of us has sinned.
Every one of us has fallen short.
Religious people.
Broken people.
Respectable people.
Addicted people.
Church people.
People who know Bible verses and people who have never opened a Bible.
Sin separates us from a holy God.
But God did not leave sinners without hope.
Jesus Christ came.
He lived the righteous life we could not live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is offered not because you deserve another chance, but because Christ paid the price.
Repent.
Turn from sin.
Come to Jesus.
Trust Him.
Stop hiding behind religious appearances.
Stop trying to clean yourself enough to approach Him.
Bring Him the truth.
The addiction.
The secret browser history.
The bitterness.
The affair nobody knows about.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The greed.
The hatred.
The compromise.
The wounds you have used as permission to wound others.
Bring the whole scandal.
Because grace does not require you to pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace takes guilty people and writes a future they could never purchase for themselves.
That is our heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin is harmless.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by promising Christians immunity from suffering.
Jesus rewrites everything by entering the wreckage, bearing our sin, defeating death, forgiving the repentant sinner, making us new and leading us home.
Maybe your Psalm 91 story will be miraculous deliverance.
Praise God.
Maybe doctors will say they cannot explain what happened.
Praise God.
Maybe the door opens.
Maybe the relationship is restored.
Maybe provision arrives at the final hour.
Tell everyone what God has done.
But perhaps your testimony will sound different.
Maybe you will say:
“I walked through something I thought would destroy me...
and Jesus never left.”
That is a miracle too.
Maybe you still cry when nobody is watching.
Maybe you still have unanswered questions.
Maybe your family is still complicated.
Maybe the medical report has not changed.
Maybe grief still visits without warning.
Maybe you thought healing meant forgetting, but God is teaching you that healing sometimes means remembering without being ruled by the wound.
You are not required to call evil good.
You are not required to enjoy suffering.
You are not required to understand everything God permits.
But you can know this:
For the person who belongs to Jesus Christ, suffering is never the final chapter.
The cross proves that God can bring redemption through what appears utterly ruined.
The empty tomb proves that endings are not always endings when God is writing the story.
So when Psalm 91 says:
“He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust,”
do not hear:
“Nothing painful will ever happen to me.”
Hear something stronger.
Whatever happens...
God remains my refuge.
If I walk through abundance...
He is God.
If I walk through loss...
He is God.
If He delivers me from the furnace...
He is God.
If He meets me inside the furnace...
He is God.
If healing comes today...
He is God.
If I must wait...
He is God.
If my prayer is answered exactly as I hoped...
He is God.
If I enter eternity still carrying questions...
Jesus Christ is still Lord.
That kind of faith cannot be destroyed by bad news.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list needs this truth.
Not another shallow promise that Christians never hurt.
They need Jesus.
They need to know that when the night becomes unbearable, God has not necessarily abandoned them.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer sees at exactly the moment they realize they are not the only Christian struggling.
Because there may come a night when Psalm 91 feels harder to believe than it does today, and you may need to remember that “I will be with him in trouble” is not a lesser promise.
It is precious.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, face difficult truths, understand the Gospel, repent, heal, grow and keep your eyes on Jesus, stay close.

Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's blessing, earn salvation, prove that you glorify God more than someone who cannot give, or place God in your debt. We are saved by grace through faith, and Christ cannot be bought.
But generous support and faithful sharing can be genuine ways believers choose to glorify God by helping sound Gospel-centered ministry reach more people.
If you have been consuming these messages quietly and thinking, “Someone needs to keep making this kind of content,” you can become one of the people helping make that possible.
Not because clicking “share” makes you righteous.
Jesus alone saves.
Do it because truth was never meant to stop with us.
Someone you know may currently believe that suffering means God abandoned them.
Someone may be one tragedy away from walking away from Christianity because nobody ever taught them what Psalm 91 actually promises.
Someone may need to discover tonight that the Gospel is not the promise of a painless life.
It is the promise of a Savior who entered our pain, carried our sin, conquered our grave and will never abandon those who are His.
Psalm 91 is still true.
The hospital room does not make it false.
The funeral does not make it false.
The unanswered question does not make it false.
The persecution does not make it false.
The scars do not make it false.
Because the deepest security of the Christian was never that trouble could not reach our body.
It is that nothing can ultimately steal us from Jesus Christ.
So dwell in the shelter of the Most High.
Pray Psalm 91.
Believe Psalm 91.
Teach Psalm 91.
But do not turn it into something God never promised.
When trouble comes, you have not necessarily fallen outside the shadow of the Almighty.
Sometimes...
the place where you finally understand the shadow
is the place where the night became darkest.
And when you cannot see the ending, remember the cross.
Humanity saw scandal.
God was accomplishing redemption.
They saw a tomb.
God was preparing resurrection.
And whatever chapter you are living right now, never confuse a painful page with the end of the story.
The nails looked like the end of Jesus' story—until the empty tomb revealed who had been holding the pen all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BACKPACK THAT NEVER CAME HOME
paragraphs:
THE BACKPACK THAT NEVER CAME HOME
When a School Becomes a Crime Scene, Where Is God? A Christian Response to the Tragedy of School Shootings, the Tears We Cannot Explain, and the Savior Who Walks Into Our Grief
There is something especially unbearable about an abandoned backpack.
A backpack is supposed to come home.
It is supposed to be dropped beside the door while someone shouts, “I’m hungry.”

It is supposed to contain unfinished homework, broken pencils, folded permission slips, snack wrappers, drawings, notebooks covered with names and doodles, and ordinary evidence that a child expected tomorrow to arrive.
But sometimes a backpack remains in a classroom after its owner does not come home.
And suddenly the ordinary becomes sacred.
A desk.
A jacket.
A lunchbox.
A photograph.
An unanswered text message.
A bedroom whose door nobody wants to open because everything inside still belongs to a future that was supposed to happen.
This is the horror hidden beneath the phrase “school shooting.”
Those two words are too small.
They cannot carry the weight of a mother discovering that the morning goodbye was the final goodbye.
They cannot explain the father who would give anything to hear one more slammed bedroom door.
They cannot describe the teacher who survives but remembers the faces of students every time silence fills a room.

They cannot capture what happens when children learn that the place where they practice multiplication, read stories, laugh with friends, and plan their futures can also become a place where they are taught how to hide.
And before Christians reach too quickly for an explanation, perhaps we should remember something astonishing about Jesus.
When Christ stood before the tomb of Lazarus, He knew resurrection was coming.
He knew exactly what He was about to do.
He knew death would not have the final word.
And still—
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek of John 11:35 is breathtakingly simple:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
Jesus wept.

The verb ἐδάκρυσεν speaks of shedding tears. The ancient text does not present a detached Messiah giving grieving people a lecture about why they should stop crying. Christ enters their sorrow. He sees Mary weeping. He sees the mourners. He sees the grave.
And the Son of God cries.
That matters.
Because somewhere tonight there is a parent who does not need a Christian stranger explaining tragedy with a sentence polished enough for social media.
They need to know whether God sees.
Somewhere there is a student who jumps when a door slams.
Somewhere there is a teacher mentally counting exits.
Somewhere there is a survivor carrying memories nobody else can see.
Somewhere there is a family staring at photographs from the last birthday, the last Christmas, the last first day of school.
And somewhere there is someone asking the question believers sometimes fear:
Where was God?
Do not shame that question.
Scripture doesn't.
The Bible contains people crying, “How long, O LORD?” The Psalms contain lament, bewilderment, fear, anger, grief, and desperate prayer. Biblical faith is not pretending tragedy does not hurt.
Christian hope is not denial.
Christian hope can stand beside a grave and cry.
Jesus did.
And the Christian answer to school shootings cannot be reduced to “everything happens for a reason.”
Scripture never asks us to call evil good.
Murder remains evil.
Human life remains sacred.
Violence remains devastating.
Death remains an enemy.
Paul does not romanticize death. He calls it “the last enemy” in 1 Corinthians 15:26.
That changes the conversation.
Christianity does not tell grieving parents that death is beautiful.
It tells them death is an enemy Christ came to defeat.
The Gospel begins in a world where something has gone terribly wrong.

Humanity was created in the image of God, possessing immeasurable dignity, yet sin entered human history and corrupted what God called good. Violence appears horrifyingly early in Scripture: Cain rises against Abel, and a brother's blood stains the ground.
God's response is not indifference.
He says:
“What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.”
Genesis 4:10.
Blood cries.
God hears.
That means the murdered are not statistics to Him.
Their names matter.
Their lives matter.
Their unfinished dreams matter.
Their families matter.
The children whose photographs briefly fill our screens and then disappear from the news cycle do not disappear from the knowledge of God.
We scroll onward.
God does not forget.
And perhaps that is one reason these tragedies should disturb Christians so deeply.
Every child sitting inside a classroom bears the image of God.
The quiet child.
The difficult child.
The brilliant child.
The lonely child.
The bullied child.
The child everyone knows.
The child almost nobody notices.
The teacher standing at the whiteboard bears God's image.
The custodian walking the hallway bears God's image.
The school secretary answering the telephone bears God's image.
Human beings are never disposable scenery in somebody else's rage.
And when violence enters a school, the damage does not end when the gunfire stops.

Psychologists studying communities affected by school shootings describe consequences that can continue long after the immediate event. Trauma may include anxiety, hypervigilance, intrusive memories, avoidance, fear, and other lasting psychological effects. The American Psychological Association has documented how the aftermath of shootings can ripple through survivors and communities for months, years, and sometimes much longer.

Even preparation for violence requires wisdom. In 2026, the American Psychological Association reported that while appropriately designed lockdown exercises can increase preparedness or confidence, highly realistic or deceptive drills can produce fear, anxiety, and emotional distress.
There is another difficulty whenever numbers about “school shootings” are discussed: not every database uses the same definition.
That distinction matters if Christians care about truth.

The K-12 School Shooting Database, for example, deliberately uses a broad definition that includes incidents in which a firearm is fired, is brandished with intent to harm, or a bullet strikes school property, regardless of whether anyone is wounded and regardless of the motive or time of day. Its methodology therefore includes situations ranging from planned attacks to accidents, domestic violence, fights, suicides, gang-related incidents, and other firearm events on school property. The database itself notes that there is no universally accepted definition across datasets.
So responsible Christians should resist sensational numbers stripped of definitions.
Truth does not need exaggeration.
Grief does not need manipulation.
One dead child is already too many.
One terrified classroom already matters.
One grieving family already deserves our attention.
And if we claim to follow the One who called children to Himself, then compassion cannot end when the headline disappears.
Jesus said:
“Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.”
Mark 10:14.
Imagine those hands.
The hands of Christ receiving children.
Now remember what those same hands would eventually endure.
Nails.
Blood.
A cross.
This is where Christianity makes its most startling claim about suffering.
God did not remain safely outside the violent world humanity created.
He entered it.
Jesus Christ was betrayed.
Arrested.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Publicly humiliated.
Falsely accused.
Tortured.
And executed.
Christianity worships a Savior who knows what violence feels like.
But Calvary reveals something even deeper.
Jesus did not merely become another victim of human evil.
He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the suffering servant:
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
Isaiah 53:5.
The Hebrew phrase describing our transgressions contains the word פְּשָׁעֵנוּ — pĕshaʿênû, “our transgressions” or rebellions.
Ours.
That word destroys the comfortable illusion that evil belongs only to monsters somewhere else.
The Gospel forces every human heart into the mirror.
Maybe you have never fired a weapon at another human being.
But have you hated?
Have you humiliated someone?
Have you secretly enjoyed another person's pain?
Have you destroyed someone with words?
Have you ignored the lonely?
Have you watched cruelty and remained silent because speaking would cost you social acceptance?
Have you carried bitterness so long that it has begun carrying you?
Jesus takes sin seriously enough to trace murder back toward the hatred growing within the human heart.
That does not make hatred legally equivalent to homicide, nor does it erase the profound distinction between angry thoughts and acts of murderous violence.
It does something more personal.
It refuses to let us discuss evil only as something “those people” possess.
Sin is humanity's disease.
And Christ is humanity's only Savior.
This is where the story moves from scandal to grace.
Because the Gospel does not say good people need improvement.
It says sinners need redemption.
Romans tells us:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
The violent.
The proud.
The bitter.
The religious hypocrite.
The secret sinner.
The person reading this while carrying something nobody knows.
All.
And yet Scripture continues with the breathtaking announcement that sinners may be justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That is Christianity.
Not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves it matters unimaginably.
Not God demanding that we repair ourselves before approaching Him.
The cross proves we cannot.
Jesus bears sin.
Jesus offers forgiveness.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus gives grace to the guilty.
Jesus receives the broken.
Jesus transforms hearts.
And Jesus walked out of the grave.
That final truth changes everything.
Because if Christ remained dead, Christianity would have nothing ultimately different to say beside a child's grave.
We could offer memories.
We could offer sympathy.
We could offer flowers.
We could say the deceased lives inside our hearts.
Beautiful sentiments, perhaps.
But the Gospel dares to say something far more radical.
Death does not get the final sentence.
Jesus said:
“I am the resurrection, and the life.”
John 11:25.
Notice where He said it.
Near a grave.
To a grieving woman.
Before Lazarus walked out.
Christ did not offer Martha an abstract philosophy.
He offered Himself.
“I am.”
That is why Christian hope is not optimism.
Optimism says maybe things will improve.
Resurrection says Someone defeated death.
And because Jesus lives, grief and hope can occupy the same heart.
You can cry and believe.
You can tremble and pray.
You can miss someone and worship.
You can ask questions and still cling to Christ.
You can need counseling and still trust God.
You can carry trauma and still be deeply loved by Jesus.

Seeking appropriate psychological or medical care after trauma is not a betrayal of faith. Christians should never shame survivors for needing help. Trauma can have serious effects, and compassionate, evidence-informed support matters.
Neither should prayer become an excuse for passivity.
Scripture repeatedly connects love with action.
“Let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
1 John 3:18.
Pray.
Yes.
Pray desperately.
Pray for grieving parents.
Pray for traumatized students.
Pray for teachers.
Pray for counselors.
Pray for first responders.
Pray for wisdom among school leaders.
Pray for people who recognize warning signs.
Pray for children living with rage, isolation, abuse, despair, or violent thoughts to encounter responsible adults willing to intervene before tragedy occurs.
Then remain awake enough to act responsibly when action is possible.

Prevention work matters. Research summarized by the CDC indicates that confidential or anonymous school reporting systems can provide pathways for students to report concerning behavior and potentially help prevent firearm violence, school shootings, and youth suicide.
Sometimes love looks like noticing.
Sometimes it looks like reporting a credible threat.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to treat another student's frightening behavior as entertainment.
Sometimes it looks like sitting beside the kid nobody sits beside.
Sometimes it means taking suicidal language seriously.
Sometimes it means a parent putting the phone down and actually listening.
Sometimes it means a church becoming a place where teenagers do not have to pretend.
Sometimes it means telling somebody:
“I see you.”
“You matter.”
“Talk to me.”
“I will stay.”
And sometimes those words arrive before darkness becomes catastrophe.
But even our best efforts cannot create a world untouched by death.
Only Christ can finally do that.
The Bible ends with an image every grieving parent should someday hear.
Not because it removes today's pain.
Because it tells us where history is going.
Revelation 21:4 says:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain.”
Read that slowly.
No more death.
No more crying.
No more pain.
Imagine a world where parents never identify their children's bodies.
Imagine schools without memorial photographs.
Imagine hallways without terror.
Imagine funerals becoming obsolete.
Imagine never hearing another breaking-news report announcing that children have been killed.
The Gospel says history is moving toward the reign of Christ in which evil will not merely be managed.
It will finally be defeated.
Until then, Christians live between tears and resurrection.
We grieve.
We protect.
We listen.
We intervene.
We comfort.
We tell the truth.
We refuse sensationalism.
We refuse indifference.
We carry one another.
And above everything else, we proclaim Jesus Christ.
Because legislation cannot resurrect the dead.
Technology cannot forgive sin.
Security cannot heal the human heart.
Counseling can provide vital help for trauma, but no therapist claims to conquer death.
Only Jesus can reconcile sinners to God.
Only Jesus carried our sin to Calvary.
Only Jesus walked from a sealed tomb alive.
Only Jesus can say:
“I am the resurrection, and the life.”
Maybe you came to this article because the title caught you.
Maybe you stayed because somewhere inside these words you found your own grief.
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you have become.
Maybe your tragedy was not a school shooting.
Maybe it was divorce.
Addiction.
Abuse.
Betrayal.
A funeral.
A diagnosis.
A child who walked away.
A secret sin slowly consuming you.
Maybe your life became a crime scene in a completely different way.
Something beautiful was shattered.
And you have been standing among the pieces asking whether God can possibly make anything holy from this.
Look toward the cross.
Christianity's central symbol is an instrument of execution transformed into the announcement of salvation.
That is what Jesus does.
He takes places of shame and writes grace across them.
He takes sinners and makes them sons and daughters.
He takes condemnation and offers forgiveness.
He takes graves and promises resurrection.
He takes stories we thought were over and writes chapters we could never have imagined.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If something hidden inside you was exposed while reading this, don't perform Christianity for another day.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Confess your sin.
Ask Him for mercy.
Trust the crucified and risen Jesus.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is Christ meeting sinners where they are and refusing to leave them there.
And if your heart is grieving rather than guilty today, you do not have to manufacture impressive words.
Sometimes the most faithful prayer sounds like:
“Jesus, help me.”
Sometimes faith is tears.
Remember:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
Jesus wept.
The Savior who asks you to bring Him your tears is not unfamiliar with tears Himself.
But when believers freely support sound Christian ministry and freely spread biblical truth, those ordinary acts can become opportunities to serve others and glorify Christ.
Remember Jesus.
Remember the tears outside Lazarus's tomb.
Remember the blood at Calvary.
Remember the empty grave.
Remember that Christianity does not promise that believers will never walk through horrifying chapters.
It promises that for everyone who belongs to Christ, the horrifying chapter will never be the final chapter.
There will come a day when classroom desks will no longer become memorials.
A day when parents will no longer bury children.
A day when fear will no longer teach children how to hide.
A day when death itself will die.

Until then, when another tragedy fills our screens, may Christians be among the first to weep, the first to listen, the first to protect, the first to serve, the first to tell the truth, and the last to abandon the broken.
Because somewhere tonight there may still be a backpack waiting beside a desk.
And somewhere there is a family learning how impossibly heavy an empty bedroom can feel.
But beyond every grave stands the One who once stood before a grave Himself.
His eyes filled with tears.
His voice called the dead to life.
And soon His own grave would be empty.
The backpack may never come home—but in Jesus Christ, death still does not get to write the last line.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HIS LEFT HAND IS UNDER MY HEAD”: The Intimacy Christians Skip Over in Song of Songs
paragraphs: “HIS LEFT HAND IS UNDER MY HEAD”: The Intimacy Christians Skip Over in Song of Songs
We learned how to serve God, fear God, obey God, defend God, and work for God. But somewhere along the way, many Christians forgot what it means to be loved without running away from the embrace.
There is a sentence in the Bible that almost sounds too intimate to read slowly.
So we usually don't.
We move past it.
We spiritualize it before we have allowed ourselves to feel the weight of what is actually happening.
Maybe because intimacy makes religious people uncomfortable.
Maybe because some of us know how to sing about God's love but have no idea how to receive love without wondering what it is going to cost us.
Maybe because being useful feels safer than being held.
Then the woman in the Song of Songs whispers:
“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.”
Song of Solomon 2:6, KJV.
The Hebrew is breathtakingly simple:
שְׂמֹאלוֹ תַּחַת לְרֹאשִׁי וִימִינוֹ תְּחַבְּקֵנִי
Semolo taḥat leroshi, wimino teḥabbeqeni.
His left hand beneath my head.
His right hand embracing me.
That final Hebrew expression comes from the verb חבק (ḥ-b-q)—to embrace, clasp, hold close.
Not merely to notice.
Not merely to tolerate.
Not merely to stand nearby.
To embrace.
And before we turn this into a metaphor, we need to respect what God actually gave us.
Song of Songs is love poetry.

It celebrates the beauty of covenantal human love, longing, desire, exclusivity, delight, and intimacy. Christians do not need to be embarrassed by that. God created the human body. God created marriage. God created affection. The Bible is not frightened by tenderness.
Neither should we be.

But Christians through the centuries have also heard something deeper resonating through this book—not by erasing its celebration of human love, but by recognizing that faithful covenant love can point beyond itself toward the God whose love gives every righteous human love its meaning.
And that is where this verse becomes almost unbearably personal.
Because some of us believe Jesus died for us...
but still do not know how to let Him love us.
Read that again.
You believe He saved you.
You believe He forgives sinners.
You believe He rose from the dead.
You believe He is coming again.
You may defend His deity, quote His words, attend church, read Scripture, pray before meals, share Christian posts, and tell everyone that God is good.
But when everything becomes quiet...
when nobody needs anything from you...
when there is nothing left to accomplish...
when you cannot impress God with your productivity...
do you know how to simply be loved by Him?
That question exposes something.
Because there are Christians who have spent years serving a Father they secretly experience as an employer.
Perform.
Produce.
Behave.
Don't fail.
Don't disappoint Him.
Read another chapter.
Pray longer.
Volunteer again.
Give more.
Try harder.
Stop struggling.
Fix yourself.
Become useful.
And perhaps nobody ever said those exact words to you.
Perhaps they did not have to.
Somewhere inside you, Christianity quietly became an endless spiritual performance review.
So when you fail, you hide.
When you sin, you withdraw.
When temptation defeats you again, you assume God must be disgusted.
When your prayer life becomes weak, you avoid prayer because you are ashamed that you have not prayed.
When you have doubts, you silence them.
When you are exhausted, you keep smiling.
“How are you?”
“Blessed.”
“How's your walk with God?”
“Good.”
But it isn't good.
You're tired.
You're ashamed.
You're lonely.
You're carrying something nobody knows about.
And perhaps the most terrifying possibility is this:
You are not merely afraid that people would reject the real you.
You are afraid God would too.
So listen again.
“His left hand is under my head…”
There is tenderness here.
Support.
Nearness.
The imagery is not of someone being interrogated from across a courtroom.
It is someone close enough to be held.
And perhaps that is exactly why this verse can disturb people who have learned religion without intimacy.
We know what to do with commandments.
We know what to do with judgment.
We know what to do with doctrine.
We know what to do with spiritual warfare.
But an embrace?
That is different.
An embrace requires proximity.
An embrace requires vulnerability.
An embrace means you cannot pretend the other person is far away.
And maybe your deepest spiritual problem is not that you have never heard that God loves you.
Maybe you have heard it ten thousand times.
Maybe the problem is that you have never believed His love could reach the version of you that you work so hard to keep hidden.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness behind your worship songs.
The marriage that looks beautiful online and feels painfully cold at home.
The jealousy you disguise as discernment.
The anger you call righteous.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The pride.
The loneliness.
The resentment.
The night you crossed a line you swore you would never cross.
The morning you woke up and wondered, “What have I become?”
The prayer you stopped praying because heaven seemed silent.
The Bible collecting dust while your phone knows the shape of your hand.
The person everyone calls strong who cries where nobody can hear.
Yes.
That person.
That is where the Gospel becomes scandalous.
Because Christianity does not announce that respectable people finally impressed God enough for Him to embrace them.
It announces something far more shocking.
“God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
While we were sinners.
Not after the cleanup.
Not after thirty consecutive days without falling.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after you repaired your reputation.
Not after you became spiritually impressive.
While.
We.
Were.
Sinners.
Christ died.
That is grace.
And grace is scandalous because grace refuses to let your worst chapter become the title of your entire story.
But grace is not permission to remain in darkness.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us out of hiding.
The Jesus who receives sinners says, “Go, and sin no more.”
The embrace of God is not an endorsement of everything destroying you.
It is the place from which transformation becomes possible.
This matters enormously when reading Song of Songs.
The intimacy Scripture celebrates is not cheap intimacy.
Immediately after the embrace of Song of Songs 2:6 comes a warning not to awaken love before its proper time.
Biblical love has boundaries precisely because biblical love has value.
Our culture often separates desire from covenant.
God does not need to despise desire in order to sanctify it.
He places holy love within truth, faithfulness, patience, commitment, and covenant.
The world says, “If you desire it, take it.”
Legalism says, “If you desire it, you should probably be ashamed.”
Biblical wisdom says something more beautiful:
Love is powerful.
Therefore do not treat it cheaply.
And perhaps that is another intimacy Christians desperately need to recover.
Not lust wearing Christian vocabulary.
Not emotional dependency renamed “God told me.”
Not manipulation disguised as spiritual leadership.
Not possessiveness baptized as protection.
Not abuse defended with isolated Bible verses.
Not sexuality severed from God's design.
Holy intimacy.
Love that does not consume another person but cherishes them.
Love that does not exploit vulnerability but protects it.
Love that does not demand access but honors covenant.
Love that can hold without owning.
Love that can desire without destroying.
Love that tells the truth.
Love that remains faithful.
And ultimately, every beautiful human embrace still leaves us with an ache no human being can completely satisfy.
Because your husband cannot be your Savior.
Your wife cannot be your Savior.
Your boyfriend cannot be your Savior.
Your girlfriend cannot be your Savior.
Your pastor cannot be your Savior.
Your children cannot be your Savior.
No human relationship was designed to carry the crushing weight of being your god.
There is only One Savior.
Jesus Christ.
And look at how He approaches broken people.
A leper approaches Him—someone society had learned not to touch.
Jesus touches him.
A sinful woman weeps at His feet.
Jesus does not pretend her sin is irrelevant, but neither does He treat her as disposable.
Peter denies Him three times.
Jesus restores him.
Thomas doubts.
Jesus comes near.
The thief beside Him has nothing left to offer—no years of ministry, no repaired reputation, no opportunity to prove himself worthy.
He has only repentance, faith, and a dying breath.
Jesus gives him paradise.
Then there is the cross.
The place where every sentimental idea about God's love is shattered and replaced with something infinitely stronger.
Nails.
Blood.
Mockery.
Thorns.
Darkness.
A crucified Messiah bearing sin.
Jesus did not merely say that sinners were loved.
He entered our catastrophe.
He carried sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately about learning how to love yourself more.
It is about discovering that the holy God loved sinners at unimaginable cost and now calls us to repent, believe, be reconciled to Him, and become new.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to earn what Jesus purchased with blood.
Perhaps that is why you are exhausted.
You keep bringing God résumés.
He keeps pointing you toward a cross.
You keep bringing promises that you will finally become better.
He keeps calling you to trust the One who said:
“It is finished.”
You keep saying, “But look what I did.”
Grace says, “Look what Christ did.”
You say, “You don't understand my past.”
The Gospel answers, “Your past is exactly why you needed a Savior.”
You say, “I ruined everything.”
Jesus specializes in resurrection.
You say, “Nobody could love me if they knew everything.”
But God already knows everything.
That does not mean everyone is automatically reconciled to God regardless of repentance or faith. Scripture never teaches that.
It means there is no advantage in hiding from the One who already sees you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Stop negotiating with the sin Jesus died to free you from.
Stop calling chains “personality.”
Stop protecting the secret that is poisoning your soul.
Stop mistaking shame for repentance.
Shame says, “Hide because you are filthy.”
Repentance says, “Run to Christ because He is merciful.”
There is a difference.
One drives you deeper into darkness.
The other brings you home.
Maybe that is why the image of a hand beneath the head is so powerful.
Some people reading this are spiritually exhausted from holding themselves up.
You have been holding the family together.
Holding the marriage together.
Holding your reputation together.
Holding your ministry together.
Holding your emotions together.
Holding your faith together.
And you are tired.
So tired.
What happens when the person who has been holding everything finally cannot hold themselves anymore?
The Gospel does not say, “Become stronger so Jesus will accept you.”
It says that salvation rests on Someone stronger than you.
Christ.
Your salvation is not anchored in the strength of your grip on Jesus.
It is anchored in the sufficiency of Jesus.
There will be nights when your emotions betray you.
Days when prayer feels dry.
Seasons when Scripture seems difficult.
Moments when temptation screams louder than worship.
Times when you cannot understand what God is doing.
But Jesus Christ does not become less faithful because you became tired.
And no, that does not make obedience optional.
Grace never makes holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes holiness possible.
The forgiven person rises differently.
The embraced prodigal does not return to the pigpen because the Father's house means nothing.
He has finally remembered where home is.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to come home.
Not back to religious performance.
Not back to pretending.
Back to Jesus.
You do not need a more convincing mask.
You need repentance.
You need grace.
You need forgiveness.
You need the blood of Christ.
You need the Holy Spirit.
You need truth.
You need the Savior.
Sit with it.
Pray.
Be honest.
Not as magic words.
Not as a performance.
As an honest confession that you are tired of hiding.
And if God has been restoring places in you that nobody else can see, leave this testimony beneath the article:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Somebody else may read your five words at 2:13 in the morning and realize they are not the only Christian still learning how to come out of hiding.
That matters.
This is how a comment section can become more than numbers.
It can become confession.
Testimony.
Prayer.
People pointing people toward Jesus.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
You may have spoken to them yesterday.
You may sit beside them in church.
You may share a surname.
You may sleep beside them every night.
They may never tell you how close they are to giving up.
There may come a night when shame tries to preach to you again.
When it does, come back and remember:
The cross has already told you what God thinks about sin.
It is deadly serious.
And the cross has already told you how far God's mercy was willing to go to rescue sinners.
All the way.
If Gospel Warrior has been helping you open Scripture again, confront hidden sin, return to prayer, understand the Gospel, heal through biblical truth, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ, stay close.

This ministry exists to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and Christ-centered truth in front of people in a world that never stops placing distractions in front of them.

Scripture gives legitimate room for believers to materially support Gospel ministry. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living through Gospel work. But Scripture is equally clear that Christian giving must not be produced by pressure or compulsion.
That would go beyond Scripture.
Pray for the ministry.
Leave a testimony.
Save the message.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Your bank account is not the measure of your devotion to Christ.
Jesus does not sell grace.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Salvation is the gift of God through Christ.
And perhaps that brings us back to the line where we began.
“His left hand is under my head…”
What if you have spent so much of your Christian life asking whether you are doing enough for God that you have forgotten to stand in wonder at what God has done for you?
The Christian faith begins not with your hand reaching high enough to heaven.
It begins with God coming down.
The Word became flesh.
Christ entered history.
Christ touched the unclean.
Christ ate with sinners.
Christ carried the cross.
Christ bore sin.
Christ entered the grave.
Christ rose victorious.
And Christ still calls sinners by grace:
Come.
Not because your scandal was small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because your sin did not matter.
Because it mattered enough for blood to be shed.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Because grace finally gives you somewhere to run when repentance breaks your heart.
Maybe you thought your story ended on the night everybody found out.
Maybe you thought it ended with the divorce.
The addiction.
The betrayal.
The relapse.
The secret.
The failure.
The church hurt.
The season when you wandered.
The prayer you stopped praying.
The person you became ashamed to see in the mirror.
But if Jesus Christ is standing in the middle of your story, the worst page does not get the final sentence.
The cross did not look like victory on Friday.
The tomb did not look temporary on Saturday.
Then Sunday came.
That is Christianity.
That is our hope.
That is why we keep telling these stories.
That is why we keep opening this Book.
That is why we keep pointing wounded people toward Jesus.
Because scandal does not have to be the end of the story when grace enters the room.

And perhaps the intimacy you have been searching for all your life begins here—not with finally finding someone who knows only your beautiful parts, but with surrendering to the Savior who already knows the darkest parts and still calls you out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
So stop running.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Let Jesus rewrite what sin tried to finish.
And remember this when shame whispers your old name tonight:
The hands strong enough to carry a cross are not too weak to hold a repentant sinner who has finally come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABNER WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH SAUL’S CONCUBINE—And the Accusation Changed a Kingdom
paragraphs: ABNER WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH SAUL’S CONCUBINE—And the Accusation Changed a Kingdom
One accusation. One furious commander. One frightened king. And a conversation about a woman that became the crack through which an entire kingdom began to change hands.
There are sentences you can take back.
