And then there are sentences that change everything.
A marriage.
A friendship.
A ministry.
A family.
A kingdom.
Sometimes the sentence is shouted in anger. Sometimes whispered behind closed doors. Sometimes typed into a message and sent before wisdom has time to stop the thumb.
And sometimes it is only a question.
“Why did you do it?”
That was essentially the question Ish-bosheth put before Abner.
But this was no ordinary confrontation between two ordinary men.
One was the surviving son of Israel’s first king.
The other was the military commander whose strength was helping keep that son on the throne.
And between them stood a woman named Rizpah.
The accusation concerned sex.
But underneath it was power.
And before the conversation was finished, Abner—the man who had been strengthening Saul’s dynasty—would declare his intention to help transfer the kingdom to David.
One accusation.
One explosion.
One political rupture.
And behind all the human anger, ambition, weakness, revenge, and bloodshed, the sovereign purpose of God continued moving forward.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps you have lived long enough to discover that some of the moments that changed your life did not arrive looking holy.
They arrived looking like betrayal.
Humiliation.
Failure.
Conflict.
Exposure.
A relationship breaking apart.
Someone saying something about you that you could not forget.
A door slamming shut.
A season collapsing so violently that you wondered where God had gone.
But 2 Samuel 3 confronts us with a startling truth:
Human beings can make a terrible mess without overthrowing the purposes of God.
The chapter begins with civil war.
Saul is dead, but Israel is divided. David reigns in Hebron over Judah, while Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, rules over much of Israel with Abner’s support.
Scripture describes the direction of history with devastating simplicity:
“David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker.”
The transition was already happening.
Slowly.
Painfully.
God had chosen David long before David possessed the whole kingdom.
And that matters.
Because there are seasons when God’s promise seems painfully slower than your suffering.
David had been anointed, but he still had to wait.
He had survived Saul’s spear.
He had lived like a fugitive.
He had hidden in caves.
He had been hunted by the very king he once served.
And even after Saul died, David did not immediately wake up ruling a united Israel.
There was another kingdom.
Another king.
Another army.
Another struggle.
Promise did not eliminate process.
Maybe somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Promise does not eliminate process.
God can have a purpose for your life while your circumstances still look completely inconsistent with it.
Then comes the confrontation.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:7 reads:
“מַדּוּעַ בָּאתָה אֶל־פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִי”
Maddua ba'tah el-pilegesh avi?
In context:
“Why have you gone in unto my father’s concubine?”
The woman was Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.
The Hebrew word used for concubine is pilegesh—פִּילֶגֶשׁ.
To modern readers, that word can sound almost incidental.
It was not.
Rizpah belonged to the household of the deceased King Saul. This accusation therefore landed in the middle of a struggle over royal authority, succession, loyalty, and power.
But here we must be careful.
Very careful.
The Bible records Ish-bosheth’s accusation.
It does not explicitly tell us that the accusation was true.
And faithful Bible teaching must never turn an accusation into a conviction simply because the accusation appears in Scripture.
Abner becomes furious.
But his response does not give us the simple courtroom answer we might expect.
He does not plainly say, “Yes, I did.”
Nor does the recorded speech give us the simple sentence, “No, I did not.”
Instead, he erupts.
“Am I a dog’s head…?”

He reminds Ish-bosheth of his loyalty to Saul’s house. He points to everything he has done to preserve the dynasty. Then he lashes out because Ish-bosheth has charged him with wrongdoing concerning this woman.
And then the conversation suddenly becomes much bigger than Rizpah.
Abner swears that he will accomplish for David what the LORD had sworn concerning David—to transfer the kingdom away from Saul’s house and establish David’s throne over Israel and Judah.
Think about what just happened.
The man helping keep Ish-bosheth on the throne has essentially announced:
I am changing sides.
And Ish-bosheth says nothing.
Scripture tells us why.
He was afraid of Abner.
That detail exposes the weakness already underneath the kingdom.
Ish-bosheth wore the crown.
Abner possessed enormous practical power.
Sometimes a person can have the title and still not have the strength.
Sometimes the visible structure remains standing even after its foundations have begun collapsing.
And sometimes one confrontation merely reveals a fracture that has existed for a long time.
Abner then sends messengers to David.
“Whose is the land?”
He offers covenant and cooperation.
He tells David, in effect, that his hand will be with him to bring Israel over to David.
Soon Abner is speaking with the elders of Israel.
And here the story becomes even more revealing.
He tells them that they had wanted David as king before.
Then he urges them to act.
The accusation did not create God’s promise to David.
It did not make David God’s chosen king.
And Abner did not invent God’s purpose.
The confrontation became part of the chain of events through which an already-existing struggle moved toward a new stage.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because when something painful becomes part of a turning point in your life, you may be tempted to call the painful thing good simply because God eventually brought good through it.
Scripture gives us a better theology than that.
God does not need evil to become good before He can overrule it.
Betrayal is still betrayal.
Sin is still sin.
Falsehood is still falsehood.
Pride is still pride.
Revenge is still revenge.
Human motives can remain painfully mixed.
Yet God remains God.
Joseph understood something similar when he looked at the brothers who had sold him and declared that they had intended evil against him, but God intended it for good.
Not because their evil secretly became righteousness.
But because their evil was never powerful enough to defeat God's sovereign purpose.
And that brings this ancient royal scandal disturbingly close to home.
Because some of you are still living inside a sentence somebody spoke over you.
“You’ll never change.”
“You destroyed everything.”
“Nobody will believe you.”
“You are exactly like your father.”
“You are exactly like your mother.”
“God could never use somebody with your past.”
Maybe the accusation was false.
Maybe part of it was true.
Maybe that is what hurts most.
Maybe you actually did what they said.
Maybe there is no clever defense.
No missing context that makes you innocent.
No villain you can blame.
Maybe when you look back at the wreckage, you know your fingerprints are on it.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from reputation management.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the public image of guilty people.
He came to save sinners.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend your scandal never happened.
The Gospel announces that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
There is a cross for guilty people.
There is blood for stained people.
There is mercy for ashamed people.
There is repentance for wandering people.
There is restoration for broken people.
There is a Savior for sinners.
His name is Jesus.
At Calvary, Christ did not die for an imaginary, sanitized version of you.
He died for sinners.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
And yet Scripture continues with the language of grace—being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that pats rebellion on the head and tells it to continue.
Grace that forgives and transforms.
Grace that calls us out of darkness.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace that does not merely cover yesterday but begins changing tomorrow.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
And perhaps that is why this story should make us examine more than Abner.
It should make us examine ourselves.
What accusation would make you explode?
What subject can nobody mention without instantly touching the wound beneath your armor?
What criticism makes you disproportionately angry?
What loss are you still trying to avenge?
What relationship are you using to prove something?
What throne are you trying desperately to keep standing even though God has been exposing how fragile it really is?
And what if the thing you are protecting is not your calling but your pride?
Be honest.
Not performatively religious.
Not Sunday-morning honest.
Alone-with-God honest.
There are people who know how to lift their hands in worship while hiding entire rooms of their heart from the One they are worshiping.
We can sing about surrender and still negotiate with Jesus over the one sin we refuse to release.
We can quote Scripture publicly while privately feeding bitterness.
We can condemn somebody else’s scandal because looking at theirs keeps us from confronting ours.
But Jesus does not call us into hiding.
He calls us into light.
And light can hurt before it heals.
Abner’s story also gives us another warning.
Knowing God’s purpose is not the same as surrendering yourself to God.
Listen carefully to Abner’s own words in the chapter.
He knew that the LORD had sworn concerning David.
That is astonishing.
Abner could speak about what God intended for David while he had spent time strengthening the competing house of Saul.
A person can know biblical truth and still resist its implications.
You can know verses and still withhold your heart.
You can understand doctrine and still protect an idol.
You can know Jesus is Lord and still spend years fighting Him for control.
Knowledge about God's will is not a substitute for obedience to God.
Eventually Abner arrives in Hebron.
David prepares a feast.
Abner promises to gather Israel so that they can covenant with David.
And then Scripture says something haunting:
David sent Abner away,
“and he went in peace.”
In Hebrew:
“וַיֵּלֶךְ בְּשָׁלוֹם”
Vayelekh b'shalom.
He went in peace.
But he would not remain in peace for long.
Joab returned.
And Joab had history with Abner.
Abner had killed Joab’s brother Asahel during the earlier conflict.
Joab heard that David had received Abner and allowed him to leave.
He sent messengers after Abner and brought him back.
Then, near the gate of Hebron, Joab took Abner aside.
And killed him.
The man who had survived wars died near a city gate.
The commander who could move tribes and influence kings could not outrun the consequences of a blood-soaked world.
David publicly distances himself from the killing and mourns Abner.
And suddenly 2 Samuel 3 is no longer merely a story about an accusation involving a concubine.
It is a story crowded with wounded people.
Rizpah.
Ish-bosheth.
Abner.
David.
Joab.
Asahel.
Michal.
Paltiel.
Families.
Soldiers.
Widows.
A divided nation.
Everyone is carrying something.
Does that sound familiar?
Look closely at the people around you.
The smiling woman may be fighting grief she has never described.
The angry man may be bleeding from something that happened twenty years ago.
The person who irritates you may be carrying a battle you cannot see.
The believer sitting beside you may be one bad night away from giving up.
The person who shared this article may have shared it because they could not find the words to tell you, “This is where I am.”
We are surrounded by people carrying invisible wars.
That is why the Gospel matters so desperately.
Jesus did not enter a clean world.
He entered ours.
A world of corrupt rulers and fractured families.
Of betrayal and political maneuvering.
Of religious hypocrisy and sexual sin.
Of money and power.
Of accusations.
Of violence.
Of graves.
And into this world came the sinless Son of God.
Not another Abner.
Not another Joab.
Not another Saul.
Not merely another David.
The greater Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
David's kingdom pointed beyond itself.
Human kings die.
Human kingdoms fracture.
Human leaders fail.
Christ remains.
Jesus stood accused.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Betrayed by a friend.
Condemned.
Crucified.
And unlike every guilty human being who has ever begged for mercy, Jesus had no hidden sin requiring forgiveness.
The innocent One died for the guilty.
The King wore thorns.
The Lord of glory was nailed to wood.
And when sinful humanity appeared to have written the ending, God overturned the grave.
Jesus rose.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because every broken relationship automatically returns.
Not because repentance magically erases every earthly scar.
But because resurrection means sin and death do not possess ultimate authority over everyone who belongs to Christ.
Maybe your life has had a Saul chapter.
Maybe an Abner chapter.
Maybe a Joab chapter.
Maybe a chapter you wish could be torn completely out of the book.
Jesus already knows.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Let Him begin changing what you thought could never change.
Stay here for a moment.
Pray.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But because sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer needed to see tonight.
Sharing a Christian article does not earn salvation.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him in faith and obedience.
But supporting and sharing faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical way to help biblical truth travel farther than it would otherwise travel.
Somebody you have never met may encounter Christ-centered truth because you refused to keep it to yourself.
Not because you need another saved post collecting digital dust.
Do you think Jesus still wants me?”
And when that moment comes, remind them:
The Gospel was made for sinners who know they need a Savior.
They are not buying God's blessing.
They are not purchasing a higher place in the Kingdom.
But their practical support can help Gospel-centered content continue being created, distributed, and placed before people who desperately need biblical truth.
Not out of guilt.
Not to prove you love God.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous.
“If God knew everything about me, would He still want me?”
And the answer of the cross is astonishing.
He already knows.
That is why Christ came.
Abner's accusation became entangled with the changing course of a kingdom.
But there is a greater Kingdom.
A greater King.
And a greater scandal of grace.
At the cross, the innocent Christ took the place of guilty sinners.
At the empty tomb, death discovered that it could not hold the King.

And in the Gospel, people with histories, failures, wounds, secrets, regrets, and shattered reputations are summoned not to pretend the past never happened, but to bring their entire lives beneath the lordship and mercy of Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the question at the end of this story is no longer:
“Did you hear what they accused Abner of doing?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What is Jesus asking you to surrender?”
Your bitterness?
Your secret sin?
Your reputation?
Your need to be vindicated?
Your anger?
Your lust?
Your pride?
Your shame?
Your obsession with what somebody said about you?
Your desperate attempt to control how your story ends?
Bring it to Christ.
Because you were never strong enough to redeem yourself.
Neither was Abner.
Neither was David.
Neither is any of us.
We need a King who does more than rearrange earthly kingdoms.
We need a King who can forgive sinners.
Cleanse consciences.
Break chains.
Raise the dead.
And make all things new.
His name is Jesus.
Because one accusation can change the direction of an earthly kingdom.
But only one King can change the eternal destiny of a sinner who comes to Him in faith.
And maybe the line you need to remember long after you close this article is this:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life, but surrendered to Jesus, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DO NOT GIVE DOGS WHAT IS HOLY” — ONE OF JESUS’ STRANGEST AND MOST IGNORED COMMANDS
paragraphs: “DO NOT GIVE DOGS WHAT IS HOLY” — ONE OF JESUS’ STRANGEST AND MOST IGNORED COMMANDS

Jesus told you to love your enemies. He told you not to judge hypocritically. But then He said something so severe that many Christians quietly skip over it: not everyone should be given continued access to what is sacred.
There is a sentence from the mouth of Jesus that sounds almost shocking when you first hear it.

Especially if you have spent years believing that being a good Christian means endlessly explaining yourself, endlessly giving people another chance to mock what you treasure, endlessly reopening doors God may be teaching you to close.
Jesus said:
“Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine…”
Matthew 7:6.
And the sentence becomes even more startling when you see it in the Greek text in which Matthew has been preserved:
“Μὴ δῶτε τὸ ἅγιον τοῖς κυσίν, μηδὲ βάλητε τοὺς μαργαρίτας ὑμῶν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν χοίρων…”
Mē dōte to hagion tois kysin, mēde balēte tous margaritas hymōn emprosthen tōn choirōn…
“Do not give what is holy to the dogs, nor cast your pearls before the pigs…”
The key words are painfully vivid.
ἅγιον — hagion — holy, sacred, set apart.
κυσίν — kysin — dogs.
μαργαρίτας — margaritas — pearls.
χοίρων — choirōn — pigs.
καταπατήσουσιν — katapatēsousin — they will trample them down.
And then comes the frightening conclusion:
“…καὶ στραφέντες ῥήξωσιν ὑμᾶς.”
“…and having turned, they may tear you.”
Jesus was not describing a minor disagreement.

He was painting a picture of something precious being offered where it will not merely be rejected but desecrated—and of the giver eventually being wounded in the process. The underlying Greek of Matthew 7:6 contains precisely this progression: holy thing, dogs; pearls, pigs; trampling; turning; tearing.
And perhaps that is why this verse hurts.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to keep placing pearls into hands that only crush them.
You gave someone truth.
They laughed.
You shared what Jesus had done in your life.
They mocked it.
You told someone something sacred about your struggle, your repentance, your marriage, your past, your recovery, your prayers, your wounds…
and later discovered that the thing you whispered through tears became entertainment in another room.
You forgave.
They interpreted forgiveness as permission.
You showed mercy.
They interpreted mercy as weakness.
You opened the door again.
They brought the same destruction back through it.
You explained yourself for the twentieth time to someone who had already decided to misunderstand you.
And somewhere inside you was a frightened Christian conscience saying:
“If I stop, am I being unloving?”
“If I walk away, am I failing Jesus?”
“If I stop arguing, have I abandoned the Gospel?”
“If I create a boundary, does that mean I have not forgiven?”
Then Matthew 7:6 stands in front of us like a locked door we never noticed before.
But be very careful here.
Because this verse has also been terribly abused.
Jesus is not giving Christians permission to walk around deciding which human beings are worthless.
He is not authorizing spiritual arrogance.
He is not telling believers to look at unbelievers with disgust.
And He certainly is not contradicting His command to love our enemies.
Look at what comes immediately before Matthew 7:6.
“Judge not…”
Then Jesus speaks about someone noticing a speck in another person's eye while ignoring the log in his own.
His command is devastatingly personal:
First deal with your own eye.
First confront your own hypocrisy.
First let truth cut you.
First repent.
Then you will be able to see clearly enough to help your brother.
And immediately after warning against hypocritical judgment, Jesus says:
“Do not give dogs what is holy…”
That placement matters.
Matthew 7 does not teach the absence of discernment.
It teaches discernment without hypocrisy.
Before I decide what someone else is doing with holy things, Jesus makes me look into the mirror.
Before I start identifying pigs, I had better start identifying planks.
That changes everything.
Christian discernment begins with repentance.
The proud person says, “Look at those terrible people.”
The disciple says, “Lord, search me first.”
The proud person uses Matthew 7:6 as a weapon.
The disciple receives Matthew 7:1–5 as surgery before ever touching verse 6.
And suddenly one of Jesus’ strangest commands becomes one of His most necessary.
Because love does not require the abandonment of wisdom.
Forgiveness does not mean unlimited access.
Grace does not require you to call evil good.
Compassion does not mean participating in another person's contempt for what is sacred.
And proclaiming Christ does not mean arguing forever with someone who only wants another opportunity to mock Him.
There is a difference between someone who doubts and someone who delights in desecration.
There is a difference between a wounded skeptic and a hardened mocker.
There is a difference between the person saying, “I don't understand,” and the person saying, “Give me another holy thing so I can spit on it.”
Jesus knows the difference.
And He teaches His disciples that there are moments when faithfulness means speaking…
and moments when faithfulness means stopping.
That is difficult for sincere Christians because we desperately want people to be saved.
You have a son who has wandered.
A daughter who no longer believes.
A husband who laughs when you mention church.
A wife who has become cold toward God.
A friend who used to pray beside you and now ridicules everything he once believed.
So you keep talking.
Another sermon.
Another message.
Another video.
Another argument.
Another late-night paragraph.
Another desperate attempt to find exactly the right sentence that will finally break through.
Maybe if I explain it better.
Maybe if I send one more Scripture.
Maybe if I answer one more objection.
Maybe if I defend Christianity one more time.
And sometimes perseverance is exactly what love requires.
But sometimes…
the person is no longer listening.
You are no longer planting.
You are simply supplying more material to be trampled.
There comes a moment when continuing the argument may cease to be faithful witness and become a refusal to accept that only the Holy Spirit can change a heart.
You are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
That sentence may free somebody reading this.
You are not the Savior.
You cannot argue someone into regeneration.
You cannot emotionally manipulate someone into repentance.
You cannot carry somebody into the kingdom on your back.
You can witness.
You can pray.
You can love.
You can answer honestly.
You can live faithfully.
You can proclaim Christ.
You can keep the door of mercy open.
But salvation belongs to God.
And sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is stop fighting the argument and start fighting on your knees.
Pray.
Love them.
Live differently in front of them.
And trust Christ with the person you cannot change.
That does not mean abandoning people.
It means refusing to confuse relentless argument with relentless love.
There is another side of this command, however, and it cuts even deeper.
Maybe the person trampling the pearl…
has been you.
Maybe you have treated holy things casually.
Maybe the Gospel became background noise.
Maybe “Jesus died for me” became so familiar that it stopped astonishing you.
Maybe grace became an excuse instead of a miracle.
Maybe you knew the Scriptures well enough to quote them while secretly protecting the very sin those Scriptures condemned.
Maybe worship played in your headphones while pornography remained hidden in your browser history.
Maybe your Bible sat beside the bed while bitterness slept inside your heart.
Maybe everyone at church thought you were strong.
But God knew.
God saw the private messages.
The secret addiction.
The jealousy.
The resentment.
The affair nobody discovered.
The money nobody knew about.
The compromise you renamed “struggle” because “sin” sounded too uncomfortable.
The prayerlessness.
The coldness.
The double life.
And perhaps the terrifying question is no longer:
“Who are the dogs and pigs?”
Perhaps the question becomes:
“What have I done with the holy things God placed in my hands?”
That is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not the story of respectable people looking down on filthy people.
Christianity is the story of sinners being rescued by a holy Savior.
Every Christian comes to Jesus empty-handed.
No résumé.
No moral trophy.
No religious performance capable of purchasing forgiveness.
Just sin.
Need.
Repentance.
And mercy.
We were not rescued because we deserved the Pearl.
We were rescued because Christ is merciful.
Jesus walked toward people stained by scandal.
Tax collectors.
Sexually broken people.
Religious hypocrites willing to repent.
Outcasts.
Failures.
Cowards.
People with histories they could not erase.
And ultimately He walked toward a cross.
There the Holy One was mocked.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The hands that healed were pierced.
The mouth that spoke life was mocked.
The King wore thorns.
And the One who had no scandal of His own carried the shame of sinners.
This is why grace should never become cheap to us.
Forgiveness cost blood.
Not ours.
His.
And resurrection declared that scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Peter's denial did not write his final chapter.
The thief's crimes did not write his final chapter.
The shame of sinners who come to Christ does not write their final chapter.
Jesus does.
This is the heartbeat of everything we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because Jesus pretends sin never happened.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
Jesus rewrites lives precisely by confronting sin, forgiving repentant sinners, giving new hearts, and calling redeemed people into a transformed way of living.
Grace is not God saying your sin was insignificant.
Grace is God revealing how serious sin was—and then showing you the scars of the Savior who paid its price.
So perhaps Matthew 7:6 is not merely about protecting pearls from other people.
Perhaps it should make us ask whether we ourselves still recognize the value of the Pearl.
Do you still tremble at the Gospel?
Does the cross still humble you?
Does forgiveness still astonish you?
Does the name of Jesus still mean more than religious vocabulary?
Or have holy things become ordinary?
There are people begging God for the Bible you barely open.
There are people longing for Christian fellowship while we casually neglect it.
There are people discovering Jesus with tears in their eyes while some of us have heard His name for decades without being moved.
Familiarity can become dangerous when familiarity produces contempt.
Do not trample what heaven calls holy.
Do not trade eternal treasure for temporary appetite.
Do not exchange Christ for the thing that will entertain you tonight and accuse you tomorrow morning.
Do not sell a pearl for another handful of mud.
And if you have already done it…
come home.
That is the Gospel.
Not “clean yourself up enough for Jesus.”
Come home.
Repent.
Confess.
Turn.
Believe.
The same Jesus who warns us about trampling holy things is the Jesus who receives sinners who turn to Him.
Your worst chapter does not have authority over Christ's ability to redeem.
Your hidden sin is not hidden from Him.
Your shame does not frighten Him.
Your past does not surprise Him.
But grace is not permission to remain buried.
Come into the light.
Somebody reading this has been pretending for too long.
You know exactly what God has been confronting.
You have postponed obedience because tomorrow always sounded easier than today.
But tomorrow is not promised.
Jesus is calling now.
Not to perform.
Not to impress Christians.
Not to manufacture tears.
To repent.
To trust Him.
To surrender what you keep defending.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs only a few words:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending.
If you are exhausted but refusing to abandon Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your soul has been running on empty and you need believers to pray with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer needed tonight.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person who has been quietly falling apart.
The person whose Facebook posts look normal but whose life you know has been heavy.
The friend drifting from Christ.
The believer drowning in shame.
The skeptic who has sincere questions.
The person who needs to discover that Christianity is not about polishing sinners until they look religious, but about sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Send it privately if their pain deserves privacy.
You can love someone without giving endless access to what they repeatedly desecrate.
You can forgive without calling destruction healthy.
You can stop an argument without stopping prayer.
You can guard what is sacred without becoming self-righteous.
And you can discover that sometimes silence is not cowardice.
Sometimes silence says:

“I have told you about Jesus. I love you. I will pray for you. My door is open when you sincerely want truth. But I will no longer turn the name of Christ into entertainment for an argument you have no intention of hearing.”
That is not hatred.
That can be discernment.
And when the person finally comes back broken and asking honest questions?
Do not stand at the door reminding them how badly they behaved.
Remember how Christ received you.
Bring the Gospel.
Bring mercy.
Bring truth.
Bring Jesus.
Because the goal was never to protect pearls so fiercely that sinners could never encounter grace.
The goal is to recognize the Pearl's worth.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you treasure Christ more deeply, consider staying close to this work. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow as well.
But hear this clearly, because biblical integrity matters more than conversion numbers:
You cannot purchase God's blessing.
It cannot purchase forgiveness.
It cannot purchase answered prayer.
And Gospel Warrior should never replace your local church, your responsibility toward your family, or generosity God has called you to elsewhere.
Scripture teaches giving from the heart rather than giving produced by pressure: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
He will not.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, building, and placing Christ-centered resources in front of people who may encounter them during the darkest night of their lives.
And financial support is not the only way to help.
Sharing matters.
Maybe you never know who.
Maybe there is no comment.
No dramatic testimony.
No message thanking you.
But perhaps somebody sitting alone at 2:13 in the morning sees what you shared…
reads…
stops…
weeps…
and prays for the first time in years.
You may never know this side of eternity.
Share anyway.
The mission is bigger than merchandise.
Bigger than engagement.
Bigger than algorithms.
If any of those things ever become the treasure, we have missed the message of Matthew 7:6 ourselves.
Jesus is the treasure.
The Gospel is the message.
People are the mission field.
Grace is the miracle.
Transformation is the evidence.
And God's glory is the goal.
Follow so we can keep walking through difficult Scriptures together.
And never forget the strange warning that began all of this.
“Do not give dogs what is holy.”
Jesus never told us that because holy things are worthless.
He told us because they are precious.
So guard what Christ calls sacred.
But never let guarding the pearl make your heart hard toward the person who does not yet recognize its value.
You once needed mercy too.
You still do.
Perhaps the person who mocks Christ today will worship Him tomorrow.
Perhaps the person who trampled the pearl will one day discover what it was worth.
Perhaps the prodigal you finally stopped arguing with will someday come home.
So discern without hatred.
Set boundaries without vengeance.
Speak truth without pride.
Forgive without becoming foolish.
Walk away when wisdom requires it.
Return with mercy when repentance opens the door.
And through everything…
keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that somebody once threw a pearl into the mud.
The greatest tragedy would be standing so close to the Pearl of greatest price that you could touch Him…
and never realizing what you had been given.
Do not spend your life fighting over pearls and wake up one day to discover that you stopped treasuring Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER FOUND A HEBREW BABY—Then Paid His Own Mother to Nurse Him
paragraphs: PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER FOUND A HEBREW BABY—Then Paid His Own Mother to Nurse Him

She thought she was rescuing an abandoned Hebrew child. She had no idea the woman she was about to hire was his own mother—or that the baby crying in her arms would one day confront Pharaoh, split Israel’s history in two, and lead a nation out of slavery.
There are moments in Scripture so astonishing that if they appeared in a movie, people would complain that the writer made the story too convenient.
Exodus 2 contains one of them.
A mother is forced to surrender her baby because a king wants children like him dead.
She places him in a basket.
The basket reaches the household of the very man who ordered Hebrew sons destroyed.
Pharaoh’s own daughter finds the child.
She realizes he is Hebrew.
She chooses compassion.
And then, through a chain of events only God could have seen from beginning to end, Pharaoh’s daughter unknowingly hires the baby’s own mother to take him home, nurse him, care for him…
and pays her to do it.
Read that again.
The mother who thought she was losing her son walked away from the Nile carrying him in her arms.
And now Egypt was paying her.
But if you stop there, you will miss the most beautiful part of the story.
Because Exodus 2 is not really a story about getting back what you lost.
It is a story about the God who remains sovereign when everything looks lost.
And maybe that is exactly why you needed to read this today.
Before Moses ever stretched his hand over the Red Sea…
before the plagues…
before Sinai…
before the burning bush…
before Pharaoh heard the words that would shake Egypt—
“Let My people go”—
there was a terrified mother trying to keep a baby alive.
Exodus tells us that Pharaoh had commanded that every Hebrew son born should be thrown into the Nile.
Then a Levite woman conceived and gave birth to a son.
She looked at him.
She knew what the decree meant.
She knew what soldiers could do if they discovered him.
And she hid him for three months.
Imagine those months.
Every cry could expose him.
Every footstep outside could make her heart stop.
Every knock could be the knock.
Scripture does not romanticize her situation.
Eventually she could hide him no longer.
So she did something that must have torn through every instinct in her body.
She made a small vessel.
The Hebrew text calls it a:
“תֵּבַת גֹּמֶא” — tevat gome’.
An ark, or basket, made of papyrus.
That word matters.
The Hebrew word tevah—תֵּבָה—is rare in the Hebrew Bible. It is also the word used for Noah’s ark.
One family once entered an ark while death surrounded the earth.
Now one Hebrew baby entered a tiny ark while death threatened Hebrew sons.
The vessel was not impressive.
But the God watching over it was.
His mother coated it with bitumen and pitch. She placed her child inside. Then she set the little ark among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.
And walked away.
Can you imagine her hands letting go?
Maybe you know something about that feeling.
Maybe you have prayed until you had nothing left to say.
Maybe you have watched a child walk somewhere you could not follow.
Maybe a relationship slipped beyond your ability to repair it.
Maybe the doctor said something you never expected.
Maybe the money ran out.
Maybe somebody you loved walked away.
Maybe you obeyed God and somehow things became harder instead of easier.
There comes a point when faith does not look like confidently holding everything together.
Sometimes faith looks like trembling hands opening.
“I cannot carry this anymore, Lord.”
And the river keeps moving.
Moses’ sister remained at a distance, watching to see what would happen.
Then Scripture shifts scenes.
Pharaoh’s daughter came down to the Nile.
She saw the basket among the reeds.
She sent her servant to retrieve it.
Then came the moment.
The Hebrew text says:
“וַתִּפְתַּח וַתִּרְאֵהוּ אֶת־הַיֶּלֶד וְהִנֵּה־נַעַר בֹּכֶה”
Vattiftach vattir’ehu et-hayyeled, vehinneh-na‘ar bokheh.
She opened it.
She saw the child.
And behold…
the boy was crying.
Then Scripture gives us one of the quietest but most consequential phrases in the chapter:
“וַתַּחְמֹל עָלָיו”
Vattachmol ‘alav.
“She had compassion on him.”
Compassion.
Inside Pharaoh’s own household.
For a child belonging to the people Pharaoh had oppressed.
She immediately recognized the danger surrounding him:
“מִיַּלְדֵי הָעִבְרִים זֶה”
“This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
She knew.
This was not simply a mysterious baby floating down a river.
She understood that he belonged to the condemned people.
Yet she spared him.
Think about the irony.
Pharaoh had turned the Nile into an instrument of death for Hebrew sons.
God used that same river as the path by which one Hebrew son entered Pharaoh’s own household.
The decree said, “Throw the boys into the river.”
Moses went into the river.
And the river carried him toward the palace.
The place designed for his destruction became part of the path toward his preservation.
Do not misunderstand this.
Scripture does not promise that every tragedy will reverse immediately, that every loss will be restored in the form we want, or that faithful believers will always understand what God is doing.
They will not.
Sometimes we live for years without understanding.
Some questions may remain unanswered in this life.
But Exodus refuses to let us confuse our inability to see God with God’s absence.
Moses’ mother could not see the palace from where she released that basket.
But God could.
And perhaps there are things happening beyond the bend of your river that you cannot see either.
Then the story becomes almost unbelievable.
Moses’ sister approaches Pharaoh’s daughter.
Imagine the courage of that girl.
She asks whether she should find a Hebrew woman to nurse the child.
Pharaoh’s daughter agrees.
And whom does the girl bring?
The Hebrew text says:
“וַתִּקְרָא אֶת־אֵם הַיָּלֶד”
Vattiqra et-em hayyaled.
“She called the mother of the child.”
His mother.
Not simply another Hebrew woman.
Not a stranger.
His own mother.
Imagine her approaching Pharaoh’s daughter while trying to control every emotion in her face.
There is her baby.
The child she placed in the river.
Alive.
Breathing.
Crying.
Waiting to be held.
Then Pharaoh’s daughter says something almost breathtaking:
“הֵילִיכִי אֶת־הַיֶּלֶד הַזֶּה וְהֵינִקִהוּ לִי וַאֲנִי אֶתֵּן אֶת־שְׂכָרֵךְ”
Heilikhi et-hayyeled hazzeh veheniqihu li, va’ani etten et-sekharekh.
“Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.”
Her wages.
The empire that threatened her son’s life would now provide the payment while she nursed him.
She arrived at the river believing she had to surrender her baby.
She returned carrying him.
There are scenes you read.
And there are scenes you feel.
This one hurts because some of us know what it is like to place something precious into God’s hands without knowing whether it will ever come back.
But we must be careful not to turn Exodus 2 into a formula saying, “Give something to God and He will return it with money attached.”
That is not the Gospel.
God is not a vending machine.
Faith is not a financial transaction.
Sometimes obedience leads through suffering.
Sometimes believers surrender things they do not receive again in this life.
The point is infinitely greater:
God was writing a redemption story while the people inside that story could see only fragments.
The mother saw a basket.
God saw an exodus.
The sister saw reeds.
God saw the Red Sea.
Pharaoh’s daughter saw a crying infant.
God saw the man through whom He would confront the mightiest ruler in the land.
Pharaoh saw disposable slaves.
God saw His covenant people.
And Moses?
Moses could not see anything.
He was just crying.
Yet God was already moving around him.
That may be where this story reaches some of us most deeply.
You have mistaken your inability to understand God for evidence that God has stopped working.
You have looked at your current chapter and assumed it must be the ending.
It is not always the ending.
The baby in the basket did not know Egypt would tremble.
Joseph in the pit did not yet see the palace.
Israel facing the sea did not yet see a road through the water.
The disciples staring at a sealed tomb did not yet see Sunday morning.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because Moses is not Jesus, and we should never blur the distinction.
But the biblical storyline unmistakably moves toward a greater Deliverer.
Moses was born under the shadow of a murderous ruler.
Jesus entered a world where Herod would order the killing of boys in Bethlehem.
Moses would lead Israel out of bondage.
Jesus came to accomplish the deeper rescue humanity desperately needed—not merely deliverance from an earthly Pharaoh, but redemption from sin and death.
Moses mediated the covenant at Sinai.
Jesus declared concerning the cup:
“This cup is the new covenant in my blood.”
Moses could lead Israel out of Egypt.
Only Christ can bring sinners home to God.
And this is where Exodus stops being merely fascinating history and starts pressing against your heart.
Because perhaps the greatest slavery in your life cannot be seen from the outside.
You can smile while enslaved.
You can attend church while enslaved.
You can quote Scripture while hiding sin.
You can post worship songs while your private life is collapsing.
You can tell everyone, “God is good,” while secretly wondering whether God still wants anything to do with you.
Maybe your Pharaoh is not sitting on a throne.
Maybe it is shame.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Greed.
An affair nobody knows about.
Secret messages you keep deleting.
The approval of people.
A wound you have turned into an identity.
A religious mask you are terrified to remove.
You keep promising yourself:
“This is the last time.”
Then you return.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until eventually you wonder whether Jesus could possibly still want you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that Christ died.
But the cross also tells us something else.
Grace is greater than the scandal you thought disqualified you.
Jesus did not come looking for people who could rescue themselves.
He came because we could not.
At Calvary, Christ bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Your salvation is not purchased by your moral résumé.
It is not purchased by religious performance.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
That distinction matters.
Because Gospel Warrior never wants your support to replace your Savior.
Christ alone saves.
So if something hidden has been eating your soul alive, stop running.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Confess.
Come to Christ.
There is mercy for the sinner who turns to Him.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is a new life that does not require pretending the old life never happened.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe only you and God know.
Maybe people still introduce you by the worst chapter of your life.
Maybe you have been carrying a sentence Jesus never gave you.
But when Christ redeems a sinner, shame does not get final authorship.
Jesus does.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But do not keep hiding from God.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop pretending you are fine.
And somebody reading the comments may realize they are not fighting alone.
There is another lesson hidden inside this story.
People matter in the work of deliverance.
God was sovereign throughout Exodus 2, yet He worked through human hands.
A mother prepared the basket.
A sister watched.
A princess showed compassion.
Servants retrieved the child.
Later, God would call Moses himself.
Divine sovereignty never made human faithfulness meaningless.
And that matters for Gospel work today.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may legitimately receive material support for that work. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel.
But Scripture also protects giving from manipulation.
“Not reluctantly or under compulsion,” Paul says, “for God loves a cheerful giver.”
Your worship belongs to God.
Your obedience belongs to God.
Your giving should be prayerful, willing, joyful, and governed by Scripture.
Not to purchase a blessing.
Not to earn salvation.
Not because God needs your money.
But because Gospel ministry requires real people willing to help carry it forward.
You are still welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep seeking Jesus.
There is another way you can help that costs nothing.
Not because we need another statistic.
Someone may have just released something they desperately wanted to keep.
Someone may be questioning whether God sees them.
Someone may be smiling publicly while privately losing the battle against sin.
Someone may be one Scripture away from finally asking for help.
You do not know who.
Neither did Moses’ mother know what waited downstream.
Sometimes you simply place truth into the current…
and trust God with where it travels.
There will probably come a night when you need to read Exodus 2 differently.
A night when your prayers seem unanswered.
A night when you cannot see beyond the reeds.
A night when all you have left is the knowledge that God can see farther downstream than you can.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer growing cold.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to them.
Even invite the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Because ultimately this ministry is not about building an audience around Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing people beyond Gospel Warrior…
to Jesus.
Back at the Nile, a mother placed her child into a tiny ark because she had reached the boundary of what she could control.
She could waterproof the basket.
She could place it carefully.
She could send his sister to watch.
But she could not command the river.
She could not control Pharaoh.
She could not arrange the princess’s schedule.
She could not force compassion into another person’s heart.
There was a line where her ability ended.
And yet God’s sovereignty did not.
Perhaps that is the line you are standing at tonight.
You have done what you can.
You have prayed.
You have cried.
You have tried to repair it.
You have tried to control the outcome.
You have replayed every possibility until your mind is exhausted.
And now there is nothing left in your hands except surrender.
Then surrender it to Christ.
Not because surrender guarantees the ending you have imagined.
But because Jesus is trustworthy even when you cannot see the ending at all.
The Nile looked like the place Moses should have died.
Instead, God used it on the road toward deliverance.
The cross looked like the place hope had died.
Then Sunday came.
That is Christianity.
Not denial of suffering.
Not pretending graves do not hurt.
Not promising every earthly story ends exactly the way we want.
Christian hope is anchored in something infinitely stronger:
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose.
And because the tomb could not keep Him, the darkest chapter is never powerful enough to overthrow the promises of God.
So repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Come home if you have wandered.
Ask for prayer if you are tired.
Support Gospel work willingly if God has given you the means and conviction to do so.
Share truth.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
And when you reach the riverbank where your own strength finally ends…
remember the basket.
Remember the crying child.
Remember the mother who thought she was saying goodbye.
Remember the princess who unknowingly returned that child to his own mother.
Remember the wages.
Remember the palace.
Remember the deliverance still hidden years beyond the reeds.
And above all—
remember Christ.
Because sometimes what feels like the place where your story is disappearing beneath the water is only the place where you finally discover that God can see farther downstream than you ever could.
The mother released the basket because she could not see what was coming; God never lost sight of the child for a single moment.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD’S ANSWER TO SEXUAL TEMPTATION ISN’T PRETENDING DESIRE DOESN’T EXIST
paragraphs:
GOD’S ANSWER TO SEXUAL TEMPTATION ISN’T PRETENDING DESIRE DOESN’T EXIST
The desire you are ashamed to admit may be the very battlefield where Jesus teaches you that holiness is not becoming less human—it is learning whom your humanity belongs to.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that happens when you love Jesus...
and still feel temptation.
You prayed.
You worshiped.
You meant every word when you told God, “I want to be pure.”
Then something appeared on your screen.
Someone walked past you.
A memory resurfaced.
Your marriage became difficult.
Loneliness settled into the room.
Your body responded before your theology had time to speak.
And suddenly you were ashamed—not only because you were tempted, but because somewhere along the way you began believing that genuinely holy people simply stopped experiencing desire.
So you wondered...
What is wrong with me?
Maybe nothing is wrong with the fact that you noticed.
Maybe the real question is what you will do next.

Because Scripture never teaches that sanctification turns human beings into people incapable of experiencing temptation. Jesus Himself “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15, KJV).
Read those final words again.
Yet without sin.
Temptation and sin cannot therefore be identical.
That distinction could rescue someone from years of unnecessary shame.
Jesus does not command you to pretend your body has no impulses. He calls you to refuse to make those impulses your master.
And that difference matters.

Sexual desire itself is not some contaminant that entered creation when humanity fell. Before Genesis ever records the serpent, shame, hiding, adultery, pornography, exploitation, or lust, God created humanity male and female and established the one-flesh union of marriage.
Then Scripture says something our shame sometimes struggles to believe:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” — Genesis 2:25, KJV
Naked.
Unashamed.
Before sin distorted sexuality, sexuality was not dirty.
God created the body.
God created marriage.
God created intimacy.
God created human beings capable of desire.
Sin did not invent desire.
Sin disorders desire.

That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a campaign to destroy human longing. The Gospel reaches deeper. Christ begins restoring people whose loves, appetites, imaginations, bodies, relationships, and desires have been disordered by sin.
And this is where some believers have quietly suffered.
We sometimes tell people what not to do without teaching them what holiness actually is.
Don’t look.
Don’t touch.
Don’t fantasize.
Don’t sleep with them.
Don’t watch that.
All of those boundaries can matter enormously.
But Scripture gives us something richer than a Christianity built entirely around the word don’t.
Listen carefully to Paul:
“Τὰς δὲ νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας φεῦγε· δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην, πίστιν, ἀγάπην, εἰρήνην...”
“Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace...” — 2 Timothy 2:22, KJV
There are two movements in that sentence.
φεῦγε — pheuge.
Flee.
Run.
Get away.
Do not negotiate with what is pulling you toward sin.
But then comes another command:
δίωκε — diōke.
Pursue.
Chase after.
Paul does not merely say, “Run away from sinful desire.”
He essentially says:
Run from this... toward that.
Toward righteousness.
Toward faith.
Toward love.
Toward peace.
Toward believers who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.
Biblical purity is therefore not merely the absence of sexual sin.
It is the presence of a greater pursuit.
You were never meant to spend your entire Christian life staring backward at the temptation you are trying not to commit.
You were meant to run toward Christ.
And perhaps that changes the battle.
Because some people reading this have been fighting sexual temptation through sheer terror.
You wake up thinking about what you must not do.
You spend the afternoon trying not to think about it.
You lie down wondering whether tonight will be another failure.
You fall.
You repent.
You promise.
You fail.
You cry.
You delete everything.
You reinstall everything.
You pray harder.
You hide deeper.
Sunday arrives, and you sing beside people who have absolutely no idea what happened Saturday night.
Then shame whispers:
If these people knew you, they would never look at you the same way.
And perhaps the cruelest whisper comes afterward:
God must be tired of you too.
But listen to the Gospel.
The answer to your sin is not pretending sin is harmless.
And the answer is not pretending temptation does not exist.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
The One who knew exactly what He was purchasing when He went to the cross.
Not the polished version of you.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version with the browser history cleaned up.
You.
The sinner.
The struggler.
The person who has made promises and broken them.
The person who may genuinely love God while simultaneously discovering how deeply sin has trained the heart to seek comfort in places that cannot save.
Christ did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was so devastating that nothing less than the blood of the Son of God could reconcile sinners to God.
That means grace is not God saying sexual sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do for themselves.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
This is where scandal becomes grace.
You brought guilt.
Christ brings righteousness.
You brought rebellion.
Christ brings reconciliation.
You brought what you were ashamed to expose.
Christ brings wounds in His hands.
And because Jesus rewrites everything, repentance does not mean you pretend yesterday never happened.
It means yesterday no longer gets to be your lord.
Maybe you need to hear something painfully practical.
When temptation comes, stop being shocked that you are being tempted.
Recognize the battlefield.
Paul wrote:
“πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος...”
“No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to humanity.”
The Greek word πειρασμός — peirasmos can refer to temptation or testing depending upon context.
Paul's point in 1 Corinthians 10:13 is not that temptation is imaginary.
Quite the opposite.
It is real.
Human.
Recognizable.
And then comes the center of the promise:
πιστὸς... ὁ Θεός — pistos... ho Theos.
God is faithful.
Notice where Paul puts your hope.
Not:
You are strong enough.
Not:
You have enough willpower.
Not:
Real Christians never struggle.
God is faithful.
And Scripture says that with the temptation He provides ἔκβασιν — ekbasin, a way out, so that it may be endured.
Sometimes that “way out” looks remarkably ordinary.
Put the phone down.
Leave the room.
End the conversation.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Install accountability.
Tell a mature believer the truth.
Do not meet that person alone.
Go to sleep instead of scrolling at 1:30 in the morning.
Stop revisiting the profile.
Stop convincing yourself that because you have not physically committed adultery, repeatedly cultivating desire for someone who is not your spouse is spiritually harmless.
Jesus takes the inner life seriously.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He moves beyond the external prohibition of adultery and confronts the deliberate lustful gaze of the heart.
Christ is not teaching that merely recognizing another person's attractiveness is adultery.
He is confronting the heart that intentionally turns another human being into an object for covetous sexual desire.
That distinction matters because otherwise sensitive Christians can become terrified by every involuntary thought or physical response.
You cannot always control the first thing that enters your awareness.
You can decide whether you invite it to dinner.
There is a difference between noticing and nurturing.
Between temptation arriving and temptation being entertained.
Between desire appearing and desire being enthroned.
You may not control every knock at the door.
But by the grace of God, you do not have to hand every visitor the keys to the house.
This is why Paul becomes startlingly direct about sexual immorality:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The command is not:
Study how close you can stand to it.
Determine precisely how much you can watch without technically crossing the line.
See how emotionally intimate you can become with someone else's spouse.
Keep the secret conversation because “nothing has happened.”
Keep the app because you are “stronger now.”
Paul says:
Flee.
Joseph did not remain in Potiphar's house giving himself a motivational speech.
He ran.
Sometimes holiness looks profoundly undignified.
Sometimes victory is leaving.
Sometimes spiritual maturity is admitting, “I cannot keep putting myself here and pretending I am invincible.”
Sometimes the most courageous thing a Christian can do is run.
But remember Paul's other word.
Pursue.
Because if you only remove the pornography without confronting the loneliness underneath it, another counterfeit comfort may eventually replace it.
If you only stop the affair without rebuilding honesty, affection, accountability, and covenant faithfulness, the heart may remain hungry for the same poison in another bottle.

If you only suppress desire while never learning to see another person as someone bearing God's image rather than existing for your consumption, you have changed behavior without necessarily retraining love.
Christian purity is not learning to hate the body.
It is learning to honor God with it.
Paul says your body is not meaningless.
“For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body...” — 1 Corinthians 6:20, KJV
Bought.
With.
A.
Price.
Your body belongs to Jesus.
Your eyes belong to Jesus.
Your imagination belongs to Jesus.
Your sexuality belongs to Jesus.
Your singleness belongs to Jesus.
Your marriage belongs to Jesus.
Your loneliness belongs to Jesus.
Even the part of your life you are most embarrassed to discuss belongs beneath the lordship of Jesus.
And perhaps tonight you do not need another promise that begins, “God, I swear I will never struggle again.”
Perhaps you need a more truthful prayer.
“Jesus, this desire is here.
You already know it.
I will not hide it from You.
I will not call sin holy, but neither will I pretend temptation means You have abandoned me.
Show me the escape.
Give me strength to take it.
Teach me what I am actually seeking beneath this temptation.
Comfort?
Validation?
Intimacy?
Control?
Escape?
To feel wanted?
And teach my heart to seek in You what sin keeps promising but can never finally give.”
Because sexual temptation frequently promises more than sex.
It whispers:
You will finally feel wanted.
You won't feel lonely tonight.
Someone desires you.
You deserve this.
Just escape for a few minutes.
Then afterward comes the invoice.
Secrecy.
Distance.
Shame.
Escalation.
Broken trust.
A divided heart.
Sometimes shattered families.
Sin advertises the moment.
It hides the aftermath.
Jesus does something completely different.
He tells you the cost of discipleship openly—and then gives you Himself.
He does not merely say, “Stop wanting.”
He says, in effect:
There is something greater to want.
“Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.” — Matthew 5:8, KJV
They shall see God.
That is the destination.
Not merely a clean browser history.
Not merely another thirty-day streak.
Not merely avoiding scandal.
God.
Knowing Him.
Loving Him.
Becoming increasingly free to see people as people instead of products for your appetite.
Learning faithfulness when nobody applauds.
Becoming the same person behind a locked door that you appear to be beneath church lights.
And when you fall?
Do not redefine sin.
Do not excuse it.
Do not make peace with it.
But do not run from Christ because you sinned against Christ.
Run to Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Confession is the death of pretending.
Repentance says:
I did this.
Grace says:
Come into the light.
Repentance says:
This must change.
Grace says:
You will not change yourself apart from Christ.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And Christian community belongs in this story too.
Remember Paul's words:
“...with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”
You were not designed to fight every battle alone.
Secrecy gives temptation oxygen.
Honest Christian fellowship can drag hidden things into daylight.
Find mature, trustworthy believers who care more about your holiness than your image.

If you are married and sexual sin has damaged your covenant, honesty and restoration may require wisdom, patience, pastoral care, and sometimes qualified counseling. Consequences do not magically disappear because forgiveness is real.
Grace is not pretending wounds never happened.
Grace is Christ meeting sinners in the wreckage and teaching them to walk in truth.
And maybe this article found you while you are standing inside that wreckage.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does know.
Maybe the relationship ended but your conscience still screams.
Maybe pornography has followed you since adolescence.
Maybe you are single and exhausted by being told simply to “wait,” as though loneliness does not ache.
Maybe you have remained sexually faithful outwardly while privately feeding fantasies you would be horrified for anyone to see.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you never would.
Then hear this carefully.
Your sexual history is not more powerful than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That sentence does not make sin small.
It makes Christ enormous.
Paul wrote to Corinth—a church surrounded by sexual disorder—and after naming serious sins, he said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus...” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Such were some of you.
There are few words more beautiful for a repentant sinner.
Were.
Not because they had never sinned.
Because Jesus changes the relationship between the redeemed sinner and the old identity.
The Gospel does not say:
Pretend the scandal never existed.
The Gospel says:
The scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So if you are fighting tonight, fight.
If you need to flee, flee.
If you need to confess, confess.
If you need accountability, seek it.
If you have sinned, repent.
If someone needs forgiveness from you, pursue what truthful restoration requires.
If you have fallen a hundred times, do not use grace as permission for number 101.
Use your need for grace as another reason to throw yourself upon Christ.
And if you are still standing, do not become proud.
The reason you stand is grace too.
Maybe someone reading this needs permission to finally stop hiding.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing even a small confession into the light becomes the first crack in a wall you have spent years building.
Then pray for someone else in those comments.
Remind somebody that repentance is possible.
Remind somebody that forgiveness is real.
Remind somebody that holiness is worth pursuing.
Because there is probably someone scrolling through Facebook tonight who thinks he is the only Christian fighting this.
There is probably a woman quietly convinced her hidden struggle makes her uniquely disgusting.
There is probably a husband drifting toward a decision that could wound his family.
There is probably a teenager learning sexuality from an algorithm before anyone has lovingly shown them God's design.
There is probably a believer one click away from returning to something Christ has been teaching them to leave behind.
Not as a badge announcing that you have conquered temptation.
Share it as a hand reaching backward toward somebody still trapped in the dark.
We do not buy grace. We receive salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Someone you know may be hiding a battle they have never had the courage to name.
Your share may become the doorway through which they discover they are not alone—and, far more importantly, that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Sexual temptation does not prove Christ has abandoned you.
It reminds you that you still need Him.
So stop pretending desire does not exist.
Bring it beneath His lordship.
Flee what corrupts it.
Pursue what makes you more like Christ.
Confess what you have hidden.
Receive the grace you cannot manufacture.
Walk with people who call upon Jesus from a pure heart.
And keep your eyes on the Savior who did not come merely to make scandalous people look respectable.
He came to make dead people alive.
The thing you thought would become the darkest final sentence of your story may become the very place where the scars of Christ teach you that grace still knows how to write.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Seven-Year-Old Boy Walked Out of Hiding and Was Crowned King. The Woman Who Wanted Him Dead Heard the Celebration.
paragraphs: A Seven-Year-Old Boy Walked Out of Hiding and Was Crowned King. The Woman Who Wanted Him Dead Heard the Celebration.

For six years, Athaliah believed she had erased David’s royal line. She was wrong. Behind the walls of the house of God, a child she thought should be dead was growing—and when seven-year-old Joash finally stepped into the light, an entire kingdom discovered that evil had not written the final chapter.
There are celebrations that sound different when you thought you had already won.
Imagine Athaliah hearing this one.
Trumpets.
Running feet.
People shouting.
A kingdom suddenly alive.

For six years she had occupied the throne of Judah. Six years earlier, after the death of her son Ahaziah, she had moved against the royal family. Scripture describes the horror without softening it: “she arose and destroyed all the seed royal” (2 Kings 11:1, KJV).
Or at least she thought she had.
Because somewhere beyond her sight, a little boy was breathing.
His name was Joash.
And that child represents one of Scripture’s most startling demonstrations that what human beings try to bury, God can preserve until the appointed moment.
But before we turn Joash into an inspirational slogan, we need to feel how dark this story actually was.
This was not a fairy tale about a lost prince.
This was blood.
Power.
Murder.
Fear.
Political calculation.
A family almost annihilated.
And a child hidden because powerful people wanted him dead.

The account appears principally in 2 Kings 11–12 and 2 Chronicles 22–24. After King Ahaziah died, his mother Athaliah seized power. Second Chronicles 22:10 says she “arose and destroyed all the seed royal of the house of Judah.”
Then Scripture gives us one of those glorious words upon which history seems to turn:
“But…”
“But Jehoshabeath, the daughter of the king, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king’s sons that were slain…” (2 Chronicles 22:11, KJV).
Athaliah was killing.
Jehoshabeath was rescuing.
Athaliah was reaching for a throne.
Someone else was reaching for a child.
History remembers armies, kings, revolutions, and public speeches. Heaven also remembers the person who quietly picks up the child everyone else has abandoned.
Jehoshabeath and her husband, Jehoiada the priest, hid Joash.

First Chronicles does not invite us to imagine that the danger was imaginary. Joash was hidden because Athaliah was killing the royal heirs. Second Kings 11:2 tells us that Jehosheba took him away secretly “from among the king’s sons which were slain,” placing Joash and his nurse in a bedchamber.
Then 2 Kings 11:3 gives us a sentence easy to read in seconds but almost impossible to comprehend emotionally:
“And he was with her hid in the house of the LORD six years. And Athaliah did reign over the land.”
Six years.
Think about that.
Six birthdays without a throne.
Six years while another person wore the crown.
Six years in which outward appearances could have made it seem that wickedness had won.
Joash was not sitting in a palace being prepared publicly for coronation.
He was hidden.
And perhaps that word touches something in you.
Hidden.
You have prayed, but nobody knows how much.
You have cried where nobody saw you.
You have watched other people move forward while your own life seemed suspended.
You have wondered whether God forgot the room where you were waiting.
Maybe you have even mistaken obscurity for abandonment.
But Scripture repeatedly refuses to equate hiddenness with uselessness.
Moses spent years away from Egypt before returning.
David was anointed before he occupied the throne.
Joseph knew the prison before the palace.
And here, Joash spent six years hidden before Judah heard the trumpet.
Sometimes the chapter nobody applauds is still part of the story God is sovereignly carrying forward.
Yet Joash’s preservation means something even larger than his personal survival.

God had made covenant promises concerning David’s dynasty. In 2 Samuel 7, the Lord promised David an enduring house and kingdom, a promise that ultimately finds its fulfillment not merely in another Judean monarch, but in Jesus Christ, the Son of David and everlasting King.
Athaliah therefore could murder descendants of David, but she could not make God unfaithful.
That distinction matters.
The hero of this story is not ultimately Joash.
It is not even Jehoshabeath.
It is not Jehoiada.
The deepest theological reality beneath the narrative is the faithfulness of God.
Human beings act.
Human beings choose.
Human beings sin.
Human beings courageously obey.
Yet above all their actions stands the God whose purposes are not overturned because a throne has been stolen.
The Hebrew language of the account makes the coronation especially vivid.
When Jehoiada finally brought Joash forward, 2 Kings 11:12 says:
וַיּוֹצִיא אֶת־בֶּן־הַמֶּלֶךְ
Vayyotzi et-ben-hammelekh.
“And he brought forth the king’s son.”
The king’s son.
For six years Athaliah had been publicly reigning.
But Scripture still knew who the boy was.
Hidden did not erase his identity.
Fear did not erase his identity.
Athaliah’s power did not erase his identity.
And when the appointed day arrived, Jehoiada brought him out.
The crown was placed upon him. The testimony was given to him. They anointed him.
Then the people clapped their hands and cried:
יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ
Yeḥi hammelekh.
“Let the king live!”
Joash was seven years old when he began to reign (2 Kings 11:21).
Seven.
The boy who had spent most of his life hidden was suddenly standing before a nation wearing a crown.
Now imagine hearing that celebration from Athaliah’s position.
Second Kings 11:13 says she heard “the noise of the guard and of the people.”
She went toward the house of the LORD.
Then she saw him.
The king.
Standing by the pillar according to custom.
Officials surrounding him.
Trumpeters beside him.
The people of the land rejoicing.
Trumpets sounding.
The child she apparently believed had disappeared with the other royal heirs was standing in public.
Alive.
Crowned.
Anointed.
And celebrated.
Athaliah tore her clothes.
Then she screamed:
קֶשֶׁר קָשֶׁר
Qesher! Qesher!
“Treason! Treason!”
There is bitter irony in that cry.
The woman who had seized power now cried treason when David’s surviving heir was crowned.
But evil has always had a remarkable ability to rename things.
Rebellion calls obedience extreme.
Bondage calls holiness restrictive.
Pride calls repentance weakness.
Darkness becomes offended when light refuses to remain hidden.
Athaliah’s reign ended. Joash’s reign began.
And if the story ended there, we could package it neatly:
The hidden boy became king.
The villain lost.
Everyone went home.
But the Bible is too honest for shallow endings.
And this is where Joash’s story becomes uncomfortable enough to reach into ours.
Second Kings 12:2 says Joash “did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him.”
Second Chronicles gives us an important parallel: “Joash did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest” (2 Chronicles 24:2).
Under Jehoiada’s influence, Joash helped restore the neglected house of the LORD. Money was collected. Workmen repaired the temple. Worship that had suffered under previous corruption was restored.
This is the part of Joash’s life we would like to freeze.
The rescued child became a king associated with restoration.
Beautiful.
But then Jehoiada died.
And something in Joash was exposed.

Second Chronicles 24 records that after Jehoiada’s death, leaders of Judah came and influenced the king. The people abandoned the house of the LORD and turned toward idols. God sent prophets to bring them back, but they would not listen.
Then Zechariah, Jehoiada’s own son, stood before the people under the Spirit of God and confronted their rebellion.
Joash responded horribly.
The king who had once needed someone courageous enough to preserve his life now ordered the death of the son of the man whose family had preserved him.
Zechariah was stoned.
By the king’s command.
This is why Joash cannot be preached faithfully as nothing more than “your comeback is coming.”
His story is more serious than that.
You can be rescued from danger and still need your heart rescued from sin.
You can experience remarkable providence and still drift.
You can stand near godly people without personally developing deep faithfulness to God.
You can repair a temple while neglecting the condition of your own heart.
You can have an extraordinary testimony about what God brought you through and still make disastrous choices afterward.
Joash’s life warns us not merely to ask, “Did I start well?”
We must ask, “Am I remaining faithful to God?”
And suddenly this ancient palace story becomes painfully personal.
Maybe your Athaliah is not a murderous queen.
Maybe it is the sin you keep protecting.
The bitterness you learned to justify.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair that began emotionally before it ever became physical.
The resentment toward someone you smile at in church.
The pride hidden beneath ministry language.
The money you worship while telling yourself you are simply ambitious.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The double life.
The unforgiveness.
The prayerlessness.
The Christianity you inherited from people around you without ever truly surrendering yourself to Christ.
Maybe you know how to look alive spiritually while something inside you has been hiding for years.
This story will not allow us merely to point at Athaliah.
It makes us examine the throne of our own hearts.
Who rules there?
That question is more important than whether your life looks successful.
Because Christianity is not primarily the story of God helping you become the king of your own life.
It is the announcement that the rightful King has come.
Jesus Christ.
Joash was a son in David’s royal line, but he was not the final Son of David.
He needed grace himself.
He sinned.
He failed.
He died.
Jesus is different.

The New Testament opens by identifying Jesus Christ as “the son of David” (Matthew 1:1). Gabriel announced concerning Him that God would give Him “the throne of his father David” and that His kingdom would have no end (Luke 1:32–33).
Joash wore a crown of royalty.
Jesus wore a crown of thorns.
Joash was hidden from someone seeking his death.
Jesus, as a child, was taken away when Herod sought to destroy Him.
Joash needed others to save his life.
Jesus came to give His life to save sinners.
Joash’s reign exposed the limitations of every merely human king.
Christ came as the sinless King we actually needed.
And at the cross, something happened infinitely greater than a palace revolution.
The One who had no sin bore sin.
The innocent One was condemned.
The King was mocked.
His hands were pierced.
His blood was poured out.
He died.
And for a moment, His enemies could have mistaken the silence of a tomb for victory.
But the grave was not the final chapter.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not positive thinking.
Not religious self-improvement.
Not “become the best version of yourself.”
Christ died for our sins and was raised.
The scandal is that sinners like us deserve judgment.
The grace is that Christ receives repentant sinners.
The scandal is Peter denying Him.
The grace is Jesus restoring Peter.
The scandal is a persecutor named Saul.
The grace is an apostle transformed by Christ.
The scandal is every hidden thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
The grace is that Jesus already knows—and still calls sinners to come into the light, repent, believe, and be made new.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But hear this carefully: grace does not mean pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
Biblical repentance is not saying, “Nobody is perfect,” and continuing unchanged.
Jesus calls us to Himself.
To confess.
To turn.
To believe.
To follow.
Perhaps that is why this story found you today.
Not because God is promising that everyone who hurt you will publicly lose while everyone watching applauds.
That is not the Gospel.
Maybe the throne that needs to fall is yours.
Maybe the thing that needs to be exposed is the secret you have defended.
Maybe you have spent years asking Jesus to improve your kingdom when He has been calling you to surrender to His.
You do not need another motivational sentence.
You need the King.
And His name is Jesus.
If something inside you is whispering, “I have gone too far,” remember what the Gospel announces.
Christ came for sinners.
Repentance is not running away from Jesus in shame.
It is turning toward the only One who can forgive you.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrates His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
