Sometimes it is church, where you lift your hands while quietly wondering whether God could still want the person you became when nobody was watching.
Be honest.
Maybe this story hit somewhere you were not expecting.
Because beneath Jacob, Leah, and Rachel is a larger biblical story about broken people desperately trying to secure through human effort what ultimately must be received from God.
And God does something astonishing with this family.
He does not call their dysfunction good.
He does not rename deception as righteousness.
He does not pretend jealousy is holy because the people involved eventually become important.
Instead, He works His redemptive purposes through people whose family history would embarrass most religious people.
And remember Leah?
The unwanted woman?
The wife who kept wondering whether her husband would finally love her?
Her fourth son was Judah.
And through the line of Judah, generations later, came David.
And ultimately, according to the flesh, came Jesus Christ.
Matthew opens the New Testament by tracing Jesus’ royal genealogy through Judah.
The woman who felt overlooked stands inside the family story leading toward the Messiah.
Let that sink in.
Human rejection did not have authority to erase God's purposes.
Jacob’s preference was not sovereign.
Leah's pain was real—but it was not the final author of her story.
God was.
And this is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a slogan.
Because Scripture does not give us a Messiah descended from a sterilized collection of people who never failed.
The biblical story contains deceivers, sexually broken people, outsiders, wounded families, moral failures, and sinners desperately dependent upon mercy.
Then Christ enters human history.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because sin matters so much that redemption required a cross.
Jesus did not come merely to make scandalous people feel better about themselves.
He came calling sinners to repentance.
He came to save.
He came to forgive.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to break sin’s claim over those who belong to Him.
At the cross, grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Grace is God dealing with sin at immeasurable cost.
The New Testament word often translated “grace” is χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Gift.
Favor.
And the Gospel announces something no human bargaining system can reproduce:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
Ephesians 2:8.
You cannot manipulate God into loving you.
You cannot seduce Him into choosing you.
You cannot impress Him into forgiving you.
You cannot purchase cleansing by religious performance.
And you cannot rewrite your past by pretending it never happened.
You come to Christ.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender the truth about yourself to the One who already knows it.
And the Gospel says that forgiveness is possible because Jesus bore sin at the cross and rose again.
Maybe you have been Leah.
Unchosen.
Compared.
Tolerated instead of treasured.
Trying to earn affection from somebody who keeps making you feel like second place.
Maybe you have been Rachel.
Loved in one area, devastated in another, staring at somebody else’s blessing until jealousy begins poisoning the blessing already in your hands.
Maybe you have been Jacob.
Manipulating people and eventually discovering how devastating manipulation feels.
Maybe you have been Laban.
Using other human beings as pieces in your strategy.
Maybe, painfully, you can recognize pieces of all of them in yourself.
That is precisely why we need Jesus.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people should try slightly harder.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners need a Savior.
Paul writes:
Romans 5:8.
While we were sinners.
Not after we repaired the family.
Not after we cleaned the browser history.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after everybody forgave us.
Not after we learned Christian vocabulary.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not excuse continuing deliberately in sin.
Grace does not give us permission to cherish the chains Christ came to break.
Grace calls us out.
Repentance means turning.
Faith means entrusting yourself to Christ.
And transformation means that Jesus does not merely become another decoration attached to your old life.
He becomes Lord.
So maybe the question is no longer, “Which person in Jacob’s household was the biggest mess?”
Maybe the question is:
What battlefield have you been hiding?
What are you bargaining for?
Whose approval has become your god?
Whose rejection still determines your worth?
What jealousy have you baptized as ambition?
What secret compromise have you been calling “complicated” because calling it sin would require repentance?
What wound have you allowed to become permission to wound other people?
And how long will you keep trying to make somebody else give you what your soul ultimately needs from God?
Jesus Christ is not frightened by the room you have kept locked.
Open it.
Bring Him the truth.
Confess the sin.
Name the wound.
Stop performing.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Maybe your story contains a bedroom battlefield.
Maybe adultery.
Pornography.
Sexual sin.
Abandonment.
Infertility.
Jealousy.
Divorce.
Rejection.
Family manipulation.
Or years spent desperately trying to be enough for someone who never knew how to love you well.
Your pain is not automatically your sin, and another person's wrongdoing against you is not yours to confess as though you caused it.
But whatever is yours—your bitterness, your deception, your lust, your pride, your unforgiveness, your rebellion—bring it honestly to Christ.
No more hiding behind everybody else’s failure.
And no more believing your failure is greater than the mercy available in Jesus.
The family in Genesis was messy.
Yet Judah came.
Centuries passed.
And from Judah's line came the Lion of the tribe of Judah.
Jesus.
The greater story was moving toward Christ even while the people inside one chapter could barely see beyond their rivalry.
Perhaps you cannot see what God can redeem from your life either.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored exactly as you want.
Biblical hope is deeper than pretending everything becomes comfortable.
It means your past does not possess greater authority than Christ.
Sin does not get the last word over the repentant sinner.
Shame does not get the last word.
Human rejection does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
Be honest.
Not as a badge proving you are spiritual.
If this ministry has fed you, challenged you, brought you back to Scripture, or helped you point someone toward Christ, you can support it here:
Share because someone else may be fighting quietly.
Tag because sometimes one name beneath one article becomes the doorway to a conversation somebody desperately needed.
Save because there may come a day when you need these words again.
Follow because discipleship is not one emotional moment—it is a lifetime of returning to Christ, His Word, His grace, His truth, His cross.
But above everything else...
Follow Jesus.
Because Leah could not make Jacob's love save her.
Rachel could not make motherhood save her.
Jacob could not outscheme the consequences of human brokenness.

And neither your relationship, your reputation, your achievements, your sexuality, your family, your money, your ministry, nor your carefully constructed image can carry the weight of being your savior.
Only Jesus can.
The story began with a man opening his eyes in the morning and discovering that everything was different from what he expected.
The Gospel reaches its climax at another morning—
a tomb opened,
death defeated,
and Jesus Christ risen.
And because He lives, the darkest room in your story does not have to become the final room.
The place where your shame says, “This is where your story ends,” may become the very place where grace teaches you to say, “Jesus is still writing.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WIFE OR CONCUBINE? Why Some Biblical Women Are Described Differently in Different Passages
paragraphs:
WIFE OR CONCUBINE? Why Some Biblical Women Are Described Differently in Different Passages
One woman can be called a “wife” in one passage and a “concubine” in another—and that does not mean the Bible contradicted itself. What if the apparent discrepancy is actually revealing something painful about the ancient world, something important about how Scripture tells the truth, and something breathtaking about the kind of people Jesus came to redeem?
You are reading your Bible when suddenly something feels wrong.
You stop.
You go back.
You read the verse again.
Wait...
Wasn’t she his wife?
Why does another passage call her his concubine?
And if you have ever noticed this, you are not asking a foolish question.
You are noticing something real.
Genesis 25:1 introduces Keturah using language commonly translated:
“Abraham took another wife, and her name was Keturah.”
The Hebrew noun behind “wife” is:
אִשָּׁה — ’iššâ
It can mean “woman” or “wife,” depending on context.
But then you reach 1 Chronicles 1:32, and suddenly Keturah is described differently:
“The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine...”
Now the Hebrew word is:
פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pîlegeš
“Concubine.”
Same Keturah.
Same Abraham.
Different description.
Contradiction?
No.
And understanding why opens a window into something much larger than vocabulary.
It opens a window into the difference between what Scripture records and what Scripture approves, between relationship and social status, between God’s design and humanity’s distortion of it.
And ultimately...
between scandal and grace.
Because the Bible does something religious propaganda usually refuses to do.
It tells the truth about its own people.
It does not airbrush Abraham.
It does not sanitize Jacob.
It does not hide David’s household.
It does not turn dysfunctional families into stained-glass saints.
Scripture can tell you that Abraham believed God—and then show you Abraham making disastrous choices.
It can call David a man after God’s heart and still devote entire chapters to the devastation caused by David’s sin.
It can preserve the names of women whom the ancient world might have preferred to leave unnamed.
That honesty matters.
And it begins all the way back at creation.
Before kings accumulated wives...
before servants were given to husbands...
before royal harems...
before concubines...
before inheritance disputes...
before human beings complicated marriage with power, politics, lust, fear, infertility, status, and survival...
there was Eden.
Genesis 2:24 gives the foundational picture:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
One man.
His wife.
One-flesh covenant union.
Jesus Himself reaches back to this creation account when questioned about marriage. He does not point His hearers toward David’s household or Solomon’s harem as the ideal.
He points backward.
To the beginning.
“Have you not read...?”
Then Christ cites Genesis and declares:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
That distinction is essential when reading the Old Testament.
The presence of something in Scripture is not automatically the endorsement of that thing by Scripture.
The Bible records murder.
It does not endorse murder.
The Bible records adultery.
It does not endorse adultery.
The Bible records deception, slavery, warfare, idolatry, polygamy, exploitation, betrayal, drunkenness, revenge, sexual violence, and grotesque abuses of power.
Its willingness to describe humanity truthfully should never be mistaken for divine approval of everything humanity does.
That brings us back to the mysterious word:
פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pîlegeš
Usually rendered “concubine.”
Its ultimate etymology is uncertain, so we should resist impressive-sounding theories that claim more certainty than the evidence permits.

But its biblical usage is clear enough to show that a pîlegeš occupied a recognized relationship with a man while generally possessing a different or secondary status from what English readers normally imagine when they hear “wife.”
That distinction explains something easily lost in translation.
“Concubine” did not necessarily mean what a modern reader might mean by “mistress.”
These women were not automatically secret adulterous partners hidden outside a household.
They could belong to an established household relationship, yet occupy a subordinate social position.
That is precisely why the Bible can sometimes use language that sounds confusing to modern ears.
A woman might be described according to her relationship in one context and according to her rank or status in another.
Keturah demonstrates this vividly.
Genesis calls her Abraham’s ’iššâ.
Chronicles calls her his pîlegeš.
Genesis 25:6 also speaks of Abraham’s “concubines” when explaining how Abraham distributed gifts while reserving the primary inheritance for Isaac.
The point is not that words suddenly ceased to mean anything.
The point is that ancient household categories do not fit perfectly into our modern English boxes.
And Keturah is not the only woman whose description demands careful reading.
Consider Hagar.
She enters Abraham’s story as Sarah’s Egyptian servant.
Genesis 16 identifies her with the Hebrew:
שִׁפְחָה — šip̄ḥâ
A female servant or maidservant.
Sarah, unable to conceive, gives Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis 16:3 then uses striking language: Sarah gives Hagar to Abram “as a wife.”
Again we encounter:
אִשָּׁה — ’iššâ
But Hagar does not thereby become socially identical to Sarah.
That becomes painfully obvious almost immediately.
Pregnancy changes the household.
Jealousy erupts.
Power is abused.
Hagar suffers.
She runs.
And then comes one of Scripture’s most beautiful reversals.
The woman who had become socially useful to Abraham’s household...
the woman caught in somebody else’s desperate attempt to manufacture God’s promise...
the woman mistreated badly enough to flee into the wilderness...
is found by God.
Not because the human arrangement was ideal.
Not because everything Abraham and Sarah had done was justified.
But because God sees people whom powerful people reduce to roles.
Hagar gives the LORD a name associated with the God who sees her.
Think about that.
People saw a servant.
People saw fertility.
People saw a solution.
People saw a problem.
God saw Hagar.
Maybe that is where this ancient question suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to be known mainly by your usefulness.
Employee.
Mother.
Father.
Provider.
Divorcee.
Widow.
Failure.
Addict.
Problem child.
Single mother.
Former inmate.
The difficult one.
The disappointing one.
The person everyone calls when they need something but somehow forget when you are bleeding.
Human beings are very good at reducing people to categories.
God keeps calling people by name.
Then there are Bilhah and Zilpah.
Their stories emerge from Jacob’s fractured household.
Rachel and Leah become trapped in a devastating competition for children and affection. Their female servants become part of that rivalry, bearing children to Jacob.
The result is not a glowing advertisement for polygamous domestic bliss.
Read the story slowly.
There is jealousy.
Competition.
Favoritism.
Bargaining.
Heartache.
Children born into rivalry.
A husband pulled through a household filled with emotional fractures.
And eventually those fractures spill into the next generation.
Joseph is favored.
His brothers resent him.
A coat becomes a symbol.
A pit appears.
A brother is sold.
A father grieves.
A family nearly destroys itself.
The Bible does not need to insert a footnote saying, “This household arrangement has consequences.”
The narrative shows you the consequences.
Then Scripture takes us somewhere even darker.
Judges 19.
A Levite has a pîlegeš.
A concubine.

But within the same narrative, familial terminology associated with marriage appears around their relationship: the woman’s father functions as the man’s father-in-law, and the text presents a recognized household bond.
Then everything collapses into horror.
The woman is subjected to brutal sexual violence.
She dies.
Her body is desecrated.
Israel descends toward civil war.
Judges 19 is not a chapter designed to make you comfortable.
It is supposed to make you recoil.
And its placement within Judges matters.
The book repeatedly drives toward the terrifying diagnosis:
“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
Judges is showing what human beings become when covenant faithfulness collapses.
So when we encounter the concubine in Judges 19, the question cannot merely be:
“What was her technical marital classification?”
There is a more haunting question.
What happens when human beings stop seeing another person as someone bearing the image of God?
She becomes negotiable.
Disposable.
A means of self-preservation.
A body rather than a person.
And suddenly an ancient story feels frighteningly contemporary.
Because our civilization may use different vocabulary, but human beings still objectify.
Still exploit.
Still consume.
Still discard.
Still hide abuse behind respectability.
Still know how to appear religious while somebody inside the house is being destroyed.
You can know Bible verses and still fail to love your wife.
You can post Christian content and still humiliate your husband.
You can raise your hands in worship and treat someone made in God’s image as disposable.
You can defend biblical marriage publicly while destroying your own marriage privately through pornography, cruelty, adultery, manipulation, neglect, pride, or unforgiveness.
That is where this stops being an ancient Hebrew word study.
Because Scripture was never given merely so we could win arguments about people who died three thousand years ago.
The Word eventually turns the light toward us.
Maybe your scandal does not involve concubines.
Maybe yours lives in browser history.
Maybe it lives inside deleted messages.
Maybe it has another person’s name attached to it.
Maybe nobody knows about the emotional affair.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is beautiful because they only see the photographs.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary well enough to conceal a heart that has wandered miles from Christ.
Maybe you have never physically committed adultery, but Jesus’ words about lust leave you nowhere comfortable to hide.
Maybe you are not the person who caused the wound.
Maybe you are Hagar in the wilderness.
Used.
Rejected.
Confused.
Wondering whether God saw what happened.
Maybe you are carrying wounds from a relationship where somebody invoked God while treating you in a way that did not resemble Him.
Hear this carefully:
The sins of biblical characters are not permission slips for ours.
“Abraham did it” is not a theology of marriage.
“David had multiple wives” is not Christ’s command.
“Solomon had concubines” does not make Solomon’s household God’s blueprint.
In fact, Solomon becomes one of Scripture’s clearest warnings.
First Kings tells us that his wives turned his heart toward other gods.
The king famous for wisdom became living proof that possessing biblical knowledge does not guarantee an undivided heart.
That should frighten every religious person just enough to become humble.
You can know truth and still wander.
You can teach truth and still wander.
You can build something impressive and still wander.
You can look spiritually successful while your heart quietly develops another altar.
And that is why Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that morally impressive people should try harder.
It is the announcement that sinners need a Savior.

The Bible's tangled marriages, broken households, abused women, compromised patriarchs, fallen kings, jealous siblings, desperate mothers, lustful men, wounded families, and catastrophic decisions all testify to one enormous truth:
Humanity cannot save itself.
We need Someone better than Abraham.
Someone purer than David.
Someone wiser than Solomon.
Someone who will not exploit the vulnerable.
Someone who will not abandon the wounded.
Someone whose covenant faithfulness will not collapse when ours does.
And then Jesus walks onto the pages of history.
Look at the women surrounding His story.
Women society whispered about.
Women carrying complicated histories.
Women considered ceremonially unclean.
Women whose reputations entered rooms before they did.
A Samaritan woman with a shattered relational history meets Him beside a well.
Jesus knows.
Everything.
And yet He speaks to her.
Not with sentimental approval of sin.
Not with contempt.
With truth.
With exposure.
With an invitation to living water.
That is Jesus.
He does not call darkness light.
He turns on the light so people can finally walk out of darkness.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
At the cross, Jesus Christ bears judgment for sinners.
The innocent One stands where the guilty should stand.
The faithful Bridegroom gives Himself for His people.
Paul later reaches for the language of marriage when describing Christ and the church:
“Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
There is the Husband humanity could never manufacture.
Faithful.
Sacrificial.
Holy.
Truthful.
Merciful.
He does not exploit His Bride.
He dies for her.
And this is why biblical marriage finally makes sense only when Christ stands at the center.
Marriage was never ultimately about male domination.
Never about collecting women.
Never about social prestige.
Never about using another human being to satisfy appetite.
Christian marriage points beyond itself toward covenant faithfulness—the mystery Paul connects to Christ and His church.
That does not erase the difficult Old Testament texts.
It helps us locate them within the whole biblical story.
Creation gives us the design.
Human sin fractures it.
Israel's history shows how deep the fracture goes.
The prophets expose unfaithfulness.
Jesus restores our eyes to God's intention.
The cross reveals covenant love at unimaginable cost.
And redemption moves toward the marriage supper of the Lamb.
From Genesis to Revelation, marriage imagery ultimately reaches beyond Abraham, Sarah, Hagar, Keturah, Jacob, Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah, David, Solomon, or any other flawed human household.
It reaches Christ.
Which means perhaps the most important question after studying “wife or concubine?” is not merely:
“What category did this particular ancient woman occupy?”
The question eventually becomes:
Where do I stand before the Bridegroom?
Because you can solve every Hebrew vocabulary question in this article and remain spiritually dead.
You can understand אִשָּׁה and פִּילֶגֶשׁ perfectly and still refuse Jesus.
You can defend marriage and never surrender your lust.
You can condemn somebody else's scandal while protecting your own.
The Gospel does not invite us merely to analyze broken people.
It calls broken people to repentance.
Including me.
Including you.
Jesus did not come because respectable people needed religious accessories.
He came because sinners needed resurrection.
So bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the marriage barely breathing behind closed doors.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the memories you cannot erase.
Bring Him the wounds somebody else caused.
Bring Him the religious hypocrisy.
Bring Him the part of your story you desperately hope nobody ever reads aloud.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Get help where the damage is deeper than you can repair alone.
And when you are the wounded rather than the offender, understand that forgiveness does not require pretending evil was acceptable or remaining in danger.
Bring the truth into the light.
Because Jesus Christ specializes in meeting people where scandal said their story should end.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted His church.
Christ transformed him.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated past.
Christ offered living water.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes.
Christ gave him paradise.
This is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves.
Dead people being made alive by Jesus Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe while reading this, something got uncomfortably close.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need prayer, ask.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.

And if Christ has already taken a chapter of your life that looked ruined and begun turning it into a testimony, tell somebody below what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed tonight.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.
Because some truths need to be reread when temptation, confusion, shame, or spiritual forgetfulness returns.
Not as religious decoration.
Let them discover what the Bible actually contains:
Broken human beings.
A holy God.
Real judgment.
Costly mercy.
And a Savior powerful enough to redeem what sin has devastated.
Grace cannot be bought.
But ministry can be supported.
If these messages keep meeting you in places nobody else sees, stay close.
But before you leave, remember the woman whose title changed depending on the passage.
“Wife.”
“Concubine.”
“Servant.”
Human history has always been full of labels.
Maybe yours is too.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Unfaithful.
Abused.
Addicted.
Ashamed.
Failure.
Too far gone.
But none of those words has the authority to write the final sentence of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
The cross gets the final word.
Grace gets the final word.
Christ gets the final word.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when Jesus takes the pen, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEXUAL SIN OFTEN BEGINS WITH ENTITLEMENT BEFORE IT BECOMES ACTION
paragraphs: SEXUAL SIN OFTEN BEGINS WITH ENTITLEMENT BEFORE IT BECOMES ACTION
The frightening moment is not always when someone crosses the line. Sometimes it happened much earlier—when the heart quietly decided, “I deserve this.”
Before the deleted messages.
Before the secret browser.
Before the affair.
Before the second account.
Before the fantasy became a habit.
Before someone else’s body became an object in your imagination.
Before the excuse, the hotel room, the hidden conversation, the compromise nobody knows about yet.
There can be another moment.
Quieter.
Almost invisible.
A thought so ordinary that nobody around you would recognize it as dangerous:
“I deserve this.”
I work hard.
My spouse does not understand me.
I have been lonely too long.
Nobody appreciates me.
My needs matter too.
I have resisted long enough.
I am stressed.
I am hurting.
I am only looking.
I am not actually touching anyone.
God knows how difficult my life has been.
And sometimes sexual sin does not begin with uncontrollable desire.
Sometimes it begins when desire becomes a demand.
That distinction matters.

Because Scripture does not teach that sexual desire itself is inherently evil. God created human beings male and female, created marriage, and created sexual intimacy to exist within His design. The problem is not that a human being can experience desire.
The danger comes when desire stops saying, “I want,” and begins saying, “Therefore, I am entitled to have.”
That is where something inside the heart can quietly dethrone God.
James describes temptation with almost terrifying precision:
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.”
The Greek word translated “desire” is ἐπιθυμία—epithymia.
The word can refer to desire, longing, or craving; context determines whether that desire is good or sinful. James is describing desire functioning as bait, drawing a person toward disobedience.
Notice the progression.
Desire.
Enticement.
Conception.
Sin.
Death.
James does not describe sin as something that suddenly materializes out of nowhere.
Something is happening inside before something happens outside.
And that should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because you can look faithful while negotiations with temptation are already happening privately in your heart.
You can worship on Sunday while feeding something on Tuesday that you would be terrified for anyone to discover.
You can know Bible verses and still be constructing excuses.
You can love your spouse and still begin resenting the boundaries protecting your marriage.
You can love Jesus and still find yourself staring at a temptation long enough to begin imagining why you should be allowed to have it.
David understood this road.
Second Samuel 11 begins almost casually.
David sees Bathsheba bathing.
But seeing is not the entire scandal.
The narrative keeps moving.
David asks about her.
He is told who she is.
“This is Bathsheba… the wife of Uriah the Hittite.”
There is the boundary.
She belongs to another marriage.
David has received the information that should stop him.
But instead of submitting desire to the boundary, the king uses his power to move past it.
He sends messengers.
He takes.
And that verb deserves our attention.
The Hebrew text uses וַיִּקָּחֶהָ—vayyiqqāḥehā—built from לָקַח, laqach, commonly meaning “to take.”
David saw.
David inquired.
David knew.
David sent.
David took.
Then came adultery.
Then pregnancy.
Then manipulation.
Then Uriah’s death.
Then concealment.
Then Nathan.
Then the sentence that shattered David’s illusion:
“You are the man.”
Second Samuel 12:7.

This story must be handled carefully. Bathsheba should not be turned into the convenient villain of David’s sin. The text concentrates enormous responsibility upon David, the king who possessed power and initiated the sequence. Whatever questions interpreters debate concerning Bathsheba’s experience, Scripture gives us no justification for shifting David’s guilt onto her.
David already had abundance.
Yet Nathan’s parable exposes the ugliness of taking what was not his to take.
That is one of entitlement’s most dangerous lies:
“What God has given me is not enough. I should be allowed to have this too.”
And perhaps this is where the story stops being ancient.
Because entitlement rarely introduces itself by saying:
“Hello. I am rebellion against God.”
It sounds much more reasonable.
“I deserve affection.”
“I deserve attention.”
“I deserve excitement.”
“I deserve to feel wanted again.”
“I deserve an escape.”
“I deserve somebody who understands me.”
“I deserve one private pleasure after everything I have endured.”
Some of those sentences begin with genuine wounds.
Loneliness is real.
Rejection hurts.
Marriages can become painfully distant.
Singleness can ache.
Betrayal can leave scars.
Stress can exhaust the soul.
Past trauma can complicate intimacy.
None of that should be mocked, minimized, or answered with shallow Christian slogans.
But pain does not turn what God calls sin into medicine.
A wound may explain why temptation feels powerful.
It cannot make disobedience holy.
And this is where the Gospel confronts us without abandoning us.
Jesus does not merely address hands.
He addresses hearts.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus takes the command against adultery deeper than outward behavior. He warns about looking in order to lust.
The Greek expression includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—pros to epithymēsai—expressing the purpose or direction of the look toward lustful desire.
Jesus is exposing something devastating.
You do not become sexually faithful merely because nobody caught you physically committing adultery.
God cares about what your heart is learning to do with another human being.
That person on the screen is not pixels created for your consumption.
That coworker is not an emotional replacement spouse.
That married person is not your secret possibility.
That stranger is not a body without a soul.
That man is somebody made in God’s image.
That woman is somebody made in God’s image.
And Christian sexual holiness is not simply about avoiding scandal.
It is about learning to see people the way Christ teaches us to see them.
With dignity.
With boundaries.
With love that refuses to consume.
This is why entitlement is so spiritually dangerous.
Entitlement can turn a person into a product.
It whispers:
“What can this body give me?”
“What can this conversation make me feel?”
“What fantasy can this person provide?”
“What can I take without anybody finding out?”
But Jesus teaches another posture entirely.
Not taking.
Giving.
Not exploiting.
Serving.
Not demanding.
Surrendering.
Not asking, “How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
But asking, “How completely can this part of my life belong to Jesus?”
Paul writes:
1 Corinthians 6:18.
The Greek is startlingly direct:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not interview it.
Not see how strong you are around it.
Not keep its number because you have “self-control.”
Not keep checking the profile.
Not preserve the conversation “just in case.”
Not return to the website to prove you can leave.
Flee.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is block the number.
Delete the account.
Move the computer.
Install accountability.
End the inappropriate friendship.
Tell your spouse the truth where doing so can be done wisely and safely.
Bring the secret into trustworthy pastoral or professional accountability.
Stop calling pornography “stress relief.”
Stop calling emotional infidelity “just friendship.”
Stop calling deliberate fantasy “harmless.”
Stop asking God to deliver you while carefully preserving access to the thing from which you are asking Him to deliver you.
But listen carefully, because this is where many Christian messages about sexual sin become cruel.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
If you have fallen sexually, you are not reading this article because Jesus has run out of mercy.

If your history contains pornography, adultery, fornication, secret fantasies, inappropriate relationships, sexual compromise, or years you desperately wish you could erase, Christianity does not announce that clean people may approach Jesus while dirty people must remain outside.
Christianity announces something far more shocking.
Christ came for sinners.
Paul writes to believers in Corinth after naming serious patterns of sin, including sexual immorality, and then says:
“And such were some of you.”
Then comes one of Scripture’s most beautiful reversals:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
1 Corinthians 6:11.
Were.
That word carries thunder.
Your sin can be part of your testimony without remaining the ruler of your identity.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
This does not mean grace makes sexual sin trivial.
Grace makes repentance possible.
The cross does not say sin does not matter.
The cross shows how profoundly sin matters—and how immeasurably God loves sinners.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable hiding chains.
He came to set captives free.
Repentance, therefore, is not merely feeling horrible about yourself.
The New Testament word μετάνοια—metanoia—speaks of repentance, a genuine turning of mind and life toward God.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, I have stopped defending this.”
“I have stopped renaming it.”
“I have stopped blaming everybody else.”
“I have stopped pretending my pain gives me permission.”
“I have stopped asking You to bless what You told me to surrender.”
“This is sin.”
“Have mercy on me.”
And He does.
First John 1:9 gives believers this promise: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because tears earn salvation.
Not because you punished yourself sufficiently.
Because Jesus Christ is enough.
The blood of Christ is enough.
The cross is enough.
The resurrection is enough.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
Nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your church does not know.
Your friends think you are strong.
People come to you for spiritual advice while you are quietly losing a war inside yourself.
You know exactly which app.
Which person.
Which folder.
Which search.
Which memory.
Which conversation.
Which fantasy.
Which hour of the night.
You have promised God, “Never again,” so many times that you are embarrassed to pray the sentence anymore.
So now you avoid Him.
Please understand what shame wants from you.
Shame wants isolation.
Sin grows comfortably in darkness.
The Gospel calls you into light.
Not public humiliation.
Not reckless disclosure to everybody.
Light.
Truth before God.
Repentance.
Wise accountability.
Necessary boundaries.
And when appropriate, trustworthy pastoral counseling or qualified professional help.
You may need to confess something.
You may need to end something.
You may need to install something.
You may need to surrender access to something.
You may need to stop protecting your reputation more fiercely than you protect your soul.
Because freedom sometimes begins with the terrifying sentence:
“I need help.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sexual history publicly.
But you can stop pretending.
And if Christ has already brought you through this kind of darkness, your testimony may become somebody else’s flashlight.
You can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
There may be somebody scrolling through those comments tonight who thought they were the only one still fighting.
Let them discover they are not alone.
And please do not read this article only for the person you wish would read it.
That is another hiding place.
“Wow. My husband needs this.”
“My wife needs this.”
“My boyfriend needs this.”
“My friend needs this.”
“My pastor needs this.”
Maybe.
But before sending it to anybody else, sit with Jesus and ask:
“Lord… is there anything here for me?”
Search me.
Expose what I have normalized.
Show me where desire became entitlement.
Show me where disappointment became permission.
Show me where I started believing that because I was hurting, I was entitled to take something You had not given me.
And then remember:
Jesus exposes wounds in order to heal.
He exposes chains in order to break them.
He exposes graves because He specializes in resurrection.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create spectators who consume another emotional Christian post and keep scrolling.
We want disciples.
People growing deeper in Scripture.
People learning to recognize lies.
People becoming dangerous to darkness because they know the truth of God and are actually living it.
You may need these words on a night when temptation sounds reasonable again.
Never use an article like this as a weapon.
Use it like a lamp.
Supporting a Christian ministry does not purchase God's favor, prove your salvation, or make God love you more. Jesus already paid what we never could.

But Scripture does teach generous, willing partnership in Gospel work. Paul praised believers who partnered with him in the Gospel, while the New Testament consistently treats Christian giving as willing rather than coerced. “God loves a cheerful giver” comes with the instruction that giving should not be “reluctantly or under compulsion” in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
One share can travel into a home we may never enter.
One share can reach a marriage silently approaching disaster.
One share can find a teenager learning to hide.
One share can reach a pastor ashamed to ask for help.
One share can find someone at 2:17 in the morning with a phone in one hand, temptation in front of them, and the Holy Spirit pressing upon their conscience.
You may never know what God does with something as simple as pressing “Share.”
Jesus is.
Discipleship is.
Truth is.
Helping people move from hiding toward healing is.
Because perhaps the deepest question is not simply:
“How do I stop committing sexual sin?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Who owns my desires?”
Jesus does not merely want the behavior everybody can see.
He wants the room nobody else enters.
The imagination.
The resentment.
The loneliness.
The craving.
The wounded ego.
The secret appetite.
The part of you that whispers, “I deserve this.”
Bring that sentence to the cross.
Because what Jesus offers is infinitely better than entitlement.
Grace.
You do not deserve forgiveness.
Neither do I.
That is why it is grace.
You do not seize it from somebody else.
You receive it from Christ.
And once you understand that you are living entirely by undeserved mercy, something begins changing inside you.
You stop asking:
“What am I entitled to take?”
And begin asking:
“What have I been given that I can surrender back to Jesus?”
Maybe tonight the scandal is still hidden.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe consequences have already arrived.
Maybe your marriage is wounded.
Maybe trust has been shattered.
Maybe you are reading these words after another failure.
Do not confuse consequences with the absence of grace.
Repentance may not erase every earthly consequence.
Forgiveness does not automatically rebuild trust overnight.
Restoration can require truth, time, boundaries, accountability, counseling, patience, and painful obedience.
But the Gospel means failure does not have to become your final identity.
Peter failed.
David fell terribly and faced terrible consequences.
Corinth contained people with histories Paul could describe only by saying:
“And such were some of you.”
That sentence is still alive.
Were.
Was.
Once.
Before Christ.
Before repentance.
Before grace began rebuilding what sin had devastated.
Maybe someday somebody will hear your testimony and struggle to believe you were once the person you are today.
Not because you became strong enough.
Because Jesus was merciful enough.
So when entitlement whispers tonight—
“You deserve this”—
remember another voice.
The voice of the One who deserved glory yet embraced a cross.
The One who had every right to judge sinners yet came to save them.
The One who knew everything you would ever hide and still stretched His hands upon Calvary.
The answer to sexual entitlement is not merely stronger willpower.
It is a greater King.
Jesus Christ.
And when Christ becomes more precious than the secret thing you thought you needed, surrender stops looking merely like deprivation.
It begins looking like freedom.
So bring Him the phone.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the entitlement.
Bring Him the scandal.
Especially the scandal.
Because the thing you are most afraid to place into the hands of Jesus may become the very place where you discover just how astonishing His grace really is.
The secret said, “Hide.”
Jesus said, “Come.”
And your next chapter does not have to be written by the thing that almost destroyed you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN JESUS PRAISED WITHOUT EVER NAMING HER
paragraphs: THE WOMAN JESUS PRAISED WITHOUT EVER NAMING HER
She walked into the story carrying a scandal. She walked out carrying words from Jesus that would follow the Gospel across the world.
There is something almost painful about the way Scripture introduces her.
No name.
No respectable family history.
No religious title.
No carefully polished testimony explaining how she arrived at this moment.
Matthew and Mark preserve her story, but neither tells us what her mother called her when she was a child.
Jesus knew her name.
History simply wasn't given it.
And somehow, that makes what happened even more powerful.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to believe nobody really sees you.
Perhaps people remember what happened to you but forget who you are.
Perhaps your mistakes have been repeated more often than your repentance.
Perhaps you have spent years quietly serving Jesus while louder Christians received the recognition.
Perhaps nobody applauded the nights you resisted temptation.
Nobody saw you close the door and cry.
Nobody knew how difficult it was for you to pray again after disappointment.
Nobody understood what it cost you just to keep believing.
Then you need to meet the unnamed woman Jesus refused to forget.
Her story appears shortly before the crucifixion.
Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, when a woman approached Him carrying an alabaster flask containing extraordinarily valuable perfume.
Matthew tells us:
“And when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, there came unto him a woman having an alabaster box of very precious ointment, and poured it on his head, as he sat at meat.”
— Matthew 26:6–7, KJV
Mark gives us another striking detail.
The perfume was nardou pistikēs polytelous — νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτελοῦς — costly pure nard.
Then she did something irreversible.
Mark says she broke the alabaster container.
She didn't merely loosen the lid.
She broke it.
And she poured the perfume over Jesus.
Immediately, the fragrance filled a room that was about to become a courtroom.
Because devotion is not always admired by people who witness it.
Sometimes it is interrogated.
Some of those present became indignant.
“What a waste.”
That is essentially their accusation.
Mark records:
“Why was this waste of the ointment made?”
— Mark 14:4, KJV
Imagine hearing those words while your offering is still running down the head of Jesus.
Waste.
Perhaps that word has been spoken over something precious in your life too.
You wasted your youth.
You wasted that opportunity.
You wasted those years.
You wasted your money.
You wasted your love.
You wasted your life.
Or perhaps people have looked at what you surrendered to Christ and considered that waste too.
Why take your faith so seriously?
Why forgive them?
Why remain sexually pure?
Why give?
Why serve?
Why pray when nobody is watching?
Why refuse the compromise everybody else accepts?
Why pour so much of yourself into Jesus?
And somewhere beneath those questions is the ancient accusation:
Why this waste?
But Jesus heard them.
And then He defended her.
“Let her alone.”
Those words matter.
The woman does not appear to defend herself.
Jesus does it for her.
Then He says something astonishing:
“She hath wrought a good work on me.”
— Mark 14:6, KJV
The Greek is beautiful:
καλὸν ἔργον ἠργάσατο ἐν ἐμοί
kalon ergon ērgasato en emoi.
She has done a beautiful — noble, good — work toward Me.
The room called it waste.
Jesus called it beautiful.
Do not move past that too quickly.
Because sometimes the difference between shame and freedom is discovering that Jesus does not describe you the way the crowd does.
People may reduce you to your worst chapter.
Jesus sees what grace is writing next.
People may remember your failure.
Jesus sees your faith.
People may measure your offering by its market value.
Jesus sees the love behind the breaking.
People may ask what you have accomplished.
Jesus may be looking at what you surrendered.
And then Jesus says something even more remarkable.
“She hath done what she could.”
— Mark 14:8, KJV
Read that again.
She did what she could.
Not what Peter could.
Not what John could.
Not what somebody richer, stronger, more educated, more respected, more articulate, or more influential could.
What she could.
There are people destroying themselves because they believe Jesus is disappointed that they cannot give Him somebody else's life.
You look at another Christian's ministry and feel insignificant.
You see someone else's family and feel behind.
You see someone else's testimony and wonder why yours is still messy.
You see someone else's spiritual discipline and feel ashamed.
You see someone else's platform and wonder whether God notices your tiny corner of obedience.
But perhaps Jesus is not asking you to become them.
Perhaps He is asking whether you will place what is actually in your hands at His feet.
She did what she could.
And apparently, to Jesus, that was beautiful.
But there is something deeper happening in Bethany.
Jesus says:
“She is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying.”
— Mark 14:8, KJV
The cross is approaching.
The disciples have heard Jesus speak about His death, yet again and again they struggle to comprehend what He means.
And here stands this unnamed woman pouring expensive perfume over the One who is going to die.
Whether she understood every theological implication of her act, Jesus Himself interpreted it in relation to His burial.
The fragrance was pointing toward a tomb.
That changes everything.
This is not merely a touching story about generosity.
It stands beneath the shadow of Calvary.
Jesus Christ came to give Himself for sinners.
The Son of God was moving toward betrayal, condemnation, crucifixion, death, burial, and resurrection.
The woman broke her alabaster vessel.
Soon Christ's body would be given.
She poured out something precious.
Soon His blood would be poured out.
She gave extravagantly.
Soon He would give infinitely more.
Her perfume was expensive.
His sacrifice was beyond price.
And suddenly her offering doesn't look extravagant anymore.
It looks like a response.
Because that is Christianity.
We do not sacrifice in order to convince God to love us.
We surrender because in Christ we discover how profoundly He already has.
“We love him, because he first loved us.”
— 1 John 4:19, KJV
The Gospel does not begin with your gift to Jesus.
It begins with Jesus giving Himself for you.
That is why the center of this story cannot ultimately be the woman.
The center must remain Christ.
She is unforgettable because of the One upon whom she poured the perfume.
And then Jesus gives her something she never asked for.
A memorial.
“Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her.”
— Mark 14:9, KJV
The Greek word translated “memorial” is μνημόσυνον — mnēmosynon.
A remembrance.
A memorial.
Something by which a person or deed is remembered.
Do you see the holy irony?
Scripture doesn't give us her name here.
Yet Jesus made sure her act would not disappear.
The world may not know what to call her.
But the Gospel remembers what she did.
And approximately two thousand years later, here you are.
Reading about her.
Jesus' words came true.
Kings disappeared.
Empires collapsed.
Generations died.
Languages changed.
Cities became ruins.
Yet a woman in Bethany broke an alabaster vessel over Jesus...
and we are still talking about it.
That should make every hidden believer tremble with hope.
Because heaven's definition of significance is radically different from ours.
We live in an age obsessed with being known.
Followers.
Views.
Reach.
Recognition.
Verification.
Platforms.
Names.
Images.
Brands.
But one of the most famous acts of devotion in the Gospel narratives was performed by a woman Matthew and Mark never name.
Maybe obscurity isn't the tragedy we think it is.
Maybe being unknown by the world is bearable when you are fully known by Christ.
Maybe your greatest spiritual legacy will not be your name.
Maybe it will be the fragrance your obedience leaves behind.
But there is another uncomfortable detail in Mark's account.
Immediately after Jesus declares that this woman's act will be remembered wherever the Gospel is proclaimed, Mark tells us:
“And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went unto the chief priests, to betray him unto them.”
— Mark 14:10, KJV
Feel the contrast.
One person is pouring something precious upon Jesus.
Another is preparing to hand Jesus over.
One moves toward surrender.
The other toward betrayal.
One considers Jesus worth the cost.
The other begins negotiating.
And suddenly the story stops being safely historical.
Because every heart must answer the question hidden inside that room:
What is Jesus worth to me?
Not what do I say He is worth on Sunday.
Not what worship song makes me emotional.
Not what Bible verse appears in my biography.
What is He worth when following Him costs something?
When repentance means deleting something.
Ending something.
Confessing something.
Forgiving someone.
Walking away from an ungodly relationship.
Returning what isn't yours.
Breaking with secret sin.
Choosing integrity when dishonesty would be profitable.
Saying no when your flesh is screaming yes.
Trusting Christ when obedience makes you look foolish.
What happens when your alabaster jar finally has to break?
Because many of us want Jesus...
without breaking the jar.
We want salvation without surrender.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
Grace without transformation.
A Savior who rescues us from hell but never interferes with our idols.
But biblical grace does not merely pardon.
Grace transforms.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could become comfortable prisoners of the sins He came to save us from.
He calls sinners to Himself.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He makes new.
And perhaps this is where the unnamed woman finds you.
Maybe your alabaster jar is not perfume.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is pornography nobody knows about.
Maybe it is bitterness you have justified for ten years.
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is your obsession with approval.
Maybe it is resentment toward God because your prayers were not answered the way you wanted.
Maybe it is the secret identity you protect because you are terrified of what would happen if somebody knew the truth.
Maybe you have mastered Christian vocabulary while your heart has slowly become cold.
You still say “God bless.”
You still share verses.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
But somewhere inside, the fragrance disappeared.
And Jesus is calling you back.
Not to religious performance.
To Himself.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because the Gospel has never depended upon pretending your story is clean.
The Gospel announces that Christ came precisely because sinners are not.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23, KJV
And yet Scripture continues:
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
— Romans 3:24, KJV
That word “freely” comes from the Greek δωρεάν — dōrean — freely, as a gift.
Grace cannot be purchased with perfume.
It cannot be purchased with money.
It cannot be purchased with religious activity.
Jesus purchased redemption.
That distinction matters.
Supporting Gospel work can be an act of gratitude, stewardship, generosity, and partnership in proclaiming truth.
But Christ alone saves.
So if this story is exposing something in you, do not merely become emotional.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Confess.
Believe.
Bring Him the hidden thing.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the years you think you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are exhausted from pretending to be.
The cross is sufficient.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is alive.
And He is still rewriting stories.
Maybe that is why you needed the woman without a name.
Because perhaps you have been waiting for recognition when what your soul actually needed was surrender.
Perhaps you wanted everybody to understand your story.
Jesus wanted your heart.
Perhaps you wanted people to defend you.
Jesus wanted you to discover that His verdict matters more.
Perhaps you wanted your name remembered.
Jesus wanted His name written across your life.
That is the transformation.
From hiding to confession.
From bondage to freedom.
From performing to surrendering.
From being consumed with your reputation to becoming consumed with Christ.
And if you are reading this with tears gathering in your eyes because something hidden has finally been touched, don't rush away from that conviction.
Be honest.
And if grace has already begun rebuilding what sin, trauma, failure, or shame tried to destroy, testify:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Your comment does not save you.
Jesus does.
But sometimes confession breaks the isolation in which darkness grows, and sometimes another struggling believer needs to see that they are not the only person still fighting.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not twenty random names.
One.
The friend quietly drifting from Jesus.
The son who stopped going to church.
The daughter carrying shame.
The husband fighting secretly.
The wife who feels spiritually exhausted.
The believer who thinks God is finished with them.
The unbeliever who assumes Christianity is merely religion for people pretending to have perfect lives.
A share cannot save a soul.
But it can carry words about the Savior to a person who desperately needs to hear them.

And if you believe Gospel-centered truth deserves to travel farther than gossip, outrage, temptation, and empty entertainment, helping distribute Scripture-centered content is one practical way to use your influence for God's glory.
There may come a night when you are the person who needs to remember:
The room called it waste.
Jesus called it beautiful.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Christ, consider following the page and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well.

We want this community to remain a place where Scripture is opened, sin is confronted, wounded people are pointed toward Christ, believers are strengthened, and the Gospel remains more important than the platform carrying it.
It does not make you more saved.
It does not replace giving to your local church, loving your neighbor, feeding the hungry, caring for your family, or obeying Christ in the ordinary places nobody sees.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for the glory of God.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Make Jesus known.
Because somewhere beyond your screen may be another unnamed person.
Someone ashamed.
Someone exhausted.
Someone secretly addicted.
Someone questioning whether God could still want them.
Someone convinced their worst chapter has become their permanent identity.
And perhaps God can use something as ordinary as your share to put the truth of Christ in front of them.
The woman in Bethany probably never imagined people thousands of years later would still be talking about what happened in that room.
She simply brought what she had.
She broke it.
She poured it out.
And Jesus remembered.
So perhaps the question isn't whether the world will remember your name.
Perhaps the question is what your life will say about His.
When your reputation is gone...
when the applause stops...
when your possessions belong to somebody else...
when your social-media accounts disappear...
when nobody remembers how many followers you had...
when your body returns to dust...
what fragrance will remain?
May it be said that you loved Jesus.
That when grace found your scandal, you stopped running.
That when Christ exposed your sin, you repented instead of hiding.
That when the world called obedience foolish, you kept pouring.
That when following Jesus became costly, you discovered that He was worth more than the jar.
And that when people forgot your name...
Jesus knew it.
Here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
You do not need the world to remember your name when your surrendered life carries the fragrance of the Name above every name.
Jesus is still receiving sinners.
Jesus is still forgiving the repentant.
Jesus is still restoring broken people.
Jesus is still worthy of everything we pour at His feet.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories the world thought were already over.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY THE SUN OBEYED: WHY DID JOSHUA COMMAND THE SUN TO STAND STILL?
paragraphs:
THE DAY THE SUN OBEYED: WHY DID JOSHUA COMMAND THE SUN TO STAND STILL?
Joshua did not command the sun to stand still because he wanted to prove how powerful his faith was. He did it because the battle was not finished—and behind one of the Bible’s most astonishing miracles is a truth about covenant, desperate prayer, divine sovereignty, and the God who fights for His people.
Imagine being so deep into the battle that quitting would undo everything.
Your muscles are burning.
Your lungs are screaming.
You have marched through the night.
Your enemies are running.
Victory appears close enough to touch...
and then you look toward the horizon.
The light is disappearing.
That is where one of the strangest, boldest, most breathtaking moments in Scripture begins.
Joshua looks toward the heavens and says words no ordinary commander would dare speak:
“Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon.”
Then Scripture records the impossible.
“And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed...”
Joshua 10:12–13.
Read those words slowly.
A man standing on a battlefield speaks toward the heavens...
and daylight does not disappear as expected.
But if we reduce this passage to “Joshua had enough faith to stop the sun,” we can miss something far greater.
Because Joshua 10 is not ultimately a story about the power of Joshua.
It is a story about the power of Joshua’s God.
And once you see why Joshua made this extraordinary request, the passage becomes even more remarkable.
Joshua was not sitting comfortably somewhere trying to manufacture a miracle.
He was exhausted.

Israel had entered into a covenant with the Gibeonites in Joshua 9 under deeply embarrassing circumstances. The Gibeonites had deceived Israel. They disguised themselves, carried worn-out provisions, pretended to have traveled from a distant land, and persuaded Israel's leaders to make a treaty with them.
Israel's leaders had failed to seek the counsel of the LORD before making that covenant.
It was a mess.
A mistake.
A humiliating decision produced through deception and insufficient discernment.
Then the consequences arrived.
When Jerusalem's king learned that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, he gathered other Amorite kings and moved against Gibeon.
Suddenly the people who had deceived Joshua were begging Joshua to rescue them.
Think about the emotional weight of that.
Joshua could have been tempted to say:
“You lied to us. Deal with the consequences.”
Instead, Israel honored the oath it had sworn.
Joshua marched to help them.
And that means the road toward one of Scripture's most astonishing miracles passed straight through the consequences of an earlier failure.
That alone should speak to somebody reading this.
Because perhaps there is something in your past you wish you could rewrite.
A decision you should never have made.
A relationship you entered without seeking God.
Words you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
A season when you were deceived.
A moment when you should have prayed first but acted instead.
And sometimes we quietly assume that because we made a mess, God can never do anything meaningful through the aftermath.
Joshua 10 destroys that assumption.
God did not call Israel's mistake good.
But Israel's failure did not place history beyond God's sovereignty.
That is one of the great patterns of redemption running through Scripture.
God does not need your past to have been perfect in order to demonstrate His faithfulness in your future.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Joshua and his warriors marched through the night from Gilgal.
Picture it.
No comfortable transportation.
No air-conditioned vehicle.
No soft bed before battle.
An overnight military march followed by combat.
Then something extraordinary happened.
The LORD threw Israel's enemies into confusion. As they fled, Scripture says God hurled great hailstones upon them, and more died from the hail than from Israel's swords.
Joshua was fighting.
Israel was fighting.
But heaven was fighting too.
Then Joshua realized the battle was not finished.
Darkness was approaching.
Escaping armies could regroup.
The opportunity before Israel was disappearing with the daylight.
And Joshua prayed one of the boldest prayers recorded in the Old Testament.
The Hebrew makes the moment even more striking:
שֶׁמֶשׁ בְּגִבְעוֹן דּוֹם וְיָרֵחַ בְּעֵמֶק אַיָּלוֹן
Shemesh bə-Giv'on dōm, və-yareach bə-emeq Ayyalon.
Approximately:
“Sun, over Gibeon, be still; and moon, over the Valley of Aijalon.”
That tiny Hebrew word translated “stand still” deserves attention.
דּוֹם — dōm.
It comes from a Hebrew verb associated with becoming silent, still, ceasing, or stopping.
It is as though Joshua speaks into creation:
Be still.
Do not continue as expected.
And the following verse explains what happened in the narrative:
וַיִּדֹּם הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְיָרֵחַ עָמָד
Vayyiddōm ha-shemesh və-yareach amad.
The sun was still, and the moon stopped/stood.
Then the text intensifies the description.
The sun did not hurry to go down “about a whole day.”
Whatever modern questions we bring concerning the precise physical mechanics of this miracle, we should not make the text claim less than it claims.
Joshua 10 presents this as an extraordinary divine intervention.
The biblical author is not giving Israel an astronomy lecture.
He is describing what the people experienced from the battlefield: daylight was extraordinarily prolonged because the LORD intervened.

Scripture often describes the heavens phenomenologically—the way human beings experience and describe them. We still say “sunrise” and “sunset” today without intending to publish a scientific model of the solar system.
So Christians do not need to force Joshua into speaking the vocabulary of modern astrophysics.
Nor should we casually explain the miracle away merely because it is supernatural.
The central theological declaration comes immediately afterward:
“And there was no day like that before it or after it, that the LORD hearkened unto the voice of a man: for the LORD fought for Israel.”
Joshua 10:14.
There it is.
The heartbeat of the passage.
The LORD fought for Israel.
Joshua spoke.
But God acted.
Joshua prayed.
But God supplied what Joshua could never manufacture.
Joshua wielded a sword.
But Joshua did not control creation.
God did.
And this distinction matters enormously.
Joshua 10 is not permission to treat prayer as a magical force by which sufficiently confident people command God to rearrange reality according to their desires.
Biblical faith is not faith in faith.
Biblical faith is trust in God.
Before Joshua ever spoke to the sun, God had already spoken to Joshua.
The LORD had told him not to fear and had promised that the enemy had been given into his hand.
Joshua's astonishing prayer therefore arose in the context of God's revealed purpose.
Joshua was not trying to persuade a reluctant God to join Joshua's private ambition.
Joshua was acting inside what God had already declared.
That changes everything.
There is a dangerous version of Christianity that makes human beings the center.
“My faith did this.”
“My declaration caused this.”
“My words created this.”
“My spiritual power accomplished this.”
Joshua 10 will not allow that interpretation.
The conclusion of the inspired writer is not:
It is:
“The LORD fought for Israel.”
That sentence should humble every believer.
Because sometimes God permits us to participate in something so extraordinary that we are tempted to confuse participation with ownership.
You prayed.
But God answered.
You preached.
But God convicted.
You encouraged someone.
But God healed what you could not reach.
You shared the Gospel.
But the Holy Spirit opened the heart.
You remained faithful.
But grace held you together when your own strength should have collapsed.
The glory belongs to God.
Always.
And there is another detail here that should stop us.
Joshua was exhausted when he asked for more daylight.
He had marched all night.
He had fought.
He had pursued.
Yet when daylight began disappearing, he did not pray:
“Lord, I have done enough.”
He essentially asked for enough light to finish what God had placed before him.
That confronts our comfortable Christianity.
We often ask God to remove the battle.
Joshua asked God for enough daylight to finish it.
We ask for easier circumstances.
Joshua asked for the opportunity to remain faithful inside difficult circumstances.
We sometimes pray, “God, make this stop.”
Sometimes the prayer God forms in us is:
“Lord, give me what I need to obey You through this.”
Maybe that is why this story is hitting you differently today.
Because your own sun feels like it is setting.
You thought you would be farther along by now.
You thought the marriage would have healed by now.
You thought your child would have returned to God by now.
You thought temptation would not still be this exhausting.
You thought you would have conquered that private sin already.
You thought grief would hurt less.
You thought your prayers would have been answered.
You thought you had more time.
And now somewhere inside you is a frightened sentence:
“Lord... I'm running out of daylight.”
Hear this carefully.
Joshua 10 does not promise that God will repeat Joshua's miracle whenever we ask.
Scripture itself says there was no day like it before or afterward.
We should never turn a unique act of God into a formula God is obligated to reproduce for us.
But the God revealed in Joshua 10 has not stopped being sovereign.
The God who ruled over Joshua's battlefield is still God when you cannot control yours.
And this is where Joshua's story ultimately pushes the Christian reader toward something even greater.
Joshua's Hebrew name is יְהוֹשֻׁעַ — Yehoshua, associated with the truth that YHWH saves.
The name Jesus comes to us through the Greek Ἰησοῦς — Iēsous, reflecting the same Hebrew naming tradition.
Joshua led God's people into the land.
But Joshua could not conquer humanity's deepest enemies.
He could defeat armies.
He could not defeat sin.
He could pursue kings.
He could not remove the guilt inside the human heart.
He could lead Israel through Canaan.
He could not lead humanity out of condemnation.
We needed a greater Deliverer.
Jesus Christ.
And centuries after Joshua fought beneath prolonged daylight, another scene unfolded outside Jerusalem.
This time something strangely opposite happened.
At the crucifixion of Jesus, darkness came over the land.
The Son of God hung on a Roman cross.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Bleeding.
Bearing shame.
To everyone watching, it looked like darkness was winning.
But Calvary was not the defeat of Jesus.
It was the place where the spotless Lamb gave Himself for sinners.
The cross exposes something we spend our lives trying to hide:
Our deepest problem was never merely that life was difficult.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We did not merely need encouragement.
We needed reconciliation with God.
We did not merely need improved circumstances.
We needed forgiveness.
We did not merely need another chance to become better versions of ourselves.
We needed resurrection life.
And Jesus came for sinners.
Liars.
Adulterers.
The proud.
The addicted.
The religious hypocrite.
The angry.
The sexually broken.
The greedy.
The bitter.
The person hiding browser history.
The person smiling at church while privately falling apart.
The person who knows exactly which sin they hope nobody ever discovers.
Maybe even you.
This is where scandal meets grace.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we like to admit.
But the cross also declares that God's grace reaches farther than repentant sinners imagine.
Jesus took the judgment sinners deserve.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
That means your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your scandal does not have to be your identity.
Your failure does not have to write the ending.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your past does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by removing repentance from Christianity.
Jesus rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth and mercy, calling them to repent and believe, forgiving those who come to Him, and beginning the transforming work of making them new.
Perhaps the miracle you need most tonight is not the sun standing still.
Perhaps it is finally surrendering while there is still daylight.
Maybe you have spent years negotiating with Jesus.
Close enough to Christianity to feel religious.
Far enough from surrender to remain in control.
You know the songs.
You know the verses.
You know when to say “Amen.”
But somewhere behind the Christian language is a room in your heart whose door you keep locked.
Jesus wants that room too.
The secret habit.
The resentment.
The relationship you know dishonors Him.
The pride.
The hidden messages.
The unforgiveness.
The double life.
The wound you converted into bitterness.
The sin you renamed so you would not have to repent of it.
You can hide from people.
You cannot hide from Christ.
And strangely, that is good news.
Because the One who sees everything is also the One who went to the cross to save sinners.
Stop pretending.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
And if you already belong to Jesus but you are exhausted from the battle, remember Joshua.
Not because God owes you another day of sunlight.
But because the battle never depended solely upon your strength.
The LORD fought for Israel.
And Christian, the risen Christ has not abandoned His people.
Maybe you are tired.
Keep looking to Jesus.
Maybe you stumbled again.
Repent and return to Jesus.
Maybe yesterday was humiliating.
Return to Jesus.
Maybe people know your scandal.
Return to Jesus.
Maybe nobody knows it except God.
Return to Jesus.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings sinners home and teaches His people to walk differently.
Be honest before God.
Not because typing three words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover they are not the only Christian fighting tears, temptation, doubt, grief, loneliness, or spiritual exhaustion.
You do not have to publish every detail.
God knows the details.
And believers can stand with one another.
Then think of one person who is running out of daylight emotionally or spiritually.
The friend whose faith has become cold.
The brother hiding an addiction.
The daughter carrying shame.
The parent silently grieving.
The believer who thinks failure has disqualified them forever.
The person who does not know Jesus at all.
There may come a night when you need to read it again and remember:
The darkness does not rule history.
God does.
Not as a superstition.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But sharing biblical truth can be an act of witness.
If you genuinely want your online presence to glorify God, let some of what passes through your hands point beyond you and toward Christ.
The goal is not merely more content.
It is deeper roots.
More Scripture.
More truth.
More Christ.
More believers equipped to stand when life becomes dark.
Because somebody you know may be fighting a battle you cannot see.
Somebody is watching the horizon.
Somebody thinks the light is almost gone.
Somebody believes their scandal has already written the final sentence of their life.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them grace is real.
Tell them repentance is still possible.
Tell them the cross is enough.
Tell them the tomb is empty.
Tell them that for everyone who turns to Christ in repentant faith, darkness does not get to write the ending.
Joshua once looked toward a setting sun and asked God for more daylight to finish the battle.
But the greater hope of the Gospel is not that God will make every earthly day longer.
It is that Jesus Christ entered our darkness, bore our sin, conquered death, rose victorious, and promises His people something infinitely greater than another afternoon.
Life with Him.
So when the horizon grows dark...
when your strength is disappearing...
when your past starts shouting...
when shame tells you the story is over...
remember this:
The setting sun never frightened the God who already knew how your story would end—and at the cross, Jesus proved that even humanity's darkest hour can become the doorway to resurrection.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A WOMAN BLED NORMALLY—AND GOD GAVE ISRAEL LAWS ABOUT IT
paragraphs: A WOMAN BLED NORMALLY—AND GOD GAVE ISRAEL LAWS ABOUT IT

Leviticus 15 sounds uncomfortable until you understand what “unclean” actually meant. Then a bleeding woman reaches for Jesus—and suddenly the ancient law becomes part of one of the most breathtaking pictures of grace in the Gospel.
There are passages in the Bible we underline.
There are passages we quote when life falls apart.
And then there are passages we quietly turn past because we have absolutely no idea what to do with them.
Leviticus 15 is one of those passages.
Blood.
Bodily discharges.
Semen.
Menstruation.
Beds becoming unclean.
Chairs becoming unclean.
People washing themselves and waiting until evening.
It doesn't exactly sound like the verse you would print on a coffee mug.
But perhaps that is precisely why we need to read it.
Because buried inside this uncomfortable chapter is something many Christians have never been properly taught:
A woman's normal menstrual period had its own purity regulations under the covenant God gave ancient Israel.
And no...
that did not mean God considered women sinful because they menstruated.
It did not mean menstruation was a moral failure.
It did not mean a woman's body disgusted God.
And it certainly does not give Christians permission to treat women experiencing menstruation as spiritually inferior, shameful, contaminated, or somehow farther from God.
If you have ever read the word “unclean” in Leviticus and automatically heard “sinful,” what comes next may change the way you read an enormous portion of your Bible.
Listen to the Hebrew of Leviticus 15:19:
וְאִשָּׁה כִּי־תִהְיֶה זָבָה דָּם יִהְיֶה זֹבָהּ בִּבְשָׂרָהּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים תִּהְיֶה בְנִדָּתָהּ וְכָל־הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּהּ יִטְמָא עַד־הָעָרֶב
Ve'ishah ki-tihyeh zavah, dam yihyeh zovah bivsarah, shiv'at yamim tihyeh beniddatah...

In context, the verse describes a woman experiencing a flow of blood and says that she remains in her נִדָּה — niddah state for seven days; one who touches her becomes טָמֵא — tamei, ritually impure, until evening.
That last distinction matters enormously.
Tamei is not another Hebrew word for “evil woman.”
Ritual impurity and moral guilt are not interchangeable categories.
We know this even from Leviticus 15 itself because the chapter does not begin with menstruation.
It begins with male bodily discharges.
Then the chapter discusses semen.
Leviticus 15:16 says that when a man has an emission of semen, he is to wash and remains ritually impure until evening.
Then comes something even more important.
Sexual intercourse itself could result in temporary ritual impurity for both the man and the woman, requiring washing and lasting until evening.
Then the chapter addresses a woman's normal menstrual bleeding.
Then it addresses prolonged or irregular bleeding.
Male.
Female.
Normal bodily processes.
