Abnormal bodily conditions.
This is not a chapter written simply to humiliate women.
It belongs to an entire biblical system governing ritual purity and Israel's relationship to God's holy dwelling among them.
The chapter itself eventually tells us why these distinctions mattered:
“You shall put the Israelites on guard against their impurity... by defiling My Tabernacle which is among them.” — Leviticus 15:31
The sanctuary is central to the logic of the chapter.
God had chosen to dwell among His covenant people.
Holy space mattered.
Purity mattered.
Approaching God's dwelling mattered.
The ordinary Israelite lived in a world where holiness was not treated casually.
And that makes something else incredibly important:
Becoming ritually impure was not necessarily the same thing as committing a sin.
Sometimes impurity came through conditions and bodily processes that were simply part of embodied human existence.
A man could become ritually impure.
A woman could become ritually impure.
A person could become ritually impure without having committed some secret act of rebellion against God.
That distinction protects Leviticus 15 from a cruel interpretation Scripture itself does not require.
A menstruating woman was not being declared morally worthless.
She was not being told that being female was sinful.
She had entered a temporary ritual condition regulated within Israel's covenant life.
And then Leviticus makes another distinction that becomes extraordinarily important when we reach the New Testament.
Normal menstruation is addressed beginning in verse 19.
But Leviticus 15:25 describes something different: a woman whose bleeding continues for many days outside or beyond the expected time of menstruation.
Now hold that thought.
Because centuries later...
a woman begins walking through a crowd.
We don't know her name.
Mark simply tells us:
Καὶ γυνὴ οὖσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος δώδεκα ἔτη...
Kai gynē ousa en rhysei haimatos dōdeka etē...
“A woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years...”
Twelve.
Years.
Not seven days.
Not another monthly cycle.
Twelve years.
Mark 5 tells us that she had suffered greatly under many physicians. She had spent everything she possessed.
Instead of improving...
she became worse.
Try not to rush past that sentence.
Twelve years of waking up and realizing the bleeding had not stopped.
Twelve years of hoping this treatment might finally work.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Twelve years of watching money disappear.
Twelve years of carrying a condition nobody around her could simply pretend did not matter.
Leviticus 15:25–30 specifically addressed prolonged bleeding outside the normal menstrual period, including purification procedures after the discharge ceased.
So when the Gospel writers tell their original readers that this woman had experienced an ongoing flow of blood for twelve years, the language lands inside a world already shaped by Torah.
Suddenly this isn't merely a medical story.
There is a purity dimension hanging over the scene.
And she walks into a crowd anyway.
Maybe that is where this story stops being ancient history for you.
Because you know what it feels like to carry something for too long.
Maybe yours isn't blood.
Maybe it's shame.
Pornography nobody knows about.
A marriage quietly collapsing behind smiling photographs.
A child you cannot stop worrying about.
An addiction you keep promising God you will defeat.
A wound from childhood you learned to joke about because telling the truth hurts too much.
A prayer that has been unanswered so long that you have stopped telling people you're still praying it.
Church hurt.
Secret resentment.
Grief.
Fear.
A double life.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you're doing fine.
You learned when to smile.
You learned the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know what worship song to post.
You know how to look spiritually alive while something inside you is hemorrhaging.
And perhaps the loneliest part is this:
Nobody can see the bleeding.
But you can.
She had been bleeding for twelve years.
And then she heard about Jesus.
That sentence changed everything.
She did not have another physician.
She did not have another payment.
She did not have another treatment plan.
She had Jesus.
So she moved through the crowd believing that if she could only touch His garment, she would be made well.
Imagine her hand shaking.
One more step.
Another body in the way.
Another step.
Then...
she touches Him.
And the bleeding stops.
Immediately.
But Jesus does something unexpected.
He stops too.
“Who touched My garments?”
The disciples almost sound bewildered.
Everybody is touching You.
Look at the crowd.
People are pressing against You from every direction.
But Jesus knew this touch was different.
Eventually the woman comes forward.
Mark says she is afraid and trembling.
She falls before Him.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most human sentences in the entire scene:
She told Him the whole truth.
Not the edited truth.
Not the church-friendly truth.
Not the version designed to preserve her reputation.
The whole truth.
Somebody reading this needs those four words.
Tell Jesus the whole truth.
Tell Him where you have fallen.
Tell Him what you keep hiding.
Tell Him what hurts.
Tell Him what you are ashamed of.
Tell Him about the anger.
Tell Him about the lust.
Tell Him about the doubt.
Tell Him about the bitterness.
Tell Him about the thing you swore you would never do again...
and did again.
He already knows.
Confession does not give an uninformed God new information.
It brings us out of hiding before the God who already sees us.
And listen carefully to the first word Jesus speaks to this trembling woman.
He does not say:
“Disgusting.”
He does not say:
“Problem.”
He does not even address her impersonally as “woman.”
He says:
Θυγάτηρ — Thygatēr.
Daughter.
Let that word sit there.
Daughter.
The woman who had been defined throughout the story by her bleeding is addressed by Jesus relationally.
Daughter.
Then He says:
ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
hē pistis sou sesōken se.
“Your faith has made you well.”
The verb translated “made you well” is σῴζω — sōzō, whose range can include saving, rescuing, delivering, or making whole depending on context.
Mark is describing genuine physical healing here; we should not flatten the story into a metaphor.
Her body was actually healed.
But Mark's language is still breathtaking.
Jesus does not merely stop a hemorrhage.
He publicly receives the trembling woman.
He calls her Daughter.
He sends her away in peace.
ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην — hypage eis eirēnēn.
Go in peace.
This is where we must be careful not to make the story say something it doesn't.
Jesus was not correcting Moses as though God's previous revelation had been evil.
He was not announcing that God's holiness had been a mistake.
The purity laws belonged to Israel's covenantal sanctuary system.
Jesus comes within Israel's story and brings it toward fulfillment.
And in Him, something astonishing keeps happening.
Jesus touches people others would avoid.
Jesus approaches the diseased.
Jesus touches lepers.
Jesus walks toward death.
And instead of impurity conquering Him...
His holiness brings cleansing, restoration, life.
That is where Leviticus begins pointing beyond itself.
Not because Leviticus was bad.
Because Leviticus taught Israel something modern people desperately want to forget:
God is holy.
We want grace without holiness.
Jesus without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Resurrection without a cross.
A Savior who comforts us but never confronts us.
But biblical grace is breathtaking precisely because biblical holiness is real.
Sin really does separate.
Guilt really does matter.
God really is holy.
And unlike menstrual impurity, sin is a moral problem.
That distinction cannot be blurred.
Your body functioning as God designed human biology to function is not the same thing as rebelling against God.
Menstruation is not a confession-worthy sin.
But pride is.
Lust is.
Hatred is.
Idolatry is.
Deception is.
Sexual immorality is.
Self-righteousness is.
Unbelief is.
Our deepest problem is not that we occasionally become socially unacceptable.
Our deepest problem is that sinners cannot make themselves righteous before a holy God.
And no amount of pretending can wash that away.
That is why Jesus did not merely come to give inspirational speeches.
He came to save sinners.
The Son of God took flesh.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose.
The scandal of Christianity is not that respectable people can improve themselves if they follow Jesus' advice.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because Jesus Christ did for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
Grace does not say your sin doesn't matter.
Grace says your sin mattered enough for Christ to die...
and His love was great enough that He came anyway.
Maybe you have spent years trying to clean yourself up before approaching Jesus.
“I'll pray when I get myself together.”
“I'll return to church when I stop doing this.”
“I'll surrender after I fix my life.”
“I'll come back to God when I'm worthy.”
Listen.
You will die waiting to become worthy enough to need no Savior.
The bleeding woman did not heal herself and then touch Jesus.
She touched Jesus because she could not heal herself.
That does not mean faith is magic.

It does not mean every physical disease will disappear immediately when someone believes hard enough. Scripture does not authorize us to condemn suffering Christians as faithless simply because healing has not come.
The point is much greater.
Jesus is the One to whom helpless people may come.
And when it comes to the guilt of sin, the Gospel makes a promise far greater than temporary physical relief.
Christ receives repentant sinners.
Not because repentance purchases grace.
Not because tears impress God.
Not because you can compensate for yesterday.
But because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Perhaps you have been hiding for twelve years in your own way.
Maybe twenty.
Maybe forty.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
And the same Christ who made a trembling woman tell “the whole truth” already knows yours.
So stop negotiating.
Stop pretending.
Stop calling chains “personality.”
Stop renaming sin so you don't have to repent of it.
Stop trying to make darkness comfortable.
Bring the whole truth to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask Him for mercy.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is reconciliation in Christ.
There is no sin so fashionable that it stops being sin...
and there is no repentant sinner so scandalous that the blood of Christ suddenly becomes insufficient.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing truth.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking sinners whose stories looked irredeemable and making grace the final word.
Peter denied Him.
Grace wasn't finished.
Paul persecuted His people.
Grace wasn't finished.
The thief was dying beside Him.
Grace wasn't finished.
And if you belong to Christ...
grace is not finished with you either.
Maybe this article exposed something you have kept hidden.
Don't perform for the comments.
Someone reading silently at two in the morning may need to know that Jesus still restores broken people.
If someone came to mind while you were reading this, don't just think about sending it.
Send it.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to hear that Christ still receives repentant sinners.
There may come a night when you need to read it again.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money buys a blessing.
It doesn't.
It shouldn't.
But voluntary, generous support of Gospel ministry is thoroughly biblical. Christians are called to generosity, and those who benefit from Gospel ministry may freely help sustain Gospel work.

So if you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior keep going, reach farther, create more biblical resources, and place Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door?”—this is one practical way.
And sharing costs you nothing.
A share helps carry the message.
Both can become practical acts of generosity when they are done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory rather than human recognition.
We want Christ glorified, not people manipulated.
We want people reading Scripture.
Learning doctrine.
Repenting.
Healing.
Growing.
Praying.
Sharing Christ.
Becoming disciples who make disciples.
Not so we can build a crowd around a page.
So we can keep pointing a crowd toward Jesus.
Because one day likes disappear.
Algorithms change.
Pages disappear.
Possessions stay behind.
Our bodies return to dust.
But Christ remains.
And perhaps that is the lesson hiding inside an uncomfortable chapter about bodies, blood, purity, washing, separation, and the holy presence of God.
Human beings are fragile.
God is holy.
We cannot save ourselves.
And still...
He comes near.
The woman reached through the crowd thinking she needed only to touch His garment.
But Jesus stopped because He intended to give her something more than an anonymous miracle.
He called her Daughter.
Maybe you came to this article curious about menstruation in Leviticus.
Maybe you stayed because somewhere along the way you realized the person bleeding wasn't only her.
It was you.
Not physically.
Somewhere deeper.
Somewhere nobody sees.
And perhaps you have become very good at hiding the wound.
But Jesus already knows the whole truth.
You do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
So come out of hiding.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where shame has been screaming.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek help where help is needed.
And keep walking toward Jesus.
Because sometimes the person everyone else sees as a problem is only one encounter away from hearing Jesus speak a new name over the story.
She came trembling with twelve years of bleeding behind her—and walked away carrying one word no disease could take from her: Daughter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BECAUSE OF THE TEMPTATION TO SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DID PAUL POINT CHRISTIANS TOWARD MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: “BECAUSE OF THE TEMPTATION TO SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DID PAUL POINT CHRISTIANS TOWARD MARRIAGE?

We live in a generation that tells us to satisfy every desire. Paul wrote to a sexually broken city and said something radically different: your body belongs to Christ—and even marriage was never meant to become permission for lust.
There are Bible verses people quote because they comfort us.
Then there are Bible verses we quietly wish would stop looking at us.
First Corinthians 7:2 is one of them.
Because Paul does not speak about sexuality as though he were discussing some distant theological puzzle.
He brings the conversation painfully close.
Close to the married Christian whose eyes have begun wandering.
Close to the single believer exhausted from fighting desires nobody knows about.
Close to the husband sleeping beside his wife while secretly feeding a fantasy life on his phone.
Close to the woman carrying desires she is ashamed to admit.
Close to the believer who loves Jesus sincerely—and still wonders why following Him has not made temptation disappear.
Close to the person who fell last night, repented this morning, and is terrified that the cycle will happen again.
Paul knew Christians like that.
He wrote to Christians like that.
And underneath his words is a truth our generation desperately needs to recover:
Jesus did not save your soul while surrendering your sexuality to the world.
He wants all of you.
Your mind.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your bedroom.
Your secret history.
Your desires.
Even the parts of you nobody sees when the door closes and the screen lights up.
That is why these words matter.
Paul writes in Greek:
Dia de tas porneias hekastos tēn heautou gynaika echetō kai hekastē ton idion andra echetō.
A careful rendering is:
“But because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.”
Notice something immediately.
Paul uses the plural πορνείας — porneias.
The word belongs to the porneia family of words and refers broadly to sexual immorality—sexual activity outside the boundaries God has established.
Paul was not writing from an ivory tower.
He was writing to Corinth.
And he was writing to people whose conversion to Christ did not magically erase their sexual histories, bodily desires, cultural conditioning, temptations, or weaknesses.
Some of them had come from profoundly sexually disordered lives.

Paul had already reminded this same church that some among them had formerly been sexually immoral, adulterers, and involved in other sins—but then came one of the most beautiful reversals in the New Testament:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:11.
Read those words again if shame has been following you.
But ye are washed.
Not “you were never dirty.”
Washed.
Christianity does not require us to pretend the stain never existed.
Christianity announces that there is a Savior powerful enough to cleanse it.
That changes how we must read 1 Corinthians 7.
Paul is not writing to pristine people who have never struggled sexually.
He is writing to redeemed sinners learning what it means for Jesus Christ to become Lord even over their bodies.
And that makes his answer astonishing.
Because Paul does not say:
“Your desires are your identity.”
He does not say:
“If you feel it strongly enough, it must be right.”
He does not say:
“Suppress everything physical because the body is evil.”
And he certainly does not say:
“Just get married and then lust becomes holy.”
Instead, Paul places sexuality inside covenant faithfulness.
Marriage.
One husband.
One wife.
Mutual responsibility.
Mutual belonging.
Mutual faithfulness.
And immediately after verse 2, Paul becomes even more startlingly practical.
The husband is to give his wife the marital affection and intimacy due to her, and the wife likewise to her husband.
Then Paul describes an extraordinary mutuality: the husband does not treat his body as though his wife does not matter, and the wife does not treat hers as though her husband does not matter.
In a world where sexual relationships could easily become about male appetite, domination, exploitation, and entitlement, Paul addresses both husband and wife.
“Each man…”
“Each woman…”
“The husband…”
“The wife…”
Again and again, reciprocity.
Christian marital intimacy is not supposed to be one person using another person.
It is covenantal self-giving.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because someone could read “because of sexual immorality” and come away with the crude idea:
So Paul is basically saying, “If you're sexually tempted, get married so you can have sex.”
No.
That is far too shallow.
Marriage is not God's loophole for lust.
A wedding ring does not sanctify selfishness.
A marriage certificate does not turn another human being into an instrument for satisfying your appetites.
And your spouse is not God's approved substitute for pornography.
Marriage is covenant.
Marriage asks something lust hates to give:
faithfulness.
Lust says, “I want your body.”
Covenant says, “I give you myself.”
Lust consumes.
Love serves.
Lust asks, “What can I get?”
Christlike love asks, “What can I give?”
Lust can survive without knowing someone's soul.
Marriage calls two people into a shared life of fidelity, sacrifice, forgiveness, responsibility, tenderness, patience, and perseverance.
This is why Paul's words become even clearer when we keep reading.

In 1 Corinthians 7:5, he warns married couples not to deprive one another except temporarily by mutual agreement for prayer, after which they should come together again so that Satan does not exploit their lack of self-control.
Paul is realistic.
Temptation exists.
Bodies exist.
Desire exists.
Weakness exists.
Satan exploits weakness.
And marriage provides a God-ordained context in which sexual desire can be expressed faithfully rather than promiscuously.
But then Paul destroys another misunderstanding.
He does not command every Christian to marry.
In fact, immediately afterward he speaks positively about singleness.
Paul himself lived unmarried and wished others could share his gift, while recognizing that God gives different gifts to different people.
Then comes 1 Corinthians 7:9:
“εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται, γαμησάτωσαν.”
Ei de ouk enkrateuontai, gamēsatōsan.
“But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry.”
Then:
“κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστιν γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι.”
Kreitton gar estin gamēsai ē pyrousthai.
“For it is better to marry than to burn.”
The point is not that unmarried Christians are incomplete.
Jesus Himself destroys that idea.
The most complete human life ever lived was lived by an unmarried man.
Jesus Christ.
So marriage cannot be necessary for human completeness.
Christ is.
And this is where the passage becomes intensely personal.
Because maybe your deepest problem is not that you need a spouse.
Maybe you have been telling yourself:
“If I could just get married, this temptation would disappear.”
But marriage does not crucify lust.

Jesus does not promise that a wedding ceremony will suddenly erase years of pornography, fantasy, objectification, emotional dependency, secret messaging, masturbation, infidelity of heart, or patterns of using other people mentally for sexual gratification.
You can bring an undisciplined heart into a marriage.
You can bring pornography into a marriage.
You can bring fantasies into a marriage.
You can bring selfishness into a marriage.
You can even lie beside the person you promised yourself to while your imagination belongs to someone else.
Marriage can provide a holy context for sexual intimacy.
But marriage is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this desperately needed.
Because you have been waiting for circumstances to save you from something only Christ can transform.
“If I find someone…”
“If I get married…”
“If my spouse becomes more affectionate…”
“If my loneliness disappears…”
“If my hormones calm down…”
“If temptation stops…”
Then I will finally become holy.
But biblical holiness does not begin when temptation disappears.
Holiness is learning whom you belong to while temptation is still speaking.
Paul had already written:
“Ye are not your own.”
And then:
“Ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
The Gospel underneath Christian sexual ethics.
You were bought.
Not with silver.
Not with gold.
Not with religious performance.
Not because you finally conquered every sexual temptation.
You were purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ.
The hands pierced on Calvary purchased the hands you keep reaching toward temptation with.
The blood poured from His body purchased the body you have sometimes used against His will.
The eyes that looked upon sinners with compassion purchased the eyes you have sometimes allowed to wander.
And Jesus does not expose your sexual sin because He enjoys humiliating you.
He exposes darkness because He intends to bring His children into light.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God. Look what you did.”
The Gospel says:
“Run to Christ. Look what He did.”
Maybe you failed.
Maybe badly.
Maybe repeatedly.
Maybe there are browser histories nobody has seen.
Messages nobody knows about.
A relationship you know you need to end.
Pornography you promised God you would stop watching.
An affair of the heart that has never become physical—but you know what you have been nurturing.
Maybe your marriage looks respectable in public while becoming painfully cold in private.
Maybe your spouse feels rejected and you have stopped talking about it.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from being told either that your desires do not matter or that satisfying them is the only way to be authentic.
Scripture offers something deeper than either lie.
Your desires matter.
But they are not your master.
Your body matters.
But it is not your god.
Sex matters.
But it cannot save you.
Marriage matters.
But it cannot complete what only Christ can complete.
And temptation may be powerful.
But temptation is not lord.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Paul's answer to Corinth was not sexual shame.
It was sexual discipleship.
For some believers, that discipleship includes faithful marriage.
For others, faithful singleness.
For every believer, it includes belonging to Jesus.
That means the Christian question is no longer merely:
“What am I allowed to do?”
The deeper question becomes:
“How can I glorify Christ with the body He redeemed?”
That question follows you into dating.
Into engagement.
Into marriage.
Into singleness.
Into loneliness.
Into the hotel room.
Into the business trip.
Into the late-night scroll.
Into the private message.
Into the moment when nobody would ever know.
Except Him.
And perhaps that sounds frightening until you remember who “Him” is.
The One who spoke with the woman caught in adultery.
The One who welcomed sexual sinners others despised.
The One who knew everything about the Samaritan woman's tangled relational history and still offered her living water.
The One who went to a cross surrounded by sinners.
The One whose blood is sufficient for sexual sinners too.
Jesus does not minimize sin.
He paid for it.
That is infinitely better.
Grace is not Jesus looking at your chains and calling them freedom.
Grace is Jesus breaking the chains and calling you to follow Him.
So if you are reading this after falling again, do not turn this article into another five minutes of religious guilt before returning to the same darkness.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
If appropriate, seek mature Christian accountability.
Remove access to what repeatedly feeds your temptation.
Stop protecting the doorway through which destruction keeps entering.
If another person is involved in an immoral relationship, stop calling disobedience “complicated” merely because obedience will hurt.
If you have sinned against your spouse, pursue truth, repentance, wisdom, and restoration rather than simply becoming better at hiding.

If your marriage is struggling sexually, do not weaponize 1 Corinthians 7 against your husband or wife. Paul's teaching about marital intimacy is mutual; it is not permission for coercion, manipulation, intimidation, or abuse.
And if you are single, do not believe the lie that your life is on hold until somebody marries you.
Jesus is not a waiting room.
You can know Him now.
Serve Him now.
Become holy now.
Love people now.
Build His kingdom now.
Live fully now.
And if God eventually leads you into marriage, do not enter it asking another sinner to become your savior.
Enter knowing you already have One.
Maybe this article exposed something.
Good.
Not because exposure feels good.
It usually doesn't.
But wounds cannot be treated while we keep pretending they aren't there.
So be honest.
Not performatively religious.
Not polished.
Honest.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting.
Someone may choose confession instead of another night of secrecy because you were brave enough to say four words.
Someone may remember that struggling is not the same thing as surrendering.
And someone desperately needs to hear what you now know:
Sexual sin can become part of your story without becoming the final sentence of your story.
Because Jesus rewrites stories.
You may never know who.
The husband who looks happy in the family photographs.
The teenager who discovered pornography years before anyone realized it.
The Christian woman too ashamed to tell anyone what she is fighting.
The single believer convinced marriage will magically fix everything.
The wounded spouse wondering whether restoration is possible.
The person who believes sexual failure has permanently disqualified them from coming home to God.
If tagging them could embarrass them, send it privately instead.
Not because every sentence will feel urgent today.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support buys a blessing.
It doesn't.
Paul taught believers to give as they had purposed in their hearts, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Christian generosity is worship precisely because it comes freely from a heart responding to grace.
Your support becomes practical partnership.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be mission.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you open your Bible again…
If something published here helped you repent…
If it helped you fight another day…
If it reminded you that Jesus had not abandoned you…
If these messages are reaching places where wounded people are hiding…
Then prayerfully consider helping keep them moving.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Point people toward Christ.
Because ultimately this is not about building an audience.
It is about reaching people.
Not collecting religious consumers.
Making disciples.
Not making sinners dependent upon a page.
Pointing sinners toward a Savior.
And perhaps tonight the sinner who most needs that Savior is you.
Then come.
You do not need to clean yourself before approaching the One whose blood cleans sinners.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come without excuses.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the fantasies.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the body you misused.
Bring Him the heart you cannot repair.
Bring Him everything.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of good people proving they never became dirty.
It is the story of guilty people discovering that the blood of Jesus Christ is stronger than their stain.
Corinth had sexual sinners.
Jesus built a church there.
Corinth had broken histories.
Jesus washed people there.
Corinth had temptation.
Jesus called people holy there.
And whatever your history is, your darkest chapter does not possess the authority to write your final sentence.
Christ does.
So when temptation whispers, “This is who you are,” remember the cross.
When shame whispers, “Hide,” remember the empty tomb.
When lust whispers, “You need this,” remember the Savior who said that whoever comes to Him will never ultimately find Him insufficient.
And when your past whispers, “There is no coming back from this,” remember three words:
But ye are washed.
That is scandal becoming grace.
That is shame meeting blood.
That is captivity meeting Christ.
That is the sinner discovering that Jesus did not come merely to improve behavior.
He came to make dead people alive.

And one day, when every secret has lost its power, every temptation has finally fallen silent, and every redeemed body stands resurrected before its Redeemer, nobody will be boasting that they were strong enough to save themselves.
We will look at the Lamb.
The scars.
The blood.
The grace.
And we will know who brought us home.
Your sin may explain a chapter of your story—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THREE WOMEN CHRISTIANS OFTEN MERGE INTO ONE—AND SCRIPTURE DOESN’T
paragraphs:
THREE WOMEN CHRISTIANS OFTEN MERGE INTO ONE—AND SCRIPTURE DOESN’T
Mary Magdalene was not called a prostitute. The woman caught in adultery was never named Mary. And the woman who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears has a story powerful enough that we should stop rewriting it.
There is a woman in the Bible almost everyone thinks they know.
She is usually imagined with a scandalous past.
A prostitute.
A woman caught in adultery.
A woman weeping at Jesus’ feet.
An alabaster jar breaking open.
Long hair wiping away tears and perfume.
Seven demons.
Then resurrection morning.
And somewhere through centuries of sermons, paintings, films, traditions, and retellings, all those images began wearing one face.
Mary Magdalene.
There is only one problem.
Scripture never puts all of those stories on Mary Magdalene.
Read the Gospels slowly and something startling happens.
The woman begins to separate.
Then another woman appears.
Then another.
And suddenly we discover that some of the most familiar things Christians have repeated about Mary Magdalene were never actually said about her in the biblical text.
This matters for more than correcting a Bible trivia mistake.
Because whenever we add something to another person’s story that God did not put there, we risk remembering a label more clearly than we remember the grace of Christ.
And maybe that cuts closer to home than we expect.
Because some of us know what it feels like when people merge the worst thing they heard about us with who we actually are.
One failure becomes your identity.
One rumor becomes your biography.
One season becomes your name.
One sin follows you into rooms you entered years after repentance.
People remember what you were.
Jesus knows who you are.
So before we talk about these women, hear the question beneath the question:
What if you have been carrying a version of someone’s story that Scripture itself never tells?
Go first to Luke 7.
Jesus is eating in the house of a Pharisee named Simon when a woman enters.
Luke does not call her Mary.
Luke does not call her Magdalene.
Luke does not call her an adulteress.
Luke describes her with the Greek words:
γυνὴ … ἁμαρτωλός — gynē … hamartōlos
A woman who was known in the city as sinful.
That is what the text gives us.
Not “prostitute.”
Not “Mary Magdalene.”
Not “the adulterous woman from John 8.”
A sinful woman.
And there is something painfully human about the scene.
She walks into a house where she knows people know her reputation.
Imagine that walk.
Imagine crossing a doorway while knowing what the people around the table think about you.
Imagine feeling eyes follow you.
Imagine knowing that before you say one word, somebody in that room has already reduced your entire existence to the thing you did.
She carries an alabaster flask of perfume.
Then she stands behind Jesus.
And she breaks.
Not the jar yet.
Her.
She weeps.
Her tears fall onto His feet.
She wipes His feet with her hair.
She kisses them.
She pours perfume over them.
And Simon watches.
But Simon does not see what Jesus sees.
Simon sees a category.
Jesus sees a woman.
Simon sees contamination.
Jesus sees faith.
Simon sees her history.
Jesus sees what grace is doing in the present.
Luke records Simon thinking that if Jesus were truly a prophet, He would know what kind of woman was touching Him.
But Jesus does know.
That is precisely the point.
Christ's holiness is not preserved by ignorance of sinners.
He knows exactly who approaches Him.
He knows what she has done.
He knows what you have done.
There has never been a confession that surprised Him.
There has never been a hidden browser history that shocked Him.
There has never been an addiction He discovered too late.
There has never been a betrayal, affair, lie, secret, relapse, private compromise, or carefully protected darkness that made Jesus suddenly reconsider whether His blood was sufficient.
He already knows.
And still He receives repentant sinners.
Jesus tells Simon about two debtors whose debts are canceled. Then He turns toward the woman while speaking to the Pharisee.
That detail is devastating.
He looks at the person everyone is judging while confronting the person doing the judging.
Then comes the heart of the scene.
Jesus tells her that her sins are forgiven and concludes:
Ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην.
Hē pistis sou sesōken se; poreuou eis eirēnēn.
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
Notice where salvation rests.
Not in the perfume.
Not in the tears as though enough crying purchases forgiveness.
Not in public humiliation.
Not in her ability to punish herself for her past.
Jesus points to faith.
Her love is the overflowing evidence of forgiven debt, not a payment large enough to force God to forgive.
That distinction is the Gospel.
We do not purchase grace with remorse.
We do not make ourselves clean enough for Christ.
We come bankrupt.
Christ forgives.
Grace creates love.
Forgiveness produces worship.
The forgiven heart stops calculating how little it can give Jesus.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years trying to repay God for what Jesus already carried to the cross.
You keep punishing yourself because guilt feels more spiritual than grace.
You believe Jesus forgives sinners in general, but when your own memories wake up at two in the morning, you quietly add an exception.
Me.
Maybe others.
But not me.
Listen again.
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
Jesus does not say, “Go pretend it never happened.”
Grace is not amnesia.
He does not say sin was harmless.
Grace never needs to lie about evil in order to defeat it.
He forgives.
That is infinitely better.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel says the Son of God considered your redemption worth His blood.
And then Luke does something extraordinarily important.
The chapter ends.
Luke 8 begins.
Jesus travels from town to town proclaiming the kingdom of God. The Twelve are with Him, along with women who had been healed.
And now Luke names one:
Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή
Maria hē kaloumenē Magdalēnē.
“Mary, the one called Magdalene.”
Luke then says:
ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει
“from whom seven demons had gone out.”
This is Mary Magdalene.
Notice what Luke does not say.
He does not say, “the sinful woman mentioned above.”
He does not say she was a prostitute.
He does not say she committed adultery.
He identifies her as Mary called Magdalene and tells us that seven demons had gone out from her.
Seven demons are not biblical shorthand for prostitution.
Demonic affliction and sexual immorality are not interchangeable categories.
We should not turn one into the other merely because later imagination found the combination dramatic.
Mary Magdalene’s actual biblical story is already astonishing.
She had known terrible bondage.
Jesus delivered her.
She followed Him.
She became part of the circle of women supporting Jesus and His ministry from their resources.
She remained near the crucifixion when so much seemed lost.
She witnessed where Jesus was laid.
And in John’s Gospel, she encounters the risen Christ.
Why would we need to manufacture another scandal for her?
Is deliverance from seven demons not enough?
Is standing near the cross not enough?
Is weeping outside an empty tomb not enough?
Is hearing the risen Jesus call her by name not enough?
Mary’s greatness is not improved by inventing a darker résumé.
Grace does not need exaggeration.
Jesus does not become more glorious when we make somebody else look worse.
Then there is another woman Christians sometimes pull into this composite portrait.
The woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11.

Whatever discussion Christians have about the textual history of that passage—and responsible modern Bibles openly note that the earliest manuscripts do not contain it—one fact is straightforward within the story as transmitted:
the woman is not named Mary Magdalene.
She is not named Mary of Bethany.
She is simply the woman brought before Jesus.
Dragging her into Mary Magdalene’s biography requires information the text never supplies.
And even inside that famous scene, notice what Christ refuses to do.
He does not join the mob.
But neither does He baptize sin as righteousness.
Mercy and holiness meet.
“Neither do I condemn you” is followed by the command to leave the life of sin.
That is the Jesus our generation desperately needs to encounter.
Not a Christ redesigned into mere affirmation.
Not a Christ reduced to condemnation.
The real Christ.
Full of grace and truth.
The Christ who receives sinners and calls sinners out of sin.
The Christ who does not throw repentant people away and does not tell them their chains are freedom.
Grace does not mean Jesus leaves you exactly where He found you.
Grace means He loves you too deeply to do that.
Then another familiar scene appears near the end of Jesus’ earthly ministry.
Bethany.
Perfume.
Jesus.
A woman.
Hair.
Feet.
And this is where careful reading matters enormously.
John names this woman.
She is Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus.
John 12:3 begins:
ἡ οὖν Μαριὰμ λαβοῦσα λίτραν μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτίμου…
Mary takes an extraordinarily costly quantity of nard, anoints Jesus’ feet, and wipes them with her hair.
The house fills with the fragrance.
John had already identified her in connection with this act when introducing Lazarus in John 11.

Matthew and Mark also recount an anointing at Bethany shortly before the Passion. They do not name the woman; they describe expensive perfume being poured on Jesus’ head, and Jesus interprets the act in relation to His burial. John explicitly names Mary of Bethany in his Bethany account. Christians have long discussed how the Gospel accounts relate in their details, but Scripture gives us no warrant to turn Mary of Bethany automatically into Mary Magdalene or Luke 7’s unnamed sinful woman.
Three portraits have been collapsed again and again:
Luke’s unnamed sinful woman.
Mary Magdalene.
Mary of Bethany.
And sometimes a fourth story—the unnamed woman caught in adultery—is folded into the same imagined biography.
But Scripture does not tell us to do that.
And something beautiful happens when we stop forcing them together.
Each woman gets her testimony back.
The unnamed woman of Luke 7 gets to remain what the Gospel makes her: a forgiven sinner whose faith erupts into extravagant love.
Mary Magdalene gets her testimony back: a woman dramatically delivered by Christ who faithfully follows Him and becomes a witness to the risen Lord.
Mary of Bethany gets her testimony back: a devoted disciple whose costly act of love points toward Jesus’ approaching burial.
The woman accused of adultery gets to remain unnamed rather than having someone else’s identity attached to her.
And Jesus stands at the center of every story.
That may be the deepest correction of all.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be obsessed with constructing scandalous biographies about broken people.
Christianity is about Jesus Christ.
We keep staring at the women.
The Gospel keeps directing us toward the Savior.
Who forgives sins?
Jesus.
Who casts out demons?
Jesus.
Who receives costly worship?
Jesus.
Who refuses self-righteous condemnation while calling sinners away from sin?
Jesus.
Who goes willingly toward burial?
Jesus.
Who dies beneath the judgment sinners deserve?
Jesus.
Who rises?
Jesus.
Who turns frightened, grieving, ashamed, wounded human beings into witnesses of grace?
Jesus.
This is why getting the story right matters.
Biblical accuracy is not cold scholarship fighting against heartfelt faith.
Truth protects people.
Truth protects testimony.
Truth protects us from turning tradition into Scripture.
And truth keeps Jesus at the center.
Maybe you have experienced the opposite.
Maybe somebody has merged several versions of you into one.
The addict you once were.
The marriage that collapsed.
The child you disappointed.
The pregnancy nobody knows about.
The years you wasted.
The church you walked away from.
The night you wish you could erase.
The secret that still makes your stomach tighten whenever somebody preaches about it.
And even after Christ began changing you, some people kept introducing you to themselves through your oldest chapter.
They remember the jar.
Jesus remembers the surrender.
They remember the demons.
Jesus sees the disciple.
They remember the accusation.
Jesus sees the person standing in need of mercy and transformation.
They remember your scandal.
Jesus knows what grace can write next.
But do not misunderstand this.
The Gospel is not, “You were secretly a good person all along.”
The Gospel is far more powerful.
We really are sinners, and Jesus really saves sinners.
Romans does not flatter humanity.
“All have sinned.”
The cross does not exist because human beings were misunderstood.
The cross exists because we were guilty.
Christ died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He rose victorious.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith is not merely given better public relations.
They are reconciled to God.
Forgiven.
Made new.
Brought from death to life.
That is why “From Scandal to Grace” is not a slogan about improving your reputation.
It is a declaration about redemption.
Jesus does not simply edit your image.
He transforms lives.
He does not merely help you hide the old chapter.
He gives you a new identity in Him.
He does not say darkness was light.
He brings you out of darkness.
He does not rewrite history by pretending sin never existed.
He rewrites what sin thought the ending would be.
The cross looked like scandal.
Then Sunday came.
A sealed tomb looked final.
Then the stone moved.
Mary Magdalene stood weeping because she thought the body of Jesus was gone.
Then a voice said her name.
“Mary.”
Imagine that moment.
The woman once tormented by seven demons hears the risen Lord speak her name.
Not her affliction.
Her name.
And perhaps that is where this entire article has been trying to take you.
Beyond correcting a misconception.
Beyond Greek vocabulary.
Beyond identifying which Mary did what.
To this:
Jesus knows your name more deeply than your scandal does.
Your sin must be confessed, not romanticized.
Your chains must be broken, not renamed.
Your past must be surrendered, not worshiped.
But none of those things possesses greater authority than the crucified and risen Son of God.
If you are hiding, come into the light.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have wandered, return.
If shame keeps whispering that Jesus will receive everybody except you, stop trusting shame as though shame were a theologian.
Look at Christ.
The woman in Luke 7 came carrying a reputation and left hearing about peace.
Mary Magdalene knew oppression and became a follower and resurrection witness.
Mary of Bethany poured out something precious before the One who was about to pour out His life.
Different women.
Different stories.
The same Savior.
And that Savior is still saving.

If this exposed something you have believed for years, don't be embarrassed that you learned something. Open the Bible again. Test everything against Scripture. Let the Word correct what tradition, movies, sermons, memes, and even sincere teachers may have blurred.
And if this reached deeper than biblical history—if it touched the part of you that is exhausted from being remembered only by your worst chapter—be honest.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “Please stand with me.”
Then send this to somebody who has been crushed by a label.
It doesn't.
Christ does.
Luke 8:1–3. John 11–12. Matthew 26:6–13. Mark 14:3–9. Read them slowly. Compare them. Let Scripture speak with its own voice.
Grace cannot be bought. Give freely, prayerfully, and willingly.
Open the Scriptures.
Know the real Jesus.
Repent when His Word exposes you.
Receive the grace He purchased at the cross.
Tell somebody what He has done.
Because the world does not need a more sensational Mary Magdalene.
It needs the Christ Mary Magdalene actually followed.
It needs the Jesus who forgives sinners without pretending sin is harmless.
The Jesus who breaks chains.
The Jesus who receives worship.
The Jesus who went willingly to His burial.
The Jesus whose tomb could not keep Him.
The Jesus who still calls broken people by name.
Share Him.
Follow Him.
And when somebody tries to reduce you forever to the chapter Christ has redeemed, remember this:
People may keep calling you by your scandal long after Jesus has called you by your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your Children Hear the Way You Talk About Their Father Too.
paragraphs:
Your Children Hear the Way You Talk About Their Father Too.
You thought you were only telling the truth about what he did. But there was a little heart in the room learning what love sounds like when it is wounded.
She thought he was playing.
That is what made it so easy.
Her little boy was sitting on the floor with two toy cars in his hands, crashing them together, making engine noises under his breath while she stood in the kitchen talking.
She was frustrated.
Maybe she had every reason to be.

Her husband had disappointed her again. Maybe he had forgotten something important. Maybe he had spoken harshly. Maybe he had come home late. Maybe he had left her carrying responsibilities that should never have been hers alone.
And now she needed to tell someone.
So she picked up her phone.
“He never thinks about anybody but himself.”
The little cars kept moving.
“He acts like another child I have to take care of.”
Crash.
“I honestly don’t know why I expected anything different.”
The little boy never looked up.
And because he never looked up, she assumed he wasn't listening.
But children do not have to look at you to hear you.
Sometimes they are building an entire understanding of marriage while sitting quietly on the carpet.
Sometimes they are learning what a husband is from the way their mother describes their father.
Sometimes they are learning what a wife is from the way their father speaks about their mother.
Sometimes they are learning what conflict means before they are old enough to spell the word.
And sometimes the sentences adults call “venting” become bricks children quietly use to build their understanding of love.
That does not mean a mother must pretend her husband never sins.
It does not mean abuse should be hidden.
It does not mean betrayal should be minimized.
It does not mean a woman should remain silent while she or her children are being harmed.

Biblical forgiveness is not permission for continued abuse, and Christian reconciliation never requires pretending evil is good. Serious mistreatment belongs in the light, and wise pastoral, professional, legal, or protective help may be necessary.
This is about something quieter.
More ordinary.
And perhaps because it is ordinary, more easily ignored.
It is about the emotional atmosphere created by our words.
Because your children hear the way you talk about their father too.
And fathers, before you quietly send this article to your wife, keep reading.
Your children hear how you talk about their mother too.
Paul wrote to believers in Ephesus:
“Πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω…”
Pas logos sapros ek tou stomatos hymōn mē ekporeuesthō…
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths…”
—Ephesians 4:29
That Greek word translated “corrupting” is σαπρός — sapros.
It can describe something rotten, spoiled, worthless, or bad.
Paul is not merely teaching Christians to avoid profanity.
He is reaching deeper.
He is confronting speech that carries decay.
Words can do that.
They can bring life into a room.
Or they can bring rot.
Paul continues:
“…ἀλλ’ εἴ τις ἀγαθὸς πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας…”
“…but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion…”
There is another important word there:
οἰκοδομή — oikodomē.
Building up.
Edification.
The language carries the idea of construction.
And that is an uncomfortable picture when you remember who may be listening.
Because every home is being built with more than lumber, concrete, furniture, and paint.
Homes are built with sentences.
A child hears:
“Your father never does anything right.”
Another brick.
“Your mother is impossible.”
Another brick.
“He is useless.”
Another brick.
“She is crazy.”
Another brick.
“I wish I had never married him.”
Another brick.
“You're just like your father.”
Another brick.
“You're becoming exactly like your mother.”
And suddenly something that sounded like an argument between adults has entered the identity of a child.
That last kind of sentence can cut especially deep.
Because if Daddy is constantly described as worthless, what does a little boy hear when someone says he looks just like Daddy?
If Mommy is constantly described as unbearable, what might a daughter feel when she recognizes her mother's personality in herself?
Children often identify with both parents.
So contempt aimed at a spouse can land somewhere you never intended it to land.
Inside your child.
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps you remember being that child.
You remember sitting in the back seat while one parent unloaded anger about the other.
You remember being asked questions you should never have been asked.
“Who do you think is right?”
You remember becoming the messenger.
“Tell your father…”
“Tell your mother…”
You remember learning when to disappear into your bedroom because you could recognize the temperature of the house from the sound of footsteps.
Maybe nobody hit anybody.
Maybe nothing was broken.
But you learned to read silence like a weather forecast.
You knew when a storm was coming.
And perhaps years later, you carried pieces of that emotional climate into your own relationships.
That is why this matters.
Children do not merely learn marriage from the wedding photographs hanging on the wall.
They learn marriage by watching what happens after disappointment.
They watch what Mommy does when Daddy fails.
They watch what Daddy does when Mommy is overwhelmed.
They listen to what parents say when the person they promised to love becomes difficult to love.
And eventually they begin answering enormous questions with tiny observations.
What happens when love gets angry?
What happens when somebody fails?
Do we humiliate them?
Do we recruit other people against them?
Do we keep a record?
Do we weaponize yesterday?
Do we apologize?
Do we forgive?
Do we repair?
Do we pray?
Do we come back to the table?
Do we tell the truth without destroying each other?
This is where the Gospel enters the room.
Not as decoration.
Not as a Christian slogan taped over dysfunction.
As rescue.
Paul does not stop with speech in Ephesians 4.
He keeps going.
“Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.”
Then comes the alternative:
“Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.”
—Ephesians 4:31–32
Look carefully at the foundation.
Paul does not merely say, “Be nicer.”
He anchors forgiveness in something infinitely greater:
“…καθὼς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐν Χριστῷ ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν.”
“…as God in Christ forgave you.”
The verb is related to χαρίζομαι — charizomai, carrying the sense of graciously giving or forgiving.
In other words, Christian forgiveness does not begin with pretending the wound was small.
It begins with remembering how enormous grace is.
That changes the entire conversation.
Because Christianity does not tell a wounded wife, “Your pain doesn't matter.”
Jesus never needed darkness renamed as light.
Sin can be called sin.
Betrayal can be called betrayal.
Cruelty can be confronted.
Boundaries can be necessary.
Trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
Reconciliation requires truth, repentance, and wisdom; forgiveness does not automatically mean immediate restoration of access or trust.
But the Gospel refuses to let another person's sin become permission for ours.
That is the difficult part.
You can be genuinely wounded and still wound others with the way you speak about your wound.
You can be right about what happened and wrong about what you do with it.
You can tell the truth in a way designed to heal.
And you can tell the truth in a way designed to humiliate.
Those are not the same thing.
Perhaps your husband really did fail you.
Perhaps your wife really did disappoint you.
Deal with it.
Speak about it.
Seek wise counsel.
Confront what needs confronting.
Get help where help is needed.
But be careful about turning your children into confidants for burdens their hearts were never designed to carry.
Your daughter does not need to become Mommy's therapist.
Your son does not need to become Daddy's defense attorney.
A child should not have to decide which parent deserves loyalty.
There is something profoundly unfair about asking little shoulders to carry adult resentment.
And perhaps right now you are remembering something you said yesterday.
Or this morning.
Maybe your child was in the next room.
Maybe you saw those little eyes change.
Maybe your teenager became quiet.
Maybe conviction is arriving before you have even finished reading.
Do not run from it.
But do not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation either.
The Gospel has something better than shame.
Repentance.
Grace.
Repair.
Jesus Christ does not expose sin merely to leave sinners staring at the wreckage.
He calls us to Himself.
At the cross, Christ bore the judgment sinners deserve. In His resurrection is the declaration that sin and death do not get the final word for those who belong to Him.
So maybe tonight the most powerful lesson about marriage your child will ever witness will not be a perfect marriage.
Maybe it will be repentance.
Maybe your child needs to hear:
“Mommy shouldn't have spoken about Daddy that way.”
Maybe:
“Daddy was angry, but what I said about your mother was wrong.”
Maybe:
“You should never feel like you have to choose between us.”
Maybe:
“Adults can disagree without trying to destroy each other's dignity.”
Maybe:
“I sinned with my words, and I asked Jesus to forgive me. I also asked your father to forgive me.”
Think about what that teaches.
Your child learns that authority can apologize.
That Christians do not have to pretend.
That repentance is not humiliation.
That saying “I was wrong” does not make a parent weak.
That grace is not something we only sing about on Sunday.
It belongs in kitchens.
Cars.
Bedrooms.
Text messages.
Arguments.
Apologies.
Marriages.
Families.
This is discipleship.
Not only Bible studies around a table.
Not only family devotionals.
Not only church attendance.
Your child is also being discipled by the way you behave when Scripture becomes inconvenient.
Anyone can quote “be kind to one another” when everyone is getting along.
The verse becomes costly when you are hurt.
Anyone can preach forgiveness when there is nothing to forgive.
The Gospel becomes visible when grace walks into an actual wound without denying the wound.
Your children are watching.
Not because they expect perfection.
They are watching to discover whether Jesus is real enough to change the way people behave when they are angry.
And mother, there is another truth you may need to hear.
Protecting your child's relationship with their father does not require lying for him.
You are not called to manufacture an imaginary man.
You are called to walk in truth.
If he has done something wrong, age-appropriate honesty may be necessary.
But there is a difference between honest explanation and character assassination.
There is a difference between seeking counsel from mature adults and unloading on a child.
There is a difference between saying, “Your father made a wrong choice,” and teaching a child, “Your father is worthless.”
Behavior can be confronted without reducing a human being made in God's image to his worst moment.
And yes, the same truth runs in the opposite direction.
Father, your wife is listening when you speak.
But so are the children.
Sarcasm about their mother teaches something.
Mocking her appearance teaches something.
Calling her emotional, stupid, lazy, crazy, useless, or impossible teaches something.
The joke everybody laughs at may still leave a wound in the child who loves the person you turned into the punchline.
Your home has an emotional vocabulary.
Someone is teaching it.
Maybe both of you are.
So ask yourself something difficult:
If my children eventually speak to their spouses the way I speak to mine, will I be proud of what I taught them?
Sit with that.
Because one day that little boy pushing cars across the floor may become somebody's husband.
One day that little girl coloring at the table may become somebody's wife.
And some of what they believe about conflict may have been learned before they knew they were learning anything at all.
But this story does not have to end in fear.
It can end in grace.
Actually, grace is where the Christian story begins again.
Maybe your home has already heard too many cruel sentences.
Jesus is still able to redeem what sin has damaged.
Maybe apologies are overdue.
Make them.
Maybe counseling is needed.
Seek it.
Maybe bitterness has become so familiar that you have started calling it personality.
Bring it before Christ.
Maybe you have been using your friends, Facebook posts, relatives, or even your children as a courtroom where your spouse is always the defendant and you are always the prosecutor.
Lay down the gavel.
You are not the Savior of your marriage.
Jesus is Lord.
And perhaps before asking Christ to change your spouse, you need to let Him search your own mouth.
Your own heart.
Your own hidden rehearsals of resentment.
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths…”
Not because words are insignificant.
Because they are powerful.
“…but only such as is good for building up…”
Build.
Build truth.
Build safety.
Build honesty.
Build repentance.
Build tenderness.
Build a home where conflict can happen without contempt becoming the family language.
Build children who know that disagreement does not require dehumanization.
Build a marriage where apologies are stronger than pride.
And when something has already been torn down?
Let Christ teach you how to rebuild.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not the polished Christianity where everybody smiles for the family photograph while resentment rots behind closed doors.
The real Gospel.
The Gospel for sinners.
The Gospel for angry mothers.
The Gospel for proud fathers.
The Gospel for wounded spouses.
The Gospel for frightened children.
The Gospel for families who wish they could rewind conversations.
The Gospel for people who cannot undo yesterday but can surrender today to Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite history by pretending the sin never happened.
He rewrites what happens next.
Repentance can happen next.
Forgiveness can happen next.
Wise boundaries can happen next.
Counseling can happen next.
A changed vocabulary can happen next.
A child hearing, “I was wrong” can happen next.
A husband kneeling before Christ can happen next.
A wife surrendering bitterness can happen next.
A family discovering that grace is more than a church word can happen next.
Maybe somebody you love needs this article.
Not so you can say, “See? This is what you've been doing.”
Please don't weaponize an article about gracious speech.
And if this exposed something in you, do not hide behind a like.
Be honest.
Your honesty may give another struggling believer permission to stop pretending too.
Not because you need another saved post.
Come back to Ephesians 4:29–32 and ask one question before the words leave your mouth:
Am I building right now, or am I spreading decay?
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow deeper in Scripture, conviction, repentance, healing, and discipleship, stay close.
If you believe this ministry is worth sustaining, you can do more than consume what it creates.
You can help carry it.
One practical way to glorify God is to steward what He has entrusted to you in ways that help spread His truth.
It is discipleship.
It is helping biblical nourishment keep reaching people.
It is choosing to support a place committed to pointing wounded, wandering, convicted, exhausted, and hungry people back to Jesus Christ.
Not to build our name.
To lift His.
Not because clicking a button earns favor with God—it does not.
But when Christ has given us grace freely, we can freely use our voices, resources, platforms, and influence to help others hear about Him.
Your child may forget what was cooking in the kitchen that night.
They may forget the toy they were holding.
They may forget what everybody was wearing.
But years from now, somewhere inside the marriage they eventually build, they may still hear the language of the home where they first learned what love sounds like when it hurts.

So give them something worth remembering: let them hear that even wounded people can surrender their words to Jesus, even broken conversations can bow before the cross, and even after the sentence you wish you could take back, grace can still write the next one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHICH DESTROYED MORE BIBLE CHARACTERS: LUST, PRIDE, OR FEAR?
paragraphs:
WHICH DESTROYED MORE BIBLE CHARACTERS: LUST, PRIDE, OR FEAR?
Samson had strength but could not master his desires. Saul wore a crown but trembled before people. Nebuchadnezzar ruled an empire but worshiped his own greatness. And somewhere inside their stories… we may recognize ourselves.
Which one destroys a person faster?
Lust?
Pride?
Or fear?
Before you answer, be careful.
Because the most dangerous sin may not be the one you can easily see in somebody else's life.
It may be the one you have learned to rename in your own.
We call lust “just attraction.”
We call pride “knowing my worth.”
We call fear “being realistic.”
And sometimes we become so skilled at giving respectable names to spiritual problems that we can sit in church, quote Scripture, sing about surrender, post verses about Jesus…
while quietly feeding the very thing that is eating us alive.
That is what makes this question uncomfortable.
The Bible does not give us a statistical table declaring that lust destroyed 37 people, pride destroyed 52, and fear destroyed 61. Scripture does something far more personal.
It gives us people.
People with names.
People with families.
People who were called by God.
People who experienced His power.
People who knew better.
And people who still fell.
Samson is one of the first names many Christians think of when lust enters the conversation.
He was set apart before birth. Judges 13 describes an extraordinary calling upon his life. Yet Judges repeatedly shows Samson being driven by what pleased his eyes.
Then came Delilah.
And the frightening thing about Samson's story is that Delilah did not defeat him in a single evening.
There were warnings.
There were opportunities to walk away.
There were moments when the trap should have become obvious.
But sin rarely needs to destroy you immediately.
Sometimes it only needs to persuade you to stay one more night.
To send one more message.
To look one more time.
To entertain one more fantasy.
To tell yourself one more lie:
“I can handle this.”
Samson kept playing near the edge until the edge became his home.

Eventually he revealed the secret connected with his Nazirite consecration. His hair was cut, the Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, bound him, and reduced Israel's feared warrior to grinding in prison.
There is a brutal irony there.
The man repeatedly governed by what looked good to his eyes eventually lost his eyes.
Yet Samson's deepest problem cannot simply be reduced to sexual desire.
Underneath the appetite was presumption.
He behaved as though consequences would always remain negotiable.
Judges 16:20 records one of Scripture's most chilling moments. Samson awakened expecting to escape as he had before.
But he did not realize that the LORD had departed from him.
Imagine becoming so accustomed to yesterday's strength that you do not recognize today's spiritual emptiness.
That is why this article is not really about Samson.
It is about us.
How many people are living on memories of what their relationship with God used to be?
You remember when prayer moved you.
You remember when Scripture convicted you.
You remember when compromise frightened you.
You remember when Jesus was not simply part of your identity—He was your treasure.
But somewhere along the road, something changed.
Maybe nobody noticed.
You still looked Christian.
Still knew the language.
Still knew when to say “Amen.”
But privately?
Something was starving.
Maybe lust found a secret room.
Maybe pornography became the place you ran when loneliness hurt.
Maybe emotional infidelity began with conversations you insisted were innocent.
Maybe you did not touch another person at all, but you have been feeding fantasies you would be terrified for your spouse—or Christ—to see.
Jesus takes the internal life seriously.
In Matthew 5:28, He warns that looking at another person with lustful intent is already adultery in the heart.
The Greek word often translated “to lust” or “to desire” is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō.

Desire itself is not automatically sinful; the New Testament can use related language for legitimate longing. Context matters. In Jesus' warning, the issue is desire directed toward someone in a way that violates covenant faithfulness and turns the heart toward adultery.
Jesus goes beneath behavior.
Into intention.
Into imagination.
Into the hidden room.
Because Christ is not interested merely in making your browser history cleaner.
He wants your heart.
But then there is pride.
And pride can be harder to detect because pride can wear religious clothing.
Nebuchadnezzar looked across Babylon and essentially celebrated the kingdom he believed he had built by his own power and for his own glory.
Daniel 4 records the result.
His greatness became the stage upon which God exposed his dependence.
Later, when his reason was restored, the king confessed the supremacy of the Most High and acknowledged that God is able to humble those who walk in pride.
That is the terrifying thing about pride.
Lust often knows it is hungry.
Fear often knows it is afraid.
Pride can believe it is righteous.
Pride can preach.
Pride can serve.
Pride can give money.
Pride can memorize Scripture.
Pride can correct everyone else's theology while remaining almost completely blind to its own heart.

The biblical languages give us vivid ways of describing this problem. One important Hebrew term associated with pride is גָּאוֹן — ga'on—which can describe exaltation, majesty, or pride depending on context. Scripture repeatedly condemns human self-exaltation that attempts to occupy the place belonging to God.
Proverbs 16:18 says:
“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.”
But pride is not merely thinking, “I am amazing.”
Sometimes pride sounds like:
“I don't need help.”
“I will never apologize first.”
“They hurt me, so they owe me.”
“I already know what the Bible says.”
“God understands why His command doesn't apply in my situation.”
“I can repent later.”
And perhaps one of pride's most dangerous sentences:
“I would never do what that person did.”
Peter once sounded remarkably confident.
When Jesus warned His disciples that they would fall away, Peter insisted that even if everyone else did, he would not.
Then came the courtyard.
A servant girl.
Questions.
Pressure.
Fear.
And the disciple who had confidently spoken of dying beside Jesus denied that he even knew Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Suddenly the question changes.
Maybe fear destroys more than we realize.
Fear does not always make you run screaming.
Sometimes fear makes you remain silent when you should speak.
Fear makes you compromise because you cannot bear rejection.
Fear makes you hide your faith because you want approval.
Fear keeps you trapped in an abusive pattern of sin because obedience seems more frightening than familiarity.
Fear makes you obey the crowd instead of Christ.
That happened catastrophically in Saul's life.
After Saul failed to carry out God's command concerning Amalek, Samuel confronted him. Saul eventually admitted:
“I feared the people and obeyed their voice.”
That confession in 1 Samuel 15:24 exposes something painfully human.
Saul was king.
Yet the king was being ruled.
Not by an army.
Not by another monarch.
By people's opinions.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that prison feels like.
You check whether they liked it.
You wonder what they said about you.
You replay criticism at 2:00 in the morning.
You change yourself depending on the room.
You know what obedience requires, but then you imagine losing friends, relationships, status, opportunities, money, applause…
and suddenly compromise begins looking reasonable.

Scripture frequently describes fear with words such as the Hebrew יָרֵא — yare'. But context is essential because biblical “fear” is not one flat concept. The same Hebrew root can be associated with terror in one context and reverent fear of God in another.
That distinction changes everything.
The Bible does not teach us to become fearless in the sense that nothing matters.
It redirects our fear.
Proverbs 29:25 says that the fear of man lays a snare, while whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.
Jesus likewise taught His followers not to fear human beings as though they possess ultimate authority over us, but to live before God with holy reverence.
And now we arrive at the uncomfortable answer.
Which destroyed more Bible characters—lust, pride, or fear?
Scripture does not give us enough information to honestly calculate a winner.
And perhaps trying to crown one misses the deeper warning.
Because lust, pride, and fear often hold hands.
Samson desired what his eyes wanted, but pride helped convince him he could keep getting away with it.
Saul feared people, but pride also appeared when he tried to preserve his honor before Israel's elders.
David's adultery with Bathsheba involved sinful desire, but what followed included an abuse of royal power and an attempt to conceal what he had done.
Peter feared association with Jesus in the courtyard, but earlier his self-confidence had made him certain that his loyalty would survive what others could not.
Different sins.
Different symptoms.
But beneath them we repeatedly find the human heart attempting to find life apart from trusting and obeying God.
Lust says:
“This desire will satisfy me more than God.”
Pride says:
“I know better than God.”
Fear says:
“What people can do to me matters more than trusting God.”
Different voices.
Same attempted coup.
God is pushed away from the center.
And self takes the throne.
That is why merely telling yourself to “stop lusting,” “stop being proud,” or “stop being afraid” will never reach Christianity's deepest answer.
You need more than behavior modification.
You need a King.
And this is where Jesus Christ enters the ruins.
Not as another biblical character who barely escaped temptation.
As the sinless Son of God.
Where Adam fell, Christ obeyed.
Where humanity reaches for forbidden satisfaction, Jesus remained faithful to His Father.
Where human beings exalt themselves, Jesus humbled Himself.

Philippians 2 tells us that Christ, though existing in the form of God, did not exploit His equality with God for selfish advantage, but humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to death—even death on a cross.
And when suffering stood before Him, Jesus did not abandon the Father's will.
In Gethsemane, He experienced genuine anguish.
Yet He prayed:
“Not my will, but yours, be done.”
Look at Him.
This is our Savior.
Not lust ruling Him.
Not pride enthroning Him.
Not fear mastering Him.
Jesus obeyed where we failed.
Then He went to the cross carrying sin that was not His.
Our lust.
Our arrogance.
Our cowardice.
Our secret browser histories.
Our hidden fantasies.
Our obsession with people's approval.
Our self-righteousness.
Our hypocrisy.
Our excuses.
Our rebellion.
Our shame.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that decent people can improve themselves enough for God to finally accept them.
The scandal is grace.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
And He rose again.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The enslaved can be freed.
The proud can be humbled without being discarded.
The fearful can learn courage.
The sexually broken can become holy.
The hypocrite can finally stop pretending.
The prodigal can come home.
This does not make sin insignificant.
Grace is not God shrugging at your rebellion.
The cross demonstrates how serious sin is.
But it also demonstrates how astonishing God's mercy is.
Romans 5:8 says that God demonstrates His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
While.
We.
Were.
Still.
Sinners.
Not after you repaired everything.
Not after you conquered every temptation.
Not after you became impressive.
Christ died for sinners.
And because He lives, repentance is not a funeral for hope.
It is a doorway home.
The New Testament word commonly translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself. It involves a genuine turning—a changed mind and direction toward God that bears fruit in life.
You stop defending what Christ calls sin.
You stop decorating the prison.
You stop negotiating with the chains.
You bring darkness into the light.
Maybe this is why you are still reading.
Not because you wanted to discover whether Samson was worse than Saul.
Because somewhere along the way, the question became personal.
Which one has been destroying you?
Lust?
Pride?
Fear?
Or some mixture you have never had the courage to name?
Do not answer publicly unless you genuinely want to.
But answer God.
No performance.
No Christian vocabulary designed to make the wound sound prettier.
Tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, I have been feeding this.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I care too much about people's approval.”
“Jesus, I thought I could control it.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you can simply comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not as magic words.
Not as public theater.
But as an honest confession that you are finished pretending darkness is light.
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer realizes there is still hope.
Then send this article to the person who came into your mind while reading.
Not to shame them.
Not to expose them.
Because you love them too much to watch them quietly lose a war nobody knows they are fighting.
Save it too.
Because temptation has an extraordinary ability to make yesterday's convictions feel distant tomorrow.
Come back when lust whispers.
Come back when pride rises.
Come back when fear tells you obedience costs too much.
And then come back to Scripture itself.
Never allow Gospel Warrior—or any Christian page, preacher, author, article, devotional, or ministry—to become a substitute for God's Word.
We want to point you toward Jesus, not make you dependent upon us.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
For daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the Christian who is tired.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending they have everything together.
Because the Gospel says something radically different.
We were sinners who needed rescue.
Christ came for us.
And grace is still rewriting stories.
It does not.
Not because financially supporting a ministry is required for salvation.
It is not.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one voluntary way of helping biblical content continue reaching people.
Jesus Christ.
Because Samson's story did not end in the prison.
Peter's story did not end beside the charcoal fire where he denied Jesus.
David's story did not end with Bathsheba.
And if you belong to Christ, your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your final sentence.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
After the resurrection, John 21 shows Jesus restoring him.
Three times Peter had denied.
Three times Jesus drew a confession of love from him and entrusted him again with caring for His sheep.
Think about that.
