Because the astonishing thing about Genesis is not that God found flawless people and built a flawless family through them.
He didn't.
He worked through sinners.
Deceivers.
Manipulators.
Jealous people.
Wounded people.
People who made disastrous choices.
People who hurt one another.
People whose homes carried consequences for generations.
And yet God remained faithful to His promise.
This does not make sin harmless.
Grace never means sin did not matter.
Grace means sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Look at Judah.
The son born when Leah said, “This time I will praise the LORD.”
Generations later, Jesus Christ came through Judah’s line.

And Jesus did what Jacob could never do for Leah, what Rachel could never do for herself, and what no husband, wife, child, romance, achievement, sexual relationship, or human approval can ever do for us.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came not merely to improve broken people but to redeem them.
At the cross, Christ carried sin.
Real sin.
Ugly sin.
Sexual sin.
Jealousy.
Idolatry.
Deception.
Pride.
Hatred.
Manipulation.
The sins we confess publicly.
And the sins we desperately hope nobody discovers.
He did not die because humanity was basically good and needed encouragement.
He died because sinners needed salvation.
And He rose because death would not have the final word.
That means repentance is not humiliation before a God eager to destroy you.
It is coming home to the God who calls sinners to turn from sin and receive mercy through Christ.
Maybe you see yourself in Leah.
Always trying to earn somebody's love.
Maybe you see yourself in Rachel.
Loved in one area but tormented by what you still do not have.
Maybe you see yourself in Jacob.
Your choices have wounded more people than you wanted to admit.
Maybe you see yourself in Laban.
You learned to manipulate people so effectively that you stopped noticing the damage.
Maybe your family resembles the entire household.
Everybody wounded.
Everybody blaming.
Everybody carrying history.
Everybody convinced somebody else started it.
Then hear this carefully:
Jesus Christ does not need a clean family history before He begins writing redemption.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
It does not have to become the title of your eternity.
Your parents' failures do not have to become your identity.
Your sexual past does not have to become your master.
Your jealousy does not have to own you.
Your rejection does not have to define you.
Your worst night does not have to become your final chapter.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus does not merely cover our shame while leaving us comfortably enslaved to the sin producing it.
He calls us to repent.
To surrender.
To come into the light.
To forgive.
To confess.
To abandon idols.
To stop asking human beings to occupy the throne that belongs to God.
And perhaps the most dangerous idol in Jacob’s house was not a carved statue.
Perhaps it was simply this:
“If I can finally get what she has, I will be okay.”
Somebody reading this has been living by that sentence.
If I get married...
If I have a child...
If my spouse changes...
If that person comes back...
If my ministry grows...
If people finally recognize me...
If I become successful...
If my body changes...
If I finally prove everybody wrong...
then I will be okay.
But Rachel had Jacob’s love and still cried.
Leah had children and still ached.
Because even good gifts become cruel gods when we ask them to do what only God can do.
Christ is not merely another blessing to add to the life you are already constructing.
Christ is Lord.
And perhaps today the prayer is not, “Jesus, give me the thing I envy.”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, forgive me for believing I needed it more than I needed You.”
Sometimes confession begins with three words.
Sometimes restoration begins when hiding ends.

And if someone came to your mind while reading this—a sister, brother, spouse, friend, wounded believer, struggling Christian, seeker, or even someone who does not yet believe in Jesus—send this to them.
Save it too.
There are truths you understand differently when the wound starts hurting again.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, and keep your eyes on Jesus, stay close.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor, proving your spirituality, or earning blessing—salvation and grace cannot be bought.
Come to Jesus.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Not to a brand.
Not to merchandise.
Not to a religious image of yourself.
Come to Christ.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who knows what happened in your family.
The One who knows what happened in your bedroom.
The One who knows whom you envy.
The One who knows whom you still resent.
The One who knows the secret you have spent years hiding.
The One who knows the thing you did.
And the thing done to you.
He knows.
And the Gospel announces that forgiveness is real, grace is costly, repentance is possible, and redemption has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Jacob’s family became a battlefield of jealousy, sex, children, rejection, rivalry, manipulation, and pain.
God did not call the dysfunction good.
He did something infinitely greater.
He continued His redemptive purpose through broken human beings until, through Judah’s line, the Savior came.
And at the cross, the story became bigger than Leah.
Bigger than Rachel.
Bigger than Jacob.
Bigger than Judah.
Bigger than your family.
Bigger than your scandal.
Because Jesus did not come merely to edit the embarrassing pages.
He came to redeem sinners.
So maybe the sentence you have feared your entire life is not the final sentence after all.
Maybe heaven is still writing.
Your family may have handed you the wound—but Jesus does not have to let the wound write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: REUBEN AND HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINE: THE SEXUAL SIN JACOB NEVER FORGOT
paragraphs: REUBEN AND HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINE: THE SEXUAL SIN JACOB NEVER FORGOT

He thought it was one night. His father carried it for years. And when Jacob finally spoke about it on his deathbed, Reuben discovered something every secret sinner eventually learns: a moment can end long before its consequences do.
There are sins committed in public that destroy a reputation overnight.
Then there are sins committed behind a curtain, in a room, in a conversation, on a screen, in a relationship nobody was supposed to know about.
For a while, life continues.
Breakfast still comes.
People still call your name.
You still laugh.
You still worship.
You still sit beside people who have absolutely no idea what happened.
And because lightning did not fall from heaven, you can begin believing the terrifying lie that perhaps nothing really changed.
Reuben may have known something about that silence.
His story is recorded with almost uncomfortable brevity.
No long explanation.
No dramatic confrontation.
No recorded speech from Reuben.
No chapter describing Jacob exploding in rage.
Just one devastating sentence.
Genesis 35:22 records:
“And it came to pass, when Israel dwelt in that land, that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Israel heard it.”
That is the King James rendering.
The Hebrew is even more arresting:
וַיֵּלֶךְ רְאוּבֵן וַיִּשְׁכַּב אֶת־בִּלְהָה פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִיו וַיִּשְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayyelekh Re’uven vayishkav et-Bilhah pilegesh aviv, vayishma Yisra’el.
In straightforward English:
“Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard.”
And Israel heard.
Four words in English.
But years later, we discover that Jacob had not forgotten.
That may be the sentence that should frighten us.
Not because Jacob was omniscient.
He was not.
Not because every earthly father remembers every offense forever.
But because Scripture is showing us that sin can have consequences long after the adrenaline, pleasure, anger, rebellion, secrecy, or impulse that produced it has disappeared.
Reuben was not some nameless outsider.
He was Jacob’s firstborn.
The first son of Leah.
When Leah gave birth to him, she named him Reuben, saying, “Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction” (Genesis 29:32).
He entered the family carrying enormous significance.
Firstborn.
Strength.
Expectation.
Inheritance.
Responsibility.
A future was sitting on his shoulders before he was old enough to understand what a future was.
Then came Bilhah.
And Scripture refuses to romanticize what happened.

Bilhah was Rachel’s servant, given to Jacob as a wife or concubine within the deeply fractured household created by Jacob’s marriages and the rivalry between Rachel and Leah. Through Bilhah, Jacob fathered Dan and Naphtali.
She was therefore not simply some unrelated woman Reuben encountered.
She belonged within his father’s household.
She had borne Reuben’s brothers.
And Genesis says Reuben slept with her.
We should be careful here.
The Bible tells us what Reuben did. It does not explicitly tell us everything going through his mind when he did it.

Some interpreters have observed that sleeping with a father’s concubine could function in the ancient world as a challenge to paternal or royal authority, and Scripture later gives a striking example when Absalom publicly sleeps with David’s concubines during his rebellion.
That historical background may help us understand the gravity of Reuben’s act.
But we should not pretend Scripture explicitly gives us Reuben’s private motive.
We do not need speculation to make his sin serious.
God’s Word already makes it serious.
He violated a sexual boundary.
He dishonored his father.
He defiled his father’s bed.
And then...
“Israel heard.”
Yet Genesis 35 records no immediate speech from Jacob.
That silence is almost unbearable.
Imagine Reuben seeing his father afterward.
Did Jacob look at him differently?
Did Reuben know Jacob knew?
Did they sit at the same meals?
Did conversations suddenly become shorter?
Did Reuben spend months wondering when his father would finally say something?
Scripture does not tell us.
So we must not pretend to know.
But Scripture does tell us something far more important.
Jacob eventually spoke.
Years passed.
Families grew.
Joseph disappeared.
Famine came.
Egypt became their refuge.
Jacob became an old man.
And finally the sons gathered around their dying father.
This should have been Reuben’s moment.
He was the firstborn.
And Jacob began beautifully:
“Reuben, thou art my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength...”
Imagine hearing that.
After all those years.
My firstborn.
My might.
The beginning of my strength.
Perhaps for one trembling second, Reuben thought the past had finally disappeared.
Then Jacob continued.
“Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed; then defiledst thou it...”
The Hebrew begins:
פַּחַז כַּמַּיִם אַל־תּוֹתַר
Pachaz kammayim, al-totar.
The expression pictures instability or recklessness like water—something uncontrolled, surging beyond its boundary.
Then Jacob names the reason.
כִּי עָלִיתָ מִשְׁכְּבֵי אָבִיךָ
Ki alita mishkevei avikha.
“Because you went up to your father’s bed...”
Then comes the devastating word:
חִלַּלְתָּ
Chillalta.
“You profaned.”
“You defiled.”
The same father who had apparently said so little when it happened had not forgotten what happened.
Years had passed.
But consequences had been waiting at the end of them.
And later Scripture removes any doubt about the historical consequence.
First Chronicles 5:1 explains that although Reuben was Israel’s firstborn, because he defiled his father’s bed, his birthright was given to Joseph’s sons.
Reuben had possessed something precious.
Then sexual sin cost him something he could not simply reclaim by wishing the night had never happened.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why that hurts.
Because you have your own “Genesis 35:22.”
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe it happened ten years ago.
Maybe it happened last night.
Maybe it was adultery.
Pornography.
An affair you justified because your marriage felt empty.
A relationship you knew dishonored Christ.
Messages you keep deleting.
A secret emotional attachment.
A sexual compromise you renamed “love” because calling it sin would force you to confront it.
Maybe your secret is not sexual at all.
But there is something in your life about which you desperately hope:
God, please don't bring that up.
And this story whispers something uncomfortable.
God does not heal us by pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is not divine amnesia.
Grace is God dealing truthfully with what sin has done and doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
That is where Reuben’s story becomes larger than Reuben.
Because if this story ended only with consequences, every one of us would eventually be crushed beneath our own history.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Not Reuben.
All.
Not the adulterer somewhere else.
All.
Not the addict.
All.
Not the hypocrite you cannot stand.
All.
You.
Me.
Every respectable churchgoer.
Every prodigal.
Every preacher.
Every person secretly scrolling through something they would never put on the sanctuary screen.
Every person carrying memories they wish they could surgically remove from their mind.
We have all crossed lines before a holy God.
And sin has consequences.
That truth must not be softened.
Reuben lost privileges attached to his firstborn status. Scripture itself connects that loss to his defilement of his father’s bed.
Forgiveness does not always erase earthly consequences.
A forgiven prisoner may still serve a sentence.
A forgiven adulterer may still have to rebuild shattered trust.
A forgiven liar may discover that credibility takes years to restore.
A forgiven addict may still need accountability.
A forgiven parent may still have painful conversations with wounded children.
Grace does not mean pretending the wound never happened.
Grace means the wound does not have to become the final word.
And now watch the biblical story carefully.
Reuben lost the birthright.
Joseph received the firstborn inheritance privilege through his sons.
But another brother rose to prominence.
Judah.
First Chronicles says that Judah prevailed among his brothers and that from him came the ruler.
And generations later...
from Judah came David.
And ultimately, according to the flesh, from Judah came Jesus Christ.
Do you see where Scripture has carried us?
From a defiled bed...
through a fractured family...
through generations of deeply imperfect people...
to Bethlehem.
To Christ.
To the cross.
God did not need a spotless human family tree to send a spotless Savior.
He sent the spotless Savior because the human family was not spotless.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not enter history because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
He entered because we could not.
The scandal does not defeat the grace of God.
Grace confronts the scandal.
Grace exposes what darkness tries to hide.
Grace calls sin what God calls it.
Grace commands repentance.
Grace refuses cheap excuses.
And then grace points trembling sinners toward a crucified and risen Christ.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally the message:
“Try harder so God will tolerate you.”
It is the announcement that the Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
The answer to your secret is not better hiding.
It is Jesus.
The answer to your shame is not pretending the past never happened.
It is Jesus.
The answer to sexual sin is not merely stronger willpower.
It is repentance, truth, wise boundaries, accountability, and ultimately a heart being transformed by Jesus Christ.
Maybe you cannot undo what you did.
Reuben could not climb backward through history and erase Bilhah from that night.
David could not resurrect Uriah.
Peter could not unsay, “I know not the man.”
Paul could not bring Stephen back.
And you cannot travel backward either.
That may be one of the hardest truths you ever accept.
You cannot change yesterday.
But because Jesus Christ lives, yesterday does not have sovereign authority over tomorrow.
Your sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have to own the ending.
Your consequences may remain.
Christ can still redeem the person walking through them.
Your reputation may have collapsed.
Christ can still rebuild character where reputation once stood.
People may remember what you did.
Christ can transform who you are becoming.
Some doors may never reopen.
Christ is still Lord over every door that remains.
This is not permission to minimize sin.
It is permission to stop believing despair is more powerful than the blood of Christ.
There is a difference between repentance and self-hatred.
Repentance turns toward God.
Self-hatred keeps staring at self.
Repentance says, “I have sinned.”
Despair says, “Therefore I am beyond redemption.”
The Gospel agrees with the first sentence and destroys the second.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say He forgives only respectable sins.
It does not say He cleanses everyone except the sexually broken.
It does not say Christ receives people whose histories are merely embarrassing but rejects those whose histories are scandalous.
Jesus touched lepers.
Jesus received notorious sinners.
Jesus confronted sexual sin without redefining it.
Jesus offered living water to the Samaritan woman whose relationship history was already known to Him.
Jesus defended the holiness of marriage.
Jesus called people to repentance.
And Jesus went to a cross where mercy and justice met.
That means the Gospel never tells you, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
It tells you something infinitely better:
“Your sin mattered enough for Christ to die—and His grace is powerful enough to save sinners who come to Him.”
Perhaps this article found you while you are standing somewhere between Reuben’s night and Jacob’s deathbed.
The sin happened.
The full consequences have not.
You still have time to repent.
Do not confuse delayed consequences with divine approval.
Do not wait until the marriage collapses.
Do not wait until somebody discovers the messages.
Do not wait until your child finds the browser history.
Do not wait until lust becomes bondage.
Do not wait until secrecy hardens into a double life.
Do not wait until the thing you once controlled begins controlling you.
Come into the light.
Today.
Not after one more night.
Not after one final conversation.
Not after one last visit.
Not after one more click.
Today.
Jesus Christ is worth more than the sin you are protecting.
And perhaps you are reading from the other side.
Everybody already knows.
Your Jacob already heard.
Your family already cried.
Your consequences already arrived.
You lost something.
Maybe a marriage.
A ministry.
Trust.
Money.
Years.
Peace.
A relationship.
Maybe there are consequences you will carry for the rest of your earthly life.
Listen carefully.
Consequences are not proof that Christ has abandoned a repentant sinner.
Sometimes grace walks with us through consequences rather than removing them.
The cross does not promise that every earthly loss will be reversed.
It promises something greater: in Christ, condemnation does not have the final word.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
No condemnation does not mean no discipline.
No consequences.
No accountability.
No restitution where restitution is possible.
It means the courtroom of eternity has a Savior standing where the repentant sinner could never stand alone.
Jesus.
Only Jesus.
Maybe that is why Reuben’s story has survived for thousands of years.
Not so we can point at an ancient man and whisper, “How disgusting.”
But so we can look into the mirror and ask:
What am I doing with the things God already sees?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Maybe you are exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
Maybe nobody around you knows how badly you need prayer.
Then don't perform here.

Or if Christ has already brought you out of a place you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the rope God uses to remind another drowning person that the shore still exists.
And please don't only read this and move on.
There may be a night when temptation returns and you need to remember Reuben.
There may be a morning when shame returns and you need to remember Jesus.
Send it privately to the believer who has been disappearing lately.
Send it to the friend trapped between shame and secrecy.
Send it to the person who thinks he has sinned too badly to come home.
Not to expose anyone.
Not to shame anyone.
But because truth shared in love can become an invitation back into the light.

If you want your life and resources to glorify God, one practical way to participate in spreading biblical truth is to help sustain work that keeps putting Christ-centered teaching in front of people who desperately need it.
Follow.
Save what strengthens you.
Share what somebody else desperately needs.
Because somewhere tonight another Reuben is standing at the entrance to a decision that could haunt him for years.
Somewhere another person is sitting inside consequences that cannot be undone.
Somewhere another believer thinks one chapter has permanently disqualified him from every chapter that could follow.
And somewhere a sinner is finally discovering the difference between hiding from God and running to Christ.
Reuben's story warns us that one moment of rebellion can reach farther than we imagined.
But the Bible does not end with Reuben.
It keeps moving.
Through Judah.
Through generations.
Through Bethlehem.
To Jesus.
To a cross.
To an empty tomb.
To the announcement that sinners can be forgiven, captives can be freed, shame can lose its throne, and human beings with histories they cannot rewrite can be made new by the Savior who can.
You cannot rewrite Genesis 35:22.
Reuben could not either.
But Jesus Christ can take a life marked by what happened in the darkness and make the rest of that life testify to what His grace did in the light.
So repent while there is time.
Come into the light.
Stop protecting the thing that is destroying you.
Bring your sin to Christ.
Receive His mercy by faith.
Walk in obedience.
Accept whatever consequences truth requires.
And then keep following Jesus.
Because your worst chapter may remain part of your history without being allowed to become the title of your eternity.
The scandal may explain where you fell—but only Jesus gets to write what grace does after you get up.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ONCE SAVED, ALWAYS SAVED? CHRISTIANS HAVE DEBATED THIS FOR CENTURIES
paragraphs: ONCE SAVED, ALWAYS SAVED? CHRISTIANS HAVE DEBATED THIS FOR CENTURIES
Jesus Promised That No One Can Snatch His Sheep From His Hand. Scripture Also Warns Believers Not to Fall Away. So What Are We Supposed to Do With Both?
There is a terrifying question some Christians only whisper.
Maybe you have whispered it too.
Not in church.
Not when the worship music was playing.
Not when everybody around you seemed certain of everything.
But at two in the morning, when the room was dark and your conscience was loud.
After the sin you promised God you would never commit again.
After months of spiritual numbness.
After realizing that the Bible on your nightstand had collected more dust than your phone.
After wondering whether the person who once wept during worship could really have become this cold.
And somewhere inside you, a question surfaced that frightened you enough to keep you awake:
Am I still saved?
Then perhaps another voice answered almost immediately.
“Once saved, always saved.”
Four words.
For some Christians, those words are a fortress.
For others, they are dangerously incomplete.

For centuries, faithful Christians who love Jesus, believe the Bible, preach the cross, and confess Christ as Lord have disagreed over precisely how Scripture’s magnificent promises of preservation fit together with its terrifying warnings about falling away.
But perhaps we have sometimes asked the question in the wrong way.
Because the deepest question is not whether you can successfully defend a theological slogan.
The deepest question is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
And before this is over, that distinction may become painfully personal.
Jesus said something in John 10 that ought to make every trembling believer stop and listen.
Speaking about His sheep, He says:
“τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν… καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.”
“My sheep hear my voice… and they follow me.”
Then comes one of the strongest promises of assurance in the New Testament:
“κἀγὼ δίδωμι αὐτοῖς ζωὴν αἰώνιον, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.”
“I give them eternal life, and they will never perish.”
And Jesus continues:
“No one will snatch them out of my hand.”

Then He speaks of the Father’s hand and declares that no one is able to snatch them from Him either. John 10:27–29 presents salvation not merely as frightened sheep desperately gripping the Shepherd, but as sheep held by the Shepherd Himself.
Notice the Greek expression:
οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται — ou mē apolōntai.
The construction οὐ μή is emphatic. Jesus is not speaking casually about the destiny of His sheep.
They will certainly not perish.
Think about that.
Your salvation, if you truly belong to Christ, does not rest upon Jesus having weak hands.
It does not rest upon Satan being unable to devise a sufficiently clever temptation.
It does not rest upon your having a flawless emotional experience every morning.
Jesus says His sheep are in His hand.
And then Scripture seems to make the fortress even stronger.

Paul writes that he is convinced that neither death nor life, angels nor rulers, present things nor future things, powers, height, depth, “nor anything else in all creation” can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Read that last category carefully.
Anything else in creation.
Paul seems to search the universe for something powerful enough to tear Christ’s people away from God’s love…
and comes back empty-handed.

That is why Christians throughout history have found enormous comfort in the doctrine often called the perseverance or preservation of the saints: God does not merely begin salvation and then stand at a distance hoping His children somehow survive.
He keeps His people.
Yet if we stop reading there, we have not allowed the whole New Testament to speak.
Because then we reach Hebrews.
And suddenly the atmosphere changes.

Hebrews 6 describes people who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, tasted the goodness of God’s word and the powers of the coming age, and then speaks of those who have “fallen away.”
The warning is severe.
Uncomfortably severe.
It speaks about the impossibility of restoring such people again to repentance while they are repudiating the Son of God and exposing Him to public disgrace.
And we cannot honor Scripture by pretending that passage is not there.
A few chapters earlier Hebrews says:
“We have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end.”
Now the tension is sitting directly in front of us.
Jesus says no one can snatch His sheep from His hand.
Hebrews tells professing believers to hold firmly to Christ.
Paul celebrates the inseparable love of God.
Other New Testament passages repeatedly call Christians to endure, remain, continue, watch, resist, overcome, and persevere.
So which is true?
Both.
The disagreement among Christians is largely over how these truths fit together.

Those who hold to what is commonly called eternal security or perseverance of the saints generally understand genuine saving faith as something God preserves to the end. When someone permanently abandons Christ, they often point to 1 John 2:19:
“They went out from us, but they did not belong to us.”
The Greek is striking:
“ἐξ ἡμῶν ἐξῆλθαν ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἡμῶν.”
Literally, the thought is that they went out from among the Christian community because they were not truly “of” them; John says that had they truly belonged, they would have remained.
From this perspective, perseverance does not purchase salvation.
Perseverance reveals genuine faith.
The person is not saved because he managed to endure through sheer spiritual willpower. He endures because the God who saved him continues His work in him.

But other Christians, including many within Wesleyan, Arminian, and related traditions, understand Scripture’s apostasy warnings as describing a genuine possibility that must be taken with full seriousness. They emphasize that the New Testament does not speak its warnings into empty air. The commands to remain faithful, on this reading, describe a real covenant responsibility rather than merely a hypothetical danger.
That position should not be caricatured as “you lose your salvation every time you sin.”
And the eternal-security position should not be caricatured as “say a prayer once and then live for Satan without consequence.”
Neither caricature does justice to serious Christian theology.
More importantly, neither caricature does justice to Scripture.
Because whatever position you ultimately reach on the theological question, one conclusion should be impossible to escape:
The Bible never presents saving grace as permission to make peace with sin.
Never.
Grace is not Jesus saying, “Your rebellion no longer matters.”
Grace is Jesus taking rebels who deserve judgment, forgiving them through His blood, reconciling them to God, giving them His Spirit, and beginning the painful, beautiful work of making them new.
That changes the question.
Perhaps instead of asking only,
“Can I lose my salvation?”
some of us desperately need to ask:
“Why am I trying to discover how far away from Jesus I can walk while still calling myself His?”
That question hurts.
Because sometimes “once saved, always saved” is not being whispered by a frightened Christian who needs assurance.
Sometimes it is being used by an unrepentant person who wants immunity.
A childhood prayer.
A baptism certificate.
An altar-call memory.
A date written in the front of a Bible.
Meanwhile there is no hunger for Christ.
No war against sin.
No repentance.
No desire for holiness.
No grief over rebellion.
No interest in His Word.
No concern about becoming like Jesus.
Just a memory.
And a slogan.
Friend, Scripture never tells you to place your confidence in the memory of having once been emotional at an altar.
It tells you to place your confidence in Jesus Christ.
There is an enormous difference.
But now somebody reading this is experiencing the opposite problem.
You are not using grace as permission to sin.
You are terrified that your sin has finally exhausted grace.
You fell.
Again.
And you hate what happened.
You wonder whether a genuine Christian could struggle the way you struggle.
You have repented so many times that even the word “sorry” feels cheap coming out of your mouth.
You imagine Jesus looking at you with disgust.
You think perhaps this was the final failure.
Listen carefully.
The very warnings of Scripture that should awaken the presumptuous should not be twisted into weapons that crush every bruised believer who is running back to Christ.
Peter denied Jesus.
Not privately.
Not accidentally.
Three times.
At the moment when loyalty mattered most, Peter insisted that he did not know Him.
Imagine the silence after the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering Jesus’ prediction.
Imagine realizing that your courage lasted exactly as long as your safety did.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
And yet Peter’s scandal was not the final chapter.
Jesus came looking for him.
Beside a charcoal fire, after the resurrection, the Savior restored the disciple who had denied Him.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Peter had denied Him three times.
Christ confronted the wound, restored the man, and recommissioned him.
“Feed My sheep.”
That is the Gospel.
Not that Peter’s denial did not matter.
It mattered terribly.
Not that sin is harmless.
It nailed the Son of God to a cross.
But Peter discovered something every broken believer eventually has to discover:
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when Jesus Christ takes the pen.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But grace does not rewrite your story by pretending the scandal was righteousness.
Grace names the darkness.
Grace exposes it.
Grace calls it sin.
Grace leads us to repentance.
Then grace does what shame never could.
Grace washes.
Grace restores.
Grace transforms.
The cross is where God demonstrates simultaneously how horrifying our sin is and how astonishing His mercy is.
If sin were trivial, Calvary would make no sense.
If sinners were beyond redemption, Calvary would make no sense either.
At the cross, both lies die.
Your sin is worse than your excuses say.
God’s grace is greater than your shame says.
And Jesus is enough.
This is why the question “Once saved, always saved?” cannot safely become a license for spiritual sleep.
If your theology of security makes you comfortable abandoning Christ, something has gone terribly wrong.
Biblical assurance does not say:
“I can walk away from Jesus because I once had Jesus.”
Biblical assurance looks toward Christ and says:
“My Shepherd is faithful. His grace is sufficient. His hands are strong. So I will keep following the One who first loved me.”
Remember how Jesus describes His sheep.
They hear His voice.
He knows them.
They follow Him.
The evidence of belonging to the Shepherd is not sinless perfection.
If perfection were the standard, none of us could stand.

The evidence is a living relationship in which the Shepherd continues calling and His sheep continue being drawn after Him—even through failure, discipline, wandering, tears, repentance, and restoration.
Sometimes the sheep limps.
Sometimes the sheep gets covered in mud.
Sometimes the Shepherd must carry it.
But the answer to wandering is never to convince yourself that the wilderness is home.
It is to hear His voice again.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not so you could win an argument between Calvinists and Arminians.
Not so you could collect another theological weapon for Facebook.
Maybe God is using this moment to ask something much closer to your heart.
Where are you with Jesus?
Not your denomination.
Not your parents.
Not your pastor.
Not the Christian version of yourself everyone else sees.
You.
When nobody is watching.
Is there hidden sin slowly becoming normal?
Have you learned Christian language while losing Christian affection?
Have you mistaken knowing theology for knowing Christ?
Have you been saying, “I’m saved,” while resisting the Savior?
Or perhaps you are on the other side of this.
You genuinely love Jesus, but your failures have convinced you He must be finished with you.
Then hear the Gospel again.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because you were easy to save.
He went because you were helpless to save yourself.
You are not justified by becoming impressive enough for God.
Salvation is by grace.
Christ is the Savior.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ intercedes.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
And the Christian life that follows is not an attempt to repay Jesus for salvation.
It is the transformed life produced by having encountered mercy.
So do not use eternal security to run away from Jesus.
And do not use the warnings of Scripture to run away from Jesus either.
Run to Jesus.
That is where both assurance and warning are meant to drive you.
If you are complacent, wake up and run to Jesus.
If you are backsliding, turn around and run to Jesus.
If you are addicted, stop hiding and run to Jesus.
If you are ashamed, run to Jesus.
If you are spiritually exhausted, run to Jesus.
If you have questions, bring them while running to Jesus.
If you fell yesterday, repent and run to Jesus.
If you have spent years pretending, today can become the day the pretending ends.
Run to Jesus.
Because Christianity is ultimately not about whether you know the correct password to eternal security.
It is about Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The reigning Christ.
The Christ who receives repentant sinners.
The Christ who breaks chains.
The Christ who disciplines those He loves.
The Christ who calls His sheep by name.
The Christ whose blood cleanses sinners.
The Christ whose resurrection announces that death does not get the last word.
The Christ whose hands still bear scars.
And those are the hands Jesus says hold His sheep.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the comments into another theological battlefield.
Make them a place of honesty.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting that battle.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Somebody may be using “once saved, always saved” to excuse a life moving farther and farther from Christ.
Somebody else may love Christ deeply and nevertheless be terrified that one terrible failure placed them beyond His mercy.
Send this to both.
Because there may come a night when you are the person who needs to read it again.

Supporting Gospel ministry can be a genuine act of Christian generosity and partnership when it is given freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully before God. We should never manipulate people into giving by suggesting otherwise.

But supporting sound Gospel work is one practical way believers can help more Scripture, discipleship resources, Christian books, encouragement, and Gospel-centered content reach people who need them.
Most importantly, your support becomes partnership in the work.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help enormously.
Send it privately to someone struggling.
Pray that every person reached will see beyond the page, beyond the ministry, beyond the writer…
and see Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A theological system is not the Savior.
Your church attendance is not the Savior.
Your ability to hold yourself together is not the Savior.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And perhaps that is the answer your exhausted soul needed more than another argument.
Can Christ truly save?
Yes.
Can Christ truly keep?
His promises give trembling believers profound reason for confidence.
Should Scripture’s warnings about unbelief, apostasy, and perseverance be taken seriously?
Absolutely.
So instead of turning assurance into presumption or warning into despair, hear the voice of the Shepherd and follow Him.
Repent where you have wandered.
Believe where fear has taken over.
Return where sin has pulled you away.
Rest where shame has exhausted you.
Keep following Jesus.
And when you stumble, do not build a house where you fell.
Get up.
Look toward the scarred hands of the Shepherd.
And come home.
Because maybe the most important question was never merely:
“Once saved, always saved?”
Maybe the question beneath the question has always been:
“Do I know the Shepherd… and am I hearing His voice today?”
Do not spend your life arguing about whether Jesus can hold His sheep while quietly refusing to follow Him.
The hands that were pierced for you are still the safest place for a repentant sinner to come home to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY KNOW YOU’RE MARRIED—SO WHY DO THEY KEEP FLIRTING WITH YOU AT CHURCH?
paragraphs: THEY KNOW YOU’RE MARRIED—SO WHY DO THEY KEEP FLIRTING WITH YOU AT CHURCH?
When attention starts feeling flattering, boundaries start feeling cruel, and something that looks innocent begins asking your heart to betray what God told you to protect.
There is a kind of temptation that does not look like temptation at first.
It does not arrive carrying a bottle.
It does not walk through the church doors announcing adultery.
It does not whisper, “Destroy your marriage.”
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it knows the worship songs.
Sometimes it says, “God bless you.”
Sometimes it serves in ministry, talks about Jesus, knows you are married…
…and keeps finding reasons to be near you anyway.
The messages become a little too personal.
The compliments become a little too warm.
The eye contact lasts a little too long.
The jokes develop a private undertone.
They seem unusually interested in how your marriage is going.
They notice when you are discouraged.
They remember details nobody else remembers.
And somewhere beneath all the Christian vocabulary, something begins happening that both of you know is not entirely innocent anymore.
But nobody has technically “done anything.”
Not yet.
And that little phrase can become one of the most dangerous lies in the room.
Because some betrayals begin long before bodies touch.
They begin when hearts start making room.
Maybe you are reading this because somebody at church keeps flirting with you even though they know you belong to someone else.
Maybe you have tried to dismiss it.
“They’re just friendly.”
“That’s just their personality.”
“I would never actually cheat.”
“We’re only talking.”
Or perhaps the truth is harder to admit.
You noticed it…
and part of you liked being noticed.

That does not mean your marriage is already destroyed. It does not mean you are beyond grace. But it may mean this is the moment to become brutally honest before something small becomes something devastating.
Because Jesus does not merely confront adultery after it reaches the bedroom.
He goes after the heart while the battle can still be won there.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus says:
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
The Greek becomes especially revealing.
Jesus speaks of looking at another person πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai — looking in a way directed toward desire or lust.
Jesus is exposing something deeper than accidental recognition of another person’s attractiveness.
There is a difference between noticing beauty and feeding desire.
There is a difference between receiving attention and cultivating it.
There is a difference between an unwanted temptation entering your mind and opening the door, pulling up a chair, and asking it to stay.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because if somebody repeatedly flirts with you knowing you are married, the question eventually stops being only:
“Why are they doing this?”
A more important question becomes:
“What am I doing with it?”
You cannot always control who becomes attracted to you.
You cannot control every comment somebody makes.
You cannot control every temptation that appears.
But you are responsible before God for what you entertain, encourage, conceal, fantasize about, and protect.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.”
The Hebrew expression begins:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
Mi-kol mishmar, netzor libbekha.
The idea is powerful: guard your heart with vigilance.
Not because the heart is worthless.
Because it is precious.
We put guards around things worth protecting.
And marriage is worth protecting before there is a crisis.
Your spouse should not have to discover an emotional relationship you kept calling friendship because admitting what it had become would have required you to end it.
Read that again.
Sometimes the most dangerous person threatening a marriage is not somebody obviously seductive.
Sometimes it is the person who “understands you.”
The person who listens when your spouse seems distracted.
The person who laughs at your jokes when home feels tense.
The person who compliments the part of you that has felt invisible.
The person who makes you feel desirable again.
And suddenly what began as attention becomes anticipation.
You start wondering whether they will be at church.
You notice what they are wearing.
You check whether they viewed your story.
You feel disappointed when they do not message.
You delete something you would rather your spouse not see.
You tell yourself nothing happened.
But your heart knows something is happening.
That is why Scripture does not merely tell believers to resist certain situations while standing as close to them as possible.
Paul tells Timothy:
“Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace…”
—2 Timothy 2:22
The Greek verb translated “flee” is φεῦγε — pheuge.
Flee.
Not negotiate.
Not investigate how close you can stand to the fire without smelling like smoke.
Flee.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is make the boundary unmistakably clear.
“I love my spouse, and this interaction is becoming inappropriate. It needs to stop.”
That may feel awkward.
Good.
Awkwardness is cheaper than adultery.
A difficult conversation is cheaper than a shattered home.
An unfollow is cheaper than months of secrecy.
Moving seats is cheaper than rebuilding trust.
Ending unnecessary private conversations is cheaper than explaining to your children why everything changed.
And if the person gets offended because you established a boundary protecting your marriage, their offense does not automatically mean your boundary was wrong.
A godly person should not need secret access to somebody else’s spouse.
But there is another side to this article that cannot be ignored.
What if you are the one doing the flirting?
What if you know that person is married?
What if you keep telling yourself it is harmless because there has been no kiss, no affair, no hotel room?
Then hear this without hatred and without humiliation:
Stop.
Not because God hates you.
Because sin destroys things God loves.
Another person’s marriage is not your opportunity.
Their loneliness is not your invitation.
Their marital struggles are not permission for you to become their emotional substitute.
Their attention is not evidence that God is “bringing you together.”
God does not need you to violate biblical faithfulness in order to accomplish His will.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled…”
Among all.
Not merely among married people.
Marriage deserves honor from the people inside it and from the people standing outside it.
That means if you know somebody is married, their covenant deserves your respect even when their marriage is struggling.
Especially then.
And church should never become camouflage for behavior we would immediately recognize as inappropriate anywhere else.
Spiritual language does not sanctify emotional adultery.
“I’m praying for you” can still become an excuse for inappropriate intimacy.
“God put you on my heart” can still be manipulated.
“Your spouse doesn’t appreciate you” can still become poison.
Even ministry can become the environment in which two people slowly give each other what should have remained protected within appropriate boundaries.
Do not baptize temptation with Christian vocabulary.
Call it what it is before it becomes what you never imagined it could become.
And if you are the married person receiving the attention, please understand something else.
Your marriage does not need to be perfect for your covenant to deserve protection.
Maybe home has been difficult.
Maybe affection has grown cold.
Maybe you feel unseen.
Maybe you have been carrying resentment for years.
Maybe the flirtation feels intoxicating precisely because somebody is giving you what you desperately wish your spouse would give you.
That pain matters.
It needs attention.
It may require confession, counseling, pastoral help, hard conversations, forgiveness, rebuilding, and time.
But another person cannot heal your marriage by becoming a secret escape from it.
They can only complicate the wound.
This is why temptation can be so deceptive.
It often offers legitimate desires through illegitimate doors.
The desire to be loved is not evil.
The desire to feel attractive is not automatically evil.
The desire to be understood is not evil.
The desire for affection is not evil.
But good desires can become dangerous when we decide God’s boundaries are preventing our happiness rather than protecting something holy.
This pattern is ancient.
Genesis 3 begins with a boundary being questioned.
“Did God actually say…?”
That question still echoes through temptation.
Did God really say this friendship is too close?
Is flirting really that serious?
Is deleting messages really wrong if nothing physical happened?
Do I really need to tell my spouse?
Do I really need to stop talking to this person?
And slowly the question changes from:
“What honors Christ?”
to:
“How much can I get away with?”
Those are very different questions.
The Christian life is not supposed to be an endless search for the nearest legal parking space beside sin.
We belong to Jesus.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 6:18
Again, Scripture says flee.
And only a few verses later:
“You were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
—1 Corinthians 6:20
You were bought with a price.
That changes everything.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your eyes belong to Christ.
Your messages belong to Christ.
Your private conversations belong to Christ.
Your marriage belongs under the lordship of Christ.
Even the parts of your life nobody else sees are lived before Christ.
But perhaps you have already crossed the line.
Perhaps this article found you too late for innocence.
There were messages.
Maybe photographs.
Maybe emotional intimacy.
Maybe touching.
Maybe kissing.
Maybe sex.
Maybe your spouse still does not know.
And now shame is screaming:
“You hypocrite.”
“You ruined everything.”
“God is finished with you.”
No.
Do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
The Gospel does not minimize your sin.
It does something infinitely more beautiful.
It tells the truth about your sin…
and then points you toward a Savior powerful enough to forgive sinners.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Confession is not pretending the wound never happened.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible.
Biblical repentance turns.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — carries the sense of a changed mind expressed in a changed direction.
Grace is not permission to continue hiding.
Grace calls you out of hiding.
You may need to end the relationship completely.
You may need to block the number.
You may need to confess.
You may need wise pastoral accountability.
You may need professional marriage counseling.
You may need to surrender your phone, your pride, your excuses, and your carefully edited version of the story.
There may be consequences.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence of sin.
Trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
Tears may come.
Questions may come.
Healing may take longer than you want.
But do not mistake a painful road back for the absence of God.
Sometimes grace looks like Jesus walking with you through the wreckage while teaching you never to build the same house of lies again.
Remember the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her sin was dragged into public view.
Religious men were ready to turn her scandal into her identity.
But after her accusers disappeared, Jesus did something extraordinary.
He neither crushed her nor celebrated her sin.
He said:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
Grace…
and truth.
Mercy…
and transformation.
No condemnation from Christ did not become permission to return unchanged.
That is the Gospel pattern.
Jesus does not save us so we can become more comfortable with the chains.
He saves us to make us free.
So if somebody keeps flirting with you at church knowing you are married, do not wait until you “feel strong enough.”
Create distance now.
Be clear now.
Protect your marriage now.
Bring darkness into light now.
If necessary, involve appropriate church leadership—not to manufacture drama, humiliate anyone, or spread gossip, but to establish wise accountability and safety.

And if the attention is persistent after you have clearly rejected it, especially if it becomes coercive, threatening, harassing, or makes you feel unsafe, this is no longer merely a question of flirtation. Seek help from trusted leadership and appropriate authorities when necessary. Christian forgiveness does not require unrestricted access to you.
Boundaries are not hatred.
Sometimes boundaries are love refusing to cooperate with destruction.
And married believer, do not only run away from temptation.
Run toward your marriage.
Flirt with your spouse again.
Listen again.
Date again.
Pray together again.
Speak appreciation again.
Have the uncomfortable conversations.
Ask where they feel lonely.
Tell them where you feel lonely.
Seek help before resentment becomes architecture.
Remember why you chose each other.
And above everything else, run toward Christ together.
Because your spouse was never meant to replace Jesus.
No husband can carry the weight of being someone’s savior.
No wife can satisfy every hunger of the human soul.
Marriage becomes distorted when we demand from another human being what only Christ can ultimately provide.
Jesus remains the center.
Jesus remains the healer.
Jesus remains the One who forgives.
Jesus remains the One who transforms.
Jesus remains the One who can take what shame called irreparable and write redemption across it.
That does not mean every marriage story ends exactly the way we want. Scripture never promises that every consequence disappears or that every human relationship will automatically be restored.
But the Gospel does promise something greater than pretending nothing happened.
In Christ, sin does not have to write the final sentence of your life.
Maybe this article is not really about somebody flirting with you.
Maybe it is about the part of you that desperately needed to know you were still desirable.
Maybe it is about loneliness.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe secrecy.
Maybe an old wound.
Maybe the marriage you stopped fighting for.
Maybe the temptation you have been feeding while praying God would remove it.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is putting His finger on something you hoped nobody would ever see.
Do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Repentance is not the doorway into humiliation.
Through Christ, repentance becomes the doorway out of slavery.
There is blood enough at the cross for adulterers.
There is blood enough for flirts.
There is blood enough for hypocrites.
There is blood enough for secret sinners.
There is blood enough for broken husbands and wounded wives.
There is blood enough for the person who crossed the boundary and suddenly realizes how far they wandered.
Jesus did not die for the imaginary version of you who never struggled.
Christ died for sinners.
And He rose again.
That means your scandal does not have greater resurrection power than your Savior.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
Jesus does.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light begins with refusing to pretend you do not have one.
Not as an accusation.
As a rescue rope.
Send it privately to the believer who needs truth without humiliation.
You may not need these words today.
You may need them on the night temptation starts sounding reasonable.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help it reach more people. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ. But voluntary generosity can support ministry and help truthful, Christ-centered resources reach people who desperately need them.
But whatever you do after reading this, remember:
Do not trade a covenant for a compliment.
Do not trade integrity for attention.
Do not trade years of trust for a few minutes of feeling desired.
Do not wait for temptation to become adultery before deciding it was dangerous.
Guard your heart.
Honor your spouse.
Respect other people’s marriages.
Run from sexual immorality.
Run toward righteousness.
And when you fall, do not run deeper into darkness.
Run toward Jesus.
Because perhaps the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is that Jesus can meet someone standing in the ashes of terrible decisions and begin writing a story that shame could never have written.
The scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when you surrender the pen to Christ, it does not get to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON’S WEDDING NIGHT DISASTER: His Bride Was Given to His Best Man
paragraphs: SAMSON’S WEDDING NIGHT DISASTER: His Bride Was Given to His Best Man

He walked away from his own wedding burning with rage. When he finally came back for his wife, another man had already taken his place. But beneath Samson’s humiliation is a terrifying warning about desire, compromise, betrayal—and the God who can still accomplish His purposes through the wreckage of broken people.
Imagine returning for your wife...
and discovering that her father had already given her to another man.
Not a stranger.
Not some distant rival.
The man who had stood beside you at your wedding.
That is essentially where Samson’s story takes us.
And somehow, the betrayal is not even the most disturbing part.
Because long before Samson lost his bride, something else was already going wrong inside him.
The disaster did not begin when another man entered the picture.
It began with what Samson allowed to rule his eyes.

Judges introduces Samson as a miracle child. Israel had again done evil before the LORD, and the Philistines oppressed them for forty years. Then the Angel of the LORD appeared to a barren woman and announced that she would bear a son who would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
Before Samson ever opened his eyes, God had placed a calling over his life.
He was to be a Nazirite from the womb.
Set apart.
Consecrated.
Marked for God.
Then Samson grew up.
And one day he went down to Timnah.
There he saw a Philistine woman.
That sounds almost harmless until you keep reading.
Samson returned to his parents and essentially said:
I saw her.
Get her for me.
His parents were troubled. Why choose a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines rather than among his own people?
But Samson insisted.
Judges 14:3 preserves the force of his reasoning:
“Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes.”
The Hebrew behind that final thought is striking:
כִּי־הִיא יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי
ki-hi yashrah be'enai
Literally, the language carries the sense that she was “right” or “pleasing” in his eyes.
That phrase should make anyone familiar with Judges uncomfortable.
Because the book eventually summarizes Israel’s spiritual collapse with hauntingly similar language:
“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
Samson was supposed to begin delivering Israel from the Philistines.
Yet Samson himself was already beginning to resemble the spiritually disordered Israel he had been called to help.
His eyes were becoming his compass.
And when your eyes become your compass, desire can start impersonating discernment.
“I want this” slowly becomes “this must be right.”
“I feel strongly about this” becomes “God must be in this.”
“I cannot stop thinking about this person” becomes “this must be God’s will.”
But intensity is not the same thing as obedience.
Attraction is not the same thing as confirmation.
Desire is a powerful servant and a terrible god.
And yet Scripture immediately prevents us from reducing Samson’s story to a simplistic moral lesson.
Judges 14:4 tells us something Samson himself apparently did not understand.
His father and mother did not know that this situation was “from the LORD,” because God was seeking an occasion against the Philistines.
That does not mean every impulse Samson had was righteous.
It means something far greater.
God was sovereign even over a deeply complicated situation.
The Lord could accomplish His purposes without declaring every human decision in the story morally good.
That distinction matters.
God’s sovereignty over human failure does not transform failure into faithfulness.
The Bible repeatedly shows a God so sovereign that even human sin cannot overthrow His purposes.
And Samson is about to become living proof.
He travels toward Timnah, and a young lion comes roaring toward him.
Then the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon Samson.
He tears the lion apart with his bare hands.
Later he passes the carcass again and discovers bees and honey inside it.
Samson takes the honey.
Then he eventually turns this bizarre experience into entertainment at his wedding feast.
“Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet.”
Thirty Philistine companions are challenged to solve the riddle.
If they solve it, Samson owes them thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing.
If they fail, they owe him the same.
It sounds like a wedding game.
Then everything turns dark.
The Philistine men cannot solve the riddle, so they threaten Samson’s bride.
Judges 14 records their threat in brutal terms: persuade your husband to tell us the answer, or we will burn you and your father’s house with fire.
Imagine being that bride.
Your wedding celebration has become a death threat.
The men surrounding you are no longer guests.
They are potential executioners.
So she weeps before Samson.
She presses him.
She accuses him of not truly loving her because he will not reveal the answer.
Day after day, the pressure continues.
Eventually Samson gives in.
He tells her.
She tells them.
And before sunset on the seventh day, the men answer Samson’s riddle:
“What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?”
Samson immediately realizes what happened.
His response is sharp and humiliating.
“If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle.”
The wedding has collapsed into manipulation, threats, betrayal, wounded pride, and rage.
Then the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon Samson. He goes to Ashkelon, kills thirty men, takes their garments, and gives the clothing to those who solved the riddle.
And Samson leaves.
Furious.
He returns to his father’s house.
The wedding is shattered.
The bride remains behind.
Then Scripture delivers the sentence that makes the whole disaster feel almost unbearable:
“And Samson’s wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.”
The Hebrew describes this man as his מֵרֵעַ—mere'a—his companion, friend, or close associate, the man who had attended him.
The man beside the groom...
became the groom.
Imagine Samson eventually discovering that.
The woman he had demanded.
The wedding he had entered.
The future he thought belonged to him.
Gone.
Another man now occupied the place Samson believed was his.
But Samson was not finished.
Judges 15 says that sometime later, during the wheat harvest, Samson returned to visit his wife carrying a young goat.
He intended to go into her room.
Her father stopped him.
“I really thought that you utterly hated her,” he explained, so he had given her to Samson’s companion.
Then, astonishingly, he offered Samson her younger sister instead.
The situation had become grotesque.
People were being treated like possessions.
Fear had produced betrayal.
Pride had produced violence.
Assumptions had produced another marriage.
And Samson exploded.
He captured three hundred foxes or jackals, tied torches between their tails, lit the torches, and released them into the Philistines’ grain fields, vineyards, and olive orchards.
The harvest burned.
The Philistines asked who had done it.
When they learned why, they retaliated with horrifying cruelty.
They burned Samson’s wife and her father.
Notice the tragedy.
The very fate she had been threatened with during the wedding feast eventually came upon her anyway.
Fear had driven her betrayal.
But compromise with evil could not finally make evil safe.
That is one of the darkest realities in this story.
Sometimes we surrender truth because we believe compromise will protect us.
We hide.
We manipulate.
We lie.
We give people what they demand.
We tell ourselves:
“I just need to survive this.”
But sin makes promises it cannot keep.
Samson’s story keeps descending.
Desire.
Secrets.
Manipulation.
Anger.
Retaliation.
Bloodshed.
Loss.
And later, another woman enters Samson’s story.
Delilah.
Again there is intimacy.
Again there is pressure.
Again there is a secret.
Again Samson is worn down by persistent questioning.
Only this time the consequences become catastrophic.
His hair is cut.
His strength leaves him.
The Philistines seize him.
His eyes—the very eyes that repeatedly helped govern his desires—are gouged out.
The man who once lived by what looked right in his eyes is eventually left unable to see at all.
He becomes a prisoner.
Bound.
Humiliated.
Grinding grain for the enemies he was born to confront.
If Samson’s story ended there, it would simply be a tragedy about wasted potential.
But Scripture gives us one more scene.
And this is where scandal begins bending toward grace.
The Philistines gather in the temple of Dagon to celebrate.
They believe their god has delivered Samson into their hands.
They bring Samson out for entertainment.
The deliverer has become the joke.
The warrior has become the spectacle.
The strong man has become dependent upon a boy to lead him by the hand.
And somewhere between the pillars...
Samson prays.
“Lord GOD, remember me.”
Think about that prayer.
Not the prayer of a man standing triumphantly over a lion.
Not the prayer of a celebrated hero.
It comes from a blind prisoner whose life bears the scars of catastrophic choices.
“Remember me.”
There is something painfully human about those words.
Maybe that is where you are.
Not physically between two pillars.
But looking at something in your life and wondering:
How did I get here?
Maybe you ignored warnings because you wanted something too badly.
Maybe loneliness convinced you to call attachment love.
Maybe you kept returning to something God was trying to expose.
Maybe anger became part of your identity.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe you have spent years blaming the person who hurt you without confronting what has been happening inside your own heart.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still smile.
You still go to church.
You still post Bible verses.
You still tell everybody, “God is good.”
But there is a room inside your heart you desperately hope nobody opens.
And this is where Samson’s story stops being ancient history.
Because the deepest question is not:
“Have you ever made a mess?”
The question is:
What do you do when the mess finally exposes you?
Samson prayed.
That does not erase everything he had done.
Grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
Biblical grace is more astonishing than that.
Grace meets guilty, shattered people with mercy they could never purchase for themselves.
And Samson’s life ultimately points beyond Samson.
Because Samson was never the Savior Israel truly needed.
He was a deeply flawed deliverer.
Jesus Christ is the greater Deliverer.
Samson repeatedly moved toward what pleased his own eyes.
Jesus could say that He came not to do His own will but the will of the Father who sent Him.
Samson's story became entangled with retaliation.
Jesus willingly gave Himself for His enemies.
Samson stretched out his arms between pillars and died while bringing judgment upon Israel’s enemies.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ stretched out His arms upon a cross and willingly bore judgment so that sinners who were enemies of God could be reconciled to Him.
The comparison is not that Samson and Jesus are moral equals.
They are not.
That is precisely the point.
Samson shows us how desperately humanity needs a better Deliverer.
And His name is Jesus.
The New Testament announces the heart of the Gospel with a word that Samson desperately needed and every one of us still needs:
χάρις
charis.
Grace.
Not permission to continue worshiping our desires.
Not religious language painted over rebellion.
Grace.
God's undeserved favor toward sinners, supremely revealed in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel says your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die...
and His grace is powerful enough that everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith can be forgiven.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the public image of broken people.
He came to save sinners.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the same Christ who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
Repentance means we stop defending the throne our desires have occupied.
We turn toward Christ.
We confess.
We surrender.
We follow.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe there are no burned fields behind you.
No ruined wedding feast.
No prison.
No crowd laughing at your downfall.
Maybe your battlefield exists entirely inside your heart.
But Jesus sees it.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The emotional affair you keep calling friendship.
The pride hiding behind ministry.
The secret messages.
The jealousy.
The rage.
The addiction to attention.
The resentment toward God.
The compromise you keep promising will be “the last time.”
Christ sees what everyone else misses.
And He still calls sinners to come.
Not to hide better.
To come.
Not to perform harder.
To come.
Not to repair yourself enough to deserve mercy.
To repent and believe the Gospel.
This is why Samson’s wedding disaster matters thousands of years later.
Because some disasters happen in one night...
but begin in the heart long before anyone can see them.
Guard what governs you.
Do not automatically trust something because it looks right in your eyes.
Bring your desires under the authority of Scripture.
Listen when godly people warn you.
Do not confuse obsession with calling.
Do not let humiliation turn into vengeance.
Do not let betrayal transform you into the kind of person who destroys everything around you.
And when you fail, do not make another idol out of your failure.
Run to Christ.
The God who worked through the wreckage of Samson's story is not threatened by the wreckage of yours.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It means consequences do not have the authority to become your savior, your identity, or your final word.
Jesus Christ gets the final word over everyone who belongs to Him.
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Being transformed.
Held by grace.
Samson appears again, surprisingly, in Hebrews 11 among people remembered in connection with faith.
That should humble us.
Scripture does not sanitize Samson's life to put him there.
The Bible leaves the ugly chapters intact.
God receives the glory precisely because biblical redemption never depends upon pretending the scandal did not happen.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by rewriting history so sin suddenly becomes virtue.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming sinners who could never redeem themselves.
So be honest.
What has been ruling your eyes lately?
What desire have you been defending because you want it too much to question it?
What secret is exhausting you?
What betrayal are you still allowing to control you?
What compromise are you hoping nobody discovers?
What would happen if instead of hiding one more day...
you brought it to Jesus?
Your testimony might become the sentence God uses to remind another wounded believer that their darkest chapter does not have to be their last.
Not because Samson's disaster is entertaining.
Not for empty engagement.
For the Gospel.

If something points people faithfully toward Jesus, repentance, forgiveness, Scripture, and eternal life, helping that truth travel farther can itself become an act of service. Glorifying God is far bigger than clicking a button, of course; Scripture calls us to offer our whole lives to Him.
Following Gospel Warrior means staying close to daily Scripture, biblical conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and Christ-centered truth.
Grace cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Not because sharing a post proves your faith.
But because if Christ-centered truth helped you, there may be someone scrolling tonight whose private life is collapsing while everybody thinks they are fine.
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
read...
and remember Jesus.
Samson thought his wedding disaster was about a stolen bride.
But underneath the scandal was a much deeper war over desire, obedience, pride, judgment, calling, and grace.
And perhaps underneath the mess you are facing right now, God is exposing something deeper too.
Do not waste the exposure.
Bring it into the light.
Bring it to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek help where you need help.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to the Savior.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Samson is not that a powerful man became broken.
It is that even from the wreckage, God remained God.
And the most unforgettable truth about your story may someday be this:
The chapter that exposed how badly you needed Jesus became the chapter where you finally stopped running from Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID THIS ABOUT MARRIAGE—AND HIS OWN DISCIPLES WONDERED IF IT WAS BETTER NOT TO MARRY
paragraphs: JESUS SAID THIS ABOUT MARRIAGE—AND HIS OWN DISCIPLES WONDERED IF IT WAS BETTER NOT TO MARRY

They had watched Jesus heal the sick, confront demons, forgive sinners, and silence religious leaders. But when He explained what marriage really meant in the eyes of God, even His disciples seemed stunned.
There is a sentence in Matthew 19 that Christians sometimes read too quickly.
We remember Jesus talking about marriage.
We remember the Pharisees asking Him about divorce.
We remember, “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
But then something extraordinary happens.
The disciples hear Jesus.
Not the Pharisees.
Not the hostile crowd.
His own disciples.
Men who had left everything to follow Him.
And their reaction is almost startling:

“If the case of the man be so with his wife, it is not good to marry.”
—Matthew 19:10, KJV
In other words:
If marriage is really that serious… maybe it is better not to get married at all.
Think about that.

Whatever Jesus had just said about marriage was so weighty that His disciples apparently realized marriage was far more serious than simply finding someone you loved, celebrating a wedding, building a home, and hoping everything worked out.
Jesus had taken them somewhere deeper.
Back before the arguments.
Back before the loopholes.
Back before the certificates of divorce.
Back before human beings started asking, “Under what circumstances can I get out?”
Jesus took them back to the beginning.
And maybe that is exactly where some of us need to go.
Because we live in a generation that has become remarkably skilled at discussing relationships while sometimes forgetting the God who created them.
We talk about compatibility.
Chemistry.
Boundaries.
Red flags.
Love languages.
Attraction.
Personal fulfillment.
We ask whether someone “makes us happy.”
And some of those conversations can be useful.
But Jesus asks something deeper.
What did God intend?
The confrontation begins when some Pharisees approach Jesus with a test:

“Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?”
—Matthew 19:3, KJV
Matthew tells us they were tempting—or testing—Him.
This was not merely an innocent request for marriage counseling.

Divorce was already the subject of serious Jewish debate. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 was central to those discussions, and different interpretations existed regarding the grounds on which a husband might divorce his wife.
But watch what Jesus does.
They want to begin with divorce.
Jesus begins with creation.

“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female…”
—Matthew 19:4, KJV
Then Jesus brings together the creation language of Genesis:

“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?”
—Matthew 19:5, KJV
And then comes the sentence that still confronts every generation:

“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
—Matthew 19:6, KJV
The Greek is powerful.
Jesus says:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν, ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω
ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō
“What therefore God joined together, let a human being not separate.”
The word translated “joined together,” συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen, carries the idea of joining or yoking together.
Notice who stands at the center of Jesus’ statement.
God.
Not merely the bride.
Not merely the groom.
Not merely the officiant.
God.
That changes the atmosphere of the entire conversation.
Marriage, in Jesus’ teaching, cannot be reduced to a private arrangement between two people that remains meaningful only while both people find it convenient.
Jesus points toward something God Himself established in creation.
And that is why the Pharisees immediately bring up Moses.
If marriage is that serious, they ask, why did Moses command a certificate of divorce?
Jesus answers:

“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
—Matthew 19:8, KJV
There is a devastating phrase buried inside that answer:
σκληροκαρδία — sklērokardia
Hardness of heart.
The word combines the ideas of hardness and heart.
Suddenly this is not merely a legal discussion.
Jesus has exposed something spiritual.
Sometimes behind the wreckage of human relationships there is something deeper than incompatibility.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Betrayal.
Lust.
Selfishness.
Cruelty.
Refusal to forgive.
Refusal to repent.
A heart becoming harder and harder until someone we once promised to love begins to feel like an enemy.
And before anyone uses this passage as ammunition against someone else, notice where the Gospel always forces us to look eventually:
inside ourselves.
Because hardness of heart is not merely “their” problem.
Every human heart is capable of becoming hard.
You can sing worship songs with a hard heart.
You can quote Scripture with a hard heart.
You can attend church while refusing to apologize.
You can know Christian vocabulary while quietly feeding resentment.
You can appear spiritually mature in public while making your spouse feel invisible at home.
You can win arguments and slowly destroy intimacy.
And sometimes the most frightening words in a marriage are not shouted.
Sometimes they are never spoken.
“I don't care anymore.”
Maybe you know that silence.
Maybe you have slept inches away from someone who felt a thousand miles away.
Maybe you remember when you could not wait to hear their voice.
Now almost every conversation becomes tension.
Maybe you are reading this after betrayal.
Maybe divorce papers have already been signed.
Maybe someone abandoned you despite your desperate attempts to save the marriage.
Maybe abuse shattered what should have been a place of safety.
Maybe you were the one who sinned.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe pornography quietly invaded your marriage.
Maybe anger poisoned your home.
Maybe your spouse begged you to change and you kept saying, “Later.”
Then later finally arrived.
And they were gone.
This is where we must handle Jesus’ words carefully.
The teaching of Matthew 19 should never become a weapon for forcing someone to remain in immediate danger or for pretending that abuse is faithfulness.
Nor should every divorced person be treated as though the circumstances of every broken marriage were identical.
