We want to know why He allowed it.
Why He delayed.
Why that relationship ended.
Why the opportunity disappeared.
Why the healing has not happened.
Why somebody who seemed faithful suffered.
Why the wicked sometimes prosper while faithful people weep.
Scripture does not pretend those questions are painless.
The Bible is filled with people asking them.
Job asked questions from the ashes.
David cried from caves.
Jeremiah lamented.
Habakkuk wrestled with what God appeared to be allowing.
The disciples panicked in a storm while Jesus was in the boat.
Even biblical faith has tears in its eyes sometimes.
Trusting God does not mean pretending the storm is sunshine.
It means recognizing that the storm is not God.
The diagnosis is not God.
The bank account is not God.
Your fear is not God.
Your disappointment is not God.
Your past is not God.
And your ability to understand what is happening is certainly not God.
There is still a throne.
And you are not sitting on it.
Neither is your crisis.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
That is why trust matters so deeply.
Trust is not merely positive thinking about God.
Trust reveals where you place the weight of your life.
Think about what happened in Eden.
The serpent’s temptation was not merely about fruit.
At its heart was an assault upon confidence in God's word and character.
God had spoken.
Then another voice whispered, in effect:
Can you really trust what God said?
Can you really trust His boundaries?
Can you really trust that He is not withholding something better from you?
That ancient whisper has never stopped.
It simply changes vocabulary.
Today it may sound like:
“God forgot you.”
“If He loved you, this wouldn't hurt.”
“You need to take control.”
“Compromise just this once.”
“You have waited long enough.”
“You know better.”
“Do whatever makes you happy.”
And beneath every variation is essentially the same invitation:
Stop trusting God. Trust something else instead.
That is why the battle over trust is ultimately a battle over worship.
Whatever receives your ultimate confidence begins functioning like your god.
Money can become that.
Relationships can become that.
Approval can become that.
Politics can become that.
Success can become that.
Your own intellect can become that.
Even ministry can become that.

And sometimes God allows the things we have leaned upon to shake—not because every hardship is a direct divine punishment, and not because suffering always means we have done something wrong, but because trials can expose where our confidence has actually been resting.
Then the uncomfortable question arrives:
If God removed everything you have been using as evidence that He loves you, would you still believe He is good?
Sit with that.
Because this is where Christianity becomes more than inspirational language.
This is where faith bleeds.
Job lost what most of us spend our lives trying to protect.
His grief was not imaginary.
His questions were not shallow.
His suffering was not solved by a motivational slogan.
Yet amid the agony, Job continued bringing his anguish into relationship with God.
Biblical trust does not require emotional numbness.
You can trust God and cry.
Trust God and grieve.
Trust God and ask questions.
Trust God while your hands shake.
Trust God while saying, “Lord, I don't understand.”
Faith is not pretending you have no wounds.
Faith is deciding where you will carry them.
And then we arrive at Jesus.
Not Christianity as a cultural identity.
Not inspirational religion.
Jesus.
The night before the cross, Christ knew suffering was coming.
Gethsemane was not theater.
Jesus prayed:

“Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt.”
— Mark 14:36
Read that carefully.
Christian surrender is not fatalism.
Jesus expressed the anguish.
He made the request.
And He surrendered Himself to the Father’s will.
That is trust at its deepest.
“Father, this hurts.”
“Father, I would choose differently.”
“Father, if there is another way…”
“Nevertheless…”
Sometimes one word separates surrender from rebellion.
Nevertheless.
I am afraid…
nevertheless.
I don't understand…
nevertheless.
I wanted another outcome…
nevertheless.
I have prayed and nothing seems to be changing…
nevertheless.
Your will above mine.
That kind of trust does not come naturally to fallen human beings.
We want control because control feels safe.
But control is often an illusion.
You cannot control tomorrow.
You cannot force another person's heart to change.
You cannot guarantee another year of life.
You cannot prevent every betrayal.
You cannot engineer a painless future.
You cannot save yourself from death.
And that is exactly where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Christianity does not say, “Trust God because nothing terrible will ever happen to you.”
Christians throughout history have suffered enormously.
Jesus Himself told His disciples that trouble would come.
The Christian claim is infinitely deeper:
Trust God because the God asking for your trust has already demonstrated His love in Jesus Christ.
Paul writes:
— Romans 5:8
The cross is where our suspicion about God's heart collides with the revelation of His grace.
Look at Christ.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
Bearing sin.
Then look at the empty tomb.
The Gospel does not tell you that God watched human suffering from a safe distance.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
Jesus carried the cross.
Jesus tasted death.
Jesus rose again.
And because He lives, suffering does not get the final word.
Sin does not get the final word.
Your history does not get the final word.
Your worst failure does not get the final word.
The grave does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is difficult for you to believe because trust has been expensive.
Someone promised forever and disappeared.
Someone who should have protected you hurt you.
Someone used Scripture while living hypocritically.
Maybe a church wounded you.
Maybe a Christian you admired failed spectacularly.
Maybe you prayed for something with everything inside you and watched the opposite happen.
Now somebody says, “Trust God,” and part of you recoils.
Because trust sounds dangerous.
Hear this carefully:
God is not asking you to pretend human betrayal never happened.
And Christianity does not require you to call abusive behavior good, remain unnecessarily exposed to unsafe people, or abandon appropriate boundaries.
People can betray you.
Religious leaders can fail you.
Institutions can disappoint you.
Christians can sin against you.
But their unfaithfulness does not redefine the character of Christ.
Jesus is not the person who betrayed you.
Do not confuse the fingerprints of broken people with the face of your Savior.
Psalm 56 captures something astonishingly human:
“What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.”
Notice the order.
David does not say, “I never become afraid because I trust God.”
He essentially says:
When I am afraid, I trust.
Fear exists.
And trust answers it.
That matters.
Because somebody reading this has been condemning themselves for feeling afraid.
Your trembling does not automatically mean faith is absent.
Sometimes faith is precisely what happens when a trembling person still reaches for God.
Hebrews 11:6 says:
“But without faith it is impossible to please him…”
The Greek word translated “faith” is πίστις — pistis, a word used for faith, trust, belief, confidence, and faithfulness depending upon context.
Biblical faith is not a magical force for obtaining everything we desire.
It is not spiritual currency with which we purchase miracles.
Christian faith has an object.
Ultimately, faith looks away from the sufficiency of self and toward God—and the New Testament centers saving faith upon Jesus Christ.
That changes everything.
Because maybe your greatest problem is not that you need more confidence in yourself.
Maybe you have spent years trying to become your own savior.
Trying harder.
Hiding better.
Performing Christianity.
Making promises to God.
Breaking them.
Feeling ashamed.
Trying again.
Falling again.
Then wondering whether God could possibly want you anymore.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Peter knew this place.
He said he would never deny Jesus.
Then pressure came.
And Peter collapsed.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine hearing yourself deny the One you swore you loved.
Imagine the shame afterward.
Imagine knowing Jesus had warned you.
Peter's confidence in Peter was shattered.
But his story did not end beside a charcoal fire of denial.
After the resurrection, John 21 records Jesus meeting Peter again.
There is another charcoal fire.
There is breakfast.
There is confrontation.
There is love.
There is restoration.
There is calling.
Peter's failure was real.
But failure did not become his final identity.
Jesus rewrote what shame wanted to make permanent.
That is the Gospel.
Not good people proving they deserve God.
Not sinners cleaning themselves enough to approach Christ.
Not religious performers collecting points.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could not rescue themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
Grace is astonishing precisely because sin is serious.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy you desperately need.
You do not have to hide.
You do not have to manufacture a respectable version of yourself before coming to Jesus.
Bring Him the truth.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The lust.
The jealousy.
The secret compromise.
The pride.
The unbelief.
The anger you are ashamed to admit.
The exhaustion.
The religious mask.
Bring Him the thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Jesus is the only Savior powerful enough to deal honestly with what sin has done.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to be painfully simple:
“Jesus, I don't know how to trust You anymore.”
Say it.
He already knows.
“Jesus, I believe; help my unbelief.”
That desperate prayer has biblical precedent.
In Mark 9:24, a father cried:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
What an extraordinary confession.
Faith and struggle standing in the same sentence.
Jesus did not need the man to perform certainty.
And maybe neither do you.
Stop performing for God.
Come honestly.
Trust does not mean you will understand everything God permits.
It means you are learning to believe that God's character is more dependable than your limited perspective.
Isaiah 55 reminds us that God's thoughts and ways transcend ours.
Romans 8 does not promise that every event will feel good; it speaks of God working in all things for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And Romans 8 ultimately directs our hope toward conformity to Christ.
God's definition of “good” is often larger than our definition of “comfortable.”
That can be painful.
But it can also set you free.
Because perhaps the question is no longer:
“God, will You give me the life I designed?”
Perhaps it becomes:
“Jesus, can I trust You with the life You are redeeming?”
There is freedom there.
Not easy answers.
Freedom.
You do not need tomorrow's grace tonight.
You need today's.
You do not need the entire map.
You need the Shepherd.
You do not need to understand every chapter while you are still living inside it.
You need to know who holds the story.
And Christian hope says the Author has scars.
So when Satan whispers that God abandoned you, look toward the cross.
When shame says your sin is too filthy, look toward the cross.
When pride says you can save yourself, look toward the cross.
When despair says death wins, look toward the empty tomb.
When your past says, “This is who you will always be,” look toward the risen Christ.
From scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God, don't manufacture a polished response.
Be honest.
Somebody reading beneath this article may need to discover that they are not the only person who has cried in the dark and still reached for Jesus.
Not because every day will feel this heavy, but because one day may come when you need these Scriptures again.
That share may travel farther than you know.
Send it to the believer who is exhausted.
The friend who stopped going to church.
The person drowning in shame.
The skeptic willing to listen.
The Christian who smiles publicly and cries privately.
Sometimes sharing Gospel truth is one simple way of placing hope where another person might actually find it.
But hear this clearly:
You cannot purchase God's favor.
Salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Financial generosity is a response to grace, never the price of it.

Scripture teaches believers to give willingly rather than under compulsion. As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says, giving should come from what a person has purposed in the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Think of it as partnership in the work—not payment to God.

Christians differ on precisely how Old Testament tithing relates to New Testament giving, but the New Testament unmistakably emphasizes willing, generous, non-compulsory giving and support for Gospel ministry.
So pray.
Give where God leads your conscience according to Scripture.
And if you choose to support Gospel Warrior, know why you are doing it:
not to purchase God's approval,
but because in Christ you already have a reason to live generously.
Leave a meaningful comment.
But before you leave, there is one question I want following you after this screen goes dark.
When everything you were leaning on begins to shake…
will you trust what you can see—or the Savior who carried a cross, walked out of a grave, and still holds your unfinished story?
Maybe you do not understand this chapter yet.
Maybe you are standing in the scandal.
Maybe your hands are shaking.
Maybe there are tears on your face while you read these words.
But if you belong to Jesus, your darkest chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
The hands holding your unfinished story are the same hands that still bear the scars.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK—YES, THAT STORY IS ACTUALLY IN GENESIS
paragraphs:
LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK—YES, THAT STORY IS ACTUALLY IN GENESIS
The Bible does not hide the scandals of broken families. It exposes them—and then, generations later, shows us something almost unbelievable: grace can reach a bloodline without ever calling its sin good.
There are Bible stories people put on nursery walls.
Noah’s ark.
David and Goliath.
Daniel surrounded by lions.
Jesus holding children in His arms.
And then there is Genesis 19.
Nobody is painting this one above the crib.
Because after the fire fell on Sodom, after Lot’s wife looked back, after a family escaped a city under judgment...
two daughters entered a cave with their father.
There was wine.
There was fear.
There was a plan.
And before Genesis 19 ends, both daughters were pregnant by their own father.
Yes.
That is actually in the Bible.
Because the most disturbing thing about this story may not be what happened inside that cave.
It may be how recognizable the road into that cave actually is.
Not because most of us will ever commit the particular sin recorded here.
But because many of us know what it is to survive something devastating and then make terrible decisions while afraid.
We know what it is to confuse desperation with permission.
We know what it is to say, “I had no other choice.”
We know what it is to survive the fire...
and still carry Sodom inside us.
That is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Lot had escaped.
But escape is not always the same thing as healing.

Genesis tells us that Lot left Zoar because he was afraid and lived with his two daughters in a cave. Then the older daughter looked at their situation and concluded that their future was disappearing. Their father was old, and in her perception there was no man available through whom they could continue the family line. Genesis records her proposal: they would give their father wine, lie with him, and preserve offspring through him.
The Hebrew makes the intention painfully direct:
לְכָה נַשְׁקֶה אֶת־אָבִינוּ יַיִן וְנִשְׁכְּבָה עִמּוֹ וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע
Lekhah nashqeh et-avinu yayin, venishkevah immo, unechayyeh me’avinu zara.
In straightforward sense:
“Come, let us make our father drink wine, and let us lie with him, so that we may preserve offspring through our father.”
The Hebrew word זֶרַע (zeraʿ) means “seed” or “offspring.” Their stated purpose was survival of the family line.
Notice what Scripture does not do.
It does not praise them.
It does not tell us that God commanded this.
It does not turn desperation into righteousness.
Genesis reports what happened.
That distinction matters enormously.
One of the most dangerous mistakes we can make when reading the Old Testament is assuming that because the Bible records an action, the Bible approves that action.
It does not.
Scripture is often brutally honest about human beings.
Abraham lies.
Jacob deceives.
Judah sleeps with a woman he believes is a prostitute.
David commits adultery and arranges a man's death.
Peter denies Jesus.
The Bible does not need sanitized heroes because the Bible is ultimately not a story about impressive people rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy God dealing with sinful people.
And Lot’s family was broken long before they entered that cave.
Earlier in the same chapter, when the men of Sodom surrounded Lot’s house and demanded his visitors, Lot horrifyingly offered his two daughters instead.
That should disturb us.
It should.
The Bible gives us no permission to defend it.
Something was profoundly disordered in this family.
Then Sodom was destroyed.
Their home disappeared.
Their mother was gone.
Their familiar world collapsed.
Now father and daughters were hiding in a cave.
Fear had become the atmosphere.
And fear can become a terrible counselor.
This does not excuse what the daughters did.
Understanding the circumstances surrounding a sin is not the same thing as declaring the sin righteous.
Later biblical law explicitly prohibits sexual relations between close relatives. Leviticus 18:6 states the principle plainly: sexual relations with close kin are forbidden.
So Genesis 19 is not a secret biblical endorsement of incest.
Far from it.
What we are witnessing is a shattered family making sinful decisions after catastrophe.
And there is another detail we must handle carefully.
Sometimes this story is retold as though we know with certainty that the daughters believed every other human being on earth had died.

The actual Hebrew can be understood as saying there was “no man in the land” or “on earth” available to them. Some later Jewish interpretation understood the daughters as believing the destruction had been worldwide like the Flood, but Genesis itself does not explicitly tell us the full extent of what they believed. The safest conclusion is simpler: from their frightened perspective, they saw no legitimate future for the family line.
So they manufactured one.
And there is the knife.
Because human beings are still doing this.
Maybe not in a cave.
Maybe not with wine.
Maybe not through incest.
But we still do it.
God seems too slow...
so we manufacture an answer.
We are afraid of being alone...
so we enter a relationship we know is pulling us away from Christ.
We are terrified of financial collapse...
so dishonesty suddenly starts sounding practical.
We are afraid our marriage cannot be restored...
so emotional intimacy with someone else starts feeling justified.
We feel unseen...
so we return to pornography.
We feel empty...
so we return to the bottle.
We feel wounded...
so revenge starts masquerading as justice.
We feel abandoned...
so compromise begins calling itself survival.
That is one of sin’s oldest lies:
“You have no other choice.”
Lot’s daughters apparently looked at an impossible future and decided they had to create their own solution.
And when fear convinces you that God cannot make a way, sin will happily offer you one.
The first night, they gave Lot wine.
The older daughter went in.
Genesis says:
וְלֹא־יָדַע בְּשִׁכְבָהּ וּבְקוּמָהּ
Velo-yada beshikhvah uvekumah.
“He did not know when she lay down or when she arose.”
The text repeats essentially the same description after the younger daughter does it the following night. Genesis emphasizes Lot’s lack of awareness during the encounters.
Two nights.
Two daughters.
One father.
Two pregnancies.
And then come the names.
The older daughter gave birth to Moab.
The younger gave birth to Ben-Ammi.

The NET Bible notes that Moab sounds like the Hebrew expression associated with “from our father,” while Ben-Ammi means “son of my people.” These sons became ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites, peoples who would repeatedly intersect—and sometimes clash—with Israel throughout biblical history.
Imagine carrying a name that keeps whispering the circumstances surrounding your beginning.
Imagine a family story you would rather nobody mention.
Imagine having something in your ancestry that you cannot rewrite.
Maybe that is why this story reaches farther than we think.
Some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to inherit a story they never chose.
Maybe your father was an alcoholic.
Maybe your mother disappeared.
Maybe adultery ripped your family apart.
Maybe abuse lived behind the smiling family photograph.
Maybe addiction keeps moving from generation to generation.
Maybe you grew up learning dysfunction so early that you thought dysfunction was normal.
Maybe there are things in your family nobody talks about.
Names.
Affairs.
Children.
Prison.
Addiction.
Violence.
Abandonment.
Secrets buried beneath Sunday clothes.
And somewhere inside you is a question you have been afraid to say aloud:
“Can anything clean come out of where I came from?”
Keep reading.
Because centuries after that cave...
a woman walked into Bethlehem.
Her name was Ruth.
And Ruth was a Moabite.
Let that settle.
Moab.
The people whose ancestral beginning Genesis traces back to that terrible night between Lot and his older daughter.
And from Moab eventually came Ruth.
But Ruth's story would not be defined merely by the scandal behind her people.
She turned toward the God of Israel.
She clung to Naomi.
She met Boaz.
Boaz married Ruth.
They had Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David.
The shepherd.
The psalmist.
The king.
Scripture explicitly traces that genealogy in Ruth 4.
But God was not finished.
Open the New Testament.
Open Matthew.
Start reading the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Generation after generation.
Then Matthew writes:
Boaz fathered Obed by...
Ruth.
And Obed fathered Jesse.
And Jesse fathered David.
Do you see it?
Genesis gives us a cave filled with shame.
Ruth gives us a Moabite woman walking in faith.
Matthew places Ruth in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
Not because the incest in Genesis somehow became good.
It never became good.
Grace does not rename evil as righteousness.
Grace does something infinitely more beautiful.
God can redeem people and histories touched by evil without ever approving the evil itself.
That is the Gospel-shaped thunder inside this story.
God does not need a spotless human history to accomplish His holy purposes.
He is holy enough to enter histories stained by human sin and bring redemption without becoming stained Himself.
And eventually, into humanity’s long history of rebellion came Jesus Christ.
Not another sinner trying to fix sinners.
The Savior.
The spotless Lamb.
The Son of God.
Jesus did not come because humanity had finally cleaned up its genealogy.
He came because we could not clean ourselves.
That is why the cross matters.
At Calvary, Jesus was not saying sin does not matter.
The cross screams that sin matters.
It cost blood.
It cost suffering.
It cost the life of the sinless Son of God.
But the cross also declares that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is possible.
Reconciliation with God is possible.
A new life is possible.
You may have done something you cannot undo.
You may carry consequences that prayer will not magically erase.
You may have wounded people.
You may have wasted years.
You may have hidden something so long that hiding has become part of your personality.
But listen carefully:
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to save sinners.
That means you do not have to sanitize your testimony before bringing it to Him.
You bring the truth.
The ugly truth.
The embarrassing truth.
The truth you wish you could delete.
You confess.
You repent.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
And you throw yourself upon the mercy of Christ.
Grace is not God pretending the cave never happened.
Grace is God refusing to let the cave have the final word.
Maybe that is why Genesis 19 had to remain in the Bible.
We would have edited it out.
God did not.
We prefer polished biographies.
Scripture gives us broken families.
We prefer heroes without stains.
Scripture gives us sinners who desperately need mercy.
We hide scandals.
God exposes sin and then shows what redemption can do.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing, “If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.”
Maybe.
People may change how they see you.
Consequences may remain.
Trust may take years to rebuild.
Biblical grace is not pretending consequences do not exist.
But your deepest question is not whether everybody will approve of you.
It is whether a holy God can forgive you.
And the Gospel answers through the blood of Jesus:
There is mercy for the repentant sinner.
There is cleansing for the guilty.
There is adoption for the outsider.
There is restoration for the broken.
There is a new identity for the person who comes to Christ.
You are not saved because your family tree is clean.
You are not saved because your past is presentable.
You are not saved because you finally became religious enough.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
So stop hiding behind the cave wall.
Bring it into the light.
Whatever “it” is.
The secret relationship.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The private messages.
The money.
The pornography.
The resentment.
The double life.
The lie everyone believes about you.
The wound you have turned into permission to wound somebody else.
Do not call bondage “coping.”
Do not call compromise “survival.”
Do not call what God calls darkness your personality.
Come to Jesus.
Not when you have repaired yourself.
Now.
Repentance does not mean merely feeling horrible about yourself.
It means turning.
Away from sin.
Toward Christ.
And perhaps the most astonishing lesson from Lot’s family is this:
Your beginning does not possess sovereign authority over your ending.
Jesus does.
The Moabite story did not end at the cave.
Ruth walked into Bethlehem.
And Ruth's name eventually appeared in Matthew’s genealogy leading to Christ.
That does not make Genesis 19 beautiful.
It makes redemption beautiful.
There is a difference.
Never glorify the scandal.
Glorify the Redeemer.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make a simple confession of dependence on Christ.
And read the comments of others with mercy.
There are wounded people behind profile pictures.
There are recovering addicts behind smiling photographs.
There are marriages fighting for restoration.
There are prodigals trying to come home.
There are believers exhausted from battles nobody else can see.
Let this become more than a comment section.
Let it become a reminder that sinners do not need another hiding place.
We need Jesus.
There will probably come a night when your past starts speaking again.
A night when shame tells you God could use somebody else, but never you.
Come back and remember Ruth.
Come back and remember the genealogy.
Come back and remember the cross.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves.
But if you genuinely want your online life to glorify God, one practical way to use what He has placed in your hands is to help put biblical truth in front of people who may never walk into a church.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or care for people in need. It is simply one voluntary way of helping truth travel farther.
Stay close for Scripture.
For conviction.
For encouragement.
For biblical truth when culture gets loud.
For reminders of grace when shame gets louder.
For discipleship that keeps pointing beyond Gospel Warrior and back to Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for people with respectable histories.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the prodigal.
Invite the person who thinks God could never want them after what they have done.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not miss Jesus because the scandal caught your attention.
Lot’s daughters are not the hero of this story.
Lot is not the hero.
Ruth is not ultimately the hero.
We are not the hero.
Jesus is.
Because Scripture is not telling us that brokenness is beautiful.
It is telling us that our Redeemer is greater than our brokenness.
The cave was real.
The sin was real.
The consequences were real.
But so was Ruth.
So was Bethlehem.
So was the genealogy.
And ultimately...
so was the cross.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It may explain some of your fears.
It may explain why certain battles are harder for you than they seem to be for somebody else.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your past is no longer qualified to be your god.
Bring the scandal to Christ.
Bring the shame to Christ.
Bring the family history to Christ.
Bring the secret to Christ.
Bring the consequences to Christ.
Bring the pieces you cannot put back together.
And let the Savior who died and rose again decide what redemption can still become.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Genesis 19 is not merely that two daughters got their father drunk and became pregnant by him.
It is that even after human beings create chapters so dark we can barely stand to read them...
God is still capable of writing grace into the generations that follow.
The cave may be part of the story—but in the hands of the Redeemer, it does not have to be the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Preached for Years—and They Still Wouldn’t Listen
paragraphs: He Preached for Years—and They Still Wouldn’t Listen

Jeremiah kept speaking while hearts kept hardening. He wept over people who would not return to God—and somewhere inside his story is a terrifying question for us: What if God has been speaking to you, too?
There comes a moment when rejection stops sounding like noise.
It starts feeling like grief.
Jeremiah knew that feeling.

He knew what it was like to carry a message from God into a culture that did not want to hear it. He knew what it was like to warn people he loved and watch them keep walking toward destruction. He knew the exhaustion of speaking truth when truth was unpopular, the loneliness of obedience when compromise would have been easier, and the strange agony of loving people enough to tell them what they desperately did not want to hear.
We often call him “the weeping prophet.”
Scripture does not formally give Jeremiah that title, but it is easy to understand why Christians have remembered him that way.
Listen to his words:
“Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!” — Jeremiah 9:1, KJV
This was not the performance of a preacher trying to manufacture emotion.
This was a broken heart.
Jeremiah was not standing at a safe distance pointing at sinful people and enjoying their downfall.
He was weeping.
That matters.
Because biblical conviction without love can easily become self-righteousness, but Jeremiah's tears reveal something deeper. He was proclaiming judgment while grieving for the people under judgment.
And perhaps that is where his story begins reaching through the centuries and touching us.
Because sometimes the most frightening form of spiritual danger is not that God has never spoken.
It is that He has spoken repeatedly...
and we have become skilled at not listening.

Jeremiah ministered during the final turbulent decades of the kingdom of Judah, through the reigns of kings including Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, as Babylon's shadow eventually swallowed Jerusalem.
But long before Jerusalem fell, something else had already been collapsing.
The people's hearts.
They still had religious language.
They still had sacred places.
They still had rituals.
They could still say things associated with God while resisting the God they claimed to worship.
That is what makes Jeremiah uncomfortable.
His message does not allow us to hide behind appearances.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still need repentance.
You can share Bible verses and still harbor bitterness.
You can attend church and still secretly negotiate with sin.
You can sing about surrender while protecting the one room in your heart where Jesus is not allowed to touch anything.
You can look alive spiritually while becoming numb inside.
And God sees beyond appearances.
Jeremiah was sent into that kind of world.
When God called him, Jeremiah immediately felt inadequate.
“Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.” — Jeremiah 1:6, KJV

The Hebrew expression translated “I am a child” contains the word נַעַר — naʿar — a term that can refer to a boy or young man. Jeremiah's protest was essentially one of inadequacy: he did not believe himself ready for what God was asking him to do.
But God did not call Jeremiah because Jeremiah felt powerful.
God called him because God had chosen him.
“Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee...” — Jeremiah 1:5, KJV
Then came the words that would change the course of his life:
“Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth.” — Jeremiah 1:9, KJV
Imagine the weight of that.
Jeremiah would speak God's message, but speaking it would cost him.
He would encounter opposition.
Mockery.
Threats.
Isolation.
Imprisonment.
His prophetic scroll would be cut apart and burned under King Jehoiakim.
At another point, Jeremiah would be lowered into a cistern where he sank into mud.
This is not the sanitized version of following God.
This is obedience when obedience hurts.
And still Jeremiah spoke.
Again.
And again.
And again.
God described Judah's stubborn refusal in haunting language:
“...they hearkened not, nor inclined their ear...” — Jeremiah 7:24, KJV
That phrase appears repeatedly in Jeremiah's message.
They would not listen.
They would not incline their ears.
God was not merely describing an information problem.
He was describing a heart problem.
The Hebrew Scriptures often use שָׁמַע — shāmaʿ — for hearing or listening, and the word can carry the sense of hearing in a way that leads toward response or obedience.
Biblical listening is more than sound reaching your ears.
It reaches your will.
That distinction should frighten anyone who has heard the Gospel hundreds of times.
Because hearing another sermon is not the same thing as surrendering.
Knowing another verse is not the same thing as obeying it.
Feeling convicted is not the same thing as repenting.
Crying during worship is not the same thing as giving Jesus the thing you keep taking back.
Maybe that is why this story feels so personal.
Because some of us are not waiting for God to speak.
We already know what He said.
Forgive.
But we keep feeding the resentment.
Flee sexual immorality.
But we keep returning to the secret screen.
Tell the truth.
But the lie protects our reputation.
Love your enemy.
But anger feels too justified to surrender.
Seek first God's kingdom.
But ambition has quietly become our master.
Do not merely hear the Word.
Do it.
And somewhere underneath all our explanations is a quieter reality:
We heard Him.
We simply did not want obedience to cost us that much.
Jeremiah knew what resistance looked like because he watched an entire people practice it.
But what makes his ministry heartbreaking is that judgment was not God's only message.
There was also an invitation.
A word that keeps appearing in Jeremiah is שׁוּב — shuv.
Return.
Turn back.
Come home.
“Return, thou backsliding Israel, saith the LORD...” — Jeremiah 3:12, KJV
Do you see the heart behind the warning?
God's call to repentance was not merely, “Feel terrible about yourself.”
It was:
Return.
That is the heartbeat of biblical repentance.
Not merely regret.
Not merely embarrassment because you got caught.
Not merely promising to behave better because consequences frightened you.
Turn.
Return.
Come back to the God against whom you have sinned.
And this is where Jeremiah stops being only an ancient story about Judah and becomes a mirror.
How long has God been calling you back?
How many times has conviction visited you?
How many sermons have made you uncomfortable for ten minutes before you returned to the same pattern?
How many times have you whispered, “Lord, I know,” while continuing to do exactly what you knew was destroying you?
Maybe nobody else knows.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
Maybe people at church think your faith is solid.
Maybe your Bible is highlighted.
Maybe you can quote Scripture better than the people around you.
But when the room gets quiet...
you know.
You know where compromise lives.
You know what you keep deleting.
You know whom you still hate.
You know what you keep hiding.
You know what Jesus has been putting His finger on.
And perhaps the saddest sentence you could ever say to God is not, “I never heard You.”
Perhaps it is:
“I heard You.
I just kept saying no.”
Jeremiah understood what persistent rebellion could eventually produce.
He watched warnings become consequences.
He watched the world around him unravel.
And when Jerusalem finally fell to Babylon, this was not Jeremiah's moment to stand over the ruins shouting, “I told you so.”
He grieved.
That is the difference between loving truth and loving being right.
Jeremiah's heart was wounded because people mattered.
Listen again:
“When I would comfort myself against sorrow, my heart is faint in me.” — Jeremiah 8:18, KJV
Then comes one of Scripture's haunting cries:
“Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?” — Jeremiah 8:22, KJV
The prophet is grieving a wound that his people cannot heal by pretending it is small.
And that image reaches us.
Because sin wounds.
Sin promises freedom and produces slavery.
Sin whispers that nobody will know and then teaches you to live divided.
Sin offers a moment and sometimes collects years.
Sin tells you that repentance can wait.
That tomorrow is safer.
That one more compromise will not matter.
That you can come back whenever you want.
But Scripture never teaches us to gamble with a hardened heart.
There is another side to Jeremiah's story that we must not miss, however.
If all we hear is judgment, we have not heard the whole book.
In the middle of Jeremiah's warnings, God speaks astonishing words of restoration.
“Yea, I have loved thee with an everlasting love...” — Jeremiah 31:3, KJV
And then something even greater.
A promise of a new covenant.
“Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant...” — Jeremiah 31:31, KJV
In Hebrew, the phrase is בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה — berit chadashah — “new covenant.”
God promised something beyond external religion.
“I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts...” — Jeremiah 31:33, KJV
And then:
“...for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.” — Jeremiah 31:34, KJV
There.
That is where the tears begin pointing toward hope.
Because centuries later, on the night before the cross, Jesus took the cup and said:
“This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.” — Luke 22:20, KJV
The Greek expression behind “new covenant” is ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη — hē kainē diathēkē.
Jeremiah had spoken of a new covenant.
Jesus declared the new covenant in His blood.
This is where the scandal meets grace.
We were not people who merely needed better habits.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed hearts transformed.
We needed reconciliation with God.
We needed a Savior.
And Jesus Christ did not come merely to make bad people look respectable.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
The One we rejected became the One who bore our sins.
The Holy One was crucified.
The guilty could be forgiven.
The rebellious could return.
The ashamed could be cleansed.
The lost could be found.
The spiritually dead could receive life.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Jesus paid a price we could never pay.
That is grace.
Grace is not God pretending your rebellion was harmless.
Grace is God dealing with sin through the sacrifice of Christ and opening the way for sinners to be reconciled to Him.
This is why repentance and grace are not enemies.
Grace gives you somewhere to run when repentance finally breaks your excuses.
You run to Christ.
Maybe you have been hiding for years.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you have been performing Christianity while privately falling apart.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you are reading this after returning to the same sin you promised God you would never touch again.
Come to Christ.
Maybe shame is telling you that God could forgive other people but surely not you.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you have ignored His voice so many times that you are afraid you have gone too far.
Do not use that fear as another excuse to remain far away.
Turn to Him now.
Confess your sin.
Trust Christ.
Ask for mercy.
There is no virtue in hiding from the Physician because you are ashamed of the wound.
And maybe someone needs to stop reading for a moment and finally become honest.
No performance.
No church language.
No pretending.
Just you and God.
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not as a magic phrase.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when hiding ends.
If your spirit is exhausted and you feel like you have been fighting the same battle for too long, comment, “pray for me.”
Let another believer see it.
Let somebody pray.
If God has been restoring you slowly, painfully, beautifully, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence that keeps another person from giving up tonight.
And if you are tired of appearing fine while your soul is begging for help, comment, “no more hiding.”
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Jeremiah reminds us that there is a terrible tragedy in repeatedly hearing God's truth while continually refusing to respond.
But the Gospel tells us something breathtaking:
The God who calls sinners to repent has provided a Savior for sinners who return to Him in faith.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by lowering God's holiness until our sin becomes comfortable.
Jesus rewrites everything through redemption.
Peter denied Him.
Grace found Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed Paul into an apostle of Christ.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward the crucified King and received a promise of paradise.
Again and again, Scripture shows us something astonishing.
The worst chapter does not have to be the final chapter when Christ becomes the center of the story.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to collect reactions.
But to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ in front of people living in a world desperately trying to drown out His voice.
If this article helped turn your attention toward Christ, do not let it die on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
Someone may have stopped going to church.
Someone may believe they have sinned too deeply to return.
Someone may need to hear one word Jeremiah proclaimed centuries ago:
Return.
Send this to the friend who has grown cold.
Share it with the believer who is exhausted.
Send it even to the person who does not yet believe in Christ.
It is a reason to run toward Him.
If Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow deeper in Scripture, consider following so these messages remain close.

Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's favor, make you more righteous, or prove that you glorify God more than someone who cannot financially contribute. The Gospel will never be for sale.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase a blessing.
Not because an algorithm is holy.
It can also carry a doorway through which someone encounters the words of Scripture and is pointed toward Jesus.
Jeremiah spent years speaking to people who repeatedly refused to listen.
His tears still ask us a question.
What will you do when God's Word reaches you?
Will you admire it?
Debate it?
Or will you finally surrender?
Because one of the greatest tragedies is not that God never called your name.
It is spending your life hearing Him say, “Return,” while continually answering, “Not yet.”
And one of the greatest wonders of grace is discovering that when a repentant sinner finally turns toward Jesus, he does not find a Savior embarrassed to receive broken people.
He finds the Christ who went to a cross for them.
So return.
While your heart can still feel conviction, return.
While His Word is in front of you, return.
While you are reading these words, return.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the religious mask.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the story you thought was too scandalous to redeem.
And discover what the Gospel has been saying all along:
Jesus Christ is greater than the chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read.
The tears of Jeremiah warn us not to keep saying “tomorrow” to the God who is calling us today.
And the blood of Jesus reminds us that sinners who return to Him do not have to write their ending alone.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but when Jesus takes hold of your story, your scandal does not get the final word. Grace does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU’RE SO BUSY SERVING GOD THAT THE PEOPLE CLOSEST TO YOU ARE GETTING WHATEVER IS LEFT
paragraphs: YOU’RE SO BUSY SERVING GOD THAT THE PEOPLE CLOSEST TO YOU ARE GETTING WHATEVER IS LEFT
What if the ministry everyone praises is quietly costing the people God entrusted to you first—and what if the most spiritual thing you could do tonight is go home, put the phone down, and love them?
The sermon was powerful.
People stayed afterward because they needed prayer.
Someone told you, “God is really using you.”
Another person sent a message saying your words came at exactly the right time.
Your notifications kept lighting up.
People needed counsel.
The ministry needed decisions.
There was another meeting.
Another message.
Another emergency.
Another person who desperately needed something from you.
And somewhere else…
someone who loves you stopped waiting.
Maybe it was your wife.
Maybe your husband.
Maybe your child.
Maybe your aging mother or father.
Maybe it was simply the people who know the version of you that never appears behind a microphone.
They have heard you tell strangers that they matter.
They have watched you make time for hurting people.

They have seen you answer calls during dinner, interrupt conversations for ministry messages, leave family moments because somebody “needed you,” and give your emotional strength to everyone outside the house.
And eventually they learned something heartbreaking:
Everybody gets the best of you.
They get what remains.
The exhausted version.
The distracted version.
The impatient version.
The version staring at a screen while saying, “I’m listening.”
The version who promises, “We’ll spend time together soon.”
Soon keeps moving.
But ministry keeps growing.
And because the thing consuming you carries God’s name, questioning it can almost feel sinful.
That is what makes this contradiction so dangerous.
Because sometimes the easiest place to hide from obedience to God…
is inside work supposedly being done for God.
Read that again.
You can become so busy doing Christian things that you stop noticing whether you are becoming like Christ.
You can preach love publicly while starving someone of it privately.
You can teach people about grace while your family walks carefully around your temper.
You can tell strangers, “I’m here whenever you need me,” while the people at your own table have stopped trying to tell you what they need.
You can have hundreds—or thousands—of people listening to you and still fail to hear the silence of one person sitting beside you.
And Scripture does not allow Christian leaders to separate these worlds.
Paul writes concerning the qualifications of an overseer:
“προϊστάμενον τοῦ ἰδίου οἴκου καλῶς…”
The phrase speaks of managing, leading, or caring for one’s own household well.
Then comes the question that should make every pastor, ministry leader, evangelist, teacher, Christian creator, volunteer, and ambitious servant of God uncomfortable enough to examine their life:
“εἰ δέ τις τοῦ ἰδίου οἴκου προστῆναι οὐκ οἶδεν, πῶς ἐκκλησίας θεοῦ ἐπιμελήσεται;”
“For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church?”
—1 Timothy 3:5
Notice the logic.
Paul does not treat the household as competition with ministry.
He treats faithfulness there as evidence relevant to ministry.
The Greek expression τοῦ ἰδίου οἴκου — tou idiou oikou means “his own household.”
His own.
Not merely the crowd.
Not merely the congregation.
Not merely the people applauding his gifting.
The people entrusted to his immediate care matter to God too.
And then Paul uses an extraordinarily tender word when speaking about caring for God’s church:
ἐπιμελήσεται — epimelēsetai.
To care for.
It is related to the language Jesus uses in the story of the Good Samaritan when the wounded man is brought to an inn and entrusted to someone’s care.
Ministry leadership, then, is not merely visibility.
It is not platform.
It is not charisma.
It is not how many people share your sermon.
It is not how many conferences invite you.
It is not how many followers recognize your name.
Biblical leadership involves care.
And Paul essentially asks:
If care repeatedly collapses among the people closest to you, why should greater spiritual responsibility automatically be considered evidence of success?
That question hurts because some people reading this genuinely love Jesus.
You are not pretending.
You really do care about souls.
You really have sacrificed.
You really have stayed awake praying for people.
You really have given money nobody knew about.
You really have answered calls when you were exhausted.
You really have cried over people walking away from Christ.
You are not necessarily a hypocrite.
Maybe you are tired.
Maybe nobody taught you boundaries.
Maybe somewhere along the way you started believing that every request was an assignment from God.
Maybe saying “no” started feeling like selfishness.
Maybe ministry became connected to your identity so deeply that being needed began to feel suspiciously similar to being loved.
And maybe the hardest possibility to admit is this:
You became everybody’s rescuer because dealing with strangers was sometimes easier than dealing with the wounds waiting at home.
Strangers usually encounter your gifting.
Family encounters your character.
The crowd sees what you can do.
Home reveals who you are becoming.
The platform celebrates your strengths.
Your closest relationships expose your weaknesses.
And God cares about both.
This does not mean your spouse or children become idols.
It does not mean Christians should abandon legitimate ministry whenever family members dislike its demands.
Jesus Himself taught that allegiance to Him comes above every human relationship.
The Gospel sometimes costs painfully.
Obedience sometimes requires sacrifice.
There will be seasons when ministry asks more from a household than usual.
There will be emergencies.
There will be late nights.
There will be inconvenient acts of mercy.
There will be missionaries, pastors, workers, volunteers, and ordinary Christians whose families sacrifice together for the kingdom.
The problem is not sacrifice.
The problem is using sacrifice for God as a permanent excuse for neglecting responsibilities God Himself gave you.
Those are not the same thing.
Jesus confronted something disturbingly similar.
In Mark 7, He rebuked people who had found a religious justification for withholding responsibility toward their parents.
They could invoke Corban—something dedicated to God—while neglecting the very command of God to honor father and mother.
Imagine the scandal of that.
Something could sound religious…
look sacrificial…
even involve something “given to God”…
and still become a mechanism for disobedience.
Jesus would not accept spirituality as camouflage for neglect.
Neither should we.
Paul becomes even more severe in 1 Timothy 5:8 when discussing responsibility toward relatives and one’s household:
“εἰ δέ τις τῶν ἰδίων καὶ μάλιστα οἰκείων οὐ προνοεῖ…”
“If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household…”
The word translated “provide,” προνοεῖ — pronoei, carries the idea of taking thought beforehand, giving consideration, making provision.
Biblical care is therefore not merely reacting after everything collapses.
It thinks ahead.
It notices.
It anticipates.
It takes responsibility.
And provision cannot honestly be reduced to money alone as though paying the bills automatically fulfills every relational responsibility Scripture gives us.
A child can have shoes and still ache for a father’s attention.
A spouse can live in a beautiful house and still feel emotionally abandoned.
A parent can receive money every month and still wonder why the child who publicly ministers compassion rarely calls.
You can provide a roof and still fail to provide presence.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You were the pastor’s kid everybody thought was lucky.
Everyone loved your father.
Everyone praised your mother.
Everyone talked about how “anointed” your family was.
But you remember waiting.
You remember church people receiving hours of conversation while you were told, “Not now.”
You remember vacations interrupted by ministry.
Birthdays shortened by emergencies.
Meals dominated by phones.
Promises postponed because the church needed something again.
And because everybody told you how blessed you were to have such godly parents, you felt guilty for being hurt.
So you buried it.
Maybe you even blamed God.
Because when you are young, it is difficult to separate God from the people constantly telling you they are neglecting you because they are serving Him.
If that is part of your story, hear something Scripture makes clear:
Jesus is not honored by hypocrisy.
Christ is not glorified when His name becomes an excuse for patterns He never commanded.
And Jesus is not the absentee father you may have unconsciously imagined Him to be.
Look at Christ.
He welcomed interruptions, yet He also withdrew.
He served crowds, yet He did not allow every demand to dictate His movements.
People searched for Him, but He remained governed by the Father’s will rather than human urgency.
He could leave crowds.
He could rest.
He could pray alone.
He could focus deeply on a smaller circle.
Even while dying on the cross—while accomplishing the greatest redemptive work in human history—Jesus noticed His mother.
Think about that.
Nails through His hands.
His body failing.
The sin of the world before Him.
The work of redemption reaching its terrible climax.
And Jesus still saw Mary.
He entrusted her care to the beloved disciple.
Even at Calvary, holy mission did not make human responsibility invisible.
And the cross reveals something else.
Biblical love is not measured primarily by how impressive it looks.
It gives itself.
Paul tells husbands:
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας…”
“Husbands, love your wives…”
Then comes the standard:
“καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
“…just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25
Ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate.
Love.
Not merely feel affection.
Not merely announce love.
Not merely post anniversary photographs with beautiful captions.
Christlike marital love moves toward self-giving.
Jesus did not give His leftovers to His bride.
He gave Himself.
And that may be the sentence somebody cannot escape tonight:
Jesus did not give His bride what was left of Him. He gave Himself for her.
So when did we start calling chronic leftovers love?
Your family does not need the version of you that only exists after everybody else has taken a piece.
Your children should not have to schedule an appointment with your calling.
Your spouse should not have to compete with strangers for your emotional presence.
Your elderly parents should not hear endless stories about how compassionate you are toward hurting people while wondering why you rarely remember them.
And no, this is not permission to shame pastors.
Do not weaponize this article against your spouse.
Do not send it to your pastor with a passive-aggressive message.
Do not use Scripture to demand unhealthy control over someone sincerely serving Christ.
This word belongs first in the mirror.
Ask yourself.
When the microphone turns off, who am I?
When nobody is watching, what version of me does my family receive?
Do strangers receive patience that my children rarely experience?
Do ministry partners receive encouragement while my spouse mostly hears correction?
Do I know what the people in my house are afraid of right now?
Do I know what they are praying about?
When did I last sit with them without checking my phone?
When did I last apologize without defending myself?
When did I last ask:
“Have I made you feel like ministry matters more to me than you do?”
And then…
actually stayed quiet long enough to hear the answer?
That conversation may terrify you more than preaching before ten thousand people.
Have it anyway.
Because repentance sometimes sounds less like shouting at an altar and more like a father sitting beside his child saying:
“I was there for everybody except you. I see it now. Please forgive me.”
Sometimes repentance sounds like a ministry leader telling a spouse:
“I kept calling my absence sacrifice when some of it was actually avoidance.”
Sometimes repentance means turning the phone off.
Canceling something.
Delegating.
Saying no.
Coming home.
Getting counseling.
Taking a Sabbath seriously.
Stepping away from a responsibility for a season.
Or admitting that a platform has become more important to your identity than you ever intended.
That admission does not have to destroy your ministry.
It may save it.
Because this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus does not merely expose contradictions.
He redeems sinners.
Peter failed publicly.
David shattered his household through terrible sin and lived with devastating consequences.
The disciples repeatedly misunderstood greatness.
Scripture does not sanitize human failure.
But neither does Scripture end the story at exposure.
At the cross, Jesus carried the guilt of sinners.
Not respectable sinners.
Not carefully branded sinners.
Sinners.
People who failed.
People who neglected.
People who lied.
People who loved applause.
People who became selfish.
People who discovered ugly things inside themselves.
People like us.
Christ died for sinners and rose again.
So conviction does not have to become condemnation.
It can become an invitation.
Repent.
Receive grace.
Then change direction.
Maybe your children cannot get back the years already lost.
Maybe your marriage has scars.
Maybe someone you love stopped expecting anything from you because disappointment became too painful.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what you surrender today.
Grace does not mean pretending damage never happened.
Grace gives us courage to tell the truth about the damage and then walk differently because Christ has forgiven us.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal is entertaining.
Not because failure deserves celebration.
But because Jesus rewrites everything surrendered to Him.
Your neglect does not need to become the final chapter.
Your pride does not need to become the final chapter.
Your child’s disappointment does not need to become the final chapter.
Your exhausted marriage does not need to become the final chapter.
Your misplaced priorities do not need to become the final chapter.
Christ can write repentance where there was defensiveness.
Presence where there was absence.
Tenderness where there was irritation.
Humility where there was reputation management.
Restoration where there were years of distance.
But you have to stop hiding.
Maybe that is why this article found you.
Not so you can think of three pastors who need to read it.
You.
Your house.
Your relationships.
Your heart.
Be honest.
Let those words become prayer rather than performance.
Not because every ministry family is broken.
Not because every busy Christian is neglectful.
But because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be doing extraordinary things publicly while something precious is quietly dying privately.

Because there may come a night when the calendar fills again, notifications multiply, people begin needing you from every direction, and you need to remember that not every demand is a divine assignment.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too. Sometimes one biblical truth shared at the right moment becomes the doorway through which someone begins looking toward Christ again.
And if Gospel Warrior is helping you grow closer to Christ, you can go beyond simply reading.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially is not a requirement for earning God’s favor, proving your faith, or purchasing spiritual blessing. Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not through financial support. But voluntary generosity can be one meaningful way believers participate in spreading biblical resources when they believe a ministry is faithfully serving Christ.
Pray.
Save what strengthens you.
Point people toward Scripture.
And above everything else, glorify Jesus with the life you live when nobody is applauding.
Because perhaps the greatest evidence that God is doing something through you will never happen underneath stage lights.
Maybe it will happen tonight.
At a dinner table.
Beside your spouse.
Inside your child’s bedroom.
During an overdue phone call to your mother.
In an apology nobody will post online.
In a quiet decision to close the laptop.
In five words your family desperately needs to hear:
“I’m here. Tell me everything.”
The crowd may never know.
There may be no applause.
No likes.
No shares.
No microphone.
No photograph.
But heaven does not confuse visibility with faithfulness.
And one day, when platforms disappear, audiences move on, algorithms forget your name, and every earthly spotlight finally goes dark, you will understand something that was true all along:
The people God entrusted to your love were never interruptions to your ministry. Loving them faithfully was part of it.
Don’t become so busy telling the world about Jesus that the people living beside you have to wonder what His love feels like.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Want Your Children to Love Jesus—But They’re Learning Christianity by Watching You
paragraphs: You Want Your Children to Love Jesus—But They’re Learning Christianity by Watching You

Your children may forget some of the family devotions you led. But they may remember for the rest of their lives what your Christianity looked like when you were angry, embarrassed, exhausted, offended, disappointed, or wrong.
There is a frightening possibility that almost no Christian parent wants to consider.
You can teach your children the right Bible stories and still teach them the wrong picture of Christianity.
You can bring them to church.
You can pray before meals.
You can put Scripture on the wall.

You can tell them that Jesus forgives sinners, that God answers prayer, that Christians should love their enemies, that money is not everything, that forgiveness matters, that holiness matters, that eternity matters.
And then they watch you.
That is where the lesson becomes real.
They watch what happens when someone humiliates you.
They hear how you speak about people when those people leave the room.
They notice whether the stranger gets Christian kindness while your spouse gets Christian leftovers.
They notice whether you can admit that you were wrong.
They notice whether “I’m sorry” exists in your vocabulary without a “but” attached to it.
They notice what happens when money gets tight.
They notice what happens when prayers seem unanswered.
They notice whether Sunday changes Monday.
And somewhere in those ordinary moments, your children are assembling an answer to a question they may never say aloud:
Is this Jesus my parents talk about actually real enough to change a human being?
That question should bring every Christian parent and grandparent to their knees.
Not because faithful parenting requires perfection.
It doesn’t.
If perfection were the requirement, none of us could disciple anyone.
The Gospel itself begins with the devastating truth that we are sinners who need mercy. Our children do not need parents pretending they have never failed.
They need to see what a sinner looks like when Jesus Christ is actually Lord.
Moses gave Israel a command that generations of believing parents have treasured:

“Thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might. And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.”
Deuteronomy 6:5–7, KJV.
The Hebrew makes the order difficult to ignore.

וְאָהַבְתָּ אֵת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ
בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ
Ve’ahavta et-YHWH Elohekha, bekhol-levavkha uvekhol-nafshekha uvekhol-me’odekha.
“And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.”
Then comes something crucial:
וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה ... עַל־לְבָבֶךָ
Vehayu haddevarim ha’elleh ... al-levavekha.
“These words ... shall be upon your heart.”
Upon your heart.
Before the words are diligently impressed upon the children, they are to live in the parent.

That does not mean parents earn their children’s salvation through exemplary behavior. They cannot. Salvation belongs to the Lord, and no amount of flawless parenting can regenerate another human heart.
It means biblical instruction was never intended to be merely information transferred from an adult mouth into a child’s brain.
God’s truth is meant to possess us.
And then, from a life possessed by that truth, we speak of Him.
At home.
On the road.
At bedtime.
In the morning.
In ordinary life.
Your kitchen becomes part of the classroom.
Your car becomes part of the classroom.
Your bank account becomes part of the classroom.
Your marriage becomes part of the classroom.
Your disappointments become part of the classroom.
Your repentance becomes part of the classroom.
Even the way you respond after losing your temper becomes part of the classroom.
And maybe that last one is where someone reading this already feels the ache.
Because you remember yesterday.
You remember what you said.
Maybe you saw your child’s face change when your voice changed.
Maybe you slammed something.
Maybe you insulted your spouse within earshot of them.
Maybe you humiliated your child and called it discipline.
Maybe you demanded respect while behaving disrespectfully.
Maybe you spent the whole drive to church tearing somebody apart and then walked through the church doors smiling.
Maybe you have been teaching your children about grace while making your home a place where nobody is allowed to fail.
Maybe your children know that Jesus forgives because their Sunday school teacher told them.
But they do not know what forgiveness feels like because resentment has been living at your dinner table for years.
That hurts.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who are in Christ Jesus, failure does not have to become the final chapter.
This is where the Gospel enters the house.
Not as decoration.
Not as a slogan.
Not as religious damage control.
As resurrection.
Your children do not need you to manufacture an image of Christian perfection.
They need to see repentance.
Imagine what happens when a father who has sinned against his child walks into the bedroom, sits beside the bed, looks that child in the eyes and says:
“I was wrong.”
No excuse.
No blame shifting.
No “You made me angry.”
No lecture disguised as an apology.
“I sinned against you. What I said was wrong. Jesus does not excuse my sin, and neither should I. Will you forgive me?”
Something enormous has just happened.
The father has not lost spiritual authority by repenting.
He has demonstrated where Christian authority comes from.
Not ego.
Not domination.
Not pretending.
Christ.
The child has just watched Christianity move from theory into flesh and blood.
They have learned that Daddy needs grace too.
That Mommy needs Jesus too.
That adults do not graduate from repentance.
That the Cross is not merely where bad people become Christians; it remains the place where Christians remember that our only boast is Christ.
Your children may someday forget the exact sermon you discussed over Sunday lunch.
They may never forget hearing you say:
“Please forgive me.”
They may forget the devotional book you used when they were eight.
They may remember watching you forgive someone who wounded you.
They may forget a hundred lessons about trusting God.
They may remember the month when money disappeared and fear entered the house—and still they watched you pray rather than worship panic.
They may forget your lecture about loving your neighbor.
They may remember how you treated the waitress who got your order wrong.
They may forget your warnings about worldly materialism.
They may remember whether possessions controlled your mood.
They may forget your explanation of Christian marriage.
They may remember how you spoke to their mother.
How you spoke to their father.
How affection looked.
How conflict looked.
How forgiveness looked.
Children are watching what Christianity does to us when Christianity costs something.
That is often where faith becomes credible.

Jesus Himself warned against a religion concerned with outward appearance while the inner life remains corrupt. His fiercest rebukes were not aimed at broken people who knew they needed mercy, but repeatedly at religious hypocrisy that performed righteousness before others while resisting the deeper reality of God’s rule.
Your home is one of the hardest places to maintain a religious performance.
Eventually the costume slips.
And maybe that is mercy.
Because perhaps the greatest spiritual gift you can give your children is not the illusion that their parent has everything together.
Perhaps it is allowing them to watch Jesus Christ deal honestly with the person you actually are.
Let them see you open the Bible because you are hungry for God, not merely because you want them to become religious.
Let them hear you pray when there is no audience.
Let them watch you give when nobody applauds.
Let them hear you refuse gossip.
Let them see you shut your mouth when your flesh desperately wants the last word.
Let them watch you honor people who cannot advance your career.
Let them see you treat cleaners, servers, laborers, drivers, employees, strangers, relatives, and difficult people as human beings bearing dignity before God.
Let them discover that your Christianity survives inconvenience.
Let them see you suffer.
This may be one of the hardest lessons of all.
Because eventually life will wound you in front of them.
A diagnosis may come.
Someone may die.
A business may collapse.
A friendship may betray you.
A prayer may appear unanswered.
The future you imagined may disappear.
And your children will watch.
They do not need to see a parent who never cries.
Jesus wept.
They do not need to see someone who pretends suffering does not hurt.
Biblical faith is not emotional anesthesia.
They need to see where you run when it hurts.
There is a difference between saying, “Christ is enough,” when everything is comfortable and whispering His name through tears when something you loved has been buried.
A child who sees that may someday remember it in a hospital corridor of their own.
Years from now, when their world is falling apart, perhaps they will remember:
I watched Mom suffer, and she still ran to Jesus.
I watched Dad break, and somehow Christ held him.
That memory can become a witness.
But parents also need to hear something equally important.
You cannot save your children.
You can teach.
You can pray.
You can model repentance.
You can discipline lovingly.
You can saturate your home with Scripture.
You can confess your hypocrisy.
You can ask forgiveness.
You can speak the Gospel faithfully.
But you cannot regenerate their hearts.
Only God can give life.
That truth should humble us, but it should also relieve us from the crushing fantasy that one parenting mistake automatically writes the ending of our children’s story.
Some parents are reading this with adult children who have walked away from Christianity.
And your heart is already accusing you.
You are replaying everything.
Every argument.
Every missed opportunity.
Every inconsistency.
Every moment when your children saw something in you that contradicted what you claimed to believe.
Where repentance is needed, repent.
If an apology is owed, give it.
Even if your child is thirty-five.
Even if the conversation is awkward.
Even if admitting your failure bruises your pride.
You can say:
“I realize there were times when the Christianity I showed you did not look much like Jesus. I cannot undo those moments. I was wrong. I am sorry. Please forgive me.”
But after genuine repentance, do not pretend you are sovereign over another person's soul.
Your failure is real.
Christ's grace is greater.
Peter failed spectacularly.
He denied Jesus.
Not privately.
Not ambiguously.
Three times.
Yet Jesus did not write Peter’s obituary at the fire where Peter failed.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him.
That is the heartbeat of everything Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim:
Your worst parenting moment does not need to become your final parenting moment.
Your family may have chapters you wish had never been written.
Alcohol.
Anger.
Infidelity.
Divorce.
Absence.
Pride.
Harshness.
Materialism.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Neglect.
Religious hypocrisy.
Years when everyone looked fine in photographs while the house was quietly bleeding.
The Gospel does not require you to rename darkness as light.
It calls you to bring darkness into the light.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
That includes parents.
And grandparents.
Pastors.
Sunday school teachers.
The people posting Bible verses.
The people writing Christian articles.
Every one of us.
But Scripture does not end at Romans 3:23.
We are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:24).
That is Christianity.
Not good parents rescuing bad children.
Not respectable families proving themselves better than broken families.
Sinners being rescued by Jesus Christ.
Your children need more than your example.
They need Christ.
They need the Son of God who lived the righteousness we could not live, bore sin at the Cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
They need to know repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
It is turning toward God.
They need to know grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
They need to know forgiveness is not cheap.
Christ was crucified.
They need to know Christianity is not primarily “become a nicer person.”
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ and a transformed life flowing from union with Him.
And perhaps one of the clearest ways they will begin to understand that is by watching grace transform you.
So tonight, before correcting your children again, ask Christ to search you.
What are they learning by watching me?
What does my anger teach them about Jesus?
What does my marriage teach them?
What does my phone use teach them?
What does my spending teach them?
What does my private life teach them?
What does my speech teach them?
What does the way I treat people who cannot benefit me teach them?
What does my reaction when I am corrected teach them?
What does my repentance teach them?
Not because your performance can save them.
Because your life should not continually contradict the Savior you are asking them to trust.
Go to Jesus.
Then, where necessary, go to your child.
Maybe tonight the most powerful family devotion will not begin with you telling your children what they did wrong.
Maybe it begins with:
“Dad needs to apologize.”
“Mom was wrong.”
“I have not shown you Christ well in this area.”
“Will you forgive me?”
And then pray together.
There are children who have heard thousands of Christian words but have rarely watched an adult genuinely repent.
Change that.
You do not need to explain everything publicly. But sometimes one honest sentence is enough to remind another exhausted parent that they are not the only one fighting for their family on their knees.
And parents, grandparents, pastors, teachers—share this.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.
We are saved by grace, through faith, and our boasting belongs in Christ, not ourselves.
Send it privately to a grandparent who has been praying for the next generation.
Save it too.
Because you may need these words again after a day when you do not parent the way you hoped you would.
It cannot purchase blessing, salvation, spiritual status, or His approval.
Jesus cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory.
Look at the people God has placed in your home.
Remember that discipleship is happening in the ordinary moments.
Your children are listening when you pray.
But they are also listening when you are angry.
They are watching you worship.
But they are also watching you apologize.
They are hearing what you say about Jesus.
But they are also discovering what you really believe when life hurts.
You will fail.
When you do, do not teach them to hide.
Teach them where sinners go.
To Jesus.
Teach them that confession is not the death of a Christian testimony.
Sometimes it is where the testimony finally becomes believable.
Teach them that shame does not get the last word.
Teach them that a father can repent.
A mother can change.
A marriage can be healed.
A wounded family can begin again.
A prodigal can come home.
