You can quote Scripture while building an identity around proving that somebody else does not deserve what God gave them.
You can stand near the altar and still want the throne.
And then the ground opens.
The judgment in Numbers 16 is intentionally terrifying.
This was not a minor disagreement in God's eyes.
The narrative describes the earth opening and swallowing members of the rebellion and their households, while fire consumes the 250 men offering incense.
The New Testament does not allow Christians to dismiss Korah as an irrelevant Old Testament curiosity either.
Jude reaches backward and uses Korah as a warning.
The Greek expression is:
τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ τοῦ Κόρε
tē antilogia tou Kore.
The key word antilogia carries the idea of contradiction, opposition, dispute, or rebellion.
Jude says people “perished in Korah's rebellion.”
Thousands of years later, Korah's name had become shorthand for a spiritual catastrophe.
But please don't miss something beautiful.
The Bible does not end Korah's family story with the grave.
Numbers 26:11 quietly records something astonishing:
“The sons of Korah did not die.”
Think about that.
Korah fell.
Yet his name did not disappear from Scripture.
Later, descendants associated with Korah's line appear in Israel's worship tradition, and several Psalms bear the heading “of the sons of Korah.”
That means the name connected with rebellion would later appear above songs of worship.
Do you see it?
Scandal...
then grace.
Judgment...
yet mercy continuing beyond the rebel's failure.
A name that could have been remembered only for a grave becomes connected with worship.
And this is where the road leads us straight to Jesus.
Because every one of us has rebelled against a greater authority than Moses.
God.
We have not merely compared ourselves with others.
We have wanted God's throne.
Every sin carries the ancient whisper of Eden:
“I will decide what is good.”
“I will decide what is evil.”
“I will rule myself.”
That is rebellion.
And if Korah's rebellion deserved judgment, what should happen to ours?
That question should make the room quiet.
Because Christianity does not say God looked at human rebellion and shrugged.
The Gospel says judgment is real.
Sin is real.
Wrath is real.
But grace is real too.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ—the sinless Son of God—stood in the place of sinners.
He did not die because our rebellion was insignificant.
He died because it was so serious that reconciliation required the giving of His life.
The One who possessed all authority did not grasp for status.
He humbled Himself.
The One who deserved the throne accepted a cross.
The One who could summon angels allowed soldiers to nail His hands open.
Korah reached upward for a position that was not his.
Jesus came downward from glory although all things were His.
Korah's path says:
“I deserve more.”
The Gospel shows Christ saying, in perfect obedience to the Father:
“Not My will, but Yours.”
Korah gathered followers around his grievance.
Jesus gathers sinners around His grace.
Korah's rebellion led toward death.
Christ entered death...
and walked out of the tomb alive.
And now the rebel can come home.
That includes you.
That includes me.
Maybe this article did not expose rebellion against a pastor.
Maybe it exposed your rebellion against God.
You have been angry about the life He allowed.
Angry about the prayer He did not answer the way you demanded.
Angry about the door He closed.
Angry that someone else was chosen.
Angry about years you believe were wasted.
Angry because obedience has cost more than you expected.
And beneath all the respectable Christian language there has been one painful sentence:
“God, I think I could have written my story better than You.”
There it is.
Korah's whisper.
But Jesus is not standing over the repentant sinner waiting to push him into the earth.
The crucified and risen Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
Grace does not tell you your rebellion was harmless.
Grace tells you Someone paid for rebels.
You do not need to keep defending yourself.
You do not need to pretend jealousy is discernment.
You do not need to call pride conviction.
You do not need to dress resentment in spiritual language.
Bring it into the light.
Call it what God calls it.
Repent.
And run to Christ.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to be painfully simple:

“Jesus, forgive me. I have wanted recognition more than faithfulness. I have compared my calling with other people's calling. I have resented blessings You gave someone else. I have questioned Your goodness because my life did not unfold according to my expectations. Clean my heart. Teach me to love Your will more than my visibility. Make me faithful with whatever You place in my hands.”
Be honest.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending the struggle is not there.
And if you are still wrestling with comparison, disappointment, jealousy, spiritual exhaustion, or resentment, comment, “Pray for me.”
Let another believer know that behind the profile picture there is a real human being still fighting to surrender.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still changes people.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not twenty random people.
One.
The friend whose disappointment is turning into bitterness.
The ministry worker who feels invisible.
The believer wounded by comparison.
The person who thinks God has forgotten them.
Save it too.
Because comparison rarely dies after one sermon.
There may come another night when somebody else's blessing feels like evidence that God has abandoned you.
Come back and remember Korah.
Come back and remember Moses facedown.
Come back and remember Jesus on the cross.
Come back and remember:
You do not need somebody else's calling to be loved by God.
You need Christ.

Supporting faithful Christian teaching can be one practical way to steward what God has entrusted to you, alongside prayer, sharing biblical truth, serving your local church, caring for people, giving generously, and living obediently before Christ.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase one sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support ministry because you love Christ and want biblical truth to reach people—not because you imagine God can be bought.
“Why did You choose them instead of me?”
They may not need another motivational quote.
They may need Korah's warning.
Moses' humility.
And above everything...
Christ's grace.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Korah was not that he believed Moses had too much power.
It was that Korah could no longer recognize the breathtaking privilege of what God had already placed in his own hands.
Don't let comparison make you despise your portion.
Don't let ambition make obedience look small.
Don't let another person's calling become an accusation against God's goodness.
Don't let disappointment turn into rebellion.
You may never stand where Moses stood.
You may never have the platform you imagined.
Your name may never become famous.
Thousands may never applaud you.
But if Jesus Christ knows your name...
if your sins are forgiven...
if the Spirit of God is transforming you...
if the Father has received you through His Son...
then you are not forgotten.
You are not living on spiritual leftovers.
You have Christ.
And Christ is not the consolation prize.
He is the treasure.
So when the old whisper returns—
“Why them?”
“Why not you?”
“Don't you deserve more?”
Remember the wilderness.
Remember the open ground.
Remember the man facedown before God.
Then look beyond Moses.
Look to Jesus.
The One who descended lower than Korah ever feared falling...
so rebels like us could be raised into everlasting life.
Because sometimes the most dangerous rebellion begins with three quiet words:
“I deserve more.”
But grace teaches the surrendered heart something infinitely better:
“In Jesus Christ, I have received mercy I could never deserve.”
And never forget this:
Korah wanted a higher place. Jesus took the lowest place to bring rebels home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?”
paragraphs:
“WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?”
Jesus Asked What Everyone Else Was Saying About Him. Then He Asked the Question That Stripped Away the Crowd, the Opinions, the religion—and made eternity suddenly personal.
There are questions you can ignore.
Questions you can postpone until life feels less complicated.
Then there is the question Jesus asked His disciples.
A question so simple that a child can understand it…
and so dangerous that a lifetime can be exposed by the answer.
Jesus looked at men who had walked beside Him, heard His teaching, watched demons flee, witnessed impossible things happen, and seen lives changed in front of them.
And He asked:
“Who do people say that the Son of Man is?”
They had answers.
Plenty of them.
People always have answers about Jesus.
Some said John the Baptist.
Others said Elijah.
Others Jeremiah.
Others one of the prophets.
Respectful answers.
Religious answers.
Impressive answers.
Wrong answers.
Then Jesus changed one word…
and suddenly there was nowhere left to hide.
“But who do YOU say that I am?”
In the Greek text of Matthew 16:15:
Ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνα με λέγετε εἶναι;
Hymeis de tina me legete einai?
“But you—who do you say that I am?”
That ὑμεῖς — hymeis, “you,” carries the emphasis.
Not Caesar.
Not the Pharisees.
Not the crowds.
Not your parents.
Not your pastor.
Not your denomination.
Not the Christian creator you follow.
Not the atheist you argued with.
Not the culture surrounding you.
Not the person sitting beside you in church.
You.
Who do you say Jesus is?
And perhaps that is why this question still makes people uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to spend years discussing Jesus without ever surrendering to Jesus.
It is possible to admire His morality while resisting His authority.
It is possible to quote Him without obeying Him.
Sing about Him without knowing Him.
Defend Christianity online while quietly living as though Christ has no claim over Monday morning.
You can own a Bible and still keep Jesus outside rooms in your heart that you refuse to unlock.
You can know worship lyrics.
You can say grace before dinner.
You can post verses.
You can wear the cross.
You can know when to say “Amen.”
And still eventually hear the footsteps of Christ approaching the place where borrowed faith can no longer answer for you.
“Who do you say I am?”
Peter answered.
“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
The Greek is breathtaking:
Σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος.
Sy ei ho Christos, ho huios tou Theou tou zōntos.
“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
—Matthew 16:16
ὁ Χριστός — ho Christos.
“The Christ.”
“The Messiah.”
“The Anointed One.”
The Greek Χριστός — Christos corresponds to the Hebrew concept מָשִׁיחַ — Mashiach, “Messiah,” the Anointed One.
Peter was not merely saying:
“You are inspirational.”
“You are a prophet.”
“You are a spiritual teacher.”
“You are a good man.”
“You make me feel better when life hurts.”
Peter was confessing the identity of Jesus.
You are the Messiah.
And Jesus answered him:
“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but My Father who is in heaven.”
Peter got the answer right.
But here is where the story becomes painfully human.
Because getting the answer right did not mean Peter understood everything the answer would cost.
Moments later Jesus began explaining that He would go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and be raised.
Peter objected.
The same Peter who had just confessed Jesus as Messiah now recoiled from the road the Messiah said He must walk.
That should humble every Christian reading this.
Because we can confess the right Christ with our mouths while still resisting the Christ who contradicts our plans.
We want Jesus as Savior…
but what happens when He exercises His authority as Lord?
We want resurrection.
We do not always want the cross.
We want forgiveness.
We hesitate at repentance.
We want promises.
We struggle with commands.
We want Jesus to heal what hurts…
but sometimes resist Him when He touches what has become an idol.
We want Christ to rescue our lives.
Sometimes we are less enthusiastic about Christ ruling them.
And Jesus refuses to be reduced to the version of Him that makes us most comfortable.
He is not asking you to manufacture an identity for Him.
Scripture reveals who He is.
The question is whether your confession agrees with that revelation—and whether your life is being brought under the truth you confess.
Maybe you have called Him Lord…
while secretly serving money.
Maybe you have called Him holy…
while protecting a hidden sin.
Maybe you have called Him sufficient…
while building your identity on human approval.
Maybe you have called Him your treasure…
while giving Him whatever remains after everything else receives your heart.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your children do not know.
Your church does not know.
Your Facebook friends definitely do not know.
You have learned how to smile while spiritually bleeding.
You know how to type “God is good” while wondering why God feels so far away.
You know how to encourage everybody else while privately asking whether you can survive another night inside your own thoughts.
You know how to look faithful.
But Jesus is not standing before your public image.
He sees you.
The real you.
The exhausted you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The addicted you.
The disappointed you.
The person who promised God, “Never again,” and somehow ended up there again.
The person carrying memories you wish could be erased.
The person wondering whether you have failed Christ too many times.
And still the question comes:
“Who do you say I am?”
Do not answer too quickly.
Because your answer matters most when the hospital calls.
When the relationship collapses.
When somebody betrays you.
When the prayer seems unanswered.
When temptation comes back.
When grief sits beside you at 2:17 in the morning and refuses to leave.
When obedience costs you something.
When God does not follow the script you wrote for Him.
Who is Jesus then?
Peter would eventually discover how deeply this question reaches.
Because the man who boldly confessed Christ would later stand in a courtyard while Jesus was being tried.
Someone recognized him.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Again.
Again.
Three times.
Think about that.
“Who do you say I am?”
“You are the Christ.”
Then later:
“I do not know the man.”
What happened to Peter?
The scandal happened.
Fear happened.
Human weakness happened.
Peter discovered that courageous declarations can collapse when discipleship becomes expensive.
Then a rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that walk into the darkness.
The man who said, “You are the Christ,” had just denied the Christ.
Maybe that is where this story finally finds you.
Not at Caesarea Philippi with the perfect confession.
But outside the courtyard…
weeping over the person you became.
Maybe you knew better.
Maybe God warned you.
Maybe you promised.
Maybe you failed anyway.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe it lives behind a password.
Maybe it has a name.
Maybe it has a face.
Maybe it happened years ago, but shame keeps replaying it as though it happened yesterday.
And perhaps you have quietly wondered:
After what I did, could Jesus possibly still want me?
Then keep reading.
Because the Gospel does not end beside Peter's tears.
Jesus was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day…
He rose.
Christianity does not rest on the idea that Jesus merely gave humanity beautiful ethical teachings. The apostolic proclamation centers on the crucified and risen Christ.
Paul summarizes the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, and He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.
The Messiah Peter confessed became the crucified and risen Savior Peter desperately needed.
And after the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
John 21 records a conversation beside the Sea of Tiberias.
There was a charcoal fire.
That detail matters.
John 18:18 also mentions a charcoal fire in the courtyard where Peter denied Jesus.
Now beside another charcoal fire stands the resurrected Christ.
Peter's worst memory has an echo.
But this time Jesus is there not to destroy Peter…
but to restore him.
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?”
Again.
Again.
Three times.
Three denials.
Three questions.

We should be careful not to force every detail beyond what Scripture explicitly states, but John's deliberate repetition is impossible to read without feeling the weight of Peter's failure and restoration.
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never fallen.
Grace is not God calling darkness light.
Grace is not Jesus shrugging at sin.
The cross itself shows us how serious sin is.
But the cross also shows us how far divine mercy goes to save sinners.
Peter's failure was real.
Christ's grace was greater.
And Jesus gave the fallen disciple work to do.
“Feed My sheep.”
That is grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not rewriting sin into virtue.
Not telling Peter that denial did not matter.
Jesus rewrote what came after Peter's failure.
Peter's scandal did not receive the final word.
Christ did.
And maybe you need that sentence more than you expected:
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
That does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
Biblical grace never eliminates repentance.
Jesus came proclaiming:
Μετανοεῖτε — Metanoeite.
“Repent.”
Turn.
Come out of hiding.
Stop negotiating with the thing that is destroying you.
Bring your sin into the light before God.
Trust Christ.
Because repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
You cannot punish yourself into salvation.
You cannot clean yourself enough to make the cross unnecessary.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith, not a trophy awarded to people who successfully repaired themselves.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith…not a result of works.”
—Ephesians 2:8–9
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
The next verse says we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to leave the old life behind.
Grace does not say, “Stay chained.”
Grace opens the prison door and says:
Follow Jesus out.
So the question remains.
Who do you say He is?
Not merely with your Facebook bio.
Not merely with your Sunday vocabulary.
Not merely with your favorite worship song.
Who does your life say He is?
If Jesus is merely a teacher, you can disagree with Him.
If He is merely an inspirational figure, you can admire Him and continue walking your own road.
If He is merely one religious option among many, you can place Him comfortably beside everything else competing for your allegiance.
But if Peter's confession is true…
If Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God…
then He cannot merely be added to your life.
Your life belongs to Him.
Jesus said:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.”
—Matthew 16:24
Notice where Matthew places that call.
In the same chapter.
Peter confesses who Jesus is.
Jesus reveals the road to the cross.
Then Jesus calls His disciples to follow.
Identity.
Cross.
Discipleship.
The Gospel does not merely ask whether you admire Jesus.
It confronts you with who Jesus is…
what He accomplished…
and whether you will follow Him.
Maybe this article found you while your faith is strong.
Then do not become proud.
Stay near Christ.
Maybe it found you while you are spiritually exhausted.
Then stop pretending.
Bring your exhaustion to Him.
Maybe it found you while you are living two lives.
One public.
One hidden.
You already know which sentence would hurt if someone read your private history aloud.
Jesus already knows.
And He still calls sinners to repent and come to Him.
Maybe you walked away from God.
Come home.
Maybe religion wounded you.
Do not confuse the failures of people claiming Christ's name with Christ Himself.
Look again at Jesus.
Maybe you do not yet believe.
Then investigate Him seriously.
Read the Gospels.
Ask the difficult questions.
But do not dismiss Jesus based on a caricature of Him you inherited from someone else.
Eventually every voice in the crowd becomes background noise.
The question comes back.
Quietly.
Personally.
Unavoidably.
“Who do YOU say I am?”
And perhaps the most dangerous answer is not “I hate Jesus.”
Perhaps it is:
“I'll deal with Him later.”
Scripture never promises you unlimited tomorrows.
Today you can turn toward Christ.
You can confess your sin.
You can ask for mercy.
You can place your trust not in your religious performance, but in the crucified and risen Son of God.
You can say:

Jesus, I have spent too long hiding behind what everyone else says about You. I need to know You. I confess that I am a sinner and cannot save myself. I believe You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Change me. Teach me to follow You—not merely with my mouth, but with my life. I surrender myself to You. Amen.
Do not mistake a prayer itself for a magical formula.
Christ saves.
The words are simply an expression of repentance and faith.
And if something inside you broke while reading this, do not immediately scroll into another distraction.
Be honest.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer needed permission to say.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “Share” proves that you are a better Christian. It does not.
Someone you know may never walk into a church this week.
But they may stop for a story about Peter.
They may recognize themselves in his failure.
And perhaps, through Scripture, they will look beyond Peter and finally see Jesus.
Because one day the person who needs to reread it may be you.
There is another practical way you can help this ministry continue.
We never want financial support confused with salvation or God's favor.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase God's blessing.

But Christians have always been able to support Gospel ministry voluntarily and generously. If you want to glorify God through your resources, one legitimate way is to support faithful Gospel work that helps spread His Word.
The goal is not collecting religious content.
The goal is becoming more deeply rooted in Christ.
Jesus is still the treasure.
He is not the means by which we build an audience.
He is the message.
He is the Christ.
The Son of the living God.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
And after every opinion has faded…
after every argument has gone silent…
after every title, possession, accomplishment, failure, secret, applause, regret, and excuse has fallen away…
the question remains.
Not:
What did your parents believe?
Not:
What did your church say?
Not:
What did Facebook say?
Not:
What did the world decide?
But:
Who do YOU say Jesus is?
Peter answered correctly.
Then Peter failed spectacularly.
Then Jesus met him in the wreckage.
That is why Peter's story is not merely a story about confession.
It is a story about grace.
A fisherman became a disciple.
A disciple became a denier.
A denier became a broken man.
A broken man met the risen Christ.
And the risen Christ was not finished with him.
That is the Gospel-shaped hope beneath every scandal surrendered to Jesus.
Your sin is serious.
Repentance matters.
Consequences can be real.
But Jesus Christ is not intimidated by the chapter you are ashamed to show Him.
He already knows it.
Bring it into His light.
And let the One who restored Peter have the final word over you.
Because sometimes the rooster crowing over your greatest failure is not the sound of your story ending—it is the sound of Jesus preparing to write what comes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT SHOULD MARRIED CHRISTIANS NEVER JOKE ABOUT?
paragraphs: WHAT SHOULD MARRIED CHRISTIANS NEVER JOKE ABOUT?
Some Jokes Last Five Seconds. The Wound They Leave in a Marriage Can Last for Years.
Everybody laughed.
Except her.
Her husband had just told the story again—the embarrassing one.
The one about something she had trusted him enough to confess in private.
The table erupted.
Someone nearly spit out their drink. Another person slapped the table. Her husband looked pleased with himself because the punchline had landed perfectly.
She smiled too.
At least, her face did.
Under the table, her hands tightened.
Nobody noticed.
On the drive home, he finally asked, “What’s wrong?”
“Nothing.”
But something was wrong.
Because sometimes the most painful sentence in a marriage begins with four innocent-sounding words:
“I was only joking.”
And sometimes the person who promised to protect your heart discovers exactly where it is tender—and then uses that tenderness to entertain a room.
That is why Christians need to ask a question deeper than, “Can married couples joke about this?”
We need to ask:
“Does the way I joke with my spouse look like Jesus?”
Because Scripture is not against laughter.
God is not threatened by joy.
“A joyful heart is good medicine” (Proverbs 17:22).
Ecclesiastes says there is “a time to laugh” (Ecclesiastes 3:4).

Jesus Himself used startling imagery, irony, exaggeration, and unforgettable verbal pictures. The Christian marriage was never intended to feel like two frightened people living under a permanent cloud of religious seriousness.
Laugh together.
Be ridiculous together.
Have inside jokes.
Tease each other affectionately when both of you genuinely enjoy it.
Grow old enough together that you can finish each other’s stories and still laugh at the stories you have heard a hundred times.
But understand something:
Not everything that produces laughter produces love.
And laughter is never permission to violate the commands God has already given us about our words.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:4 about speech that does not belong among God’s people, including what many English translations render as “crude joking.” The Greek word is εὐτραπελία—eutrapelia.

The word can carry the idea of clever or witty speech, but in Paul’s immediate context it is associated with speech that has become morally inappropriate, shameful, or indecent. Paul does not condemn every clever joke. He contrasts degrading speech with thanksgiving.
That distinction matters.
The biblical question is not simply, “Was it funny?”
The biblical question is, “What did the joke do?”
Did it honor?
Did it humiliate?
Did it protect?
Did it expose?
Did it strengthen intimacy?
Did it turn something sacred into entertainment?
Did your spouse laugh because it was genuinely funny—or because everyone was watching and laughing was less painful than admitting you embarrassed them?
There are places in your spouse’s heart where comedy should enter carefully.
And there are some things Christian husbands and wives should refuse to turn into weapons disguised as punchlines.
Do not casually joke about divorce as though covenant abandonment is entertainment.
“I should’ve married someone else.”
“I’m trading you in.”
“One more argument and I’m filing for divorce.”
“Maybe my next husband will listen.”
“Maybe my next wife will actually cook.”
People laugh.
But the heart remembers.

Marriage in Scripture is covenantal, not disposable. Jesus takes marriage with profound seriousness in Matthew 19:4–6, pointing back to creation and declaring that husband and wife become “one flesh.”
The Greek expression is σὰρξ μία—sarx mia—“one flesh.”
Not two competitors temporarily sharing an address.
One flesh.

This does not mean every mention of divorce is sinful, nor does it erase the difficult biblical and pastoral questions surrounding abuse, abandonment, adultery, separation, or divorce. Those circumstances require truth, wisdom, safety, pastoral care, and sometimes professional or legal help.
But repeatedly threatening the covenant for comedy is something else.
Imagine building a house with someone and periodically joking that you might burn it down.
Eventually, they may stop sleeping peacefully inside it.
The same principle applies to adultery.
Be extraordinarily careful about jokes suggesting that you want someone else sexually or romantically.
“Your sister is looking good.”
“If he asked me out, you’d better watch yourself.”
“That actress is my real wife.”
“I only married you because she rejected me.”
Maybe everyone understands the joke.
Maybe your spouse even laughs.
But marriage is not merely a legal arrangement. It is a place where emotional and sexual exclusivity should be cultivated and protected.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage should be held in honor and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
Jesus goes even deeper in Matthew 5:27–28, addressing lust at the level of the heart.
So why would a Christian repeatedly make entertainment out of the very betrayal Scripture tells us to guard against?
Faithfulness should feel safe in your marriage.
Not fragile.
Not negotiable.
Not something your spouse has to compete for.
And never use your spouse’s body as a comedy routine.
Weight.
Age.
Hair loss.
Wrinkles.
Sexual performance.
Infertility.
Pregnancy changes.
Physical disabilities.
Medical struggles.
Features they already dislike about themselves.
There is a world of difference between affectionate teasing shared by two secure people and repeatedly targeting an insecurity because you know it gets laughs.
Your spouse gave you access that strangers do not have.
You know where they are insecure.
You know what happened in childhood.
You know what their former partner said.
You know what they see when they stare too long into the mirror.
You know what makes them feel unwanted.
That knowledge makes you powerful.
Christian love asks what you will do with that power.
Proverbs 12:18 says that reckless words can pierce like a sword, while the tongue of the wise brings healing.
A sword does not become harmless because the person swinging it is smiling.
Read that again.
A sword does not become harmless because the person swinging it is smiling.
Some spouses have become experts at stabbing lovingly.
They insult, then grin.
They expose, then laugh.
They belittle, then say, “You’re too sensitive.”
They wound, then make the wounded person feel guilty for bleeding.
That is not the tenderness Scripture calls husbands and wives toward.
Ephesians 4:29 gives Christians a radically different standard for speech: our words should build others up according to their needs and give grace to those who hear.
Grace.
Even in humor.
Especially at home.
Your spouse should not have to develop thicker skin just to survive your personality.
And please—do not turn private sexual intimacy into public entertainment.
There are things a husband knows about his wife that belong inside the sanctuary of their covenant.
There are things a wife knows about her husband that should never become material for the group chat.
The bedroom should not become tomorrow morning’s comedy content.
Your spouse’s private fears, sexual vulnerabilities, embarrassing moments, deeply personal disclosures, past trauma, failures they confessed to you, and struggles entrusted to you deserve discretion.
Love does not merely ask, “Is this technically true?”
Love asks, “Was this mine to tell?”
Proverbs 11:13 contrasts gossip with the trustworthiness of someone who keeps confidence.
There is something breathtaking about being married to someone who knows the ugliest chapter of your story and makes you feel safer because they know it—not more exposed.
That is intimacy.
Your spouse should be able to hand you something fragile without wondering whether you will eventually hand it to an audience.
And never joke about abuse, violence, coercion, or terror in a way that normalizes them.
“I’m going to kill you.”
“She needs a good slap.”
“I keep him in line.”
“He knows what happens when I get angry.”
Christian marriage is not permission for domination, intimidation, or cruelty.

Colossians 3:19 tells husbands to love their wives and not be harsh with them. First Peter 3:7 commands husbands to live with their wives with understanding and honor. Ephesians 5 places Christian marriage beneath the enormous shadow of Christ’s self-giving love.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
The Greek verb translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶτε—agapate—from ἀγαπάω, agapaō.
Whatever debates surround the nuances of Greek words for love, Paul makes his intended meaning unmistakable by giving us the model:
Christ.
He gave Himself.
That destroys the fantasy that biblical headship is a license for humiliation, fear, or selfish control.
Jesus does not stand over His bride looking for vulnerabilities He can exploit.
He gives Himself for her.
Christian marriage therefore keeps returning to one terrifyingly beautiful question:
Does the way I treat my spouse resemble the way Christ loves His people?
That includes our jokes.
And there is another kind of humor that can quietly poison a marriage: contempt.
“My husband is basically another child.”
“My wife never stops talking.”
“You know husbands. They’re useless.”
“You know wives. They’re crazy.”
It becomes socially acceptable because everyone recognizes the stereotype.
But your husband is not “men.”
Your wife is not “women.”
This is the person whose hand you held while making promises before God.
When contempt becomes entertainment, disrespect becomes easier.
Then resentment becomes normal.
Then tenderness becomes awkward.
Then one day two people can sleep inches apart while living emotionally miles away.
It rarely happens all at once.
Sometimes marriages bleed through paper cuts.
One sarcastic comment.
One public embarrassment.
One private insecurity turned into a punchline.
One comparison.
One “joke” about another woman.
One “joke” about another man.
One “joke” about divorce.
One “joke” about sex.
One “joke” about failure.
Then another.
Then another.
Until somebody stops telling you what hurts because telling you has become dangerous too.
But this is where the Gospel interrupts the story.
Because perhaps while reading this, you did not think about what your spouse has done to you.
You thought about what you have done to your spouse.
You remembered their face.
That dinner.
That argument.
That joke.
That secret.
That moment everyone laughed.
And suddenly you remember that your spouse did not.
What do you do now?
Not defensiveness.
Not, “But I didn’t mean it that way.”
Not, “You joke about me too.”
Not, “Everyone knew I was kidding.”
Not, “You need to stop being so sensitive.”
Repent.
That word frightens people because we have reduced repentance to religious humiliation.
But biblical repentance is an invitation to turn.
The New Testament commonly uses μετάνοια—metanoia—for repentance, carrying the sense of a changed mind and turning expressed in a changed direction.
Repentance says:
“I see what my words have been doing.”
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“I will not hide behind humor.”
“Please forgive me.”
And then repentance produces fruit.
The joke stops.
The secret stays private.
The flirting disguised as humor ends.
The public humiliation ends.
The contempt ends.
The threats end.
You begin learning how to make the person you married feel safe in your words again.
Maybe you are the wounded spouse.
Perhaps you have laughed publicly and cried privately.
Perhaps everyone thinks your husband is hilarious, but you know what it feels like to be the material.
Perhaps your wife knows exactly which insecurity will silence you.
Perhaps “I was joking” has been used so often that you have begun wondering whether you are simply too sensitive.
Your pain should not automatically be dismissed merely because somebody else laughed.
At the same time, every awkward joke is not abuse, every insensitive comment is not evidence of a doomed marriage, and spouses must leave room for misunderstanding, forgiveness, maturity, and growth.
Christians should resist both extremes.
We should not call every imperfect sentence abuse.
And we should not call cruelty humor merely because someone laughed.
The Gospel gives us something better than both hypersensitivity and hardness.
It gives us truth wrapped in grace.
Jesus exposes sin without abandoning sinners who come to Him.
That is the heartbeat of the Christian story.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met Thomas.
The woman caught in adultery stood beneath the weight of public shame, and Jesus neither celebrated her sin nor surrendered her to condemnation. He called her toward a different life.
The cross itself announces something astonishing:
Your worst moment does not have to write your final chapter.
That is why there is hope for the husband whose tongue has been cruel.
There is hope for the wife whose sarcasm became a weapon.
There is hope for the marriage that has accumulated years of little wounds.
There is hope for the couple who has forgotten how to speak gently.
Not because words do not matter.
They matter enormously.
But because Jesus Christ is still in the business of transforming people.
You may not be able to retrieve every sentence you have spoken.
You cannot walk back into every room and catch every joke before it leaves your mouth.
You cannot erase every memory.
But through Christ, you can become someone who speaks differently tomorrow.
Confess your sin to God.
Confess specifically to your spouse where appropriate.
Ask forgiveness without demanding immediate emotional recovery.
Listen when they tell you what your words have done.
Do not argue with their wound.
And then begin rebuilding.
Slowly.
Tenderly.
Consistently.
Let your spouse discover that their weakness is safe with you.
Let them discover that their body is safe with you.
Let them discover that their history is safe with you.
Let them discover that their failures are safe with you.
Let them discover that the marriage covenant is not something you threaten whenever you need a punchline.
Then laugh.
Please laugh.
Laugh until your stomach hurts.
Laugh about the burnt dinner.
Laugh about getting lost on vacation.
Laugh about the ridiculous thing you both misunderstood.
Laugh about the harmless quirks you both genuinely enjoy teasing each other about.
Laugh about growing older together.
Build a home filled with joy.
But make sure the laughter leaves both people standing.
Because Christian humor should never require the sacrifice of your spouse’s dignity.
Before you make your husband the punchline, remember who he is.
Before you embarrass your wife for applause, remember who she is.
Not your content.
Not your target.
Not your emotional punching bag.
Not your comedy prop.
Someone made in the image of God.
Someone you promised to love.
Someone whose heart has been placed unusually close to your hands.
Handle it accordingly.
And if this article exposed something in you, resist the temptation to immediately send it to your spouse as ammunition.
Read it again for yourself first.
Ask Jesus:
“Lord, what needs to change in me?”
Maybe the most Christlike thing you do tonight will not be winning an argument about whose jokes are worse.
Maybe it will be walking into the room, sitting beside the person you love, and saying:

“I realize some of the things I’ve called jokes have hurt you. I’m sorry. I don’t want my humor to cost you your sense of safety with me. Will you forgive me? And will you help me understand where I need to change?”
That conversation may not fix everything tonight.
But grace often begins with somebody finally telling the truth.
And if your marriage needs prayer, there is no shame in simply commenting, “pray for us.”
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become reminders that Christian marriages are filled with real people who need real grace from a real Savior.
Supporting a ministry is not a requirement for earning God’s favor, proving your faith, or glorifying God—Christians glorify God through lives surrendered to Him.
Take it home.
Take it into your marriage.
Take it before Christ.
Because perhaps the question was never merely, “What should married Christians never joke about?”
Perhaps the deeper question has always been:
“Does the person who knows me most intimately experience more of Christ because of the way I speak to them?”
Your marriage does not need two perfect people.
It needs two people who keep bringing their imperfect hearts to a perfect Savior.
Two people willing to repent.
Two people willing to forgive.
Two people learning when to laugh and when something is too sacred to become a joke.
Two people discovering that grace does not merely forgive what happened yesterday.
Grace teaches us how to love differently tomorrow.
And remember this:
The mouth that once made your spouse feel small can, surrendered to Jesus, become the mouth that spends the rest of your marriage reminding them they are deeply loved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABIGAIL’S STORY COMPLICATES THE WAY CHURCHES TALK ABOUT MARRIAGE
paragraphs: ABIGAIL’S STORY COMPLICATES THE WAY CHURCHES TALK ABOUT MARRIAGE
She was a faithful woman married to a foolish man. And when his choices threatened an entire household, Scripture does not portray her wisdom, courage, or intervention as rebellion.
There are Bible stories we love because they fit neatly into sermons.

And then there are Bible stories that walk into the room, sit down in the uncomfortable chair nobody wants to acknowledge, and quietly ask whether some of our favorite Christian slogans have actually said everything the Bible says.
Abigail’s story is one of those stories.
Because somewhere tonight, a woman may be sitting in a church pew beside a husband everyone else respects while privately carrying the consequences of decisions she did not make.
Somewhere, a husband may be desperately trying to understand the difference between biblical covenant faithfulness and enabling destructive behavior.
Somewhere, someone has been told that being godly means never speaking, never resisting, never seeking help, never exposing what is happening behind closed doors.
And somewhere, perhaps, a sincere pastor has reduced an enormously complicated situation to a sentence that sounded biblical:
“Just submit.”
Then Abigail walks into 1 Samuel 25.
And suddenly the conversation gets harder.
Not because Scripture contradicts Scripture.
It doesn’t.
But because Scripture is often far more honest about broken human relationships than our slogans are.
Listen carefully to how the biblical writer introduces this marriage.
Abigail is described in Hebrew as:
טוֹבַת־שֶׂכֶל — tovat-sekhel
A woman of good understanding. Good judgment. Discernment.
Her husband Nabal, however, is described as:
קָשֶׁה וְרַע מַעֲלָלִים — qasheh vera ma‘alalim
Harsh…and evil in his deeds.
That contrast is not something modern readers invented.
It is sitting there in the Hebrew text.
The narrator deliberately places a discerning woman beside a harsh man whose conduct is evil.
And that matters.
Because sometimes we talk about marriage as though putting a wedding ring on someone magically sanctifies everything that person subsequently does.
Scripture never teaches that.
Marriage is sacred.
Sin is not.
Covenant is sacred.
Cruelty is not.
Faithfulness is sacred.
Foolishness does not become holy simply because the fool committing it happens to be someone’s spouse.
And Abigail knew something terrible was coming.

David and his men had been living in the wilderness. During that period, David’s men had protected Nabal’s shepherds and possessions. When sheep-shearing season arrived—a time associated with celebration and abundance—David sent men requesting provisions.
Nabal responded with contempt.
“Who is David?”
Essentially: Why should I care about him?
He insulted the future king and sent David’s messengers away empty-handed.
And David became furious.
Not mildly irritated.
Not disappointed.
Furious.
He strapped on his sword.
His men strapped on theirs.
And David headed toward Nabal’s household intending bloodshed.
Now notice what happens next.
One of Nabal’s servants does not go to Nabal.
He goes to Abigail.
That detail should make us uncomfortable.
Why?
Because the servant explains that Nabal is essentially impossible to reason with.
The household knows what kind of man he is.
They know disaster is coming.
And they know the person most capable of doing something about it is Abigail.
There are homes like that.
Everyone knows who the dangerous person is.
Everyone knows who absorbs the consequences.
Everyone knows who cleans up the emotional wreckage afterward.
Everyone knows who must calculate every sentence before speaking.
But outside the house?
Nobody knows.
Sometimes the person holding a household together looks so capable that nobody realizes how exhausted they are.
Abigail immediately acts.
She gathers bread.
Wine.
Sheep.
Grain.
Raisins.
Figs.
She loads donkeys.
And Scripture says something extraordinarily important:
She does not tell Nabal what she is doing.
Read that again.
Abigail takes decisive action to prevent catastrophe without first obtaining the approval of the husband whose foolishness created the catastrophe.
And the biblical narrator does not interrupt the story to condemn her.
Instead, Abigail rides directly toward danger.
Imagine that scene.
Dust beneath the animals.
Food strapped down.
Servants moving quickly.
David approaching from the opposite direction with hundreds of armed men.
One woman riding between male arrogance and male vengeance.
Nabal has behaved wickedly.
David is about to respond wickedly.
And Abigail steps into the space between them.
She gets off the donkey.
She bows before David.
Then she begins talking.
And what comes out of her mouth is astonishing.
She does not merely beg.
She reasons.
She appeals to David’s future.
His calling.
His conscience.
His relationship with God.
She essentially tells the future king:
Do not become the kind of man who will someday regret what he did today.
Think about that.
David had been anointed.
David had defeated Goliath.
David had written songs to God.
David was the hero of Israel.
And Abigail still confronted the direction he was going.
Because being chosen by God does not mean every impulse you have comes from God.
That sentence alone could save churches from enormous amounts of spiritual damage.
Anointing does not eliminate accountability.
Leadership does not eliminate accountability.
Marriage does not eliminate accountability.
Pastoral authority does not eliminate accountability.
Being male does not eliminate accountability.
Being female does not eliminate accountability.
Nobody becomes incapable of sin because they possess a biblical title.
And Abigail refuses to treat David’s rage as righteousness simply because David is God’s anointed.
She reminds him that God Himself is capable of dealing with his enemies.
She speaks of David’s life being kept securely with the LORD.
And then she warns him against acquiring needless bloodguilt.
In 1 Samuel 25:31, she speaks about this becoming a future פּוּקָה — puqah, a staggering or stumbling of conscience, together with the grief of having shed blood without cause.
In other words:
David…
You are about to become someone you do not need to become.
You are angry now.
But tomorrow exists.
Your calling exists.
Your conscience exists.
Your future exists.
God’s judgment exists.
Do not sacrifice tomorrow because your anger is screaming today.
And David stops.
That may be one of the most beautiful moments in the entire chapter.
A powerful man listens to a wise woman.
He does not say, “Know your place.”
He does not say, “God chose me, so don't question me.”
He does not accuse her of rebellion.
He listens.
Then David says:
בָּרוּךְ טַעְמֵךְ וּבְרוּכָה אָתְּ — barukh ta‘mekh uverukhah att
“Blessed be your discernment, and blessed are you.”
David recognizes that God has used Abigail to stop him from bloodshed.
Pause there.
Because this story is not simply about a wonderful woman and a terrible husband.
David needs correction too.
Nabal is wrong.
David is becoming wrong.
Abigail stands between two forms of destructive masculinity and refuses to surrender her discernment to either one.
That complicates the way churches talk about marriage.
Especially when we speak about submission.
Yes, Scripture teaches wives to submit to their husbands.
We should not erase that because contemporary culture dislikes it.
Ephesians 5 says it.
But Christians cannot faithfully quote Ephesians 5:22 while pretending Ephesians 5:25 does not exist.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
The model for Christian husbandhood is not domination.
It is crucifixion.
Christ does not crush His bride.
He gives Himself for her.
Christ does not manipulate His bride.
He sanctifies her.
Christ does not use authority to feed His ego.
He lays down His life.

So whenever “submission” is taught in a way that protects selfishness, intimidation, violence, sexual coercion, manipulation, criminal behavior, or unrepentant cruelty, something has gone catastrophically wrong.
Biblical submission is never permission to sin.
And biblical marriage never makes evil good.
Abigail understood that honoring God sometimes means refusing to cooperate with another person's foolishness.
But we must also be careful here.
Abigail’s story is not permission to label every disagreement “abuse.”
It does not teach that a wife should secretly undermine her husband whenever she believes she knows better.
It does not erase the Bible’s teaching about covenant, reconciliation, patience, forgiveness, mutual responsibility, or marital faithfulness.
And 1 Samuel 25 is not primarily a divorce manual.
We should not force the passage to answer questions it was not directly written to answer.
But neither should we silence what it actually shows us.
Abigail is not condemned for recognizing reality.
She is not condemned for exercising discernment.
She is not condemned for protecting her household.
She is not condemned for speaking truth to David.
She is not condemned for taking action when Nabal cannot be reasoned with.
In fact, David blesses her discernment.
That means churches must become places where people can tell the truth about what is happening inside their homes.
Not gossip.
Truth.
Not revenge.
Truth.
Not character assassination.
Truth.
There is a difference.
Because sometimes Christians become so frightened of “breaking up a marriage” that they unintentionally help conceal the very sins destroying the marriage.
We must do better.
If someone is in immediate physical danger, seeking safety is not spiritual failure.
If criminal violence is occurring, contacting appropriate civil authorities is not a betrayal of Christ.
Romans 13 recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining wrongdoing.
If abuse is happening, wise pastoral care should not consist merely of sending someone home with instructions to become more compliant.
Churches should care about repentance.
Real repentance.
The kind that produces fruit.
The kind John the Baptist demanded when he said, “Bear fruit in keeping with repentance.”
Not tears without transformation.
Not apologies followed by repetition.
Not Bible verses used as camouflage.
Not “God forgave me, so why can't you?”
Repentance turns.
Grace forgives sinners, but grace never teaches sinners that their sin does not matter.
And that is where Abigail’s story unexpectedly begins pointing beyond Abigail.
Because eventually we realize something uncomfortable.
We are not always Abigail.
Sometimes we are Nabal.
Hard.
Proud.
Impossible to correct.
Certain that our money, status, personality, pain, or position gives us the right to treat others however we want.
And sometimes…
we are David.
Wounded.
Humiliated.
Angry.
Convinced that because somebody sinned against us, we now have permission to sin against them.
That is the terrifying genius of 1 Samuel 25.
You begin reading believing you know who the villain is.
Then suddenly David has a sword in his hand.
And if we are willing to be honest before God, sometimes so do we.
Maybe yours is not made of steel.
Maybe your sword is your tongue.
Your silence.
Your temper.
Your Facebook post.
Your manipulation.
Your threat.
Your revenge.
Your ability to make someone feel tiny.
Your determination to make them hurt because they hurt you.
And somewhere between the insult and the retaliation, God whispers:
Put the sword down.
This is where the Gospel enters the story.
Because Abigail can stop David from committing bloodshed that afternoon.
But Abigail cannot cleanse David’s heart.
And she cannot cleanse ours.
We need someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
David was a king who sometimes needed someone to stop him from shedding another person's blood.
Jesus is the King who willingly shed His own blood to save His enemies.
David reached for a sword after being insulted.
Jesus, when reviled, did not revile in return.
David was prepared to destroy the guilty man along with his household.
Jesus stood in the place of guilty people and allowed judgment to fall upon Himself.
At Calvary, the innocent Christ received what sinners deserved.
The nails entered His hands.
The crown pierced His head.
His blood fell.
And the Son of God died not because our sin was small…
but because His mercy was greater.
This is Christianity.
Not pretending everything is okay.
Not protecting appearances.
Not baptizing dysfunction.
Not calling darkness light.
The Gospel tells the horrifying truth about our sin and then announces an even greater truth about our Savior.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
That is scandalous grace.
Nabal needs grace.
David needs grace.
Abigail needs grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years trying to rescue everyone around you.
Jesus sees you.
Maybe someone used Scripture to keep you silent while protecting their own sin.
Jesus is not threatened by truth.
Maybe you are the one who has wounded the people closest to you and have become very skilled at explaining why it was actually their fault.
Then stop explaining.
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Confess what you have done.
Seek forgiveness.
Accept accountability.
Make restitution where possible.
Get help.
Bring your behavior into the light.
Because the Gospel does not merely offer you forgiveness from the penalty of sin.
Jesus intends to transform you.
And perhaps that is the word someone reading this desperately needed.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
David put down the sword.
Later, Nabal died, and Scripture explicitly presents his death as an act of the LORD—not Abigail’s revenge and not David's hand.
David did not have to become Nabal’s judge.
God remained God.
Eventually Abigail became David’s wife.
But even that is not the deepest ending of the story.
Because Abigail’s ultimate significance is not that one difficult marriage ended and another marriage began.
Her story matters because, for one extraordinary moment, a woman of discernment stood between foolishness and bloodshed and trusted that God could handle what human vengeance could not.
And generations later, the Son of David would come.
Jesus Christ.
The greater King.
The perfectly righteous King.
The Bridegroom who never abuses His bride.
The Savior who never manipulates the broken.
The Shepherd who does not devour His sheep.
The Lord who tells sinners the truth while opening His arms to receive those who repent.
That is why churches must speak carefully about marriage.
We should defend marriage fiercely.
And we should defend it biblically.
Which means we cannot defend the institution while ignoring the character of the God who created it.
Marriage is meant to tell the truth about Christ and His Church.
So our teaching must sound like Christ.
Our leadership must look like Christ.
Our marriages must increasingly reflect Christ.
Our repentance must lead us toward Christ.
And our treatment of wounded people must carry the compassion and truth of Christ.
If this article exposed something in you, don't rush past that discomfort.
Maybe your prayer needs to be:
“Jesus, show me where I have confused control with leadership.”
Or:
“Jesus, show me where fear has kept me silent.”
Or simply:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
There are moments when two words are enough for another believer to know they need to stand beside you in prayer.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't weaponize this article against them.
Pray first.
Then, if sharing it would genuinely serve them, send it with love.
Save it too.
There are truths you understand differently when you return to them after the emotion has settled.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you see Scripture more clearly, following this ministry helps you stay connected to daily biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.

If glorifying God matters to us, it should eventually touch what we do with our voice, influence, time, generosity, and resources. The Gospel is grace, not merchandise. But when Christ-centered ministry genuinely strengthens you, voluntarily supporting and sharing that work can help put biblical truth in front of another person who needs it.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is sitting behind a carefully maintained Christian appearance wondering whether God sees what nobody else sees.
He does.
And somewhere else, somebody is holding the sword of anger, convinced retaliation will finally make the pain disappear.
Jesus is calling them to put it down.

And somewhere, perhaps inside your own heart, Christ is exposing what has been hidden—not to destroy you, but to bring you into the light where repentance becomes possible and grace becomes more than a religious word.
Remember Abigail.
Remember David lowering the sword.
Remember that God remained God even when human beings were losing control.
And above all…
remember Jesus.
Because sometimes grace does not merely rescue you from the person coming toward you with a sword—it rescues you from becoming the person holding one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WOULD GOD GIVE YOU THE FREEDOM TO BREAK HIS HEART?
paragraphs: WHY WOULD GOD GIVE YOU THE FREEDOM TO BREAK HIS HEART?
If God already knew what you would choose, why give you a choice at all? The answer leads from Eden’s rebellion to a bloodstained cross—and may change the way you understand every decision you make.
There is something terrifying about the love of God.
He lets you say no.
Think about that.

The God who formed galaxies could have created creatures incapable of rebellion. He could have made humanity like a universe of obedient machinery—every movement predetermined, every response automatic, every knee bending because no other movement was possible.
No betrayal.
No rebellion.
No adultery.
No hatred.
No war.
No prodigal sons walking away from home.
No Peter denying Jesus beside a charcoal fire.
No Judas disappearing into the night.
No forbidden fruit.
No cross.
So why didn't He?
Why would a holy God create human beings capable of looking into the face of their Creator and saying...
No.
Maybe that question has become painfully personal for you.
Maybe you have wondered why God allowed someone to make a choice that shattered your life.
Why did He let that person leave?
Why didn't He stop the betrayal?
Why didn't He force your child to come home?
Why didn't He prevent the decision that destroyed the marriage?
Why doesn't God simply overpower the stubborn heart of someone you desperately love?
And perhaps there is another question you are more afraid to ask.
Why did God allow you to make the choices you now regret?
The relationship.
The secret.
The addiction.
The years you wasted.
The compromise nobody knows about.
The moment you knew what was right...
and still chose something else.
If God knew what you were going to do, why did He allow you to choose?

The Bible does not answer every philosophical question about human freedom in one neat sentence. Christians have wrestled for centuries with how God's sovereignty and genuine human responsibility fit together. Scripture strongly teaches both God's sovereign purpose and humanity's accountability before Him.
We should be careful not to pretend the mystery is smaller than Scripture makes it.
But Scripture does reveal something breathtaking.
God repeatedly addresses human beings as people whose responses matter.
Near the end of Moses' life, Israel stood before a decision.
God had rescued them, carried them, disciplined them, provided for them and revealed His covenant to them.
Then Moses spoke words that still feel almost dangerous:
“I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life...” — Deuteronomy 30:19.
The ancient Greek Septuagint renders that command:
“ἔκλεξαι τὴν ζωήν”
eklexai tēn zōēn.
“Choose life.”
But notice what comes immediately afterward.
Choosing life is not presented merely as choosing a better lifestyle.
Moses continues by describing loving the LORD, listening to His voice and holding fast to Him, “for he is your life.”
That changes everything.
God was not merely placing two abstract philosophical buttons before Israel.
He was calling them into covenant faithfulness.
Choose life...
because God Himself is your life.
And there, buried inside that ancient scene, is something we desperately need to understand.
Biblical freedom is not merely the freedom to do whatever you want.
Our culture often imagines freedom as the absence of restraint.
“If I want it, I should have it.”
“If I feel it, I should follow it.”
“If it makes me happy, nobody should question it.”
But Scripture gives us a far more unsettling picture.
Human beings can choose...
and human beings can choose terribly.
Freedom does not guarantee wisdom.
Ask Adam and Eve.
The serpent did not need to drag Eve toward the forbidden fruit.
He needed to distort what she believed about God.
“Did God actually say...?”
That ancient whisper still works.
Sin frequently begins when we start wondering whether God's boundaries are keeping us from happiness rather than protecting us from destruction.
The forbidden thing begins looking beautiful.
Necessary.
Deserved.
Harmless.
Then we reach.
And humanity has been reaching ever since.
We reach for approval.
Bodies.
Money.
Status.
Pornography.
Revenge.
Control.
Attention.
Power.
Secret conversations.
Another drink.
Another lie.
Another compromise.
Another night telling ourselves:
“I can stop whenever I want.”
Then one day we discover something horrifying.
The freedom we used to choose our chains eventually begins to feel like slavery.
Jesus said, “everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34).
That is the scandal of human rebellion.
We were made for God, yet our desires became disordered by sin.
We wanted freedom from God...
and discovered bondage without Him.
This is why the Christian message cannot be reduced to “God gave everybody free will, so just make better choices.”
If better choices could save us, Calvary would be unnecessary.
Scripture's diagnosis goes much deeper.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Humanity's problem is not simply that occasionally we select the wrong option.
Something inside us has gone wrong.
We don't merely commit sins.
We need rescue from sin.
And this is where the question “Why does God give free will?” becomes something far more personal than philosophy.
Because eventually the question stops being:
“Why did God allow Adam to choose wrongly?”
It becomes:
“Why have I chosen wrongly when I knew better?”
You knew that bitterness was poisoning you.
You kept drinking it.
You knew that relationship was pulling you away from Christ.
You stayed.
You knew what was happening behind that locked screen.
You returned.
You knew pride was destroying your marriage.
You refused to apologize.
You knew you were drifting.
You kept telling everybody you were fine.
Some of the deepest wounds in our lives were inflicted by other people's choices.
Others came from our own.
And sometimes the hardest person to forgive is the person staring back from the mirror.
But now comes the part the enemy hopes you never understand.
Your worst decision does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Because Christianity is not primarily the story of humanity successfully choosing God.
It is the story of God coming after sinners.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son...” — John 3:16.
We ran.
He came.
We sinned.
He pursued.
We hid.
He called.
We rebelled.
Christ stepped into human history.
And at the center of Christianity stands the most shocking collision imaginable between human rebellion and divine redemption.
The cross.
Look carefully at Calvary.
Human beings exercise their wills there.
Judas chooses betrayal.
Religious leaders choose accusation.
Pilate chooses political convenience.
The crowd chooses Barabbas.
Soldiers choose cruelty.
Peter has already chosen denial.
Human sin seems to be writing the ending.
Then Jesus reveals that another purpose has been moving through the story all along.
The Son of God willingly gives Himself.
Human evil does not defeat God's redemptive purpose.
God turns history's darkest act into the place where salvation is accomplished.
This does not make evil good.
It reveals that evil does not get the last word.
The cross exposes both the horror of sin and the magnitude of grace.
God does not stand far away from the consequences of human rebellion.
In Jesus Christ, He enters our suffering.
He bears shame.
He experiences rejection.
He is mocked.
He is wounded.
He is crucified.
And the hands stretched across the wood are not the hands of a God indifferent to what human beings have done.
They are the hands of the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
That is why grace is so scandalous.
Grace does not say your choices did not matter.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross...
and His mercy is greater still.
Maybe you need to read that again.
Your sin matters.
Your choices matter.
Repentance matters.
But your failure does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
The Gospel is God rewriting what the scandal gets to mean.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
The sound of his own voice:
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine seeing Jesus crucified afterward.
Imagine wondering whether your cowardice would forever define you.
Then the risen Christ comes looking for Peter.
Jesus does not pretend Peter never failed.
He restores him.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Failure had spoken three times.
Grace would speak again.
Peter's denial was real.
But it wasn't final.
That is Gospel Warrior territory.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by pretending sin is harmless.
Not by telling us that whatever we choose is acceptable.
Jesus rewrites everything through repentance, forgiveness, restoration and a new life centered on Him.
This is why grace never means, “My choices don't matter.”
Grace means I no longer have to remain the person my sinful choices were turning me into.
You can repent.
You can return.
You can confess.
You can surrender.
You can come home.
And notice the final invitation of Scripture.
Near the end of Revelation comes this astonishing call:
“Let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.”
The Greek expression includes:
“ὁ θέλων”
ho thelōn — “the one willing,” “the one desiring.”
And then:
“λαβέτω...δωρεάν”
“let him take...freely.”
What a way for the biblical story to approach its ending.
Come.
Take.
Drink.
Freely.
The Gospel is not Christ standing behind a locked door laughing while thirsty sinners search for a key.
The invitation goes out.
Come.
But do not confuse invitation with human boasting.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot earn the blood.
You cannot perform enough religious acts to force God into your debt.
Grace is grace precisely because the sinner comes empty-handed.
So perhaps the deeper question is not merely:
“Why does God give us the ability to choose?”
Perhaps tonight the question is:
“What are you doing with the choices sitting in front of you?”
Because you are choosing something.
Every day.
Sometimes without realizing it.
Every secret click is a choice.
Every grudge you feed is a choice.
Every compromise you excuse is a choice.
Every prayer you postpone is a choice.
Every time conviction whispers and you silence it...
something is being formed inside you.
And every time you turn toward Christ, confess your sin, forgive someone, resist temptation, open Scripture when your flesh wants distraction, pray when you feel empty, obey when obedience hurts...
something is being formed inside you too.
Do not misunderstand me.
We are not saved because we accumulated enough good decisions.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith, not something we can boast that we earned.
But the grace that saves us does not leave us comfortably chained to the life from which Christ came to rescue us.
Jesus calls us to follow Him.
That means some things must be left behind.
Maybe this article found you while you are standing at one of those invisible crossroads.
Nobody else knows.
But you know.
There is something God has been putting His finger on.
Something you keep defending.
Something you keep postponing.
Something you keep hiding.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need sophisticated theology.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus...I chose wrong.”
Those words can feel terrifying.
But confession is not the end of hope.
It can be the doorway back into the light.
John writes that light came into the world, yet people loved darkness rather than light because their works were evil.
Darkness says:
Hide.
Grace says:
Come into the light.
Shame says:
Run from God.
The Gospel says:
Run to Christ.
Pride says:
Explain yourself.
Repentance says:
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
The enemy wants your worst chapter to become your identity.
Jesus calls sinners into something new.
Maybe you cannot undo what happened.
Maybe you cannot recover every year.
Maybe that relationship will never return.
Maybe consequences remain.
Grace is not a time machine.
But Jesus is a Redeemer.
He can take a life scarred by sinful choices and make it a testimony to mercy.
He can take the man who denied Him and make him a preacher of Christ.
He can take persecutors and make them proclaimers.
He can take prodigals and bring them home.
And He can take your scandal...
yes, even that one...
and refuse to let it write the final line.
Just be honest.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person still fighting.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend quietly drifting.
The son who stopped praying.
The daughter carrying shame.
The husband fighting privately.
The wife who feels forgotten.
The believer who still attends church but knows something inside has grown cold.
The skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely a list of religious rules.
Send this privately if that would serve them better.
Sometimes evangelism begins with something as simple as placing truth where a wounded person might unexpectedly find it.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction made painfully clear.
You may need these words again on a night when darkness starts negotiating with you.
We want this space to remain somewhere people encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship and, above everything else, Jesus Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It never could.
Not because supporting this ministry replaces belonging to and faithfully supporting a local church.
It doesn't.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should be decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
But voluntary generosity can be one meaningful way Christians use what God has entrusted to them for ministry and Gospel work.
Some believers faithfully describe part of their giving as an offering to ministries they believe are bearing Gospel fruit.
We would rather invite you to give freely, prayerfully and joyfully.
We want people to have reasons to stay close to Scripture long after a social-media post disappears from their feed.
If you cannot financially support the ministry, you are not less valuable here.
Pray.
Share.
Invite others to follow.
Use what is freely available.
Take the Gospel farther than an algorithm ever could.
Because ultimately this ministry is not about building an audience around Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing people beyond Gospel Warrior...
to Jesus.
The One who met sinners at wells.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who ate with people respectable religion avoided.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who still calls:
Come.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful thing about the frightening gift of choice.
God does not tell us that every choice is equally good.
He does something far more loving.
He tells us where life is found.
He warns us where death leads.
And then the Gospel reveals that the Life we desperately need is not merely a principle.
He has a name.
Jesus Christ.
So when you stand at the crossroads again...
when the screen is glowing...
when anger is rising...
when temptation whispers...
when pride tells you not to apologize...
when shame tells you not to pray...
when your past tells you there is no point coming home...
remember Moses' ancient words:
Choose life.
And remember what the next verse reveals:
He is your life.
You may have made choices that broke things.
You may carry consequences.
You may have chapters you wish could be burned from the book.
But while Christ is calling you, your story does not have to end where your rebellion left you.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive grace.
Follow Jesus.
Then get up and walk with Him.
Because perhaps the choice you regret most is not where your story ends.
Perhaps it is the place where, years from now, you will point backward with tears in your eyes and say:
“That was where I finally discovered that my sin could write a scandal—but only Jesus Christ could write the ending.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Ezekiel Uses Sexual Imagery So Graphic Many Churches Skip the Chapter
paragraphs: Ezekiel Uses Sexual Imagery So Graphic Many Churches Skip the Chapter
The Bible does not sanitize spiritual adultery. Ezekiel makes it disturbing on purpose—and buried beneath the shame is one of Scripture’s most breathtaking movements from scandal to grace.
There are chapters of the Bible people underline.
There are chapters they turn into wall art.
There are chapters preached at weddings, funerals, conferences, and Sunday services.
And then there is Ezekiel 16.
A chapter so uncomfortable that reading portions of it aloud can make an entire room suddenly interested in the floor.
And Ezekiel 23 goes further still.
The language becomes sexual. Graphic. Humiliating. At points, shocking enough that modern readers may wonder why words like these are even in Holy Scripture.
But perhaps the more dangerous question is not, “Why would God allow language this disturbing in the Bible?”
Perhaps it is...
What was happening in the human heart that required language this disturbing to expose it?
Because Ezekiel was not writing pornography.
He was prosecuting idolatry.
And when you understand what God was exposing, the chapter stops being merely about ancient Jerusalem.
It starts reading your heart.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Jerusalem had been loved.
Chosen.
Covered.
Adorned.
Provided for.
Yet she took the very gifts God had given her and used them in spiritual unfaithfulness.
Ezekiel describes Jerusalem metaphorically as a woman whom God rescued, cared for, entered into covenant with, clothed, adorned, and established. Then comes the devastating turn.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:15 says:
וַתִּבְטְחִי בְיָפְיֵךְ ... וַתִּזְנִי
Vattivtechi veyofyekh ... vattizni.
In context:
“But you trusted in your beauty ... and prostituted yourself.”
That final Hebrew verb comes from the root זנה — zanah, a word associated with prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness.
That matters.
God could have described Israel merely as “disobedient.”
He could have said they had “made poor choices.”
He could have softened it into the kind of religious vocabulary that allows people to feel convicted for eleven minutes and then go home unchanged.
He did not.
Through Ezekiel, covenant betrayal is portrayed as adultery.
Why?
Because idolatry is not merely breaking a regulation.
It is betraying a relationship.
That changes everything.
Imagine a husband discovering that the person to whom he gave his heart has been secretly giving herself to someone else.
Imagine the photographs.
The messages.
The lies.
The realization that some of the gifts he bought her were worn while she went to meet another man.
Now imagine someone walking into the room and saying:
“Relax. She merely violated a technical requirement of the marriage contract.”
You would know immediately how absurd that sounds.
Because betrayal is personal.
And that is precisely what respectable religion sometimes allows us to forget about sin.
We reduce sin to rule-breaking.
God reveals it as rebellion against the One who loved us.
We call it a habit.
God sees what it worships.
We call it a private struggle.
God sees what it is doing to our soul.
We call it “just entertainment.”
“Just flirting.”
“Just bitterness.”
“Just ambition.”
“Just another purchase.”
“Just one more drink.”
“Just another fantasy.”
“Just the way I am.”
“Just something nobody knows about.”
But Ezekiel tears the word just away.
Jerusalem's tragedy was not merely that she sinned.
She received gifts from God and then used those gifts apart from God.
And that possibility has not disappeared.
The body God gave you can become an instrument of lust.
The mind God gave you can become consumed by pride.
The money God entrusted to you can become your security.
The career God allowed you to build can become your identity.
The influence God permitted you to have can become an altar where you worship applause.
Even ministry can become something we secretly use to make people notice us instead of Jesus.
That is when Ezekiel gets frighteningly close.
Because idols are not always statues.
Sometimes they have screens.
Sometimes they have bank accounts.
Sometimes they have follower counts.
Sometimes they have another person's face.
Sometimes the idol looking back at us from the mirror is ourselves.
And sometimes the most dangerous idols are good things that quietly inherited the place belonging only to God.
Ezekiel refuses to make this pretty.
In chapter 23, he portrays Samaria and Jerusalem through two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, whose sexual promiscuity symbolizes their idolatry and their faithless pursuit of foreign powers.
Then Ezekiel 23:20 uses imagery so explicit that its force survives even across thousands of years.
The Hebrew reads:
אֲשֶׁר בְּשַׂר חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם וְזִרְמַת סוּסִים זִרְמָתָם
A close rendering is:
“whose flesh was like the flesh of donkeys, and whose emission was like that of horses.”
Yes.
