The deepest human problem hiding beneath the visible human crisis.
And if we rush too quickly to the moment when the man walks, we may miss the scandal of the moment when Jesus forgives.
The word Τέκνον — Teknon is tender.
“Child.”
Jesus does not begin by humiliating him.
He does not announce a catalog of the man’s sins to the room.
He does not make the broken man perform for mercy.
He addresses him with tenderness.
Then comes that extraordinary declaration:
ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι.
“Your sins are forgiven.”
The verb comes from ἀφίημι — aphiēmi, carrying the sense of releasing, letting go, sending away, forgiving.
Think about that.
The man was physically carried into the presence of Jesus because he could not walk.
And Jesus spoke of another burden being released.
His sins.
There is something here that our generation desperately needs to hear.
We often come to God asking Him to change the thing hurting us most.
“Jesus, fix my marriage.”
“Jesus, heal my body.”
“Jesus, rescue my child.”
“Jesus, give me work.”
“Jesus, remove this anxiety.”
“Jesus, get me out of debt.”
“Jesus, make the loneliness stop.”
“Jesus, restore what I lost.”
These are not necessarily wrong prayers.
Jesus cares about human suffering.
The Gospels repeatedly show Him responding with compassion to the sick, grieving, marginalized, and desperate.
And in this very story, Jesus eventually heals the man's paralysis.
But Christ refuses to let the visible crisis convince us that the visible crisis is always the deepest crisis.
Sometimes we want Jesus to repair our circumstances while He is confronting our eternity.
We want relief.
Jesus offers reconciliation.
We want the situation changed.
Jesus wants sinners brought home to God.
We want Him to make life comfortable again.
Jesus came to make dead people alive.
And please understand what this passage does not give us permission to say.
It does not say that this man's paralysis was caused by some particular personal sin he committed.
We should never look at a disabled or sick person and casually conclude, “You must have sinned.”
Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic connection elsewhere.
When His disciples encountered a man blind from birth, they asked:
“Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus answered:
“Neither this man nor his parents sinned…”
That is John 9.
So Mark 2 should never become a weapon used to shame suffering people.
Jesus is doing something much greater here.
He is revealing who He is.
Because the moment Jesus declares the man's sins forgiven, some scribes sitting nearby begin reasoning in their hearts:
“Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
Their theology has collided with the Man standing in front of them.
And their underlying premise contains something profoundly important.
Ultimately, forgiveness belongs to God.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal God as the One who forgives His people.
Psalm 103 celebrates the LORD:
הַסֹּלֵחַ לְכָל־עֲוֹנֵכִי
ha-solēaḥ le-khol-avonekhî
“Who forgives all your iniquity.”
The scribes understand the gravity of what they have heard.
Jesus has not merely offered encouragement.
He has pronounced forgiveness.
And Mark tells us Jesus immediately knows what they are reasoning within themselves.
So He asks:
“Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk’?”
It is a devastating question.
Anyone can say invisible sins have been forgiven.
How would the room verify it?
But telling a visibly paralyzed man to stand up creates an immediate test.
Either he gets up…
or he does not.
Then Jesus reveals why the visible miracle is about to happen:
“But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…”
There it is.
The healing is not merely a spectacle.
It is a sign.
Jesus turns to the paralyzed man.
“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.”
And the impossible happens.
The man rises.
The mat that carried him into the house is now carried out by him.
Imagine that moment.
The hands that had gripped the corners of his stretcher no longer need to carry him.
The crowd that prevented him from entering now watches him leave on his own feet.
The object that once testified to his helplessness is tucked beneath his arm.
He walks out.
But never forget this:
The greatest words Jesus spoke to him were spoken before his legs moved.
“Your sins are forgiven.”
That is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because eventually every healed body dies.
Every strong body weakens.
Every beautiful face ages.
Every possession changes hands.
Every career ends.
Every earthly achievement eventually becomes somebody else's memory.
Even Lazarus, after being raised, eventually faced physical death again.
Physical healing is precious.
But physical healing is not the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to make our temporary lives more comfortable before the grave.
He came to save sinners.
The angel's announcement concerning Him in Matthew 1:21 was breathtakingly specific:
“You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”
That is why the cross stands at the center of Christianity.
Our problem was deeper than bad habits.
Deeper than disappointment.
Deeper than trauma.
Deeper than financial trouble.
Deeper than physical weakness.
Humanity stood guilty before a holy God.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Yet the Gospel does not stop at guilt.
That same passage moves immediately toward grace:
and sinners are “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
This is Christianity.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not pretending judgment is imaginary.
Not telling wounded people to repair themselves until God becomes impressed.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The forgiveness announced in that crowded house points us toward the staggering reality accomplished through Christ.
The One who had authority to say, “Your sins are forgiven,” would eventually allow nails to be driven through His hands.
The One who commanded a paralyzed man to rise would Himself rise from the grave.
The One who told that man to go home would make a way for sinners to come home to God.
That is why grace is so scandalous.
We spend years trying to hide the evidence.
Jesus already knows.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair you buried.
The bitterness you have learned to justify.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The pride disguised as confidence.
The jealousy hidden beneath congratulations.
The hatred.
The lies.
The years spent performing Christianity while your heart wandered miles from Christ.
Maybe everybody thinks you are fine.
Maybe you still go to church.
Maybe you know when to raise your hands.
Maybe you can quote Scripture.
And somewhere underneath all that performance is an exhausted soul whispering:
“If people knew everything about me, would anybody still love me?”
Look again at the man on the mat.
Jesus knew more about him than anyone in that room.
And Jesus called him:
Τέκνον.
Child.
This is not permission to remain in sin.
Grace never turns rebellion into righteousness by simply renaming it.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and faith.
But repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
It is not self-punishment.
It is not promising God that this time you will become worthy.
The Gospel is better.
We turn from sin and entrust ourselves to Christ because salvation is found in Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe you have been asking Jesus to fix everything except the thing between you and God.
Maybe you have spent years praying for the circumstances around you while resisting the Lordship of Christ within you.
Maybe your prayer has been:
“Jesus, make me happy.”
And Christ is calling you deeper:
“Come to Me.”
Maybe you have been trying to walk before receiving what only grace can give.
Maybe shame has convinced you that Jesus wants nothing to do with you until you become respectable.
But look at the Gospel.
People did not clean themselves before coming to Jesus.
They came needy.
Blind.
Bleeding.
Possessed.
Diseased.
Despised.
Grieving.
Guilty.
Broken.
And sinners still come that way.
You do not crawl toward Christ carrying a résumé.
You come carrying need.
You come confessing sin.
You come empty-handed.
And the glory of the Gospel is not that broken sinners finally become impressive enough for Jesus.
The glory of the Gospel is Jesus Himself.
His righteousness.
His cross.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
His victory.
His grace.
Maybe your “mat” is different from the man's in Mark 2.
Maybe nobody sees yours.
Maybe you have carried shame for fifteen years.
Maybe somebody hurt you and you built an entire identity around the wound.
Maybe you committed something you cannot undo.
Maybe you keep replaying a night you desperately wish you could erase.
Maybe you wonder whether God could forgive that.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend it never happened.
The Gospel tells you something infinitely greater.
Your past does not have more saving authority than Jesus.
Your shame does not outrank His grace.
Your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
And His sacrifice is sufficient enough that sinners who trust Him can truly be forgiven.
That is the scandal.
That is grace.
That is why we keep saying:
He does not rewrite history by pretending evil was good.
He rewrites the sinner's future through redemption.
Peter's denial was real.
Paul's persecution of Christians was real.
The thief's guilt was real.
The Samaritan woman's broken history was real.
The prodigal's rebellion in Jesus' parable was real.
Grace does not require us to lie about the scandal.
Grace reveals that the scandal does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been lying spiritually on a mat for years.
You have watched other people walk.
Watched other people testify.
Watched other people seem joyful.
And quietly wondered whether Jesus has forgotten you.
He has not promised that every suffering will disappear in this present life.
Christian faith does not guarantee that every believer will receive immediate physical healing, financial prosperity, restored relationships, or freedom from every earthly hardship.
Some faithful Christians carry suffering for decades.
Some die waiting for healing.
Paul himself pleaded three times for his “thorn” to depart, and God's answer was:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Christian hope is not built on the promise that nothing painful will happen.
It is built on Christ.
And because Christ rose, suffering does not have the final word.
Sin does not have the final word.
Death does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
One day resurrection will accomplish what temporary healing never could.
For those who belong to Christ, Revelation points toward a future in which death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, crying, nor pain anymore.
Until then, sometimes Jesus changes the circumstance.
Sometimes He gives grace to endure it.
But the sinner who comes to Christ receives something this world could never manufacture:
reconciliation with God.
If Jesus exposed everything hidden in your heart tonight…
would you run from Him?
Or finally run to Him?
There are people reading this who need to stop performing.
No more hiding behind Christian vocabulary.
No more secret agreement with sin.
No more pretending that knowing about Jesus is the same as belonging to Jesus.
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not become a spectator to their pain.
Pray for them.
Remind them of Christ.
We need Christian communities where confession is met with truth and grace rather than gossip.
And think about the four friends for a moment.
The paralyzed man reached Jesus because somebody was willing to carry him.
Who are you carrying?
Whose name came into your mind while reading this?
Do not merely think about them.
Send this to them.

Supporting a ministry does not purchase God's favor, prove your salvation, or make you more righteous. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and financial support is one voluntary way believers can help Gospel-centered resources reach more people.
But the merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The mission is not building consumers.
It is helping make disciples.
It is putting biblical truth in front of exhausted Christians at midnight.
It is reaching the person quietly losing faith.
It is confronting comfortable Christianity with the Gospel.
It is reminding ashamed sinners that repentance has a destination—and His name is Jesus Christ.
And comment.
Not for an algorithm alone.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“No more hiding.”
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Because perhaps you entered this story staring at a paralyzed man's legs…
only to realize Jesus was speaking to your heart.
The crowd saw a man who could not walk.
Jesus saw a sinner who needed forgiveness.
Then Christ did what nobody in the room could do.
He dealt with both.
And centuries later, the question is no longer merely whether Jesus can make a paralyzed man stand.
Mark has already told us what happened.
The question is whether you will trust the authority of the One who told him:
“Your sins are forgiven.”
Bring Him the sin.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the secret you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the exhausted faith.
Bring Him the mat.
Because the most beautiful part of your story may not be the moment everybody watches you stand.
It may be the moment, while you are still lying helpless before Christ, when you finally understand that grace came looking for you before you had anything impressive to offer.
The mat may explain how you arrived broken, but Jesus gets the final word over who you become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE GOOD THING YOU DID FOR GOD WAS REALLY FOR THE APPLAUSE?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE GOOD THING YOU DID FOR GOD WAS REALLY FOR THE APPLAUSE?
What Jesus Really Meant When He Warned Against Practicing Righteousness to Be Seen—and Why His Words May Expose Something in Us We Never Wanted to Admit
There is a terrifying possibility hidden inside the Christian life.
You can do the right thing…
for the wrong reason.
You can give.
You can pray.
You can fast.
You can serve.
You can post Scripture.
You can defend biblical truth.
You can tell people about Jesus.
You can raise your hands during worship, volunteer at church, help someone who is suffering, give money to someone who desperately needs it, and say words that are completely true…
while somewhere underneath all of it, almost invisible even to you, your heart is whispering:
I hope somebody notices.
That is where Jesus takes us in Matthew 6.
Not merely into our behavior.
Into our motives.
Into that hidden room inside the human heart where nobody sees the difference between worship and performance.
Nobody…
except God.
And perhaps that is why the warning of Jesus is so uncomfortable.
Because He does not merely ask:
“What did you do?”
He confronts us with the far more frightening question:
“Who were you hoping would see you do it?”
Matthew records Jesus saying:
“Προσέχετε δὲ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν μὴ ποιεῖν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς…”
Prosechete de tēn dikaiosynēn hymōn mē poiein emprosthen tōn anthrōpōn pros to theathēnai autois…
A careful rendering is:
“Beware of practicing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them…”
—Matthew 6:1
Slow down.
Because one small Greek expression changes how we understand this entire warning:
πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς
pros to theathēnai autois
“In order to be seen by them.”
Jesus was not issuing a blanket prohibition against anyone ever seeing you do something righteous.
That cannot be what He meant.
Only moments earlier in the same Sermon on the Mount, Jesus had told His disciples to let their light shine before others so that people would see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven.
So Matthew 5 does not say, “Make sure nobody sees.”
And Matthew 6 does not contradict Matthew 5.
The difference is devastatingly simple.
In Matthew 5, people see the works…
and glorify God.
In Matthew 6, people see the works…
and the performer wants them to glorify him.
Same visibility.
Different audience of the heart.
That is the issue.
You can perform a good deed publicly without performing it for publicity.
And you can perform a good deed secretly while still fantasizing about being praised for it.
Jesus goes deeper than location.
He goes after intention.
He is exposing the theater hidden inside the human heart.
And suddenly this two-thousand-year-old sermon feels painfully modern.
Because we live in an age where almost everything can become content.
The meal.
The workout.
The vacation.
The grief.
The generosity.
The prayer.
The Bible study.
The ministry.
Even compassion can become content.
Even repentance can become branding.
Even humility can become a performance of humility.
You can help someone and immediately feel the temptation to tell everyone that you helped.
You can read your Bible and wonder whether the open Bible would make a good photograph.
You can give generously and secretly hope your name is mentioned.
You can write something about Jesus and repeatedly check whether people reacted to it.
You can preach against pride while feeding your own.
You can even say, “All glory to God,” while quietly wondering how many people admired the person who said it.
That is how subtle this becomes.
The problem is not that someone saw.
The problem is that being seen became the reward you were seeking.
Jesus continues His warning by speaking about giving.
When you give to the needy, He says, do not announce it like the hypocrites who seek honor from others.
Then comes one of the most sobering statements in the passage:
“They have received their reward.”
Think about that.
Jesus does not say they received nothing.
They received exactly what they wanted.
Attention.
Recognition.
Admiration.
Applause.
And that was the tragedy.
They traded the pleasure of the Father for the praise of the crowd.
They received their reward…
and it was painfully small.
A compliment.
A reputation.
A reaction.
A few seconds of admiration from people who will eventually forget their name.
Imagine standing before eternity having exchanged something heavenly for something that disappeared before bedtime.
But before we turn this passage into a weapon against somebody else, Jesus forces us to bring it home.
Because it is incredibly easy to read Matthew 6 and immediately think of a religious hypocrite we know.
A preacher.
A church leader.
A Christian influencer.
Someone who posts every good deed.
Someone whose spirituality always seems to have a camera nearby.
But Jesus did not give this warning so that we could become experts at diagnosing everybody else's motives.
He gave it so that we would examine our own.
So forget everyone else for a moment.
What happens inside you when nobody notices?
When you serve and nobody thanks you?
When you give and nobody knows?
When you sacrifice and somebody else gets the credit?
When you pray and there is nobody nearby to hear how spiritual you sound?
When you obey God and it produces no likes, no recognition, no platform, no applause?
Does obedience still feel worthwhile?
That question can uncover things years of religious activity managed to hide.
Because sometimes we do not realize how addicted we have become to human approval until God allows us to obey Him without receiving any.
And silence from people can become spiritual surgery.
Suddenly you discover whether Jesus was really enough.
Jesus then turns toward prayer.
He describes people who love praying where others can see them.
Notice the problem again.
Prayer itself is good.
Public prayer itself is not inherently sinful. Jesus Himself prayed where others could hear Him.
The poison is the audience of the heart.
A prayer supposedly addressed to God can secretly become a speech performed for people.
The lips say, “Father…”
while the heart says, “Everybody, listen to me.”
That should shake every Christian who has ever prayed publicly.
Every pastor.
Every worship leader.
Every ministry worker.
Every content creator.
Every person who has ever typed a prayer beneath a photograph.
Including us.
Especially us.
Because religious performance is dangerous precisely because it can look almost identical to genuine devotion.
Two people can pray the same words.
One is worshiping.
The other is performing.
Two people can give the same amount.
One wants the hungry person helped.
The other wants the room impressed.
Two people can share the same Bible verse.
One desperately wants someone to encounter Christ.
The other desperately wants engagement.
But heaven can.
That is why Jesus repeatedly brings the Father into the conversation.
Your Father sees.
Your Father knows.
Your Father rewards.
This is not merely a sermon against hypocrisy.
It is an invitation into freedom.
You do not have to spend your life auditioning anymore.
You already have an audience.
The only Audience whose judgment ultimately matters.
Your Father sees the prayer nobody applauded.
He sees the money quietly given.
He sees the temptation resisted at 2:17 in the morning when nobody would ever have known.
He sees the apology.
He sees the forgiveness.
He sees the meal you bought.
He sees you closing the door and weeping before Him.
He sees the Christian who serves for twenty years without becoming famous.
He sees the mother praying over her sleeping children.
He sees the exhausted father opening Scripture before work.
He sees the teenager refusing what everyone else is doing because Christ matters more.
He sees the believer who could have announced the sacrifice but chose silence.
He sees.
And when the approval of God becomes enough, the addiction to human applause begins losing its power.
Then Jesus speaks about fasting.
Again, He confronts people who deliberately alter their appearance so others will recognize their spirituality.
Different century.
Same heart.
They wanted suffering to become a costume.
They wanted sacrifice to become advertising.
They wanted people to look at them and think:
Wow. That person must really love God.
Jesus tells His followers, essentially, not to turn devotion into theater.
There is something almost breathtaking about His alternative.
Live before the Father.
Give before the Father.
Pray before the Father.
Fast before the Father.
Stop needing every act of obedience to produce witnesses.
Some of the holiest moments of your life may happen where nobody can photograph them.
Some of your greatest victories may receive no comments.
Some of your deepest worship may never be heard by another human being.
Some of your most costly obedience may never become a testimony you tell publicly.
And it still matters.
Because God saw it.
But there is another danger here.
We can misunderstand Jesus and become afraid of doing anything publicly for God.
That is not what this passage teaches.
Remember Matthew 5:16.
Jesus wants good works to become visible in ways that cause people to glorify the Father.
Christianity was never meant to become invisible.
The Gospel is supposed to be proclaimed.
Mercy is supposed to spread.
Truth is supposed to be spoken.
People are supposed to hear about Jesus.
Testimonies can encourage believers.
Public generosity can sometimes inspire generosity.
Sharing Scripture can put God's Word in front of someone who desperately needs it.
A Christian ministry can invite people to participate in its mission.
The question is not merely:
“Will people see this?”
The question is:
“Whose glory am I seeking when they do?”
There is an enormous difference between making Christ visible and making yourself impressive.
And only God perfectly knows where that line runs through your heart.
Which means Matthew 6 should produce humility rather than suspicion.
“Search me, O God.”
Not:
“Search them, O God.”
Search me.
Why did I post that?
Why did I say that?
Why did it bother me when nobody thanked me?
Why was I disappointed when my name was not mentioned?
Why did I need people to know how much I sacrificed?
Why did being overlooked hurt so badly?
Why did somebody else's recognition feel like my rejection?
Why do I want people to think I am spiritually mature?
Why do I sometimes want the appearance of holiness more than the painful process of actually becoming holy?
Those questions hurt.
But sometimes grace begins where pretending ends.
And this is where we must be careful not to turn the Sermon on the Mount into another ladder by which sinners try to climb toward God.
Because if Matthew 6 only leaves you thinking, I need to purify my motives enough so God will accept me, you have not yet reached the Gospel.
Who among us has perfectly pure motives?
Who has never wanted approval?
Who has never enjoyed recognition too much?
Who has never mixed worship with ego?
Who has never wanted to appear better than he really was?
If acceptance before God depended upon perfectly unmixed motives, every one of us would be exposed.
We need more than behavioral adjustment.
We need mercy.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And that is where Jesus becomes infinitely more than a moral teacher telling hypocrites to behave better.
The One preaching this sermon would eventually walk toward a cross.
Not surrounded by admirers.
Surrounded by mockers.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Humiliated.
His public image destroyed.
No earthly applause.
No attempt to impress the crowd.
He obeyed the Father all the way to death.
Jesus did not merely teach a righteousness deeper than performance.
He ultimately became the hope of performers, hypocrites, approval-addicts, sinners, and people like us whose motives have never been as pure as we pretend.
At the cross, our masks become useless.
We cannot impress God there.
We cannot perform our way into forgiveness.
We cannot accumulate enough Christian activity to erase our sin.
We come empty-handed.
We repent.
We believe.
We receive grace.
Christ died for sinners and rose again, and the Gospel does not merely polish our religious image.
It gives us a new life.
That is why the answer to spiritual performance is not better spiritual performance.
It is Jesus.
It is learning that because of Christ, you do not have to manufacture a righteous identity before other people.
Your salvation is not secured by their applause.
Your worth is not measured by their reaction.
Your standing before God is not determined by whether people think you are impressive.
Come to Christ honestly.
No costume.
No stage.
No carefully edited spiritual image.
Just the truth.
“Jesus, there is pride in me.”
“Jesus, I wanted people to notice.”
“Jesus, sometimes I wanted the reputation of holiness more than holiness.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That prayer may be more beautiful before heaven than a thousand impressive performances.
Because repentance kills the illusion.
Grace meets the sinner underneath the costume.
And Jesus begins rewriting what pride tried to author.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal was never something that made headlines.
Maybe your scandal has lived quietly inside your motives.
The craving to be admired.
The obsession with being recognized.
The secret jealousy when somebody else receives attention.
The Christian image you have worked hard to protect.
The terror that people might discover you are weaker than they think.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling you closer.
Not closer to the stage.
Closer to Himself.
Maybe the freedom you desperately need begins when you stop asking:
“Did they see me?”
and start asking:
“Did He?”
Because your Father sees what is done in secret.
And that can become enough.
So do something this week that only God knows about.
Encourage someone anonymously if appropriate.
Give without announcing the amount.
Pray for someone who may never discover you prayed.
Serve where there is no photograph.
Forgive without turning your forgiveness into a testimony about how gracious you are.
Open your Bible without posting it.
Sit with Jesus when nobody is watching.
And when your flesh whispers, But nobody knows…
answer it:
My Father knows.
That is enough.
And ironically, this truth also changes how we share the Gospel publicly.
Sharing something about Christ is not automatically spiritual performance.
If your purpose is genuinely to help someone see Jesus, sharing can become service.
And if these words exposed something uncomfortable, do not hide behind silence simply to preserve an image.
Be honest.
Your honesty may give somebody else permission to stop pretending too.

And if Gospel Warrior is helping you grow deeper in Scripture, you can follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well—not to build a personality cult, but so more people can encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the message of Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus.
It does not.
And certainly not because God can be manipulated into blessing someone who financially supports a ministry.
He cannot.
Support Christian work because you have already received grace—not because you are trying to purchase it.
Your support helps us keep putting Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, discipleship materials, and Christian resources in front of people who may desperately need them.
But remember the warning that began this entire conversation.
Do not share it so people will think you are righteous.
Do not comment because everyone else is commenting.
Do not perform.
Love.
Do not advertise yourself.
Point to Jesus.
Do not chase the reward of being seen.
Live before the Father who already sees.
Because one day the likes disappear.
The applause stops.
The audience goes home.
The reputation fades.
The platform belongs to somebody else.
And eventually every carefully constructed version of ourselves falls away.
Then only truth remains.
Christ remains.
Grace remains.
And perhaps one of the greatest freedoms Jesus can give you in this life is the ability to do something beautiful for Him…
and be completely at peace when nobody knows.
When you no longer need the crowd to see you, you finally discover how deeply the Father always has.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ACHSAH GOT MARRIED—Then Immediately Asked Her Father for Springs of Water
paragraphs: ACHSAH GOT MARRIED—Then Immediately Asked Her Father for Springs of Water

She had the land. She had the husband. She had the inheritance. But Achsah understood something many of us discover painfully late: having what looks like a blessing means very little if there is no water to keep it alive.
There is a woman hidden in Joshua 15 whose story takes only a handful of verses to tell.
No long biography.
No book bearing her name.
No recorded sermon.
No spectacular miracle.
Just a marriage...
a piece of land...
a woman getting down from a donkey...
and one request to her father.
Yet once you understand what she asked for, her story becomes almost impossible to forget.
Her name was Achsah.
And she refused to inherit dry ground without asking for water.

Joshua 15 places us in the days when Israel was taking possession of the land God had promised. Caleb—the same Caleb who decades earlier believed God when almost everyone around him was terrified of giants—had received his inheritance.
Then Caleb made an offer.
The man who captured Kiriath-sepher would receive his daughter Achsah in marriage.
Othniel took the city.
Achsah became his wife.
And if this were a modern story, perhaps that is where we would expect the beautiful ending.
Battle won.
Marriage celebrated.
Property received.
Everybody goes home.
But Achsah did something after the wedding that Scripture considered important enough to preserve not once, but twice—the scene appears again in Judges 1.
She went to her father.
Caleb looked at his daughter and essentially asked:
What do you want?
And Achsah answered with words that deserve to be heard in the language in which they came down to us:
תְּנָה־לִּי בְרָכָה
Tenah-li berakhah.
“Give me a blessing.”
Then:
וְנָתַתָּה לִי גֻּלֹּת מָיִם
Ve-natattah li gulloth mayim.
“Give me springs of water.”
The Hebrew text of Joshua 15:19 uses בְּרָכָה — berakhah, a blessing, gift, or favor, and גֻּלֹּת מָיִם — gulloth mayim, referring here to springs or pools of water.
Achsah had been given land in the Negev—the dry southern country.
But she understood something brutally practical.
Land without water could become a possession that could not sustain what was supposed to grow there.
So she asked.
Not because the land was worthless.
Because the land needed water.
And Caleb did not rebuke her.
He did not say, “Ungrateful daughter. Haven't I already given you enough?”
He did not shame her for asking.
Scripture simply tells us that Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
She asked for water.
Her father gave generously.
And somewhere inside that ancient scene is a question that may be far more personal than we want it to be:
What if you have been trying to survive on dry ground while being too ashamed to ask your Father for what you desperately need?
Maybe you have the job.
But no peace.
The marriage.
But no intimacy.
The ministry.
But no fire.
The house.
But no rest inside it.
The Bible on your nightstand.
But weeks have passed since you opened it with hunger.
The Christian posts.
The worship playlist.
The Sunday attendance.
The smile everybody recognizes.
But somewhere beneath all of it...
you are thirsty.
And nobody knows.
You learned how to look planted while your roots were drying out.
You learned Christian vocabulary while quietly losing Christian joy.
You know how to say, “God is good,” even on days when your soul feels numb.
You tell people, “I'm okay.”
You keep working.
Keep serving.
Keep posting.
Keep showing up.
Keep laughing.
But late at night, when the noise dies and there is nobody left to impress, something inside you whispers:
I need water.
That is why Achsah's little story can hit so hard.
She did not pretend dry ground was enough.
She recognized what she had received, recognized what it needed, and went to the one who could give it.
Please understand the difference.
This passage is not teaching that God owes Christians houses, money, promotions, marriages, businesses, or whatever else we decide to call our “springs.”
Joshua 15 is not a blank check for prosperity theology.
Achsah was speaking to her earthly father about actual land and actual water within an actual inheritance.
We should honor the text enough to say that clearly.
But the rest of Scripture reveals something astonishing about believers coming to our heavenly Father with our need.
Because when the Bible finally brings us to Jesus Christ, thirsty people are still being invited to come.
And now the water becomes infinitely deeper.
Jesus met a Samaritan woman beside a well in John 4.
She came carrying a water jar.
But Christ saw another thirst.
A thirst no bucket could reach.
A thirst hidden underneath relationships, disappointment, shame, history, and the exhausting human attempt to find in created things what only God can ultimately give.
Jesus told her that whoever drank the water He gives would have within them a spring welling up to eternal life.
Later, in John 7, Jesus stood and cried out that anyone who thirsts should come to Him and drink, and John explains the statement in connection with the Holy Spirit.
That is not permission to turn Achsah into an allegory where every detail secretly predicts Jesus.
We do not need to manipulate the Old Testament to make it powerful.
The connection is more beautiful when we let Scripture speak honestly.
Achsah needed literal water for literal dry land.
You and I have a deeper thirst that literal water cannot cure.
And Jesus Christ presents Himself as the One to whom the thirsty may come.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe your problem is not that God has given you nothing.
Maybe your problem is that you have been trying to make good things do what only Christ can do.
You expected marriage to save you from loneliness.
Then discovered another human being cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
You expected success to silence insecurity.
Then reached another milestone and heard the same old voice asking, “Is this all?”
You thought money would make you feel safe.
Attention would make you feel valuable.
Sex would make you feel loved.
Achievement would make you feel significant.
Ministry would make you feel close to God.
Religious activity would make you holy.
And perhaps you discovered something frightening:
You can possess the field...
and still be thirsty.
You can receive what you prayed for...
and discover that receiving it did not heal what was broken inside you.
You can finally arrive at the place you begged God to take you...
only to discover you brought your wounded heart with you.
Somebody needs to hear this before wasting another decade drinking from wells that cannot save them.
Your deepest need is not a better image.
Not another distraction.
Not another secret relationship.
Not another purchase.
Not another night numbing yourself.
Not another religious performance designed to convince everyone—including yourself—that everything is fine.
You need Christ.
Not Christianity as decoration.
Not Jesus as an accessory to the life you already planned.
Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Lord.
Savior.
King.
The One before whom hidden sin can finally be confessed because grace is not permission to remain in darkness—grace is God's mercy meeting sinners and bringing them into a new life.
And this is where the story becomes painfully beautiful.
Achsah asked her father for a berakhah.
A blessing.
And the Gospel tells sinners that something far greater than fertile acreage has been opened to us through Jesus Christ.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Mercy.
Adoption.
New life.
Access to God.
Not because we captured enough cities.
Not because we became religious enough.
Not because we cleaned ourselves up before approaching Him.
But because Jesus did what we could never do.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
He remained righteous where we sinned.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now Hebrews tells believers to approach God's throne of grace with confidence so that we may receive mercy and find grace in our time of need.
Do you see it?
The Gospel does not tell the thirsty sinner:
Pretend you aren't thirsty.
It says:
Come.
The Gospel does not say:
Hide until you deserve water.
It says:
Come to Christ.
The Gospel does not say:
Repair yourself and perhaps God will receive you afterward.
It announces that Jesus came for sinners, and repentance means we stop defending the very sin that is destroying us and turn toward the Savior who alone can forgive and transform us.
Some of us have spent years standing on dry ground because pride would rather die thirsty than admit need.
We do it with God.
We do it with people.
We do it in church.
We are terrified somebody might discover the Christian they admire is struggling.
So we become experts at spiritual cosmetics.
We cover envy with smiles.
Pornography with privacy.
Bitterness with silence.
Prayerlessness with busyness.
Pride with “discernment.”
Unforgiveness with “boundaries” when what we really mean is vengeance.
Fear with control.
Emptiness with entertainment.
And sometimes even ministry becomes camouflage.
We can speak about living water while our own souls are cracking beneath our feet.
But Achsah got off the donkey.
There is something about that moment.
She came down.
She approached.
She answered honestly.
“I need a blessing.”
“I need water.”
There was no impressive speech.
No performance.
Just need brought into relationship.
What would happen if you stopped pretending tonight?
What if your most spiritual prayer was not eloquent at all?
What if it sounded more like:
“Father, I am dry.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Lord, I have been hiding.”
“I keep returning to this sin.”
“My marriage is hurting.”
“I am angry.”
“I am jealous.”
“I don't know how to forgive.”
“I have been performing Christianity instead of walking with Christ.”
“I've been trying to satisfy my soul everywhere except in You.”
“Have mercy on me.”
Those prayers may not impress anybody.
But God is not asking you to impress Him.
The Gospel destroys the illusion that you can.
You come empty-handed.
You come because Christ is sufficient.
You come because mercy is mercy precisely because you could never purchase it.
And maybe your scandal is bigger than thirst.
Maybe you crossed lines.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Maybe you became the person you once promised yourself you would never become.
Maybe your browser history tells one story and your Sunday clothes tell another.
Maybe people know one version of you while God knows everything.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending sin never mattered.
The cross proves sin matters more than we wanted to believe.
Grace was not cheap.
Christ was crucified.
But the cross also proves your sin does not have to write the final sentence.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is real.
Restoration is real.
Transformation is real.
There can be a new chapter because there is a risen Christ.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not scandal to excuses.
Not scandal to image management.
Not scandal to pretending consequences do not exist.
Scandal...
to repentance.
Scandal...
to the cross.
Scandal...
to mercy.
Scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe not by erasing every earthly consequence.
Maybe not by returning every opportunity sin destroyed.
Maybe not by making your past disappear from human memory.
But Jesus can change what your past means for your eternity.
The forgiven adulterer does not have to remain defined by adultery.
The former addict does not have to worship the chains Christ broke.
The liar can learn truth.
The bitter can forgive.
The proud can bow.
The sexually broken can walk in holiness.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The thirsty can come.
And the person who thought, “God could never want me after what I've done,” can discover that the entire Gospel is about a Savior who came to seek and save the lost.
So perhaps Achsah's question reaches us differently now.
She knew what her ground needed.
Do you?
What have you been calling “fine” that is actually dry?
What sin are you protecting?
What wound are you hiding?
What substitute have you been drinking from?
What conversation with God have you postponed because honesty terrifies you?
What if today is the day you stop decorating the desert?
Come to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
Come because He is Savior.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust Him.
Ask for mercy.
Open His Word again.
Pray again.
Return again.
And when you stumble, do not make peace with sin—but do not run away from Christ either.
Run toward Him.
There is another detail I cannot shake.
Achsah asked for springs.
Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
The text does not tell us to turn those two springs into some secret spiritual formula. We should resist inventing meanings Scripture itself never gives them.
But we should not miss the simple beauty either.
Her father heard her request.
And he gave.

That should make every Christian think about how much greater our heavenly Father is—not because He promises to grant every earthly desire, but because in Christ He has given us what sinners need most.
And if you are reading this while exhausted, ashamed, spiritually dry, or barely holding onto faith, perhaps your next move is not to manufacture strength.
Perhaps your next move is to come honestly before God.
“Father...
I need You.”
That may be the sentence your pride has been avoiding for years.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn this moment into another emotional experience you forget tomorrow.
Respond.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask a mature believer for help if you are trapped in something you cannot fight alone.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship.
Return—not to religious performance, but to Jesus Christ.

If Christ has already brought you through a season where your soul felt completely dry, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because saving a Facebook post is spiritual obedience, but because tomorrow's emotions may not remember what tonight's conviction understood.
Come back to these Scriptures.
Open Joshua 15:16–19 yourself.
Read Judges 1:12–15.
Then go to John 4, John 7, and Hebrews 4.
Test what you have read here against the Word of God.
Never outsource your Bible to a Facebook page.
Send it privately to the person who may never comment publicly but desperately needs to hear that thirst is not cured by pretending.

Invite your family, your Christian friends, the believer who has drifted, the person wrestling with faith, and even the unbeliever who wonders whether Jesus could possibly receive someone with their history.
And there is something else we want you to use whether you ever purchase anything or not.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Our products can sit on shelves.
Our articles can disappear from feeds.
Our page can someday cease to exist.
But the Gospel remains:
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the grave.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
Christ forgives.
Christ restores.
Christ transforms.
And Christ is still calling thirsty people to come.
Achsah had the courage to look at dry ground and admit:
I need water.
Maybe tonight...
so do you.
Don't spend another year trying to convince everyone that your desert is a garden.
Go to the Father.
Go through Christ.
Bring the truth.
Bring the thirst.
Bring the sin you finally stopped defending.
Bring the shame you cannot wash away yourself.
Bring the broken pieces.
Bring the empty cup.
Because the most dangerous kind of dryness is not knowing you are thirsty.
And the most beautiful moment may be the moment you finally stop pretending you aren't.
You may have been handed dry ground—but in Jesus Christ, dryness does not get to write the last line of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID’S DEATHBED AND THE YOUNG WOMAN BESIDE HIM: The Strange Story of Abishag
paragraphs: DAVID’S DEATHBED AND THE YOUNG WOMAN BESIDE HIM: The Strange Story of Abishag

She entered Scripture beside a dying king, barely spoke in the recorded story, and somehow became connected to a struggle for Israel’s throne. But hidden inside this strange account is something far bigger than Abishag, David, or Solomon: a haunting picture of fading human glory—and our desperate need for the King whose throne will never grow cold.
There is a young woman standing beside the bed of one of the most famous men in the Bible.
She is beautiful.
He is dying.
And almost nobody talks about her.
The old man beneath the blankets is David.
David.
The shepherd boy who faced Goliath.
The fugitive who survived Saul.
The warrior who united a kingdom.
The poet who sang, “The LORD is my shepherd.”
The king whose name would become inseparable from Israel’s hope for the Messiah.
But when 1 Kings opens, we do not meet David holding a sword.
We meet him beneath blankets.
And he cannot get warm.
That detail should stop us.
Because Scripture has a way of stripping human glory down to the truth.
The Hebrew says:
“וְהַמֶּלֶךְ דָּוִד זָקֵן, בָּא בַּיָּמִים”
Vehammelekh David zaqen, ba bayyamim.
“King David was old, advanced in days.”
Then comes the painful sentence:
“וְלֹא יִחַם לוֹ”
Velo yicham lo.
He could not get warm.
The man who once made armies tremble could not command warmth into his own body.
The man who had survived lions, bears, giants, spears, rebellions, betrayal, warfare, grief, scandal, and consequences was now losing a battle every human being eventually loses.
Time.
No title could stop it.
No palace could stop it.
No army could stop it.
No reputation could stop it.
David was still king.
But David was dying.
And maybe that is where this story begins speaking directly to us.
Because we spend so much of life trying to become something.
Successful.
Admired.
Secure.
Beautiful.
Influential.
Comfortable.
Remembered.
We build names people will recognize and lives people will envy.
Then Scripture quietly walks us into David’s bedroom and whispers:
Look again.
This is where earthly glory eventually goes.
The crown remains.
The body weakens.
The achievements remain.
The heartbeat slows.
People may still call you important while your lungs are taking their final breaths.
And suddenly the questions that consumed your life become embarrassingly small beside the question that actually matters:
Who are you before God?
David’s servants proposed an unusual solution. They would search for a young virgin who could attend the king, lie close to him, and provide warmth.
They searched throughout Israel.
And they found her.
Abishag.
“אֲבִישַׁג הַשּׁוּנַמִּית”
Avishag ha-Shunammit.
Abishag the Shunammite.
She came from Shunem, and Scripture emphasizes something immediately about her.
She was extraordinarily beautiful.
But read carefully.
Because this is where careless retellings can turn Scripture into something Scripture never says.
Abishag was brought to David as an attendant and caregiver. The Hebrew describes her as a sokhenet—an attendant or one caring closely for the king—and says she ministered to him.
Then the biblical writer deliberately adds:
Vehammelekh lo yeda‘ah.
Literally:
“The king did not know her.”
In biblical Hebrew, “know” can function as a discreet expression for sexual relations, and that is clearly the meaning here.
David did not have sexual relations with Abishag.
That matters.
The text wants us to know it.
Abishag shared proximity to the king without becoming another sexual conquest.
And the contrast with an earlier chapter in David’s life is difficult to miss, even though Scripture does not explicitly tell us to equate the two scenes.
Years earlier, David had been in royal comfort when he saw another beautiful woman.
Bathsheba.
That encounter became one of the darkest scandals of his life.
Adultery.
Deception.
Uriah’s death.
Nathan’s confrontation.
Consequences that tore through David’s household.
David eventually confessed his sin, and God forgave him—but forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence.
Now, near the end of his life, another beautiful woman is near his bed.
But this time Scripture explicitly says:
He did not know her.
Do not misunderstand that.
The Bible is not presenting David’s old age as though one final act of restraint somehow paid for Bathsheba.
David could never undo his own sin.
Neither can we.
That is exactly why grace is grace.
You cannot go backward and become the person who never sinned.
You cannot climb into yesterday and unsay the words.
You cannot reopen the moment before the affair.
Before the addiction.
Before the betrayal.
Before the secret.
Before the compromise.
Before you became the person you promised yourself you would never become.
Some of you reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You love Jesus now.
But there are memories you wish had never happened.
People may know the cleaned-up version of you.
God knows the whole story.
The private browser history.
The message you deleted.
The person you used.
The lie you protected.
The bitterness you fed.
The marriage you damaged.
The years you wasted.
The faith you performed publicly while starving privately.
And sometimes the enemy takes those memories and whispers:
“That is who you really are.”
But David’s story refuses both cheap excuses and hopeless condemnation.
Sin matters.
Consequences matter.
Repentance matters.
Grace matters.
David was not saved because David managed to become impressive again.
David needed mercy.
Just like us.
And that is where the story begins turning toward Someone greater than David.
But first, the room around the dying king becomes dangerous.
While David grows weak, one of his sons sees opportunity.
Adonijah.
Scripture says:
“וַאֲדֹנִיָּה בֶן־חַגִּית מִתְנַשֵּׂא לֵאמֹר אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ”
Adonijah exalted himself, saying:
“I will be king.”
Notice the heart of rebellion.
“I will.”
God had His purposes.
David had not yet died.
Solomon was the son David would publicly designate to succeed him.
But Adonijah was already reaching for the throne.
And Scripture gives us a painful detail about David’s parenting: his father had not confronted him by asking why he behaved as he did.
That single observation should make every parent uncomfortable.
Because sometimes love becomes distorted into avoiding necessary confrontation.
Sometimes we call something “grace” when we are actually afraid to speak truth.
Sometimes we protect people from discomfort until they become strangers to correction.
Adonijah wanted a crown.
He gathered chariots.
Horsemen.
Fifty men running before him.
He built the appearance of kingship before possessing the authority of kingship.
And human beings are still doing this.
We want the appearance.
The platform.
The applause.
The relationship.
The ministry.
The recognition.
The title.
The influence.
We want to look chosen.
But there is a terrifying difference between what you can manufacture and what God has actually given you.
Adonijah could organize a procession.
He could not manufacture God’s appointment.
Eventually David acted.
Solomon was publicly installed as king.
Adonijah’s attempted seizure collapsed.
And for a moment, it seemed the crisis had passed.
But Abishag’s story was not finished.
After David died, Adonijah approached Bathsheba.
He asked her for something that sounded almost strangely modest.
He wanted Abishag.
“Give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.”
Just one woman.
That was all.
Or was it?
Bathsheba carried the request to Solomon.
And Solomon immediately recognized enormous political implications in it.
His response is explosive.
In Hebrew:
“וְלָמָה אַתְּ שֹׁאֶלֶת אֶת־אֲבִישַׁג הַשֻּׁנַמִּית לַאֲדֹנִיָּהוּ וְשַׁאֲלִי־לוֹ אֶת־הַמְּלוּכָה”
“Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also.”
Read that again.
Ask for Abishag?
You might as well ask for the kingdom.

Whatever Adonijah may personally have intended, Solomon understood the request as bound up with a renewed claim to royal power. In the world of ancient monarchy, relationships involving women associated with a former king could carry dynastic significance. More importantly, we do not have to guess how Solomon interpreted this particular request—the biblical text tells us.
To Solomon, Abishag was not merely a beautiful young woman someone wanted to marry.
The request touched the throne.
And suddenly the young woman who entered the story to warm an old man’s body stands near the center of a deadly struggle over kingship.
Think about Abishag for a moment.
Not as a symbol.
As a human being.
Scripture tells us very little about her inner life.
We are never given a recorded speech from her.
We are not told what she thought when royal servants arrived.
We are not told how she felt entering David’s chambers.
We are not told whether she was frightened.
Honored.
Confused.
Overwhelmed.
We are not told what she thought when David died.
We are not told what she thought when Adonijah asked for her.
And that silence should make us careful.
We should not invent emotions and call them Scripture.
But perhaps the silence itself reminds us of something painfully human.
Some people appear in other people’s stories while carrying stories nobody asks them to tell.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Everybody remembers what happened around you.
Few people ask what happened inside you.
You were the child in the divorce.
The spouse beside the addiction.
The person abandoned after somebody else made the decision.
The believer quietly holding the family together.
The woman whose pain became somebody else’s gossip.
The man everyone thought was strong because nobody saw him collapse.
You served.
You stayed.
You carried things.
You watched powerful personalities make decisions that changed your life.
And somehow your name became attached to a story you never asked to enter.
God sees people whose voices human history barely records.
Abishag may occupy only a small amount of biblical space.
But God knew her completely.
And He knows you.
Still, there is an even deeper ache running through this chapter.
David is dying.
Adonijah wants the throne.
Solomon receives the throne.
People maneuver around power.
And eventually Solomon will die too.
Every human king dies.
Every earthly throne eventually belongs to someone else.
Every empire becomes history.
Every celebrity becomes an old photograph.
Every billionaire eventually leaves every dollar behind.
Every body praised for its beauty returns to dust.
Every hand gripping power eventually opens.
David could not remain king forever.
Solomon could not remain king forever.
Israel needed something no ordinary son of David could finally provide.
A King death could not keep.
And centuries later, another Son of David came.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the Bible’s larger story becomes breathtaking.
Jesus is repeatedly identified in the New Testament with David’s royal line and messianic hope.
But Jesus did what David never could.
David defeated Goliath.
Jesus defeated the greater enemies—sin and death.
David ruled Jerusalem.
Jesus announced the kingdom of God.
David committed grievous sin and needed forgiveness.
Jesus was without sin and became the sacrifice through whom sinners receive forgiveness.
David eventually lay beneath blankets unable to keep himself warm.
Jesus willingly went to a cross.
David entered the grave and remained there.
Jesus entered the grave and rose.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of sinful people successfully repairing themselves.
It is the announcement that God came to rescue sinners who could not rescue themselves.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe beneath everything people see, you are tired.
Tired of managing appearances.
Tired of promising God you will change and returning to the same chains.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of carrying shame into worship.
Tired of knowing Bible verses while secretly wondering whether Jesus could still want someone who has done what you have done.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Christ is sufficient.
Repentance is not pretending the darkness never happened.
Repentance turns from sin toward God.
Grace is not God announcing that holiness no longer matters.
Grace is God giving guilty people what they could never earn through Jesus Christ.
The cross does not minimize your sin.
The cross reveals how deadly sin is.
And then it reveals how far God was willing to go to save sinners.
David knew something about this.
After his sin was exposed, Psalm 51 records the cry of a man who could no longer hide behind a crown:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
That is not the prayer of a man polishing his reputation.
That is the prayer of someone who knows he needs God to do what he cannot do for himself.
Maybe that needs to become your prayer tonight.
Not:
“God, make me look better.”
Not:
“God, make everybody forget.”
Not:
“God, protect my reputation.”
But:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
“Clean me.”
“Change me.”
“I am tired of hiding.”
Sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we spent years building.
And please hear this too:
Do not turn Abishag into gossip.
Do not turn David’s weakness into entertainment.
Do not turn Adonijah’s ambition into merely another strange Bible story.
Let the text turn the mirror toward us.
Because somewhere inside these chapters, most of us recognize ourselves.
We know what it is to want what God has not given.
We know what it is to manufacture appearances.
We know what it is to carry consequences.
We know what it is to grow tired.
We know what it is to need mercy.
And every one of us is moving toward the same unavoidable appointment David faced.
Death.
The question is not whether your body will eventually fail.
The question is whether you belong to the King who conquered the grave.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave better.
He came calling sinners to repentance, forgiving those who come to Him, reconciling us to God, and making His people new.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message will always return here:
Not because scandal becomes irrelevant.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because Christians should romanticize sin.
But because Jesus Christ can write redemption into lives human beings would have discarded.
Your worst chapter does not have authority over Christ.
Your shame does not sit on the throne.
Your addiction does not sit on the throne.
Your past does not sit on the throne.
Your critics do not sit on the throne.
Your success does not sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
If this article made you think of someone who has been running from God, share it with them.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus. Salvation cannot be bought, and grace cannot be purchased.
Christ cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Eternal life cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So before you leave this story, picture that bedroom one final time.
David beneath the blankets.
Abishag beside him.
The palace whispering.
A son reaching for a crown.
Another son preparing to inherit it.
An old king breathing toward eternity.
Everything humans fight to possess slipping through human fingers.
Then look beyond Jerusalem.
Beyond David.
Beyond Solomon.
Beyond every earthly throne.
Look toward a hill outside Jerusalem where the true Son of David wore a crown made of thorns.
Look toward a sealed tomb that could not keep Him.
And understand the difference.
David needed someone beside him because he was dying.
Jesus came beside us because we were dying.
David could not hold onto his kingdom.
Jesus says His kingdom will never end.
David’s body grew cold.
Jesus walked out of the grave alive.
That is our hope.
Not that we lived without scandal.
Not that we never failed.
Not that our story remained clean enough to impress religious people.
Our hope is that sinners can repent, ruined people can be redeemed, guilty people can be forgiven, dead hearts can be made alive, and shattered stories can be placed into the hands of Jesus Christ.
But above everything else...
Come to Jesus.
Because one day every blanket will be useless.
Every title will disappear.
Every possession will belong to somebody else.
Every human throne will be empty.
And on that day, the only story that will finally matter is whether your story was surrendered to the King who walked out of His grave.
The crown eventually falls from every human head—but grace still belongs to the sinner who falls at the feet of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SOMEONE FOLLOW CHRIST WITHOUT EVER MARRYING OR HAVING SEX?
paragraphs:
CAN SOMEONE FOLLOW CHRIST WITHOUT EVER MARRYING OR HAVING SEX?
Jesus never married. Paul called singleness a gift. And somewhere along the way, many Christians started treating marriage as though it were the finish line of faithfulness.
There is a question some Christians are almost afraid to ask out loud.
Not because Scripture is silent about it.
But because church culture sometimes isn't.
Can someone really follow Jesus for an entire lifetime without ever getting married… without ever having sex… without ever building the kind of romantic life everyone seems to expect?
And underneath that question is usually another one.
Would my life still be complete?
Maybe you have watched the engagements appear on your feed.
Then the weddings.
Then the pregnancy announcements.
Then the family photographs.
And you smiled.
You congratulated them.
You meant it.
But later, when nobody was watching, something inside you whispered:
What about me?
Maybe you have prayed for a husband for years.
Maybe you have prayed for a wife.
Maybe marriage simply isn't something you desire.
Maybe circumstances have left you single much longer than you expected.
Maybe you have experienced heartbreak so severe that the future you imagined disappeared with someone who walked away.
Maybe you are widowed.
Maybe you are divorced and trying to understand what obedience to Christ looks like now.
Maybe sexual temptation has become exhausting, and part of you secretly wonders whether a person can actually live without sexual expression without becoming incomplete.
Or perhaps you have heard well-meaning Christians talk about marriage so often that you have quietly begun believing something the Bible never actually says:
Jesus is enough for salvation… but perhaps He isn't enough for a full human life.
That thought needs to be brought into the light.
Because standing at the center of Christianity is a Man who never married.
Jesus Christ lived without a wife.
He lived without sexual intercourse.
And Christians confess that His humanity was not defective, unfinished, emotionally meaningless, or less than fully human.
He was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
He loved deeply.
He wept.
He celebrated.
He ate at tables with friends.
He welcomed children.
He experienced betrayal.
He knew loneliness.
He formed profound relationships.
He poured Himself into people.
He gave and received friendship.
And He lived a completely sexually chaste life.
If lifelong celibacy automatically made someone less human, Christianity would immediately have an enormous theological problem.
Because our picture of perfect humanity is Jesus.
And Jesus was single.
That does not make marriage insignificant.
Quite the opposite.
Scripture speaks beautifully about marriage.
Genesis says:
“It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18).
The Hebrew expression translated “not good” is לֹא־טוֹב — lo-tov.
Marriage then appears within God's good creation, and Genesis 2:24 describes man and woman becoming בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad, “one flesh.”
Jesus Himself affirmed this creation pattern when discussing marriage in Matthew 19:4–6.
Marriage matters.
Sex matters.
The body matters.
Christianity does not solve the question by pretending sexuality is dirty.

Sex within the covenant of marriage is not something Christianity needs to apologize for. Hebrews 13:4 tells believers to honor marriage, and Scripture can speak about marital intimacy without embarrassment.
But here is where something remarkable happens.
In the same chapter where Jesus strongly affirms marriage, He also makes room for people who will not marry.
After discussing marriage and divorce, Jesus speaks of those who have “made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12).
The Greek wording includes:
εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν
— language describing voluntary renunciation “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”
Jesus is not commanding bodily mutilation.
He is describing a radical form of renunciation: there are people for whom marriage and sexual relations will not define their earthly calling.
And Jesus does not describe such people as failures.
He connects their sacrifice with the kingdom.
Think about that.
What the world may call missing out, Jesus can receive as consecration.
What people may pity, Christ can fill with purpose.
What looks empty from the outside may actually contain a hidden altar.
Then Paul says something equally startling.
In 1 Corinthians 7, while affirming marriage and recognizing sexual desire realistically, Paul writes:
θέλω δὲ πάντας ἀνθρώπους εἶναι ὡς καὶ ἐμαυτόν
“I wish that all were as I myself am.”
But Paul immediately adds:
ἀλλὰ ἕκαστος ἴδιον ἔχει χάρισμα ἐκ θεοῦ
“But each has his own gift from God” (1 Corinthians 7:7).
That word χάρισμα — charisma matters.
Gift.
Grace-gift.

Paul does not establish singleness as a superior spiritual caste, nor does he command every Christian to remain unmarried. In the same chapter he explicitly says that if someone marries, that person has not sinned (1 Corinthians 7:28).
Marriage can glorify God.
Singleness can glorify God.
Faithfulness is the issue.

Paul later explains that the unmarried believer may have a distinctive freedom to be concerned with “the things of the Lord,” while marriage necessarily brings legitimate responsibilities toward one's spouse (1 Corinthians 7:32–35).
Paul's concern is not to put a noose around anyone.
He explicitly says the opposite.
His concern is undivided devotion to the Lord.
And suddenly the question changes.
It is no longer merely:
Can I survive without sex?
It becomes:
Can my body belong so completely to Jesus that even my desires come underneath His lordship?
That question is not only for single Christians.
It is for everyone.
Marriage is not God's permission slip for unlimited sexual desire.
Married Christians must practice self-control too.
A husband does not cease belonging to Christ when he receives a wife.
A wife does not cease belonging to Christ when she receives a husband.
Single or married, the Christian confession remains:
Jesus is Lord.
Our bodies are not outside His authority.
Paul tells the Corinthians:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
That confronts our age because modern culture often treats sexual expression almost like food or oxygen—as though denying a sexual desire must necessarily mean denying someone's humanity.
Christianity tells a different story.
Sex is powerful.
Sex is meaningful.
Sex is good in its God-given place.
But sex is not God.
And you will not die spiritually because you never have it.
You can live without sex.
You cannot live without God.
That distinction can feel brutal when desire is burning through your body at two in the morning.
Christian teaching about chastity is easy to discuss abstractly.
It becomes much harder when loneliness has a name.
When you want someone's hand in yours.
When you want someone to notice you came home.
When you want someone beside you when life falls apart.
When you are tired of sleeping alone.
When you don't merely want sex—you want to be known.
That is where shallow Christian answers can become cruel.
Telling a lonely person, “Jesus is all you need,” can be theologically true while being pastorally careless if what we mean is, “Stop needing people.”
That isn't Christianity.
Jesus Himself built community.

The New Testament repeatedly commands believers to bear one another's burdens, love one another, encourage one another, practice hospitality, gather together, care for widows, welcome strangers, and live as one body.
Biblical singleness is not supposed to mean biblical isolation.
A church that celebrates married families while leaving single believers emotionally stranded has misunderstood something about being the family of God.
Jesus said something astonishing in Mark 10.

Speaking about sacrifices made for Him and the Gospel, He promised that those who leave houses or family relationships for His sake will receive, even in this present age, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children—along with persecutions—and in the age to come eternal life (Mark 10:29–30).
The Gospel does not merely remove things.
It creates a family.
This means the single Christian should not be treated as someone waiting in the church lobby until “real adulthood” begins.
Your life is happening now.
Your calling is happening now.
Your usefulness is happening now.
Your worship is happening now.
You do not become complete when someone places a ring on your finger.
Marriage cannot accomplish what only Christ can accomplish.
A spouse cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Sex cannot cleanse your conscience.
Romance cannot reconcile you to God.
Children cannot justify you.
And marriage cannot resurrect you from the dead.
Only Jesus can.
Perhaps that is why this question reaches deeper than sexuality.
Because eventually every human being discovers that even God's best earthly gifts cannot bear the weight of becoming God.
Some married people are desperately lonely.
Some sexually active people feel profoundly empty.
Some people received the relationship they begged God for and discovered that another human being could never heal everything broken inside them.
The Gospel begins where our substitutes collapse.
We were created for God, yet sin has separated humanity from Him.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve our romantic lives.
He came to rescue sinners.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And He calls sinners not merely into behavior modification but into repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance: a turning, a changed mind expressed in a changed direction toward God.
Grace does not say:
“Your desires don't matter.”
Grace says:
“Your desires don't have to be your master anymore.”
That is freedom.
Not the absence of desire.
Not emotional numbness.
Not pretending temptation never comes.
Freedom is being able to feel something powerfully without having to obey it.
Jesus never promised that following Him would mean getting everything we naturally desire.
He said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).
That sentence belongs to every disciple.
For one person, obedience may involve remaining sexually faithful inside a difficult marriage.
For another, fleeing pornography.
For another, refusing adultery.
For another, ending a sexually immoral relationship.
For another, waiting until marriage.
For another, accepting that marriage may never come.
Different crosses.
Same Lord.
And none of us carries our cross to purchase God's love.
We obey because Christ loved us first.
The cross is not a transaction where enough sexual restraint earns heaven.
Salvation is grace.
Paul writes:
That Greek word for grace is χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Undeserved favor.
Gift.
Christian chastity only makes sense downstream from that grace.
Otherwise it becomes miserable religious scorekeeping.
You are not trying to make Jesus love you by being pure enough.
You are learning to surrender your body because the One who already loved you gave His body for you.
And if you fail?
This is where scandal meets grace.
Maybe your sexual history isn't clean.
Maybe you have slept with people you weren't married to.
Maybe pornography has owned years of your life.
Maybe secret messages became secret meetings.
Maybe your browser history would embarrass you.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you promised God you would never cross.
Maybe you have repented before and then fallen again.
Maybe reading an article about chastity makes shame start screaming your name.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that clean people can come to Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can.
Paul's words to the Corinthian church are staggering because after naming patterns of serious sin, including sexual sin, he says:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not possess the authority to write your final chapter.
Jesus does.
Repentance is real.
Consequences can be real.
Healing may take time.
Temptation may require boundaries, accountability, prayer, community, counseling, confession, and painfully practical decisions.
But grace is real too.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because your story became scandalous.
Peter had his scandal.
The woman at the well had hers.
The Corinthian church had plenty.
The Bible does not sanitize human beings before introducing them to grace.
It shows what happens when grace invades human wreckage.
So can someone follow Jesus without ever marrying?
Yes.
Can someone follow Jesus without ever having sex?
Yes.
Jesus Himself destroys the idea that sex is required for a fully meaningful human existence.
Paul shows that unmarried devotion can become a remarkable arena of kingdom service.
But Scripture also refuses to turn singleness into a universal command.
Some believers will marry.
Some will remain unmarried.
Some desperately want marriage and have not received it.
Some may experience seasons of singleness before marriage.
Some will lose spouses and face singleness again.
The Christian hope is not ultimately that everyone gets married.
It is far greater.
There is a wedding coming.
Revelation calls it “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).
And the Bridegroom is Christ.
Even earthly marriage points beyond itself.
Jesus taught that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30).
That means marriage—beautiful, holy, precious marriage—is temporary.
Christ is eternal.
One day the Christian who spent decades wondering whether something was missing will stand before the One for whom every earthly shadow existed.
No loneliness.
No pornography.
No lust.
No adultery.
No abandonment.
No rejection.
No unwanted bed.
No aching memory.
No desperate scrolling at midnight hoping someone will make you feel desirable.
No shame.
No funeral separating husband from wife.
No wedding ring necessary to prove you were loved.
Christ.
Fully known.
Fully redeemed.
Finally home.
So perhaps the question was never only:
Can I live without marriage or sex?
Perhaps the deeper question has always been:
If Jesus asks for every room in my life—even the room where my deepest desires live—will I still call Him Lord?
That is where discipleship becomes personal.
And maybe this article found you because that room has been locked for a long time.
You let Jesus into Sunday.
You let Him into your prayers.
You let Him into your theology.
But sexuality?
Loneliness?
Pornography?
Dating?
The person you cannot release?
The fantasy you keep feeding?
The fear that nobody will ever choose you?
You kept that door closed.
Christ is not standing there because He wants to destroy your humanity.
He is Lord of that room because He loves you too much to surrender any part of you to another master.
Bring it into the light.
Repent where repentance is necessary.
Grieve where grief is necessary.
Ask for help where help is necessary.
And stop measuring the value of your life by whether somebody eventually sleeps beside you.
The deepest proof that your life matters is not that another human being desires you.
The Son of God gave Himself for you.
You can simply write, “Jesus, I surrender this too.”
If you know somebody who believes they are incomplete because they are unmarried, send this to them.
Save it too.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what God made clear today.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, repentance, grace, and Jesus Christ, stay close.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor.
Sharing a post cannot save you.
Buying a Christian book cannot save you.
Being married cannot save you.
Being celibate cannot save you.
