Maybe you have been trying to clean yourself before returning to Jesus.
Come filthy.
Come ashamed.
Come tired.
Come with the confession you have rehearsed a hundred times but never spoken.
Come with the addiction.
Come with the pride.
Come with the religious hypocrisy.
Come with the wounds.
Come with the questions.
But come to Christ.
Repentance is not paying God back.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior whose grace you could never purchase.
And when you belong to Christ, Romans 12:1 becomes a daily answer to mercy:
“Here I am.”
My body.
My plans.
My ambitions.
My sexuality.
My finances.
My relationships.
My career.
My wounds.
My future.
My influence.
My platform.
My ordinary Tuesday afternoon.
All of it.
Yours.
This is where worship leaves the church building.
The mother quietly caring for her children can worship.
The student refusing to cheat can worship.
The businessman choosing integrity over a profitable lie can worship.
The young believer deleting what keeps dragging him toward sin can worship.
The wounded Christian choosing the long road toward forgiveness can worship.
The exhausted believer opening Scripture again can worship.
The person who has fallen and finally stops hiding can worship through confession and repentance.
The Christian who has almost nothing but still asks, “Lord, how can what I have serve You?” can worship.
Your life becomes the sanctuary.
Not because every ordinary action automatically becomes holy, but because the ordinary life increasingly comes under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that brings us somewhere uncomfortable even for Gospel Warrior.
It does not.
Jesus Christ saves.
Your share cannot purchase forgiveness.
Your money cannot purchase God's favor.
The Gospel is not for sale.
But a life surrendered to Christ does begin asking a different question about everything it possesses:
“How can I use what God has entrusted to me for His glory?”
Sometimes that means giving.
Sometimes serving.
Sometimes supporting faithful ministry.
Sometimes helping someone privately who can never repay you.
Sometimes sharing biblical truth with the person God keeps putting on your heart.
Sometimes using your online presence for something greater than yourself.
If this article brought you back to Scripture, don't let it die silently on your screen.
Someone may need Romans 12:1 tonight.
Someone may need to discover that Christianity is more than pretending to be okay.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is still possible.
Someone may need to remember that Jesus still receives sinners.
Send this to the believer who is exhausted from fighting alone.
Send it to the person drifting from God.
Send it to the friend carrying shame.
Even send it, with gentleness rather than superiority, to someone who does not yet believe.
Be honest.
Or tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may need evidence that Christ still restores people who thought they had gone too far.
Because surrender has a strange habit of feeling obvious when conviction is burning and negotiable when temptation returns.
Come back.
Read Romans 12 again.
Remember the mercy.
Remember the altar.
Remember the cross.
If you genuinely want to glorify God, then let that desire reach beyond words. Ask Him how your time, influence, sharing, generosity, and resources can serve His purposes.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe but is willing to listen.
But before you leave, return once more to the altar.
Romans 12:1 is not asking whether you once gave your life to Jesus during an emotional moment years ago.
It confronts us today.
Right now.
What is still withheld?
What are you protecting?
What keeps climbing down from the altar?
What would obedience look like before you go to sleep tonight?
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic answer.
Maybe the next act of surrender is simply confession.
Maybe it is an apology.
Maybe it is deleting something.
Maybe it is forgiving.
Maybe it is opening your Bible.
Maybe it is asking for help.
Maybe it is giving generously.
Maybe it is walking away from what keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is kneeling beside your bed and finally saying the words you have been afraid to say:
“Jesus, I don't want to keep giving You pieces of me.”
Because the deepest beauty of Romans 12:1 is not that God found flawless people and put them on an altar.
He found sinners.
He showed them mercy.
Christ redeemed them.
And grace began turning rescued lives into worship.
Your worst chapter does not need to be your last chapter.
Your failure does not have authority to write the ending.
Your shame does not sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
And the Christ who calls you to surrender is the Christ whose hands still bear the testimony of how far love went to redeem sinners.
So bring Him the chapter you wish had never happened.
Bring Him the habit you are ashamed to name.
Bring Him the future you are afraid to release.
Bring Him your body.
Bring Him your plans.
Bring Him your yes.
And tomorrow morning, when you discover that a living sacrifice is still very much alive...
give Him your yes again.
Because sometimes the thing you keep dragging off the altar is the very thing Jesus is asking you to trust Him enough to surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PSALM 23 WAS NEVER JUST FOR FUNERALS: THE TERRIFYINGLY BEAUTIFUL TRUTH HIDDEN IN THE SHEPHERD PSALM
paragraphs: PSALM 23 WAS NEVER JUST FOR FUNERALS: THE TERRIFYINGLY BEAUTIFUL TRUTH HIDDEN IN THE SHEPHERD PSALM
You may have heard it beside a coffin. David wrote it for people who were still breathing—and still walking through valleys.
There is something almost tragic about the way many people first encounter Psalm 23.
They hear it when somebody dies.

A pastor stands beside a grieving family. Flowers surround a coffin. Someone is trying not to cry. Someone else is staring at the floor because looking at the photograph of the person they lost hurts too much.
Then come the familiar words:
“The LORD is my shepherd…”
And because generations of us have heard Psalm 23 in moments like these, we can unconsciously begin treating it as though David wrote a funeral poem.
He didn’t.
Psalm 23 certainly speaks powerfully into death, grief, and mortality.
But it was written for the living.
For frightened people.
For exhausted people.
For people being pursued.
For people surrounded by enemies.
For people who have discovered that following God does not mean avoiding every dark valley.

And perhaps that is why Psalm 23 becomes much more unsettling—and much more beautiful—when you stop reading it as something meant merely to comfort you when someone dies and begin reading it as something meant to teach you how to live while everything around you feels like it is falling apart.
The Hebrew begins:
מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
Mizmor leDavid. YHWH ro‘i, lo echsar.
“A psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not lack.”
Slow down.
David does not merely say God is a shepherd.
He makes it personal.
יְהוָה רֹעִי
YHWH ro‘i.
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
That little word changes everything.
Because sheep do not merely admire shepherds.
They depend upon them.
A sheep separated from its shepherd is not experiencing independence. It is experiencing danger.
And suddenly Psalm 23 asks a question considerably more uncomfortable than, “Do you believe in God?”
It asks:
Who is actually shepherding your life?
Because something is.
Your appetite can shepherd you.
Money can shepherd you.
Approval can shepherd you.
Sexual desire can shepherd you.
Resentment can shepherd you.
Fear can shepherd you.
Your political tribe can shepherd you.
Your career can shepherd you.
Your trauma can shepherd you.
Your phone can shepherd you.
Even your desperate need to make everybody think you are okay can shepherd you.
We live in a culture obsessed with independence, yet almost everyone is following something.
David's freedom begins with surrender.
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
Not my feelings.
Not my cravings.
Not the crowd.
Not my past.
Not even myself.
The LORD.
And then comes the declaration:
לֹא אֶחְסָר
Lo echsar.
“I shall not lack.”
That does not mean the believer will receive everything he wants.
David's own life destroys that interpretation.
He experienced danger, betrayal, family catastrophe, warfare, grief, sin, consequences, enemies, and seasons of profound anguish.
Psalm 23 is not prosperity theology hiding inside beautiful poetry.
David is saying something deeper.
If the Shepherd is truly enough, then even when life removes things from me, it cannot remove the One upon whom my soul ultimately depends.
That is why the next line is so beautiful:
בִּנְאוֹת דֶּשֶׁא יַרְבִּיצֵנִי
“He makes me lie down in green pastures.”
Notice something almost uncomfortable.
“He makes me lie down.”
Some of us know exactly what it is like to refuse rest.
We keep moving because silence makes us think.
We keep working because stopping makes us feel.
We keep scrolling because being alone with our thoughts feels unbearable.
We stay busy because somewhere beneath the noise there is grief we haven't processed, sin we haven't confessed, forgiveness we haven't extended, or emptiness we haven't wanted to admit.
And sometimes the Shepherd loves His sheep enough to interrupt them.
The interruption may not feel loving while it is happening.
A closed door.
A season of waiting.
A plan that collapses.
A relationship that exposes what is inside you.
A moment when your strength finally reaches its limit.
Not every hardship should be simplistically described as God “making you lie down.” Scripture does not authorize us to call every tragedy a direct divine intervention.
But Scripture does teach us that God can meet His people in weakness and use suffering without being defeated by it.
And some people reading this know the strange mercy of finally reaching the place where they could no longer pretend they were strong.
You thought you were falling apart.
But perhaps, in that place, you finally stopped running long enough to hear the Shepherd.
Then David writes:
עַל־מֵי מְנֻחוֹת יְנַהֲלֵנִי
Al mei menuchot yenahaleni.
“He leads me beside waters of rest.”
Not waters of panic.
Not waters of endless striving.
Rest.
But then Psalm 23 says something commonly translated:
“He restores my soul.”
The Hebrew is:
נַפְשִׁי יְשׁוֹבֵב
Nafshi yeshovev.
The word nefesh can speak of one's life, self, or living being—not merely “soul” in the later popular sense of an invisible component trapped inside a body.
David is describing restoration at the level of the person.
God brings back what has become depleted.
He revives.
He restores.
He turns the wandering life back toward Himself.
Maybe you need that more than you have admitted.
Because there is a kind of exhaustion sleep cannot cure.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up tired.
You can take a vacation and remain empty.
You can laugh with friends and drive home feeling strangely hollow.
You can sit inside a church while your heart feels miles away from God.
You can even post Bible verses while secretly losing the battle nobody online knows you are fighting.
And that is where Psalm 23 stops being decoration and becomes confrontation.
The Shepherd does not merely want to improve your circumstances.
He wants you.
“He leads me in paths of righteousness for His name's sake.”
The Shepherd comforts—but He also leads.
And His leading has moral direction.
Righteousness.
That means Psalm 23 cannot honestly be reduced to:
“God loves me, therefore I can continue living however I want.”
No.
Grace does not merely soothe wandering sheep.
Grace brings wandering sheep home.
Jesus did not go to the cross so we could decorate our rebellion with Christian vocabulary.
He came to save sinners.
Forgive sinners.
Cleanse sinners.
Transform sinners.
And call sinners to follow Him.
Then the landscape changes.
The pasture disappears.
The quiet water disappears.
Suddenly David is walking somewhere terrifying.
גַּם כִּי־אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת
Gam ki elekh begei tsalmavet…
“Even though I walk through a valley of deepest darkness…”
The famous traditional translation says:
“the valley of the shadow of death.”
And that translation has comforted countless grieving people.
But the Hebrew expression צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet) can carry the broader sense of deep or deathlike darkness.
That matters.
Because this valley is not reserved for the cemetery.
You can walk through tsalmavet while still alive.
The diagnosis.
The divorce papers.
The betrayal.
The depression nobody sees.
The night your child calls crying.
The financial collapse.
The temptation you thought you had conquered.
The funeral you were not ready to attend.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The season when heaven appears silent.
The moment you look at your own life and whisper:
“How did I get here?”
Psalm 23 never promises you will not enter that valley.
Read that again.
God never promised His sheep a valley-free existence.
Christianity does not mean Jesus hands you a map around suffering.
Sometimes He leads you through it.
But there is one word in the verse that changes the entire valley.
עִמָּדִי
Immadi.
“With me.”
“I will fear no evil, for You are with me.”
David's confidence is not that the valley isn't dangerous.
His confidence is that he isn't abandoned.
And there is something extraordinary happening grammatically and relationally in the psalm.
Before the valley, David speaks about God.
“He makes me…”
“He leads me…”
“He restores…”
Then inside the darkness, David begins speaking to God.
“You are with me.”
“Your rod…”
“Your staff…”
Sometimes suffering turns theology into prayer.
It is easy to talk about God beside green pastures.
The valley teaches you to talk to Him.
And perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
There are prayers you pray when life is comfortable.
And there are prayers you pray at 2:17 in the morning when nobody else is awake.
“Jesus…”
That is sometimes the whole prayer.
“Jesus, help me.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, don't let me go.”
“Jesus, I don't know what to do.”
And somehow the Shepherd hears prayers that barely have enough strength to become sentences.
David continues:
“Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.”
We often imagine comfort as softness.
But shepherding included protection and guidance.
The Shepherd's comfort is not sentimental indulgence.
Sometimes His protection comforts.
Sometimes His correction comforts.
That means one of the most loving things God can do is refuse to let us comfortably destroy ourselves.
Some of us pray:
“Lord, lead me.”
But what we mean is:
“Lord, approve the direction I already chose.”
Those are not the same prayer.
The Shepherd has a staff because sheep wander.
And this is where Psalm 23 points us beyond David toward Jesus Christ.
Centuries later Jesus would say:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
Do not miss how shocking that is.
Psalm 23 says:
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
Then in John 10 Jesus identifies Himself as the Good Shepherd and describes His mission in terms of laying down His life for the sheep.
The Shepherd enters the danger.
The Shepherd bears the cost.
The Shepherd gives His life.
And at the cross we discover just how far the Shepherd is willing to go to rescue sinners.
Jesus did not merely stand outside our darkness shouting directions.
He entered human suffering.
He was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And He bore sin so that guilty people could be reconciled to God.
The Shepherd became the sacrifice.
And death did not get the final word.
Christ rose.
That is why Christian hope is not:
“Nothing bad will happen to me.”
Christian hope is:
Whatever happens, Jesus Christ has already walked into death and come out victorious.
Then Psalm 23 changes scenes again.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.”
Notice what God does not necessarily do first.
He does not immediately remove the enemies.
He prepares a table while they are still there.
Imagine it.
Danger nearby.
Enemies watching.
And God says:
Sit.
Eat.
You are under My care.
There is something almost defiant about that peace.
Biblical peace is not always the absence of conflict.
Sometimes it is the presence of God in the middle of conflict.
Your enemies do not get to determine whether God can sustain you.
Your critics do not get to cancel God's faithfulness.
Your past does not get the final vote on your future.
Your worst chapter does not get to write the ending.
And your scandal does not have authority greater than His grace.
That does not mean consequences disappear.
David knew consequences.
Repentance does not magically erase every earthly result of our decisions.
But grace means your sin does not have to become your final identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a complicated history.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to repair his reputation.
Yet Christ kept rewriting stories.
Not by pretending sin was harmless.
By dealing with sin through grace.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Then David says:
“You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.”
Not barely enough.
Overflow.
Not because David's circumstances were always easy.
Because the Shepherd's goodness was greater than the wilderness.
And then comes perhaps one of the most misunderstood beautiful lines in the entire psalm:
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.”
The Hebrew says:
אַךְ טוֹב וָחֶסֶד יִרְדְּפוּנִי
Akh tov va-chesed yirdefuni.
Goodness and chesed.
חֶסֶד — chesed.
A word rich with the idea of steadfast, faithful, covenant love.
But look at the verb:
יִרְדְּפוּנִי
yirdefuni.
It can mean pursue me.
Not merely casually follow several steps behind.
Pursue.
David knew what being pursued felt like.
Enemies had pursued him.
Danger had pursued him.
Consequences had pursued him.
But David reaches the end of Psalm 23 and realizes:
Something else has been chasing me.
God's goodness.
God's steadfast love.
Perhaps you have spent years believing your past is chasing you.
Perhaps shame keeps whispering:
“You will always be what you did.”
Perhaps your memories keep replaying the person you used to be.
Perhaps there is something you have never told anyone because you are terrified that if people knew the entire story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel tells you that Christ's blood is sufficient.
Repentance means we stop defending our sin and bring it into the light before God.
Grace means the sinner who comes to Christ does not find a Savior reluctant to forgive.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe this article found you while you are walking through your valley.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing fine.
Maybe you have mastered the smile.
The church smile.
The family smile.
The Facebook smile.
But God knows what happens after the screen goes dark.
He knows what you cried about.
He knows what you are afraid of.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows what you keep trying to forget.
He knows the temptation.
He knows the secret.
He knows the exhaustion.
And still the Shepherd calls.
Not:
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will receive you.”
But:
“Come.”
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Me.
You may have spent years running from God only to discover that His mercy has been pursuing you through every mile.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't hide behind religious language.

And if you have lived long enough to know that your worst chapter was not your final chapter, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another wounded person realize they are not alone.
Send this to the person who has stopped talking about what hurts.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
We glorify God through faith, worship, obedience, love, generosity, holiness, and lives surrendered to Christ.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can itself become one practical expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
Not to glorify an algorithm.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Because somewhere tonight somebody is walking through tsalmavet.
Deep darkness.
They are wondering whether God abandoned them.
They are wondering whether their sin disqualified them.
They are wondering whether they can ever come home.
And perhaps what they need is not another motivational quote.
Perhaps they need to hear:
The Shepherd is still calling.
The Shepherd still restores.
The Shepherd still leads.
The Shepherd still corrects.
The Shepherd still protects.
The Shepherd still prepares tables in hostile territory.
The Shepherd still pursues His people with goodness and steadfast love.
And Jesus Christ—the Good Shepherd—still saves sinners.
Psalm 23 was never merely a beautiful passage to read when somebody's journey ends.
It is a declaration for those of us whose journey is still happening.
For the pasture.
For the wilderness.
For the table.
For the enemy.
For the failure.
For the restoration.
For the valley.
Even for the grave.
Because the Christian does not walk into darkness alone.
The Shepherd has already gone ahead.
And maybe that is what you need to remember tonight:
The valley may become part of your story, but because of Jesus, the valley never gets to be your Shepherd.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE COMPARE IDOLATRY TO SEXUAL UNFAITHFULNESS?
paragraphs: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE COMPARE IDOLATRY TO SEXUAL UNFAITHFULNESS?

Because God does not describe idolatry merely as breaking a rule. He describes it as betraying a covenant—and once you understand that, some of the Bible’s most uncomfortable passages begin to sound painfully personal.
There is a reason Scripture sometimes speaks about idolatry in language so intimate, severe, and even shocking that modern readers instinctively want to soften it.
God could have called idolatry foolishness.
He does.
He could have called it rebellion.
He does.
He could have called it spiritual blindness, wickedness, vanity, or sin.
He does all of that too.
But again and again, especially through the prophets, God reaches for another image.
Adultery.
Unfaithfulness.
Whoring after other gods.
A bride abandoning her husband.
And that language can make us uncomfortable.
Maybe it is supposed to.
Because the biblical God is not presenting Himself as an impersonal ruler whose subjects happened to violate an obscure regulation.
He is revealing the heartbreak of covenant betrayal.
This is why understanding the biblical language matters.

In the Old Testament, one important Hebrew verb is זָנָה — zanah — a word that can refer literally to prostitution or sexual immorality, but which the prophets also employ metaphorically for Israel’s religious unfaithfulness.
That metaphor appears with devastating force throughout the prophets.
God tells Jeremiah:
“Thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again to me, saith the LORD.”
— Jeremiah 3:1, KJV
Notice the astonishing ending.
Return.
The betrayal is real.
The judgment is real.
Yet so is the invitation.
Return.
That single word tells us something essential about the entire biblical story.
God exposes Israel’s spiritual adultery not because He delights in humiliating His people, but because covenant love refuses to pretend betrayal is harmless.
And perhaps this is where the passage becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because idolatry did not disappear when human beings stopped bowing before carved statues.
An idol can have a screen.
An idol can have a salary.
An idol can wear your dream body.
An idol can carry your surname.
An idol can be approval.
Romance.
Sex.
Success.
Politics.
Comfort.
Influence.
A ministry.
A reputation.
Even something good can become spiritually destructive when we ask it to occupy the place belonging to God alone.
The frightening thing about idols is that they rarely introduce themselves by saying, “I am here to replace God.”
They whisper something far more believable.
“You need me to be okay.”
That is where idolatry begins to expose the heart.
What do you believe you absolutely must possess before life can have meaning?
Whose approval can destroy you when you lose it?
What consumes your imagination?
What controls your obedience?
What are you unwilling to surrender even when Christ puts His finger on it?
What do you run toward when you are afraid, lonely, ashamed, rejected, exhausted, or empty?
Sometimes the clearest evidence of an idol is not what we worship on Sunday.
It is what we cannot imagine living without on Monday.
And suddenly the prophetic metaphor does not seem ancient anymore.
It feels invasive.
Personal.
Almost unbearably close.
The book of Hosea makes that closeness impossible to escape.

Hosea’s marriage becomes a living prophetic sign through which Israel is confronted with its covenant unfaithfulness. The story is intentionally painful because Israel’s relationship with God was never meant to be understood as a cold contract.
God had loved them.
Redeemed them.
Provided for them.
Called them His people.
Yet they repeatedly pursued other gods.
Hosea 2 depicts Israel chasing her “lovers,” believing they were the source of her bread, water, wool, flax, oil, and drink.
Then comes the devastating revelation.
She had failed to recognize who had actually provided for her.
God says:
“For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal.”
— Hosea 2:8, KJV
Read that slowly.
God gave the gifts.
The gifts were taken.
And the gifts were used in devotion to another.
That is one of Scripture’s most penetrating pictures of idolatry.
God gives breath...
and we use that breath to boast about ourselves.
God gives bodies...
and we use those bodies as though He has no claim upon them.
God gives intelligence...
and we use it to explain why we do not need Him.
God gives money...
and money becomes our security.
God gives relationships...
and relationships become our savior.
God gives influence...
and influence becomes our identity.
God gives ministry...
and eventually we can become more addicted to being seen serving Jesus than to Jesus Himself.
That last idol can hide beneath religious clothing.
You can sing worship songs and worship recognition.
You can preach Christ and secretly worship applause.
You can defend biblical truth and worship being right.
You can build a Christian platform while slowly allowing the platform to occupy the throne that belongs to Christ.
Idolatry is frightening precisely because religious activity does not automatically cure it.
Sometimes religious activity simply gives it somewhere sophisticated to hide.
Ezekiel uses similarly severe imagery.
In Ezekiel 16, Jerusalem is portrayed as a woman whom God rescued, cared for, adorned, and entered into covenant with, only for her to trust in her beauty and become unfaithful.
The imagery is deliberately disturbing.
God says:
“But thou didst trust in thine own beauty, and playedst the harlot because of thy renown...”
— Ezekiel 16:15, KJV
There it is again.
The gift becomes the rival.
Beauty was not the ultimate problem.
Trusting in beauty was.
Renown was not necessarily the ultimate problem.
Building identity upon renown was.
And this is where the prophets stop being archaeological artifacts and begin reading our hearts.
Because human beings still do this.
We receive something from God...
then gradually begin trusting the thing instead of the One who gave it.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe something good slowly became ultimate.
Maybe you told yourself you could stop anytime.
Maybe nobody around you knows how much of your heart it actually controls.
Maybe there is something you would surrender to Jesus...
except that one thing.
And if something inside you is already naming it, do not silence that conviction too quickly.
Because conviction can be mercy.
The Bible’s marriage imagery helps explain why.
Biblically, covenant is relational.
Israel belonged to Yahweh.
That exclusivity is embedded in the covenant itself:
“Thou shalt have no other gods before me.”
— Exodus 20:3, KJV
This is not divine insecurity.
It is covenant reality.
A husband or wife who expects marital fidelity is not demanding an arbitrary privilege. Exclusivity belongs to what marriage is.
Likewise, Israel could not remain covenantally faithful to Yahweh while simultaneously giving divine allegiance to Baal.
The prophets therefore describe idolatry using marital betrayal because both involve giving to another what covenant love has pledged exclusively.
And Scripture carries this relational understanding into the New Testament.
James writes:
— James 4:4, KJV
The Greek text begins with one explosive word:
μοιχαλίδες — moichalides.
Literally, “adulteresses.”
James is using prophetic covenant language.
He is not merely saying, “You made a poor spiritual choice.”
He is exposing divided loyalty.
And divided loyalty is one of the most dangerous conditions in Christianity because it can survive underneath an outwardly religious life.
Jesus said:
“No man can serve two masters...”
— Matthew 6:24, KJV
Not “should not.”
Cannot.
Eventually one master wins.
That is why idolatry is not merely having something you enjoy very much.
Scripture does not teach that affection itself is sinful.
The deeper question is allegiance.
Worship.
Trust.
Identity.
Obedience.
Who owns the throne?
And sometimes we discover the answer only when God threatens the thing sitting on it.
Take away applause and see what happens.
Take away control.
Take away money.
Take away the relationship.
Take away visibility.
Take away the dream.
Take away the version of your future you secretly told God He was obligated to provide.
What happens inside you?
Grief is not automatically idolatry.
Pain is not automatically idolatry.
Jesus Himself grieved.
But sometimes loss reveals that we were asking created things to carry the weight of God.
And created things collapse underneath divine weight.
That is one reason idols eventually wound their worshipers.
They cannot fulfill the promises we force them to make.
Money can help you live.
It cannot tell you why you are alive.
Sex can create profound bodily intimacy within its God-given context.
It cannot cleanse guilt.
Achievement can earn recognition.
It cannot justify you before God.
Another person can love you deeply.
They cannot become your Messiah.
Politics can address real questions of public life.
It cannot resurrect the dead.
A career can give you meaningful work.
It cannot reconcile you to your Creator.
Followers can know your name.
They cannot write it in the Book of Life.
Only Jesus can occupy the place of Jesus.
And this is where the Gospel changes the entire story.
Because if Scripture ended merely by exposing spiritual adultery, every one of us would stand condemned.
Who among us has loved God perfectly?
Who has never looked to something created for what only the Creator can ultimately provide?
Who has never trusted something else?
Desired something else?
Run somewhere else?
Hidden something?
Who has never allowed the heart to wander?
The Gospel does not announce that faithful people saved themselves from unfaithful people.
The Gospel announces that the Faithful One came for the unfaithful.
Jesus Christ enters the story.
And suddenly Scripture's marriage imagery reaches its breathtaking climax.
Paul writes:
— Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Then Paul says that the mystery ultimately speaks of “Christ and the church.”
The Bridegroom does not merely demand faithfulness.
He gives Himself for His bride.
Jesus goes to the cross.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because sin was so serious that reconciliation required a cost we could never pay ourselves.
At Calvary, grace does not pretend betrayal never happened.
Grace pays for the betrayer.
Christ bears sin.
Christ receives judgment.
Christ sheds His blood.
Christ dies.
Christ rises.
And sinners who repent and believe are not merely tolerated.
They are forgiven.
Cleansed.
Reconciled.
Redeemed.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “be a better person.”
The Gospel is infinitely more scandalous than self-improvement.
The guilty are offered pardon through the innocent Christ.
The wandering are called home.
The spiritually unfaithful can be washed.
The ashamed can be clothed in righteousness they did not earn.
The dead can live.
The sinner does not rewrite his own ending.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps you have been reading this while thinking about someone else's idol.
Do not leave that way.
Ask the harder question.
What is mine?
What receives the affection, trust, obedience, imagination, money, time, or identity that rightly belongs under Christ's lordship?
Do not answer publicly before answering privately before God.
Maybe your idol is success.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is a relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe it is being admired.
Maybe it is your appearance.
Maybe it is control.
Maybe it is comfort.
Maybe it is resentment you refuse to release because anger has become part of who you think you are.
Maybe your idol is even the image of yourself as “a good Christian.”
Whatever it is, Jesus is not asking you to decorate the idol.
He calls you to repent.
The New Testament word often translated “repentance” is connected with μετάνοια — metanoia — a change of mind that, in biblical proclamation, is inseparable from turning toward God.
Repentance is not performing sadness so God will love you.
Repentance is agreeing with God about your sin and turning from rebellion toward Him.
And the astonishing news is that the God who commands repentance is the God who receives repentant sinners.
“Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts.”
— Malachi 3:7, KJV
Maybe you have wandered farther than anyone knows.
Return.
Maybe you have maintained the appearance of Christianity while your private heart has been worshiping something else.
Return.
Maybe shame keeps telling you that you need to clean yourself before approaching Christ.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you have failed in the same place so many times that you have started believing repentance is pointless.
Return.
Not because your sin is small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
Do not confuse grace with permission to continue worshiping idols.
The same Jesus who forgives sinners also calls sinners to follow Him.
Grace does not make idols safe.
Grace breaks their claim.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace restores what sin devastated.
Grace puts Jesus back at the center.
And perhaps that is why Scripture's language of spiritual adultery is ultimately more hopeful than it first appears.
You cannot commit adultery against someone with whom there is no relationship.
The metaphor hurts because covenant matters.
Betrayal hurts because love matters.
And the God who exposes His people's unfaithfulness repeatedly reveals something astonishing about His own character:
He remains faithful.
Paul writes:
— 2 Timothy 2:13, KJV
That verse is not permission for apostasy or comfortable rebellion.
It is a declaration about God's character.
Our instability does not make God unstable.
Our lies do not make Him false.
Our wandering does not make Him cease to be who He is.
And the ultimate proof stands outside Jerusalem.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A risen Christ.
So perhaps today is not the day to keep hiding.
Perhaps today is the day to tell Jesus the truth He already knows.
“Lord, this has become too important to me.”
“Lord, I have been looking to this person to save me.”
“Lord, I have been worshiping approval.”
“Lord, I have loved my secret sin.”
“Lord, I have wanted Your gifts more than I wanted You.”
“Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
You do not need eloquent words.
You need an honest heart before a merciful Savior.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing a sentence saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging our need for Him becomes a small act of refusing to hide anymore.
And if Christ has already begun tearing idols from your heart and healing places nobody knew were wounded, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence another struggling believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because every word here deserves preservation, but because the Scriptures underneath it deserve to be returned to when your heart begins forgetting.
Invite your family.
Your friends.
The believer who has grown cold.
The Christian who is secretly exhausted.
The seeker who thinks Christianity is merely a religion of rules.
Even the person who does not yet believe.
Let them see the Gospel for what it actually announces:
There is grace for sinners because there is a Savior for sinners.
Scripture calls Christians to give willingly rather than under compulsion.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to earn His favor.
Not because clicking “share” proves your faith.
Do it, if you choose, as mission.
They may never tell you.
They may never walk into a church and admit it.
But they might read what you share at 1:17 in the morning when the room is dark and the thing they thought would satisfy them has failed them again.
And perhaps somewhere between Hosea's heartbreak and Calvary's blood, they will finally understand:
God is not exposing their idol because He wants to destroy them.
He is exposing what is destroying them because He calls them back to Himself.
That is the wound and wonder of Scripture's adultery metaphor.
Idolatry is not merely breaking God's rule.
It is giving another lover the heart that belongs to Him.
But the Gospel announces something almost too beautiful for traitors to believe.
The Bridegroom came looking for the unfaithful.
He bore their shame.
He paid their debt.
He rose from the grave.
And He still says:
Return.
The idol will ask you to sacrifice everything and still leave you empty; Jesus sacrificed Himself to bring empty sinners home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED” — THE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO SILENCE YOU
paragraphs: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED” — THE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO SILENCE YOU
What if one of the Bible verses you were taught to fear was never saying what you were told it said?
Maybe you have heard it from a pulpit.
Maybe someone whispered it after you asked an uncomfortable question.

Maybe you watched something happen in a church that did not seem right. Money disappeared without explanation. A leader behaved in a way that troubled your conscience. Someone was wounded. Someone finally spoke. Someone asked for accountability.
And suddenly four words entered the room like a spiritual threat:
“Touch not Mine anointed.”
Conversation over.
Questions became rebellion.
Discernment became dishonor.
Accountability became persecution.
And somewhere inside you, fear whispered, “What if questioning this person means I am questioning God?”
But what if that fear came from a verse removed from its context?
What if Psalm 105:15 was never given to make Christian leaders untouchable?
And what if reading the words surrounding it changes the entire conversation?
The King James Version reads:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.” — Psalm 105:15
Those words are Scripture. They are holy. They should not be mocked, dismissed, or explained away.
But because they are Scripture, we must care enough about them to ask what God actually meant.
The Hebrew is striking:
אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי וְלִנְבִיאַי אַל־תָּרֵעוּ
’Al-tigge‘u vimshichai, velinvi’ai ’al-tare‘u.
In straightforward English:
“Do not touch My anointed ones, and do My prophets no harm.”
Notice something easily missed.
“Anointed” is plural.
בִמְשִׁיחָי — vimshichai — “My anointed ones.”
The underlying word is related to מָשִׁיחַ, mashiach, “anointed one,” the word from which we get “Messiah.”
But Psalm 105 is not describing a modern preacher standing behind a pulpit and warning people not to question him.
Read backward.
That is where the walls begin to move.

The psalm remembers God’s covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It speaks about people who were few in number, strangers and sojourners, wandering from nation to nation and from kingdom to kingdom. God protected them and rebuked kings on their behalf.
Then comes the famous declaration:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”

The “anointed ones” in this immediate context are the patriarchal covenant family God was preserving—particularly Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—not a special class of modern Christian leaders who have been granted immunity from examination.
That changes everything.
The verse so often used by powerful people to protect themselves originally appears in a song celebrating God protecting vulnerable covenant people as they wandered among powerful kings.
Sit with that.
A text about God protecting His servants from powerful rulers can become dangerously distorted when powerful religious figures use it to protect themselves from legitimate accountability.
That is not a small interpretive mistake.
It can turn comfort into intimidation.
It can turn Scripture into a shield for human power.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You were not trying to destroy the church.
You were trying to understand what happened.
You were not trying to dishonor God.
You were trying to reconcile what you saw with what Scripture says.
You were told not to gossip—and rightly so.
But eventually “gossip” seemed to mean anything that made leadership uncomfortable.
You were told to honor spiritual authority—and Christians absolutely should honor faithful leadership.
But eventually “honor” seemed to mean silence.
You were told, “David would not touch Saul.”
And that story deserves to be taken seriously too.
Saul really was the LORD’s anointed king.
David really did refuse to kill him.
When David had an opportunity to strike Saul, he refused to “put forth” his hand against the LORD’s anointed.
But notice what David did not do.
David did not pretend Saul was behaving righteously.
David did not surrender himself to Saul so Saul could murder him.
David did not call Saul’s persecution acceptable because Saul held an anointed office.
David spared Saul’s life while still confronting Saul with the truth.
He essentially said: Look at what you are doing. I have not sinned against you, yet you are hunting me to take my life. Let the LORD judge between us.
That is a world away from saying, “A spiritual leader must never be questioned.”
David refused vengeance.
He did not refuse discernment.
He refused murder.
He did not deny wrongdoing.
He honored the office without pretending the man occupying it could do no wrong.
There is a lesson there for both wounded church members and angry critics.
Biblical accountability is not permission for a mob.
Christians must not confuse legitimate correction with gossip, slander, character assassination, rumor, online humiliation, or the thrill of watching somebody fall.
A pastor is not fair game simply because he is visible.
An accusation is not automatically true because it is dramatic.
A viral post is not evidence.
A suspicion is not a conviction.
Scripture protects leaders from reckless accusations too.
Paul tells Timothy:
“Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses.” — 1 Timothy 5:19
That should make us careful.
But keep reading.
The next verse says:
“Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.” — 1 Timothy 5:20
There it is.
Both truths standing beside each other.
Do not casually receive accusations against an elder.
And when sin is established and persists, leadership is not exempt from correction.
Scripture protects faithful leaders from slander without protecting sinful leaders from accountability.
The Bible refuses both extremes.
It will not give us permission to destroy pastors with unverified accusations.
And it will not give pastors permission to use their position to escape biblical accountability.
That balance matters because Jesus loves His church too much for either abuse.
This is where the issue becomes painfully personal.
Because spiritual abuse often does not begin with somebody announcing, “I intend to manipulate you.”
It can begin with biblical language.
“Honor.”
“Submission.”
“Authority.”
“Covering.”
“Rebellion.”
“Anointing.”
Words that may contain legitimate biblical ideas can become dangerous when detached from the rest of Scripture and placed into the hands of someone who refuses correction.
And there is a devastating irony here.
A leader may quote “Touch not Mine anointed” to defend himself while forgetting that Scripture repeatedly records God Himself confronting leaders.
Nathan confronted David.
David was king.
David was anointed.
David was also guilty.
Nathan did not walk into the throne room and say, “Because you are anointed, adultery and bloodshed are none of my business.”
He said:
“Thou art the man.”
And David eventually said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
That is what godly leadership looks like when confronted by truth—not perfection, but repentance.
The truly terrifying sign is not merely that a Christian leader can sin.
Every Christian leader is still a sinner dependent upon grace.
The terrifying sign is when someone begins acting as though his calling places him beyond correction.
Because the Gospel never creates untouchable celebrities.
It creates servants.
Jesus Himself overturned the worldly model of leadership.
The rulers of the Gentiles exercise dominion over people, He taught His disciples, but “it shall not be so among you.” Greatness in His kingdom looks like service.
Then look at Christ.
The One who actually possessed all authority washed feet.
The One before whom angels worship did not need manipulation to preserve His importance.
The King wore a towel.
Then He wore thorns.
Then He carried a cross.
That is Christian authority.
Not “How dare you question me?”
But “How can I serve?”
Not “Protect my reputation at all costs.”
But “Christ must be honored at all costs.”
Not “I am too anointed to repent.”
But “Search me, O God.”
And perhaps the most sobering part is that Jesus Christ is the Anointed One in the ultimate messianic sense.
Χριστός — Christos.
Christ.
The Anointed One.
The Messiah.
Christianity was never supposed to revolve around protecting the personal kingdoms of charismatic personalities.
It revolves around Jesus.
The pastor did not die for you.
The apostle did not die for you.
The prophet did not die for you.
The denomination did not die for you.
The ministry brand did not shed its blood for you.
Jesus Christ did.
There is only one name before which every knee will ultimately bow.
Jesus.
And when a ministry begins making people more afraid of questioning a human leader than of disobeying Christ, something has gone terribly wrong.
But there is another side to this article, and it may hurt differently.
Perhaps you have used legitimate concerns as permission for bitterness.
Perhaps somebody wounded you in church, and slowly your pain became contempt for the entire body of Christ.
Perhaps “discernment” became the respectable Christian word you used for constantly searching for somebody to expose.
Perhaps you enjoy watching ministers fall.
Perhaps you share accusations before checking whether they are true.
Perhaps you have spoken about servants of God in ways you would never want others to speak about you.
Then this article is not permission to continue.
Jesus calls you to repentance too.
Truth without love becomes cruelty.
Love without truth becomes sentimentality.
Biblical Christianity permits neither.
We do not protect wolves by silencing sheep.
But neither do we become wolves while claiming to protect sheep.
We tell the truth.
We seek evidence.
We reject gossip.
We protect the vulnerable.
We honor faithful shepherds.
We confront proven sin biblically.
We forgive where repentance is real.
We refuse vengeance.
And above everything else, we remain under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the answer to abusive authority is not rebellion against all authority.
The answer is Christlike authority.
The answer to spiritual manipulation is not abandoning Scripture.
The answer is reading Scripture faithfully.
The answer to a distorted gospel is not no gospel.
It is the true Gospel.
And this is where scandal meets grace.
David, the man who refused to kill Saul, later became the king confronted for his own horrifying sin.
Think about that.
The man who once respected another anointed king eventually became an anointed king who needed someone courageous enough to confront him.
That alone should destroy our appetite for simplistic categories.
Today you may be David hiding from Saul.
Tomorrow you may be David standing before Nathan.
Sometimes you are the wounded person who needs protection.
Sometimes you are the sinner who needs confrontation.
Sometimes you need courage to speak.
Sometimes you need humility to listen.
Every one of us desperately needs Jesus.
That is why grace is not pretending sin never happened.
Grace tells the truth about sin and then points trembling sinners toward a Savior whose blood is greater than their shame.
The cross does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves sin matters so much that the Son of God gave Himself to save sinners from it.
Jesus does not merely expose darkness.
He calls people out of it.
He does not merely uncover scandal.
He offers grace.
He does not merely say, “You are guilty.”
To the repentant sinner He offers forgiveness, cleansing, restoration, and a completely new identity in Him.
So if you are a pastor reading this, do not fear biblical accountability.
Fear becoming the kind of leader who no longer believes he needs it.
Surround yourself with people who love Jesus more than they love your approval.
Give them permission to tell you the truth.
Do not build a throne where Christ placed a cross.
If you are a church member reading this, honor your leaders.
Pray for them.
Do not spread rumors.
Do not confuse disagreement with abuse.
Do not weaponize accusations.
But never surrender your conscience to a human being.
Test teaching by Scripture.
Christ alone is Lord of the conscience.
And if you have been spiritually wounded, hear this carefully:
You do not have to choose between truth and Jesus.
Jesus is the truth.
What somebody did while carrying a Bible does not redefine the Bible.
What somebody did while standing behind a pulpit does not redefine Christ.
What somebody did in the name of God does not change the character of God.
Do not let the person who wounded you steal Jesus from you too.
Bring the wound to Him.
Bring the anger.
Bring the confusion.
Bring the questions you were told you were not allowed to ask.
Bring the bitterness you are embarrassed to admit.
Bring everything into the light.
And then look at the cross.
There hangs the true Anointed One.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Crucified.
Not exploiting sheep but dying for them.
Not demanding that others bleed to preserve His kingdom but shedding His own blood to bring sinners into His kingdom.
That is your Shepherd.
That is your King.
That is Jesus.
Maybe you came into this article angry at a pastor.
Maybe you came here defending one.
Maybe you came here because somebody sent this to you and you were ready to argue.
But perhaps the Holy Spirit has turned the mirror around.
Because eventually this stops being about “them.”
What do you do when Scripture corrects you?
Can you repent?
Can you forgive?
Can you admit you were wrong?
Can you refuse revenge when somebody really has wronged you?
Can you honor faithful leadership without idolizing it?
Can you expose darkness without enjoying another person's destruction?
Can you follow Jesus when doing so costs you your pride?
That is the deeper test.
And maybe your next prayer needs to be very simple:

“Jesus, show me where I have believed people more than Your Word. Show me where I have confused honor with fear, discernment with bitterness, loyalty with idolatry, or accountability with revenge. Forgive me. Heal what has been wounded. Expose what needs to be exposed in me. Teach me to love truth without losing love. I belong to You.”
If this uncovered something you have been afraid to admit, do not hide behind religious language.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not alone.
And if you know a believer who has been frightened into silence by a verse taken out of context, send this to them personally.
Save it too.
Because eventually somebody may quote those four words again, and you will want to remember the verses surrounding them.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is nothing more than religious power to follow as well. Let them encounter the Jesus who confronts sin while opening His arms to sinners.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus. It does not.
And never because anyone should manipulate you into believing God will be disappointed with you if you cannot financially support a ministry.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.

But one practical way believers who are able can participate in spreading biblical teaching is by supporting ministries whose work they prayerfully believe is bearing faithful fruit. Your sharing matters too.
You belong to Jesus before you belong to any ministry.
Follow Christ before personalities.
Know Scripture beyond quotations.
Honor godly leaders without worshiping them.
Refuse slander without surrendering discernment.
Protect the wounded without becoming consumed by vengeance.
And when scandal reveals how broken human beings can become—even inside churches—run toward the Savior whose grace is powerful enough to expose sin without abandoning the repentant sinner.
Because perhaps the most dangerous misuse of “Touch not Mine anointed” is not simply misunderstanding an ancient verse.
It is allowing a human voice to become so powerful that you become afraid to hear what God actually said.
So open the Bible.
Read before the verse.
Read after the verse.
Look at Jesus.
And never again confuse protecting someone's platform with protecting the Gospel.
The Gospel does not need an untouchable man.
It already has an unconquerable Christ.
And please, do not leave without answering the question Scripture has quietly placed before all of us:
When truth finally reaches your door, will you protect your image—or will you let Jesus rewrite your story?
Because the hands pierced for you are the only hands worthy of holding the throne of your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Confessed the Same Sin Again—and Now You’re Wondering Whether Jesus Is Tired of Hearing Your Voice
paragraphs: You Confessed the Same Sin Again—and Now You’re Wondering Whether Jesus Is Tired of Hearing Your Voice

When the same failure brings you back to your knees, Scripture does not tell you to pretend the sin is small—but neither does it tell the repentant sinner that Jesus has grown tired of hearing their confession.
You knew what you were doing.
That may be the part that hurts the most.
It wasn’t ignorance this time.
You had already confessed it.
You had already cried about it.
You had already promised God you wanted to change.

Maybe there was even a night when you sat alone with your Bible open, tears falling onto pages you could barely read, and whispered, “Jesus, please forgive me. I don’t want to be this person anymore.”
And you meant it.
Then days passed.
Maybe weeks.
Maybe months.
And somehow you found yourself standing in the wreckage of the same sin again.
The same screen.
The same conversation.
The same bottle.
The same rage.
The same secret.
The same lust.
The same bitterness.
The same dishonesty.
The same compromise.
The same pattern you swore you would never return to.
Only this time, something feels different.
You are almost afraid to pray.
Because what exactly are you supposed to say now?
“Lord, forgive me”?
Again?
You said that last time.
And the time before that.
Perhaps the most terrifying thought is not simply, “I sinned again.”
It is this:
“What if Jesus is tired of hearing my voice?”
If you have ever stared at the ceiling after another failure and wondered whether you have finally exhausted the patience of God, you need to hear what Scripture actually says—not what shame says.
Because shame has a voice.
And it can sound frighteningly religious.
Shame says, “Don’t pray now. You’re a hypocrite.”
Shame says, “God has heard this apology before.”
Shame says, “Clean yourself up first, then come back.”
Shame says, “Real Christians wouldn’t struggle like this.”
Shame says, “Maybe grace worked for you the first ten times, but surely there is a limit.”
And somewhere between conviction and despair, a struggling believer can begin treating distance from God as though distance itself were repentance.
But hiding from the One you sinned against is not the cure for sin.
It is one of sin’s oldest consequences.
Adam and Eve sinned, heard the sound of God, and hid.
Human beings have been hiding ever since.
We hide behind religion.
We hide behind busyness.
We hide behind church attendance.
We hide behind jokes.
We hide behind carefully edited photographs and Sunday smiles.
Sometimes we even hide behind self-hatred because condemning ourselves can feel strangely more spiritual than receiving mercy.
Then John writes words that leave nowhere for our pretending to survive:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
That is 1 John 1:8.
Notice the honesty.
Christianity does not require you to pretend that sin disappeared the moment you believed.
John does not say sin is imaginary.
He does not call rebellion harmless.
He does not tell us to rename sin “a mistake,” “a season,” or “just being human” so we can feel better about ourselves.
He says that denying our sin is self-deception.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking promises in the New Testament:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
The Greek begins:
“ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν…”
ean homologōmen tas hamartias hēmōn…
“If we confess our sins…”
That word translated “confess” comes from ὁμολογέω — homologeō.
It carries the sense of acknowledging, admitting, declaring, agreeing.
Biblical confession is not negotiating with God.
It is not saying, “Yes, Lord, but You need to understand why I did it.”
It is not dressing rebellion in softer vocabulary.
It is stepping into the light and agreeing with God about what happened.
“Yes, Lord.
It was sin.
I did it.
I cannot blame my childhood, my spouse, my loneliness, my stress, my hormones, my friends, my circumstances, or the devil for the choices that belonged to me.
Have mercy on me.”
But look carefully at what John says next.
He does not say God forgives because your apology was emotionally impressive.
He does not say God forgives because you cried enough.
He does not say God forgives because you punished yourself long enough.
He does not say God forgives because this time you finally found the perfect words.
He says:
“πιστός ἐστιν καὶ δίκαιος…”
pistos estin kai dikaios.
“He is faithful and just.”
That changes everything.
Your hope is not ultimately anchored in the intensity of your remorse.
Your hope is anchored in the character of God and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
John has already pointed directly to that foundation:
“The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.”
And shortly afterward he writes:
The Christian answer to guilt is therefore not, “Sin doesn’t matter.”
The answer is that sin mattered so terribly that the Son of God went to the cross.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace is purchased mercy.
At Calvary, Jesus did not make peace with our sin.
He bore sin.
The cross simultaneously destroys two lies we desperately want to believe.
The first says, “My sin isn't really that serious.”
Look at the cross.
It is.
The second says, “My sin is too terrible for Christ to forgive.”
Look again at the cross.
His sacrifice is enough.
This is where exhausted believers often become confused.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin.
You should not look at repeated failure and casually say, “Grace covers it, so it doesn't matter.”
Paul confronted that distortion directly:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace is never permission to cherish what nailed Christ to the cross.
If you are arranging your life so that you can protect your sin from Jesus, refusing repentance while demanding reassurance, Scripture gives you no reason to become comfortable.
But perhaps that is not why you are reading this.
Perhaps you hate what this sin is doing to you.
Perhaps you have prayed against it.
Perhaps you have deleted things and then downloaded them again.
Perhaps you have walked away and then crawled back.
Perhaps you have made progress nobody saw, only to collapse again.
Perhaps you are exhausted from fighting yourself.
And now your repeated failure has convinced you that your struggle itself proves Jesus wants nothing more to do with you.
Listen carefully.
The fact that sin must be fought seriously does not mean the wounded soldier should run away from the Physician.
Peter knew something about repeated failure.
He did not merely have a bad moment.
Jesus warned him.
Peter confidently insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then pressure arrived.
And Peter denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine that sound.
One ordinary sound suddenly carrying the weight of every confident promise Peter had just shattered.
Scripture says Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter Jesus wrote over his life.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
There was a charcoal fire.
There were questions.
There was pain.
There was restoration.
There was a calling.
“Feed my sheep.”
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial had never happened.
He restored the man who had failed Him and called him forward into faithful obedience.
That is grace.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your past will not have the final word because Jesus does.”
This is why repentance is so much more beautiful than endless self-condemnation.
Repentance turns toward God.
Condemnation curls inward.
Repentance says, “Jesus, I sinned. Change me.”
Condemnation says, “I sinned. Therefore I should disappear.”
Repentance exposes sin to the light.
Shame builds another hiding place.
And the Gospel keeps calling you out of hiding.
Not because God has become casual about holiness.
Because Christ has made a way for sinners to come home.
Maybe you need to stop making dramatic promises tonight.
Maybe God does not need another, “I swear I will never do this again.”
Maybe what you need is smaller, harder, and more honest.
“Jesus, I sinned.
I have no excuse.
Thank You that Your mercy is not built on my ability to impress You.
Show me what repentance requires now.
Show me what needs to be confessed.
Show me what needs to be deleted.
Show me whom I need to apologize to.
Show me what access needs to disappear.
Show me what boundary needs to be built.
Show me whom I need to ask for help.
And give me grace to obey You in the next decision.”
Because repentance has feet.
Sometimes repentance means closing the door you keep asking God to help you resist walking through.
Sometimes it means telling a trusted mature Christian what you have carefully kept hidden.
Sometimes it means accountability.
Sometimes it means returning money.
Sometimes it means ending the secret conversation.
Sometimes it means admitting that your “boundary problem” is actually a willingness problem.
Sometimes it means confessing to someone you hurt.
Sometimes it means getting rid of the object, application, contact, environment, or habit that keeps feeding what you claim you want starved.
Jesus spoke radically about dealing with sin because sin destroys.
So do not trivialize your repeated failure.
But do not worship your failure either.
Your sin is not more powerful than Christ.
Your shame is not your savior.
Your tears do not purchase forgiveness.
Your self-hatred cannot add one drop to the blood Jesus shed.
And repeatedly replaying your worst moment does not make you holier.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Get up.
Obey again.
And when you stumble, do not turn your stumbling into an excuse for surrender.
Return to Christ.
Again.
Not casually.
Not presumptuously.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because Jesus does.
Perhaps someone reading this has not prayed honestly in months.
You still attend church.
You still know when to say amen.
You still share Bible verses.
People may even come to you for spiritual advice.
But privately, you have begun believing that God tolerates everyone except you.
You think other people's testimonies prove grace works, while your repeated failures prove you are the exception.
You are not the exception to the Gospel.
Christ came for sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not sanitized sinners.
Sinners.
Paul described Christ's coming into the world as coming “to save sinners.”
The Gospel does not begin when you finally become impressive enough for Jesus.
It begins with Jesus doing what you could never do for yourself.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the grave.
And He calls people not merely to feel bad about themselves but to repent, believe, follow Him, and walk in newness of life.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need eloquence.
Perhaps it needs honesty.
“Jesus, here I am again.”
And perhaps you expect heaven to answer:
“Again?”
But 1 John points your trembling heart somewhere else.
“He is faithful and just…”
Your confidence rests in Him.
This does not mean every person who repeats religious words possesses genuine repentance.
Scripture repeatedly warns against empty profession and deliberate, hardened rebellion.
But neither should the believer who is grieved by sin be taught to measure Christ's mercy by the number of times they have needed it.
The answer to repeated sin is not less Jesus.
It is deeper surrender to Jesus.
More truth.
More light.
More obedience.
More dependence.
More ruthless honesty about what keeps leading you back into darkness.
You may need help.
Ask for it.
You may need accountability.
Seek it.
You may need to confess something embarrassing.
Bring it into the light with wise, trustworthy believers.
You may need to stop asking God to remove a temptation while continually preserving easy access to it.
Close the door.
You may need to forgive someone.
You may need to make restitution.
You may need to stop confusing temptation with defeat.
You may need to learn that sanctification is not always spectacular.
Sometimes holiness looks like one unseen “no.”
Then another.
Then another.
Until, by the grace of God, the chains that once felt inevitable no longer rule you the way they once did.
And when progress feels painfully slow, remember this:
Jesus is not merely interested in making you feel forgiven.
He is transforming His people.
Grace pardons.
Grace also trains.
Titus says that the grace of God teaches believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
The grace that receives the repentant sinner is the same grace that refuses to leave that sinner unchanged.
That is the beauty of the Gospel Warrior message:
Not from scandal to pretending.
Not from scandal to reputation management.
Not from scandal to endless self-loathing.
He rewrites Peter the denier into Peter the shepherd.
He rewrites persecutors into preachers.
He rewrites rebels into sons and daughters.
He takes what sin has disfigured and begins the long, holy work of restoration.
And no, that does not mean your consequences magically disappear.
Forgiveness does not always erase earthly consequences.
Grace does not make wisdom unnecessary.
Restoration may take time.
Trust may have to be rebuilt.
Some scars remain.
But scars are not proof that grace failed.
Sometimes scars become evidence that the wound did not get the final word.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write your private sin publicly.
But you can say something honest.
Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer finally believes that restoration is possible.
Then think of one person who needs this.
Not fifty.
One.
The person who stopped talking about God because they are ashamed.
The friend whose smile has become suspiciously practiced.
The believer who keeps disappearing.
The son or daughter who thinks they have gone too far.
The person who assumes that because Christians disappointed them, Jesus must have abandoned them too.
Better yet, send this to them personally.

We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him. But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement and discipleship reach people who need it.
Not because you expect to fail.
On that night, read 1 John 1 again.
Read it slowly.
Remember that confession does not surprise God.
Remember that forgiveness is not founded upon your emotional performance.
Remember that Jesus Christ is righteous.
Remember His blood.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that repentance means turning toward Him, not running away from Him.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Invite the person who thinks Christians are supposed to have everything together.
Let them discover what Christianity actually announces:
We do not have a Savior because we successfully saved ourselves.
We have a Savior because we desperately needed one.
Maybe you failed again.
Maybe you are ashamed.
Maybe your prayer tonight feels painfully familiar.
But do not let familiarity convince you that confession is meaningless.
Call sin what God calls it.
Bring it into the light.
Turn from it.
Take whatever practical steps repentance requires.
Trust the sufficiency of Christ.
Then get up and walk with Him again.
Because the most important sentence over your life does not have to be:
“I did it again.”
In Christ, another sentence can follow.
“I came home again.”
And one day, when Christ's work in His people is complete, the fight itself will finally be over.
Until then, do not confuse the voice telling you to hide with the voice of the Savior calling sinners into the light.
The rooster may remind you where you failed—but the risen Jesus is still standing on the other side of your worst night, calling you to follow Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL SERVED GOD WITH TEARS—AND THAT CHANGES WHAT FAITHFULNESS LOOKS LIKE
paragraphs: PAUL SERVED GOD WITH TEARS—AND THAT CHANGES WHAT FAITHFULNESS LOOKS LIKE

We were taught to recognize faith by strength. Paul showed the Ephesian elders something far more uncomfortable: sometimes the clearest evidence that you have not abandoned God is the tears on your face while you keep serving Him.
There are tears nobody at church ever sees.
You wipe them away before walking through the door.
You straighten your clothes. Fix your face. Open your Bible. Smile when someone asks how you are doing.
“I'm good.”
But you are not good.
Something inside you is exhausted.
You have prayed about the same thing so many times that you are beginning to feel embarrassed mentioning it to God again.
You have worshiped while wondering why heaven seems silent.
You have encouraged people while privately needing someone to encourage you.
You have served while hurting.
Given while empty.
Loved while disappointed.
Forgiven while still bleeding from what happened.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps you quietly started believing something terrifying:
Maybe if my faith were stronger, I wouldn't hurt this much.
Then Paul stands on a shoreline near Miletus and destroys that illusion.
He is saying goodbye to men he loves.

Luke tells us that Paul summoned the elders of the church in Ephesus. These were not strangers listening to a polished testimony. These men had watched his life. They knew what happened when the meetings ended. They knew what his ministry actually cost.
So Paul could not impress them with religious performance.
Instead, he reminded them of something they had already witnessed.
In the Greek text of Acts 20:19, Paul describes himself this way:
δουλεύων τῷ Κυρίῳ μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης καὶ δακρύων
douleuōn tō Kyriō meta pasēs tapeinophrosynēs kai dakryōn
Literally, the thought is:
“Serving the Lord with all humility and with tears.”
With tears.
Do not rush past those two words.
The apostle Paul—the missionary, preacher, church planter, theologian, prisoner, defender of the Gospel—did not tell these elders, “You remember how powerful I looked.”
He reminded them that they had seen him cry.
And the Greek makes something especially beautiful clear.
The word δουλεύων (douleuōn) comes from douleuō, carrying the idea of serving as a servant. Paul understood himself as belonging to the Lord.
But notice what stands beside his service.
δακρύων.
dakryōn.
Tears.
His tears were not evidence that he had stopped serving.
They accompanied his service.
That distinction may be exactly what somebody reading this needs tonight.
You can be hurting and faithful at the same time.
You can be grieving and obedient at the same time.
You can have questions and still follow Jesus.
You can cry during the prayer and still mean every word of it.
You can walk into tomorrow without understanding what God is doing and still whisper, “Jesus, I belong to You.”
Faithfulness is not emotional numbness.
Paul's tears prove it.

And these were not theatrical tears manufactured to make a sermon more moving. Acts places them inside the pressure of real ministry. Paul speaks about trials and opposition. He reminds the elders that he withheld nothing profitable from them, teaching publicly and from house to house. Then he summarizes the heartbeat of his message: repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
That matters.
Because biblical Christianity is not merely learning how to survive difficult emotions.
The center is Jesus.
The call is repentance.
The promise is grace.
Paul did not spend three years telling people simply to believe in themselves, discover their potential, protect their peace, or manifest a better future.
He pointed sinners toward God.
He pointed them toward Christ.

Repentance means we cannot merely blame everything outside ourselves. Somewhere beneath our wounds are sins we must confess, idols we must surrender, bitterness we must release, pride we must crucify, secret compromises we must drag into the light.
And faith means we do not save ourselves after discovering what is wrong with us.
We run to Jesus.
That is the Gospel.
Not “repair yourself until God accepts you.”
Christ came for sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the grave.
Forgiveness is not purchased by our tears.
Grace is not God's reward for people who suffer beautifully.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why Paul's tears are so powerful.
They belonged to a man who knew grace.
Before Paul became the man crying over churches, he was the man persecuting the church.
Think about that.
There had been another version of Paul.
A feared version.
A violent version.
A man whose religious zeal had become persecution.
Acts introduces Saul approving the killing of Stephen, and then describes him ravaging the church and dragging believers away.
If you had frozen Paul's story there, you might have thought you knew how it ended.
Enemy.
Persecutor.
Destroyer.
Scandal.
But Jesus had not finished writing.
On the road to Damascus, Saul encountered the risen Christ.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The man once associated with suffering inflicted upon Christians eventually became a man willing to suffer for Christ.
The hands connected with persecution would become hands that worked to support ministry.
The mouth that once opposed Jesus would proclaim Him.
The eyes once burning with hostility would fill with tears over Christ's people.
That is not self-improvement.
That is grace.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely polish reputations.
He resurrects lives.
And maybe you need that because there is a chapter of your own story you desperately wish could be torn out.
Something you did.
Something you became.
Someone you hurt.
Years you wasted.
A secret nobody knows.
A season when you walked away from God.
A marriage damaged by your choices.
A child you failed.
An addiction you kept feeding.
A compromise you kept defending.
A version of yourself that still appears in your memories at two in the morning and whispers:
“After everything you've done, who do you think you are to come back to God?”
Look again at Paul.
The Gospel does not pretend the scandal never happened.
The Gospel declares that the scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending sin does not matter.
Not by erasing repentance.
Jesus transforms sinners through grace.
The cross proves simultaneously how serious our sin is and how extraordinary God's mercy is.
Paul knew this personally.
So when this man speaks about grace, he is not discussing an abstract doctrine.
He is describing the reason he is standing there at all.
Then the farewell becomes even heavier.
Paul tells the elders that he is going toward Jerusalem without knowing exactly what will happen there. What he does know is sobering: imprisonment and afflictions await him.
Imagine knowing suffering is ahead...
and walking forward anyway.
Most of us want God to show us the safe road.
Paul was willing to obey on the dangerous one.
Acts 20:24 reveals why. His overriding concern was finishing the course and ministry he had received from the Lord Jesus: bearing witness to the Gospel of God's grace.
There it is again.
Grace.
The former persecutor is now willing to suffer so other people can hear about the grace that rescued him.
Maybe this is where Paul's story stops being comfortable.
Because many of us are willing to follow Jesus as long as following Jesus does not cost too much.
We want Christianity with manageable inconvenience.
We want a cross that matches the furniture.
We want resurrection without dying to ourselves.
We want Jesus as Savior while quietly negotiating whether He may truly be Lord.
But Paul says, in effect:
My life is not the treasure I am protecting.
Christ gave me a mission.
I intend to finish it.
And still...
he cried.
Do you see the strange beauty?
Courage and tears occupied the same body.
Conviction and tenderness lived in the same man.
Paul did not become courageous by becoming emotionally cold.
He became courageous because Christ mattered more than his comfort.
Later in the same farewell, Paul returns to the tears.
He tells the elders to remember that for three years he had warned them night and day “with tears.”
Three years.
Night and day.
With tears.
These were shepherd's tears.
Tears for people.
Tears because truth matters.
Tears because souls matter.
Tears because deception destroys.
