Tears because Paul understood that ministry is not content production. People are not numbers. Congregations are not audiences. The Gospel is not a brand.
These were human beings for whom Christ died.
That should confront every Christian who has learned how to discuss theology without loving people.
You can win an argument and lose tenderness.
You can know doctrine and become proud.
You can defend truth while secretly enjoying humiliating the person who is wrong.
Paul would not recognize that as spiritual maturity.
His doctrine had tears in it.
His warnings had tears in them.
His leadership had tears in it.
His courage had tears in it.
His ministry had tears in it.
And then something happens at the end of Acts 20 that is almost unbearably human.
Paul finishes speaking.
He kneels.
They pray.
And everybody begins crying.
These grown men embrace Paul and kiss him.
They know this is goodbye.
Luke tells us what hurt them most: Paul had said they would not see his face again.
Notice that Scripture does not sanitize the scene.
Nobody says, “Stop crying. Paul is going to heaven someday.”
Nobody rebukes them for grief.
Nobody tells them that strong Christians should smile because God has a plan.
They weep.
Because love makes goodbye hurt.
Christian hope does not require us to pretend loss is painless.
Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus's tomb.
The Son of God knew resurrection was coming, and still He wept.
That means tears and faith are not enemies.
Sometimes tears are what love looks like when words can no longer carry the weight.
So perhaps you have misunderstood your tears.
Maybe you thought crying meant God was disappointed with you.
Maybe somebody taught you that mature believers never collapse.
Maybe you have been hiding because everyone thinks you are the strong one.
Pastors cry.
Mothers cry.
Fathers cry.
Missionaries cry.
Leaders cry.
People who know Scripture cry.
People filled with faith cry.
People walking in obedience cry.
Paul served the Lord...
with tears.
But there is another side of this message that we cannot avoid.
Not every tear proves faithfulness.
We can cry over consequences without repenting of sin.
We can feel emotional during worship and refuse to surrender.
We can be moved by Jesus without actually following Jesus.
Paul's message was not merely tears.
It was repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus.
So this is where the question becomes personal.
What are your tears producing?
Are they pushing you toward Jesus...
or merely deeper into yourself?
Are you asking God only to remove the pain...
or are you willing to let Him expose what needs to change?
Are you asking Jesus to comfort you while refusing to surrender the thing He has already told you to release?
Because grace comforts us, yes.
But grace also transforms us.
Jesus did not die merely to make us feel better while we remain enslaved to the same sin.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile.
To make us new.
Maybe you have been pretending for too long.
Tonight, you do not need another performance.
You need Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Tell Him you are tired.
Tell Him where you sinned.
Tell Him what you are afraid of.
Tell Him what you have been hiding.
Tell Him about the anger.
The pornography.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The bitterness.
The affair.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The unbelief.
The resentment toward God.
The shame.
Bring it into the light.
Repentance is not running away from God because you have been exposed.
It is turning toward Him because Christ opened the way home.
You may come with tears.
Just come.
There is something else Paul tells those elders before he leaves.
He commends them to God and to “the word of His grace.”
Paul knows he cannot stay.
He cannot protect them forever.
He cannot answer every future question.
He cannot prevent every wolf from coming.
So eventually Paul must release the people he loves into hands stronger than his own.
God's hands.
Perhaps you need to do that too.
There is someone you cannot fix.
A child you cannot control.
A spouse you cannot change.
A loved one you cannot force to believe.
A situation you cannot hold together no matter how tightly your fingers are wrapped around it.
You have prayed.
You have warned.
You have cried.
You have tried.
There comes a moment when faith sounds like:
“Jesus, I cannot carry this person as if I were their savior. You are the Savior. I entrust them to You.”
That surrender may come with tears.
Let it.
Paul's did.
And perhaps this is the sentence you should remember tomorrow when the pain returns:
You do not have to stop crying before you can keep following Jesus.
Cry...
and pray.
Cry...
and obey.
Cry...
and forgive.
Cry...
and repent.
Cry...
and open the Bible again.
Cry...
and show up.
Cry...
and worship.
Cry...
and keep your eyes on Christ.
Because sometimes faith does not look like walking through the fire without tears.
Sometimes faith looks like walking through the fire while the tears are still falling, because you have decided Jesus is worthy even here.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Do not keep this message trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves, and grace cannot be bought.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and Jesus Christ, supporting and sharing that work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement reach someone else. If you want your support to glorify God, let it come from gratitude rather than guilt—from a desire to see Christ proclaimed rather than from any thought that you can purchase His approval.
Look at Jesus.
Paul's tears matter because Paul's Lord matters.
The Savior Paul proclaimed is the Savior who received sinners.
The Savior who touched lepers.
The Savior who welcomed the broken.
The Savior who called people to repentance.
The Savior who wept.
The Savior who carried the cross.
The Savior whose blood was shed for sinners.
The Savior who was buried.
The Savior who rose.
The Savior who confronted a persecutor named Saul and turned his entire story around.
And He is still saving sinners.
Still restoring wanderers.
Still breaking chains.
Still forgiving the repentant.
Still rebuilding what sin shattered.
Still receiving people who finally stop pretending.
So if your face is wet with tears while you read these final words, perhaps you do not need to wipe them away yet.
Talk to Jesus.
The tears are not too much for Him.
The past is not too scandalous for His grace.
The wound is not hidden from His eyes.
The sin is not something you need to disguise.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Come exhausted if necessary.
But come to Christ.
And tomorrow, when you wake up and discover that everything has not magically become easy, remember an apostle standing before beloved elders saying that he served the Lord with humility...
and tears.
Then remember something even greater.
Paul's story did not begin with Paul's faithfulness.
It began with Christ's mercy.
And yours does too.
And before you leave, comment one sentence—not for an algorithm, but as an honest confession before a community that also knows what it means to struggle:
“Jesus, I will serve You even through my tears.”
Because one day you may discover that the tears you thought proved you were falling apart were falling from the face of someone Christ was teaching to depend completely on Him.
Your tears do not get the final sentence. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Nobody Saw What You Almost Did Last Night. God Saw the Battle You Chose Not to Lose.
paragraphs: Nobody Saw What You Almost Did Last Night. God Saw the Battle You Chose Not to Lose.

There are victories nobody applauds because nobody knows there was a war—and some of the holiest moments of your life may be the sins you almost committed, the doors you almost opened, and the temptations you finally carried to Jesus instead.
Nobody knows.
That may be the hardest part.
Nobody knows how close you came last night.
They saw you this morning.

They saw the normal profile picture. The ordinary smile. The “Good morning.” The coffee. The work. The family routine. Maybe they saw you at church last Sunday with your Bible open and your hands raised.
But they did not see the moment when the room became quiet and the battle became loud.
They did not see your finger hovering over the screen.
They did not see the message you almost sent.
The website you almost opened.
The number you almost called.
The conversation you almost returned to.
The drink you almost reached for.
The lie you almost told.
The bitterness you almost fed.
The fantasy you almost entertained.
The old relationship you almost resurrected.
The secret habit that whispered your name again.
Nobody saw how badly part of you wanted to surrender.
Nobody saw you sitting there negotiating with temptation.
Nobody heard the arguments running through your mind.
“Just once.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You've already messed up before.”
“You can repent afterward.”
“You deserve this.”
“You're lonely.”
“You're tired.”
“You're stressed.”
“God will forgive you anyway.”
And maybe nobody saw the moment when your hand stopped.
When something inside you remembered Jesus.
When you closed the screen.
Put down the phone.
Walked out of the room.
Deleted the message.
Turned the car around.
Started praying.
Started crying.
Called somebody.
Opened your Bible.
Or simply whispered through clenched teeth:
“Jesus... help me.”
Nobody applauded.
There was no worship band playing behind you.
No pastor saw it.
No friend congratulated you.
Nobody posted about your spiritual maturity.
Nobody knew that what looked like an ordinary Tuesday night was a battlefield.
But heaven was not blind.
God saw you.
And before we turn that sentence into sentimental encouragement, we need to understand something deeper.
God did not merely see your victory.
He was faithful in your battle.
Paul wrote something extraordinary to believers surrounded by temptation:
“πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος· πιστὸς δὲ ὁ θεός...”
Peirasmos hymas ouk eilēphen ei mē anthrōpinos; pistos de ho Theos...
“No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to mankind. And God is faithful...” — 1 Corinthians 10:13.
Read those final words again.
πιστὸς δὲ ὁ θεός — pistos de ho Theos.
God is faithful.
That is the center of the verse.
Not your willpower.
Not your personality.
Not your impressive self-control.
God.
Is.
Faithful.

The Greek word πειρασμός — peirasmos can carry the sense of temptation, trial, or testing depending upon context. And εἴληφεν — eilēphen carries the idea of something having taken hold of or seized you.
Paul is speaking to people who knew what it meant to be confronted by pressure.
But notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Christians will never feel powerful temptation.
It does not say mature believers stop experiencing ugly desires.
It does not say temptation itself proves you have been abandoned by God.
And it certainly does not say, “If you really love Jesus, temptation will never feel attractive again.”
Sometimes temptation feels attractive precisely because it is temptation.
That is why the battle hurts.
If sin always arrived looking like death, fewer people would embrace it.
But sin knows how to dress a grave like a bedroom.
It knows how to disguise chains as comfort.
It knows how to make poison taste like relief.
It whispers about the next five minutes while hiding the next five years.
And some of you understand that more deeply than anyone around you realizes.
You love Jesus.
And you are still fighting.
You believe the Bible.
And you are still fighting.
You pray.
And you are still fighting.
You worship.
And sometimes, late at night, you are still fighting things you wish had disappeared years ago.
Listen carefully:
The existence of temptation is not the same thing as surrender to temptation.
Jesus Himself “has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
Temptation and sin must therefore not be confused.
The enemy would love to convince you that because an ungodly thought entered the battlefield, you might as well hand it the kingdom.
No.
Take it to Christ.
Run to Christ.
Expose it before Christ.
Because secrecy is where temptation often grows teeth.
And here is where 1 Corinthians 10:13 becomes breathtaking.
Paul continues:
“ἀλλὰ ποιήσει σὺν τῷ πειρασμῷ καὶ τὴν ἔκβασιν...”
alla poiēsei syn tō peirasmō kai tēn ekbasin...
“But with the temptation He will also provide the way of escape...”
That word translated “way of escape” is ἔκβασις — ekbasis.
An exit.
A way out.
But keep reading, because the end of Paul's sentence protects us from misunderstanding the promise:
“τοῦ δύνασθαι ὑπενεγκεῖν.”
So that you may be able to endure it.
God's promise is not that temptation will never hurt.
His promise is not that obedience will always feel effortless.
Sometimes the “escape” is a door you must actually walk through.
Sometimes it looks embarrassingly ordinary.
Block the number.
Leave the room.
Turn off the device.
Confess to a mature believer.
Stop going to the place where you repeatedly fall.
Do not answer the message.
Do not keep staring.
Do not continue the conversation.
Pray while your flesh is screaming.
Run.
In fact, Paul's very next words after 1 Corinthians 10:13 are:
“Therefore, my dear friends, flee from idolatry.”
Flee.
There are moments when spiritual maturity does not look like standing inches away from sin proving how strong you are.
It looks like running because you finally understand how weak you can be.
Joseph did not negotiate with Potiphar's wife.
He ran.
And sometimes victory leaves your coat behind.
Sometimes obedience looks undignified.
Sometimes holiness looks like getting out of there before you change your mind.
Maybe that was you last night.
Maybe you ran.
Maybe barely.
Maybe you were shaking.
Maybe part of you hated walking away.
Maybe nobody knows how close it was.
And today you almost feel ridiculous calling it a victory because all you did was close an app.
All you did was delete a message.
All you did was say no.
All you did was walk away.
“All you did?”
You chose obedience when disobedience was available.
Do not worship yourself for that.
Thank God.
Because Scripture does not point us toward self-congratulation.
“God is faithful.”
The strength to endure does not make us our own saviors.
It gives us another reason to worship the Savior.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop pretending.
Because maybe you did not walk away last night.
Maybe you fell.
Maybe you clicked.
Maybe you went.
Maybe you drank.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you returned.
Maybe you slept with someone.
Maybe you watched it.
Maybe you exploded in anger.
Maybe you betrayed something you promised God you would never betray again.
And now you are reading an article about victory while sitting in the wreckage of defeat.
Then this is where the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people successfully rescued themselves from sin.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners needed a Savior—and Jesus Christ came.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride cannot survive there because your sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
Despair cannot have the final word there because Christ willingly died for sinners and rose again.
Your scandal does not surprise Jesus.
But His grace must never become your permission to keep loving the thing that crucified Him.
Grace does not say, “Sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says sin mattered so much that the Son of God bore judgment for sinners—and His mercy is so astonishing that guilty people can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and transformed.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
So if you fell, stop hiding.
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Where another person has been harmed, pursue biblical repentance and appropriate accountability.
Where secrecy has protected an enslaving pattern, seek mature Christian help.
Cut off what keeps dragging you backward.
And look again toward Christ.
Not because repentance purchases forgiveness.
Not because tears earn salvation.
Not because promising harder will erase yesterday.
Come because Jesus saves sinners.
Come because the blood of Christ is sufficient.
Come because resurrection means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not scandal ignored.
Not scandal celebrated.
Not scandal renamed so nobody feels uncomfortable.
Scandal confronted by truth.
Scandal carried into the light.
Scandal met by repentance.
Scandal brought beneath the cross.
And sinners transformed by grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But there is another person reading this.
You did resist last night.
And today nobody knows.
You probably will never receive recognition for it.
Good.
Let that hidden victory become worship instead of performance.
Jesus spoke of a Father “who sees what is done in secret” (Matthew 6:4).
That truth reaches farther than secret sin.
Your Father is not absent from the hidden places.
There are acts of faithfulness that will never become testimonies on a stage.
There are prayers nobody will hear.
Tears nobody will photograph.
Temptations nobody will know you resisted.
Sacrifices nobody will understand.
And moments when you will choose Christ with absolutely no audience except God.
Those moments matter.
Not because they earn His love.
If you belong to Christ, obedience is not an audition for adoption.
It is the fruit of grace.
Jesus said, “If you love me, keep my commands” (John 14:15).
Not, “Obey so I might eventually love you.”
Love comes first.
Grace comes first.
Christ comes first.
Then the redeemed heart begins learning to say no to what once owned it.
Sometimes loudly.
Sometimes beautifully.
Sometimes with trembling hands at 1:47 in the morning.
Maybe you need to hear this:
You are not strange because the battle was intense.
Paul called temptation anthrōpinos—human, common to mankind.
Your particular circumstances may be deeply personal, but temptation itself is not evidence that you are uniquely beyond hope.
Other believers are fighting too.
The man sitting three rows ahead of you at church may be fighting.
The woman who seems completely composed may be fighting.
The teenager who never says much may be fighting.
The pastor needs vigilance too.
The longtime believer needs vigilance too.
That is why the verse immediately before 1 Corinthians 10:13 warns:
“If you think you are standing firm, be careful that you don't fall!”
Christian maturity does not say, “I could never.”
Christian maturity says, “Apart from Christ, I must never become arrogant about what I am capable of.”
So guard the door.
Watch your heart.
Know your patterns.
Do not romanticize your weakness.
Do not pet the temptation you are asking God to kill.
Do not repeatedly walk to the edge of the cliff and call your survival spiritual maturity.
Use the escape God provides.
And when you escape, worship the One who was faithful.
There may come another night.
Another notification.
Another memory.
Another lonely hour.
Another argument.
Another opportunity nobody would discover.
And when that moment comes, remember this:
You are not deciding merely what you will do for ten minutes.
You are deciding what you will feed.
Every surrendered temptation becomes another opportunity to say:
“Jesus, You are worth more than this.”
More than the screen.
More than the affair.
More than revenge.
More than applause.
More than the secret addiction.
More than the fantasy.
More than being right.
More than whatever temporary relief sin is promising.
Jesus is better.
Not merely because sin has consequences.
Jesus is better because Jesus is Jesus.
Holy.
Crucified.
Risen.
Merciful.
Faithful.
King.
The One who knew every scandalous thing about humanity and still stretched His arms across a cross.
The One who was buried.
The One who rose.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness.
The One who does not merely improve behavior but gives new life.
And maybe tonight, when temptation returns, nobody will see you choose Him again.
Choose Him anyway.
Maybe your hands will shake.
Choose Him anyway.
Maybe tears will fall.
Choose Him anyway.
Maybe you have to call someone and admit, “I am dangerously close to falling.”
Call them.
Maybe you need to put your phone outside the bedroom.
Put it there.
Maybe you need to end a relationship that continually pulls you away from Christ.
Obey.
Maybe you need pastoral help, Christian counseling, accountability, or practical safeguards because this has become a repeating pattern.
Get help.
There is no trophy for fighting alone.
The body of Christ exists for a reason.
And if this article found you during a private battle, do something brave right now.
Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of your sin. Wisdom matters. Privacy matters. But stop believing the lie that you are the only Christian fighting a war nobody sees.
And if Christ has already delivered you from something that once controlled you, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony might become another believer's reminder that chains really can break.
Then think of one person who has been unusually quiet lately.
One friend.
One son.
One daughter.
One husband.
One wife.
One believer who seems tired.
One person who keeps smiling but whose eyes tell another story.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “Share” makes someone spiritually superior. It does not.
But if these words can place Scripture in front of one person sitting alone with temptation tonight, sharing becomes an opportunity to serve.
You may never know.
Share it anyway.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions feel distant.
Come back when the room becomes quiet again.
Come back when the old voice returns.
Come back and read those words:
πιστὸς δὲ ὁ θεός.
God is faithful.
And stay connected with Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker who does not yet understand grace.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely religious people pretending they never struggle.
Let them see what the Gospel actually announces:
We needed rescue.
Jesus came.
Jesus died for sinners.
Jesus rose.
Jesus saves.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Do it as an act of willing support for Gospel ministry—not as a purchase of God's favor, because grace cannot be bought.
Share.
And if God has used it to confront something hidden, do not merely react to an article.
Respond to Jesus.
Because eventually the phone goes dark.
The comments stop.
The article ends.
And you are alone again with the choice.
Nobody may ever know how close you came.
Nobody may ever applaud the sin you refused.
Nobody may ever understand how much that little “no” cost you.
But when the temptation comes again, remember the words that were true before the battle began and will remain true after it ends:
πιστὸς δὲ ὁ θεός.
God is faithful.

And perhaps the victory nobody ever celebrates on earth will be the night you quietly discovered that what sin promised for a moment could never compare with the Christ who gave Himself to have you forever.
Some of the loudest victories in your life will make no sound at all—just a trembling sinner closing one door and running home to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAUL’S DAUGHTER MERAB HAD FIVE SONS — AND ONE WORD IN 2 SAMUEL 21 OPENS ONE OF THE BIBLE’S MOST DIFFICULT TEXTUAL QUESTIONS
paragraphs: SAUL’S DAUGHTER MERAB HAD FIVE SONS — AND ONE WORD IN 2 SAMUEL 21 OPENS ONE OF THE BIBLE’S MOST DIFFICULT TEXTUAL QUESTIONS
The Hebrew text appears to say Michal had five sons.
But another passage says Michal had no children.
And the man those five sons belonged to was married—not to Michal—but to her sister Merab.
So what happened?
Did somebody make a mistake?
Has the Bible contradicted itself?

Or are we standing at one of those rare places where God has allowed us to see something most Christians never think about—the long, human, painstaking history through which the biblical manuscripts were copied and preserved?
Stay with this one.

Because before we reach the end, five sons will die, a grieving woman will stand beneath an open sky guarding the dead, an ancient covenant will come back demanding an accounting, and a single Hebrew name will force us to ask what we really mean when we say we trust the Bible.
And somehow, beyond all of that darkness, we will find ourselves looking toward Jesus.
It begins with a famine.
Not for a few weeks.
Not for one bad agricultural season.
Three years.

The opening words of 2 Samuel 21 are heavy with desperation. Israel's ground will not give what the people need. Eventually David seeks the LORD, and the answer reaches backward into Israel's history.
There is bloodguilt connected with Saul and his house because Saul had attacked the Gibeonites.
That detail matters.

The Gibeonites were protected by an oath Israel had made generations earlier in Joshua 9. The circumstances surrounding that covenant were messy—the Gibeonites had deceived Israel—but Israel had nevertheless sworn an oath before the LORD to preserve them.
Saul's later zeal for Israel and Judah did not give him permission to treat that oath as disposable.
Religious enthusiasm does not transform disobedience into obedience.
That alone should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to become so convinced that we are defending God's interests that we begin violating God's character.
It is possible to say, “I am doing this for God,” while God is saying, “I never authorized this.”
Saul's actions were in the past.
But the consequences were not.

The Gibeonites demanded satisfaction involving seven male descendants from Saul's house. David spared Jonathan's son Mephibosheth because of his covenant with Jonathan, but seven others were handed over.
Two were sons of Rizpah.
Then comes the sentence that has caused readers, translators, scribes, and scholars to stop and look again.
The traditional Masoretic Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 21:8 contains these words:
חֲמֵשֶׁת בְּנֵי מִיכַל בַּת־שָׁאוּל
ḥămēšet bənê Mîḵal bat-Šāʾûl
“The five sons of Michal, the daughter of Saul…”
There is the problem.
מִיכַל
Mîḵal.
Michal.
Not Merab.
And if you have read the earlier chapters of Samuel carefully, your mind immediately says:
Wait.
Michal?
Because 2 Samuel 6:23 had already told us that Michal, Saul's daughter, had no child to the day of her death.
And there is another difficulty.
The five sons in 2 Samuel 21:8 are connected with a man named Adriel.
But go backward to 1 Samuel 18:19.
The Hebrew says:
מֵרַב בַּת־שָׁאוּל
Mērāḇ bat-Šāʾûl.
“Merab, Saul's daughter.”
And the verse says she was given:
לְעַדְרִיאֵל הַמְּחֹלָתִי לְאִשָּׁה
ləʿAḏrîʾēl hamməḥōlāṯî ləʾiššāh
“to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife.”
There it is.
Adriel's wife was Merab.
Not Michal.
Now the tension becomes impossible to miss.
First Samuel identifies Merab as Adriel's wife.
Second Samuel 6 says Michal remained childless.
Yet the traditional Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 21:8 appears to call these five boys “the sons of Michal” in connection with Adriel.
And this is where we must resist two temptations.
The skeptic may want to shout, “Contradiction!”
The frightened Christian may want to pretend there is nothing here worth discussing.
Neither response does justice to the evidence.
Because something fascinating happened in the transmission history of this verse.

Most Hebrew manuscripts behind the Masoretic textual tradition read “Michal” here. Yet two Hebrew manuscripts, together with witnesses in the ancient Greek Septuagint tradition, support the reading “Merab.” This is why several modern English translations print “Merab” in the verse and place a textual note at the bottom explaining that the traditional Masoretic reading is “Michal.”
That footnote is not your Bible secretly confessing defeat.
It is evidence that translators are showing you their work.
They are telling you where the surviving manuscript evidence contains a variation instead of quietly pretending the variation does not exist.
And there is strong contextual reason for the reading “Merab.”
First Samuel 18:19 explicitly identifies Merab as the woman given to Adriel as his wife.
Second Samuel 6:23 explicitly reports Michal's childlessness.
Then 2 Samuel 21:8 identifies Adriel as the father connected with these five sons.
Put those pieces together, and it is easy to understand why many textual critics and modern translations regard “Merab” as the reading that best fits the historical context.
Could “Michal” nevertheless be explained?

Some interpreters historically proposed that Merab bore the children while Michal later raised them, so they could in some sense be associated with Michal. This attempts to preserve the traditional reading without making Michal their biological mother.
But Scripture never explicitly tells us that Michal adopted or raised Merab's five sons.
That distinction matters.
We should never turn a possible explanation into a revealed fact simply because it solves a difficult verse.
There is a difference between saying, “This could have happened,” and saying, “The Bible says this happened.”
It doesn't.

Another possibility—and the one reflected in many modern translations—is much simpler: at some point in the history of textual transmission, “Merab” and “Michal” became confused in this verse, while other manuscript witnesses preserved the reading “Merab.”
Christians do not need to panic at that sentence.
Ancient Scripture was copied by human hands.
Before printing presses, before photocopiers, before digital files, before cloud backups, scribes copied texts letter by letter, word by word, generation after generation.
The astonishing reality is not that manuscript variations exist.
The astonishing reality is how much evidence survives that allows scholars to identify, compare, and evaluate them.
And notice something extraordinary here.
We know there is a textual question precisely because the evidence was preserved.
Nobody successfully erased the difficulty.
Nobody standardized every surviving witness so future generations would never discover it.
The variant survived.
The evidence survived.
The earlier identification of Merab survived.
The statement concerning Michal's childlessness survived.
And now you can open an ordinary modern Bible and often find a footnote telling you about it.
That is not what concealment looks like.
That is transparency.
But if we stop with the textual problem, we will miss the human horror inside the passage.
Because these are not merely five names in a textual apparatus.
They were sons.
Five of them.
Merab's story had already contained heartbreak.
Saul had initially promised his elder daughter Merab to David, but when the appointed time came, she was instead given to Adriel the Meholathite.
Years pass.
Kings rise.
Wars are fought.
Saul dies.
David reigns.
And then the consequences of Saul's violence against the Gibeonites reach into another generation.
Seven descendants of Saul's house die.
The text is severe.
It should disturb us.
The Bible does not sanitize the brutal realities of the ancient world.
And then a woman named Rizpah does something almost impossible to forget.
Two of the dead were her sons.
The bodies remained exposed.
So Rizpah took sackcloth and spread it upon a rock.
And she stayed.
Through daylight.
Through darkness.
Through heat.
Through exhaustion.
She drove away the birds during the day.
She kept the wild animals away at night.
Imagine that mother.
Everyone else goes home.
She stays.
Night falls.
She stays.
The sun comes up again.
She stays.
Birds circle overhead.
She stays.
Animals move in the darkness.
She stays.
She cannot bring her sons back.
She cannot reverse the judgment.
She cannot rewrite yesterday.
But she can refuse to abandon their bodies.
There are griefs for which language becomes too small.
Some of you know that.
You know what it means to keep functioning after something inside you collapsed.
You answered messages.
You went to work.
You smiled when somebody greeted you.
You said, “I'm okay.”
But somewhere inside your soul, you were sitting on Rizpah's rock.
Guarding what remained of something you loved.
Maybe it was a marriage.
Maybe a child.
Maybe a parent.
Maybe your innocence.
Maybe your reputation.
Maybe a ministry.
Maybe years you cannot recover.
Maybe your relationship with God has felt like that.
You still know the songs.
You still know the verses.
You still know how Christians are supposed to answer when someone asks how you're doing.
But deep inside, you have been fighting the birds away from something that died.
And perhaps nobody noticed.
David eventually noticed Rizpah.
When he heard what she had done, something changed.
He retrieved the remains of Saul and Jonathan. The bones of those who had been executed were gathered. Saul's family finally received burial in the family tomb.
Then comes the quiet sentence:
After that, God responded to the plea for the land.
The rain came.
But there is something even deeper here.
Second Samuel 21 is about bloodguilt, covenant, judgment, grief, death, burial, and restoration.
Those themes do not end with Saul's family.
They push the Christian reader forward.
Toward another Son.
Another King.
Another death.
Another moment when bloodguilt demanded an answer.
But here we must be careful.
Jesus is not merely another victim in the story of 2 Samuel 21, and the execution of Saul's descendants is not a simple one-to-one picture of the cross.
The Gospel is greater.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ willingly gives Himself.
“No one takes it from me,” Jesus says concerning His life, “but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).
He is not dying for His own sin.
He has none.
He bears the sins of others.
Peter writes:
Paul says that God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).
And suddenly the deepest scandal in Scripture becomes the doorway into grace.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because it mattered so much that redemption cost blood.
Not because justice disappeared.
Because at the cross, justice and mercy meet in Christ.
You and I have something far worse than a difficult manuscript reading.
We have a sin problem.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Envied.
Hated.
Manipulated.
Hidden.
Pretended.
Used religious language while protecting private rebellion.
We have wanted God's blessings while resisting God's authority.
And some of us have become extraordinarily skilled at appearing spiritually alive while secretly starving.
You can fool a congregation.
You can fool your Facebook friends.
You can fool your family.
You can sometimes fool yourself.
But you cannot fool Jesus.
And here is the Gospel:
You do not have to.
You can come into the light.
The Jesus who already knows the worst thing about you is the same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness to everyone who comes to Him in faith.
The cross says your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
The empty tomb says God's grace is greater than your sin can defeat.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of respectable people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of dead sinners receiving life.
Guilty people receiving pardon.
Prodigals coming home.
Ashes becoming testimony.
Scandal becoming grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have spent years believing your worst chapter became your final identity.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Abandoned.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Unclean.
Unworthy.
Too far gone.
But Jesus has never needed a clean past to create a redeemed future.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a shattered relational history.
The thief beside Jesus had almost no earthly future remaining.
Grace found them anyway.
Grace does not mean your past did not happen.
Grace means your past no longer gets the authority to tell you who Christ can make you.
And maybe that is why this strange textual question in 2 Samuel 21 matters more than we first imagined.
At first we came looking for the answer to one question:
Merab or Michal?
But Scripture turned the question toward us.
What has been written across your life that you believe can never change?
What shame have you mistaken for your identity?
What hidden sin are you still defending?
What dead thing are you still guarding alone?
What covenant with sin are you protecting while asking God for rain?
Maybe the most important word you need today is not Merab.
Not Michal.
Not even David.
It is Jesus.
Ἰησοῦς.
Iēsous.
Jesus.
The One whose name announces salvation.
The One who does not merely edit your public image.
He transforms hearts.
He forgives sin.
He receives the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He gives new life.
Be honest before God.
If you need mercy, you can simply comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you cannot even explain what is happening inside you right now, comment, “pray for me.”
Someone reading silently may need to discover that Christians are not people without scars. We are people whose scars no longer have the final word.
Then send this to somebody.
Not because an algorithm needs another share.
Because a person may need the truth.
Send it privately to the person who has been quietly carrying shame.
Because there will be a day when the accusation returns.
A day when your past starts speaking loudly again.

A day when you need to remember that Christianity does not require us to pretend difficult questions do not exist—and the Gospel does not require us to pretend our difficult past does not exist either.
Truth can withstand examination.
And grace can withstand your confession.
It doesn't.
Not because giving can purchase forgiveness.
It cannot.
It isn't.
Jesus purchased redemption. We cannot.
Christian giving must never be manipulated through fear, guilt, or promises that money can buy spiritual blessing.

But Scripture does teach believers to support Gospel ministry generously and willingly. Paul describes Christian giving as something decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7), and he teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for Gospel work (1 Corinthians 9:14).

Some believers may include ministry support within what they personally call their tithes and offerings; others understand New Covenant giving differently. We will not bind your conscience where Scripture does not.
Give first to God with a willing heart.
Support your local church faithfully.
Care for people in need.

Your support helps us keep producing Christ-centered biblical content, reaching struggling believers, answering difficult questions, encouraging seekers, and putting resources into the hands of people hungry for God's Word.
And there is far more waiting for those who want to go deeper.
Pray about becoming one of the people who helps carry it.
And whether you are able to support financially or not, you can still help.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the skeptic with difficult questions.
Invite the person who would never walk into a church building but might stop long enough to read about Jesus on a screen.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is sitting on their own version of Rizpah's rock.
Guarding what remains.
Fighting through another night.
Wondering whether God still sees them.
Maybe your share reaches them.
Maybe your comment gives them courage to confess.
Maybe your testimony reminds them that grace still exists.
Maybe Scripture leads them to Christ.
And if that happens, every click becomes insignificant compared with one soul turning toward Jesus.
We began with five sons and one disputed name.
We end with a Savior whose name is not disputed by heaven.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
King.
And still calling sinners home.
Your darkest chapter may be true—but in the hands of Jesus, it does not have to be the last chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE “SONS OF GOD” SAW THAT HUMAN WOMEN WERE BEAUTIFUL AND TOOK WIVES—WHO WERE THESE MYSTERIOUS MEN?
paragraphs: THE “SONS OF GOD” SAW THAT HUMAN WOMEN WERE BEAUTIFUL AND TOOK WIVES—WHO WERE THESE MYSTERIOUS MEN?

Genesis 6 contains four of the strangest verses in the Bible. But what if our obsession with the mysterious “sons of God” has caused us to miss the terrifying warning—and the breathtaking grace—standing right beside them?
There are passages in Scripture that comfort you.
There are passages that correct you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading, move your eyes back to the beginning of the sentence, and whisper…
“Wait. What did I just read?”
Genesis 6:1–4 is one of those passages.
Humanity is multiplying. Daughters are being born. Civilization is expanding.
Then, without warning, the biblical narrative gives us one of the most mysterious statements in the Old Testament:
וַיִּרְאוּ בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת־בְּנוֹת הָאָדָם כִּי טֹבֹת הֵנָּה
Vayyir'u bene-ha'elohim et-benot ha'adam ki tovot hennah.
In straightforward English:

“The sons of God saw the daughters of man, that they were good/beautiful…”
—Genesis 6:2
And then:
וַיִּקְחוּ לָהֶם נָשִׁים מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בָּחָרוּ
Vayyiqchu lahem nashim mikkol asher bacharu.
“…and they took for themselves women/wives from whomever they chose.”
Who were these “sons of God”?
Angels?
Fallen heavenly beings?
Powerful human rulers?
Descendants of Seth?
And what in the world were the Nephilim?
Giants?
Warriors?
Hybrid offspring?
Ancient tyrants whose reputations became legendary?
Those questions have fascinated readers for centuries.
But before chasing giants, angels, bloodlines, ancient legends, or sensational theories, we need to do something much less exciting—and much more important.
We need to listen to what the Bible actually says.
The Hebrew expression translated “sons of God” is:
בְנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים — bene ha'elohim.
Bene means “sons of,” while ha'elohim contains the familiar word Elohim.
The expression itself is real.
The mystery surrounding its precise identification is also real.
And Christians should be careful not to transform biblical mystery into dogmatic certainty where Scripture itself has not given us that certainty.
One ancient interpretation understands these “sons of God” as heavenly beings.
That interpretation did not originate with modern conspiracy videos.
Similar “sons of God” language elsewhere in the Old Testament can describe members of the heavenly assembly. Job 1:6, for example, describes the bene ha'elohim presenting themselves before the LORD.
That makes the heavenly-being interpretation a serious reading rather than something we should simply laugh away.
Ancient Jewish interpretation also developed the idea of rebellious heavenly beings associated with the events surrounding Genesis 6. Later Jewish writings expanded that tradition dramatically.
Some Christians also connect Genesis 6 with passages such as Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4, which speak of angels who sinned and were judged.
Yet caution is necessary.
Genesis 6 itself never stops and says:
“By sons of God, Moses means fallen angels.”
That explanatory sentence simply isn't there.

And Jesus taught that angels in heaven “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). Christians differ over how directly that statement should be applied to Genesis 6, particularly because Jesus specifically speaks about angels in heaven.
So the heavenly-being interpretation has ancient roots and textual arguments behind it—but questions remain.
There is another historic interpretation.
Some readers understand the “sons of God” as powerful rulers, nobles, judges, or warrior-kings who abused their position.
That possibility becomes especially interesting when you slow down over the verbs.
They saw.
They desired.
They took.
From whomever they chose.
There is something chilling about that sequence.
Beauty was observed.
Desire awakened.
Power reached out.
And women were taken.
Whatever else Genesis 6:2 means, this is hardly presented as a beautiful biblical romance.
It sounds disturbingly like a world in which those possessing power believed desire gave them permission.
And suddenly this strange ancient passage doesn't feel quite so ancient anymore.
How much human evil has begun with the same lie?
“I want it, therefore I deserve it.”
“I can take it, therefore I am allowed to have it.”
“I have power, therefore nobody can tell me no.”
That spirit has destroyed marriages.
It has corrupted ministries.
It has exploited women.
It has destroyed men.
It has poisoned businesses.
It has turned authority into domination.
It has transformed blessing into entitlement.
And it has whispered to countless human hearts:
If you want it badly enough, take it.
Genesis knows that voice.
It has heard it before.
Eve saw that the tree was good.
She took its fruit.
Genesis 6 tells us that the sons of God saw the daughters of humanity were desirable.
And they took.
See.
Desire.
Take.
The vocabulary should make us uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the greatest monster hiding in Genesis 6 isn't a giant.
Perhaps it is uncontrolled desire.

There is also a third major interpretation Christians have held: that the “sons of God” represent the godly line associated with Seth while the “daughters of man” represent women from an ungodly human line, often associated with Cain.

On this reading, Genesis describes the collapse of spiritual separation as people belonging to a covenant-conscious lineage abandon faithfulness and choose relationships according to outward attraction rather than devotion to God.
This interpretation became especially influential within portions of Christian tradition.
Yet it also faces questions because Genesis 6 does not explicitly call the men “sons of Seth” or explicitly identify the women as “daughters of Cain.”
Again…
Humility.
Sometimes faithfulness to Scripture means refusing to say more than Scripture says.
The Bible does not become less authoritative because we admit that one difficult passage is difficult.
Quite the opposite.
We honor Scripture when we allow Scripture to speak in its own words instead of forcing it to say whatever makes our theory work.
Then Genesis introduces another famous word:
הַנְּפִלִים — ha-Nephilim.
“The Nephilim.”
Genesis 6:4 says:
הַנְּפִלִים הָיוּ בָאָרֶץ בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם
Ha-nephilim hayu va'aretz bayyamim hahem.
“The Nephilim were on the earth in those days…”
The exact derivation and meaning of Nephilim have been debated for centuries.
It is commonly connected with the Hebrew root n-f-l, associated with “falling,” although proposed explanations of the name differ.
And notice something people often overlook.
Genesis does not give us a detailed anatomy lesson.
It doesn't tell us their exact height.
It doesn't give us their skeletal measurements.
It doesn't provide a chart explaining supernatural genetics.
Instead it continues:
הֵמָּה הַגִּבֹּרִים אֲשֶׁר מֵעוֹלָם אַנְשֵׁי הַשֵּׁם
Hemmah haggibborim asher me'olam anshei hashem.
They were the gibborim—the mighty ones, warriors, powerful men of ancient times—“men of the name,” commonly rendered “men of renown.”
And there is an irony here that is almost painful.
They had a name.
They had reputation.
They had power.
They had renown.
People knew who they were.
Perhaps people feared them.
Perhaps people celebrated them.
Perhaps mothers told stories about them.
Perhaps generations remembered their exploits.
They were the celebrities of a dying world.
And none of their fame could save them.
Read that again.
They were famous in a world God was about to judge.
That sentence should haunt us.
Because we live in a civilization obsessed with becoming anshei hashem—people of the name.
We want followers.
Recognition.
Influence.
Status.
Verification.
Applause.
People knowing who we are.
Even Christians can secretly become intoxicated by being known.
We can build platforms while neglecting prayer.
We can defend reputations while hiding sin.
We can learn how to appear spiritual without becoming holy.
We can make our names recognizable while the name of Jesus becomes increasingly decorative in our lives.
And Genesis whispers from the ruins of the ancient world:
Being known by everybody means nothing if you are not walking with God.
Because immediately after this strange account comes the sentence that explains the spiritual condition of the world.
Genesis 6:5:
וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי רַבָּה רָעַת הָאָדָם בָּאָרֶץ
Vayyar YHWH ki rabbah ra'at ha'adam ba'aretz.
“The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth…”
Notice the repeated idea.
They saw.
And God saw.
Humanity saw what it desired.
God saw what humanity had become.
They looked outward and saw beauty to possess.
God looked inward and saw hearts corrupted by evil.
That is where Genesis 6 becomes frighteningly personal.
Because you and I can control what people see.
God sees what people never see.
He sees the browser history nobody knows about.
He sees the private resentment beneath the worship song.
He sees the jealousy hidden underneath congratulations.
He sees the secret conversation.
The compromise.
The fantasy.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The pride disguised as ministry.
The hunger for applause disguised as “influence.”
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Him.
The thing you keep deleting.
The thing you keep returning to.
The thing you promised Jesus you would surrender.
People see the profile.
God sees the heart.
And perhaps that is why this story bothers us.
We came looking for mysterious beings.
Scripture turned the mirror toward us.
We wanted to ask:
“Who were the sons of God?”
God may be asking:
“What are you becoming?”
Because the ultimate story of Genesis 6 is not merely about mysterious beings.
It is about a world collapsing beneath the weight of rebellion.
Humanity had multiplied technologically, socially, culturally, and physically…
while deteriorating spiritually.
And then comes judgment.
The Flood.
The undoing of a corrupted world.
Sin is not harmless.
God's patience should never be confused with God's approval.
The God of Scripture is holy.
He sees exploitation.
He sees violence.
He sees sexual corruption.
He sees injustice.
He sees what powerful people do when nobody can stop them.
And He sees what ordinary people hide when nobody is watching.
But if Genesis 6 ended only with human corruption, we would have reason to despair.
It doesn't.
Hidden near the approaching storm is one of the most beautiful sentences in Genesis.
וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה
Ve-Noach matza chen be'einei YHWH.

“But Noah found favor/grace in the eyes of the LORD.”
—Genesis 6:8
There it is.
חֵן — chen.
Favor.
Grace.
Human wickedness was great.
But grace was still there.
Judgment was approaching.
But grace was still there.
Civilization was corrupt.
But grace was still there.
The famous had their names.
The mighty had their strength.
The powerful took what they wanted.
But one man's story became marked by something infinitely greater.
Grace.
And now the entire mystery begins pointing beyond Noah.
Because Noah's ark could preserve human life through water…
but Noah could not cure the human heart.
The Flood judged a wicked generation.
It did not remove sin from human nature.
Humanity needed something greater than an ark.
We needed a Savior.
And eventually another Son would enter humanity's darkness.
Not a mysterious “son of God” taking whatever pleased Him.
The eternal Son of God giving Himself for sinners who had nothing worthy to offer Him.
Jesus did not come to exploit humanity.
He came to rescue humanity.
He did not come demanding that sinners bleed for Him.
He bled for sinners.
He did not come merely to condemn the guilty from a safe distance.
He stepped into our judgment.
The cross tells the truth Genesis 6 already forces us to confront:
Sin is worse than we imagine.
And grace is greater than we deserve.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ carried the judgment our rebellion deserved.
The innocent One stood where the guilty should have stood.
The Holy One was numbered with transgressors.
The One with the greatest Name humbled Himself.
The King wore thorns.
The Creator was nailed to wood.
The Son of God entered death…
and three days later walked out of the grave.
That is the Gospel.
Not “become good enough and maybe God will accept you.”
Not “hide your scandal carefully enough and religious people will respect you.”
Not “build such a powerful name that nobody remembers your failures.”
No.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Trust Jesus Christ.
Receive the mercy you cannot purchase.
Let Him begin changing what sin has distorted.
Maybe your scandal isn't Genesis 6.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe you have spent years carefully managing appearances.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe pornography has become your secret prison.
Maybe bitterness has lived inside you so long that it feels like personality.
Maybe you have wandered from Christ while still posting Christian verses.
Maybe you know exactly how to sound saved while privately wondering how far your heart has gone.
Then hear this.
Your sin matters.
Repentance matters.
Judgment is real.
But your story does not have to end where your sin wrote its darkest sentence.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives the repentant.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still receives prodigals.
Jesus still turns graves into testimonies.
Jesus still rewrites stories.
That is why our message will always be:
Not because scandal doesn't matter.
But because scandal does not have the final word when Jesus Christ takes hold of a surrendered life.
So maybe the question you need to answer tonight isn't whether the sons of God were angels, rulers, or descendants of Seth.
Study that question.
Search the Scriptures.
Think carefully.
Hold your conclusions with biblical conviction and appropriate humility.
But don't become so fascinated with the identity of the Nephilim that you ignore the condition of your own heart.
The ancient world had mighty men.
God looked for righteousness.
The ancient world celebrated names.
God looked at hearts.
The ancient world followed desire.
God called humanity to account.
And somewhere tonight, perhaps while reading these words, somebody knows that God has just touched the place they have been trying hardest to hide.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Ask for help if you need help.
Come home.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, you don't have to explain your whole story publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded person from giving up tonight.
Not because every difficult question in Genesis 6 has been solved in a few paragraphs.
“See it. Want it. Take it.”
And you may need to remember that God sees farther than desire does.
Not merely to help an algorithm.
And yes—even send it privately to the person who would never call themselves a Christian but keeps asking questions about the Bible.
One share can open a conversation.
One conversation can lead someone back to Scripture.
And God can use Scripture to lead a sinner to Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
And not because anyone should give under spiritual pressure.
Scripture teaches, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Christian generosity is worship when it rises freely from a heart grateful to God.
But the greatest reason to stay connected isn't merchandise.
It's growth.
It's being sharpened.
Convicted.
Encouraged.
Corrected.
Comforted.
Pointed repeatedly toward Jesus Christ.
Jesus Christ is worth following.
Your eternity is worth taking seriously.
Your hidden life is worth surrendering.
Your Bible is worth opening.
Your family is worth praying for.
Your sin is worth confessing.
The Gospel is worth sharing.
And the grace of Christ is greater than the version of you that you are ashamed for anyone else to meet.
Save what strengthens you.
Share what somebody else needs.
And comment—not for empty engagement, but because sometimes saying “Jesus, I need You” in front of others becomes the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
The “sons of God” in Genesis 6 may remain one of Scripture's most debated mysteries.
But the most important truth in the chapter isn't mysterious at all.
Humanity falls.
God sees.
Sin brings judgment.
Grace appears.
And ultimately…
Christ comes.
The ancient mighty men became memories.
The men of renown lost their world.
But the name above every name remains.
Jesus.
And when the last secret has been exposed, the last reputation has faded, and every human name has been stripped of its earthly applause, that is the Name that will still matter.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I AM THE GOOD SHEPHERD”: THE OLD TESTAMENT PASSAGE THAT MAKES JESUS’ WORDS ALMOST TERRIFYINGLY BOLD
paragraphs: “I AM THE GOOD SHEPHERD”: THE OLD TESTAMENT PASSAGE THAT MAKES JESUS’ WORDS ALMOST TERRIFYINGLY BOLD

Jesus was not merely saying He cared about sheep. Ezekiel 34 had already declared that God Himself would come looking for His scattered flock. So when Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd,” the question was far bigger than most of us realize: Who, exactly, was standing before them?
There are sentences in the Bible that sound gentle only because we have heard them too many times.
“I am the good shepherd” is one of them.
We embroider it on blankets.
Print it beneath paintings of Jesus carrying a lamb.
Read it at funerals.
Whisper it to frightened children.
And none of that is wrong.
But familiarity can quietly remove the thunder from words that originally shook the ground.
Because when Jesus said:
“I am the good shepherd.”
He was not simply saying:
“I am kind.”
He was not merely saying:
“I will take care of you.”
And He certainly was not inventing a beautiful pastoral metaphor out of nowhere.
There was an ancient accusation hanging behind those words.
A devastated flock.
Corrupt shepherds.
Scattered sheep.
Predators.
Wounds.
Exploitation.
Judgment.
And then came a promise so staggering that centuries later, when Jesus opened His mouth in John 10, anyone soaked in Israel’s Scriptures had reason to feel the weight of what He was saying.
To understand why, you have to go backward.
Back to Ezekiel 34.
And once you see what is there, “I am the good shepherd” may never sound tame again.
God speaks through Ezekiel against the shepherds of Israel.
The Hebrew word is רֹעִים — ro‘im — “shepherds,” from the verb רעה (ra‘ah), to shepherd, tend, or pasture.
But these shepherds were not caring for the flock.
They were feeding themselves.
“You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep.”
Then comes an indictment that sounds painfully modern.
“The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought.”
Instead, God says, they ruled the flock “with force and harshness.”
So the sheep scattered.
That is the scandal of Ezekiel 34.
People entrusted with the sheep were using the sheep.
The shepherds benefited.
The flock bled.
And perhaps that is where this ancient chapter stops feeling ancient.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to be wounded by somebody who was supposed to protect you.
Maybe your wound did not come from an obvious enemy.
Maybe it came from someone carrying a Bible.
Maybe from someone who could quote Scripture while manipulating you.
Maybe from a church leader whose public holiness concealed private cruelty.
Maybe from a Christian parent who taught grace but made home feel like judgment.
Maybe from someone who told you to forgive while refusing to repent.
Maybe you were not shepherded.
You were managed.
Used.
Silenced.
Shamed.
And eventually you wandered.
Not necessarily because you stopped believing God existed.
Sometimes wounded sheep wander because they no longer know whom they can trust.
God sees that.
Ezekiel 34 does not minimize abusive shepherding to protect religious reputations.
God exposes it.
But here is where the chapter becomes astonishing.
God does not merely announce that He will replace bad shepherds with better management.
He says:
הִנְנִי־אָנִי וְדָרַשְׁתִּי אֶת־צֹאנִי
Hineni ani, vedarashti et-tsoni.
“Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep.”
Listen to the emphasis.
“I myself.”
God says He is coming after His sheep.
Then the language keeps building.
“I will rescue them.”
“I will bring them out.”
“I will gather them.”
“I will feed them.”
“I will seek the lost.”
“I will bring back the strayed.”
“I will bind up the injured.”
“I will strengthen the weak.”
The shepherds failed.
So God Himself declares that He will shepherd His people.
Do not rush past that.
Because centuries later Jesus stands in Israel and says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός.
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
The Greek adjective καλός (kalos) can carry the sense of good, noble, beautiful, excellent, worthy—the shepherd who is everything a shepherd ought to be.
But the force of John 10 becomes even richer when heard against Israel’s Scriptures.
Ezekiel had announced that God Himself would search for His sheep.
Jesus announces:
“I am the good shepherd.”
Ezekiel describes God rescuing His scattered flock.
Jesus says His sheep hear His voice.
Ezekiel promises that God will gather His sheep.
Jesus speaks of gathering His sheep into one flock.
Ezekiel condemns shepherds who consume the flock for themselves.
Jesus says:
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
There is the reversal.
False shepherds sacrifice the sheep to save themselves.
Jesus sacrifices Himself to save the sheep.
Read that again.
False shepherds sacrifice the sheep to save themselves.
Jesus sacrifices Himself to save the sheep.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where Christianity stops being merely a philosophy about becoming a better person.
The Shepherd came for His sheep.
Not because the sheep had successfully found their own way home.
Because they were lost.
Isaiah had already described humanity this way:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way.”
That is sin.
We often reduce sin to a collection of especially ugly behaviors committed by especially terrible people.
Scripture goes deeper.
Sin is humanity wandering from its Shepherd.
Our way.
Our throne.
Our truth.
Our desires.
Our terms.
Our lives without rightful submission to the God who gave them.
Some sheep wander through rebellion.
Some through pride.
Some through lust.
Some through bitterness.
Some through money.
Some through religious hypocrisy.
Some become experts at looking close to the Shepherd while their hearts are miles away.
And maybe that last one is the most frightening.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still be lost.
You can sing worship songs while protecting a secret sin.
You can post Bible verses and quietly hate someone.
You can know how to say “God is good” while refusing to surrender the one room of your heart where you have hung a sign saying:
DO NOT ENTER.
You can look clean enough to fool people.
But sheep do not save themselves by looking clean.
They need a Shepherd.
And Jesus did not say the good shepherd gives the sheep motivational advice.
He said:
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
That sentence takes us toward a hill outside Jerusalem.
Toward nails.
Toward blood.
Toward darkness.
Toward the sinless Son of God willingly giving Himself for sinners.
Jesus says something remarkable in John 10:
“No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.”
The cross was not Jesus losing control of His mission.
The cross was central to His mission.
The Shepherd walked toward the wolves.
He placed Himself between judgment and His sheep.
The One without sin bore sin.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The Shepherd became the sacrifice.
And if you have spent years believing Christianity is essentially God telling bad people to behave better, look at the cross again.
Christianity begins with something far more devastating:
You could not rescue yourself.
And something infinitely more beautiful:
Jesus came anyway.
That is grace.
Grace does not pretend your wandering was harmless.
Grace tells the truth about how lost you were and then shows you how far the Shepherd was willing to go to bring sinners home.
Maybe you have wandered farther than anyone knows.
Maybe the version of you people see on Facebook is not the version of you that appears when the screen goes dark.
Maybe there are searches you delete.
Messages you hide.
Memories you numb.
Habits you keep promising to stop.
Maybe you have become skilled at saying “I’m okay” because explaining the truth feels exhausting.
Maybe you once burned for Christ.
Now you barely feel anything.
You still believe.
At least you think you do.
But prayer feels mechanical.
Scripture stays closed.
Compromise has become easier.
Conviction has become quieter.
And somewhere inside you is a frightening question:
Have I gone too far?
Hear Ezekiel again.
“I will seek the lost.”
Not merely the impressive.
Not merely the disciplined.
Not merely the people who never made a public mess of their lives.
The lost.
“I will bring back the strayed.”
The strayed.
The ones who left the path.
The ones who made choices they regret.
The ones whose testimony contains chapters they wish they could tear out.
The ones whose story became a scandal.
And this is precisely where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Jesus rewrites lives by confronting sin, forgiving repentant sinners, restoring the broken, and transforming those who come to Him.
Grace is not God saying your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it mattered terribly.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty sinners could never provide for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new Master.
A new direction.
A new life.
The Shepherd does not merely find us so we can continue wandering with religious reassurance.
He brings us under His shepherding.
Jesus says:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
Notice the movement.
They hear.
He knows.
They follow.
Real grace does not only comfort.
Grace transforms.
Jesus does not save us so sin can remain king with Christian decorations hanging around its throne.
He calls us to repentance.
To surrender.
To follow.
And there may be something in your life right now that you already know the Shepherd has been confronting.
You do not need another sign.
You need surrender.
Maybe it is pornography.
An affair.
Pride.
Greed.
Unforgiveness.
Dishonesty.
A relationship pulling you away from Christ.
A secret addiction.
A double life.
A wound you have turned into an excuse to wound others.
But the Shepherd knows.
And remarkably, being fully known by Christ does not mean you are beyond His reach.
Jesus knows His sheep.
The terrifying beauty of the Gospel is that Christ knows what we desperately hope nobody discovers, yet He still calls sinners to come into the light, repent, believe, and follow Him.
Do not confuse that invitation with permission to remain unchanged.
The Shepherd who carries wounded sheep also leads them.
His grace comforts us.
His truth confronts us.
His mercy forgives us.
His Spirit transforms us.
And sometimes following Him means finally admitting:
“Jesus, I have been wandering.”
Maybe that is your prayer tonight.
Not polished.
Not impressive.
Just true.
Jesus, I have been wandering.
Forgive me.
Bring me back.
I surrender.
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing our struggle into the light is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building.
There are believers reading beside you who understand what it means to limp behind the Shepherd.
Let somebody else who is drowning discover that grace still reaches people in deep water.
And do not only comment.
Look at your friends.
Your family.
That person who stopped attending church.
That person who jokes about Christianity because getting serious about God would hurt too much.
That believer who seems strong but has been strangely quiet.
Not as an algorithm trick.
As mission.

We cannot know whose screen this will appear on at 2:13 in the morning when temptation has won again, the marriage feels dead, shame is suffocating them, or they are wondering whether God could possibly want them back.
A share can become a doorway through which someone encounters Scripture.
Return to Ezekiel 34 and John 10 when you forget what kind of Shepherd Jesus is.
There is also a practical way to help this ministry continue producing and distributing Christ-centered resources.
It does not.
It cannot.
Christ purchased redemption; we cannot purchase righteousness.
The Gospel does not need to be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
What matters eternally is whether you belong to the Shepherd.
Because Ezekiel 34 eventually contains another detail we cannot ignore.
After God promises, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep,” He also promises:
“I will set up over them one shepherd, my servant David.”
Ezekiel was writing long after the historical King David had lived.
The promise therefore looks forward—to the Davidic shepherd-king God would appoint over His people.
Then Jesus arrives.
Son of David.
Messiah.
Shepherd.
King.
And He says:
“I am the good shepherd.”
This is why the statement is explosive.
John 10 is not giving us a sentimental picture of a religious teacher who happens to be unusually compassionate.
Jesus stands inside Israel’s great shepherd promises and presents Himself as their fulfillment.
The promised Shepherd-King has come.
And the divine rescue promised in Ezekiel is coming into focus in Him.
Then John takes us even deeper.
Jesus says:
“I and the Father are one.”
His opponents understand enough of the claim that they pick up stones.
The Shepherd is not merely offering therapy for wounded sheep.
He is revealing Himself.
Calling.
Gathering.
Giving His life.
Taking it up again.
And offering His sheep eternal life.
So perhaps the most important question this article can leave with you is not:
Did this make me emotional?
Not:
Did I enjoy reading this?
Not even:
Do I agree that Jesus is the Good Shepherd?
The question is:
Am I following His voice?
Because you can admire a shepherd without belonging to his flock.
You can admire Jesus historically.
Quote Jesus culturally.
Post Jesus publicly.
Study Jesus academically.
Sing about Jesus emotionally.
And still refuse to follow Jesus personally.
Christ does not call us merely to admire Him.
“Follow me.”
There is the invitation.
And there is the cost.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Let Him expose what must be exposed.
Let Him forgive what you cannot undo.
Let Him heal what others broke.
Let Him remove what is destroying you.
Let Him lead where you would not naturally go.
Let Him become more than the Shepherd in a painting hanging on your wall.
Let Him be your Shepherd.
Maybe your story is messy.
Good.
The Bible is full of people whose lives would have destroyed their reputations if social media had existed.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Cowards.
Persecutors.
Outcasts.
People possessed by demons.
People publicly disgraced.
People privately shattered.
Grace does not require a spotless résumé.
It requires a Savior.
And Jesus Christ is still in the business of finding people whose stories look finished.
That is why shame does not get the final sentence.
Your failure does not get the final sentence.
Your addiction does not get the final sentence.
Your betrayal does not get the final sentence.
Your past does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
But biblical grace is not Jesus editing your old life until it becomes socially acceptable.
It is Christ bringing sinners from death to life and teaching rescued sheep to follow their Shepherd.
So come home.
Not to religious performance.
Not to pretending.
Not to the approval of people.
To Christ.
The Shepherd who knows your name.
The Shepherd who sees your wounds.
The Shepherd who confronts your wandering.
The Shepherd who laid down His life.
The Shepherd who rose again.
The Shepherd who still calls.
And if your heart is whispering, “But you don't know what I've done”…
You are right.
I don't.
But Jesus does.
And the question has never been whether your sin is too ugly to shock Him.
The question is whether you will keep running from the only Shepherd who can save you.
But long after you close this article, remember this:
The Shepherd did not wait for the lost sheep to become worthy of being found—He came looking, laid down His life, rose again, and still calls the wandering home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Asked God for Purpose. He Gave You People to Love, Work to Do, and Obedience You Called “Too Ordinary.”
paragraphs: You Asked God for Purpose. He Gave You People to Love, Work to Do, and Obedience You Called “Too Ordinary.”
Maybe you haven't missed your calling. Maybe you've been standing inside it while waiting for something more impressive to arrive.
You prayed for purpose.
You asked God to show you why you're here.

You watched testimonies of people who seemed to have discovered the thing they were born to do. Someone launched a ministry. Someone wrote the book. Someone moved across the world. Someone built the business. Someone stood beneath stage lights and told thousands of people how God called them.
And somewhere between their breakthrough and your ordinary Tuesday morning, a quiet fear began growing inside you.
What if I'm wasting my life?
Because your life doesn't feel spectacular.
You wake up.
You make the coffee.
You answer messages.
You go to work.
You study.
You wash dishes.
You care for children or aging parents.
You sit in traffic.
You pay bills.
You help somebody who may never thank you.
You fight temptations nobody knows you're fighting.
You forgive someone who doesn't realize how deeply they wounded you.
You pray when you don't feel anything.
You open your Bible when heaven seems silent.
You show up again.
And again.
And again.
And because none of it looks dramatic enough to become a testimony video, you quietly wonder whether any of it matters.
But what if the problem isn't that God hasn't given you purpose?
What if He already has...
and you dismissed much of it because it looked too ordinary?
Paul writes:
Then only a few verses later:
“And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men; knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.”
— Colossians 3:17, 23–24
There is something almost unsettling about those words.
Paul doesn't say, “Whatever spectacular thing you eventually discover…”
He says:
Whatever you do.
The Greek is startlingly comprehensive.
πᾶν ὅ τι ἐὰν ποιῆτε
pan ho ti ean poiēte
In context, the thought is essentially: whatever you may do.
Not only preaching.
Not only missions.
Not only ministry platforms.
Not only the moments people applaud.
Whatever you do.
And then Paul says:
ἐκ ψυχῆς ἐργάζεσθε
ek psychēs ergazesthe
Literally carrying the sense of working “from the soul”—wholeheartedly, from the inner person.
Why?
τῷ κυρίῳ
for the Lord.
Then comes the line that changes the entire room:
τῷ κυρίῳ Χριστῷ δουλεύετε
tō Kyriō Christō douleuete.
You are serving the Lord Christ.
Read that slowly.
Because somebody desperately needs to hear it before another year disappears while they wait for their “real purpose” to begin.
You are serving Christ.
The context of Colossians 3 isn't a conference filled with celebrity Christians discovering their dreams.
Paul is speaking directly into households.
Marriage.
Parenting.
Family relationships.
Work.
Authority.
Responsibility.
Daily conduct.
The painfully ordinary architecture of human life.
And into that ordinary world, Paul places Jesus Christ at the center.
That means Christianity does something astonishing to ordinary life.
It makes the ordinary holy when the ordinary is surrendered to Christ.
You wanted God to give you a mission.
He gave you someone difficult to love.
You wanted Him to use you.
He gave you work requiring integrity when nobody was watching.
You wanted a platform.
He gave you a family.
You wanted influence.
He gave you one hurting friend who needed somebody to listen.
You wanted a spiritual breakthrough.
He showed you something you needed to repent of.
You wanted to change the world.
He asked you to change the way you speak to the people living in your house.
And you almost missed Him...
because obedience wasn't wearing stage lights.
There is a generation exhausted by the pressure to become extraordinary.
We have been taught to optimize ourselves, brand ourselves, discover ourselves, monetize ourselves, distinguish ourselves, and somehow construct lives impressive enough to prove that we existed.
Even purpose can become another form of anxiety.
What's my calling?
What's my destiny?
What's God's big plan for me?
Those aren't necessarily wrong questions.

God genuinely calls people into particular assignments. Scripture contains dramatic commissions. Moses had the burning bush. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up. Jeremiah was appointed to prophetic ministry. Paul encountered the risen Christ on the road to Damascus.
But here's what we conveniently forget.
Moses spent decades in obscurity before the burning bush.
David knew what it meant to tend sheep before wearing a crown.
Jesus Himself spent most of His earthly life outside the public ministry recorded in detail in the Gospels.
Think about that.
The eternal Son of God entered human history...
and for years there were no crowds following Him.
No feeding of five thousand.
No Sermon on the Mount.
No public miracles recorded from those hidden years.
There was ordinary human life in Nazareth.
Then, when His public ministry began, Jesus didn't spend His days chasing applause.
He touched people society avoided.
He welcomed children.
He ate with sinners.
He washed feet.
He stopped for people everyone else was walking past.
And ultimately, He obeyed the Father all the way to a Roman cross.
The world saw scandal.
Heaven was accomplishing redemption.
The cross itself should permanently destroy our assumption that God's greatest purposes must look impressive to human eyes.
To Rome, crucifixion was humiliation.
To spectators, Jesus looked defeated.
To His frightened disciples, everything appeared to be collapsing.
Yet through the very place that looked like shame, God was accomplishing salvation.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
The stone didn't get the final word.
Sin didn't get the final word.
Death didn't get the final word.
And your culture doesn't get the final word about what makes a life meaningful either.
Jesus does.
That is why the Gospel doesn't merely give you a better “purpose strategy.”
It gives you a new Lord.
