Then one day you realize the thing you thought you controlled has begun controlling you.
The prodigal finally sees where his rebellion has taken him.
Then he gets up.
He turns toward home.
And here comes the scandal.
The father sees him.
The father runs.
Not because rebellion suddenly became righteous.
Not because the pigpen was secretly holy.
Not because sin did not matter.
The father runs toward a son who is coming home.
That is grace.
Grace does not stand at the door saying, “Clean yourself perfectly and perhaps I will consider loving you.”
Grace runs toward the repentant sinner.
Grace embraces.
Grace restores.
Grace clothes shame.
Grace welcomes the undeserving.
And Christianity becomes distorted whenever we separate what God has joined together.
If we preach repentance without grace, broken sinners may hear nothing but condemnation and imagine they must somehow become worthy enough for God.
But if we preach grace in a way that eliminates repentance, sinners can begin imagining that Jesus came merely to make rebellion more comfortable.
Neither is the Gospel.
Jesus does not say, “Fix yourself, then come.”
He says, in effect, “Come to Me—and I will not leave you where I found you.”
This is why the risen Christ's words in Luke 24 are so important.
Jesus tells His disciples that the message going out from Jerusalem to the nations will include μετάνοιαν — metanoian, repentance, in connection with the forgiveness of sins in His name.
Repentance was not an embarrassing leftover from a primitive religion that the apostles needed to outgrow.
It belonged to the mission Christ gave them.
And notice where forgiveness is found.
Not in our moral perfection.
Not in our religious performance.
Not in punishing ourselves enough.
Not in proving how sorry we are.
In His name.
Jesus Christ.
That changes everything.
Because Christian repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with tears.
You cannot cry enough to buy the blood of Christ.
You cannot perform enough religious acts to earn the cross.
You cannot hate yourself into holiness.
You cannot pay a debt that Christ alone could bear.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He died for sinners.
The cross tells the truth about us more brutally than our culture wants to hear—and tells the truth about God's mercy more beautifully than our shame dares to believe.
Our sin was serious enough that redemption required the sacrifice of the Son of God.
And His love was great enough that He willingly gave Himself.
That is why repentance and grace are not enemies.
Repentance says, “I was wrong.”
Grace says, “Come home.”
Repentance says, “My sin is real.”
Grace says, “So is His blood.”
Repentance stops defending the wound.
Grace begins healing it.
Repentance brings the darkness into the light.
Grace says the darkness does not get the final word.
And suddenly this conversation becomes uncomfortable again.
Because it is much easier to debate what “modern Christianity” is doing wrong than to ask what I am refusing to surrender.
So forget everyone else for a moment.
What is yours?
What are you defending that Jesus is confronting?
What do you keep renaming so you do not have to repent of it?
You call it “coping.”
God knows when it has become bondage.
You call it “just looking.”
God sees what it is doing to your heart.
You call it “venting.”
God hears the cruelty.
You call it “protecting my peace.”
Perhaps sometimes it is.
And perhaps sometimes it is unforgiveness wearing therapeutic vocabulary.
You call it “love.”
But if it requires disobedience to Christ, love is not an adequate justification.
You call it “my truth.”
Jesus asks whether it is the truth.
You call it “just who I am.”
Jesus calls people to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him.
And that is where many people want Christianity to stop talking.
Because we love resurrection.
We just do not always love crucifixion.
We love forgiveness.
We struggle with confession.
We love promises.
We avoid commands.
We love a Savior.
But the New Testament will not allow us to separate Savior from Lord.
Still, hear this carefully:
Repentance does not mean that genuine Christians never stumble again.
If that were the standard, none of us could stand.

The Christian life is not sinless perfection achieved through human strength. Believers still battle the flesh. They still need confession. They still need the Spirit's power. They still fall and need to get back up.
The crucial difference is not between “people who have ever sinned” and “people who have never sinned.”
The difference is between making peace with sin and making war against it.
There is a world of difference between falling into the mud and building your house there.
The believer may cry, “Lord, I failed again.”
The hardened heart eventually says, “Stop telling me this is wrong.”
One grieves the chains.
The other decorates them.
Maybe that distinction just exposed something you have been hiding.
Maybe you are exhausted.
You genuinely love Jesus, but there is a battle you keep losing.
You promised God it was the last time.
Then it happened again.
And afterward you could barely pray because shame told you:
God must be sick of you by now.
Listen carefully.
Shame wants you hiding.
Jesus calls you into the light.
The answer to repeated failure is not to redefine sin until it stops hurting.
And the answer is not to run from Christ because you are ashamed.
Run to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Remove access where wisdom requires it.
Tell a mature believer when secrecy is feeding the bondage.
Make restitution when repentance requires making something right.
Seek reconciliation where Scripture calls for it.
Cut off what repeatedly pulls you away from God.
Not because those actions purchase salvation.
Because grace teaches redeemed people to stop embracing the chains from which Christ is freeing them.
This is where Christianity becomes more than inspirational content.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your mood.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came for the liar.
The adulterer.
The sexually broken.
The greedy.
The self-righteous.
The bitter.
The addicted.
The hypocrite.
The religious performer.
The person with a secret browser history.
The person smiling in church while quietly collapsing inside.
The person everyone thinks is strong.
The person who has almost stopped believing change is possible.
People like us.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Not privately in his thoughts.
Openly.
Three times.
Imagine living with that memory.
Imagine hearing the rooster in your dreams.
Imagine remembering His face.
Peter could have become nothing more than the worst moment of his life.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
David committed grievous sin and could not undo the devastation his choices caused.
Yet Psalm 51 gives us the language of a crushed man coming before God without excuses, pleading for cleansing and renewal.
Paul had persecuted Christ's people.
Then grace intercepted him.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people with chapters they would never have chosen to publish.
Yet God met sinners in their ruin.
Not by calling darkness light.
By bringing them into the light.
That is our theme because that is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing sin into virtue.
Not by telling us consequences are imaginary.
Jesus rewrites everything through redemption.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can become humble.
The sexually enslaved can learn purity.
The bitter can forgive.
The greedy can become generous.
The coward can become courageous.
The self-righteous can discover mercy.
The ashamed can discover that their worst chapter does not have to become their final chapter.
This is what cheap grace cannot give you.
Cheap grace can excuse your chains.
Jesus came to break them.
And perhaps this is why repentance has become difficult to preach.
Repentance confronts the modern idol of absolute self-sovereignty.
It tells me that my desires are not automatically authoritative simply because they are mine.
It tells me feelings can be real without being lord.
It tells me sincerity cannot transform disobedience into obedience.
It tells me I am not the final judge of good and evil.
God is God.
I am not.
And strangely, surrendering that throne is where freedom begins.
Because being your own god is exhausting.
You must justify everything.
Control everything.
Define everything.
Protect everything.
Save yourself.
But the Gospel announces something infinitely better:
You do not need to save yourself.
There is a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
Repentance therefore is not merely the funeral of the old life.
In Christ, it opens toward resurrection.
It is turning from the far country because you finally remember there is a Father's house.
It is dropping the weapon because you discovered the King you fought against is the One who died to reconcile His enemies.
It is opening your clenched fist.
It is saying:
“Jesus, no more negotiations.
No more secret rooms.
No more pretending.
No more calling bondage freedom.
No more asking You to be Lord of everything except the thing I love more than You.
I am Yours.”
Maybe you cannot honestly say all of that yet.
Then start with honesty.
“Jesus, I want to want You more.”
“Jesus, I am afraid to surrender this.”
“Jesus, I know this is destroying me.”
“Jesus, I keep returning to it.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There are prayers heaven does not despise.
A broken, contrite heart is not impressive.
It is honest.
And perhaps honesty before God is where your return begins.
So has modern Christianity made repentance optional?
No single sentence can fairly describe every modern church, denomination, pastor, or Christian. Many believers and churches still preach repentance clearly and faithfully.
But wherever Christianity promises forgiveness while teaching people that turning from sin is unnecessary, it has departed from the pattern we see in Jesus' commission and apostolic preaching.
Wherever “grace” becomes permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin, something precious has been distorted.
Biblical grace does not tell the prodigal that the pigpen is actually his promised land.
It brings him home.
And if these words are exposing you, do not waste that moment by becoming defensive.
You do not need another religious performance.
You need Jesus.
Come to Him.
Not after you clean everything.
Now.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the pride.
Bring the secret.
Bring the affair.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the hypocrisy.
Bring the wounds.
Bring the shame.
Bring the parts of your story you would delete if life had an edit button.
Bring them into His light.
Repentance is not God saying, “I do not want you.”
It is God calling:
“Turn around.”
And when you turn, you discover the astonishing center of Christianity was never your ability to rescue yourself.
It was Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Merciful.
Holy.
Calling sinners home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting.

Your support helps us keep producing Christ-centered biblical content intended to reach believers, seekers, struggling Christians, and people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
And do not keep the resources to yourself.
Christ is calling.
Not to a brand.
Not to merchandise.
Not to an algorithm.
To Himself.
Maybe your life has become a scandal.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you have spent years believing that because you knew better, failed again, promised again, cried again, and fell again, God could never possibly do anything beautiful with what remains.
Peter's failure was not his final chapter.
The prodigal's pigpen was not his final address.
The cross looked like the end until Sunday morning.
And your darkest chapter does not possess the authority to write the last sentence.
Jesus does.
So turn around.
Come home.
Because perhaps the most dangerous lie sin ever told you was that repentance meant the end of your life—when surrender to Jesus may be where life finally begins.
The sin you are terrified to bring into the light may be standing at the doorway of the chapter where grace begins rewriting everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ELKANAH HAD TWO WIVES—One Had Children, the Other Was Tormented for Having None
paragraphs: ELKANAH HAD TWO WIVES—One Had Children, the Other Was Tormented for Having None

One woman walked into the house with children around her feet. The other walked in carrying an emptiness nobody could see. Then the woman who already had what Hannah desperately wanted began tormenting her because she did not have it.
There are some Bible stories we have heard so many times that we accidentally clean them up.
We turn them into inspirational quotes.
We skip over the uncomfortable sentences.
We rush toward the miracle because sitting inside the pain makes us uncomfortable.
But 1 Samuel 1 does not begin with a miracle.
It begins with a complicated home.
A husband.
Two wives.
Children.
Jealousy.
Provocation.
Tears.
A woman who could not eat.
A woman praying so desperately that a priest thought she was drunk.
And somewhere inside that scandalous, painful household was a woman named Hannah whose tears were about to become part of one of the most consequential stories in Israel.
But before Samuel ever cried in his mother's arms...
Hannah cried without him.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not at the miracle.
At the waiting.
Elkanah had two wives.
Scripture says:
“He had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah: and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.” — 1 Samuel 1:2, KJV
That last sentence lands with almost brutal simplicity.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah had none.
The Hebrew names the women plainly:
חַנָּה — Ḥannah
פְּנִנָּה — Peninnah
And the text immediately establishes the wound around which much of the chapter will turn.
One had what the other desperately wanted.
Before going any further, we need to say something the passage itself requires us to understand carefully.
The Bible's description of Elkanah having two wives is not the same thing as God's endorsement of polygamy.
Scripture often tells us truthfully what human beings did without declaring everything they did to be God's design.
Jesus points us back to creation itself when speaking about marriage: “the two shall become one flesh” (Matthew 19:4–6; compare Genesis 2:24).
And throughout the Old Testament, households fractured by multiple wives repeatedly reveal rivalry, grief, favoritism, and conflict.
Elkanah's household was no exception.
Every year he traveled from Ramah to Shiloh to worship and sacrifice to the LORD.
And when the time came to distribute portions from the sacrifice, Scripture tells us that he gave portions to Peninnah and her sons and daughters.
Then comes Hannah.
“But unto Hannah he gave a worthy portion; for he loved Hannah: but the LORD had shut up her womb.” — 1 Samuel 1:5, KJV
The Hebrew text contains a famously difficult expression:
מָנָה אַחַת אַפָּיִם — mānāh ʾaḥat ʾappāyim
Translations handle the phrase differently. The KJV has “a worthy portion,” while many modern translations understand it as some form of special or double portion.
The precise expression is debated.
The emotional point is not.
Elkanah loved Hannah.
And Hannah was hurting.
Love did not make the infertility disappear.
A special portion did not silence the ache.
And perhaps somebody reading this understands that more deeply than anyone around you realizes.
People can love you...
and still be unable to fix what hurts.
Someone can put an arm around you and still not understand what happens when the bedroom door closes.
They can tell you how blessed you are.
They can remind you of everything you still have.
They can genuinely mean well.
And still...
there is that empty chair.
That unanswered prayer.
That pregnancy test.
That diagnosis.
That relationship that never came.
That child who walked away.
That marriage you prayed would heal.
That opportunity everyone else seems to receive effortlessly.
That prayer you have whispered so many times that sometimes you wonder whether you have any words left.
And then there is the additional pain nobody asked for:
watching somebody else receive what you have been begging God for.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
But the story gets worse.
Peninnah did not simply enjoy her blessing.
She weaponized Hannah's wound.
First Samuel 1:6 says:
“And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb.”
Listen to the Hebrew:
וְכִעֲסַתָּה צָרָתָהּ גַּם־כַּעַס
ve-khiʿasattāh tsārātāh gam-kaʿas
The language communicates intense provocation and vexation. Peninnah is described in relation to Hannah as her rival, and the text portrays repeated, deliberate provocation.
Not accidental insensitivity.
Not one careless comment.
This happened repeatedly.
Year after year.
Imagine it.
Hannah was already carrying grief inside her own body.
Then someone kept touching the bruise.
She did not need Peninnah to remind her that she was childless.
She knew.
She woke up knowing.
She went to sleep knowing.
And perhaps the cruelest wounds are sometimes not the wounds themselves...
but the people who discover where you bleed and keep pressing there.
Maybe someone has done that to you.
They know about your past, so they bring it up when they want to humiliate you.
They know your marriage is struggling, so they parade theirs in front of you.
They know you are lonely, so they make jokes about your singleness.
They know you are recovering, so they keep naming the person you used to be.
They know your child is struggling.
They know your finances collapsed.
They know you failed.
They know you relapsed.
They know you are ashamed.
And somehow your wound became their weapon.
But listen carefully:
Your wound is not your name.
Your waiting is not your identity.
Your humiliation does not get the final sentence.
Hannah's story had not ended simply because Peninnah thought she understood it.
And neither has yours.
Scripture says the provocation continued year after year until Hannah wept and would not eat.
Elkanah saw her.
And like many people who love someone they cannot fully understand, he tried to comfort her:
“Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?” — 1 Samuel 1:8, KJV
There is something painfully human about that question.
Elkanah loved her.
But love does not always equal understanding.
He was essentially saying, “You have me.”
Hannah's heart was saying, “But you are not what I am grieving.”
Sometimes people try to make suffering disappear by reminding us of other blessings.
And gratitude matters deeply.
But biblical faith does not require pretending grief does not exist.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Faith can worship while crying.
Faith can trust while hurting.
Faith can say, “God is good,” while simultaneously asking, “How long, O LORD?”
Hannah finally did something with her pain that Peninnah could never prevent.
She took it somewhere Peninnah could not follow.
Into the presence of God.
First Samuel says Hannah was in “bitterness of soul.”
The Hebrew expression is:
מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — marat nāfesh
Deeply bitter in soul.
She was not strolling casually into prayer.
She was shattered.
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.” — 1 Samuel 1:10, KJV
Do not miss this.
Hannah did not wait until she became emotionally presentable before approaching God.
She brought Him the wreckage.
The tears.
The disappointment.
The unanswered questions.
The longing.
The bitterness.
She prayed from inside it.
Somebody needs permission to do that again.
You do not have to sanitize your tears before bringing them to Jesus.
You do not need Christian vocabulary impressive enough to hide how exhausted you are.
You do not need to tell God you are fine when you are falling apart.
He already knows.
Prayer is not performing strength before God.
Prayer is coming because you know you need Him.
Hannah poured herself out so intensely that her lips moved while her voice could not be heard.
Eli the priest watched her and reached the wrong conclusion.
He thought she was drunk.
Think about that.
Hannah was already misunderstood at home.
Now she was misunderstood at the place of worship.
She was hurting...
and the spiritual leader in the room initially misread her pain.
Maybe you know what that feels like too.
Sometimes the person barely holding themselves together is mistaken for being distant.
Difficult.
Cold.
Unspiritual.
Unfriendly.
Weak.
Maybe nobody knows the battle taking place underneath your silence.
Eli told her to put away her wine.
Hannah answered:
“No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit... but have poured out my soul before the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 1:15, KJV
There it is.
One of the most beautiful descriptions of prayer in Scripture.
I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
Not polished it.
Not edited it.
Not disguised it.
Poured it out.
There are moments when prayer sounds less like a sermon and more like:
“Jesus, help me.”
“Lord, I don't understand.”
“Father, I'm tired.”
“God, please don't let me become bitter.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
And heaven is not offended by the broken prayer of a broken person coming honestly before God.
Hannah made a vow concerning the son for whom she prayed, promising that if God gave her a son, she would give him to the LORD.
Eventually Scripture says:
“And the LORD remembered her.” — 1 Samuel 1:19, KJV
That phrase does not mean God had forgotten Hannah and suddenly remembered she existed.
In biblical language, God's “remembering” often signals His movement toward someone according to His covenant purposes.
Then Hannah conceived.
She bore a son.
She called him Samuel.
The text connects his name with her declaration:
“Because I have asked him of the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 1:20, KJV
Imagine holding the child you once cried over before he even existed.
Imagine looking into the face of an answered prayer.
But we must be careful here.
Hannah's story is not permission to tell every grieving woman, “If you pray hard enough, God will give you a baby.”
It is not a formula.
Scripture never gives us the right to turn one person's miracle into a guarantee God has made to everybody.
Some prayers receive the answer we desperately wanted.
Some receive an answer we never expected.
Some remain unanswered in the way we hoped throughout this earthly life.
Christian hope ultimately rests somewhere greater than getting the earthly outcome we desire.
It rests in God Himself.
And ultimately, it rests in Jesus Christ.
Because the Bible is not fundamentally the story of human beings discovering techniques for obtaining their dreams.
It is the story of the holy God redeeming sinners.
And that story leads us to Christ.
Hannah received Samuel.
But humanity needed something infinitely greater.
We needed a Savior.
We had a problem deeper than infertility, loneliness, rejection, poverty, sickness, disappointment, or humiliation.
We had sin.
And no amount of self-improvement could remove our guilt before a holy God.
Then Jesus came.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He touched the rejected.
He welcomed the broken.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He carried the cross.
And on that cross, Christ bore sin and suffered in the place of sinners.
Then He rose from the grave.
That is the Gospel.
Not that Christians always get the ending they requested.
But that in Christ, sin and death do not get the final word.
Grace does.
Hannah's humiliation was not the final chapter of Hannah.
Peter's denial was not the final chapter of Peter.
The thief's criminal past was not the final chapter of the thief who turned to the crucified Christ.
And if you belong to Jesus, your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
That authority belongs to Christ.
Maybe your scandal is something everybody knows.
Maybe yours is hidden.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Addiction.
Pride.
An affair.
A broken marriage.
A secret habit.
Years of pretending.
Bitterness.
Abortion.
Greed.
Pornography.
Dishonesty.
Religious hypocrisy.
Or perhaps you were the one wounded by somebody else's sin, and now bitterness is slowly building a home inside you.
Do not confuse grace with pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost Jesus blood.
The Gospel calls us to repentance.
To turn.
To stop defending what Christ died to save us from.
To come into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
You do not need another mask.
You need Jesus.
You do not need a better reputation while your soul dies quietly behind it.
You need Jesus.
You do not need everyone on Facebook believing you have everything together.
You need Jesus.
And perhaps the deepest question in Hannah's story is not simply:
“When will my prayer finally be answered?”
Maybe another question is:
“What will I do with my heart while I wait?”
Will pain make you run from God...
or pour yourself out before Him?
Will somebody else's blessing become your bitterness?
Will somebody else's cruelty determine who you become?
Will your unanswered prayer become evidence, in your mind, that God has abandoned you?
Or will you bring the questions, tears, anger, confusion, repentance, and longing into His presence?
Hannah went into worship carrying something she could not fix.
And she poured out her soul.
Maybe today that needs to be you.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Let believers who see those words pray instead of judge.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only person crying behind a smiling profile picture.
Not to expose them.
To remind them:
“You are not alone.”
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, sharing it is one simple way you can put that truth in front of somebody who may desperately need it tonight.
There may be a husband who cannot understand why his wife keeps crying.
There may be a Peninnah who needs to repent because she has been using another person's weakness to make herself feel powerful.
There may be someone who has not prayed honestly in years.
Your share could place Scripture in front of them.
Not so we can build an impressive number on a screen.
So more people can encounter Scripture.
So wounded people can hear about grace.
So comfortable hearts can be confronted with repentance.
So sinners can hear that forgiveness is available through Jesus Christ.
So people who believe their story is already ruined can discover that the cross says otherwise.
Because there may come a night when you become Hannah again.
A night when somebody else's life seems full while yours feels painfully empty.
A night when someone presses the bruise.
A night when even people who love you cannot understand you.
A night when your prayer is barely audible.
Come back and remember:
Hannah was not invisible to God.
But do not stop at Hannah.
Look beyond Shiloh.
Look toward Calvary.
There you find the greater evidence that suffering does not mean God is absent.
There you find Jesus rejected, mocked, wounded, crucified...
and then the empty tomb.
The Christian story moves through death toward resurrection.
Through repentance toward forgiveness.
Through guilt toward grace.
Through the old life toward new creation in Christ.
So bring Him the chapter you wish had never been written.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the waiting.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the sin—and repent.
Bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the parts of your story you thought disqualified you forever.
Because the Gospel does not tell us that our past was insignificant.
It tells us something far more astonishing.
Jesus Christ is greater.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades is this:
The place where you thought your story was over may become the very place where grace teaches you that Jesus still holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SEXUAL SCANDAL PAUL SAID EVEN THE PAGANS WOULDN’T TOLERATE
paragraphs: THE SEXUAL SCANDAL PAUL SAID EVEN THE PAGANS WOULDN’T TOLERATE

The terrifying part of 1 Corinthians 5 isn’t simply what one man did in secret. It’s what an entire church learned to tolerate in public—and what Paul did next reveals the difference between grace that saves and “grace” that quietly lets sin destroy us.
There are passages in the Bible we love to underline.
There are passages we put on coffee mugs.
There are passages we whisper when we cannot sleep.
And then there are passages like 1 Corinthians 5.
Passages that walk into the room, turn on the light, and expose what everyone hoped would remain comfortably hidden.
Paul had heard something about the church in Corinth.
Something sexual.
Something public.
Something so disturbing that the apostle did not soften his opening sentence with pleasantries.
He wrote:
“Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία…”
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you…”
Then Paul makes the accusation even more devastating.
“…καὶ τοιαύτη πορνεία ἥτις οὐδὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν…”
…kai toiautē porneia hētis oude en tois ethnesin…
Sexual immorality of such a kind that it was not even found among the Gentiles.
And then Paul names it.
“…ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.”
A man had his father’s wife.
—1 Corinthians 5:1
Read that again.
Slowly.
Paul was writing to Christians.
Not to a pagan temple.
Not to a Roman brothel.
Not to people who had never heard the Gospel.
To the church.
And somewhere inside that congregation was a man involved with his father’s wife.

The language strongly indicates a relationship with his stepmother or a woman who was his father’s wife. Whatever the precise surrounding circumstances, the relationship itself was explicitly forbidden by Scripture. Leviticus 18:8 had already declared that a man must not uncover the nakedness of his father’s wife.
Paul’s shock was therefore not difficult to understand.
But here is where the passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because the sexual scandal was not the only scandal.
The church’s reaction was another.
“And you are arrogant!”
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 5:2.
Imagine expecting sympathy and receiving that sentence.
Imagine Paul walking into the congregation while everybody is discussing the sinful man and saying, in effect:
Why are all of you acting as though he is the only problem?
That changes everything.
Because Paul’s deepest confrontation was not merely directed toward a sexually immoral individual.
He confronted a spiritually complacent church.
They knew.
And somehow they had learned to live with what they knew.
That may be the part of this chapter modern Christians desperately need to hear.
We have become remarkably skilled at being horrified by everybody else’s sin while negotiating private treaties with our own.
We condemn what disgusts us.
We rationalize what attracts us.
We can recognize rebellion immediately when someone else commits it, yet when our own desires are involved, suddenly everything becomes complicated.
“It’s just a struggle.”
“God understands.”
“We love each other.”
“Nobody knows.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“It isn’t hurting anybody.”
“I prayed about it.”
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
He does.
And that should comfort the repentant sinner.
But it should terrify the person determined to keep hiding.
Because God knows the heart beneath the explanation.
He knows whether you are fighting sin or feeding it.
He knows whether you stumbled and are crawling back toward Him—or whether you have decorated your chains and renamed them freedom.
He knows.
The Greek word Paul uses is πορνεία—porneia.
It is the word commonly translated “sexual immorality.”
Paul does not treat sexual sin as an embarrassing little imperfection Christians should simply stop talking about.
Neither does he treat sexually broken people as disposable human beings.
That distinction matters enormously.
Biblical Christianity does not require us to choose between truth and compassion.
Jesus gives us both.
Truth without grace can become cruelty.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
But Jesus Christ came “full of grace and truth.”
And some of us need both desperately tonight.
Because maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody found the messages.
Nobody discovered the browser history.
Nobody knows about the relationship.
Nobody knows what happens when you are alone.
Nobody knows about the emotional affair you keep insisting is only friendship.
Nobody knows what you watch after your family goes to sleep.
Nobody knows the person you become behind a locked screen.
Nobody knows the memory you keep revisiting.
Nobody knows how many times you promised God, “This is the last time.”
Nobody knows.
Except God.
And perhaps reading that makes your stomach tighten.
Perhaps you expected another article about some ancient Corinthian pervert and suddenly realized Scripture has turned the mirror around.
That is what the Word of God does.
We approach it intending to examine the text.
Then the text examines us.
And please hear this carefully:
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation says, “Run away from God. You are filthy.”
Conviction says, “Run toward God. You cannot keep living like this.”
The enemy wants your shame to become a hiding place.
Jesus wants your conviction to become a doorway home.
That is why Paul’s response in 1 Corinthians 5 sounds so severe.
He commands the church to deal decisively with the man’s open, unrepentant sin.
Modern ears sometimes recoil at that.
Where is the compassion?
Where is the mercy?
Where is grace?
Look closer.
Grace is precisely why Paul refuses to pretend nothing is wrong.
If someone you love is walking toward destruction, silence is not necessarily kindness.
Sometimes silence is cowardice wearing the clothes of compassion.
Paul even describes the disciplinary action as having a redemptive purpose: “…so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.”
That changes the emotional temperature of the entire chapter.
The goal was not humiliation for entertainment.
Not revenge.
Not gossip.
Not religious superiority.
Not, “Look how disgusting this man is.”
The goal was salvation.
Restoration.
Awakening.
Repentance.
Paul was willing to make the man uncomfortable because eternity mattered more than maintaining appearances.
And perhaps that is where some churches have failed.
Some churches have failed by becoming harsh places where broken people are publicly crushed.
Others have failed in the opposite direction—becoming places where almost nothing can be confronted because confrontation itself is considered unloving.
Paul allows neither extreme.
The church must not delight in exposing sinners.
But neither may the church celebrate, normalize, protect, or casually tolerate unrepentant sin among those professing Christ.
Why?
Paul gives an unforgettable picture.
“A little leaven leavens the whole lump.”
Sin rarely remains neatly contained.
What we tolerate begins teaching us.
What we repeatedly excuse begins reshaping our conscience.
What once made us blush eventually makes us shrug.
What once made us repent eventually becomes something we defend.
And one of the most dangerous moments in your spiritual life is not necessarily when you fall.
It may be when falling no longer bothers you.
When prayer becomes quieter.
When conviction becomes easier to dismiss.
When Scripture becomes something you avoid because you already know what it will say.
When worship continues from your mouth while surrender quietly disappears from your life.
That is dangerous.
Because Christianity was never meant to become sophisticated sin management.
Jesus did not die so we could become more comfortable inside the prison.
He came to bring prisoners out.
Paul eventually writes in the next chapter:
Not negotiate with it.
Not schedule it.
Not keep it available for difficult nights.
Not follow it secretly while posting Bible verses publicly.
Flee.
There are moments when victory looks remarkably unspiritual.
Delete the number.
End the affair.
Block the account.
Confess to a trustworthy mature believer.
Move the computer.
Stop entering the environment where you repeatedly fall.
Tell your spouse the truth where appropriate and seek wise pastoral or professional help.
Get accountability.
Stop calling bondage “privacy.”
Stop calling lust “love.”
Stop calling secrecy “protection.”
Stop waiting for temptation to become weaker while continuing to feed it.
Run.
Because Jesus is better than what is killing you.
And this is where the scandal in Corinth becomes something breathtaking.
Paul does not end the Corinthian story with sexual sinners being beyond redemption.
In 1 Corinthians 6, immediately after naming sins that characterized people outside God’s kingdom, Paul tells the believers something astonishing:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That single word carries an ocean of grace.
Some of them had been sexually immoral.
Some idolaters.
Some adulterers.
Some thieves.
Some greedy.
Some drunkards.
Some revilers.
Some swindlers.
Paul does not say those histories were imaginary.
He says those histories were no longer their identity.
“And such were some of you.”
Then comes the Gospel:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for avoiding scandal.
Dead people being made alive.
Guilty people being justified.
Dirty people being washed.
Captives being liberated.
Prodigals coming home.
Sinners receiving mercy they could never purchase.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross proves your sin was so serious that the Son of God gave His life for sinners.
But the resurrection declares something equally glorious:
Your sin does not get the final word when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your story.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere beneath the respectable version of yourself is something you desperately wish could be rewritten.
A sexual past.
An abortion.
An affair.
Pornography.
Promiscuity.
A betrayal.
A secret relationship.
Years of lust.
Something done to you.
Something done by you.
A marriage you damaged.
A family you wounded.
A promise you broke.
A season you would erase if heaven allowed editing.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend it never happened.
The Gospel announces that Jesus can write something after it.
That is grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
There was something after the denial.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
There was something after the accusation.
The thief was dying beside Christ with nothing left to offer.
There was something after the criminal record.
Paul himself had persecuted the church.
There was something after the violence.
The cross stands forever as God’s declaration that your worst chapter does not possess sovereign authority over the ending.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But do not misunderstand what “rewrites” means.
Jesus does not rewrite sin by calling evil good.
He rewrites sinners by making them new.
Grace is not Jesus helping us hide the old life.
Grace is Jesus calling the old life into the grave and raising us to walk in newness of life.
That means repentance matters.
Real repentance.
Not religious embarrassment because you got caught.
Not tears because consequences arrived.
Not deleting evidence while preserving desire.
Repentance is the heart turning toward God.
It is agreeing with God about sin.
It is bringing darkness into His light.
It is abandoning the fantasy that rebellion can give us what only Christ can provide.
And sometimes repentance hurts.
Sometimes obedience costs relationships.
Sometimes confession destroys an image you spent years building.
Sometimes holiness means grieving something your flesh desperately wants.
Sometimes following Jesus feels like losing something before you understand what you are gaining.
But there is no sexual pleasure, secret relationship, hidden fantasy, applause, reputation, or temporary comfort worth trading intimacy with Christ for.
None.
Jesus is better.
Better than the fantasy.
Better than the affair.
Better than the approval.
Better than the secret.
Better than the addiction.
Better than the counterfeit intimacy.
Better than the version of yourself you are desperately trying to protect.
And if you have fallen again…
Come home.
If you have fallen fifty times…
Come home.
If you are ashamed to pray because you promised God last time would be the last time…
Come home.
Do not use grace as permission to remain in sin.
But do not let shame convince you that repentance is no longer available.
Confess.
Turn.
Seek help.
Cut off access.
Make restitution where wisdom and righteousness require it.
Walk in the light.
And believe the Gospel.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
That sentence has not expired.
Maybe the person who most needs this article is not you.
Maybe while reading, a face appeared in your mind.
Someone drifting.
Someone trapped.
Someone who still attends church but is slowly disappearing inside.
Someone whose marriage is cracking.
Someone hiding pornography.
Someone convinced that sexual sin has made them permanently filthy.
Someone who thinks God is finished with them.
Someone who needs conviction before destruction comes.
Or someone who needs grace before shame convinces them to give up.
Send this to them.
Not as a weapon.
As a rescue rope.
If something hidden was exposed while you were reading, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your life. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Or comment, “Christ is still healing me,” if your testimony is not finished yet.
Someone else may read your three words and realize they are not the only person fighting to come back into the light.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Christ, consider staying close to this ministry.
Not because supporting a ministry earns salvation—it never will.
But one genuine way believers may glorify God is by freely supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work so biblical truth can reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
But whether you ever spend a cent or not, do not leave this message without hearing the most important invitation.
Come to Jesus.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Not to merchandise.
To Jesus.
Because Paul’s scandalous chapter is ultimately not merely a warning about a man sleeping with his father’s wife.
It is a warning about what happens when sin becomes comfortable.
And it is an invitation to remember what the blood of Christ can do with people who finally stop hiding.
The Corinthian church needed truth strong enough to confront them.
The sinful man needed discipline serious enough to awaken him.
And every one of us needs grace powerful enough to save us.
Maybe your scandal never made the news.
Maybe nobody whispered your name.
Maybe your family never discovered it.
Maybe your church never knew.
Maybe your secret is still sitting safely behind a password.
But there is a far more important question than whether people know.
Does Jesus have all of you?
The room nobody enters.
The memory nobody knows.
The browser history.
The private messages.
The relationship.
The wound.
The appetite.
The shame.
The thing you keep promising to surrender tomorrow.
Does He have that too?
Because Jesus did not endure the cross merely to improve the public version of you.
He came for the person underneath it.
The real one.
The ashamed one.
The tempted one.
The guilty one.
The exhausted one.
The one still hiding.
The one reading these final words with a strange heaviness in the chest because somewhere inside, you know this stopped being an article about Corinth several paragraphs ago.
This became about you.
And perhaps tonight the Holy Spirit is not exposing you to destroy you.
Perhaps He is calling you out of the darkness because Jesus intends to heal what darkness has been consuming.
So stop running.
Stop negotiating.
Stop pretending.
Bring the scandal into the light of the cross.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Because the most unforgettable thing about your story does not have to be the night you fell.
It can be the moment Jesus found you there…and you finally stopped hiding.
And comment something honest.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“No more hiding.”
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of walking back into the light.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but once the pen is surrendered to Jesus, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY COULD NOT BE CURSED—SO THEY WERE SEDUCED
paragraphs: THEY COULD NOT BE CURSED—SO THEY WERE SEDUCED
Israel Survived the Enemy Outside the Camp. Then Desire Opened the Door From Within.
There are some battles Satan does not need to win by attacking you.
He only needs to make sin attractive enough that you stop fighting him.
That may be one of the most frightening lessons hidden inside Numbers 25.
Israel was standing near the edge of promise.
Behind them were years of wilderness.
Graves.
Failures.
Miracles.
Manna.
Judgment.
Mercy.
Ahead of them was the land God had promised.
And immediately before the scandal at Peor, something extraordinary had happened.
A pagan king named Balak had wanted Israel cursed. Balaam had been summoned. Money, prestige, pressure, and political expectation surrounded him.
But when Balaam opened his mouth, God would not permit him to curse the people God had blessed.
The enemy wanted a curse.
God turned it into blessing.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Israel could not be destroyed by the curse spoken over them.
Then Numbers 25 opens with a sentence so quiet that you can almost miss the catastrophe hiding inside it.
Israel was staying at Shittim.
And the people began committing sexual immorality with the women of Moab.
No invading army.
No chariots charging through the camp.
No giant standing in a valley screaming threats.
No visible battlefield.
Just invitations.
Meals.
Desire.
Compromise.
And worship.
That is what makes Peor terrifying.
Because sometimes the thing that devastates a person spiritually does not enter their life looking like an enemy.
Sometimes it smiles.
Sometimes it makes you feel wanted.
Sometimes it says, “It’s only this once.”
Sometimes it begins with something you believe you can control.
Then somewhere between attraction and appetite, you discover that what you thought you were merely enjoying has begun demanding your worship.
Numbers 25:1 uses language that should make us uncomfortable.
The Hebrew says:
וַיָּחֶל הָעָם לִזְנוֹת אֶל־בְּנוֹת מוֹאָב
Vayyāḥel hā‘ām liznōt ’el-benōt Mō’āv.
In context, the people began to prostitute themselves or engage in sexual immorality with the daughters of Moab.
The verb connected with זנה — zanah carries the idea of prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness and can also become a powerful biblical image for spiritual unfaithfulness.
But watch what happens next.
The women invited the people to sacrifices offered to their gods. Israel ate.
Then Israel bowed down.
Sexual compromise did not remain merely sexual.
Desire became participation.
Participation became worship.
And Numbers 25:3 says:
וַיִּצָּמֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַעַל פְּעוֹר
Vayyitstsāmed Yisrā’ēl le-Va‘al Pe‘ōr.
Israel joined himself to Baal of Peor.
The verb צמד — tsamad carries the sense of joining, binding, or attaching oneself.
Do not rush past that.
They did not wake up one morning planning to abandon Yahweh.
The descent happened through a chain of compromised desires.
Invitation.
Appetite.
Participation.
Bowing.
Attachment.
That is how many spiritual disasters still happen.
Almost nobody planning adultery begins by saying, “Today I will destroy my marriage.”
It begins with a conversation they should have ended.
A message they should not have answered.
An emotional intimacy they rationalized.
A secret they protected.
A boundary they moved.
Then moved again.
Almost nobody who becomes trapped in pornography began by praying, “God, let this enslave my mind.”
It began with curiosity.
A click.
Another click.
A private habit.
A promise to stop.
Another failure.
Another deleted history.
Another night telling God, “This is the last time.”
Almost nobody who becomes spiritually cold announces, “Today I am abandoning Jesus.”
You simply stop praying.
Then Scripture becomes occasional.
Conviction becomes irritating.
Worship becomes mechanical.
Sin becomes manageable.
Repentance becomes tomorrow.
And tomorrow becomes months.
You are still around Christian things.
Still know Christian language.
Still perhaps post Christian verses.
Still say you love God.
But something else has quietly attached itself to your heart.
Peor is not merely an ancient scandal.
Peor asks an unbearable question:
What has your heart become attached to that your mouth still refuses to call an idol?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe the people who follow you online would never imagine it.
Maybe you have learned how to worship publicly while negotiating privately with something that is slowly hollowing you out.
That is why this chapter should not be weaponized merely against “those immoral people out there.”
Numbers 25 was not primarily about pagans behaving like pagans.
It was about covenant people compromising with pagan worship.
People who had seen miracles.
People who had eaten manna.
People whose camp contained the tabernacle.
People who belonged to the community God had rescued from Egypt.
And they fell.

Paul later reached back into Israel’s wilderness history when warning the Corinthian church about idolatry and sexual immorality. In 1 Corinthians 10, he did not present these events as irrelevant archaeological curiosities.
They were warnings.
“Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.”
That sentence destroys spiritual arrogance.
You can love Jesus and still need boundaries.
You can know Scripture and still need accountability.
You can have years of Christian experience and still need to flee temptation.
You can preach against sin and still need to guard your own heart.
You can survive yesterday’s battle and fall to tomorrow’s invitation.
Spiritual maturity is not reaching a place where temptation becomes harmless.
Sometimes maturity means finally becoming humble enough to know what you must run from.
And there is another disturbing layer to Peor.

Numbers 25 itself describes the Moabite women inviting Israel into sacrifice and idolatry. Later, Numbers 31:16 connects the Peor catastrophe with the counsel of Balaam, saying that the Israelites were induced into unfaithfulness in the Peor incident through Balaam’s counsel.
That matters because Balaam had previously been unable to pronounce the curse Balak wanted.
What could not be accomplished by cursing Israel from a mountain became associated with enticing Israel into unfaithfulness.
Think about that.
If destruction cannot come through what frightens you...
perhaps temptation will come through what attracts you.
Some believers are watching constantly for the devil at the front door while leaving another door open for their favorite sin.
We prepare ourselves for persecution while making peace with compromise.
We rebuke demons but entertain lust.
We pray against attacks but refuse accountability.
We ask God to protect our families while secretly feeding habits capable of destroying them.
We want victory without surrender.
Deliverance without confession.
Grace without repentance.
Jesus without a cross.
But Jesus loves us too deeply to baptize the thing that is killing us.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing through Christ what sinners could never do for themselves—and then calling the forgiven person out of darkness and into a transformed life.
Peor became catastrophic.
God's judgment fell, and Numbers 25 records a plague in which twenty-four thousand died.
We should not soften that merely because divine judgment makes modern readers uncomfortable.

But neither should we carelessly take an Old Covenant historical judgment and begin declaring that every modern disease, tragedy, or death is God's direct punishment for someone's particular sexual sin.
Scripture does not give us permission to make that leap.
The text tells us what happened at Peor.
And what happened at Peor tells us something Christianity desperately needs to recover:
God's grace does not make idolatry harmless.
Sin is not dangerous merely because God has rules.
God's commands reveal that the One who created us knows what destroys us.
Sin promises freedom while creating chains.
It promises intimacy while producing shame.
It promises pleasure while demanding increasing control.
It promises secrecy while slowly rearranging the architecture of your soul.
And eventually the question stops being, “Do I still believe in God?”
The deeper question becomes:
What actually controls me?
What do you obey when nobody is watching?
What determines your decisions?
What receives your imagination?
What do you repeatedly sacrifice your peace, marriage, integrity, time, money, calling, and communion with God to keep?
That may be where your Peor is hiding.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to stop pretending.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You know the conversation you need to end.
You know the relationship that crossed the boundary.
You know the browser history.
You know the second account.
You know the bottle.
You know the obsession.
You know the money.
You know the bitterness.
You know the secret fantasy.
You know the compromise you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would force you to make a decision.
And maybe you are exhausted.
Exhausted from hiding.
Exhausted from promising God that this time will be different.
Exhausted from crying after the sin and craving it again three days later.
Exhausted from appearing strong while privately wondering whether God could possibly still want you.
Then hear the Gospel before shame convinces you to run farther.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who successfully hid their scandals.
He came for sinners.
Real sinners.
Guilty sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Religious sinners.
Sexually broken sinners.
Idolaters.
Liars.
Adulterers.
The proud.
The addicted.
The self-righteous.
People whose lives cannot be repaired by better public relations.
The cross is not God's announcement that sin was never serious.
Look at the cross.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And grace is so astonishing that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
There is the scandal.
And there is the grace.
Jesus does not merely improve the image of guilty people.
He saves.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He makes new.
The answer to Peor is not becoming better at hiding Peor.
The answer is repentance and Jesus Christ.
The New Testament word often translated repentance is μετάνοια — metanoia, carrying the idea of a changed mind, a turning of one's thinking and direction.
Biblical repentance is deeper than feeling terrible after being caught.
Judas experienced terrible remorse.
Repentance is not simply hating consequences.
It is coming into agreement with God about your sin and turning toward Him.
You stop defending what crucified Christ.
You stop calling bondage freedom.
You stop negotiating with the idol.
You bring darkness into light.
And when you fall, you do not make peace with the ground.
You run again to Christ.
This is why the Gospel is different from religious shame.
Shame whispers:
“Hide.”
Jesus calls:
“Come.”
Shame says:
“Clean yourself before God sees you.”
The Gospel says God already sees you, and Christ came precisely because you could never cleanse yourself.
Shame says:
“Your scandal is your identity.”
The Gospel says that for those who belong to Christ, the deepest verdict over their lives is no longer their worst chapter.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a new life.
There is a cross stained with the blood of Jesus and an empty tomb declaring that sin and death do not get the final sentence.
But do not confuse forgiveness with permission to return comfortably to the idol.
Jesus saves us from sin, not so that we can build a theology allowing us to remain peacefully enslaved by it.
Maybe your first act of repentance after reading this needs to be brutally practical.
Delete the number.
End the affair.
Confess to your spouse.
Call a mature believer.
Install accountability.
Leave the room.
Cancel the secret account.
Stop meeting the person privately.
Tell your pastor.
Ask for help.
Get appropriate professional help where addiction or destructive behavior requires it.
Not because those actions purchase God's forgiveness.
Christ cannot be purchased.
Do them because repentance eventually grows legs.
There are moments when faith looks profoundly spiritual.
And there are moments when faith looks like blocking a phone number while your hands are shaking.
Someone reading this has been asking God to remove a temptation while continuing to preserve access to it.
You cannot continually feed what you keep praying will starve.
And perhaps that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Peor teaches us that the most dangerous idol may not be the one you openly worship.
It may be the one you keep refusing to surrender.
Yet Numbers 25 is not the end of the Bible.
Peor does not get the last word.
Israel's failures do not stop God's redemptive purpose.
Human sin does not surprise God into abandoning His plan.
Generation after generation would fail.
Kings would fail.
Priests would fail.
People would fail.
Then, in the fullness of time, came Jesus.
Where humanity repeatedly surrendered to temptation, Christ remained faithful.
Where sinners deserve judgment, Christ willingly bore judgment for His people.
Where sin separates, His blood reconciles.
Where guilt accuses, His grace answers.
Where death seems final, resurrection declares otherwise.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people climbing successfully toward God.
It is the story of the holy God coming to rescue sinners who could never climb high enough.
Maybe you came into this article expecting a story about sexually immoral Israelites thousands of years ago.
And somewhere along the way...
Peor found your address.
Respond.
No elaborate explanation is required.
Someone may need your honesty more than your image of perfection.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be smiling in photographs while losing a war nobody knows exists.
Send it privately to the friend who has gone quiet.
Send it to the believer drifting from Christ.
Send it to the person who does not believe yet.
You do not know where one shared message might land at two o'clock in the morning.
Not every message is for the moment you first read it.
Some truths need to be waiting for you when temptation returns.

Gospel Warrior exists to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and Christ-centered spiritual nourishment in front of people who desperately need it.
Do it freely.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it as an act of voluntary generosity to Gospel work—not as payment for God's blessing, not as a purchase of salvation, and not because anyone has the authority to sell you grace.

Scripture teaches cheerful, willing generosity rather than giving under compulsion. The New Testament also shows believers materially supporting Gospel ministry. That makes Christian financial support something far more beautiful than religious pressure: worship flowing from a willing heart.

If you have a biblical conviction concerning tithes and offerings, honor that conviction faithfully in the church and ministries God has called you to support. It can, however, be an additional offering of generosity toward Gospel ministry if God genuinely puts that on your heart.
It should be mission.
If this ministry is feeding you spiritually and you believe its Christ-centered work should continue reaching others, your monthly support helps make that continuation possible.
And whether you ever give one cent or not, hear this clearly:
The Gospel itself remains priceless and cannot be bought.
Jesus is not merchandise.
Forgiveness is not behind a paywall.
Christ gave Himself for sinners.
So support the work if God leads you.
And above everything else...
surrender to Jesus.
Because Peor still whispers.
Temptation still dresses itself beautifully.
Idols still ask for our hearts without introducing themselves as gods.
And human beings are still remarkably skilled at hiding chains underneath respectable clothing.
But Jesus Christ is still saving sinners.
Still receiving the repentant.
Still breaking chains.
Still restoring ruined lives.
Still calling prodigals home.
Still transforming people whose stories looked beyond redemption.
So perhaps the question after Numbers 25 is not merely:
“How could Israel have fallen so far?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What am I allowing close enough to my heart that could eventually make me bow?”
Be honest.
Then bring the answer to Jesus.
Because perhaps somebody's midnight prayer will be answered through something you helped us place in front of them.
And remember this when temptation tells you that your failure deserves the final word:
The place where your sin tried to write “THE END” may become the very place where the scars of grace begin telling the world what Jesus can rewrite.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH DAVID’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP BEFORE ISRAEL
paragraphs: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH DAVID’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP BEFORE ISRAEL

David committed his sin in secret. Years later, his own son turned a rooftop into a public declaration of rebellion. But buried beneath one of the darkest scandals in the Bible is a terrifying warning about sin—and an astonishing reason sinners can still run to Jesus.
There are passages in the Bible that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you stare at the page and whisper...
“God actually allowed this story to remain in Scripture?”
Second Samuel 16 is one of them.
A king is running for his life.
A son has betrayed his father.
A trusted counselor has become an architect of rebellion.
Ten women have been left behind in a palace that is about to fall into enemy hands.
And then someone carries a tent onto a rooftop.
Not just any rooftop.
David’s rooftop.
And what happens there is so shameful that many Christians can read through the story of David for years without stopping long enough to understand why this horrifying scene matters.
Because this was not merely about sex.
It was about a throne.
It was about rebellion.
It was about humiliation.
It was about consequences.
And, when we follow the biblical story all the way through, it forces us to confront a truth we desperately need:
God can forgive sin completely without pretending sin was harmless.
David had once stood at the summit of Israel.
The shepherd boy nobody expected became the giant killer nobody could ignore.
The fugitive became king.
The songwriter became warrior.
The forgotten son became the man Scripture describes as a man after God's own heart.
But being used by God never made David incapable of falling.
One evening, David was walking on the roof of his palace when he saw Bathsheba.
That rooftop became connected to one of the darkest chapters of his life.
Desire became action.
Action became concealment.
Concealment became manipulation.
And manipulation eventually became bloodshed.
Uriah died.
David's secret remained hidden from human eyes for a time.
But never from God's.
Then Nathan the prophet walked into David's world carrying a message no crown could silence.
“You are the man.”
And the Lord announced consequences that would reach into David's own household.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 is chilling:
כִּי אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ בַסָּתֶר ... נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנֶגֶד הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Ki attah asita basater ... neged kol-Yisrael weneged hashemesh.
The sense is:
“You did it secretly ... [but this will occur] before all Israel and before the sun.”
David had hidden his sin.
God was telling him that the consequences would not remain hidden.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Years pass.
David's family begins tearing itself apart.
Amnon violates Tamar.
Absalom burns with anger.
Amnon dies at Absalom's command.
Absalom becomes estranged from David.
Eventually the handsome, charismatic prince begins stealing the hearts of Israel.
Then rebellion erupts.
David—the giant killer, warrior, king—is forced to flee Jerusalem because his own son wants his throne.
Imagine that walk.
David once entered Jerusalem as king.
Now he leaves it weeping.
The crown is still his, but the city is slipping from his hands.
Second Samuel 15 tells us that David fled with his household but left ten concubines behind to care for the palace.
Ten women.
Remember them.
Because biblical scandals are often told through famous men's names while nearly forgotten people bear terrible consequences in the background.
Absalom enters Jerusalem.
David is gone.
The palace is his.
But taking a palace is not enough.
Absalom needs Israel to believe there will be no reconciliation between father and son.
That is when Ahithophel gives him horrifying advice.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 16:21 begins:
בּוֹא אֶל־פִּלַגְשֵׁי אָבִיךָ
Bo el-pilagshei avikha.
“Go in to your father's concubines.”
Why?
Ahithophel explains that when Israel hears what Absalom has done, everyone will know the rupture with David is complete.
Then comes verse 22:
וַיַּטּוּ לְאַבְשָׁלוֹם הָאֹהֶל עַל־הַגָּג וַיָּבֹא אַבְשָׁלוֹם אֶל־פִּלַגְשֵׁי אָבִיו לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayyattu le-Avshalom ha'ohel al-haggag, vayyavo Avshalom el-pilagshei aviv le'einei kol-Yisrael.
They spread a tent for Absalom “on the roof,” and Absalom went in to his father's concubines “before the eyes of all Israel.”
There it is.
עַל־הַגָּג — al-haggag.
“On the roof.”
And:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — le'einei kol-Yisrael.
“Before the eyes of all Israel.”
The biblical text does not describe the women's thoughts, words, or consent, so we should not manufacture details Scripture does not give us.
But Scripture leaves no doubt about Absalom's purpose.
These women were being drawn into a public political act designed to disgrace David and demonstrate Absalom's irreversible rejection of his father.
The bedroom had become propaganda.
Sex had become a declaration of power.
The rooftop had become a stage.
And Israel was the audience.
Now remember Nathan's words.
David had sinned בַסָּתֶר — basater.
“In secret.”
But the consequences would unfold:
נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — neged kol-Yisrael.
“Before all Israel.”
Then years later, the narrator describes Absalom's rooftop scandal:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — le'einei kol-Yisrael.
“Before the eyes of all Israel.”
The connection is difficult to miss.
What David tried to bury had consequences that eventually walked into daylight.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been hiding.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your parents don't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your friends see your Bible verses, your Sunday smile, your worship playlist, your Christian posts...
but they don't see what happens when the door closes.
They don't see the messages.
They don't see the addiction.
They don't see the browser history.
They don't hear the bitterness.
They don't know about the relationship.
They don't know what happened years ago.
They don't know the compromise you have renamed “struggling” because calling it sin would require you to confront it.
And perhaps you have mistaken secrecy for safety.
David's story destroys that illusion.
Sin does not become harmless because nobody applauds it, photographs it, exposes it, or discovers it.
God already sees.
That sounds terrifying.
Until you understand the Gospel.
Because the God who sees what you hide is also the God to whom you can finally stop hiding.
David's story is not simply the story of a wicked man getting what he deserved.
That would be too shallow.
David sinned grievously.
David was confronted.
David repented.
David was forgiven.
And David still experienced devastating temporal consequences.
Those truths belong together.
Listen to David when Nathan confronts him:
חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה
Chatati la-YHWH.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
No speech.
No public-relations campaign.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No blaming stress.
No blaming kingship.
No blaming loneliness.
No rewriting the definition of holiness.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
And Nathan responds with extraordinary words:
גַּם־יְהוָה הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ
The LORD has put away David's sin.
That is grace.
But grace did not transform evil into good.
Forgiveness did not mean consequences vanished.
David was forgiven, yet his house still bled.
That distinction matters enormously.
Some people think repentance means saying “sorry” and demanding that every consequence disappear.
Scripture teaches something deeper.
God's forgiveness is real.
God's discipline is real.
God's mercy is real.
And the damage caused by sin can also be painfully real.
You may be forgiven and still need to rebuild trust.
Forgiven and still need accountability.
Forgiven and still need to confess.
Forgiven and still need to repair what you can.
Forgiven and still have scars.
Forgiven and still have people who need time to heal from what you did.
Grace is not God pretending the wreckage never happened.
Grace is God refusing to abandon the repentant sinner in the wreckage.
And there is another uncomfortable part of this story we should not rush past.
The ten women.
After the rebellion was eventually crushed and David returned to Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 20:3 tells us what became of them.
David provided for them, but he no longer went in to them, and they lived secluded “in widowhood” until their deaths.
The Bible does not give us their conversations.
It does not record their prayers.
It does not tell us what they felt when Absalom entered Jerusalem or when the tent was raised.
So we should resist filling silence with imagination and calling it Scripture.
But their presence reminds us of something sobering:
Powerful people's sins rarely hurt only powerful people.
Other people get caught in the blast radius.
Children.
Spouses.
Families.
Churches.
Friends.
People whose names never become famous enough to appear in the headline.
That is why repentance cannot merely mean, “God, make me feel better.”
Real repentance asks:
“Lord, what has my sin done?”
“Whom have I wounded?”
“What must I confess?”
“What must I stop?”
“What must I surrender?”
“What needs to change?”
And then comes the question that makes this ancient scandal suddenly personal.
What rooftop are you building?
Maybe yours isn't made of stone.
Maybe yours glows in your hand at two in the morning.
Maybe it is a secret conversation.
Maybe it is resentment rehearsed until hatred feels justified.
Maybe it is pride disguised as ministry.
Maybe it is pornography hidden behind passwords.
Maybe it is emotional infidelity you keep calling friendship.
Maybe it is greed disguised as ambition.
Maybe it is unforgiveness you protect because releasing it feels like letting the person escape justice.
Maybe everyone thinks you are close to Jesus while privately you know you have been drifting for months.
You do not need another hiding place.
You need Christ.
Because eventually the story of David forces us to look beyond David.
David was Israel's king.
But David could not save Israel from sin.
David defeated Goliath but could not defeat the corruption inside his own heart.
David wore a crown but needed mercy.
David wrote psalms but needed forgiveness.
David shepherded a nation but needed a Shepherd himself.
The Bible was preparing us for another King.
Another Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
And look at the contrast.
Absalom wanted his father's throne.
Jesus willingly submitted to His Father.
Absalom exalted himself publicly.
Jesus humbled Himself.
Absalom entered Jerusalem seeking a kingdom through rebellion.
Jesus entered Jerusalem as the rightful King and walked toward a cross.
Absalom's path toward a throne brought shame upon others.
Jesus took our shame upon Himself.
And here the scandal of David's family finally opens toward the scandalous beauty of grace.
David deserved judgment.
So do we.
Yet the Gospel announces that God did not leave sinners without hope.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin's judgment for all who trust in Him.
Not because sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
Not because God suddenly stopped being holy.
Because Christ satisfied what holiness required.
The cross does not tell us that our sin did not matter.
The cross tells us our sin mattered so much that redemption cost the blood of the Son of God.
And the empty tomb tells us sin does not get the final word.
Your scandal does not have to become your final sentence.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your identity.
Your secret does not have to become your master.
Your shame does not have to become your name.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Not cleaned-up sinners.
Not people with respectable testimonies.
Sinners.
People who have ruined things.
People who knew better.
People who promised God they would never do it again and then did.
People who have carried shame so long they have forgotten what freedom feels like.
People afraid that if anyone really knew them, they would walk away.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to repent and come.
That does not mean, “Continue living however you want because grace will cover it.”
Paul crushes that distortion in Romans 6.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace brings the prodigal home.
Grace turns persecutors into apostles.
Grace transforms the sexually immoral, idolaters, thieves, greedy, drunkards, revilers, and swindlers so Paul can speak of believers and say:
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
That word carries a resurrection inside it.
You may have been that person.
But in Christ, that does not have to be where the sentence ends.
Maybe this article found you while you are still standing on your own secret rooftop.
Come down.
Stop hiding.
Stop negotiating.
Stop saying tomorrow.
Bring the sin into God's light.
Repent.
If another person needs to know, seek godly wisdom and tell the truth appropriately.
Get accountability.
Remove access to whatever repeatedly pulls you back.
Open your Bible again.
Pray even when prayer feels awkward.
Return to fellowship.
And above everything else, fix your eyes on Jesus.
You are not saved because you managed to become impressive enough for God.
You are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
The King who knew every hidden room of your heart loved sinners enough to go to a cross.
And He did not stay dead.
Jesus rose.
That means there is hope for people with histories.
Hope for broken families.
Hope for addicts.
Hope for adulterers who repent.
Hope for hypocrites who finally become honest.
Hope for prodigals.
Hope for the ashamed.
Hope for people whose consequences cannot be completely undone.
Hope even when yesterday cannot be rewritten...
because Jesus can rewrite what happens next.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain Christians with shocking Bible stories.
Not to turn biblical scandal into religious gossip.
But to take people through the difficult pages of Scripture until those pages expose our hearts and point us toward Jesus Christ.
Be honest before God.
Somebody reading beneath this article may need evidence that God still restores broken people.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend whose smile has been hiding a war.
The husband trying to return to God.
The wife carrying silent wounds.
The son who walked away.
The daughter drowning in shame.
The believer who thinks failure has permanently disqualified them.
The unbeliever who thinks Christianity is for people who have never made a mess of their lives.
Send this article privately if that would be wiser.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and Jesus Christ, supporting and sharing that work is one practical way you can help biblical truth reach another screen, another home, another wounded heart.
Because temptation has a way of making us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.
Because somebody else's secret may be killing them quietly.
There are people scrolling Facebook tonight who do not need another argument.
They need to discover that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
David's story began this chapter with a kingdom collapsing.
Absalom turned a rooftop into a monument to rebellion.
A father's hidden sin had produced consequences he could no longer hide.
But neither David's scandal nor Absalom's rebellion would be the final word of Scripture.
Another Son of David was coming.
Another King.
A sinless King.
A King betrayed by people He loved.
A King publicly humiliated.
A King stripped and exposed to shame.
A King crowned with thorns.
A King lifted up before watching crowds.
But unlike David, He was suffering with no secret sin of His own to answer for.
He was the spotless Lamb.
And on the third day...
the grave was empty.
So when the enemy whispers, “Look at what you did,” don't answer by pretending you never did it.
Repent.
Confess.
Then point to Christ.
“Yes. I sinned.
Yes. I need mercy.
Yes. I may carry consequences.
But Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
Jesus Christ is still transforming lives.
And my sin will not be greater than my Savior.”
The rooftop may expose the scandal—but the cross reveals how far God was willing to go to redeem the repentant sinner.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS SEXUAL FRUSTRATION A TEST FROM GOD?
paragraphs:
IS SEXUAL FRUSTRATION A TEST FROM GOD?
When your body wants what your convictions cannot permit, the battle may reveal something deeper than desire—and what you do with that desire can either drive you into hiding or drive you closer to Jesus.
There are prayers Christians whisper that almost never make it into church conversations.
“God… how long?”
“How long do I have to be alone?”
“How long do I have to keep saying no?”
“How long do I have to carry desires that feel completely natural when there seems to be no righteous place for them to go?”
Maybe nobody knows how difficult this has become for you.
You worship.
You pray.
You try to guard your eyes.
You try to keep your thoughts clean.
You genuinely love Jesus.
And yet there are nights when your body seems to be arguing with everything your spirit believes.
You do not necessarily want rebellion.
You want relief.
And sometimes that distinction makes the struggle even more confusing.
Because you begin wondering…
“If God created sexuality, why does obedience sometimes hurt this much?”
“Why would God give me these desires and then tell me to wait?”
“Is this frustration punishment?”
“Is Satan attacking me?”
“Is God testing me?”
