Or a sinner convinced that what they have done has already disqualified them from grace.
Let them hear this before the fire spreads:
Jesus Christ still saves.
Jesus still forgives repentant sinners.
Jesus still restores broken people.
Jesus still teaches His people to walk in holiness.
Jesus still calls what is dark, dark.
And then He does something scandalously beautiful.
He calls sinners into the light.
Your hidden conversation does not have to become your next catastrophe.
Your failure does not have to become your final identity.
Your scandal does not get the last sentence.
Because when everything hidden finally comes into the light, you may discover that Jesus was not waiting there to help you hide better—He was waiting to teach you how to become free.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY JESUS TOLD A MAN TO “LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR DEAD”
paragraphs:
WHY JESUS TOLD A MAN TO “LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR DEAD”
One of Jesus’ Harshest-Sounding Commands Wasn’t About Disrespecting the Dead—It Was About the Terrifying Danger of Saying “Jesus, But First…”
There are words of Jesus that comfort you immediately.
“Come to Me.”
“Do not be afraid.”
“Your sins are forgiven.”
And then there are words that stop you cold.
Words you read twice because they almost do not sound like the Jesus you thought you knew.
A man tells Jesus that he wants to follow Him, but asks permission to do something seemingly honorable first.
Bury his father.
And Jesus answers:
“Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God.” — Luke 9:60, KJV
At first, it sounds almost cruel.
Was Jesus telling a grieving son to abandon his dead father?
Was He condemning funerals?
Was He teaching Christians to neglect their families?
No.
But what Jesus was saying may be even more uncomfortable than those interpretations.
Because hidden inside this encounter is a warning about one of the most dangerous words you can ever place between yourself and Jesus.
Not “never.”
Not “no.”
Just...
“first.”
And before you finish reading this, you may realize that the unnamed man standing beside Jesus two thousand years ago sounds disturbingly familiar.
Because some of us have never actually told Jesus no.
We have simply spent years telling Him...
“Not yet.”
Luke places the encounter in a section filled with the cost and urgency of discipleship. Jesus is traveling toward Jerusalem. Along the road, people encounter Him and speak about following Him.
One man confidently declares that he will follow Jesus wherever He goes.
Jesus warns him that following the Son of Man offers no guarantee of earthly comfort.
Then Jesus turns to another man.
This time, the man does not initiate the conversation.
Jesus does.
Two words fall upon his life:
“Follow me.” — Luke 9:59, KJV
Imagine hearing that personally.
Not from a preacher.
Not from a devotional.
Not through a screen.
Jesus Christ looks at you and says:
Follow Me.
And the man responds:
“Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.”
There it is.
“Lord... first.”
Those words belong together far less comfortably than we imagine.
The Greek text makes the tension painfully clear:
Κύριε, ἐπίτρεψόν μοι ἀπελθόντι πρῶτον θάψαι τὸν πατέρα μου.
Kyrie, epitrepson moi apelthonti prōton thapsai ton patera mou.
A straightforward rendering is:
“Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.”
Then comes Jesus’ shocking response:
Ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς· σὺ δὲ ἀπελθὼν διάγγελλε τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.
Aphes tous nekrous thapsai tous heautōn nekrous; sy de apelthōn diangelle tēn basileian tou theou.
“Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.”
The word repeated is νεκρός — nekros — “dead.”
Jesus deliberately uses “dead” in two senses.
The physically dead obviously cannot conduct funerals.

So the force of the saying is commonly understood as a contrast between those who are physically alive yet outside the urgent call of discipleship, and those who have been summoned to proclaim God’s kingdom.
Jesus is not confused about death.
He is exposing another kind of death.
A person can breathe...
work...
eat...
laugh...
build a career...
raise children...
scroll through a phone...
sit in church...
sing worship songs...
and still be spiritually dead apart from the life God gives.
The New Testament repeatedly develops that reality.
Paul later writes of people being “dead in trespasses and sins” before God makes them alive with Christ.
Jesus Himself speaks elsewhere of the dead hearing the voice of the Son of God and living.
So when Jesus says, “Let the dead bury their dead,” He is not mocking grief.
He is confronting spiritual priority.
And we should be careful about claiming more than Scripture tells us.

Luke does not explicitly say whether the man's father was lying dead at that moment. Some interpreters have suggested that “bury my father” could mean remaining with his family until his father eventually died. That is possible, and some Bible notes explicitly recognize that the father was not necessarily already dead.
But Scripture does not settle that historical detail for us.
We do not need speculation to feel the force of Jesus' command.
The point Luke gives us is already devastatingly clear:
Jesus called.
The man answered...
“first.”
And perhaps that is where this ancient road suddenly enters your house.
Because what is your “first”?
“Jesus, I will follow You, but first let me get my life together.”
“Jesus, I will surrender this relationship, but first let me see where it goes.”
“Jesus, I know I need to forgive, but first let them apologize.”
“Jesus, I know this habit is destroying me, but first give me one more night.”
“Jesus, I know I should repent, but first let me enjoy myself while I am young.”
“Jesus, I will serve You when life becomes less busy.”
“Jesus, I will open my Bible when I have more time.”
“Jesus, I will tell people about You when I become more confident.”
“Jesus, I will come back to church when I stop feeling ashamed.”
“Jesus, I will surrender everything...
eventually.”
And eventually becomes next month.
Next month becomes next year.
Next year becomes someday.
Someday becomes a lifetime.
Then one day you realize something terrifying:
You never consciously abandoned Jesus.
You just kept postponing Him.
That is why this passage cuts so deeply.
The man's request does not sound wicked.
That matters.
Sin does not always approach wearing the face of obvious rebellion.
Sometimes what competes with obedience is something respectable.
Family.
Career.
Comfort.
Security.
Reputation.
Tradition.
Plans.
Responsibilities.
Things that may be legitimate in themselves can become spiritually destructive when they are placed above the direct claim of Christ.
Jesus is not teaching that parents do not matter.

The same Scriptures command people to honor father and mother. Jesus condemned religious hypocrisy that allowed people to evade legitimate responsibilities toward their parents. At the cross, while suffering unimaginably, Jesus made provision for His mother.
So Luke 9 cannot responsibly be interpreted as Jesus suddenly becoming anti-family.
Something deeper is happening.
Jesus is establishing supremacy.
There is a difference between loving your family...
and allowing family to outrank Christ.
There is a difference between having responsibilities...
and using responsibilities as respectable camouflage for delayed obedience.
There is a difference between saying, “Jesus is important to me”...
and saying, “Jesus is Lord.”
Lordship means Jesus does not simply receive whatever part of your life remains after everything else has taken its share.
He gets the throne.
This becomes even clearer because Luke immediately tells us about another would-be disciple.
Another man says:
“I will follow thee, Lord; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house.”
Again.
“I will follow You...”
“But first.”
Jesus responds with another uncompromising image:
“No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” — Luke 9:62, KJV
Do you see the pattern?
One person wants discipleship without insecurity.
Another wants discipleship after burial.
Another wants discipleship after farewell.
Jesus keeps cutting through every condition placed in front of obedience.
Not because He lacks compassion.
Because He knows something we desperately try to forget:
Delayed surrender can become disguised refusal.
We imagine rebellion always screams:
“I hate God!”
But sometimes rebellion whispers:
“I'll obey tomorrow.”
And tomorrow is one of Satan's most effective counterfeits of repentance.
Because tomorrow feels responsible.
Tomorrow feels possible.
Tomorrow lets your conscience quiet down without requiring your life to change today.
You can cry during worship today and promise surrender tomorrow.
You can feel conviction today and repent tomorrow.
You can know the relationship is sinful today and leave tomorrow.
You can know you need Christ today and decide tomorrow.
You can feel the Holy Spirit exposing something today...
and keep it hidden until tomorrow.
But Scripture never promises you tomorrow.
Jesus calls people in the present tense.
“Follow Me.”
Maybe that is why these words bother us.
We prefer a Jesus who advises.
Jesus commands.
We prefer a Jesus who fits into our existing priorities.
Jesus rearranges them.
We prefer Christianity as an improvement to our lives.
Jesus calls us to lose our lives for His sake.
We want Jesus as Savior from hell while quietly resisting Jesus as Lord over Monday morning.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
Grace without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without a cross.
But that is not the Gospel Jesus preached.
And strangely...
that is good news.
Because the Jesus who demands everything is the Jesus who gave everything.
The One telling this man to follow Him was walking toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward mocking.
Toward scourging.
Toward nails.
Toward a Roman cross.
Jesus was not standing safely at a distance demanding sacrifice from other people.
He was walking toward His own.
The hands commanding, “Follow Me,” would soon be pierced.
The feet walking toward Jerusalem would soon be nailed to wood.
The voice proclaiming God's kingdom would cry out beneath the weight of suffering.
And the sinless Son of God would give His life for sinners.
Then the grave would receive Him.
And the grave would fail to keep Him.
That changes everything.
Christian discipleship is not surrender to a tyrant demanding your life for his ego.
It is surrender to the Savior who gave His life to rescue yours.
Jesus is worthy of first place because there is no one like Him.
He carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now the risen Christ does not merely offer you improved behavior.
He offers life.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new identity.
A new future.
Grace does not mean Jesus lowers the cost of discipleship until nothing has to change.
Grace means you could never purchase salvation at all.
Christ purchased redemption.
And the grace that saves us begins transforming us.
That is where scandal becomes grace.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe there was no headline.
No viral exposure.
No public collapse.
Maybe your scandal lives behind a locked phone.
Inside deleted messages.
Inside bitterness nobody can see.
Inside pornography you keep promising to quit.
Inside pride dressed as spirituality.
Inside resentment toward someone you smile at every Sunday.
Inside a relationship you know dishonors Christ.
Inside money that owns you.
Inside secret compromise.
Inside years of saying:
“Jesus...
first let me...”
And perhaps you have assumed that because you delayed so long, Jesus must finally be finished with you.
Look again at the Gospel.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus reached the end of a ruined life with nothing left to offer.
Christ's grace reached sinners in places respectable religion would have considered hopeless.
This does not make sin small.
It makes the Savior enormous.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending your scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by taking guilty sinners, forgiving those who repent and believe, making them His own, and beginning a transformation only grace could produce.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But you cannot keep gripping the old pages while asking Jesus to write the new ones.
Repentance means turning.
Faith means trusting Christ.
Following means He leads.
And maybe the sentence you need today is not complicated.
Stop negotiating with the One who died for you.
Stop giving Jesus conditions.
Stop treating surrender like an appointment you can reschedule indefinitely.
Stop saying:
“Lord, first...”
Maybe today the prayer becomes:
“Lord, You first.”
You first before my reputation.
You first before my appetite.
You first before my relationship.
You first before my ambition.
You first before my comfort.
You first before the secret thing I am terrified to surrender.
Not because surrender purchases His love.
Because in Christ you have encountered a love worth surrendering everything to.
Be honest.
There is no prize for pretending you are stronger than you are.
The Gospel begins with the collapse of self-salvation and the discovery that Christ is enough.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, do not immediately assume this article is only for them.
Let God search you first.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you encounter Scripture, repent more deeply, understand the Gospel, and keep Jesus before people who desperately need Him, then supporting this work can become one practical expression of generosity and participation in spreading biblical truth.
Your support helps this ministry continue putting the message of Jesus in front of people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
And that is why sharing matters too.
It can also become a doorway.
Somebody you know may be silently losing a battle you know nothing about.
Somebody may be questioning whether God could forgive them.
Somebody may be one night away from making another destructive decision.
Somebody may have stopped praying.
Somebody may be ashamed to return to church.
Somebody may not know Jesus at all.
You cannot know where a shared Gospel message will travel.
Return to Luke 9:57–62 when your obedience begins accumulating conditions again.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person who has become lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who keeps asking difficult questions.
Those things cannot be sold.
You are supporting the work while receiving deeper opportunities for Christian nourishment and resources created to keep pointing people toward Jesus.
But never confuse the invitation.
The question beneath this entire article is whether you are following Jesus.
Because eventually every excuse runs out.
Every possession changes hands.
Every career ends.
Every applause fades.
Every body returns to dust unless Christ returns first.
And suddenly the strange words spoken beside an ancient road do not sound so strange anymore.
“Follow Me.”
The man wanted something first.
Jesus wanted the man.
And perhaps right now...
He is putting His finger on your “first.”
That relationship.
That habit.
That grudge.
That fear.
That ambition.
That secret.
That delay.
That carefully protected corner of your life where you have placed a tiny sign saying:
“Everything but this, Lord.”
What happens next is between you and Jesus.
You can close this article.
You can scroll.
You can tell yourself you will think about it later.
You can feel convicted for five minutes and return unchanged to the same life.
Or you can stop.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Surrender.
Come to Christ again with empty hands.
Not:
“Lord, first...”
But:
“Lord...
You first.”
And if you have wandered, come home.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you are ashamed, run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
If you have never trusted Him, do not imagine that cleaning yourself up first will make you worthy.
You cannot rewrite yourself into righteousness.
That is why you need a Savior.
Jesus Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
The cross says your sin is more serious than you wanted to believe.
The cross also says God's grace is greater than you dared to hope.
And the empty tomb declares that death itself does not get the final sentence.
So share this if someone needs to hear it.
And comment something real.
“Jesus, You first.”
“Pray for me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or tell your testimony.
Because someone reading the comments may need evidence that grace still reaches people in wreckage.
There is still time to stop saying “Jesus, but first”—but do not make the mistake of assuming there will always be another tomorrow in which to say, “Jesus, You first.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SOLOMON’S 1,000 WOMEN: Why Did God Allow a King to Have 700 Wives and 300 Concubines?
paragraphs: SOLOMON’S 1,000 WOMEN: Why Did God Allow a King to Have 700 Wives and 300 Concubines?

He was the wisest king of his generation. He built the Temple. He spoke thousands of proverbs. Kings crossed borders to hear him. Yet the man who knew so much about God slowly gave his heart to what God had warned him about all along.
There is something almost uncomfortable about Solomon’s story.
Seven hundred wives.
Three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
And one haunting question:
Why did God allow it?
Maybe you have wondered this yourself.
If Solomon was blessed by God… if God gave him extraordinary wisdom… if Solomon built the magnificent Temple in Jerusalem… if Scripture preserves his words for generations of believers…
then why do we eventually find him surrounded by a thousand women?
Did God approve of this?
Did biblical kings somehow receive an exemption from God’s design for marriage?
And perhaps the harder question underneath all of those questions is this:
Why would God continue dealing with a man who knew better…and still wandered?
That question is much closer to us than we might want to admit.
Because most of us will never have seven hundred wives or three hundred concubines.
But many of us know what it is like to receive a warning from God…
and keep walking toward the thing He warned us about.
That is where Solomon’s story stops being ancient history.
It becomes a mirror.
Long before Solomon was born, God had already spoken about Israel’s future kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says of the king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.”
The Hebrew is striking.
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim, ve-lo yasur levavo.
In context, the warning is essentially:
He must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn aside.
Notice what God warned about.
Not merely scandal.
Not merely sexuality.
Not merely political complications.
The heart.
לְבָבוֹ — levavo — his heart.
God warned Israel’s kings about the destination before Solomon ever began the journey.
And centuries later, Scripture records something chillingly close to the language of that warning.
“King Solomon loved many strange women…”
Then comes the devastating total:
“And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines…”
And then 1 Kings 11:3 gives us the sentence that explains the tragedy:
“and his wives turned away his heart.”
There it is.
The warning.
Then the fulfillment.
God had said, in effect, “Do not multiply wives, lest his heart turn away.”
Solomon multiplied wives.
His heart turned away.
So we need to establish something immediately:
The Bible recording Solomon’s behavior does not mean God endorsed Solomon’s behavior.
Scripture often describes human sin with brutal honesty without prescribing it as God’s will.
The Bible tells us Cain murdered Abel.
That does not make murder holy.
It tells us David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged Uriah’s death.
That does not mean adultery and murder received divine approval.
It tells us Peter denied Jesus three times.
That does not mean denying Christ became acceptable.
And when Scripture tells us Solomon accumulated seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, it is not giving believers a model to imitate.
It is showing us what happened when a powerful man ignored a warning God had already given.
God’s patience must never be confused with God’s permission in the moral sense.
And God’s permission in providence must never be confused with His approval.
Sometimes one of the most frightening judgments God can allow is for a human being to keep walking down the road he stubbornly insists on traveling.
Solomon did not begin as the obvious villain of his story.
That is what makes this so unsettling.
He began with extraordinary promise.
When God appeared to Solomon and invited him to ask what he desired, Solomon did not initially ask for wealth, military domination, or long life.
He asked for an understanding heart so he could govern God’s people.
God was pleased with the request.
God gave him wisdom.
God gave him riches and honor.
Solomon built the Temple.
At its dedication, Solomon prayed one of the great prayers recorded in the Old Testament.
He knew theology.
He knew worship.
He knew wisdom.
He knew the commandments.
And apparently, knowing was not enough.
Read that slowly.
Knowing was not enough.
You can know Scripture and still need to obey Scripture.
You can speak beautifully about God while quietly allowing something else to occupy territory in your heart.
You can recognize wisdom and still refuse to live wisely.
You can have yesterday’s testimony and still face today’s temptation.
You can be used by God publicly while neglecting your heart privately.
Solomon’s downfall is frightening precisely because he was not ignorant.
He was wise.
Yet wisdom that is admired but not obeyed cannot save a person from the consequences of rebellion.
And perhaps that is where Solomon reaches across three thousand years and puts his hand on our shoulder.
Because your danger may not look like his.
Maybe your “thousand” is hidden inside your phone.
Maybe it is pornography that you keep promising will be the last time.
Maybe it is a relationship you already know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe applause.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe ambition.
Maybe the secret conversation you would never want your spouse to read.
Maybe the addiction you have learned to disguise.
Maybe you still sing in church while something inside you has been slowly drifting away from the God you sing about.
Nobody wakes up one morning with a completely hardened heart.
Drift usually happens by degrees.
A compromise.
Then an explanation.
Then another compromise.
Then a justification.
Then a habit.
Then eventually you look back and realize you have traveled miles from the place where you first stopped listening.
Solomon’s thousand women were not merely a sexual statistic.
They became part of a spiritual catastrophe.
First Kings specifically emphasizes that many of Solomon’s wives were foreign women from nations concerning which Israel had been warned because of the danger of being turned toward their gods.
This point must be handled carefully.
The biblical issue is not ethnicity.
Ruth was a Moabite, yet she turned toward the God of Israel and became part of the covenant community—and eventually part of the messianic line.
The issue in 1 Kings 11 is idolatry.
Solomon “clave unto these in love,” and as he grew older, his wives turned his heart after other gods.
The man who built a house for the name of the LORD eventually built high places associated with false worship.
Think about that tragedy.
Hands that helped construct the Temple of the LORD…
also constructed places connected with idolatry.
A heart that once prayed toward heaven…
became divided among rival loves.
This is what sin does.
It rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I have come to destroy you.”
It usually whispers:
“You can handle this.”
“You deserve this.”
“This is different.”
“God understands.”
“You can stop whenever you want.”
“It isn't affecting your faith.”
Until one day the thing you thought you possessed begins possessing you.
And Solomon proves something every generation desperately needs to remember:
A gift from God is not a substitute for faithfulness to God.
Intelligence will not protect a disobedient heart.
Success will not protect it.
Ministry will not protect it.
Money will not protect it.
Biblical knowledge will not protect it.
A reputation will not protect it.
You can be surrounded by evidence of God’s blessings and still allow your affections to wander.
But Solomon’s story contains another uncomfortable dimension.
Why did God not simply stop him?
Why allow Solomon to make these decisions at all?

Because throughout Scripture, God deals with human beings as morally responsible creatures. His sovereignty does not turn people into puppets, nor does His patience mean He approves of every decision He permits people to make.
God warned.
Solomon chose.
And consequences followed.
By 1 Kings 11:9, the language becomes heartbreaking:
“And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the LORD God of Israel…”
God’s response destroys the idea that Solomon’s marriages and subsequent idolatry carried divine approval.
The Lord confronts him and announces judgment upon his kingdom.
The kingdom will be torn.
Yet even there, astonishingly, judgment is restrained because of God’s covenant dealings connected with David.
Justice and mercy stand beside one another.
Solomon sins.
God does not call evil good.
Consequences come.
Yet God’s covenant purposes are not destroyed by Solomon’s failure.
And now we begin moving toward the greater King.
Because if Solomon’s story ended merely with the warning “do better,” we would still be in terrible trouble.
You and I need more than Solomon’s wisdom.
We need Solomon’s greater Son.
Jesus Himself said:
“behold, a greater than Solomon is here.”
The Greek expression is powerful:
πλεῖον Σολομῶνος ὧδε
pleion Solomōnos hōde
Something greater than Solomon is here.
Jesus is not another Solomon.
He is greater.
Solomon possessed wisdom given by God.
Christ is presented in the New Testament as the One in whom are hidden “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”
Solomon built a temple.
Jesus spoke of His body as the temple that would be raised.
Solomon’s kingdom fractured.
Christ’s kingdom endures.
Solomon’s heart turned.
Jesus remained obedient to the Father even unto death.
Solomon’s compromises helped bring judgment upon his kingdom.
Jesus took judgment upon Himself for sinners.
And suddenly the scandal of Solomon’s failure begins pointing us toward the necessity of grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls sin harmless.
Not grace that says repentance does not matter.
Real grace.
Grace purchased at a cross.
Grace where sin is taken so seriously that the Son of God bears its judgment.
Grace where sinners are loved so deeply that forgiveness is offered through Christ.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
God does not save us by pretending our rebellion was acceptable.
He saves sinners through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, righteousness and mercy are not enemies.
Christ bears sin.
Christ sheds His blood.
Christ dies.
Christ rises.
And people whose hearts have wandered can be called home.
That means the deepest question in this story may not actually be:
“How could Solomon have one thousand women?”
The question may be:
What is turning your heart right now?
Because Scripture did not preserve Solomon’s story so we could stare safely at another man’s scandal.
It preserved it as warning.
What have you multiplied in your life that is slowly subtracting God from the center?
What started small?
What have you renamed so you would not have to call it sin?
What warning from Scripture do you already understand intellectually but keep negotiating with privately?
What relationship has become more authoritative than Jesus?
What appetite keeps demanding another sacrifice?
What do you defend immediately because somewhere inside you know God has already touched the nerve?
This is where we stop talking about Solomon.
This is where the room becomes quiet.
Because maybe you know.
You know exactly what it is.
And perhaps nobody else knows.
But Christ does.
And here is what makes the Gospel breathtaking:
He is still calling you.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Because His grace is greater.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning house.
The New Testament word commonly translated “repent” is connected with μετανοέω — metanoeō: to repent, to change one’s mind, to turn in a transformed direction.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Peter wept bitterly.
But the Gospel calls us beyond emotion toward Christ.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
Confess.
Turn.
Ask for mercy.
Cut off the road that keeps carrying you back toward destruction.
And when you fall, do not run away from the only One who can cleanse you.
Run toward Him.
Maybe this article found you while you are exhausted from pretending.
Maybe people think you are strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you post Bible verses while fighting something nobody sees.
Maybe you love Jesus genuinely, but there is an area you have repeatedly refused to surrender.
Then hear this without theatrics:
Do not wait until your compromise becomes your captivity.
Solomon had wisdom.
He had wealth.
He had influence.
He had access.
He had almost everything the human heart imagines will finally satisfy it.
Yet Ecclesiastes—traditionally associated with Solomon—opens with the haunting cry:
“Vanity of vanities…all is vanity.”
Everything underneath the sun eventually fails when we ask it to become what only God can be.
Another woman cannot do it.
Another relationship cannot do it.
Another promotion cannot do it.
Another purchase cannot do it.
Another sexual experience cannot do it.
Another million cannot do it.
Another thousand cannot do it.
If one idol cannot satisfy the human heart, multiplying the idol will not heal the hunger.
Only God can occupy God's place.
That is why Jesus is not an accessory to the good life.
Jesus is life.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop hiding right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Not as a magical formula.
Not to perform spirituality for strangers.
Let it be an honest confession that says, “I am finished pretending that I do not need grace.”
Someone else reading those words may discover they are not the only believer fighting through the night.
If you need prayer, simply write:
You do not have to tell strangers every detail.
God knows the detail.
But sometimes healing begins when hiding ends.
Someone may be standing at the same prison door you once thought would never open.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose heart has been drifting.
The friend who stopped going to church.
The husband hiding pain behind silence.
The wife quietly carrying spiritual exhaustion.
The son who thinks he has gone too far.
The daughter who believes Christianity is only for people who have never made catastrophic mistakes.
The believer whose compromise is slowly becoming bondage.
Or send this privately if their struggle should remain private.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be treated as purchasing God’s favor, proving your devotion, or earning spiritual merit; salvation and grace cannot be bought.
There will probably come a night when its question hits differently:
What is turning my heart?
But before you leave, remember the man at the center of this story.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom and still discovered that a human heart can wander.
So guard yours.
Do not confuse God’s patience with approval.
Do not mistake His blessings for permission to ignore His Word.
Do not allow the gifts He gave you to become substitutes for the God who gave them.
And above everything else, do not let shame convince you that because you wandered, you can never come home.
The Bible is filled with deeply flawed people precisely because its ultimate Hero is not Solomon.
Not David.
Not Peter.
Not you.
Not me.
Jesus Christ.
The King whose heart never turned away.
The King who did not exploit His power but humbled Himself.
The King who came looking for sinners.
The King who carried a cross.
The King who was buried.
The King who rose.
The King who still receives repentant people with scarred histories and divided hearts and begins making them new.
Solomon’s thousand women tell us what happens when the heart keeps reaching for what cannot satisfy.
The cross tells us what God was willing to do to bring wandering hearts home.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy Christ offers.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
The scandal may explain where you have been—but grace can change where you are going.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SACRIFICE THAT KEEPS CLIMBING OFF THE ALTAR
paragraphs:
THE SACRIFICE THAT KEEPS CLIMBING OFF THE ALTAR
Understanding Romans 12:1 — What Becoming a “Living Sacrifice” Looks Like Today
There is something almost unsettling about the phrase Paul uses.
A living sacrifice.
Not a dead sacrifice.
Not something surrendered once and forgotten.
Living.
Breathing.
Thinking.
Wanting.
Remembering.
Still carrying desires. Still feeling temptation. Still capable of crawling away.
And perhaps that is exactly why Romans 12:1 reaches so deeply into the modern Christian heart.
Because dying once sounds dramatic.
But surrendering again tomorrow morning?
When nobody applauds?
When the temptation comes back?
When forgiveness still hurts?
When obedience costs you something?
When God touches the part of your life you quietly hoped Christianity would allow you to keep?
That is where the altar becomes real.
Paul writes:
—Romans 12:1, KJV
The Greek text contains this remarkable phrase:
παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν
parastēsai ta sōmata hymōn thysian zōsan
Literally, Paul is calling believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice.
And before we turn those words into another inspirational Christian slogan, we need to notice something important.
Paul does not begin with the sacrifice.
He begins with mercy.
“Therefore…”
That word matters.
Romans 12 does not fall out of the sky as an isolated command demanding that frightened people somehow earn God's approval through extreme devotion.
Paul has already spent eleven chapters unfolding the catastrophe of human sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
Humanity is guilty.
Sin is real.
Judgment is deserved.
Our religious performance cannot justify us.
And yet God acted.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ was raised.
Justification comes through faith.
There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Nothing can separate God's people from the love of God in Christ.
Then comes Romans 12.
Therefore.
In other words:
Because of what God has done…
Because Christ has shown mercy…
Because salvation cannot be purchased by your goodness…
Because Jesus gave Himself for sinners…
Now give yourself to Him.
Christian surrender is not the entrance fee for mercy.
It is the response to mercy already received.
That changes everything.
Because without the first eleven chapters of Romans, “be a living sacrifice” can become spiritual exhaustion.
Try harder.
Sacrifice more.
Prove yourself.
Make God proud.
Maybe then He will love you.
But that is not Paul's Gospel.
The altar of Romans 12 is not where you purchase God's mercy.
It is where a person overwhelmed by God's mercy finally whispers:
“Jesus, after everything You have done for me… how could I keep pretending my life belongs only to me?”
And suddenly this verse becomes painfully personal.
Because most of us are willing to give God something.
The question is whether we are willing to give Him ourselves.
We give Him Sunday morning but guard Monday afternoon.
We give Him worship songs but protect our bitterness.
We give Him public Christianity while hiding private compromises.
We ask Him to bless our plans without asking whether our plans honor Him.
We surrender our crisis because we desperately need Him…
then reclaim control when life becomes comfortable again.
We say, “Lord, use me.”
But sometimes what we really mean is:
“Use me without inconveniencing me.”
“Change me without exposing me.”
“Lead me wherever You want, provided it is somewhere I already wanted to go.”
“Forgive my sins, but please do not touch the one I am emotionally attached to.”
And Romans 12:1 quietly walks into that carefully negotiated Christianity and places one word on the table:
Bodies.
“Present your bodies…”
Not merely your religious thoughts.
Not merely your church attendance.
Not merely your Christian vocabulary.
Your body.
Your eyes.
Your mouth.
Your hands.
Your sexuality.
Your appetite.
Your energy.
Your money-making ability.
Your schedule.
Your phone at 1:17 in the morning.
Your conversations when the pastor is nowhere nearby.
Your behavior toward the person who wounded you.
Your integrity when dishonesty would be profitable.
Your physical presence beside somebody who needs compassion.
Your willingness to walk away from what feeds your flesh even when part of you desperately wants to stay.
Christianity is profoundly spiritual, but biblical spirituality is never permission to separate “spiritual life” from embodied life.
Jesus purchased the whole person.
Paul uses παραστῆσαι — parastēsai, from paristēmi, language that can carry the idea of presenting, placing at someone's disposal, or offering oneself.
Earlier in Romans, Paul had already used similar language:
“Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God…”
—Romans 6:13, KJV
There it is again.
Who gets your hands?
Who gets your mouth?
Who gets your imagination?
Who gets your strength?
Who gets your body?
Who gets you?
Because something will.
The modern world loves telling us, “Your body belongs to you.”
Scripture confronts the Christian with something far more radical.
“You are not your own.”
Paul tells believers elsewhere:
“For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body…”
—1 Corinthians 6:20, KJV
Bought.
With a price.
And the price was not silver.
Not gold.
Not religious achievement.
It was Christ Himself.
So when Paul says θυσίαν ζῶσαν — thysian zōsan, “a living sacrifice,” he creates an image his original hearers would have understood with uncomfortable clarity.
Sacrifice meant cost.
Sacrifice meant something was placed before God.
But this sacrifice lives.
That means the Christian altar is not merely one emotional moment at conversion.
There may be unforgettable moments of surrender.
But then Tuesday comes.
The alarm rings.
The old anger returns.
Someone insults you.
Someone attractive messages you.
The loneliness comes back.
Money gets tight.
Your pride gets wounded.
Your prayers appear unanswered.
Nobody notices your obedience.
And the sacrifice is still alive.
This is where surrender stops being poetry.
A living sacrifice may look like closing the browser when nobody would ever know what you watched.
It may look like refusing to participate in gossip even though silence makes you feel excluded.
It may look like returning money that you could probably get away with keeping.
It may look like apologizing without attaching a defense to the apology.
It may mean ending a relationship that repeatedly pulls you away from Christ.
It may mean staying faithful in a marriage when feelings are wounded and choosing the hard work of biblical love, truth, repentance, forgiveness, and appropriate boundaries.
It may look like serving somebody who cannot improve your reputation.
It may mean telling the truth when lying would save your image.
It may mean forgiving someone while still wisely refusing to pretend that trust has automatically been restored.
It may mean giving generously instead of worshiping financial security.
It may mean refusing to make political allegiance, career success, romance, popularity, comfort, possessions, pleasure, or even ministry itself into an idol.
Sometimes the altar is dramatic.
Most days…
it looks remarkably ordinary.
That may be one of the hardest truths to accept.
We imagine surrender happening under bright lights while emotional music plays.
But some of the holiest sacrifices God receives happen in kitchens.
Bedrooms.
Offices.
Cars.
Hospital corridors.
School hallways.
Quiet bank transfers.
Deleted messages.
Unsent angry replies.
Closed doors.
Private prayers.
Moments when nobody on earth realizes that a war just happened inside somebody's heart…
and Jesus won.
Paul calls this sacrifice ἁγίαν — hagian.
Holy.
Set apart for God.
And εὐάρεστον τῷ θεῷ — euareston tō theō.
Pleasing to God.
Then comes a phrase translated in several ways:
τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν ὑμῶν — tēn logikēn latreian hymōn.
The KJV says “your reasonable service.”
Other major translations render the phrase along the lines of “spiritual worship” or “true and proper worship.”

The Greek adjective λογικός — logikos has generated considerable discussion because its semantic range does not map neatly onto one English expression. The point should therefore not be reduced to a clever claim that only one English rendering is possible.
But the larger context is unmistakable.
Paul is describing worship that encompasses the surrendered life.
Worship is not merely what comes out of your mouth during a song.
Worship is what happens when your whole embodied existence is offered to God because His mercy has captured you.
Which means you can sing with your hands raised…
and still refuse the altar.
You can know every lyric.
Quote verses.
Share Christian posts.
Wear Christian clothing.
Own several Bibles.
Say “God first” in your biography.
And still maintain carefully guarded rooms where Jesus is treated more like a visitor than Lord.
That is why Romans 12:1 is dangerous to comfortable Christianity.
It asks a question we cannot answer with aesthetics:
What does Jesus actually have permission to change?
Your habits?
Your relationships?
Your spending?
Your ambitions?
Your entertainment?
Your temper?
Your secret life?
Your sexuality?
Your pride?
Your resentment?
Your need to be admired?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your obsession with controlling what happens next?
There are people reading this right now who love Jesus…
but are exhausted from repeatedly climbing off the altar.
You surrender.
Then take it back.
Repent.
Then stumble.
Promise God you are finished.
Then discover that temptation remembers your address.
And somewhere along the way you begin wondering whether God must finally be tired of you.
Listen carefully.
Romans 12:1 begins with the mercies of God.
Not your flawless record.
Not your heroic discipline.
Not your ability to maintain a perfect spiritual streak.
Mercy.
This does not make sin harmless.
Grace never turns rebellion into righteousness.
The Gospel calls us to repentance.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could decorate our chains with Christian vocabulary and continue loving the slavery He came to break.
But when a believer falls, the answer is not to hide from Christ.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Bring the wounded, embarrassed, trembling sacrifice back onto the altar.
Again.
Not because repeated sin should be treated casually.
But because your hope was never your ability to save yourself.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you have spent years hiding.
People think you are strong.
Your family thinks you are fine.
Your church friends see the polished version.
You encourage everyone else while quietly wondering who would stay if they knew everything.
Jesus already knows.
That should terrify hypocrisy.
But for the repentant sinner, it is also breathtakingly beautiful.
Because the One who knows the entire story is the One who went to the cross.
The scandal is not merely that you sinned.
The greater scandal of grace is that the holy Son of God willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.”
—Romans 5:6, KJV
Not the impressive.
Not the cleaned-up.
Not people who had finally made themselves worthy.
The ungodly.
And this is where your scandal can collide with His grace.
Maybe your past is ugly.
Maybe your present is messy.
Maybe there are chapters you would burn before letting another human being read them.
But the Gospel does not say your sin gets the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Repentance is not pretending the old chapter never happened.
Grace does something better.
It takes guilty people, washes them through Christ, reconciles them to God, and begins transforming lives that once seemed irredeemable.
That is our heartbeat:
Not because Jesus edits sin into something respectable.
He does not.
He calls sin what it is.
He calls sinners to repent.
Then He does what our self-improvement could never accomplish.
He forgives.
Cleanses.
Redeems.
Restores.
Transforms.
And now the forgiven sinner climbs onto the altar not to become loved…
but because in Christ, mercy has already found them.
So what does becoming a living sacrifice look like today?
It looks like waking tomorrow morning and saying:
“Jesus, my body belongs to You.”
“My plans belong to You.”
“My mouth belongs to You.”
“My sexuality belongs to You.”
“My career belongs to You.”
“My money belongs to You.”
“My wounds belong to You.”
“My future belongs to You.”
“My reputation belongs to You.”
“My gifts belong to You.”
“My weakness belongs to You.”
“Even the parts of me that are still learning how to surrender belong to You.”
And then you live the prayer.
Imperfectly perhaps.
Sometimes painfully.
Always dependent upon grace.
Because Romans 12:1 is immediately followed by Romans 12:2, where Paul speaks of refusing conformity to this age and being transformed through the renewing of the mind.
God is not merely interested in restraining behavior.
He transforms people.
The Gospel does not merely teach your old self some religious manners.
Christ makes His people new.
And that transformation continues.
So maybe the question today is not whether you have ever “given your life to Jesus.”
Maybe the uncomfortable question is:
What did you take back?
What is sitting in your hands right now that once belonged on the altar?
A relationship?
An addiction?
A grudge?
A dream?
A secret?
A reputation?
A fear?
Control?
You do not need another inspirational sentence telling you that you are powerful enough to fix yourself.
You need mercy.
You need repentance.
You need Christ.
And perhaps right now, somewhere nobody else can see you, your prayer needs to become painfully simple:
“Jesus, I keep crawling off the altar.
Have mercy on me.
Forgive what I have excused.
Expose what I have hidden.
Break what enslaves me.
Renew my mind.
Teach me obedience.
Take what I keep trying to reclaim.
I am Yours.”
If that prayer exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn this into another article you emotionally react to and then forget.
There is no trophy for pretending.
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of coming back into the light.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore that name.
Not to embarrass them.
Not because you assume you know their secret struggle.
It is life under the mercy and lordship of Jesus Christ.
Somebody you know may never walk through the doors of your church.
They may ignore an invitation to a Bible study.
If you genuinely want your online life to glorify God, then use what He has placed in your hands for His purposes.
A profile can advertise ourselves.
Or it can point toward Christ.
A share button looks insignificant until you remember there is a human soul on the other side of the screen.
Because the altar is waiting tomorrow.
There may come a morning when surrender feels harder than it does right now.
Come back.
Read Romans 12 again.
Remember the order.
Mercy first.
Then surrender.
Financial support is not what glorifies God by itself.
But generosity, stewardship, sharing truth, supporting faithful Gospel work, and using what God has entrusted to us for His purposes can certainly be ways believers glorify Him.
And there is something larger behind these articles.
The goal is not merely more content.
It is deeper discipleship.
More Scripture.
More truth.
More repentance.
More healing rooted in Christ.
More spiritual nourishment.
More believers equipped to stand when culture tells them to bow.
More wounded people discovering that their darkest chapter does not have authority over the final chapter Jesus writes.
Then invite someone else.
And please do not leave without answering the question Romans 12:1 has quietly been asking you from the beginning.
Not:
“How religious are you?”
Not:
“How emotional did this make you?”
Not even:
“How much Scripture do you know?”
But:
What is still missing from the altar?
Name it before God.
Bring it into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy purchased by Christ.
And present yourself again.
Alive.
Breathing.
Still tempted.
Still growing.
Still dependent.
But His.
Because perhaps the most beautiful thing about a living sacrifice is not that it never struggles to crawl away.
It is that the mercy of God keeps teaching surrendered hearts where they belong.
The altar was never where Jesus asked you to earn His love; it is where His mercy finally becomes too beautiful to keep anything back.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SATAN EXPLOIT SEXUAL TEMPTATION? THE BATTLE YOU THOUGHT WAS ONLY ABOUT YOUR BODY MAY BE REACHING FOR YOUR SOUL
paragraphs: CAN SATAN EXPLOIT SEXUAL TEMPTATION? THE BATTLE YOU THOUGHT WAS ONLY ABOUT YOUR BODY MAY BE REACHING FOR YOUR SOUL
Scripture gives a disturbing answer—but it also reveals why sexual temptation does not have to become your identity, your master, or the final chapter of your story.
There is a moment in temptation that almost nobody talks about.
Not the moment after.
Not the guilt.
Not the browser history you deleted.
Not the message you wish you had never sent.
Not the relationship that crossed a boundary.
Not the secret fantasy you would be horrified for anyone at church to discover.
I mean the moment before all of that.
That strange, quiet moment when something enters your mind and begins negotiating.
Just once.
Nobody will know.
You deserve this.
You can repent afterward.
It isn't hurting anyone.
You're lonely.
Your marriage is struggling.
You've been strong long enough.
God understands.
And sometimes the most dangerous temptation does not feel like rebellion at first.
It feels like relief.
That is precisely why the question matters:
Can Satan exploit sexual temptation?
The biblical answer is yes.
But perhaps not in the simplistic way people sometimes imagine.

The Bible does not teach that every sexual thought is Satan personally whispering into your ear. Scripture refuses to let us escape responsibility that easily. James writes that each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.
The Greek is painfully revealing:
ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος
hekastos de peirazetai hypo tēs idias epithymias exelkomenos kai deleazomenos
“But each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.”
—James 1:14

That word ἐπιθυμία — epithymia speaks of desire, craving, or longing. Desire itself must be understood according to its context, but James is describing desire that has become an enticement away from obedience to God.
Then he gives us the progression.
Desire conceives.
Sin is born.
Sin grows.
And death follows.
James does not say, “The devil made you do it.”
He reaches closer.
Your desires matter.
Your choices matter.
What you repeatedly entertain matters.
But that is not the entire biblical picture.
Because in one of the New Testament's most striking passages concerning marriage and sexual self-control, Paul explicitly warns believers that Satan can exploit sexual vulnerability.
Speaking to husbands and wives about mutually agreed periods of abstinence for prayer, Paul tells them to come together again:
ἵνα μὴ πειράζῃ ὑμᾶς ὁ Σατανᾶς διὰ τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν
hina mē peirazē hymas ho Satanas dia tēn akrasian hymōn
“So that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”
—1 Corinthians 7:5
Read that again.
Paul does not treat sexual vulnerability as imaginary.
He does not treat Satan as imaginary.
And he does not treat human weakness as imaginary.
He places spiritual attack and human vulnerability in the same sentence.
That changes the conversation.
Satan does not need to manufacture every desire in order to exploit one.
He does not need to create loneliness to weaponize loneliness.
He does not need to invent marital frustration to exploit marital frustration.
He does not need to create your wounds to tempt you toward sinful ways of medicating them.
He does not need to create sexual desire—God created human sexuality. What the enemy can exploit is desire detached from God's design, truth, covenant faithfulness, holiness, love, and self-control.
This is where many Christians become confused.
Sex itself is not the enemy.
Your body is not the enemy.
Marriage is not dirty.
Sexual desire is not proof that you are spiritually defective.
God created humanity male and female, and Genesis presents the marital union of husband and wife without shame before sin enters the world.
Genesis 2:25 says:
וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ
Vayyihyu sheneihem arummim, ha'adam ve'ishto, velo yitboshashu.
“The man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
Sexuality existed before the Fall.
Shame was not its creator.
Satan was not its creator.
God was.
The corruption comes when something God designed is pulled outside His will and made to serve another master.
And isn't that often how temptation works?
The enemy rarely needs to persuade you that evil is beautiful.
He only needs to take something good and persuade you to pursue it in a way God has forbidden.
Appetite without obedience.
Pleasure without holiness.
Intimacy without covenant faithfulness.
A body without seeing the person made in God's image.
Desire without self-control.
Secrecy without accountability.
Pleasure without asking what it is doing to your soul.
And eventually, what began as “I want this” can become “I need this.”
Then “I need this” becomes “I can't stop this.”
Then “I can't stop this” becomes “This is just who I am.”
That last sentence can become a prison.
Because once sin persuades you that your bondage is your identity, you may stop fighting what Christ came to redeem.
Maybe nobody knows your battle.
Maybe people see you worship while you remember what you watched last night.
Maybe your spouse thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you keep deleting and reinstalling the same app.
Maybe you promised God, with tears in your eyes, that it was the last time.
And then it happened again.
Maybe your struggle is pornography.
Maybe it is adultery.
Maybe it is lust.
Maybe it is sexual messaging you keep rationalizing because nothing “physical” has happened.
Maybe it is fantasizing about someone who is not your spouse.
Maybe you are emotionally starving and have begun looking toward forbidden places for something that feels like affection.
Maybe you crossed a line years ago and Satan has discovered something even more useful than the temptation itself:
your shame.
First comes the invitation:
“Do it.”
Then, after you fall, comes the accusation:
“How could someone like you call yourself a Christian?”
Do you see the trap?
Temptation tries to lead you toward sin.
Accusation then tries to keep you away from the Savior.
Revelation calls Satan “the accuser,” and this pattern is worth recognizing. The enemy wants sin to appear small before you commit it and forgiveness to appear impossible afterward.
But the Gospel destroys both lies.
Sin is more serious than temptation tells you.
Grace is greater than accusation tells you.
Jesus does not minimize sexual sin.
He goes deeper than outward behavior.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Christ takes the commandment against adultery and exposes lustful intent in the heart. Christianity therefore cannot be reduced to, “At least I didn't physically do anything.”
Jesus wants the heart.
The imagination.
The eyes.
The desires.
The secret room nobody else enters.
Not because He delights in humiliating you.
Because He came to make you whole.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6 that believers are to flee sexual immorality. The Greek command is strikingly direct:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can get.
Not keep it in your phone because you think you are spiritually strong enough.
Flee.
There are battles where standing your ground is courage.
There are temptations where running is wisdom.
Joseph understood this centuries before Paul wrote those words.
When Potiphar's wife repeatedly attempted to seduce him, Joseph did not remain in the room to prove his spiritual maturity.
He ran.
He left his garment behind.
There are moments when protecting your soul matters more than protecting your appearance.
Sometimes victory looks remarkably undramatic.
Close the tab.
Delete the contact.
Leave the room.
Stop the conversation.
Cancel the secret meeting.
Move the phone out of the bedroom.
Tell your spouse the truth where appropriate and safe.
Call a mature Christian you trust.
Ask for accountability.
Stop feeding what you keep begging God to kill.
And pray.
Not as a substitute for practical obedience, but as part of it.
Jesus told His disciples:
γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσεύχεσθε, ἵνα μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς πειρασμόν
Grēgoreite kai proseuchesthe, hina mē eiselthēte eis peirasmon.
“Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation.”
—Matthew 26:41
Watch.
And pray.
Spiritual vigilance and dependence on God belong together.
There is another truth someone desperately needs to hear.
Being tempted is not identical to committing sin.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet remained without sin. Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
So the arrival of temptation is not the same thing as surrender to temptation.
That distinction matters enormously to Christians trapped in obsessive shame.
The question is not merely whether temptation knocks.
The question is what happens when it arrives.
Do you entertain it?
Feed it?
Return to it?
Arrange circumstances around it?
Hide it?
Or do you bring the battle into the light and turn toward Christ?

Paul tells the Thessalonians that God's will includes their sanctification and abstaining from sexual immorality, learning to possess or control one's own body in holiness and honor (1 Thessalonians 4:3–5).
Biblical sexual holiness is therefore not merely God saying “no.”
It is God saying:
Your body has meaning.
Other people's bodies have meaning.
Sex has meaning.
Covenant has meaning.
Faithfulness has meaning.
What you do when nobody is watching has meaning.
And according to 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, the Christian's body belongs to God.
“You were bought with a price.”
That price was not silver.
It was not gold.
It was Christ.
Now we arrive at the place where shame desperately wants to stop you from reading.
What if you already failed?
What if this is not theoretical?
What if sexual sin has already damaged your conscience, your marriage, your relationships, or the way you see yourself?
What if you knew better?
What if you were a Christian when you did it?
What if you have repented before and fallen again?
Does Jesus still want you?
Look at the people Jesus met.
Look at the scandal surrounding His ministry.
Look at the woman in John 8 brought before Him in the aftermath of adultery.
Jesus did not call evil good.
Neither did He hand a broken sinner over to self-righteous executioners.
His response held mercy and holiness together.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
And then:
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Grace did not erase repentance.
Repentance did not erase grace.
That is Jesus.
The Christ who refuses to redefine darkness as light is the same Christ who kneels beside people everybody else is ready to destroy.
This is why the Gospel is neither permissiveness nor hopeless condemnation.
At the cross, Jesus does not pretend sin is harmless.
He demonstrates just how costly sin is.
And then He bears the judgment sinners could never remove from themselves.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
—2 Corinthians 5:21
This is where sexual shame meets something stronger than itself.
The blood of Christ.
If you are in Christ, your worst sexual failure does not possess greater saving power than His cross.
But grace is not permission to return comfortably to bondage.
Romans 6 asks the question directly: should Christians continue in sin so that grace may increase?
Paul's answer is emphatic.
By no means.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace begins transforming.
Repentance is not saying, “I'm sorry I got caught.”
It is not crying tonight while preserving tomorrow's opportunity to repeat the same sin.
Biblical repentance involves turning.
Confession.
Truth.
Changed direction.
And sometimes painfully practical decisions.
Some people reading this need to stop calling an affair a “connection.”
Some need to stop calling pornography “stress relief.”
Some need to stop calling lust “just being human.”
Some need to stop blaming Satan for choices they are actively protecting.
And some need to stop believing Satan's accusation that because they have failed sexually, God could never restore them.
Both lies keep you imprisoned.
One makes sin too small.
The other makes Jesus too small.
Neither is the Gospel.
Listen carefully.
Satan may exploit sexual temptation.
Your own disordered desires can entice you.
The world can normalize what God forbids.
Habits can strengthen pathways of temptation.
Secrecy can give sin room to grow.
But none of those realities makes obedience impossible for the person who belongs to Christ.

First Corinthians 10:13 tells believers that temptation is common to humanity and that God is faithful; He will not allow His people to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation provides a way of escape so they can endure it.
Sometimes the way of escape is not spectacular.
It is the door you need to walk through.
The confession you need to make.
The boundary you need to establish.
The relationship you need to end.
The device you need to surrender.
The accountability you have been avoiding.
The Scripture you need to obey instead of merely highlighting.
The prayer you need to pray before temptation becomes a plan.

And if your struggle has become compulsive or deeply entrenched, seeking wise pastoral care and qualified professional help is not an admission that Jesus is insufficient. It can be one of the means through which you stop hiding and begin walking truthfully toward healing and obedience.
You do not defeat darkness by becoming better at hiding in it.
You bring darkness into the light.
First John 1:9 gives repentant sinners extraordinary hope: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Not some unrighteousness.
All.

That does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear. Betrayal can leave wounds. Trust may require a long rebuilding process. Relationships may carry scars. Forgiveness from God does not make every temporal consequence vanish.
But consequences are not the same thing as condemnation.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not so you could study Satan.
So you could finally stop hiding from Jesus.
Perhaps the question underneath “Can Satan exploit sexual temptation?” was always more personal:
“Can Jesus still rescue me here?”
Yes.
Not by pretending your sin does not matter.
By doing something infinitely greater.
Forgiving it.
Cleansing you.
Teaching you to walk differently.
Giving you His Spirit.
Calling you out of darkness.
Restoring what shame told you was permanently destroyed.
Your story does not have to end in the room where you fell.
Peter's story did not end beside the fire where he denied Christ.
Paul's story did not end with Christians terrified of his name.
The cross itself looked like history's greatest defeat until an empty tomb announced that God was writing something no darkness could stop.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting for holiness.
Send it privately to the believer who has slowly disappeared into shame.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, not by financial contribution.
Leave thinking about Jesus.
The One who was tempted yet never sinned.
The One who touched people religious society avoided.
The One who told sinners the truth without abandoning them to their shame.
The One who carried our sin to Calvary.
The One who rose.
The One who still receives the repentant.
The One who can teach your eyes to look differently, your mind to think differently, your body to live differently, and your heart to desire holiness more deeply.
Sexual temptation may know where you are vulnerable.
Satan may know where you have fallen before.
Your past may know your name.
But none of them gets to write the final sentence of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
The place where shame keeps pointing and saying, “This is where your story ended,” may become the very place where Jesus writes, “This is where grace found you.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEMEN, WASHING, AND RITUAL PURITY: THE BIBLE PASSAGE NOBODY VOLUNTEERS TO TEACH
paragraphs:
SEMEN, WASHING, AND RITUAL PURITY: THE BIBLE PASSAGE NOBODY VOLUNTEERS TO TEACH
Leviticus says a man who releases semen must wash and remain “unclean until evening.” But if you think that means sex is dirty, semen is sinful, or God is ashamed of the human body, you may have completely misunderstood one of the Bible’s most uncomfortable passages.
There are Bible passages people underline.
There are passages people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses printed on coffee mugs, stitched onto shirts, written inside wedding cards, and posted over sunsets on Facebook.
And then there is Leviticus 15.
Nobody seems to volunteer for that sermon.
Nobody walks into a Christian bookstore asking where the inspirational merchandise about bodily discharges is kept.
Yet there it is.
In the Bible.
Not hidden in some forbidden manuscript.
Not added by an embarrassed medieval theologian.
Right there in Scripture.
And perhaps our discomfort with it reveals something important—not about the Bible, but about us.
Because God is willing to speak about parts of embodied human existence that religious people sometimes prefer to pretend do not exist.
Leviticus 15:16 begins:
“וְאִישׁ כִּי־תֵצֵא מִמֶּנּוּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע…”
Ve’ish ki-tetze mimennu shikhvat-zara…
The central Hebrew expression is שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע — shikhvat zeraʿ, an expression referring to an emission of semen, literally built around the ideas of “lying” and “seed.”
The verse continues:
“וְרָחַץ בַּמַּיִם אֶת־כָּל־בְּשָׂרוֹ וְטָמֵא עַד־הָעָרֶב”
Verachatz bammayim et-kol-besaro, vetame ad-ha‘arev.
In straightforward English:
He is to wash his whole body with water and remain ritually impure until evening.
That last sentence is where centuries of unnecessary shame can begin if we read the Bible carelessly.
Because Scripture does not say:
“He has sinned.”
It does not say:
“God is disgusted with him.”
It does not say:
“His sexuality has made him morally corrupt.”
It says he becomes טָמֵא — tameʾ.
Ritually impure.
That distinction matters enormously.
In the world of Leviticus, “unclean” does not automatically mean “sinful.”
Read that again, especially if someone once used religious language to make you ashamed of having a human body.
Ritual impurity and moral guilt are not identical categories.
A person could become ritually impure through ordinary bodily circumstances without having committed a moral transgression.
That changes everything.

Leviticus 15 is concerned with bodily discharges. It discusses abnormal male discharge, seminal emission, menstruation, abnormal female bleeding, washing, waiting, and the boundaries surrounding Israel’s sanctuary.
The chapter eventually tells us why these regulations mattered so seriously: Israel was to be guarded from impurity because God’s tabernacle stood among them.
This is sacred-space language.
God had chosen to dwell among His people.
And approaching His sanctuary was not treated casually.
There were boundaries between common and holy, clean and unclean, ordinary human existence and the concentrated holiness associated with God’s dwelling place.
That means Leviticus 15:16 is not God announcing that semen is evil.
In fact, the next verses make that interpretation extremely difficult.
If semen gets onto clothing or leather, the affected material is washed and remains impure until evening.
Then comes verse 18.
A man and woman have sexual relations involving seminal emission, and both wash and remain impure until evening.
Notice what the passage does not do.
It does not condemn the married couple for having sex.
It does not command a sacrifice for sexual immorality merely because intercourse occurred.
It does not describe marital intimacy itself as rebellion against God.
Instead, it places the bodily event within Israel’s ritual purity system.
There is an enormous difference between saying, “Your body has entered a temporary ritual condition,” and saying, “You have committed moral evil.”
Confuse those categories and you can manufacture shame God never commanded.
And some people reading this know exactly what religious shame feels like.
Maybe nobody explained the difference to you.
Maybe Christianity was introduced to you mostly through warnings.
Don’t touch.
Don’t feel.
Don’t desire.
Don’t ask.
Don’t admit.
Don’t talk about your body.
And certainly don’t tell anyone what you are struggling with.
So you learned something churches rarely realize they are teaching.
You learned how to hide.
You learned how to smile while carrying questions you thought would disgust everybody in the room.
Maybe your struggle went beyond innocent questions.
Maybe pornography became the place you ran when loneliness became unbearable.
Maybe lust started quietly and became a prison.
Maybe masturbation became tangled with compulsion, fantasy, secrecy, shame, or habits you desperately wanted to escape.
Maybe sexual sin really did enter the picture.
If so, Scripture does not help us by pretending sin is harmless.
Jesus certainly did not.
Christ takes sexual holiness deeper than external behavior. He confronts lust within the heart. The apostles call believers away from sexual immorality and toward holiness.
Grace never requires us to rename darkness as light.
But neither does holiness require us to call everything about the human body dirty.
There is a difference between having a body and using that body sinfully.
There is a difference between biological function and lust.
There is a difference between ritual impurity under the Mosaic covenant and moral rebellion against God.
There is a difference between conviction and humiliation.
And somebody desperately needs that distinction tonight.
Because conviction says:
“Come home.”
Shame says:
“Hide.”
Conviction exposes the wound because God intends to heal.
Condemnation whispers that you are the wound and therefore should never let anyone see you.
One voice leads you toward Christ.
The other makes you run into the shadows.
And humanity has been running into shadows for a very long time.
Long before Leviticus.
Long before Israel.
Long before the tabernacle.
There was a garden.
There was nakedness without shame.
There was intimacy without corruption.
There was humanity standing before God with nothing to conceal.
Then sin entered.
And suddenly Adam and Eve realized they were naked.
They covered themselves.
They hid.
Listen carefully to the movement of the story.
Sin.
Shame.
Covering.
Hiding.
Then God came looking.
“Where are you?”
God was not confused about Adam’s GPS coordinates.
The question exposed a spiritual catastrophe.
Adam had moved from fellowship into hiding.
And humanity has been sewing fig leaves ever since.
Some fig leaves look religious.
Some look respectable.
Some look like Sunday clothes and Christian vocabulary.
Some look like browser histories being erased at 2:13 in the morning.
Some look like marriages where nobody tells the truth anymore.
Some look like pastors terrified somebody will discover they are struggling.
Some look like teenagers convinced God hates them because nobody ever explained the difference between temptation, bodily development, lust, ritual categories, and deliberate sin.
Some look like grown adults still carrying shame somebody handed them when they were fourteen.
And then Scripture does something astonishing.
It keeps moving toward Jesus.
The purity laws of Leviticus teach us that the presence of the holy God is not trivial.
God is not merely a spiritual accessory.
His holiness is not decorative.
Sin is not imaginary.
Defilement is not meaningless.
Human beings cannot stroll into divine holiness on whatever terms they invent.
But the biblical story does not end with humanity standing outside.
It moves toward a Savior who comes to us.
And when Jesus arrives, something breathtaking begins happening around purity.
People everyone else avoids start approaching Him.
Lepers.
Bleeding people.
Broken people.
People carrying scandal.
People carrying histories.
People carrying bodies that have failed them.
People carrying sins they cannot undo.
In Mark 5, a woman has suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
Twelve years.
Think about that.
Not twelve minutes of embarrassment.
Not twelve days.
Twelve years.
She has suffered physically and financially. She has spent what she had seeking help.
Then she moves through a crowd toward Jesus.
She touches His garment.
And instead of her uncleanness overpowering Christ, Christ’s power overwhelms her condition.
The bleeding stops.
Jesus does not recoil.
He does not say, “How dare you touch Me?”
He calls her:
“Daughter.”
Imagine how that word sounded after twelve years of suffering.
Daughter.
That is what Jesus does with people who have been reduced to their condition.
The crowd sees the problem.
Jesus sees the person.
Religion can sometimes turn people into labels.
Addict.
Impure.
Divorced.
Pornographer.
Adulterer.
Failure.
Backslider.
Dirty.
Jesus does not deny sin or suffering, but neither does He reduce human beings to their worst chapter.
He restores people.
And eventually He goes somewhere even more shocking.
To the cross.
There, the One who is truly clean stands where the unclean belong.
The sinless One bears sin.
The righteous One is numbered with transgressors.
The beloved Son enters our disgrace.
Jesus does not save us by pretending we were already clean.
He saves us by doing what we could never do for ourselves.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally the story of dirty people learning how to scrub harder.
It is the story of a holy Savior cleansing people who could never cleanse themselves from sin.
Water could wash Israelite skin.
Time could bring ritual impurity to its appointed end.
Priestly procedures could restore ceremonial access where the Law prescribed them.
But soap cannot wash guilt from a conscience.
A shower cannot cleanse adultery.
A bath cannot remove pornography from the heart.
Water cannot erase hatred.
Religious performance cannot undo rebellion.
You need something deeper.
You need redemption.
You need forgiveness.
You need Christ.
The New Testament takes us there with extraordinary force.
Hebrews speaks about purification reaching the conscience and points us toward the blood of Christ.
First John declares that the blood of Jesus cleanses from sin.
Paul tells believers that some of them once lived in devastating forms of sin, and then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in Scripture:
“But you were washed…”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not because they successfully edited their past.
Not because nobody found out.
Not because their scandal suddenly became acceptable.
Because Jesus Christ intervened.
This is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Not from scandal to pretending.
Not from scandal to public relations.
Not from scandal to religious camouflage.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that sounds beautiful until your own scandal enters the sentence.
Then suddenly theology becomes personal.
What about what you watched?
What about what you did?
What about the affair?
What about the fantasy?
What about the person you used?
What about the years you wasted?
What about the secret account?
What about what happened behind the locked door?
What about the promises to God you broke again three days later?
What about the thing you cannot bring yourself to type into a comment because even seeing the words makes your stomach turn?
The Gospel does not tell you your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it matters more than you imagined.
But the cross also proves something else.
God’s mercy is greater than your ability to destroy yourself.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean every broken relationship will automatically be restored.
Biblical grace is not permission to keep worshiping the thing that is killing you.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
Real repentance.
The kind that stops negotiating with darkness.
The kind that brings secrets into the light.
The kind that confesses.
The kind that seeks accountability.
The kind that cuts off access when necessary.
The kind that says, “Jesus, I cannot keep calling You Lord while protecting the very thing You are telling me to surrender.”
But repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
Repentance runs toward the Savior because grace has opened the door.
And perhaps that is why this strange passage about semen, washing, and ritual purity matters more than we thought.
It reminds us that the Bible is remarkably unafraid of embodied humanity.
God knows we bleed.
God knows we sweat.
God knows bodies produce fluids.
God invented human reproduction.
God designed marriage.
God created sexuality with purpose and boundaries.
And God also knows how sin can invade His gifts, distort desire, exploit bodies, enslave imagination, wound marriages, and turn intimacy into consumption.
He is neither embarrassed by your humanity nor indifferent to your holiness.
He wants all of you.
Not merely the church version.
Not merely the Facebook version.
Not merely the version holding a Bible in your profile picture.
You.
The person nobody else sees.
The thoughts you delete.
The history you conceal.
The appetite you keep feeding.
The wound underneath the appetite.
The loneliness underneath the behavior.
The shame underneath the smile.
Jesus does not stand outside your locked room shouting, “Clean yourself before I come in.”
