He calls you into the light.
And yes, coming into the light can hurt.
Because light exposes.
But the same light that exposes the infection shows the surgeon where to heal.
So stop confusing hiding with holiness.
Somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
You love Jesus.
At least you believe you do.
But there is an area of your life you keep fencing off from Him.
You worship with it.
Sleep with it.
Wake up with it.
Delete it.
Confess it.
Return to it.
Hate it.
Miss it.
Promise to quit it.
Then hide it again.
And you are exhausted.
If that is you, perhaps your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
Maybe it needs five words:
“Jesus, no more hiding. Help me.”
You do not have to publish graphic details of your struggle.
You do not owe strangers your private history.
But sometimes publicly admitting that you need Christ is the first crack in a wall secrecy has been building for years.
Someone reading the comments may discover hope because you were brave enough to admit that grace is still doing surgery.
And please—share this.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Someone may believe bodily temptation means God hates them.
Someone may be confusing ritual impurity with moral guilt.
Someone else may actually be trapped in sexual sin and desperately needs to hear that grace does not mean surrendering to bondage—it means there is still a road home through Jesus Christ.
And when it does, come back and remember:
ritual impurity was not automatically moral guilt.
Human embodiment is not automatically sexual sin.
Sexual sin is real and must not be excused.
Repentance is necessary.
Grace is real.
Christ is sufficient.
And hiding is not your only option anymore.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture more deeply, stay close to this ministry.
We are trying to build something deeper than inspirational scrolling.
We are saved by grace, not by purchasing access, supporting a ministry, sharing a post, or performing religious works.
But redeemed people can freely choose to support Gospel work out of gratitude, generosity, and a desire to help others hear truth.
But before you leave this page, remember the man in Leviticus.
He washed.
He waited.
Evening came.
His temporary ritual condition ended.
And remember the bleeding woman.
Twelve years.
Then Jesus.
Remember the sinners Paul described.
Then came those astonishing words:
“But you were washed.”
And now remember yourself.
Your story may contain pages you wish had never been written.
There may be stains you cannot erase by replaying them.
There may be consequences you still have to face.
There may be repentance you still need to make.
There may be help you need to seek.
There may be a confession that cannot remain postponed forever.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your scandal does not possess the authority to write the final sentence.
Christ does.
So come out of hiding.
Bring the body.
Bring the questions.
Bring the temptation.
Bring the failure.
Bring the wounds.
Bring the guilt that actually is guilt.
Bring the shame that never belonged there.
Bring the secrets.
Bring the years.
Bring the shattered pieces.
Bring everything into the light of Christ.
Because the Savior who calls you to holiness is the same Savior who carried a cross for sinners.
And when Jesus cleanses what sin has stained, your worst chapter discovers it was never holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE SAID, “THE FIRST WILL BE LAST”
paragraphs:
WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE SAID, “THE FIRST WILL BE LAST”
The terrifying warning—and breathtaking hope—hidden inside one of Jesus’ most misunderstood statements
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that should make successful people uncomfortable...
and exhausted people lift their heads.
It should disturb the Christian who secretly keeps score.
It should give hope to the believer who feels forgotten.
It should confront the person who has spent years building an impressive religious life while quietly asking God, “Surely all of this means I deserve something.”
And it should reach the person reading this who feels as though everybody else got ahead while you were simply trying to survive.
Jesus said:
“Many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
In the Greek of Mark 10:31:
Πολλοὶ δὲ ἔσονται πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι καὶ οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι.
Polloi de esontai prōtoi eschatoi kai hoi eschatoi prōtoi.
Literally, the words revolve around two startling opposites:
πρῶτοι — prōtoi — first.
ἔσχατοι — eschatoi — last.
First.
Last.
Last.
First.
Jesus turns the order upside down in a single sentence.
But if you have ever heard those words reduced to “the underdog eventually wins,” you have not yet felt their full weight.
Jesus was not offering a motivational slogan about late bloomers.
He was exposing the way human beings measure greatness, goodness, sacrifice, status, reward—and even salvation itself.
And the story surrounding those words makes them almost impossible to escape.
A man came running to Jesus.
Not crawling.
Not mocking.
Running.
He knelt before Him.
He asked about eternal life.
From the outside, he looked like the kind of man religious people would have wanted sitting in the front row.
Moral.
Serious.
Respectful.
Successful.
Apparently disciplined.
And wealthy.
When Jesus reminded him of God's commandments, the man said that he had kept them from his youth.
Then Mark records one of the most beautiful details in the entire encounter.
Jesus looked at him...
and loved him.
Do not rush past that.
Before Jesus exposed his idol, Jesus loved him.
Before Jesus put His finger on the place the man did not want touched, Jesus loved him.
Before the man's sorrowful departure, Jesus loved him.
That matters because biblical conviction is not Jesus trying to destroy you.
Sometimes His love is precisely why He refuses to leave your idols unnamed.
Then came the sentence that opened the man's heart like a surgeon's blade.
One thing was lacking.
Sell what you have.
Give to the poor.
Treasure will be waiting in heaven.
Then...
“Come, follow Me.”
The tragedy is not simply that the man possessed wealth.
The tragedy is that when Jesus stood on one side and his possessions stood on the other, he could not let go.
He walked away grieving.
Imagine that scene.
He came running.
He left sorrowful.
He came asking about eternal life.
He left holding the very thing that revealed what ruled his heart.
He knelt before Jesus...
but he could not surrender to Jesus.
And suddenly this story becomes painfully modern.
Because you do not need to be wealthy to understand him.
Some people cannot surrender money.
Others cannot surrender an image.
A relationship.
A secret sin.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Control.
Recognition.
A career.
A dream.
A reputation.
A ministry.
A political identity.
The need to be admired.
The need to win every argument.
The need for people to think you are spiritually stronger than you really are.
You can kneel physically while something else still occupies the throne internally.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still protect the one room of your heart where Jesus is not allowed to rearrange the furniture.
You can sing, “I surrender all,” while quietly adding...
“except this.”
And perhaps that is why this encounter hurts.
Because the rich man is easier to criticize when we imagine his idol as money.
It becomes much harder when we give the idol our own name.
Jesus then told His disciples how difficult it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God.
The disciples were astonished.
Jesus intensified the picture with the camel and the eye of a needle.
Then they asked the question underneath every human attempt to make ourselves acceptable before God:
Who, then, can be saved?
Jesus answered that with man it is impossible...
but not with God.
That is the Gospel hiding in plain sight.
Human beings do not climb into the kingdom by becoming impressive enough.
We do not purchase salvation.
We do not outperform our neighbors into heaven.
We do not accumulate enough morality until God owes us eternal life.
Salvation is not the trophy waiting at the finish line of human achievement.
What is impossible for fallen humanity, God accomplishes.
And ultimately He accomplishes salvation through Jesus Christ.
The Son of God came for sinners.
He lived without sin.
He went to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose again.
And the sinner who turns to Christ in repentance and faith does not stand before God boasting, “Look what I achieved.”
The Christian stands there amazed:
“Look what Christ has done.”
But Peter had been listening.
And Peter noticed something.
The wealthy man would not leave everything.
The disciples had.
So Peter essentially said:
Look...
we left everything.
There it is.
The scoreboard.
Maybe Peter did not intend arrogance. Maybe it was bewilderment. Maybe genuine sacrifice and a very human question were tangled together.
We left our nets.
Our homes.
Our old lives.
We followed You.
What does that mean for us?
Jesus did not deny their sacrifice.

He promised that no one who had left home, family, or fields for His sake and for the Gospel would ultimately lose by following Him. He spoke of God's provision, a new family among His people, persecution in this age, and eternal life in the age to come.
Notice the word Jesus did not hide:
persecutions.
Christian discipleship is not a prosperity contract.
Jesus did not promise His followers a pain-free road decorated with luxury because they surrendered something.
He promised that following Him is worth everything...
even when following Him costs everything.
And then He said it:
“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
Now the sentence lands differently.
Jesus is confronting the instinct to turn discipleship into a ranking system.
The kingdom of God does not operate according to our little ladders.
The person who appears first by earthly standards may discover that heaven was never impressed by the things earth applauded.
And the person who appears last—unnoticed, unimpressive, overlooked, poor, broken, serving without applause, repenting where nobody can see—may discover that God saw everything.
But there is another danger.
Even the “last” can become proud of being last.
We can make sacrifice another status symbol.
We can start thinking:
I suffered more.
I gave more.
I served longer.
I sacrificed more.
I have been a Christian longer.
I know more Scripture.
I pray more.
I volunteer more.
I gave up things they never gave up.
Therefore...
God owes me more.
And Jesus destroys that mathematics.
Matthew's Gospel makes the point even harder to miss.
After the statement about the first and last at the end of Matthew 19, Jesus tells a story about a landowner hiring workers for his vineyard.
Some begin early.
Others arrive later.
Some have endured the burden of the day.
Others have worked only a fraction of that time.
Yet the landowner gives the later workers the agreed daily wage as well.
The early workers become angry.
Why?
Because comparison transformed generosity into an insult.
They were content with what they had been promised...
until they saw grace given to somebody else.
Read that again.
They were content...
until grace reached someone they believed deserved less.
And suddenly the parable stops being ancient.
Because there is a frightening little Pharisee hiding inside the human heart that does not merely want grace.
It wants more grace than the other person.
We celebrate the prodigal son until God throws a party for somebody whose sins hurt us.
We preach forgiveness until Jesus forgives the person we had already sentenced in our mind.
We sing about amazing grace until grace becomes amazing for somebody we think should have suffered longer.
We love testimonies of redemption...
provided the redeemed person's past is respectable enough.
But grace cannot be grace while simultaneously being wages we believe God owes us.
Jesus concludes the vineyard parable with the same reversal:
“The last will be first, and the first last.”
This does not mean obedience is meaningless.
It does not mean faithfulness is irrelevant.
It does not mean every person receives identical responsibilities or rewards regardless of faithfulness.
And it certainly does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means God's kingdom cannot be reduced to human entitlement.
Nobody enters eternal life because God finally looked at their résumé and admitted He was impressed.
We need mercy.
All of us.
The lifelong church member needs mercy.
The addict walking through the doors trembling needs mercy.
The preacher needs mercy.
The prisoner needs mercy.
The respectable businessman needs mercy.
The woman carrying a past she cannot bear to discuss needs mercy.
The person baptized decades ago needs mercy.
The dying thief had nothing left to build.
No decades of ministry.
No missionary journeys.
No opportunity to repair his reputation.
No lifetime left to prove that his repentance was real through years of visible service.
He had a crucified Savior beside him...
and a desperate cry of faith.
Jesus promised him paradise.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that removes repentance.
Grace purchased at the immeasurable cost of Christ's blood.
Grace that means nobody can stand at the foot of the cross and brag about how much better they climbed there than everyone else.
Maybe you have spent your life feeling last.
Maybe nobody knows how hard you have fought simply to remain faithful.
Maybe your prayers seem unanswered.
Maybe someone younger passed you.
Someone less experienced received the opportunity.
Someone else got married.
Someone else had the child.
Someone else's ministry grew.
Someone else's business succeeded.
Someone else's testimony received applause while yours seems to be happening in a room where nobody is watching.
Maybe you have quietly asked God:
“Did You forget me?”
Listen carefully.
Jesus' words do not promise that every earthly disappointment will reverse exactly the way you want.
Christian hope is deeper than “your turn is coming.”
Sometimes your earthly turn never comes.
Some faithful Christians die unknown.
Some prayers are answered differently from what we begged for.
Some wounds remain scars until resurrection.
Some obedience receives almost no applause on earth.
But if you belong to Christ, being overlooked by the world does not mean being overlooked by God.
That changes everything.
The secret prayer matters.
The temptation you resisted when nobody would have discovered the sin matters.
The money you quietly gave matters.
The person you forgave matters.
The Gospel conversation nobody applauded matters.
The tears you cried before God matter.
The decision to keep following Jesus when your emotions were screaming at you to quit matters.
He sees.
And perhaps an even more dangerous question remains.
What if you are “first”?
What if people admire your faith?
What if you have influence?
Money?
Knowledge?
A platform?
A title?
A successful ministry?
A respected family?
Thousands of followers?
What if people quote you?
What if people call you “man of God” or “woman of God”?
Then Jesus' words are not permission to hate what God has entrusted to you.
They are a warning never to confuse stewardship with superiority.
The higher you rise, the more carefully you should remember who put breath in your lungs.
Who gave the ability.
Who opened the door.
Who provided the opportunity.
Who forgave your sins.
Who carried you when nobody knew you were falling apart.
Who saved you.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people becoming slightly better.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the world's definitions of first and last collapse completely.
Look at Jesus.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Crowned with thorns.
Crucified between criminals.
To the watching world, He looked defeated.
Last.
Finished.
A scandal hanging on Roman timber.
But death could not hold Him.
The stone moved.
The tomb emptied.
Christ rose.
And the One men rejected is Lord.
This is the kingdom's great reversal.
The King became the suffering Servant.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
The sinless One bore the judgment sinners deserved.
And those who come to Him empty-handed receive what they could never earn.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Adoption.
New life.
Hope.
A future resurrection.
Eternal life with Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So maybe the question is no longer:
“Am I first?”
Maybe it is not even:
“Am I last?”
Maybe the question is:
Do I belong to Jesus?
Because you can be first in the world and lost.
You can be last in the world and belong to the King.
You can have everything people spend their lives chasing and still discover that none of it could save you.
And you can come to Christ with a shattered history, empty hands, a ruined reputation, tears running down your face, and nothing impressive left to offer...
and discover that grace was never waiting for you to become impressive.
It was calling you to surrender.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding behind your achievements.
Stop hiding behind your failures.
Stop telling yourself you are too good to need saving.
Stop telling yourself you are too ruined to be saved.
Both lies keep your eyes on you.
Look at Christ.
Talk to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
If there is sin, confess it.
If there is pride, surrender it.
If there is bitterness, bring it into His light.
If you have been trying to earn what only grace can give, stop negotiating and come empty-handed.
And if you have never truly trusted Christ, do not confuse knowing Christian language with knowing Jesus.
Turn to Him.
He is not asking you to clean yourself sufficiently so you can become worthy of the cross.
The cross is precisely where unworthy sinners discover how astonishing the mercy of God really is.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, be brave enough to say it.
You do not have to explain the whole battle.
Sometimes two honest words are the beginning of somebody finally stepping out of hiding.
And read the other comments too.
Someone there may need to know they are not the only believer still fighting.
We are saved by grace, not by supporting a page.
But if Gospel Warrior is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, call sin what Scripture calls it, and keep your eyes on the Gospel, you can help sustain and extend this work.
One practical way to glorify God is to steward what He has given you toward making Christ known.
But the deepest reason to stay is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
But please remember this after the link disappears from your screen.
Your sharing cannot save you.
Your religious accomplishments cannot save you.
Being first cannot save you.
Being last cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
So when the world tells you to climb higher, become louder, outrun everyone, prove yourself, collect applause, protect your position, and make certain nobody gets ahead of you...
remember the words of the King.
The first may become last.
The last may become first.
And at the end of everything, the greatest question will never be how impressive you looked standing in line.
It will be whether you belonged to the One standing at the center of eternity.
One day every scoreboard you spent your life watching will disappear—and only what Christ says about you will matter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” ACTUALLY PROMISES
paragraphs: WHAT “IF GOD IS FOR US, WHO CAN BE AGAINST US?” ACTUALLY PROMISES
Romans 8:31 is not God promising that nobody will fight you. It is God declaring that, because you belong to Christ, nobody who fights you can overturn what He has determined to finish.
There is a version of Christianity that sounds wonderful until your life falls apart.
It tells you that if God is really with you, doors will open.
People will favor you.
Enemies will disappear.
Your prayers will quickly produce visible answers.
Your finances will improve.
Your family will come together.
Your sickness will leave.
Your reputation will recover.
And eventually everything will start looking like proof that God is on your side.
Then something terrible happens.
The door closes.
The diagnosis comes.
The marriage trembles.
Someone you trusted betrays you.
You lose something you begged God to preserve.
People misunderstand you.
Your prayers seem to hit the ceiling.
You are trying to obey Jesus, yet somehow life becomes harder instead of easier.
And suddenly one frightening question crawls into your mind:
If God is really for me… why does it feel like so much is against me?
That question is exactly why Romans 8:31 must be understood correctly.
Because Paul never wrote,
“If God is for us, nothing painful will ever happen to us.”
He wrote:

“If God be for us, who can be against us?”
—Romans 8:31
The Greek is even more striking:
εἰ ὁ θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, τίς καθ’ ἡμῶν;
ei ho Theos hyper hēmōn, tis kath’ hēmōn?
Literally, the force is:
If God is for us, who is against us?
The contrast is powerful.
ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν — hyper hēmōn — “for us,” “on our behalf.”
Then:
καθ’ ἡμῶν — kath’ hēmōn — “against us.”
Paul is placing every opposing power on one side…
and God on the other.
But here is where this verse becomes far more powerful than the inspirational slogan we sometimes make it.
Paul is not pretending nobody is against Christians.
Paul knew people could be against him.
He had enemies.
He experienced persecution.
He was beaten.
He was imprisoned.
He was rejected.
He suffered.
He knew what it was to be hated for preaching Christ.
So Romans 8:31 cannot possibly mean, “Nobody will oppose you.”
The very chapter containing this triumphant declaration speaks openly about suffering.
Paul writes that believers are children and heirs of God, “if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together” (Romans 8:17).
A few verses later he describes creation groaning.
Then believers groaning.
Then weakness so deep that sometimes we do not even know what we should pray for as we ought.
And still…
right there…
in a chapter filled with suffering, weakness, groaning, waiting, persecution, and uncertainty…
Paul asks:
“If God be for us, who can be against us?”
That changes everything.
Because the promise is not that you will have no enemies.
The promise is that no enemy can successfully overturn God’s saving purpose for those who are in Christ.
People can oppose you.
They cannot dethrone Christ.
People can accuse you.
They cannot reverse the justification God gives in Christ.
Suffering can wound you.
It cannot separate you from Christ’s love.
Death can take your earthly life.
It cannot cancel resurrection.
The devil may accuse.
He cannot produce a condemnation greater than the verdict secured through Jesus Christ.
Your past can haunt your memory.
It cannot rewrite the Gospel.
And your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
That belongs to Jesus.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
Because perhaps you have been interpreting opposition as abandonment.
You thought the battle meant God had left.
You thought the silence meant He stopped caring.
You thought the failure meant your story was over.
You thought the scandal permanently defined you.
You thought what you did was too ugly.
Or perhaps what someone did to you was so devastating that you cannot imagine anything beautiful growing from the wreckage.
But Romans 8 does not begin with your ability to hold yourself together.
It begins with a verdict:

“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
Read that carefully.
In Christ Jesus.
That is the center of the entire promise.
Romans 8:31 is not a motivational slogan about believing in yourself.
It is not God endorsing every ambition you have.
It does not mean every plan you make automatically becomes God's plan.
It does not mean you can attach Jesus’ name to whatever you want and declare that nobody can stop you.
God being “for us” does not mean God becomes the servant of our agenda.
It means that in Christ, God is accomplishing His redemptive purpose for His people.
And Paul anchors that confidence not in our circumstances…
but in the cross.
Immediately after asking, “If God be for us, who can be against us?” Paul writes:
—Romans 8:32
There it is.
The proof that God is for you is not that nothing bad happened today.
Look at Calvary.
The proof is Jesus.
“He that spared not his own Son…”
God’s love is not ultimately measured by the ease of your week.
It was demonstrated at a bloodstained cross.
Think about that.
The greatest evidence that God was accomplishing salvation looked, for a moment, like absolute catastrophe.
Jesus was betrayed.
Jesus was falsely accused.
Jesus was mocked.
Jesus was beaten.
Jesus was crucified.
His followers scattered.
His body was placed in a tomb.
If someone had judged God's faithfulness merely by Friday afternoon, everything would have looked lost.
But Friday was not the end of the story.
Sunday was coming.
The stone moved.
The tomb emptied.
Christ rose.
Death lost its claim.

And what appeared to be the darkest scandal in human history became the stage upon which the grace, justice, mercy, wisdom, and saving power of God were revealed through the crucified and risen Christ.
So maybe you should be careful about calling your present chapter the ending.
You do not know what God is still doing.
This does not mean every tragedy will become comfortable in this life.
Romans 8 offers something stronger than shallow optimism.
It points beyond present suffering toward resurrection glory.
Paul says:

“For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.”
—Romans 8:18
Christian hope is not pretending suffering does not hurt.
It is knowing suffering does not win.
And that is why Romans 8:31 sits where it does.
Paul has just written:

“And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.”
—Romans 8:28
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say all things are good.
Betrayal is not good.
Abuse is not good.
Sin is not good.
Death is an enemy.
Injustice is not suddenly righteous because God is sovereign.
The promise is that God is so sovereign, wise, and powerful that evil cannot ultimately frustrate His saving purpose.
And Paul immediately defines the trajectory of that purpose:

“For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son…”
—Romans 8:29
There is the “good” toward which Romans 8 is moving.
Christlikeness.
Redemption.
Final glory.
God is not merely committed to making you comfortable.
He is conforming His people to His Son and bringing His redemptive purpose to completion.
That means sometimes the answer to “If God is for me, why is this happening?” is not something we will completely understand on this side of eternity.
Christian faith does not require us to manufacture explanations God has not revealed.
Sometimes we grieve.
Sometimes we wait.
Sometimes we pray through tears.
Sometimes all we can say is, “Jesus, I still trust You.”
And Romans 8 tells us something breathtaking about those moments.
When your prayers collapse into groaning, God has not abandoned you.

“Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities…”
—Romans 8:26
Even your weakness occurs within the presence of God.
Then Paul takes us into what sounds almost like a heavenly courtroom.

“Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth.”
—Romans 8:33

“Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again…”
—Romans 8:34
Can you feel what Paul is doing?
Who can bring the decisive accusation?
God justifies.
Who can issue the final condemnation?
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ intercedes.
The believer’s confidence is not:
“I have never failed.”
It is:
“Christ died.”
It is not:
“My record is clean.”
It is:
“God justifies.”
It is not:
“I am strong enough to save myself.”
It is:
“Christ is risen.”
This is where Romans 8 becomes intensely personal.
Because some of the loudest voices “against us” do not come from other people.
Sometimes they come from inside our own heads.
Look what you did.
Remember who you were.
God could never want somebody like you.
You ruined everything.
You should hide.
If people really knew you…
And perhaps there really are things in your past that were sinful.
The Gospel does not ask you to rename darkness as light.
Repentance does not make excuses.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how seriously God takes sin.
Jesus Christ bore sin’s judgment so that guilty sinners who repent and believe can be forgiven, reconciled, justified, and transformed.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not permission to continue worshiping the sin Jesus died to save us from.
Grace that finds sinners in the wreckage…
calls them to repentance…
washes them…
forgives them…
and begins making them new.
You may have made a scandal of your life.
But Jesus specializes in resurrection.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
“I do not know the man.”
Then the rooster crowed.
Peter remembered.
And he wept bitterly.
Yet Jesus was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him and called him again into faithful service.
Peter’s denial was real.
So was Christ’s grace.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the worst chapter surrendered to Him.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And then Romans 8 reaches its thunderous conclusion.
Paul asks:

“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?”
—Romans 8:35
Then notice the list.
Tribulation.
Distress.
Persecution.
Famine.
Nakedness.
Peril.
Sword.
Do you see it now?
“If God is for us” never meant these things would not come.
Paul literally lists terrifying things that can come.
And then declares:

“Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.”
—Romans 8:37
Not always away from these things.
Sometimes in them.
That distinction matters.
Christian victory is not always God removing the furnace.
Sometimes it is discovering that Christ remains Lord in the flames.
And finally Paul says:
“For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,

Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
—Romans 8:38–39
There is the promise.
Death cannot do it.
Life cannot do it.
Spiritual powers cannot do it.
The present cannot do it.
The future cannot do it.
Nothing in all creation can successfully tear those who belong to Christ away from the saving love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
So when you say,
“If God is for us, who can be against us?”
do not say it as though Christians have no enemies.
Say it while your hands are trembling.
Say it when people walk away.
Say it when obedience costs you something.
Say it when you cannot understand what God is doing.
Say it when your past starts screaming.
Say it when repentance hurts.
Say it when the future terrifies you.
Say it at the hospital.
Say it beside the grave.
Say it when the prayer has not yet been answered.
Say it when everything visible appears to contradict what you believe.
Not because you know tomorrow.
But because you know Christ.
If God is for us, opposition can be real without being ultimate.
That is the difference.
Your enemy may have a voice.
He does not have the final verdict.
Your suffering may have a chapter.
It does not own the ending.
Your sin may belong to your testimony.
It does not have to remain your identity.
Your scars may explain where you have been.
They do not determine where Christ is taking you.
And if you are reading this while far from God, Romans 8 is not an invitation to borrow Christian promises while rejecting the Christ at their center.
Come to Him.
Stop hiding.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
You do not need to clean yourself sufficiently before approaching Jesus.
You come because you need mercy.
Confess your sin.
Turn toward Christ.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
There is grace for sinners.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is a new life that does not require you to pretend your old life never happened.
Maybe this exposed something you have kept hidden for years.
If it did, be honest.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting that battle.
And perhaps your honesty will give someone else courage to stop hiding.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.
But if Christ has used this message to remind you of truth, you can help place that truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
Send it to the believer who thinks suffering means God abandoned them.
Send it to the person drowning in shame.
Send it to the lukewarm Christian who needs to remember what the Gospel actually promises.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely positive thinking.
Because there may come a night when Romans 8:31 feels much harder to believe than it does today.
You may need to come back and remember:
God never promised you an opposition-free life.
He gave you something infinitely stronger.
Jesus Christ.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
It is simply one practical way to support the continued creation and distribution of Christ-centered content so more people can encounter biblical truth.
Remember Jesus.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that Christianity does not promise the absence of suffering.
It promises the presence, saving love, intercession, resurrection victory, and final triumph of Christ.
So when tomorrow becomes frightening…
when another accusation comes…
when the past knocks again…
when the enemy whispers that everything is over…
remember Romans 8.
εἰ ὁ θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, τίς καθ’ ἡμῶν;
If God is for us, who can be against us?
Not:
“Who can oppose us?”
Many can.
But ultimately:
Who can oppose the saving purpose of God in Christ and win?
That is why the battered believer can still worship.
That is why the repentant sinner can come home.
That is why the ashamed can stop hiding.
That is why the grieving can still hope.
That is why the persecuted Church can still sing.
That is why death itself does not get the final word.
Because the final word belongs to the crucified and risen King.
And maybe the chapter you thought proved God had abandoned you will someday become the chapter where you finally understood what it meant for Him to hold you.
Your darkest chapter may still carry your fingerprints—but because of Jesus, it does not get to hold the pen that writes your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Church Hurt Can Explain Why You Pulled Away. It Cannot Make Jesus Guilty of What People Did.
paragraphs: Church Hurt Can Explain Why You Pulled Away. It Cannot Make Jesus Guilty of What People Did.

What happened under the name of Christianity may have wounded your faith deeply. But before you walk away from Jesus because of what people did, look again at the One Scripture actually tells you to look at.
Maybe you did not stop going to church because you stopped believing in God.
Maybe you stopped because believing started to hurt.
You trusted someone who carried a Bible.

You opened your life to people who prayed with you, worshiped beside you, called you “brother” or “sister,” spoke about grace, preached about holiness, and told you that church was supposed to be family.
Then something happened.
Maybe a pastor manipulated you.
Maybe somebody used Scripture to control you.
Maybe private pain became public gossip.
Maybe you watched hypocrisy flourish while honesty was punished.
Maybe leadership protected a reputation instead of protecting the wounded.
Maybe you asked legitimate questions and were labeled rebellious.
Maybe somebody demanded forgiveness while refusing accountability.
Maybe you were told to “honor authority” when what they really wanted was silence.
Maybe you watched people preach compassion from a platform and practice cruelty behind closed doors.
Or maybe nobody did anything dramatic enough to make headlines.
They simply disappointed you again.
And again.
And again.
Until one Sunday you realized you were sitting in a room full of worship songs while something inside you had gone numb.
So you pulled away.
First from the people.
Then from church.
Then prayer became harder.
Your Bible stayed closed longer.
The name of Jesus became tangled in your mind with the faces of people who hurt you.
And eventually you began wondering something you may have been afraid to say aloud:
“If Christianity produced this… why should I still want Christ?”
That question deserves more than a religious cliché.
And your wounds deserve more than someone telling you to “just get over it.”
Spiritual abuse is real.
Betrayal is real.
Hypocrisy is real.
Church wounds can be devastating precisely because they happen in places where people expected safety, truth, holiness, family, and God.
Jesus Himself never taught us to pretend religious corruption was harmless.
He confronted it.

Some of His strongest recorded words were spoken not to obvious outsiders but to religious leaders whose outward spirituality concealed inward corruption. In Matthew 23, Christ repeatedly denounced hypocrisy among the scribes and Pharisees. He spoke of leaders who placed heavy burdens on others. He condemned religious performance that looked righteous outwardly while corruption remained within.
Jesus was not impressed by religious appearances.
And He did not confuse religious position with godly character.
That matters when you have been hurt by somebody who carried His name.
Because Christianity does not require you to call evil good simply because the person doing it knew Bible verses.
But there is another truth wounded hearts desperately need.
What happened to you may explain why you pulled away.
It may explain why you became suspicious.
It may explain why worship became complicated.
It may explain why entering another church building makes your chest tighten.
It may explain why words like “pastor,” “ministry,” “submission,” “church family,” or even “Christian” now carry memories they were never supposed to carry.
Your wound may explain your distance.
But your wound cannot change who Jesus is.
And the people who misrepresented Him do not get to redefine Him.
That distinction could become one of the most important distinctions of your spiritual life:
Jesus is not guilty of what somebody did while using His name.
Think about that carefully.
If a doctor commits malpractice, medicine itself has not committed malpractice.
If a judge becomes corrupt, justice itself has not become corrupt.
And if someone invokes Christ while behaving contrary to Christ, their hypocrisy is not evidence that Jesus shares their hypocrisy.
In fact, sometimes their behavior is condemned by the very Christ they claimed to represent.
This is why Hebrews gives wounded, exhausted believers such an important direction.
Hebrews 12:2 begins:
ἀφορῶντες εἰς τὸν τῆς πίστεως ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν Ἰησοῦν
aphorōntes eis ton tēs pisteōs archēgon kai teleiōtēn Iēsoun
The central movement is breathtaking.
ἀφορῶντες — aphorōntes.
The idea is to look away toward something, to direct one's attention toward.
And where does Hebrews direct the eyes?
εἰς… Ἰησοῦν — eis… Iēsoun.
Toward Jesus.
Hebrews does not tell suffering believers to anchor their faith in the perfection of other Christians.
It points them to Jesus.
Not the pastor who failed you.
Jesus.
Not the Christian who betrayed you.
Jesus.
Not the ministry that disappointed you.
Jesus.
Not the leader who demanded standards privately ignored.
Jesus.
Not the people who weaponized Scripture.
Jesus.
Not even your memory of what Christianity was supposed to look like.
Jesus Himself.
Hebrews calls Him ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν—the pioneer/founder and perfecter of faith.
Then the text takes us directly into the scandal at the center of Christianity.
Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him,” endured the cross.
And Hebrews uses a devastating expression:
αἰσχύνης καταφρονήσας
aischynēs kataphronēsas
Despising—disregarding—the shame.
The cross was not polished religion.
It was humiliation.
Rejection.
Mockery.
Violence.
Shame.
Jesus knows what it means to be wounded by human beings.
He knows betrayal from the inside.
Judas did not betray a stranger.
He betrayed Someone whose table he had shared.
Peter did not deny someone he barely knew.
He denied the Lord he had promised to follow.
Religious leaders did not merely misunderstand Jesus.
They participated in His condemnation.
Soldiers mocked Him.
Crowds turned.
His clothing was divided.
His body was pierced.
And while Jesus hung on the cross, the people looking at Him could have concluded that everything had ended in disgrace.
But they were watching grace move through scandal.
The cross looked like defeat before the resurrection revealed victory.
And this is where your story may meet His.
Because sometimes church hurt leaves you standing among the ruins of what you thought your faith would become.
You may have lost relationships.
Trust.
Community.
Confidence.
Years.
Maybe even part of your ability to recognize yourself.
And perhaps someone reading this still loves Jesus but does not know how to trust Christians again.
You do not have to pretend that rebuilding trust is instantaneous.
Forgiveness and trust are not identical.
Forgiveness does not mean calling abuse acceptable.
Forgiveness does not automatically require restoring someone to leadership.
Forgiveness does not mean refusing appropriate boundaries.
Forgiveness does not require concealing crimes or shielding wrongdoing from legitimate accountability.
Biblical grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant abuse.

Jesus told His disciples that if a brother sins, there is a place for rebuke and repentance (Luke 17:3). Matthew 18 includes confrontation and accountability rather than pretending sin never occurred. The New Testament establishes serious qualifications for church leadership in passages such as 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1.
Grace does not make holiness irrelevant.
Grace teaches us how desperately we need it.
So perhaps your next step is not pretending nothing happened.
Perhaps your next step is separating two faces that pain has fused together:
the face of the person who hurt you…
and the face of Jesus Christ.
They are not the same.
Read the Gospels again without forcing Jesus to wear the personality of the Christians who wounded you.
Watch Him touch people others avoided.
Watch Him welcome the broken.
Watch Him confront hypocrisy.
Watch Him tell the truth without becoming corrupt.
Watch Him weep.
Watch Him forgive.
Watch Him defend the sanctity of God's house.
Watch Him kneel before His disciples and wash their feet.
Watch Him walk toward a cross He did not deserve for sinners who could never deserve Him.
Then ask yourself:
“Is this the Jesus I rejected…
or did I reject a distorted picture of Him painted by somebody else's behavior?”
That question may hurt.
But it may also open a door.
Because perhaps you thought leaving those people meant you had to leave Him too.
Perhaps somebody behaved so badly in the name of Jesus that eventually hearing His name reminded you of them.
But they do not own His name.
They did not die for you.
They did not carry your sin.
They did not conquer death.
They are not your Savior.
Jesus is.
And Hebrews continues:
ἀναλογίσασθε γὰρ τὸν τοιαύτην ὑπομεμενηκότα… ἀντιλογίαν
“Consider him who endured” such hostility from sinners against Himself, so that you may not grow weary and lose heart.
Consider Him.
There it is again.
Your attention is being redirected.
The writer knows believers can become exhausted.
The text does not mock weariness.
It addresses it.
“Consider Him.”
When Christians disappoint you, consider Him.
When hypocrisy disgusts you, consider Him.
When memories return, consider Him.
When you are tempted to conclude that every Christian is fake, consider Him.
When you wonder whether grace was ever real, consider Him.
When the church failed to look like Christ, do not use the failure to resemble Christ as evidence against Christ.
Use Christ as the standard that exposes the failure.
That changes everything.
You can say, “What they did was wrong,” precisely because Jesus gives you a standard by which wrong can be named.
You can say, “That leadership was abusive,” without saying, “Therefore Christ is abusive.”
You can say, “That church handled my pain terribly,” without saying, “Therefore Jesus does not care about my pain.”
You can say, “I need boundaries,” without saying, “I no longer need Jesus.”
And you can seek a healthy Christian community again without pretending every church is healthy.
The New Testament never presents Christians as incapable of sin.
Quite the opposite.
The early church had conflict, hypocrisy, immaturity, doctrinal errors, favoritism, sexual sin, selfishness, and division serious enough that apostolic letters confronted them openly.
The existence of sinful Christians was never Christianity's claim.
Christianity's claim is that sinners need a Savior.
That includes people in pews.
That includes people behind pulpits.
That includes the person who wounded you.
And painfully, humblingly, it includes you and me.
Church hurt can produce another danger if we are not careful.
We can move from recognizing somebody else's sin to believing our pain makes repentance unnecessary for us.
It does not.
Their sin does not make ours righteous.
Their hypocrisy cannot become our permission to live apart from Christ.
Their failure cannot save us.
And our bitterness cannot heal us.
Jesus still calls every one of us—wounded and wounder, betrayed and betrayer—to repentance, faith, grace, truth, forgiveness, holiness, and reconciliation with God.
Not cheap reconciliation.
Not pretending.
Not spiritual theater.
The real thing.
The Gospel.
We have all sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).
The wages of sin is death, but God's gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23).
God demonstrates His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
That means your deepest hope was never supposed to rest on finding Christians who never fail.
Your deepest hope rests on the Christ who never does.
And maybe that is where healing begins.
Not with, “It didn't matter.”
It mattered.
Not with, “They didn't hurt me.”
They may have hurt you terribly.
Not with, “I should trust everyone again.”
Wisdom may require boundaries, discernment, accountability, time, and in serious situations professional, pastoral, legal, or safeguarding help from trustworthy people.
Healing begins somewhere deeper:
“They hurt me.
But they are not Jesus.
And I will not let their sin have the final word over my relationship with Him.”
Read that again.
Because somebody's misconduct may have already taken enough from you.
Do not voluntarily hand it your Savior too.
Do not let the person who wounded you become the permanent interpreter of Jesus in your mind.
Do not allow hypocrisy to steal Christ from you.
Do not allow spiritual manipulation to convince you that genuine spiritual authority does not exist.
Do not allow counterfeit Christianity to make you abandon the real Christ.
Come back to the source.
Open Matthew.
Open Mark.
Open Luke.
Open John.
Look at Jesus.
Not through their eyes.
Not through your former leader's personality.
Not through denominational politics.
Not through social media Christians.
Look at Him in Scripture.
You may discover something startling.
Jesus may be far more offended by what happened to you than the people who used His name to excuse it.
And He may also love the people who hurt you enough to call them to repentance.
That is the scandal of grace.
Grace is not God declaring evil unimportant.
Grace is God confronting sin so seriously that the Son of God went to the cross to save sinners from it.
At Calvary, justice and mercy are not cheapened.
Sin is exposed as deadly.
Love is revealed as costly.
Forgiveness is purchased at an unimaginable price.
And guilty people are offered what they could never earn.
That includes you.
That includes me.
That even includes the people we struggle to imagine receiving mercy.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately a story about good church people finding God.
It is the story of a holy God coming after sinners.
It is scandal becoming grace.
Shame meeting mercy.
Guilt meeting forgiveness.
Death meeting resurrection.
Prodigals coming home.
Failures becoming testimonies.
Broken people discovering that Jesus is still Jesus even after Christians have failed to look like Him.
Maybe you are reading this with tears you did not expect.
Maybe anger.
Maybe resistance.
Maybe relief.
Maybe you have not prayed sincerely in months or years.
You do not need an impressive prayer.
You can begin with honesty.

“Jesus, people hurt me, and somewhere along the way I blamed You for it. I don't know how to trust again. I don't know how to return. But if You are truly who Scripture says You are, help me see You clearly. Expose what is false in me. Heal what is wounded. Forgive my sin. Lead me into truth. Teach me to forgive without calling evil good. Give me wisdom, courage, and healthy boundaries. Bring trustworthy believers into my life. Restore what You desire to restore. I surrender myself to You again. Amen.”
And if you cannot pray all of that yet, perhaps you can whisper only this:
“Jesus, help me look at You again.”
That is enough of a beginning to turn your face toward Him.
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may have disappeared from church years ago, and everybody assumed they became rebellious.
Maybe they were wounded.
Someone you love may still believe in God but secretly cannot separate Jesus from the Christians who hurt them.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too—not to build a personality around a page, but to keep Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ moving through feeds increasingly crowded with everything else.
Supporting Gospel work is not a way to purchase God's favor, prove that you glorify God, or earn spiritual merit.
Come back to Jesus.
Not back to pretending.
Not back to unsafe environments.
Not back to unquestioning loyalty to human leaders.
Not back to religious performance.
Back to Jesus.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who despised its shame.
The One who endured hostility from sinners.
The One Hebrews tells weary believers to consider so they will not lose heart.
The One who still calls sinners to repentance.
The One who still forgives.
The One who still restores.
The One who still transforms.
The One who cannot be made guilty by somebody else's hypocrisy.
Perhaps the people who hurt you wrote a chapter you never wanted in your story.
They do not get to write the ending.
Do not let the hands that wounded your faith become the hands that permanently cover your eyes from seeing Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD KNEW SATAN WOULD REBEL—SO WHY DID HE CREATE HIM? THE ANSWER LEADS TO A CROSS, AN EMPTY TOMB, AND A TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT YOUR OWN HEART
paragraphs: GOD KNEW SATAN WOULD REBEL—SO WHY DID HE CREATE HIM? THE ANSWER LEADS TO A CROSS, AN EMPTY TOMB, AND A TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT YOUR OWN HEART

If God knew the devil would become the enemy, knew Eden would be invaded by temptation, knew humanity would fall, knew history would bleed, and knew His own Son would be crucified… why create Satan at all? Perhaps the most unsettling part of the answer is that Scripture eventually turns the question around—and asks what you are doing with the freedom, mercy, and Christ you have been given.
There is a question many Christians are almost afraid to ask.
Not because they do not believe in God.
Sometimes because they do.
They believe He knows everything.
They believe He is sovereign.
They believe nothing catches Him by surprise.

And then one night, perhaps after watching another family collapse, another innocent person suffer, another addiction consume someone, another war fill graves, another believer lose a battle they promised themselves they would never fight again, the question crawls out of the darkness:
If God knew Satan would rebel…
why did God create him?
Why create the being who would become the devil?
Why not simply refuse to create him?
Why allow the possibility of rebellion when God already knew where rebellion would lead?
And beneath that theological question is usually another question—one much more personal.
God, if You knew all of this would hurt so badly…
why did You allow the story to begin?
We need to be careful here.
Because Scripture gives us truths from which we can reason, but it does not give us a verse saying, “Here are all of God’s reasons for creating the angel who became Satan.”
So we must never pretend God revealed what He did not reveal.
Mystery should make Christians humble, not imaginative.
But Scripture does tell us enough to destroy several dangerous misunderstandings.
The first is enormous:
God did not create an evil rival god.
There are not two eternal powers staring each other down across the universe—one good and one evil—hoping to see which one wins.
Satan is not God’s opposite.
God has no opposite.
The devil is a creature.
God is Creator.
And that difference is infinite.
Paul writes about Christ:
Hoti en autō ektisthē ta panta…
“For in Him all things were created…”
Then Paul expands the statement:
“…things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him.”
Colossians 1:16.
Read those final words again.
Through Him.
For Him.
Jesus Christ is not one spiritual power competing with Satan.
Christ is Lord over creation.
The devil is created.
Jesus is not.
The devil's existence is dependent.
Christ's glory is not.

The devil does not possess unlimited power, unlimited knowledge, or unlimited presence. Scripture never presents him as God's equal. He operates as a rebellious creature beneath the sovereignty of the God he hates.
And Scripture refuses to blame God for evil.
James says plainly:
“God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one.”
James 1:13.
First John declares:
“God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.”
1 John 1:5.
So whatever we say next, one boundary cannot move:
God is not morally evil.
He does not become the author of sin merely because He knew rebellion would occur.
Knowing an act will happen is not the same thing as morally committing that act.
This matters because people sometimes imagine that God created “Satan” already evil—as though wickedness rolled directly off the Creator's assembly line.
That is not the biblical picture.
Even the name we commonly use tells part of the story.
The Hebrew word שָׂטָן—satan—carries the sense of an adversary or accuser. The Greek New Testament frequently uses διάβολος—diabolos—meaning slanderer or accuser.
These words describe opposition.
They do not make evil eternal.
God alone is eternal and uncreated.
Christian theology therefore understands Satan as a created spiritual being who rebelled against God, not as an eternally evil counterpart to Him.
Jesus says of the devil in John 8:44 that “he was a murderer from the beginning” and that he “does not stand in the truth.”
Notice the language.
He does not stand in the truth.
There is rebellion.
Departure.
Corruption.
Something created is turning against the One for whom creation exists.
And here we need another careful distinction.

Christians have historically connected Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 with Satan's fall. There may be typological or theological connections worth considering, but we should not pretend their immediate historical contexts do not exist.
Isaiah 14 directly speaks concerning the king of Babylon.
Ezekiel 28 addresses the ruler and king of Tyre.
So when someone confidently declares that every line in those passages is simply God's direct biography of Satan before Eden, they are saying more than the texts themselves explicitly say.
Biblical faith does not need exaggeration to survive.
Truth is powerful enough.
What Scripture unmistakably establishes elsewhere is that the devil sins, deceives, opposes God, and stands condemned.
First John 3:8 gives us one of the most astonishing statements in the New Testament:
“ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ὁ διάβολος ἁμαρτάνει…”
Ap’ archēs ho diabolos hamartanei…
“The devil has been sinning from the beginning.”
But John does not stop there.
The second half changes everything:
“εἰς τοῦτο ἐφανερώθη ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, ἵνα λύσῃ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ διαβόλου.”
Eis touto ephanerōthē ho huios tou Theou, hina lysē ta erga tou diabolou.
“For this purpose the Son of God was revealed: to destroy the works of the devil.”
1 John 3:8.
There.
That is where the question begins moving toward Jesus.
Not toward Satan.
Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of how powerful the devil became.
It is the story of what God did about sin.
The devil rebelled.
Humanity rebelled.
And God did something Satan could never have predicted into existence, demanded, deserved, or forced.
God came for sinners.
Think about that.
The scandal of Christianity is not merely that an angel rebelled against God.
The greater scandal is that human beings joined the rebellion—and God loved His enemies enough to send His Son.
Maybe this is where the question gets uncomfortable.
Because asking why God allowed Satan to rebel can sometimes keep the rebellion safely outside ourselves.
Satan rebelled.
Adam rebelled.
Eve rebelled.
They did it.
But then Scripture walks across the room, sits beside us, and says:
You have rebelled too.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
The most frightening evidence that rebellion is real is not merely somewhere in the ancient history of angels.
It has appeared in your heart.
And mine.
Every time we knew what God said and chose differently.
Every secret we protected.
Every appetite we enthroned.
Every person we refused to forgive while celebrating the forgiveness God gave us.
Every moment we wanted God's gifts without God's authority.
Every time we whispered with our lives:
Not Your will.
Mine.
Suddenly Satan's rebellion stops being an interesting theological puzzle.
Because rebellion has our fingerprints on it too.
Perhaps you have never shaken your fist toward heaven.
Maybe your rebellion looked respectable.
You attended church.
You knew the songs.
You posted Scripture.
You said, “God bless you.”
People thought you were doing well.
But behind the screen…
behind the smile…
behind the Sunday clothes…
there was another version of you.
Pornography nobody knew about.
Bitterness you kept feeding.
An affair living inside messages you kept deleting.
Money controlling you.
Pride disguised as discernment.
Jealousy disguised as concern.
Gossip disguised as prayer requests.
A relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
An addiction you promised God “one last time” about so many times that you stopped believing yourself.
Or maybe nothing outwardly scandalous happened.
Maybe you simply became cold.
Prayer became rare.
Scripture became optional.
Jesus became somebody you believed in but barely followed.
And somehow you learned how to look alive while spiritually falling asleep.
That is why this question matters.
Because evil is not merely something to explain.
It is something from which we need to be rescued.
But now we arrive at the hardest part.
If God knew rebellion would happen, why create a world in which it could happen at all?
The Bible does not give us permission to claim exhaustive knowledge of God's secret counsel.
Deuteronomy 29:29 reminds us that “the secret things belong to the LORD our God.”
There are places where faithful theology must bow.
Yet Scripture does reveal the destination toward which God's redemptive plan moves.
His glory.
His justice.
His mercy.
His grace.
And the supremacy of Jesus Christ.
God's foreknowledge of evil does not mean evil defeats His purpose.
God can permit what He hates morally while sovereignly directing history toward purposes that remain holy.
The clearest proof is not Satan's rebellion.
It is the cross.
Because if there was ever an event that looked like evil had finally won…
it was Calvary.
Jesus betrayed.
Jesus falsely accused.
Jesus mocked.
Jesus beaten.
Jesus stripped.
Jesus nailed to wood.
Human wickedness gathered around the only perfectly innocent Man who ever lived.

And Acts 2:23 says something staggering: Jesus was delivered up according to God's “definite plan and foreknowledge,” while those who crucified Him were still held responsible for their wicked actions.
Do not rush past that tension.
God remained sovereign.
Human beings remained responsible.
Evil remained evil.
And God's purpose remained good.
At the cross, wicked people committed wicked acts—and God accomplished salvation without becoming wicked Himself.
What looked like hell's greatest victory became the place where God displayed the glory of His grace.
Satan could tempt.
Satan could accuse.
Satan could deceive.
But Satan could not make God stop being God.
And he could not turn the cross into God's defeat.
Colossians 2 says that Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them through the cross.
Hebrews 2:14 says that through death Christ would destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil.
Do you see the reversal?
The instrument of shame became the throne of sacrificial love.
The apparent defeat became victory.
The blood became cleansing.
The grave received Jesus…
and then had to give Him back.
This is the Gospel pattern.
God does not call evil good.
He conquers evil with good.
He does not excuse rebellion.
He judges sin.
But for sinners who come to Christ, He does something almost impossible to comprehend.
He gives grace.
This is why the question, “Why did God create Satan knowing he would rebel?” cannot end with Satan.
Scripture carries us farther.
To Christ.
To Calvary.
To an empty tomb.
And eventually…
to you.
Because you already know something about rebellion.
The real question is what you will do with the mercy standing in front of you now.
Maybe you have spent years blaming the devil for chains you keep unlocking yourself.
Maybe you have been asking God philosophical questions because repentance feels more frightening than intellectual uncertainty.
Questions are not sinful.
God is not threatened by honest questions.
But sometimes the question underneath our questions is:
Can I keep control of my life and still have Jesus?
And Christianity answers:
No.
Jesus did not die merely to improve the life you refuse to surrender.
He came to save you.
He calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with religious behavior.
It is not cleaning yourself up enough to make Jesus tolerate you.
The Gospel is infinitely better.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
Grace does not tell you your rebellion does not matter.
Grace tells you your rebellion mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His love was so great that He went willingly.
That is scandalous grace.
You brought sin.
Christ brings righteousness.
You brought guilt.
Christ brings pardon.
You brought wounds.
Christ brings redemption.
You brought a history you cannot rewrite.
Jesus brings resurrection.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner caught inside it.
And there is one more thing Scripture wants you to know about Satan.
He loses.
Not “maybe.”
Not “if Christians perform well enough.”
He loses.

Revelation 20:10 describes the devil's final judgment. Revelation 21 then moves our eyes toward the breathtaking future God has promised His people—a renewed creation where death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
The Bible begins with a serpent entering a garden.
It ends with the serpent defeated and God's people dwelling with Him.
So why did God create a being He knew would rebel?
We cannot truthfully give an exhaustive answer God Himself has not exhaustively revealed.
But we can say what Scripture allows us to say.
God did not create an equal evil deity.
He created the spiritual realm, and rebellion belongs morally to the rebel, not to the holy Creator.
God knew evil would enter His creation without Himself becoming evil.
He remains sovereign without making creatures morally innocent of their rebellion.
And He has demonstrated in history that evil cannot overthrow His purpose.
Above all, the Gospel reveals something far greater than Satan's rebellion:
Jesus Christ came to destroy the works of the devil, save sinners, display God's grace, defeat death, and bring His redeemed people home.
Perhaps we have been staring at the wrong character.
Satan is not the hero of this question.
He is not even the most interesting character.
Jesus is.
The question begins:
“Why did God create Satan?”
The Gospel eventually asks:
“Why would the holy Son of God die for rebels like us?”
And suddenly the room becomes quiet.
Because one mystery produces questions.
The other brings us to our knees.
Maybe God has used these words to uncover something you have kept buried.
Don't hide behind theology now.
Come to Christ.
Confess the sin.
Turn from it.
Ask for mercy.
You do not need to pretend you are clean before approaching the One whose blood cleanses sinners.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people in dark places.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not. Salvation is by grace, not social-media activity.

But if this truth has helped you, sharing it can become one simple way of helping put the Gospel in front of someone who may never walk through a church door but will stop for a question they have secretly asked themselves.
Send it to the family member who walked away from church.
Share it with the skeptic who thinks Christians are afraid of hard questions.
Not to buy favor from God.
Not to prove that you are a better Christian.
Not because God needs your money.
But because glorifying God includes willingly using what He has entrusted to us to help advance truthful, Christ-centered ministry.
Your money cannot purchase grace.
Your sharing cannot purchase forgiveness.
Your comments cannot purchase heaven.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So support the Gospel because you love Christ—not because you are trying to make Christ love you.
Share because somebody needs truth.
Tag because somebody you know may be fighting silently.
Save because truth forgotten in comfortable seasons becomes desperately precious in painful ones.
Follow because your soul needs more than an algorithm can give it.
But above everything…
follow Jesus.
Satan rebelled.
Humanity fell.
Sin scarred the story.
The cross looked like defeat.
The tomb looked final.
Then Sunday came.
And perhaps that is the answer your wounded heart needed more than a philosophical explanation:
God never promised that evil would never enter the story.
He promised that evil would not have the final word.
The serpent may appear in the opening chapters of your broken story—but Jesus Christ owns the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TRUTH ABOUT “WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED”
paragraphs:
THE TRUTH ABOUT “WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED”
The Verse We Quote for Comfort Was Spoken in a Much Harder Room—And What Jesus Actually Meant May Change the Way You Handle Sin, Conflict, Forgiveness, and the Church Forever
“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”
—Matthew 18:20, KJV
You have probably heard that verse in a nearly empty prayer meeting.
Maybe the room was quiet.
Maybe only three people came.
Maybe someone looked around at all the empty chairs and smiled before saying, “Well, the Bible says where two or three are gathered, Jesus is here.”
And there is something beautiful in that confession.
Jesus really is with His people.

A small gathering is not an insignificant gathering simply because it is small. The kingdom of God has never depended upon impressive attendance numbers, expensive buildings, packed auditoriums, or human applause.
But there is something about Matthew 18:20 that many Christians have never been told.
Jesus did not originally speak those famous words because attendance was low.
He was talking about something far more uncomfortable.
Sin.
Confrontation.
Witnesses.
Broken relationships.
Church discipline.
Prayer.
Authority.
Restoration.
And when you put the verse back where Jesus put it, “where two or three are gathered” stops sounding merely like encouragement for a poorly attended meeting.
It becomes something breathtakingly serious.

Because Jesus was describing what His followers are supposed to do when sin tears relationships apart—and He promises that when His people faithfully act under His name and authority, He is not standing at a distance.
He is there.
And perhaps somebody reading this right now needs to know that, because there is a name you have been trying not to think about.
Someone hurt you.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone lied.
Someone sinned.
Or perhaps the person whose name makes you uncomfortable...
is you.
Keep reading.
Because before this passage ends, Jesus may bring you face-to-face with something you have spent years avoiding.
Matthew 18:20 cannot be understood faithfully by ripping it away from Matthew 18:15–19.
Jesus begins:
“Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone...”
Notice the first movement of Jesus.
Not Facebook.
Not the group chat.
Not gossip disguised as a prayer request.
Not calling five people to explain your side before speaking to the person involved.
Jesus sends the offended believer toward the offender.
Privately.
Quietly.
Redemptively.
Why?
Because the objective is not humiliation.
The objective is restoration.
Jesus says that if the brother listens, “thou hast gained thy brother.”
Gained.
That word matters.
The Greek verb is κερδαίνω—kerdainō—carrying the idea of gaining or winning.
Jesus does not describe the confrontation as winning an argument.
He describes it as winning a brother.
There is a devastating difference.
Some of us have “won” arguments and lost relationships.
We proved our point.
We collected screenshots.
We rehearsed the offense.
We found people who agreed with us.
We walked away feeling vindicated...
and somehow nobody looked more like Jesus afterward.
But Christ's concern is not merely, “Were you right?”
His concern includes, “Did you seek your brother?”

That does not mean ignoring abuse, concealing crimes, tolerating danger, refusing legitimate authorities, or remaining in unsafe circumstances. Scripture never requires someone to place themselves in danger in order to prove forgiveness. Serious wrongdoing may require pastoral, legal, protective, or civil intervention.
But for ordinary interpersonal sin within the Christian community, Jesus establishes something radically different from our culture of public humiliation.
Go first.
Speak truth.
Seek restoration.
And if the person refuses to listen?
Jesus continues:
“But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more...”
And then comes the sentence that unlocks much of what follows:
“...that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.”
Two or three.
There it is.
Before Jesus says, “where two or three are gathered,” He has already spoken about “two or three witnesses.”
And He is reaching backward into Israel's Scriptures.
Deuteronomy 19:15 says:
“...at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.”
The Hebrew behind the expression includes:
עַל־פִּי שְׁנֵי עֵדִים אוֹ עַל־פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה־עֵדִים
ʿal-pî shənê ʿēdîm... ʿal-pî shəlōšāh-ʿēdîm
Literally, the expression uses the imagery of something being established “upon the mouth” of two or three witnesses—that is, upon their testimony.
This was about justice.
Truth mattered too much for someone's life or reputation to be destroyed casually by one unsupported accusation.
And Jesus brings that principle into the life of His covenant community.
Matthew records His words in Greek:
ἵνα ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων ἢ τριῶν σταθῇ πᾶν ῥῆμα
Hina epi stomatos dyo martyrōn ē triōn stathē pan rhēma.
So that, in essence, every matter may be established upon the testimony of two or three witnesses.
Do you see what is happening?
Jesus is building a process in which truth matters...
justice matters...
the sinner matters...
the wounded person matters...
the church matters...
and restoration matters.
Then the situation becomes even more serious.
If the person still refuses correction, Jesus says to tell it to the church. If that person ultimately refuses even the church's correction, the relationship changes in a profound way.
Then Jesus speaks about “binding” and “loosing.”
Then He speaks about two agreeing in prayer.
And then...
only then...
comes the verse printed on countless church posters:
“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”
The Greek is beautiful:
οὗ γάρ εἰσιν δύο ἢ τρεῖς συνηγμένοι εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα, ἐκεῖ εἰμι ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν.
Hou gar eisin dyo ē treis synēgmenoi eis to emon onoma, ekei eimi en mesō autōn.
“For where two or three are gathered in My name, there I am in their midst.”
But notice something many of us were never taught to notice.
Jesus does not merely say “two or three.”
He says they are gathered in His name.
That changes everything.
The power is not in the number.
Two is not a magical spiritual threshold.
Three does not summon Jesus into a room.
Jesus is not standing outside your prayer closet saying, “Find one more Christian and then I can enter.”
The glorious truth of Scripture is much greater than that.
A believer praying alone is not abandoned by Christ.
Jesus taught His disciples to enter their room, shut the door, and pray to their Father in secret.
Paul could say, “Christ liveth in me.”
The risen Christ promised His disciples, “I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.”
So Matthew 18:20 cannot reasonably mean that Jesus becomes present only after Christian number two walks through the door.
The emphasis is His name.
His authority.
His truth.
His people acting as His people.
His disciples dealing with painful realities according to the heart and commands of their King.
And suddenly the verse becomes both more comforting...
and more terrifying.
Because we love claiming Christ's presence when we sing.
But what about when we confront?
We love claiming His presence when everybody agrees.
But what about when somebody must repent?
We love claiming His presence in worship.
But what about when reconciliation requires us to swallow our pride, knock on a door, and say:
“I was wrong.”
What if “Jesus is in the midst” means He is standing spiritually at the center of conversations where nobody gets to manipulate the truth?
What if He is present when wounded believers refuse revenge?
What if He is present when mature witnesses patiently establish what actually happened?
What if He is present when a church refuses both cheap grace and cruel condemnation?
What if He is present when a sinner finally stops defending himself...
and breaks?
“I did it.”
“I lied.”
“I betrayed you.”
“I sinned.”
“I need forgiveness.”
That room may not look like revival.
Nobody may be singing.
There may be tears on the table.
Hands trembling.
Years of pain surfacing in sentences nobody wanted to say.
But Christ can be there.
Because Jesus is not only Lord of the sanctuary.
He is Lord of the uncomfortable room.
And this is where the Gospel becomes astonishing.
Because Matthew 18 is not ultimately a manual teaching righteous people how to dispose of terrible sinners.
It is instruction given to people who themselves survive entirely by mercy.
Only a few verses earlier, Jesus tells of the shepherd seeking the wandering sheep.
Immediately after this section, Peter asks Him:
“Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?”
Do you see the heartbeat running through the chapter?
The wandering sheep.
The sinning brother.
The witnesses.
The church.
Forgiveness.
Restoration.
Then Jesus tells the terrifying parable of the unforgiving servant—a man forgiven an enormous debt who refuses mercy to someone indebted to him.
The chapter will not allow us to separate truth from grace.
Truth without grace becomes brutality.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
Jesus gives us neither.
He gives us Himself.
“Grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.”
And nowhere is that union clearer than the cross.
Think about it.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He did not sweep rebellion underneath the universe's carpet.
He did not look at humanity's wickedness and say, “It doesn't matter.”
It mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross.
And yet sinners mattered so much that the Son of God willingly went to the cross for them.
That is Christianity.
Not God lowering His holiness until sinners become acceptable.
God providing a Savior who bears judgment so guilty sinners can be forgiven, reconciled, transformed, and brought home.
This is why biblical confrontation should never sound like:
“How dare someone like you sin?”
It should sound more like:
“Come back.”
Because every Christian confronting another Christian must remember that he is one beggar speaking to another beggar about the Bread of Life.
Every forgiven believer carries a scandal in his testimony.
Maybe yours never appeared in a newspaper.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you learned how to dress it in church clothes.
But heaven knows what grace rescued you from.
The thoughts.
The lust.
The pride.
The bitterness.
The dishonesty.
The secret addiction.
The unforgiveness.
The hypocrisy.
The nights when you knew exactly what God wanted...
and chose something else.
Then Jesus came near.
Not because your sin was small.
Because His mercy is great.
That is the scandal of grace.
The holy Son of God receives repentant sinners.
Liars can become truth-tellers.
The sexually broken can become pure.
The proud can become humble.
The bitter can forgive.
The addicted can begin walking in freedom.
The wandering sheep can come home.
The guilty can be washed.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
Not because Jesus rewrites God's definition of sin.
Because Jesus rewrites the sinner's story.
From scandal...
to grace.
And maybe now Matthew 18 is no longer about somebody else.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has brought a face into your mind.
Maybe you have been waiting for them to apologize first.
Maybe you have been telling everyone except them.
Maybe your version of the story has slowly become more important to you than reconciliation.
Maybe you know you sinned and have been hiding behind explanations.
Maybe you have called stubbornness “discernment.”
Maybe you have called gossip “processing.”
Maybe you have called bitterness “boundaries.”
Maybe you have called cowardice “keeping the peace.”
And maybe Jesus is asking you to stop hiding behind Christian vocabulary.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
