But emotional neglect should not be romanticized as maturity.
Christian marriage is covenant companionship.
Genesis says:
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
Marriage was never designed merely to produce two exhausted roommates who share expenses and occasionally attend church together.
Your spouse is a human soul.
Still changing.
Still struggling.
Still carrying questions.
Still carrying memories you do not completely understand.
Still becoming someone.
You have not finished knowing them.
And they have not finished knowing you.
That is why continuing to “date” your spouse can be much more than preserving romance.
It can be an act of curiosity.
A declaration:
“I refuse to assume I already know everything about you.”
Ask your wife what she dreams about now.
Not what she dreamed about when you were twenty-three.
Now.
Ask your husband what has been frightening him lately.
Not what he is accomplishing.
What is frightening him.
Ask what has made your spouse feel unseen.
Ask when they feel closest to you.
Ask what they miss about the beginning of your relationship.
Ask where you have wounded them.
Then be brave enough not to defend yourself immediately.
Listen.
There may be tears.
There may be silence.
There may be things you did not want to hear.
But sometimes healing begins when somebody finally feels safe enough to tell the truth.
And perhaps this article is landing painfully because you know exactly when the distance began.
After the baby.
After the betrayal.
After the funeral.
After the business failed.
After the argument nobody resolved.
After pornography entered the marriage.
After trust was damaged.
After depression swallowed a season.
After one of you became consumed with work.
After ministry became more important than the marriage.
After the words were spoken that neither of you could take back.
And now “go on a date” sounds painfully simplistic.
Fair enough.
Some wounds cannot be repaired over dinner.
Some marriages need much more than romance.
They need repentance.
Truth.
Accountability.
Counseling.
Boundaries.
Patience.
Forgiveness.
And sometimes a long rebuilding of trust.
But even there, the Gospel speaks.
Because Christianity is built around a truth scandalous enough to offend human pride:
Broken things are not beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
The cross itself looked like the end.
The Messiah betrayed.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Buried.
A stone rolled across the entrance.
Finished.
Except Jesus specializes in stories everybody else thinks are finished.
The tomb opened.
Death lost.
Christ rose.
And while marriage is not the Gospel and no earthly marriage is promised a painless outcome, Christian hope means brokenness does not have to have the final word.
This is our heartbeat:
Maybe your marriage has a chapter you wish nobody knew.
Jesus already knows.
Maybe there has been failure.
He knows.
Maybe there has been coldness.
He knows.
Maybe you have been pretending at church.
He knows.
Maybe everyone sees the smiling Facebook photographs while you know what the house feels like after the camera is gone.
He knows that too.
And Christ does not call sinners into hiding.
He calls us into the light.
The answer is not pretending your marriage is perfect.
The answer is bringing the truth before Jesus.
Repentance where repentance is needed.
Forgiveness where forgiveness is possible.
Wisdom where wisdom is necessary.
Help where help is needed.
And grace everywhere.
Maybe your next date should begin before you ever leave the house.
Maybe it begins with:
“I’m sorry I stopped pursuing you.”
Maybe:
“I think I have taken you for granted.”
Maybe:
“I've been physically present but emotionally absent.”
Maybe:
“I miss us.”
Maybe:
“I want Christ to become the center of our marriage again.”
Maybe:
“Will you forgive me?”
And perhaps the most beautiful answer will not be dramatic.
Maybe your spouse simply reaches across the table.
Maybe there are tears.
Maybe there is awkward silence.
Maybe rebuilding feels slower than you hoped.
But small acts of faithfulness matter.
Do not despise them.
You do not rebuild ten years of distance in ten minutes.
You begin with the next faithful step.
And then another.
And another.
Pray together again.
Talk again.
Laugh again.
Touch again.
Listen again.
Confess again.
Forgive again.
Seek help when you need it.
Put the phones down.
Look at each other.
Remember the person behind the responsibilities.
And please remember this:
Jesus is not merely interested in making your marriage more romantic.
He wants to make you more like Him.
Marriage can expose selfishness with ruthless precision.
It reveals impatience.
Pride.
Entitlement.
Bitterness.
Lust.
Control.
Fear.
Insecurity.
Our hunger to be served instead of serving.
And those revelations can feel scandalous.
But exposure in the hands of Christ can become an invitation to grace.
Because Jesus did not go to the cross for the polished version of you.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned how to be perfect husbands and wives.
Christ died for sinners.
That is the foundation beneath every Christian marriage.
Not “we are good people.”
But:
“Jesus is a great Savior.”
So if this article exposed something uncomfortable, do not waste that conviction.
Go talk to your spouse.
And go talk to God.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to know that another chapter can still be written.
Not because sharing a post somehow earns favor with God. It does not.
And stay close.
Not because you need another post buried in a folder.
There may come a night when you are angry.
A night when you feel invisible.
A night when both of you are exhausted and you begin wondering where the people in those wedding photographs went.
Come back then.
Remember:
Your spouse is not merely the person helping you survive adulthood.
That is your beloved.
A soul entrusted to your covenant love.
A person still worth discovering.
Still worth listening to.
Still worth praying with.
Still worth pursuing.
And perhaps tonight you do not need an expensive reservation.
Maybe you just need two chairs.
Two cups of coffee.
Two phones turned face down.
One honest conversation.
And enough humility to say:
“I don't want us to become strangers.”
Then listen.
Because maybe the marriage you thought was simply growing old has actually been waiting for someone to start pursuing again.
Maybe that someone is you.

And maybe years from now, when somebody asks when everything began changing, you will remember an ordinary night when pride finally surrendered, two hearts became honest, and Jesus was invited into the rooms you had kept locked.

Sometimes the most romantic thing you can do is look again at the person you promised never to stop choosing—and choose them again under the grace of the Christ who first chose to love sinners like you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE HAD TO HIRE HER OWN HUSBAND FOR ONE NIGHT—AND GOD PUT HER SON IN THE BLOODLINE OF JESUS
paragraphs: SHE HAD TO HIRE HER OWN HUSBAND FOR ONE NIGHT—AND GOD PUT HER SON IN THE BLOODLINE OF JESUS

Leah walked into the evening carrying a sentence no wife should ever have to say: “You must come in to me tonight—I have hired you.” But Genesis 30 is not ultimately a scandalous story about sex, mandrakes, jealousy, or a desperate woman competing for a man. It is the story of what God can do with the person who has spent years wondering, “Why am I never the one they choose?”
There are Bible verses we read slowly because they comfort us.
And then there are Bible verses that make us stop and ask...
Did she really just say that?
Genesis 30:16 is one of them.
Jacob comes home from the field in the evening.
Before he can settle in, Leah goes out to meet him.
Not Rachel.
Leah.
The woman who knew what it felt like to sleep beside a man whose heart belonged somewhere else.
And she says:
“Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son's mandrakes.”
The ancient Hebrew is even more striking:
אֵלַי תָּבוֹא כִּי שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ בְּדוּדָאֵי בְנִי
Elai tavo, ki sakhor sekhartikha beduda'ei beni.
The heart of the sentence is:
שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ — sakhor sekhartikha
“I have surely hired you.”
The Hebrew intensifies the idea of hiring. Leah is not speaking metaphorically about romance. A transaction has taken place.
And when you understand what happened before Jacob arrived from that field, the sentence becomes almost unbearably human.
Leah's son Reuben had found דּוּדָאִים — duda'im, traditionally translated “mandrakes,” and brought them to his mother.
Rachel wanted them.
Leah responded with words carrying years of accumulated pain:
“Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also?”
Listen to that again.
“My husband.”
That is what makes the scene hurt.
Legally, Jacob was Leah's husband.
Emotionally, Leah knew exactly where she stood.
Rachel then proposed an exchange: Jacob could spend that night with Leah in return for Reuben's mandrakes.
And Leah agreed.
So when Jacob returned from the field, Leah walked toward him and announced that extraordinary sentence.
She had, in effect, negotiated for a night with her own husband.
Imagine carrying that humiliation.
Imagine loving someone while knowing you are not the one he wanted.
Imagine having to negotiate for affection that you desperately wished would be freely given.
Imagine wondering whether another pregnancy might finally make somebody look at you differently.
Some people reading this know exactly what that feels like, even if mandrakes have never entered your story.
You have tried to earn what you desperately wanted someone to give freely.
You performed for love.
You became useful so people would keep you around.
You stayed silent because you were afraid honesty would make somebody leave.
You changed yourself.
Lowered your standards.
Overworked.
Overgave.
Overexplained.
Apologized when you had done nothing wrong.
You kept asking yourself:
What else do I need to become before somebody finally chooses me?
And that is why Genesis 30 cannot be understood properly without Genesis 29.
Because before Leah ever said, “I have hired you,” Scripture had already told us something devastating about her marriage.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Genesis says that after the deception surrounding his marriage to Leah, Jacob also married Rachel, and “he loved also Rachel more than Leah.”
Then comes one of the most tender sentences in Leah's entire story:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb...”
Genesis 29:31.

Some English translations render the Hebrew relationally as “unloved.” The Hebrew is stronger: שְׂנוּאָה — senu'ah, from a word associated with being hated. In this family context, the point is the painful disparity of affection between the sisters.
But notice the first movement of the verse.
The LORD saw Leah.
Jacob may have looked past her.
God did not.
Rachel may have occupied Jacob's heart.
Leah still occupied God's attention.
The woman who felt invisible was being watched by heaven.
And somebody reading this needs to sit with that for a moment.
God sees what rejection does to you when everybody else only sees your reaction to it.
He sees the nights when you ask what is wrong with you.
He sees you scrolling through somebody else's life wondering why they seem effortlessly loved while you feel perpetually tolerated.
He sees the marriage nobody knows is lonely.
He sees the child who spent years trying to make a parent proud.
He sees the believer serving everybody at church while quietly wondering whether anybody would notice if they disappeared.
He sees the person behind the smile.
He sees you.
Leah's children even became markers along the road of her longing.
When Reuben was born, Leah essentially hoped:
Now my husband will love me.
Then Simeon.
God had heard that she was unloved.
Then Levi.
Perhaps now, she hoped, her husband would finally become attached to her.
Can you hear the progression?
Love me.
Hear me.
Attach yourself to me.
Please.
Choose me.
Please.
Stay.
It is painfully recognizable.
We still do it.
Only we give our Reubens different names.
Career.
Money.
Beauty.
Sex.
Marriage.
Followers.
Success.
Ministry.
Achievement.
Recognition.
Maybe if I become attractive enough...
Maybe if I earn enough...
Maybe if my ministry grows enough...
Maybe if people applaud enough...
Maybe if I sacrifice enough...
Maybe if I become indispensable...
Then I will finally know that I matter.
But there is a terrifying problem with building your identity on human approval.
Even when you get it, you have to keep earning it.
That is slavery dressed like validation.
Then something happens with Leah's fourth son.
Something changes.
She gives birth again.
But this time the recorded words are different.
No “maybe Jacob will love me.”
No “maybe he will become attached to me.”
Instead:
“This time will I praise the LORD.”
And she called his name Judah.
יְהוּדָה — Yehudah.
Judah.
Praise.
Do not romanticize Leah's transformation as though every wound suddenly disappeared. Genesis 30 shows that the family conflict continued.
Leah was still human.
Still living inside a fractured household.
Still competing.
Still longing.
Still capable of desperation.
And eventually she would stand in that field at sunset and tell Jacob that she had hired him for the night.
The Bible is astonishingly honest.
It does not airbrush its people before putting them on the page.
That matters.
Because Christianity is not the story of impressive people finally becoming good enough for God.
It is the story of a holy God entering the wreckage of sinners and accomplishing redemption that sinners could never manufacture for themselves.
And this is where Leah's story becomes far greater than Leah could possibly have understood that evening.
Because Judah was not merely another son.
Judah became a tribe.
Genesis 49 would later speak of royal authority in connection with Judah.
Centuries passed.
Kings rose.
Kings fell.
Israel fractured.
Judgment came.
Exile came.
Generations disappeared into graves.
And then Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
And then...
“Jacob begat Judas [Judah] and his brethren.”
Follow that line far enough and you arrive at Jesus Christ.
The New Testament says it plainly:
“For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda.”
Hebrews 7:14.
Do you see what happened?
The woman wondering whether her husband would ever truly love her became the mother of Judah.
And through Judah's line, according to the flesh, came the Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
The Lion of the tribe of Judah.
Leah could not see Bethlehem from her heartbreak.
She could not see the manger.
She could not see Calvary.
She could not see the empty tomb.
She could not see Revelation declaring Christ “the Lion of the tribe of Juda.”
She saw Jacob walking home from a field.
God saw generations.
She saw rejection.
God was writing redemption.
She saw one painful night.
God saw a bloodline through which the promised Messiah would enter history.
That does not mean God approved of every action in that household.
The Bible frequently describes broken human behavior without prescribing it.
Genesis does not command polygamy, marital rivalry, bargaining for intimacy, reproductive competition, or favoritism.
It shows us what fallen human beings actually look like.
And that distinction matters.
The scandal is real.
So is the grace.
Maybe that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
We prefer Bible characters after we have cleaned them up.
God gives us Scripture before the cleanup.
Deception.
Jealousy.
Favoritism.
Sexual brokenness.
Family dysfunction.
Desperation.
Competition.
Manipulation.
Tears.
Longing.
People trying to get from other people what only God can ultimately secure in them.
And right through that mess runs the sovereign purpose of God.
That does not make evil good.
It means evil, failure, rejection, and human brokenness do not possess enough power to make God stop being God.
And then Jesus comes.
Not because humanity finally deserves Him.
Because we don't.
Jesus comes into the scandal.
He bears sin.
He touches lepers.
He eats with sinners.
He receives the rejected.
He calls the weary.
He confronts the self-righteous.
He forgives repentant sinners.
And finally, the sinless Son of God goes to a cross.
There, the One who deserved acceptance experienced rejection.
The One without sin bore sin.
The innocent One died for the guilty.
And three days later, the grave discovered that it could not keep Him.
This is the Gospel.
Not “try harder until God loves you.”
Not “be impressive enough and Jesus will choose you.”
Not “perform until heaven accepts you.”
Christ came for sinners.
Grace is not a salary.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased with mandrakes, money, religious performance, good works, church attendance, tears, or promises to do better.
Jesus paid what we could never pay.
The Gospel does not say:
Earn Me.
Jesus says:
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Maybe you have been living like Leah without realizing it.
Hiring people emotionally.
Trading pieces of yourself for moments of affection.
Trying to purchase belonging with usefulness.
Trying to make somebody choose you.
Trying to earn from human beings a verdict about your worth that they were never qualified to give.
And maybe underneath all of it is an even deeper tragedy.
You have been trying to earn God's love too.
Listen carefully.
You cannot purchase the blood of Jesus.
You cannot earn the resurrection.
You cannot negotiate yourself into grace.
Repentance is not paying God back.
Faith is not hiring Jesus.
Salvation is grace.
And when Christ saves, He does not merely improve the old life.
He begins making us new.
Your wounds may explain some of your behavior.
They do not have to rule it forever.
Your rejection may be part of your history.
It does not have to become your identity.
Your sin may be real.
Grace is real too.
Your past may contain chapters you would never voluntarily read aloud.
Jesus Christ is still writing.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Not because the scandal never happened.
Because scandal does not get the final word when Christ enters the story.
If this exposed the exhausting way you have been trying to earn love, stop hiding behind religious language for a moment.
Be honest.
And if you have never truly surrendered yourself to Jesus Christ, do not turn this into another inspirational story and keep scrolling.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace brings us to the One who forgives us and then teaches us to walk in newness of life.
And think of one person who needs Leah's story tonight.
Not fifty people.
One.
The woman who keeps asking why she was not enough.
The husband silently living with rejection.
The teenager comparing herself with everybody on her screen.
The believer who thinks his past disqualified him.
The person who smiles publicly and falls apart privately.
Or send this privately.
Save this too.
Because there may come a night when the person needing to read it again is you.
It does not.
It is not.
And never because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
But Christian ministry does require real people who freely decide, before God, to help sustain the work.
Think of it as voluntary ministry support—an offering of encouragement toward work you believe is bearing Gospel fruit.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing:
A share helps carry the message beyond the people we can reach ourselves.
Both matter, but neither earns a single ounce of God's grace.
Grace has already been purchased at a price infinitely greater than ours.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is having another stream of Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, accountability, and spiritual nourishment continually pointing you back toward Christ.
Who are you still trying to hire to love you?
Whose approval controls your peace?
Whose rejection still determines what you believe about yourself?
What achievement are you secretly hoping will finally make you feel worthy?
What relationship have you turned into an altar?
What human voice has become louder in your heart than the voice of God?
Leah once looked at a child and thought:
Maybe now my husband will love me.
Then another:
Maybe now he will hear me.
Then another:
Maybe now he will attach himself to me.
And then came Judah.
“This time will I praise the LORD.”
Centuries later, from the line of Judah came Jesus.
Perhaps that is where your healing begins too.
Not when everybody who rejected you finally realizes what they lost.
Not when the person who abandoned you comes crawling back.
Not when everybody apologizes.
Not when you finally become attractive, successful, wealthy, famous, married, admired, followed, or needed enough.
But when Jesus becomes more precious than the approval you have been begging other people to give you.
Leah walked toward Jacob that evening believing she had negotiated for one night.
She could not possibly have known how enormous the story surrounding her would become.
And maybe you cannot see what God is doing from where you are standing either.
You only see the rejection.
The unanswered prayer.
The broken relationship.
The embarrassing chapter.
The years you wish you could recover.
The thing you wish you had never done.
The thing somebody did to you.
The nights you spent asking why you were never enough.
But Scripture keeps whispering through Leah's complicated story:
God sees.
God hears.
And God's redemptive purposes are larger than the chapter currently hurting you.
So repent where you have sinned.
Forgive as Christ commands.
Seek healing where you are wounded.
Stop worshiping human approval.
Stop bargaining away pieces of yourself to be chosen.
And run to Jesus.
Because the deepest miracle in Leah's story is not that an unwanted woman finally obtained another night with Jacob.

It is that God was moving history toward the day when a descendant of Judah would stretch out His hands on a Roman cross and make redemption available to people whose lives were covered in scandals of their own.
That descendant is Jesus Christ.
And the hands stretched out on Calvary are still more powerful than the hands that rejected you.
And comment something honest.
“No more hiding.”
“Jesus, heal me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or simply:
“I choose Jesus.”

Because somewhere beneath the strange bargain, the mandrakes, the rivalry, the rejection, the marriage wounds, and one woman's desperate sentence is a truth hell would love for wounded people to forget:
The chapter where you felt unwanted may become the very place where you discover that Jesus was never looking away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Keep Calling It “Waiting on God”—But Deep Down, You Know You’re Afraid to Obey.
paragraphs: You Keep Calling It “Waiting on God”—But Deep Down, You Know You’re Afraid to Obey.
Sometimes the silence you are blaming on God is happening after He has already spoken—and what feels like spiritual patience may actually be fear wearing the clothes of faith.
There is a prayer you can keep praying long after you already know the answer.
“Lord, show me what to do.”
You whisper it in the morning.
You pray it before sleeping.
You ask for confirmation.
Then another confirmation.
Then a sermon.
Then a sign.
Then “peace.”
Then the perfect timing.
And because all of this sounds spiritual, almost nobody questions it.
Not even you.
But somewhere underneath all those prayers is a possibility you have been trying not to touch:
What if God has already made the next faithful step clear?
What if the problem is no longer that you do not know?
What if you are afraid of what obedience might cost you?
That question hurts because fear knows how to speak Christian.
Fear does not always scream, “I refuse to obey God.”
Sometimes fear whispers,
“I’m still praying about it.”
“I’m waiting on the Lord.”
“I just need another confirmation.”
“I don’t have peace yet.”
“Maybe this isn’t the right season.”
And sometimes those statements are completely legitimate. Scripture does call believers to pray, seek wisdom, wait upon the Lord, test what they hear, and refuse reckless decisions.
There are seasons when waiting is obedience.
But there are also moments when waiting becomes a respectable name for delay.
That distinction matters.
Because James writes something brutally simple:
—James 1:22, KJV
The Greek is even more revealing:
“Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταὶ παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτούς.”
Ginesthe de poiētai logou kai mē monon akroatai paralogizomenoi heautous.
In context, James is not attacking careful discernment. He is confronting the dangerous gap between receiving God’s Word and actually living according to it.
The word translated “doers,” ποιηταί (poiētai), speaks of those who do, make, or practice something.
Not merely admirers of the Word.
Not collectors of sermons.
Not people endlessly fascinated by biblical truth.
Doers.
And then comes the uncomfortable word:
παραλογιζόμενοι (paralogizomenoi).
Deceiving yourselves.
Misreasoning.
Drawing a false conclusion through faulty reasoning.
That means James recognizes something frightening about the human heart:
You can hear truth and still construct an argument convincing enough to make disobedience feel reasonable.
You can even make it sound spiritual.
And maybe that is where this becomes personal.
Maybe you already know you need to forgive someone.
But you keep waiting until you “feel ready.”
Maybe you know you need to confess what you have hidden.
But you are terrified of what honesty could cost.
Maybe you know that relationship keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you know the business practice is dishonest.
Maybe you know the apology needs to happen.
Maybe you know you need to stop returning to that secret sin.
Maybe Scripture has already settled the moral question, but you keep asking God to give you a different answer because the biblical one is painful.
Maybe obedience could cost you comfort.
Reputation.
Money.
Control.
A relationship.
An opportunity.
Someone’s approval.
And suddenly “waiting on God” becomes safer than walking with God.
Read that again.
Because there is a difference between waiting for God and waiting instead of obeying God.
Scripture honors the first.
It does not authorize the second.
Abraham knew something about this.
Genesis 12 records God telling Abram to leave his country, kindred, and father’s house for a land God would show him.
Imagine that conversation happening today.
“But Lord, where exactly?”
“What is the five-year plan?”
“What happens financially?”
“Can You show me the entire route first?”
“What if my family thinks I’ve lost my mind?”
“Can I have three confirmations?”
But Scripture gives us a stunning sentence:
“So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him…”
—Genesis 12:4, KJV
He did not possess the entire map.
He possessed a word from God sufficient for the step God required.
That is faith.
Biblical faith is not knowing everything that will happen.
It is trusting the God who knows everything that will happen.
And perhaps this is why obedience can feel terrifying.
We want God to reveal enough of tomorrow that obedience today no longer requires trust.
But then it would not be faith.
Hebrews 11:8 says of Abraham:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”
Notice the order.
Called.
Obeyed.
Went.
Not knowing.
We often want the order reversed.
Knowing.
Understanding.
Feeling safe.
Receiving guarantees.
Then obeying.
But faith sometimes walks while questions are still unanswered.
This does not mean every strong feeling, inner impression, dream, coincidence, or personal desire is God's command.
That distinction is crucial.
Christians are not commanded to obey every thought that enters their minds.
We test everything against Scripture.
We seek wisdom.
We pray.
We welcome mature biblical counsel.
And when Scripture has not prescribed a specific choice—Which job? Which city? Which house? Which legitimate opportunity?—careful discernment may be exactly what faithfulness requires.
But when God has already spoken clearly in His Word, “I’m waiting for confirmation” can become dangerous.
You do not need another sign to determine whether you should repent of known sin.
You do not need another prophecy to discover whether Christians are called to forgive.
You do not need another dream to determine whether dishonesty is wrong.
You do not need a mystical feeling before loving your enemy.
You do not need perfect emotional certainty before doing what Scripture has plainly commanded.
Sometimes we are not waiting for clarity.
We are waiting for obedience to become painless.
And it may never become painless.
Ask Jesus.
Gethsemane destroys the shallow idea that obedience always feels peaceful.
Jesus knew exactly what obedience would cost.
He was not confused about His mission.
He was approaching betrayal, humiliation, torture, crucifixion, and the bearing of sin according to the saving purpose of God.
Matthew records Him praying:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
—Matthew 26:39, KJV
Do not rush past that.
Jesus did not teach us that faithful obedience means the absence of anguish.
He showed us perfect obedience in the presence of anguish.
The Son submitted to the Father even when the road before Him led to a cross.
And because He did…
sinners like us have hope.
This is where Christianity separates itself from motivational self-improvement.
The Gospel is not simply:
“Stop being afraid and obey harder.”
If that were the message, frightened sinners would merely receive another burden.
The Gospel begins with what Christ has done.
Jesus obeyed where we have failed.
Jesus remained faithful where we have compromised.
Jesus went to the cross for sinners—including procrastinating, frightened, excuse-making, self-deceiving sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the scandal of grace is that the person who finally admits, “Lord, I have been hiding behind excuses,” does not discover a Savior standing far away with folded arms.
The repentant sinner discovers Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen in victory.
Full of truth.
Full of grace.
Calling us out of darkness.
Not so we can remain unchanged, but so grace can produce what fear never could.
A surrendered life.
This is why grace must never become another excuse for disobedience.
Grace does not say, “Your rebellion does not matter.”
Grace says, “Your rebellion mattered enough that Christ shed His blood—and His mercy is great enough to forgive you and transform you.”
Jesus does not merely forgive us from something.
He calls us into something.
Follow Me.
That invitation has always carried a cost.
Peter had to leave nets.
Matthew had to leave the tax booth.
Zacchaeus could not encounter Christ and continue treating money the same way.
Paul could not meet the risen Jesus and continue persecuting His church.
Again and again, grace interrupts a life and produces movement.
Not perfect movement.
Not fearless movement.
But surrendered movement.
And perhaps that is what you have been avoiding.
You keep asking God to remove the fear before you obey.
Perhaps courage will come differently.
Perhaps courage will meet you while your hands are still shaking.
Peter did not discover that water was solid before stepping out of the boat.
Abraham did not receive the entire itinerary before leaving.
The servants at Cana filled the waterpots before they saw what Jesus would do.
Obedience frequently begins before outcomes are visible.
And there is something else you need to hear.
Delayed obedience can become dangerous because repeated resistance can train your heart to become comfortable with conviction.
The first time God’s Word confronts something in you, it hurts.
The tenth time, perhaps a little less.
Eventually, you can learn how to hear a sermon about your exact compromise, say “Amen,” feel convicted for five minutes, and continue living exactly the same way.
That is why James does not merely warn about ignorance.
He warns about self-deception.
You can become so familiar with truth that hearing it begins to feel like obeying it.
You highlight the verse.
Save the sermon.
Post the quote.
Cry during worship.
And still refuse the thing Christ is putting His finger on.
That is terrifying.
Because proximity to truth is not the same thing as surrender to truth.
James continues with the picture of someone looking into a mirror and then walking away, immediately forgetting what he saw.
Scripture does not merely give us information about God.
It exposes us before God.
And sometimes the reflection is uncomfortable.
Maybe the mirror is showing you fear.
Maybe pride.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe lust.
Maybe dishonesty.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe a relationship you have made into an idol.
Maybe a secret habit you keep promising to surrender “eventually.”
Maybe an apology you owe.
Maybe restitution needs to happen.
Maybe you need to ask for help because the private battle is becoming stronger than your private resistance.
Maybe your next act of obedience is not dramatic at all.
Maybe it is one phone call.
One confession.
One boundary.
One conversation.
One deleted number.
One honest sentence.
One act of forgiveness.
One decision to stop hiding.
One trembling prayer:
“Jesus, I surrender.”
And maybe you are afraid that if you surrender, everything will fall apart.
But what if the thing falling apart is the prison you have mistaken for protection?
What if obedience does cost something?
It probably will.
Jesus never advertised discipleship as painless.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
—Matthew 16:24, KJV
A cross is not comfortable.
Self-denial is not comfortable.
Repentance is not comfortable.
Confession can be humiliating.
Forgiveness can feel unfair.
Leaving sin can feel like losing something you cannot live without.
But sin has always lied about what it gives and hidden what it takes.
Jesus tells the truth about both the cost and the destination.
He calls us to Himself.
And this is the moment where you need to stop thinking about everybody else who should read this.
Not your spouse.
Not your friend.
Not the lukewarm Christian you have been worried about.
You.
What have you been calling “waiting on God” that may actually be fear of obeying what God has already made clear?
Do not answer publicly if doing so would expose something that should remain private.
But answer God.
Be painfully honest.
“Lord, I am scared.”
That is a prayer God can work with.
“Lord, I know what Your Word says, but I don't know if I have the courage.”
Bring Him that.
“Lord Jesus, I have been asking for another answer because I don't like the answer Scripture already gave me.”
Bring Him that too.
Repentance begins in truth.
You do not have to impress Jesus with religious language.
He already knows.
He knows what you are afraid of losing.
He knows the conversation you dread.
He knows the consequences you cannot predict.
He knows how long you have been postponing this.
And He knows every failure that brought you here.
Still, grace calls.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that blesses our hiding.
Grace that opens the prison door and says,
“Come out.”
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment when another excuse was forming.
Maybe tonight you were going to tell yourself, “Next week.”
Maybe after one more prayer.
One more sign.
One more Sunday.
One more confirmation.
One more comfortable delay.
But perhaps your next prayer should not be,
“God, tell me what to do.”
Perhaps it should be,
“God, give me courage to obey what You have already shown me through Your Word.”
That changes everything.
And please understand this carefully:
You are not saved because you finally become courageous enough.
You are not justified before God by accumulating impressive acts of obedience.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works that give us grounds for boasting, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But the passage does not stop there.
Ephesians 2:10 says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
Grace saves.
And saving grace transforms.
We do not obey so Christ will love us enough to save us.

We obey because Christ is Lord, because His grace has captured us, and because genuine faith cannot be content forever with merely hearing the voice of the Shepherd while continually refusing to follow Him.
So if fear has been hiding behind spiritual vocabulary, bring it into the light.
No performance.
No pretending.
No religious costume.
Just truth.
“Jesus, I am afraid.”
Then ask Him for strength.
Open Scripture.
Seek wise biblical counsel where discernment is genuinely needed.
Make sure what you are calling “God's will” actually agrees with God's Word.
And when Scripture has made your responsibility clear…
take the next faithful step.
Not every step for the next twenty years.
The next one.
You may still tremble.
Obey trembling.
You may still cry.
Obey crying.
You may not know how everything ends.
Obey trusting Christ with the ending.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding behind spiritual language, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can make a simple confession of dependence:
Let other believers know they are not the only ones trembling between conviction and obedience.
And think of the person who has been saying for months, “I’m still praying about it,” when you both know the real battle is fear.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But if Gospel-centered truth has strengthened you, you can help put that truth in front of someone who may never have searched for it themselves.
That kind of support matters.

Invite your family. Invite the friend quietly struggling with faith. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the seeker with difficult questions. Even invite the unbeliever who thinks grace could never possibly be for someone like them.
Because fear has a way of returning with better arguments.
And when it does, come back and remember:
Waiting on God is holy when God has told you to wait.
But when His Word has already made obedience clear, fear does not become faith merely because we give it a spiritual name.
Jesus is not asking you to know the entire road.
He is calling you to trust the One who does.
And perhaps years from now, when you look back at the moment everything began to change, you will realize the miracle was not that God finally gave you another sign.
The miracle was that grace finally gave your trembling heart the courage to stop hiding and say yes to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS SEX ONLY FOR HAVING CHILDREN?
paragraphs:
IS SEX ONLY FOR HAVING CHILDREN?
What Scripture Actually Shows About Marital Pleasure—and Why the Bible Is Far Less Embarrassed About Married Desire Than Many Christians Are
There are married Christians who can pray together without shame.
They can worship together.
Read Scripture together.
Raise children together.
Serve in church together.
And yet when the bedroom door closes, something strange happens.
They suddenly become embarrassed by something God Himself created.
A husband wonders whether enjoying his wife too much is somehow “carnal.”
A wife has spent years feeling guilty for wanting to be desired.
A couple knows that sex can produce children—but somewhere along the way they absorbed the idea that reproduction must therefore be the only truly holy reason for sexual intimacy.
And sometimes nobody ever explicitly taught them this.
They simply inherited it.
From silence.
From awkwardness.
From shame.

From the strange assumption that holiness requires Christians to speak confidently about adultery, lust, fornication, and sexual sin—but almost whisper when Scripture speaks about the beauty of sexual love inside marriage.
So we need to ask the question plainly:
Is sex only for having children?
And perhaps an even more uncomfortable question:
Does the Bible actually permit a husband and wife to desire, enjoy, and delight in one another sexually—even when conception is not the immediate purpose of their intimacy?
The answer should not come from modern sexual culture.
It should not come from pornography.
It should not come from reactionary purity culture.
It should not come from whatever makes us personally comfortable.
It must come from Scripture.
And once Scripture is allowed to speak for itself, something beautiful emerges:
The Bible honors procreation profoundly, but it does not reduce marital sexuality to procreation.
Children are unquestionably presented as a blessing from God. Genesis establishes the procreative dimension of marriage immediately:
“Be fruitful and multiply.”
In Hebrew:
פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ — perû ûrevû
“Be fruitful and multiply.”
Genesis 1:28.

Human sexuality has an undeniable relationship to fruitfulness. Christianity has no reason to apologize for that. Children are not accidents that interrupt the “real” purpose of marriage. Psalm 127 calls children a heritage from the LORD.
But here is where careful Bible reading matters.
Something may have more than one God-given purpose.
Food sustains life, yet Scripture also allows feasting.
Speech communicates information, yet Scripture also gives us poetry and song.
Marriage can produce children, but Scripture also presents marriage as companionship, covenant union, mutual belonging, comfort, delight—and, yes, sexual pleasure.
Go back to the beginning.
Before sin.
Before shame.
Before adultery.
Before pornography.
Before humanity learned to exploit bodies.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
“One flesh.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not describe the woman merely as a reproductive instrument.
Genesis 2 first presents the crisis of human aloneness:
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
God's answer is relational.
Personal.
Covenantal.
Adam receives someone with whom he can share life.
And his response to Eve is almost poetry:
“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Then Scripture gives us one of the most revealing descriptions of innocent embodied existence anywhere in the Bible:
“And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ — velo yitboshashu
They were not ashamed.
That sentence is breathtaking when you remember where it occurs.
Genesis 2:25 comes before the Fall.
Nakedness existed before shame.
The body existed before lust corrupted the gaze.
Sexual difference existed before sexual exploitation.
Marriage existed before adultery.
Desire itself is not the enemy.
Sin is.
And Christianity does something radically different from both sexual repression and sexual permissiveness.
The world often says, “If you desire it, fulfill it.”
Religious shame can imply, “If you desire it, distrust it.”
Scripture says something far richer:
Desire must be brought under the lordship of God.
Some desires must be denied.
Some desires must be crucified.
Some desires must be redirected.
But some desires can be received with thanksgiving because God Himself placed them within a covenant where they can become expressions of faithful love.
And this is where Proverbs becomes almost impossible to misunderstand.
Proverbs 5 warns a young man against adultery. The chapter does not respond to dangerous sexual desire by commanding him to become sexually indifferent.
Instead, Scripture redirects his desire toward his wife.
Then come words Christians sometimes seem embarrassed to read aloud:
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth…”
And then:
“Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:18–19.
Not pornography.
Not secular romance literature.
Not a modern marriage counselor trying to make Christianity more sexually permissive.
Proverbs.
Wisdom literature.
Scripture.
The Hebrew is striking.
The text uses language of rejoicing, delight, and being continually captivated by marital love.
The sexual imagery is not incidental.
The wife is not being described merely as the potential mother of the husband's future children.
The husband is told to rejoice in her.
To delight in her.
To remain captivated by her love.
Why?
Because biblical holiness is not merely the suppression of forbidden desire.
It also includes the proper celebration of righteous desire.
God does not simply tell the married man where he must not drink.
The imagery of Proverbs 5 tells him to drink from his own cistern.
Faithfulness is not portrayed as lifeless deprivation.
It is covenant delight.
And then there is the Song of Songs.
Perhaps nowhere does our discomfort become more obvious.
Because if marital sexual pleasure were legitimate only when directly oriented toward conception, the Song of Songs would be extraordinarily difficult to explain.
Read it carefully.
The lovers admire each other's bodies.
They long for one another.
They speak of kisses.
Fragrance.
Touch.
Beauty.
Gardens.
Fruit.
Spices.
Longing.
Belonging.
The woman is not merely tolerated as the object of male desire.
She speaks.
She desires.
She initiates.
She longs.
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.”
And later:
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
Song of Songs 7:10.
The Hebrew word translated “desire” there is:
תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah
The Song does not treat mutual marital attraction as something embarrassing that mature believers eventually outgrow.
It places covenantal desire inside biblical poetry.
That does not mean every line of the Song should be crudely literalized. Nor does it settle every theological question Christians have debated about sexuality.
But we should not erase what is plainly present.
The Song celebrates the beauty of love between bride and bridegroom in embodied, passionate language.
And notably, its expressions of desire are not constantly justified by references to conception.
The lovers delight in one another.
That matters.
Because some Christians have unconsciously turned marriage into a place where sex may be technically permitted while pleasure remains spiritually suspicious.
Scripture does not require us to make that move.
Then Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 7 that becomes even more significant when we remember the ancient world in which he wrote.
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
Then:
“For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
The Greek word translated “likewise” is:
ὁμοίως — homoiōs
Likewise.
Similarly.
In the same manner.
Paul establishes reciprocity.
The husband's body belongs, covenantally, to his wife just as her body belongs, covenantally, to him.
That passage has sometimes been horribly misused as though marriage creates permission for coercion.
It does not.
Read Paul's logic carefully.
The command is reciprocal.
Neither spouse is given unilateral selfish ownership while the other becomes an object.
Christian marital intimacy is shaped by mutuality.
And Paul's next instruction is equally revealing:
“Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again…”
Agreement.
Temporary abstinence.
Then reunion.
Why does Paul encourage reunion?
Among his stated concerns is sexual temptation and lack of self-control.
In other words, sexual intimacy within marriage has a purpose beyond conceiving children.
It can serve marital faithfulness.
Mutual giving.
Union.
Protection against temptation.
And embodied intimacy between husband and wife.
Paul does not say:
“Come together again only when you intend to conceive.”
That sentence is simply not in the text.
This does not diminish children.
It simply refuses to make Scripture say less—or more—than Scripture actually says.
Hebrews 13:4 gives us another important boundary:
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled…”
The Greek word translated “bed” is:
κοίτη — koitē
In context, the marriage bed is treated as something that can remain undefiled precisely because sexual immorality is being contrasted with the honorable covenant of marriage.
The Bible therefore refuses two opposite errors.
It refuses to worship sex.
And it refuses to demonize sex.
Outside God's boundaries, sexuality can become profoundly destructive.
Adultery destroys trust.
Pornography trains people to consume bodies rather than love persons.
Lust turns a human being into an object inside the imagination.
Sexual exploitation wounds people God made in His image.
Fornication contradicts God's design for sexual union within marriage.
But the abuse of something does not prove that its proper use is shameful.
Fire can destroy a house.
Fire can also warm one.
The issue is not whether fire exists.
The issue is whether it remains where it belongs.
And this is where the Gospel enters the bedroom in ways many Christians desperately need.
Because maybe your problem is not theological curiosity.
Maybe this article touched a wound.
Maybe sexuality has never felt innocent to you.
Maybe you carry memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe someone crossed yours.
Maybe pornography reshaped your imagination.
Maybe adultery shattered your marriage.
Maybe you were sexually reckless before coming to Christ.
Maybe you were taught that your body itself was dirty.
Maybe your marriage now contains years of rejection, resentment, exhaustion, misunderstanding, physical changes, infertility, trauma, mismatched desire, or silence.
Maybe you are reading an article about marital pleasure while quietly thinking:
You don't know my story.
No.
But Jesus does.
And the Christian message is not that sexually unbroken people get to approach God while everyone else remains permanently stained.
The Gospel is that sinners can be washed.
Paul writes to believers in Corinth after naming serious patterns of sin, including sexual sin, and then says:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified…”
1 Corinthians 6:11.
Were.
That word carries hope.
Your sin may belong to your history without being allowed to own your identity.
What you did matters.
What happened to you matters.
Repentance matters.
Healing matters.
Consequences can be real.
Trust may need rebuilding.
But Jesus Christ is not intimidated by the chapter you wish nobody knew.
At the cross, Christ does not pretend sin is harmless.
He demonstrates how serious it is.
And in His resurrection, He demonstrates that sin and death do not get the final word.
This is why grace is not permission to continue destroying ourselves.
Grace calls us home.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace transforms.
Grace takes sexuality away from both shame and idolatry and places the whole person under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
So, is sex only for having children?
Scripture does not present it that way.
Procreation is a beautiful and significant good associated with marriage and sexual union.
But Scripture also presents marital intimacy in connection with one-flesh union, companionship, mutual belonging, delight, desire, faithfulness, and reciprocal conjugal responsibility.
There is no biblical requirement that married couples feel guilty because they experience pleasure in one another.
But there is also something important that must be said.
Biblical marital pleasure is not selfish consumption with a wedding ring added to it.
Marriage does not baptize selfishness.
A husband does not honor God by treating his wife's body as an entitlement.
A wife does not honor God by treating intimacy as a weapon of manipulation.
Neither spouse should use Scripture to pressure, humiliate, threaten, or coerce the other.
Christlike love asks something deeper:
How can I love you faithfully?
Not merely:
What can I get from you?
Ephesians 5 ultimately places Christian marriage beneath the enormous reality of Christ and His Church.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That is not the language of consumption.
It is sacrifice.
Christ gives Himself.
So Christian intimacy should never become the opposite of Christlike love.
The bedroom is not a theological exemption where selfishness suddenly becomes holy.
Tenderness matters.
Patience matters.
Communication matters.
Consent matters.
Faithfulness matters.
The wellbeing of your spouse matters.
And sometimes love looks passionate.
Sometimes it looks patient.
Sometimes it looks like listening.
Sometimes it means recognizing pain, illness, postpartum recovery, disability, trauma, grief, exhaustion, age, hormonal changes, or emotional wounds that affect intimacy.
A biblical theology of marital pleasure should make husbands and wives more loving, not more demanding.
More tender.
Not more entitled.
More honest.
Not more manipulative.
Because ultimately marriage itself points beyond marriage.
Sex is not God.
Romance is not God.
Your spouse is not your Savior.
Marriage cannot carry the weight of your soul.
Even the happiest marriage on earth is temporary.
Jesus taught that resurrection life cannot simply be reduced to the continuation of earthly marriage as we presently experience it.
Marriage is precious.
But Christ is ultimate.
Sexual pleasure is a gift.
But Christ is the Giver.
Children are a blessing.
But Christ is Lord.
And perhaps that is the freedom somebody needed today.
You do not have to worship sexuality.
You do not have to fear it.
You do not have to call evil what God designed for good.
And you do not have to call good what God calls sin.
You can bring your sexuality—your desires, failures, wounds, marriage, singleness, temptations, memories, questions, and body—to Jesus Christ.
All of it.
Nothing hidden.
Nothing dressed up.
Nothing pretending.
Because Christianity is not the story of people who successfully kept their scandals secret.
It is the story of sinners meeting a Savior whose grace is greater than the identities sin tried to give them.
You can simply write “Christ is still healing me.”
And if grace has already restored something you once thought was permanently destroyed, tell your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that restoration is possible.
Send it privately to someone who would never publicly admit that this subject has been hurting them.

Supporting Christian ministry should never be presented as though paying money earns God's favor—it does not. Salvation is by grace, and God's glory cannot be purchased. But when you freely choose to support biblical work you believe is bearing good fruit, that generosity can itself become an act of stewardship and participation in Gospel ministry.
And don't keep the message trapped on this page.

One share can reach a marriage you never knew was struggling. One tag can reach someone carrying shame in silence. One honest comment can make another believer realize they are not the only person still fighting. One saved article can become something someone returns to on a difficult night.
But remember this before you leave.
The greatest intimacy you will ever experience is not ultimately found in another human being knowing your body.
It is found in Jesus Christ knowing the darkest rooms of your soul…
and still calling you out of hiding and into His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID THE HIGH PRIEST WEAR TWELVE STONES? THE ANSWER MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU THINK GOD SEES YOU
paragraphs: WHY DID THE HIGH PRIEST WEAR TWELVE STONES? THE ANSWER MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU THINK GOD SEES YOU

He carried their names over his heart—and thousands of years later, that ancient picture points us toward something breathtaking about Jesus Christ, guilt, remembrance, and the grace that refuses to forget His people.
Imagine standing outside the Tabernacle.

Smoke rises from the altar. Blood has been shed. The smell of sacrifice hangs in the wilderness air. Somewhere behind the curtains is a place ordinary Israelites cannot simply walk into whenever they please.
And then you see him.
The high priest.

His garments are unlike those of anyone else in Israel. Gold catches the desert light. Blue, purple, and scarlet thread run through carefully woven fabric. Upon his shoulders are stones engraved with names.
But then your eyes move toward his chest.
There, over his heart, rests something extraordinary.
Twelve precious stones.
Twelve names.
Twelve tribes.
Not decoration.
Not religious jewelry.
Not an ancient attempt to make the priest appear impressive.
God commanded it.
And hidden inside that command is one of the most beautiful pictures in the Old Testament of what it means to be represented before God.
Because when the high priest entered before the LORD, Israel was not merely waiting outside.
Their names went in with him.
That changes everything.
Exodus 28 describes the priestly breastpiece, traditionally called the breastplate of judgment. The Hebrew expression is:
חֹשֶׁן מִשְׁפָּט
ḥōšen mišpāṭ.

The second word, מִשְׁפָּט, mishpat, carries the sense of judgment, justice, or judicial decision. This was therefore not merely an ornamental breastpiece. It belonged to the solemn priestly ministry established by God.
The LORD commanded that precious stones be mounted upon it in four rows.
Then Scripture gives the detail we cannot afford to miss:
וְהָאֲבָנִים תִּהְיֶיןָ עַל־שְׁמֹת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה עַל־שְׁמֹתָם
“Veha’avanim tihyena al-shemot benei-Yisrael, sheteim esreh al-shemotam…”

The sense of Exodus 28:21 is that the stones were to correspond to the names of the sons of Israel—twelve stones according to their names—engraved like seals, each bearing the name of one of the twelve tribes.
Then comes the sentence that makes the entire scene breathe.
Exodus 28:29 says that Aaron was to bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment:
עַל־לִבּוֹ
‘al-libbo.
“Over his heart.”
When he went into the Holy Place.
Over his heart.
Read that again slowly.
Their names were not lying forgotten somewhere in the camp.
They were being carried before the LORD.
The text says Aaron would bear their names “for a memorial before the LORD continually.”
לְזִכָּרֹן לִפְנֵי־יְהוָה תָּמִיד
Lezikkaron lifnei-YHWH tamid.
“For a memorial before the LORD continually.”
The point was not that an all-knowing God might accidentally forget Israel unless Aaron wore gemstones.
Biblically, “memorial” language is covenantal and relational. God was establishing a visible, priestly sign that His covenant people were being represented before Him.
Twelve tribes.
Different histories.
Different failures.
Different personalities.
Different futures.
One priest carrying their names.
And maybe that is where this ancient passage suddenly becomes uncomfortable.
Because we know what those tribes were actually like.
These were not twelve tribes of flawless saints.
Their family story contained jealousy, deception, sexual sin, violence, betrayal, fear, idolatry, rebellion, and staggering moments of unbelief.
Read Genesis.
Read Exodus.
Keep reading through Israel’s history.
This is not the story of human beings proving that they deserved to have their names carried before a holy God.
It is the story of a holy God remaining faithful to His covenant purposes despite the terrifying reality of human sin.
The stones were precious, but the people whose names were engraved upon them were deeply flawed.
That sounds painfully familiar.
We polish our Christian appearance.
We know when to say, “God is good.”
We post the verse.
We attend the service.
We lift our hands.
We tell people we are blessed.
But there are names for things happening inside us that never make it into the Facebook caption.
Shame.
Jealousy.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Secret compromise.
Prayerlessness.
Pride.
Unforgiveness.
Fear.
The marriage nobody knows is struggling.
The child you cry about when everyone else is asleep.
The temptation you promised God you would never return to.
The resentment you keep dressing up as “discernment.”
The spiritual exhaustion hidden behind ministry activity.
The private version of you that feels completely different from the public one.
And eventually a question begins whispering from somewhere deep inside:
Would God still want my name near His presence if everyone knew the whole story?
The Gospel answers that question in a way cheap religion never could.
But before we rush to the answer, we need to understand something.
The twelve stones did not mean sin did not matter.
The entire Tabernacle system screamed the opposite.
God is holy.
Sin is serious.
Atonement matters.
Access to God cannot be manufactured by human sincerity.
Blood was shed.
Sacrifices were offered.
Priests were appointed.
Boundaries existed.
The breastpiece cannot honestly be turned into a sentimental message saying, “God thinks you are precious, therefore everything you do is fine.”
That is not biblical grace.
Biblical grace never needs to pretend sin is harmless.
Grace is astonishing precisely because sin is not harmless.
The high priest carried the names of Israel before God, but even that high priest was himself a sinner.
Aaron needed atonement too.
The priest carrying everyone else’s names still needed mercy for his own.
And that is where the Old Testament creates a hunger it cannot finally satisfy.
We need a better priest.
A priest who does not need cleansing for His own sins.
A priest whose ministry does not end in death.
A priest who does not enter an earthly sanctuary again and again with sacrifices that can never become the final answer to human guilt.
We need someone greater.
And then Jesus comes.
The New Testament does not tell us that Jesus literally wears Aaron’s twelve-stone breastpiece in heaven, so we should not claim what Scripture does not claim.
What Scripture does tell us is infinitely greater.
Hebrews calls Jesus our great High Priest.
The Greek says:
ἔχοντες οὖν ἀρχιερέα μέγαν
Echontes oun archierea megan.
“Therefore, having a great high priest…”
And Hebrews 4:14 identifies Him:
Ἰησοῦν τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ
Iēsoun ton huion tou Theou.
“Jesus, the Son of God.”
Aaron carried Israel’s names into the earthly sanctuary.
Jesus entered the greater and perfect heavenly reality as the true and final High Priest.
Hebrews 9:24 says Christ entered heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.
On our behalf.
Sit with those words.
The Christian hope is not that you become impressive enough to walk into God’s presence carrying a résumé of spiritual accomplishments.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 7:25 declares that He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him because He always lives to intercede for them.
The Greek expression is stunning:
πάντοτε ζῶν εἰς τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν
Pantote zōn eis to entynchanein hyper autōn.
“Always living to intercede for them.”
Always living.
Always interceding.
Your salvation does not rest upon your ability to keep yourself impressive enough for Jesus.
It rests upon the sufficiency of Christ.
That does not give us permission to cherish sin.
It gives us a reason to finally stop hiding it.
Because the Gospel is not Jesus helping respectable people become slightly better.
The Gospel is Jesus Christ saving sinners.
Maybe you have spent years trying to hide the part of your story you think would make God turn His face away.
Maybe you have wondered whether you have failed too many times.
Maybe you repented, fell again, cried again, promised again, and now you are almost embarrassed to pray.
Maybe your Bible has been closed for weeks.
Maybe your heart has become cold and you know it.
Maybe nobody around you knows.
But you know.
And God knows.
Here is where grace becomes scandalous.
Christ did not die for the fictional version of you.
He died for sinners.
Romans 5:8 does not say God waited for us to become presentable.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is the scandal.
Not that sin is insignificant.
But that the Son of God willingly came for people who could never cleanse themselves.
The cross simultaneously destroys our excuses and destroys our despair.
It tells our pride:
Your sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
Then it tells our shame:
His sacrifice was sufficient enough that you do not have to remain condemned when you come to Him in faith.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace stops being a religious theory and becomes personal.
You stop defending what Jesus died to forgive.
You stop calling darkness “just who I am.”
You stop hiding behind church language.
You stop blaming everyone else.
You bring the truth into the light.
You confess.
You turn.
You come to Christ.
And you discover that the hands receiving repentant sinners are scarred hands.
Somebody reading this has been running from God because you think returning means pretending you never left.
It does not.
Come home telling the truth.
The same Bible that commands repentance also tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because tears earn salvation.
Not because you punished yourself long enough.
Because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
This is what religious performance cannot understand.
Religion says, “Clean yourself up, then come closer.”
The Gospel announces that sinners must come to Christ because they cannot cleanse themselves.
And Christ does not merely improve the old story.
He gives new life.
This is why the image of those names carried before God is so powerful.
Not because Christians should pretend every detail of Aaron’s breastpiece is secretly a coded prediction.
We do not need to force the text.
The biblical pattern is already beautiful enough.
God established a priesthood in which His covenant people were represented before Him.
That priesthood was temporary and imperfect.
Then Hebrews directs our eyes to the greater High Priest whose sacrifice is sufficient and whose priesthood does not pass away.
Jesus.
The One who does not merely carry stones.
The One who carried a cross.
The One who did not merely enter a sanctuary made with hands.
The One who entered heaven itself on behalf of His people.
The One who did not offer the blood of another.
The One who offered Himself.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who lives.
The One who intercedes.
The One who saves.
Suddenly the question is no longer merely, “Why did the high priest wear twelve stones?”
The deeper question becomes:
Who is representing you before God?
Your morality?
Your church attendance?
Your generosity?
Your theology?
Your reputation?
Your family name?
Your ministry?
Your religious achievements?
None of them can bear the weight of your eternity.
Only Christ can.
There is no stone expensive enough to purchase forgiveness.
No religious garment beautiful enough to cover guilt.
No human priest holy enough to become the final mediator.
No amount of self-improvement powerful enough to resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
We need Jesus.
And perhaps you needed to hear that today because you have quietly made Christianity about your ability to hold onto God.
The Gospel begins somewhere far more secure.
Christ is mighty to save those who come to God through Him.
So come.
Not tomorrow when you feel spiritual again.
Not after you have gone seven days without failing.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Come honestly.
Repent honestly.
Believe honestly.
Bring the hidden thing into His light.
You do not need another Christian performance.
You need Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write the details publicly. But if you want to mark this moment, comment, “no more hiding.”
If your faith has been battered and you are still clinging to Jesus, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you are exhausted and need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”

And if you know from experience that grace has met you in places nobody else could see, leave a testimony. Someone scrolling through the comments tonight may need evidence that Jesus still restores broken lives.
Then think of one person whose name came into your mind while reading this.
You know who they are.
The friend who is drifting.
The son who stopped believing.
The daughter carrying shame.
The believer quietly fighting temptation.
The person who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Or send this privately with one sentence:
“I thought about you while reading this.”
Not as a religious performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
But if Christ has given us truth worth hearing, we should not be ashamed to help truth travel.
If you genuinely want your Facebook presence to glorify God, use it intentionally. Let somebody encounter Scripture between the arguments, advertisements, tragedies, memes, and noise.
One share may place the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
One saved article may become something you return to on the night shame starts speaking again.
One tag may remind someone they have not been forgotten.
One honest comment may give another struggling believer enough courage to stop pretending.
And one decision to keep receiving biblical teaching may help turn occasional inspiration into consistent discipleship.
That is why I want to invite you to stay close to Gospel Warrior.
It does not purchase blessing, salvation, forgiveness, spiritual status, or divine favor. Jesus cannot be bought.

It is simply a practical way to stand behind the work, help Gospel-centered content continue reaching people, and participate in putting Scripture, discipleship, encouragement, and the message of Christ in front of more souls.
If you have been asking how you can help Gospel Warrior keep spreading Christ-centered truth, this is one tangible way.
Not because God needs an algorithm.
Because people need Jesus.
Somewhere tonight there is a person carrying a secret and wondering whether their name has become synonymous with their worst mistake.
Let this reach them.
Let them discover that Christianity is not the announcement that good people can congratulate themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The ancient high priest walked toward the Holy Place carrying twelve names over his heart.
But the biblical story did not end in the Tabernacle.
It moved toward a hill outside Jerusalem.
Toward nails.
Toward blood.
Toward a torn veil.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward a risen High Priest.
Toward grace.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your past.
Your failure may have consequences.
Your wounds may take time to heal.
Repentance may require painful honesty.
Restoration may require rebuilding what sin damaged.
Grace does not erase truth.
Grace brings truth to the cross and refuses to let sin have the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
So when shame whispers, “Look what you did,” look toward Jesus.
When pride whispers, “Look how good you are,” look toward Jesus.
When religion whispers, “Try harder so God will finally accept you,” look toward Jesus.
When despair whispers, “There is no way back,” look toward Jesus.
Our hope is not that our story contains no scandal.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ entered the story.
And once Jesus becomes the center, your darkest chapter no longer gets to write the final sentence.
Remember this when you forget everything else:
Your sin may have written a chapter in blood and tears—but at the cross, Jesus proved that your worst chapter does not have to become your final one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TEN WOMEN DAVID LEFT BEHIND: What Happened After Absalom Used Them?
paragraphs:
THE TEN WOMEN DAVID LEFT BEHIND: What Happened After Absalom Used Them?
They survived the rooftop. Then came a sentence in Scripture so quiet—and so devastating—that most readers pass over it without realizing what happened to them next.
There were ten of them.
We do not know their names.
We do not know their ages.
We do not know which one trembled first when Jerusalem realized Absalom was coming.
We are not told what they whispered to one another inside David’s palace while the king fled.
We are not told whether any of them begged to leave with him.
We are not told whether they understood what was about to happen.
Scripture gives us almost none of those details.
And that restraint matters.
Because we must never invent a story and then call it the Bible.
But what Scripture does tell us is disturbing enough.
David was fleeing Jerusalem from his own son.

Absalom had stolen the hearts of many Israelites. The conspiracy was strengthening. Messengers arrived with the terrifying news that the people were turning toward Absalom, and David knew Jerusalem could become a battlefield.
So David ran.
His household went with him.
Almost all of it.
Then comes one sentence.
A sentence that sounds almost administrative until you know what happens next:
“And the king went forth, and all his household after him. And the king left ten women, which were concubines, to keep the house.”
—2 Samuel 15:16, KJV
Ten women.
Left behind.
To keep the house.
And if you have ever been the person everybody expected to remain strong while somebody else escaped…
If you have ever been left holding together a home somebody else walked away from…
If someone else’s war entered your life and you paid a price for decisions you did not make…
Do not rush past these women.
Because the Bible does not.
David escaped Jerusalem.
The ten remained.
Then Absalom arrived.
And what happened next was not presented in Scripture as romance.
It was political.
It was public.
It was an act designed to communicate that Absalom had irreversibly broken with his father and was claiming royal authority.

Ahithophel advised Absalom to go in to the concubines David had left behind. The purpose stated in the text was political: all Israel would hear of the rupture between father and son, strengthening Absalom’s supporters.
Then Scripture records:
“So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the top of the house, and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.”
—2 Samuel 16:22, KJV
On the roof.
In public view.
Ten women became entangled in a rebellion between powerful men.
And there is something especially chilling about the location.
The rooftop.
Because years earlier, another rooftop had appeared in David’s story.
David had seen Bathsheba bathing.
What followed included adultery, pregnancy, deception, Uriah’s death, and finally Nathan the prophet standing before David with the judgment of God.
Nathan told him that what David had done secretly would bring consequences into the open.
God declared that calamity would arise from David’s own household and that what David had done secretly would be answered before Israel in broad daylight.
Then David said five devastating words:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
And Nathan answered with something equally astonishing:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin.”
Do not miss the tension.
David was forgiven.
David was also living through consequences.
Those are not contradictions.
Grace does not mean sin was harmless.
Forgiveness does not transform evil into good.
God’s mercy toward David does not require us to pretend that nobody else was wounded by the wreckage surrounding his sin.
That is one reason these ten forgotten women matter.
They force us to look at something uncomfortable.
Sin rarely stays inside the person committing it.
We call something “private.”
God sees where the cracks are traveling.
A father’s sin can wound a household.
A leader’s corruption can wound people without power.
A husband’s secrecy can devastate a wife.
A parent’s addiction can shape a child’s memories.
A moment of lust can become years of consequences.
One person can repent and genuinely receive forgiveness while other people are still carrying scars created in the catastrophe.
That does not make grace less glorious.
It shows us why grace was so desperately necessary.
David’s sin had been forgiven.
But David’s house was bleeding.
Amnon violated Tamar.
Absalom murdered Amnon.
Absalom rebelled against David.
David fled Jerusalem.
And now ten women stood in the middle of a conflict they had not created.
They became part of Absalom’s political declaration against his father.
And then…
Absalom died.
David returned.
The rebellion was over.
The king came home.
You might expect that to be the moment everything becomes normal again.
But then Scripture gives us one of the saddest verses in David’s story.

“And David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in ward, and fed them, but went not in unto them. So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood.”
—2 Samuel 20:3, KJV
Read those final words again.
“Living in widowhood.”
The Hebrew is haunting:
אַלְמְנוּת חַיּוּת
ʾalmenût ḥayyût

The wording conveys the extraordinary condition described in the verse: widowhood while still living, even though David himself remained alive. The text also says they were צְרֻרוֹת — ṣərurôt, “shut up,” “confined,” or kept under restraint until their deaths.
Alive.
Provided for.
Yet separated.
David fed them.
David supported them.
But he did not resume sexual relations with them.
And they remained that way until death.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us every reason David made that decision.
So we should be careful where the Bible is careful.
We should not pretend we know exactly what David thought.
We should not manufacture conversations between David and these women.
We should not turn speculation into revelation.
But we can say what the text says.
They had been left behind.
Absalom publicly went in to them.
David later placed them under confinement, continued providing for them, did not return to them sexually, and they remained in that condition until death.
Ten women.
And Scripture never gives us one of their names.
That may be the part that reaches somebody reading this right now.
Because maybe you know what it feels like to become the unnamed person in somebody else’s story.
Everybody remembers the person who betrayed you.
Nobody remembers what betrayal did to you.
Everybody talks about the divorce.
Nobody knows what happened when you shut the bedroom door.
Everybody knows the scandal.
Nobody knows the person who had to wake up the next morning and continue living.
Everybody remembers the pastor who fell, the marriage that collapsed, the family that exploded, the addiction that was exposed, the affair that became public, the friendship that shattered.
But somebody else had to survive the aftermath.
Maybe that somebody was you.
You were not the headline.
You were the collateral damage.
And sometimes the deepest pain is not merely what happened.
It is what happened afterward.
Life continued.
People moved on.
Someone apologized.
