What if grace means your identity no longer has to be negotiated with your past?
Esther had two names in the biblical narrative: Hadassah and Esther.
But long before any earthly title could define her, she belonged to a people whose existence was tied to promises far older than Persia.
And Christian, your deepest identity is not “abandoned.”
Not “divorced.”
Not “betrayed.”
Not “addicted.”
Not “failure.”
Not “damaged.”
Not even “successful.”
If you are in Christ, Scripture gives you a deeper identity.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Adopted.
Beloved in Christ.
A child of God.
Paul writes that believers have received “the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15).
And there is the word an orphaned heart longs to hear.
Father.
Not because earthly fathers do not matter.
They do.
Their presence matters.
Their absence hurts.
But the Gospel announces that through Jesus Christ, sinners who were alienated from God can be reconciled to Him and brought into His family by grace.
That is bigger than a crown.
And it means you do not have to romanticize your wounds to believe God can redeem your life.
Esther's parents dying was tragic.
The threatened extermination of her people was evil.
Fear was real.
Risk was real.
Grief was real.
Yet tragedy did not possess sovereign authority over the conclusion.
There came a moment when Mordecai challenged Esther with words that have echoed through centuries:
“Who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14).
Notice the humility of the wording.
“Who knows...?”
Not a prosperity slogan.
Not a promise that every ambition is God's calling.
A question.
A possibility.
A summons to responsibility.
Esther had reached a moment when privilege could no longer be separated from responsibility.
The palace that sheltered her could not become an excuse to forget the people outside it.
And that is where this story turns toward us.
What if the thing God has entrusted to you was never meant to end with you?
Your voice.
Your testimony.
Your resources.
Your platform.
Your restored marriage.
Your recovery.
Your business.
Your second chance.
Your Bible knowledge.
Your influence.
Your survival.
Grace does not merely ask, “What did God bring me out of?”
Grace eventually asks, “Who can I serve now that He has brought me through?”
Esther could have protected her comfort.
Instead, she risked it.
She told Mordecai to gather the Jews of Susa and fast for her. Then she prepared to approach the king despite the danger.
“And if I perish, I perish.”
Those words are powerful not because Esther had stopped valuing her life.
They are powerful because something had become more important than preserving her comfort.
That is conviction.
And perhaps that is where this article has found you.
Because following Jesus was never meant to become another method of protecting our comfort.
Christ calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
That does not mean manufacturing suffering or acting recklessly.
It means Jesus becomes Lord.
Our money belongs to Him.
Our influence belongs to Him.
Our reputation belongs to Him.
Our platforms belong to Him.
Our stories belong to Him.
Even the scars we would rather hide can become places from which we testify to His mercy.
So ask yourself something uncomfortable.
What have you survived that you are still ashamed to talk about?
What has Jesus forgiven that you still secretly use to condemn yourself?
What part of your story do you keep hiding because you are afraid somebody will discover that the person they admire once fell apart?
The Gospel does not require you to pretend your scandal never happened.
It declares that your scandal does not have greater authority than Christ's grace.
Repentance is not pretending.
Grace is not denial.
Forgiveness is not God calling sin harmless.
At the cross, we discover how serious sin truly is—and how astonishing God's mercy truly is.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by editing evil until it looks innocent.
He rewrites everything by redeeming sinners.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He makes dead hearts alive.
He takes people whose stories seem permanently stained and makes them testimonies to the power of grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your “before” is ugly.
Maybe there are chapters you wish could be burned.
Maybe you were the betrayed one.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you were abandoned.
Maybe you were the person who walked away.
Maybe you were wounded.
Maybe you wounded people.
There is a dangerous temptation in Christian storytelling to divide humanity into innocent Esthers and evil Hamans while quietly placing ourselves among the heroes.
But the Gospel will not let us do that.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
We do not merely need inspiration.
We need salvation.
And that is why Jesus is better than every earthly rescue story.
He does not simply move us from obscurity to influence.
He moves sinners from death to life.
He does not merely improve reputations.
He gives new hearts.
He does not merely offer a second chance to become impressive.
He offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life to everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
So perhaps the most important question is not whether you will ever have an Esther moment.
Perhaps it is whether Jesus truly has your heart.
Not your Christian image.
Not the verse in your bio.
Not your church attendance.
Not the version of you everybody sees on Facebook.
Your heart.
The hidden room.
The secret habit.
The resentment.
The compromise.
The pride.
The thing you keep excusing because nobody knows.
Jesus already knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Receive mercy.
Trust Christ.
Stop trying to become good enough to erase your past.
You cannot.
That is why there was a cross.

You do not have to tell strangers every private detail of your life, but you can simply write, “Jesus, have mercy on me,” or “No more hiding.” If you are exhausted but still fighting to hold onto Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Sometimes one honest sentence is where pretending finally begins to die.
Send this privately to the person who needs hope.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for supporting a ministry.
But grace produces generosity.

That support is not a way to prove that you glorify God. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and Christian giving must be willing rather than coerced. But financial support can be one practical way of participating in Gospel-centered ministry when it is given freely, wisely, and cheerfully.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who is searching.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who is willing to listen.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Because there are still Esthers sitting in ordinary rooms who cannot imagine what obedience may cost them.
There are still Mordecais wondering whether anybody sees their faithfulness.
There are still wounded people convinced the first chapter has already determined the ending.
There are still sinners hiding from God because shame has convinced them that grace could never reach this far.
But the Gospel says otherwise.
Esther was an orphan before she ever became a queen.
Her beginning did not reveal everything her life would become.
And your darkest chapter does not possess the authority to overrule Jesus Christ.
Maybe there will never be a palace.
Maybe nobody will ever put a crown on your head.
Maybe the world will never applaud your testimony.
That is okay.
There is something infinitely greater than being noticed by a king.
There is being reconciled to the King of kings.
So bring Him the orphaned places.
Bring Him the angry places.
Bring Him the ashamed places.
Bring Him the secret places.
Bring Him the sins you need to confess and the wounds you cannot heal by yourself.
Come to Christ without pretending.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Come empty-handed.
Grace has always been for people who cannot save themselves.
And perhaps that is what makes Esther's first chapter so difficult to forget.
Before anyone saw a queen, there was a grieving girl.
Before the royal robes, there was loss.
Before courage became visible, there were years nobody celebrates.
And behind a story in which God's name is never explicitly mentioned, providence was quietly moving toward deliverance.
So when you cannot see what God is doing, do not confuse hiddenness with abandonment.
When your past whispers that you will always be what happened to you, remember the cross.
When shame says your story is finished, remember the empty tomb.
And when the world tells you that your worth depends upon finally receiving a crown, remember the Savior who wore thorns to bring sinners home.
The crown was never the greatest miracle in Esther's story—and your greatest miracle will never be becoming impressive; it will be discovering that grace found you when you had nothing left to prove.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF SEX MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE FLESH”… WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THERE’S A THIRD?
paragraphs:
IF SEX MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE FLESH”… WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THERE’S A THIRD?
What adultery, sexual history, multiple partners, and polygamy reveal about one of the Bible’s most misunderstood—and painfully personal—truths
There is a question Christians sometimes whisper because saying it out loud feels dangerous.
If sex makes two people “one flesh”…
what happens when one of them sleeps with somebody else?
Does that person now become “one flesh” with two people?
What if there have been ten partners?
What about someone who lived promiscuously before coming to Christ?
What about adultery?
And perhaps the question that makes everything even more uncomfortable:
What about the men in the Bible who had multiple wives?
If “one flesh” means what Christians often say it means, how does any of this fit together?
Stay with me, because somewhere inside this question is something much bigger than sex.
It is about covenant.
It is about betrayal.
It is about why sexual sin can hurt so deeply.
It is about why God designed marriage the way He did.
And ultimately, it is about whether your past can still follow you after Jesus has called you His.
We have to begin where Scripture begins.
Before adultery.
Before pornography.
Before broken marriages.
Before Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, or any of the complicated relationships that followed.
There was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 says in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzāḇ-’îš ’eṯ-’āḇîw wə’eṯ-’immô, wəḏāḇaq bə’ištô; wəhāyû ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
In straightforward English:
“Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.”
Look carefully.
There is movement in the verse.
He leaves.
He clings.
They become.
The Hebrew verb דָּבַק — dābaq — carries the idea of clinging, adhering, holding fast.
And then comes the phrase that has echoed through thousands of years:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
The Bible does not introduce sex as merely two bodies experiencing pleasure.
God places sexual union inside something larger: the covenantal union of husband and wife.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because years later, Jesus reaches all the way back to this creation account when people question Him about marriage.
He does not begin with whatever human beings had normalized.
He goes back to creation.
He speaks of the Creator making them male and female, of a man leaving father and mother and being joined to his wife, and of the two becoming one flesh.
Then Jesus draws the conclusion:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Notice where Christ takes us.
Back to God’s design.
Not merely sexual chemistry.
Not merely attraction.
Not merely desire.
God joining husband and wife in a union that human beings are not supposed to tear apart.
But now we reach the uncomfortable part.
Because Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 6 that prevents us from treating sex casually even outside marriage.
He is warning Christians about sexual immorality, and specifically about intercourse with a prostitute.
And Paul writes:
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν; Ἔσονται γάρ, φησίν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.
The shocking point is essentially this:
Do you not know that the person joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, Scripture says, “the two will become one flesh.”
Read that again.
Paul takes language rooted in Genesis and applies it to an immoral sexual encounter.
That destroys one popular Christian oversimplification.
You sometimes hear:
“Sex makes you married in God’s eyes.”
But Paul does not call the prostitute the man’s wife.
He tells the man to flee sexual immorality.
If intercourse automatically constituted a complete biblical marriage covenant, Paul’s argument would become extraordinarily strange.
Instead, Scripture gives us a more careful—and more sobering—picture.
Sex does not appear to be identical to marriage.
But sex is profoundly connected to the one-flesh reality for which marriage was designed.
That is why casual sex is not actually casual in biblical theology.
The body participates in something that was designed to speak the language of covenant even when the people involved refuse the covenant surrounding it.
Think about that.
The body can say something the heart refuses to promise.
“I give myself to you.”
And then morning comes.
One person gets dressed.
Someone checks a phone.
Someone says, “Last night was fun.”
And two people walk away pretending nothing profound happened.
But Scripture refuses to make sex that small.
Paul’s Greek word for being “joined” in 1 Corinthians 6:16 is κολλώμενος — kollōmenos, from kollaō, language associated with joining or adhering.
This is why Paul does not say:
“It doesn't matter. It was only physical.”
He argues almost exactly the opposite.
Your body matters.
And immediately after discussing sexual immorality, Paul reminds believers that their bodies belong to Christ and are temples of the Holy Spirit.
Christian sexual ethics therefore does not begin with God hating pleasure.
It begins with God assigning extraordinary dignity to the human body.
Your body matters because you matter.
And sex matters because God designed it to unite persons in a way that is meant to belong inside covenant faithfulness.
So what happens when someone has sex with another person?
According to Paul, something genuinely bodily and morally significant happens.
A one-body, one-flesh reality is involved.
But that does not mean every sexual partner becomes another permanent spouse in some invisible heavenly marriage registry.
Scripture never tells sexually immoral converts that they must locate every previous sexual partner and treat each person as a continuing spouse.
Instead, Scripture tells sinners something far more powerful:
Repent.
Flee sexual immorality.
Belong to Christ.
And this becomes breathtaking when we remember whom Paul was addressing.
Immediately before this discussion, Paul lists serious sins from which members of the Corinthian church had come.
Then come three of the most beautiful words ever spoken over a ruined past:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Something happened.
They were washed.
They were sanctified.
They were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you understand what that means for the person reading this who has been silently counting?
Two partners.
Five.
Twenty.
Maybe you cannot remember.
Maybe you can remember every face.
Maybe your sin was adultery.
Maybe someone committed adultery against you.
Maybe pornography rewired your expectations of intimacy.
Maybe somebody used your body and disappeared.
Maybe you willingly participated in things you now deeply regret.
Maybe you were sexually sinned against—and this distinction is essential: what someone did to you without your consent is not your sexual sin. The shame belongs to the offender, not the victim.
And maybe the hardest person for you to forgive is the person you used to be.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross only for people with clean histories.
The Gospel is not:
“Jesus saves everyone except people who made sexual mistakes.”
The Gospel is that sinners can be washed.
Not excused.
Washed.
Not told that sin was harmless.
Forgiven.
Not told that rebellion did not matter.
Redeemed.
Grace does not need to pretend sin was small in order to prove that Christ is greater.
That brings us to adultery.
What happens when a married person sleeps with someone else?
They do not somehow become “half married” to two people.
Rather, adultery takes something designed to express exclusive marital union and directs it toward someone outside that covenant.
That is part of why betrayal can feel almost physical to the betrayed spouse.
Something that belonged inside the exclusivity of the marriage was given elsewhere.
The marriage covenant has been violated.
One-flesh sexuality has been taken outside the covenant where God intended it to flourish.
Jesus treats adultery seriously precisely because marriage is serious.
But even here we must never preach condemnation more loudly than the cross.
Adultery can destroy trust.
It can devastate families.
It can produce consequences that forgiveness does not instantly erase.
Repentance does not mean pretending damage never happened.
Reconciliation may require confession, truth, accountability, changed behavior, rebuilding trust, pastoral wisdom, and time.
But adultery is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
There are people reading this who desperately need that sentence.
Adultery is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Sexual immorality is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Pornography is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Your past is not stronger than the blood of Christ.
Now we come to polygamy.
Someone will immediately say:
“But Abraham had more than one woman.”
“Jacob had Leah and Rachel.”
“David had multiple wives.”
“Solomon had hundreds.”
Yes.
The Bible records polygamy.
But recording something is not the same as prescribing it.
That distinction protects us from terrible theology.
Scripture records murder.
Scripture records deception.
Scripture records incest.
Scripture records idolatry.
Narrative description does not automatically equal divine endorsement.
Even Israel’s law recognizes situations in which a man has two wives and regulates inheritance rights so that favoritism does not deprive the rightful firstborn.
That legislation shows that Scripture addresses polygamous realities within fallen human society.
But regulation of a broken situation is not the same thing as establishing that situation as the creation ideal.
And what is fascinating is what repeatedly happens when polygamy appears in biblical narratives.
Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar?
Pain.
Jacob, Leah, and Rachel?
Rivalry.
Hannah and Peninnah?
Provocation and grief.
Solomon’s many wives?
His heart is eventually turned toward other gods.
The Bible hardly needs to interrupt every story and shout, “THIS IS COMPLICATED.”
The stories themselves bleed.
And when Jesus is asked about marriage, He does something decisive.
He returns to the beginning.
One man.
His wife.
The two.
One flesh.
Jesus does not build His theology of marriage from Solomon’s palace.
He builds it from Eden.
That is enormously important.
We should not allow humanity’s later arrangements to redefine God’s original pattern.
Yet there is another danger here.
Some Christians become fascinated with whether previous partners create mysterious “soul ties” that must be individually broken through special formulas or rituals.
We should be careful.
The Bible absolutely treats sexual union as spiritually and morally serious.
Paul unquestionably uses Genesis one-flesh language in discussing prostitution.
But Scripture does not give Christians an elaborate doctrine requiring special “soul-tie breaking” ceremonies for every previous sexual partner.
Our confidence must rest somewhere much stronger.
Christ.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Sanctification.
The indwelling Holy Spirit.
The authority of Jesus Christ over the believer’s life.
You do not need to invent a ritual stronger than the Gospel.
You need Jesus.
And maybe that is where this entire conversation was always heading.
Because perhaps you clicked this article expecting an argument about sex.
Instead, Scripture has been quietly asking:
Who owns you now?
Your past?
Your desires?
Your wounds?
Your spouse?
Your former partners?
Your shame?
Or Christ?
Paul’s answer is astonishing.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
Your body.
The body that sinned.
The body that was hurt.
The body that remembers.
The body you sometimes hate.
The body you sometimes used for validation because you desperately wanted somebody to tell you that you were desirable.
That body can now glorify God.
Maybe nobody ever explained holiness to you this way.
Holiness is not God saying:
“Your body is disgusting.”
Holiness is God saying:
“Your body is too valuable to surrender to everything that wants access to it.”
There is a difference.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been living divided.
Church on Sunday.
Secret messages Monday night.
Worship music playing while pornography remains hidden in another tab.
A wedding ring on the hand while another person lives in the imagination.
A Bible beside the bed where somebody who is not your spouse sometimes sleeps.
Nobody knows.
Except you.
And God.
Maybe this is the moment you stop hiding.
Not because Christians are supposed to pretend temptation disappears.
But because Jesus did not die so that we could decorate our chains with Bible verses.
He came to set captives free.
Repentance means turning.
Sometimes trembling.
Sometimes crying.
Sometimes deleting a number.
Sometimes confessing what pride desperately wants hidden.
Sometimes installing accountability.
Sometimes ending a relationship you already know dishonors Christ.
Sometimes finally telling a trusted mature Christian, pastor, counselor, or spouse the truth that secrecy has been feeding.
But repentance does not walk toward punishment hoping God might eventually become merciful.
Repentance runs toward the God whose mercy is already calling the sinner home.
That is the scandal.
We sinned.
He pursued.
We hid.
He called.
We wandered.
He came looking.
We carried shame.
He carried a cross.
And when Christ stretched out His hands at Calvary, He did not say:
“Clean yourself up and then come back.”
He paid for sinners who could never make themselves clean enough.
That is why the Christian story can never end with sexual failure.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe your history is complicated.
Maybe you are single and tired of waiting.
Maybe you crossed boundaries last night.
Maybe your spouse does not know what you have done.
Maybe you have remained sexually faithful but secretly carry arrogance toward people whose stories are messier than yours.
Then every one of us needs the same Savior.
The sexually broken need Jesus.
The sexually proud need Jesus.
The adulterer needs Jesus.
The betrayed spouse needs Jesus.
The virgin needs Jesus.
The person with fifty former partners needs Jesus.
The person who has never kissed anyone needs Jesus.
Nobody enters the Kingdom because his or her sexual résumé was impressive.
We enter through Christ.
And Christ does not merely forgive.
He transforms.
So yes, sex creates a profound one-flesh bodily union.
Yes, sexual activity outside marriage takes something God designed for covenant and tears it away from its intended home.
Yes, adultery violates marital exclusivity.
Yes, Scripture records polygamy while the creation pattern to which Jesus points remains the union of the two becoming one flesh.
But there is something even greater you must remember.
Your sexual history is not your identity.
Jesus is not standing over repentant sinners counting bodies.
He is calling people out of darkness and into Himself.
So stop asking only:
“What did I become connected to?”
Start asking:
“Whom do I belong to now?”
If you belong to Christ, then live like someone purchased at immeasurable cost.
If you are married, honor your covenant.
If you are single, honor Christ with your body.
If you are sexually tempted, run toward God instead of negotiating with temptation.
If you have fallen, repent rather than hiding.
If you have been betrayed, know that another person's sin does not reduce your worth.
If you have a past, remember that the Gospel was written for people with pasts.
Just be honest.
Someone reading your three words may realize they are not the only Christian fighting for purity.
It is an invitation to belong completely to Jesus.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but needs grace desperately.
Not because paying for something earns favor with God. It never does.
Scripture never teaches that, and we will not manipulate you by pretending it does.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach another person.
And beyond that, stay close because discipleship cannot survive on emotional moments alone.
Jesus is still calling people.
Leave the comment you almost decided not to leave.
Come back to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most important “one flesh” question was never how many people your past connected you to.
Perhaps it was whether your whole life belongs to Christ today.
Your past may explain some of your scars—but it does not get to write the final sentence after Jesus picks up the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE FOR SICKNESS WAS FIRST TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING EVEN MORE DEADLY
paragraphs: “BY HIS STRIPES WE ARE HEALED” — THE VERSE WE QUOTE FOR SICKNESS WAS FIRST TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING EVEN MORE DEADLY

Isaiah 53:5 is often spoken over hospital beds, cancer diagnoses, chronic pain, and bodies desperate for healing. God absolutely can heal the sick. But what if the wound Isaiah was ultimately staring at was deeper than the sickness in your body? What if the greatest miracle promised in this passage is the healing of something every human being desperately needs healed?
There are Bible verses we read.
And then there are Bible verses we reach for when our hands are shaking.
Isaiah 53:5 is one of them.
The diagnosis comes back.
The doctor sits down.
The pain will not leave.
Someone you love is lying beneath hospital lights while machines make sounds you never wanted to understand.
And somewhere between fear and faith, someone whispers:
“By His stripes we are healed.”
Maybe you have whispered it too.
Maybe you prayed it until your voice cracked.
Maybe you believed with everything inside you that the next scan would be clear, the next test would be different, the tumor would disappear, the pain would stop, the miracle would come.
And sometimes it does.
God heals.
We should never become so intellectually sophisticated that we explain away the God who created the human body and remains perfectly capable of restoring it.
Jesus healed the sick. The apostles prayed for healing. James tells suffering believers to pray. Christians have every biblical reason to bring sickness boldly before God.
But there is another side of this verse that we cannot afford to miss.
Because Isaiah 53:5 was never meant to become a slogan that makes a suffering Christian feel spiritually defective when the hospital room remains occupied.
And when you read the verse in its own language…
then keep reading the surrounding verses…
then watch how the New Testament itself interprets Isaiah…
something breathtaking happens.
You discover that “by His stripes we are healed” reaches deeper than the skin.
Deeper than the bloodstream.
Deeper than the tumor.
Deeper than the disease.
Isaiah is bringing us face-to-face with the sickness beneath every sickness.
Sin.
And the Servant who would be wounded to bring sinners home.
Listen to Isaiah.
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
Isaiah 53:5, KJV.
Now look beneath the English.
The final Hebrew words are:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
uvaḥavurato nirpa-lanu.
A careful sense of the phrase is:
“And by His wound, healing has come to us.”
The Hebrew word often translated “stripes” is חַבּוּרָה — ḥabburah — carrying the idea of a wound, bruise, welt, or injury produced by a blow.
But do not isolate those words from everything Isaiah has just said.
The Servant is wounded…
Why?
Because of our transgressions.
He is crushed…
Why?
Because of our iniquities.
Punishment falls upon Him…
Why?
So that peace might come to us.
Then Isaiah says that through His wound we are healed.
Do you see the movement?
Our rebellion.
His wounds.
Our guilt.
His suffering.
Our alienation.
His punishment.
Our peace.
His blood.
Our healing.
This is not primarily the language of a medical transaction.
It is the language of substitution.
Someone innocent is suffering because someone guilty needs peace with God.
And the guilty ones are us.
That is why the next verse matters so much.
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way…”
Isaiah does not immediately say, “All we like sheep became physically ill.”
He says we wandered.
We rebelled.
We chose our own way.
That is the disease Isaiah is exposing.
The human heart walked away from its Shepherd.
And then comes one of the most astonishing statements in the Old Testament:
“…and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Our iniquity.
On Him.
Stop there.
Because Christianity becomes meaningless when we make the cross merely an inspirational story about enduring suffering.
Jesus did not die merely to show you how much suffering a person could survive.
He was not simply history's greatest example of perseverance.
The cross was substitution.
The righteous One stood where the unrighteous belonged.
The innocent suffered for the guilty.
The Shepherd was struck for wandering sheep.
Jesus Christ stepped into the courtroom carrying nothing deserving condemnation…
while we entered carrying everything.
And somehow…
He took our sentence.
This is where “by His stripes we are healed” becomes far more uncomfortable than the inspirational quote printed on a coffee mug.
Because before you can celebrate the healing, you must admit the disease.
We were not merely wounded people needing encouragement.
We were sinners needing reconciliation.
That distinction matters.
Because our culture is comfortable saying, “I’m hurting.”
We are less comfortable saying, “I have sinned.”
We will talk about trauma.
We will talk about rejection.
We will talk about what people did to us.
And those wounds can be painfully real.
But Scripture also asks a question our generation desperately wants to avoid:
What have we done against God?
Not only…
Who hurt you?
But…
Who have you hurt?
Not only…
Who betrayed you?
But…
Where have you betrayed God?
Not only…
What happened to you?
But…
What has been happening inside you?
The secret bitterness.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair hidden behind deleted messages.
The pride disguised as confidence.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The greed disguised as ambition.
The unforgiveness you keep calling “boundaries” even though deep inside you know hatred has been feeding there for years.
The religious performance.
The Sunday worship with the Monday compromise.
The Bible verses posted publicly while private sin remains protected.
The smiling profile picture.
The exhausted soul.
The Christian vocabulary.
The hidden chains.
Maybe that is why this verse feels different when we stop treating it merely as a promise about circumstances.
Because Isaiah is not allowing us to stand at the cross pointing at everyone else's wounds.
He makes us look at our own sin.
And then…
he makes us look at Jesus.
This is where the story turns.
Because Christianity does not say, “Look how terrible you are; now fix yourself.”
Christianity says:
Look how devastating sin is.
Now look at what Christ did about it.
Centuries after Isaiah wrote those words, Peter reached back into Isaiah 53 while explaining what happened at the cross.
He wrote that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness,” and then echoed Isaiah:
“by whose stripes ye were healed.”
1 Peter 2:24, KJV.
The Greek expression includes:
οὗ τῷ μώλωπι ἰάθητε
hou tō mōlōpi iathēte.
“By whose wound you were healed.”
And Peter does something enormously important.
He tells us what kind of healing he has in view.
Christ bore…
our sins.
So that we might…
die to sins.
And live…
to righteousness.
Then Peter continues:
“For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.”
There it is again.
Isaiah's wandering sheep.
Peter's returning sheep.
Sin.
The cross.
Healing.
Return.
The Shepherd.
Peter himself connects the “healing” language with Christ bearing sin and wandering sinners returning to their Shepherd.
That does not make physical healing unimportant.
It makes salvation immeasurably bigger.
Because imagine receiving a perfectly healthy body…
and remaining separated from God.
Imagine being healed of cancer…
but never forgiven.
Imagine getting another fifty years…
and entering eternity without Christ.
What would you really have gained?
Jesus once asked what it profits someone to gain the whole world and lose his soul.
We might ask something equally sobering:
What good is a healed body if the soul remains unreconciled to its Creator?
Your body matters to God.
Your suffering matters.
Your diagnosis matters.
Your tears matter.
Pray for healing.
Ask boldly.
Gather believers around you.
Call the elders.
Trust the God who raises the dead.
But never reduce the cross to a guarantee that every faithful Christian must experience immediate physical healing in this present life.
Because some extraordinary believers have prayed faithfully…
and still died.
Paul knew bodily weakness.
Timothy apparently experienced recurring physical problems.
Trophimus was left sick.
And eventually every apostle died.
The Gospel does not promise Christians exemption from mortality before the resurrection.
It promises something greater:
Death itself will not have the final word.
That is Christian healing in its ultimate horizon.
Christ does not merely patch up Adam's dying world.
He makes all things new.
There is coming a resurrection.
There is coming a day when what Revelation describes becomes reality: death will be no more. Mourning will end. Crying will end. Pain will end.
Not because Christians learned the correct formula.
Not because they accumulated enough faith points.
But because the Lamb conquered.
So yes…
for the Christian, complete physical healing is coming.
Sometimes God graciously gives us a foretaste now.
Sometimes cancer disappears.
Sometimes doctors cannot explain what happened.
Sometimes treatment succeeds.
Sometimes recovery comes slowly through medicine, surgery, therapy, rest, and the ordinary providence of God.
Sometimes we pray desperately…
and the answer we wanted does not come before death.
But resurrection means sickness still loses.
Cancer does not get the final sentence.
Alzheimer's does not write the ending.
Paralysis does not write the ending.
Chronic pain does not write the ending.
The cemetery does not write the ending.
Jesus does.
And perhaps someone reading this needs that truth because you have been quietly blaming yourself.
You prayed.
They were not healed.
And somewhere along the way you began wondering whether you failed.
Maybe you did not have enough faith.
Maybe you said the wrong prayer.
Maybe God was disappointed with you.
Hear this carefully:
Isaiah 53:5 is not a weapon meant to beat suffering Christians with guilt.
It is a window into the suffering Servant who carried our guilt.
Jesus is not standing beside your hospital bed accusing you because you are still sick.
He knows suffering.
He knows pain.
He knows what it is to groan.
He knows what it is to bleed.
And ultimately, He entered death itself.
The astonishing claim of Christianity is not that God watched human suffering safely from heaven.
God the Son entered our world.
Jesus touched lepers.
Jesus wept beside a tomb.
Jesus sweat in anguish.
Jesus was struck.
Jesus was scourged.
Jesus was crucified.
And then Jesus walked out of the grave.
The scars remained.
But death did not.
Maybe that is the image you need tonight.
The risen Jesus still bearing scars.
Because scars tell you something.
The wound was real.
But the wound did not win.
And perhaps your story has scars too.
Some were inflicted upon you.
Some came from choices you made.
Some came from sins you still struggle to forgive yourself for.
There are chapters you would delete if life had an edit button.
There are nights you wish nobody knew about.
Relationships you destroyed.
Promises you broke.
Years you wasted.
Maybe even Christianity you performed while your heart wandered far from Christ.
And you have quietly wondered:
Could Jesus really want someone like me?
Isaiah 53 answers from seven centuries before the crucifixion:
That is exactly why the Servant was wounded.
Not for imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
Not polished sinners.
Guilty ones.
Not people who almost had their lives together.
Sheep who had gone astray.
People like us.
This is the scandal of grace.
The wound belonged to Him.
The transgression belonged to us.
The crushing belonged to Him.
The iniquity belonged to us.
The chastisement belonged to Him.
The peace comes to us.
We wandered.
He came looking.
We sinned.
He carried it.
We deserved judgment.
He stood in our place.
And the resurrection declares that sin, Satan, condemnation, and death will not have the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
That is why grace is scandalous.
Because Jesus does not merely improve respectable people.
He redeems sinners.
He takes stories that should have ended in shame and writes mercy across them.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Grace is not Jesus giving us permission to remain comfortably chained to the sins for which He died.
Peter says Christ bore our sins so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.
Grace forgives you.
And grace begins changing you.
Jesus does not save us so we can proudly decorate our prison cells with Bible verses.
He opens the door.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
It is the turning of a heart that has finally realized the Shepherd is better than wandering.
Maybe that is your moment right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
You may have opened this expecting an article about physical healing.
And somehow God has brought the conversation somewhere deeper.
Your soul.
Your sin.
Your Shepherd.
Jesus.
Perhaps the healing you desperately need tonight begins with three words nobody around you can see:
“I need You.”
Jesus, I have wandered.
Jesus, I have sinned.
Jesus, I cannot save myself.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, bring me home.
There is no magic in repeating words.
Salvation is not a formula.
Come to Christ with genuine repentance and faith.
Trust the One who bore sin on the cross and rose from the dead.
Stop hiding behind religion.
Stop bargaining.
Stop pretending.
Bring Him the real story.
The addiction.
The shame.
The anger.
The secret.
The failure.
The unbelief.
The years you cannot recover.
The person you became while everybody thought you were okay.
Bring it into His light.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people can become slightly better.

It is the announcement that guilty sinners can be forgiven, wandering sheep can come home, enemies can receive peace with God, and spiritually dead people can receive life because Jesus Christ died and rose again.

And if Christ has already begun rebuilding a life you once thought was beyond redemption, tell someone what He has done. Your testimony might become the sentence God uses to interrupt another person's despair.
Not because an algorithm needs another save.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only a religion for people who have their lives together.
Because perhaps they need to discover what we discovered in Isaiah 53.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of people who healed themselves.
It is the story of wounded sinners meeting a wounded Savior…
and discovering that His wounds were not the end of His story.
And because He rose…
our wounds do not have to be the end of ours.
So the next time you hear someone whisper:
“By His stripes we are healed…”
remember the hospital room.
Pray for the body.
Ask God for the miracle.
Believe that He is able.
But then look farther.
Look toward Calvary.
See the Servant pierced for transgressions.
See Him crushed for iniquities.
See the punishment that brings peace falling upon Him.
See wandering sheep being carried home.
See sinners forgiven.
See enemies reconciled.
See shame losing its claim.
See the tomb opening.
See the risen Christ.
And understand:
The greatest healing Isaiah promised was never merely about getting you out of a hospital.
It was about bringing you home to God.
Your sickness may have wounded your body.
People may have wounded your heart.
Sin may have devastated years of your story.
But if you belong to Jesus, none of those things gets to write your final chapter.
The scars may explain where you have been. Only Jesus gets to decide where your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Never Touched Them—but Jesus Still Wants to Talk About What Happened in Your Heart
paragraphs: You Never Touched Them—but Jesus Still Wants to Talk About What Happened in Your Heart

You may have kept your hands clean, your messages deleted, your reputation intact, and your secret invisible. But Jesus has never been interested only in what your hands did. He loves you enough to confront what your heart became.
There are sins nobody can screenshot.
No hotel receipt.
No secret child.
No eyewitness.
No confession whispered through tears to a spouse.
No physical affair anyone could uncover.
Nothing happened.
At least, that is what you keep telling yourself.
You never touched them.
You never kissed them.
You never crossed that final physical line.
And maybe because you did not cross it, you have quietly built a courtroom inside your own mind where you are both defendant and judge.
Your verdict?
“I didn’t actually do anything.”
Then Jesus walks into the courtroom.
And suddenly the question changes.
Not:
“Did you touch them?”
But:
“What happened in your heart?”
That question is terrifying.
And strangely beautiful.
Because Jesus Christ does not expose the heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposes what is killing us because He came to save sinners.
Maybe it started innocently.
A conversation.
A friendship.
Someone at work who listened a little more carefully than your spouse seemed to.
Someone online whose attention made you feel attractive again.
Someone at church who understood your struggles.
Someone from your past who suddenly appeared in your notifications.
You told yourself there was nothing wrong with talking.
And perhaps, initially, there wasn’t.
But somewhere along the way, something shifted.
You began waiting for their name to appear.
You started dressing with the possibility of seeing them somewhere in the back of your mind.
You replayed conversations after they ended.
You imagined conversations that had never happened.
You wondered what life might feel like with them.
You compared their tenderness with your spouse’s weaknesses.
Or, if you were single, you allowed desire to turn another human being into the private theater of your imagination.
Nobody knew.
You smiled normally.
You worshiped normally.
You went home normally.
You may even have prayed normally.
But there was another room inside you.
A room you would have been horrified for anyone else to enter.
And this is exactly where the words of Jesus become painfully relevant.
Jesus said:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:28.
The Greek is devastatingly precise:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial expression is πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—pros to epithymēsai—looking in such a way as to desire, covet, or lust after.
Jesus is not declaring that noticing another person's beauty is automatically adultery.
He is going deeper.
He is confronting the cultivated gaze.
The entertained desire.
The inward consent.
The heart that does not merely experience temptation but begins feeding it.
Then comes the phrase we desperately wish Jesus had omitted:
ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ
en tē kardia autou.
“In his heart.”
There.
That is the room.
That is where Jesus is standing.
And perhaps you immediately feel defensive.
“But I never touched them.”
Jesus knows.
“But I never slept with them.”
Jesus knows.
“I never even told them how I felt.”
Jesus knows that too.
But He also knows what you imagined when nobody was watching.
He knows which conversations you replayed.
He knows whether you secretly wanted their marriage to fail.
He knows whether you compared your spouse to them.
He knows what you searched.
He knows why you returned to that profile.
He knows what you hoped would happen.
He knows the difference between temptation arriving at your door and you quietly pulling out a chair for it.
And before shame convinces you to stop reading, you need to understand something enormously important.
Jesus did not preach Matthew 5 so that respectable sinners could learn to hate themselves more efficiently.
He was demolishing our obsession with external righteousness.
Earlier in the same sermon, He warned that unless our righteousness exceeded that of the scribes and Pharisees, we would not enter the kingdom of heaven.
Then He began pressing beyond behavior into the heart.
Murder?
Look at anger.
Adultery?
Look at lust.
Religious performance?
Look at motive.
Jesus keeps taking the human finger pointing outward and turning it toward the human heart.
Why?
Because the deepest human problem cannot be solved merely by keeping our bodies away from certain locations.
We need new hearts.
That is why this hurts.
Some of us have spent years congratulating ourselves for sins we almost committed physically while secretly nourishing them emotionally.
You remained faithful with your body while becoming unfaithful in fantasy.
You never climbed into their bed.
But you built an imaginary life with them.
You never said, “I love you.”
But you desperately wanted them to say it.
You never removed your wedding ring.
But somewhere inside your imagination, you temporarily removed your covenant.
Perhaps your struggle is pornography.
Perhaps it is someone you know.
Perhaps it is an ex.
Perhaps it is a celebrity.
Perhaps it is the person whose profile you keep checking and would be embarrassed to explain why.
Perhaps there is no particular person at all—only an imagination you have trained to consume bodies without ever considering souls.
And maybe your secret defense has always been:
“At least I haven't actually cheated.”
But Christianity is not ultimately about becoming skillful enough to remain technically innocent.
Jesus wants truth in the inward person.
And here is where the story could become another piece of religious shame.
It could leave you exposed, frightened, and disgusted with yourself.
But that would stop before reaching the Gospel.
Because the same Jesus who exposes lust is the Jesus who receives sinners.
The same Christ who refuses to rename darkness also refuses to abandon the repentant person trapped inside it.
He does not say sin is harmless.
He does something infinitely better.
He bears its judgment.
At the cross, Jesus was not crucified merely for the sins that became visible.
He died for sinners.
For what was done with hands.
For what was spoken with mouths.
For what was entertained in hearts.
For secret rebellion.
For respectable rebellion.
For the darkness everybody discovered.
And the darkness nobody ever did.
Scripture says:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον
pantes gar hēmarton.
“For all have sinned.”
Romans 3:23.
All.
The adulterer.
The fantasizer.
The pornography addict.
The religious hypocrite.
The lonely spouse who allowed emotional hunger to become secret idolatry.
The single believer who repeatedly feeds lust and then promises God, “This was the last time.”
The pastor.
The teenager.
The husband.
The wife.
The person reading this while thinking, “Nobody knows.”
All have sinned.
But Romans does not end there.
The astonishing announcement of Christianity is not that sinful people can clean themselves sufficiently for God to tolerate them.
The announcement is Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after our search history became clean enough.
Not after temptation disappeared.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Christ moved toward sinners while they were sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
Repentance is not pretending you were never dirty.
Repentance is finally agreeing with God about the dirt and running toward the One who can wash you.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε—metanoeite—a call to turn, to change one's mind and direction in response to God's kingdom.
Repentance is more than feeling horrible after sin.
You can hate the consequences of sin and still love the sin.
You can cry after pornography and return tomorrow.
You can feel guilty about emotional infidelity while continuing to protect the relationship that feeds it.
You can delete the messages while secretly hoping they message again.
Repentance eventually asks harder questions.
What needs to end?
What access needs to disappear?
What confession needs to happen?
What boundary have I been calling “legalistic” because obedience would cost me something I enjoy?
What am I protecting that is competing with Christ?
Jesus uses startling language immediately after addressing lust.
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
He was not establishing self-mutilation as the cure for lust.
A person could lose an eye and still possess a lustful heart.
His language communicates the radical seriousness with which disciples must deal with sin.
In modern terms, perhaps your “right eye” is an account you need to unfollow.
An app.
A private conversation.
A friendship whose boundaries you deliberately blurred.
A phone taken into places where you repeatedly fall.
A streaming habit.
A secret password.
An emotional dependency.
A fantasy you keep revisiting because reality disappoints you.
Grace does not teach us to pet the thing Christ died to free us from.
Grace teaches us to bring it into the light.
And bringing something into the light can hurt.
There may be consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Accountability may become uncomfortable.
Depending on what has happened, wise pastoral counsel or professional Christian counseling may be needed.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence.
But consequence is not the same thing as condemnation.
For the person who belongs to Jesus Christ, Romans 8:1 announces:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
For whom?
“For those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Read that carefully.
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction says, “Come out of hiding.”
Condemnation says, “There is no point coming home.”
Conviction points toward Christ.
Condemnation tells you to run from Him.
The Gospel says run toward Him.
You may have failed again last night.
Run toward Him.
You may have spent months feeding something you knew was wrong.
Run toward Him.
You may have betrayed someone emotionally even though your bodies never touched.
Stop defending it.
Run toward Him.
You may be reading this with tears because you finally have language for something you have hidden even from yourself.
Run toward Him.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
The scandal of Christianity has always been grace.
Grace for people who do not deserve grace.
Mercy for people who cannot rewrite yesterday.
A Savior wounded for sinners who cannot save themselves.
And resurrection declaring that sin and death do not get the final word.
This is why our words at Gospel Warrior remain:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything because He enters ruined stories with nail-scarred hands.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted His church.
Jesus transformed him into a witness of the Gospel he once tried to destroy.
The cross itself looked like history's greatest defeat until resurrection morning revealed what God was doing.
Jesus specializes in stories where everyone else thinks the final chapter has already been written.
Maybe that includes yours.
But please hear this carefully.
Jesus is not offering you permission to continue feeding lust because grace is available.
Paul confronted precisely that distortion:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!”
Romans 6:1–2.
Grace forgives.
Grace also trains.
Grace restores.
Grace also transforms.
Grace receives you covered in mud and loves you too deeply to convince you the mud is your permanent home.
So perhaps today your prayer does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe it sounds more like this:
Jesus, I sinned.
Not merely with what I did.
With what I wanted.
With what I watched.
With what I imagined.
With what I protected.
With what I secretly hoped would happen.
I have spent too much time defending myself instead of surrendering myself.
Forgive me.
Clean me.
Change what I love.
Teach my eyes to see people as souls, not objects.
Teach my heart to desire holiness more than secrecy.
Give me courage to close every door that keeps leading me away from You.
And when temptation whispers that I will always be this person, remind me that my identity is not written by my worst moment.
It is found in Christ.
Amen.
And now comes the difficult part.
Get up differently.
Repentance has feet.
If someone needs to be blocked, do it.
If something needs to be deleted, delete it.
If trusted Christian accountability is needed, seek it.
If you need pastoral help, ask.
If your marriage has been neglected, stop feeding imaginary intimacy while starving covenant intimacy.
If pornography has become compulsive, stop treating repeated secrecy as a private inconvenience and seek serious, trustworthy help.
And if you fall, do not transform failure into permission to remain fallen.
Confess.
Return.
Fight again.
Not to purchase God's love.
Because in Christ, grace has taught you that sin is no longer your master.
Maybe someone you love is fighting this battle silently.
Not because sharing an article earns favor with God—it does not.
Christ alone saves.
But if these words can place Scripture in front of one person who is hiding, sharing becomes an opportunity to serve.
Send this privately to the husband who is fighting for purity.
The wife carrying secret shame.
The young believer being discipled more aggressively by pornography than by Scripture.
The friend who thinks because nobody touched anybody, nothing happened.
Because temptation has an astonishing ability to make yesterday's conviction feel unreasonable tomorrow.
Come back when your heart starts negotiating again.
And please do not hide behind a polished comment section.
If this exposed something you have been defending, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
And if Christ has already begun restoring an area of your life you once believed could never change, tell someone beneath this article.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason to stop hiding.
Do it as support for Gospel work, not as payment to God.
No purchase can earn blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or spiritual status.
Those belong to the realm of grace, and salvation is God's gift in Christ.

But financial support can help Gospel-centered work continue reaching people, producing biblical resources, and placing Christ-centered truth before more eyes. Giving and supporting Christian ministry can therefore become one practical expression of stewardship and partnership in Gospel work when it is done freely, wisely, cheerfully, and for God's glory—not under spiritual coercion.
Not because clicking “Share” makes you righteous.
Jesus does that which you could never do for yourself.
Share because somewhere behind another perfectly normal profile may be a person whispering:
“I never touched them. Surely this doesn't count.”
And perhaps God will use the truth of His Word appearing on their screen to interrupt a secret compromise before it becomes a public catastrophe.
One more thing.
You never touched them.
Maybe nobody ever discovered it.
Maybe nobody ever will.
But Jesus saw the heart.
And remarkably, He did not turn His face away.
He is calling you out of darkness because He intends something better than helping you become more talented at hiding.
He wants your heart.
Not the edited version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version your spouse sees.
Not the version your followers see.
The real one.
The wandering one.
The wounded one.
The lustful one.
The lonely one.
The ashamed one.
Bring that heart to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive mercy.
Then let the Spirit teach that same heart how to love what is holy.
Because one day you may discover that the most beautiful part of your story was not that nobody ever found out what happened inside you.
It was that Jesus already knew—and instead of leaving you there, He called you home.
The heart you were terrified Jesus would expose may become the very place where you remember how deeply you needed His cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ESAU MARRIED TWO HITTITE WOMEN—And They Made Life Bitter for His Parents
paragraphs:
ESAU MARRIED TWO HITTITE WOMEN—And They Made Life Bitter for His Parents
Genesis records the wedding in one sentence. Then, in the next, Scripture tells us what happened inside the home: “bitterness of spirit.” And buried inside those two verses is a warning for every person who thinks a private decision can never wound the people who love them.
There are weddings where parents cry because they are happy.
And then there are tears nobody photographs.
No one posts them.
No one sees the mother lying awake afterward.
No one hears the father wondering where things changed.
No one sees what happens when somebody you raised, prayed over, protected, corrected, forgave, and loved becomes old enough to make decisions you can no longer make for them.
Genesis gives us one of those moments.
Almost brutally.
No long explanation.
No dramatic speech.
Just two verses.
“When Esau was forty years old, he took to wife Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite…”
Then comes the sentence that changes the emotional temperature of the entire scene:
“וַתִּהְיֶיןָ מֹרַת רוּחַ לְיִצְחָק וּלְרִבְקָה”
Vattihyena morat ruaḥ le-Yitzḥaq u-le-Rivqah.
Literally, the Hebrew carries the sense that they became “bitterness of spirit” to Isaac and Rebekah.
Genesis 26:34–35.
Not merely an inconvenience.
Not simply an awkward disagreement between generations.
Bitterness of spirit.
Imagine those words inside a home.
Esau was forty years old.
That detail matters.
This was not a child who did not know better.
This was a grown man making grown decisions.
And that may be exactly where this passage begins hurting some of us.
Because eventually your children grow beyond the reach of your hands.
You can teach them.
You can warn them.
You can pray for them.
You can show them truth.
You can tell them what God has done in your family.
But there comes a day when they make choices while you stand close enough to watch and too far away to choose for them.
Some parents reading this know that pain.
Your son is alive, but you barely recognize the direction of his life.
Your daughter still calls you “Mom,” but she no longer wants the God you taught her to love.
Maybe someone you raised has walked into a relationship that is pulling them farther from Christ.
Maybe you watched somebody you love trade conviction for companionship.
Maybe your family photographs still look beautiful while something underneath them is breaking.
And perhaps nobody knows.
You smile at church.
You answer, “We’re doing fine.”
You change the subject when somebody asks about your children.
Then you go home carrying what Genesis calls מֹרַת רוּחַ — morat ruaḥ.
Bitterness of spirit.
But we need to be careful here.
Genesis 26 is not giving Christians permission to despise people because of ethnicity, nationality, family background, or because they are “outsiders.”
That would badly mishandle the passage.
The issue belongs to the unfolding covenant story.

Abraham had previously been deeply concerned that Isaac not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. Later, Rebekah herself would say concerning Esau’s Hittite wives, “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth” (Genesis 27:46). And Genesis 28 tells us that Esau eventually recognized that “the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father.”
Something deeper than parental preference was happening.
Esau was living inside a family carrying covenant promises from God while repeatedly showing how little spiritual inheritance seemed to weigh upon him.
And we had already seen it.
Before these marriages, Esau came home exhausted.
Jacob had food.
Esau had a birthright.
One satisfied his stomach for a few hours.
The other represented inheritance, privilege, responsibility, and covenant significance.
And Esau said, essentially, What good is the birthright to me if I am about to die?
He traded what was sacred for what was immediate.
Genesis 25 ends that episode with terrifying simplicity:
“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
That is the shadow standing behind Genesis 26.
The marriages did not suddenly create Esau’s spiritual problem.
They revealed something that had already been growing.
And that is where this ancient story walks straight into our lives.
Because most spiritual disasters do not begin on the day everybody notices them.
They begin quietly.
A compromise nobody confronts.
A conviction repeatedly ignored.
A prayer life slowly abandoned.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ, but loneliness makes you afraid to let go.
A habit you keep defending.
A resentment you keep feeding.
A secret browser history.
A conversation you would immediately delete if your spouse picked up your phone.
A church attendance that remains while your hunger for God disappears.
Nobody wakes up one morning planning to become spiritually cold.
We drift there through decisions.
One appetite.
One justification.
One compromise.
One “just this once.”
One “God understands.”
One “everybody does it.”
One “I can stop whenever I want.”
Until something that once disturbed your conscience becomes normal.
That is one of the frightening things about Esau.
He does not appear to wake up every morning announcing war against God.
He simply keeps choosing what is immediately desirable without adequately treasuring what is spiritually weighty.
And Scripture later remembers him for it.
Hebrews 12 warns believers not to become “profane” like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright.
Think about that.
One meal.
The food disappeared.
The decision remained.
Somebody reading this needs that sentence.
The appetite will pass. The consequences may remain.
That relationship feels impossible to surrender right now.
That temptation feels unbearable right now.
That anger feels justified right now.
That secret sin feels comforting right now.
That compromise feels profitable right now.
But “right now” is a dangerous god.
Esau teaches us what happens when immediate appetite becomes more authoritative than eternal truth.
And before we point at him too confidently, we should look in the mirror.
How many times have we done our own version of the same thing?
We knew what Scripture said.
But we wanted something.
We knew what obedience required.
But obedience was expensive.
We knew the Holy Spirit was convicting us.
But compromise felt easier.
So we chose the bowl.
Different bowl.
Same temptation.
And sometimes other people end up tasting the bitterness of decisions they never made.
Isaac and Rebekah did.
That is another uncomfortable truth hidden inside Genesis 26.
Sin loves telling us:
“This is my life. My decision. It affects nobody but me.”
Scripture repeatedly destroys that illusion.
Our choices ripple.
A father's hidden addiction can eventually enter the emotional atmosphere of his home.
A mother's bitterness can shape how her children understand forgiveness.
A spouse's secret betrayal can fracture somebody else's ability to trust.
A young person's rebellion can leave praying parents awake at two in the morning.
And parents can wound children too.
This passage must never become ammunition for parents who want to control adult sons and daughters under the banner of “honoring God.”
Isaac and Rebekah themselves were not a flawless family.
Keep reading Genesis.
Favoritism entered that house.
Isaac favored Esau.
Rebekah favored Jacob.
Deception followed.
Manipulation followed.
Heartbreak followed.
The Bible does not airbrush its families.
That is one reason Scripture feels so painfully real.
God does not give us polished families pretending everything is fine.
He gives us tents full of tension.
Parents with weaknesses.
Children making destructive decisions.
Brothers fighting.
Spouses grieving.
People deceiving one another.
People running away.
People carrying consequences.
And somehow…
God keeps writing.
That may be the most beautiful thing in the entire story.
Because if Genesis were only about human faithfulness, the story would collapse almost immediately.
Abraham failed.
Isaac failed.
Rebekah failed.
Jacob failed spectacularly.
Esau made devastating choices.
The family became messy enough that if their story happened today, people would probably argue about them endlessly in comment sections.
Yet the covenant promise did not survive because this family was impressive.
It survived because God is faithful.
And eventually, generations later, from the covenant line would come Jesus Christ.
That is where this story must ultimately take us.
Not merely:
“Choose better relationships.”
Not merely:
“Listen to your parents.”
Not merely:
“Don't become like Esau.”
Those lessons can have their place.
But Christianity is not a self-improvement program for people trying harder not to embarrass their families.
The Gospel goes much deeper.
Because the deepest problem is not that Esau once made terrible decisions.
The deeper problem is that something of Esau lives inside every sinner.
We have all preferred lesser things to God.
We have all exchanged holiness for appetite in one form or another.
We have all sinned.
We have all wounded others.
We have all chosen things we later wished we could unchoose.
And some of you are reading this article carrying exactly that kind of regret.
You are not Isaac or Rebekah in this story.
You feel like Esau.
You were the one who made life bitter.
You were the child who rebelled.
You were the spouse who betrayed.
You were the parent who failed.
You were the person who ignored every warning until the consequences finally arrived.
And now you would give almost anything to return to the moment before everything changed.
Listen carefully.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what yesterday did to you.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Grace is not pretending sin never mattered.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin mattered so much that our reconciliation with God required a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to improve sinners.
He came to save them.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore sin for sinners.
The One who never traded righteousness for appetite carried the judgment deserved by people who have.
The One perfectly obedient to the Father died for the disobedient.
And He rose again.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
You do not have to keep defending the thing destroying you.
You do not have to rename darkness so you can continue living inside it.
You do not have to pretend the bitterness isn't bitter.
You can confess.
You can turn.
You can come to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise in 1 John 1:9 is not sentimental optimism.
It rests on Jesus.
Maybe you have become Esau in somebody else's story.
Then repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not when life becomes easier.
Now.
Call the person you wounded if reconciliation is appropriate and safe.
Tell the truth.
Stop hiding.
Bring the secret into the light.
Ask forgiveness without demanding that the wounded person immediately trust you again.
Accept that repentance may require restitution, changed behavior, boundaries, accountability, patience, and time.
Grace is free.
Transformation will cost your pride.
And maybe you are Isaac or Rebekah.
You are watching someone you love make decisions that hurt.
Then hear this too:
You cannot be their Holy Spirit.
You cannot repent for them.
You cannot force regeneration.
You can speak truth.
You can establish wise boundaries.
You can refuse to finance destruction.
You can refuse to call evil good simply to keep the peace.
But you can also keep praying.
Keep loving without enabling.
Keep your heart from becoming poisoned by the bitterness of what happened.
Because there is another danger here.
Someone else's rebellion can become your bitterness.
And suddenly their sin has wounded your heart twice.
Once through what they did.
Then again through what you allowed their decision to turn you into.
Give that bitterness to Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again if necessary.
Some prayers are prayed with confidence.
Others come out as tears.
God hears both.
And please remember something Genesis itself teaches repeatedly:
God can still be working in a family that looks completely broken.
You may be looking at chapter 26 while God already knows chapter 33.
You may be staring at the scandal while God is still writing.
That does not guarantee every relationship will be restored exactly as we want it in this life.
The Bible never promises that.
But it does mean human failure does not dethrone God.
Your child's rebellion is not stronger than God.
Your past is not stronger than Christ's blood.
Your shame is not stronger than grace.
Your family history is not sovereign.
Jesus is.
Maybe that is why you found this today.
Not so you could criticize Esau.
But so Esau's story could expose something in you.
What are you trading?
What temporary appetite has become more precious than obedience?
What relationship are you protecting even though it is pulling you farther from Christ?
What secret are you defending?
Whose heart is becoming bitter because you refuse to repent?
Or whose choices have made your spirit bitter?
Sit with them.
Because sometimes the most dangerous sentence a Christian can say is:
“It's not that serious.”
Esau probably wanted dinner.
He could not see Hebrews 12 being written centuries later.
You cannot see every consequence attached to today's compromise either.
So choose Christ.
Not because obedience purchases His love.
Because in Christ you have encountered a love worth obeying.
Choose the Savior over the appetite.
Choose truth over secrecy.
Choose repentance over reputation.
Choose holiness over the thing you keep telling yourself you cannot live without.
And if you have already failed…
Come anyway.
Come ashamed.
Come trembling.
Come with consequences behind you.
Come with the smell of yesterday still on your clothes.
Come with nothing impressive to show God.
Just come to Jesus.
The Gospel was never good news because good people finally became perfect.
It is good news because a perfect Savior came looking for sinners.
This is Gospel Warrior.
And if something inside you was exposed while reading this, don't reduce this moment to another piece of content you consumed and forgot.
You do not need to explain everything publicly. God knows the details. But sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And look through those comments.
Somebody there may need encouragement.
Pray for them.
Remind them of Christ.
Let this become more than content. Let believers carry one another's burdens.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
But if Gospel-centered truth has helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone who may desperately need it tonight.
Someone may be hiding a compromise.
Someone may be a parent crying over a child.
Someone may believe their scandal has placed them beyond grace.
Let them hear about Jesus.

Supporting Gospel ministry does not make God love you more, and it should never replace faithful giving, serving, or involvement in a biblical local church. But when believers voluntarily support sound Christian work, they help make more Gospel-centered resources possible.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the One sinners need.
So share the article if it can reach somebody.
But above everything…
Follow Jesus.
Esau's story leaves us with bitterness in a family's home.
The Gospel takes us somewhere Esau could never have imagined.
To a cross.
To an empty tomb.
To sinners being forgiven.
To rebels becoming sons and daughters.
To shame losing its final word.
To people discovering that the worst chapter they wrote does not have to become the final chapter of their lives.
Because when Jesus enters the story, repentance can replace rebellion.
Grace can meet guilt.
Forgiveness can confront failure.
Redemption can rise out of wreckage.
And scars that once screamed only of what happened can someday testify to what Christ has done.
Maybe the bitter chapter is real—but it still doesn't get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Never Slept With Them—but Your Spouse Would Be Devastated If They Read the Messages
paragraphs: You Never Slept With Them—but Your Spouse Would Be Devastated If They Read the Messages

You may never have touched their body. But if you have to hide the conversation, delete the evidence, change the name, turn the phone over, or pray your spouse never reads what was said… the question is no longer merely, “Did I commit adultery?” The deeper question is: “What has my heart already begun giving away?”
There is a particular sound a phone makes when it vibrates beside you.
Usually, it means nothing.
But sometimes…
you know exactly who it is before you even look.
And something inside you changes.
Your spouse is sitting a few feet away.
Maybe watching television.
Maybe folding clothes.
Maybe feeding the baby.
Maybe exhausted from another ordinary day of building a life with you.
Then your screen lights up.
A name appears.
And instinctively…
you turn the phone over.
That tiny movement may last less than a second.
But sometimes a whole spiritual battle fits inside one second.
Because your spouse asks,
“Who was that?”
And you say,
“Nobody.”
Nobody.
But “nobody” has been making you smile lately.
“Nobody” understands you.
“Nobody” listens when your spouse seems too tired.
“Nobody” notices things about you that you wish your husband or wife noticed.
“Nobody” sends messages you reread after everyone goes to sleep.
And technically…
you have never slept together.
You have never kissed.
Maybe you have never even held hands.
So you have built yourself a courtroom inside your conscience, presented the evidence, acted as your own defense attorney, and announced the verdict:
“I haven’t cheated.”
But there is one question you desperately hope nobody asks.
Would you hand your spouse your unlocked phone and let them read the entire conversation?
Not selected messages.
Not the cleaned-up version.
Not after deleting the dangerous parts.
Everything.
Every joke.
Every late-night confession.
Every heart emoji.
Every “I wish things were different.”
Every complaint about your marriage.
Every message you deleted because you knew how it would look.
Every sentence that sounded innocent when viewed alone but becomes painfully obvious when read from beginning to end.
Would you hand them the phone?
Because sometimes the most revealing evidence is not what happened in a bedroom.
Sometimes it is what you are terrified will be discovered on a screen.
And Jesus does something deeply uncomfortable with our favorite defenses.
He goes beneath behavior.
He goes after the heart.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus recalls the commandment against adultery and then says:

ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν
egō de legō hymin
“But I say to you…”

He continues that whoever looks at a woman πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν—pros to epithymēsai autēn—with the purpose or movement of desiring her, has already committed adultery with her ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ—en tē kardia autou—
“in his heart.”

Jesus was not teaching that temptation itself makes a person identical to someone who has physically committed adultery, nor was He erasing meaningful distinctions between temptation, lustful intention, emotional betrayal, and physical sexual sin.
He was destroying the comforting lie that sexual faithfulness can be measured only by what our bodies have done.
Jesus takes the conversation somewhere we would often rather not go.
The heart.
That private territory where attraction is entertained.
Where fantasies are fed.
Where another person slowly becomes emotionally precious.
Where attention that belongs inside a covenant starts flowing somewhere else.
Where secrecy begins feeling necessary.
And where we can remain physically faithful while becoming increasingly divided within.
This is why the sentence “But nothing happened” can sometimes hide an enormous amount of something.
Nothing happened?
Then why delete the messages?
Nothing happened?
Then why does your heartbeat change when their name appears?
Nothing happened?
Then why have you told them things about your marriage that you have never had the courage to tell your spouse?
Nothing happened?
Then why would your husband be shattered if he saw it?
Why would your wife cry?
Why would you need fifteen minutes to “explain the context”?
Why does secrecy feel necessary to keep the relationship alive?
Maybe you never slept with them.
But perhaps you started building a room for them inside your heart.
And your spouse does not have the key.
That is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because these things rarely begin with somebody waking up one morning and announcing,
“Today I will betray my marriage.”
It often begins much smaller.
A compliment.
A private joke.
A coworker who listens.
An old flame who suddenly follows you again.
A message from someone you knew years ago.
“You look amazing. You haven’t changed.”
You smile.
You answer.
Nothing terrible happens.
Then another message comes.
Then another.
Soon they know you had an argument with your spouse.
They know you feel lonely.
They know what your spouse supposedly “doesn’t understand” about you.
