And then Scripture gives us three words that may have altered the course of Christian history:
“But Barnabas took him...”
Barnabas took him.
Everybody else saw danger.
Barnabas saw what Christ was doing.
Everybody else remembered Saul's reputation.
Barnabas listened to Saul's testimony.
Everybody else backed away.
Barnabas stepped closer.
He brought Saul to the apostles and explained what had happened—how Saul had seen the Lord and had boldly preached in the name of Jesus.
Barnabas became a bridge between a redeemed man and a frightened church.
Don't misunderstand this.
Biblical grace is not gullibility.
Christian forgiveness does not mean pretending evil never happened. Wisdom still matters. Accountability matters. Truth matters. Repentance matters.
But Barnabas understood something the church can easily forget:
If Jesus truly transforms someone, we cannot permanently chain that person to the identity Christ has redeemed them from.
Saul's past was real.
So was Christ's grace.
And grace had the final word.
The man once feared as a persecutor would become Paul the missionary, proclaiming Christ across cities and cultures.
Barnabas didn't create Paul's calling.
Jesus did.
Barnabas simply refused to stand in the way of what Jesus was creating.
There is a difference.
And somebody reading this needs to hear it.
You do not need to become somebody's savior.
You already have one.
His name is Jesus Christ.
But you may be called to become somebody's Barnabas.
The person who says:
“I know what you did. But I also see what Christ is doing.”
“I know you failed. But failure doesn't have to become your final identity.”
“I know everyone has given up on you. I haven't.”
“I know your story is messy. Come with me anyway.”
Maybe somebody once did that for you.
Maybe one phone call kept you alive spiritually.
One pastor answered when everybody else was tired of your problems.
One friend sat beside you after your marriage collapsed.
One believer looked past your addiction.
One person invited you back after you disappeared.
One Christian refused to treat your scandal as the end of your story.
You may not remember every sermon you heard during that season.
But you remember who stayed.
That is Barnabas-shaped Christianity.
And his story wasn't finished.
Later, the Gospel began spreading powerfully in Antioch.
When Barnabas arrived and saw the grace of God, Acts tells us that he was glad and encouraged the believers to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose.
Then Scripture gives one of the most beautiful descriptions ever written about a man:
Barnabas was “a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.”
And many people were brought to the Lord.
Notice what Barnabas did next.
He could have enjoyed the growing ministry.
He could have protected his influence.
He could have become the celebrity.
Instead...
he went looking for Saul.
Barnabas traveled to Tarsus to find him.
Let that sink in.
Barnabas saw a growing work of God and thought:
Someone else needs to be here.
That is rare.
We live in a world obsessed with platforms.
Followers.
Recognition.
Credit.
Visibility.
Being quoted.
Being noticed.
Being the person in the photograph.
Barnabas saw a thriving ministry and deliberately brought in someone whose gifts might eventually eclipse his own visibility.
That takes security.
That takes humility.
That takes a man whose identity is rooted somewhere deeper than applause.
It takes somebody who knows that the Kingdom belongs to Jesus.
Not us.
Barnabas found Saul, brought him to Antioch, and together they taught a great many people.
And it was there, at Antioch, that the disciples were first called Christians.
But then comes the part of Barnabas's story that makes him painfully human.
Because encouragement does not mean avoiding conflict.
Paul and Barnabas eventually had one.
A serious one.
A man named John Mark had accompanied them previously but had left them during the mission.
Later Barnabas wanted to take Mark again.
Paul did not.
Paul apparently saw Mark's previous departure as reason not to bring him.
Barnabas saw something worth giving another opportunity.
Acts 15 says the disagreement became sharp.
So sharp that Paul and Barnabas separated.
Paul took Silas.
Barnabas took Mark.
And Scripture does something beautiful here.
It does not turn either man into a cartoon villain.
These were faithful servants of Christ navigating a real disagreement.
But Barnabas did what Barnabas had done before.
He took the man others hesitated to take.
First Saul.
Now Mark.
Do you see the pattern?
Barnabas kept finding people standing dangerously close to being defined by yesterday.
And he kept walking toward them.
He did it for Saul when Saul's problem was a terrible past.
He did it for Mark when Mark's problem was a disappointing failure.
Those are not the same thing.
But Barnabas knew something about restoration.
A person's worst chapter does not necessarily reveal how Jesus intends to finish the book.
And years later...
something remarkable appears in Paul's own writing.
The Paul who once refused to take Mark would eventually tell Timothy:
“Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.”
Read that again.
Profitable to me for the ministry.
The rejected worker became useful again.
The man who once turned back was wanted again.
The failure wasn't final.
Imagine what might have happened if Mark had been abandoned permanently at his weakest moment.
We cannot know the alternate history.
Scripture does not tell us.
So we should not invent it.
But Scripture does show us that Mark was restored to usefulness—and Barnabas had been willing to walk with him when his reliability was being questioned.
That should terrify some of us.
Because perhaps we have been so busy identifying people's failures that we haven't noticed what Jesus may still be building in them.
Maybe the person you wrote off isn't finished.
Maybe the son who walked away isn't finished.
Maybe the woman whose marriage collapsed isn't finished.
Maybe the pastor who burned out isn't finished.
Maybe the addict fighting through another day isn't finished.
Maybe the teenager questioning everything isn't finished.
Maybe the Christian who disappeared because shame swallowed them isn't finished.
Maybe...
you're not finished.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin doesn't matter.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God went to a cross.
Jesus did not come to tell us our rebellion was harmless.
He came because we were helpless to save ourselves from it.
At Calvary, Christ bore sin.
Our shame.
Our guilt.
Our condemnation.

The holy Son of God died and rose again so sinners could be reconciled to God—not through religious performance, reputation management, or pretending to be good enough, but through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace walks into darkness and brings sinners into the light.
Repentance does not mean explaining your sin.
It means turning from it toward Christ.
Forgiveness does not mean your past never happened.
It means your past no longer has authority to pronounce the final verdict over someone Jesus has redeemed.
That is why Barnabas matters.
His life points beyond himself.
Toward Christ.
Barnabas encouraged because he had encountered the Gospel of Jesus.
Barnabas gave because Christ had become more valuable than possessions.
Barnabas welcomed because Christ welcomes repentant sinners.
Barnabas restored because Christ restores broken people.
Barnabas could step away from the spotlight because Jesus was the center.
And maybe this article found you because God is putting one uncomfortable question in front of you:
Who needs you to become Barnabas right now?
Not their savior.
Their encourager.
Maybe somebody needs a message tonight.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
“I haven't forgotten you.”
Maybe somebody needs you to say:
“Come back to church with me.”
Maybe somebody needs:
“I know you've messed up. But Jesus is still calling you.”
Maybe somebody needs you to stop gossiping about the chapter God is trying to heal.
Maybe the person who needs encouragement lives under your roof.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your child.
Your father.
Your mother.
Maybe you have been encouraging strangers online while starving your own family of grace.
Or perhaps you are the Saul in this story.
You came to Jesus carrying a history that makes people uncomfortable.
Keep walking with Christ.
Or maybe you're Mark.
You failed.
You left.
You disappointed somebody who trusted you.
And now every time you think about serving God again, a voice whispers:
You had your chance.
Listen carefully.
Your failure may have consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Repentance may require painful honesty.
Restoration may take time.
But none of that means Jesus is finished with you.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Mark turned back.
Paul persecuted believers.
And the church itself is made of people whose only hope is the mercy of Jesus Christ.
There are no trophies of human perfection at the foot of the cross.
Only sinners who needed a Savior.
So come home.
Stop negotiating with the sin Jesus is telling you to surrender.
Stop protecting what is killing your fellowship with God.
Stop pretending.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already restored you from something you thought would destroy your life, tell somebody what Jesus did. Your testimony may become another person's Barnabas moment.
Then think of one specific person who needs this message.
Not your entire friends list.
One person.
You already know their name.
Send this to the believer who thinks failure disqualified them forever.
If Christ has given you truth that can point another wounded person toward Him, don't bury it.
Because eventually you may become the person who needs to read it again.
Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's favor. It does not earn salvation. It does not make anyone more spiritual.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But believers who have freely received can freely choose to help Gospel-centered ministry reach others.
And whether you ever spend a cent or not, keep pursuing Christ.
Because Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Barnabas's story leaves us with something we desperately need in an age that enjoys public humiliation.
The world knows how to expose people.
Jesus knows how to redeem them.
The world knows how to screenshot your worst moment.
Jesus knows how to write your next chapter.
The world says:
“Remember what they did.”
Grace says:
“Look what Christ is doing.”
Barnabas was born Joseph.
But grace shaped his life so deeply that people eventually knew him by what flowed through him.
Encouragement.
Perhaps that is the question you should carry after closing this article.
Not:
“Will people remember my name?”
But:
“When people remember how I treated them at their lowest, will they remember something that looked like Jesus?”
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is standing outside a door.
Somebody is ashamed.
Somebody failed.
Somebody believes their usefulness to God ended in their worst chapter.
And perhaps God is not asking you to preach them a sermon.
Perhaps He is simply asking you to walk toward them...
take them by the hand...
and remind them that Jesus Christ is still writing.
Never confuse the chapter where someone fell with the chapter where Jesus intends to finish their story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH”: WHY DOES THE BIBLE OPEN A LOVE SONG LIKE THIS?
paragraphs: “KISS ME WITH THE KISSES OF HIS MOUTH”: WHY DOES THE BIBLE OPEN A LOVE SONG LIKE THIS?

The first sentence of the Song of Songs sounds almost too intimate to be Scripture. But perhaps what makes us uncomfortable is exactly what exposes how little we understand about holy love—and how desperately the human heart was created to be fully known, faithfully loved, and ultimately redeemed.
“Kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
Wait.
That is in the Bible?
Not buried somewhere in an obscure manuscript. Not hidden behind a theological metaphor. Not something added by a modern writer trying to make Scripture provocative.
It is essentially how the Song of Songs begins.

Before we sanitize it, spiritualize it, turn it into a sermon illustration, or rush past it because it makes respectable Christians slightly uncomfortable, we need to hear what the Hebrew actually says.
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqēnî minnĕshîqôth pîhû.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
Then:
כִּי־טוֹבִים דֹּדֶיךָ מִיָּיִן
Kî-tôvîm dōdeykhā miyyāyin.
“For your love is better than wine.”
Song of Songs 1:2.
There is no need to make the Hebrew less intimate than it is.
The woman desires the man she loves.
She speaks first.
She longs for his kiss.
And God allowed those words into Holy Scripture.
That alone should make us pay attention.
Because perhaps one of our problems is that we have sometimes confused holiness with emotional coldness.
We imagine that anything deeply passionate must somehow be less spiritual.
But the Bible does not begin the Song of Songs with two detached people discussing abstract principles of romance.
It begins with longing.
Desire.
Anticipation.
A woman who does not merely want to know that she is loved intellectually.
She wants love brought near.
“Kiss me…”
There is something painfully human about that sentence.
Because beneath all the things we spend our lives chasing, there remains a hunger most of us rarely admit aloud.
We want to be wanted.
Not tolerated.
Not merely useful.
Not noticed only when somebody needs something.
Wanted.
Known without being discarded.
Seen without being abandoned.
Loved without having to perform every second to keep that love alive.
Maybe that is why these ancient words still feel strangely modern.
You can have thousands of Facebook friends and still wonder whether anybody actually knows you.
You can sleep beside someone and feel miles away.
You can sit in church surrounded by worshippers while privately wondering whether God has become tired of you.
You can smile for the photograph.
Post the Bible verse.
Say, “God is good.”
Answer, “I’m blessed.”
And still carry a silent question underneath all of it:
Does anybody really love the person underneath this version of me?
Song of Songs begins where many of us are afraid to begin.
With desire.
But we need to understand the book carefully.

The Song of Songs is genuine love poetry. Its language celebrates the attraction, delight, exclusivity, longing, beauty, and covenantal dimensions of human love. We do not honor Scripture by pretending the man and woman are not actually speaking about one another.
The kisses are kisses.
The attraction is real.
The poetry is intentionally intimate.
God is not embarrassed by the love He designed.
Yet Christians throughout history have also heard something deeper echoing through this biblical portrait of faithful love.
Not because every romantic sentence should automatically be converted into a secret code about Jesus.
That would flatten the actual poetry.
Rather, because the whole biblical story eventually reveals a mystery larger than any human romance.
Marriage itself can point beyond itself.
Paul writes that a husband and wife becoming “one flesh” carries a profound mystery, and he connects that mystery to Christ and the church in Ephesians 5:31–32.
That changes how Christians can hear the Song.
The Song is not transformed into a decoder ring where every kiss, fragrance, garden, breast, spice, and vineyard must have an invented spiritual equivalent.
But neither must Christian readers stop at human romance.
Human covenant love can become a window.
And beyond that window stands the Bridegroom.
Jesus Christ.
Suddenly the deepest ache beneath the poetry becomes familiar.
Because Scripture tells another love story.
One far more scandalous.
Except in this story, the Bride was not spotless.
We were not waiting beautifully in a garden, deserving to be pursued.
We ran.
We rebelled.
We sinned.
We hid.
Humanity's oldest instinct after sin was not to run toward God.
It was to hide from Him.
Adam and Eve heard God walking in the garden and concealed themselves.
And we have been sewing fig leaves ever since.
Different leaves.
Same hiding.
Success.
Religion.
Money.
Sex.
Achievement.
Entertainment.
Ministry.
Busyness.
Relationships.
Followers.
Reputation.
Even theological knowledge can become another leaf if we use knowledge about God to avoid surrendering ourselves to God.
We desperately want intimacy while simultaneously fearing what intimacy requires:
being known.
That is the terrifying contradiction inside the human heart.
“Love me…”
But don't look too closely.
“Come near…”
But not near enough to discover what I did.
“Know me…”
But only the version I have carefully prepared for you.
And then comes Jesus.
Not merely offering advice from heaven.
Coming near.
“The Word became flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
Think about that.
The God humanity ran from became flesh and entered the neighborhood of the fugitives.
He touched lepers.
He ate with sinners.
He received the disgraced.
He spoke with people respectable society preferred to avoid.
He let a woman with a shattered reputation weep at His feet.
He restored failures.
He confronted hypocrites.
He welcomed children.
He called sinners to repentance.
He did not redefine darkness as light to make people comfortable.
He stepped into our darkness to bring us into His light.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do to rescue us from what sin has done.
And the cross proves the cost.
This is where the love story becomes almost unbearable.
The One who never sinned was betrayed with a kiss.
A kiss.
Judas approached Jesus in Gethsemane and used an act normally associated with affection as the signal of betrayal.
Imagine the contrast.
Song of Songs opens with:
“Let him kiss me…”
The Gospels move toward a garden where the Son of God receives a traitor's kiss.
Human love longs for intimacy.
Human sin corrupts even intimacy.
And Jesus walks straight through our corruption toward the cross.
He knows what counterfeit affection feels like.
He knows the difference between lips that approach Him and hearts that belong to Him.
That should disturb every comfortable Christian.
Because it is possible to sing His name without surrendering to Him.
It is possible to post Scripture while privately feeding the sin Scripture condemns.
It is possible to say “Lord” publicly while protecting an idol privately.
Judas was physically close enough to kiss Jesus.
And still infinitely far from Him in his heart.
So perhaps the frightening question is not simply:
“Do I believe in Jesus?”
Perhaps tonight the question becomes:
Have I merely learned how to stay close enough to Christianity to look faithful while keeping Jesus away from the rooms in my heart I refuse to surrender?
That secret addiction.
That bitterness.
That relationship you know is dragging you from God.
That pornography nobody knows about.
That affair living first in messages and imagination.
That pride dressed like discernment.
That unforgiveness you have renamed “boundaries” when what you really mean is hatred.
That hunger for approval.
That hidden dishonesty.
That carefully maintained Christian image.
You can fool an audience.
You cannot fool Christ.
And strangely, that is not only terrifying.
It is beautiful.
Because the Jesus who already knows the truth about you is the same Jesus who calls sinners to come.
You do not have to clean yourself into acceptability before approaching the cross.
You come confessing that you cannot clean yourself.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
That is Gospel.
Not pretending.
Not image management.
Not religious cosmetics.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
New life.
The Bridegroom does not merely make sinful people feel better about remaining chained.
He breaks chains.
He calls the dead to life.
He forgives the guilty.
He cleanses the stained.
He restores the broken.
He teaches people who spent their lives searching for love in destructive places what love actually is.
And perhaps now we understand why Song of Songs can hurt so beautifully.
“For your love is better than wine.”
Wine represented pleasure, celebration, abundance.
Yet the beloved says there is something better.
Your love.
Now carry that longing carefully into the greater biblical story.
How many “wines” have you tasted trying to satisfy something only God could ultimately fill?
Approval tasted good for a moment.
Then you needed another compliment.
Money promised security.
Then you needed more.
Sex promised intimacy.
Without covenant and holiness, it could leave another wound.
Social media promised connection.
Then you found yourself staring at a screen wondering why everyone else's life looked happier.
Success promised significance.
Then yesterday's achievement became today's minimum expectation.
Sin always makes extravagant promises.
Then sends an invoice.
Jesus tells the truth before He asks for your life.
Following Him means denying yourself and taking up your cross.
Repentance may hurt.
Obedience may cost you relationships, habits, opportunities, pleasures, reputations, and versions of yourself you thought you needed.
But Christ does not empty your hands merely to leave them empty.
He calls you from death into life.
From slavery into freedom.
From condemnation into justification.
From estrangement into reconciliation.
From orphan-hearted wandering into adoption.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have spent years believing your scandal is the final chapter.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Sexual sin.
Abortion.
Infidelity.
Prison.
Failure.
A secret nobody knows.
Something done to you.
Something done by you.
A season when you walked away from God.
A prayer you stopped praying because you became convinced heaven had stopped listening.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Christ is sufficient.
There is a difference.
The cross does not minimize your guilt.
The cross demonstrates how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's mercy is.
Jesus did not bleed because humanity needed motivational content.
He came to save sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And because the tomb is empty, your past does not possess sovereign authority over your future.
Christ does.
Maybe this article reached you while nobody knows what is happening inside you.
Maybe you almost scrolled away.
Maybe that opening sentence about a kiss caught your attention for one reason, but somewhere along the way another sentence found the wound.
If that happened, don't hide now.
You do not need to confess private details publicly.
But you can take one honest step.
And if you cannot find impressive words at all, just write:
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way home.
And somebody needs to hear what you just heard.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because there may be one person among your friends who is smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
You may never know that your share reached them at 2:13 in the morning when temptation was winning.

You may never know that someone opened it after an argument, after falling back into addiction, after considering walking away from their marriage, or after becoming convinced that God could never want them again.
Share it anyway.
There are truths you do not save because you have forgotten them.
You save them because you know there will be a night when you will need to remember them again.
There is another way you can help this work continue.
But hear this carefully.
It does not buy forgiveness.
It does not make God love you more.
And it should never replace faithful generosity to your local church or other responsibilities God has placed before you.
Scripture says giving should not be “grudgingly, or of necessity,” because “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Prayerfully.
Joyfully.
As voluntary support for continuing and expanding Gospel-centered work.

Supporting Christian ministry is biblical; Paul teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), while Christian generosity must remain willing rather than coerced.
So if you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior reach more people?” this is one practical answer.
It is mission.
It is another wounded person encountering Scripture.
Another believer being called back from compromise.
Another exhausted Christian remembering grace.
Another seeker hearing clearly that Christianity is not fundamentally about becoming impressive enough for God.
It is about Christ saving sinners who could never save themselves.
Pray.
Share.
Save Gospel-centered resources.
Follow.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe at all but is willing to listen.
Because somewhere beyond your screen is a human being whose polished profile is hiding an aching soul.
And perhaps now we finally understand why the Bible dares to begin this love song with such vulnerable words.
“Kiss me…”
It is the language of nearness.
And underneath so much of human sin is a desperate, disordered search for nearness.
We keep trying to satisfy eternal hunger with temporary things.
Another body.
Another relationship.
Another achievement.
Another purchase.
Another drink.
Another notification.
Another person telling us we matter.
Another distraction so we do not have to sit quietly long enough to hear the emptiness.
Yet Scripture keeps drawing us toward something greater.
Human love is beautiful when received according to God's design.
Marriage is beautiful.
Desire within its holy covenant is beautiful.
A husband delighting in his wife is beautiful.
A wife desiring her husband is beautiful.
God is not embarrassed by any of it.
But even the greatest human love cannot carry the weight of being God.
Your spouse cannot redeem you.
Your boyfriend cannot justify you.
Your girlfriend cannot resurrect you.
Your children cannot become your savior.
Your followers cannot give you eternal life.
Only Christ can bear that weight.
And this is the breathtaking reversal of the Gospel:
We spend our lives crying,
“Someone come close enough to prove I am worth loving.”
Then Jesus Christ comes closer than we imagined…
and shows us something far greater.
Not that we were secretly innocent.
Not that our rebellion never mattered.
Not that every desire we carried was holy.
But that while we were sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
He knew.
And came anyway.
He saw the scandal.
And brought grace.
He saw the grave.
And brought resurrection.
He saw what sin had written over your life…
and stepped into history with nail-scarred hands.
So perhaps the deepest question after reading Song of Songs 1:2 is not whether Christians are allowed to talk about kissing.
Perhaps it is this:
What have you been kissing because your soul was starving for a love only God could ultimately give?
Don't answer too quickly.
Sit there.
Let it hurt.
Then bring the answer to Jesus.
Because repentance is not the moment God discovers your scandal.
It is the moment you stop running from the One who already knows—and turn toward the Savior who died and rose to redeem sinners.
Come out of hiding.
Come home.
And remember this when your past whispers your old name tonight:
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you, but grace gets to tell the world what Jesus did with you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE MARRIAGE BED” SHOULD BE HONORED: What Exactly Is Hebrews 13:4 Protecting?
paragraphs: “THE MARRIAGE BED” SHOULD BE HONORED: What Exactly Is Hebrews 13:4 Protecting?
We quote this verse when marriages are already bleeding. But what if God gave it to us before the wound—to protect something the world keeps teaching us to treat as disposable?
There is a sentence in Scripture that people often whisper when they would rather not talk about what it actually means.
It appears near the end of Hebrews.
No long introduction.
No attempt to soften the language.
Just a startlingly direct declaration about marriage, sexuality, purity, and judgment:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.” — Hebrews 13:4, KJV
And underneath the English translation stands the Greek text:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος, πόρνους γὰρ καὶ μοιχοὺς κρινεῖ ὁ Θεός.
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos, pornous gar kai moichous krinei ho Theos.
The wording is compact.
But it carries enormous weight.
Τίμιος — timios.
Precious. Honored. Valuable. Something regarded as worthy rather than common.
γάμος — gamos.
Marriage.
κοίτη — koitē.
Literally a bed, and in this context the marriage bed—the intimate sexual dimension of married life.
ἀμίαντος — amiantos.
Undefiled. Unstained.
Then Scripture turns from what should be honored to what God Himself will judge:
πόρνους — pornous.
Those practicing sexual immorality.
And μοιχούς — moichous.
Adulterers.

The basic meaning is not hidden behind some mysterious theological code. Major English translations consistently render the verse as honoring marriage and keeping the marriage bed undefiled, followed by the warning that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
But perhaps the question we have not asked deeply enough is this:
Why does God care so much about what happens in a marriage bed?
Why should heaven care about something occurring behind a closed bedroom door?
Because the bed is not ultimately the point.
Covenant is.
And once you understand that, Hebrews 13:4 stops sounding like an isolated prohibition about sex and starts sounding like God standing guard over something precious.
Read what surrounds it.
Hebrews 13 begins:
“Let brotherly love continue.”
Then comes hospitality.
Then compassion for prisoners.
Then remembering those who are mistreated.
Then marriage.
Then, immediately afterward, freedom from the love of money and contentment in God.
The Greek text itself places the commands in precisely this sequence.
This is not a random collection of religious rules.
It is a picture of what a life transformed by Christ looks like.
Love people.
Welcome strangers.
Remember suffering people.
Honor marriage.
Reject sexual unfaithfulness.
Do not worship money.
Trust God.
In other words, Christianity does not merely ask what you believe while sitting in church.
It asks what happens to your love, your home, your body, your sexuality, your money, your loyalties, and your secret life when Jesus becomes Lord.
And that is where this verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because some betrayals happen long before another person enters the bedroom.
Sometimes adultery begins as permission.
A conversation you know you should end.
A message you delete.
A fantasy you repeatedly feed.
A relationship you deliberately keep hidden.
A screen nobody knows you are watching.
An emotional intimacy being given to someone who is not your spouse.
A secret world slowly becoming more exciting than the covenant waiting for you at home.
Not every temptation is adultery.
Not every struggle means someone has committed the same sin.
But Jesus went directly beneath external behavior and exposed the desires of the heart.
“You have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
— Matthew 5:27–28, KJV
Jesus was not making physical adultery meaningless.
He was making holiness deeper.
The Pharisee could congratulate himself because his body had never crossed a particular boundary.
Jesus walked into the hidden room of the heart.
That is terrifying.
And strangely beautiful.
Because Jesus is interested in more than controlling behavior.
He wants the heart.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been watching.
Maybe nobody knows who you have been messaging.
Maybe your spouse thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you have mastered the art of turning the screen over when someone walks into the room.
Maybe there is no affair.
Not physically.
Not yet.
But you know something has begun moving inside you.
You know why that conversation feels different.
You know why you erased the history.
You know why you would panic if your spouse held your phone for five uninterrupted minutes.
And perhaps Hebrews 13:4 is not God trying to ruin your happiness.
Perhaps it is God interrupting you before temporary excitement burns down something you will someday beg Him to restore.
The command is not merely “Do not commit adultery.”
It is:
Honor marriage.
That reaches farther.
To honor something means you stop treating it as cheap.
Marriage cannot be sacred in the ceremony and disposable in ordinary life.
You cannot publicly celebrate covenant while privately starving it.
You cannot promise faithfulness at the altar and then continuously give the deepest parts of yourself to everyone except the person standing beside you.
And husbands and wives both need to hear this.
Hebrews 13:4 is not ammunition for men to control women.
It is not ammunition for women to control men.
It is not permission for one spouse to demand sexual access regardless of the other person's dignity, wellbeing, consent, suffering, or circumstances.
The command to honor marriage applies to the whole covenant.
Scripture's vision of marital intimacy is never properly understood through selfish entitlement.
Paul tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Think about the standard.
Not domination.
Christ.
Not “What can I get?”
“What can I give?”
Not exploitation.
Sacrifice.
Not selfishness wearing a wedding ring.
Christlike love.
And this is why “the marriage bed” cannot biblically become an excuse for degradation, coercion, manipulation, violence, humiliation, or abuse.
Something does not become holy merely because married people do it.
Marriage itself must be honored.
The other person remains an image-bearer of God.
A husband does not become his wife's god.
A wife does not become her husband's possession.
Both belong ultimately to Christ.
Marriage does not erase human dignity.
It should become one of the places where dignity is most fiercely protected.
And yet there is another mistake Christians sometimes make.
We can become so afraid of sexual sin that we accidentally begin treating sex itself as dirty.
Hebrews 13:4 does not do that.
Notice the astonishing contrast.
The marriage bed is not condemned.
It is called ἀμίαντος — amiantos — undefiled.
Sexual intimacy within marriage is not presented as God's embarrassing concession to human weakness.
Scripture can speak of married intimacy with joy.
Proverbs tells the husband to rejoice with the wife of his youth.
First Corinthians recognizes mutual marital intimacy.
Genesis describes husband and wife becoming one flesh.
The biblical story does not teach that sex is inherently filthy.
It teaches that something powerful and meaningful should not be ripped away from the covenant in which God designed it to flourish.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the curtains can destroy it.
The problem is not that fire exists.
The question is where it burns.
And perhaps that is why sexual sin can leave wounds that people carry for years.
Because bodies are not meaningless.
People are not products.
Intimacy is not merely recreation.
And another human being was never created to become content for our consumption.
The culture can call something casual.
The heart may discover that it was never casual at all.
And now somebody reading this feels shame rising.
Because this is no longer an article about somebody else.
You crossed the line.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe yesterday.
Maybe the person sleeping beside you still does not know.
Maybe the marriage ended because of what happened.
Maybe pornography rewired your expectations.
Maybe lust became a hiding place.
Maybe you gave yourself to people who disappeared.
Maybe someone used you.
Maybe you used someone.
Maybe you knew Scripture and rebelled anyway.
And now the words hit:
“God will judge.”
Do not erase those words.
Christianity loses something essential when we turn every warning into something harmless.
Hebrews really does warn about divine judgment.
God takes sexual sin seriously.
God takes adultery seriously.
God takes covenant seriously.
But if you stop reading the Bible at judgment, you have not yet reached the heart of the Gospel.
Because the same Bible that exposes sinners introduces us to a Savior who receives sinners.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity was already clean.
He came because we were not.
The Gospel is not:
Clean yourself up enough and maybe Jesus will tolerate you.
The Gospel is that the holy Son of God came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Grace does not tell adultery that adultery was harmless.
Grace tells the adulterer that sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Grace does not call pornography innocent.
Grace says chains can be broken.
Grace does not tell the sexually broken, “Pretend nothing happened.”
Grace says:
Bring what happened into the light.
Repentance is not pretending.
Repentance turns.
It stops defending darkness.
It stops renaming rebellion.
It stops asking how close to the edge we can walk while still calling ourselves faithful.
It comes into the light and says:
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“This is what I became.”
“This is what I have hidden.”
“I cannot save myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
And there—in the place where scandal meets the blood of Christ—the Gospel begins rewriting what sin tried to finish.
Some consequences may remain.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence.
Trust broken in five minutes may require years to rebuild.
Some marriages will require deep pastoral help, wise counseling, confession, boundaries, accountability, patience, and sustained evidence of repentance.
Forgiveness and immediate restoration of trust are not identical things.
And someone being abused should never be told that “honoring marriage” means silently remaining available for further abuse.
Truth matters.
Safety matters.
Justice matters.
Repentance matters.
And grace matters.
Real grace is strong enough to tell the truth.
Maybe the most powerful thing you can do after reading this is not promise that you will never struggle again.
Maybe it is finally stop hiding.
Tell the truth.
Close the secret account.
Delete the number you keep returning to.
Put accountability around the device.
Confess where confession is biblically and wisely required.
Seek mature pastoral help.
Get qualified professional help when the situation requires it.
Stop feeding what you keep asking God to kill.
And if your marriage is hurting, stop waiting for catastrophe before you begin protecting covenant.
Talk.
Listen.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Put the phone down.
Look at each other.
Become curious about the pain underneath the silence.
Learn to apologize without adding “but.”
Date your spouse again.
Guard each other's dignity.
Fight the problem instead of fighting each other.
Remember why you chose one another.
And when feelings fluctuate—and they will—remember that covenant was designed to carry something emotion alone cannot carry.
Marriage is not sustained by romance alone.
It needs truth.
Mercy.
Faithfulness.
Patience.
Forgiveness.
Repentance.
And Christ.
Especially Christ.
Because eventually every marriage discovers that two imperfect people cannot build heaven by themselves.
You need grace in the room.
You need Jesus at the table.
You need Jesus in the arguments.
You need Jesus in the disappointment.
You need Jesus when attraction changes.
You need Jesus when temptation whispers.
You need Jesus when forgiveness feels impossible.
You need Jesus when the marriage bed becomes complicated by grief, sickness, trauma, exhaustion, aging, childbirth, distance, disappointment, or wounds nobody else can see.
Hebrews 13:4 is protecting far more than furniture in a bedroom.
It is calling God's people to honor covenant.
To refuse sexual betrayal.
To reject the commodification of bodies.
To treat marital intimacy as something worthy of faithfulness rather than consumption.
And ultimately, it reminds us that our hidden lives still matter before God.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear tonight.
Not:
“You are beyond hope.”
But:
Stop running.
The One calling you out of darkness is the same Christ whose hands were pierced for sinners.
Come home.
Not to religious performance.
To Jesus.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
And begin walking differently.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make one honest declaration:
Let other believers know they are not fighting alone.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need your testimony.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.
Someone in your circle may be one secret conversation away from destroying a covenant.
Someone else may already believe his or her failure is beyond the reach of Christ.
Your share may put this message in front of them before another choice is made.
And even send it privately to the person you know will never comment publicly but desperately needs to read it.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, confront hidden sin, understand the Gospel, strengthen your marriage, or walk closer to Jesus Christ, you can also help keep this ministry moving.
Following costs nothing, but it helps you stay connected to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.

Biblical tithes and offerings deserve to be taught in their own biblical context, and believers should faithfully support their local church and Christian ministry according to conscience, Scripture, wisdom, and cheerful generosity.
If this ministry glorifies Christ and genuinely helps people encounter His Word, your support helps us keep doing that work.
And there is much more available even without paying.
That matters because this ministry should never become merely another content machine.
We want people in the Word.
We want wounded believers restored.
We want secret sin dragged into the light.
We want marriages strengthened.
We want prodigals coming home.
We want unbelievers meeting Jesus.
We want Christians becoming disciples rather than spectators.
And above everything else, we want Christ glorified.
Share because someone you love may need this message.
Follow because tomorrow's message may meet you—or somebody you love—exactly where the battle is happening.
And comment because there should be no shame in admitting that we still need grace.
“No more hiding.”
“Pray for us.”
“Jesus still restores.”
Whatever your story has been, do not confuse your worst chapter with your final chapter.
Hebrews 13:4 reminds us that covenant matters.
Purity matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Judgment is real.
But the Bible does not end with sinners standing helpless beneath judgment.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
And Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still cleanses.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still teaches wounded people how to walk again.
Jesus still rebuilds lives that sin tried to demolish.
Jesus still writes redemption into places we thought could contain only regret.
So honor marriage.
Guard the marriage bed.
Run from sexual immorality.
Tell the truth.
Repent quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Seek help when you need it.
Protect the covenant before you have to rescue it from the wreckage.
And when shame tells you that your scandal has already written the ending, look again toward the cross.
Because the nails in His hands tell another story.
Your scandal may explain the chapter that broke you, but it does not have authority to write the ending Jesus purchased with His blood.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN WHO MADE HANNAH CRY: WHEN THE PEOPLE CLOSEST TO YOU KNOW EXACTLY WHERE TO HURT YOU
paragraphs: THE WOMAN WHO MADE HANNAH CRY: WHEN THE PEOPLE CLOSEST TO YOU KNOW EXACTLY WHERE TO HURT YOU
What Hannah and Peninnah teach us about jealousy, unanswered prayer, family wounds, cruel comparison—and the God who can write redemption in the very place where you thought your story was ruined.
Some wounds come from enemies.
Those are painful.
But there is another kind of wound that seems to travel deeper because it comes from someone sitting at the same table.
Someone who knows your weakness.
Someone who has watched you pray.
Someone who knows what you desperately want but still do not have.
Someone who does not need to invent a lie about you because the truth of your pain is already enough ammunition.
That was Hannah's world.
And maybe, in a way you have never admitted aloud, it has been yours too.
Before you finish this article, you may recognize Hannah.
You may recognize Peninnah.
More unsettlingly, you may recognize a little of both women inside your own heart.
Because 1 Samuel does not introduce Hannah in a peaceful home where everyone understands each other. It introduces us to a complicated household.
Elkanah had two wives.
One was Hannah.
The other was Peninnah.
Then Scripture gives us one devastating contrast:
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
In Hebrew, Hannah's name is written חַנָּה — Ḥannah, associated with grace or favor.
Yet the woman whose very name carried the sound of grace was living through circumstances that did not feel gracious at all.
Have you ever experienced that contradiction?
You know God is good, but your life hurts.
You believe He hears prayer, but the answer has not come.
You worship Him while secretly wondering why somebody else received the thing you have begged Him for.
You congratulate people while something inside you breaks.
You smile at another pregnancy announcement while carrying infertility.
You applaud another wedding while wondering whether you will ever be chosen.
You celebrate someone else's promotion while your bills keep arriving.
You watch another family laughing together while yours barely speaks.
You see someone's children walking with God while you lie awake wondering where your own child went spiritually.
You say, "I'm happy for you."
And perhaps you really are.
But later, when nobody is watching...
you cry.
That is why Hannah's story refuses to become a shallow motivational slogan.
Scripture says Elkanah loved Hannah, yet "the LORD had closed her womb" (1 Samuel 1:5).
Those words require humility.

The biblical text does not present Hannah's infertility as proof that she lacked faith, nor does it tell us that she had committed some secret sin that caused it. Scripture simply places her suffering beneath the mysterious sovereignty of God.
That distinction matters.
Because suffering people have endured enough pain without Christians adding accusations God never made.
Not every unanswered prayer means you did something wrong.
Not every delay means your faith is defective.
Not every barren season is divine punishment.
And not every painful chapter gives us permission to pretend we understand everything God is doing.
But Hannah's empty arms were not the only thing hurting her.
There was Peninnah.
The Hebrew text describes Peninnah with the word צָרָתָהּ — tsaratah — her rival, adversary, or competing wife.
Then comes one of the most painful sentences in the chapter:
"וְכִעֲסַתָּה צָרָתָהּ גַּם־כַּעַס"
Ve-khi'asatah tsaratah gam-ka'as...
Her rival repeatedly provoked her bitterly.
The language carries the idea of vexing, provoking, causing grief or anger.
Peninnah did not accidentally stumble onto Hannah's wound.
She pressed it.
And Scripture says this happened "year by year."
Think about that.
Not once.
Not one insensitive remark everybody regretted afterward.
Not one terrible holiday.
Year...
after...
year.
Hannah knew what was coming.
The journey to worship should have been sacred, yet even there she encountered torment.
Peninnah possessed what Hannah desperately wanted, and instead of receiving her blessing with humility, she apparently weaponized it against the woman who lacked it.
There is something frighteningly contemporary about that.
Because human beings are still doing this.
We turn marriages into status symbols.
Children into trophies.
Ministry into competition.
Money into identity.
Beauty into superiority.
Education into arrogance.
Followers into validation.
Spiritual gifts into rankings.
Even testimonies can become weapons when we use what God has given us to make another wounded person feel spiritually inferior.
Sometimes the person hurting you is not miserable because she has nothing.
Sometimes she is hurting you while holding the very thing you wish you had.
And sometimes having more does not heal an insecure heart.
Peninnah had children.
Yet Hannah had Elkanah's special affection.
The text says he loved Hannah.
Perhaps somewhere inside this fractured household lived the poisonous machinery of comparison.
One woman could look across the room and think, "She has his heart."
The other could look back and think, "She has the children."
And suddenly everybody is measuring.
Everybody is noticing.
Everybody is hurting.
This is what comparison does to families.
It teaches wounded people to stare at another person's portion until they become blind to their own.
It whispers:
Why does Mom treat her differently?
Why does Dad always praise him?
Why did she get married first?
Why does his career succeed?
Why are their children doing better?
Why does everybody listen to her?
Why did God give them what He withheld from me?
Comparison can turn brothers into competitors, sisters into strangers, spouses into scorekeepers, parents into judges, and homes into emotional battlefields.
And if comparison remains unconfessed long enough, another person's blessing can begin to feel like your humiliation.
But there is something remarkable about Hannah.
We are never told that she destroyed Peninnah in return.
She cried.
She stopped eating.
She hurt deeply.
Then she went somewhere with her pain.
To God.
First Samuel 1:10 says Hannah was "bitter of soul"—מָרַת נָפֶשׁ, marat nephesh.
This is not sanitized spirituality.
Her soul hurt.
She wept bitterly.
And she prayed.
Please do not miss that order.
Hannah did not wait until she felt emotionally impressive before approaching God.
She came broken.
Her prayer was so intense and inward that Eli saw her lips moving without hearing her voice and wrongly assumed she was drunk.
Even the priest misunderstood her.
Imagine that.
Tormented at home.
Misunderstood at church.
Still praying.
Somebody reading this knows that loneliness.
You tried explaining what happened in your family, and people minimized it.
You told someone you were struggling, and they gave you a cliché.
You came to church carrying something almost unbearable, and everyone around you saw your clothes but not your battle.
You worshipped while exhausted.
You sang while grieving.
You smiled while unraveling.
And perhaps you wondered:
Does anybody actually see me?
God did.
Hannah told Eli:
"I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD."
The Hebrew imagery is powerful.
שָׁפַכְתִּי אֶת־נַפְשִׁי לִפְנֵי יְהוָה
Shafakhti et-nafshi lifnei YHWH.
"I poured out my soul before the LORD."
Not polished it.
Not edited it.
Not disguised it.
Poured it out.
There are moments when prayer is not eloquent.
Prayer is tears falling onto a pillow.
Prayer is sitting in your car because you cannot walk inside yet.
Prayer is whispering "Jesus" because every other sentence feels impossible.
Prayer is telling God, "I don't understand."
Prayer is admitting, "I'm jealous."
"I'm angry."
"I'm tired."
"I'm scared."
"I feel forgotten."
"I don't know how much longer I can carry this."
God is not frightened by honest grief.
Biblical faith does not require pretending that pain does not hurt.
But Hannah teaches us something else.
Pain must have somewhere holy to go.
Because pain that is never surrendered can become bitterness.
And bitterness eventually looks for someone to punish.
Maybe that is part of what makes Peninnah such a warning.
We know considerably less about her inner life than we know about Hannah's, so we should resist inventing motives Scripture does not reveal.
But we do know what she did.
She provoked a hurting woman.
Repeatedly.
And that should force an uncomfortable question:
Have you become someone's Peninnah?
Not because you have two husbands or live in an ancient Israelite household.
But because you know where somebody hurts...
and sometimes you press there.
Maybe during arguments you bring up the failure your spouse already regrets.
Maybe you compare your children.
Maybe you make jokes about someone's weight, income, singleness, education, infertility, past, addiction, divorce, parenting, or mistakes.
Maybe you post things partly because you know a particular person will see them.
Maybe you call it honesty when it is actually cruelty.
Maybe you tell yourself, "I'm only telling the truth."
But truth without love can still be wielded like a knife.
Being wounded does not give us permission to wound.
Being jealous does not excuse cruelty.
Being overlooked does not authorize revenge.
And being blessed never gives us the right to humiliate someone whose prayer remains unanswered.
This is where the story becomes more than Hannah versus Peninnah.
Because if we only read Scripture asking, "Which character am I?" we can still miss the greater story.
The Bible is ultimately moving us toward Christ.
Hannah eventually conceived and gave birth to Samuel.
But Samuel was not merely Hannah's personal happy ending.
He would become a prophet and judge in Israel. He would anoint David.
And through David's royal line, Scripture moves forward toward Jesus Christ.
Do you see the breathtaking movement?
A woman crying because she could not have a child...
prays.
A child is eventually born.
That child becomes part of Israel's redemptive history.
Samuel anoints David.
And generations later, Jesus Christ comes as the promised Son of David.
Hannah could see her pain.
God could see history.
Hannah could see an empty womb.
God could see Samuel.
Hannah could see Peninnah.
God could see generations.
That does not mean every Christian will eventually receive the exact earthly thing for which they pray.
Christian hope is deeper than that.
Some prayers are answered differently than we desire.
Some losses remain losses in this life.
Some wombs remain empty.
Some marriages are not restored.
Some prodigals take years to return, and some situations remain painfully unresolved.
The Gospel is not "follow God and eventually He will give you your preferred ending."
The Gospel is infinitely greater.
God has given us His Son.
Jesus entered our broken world, bore sin at the cross, died in the place of sinners, and rose again.
Our deepest problem was never merely that life hurts.
Our deepest problem is sin separating humanity from a holy God.
And our greatest hope is not that every circumstance becomes comfortable.
Our greatest hope is Christ.
At the cross, Jesus carried what we could never carry away ourselves.
Sin.
Guilt.
Condemnation.
Our rebellion against God.
And because He rose from the dead, grace has the final word for everyone who belongs to Him.
That is why family pain does not have to become your identity.
What your father said is not your identity.
What your mother failed to give you is not your identity.
What your sibling did is not your identity.
What your former spouse called you is not your identity.
What happened behind the closed doors of your childhood home is not your identity.
Even what you yourself have done is not beyond the reach of Christ's redeeming grace when you repent and come to Him.
Maybe your family story contains scandal.
Betrayal.
Favoritism.
Jealousy.
Abandonment.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Infidelity.
Years of silence.
Manipulation.
Cruel words.
Funerals where relatives still refused to speak.
Christmas dinners where everyone pretended.
Church photographs where everybody smiled.
Secrets nobody mentions.
Jesus is not intimidated by messy family histories.
Look at the genealogy through which He entered the world.
Scripture does not airbrush human brokenness before announcing the Savior.
God brings redemption into real human history.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by promising every relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
But by refusing to allow sin, shame, bitterness, or another person's cruelty to have ultimate authority over the person Christ redeems.
And perhaps the most important question now is not:
"Who was your Peninnah?"
You probably already know.
The harder question may be:
"What are you going to do with the wound?"
Will you rehearse it until it becomes your personality?
Will you retaliate?
Will you become cruel because someone was cruel to you?
Will you spend another decade waiting for an apology before allowing yourself to live?
Or will you pour your soul before the Lord?
Forgiveness does not mean pretending abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean refusing wise boundaries.
It does not mean immediately trusting an unsafe person.
It does not erase justice or accountability.
Christian forgiveness means relinquishing personal vengeance into God's hands and refusing to let hatred become your master.
Sometimes reconciliation becomes possible.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
But bitterness must never become your god.
Jesus did not rescue you so the person who wounded you could continue living rent-free inside your soul.
And if, while reading this, the Holy Spirit has shown you that you have been the one doing the wounding...
do not hide behind shame.
Repent.
There is grace for Peninnah-shaped hearts too.
That may be one of the most beautiful truths in Christianity.
The Gospel is not merely good news for victims who need healing.
It is good news for guilty people who need forgiveness.
At the cross, there is mercy for the person who cried...
and mercy for the person who caused tears when that sinner genuinely repents and trusts Christ.
Maybe you need to apologize.
Maybe you need to stop comparing your children.
Maybe you need to call your sister.
Maybe you need to confess what jealousy has been turning you into.
Maybe you need to forgive without waiting for the other person to become worthy of forgiveness.
Maybe tonight you simply need to shut the door, kneel beside your bed, and finally pour out the sentence you have been afraid to say to God.
Whatever it is...
do not waste your pain by letting it teach you cruelty.
Let it drive you toward Christ.
You do not owe strangers your private story. But sometimes three honest words are enough to tell another wounded believer, "You're not the only one still fighting."
And if you know somebody who has been carrying family pain quietly, send this to them.
Not as an accusation.
As a hand on their shoulder.

Invite your family, your Christian friends, the exhausted believer, the person drifting from God, the seeker, and even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say to broken families. Let them encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

If you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting Gospel-centered work, don't reduce that desire merely to words. Pray. Live the Gospel. Serve your local church. Give generously where God leads. Share biblical truth.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
No ministry replaces Him.
No merchandise makes you faithful.
No Facebook page can forgive your sins.
Christ alone saves.
Turn from sin. Trust Him. Follow Him.
And when your family story becomes painful again, remember Hannah.
Remember the woman who walked toward worship while carrying a wound.
Remember the tears.
Remember the silent moving lips.
Remember the soul poured out before God.
Remember that the chapter that made Hannah weep was not the final chapter God was writing.
And perhaps that is what somebody desperately needed to hear tonight.
The person who wounded you may have touched a chapter of your story—but only Jesus Christ has the authority to write its ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE IS THE ONE THAT CAN QUOTE THE BIBLE
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE IS THE ONE THAT CAN QUOTE THE BIBLE
When Scripture becomes a shield for what we secretly refuse to surrender, we are no longer letting the Word correct us—we are trying to make the Word agree with us.
There is a frightening moment in the Bible that many Christians read too quickly.
The devil quotes Scripture.
Not an atheist.
Not a pagan philosopher.
Not someone standing outside the faith mocking the Bible.
Satan himself.
Jesus has been fasting in the wilderness. He is hungry. He is physically weakened. Then the tempter comes.
First, Satan challenges Jesus to turn stones into bread. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy.
Then something chilling happens.
The devil changes tactics.
If Jesus is going to answer with Scripture...
Satan will use Scripture too.
He takes Jesus to the holy city, sets Him on the pinnacle of the temple, and essentially says:
If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down.
Then he quotes Psalm 91.
In the Greek text of Matthew 4:6, the temptation includes these words:
γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι...
gegraptai gar hoti...
“For it is written...”
Think about that.
“It is written.”
Those are sacred-sounding words.
Those are words you would expect from a preacher.
Those are words that sound biblical.
And they came from the mouth of the tempter.
That should disturb every person who has ever opened a Bible.
Because apparently, quoting Scripture does not automatically mean someone is submitting to Scripture.
You can have a verse in your mouth while rebellion is still hiding in your heart.
You can quote something that is completely true and still use it in a completely false way.
You can know where the verse is located.
You can memorize it.
Post it.
Preach it.
Build an argument around it.
Turn it into a caption.
Put it over a beautiful photograph.
Win an argument with it.
And still completely miss what God is saying.
That is why one of the most dangerous questions you can ask is not merely:
“Can I find a Bible verse supporting what I believe?”
A more searching question is:
“If Scripture contradicts what I desperately want to believe, will I surrender?”
Because sometimes we do not approach the Bible looking for truth.
Sometimes we approach it looking for permission.
And those are not the same thing.
Sometimes we have already decided what we want.
We already know the relationship we refuse to leave.
The resentment we refuse to release.
The behavior we refuse to confront.
The doctrine we desperately want to be true.
The lifestyle we do not want questioned.
The political or cultural position we want baptized.
The money we want to keep.
The person we want condemned.
The sin we want renamed.
The compromise we want excused.
Then we open Scripture—not asking God to transform us, but searching for a sentence we can recruit to defend the person we have already decided to remain.
We do not always say that out loud.
We can make it sound spiritual.
“I prayed about it.”
“I have peace about it.”
“God knows my heart.”
“Jesus said not to judge.”
“We're under grace.”
“God wants me happy.”
“This verse speaks to me differently.”
And sometimes there may be legitimate truths buried inside those statements.
But a true sentence can become spiritually destructive when it is ripped from its biblical context and made to carry a meaning God never gave it.
That is exactly why the wilderness temptation matters.
Satan did not invent Psalm 91.
The words were Scripture.
The manipulation was in how Scripture was being used.
And Jesus did not respond by denying Psalm 91.
He answered Scripture with Scripture, correctly understood.
Matthew 4:7 records Jesus saying:
Πάλιν γέγραπται· Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου.
Palin gegraptai: Ouk ekpeiraseis Kyrion ton Theon sou.
“Again, it is written: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”
Jesus draws from Deuteronomy 6:16.
In other words, one biblical passage cannot legitimately be interpreted in a way that contradicts what God has revealed elsewhere.
Scripture is not a collection of inspirational fragments waiting for us to assign them whatever meaning makes us comfortable.
It is revelation that must be heard in context.
That distinction can expose us.
Because twisting Scripture is not merely something cult leaders, false teachers, televangelists, politicians, influencers, or people from “that other denomination” can do.
We can do it too.
I can.
You can.
Anyone can.
And sometimes the person we are most determined to deceive is the one staring back from the mirror.
We know how to condemn sins that do not tempt us.
We know how to find verses about somebody else's pride while ignoring our own.
We know how to preach forgiveness when we need forgiveness and justice when someone has wounded us.
We know how to speak about grace when consequences reach our doorstep and holiness when another person's failure becomes public.
We can become incredibly sophisticated attorneys defending ourselves before God.
Verse after verse.
Argument after argument.
Explanation after explanation.
But God did not give us Scripture so that we could win our case against Him.
He gave us His Word so that truth could expose us, lead us to Christ, renew our minds, correct our paths, and teach us how to live as people redeemed by grace.
There is an uncomfortable prayer hidden inside real Bible reading:
“Lord, prove me wrong wherever I am wrong.”
That prayer costs something.
Because we usually enjoy Scripture when Scripture confirms us.
But discipleship begins to hurt when Scripture confronts us.
The writer of Hebrews describes the Word of God as ζῶν... καὶ ἐνεργής—zōn kai energēs—“living and active” (Hebrews 4:12).
Then comes the image of penetration and exposure.
The Word reaches beneath appearances.
Beneath excuses.
Beneath religious performance.
Beneath the polished explanation we have repeated so many times that even we have started believing it.
Hebrews 4:13 then brings us before the God to whom we must give account.
That is what makes Scripture dangerous to hypocrisy.
The Bible does not exist merely for us to examine it.
Eventually...
it examines us.
That is why Paul told Timothy that all Scripture is θεόπνευστος—theopneustos—“God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16).
And notice what God-breathed Scripture does.
It teaches.
It reproves.
It corrects.
It trains in righteousness.
Correction is part of the gift.
We often want inspiration without correction.
Comfort without repentance.
Promises without commands.
Grace without transformation.
A Savior without a Lord.
But biblical grace never needed sin to become harmless in order for sinners to become loved.
That is part of what makes the Gospel breathtaking.
God does not have to pretend darkness is light to rescue people from darkness.
He does not have to rename rebellion to offer mercy to rebels.
He does not have to distort holiness to welcome sinners home.
At the cross, both realities stand together with terrifying beauty:
Sin is more serious than we wanted to admit, and God's grace is greater than we dared to believe.
Look at Jesus.
He does not say your sin was imaginary.
He bears sin.
He does not say guilt does not matter.
He pays the debt sinners could never pay for themselves.
He does not tell humanity to save itself through better arguments, better behavior, religious performance, or carefully selected Bible verses.
He gives Himself.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that God finally decided sin did not matter.
The scandal is that the Holy One loved sinners enough that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
συνίστησιν δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην εἰς ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός...
God demonstrates His own love toward us...
And how?
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν...
“while we were still sinners...”
Christ died for us.
Not after we successfully rewrote our story.
Not after we made our sins sound respectable.
Not after we found enough verses to silence conviction.
Christ came for sinners.
This is where Scripture twisting becomes especially tragic.
When we manipulate God's Word to make ourselves feel less guilty, we may think we are protecting ourselves from condemnation.
But we can actually be hiding from the very grace that could set us free.
Because you cannot confess what you insist on calling righteous.
You cannot repent of what you refuse to acknowledge.
You cannot bring something into the light while spending your energy proving that it belongs in the darkness.
And you do not need to manipulate Scripture to make Jesus love you.
Read that again.
You do not need to manipulate Scripture to make Jesus love you.
You do not have to prove that your sin was never sinful before you are allowed to approach the cross.
That is not Christianity.
The invitation of the Gospel is far more astonishing:
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Confess.
Repent.
Trust Christ.
Receive mercy.
Be transformed.
The apostle John writes:
ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν...
ean homologōmen tas hamartias hēmōn...
“If we confess our sins...” (1 John 1:9).
The verb translated “confess” comes from ὁμολογέω — homologeō, carrying the sense of acknowledging or confessing.
Christian confession is not negotiating with God until He adopts our preferred definition of righteousness.
It is coming into agreement with the truth.
No spin.
No carefully cropped verses.
No theological camouflage.
No “but everybody does it.”
No “at least I'm not as bad as...”
No hiding behind another person's hypocrisy.
Just truth.
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“This is what I've become.”
“This is what I've been defending.”
“This is what I've been hiding.”
“This is what I keep returning to.”
“This is what I wanted Your Word to approve.”
“Have mercy on me.”
And this is where the story changes.
Because the person who comes to Christ in repentance does not encounter a Savior reluctantly standing with crossed arms.
Jesus came precisely to save sinners.
The cross is where our excuses can finally die because our hope no longer depends upon our excuses surviving.
You can stop defending yourself when Christ becomes your hope.
You can finally admit, “I was wrong.”
You can finally say, “That verse did not mean what I wanted it to mean.”
You can finally confess, “I wasn't searching for God's will. I was searching for God's signature underneath mine.”
And strangely...
that humiliating moment can become the beginning of freedom.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
Maybe this article has brought a particular issue to mind.
Not someone else's.
Yours.
Maybe there is something you have been defending for years.
Maybe you have collected arguments around it.
Maybe you follow teachers who never challenge it.
Maybe you immediately become angry when someone brings up the passages you avoid.
Maybe somewhere underneath all the theology, debates, posts, podcasts, and explanations...
you already know.
You are tired.
Tired of defending it.
Tired of hiding it.
Tired of rearranging Scripture around it.
Tired of trying to make conviction disappear.
Then hear this carefully.
Conviction that drives you toward Christ is not your enemy.
There is a difference between hopeless condemnation and the gracious exposure that calls a sinner home.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
But that glorious promise was never permission to make peace with sin.
Paul had already asked in Romans 6:1–2 whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
His response is emphatic:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
Grace does not teach us how to become comfortable prisoners.
Grace opens the prison door.
Titus 2:11–12 says God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace changes us.
Grace brings us home.
And maybe the greatest evidence that you are beginning to understand grace is that you no longer need to call darkness light before you believe God can forgive you.
You can finally tell the truth.
That is freedom.
So the next time you open your Bible, resist the temptation to ask only:
“What verse supports me?”
Ask:
“Lord Jesus, what is true?”
“What did this passage mean in its context?”
“What does the rest of Scripture reveal?”
“Am I reading this to hear You, or am I searching for ammunition?”
“Is there something I desperately need this verse to permit?”
“Would I still accept this interpretation if it cost me something I wanted?”
“Am I willing to obey if the answer is no?”
Those questions can hurt.
But some wounds are surgical.
Sometimes grace has to cut away the lie we have been protecting before healing reaches what has been buried underneath it.
And please do not use this message as another weapon.
Do not finish reading and immediately think:
“I know exactly who needs this.”
Maybe they do.
But before sending it to them...
sit with it yourself.
Let Scripture search you.
Let it search me.
Psalm 139 ends with one of the most dangerous prayers a believer can sincerely pray.
In Hebrew:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
ḥoqreni El, veda levavi.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
Then:
וּרְאֵה אִם־דֶּרֶךְ־עֹצֶב בִּי
“See if there is any grievous way in me...”
And lead me in the everlasting way.
Not:
“Search my enemies.”
Not:
“Expose my denomination's enemies.”
Not:
“Prove that everybody arguing with me is wrong.”
Search me.
That prayer changes everything.
Because Christianity was never meant to be the art of becoming better at defending ourselves.
It is the miracle of surrendering ourselves to Christ.
Maybe your scandal is real.
Maybe the thing you have hidden would embarrass you if people knew.
Maybe you distorted Scripture because admitting the truth felt unbearable.
Maybe religion became camouflage.
But Jesus Christ is still in the business of rewriting stories.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church had serious moral disorder.
The New Testament does not sanitize human failure.
And yet grace kept moving.
Not grace that pretended nothing happened.
Grace that redeemed people through Jesus Christ.
That is not permission to remain in the scandal.
It is the proclamation that the scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Jesus does.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain the details publicly. But you can make one small declaration of surrender.
“Jesus, search me.”
Let those words become more than engagement beneath an article.
Let them become a prayer.

Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership, but it is not a test of whether you truly glorify God; Scripture calls believers to glorify God with the whole of life.
Open your Bible without demanding that it agree with you.
Come before Jesus without your defense.
Bring Him the secret.
The compromise.
The stubborn belief.
The carefully protected sin.
The shame.
The scandal.
And whisper the prayer that our pride fears but our souls desperately need:
“Jesus... if I am wrong, correct me. If I am hiding, expose me. If I have twisted Your Word to protect what You are asking me to surrender, forgive me. Teach me Your truth. Lead me home.”
Because perhaps the greatest danger is not discovering that you misunderstood a verse.
Perhaps the greatest danger is spending your whole life using the Bible to protect yourself from the God who gave it to you.
And perhaps one of the greatest mercies is the moment Jesus loves you enough to tear your favorite excuse apart...
only for you to discover that underneath it was not rejection waiting for you.
It was a cross.
An empty tomb.
And a Savior calling you out of hiding.
You never needed Jesus to rewrite the truth—you needed Jesus to rewrite you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re Afraid of Dying—but Maybe What Terrifies You Most Is Finally Losing Control
paragraphs: You’re Afraid of Dying—but Maybe What Terrifies You Most Is Finally Losing Control

You can control the appointment. The medication. The retirement account. The locks on the door. The food you eat. The people you call. But eventually every human being reaches a door that cannot be negotiated with—and Hebrews says Jesus Christ walked through that door first so fear would no longer have to own you.
There is a thought most of us know how to push away.
Until 2:13 in the morning.
Until the doctor says, “We found something.”
Until someone your age dies.
Until you stand beside a hospital bed watching a chest rise... fall... rise... fall...
Until you attend the funeral of someone who was laughing in photographs only weeks before.
Until your parents begin looking older.
Until your children start asking questions about what happens when people die.
Until you notice that the face in the mirror is changing too.
Then suddenly the thought you have spent years keeping outside gets through the door.
One day, I am going to die.
And perhaps what makes that sentence so terrifying is not merely death itself.
Perhaps it is the unbearable realization that, when that moment comes, you will finally encounter something you cannot control.
We spend enormous portions of our lives trying to manage uncertainty.
Calendars.
Insurance.
Savings.
Checkups.
Security systems.
Passwords.
Backup plans.
Five-year plans.

We monitor our bodies. We make plans for tomorrow. We worry about our children. We try to protect what we love. None of those things are inherently wrong. Scripture does not condemn wisdom, stewardship, preparation, or legitimate care for life.
But underneath good preparation can sometimes hide another hunger.
If I can control enough, perhaps nothing can truly hurt me.
Then death whispers the sentence human pride hates hearing:
You are not God.
You cannot negotiate another century into your lungs.
You cannot command your heart to beat forever.
You cannot accumulate enough money to purchase immortality.

You cannot become successful enough, attractive enough, careful enough, powerful enough, religious enough, or admired enough to make your body exempt from the sentence that has followed humanity since Eden.
And this is precisely where Christianity refuses to offer us sentimental comfort.
The Gospel does not tell us death is imaginary.
It tells us death has been confronted.
Hebrews 2:14–15 says of Jesus:

“Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.”
Listen closely to the language.
The New Testament was written here in Greek, and the words are startling:
“ἵνα διὰ τοῦ θανάτου καταργήσῃ... καὶ ἀπαλλάξῃ τούτους... φόβῳ θανάτου... δουλείας.”
At the heart of the passage are words about death, liberation, fear, and slavery.
Thanatos — θάνατος — death.
Phobos — φόβος — fear.
Douleia — δουλεία — slavery or bondage.
And then there is that powerful verb associated with what Christ accomplished: katargeō — καταργέω.
