You can change your surroundings without immediately changing every instinct of your heart.
And Genesis 19 refuses to let us pretend otherwise.

The chapter begins with judgment falling upon Sodom and Gomorrah. Lot and his family are urged out of the doomed city. His wife looks back and dies. Eventually Lot leaves Zoar and lives in a cave in the mountains with his two daughters.
Think about the emotional wreckage surrounding that cave.
Their home was gone.
Their mother was gone.
The cities they knew had been destroyed.
Their future appeared uncertain.
And the daughters began interpreting reality through fear.
The older daughter said to the younger:
“Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth.”
The Hebrew expression behind “there is not a man” is:
אֵין אִישׁ
’ên ’îš — “there is no man.”

But taken in context, their conclusion should not be read as an objective statement that literally every man on the planet had died. Lot and his daughters had recently been in Zoar. The narrative itself gives us no reason to believe humanity had disappeared.
Their perception had narrowed.
Their world had become a cave.
And fear has a terrifying ability to make a cave feel like the entire universe.
That is still happening.
“I’ll always be alone.”
“Nobody will ever love me.”
“I’ll never recover.”
“There is no other way.”
“My marriage can never heal.”
“My child will never come back.”
“God cannot possibly redeem this.”
Fear loves absolute language.
Never.
Nobody.
Nothing.
Impossible.
Finished.
And when fear convinces you that God has no future for you, sin begins offering counterfeit futures.
The daughters decided they needed to preserve their family line.
Then came the plan:
“Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father.”
The Hebrew phrase translated “preserve seed” is:
וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע
uneḥayyeh me’avinu zera‘
The idea is to preserve or keep offspring alive through their father.
Their desired outcome may have been survival.
Their method was profoundly wrong.
That distinction matters.
The Bible repeatedly shows human beings attempting to accomplish something they consider necessary through methods God never authorized.
A desperate motive does not sanctify a sinful method.
Fear does not transform evil into righteousness.
Trauma can help us understand why people make destructive choices without making those choices good.
And Scripture does something remarkably honest here.
It tells us what happened without telling us to imitate it.
The Bible is sometimes misunderstood precisely because readers assume that whatever Scripture records, Scripture recommends.
It does not.
The Bible contains murder, adultery, betrayal, incest, drunkenness, exploitation, cowardice, idolatry, deception, and horrifying failures because it is telling the truth about humanity.
God does not airbrush the family album.
And thank God He does not.
Because if Scripture were merely a collection of polished saints behaving beautifully, people like us would eventually wonder whether there was room inside it for our families.
Our secrets.
Our failures.
Our shame.
But Scripture opens closets.
It enters caves.
It walks into dysfunctional homes.
It exposes drunken fathers, frightened daughters, adulterous kings, lying patriarchs, violent brothers, compromised disciples, religious hypocrites, prostitutes, persecutors, thieves, and sinners.
Not because God celebrates the darkness.
Because redemption means nothing if we refuse to admit how dark darkness actually is.
The daughters made Lot drunk.
Then the older daughter lay with him.
Genesis emphasizes that Lot “did not know when she lay down or when she arose.”
The following night, they repeated the plan with the younger daughter.
Again Lot became intoxicated.
Again the text says he did not know when she lay down or arose.
We should be careful here.

The narrative portrays the daughters as deliberately engineering these encounters while Lot is severely intoxicated and unaware of what is occurring. That makes the episode not merely sexually immoral but exploitative.
Yet Lot should not be transformed into an innocent spiritual hero either.
His story has been moving through compromise for years.
Earlier in Genesis, Lot chose the fertile Jordan plain and pitched his tents near Sodom.
Then Genesis 14 finds him living in Sodom.
By Genesis 19, Lot is sitting at Sodom’s gate.
Near Sodom became in Sodom.
In Sodom became established in Sodom.
That progression should haunt us.
Most spiritual catastrophes do not begin with someone waking up and deciding:
“Today I will destroy my life.”
They begin with proximity.
One compromise.
One rationalization.
One boundary moved six inches.
One secret nobody supposedly needs to know.
One more drink.
One more message.
One more private conversation.
One more night.
One more excuse.
Until something that once horrified you barely troubles you anymore.
That is why Scripture warns:
“Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.”
Proverbs 20:1.
And the New Testament gives believers an entirely different command:
“Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit.”
Ephesians 5:18.
The Greek contrasts intoxication with another controlling influence.
καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ
kai mē methyskesthe oinō
“Do not become drunk with wine.”
Instead:
πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι
plērousthe en pneumati
“Be filled with the Spirit.”
That contrast reaches far beyond alcohol.
Something will influence the direction of your life.
Something will speak loudly when you are afraid.
Something will shape what you do with loneliness.
Something will tell you where to run when your heart hurts.
And whatever repeatedly becomes your refuge can eventually become your master.
For some people it is alcohol.
For others pornography.
Attention.
Food.
Money.
Work.
Relationships.
Approval.
Anger.
Scrolling until two in the morning because silence would force you to feel something you have spent years avoiding.
Some caves have Wi-Fi.
They are still caves.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that means.
You love Jesus.
But there is something you keep returning to when life becomes unbearable.
Nobody at church knows.
Your family may not know.
Your friends see the edited version of you.
But Christ sees the exhausted person underneath it.
And the Gospel does not begin by asking you to become better at hiding.
It asks you to come into the light.
The children born from those two nights were named Moab and Ben-ammi.
Genesis identifies them as ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.
And here the story could have remained merely tragic.
Except the Bible keeps going.
Generations pass.
Then another woman appears.
A Moabite woman.
Her name is Ruth.
Yes.
Ruth.
The same Ruth who tells Naomi:
“Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.”
Ruth 1:16.
Do not rush past what Scripture has just done.
Genesis tells us Moab's scandalous beginning.
The book of Ruth introduces us to a faithful Moabite woman who turns to the God of Israel.
Ruth eventually marries Boaz.
They have Obed.
Obed fathers Jesse.
Jesse fathers David.
And Matthew begins the New Testament by tracing the royal genealogy forward until we arrive at Jesus Christ.
Matthew explicitly includes Ruth in that genealogy.
Do you see why grace is so astonishing?
God does not call the cave good.
He does not rename sin righteousness.
He does not pretend Genesis 19 never happened.
Instead, across generations, God demonstrates something far greater:
Human sin does not possess the authority to cancel God's redemptive purposes.
Moab's beginning was scandalous.
But scandal did not get the final sentence.
Grace kept writing.
And eventually, within the unfolding biblical story, a woman from Moab appears in the messianic genealogy.
Ruth did not become worthy because her ancestry suddenly became clean.
She found refuge under the wings of Israel's God.
And this is where the story stops being about somebody else's dysfunctional family.
Because you have a genealogy too.
Maybe nobody knows everything in yours.
Alcoholism.
Adultery.
Abuse.
Abandonment.
Addiction.
Divorce.
Infidelity.
Violence.
Secrets.
A father nobody talks about.
A mother whose wounds became your wounds.
A childhood you survived but never really processed.
Maybe you inherited patterns you swore you would never repeat—and then one day heard yourself speaking exactly like the person who hurt you.
And you wondered:
“Is this all I am?”
No.
Your family history may explain part of your story.
It does not have to become your destiny.
Jesus Christ does not merely renovate respectable people.
He redeems sinners.
The Gospel is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin matters so profoundly that redemption required the blood of Christ.
Jesus carried our sins in His body on the tree.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not, “Hide your scandal better.”
It is:
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.

The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετάνοια (metanoia), with the related verb μετανοέω (metanoeō). Biblical repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because consequences arrived. It is a turning of heart and life toward God.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel temporarily inspirational.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Reconcile.
Transform.
That means grace never requires you to pretend the cave was beautiful.
Grace allows you to finally tell the truth about the cave because you have discovered Someone greater than it.
Some of you have spent years thinking:
“If people knew what happened to me, they would look at me differently.”
Maybe they would.
Jesus already knows.
“If people knew what I did…”
Jesus already knows.
“If God saw the thoughts I fight…”
He does.
“If He knew how many times I promised I would stop…”
He was there every time.
And still the crucified and risen Christ calls sinners to Himself.
Not so we can continue comfortably in darkness.
So we can finally leave it.
That is grace.
Grace does not say sin was harmless.
Grace says sin does not have to have you anymore.
Grace does not say repentance is unnecessary.
Grace makes repentance possible because there is somewhere to return.
Grace does not erase justice.
At Calvary, we discover how seriously God takes both sin and salvation.
Maybe your cave is not sexual sin.
Maybe your cave is resentment.
You replay the betrayal every night.
Maybe it is pride.
Nobody can correct you anymore.
Maybe it is secret pornography.
You delete the history but cannot delete what it is doing to your soul.
Maybe it is alcohol.
You keep calling it relaxation even though somewhere inside you know you have started needing it.
Maybe it is bitterness toward God.
You still sing worship songs, but privately you are furious with Him.
Maybe it is religious performance.
You know how to sound Christian while your prayer life is almost dead.
Then hear this carefully:
Jesus is not standing outside your cave waiting to humiliate you.
He is calling you out of darkness.
The One calling you is the same Savior who ate with sinners, touched the unclean, restored failures, forgave the repentant, and willingly went to the cross.
But He loves you too much to bless the darkness destroying you.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent where repentance is necessary.
Seek help where help is necessary.
Make the phone call.
Tell the truth.
Break access to what repeatedly pulls you back.
Ask mature believers to walk with you.
And when your past whispers, “Look where you came from,” remember Ruth.
When shame whispers, “Your family is too broken,” remember Ruth.
When the enemy whispers, “Nothing clean can ever come from something this ugly,” remember Ruth.
And then look beyond Ruth.
Look at Jesus.
Because Ruth is not the Savior of this story.
Jesus is.
Ruth points forward into a genealogy that ultimately announces the arrival of Christ.
And Christ is where every Christian testimony finally has to land.
Not:
“Look how strong I became.”
But:
“Look what Jesus did with someone who could not save himself.”
Maybe this article exposed something you have kept buried.
Talk to God.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
If words are difficult, begin simply:
“Jesus, have mercy on me. Bring me into the light.”
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need the light is one small way of refusing to keep pretending.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars do not get the final word.
Not as a badge proving how spiritual you are.
There may come a night when shame starts talking again, and you need to remember that Genesis did not end at the cave.
And stay connected with Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Scripture calls believers to glorify God with their lives, their obedience, their love, their generosity, and the proclamation of Christ.
Come to Christ.
Because merchandise cannot redeem you.
A ministry cannot redeem you.
A pastor cannot redeem you.
A church building cannot redeem you.
Jesus Christ can.
Two daughters.
Two nights.
Too much wine.
Their own father.
A cave filled with consequences.
A family line carrying a scandal nobody would choose as its beginning.
Then generations later…
Ruth.
Boaz.
Obed.
Jesse.
David.
And eventually, in the messianic genealogy recorded by Matthew:
Jesus Christ.
That does not make what happened in the cave good.
It makes grace breathtaking.
God did not need to rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
He demonstrated His sovereignty by writing redemption through history despite human sin.
Maybe that is what you needed tonight.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But yesterday does not get to be your god.
Your family's worst chapter does not outrank Jesus.
Your greatest failure does not outrank Jesus.
Your deepest wound does not outrank Jesus.
Your shame does not outrank Jesus.
Your cave does not outrank Jesus.
Repentance can begin today.
Forgiveness can be received today.
A different pattern can begin today.
And through Christ, the sentence you thought ended with your scandal may yet become a testimony of His grace.
The cave may explain where the wound began—but Jesus still decides where redemption leads.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAUL WENT LOOKING FOR MISSING DONKEYS—AND CAME HOME ANOINTED AS ISRAEL’S KING
paragraphs:
SAUL WENT LOOKING FOR MISSING DONKEYS—AND CAME HOME ANOINTED AS ISRAEL’S KING
He thought he was searching for something his father had lost. He had no idea God was using the loss to lead him toward a calling he never went looking for.
Imagine leaving home in the morning looking for donkeys…
…and returning with the knowledge that you have been chosen to become king.
Not promoted.
Not noticed by an influential man.
Not handed a better job.
Anointed king of Israel.

That sounds almost absurd until you realize how often God has used ordinary frustrations, inconvenient detours, unanswered questions, closed doors, and seemingly meaningless losses to move people into places they never would have entered voluntarily.
And maybe that is why Saul’s story in 1 Samuel 9–10 feels strangely personal.
Because some of us are still staring at the missing donkeys.
We are frustrated about what disappeared.
Confused about what changed.
Exhausted from searching.
Wondering why God allowed something that seemed stable to suddenly become uncertain.
We keep asking, “Where did it go?”
While God may be doing something much deeper than returning what was lost.
The story begins without trumpets.
There is no throne.
No palace.
No royal procession.
There are missing animals.
Kish, Saul’s father, had lost some donkeys, and he told his son to take a servant and go search for them.
So Saul went.
That is important.
Before Saul ever carried the title of king, Scripture shows him carrying out an ordinary responsibility for his father.
He did not wake up chasing greatness.
He went looking for donkeys.
Through the hill country of Ephraim.
Through Shalishah.
Through Shaalim.
Through the territory of Benjamin.
Again and again…
nothing.
Imagine the frustration.
Another hill.
Another road.
Another village.
Another disappointment.
No donkeys.
Eventually Saul became concerned that his father would stop worrying about the animals and start worrying about him.
From Saul’s perspective, the mission was failing.
But from heaven’s perspective, the journey was approaching its appointed destination.
That distinction can change the way you understand some of the most confusing seasons of your life.
Something can look unsuccessful from where you are standing while still being used within the providence of God.
Saul could not see what the reader is allowed to see.
Before Saul arrives, God has already spoken to Samuel.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 9:15 uses an intimate expression:
וַיהוָה גָּלָה אֶת־אֹזֶן שְׁמוּאֵל
VaYHWH galah et-ozen Shemu’el.
Literally, the LORD had “uncovered Samuel’s ear.”
In other words, God privately revealed to Samuel what was about to happen.
And what God told Samuel is astonishing.
Approximately a day before Saul arrived, the LORD told Samuel that a man from Benjamin would come to him and that Samuel was to anoint him as ruler over Israel.
Saul was searching.
Samuel was expecting.
Saul saw missing donkeys.
Samuel had received revelation.
Saul thought he was trying to solve a family problem.
God was moving the story toward an anointing.
Do not misunderstand this passage.
It does not teach that every inconvenience means God is secretly preparing you for fame, promotion, wealth, leadership, or some spectacular earthly breakthrough.
That is not the Gospel.
Sometimes a lost thing is simply lost.
Sometimes suffering remains painful.
Sometimes what disappears does not come back.
And Saul’s later life itself warns us against turning his anointing into a simplistic prosperity slogan.
But 1 Samuel 9 does show something beautiful about divine providence:
God can accomplish purposes people cannot yet see through circumstances that appear painfully ordinary.
That matters when your life does not make sense.
Because perhaps you have had your own “missing donkeys.”
The relationship you thought would last.
The opportunity you were sure was yours.
The plan that collapsed.
The prayer that did not unfold the way you expected.
The season that has gone on longer than you imagined.
The door that closed without explanation.
The thing you have been desperately trying to recover.
And you keep thinking:
“If I could just get this back, everything would be okay.”
Saul probably wanted something similarly simple.
Find the animals.
Return home.
Mission accomplished.
But then his servant suggested they visit the man of God.
One apparently small suggestion changed the direction of the journey.
And when Saul finally met Samuel, Samuel said something Saul could never have expected.
Do not worry about the donkeys.
They had been found.
Think about that.
The problem Saul had been chasing was already being resolved while Saul was being led toward something he did not know existed.
Then Samuel spoke words that must have stopped him cold.
He pointed toward Saul and his father’s household in connection with “all the desire of Israel.”
Saul’s response reveals how unlikely this must have sounded to him.
He essentially asked:
Why me?
He was from Benjamin—the smallest tribe of Israel—and from a comparatively insignificant family within Benjamin.
Whether Saul’s words reflected genuine humility, social convention, or something more complicated, the shock in the scene is unmistakable.
He came asking about donkeys.
Samuel began speaking about Israel.
He came carrying the concerns of his father’s house.
Suddenly he was being confronted with a calling involving an entire nation.
Then Samuel took a flask of oil.
And poured it over Saul’s head.
The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 10:1 says:
וַיִּקַּח שְׁמוּאֵל אֶת־פַּךְ הַשֶּׁמֶן וַיִּצֹק עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ
Vayyiqqach Shemu’el et-pakh hashemen, vayitzok al-rosho.
Samuel took the flask of oil…
and poured it upon Saul’s head.
The ordinary search had arrived at an extraordinary moment.
Oil running down his head.
Samuel kissing him.
Words of divine appointment ringing in his ears.
The man who had walked into the region looking for his father’s animals was being anointed as ruler over the LORD’s inheritance.
And then God gave him confirming signs.
He would meet men who would tell him the donkeys had been found.
He would encounter others carrying goats, bread, and wine.
He would meet a company of prophets.
And something would happen inside Saul himself.
One of the most striking statements appears in 1 Samuel 10:6:
וְצָלְחָה עָלֶיךָ רוּחַ יְהוָה
Vetzalchah alekha Ruach YHWH.
“The Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you.”
Samuel continued:
וְנֶהְפַּכְתָּ לְאִישׁ אַחֵר
Venehpákhta le’ish acher.
“You shall be turned into another man.”
And shortly afterward Scripture says:
וַיַּהֲפָךְ־לוֹ אֱלֹהִים לֵב אַחֵר
Vayyahafoḵ-lo Elohim lev acher.
“God changed for him another heart,” or more naturally, “God gave him another heart.”
There is something breathtaking about that moment.
But there is also something sobering about it.
Because if you know the rest of Saul’s story, you know that an extraordinary beginning did not guarantee an extraordinary ending.
Saul was genuinely chosen.
Genuinely anointed.
Genuinely empowered for the role God had given him.
And yet Saul would later disobey.
He would become increasingly consumed with preserving his position.
Fear would distort him.
Jealousy would poison him.
David would become a threat in Saul’s eyes.
The man who once seemed small in his own estimation would eventually fight desperately to hold onto a throne God had told him he would lose.
And this is where the story stops being merely inspirational.
This is where it becomes a warning.
Because finding your calling is not the same thing as faithfully walking with God.
Being used by God is not permission to stop obeying God.
Yesterday’s anointing cannot become tomorrow’s excuse for rebellion.
A powerful beginning cannot substitute for continuing faithfulness.
You can receive responsibility and still mishandle it.
You can experience the mercy of God and still need daily surrender.
You can be surrounded by religious activity while your heart quietly begins protecting an idol.
For Saul, eventually, the throne became something he was desperate to preserve.
And before we condemn him too quickly, we should ask what throne we are protecting.
Reputation?
Approval?
Control?
Money?
Influence?
A relationship?
An image?
A ministry?
The need to always appear strong?
What do you become defensive about when obedience to God threatens it?
That question hurts.
It is supposed to.
Because Scripture was not given merely so we could stand safely outside its stories and criticize everyone who failed.
The Word exposes us.
Saul’s tragedy whispers a warning across the centuries:
You can be close to holy things while still resisting the Holy One.
You can know that God has called you to obedience and still negotiate with Him.
You can begin with humility and slowly become addicted to protecting yourself.
And perhaps the saddest irony is that Saul went looking for animals that belonged to his father…
then spent years trying to hold onto a kingdom that ultimately belonged to God.
That is what sin does.
It convinces us to clutch what was never truly ours.
But this story belongs inside a much larger biblical story.
Because Saul was not Israel’s ultimate king.
Neither was David.
Israel’s kings, even the greatest of them, pointed beyond themselves toward the need for a King who would not collapse beneath the weight of human sin.
And eventually another King came.
Jesus Christ.
He did not need Samuel’s flask of oil to establish His identity.
He is the Messiah—the Christ.
Both titles carry the idea of the Anointed One.
The Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ, mashiach.
The Greek Χριστός, Christos.
Jesus is the true and greater King.
Saul received a kingdom and eventually grasped to preserve it.
Jesus possessed divine glory and humbled Himself.
Saul’s fear drove him toward destructive self-preservation.
Jesus willingly walked toward the cross.
Saul pursued David, seeking his death.
Jesus pursued sinners knowing His pursuit would lead to His own death.
Saul's kingdom fractured.
Christ’s kingdom will never end.
And here is where your story enters the Gospel.
You may have come here because the title sounded strange.
Missing donkeys.
A future king.
An unbelievable detour.
But perhaps underneath everything else, you are searching too.
Maybe you are searching for peace.
For identity.
For forgiveness.
For something that will finally silence the shame.
Maybe you have spent years trying to recover a version of yourself you lost somewhere along the way.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Or what was done to you.
Maybe you can smile convincingly.
Post beautifully.
Attend church.
Quote Scripture.
Say, “God is good.”
And still lie awake at night wondering whether Jesus could possibly want the person behind the presentation.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not that God discovered you were secretly good.
The Gospel is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
You do not have to manufacture innocence before approaching Jesus.
You come guilty.
He offers grace.
You come stained.
He cleanses.
You come unable to purchase your redemption.
Christ has paid the price.
You come carrying sin that must be confessed and forsaken.
He does not call you to hide it more successfully.
He calls you to repent and believe.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that pretends sin does not matter.
Grace purchased at the cross, where we discover exactly how serious sin is—and exactly how far the love of God went to rescue sinners.
Jesus does not merely improve the public version of you.
He calls the real you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The addicted you.
The exhausted you.
The secretly jealous you.
The religious you.
The wandering you.
The person underneath all the defenses.
And He calls you not merely into a better mood but into repentance, faith, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life under His lordship.
Maybe your greatest problem is not the “missing donkey” you have been begging God to return.
Maybe your greatest need is the King.
Jesus.
Because you can recover what you lost and still lose your soul.
You can get the relationship back.
Get the money.
Get the opportunity.
Get the recognition.
Get the answer you wanted.
And still remain separated from God.
But if you have Christ, then even when earthly circumstances remain painful, you possess something suffering cannot ultimately steal.
Forgiveness.
Adoption.
Hope.
Eternal life.
A Savior who entered death and walked out of the grave.
This is where Saul’s story leaves us trembling.
He found the donkeys.
He received the crown.
Yet the crown could not save his heart.
And neither can whatever you are chasing save yours.
Only Christ can.
So stop hiding behind religion.
Stop promising God that someday you will surrender.
Stop treating repentance as something you will do when life becomes convenient.
If the Spirit of God is exposing something while you read this, bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
There is mercy for repentant sinners.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is no sin you can cleanse by pretending it never happened.
But there is cleansing in Jesus Christ for those who come to Him.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer needed to see to realize they are not the only one struggling.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
If the Gospel has given you something worth sharing, let your sharing become one simple way of making that truth visible.
Because one day you may become so focused on what disappeared that you need to remember Saul walking mile after mile searching for donkeys, unaware of what awaited him.

But if this ministry genuinely helps you grow in Christ and you want to help us reach more people with the Gospel, you can glorify God through generous, willing stewardship—including supporting Gospel work and sharing biblical truth with others.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A Christian book cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your generosity cannot save you.
Your good works cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
Everything else must remain beneath Him.
So share because the Gospel is worth sharing.
Support Gospel work because you genuinely want others to hear.
Give freely, not under compulsion.
Follow because you want to stay close to biblical truth.
Save what helps you remember Christ.
And through all of it…
worship Jesus.
Because perhaps the most haunting lesson from Saul is not that an ordinary man once went searching for missing donkeys and came home anointed to be king.
It is that a person can receive something extraordinary from God and still eventually lose sight of God Himself.
Do not make that mistake.
Do not become so obsessed with finding what you lost that you miss what God is revealing through His Word.
Do not become so fascinated with your calling that you neglect the One who called you.
Do not become so protective of your little kingdom that you resist the true King.
And do not allow shame to convince you that your worst chapter must become the final chapter.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted the church before Christ confronted him.
Sinners have fallen at the feet of Jesus for centuries and discovered that His grace is greater than the identities their sins had written over them.
The cross still stands.
The tomb is still empty.
Christ still saves.
Repentance is still possible.
Grace is still offered.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Maybe you started reading because a man went looking for donkeys.
Maybe you reached the end because somewhere between Saul’s search and Saul’s anointing, God’s Word started searching you.
So here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this page:
You may spend half your life searching for what went missing, only to discover that your deepest need was never the thing you lost—it was the King who came looking for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOW PORN CHANGES THE WAY YOU SEE GOD
paragraphs: HOW PORN CHANGES THE WAY YOU SEE GOD

Porn does more than train your eyes to look at people differently. If you let it remain in the darkness, it can slowly distort the way you imagine holiness, intimacy, forgiveness—and even the face of God.
There is a moment after the screen goes dark that almost nobody talks about.
The room looks exactly the same.
The phone is still in your hand.
The door is still locked.
Nobody may know.
But something inside you feels different.
For a few minutes, maybe there was excitement. Escape. Relief. A temporary silencing of loneliness, stress, rejection, boredom, anger, or pain.
Then the silence returns.
And sometimes the silence is worse than what you were trying to escape.
You don't necessarily stop believing in God.
You may still believe every word of the Gospel.
You may still pray.
Still worship.
Still go to church.
Still post Bible verses.
Still tell other people that Jesus saves.
But when you think about God looking at you...
something has changed.
You imagine disappointment before mercy.
Disgust before compassion.
Distance before invitation.
You begin hiding from the very One you desperately need.
And that may be one of pornography's most spiritually destructive consequences.
Porn can distort more than the way you see sex.
It can distort the way you see yourself.
The way you see another human body.
The way you understand intimacy.
And eventually, if shame is allowed to preach louder than Scripture, it can distort the way you see God.
This story, however, did not begin with pornography.
It began in a garden.
Before humanity ever learned how to hide, Scripture says Adam and Eve were naked and felt no shame.
Genesis 2:25 uses the Hebrew idea expressed by עֲרוּמִּים... וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ — ʿarummim... velo yitboshashu.
They were naked...
and they were not ashamed.
There was exposure without exploitation.
Vulnerability without fear.
Bodies without commodification.
Intimacy without hiding.
Then sin entered.
And one of humanity's earliest instincts after rebellion was remarkably familiar:
cover yourself.
Hide.
Genesis 3:10 records Adam saying that he was afraid because he was naked, so he hid.
Notice the movement.
Sin.
Shame.
Fear.
Hiding.
Thousands of years later, the technology has changed.
The human heart hasn't.
Pornography frequently survives through secrecy.
Delete the history.
Close the tab.
Hide the account.
Clear the search.
Make another promise.
Swear this was the last time.
Then carry the shame into prayer.
And slowly you may begin doing spiritually what Adam did physically.
You hide from God.
Not because God cannot see you.
Because shame has convinced you that being seen means being rejected.
But the Gospel tells a radically different story.

Jesus said in Matthew 5:28 that whoever looks at a woman πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν — pros to epithymēsai autēn, commonly understood as looking at her with lustful intent, has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
Jesus takes the issue deeper than behavior.
He goes after the heart.
That matters because pornography trains the gaze toward something Christ refuses to reduce human beings into:
objects for consumption.
The person on the screen bears God's image.
That body belongs to a human story.
Someone with fears.
Someone with a childhood.
Someone with wounds you cannot see.
Someone who will stand before God.
Someone Jesus commands you to regard as a neighbor rather than a product.
Pornography says:
consume.
Jesus says:
love.
Pornography says:
take without relationship.
Jesus teaches self-giving love.
Pornography can train desire to ask, "What can this body give me?"
Christ transforms the heart until it begins asking, "How can I honor the person God created?"
That difference reaches far beyond sexuality.
Because eventually the consumer mentality can creep into your relationship with God.
You begin approaching Him primarily for another emotional experience.
Another feeling.
Another quick relief.
Another promise that will make the discomfort disappear.
But God is not another object for consumption.
He is Lord.
Father.
Creator.
Redeemer.
And He loves you too much merely to help you manage the darkness you refuse to surrender.
He wants to bring you into the light.
That sounds terrifying when you're hiding something.
Because shame whispers:
"If God really saw everything, He would want nothing to do with you."
But Scripture says something astonishing.
Ὁ Θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν — Ho Theos phōs estin.
"God is light."
That's 1 John 1:5.
And our instinct is often to hear that and panic.
Because if God is light...
He sees it.
Every search.
Every fantasy.
Every relapse.
Every secret.
Every promise you broke.
Every time you prayed for forgiveness and returned to the same screen.
Every rationalization.
Everything.
But keep reading John's message.
The light isn't merely where sinners are exposed.
In Christ, it is where sinners can be cleansed.
First John 1:7 teaches that as we walk in the light, the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin.
Then verse 9 gives one of Scripture's great promises to repentant sinners: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
The Greek word translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō.
It carries the sense of acknowledging or confessing.
No pretending.
No renaming lust as "just stress."
No calling bondage "just something everybody does."
No hiding behind loneliness.
No blaming your spouse.
No blaming singleness.
No bargaining with God.
You bring the truth into the light.
"This is sin."
"I have wanted what dishonors You."
"I have used people in my imagination."
"I have run toward counterfeit intimacy instead of You."
"Jesus, have mercy on me."
And something extraordinary happens when confession meets the Gospel.
You discover that God already knew.
And Christ still went to the cross.
Read that again.
Jesus did not discover your darkest moment after Calvary.
Romans 5:8 says God demonstrates His love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after you finally became disciplined.
Not after ninety clean days.
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you became worthy of being loved.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
This does not make pornography insignificant.
Grace never needs to minimize sin in order to forgive sinners.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And God's mercy is so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
That is where pornography's distorted picture of God begins to crack.
Maybe you have imagined God standing over you with folded arms, waiting for your next failure.
Maybe you've begun believing He is exhausted by you.
Maybe you think you've confessed too many times.
Maybe you no longer know whether your repentance is real because you hate what you're doing...
and somehow keep returning.
Listen carefully.
Repeated sin should never be treated casually.
Jesus calls us to repentance.
Real repentance does not merely ask God to remove consequences while protecting the idol.
Jesus used intentionally severe imagery when speaking about sin in Matthew 5:29–30: if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out; if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off.
Christ was not commanding bodily mutilation.
He was communicating the radical seriousness with which sin should be confronted.
So if pornography owns a doorway into your life...
close the doorway.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Delete what needs deleting.
Install accountability where secrecy has flourished.
Move the device.
Stop taking the phone into the room where you repeatedly fall.
Tell a mature Christian you trust.
Confess.
Ask for prayer.
Seek pastoral help.

If the pattern feels compulsive or deeply connected to trauma, loneliness, anxiety, or other wounds, getting help from a qualified professional can be part of dealing truthfully with what is happening.
Stop protecting the environment in which your secret keeps surviving.
Because repentance sometimes looks less dramatic than tears at an altar.
Sometimes repentance looks like handing someone your password.
Sometimes it looks like leaving the phone outside the bedroom.
Sometimes it looks like admitting to another believer:
"I need help."
And perhaps that terrifies you.
Because pornography taught you to hide.
Jesus calls you into light.
Pornography offers intimacy without being known.
The Gospel gives you something far more frightening...
and infinitely more beautiful:
to be completely known by God and, in Christ, still invited to come near.
Hebrews 4 does not tell struggling believers to run away from God's throne.
It tells them to approach.
The Greek expression is breathtaking:
προσερχώμεθα οὖν μετὰ παρρησίας τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος — proserchōmetha oun meta parrēsias tō thronō tēs charitos.
"Let us therefore draw near with confidence to the throne of grace."
Think about that.
You fell.
And the enemy says, "Run."
Jesus says, "Come."
You feel filthy.
Shame says, "Hide."
Grace says, "Come."
You think God cannot possibly want to hear another confession.
Scripture says:
Come.
Not confidently because your performance is impressive.
Confidently because your High Priest is Jesus.
The throne you approach is called the throne of χάριτος — charitos.
Grace.
This is where pornography profoundly distorts our perception of God.
Porn teaches transaction.
God reveals covenant.
Porn teaches consumption.
Jesus demonstrates sacrifice.
Porn offers bodies without persons.
Christ restores persons—including the person looking back at you in the mirror.
Porn says desire must be immediately satisfied.
Jesus teaches that desire can be submitted to the Father.
Porn tells you intimacy can exist without holiness.
God designed covenant intimacy to involve faithfulness, dignity, responsibility, love, and self-giving.
Porn says secrecy will protect you.
Jesus says truth will bring you into freedom.
And shame says your scandal is the end of your story.
The cross says otherwise.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Peter publicly denied Jesus.
Paul had participated in violent persecution of Christians.
The Corinthian church included people whose former lives were marked by serious sexual sin.
Scripture does not sanitize human failure.
But neither does it permit failure to have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
First Corinthians 6:11 contains three breathtaking declarations about believers whose pasts included serious sin:
You were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That does not mean Christians become incapable of temptation.
It means sin is no longer entitled to define their identity.
Maybe pornography has been telling you who you are.
Dirty.
Perverted.
Fake.
Unworthy.
Hopeless.
Too far gone.
Maybe you secretly wonder whether a real Christian could struggle like this.
The correct response is not to excuse the sin.
And it is not to surrender your identity to the sin.
Your sin tells the truth about your need for a Savior.
It does not have authority to rewrite what Christ has accomplished for those who belong to Him.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction exposes sin and pulls you toward repentance.
Condemnation tells you there is no point returning.
Conviction says:
"This must come into the light."
Condemnation says:
"Stay hidden. God doesn't want you anymore."
Romans 8:1 answers that lie:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα — Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
"There is therefore now no condemnation..."
for those who are in Christ Jesus.
No condemnation does not mean no correction.
No discipline.
No battle.
No consequences.
No repentance.
It means that for the person united to Christ, the courtroom verdict has changed because Christ bore the condemnation of sin.
So stop confusing the voice telling you to surrender your sin with the voice telling you to surrender your hope.
They are not the same voice.
Jesus exposes what is killing you because He loves you.
The enemy accuses you in order to convince you that hiding is safer than coming home.
And perhaps that is exactly what you needed to hear tonight.
You do not need another secret promise whispered over a glowing screen.
You need Jesus.
Not Jesus added to your coping mechanisms.
Not Jesus as motivational content.
Not Jesus as the emergency button after pornography.
Jesus as Lord.
Jesus as Savior.
Jesus as the One who has authority over your body, imagination, sexuality, phone, loneliness, desires, relationships, habits, wounds, and future.
You may need to stop asking only:
"How do I stop watching porn?"
and begin asking:
"What am I really searching for when I open it?"
Comfort?
Control?
Escape?
Affection?
Validation?
Novelty?
Numbness?
A substitute for intimacy?
Then ask the harder question:
"What have I started believing about God that makes this counterfeit refuge feel safer than running to Him?"
Because sometimes underneath the sexual struggle sits a theological wound.
You may believe God is distant.
So you medicate loneliness.
You may believe God is withholding something good.
So you take what you want.
You may believe God only loves the cleaned-up version of you.
So you hide the wounded version.
You may believe holiness is merely deprivation.
So sin begins looking like freedom.
But Satan has been selling that lie since Eden:
God is keeping something good from you.
The Gospel answers:
Look at the cross.
The God you suspect of withholding Himself...
gave Himself.
The Son of God was not dragged unwillingly into redemption.
Christ loved and gave Himself.
He took shame.
He bore sin.
He endured the cross.
He rose from the grave.
And now He does not merely offer behavior modification.
He offers resurrection life.
So maybe your next step isn't another dramatic vow that you'll never fail again.
Maybe it is simply the most honest prayer you've prayed in years:
"Jesus, I don't want to hide anymore."
You don't have to explain everything publicly.
But somebody reading those words may realize they aren't the only believer fighting in the darkness.
And somebody may pray for you tonight.
Your testimony might become somebody else's reason not to give up.
Come back to it when shame tries to convince you that God is only waiting to reject you.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that Jesus still receives sinners who come into the light.
But hear this clearly:
You do not earn salvation by supporting a ministry.
You do not glorify God because money changed hands.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.
Support matters when it flows from gratitude and becomes a means of helping biblical truth travel farther.
Because pornography's greatest lie may not simply be that a screen can satisfy you.
Its crueler lie may be what it whispers afterward:
"After what you've done, don't let God see you."
But He already sees you.
And the wonder of the Gospel is not that you managed to hide your scandal well enough for Jesus to love you.
The wonder is that Jesus walked directly into the scandal, carried sin to the cross, defeated death, and now calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
So turn off the screen.
Open the door.
Tell the truth.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Run toward Christ.
Not because your sin isn't serious.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Because His kindness leads sinners toward repentance.
Not because the battle will necessarily disappear tomorrow.
Because you no longer have to fight it while pretending nobody knows.
The screen does not get to name you.
Your worst night does not get to name you.
Your browser history does not get to name you.
Your relapse does not get to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
And maybe the most beautiful thing you will ever discover is this:
The God you were terrified would see your darkness is the very God who entered it to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EVERYONE SAW A SHEPHERD BOY—GOD SAW ISRAEL’S NEXT KING
paragraphs: EVERYONE SAW A SHEPHERD BOY—GOD SAW ISRAEL’S NEXT KING

They almost finished choosing without even calling David into the room. But when people overlook you, God does not lose sight of you—and sometimes the field where nobody applauds you is exactly where God is preparing you for what comes next.
There was an empty seat at Jesse’s house.
Not because someone was late.
Because apparently, no one thought the missing person needed to be there.
Samuel had come to Bethlehem carrying a horn of oil. God had sent him to the household of Jesse because one of Jesse’s sons had been chosen for something extraordinary.
A king was somewhere in that family.
Imagine the atmosphere.

Samuel was not an ordinary visitor. He was the prophet of the LORD. His arrival mattered. Jesse’s sons passed before him, beginning with Eliab, whose appearance was impressive enough that Samuel apparently thought the search might already be over.
Surely this was the one.
Tall enough.
Strong enough.
Impressive enough.
King enough.
And then God interrupted Samuel’s assumption.
The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 16:7 carries a truth that still cuts through every culture obsessed with appearance:
“כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַיהוָה יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב”
Ki ha’adam yir’eh la‘einayim, vaYHWH yir’eh lalevav.
In context, the sense is:
Human beings look at what is visible to the eyes, but the LORD looks at the heart.
The contrast is devastatingly simple.
People see what appears before them.
God sees deeper.

The Hebrew word לֵבָב — levav, “heart,” is not merely talking about emotion. In biblical Hebrew, the heart can encompass the inner person—the center of thought, intention, desire, will, and character.
God was not searching Bethlehem for the best résumé.
He was looking where human eyes could not.
And maybe that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us know what it feels like to be the person nobody called.
You watched somebody else get chosen.
Somebody else got the opportunity.
Somebody else received the recognition.
Somebody else was celebrated publicly while you quietly wondered whether your life mattered at all.
You smiled when they succeeded.
You congratulated them.
You tried to be mature about it.
Then you went home carrying a question you were almost ashamed to say aloud:
“God… do You even see me?”
David would understand the question.
Because while the prophet stood inside Jesse’s house examining potential kings, David was apparently still outside tending sheep.
Think about that.
Samuel knew God had chosen one of Jesse’s sons.
Jesse gathered his sons.
And David was still with the sheep.
He was not merely standing at the back of the line.
He was not in the line.
One son passed before Samuel.
No.
Another.
No.
Another.
Still no.
Seven sons passed before Samuel, and God rejected every one of them for this particular calling.
The oil remained in the horn.
The room must have become increasingly uncomfortable.
Finally Samuel asked Jesse the question that changed everything:
Are these all your sons?
And Jesse essentially answered:
There is still the youngest.
He is tending the sheep.
There is something heartbreaking hidden inside that sentence.
There was another son.
He simply had not been summoned.
David was close enough to belong to the family but apparently far enough from everyone’s expectations that when a king was being sought among Jesse’s sons, he remained in the field.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Present, but overlooked.
Faithful, but unnoticed.
Working, but uncelebrated.
Serving while someone else is seen.
Praying while someone else is promoted.
Trying to obey God while it seems everyone else is moving forward faster than you.
And this is where we must be careful not to turn David’s story into a shallow motivational slogan.
The message is not, “Everyone who gets overlooked is secretly destined to become famous.”
Scripture promises no such thing.
God does not owe us a platform.
He does not owe us applause.
He does not promise every faithful Christian earthly prominence.
The Gospel is far greater than self-actualization.
The breathtaking truth is this:
Your value before God has never depended upon human recognition.
And God can accomplish His purposes without asking permission from the people who underestimated you.
Samuel said:
“Send and get him.”
Suddenly the shepherd nobody had invited became the person everyone had to wait for.
David left the sheep.
Perhaps dust clung to his clothes.
Perhaps the smell of the field followed him into the room.
He walked through a doorway without fully understanding that his life was about to change.
Then God spoke.
“Rise and anoint him; this is the one.”
The Hebrew carries the force of divine identification:
קוּם מְשָׁחֵהוּ כִּי־זֶה הוּא
Qum, meshachehu, ki-zeh hu.
“Rise. Anoint him. For this is he.”
Not Eliab.
Not the man Samuel expected.
David.
The shepherd.
The forgotten son from the field.
And Samuel took the horn.
Oil began to fall over David’s head.
In front of the brothers who had already been considered.
In front of the family that had left him with the sheep.
Scripture says Samuel anointed David. The Hebrew verb comes from מָשַׁח — mashach, “to anoint.” From the related noun מָשִׁיחַ — mashiach comes the familiar word “anointed one” or “messiah.”
David was being set apart as Israel’s future king.
Then something even greater happened.
1 Samuel 16:13 tells us:
וַתִּצְלַח רוּחַ־יְהוָה אֶל־דָּוִד מֵהַיּוֹם הַהוּא וָמָעְלָה
Vattitzlach Ruach-YHWH el-David mehayom hahu vama‘lah.
The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon David from that day forward.

The Hebrew verb translated in various English versions as “came powerfully,” “came mightily,” or “rushed upon” communicates forceful divine empowerment. David’s future would ultimately depend not merely upon natural talent but upon God’s empowering presence.
But here is the part we sometimes skip.
David was anointed...
and then he did not immediately sit on Israel’s throne.
There was oil on his head before there was a crown on it.
Calling came before coronation.
Promise came before possession.
Anointing came before adversity.
There would still be waiting.
There would still be Goliath.
There would still be Saul.
There would still be caves.
There would still be betrayal.
There would still be fear.
There would still be nights when the future king looked nothing like a king.
That matters.
Because sometimes we think God’s presence should eliminate the difficult middle.
Instead, Scripture repeatedly shows God forming His servants inside it.
Maybe you are living in that middle right now.
You know God has been faithful, but your circumstances are confusing.
You have prayed, but nothing seems to move.
You have tried to obey, but doors keep closing.
You thought surrender would make everything easier.
Instead, obedience led you somewhere lonely.
Do not confuse hiddenness with abandonment.
But also do not romanticize hiddenness.
Use it.
Let God search you there.
Because David’s story contains another warning we desperately need.
The same David whose heart God saw in 1 Samuel 16 would later commit terrible sin.
He would abuse royal power in the matter involving Bathsheba and Uriah.
The shepherd became king.
The overlooked became powerful.
And power did not make him immune to sin.
That destroys another popular misunderstanding of this passage.
“God looks at the heart” does not mean, “God knows I am basically a good person, so my behavior does not matter.”
Quite the opposite.
If God sees the heart, then nothing is hidden.
Not lust.
Not envy.
Not pride.
Not bitterness.
Not secret messages.
Not private addictions.
Not religious hypocrisy.
Not the resentment behind the smile.
Not the sin hidden beneath ministry language.
People may see your Christian posts.
God sees your heart.
People may hear your worship.
God sees your heart.
People may admire your Bible knowledge.
God sees your heart.
People may call you anointed.
God sees your heart.
And suddenly 1 Samuel 16:7 stops being merely comforting.
It becomes terrifying.
Because the God who sees past the rejection that wounded you also sees past the image you created to hide what is destroying you.
He sees both.
Your wounds...
and your sin.
Your rejection...
and your rebellion.
Your tears...
and your secrets.
And He still calls you toward Himself.
That is where David’s story must lead us beyond David.
Because David is not the final Hero of Scripture.
Jesus is.
David was an anointed king.
Jesus is the Christ.
The Greek title Χριστός — Christos means “Anointed One,” corresponding conceptually to Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ — Mashiach.
Jesus is the promised Son of David whose kingdom ultimately surpasses David’s.
David defeated Goliath.
Jesus defeated what no human warrior could defeat for us.
Sin.
Death.
Condemnation.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus provides it.
David fell into sin.
Jesus remained without sin.
David’s kingdom eventually fractured.
Christ’s kingdom will never end.
And this is where your story collides with the Gospel.
God does not merely see a better version of you waiting to emerge.
He sees a sinner who needs a Savior.
So do I.
So does every person reading this.
The deepest problem in our lives is not that people failed to recognize our potential.
It is that sin separated humanity from the holy God who created us.
We do not primarily need recognition.
We need reconciliation.
We do not primarily need promotion.
We need pardon.
We do not primarily need somebody to notice us.
We need Jesus to save us.
And He came.
The promised King entered human history not surrounded by earthly splendor but in humility.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The true King wore a crown made of thorns.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin and judgment so guilty people could be forgiven through Him.
Then the grave received Him.
For a moment, it looked as though darkness had won.
But the story was not finished.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
The rejected King lives.
And now grace reaches people whose stories look impossible to rewrite.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Addicts.
Hypocrites.
The bitter.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The spiritually exhausted.
The person who keeps promising God, “This is the last time,” only to fall again.
The person who looks fine at church and falls apart alone.
The person convinced that if everyone knew the whole story, nobody would stay.
Jesus already knows the whole story.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it mattered enough for Christ to die.
But the resurrection announces that sin does not have to write your final chapter.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Stop defending what Jesus died to forgive.
Stop hiding what Christ is calling you to surrender.
You may have been ignored by people.
Jesus sees you.
You may have been abandoned.
Jesus sees you.
You may have been underestimated.
Jesus sees you.
You may also have sinned terribly.
Jesus sees that too.
And if you come to Him in repentance and faith, you will discover that being fully known by Christ does not have to end in rejection.
It can end in redemption.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the scandal never happened.
God redeeming sinners through the blood of Jesus Christ.
David himself would eventually learn how desperately he needed that mercy.
After his devastating sin, he prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
The man whose heart God saw knew his heart still needed cleansing.
Maybe that needs to become your prayer today.
Not:
“God, make everybody recognize me.”
But:
“God, make my heart clean.”
Not:
“God, prove them wrong.”
But:
“Jesus, make me Yours.”
Not:
“Lord, give me a platform.”
But:
“Lord, give me a heart that can be trusted whether anyone sees me or not.”
Because perhaps the field is doing something the palace could never do.
Perhaps the silence is revealing whether you worship God for God—or worship Him for what you hope He will give you.
Perhaps obscurity is exposing your hunger for human applause.
Perhaps waiting is teaching you obedience.
Perhaps this season is less about God showing everyone who you are and more about God showing you who He is.
And maybe you needed to hear this today:
You do not need to force open every door.
You do not need to manipulate people into seeing your worth.
You do not need to become bitter because somebody chose someone else.
You do not need to spend your life auditioning for people who were never assigned to determine your identity.
Stay faithful.
Stay humble.
Stay repentant.
Stay close to Jesus.
Because human beings still look at what is before their eyes.
But the LORD sees the heart.
Be honest.
Let believers reading the comments know where somebody needs prayer.
Maybe your comment becomes the place where another Christian stops scrolling and starts interceding.
And think of one person who feels forgotten right now.
Not twenty people.
One.
The friend whose smile has been hiding exhaustion.
The son who thinks he disappointed everyone.
The daughter who feels invisible.
The believer who has quietly started drifting away from God.
The person everybody assumes is okay.
If this spoke to you, save it too.
There may come a night when rejection feels louder than truth, and you will need to remember again:
God sees deeper.
Come to Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A Christian book cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
So if this article reaches nothing except your wounded pride, it has not gone deep enough.
Let it reach your heart.
Let Christ confront the secret sin.
Let Him touch the rejection.
Let Him expose the bitterness.
Let Him dismantle the performance.
Let Him call you out of hiding.
The shepherd boy eventually became a king.
But the greater Son of David became the crucified and risen Savior through whom sinners can become children of God.
That is the story worth giving your life to.
Maybe everyone else has only seen your field.
God sees the person standing in it.
Maybe people remember your worst chapter.
Christ still knows how redemption is written.
Maybe your past looks scandalous.
Maybe your present feels forgotten.
Maybe your future looks impossible.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where bitterness has taken root.
Wait where God has not yet opened the door.
Obey where Scripture has already made His will clear.
And remember the room in Bethlehem.
Seven impressive sons passed before the prophet.
The oil did not move.
Then someone finally remembered the shepherd.
David walked in.
God said:
This is the one.
The world had seen a boy tending sheep.
God had seen Israel’s next king.
And yet even Israel’s next king would eventually need mercy.
That is why the greatest hope in this story is not that you might secretly be another David.
It is that there is already a greater King than David.
His name is Jesus.
He sees the heart no human being can see.
He knows the sin no audience knows.
He knows the wound nobody noticed.
And for everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith, His grace can reach places shame said were beyond redemption.
So share this if someone needs that truth.
And comment something real—not something impressive.
“Jesus, search my heart.”
“Pray for me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“No more hiding.”
Because maybe the most important thing God does after this article is not changing how everybody else sees you.
Maybe it is changing what is happening inside the heart only He can fully see.
You were never hidden from the eyes that mattered most—and the King who sees your entire story still calls sinners out of hiding and into His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Spiritual Burnout Can Happen While Everyone Is Still Complimenting Your Faithfulness
paragraphs:
Spiritual Burnout Can Happen While Everyone Is Still Complimenting Your Faithfulness
The frightening part is that you can still be serving Jesus in public while quietly losing your joy in being with Jesus in private.
Nobody noticed because you never stopped showing up.
You still answered the message.
Still volunteered.
Still preached.
Still led worship.
Still cared for everybody.
Still checked on the person who was falling apart while nobody thought to ask whether you were falling apart too.
You still smiled when someone said, “I don’t know how you do it.”
And perhaps that compliment hurt more than they realized.
Because you didn’t know how you were doing it either.
You were just doing it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
People called you faithful.
Dependable.
Strong.
Committed.
Anointed.
A blessing.
But somewhere underneath all that Christian activity, something had begun changing.
Prayer started feeling like another responsibility.
Scripture became something you needed to prepare for other people instead of bread you desperately needed yourself.
Worship became something you helped create while struggling to experience it.
Someone asked for another favor, and you said yes with your mouth while resentment whispered inside your chest.
Then came the guilt.
Because faithful Christians aren't supposed to feel that way... right?
So you buried the exhaustion.
You rebuked yourself.
You called your limits selfishness.
You confused being needed with being obedient.
And because people kept complimenting your faithfulness, you assumed the exhaustion must be holy.
But then you arrive at Mark 6.
And Jesus says something that exhausted Christians desperately need to hear.
The apostles had been sent out into ministry. They had preached repentance. They had ministered powerfully. They returned to Jesus carrying stories of everything they had accomplished.
Mark records:
“Καὶ συνάγονται οἱ ἀπόστολοι πρὸς τὸν Ἰησοῦν…”
The apostles gather to Jesus.
That matters.
Before they were workers reporting results, they were disciples returning to Christ.
They told Him what they had done and what they had taught.
And Jesus listened.
But notice what He did not say.
He did not immediately say:
Wonderful. Now go do more.
He did not reward fruitful ministry with endless ministry.
He did not tell exhausted disciples that needing rest proved they lacked dedication.
Instead, Mark records His words:
“Δεῦτε ὑμεῖς αὐτοὶ κατ’ ἰδίαν εἰς ἔρημον τόπον καὶ ἀναπαύσασθε ὀλίγον.”
In context, the sense is:
Come away yourselves, privately, into a deserted or solitary place...
and rest a little.
That word translated “rest” is ἀναπαύσασθε — anapausasthe.
Jesus is commanding His disciples to rest.
Not because the mission no longer mattered.
Because the people carrying the mission mattered to Him too.
Then Mark gives us a painfully ordinary detail.
There were so many people coming and going that the disciples did not even have opportunity to eat.
Think about that.
These men were not exhausted because they had abandoned God's work.
They were exhausted in the middle of God's work.
They were not running from ministry.
They had been doing ministry.
They were not spiritually useless.
They had been fruitful.
And Jesus looked at fruitful, needed, busy disciples surrounded by legitimate human need...
and told them to come away.
That should confront some of us.
Because we have baptized exhaustion.
We have made depletion look like devotion.
We have sometimes treated a destroyed schedule as proof of a surrendered life.
We have quietly created Christian cultures where the person who never says no appears more spiritual than the person who understands human limitations.
But Jesus never taught that your value increases according to how exhausted you become for Him.
You are not the Messiah.
Jesus is.
Read that again if you need to.
You are not the Messiah.
Jesus is.
The church does not ultimately belong to you.
The ministry does not ultimately belong to you.
Your family is not sustained by your omnipotence.
Your friends do not need you to become omnipresent.
You cannot answer every message, solve every crisis, carry every burden, accept every opportunity, satisfy every expectation, rescue every hurting person, and remain emotionally untouched.
You are a creature.
He is God.
And sometimes one of the most spiritually dangerous things a sincere Christian can do is attempt to possess attributes God never gave human beings.
Omnipresence belongs to God.
You cannot be everywhere.
Omnipotence belongs to God.
You cannot fix everything.
Omniscience belongs to God.
You will not know everything.
The kingdom has a King.
And His name is Jesus.
Maybe your exhaustion has become so normal that you no longer call it exhaustion.
You call it responsibility.
You wake up already tired.
You serve while irritated.
You help people while secretly wishing they would stop needing you.
You say, “Of course,” when someone asks for something else, then sit alone wondering why you are becoming angry at people you genuinely love.
Your body is present at church.
Your hands are serving.
Your mouth is saying the correct Christian things.
But inside, you are whispering:
“I don't want anyone to need anything else from me.”
And immediately you feel ashamed.
Please understand the distinction.
Resentment should not be nurtured or justified as righteousness. Sin must still be brought honestly before Christ.
But sometimes resentment is also exposing something.
Perhaps you have repeatedly said yes when wisdom required no.
Perhaps you have made promises Jesus never asked you to make.
Perhaps you are trying to maintain an image of yourself as “the dependable Christian.”
Perhaps you secretly fear that if you stop producing, people will stop appreciating you.
That question can go very deep:
Who are you when nobody needs you?
Who are you when you aren't preaching?
When you aren't leading?
When you aren't volunteering?
When you aren't caregiving?
When you aren't fixing somebody else's emergency?
When you aren't being thanked?
When there is nothing impressive to report?
Can you still sit before Jesus and believe you are loved?
Because there is a subtle tragedy that can happen in Christian service.
You can become so occupied doing things for Jesus that being with Jesus begins to feel unproductive.
Silence feels wasteful.
Rest feels guilty.
A quiet morning feels irresponsible.
Prayer without an agenda feels strange.
Reading Scripture without preparing a sermon, devotional, post, lesson, or Bible study feels almost indulgent.
Slowly...
almost invisibly...
relationship becomes output.
Communion becomes production.
And eventually you know how to speak about Jesus while barely speaking to Jesus.
That is dangerous.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the story of exhausted human beings proving their worth to God through religious productivity.
It is the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Christ came for sinners who could not save themselves.
He lived the righteous life we failed to live.
He went to the cross bearing sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Salvation is not the trophy presented to the most productive religious worker.
It is grace received through faith in Christ.
The exhausted pastor needs that Gospel.
The worship leader needs it.
The mother caring for everyone needs it.
The father carrying responsibilities nobody sees needs it.
The ministry volunteer stacking chairs after everybody leaves needs it.
The caregiver changing sheets at two in the morning needs it.
The Christian friend who somehow became everyone's emergency contact needs it.
The person who keeps answering, keeps serving, keeps smiling, keeps saying “I'm okay”...
needs it.
You are not saved because you exhausted yourself sufficiently for Jesus.
You are saved by Jesus.
And maybe the scandal of grace for you right now is discovering that Jesus does not only meet you when you have something impressive to offer Him.
He meets empty people.
Weak people.
Tired people.
People who finally admit:
“Lord, I cannot keep pretending.”
There is something breathtaking about Mark 6.
Jesus knew the crowd existed when He told the disciples to rest.
The needs were real.
The people mattered.
And still He said:
Come away.
The presence of need does not automatically constitute God's personal command for you to meet every need.
That distinction can save a Christian from years of unnecessary guilt.
There will always be another need.
Another email.
Another person.
Another project.
Another ministry opportunity.
Another emergency.
Another request.
Another reason to postpone your soul.
If you wait until nobody needs anything from you before you rest, you may never rest.
Jesus Himself lived with human limitations in His earthly ministry. He slept. He withdrew. He prayed. He did not allow every demand of every crowd to determine His movements.
And here, He invites His disciples away.
Yet there is another beautiful detail.
The crowd follows.
The planned solitude gets interrupted.
Mark tells us that people recognized them and reached the destination.
And when Jesus saw the crowd, He had compassion on them.
That keeps us from turning biblical rest into selfish isolation.
Jesus is neither teaching relentless exhaustion nor indifferent self-protection.
He is Lord over both service and rest.
Sometimes love will interrupt your plans.
Sometimes genuine sacrifice will cost you sleep.
Sometimes obedience will be uncomfortable.
Christian discipleship absolutely includes self-denial.
Jesus said to take up the cross.
But taking up your cross is not the same thing as inventing crosses Jesus never gave you and then resenting everyone because you are carrying them.
Some of us need to hear that sentence twice.
Taking up your cross is not the same thing as inventing crosses Jesus never gave you.
There is a difference between sacrifice and savior-complex.
Between obedience and compulsive availability.
Between faithfulness and fear-driven performance.
Between serving because Christ called you and serving because you cannot bear disappointing anybody.
And perhaps the question is not simply:
“Am I doing enough for God?”
Perhaps tonight the more revealing question is:
“Why am I terrified of stopping?”
Maybe because stopping would make you feel the grief you've been outrunning.
Maybe silence would expose loneliness.
Maybe rest would uncover disappointment with God you have been afraid to admit.
Maybe your usefulness has become part of your identity.
Maybe applause became oxygen.
Maybe being “the strong one” became the hiding place where you never had to admit that you needed help too.
Maybe you don't know how to receive anymore.
Only give.
And Jesus is standing beside the exhausted version of you that everybody else keeps complimenting.
He sees beneath the faithfulness everyone applauds.
He sees the fatigue.
The resentment.
The loneliness.
The tears you keep postponing.
The prayers that have become difficult.
The places where your love has grown thin.
The sins exhaustion has helped expose.
The bitterness you don't want anyone to know exists.
And His invitation is not:
Pretend better.
It is:
Come.
Come away.
Not away from Jesus.
Away with Jesus.
That difference is everything.
Biblical rest is not ultimately escape from responsibility.
It is refusal to live as though everything depends on you.
It is an embodied confession:
God is God.
I am not.
Christ is Savior.
I am not.
The kingdom belongs to Him.
I belong to Him too.
Maybe repentance for you will not begin with doing something dramatic.
Maybe it begins with telling Jesus the truth.
“Lord, I am tired.”
“I have become resentful.”
“I've been serving people while quietly becoming angry at them.”
“I've cared more about being seen as faithful than actually remaining close to You.”
“I've neglected my family while telling myself it was ministry.”
“I've neglected my body and called it sacrifice.”
“I've stopped praying unless I need something for somebody else.”
“I've made productivity part of my identity.”
“I don't know how to stop.”
Bring that into the light.
There is grace there.
Not grace that celebrates sin.
Grace that forgives sinners.
Grace that confronts what is killing us and then leads us home.
The same Jesus who calls sinners to repentance is the Jesus who receives the weary.
The same Christ who commands obedience is the Christ whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light.
The same Savior who calls us to take up our cross first carried the cross we could never carry.
And at Calvary, Jesus did not whisper:
“Try harder.”
He accomplished redemption.
This is where burnout meets the Gospel.
You do not have to become less human to become more holy.
Jesus does not need you to pretend you have infinite capacity.
You need Christ.
You need grace.
You need repentance where exhaustion has exposed sin.
You need forgiveness where resentment has poisoned love.
You need wisdom about boundaries.
You need courage to disappoint people when obeying God requires it.
You need humility to receive help.
You need brothers and sisters who know the person behind the ministry.
You may need sleep.
You may need food.
You may need a day where nobody applauds you.
You may need to sit before Scripture without turning what you read into content.
You may need to pray without producing anything afterward.
You may need to remember what it felt like when Jesus Himself was enough.
And if this article feels strangely personal, don't rush away from that discomfort.
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you really are.
You don't need to tell the entire internet everything.
But perhaps you need to stop hiding completely.
Not because a comment magically fixes burnout.
Because sometimes three honest words are the first crack in the wall.
Someone else reading the comments may realize they are not the only Christian struggling to keep going.
Let that be more than engagement.
Let it become prayer.
Then think of one person who needs this.
Not fifty.
One.
The pastor who keeps pouring out.
The volunteer who never says no.
The caregiver who is disappearing underneath everyone else's needs.
The mother nobody checks on because she always seems strong.
The father silently carrying more than anyone realizes.
The ministry leader everybody assumes is fine.
The dependable Christian friend who always answers your calls.
Not to diagnose them.
To remind them they are seen.
Sharing biblical encouragement can be one simple way of glorifying God by putting truth where someone else may encounter it. Grace cannot be bought.
But the deeper reason to stay close is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is Scripture.
It is continuing to be reminded, in a noisy world, that Jesus Christ is still the center.
Because exhaustion has a strange way of making us forget truths we were certain we understood.
And before you leave...
go back to the boat.
See the exhausted disciples.
Listen to the noise of people coming and going.
Feel the pressure of needs everywhere.
They have done real ministry.
They have taught.
They have served.
They have been faithful.
And standing in the middle of all that unfinished work is Jesus.
He knows there are still hungry people.
He knows there is still ministry ahead.
He knows the crowd will follow.
Yet His disciples hear something from His mouth that some of us desperately need permission to hear from Scripture:
Come away.
Rest a little.
Maybe everyone around you is still complimenting your faithfulness.
Maybe they have no idea how close you are to empty.
But Jesus does.
And perhaps the most important thing you accomplish tonight will not be another task completed for Him.
Perhaps it will be returning to Him.
Because your usefulness was never your Savior.
Your endurance was never your Savior.
Your reputation for being dependable was never your Savior.
Your ministry was never your Savior.
Jesus is.
And when exhausted faithfulness finally collapses at His feet, grace does not look at the wreckage and say, “You should have performed better.”
Grace begins rebuilding the person underneath the performance.
You spent so long carrying things for Jesus that you almost forgot Jesus was willing to carry you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS THOUGHT JESUS HAD BLASPHEMED. THEN THE PARALYZED MAN STOOD UP.
paragraphs: THE RELIGIOUS LEADERS THOUGHT JESUS HAD BLASPHEMED. THEN THE PARALYZED MAN STOOD UP.
They came expecting to see a healing. Jesus did something far more scandalous first: He forgave the man’s sins.
The room was already full when they arrived.
Not comfortably full.
Full enough that nobody was squeezing through the doorway.
Jesus was teaching inside a house in Capernaum, and word had spread so quickly that people crowded around Him until there was no room left, “not even at the door” (Mark 2:2).
Some came because they believed.
Some came because they were curious.
Some came because they had heard stories about miracles.
And some were watching Jesus very carefully.
Then four men appeared carrying a paralyzed man.
Imagine being the man on that mat.
Everybody else walked into the story.
You had to be carried.
Everybody else could push through a crowd.
You could not even get yourself through the door.
