If salvation is really by grace…
where do good works fit?
If my works cannot save me, does it matter how I live?
If obedience matters, how can salvation still be completely by grace?
And if I keep failing after coming to Christ, does that mean I was never saved—or that I need to somehow work harder until God accepts me again?
Maybe you have quietly lived somewhere between those questions.
Trying to love Jesus while secretly keeping score.
Bible read today.
Check.
Prayer accomplished.
Check.
Church attended.
Check.
Temptation resisted.
Check.
Good Christian.
Then another day comes.
You lose your temper.
You return to something you promised God you would leave behind.
You neglect prayer.
You say something you regret.
You entertain the thought.
You click the thing.
You hide the wound.
You become spiritually cold.
And suddenly the scoreboard changes.
Bad Christian.
Disappointing Christian.
Maybe-not-even-a-Christian Christian.
Then shame starts preaching.
“God must be tired of you.”
“You need to make this up to Him.”
“Do something spiritual.”
“Try harder.”
“Become worthy again.”
But beneath all that religious noise stands a blood-stained cross declaring something radically different.
You were never worthy enough to purchase salvation in the first place.
And that is exactly why Jesus came.
Paul writes:
“Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί” — tē gar chariti — “for by grace.”
“ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι” — este sesōsmenoi — “you have been saved.”
“διὰ πίστεως” — dia pisteōs — “through faith.”
Then Paul drives the point home:
“οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν” — ouk ex hymōn — “not from yourselves.”
“θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον” — theou to dōron — “the gift of God.”
“οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων” — ouk ex ergōn — “not from works.”
And why?
“ἵνα μή τις καυχήσηται” — hina mē tis kauchēsētai — “so that no one may boast.”
That is Ephesians 2:8–9.
And every phrase removes another brick from the little throne human pride keeps trying to build.
Grace.
Saved.
Through faith.
Not from yourselves.
Gift.
Not from works.
No boasting.
Paul leaves nowhere for human beings to stand before God and say, “Jesus helped me, but I helped save myself too.”
No.
The Gospel does not say Jesus made salvation possible for sufficiently impressive people.
The Gospel says spiritually dead people needed to be made alive.
That context matters enormously.
Because Ephesians 2 does not begin with humanity being described as slightly damaged, spiritually confused, or mostly good but needing improvement.
It begins with death.
“And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1).
Dead.
That is the diagnosis.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in all of Scripture:
“But God…”
“But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us…” (Ephesians 2:4).
You were dead.
But God.
You were guilty.
But God.
You were unable to resurrect yourself.
But God.
You could not climb high enough to reach Him.
So in Christ, God came down to rescue sinners.
This is why grace is so offensive to human pride.
We would often rather receive a ladder than a Savior.
Give us commandments to accomplish.
Give us religious achievements to display.
Give us something allowing us to look across the room and think, “At least I am better than that person.”
Grace destroys that game.
At the foot of the cross, the respectable sinner and the scandalous sinner arrive with the same empty hands.
The religious man cannot boast.
The addict cannot despair that his past places him beyond Christ’s reach.
The churchgoer cannot purchase heaven with attendance.
The adulterer cannot cleanse himself by promising to become better.
The generous cannot donate enough to erase guilt.
The preacher cannot preach himself into heaven.
And the broken person cannot sin so spectacularly that the blood of Christ becomes insufficient for everyone who truly comes to Him in repentant faith.
Salvation is not wages.
It is gift.
Romans 6:23 says, “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Wages are earned.
A gift is received.
That distinction changes everything.
You do not obey so that Christ will finally decide to save you.
You come to Christ because you cannot save yourself.
You do not repent because you have successfully repaired yourself.
You repent because you finally stop defending the sin from which you need Him to rescue you.
You do not bring God a résumé.
You bring Him your need.
But this is precisely where another dangerous misunderstanding can appear.
Some people stop reading at Ephesians 2:9.
Paul did not.
The next sentence matters.
A lot.
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10).
There it is.
Good works.
They were never thrown away.
They were simply put in their proper place.
Works are not the root of salvation.
They are its fruit.
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Read that slowly.
Not saved by them.
Saved for them.
Ephesians 2:8–9 protects the Gospel from legalism.
Ephesians 2:10 protects grace from becoming an excuse for lawlessness.
The same Paul who says salvation is “not from works” immediately says that those created in Christ Jesus are created “for good works.”
There is no contradiction.
There is an order.
Grace comes first.
Salvation comes from God.
Then the life touched by grace begins to change.
This is why biblical Christianity can simultaneously proclaim that salvation is completely undeserved and insist that genuine faith does not leave a person comfortably unchanged.
Good works are not the price of adoption.
They are the family resemblance that begins appearing in the adopted child.
Imagine an apple tree.
You do not tape apples onto a dead tree and declare it alive.
Life must exist first.
But when the tree is genuinely alive and healthy, fruit eventually appears.
Jesus Himself used the language of fruit when speaking about the reality revealed through a person's life.
This also helps us understand James.
James writes:
At first glance someone might think James is contradicting Paul.
Paul: not by works.
James: faith without works is dead.
But they are confronting different errors.
Paul destroys the idea that works can earn justification before God.
James destroys the idea that merely claiming to possess faith, while producing no evidence of living faith, should automatically be treated as saving faith.
Paul asks, in effect, “Can your works earn your salvation?”
No.
James asks, “Can a faith that never produces fruit reasonably be called living faith?”
No.
Good works do not purchase salvation.
They reveal the transforming activity that salvation produces.
Even here, we need humility.
Christians still stumble.
Christians still need confession.
Christians still wage war against the flesh.
Sanctification is not the claim that every genuine believer instantly becomes flawless.
John wrote to believers:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).
Then immediately:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
The Christian life is therefore not sinless perfection.
But neither is it peaceful surrender to sin.
There is a difference between falling in battle and making peace with the enemy.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and building a home inside it while demanding that grace never confront you.
Grace forgives.
Grace also teaches.
Titus 2:11–12 says:
“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly…”
Notice what teaches the believer to reject ungodliness.
Grace.
Biblical grace is not God shrugging at sin.
Grace is God rescuing sinners from sin's guilt, breaking sin's dominion, teaching His people a new way to live, and ultimately bringing them into the presence of Christ.
Grace does not whisper, “Your sin does not matter.”
Grace points toward the crucified Son of God and says, “Your sin mattered enough for this.”
Then grace looks at the forgiven sinner and says, “Now follow Him.”
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove something to God.
Maybe nobody else knows.
People see your Christianity.
God sees the exhaustion beneath it.
You serve because you are afraid to disappoint Him.
You give because you are afraid He will stop blessing you.
You pray because missing a day makes you feel spiritually disqualified.
You compare yourself with Christians who seem stronger.
And whenever you fail, you crawl back toward God like an employee expecting termination instead of a child running toward a Father.
Listen carefully.
Your obedience matters deeply.
But your obedience is a terrible savior.
There was only One qualified for that position.
Jesus Christ.
He lived the righteousness you could not produce.
He bore sin on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Your hope is not that you will eventually become impressive enough to make Calvary unnecessary.
Your hope is Christ.
Christ when you are strong.
Christ when you are trembling.
Christ when temptation screams.
Christ when repentance hurts.
Christ when you have nothing impressive left to say about yourself.
Christ.
That is why the Gospel is such devastating news for pride and such breathtaking news for broken people.
The Gospel closes the courtroom door on boasting.
Nobody will stand before God and say, “Look what I did to deserve this.”
The redeemed will forever have reason to say, in essence, “Look what Christ has done.”
But there is another side.

If you claim to have encountered this grace while deliberately refusing Christ's lordship, refusing repentance, loving darkness, and using “grace” as permission to remain untouched by the Savior you profess, Scripture gives no encouragement for that kind of presumption.
Jesus did not die merely to improve our vocabulary.
He saves people.
He changes people.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes through battles nobody else can see.
But grace moves us toward Christ.
This means your good works matter enormously—just not as currency for heaven.
Feed someone because Christ loved you.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Give because your treasure no longer owns you.
Serve because your King became a servant.
Tell the truth because you belong to the One who is Truth.
Fight lust because your body belongs to Christ.
Care for the forgotten because your Savior came looking for you when you were lost.
Open Scripture because you want to know the God who rescued you.
Pray because through Christ you have access to the Father.
Do you see the difference?
Legalism says, “I obey so God will love me.”
The Gospel says, “In Christ I have encountered a love I could never earn, therefore I want my life to belong to Him.”
Legalism asks, “How much must I do before I am enough?”
Grace says, “Christ is enough; now let my life become an offering of gratitude to Him.”
And that brings us to something uncomfortable even for Christian ministries to say.
You do not need to buy a book to receive God's forgiveness.
You cannot purchase grace from us.
We cannot sell you favor with God.
Jesus Christ alone saves.

But if Gospel-centered teaching has strengthened you, if these articles have helped you open your Bible again, if they have reached you during nights when you were struggling, or if you believe resources like this should continue reaching believers, seekers, wounded Christians, and people who may never walk into a church building, then supporting this work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
Not to earn God's love.
Because in Christ, grace has already taught you that His love cannot be bought.
Someone you know may still believe God only loves good people.
Someone may have failed last night and believes Jesus wants nothing more to do with them.
Someone may be hiding behind religious performance.
Someone may be using grace as an excuse not to repent.
Someone may desperately need to understand the difference between being saved by works and being saved for good works.
What have you been trusting more—Christ's finished work or your own performance?
If this exposed a hidden attempt to earn God's acceptance, comment, “Jesus, I trust Your grace.”
If you are still fighting sin and refusing to surrender your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If shame has exhausted your spirit lately, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ is rebuilding areas of your life nobody else can see, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if grace has finally made you tired of pretending, comment, “no more hiding.”
Your honesty may become the sentence another struggling believer needs to read tonight.
Let it be gratitude.
Let it be generosity.
Let it be partnership.
Let it be one small way of saying, “If Christ-centered truth helped reach me, I want to help it reach someone else.”
Because ultimately Ephesians 2:8–10 leaves us with something far greater than a theological slogan.
It leaves us with a completely different life.
We were dead.
God made us alive.
We were guilty.
Christ became our hope.
We could not earn salvation.
God gave grace.
We could not boast.
Christ received the glory.
And now the people who could never save themselves are sent into the world to live lives shaped by the Savior who did.
Your works cannot carry you to the cross.
The cross carries you into a life of good works.
Your obedience cannot rewrite your guilty verdict.
Jesus can.
Your past does not become beautiful because the scandal was imaginary.
The scandal was real.
The sin was real.
The guilt was real.
The wounds were real.
The cross was real.
The grave was real.
And the resurrection was real.
That is why grace is not sentimental Christianity.
Grace cost blood.
Grace entered our scandal.
Grace met sinners where they actually were.
Grace did not call evil good.
Grace conquered evil with something we could never manufacture for ourselves—the saving work of Jesus Christ.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what you have hidden.
Stop bargaining with God.
Stop trying to impress the One who already knows everything.
Stop treating good works as payment.
Stop treating grace as permission.
Come again to Christ.
Then rise.
Obey.
Love.
Serve.
Give.
Forgive.
Fight sin.
Walk in the good works God has prepared for His people.
Not desperately trying to become your own savior.
But because you finally understand that you already needed One.
And His name is Jesus.
But whatever you do, never confuse the response with the Rescue.
The Rescue is Jesus.
And when all your religious trophies have fallen from your hands, when your excuses have finally gone silent, and when you have nothing left to offer God except empty hands of faith, remember this:
The hands that could never earn salvation are exactly the hands grace teaches to serve after they have received it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU NEVER TOUCHED THEM—SO WHY DID JESUS CALL IT ADULTERY?
paragraphs:
YOU NEVER TOUCHED THEM—SO WHY DID JESUS CALL IT ADULTERY?
What Jesus Meant When He Said Lust Can Begin in the Heart—and Why His Terrifying Words Were Never Meant to Leave the Guilty Without Hope
There are sins nobody sees.
No hotel room.
No secret apartment.
No physical affair.
No incriminating message your spouse accidentally discovers.
No church scandal.
No public confession.
Nothing anyone could screenshot and send around.

You can sit in church with your Bible open, sing about holiness, hug your family afterward, shake the pastor’s hand, post a Scripture verse before bed—and still carry a private world inside you that nobody knows exists.
Except Jesus.
And perhaps that is why His words in the Sermon on the Mount can feel so frighteningly personal.
Jesus said:
“Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις.”
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’”
Then He went deeper.
“ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28.
Read those words slowly.
Because Jesus just walked past the locked door.
Past the browser history.
Past the outward reputation.
Past the carefully managed Christian image.
Straight into the heart.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Have I ever physically committed adultery?”
The question becomes:
“What have I been allowing my heart to do when nobody is watching?”
That question changes everything.
But before shame takes this passage somewhere Jesus did not take it, something important needs to be understood.
Jesus was not saying that noticing that another human being is physically attractive is automatically adultery.
He was not declaring that every involuntary thought, temptation, or momentary awareness makes someone guilty of the completed sin He describes.
The Greek wording matters.
Matthew records:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
The word translated “looking” comes from βλέπω—blepō.
But the force of the sentence does not rest on seeing alone.
The crucial expression is:
“πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι”
pros to epithymēsai.
It expresses looking directed toward desire—looking with the purpose of lusting.
That is different from simply possessing eyes.
Different from recognizing beauty.
Different from temptation arriving unexpectedly.

Jesus is exposing something deeper: the deliberate gaze that welcomes lust, feeds it, returns to it, imagines, consumes, and inwardly turns another person into the object of sexual desire outside the holiness God intended.
Temptation may knock.
Jesus is talking about opening the door, pulling up a chair, and feeding it dinner.
And some people reading this know exactly what that means.
Because sometimes the first look really was accidental.
But the second wasn't.
Sometimes the image appeared unexpectedly.
But going back wasn't accidental.
Sometimes the thought entered without permission.
But keeping it alive became a choice.
Sometimes you told yourself:
“I would never actually do anything.”
And perhaps you haven't.
But Jesus refuses to let physical restraint become camouflage for inward surrender.
Because Jesus does not merely want faithful bodies.
He wants faithful hearts.
The word Matthew uses is καρδίᾳ—kardia.
Heart.
In biblical thought, the heart is not merely the place of romantic emotion. It describes the inner person—the realm of desire, intention, thought, will, and moral direction.
Jesus is saying something devastatingly simple:
Sin does not suddenly become serious when somebody catches you.
It was already serious when your heart began making peace with it.
That is uncomfortable because human beings are remarkably skilled at measuring righteousness by comparison.
“At least I never cheated.”
“At least I never slept with anyone.”
“At least nobody got hurt.”
“At least my spouse doesn't know.”
“At least it's only pornography.”
“At least it's only fantasy.”
“At least it's only looking.”
“At least it's only in my mind.”
And Jesus quietly removes the words “at least.”
Because the kingdom of God is not built upon learning how close we can stand to darkness without technically stepping into it.
Jesus wants the heart.
All of it.
The hidden room too.
Especially the hidden room.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop pretending.
Maybe nobody knows what happens after midnight.
Maybe nobody knows what you erase.
Maybe your spouse thinks everything is fine.
Maybe your parents think you're fine.
Maybe the people at church think you're strong.
Maybe you are the person others ask for spiritual advice.
Yet there is a private battle behind the screen.
Pornography.
Fantasy.
Secret messages.
Replaying someone's body in your imagination.
Following accounts you know awaken something destructive.
Returning to pictures you know you should leave alone.
Emotionally feeding an attraction toward someone who does not belong to you.
Looking longer because something inside you wants more.
And afterward comes the familiar silence.
Delete.
Close.
Clear history.
Put the phone down.
Promise God again.
“Never again.”
Then morning comes.
Life continues.
Nobody knows.
But you know.
And God knows.
This is where many people make another dangerous mistake.
They hear Jesus exposing their sin and assume He is pushing them away.
But look at who is speaking.
This is Jesus Christ.
The One who exposes darkness because He came to rescue people from darkness.
The One who tells the truth about sin because lies cannot heal us.
The One who refuses to rename bondage “freedom” simply to protect our feelings.
Jesus does not expose the wound because He enjoys watching us bleed.
The Great Physician exposes the wound because hidden wounds cannot be treated while we insist they aren't there.
That is why the next words of Jesus sound so severe.
“If your right eye causes you to sin…”
The Greek says:
“εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ὁ δεξιὸς σκανδαλίζει σε…”
And Jesus continues with shocking imagery about tearing it out and throwing it away. Then He says essentially the same concerning the right hand.
Matthew 5:29–30.
Jesus is using deliberately radical language to communicate the deadly seriousness of sin.
The answer is not literal self-mutilation.
Removing an eye cannot remove lust from the heart.
A blind person can still lust.
Removing a hand cannot regenerate the soul.
Jesus has already identified the battlefield.
The heart.
His language demands ruthless repentance.
Whatever continually feeds the sin must stop being treated as harmless.
That might mean deleting an app.
Ending a secret conversation.
Unfollowing an account.
Installing accountability software.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Confessing to a mature believer.
Ending access to something you repeatedly use for sin.
Walking away from a relationship that survives on secrecy.
Changing routines.
Stopping the excuses.
Not because these actions purchase forgiveness.
They don't.
Not because discipline saves you.
It cannot.
But genuine repentance does not keep building comfortable furniture inside the room it claims to be leaving.
Jesus takes sin seriously because sin destroys what God loves.
Lust teaches us to consume people who bear God's image.
It separates bodies from souls.
It trains the imagination to ask, “What can this person give me?” instead of, “How should this person be honored before God?”
It can slowly teach husbands to compare their wives with fantasies no real woman was created to satisfy.
It can teach wives to emotionally or sexually fantasize about someone other than the covenant partner beside them.
It can train single people to rehearse intimacy without covenant, sacrifice, responsibility, or love.
And pornography magnifies the deception by turning someone's body into content.
Swipe.
Watch.
Consume.
Close.
Find another.
But there is a human being on that screen.
A person made in the image of God.
A person with a childhood.
A person with wounds you cannot see.
A person Jesus commands you not merely to avoid touching unlawfully, but to learn to see differently.
Christian purity is not pretending bodies aren't beautiful.
It is learning to see human beings as more than bodies.
It is recovering holy vision.
And if this article is hurting right now, please keep reading.
Because conviction is not the end of this story.
The Gospel is.
Maybe you've already failed.
Maybe repeatedly.
Maybe you stopped counting years ago.
Maybe pornography has followed you from adolescence into marriage.
Maybe you committed actual adultery.
Maybe your marriage shattered because of what you did.
Maybe someone trusted you and you betrayed them.
Maybe you were exposed publicly.
Maybe your scandal has a name.
Maybe yours has never left the heart.
Either way, Christianity does not begin with good people congratulating themselves for being cleaner than everybody else.
It begins with sinners who need a Savior.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not lower God's standard until our sin becomes acceptable.
He does something infinitely more costly.
He bears the judgment sinners deserve.
The same Jesus who preached Matthew 5 would eventually walk toward a cross.
He would be stripped.
Mocked.
Shamed.
Crucified.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because sin was so serious that redemption would cost blood.
And because His love was so great that He willingly gave His life.
At the cross, holiness and mercy are not enemies.
They meet.
Christ died for sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And therefore the person trapped in lust does not have to choose between pretending to be innocent and drowning forever in condemnation.
There is another way.
Confession.
Repentance.
Faith.
Grace.
Transformation.
Jesus.
The Gospel does not say:
“Clean yourself up enough and maybe Christ will receive you.”
The Gospel announces that sinners can come to Christ because Christ is the Savior sinners desperately need.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace actually makes real repentance possible.
You stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
You bring the hidden thing into His light.
You call sin what God calls it.
You ask forgiveness.
You turn.
And when you stumble, you do not turn your failure into permission to surrender.
You run back to Christ.
Again.
Not casually.
Not cheaply.
Not treating grace as a license.
But believing that the blood of Jesus is stronger than the shame telling you to hide.
There is a difference between a believer battling sin and a person making peace with sin.
Battle means there may be scars.
Battle means sometimes you crawl.
Battle means sometimes you need another Christian beside you.
Battle means confession may be humiliating.
Battle means boundaries may feel inconvenient.
Battle means you stop asking, “How much can I get away with?”
And begin asking:
“What must I remove because Jesus is worth more?”
Somebody needs that question tonight.
Not:
“How close can I get?”
But:
“How free do I actually want to become?”
Because perhaps the deepest tragedy of lust is not simply that it makes us desire something forbidden.
It can make us forget that Christ Himself is better.
Better than the image.
Better than the fantasy.
Better than five minutes of secret pleasure followed by another night of shame.
Better than the person you've been imagining.
Better than the affair.
Better than the hidden account.
Better than the version of yourself you keep feeding in darkness.
Jesus is better.
And purity is not God withholding happiness from you.
Purity is God teaching your desires that they were created for something holier than consumption.
So tonight, perhaps repentance begins quietly.
Maybe nobody applauds.
Maybe there is no dramatic music.
Maybe it is simply you sitting alone with God and finally refusing to lie.
“Jesus… this has owned part of me.”
“This is what I've been watching.”
“This is who I've been fantasizing about.”
“This is what I've been hiding.”
“I cannot keep calling slavery freedom.”
“Forgive me.”
“Clean me.”
“Teach me to see people differently.”
“Give me a heart that wants You more than this.”
And then get up and make repentance practical.
Delete what needs deleting.
End what needs ending.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek mature Christian accountability.

If your sexual behavior has become compulsive and you repeatedly cannot stop despite serious consequences, seeking help from a qualified Christian counselor or other appropriate professional is not spiritual defeat. Wisdom does not compete with prayer.
Bring the darkness into light.
Because the enemy loves secrecy.
Christ calls people into truth.
And hear this carefully:
Your worst sexual sin does not have to become the final sentence of your life.
Peter's denial was not his final chapter.
The Samaritan woman's broken relational history was not the end of her story.

The sexually immoral in Corinth were not told that transformation was impossible; Paul reminded believers that some of them had once lived in grievous sins, but had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
The Gospel specializes in impossible rewrites.
That is why we keep saying it:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by making sin respectable.

He rewrites everything by forgiving sinners, cleansing the guilty, transforming hearts, restoring what can be restored, teaching His people holiness, and giving new identities to people who thought their worst chapter had already named them forever.
Maybe your scandal happened with another person.
Maybe yours happened behind a locked screen.
Maybe yours happened entirely inside your imagination.
Jesus still sees the heart.
And Jesus still saves sinners who come to Him.
So be honest.
Did this expose something you have been hiding?
You don't need to describe the details publicly.
But you can stop hiding spiritually.
Your testimony may become the sentence somebody else desperately needed to read tonight.
And please don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It never could.
Christ alone saves, by grace, received through faith.
But if you want your digital life to glorify God, one practical way is to use the reach He has placed in your hands to put biblical truth in front of someone who may never walk through a church door.
There may be a husband silently losing a battle nobody knows about.
A wife carrying betrayal she cannot explain.
A teenager learning sexuality from pornography.
A believer convinced God could never want them again.
A friend smiling publicly while privately drowning.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for supporting your local church, caring for your family, helping the needy, or practicing generosity wherever God calls you.
But if this ministry has genuinely served you and you want to help it reach more people, your support allows you to participate practically in that mission.
Go to Jesus.
The point was never to make you stare endlessly at your dirt.
The point was to make you see your need for the Savior.
The Savior who sees the browser history.
The Savior who sees the fantasy.
The Savior who sees the second look.
The Savior who sees the affair.
The Savior who sees the tears afterward.
The Savior who sees the years of hiding.
And still calls sinners to come into the light.
Not so they can remain what they were.
So He can transform them.
Perhaps you came to this article wondering whether a hidden look could really matter that much.
Now you know why Jesus went after the heart.
Because long before sin becomes a scandal people can see, it often becomes a secret the heart has learned to protect.
And grace begins when you stop protecting what is destroying you.
Remember this when temptation whispers your name again:
Jesus did not expose your hidden room so you would die inside it. He opened the door because He intends to lead you out.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS “FOLLOW YOUR HEART” BIBLICAL?
paragraphs:
IS “FOLLOW YOUR HEART” BIBLICAL?
The advice sounds beautiful. It feels empowering. Millions repeat it as wisdom. But what if the heart you’ve been told to trust is the very thing Jesus came to transform?
“Follow your heart.”
You’ve heard it in movies.
You’ve seen it printed on shirts, journals, coffee mugs, graduation cards, Instagram captions, and inspirational posts.
Maybe someone whispered it to you when you were confused.
“Just follow your heart.”
Maybe you whispered it to yourself.
And perhaps that is what makes this conversation uncomfortable.
Because “follow your heart” sounds compassionate.
It sounds courageous.
It sounds almost spiritual.
But there is one devastating problem.
Jesus never told you to follow your heart.
He said something far more costly.
“Follow Me.”
And there is an enormous difference between the two.
One puts your feelings on the throne.
The other puts Jesus Christ there.
One asks, “What does my heart want?”
The other asks, “Lord, what do You want?”
One assumes the deepest desires inside us must be trustworthy because they feel sincere.
The other recognizes something Scripture repeatedly teaches us:
Sincerity does not make something holy.
You can sincerely want something that destroys you.
You can sincerely love someone you should not be sleeping with.
You can sincerely believe bitterness is justified.
You can sincerely feel that revenge would bring closure.
You can sincerely desire money, recognition, attention, control, or pleasure.
You can sincerely believe walking away from obedience will finally make you happy.
And you can be completely sincere...
and completely wrong.
That is why one of the most culturally celebrated pieces of advice becomes spiritually dangerous when it replaces the authority of God:
“Follow your heart.”
Jeremiah gives us a disturbing diagnosis.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?”
Jeremiah 17:9
The Hebrew is even more striking.
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל
ʿāqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl
The word translated “heart” is לֵב — lev.
In biblical Hebrew, the heart is not merely the place where romantic emotions live. It can describe the inner person—the center of thought, desire, intention, will, and moral decision.
And Jeremiah describes this heart with עָקֹב — ʿāqōḇ, a word carrying the sense of being deceitful, insidious, or difficult to trust.
Then comes language traditionally rendered “desperately wicked,” though many modern translations render the Hebrew אָנֻשׁ — ʾānush along the lines of “desperately sick” or “incurably sick.”
Either way, Jeremiah’s point is devastatingly clear.
Our fallen inner life cannot function as our ultimate moral compass.
Read that again.
Your feelings are real, but they are not God.
Your desires matter, but they are not Scripture.
Your emotions deserve to be acknowledged, but they were never designed to sit on the throne.
And maybe this is where the article stops being about “culture”...
and starts being about you.
Because there was probably a moment when your heart told you something.
“You deserve this.”
“God will understand.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You need this relationship.”
“You can repent later.”
“Just one more time.”
“You’ve suffered enough. Do whatever makes you happy.”
“Forgiveness is weakness.”
“Your identity is whatever you feel it is.”
“God’s way is too restrictive.”
“Choose yourself.”
And somewhere beneath all the excuses, there was another voice.
Quieter.
Holier.
Painfully clear.
You knew what Scripture said.
But you wanted what your heart said.
That is the battle.
And it is older than you think.
Go back to the beginning.
The serpent did not merely offer Eve fruit.
He challenged whether God should have the final authority over what was good.
Genesis says that Eve saw the tree was good for food, pleasant to the eyes, and desirable for gaining wisdom.
It looked good.
It felt desirable.
It appeared reasonable.
And it was still rebellion.
HELLO. I AM HERE TO DESTROY YOU.
It often arrives looking beautiful.
Reasonable.
Comforting.
Liberating.
Even loving.
Sin can make chains look like wings.
It can make poison taste like freedom.
It can make disobedience feel like self-discovery.
Then, after you have followed it far enough, you look around and wonder:
“How did I get here?”
Maybe you know that feeling.
Maybe you followed your heart into a relationship and came out shattered.
Maybe you followed your anger until people you loved stopped recognizing you.
Maybe you followed your appetite until pleasure became slavery.
Maybe you followed ambition until success became your god.
Maybe you followed insecurity until strangers on a screen controlled how valuable you felt.
Maybe you followed loneliness into somebody’s bed.
Maybe you followed disappointment until you stopped praying.
Maybe you followed shame until you convinced yourself that God no longer wanted you.
Maybe your heart led you somewhere you swore you would never go.
And now you are reading an article about whether you should follow your heart...
while quietly wondering whether Jesus would still take you back.
Listen carefully.
That is where the Gospel enters the story.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people should learn to trust themselves more.
Christianity announces that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not come merely to validate everything already inside us.
He came to save us.
Forgive us.
Cleanse us.
Reconcile us to God.
Give us His Spirit.
Teach us obedience.
And transform us from the inside out.
This is why the biblical answer is deeper than simply saying:
“Never trust your feelings.”
Christianity does not teach emotional self-hatred.
God created human emotion.
Jesus Himself wept.
Jesus experienced compassion.
Jesus experienced sorrow.
Jesus loved.
Jesus grieved.
And in Gethsemane, Jesus showed us something extraordinarily important about the relationship between desire and obedience.
Facing the horror of the cross, He prayed:
“Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.”
Luke 22:42
That is not emotional denial.
That is holy surrender.
Jesus expressed the anguish truthfully...
and submitted Himself perfectly to the Father.
There is the pattern.
You do not have to pretend you feel nothing.
You bring what you feel before God.
You test what you feel against His truth.
And where your desires conflict with His will...
you surrender.
Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
Luke 9:23
The Greek makes the central command impossible to miss.
ἀκολουθείτω μοι
akoloutheitō moi
“Let him follow Me.”
Not:
Follow your impulses.
Follow your appetites.
Follow whatever makes you comfortable.
Follow whatever culture celebrates.
Follow whatever version of yourself demands the least surrender.
Follow Me.
Jesus Christ becomes the direction of the Christian life.
That means sometimes following Jesus will feel wonderful.
Sometimes it will feel terrifying.
Sometimes obedience will bring immediate peace.
Sometimes obedience will make you cry.
Sometimes following Jesus means walking away from something your flesh desperately wants.
Sometimes it means forgiving somebody your emotions want to punish.
Sometimes it means confessing something your pride desperately wants hidden.
Sometimes it means remaining sexually pure when your body screams otherwise.
Sometimes it means telling the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
Sometimes it means staying faithful when nobody applauds you.
Sometimes it means saying:
“Jesus, I want this...
but I want You more.”
That sentence can break chains.
Because the Christian life is not about becoming heartless.
It is about receiving a new heart.
Centuries before Christ, God promised through Ezekiel:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.”
Ezekiel 36:26
The Hebrew phrase is breathtaking:
לֵב חָדָשׁ
lev chadash
“A new heart.”
Notice the Gospel-shaped difference.
God’s answer to the corruption within humanity is not:
“Follow it harder.”
His answer is transformation.
This reaches its fulfillment in the new life Christ gives His people.
The apostle Paul writes:
2 Corinthians 5:17
That changes the question entirely.
The question is no longer simply:
“Should Christians follow their hearts?”
The better question becomes:
Who is forming your heart?
Because a heart surrendered to Christ should increasingly desire what pleases Christ.
The goal is not that you spend your entire Christian life terrified of every emotion.
The goal is sanctification.
God changes what you love.
He changes what you hunger for.
He changes what disgusts you.
He changes what satisfies you.
He teaches your heart to beat differently.
Psalm 37:4 says:
“Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.”
That verse is sometimes treated as though God were promising to finance whatever dreams happen to occupy our imagination.
But notice the order.
Delight yourself in the LORD.
God comes first.
As He increasingly becomes your delight, your desires themselves are being brought beneath His rule.
And Psalm 51 shows us what to pray when our hearts have gone terribly wrong.
After David’s devastating sin, he did not pray:
“God, help me trust myself again.”
He prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Psalm 51:10
The Hebrew is unforgettable:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
lev tahor bera-li Elohim
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
That word בְּרָא — bara, “create,” matters.
David knew he needed something deeper than reputation management.
He needed God to work within him.
Maybe you do too.
Maybe behind your carefully edited photographs, church attendance, Bible verses, Christian captions, smiles, and “I’m blessed” answers...
your heart is exhausted from hiding.
There are things nobody knows.
Search histories.
Messages.
Fantasies.
Resentments.
Compromises.
Secret addictions.
Jealousies.
Questions.
A relationship you know is pulling you from Christ.
A wound you turned into bitterness.
A habit you keep promising God you will stop.
Perhaps you have spent so long defending what your heart wants that you have stopped asking whether God calls it good.
You do not need another motivational slogan.
You need Jesus.
And here is the scandal of grace:
He already knows.
Jesus is not discovering your darkness while reading this article.
He knows.
The cross proves that Christianity does not minimize sin.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
But the cross also proves that God's grace reaches people who cannot rescue themselves.
Christ “died for our sins according to the scriptures.”
He was buried.
He rose again.
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is good news about what Jesus Christ has done.
You do not clean yourself enough to become worthy of the cross.
You come to Christ because you aren't.
Repentance means you stop negotiating with the sin Jesus died to save you from.
You turn toward Christ.
You confess.
You surrender.
You believe.
You follow.
And when you stumble, you do not make peace with the darkness.
You run again toward the Light.
First John tells believers:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is grace.
There is still a Savior.
Maybe your heart has lied to you for years.
Maybe it told you that you were too dirty.
Too damaged.
Too addicted.
Too compromised.
Too hypocritical.
Too far gone.
Maybe the same heart that once whispered, “Do it,” now whispers:
“God could never forgive you for doing it.”
Do you see the cruelty?
First sin seduces.
Then shame condemns.
But Jesus interrupts both.
The cross says your sin is worse than your excuses admit...
and His grace is greater than your shame wants you to believe.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Not calling darkness light.
Not rewriting God's commandments to make ourselves comfortable.
Grace looks directly at the wreckage...
and announces that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting truth.
By rewriting lives.
He turns rebels into sons and daughters.
The ashamed into witnesses.
The addicted into testimonies of freedom.
The sexually broken into stories of redemption.
The bitter into forgivers.
The proud into worshipers.
The spiritually dead into people made alive in Christ.
The scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Jesus can write grace where you thought only shame remained.
So perhaps we need to retire the sentence:
“Follow your heart.”
Replace it with something far safer.
Bring your heart to Jesus.
When your heart says something, test it.
Does this agree with Scripture?
Does this glorify Christ?
Does this require me to disobey something God has clearly revealed?
Is this drawing me toward holiness or merely toward comfort?
Am I calling something “peace” because God approves it—or because I finally stopped resisting temptation?
Am I asking God to guide me...
or asking Him to approve a decision I already made?
Those questions hurt.
But some wounds are surgical.
Hebrews describes God's Word as “quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword.”
Sometimes Scripture comforts you.
Sometimes Scripture confronts you.
Sometimes it feels like God has placed His finger directly on the thing you hoped nobody would mention.
Do not run.
Conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It can become an invitation home.
Maybe this article found you at exactly the uncomfortable moment when you needed to stop calling disobedience “following your heart.”
Then be honest before God.
You do not need impressive religious language.
“Jesus, I have followed myself more than I have followed You. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to want what You want. I surrender.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light begins with refusing to keep pretending.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer in a battle.
Let believers pray for believers.
Let testimonies meet confession.
Let grace meet honesty.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because somebody you know may be following a heart that is quietly leading them away from Jesus.
There may be a night when your feelings become louder than your faith and you need to read these truths again.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to become another destination for religious entertainment.
We want people opening Scripture.
Knowing Christ.
Repenting honestly.
Growing deeper.
Living differently.
And helping others do the same.
Supporting a ministry does not earn God's favor, purchase spiritual blessing, or make someone more faithful than those who cannot give.
Grace cannot be bought.
But generosity can be one voluntary way believers help Gospel-centered work reach others.
do not miss the greater invitation.
Jesus is calling you to something infinitely more important than supporting a page.
He is calling you to follow Him.
Your heart will change.
Your feelings will rise and fall.
Culture will reinvent morality.
Popular advice will come and go.
But Jesus Christ remains Lord.
So when your heart whispers one thing and Christ says another...
follow Christ.
When obedience costs you...
follow Christ.
When nobody understands...
follow Christ.
When temptation feels beautiful...
follow Christ.
When repentance feels humiliating...
follow Christ.
When shame tells you there is no road home...
run to Christ.
And someday, after grace has carried you farther than your feelings ever could, you may look back at the places your heart wanted to take you and whisper:
“Thank You, Jesus, for loving me enough not to leave me there.”
Because perhaps the greatest freedom was never getting everything your heart wanted.
Perhaps the greatest freedom was finally giving your heart to the One who knew how to make it new.
Your heart was never meant to be your Savior. It was meant to belong to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE’S STRANGEST FAILED-MARRIAGE CONVERSATION MIGHT BE IN JUDGES 15
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S STRANGEST FAILED-MARRIAGE CONVERSATION MIGHT BE IN JUDGES 15

He came back carrying a young goat, expecting to see his wife. Her father met him at the door and essentially said, “I thought you hated her, so I gave her to your friend.” What follows is not a strange Bible story meant to entertain us. It is a terrifying picture of what happens when wounded people keep answering wounds with wounds—and why we desperately need a Savior greater than Samson.
There are sentences in the Bible so strange that you almost have to read them twice.
Judges 15 opens with one of them.
Samson shows up at his wife’s home carrying a young goat.
That is already a sentence most modern readers were not expecting.
But the goat is not the strangest part.
The door is.

Because Samson apparently arrives believing that whatever happened between him and his wife can somehow continue. He has been angry. He has walked away. His wedding celebration ended disastrously. Blood has already been spilled.
But now he comes back.
And the man standing between Samson and his wife has news for him.
She has been given to someone else.
Not just anyone else.
His companion.
His wedding companion.
And then, as though this shattered relationship can be repaired by exchanging one woman for another, her father offers Samson her younger sister instead.
It is bizarre.
It is painful.
It is morally chaotic.
And buried inside this strange ancient conversation is something painfully modern.
Because some of us know what it is like to discover that while we were angry, something died.
While we were refusing to speak, somebody made a decision.
While we were rehearsing what they did to us, the relationship changed.
While we were telling ourselves, “I’ll deal with it later,” later arrived without asking permission.
And suddenly you are standing at a door you thought would still open.
But it doesn’t.
Judges records the moment in Hebrew:
“אָמֹר אָמַרְתִּי כִּי־שָׂנֹא שְׂנֵאתָהּ”
Amor amarti ki-sano s’netah.
The father’s words carry an emphatic sense: “I really thought that you utterly hated her.”
The Hebrew construction intensifies the statement.
Not merely dislike.
Not merely frustration.
He thought Samson hated her.
So he gave her away.
That does not make the father’s decision righteous. Scripture records what happened; it does not thereby endorse everything its characters do.
That distinction matters enormously in Judges.

Judges is deliberately filled with human beings doing horrifying, impulsive, compromised things. The book increasingly shows what life looks like when God’s people descend into spiritual and moral disorder.
And Samson is standing right in the middle of that disorder.
His story is uncomfortable because Samson can be extraordinarily gifted and extraordinarily uncontrolled almost in the same breath.
Called by God.
Set apart from birth.
Empowered by the Spirit.
And still capable of terrible choices.
That should disturb every Christian who has ever confused gifting with maturity.
You can know Scripture and still need repentance.
You can have influence and still have wounds controlling you.
You can be used by God and still have areas of your heart you have refused to surrender to God.
You can win battles publicly while losing wars privately.
Samson had strength that terrified armies.
But strength was never the same thing as holiness.
And perhaps that is why this strange doorway scene hurts so much.
He arrives carrying something that looks almost ordinary.
A gift.
A visit.
Maybe an expectation that the relationship is still there.
But relationships do not survive merely because one person eventually comes back.
Something catastrophic happened before Judges 15 ever began.
Go backward one chapter.
Samson had married a Philistine woman from Timnah despite his parents’ objections. During the wedding feast he gave thirty men a riddle. The men could not solve it, so they threatened Samson’s wife:
Get the answer from your husband…
or we will burn you and your father’s household.
Imagine her fear.
She pressures Samson until he finally reveals the answer. She gives it to the men. They answer Samson’s riddle.
Samson realizes what happened.
His response is not quiet reconciliation.
Judges 14:19 says that he went to Ashkelon, killed thirty men, took their belongings, paid what he owed from the wager, and returned angrily to his father’s house.
Then comes the sentence that sets up everything in chapter 15:
Samson’s wife was given to his companion.
Now Samson comes back.
That context changes the entire scene.
This is not simply “Samson’s wife was stolen.”
The story is a collision of fear, betrayal, threats, anger, vengeance, assumptions, abandonment, exploitation, and violence.
Almost everybody is reacting.
Almost nobody is healing.
And that is where Judges 15 suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because maybe your weapon was never Samson’s jawbone.
Maybe it was silence.
Maybe you punished someone by disappearing.
Maybe you wanted them to feel what you felt.
Maybe you withheld affection.
Maybe you kept screenshots.
Maybe you told everybody except the person you were actually angry with.
Maybe you learned to say “I’m fine” while quietly building a courtroom inside your head.
Maybe somebody betrayed you, and somewhere along the way their sin became permission for yours.
That is where wounded hearts become dangerous.
Pain begins as something that happened to us.
Then, if we refuse to surrender it to God, pain can become something operating through us.
Samson hears what happened to his wife, and the story does not become a reconciliation story.
It becomes retaliation.

He catches three hundred animals—traditionally translated “foxes,” though the Hebrew word שׁוּעָלִים (shu'alim) can refer to foxes or jackals—pairs them, attaches torches, and releases them into Philistine agricultural land.
Grain burns.
Vineyards burn.
Olive groves burn.
Then the Philistines ask why.
They discover that Samson did it because his wife had been given to his companion.
And their response?
More fire.
They burn the woman and her father.
Read that slowly.
A woman who had previously been threatened with burning in Judges 14 is eventually killed by fire in Judges 15.
The thing she feared still found her.
Then Samson sees what they have done and retaliates again.
Violence answers violence.
Revenge answers revenge.
Wounded people wound other people, who wound more people, who create new wounds requiring new revenge.
And suddenly everybody has a reason.
That may be one of the most frightening things about sin.
Everybody eventually has a reason.
“I did this because they did that.”
“I said that because she said this.”
“I cheated because I felt neglected.”
“I became cold because he hurt me.”
“I destroyed their reputation because they destroyed mine.”
“I stopped praying because God disappointed me.”
“I became bitter because nobody apologized.”
Human beings are remarkably skilled at turning pain into permission.
Samson himself says in Judges 15:3, in effect, that this time he considers himself justified in harming the Philistines.
Later the Philistines explain that they have come to capture Samson “to do to him as he did to us.”
And Samson eventually expresses the same logic:
“As they did unto me, so have I done unto them.”
There it is.
The entire cycle of vengeance compressed into one sentence.
They did it to me.
So I did it to them.
And somewhere tonight, somebody reading this is living by exactly that sentence.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe you worship with your hands raised.
Maybe you post verses.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
But deep inside you is a list.
Names.
Moments.
Betrayals.
Things said to you when you were twelve.
What your father did.
What your mother never did.
What your spouse hid.
What your friend said.
What that church leader mishandled.
What that person took from you.
And you may not be burning anyone’s fields.
But perhaps you have been carrying a torch.
That is where this story must eventually take us beyond Samson.
Because if Judges 15 were merely a lesson about controlling anger, it would not go deep enough.
The Bible’s answer to humanity’s cycle of sin is not simply “try harder to be nicer.”
We need rescue.
We need another Deliverer.
Samson was a deliverer in Israel, but he was a deeply flawed one.
And his imperfections make us long for Someone better.
Someone who would possess power without being corrupted by power.
Someone betrayed by people closest to Him without becoming consumed by revenge.
Someone falsely accused without retaliating in kind.
Someone mocked without needing to prove Himself.
Someone struck without surrendering Himself to hatred.
Someone abandoned by friends and still capable of saying words of forgiveness.
Someone who would not merely kill His enemies to save His people…
but would lay down His own life for sinners who had made themselves enemies of God.
Jesus Christ.
Samson carried wounds and set fields on fire.
Jesus carried a cross and opened the way to reconciliation.
Samson's story repeatedly spirals through retaliation.
Jesus breaks the logic of retaliation.
At Calvary, the cycle encounters something radically different.
Grace.
Not grace pretending evil does not matter.
Grace because evil matters so much that the Son of God bears judgment for sin.
The cross does not tell victims that their wounds are imaginary.
The cross tells us sin is so serious that redemption required blood.
But not yours.
His.
Jesus did not come to teach us how to hide our scandal better.
He came to save sinners.
That includes the sexually broken.
The furious.
The betrayed.
The betrayer.
The abandoned.
The religious hypocrite.
The addict.
The person who destroyed their marriage.
The person whose marriage was destroyed by someone else.
The person who cannot undo what happened.
The person ashamed of what they became after what happened.
The person thinking, “If everybody knew the whole story, nobody would look at me the same.”
Christ already knows the whole story.
And still the Gospel says:
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Be washed.
Be forgiven.
Be made new.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
It does not mean reconciliation is always immediately possible or safe, especially where abuse, coercion, or danger exists.
Biblical forgiveness is not permission for continued abuse.
But it does mean your sin does not have to write the final chapter of your life.
Neither does what somebody else did to you.
What happened to you matters.
What you did matters.
But neither one is greater than Jesus.
There are scandals grace does not excuse but can redeem.
There are stains Christ can cleanse.
There are chains He can break.
There are bitter hearts He can soften.
There are people who have spent years telling themselves, “This is just who I am now,” whom Christ can transform.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By entering the wreckage and making redemption possible.
Think again about that door in Judges 15.
Samson arrived expecting access to something that had changed while he was away.
Some of us keep doing that spiritually.
We keep assuming tomorrow belongs to us.
“I'll repent eventually.”
“I'll forgive later.”
“I'll deal with the pornography later.”
“I'll apologize when I'm ready.”
“I'll come back to God after I fix myself.”
“I'll surrender once life settles down.”
But you do not own tomorrow.
The Gospel does not call you to someday.
It calls you now.
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
Maybe your greatest danger is not that God has stopped calling.
Maybe it is that you have become frighteningly skilled at postponing your answer.
And maybe underneath all the Christian language, you are tired.
Tired of being angry.
Tired of replaying it.
Tired of secretly wanting somebody to suffer because you suffered.
Tired of pretending the marriage is fine.
Tired of hiding the addiction.
Tired of carrying shame into worship.
Tired of telling everybody “God is good” while privately wondering whether He could still want someone like you.
He does not ask you to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
Come because you cannot clean yourself.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who paid what you could never pay.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Romans 5 points us to the staggering reality that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
This is Christianity.
Not damaged people pretending they were never damaged.
Not guilty people pretending they never sinned.
Not strong people proving how strong they are.
Dead people receiving life.
Guilty people receiving pardon.
Enemies being reconciled.
Prodigals coming home.
Sinners becoming saints not because they successfully rewrote themselves…
but because Jesus saves.
So be honest.
What torch are you carrying?
Whose field are you still secretly trying to burn?
Whose name still changes your heartbeat?
What wound have you turned into permission?
What sin have you renamed “coping”?
What bitterness have you renamed “boundaries”?
What vengeance have you renamed “justice”?
And what would happen if, instead of carrying it for another year, you finally brought it into the light before Christ?
Not Facebook first.
Not your friends first.
Jesus.
“Lord, this is what they did.”
“Lord, this is what I did.”
“Lord, I hate what this has made me.”
“Lord, I cannot change myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
That prayer is not weakness.
That is where surrender begins.
Be real.
And if God has already brought you through a season you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what Jesus did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needs tonight.
Not because every paragraph feels comfortable.
We need grace too.

Following Gospel Warrior is not about building an audience around a page. The goal is to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the Gospel in front of people who are being discipled every day by everything else on their screens.
But if you want to help this particular work reach more people, your support matters.
Deeper discipleship.
Biblical nourishment.
Spiritual sharpening.
Encouragement when faith feels exhausted.
Truth when culture becomes noisy.
A place that continually points beyond Gospel Warrior and back to Jesus Christ.
Come to Christ.
Because Judges 15 leaves us staring at a world where everybody has been hurt, everybody has an explanation, and retaliation keeps producing another funeral.
The Gospel shows us another way.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A Savior.
Forgiveness that cost Him everything.
Grace strong enough to tell the truth about our sin without abandoning the sinner who repents and believes.
Perhaps you walked into this article thinking about Samson's strange marriage.
Perhaps somewhere along the way, you realized Scripture was talking about your heart.
That is not the moment to run.
That is the moment to come home.
Because the most frightening thing about carrying a torch long enough is that eventually you forget you were once only trying to illuminate your pain…
and start using it to burn everything around you.
Put the torch down.
Bring the wound to Jesus.
Bring the sin to Jesus.
Bring the failed marriage.
Bring the betrayal.
Bring the rage.
Bring the secret.
Bring the shame.
Bring the years you cannot recover.
Bring the version of yourself you wish nobody had ever met.
The hands stretched out on Calvary already know what human beings are capable of.
And those scarred hands are still able to save.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story.
It does not have authority to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR OWN DEAD” — WHY WOULD JESUS SAY SOMETHING THAT SOUNDS SO HARSH?
paragraphs:
“LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR OWN DEAD” — WHY WOULD JESUS SAY SOMETHING THAT SOUNDS SO HARSH?
One of Jesus’ most disturbing sentences may actually be one of His most urgent invitations to life—and the word hidden inside the disciple’s response may expose the excuse standing between you and Christ.
There are words of Jesus we love putting on walls.
“Come to me.”
“Do not be afraid.”
“Peace be with you.”
And then there are words like these.
“Let the dead bury their own dead.”
You read that sentence and something inside you almost recoils.
Jesus…
Really?
A man wants to bury his father, and that is Your answer?
Where is the compassion?
Where is the tenderness?
Where is the Jesus who wept at Lazarus’ tomb?

Maybe you have buried someone you loved. Maybe you have stood beside a coffin wishing you could hear one more laugh, receive one more embrace, say one more sentence you assumed you would have time to say.
If so, these words can sound especially brutal.
But before we accuse Jesus of lacking compassion, we need to slow down.
Because the Jesus who spoke these words is also the Jesus who wept when Lazarus died.
The Jesus who noticed a grieving widow walking behind the body of her only son.
The Jesus who, while hanging from a cross and struggling for breath, still made provision for His mother.
So whatever Luke 9:60 means, it cannot honestly mean that Jesus considers grief meaningless or that honoring family is sinful.
Something deeper is happening.
And when you see it, this strange sentence stops looking like an attack on grieving people.
It becomes a terrifyingly personal question:
What have you placed between the words “Lord” and “follow”?
Luke records the encounter with almost uncomfortable simplicity.
Jesus says to a man:
“Follow me.”
The man answers:
“Lord, first let me go and bury my father.”
Then comes the sentence that has disturbed readers for centuries:
“Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God.”
Matthew preserves the same piercing exchange and places the emphasis directly on Jesus’ call:
“Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
Matthew 8:22.
But there is something in the conversation that is easy to miss.
The New Testament was written here in Greek, and Luke’s Greek makes the collision startling.
Jesus’ invitation is:
Ἀκολούθει μοι — Akolouthei moi.
“Follow Me.”
But the man’s response contains a tiny word carrying enormous weight:
πρῶτον — prōton.
“First.”
Lord…
first.
That may be where this entire story opens.
The problem is not merely that the man wants to bury his father.
The problem exposed by the narrative is the question of priority.
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
The man effectively answers, “Yes, Lord…but first.”
And suddenly this ancient conversation becomes painfully modern.
“Lord, I’ll follow You…but first let me get my life together.”
“Jesus, I’ll surrender…but first let me enjoy this relationship.”
“I’ll forgive…but first they need to apologize.”
“I’ll repent…but first let me have a little more time.”
“I’ll serve You…but first let me become financially secure.”
“I’ll tell people about You…but first let me stop being afraid of what they think.”
“I’ll come back to church…but first I need to fix myself.”
“I’ll open my Bible again…but first life needs to calm down.”
“I’ll follow You, Lord…
but first.”
And perhaps some of the most dangerous words a human being can say to Jesus are not, “I hate You.”
They are:
“Not yet.”
Because “not yet” feels nothing like rebellion.
It feels reasonable.
Responsible.
Temporary.
Even respectable.
That is what makes it dangerous.
We need to be careful, however, not to manufacture historical certainty Scripture itself does not give us.
Was the man’s father already dead?
Was the funeral happening immediately?
Was “bury my father” a way of asking to remain home until his father eventually died?
Was Jesus’ statement connected with burial practices in which remains could later be gathered and reinterred?

Interpreters have proposed several possibilities. Ancient Jewish burial customs can illuminate the passage, and some commentators argue that the request may involve obligations extending beyond an immediate funeral. But the text itself does not give us enough information to declare every historical detail with certainty.
And perhaps we should not become so fascinated with reconstructing the man’s family circumstances that we miss what Luke actually tells us.
Jesus gives the meaning of the moment through the contrast:
The dead may bury their dead.
“But you…”
You have been called somewhere else.
You have been summoned to announce the Kingdom of God.
That “but you” changes everything.
The Greek of Luke 9:60 reads:
Ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς· σὺ δὲ ἀπελθὼν διάγγελλε τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ.
In straightforward English:
“Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, having gone, proclaim the kingdom of God.”
The shock is deliberate.
Jesus speaks of “dead” people burying “dead” people.
Obviously a physically dead person cannot conduct a funeral.

That is precisely why interpreters have long understood the first use of “dead” as referring in some sense to those outside the life and calling of the Kingdom, while the second refers to the physically deceased. Luke’s command immediately turns the disciple toward proclamation of God’s Kingdom.
Jesus is forcing a distinction between two kinds of existence.
There is breathing.
And there is life.
There is existing.
And there is following Christ.
There is maintaining everything expected of you.
And there is hearing the King call your name.
This is not Jesus saying funerals do not matter.
This is Jesus saying He matters ultimately.
That difference is enormous.
The same Lord who commands people to honor father and mother will not allow even something honorable to become greater than obedience to Him.
Because good things can become dangerous things when they become first things.
Family is good.
Work is good.
Responsibility is good.
Security is good.
Reputation can be good.
Planning can be wise.
But none of them can occupy the throne.
Only Christ belongs there.
And this is where the passage stops being an ancient theological puzzle and begins walking through your front door.
Because your “father’s burial” may not look anything like this man’s.
Yours might be the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The secret habit you keep promising to surrender eventually.
The resentment you have rehearsed for so long that anger now feels like part of your identity.
The career that has slowly become your god.
The approval of people whose opinions have become louder than Scripture.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The compromise you have renamed “struggling” because calling it sin would require repentance.
The church wound you now use as permission to stay far from Jesus.
The shame that whispers you need to clean yourself before you can come home.
The comfortable Christianity where Jesus can inspire you, encourage you, bless you, protect you and forgive you…
as long as He never interrupts your plans.
Then Christ walks directly into all of it.
And says:
Follow Me.
Not when you become impressive.
Not when your history becomes less embarrassing.
Not when temptation disappears.
Not when everybody understands.
Not after you have repaired yourself.
Follow Me.
And perhaps you whisper:
“Lord…”
That sounds promising.
“…first…”
And heaven suddenly touches the nerve.
Because Jesus is not applying for second place in your life.
He is Lord.
There is something else here we desperately need to understand.
Jesus’ severity is not the opposite of His love.
Sometimes it is an expression of it.
A doctor who discovers something deadly inside you does not love you by pretending everything is fine.
A firefighter does not whisper politely while your bedroom fills with smoke.
And Christ does not flatter us while we sleep spiritually beside things that are killing us.
Grace is tender.
But grace is not tame.
Jesus receives sinners, but He does not tell us our chains are jewelry.
He forgives the guilty, but He does not rename darkness light.
He welcomes the broken, but He loves them too much to leave them worshiping what broke them.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “Jesus makes me feel better.”
Jesus did not merely come to improve your mood.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He came to forgive.
To redeem.
To resurrect.
To make dead hearts alive.
And eventually His road leads to another shocking scene.
Not a funeral.
A cross.
There, the One who told a man to leave the dead and proclaim the Kingdom would Himself be numbered among the dead.
Nails through His hands.
Blood running down wood.
Mockery around Him.
Darkness overhead.
His disciples scattered.
His body placed inside a borrowed tomb.
If Luke 9 were the only picture we possessed of Jesus, someone might accuse Him of being indifferent toward death.
But Calvary destroys that accusation.
Jesus does not stand safely outside human death and shout instructions at us.
He enters it.
He bears sin.
He tastes death.
He is buried.
And on the third day, the tomb loses.
That is the Gospel.
Not that good people learn how to become slightly better people.
Not that religious people earn enough points for heaven.
Not that broken people pretend they were never broken.
The Gospel announces that sinners who cannot save themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The crucified Christ rises.
Grace walks out of the grave.
And suddenly “let the dead bury their own dead” sounds different.
Because the Man saying it is walking toward the place where He will conquer death.
He is calling this disciple away from death toward the announcement of a Kingdom where death will not have the final word.
That is why following Jesus cannot permanently remain somewhere near the bottom of your schedule.
If Christ really rose from the dead, Christianity cannot merely be your inspirational accessory.
If Christ really bore our sins, repentance cannot be treated as an optional religious hobby.
If Christ really is Lord, “later” cannot safely become the permanent answer to His call.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe something inside you has been uncomfortable for several paragraphs.
Not because you hate Jesus.
Because you know exactly what your “first” is.
You already thought of it.
That name.
That habit.
That wound.
That secret.
That excuse.
That compromise.
That room inside your heart where you keep telling Christ:
“Everything is Yours…
except this.”
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not calling you to earn His grace.
You cannot.
He is not telling you to become worthy enough to approach Him.
You cannot do that either.
The scandal of grace is that Christ came for sinners.
Real ones.
Messy ones.
Ashamed ones.
People with histories.
People with addictions.
People who failed after promising God they never would again.
People who knew better and still chose wrong.
People who have sat in church while hiding things that would shock everyone sitting beside them.
People like us.
Repentance does not mean purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Look at the cross.
It mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
And the cross is not God declaring that you are beyond redemption.
Look at the empty tomb.
Jesus rewrites endings.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, build a ministry, repay society or impress religious people.
He had a dying body, a guilty history and faith placed in a crucified King.
Grace met him there.
Your scandal does not have to write your final chapter either.
But grace is not permission to keep running.
Grace calls you home.
So maybe today the prayer is not complicated.
“Jesus, no more ‘but first.’”
No more negotiating.
No more pretending.
No more hiding.
No more trying to make peace with the thing Christ is calling you to surrender.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light is the first honest moment we have allowed ourselves in a very long time.
Let believers who see your words pray with you.
Your testimony may become the reason somebody else realizes they are not beyond the reach of grace.
Someone reading those three words may need them tonight.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It does not.

But if this message is faithful to Scripture and you believe someone in your circle needs to hear it, sharing it is one practical way you can help place biblical truth in front of another human being.
Send it privately to the person whose faith has gone quiet.
Send it to the believer carrying secret shame.
Send it to the person who believes Jesus could forgive everyone except them.
Even send it to the skeptical friend who thinks Christianity is only condemnation and rules.
Let them encounter the scandal of a Savior who tells sinners the truth and then goes to the cross to save them.
Because there may come a night when you need to read it again.
Your support helps Gospel-centered teaching keep reaching people.
But before you leave this article, go back to that road in Luke one last time.
Imagine the dust.
Imagine Jesus standing there.
Imagine the disciple facing Him.
No stage.
No microphone.
No audience.
Just a man…
and Christ.
“Follow Me.”
“Lord, first…”
We never hear the rest of this man’s story.
Luke does not tell us whether he followed.
Maybe that silence is intentional.
Because eventually the question stops being about him.
It becomes about us.
Jesus has already walked toward Jerusalem.
Already carried the cross.
Already entered death.
Already risen.
Already opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And now, across centuries, through the pages of Scripture, His call still reaches people buried beneath shame, distraction, religion, ambition, grief, compromise and delay.
Follow Me.
Maybe you have spent years explaining why today cannot be the day.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are spiritually fine.
Maybe nobody knows what happens when the screen goes dark and you are alone with your thoughts.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary while slowly drifting from Christ Himself.
Maybe you have been standing beside your excuse for so long that you started calling it wisdom.
But Jesus is still calling.
Not toward condemnation for everyone who comes to Him in faith.
Toward life.
Toward repentance.
Toward forgiveness.
Toward grace.
Toward Himself.
So when Christ says, “Follow Me,” may our answer finally lose two devastating words.
Not:
“Lord, but first…”
Just:
“Lord.”
And perhaps the sentence that sounded cruel at the beginning was actually the sound of Life Himself calling a human being out of the kingdom of death.
And comment honestly before you leave.
What is your “but first”?
You do not need to tell the whole story.
Maybe all you can write is:
Sometimes surrender begins when the sentence we have spent years avoiding finally leaves our heart.
And remember this when your past starts shouting louder than the cross:
The grave may describe where you have been—but when Jesus calls your name, it does not get to decide where your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD SAW WHAT EVERYONE ELSE MISSED
paragraphs: GOD SAW WHAT EVERYONE ELSE MISSED
Why God Looks at the Heart While People Look at Appearance—and Why the Person Everyone Overlooks May Be the Very Person God Is Preparing
There is a particular kind of pain that almost nobody sees.
It happens when people look directly at you…
and still don’t really see you.
They see your face.
Your clothes.
Your body.
Your age.
Your job.
Your failures.
Your reputation.
Your past.
Your bank account.
Your education.
Your followers.
Your mistakes.
They notice whether you walked into the room confidently or quietly. They notice whether your life looks successful enough to admire. They notice the chapter everybody can see.
But they cannot see the nights you cried and still prayed.
They cannot see how hard you fought not to become bitter.
