They cannot see the temptation you resisted when nobody would have known.
They cannot see the apology you whispered to God after everybody else went to sleep.
They cannot see the wounds underneath your smile.
They cannot see the private battles behind your public face.
And sometimes, after being judged by what people can see for long enough, you begin doing something even more painful.
You start judging yourself the same way.
That is where this story becomes dangerous.
Because Scripture reveals something about God that can completely dismantle the courtroom you have been carrying around inside your head.
The prophet Samuel once walked into a house looking for Israel’s next king.
God had sent him to Bethlehem, to the household of Jesse, because one of Jesse’s sons had been chosen by God.
Samuel saw Eliab.
And Eliab looked right.
Apparently, impressively right.
Samuel thought:
“Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.”
But God interrupted Samuel’s conclusion.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 16:7 says:
“אַל־תַּבֵּט אֶל־מַרְאֵהוּ וְאֶל־גְּבֹהַּ קוֹמָתוֹ”
’Al-tabbet el-mar’ehu ve’el-gevoah qomato…
“Do not look at his appearance or at the height of his stature…”
Then comes the line that exposes something deeply human:
“כִּי לֹא אֲשֶׁר יִרְאֶה הָאָדָם”
Ki lo asher yir’eh ha’adam…
God’s way of seeing is not limited to the way human beings see.
And then:
“כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַיהוָה יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב”
Ki ha’adam yir’eh la‘einayim, vaYHWH yir’eh lalevav.
“For man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
—1 Samuel 16:7
Read that again slowly.
People look at what is before their eyes.
God looks at the heart.
The Hebrew word translated “heart” here is לֵבָב — levav.

In biblical Hebrew, the heart is not merely the place of emotion in the modern sentimental sense. It can encompass the inner person—the will, desires, thoughts, intentions, understanding, and moral orientation.
In other words, God sees deeper than presentation.
He sees the person underneath it.
That should comfort you.
And it should terrify you.
Because this verse is often quoted as though it simply means, “Don’t worry about what people think because God knows you are a good person.”
That is not what the Bible says.
God looking at your heart does not automatically mean God approves of what He finds there.
The same God who sees sincerity also sees hypocrisy.
He sees compassion—and envy.
He sees generosity—and the secret desire to be praised for it.
He sees worship—and the pride hiding underneath religious performance.
He sees the Bible verse you posted publicly and the bitterness you protected privately.
He sees the church attendance.
He also sees what happens after church.
He sees the hands raised in worship.
He also sees what those hands reach for when nobody is watching.
People can be fooled by appearances.
God cannot.
And suddenly 1 Samuel 16:7 stops being merely comforting.
It becomes a mirror.
Because some of us have spent years trying to convince people that we are okay while avoiding the God who already knows we are not.
We learned how to smile.
How to say, “God is good.”
How to post Scripture.
How to look strong.
How to answer, “I’m blessed.”
How to appear spiritually mature.
Meanwhile something underneath the appearance has been starving.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe people think your marriage is fine.
God sees the distance.
Maybe people think you are confident.
God sees the insecurity eating you alive.
Maybe people call you successful.
God sees how desperately you need approval.
Maybe everybody thinks you have moved on.
God still sees the wound.
Maybe people believe you are spiritually strong.
God sees how exhausted your faith has become.
Maybe nobody knows about the addiction.
The resentment.
The jealousy.
The secret messages.
The pornography.
The pride.
The unforgiveness.
The double life.
The compromises you keep promising will be the last ones.
God sees it.
But here is where the Gospel changes the entire story.
The God who sees everything did not wait for sinners to make themselves presentable before coming to rescue them.
He came toward us.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had perfected their appearance.
He repeatedly moved toward people whose lives carried scandal.
Tax collectors.
Outcasts.
The morally compromised.
The socially despised.
The ashamed.
The spiritually desperate.
The people religious society knew how to label but did not know how to restore.
And Jesus never confused compassion with approval of sin.
He did something infinitely greater.
He called sinners to repentance while offering them mercy.
That matters.
Because biblical grace is not God pretending your heart is clean.
Grace is God knowing exactly how desperately you need cleansing—and providing what you could never provide for yourself through Jesus Christ.
The problem goes deeper than appearances.
Jesus said:
“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts…”
—Mark 7:21
The problem is not merely that other people misunderstand our hearts.
The deeper problem is that our hearts need redemption.
We do not merely need better self-esteem.
We need a Savior.
We do not merely need people to recognize our hidden goodness.
We need Christ to deal with our hidden sin.
We do not merely need someone to tell us, “You are enough.”
We need the One who was enough when we never could be.
This is why the cross is so devastatingly beautiful.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the edited version of you.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the version that knows exactly when to say “Amen.”
Christ died for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after the reputation was repaired.
Not after every habit disappeared.
Not after everybody started respecting us.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up enough to deserve Him.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
This is the scandal of grace.
God sees deeper than everyone else…
and still calls sinners to come to Christ.
But grace does not leave us where it finds us.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus rewrites everything.
David eventually walked into Samuel’s presence after his older brothers had been considered.
The one who had apparently not even been Jesse’s first thought when Samuel asked to see his sons was the one God had chosen.
But do not romanticize David.
His later life would prove why “God looks at the heart” cannot mean “God chooses flawless people.”
David would fail catastrophically.
Adultery.
Deception.
The arranged death of Uriah.
Consequences that would tear through his household.
The man chosen in 1 Samuel 16 would later become the broken man crying in Psalm 51:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
Notice what David did not pray.
“God, improve my image.”
He prayed for a clean heart.
That is repentance.
Repentance stops negotiating with appearances.
It stops asking, “How do I keep people from finding out?”
And starts asking, “God, what must change inside me?”
Maybe that is why you are reading this.
Maybe you have been obsessing over what people think while God has been dealing with something much deeper.
You want people to understand you.
God wants your heart.
You want vindication.
God wants surrender.
You want your reputation repaired.
God wants your character transformed.
You want the people who rejected you to regret it.
God may be asking you to forgive them.
You want somebody to recognize your worth.
God is pointing you toward the cross, where your value and your desperate need for grace collide.
And maybe…
just maybe…
the rejection that made you question your worth exposed how much of your worth you had placed in human approval.
That hurts.
Because human approval is addictive.
One compliment can lift us.
One insult can ruin the day.
One person unfollows us and suddenly we wonder what we did wrong.
One person overlooks us and suddenly we feel invisible.
One person chooses somebody else and suddenly we question everything about ourselves.
We say we live for God.
Yet sometimes strangers can control our emotions with a facial expression.
Samuel almost made the same mistake in another form.
He saw Eliab and immediately concluded that the impressive exterior must indicate God’s choice.
God corrected him.
Because heaven does not conduct its evaluations according to human eyesight.
That means you should be careful when people applaud you.
And careful when people reject you.
Neither necessarily tells you what God thinks.
Popularity is not proof of divine approval.
Rejection is not proof of divine abandonment.
Beauty is not holiness.
Success is not righteousness.
Charisma is not character.
Religious vocabulary is not spiritual maturity.
A platform is not anointing.
And being overlooked does not mean God has overlooked you.
That last sentence is for somebody who has spent too many nights wondering why nobody seems to notice.
God sees you.
But remember what that means.
He sees the pain you cannot explain.
And He sees the sin you cannot excuse.
He sees the good nobody applauded.
And He sees the compromise nobody discovered.
He sees the prayers.
He sees the motives.
He sees the tears.
He sees the pride.
He sees the obedience.
He sees the resentment.
Nothing is hidden.
Yet for those who come to Christ, being fully known does not have to end in hopelessness.
It can become the doorway to grace.
The apostle John writes:
—1 John 1:9
Not hide.
Confess.
Not curate.
Confess.
Not defend.
Confess.
Not compare your sin with somebody worse.
Confess.
There is freedom in finally becoming honest before the God from whom you were never hidden anyway.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to become painfully simple:
“Jesus, You see my heart.
You see what everyone else misses.
You see what I wish people understood.
And You see what I desperately hope nobody discovers.
Forgive me.
Clean me.
Change me.
Teach me to care more about who I am before You than how I appear before people.
Give me a clean heart.
Make me more like You.”
That prayer is more valuable than maintaining an impressive religious appearance while your soul quietly collapses.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops pretending.
Somebody reading underneath this article may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter when a sinner turns to Christ.
This is also why sharing truth matters.
If someone came into your mind while reading this, do not immediately assume they are the person who needs correcting.
Ask God whether you needed this first.
Then send it to them.

If you want to glorify God, support Gospel work not merely with words but through faithful participation—sharing biblical truth, encouraging others toward Christ, praying, serving, giving where God leads, and helping sound Gospel-centered resources reach people who might never walk into a church.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God's grace is not a transaction.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that nobody can boast.
But Christians can freely choose to support Gospel ministry so that biblical teaching, encouragement, discipleship resources, and Christ-centered content can continue reaching more people.
Not because you need another post sitting inside a collection.
Come back then.
Remember Samuel.
Remember David.
Remember the heart.
Remember the cross.
Remember that neither applause nor rejection gets the final word over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
But before you leave, there is one final truth I hope follows you long after this article disappears from your screen.
People may remember the version of you they once saw.
Some will remember your worst season.
Some will remember your failure.
Some will remember the rumor.
Some will remember the awkward version.
Some will remember the broken version.
Some will judge your entire life from one chapter.
But Jesus Christ is not limited to the chapter where everybody else stopped reading.
Peter denied Him and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians and became a servant of Christ.
David fell terribly and discovered the agony of repentance and the mercy of God.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to let human failure have the final word where genuine repentance meets divine grace.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It proves grace is astonishing.
So stop spending your entire life decorating an exterior while neglecting the person God sees underneath.
Let Him search you.
Let His Word expose you.
Let conviction lead you to repentance.
Let repentance drive you toward Christ rather than away from Him.
Let grace humble you.
Let forgiveness free you.
Let the Holy Spirit transform you.
And when people misunderstand you, resist the temptation to build your identity around proving them wrong.
Live before God.
When people praise you, do not become intoxicated by applause.
Live before God.
When nobody notices your obedience, keep obeying.
Live before God.
When your secret heart begins wandering from Christ, do not hide behind your reputation.
Run back to Jesus.
Because someday every mask will be useless.
Every carefully managed appearance will disappear.
Every human opinion will lose its power.
And what will matter infinitely more than whether people thought you looked Christian…
is whether you belonged to Christ.
So ask yourself the question that may be harder than anything else in this article:
If everybody could see my heart as clearly as God does, what would I desperately want to hide?
Whatever your answer is…
take it to Jesus.
Today.
There is no reason to keep hiding from the One who already sees you.
And there is no better place for a repentant sinner to run than the Savior whose blood was shed to forgive, cleanse, redeem, and make all things new.
People look at appearances.
God sees the heart.
And the most breathtaking part of the Gospel is not merely that Jesus sees beyond your appearance.
It is that He sees the sinner beneath it, calls that sinner to repentance, offers grace to the undeserving, and begins transforming the heart from the inside out.
Because perhaps the person who reads what you shared tonight will finally stop running tomorrow.
Perhaps the person you tag will realize God has not forgotten them.
And perhaps your support will help put the Gospel in front of one more heart that desperately needs Jesus.
You never know what God may do with one surrendered act of obedience.
But never forget this:
The world may judge you by the chapter it witnessed, but Jesus can transform the heart that wrote it—and grace can change how the story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Cigarette Isn’t Your Savior, Even If It’s Where You Run Every Time Life Hurts
paragraphs: The Cigarette Isn’t Your Savior, Even If It’s Where You Run Every Time Life Hurts
Maybe the deepest question isn't why you smoke. Maybe it's why, when your heart starts hurting, your hand already knows where to reach.
There is a moment nobody sees.
The argument is over.
The house is finally quiet.
The children are asleep.
Your phone screen goes dark.
The bad news is still sitting inside your chest.

Maybe somebody disappointed you again. Maybe the bills are piling up. Maybe your marriage feels colder than it used to. Maybe grief came back without warning. Maybe anxiety has been whispering all day. Maybe you are carrying something you have never told another human being.
So you step outside.
You reach into your pocket.
One cigarette.
One lighter.
Click.
Flame.
Inhale.
Exhale.
And for a few minutes, the world becomes quieter.
That is why an article about smoking can completely miss the human being holding the cigarette.
Because sometimes the cigarette isn't merely something you smoke.
Sometimes it is where you go.
That distinction matters.
Especially to Jesus.
Because Christ does not look at struggling people the way religious spectators sometimes do.
People see smoke.
Jesus sees the wound underneath it.
People smell tobacco.
Jesus knows what happened before you lit it.
He knows the conversation.
The rejection.
The loneliness.
The pressure.
The memory.
The funeral.
The betrayal.
The panic.
The exhaustion.
The night you couldn't sleep.
The thing you desperately wanted to stop thinking about.
He knows every cigarette you smoked while trying not to cry.
And if you love someone who smokes, understand this before saying another word to them:
You may be looking at a habit while they are experiencing a refuge.
That doesn't make the dependence harmless.
It makes the person human.
And perhaps that is exactly where this conversation has to begin.
Not with contempt.
Not with disgust.
Not with Christians standing at a distance pointing fingers.
But with truth spoken close enough to hear the heartbeat underneath the struggle.
Because Scripture gives us a sentence that reaches far deeper than cigarettes.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
Panta moi exestin, all’ ou panta sympherei. Panta moi exestin, all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
A careful rendering of the thought is:
“All things are permissible for me, but not all things are beneficial. All things are permissible for me, but I will not be mastered by anything.”
Notice that last movement.
“οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.”
“I will not be mastered by anything.”
Paul was not writing a first-century anti-smoking campaign. Cigarettes are not the subject of 1 Corinthians 6:12, and we should never pretend Scripture says something it does not say.
The immediate context moves into questions concerning the body, sexual immorality, union with Christ, and the astonishing reality that the believer belongs to God.
But the principle Paul articulates is devastatingly relevant:
Christian freedom is not permission to become someone else's slave.
And that forces a harder question than simply:
“Do you smoke?”
The deeper question is:
“What has mastered you?”
Because mastery does not always announce itself.
Sometimes it arrives quietly.
“I just need one.”
“I can't deal with this right now without smoking.”
“I'll quit after things calm down.”
“This is the only thing that relaxes me.”
“I deserve this.”
“Just five minutes.”
Then five minutes becomes years.
And somewhere along the way, something that seemed to serve you begins giving orders.
Wake up.
Smoke.
Stress.
Smoke.
Eat.
Smoke.
Drive.
Smoke.
Fight with somebody.
Smoke.
Feel lonely.
Smoke.
Receive terrible news.
Smoke.
Feel anxious.
Smoke.
Try to quit.
Think about smoking.
Smoke.
And suddenly Paul's words don't sound ancient anymore.
“I will not be mastered by anything.”
Maybe that sentence makes you uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because God wants to humiliate you.
Because sometimes discomfort is mercy knocking on a locked door.
There is an enormous difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation says, “Look at you. You're disgusting. Hide from God.”
Conviction says, “This thing is mastering you. Come back to Me.”
Condemnation drives Adam behind the trees.
Grace calls, “Where are you?”
And perhaps Jesus is asking someone reading this that question right now.
Not because He doesn't know where you are.
Because He wants you to recognize where you've been hiding.
Maybe behind anger.
Maybe behind pornography.
Maybe behind alcohol.
Maybe behind food.
Maybe behind endless scrolling.
Maybe behind work.
Maybe behind relationships.
Maybe behind pills.
Maybe behind applause.
Maybe behind nicotine.
Different hiding places.
Same aching human heart.
We run toward something because, for a moment, we don't want to feel what we are feeling.
That is why merely telling somebody, “Just stop smoking,” can sometimes be like telling a drowning person, “Just stop grabbing things.”
There is a deeper question:
What are they trying not to drown in?
Maybe you started because everyone else did.
Maybe you were sixteen.
Maybe twenty-five.
Maybe forty.
Maybe you thought you could quit whenever you wanted.
But then life happened.
The cigarette became associated with relief.
A break.
A breath.
A transition.
A reward.
A companion.
Something predictable when everything else felt unpredictable.
And eventually your body began asking for what your emotions had already learned to associate with comfort.
That deserves honesty.
But it also deserves compassion.
Because shame rarely produces the kind of transformation Jesus produces.
Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel filthy enough to behave better.
He came to save.
To redeem.
To reconcile.
To make new.
To break chains deeper than behavior.
The Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up enough so Jesus will tolerate you.”
The Gospel is that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride cannot survive because our sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
Despair cannot survive because Christ loved us enough to die anyway.
So hear this carefully if you are smoking while reading these words.
Put away the religious performance for a moment.
Jesus Christ is not waiting for you to become nicotine-free before you are allowed to approach Him.
Come to Him now.
With the craving.
With the pack.
With the failed attempts.
With the embarrassment.
With the irritability.
With the fear that you'll fail again.
Come honestly.
Christian repentance isn't pretending temptation disappeared.
Repentance is turning toward God in the middle of the truth.
You can say:
“Jesus, I don't know how to let this go.”
That is a real prayer.
“Jesus, I'm afraid of who I'll be without this.”
Real prayer.
“Jesus, I keep running here when I'm stressed.”
Real prayer.
“Jesus, part of me wants freedom and another part of me wants another cigarette.”
That may be more spiritually honest than a thousand polished religious sentences.
Because Christ already knows.
You aren't informing Him.
You're surrendering.
And surrender is where things begin changing.
Perhaps tonight, when the familiar pressure comes and your hand automatically reaches for the familiar refuge, something different can happen.
Maybe before you light it, you stop.
Not with dramatic promises.
Not “God, I'll never do this again.”
Just stop.
Ten seconds.
And ask yourself:
“What am I actually feeling right now?”
Angry?
Rejected?
Afraid?
Lonely?
Restless?
Ashamed?
Overwhelmed?
Bored?
Grieving?
Then take the next question somewhere deeper:
“What am I asking this cigarette to do for me right now?”
Calm me?
Comfort me?
Distract me?
Reward me?
Give me a break?
Help me survive this moment?
Then comes the question that may change everything:
“Have I learned to ask this cigarette for something my soul ultimately needs to seek in God?”

That question is not meant to oversimplify physical dependence. Bodies matter. Withdrawal is real. Habits become deeply established. Seeking appropriate medical help and practical support when breaking dependence is not evidence of weak faith.
But neither should we ignore the spiritual dimensions of where we repeatedly seek refuge.
The Psalms repeatedly describe God as refuge.
Not nicotine.
Not another person.
Not money.
Not sex.
Not success.
Not entertainment.
God.
This does not mean believers never experience anxiety.
It means anxiety no longer has to decide where we worship.
And worship is sometimes revealed by where we instinctively run when life hurts.
That may sting.
Because idols are not always statues.
Sometimes an idol looks like whatever we believe we cannot live without.
Whatever controls us.
Whatever repeatedly receives our trust.
Whatever we obey even while telling ourselves we are free.
And before anyone becomes self-righteous toward smokers, remember:
A person can never touch a cigarette and still be mastered.
You can be mastered by money.
Mastered by lust.
Mastered by people's approval.
Mastered by resentment.
Mastered by your phone.
Mastered by food.
Mastered by ambition.
Mastered by attention.
Mastered by fear.
Mastered by the desperate need to control everything.
So this isn't an article where clean-lunged Christians get to throw stones at smokers.
Everybody needs to put the stone down.
Everybody needs Jesus.
Because the scandal of Christianity isn't that bad people need grace.
The scandal is that all of us do.
The respectable churchgoer.
The chain-smoker standing outside the building.
The pastor.
The addict.
The person hiding pornography.
The successful businessman worshiping money.
The exhausted mother secretly falling apart.
The teenager who doesn't know how to stop.
The believer who keeps promising God, “This is the last time.”
Every one of us approaches the cross empty-handed.
And that cross tells us something astonishing.
Your body matters to God.
Paul continues his argument until he reaches this breathtaking reality: the believer's body belongs to God, has been bought at a price, and therefore God is to be glorified in the body.
That changes stewardship.
Your body isn't garbage.
Your body isn't disposable.
Your body isn't merely an inconvenience carrying your soul around until heaven.
Christ's resurrection itself tells us Christianity takes embodied human existence seriously.
So caring for your body isn't vanity.
It can become gratitude.
Not:
“I need to take care of myself so God will love me.”
But:
“Because God has loved me at immeasurable cost, I want even my body to become an offering of gratitude.”
That's a completely different motivation.
Grace first.
Transformation follows.
Never reverse them.
And maybe that is what somebody needs to hear tonight.
You have tried hatred.
You hated yourself after smoking.
You hated the smell.
You hated needing it.
You hated buying another pack.
You hated telling yourself you'd quit Monday.
You hated reaching Wednesday and starting again.
You hated disappointing people.
You hated disappointing yourself.
Maybe hatred hasn't freed you.
So try bringing the whole mess into the light of Christ.
Not because grace makes bondage acceptable.
Because grace makes freedom possible without requiring you to despise yourself on the journey.
There may be setbacks.
There may be cravings.
There may be mornings when victory feels close and nights when it feels impossible.
But your struggle does not get to rename you.
If you belong to Jesus, your deepest identity isn't “smoker.”
It isn't “addict.”
It isn't “failure.”
It isn't “hopeless.”
You belong to Christ.
And belonging changes the battle.
You aren't fighting to become worthy of being loved.
You are learning to live from the love demonstrated at Calvary.
You aren't trying to purchase forgiveness through perfect behavior.
Jesus already paid a price you could never pay.
You aren't trying to impress God with your willpower.
You're learning dependence of another kind.
Dependence upon Christ.
And maybe that's the beautiful irony.
Freedom isn't becoming a person who needs absolutely nothing.
Human beings were never created for that.
Freedom is discovering whom you were created to need.
Jesus.
When anxiety comes...
Jesus.
When grief comes...
Jesus.
When the craving comes...
Jesus.
When you fail...
Jesus.
When shame says, “Don't pray now. Look what you just did”...
Jesus.
Especially then.
Run toward Him instead of away.
Because the Savior already knows the worst chapter and still chose the cross.
That's why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes Peter's denial and writes restoration.
He takes Paul's persecution and writes apostleship.
He takes shame and writes testimony.
He takes rebellion and writes redemption.
He takes prodigals and brings them home.
And He can take the place where you've been hiding and turn it into the place where your testimony begins.
Maybe someday somebody will ask you:
“How did you finally start becoming free?”
And perhaps your answer won't be:
“I became stronger.”
Maybe it will be:
“I finally admitted I wasn't.”
“I stopped hiding.”
“I asked for help.”
“I started bringing my cravings to Jesus instead of pretending they weren't there.”
“I learned that falling wasn't permission to stay down.”
“I discovered that grace wasn't God's permission for my chains. Grace was God's invitation out of them.”
And if you're reading this because you love someone who smokes, please don't weaponize this article.
Love them.
Pray for them.
Listen to them.
Ask what happens inside them before they reach for the cigarette.
Don't reduce a whole human being made in God's image to the habit you desperately want them to stop.
Truth without love can become a hammer.
Love without truth can become permission to remain chained.
Jesus gives us something better.
Grace and truth.
Maybe send this to them with only one sentence:
“I love you. I'm not judging you. I'll walk with you.”
And if you're the person struggling, perhaps this is your moment to stop pretending.
You don't even have to explain what it is.
Maybe nicotine isn't your struggle.
Maybe something else has mastered you.
Somebody reading silently tonight may desperately need evidence that another chapter can be written.
Not because every sentence will suddenly make cravings disappear, but because there may come a night when you need to remember the question:
“What am I asking this thing to do for me that I need to bring before Jesus?”
It doesn't.
Not because supporting a Christian ministry earns spiritual merit. It doesn't.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, witness, and lives surrendered to Him—not through a Facebook transaction.
Come to Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church cannot save you.
Willpower cannot save you.
And that cigarette certainly cannot save you.
Jesus Christ can.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
He receives those who repent and trust Him.
And maybe tonight, instead of making another enormous promise about what you'll never do again, your prayer can simply be:
“Jesus, this has become somewhere I run when life hurts. Teach me to run to You.”
Then tomorrow...
pray it again.
And if you stumble...
pray it again.
If you need help...
ask for it.
If shame tells you to hide...
come into the light.
Because the cigarette may have been there during some of the hardest moments of your life.
But it did not bleed for you.
It did not carry your sin.
It did not walk out of a tomb.
It cannot forgive you.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
It cannot give you eternal life.
It cannot call you by name.
It cannot make you new.
Christ can.
So perhaps the next chapter doesn't begin when you finally become strong enough to say, “I don't need a cigarette.”
Perhaps it begins when your exhausted heart finally whispers:
“Jesus, I need You more.”
And remember this when the flame flickers in the darkness:
What you kept reaching for when you were hurting may have numbed the pain for a moment—but only the hands pierced for you can hold your life without becoming your chains.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE ALGORITHM KNOWS WHAT MAKES YOU WEAK
paragraphs:
THE ALGORITHM KNOWS WHAT MAKES YOU WEAK
Can Social Media Strengthen Temptation—and Keep Putting the Same Door Back in Front of You?
You told yourself you were only going to check one notification.
That was twenty-seven minutes ago.
Your thumb is still moving.
Scroll.
Scroll.
Scroll.
Then something appears.
Maybe it is not pornography.
Maybe it is not obviously sinful at all.
Maybe it is the photograph that awakens envy.
The video that feeds lust.
The argument that makes anger feel righteous.
The body that makes you despise your own.
The lifestyle that suddenly makes everything God has given you feel inadequate.
The celebrity gossip you know you should not care about.
The outrage that makes contempt strangely pleasurable.
The former relationship you keep checking even though you promised yourself you were finished.
The person whose profile you should have stopped visiting months ago.
The content that touches a weakness nobody at church knows you have.
And something inside you whispers:
Just one more.
Here is the disturbing question.
What happens when temptation meets technology capable of learning what keeps your attention?
Not reading your soul.
Not knowing your heart the way God knows it.
But observing behavior.
What you watch.
What you replay.
What you search.
What holds your attention.
What you return to.
And then placing more content in front of you that resembles what previously kept you engaged.
Suddenly an ancient spiritual battle is happening inside an extraordinarily modern environment.
The temptation is ancient.
The delivery system is new.
And perhaps that is why some Christians are losing battles they do not even realize they have been training themselves to fight poorly.

Research does not justify the simplistic claim that “the algorithm makes people sin.” Human beings remain morally responsible for their choices, and researchers continue debating exactly how recommendation systems affect different users. But there is legitimate evidence that recommendation systems can facilitate pathways toward certain kinds of problematic content. A systematic review examining YouTube recommendation research found that 14 of 23 included studies implicated the recommendation system in pathways toward problematic content, seven reported mixed findings, and two did not implicate it. The authors themselves warned that limited access to recommendation systems makes sweeping causal conclusions difficult.
That distinction matters.
Because the Bible never allows us to outsource responsibility for sin.
Not to Satan.
Not to culture.
Not to our childhood.
Not to our hormones.
And certainly not to an algorithm.
But Scripture also never tells us to be careless about environments that repeatedly place temptation before us.
Jesus said something far more severe.
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
Matthew 5:29.
The Greek is deliberately forceful:
εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ὁ δεξιὸς σκανδαλίζει σε
ei de ho ophthalmos sou ho dexios skandalizei se
“If your right eye causes you to stumble…”
That word is worth noticing.
σκανδαλίζει — skandalizei.
It comes from the same word family behind skandalon—a stumbling block, something that becomes an occasion for falling.
Jesus was not commanding routine bodily mutilation. He was using shocking language to teach the seriousness with which His disciples must deal with occasions of sin.
In other words:
Do not negotiate indefinitely with what repeatedly drags you toward destruction.
And suddenly that teaching feels painfully contemporary.
Because what if the thing in your hand is not inherently evil…
but you have trained it to keep bringing your stumbling blocks back?
Think about that.
The phone is not your enemy.
Technology is not Satan.
Social media itself is not automatically sinful.

The same platforms carrying lust, vanity, rage, deception, gossip, and envy can also carry Scripture, testimonies, encouragement, education, friendship, prayer, evangelism, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
The question is not merely:
“Is social media bad?”
That question is too easy.
The harder question is:
What is social media becoming in me?
Because James describes temptation with terrifying intimacy.
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
James 1:14.
The Greek says:
ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας
hypo tēs idias epithymias
“by his own desire.”
Notice what James does not say.
He does not say temptation proves you are uniquely disgusting.
He does not say temptation itself means you have already committed the sin.
He does not blame an external system for everything happening inside the human heart.
He goes deeper.
Desire can lure us.
Desire can entice us.
Then, James says, desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when fully grown brings forth death.
There is a progression.
A seed.
A conception.
A birth.
A destination.
And now imagine placing that ancient description beside a personalized digital feed.
You linger.
The system receives behavioral information.
You click.
More related content becomes available.
You watch.
You search again.
Your preferences become increasingly legible to the system.
That does not mean the algorithm understands your spiritual condition.
It means something more ordinary—and still worth taking seriously:
personalized recommendation technologies can respond to patterns in behavior.

Research into recommender systems has repeatedly found that algorithmic pathways can expose users to content related to what they have already consumed, although the strength, direction, and consequences of that effect vary considerably. One large audit of YouTube using 100,000 automated accounts found evidence of increasingly congenial recommendations in some contexts and a growing proportion of recommendations from channels the researchers categorized as problematic deeper in certain recommendation trails, while not finding a meaningful overall increase in ideological extremity itself.
The science deserves that nuance.
The spiritual principle deserves equal clarity.
An algorithm does not need to create your desire to repeatedly place opportunities before that desire.
And temptation loves repetition.
Maybe your weakness is lust.
You clicked once.
Then again.
Then lingered.
Soon your feed seems to know exactly what kind of image makes you stop.
You call it coincidence.
You call it entertainment.
You call it harmless.
But Jesus calls you to guard your heart and deal seriously with whatever repeatedly becomes an occasion for sin.
Maybe lust is not your battle.
Maybe yours is envy.
Someone posts the house.
The vacation.
The engagement.
The pregnancy announcement.
The promotion.
The perfect marriage photograph taken seven minutes after an argument nobody online will ever see.
You smile.
Then something happens inside you.
“Why not me?”
Scroll.
“God, when is it my turn?”
Scroll.
“Maybe I chose the wrong life.”
Scroll.
“Maybe God forgot me.”
Scroll.
And eventually another person's highlight reel becomes evidence in a trial you have secretly opened against the goodness of God.

Research has found an association between problematic social-media use and social comparison, though association does not by itself prove that one causes the other. A recent meta-analysis reported a modest positive relationship between the two.
Scripture understood the danger of comparison long before smartphones existed.
Paul wrote that people “measuring themselves by one another and comparing themselves with one another” are “without understanding” (2 Corinthians 10:12).
The interface changed.
The human heart did not.
Maybe your weakness is anger.
You watch one video that makes you furious.
Then another appears.
Then another.
Soon you are not opening social media to understand people.
You are opening it to become angry at them.
And anger feels good when you can call it righteousness.
That is one of the most dangerous temptations of all.
Because some sins arrive wearing horns.
Others arrive carrying a Bible verse.
James warns:
“The anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.”
James 1:20.
You can win every comment-section battle and slowly lose tenderness toward human beings made in the image of God.
You can defend truth while becoming addicted to contempt.
You can speak about Jesus while sounding nothing like Him.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that eventually you stop noticing.
The feed feels normal.
The anger feels normal.
The lust feels normal.
The comparison feels normal.
The compulsive checking feels normal.
The secret profile visits feel normal.
The midnight scrolling feels normal.

Researchers have also found meaningful associations between problematic social-media use and depression, anxiety, and stress among adolescents and young adults, although these findings should not be misrepresented as proof that social media alone causes those conditions.
So this is not an invitation to panic about technology.
It is an invitation to wake up.
Because Scripture has a word for this.
Watchfulness.
Jesus told His disciples:
“Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Matthew 26:41.
In Greek:
γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσεύχεσθε
grēgoreite kai proseuchesthe
“Keep watch and pray.”
Not merely pray.
Watch.
There are moments when Christians pray for deliverance from temptations they continue deliberately carrying in their pockets.
We ask God to rescue us from lust while refusing to unfollow what continually awakens lust.
We ask God to heal our envy while consuming hours of content designed around lifestyles we desperately covet.
We ask God to give us peace while beginning and ending every day submerged in outrage.
We ask God to restore our marriages while secretly watching people who make our spouses seem less desirable.
We ask God to make us content while voluntarily studying everybody else's possessions.
We ask God to renew our minds while handing those minds to an endless feed.
And perhaps tonight the Holy Spirit is not merely asking you to pray harder.
Perhaps obedience looks like pressing unfollow.
Perhaps repentance looks like deleting something.
Perhaps wisdom looks like changing what you watch.
Perhaps freedom begins when you stop saying:
“I can handle it.”
Paul gave believers a devastatingly practical command:
“Make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.”
Romans 13:14.
The Greek phrase is:
τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν μὴ ποιεῖσθε
tēs sarkos pronoian mē poieisthe
Do not make provision for the flesh.
Do not prepare its supplies.
Do not keep stocking the room where your weakness lives.
That changes the question.
Instead of asking,
“How close can I get without technically sinning?”
ask,
“Why am I making arrangements for the thing I keep begging Jesus to free me from?”
That question hurts.
I know.
Because there are things we do not want to call idols because we enjoy them too much.
Things we call “just entertainment.”
Things we call “just scrolling.”
Things we call “just curiosity.”
But if you cannot put it down when Christ calls you away from it…
you should at least be willing to ask whether you possess it—
or it possesses you.
And here comes the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not the story of disciplined people successfully cleaning themselves up enough for God.
It is the story of sinners who could not save themselves being pursued by a Savior who could.
Jesus did not go to the cross because your temptations were small.
He went because sin is deadly.
And He did not rise from the grave merely so you could be forgiven while remaining permanently enslaved.
Christ came to redeem.
To cleanse.
To restore.
To transform.
To make dead people alive.
The Christian response to temptation is therefore not:
“I am disgusting.”
It is:
“I need Jesus.”
Not:
“I'll hide this better.”
But:
“I will bring this into the light.”
Not:
“I promise I'll never struggle again.”
But:
“I will stop defending what Christ is calling me to surrender.”
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is the scandal.
God already knows what you watched.
What you searched.
Who you stalked.
What you imagined.
What you envied.
What you deleted from your history.
What you would be horrified for your pastor, spouse, children, parents, or friends to see.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the blood of Jesus matters infinitely more than your attempt to hide it.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
The scandal is not simply that you fell.
The greater scandal is that the holy Son of God willingly took the place of sinners.
The grace is not permission to keep crawling toward the chains.
Grace breaks chains.
“For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.”
Romans 6:14.
Maybe tonight you need to retrain more than an algorithm.
Maybe you need to retrain your attention.
Fill your eyes with what is true.
Fill your mind with Scripture.
Fill your quiet moments with prayer again.
Follow accounts that make you hunger for Christ instead of envy strangers.
Stop feeding what you are trying to starve.
Start feeding what you are praying will grow.
And when temptation comes—and it will—remember Paul's promise in 1 Corinthians 10:13: temptation is common to humanity, God is faithful, and He provides a way of escape so His people can endure it.
Sometimes that escape will look dramatic.
Sometimes it will look embarrassingly ordinary.
Close the app.
Put down the phone.
Walk out of the room.
Call a mature believer.
Confess.
Block the account.
Install accountability.
Stop following the person.
Do not reopen the message.
Go pray.
Open Scripture.
Go outside.
Talk to your spouse.
Tell someone the truth.
Run.
Not because running makes you weak.
Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife.
Sometimes running is what spiritual warfare looks like when you actually intend to win.
Be honest.
Then pray for somebody else who comments.
Turn a comment section into something the internet rarely becomes:
a place where people stop pretending.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ purchased redemption with His blood; we cannot purchase what grace gives freely.

But if this ministry is helping people confront sin, return to Scripture, discover the Gospel, and grow deeper in Christ, supporting and sharing that work can be one practical way of helping put truth into feeds already overflowing with everything else.
Send it privately to the friend whose battle nobody else sees. Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about pretending to be good.
Someone may need these words at 1:43 tomorrow morning when temptation is sitting six inches from their face.
You may not need it most today.
You may need it on the night when “just one look” sounds reasonable again.

But it is a tangible way to support the continued creation and distribution of Christ-centered resources while receiving deeper biblical nourishment, discipleship, encouragement, accountability, and spiritual sharpening.
Your support helps us keep putting biblical truth where temptation, confusion, despair, and spiritual hunger are already fighting for people's attention.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the One who forgives.
Jesus is the One who transforms.
Jesus is the One worth following when every algorithm on earth is competing to tell you what deserves your attention.
So tonight, before you scroll again, ask yourself one question:
What am I teaching my feed to feed me—and what is that feeding in my soul?
Then ask an even greater question:
What would happen if I became as intentional about seeking Jesus as the digital world is about seeking my attention?
Your flesh may remember what once made you fall.
Your past may remember every scandal.
But the Gospel announces something stronger than all three.
In Christ, your worst pattern does not have to become your final chapter.
The feed may learn your weakness—but Jesus knows your name, bore your sin, conquered the grave, and is still calling you out of hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL CONFRONTED ELYMAS THE SORCERER—AND THE MAN SUDDENLY BECAME BLIND
paragraphs: PAUL CONFRONTED ELYMAS THE SORCERER—AND THE MAN SUDDENLY BECAME BLIND
He tried to turn one man away from Jesus. Then Paul looked straight at him, spoke words no one in that room could ignore—and darkness fell over his eyes.
There are moments in Scripture that feel almost too intense to read casually.
This is one of them.
A sorcerer stands before an apostle.
A powerful government official is listening.
The Gospel is being preached.
Someone desperately wants to stop it.
Then Paul turns.
Looks directly at the man opposing the message.
And says something terrifying.
Moments later, the sorcerer cannot see.
But if all we remember from this story is, “Paul made a sorcerer blind,” we have missed what Luke was actually showing us.
Because Acts 13 is not ultimately a story about an apostle displaying supernatural power.
It is about Jesus Christ breaking through deception to reach someone who wanted to hear the Word of God.
And buried inside this confrontation is a warning for every person who has ever resisted truth, distorted truth, hidden from truth—or stood in the way while someone else was trying to find Jesus.
Maybe even you.
The story begins in Acts 13:4–12.

Barnabas and Saul have been sent out by the Holy Spirit. They travel to Cyprus and eventually reach Paphos, where they encounter a Jewish man described as a magician and false prophet named Bar-Jesus.
That name itself catches your attention.
“Bar-Jesus” comes from an Aramaic naming construction: בַּר, bar, meaning “son,” followed by Jesus/Joshua—essentially, “son of Jesus” or “son of Joshua.”
But Luke also calls him Elymas, explaining that this was connected with his identity as a magician.
He was associated with Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul of Cyprus.
And Sergius Paulus wanted to hear something.
Not another spell.
Not another performance.
Not another spiritual counterfeit.
He wanted to hear the Word of God.
Acts 13:7 says that the proconsul “called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God.”
Then Elymas interfered.
Luke writes in Greek:
ἀνθίστατο δὲ αὐτοῖς Ἐλύμας ὁ μάγος
anthistato de autois Elymas ho magos
Elymas the magician “opposed them.”
But Luke goes further.
Elymas was:
ζητῶν διαστρέψαι τὸν ἀνθύπατον ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως
“seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.”
That changes the atmosphere of the entire story.
This was not merely a theological disagreement.
A man wanted to hear God's Word, and another man was actively trying to turn him away from faith.
Think about how serious that is.
Someone is leaning toward the light…
and someone else is pulling him toward darkness.
Someone is beginning to listen…
and someone else is whispering, “Don't.”
Someone is wondering whether Jesus really is Lord…
and someone else is trying to make sure he never finds out.
Then Saul—whom Luke now also identifies as Paul—turns toward Elymas.
Acts says Paul was:
πλησθεὶς πνεύματος ἁγίου
plēstheis pneumatos hagiou
“filled with the Holy Spirit.”
That detail matters enormously.
Paul's confrontation is not presented as an uncontrolled explosion of personal rage.
Luke deliberately tells us that Paul is filled with the Holy Spirit.
Then Paul fixes his eyes on Elymas.
And the words come.
“Thou child of the devil, thou enemy of all righteousness, wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?”
The Greek is even more vivid:
ὦ πλήρης παντὸς δόλου καὶ πάσης ῥᾳδιουργίας, υἱὲ διαβόλου, ἐχθρὲ πάσης δικαιοσύνης
The language speaks of someone filled with deceit and wrongdoing, a “son of the devil,” an enemy of righteousness.
Then Paul asks:
οὐ παύσῃ διαστρέφων τὰς ὁδοὺς τοῦ κυρίου τὰς εὐθείας;
“Will you not stop making crooked the straight ways of the Lord?”
There is the heart of the confrontation.
God's way is straight.
Elymas is trying to twist it.
Truth is being proclaimed.
Elymas is trying to distort it.
Someone is trying to come toward faith.
Elymas is trying to turn him away.
Then Paul says:
“And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon thee, and thou shalt be blind, not seeing the sun for a season.”
For a season.
Do not rush past those words.
Paul does not announce that Elymas will be permanently blind.
The Greek says:
ἄχρι καιροῦ
achri kairou
“until a time,” or “for a season.”
And immediately Luke tells us:
παραχρῆμά τε ἔπεσεν ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν ἀχλὺς καὶ σκότος
“Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him.”
Then comes one of the most haunting images in Acts.
Elymas begins:
περιάγων ἐζήτει χειραγωγούς
He went about looking for people to lead him by the hand.
The man who had been trying to lead someone else away from faith…
now needed someone to lead him by the hand.
Read that again.
The man attempting to redirect another man's spiritual sight suddenly lost his physical sight.
The man trying to keep Sergius Paulus in darkness was himself surrounded by darkness.
The man who behaved as though he could guide another person's soul could no longer guide his own footsteps.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us that every detail is intended as symbolism, so we should not force the passage beyond what Luke actually says.
But the narrative contrast is impossible to ignore.
And there is another astonishing connection.
Paul knew something about blindness.
Before he was Paul the missionary, he was Saul the persecutor.
Before he traveled from city to city proclaiming Jesus, he was hunting people who belonged to Jesus.
Acts 9 describes Saul approaching Damascus with authority to arrest followers of Christ.
Then heaven interrupted him.
A light flashed.
Saul fell.
Jesus spoke.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?”
And when Saul rose from the ground…
he could not see.
The future apostle had to be led by the hand.
Sound familiar?
The man confronting Elymas had once been the blind man.
Paul knew what it was to believe you were defending God while actually opposing what God was doing.
He knew what it was to possess religious knowledge and still fail to recognize Jesus.
He knew what it was to walk confidently in the wrong direction.
He knew what it was to be stopped.
Blinded.
Led helplessly by another person's hand.
And then shown mercy.
That is why we should be careful not to read Acts 13 as permission for Christians to become cruel toward people who oppose them.
Paul's authority as an apostle in this specific Spirit-directed confrontation is not a blank check for believers to pronounce curses upon everyone who irritates them.
The Gospel does not create arrogant people celebrating another person's destruction.
The Gospel creates people who remember where Jesus found them.
Paul could look at a man walking in darkness because Paul himself had once walked in darkness.
So have we.
Maybe your darkness never involved sorcery.
Maybe nobody would ever have called you a false prophet.
Maybe you have attended church for years.
Maybe you know worship songs.
Maybe your Bible has highlighted verses.
Maybe people think you're strong in the faith.
But darkness has quieter forms.
The secret habit nobody knows about.
The bitterness you have renamed “discernment.”
The lust you keep promising God you will quit.
The relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
The pride that makes repentance feel humiliating.
The jealousy you hide behind silence.
The unforgiveness you keep rehearsing.
The private messages you would panic if your spouse saw.
The double life.
The compromise.
The spiritual performance.
The smiling profile picture posted hours after you cried alone.
The “I'm fine” you keep saying because telling the truth feels too dangerous.
And sometimes the most frightening darkness is not knowing that you are in darkness.
Elymas could see physically before Paul spoke.
But spiritually, he was fighting against the light standing directly in front of him.
That should make every one of us ask a frightening question:
What if the thing I keep defending is the very thing Jesus is trying to expose?
What if I have become so skilled at explaining my compromise that I no longer call it compromise?
What if conviction keeps knocking and I keep calling it discomfort?
What if God has been trying to straighten something that I keep making crooked?
There is a strange mercy in being interrupted by God.
Ask Saul.
He was on his way to persecute Christians when Jesus stopped him.
Had Christ allowed Saul to continue uninterrupted, Saul would have continued believing he was right.
Sometimes grace does not initially feel gentle.
Sometimes grace knocks you down.
Sometimes grace exposes what you buried.
Sometimes grace destroys the excuse that was helping you sleep at night.
Sometimes grace allows the mask to crack.
Not because Jesus enjoys humiliating sinners.
Because Jesus came to save sinners.
There is an enormous difference.
The Christ who confronted Saul was the Christ who would transform Saul.
The persecutor would become a preacher.
The enemy would become a servant.
The man breathing threats against Christians would eventually suffer for the name he once tried to erase.
That is scandalous grace.
And perhaps that is why this story belongs so beautifully inside the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people finally earned God's approval.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God bears sin.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
The spiritually dead are offered life.
Enemies can become children.
People with histories they cannot rewrite encounter a Savior who can redeem what their sin has shattered.
Paul himself would later write:
Not after we cleaned ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we finally deserved Him.
“While we were yet sinners.”
That is where grace finds people.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus forgives sinners, and Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
The Gospel does not say, “Your darkness doesn't matter.”
The Gospel says the Light has come.
Christ does not merely decorate our old lives with religious language.
He makes us new.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back for salvation.
It is the turning of a heart that has encountered the truth.
And maybe that is exactly where this story has found you.
Not standing beside Paul.
Standing closer to Elymas than you wanted to admit.
You have been resisting.
Twisting.
Running.
Hiding.
Or perhaps you have been quietly steering someone else away from Jesus because their growing faith makes you uncomfortable.
Maybe you mocked their conversion.
Maybe you discouraged their hunger for Scripture.
Maybe you told them not to take Christianity “too seriously.”
Maybe your children watched you claim Christ publicly while contradicting Him privately.
Maybe someone learned cynicism about Christianity by watching your hypocrisy.
That realization hurts.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The answer is not to hide harder.
The answer is Christ.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Stop negotiating with the thing Jesus died to free you from.
You do not need another mask.
You need mercy.
You do not need to convince everybody that you have your life together.
You need Jesus.
And the astonishing thing about Jesus is that your worst chapter does not intimidate Him.
Ask Peter after the denial.
Ask the thief dying beside Him.
Ask Saul on the Damascus road.
The Gospel is filled with people whose stories should have ended in shame…
but grace entered the story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the necessity of repentance.
Jesus rewrites everything by doing something infinitely greater:
He redeems sinners.
Then notice what happens at the end of the confrontation with Elymas.
Acts 13:12 says:
τότε ἰδὼν ὁ ἀνθύπατος τὸ γεγονὸς ἐπίστευσεν
“Then the proconsul, when he saw what had happened, believed…”
But Luke adds something important.
He was:
ἐκπλησσόμενος ἐπὶ τῇ διδαχῇ τοῦ κυρίου
astonished at “the teaching of the Lord.”
Do not reduce the ending to supernatural spectacle.
Luke points us back to the teaching of the Lord.
The miracle did not become the center.
God's truth remained the center.
Jesus remained the center.
That matters in an age where people can become fascinated by manifestations, personalities, controversies, signs, experiences, and sensational stories while barely opening their Bibles.
Christianity is not a circus.
The Gospel is not entertainment.
And spiritual power is never supposed to replace Christ.
Signs in Scripture point beyond themselves.
And this frightening sign in Acts 13 served a Gospel advance: opposition was confronted, the proconsul saw what happened, and he believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Maybe you began reading because the title said a sorcerer suddenly became blind.
But perhaps you stayed because somewhere along the way the story stopped being about Elymas.
It became about you.
About me.
About the things we hide.
About the truth we resist.
About the people we influence.
About whether our lives are pointing someone toward Jesus or quietly pulling them away.
So be honest before God.
What are you making crooked that He has called straight?
What are you defending that Scripture has already confronted?
Where have you been pretending?
What would repentance actually look like tonight?
Not tomorrow.
Not when life becomes easier.
Tonight.
You can close an article.
You can silence a preacher.
You can avoid the Christian friend who keeps asking how your soul is doing.
You can scroll until conviction becomes background noise.
But you cannot heal yourself by hiding from the One who already sees you.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to come.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may need to know that failure does not have to be the final chapter when a sinner turns to Jesus.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Because there may come a night when you need to read it again.
And think about one person who has been drifting from Christ.
One.
Send this article privately if that would honor them better.
Not as religious performance.
Not to prove that you are a good Christian.
Share because another Sergius Paulus may be listening.
Someone may be closer to asking about Jesus than you realize.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has become lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
But never confuse resources with the Savior.
Books cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Paul cannot save you.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And perhaps the deepest warning from Elymas is not that a man once became physically blind.
It is that a person can have functioning eyes and still resist the Light.
So don't wait for darkness to teach you the value of sight.
Turn toward Christ while you can see Him calling.
Repent where you have sinned.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Walk away from what is destroying you.
Stop making crooked what God has called straight.
And if your story is stained with things you wish you could erase, remember the former persecutor who became an apostle.
Remember Peter.
Remember the thief beside the cross.
Remember the blood shed at Calvary.
Remember the empty tomb.
Your sin is serious.
The cross proves that.
But for everyone who comes to Christ in repentant faith, sin does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is still walking through the dark with their hands stretched out, desperately searching for someone to lead them.
May the hand they finally reach belong to someone who leads them straight to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS TITHE 10%—OR IS THAT AN OLD COVENANT REQUIREMENT?
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS TITHE 10%—OR IS THAT AN OLD COVENANT REQUIREMENT?
What if the question God is asking is not, “Did you give Me exactly ten percent?” but something far more uncomfortable: “After everything My Son gave for you… how much of you actually belongs to Me?”
There is a moment that happens in churches almost everywhere.
The sermon ends.
The music softens.
Someone begins talking about giving.
And suddenly, people get uncomfortable.
Some reach for their wallets.
Some reach for their phones.
Some feel grateful.
Some feel guilty.
Some quietly calculate ten percent.
And some sit there wondering something they have been afraid to ask out loud:
“Does God actually require Christians to tithe ten percent?”
Maybe you were taught that if you do not tithe, you are robbing God.
Maybe someone quoted Malachi 3 and told you that financial hardship might be happening because you withheld God’s ten percent.
Maybe you were taught that the first ten percent belongs to your local church and anything beyond that is an offering.
Or perhaps you came from the opposite side.
“Jesus fulfilled the Law. Tithing is Old Testament. Christians are under grace. I can give whatever I want—or nothing at all.”
Both positions can sound biblical when isolated verses are placed behind them.
But Scripture deserves something better than slogans.
And so does your conscience.
Because this question is not ultimately about percentages.
It is about worship.
It is about ownership.
It is about grace.
And before this is finished, the uncomfortable question may no longer be whether God wants ten percent of your money.
The question may become:
What happened to the other ninety percent?
To understand tithing, we first have to understand the word itself.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “tithe” is מַעֲשֵׂר — ma‘aser.
It means a tenth.
That matters because biblical tithing was not originally a vague synonym for “giving money to God.” It referred to something specific within Israel’s covenant life.

Leviticus says that the tithe of the land belonged to the LORD and was holy to Him. Leviticus 27:30 specifically speaks of the produce of the land, while the following verses also address herd and flock.
This was part of Israel’s covenant structure.
It supported worship.
It supported those assigned to sacred service.
It was intertwined with Israel’s agricultural life and covenant obligations.
And yes, the Old Testament takes it seriously.
Then comes the passage almost everyone has heard during a sermon about giving.
Malachi 3:10.
The Hebrew begins:
הָבִיאוּ אֶת־כָּל־הַמַּעֲשֵׂר אֶל־בֵּית הָאוֹצָר
Havi'u et-kol-hamma'aser el-beit ha'otzar.
“Bring the full tithe into the storehouse…”
The word הַמַּעֲשֵׂר — hamma‘aser means “the tithe” or “the tenth.”

And God says there should be food in His house. The historical picture is not simply a modern Christian placing ten percent of a salary into an offering envelope. Malachi addresses Israel within its covenant setting, with the tithe being brought into the storehouse and providing food connected with the life of God’s house.
That context matters.
We should never weaken Scripture.
But neither should we move a command from one covenant setting into another without asking how the New Testament handles it.
Someone may immediately object:
“But Abraham tithed before Moses.”
Correct.

Genesis records Abraham giving Melchizedek a tenth after the battle, and Hebrews 7 deliberately remembers that event. The Greek text uses δεκάτην — dekatēn, “a tenth.” Hebrews says Abraham apportioned a tenth of everything to Melchizedek.
That demonstrates something important.
Giving a tenth existed before the Mosaic Law.
But there is a difference between showing that Abraham once gave a tenth and establishing a universal command requiring every Christian to give exactly ten percent of every paycheck.
The text must be allowed to say what it says.
Not less.
Not more.
Then Jesus enters the conversation.
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus confronts the scribes and Pharisees because they meticulously tithed even small herbs while neglecting “the weightier matters of the law”—justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
He tells them they should have practiced those things without neglecting the others.
So Jesus certainly did not mock tithing.
He did not praise disobedience.
But notice the setting.
He is speaking before the cross, to people living within Israel’s covenant world, while confronting teachers of the Law about their hypocritical observance of that Law.
And then something happens that changes everything.
The cross.
The resurrection.
The New Covenant.
Jesus does not merely arrive to improve religious bookkeeping.
He gives Himself.
His blood is poured out.
His body is broken.
The sinless One dies for sinners.
The debt we could never pay is answered not by ten percent of Christ…
but by all of Christ.
And when the apostles begin teaching New Covenant churches how to give, something fascinating happens.
They speak about generosity repeatedly.
They speak about supporting ministry.
They speak about helping believers in need.
They speak about sharing materially.
They speak about giving regularly and intentionally.
They speak about generosity so radical that it can hurt.

But in the central New Testament instructions to churches about giving, the emphasis shifts from calculating a mandatory percentage toward willing, purposeful, proportionate, generous giving flowing from grace.
Paul tells the Corinthians:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ
hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia
“Each one as he has purposed in the heart…”
Then come words that should terrify anyone who has ever tried to manipulate Christians into opening their wallets:
μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs
“not from grief or from necessity/compulsion.”
And then:
ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ Θεός
hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos
“For God loves a cheerful giver.”
That is 2 Corinthians 9:7. The Greek text explicitly contrasts giving from the heart with giving under ἀνάγκη — anankē, necessity or compulsion.
Read that again.
God does not need to emotionally extort His children.
Grace does not put a spiritual gun against your conscience.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be manufactured through panic.
And Paul gives another principle in 1 Corinthians 16.
Speaking about a collection for believers, he tells Christians to set something aside regularly, ὅ τι ἂν εὐοδῶται—in keeping with how one is prospering.
That sounds less like careless spontaneity and more like intentional generosity.
Regular.
Thoughtful.
Proportionate.
Purposeful.
So does that mean Christians should never give ten percent?
Not at all.
Ten percent can be an excellent discipline.
For some believers, it may be a helpful starting point.
For someone learning to put God ahead of consumption, deliberately setting aside ten percent may train the heart away from greed.
But we should be careful about calling a useful benchmark a universal New Covenant command when the apostolic instructions themselves do not impose that percentage on the churches.
And here is where grace becomes far more challenging than a calculator.
Because legalism asks:
“What is the minimum I have to give?”
Grace asks:
“How can everything God has entrusted to me serve Christ?”
That is a much more dangerous question.
Ten percent can actually become comfortable.
Imagine earning $100.
“Ten belongs to God.”
Then what?
Does the remaining $90 belong entirely to you?
Imagine earning $10,000.
“One thousand for God.”
And the other $9,000?
Is Jesus Lord of that too?
This is where the Gospel destroys our little accounting system.
Because the Christian does not belong ten percent to Jesus.
The Christian belongs to Jesus.
Your money belongs to Jesus.
Your house belongs to Jesus.
Your career belongs to Jesus.
Your business belongs to Jesus.
Your talents belong to Jesus.
Your Saturday belongs to Jesus.
Your retirement belongs to Jesus.
Your influence belongs to Jesus.
Your phone belongs to Jesus.
Your plans belong to Jesus.
Even the breath currently moving through your lungs is mercy.
Christian stewardship begins when we stop asking how little we can surrender while still considering ourselves obedient.
And this is where the story gets painfully personal.
Because some people give ten percent faithfully…
and still worship money.
They tithe while ignoring a struggling family member.
They tithe while exploiting employees.
They tithe while drowning themselves in luxury.
They tithe while refusing generosity unless there is a tax deduction, recognition, applause, or promised blessing attached.
Jesus confronted precisely that kind of religious mathematics when He rebuked people who carefully counted herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
You can calculate ten percent perfectly…
and still withhold your heart.
But the opposite error is just as dangerous.
Some Christians hear “we are not under the Old Covenant tithe” and quietly translate that into:
“Wonderful. I don't have to give.”
But if grace makes us less generous than people living under the Law, perhaps we have misunderstood grace.
Look at Jesus.
He did not ask what percentage of Himself He was required to surrender.
He gave Himself.
This is the heartbeat beneath Christian generosity.
Paul's appeal to generosity in 2 Corinthians does not end with money.
It rises until it reaches worship.

The ministry of generous giving supplies needs and causes thanksgiving to overflow toward God. Paul says this generosity becomes evidence connected with their confession of the Gospel of Christ, and he finally erupts:
“Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!”
There it is.
Behind every truly Christian gift stands a greater Gift.
Jesus.
We give because God first gave.
We love because we have been loved.
We open our hands because Christ opened His arms on a cross.
We stop clutching temporary treasures because an eternal treasure has taken hold of us.
Maybe you cannot give ten percent right now.
Maybe you are drowning in debt.
Maybe you are buying groceries with trembling hands.
Maybe you are supporting elderly parents.
Maybe medical bills have swallowed what little margin you once had.
Do not let another human being weaponize Scripture to manufacture shame where Scripture gives room for willing, proportionate generosity.
God sees the heart.
And remember the widow Jesus watched giving two small coins.
Human beings saw an insignificant amount.
Jesus saw sacrifice.
But perhaps your situation is different.
Perhaps you could give far more than ten percent and barely notice.
Perhaps God has prospered you, but your lifestyle expanded every time your income did.
A larger house.
Another upgrade.
Another gadget.
Another vacation.
Another package arriving at the door.
And somewhere between “God blessed me” and “I deserve this,” generosity became whatever was left over.
Then maybe the question “Do Christians have to tithe?” is protecting you from the question your heart does not want to hear:
How much is enough for me?
There are believers for whom ten percent would be an enormous act of faith.
There are others for whom ten percent may be remarkably easy.
The New Testament does not lower the vision of generosity.
It takes the ruler away and aims at the heart.
Give deliberately.
Give willingly.
Give proportionately.
Give generously.
Give sacrificially when God leads.
Support faithful Gospel ministry.
Care for people in need.
Provide for your responsibilities.
Do not give because someone frightened you.
Do not give because someone promised that God would make you rich.
Do not give because you think money can purchase divine favor.
You cannot buy what Jesus purchased with blood.
Give because Christ is worthy.
And if ten percent helps you begin living generously, begin there.
If you can joyfully do more, do not let ten percent become the ceiling of your obedience.
And if you genuinely cannot reach that number, do not pretend before God. Begin faithfully with what you can give, ask Him for wisdom, order your finances carefully, and grow in generosity.
But whatever the percentage…
do not give God leftovers.
Give Him your heart.
And now I need to say something important about Gospel Warrior itself.
If these articles have helped you return to Scripture…
if something here has confronted sin without hiding grace…
if these messages have reached you at two in the morning when nobody knew you were struggling…
if they have helped you remember that Jesus has not finished writing your story…
then you can help this ministry continue and expand.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces your responsibility to your local church, your family, believers in need, or wherever else God is calling you to give.
It does not.
But voluntary support of Gospel work is thoroughly consistent with the New Testament vision of believers using their resources to serve Christ, meet needs, and advance faithful ministry.
But please hear this clearly.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot purchase salvation.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Christ already paid the price we could never pay.
And money is not the only way you can help.
That costs nothing.
One share could place this message in front of them tonight.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is nothing more than rules.
Invite even the unbeliever who has questions nobody in church ever allowed them to ask.
And I want you to do something even more important than sharing.
Has giving been worship for you…
or has it been guilt?
Have you used “grace” as an excuse to keep everything for yourself?
Have you been afraid that God would punish you financially if you missed ten percent?
Has money quietly become the part of your life you do not want Jesus touching?
No pretending.
No performance.
There may be someone reading your comment who thought they were the only one struggling.
And perhaps this is the scandal underneath the entire question.
We keep asking how much we owe God.
Ten percent?
Five?
Twenty?
But the Gospel announces something far more astonishing.
You owed a debt you could never repay.
And instead of demanding payment from your empty hands…
God gave.
Christ came.
Christ obeyed.
Christ suffered.
Christ was crucified.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
And sinners who bring nothing but repentance and faith receive forgiveness they could never afford.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that does not merely change where you go when you die.
Grace changes what you live for while you are still breathing.
Including what you do with money.
So should Christians tithe ten percent?

Christians are not given a simple New Testament command imposing ten percent on every believer in the same covenantal form in which Israel received its tithing laws. Yet Christians are unmistakably called to something that can be even more searching: intentional, willing, proportionate, cheerful, generous, sometimes deeply sacrificial stewardship under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Ten percent can be a wise beginning.
It should never become an excuse to tell Jesus:
“The rest is mine.”
Because maybe the most important number in Christian giving was never ten.
Maybe it was one hundred.
Not necessarily one hundred percent placed in an offering.
But one hundred percent surrendered to the ownership of Christ.
Your spending surrendered.
Your saving surrendered.
Your giving surrendered.
Your earning surrendered.
Your plans surrendered.
Your future surrendered.
Your heart surrendered.
All of it placed beneath the pierced hands of the One who gave everything to redeem you.
And perhaps when we finally understand that…
we stop asking:
“Jesus, how much do I have to give You?”
And begin asking:
“Jesus, everything I have came from You. How do You want me to use it?”
That question cannot be answered by a calculator.
It can only be answered by a surrendered heart.
The Gospel never asks you to purchase grace. It reveals a Savior whose grace was so costly that, once you truly see Him, clenched hands begin to open.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SIN WE COMMIT WITH SOMEONE ELSE’S STORY
paragraphs:
THE SIN WE COMMIT WITH SOMEONE ELSE’S STORY
Why Gossip Is More Spiritually Dangerous Than We Admit—and Why Jesus Wants More Than Your Silence. He Wants Your Heart.
There is a terrifying kind of sin that rarely feels like sin while you are committing it.
You don’t have to sneak into a dark room.
You don’t have to hide a bottle.
You don’t have to erase your browser history.
You don’t even have to raise your voice.
Sometimes all you have to do is lean a little closer and say:
“Please don’t tell anyone I told you this…”
