A faithful shepherd doesn't chain the sheep to himself—he keeps pointing them toward the Shepherd whose scars prove who they belong to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SEXUAL DESIRE EXIST WITHOUT BECOMING SEXUAL SIN?
paragraphs: CAN SEXUAL DESIRE EXIST WITHOUT BECOMING SEXUAL SIN?
The Desire You’re Ashamed to Admit May Not Be the Sin You Think It Is—But What You Do With It Can Either Feed the Darkness or Lead You Straight Into the Grace of Jesus Christ
There is a moment many Christians never talk about.
You notice someone.
Something happens inside you.
Attraction.
Desire.
A physical response you did not schedule, request, or consciously manufacture.
And almost immediately, another feeling arrives.
Shame.
“Did I just sin?”
“Does God think I’m disgusting?”
“If I were really holy, would I even feel this?”
So you look away.
You pray harder.
Maybe you rebuke yourself.
Maybe you have spent years secretly wondering whether every flicker of sexual attraction proves there is something spiritually wrong with you.
And perhaps nobody ever taught you how to distinguish between experiencing sexual desire and deliberately turning another human being into material for lust.
That distinction matters.
Because confusing temptation with sin can bury a sincere Christian beneath unnecessary condemnation.
But confusing desire with permission can lead that same Christian into bondage.
The Gospel gives us something better than either extreme.
Truth.
And grace.
So here is the question we need enough courage to ask:
Can sexual desire exist without becoming sexual sin?
Yes.
But that answer needs to be understood carefully, because the distance between desire and sin can sometimes be only a few deliberate thoughts apart.
And Jesus cares deeply about what happens there.
Sexuality itself did not begin in a nightclub, pornography studio, dating app, or fallen human imagination.
It appears in Scripture before the fall.

Before shame entered the human story, God created humanity male and female, blessed them, and told them to “be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:27–28). Genesis 2 presents marital union without embarrassment: “the two shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad — “one flesh.”
Sexual union, therefore, is not something Satan invented that Christians reluctantly tolerate.
God created human sexuality.
Sin distorted it.
That difference changes everything.
The Christian answer to sexual brokenness is therefore not, “Your body is evil.”
It is, “Your whole person belongs to God.”
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 6:20
Christian holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is the redemption of what we do with the body.
And this is where many wounded consciences need to hear something clearly:
Noticing beauty is not automatically lust.
Experiencing attraction is not automatically sexual immorality.
Feeling temptation is not identical to committing sin.
If temptation itself were sin, we would have an enormous theological problem.
Hebrews says Jesus was:
“tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin.”
The Greek is striking:
πεπειρασμένον δὲ κατὰ πάντα καθ’ ὁμοιότητα χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας
The final words, χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας — chōris hamartias, mean “without sin.”
Jesus was genuinely tempted.
Jesus remained completely sinless.
Therefore temptation and sin cannot simply be identical.

That does not mean Jesus experienced every specific fallen desire exactly as sinful humanity experiences it. Scripture is affirming the reality of His temptation and His sinlessness, not giving us permission to project every human experience onto Christ.
But it establishes something enormously important:
The presence of temptation does not itself prove the presence of guilt.
James helps us see what can happen next.
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin…”
The Greek word translated “desire” is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia.
And here is something fascinating.
The word itself is not automatically evil in every context.
It describes strong desire or longing, and context determines its moral character.
Jesus Himself says in Luke 22:15:
ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα
Literally, an emphatic expression of desire: “I have earnestly desired…”
So the mere existence of strong desire is not the entire moral question.
The question becomes:
What is desired?
How is it desired?
What do you choose to do with that desire?
That brings us to some of the most searching words Jesus ever spoke about sexuality.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
—Matthew 5:27–28
The Greek phrase deserves careful attention:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
It describes looking in relation to desiring or lusting after her.
Jesus is going beneath the externally visible act of adultery and exposing the heart from which sexual sin can grow.
He is not giving men permission to say, “As long as I don’t touch her, I can mentally consume her.”
He brings holiness all the way into the imagination.
But neither should we carelessly turn His teaching into:
“If your brain recognizes that someone is sexually attractive, you have already committed adultery.”
There is a meaningful moral distinction between recognizing attraction and choosing to cultivate lust.
You can notice without possessing.
You can feel without feeding.
You can be tempted without surrendering.
You can recognize someone’s beauty without mentally undressing them.
You can experience a bodily response without giving that response authority over your imagination.
And perhaps that is where this article just found you.
Because maybe your greatest battle has never been the first look.
It has been what happens after it.
The second look.
Then another.
The imagination you permit to remain.
The fantasy you begin directing.
The private storyline where the other person stops being someone made in the image of God and becomes someone existing for your consumption.
That is where desire can become something darker.
The body says:
“I am attracted.”
Lust answers:
“Then I will take possession of this person inside my imagination.”
And pornography takes that logic even further.
It trains the eyes to consume bodies while forgetting souls.
A person becomes an image.
An image becomes stimulation.
Stimulation becomes repetition.
Repetition becomes habit.
Habit can become bondage.
And somewhere in that cycle, someone who once wanted intimacy can discover that they have been training themselves for consumption instead.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
You promised yourself it was the last time.
Then there was another last time.
And another.
You cleared the history.
Closed the browser.
Deleted the app.
Prayed.
Cried.
Felt clean for a few days.
Then temptation returned.
And after falling again, perhaps you could barely pray because you imagined Jesus looking at you with the same disgust you felt toward yourself.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that sexual sin is harmless.
But neither does the Gospel tell the repentant sinner that sexual sin is stronger than the blood of Christ.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not redefine darkness as light.
He enters our darkness and calls us into the light.
“For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.”
—John 3:17
And later:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Notice that Scripture does not say:
“If we pretend.”
“If we excuse.”
“If we rename.”
“If we hide.”
It says:
If we confess.
The Greek verb is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō.
To confess is to acknowledge—to say the truth about our sin before God rather than constructing another name for it.
And strangely enough, freedom often begins when hiding ends.
Somebody reading this has spent years hiding.
Nobody knows about the messages.
Nobody knows about the pornography.
Nobody knows about the fantasy.
Nobody knows about the emotional affair.
Nobody knows what happens when loneliness meets a locked bedroom door and a glowing screen.
Everybody sees the Bible verses you post.
Almost nobody sees the battle you fight at 1:17 in the morning.
And you have become exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
One visible.
One secret.
But Jesus already knows both.
And He is still calling you.
Not deeper into hiding.
Into repentance.
The beautiful thing about biblical repentance is that it is more than feeling terrible.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It carries the idea of changing one’s mind, turning from sin toward God.
Repentance is not merely:
“I hate myself because I failed.”
It is:
“Jesus, I agree with You about this. I do not want this sin ruling me anymore. Teach me to walk in Your light.”
There is an enormous difference between conviction and hopeless condemnation.
Conviction says:
“This must come into the light.”
Hopeless condemnation whispers:
“You might as well stay in the darkness because someone like you will never change.”
One draws you toward Christ.
The other makes hiding feel inevitable.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Not because sin became insignificant.
Because Christ became our righteousness.
This means your sexual history does not have to become your permanent identity.
What you watched is not your name.
What you did is not your name.
What someone did to you is not your name.
The temptation you are fighting is not your name.
The failure you confessed is not your name.
Your deepest identity, if you belong to Christ, is not the darkest chapter you wish you could erase.
You belong to Jesus.
And Jesus is still writing.
But grace is not permission to return comfortably to chains.
Paul anticipates that distortion:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!”
—Romans 6:1–2
Grace forgives us.
And grace begins teaching us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Think about that.
Grace trains.
Not merely forgives.
Not merely wipes yesterday clean.
Grace begins discipling tomorrow.
So what should you do when sexual desire appears?
You do not necessarily have to panic because attraction exists.
You bring desire under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
You learn to see the person in front of you as a human being bearing God’s image, not as a body provided for your imagination.
You stop negotiating with fantasies that you already know are pulling you away from Christ.
You flee what Scripture tells you to flee.
Paul does not tell Timothy to stand around admiring temptation while proving how spiritually strong he is.
He says:
“Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace…”
—2 Timothy 2:22
Sometimes holiness looks very spiritual.
Sometimes holiness looks like closing the tab.
Walking away.
Putting the phone outside the bedroom.
Ending the secret conversation.
Installing accountability.
Calling a trusted Christian friend before you fall rather than afterward.
Changing the environment where you repeatedly compromise.
Refusing to revisit the profile.
Stopping the flirtation you keep calling innocent.
Confessing to mature believers who can help you walk in the light.
And if the pattern has become compulsive or deeply entrenched, getting wise pastoral and professional help is not evidence that Jesus failed you.
It may be one of the means through which healing and disciplined obedience begin taking shape.
Sexual holiness is not achieved by pretending sexuality does not exist.
It is learned by surrendering sexuality to the One who created it.
That includes single Christians.
Widows and widowers.
Married Christians.
Young adults.
Older adults.
People experiencing unwanted desires.
People carrying sexual regrets.
People whose marriages are struggling.
People who have been sexually wounded.
People who have sinned sexually.
People who have been sinned against sexually.
The Gospel is not reserved for people with uncomplicated stories.
Jesus has always been extraordinarily good at walking into complicated stories.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Her humiliation became public entertainment.
Her sin was dragged into daylight while the people around her prepared judgment.
Jesus did not call adultery righteousness.
Neither did He hand her over to the crowd’s cruelty.
He told her:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
—John 8:11
Grace.
And truth.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
Grace.
“Sin no more.”
Truth.
We keep trying to separate what Jesus holds together.
Some want grace without repentance.
Others preach repentance without tenderness.
Jesus gives us holy mercy.
He forgives sinners and calls forgiven sinners into transformed lives.
Maybe that is exactly what you need tonight.
Not someone screaming that sexual desire makes you filthy.
Not someone telling you sexual boundaries no longer matter.
You need Jesus.
The Jesus who knows what you clicked.
The Jesus who knows what you imagined.
The Jesus who knows what happened to you.
The Jesus who knows what you did.
The Jesus who knows what you almost did.
The Jesus who knows the battle you have never told another person about.
And still says:
Come into the light.
There is forgiveness here.
There is cleansing here.
There is a cross here.
There is an empty tomb here.
There is power to begin again here.
And if you fall?
Do not turn your fall into permission to keep falling.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His forgiveness.
Get back into the fight.
Perhaps someone needs to say this publicly for the first time.
You do not need to publish intimate details.
You do not owe strangers your private history.
But sometimes three honest words can become the first crack in a wall that shame has spent years building.
You may need to read it again on a night when temptation is louder than conviction.
Send it privately to the friend who has been disappearing behind shame.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, healing, or discipleship, consider following and supporting this ministry so this work can continue reaching people who desperately need Christ-centered truth.
Financial support should never be treated as purchasing God’s favor, forgiveness, blessing, or salvation.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Giving cannot replace repentance.
Scripture says:
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
And there is much more available beyond a single article.
Give Jesus your heart.
Give Him the room you keep locking.
Give Him the search history.
Give Him the fantasy.
Give Him the loneliness.
Give Him the relationship.
Give Him the attraction.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him your body.
Give Him your future.
Because the goal of Christianity is not to become a person incapable of experiencing desire.
The goal is to become a person whose desires, body, imagination, relationships, sexuality, and whole life increasingly come under the beautiful lordship of Jesus Christ.
Sexual desire can exist without becoming sexual sin.
But desire was never meant to become your master.
Christ is Lord.
And when temptation comes, your story does not have to end where your desire begins.
There is another road.
Sometimes narrow.
Sometimes costly.
Sometimes walked with trembling hands and tears in your eyes.
But it leads toward freedom.
And if you already crossed the line…
If you already failed…
If your story contains chapters you would burn before letting another human being read them…
Look at the cross.
Your scandal may explain part of your past.
It does not have authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
The chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read may become the very page where people discover how astonishingly far the grace of Jesus Christ can reach.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHY DO YOU CALL ME ‘LORD, LORD’… AND STILL IGNORE ME?”
paragraphs:
“WHY DO YOU CALL ME ‘LORD, LORD’… AND STILL IGNORE ME?”
The terrifying question Jesus asked religious people—and the difference between knowing His name and actually surrendering your life to Him.
There are words of Jesus that comfort you.
And then there are words of Jesus that corner you.
Words that leave nowhere to hide.
No theological loophole.
No carefully polished Christian image.
No church attendance record.
No worship playlist.
No Bible verse in your biography.
No cross hanging around your neck.
Just you…
and Jesus.
And one question.
“Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
That question appears in Luke 6:46, and perhaps we have heard it so many times that we no longer feel how devastating it actually is.
But imagine hearing it from Christ Himself.
Not from an angry preacher.
Not from someone trying to shame you.
Not from someone who knows only the public version of your life.
Jesus.
The One who knows what happens after everyone else goes home.
The One who knows what you delete.
What you hide.
What you secretly excuse.
What you keep promising to surrender.
What you refuse to forgive.
What you repeatedly justify.
What you know He has told you…
and what you continue refusing to do.
Then He asks:
“Why?”
The Greek text preserves the force of His question:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
A faithful rendering is:
“Why do you call Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
That repeated Κύριε κύριε—Kyrie, kyrie—“Lord, Lord” matters.
Jesus is confronting an unbearable contradiction between confession and conduct.
Their mouths are saying one thing.
Their lives are saying another.
And suddenly Christianity becomes painfully personal.
Because it is possible to say “Lord” beautifully…
while quietly living as though you are lord.
That is the scandal.
We can sing about surrender while negotiating the terms of our obedience.
We can raise our hands on Sunday while holding tightly to the very thing Christ has commanded us to release.
We can post Scripture publicly and entertain sin privately.
We can defend biblical truth in comment sections while refusing to practice biblical forgiveness in our own homes.
We can tell the world that Jesus is King while treating His commands as suggestions to be followed whenever they agree with our feelings.
And Jesus asks:
Why do you call Me Lord?
The word κύριος—kyrios can mean “lord,” “master,” or one possessing authority.
So calling Jesus “Lord” is not merely attaching a religious title to His name.
Lordship has consequences.
If He is Lord, I am not.
If He is Master, I do not get to rewrite His commands whenever obedience becomes uncomfortable.
If He is King, Christianity cannot merely be Jesus decorating the life I already wanted.
He has authority over it.
My sexuality.
My money.
My anger.
My relationships.
My ambitions.
My grudges.
My secret habits.
My speech.
My treatment of enemies.
My private thoughts.
My public behavior.
My plans for tomorrow.
Everything.
And that is precisely where Christianity becomes more uncomfortable than religious culture sometimes allows.
Because many people want Jesus as Savior without wanting Jesus as Lord.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
Grace without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without a cross.
We want Christ to rescue us from hell while leaving the throne of our present life untouched.
But the biblical Jesus does not merely offer improvement.
He calls us to follow Him.
And following implies movement.
It means when Jesus goes one direction and my sinful desires go another, somebody has to lose.
Biblical repentance means I stop insisting that somebody must always be Jesus.
This is why Luke 6:46 cannot be ripped out of its context and turned into a slogan about “trying harder.”
Jesus immediately tells a story.
He says that the person who comes to Him, hears His words, and does them is like a man building a house who dug deep and laid its foundation upon rock.
Then the flood came.
The river slammed against the house.
But it could not shake it because it had been well built.
Then Jesus describes another person.
This person also hears.
That detail should haunt us.
The foolish person is not ignorant of the words.
He hears them.
But he does not act upon them.
Jesus says this person resembles someone who builds a house on the ground without a foundation.
The river crashes against it…
and immediately it collapses.
Jesus concludes that its ruin is great.
Notice the difference.
Both heard.
Both built.
Both experienced the storm.
Only one obeyed.
The dividing line was not exposure to Jesus' teaching.
It was what they did after hearing it.
That means one of the greatest dangers in Christianity is becoming so familiar with truth that familiarity begins impersonating obedience.
You know the verse.
You know the sermon.
You know the worship song.
You know the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say amen.
You may even know enough theology to correct somebody else's doctrine.
But knowing what Jesus said and submitting to what Jesus said are not identical things.
James later expresses the same danger:
“Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.”
That final phrase is terrifying.
Deceiving yourselves.
There is a kind of deception that does not require somebody else lying to you.
You can do it to yourself.
You can mistake conviction for repentance.
You can feel guilty and assume you have changed.
You can cry during worship and assume tears equal surrender.
You can agree with a sermon and assume agreement equals obedience.
You can know that something is wrong…
hate yourself afterward…
promise God you will never do it again…
and still protect the doorway through which you keep returning to it.
Jesus is not asking whether His words moved you emotionally.
He is asking whether His words moved you obediently.
And before anyone turns this into salvation by moral performance, we need to hear the rest of the Gospel.
Because Jesus did not come looking for people who had already achieved flawless obedience.
If that were the requirement for approaching Him, nobody would come.
Scripture says plainly:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples fled.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The woman caught in adultery stood exposed.
The thief beside Jesus was literally dying under criminal condemnation.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people successfully climbed their way to God.
Christianity is the announcement that God came down to sinners.
Jesus Christ lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The answer to hypocrisy is therefore not pretending harder.
It is repentance.
It is grace.
It is coming into the light.
It is admitting:
“Jesus, I have called You Lord with my mouth while fighting Your authority with my life.”
And here is where scandal begins becoming grace.
Because the same Christ who exposes hypocrisy also receives repentant sinners.
Jesus does not expose you because He enjoys humiliation.
He exposes what is killing you because darkness survives by remaining hidden.
Grace does not say your rebellion does not matter.
Grace says your rebellion mattered enough that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is greater than the sin you finally stop defending.
Think about Peter.
He said he would never abandon Jesus.
Then, within hours, he denied even knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
The sound of the rooster.
The realization.
The collapse of everything Peter thought he was.
Yet Peter's scandal was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
Not because denial suddenly became acceptable.
Not because truth no longer mattered.
But because failure surrendered to Christ does not have to become your identity forever.
Jesus rewrites people.
That does not mean He calls evil good.
It means He takes sinners who have finally stopped pretending and begins transforming them by grace.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Not from scandal to pretending the scandal never happened.
Not from scandal to self-righteousness.
Not from scandal to religious reputation management.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal is hidden.
Nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your church does not know.
Your friends would never suspect it.
Maybe there is an addiction behind the worship songs.
Pornography behind the Bible app.
Bitterness behind the smile.
Jealousy behind the congratulations.
Pride behind the ministry.
A secret relationship behind the Christian image.
Greed behind the generosity people see.
Unforgiveness buried beneath years of religious language.
Or maybe your rebellion looks respectable.
That can be even harder to recognize.
Maybe you are not living in some spectacular public scandal.
Maybe you simply keep telling Jesus:
“Later.”
Later I will forgive.
Later I will reconcile.
Later I will stop.
Later I will confess.
Later I will obey.
Later I will surrender this relationship.
Later I will seek God seriously.
Later I will become the person Christ is calling me to become.
Later.
But delayed obedience can become dressed-up disobedience.
Jesus' question remains:
Why call Me Lord…
if you have already decided which commands you will ignore?
And this is where the article stops being about “those hypocritical Christians.”
It becomes about me.
It becomes about you.
What has Jesus already made clear that you keep negotiating?
Don't answer publicly for appearances.
Answer before God.
What are you defending that Scripture is confronting?
Who are you refusing to forgive?
What are you hiding?
Where are you deliberately compromising?
What relationship has become more authoritative than Christ?
What appetite gets the final vote?
What command do you secretly wish Jesus had never given?
Because sometimes the command that irritates us most reveals the throne we are protecting most fiercely.
And perhaps right now you feel exposed.
Good.
Not condemned beyond hope.
Exposed.
There is a difference.
The enemy wants exposure to drive you away from Christ in shame.
The Gospel calls exposed sinners toward Christ in repentance.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That promise is not permission to make peace with sin.
It is freedom to stop hiding from the Savior.
You don't have to clean yourself perfectly before approaching Jesus.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Bring Him the ugly thing.
The repeated thing.
The thing you said you would never do again.
The thing you are ashamed to name.
Bring the ruins.
Bring the hypocrisy.
Bring the double life.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the secret.
Bring the scandal.
But don't bring it so you can ask Jesus to bless it.
Bring it so you can surrender it.
That is the difference.
Jesus does not merely want to become another voice in your life.
He is Lord.
And genuine faith does not produce sinless perfection overnight, but it does change our relationship with obedience.
The Christian still stumbles.
The Christian still needs grace.
The Christian still confesses sin.
The Christian still fights the flesh.
But the direction changes.
We stop making peace treaties with the sins Christ died to redeem us from.
We fall…
and return.
We fail…
and confess.
We wander…
and hear the Shepherd calling.
We discover another room in our hearts that we have kept locked…
and eventually hand Him the key.
This is sanctification.
Not earning Christ's love.
Living because we have received it.
Jesus said elsewhere:
“If you love Me, keep My commandments.”
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase His grace.
Obedience is fruit growing from a life captured by His grace.
You cannot buy the cross.
You cannot earn resurrection.
You cannot accumulate enough Christian achievements to make God indebted to you.
Salvation is grace.
Yet the grace that forgives also transforms.
Christ does not merely pardon rebels and leave rebellion enthroned.
He makes disciples.
So maybe tonight your prayer does not need sophisticated theology.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, You are Lord.
Forgive me for the places where I have only called You Lord.
Show me where my confession and my life contradict each other.
Expose what I keep hiding.
Give me strength to obey where I have been resisting.
I cannot save myself.
I need Your mercy.
I need Your Spirit.
I need Your grace.
Teach me to follow You.”
And then…
when He shows you something…
don't merely admire the conviction.
Respond.
Make the apology.
End the sinful arrangement.
Delete what needs deleting.
Return what needs returning.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive whom Christ commands you to forgive.
Seek wise, mature Christian accountability where you need help.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Come back to fellowship.
Take the next faithful step.
Not because these actions purchase salvation.
Because when the King calls, disciples follow.
And if you stumbled yesterday?
Return today.
If you fell this morning?
Return now.
If you have spent years performing Christianity while secretly starving spiritually?
Return.
The cross still stands.
The tomb is still empty.
Jesus is still Lord.
Grace is still grace.
And repentance is still one of God's great mercies because it means your present direction does not have to become your final destination.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to tell strangers every private detail. But you can refuse to hide from God anymore.
Sometimes one honest sentence is where the mask finally begins to crack.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It doesn't.
Christ alone saves.
But if biblical truth has helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone you may never realize is quietly drowning.
Send it privately to the friend whose faith has gone cold.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Invite even the person who says they no longer believe.
Let them encounter Christ rather than another performance of Christianity.
Because one day the storm may hit your own house, and you may need to remember what Jesus said about foundations.
Those cannot be purchased.
Your support helps us keep creating Scripture-centered content intended to point people toward Jesus, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformed lives.
If you believe this ministry should keep reaching people with Christ-centered truth, you can support the mission here:
Jesus is calling you.
Not to become a customer.
Not to become a statistic.
Not to become another follower on a page.
To become His disciple.
The question was never merely whether your lips could pronounce the word “Lord.”
The question is whether the One you call Lord actually has your life.
Because eventually every house meets a storm.
And when the waters rise, the foundation underneath everything you have built will matter far more than the Christian name painted across the front door.
So when Jesus asks,
“Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
don't waste the question by applying it only to somebody else.
Let it search you.
Let it expose you.
Let it bring you to repentance.
Then let grace lead you home.
The most dangerous distance in Christianity may be the few inches between a mouth that says “Lord” and a heart that still whispers, “I will rule myself.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY GOD WALKED OUT OF HIS OWN TEMPLE
paragraphs:
THE DAY GOD WALKED OUT OF HIS OWN TEMPLE
Ezekiel Watched the Glory of God Leave Jerusalem—And the Most Terrifying Part Was That the Religious People Were Still There
There are frightening verses in the Bible.
Verses about judgment.
Verses about fire.
Verses about nations falling and kings trembling.
But there is something uniquely terrifying about Ezekiel 10–11.
Because Ezekiel saw something happen that should make every religious heart go quiet.
He watched the glory of God leave the temple.
Not because Babylon was stronger than God.
Not because heaven had lost control.
Not because the Lord had been defeated.
God left a place that still carried His name.
Sit with that.
The building remained.
The priests remained.
The religious system remained.
Jerusalem remained.
People could still point toward the temple and say, “There it is.”
And yet Ezekiel saw what human eyes could not see.
The glory was moving.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps one of the greatest spiritual dangers is not openly rejecting God.
Perhaps it is becoming so accustomed to the things of God that we no longer notice when our hearts have wandered from God Himself.
You can still know the songs.
Still carry the Bible.
Still post the verse.
Still say “God is good.”
Still attend church.
Still know when to raise your hands.
Still have Christian language decorating a life that has quietly learned how to resist the Lord.
And Ezekiel’s vision forces a disturbing question upon us:
What if we have mistaken proximity to holy things for intimacy with the Holy One?
Ezekiel had already been shown what was happening beneath Jerusalem’s religious appearance.
In Ezekiel 8, God brought the prophet, in a vision, into scenes of escalating abomination connected with the temple. Idolatry had invaded the place associated with the worship of YHWH.
This matters because Ezekiel 10 is not the story of an impatient God suddenly exploding over one mistake.
The departure of the glory comes in the context of persistent covenant rebellion and desecration.
The people had not merely stumbled.
Their worship had become corrupted.
And then Ezekiel sees it.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 10:18 reads:
וַיֵּצֵא כְּבוֹד־יְהוָה מֵעַל מִפְתַּן הַבָּיִת
Vayyēṣēʾ kevōd-YHWH mēʿal miptan habbāyit.
“And the glory of YHWH departed from over the threshold of the house.”
The word that should stop us is:
כְּבוֹד
Kavod.
Glory.
It carries the idea of weightiness, honor, significance, majesty.
This was not merely beautiful light disappearing from a building.
Ezekiel was witnessing the visible manifestation of the divine glory withdrawing from the defiled sanctuary.
And notice something heartbreaking.
The glory does not simply disappear instantaneously.
Ezekiel watches its movement.
Earlier, the glory moves toward the threshold.
Then in Ezekiel 10:18 it departs from the threshold and stands over the cherubim.
The cherubim rise.
The wheels accompany them.
The glory of the God of Israel is above them.
Then the movement continues.
Toward the east.
Until Ezekiel 11:23 says that the glory of YHWH went up from the midst of the city and stood over the mountain east of Jerusalem.
It feels almost painfully deliberate.
Threshold.
Cherubim.
Gate.
City.
Mountain.
Departure.
And I cannot read that without wondering how many times God had warned His people before this moment.
How many prophets had spoken?
How many calls to repentance had been ignored?
How many compromises had once troubled consciences but eventually became normal?
That is how spiritual numbness works.
Rarely does a person wake up one morning and decide, “Today I will harden my heart against God.”
It usually happens more quietly.
One compromise.
One rationalization.
One hidden habit.
One conviction postponed.
One apology never made.
One sin renamed so we no longer have to call it sin.
One season of prayerlessness excused because life is busy.
One secret resentment fed because we believe we deserve it.
One private appetite protected from the lordship of Christ.
Then another.
Then another.
Until what once made us tremble barely makes us uncomfortable.
That may be why this story feels so modern.
We know how to maintain appearances.
Someone asks how we are spiritually.
“Good.”
But we have not prayed honestly in weeks.
“Blessed.”
But bitterness is eating us alive.
“God is faithful.”
True words.
But sometimes spoken by lips belonging to a heart running from Him.
We can curate Christianity.
God cannot be curated.
He sees behind the caption.
Behind the church clothes.
Behind the ministry title.
Behind the worship playlist.
Behind the smiling family picture.
Behind the “Amen.”
Behind the theology we can explain to everyone else.
He sees us.
And perhaps somebody reading this has become exhausted from pretending.
You still love Jesus—or at least desperately want to.
But something has grown cold.
Prayer feels different.
Something you once fought has slowly become something you tolerate.
You remember when conviction came quickly.
Now you can excuse things that once brought you to your knees.
Do not respond to that realization by running farther from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Because Ezekiel’s vision is terrifying, but terror is not the final word.
Buried inside these chapters of judgment is one of the most astonishing demonstrations of grace in the book.
The people have been scattered.
Jerusalem looks privileged because the temple is there.
The exiles look abandoned because they are far away.
Then God says something nobody expecting a merely location-bound theology would anticipate.
Ezekiel 11:16 contains this extraordinary expression:
וָאֱהִי לָהֶם לְמִקְדָּשׁ מְעַט
Vāʾĕhî lāhem ləmiqdāš məʿaṭ.
God declares that He has been for them a miqdāš meʿaṭ among the countries where they have gone.
A sanctuary.
God's presence was not trapped inside Jerusalem.
The temple could be judged.
Jerusalem could fall.
The people could be scattered.
But YHWH had not ceased to be God.
The exiles discovered something devastating and beautiful:
You can lose the place you thought you needed and discover that God Himself is what you needed most.
Maybe you know something about exile.
Not Babylon.
Your exile had another name.
Divorce.
Grief.
Failure.
Rejection.
Bankruptcy.
Loneliness.
A child who walked away.
A dream that died.
A church wound you still struggle to talk about.
A season when everything familiar disappeared so quickly that you wondered whether God disappeared with it.
Perhaps you whispered prayers from a room nobody knew was breaking you.
“God, where are You?”
Ezekiel gives us an answer that does not make suffering painless, but it makes despair impossible for those who belong to God.
He is not confined to the place where your life made sense.
He can meet people in exile.
He can preserve His people in Babylon.
He can speak beside the Chebar canal.
He can be sanctuary to the scattered.
And He can meet you in the place you never wanted to be.
But grace does not mean God looks at our idols and says they do not matter.
The same God who promises His presence also promises transformation.
Listen to Ezekiel 11:19:
וְנָתַתִּי לָהֶם לֵב אֶחָד וְרוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם
Wənāṯattî lāhem lēḇ ʾeḥāḏ, wərûaḥ ḥăḏāšāh ʾettēn bəqirbəḵem.
God promises to give them one heart and to put a new spirit within them.
Then comes the picture that exposes the real problem:
He will remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh.
לֵב הָאֶבֶן
Lēv hāʾeven.
The heart of stone.
לֵב בָּשָׂר
Lēv bāśār.
A heart of flesh.
There is the battlefield.
God was not merely interested in repairing a damaged religious institution.
He was addressing damaged worshipers.
The deepest problem was never architecture.
It was the human heart.
And thousands of years later, our deepest problem remains the same.
We do not merely need improved circumstances.
We need transformed hearts.
We do not merely need inspiration.
We need redemption.
We do not merely need another religious routine.
We need God to do what sinners cannot accomplish by self-improvement.
We need hearts awakened to Him.
And this is where Ezekiel's vision ultimately makes the Christian heart look toward Jesus Christ.
We must be careful here.

Ezekiel 10–11 is first a prophetic vision concerning YHWH, Jerusalem, judgment, exile, and restoration. We should not erase that historical and covenant context just to manufacture a Christian illustration.
But when Christians read Ezekiel within the whole canon of Scripture, something breathtaking emerges.
The story of God's presence with His people does not end on the mountain east of Jerusalem.
The Gospel announces that the eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Jesus stood among sinners.
Touched lepers.
Ate with people whose reputations made religious society uncomfortable.
Called the guilty to repentance.
Forgave sins.
Confronted hypocrisy.
Wept.
Bled.
And went to the cross.
This is not a Gospel in which God shrugs at sin.
The cross destroys that illusion.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God cannot be achieved through our moral effort, religious reputation, charitable works, or spiritual performance.
Christ bore sin and judgment.
The sinless One gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Grace is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is God accomplishing redemption that sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up enough so Jesus will finally accept your application.
Biblical repentance turns from sin toward God.
Faith rests in Christ.
And the Gospel announces something almost too beautiful for guilty people to believe:
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Peter's denial was not his final chapter.
The thief's criminal past was not his final chapter.
Paul's persecution of Christians was not his final chapter.
And if you come to Christ, your scandal does not have to write the ending either.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that sentence sounds beautiful until the scandal is yours.
It is easier to believe grace for somebody else.
Harder when you remember what you did.
Harder at 2:17 in the morning when memories return without permission.
Harder when you remember the person you hurt.
The marriage you damaged.
The years you wasted.
The addiction you hid.
The lie everybody believed.
The secret nobody knows.
The promise to God you broke again.
And again.
And again.
There are people who know Jesus forgives sins theologically but still live as though their particular sin was somehow printed in ink darker than His blood can cover.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not pretending your sin was small.
The answer is realizing your Savior is greater.
Confess it.
Bring it into His light.
Repent.
Stop negotiating with the thing crucifying your spiritual life.
Stop decorating chains Jesus calls you to leave.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop waiting until you feel worthy enough to come home.
You will never repent because you became worthy of grace.
You repent because the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of you.
Sometimes the mercy of God feels painful when it touches the thing we have spent years protecting.
Not because typing three words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need Him is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not fighting alone.
Pray for one another.
Encourage one another.
Point one another back to Christ.
Because Ezekiel's message is not simply, “Look how terrible these people became.”
The dangerous way to read Scripture is always to imagine ourselves standing safely outside the warning.
Ezekiel asks us to look inward.
What have I allowed into the temple of my attention?
What has captured my affection?
What gets the first of my thoughts and the best of my energy?
What sin have I renamed?
What idol would make me angry if Jesus asked me to surrender it?
Where am I performing Christianity instead of walking with Christ?
These are uncomfortable questions.
Not because every word needs to be remembered, but because there may come a night when you need these questions again.
A night when compromise looks attractive.
A night when shame tells you to hide.
A night when you need to remember that the God who judges idolatry is also the God who promises a new heart.
Not as a superstition.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
Someone may be drifting and nobody knows.
Someone may have become comfortable with compromise.
Someone may believe their scandal disqualified them permanently from grace.
Someone may need to hear tonight that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Let them see a God whose holiness is terrifying, whose judgment is righteous, whose mercy reaches exiles, and whose saving grace meets sinners in Jesus Christ.
We also want to ask something of those who believe this work should continue.
It cannot.
Not because financial support proves your faith.
It does not.
And not because God needs an algorithm.
He does not.
Support should flow from willing gratitude and faithful stewardship, never spiritual coercion.
A share can put the message in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
A comment can become the beginning of a conversation.
A tag can tell somebody, “I was thinking about you.”
A saved article can return to you when your heart needs the reminder.
And a life surrendered to Jesus can become something no algorithm could ever manufacture:
a testimony.
But before you leave, return once more to Ezekiel.
Picture the prophet watching.
The glory rises.
Moves toward the threshold.
Moves toward the gate.
Moves outside the city.
The holy presence Israel had treated casually was not casual at all.
That should make us tremble.
Yet Ezekiel's book does not finish with God's glory gone forever.
Later, in Ezekiel 43, the prophet sees the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east.
The direction from which the glory had departed becomes the direction associated with its return.
Judgment was real.
But abandonment was not the final sentence of Ezekiel's story.
Restoration was coming.
And the book eventually ends with a city bearing an extraordinary name:
יְהוָה שָׁמָּה
YHWH Shammah.
“The LORD is there.”
There.
After judgment.
There.
After exile.
There.
After everything seemed ruined.
There.
God's story moved toward restored presence.
And for Christians, every longing for God's presence reaches its ultimate hope in Christ and in the biblical promise of God dwelling with His redeemed people.
So maybe you arrived at this article afraid because something in you has grown cold.
Do not merely become emotional.
Come home.
Maybe you arrived ashamed.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you arrived angry at God.
Tell Him the truth and open His Word.
Maybe you arrived hiding something.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe you arrived convinced you have ruined too much.
Look at the cross before you decide what grace can and cannot redeem.
Maybe you have been performing religion while your heart has slowly turned to stone.
Then pray for what only God can give.
A heart alive toward Him.
A spirit responsive to Him.
A life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And if you have a testimony of grace, tell it.
Somebody needs to know Christians are not people without scandals.
We are people who have discovered that our scandals are not stronger than our Savior.
Ezekiel watched the glory leave a temple people thought could never lose it.
But Scripture would not let departure have the final word.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody needs tonight:
The chapter where everything holy seemed to be leaving was not the chapter where God stopped writing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABIMELECH’S HOUSEHOLD WOMEN BECAME INFERTILE — And the Sarah Crisis Reveals What Happens When God Steps Into a Hidden Compromise
paragraphs: ABIMELECH’S HOUSEHOLD WOMEN BECAME INFERTILE — And the Sarah Crisis Reveals What Happens When God Steps Into a Hidden Compromise

Genesis 20:17–18 is more disturbing than it first appears. A frightened husband concealed the truth. A king unknowingly took another man’s wife. An entire household suddenly felt consequences it did not understand. Then one prayer changed everything. But beneath the scandal is something even greater: the relentless grace of a God who protects His promise when human beings make a complete mess of the story.
Imagine living inside Abimelech’s household.
Everything appears normal.
Then something begins happening among the women.
Pregnancies stop.
Wombs remain closed.
Something is wrong.
But nobody knows why.
No one can see the conversation that happened outside the palace. No one knows what Abraham said about Sarah. No one understands the danger hanging over the king’s house.
They only know something has changed.
And then Scripture gives us one of those sentences that can make you stop reading and stare at the page.
“For the LORD had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham’s wife.”
Genesis 20:18.
The Hebrew is even more striking:
כִּי־עָצֹר עָצַר יְהוָה בְּעַד כָּל־רֶחֶם לְבֵית אֲבִימֶלֶךְ בְּעַד שָׂרָה אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָהָם
Ki-‘atzor ‘atzar YHWH be‘ad kol-rechem leveit Avimelekh, be‘ad Sarah eshet Avraham.

The construction עָצֹר עָצַר (‘atzor ‘atzar) intensifies the idea of restraining or closing. The text says that YHWH had closed “every womb”—כָּל־רֶחֶם (kol-rechem)—belonging to the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.
This was not merely an unfortunate fertility problem occurring in the background of the story.
Genesis explicitly connects what happened in Abimelech’s household to the Sarah crisis.
But before anyone turns this passage into a simplistic formula—“someone sins and therefore somebody becomes infertile”—we need to stay painfully close to the text.
Genesis 20 does not teach that infertility in general is evidence that someone has sinned.
It does not give Christians permission to look at a woman struggling to conceive and whisper, “What did she do?”
Please never weaponize this passage against someone carrying the private grief of infertility.
That would be cruel.
And it would be bad biblical interpretation.
Genesis is describing a specific divine intervention at a specific moment in redemptive history involving Abraham, Sarah, Abimelech, and the covenant promise of God.
And the circumstances that brought everyone there were messy.
Very messy.
Abraham had entered Gerar with Sarah.
And Abraham said something that should sound painfully familiar to anyone who has already read Genesis 12.
“She is my sister.”
Technically, there was truth buried inside the statement. Genesis 20:12 tells us Sarah was Abraham’s half-sister.
But Abraham was withholding the truth that mattered most.
She was also his wife.
That is what makes this story uncomfortable.
Abraham was not a cartoon villain.
He was the man God had called.
The man who believed God.
The man whose faith would become foundational to the biblical story.
And yet here he is...
afraid.
Again.
Abraham later explains his reasoning:
“Because I thought, Surely the fear of God is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife’s sake.”
Genesis 20:11.
Fear began writing the script.
And fear has written some terrible scripts in the lives of otherwise faithful people.
Fear says:
Tell enough truth to protect yourself.
Hide enough truth to control what happens next.
Make the compromise look reasonable.
Convince yourself you had no choice.
Have you ever done that?
Not necessarily with a king.
Not necessarily with a marriage.
But with your reputation?
Your browser history?
Your finances?
Your relationship?
Your addiction?
Your private conversations?
Your secret resentment?
Your spiritual life?
Have you ever constructed a version of the truth designed less to reveal reality and more to protect yourself from its consequences?
That is where this ancient scandal suddenly becomes uncomfortably modern.
Because some lies are spoken with completely false words.
Others are constructed from carefully selected truths.
Abraham’s fear placed Sarah in a devastating position.
Abimelech took Sarah into his household.
Then God intervened.
Before Abimelech slept with her, God came to him in a dream and gave him a terrifying warning:
“Behold, thou art but a dead man, for the woman which thou hast taken; for she is a man’s wife.”
Genesis 20:3.
Imagine hearing that from God.
Abimelech protested that he had acted without knowing the truth.
And remarkably, God acknowledged it.
God told him:
“Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart; for I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her.”
Genesis 20:6.
Do not miss that.
Abimelech did not know the entire situation.
God did.
Abraham had created confusion.
God entered the confusion.
Sarah was vulnerable.
God protected Sarah.
Abimelech was approaching an act whose full significance he did not understand.
God restrained him.
The covenant appeared endangered by human fear.
God did not lose control.
That is one of the great currents running beneath Genesis 20.
Human beings are making a mess.
God is preserving His purpose.
And perhaps that is where this story finds some of us.
You love Jesus...
but you have made a mess.
You knew better...
but fear won.
You believed God...
until the pressure became personal.
You trusted Him on Sunday...
then tried to manipulate the outcome on Tuesday.
You have a testimony, but there is a chapter you hope nobody reads.
Welcome to the uncomfortable honesty of Scripture.
The Bible does not airbrush its heroes.
Abraham’s failures are left on the page.
Why?
Because ultimately the Bible is not a monument to the flawless performance of Abraham.
It is the revelation of the faithfulness of God.
And Genesis 20 refuses to let Abraham become the savior of his own story.
He needs grace too.
That matters enormously.
Because some people secretly believe Christianity is about good people proving they deserve God.
It is not.
The Gospel eventually brings us to exactly the opposite conclusion.
We are sinners who need a Savior.
Abraham needed grace.
Sarah needed God’s protection.
Abimelech needed warning.
His household needed healing.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And the ultimate answer is not Abraham.
It is Jesus Christ.
But watch what happens before we get there.
God tells Abimelech to return Sarah.
Then God says something surprising about the very man whose fear helped create the crisis:
“He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live.”
Genesis 20:7.
Read that again.
The compromised prophet is still called to pray.
That does not excuse Abraham.
Grace never means sin suddenly becomes righteous.
But God is already showing us something about restoration.
Failure does not have to be the final sentence.
Abimelech confronts Abraham.
Sarah is restored.
And then comes Genesis 20:17:
וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל אַבְרָהָם אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים וַיִּרְפָּא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וְאֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ וְאַמְהֹתָיו וַיֵּלֵדוּ
Vayyitpallel Avraham el-ha’Elohim, vayirpa Elohim et-Avimelekh ve’et-ishto ve’amhotav, vayeledu.
“And Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children.”
The verb וַיִּרְפָּא (vayirpa) comes from רפא (rapha’), “to heal.”
Abraham prayed.
God healed.
The closed wombs opened.
Life could continue.
The judgment was real.
So was the mercy.
That tension matters.
Modern Christianity can sometimes speak about grace as though grace means God simply shrugs at sin.
Genesis 20 will not allow that.
God takes wrongdoing seriously.
He identifies Sarah unmistakably as another man’s wife.
He warns Abimelech.
He restrains sin.
He requires Sarah’s restoration.
There are consequences inside the household.
And yet judgment is not where the story ends.
Healing comes.
Restoration comes.
Mercy comes.
That is why the Gospel is so much greater than pretending our scandals never happened.
Jesus does not save us by rewriting history so that we were secretly innocent all along.
He saves sinners.
At the cross, sin is not called harmless.
It is exposed as so serious that redemption costs the blood of Christ.
And grace is revealed as so astonishing that the Son of God willingly gives Himself for sinners.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
Isaiah 53:5.
The scandal of Genesis 20 therefore whispers toward the greater story Scripture will eventually unveil.
Human failure.
Divine intervention.
Judgment.
Mercy.
Restoration.
And ultimately...
Christ.
There is another detail we cannot ignore.
Sarah is not merely Abraham’s wife.
She stands inside the unfolding covenant promise.
God had already declared that Sarah would bear Isaac.
Genesis 17:19 says:
“Sarah thy wife shall bear thee a son indeed; and thou shalt call his name Isaac: and I will establish my covenant with him.”
Then in Genesis 18, God again promises that Sarah will have a son.
And suddenly, in Genesis 20, Sarah is inside another king’s household.
Do you see the narrative tension?
God has promised a son through Abraham and Sarah.
Yet Abraham’s fear creates circumstances that could throw the identity and integrity of the promised line into confusion.
But God intervenes before Abimelech touches her.
The promise will not be hijacked by Abraham’s fear.
The covenant will not collapse because the covenant bearer panicked.
God remains faithful even when human faithfulness trembles.
Then Genesis 21 begins.
“And the LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did unto Sarah as he had spoken.”
As He had said.
As He had spoken.
That is the heartbeat.
God keeps His word.
Not because Abraham performed perfectly.
Not because Sarah never struggled.
Not because every human decision was wise.
God keeps His word because God is faithful.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction.
God’s faithfulness is not permission to continue living in compromise.
It is the reason you can repent without believing your story is over.
Repentance is not running away from grace.
Repentance is turning toward the God of grace.
Maybe you have been carrying something.
Something you have learned to hide so well that people compliment the version of you they see while you quietly grieve the person you know exists underneath.
Maybe there is an Abraham-sized compromise hiding inside a respectable Christian life.
Maybe fear made you dishonest.
Maybe loneliness made you vulnerable.
Maybe lust became a secret room.
Maybe bitterness became your companion.
Maybe pride made repentance feel humiliating.
Maybe you keep saying, “It’s complicated,” because calling it sin would mean admitting something needs to change.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to hide better.
The answer is Jesus.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
There is no freedom in endlessly protecting the version of yourself that is killing your fellowship with God.
Bring it into His light.
Name the sin.
Stop negotiating with it.
Stop dressing bondage in respectable language.
Repent.
Not because Christ is waiting for an excuse to destroy you.
Because Christ died and rose again to save sinners.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing at the cross.
There is reconciliation with God through Christ.
There is a new life that does not require you to pretend the old wounds never existed.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful things about Genesis 20 is that the chapter does not end with closed wombs.
It ends with healing.
Think about that.
The scandal was real.
But so was the restoration.
Abraham’s fear was real.
But it did not become sovereign.
The crisis was real.
But the crisis did not get the last word.
God did.

That is the message Gospel Warrior exists to keep declaring in a world full of hidden wounds, exhausted believers, skeptical seekers, prodigals, struggling Christians, and people who think their worst chapter has permanently disqualified them:
Jesus Christ still saves.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus still restores broken people.
Jesus still turns shame into testimony.
Jesus still takes stories that look ruined and writes redemption across pages we thought were finished.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest before God.
And if you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “no more hiding.”
If you are exhausted but you have not abandoned Jesus, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your spirit has been worn thin and you desperately need prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
Somebody reading underneath this article may need evidence that Christians are not people without scars—we are people whose scars no longer have to tell the story without the cross.
Do not make the comments a performance.
Make them a place of honesty.
There is still grace.
Save it too.
There are truths you do not save because you have forgotten them.
You save them because there will be days when pain tries to make you forget.
Scripture deserves greater care than that.
The New Testament principle for Christian giving is beautifully free of manipulation:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
2 Corinthians 9:7.
God’s grace is not for sale.
If Gospel Warrior has strengthened you, your monthly support helps us keep building and expanding the work so more people can encounter biblical truth and be pointed toward Christ.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel ministry is not merchandise.
It is mission.
It is another article reaching a broken person.
Another devotional reaching someone fighting temptation.
Another Christian resource strengthening a believer.
Another seeker hearing that Christianity is not fundamentally the story of human beings becoming impressive enough for God.
It is the story of the holy God coming to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
And whether you are able to support financially or not, you can still help.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Because ministry is not ultimately measured by how impressive a page looks.
It is measured by faithfulness to Christ and by whether people are being pointed toward Him.
Genesis 20 began with fear.
It moved through deception.
A woman was placed in danger.
A king received a terrifying warning.
A household experienced closed wombs.
A prophet who had failed was confronted.
Then Abraham prayed.
God healed.
Sarah was restored.
And the promise continued.
Then the next chapter opened with words every wounded believer should remember:
“The LORD visited Sarah as he had said.”
As He had said.
Maybe that is the sentence you need tonight.
Your failure is not more powerful than God.
Your secret is not too dark for the light of Christ.
Your shame does not possess greater authority than the blood shed at Calvary.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean repentance makes yesterday nonexistent.
It means that when a sinner turns to Jesus Christ, yesterday no longer has the authority to determine eternity.
So come out of hiding.
Bring Him the chapter you wish you could tear from the book.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the thing you cannot repair yourself.
And trust the Savior who was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
Because the most unforgettable truth in Abraham’s scandal is not that Abraham nearly ruined everything.
It is that God remained faithful.
And the most unforgettable truth about your story may not be what you did in the chapter you are ashamed of.
It may be what Jesus did after you finally surrendered the pen.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence when the risen Christ is still writing redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DO NOT WORRY ABOUT TOMORROW” — JESUS NEVER TOLD YOU TO STOP PLANNING
paragraphs: “DO NOT WORRY ABOUT TOMORROW” — JESUS NEVER TOLD YOU TO STOP PLANNING
You can prepare for tomorrow without carrying tomorrow. The difference may be exactly what your exhausted soul needs to hear tonight.
There is a version of tomorrow already living inside your head.
It has conversations that have not happened.
Bills that are not yet due.
Test results you have not received.
Doors that have not closed.
People who have not left.
Problems that have not arrived.
Failures that have not occurred.
And somehow…
you are already exhausted from surviving them.
Your body is sitting in today, but your mind has traveled three weeks ahead.
You are lying in bed, but internally you are running.
Calculating.
Rehearsing.
Predicting.
“What if I lose the job?”
“What if the money does not come?”
“What if my child makes the wrong decision?”
“What if the doctor calls?”
“What if this relationship falls apart?”
“What if I never recover?”
“What if God does not come through the way I desperately need Him to?”
And perhaps the strangest part is that you call it “being responsible.”
You tell yourself you are planning.
You tell yourself you are preparing.
You tell yourself that thinking about the problem one hundred more times might finally produce control.
But somewhere between preparation and obsession, planning became panic.
And somewhere between wisdom and fear, tomorrow became your master.
Then Jesus says something that almost sounds impossible:
“Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself.”
That is Matthew 6:34 in the King James Version.

But if you have ever read those words while staring at overdue bills, raising children, running a business, trying to save money, preparing for an uncertain future, or simply attempting to behave like a responsible adult, you may have quietly wondered:
Jesus… are You really telling me not to think about tomorrow?
No.
And understanding what He actually said may set someone free tonight.
Matthew was written in Greek, and the crucial words in Matthew 6:34 read:
“μὴ οὖν μεριμνήσητε εἰς τὴν αὔριον”
Mē oun merimnēsēte eis tēn aurion.
The heart of the sentence is the verb μεριμνάω — merimnaō.
It carries the sense of being anxious, worried, troubled, or consumed with care.
That matters.
Jesus was not condemning foresight.
He was confronting anxiety.
He was not saying, “Never make plans.”
He was saying, in effect, “Do not surrender your heart to anxious preoccupation about tomorrow.”
There is an enormous difference.
Planning looks toward tomorrow and asks, “What can I wisely do today?”
Worry looks toward tomorrow and asks, “How can I control everything that might happen?”
Planning can finish its work and sleep.
Worry keeps holding meetings at 2:13 in the morning.
Planning makes a budget.
Worry checks the bank account fourteen times.
Planning prepares for the medical appointment.
Worry mentally attends your own funeral before the doctor has even given you a diagnosis.
Planning teaches your children wisdom.
Worry tries to control every decision they will make for the next twenty years.
Planning says, “If the Lord wills, this is what I intend to do.”
Worry whispers, “Unless I personally hold every piece together, everything will collapse.”
And maybe that is why worry is so exhausting.
You were never designed to be God.
Read the entire movement of Jesus’ words in Matthew 6:25–34 and something beautiful happens.
Jesus points upward.
Look at the birds.
Then outward.
Look at the flowers.
Then inward.
Look at your anxiety.
Then upward again.
Look at your Father.
The birds are not Jesus’ argument against work. Birds spend enormous energy gathering food.
The flowers are not His argument against reality. Grass withers.
His argument is about the character of the Father.
“Your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.”
Before Jesus tells frightened people not to worry, He gives them something stronger than positive thinking.
He gives them a Father.
That changes everything.
Christian peace is not pretending tomorrow will be painless.
Jesus never promised that.
In fact, the final words of Matthew 6:34 destroy the shallow idea that Christianity means nothing difficult will happen:
“ἀρκετὸν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἡ κακία αὐτῆς.”
Arketon tē hēmera hē kakia autēs.
“Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.”
Jesus acknowledges trouble.
That is what makes His command so astonishing.
He does not say, “Do not worry because nothing bad will happen.”
He essentially says, “Today already contains enough trouble. Do not drag tomorrow’s trouble into it as well.”
Somebody needs to read that twice.
You may be suffering today from something that has not happened.
You may be grieving an imaginary funeral.
Fighting an imaginary argument.
Enduring an imaginary bankruptcy.
Surviving an imaginary rejection.
Feeling the pain of an imaginary betrayal.
You have borrowed trouble from a day God has not yet given you.
And because you borrowed tomorrow’s trouble, you are spending today’s strength on something that may never happen.
But there is another side to this.
Some Christians have misunderstood Jesus’ words and treated irresponsibility as faith.
“I do not need to save. God will provide.”
“I do not need to prepare. God will handle it.”
“I do not need to make wise decisions. I am trusting Jesus.”
That is not what Matthew 6 teaches.
The Bible repeatedly commends wisdom, diligence, stewardship, preparation, and thoughtful action.
Joseph prepared Egypt for seven years of famine.
Proverbs points us toward the ant that prepares its provisions.
Jesus Himself spoke about counting the cost before building a tower.
James did not condemn making plans; he corrected the arrogance of planning as though God were irrelevant: “If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.”
Biblical faith is not careless.
It simply refuses to make an idol out of control.
So make the appointment.
Build the emergency fund.
Study for the examination.
Prepare the presentation.
Write the business plan.
Buy what is needed.
Save wisely.
Teach your children.
Think about retirement.
Set the alarm.
Apply for the job.
Have the difficult conversation.
Plan for tomorrow.
Just do not worship tomorrow.
Do not give tomorrow authority over your peace today.
Do not let a calendar date that has not arrived become more powerful in your imagination than the Father who is already there.
Because perhaps this is the deeper wound beneath our worry:
We do not merely fear tomorrow.
Sometimes we fear that when tomorrow comes, God will somehow not be enough.
That is where this becomes painfully personal.
You can believe God exists and still struggle to trust Him.
You can sing worship songs on Sunday and panic on Monday.
You can quote Scripture publicly and secretly imagine catastrophe at night.
You can tell everybody else, “God has a plan,” while privately wondering whether His plan for you has somehow fallen apart.
Faith and fear can fight inside the same chest.
Peter knew Jesus and still sank.
The father in Mark 9 cried, “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
So if you are anxious tonight, Jesus is not standing over you with folded arms, disgusted that you are struggling.
Look at how He speaks in Matthew 6.
“Your heavenly Father…”
He brings the anxious heart back to relationship.
Your Father knows.
Your Father sees.
Your Father has not misplaced you.
And this does not mean you will receive everything you want.
It does not mean every illness disappears.
It does not mean every business succeeds.
It does not mean every relationship survives.
It does not mean every prayer receives the answer you imagined.
Christian hope is much deeper than “Everything will work out exactly how I want.”
Christian hope says:
Whatever tomorrow contains, Christ will still be Christ.
And ultimately, your greatest problem was never tomorrow.
It was sin.
The deepest disaster threatening humanity was not unemployment, sickness, rejection, debt, aging, loneliness, or death.
It was separation from a holy God because of sin.
And that is exactly where the Gospel becomes more than motivational advice.
Jesus did not come merely to make anxious people calmer.
He came to save sinners.
The Christ speaking about tomorrow in Matthew 6 was walking toward a cross.
There would come a tomorrow when He would be betrayed.
A tomorrow when He would be falsely accused.
A tomorrow when Roman soldiers would beat Him.
A tomorrow when nails would tear through flesh.
A tomorrow when darkness would fall.
A tomorrow when the sinless Son of God would give His life for sinners.
And Jesus knew it was coming.
Yet He continued obeying the Father.
That is not denial.
That is trust.
At Calvary, the One who taught us not to be mastered by tomorrow carried something infinitely heavier than tomorrow.
He carried our sin.
Our shame.
Our rebellion.
Our guilt.
Our record.
Our scandal.
The secret things.
The things nobody knows.
The things you wish you could erase.
The decisions you would give almost anything to undo.
And this is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin acceptable.
Not by teaching us to excuse rebellion.
He rewrites the story through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and grace purchased by His blood.
At the cross, sin is not minimized.
It is judged.
And grace is not cheap.
It cost Christ everything.
Then came another tomorrow.
The stone was rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly the future of everyone who belongs to Him could never again be defined merely by what happens tomorrow.
Because resurrection had entered the story.
Maybe that is the tomorrow you have forgotten.
You have imagined a hundred terrible tomorrows.
Have you remembered the final one?
The day when faith becomes sight.
The day when Christ gathers His people.
The day when death does not get the final sentence.
The day when every redeemed sinner discovers that Jesus was more faithful than fear ever allowed them to imagine.
Until then, He gives us today.
Daily bread.
Notice the language.
Not monthly bread.
Not lifetime bread.
“Give us this day our daily bread.”
There is something almost offensive about daily dependence to people obsessed with control.
We want lifetime guarantees.
God often gives daily grace.
We want the entire map.
He gives enough light for the next faithful step.
We want to know how everything ends.
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Maybe you do not need an answer for the next ten years tonight.
Maybe you need grace for Monday.
Maybe you do not need enough strength to survive everything your imagination can manufacture.
Maybe you need strength for this conversation.
This appointment.
This decision.
This temptation.
This lonely evening.
This single act of obedience.
Today.
Because tomorrow has not asked you to live it yet.
So stop demanding tomorrow’s grace before tomorrow arrives.
When tomorrow becomes today, the God who met you today will still be God.
That does not make planning unnecessary.
It makes panic unnecessary.
Prepare what you can.
Entrust what you cannot.
Then breathe.
Not because life is predictable.
Because Jesus is faithful.
And perhaps you have been carrying something while reading this.
Something specific.
A name appeared in your mind.
A diagnosis.
A deadline.
A debt.
A marriage.
A child.
A mistake.
A decision.
A secret fear you have not admitted to anyone.
Do not hide behind religious language.
Bring it to Christ.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to forgive, forgive.
If you need to apologize, apologize.
If you need to make a responsible plan, make one.
If you need professional help, seek it.
If there is work God has placed in front of you, do it.
But after obedience has done everything obedience can do…
release the outcome.
Your clenched fist cannot control tomorrow anyway.
Open it.
“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.”
There is the invitation.
Not pretending.
Casting.
Not suppressing.
Surrendering.
Not “I am fine.”
“Father, I am afraid.”
There is a difference between surrender and denial.
And maybe somebody reading this has been pretending for too long.
Not because typing a sentence magically removes anxiety.
It does not.
But sometimes confession is the moment we stop pretending.
No explanation required.
And if Christ has already carried you through a tomorrow you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody.
There is someone scrolling through these words who may desperately need evidence that another believer cried, trembled, prayed, survived—and discovered that God had not abandoned them.
Do not keep that testimony locked inside you.
And think of one person who is living three months ahead in fear right now.
You know who they are.
The friend whose marriage is shaking.
The mother worried about her child.
The father carrying financial pressure silently.
The believer whose faith is tired.
The person waiting for medical results.
The person smiling online while privately falling apart.
Better yet, send this directly to them.
Not merely to help an algorithm.
One share can place Scripture in front of someone you may never have known was desperate for it.
Because anxiety has a strange habit of forgetting yesterday’s lessons when tomorrow becomes frightening again.
Come back when your mind starts running ahead of grace.
Read Matthew 6 again.
Look at the birds again.
Look at the flowers again.
Look at the Father again.
Then look at Christ.
And I want to say this carefully because biblical truth matters more than fundraising:
You do not buy a blessing.
And no faithful Christian ministry should pressure you into giving.

Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing rather than compelled: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But voluntary financial support is a real way believers can help Gospel-centered work continue and expand.
Call it what Scripture clearly allows us to call it:
Generosity.
Partnership.
Support.
Giving from a willing heart.
A practical decision to help Gospel-centered ministry continue.
And if you decide before God that this is where you want part of your Christian giving to go, then give freely, prayerfully, joyfully, and without compulsion.
But the deepest reason to stay connected should never be merchandise.
It should be Jesus.
Stay close to Scripture.
Stay teachable.
Stay hungry for Christ.
Your support can help keep Gospel-centered content moving outward.
Your share can put truth on another screen.
Your tag can reach the person who would never have searched for this themselves.
Your comment can become a testimony somebody else needed to read.
But Jesus alone saves.
Jesus alone deserves the glory.
And that distinction must never be blurred.
So tomorrow morning, plan.
Make your list.
Set your goals.
Check your calendar.
Go to work.
Pay what you can.
Save what you can.
Prepare wisely.
Make the phone call.
Schedule the appointment.
Do the next responsible thing.
But before you walk into tomorrow, remember:
You are not walking there alone.
The Father you trust today will not disappear at midnight.
Christ will already be Lord when morning arrives.
Grace will already be there.
And whatever tomorrow eventually brings, it will never be stronger than the Savior who conquered the grave.
So tonight…
put tomorrow back where it belongs.
Not in your hands.
In His.
You do not have to carry tomorrow tonight—the hands already holding tomorrow still bear the scars that prove how far His love was willing to go for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN HAVE TATTOOS OR BODY PIERCINGS? THE BIBLE’S ANSWER MAY EXPOSE A DEEPER QUESTION
