paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN HAVE TATTOOS OR BODY PIERCINGS? THE BIBLE’S ANSWER MAY EXPOSE A DEEPER QUESTION
Before you ask whether God allows ink on your skin or metal through your body, there is a question far more uncomfortable: Who does your body belong to—and what does your heart want people to see?
Maybe you already have one.
A tattoo hidden beneath your sleeve.
A name across your chest.
A verse on your arm.
A cross behind your ear.
A piercing your parents hated.
Maybe you got it before you knew Christ.
Maybe you got it after.
Maybe it represents someone you lost.
Maybe it reminds you of something you survived.
Maybe you are sitting in a tattoo shop right now, staring at the design you have wanted for months, wondering whether pressing “go” will somehow put distance between you and God.
Or maybe you would never get tattooed.
And perhaps that is exactly why you need to keep reading.
Because this conversation is not only about people with ink.
It is also about people with stones in their hands.
Some Christians have been made to feel as though a tattoo automatically announces rebellion, while others dismiss every biblical concern by saying, “God only cares about the heart.”
Neither response is careful enough.
God absolutely cares about the heart.
But the God who cares about your heart also cares about what you do with your body.
And Scripture takes us somewhere much deeper than the internet argument of “tattoos are sinful” versus “tattoos are completely fine.”
The Bible asks something more searching.
Something that reaches beneath the ink.
Beneath the piercing.
Beneath the clothes.
Beneath the Christian image.
Beneath the excuses.
Who owns you?
That question changes everything.
The verse almost everyone reaches for first is Leviticus 19:28. In Hebrew, part of the command reads:
וּכְתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע לֹא תִתְּנוּ בָּכֶם
ukhetovet qa‘aqa lo tittenu bakhem
The expression כְּתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע — ketovet qa‘aqa refers to an inscribed or tattooed mark. The verse also prohibits making cuts in the flesh “for the dead.”
That matters.
We should not erase the verse because it makes modern people uncomfortable. God really gave this command to Israel.
But we should not rip one line out of Leviticus and pretend context does not exist either.

The surrounding passage contains commands given to Israel as God's covenant people, distinguishing their life and worship from the practices surrounding them. Leviticus 19:28 specifically connects cutting the flesh with practices associated with the dead and then prohibits the tattooed marking.
So does that mean every person who walks into a modern tattoo studio is consciously performing an ancient pagan mourning ritual?
Obviously not.
But does that make Leviticus 19:28 meaningless?
Absolutely not.
It reveals something about God's concern for His people: they were not to imitate practices tied to idolatry, pagan worship, death rituals, or identities that contradicted belonging to Him.
God was teaching His people:
You are Mine.
Do not let the surrounding culture disciple your body into proclaiming allegiance to another god.
And suddenly this ancient command begins asking a frighteningly modern question.
What is discipling your desires?
Culture?
Pain?
Fashion?
Sexual attention?
Rebellion?
Grief?
Your friends?
Your need to belong?
Your hunger to be noticed?
Or Christ?

The New Testament does not give Christians a verse saying, “You shall never receive a modern tattoo,” nor does it give us a blanket command saying every tattoo and every piercing is automatically righteous.
That distinction matters.
Gentile believers were not simply placed wholesale under Israel's Mosaic covenant when the early church wrestled with this very question in Acts 15.
But freedom from the Mosaic covenant is not freedom from holiness.
Grace does not mean, “My body, my rules.”
In fact, Paul says almost the opposite.
Writing to believers in Corinth, he asks:
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν…
ē ouk oidate hoti to sōma hymōn naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos estin…
“Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you…?”
Then comes the line that destroys both careless legalism and careless license:
οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν
ouk este heautōn.
You are not your own.
And then:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore, Paul says, glorify God in your body.
Read that again.
Not because Paul was discussing tattoos in 1 Corinthians 6—he wasn't. The immediate context concerns sexual immorality and the believer's bodily union with Christ.
That actually makes the principle stronger when properly understood, not weaker.
Paul refuses to separate Christianity into a “spiritual” part that belongs to Jesus and a physical part over which we remain sovereign.
Christ purchased the person.
Your mind.
Your sexuality.
Your hands.
Your eyes.
Your ambitions.
Your money.
Your relationships.
Your body.
All of you.
The Christian question therefore cannot merely be:
“Am I allowed to get this?”
It must become:
“Can I sincerely glorify Jesus Christ by doing this?”
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Christian maturity does not spend its entire life searching for the fence so it can stand one millimeter away from disobedience.
It begins asking what pleases the One who died for us.
Suppose you want a tattoo.
Before the needle touches your skin, sit before Jesus long enough to ask yourself questions nobody on social media can answer for you.
Why do I want this?
What am I trying to communicate?
Would I still want it if nobody ever saw it?
Am I doing this from rebellion?
Am I trying to provoke somebody?
Am I chasing attention?
Am I copying a culture whose values are slowly becoming mine?
Does the imagery honor what Scripture calls good?
Would this damage my witness in the particular situation where God has placed me?
Am I violating my conscience?
Can I pray before doing this—not a five-second prayer asking God to approve a decision I have already made, but an honest prayer of surrender?
“Jesus, if this does not honor You, I don't want it.”
That last sentence may reveal more than a thousand arguments.
Because sometimes we do not actually want God's answer.
We want God's signature beneath ours.
We make the decision.
Then we ask Heaven to cosign it.
But discipleship works the other way around.
Jesus is Lord.
We follow.
The same principle applies to piercings.

Scripture itself does not treat jewelry or bodily adornment as intrinsically evil. Biblical narratives even contain positive references to jewelry, including nose rings and earrings. The mere existence of a piercing therefore cannot honestly be declared universally sinful from Scripture.
At the same time, Scripture repeatedly warns God's people about vanity, sensuality, pride, ostentation, and making external appearance more important than the hidden person of the heart.
So the hole itself may not be the deepest issue.
The heart can be.
And here is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable for everyone.
Because an untattooed Christian can be consumed with vanity.
A woman with pierced ears can love Jesus deeply.
A tattooed man can preach Christ faithfully.
A person without a single mark can secretly worship people's approval.
Someone covered in Christian symbols can still live nothing like Christ.
And somebody carrying a tattoo from a terrible chapter of life may now belong completely to Jesus.
Skin does not tell the whole story.
The heart matters.
But please do not twist that into the slogan, “God doesn't care what I do with my body because He knows my heart.”
That is not biblical Christianity.
The heart and body belong to the same Lord.
Romans 12:1 urges believers, in view of God's mercies, to present their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God.
There it is again.
Your body matters precisely because worship is bigger than singing.
Worship walks.
Worship spends.
Worship speaks.
Worship dresses.
Worship dates.
Worship works.
Worship suffers.
Worship decides.
Worship lives inside a body.
So can a Christian have a tattoo?
Can a Christian have body piercings?

There is no faithful reason to invent a universal New Testament prohibition that Scripture itself does not explicitly give. But neither should Christians turn that absence into permission to do anything for any reason.
A tattoo or piercing can involve matters of conscience, motive, content, cultural meaning, wisdom, stewardship, witness, maturity, and love for others.
Romans 14 becomes enormously important here.

Paul teaches believers not to despise or condemn one another over disputable matters, while also insisting that each person act from faith before the Lord. Christian liberty is never permission to violate conscience.
And 1 Corinthians 10:31 gives us a breathtakingly simple standard:
Whether you eat or drink—or whatever you do—
do everything for the glory of God.
Whatever.
That word follows you all the way into the tattoo shop.
It follows you into the piercing studio.
It follows you into your wardrobe.
Your relationship.
Your browser history.
Your bank account.
Your private messages.
Your secret habits.
Your ambitions.
Your Sunday worship.
Everything.
And perhaps you came to this article terrified because you already have tattoos.
Maybe some are vulgar.
Maybe one carries the name of somebody who broke you.
Maybe your skin still bears symbols from the person you were before Christ.
Maybe every time you look in the mirror, you remember nights you wish you could erase.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Jesus did not go to the cross because your skin was clean.
He went because your soul needed redemption.
You do not scrub yourself clean enough to become worthy of Him.
You come to Him in repentance and faith.
And He saves sinners.
Real sinners.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People with regrets.
People whose bodies remember things their mouths struggle to explain.
The Gospel is not God pretending your past never happened.
It is God refusing to let your past have the final word.
Maybe you cannot erase every mark.
But Christ can redeem the person carrying them.

There is something painfully beautiful about a believer standing in worship with scars from self-destruction, old tattoos from rebellion, memories of addiction, evidence of a former life—and hands raised to Jesus.
Not because the past was good.
But because the past lost ownership.
That body belongs to Another now.
You were bought with a price.
Perhaps that is the tattoo every Christian needs written somewhere deeper than skin.
Bought.
Purchased.
Redeemed.
His.
Not because silver changed hands.
Not because gold purchased you.
But because the spotless Lamb of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus Christ was pierced too.
Not for decoration.
For our transgressions.
His body was wounded.
His blood was poured out.
The sinless Son of God carried shame He did not deserve so guilty people could receive grace they could never earn.
And suddenly the tattoo debate becomes very small beside Calvary.
Because Christianity is ultimately not about whether your body has ink.
It is about whether your life belongs to the One whose body was broken for you.
Maybe you have been judging somebody because of how they look.
Repent.
Maybe you have used “Christian freedom” to excuse decisions you know were driven by rebellion.
Repent.
Maybe you have been desperately trying to appear holy while hiding sins far deeper than somebody else's tattoo.
Repent.
Maybe you have believed your past makes you permanently dirty.
Come to Christ.
The same Jesus who forgave prostitutes, tax collectors, rebels, religious hypocrites, and criminals still receives sinners who come to Him.
There is grace here.
But grace is not God's permission to remain unchanged.
Grace forgives us and begins transforming us.
Jesus does not merely rewrite our destination.
He rewrites our desires.
So if you are considering a tattoo or piercing, do not merely ask strangers online whether Christianity permits it.
Bring your desire before Christ.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Examine your motive.
Seek wise counsel from mature believers who know you personally.
Consider your conscience.
Consider your witness.
Consider permanence.
Consider stewardship.
Consider whether the imagery itself conflicts with biblical truth.
And be willing to walk away.
Not because ink possesses some mystical power to separate you from God, but because anything you cannot surrender has already begun revealing its power over you.

And if after sincere prayer, biblical reflection, examination of motive, wise counsel, and a clear conscience you believe you can proceed while genuinely glorifying Christ, do not turn your freedom into a weapon against Christians whose consciences lead them differently.
Likewise, if your conscience tells you not to do it, obey that conscience before God without turning your personal conviction into a commandment Scripture never gave to every believer.
This is where mature Christians become different from religious crowds.
We can hold conviction without cruelty.
Freedom without arrogance.
Holiness without legalism.
Grace without compromise.
Truth without throwing stones.
Perhaps somebody reading this has spent years avoiding church because Christians looked at your tattoos before they looked into your eyes.
If that is you, please understand something.
Jesus sees farther than skin.
But He also sees farther than the story you tell everyone else.
He sees the wounds beneath the confidence.
The nights beneath the smile.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The shame you buried.
The things you did.
The things done to you.
The person you became just to survive.
And still He calls sinners to Himself.
Not to celebrate our darkness.
To bring us out of it.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture religious arguments.
Not to create another Christian corner of the internet where everyone screams and nobody gets discipled.

We want people to meet Jesus Christ in Scripture, wrestle honestly with sin, understand grace, repent where repentance is needed, heal where wounds have remained hidden, and become men and women whose entire lives say:
I belong to Jesus.
Your honesty may become the exact testimony another wounded person needs tonight.
We need Scripture.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider staying closer to this ministry.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus.
It does not.
Christ alone saves, entirely by grace.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot tattoo enough Bible verses onto your body to make yourself righteous.
You cannot remove enough piercings to cleanse your conscience.
You cannot dress conservatively enough to erase your sin.
You cannot perform your way into God's family.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
The cross is enough.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Then take your whole life—your body, your story, your scars, your decisions, your future—and lay it before the One who purchased you.
Maybe the question that brought you here was:
“Can Christians have tattoos or body piercings?”
But perhaps the question Jesus wanted you to leave with was never simply about tattoos.
Perhaps it was this:
If I belong to Christ, what part of me still refuses to belong to Him?
Sit with that.
Because you may never have allowed a tattoo needle to touch your skin and still have entire rooms in your heart marked KEEP OUT, JESUS.
And that is the mark we should fear most.
Give Him the room.
Give Him the secret.
Give Him the rebellion.
Give Him the regret.
Give Him the body.
Give Him the future.
Give Him all of you.
Because at the end of this conversation, the most important mark on a Christian is not the one another human being can see on the skin.
It is the invisible declaration written across a surrendered life: “This one belongs to Jesus.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY ONE CENSUS ENDED WITH 70,000 DEAD
paragraphs: WHY ONE CENSUS ENDED WITH 70,000 DEAD

David only wanted a number. Before the story was over, seventy thousand people were dead, an angel stood over Jerusalem, and a king who had counted his strength was lying before God confessing his sin. But hidden inside this terrifying chapter is something even greater than judgment: an altar, a sacrifice, mercy—and a road that ultimately points us toward Jesus Christ.
There are Bible stories we love to put on children's walls.
David and Goliath.
Noah and the rainbow.
Daniel among the lions.
And then there are passages like 2 Samuel 24.
Passages that make you stop.
Passages that refuse to become sentimental.

Passages where, if we are willing to stay long enough instead of running toward an easy explanation, Scripture puts its hand around some of our deepest assumptions about God, sin, power, judgment, mercy, and ourselves.
This is one of those passages.
A king ordered a census.
And seventy thousand people died.
Read that again.
Seventy thousand.
Not seventy.
Not seven hundred.
Seventy thousand human beings.
Somebody's father.
Somebody's son.
Somebody's neighbor.
Somebody who had probably gone to sleep the night before expecting tomorrow to arrive.
The disturbing question almost asks itself:
Why?
Why would a census lead to catastrophe?
Why was David's decision so serious?
Why did Israel suffer?
And perhaps the question underneath all the other questions is the one many Christians are frightened to say aloud:
What does this tell us about God?
Don't run from that question.
The Bible doesn't.
The story begins before David ever starts counting.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 24:1 says:
"וַיֹּסֶף אַף־יְהוָה לַחֲרוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל"
Vayyosef aph-YHWH lacharot b'Yisrael.
In context: the anger of the LORD again burned against Israel.
That first sentence matters enormously.
The disaster did not begin because an otherwise innocent nation happened to be standing nearby when David made an administrative mistake.
God's anger against Israel was already present.
Why?
The chapter does not tell us.
And biblical faithfulness requires enough humility to stop where Scripture stops.
We can speculate.
We cannot turn speculation into revelation.
Something had already brought Israel under divine displeasure, but God did not choose to tell us in this passage exactly what it was.
Then comes one of the most difficult statements in the story.
Second Samuel says David was incited to number Israel and Judah.
Yet when the same event is retold in 1 Chronicles 21:1, we read:
"וַיַּעֲמֹד שָׂטָן עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל"
Vaya'amod satan al-Yisrael.
An adversary—satan—stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel.
This deserves careful handling.

The Hebrew word satan fundamentally carries the sense of an adversary or accuser. Christian readers commonly understand the Chronicler's wording as referring to Satan. Whatever questions we bring to the relationship between Samuel and Chronicles, neither account gives us permission to conclude that David was therefore an innocent puppet.
Because David himself doesn't.
That becomes crucial.
David sends Joab through Israel to count the fighting men.
Joab—of all people—objects.
Think about the irony.
Joab was hardly the tender conscience of David's kingdom. He was a hardened military commander.
Yet even Joab senses something is wrong.
He effectively asks his king:
Why do you want this?
But David's command prevails.
So the machinery begins.
Men travel.
Tribes are visited.
Numbers accumulate.
Human lives become military totals.
Eventually Joab returns with the figures.
And then something happens inside David that no spreadsheet could measure.
His heart strikes him.
The Hebrew says:
"וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד אֹתוֹ"
Vayyakh lev-David oto.
David's heart struck him.
The king who wanted to know how many men belonged to him suddenly had to face the man he himself had become.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story becomes frighteningly modern.
Because we count too.
Followers.
Views.
Money.
Sales.
Achievements.
Church attendance.
Influence.
Connections.
Properties.
Awards.
People who know our name.
Numbers are not inherently evil.
Scripture itself contains censuses commanded by God. Israel is numbered in the Torah. Therefore, we cannot faithfully preach that counting itself was the sin.

Exodus 30:11–16 also provides significant background: when Israel was numbered, each counted Israelite was to give the prescribed ransom offering, and the text explicitly associates this provision with avoiding plague. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters therefore understand David's census in light of a failure to observe those requirements.
Others have seen something else operating in David's heart: royal pride, military ambition, or confidence in the size of his army rather than confidence in God.
Second Samuel does not explicitly tell us, “David's precise motive was pride.”
So we should not pretend that it does.
But the narrative makes one fact unmistakable:
David knew he had sinned.
He doesn't blame Joab.
He doesn't blame the political climate.
He doesn't hide behind divine sovereignty.
He confesses.
"חָטָאתִי מְאֹד"
Chatati me'od.
“I have sinned greatly.”
Four words in English.
A shattered kingdom inside them.
And there is something painfully familiar about David here.
Sometimes we know.
Before anyone exposes us.
Before the consequences arrive.
Before the screenshots surface.
Before the marriage breaks.
Before the addiction becomes visible.
Before the secret becomes public.
Before anyone else knows what happened in the hotel room, browser history, private messages, bank account, office, relationship, or imagination...
the heart knows.
You can silence conviction with noise.
You can bury it beneath ministry.
You can cover it with success.
You can rename greed “ambition.”
You can rename lust “connection.”
You can rename bitterness “discernment.”
You can rename pride “confidence.”
You can rename compromise “survival.”
But somewhere beneath all those carefully chosen words...
the heart knows.
David's did.
Then Gad the prophet arrives.
Judgment is coming, and David is presented with three alternatives: famine, fleeing before enemies, or pestilence.
David answers with one of the most haunting declarations of faith in the chapter:
“Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great.”
Do not miss the paradox.
David fears God's judgment...
yet runs toward God's mercy.
He knows something about God that shame constantly tries to make sinners forget.
The God against whom you have sinned is still the only One who can save you.
So pestilence comes.
From Dan to Beersheba, death moves through the land.
Seventy thousand die.
There is no responsible way to make that number emotionally comfortable.
Nor should we.
Biblical judgment is supposed to disturb us.
Sin is not adorable.
Rebellion against a holy God is not a personality quirk.
The modern instinct is often to minimize sin until grace becomes unnecessary.
Scripture does the opposite.
It reveals the horror of sin so that mercy can be seen for the miracle it actually is.
Then the destroying angel stretches his hand toward Jerusalem.
And suddenly...
God says enough.
The Hebrew expression in 2 Samuel 24:16 is arresting:
"רַב עַתָּה הֶרֶף יָדֶךָ"
Rav, attah hereph yadekha.
“Enough; now stay your hand.”
Enough.
Mercy interrupts destruction.
The sword stops.
And David sees the angel.
At that moment the king does something that reveals the shepherd still buried underneath the crown.
He cries:
“I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done?”
David no longer sounds like a king counting assets.
He sounds like a shepherd grieving sheep.
Something has broken in him.
Earlier he wanted to know how many people he possessed.
Now he is begging God to let judgment fall upon him instead.
Do you see the movement?
From counting people...
to pleading for people.
From power...
to repentance.
From control...
to surrender.
From throne...
to altar.
And this is where the story begins turning toward something astonishing.
God sends David to the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.
David is told to build an altar there.
Araunah offers the property, the oxen, and the wood.
David could have accepted everything for free.
Instead he says words believers have repeated for generations:
“I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing.”
David buys the site.
An altar rises.
Sacrifices are offered.
And 2 Samuel ends the account by telling us that the LORD answered the plea for the land...
and the plague stopped.
But the story does not really disappear there.
Chronicles gives that location enormous significance.
The threshing floor associated with David's sacrifice becomes identified with the place where Solomon would build the temple.
Think about that.
A place associated with judgment becomes a place associated with worship.
A place where a sword was raised becomes a place where sacrifices would be offered.
A place stained by the memory of sin becomes connected to the house where generations would seek the God of Israel.
Scandal...
rewritten by grace.
Not because the scandal didn't matter.
Because grace had the final word.
And still...
there was a problem.
Animal sacrifices could point beyond themselves, but they could never become the final answer to human sin.
David could ask for judgment to fall upon himself instead of the sheep.
But David was himself a sinner.
Israel needed something greater than David.
We do too.
Then, generations later, another Son of David appeared.
Jesus Christ.
He did not need to say, “I have sinned.”
He had not.
He did not stand before God as another guilty king.
He stood as the spotless Lamb.
David essentially cried, “Let Your hand be against me.”
At Calvary, the greater Son of David actually gave Himself.
Jesus said:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
David saw endangered sheep and wished to stand between them and judgment.
Jesus came to do what David could never finally accomplish.
The Shepherd gave His life for the sheep.
At the cross, God did not shrug at evil.
He did not declare sin imaginary.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
The Gospel is infinitely more costly than that.
Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Paul writes that God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).
And Romans 5:8 delivers the sentence every ashamed sinner needs to hear:
While we were still sinners...
Christ died for us.
That is Christianity.
Not bad people becoming impressive.
Not religious people accumulating spiritual statistics.
Not sinners cleaning themselves until God can tolerate them.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ receiving repentant sinners.
Christ forgiving the guilty.
Christ making dead hearts alive.
Christ rewriting stories.
Maybe your census isn't an army.
Maybe you're counting everything you think proves you matter.
Your bank balance.
Your accomplishments.
Your followers.
Your children's success.
Your ministry.
Your reputation.
Your possessions.
Your attractiveness.
Your intelligence.
Your years of service.
Even your good deeds.
And perhaps underneath all that counting is a frightened human heart whispering:
If the number becomes large enough, maybe I'll finally be secure.
But numbers make terrible saviors.
Your strength cannot forgive you.
Your reputation cannot cleanse you.
Your money cannot resurrect you.
Your followers cannot stand before God's judgment for you.
Your religious record cannot bear your sins.
Only Jesus can.
And maybe the most dangerous census is the one happening secretly inside the human heart:
Look how much I have.
Look how far I've come.
Look how many people need me.
Look how successful I am.
Look how spiritual I am.
Look how much better I am than them.
Until mercy comes and destroys the illusion:
You were never saved because you had enough.
You are saved because Christ is enough.
Maybe your heart is striking you right now.
Not because of a census.
Because of something you haven't surrendered.
A hidden relationship.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Pride.
Hatred.
Greed.
Dishonesty.
A secret addiction.
A hardened heart.
A faith you perform publicly but barely live privately.
Maybe everyone thinks you're fine.
God knows.
And so do you.
Please understand the difference between condemnation that drives you away from Christ and conviction that calls you home.
David's heart struck him...
and David confessed.
The answer to exposed sin isn't better hiding.
It is repentance.
Bring it into the light.
Call sin what God calls it.
Turn from it.
Run to Jesus.
There is forgiveness in Him.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Blood-bought forgiveness.
Cross-shaped forgiveness.
Resurrection-backed forgiveness.
Grace strong enough to forgive your past and powerful enough to begin transforming your future.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not “Jesus makes consequences disappear.”
Not “Jesus calls evil good.”
Not “Jesus gives us permission to continue destroying ourselves.”
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus takes sinners who finally stop defending themselves and teaches them to become sons and daughters who walk in the light.
Be honest.

And if God has been restoring areas of your life you thought were beyond redemption, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded person realizes that coming home is still possible.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if you genuinely want your life and resources to glorify God, one practical expression of that desire is helping sound Gospel-centered truth reach people who may never walk into a church but will stop for something a friend shared.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
It is not a spiritual transaction.
It does not buy favor, forgiveness, healing, answered prayer, or salvation.
Jesus already paid the price salvation required.
But before you leave this story, return once more to David.
A king stood over the results of his census.
The numbers were enormous.
His kingdom looked strong.
And none of it could save him.
Then came conviction.
Confession.
Judgment.
Mercy.
An altar.
A sacrifice.
And eventually, through the unfolding story of Scripture, the world would meet the Son of David whose sacrifice no other sacrifice could equal.
Maybe you arrived here thinking this was a story about seventy thousand dead people.
Perhaps it is also a warning about something inside every living person.
We desperately want something we can count...
because counting gives us the illusion that we are in control.
God keeps calling us to something we cannot manufacture:
trust.
David counted soldiers.
God showed him mercy.
And at Calvary, God showed us just how far that mercy would go.
So stop bringing Jesus the numbers that supposedly prove your worth.
Bring Him your sin.
Bring Him your pride.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shattered marriage.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him your failure.
Bring Him the part of your story you desperately wish could be rewritten.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Christ.
Because the final hope of 2 Samuel 24 isn't found in the census.
It isn't found in seventy thousand deaths.
It isn't even finally found in David.
Our hope is found in the greater Son of David...
Jesus Christ.
The King who became the sacrifice.
The Shepherd who died for His sheep.
The Savior who walked out of the grave.
And the Lord who is still taking stories that should have ended in judgment and, through repentance and faith, writing something sinners could never have written for themselves:
Grace.
You may have spent years counting everything you thought made you safe—only to discover that the one thing you could never count was how far Jesus was willing to go to bring a repentant sinner home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your Children May Forget the Sermons. They Won’t Forget What Happened When You Got Angry.
paragraphs: Your Children May Forget the Sermons. They Won’t Forget What Happened When You Got Angry.

You can teach them Bible verses every night, take them to church every Sunday, and tell them about the love of God—but one frightening moment of uncontrolled anger can preach a sermon their heart remembers for years.
There are sermons your children may forget.
They may forget the preacher’s three points.
They may forget the Sunday school lesson about patience.
They may forget the memory verse you practiced with them in the car.
They may even forget some of those nights when you opened the Bible at the dinner table and tried, with all the sincerity you had, to teach them who God is.
But there are other moments children remember with terrifying clarity.
The sound of your footsteps coming down the hallway.
The change in your voice.
The slammed door.
The plate hitting the table harder than necessary.
The sentence you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
The look on your face when something small suddenly became something enormous.
And sometimes…
the silence afterward.
That terrible silence when everybody in the house knows something happened, but nobody knows whether it is safe to talk about it.
Years later, your child may not remember what started the argument.
But they may remember how small they felt standing in front of you.

That is why one quiet sentence in Colossians deserves the attention of every Christian father, every Christian mother, every grandparent, guardian, and every believer entrusted with the heart of a child.
Paul writes:
Hoi pateres, mē erethizete ta tekna hymōn, hina mē athymōsin.
A faithful rendering is:
“Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they may not become discouraged.”
The Greek matters.
Paul uses ἐρεθίζετε — erethizete.
It carries the idea of provoking, irritating, stirring up, exasperating.
Then comes the consequence Paul is concerned about:
ἀθυμῶσιν — athymōsin.
To become discouraged.
To become disheartened.
To lose heart.
Paul is not merely concerned about whether children obey.
He is concerned about what can happen inside them while adults are trying to make them obey.
Read that again.
Because some parents have won arguments while slowly losing access to their child’s heart.
Some have corrected behavior while crushing courage.
Some have demanded respect while behaving in ways for which they themselves desperately needed to repent.
Some have been so determined to establish authority that they forgot Christian authority is never permission for uncontrolled flesh.
And Scripture does not only speak to the child.
That matters.
Because it is easy to quote, “Children, obey your parents.”
It is considerably more uncomfortable when the Bible turns toward the parent.
But it does.
“Fathers…”
God sees you too.
Not merely the child who disobeyed.
Not merely the teenager who talked back.
Not merely the spilled drink, unfinished homework, broken rule, messy bedroom, forgotten chore, bad grade, disrespectful tone, scratched car, missed curfew, or embarrassing scene in public.
God sees what happens inside you when those things happen.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Something happens.
Your body tightens.
Your patience disappears.
Your voice changes.
You tell yourself you are “correcting” them.
But somewhere inside, correction has stopped being correction.
Now you are unloading.
Yesterday’s stress.
Money problems.
Exhaustion.
Pressure at work.
Conflict in your marriage.
Your own childhood wounds.
The disappointment you never processed.
The fear that you are failing as a parent.
The frustration that nobody seems to listen until you become loud.
And suddenly your child is standing in front of an emotional storm they did not create.
They may have done something wrong.
Absolutely.
Biblical parenting does not mean pretending disobedience does not matter. Scripture teaches correction, instruction, discipline, boundaries, obedience, and parental authority.
But biblical authority and uncontrolled anger are not the same thing.
The child may genuinely need correction.
The parent may simultaneously need repentance.
Those truths can exist in the same room.
That is one of the hardest lessons Christian parents ever learn.
Being right about what your child did does not automatically make you right about how you responded.
You can have the correct rule…
and the wrong spirit.
You can defend a biblical standard…
with an unbiblical temper.
You can demand an apology…
while owing one yourself.
You can tell your child to control their emotions while demonstrating that you cannot control yours.
And children notice contradictions adults imagine they cannot see.
They notice how Dad behaves when inconvenienced.
They notice how Mom speaks when exhausted.
They notice whether Christianity survives traffic.
Whether grace survives spilled milk.
Whether patience survives disrespect.
Whether humility survives being challenged.
Whether Jesus is still Lord when the house gets loud.
That may be where some of the deepest discipleship happens.
Not when everybody is dressed nicely for church.
When somebody spills something.
When somebody lies.
When somebody breaks the expensive thing.
When your teenager says the sentence that hits the nerve you thought was healed.
When you are tired.
When nobody is watching.
When you have every opportunity to explode.
Because your children are not merely listening to what you say about Jesus.
They are watching what Jesus is doing to you.
James gives Christians a brutally practical command: be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. The Greek says βραδὺς εἰς ὀργήν — bradys eis orgēn—slow toward anger.
Slow.
Not incapable of recognizing wrong.
Not passive toward sin.
Not afraid to exercise authority.
Slow to anger.
Why?
James continues by warning that human anger does not produce the righteousness God requires.
That sentence should stop us.
Because how many times have we used anger in an attempt to manufacture righteousness?
We become louder because we want immediate obedience.
We intimidate because patience feels inefficient.
We shame because shame gets a reaction.
We threaten because fear produces fast compliance.
And sometimes it works.
For the moment.
The child becomes quiet.
The teenager walks away.
The room freezes.
You “win.”
But Colossians asks a deeper question:
What is happening to their heart?
Hina mē athymōsin.
So they do not become discouraged.
So they do not lose heart.

This does not mean every raised voice permanently damages a child. It does not mean faithful parents never become angry, never fail, or never need to speak firmly. Scripture itself distinguishes anger from sin when it commands believers not to sin in their anger.
The issue is not perfection.
The issue is what rules the home when imperfection appears.
Pride?
Or repentance?
Fear?
Or grace?
Image management?
Or truth?
Because there is another sermon your children may remember for the rest of their lives.
It begins after you failed.
You walk back into the room.
Your child expects another lecture.
Instead, you sit down.
Maybe your voice shakes.
Maybe this feels humiliating because nobody ever apologized to you when you were a child.
Maybe your father believed admitting wrong would weaken his authority.
Maybe your mother never said the words you spent decades wishing you could hear.
But now the Gospel gives you another way.
You look into your child’s eyes and say:
“What you did was wrong, and we still need to deal with it. But the way I spoke to you was wrong too. I sinned in my anger. I should not have treated you that way. Please forgive me.”
Imagine what just happened.
You did not surrender your authority.
You demonstrated where your authority ultimately comes from.
You showed your child that Dad answers to Jesus.
Mom answers to Jesus.
Everybody in this house stands beneath the Word of God.
You showed them that Christianity is not a system where powerful people use Scripture to control weaker people.
It is a kingdom where sinners bow before a holy King.
Including parents.
Especially parents.
And suddenly your failure becomes a doorway into something beautiful.
Your child learns what repentance looks like before they can spell theology.
They learn that confession is not humiliation.
They learn that authority can admit wrong.
They learn that love does not disappear after conflict.
They learn that forgiveness is more than something Christians talk about.
They watch it happen three feet away.
This is where the Gospel enters the living room.
Because Christianity was never the announcement that good families finally learned how to behave perfectly.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners have a Savior.
Jesus Christ did not come for parents who never lose patience.
He came for sinners.
He came for the father ashamed of what he shouted last night.
He came for the mother crying in the bathroom because she became the kind of parent she swore she would never become.
He came for the adult child still carrying memories of a home where anger felt more powerful than affection.
He came for families carrying wounds nobody discusses at church.
He came for the guilty.
The exhausted.
The ashamed.
The wounded.
The ones who need forgiveness.
The ones who need to forgive.
The ones who do not know how.
And He did not come merely to make us feel better about what happened.
He came to redeem us.
At the cross, Jesus does not excuse sin.
He bears its judgment.
Grace does not say your anger did not matter.
Grace says your anger mattered so much that Christ had to die for sin—and His mercy is so great that repentant sinners can actually be forgiven and changed.
That is the difference between shame and conviction.
Shame whispers:
“Hide.”
Jesus calls:
“Come.”
Shame says:
“Pretend it never happened.”
Jesus says:
“Confess.”
Shame says:
“You ruined everything.”
The Gospel says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
And maybe someone reading this needs that sentence desperately.
You cannot go backward.
You cannot become the parent you were ten years ago and unsay every word.
You cannot climb into your child’s memories and delete every frightening night.
You cannot erase the moment they saw you lose control.
But you can repent today.
You can ask forgiveness today.
You can seek reconciliation today.
You can get help today.
You can break patterns today.
You can stop defending what God is asking you to confess.
And if your children are grown?
Call them.
Not to explain yourself.
Not to tell them how difficult they were.
Not to remind them that you provided food and paid the bills.
Not to demand that they acknowledge everything you did right before you acknowledge what you did wrong.
Just tell the truth.

“I have been thinking about some things from when you were growing up. There were times my anger hurt you. I cannot change those moments, and I don't want to make excuses for them. I am sorry. If there are things you need to tell me, I want to listen.”
Then listen.
Really listen.
You may hear things differently than they remember them.
You may disagree with parts of their interpretation.
But reconciliation does not begin with winning the historical argument.
Sometimes it begins with enough humility to hear the pain.
And if you are the adult child reading this rather than the parent…
perhaps your hands are shaking a little.
Because you remember.
You remember the footsteps.
The shouting.
The unpredictable moods.
The words nobody should have said to a child.
Maybe you became excellent at reading faces because childhood taught you to detect danger before anyone spoke.
Maybe you became quiet.
Maybe funny.
Maybe invisible.
Maybe successful.
Maybe rebellious.
Maybe religious.
Anything that helped you survive emotionally.
And perhaps the most complicated part is that the person who frightened you also took you to church.
So somewhere along the way, authority, anger, Christianity, and God became tangled together in your heart.
Hear this carefully:
Your earthly parent is not the measure of your heavenly Father.
Jesus reveals God perfectly.
Look at Christ.
Look at the One who welcomed children.
Look at the One who touched people others avoided.
Look at the One who confronted hypocrisy yet showed astonishing tenderness to the broken.
Look at the Savior who knew every sinful thing about His people and still went willingly toward the cross.
If somebody used Christian authority badly, Jesus is not asking you to pretend it was good.
He is inviting you to discover what His authority actually looks like.
Holy.
True.
Strong.
Merciful.
Never sinful.
And if this article exposed something hidden in your own parenting, do not run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
Maybe tonight does not need another promise that you will “try harder.”
Maybe it needs confession.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Perhaps those are the three most important words you could say.
And perhaps your child needs to hear the next ones.
“Please forgive me too.”
There is no prize for pretending.
We are not building a community of perfect Christians.
We are gathering around a perfect Christ.
And if you know a father who loves Jesus but is exhausted…
If you know a mother quietly wondering whether she is failing…
send this to her.
Not because every sentence is easy to hear.
Because the next time anger rises, you may need to remember one Greek word:
athymōsin.
Discouraged.
Lose heart.
Before you raise your voice, remember the heart standing in front of you.
Before you unload your frustration, remember whose little soul has been entrusted to your care.
Before you demand repentance, remember that the cross has made repentance possible for you too.
We want this ministry to remain a place where Scripture is not merely posted—it is opened, wrestled with, lived, and brought into the rooms where people actually hurt.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces generosity to your local church or other faithful Christian giving.
It does not.
The New Testament teaches generosity that comes from the heart rather than compulsion. Give freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully.
One share may put this message in front of the parent who was about to explode tonight.
One tag may reach the father who has never learned how to apologize.
One saved article may be reopened five minutes before somebody repeats the pattern that wounded them as a child.
One honest comment may make another believer realize they are not the only Christian struggling with anger.
One invitation to follow may lead someone toward Scripture who has been surviving on spiritual crumbs.
Never underestimate what God can do with something faithfully placed in another person's path.
Your children may forget many of your sermons.
But imagine what happens if one of their strongest memories becomes this:
“My parent sometimes failed. But when they did, they came back. They admitted it. They asked forgiveness. They kept running to Jesus. And over the years…I watched Christ change them.”
That is a sermon too.
Maybe one of the most powerful you will ever preach.
Because your children do not need you to convince them that you are flawless.
They need to see what a sinner looks like when grace becomes real.
Tonight, the loudest sermon in your house may never come from a Bible held in your hand.
It may come from the moment you lower your voice, bend your pride, walk back through the door, look your child in the eyes, and say:
“I was wrong. Jesus is still changing me. Will you forgive me?”
Some children will forget the night you lost your temper—but they may spend a lifetime remembering the night grace brought you back through the door.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID’S SON TURNED SEX INTO A PUBLIC DECLARATION OF REBELLION
paragraphs:
DAVID’S SON TURNED SEX INTO A PUBLIC DECLARATION OF REBELLION
Absalom did not climb onto that rooftop because he lost control of his lust. He went there to send a message to his father, to Israel, and to heaven: “David’s throne is mine now.” But the darkest scandal in David’s house was already exposing something terrifying about sin—and something breathtaking about the grace of Jesus Christ.
There are sins committed in darkness because the sinner desperately hopes no one will ever know.
Then there are sins committed where everybody can see because being seen is the entire point.
Absalom chose the second kind.
Picture Jerusalem.
David—the warrior king who once stood before Goliath, the shepherd who wrote songs of worship, the man God had lifted from obscurity to a throne—is fleeing his own capital.
Not because a foreign army has broken through the gates.
Not because the Philistines have returned.
His own son has turned against him.
And while David is leaving Jerusalem humiliated, barefoot and weeping, Absalom is entering the city as though the kingdom already belongs to him.
Then comes one of the most disturbing moments in David’s story.
Ahithophel, Absalom’s counselor, gives him advice designed to make reconciliation with his father politically unthinkable:
“Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.”
—2 Samuel 16:21, KJV
And Absalom does it.
Not secretly.
Not somewhere behind a locked palace door.
A tent is erected on the roof.
The biblical narrator then delivers the horrifying sentence with almost unbearable restraint:
“So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.”
—2 Samuel 16:22, KJV
“In the sight of all Israel.”
That detail changes everything.
This was sexual sin, certainly—but it was also political theater.
Absalom was weaponizing sex as a public declaration of rebellion.

The women were caught inside a power struggle they did not create. Scripture later tells us that David provided for these ten women but separated them from ordinary marital life, and they remained in confinement “living in widowhood” until their deaths. Their suffering should not disappear merely because kings and princes dominate the narrative. Powerful men made decisions, and women lived with the consequences. See 2 Samuel 20:3.
But to understand just how outrageous Absalom’s action was, listen to the language of the Torah.
Leviticus 18:8 says:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא
“‘Ervat eshet-avikha lo tegalleh; ‘ervat avikha hi.”
Literally, the sense is:
“The nakedness of your father’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your father’s nakedness.”

The Hebrew word עֶרְוָה—‘ervah—carries the idea of nakedness or exposed nakedness, and in this legal context “uncovering nakedness” functions as sexual language. The command is not ambiguous. Sexual relations with one’s father’s wife violated a boundary God had explicitly established.
Absalom did not merely cross a social line.
He trampled a divine boundary.
And he did it publicly.
He turned what God had forbidden into a political announcement.
The message was unmistakable:
My father is finished.
His household is mine.
His royal privileges are mine.
His authority is mine.
His throne will be mine.
There would be no quiet reconciliation after this.
That was precisely the strategy.
Ahithophel wanted all Israel to hear what Absalom had done so that Absalom’s supporters would understand that the rupture between father and son had become irreversible.
This is what rebellion eventually does.
At first, rebellion whispers.
Later, it demands a microphone.
At first, sin wants a hidden room.
Eventually, if continually fed, it can begin demanding the rooftop.
And before we point at Absalom with too much confidence, there is something painfully familiar here.
Maybe your rebellion never involved a palace.
Maybe nobody erected a tent.
Maybe thousands of people never watched your worst decision.
But rebellion does not require a crown.
Sometimes rebellion sounds like:
“God, I know what You said…but I want this.”
“I know this relationship is pulling me away from Christ…but I don't want to surrender it.”
“I know I should forgive…but I want them to suffer.”
“I know nobody knows what I watch when I am alone.”
“I know what I keep deleting.”
“I know what I keep hiding.”
“I know this bitterness is poisoning me.”
“I know this compromise is becoming normal.”
“I know I have learned how to look Christian while protecting something from Christ.”
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because there may be a little rooftop inside every human heart.
A place where we want the throne.
A place where we tell God, perhaps without saying the words:
This part belongs to me.
You may have my Sundays.
You may have my worship songs.
You may have the Bible sitting beside my bed.
You may have the Christian language I use around Christian people.
But You cannot have this.
And Jesus does not come merely to negotiate visitation rights over the rooms of your heart.
He is Lord.
That is why the Gospel is simultaneously terrifying to our pride and beautiful to our souls.
Christ does not merely offer to improve the kingdom you have built around yourself.
He calls you to surrender the throne.
But there is another layer to Absalom’s rooftop that makes this story even more sobering.
Years earlier, David had committed his own sexual sin.
He took Bathsheba and then arranged circumstances that led to the death of her husband, Uriah.
David tried to conceal what he had done.
Then Nathan the prophet confronted him.
And Nathan declared:
“Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house…”
Then came these chilling words:
“For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.”
—2 Samuel 12:11–12, KJV
Read that again.
David sinned secretly.
Years later, disgrace erupted publicly from inside his own household.
The biblical narrative itself connects these events.
What happened on Absalom’s rooftop echoes Nathan’s judgment with frightening precision.
David had hidden sexual sin.
Now sexual humiliation entered his family tragedy in full public view.

That does not mean Absalom was an innocent puppet with no moral responsibility. Scripture portrays him as making choices, receiving counsel, and acting. Nor does it make God the moral author of Absalom’s wickedness. The narrative holds human rebellion and divine judgment together without turning evil into righteousness.
But it does teach something our generation desperately needs to remember:
Forgiven sin can still leave consequences.
David had confessed.
When Nathan confronted him, David said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
And Nathan answered:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.”
—2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
That is grace.
Real grace.
David's guilt was not beyond God's forgiveness.
But forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence of everything David had done.
Somebody reading this needs that distinction.
Perhaps Jesus has forgiven you, but you are still rebuilding trust.
Perhaps you repented, but the consequences did not disappear the following morning.
Perhaps God restored your fellowship with Him, but you still have apologies to make.
Perhaps the blood of Christ has washed your guilt, but wisdom requires boundaries because of what happened.
Perhaps you are wondering whether consequences mean God did not forgive you.
Not necessarily.
Grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
Grace is God refusing to let sin have the final word over the repentant sinner.
And David's story proves something else.
You can love God deeply and still make devastating choices.
You can write worship songs and still need repentance.
You can defeat giants in one season and lose battles with your own desires in another.
You can know Scripture and still disobey it.
You can have a testimony and still need accountability.
You can be used by God and still desperately need the mercy of God.
That should destroy spiritual arrogance.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people standing above bad people.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners need a Savior.
David needed one.
Absalom needed one.
You need one.
I need one.
And that is where this scandal begins pointing beyond David.
Because another Son of David would eventually enter Jerusalem.
But He would be nothing like Absalom.
Absalom entered Jerusalem grasping for his father’s throne.
Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing He was going toward a cross.
Absalom used people to strengthen his claim to power.
Jesus laid down His life to rescue sinners.
Absalom publicly humiliated his father.
Jesus publicly honored His Father.
Absalom sought a kingdom through rebellion.
Jesus said, “Not my will, but thine, be done.”
Absalom wanted the crown without submission.
Jesus accepted thorns before glory.
And this is the difference between the rebel son and the obedient Son.
Absalom climbed upward by violating others.
Jesus came downward to save others.
The eternal Son “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant,” and humbled Himself “unto death, even the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:7–8).
Think about that.
The true King did not need to steal a throne.
The throne already belonged to Him.
Yet He came for rebels.
People like David.
People like us.
People who have taken God's gifts and used them against the Giver.
People who have wanted God's blessings while resisting God's authority.
People who know how to hide.
People who have made promises to God and broken them.
People whose private search history would embarrass them.
People carrying sexual shame.
People carrying adultery.
People carrying pornography.
People carrying bitterness.
People carrying secret addictions.
People carrying memories they wish they could erase.
People who look clean in church photographs while quietly wondering whether God could still want them.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required the death of Christ.
But the cross also declares something astonishing:
Your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
David committed terrible sin, but Scripture does not end his story at Bathsheba.
Peter denied Jesus, but Scripture does not end his story beside the charcoal fire of denial.
Paul persecuted the church, but Scripture does not end his story holding the coats of those who killed Stephen.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet Jesus could still say, “Today shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
This is what grace does.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace enters the darkness and brings the sinner into the light.
Grace does not say, “Nothing happened.”
Grace says, “Something terrible happened—and Jesus is greater.”
Grace does not remove repentance.
Grace produces it.
Grace does not teach us to excuse rebellion.
Grace brings rebels home.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe it is private.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe people still mention what you did.
Maybe your marriage carries scars.
Maybe your children remember things you wish they could forget.
Maybe you damaged someone's trust.
Maybe someone damaged yours.
Maybe you are not David in this story.
Maybe you feel like one of the people who suffered because someone powerful chose sin.
And if that is you, hear this carefully: another person's sin against you is not proof that God abandoned you.
Jesus sees wounded people too.

The women in 2 Samuel 16 were not props. They were human beings caught inside the devastation of male ambition, family collapse, and political rebellion. The later text records the painful consequences that continued in their lives.
Scripture is brutally honest about what sin does to people.
That honesty matters.
Because some wounds cannot be healed by pretending they never happened.
Christ does not ask you to call evil good.
He asks you to bring your wounds to the One who was wounded.
He was betrayed.
Publicly humiliated.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Condemned.
And crucified.
Jesus understands shame from the inside of human suffering.
Yet shame did not defeat Him.
Death did not defeat Him.
The grave did not keep Him.
And if you belong to Him, your darkest chapter does not get permission to write the final sentence.
That belongs to Jesus.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not because you needed another shocking Bible story.
Because somewhere underneath your smile, your work, your family photographs, your church attendance, your jokes, your scrolling, and your “I'm fine”…
there is something you are tired of hiding.
Then stop running toward the rooftop.
Run toward the cross.
You do not need to make yourself clean enough to approach Jesus.
Come confessing.
Come surrendering.
Come without excuses.
Come without blaming everybody else.
Come without editing the story so you look better.
Call sin what God calls it.
And trust the Christ who died for sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Not some unrighteousness.
“All unrighteousness.”
That does not make repentance cheap.
It makes Christ precious.
And maybe the most dangerous person reading this is not the person crying over obvious failure.
Maybe it is the person thinking, “At least I have never done anything like Absalom.”
Be careful.
The seed of rebellion is not measured by how spectacularly it becomes visible.
You can rebel against God quietly.
Respectably.
Religiously.
You can sit in church while protecting your throne.
You can sing “I surrender all” while mentally adding, “except that.”
You can post Scripture and refuse reconciliation.
You can preach purity while feeding secret lust.
You can talk about grace while refusing to forgive.
You can defend biblical truth while ignoring the truth about yourself.
So don't merely ask:
“How could Absalom do that?”
Ask:
“Jesus, where am I resisting You?”
That question can change a life.
Be real.
Your honesty may become the permission someone else needed to stop pretending.
Return to it when hidden compromise starts trying to sound harmless again.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
Share it with the person who thinks their past has permanently disqualified them from the mercy of Christ.
Salvation is by grace, and Christian giving and support are responses of love, not payments for blessing.
But before you leave, remember the rooftop.
Remember David.
Remember Absalom.
Remember the terrible distance sin can travel once the human heart decides God's throne belongs to us.
Then remember another hill.
Not a palace roof in Jerusalem where a rebellious son publicly declared war against his father.
A hill outside Jerusalem where the obedient Son stretched out His hands to reconcile rebels to His Father.
One rooftop displayed the ugliness of human rebellion.
One cross displayed the staggering cost of divine mercy.

And when Satan whispers that what you did is too filthy, too public, too secret, too sexual, too shameful, too hypocritical, too complicated, or simply too late for redemption, point him toward the empty tomb.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of sinners becoming impressive enough for Jesus.
It is the story of Jesus being powerful enough to save sinners.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but surrender it to Christ, and it does not get to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM’S CONCUBINES: THE WOMEN AND CHILDREN EVERYONE FORGETS AFTER SARAH
paragraphs: ABRAHAM’S CONCUBINES: THE WOMEN AND CHILDREN EVERYONE FORGETS AFTER SARAH

We remember Sarah. We remember Isaac. We remember the promise. But buried near the end of Abraham’s story is one uncomfortable sentence about other women, other sons, gifts placed into departing hands—and a family separation Scripture refuses to erase.
Most people think they know how Abraham’s story ends.
Sarah dies.
Isaac remains.
Abraham grows old.
The patriarch dies in faith.
Curtain closed.
Except the Bible does something strange before Abraham leaves the stage.
It opens another door.
And standing behind that door are people many Christians barely remember.
A woman named Keturah.
Six sons.
Grandsons.
Entire family lines.
And then one sentence that should make us stop reading so quickly:
“But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts…”
Genesis 25:6.
Sons.
Concubines.
Plural.
Suddenly the ending of Abraham’s life feels more complicated than the version many of us remember from Sunday school.
Because Abraham’s household was not a polished family portrait.
It contained promise and pain.
Faith and human failure.
Miraculous intervention and complicated consequences.
A beloved wife named Sarah.
An Egyptian servant named Hagar.
A woman named Keturah.
Isaac, the covenant son.
Ishmael, the son Abraham loved but who was not the covenant heir.
Other sons whose names rarely survive in Christian memory.
And through all of it, a God whose redemptive purpose continued despite the tangled humanity of the people He called.
That matters.
Because perhaps you came to Jesus carrying a tangled story too.
Before going further, however, we need to be precise about what Scripture actually says.
Genesis 25 introduces Keturah with these words:
“Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.”
The Hebrew begins:
וַיֹּסֶף אַבְרָהָם וַיִּקַּח אִשָּׁה וּשְׁמָהּ קְטוּרָה
Vayyosef Avraham vayyiqqach ishah, ushemah Qeturah.
In straightforward sense: Abraham again took a woman as wife, and her name was Keturah.
The important word is אִשָּׁה — ishah.
Depending on context, it can mean “woman” or “wife.”
So Genesis 25:1 presents Keturah as Abraham’s wife.
But Scripture gives us another description.
First Chronicles 1:32 calls her:
קְטוּרָה פִּילֶגֶשׁ אַבְרָהָם
Keturah, Abraham’s pilegesh—his concubine.
That is not a contradiction that needs to be hidden.
It gives us a fuller picture of her status.

A concubine in the ancient world was not simply what modern readers might imagine when hearing words such as “mistress” or “affair.” She occupied a recognized but subordinate marital or household status and did not possess the same standing as the principal wife.
Keturah could therefore be described as a wife in Genesis while Chronicles identifies her more specifically as a concubine.
And then Genesis 25:6 makes the picture even more intriguing by speaking of Abraham’s “concubines” in the plural.
The Hebrew expression is:
בְּנֵי הַפִּילַגְשִׁים
benei happilagshim—
“the sons of the concubines.”
We should not pretend the Bible tells us more than it does.
It does not give us a neat list saying, “These were all Abraham’s concubines.”
Keturah is explicitly called his concubine in Chronicles.
Hagar requires slightly more careful language.
Genesis identifies Hagar as Sarah’s Egyptian servant, and Genesis 16:3 says Sarah gave Hagar to Abram:
לְאִשָּׁה
le’ishah—
“as a wife.”

That makes the story considerably more complex than reducing Hagar to merely Abraham’s secret lover. She entered a recognized relationship within the household through an ancient arrangement initiated by Sarah—an arrangement Scripture records without requiring us to treat the arrangement itself as God’s ideal.
And that distinction is crucial.
The Bible often tells us what happened without telling us to imitate everything that happened.
Abraham is a towering man of faith.
Abraham is also a man whose household reveals what happens when frightened human beings try to accomplish divine promises through human solutions.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
Waiting became painful.
Pain became pressure.
And pressure whispered the same dangerous sentence it still whispers today:
“Maybe God needs your help.”
So Hagar entered the story.
And Ishmael was born.
This is where we need to resist the temptation to turn Hagar into a villain.
She was an Egyptian servant caught inside decisions made by people with far more power than she possessed.
Genesis does not hide the ugliness that followed.
Pregnancy changed relationships.
Contempt appeared.
Sarah became harsh.
Hagar fled.
And then something astonishing happened.
God found her.
Not Abraham.
Not Sarah.
God.
An Egyptian servant woman running through the wilderness became the recipient of divine attention.
The angel of the LORD met her near a spring.
God heard her suffering.
God spoke about her unborn child.
God gave promises concerning Ishmael’s future.
And Hagar responded with one of Scripture’s most unforgettable declarations about God:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro’i.
“You are a God who sees me.”
Think about that.
The woman human beings pushed toward the margins discovered that heaven had not lost sight of her.
Maybe that is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to become collateral damage in somebody else’s choices.
Someone else made the decision.
You inherited the wound.
Someone else broke the covenant.
You lived with the consequences.
Someone else created the chaos.
You grew up inside it.
Someone else walked away.
You spent years wondering why you were apparently so easy to leave.
And somewhere inside you is a question you rarely say aloud:
“Does God see what happened to me?”
Hagar’s story answers from the wilderness.
Yes.
He sees.
But seeing Hagar does not mean God abandoned His covenant concerning Isaac.
That is another truth modern readers sometimes struggle to hold simultaneously.
God could care deeply for Ishmael while maintaining that Isaac was the covenant son through whom the particular covenant line would continue.
Grace toward one person did not require God to rewrite what He had promised concerning another.
Genesis eventually reaches Sarah’s death.
Then, almost unexpectedly, Keturah appears.
She bears Abraham six sons:
Zimran.
Jokshan.
Medan.
Midian.
Ishbak.
Shuah.
Then the genealogy expands again.
Jokshan fathers Sheba and Dedan.
Midian fathers Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah.
Names.
Names.
Names.
Names modern readers hurry past.
But God did not hurry past them.
Scripture recorded them.
That alone should humble us.
Because human beings measure significance by spotlight.
God does not.
We remember the person standing in the center of the photograph.
God remembers the people whose names barely fit into the caption.
We remember Isaac because the covenant narrative continues through Isaac.
But God remembered Ishmael.
God recorded Keturah.
God recorded Zimran.
God recorded Jokshan.
God recorded Medan.
God recorded Midian.
God recorded Ishbak.
God recorded Shuah.
People we forget remained visible to God.
Then comes the painful sentence.
Abraham gave everything he had to Isaac.
But to the sons of his concubines he gave gifts while he was still alive.
Then he sent them away from Isaac.
Eastward.
Away.
Imagine that moment without romanticizing it.
Possessions being gathered.
Gifts being distributed.
Camels being prepared.
Perhaps mothers watching.
Perhaps sons looking back.
Perhaps questions nobody knew how to answer.
Scripture does not tell us their private emotions, so we should not invent them as history.
But Scripture does tell us what happened.
Isaac received Abraham’s estate.
The other sons received gifts.
Then Abraham sent them eastward, away from Isaac.
Why?
The text places this separation alongside Isaac’s unique inheritance and covenant role.
Earlier God had already declared concerning Sarah:
“I will establish my covenant with him for an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him.”
The covenant would continue through Isaac.
Not because Isaac was morally superior as a baby.
Not because Ishmael was worthless.
Not because Keturah’s children were invisible.
But because God had sovereignly chosen the covenant line through which His redemptive purpose would advance.
Isaac.
Then Jacob.
Then Israel.
Then Judah.
Then generation after generation...
until eventually another genealogy opens:
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”
There He is.
Jesus.
Suddenly Abraham’s complicated household belongs to a story much larger than Abraham.
The promise was moving somewhere.
Toward Christ.
This is why we must be careful when preaching Abraham.
The point is not that Abraham was flawless.
He was not.
The point is that God was faithful.
The Bible does not need Abraham to look perfect in order for God to look glorious.
That may be one of the most liberating truths in Scripture.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that God finally found enough impressive people to build His kingdom.
Christianity is the announcement that the holy God entered the wreckage of human history to redeem sinners through Jesus Christ.
Abraham believed God.
Abraham also experienced fear.
He obeyed magnificently at times.
He failed painfully at others.
His family experienced consequences.
Yet God remained faithful to His promise.
And eventually Jesus stepped into Abraham’s bloodline.
Not because every chapter before Him was clean.
But because grace had been moving through the mess all along.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not come from a Bible filled with airbrushed people.
He enters a biblical history filled with barrenness, jealousy, favoritism, sexual brokenness, family conflict, deception, exile, grief, failure, and sin.
Then at Calvary, the Son of God carries human sin upon Himself.
The scandal becomes the place where grace speaks.
The cross looked like defeat.
God made it the place of victory.
The condemned Christ became the risen Lord.
The grave received Him.
The grave could not keep Him.
And now everyone who comes to Christ in repentance and faith discovers something Abraham’s complicated household whispers from thousands of years ago:
Your history is real.
But your history does not have to become your master.
Maybe your family tree embarrasses you.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother wounded you.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe you were the one who caused the collapse.
Maybe there is a child you barely speak to anymore.
Maybe your past contains sexual sin.
Maybe you manipulated people.
Maybe you were manipulated.
Maybe you waited for God, became impatient, and created an Ishmael-sized consequence you cannot simply erase.
The Gospel does not ask you to rename darkness as light.
Repentance means bringing the truth into the presence of God.
No excuses.
No religious costume.
No carefully edited testimony.
Sin is sin.
Wounds are wounds.
Consequences can remain consequences.
But Jesus Christ is still Jesus Christ.
And grace is not God pretending your past never happened.
Grace is God refusing to let your past have the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
There is an enormous difference.
God did not delete Hagar from Genesis.
He met her.
God did not erase Ishmael.
He heard him.
God did not erase Keturah.
He recorded her.
God did not erase her sons.
He named them.
God did not rewrite Abraham’s story by pretending its painful chapters never existed.
He carried His promise through them.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needed tonight.
You keep asking God to erase the chapter.
Maybe redemption is not erasure.
Maybe redemption is Christ taking a chapter that should have ended in shame and making it testify to mercy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing yesterday’s facts.
By changing what yesterday gets to mean for your eternity.
If you have been hiding something from God, stop running.
He already sees you.
If you have been excusing sin because someone else hurt you first, stop.
Their sin does not sanctify yours.
If you have been convinced you are beyond forgiveness, look at the cross again.
Christ did not shed symbolic blood for imaginary sinners.
He died for real sinners carrying real guilt.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring the secret into His light.
Come home.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to explain your entire story publicly.
Just comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If your faith has been exhausted and you are still trying to hold on, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
And if you have watched Jesus begin redeeming something in your life that once looked impossible to redeem, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence somebody else desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if biblical truth helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone you may never realize was silently drowning.
Send it privately to the person whose family is breaking apart.
Not to purchase God’s favor.
Not to prove that you love Jesus.
Not because financial support makes anyone more spiritual.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But ministry does require people willing to help carry it.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
Thousands.
Free.
Because not everyone can afford a shelf full of Christian books, but everyone should be encouraged to open Scripture, seek Christ, grow in truth, and become deeply rooted in the Gospel.
Leave asking something deeper about yourself.
Which chapter are you still hiding?
Which consequence have you mistaken for a life sentence?
Which wound has become your identity?
Which failure convinced you that Jesus could forgive everybody except you?
Abraham’s story did not end with Hagar running into the wilderness.
It did not end with Sarah’s grave.
It did not end with Keturah’s sons traveling east.
It did not even end inside the cave where Isaac and Ishmael together buried their father.
The promise kept moving.
Generation after generation.
Until Bethlehem.
Until a carpenter’s home.
Until Galilee.
Until blind eyes opened.
Until lepers were cleansed.
Until sinners sat at the table.
Until nails entered holy hands.
Until blood ran down a Roman cross.
Until a stone sealed a borrowed tomb.
Until Sunday morning.
That is where every story of biblical redemption ultimately points.
Not Abraham.
Jesus.
Not human faithfulness.
His faithfulness.
Not our ability to repair ourselves.
His power to save.
So if your family history looks more like Genesis than a Christian greeting card, you may be closer to understanding grace than you realize.
The Bible was never frightened by broken families.
Jesus entered one long human history filled with broken people to rescue broken people.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the family secret.
Bring Him the consequence.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish nobody knew.
Then repent where you must repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is righteous and possible.
Make restitution where repentance requires it.
And trust the Savior who carried sin and shame to the cross.
Because the forgotten women around Abraham’s household remind us of something we dare not forget:
God sees people standing outside the spotlight.
He hears cries from the wilderness.
He remembers names other people skip.
And His redemptive purpose is not defeated by the tangled histories of human beings.
So comment if you need prayer.
Share if someone in your world needs this truth.
Because somewhere tonight, another Hagar is convinced nobody sees her.
Another Ishmael feels pushed outside the promise.
Another family is living with consequences nobody posts about.
Another believer thinks one terrible chapter has destroyed the entire book.
And somebody needs to tell them:
