The chapter that embarrasses you may be the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need the Savior who refuses to abandon repentant sinners to their shame.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF THE BIBLE NEVER SAYS “MASTURBATION,” WHY DOES YOUR CONSCIENCE KEEP ASKING GOD ABOUT IT?
paragraphs: IF THE BIBLE NEVER SAYS “MASTURBATION,” WHY DOES YOUR CONSCIENCE KEEP ASKING GOD ABOUT IT?

Scripture never directly names the act. That does not mean Scripture has nothing to say about the desire behind it, the imagination feeding it, the mastery it can acquire, the body involved in it—or the Christ who can meet you in the room where nobody else knows you are struggling.
There is a moment after the screen goes dark.
After the fantasy dissolves.
After the body settles.
After whatever relief you were chasing lasts far less time than you hoped it would.
And then there is silence.
Maybe you know that silence.
You lie there staring at the ceiling.
Maybe you whisper, “God, I’m sorry.”
Maybe you promise this was the last time.
Maybe you do not even know anymore whether you should feel guilty.
Because somewhere along the way you discovered something that confused you:
The Bible never directly says, “You shall not masturbate.”
And suddenly a question you thought was simple became complicated.
If Scripture never specifically names masturbation, is it actually sinful?
Or have Christians created a commandment God never gave?
That deserves a serious answer.
Not panic.
Not shame disguised as holiness.
Not somebody screaming at you from a pulpit.
And certainly not the lazy answer, “Well, everybody knows it’s wrong.”
If we are going to call something sin, we should care deeply about whether God actually calls it sin.
But we should also be careful about another mistake.
The absence of a modern word from Scripture does not necessarily mean the absence of biblical principles capable of judging the thing that word describes.
So perhaps the deepest question is not simply:
“Where does the Bible mention masturbation?”
Perhaps it is:
“What does masturbation become when I place my desires, imagination, body, habits, motives, conscience, and relationship with Christ underneath everything Scripture actually says?”
That question is harder.
Because now we cannot hide behind vocabulary.
And we cannot hide behind shame either.
We have to walk into the light.
First, something needs to be said clearly because Christians sometimes overstate the biblical evidence.
Scripture does not directly name masturbation as a distinct sexual act and then issue an explicit command saying, “Do not masturbate.”
We should admit that.

The story of Onan in Genesis 38 is also frequently used as though it were a straightforward prohibition of masturbation, but that is not what the narrative describes. Onan deliberately refused his obligation concerning offspring while exploiting the sexual relationship, and God's judgment falls within that context. Turning the passage into a simple proof text about masturbation asks the text to say more than it actually says.
Biblical faithfulness does not require us to exaggerate Scripture.
It requires us to submit to Scripture.
And once we do that, something uncomfortable happens.
The Bible may not directly name masturbation...

but it speaks relentlessly about the heart that desires, the eyes that look, the mind that imagines, the body that belongs to God, sexual holiness, self-control, enslavement, conscience, love of neighbor, marriage, and what Christians do with their bodies.
Jesus takes us immediately beneath external behavior.
Matthew 5:28 contains these words:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν...”
The crucial expression includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—pros to epithymēsai—speaking in context of looking at a woman with the purpose or orientation of desiring her lustfully.
Jesus continues by locating the adultery “ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ”—en tē kardia autou—“in his heart.”
Notice where Jesus takes the conversation.
The heart.
Not merely what your hands have done.
Not merely whether another person's body was physically present.
The heart.
That matters enormously.
Because for many people masturbation is not an isolated physiological event.
There is a face attached to it.
A video attached to it.
A memory attached to it.
A fantasy attached to it.
Someone else's body has been pulled into the imagination and transformed into material for personal sexual gratification.
Sometimes it is pornography.
Sometimes it is someone at work.
Someone at church.
Someone else's spouse.
An ex.
A stranger.
A person on social media who has absolutely no idea what role they are playing inside your imagination.
And suddenly the question changes.
“Did my body technically violate an explicitly named command?”
becomes:
“What am I deliberately teaching my heart to desire?”
That is much closer to Jesus' concern.
And this is where pornography makes the moral issue substantially clearer.

Pornography does not merely involve sexual release. It ordinarily involves intentionally seeking sexual stimulation through viewing other people sexually. It can train the mind to consume bodies rather than love persons.
You can close the browser history.
But you cannot pretend nothing happened inside the heart.
Still, we need another layer of honesty.
Not every instance of masturbation necessarily involves pornography or consciously fantasizing about a particular person.
That distinction matters.
A Christian seeking biblical truth should not be frightened into claiming more than Scripture establishes.
So imagine someone saying:
“I don't watch pornography. I deliberately avoid fantasizing about another person. What then?”
Now we need more than Matthew 5:28.
Paul gives us another question.
“Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν· ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει.”
“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are beneficial.”
Then comes the line that reaches into countless secret habits:
“ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.”
All’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
“I will not be mastered by anything.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:12.
Read that slowly.
I will not be mastered by anything.
Now stop asking only:
“Can I do this?”
Ask:
“Can I stop?”
That question has exposed more bondage than arguments ever will.
Can you leave it alone?
For a week?
A month?
Can you experience stress without running toward it?
Can you feel lonely without needing it?
Can you go to bed without depending upon it?
When temptation arrives, do you experience genuine freedom to say no—or does your mind immediately begin negotiating?
“I need this.”
“I can't sleep without it.”
“Just tonight.”
“I've already messed up anyway.”
“Tomorrow I'll stop.”
You may recognize that voice.
It has spoken through countless compulsions.
And Paul offers a Christian vision of freedom far greater than permission.
The Christian question is not merely, “Am I technically allowed?”
The Christian question is, “Is anything beginning to own what Jesus purchased?”
Because a few verses later Paul says something astonishing:
“οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν”
ouk este heautōn.
“You are not your own.”
Then:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς”
ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“You were bought with a price.”
And therefore:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
“Glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
The body of the Christian is not dirty.
That is important.
Christianity does not teach that bodies are disgusting or sexual desire itself is inherently evil.
God created embodied human beings.
God created marriage.
God created sexual union for marriage.
The Christian hope is even bodily resurrection.
Your body matters precisely because God says it matters.
Paul's argument is not:
“Hate your body.”
It is:
“Your body belongs to the Lord.”
That changes everything.
Sexual desire is not an enemy merely because it is powerful.
But a good desire can become disordered.
Hunger is good.
Gluttony is not.
Rest is good.
Sloth is not.
Money can serve good purposes.
Greed corrupts.
Sexual desire belongs within God's good creation, yet desire detached from God's purposes can begin ruling the person who was supposed to steward it.
That is why 1 Thessalonians 4 speaks so directly:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν”
Touto gar estin thelēma tou Theou, ho hagiasmos hymōn.
“This is the will of God: your sanctification.”
Paul then speaks of abstaining from πορνεία—porneia, sexual immorality, and continues:
“μὴ ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας”
mē en pathei epithymias—
not in the passion of lustful desire.
Notice again that Christianity is reaching deeper than anatomy.
God wants the person.
Your desires.
Your imagination.
Your habits.
Your sexuality.
Your loneliness.
Your wounded places.
Even the parts of you nobody sees.
And maybe this is where this article stops being theological information and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because perhaps masturbation was never really just about sex for you.
Maybe it became anesthesia.
You were lonely.
You discovered relief.
You were rejected.
You discovered relief.
You were anxious.
Relief.
Depressed.
Relief.
Bored.
Relief.
Heartbroken.
Relief.
You felt unwanted, but for a few minutes fantasy allowed you to construct a world in which you were desired.
Then the feeling disappeared.
And whatever ache existed before was still waiting afterward.
So you returned.
Again.
And again.
Until something meant to soothe you started controlling you.
And perhaps you hate yourself for it.
Listen carefully.
Self-hatred is not repentance.
Shame saying, “Hide from God,” is not the voice you need to obey.
The Gospel does something radically different.
It tells the truth about sin without surrendering the sinner to despair.
This is where Jesus becomes more than the closing paragraph of an article about sexual ethics.
Jesus is the center of the entire answer.
Because Christianity's ultimate answer to sexual brokenness is not merely:
“Try harder.”
It is:
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the fantasies.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the loneliness beneath the relapse.
Bring Him the memory you are ashamed of.
Bring Him the habit you have confessed fifty times.
Bring Him the part of you that wonders whether confession number fifty-one could possibly be sincere.
Come into the light.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves exactly how seriously God takes sin—and how astonishingly far His mercy goes to redeem sinners.
Paul wrote something immediately before his teaching about the Christian body that struggling believers desperately need to remember:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε”
kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then Paul piles grace upon grace:
“ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε”
“But you were washed.”
“ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε”
“You were sanctified.”
“ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε”
“You were justified.”
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the stain never existed.
Washed.
Not calling bondage freedom.
Sanctified.
Not declaring guilty people innocent because their sin was insignificant.
Justified because Christ is sufficient.
Maybe you failed last night.
Maybe ten minutes ago.
Maybe you are reading this immediately after doing the very thing you promised God you would never do again.
Your next move should not be running farther from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Confess honestly.
Repent genuinely.
Receive His mercy gratefully.
Then begin taking obedience seriously.
If pornography feeds the cycle, remove access.
If social media accounts repeatedly awaken lust, unfollow them.
If isolation strengthens temptation, stop fighting completely alone.
Find a mature, trustworthy believer who understands both holiness and grace.
Pray before temptation becomes overwhelming, not merely afterward.
Fill your imagination with what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and commendable.
And when necessary, make practical boundaries inconvenient enough that your future tempted self cannot casually overthrow the convictions of your present clear-minded self.
This is not earning salvation.
It is learning to fight from the identity Christ has given you.
And if you fall?
Do not rename darkness as light.
But do not make an idol out of your failure either.
Get up.
Confess.
Return.
Fight again.
Grace is not God's permission to remain chained.
Grace is God's power and mercy meeting sinners while Christ leads them into freedom.
So...
Is masturbation always and explicitly identified by name as sin in Scripture?
No.
The Bible does not give us that sentence, and Christians should be truthful about that.
Does that therefore mean every conceivable instance is automatically morally harmless?
That conclusion goes beyond the evidence too.

Instead, Christians should examine the practice underneath the larger biblical theology of sexuality, desire, holiness, freedom, conscience, marriage, love, self-control, and the body belonging to Christ.
If it requires pornography, deliberately cultivated lust, or mentally using another person for sexual gratification, Jesus' teaching about lust becomes directly relevant.
If it masters you, Paul's refusal to “be mastered by anything” becomes painfully relevant.
If it trains sexuality inward toward repeated self-gratification rather than toward God's purposes for sexual love, that deserves serious Christian examination.
If you cannot bring the practice before God with a clear conscience and thanksgiving, do not silence your conscience merely because you cannot locate a verse containing the modern English word.
And if abstaining from it exposes an inability to control your desires, do not panic.
Pay attention.
You may have discovered where the battle actually is.
Yet do not turn personal conviction into careless condemnation of everyone else.
Romans 14 gives Christians important categories concerning conscience in matters where Scripture does not issue the exact explicit prohibition someone may be demanding.
We must neither invent commandments nor search for loopholes around holiness.
We belong to Jesus.
That is higher than loophole Christianity.
Perhaps, then, the most revealing question is not:
“Can I masturbate and still be a Christian?”
Ask something far more dangerous:
“Jesus, what would You have me surrender so that even my hidden sexuality glorifies You?”
Then wait.
Because sometimes we already know what answer we are afraid He will give.
And perhaps underneath this entire struggle is something even deeper.
You do not merely need greater sexual discipline.
You need a greater affection.
You need Christ to become more beautiful than the thing you keep reaching for in secret.
Rules can restrain hands for a while.
Only grace can transform hearts.
Jesus does not merely want to interrupt your behavior.
He wants you.
All of you.
Including the room where the door is locked.
Including the midnight version of you.
Including your browser.
Your imagination.
Your hormones.
Your wounds.
Your loneliness.
Your longing to be loved.
Your failures.
Your sexuality.
Your future marriage, if God gives you one.
Your singleness, however long it lasts.
Your entire body.
Because the body you keep thinking of as the scene of your shame can become a place where Christ is glorified.
That is redemption.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to gather perfect Christians pretending they never struggle.
We want to keep pointing wounded, tempted, exhausted, convicted, growing people toward Jesus Christ and the truth of Scripture.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sexual details publicly.
But you can step toward the light.

And if Jesus has already been freeing you from sexual bondage, consider leaving a testimony that gives someone else hope. Somebody reading quietly may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to become their identity.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns God's favor. It does not.
But if this truth helped you, sharing it can place biblical hope in front of someone you may never know was struggling.
That is one meaningful way your platform can glorify God: use what you have to point someone toward Christ.
Leave the honest comment.
But above everything else...
Go back to Jesus.
Because your greatest victory will never be simply being able to say:
“I stopped masturbating.”
The greater testimony is:
“Jesus became Lord even over the part of my life I thought I would always have to hide.”
Maybe nobody knows what happened behind your closed door.
Jesus does.
And the hands that were pierced for sinners are not calling the repentant deeper into hiding.
They are calling you home.
Your secret may explain where the story became painful—but Jesus still gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON DEMANDED A PHILISTINE WOMAN—EVEN AFTER HIS PARENTS QUESTIONED THE MARRIAGE
paragraphs: SAMSON DEMANDED A PHILISTINE WOMAN—EVEN AFTER HIS PARENTS QUESTIONED THE MARRIAGE
He saw what he wanted. His parents saw the danger. God saw a battlefield. And buried inside Samson’s scandal is a warning for every believer who has ever confused desire with destiny.
There are moments in Scripture that make you uncomfortable because the people God uses do not behave the way you expect people used by God to behave.
Samson is one of those people.
Before Delilah.
Before the haircut.
Before the blinded warrior stood between the pillars of a Philistine temple.
Before the name Samson became synonymous with extraordinary strength and catastrophic weakness...
there was a woman.
And one sentence.
A sentence that should make every believer who has ever desperately wanted something stop and examine the heart.
Samson went down to Timnah.
He saw a Philistine woman.
Then he went home and essentially told his parents:
Get her for me.
I want her as my wife.
His parents questioned him.
Samson insisted.
And then Scripture says something so startling that, if we read it carelessly, we can completely misunderstand both Samson and God.
Because Judges 14:4 tells us that something in this unfolding confrontation was “from the LORD.”
Wait.
What?
Did God approve Samson’s every desire?
Was Samson’s attraction automatically holy because God would ultimately use the situation?
Does the fact that God can accomplish His purposes through a broken decision mean the brokenness suddenly becomes righteousness?
No.
And this is where Samson’s story stops being an ancient story about a strong man with terrible relationship problems...
and starts walking uncomfortably close to your own front door.
Samson’s story did not begin with a woman.
It began with God.

Israel had again fallen into evil, and the Philistines oppressed them for forty years. Into that darkness, the angel of the LORD announced the birth of a child who would be specially consecrated to God.
Judges 13 says Samson would be a Nazirite to God from the womb and would “begin to deliver Israel” from Philistine domination.
Think about that.
Before Samson could walk, there was calling.
Before Samson could choose anything, there was consecration.
Before Samson ever saw the woman in Timnah, God had already declared that his life belonged to a purpose greater than his appetites.
That makes what happens next so painful.
Judges 14 opens almost abruptly:
Samson goes down to Timnah.
He sees a Philistine woman.
He returns to his parents.
And he wants her.
The Hebrew makes his insistence particularly revealing.
When his parents object, Samson says:
אוֹתָהּ קַח־לִי כִּי־הִיא יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי
’Otah qach-li, ki-hi yashrah be‘enai.
The sense is:
“Get her for me, because she is right in my eyes.”
Or, idiomatically, “She is right for me.”
That expression should make readers of Judges uneasy.
בְּעֵינַי — be‘enai
“In my eyes.”
Samson saw something.
Samson wanted something.
And what he saw looked right to him.
That sounds frighteningly familiar.
Because some of the most dangerous words a human heart can whisper are:
“But it feels right to me.”
I know what Scripture says...
but this feels right.
I know people who love me are warning me...
but this feels right.
I know I am becoming spiritually colder...
but this feels right.
I know I have started hiding things...
but this feels right.
I know I cannot pray about this with the same honesty anymore...
but surely God understands.
Samson’s parents saw a problem their son did not appear interested in seeing.
They asked why he needed to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines rather than from among his own people. Judges 14 explicitly records their objection and Samson’s continued insistence.
But then comes the sentence that changes the entire scene.
וְאָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ לֹא יָדְעוּ כִּי מֵיְהוָה הִיא
Ve’aviv ve’immo lo yade‘u ki meYHWH hi...
His father and mother did not know that this was “from the LORD.”
The verse continues by explaining that an occasion was being sought against the Philistines, who were ruling over Israel.
This is one of those verses where humility matters.
We should not make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
The text does not give us permission to transform Samson’s impulses into a model of godly romantic discernment.
Rather, it reveals something far greater about the sovereignty of God:
God was capable of using this explosive situation in His larger purpose against Israel’s oppressors.
That distinction matters enormously.
God using something does not necessarily mean God morally endorses everything human beings did within it.
God is sovereign enough to accomplish His purposes even through tangled motives, human weakness, disastrous consequences, hostile enemies, and situations that seem completely out of control.
That is not permission to sin.
It is a reason to worship.
Because if God could work through Samson’s complicated story, your failures have not somehow become stronger than His sovereignty.
But do not twist grace into permission.
There is a dangerous counterfeit gospel that whispers:
“God can use my mistakes, so my choices do not really matter.”
Samson’s life destroys that lie.
Yes, God used Samson.
And Samson suffered terribly.
Those two realities stand beside each other.

The Spirit of the LORD empowered Samson with extraordinary strength. Judges records the Spirit coming powerfully upon him repeatedly. Yet the narrative also exposes a man whose appetites and impulses repeatedly brought devastation into his life.
Calling did not make him consequence-proof.
Giftedness did not make him spiritually invincible.
Strength did not make him wise.
And being used by God did not mean every choice he made pleased God.
Someone reading this needs that sentence.
Because perhaps people admire your ministry.
Your talent.
Your intelligence.
Your generosity.
Your Bible knowledge.
Your ability to encourage everyone else.
Perhaps people see strength when they look at you.
But there is something you keep allowing because it looks right in your own eyes.
Nobody sees it.
Yet.
Maybe it is a relationship you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
Maybe it is pornography you promised would be “just one more time.”
Maybe it is resentment you have learned to disguise as discernment.
Maybe it is secret flirting you insist is harmless.
Maybe it is money becoming your real security.
Maybe it is pride hiding underneath ministry.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Maybe it is an addiction.
Maybe you keep asking God to bless something you have never genuinely surrendered to Him.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that your life still appears strong.
Samson was strong too.
That is the warning.
You can possess remarkable gifts while carrying dangerous weaknesses.
You can experience God’s mercy while still needing repentance.
You can know Scripture and still rationalize desire.
You can look powerful publicly while becoming vulnerable privately.
And sometimes the enemy does not need to destroy your strength.
He only needs to convince you that because you are strong in one area, you cannot fall in another.
Samson could tear apart a lion.
But physical strength could not automatically govern his heart.
Imagine that.

A lion comes roaring toward him near the vineyards of Timnah, and the Spirit of the LORD comes powerfully upon Samson. With no weapon in his hands, Samson tears the animal apart. Judges 14 records the extraordinary event plainly.
He could defeat what terrified ordinary men.
Yet the greater battle was always closer.
Inside.
That is where many of us lose.
We are fighting demons “out there” while refusing to confront desires “in here.”
We rebuke darkness but excuse pride.
We quote Scripture publicly and negotiate with temptation privately.
We want victory over circumstances while resisting Christ’s lordship over our appetites.
We want Samson’s strength without Samson’s warning.
But Scripture loves us too much to give us sanitized heroes.
The Bible does not airbrush Samson.
It does not hide Abraham’s fear.
It does not hide Jacob’s deception.
It does not hide David’s adultery.
It does not hide Peter’s denial.
And it does not hide Samson’s appetite.
Why?
Because the Bible is ultimately not the story of impressive human beings rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy and faithful God working through a fallen world while moving history toward the One Savior who does not fail.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where Samson’s story becomes even more powerful.
Samson was a deliverer.
But Samson needed deliverance.
Jesus is different.
Samson was announced before birth as one who would begin Israel’s deliverance from the Philistines.
Jesus came to accomplish the deeper rescue humanity could never accomplish for itself.
Samson’s enemies bound him.
Jesus willingly submitted Himself to arrest.
Samson’s story became entangled with personal vengeance.
Jesus prayed for His executioners.
Samson ultimately died while destroying enemies.
Jesus died to save His enemies.
Samson’s death brought judgment upon Philistine oppressors.
Christ’s death bore judgment for sinners who trust in Him.
Samson stretched out his arms between pillars and died.
Centuries later, outside Jerusalem, Jesus Christ stretched out His arms upon a cross.
But Jesus was not another flawed judge.
He was the sinless Son of God.
The Lamb of God.
The true Savior.
Samson could begin a temporary deliverance.
Jesus could cry:
“It is finished.”
And that is why your scandal does not have to be your final chapter.
Maybe you have made choices because they were right in your own eyes.
Maybe your parents warned you.
Maybe your pastor warned you.
Maybe your spouse pleaded with you.
Maybe Scripture convicted you.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has been pressing the same wound for months.
And you kept saying:
I know.
But I want it.
Perhaps you got what you wanted.
And now you are living with what wanting it cost.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin did not matter.
The Gospel says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace is God offering guilty sinners forgiveness purchased by the blood of His Son.
That means you do not need another excuse.
You need Jesus.
You do not need to convince yourself that everything was “meant to happen.”
You need repentance.
You do not need to rewrite your past until your sin looks innocent.
Bring the truth into the light.
Call sin what God calls it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
Because one of the most beautiful truths in all Scripture is that God does extraordinary things with people whose stories contain chapters they wish they could erase.
Not because scandal becomes righteousness.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because grace is greater than the finality we assign to our failures.
Even Samson’s story did not end in Judges 14.
There would be anger.
Violence.
Loss.
More compromise.
Delilah.
Betrayal.
Chains.
Blindness.
Humiliation.
A man once feared for supernatural strength would eventually be led around by others.
And yet...
even there...
Samson prayed.
At the end of his ruined strength, Samson turned again toward the God who had never ceased to be God.
And centuries later, Hebrews 11 would actually include Samson among people remembered in connection with faith.
What astonishing mercy.
Not a perfect man.
Not an uncomplicated story.
Not a spotless record.
A broken man whose name still appears in the biblical testimony of faith.
That is not permission to imitate Samson’s sins.
It is permission to stop believing that failure places you beyond the reach of God’s mercy.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not because you need to hear that Samson was strong.
You already know that.
Maybe you needed to discover that the strongest man in the room could still desperately need grace.
And so can you.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe your children barely recognize the person you have become.
Maybe lust has eaten years of your spiritual life.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe you returned to the thing Christ delivered you from.
Maybe you feel like a hypocrite walking into church.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well while you are exhausted from maintaining the appearance.
Then stop performing.
Come home.
Jesus already knows the chapter you are hiding.
He saw the decision.
He saw the message.
He saw the browser history.
He heard the lie.
He knows the resentment.
He knows why you did it.
He knows what happened afterward.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up enough so Christ might tolerate you.”
It is:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing.
There is mercy.
There is restoration.
There is a new way to live.
And there is something Samson desperately teaches us:
Do not wait until the pillars are around you to surrender what God is confronting today.
Do not wait until desire becomes bondage.
Do not wait until compromise becomes identity.
Do not wait until secrecy becomes captivity.
Do not wait until you lose something precious before deciding that obedience was precious all along.
Ask yourself the question Samson’s story forces upon us:
What looks right in my eyes right now that I have never honestly placed before the eyes of God?
Stay there for a moment.
What is it?
A person?
A relationship?
A habit?
A secret?
An ambition?
An offense you refuse to forgive?
Something you desperately want God to approve?
You do not have to tell the entire internet what happened.
But you should stop lying to God about it.
Not as a performance.
As a confession.
Let other believers stand with you.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that repentance is not the end of a person’s story.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who looks strong but is quietly losing a battle nobody knows exists.
Not for numbers.
Not for applause.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday’s conviction difficult to remember tomorrow.
Come back when something begins looking “right in your eyes” and ask again whether it is right before God.
Supporting Gospel work can be a genuine way to glorify God when it is done freely, gratefully, wisely, and for the advance of Christ-centered ministry.
It is discipleship.
It is helping truth keep moving.
It is standing behind a mission that wants to put Christ before another exhausted believer at two in the morning...
another marriage hanging by a thread...
another person hiding an addiction...
another Christian drifting into compromise...
another skeptic wondering whether grace could possibly be real...
another Samson who still thinks strength means he cannot fall.

One shared article cannot save anyone—Jesus saves—but God can use a shared truth, a Scripture passage, a testimony, or a faithful invitation to put the Gospel in front of someone at the moment they desperately need to hear it.
Samson wanted what looked right in his own eyes.
His story reminds us how dangerous that can become.
But Samson's failures were never bigger than God's sovereignty.
And your worst chapter is not greater than the grace offered to you in Jesus Christ.
So repent while your heart can still hear the warning.
Return while grace is calling.
Stop defending what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy is not discovering that something you wanted was wrong.
Perhaps it is discovering it was wrong...
and still refusing to let it go.
You may have written a chapter in your life that you would give anything to erase—but at the cross, Jesus proves that your darkest chapter does not have to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Apology You Keep Waiting For May Never Come. What Will You Do With Your Heart Until Then?
paragraphs: The Apology You Keep Waiting For May Never Come. What Will You Do With Your Heart Until Then?

When the person who wounded you refuses to admit what they did, Jesus does not ask you to call evil good. He calls you to place justice in hands strong enough to carry it—so the person who hurt you does not keep owning your heart.
Maybe you have already imagined the conversation.
More times than you would admit.
They finally sit across from you.
Their defenses are gone.
Their voice is different now.
And at last, they say the words you have needed to hear:
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“You didn’t deserve what I did.”
“I lied.”
“I betrayed you.”
“I should have protected you.”
“I should have believed you.”
“I should never have treated you that way.”
“Please forgive me.”
And somewhere inside that imagined moment, something in your chest finally loosens.
Because perhaps you have spent months—or years—believing that healing begins when they finally understand what they did to you.
But what happens if they never do?
What happens if the apology never comes?
What happens if the person who broke something inside you sleeps peacefully while you are still trying to understand how to live with the pieces?
What happens if they rewrite the story?
What happens if they minimize it?
What happens if they blame you?
What happens if they move forward with their life while you are still carrying consequences they helped create?
And what happens if they die without ever saying they were sorry?
That question can feel almost unbearable.
Because unresolved injustice creates a peculiar kind of prison.
The door may be open, but your heart keeps waiting for someone else to walk into the room and unlock it.
This is where the Gospel speaks with startling tenderness—and startling strength.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.’”
The Greek begins with one word that matters more than we sometimes realize:
Ἀγαπητοί — agapētoi.
“Beloved.”
Before Paul speaks about vengeance, he speaks about identity.
Beloved.
Not forgotten.
Not invisible.
Not disposable.
Beloved.
God does not begin His instruction to wounded Christians by scolding them for being hurt.
He addresses them as people who are loved.
Then comes the difficult command:
μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες — mē heautous ekdikountes
Do not avenge yourselves.
And then:
δότε τόπον τῇ ὀργῇ — dote topon tē orgē
Literally, “give place to wrath.”
In context, Paul is telling believers to step away from personal vengeance and leave judgment to God.
Then he reaches back into the Hebrew Scriptures, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35:
לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם — li naqam veshillem
“Vengeance is Mine, and recompense.”
This does not mean God is asking you to pretend nothing happened.
It means something almost frighteningly freeing:
You are not the final court.
You do not have to become the executioner of the person who wounded you in order for their wrong to matter.
God saw it.
God knows it.
And God does not need the offender's cooperation before He can begin healing you.
Read that again.
God does not need their apology before He can begin restoring your heart.
Somebody reading this has spent years emotionally standing beside a mailbox waiting for a letter that may never arrive.
Maybe it was your father.
Your mother.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your ex.
A sibling.
A pastor.
A church leader.
A friend you trusted with things you had never told anyone.
Maybe someone publicly humiliated you and privately acted as though nothing happened.
Maybe somebody betrayed your confidence.
Maybe someone abandoned you when you needed them most.
Maybe they cheated.
Maybe they lied about you.
Maybe they manipulated you and then convinced everyone else that you were the problem.
Maybe you confronted them—and instead of repentance, you received excuses.
Maybe the wound became even deeper because they refused to acknowledge that there was a wound at all.
There are injuries caused by what people do.
And then there are injuries caused by their refusal to admit they did it.
Sometimes the second wound hurts almost as much as the first.
Because an apology says:
I see what happened.
I acknowledge your pain.
I accept responsibility.
And when those words never come, part of us begins screaming:
“Does anybody see this?”
Jesus does.
That changes everything.
But it does not make everything easy.
Christian forgiveness is often spoken about so carelessly that wounded people begin believing Scripture requires them to become emotionally dishonest.
It does not.
Forgiveness does not require calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not require pretending betrayal did not matter.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
Forgiveness does not mean every broken relationship must return to exactly what it was before.
Forgiveness does not require placing yourself back into an unsafe situation merely to prove that you are spiritual.
Scripture itself distinguishes forgiveness from reconciliation.
Romans 12:18 says:
“If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.”
Those words matter:
If possible.
So far as it depends on you.
Reconciliation involves more than one heart.
Trust involves demonstrated faithfulness.
Repentance bears fruit.
Consequences may remain.
Boundaries may remain.
Wisdom may require distance.
You can forgive someone and still recognize that giving them the same access to your life would be foolish.
You can release vengeance without restoring privileges.
You can pray for somebody without pretending they are trustworthy.
You can refuse hatred while refusing manipulation.
You can desire their salvation while recognizing that reconciliation may require repentance and change.
And yes—you can forgive while tears are still running down your face.
Forgiveness is not amnesia.
It is surrendering the throne.
It is saying:
“God, I will not spend the rest of my life trying to become You.”
Because that is what vengeance quietly asks of us.
It asks us to become judge, jury, historian, prosecutor, and executioner.
It asks us to keep reopening the courtroom every night.
It asks us to rehearse the evidence.
Exhibit A.
Exhibit B.
Exhibit C.
Remember what they said?
Remember what they did?
Remember how nobody defended you?
Remember how they got away with it?
Again.
Again.
Again.
And every rehearsal feels as though we are preserving justice.
But sometimes we are only preserving the wound.
There is a difference between remembering what happened wisely and continually drinking from what happened bitterly.
You may have every reason to be angry.
The question is what your anger is becoming.
Paul does not tell believers that evil is imaginary.
Just two verses later, Romans 12:21 says:
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”
Notice the assumption.
Evil exists.
Something really happened.
Something really was wrong.
But now there is another danger.
The evil that happened to you can begin producing evil inside you.
The betrayal can become bitterness.
The injustice can become obsession.
The rejection can become an identity.
The wound can become a permanent address.
And suddenly, someone who may no longer even be present in your life is still determining what kind of person you are becoming.
That is too much power to give them.
Maybe this is where Jesus is meeting you.
Not asking you to deny what happened.
Not asking you to manufacture warm feelings toward someone who devastated you.
Not asking you to pretend justice does not matter.
He is asking you to hand Him the case.
All of it.
The evidence.
The unanswered questions.
The conversations you never got to have.
The confession they never made.
The reputation they damaged.
The years you cannot recover.
The money you lost.
The childhood you should have had.
The marriage you thought would survive.
The friendship you believed would last.
The church experience that left you afraid to trust Christians again.
The words you still hear when the room becomes quiet.
Give Him the case.
Because the hands that were pierced for you are strong enough to hold what happened to you.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from shallow positivity.
The Gospel never says injustice does not matter.
Look at the cross.
The cross tells us sin matters so profoundly that reconciliation with God required something far greater than pretending it never happened.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, bore sin at Calvary.
Justice was not dismissed.
Grace was purchased at immeasurable cost.
Romans 5:8 tells us:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
And now comes the uncomfortable part.
The Gospel does not permit us to divide humanity neatly into innocent people like us and sinners like them.
They sinned against you.
Perhaps terribly.
But you also need grace.
So do I.
We may not have committed their particular sin, and saying that does not minimize what they did.
But before the holiness of God, every one of us stands in desperate need of mercy.
That is why the Christian does not surrender vengeance because evil does not deserve judgment.
We surrender vengeance because judgment belongs ultimately to God.
And because at the cross, we discovered that the Judge we entrust ourselves to is also the Savior who offered mercy to us.
This is scandalous grace.
Jesus does not merely rescue respectable people.
He saves sinners.
Liars can repent.
Adulterers can repent.
Abusers can repent.
The proud can repent.
The bitter can repent.
The people who wounded us can repent.
And wounded people who have begun living from hatred can repent too.
Nobody is beyond the reach of Christ while there is still breath and opportunity to turn to Him.
But grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings sinners out of darkness.
That distinction matters.
The Jesus who said, “Father, forgive them,” while being crucified is the same Jesus Scripture presents as the righteous Judge.
Mercy and justice do not become enemies in Him.
So perhaps the prayer tonight is not:
“Jesus, make me forget.”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, make me free.”
Free from needing their remorse before you can breathe again.
Free from checking whether life has punished them yet.
Free from imaginary arguments in the shower.
Free from stalking their happiness and secretly resenting every photograph where they appear to be doing fine.
Free from hoping their life collapses just so your pain will finally feel validated.
Free from needing everyone to understand your side before you can have peace.
Free from allowing the worst thing somebody did to you to become the central story of who you are.
Because you are more than what happened to you.
If you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not “betrayed.”
Not “abandoned.”
Not “divorced.”
Not “rejected.”
Not “humiliated.”
Not “forgotten.”
Not “the one they hurt.”
In Christ, you are His.
And perhaps that is why Romans begins this painful instruction with:
Ἀγαπητοί.
Beloved.
Before God asks you to release vengeance, He reminds you that you are loved.
Because releasing vengeance without knowing you are loved feels like losing.
But releasing vengeance into the hands of a Father who sees everything is different.
It becomes trust.
Maybe they never say sorry.
God is still God.
Maybe they never admit the truth.
God still knows it.
Maybe people believe their version.
God is not confused.
Maybe earthly justice comes.
Maybe it does not come in the form or timing you hoped for.
God remains righteous.

And none of this means you should remain silent about ongoing harm. Depending on what happened, wisdom may include confronting wrongdoing, seeking pastoral or professional counsel, reporting crimes or abuse to appropriate authorities, establishing boundaries, pursuing lawful justice, or getting somewhere safe.
Romans 12:19 is not a command to protect wrongdoing from consequences.
It is a command not to seize God's place through personal vengeance.
There is a profound difference between seeking legitimate justice and being consumed by revenge.
One says, “This wrong must be addressed appropriately.”
The other says, “I cannot rest until I personally make you hurt.”
Jesus wants more for your heart than that prison.
And perhaps the most difficult realization is this:
The apology you keep waiting for may never come.
But Jesus already came.
The person who wounded you may never kneel before you in repentance.
But Christ already carried a cross for sinners.
They may never give you the words you thought you needed in order to move forward.
But Christ can meet you in the place those words never reached.
He can heal without rewriting history.
He can restore without pretending.
He can soften your heart without making you naive.
He can teach you forgiveness without destroying your boundaries.
He can remove hatred without requiring foolish trust.
He can give you peace while the unanswered questions remain unanswered.
That is the miracle.
Not that the past suddenly becomes acceptable.
But that the past stops being your master.
There comes a moment when you realize healing is not getting the person who wounded you to finally become the person you needed them to be.
Healing is discovering that Jesus is sufficient even where they failed you.
Maybe your hands have been clenched around this story for years.
Maybe nobody knows how angry you still are.
Maybe you smile when their name is mentioned, but something inside you turns cold.
Maybe you have prayed about it before and then picked the case right back up.
Bring it again.
Jesus is not intimidated by how many times you have struggled to release it.
Tell Him the truth.
“Lord, what they did was wrong.”
“Lord, I still want them to admit it.”
“Lord, part of me still wants them to hurt.”
“Lord, I do not know how to forgive this.”
“Lord, I am tired.”
“Lord, judge rightly.”
“Lord, protect me from becoming what pain is trying to turn me into.”
“Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
And surrender is sometimes where healing finally stops waiting for permission from the person who caused the wound.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
You do not have to pretend to be farther along than you are.
Not as a performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
But if this truth can reach one wounded person through you, sharing becomes a simple act of service.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's blessing, prove your devotion, or make you more righteous. Jesus alone saves, and His grace cannot be bought.
But one genuine way believers can glorify God is by willingly supporting faithful Gospel work and helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it.
But before you leave this page, there is one more question.
Not for the person who hurt you.
For you.
If the apology never comes...
will you allow their silence to decide how the rest of your heart lives?
Or will you place the case into the scarred hands of Jesus and finally let the Judge be Judge, the Savior be Savior, and your wounded heart begin learning how to live again?
The scandal may be part of your history.
It does not have to become your identity.
Because Jesus still redeems what people thought they permanently ruined.
You may never hear them say, “I’m sorry”—but you can still live long enough to hear your own heart say, “Jesus, I’m finally letting You carry this.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A ROMAN CENTURION TOLD JESUS, “YOU DON’T EVEN NEED TO ENTER MY HOUSE.”
paragraphs:
A ROMAN CENTURION TOLD JESUS, “YOU DON’T EVEN NEED TO ENTER MY HOUSE.”
He had soldiers who obeyed his commands, influence in the city, and enough respect that Jewish elders spoke on his behalf. But when someone he loved was dying, this powerful Roman officer discovered that there are battles human authority cannot win—and then he said something about Jesus that made Christ marvel.
There was a man lying inside a house in Capernaum who could not get up.
Outside that house stood a Roman officer accustomed to giving orders.
Inside it lay someone he could not command back to health.
And somewhere between those two realities, one of the most remarkable confessions of faith recorded in the Gospels was born:
Jesus did not even have to enter the house.
Think about that.
The centurion did not ask Jesus to perform a ceremony.
He did not demand a sign.
He did not tell Christ exactly how the miracle needed to happen.
He did not say, “Jesus, if You really have power, prove it by coming here.”
His faith reached a startling conclusion:
If Jesus has authority, distance is irrelevant.
And perhaps that is exactly where this story finds you.
Because eventually almost everyone discovers something they cannot command.
You can command employees and still not command peace into your marriage.
You can manage a company and still be unable to make your child come home.
You can organize everybody else's problems and lie awake helpless before your own.
You can have money and discover there are things money cannot purchase.
You can have followers and still feel unbearably alone.
You can smile for the photograph while privately carrying something that terrifies you.
You can even know Scripture, attend church, sing worship songs, and still find yourself staring at a situation you cannot fix.
That is where the centurion stood.
Matthew tells us that when Jesus entered Capernaum, a ἑκατόνταρχος — hekatontarchos, a centurion, appealed to Him.
This was not an insignificant man.
A centurion was a military officer accustomed to authority. He understood commands. He understood rank. He understood what happened when someone with legitimate authority spoke.
Yet Matthew 8:6 records him coming to Jesus concerning his παῖς — pais, his servant, lying at home paralyzed and suffering terribly.
Luke gives us another angle on the same encounter.
Luke 7 calls the servant a δοῦλος — doulos, a slave or bondservant, and says that he was ἔντιμος — entimos to the centurion: valued, honored, precious to him.
This matters.
The powerful man was pleading for someone beneath him socially.
And suddenly the uniform seems less important.
The rank fades.
The military authority becomes irrelevant.
Because suffering has a way of stripping away the illusion that control makes us invincible.
Maybe you already know that.
Maybe you learned it beside a hospital bed.
Maybe you learned it when somebody walked away.
Maybe you learned it when the diagnosis arrived.
Maybe you learned it when the addiction returned.
Maybe you learned it when the money disappeared.
Maybe you learned it at 2:13 in the morning when everyone else was asleep and you finally admitted:
“God, I cannot fix this.”
There are moments when all your accomplishments stand outside a locked door and cannot enter.
The centurion had reached one of those doors.
And then he heard about Jesus.

Luke tells us that Jewish elders approached Christ on the centurion's behalf. They pleaded earnestly and argued that the officer deserved Jesus' help because he loved their nation and had helped provide their synagogue.
Notice their language.
He is worthy.
Then listen to the centurion's language.
I am not worthy.
That contrast is almost impossible to miss.
Other people were presenting his résumé.
He was confessing his insufficiency.
They were talking about what he had done.
He was looking at who Jesus was.
That is where grace begins to become beautiful.
Religion is constantly tempted to approach God carrying a résumé.
“I have been good.”
“I helped people.”
“I gave money.”
“I went to church.”
“I never did what those people did.”
“I deserve this.”
Grace drops the résumé.
Grace realizes that Jesus is not our debtor.
The centurion had done admirable things, yet when Christ approached, he did not hide behind them.
Luke records his message:
Κύριε, μὴ σκύλλου· οὐ γὰρ ἱκανός εἰμι…
“Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy…”
And Matthew preserves the heart of his confession:
μόνον εἰπὲ λόγῳ
“Only speak a word.”
Only speak.
A word.
That was enough.
He understood something many people who had spent their entire lives surrounded by religious privilege had failed to understand.
Jesus possessed authority unlike anyone else.
The centurion explained it using the world he knew.
He essentially said:
I understand authority.
I am a man under authority, and soldiers are under me.
I tell one man, “Go,” and he goes.
I tell another, “Come,” and he comes.
I tell my servant, “Do this,” and he does it.
Therefore…
Jesus, if sickness is under Your authority, You do not need to walk into my house.
You only need to speak.
Do you see it?
He was not merely believing Jesus had healing ability.
He recognized authority.
That distinction changes the entire scene.
Jesus was not a wandering miracle worker whom the centurion hoped might possess enough spiritual power to defeat the illness.
The centurion saw a King.
And kings do not negotiate with subjects.
They command.
This Roman officer knew what an authoritative word could accomplish because every day men moved when he spoke.
But now he stood before Someone whose authority reached where Rome's authority stopped.
Rome could command soldiers.
Jesus could command disease.
Rome could occupy territory.
Jesus possessed authority over creation.
Rome could place guards at a tomb.
It would eventually discover that even a sealed tomb could not imprison the Son of God.
The centurion saw enough to say:
Just speak.
And Matthew tells us something extraordinary happened.
Jesus marveled.
The Greek verb is ἐθαύμασεν — ethaumasen.
He marveled.
The centurion came amazed by Christ's authority, and Christ publicly marveled at the centurion's faith.
Jesus turned to those following Him and declared that He had not found faith like this in Israel.
Pause there.
A Gentile.
A Roman officer.
A man belonging to the machinery of an occupying power.
Not one of the Twelve.
Not a rabbi.
Not someone whose background would have made him the obvious hero of a Jewish religious story.
Yet Jesus held his faith before the crowd.
That is scandalous grace.
And then Christ widened the horizon even further.
Matthew records Jesus saying that many would come from east and west and recline at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.
The kingdom would not be possessed through ancestry, proximity to religion, or outward privilege.
People would come from places the crowd never expected.
Outsiders would be welcomed.
And the warning running through Christ's words is equally serious: being close to religious things is not the same as belonging to Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Jesus.
You can own a Bible and never surrender.
You can sing about grace while secretly trusting your goodness.
You can sit in church while your heart remains miles away.
You can know how Christians are supposed to look and still never come to the place where the centurion came:
“Lord… I am not worthy.”
That confession does not end in despair when it is spoken before Jesus.
It becomes the doorway to grace.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that worthy people finally found God.
It is the announcement that God came for sinners.
Jesus Christ came into this world not merely to improve respectable people but to save the lost.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly toward the cross.
There the sinless Son of God bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The deepest human problem is therefore greater than the illness inside the centurion's house.
Our greatest problem is sin and separation from God.
And our greatest need is not merely for Jesus to repair our circumstances.
We need Jesus to reconcile us to God.
Sometimes Christ changes the circumstance.
Sometimes He carries us through it.
Sometimes prayers for physical healing are answered in ways that leave us stunned with gratitude.
Sometimes faithful believers continue suffering while trusting God.
This passage must never be twisted into the cruel idea that anyone who remains sick simply “didn't have enough faith.”
The centurion's story teaches us the authority of Christ; it does not give us permission to turn faith into a formula by which we control Him.
Biblical faith does not say:
“If I believe intensely enough, God must obey me.”
Biblical faith says:
“Jesus is Lord. I trust Him.”
There is an enormous difference.
The centurion did not place Jesus beneath his authority.
He placed himself beneath Jesus'.
Maybe that is the sentence someone reading this desperately needs.
Faith is not getting Jesus under your authority.
Faith is discovering the peace of coming under His.
And there may be something in your life right now that you desperately wish Jesus would change.
A child you have been praying for.
A marriage hanging by threads.
A body that hurts.
A secret addiction.
A grief you cannot explain to people anymore because you are tired of hearing yourself explain it.
A private sin hidden beneath a public Christian appearance.
A fear you cannot silence.
A person you cannot rescue.
A prayer that seems to have traveled upward and disappeared.
You keep thinking:
“If Jesus would just come into this situation…”
But the centurion reminds us that Christ does not cease to be Lord because you cannot see what He is doing.
Jesus did not need to stand inside that house to possess authority over what was happening inside it.
And Jesus does not have to fit inside your understanding before He can be trusted.
That does not mean pretending pain does not hurt.
Christian faith is not emotional denial.
Sometimes faith cries.
Sometimes faith trembles.
Sometimes faith says, like another desperate man in the Gospels, “I believe; help my unbelief.”
Faith can have tears in its eyes.
Faith can whisper.
Faith can crawl.
Faith can arrive exhausted.
But faith still reaches toward Christ.
And perhaps that is what you need to do now.
Not perform.
Not impress Him.
Not pretend.
Come.
Tell Him what hurts.
Tell Him what you have hidden.
Tell Him where you sinned.
Tell Him where you are afraid.
Tell Him where you stopped trusting.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask forgiveness where you have sinned.
Stop defending what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy that forgives and begins transforming sinners who come to Christ.
This is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the story of the outsider.
He rewrites the story of the ashamed.
He rewrites the story of the sinner.
He rewrites the story of the person everybody else has already categorized.
He rewrites the story of the one who finally realizes, “I cannot save myself.”
At the cross, scandal and grace collide.
Our sin is exposed as worse than our excuses admit.
God's mercy is revealed as greater than our shame imagined.
And resurrection announces that Jesus is not merely someone who once spoke healing into a house in Capernaum.
Jesus Christ is alive.
So perhaps the question this ancient Roman officer leaves in your hands is not simply:
“Do I believe Jesus can give me what I want?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
Do I recognize who Jesus is?
The centurion did.
And Jesus answered him.
Matthew says Christ told him to go, and that it would be done according to his faith.
His servant was healed.
Luke says those who returned to the house found the servant well.
Imagine that walk back.
Imagine approaching the doorway.
Imagine wondering whether the word spoken at a distance had reached the room.
Then the door opens.
The servant is alive.
Well.
The centurion had been right about one thing:
Jesus never needed to enter the house.
His authority was already there.
And maybe tonight you need to stop measuring Christ's nearness only by what your eyes can see.
Maybe you cannot see the answer yet.
Maybe the room still feels silent.
Maybe the prodigal is still gone.
Maybe the test results still frighten you.
Maybe the relationship remains fractured.
Maybe grief still sits beside you at dinner.
But do not confuse an unanswered question with an absent Christ.
Bring your need to Him.
And above all, bring yourself.
Because even if every earthly problem disappeared tomorrow, you would still need a Savior.
Jesus did not ultimately come merely to give us easier lives.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
And the same Jesus who possessed authority over sickness walked willingly toward a cross where men appeared to have authority over Him.
Soldiers mocked Him.
Soldiers struck Him.
Soldiers crucified Him.
And yet Scripture reveals something breathtaking:
They were not taking His life from Him as though He were powerless.
He laid it down.
The Commander of heaven submitted Himself to death.
The One who could speak healing with a word remained on the cross.
Why?
For sinners.
For rebels.
For outsiders.
For religious hypocrites.
For people carrying shame.
For people who have ruined things.
For people whose private lives would scandalize everyone who admires their public lives.
For people like us.
Then death met an authority it could not overthrow.
Jesus rose.
And that is why Christianity does not ultimately tell you to believe harder in yourself.
It tells you to repent and believe in Christ.
Talk to Jesus.
And believers reading those words—do not turn somebody's vulnerability into entertainment.
Pray for them.
Let the comments beneath this article become something rarer than another internet argument.
Let them become a place where people remember they are not fighting alone.

Supporting Gospel ministry can be one practical way to steward what God has entrusted to us, but our support must always flow from grace, never as payment for grace. God's glory cannot be purchased, and salvation cannot be bought.
And beyond supporting the work, stay because you want to keep growing.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the believer who is tired.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Invite the Christian who has become comfortable around Jesus but has forgotten how astonishing He is.
But before you leave, remember the house in Capernaum.
A suffering servant was inside.
A powerful officer stood outside unable to fix him.
Jesus was still some distance away.
And yet one sentence from Christ was enough.
The centurion understood what desperation had finally taught him:
There are places your strength cannot reach.
There are wounds your money cannot heal.
There are battles your reputation cannot win.
There are sins your good deeds cannot erase.
There is a death you cannot defeat.
But there is a Savior whose authority reaches farther than your hands ever could.
So when your strength finally runs out…
when the door stays closed…
when the room is beyond your reach…
when all you have left is Jesus…
remember:
The house was beyond the centurion's reach—but it was never beyond Christ's authority.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JEREMIAH NEVER MARRY? God Gave Him a Command Most Prophets Never Received
paragraphs: WHY DID JEREMIAH NEVER MARRY? God Gave Him a Command Most Prophets Never Received

One sentence from God changed Jeremiah’s future—and behind that painful command is a warning about judgment, a revelation about obedience, and a breathtaking reminder that when everything seems to be ending, God is still writing redemption.
There are commands from God that change what you do.
Then there are commands that seem to change the life you thought you were going to have.
Jeremiah received one of those.

Imagine being a young man carrying the Word of God to a nation that does not want to hear it. Imagine being mocked because you tell the truth. Imagine watching the people you love keep walking toward destruction while accusing you of being the problem for warning them.
And then imagine hearing God tell you something deeply personal.
Not about your sermon.
Not about the king.
Not about Babylon.
About your own home.
Your own future.
Your own possibility of holding a wife in your arms and hearing children running through your house.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 16:2 is startlingly direct:
לֹא־תִקַּח לְךָ אִשָּׁה וְלֹא־יִהְיוּ לְךָ בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה
Lo tiqqaḥ lekha ishah, velo yihyu lekha banim uvanot bammaqom hazzeh.
A close translation is:
“You shall not take for yourself a wife, and you shall not have sons and daughters in this place.”
Jeremiah 16:2.
Read it again.
God was not merely telling Jeremiah where to preach.
God was touching the prophet’s personal future.
And before going any further, we need to be careful with Scripture.

The Bible explicitly tells us that Jeremiah was commanded not to take a wife or have sons and daughters “in this place.” It does not give us a later account of Jeremiah marrying, and he is ordinarily understood from the biblical record as unmarried during the ministry described to us. But Scripture does not explicitly give us the sentence, “Jeremiah never married at any point until the day he died.”
That distinction matters.
We should never make the Bible say more than God chose to say.
But what God did say is already devastating enough.
Because immediately after the command, God explained why.

The children born in that land, and the mothers and fathers who bore them, were approaching catastrophe. Jeremiah 16:3–4 describes coming death through disease, sword, and famine. The judgment descending upon Judah would be so severe that ordinary mourning and burial would collapse under the weight of disaster.
Jeremiah’s unmarried life was therefore not presented as punishment for being defective, undesirable, unspiritual, or incapable of love.
It became a living sign.
His empty nursery preached.
His absent wedding feast preached.
The family he was commanded not to establish in that place preached.
Every time somebody could have asked, “Jeremiah, when are you going to settle down?”
his life itself carried an answer:
Judgment is coming.
That is what makes this passage so uncomfortable.
We often imagine prophetic ministry as standing before crowds and speaking mighty words.
But sometimes the message cost the messenger something before it ever cost the audience anything.
Jeremiah did not merely announce the warning.
In a profound sense, he had to live inside it.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe you have obeyed God and still lost something.
Maybe you thought obedience would immediately make life easier.
Maybe you prayed.
You waited.
You tried to remain faithful.
You watched somebody else receive what you begged God for.
They got married.
They had the child.
They received the opportunity.
Their ministry grew.
Their family reconciled.
Their prayer seemed to receive an answer while yours seemed to disappear into heaven without an echo.
And somewhere beneath all your Christian vocabulary is a question you are almost afraid to say aloud:
“Jesus, if I belong to You, why does obedience sometimes hurt this much?”
Jeremiah would understand the question.
But Jeremiah’s story also warns us against a dangerous conclusion.
Pain is not proof that God has abandoned you.
And sacrifice is not a currency by which we purchase His love.
The Gospel destroys that idea.
We do not suffer enough to make God love us.
We do not obey enough to make Christ save us.
We do not become worthy enough to earn grace.
At the center of Christianity is not a human being desperately climbing toward God.
At the center is God coming down to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ entered our world.
He lived without sin.
He willingly went to the cross.
He bore judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Jeremiah carried a warning of judgment.
Jesus carried judgment itself for His people.
That is where the road eventually leads.
To Christ.
Always to Christ.
And there is another detail in Jeremiah 16 that makes the chapter even more extraordinary.
God did not stop with destruction.
After announcing terrible judgment and exile, He also spoke about restoration.

Jeremiah 16:14–15 says that days were coming when Israel’s deliverance would be remembered in terms so dramatic that the return God would accomplish would stand beside the memory of the exodus from Egypt.
Think about that.
The same chapter containing:
“You shall not take for yourself a wife…”
also contains:
“I will bring them back.”
That is the heartbeat many people miss.
Judgment was real.
Sin was serious.
Consequences were coming.
But judgment was not evidence that God had forgotten His covenant purposes.
God was still writing.
And that is why Jeremiah’s story belongs so naturally beside the Gospel.
Not because Jeremiah was Jesus.
He was not.
Not because every detail of Jeremiah’s singleness secretly predicts Christ.
Scripture does not require us to make that claim.
But Jeremiah’s ministry forces us to confront realities that find their ultimate answer in Christ:
Sin is serious.
Judgment is real.
Obedience can be costly.
Human rebellion destroys.
God keeps His word.
And mercy is far greater than rebellious people deserve.
Jeremiah knew rejection.
Jesus was rejected.
Jeremiah wept over a rebellious people.
Jesus wept over Jerusalem.
Jeremiah proclaimed coming judgment.
Jesus warned of judgment while offering Himself as the Savior of sinners.
And at Calvary, something happened infinitely greater than Jeremiah could accomplish.
The innocent Son of God gave Himself for the guilty.
That is scandalous grace.
The holy One for sinners.
The righteous One for rebels.
The beloved Son bearing the curse.
The King wearing thorns.
The hands that could have judged the world stretched across wood.
The mouth that spoke creation into existence saying:
“It is finished.”
The Greek of John 19:30 gives us one unforgettable word:
τετέλεσται — tetelestai.
“It has been finished.”
Not “I tried.”
Not “Do the rest yourself.”
Not “Become worthy and perhaps God will accept you.”
Finished.
Christ’s saving work is not an invitation to decorate our old rebellion with religious language.
It is a call to repent and believe.
Grace does not tell us sin does not matter.
Grace tells us sin mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishing that sinners who come to Him can be forgiven.
Maybe that is why Jeremiah’s command reaches deeper than an interesting Bible question.
Because eventually this stops being about whether Jeremiah had a wedding.
It becomes about whether we trust God when following Him costs us the future we imagined.
There are people reading this who are carrying an invisible funeral for a life that never happened.
The marriage that ended.
The relationship that never became what you hoped.
The child you prayed for.
The door that closed.
The years you cannot recover.
The betrayal nobody knows still hurts.
The ministry opportunity that disappeared.
The person you begged God to change.
The version of yourself you thought you would be by now.
You still go to church.
You still know the verses.
You still say, “God is good.”
But there are nights when your soul whispers:
“Then why did He allow this?”
Jeremiah does not give us permission to invent easy answers to every tragedy.
Neither should anyone else.
Not every loss means God specifically commanded that loss as He specifically commanded Jeremiah not to marry in Jeremiah 16.
Please do not misuse his story that way.
Someone else's heartbreak should never become an opportunity for Christians to casually announce, “God took that from you for a reason,” when God has not revealed such a reason.
Sometimes faith means refusing to invent explanations God has not given.
But biblical faith can say something stronger.
Even when you do not know why, you can know Who.
Christ has not changed.
His cross has not changed.
His resurrection has not changed.
His promise to receive those who come to Him has not changed.
Your unanswered question does not make Jesus less risen.
Your tears do not erase the empty tomb.
Your disappointment does not cancel the Gospel.
And your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
That belongs to God.
Maybe you have a scandal in your story.
Something you did.
Something done to you.
Something you would erase if heaven gave you an eraser.
Maybe people know.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your Facebook photographs look peaceful while your private life feels like a war zone.
Maybe you have become exceptionally good at saying “I’m blessed” while quietly bleeding.
But hear this carefully:
Jesus Christ did not come only for people with respectable histories.
He came for sinners.
He came calling people to repentance.
He came bringing forgiveness.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He came to make dead people alive.
You do not need better camouflage.
You need Christ.
You do not need another religious mask.
You need Christ.
You do not need to convince everybody that you have never fallen.
You need the Savior who died for sinners and rose victorious over death.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the version of you that nobody on social media sees.
Repentance is not pretending the darkness never existed.
Repentance turns from sin toward the God whose mercy is found in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs permission to stop pretending tonight.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop defending the darkness.
You do not have to publish your entire story.
God already knows it.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that Christians are not a museum of people who never broke.
We are people desperately dependent upon the grace of Jesus Christ.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not merchandise.

If you want to glorify God through what you do online, one meaningful way is to use the reach He has entrusted to you to point people toward Christ. That may include sharing biblical truth, encouraging struggling believers, and supporting ministries you prayerfully believe are faithfully serving the Gospel.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the believer who feels spiritually numb.
Invite the person who has not yet believed.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
And you cannot buy your way into His kingdom.
We support Christian work because grace has already been freely given—not because money purchases grace.
The greatest response to Jeremiah 16 is not clicking anything.
It is asking:
Do I belong to Jesus Christ?
Have I repented?
Am I trusting Christ—or merely Christian culture?
Have I surrendered my life to Him, or have I simply learned how to appear religious?
Because one day every Facebook post will disappear.
Every platform will become obsolete.
Every follower count will become irrelevant.
Every possession will belong to somebody else.
Every applause will become silent.
But Christ will still be King.
Jeremiah lived during a generation that believed normal life would continue while judgment approached.
People still married.
Families still made plans.
Life still looked like life.
And standing among them was one lonely prophet whose very household—or lack of one—was screaming:
Do not mistake normality for safety.
That warning still deserves to disturb us.
You can have plans and still need Christ.
You can have a family and still need Christ.
You can have a ministry and still need Christ.
You can quote Scripture and still need Christ.
You can look successful and still need Christ.
You can have thousands of followers and still stand before God with nothing capable of saving you except the mercy found in His Son.
So do not waste the discomfort of Jeremiah’s story.
Let it ask you the question we spend our lives avoiding:
If following God costs more than you expected, is Jesus still worth everything to you?
For Jeremiah, obedience entered the rooms nobody else could see.
And for us, genuine discipleship eventually does the same.
Jesus does not merely want the polished Sunday version of you.
He calls you entirely.
Your public life.
Your private life.
Your plans.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your future.
Your repentance.
Your surrender.
And here is the wonder at the center of everything:
The God who sees the ugliest chapter is still able to write redemption.
Peter denied Christ.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted believers.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply sinful pasts.
Yet the New Testament does not end with human scandal having the final word.
Grace does.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that celebrates rebellion.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that calls sinners out of darkness.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace that makes enemies children.
Grace purchased at a cross we could never deserve and vindicated by a resurrection we could never accomplish.
Maybe your life does not look like what you imagined.
Jeremiah's certainly did not.
But the question is not whether every dream came true.
The question is whether Christ has become more precious than the dream.
And maybe tonight, somewhere between Jeremiah’s empty house and Christ’s empty tomb, you finally understand:
An empty place does not always mean an absent God.
Sometimes the place that hurts most becomes the place where you discover that when everything else can be taken away, Jesus is still enough.
If this reached somewhere deeper than you expected, do not rush past it.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Ask for help where you are weak.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to Christian fellowship.
Most importantly, return your eyes to Jesus.
Then save these words.
Share them.
“I’m still fighting.”
Or:
“Pray for me.”
Or, if grace has found you in a chapter you thought could never be redeemed:
“Jesus is still rewriting my story.”
Because perhaps someone scrolling tonight is one testimony away from realizing they do not have to keep running from Christ.
Jeremiah reminds us that obedience can cost something.
Calvary reminds us that our salvation cost Christ everything.
And the empty tomb reminds us that when human beings think the story is over, God is not finished.
The chapter you wanted to hide may become the very place where people see what the grace of Jesus Christ can do.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY MOSES TOOK HIS WIFE AND SONS BACK TO MIDIAN
paragraphs: WHY MOSES TOOK HIS WIFE AND SONS BACK TO MIDIAN
The Family Moses Brought Toward Egypt Suddenly Disappears From the Story—And One Hebrew Phrase Reveals a Painful Chapter the Bible Never Fully Explains
There is a moment in the life of Moses that most people read straight past.
God had called him from the burning bush.
Egypt was waiting.
Pharaoh was waiting.
Israel was groaning.
History was about to split open beneath the footsteps of one reluctant shepherd carrying the command of God.
And Moses did not initially leave Midian alone.
Exodus says:
