That question exposes something in all of us.
Because sin loves turning covenant into entitlement.
We read about the responsibility of another person and immediately start making a list.
What she owes me.
What he owes me.
What I deserve.
What I am not receiving.
But grace turns the mirror around.
How am I loving?
How am I serving?
How am I listening?
How am I protecting the person who trusted me with the most vulnerable parts of his or her life?
How am I becoming more like Jesus inside the place where nobody else sees me?
That is where this passage stops being an argument about somebody else's body and becomes an examination of your own heart.
Marriage in Scripture is extraordinarily intimate.
Genesis speaks of husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
Jesus Himself repeats that language when speaking about marriage.
Paul later employs marriage as an image pointing beyond itself toward Christ and His church.
Christian marriage, therefore, is not merely a contractual arrangement between two consumers trying to extract maximum personal satisfaction from one another.
It is covenant.
And covenant says something radically different from selfishness.
Selfishness asks, “What can I take?”
Covenant asks, “How can I faithfully give?”
Selfishness keeps score.
Covenant remembers promises.
Lust reduces another person to a body.
Love remembers that there is a soul living inside that body.
That distinction matters.
Deeply.
Because there may be someone reading this who has spent years believing that Scripture justified something that wounded them.
Perhaps somebody quoted a verse while ignoring everything around it.
Perhaps biblical language was used to silence your fear, pain, exhaustion, illness, trauma, or distress.
If that happened, twisting Scripture does not make the twisting holy.
A wedding vow does not transform cruelty into Christlikeness.
Paul's language about mutual marital responsibility cannot responsibly be separated from the New Testament's commands to love, honor, gentleness, self-control, and self-giving care.
Marriage does involve profound mutual obligations.
But obligation is not the same thing as permission to become cruel.
Mutuality is not domination.
Covenant is not exploitation.
And Christlike love never gives us permission to stop seeing the person standing in front of us as someone made in the image of God.
There is another side of this passage we should not hide, either.
Sometimes modern readers become so concerned about correcting abusive interpretations that they erase Paul's actual challenge altogether.
Paul really does teach mutual marital responsibility.
He does not present marriage as two completely independent lives occasionally intersecting when convenient.
Marriage involves giving yourself.
It involves sacrifice.
It involves learning that your preferences are no longer the only preferences in the room.
That truth confronts husbands.
And wives.
Sometimes intimacy becomes a battlefield not because someone is being harmed, but because resentment has been allowed to grow.
Weeks become months.
Nobody talks.
Nobody apologizes.
Nobody reaches.
The bed becomes cold long before the marriage officially does.
One spouse waits for the other to move first.
Pride whispers:
“Let them suffer.”
And suddenly physical distance is only the visible symptom of a much deeper spiritual distance.
That is also something Paul's words can confront.
Not with coercion.
With reconciliation.
Not with demands.
With conversation.
Not with humiliation.
With tenderness.
Not with “Give me what I deserve.”
But with:
“What happened to us?”
That may be one of the hardest questions two people ever ask.
Because sometimes the answer is exhaustion.
Sometimes childbirth.
Sometimes illness.
Sometimes grief.
Sometimes unresolved conflict.
Sometimes betrayal.
Sometimes pornography.
Sometimes insecurity.
Sometimes years of feeling unseen.
Sometimes wounds nobody knew how to name.
And sometimes both people are lying inches apart while emotionally living a thousand miles away.
That is when Christians need more than a weaponized verse.
They need truth.
They need repentance.
They need forgiveness.
They may need wise pastoral help.
In serious situations they may need qualified professional help.
And above everything, they need Jesus.
Because Jesus does something human pride cannot do.
He brings dead things back to life.
Maybe your marriage does not need another winner.
Maybe it needs two people willing to kneel.
Maybe the breakthrough begins when somebody finally stops saying:
“You need to change.”
And whispers:
“Lord, begin with me.”
That prayer is terrifying.
Because Jesus has a habit of answering it.
He exposes pride.
He uncovers hidden resentment.
He confronts secret lust.
He reaches into the places where we have carefully preserved our excuses.
But He does not expose us merely to humiliate us.
He exposes what is killing us so grace can begin healing what we kept hiding.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the story of good people successfully keeping themselves clean.
It is the story of sinners meeting a Savior.
It is Peter after denial.
Thomas after doubt.
The woman caught in public disgrace.
A thief dying beside Jesus with nothing left to offer.
It is scandal colliding with mercy.
Sin meeting holiness.
Guilt meeting a cross.
Death meeting an empty tomb.
And sinners discovering that the final sentence over their lives does not have to be written by their worst chapter.
Jesus rewrites everything.
That includes marriage.
That includes sexuality.
That includes shame.
That includes the memories you wish you could erase.
That includes the years you wasted.
That includes what happened behind closed doors.
That includes what you did.
And it includes what was done to you.
The Gospel never asks us to pretend sin did not matter.
The cross proves exactly how seriously God takes sin.
But the resurrection proves sin does not get the final word over everyone who comes to Christ.
Maybe you have failed your spouse.
Repent.
Not theatrically.
Not with another promise you will forget next Tuesday.
Repent honestly.
Confess what needs confessing.
Ask forgiveness without demanding immediate restoration of trust.
Accept that forgiveness and rebuilt trust are related but not identical processes.
Become faithful when nobody applauds you.
Maybe you have used Scripture to win arguments instead of becoming like Christ.
Repent.
Maybe you have withheld affection to punish.
Repent.
Maybe pornography has quietly discipled your expectations more than Scripture has.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe resentment has been sleeping beside you every night.
Name it.
Maybe you have become so accustomed to surviving that you no longer remember how to be vulnerable.
Tell the truth.

And if you are reading this while carrying abuse, coercion, threats, or fear, understand this clearly: Christian teaching about marriage must never be twisted into an instruction to silently endure violence or sexual coercion. Seek safety and trustworthy help. Scripture does not make another person's sin holy simply because that person is your spouse.
Now read Paul's words again.
The wife…
and likewise the husband.
One another.
Mutual agreement.
Paul's language keeps pulling us away from selfish power and back toward reciprocal covenant responsibility.
And beneath all of it stands something even bigger.
For the Christian, our bodies ultimately belong to God.

Only a few verses earlier, in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, Paul reminds believers that they are not ultimately autonomous possessions unto themselves; they were “bought with a price,” and therefore are called to glorify God with their bodies.
Before your body becomes a question about what your husband wants…
before it becomes a question about what your wife wants…
there is a deeper question:
What would glorify Christ?
That question changes bedrooms.
It changes arguments.
It changes apologies.
It changes the way a husband looks at his wife.
It changes the way a wife looks at her husband.
Because suddenly the person beside you is no longer merely the person from whom you want something.
This is someone Christ commands you to love.
Someone with fears.
Someone with history.
Someone with wounds.
Someone with weaknesses.
Someone who may be fighting battles you stopped asking about.
Someone who will one day stand before God just as you will.
And perhaps tonight the most spiritual thing you can do is not quote another verse at them.
Perhaps it is to listen.
Perhaps it is to apologize.
Perhaps it is to pray together after months of avoiding it.
Perhaps it is to say:
“I have been selfish.”
“I haven't been listening.”
“I miss us.”
“I need help.”
“Will you forgive me?”
“Can we begin again?”
There are moments when heaven seems to enter a home through sentences that small.
Because grace often begins where pretending ends.
And maybe that is why you found this article.
Not so you could send it to your spouse and say, “See? I was right.”
Please don't waste it like that.
Let the Word examine you first.

And if God has already restored something in your marriage that once looked impossible, tell that testimony too. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that broken chapters do not always become final chapters.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because there are truths we need to return to when emotion gets loud.
A share may seem tiny, but truth travels through ordinary people willing to carry it.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, helping you understand Scripture in context, calling you toward repentance, or pointing you back to Jesus, consider following and supporting this ministry so this work can continue reaching people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.

Supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of generosity, but it should never be manipulated out of you. Scripture says giving should not be done “reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is simply one voluntary way you can help this particular ministry keep writing, teaching, creating, reaching, and expanding.
If you choose to make Gospel Warrior part of your regular Christian giving, let it come from conviction and generosity before God—not pressure.
And there is much more than one article waiting for you.
Because somebody you know may be smiling publicly while their marriage is bleeding privately.
Somebody may have had Scripture weaponized against them.
Somebody may be one honest conversation away from repentance.
Somebody may be one prayer away from finally asking for help.
Somebody may need to discover that Jesus did not come merely to help us win arguments.
He came to save sinners.
So before you use Paul's words to claim another person's body, remember the body of Christ.
Pierced.
Wounded.
Given.
A Savior who did not conquer His Bride by crushing her, but loved His people at the cost of Himself.
And perhaps that is the image Christian husbands and wives most desperately need to recover.
Not entitlement.
Not domination.
Not scorekeeping.
Christ.
Because when Jesus becomes the center, the question slowly changes from “What does my spouse owe me?” into something infinitely more difficult and infinitely more beautiful:
“How can my life look more like His?”
And when grace finally enters the room, even the chapter you thought would destroy everything may become the place where Christ begins writing something new.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your marriage's final sentence when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE HEART IS DECEITFUL ABOVE ALL THINGS” — BUT JEREMIAH 17:9 IS ONLY PART OF THE MESSAGE
paragraphs: “THE HEART IS DECEITFUL ABOVE ALL THINGS” — BUT JEREMIAH 17:9 IS ONLY PART OF THE MESSAGE

You have probably heard this verse used to tell you never to trust your heart. But keep reading. The next words reveal who can search the heart no human being can fully understand—and a few verses later, Jeremiah cries out for the only healing deep enough to reach it.
There are Bible verses we quote so often that eventually we stop hearing them.
They become captions.
Church phrases.
Words printed across coffee mugs, devotionals, T-shirts, and social media graphics.
And somewhere between memorizing the verse and repeating it, we can accidentally stop asking what God was actually saying.
Jeremiah 17:9 may be one of those verses.
“The heart is deceitful above all things…”
You have probably heard it.
Maybe you have quoted it.
Maybe somebody quoted it to you after you made a terrible decision.
Maybe you followed your feelings into a relationship that wounded you.
Maybe you trusted someone you should not have trusted.
Maybe you convinced yourself that something sinful was harmless because it felt right at the time.
Maybe you looked straight at a warning sign and renamed it “peace.”
Maybe you prayed for God’s will while secretly begging Him to approve the decision you had already made.
Then everything collapsed.
And suddenly Jeremiah 17:9 sounded painfully personal.
The Hebrew text reads:
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿāqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl, wəʾānuš hūʾ; mî yēḏāʿennū?
The heart is deceitful—crooked, insidious—above all, and desperately sick, grievously afflicted. Who can know it?
The Hebrew word translated “heart” is לֵב — lev.
In biblical Hebrew, the heart is more than the place where emotions happen. It is associated with the inner person—with thought, desire, intention, decision, understanding, and will.
And Jeremiah says something disturbing about it.
עָקֹב — ʿāqōḇ.
Deceitful.
Crooked.
Treacherous.
Something capable of misleading.
Then comes אָנֻשׁ — ʾānûš, a word carrying the sense of being desperately sick, grievously afflicted, even incurable in certain contexts.
And then Jeremiah asks the terrifying question:
מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ — mî yēḏāʿennū?
Who can know it?
That question should make us uncomfortable.
Because we spend enormous portions of our lives trusting the very thing Scripture warns can deceive us.
“I know myself.”
Do you?
“I know why I did it.”
Do you?
“My intentions were good.”
Were all of them?
“I prayed about it.”
Yes—but did you surrender it?
“I have peace about it.”
But is every feeling of relief the peace of God?
“It makes me happy.”
But when did happiness become the final test of holiness?
“My heart says…”
And Jeremiah quietly interrupts:
Your heart can lie to you.
That is the scandal.
Not merely that other people can deceive you.
Not merely that Satan can tempt you.
Not merely that culture can mislead you.
You can participate in deceiving yourself.
You can call pride “standards.”
You can call bitterness “discernment.”
You can call lust “chemistry.”
You can call envy “ambition.”
You can call gossip “concern.”
You can call cowardice “waiting on God.”
You can call disobedience “following your heart.”
You can call an idol “a blessing.”
You can even use spiritual vocabulary to protect something God has been asking you to surrender.
That is why this verse hurts.
Because Jeremiah does not merely expose the person sitting beside you.
He exposes you.
He exposes me.

He reaches past the Christian vocabulary, the worship playlist, the Bible highlighted in five colors, the church attendance, the Facebook Scripture posts, the ministry position, the theological arguments, the public testimony…
…and puts his finger on the place nobody else can see.
The heart.
But here is where we have to be extremely careful.
Because Jeremiah 17:9 is true.
Completely true.
But Jeremiah 17:9 is not the whole message.
Stop ending the sermon one verse too early.
Because the very next verse says:
אֲנִי יְהוָה חֹקֵר לֵב בֹּחֵן כְּלָיוֹת
ʾănî YHWH, ḥōqēr lēḇ, bōḥēn kəlāyōṯ…
“I, YHWH, search the heart…”
Jeremiah asks:
Who can know the heart?
And God answers.
I can.
That changes everything.
You may not completely understand your own heart.
God does.
You may have buried something so deeply that you have constructed an entire personality around avoiding it.
God sees it.
You may have become so skilled at explaining your behavior that everybody around you believes your explanation.
God sees underneath it.
You may have convinced your family.
Your spouse.
Your pastor.
Your friends.
Your followers.
Maybe even yourself.
But there is One before whom every locked room of the soul stands open.
And strangely…
that should not only terrify you.
For the person who comes to God in repentance, it can also become one of the most comforting truths imaginable.
Because the God who sees the worst thing inside you is the same God from whom you never needed to hide it.
Think about that.
We spend years terrified that if people knew everything about us, they might leave.
So we edit ourselves.
We reveal the acceptable wounds.
We confess the respectable struggles.
We tell testimonies about battles we have already won.
But there are rooms we keep locked.
The addiction nobody knows returned.
The resentment toward someone we publicly forgave.
The private messages.
The secret browsing.
The jealousy.
The fantasies.
The money.
The compromise.
The prayerlessness.
The resentment toward God Himself.
The strange emptiness we feel even while telling everyone how blessed we are.
And sometimes the most exhausting part of sin is not merely committing it.
It is maintaining the person you pretend to be afterward.
Smiling while hiding.
Serving while hiding.
Posting Scripture while hiding.
Singing while hiding.
Telling everybody “God is good” while quietly wondering how long you can keep living two lives.
But God already knows.
אֲנִי יְהוָה חֹקֵר לֵב
“I, YHWH, search the heart.”
He was never fooled by the mask.
And He is not waiting for your confession because He needs information.
He is calling you into confession because you need freedom.
That is why Jeremiah 17 must be read in context.
Before verse 9 ever describes the deceptive heart, verses 5–8 describe two radically different places of trust.
One person trusts in humanity and makes flesh his strength while his heart turns away from the LORD.
Then comes the contrast:
בָּרוּךְ הַגֶּבֶר אֲשֶׁר יִבְטַח בַּיהוָה וְהָיָה יְהוָה מִבְטַחוֹ
Bārûḵ haggeḇer ʾăšer yiḇṭaḥ baYHWH, wəhāyâ YHWH miḇṭaḥô.
Blessed is the person who trusts in YHWH, whose confidence is YHWH.
Notice the issue.
Jeremiah is talking about trust.
Where will you place the weight of your life?
In human strength?
In yourself?
In the impulses of your own heart?
Or in the LORD?
The answer to a deceptive heart is not learning to hate yourself.
The answer is learning where your trust belongs.
Not:
“Believe in yourself harder.”
Not:
“Follow your heart wherever it leads.”
Not even:
“Become suspicious of every emotion you ever experience.”
The biblical answer is deeper.
Trust the LORD.
Bring the heart beneath the authority of the God who searches it.
Let His Word contradict you.
Let His holiness confront you.
Let His Spirit convict you.
Let His wisdom overrule your impulses.
Let God tell you when the thing you desperately want is destroying you.
Because sometimes grace sounds like comfort.
And sometimes grace sounds like:
“No.”
Sometimes grace closes the door you were begging God to open.
Sometimes grace exposes the relationship.
Sometimes grace interrupts the affair.
Sometimes grace destroys the excuse.
Sometimes grace allows the consequences to become painful enough that pretending is no longer possible.
Sometimes the mercy of God is that He refuses to let you remain comfortably deceived.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Something has been bothering you.
Quietly.
You have been explaining it away.
But late at night, when the notifications stop and there is nobody left to impress, you know.
Something is wrong.
You keep calling it complicated.
God keeps calling you closer.
You keep defending yourself.
God keeps touching the wound.
You keep saying, “That is just who I am.”
Jesus keeps saying, “Follow Me.”
And maybe the reason this article found you tonight is not so you can send Jeremiah 17:9 to somebody else.
Maybe God is asking you to stop reading it with another person’s face in mind.
Maybe this one is about you.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
But do not run.
Because Jeremiah does not end with diagnosis.
Only a few verses later comes one of the most beautiful cries in the chapter:
רְפָאֵנִי יְהוָה וְאֵרָפֵא הוֹשִׁיעֵנִי וְאִוָּשֵׁעָה כִּי תְהִלָּתִי אָתָּה
Rəp̄āʾēnî YHWH wəʾērā-p̄ēʾ; hōšîʿēnî wəʾiwwāšēʿâ, kî təhillāṯî ʾāttâ.
“Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for You are my praise.”
There it is.
The movement of the passage.
The heart is sick.
God searches the heart.
And the prophet cries:
Heal me.
Not “teach me to hide it better.”
Heal me.
Not “help me manage appearances.”
Heal me.
Not “give me enough religious activity that nobody notices.”
Heal me.
Not “make everybody believe I am okay.”
Heal me.
And then:
Save me.
That cry ultimately finds its deepest Christian answer in Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people should try harder to develop better hearts.
The Gospel is far more devastating than that…
and infinitely more beautiful.
We needed rescue.
Jesus said that evil proceeds from within, from the human heart. He did not flatter humanity about its condition.
But Christ did something infinitely greater than diagnose us.
He came for sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He ate with the despised.
He confronted hypocrites.
He forgave the guilty.
He called the wandering home.
And then He went to the cross.
The sin we rationalized…
He carried.
The guilt we hid…
He bore.
The judgment we deserved…
He faced.
The righteousness we could never manufacture…
is found in Him.
And the story did not end inside a sealed tomb.
Jesus rose.
That means your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your life.
Your scandal does not have the final word.
Your addiction does not have the final word.
Your adultery does not have the final word.
Your pornography does not have the final word.
Your pride does not have the final word.
Your failure does not have the final word.
Your secret does not have the final word.
Your shame does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
But grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is not permission to keep hugging the thing that crucified your Savior.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace produces repentance.
Grace takes the person who finally stops saying, “I’m fine,” and teaches him to pray:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Maybe you need that prayer tonight.
No polished language.
No performance.
Just honesty.
Jesus, my heart has deceived me.
I have wanted things You told me to surrender.
I have defended things Your Word calls sin.
I have blamed people for choices that were mine.
I have hidden.
I have performed.
I have tried to look alive spiritually while parts of me were dying.
Search me.
Expose what needs exposing.
Forgive what needs forgiving.
Break what needs breaking.
Heal what needs healing.
Teach me to trust You more than I trust myself.
And when my heart tells me something different from Your Word…
give me grace to believe You.
That is repentance.
Not theatrical shame.
Not self-hatred.
Turning.
Coming home.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your private struggle. But perhaps you do need to stop pretending before God.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer realizes that failure does not have to be final.
Then think of one person who needs this.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Not somebody you want to attack with a Bible verse.
Somebody you love.
Somebody quietly drifting.
Somebody smiling while drowning.
Somebody who has mistaken feelings for truth.
Somebody who thinks their secret has made them unreachable.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when your own heart begins negotiating with something God has already spoken about, and you will need the reminder again:
Your heart is not your Savior. Jesus is.
Supporting Gospel Warrior is not a purchase of God’s favor. It cannot buy salvation.

Scripture gives us an important safeguard: Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through spiritual pressure. Paul teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves cheerful giving.
He will not.
You cannot purchase grace.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But if Gospel Warrior is feeding your faith, strengthening believers, reaching struggling Christians and seekers, and putting Christ-centered resources into people's hands, then you can freely choose to become one of the people who helps carry that mission forward.
another prodigal can remember the Father’s house…
another ashamed Christian can discover that repentance still has a door…
another seeker can hear about Jesus…
another wounded soul can realize:
God is not finished writing.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help.
Because sometimes evangelism begins with something as ordinary as pressing “share.”
Someone scrolls.
Someone stops.
Someone reads.
Someone remembers.
Someone repents.
Someone whispers the name of Jesus again after years of running.
And suddenly what looked like a simple Facebook share became part of a story only eternity will fully reveal.
But before you leave, remember the verse we started with.
“The heart is deceitful above all things…”
Yes.
That is Scripture.
But do not stop there.
The God who says the heart is difficult for us to understand immediately declares:
I search the heart.
And the prophet who knows the sickness of the human heart eventually cries:
Heal me, LORD, and I will be healed. Save me, and I will be saved.
That is the message.
Your heart can deceive you.
God cannot.
Your feelings can change.
God’s truth does not.
Your sin can scar you.
Christ can redeem you.
Your past can accuse you.
The cross announces that forgiveness is real for those who come to Christ.
Your heart is not trustworthy enough to become your god.
But it is not too hidden for God to search.
Not too wounded for Him to reach.
Not too sinful for Christ to confront.
Not too stained for grace.
Not too far gone to repent.
And not beyond the reach of the Savior who still calls sinners home.
So perhaps tonight the bravest prayer you can pray is not:
“God, follow my heart.”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, search my heart…and teach my heart to follow You.”
Because maybe the most dangerous lie your heart ever told you was not that your sin was harmless.
Maybe it was telling you that after everything you have done, Jesus would never want you back.
He still calls sinners to come.
He still forgives those who repent and believe.
He still saves.
He still heals.
He still rewrites stories.
And when Jesus takes the pen, the scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FOR I KNOW THE PLANS I HAVE FOR YOU” — JEREMIAH 29:11 IS NOT SAYING WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK
paragraphs: “FOR I KNOW THE PLANS I HAVE FOR YOU” — JEREMIAH 29:11 IS NOT SAYING WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK

We turned one of Scripture’s most painful promises into a slogan about getting the life we wanted. But when you put Jeremiah 29:11 back into Babylon, the verse becomes harder, deeper—and far more beautiful.
You have probably seen it on a graduation card.
Printed beneath a sunrise.
Framed above a desk.
Posted after someone got the job.
Quoted when the relationship finally worked out.
Whispered when somebody desperately needed to believe that the next chapter of life would be better than the last.
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
And somewhere along the way, many of us began hearing something God never actually said.
You are going to get the future you imagined.
This disappointment will disappear soon.
Your career will work out.
Your dream will happen.
The person will come back.
The diagnosis will change.
The door will open.
The money will arrive.
Everything is about to fall into place.
But what if I told you Jeremiah 29:11 was originally spoken to people whose lives had already fallen apart?
Not people standing at the doorway of their dream.
Exiles.
People who had lost their homeland.
People living under the shadow of Babylon.
People who wanted to go home.
And God essentially told them:
Not yet.
That changes the verse.
And perhaps it needs to change the way some of us understand God.
Because the Bible does not become less comforting when we read it correctly.
It becomes more comforting.
The Hebrew of Jeremiah 29:11 reads:
כִּי אָנֹכִי יָדַעְתִּי אֶת־הַמַּחֲשָׁבֹת אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי חֹשֵׁב עֲלֵיכֶם נְאֻם־יְהוָה מַחְשְׁבוֹת שָׁלוֹם וְלֹא לְרָעָה לָתֵת לָכֶם אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה
Ki anokhi yada'ti et-hamachashavot asher anokhi choshev aleikhem, ne'um-YHWH; machshevot shalom velo lera'ah, latet lakhem acharit vetikvah.
A careful sense of the verse is:
“For I know the plans—or intentions—I am planning concerning you,” declares the LORD, “plans of shalom and not of calamity, to give you a future and a hope.”
Notice that word.
Shalom.
שָׁלוֹם
We often reduce shalom to “peace,” but biblical shalom can carry the richer sense of welfare, wholeness, well-being, soundness, things being put right.
And that matters enormously.
God was not promising His exiled people immediate comfort.
He was declaring that catastrophe would not have the final word over His covenant purposes.
There would be an acharit—אַחֲרִית—a future, an outcome, an end beyond what they could presently see.
There would be tikvah—תִּקְוָה—hope.
But here is the detail that rarely makes it onto the coffee mug.
One verse earlier, God tells them how long Babylon will last.
Seventy years.
Read that slowly.
Seventy.
Years.

The people receiving Jeremiah’s letter were being warned against false hopes of an immediate escape. God told the exiles to build houses and live in them. Plant gardens. Eat their produce. Marry. Have children. Multiply. Seek the shalom of the city where they had been carried into exile. Pray for it.
In other words:
You are going to be here for a while.
Imagine receiving that message when you had been praying every night to leave.
Imagine begging God to open the prison door…
and God telling you to plant a garden outside it.
Imagine asking God when your old life is coming back…
and hearing Him tell you to become faithful in the life you never wanted.
That is Jeremiah 29:11.
And suddenly the verse stops sounding like motivational Christianity.
It starts sounding like something strong enough to keep a human soul alive when God does not remove Babylon.
Maybe that is why this verse needs to be rescued from the way we sometimes use it.
Because somebody reading this is living in a Babylon you never chose.
You prayed.
Nothing moved.
You believed.
The door stayed closed.
You tried to remain faithful, but the marriage still fractured.
You asked God for healing, but you are still waiting.
You raised the child in church, and now you barely recognize the person they have become.
You thought obedience would produce a straight road.
Instead, obedience led you into a wilderness.
You watched other people testify about answered prayers while yours seemed to disappear into the ceiling.
And perhaps someone handed you Jeremiah 29:11 as though it meant:
“Don't worry. God is about to give you what you want.”
Then He didn't.
And somewhere inside you, something cracked.
Maybe you wondered whether God had forgotten His promise.
But what if the promise was even greater than what you thought?
God never promised Israel that Babylon was imaginary.
He promised Babylon would not be final.
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Biblical hope is not pretending the furnace is cold.
Biblical hope is discovering that God remains God inside the fire.
It is not believing Christians will never enter valleys.
It is knowing the Shepherd enters valleys with His sheep.
It is not believing every earthly story receives the ending we request.
It is trusting that no earthly chapter can overthrow the redemptive purposes of God.
And Jeremiah's message gets even more uncomfortable.
Before the promise comes a warning.
False prophets were telling the people what they wanted to hear.
God warned the exiles not to be deceived by them.
Think about that.
There were voices offering quick deliverance.
Jeremiah offered faithful endurance.
There were voices saying Babylon would soon disappear.
God said:
Build.
Plant.
Live.
Pray.
Wait.
And then came:
“I know the plans…”
Maybe some of us have unknowingly preferred the false prophet's version of Jeremiah 29:11.
The version where God exists to guarantee our timeline.
The version where faith means getting promoted.
The version where favor means becoming comfortable.
The version where suffering must mean something has gone wrong.
The version where God's plan is automatically identified with whatever future we happen to desire most.
But Scripture refuses to make God the servant of our dreams.
God is not writing our story merely to make us impressive.
He is drawing His people back to Himself.
And that becomes unmistakable when you keep reading.
Jeremiah 29 does not stop at verse 11.
God continues:
“You will call upon Me…”
“You will pray to Me…”
“You will seek Me…”
And then comes one of the most beautiful statements in the chapter:
וּבִקַּשְׁתֶּם אֹתִי וּמְצָאתֶם כִּי תִדְרְשֻׁנִי בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם
Uviqqashtem oti umetzatem, ki tidreshuni bekhol-levavkhem.
“You will seek Me and find Me when you seek Me with all your heart.”
There it is.
Maybe the greatest gift in Jeremiah 29 was never simply getting out of Babylon.
It was getting Israel's heart back toward God.
We want God's plans.
God wants our hearts.
We want the future.
God says:
Seek Me.
We want the breakthrough.
God says:
Call upon Me.
We want Babylon removed.
God says:
Do not waste Babylon.
There are things God can form in exile that comfort could never teach us.
Not because suffering is inherently good.
Not because tragedy should be romanticized.
Not because every painful event can casually be labeled “God's plan.”
Scripture never gives us permission to call evil good.
But Scripture repeatedly shows us a God so sovereign, wise, and redemptive that evil does not get the privilege of writing the final sentence.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because Christians cannot read the story of exile, promise, restoration, hope, judgment, mercy, and homecoming without eventually seeing the entire biblical story rushing toward Christ.
Humanity has a deeper Babylon.
Sin.
We have not merely experienced brokenness.
We have participated in it.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Hated.
Envied.
Hidden.
Manipulated.
Worshiped ourselves.
Excused what God calls sin.
Built private idols while publicly appearing religious.
We have wanted God's blessings while resisting God's authority.
And no motivational interpretation of Jeremiah 29:11 can solve that problem.
We do not merely need better plans.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve our earthly circumstances.
He came to rescue sinners.
The cross destroys the fantasy that God's love means the absence of suffering.
Look at Jesus.
The sinless Son of God betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
If suffering automatically meant God had abandoned His plan, Calvary would appear to be history's greatest failure.
Instead, Calvary became the center of redemption.
What looked like scandal became grace.
What looked like defeat became victory.
What looked like the end became the doorway to resurrection.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the nails never pierced Him.
By rising with the scars.
And maybe somebody needs that distinction tonight.
God's plan for you does not necessarily mean you will get everything you have been asking for.
It means that for those who belong to Christ, your suffering cannot cancel God's faithfulness.
Your disappointment cannot dethrone Jesus.
Your past cannot overpower the blood of Christ.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority over your final identity.
Your sin does not have to become your destiny if you turn to Christ in repentance and faith.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe your marriage did not survive.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe the business failed.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe somebody walked away.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe your body was not healed when you begged for healing.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you are rebuilding from consequences you caused yourself.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you wasted years.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you are reading this with tears nobody knows about.
Jesus is still Lord.
Christian hope is not:
“Everything I want will eventually happen.”
Christian hope is:
“Whatever happens, Christ will remain faithful, death will not have the last word, resurrection is real, and everyone who belongs to Jesus has a future no Babylon can steal.”
That is stronger than a slogan.
That can survive a funeral.
That can survive rejection.
That can survive bankruptcy.
That can survive betrayal.
That can survive unanswered questions.
That can survive the night when you cannot feel God at all.
Because Christian hope ultimately rests not in circumstances but in a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where Jeremiah 29:11 becomes personal without becoming selfish.

The original “you” belongs in its historical setting. Jeremiah was writing God's word to the Judean exiles as a people. We should not rip that covenant promise from its context and pretend every detail was directly addressed to twenty-first-century individuals.
But the God revealed there is still the God Christians worship.
A God who keeps covenant.
A God who judges sin seriously.
A God who refuses to abandon His redemptive purposes.
A God who calls His people to seek Him wholeheartedly.
And the New Testament gives believers promises even greater than the shallow version we sometimes try to manufacture from Jeremiah 29:11.
In Christ, God does not promise that every circumstance will become pleasant.
He promises that nothing can separate His people from His love.
He does not promise exemption from tribulation.
Jesus explicitly told His disciples that they would have trouble in this world.
He does not promise Christians a life untouched by grief.
He promises resurrection.
He promises forgiveness through Christ.
He promises His presence.
He promises an inheritance that cannot be destroyed.
He promises that the story of everyone united to Jesus ends not in exile but home.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“What plans does God have for my dream?”
Perhaps the question becomes:
“Jesus, what are You doing with my heart while I wait?”
That question is harder.
And holier.
Because maybe you have spent years asking God to change your surroundings while He has been exposing what lives inside you.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
Secret sin.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The relationship you know dishonors Him.
The resentment you keep feeding.
The version of Christianity that wants blessing without surrender.
What if your greatest danger is not that God's plan will fail?
What if your greatest danger is becoming so obsessed with escaping Babylon that you miss God's invitation to seek Him there?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Maybe you do not need another inspirational quote tonight.
Maybe you need repentance.
Maybe you need to stop negotiating with the sin Jesus died to save you from.
Maybe you need to stop calling disobedience “a complicated season.”
Maybe you need to forgive.
Maybe you need to confess.
Maybe you need to come home.
Not to religion.
To Christ.
If that is you, do not hide behind Christian language.
Jesus already knows.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him your unbelief.
Bring Him the broken pieces.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people can improve themselves.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life are offered through Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
And if you are already His but exhausted from waiting, hear this carefully:
Your waiting is not proof that God has forgotten you.
Jeremiah's exiles had to learn that a delayed promise was not an abandoned promise.
Plant the garden.
Pray.
Stay faithful.
Seek God.
Love people.
Obey what Scripture has already made clear.
Stop demanding that God show you the entire map before you take the next faithful step.
And when tomorrow still looks like Babylon…
remember who holds tomorrow.
Pray for somebody.
Encourage somebody.
Remind somebody that Jesus has not finished writing their story.
Not because God needs our money.
Not because clicking a button proves our faith.
But because Christians have always used their time, resources, voices, generosity, and opportunities to help truthful ministry reach others.
If you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting this work, do it freely, prayerfully, and for Christ—not from guilt.
If you have been consuming truth quietly, perhaps today is the day to help carry it farther.
Follow.
But never confuse the ministry with the Messiah.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your generosity cannot save you.
Your morality cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And perhaps that is the truth Jeremiah 29:11 has been trying to teach us beneath all our inspirational posters.
God's faithfulness is bigger than the future you planned.
Sometimes He does open the door.
Sometimes He makes us faithful while the door remains closed.
Sometimes He restores what was lost.
Sometimes He teaches us that Christ Himself is better than what we lost.
Sometimes He leads us home quickly.
Sometimes the road runs through Babylon.
But for those who belong to Jesus, Babylon never gets to write the ending.
So the next time you read:
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
do not hear:
“God owes me the life I imagined.”
Hear something stronger.
The God who sees the entire story has not surrendered His throne because you cannot understand this chapter.
The God who brought redemption through a cross can be trusted when your story looks nothing like the one you would have written.
And the Savior who walked out of a grave is still writing stories that graves, failures, scandals, sins, betrayals, disappointments, and exiles cannot finish.
You may be standing in a chapter you never would have chosen—but if Jesus holds the pen, Babylon does not get the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DANIEL WAS THROWN INTO THE LIONS’ DEN BECAUSE HE WOULDN’T STOP PRAYING
paragraphs: DANIEL WAS THROWN INTO THE LIONS’ DEN BECAUSE HE WOULDN’T STOP PRAYING
They could find nothing corrupt in his life—so they weaponized the one thing they knew he would never surrender: his devotion to God.
There is something terrifying about Daniel 6 that we sometimes miss because we already know how the story ends.
We know about the angel.
We know about the lions.
We know Daniel survives.
Daniel did not.
Not yet.
When Daniel walked toward that den, he did not have the privilege of turning the page and reading the ending.
He only had God.
And maybe that is why this story needs to find you today.
Because somewhere between the prayers you have prayed and the answers you are still waiting for, you may have quietly started believing that faithfulness should keep you away from lions’ dens.
Daniel discovered something far more unsettling.
Sometimes faithfulness is exactly what gets you thrown into one.

Daniel was not a reckless young man trying to prove how spiritual he was. By this stage of the biblical story, he had spent years living as an exile, serving through changing kingdoms and rulers. He had survived Babylon. He had watched power change hands. He had lived long enough to understand that earthly kingdoms rise, tremble, boast, and eventually disappear.
But Daniel’s God remained.
And Daniel had become so trustworthy in government that his enemies faced an embarrassing problem.
They wanted to destroy him...
but they could not find enough dirt.
Daniel 6 says his opponents searched for grounds to accuse him concerning his administration, yet they could find no corruption or negligence because he was faithful.
Imagine being hated so deeply that people investigate your life hoping to find your scandal...
and the closest thing they can find to a scandal is your obedience to God.
So they changed tactics.
If they could not make Daniel compromise, they would make his faithfulness illegal.
They persuaded King Darius to establish a decree: for thirty days, anyone making a petition to any god or human being except the king would be thrown into the lions’ den.
Thirty days.
That was all.
Daniel could have reasoned with himself.
God understands.
It’s only thirty days.
I can pray silently.
I can close the windows.
I can change my routine.
I can survive this month and return to normal afterward.
And that is where this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because most compromise does not introduce itself by saying, “Abandon God forever.”
It whispers...
“Just this once.”
“Keep your faith private.”
“Don’t make trouble.”
“God knows your heart.”
“Everybody else is doing it.”
“You can obey later.”
But Daniel had spent too many years with God to suddenly treat prayer as disposable.
The biblical text makes the moment almost breathtakingly simple.
Daniel learned that the decree had been signed.
He went home.
He entered his upstairs room.
His windows opened toward Jerusalem.
He knelt.
And he prayed.
Three times that day.
Not because Daniel had suddenly become courageous.
Because this was what Daniel had already been doing.
Scripture emphasizes that he prayed and gave thanks before his God “just as he had been accustomed to do previously.”
That changes everything.
The lions’ den did not create Daniel’s prayer life.
His prayer life prepared Daniel for the lions’ den.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that before your next crisis arrives.
You cannot expect emergency faith to consistently replace everyday communion with God.
Private surrender matters.
The prayers nobody applauds matter.
Opening Scripture when nobody knows matters.
Repenting when nobody catches you matters.
Worshiping when nothing dramatic happens matters.
Seeking God on ordinary Tuesdays matters.
Because sometimes the faith that stands when everybody is watching was built during thousands of moments when nobody was.
The book of Daniel from Daniel 2:4b through chapter 7 is substantially written in Biblical Aramaic, so here we can actually hear part of Daniel’s story in the language preserved in the ancient text.
Daniel’s accusers describe him this way:
וְזִמְנִין תְּלָתָה בְּיוֹמָא בָּעֵא בָּעוּתֵהּ
we-zimnîn telāṯāh be-yômā bāʿē bāʿûṯēh
The sense is:
Three times a day, he makes his petition.
The repetition built around the Aramaic root for asking or petitioning underscores what his enemies observed.
Daniel kept praying.
They knew where they would find him.
Think about that.
His enemies understood his spiritual habits well enough to build a trap around them.
If someone wanted to trap you by predicting your devotion to Jesus Christ...
would there be enough evidence to know where to wait?
That question hurts.
Because some of us are terrified of lions we have never faced while barely praying to the God who shuts lions’ mouths.
Some of us reach for our phones before we reach for God.
Some know how to scroll for an hour but struggle to pray for five minutes.
Some can argue Christianity publicly while neglecting Christ privately.

Some still say “I believe in God,” but underneath the Christian vocabulary, prayer has become occasional, repentance has become uncomfortable, Scripture has become distant, and Jesus has slowly been pushed toward the edges of life.
Then trouble comes.
And suddenly we wonder where God is.
Daniel teaches us to ask another question:
Where were we before the trouble came?
Because Daniel did not suddenly discover God at the mouth of the lions’ den.
He knew Him upstairs.
On his knees.
Before the accusation.
Before the arrest.
Before the stone.
Before the lions.
That is where courage was born.
And then they caught him.
Exactly where they expected.
Praying.
Daniel was brought before the king. Darius realized what had happened and tried to rescue him, but the decree stood.
Then came the sentence.
Daniel was taken to the lions’ den.
Try to forget the children’s Bible illustrations for a moment.
These were not friendly animals sitting peacefully around a smiling prophet.
The narrative itself later makes the danger unmistakable: when Daniel’s accusers were cast into the den, the lions overpowered them before they reached its floor.
Daniel was being handed over to death.
A stone was placed over the opening.
The king sealed it.
Night fell.
And Scripture records no speech from Daniel as the stone closes.
No dramatic sermon.
No boast.
No promise that everything will be fine.
Just darkness.
Maybe that is where this story meets you.
Not at the miracle.
At the stone.
You prayed for your marriage...
and there is a stone.
You prayed for your child...
and there is a stone.
You prayed for restoration...
and there is a stone.
You begged God to open a door...
and instead another one slammed shut.
You tried to obey Jesus, and somehow obedience did not make life easier.
You gave up something sinful and still felt lonely.
You forgave someone and still cried afterward.
You started following Christ seriously and discovered that surrender did not exempt you from suffering.
And somewhere inside you a question formed that you were almost afraid to say aloud:
God, I obeyed You. Why am I here?
Daniel’s story does not give us permission to promise that every faithful Christian will escape every earthly tragedy.
The Bible never teaches that.
Some believers are delivered from suffering.
Others glorify Christ through suffering.

Hebrews 11 deliberately places extraordinary deliverance and extraordinary endurance beside each other. Some, through faith, “shut the mouths of lions”; others suffered, were imprisoned, mistreated, and killed.
Same chapter.
Same faith.
Same God.
That protects Daniel’s story from becoming a prosperity slogan.
The message is not:
“If you pray hard enough, nothing bad can happen to you.”
The message is far deeper:
No earthly power can dethrone the God to whom you belong.
Daniel could be thrown down.
God could not.
Daniel could be sealed inside.
God could not.
Daniel could be condemned by human law.
God remained King.
And somewhere in the darkness of that den, heaven moved.
Daniel later explained it in the Aramaic preserved in Scripture:
אֱלָהִי שְׁלַח מַלְאֲכֵהּ, וּסְגַר פֻּם אַרְיָוָתָא
ʾĔlāhî šelaḥ malʾăḵēh ûseḡar pum ʾaryāwāṯā.
“My God sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths.”
Read those words again.
My God.
Not merely “the God.”
My God.
The God Daniel knew before the den was the God Daniel discovered inside the den.
God did not prevent Daniel from entering.
God met him there.
And sometimes that is the miracle we do not want...
until it becomes the miracle we desperately need.
We want the God who keeps us from every den.
But Scripture repeatedly introduces us to the God who enters impossible places with His people.
Joseph had a prison.
Moses had a wilderness.
David had caves.
Jeremiah had a cistern.
Paul and Silas had a jail.
Daniel had lions.
And Jesus Christ had a tomb.
That does not mean these events are identical. Daniel is not Jesus, and we should not force every detail into an allegory the biblical text itself does not make.
But Daniel’s deliverance participates in a great biblical pattern that reaches its glorious climax in Christ:
Human power says, “It is finished.”
A stone closes the place of death.
And God has the final word.
Daniel came out of the den alive.
Jesus did something infinitely greater.
Jesus entered death itself.
Not because He was trapped by political rivals.
Not because He had sinned.
The New Testament presents Christ as the sinless Son of God who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Our deepest problem is not that there are lions around us.
Our deepest problem is that there is sin within us.
We have broken God’s commands.
We have loved created things more than the Creator.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Envied.
Hated.
Hidden.
Compromised.
Worshiped ourselves.
Excused what God calls sin.
And no amount of religious performance can erase our guilt.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of courageous people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of God coming for people who could never rescue themselves.
Jesus Christ lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
At the cross, He gave Himself for sinners.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day...
the stone did not get the last word.
Christ rose.
That is the heartbeat beneath every true story of redemption.
The enemy says ruined.
Jesus says redeemed.
Sin says condemned.
In Christ there is forgiveness.
Shame says hide.
Jesus calls sinners into the light.
Your past says this is who you will always be.
Grace says Jesus is still writing.
That is why the Gospel is bigger than inspiration.
Daniel does not merely challenge you to “be brave.”
Jesus calls you to repent and believe.
Maybe your lions’ den is not persecution.
Maybe it is the secret nobody knows.
The browser history.
The bitterness.
The affair you are emotionally drifting toward.
The addiction you keep renaming a “struggle” because calling it sin would force you to confront it.
The pride behind the Christian image.
The resentment toward God.
The prayerlessness.
The exhaustion.
The church hurt you never healed from.
The grief that changed you.
The private compromise you promised would happen only once.
And maybe you have become very good at looking alive spiritually while something inside you is starving.
No more pretending.
Christ already knows.
And still He calls you.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up so Jesus will finally tolerate you.
It is turning from sin and coming to the Savior because you finally understand that you cannot save yourself.
Grace does not tell you your sin does not matter.
Grace tells you your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishing that sinners who come to Him can truly be forgiven.
Maybe tonight your greatest act of courage is not standing before lions.
Maybe it is kneeling again.
Maybe it is whispering:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Maybe it is finally confessing what you have hidden.
Maybe it is returning to Scripture.
Maybe it is praying after months of silence.
Maybe it is surrendering the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is asking another believer for help.
Maybe it is admitting that your Christianity has become public performance without private communion.
Daniel opened his windows and prayed because God was not a religious accessory to him.
God was his life.
And when morning came, Darius rushed toward the den.
The king cried out anxiously:
Was Daniel’s God—the God he served continually—able to rescue him?
From inside a place that should have contained a corpse came a voice.
Daniel was alive.
The lions had not consumed him.
God had shut their mouths.
And suddenly the place designed to prove Daniel’s destruction became the place from which God’s power was proclaimed.
That is scandal becoming testimony.
That is darkness being forced to surrender the final sentence.
That is why we keep saying:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing consequences with sentimental religion.

Jesus rewrites everything by bringing sinners through repentance into forgiveness, captives into freedom, shame into testimony, death into resurrection hope, and broken lives into stories that point beyond themselves to the mercy of God.
And if Christ has rescued you, do not keep that rescue to yourself.
Someone on your Facebook feed is smiling in photographs and quietly losing the battle inside.
Someone you know has stopped praying.
Someone thinks they have sinned too badly to come home.
Someone believes God abandoned them because the stone has not moved yet.
Someone is one honest Gospel message away from remembering that Jesus Christ still receives sinners.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not. Salvation is by grace, not by social-media activity.
Send this to the person whose faith has been hanging by a thread.
Somebody else may need to see evidence that Christians still hurt, still struggle, still enter dens—and still cling to Christ.
Because there may come a night when you need these words more than you need them today.

Supporting Christian ministry does not purchase God’s blessing, prove salvation, or make someone more faithful than believers who cannot financially contribute. We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him.
Return to Jesus.
Pray again.
Repent again.
Open the Bible again.
Stop hiding.
Stop negotiating with the sin Christ died to free you from.
And when obedience costs you something, remember Daniel.
The decree was signed.
Daniel knew.
The windows remained open.
His knees still bent.
His prayers still rose.
The stone still fell.
The night still came.
The lions were still real.
But they were never sovereign.
God was.
And He still is.
So when the world asks whether your God is worth trusting when obedience becomes expensive, may your life answer before your mouth ever does.
And when your own lions begin roaring so loudly that you can barely hear your faith anymore, remember this:
The loudest roar in your darkest night still does not get to write the final sentence—Jesus does.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is standing at an open window deciding whether they will keep praying.
May they discover that the God of Daniel still lives...
and may they ultimately discover something even greater:
Jesus Christ crucified.
Jesus Christ risen.
Jesus Christ forgiving sinners.
Jesus Christ restoring the broken.
Jesus Christ reigning.
Jesus Christ still rewriting stories.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “CALL THOSE THINGS INTO EXISTENCE” — DID GOD REALLY GIVE CHRISTIANS CREATIVE POWER THROUGH THEIR WORDS?
paragraphs:
“CALL THOSE THINGS INTO EXISTENCE” — DID GOD REALLY GIVE CHRISTIANS CREATIVE POWER THROUGH THEIR WORDS?
Millions of Christians have been told to “speak it into existence.” But what if the verse behind that teaching was never describing your power at all—and what if what Scripture actually promises is far more beautiful?
Maybe you have done it.
You stood in front of a mirror and declared that the sickness was gone.
You spoke prosperity over an empty bank account.
You declared that the relationship would return.
You announced that the job was already yours.
You refused to say anything “negative” because someone warned you that your words might create the very thing you feared.
And somewhere underneath all those declarations was a sentence you had heard preached with breathtaking confidence:
“Call those things which be not as though they were.”
It sounded biblical.
It sounded powerful.
It sounded almost impossible to question because, after all, those words really are connected to Romans 4:17.
But there is a question every follower of Jesus eventually has to be brave enough to ask:
Did God actually give Christians the ability to create reality with their words?
Or have we quietly taken something Scripture says about God…and made it about us?
That question matters more than it first appears.
Because when theology is slightly wrong in comfortable seasons, it can become devastating theology in seasons of suffering.
Imagine the mother praying beside a hospital bed who has been told that acknowledging the seriousness of her child's condition demonstrates unbelief.
Imagine the Christian whose business collapses despite months of declarations.
Imagine the woman desperately praying for a marriage while being told she simply has to “speak” restoration.
Imagine someone grieving a death while secretly wondering whether they failed because their faith was not strong enough.
That is where this teaching stops being merely theoretical.
It enters hospital rooms.
Funerals.
Divorce courts.
Empty bedrooms.
Unemployment lines.
And terrified midnight prayers.
So we need to open the Bible carefully.
Not to destroy faith.
To rescue faith from something God never asked it to carry.
Romans 4:17 contains the famous language. In the Greek text we read:
“θεοῦ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος τοὺς νεκροὺς καὶ καλοῦντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα”
The crucial words are:
“καλοῦντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα”
kalountos ta mē onta hōs onta.
The idea is of calling the things that are not as though they are—or, as some translations express the thought, calling into being that which does not exist.
But slow down.
Because one grammatical observation changes the entire conversation.
Who is doing the calling?
Read the words immediately before the famous phrase:
“θεοῦ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος…”
theou tou zōopoiountos…
God—the One giving life.
Paul is describing God.
Romans 4:17 is not primarily a command telling Abraham how to speak.
It is a revelation describing the God Abraham believed.
That difference is enormous.

Abraham's faith was extraordinary not because Abraham discovered a divine mechanism for manufacturing reality with vocabulary, but because Abraham trusted the God whose power was greater than Abraham's impossibility.
Paul's focus is not the creative sovereignty of Abraham's mouth.
It is the sovereign power of Abraham's God.
The same God introduced in the opening chapter of Scripture.
“וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר וַיְהִי־אוֹר”
Vayomer Elohim, yehi or; vayehi or.
“And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.”
Notice who speaks creation into existence.
God.
Genesis does not introduce humanity as independent creators whose sentences possess God's sovereign power. It introduces the LORD as Creator and humanity as His creation.
That distinction does not diminish human dignity.
It establishes it correctly.
We bear God's image.
We are not God.
And sometimes one of the most spiritually dangerous things we can do is take something glorious about God and subtly relocate it into ourselves.
It happened in Eden.
The temptation was not merely about fruit.
It was about the ancient desire to cross the Creator-creature boundary.
“You will be like God.”
Humanity has been reaching for that sentence ever since.
Sometimes through pride.
Sometimes through religion.
And sometimes through Christian vocabulary.
That does not mean your words are powerless.
Far from it.
Scripture treats human speech with frightening seriousness.
Proverbs 18:21 says that death and life are in the power of the tongue and that those who love it will eat its fruit. The Hebrew expression includes:
“מָוֶת וְחַיִּים בְּיַד־לָשׁוֹן”
Maveth vechayyim beyad-lashon.
Death and life are “in the hand”—that is, within the power or agency—of the tongue.
Words can destroy reputations.
Words can fracture marriages.
Words can crush children.
Words can spread lies.
Words can ignite hatred.
Words can manipulate.
Words can also confess truth.
Comfort the grieving.
Defend the vulnerable.
Proclaim Christ.
Ask forgiveness.
Restore relationships.
Bless rather than curse.
Speak courage into someone who has almost surrendered.
Tell a sinner that there really is mercy at the cross.
Words matter enormously.
But “words have consequences” is not the same statement as “human words possess God's sovereign creative power.”
That distinction protects us from turning biblical faith into a Christianized version of manifestation.
The Gospel is not “believe strongly enough in your desired future and your words will attract it.”
The Gospel is not “the universe responds to your frequency.”
The Gospel is not “your mouth creates your reality.”
Christianity begins somewhere completely different.
God is God.
We are sinners.
Christ is Lord.
We cannot save ourselves.
And our hope rests not in mastering spiritual laws but in being reconciled to the Father through Jesus Christ.
Even Mark 11, another passage frequently brought into this discussion, begins with words we dare not rush past.
“Ἔχετε πίστιν θεοῦ.”
Echete pistin theou.
“Have faith in God.”
Then Jesus speaks about commanding a mountain and believing in prayer.
But notice where Jesus places the faith.
Not in faith itself.
Not in verbal technique.
Not in personal creative energy.
In God.
Jesus directs His disciples away from self-reliance and toward the Father.
And the wider biblical teaching about prayer refuses to turn God into a machine controlled by the correct confession.
First John 5:14 says that our confidence is that when we ask according to His will, He hears us.
That phrase matters:
“according to His will.”
Christian prayer is bold.
Christian prayer can be audacious.
Christian prayer expects miracles because our God can do what we cannot.
We can pray for healing.
We can pray for provision.
We can pray for reconciliation.
We can ask God to open doors no human being can open.
We can plead for prodigals to come home.
We can pray against circumstances that look utterly impossible.
But prayer is not the throne commanding the King.
Prayer is the child approaching the Father.
There is authority in Christ.
There is confidence before God.
There is genuine power in prayer.
There are gifts of the Holy Spirit.
There is supernatural intervention.
There is nothing weak about biblical Christianity.
But biblical authority is delegated authority.
We never become sovereign.
Jesus remains Lord.
That becomes painfully important when God's answer is not the answer we wanted.
Jesus Himself shows us what faithful prayer looks like when suffering is approaching.
Gethsemane.
Darkness.
Agony.
The cross drawing closer.
Jesus does not pretend suffering is pleasant.
He does not rename agony as comfort.
He does not teach us that acknowledging pain creates pain.
He pours out His heart before the Father.
And then comes surrender:
“Not my will, but Yours, be done.”
That is not weak faith.
That is perfect faith.
Maybe this is where someone reading these words needs to be released from a burden you have carried for years.
Maybe somebody convinced you that your tragedy happened because you “spoke negatively.”
Maybe you have replayed your sentences trying to discover which words supposedly opened the door.
Maybe someone became sick and you blamed yourself.
Maybe you prayed for healing and healing did not come in the way you begged for it.
Maybe your marriage ended.
Maybe the pregnancy was lost.
Maybe the business failed.
Maybe the person died.
And somewhere in your grief came another wound:
Was my faith too weak?
Listen carefully.
Biblical faith is not pretending the grave is empty when the body is still inside it.
Biblical faith can stand outside Lazarus's tomb and weep.
Jesus did.
Faith can tell the truth about pain without surrendering hope in God.
Abraham himself is the example in Romans 4.
Paul does not portray him as a man refusing to acknowledge reality. Abraham knew the condition of his body. He knew Sarah's barrenness. The impossibility was real.
But the impossibility was not sovereign.
God was.
That is faith.
Not denying reality.
Trusting God beyond reality.
There is a world of difference.
You do not have to call cancer “health” to believe God can heal.
You can say, “This diagnosis is terrifying, but my God is still God.”
You do not have to call poverty “wealth.”
You can say, “I don't know where the provision will come from, but Father, give me this day my daily bread.”
You do not have to pretend your marriage is healthy when it is breaking.
You can tell the truth, seek help, repent where necessary, establish wise boundaries where necessary, and beg Christ for restoration.
You do not have to say, “I am not hurting.”
You can say, “Jesus, I am hurting so badly that I barely know how to pray.”
That is not unbelief.
Sometimes that is the most honest faith you have left.
The Psalms are filled with believers crying, questioning, grieving, remembering, pleading and hoping.
God never required His children to lie about their wounds in order to prove they trusted Him.
And that brings us to something even deeper.
Perhaps the greatest miracle Christianity offers is not that you can speak whatever future you desire into existence.
It is that God can take a future you destroyed and write redemption into it.
That is the heartbeat of grace.
Peter could not unsay his denial.
Three times.
“I don't know Him.”
Words.
Terrible words.
Words spoken by a man who had promised Jesus he would never abandon Him.
Peter's tongue produced something devastating.
But Peter's failure did not get the final sentence.
Jesus met him again.
Grace walked onto the shore.
A charcoal fire burned.
And the disciple who had denied Christ was restored by Christ.
That is our story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you preached one thing and lived another.
Maybe you have been carrying pornography behind a Christian smile.
Maybe bitterness has been eating you alive.
Maybe pride made you cruel.
Maybe you have manipulated people.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you walked away from God and still know exactly how to look spiritual when people are watching.
Maybe your mouth has worshiped Jesus on Sunday and destroyed people by Monday.
Then perhaps the question you most desperately need answered is not:
“How can I speak my dream into existence?”
Perhaps it is:
“Can Jesus still redeem someone like me?”
Yes.
Not because your words possess creative sovereignty.
Because His grace is greater than your sin.
You cannot declare yourself righteous.
Christ justifies the ungodly who trust Him.
You cannot speak away your guilt.
Christ carried guilt to the cross.
You cannot manifest resurrection.
Jesus walked out of the tomb.
You cannot create a new heart by positive confession.
God saves.
God forgives.
God regenerates.
God restores.
God transforms.
And suddenly Romans 4:17 becomes far more beautiful than a formula for getting things.
The God “who gives life to the dead” is the center of the sentence.
That is the God Abraham trusted.
And that is the God sinners desperately need.
Because spiritually, our problem was never merely that we lacked enough positive declarations.
We needed resurrection.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your vocabulary.
He came to save you.
He lived the righteousness you failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him finds something no motivational confession could manufacture:
grace.
Real grace.
Grace for the ashamed.
Grace for the addict.
Grace for the hypocrite finally tired of pretending.
Grace for the religious person discovering that religion cannot save.
Grace for the person whose life looks nothing like the testimony they wish they had.
Grace for scandals.
Grace for ruins.
Grace for people who have finally reached the end of themselves.
But grace does not leave us unchanged.
Jesus does not simply rewrite our ending while permitting us to remain in love with the sin destroying us.
Grace calls us to repentance.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace brings hidden things into light.
Grace transforms our speech because grace transforms our hearts.
So should Christians speak differently?
Absolutely.
Speak truth.
Speak Scripture.
Speak encouragement.
Speak blessing rather than cursing.
Confess Christ.
Confess sin.
Pray boldly.
Ask courageously.
Refuse gossip.
Reject slander.
Stop rehearsing hopelessness as though God were absent.
Tell your soul what is true about God.
Tell frightened believers that Christ has not abandoned them.
Tell sinners there is forgiveness.
Tell the brokenhearted there is a Savior.
Tell the world that the tomb is empty.
But never confuse declaring God's truth with possessing God's sovereignty.
Your confidence is not:
“My words control tomorrow.”
Your confidence is:
“My Father already holds tomorrow.”
That is stronger.
Because if your hope rests on the perfection of your confession, then eventually you will become terrified of your own mouth.
But if your hope rests in Jesus Christ, you can pray through tears.
You can stumble over sentences.
You can whisper, “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.”
You can come empty-handed.
You can admit that you do not understand.
You can tell God exactly how frightened you are.
And you can still be held.
Maybe that is the word somebody desperately needs tonight.
You do not need magical words.
You need Christ.
You do not need to become your own creator.
You need to trust your Creator.
You do not need enough spiritual power to control every chapter.
You need the Savior who already knows how the story ends.
And if this exposed something you have believed, don't hide from the conviction.
Bring it to Scripture.
Bring it to Jesus.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only unfinished person following a perfect Savior.
Let them see the difference.
We want this community to remain a place for Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, repentance, grace and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Not to a formula.
Not to manifestation.
Not to the illusion that you can control the universe if only you learn the correct words.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive grace.
Trust the Father.
Pray boldly.
Speak truth.
Love people.
And when circumstances refuse to obey your voice, remember that they have never escaped His authority.
You were never asked to become God.
You were invited to become His child.
And perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying into every impossible room you will ever enter:
You don't have to speak your future into existence when your future is already in the hands of the God who gives life to the dead.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TEST ME IN THIS” — The Verse Prosperity Preachers Love… But Malachi Was Never a Get-Rich Formula
paragraphs:
“TEST ME IN THIS” — The Verse Prosperity Preachers Love… But Malachi Was Never a Get-Rich Formula
God really did say, “Test Me.” But before you turn Malachi 3:10 into a promise that giving money will make you rich, you need to hear what God was actually confronting—and why the truth is far more dangerous to your heart than a prosperity sermon.
There is something almost shocking about Malachi 3:10.
God says:
“Test Me in this.”
Those words sound daring.
Almost reckless.

Especially when they are pulled out of their setting, placed beneath a giving envelope, projected onto a church screen, or followed by a testimony about somebody who gave their last hundred dollars and mysteriously received a thousand the next week.
You have probably heard some version of it.
“Give, and God will give you more.”
“Sow your seed.”
“Release what is in your hand so God can release what is in His.”
“God said to test Him. Try Him. Give your tithe and watch what happens to your finances.”
And then Malachi 3:10 appears:
“Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse... Test me in this... and see if I will not throw open the floodgates of heaven and pour out so much blessing...”
It sounds almost mathematical.
You give.
God multiplies.
You tithe.
God increases your income.
You sow $100.
He sends $1,000.
Christianity becomes an investment strategy with heaven as the bank.
But there is a problem.
That is not what Malachi was saying.
And if we reduce this passage to a divine wealth formula, we may actually repeat the very spiritual sickness Malachi was confronting.
Because Malachi 3 is not primarily about people discovering the secret to becoming wealthy.
It is about covenant unfaithfulness.
It is about worship.
It is about a people who belonged to God while withholding from God.
And underneath the money was something much deeper.
Their hearts.
Listen to the Hebrew.
Malachi 3:10 begins:
הָבִיאוּ אֶת־כָּל־הַמַּעֲשֵׂר אֶל־בֵּית הָאוֹצָר
Hāḇîʾû ʾeṯ-kol-hammaʿăśēr ʾel-bêṯ hāʾôṣār.
“Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse.”
The word מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿăśēr) means “tenth” or “tithe.”
The storehouse—בֵּית הָאוֹצָר (bêṯ hāʾôṣār)—belongs to the world of Israel’s covenant worship and temple economy.
This was not Malachi introducing a twenty-first-century fundraising technique.
He was speaking to covenant Israel.
That matters enormously.
The Old Testament tithe existed within Israel’s covenant life, involving agricultural produce, livestock, support for the Levites, worship, communal celebration, and provision for vulnerable people.
Read Numbers 18.
Read Deuteronomy 14.
Read Nehemiah 10 and 13.
Then return to Malachi.
Suddenly the passage begins breathing in its own world again.
God was not standing before modern Christians saying:
“Transfer ten percent to a ministry and I guarantee financial multiplication.”
He was confronting His covenant people because something had gone terribly wrong in their relationship with Him.
And Malachi had already exposed it.
They were offering polluted sacrifices.
They were dishonoring God.
Priests had corrupted their responsibilities.
Covenant faithfulness was collapsing.
Justice was being violated.
And then God says:
“Will a man rob God?”
The Hebrew is piercing:
הֲיִקְבַּע אָדָם אֱלֹהִים
Hayiqbaʿ ʾādām ʾĕlōhîm?
“Will a human being rob God?”
And Israel essentially responds:
“What are You talking about?”
God answers:
“In tithes and contributions.”
That exchange reveals something uncomfortable.
Their giving problem was a worship problem.
Their worship problem was a heart problem.
And heart problems have a strange ability to hide behind religious appearances.
You can sing while withholding yourself.
You can pray while protecting an idol.
You can attend church while quietly telling Jesus:
“You may have this part of me, Lord.
Just don't touch that part.”
Money merely has a remarkable ability to reveal where that boundary has been drawn.
That is why Jesus spoke about money so penetratingly.
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Notice the order.
Treasure.
Then heart.
Jesus understood something we desperately want to avoid.
Our bank statements can sometimes expose our theology more honestly than our worship songs.
But that still does not make Malachi 3:10 a get-rich formula.
Now we reach the famous words:
וּבְחָנוּנִי נָא בָּזֹאת
Ûḇəḥānûnî nāʾ bāzōʾṯ.
“Test Me, please, in this.”
The verb comes from בחן (bḥn), carrying the idea of examining, testing, or proving.
Yes.
God really does invite Israel to test Him here.
We should not explain that away simply because the verse has been abused.
But we must allow God to define the test.
Not the prosperity preacher.
Not the fundraiser.
Not our desire for financial security.
God.
Israel had withheld what belonged within its covenant obligations, and God called the nation to return to covenant faithfulness and discover that He Himself remained faithful.
That is dramatically different from saying:
“Give God money and He is contractually obligated to make you rich.”
Then comes the image everybody remembers:
אֲרֻבּוֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם
ʾărubbôṯ haššāmayim.
The “windows” or “floodgates of heaven.”
That language is powerful.
But keep reading.
God speaks about rebuking the “devourer,” protecting the fruit of the ground, preventing the vine from failing, and the nations recognizing Israel's blessed condition.
This is agricultural covenant language.
Land.
Crops.
Harvest.
Fruitfulness.
Protection.
