Babylon persecutes those she cannot seduce.
And the Lamb?
The Lamb conquers.
Revelation 17:14 gives away the ending before Babylon even falls:
The Lamb will overcome them.
Why?
Because He is Lord of lords and King of kings.
There is the center of the chapter.
Not the prostitute.
Not Babylon.
Not the beast.
Not Rome.
Not Satan.
Jesus Christ.
This is something we repeatedly get wrong when reading Revelation.
We become fascinated with the beast and forget the Lamb.
We chase timelines and overlook worship.
We argue over symbols while ignoring repentance.
We attempt to identify Babylon while Babylon's values quietly colonize our hearts.
But Revelation was not written merely to satisfy curiosity about tomorrow.
It was written to produce faithfulness today.
And that means the appropriate response to Revelation 17 is not:
“Who can I accuse of being Babylon?”
It is:
“Jesus, show me where I have been drinking from her cup.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because Christ may expose something.
Maybe your Christianity has become a performance.
Maybe you know worship songs but barely know the One being worshiped.
Maybe your Bible gathers dust while your screen receives hours of your attention.
Maybe pornography has been discipling your imagination.
Maybe money has been discipling your decisions.
Maybe outrage has been discipling your emotions.
Maybe approval has been discipling your identity.
Maybe comfort has been discipling your obedience.
Maybe you have learned how to appear spiritually alive while privately becoming numb.
Nobody knows.
You still smile.
Still post Scripture.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still attend church.
Still encourage other people.
But somewhere inside you...
something has gone quiet.
You remember when conviction came quickly.
You remember when prayer felt less complicated.
You remember when you wanted Jesus more than you wanted the appearance of wanting Jesus.
And perhaps reading this has uncovered the thing you have been trying not to name.
Listen carefully.
Exposure is not always condemnation.
Sometimes exposure is mercy.
Jesus exposes what He intends to heal.
The Gospel is not the announcement that clean people are welcomed while dirty people are rejected.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can come home because Jesus Christ took judgment upon Himself.
That is why the imagery of Revelation must never become an excuse for Christians to shame sexually broken people.
Jesus was repeatedly compassionate toward people carrying sexual shame while remaining absolutely truthful about sin.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Remember the Samaritan woman whose relational history Jesus already knew.
Christ did not need their secrets explained to Him.
He knew.
And still He engaged them.
Still He called.
Still He offered grace.
Still He called people away from sin.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus does not save us because our history is respectable.
He saves us because His blood is sufficient.
You may have committed sexual sin.
You may have betrayed someone.
You may have lived for money.
You may have worshiped success.
You may have sold pieces of your conscience for acceptance.
You may have consumed things privately you would be horrified for anyone to discover.
You may have spent years drinking from Babylon's cup.
But Babylon does not get the final word over your identity.
Jesus does.
The cross means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning building.
That is why another voice eventually thunders in Revelation:
“Come out of her, my people.”
Notice those words.
My people.
There is ownership there.
Affection.
A summons.
God is calling His people away from participation in Babylon.
Come out.
Not because Babylon has nothing attractive to offer.
Come out precisely because it does.
Come out before luxury becomes your master.
Come out before compromise becomes normal.
Come out before your conscience stops hurting.
Come out before you exchange eternal treasure for temporary applause.
Come out before the golden cup convinces you that poison is wine.
Come out because Babylon falls.
That is the unavoidable message of Revelation 18.
Merchants mourn.
Kings mourn.
The economic machine that seemed untouchable collapses.
What looked permanent disappears.
What appeared invincible receives judgment.
And heaven does not mourn Babylon as though God's kingdom has suffered defeat.
Because Babylon was never eternal.
Jesus is.
That is the choice Revelation places before us.
Two kingdoms.
Two allegiances.
Two visions of reality.
Babylon says, “Take.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Babylon says, “Make yourself great.”
Jesus says, “Deny yourself.”
Babylon says, “Protect your image.”
Jesus says, “Walk in the light.”
Babylon says, “Buy enough and you will matter.”
Jesus says you were worth His blood before you could purchase anything.
Babylon says, “Use people.”
Jesus says, “Love one another.”
Babylon says, “Worship power.”
Jesus washes feet.
Babylon wears scarlet.
Jesus wore our shame.
Babylon holds a golden cup filled with corruption.
Jesus took another cup—the cup of suffering—and drank what sinners deserved.
Do you see it?
Revelation is ultimately presenting competing loves.
Babylon seduces.
Christ redeems.
Babylon intoxicates.
Christ awakens.
Babylon enslaves.
Christ liberates.
Babylon consumes her lovers.
Christ gives Himself for His bride.
And when Babylon's beauty has turned to ashes...
the Lamb is still standing.
Maybe you needed that sentence tonight.
Maybe everything you trusted has been shaking.
Maybe something you thought would satisfy you has left you emptier.
Maybe sin promised pleasure and handed you chains.
Maybe success gave you applause but stole your peace.
Maybe religion gave you an image while your heart remained far from God.
Then hear the Gospel again.
You can come home.
Not after you repair yourself.
Not after you become impressive.
Not after you erase your history.
Come to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Surrender.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is no scandal so filthy that His grace becomes insufficient for the genuinely repentant sinner.
There is no chain so respectable that Jesus will allow us to keep calling it freedom.
Grace does not merely forgive the old life.
Grace begins transforming us into something new.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Stay here for a moment.
Talk to Him.
You do not need impressive words.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Sometimes surrender begins with four words spoken honestly.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need mercy is one small way of refusing to hide anymore.
Someone reading may desperately need proof that chains really can break.
Not merely because an algorithm rewards sharing.
They may never tell you.
They may look successful.
They may post smiling photographs.
They may laugh at work.
They may sit beside you in church.
And they may be silently wondering whether Jesus would still receive them if anyone knew the truth.
Send it privately to someone who needs grace more than another lecture.
There is also a practical reality behind this ministry.
Biblical content, discipleship resources, books, research, outreach, and the continued building of resources for believers require people willing to stand behind the work.
It does not make someone a better Christian.
It does not earn spiritual blessing.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people with Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the hope found in Jesus Christ.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
“Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved.”
Our mission is simply to keep pointing people toward Him.
Because someday Babylon's music stops.
The merchants stop selling.
The applause stops.
The screens go dark.
The gold changes hands.
The houses belong to somebody else.
The titles disappear.
The followers forget.
The body returns to dust.
And every glittering thing this world told us we could not live without will finally reveal how temporary it always was.
But Jesus Christ will still be King.
So before you take another drink from the cup this world keeps passing around...
look inside it.
Then look at the Lamb.
And choose carefully what gets your heart.
Because the most dangerous thing about Babylon was never that she looked evil—it was that she looked beautiful enough to make people forget they were made for God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “CALEB PROMISED HIS DAUGHTER TO THE MAN WHO CAPTURED A CITY”
paragraphs: “CALEB PROMISED HIS DAUGHTER TO THE MAN WHO CAPTURED A CITY”
The strange story of Achsah, Othniel, a conquered city, two springs of water—and the uncomfortable question of what real faith does when God places an inheritance in front of you.
There are verses in the Bible we underline.
There are verses we frame.
There are verses we whisper when the hospital room gets quiet, when the marriage is shaking, when the money is disappearing, when fear crawls into bed beside us at two in the morning.
And then...
there are verses like this one.
Verses that make you stop.
Read them again.
And wonder:
“Wait... Caleb did WHAT?”
Joshua 15:16 records these startling words:
“Caleb said, ‘He that smiteth Kiriath-sepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.’”
The Hebrew is even more direct:
וַיֹּאמֶר כָּלֵב אֲשֶׁר־יַכֶּה אֶת־קִרְיַת־סֵפֶר וּלְכָדָהּ וְנָתַתִּי לוֹ אֶת־עַכְסָה בִתִּי לְאִשָּׁה
Vayyomer Kalev, asher-yakkeh et-Qiryat-Sefer ulekadah, venatatti lo et-Aksah bitti le'ishah.
In straightforward English:
“And Caleb said, whoever attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as a wife.”

That really is what the Hebrew says. The verbs יַכֶּה (yakkeh) and וּלְכָדָהּ (ulekadah) carry the sense of striking/attacking and capturing the city, while לְאִשָּׁה (le'ishah) means “as a wife.” Joshua 15:16–17 then identifies the victor as Othniel son of Kenaz, a relative of Caleb, and says Caleb fulfilled the promise.
It sounds almost like the opening scene of an ancient war epic.
A fortified city stands unconquered.
Caleb looks at the men around him.
Then he makes an announcement that would stop almost any modern reader cold:
Capture that city...
and you will marry my daughter.

But before we rush to condemn Caleb, defend Caleb, romanticize Othniel, or turn Achsah into a helpless character the Bible itself never describes her as being, we need to do something increasingly rare.
We need to let Scripture speak before our assumptions speak for it.
Because the Bible tells us what Caleb announced.
It tells us who captured the city.
It tells us that Achsah became Othniel's wife.
But it does not tell us every conversation that happened inside that family.
It does not record Achsah's response to the proposed marriage.
It does not tell us everything about the customs surrounding the arrangement.
It does not give us permission to invent a romance between Achsah and Othniel.
And it certainly does not command Christian fathers today to offer their daughters as rewards for military victories.
This is narrative.
It describes something that happened in Israel's conquest of Canaan; it is not automatically a prescription for Christian courtship.
That distinction matters.
But something else matters too.
If you stop reading at verse 17, you may completely misunderstand the woman at the center of this story.
Because Achsah does not disappear.
She speaks.
She acts.
She asks.
And suddenly the woman who can initially appear to modern readers as merely part of Caleb's promise becomes one of the most memorable personalities in the scene.
After Othniel captures Kiriath-sepher, Achsah approaches her father.
Caleb asks her:
“What wouldest thou?”
And Achsah answers:
“Give me a blessing.”
Then she explains the problem.
She has been given land in the Negev—the dry country—and she needs water.
“Give me also springs of water.”
And Caleb responds by giving her the upper springs and the lower springs.
The Hebrew preserves the force of her request:
תְּנָה־לִּי בְרָכָה
Tenah-li berakhah.
“Give me a blessing.”
Then:
וְנָתַתָּה לִי גֻּלֹּת מָיִם
Venatattah li gullot mayim.
“Give me springs of water.”
And Caleb gives them to her.
Not one spring.
The text says he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
Do you see her differently now?
Achsah is not silent in the scene Scripture actually records.
She understands what she has received.
She recognizes what it lacks.
And she has enough confidence to approach her father and ask for what is necessary.
She had land.
But land without water in a dry country could become an inheritance that could not flourish.
So she asked for springs.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story begins crawling uncomfortably close to our own lives.
Because some of us have been standing on land God has given us...
while dying of thirst.
You have the job.
But no peace.
You have the house.
But something inside that house is breaking.
You have the marriage photographs.
But intimacy disappeared years ago.
You have the Bible app.
The worship playlist.
The Christian posts.
The church attendance.
Maybe even a ministry.
And yet somewhere underneath everything visible...
your soul is dry.
You learned how to look blessed while secretly becoming thirsty.
You learned the Christian vocabulary.
“I’m good.”
“God is faithful.”
“Just busy.”
“Keep me in prayer.”
But behind the language there are nights when you wonder why you cannot feel what you once felt.
Prayer became shorter.
Temptation became easier.
Conviction became quieter.
Your Bible stayed closed longer.
And gradually you became skilled at surviving spiritually without admitting that something inside you desperately needed water.
Achsah's words suddenly become painfully personal:
“Give me a blessing... give me also springs of water.”
Not more appearances.
Not another religious performance.
Water.
And that is where this story must ultimately lead beyond Caleb, beyond Othniel, beyond Achsah, beyond Kiriath-sepher...
to Jesus Christ.
Because centuries later, another thirsty person would meet someone beside water.
A Samaritan woman came to Jacob's well carrying a jar.
She expected water.
Instead, she encountered Jesus.
And Christ told her that whoever drank the water He gave would not remain trapped in the same thirst forever; the water He gives becomes a spring welling up to eternal life.
Then, in John 7, Jesus cried out that anyone who thirsts should come to Him and drink.
This is the Gospel.
Christianity is not Jesus helping reasonably good people become slightly better versions of themselves.
The Gospel begins with a far more devastating diagnosis.
We have sinned.
Not merely stumbled.
Not merely developed bad habits.
We have rebelled against the holy God who created us.
We have loved things He hates.
Ignored things He commands.
Worshiped ourselves.
Hidden our darkness.
Justified our pride.
Excused our lust.
Fed our bitterness.
Protected secret sins while asking God to bless public lives.
Romans says that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
And the wages of sin is death.
That is the scandal.
But it is not the end of the story.
Because God did not wait for sinners to conquer enough cities, clean themselves up, prove themselves worthy, or earn their way home.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteous life we could never live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Grace is not God pretending your sin was insignificant.
Grace is God dealing with sin at the cross at a cost we could never pay ourselves.
You do not purchase that grace.
You do not earn it through religious activity.
You do not buy enough Christian books to deserve it.
You cannot donate your way into heaven.
Salvation is the gift of God received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that matters enough to say plainly.
Because no ministry deserves the place that belongs to Christ alone.
Not this ministry.
Not any preacher.
Not any church.
Not any platform.
Jesus saves.
But when grace truly reaches a person, something changes.
We begin asking a different question.
Not:
“How little can I give God and still call myself Christian?”
But:
“Lord, after everything You have done for me... what part of my life still belongs to me?”
That question reaches deeper than money.
Your reputation.
Your time.
Your plans.
Your sexuality.
Your ambition.
Your wounds.
Your grudges.
Your private browser history.
Your relationships.
Your future.
Your platform.
Your possessions.
Your voice.
Your whole life.
The Christian response to grace is not purchasing God's favor.
It is surrender.
And suddenly Caleb's story carries another echo.
Long before Kiriath-sepher, Caleb himself had stood before something frightening.
He had seen giants.
He had seen fortified cities.
He had heard the fearful report of the other spies.
Yet Caleb refused to let the size of the enemy become larger in his imagination than the faithfulness of God.
Decades passed.
Forty-five years.
Then at eighty-five years old, Caleb stood before Joshua and essentially said:
Give me the mountain.
Joshua 14 says he had followed the LORD wholeheartedly. Caleb himself acknowledged that victory depended upon the LORD being with him.
Do not miss that.
Biblical courage is not pretending giants are small.
Biblical courage knows giants are real...
and believes God is greater.
There is a counterfeit faith that says, “Nothing bad will happen.”
Biblical faith says:
“Even if the battle is real, God remains God.”
And maybe there is a Kiriath-sepher standing in your life right now.
Something fortified.
Something you have walked around so long that you started calling captivity normal.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Adultery.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Secret messages.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
An unforgiving heart.
A double life.
A prayerlessness nobody sees.
A church wound that slowly became an excuse to abandon Jesus.
A private compromise you promised would happen only once.
Except once became occasionally.
Occasionally became regularly.
Regularly became secretly.
And secretly became slavery.
There are cities in the human heart that do not surrender because we rename them.
Some things must be brought into the light.
Some things must be confessed.
Some things must be cut off.
Some things require repentance.
And repentance is more than feeling terrible after sinning.
It is turning.
You cannot keep hugging the chains while asking Jesus to make captivity comfortable.
Christ came to forgive sinners...
and to transform them.
Maybe you have spent years believing the worst chapter of your life became the title of your entire story.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Rejected.
Unfaithful.
Abused.
Betrayed.
Bankrupt.
Ashamed.
Backslidden.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Too far gone.
But the Gospel has never depended upon your worst chapter having the final word.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated history to a well and walked away telling people about Christ.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace reached him before death did.
That is why we keep saying it:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because Christianity teaches us to pretend wounds never happened.
Jesus rewrites everything because when Christ redeems a sinner, sin no longer possesses the authority to write the ending.
Your scars may remain.
But scars are not the same thing as open wounds.
Your testimony may contain chapters you wish had never existed.
But Jesus is capable of taking the chapter Satan wanted to use as your obituary and making it part of the testimony that points somebody else toward the cross.
Look again at Achsah.
“Give me a blessing.”
She knew where to go.
She knew what she needed.
She asked.
And her father gave her springs.
There are people reading this who need to stop performing and finally ask.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I cannot defeat this by pretending anymore.”
“Jesus, my heart is dry.”
“Jesus, bring me back.”
“Jesus, I need mercy.”
You do not need impressive language.
The tax collector in Jesus' parable prayed essentially:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
Sometimes the beginning of restoration sounds less like a sermon...
and more like surrender.
So be honest.
Not because typing words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing what has been hidden into the light begins with finally refusing to pretend.
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply write:
And if God has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell us.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need the testimony you almost decided not to share.
Your scars might become somebody else's evidence that surviving is possible.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
Somebody scrolling tonight may be smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Somebody you love may never walk through the doors of your church...
but they might read something you place in front of them.
Send this to the believer who feels ashamed to come back.
There may come a night when you are the one who needs to remember it.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not because salvation is for sale.

But because Gospel work is carried forward when believers voluntarily decide that biblical teaching, discipleship resources, evangelistic content, and Christ-centered encouragement are worth helping sustain.
Support ministries when you prayerfully choose to.
Share truth freely.
Give generously.
Serve faithfully.
But worship Jesus alone.
Because one day Gospel Warrior will disappear.
Every Facebook page will disappear.
Every book will eventually crumble.
Every platform will become obsolete.
Every follower count will become meaningless.
But Christ will remain.
And perhaps that is what makes this strange ancient story worth remembering.
A city had to be confronted.
A warrior stepped forward.
A daughter received land.
Then she realized land was not enough.
She needed water.
And she asked for springs.
Maybe you have spent years asking God for land when what your soul actually needed was Living Water.
Maybe you have chased success, recognition, relationships, money, comfort, applause, influence, and religious appearance...
only to discover that a human soul can possess enormous territory and still die thirsty.
So come to Christ.
Not the polished version of you.
You.
The ashamed you.
The tired you.
The addicted you.
The angry you.
The doubting you.
The wounded you.
The you who promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Come empty-handed.
Because Christianity was never the announcement that good people had finally climbed high enough to reach God.
It is the announcement that in Jesus Christ...
God came down to rescue sinners.
The cross says your sin is worse than your excuses wanted to admit.
The cross also says God's grace is greater than your shame wanted you to believe.
And the empty tomb declares that death itself does not get the final sentence.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be complicated.
“Father...
I have the land.
But I need the water.
I have the appearance.
But I need Jesus.
I have been hiding.
I am tired.
Forgive me.
Cleanse me.
Change me.
I surrender.”
And when you rise from that prayer, do not merely admire the city that needs confronting.
Walk with Christ toward it.
Do not merely talk about the chains.
Bring them into the light.
Do not merely repost the Gospel.
Live like you have actually been rescued by it.
There are still fortified cities.
There are still thirsty hearts.
There are still people hiding behind smiles.
There are still prodigals wondering whether the Father would receive them.
There are still sinners convinced they have gone too far.
And there is still a Savior whose grace reaches farther.
Never let the chapter where you fell convince you that Jesus has finished writing your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MICAIAH SAW THE SHEEP SCATTERED — THEN THE SHEPHERD CAME
paragraphs: MICAIAH SAW THE SHEEP SCATTERED — THEN THE SHEPHERD CAME
When everyone around you is saying what you want to hear, the most merciful voice in the room may be the one that breaks your heart.
There is a terrifying moment in 1 Kings 22 that almost feels too familiar.
A king wants reassurance.
An army is preparing for battle.
Hundreds of prophetic voices are telling him essentially the same thing.
Go.
Fight.
You will succeed.
Victory is coming.
Then one unwanted prophet opens his mouth.
Micaiah.
And suddenly the atmosphere changes.
Because Micaiah sees something no flattering voice wants to talk about.
Not victory.
Not celebration.
Not a triumphant king returning from war.
Sheep.
Scattered sheep.
Sheep wandering across mountains with nobody leading them home.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story still reaches into the places we try hardest to hide.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to be one of those sheep.
You can look successful and still be scattered inside.
You can sit in church and still feel spiritually homeless.
You can know worship songs, quote Bible verses, post Christian content, tell everybody “God is good,” and still quietly wonder how you wandered this far from the Shepherd.
That is where Micaiah's vision becomes painfully personal.
The Hebrew of 1 Kings 22:17 reads:
וַיֹּאמֶר רָאִיתִי אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל נְפֹצִים אֶל־הֶהָרִים כַּצֹּאן אֲשֶׁר אֵין־לָהֶם רֹעֶה וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה לֹא־אֲדֹנִים לָאֵלֶּה יָשׁוּבוּ אִישׁ־לְבֵיתוֹ בְּשָׁלוֹם׃
A close translation is:
“I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, like sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, ‘These have no master; let each return to his house in peace.’”
The imagery is devastating.
The Hebrew word נְפֹצִים, nefoṣim, carries the sense of being scattered or dispersed.
And then comes the image כַּצֹּאן אֲשֶׁר אֵין־לָהֶם רֹעֶה — “like sheep for whom there is no shepherd.”
רֹעֶה, ro‘eh, is “shepherd.”
This was not merely a picturesque description of frightened soldiers.
Micaiah was standing before King Ahab.
The shepherd of Israel was about to fall.
The people who had followed him into battle would be left without their king.
To understand how chilling this moment is, you have to hear all the voices surrounding Micaiah.
Ahab, king of Israel, wants to recover Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, is with him, but Jehoshaphat asks that they first inquire for the word of the LORD.
So the prophets are assembled.
About four hundred men.
Their message overwhelmingly points in the direction Ahab wants.
Go up.
The Lord will give it into the king's hand.
One prophet, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah, even makes iron horns and dramatically declares that Israel will gore the Arameans until they are destroyed.
It is loud.
Confident.
Religious.
Impressive.
There is only one problem.
Jehoshaphat senses that something is missing.
“Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?”
There is.
Ahab knows exactly who he is.
And Ahab does not want him.
Listen carefully to the king's reason.
“I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil.”
That sentence should frighten every person who has ever wanted God to agree with them more than they wanted God to correct them.
Ahab did not primarily want truth.
He wanted confirmation.
And there is a difference.
A dangerous difference.
Sometimes we do the same thing with Scripture.
We do not open the Bible asking, “Lord, what is true?”
We open it hoping to find permission for what we have already decided.
We search for teachers who will never confront our favorite sin.
We keep friends who affirm everything.
We avoid Christians who love us enough to ask uncomfortable questions.
We call conviction “judgment.”
We call correction “negativity.”
We call compromise “grace.”
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, we build a spiritual echo chamber where God is supposedly always saying exactly what we already wanted to hear.
But God loves us too much to become the echo of our desires.
Micaiah arrives.
Even the messenger bringing him to the king pressures him beforehand. The other prophets are speaking favorably, so Micaiah is encouraged to make his message agree with theirs.
Imagine that pressure.
Hundreds against one.
The king wants one answer.
The room wants one answer.
The political momentum wants one answer.
The military plan is already moving toward one answer.
Just say what everybody else is saying.
Micaiah responds:
“As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak.”
That is courage.
Not loudness.
Not arrogance.
Not enjoying confrontation.
Courage is being more afraid of misrepresenting God than of disappointing people.
When Micaiah initially tells Ahab to go and prosper, the king recognizes that something is wrong and demands the truth. Then Micaiah gives him the vision he did not want.
Israel scattered across the mountains.
Sheep without a shepherd.
Ahab understands.
The message concerns him.
And yet the tragedy of the chapter is not merely that Ahab hears a warning.
The tragedy is that he hears it and still goes.
Think about that.
He was warned.
And still went.
He heard the word.
And still went.
He knew Micaiah had spoken against the battle.
And still went.
Then Ahab tries something almost painfully human.
He disguises himself.
He tells Jehoshaphat that he himself will enter the battle disguised while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes.
Perhaps a disguise can confuse the enemy.
But no disguise can hide a man from the sovereignty of God.
Then comes one of Scripture's most sobering details.
An Aramean soldier draws his bow “at random.”
No carefully identified royal target.
No humanly calculated shot at Ahab.
Just an arrow released into the chaos of battle.
And it strikes the king between the scale armor and the breastplate.
The disguised king is found by an arrow that did not know his name.
Ahab remains propped up in his chariot while the battle rages.
His blood pours into the bottom of the chariot.
By evening, he is dead.
Then the cry goes through the army:
“Every man to his city, and every man to his country!”
The sheep scatter.
Micaiah's word stands.
The king who hated the truth could reject the prophet.
He could imprison the prophet.
He could disguise himself.
He could go into battle anyway.
But he could not make the Word of God untrue.
And this is where the story stops being merely about Ahab.
Because there is an Ahab-shaped temptation inside the human heart.
We want God near enough to bless us but not always near enough to rule us.
We want promises without repentance.
Comfort without correction.
A Savior without a Lord.
A shepherd who carries us when we hurt but never uses His staff to pull us away from the cliff.
Yet Scripture does not give us that Jesus.
And thank God it does not.
Because a shepherd who refuses to warn sheep about a cliff does not love the sheep.
Maybe you have been running.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your family thinks you are fine.
Your church friends think you are fine.
You learned how to smile while your soul was bleeding.
You learned how to say, “I'm blessed,” while something inside you was slowly collapsing.
Maybe the sin you promised would happen once became a pattern.
Maybe bitterness moved into your heart and started rearranging the furniture.
Maybe pornography became the place you disappear when loneliness gets too loud.
Maybe pride convinced you that everybody else needs correction except you.
Maybe disappointment with God hardened into distance from God.
Maybe you stopped praying because you were ashamed of what you had become.
Maybe you are not openly rebelling.
You are simply drifting.
And drifting feels harmless until you look up and cannot remember where the Shepherd is.
But the Bible's story of sheep does not end on the mountains of 1 Kings 22.
That is where the Gospel begins to shine.
Centuries later, Jesus looks at crowds of exhausted, hurting people.
Matthew 9:36 says He had compassion on them because they were “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.”
There is the image again.
Sheep.
Without a shepherd.
But something has changed.
This time the Shepherd is standing in front of them.
Jesus does not merely diagnose the scattered condition.
He comes to rescue the scattered.
He later declares in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
Do not rush past that.
The Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
The Gospel is not the story of lost sheep somehow becoming intelligent enough to navigate themselves home.
It is the story of the Shepherd coming for sinners.
Isaiah had already confessed the human condition:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way.”
That is us.
Not merely Ahab.
Us.
We wandered.
We sinned.
We chose our own way.
We wanted autonomy.
We wanted to decide good and evil for ourselves.
We wanted God when convenient and ourselves on the throne when He was not.
Yet Isaiah continues with the astonishing announcement that “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
The sheep wandered.
The Shepherd bore the judgment.
This is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Christ did not die because humanity was basically good and needed encouragement.
He died because sinners needed reconciliation with a holy God.
He carried sin.
He endured judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
Grace is not God pretending your rebellion never mattered.
Grace is God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost and offering forgiveness to sinners through Jesus Christ.
That means your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your life.
Your adultery does not get the last word.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your secret compromise does not get the last word.
Your years of wandering do not get the last word.
Your hypocrisy does not get the last word.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your failure does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
This is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because Jesus edits sin until it looks respectable.
Not because grace teaches us to rename darkness.
Jesus rewrites everything because He forgives sinners, makes the spiritually dead alive, calls wanderers home, gives His Spirit to His people, and begins transforming those who belong to Him.
Peter later writes to believers:
Returned.
Maybe that is the word somebody reading this needs tonight.
Returned.
Not pretended.
Not performed.
Not polished.
Returned.
You do not need another disguise.
Ahab wore one.
It did not save him.
And yours will not save you either.
The Christian disguise cannot save you.
The church attendance cannot save you.
The Bible verses in your bio cannot save you.
Religious vocabulary cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your good deeds cannot erase your guilt.
Only Christ saves.
So come into the light.
Repent.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Biblical repentance turns from sin toward God.
Stop defending what Christ died to deliver you from.
Stop negotiating with the thing destroying your fellowship with God.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy enough to come home.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
That is why it is grace.
Come because Christ is merciful.
Come because His blood is sufficient.
Come because the risen Jesus still receives sinners who turn to Him in faith.
Come because the Good Shepherd still calls wandering sheep.
And maybe, beneath everything else, this is what hurts most about Micaiah's story:
Ahab received a warning before the arrow came.
There was mercy even in the warning.
The hard word was not evidence that God had failed to speak.
It was evidence that Ahab had been given truth before judgment arrived.
Some warnings are mercy wearing uncomfortable clothes.
Perhaps this article is uncomfortable for you.
Perhaps a name came into your mind.
Perhaps a hidden habit did.
Perhaps you immediately knew the area where you have been asking God to approve something He has already told you to surrender.
Do not waste that conviction.
Do not scroll quickly enough to silence it.
Bring it to Jesus.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is restoration.
There is a Shepherd.
And if you belong to Him, there is a way home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
If your soul has been scattered lately and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if you know the Shepherd has been patiently restoring you, tell somebody beneath this article, “Christ is still healing me.”
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer needed to see.
Do not turn the comments into a place for pretending.
Let them become a place where people point one another toward Christ.
And think of one person who needs this message.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend whose faith has become quiet.
The brother hiding behind jokes.
The daughter who stopped talking about God.
The father carrying private shame.
The Christian who has become comfortable with compromise.
The person who does not yet know Christ.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by supporting a page, purchasing a product, or performing religious works.
If you desire to glorify God, glorify Him first through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, holiness, generosity, worship, and a life surrendered to Him.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is having another place in your daily life calling you away from spiritual numbness and back toward Scripture.
It is being reminded of Jesus when the world has spent all day teaching your heart to forget Him.
There may come a night when you need to read it again.
A night when compromise starts sounding reasonable.
A night when shame tells you to hide.
A night when everybody around you is saying what you want to hear and you desperately need someone who loves you enough to tell you the truth.
Micaiah saw Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd.
But Scripture eventually reveals something infinitely greater.
The Shepherd came.
His name is Jesus.
He came for wanderers.
He came for sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
He came for people whose public image and private life stopped matching a long time ago.
He came not merely to improve them but to redeem them.
And the hands of the Good Shepherd bear scars.
So when conviction comes, do not mistake the Shepherd's voice for rejection.
When His Word exposes you, do not run farther into the mountains.
When Christ calls you away from sin, do not resent Him for ruining the illusion that everything is fine.
The Shepherd is not trying to destroy you by calling you out of darkness.
He is calling you home.
Where have you been asking the Shepherd to follow you instead of surrendering and following Him?
If you cannot explain it yet, just write:
Because the most dangerous place for a sheep is not admitting that it wandered.
It is becoming comfortable without the Shepherd.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN DESCRIBED THE MAN SHE LOVED FROM HEAD TO TOE — BUT THE LAST THING SHE SAID ABOUT HIM CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: THE WOMAN DESCRIBED THE MAN SHE LOVED FROM HEAD TO TOE — BUT THE LAST THING SHE SAID ABOUT HIM CHANGES EVERYTHING

Song of Songs 5:10–16 is breathtakingly intimate. But beneath the gold, ravens, doves, spices, ivory, marble, and cedars is something our generation desperately needs to remember: when love is real, you don't merely recognize the one you love—you know why he is precious to you.
She had lost sight of him.
That is where the story really begins.
And maybe that is why this ancient love poem can hit a modern heart with such unexpected force.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to realize the value of someone after distance has entered the room.
Earlier in Song of Songs 5, the woman hears her beloved knocking.
She hesitates.
Then she rises.
But when she finally opens the door...
he is gone.
She searches for him.
She calls for him.
There is no answer.
She moves through the city looking for the man she loves, and the night becomes brutal. The watchmen find her. They strike her. They wound her. They take away her covering.
Then she cries to the daughters of Jerusalem that she is sick with love.
And they ask her what is essentially one devastating question:
What makes your beloved so special?
Why him?
Why are you searching like this?
Why does this man matter so much?
And suddenly this wounded woman begins to speak.
Not vaguely.
Not casually.
Not with a generic, "He's wonderful."
She remembers him.
From his head...
to his hair...
to his eyes...
to his cheeks...
to his lips...
to his hands...
to his body...
to his legs...
to his appearance...
to his mouth.
It is one of Scripture's most striking poetic portraits of romantic admiration.
The Hebrew begins:
"דּוֹדִי צַח וְאָדוֹם דָּגוּל מֵרְבָבָה"
Dodi tsach ve'adom, dagul mer'vavah.
"My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand."
The word דּוֹדִי — dodi — means "my beloved."
Not merely a beloved.
Mine.
There is relationship in that word.
Affection.
Attachment.
History.
She is not describing a stranger she happens to find attractive. She is remembering the one her heart knows.
Then comes the extraordinary expression:
דָּגוּל מֵרְבָבָה
dagul mer'vavah.
He is conspicuous, distinguished, outstanding among a multitude.
Put him among ten thousand...
she would still know him.
And perhaps that is where this ancient poem begins asking us uncomfortable questions.
What has captured your eyes so completely that you can recognize it among ten thousand distractions?
What does your heart know that well?
We can recognize the notification sound of our phone from across a crowded room.
We recognize the logo of the brands we love.
We know the voices of celebrities.
The faces of athletes.
The lyrics of songs.
The details of fictional worlds.
We can scroll through hundreds of faces and stop instantly when we see someone important to us.
But if someone asked us tonight...
"What is so beautiful about Christ?"
Would we know what to say?
Not the Sunday-school answer.
Not the church answer.
Not something copied from somebody else's testimony.
If somebody looked directly into your eyes and asked:
"Why Jesus?"
Could you talk about Him like someone you actually know?
That question matters.
Because Christianity was never meant to be merely information about Christ.
It is reconciliation to God through Christ.
It is knowing Him.
Loving Him.
Following Him.
Trusting Him.
Being forgiven by Him.
Being transformed by Him.
The woman continues.
"רֹאשׁוֹ כֶּתֶם פָּז"
Roshó ketem paz.
"His head is finest gold."
Then:
"קְוֻצּוֹתָיו תַּלְתַּלִּים שְׁחֹרוֹת כָּעוֹרֵב"
His locks are curled, black like a raven.
She sees beauty in detail.
His eyes are compared to doves beside streams of water.
His cheeks to beds of spices.
His lips to lilies dripping myrrh.
His hands to gold.
His body to polished ivory adorned with precious stones.
His legs to marble pillars resting upon bases of gold.
His appearance to Lebanon.
Majestic like cedars.
This is extravagant Hebrew love poetry.
The images are not intended to produce a police sketch.
They communicate admiration, strength, beauty, preciousness, fragrance, dignity, vitality, and desire.
And we should be careful here.

Song of Songs, in its immediate literary setting, celebrates the love and desire between a man and a woman. We do not need to pretend every body part secretly represents Jesus in order to make the passage spiritual.
Scripture deserves better than forcing meanings into it.

But Christians cannot read about love, covenant, longing, beauty, faithfulness, bridegroom, and bride without eventually remembering that the larger biblical story leads us to Christ—the Bridegroom who loved His people and gave Himself for them.
The New Testament gives us that language.
And there the metaphor becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Because Jesus did not merely describe His love.
He demonstrated it.
At the cross.
Think about the difference.
The woman in Song of Songs describes the beauty of the man she loves from head to toe.
But when the Gospel shows us Jesus from head to toe...
what do we see?
A head crowned with thorns.
A face mocked and struck.
A mouth tasting suffering.
Hands pierced.
A body wounded.
Feet nailed.
Blood.
Shame.
Rejection.
A cross.
And somehow...
this is where divine love becomes impossible to dismiss.
Not because suffering itself is beautiful.
But because of who willingly endured it, and why.
"For God so loved the world..."
That is the scandal.
The Holy One came for sinners.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The King wore thorns.
The Creator was rejected by creatures.
The One through whom all things were made stretched His hands upon wood.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because humanity was already lovely.
He went because God is love.
He went for rebels.
For liars.
For adulterers.
For hypocrites.
For addicts.
For religious pretenders.
For proud people.
For broken people.
For people carrying secrets they hope nobody ever discovers.
For people who promised God, "Never again," and then did it again.
For people who know how to smile at church while privately falling apart.
Maybe...
for you.
And for me.
That is why grace is so shocking.
We spend our lives trying to make ourselves desirable enough to be loved.
Jesus came knowing the worst.
He knew what was underneath the polished photograph.
He knew the hidden browser history.
The resentment.
The envy.
The lust.
The secret conversation.
The pride disguised as spirituality.
The unforgiveness we renamed "boundaries" because we did not want to admit hatred had begun growing inside us.
He knew every room of the heart we kept locked.
And still...
Christ went to the cross.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Because biblical grace never says your sin did not matter.
The cross says it mattered so much that redemption cost blood.
And grace says God loved sinners enough to pay the price Himself in the person and work of Jesus Christ.
This is where Christianity becomes more than religion.
You are not saved because you became impressive.
You are saved by grace through faith.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the risen Jesus still calls sinners to repent, believe, come home, and follow Him.
Maybe you have spent years trying to clean yourself before returning to God.
Maybe you thought:
"When I stop struggling..."
"When I fix my marriage..."
"When I defeat this addiction..."
"When I become disciplined again..."
"When I finally feel worthy..."
"Then I'll come back."
Listen carefully.
If you could make yourself worthy of the cross...
you would not need the cross.
You come because you are needy.
You come because He is merciful.
You repent because sin destroys.
You believe because Christ saves.
You surrender because Jesus is Lord.
And then grace begins rewriting what sin tried to make permanent.
Your scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Peter's denial wasn't the final chapter.
The thief's crimes weren't the final chapter.
The Samaritan woman's history wasn't the final chapter.
Paul's persecution of believers wasn't the final chapter.
The cross itself looked like the final chapter on Friday.
Then Sunday came.
This is what Jesus does.
He walks into stories everyone else has already concluded...
and writes resurrection where people expected a period.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now we finally reach the line in Song of Songs that may be more beautiful than every physical description preceding it.
After describing him from head to toe, she says:
"חִכּוֹ מַמְתַקִּים וְכֻלּוֹ מַחֲמַדִּים"
Chikko mamtakkim, vechullo machamadim.
His mouth is sweetness...
and all of him is delightful.
Then she finishes:
"זֶה דוֹדִי וְזֶה רֵעִי"
Zeh dodi vezeh re'i.
"This is my beloved, and this is my friend."
Friend.
Do not rush past that.
After the poetry...
after the attraction...
after the gold...
after the ivory...
after the spices...
after the cedars...
she says:
This is my beloved.
And this is my friend.
Maybe that is part of what so many hearts are starving for.
To be known without performing.
To be loved without pretending.
To have someone close enough to know the truth.
Human relationships can give us beautiful glimpses of this, but no human being can carry the weight of being our savior.
Jesus can.
And Christ offers something deeper than sentimental spirituality.
He offers reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
New life.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new identity.
A new direction.
Not permission to remain enslaved to the old life.
Freedom to begin walking out of it.
So perhaps the question tonight is not merely:
"Do you believe Jesus exists?"
The demons know that.
The question is closer.
Do you know Him?
Has the Gospel moved from information in your head to the treasure of your heart?
If someone asked why Jesus is precious to you...
could you answer?
Could you remember the pit He pulled you from?
Could you remember the night you thought you would never survive?
Could you remember the prayer nobody heard?
Could you remember the shame you carried?
Could you remember how many times mercy found you after you had already given up on yourself?
Maybe your answer would not sound theological.
Maybe it would simply be:
"He didn't leave me."
Maybe:
"He forgave me."
Maybe:
"He found me when I wasn't looking for Him."
Maybe:
"I should have been destroyed by the life I was living, but Jesus had mercy on me."
Maybe:
"I'm still struggling... but I'm not who I used to be."
Not because a comment proves your faith.
It doesn't.
But because somebody reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who have never been wounded.
We are people learning where to bring our wounds.
You do not have to publish the details.
God already knows them.
But sometimes there is something powerful about finally refusing to pretend.
Let believers who see it pray.
Let the comment section become something better than arguments and noise.
Let it become a place where somebody discovers they are not the only person fighting to hold onto faith.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them publicly.
Because you love them.
Send this article privately if that would be kinder.
You may never know who reads without reacting.
Who cries without commenting.
Who has been asking God for a sign that they should come home.
Sometimes sharing one Gospel-centered message is a very small act.
And God can use very small acts.
There may come a night when you need to read it again.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, helping you return to Scripture, pointing you toward repentance, encouraging you when you wanted to quit, or helping you keep Jesus in front of your eyes, consider staying close to this ministry.
We want this community to remain a place filled with Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money buys blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or a better standing before God.
It cannot.
Your local church, conscience, responsibilities, and convictions about Christian giving deserve to be treated faithfully and seriously.

Scripture teaches generosity as something that should come from the heart rather than manipulation or compulsion. As Paul wrote, giving is not to be done "under compulsion," because God loves a cheerful giver.
a willing act of support.
A practical way of saying, "I want Gospel-centered content like this to keep reaching people."
And please remember: financial support is not the only meaningful way to help.
Sharing costs nothing.
A tag can reach one hurting friend.
A comment can encourage another believer.
A saved article can return to you at exactly the moment you need it.
A follow can keep Scripture and Gospel-centered encouragement appearing in the middle of an online world fighting relentlessly for your attention.
But every one of those things must remain secondary to the most important response of all.
Jesus does not primarily want your click.
He wants you.
Not your religious performance.
You.
Not the cleaned-up version.
You.
Not the person you promise to become next month.
You.
The sinner who needs mercy.
The wounded person who needs healing.
The wanderer who needs home.
The believer who has grown cold.
The Christian who knows the vocabulary but quietly realizes the fire has almost disappeared.
Come back.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Put away what is poisoning your soul.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Seek Christ again.
Not because your persistence earns His grace...
but because grace has opened the door.
The woman in Song of Songs could describe the man she loved from head to toe because love had taught her to notice him.
Maybe our deepest problem is not that Jesus has become less beautiful.
Maybe we have simply been staring at everything else for too long.
Look again.
Look at Bethlehem.
Look at the compassion of Christ.
Look at Him touching lepers.
Receiving outcasts.
Calling sinners.
Confronting hypocrisy.
Weeping with mourners.
Welcoming children.
Forgiving the guilty.
Look at Gethsemane.
Look at Calvary.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the risen Christ.
And then ask yourself:
Among the ten thousand things competing for my heart...
who is Jesus to me?
When everything temporary has lost its shine...
when applause goes quiet...
when beauty fades...
when money cannot stop death...
when followers cannot heal loneliness...
when possessions cannot cleanse guilt...
when the world cannot give your soul what it keeps promising...
there will still be Jesus.
Crucified.
Risen.
Merciful.
Holy.
Calling.
And perhaps one day you will realize that the greatest testimony of your entire life was never:
"I found Jesus."
It was this:
Jesus came looking for me.
So share this if somebody needs to come home.
Because after all the gold...
after all the poetry...
after every beautiful metaphor...
the woman ultimately knew what mattered.
"This is my beloved, and this is my friend."

And when your own story finally reaches its last page, may the greatest thing anyone can say about you be that somewhere between your wounds and your wandering, your failures and your forgiveness, your scandal and your restoration...
you discovered that Jesus was more beautiful than everything you once thought you couldn't live without.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD MARRIED PEOPLE KEEP THEIR EXES ON SOCIAL MEDIA? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHETHER YOU STILL LOVE THEM—IT’S WHY YOU STILL NEED THE DOOR OPEN
paragraphs: SHOULD MARRIED PEOPLE KEEP THEIR EXES ON SOCIAL MEDIA? THE QUESTION ISN’T WHETHER YOU STILL LOVE THEM—IT’S WHY YOU STILL NEED THE DOOR OPEN
That “harmless” follow may mean absolutely nothing. But if protecting it matters more to you than protecting your spouse’s heart, something deeper may already be happening.
It’s only a follow.
That’s what you tell yourself.
You don’t message them.
You’re not cheating.
You don’t meet secretly.
You’re married now. You love your spouse. That relationship ended years ago.
So why should it matter that your ex can still see your life?
Why should it matter that you can still see theirs?
Then one night, while your spouse is sleeping beside you, you’re scrolling.
And there they are.
Your ex.
Older now.
Different.
Maybe married.
Maybe single.
Maybe smiling beside someone else.
You don’t touch the message button.
You barely pause.
But something inside you does.
And sometimes the most dangerous doors are not the ones we walk through.
They are the ones we insist on keeping unlocked.
So let’s deal with this carefully, because Christians can make two opposite mistakes here.
One is pretending boundaries do not matter.
The other is inventing commandments God never gave.
The Bible does not say, “Thou shalt unfriend your ex.”
There is no verse commanding every married Christian to remove every former boyfriend, girlfriend, fiancé, or romantic interest from every social-media platform.
We must be honest about that.
Following an ex is not automatically adultery.
Being followed by an ex is not automatically emotional unfaithfulness.
Some people may have legitimate reasons for limited contact, especially when children, family responsibilities, work, ministry, or unavoidable community connections are involved.
But biblical wisdom asks a deeper question than:
“Am I technically allowed to do this?”
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:23:
The Christian life is not merely about discovering how close we can stand to a cliff without falling.
It is about asking what glorifies Christ.
What builds others up.
What protects what God has entrusted to us.
What makes love stronger rather than merely proving that something is technically permissible.
And marriage changes the question.
Because once you have entered a marriage covenant, the issue is no longer simply:
“Do I have feelings for my ex?”
A more mature question is:
“Does keeping this connection help me love my spouse faithfully, transparently, sacrificially, and securely before Christ?”
There is a line in Proverbs that becomes painfully relevant here.
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
Mikkol-mishmar netzor libbekha.
“Guard your heart with all diligence…”
Proverbs 4:23.
The Hebrew verb נְצֹר (netzor) carries the sense of guarding, watching, preserving.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
“Trust your heart.”
It says guard it.
Why?
Because human hearts drift.
Memories romanticize.
Loneliness exaggerates.
Disappointment rewrites history.
And social media has given previous relationships something earlier generations rarely possessed:
persistent visibility.
Once, someone could leave your life.
Today, they can remain in your pocket.
Their birthday.
Their vacation.
Their marriage.
Their divorce.
Their new haircut.
Their heartbreak.
Their late-night story.
Their “remember this?” photograph.
Their message notification.
Their name appearing when your marriage is going through its worst month.
That does not mean everyone will fall into sin.
Sometimes it arrives disguised as nostalgia.
Sometimes curiosity.
Sometimes closure.
Sometimes concern.
Sometimes, “I was just checking how they were doing.”
Sometimes, “We’re only friends.”
And sometimes that is genuinely true.
But sometimes “friendship” becomes the respectable word we use because we are uncomfortable admitting that a tiny part of us enjoys knowing the door is still there.
That is where this article stops being about your ex.
Because perhaps the real question is not:
“Should married people keep exes on social media?”
Perhaps the real question is:
“Why do I need to?”
That question can hurt.
Especially when the answer underneath it is something we never intended to say aloud.
Maybe you enjoy being remembered.
Maybe you like knowing they still watch your stories.
Maybe their likes still give you something.
Maybe you occasionally wonder what life would have been like.
Maybe nothing inappropriate has happened—but you know you would feel uncomfortable if your spouse saw every interaction.
Maybe you compare.
Maybe when your marriage becomes difficult, memories of your ex become strangely selective.
You remember the laughter but forget the dysfunction.
You remember the chemistry but forget why it ended.
You remember being wanted but forget being wounded.

You compare somebody else’s carefully edited social-media presence with the exhausted human being sleeping beside you—the person who pays bills with you, raises children with you, sees your worst moods, knows your weaknesses, carries burdens with you, and has to love the version of you that never appears in photographs.
That comparison is brutally unfair.
Your ex gets remembered in highlights.
Your spouse has to live with the behind-the-scenes footage.
And suddenly yesterday begins competing with the covenant God has placed in your hands today.
This is why boundaries are not automatically insecurity.
Sometimes boundaries are love wearing work clothes.
Paul gives husbands an astonishing standard in Ephesians 5:25:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Look at those words.
ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate.
Love.
παρέδωκεν — paredōken.
Gave Himself up.
Christian marital love is therefore not built around:
“What am I entitled to keep?”
Its model is Christ asking, in effect:
“What am I willing to give?”
Jesus did not love His church by defending His convenience.
He gave Himself.

That does not mean your spouse gets unlimited control over your friendships, your phone, or your life. Scripture should never be twisted into justification for coercion, isolation, jealousy, surveillance, or abuse.
But neither should “You’re just insecure” become an automatic weapon for dismissing a spouse’s legitimate pain.
Imagine your husband or wife saying quietly:
“This relationship makes me uncomfortable.”
And your immediate response is:
“You need to trust me.”
Perhaps they do.
But another question deserves to be asked.
Why is maintaining access to your ex more important than addressing the heart of the person you vowed to love?
That does not automatically mean you must delete someone whenever your spouse feels uncomfortable. Couples need wisdom, honesty, context, and sometimes pastoral counsel.
But if removing an unnecessary connection would cost you almost nothing and bring genuine peace to your marriage, why does surrendering it feel so expensive?
Sometimes our resistance reveals more than the connection itself.
“I haven’t done anything.”
Maybe you haven’t.
Thank God.
But faithfulness is bigger than proving you have not committed adultery.
Jesus takes sexual purity into the interior life in Matthew 5:27–30. He confronts lust at the level of the heart and then uses deliberately severe imagery about removing what causes one to stumble.
Jesus is not commanding bodily mutilation. His shocking language emphasizes the seriousness with which disciples should treat sin.
In other words:
Do not pet what you should flee.
Do not feed what you should starve.
Do not preserve convenient access to something you already know repeatedly pulls your heart away from faithfulness.
There are marriages that did not collapse in a hotel room.
They began collapsing much earlier.
A notification.
A private joke.
A reaction to a story.
“How have you been?”
“I’ve been thinking about you.”
“Do you ever wonder what would have happened if…?”
Then deleting messages.
Turning the phone over.
Changing passwords.
Calling emotional intimacy “catching up.”
And by the time bodies cross a boundary, hearts may have been trespassing for months.
But hear this carefully:
This article is not accusing everyone who follows an ex of secretly wanting an affair.
That would be unfair.
The issue is not paranoia.
The issue is wisdom.
For some married couples, an ex remaining somewhere on a friends list genuinely carries no emotional significance whatsoever.
For others, it is gasoline sitting beside a fire nobody believes will spread.
Only you, your spouse, and ultimately God know which situation you are dealing with.
And God sees what nobody scrolling your profile can see.
He sees whether you search their name.
He sees whether you wait for their reaction.
He sees whether you compare your spouse with them.
He sees whether you revisit photographs.
He sees the conversation you deleted.
He sees the fantasy you immediately pushed away.
He sees the fantasy you did not push away.
He sees the wounded part of you that still wants an old person to regret losing you.
He sees everything.
And remarkably, the Gospel does not end there.
Because Jesus did not come merely to expose hidden rooms.
He came to redeem the people hiding inside them.
Maybe you have already crossed a line.
Maybe this article is no longer theoretical for you.
Maybe you kept the ex.
Then came the message.
Then another.
Maybe you told yourself your spouse would misunderstand, so you hid it.
Maybe emotional intimacy formed.
Maybe sexual conversation happened.
Maybe photographs were exchanged.
Maybe you met.
Maybe adultery happened.
And now you are reading this with your stomach tightening because this stopped being an article about social media several paragraphs ago.
Now it is about you.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But Jesus Christ is greater than your scandal.
The answer is not better hiding.
The answer is repentance.
Confession.
Truth.
Turning away from sin and toward Christ.
The Gospel does not say your betrayal was insignificant.
The Gospel says Christ's blood is sufficient for sinners who come to Him.
At the cross, Jesus does something human beings could never accomplish for themselves.
He bears sin.
He offers forgiveness.
He calls sinners out of darkness.
He gives new life.
Grace does not rename adultery as harmless.
Grace takes guilty people who repent and begins rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
That is the difference between cheap permission and costly grace.
Cheap permission whispers:
“Everybody does it. Hide it better.”
Jesus says:
“Come into the light.”
Maybe your next act of worship is unfollowing somebody.
Maybe it is blocking somebody.
Maybe it is showing your spouse a conversation you have hidden.
Maybe it is ending emotional dependence on someone who does not belong in the intimate space of your marriage.
Maybe it is admitting you still carry feelings from a previous relationship and getting mature pastoral or professional help rather than pretending they do not exist.
Maybe the problem is not an ex at all.
Maybe the problem is your own jealousy, and Christ needs to heal your fear rather than requiring your spouse to spend a lifetime proving innocence.
Wisdom looks different in different circumstances.
But secrecy should always concern us.
If you would panic if your spouse picked up your phone…
If you repeatedly delete conversations…
If you speak to an ex about marital problems you refuse to discuss honestly with your spouse…
If you seek emotional affirmation from an ex…
If you fantasize about being with them…
If you hide the frequency or tone of your communication…
If their attention gives you something you should be cultivating within your marriage…
You are no longer dealing with an innocent question about a friends list.
Something needs to come into the light.
And maybe you are the spouse on the other side.
You saw the name.
You noticed the messages.
You felt foolish for being bothered.
You wondered whether speaking up would make you look controlling.
You tried to convince yourself it meant nothing.
Please remember this too:
Biblical love does not require pretending pain does not exist.
Speak truthfully.
Do not retaliate.
Do not manipulate.
Do not publicly humiliate your spouse.
Do not manufacture evidence.
Do not make accusations you cannot support.
But do not build peace on pretending.
Healthy marriages need truth.
And truth can hurt before it heals.
So should married people keep their exes on social media?
There is no universal biblical command requiring every married Christian to delete every ex.
But there is a universal call to holiness, wisdom, love, truth, purity, and faithfulness.
Therefore, ask better questions.
Does this connection strengthen my marriage or quietly weaken it?
Would I behave exactly the same way if my spouse were sitting beside me?
Am I protecting this connection because it is necessary—or because I enjoy what it gives me?
Would I be comfortable if my spouse interacted with their ex exactly as I interact with mine?
Is there secrecy?
Is there nostalgia becoming fantasy?
Is my spouse's concern reasonable?
Does keeping this person near help me become more faithful to Jesus?
And perhaps the hardest:
If Christ asked me to surrender this connection for the good of my marriage, why would I hesitate?
Marriage is already difficult enough without keeping unnecessary ghosts seated at the table.
Your spouse should not have to compete with a memory.
Your marriage should not have to survive a relationship you refuse to bury.
And you do not need to prove spiritual maturity by standing unnecessarily close to temptation.
Sometimes maturity looks remarkably unimpressive.
Unfollow.
Delete.
Block.
Tell the truth.
Put the phone down.
Turn toward your spouse.
Pray together.
Get help.
Forgive where repentance is real.
Rebuild what secrecy damaged.
And when necessary, establish boundaries strong enough that tomorrow's weakness cannot easily undo today's conviction.
But above everything else…
Turn toward Jesus.
Because you can delete every ex and still possess an unfaithful heart.
You can have perfect social-media boundaries and still be proud, lustful, selfish, bitter, dishonest, or emotionally absent.
Christianity is not behavior modification with Bible verses attached.
We need Christ.
We need His forgiveness.
We need His Spirit transforming our desires.
We need the Savior who does not merely clean our profile but changes our hearts.
And perhaps that is why this subject matters far beyond Facebook.
Sooner or later every disciple encounters something that forces the question:
Do I want Jesus only when He comforts me…
or is He Lord when obedience costs me something?
Be honest before God first. Then, if it reflects where you truly are, comment, “no more hiding.”
If your marriage has been fighting through wounds, temptation, mistrust, or restoration, comment, “Christ is still healing us.”
If you are struggling and need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance, forgiveness, wise boundaries, patient rebuilding, and the grace of Christ can still write another chapter.
Not because every sentence applies to every marriage, but because there may come a night when you need to remember the question:
“Is this worth risking what God has entrusted to me?”
Not because God needs your money.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by financial support.
But if God has given you the ability and desire to support Gospel-centered work, voluntary generosity can itself be offered for His glory.
Give Jesus the room you keep locking.
Give Him the conversation.
Give Him the temptation.
Give Him the nostalgia.
Give Him the marriage.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the secret.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where biblical forgiveness is needed.
Seek wisdom where the situation is complicated.
And remember this:
Some doors need to close not because you still love the person behind them, but because you finally understand the value of the person God has placed beside you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR MOUTH IS TELLING THE TRUTH ABOUT YOUR HEART
paragraphs: YOUR MOUTH IS TELLING THE TRUTH ABOUT YOUR HEART
Understanding “Out of the Abundance of the Heart the Mouth Speaks”—and Why Jesus Was Talking About Something Far Deeper Than Bad Words
There are things you have said that you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Words spoken in anger.
Words whispered when nobody else was listening.
That cruel sentence you fired at someone you love.
That gossip you dressed up as “concern.”
That sarcastic comment you said was only a joke.
That bitter sentence about the person who hurt you.
That private conversation where a version of you appeared that nobody at church would recognize.
And afterward came the explanation.
“I didn't mean it.”
“I was just angry.”
“I was exhausted.”
“They pushed me too far.”
“That isn't really who I am.”
Maybe.
But Jesus said something uncomfortable enough to make us stop before dismissing our words so quickly.
“For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.” — Luke 6:45
The Greek is piercing:
“ἐκ γὰρ περισσεύματος καρδίας λαλεῖ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ.”
Ek gar perisseumatos kardias lalei to stoma autou.
In straightforward English:
“For out of the abundance—the overflow—of the heart, his mouth speaks.”
Jesus was not merely giving etiquette lessons.
He was not saying, “Christians should use nicer vocabulary.”
He was revealing something about the human heart.
Your mouth can become a spillway.
And sometimes what spills out tells you what has been accumulating within.
That is why this verse should not merely make us watch our mouths.
It should make us examine our hearts.
Because Jesus did not begin His illustration with speech.
He began with a tree.
“No good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit.”
Then He speaks of treasure.
The good person brings good from the good treasure of the heart, while evil comes from evil treasure.
Then comes the mouth.
In other words, Jesus moves beneath the visible fruit to its hidden source.
Fruit tells you something about the tree.
Words tell you something about the treasury.
The mouth reveals something about the heart.
The Greek word translated “treasure” is θησαυρός — thēsauros.
A treasury.
A storehouse.
Something accumulated and kept.
And suddenly Luke 6:45 becomes painfully personal.
What have you been storing?
Not merely what did you say today.
What have you been depositing into your inner treasury for months?
Resentment?
Envy?
Lust?
Fear?
Self-pity?
Pride?
The need to be admired?
The need to win every argument?
Quiet jealousy toward somebody whose life appears better than yours?
Anger toward the person who wounded you five years ago?
You can hide a treasury for a while.
Then somebody bumps into you hard enough...
and something spills.
A husband explodes at his wife and says, “She made me angry.”
A woman destroys somebody's reputation and says, “I was only telling the truth.”
A believer humiliates another believer online and calls it “defending sound doctrine.”
Someone repeatedly complains about everybody around them but never considers whether discontent has quietly occupied the heart.
Someone makes sexual jokes constantly and insists, “They're only jokes.”
Someone cannot celebrate another person's blessing without immediately finding something wrong with it.
Someone speaks about money constantly.
Someone talks endlessly about themselves.
Someone's conversation repeatedly tears people down.
And Jesus quietly brings us back to the same terrifying possibility:
What if the mouth isn't creating the problem?
What if the mouth is exposing it?
A bottle filled with water does not suddenly produce orange juice because someone shakes it.
Pressure reveals what was already inside.
And life has a way of shaking us.
Traffic.
Bills.
Marriage.
Children.
Rejection.
Church conflict.
Politics.
Social media.
Exhaustion.
Betrayal.
Waiting.
Disappointment.
Someone disrespecting you.
Someone receiving the opportunity you prayed for.
Someone correcting you.
Someone saying “no.”
Someone touching the wound you thought you had buried.
Then suddenly...
the heart spills through the mouth.
This does not mean every careless sentence perfectly defines everything about a person.
Scripture gives room for stumbling. James says, “we all stumble in many ways” and then immediately discusses speech. Peter himself denied Jesus with his mouth and was later restored by Christ.
So Luke 6:45 should never become a weapon for mercilessly diagnosing everyone around us from one sentence.
Jesus' teaching should first become a mirror.
Not binoculars.
Before asking, “What does their mouth reveal about their heart?”
Ask:
“Lord... what does mine reveal about mine?”
That question gets uncomfortable quickly.
Because some of us have learned Christian vocabulary without allowing Christ into certain locked rooms of the heart.
We know when to say, “God bless you.”
We know when to post the verse.
We know when to lift our hands.
We know when to say, “I'll pray for you.”
But Jesus is not impressed by religious vocabulary disconnected from spiritual reality.
Matthew records Jesus using essentially the same truth in an even sharper confrontation:
“How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” — Matthew 12:34
And shortly afterward Jesus warns that people will give account for their careless words.
That should sober us.
But please don't miss what Jesus is exposing.
The Pharisees' fundamental problem was not that they needed vocabulary training.
They needed hearts that were right before God.
And that distinction changes everything.
Christianity is not primarily Jesus teaching rotten trees how to tape attractive fruit onto their branches.
Jesus came to save sinners.
He came to make us new.
That is why simply trying harder to “speak positively” can never reach the deepest problem.
You can filter vocabulary while resentment remains alive underneath.
You can stop cursing while pride remains untouched.
You can learn church language while secretly despising people.
You can speak softly while manipulating everybody around you.
You can quote Scripture while using Scripture to exalt yourself.
The Gospel goes deeper.
Jesus does not merely want cleaner sentences.
He wants you.
The real you.
The angry you.
The jealous you.
The ashamed you.
The wounded you.
The version nobody sees.
The version that occasionally escapes through your mouth.
And here is where conviction can either drive you toward hiding...
or toward Christ.
Maybe something ugly came out of you recently.
Something so ugly that afterward you sat there thinking:
“Where did that come from?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“Lord, what are You showing me?”
Maybe that explosion revealed resentment you never surrendered.
Maybe the gossip revealed envy.
Maybe the constant criticism revealed pride.
Maybe the cruel joke revealed contempt.
Maybe the defensiveness revealed an identity built upon needing other people's approval.
Maybe the boasting revealed insecurity.
Maybe the endless complaining revealed that circumstances have become more influential over your joy than the promises of God.
Don't waste the revelation.
Don't merely apologize for the sentence and leave the source untouched.
Follow the words upstream.
Back through the mouth.
Back into the heart.
And meet Jesus there.
Because the Christian response to exposed sin is not:
“I need to hide this better.”
It is:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
This is repentance.
Not image management.
Not learning to sound holy.
Not becoming better at suppressing evidence.
Repentance brings what darkness has been protecting into the light of God.
“Lord, this bitterness is mine.”
“This jealousy is mine.”
“This pride is mine.”
“This anger is mine.”
“I cannot blame my spouse anymore.”
“I cannot blame my childhood forever.”
“I cannot blame social media.”
“I cannot blame stress.”
“They may explain the pressure...
but the pressure exposed something inside me.”
And there, at the place where excuses finally die, grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus already knows.
Before your confession, He knows.
Before the mask falls, He knows.
Before everybody discovers what you are ashamed of, Christ knows exactly what resides within the human heart.
