And He still went to the cross.
The Gospel is not God discovering good people and rewarding them.
The Gospel is God saving sinners through Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for the polished imaginary version of you.
Christ died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He shed His blood.
He rose from the grave.
And now forgiveness is not offered because you finally learned how to appear respectable.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ.
That means your ugliest moment does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
Peter's mouth once said:
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine carrying that sentence after the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering Jesus' face.
Imagine realizing that the mouth that once declared loyalty had just denied Him.
Peter wept bitterly.
But Jesus wasn't finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him.
The mouth that denied Jesus would eventually proclaim Jesus.
That is grace.
Not pretending the denial never happened.
Not calling evil good.
Not minimizing failure.
Grace confronts the scandal...
and then Jesus begins rewriting the story.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You said terrible things.
You wounded people.
You lied.
You gossiped.
You manipulated.
You cursed.
You denied Christ by the way you lived.
You cannot undo yesterday.
But you can bring yesterday to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask forgiveness from the people you wounded where appropriate.
Stop defending what God is confronting.
And believe the Gospel.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
There is another beautiful side to Luke 6:45 too.
If the mouth speaks from what fills the heart...
then imagine what happens when the heart is increasingly filled with Christ's truth.
When Scripture begins occupying rooms once inhabited by lies.
When gratitude begins displacing entitlement.
When forgiveness begins replacing revenge.
When humility starts suffocating pride.
When compassion replaces contempt.
When worship becomes louder inside you than worry.
When the Gospel becomes more precious than your reputation.
Something begins changing.
Not perfectly.
Not overnight.
But genuinely.
Your words begin changing because the treasury is changing.
The person who once always needed the last word begins learning silence.
The parent who once screamed begins apologizing.
The husband who once used words as weapons begins using them to build.
The woman who once lived on gossip begins refusing conversations that destroy people.
The believer who once used social media to prove superiority begins asking, “Will this glorify Christ?”
The wounded person who once cursed an enemy begins praying for them.
That is not mere behavior modification.
That is fruit.
And fruit points toward what is happening at the root.
This is why what you repeatedly consume matters.
What you watch.
What you replay.
Whose voices disciple you.
The arguments you feed upon.
The fantasies you entertain.
The grievances you rehearse.
The Scriptures you neglect.
The truth you meditate upon.
The worship you sing when nobody is watching.
Every day, something is entering the treasury.
And eventually...
treasuries spend what they contain.
So perhaps before asking God, “Please control my tongue,” we should also pray:
“Jesus, transform my heart.”
Because you can put a guard at the door...
but Christ wants the house.
You can police the vocabulary...
but Jesus wants the treasury.
You can manage appearances...
but Jesus wants the tree.
And maybe this article has exposed something you have been trying not to name.
Don't run from that conviction.
Run to Christ with it.
If your words have revealed bitterness, confess it.
If they have revealed jealousy, confess it.
If they have revealed lust, confess it.
If they have revealed pride, confess it.
If they have revealed unbelief, fear, hatred, resentment, or unforgiveness, bring it honestly before God.
And if someone else has been wounded by your words, repentance may require more than silently praying about it.
You may need to say:
“I was wrong.”
Not...
“I'm sorry you were offended.”
Not...
“I'm sorry, but you made me angry.”
Simply:
“I sinned against you with my words. Please forgive me.”
There is extraordinary freedom in no longer having to defend the old you.
Because Christ is forming something new.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes public honesty becomes a small declaration that we are finished pretending.
Let other believers see it.
Let somebody pray.
Let the comment section become more than reactions and emojis. Let it become a place where people stop performing for a moment and admit that we desperately need Jesus.
Somebody who thinks they can never change may need to hear what God's grace has done in you.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose anger is eating them alive.
The friend who loves Jesus but has become bitter.
The husband and wife barely speaking without hurting each other.
The believer whose online words no longer resemble the Christ they profess.
The person carrying shame because of something terrible they said.
Or send this privately.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God. It doesn't.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if something points people toward Jesus Christ, repentance, forgiveness, and biblical truth, sharing it can become one simple way of putting truth where someone else may encounter it.
If you want your Facebook presence to glorify God, don't only use it to show people where you went, what you bought, what made you laugh, or what made you angry.
Let some of what you share point people toward Christ.
Someone scrolling tonight may be one sentence away from finally admitting:
“I need Jesus.”
Because there will probably come another moment when somebody presses exactly the wrong button...
and what is inside you wants to spill everywhere.
Come back.
Read Luke 6:43–45 again.
Remember the tree.
Remember the treasury.
Remember the mouth.
Remember the heart.
And remember the Savior who changes sinners from the inside out.
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is done freely, worshipfully, and for God's glory.
Pray.
Send it to someone.

Because supporting Gospel ministry is not only financial. Sometimes you glorify God simply by refusing to keep life-giving truth to yourself and faithfully placing the message of Jesus where another human being can see it.
But above everything else...
don't leave this article merely thinking about your mouth.
Go deeper.
Ask Jesus about your heart.
Because eventually the cup spills.
Eventually the tree produces fruit.
Eventually the treasury opens.
And when it does, the question will not merely be, “What words came out?”
The deeper question will be:
“What had I been storing inside?”
So fill your heart with Christ.
Fill it with His Word.
Fill it with gratitude for the cross.
Fill it with remembrance of mercy.
Fill it with the Gospel until grace begins spilling into conversations where anger once lived.
And when something ugly spills out again—as you continue growing and stumbling—don't hide the evidence.
Take it back to Jesus.
Repent quickly.
Receive His grace.
Make things right.
Keep walking.
Because the most beautiful testimony is not, “I have never failed.”
It is:
“Jesus found me in my failure, forgave me, and He is changing me.”
Your mouth may reveal what has been living in your heart...
but when that heart is surrendered to Jesus, yesterday's overflow does not have to become tomorrow's identity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD TOLD EZEKIEL HIS WIFE WOULD DIE—AND THEN TOLD HIM NOT TO PUBLICLY MOURN
paragraphs: GOD TOLD EZEKIEL HIS WIFE WOULD DIE—AND THEN TOLD HIM NOT TO PUBLICLY MOURN

The terrifying night when a prophet lost “the delight of his eyes,” a nation was shown what it was about to lose, and God exposed the deadly difference between loving His gifts and truly belonging to Him.
There are passages in the Bible that comfort you.
There are passages that correct you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading for a moment because you are not sure you were prepared for what you just saw.
Ezekiel 24:15–24 is one of them.
God speaks.
A wife is going to die.
A husband already knows.
And when the death comes, the grieving prophet will not be permitted to mourn publicly in the ordinary way.
If you have ever buried someone you loved, this story may feel almost unbearable.
If you have ever sat beside a hospital bed knowing you were running out of time...
if you have ever stared at an empty chair that used to belong to somebody...
if you have ever instinctively reached for a phone to call someone who is no longer alive...
then do not rush through this passage.
There is something here that hurts.
And there is something underneath the hurt that is even more frightening.
Because Ezekiel's tragedy was about to become a mirror.
And Israel was going to see itself inside it.
The Hebrew begins with God's devastating announcement:
“בֶּן־אָדָם הִנְנִי לֹקֵחַ מִמְּךָ אֶת־מַחְמַד עֵינֶיךָ”
Ben-adam, hineni loqeakh mimkha et-makhmad einekha...
“Son of man, behold, I am taking from you the delight of your eyes...”
That expression deserves to be felt before it is explained.
מַחְמַד עֵינֶיךָ — makhmad einekha.
The delight of your eyes.
The precious one your eyes loved to behold.
God does not introduce Ezekiel's wife as an inconvenience, an attachment the prophet should have spiritually outgrown, or someone whose death should not matter.
He calls her the delight of Ezekiel's eyes.
Scripture does not even give us her name.
We are not told how they met.
We do not hear her voice.
We are not shown their wedding.
We do not know how many evenings she waited while Ezekiel carried the crushing burden of prophetic ministry.
We do not know how often she saw the man behind the prophet.
But one phrase tells us enough.
She was precious to him.
And then came the sentence no husband would want to hear.
God told Ezekiel that she would be taken “בְּמַגֵּפָה” — bemaggefah — by a sudden blow or stroke.
Then came an instruction that sounds almost impossible:
“וְלֹא תִסְפֹּד וְלֹא תִבְכֶּה וְלוֹא תָבוֹא דִּמְעָתֶךָ”
He was not to perform the normal public lamentation. He was not to weep publicly or allow the customary outward display of tears.
But read the next Hebrew words carefully, because they protect us from a cruel misunderstanding of this passage:
“הֵאָנֵק דֹּם”
He'aneq dom.
Groan silently.
The prophet was not commanded to stop loving.
He was not transformed into stone.
God was not teaching that holiness means emotional numbness.
There was a groan.
There was pain.
There was grief.
But for this extraordinary prophetic sign, the normal public rituals of mourning were withheld.

Ezekiel was to keep his head covering on. His sandals remained on his feet. He was not to cover his upper lip in the customary manner of mourning. He was not to eat the customary food brought by mourners or comforters.
Then Scripture gives us one of the coldest, shortest sentences imaginable:
“וַתָּמָת אִשְׁתִּי בָּעָרֶב”
Vattamat ishti ba'arev.
“My wife died in the evening.”
That is almost all we get.
No dramatic speech.
No description of Ezekiel holding her hand.
No account of her final breath.
Just:
My wife died in the evening.
Sometimes grief really does sound like that.
The sentences become shorter because there are no words large enough for what happened.
She died.
He was gone.
The diagnosis came back.
The marriage ended.
The child never came home.
The phone rang.
Everything changed.
And somehow morning still arrived.
Ezekiel says:
“וָאַעַשׂ בַּבֹּקֶר כַּאֲשֶׁר צֻוֵּיתִי”
Va'as babboqer ka'asher tsuvveiti.
“In the morning I did as I was commanded.”
Think about that morning.
The bed is different.
The house is different.
The silence is different.
Yesterday, his wife was alive.
Today, Ezekiel must stand before people.
And they notice something strange.
A man has suffered devastating loss, yet the expected public signs of mourning are absent.
So they ask the obvious question:
What does this mean for us?
There.
That is the doorway into the passage.
Ezekiel's private agony had become a public prophecy.
God explains that what Ezekiel's wife was to Ezekiel, the sanctuary had become to the people in another devastating sense.
God calls the sanctuary:
“מַחְמַד עֵינֵיכֶם”
Makhmad eineikhem.
“The delight of your eyes.”
It is the same core expression.
Ezekiel's beloved wife was the delight of his eyes.
The sanctuary was the delight of theirs.
But Israel's relationship with God had become catastrophically corrupted.
They treasured the sanctuary while rebelling against the God whose sanctuary it was.
They loved the visible symbol while resisting the Holy One it represented.
They could admire sacred things and still tolerate sin.
They could possess religious identity without covenant faithfulness.
They could look toward the Temple and assume its existence somehow guaranteed their security while their hearts remained rebellious.
And that should frighten every religious person who reads this.
Because it is possible to love Christian things without truly loving Christ.
You can love worship music and resist worship.
You can love Bible quotations and refuse biblical correction.
You can love church culture while hiding secret sin.
You can repost sermons while refusing repentance.
You can defend Christianity online while treating people cruelly offline.
You can know Christian vocabulary, Christian personalities, Christian controversies, Christian books, Christian conferences and Christian arguments...
and still keep Jesus standing outside rooms in your heart you refuse to surrender.
The terrifying possibility in Ezekiel 24 is not merely that people can lose something precious.
It is that people can become so attached to the things associated with God that they mistake those things for faithfulness to God Himself.
Israel apparently believed Jerusalem and the sanctuary represented security.
But no sacred building could turn rebellion into righteousness.
No religious symbol could make unrepented sin holy.
No history with God could become permission to live without God.
And no amount of outward Christianity can substitute for reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is where this ancient tragedy becomes painfully personal.
What is the “delight of your eyes”?
The thing you quietly believe you cannot live without?
Your marriage?
Your children?
Your ministry?
Your reputation?
Your income?
Your health?
Your church position?
Your plans?
Your followers?
Your comfort?
Your political certainty?
Your dream for the future?
Even good gifts become dangerous when our hearts begin demanding from them what only God can provide.
That does not mean loving your spouse deeply is idolatry. Ezekiel's wife being called “the delight of his eyes” shows the preciousness of the relationship rather than condemning it.
It means every created gift remains a gift.
Not God.
And eventually every human being discovers how fragile the things we hold are.
A doctor can change your vocabulary in thirty seconds.
A phone call can divide your life into before and after.
A betrayal can destroy plans that took twenty years to build.
A funeral can reduce decades of possessions to boxes somebody else must sort through.
A financial collapse can erase numbers you thought meant security.
A grave can teach what prosperity sometimes lets us forget:
We are not sovereign.
And Ezekiel's story becomes even more sobering because the judgment coming upon Jerusalem was not random cruelty.
God had warned His people repeatedly.
Ezekiel's ministry is filled with exposure of idolatry, injustice, bloodshed, corruption and covenant rebellion.
Judgment did not fall because God suddenly became temperamental.
Judgment came after persistent rebellion against the God who had called His people to Himself.
That distinction matters.
This chapter should never be weaponized against a grieving Christian.
If someone you love has died, Ezekiel 24 does not give another believer permission to walk into your grief and say, “Stop crying. Ezekiel didn't.”
That would completely miss what was happening.
Ezekiel was given an exceptional prophetic command because his behavior itself was a sign to the exiles.
Elsewhere Scripture openly permits and portrays godly grief.
Abraham mourned Sarah.
Joseph mourned Jacob.
David grieved.
The early believers mourned Stephen.
And then there is Jesus.
Standing outside the tomb of Lazarus, knowing resurrection was moments away, Jesus wept.
The shortest tears in Scripture destroy the lie that faith and grief cannot occupy the same heart.
Jesus knew Lazarus would rise.
Jesus still wept.
Christian hope does not require pretending death does not hurt.
The Gospel does not tell us death is harmless.
The Gospel announces that death has met its conqueror.
And this is where Ezekiel's dark morning begins pointing beyond itself.
Jerusalem would fall.
The sanctuary would be devastated.
The people would discover that their religious confidence could not save them.
But God's redemptive purpose was not finished.
Ezekiel himself would later speak of cleansing.
A new heart.
A new spirit.
Dry bones receiving life.
A restored people.
A shepherd.
And the biblical story keeps moving until all our false refuges are confronted by the One true Savior.
Jesus Christ.
Not a building.
Not a ritual.
Not religious reputation.
Christ.
And there is another scene of unimaginable grief waiting in the Gospel.
At Calvary, God did not merely send another prophet to perform a sign.
The Son of God gave Himself.
Jesus was not a sinner receiving deserved judgment. He was the righteous One.
He willingly laid down His life.
At the cross, our sin is not minimized, excused or renamed.
It is exposed as so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required what we could never provide for ourselves.
And grace is revealed as so astonishing that God provided the Lamb.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus shed His blood.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And Jesus rose.
That is why Christianity does not tell broken people, “Try harder until God likes you.”
It announces something infinitely better.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Trust Him.
Receive mercy you could never purchase.
Receive forgiveness you could never earn.
Let the One who conquered the grave become Lord over the places you have kept locked.
Maybe you have spent years around Christianity while secretly running from Christ.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
Maybe you know exactly what to say when somebody asks how you are doing.
“Blessed.”
“God is good.”
“I'm okay.”
But you are not okay.
There is resentment you never surrendered.
Pornography nobody knows about.
An affair hidden behind passwords.
Bitterness you have renamed discernment.
Pride you have renamed standards.
Greed you have renamed ambition.
Fear you have renamed wisdom.
A prayer life that has almost disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust while your thumb spends hours scrolling.
You do not need another religious performance.
You need Jesus.
Not the edited Jesus who exists to approve everything you already want.
The crucified and risen Christ.
The Savior who loves sinners enough to receive them and loves them too much to leave them enslaved.
Repentance is not God standing over you enjoying your humiliation.
Repentance is turning from the road that is killing you toward the Savior who died to give you life.
Grace does not say sin never mattered.
Grace says sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and you were loved so deeply that He went willingly.
Perhaps the most frightening question raised by Ezekiel's story is not, “What if God takes something I love?”
Perhaps it is:
“What if I have built my identity around God's gifts while my heart has been drifting away from God Himself?”
Do not answer that question for your spouse.
Do not answer it for the person you think needs to read this.
Answer it for yourself.
If everything visible disappeared...
would Christ still be enough?
If the applause stopped?
If the money vanished?
If the position disappeared?
If the ministry ended?
If the plan collapsed?
Would you still say:
Jesus, I am Yours?
That question reaches deeper than religious appearance.
And if it exposed something hidden in you, do not hide again.
There is no trophy for pretending.
The church should be a place where wounded people can tell the truth while being pointed toward Christ.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, do not merely think about them.
Not as an accusation.
Not as a public rebuke.
As a hand reaching through the darkness saying, “I thought of you. I want you to know you are not alone.”
There are truths you do not realize you will need again until the phone rings, the diagnosis arrives, the relationship breaks, or the thing you thought could never disappear suddenly does.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But if Gospel-centered truth has strengthened you, sharing it can put that truth in front of somebody you may never know was struggling.
Your share could reach a grieving widow.
A backslidden believer.
A man hiding an addiction.
A teenager quietly questioning whether God still wants them.
A person sitting alone tonight wondering whether there is any road home.
Use what God has placed in your hands for His glory.
But before you leave this page, go back to that house in Babylon one final time.
Evening.
A prophet.
A wife who had been the delight of his eyes.
Then silence.
Morning comes.
Ezekiel gets up.
He obeys.
The people stare.
And through one man's unbearable loss, God forces an entire community to confront what they had loved, what they had trusted, and how far their hearts had wandered.
Thousands of years later, the question still reaches us.
What are you trusting that cannot survive the grave?
Your possessions cannot.
Your reputation cannot.
Your body cannot.
Your achievements cannot.
Even the people you treasure cannot remain with you forever in this present mortal life.
But Jesus Christ walked into death and came out alive.
So when everything temporary finally proves temporary, the Christian's ultimate hope is not that nothing painful will ever be taken away.
Our hope is a Person whom death could not keep.
Jesus.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who forgives the guilty.
The One who restores the fallen.
The One who gives new hearts.
The One who meets mourners beside graves.
The One who turns ruined stories toward redemption.
The One who still calls prodigals home.
So cry when you need to cry.
Groan when words disappear.
Grieve what was precious.
But do not build your eternity upon something death can steal.
Build upon Christ.
And if your story currently looks more like scandal than grace, more like ashes than restoration, more like failure than testimony...
do not write the final sentence yet.
Jesus is still holding the pen.
The grave may close over what your eyes once delighted in—but it cannot close over the Christ who rose to bring broken sinners home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Ezekiel Shaved His Head With a Sword—and What He Did With the Hair Was a Terrifying Warning From God
paragraphs: Ezekiel Shaved His Head With a Sword—and What He Did With the Hair Was a Terrifying Warning From God

He burned one-third. Struck one-third with a sword. Scattered one-third into the wind. But then God told him to save a few strands—and hidden inside that terrifying act is a truth about judgment, mercy, repentance, and Jesus Christ that we desperately need to hear.
Imagine seeing a man of God sitting in public with a sharpened sword in his hand.
Not holding it against an enemy.
Holding it against his own head.
Then the blade begins to move.
Hair falls.
His beard disappears.
People stare.
And when the last strands have fallen, he does something even stranger.
He gathers the hair.
He brings out scales.
He weighs it.
Carefully.
Deliberately.
Then he divides it into three portions.
If you had been watching Ezekiel that day, you might have wondered whether the prophet had finally lost his mind.
But Ezekiel was not performing madness.
He was preaching.
Without a pulpit.
Without a microphone.
Without even needing a sermon.
His own body had become the message.
And the hair falling from his head was telling Jerusalem what words alone had failed to make them understand.
Judgment was coming.
The Hebrew text begins with a command that sounds almost violent even before we understand its meaning:
“וְאַתָּה בֶן־אָדָם קַח־לְךָ חֶרֶב חַדָּה”
Ve’attah ben-adam, qach-lekha cherev chaddah...
“And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword...” — Ezekiel 5:1.
Then comes the shocking instruction:
“תַּעַר הַגַּלָּבִים”
ta'ar ha-gallavim — a barber’s razor.
God tells Ezekiel to use the sword like a razor and pass it over his head and beard. Then Ezekiel is commanded to take “מֹאזְנֵי מִשְׁקָל” — moznei mishqal — weighing scales, and divide the hair.
Nothing about this scene is accidental.
The sword matters.
The shaving matters.
The scales matter.
The three portions matter.
Even the few hairs that remain matter.
Ezekiel had already been acting out Jerusalem’s coming siege. Now the prophet’s shaved hair would become a miniature picture of what was going to happen to its people.
God commands him to burn one-third in the fire.
Another third is to be struck with the sword.
The final third is scattered into the wind.
Then comes the chilling sentence:
“וְחֶרֶב אָרִיק אַחֲרֵיהֶם”
vecherev ariq achareihem.
“And I will draw out a sword after them.”

Later in the chapter, God Himself explains the symbolism. One-third would perish through pestilence and famine; one-third would fall by the sword; another third would be scattered to the winds, with the sword pursuing them.
The strange performance was a prophetic sign of Jerusalem’s coming catastrophe.
This was not random cruelty from an unpredictable God.
That point matters.
Because if we rip Ezekiel 5 from everything surrounding it, we can turn God into a caricature.
The chapter itself tells us why judgment was coming.
Jerusalem had rebelled against God’s judgments and rejected His statutes. God speaks of the defilement of His sanctuary and of the abominations committed among His people.
These were covenant people who possessed extraordinary spiritual privilege but had persistently rebelled against the God who had called them.
Their greatest danger was not simply that Babylon existed.
Their greatest danger was that they had become comfortable with rebellion while still carrying the identity of God’s people.
And suddenly Ezekiel’s shaved head stops feeling quite so ancient.
Because that temptation survived Jerusalem.
It walked into churches.
It entered homes.
It learned Christian vocabulary.
It discovered how to lift its hands during worship.
It learned how to post Bible verses.
It learned how to say, “God knows my heart.”
It learned how to appear spiritually alive while protecting rooms of the heart from the lordship of God.
That is what makes Ezekiel uncomfortable.
He forces us to confront a question modern Christianity can easily avoid:
What if my greatest spiritual danger is not that I openly reject God...
but that I have learned how to live near holy things while quietly resisting Him?
You can know worship songs and still hide bitterness.
You can own several Bibles and refuse to forgive.
You can post about Jesus and secretly feed an addiction.
You can attend church faithfully while pride slowly hardens your heart.
You can speak about grace while refusing repentance.
You can convince everyone around you that you are doing fine while privately becoming someone you never imagined you would be.
And perhaps the most frightening stage of sin is not when sin shocks you.
It is when it no longer does.
That is where Ezekiel’s sword begins cutting closer than hair.
Because God cared enough about His people to expose what they had normalized.
Biblical judgment is never permission for Christians to become self-righteous spectators pointing fingers at everyone else.
Ezekiel 5 should first make us examine ourselves.
“Search me, O God.”
That is the posture.
Not, “Lord, show me who needs this article.”
Lord...
show me where I need it.
Show me what I excuse because everybody else excuses it.
Show me what I call weakness when You call it sin.
Show me where I use grace as camouflage instead of running to grace for transformation.
Show me where Christianity has become something I display rather than Someone I follow.
Because there is another detail in Ezekiel’s terrifying sign-act that is easy to miss.
God tells him not to destroy every strand.
“וְלָקַחְתָּ מִשָּׁם מְעַט בְּמִסְפָּר”
Velaqachta misham me'at bemispar.
“Take from there a few in number.”
Then Ezekiel is commanded to bind those few hairs into the folds of his garment.
Pause there.
Almost everything in the scene screams destruction.
Fire.
Sword.
Scattering.
Judgment.
But hidden in the prophet’s garment...
are a few hairs.
Preserved.
Held close.
Not forgotten.
There is severity in Ezekiel 5, and we should never soften what God has made severe. Even some of those hairs are subsequently placed into the fire as the sign continues.
So we must not turn those strands into a sentimental promise that judgment does not matter.
It does.
But throughout the book of Ezekiel, judgment is not the end of the biblical story.
God will later speak of gathering His scattered people.
He will speak of cleansing.
He will promise a new heart.
A new spirit.
He will say:
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.”
The God who exposes rebellion is also the God who can transform rebels.
And this is where the road eventually carries us beyond Ezekiel...
to Jesus.
Because Christianity does not teach that God simply looked at human rebellion and decided sin did not matter after all.
The cross says exactly the opposite.
Sin mattered enough that redemption cost blood.
Grace is not God pretending evil is harmless.
Grace is God providing what sinners could never provide for themselves.
At Calvary, judgment and mercy meet in a way Ezekiel could only anticipate from afar.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, willingly gives Himself for sinners.
Isaiah had spoken of the Servant being wounded for our transgressions.
John the Baptist would point at Jesus and declare Him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
Paul would write that God made the One who knew no sin to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Peter would say that Christ Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.
The Gospel is not:
“You were actually good enough all along.”
The Gospel is:
You were guilty...
and Christ came for the guilty.
You wandered...
and the Shepherd came looking.
You sinned...
and the Savior carried sin to the cross.
You could not cleanse yourself...
so Jesus shed His blood.
You could not resurrect your dead heart...
so the risen Christ offers life.
That changes how we read Ezekiel.
Because when you understand the holiness of God, the cross becomes astonishing.
We often want grace without understanding judgment.
But cheap grace produces casual Christianity.
Ezekiel will not let us have casual Christianity.
The sword tells us God is holy.
The scales tell us God is just.
The fire tells us rebellion has consequences.
The scattering tells us sin destroys.
And the larger biblical story tells us something almost unbelievable:
the holy God against whom humanity sinned became the God who came near to save sinners.
Jesus did not come because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He came because we needed redemption.
Maybe you know exactly what that means.
Maybe there is something on your phone you hope nobody ever sees.
Maybe your marriage looks healthy in photographs while resentment has been eating both of you alive.
Maybe nobody knows how tired you are.
Maybe you have been drinking secretly.
Maybe pornography has become the prison you keep promising yourself you will leave tomorrow.
Maybe pride is destroying relationships while you keep blaming everyone else.
Maybe you stopped praying months ago but still know exactly how to sound Christian.
Maybe you are angry with God.
Maybe you have walked so far from Him that returning feels embarrassing.
Maybe you have convinced yourself that because you failed again, Jesus must finally be finished with you.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Repentance is not God telling you to clean yourself up before you approach Christ.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ who alone can save you.
You do not have to hide from the Physician because you are sick.
You go to Him because you are sick.
You do not avoid the Savior because you sinned.
You run to Him because you sinned.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Stop renaming it.
Stop defending it.
Stop negotiating with what is killing you.
And come to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel spiritual enough.
Not when you have successfully punished yourself with enough guilt.
Now.
There is a world of difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction exposes sin so that you will turn toward Christ.
Condemnation whispers that because you have sinned, there is no point returning.
But Scripture says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance hopeful.
Because the Christian does not repent hoping to persuade an unwilling God to become merciful.
We repent because in Jesus Christ we have encountered a Savior who has already demonstrated the staggering depth of His mercy at the cross.
Maybe you have been hiding.
No more hiding.
Maybe you have been performing.
No more pretending.
Maybe Christianity became routine while your heart drifted.
Come home.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret nobody knows.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling sinners to repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and life.
That is why the most important question raised by Ezekiel’s shaved head is not:
“Wasn’t that strange?”
The question is:
What was God desperate for His people to understand?
Sin is serious.
God is holy.
Judgment is real.
Religious identity cannot substitute for obedience.
And mercy should never be presumed upon.
Yet when we follow the biblical story to Christ, we discover that the God who judges sin has made a way for sinners to be reconciled to Himself.
Not through our religious performance.
Not through money.
Not through buying Christian merchandise.
Not through sharing an article.
Through Jesus Christ alone.
That distinction matters enormously.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
But grace does something to people.
Grace makes us want others to hear.
When you have found bread, you want another starving person to know where it is.
When you have been pulled from darkness, you want someone still stumbling there to see the light.
When Christ has forgiven you, restored you, confronted you, carried you, and refused to abandon you...
you stop wanting the Gospel to end with you.
So if this article brought Scripture into a place in your heart you have been avoiding, do something with that conviction.
First, respond to Jesus.
Then think of the person who needs this truth.
Send it privately to the believer who stopped coming to church.
Share it with the person who thinks their past has disqualified them from grace.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity teaches that good people save themselves.
Let them see something better.
Christ saves sinners.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, be honest enough to say it.
Sometimes another believer needs to discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Sometimes confession becomes the first crack through which light enters a locked room.
There may come a night when temptation starts talking again.
A night when shame tells you not to pray.
A night when your past starts introducing itself as your future.
Come back and remember the sword, the scales, the scattered hair...
and then remember the cross.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the person who has become lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbeliever who has questions about Jesus.
We want it to keep pointing people back to the Word of God and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
Not because God’s grace can be purchased.
Not because clicking a button proves that you love Jesus.
But because Gospel work requires people willing to pray, participate, share, give, and help biblical resources reach farther than they could otherwise reach.
Follow.
Pray.
Tell someone about Jesus.
And somewhere between the falling hair and the scattered strands...
they may realize God takes sin seriously.
Then somewhere between judgment and mercy...
they may finally understand why Jesus went to the cross.
And somewhere between shame and surrender...
they may whisper the prayer they thought they would never pray again:
“Jesus...
have mercy on me.”
Ezekiel once watched his hair fall to the ground because God wanted Jerusalem to understand that rebellion eventually costs more than sinners imagine.
Centuries later, outside Jerusalem, another scene unfolded.
There was rejection.
There was humiliation.
There was blood.
There was a cross.
But this time the One suffering was not acting out the judgment of another people.
Jesus Christ was giving Himself for sinners.
And three days later, the tomb was empty.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sin can be confessed.
Your chains can be broken.
Your wandering can end.
Your shame does not have to name you forever.
Your failure does not outrank the mercy of Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend the scandal never happened.
It tells you that Jesus can redeem what sin tried to destroy.
So come out of hiding.
Repent.
Believe.
Return.
And when Christ begins rewriting what you thought was already ruined, do not keep the story to yourself.
Someone else needs to know that the God who exposes sin is also the God who saves sinners.
Someone else needs to know that judgment is not a joke...
but neither is grace.
Someone else needs to know that Jesus still receives people who finally stop running.
And perhaps the few strands held close inside Ezekiel’s garment should leave us with an image we will not easily forget:
When everything seems scattered beyond recovery, never assume God has reached the end of the story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your Spouse Should Not Have to Compete With a Screen for Your Eyes, Your Laughter, and Your Attention
paragraphs: Your Spouse Should Not Have to Compete With a Screen for Your Eyes, Your Laughter, and Your Attention

Some marriages do not begin breaking with an affair, a screaming match, or divorce papers. Sometimes the distance begins with two people sitting inches apart… while one of them keeps giving the best of their attention to something glowing in their hand.
Your spouse says something.
“Hmm?”
They repeat it.
You answer without looking up.
A few seconds later, you laugh.
But not because of anything they said.
Something on the screen made you laugh.
And across the room—or perhaps only twelve inches away—the person you once could not stop looking at quietly feels something they may not even know how to explain.
I miss you.
Except you are right there.
That may be one of the strangest forms of loneliness in modern marriage.
To be beside someone who is somewhere else.
To sleep next to someone whose final attention before closing their eyes belongs to a screen.
To wake beside someone whose first reach of the morning is not toward you, not toward prayer, not toward the Word of God…
but toward a phone.
No affair.
No secret hotel room.
No dramatic betrayal.
Nothing that looks scandalous enough to make people gasp.
Just five minutes here.
Ten minutes there.
One more video.
One more notification.
One more comment.
One more scroll.
One more “hold on.”
One more “I’m listening” while your eyes say you are not.
And that is precisely why this can become dangerous.
Because some forms of marital neglect do not arrive like an explosion.
They accumulate like dust.
Almost invisible.
Until one day somebody realizes they have been emotionally starving in a house full of food.
Scripture spoke to the heart of this problem long before smartphones existed.
Paul wrote in Philippians 2:4:
“μὴ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστοι σκοποῦντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἑτέρων ἕκαστοι.”
A faithful sense of the Greek is:
Do not each look only to your own things, but also to the things of others.
That word translated “looking,” σκοποῦντες — skopountes, comes from skopeō: to look at, pay attention to, take notice of, or carefully regard.
And notice the context.

Paul is not giving married couples a command specifically about phones. He is teaching the church the Christ-shaped posture of humility. In the surrounding verses, believers are called away from selfish ambition and empty glory, toward considering others and their concerns. Then Paul brings everything to its breathtaking center:
Jesus Christ.
“τοῦτο φρονεῖτε ἐν ὑμῖν ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ…”
Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.
Then Paul points us toward the humility of the Son of God—the One who took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient even to death on a cross.
So Philippians 2:4 is bigger than digital etiquette.
This is not merely…
Put your phone down because phones are bad.
Phones are tools.
Social media is a tool.
Technology is a tool.
The deeper question is:
What receives your attention so consistently that the person God entrusted to your covenant begins receiving what is left over?
That question hurts.
Because perhaps you would never cheat on your spouse.
But would you repeatedly ignore them?
Perhaps you would never abandon your marriage.
But have you gradually stopped being present inside it?
Perhaps you would never flirt with somebody else across a dinner table.
But do you spend dinner staring into a device while the person you promised your life to eats across from you?
You can be faithful with your body and still become careless with your presence.
You can provide financially and still leave someone emotionally hungry.
You can say “I love you” every morning and slowly train your spouse to believe that everything on your screen is more interesting than whatever is happening inside their heart.
And sometimes the neglected spouse stops complaining.
That is not always good news.
Sometimes people stop complaining because something improved.
Sometimes they stop because they became tired of asking.
There is a difference.
There is a kind of silence that is peace.
And there is another kind of silence that is resignation.
Maybe your husband used to tell you about his day in detail.
Now he says, “It was fine.”
Maybe your wife used to crawl close to you on the couch.
Now she sits at the other end with her own phone.
Maybe you think, See? She does it too.
Maybe you think, He is just as bad.
Perhaps.
But Philippians 2 does not invite us to wait until somebody else becomes humble first.
Jesus did not love us because we had finally become lovable enough.
The Gospel confronts the exhausting mathematics of marriage:
I will give when you give.
I will listen when you listen.
I will apologize when you apologize.
I will change when you change.
Christ interrupts that cycle.
The cross says grace moves first.
And perhaps tonight repentance looks surprisingly ordinary.
Maybe there are no tears at an altar.
No dramatic music.
No public confession.
Maybe repentance sounds like a phone being placed facedown on a table.
And then a sentence:
“Talk to me. I want to hear you.”
Maybe it looks like noticing the expression on your spouse's face instead of the notification at the top of your screen.
Maybe it sounds like:
“I think I have been here physically without really being here. I’m sorry.”
Do not underestimate those words.
Because one of the most healing experiences in a marriage is not having a perfect spouse.
It is having a spouse who can still be convicted.
A spouse who can recognize hurt without immediately defending themselves.
A spouse who can say:
“I see what I have been doing.”
“I understand why that hurt.”
“I don't want you begging for my attention anymore.”
“Please forgive me.”
There is something deeply Christlike about turning toward someone.
Jesus repeatedly noticed people others overlooked.
The desperate.
The grieving.
The ashamed.
The socially inconvenient.
The people everyone else had learned to walk past.
He saw them.
And although marriage is not the direct subject of every Gospel scene where Jesus notices someone, His character exposes something in us:
Love pays attention.
Love notices.
Love is not merely an emotion hidden somewhere inside your chest.
Biblical love moves outward.
It serves.
It listens.
It considers.
It gives.
And yes, sometimes love says:
“This can wait.”
That email can wait.
That reel can wait.
That argument in the comment section can wait.
That video can wait.
That notification can wait.
The person sitting in front of you will not always be sitting there.
Read that again.
Not because tragedy is guaranteed tomorrow.
But because marriage is mortal.
Life moves.
Bodies age.
Children grow.
Seasons disappear.
The ordinary Tuesday nights you barely notice today may become memories you would someday give almost anything to revisit.
One day you may miss the voice interrupting your scrolling.
You may miss the question you once found inconvenient.
You may miss hearing your name called from another room.
You may miss those feet on your side of the bed.
You may even miss the stories you thought you had heard a thousand times.
So why wait until absence teaches you the value of presence?
Your spouse should not have to become more entertaining than the internet to deserve your eyes.
They should not have to compete with an algorithm engineered to keep offering you something new.
They should not need perfect hair, perfect conversation, perfect humor, perfect energy, or perfect sexuality to hold the attention of the person who made a covenant with them.
Marriage is not an endless audition.
Your husband should not have to perform for your attention.
Your wife should not have to become content.
And perhaps this article is making you uncomfortable because you know exactly which side of this conversation you are on.
Maybe you are the one holding the phone.
If so, conviction is not condemnation.
In Christ, exposure can become the doorway to repentance.
Do something with what God is showing you.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
Put it down.
Look at them.
Ask a real question.
Then listen long enough for the first answer to become the second answer.
Because “How are you?” often gets “fine.”
But presence sometimes eventually gets the truth.
Or maybe you are the spouse who has been staring at the side of somebody's face for months.
You have tried joking about it.
You have tried competing with it.
You have tried becoming quiet.
You have wondered whether you are boring.
Unattractive.
Too needy.
Too emotional.
Too much.
Please hear this carefully: this article is not permission to weaponize Scripture against your spouse.
Do not shove Philippians 2:4 across the table like ammunition.
The Word of God is not a club for winning marital arguments.
It is first a mirror.
Before saying, “This verse describes you,” ask:
“Lord, where does this verse expose me?”
Maybe your distraction is not a phone.
Maybe it is work.
Gaming.
Television.
Sports.
Ministry.
Friends.
Hobbies.
Even something good can become disordered when it continually receives the attention that love requires us to steward elsewhere.
And yes…
even ministry.
You can speak about Jesus publicly while neglecting the person you vowed to love privately.
You can answer strangers in a comment section while refusing to answer the ache sitting beside you.
You can encourage thousands and ignore one.
That should sober every Christian with a platform—including us.
Because the Gospel does not merely transform what we post.
The Gospel must transform how we live when nobody is watching.
Jesus did not die merely to improve our online behavior.
He died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He calls us to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He reconciles us to God.
And the grace that saves us begins reshaping the ordinary corners of our lives—including the way we speak, listen, forgive, serve, repent, and love inside marriage.
This is where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Sometimes the scandal is obvious.
Adultery.
Pornography.
Deception.
Abandonment.
Betrayal.
Sometimes it is quieter.
A thousand tiny moments of indifference.
A marriage slowly disappearing behind two illuminated screens.
But grace can enter there too.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin did not happen.
Not by calling neglect harmless.
Not by demanding that wounded people fake healing.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace repents.
Grace forgives.
Grace rebuilds.
Grace teaches us to love differently.
Maybe your marriage does not need another expensive vacation as desperately as it needs twenty uninterrupted minutes tonight.
Maybe you do not need a new spouse.
Maybe you need new habits.
Maybe the first battlefield is not the bedroom.
Maybe it is the dinner table.
Maybe restoration begins with two phones placed somewhere neither person can reach without standing up.
And maybe the first conversation is awkward.
Have it anyway.
“Have I made you feel like my phone matters more than you?”
Then do something terrifying.
Do not defend yourself.
Listen.
If the answer hurts, listen.
If your spouse cries, listen.
If they say, “I stopped telling you things because you never seemed interested,” listen.
If they say, “I feel alone even when you're here,” do not immediately explain your intentions.
Intentions matter.
But so does impact.
Then ask:
“What would being more present look like to you?”
That is not weakness.
That is love learning how to pay attention again.
And if both of you have failed?
Welcome to marriage between two sinners who need Jesus.
There is grace for that.
The Christian marriage was never supposed to be the story of two flawless human beings.
It is two people continually discovering how desperately they need the mercy of Christ.
Confessing.
Forgiving.
Learning.
Failing.
Getting back up.
Returning to Jesus.
Returning to each other.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Perhaps you need to send this article to your spouse.
But before you do, ask yourself whether you are sending it as an accusation…
or an invitation.
There is a difference between:
“READ THIS. THIS IS YOU.”
and:
“I read this and realized there are things I need to change too. Can we talk tonight?”
One starts a trial.
The other may start healing.
And perhaps you know another couple living this without having words for it.
Not to shame anyone.
Send it privately to a couple you love.
Save it before the feed carries it away, because conviction is easy to feel for three minutes and easier to forget by morning.
Maybe your marriage has survived this.
Maybe you are fighting through it now.
Maybe you have been the distracted spouse.
Maybe you have been the lonely one.
Maybe both are true.
You do not have to tell strangers every private detail.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the moment pretending finally loses its grip.
And if you know Christ has already begun restoring something you thought was dying, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become another couple's reason not to give up.
It does not.
It does not.
Christian giving must not be manipulated. Scripture says giving is to come from what a person has determined in the heart, not from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
But voluntary support can still become a meaningful offering toward Gospel work.
It helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep building.
Keep pointing wounded people toward Jesus.

And sometimes glorifying God with what He has entrusted to us includes freely supporting Gospel work we believe is bearing good fruit—not under pressure, not to purchase blessing, but from gratitude and willing generosity.
One share can enter a home we have never seen.
One tag can reach a husband who has stopped noticing the distance.
One private message can reach a wife who thought nobody understood.
One comment can make another believer brave enough to admit, “Us too.”
One saved article can be reopened on the night somebody finally decides to put the phone down and have the conversation.
Put the screen down long enough to see the soul beside you.
Look into the eyes you once searched across crowded rooms.
Listen to the voice you once stayed awake late just to hear.
Ask what has been hurting.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive what can be forgiven.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help when wounds run deeper than a conversation can repair.
And bring the marriage back beneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Because the goal is not merely less screen time.
The goal is more Christlike love.
Not merely fewer notifications.
More attention.
Not merely digital boundaries.
A heart being transformed.
Not merely saving a marriage's appearance.
Learning again to see the person inside it.
Your phone will eventually become obsolete.
The posts will disappear down the feed.
The videos will be forgotten.
Today's urgent notification will become tomorrow's digital dust.
But the person sitting beside you is carrying a soul.
A story.
Fears they may not have told you.
Prayers you may not know they pray.
Wounds you may not realize you caused.
Love they may still be desperately trying to give you.
So tonight, when the screen lights up…
perhaps let it wait.
Turn toward them.
Look.
Listen.
Stay.
And remember this:
Do not wait until an empty chair teaches you how precious the person sitting in it was.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Jealousy Always a Sin? The Answer May Expose What Your Heart Loves Most
paragraphs: Is Jealousy Always a Sin? The Answer May Expose What Your Heart Loves Most

We usually think jealousy is something Christians should immediately repent of. But Scripture describes God Himself as jealous. So what separates sinful jealousy from holy jealousy—and what if the jealousy you keep excusing is actually revealing the throne of your heart?
There is a kind of jealousy that destroys relationships.
And there is a kind of jealousy that reveals love.
If that sounds uncomfortable, good.
Because somewhere along the way, many Christians learned to treat the word jealousy as though it automatically belongs beside words like hatred, bitterness, pride, and envy.
We hear, “God is jealous,” and almost instinctively feel the need to explain it away.
Because we know what human jealousy looks like.
A husband scrolling through his wife’s phone while she sleeps.
A woman quietly resenting another woman because she is prettier, more successful, more admired, or seemingly more blessed.
A believer smiling when someone announces good news while secretly wondering:
Why does God keep doing that for them and not for me?
A ministry leader watching someone else grow faster.
A friend becoming strangely cold when your life starts getting better.
A sibling silently keeping score.
A Christian congratulating someone publicly while privately hoping they fail.
We know that jealousy.
It is ugly.
But then you open your Bible.
And suddenly God says something startling.
In Exodus 34:14, the Hebrew text says:
כִּי יְהוָה קַנָּא שְׁמוֹ אֵל קַנָּא הוּא
Ki YHWH qannā shemo, El qannā hu.
“For the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.”
Not merely that God occasionally feels jealousy.
The text associates jealousy with His very name.
So now we have a problem.
If jealousy is always sinful, how can the perfectly holy God be jealous?
He cannot sin.
Scripture says plainly that God cannot be tempted with evil and does not tempt anyone with evil (James 1:13).
So perhaps our definition is too shallow.
Perhaps not everything called jealousy is the same thing.
And perhaps understanding the difference will expose something in us that we would rather leave hidden.
Because jealousy is not ultimately understood merely by asking:
“Do I feel jealous?”
The deeper question is:
“What does my jealousy believe belongs to me?”
That question changes everything.
Imagine watching someone walk into your house, put their arm around your spouse, and begin trying to seduce them away from you.
Would you shrug?
Would you smile politely and say:
“I don't want to be possessive.”
Of course not.
There is a form of jealousy that can arise because something precious is being violated.
Marriage involves covenant.
Faithfulness matters precisely because love matters.
And this begins to help us understand biblical language about God.
Throughout Scripture, God frequently describes His relationship with His covenant people using the language of marital faithfulness.
Israel's idolatry was therefore not presented merely as breaking an arbitrary religious regulation.
It was spiritual adultery.
God had rescued them.
Loved them.
Claimed them as His covenant people.
And they repeatedly ran toward other gods.
That is why Exodus 20:5 says:
כִּי אָנֹכִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵל קַנָּא
Ki anokhi YHWH Elohekha, El qannā.
“For I the LORD your God am a jealous God.”
The Hebrew word קַנָּא — qannā carries the sense of jealousy or zeal and, in Scripture, is especially associated with God's insistence upon the exclusive worship rightly belonging to Him.
God's jealousy is not insecurity.
He is not looking down from heaven worried that another god might outperform Him.
There is no competitor who threatens His throne.
Isaiah declares:
“I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God.” (Isaiah 45:5)
God does not need our worship because His ego is fragile.
God commands our worship because He alone is God.
Giving worship to an idol is not simply violating God's preference.
It is giving creation what belongs to the Creator.
And because God loves His people, He refuses to pretend that our idols are harmless.
That is holy jealousy.
But human jealousy can become something very different.
Scripture gives us another word worth seeing.
In Galatians 5:20, among the works of the flesh, Paul includes:
ζῆλος — zēlos
The Greek word can carry the idea of zeal or jealousy depending upon its context.
That matters.
Because Scripture does not teach that every intense desire or every form of zeal is automatically evil.
Paul can even say:
ζηλῶ γὰρ ὑμᾶς θεοῦ ζήλῳ
“For I feel a divine jealousy for you.” (2 Corinthians 11:2)
The same family of Greek words can therefore appear in very different moral contexts.
The emotion alone does not settle the question.
Its object matters.
Its motive matters.
Its expression matters.
And above everything else, whether it agrees with God's holiness matters.
This is where the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes what we call jealousy is actually envy wearing a more respectable outfit.
You see someone receive what you wanted.
The promotion.
The marriage.
The baby.
The ministry opportunity.
The beautiful home.
The successful business.
The recognition.
The healing.
The attention.
The platform.
The answered prayer.
And something twists inside you.
You don't necessarily want to steal it from them.
But their happiness somehow makes your disappointment hurt more.
Everyone else sees a celebration.
You see a reminder of everything you don't have.
And you whisper:
“God, when is it my turn?”
There is nothing inherently sinful about grieving an unmet desire.
There is nothing inherently sinful about wanting marriage, children, meaningful work, fruitful ministry, friendship, stability, or other good gifts.
The danger begins when another person's blessing becomes an accusation against God's goodness.
When gratitude dies because someone else received more.
When love becomes difficult because another person's flourishing threatens your sense of worth.
When you cannot celebrate what God has done for them because you are consumed by what He has not yet done for you.
James describes the destructive trajectory with frightening clarity:
“For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.” (James 3:16)
Jealousy can become a window into worship.
Because sometimes jealousy says:
I don't merely want what they have.
I need what they have in order to believe I matter.
And suddenly the issue is deeper than emotion.
Now we are standing before an idol.
Maybe your idol is approval.
Maybe beauty.
Maybe marriage.
Maybe money.
Maybe influence.
Maybe ministry success.
Maybe being needed.
Maybe being noticed.
Maybe winning.
Maybe being the person everyone envies instead of the person doing the envying.
And idols make terrible masters because they always demand another sacrifice.
You finally get the thing you thought would silence your jealousy...
and then someone gets more.
A larger house.
A happier marriage.
A bigger audience.
A better body.
A more successful child.
A more impressive career.
More applause.
More money.
More influence.
And the finish line moves again.
This is why comparison can become spiritual slavery.
There will always be somebody ahead of you according to whatever scoreboard you choose.
But Jesus never invited you to build your identity on a scoreboard.
There is a moment after Christ's resurrection when Peter asks Jesus about another disciple.
Essentially:
What about him?
Jesus answers:
“If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!” (John 21:22)
Read those final words again.
You follow Me.
Not their calling.
Not their timeline.
Not their marriage.
Not their ministry.
Not their blessing.
Not their audience.
Not their life.
Me.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this desperately needs today.
You have spent so much time watching what Jesus is doing with somebody else that you are missing what Jesus is doing with you.
You keep staring sideways while Christ is calling you forward.
And perhaps jealousy has been quietly stealing years from your life.
But there is another side to this.
Because some Christians become so afraid of jealousy that they mistake indifference for maturity.
There are things worth being jealous for in the biblical sense of holy zeal.
Paul's “divine jealousy” for the Corinthian believers was connected to his desire to present them faithfully to Christ.
He feared that they were being spiritually deceived.
His concern was not:
They belong to me.
His concern was:
They belong to Christ.
That distinction is enormous.
Sinful jealousy says:
“You are mine for my glory.”
Godly zeal says:
“You belong to God for His glory.”
Sinful jealousy wants possession.
Holy jealousy wants faithfulness.
Sinful jealousy is threatened by another person's flourishing.
Holy zeal grieves when another person's soul is being pulled away from Christ.
Sinful jealousy asks:
“How does this affect my importance?”
Holy zeal asks:
“How does this affect God's glory and this person's good?”
Even then, we must be careful.
Human beings can disguise control as spiritual concern.
We can call possessiveness “discernment.”
We can call insecurity “boundaries.”
We can call pride “righteous anger.”
We can call rivalry “protecting the truth.”
We can even claim to be defending God when what we are really defending is our reputation.
The human heart is frighteningly talented at baptizing its own motives.
That is why jealousy must be brought into the light.
Not merely managed.
Not renamed.
Not justified.
Brought before Christ.
Ask yourself something uncomfortable.
When someone else succeeds, what happens inside you?
When someone else receives praise, do you feel diminished?
When someone else is chosen, do you secretly want them to fail?
When someone else's prayer is answered while yours remains unanswered, do you begin questioning whether God loves you?
When somebody you love gives attention to someone else, is your first impulse love—or control?
When someone grows spiritually, do you celebrate them or compete with them?
And perhaps the hardest question:
Would you still want God to bless them if His blessing on their life never made your life look more impressive?
That one reaches deep.
Because the Gospel does not merely teach us how to behave when jealousy appears.
The Gospel dismantles the reason jealousy has so much power over us.
At the cross, your worth is no longer something you have to win.
You don't have to outperform somebody to become lovable.
You don't have to become more attractive than her.
More successful than him.
More spiritual than them.
More admired.
More followed.
More accomplished.
More impressive.
If you belong to Christ, your identity is rooted somewhere comparison cannot reach.
You are redeemed not because you defeated your competition, but because Christ defeated sin and death.
You are forgiven not because you finally became impressive enough, but because Jesus was pierced for sinners.
You are welcomed not because your résumé impressed heaven, but because the Son opened the way.
This is grace.
And grace murders the scoreboard.
At Calvary, there is no podium where the most impressive sinner gets the closest seat to Jesus.
There is only mercy.
The proud need it.
The jealous need it.
The envious need it.
The insecure need it.
The secretly bitter need it.
The person smiling while dying inside needs it.
And perhaps that person is you.
Maybe you have been carrying jealousy nobody knows about.
You never acted on it publicly.
You never posted anything cruel.
You never started a fight.
You simply learned to hide it.
But God sees the part of your heart you keep editing before other people see you.
And here is the scandal of grace:
Jesus already knows.
He knows the ugly thought.
The resentment.
The comparison.
The secret satisfaction when somebody you envied stumbled.
The silent question asking why God gave them what you deserved.
He knows.
And still the Gospel says:
Come.
Not because jealousy doesn't matter.
Because grace does.
Repentance is not pretending the sin wasn't there.
Repentance is bringing it into the light, agreeing with God about it, turning from it, and running toward Christ.
First John 1:9 gives sinners astonishing hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
That means jealousy does not have to become your identity.
Envy does not get the final chapter.
Bitterness does not own your future.
Christ can teach you to celebrate another person's blessing without interpreting it as your rejection.
He can teach you to pray sincerely for someone you once secretly competed against.
He can teach you to look at another person's success and say:
“Thank You, Lord, for being good to them.”
And mean it.
That is freedom.
Not having everything everyone else has.
Being so satisfied in Christ that somebody else's blessing no longer feels like your curse.
So is jealousy always a sin?
No.
Scripture itself prevents us from saying that.
God possesses perfect, holy jealousy for His own glory and covenant faithfulness. Paul could speak of a “divine jealousy” concerning believers' faithfulness to Christ.

But the jealousy that grows from envy, selfish ambition, covetousness, insecurity, rivalry, pride, controlling possessiveness, resentment, or a desire to deprive another person of good is sinful and must not be excused.
The question is not simply whether jealousy exists.
The question is what kind of jealousy it is—and what it reveals about what you worship.
Jesus is not asking you to clean yourself before coming to Him.
He is calling you to repent and come honestly.
Maybe your prayer today needs to be painfully simple:
Jesus, I have compared.
I have envied.
I have resented.
I have treated another person's blessing as evidence that You forgot me.
Forgive me.
Teach me to want Your glory more than my recognition.
Teach me to rejoice when others rejoice.
Teach me to trust Your wisdom when my story looks different.
And become more precious to me than everything I keep comparing.
Not as performance.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop hiding.
Not as a transaction with God. We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in loving obedience, not through supporting a page.
But if this ministry is genuinely helping people see Jesus more clearly, supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work can be one practical way to help truth reach someone you may never meet.
Let this find them.
Save it too.
Because jealousy rarely disappears after one confrontation.
Sometimes it returns the next time somebody gets what you prayed for.
And when it does, come back and remember:
Their blessing is not proof of your abandonment.
Share because someone needs the Gospel more than you need to protect your reach.
Tag because sometimes love looks like making sure somebody doesn't walk through a battle alone.
Save because tomorrow's temptation may require today's truth.
And above all...
Look at Jesus.
The One who knew exactly how corrupted our hearts could become and went to the cross anyway.
The One who took sinners covered in pride, envy, rivalry, lust, bitterness, jealousy, and shame...
and offered them something comparison could never earn.
Grace.
Maybe you spent years believing someone else's beautiful chapter meant God had abandoned your story.
But the hands holding your story still carry nail scars.
And when you finally stop staring at everybody else's blessings, you may discover that Jesus Himself was the Treasure jealousy kept distracting you from.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOTHER WHO NAMED HER SON “NO GLORY”
paragraphs: THE MOTHER WHO NAMED HER SON “NO GLORY”
She was dying. Her husband was dead. Israel had been shattered. Yet the tragedy that broke her heart most deeply was something many Christians today barely notice when it happens: the glory was gone.
There are names a mother whispers because she has dreamed of them for years.
Names spoken over a swollen belly.
Names written secretly on paper.
Names carrying prayers, hopes, inheritance, promise.
And then there is the name one dying mother gave her newborn son.
Ichabod.
A name forever attached to one of the darkest days in Israel’s history.
A name commonly understood along the lines of “No glory,” “Where is the glory?” or “Alas, the glory.”
But Scripture itself tells us exactly what was crushing this woman’s soul.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 4:21 says:
וַתִּקְרָא לַנַּעַר אִיכָבוֹד לֵאמֹר גָּלָה כָבוֹד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
Vattiqra lanna'ar I-khavod lemor: galah khavod mi-Yisrael.
“She named the boy Ichabod, saying, ‘The glory has departed from Israel.’”
גָּלָה כָבוֹד — galah kavod.
The glory has departed.
The verb גָּלָה — galah can carry the sense of going away, being removed, or going into exile.
And כָּבוֹד — kavod, “glory,” comes from a Hebrew word-family associated with weight or heaviness and, by extension, honor, splendor, significance, and glory.
In other words, this was not merely a woman saying, “Something bad happened today.”
Something weighty had been lost.
And if you understand why, this ancient mother’s final words may expose something terrifying about modern Christianity—and perhaps something about your own heart.
Because the tragedy of 1 Samuel 4 did not begin when Israel lost a battle.
It began when people learned how to carry the things of God while their hearts were drifting from the God those things represented.
That should frighten us more than losing money.
More than losing influence.
More than losing popularity.
More than losing comfort.
Because it is possible to keep the religious language while losing reverence.
Possible to sing worship songs while protecting secret sin.
Possible to quote Scripture while refusing to obey it.
Possible to know how church works while barely knowing what trembling before a holy God feels like anymore.
Israel discovered this painfully.
Before Ichabod was born, the spiritual condition of Israel was already diseased.

Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests, but their behavior dishonored the LORD. They abused their priestly position, treated the LORD's offering with contempt, and persisted in sexual immorality around the sanctuary.
They had proximity to holy things without holy hearts.
That is one of Scripture's most terrifying warnings.
You can stand near an altar and still be far from God.
You can hold a Bible and still resist its Author.
You can have Christian content filling your phone while lust, bitterness, greed, pride, unforgiveness, hypocrisy, or secret compromise is quietly consuming your soul.
You can even become skilled at appearing spiritually alive.
And then Israel went to war.
They were defeated by the Philistines.
Thousands died.
But instead of first asking what their defeat revealed about their relationship with God, Israel reached for something religious.
The ark.
“Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD,” they essentially reasoned, so that it might save them from their enemies.
Do you see the danger?
They wanted God's power without confronting their rebellion.
They wanted victory without repentance.
They wanted the symbol of God's presence without surrendering to the God whose presence made it holy.
The ark was not a magical object.
God could not be manipulated.
Yet Israel treated what was sacred almost like a spiritual weapon they could deploy whenever life became desperate.
And we are capable of doing the same thing.
We ignore God until the diagnosis comes.
Then we pray.
We compromise until the marriage starts collapsing.
Then we pray.
We feed an addiction privately until its consequences become public.
Then we pray.
We build our lives around ourselves, sprinkle Christian language over our ambitions, and when everything begins falling apart we suddenly reach for God as though He were an emergency lever.
Prayer is good.
Running to God is good.
The prodigal is always right to come home.
But there is a difference between desperately wanting God and desperately wanting God to remove the consequences while we keep the idols.
Israel carried the ark into battle.
The people shouted so loudly that the earth shook.
Imagine the scene.
Thousands of voices.
Religious excitement.
Confidence.
Noise.
The visible symbol of God's covenant presence standing among them.
It probably looked like revival.
Then the Philistines attacked.
Israel was crushed.
Thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fell.
Hophni died.
Phinehas died.
And the ark of God was captured.
A messenger ran from the battlefield to Shiloh with his clothes torn and dust upon his head.
Eli was waiting.
Scripture says his heart trembled for the ark of God.
Then the report came.
Israel has fled.
Your sons are dead.
The ark has been captured.
When Eli heard about the ark, the old priest fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died.
But the story was not finished.
Somewhere nearby was Phinehas's pregnant wife.
Imagine what reached her ears in a matter of moments.
Her nation had suffered catastrophic defeat.
Her husband was dead.
Her brother-in-law was dead.
Her father-in-law was dead.
The ark of God had been captured.
The shock sent her into labor.
She gave birth while dying.
Women stood around her trying desperately to give her one reason to hold on.
“Do not be afraid. You have given birth to a son.”
Normally those words should have pierced darkness with joy.
A son.
Life arriving while death surrounded her.
A future.
A reason to smile.
But Scripture says she did not answer.
She did not set her heart upon it.
Her body was fading.
And then she named him.
Ichabod.
Not because her husband was dead alone.
Not because Eli was dead alone.
Not simply because Israel lost a battle.
Her final explanation keeps returning to the ark.
גָּלָה כָבוֹד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
Galah kavod mi-Yisrael.
“The glory has departed from Israel.”
Then Scripture repeats her final thought:
גָּלָה כָבוֹד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל כִּי נִלְקַח אֲרוֹן הָאֱלֹהִים
“The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured.”
And she died.
A baby entered the world carrying the vocabulary of a national spiritual catastrophe.
Every time someone called his name, the tragedy would echo again.
Ichabod.
Where is the glory?
No glory.
The glory has departed.
But here is where we must read the whole biblical story carefully.
The Philistines had captured the ark.
They had not captured God.
That distinction changes everything.
In the very next chapter, the Philistines put the ark inside the temple of their god Dagon.
They apparently thought Israel's God had been defeated.
Then morning came.
Dagon was lying face-down before the ark of the LORD.
They put their idol back up.
The next morning?
Dagon was down again—this time with his head and hands severed.
The message is almost impossible to miss.
Israel had been defeated.
YHWH had not.
Israel's priests had disgraced His name.
God remained holy.
The ark had been captured.
God remained sovereign.
No Philistine army had dragged the LORD into captivity.
The God of Israel did not need Israel's army to rescue Him.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs those words.
Because something has been captured in your life.
Something has died.
Something collapsed.
Maybe your marriage did not become what you prayed it would become.
Maybe your child walked away.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe the addiction returned.
Maybe you promised Jesus, “Never again,” and then found yourself crying over the same sin.
Maybe people know your Christian face but not your private war.
Maybe you look spiritually alive online while inside you keep whispering:
Where is the glory?
Where did the fire go?
Where did my hunger for Scripture go?
Why can I scroll for two hours but struggle to pray for ten minutes?
Why does temptation excite me more than holiness?
Why do I miss the person I used to be with God?
Be honest.
This may be hitting harder than you expected.
And perhaps that discomfort is mercy.
Because conviction is not Jesus throwing you away.
Conviction can be Jesus exposing what is killing you so that you will finally bring it into His light.
The answer to Ichabod is not pretending there was never a scandal.
Christianity is not a religion of pretending the scandal did not happen.
It is the announcement that God entered our scandal to redeem sinners.
And this is where the road eventually leads us far beyond Shiloh.
To Jesus Christ.
Israel's story teaches us that sacred objects cannot save sinners.
Priestly ancestry cannot save sinners.
Religious excitement cannot save sinners.
Our reputation cannot save us.
Our church attendance cannot wash away guilt.
Our good works cannot erase rebellion.
We need more than the appearance of glory.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And the Gospel declares that the eternal Son of God came to us.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He called sinners to repentance.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He exposed darkness.
He forgave.
He healed.
And then He walked willingly toward the cross.
There, something happened that makes Ichabod's story tremble with deeper significance.
Jesus cried:
Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ, λεμὰ σαβαχθανί;
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
Mark preserves the cry in transliterated Semitic form and explains it:
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Jesus was invoking Psalm 22 as He suffered on the cross.
The sinless Christ was bearing sin.
The One who deserved glory accepted shame.
The Holy One stood in the place of the guilty.
