Second Kings 1 opens after the death of Ahab. Ahaziah, his son, is king over Israel. He possesses what most people spend their lives trying to obtain—position, influence, servants, authority, access.
Then gravity humiliates a king.
Scripture says:
וַיִּפֹּל אֲחַזְיָה בְּעַד הַשְּׂבָכָה בַּעֲלִיָּתוֹ אֲשֶׁר בְּשֹׁמְרוֹן וַיָּחַל
Vayyippol ’Achazyah… vayyachal.
In context: Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper chamber in Samaria and became sick or injured. — 2 Kings 1:2.
The Hebrew verb וַיִּפֹּל — vayyippol comes from naphal, “to fall.”
The king fell.
Not metaphorically.
Physically.
Painfully.
Suddenly.
A man who could command other men could not command his own body to remain standing.
A crown could not stop gravity.
A palace could not guarantee safety.
Power could not negotiate with mortality.
And now Ahaziah is lying wounded.
Imagine the room.
Servants moving quietly.
Whispers outside the chamber.
A king who once gave orders from a throne now giving orders from a bed.
He wants to know one thing.
Am I going to survive this?
That question itself was not sinful.
There is nothing wrong with wanting to live.
There is nothing wrong with seeking help when we are sick. Scripture does not teach Christians to reject legitimate medical care. Luke himself was called “the beloved physician” in Colossians 4:14.
The scandal was not that Ahaziah wanted an answer.
The scandal was where he went looking for one.
He called his messengers.
And instead of telling them to seek the LORD, the God of Israel, he said:
לְכוּ דִרְשׁוּ בְּבַעַל זְבוּב אֱלֹהֵי עֶקְרוֹן
Lekhu dirshu be-Va‘al Zevuv, elohei ‘Eqron.
“Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron…”
He wanted to know whether he would recover.
But he wanted the answer from the wrong god.
And perhaps this is where an ancient king suddenly begins looking uncomfortably modern.
Because we may never send servants to Ekron.
We may never bow before a carved statue called Baal-zebub.
But when life falls apart, where does your heart run first?
When fear enters the room, what becomes your functional savior?
Money?
Control?
A relationship?
Approval?
Horoscopes?
Manifestation?
Psychics?
Superstition?
Endless scrolling?
Alcohol?
Pornography?
Work?
Your own intelligence?
Another human being whom you secretly expect to give you the security only God can give?
Even good things can become idols when we demand from them what belongs ultimately to God.
And suddenly Ahaziah's messengers are not so distant from us.
Because idolatry is not merely kneeling before something made of stone.
At its heart, idolatry gives created things the trust, worship, allegiance, hope, or ultimate dependence that belongs to the Creator.
That is why God interrupts the journey.
The messengers are traveling toward Ekron when the angel of the LORD sends Elijah the Tishbite to intercept them.
And God gives Elijah a question.
Not a long speech.
Not a philosophical argument.
A question.
A devastating one.
הֲמִבְּלִי אֵין־אֱלֹהִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
Hamibbeli ein-Elohim be-Yisra’el?
In context:
“Is it because there is no God in Israel…?” — 2 Kings 1:3.
Read that slowly.
Is there no God in Israel?
That question cuts deeper than Ahaziah's physical wound.
God was not absent.
God was not dead.
God had not surrendered His throne.
God had not lost His voice.
Yet the king behaved as though the living God were unavailable.
That was the indictment.
And maybe the Spirit of God is pressing the same question against some hearts reading this:
Is there no God when you are afraid?
Is there no God when your marriage is breaking?
Is there no God when the doctor gives you news you never wanted to hear?
Is there no God when somebody leaves?
Is there no God when you lose your job?
Is there no God when temptation screams louder than Scripture?
Is there no God when you cannot feel Him?
Is there no God when heaven seems silent?
Is there no God when you have prayed for months and nothing appears to be changing?
We often imagine that rejecting God means standing in His face and shouting, “I do not believe You exist.”
Sometimes it is quieter than that.
Sometimes we confess Him with our mouths while living as though He is irrelevant to our crisis.
We pray after we have exhausted every other option.
We open Scripture after everything else fails.
We seek God's wisdom after doing exactly what we already wanted to do.
We ask Him to bless decisions we never invited Him into.
We call Jesus “Lord,” but when panic comes, something else gets the first call.
And this story forces an uncomfortable question:
Where do your messengers go when you are wounded?
Ahaziah's crisis did not create the deepest problem in his heart.
It exposed it.
That matters.

Pain is not proof that God has abandoned you. Scripture repeatedly shows faithful people suffering deeply. Job suffered. David suffered. Paul suffered. The apostles suffered. Above all, Jesus Christ—the sinless Son of God—suffered.
So we must never turn Ahaziah's story into the cruel formula that every injured or sick person is being personally punished for some secret sin.
That is not what Scripture teaches.
Ahaziah's judgment is explicitly connected to his rejection of the LORD and his decision to seek the pagan deity of Ekron instead of seeking the word of Israel's God.
Elijah eventually stands before him and repeats the charge.
Because you sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub…
because you acted as though there were no God in Israel whose word could be sought…
you will not rise from the bed on which you are lying.
You will die.
And 2 Kings 1:17 records the terrifying conclusion:
וַיָּמָת כִּדְבַר יְהוָה
Vayyamat kidvar YHWH.
“He died according to the word of the LORD.”
The king wanted a word about his future.
He received one.
Just not from the god he chose.
There is something sobering here that modern Christianity must not soften.
God is gracious.
God is compassionate.
God is patient.
God forgives sinners.
But grace does not mean God has stopped being holy.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sin never mattered.
The Gospel is the announcement that sin mattered so much that the Son of God went to a cross to bear judgment for sinners.
And this is where Ahaziah's story leaves us standing at an enormous crossroads.
Because if the Bible ended with rebellious kings dying under judgment, none of us would have much reason for hope.
We have all sent the messengers of our hearts somewhere they did not belong.
We have all trusted substitutes.
We have all loved created things more than the Creator.
We have all sinned and fallen short of the glory of God.
Maybe your false god never had a temple.
Maybe it had a contact name in your phone.
Maybe it had a bank balance.
Maybe it had a bottle.
Maybe it had a browser history.
Maybe it had your face.
Maybe your idol was simply you—your ability to control everything, understand everything, fix everything, and survive without surrender.
And eventually every false god makes the same confession:
I cannot save you.
Money can pay a hospital bill, but it cannot purchase eternal life.
Popularity can surround you with people while leaving your soul unbearably lonely.
Pleasure can numb pain for a night and multiply it by morning.
Human approval can applaud you today and crucify your reputation tomorrow.
Your body will eventually weaken.
Your achievements will eventually belong to history.
Every earthly throne eventually becomes vacant.
Every human heart eventually stops beating.
So where do sinners go?
Not Ekron.
Not another idol.
Not deeper into ourselves.
We go to Jesus.
And here the story becomes more than a warning.
It becomes an invitation.
Ahaziah lay on a bed facing death because he rejected the word of God.
Centuries later, another King would walk deliberately toward death in obedience to the Father.
Jesus Christ did not fall accidentally into suffering.
He willingly gave Himself.
He was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crowned with thorns.
Nailed to a cross.
And there, the true King bore the judgment sinners deserved.
Isaiah had foretold that the suffering Servant would be pierced for our transgressions.
The New Testament declares that Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is the center of Christianity.
Not “be a better Ahaziah.”
Not “try harder.”
Not “be religious enough so bad things never happen.”
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
Lord.
The Gospel does not merely tell wounded people to climb back toward God.
It announces that God came down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And perhaps you have been sending messengers everywhere because you are terrified of what will happen if you finally become honest with Jesus.
Maybe you think repentance means walking toward someone eager to humiliate you.
Look at the cross.
The Savior already knows the worst thing about you.
He knew it when He stretched out His hands.
Repentance is not pretending your sin was small.
It is agreeing with God about your sin and turning from it toward the Savior whose grace is greater.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Jesus said that whoever comes to Him He will never cast out.
The same Bible that warns us about Ahaziah also gives us Peter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Jesus restored him.
It gives us Paul.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Jesus transformed him.
It gives us a criminal dying beside Christ with nothing left to offer—no ministry résumé, no years of restitution, no religious accomplishments—and he turned to Jesus in faith.
Jesus gave him hope beyond the grave.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not permission to continue worshiping our idols.
Grace that calls sinners out of darkness.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace that takes people whose stories looked ruined and makes them witnesses to the mercy of Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But do not misunderstand that sentence.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites sinners by redeeming them.
He does not call darkness light.
He brings people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
He does not tell us our idols are harmless.
He calls us to turn from idols to the living God.
And that means this article cannot end with Ahaziah.
It has to end with you.
Where are your messengers going?
When you cannot sleep tonight, where will your mind run?
When fear comes tomorrow, what will you worship for security?
When temptation returns, whose voice will carry authority?
When guilt reminds you of what you did, will you hide from Christ—or run toward the One who died for sinners?
When success comes, will you remember the God you begged for help during the storm?
Maybe you have been away from God for years.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You still know how Christians talk.
You know when to say “Amen.”
But privately, your heart has been sending messengers to Ekron.
No more hiding.
Come home.
Not because you can repair yourself before approaching Jesus.
Come because you cannot.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the exhausted version of yourself nobody else gets to see.
You do not need another false god promising what it cannot deliver.
You need Christ.
Be honest.
Your comment does not save you.
Jesus does.
But sometimes publicly admitting, I need Christ, is the first crack in a wall of pretending that has stood for years.
And please do not keep this message trapped on your screen.
Someone may be sending their messengers toward an idol.
Someone may look perfectly fine in their profile picture while quietly wondering whether life is worth continuing.
Someone may need to be reminded tonight:
There is still a God to seek.
Send this privately to the person whose faith has become tired.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to their brokenness.
Supporting Christian ministry can be a meaningful act of generosity when it is done freely, cheerfully, and for God's glory—not from guilt or the belief that payment purchases God's blessing.
And your sharing can carry this message into a home we may never enter, onto a screen we may never see, and into the life of someone we may never meet.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Eternal life is God's gift in Christ, received through faith.
His servants are waiting.
The road to Ekron is open.
The false god is waiting to be consulted.
And then heaven interrupts the journey with one question:
הֲמִבְּלִי אֵין־אֱלֹהִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
Is there no God in Israel?
There is.
And Christian, there is still a God when your life falls through the lattice.
There is still a God when the diagnosis comes.
There is still a God when your plans collapse.
There is still a God when you are ashamed of what you have become.
There is still a God when your prayers feel weak.
There is still a God when your faith feels smaller than your fear.
There is still a God when everyone else leaves.
And there is still a Savior whose hands bear the scars of how far He was willing to go to redeem sinners.
Do not send your heart to Ekron.
Run to Jesus.
Because the most dangerous thing about falling is not hitting the ground.
It is discovering, while you are lying there broken, that your heart has been calling the wrong god—and refusing the invitation to finally come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID PAUL MENTION ALEXANDER THE COPPERSMITH?
paragraphs: WHY DID PAUL MENTION ALEXANDER THE COPPERSMITH?

The name Paul carried into one of his final letters reveals something frightening about betrayal, something beautiful about forgiveness, and something every wounded Christian needs to understand before pain turns into poison.
There is a name sitting near the end of Paul’s final letter that almost feels out of place.
Alexander.
Not Peter.
Not John.
Not Timothy.
Not one of the heroes whose names Christians teach their children.
Alexander the coppersmith.
Paul is nearing the end of his race. He has already written words that sound almost like a man hearing eternity approaching:
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.”
—2 Timothy 4:7, KJV
And then, surrounded by instructions, memories, loneliness, names of friends, and the approaching shadow of death, Paul remembers one man who hurt him.
He writes:
—2 Timothy 4:14–15, KJV
Why?
Why preserve Alexander’s name?
Why allow the memory of someone who wounded an apostle to remain in Holy Scripture for generations?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
Why does Paul sound so different here from the sanitized version of Christianity many of us have learned to perform?
Because Paul does not say, “Nothing happened.”
He does not pretend Alexander was misunderstood.
He does not call evil good so that he can appear forgiving.
He names the harm.
And then he refuses to become its judge.
That distinction may save somebody reading this from becoming the very thing that wounded them.
The Greek is painfully direct:
“Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ χαλκεὺς πολλά μοι κακὰ ἐνεδείξατο· ἀποδώσει αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ.”
Alexandros ho chalkeus polla moi kaka enedeixato; apodōsei autō ho Kyrios kata ta erga autou.
Alexander the metalworker did Paul great harm; the Lord would render to him according to his works.

The word χαλκεύς (chalkeus) identifies Alexander as a smith or metalworker. Although traditionally rendered “coppersmith,” the term could be used more generally for someone who worked metal. The expression πολλά μοι κακά is equally difficult to soften: many evils, much harm, great injury done to Paul.
Paul was not imagining the wound.
He was not exaggerating forgiveness by denying reality.
Alexander hurt him.
That matters.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christians learned that forgiveness means pretending nothing happened.
Someone betrayed you?
Smile.
Someone lied about you?
Stay quiet.
Someone manipulated you?
Call it grace.
Someone repeatedly harms you?
Keep giving them unrestricted access because “Christians forgive.”
But that is not what Paul does.
Immediately after entrusting Alexander to God's judgment, Paul tells Timothy:
“Of whom be thou ware also.”
In Greek:
“ὃν καὶ σὺ φυλάσσου”
hon kai sy phylassou.
You also—guard yourself against him.
Read that again if you have spent years confusing forgiveness with unlimited access.
Paul can leave vengeance with God and still warn Timothy.
He can refuse personal retaliation and still recognize danger.
He can forgive without becoming foolish.
He can trust divine justice without pretending evil is harmless.
There is no contradiction.
There is maturity.
And maybe that is why Alexander’s name survived.
Not so Christians would spend two thousand years hating a man they never met.
But so wounded believers could learn what to do when another human being leaves damage behind.
There is something else we must handle carefully.

The New Testament mentions other men named Alexander. First Timothy 1:20 names “Hymenaeus and Alexander,” whom Paul says he delivered unto Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme. Acts 19:33 also mentions an Alexander during the Ephesian riot.
Was Alexander the coppersmith one of these men?
Possibly.
But Scripture does not explicitly tell us.
Interpreters have disagreed over the identification, and responsible reading should resist turning possibility into certainty.
We do not need speculation to make Paul's warning more dramatic.
What Scripture actually says is already devastating enough.
Alexander harmed Paul.
Alexander strongly opposed the apostolic message.
Timothy needed to be warned.
And judgment belonged to the Lord.
That last part changes everything.
“ἀποδώσει αὐτῷ ὁ κύριος”
apodōsei autō ho Kyrios.
“The Lord will repay him.”
Notice who is missing from the role of executioner.
Paul.
Paul does not say, “I will make Alexander pay.”
He says, in effect, “The Lord sees.”
There are wounds you cannot repair by getting even.
There are lies you cannot chase down fast enough.
There are people who may never apologize.
There are conversations where you will never receive closure.
There are betrayals where the person who destroyed your trust may continue living as though nothing happened.
And there is something terrifyingly seductive about revenge when you have been genuinely wronged.
You replay the conversation.
You imagine the day they finally understand what they did.
You want the truth exposed.
You want them embarrassed.
You want them to hurt just enough to understand your hurt.
Maybe you would never say it aloud.
But heaven has heard the conversations you have held inside your head.
Paul gives us another road.
Tell the truth about evil.
Protect others when protection is necessary.
Use wisdom.
Set appropriate boundaries.
But do not climb onto God's throne.
“The Lord will repay.”
Those words are not permission for vindictiveness.
They are liberation from it.
You do not have to become someone's judge in order for justice to exist.
God saw what happened when nobody else did.
God heard the conversation you could never prove happened.
God knows what was said behind the closed door.
God knows what was deliberately twisted.
God knows what it cost you.
And because He knows perfectly, you are free to surrender judgment perfectly to Him.
But the passage becomes even more astonishing when you keep reading.
After warning Timothy about Alexander, Paul writes:
—2 Timothy 4:16, KJV
Do you see it?
Alexander opposed him.
Others abandoned him.
Yet Paul's responses are not identical.
Concerning Alexander, Timothy needs a warning.
Concerning those who deserted him, Paul asks that their failure not be charged against them.
Biblical forgiveness is not moral blindness.
Grace has discernment.
Paul does not flatten every situation into the same category.
Some people were weak.
Alexander was actively dangerous.
Some needed mercy for abandoning him.
One needed to be watched.
That distinction matters enormously in real life.
The person who failed you in weakness is not necessarily the same as the person committed to harming you.
The friend who panicked is not necessarily the same as the manipulator who planned.
The believer who stumbled is not necessarily the same as the person who continues deliberately opposing truth.
Christian love does not require us to erase discernment.
And then comes perhaps the most beautiful sentence in the entire scene.
Paul has been harmed.
Paul has been opposed.
Paul has been deserted.
Human support disappears.
And he writes:
—2 Timothy 4:17, KJV
There it is.
That is the center.
Not Alexander.
Jesus.
Alexander may explain the wound.
Jesus explains why the wound did not win.
People left.
“The Lord stood with me.”
People weakened him.
The Lord “strengthened me.”
Someone opposed the message.
Yet Paul says the preaching continued through him.
This is Christianity at its deepest.
Not the promise that nobody will betray you.
Not the promise that faithful Christians never become lonely.
Not the promise that obedience protects you from malicious people.
The promise is Christ Himself.
When everybody else steps away, Christ does not.
When somebody drags your name through the dirt, Christ does not forget your name.
When your strength collapses, Christ remains.
When people leave you standing alone in the room you thought they would enter with you—
Jesus stands there.
Maybe your Alexander had another name.
Maybe it was someone you trusted.
Someone from church.
Someone you loved.
Someone you defended.
Someone you helped.
Someone who knew exactly where you were vulnerable because you were foolish enough—or loving enough—to let them close.
And maybe what hurts most is not merely what they did.
It is who did it.
Strangers can wound you.
But betrayal requires proximity.
Judas needed to be close enough to kiss Jesus.
Peter needed to know Jesus before denying that he knew Him.
The deepest wounds often come carrying familiar voices.
And this is where the Gospel confronts us.
Because eventually every wounded person faces a decision.
Will what they did to me determine who I become?
Paul's answer is no.
Not because the wound was imaginary.
Because Jesus was greater.
This is where Alexander's story unexpectedly brings us toward Calvary.
Jesus Christ knows betrayal more deeply than any of us.
He was betrayed for silver.
Abandoned by friends.
Denied by Peter.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And while hanging beneath the judgment our sins deserved, Christ was not merely giving humanity an inspiring example of endurance.
He was accomplishing redemption.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
—2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
At the cross, God does not pretend sin does not matter.
The cross proves how seriously God takes it.
And simultaneously, the cross reveals how unimaginably far His grace is willing to go to rescue sinners.
That includes people wounded by Alexanders.
And it includes people who have behaved like Alexander.
That second sentence is harder.
Because while reading this, perhaps you instinctively identified with Paul.
But what if you have been Alexander in somebody else's story?
What if you were the one who damaged them?
What if your words opposed truth?
What if you betrayed someone's confidence?
What if you destroyed a reputation?
What if the person reading Paul's warning and thinking of an enemy should actually be thinking of himself?
That is where Christianity becomes more than emotional therapy.
The Gospel does not exist merely to help victims feel stronger.
It calls sinners to repentance.
All sinners.
Including us.
You may have been betrayed.
You may also have betrayed.
You may have been lied about.
You may also have lied.
You may carry scars from someone else's sin while somebody else carries scars from yours.
And neither revenge nor denial can cleanse that.
Only Christ can.
The Gospel does not say, “You weren't that bad.”
It says something far more glorious.
You were guilty, and Christ died for sinners.
You were unable to save yourself, and the Son of God came for you.
You had a debt you could never repay, and Jesus carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is offered not because sin was insignificant but because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
Repentance therefore is not humiliation without hope.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior whose grace is greater than your scandal.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing evil out of your history.
Not by calling darkness light.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming sinners who could never rewrite themselves.
Look at Paul himself.
Before he became the wounded apostle warning Timothy about an opponent, Paul had been the opponent.
Before people persecuted Paul, Paul persecuted Christians.
Before Paul suffered for the name of Jesus, he tried to destroy those who called upon that Name.
Acts tells us Saul was “breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord.”
If Paul's biography had ended there, his name would have belonged to scandal.
Then Jesus met him.
Grace interrupted the story.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy became an apostle.
The man who once tried to silence the Gospel eventually suffered because he refused to stop proclaiming it.
That is what Jesus does.
So perhaps the greatest lesson from Alexander is not, “Watch out for bad people.”
It is this:
Do not let another person's sin become the author of your remaining chapters.
Alexander did Paul harm.
But Alexander did not get Paul's ending.
Jesus did.
That may be the word somebody desperately needs tonight.
What happened to you was real.
But it does not own the ending.
What they called you does not own the ending.
What they exposed does not own the ending.
What you lost does not own the ending.
Even your own worst sin does not have to own the ending if you come to Christ in genuine repentance and faith.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still transforms.
Jesus still takes lives buried beneath shame and writes grace where everyone expected only scandal.
Maybe you have spent years secretly waiting for your Alexander to suffer.
Give the courtroom back to God.
Maybe you keep allowing a dangerous person into your life because you thought boundaries meant unforgiveness.
Remember Paul's words:
“ὃν καὶ σὺ φυλάσσου.”
Guard yourself.
Maybe you abandoned somebody when courage was required.
Repent.
Maybe you have been somebody else's Alexander.
Do not hide behind explanations.
Confess your sin.
Where appropriate and possible, seek reconciliation and make right what you can.
But above everything else, run to Christ.
There is mercy at His cross for repentant sinners.
There is cleansing for guilty consciences.
There is strength for wounded hearts.
There is freedom from revenge.
There is grace powerful enough to prevent yesterday's scandal from becoming tomorrow's identity.
Be honest.
There may be another believer reading the comments who needs to discover that they are not the only one still fighting.
And think of one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to attack indirectly.
Someone you genuinely want to help.
Save it too.

Because eventually a name may come back into your mind, an old wound may reopen, or the temptation to retaliate may return. On that day, remember the imprisoned apostle who named the evil, warned his brother, surrendered judgment to God, and kept preaching Christ.
Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership, though our first calling is always obedience to Christ—not allegiance to a page, platform, or ministry.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling silently.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually cold.
Invite the seeker with difficult questions.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Use them.
Share them.
Let truth travel farther than scandal.
Let Scripture travel farther than gossip.
Let the Gospel travel farther than the wound.
Because perhaps that is the final irony of Alexander the coppersmith.
He opposed Paul's words.
Yet nearly two thousand years later, we are still reading Paul's words.
Alexander could hurt the messenger.
He could not stop the message.
And neither can your Alexander.
The person who wounded you does not have enough authority to cancel what Jesus intends to do through a surrendered life.
So forgive without pretending.
Discern without becoming bitter.
Warn when love requires warning.
Repent when you discover Alexander in yourself.
Leave vengeance to God.
Stay near Jesus.
Keep preaching Christ.
Keep walking.
Keep loving.
Keep telling the truth.
And when everyone else disappears, remember the sentence Paul left behind for every lonely Christian who would someday wonder whether they could survive being abandoned:
“The Lord stood with me.”
Alexander may have been part of Paul's pain—but Jesus was the Author of Paul's ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BUSINESSWOMAN WHO OPENED HER HOME TO THE GOSPEL—AND HELPED CHANGE THE SPIRITUAL STORY OF EUROPE
paragraphs: THE BUSINESSWOMAN WHO OPENED HER HOME TO THE GOSPEL—AND HELPED CHANGE THE SPIRITUAL STORY OF EUROPE

She had money. She had influence. She had religion. But one morning beside a river, Lydia discovered that you can worship God, build a successful life, and still desperately need your heart opened by the Lord.
There are moments that look painfully ordinary while they are happening.
No stadium.
No cathedral.
No worship band.
No flashing lights.
No crowd waiting for a miracle.
Just a riverbank.
A handful of women.
A traveling Jewish missionary named Paul.
And a businesswoman who had absolutely no idea that before the day was over, the story of her household would be different.
Her name was Lydia.
And if you have ever built a life that looked successful from the outside while quietly wondering whether something was still missing inside, you need to stay with her story.
Because Lydia was not introduced as a woman whose life was collapsing.
That is what makes her story dangerous.
Sometimes we imagine that Jesus is primarily for people standing in the wreckage of obvious disaster.
The addict.
The criminal.
The adulterer.
The person whose scandal has become public.
But what happens when the person who needs Christ is respectable?
What happens when she works hard?
What happens when she owns or manages a thriving enterprise, worships God, behaves morally, opens her home generously, and probably appears more spiritually responsible than many people around her?
What happens when there is no spectacular scandal to expose?
Acts 16 answers with a sentence so quiet that you can read past it without realizing how devastating it is:
“The Lord opened her heart.”
That sentence changes everything.

Paul had received a vision calling him toward Macedonia. He and his companions crossed the Aegean and eventually arrived in Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia. On the Sabbath, instead of entering a synagogue, Luke tells us that they went outside the city gate toward a river where they expected to find a place of prayer. There they sat down and spoke with women who had gathered.
And among them was Lydia.
The Greek text introduces her this way:
“καί τις γυνὴ ὀνόματι Λυδία, πορφυρόπωλις πόλεως Θυατείρων, σεβομένη τὸν Θεόν, ἤκουεν…”
Kai tis gynē onomati Lydia, porphyropōlis poleōs Thyateirōn, sebomenē ton Theon, ēkouen…
In straightforward English:
“A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, was listening…”
That word Luke uses for her occupation is striking:
πορφυρόπωλις — porphyropōlis.
A seller or dealer in purple.

Lydia was involved in the purple-goods trade and came from Thyatira. We should be careful not to turn the sparse biblical description into an invented biography. Scripture never tells us her income, the size of her business, or precisely what social rank she occupied.
But Luke deliberately tells us what she did.
She was a merchant.
A businesswoman.
She dealt in purple goods.
And later in the story, we discover that she possessed a household and was able to offer hospitality to Paul and his companions.
She was not introduced as helpless.
She was not introduced as destitute.
She was not introduced as irreligious.
Luke says she was σεβομένη τὸν Θεόν — sebomenē ton Theon.
A woman “worshiping God.”
And that is where Lydia stops being merely an ancient woman beside an ancient river.
Because she begins to look disturbingly familiar.
Maybe she looks like you.
You believe in God.
You pray.
You post Bible verses.
You try to be decent.
Maybe you attend church.
Maybe you give.
Maybe you run a company, lead a team, raise children, pay bills, help relatives, encourage friends, and carry responsibilities nobody notices.
People may even look at you and think:
“She has it together.”
But there is a terrifying difference between being near the things of God and having your heart conquered by the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still need Christ.
You can admire Jesus and still need to surrender to Jesus.
You can respect Scripture and still resist what Scripture is exposing.
You can sit among praying people while hiding rooms in your heart that you have never fully handed to God.
Lydia was listening.
Then something happened that no marketing strategy could manufacture, no preacher could force, and no emotional manipulation could produce.
Luke writes:
Hēs ho Kyrios diēnoixen tēn kardian…
“The Lord opened her heart…”
Do not rush past that.
ὁ Κύριος — ho Kyrios — the Lord.
The Lord did it.
Paul preached.
Lydia listened.
But God opened the heart.
The Greek verb διήνοιξεν — diēnoixen carries the basic sense of opening something so that what was previously closed becomes accessible or understandable.
This is grace.
Christian conversion is not ultimately the story of a clever preacher successfully selling Jesus to a reluctant customer.
Jesus Christ is not a product.
The Gospel is not a sales pitch.
Salvation is not spiritual self-improvement.
God confronts us with the truth about His Son, exposes our sin, calls us to repentance and faith, and gives what we could never purchase with our achievements.
Grace.
Lydia sold purple.
But grace could not be bought.
She understood commerce.
But salvation was not a transaction she could negotiate.
She may have known what valuable things cost.
Then she encountered the Gospel of the One whose blood purchased sinners.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
Lord.

This is the center of Paul's Gospel. Humanity's deepest problem is not merely that we need better circumstances. We are sinners alienated from a holy God. Yet God acted in mercy through Jesus Christ. Christ died for our sins and rose again, and forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
That means Lydia's greatest need was not another customer.
Not another profitable contract.
Not greater status.
Not greater religious discipline.
Her deepest need was the same as yours.
Jesus.
And perhaps that is exactly where this article has found you.
Maybe your business is growing while your prayer life is dying.
Maybe your career looks impressive while your marriage is bleeding.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong because nobody has ever seen you cry in the car before walking into work.
Maybe you have become so good at functioning that you no longer know how to admit you are exhausted.
Maybe you know how to make money but have forgotten how to be still before God.
Maybe you know how to close deals but cannot close the distance that sin has created between your public confession and your private life.
Maybe there is pornography nobody knows about.
An affair hidden behind deleted messages.
Bitterness you have baptized as “discernment.”
Pride disguised as confidence.
Greed renamed ambition.
A secret addiction.
A private compromise.
A wound you have turned into an identity.
Or perhaps there is nothing outwardly scandalous at all.
Maybe you are simply spiritually asleep.
And sometimes that is the scandal nobody sees.
You have learned how to look alive around Christians while slowly becoming numb to Christ.
Lydia's story whispers something uncomfortable:
Being respectable does not mean your heart does not need opening.
And being religious does not mean you do not need the Gospel.
But here comes the beauty.
Jesus does not expose the heart merely to humiliate it.
He opens what sin has closed so grace can enter.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
This is where shame loses the right to write the final chapter.
This is where the person you were does not have to become the person you die as.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
After Lydia responds to Paul's message, Acts tells us that she and her household were baptized.
Then something immediately becomes visible.
Her faith begins affecting what she possesses.
Her house becomes available to the mission.
She urges Paul and his companions:
“If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.”
Think about that.
The Gospel reached her heart...
and then reached her home.
Grace moved inward...
and then outward.
Conversion did not make Lydia less responsible with what she possessed.
It gave what she possessed a new King.
Her resources could serve Christ.
Her table could serve Christ.
Her rooms could serve Christ.
Her influence could serve Christ.
Her hospitality could serve Christ.
This is one of the great questions every Christian eventually faces:
If Jesus owns my heart, what does that mean for what I own?
Not because giving purchases salvation.
It cannot.
Not because generosity earns God's love.
It does not.
Never.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works. Good works are the fruit of salvation, not its price.
But genuine grace does something to our hands.
The Gospel changes what we do with our time.
Our homes.
Our businesses.
Our platforms.
Our money.
Our influence.
Our voices.
Our opportunities.
The question stops being only, “What can this do for me?”
And gradually becomes:
“How can what God entrusted to me glorify Christ?”
That is why Lydia's story should make us uncomfortable with spectator Christianity.
Imagine if Lydia had said:
“That was a beautiful message, Paul. Very inspiring.”
And gone home.
Imagine if she had encountered truth but refused to let truth rearrange anything.
Instead, the woman whose heart was opened opened her home.

And Acts later gives us one more beautiful glimpse. After Paul and Silas were beaten, imprisoned, miraculously released, and eventually left the prison, Acts 16:40 says they went to Lydia's house. There they met with “the brothers,” encouraged them, and departed.
Do not claim more than Scripture claims.
The Bible does not explicitly call Lydia the pastor of the Philippian church. It does not explicitly tell us precisely how the congregation developed within her household.
But Acts unquestionably places her home in the unfolding Christian community at Philippi.
The woman beside the river had become part of something bigger than herself.
Her story was now entangled with the advance of the Gospel.

And this is why she is often described as Paul's first recorded European convert. More precisely, she is the first person Luke explicitly records responding to Paul's preaching after the missionary party enters Macedonia in Acts 16. We should not pretend Scripture tells us things it does not. But we should not miss the extraordinary significance of what it does tell us.
Paul had seen a Macedonian man in his vision saying:
“Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
Then Paul crossed the sea.
And one of the first people Luke shows us receiving the message is...
a woman.
A businesswoman.
Beside a river.
God's providence rarely submits to our expectations.
You think God needs a stage.
He chooses a riverbank.
You think He needs thousands.
He starts with a handful.
You think the important person will look obviously important.
He opens the heart of a merchant listening among praying women.
You think your ordinary obedience cannot possibly matter.
Then Lydia opens her door.
And two thousand years later, Christians are still reading her name.
Never underestimate what Jesus can do with one surrendered heart.
That includes yours.
Perhaps nobody will write books about you.
Perhaps your name will never trend.
Perhaps your testimony will never reach millions.
But somewhere there may be a child watching you.
A spouse watching you.
An employee.
A customer.
A friend.
A brother who has walked away from God.
A daughter who secretly wonders whether Christianity is real.
A coworker who would never walk into a church but might read something you shared because it came from you.
But what if one person encounters the Gospel there because you were willing to share it?
That is why, if this article has genuinely pointed you toward Christ, do not let it die quietly on your screen.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
Do it because someone connected to you may desperately need the truth you just read.
And if Lydia's story exposed something inside you, do not hide behind a reaction button.
Be honest.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Because there may come a night when the business is quiet, the children are asleep, the notifications stop, and the questions you have avoided become loud again.
On that night, remember Lydia.
Remember the river.
Remember the listening woman.
Remember the Lord who opened her heart.
And remember that Christianity does not ultimately begin with what you can accomplish for God.
It begins with what God has done for sinners through Jesus Christ.
Christ took the scandal of human sin seriously enough to go to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And because He lives, your worst chapter does not have authority to declare itself your final chapter.
Repentance is not God asking you to clean yourself before approaching Jesus.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace brings us to Christ and begins transforming what sin had distorted.
Forgiveness does not mean sin was insignificant.
The cross proves exactly how serious sin is.
But the resurrection declares that sin and death do not get the last word over those who belong to Christ.
Maybe you have spent years selling people an image of yourself.
Strong.
Successful.
Spiritual.
Happy.
Fine.
Maybe the exhausting business you really need to close is the business of pretending.
Come to Jesus without the résumé.
Without the filters.
Without the carefully managed reputation.
Without bargaining.
Without pretending that being “better than most people” can reconcile you to a holy God.
Come as a sinner who needs mercy.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
And let Him begin changing everything.
Do it as support for Gospel ministry, not as payment for God's favor.

If you genuinely want to glorify God through what He has entrusted to you, one practical expression can be helping sound Gospel-centered work continue and helping its message reach people who may never enter a church building. Lydia reminds us that resources placed under Christ's lordship can become instruments of hospitality, ministry, encouragement, and Gospel advance.
Jesus Christ.
Scripture.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Redemption.
Transformation.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to earn heaven.
Not because an algorithm is holy.
But because someone you know may be sitting beside their own invisible river right now.
Successful on the outside.
Searching underneath.
And perhaps God will use a simple act of obedience from you to place the truth of Jesus Christ in front of them.
That is how Lydia's story began.
A messenger obeyed.
A woman listened.
The Lord opened a heart.
A household was baptized.
A door opened.
Believers gathered.
And the Gospel kept moving.
You may think your life is too ordinary to matter.
So did that riverbank look.
You may think your home is merely a home.
Lydia's became a place where believers gathered.
Put them into the hands of Jesus before deciding what He can do with them.
And please remember this when shame starts reciting your old chapters back to you:
The world may remember what you were, but Jesus is still writing what grace is making you become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THERE WAS ONLY ONE WAY IN
paragraphs: THERE WAS ONLY ONE WAY IN
Why the Tabernacle Had One Entrance—and Why Jesus Said, “I Am the Door”
Imagine standing in the wilderness thousands of years ago.
Dust beneath your feet.
The heat pressing against your skin.
The tents of Israel stretching across the desert.
And there, at the center of the camp, stands something unlike everything around it.
The Tabernacle.
The dwelling place God commanded Israel to build.
You can walk around it.
You can study its curtains.
You can admire its dimensions.
You can stand close enough to know that something holy is beyond those walls.
But there is something you cannot do.
You cannot invent your own entrance.
That detail should make every person who has ever said, “I think there are many ways to God,” stop for a moment.
Because the Tabernacle did not have an entrance wherever somebody happened to prefer one.
God prescribed the way of approach.

Exodus describes the courtyard and then specifies its gate. Exodus 27:13–16 places the entrance on the eastern side of the courtyard and describes its screen in careful detail. The Hebrew expression includes שַׁעַר הֶחָצֵר — shaʿar heḥatser — “the gate of the court,” with its screen, מָסָךְ — masakh.
Not five gates.
Not a collection of equally valid entrances designed around personal preference.
One prescribed gateway into the courtyard.
And centuries later, standing among people who knew the imagery of shepherds, gates, sacrifice, covenant, and Israel’s Scriptures, Jesus spoke words that should still shake us:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα.
Egō eimi hē thyra.
“I am the door.”
Not merely, “I can show you a door.”
Not, “I know where the door is.”
Not even, “I am one door among many.”
“I am the door.”
The Greek word θύρα — thyra — means a door, gate, or entrance.
And Jesus continues in John 10:9:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα· δι’ ἐμοῦ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθῃ σωθήσεται.
“I am the door. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved.”
Read that slowly.
Through Me.
There is something both comforting and offensive to human pride about those words.
Comforting because the entrance is open.
Offensive because we do not get to redesign it.
We want God.
But sometimes we want God without surrender.
We want heaven without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Resurrection without a cross.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
Grace without admitting that we desperately need grace.
We want to approach God carrying our résumé.
“I’m a good person.”
“I help people.”
“I go to church.”
“My family is Christian.”
“I was baptized.”
“I give.”
“I pray sometimes.”
“I’m not as bad as that person.”
And standing silently behind all of those sentences is the terrifying assumption that perhaps our goodness can become another entrance.
But Scripture keeps dismantling the entrances we build for ourselves.
Religion cannot become the door.
Morality cannot become the door.
Christian parents cannot become the door.
Church attendance cannot become the door.
Money cannot become the door.
Good intentions cannot become the door.
Your ministry cannot become the door.
Even your tears cannot become the door.
There is a Door.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
This is where the Tabernacle becomes breathtaking.

The Tabernacle was not merely an ancient religious tent filled with mysterious furniture. Hebrews explains that the earthly sanctuary belonged to a divinely ordered system that pointed beyond itself. The Holy Spirit was teaching something through its restrictions, sacrifices, priesthood, blood, curtains, and limited access.
There was an entrance.
Then an altar.
Then washing.
Then the Holy Place.
Then another veil.
And beyond that veil stood the Most Holy Place, associated uniquely with the presence of God.
The message was impossible to miss:
God is holy.
Sin is serious.
Access to God cannot be treated casually.
And sinful humanity cannot simply stroll into the presence of infinite holiness on its own terms.
Hebrews 9 says that under that arrangement the priests repeatedly entered the outer section, while only the high priest entered the inner sanctuary, and only once each year, “not without blood.”
Then Hebrews says something astonishing.
The Holy Spirit was indicating through this arrangement that the way into the holy places had not yet been fully opened while that first arrangement remained.
Then come two words upon which eternity seems to turn:
“But Christ…”
Christ came.
And suddenly the shadows began giving way to their fulfillment.
Hebrews 9 presents Jesus as the great High Priest who entered not by the blood of goats and calves, but by His own blood, securing eternal redemption.
Think about what that means.
Jesus did not merely stand outside the entrance telling sinners how to behave better.
He came for them.
He did not shout instructions toward drowning humanity from the safety of heaven.
He entered our world.
He took flesh.
He walked among sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He received the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called sinners to repentance.
He wept.
He was betrayed.
He was mocked.
He was beaten.
And then the One who said, “I am the door” allowed Himself to be nailed to a Roman cross.
The Door was wounded so sinners could enter.
That is the scandal of grace.
We spend our lives trying to convince everybody that we are worth saving.
The Gospel begins when we finally admit that we cannot save ourselves.
Maybe that is where this becomes personal.
Because perhaps you know how to look Christian while quietly falling apart.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which Bible verses to post.
You know how to smile when somebody asks, “How are you?”
But there are rooms inside you nobody sees.
The addiction you keep promising will be the last time.
The bitterness you justify because they really did hurt you.
The pornography hidden behind deleted history.
The affair nobody knows about.
The jealousy disguised as discernment.
The anger you call righteous even when it is poisoning your family.
The secret messages.
The dishonesty.
The unforgiveness.
The pride.
The prayerlessness.
The coldness.
The exhausting performance of pretending you are spiritually alive while privately wondering why God feels so far away.
And perhaps your greatest fear is not merely that people will discover what you have done.
Perhaps your greatest fear is that if God truly knows you, He will not want you.
But He already knows.
Every room.
Every search.
Every thought.
Every compromise.
Every excuse.
Every night you cried and told nobody.
Every time you promised Him you would change and then returned to the same chains.
He knows.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that God finally discovered how sinful you are.
The Gospel is the announcement that while you were still a sinner, Christ died for sinners.
You do not clean yourself enough to become worthy of the Door.
You come through the Door because you never could make yourself worthy.
Grace does not tell you your sin does not matter.
Look at Calvary.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God shed His blood.
But grace also tells you that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Look again at Calvary.
Jesus shed His blood.
And then He rose.
This is why Christianity cannot honestly be reduced to “be a nicer person.”
The Gospel is not behavior modification for respectable sinners.
It is resurrection for the spiritually dead.
It is reconciliation for enemies.
Forgiveness for the guilty.
Freedom for captives.
A new heart for people exhausted from trying to repair the old one.
And this also explains why Jesus’ claim is so exclusive and yet His invitation is so astonishingly wide.
Jesus later says in John 14:6:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ὁδὸς καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια καὶ ἡ ζωή.
Egō eimi hē hodos kai hē alētheia kai hē zōē.
“I am the way and the truth and the life.”
Then He says that no one comes to the Father except through Him.
Christianity did not invent that exclusivity centuries later.
Jesus placed Himself at the center of access to the Father.
But do not miss the other side of the sentence.
The Door is exclusive.
The invitation is expansive.
Jesus says, “If anyone enters through Me…”
Anyone.
The ashamed.
The religious.
The irreligious.
The addict.
The skeptic.
The church kid who secretly wandered away.
The prisoner.
The businessman.
The prostitute.
The pastor who has become spiritually empty.
The person reading this with tears forming because nobody knows how tired you have become.
Anyone.
The question is not whether your past is ugly.
The question is whether you will come to Christ.
Maybe your story is scandalous.
Good.
The Bible is full of people whose stories would make terrible religious publicity campaigns.
David committed adultery and arranged a man’s death.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes, not building a religious résumé.
Scripture does not airbrush humanity so we can admire heroes.
It exposes human need so we can behold a Savior.
That is why grace is so shocking.
Jesus does not merely edit respectable stories.
He resurrects ruined ones.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But be careful here.
Grace does not mean Jesus helps you continue peacefully in rebellion.
The Door does not lead into a prettier version of your old captivity.
Jesus calls us to repent.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness by feeling sufficiently terrible.
It is the turning of the heart toward God—a surrender that stops defending the very sin Christ came to save us from.
Real grace forgives.
And real grace transforms.
The Jesus who welcomes sinners also says, in effect, leave the darkness and follow Me.
Maybe you have been standing near the entrance for years.
Close enough to Christianity to recognize its language.
Close enough to church to know its music.
Close enough to believers to imitate their vocabulary.
But proximity to the Door is not the same as entering through the Door.
You can admire Jesus and still refuse Him.
Study Jesus and still resist Him.
Post about Jesus and still hide from Him.
Know theology about Jesus without actually trusting Jesus.
And perhaps that is why these words have found you today.
Not so you can win another theological argument.
So you can answer the question your soul has been avoiding.
Have you actually entrusted yourself to Christ?
Not your image.
Not your denomination.
Not your achievements.
Christ.
Because the wonder of the Gospel is not that sinners finally discovered a way to climb into heaven.
Heaven came down looking for sinners.
And the Door has a name.
Jesus.

Hebrews moves the imagery even further. Because of the blood of Jesus, believers have confidence to draw near to God. Christ has done what the old sacrifices could never finally accomplish. The shadows pointed forward; Jesus accomplished redemption.
The sacrifice is not waiting for you to complete it.
Jesus cried, “It is finished.”
The price of redemption is not your religious performance.
Christ gave Himself.
This destroys both despair and pride at the same time.
Despair says, “I am too filthy.”
The cross answers, “His blood is enough.”
Pride says, “I am good enough.”
The cross answers, “You needed His blood too.”
At Calvary, the openly broken and the secretly self-righteous discover the same truth:
Everybody needs Jesus.
So what do you do?
Come.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without pretending.
Come believing that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose from the dead.
Bring Him the thing you keep hiding.
Name the sin you keep renaming.
Stop negotiating with the darkness that is destroying you.
You do not need another secret entrance.
You need the Door God has already provided.
And if something inside you is breaking while you read this, do not rush past it.
Talk to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Ask for mercy.
Turn from your sin and place your trust in Him.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
If you are exhausted but still fighting to hold onto your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, comment, “pray for me.”
Somebody scrolling silently may need to see that Jesus still restores broken people.
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who would never walk into a church this week but would read something you shared at two in the morning.
Someone is smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Someone has convinced himself he has sinned too much.
Someone thinks Christianity is only for clean people.
Someone believes God could never forgive what she did.
Someone is standing near the Door without realizing it is still open.
Not as a superstition.
Not to prove that you love God.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual favor.
Send this privately to somebody who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
There is a Door.
His name is Jesus.
If you genuinely want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, one practical expression can be supporting faithful Gospel ministry and helping sound biblical teaching travel farther.
And there is something else I do not want you to miss.
Use them.
Share them.
Put them in the hands of someone hungry for Scripture.
Invite the friend drifting from Christ.
Invite the new believer who does not know where to begin.
Invite the exhausted Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm believer who needs awakening.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who keeps asking difficult questions.
Because this was never ultimately about a tent in the wilderness.
The Tabernacle matters because God was teaching His people about holiness, sacrifice, access, and His presence.
The altar mattered.
The blood mattered.
The priesthood mattered.
The veil mattered.
The entrance mattered.
But they were never the final destination.
Christ is.
The ancient worshiper approached through the entrance God prescribed.
And when the fullness of redemption came, Jesus stood before a broken world and said words no mere religious teacher had the right to say:
“I am the door.”
Maybe you have spent years searching for another entrance because surrender frightened you.
Maybe you thought your scandal disqualified you.
Maybe religion wounded you.
Maybe hypocrisy disgusted you.
Maybe suffering confused you.
Maybe sin chained you.
Maybe shame convinced you to hide.
But Christianity does not finally ask you to trust Christians to be perfect.
It asks you to look at Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Merciful.
Holy.
Calling sinners home.
The most important question is no longer whether you have a scandal in your story.
We all do.
The question is who gets to write the ending.
Your sin?
Your shame?
Your past?
Other people?
Or Jesus Christ?
The entrance is not hidden.
The invitation has been spoken.
The blood has been shed.
Christ has risen.
And the Door is still open.
Do not spend your entire life standing outside the grace you were invited to enter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Thief Beside Jesus Had No Time Left to Repair His Reputation—Only Enough Time to Receive Mercy
paragraphs: The Thief Beside Jesus Had No Time Left to Repair His Reputation—Only Enough Time to Receive Mercy

He could not undo what he had done. He could not rebuild the life he had destroyed. He could not climb down from the cross and prove that he had changed. All he had left was a dying breath, a guilty past, and Jesus beside him—and somehow, that was enough.
There is something terrifying about running out of time.
Not running late.
Running out.

No tomorrow to fix what happened yesterday. No second career. No restored reputation. No opportunity to return what was taken, repair every relationship, apologize to everyone wounded, or spend the next twenty years proving that you have become a different person.
Imagine knowing that your final chapter has already begun.
Your hands cannot move.
Your feet cannot run.
Your sentence has been pronounced.
People are watching you die.
And whatever reputation you once had is now buried beneath one word:
Criminal.
That was the man hanging beside Jesus.
We are not told his name.

We do not know his childhood. We do not know the face of his mother. We do not know what choices brought him to that cross or how many warnings he ignored before Rome finally drove iron through his existence.
Luke simply identifies the condemned men as κακοῦργοι—kakourgoi—criminals, evildoers.
That is how history meets him.
Not as a misunderstood hero.
Not as a basically good man who made one harmless mistake.
A condemned criminal.
And this matters, because the beauty of this story disappears if we sanitize the man Jesus saved.
Grace becomes cheap sentimentality when sin is made insignificant.
The Gospel does something far more astonishing.
It tells the truth about human guilt...
and then tells an even greater truth about the mercy of Christ.
Three crosses stood at Calvary.
On one cross hung rebellion.
On another hung repentance.
And in the middle hung Redemption Himself.
One dying criminal looked at the crucified Jesus and mocked Him:
“If You are the Christ, save Yourself and us.”
He wanted rescue without surrender.
Deliverance without repentance.
A kingdom without a King.
He wanted Jesus to remove his cross, but there is no indication in Luke’s account that he wanted Jesus to rule his heart.
And then the other criminal spoke.
Listen carefully, because these may have been among the most important words he ever said.
“Do you not even fear God...?”
Then comes the confession that makes this scene so uncomfortable for a culture obsessed with self-justification:
“We indeed justly...”
In Luke’s Greek:
καὶ ἡμεῖς μὲν δικαίως
Kai hēmeis men dikaiōs.
In context: “And we indeed justly...”
He does not blame Rome.
He does not blame his childhood.
He does not compare himself with someone worse.
He does not say, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
He does not rename evil as trauma, weakness, complexity, or circumstance.
He admits guilt.
“We indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve.”
Then he looks toward the bleeding Man hanging beside him and says something extraordinary:
“This Man has done nothing wrong.”
Think about that.
A condemned man recognizes the innocence of Jesus while many surrounding Him reject Him.
But he sees more than innocence.
He sees a King.
Jesus has been beaten.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Nailed to wood.
There is no visible palace.
No earthly throne.
No army charging over the hill.
No crown except thorns.
No appearance of victory.
And this dying criminal says:
Ἰησοῦ, μνήσθητί μου...
Iēsou, mnēsthēti mou...
“Jesus, remember me...”
And he connects that plea with Christ’s kingdom.
That is staggering faith.
He looks at a crucified Man...
and sees a coming King.
Everyone else can see nails.
He sees a kingdom.
Everyone else can see humiliation.
He sees royalty.
Everyone else can see apparent defeat.
He believes Jesus still has a future—and somehow dares to ask for a place in it.
“Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.”
Notice what he does not say.
“Jesus, look at all the good I have done.”
He has no résumé.
“Jesus, give me a few years and I will prove myself.”
He has no years.
“Jesus, let me repair my reputation first.”
Too late.
“Jesus, let me perform enough religious works to balance the scales.”
His hands are nailed down.
He cannot be baptized before his death.
He cannot give money to the poor.
He cannot go on pilgrimage.
He cannot spend decades building a respectable Christian testimony.
He cannot descend from his cross and knock on the doors of everyone he hurt.
He cannot demonstrate a lifetime of subsequent obedience.
He has nothing to offer Jesus as the price of mercy.
Nothing.
Except the empty hands of faith.
And empty hands, strangely enough, are exactly the kind of hands capable of receiving a gift.
Then Jesus speaks.
And if you have ever believed that your past has permanently disqualified you from coming home to God, do not rush past these words.
In the Greek text of Luke 23:43:
Ἀμήν σοι λέγω σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.
Amēn soi legō sēmeron met’ emou esē en tō paradeisō.
“Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in paradise.”
Read the heart of that promise again.
σήμερον — sēmeron.
Today.
μετ’ ἐμοῦ — met’ emou.
With Me.
ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ — en tō paradeisō.
In paradise.
The criminal asked Jesus to remember him.
Jesus promised him presence.
He asked for mercy sometime in the coming kingdom.
Christ answered with something breathtaking:
Today.
With Me.
Paradise.
Jesus did not pretend the man was innocent.
The man himself had already admitted the opposite.
Jesus did not rewrite his earthly history by pretending his crimes never happened.
He did something infinitely greater.
He rewrote his eternity.
That is grace after ruin.
And maybe this is where the story stops being about an unnamed criminal two thousand years ago.
Maybe this is where it finds you.
Because some people reading this are carrying things nobody around them knows.
There are photographs you hope nobody ever sees.
Messages you wish you had never sent.
Relationships you destroyed.
Promises you broke.
Money you wasted.
Years you cannot recover.
Secret addictions.
Private compromises.
A marriage wounded by your choices.
Children you failed.
Parents you dishonored.
People you betrayed.
Bodies you used.
People who used you.
A faith you abandoned.
A season when you knew exactly what God was telling you...
and chose the opposite.
Perhaps everybody around you thinks you are doing fine.
But you know.
And sometimes, late at night, the prosecutor in your mind opens the old files.
Remember this?
Remember her?
Remember him?
Remember what you did?
Remember what you became?
Remember how many times God warned you?
And eventually shame whispers its most poisonous sentence:
“Jesus might forgive people...
but surely not people like you.”
Look at the cross.
There is literally a man dying beside Jesus whose life is already beyond earthly repair.
He cannot rehabilitate his public image.
He cannot construct a respectable Christian future before coming to Christ.
He cannot earn his way into paradise.
And Jesus does not say:
“Too late.”
Jesus does not say:
“Your record is too long.”
Jesus does not say:
“Clean yourself up and then come back.”
Jesus does not say:
“Convince Me that you deserve another chance.”
The guilty man turns toward Christ in repentance and faith...
and mercy meets him before death does.
This does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
The thief demonstrates the opposite.
He stops defending himself.
He acknowledges that his judgment is deserved.
He recognizes Jesus’ innocence.
He appeals personally to Jesus.
He recognizes Christ’s kingdom.
He entrusts his dying future to the crucified King.
Grace did not teach him that sin did not matter.
Grace taught him where a guilty sinner must go.
To Jesus.
This is why biblical grace is so scandalous.
Religion constructed around human merit says, “Become worthy, then perhaps you can approach.”
The Gospel announces that sinners who could never make themselves worthy are invited to come to the worthy Christ.
We are not saved because our past becomes impressive.
We are saved because Jesus is sufficient.
We are not justified because we finally accumulate enough evidence for our defense.
Scripture says that God justifies the ungodly who believe.
We are not redeemed because we managed to erase every stain.
We are redeemed because Christ shed His blood for sinners.
The thief had no time left to build a testimony.
Jesus became his testimony.
He had no time to repair his reputation.
Jesus became his righteousness.
He had no future achievements to present.
Jesus became his hope.
He could not come down from his cross.
So Christ carried salvation all the way to him.
And here is where we must be careful.
The thief on the cross is not permission to deliberately postpone repentance.
Nobody reading this has been promised a final hour in which repentance will suddenly become convenient.
Scripture says, “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
The thief proves that it is never too late while breath remains to turn to Christ.
He does not prove that it is safe to wait.
Those are very different messages.
Do not gamble eternity on another tomorrow.
If Christ is confronting your heart today, answer Him today.
You do not need a polished prayer.
The criminal did not have one.
You do not need theological vocabulary impressive enough to make heaven listen.
He simply cried:
“Jesus, remember me.”
Maybe your prayer tonight sounds more like:
Jesus...
I have sinned.
I have stopped making excuses.
I cannot undo what I have done.
I cannot save myself.
I believe You are the crucified and risen Lord.
I believe You died for sinners.
Have mercy on me.
Forgive me.
Take what remains of my life.
I surrender to You.
Remember me.
Save me.
And understand this clearly: words themselves are not magic.
Jesus saves.
Christ is not a religious formula to repeat while clinging stubbornly to sin.
The Gospel calls us to repentance and faith—to turn from sin and entrust ourselves to Jesus Christ.
The thief had almost nothing left.
But what remained, he turned toward Jesus.
Maybe that is what you need to do now.
Not when your addiction disappears.
Not when your marriage is fixed.
Not when everybody respects you again.
Not after you have attended church long enough to stop feeling ashamed.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Come guilty.
Come exposed.
Come tired.
Come ashamed.
Come with the wreckage.
But come to Christ.
Because the cross was never erected for people who could save themselves.
And please hear this distinction.
Coming to Jesus does not guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears.
Grace does not always restore a ruined reputation overnight.
Forgiveness does not necessarily erase prison sentences, broken trust, financial consequences, wounded relationships, or the long process of restitution and reconciliation.
The thief was forgiven...
and he still died on his cross.
That matters.
Jesus did not promise him freedom from every temporal consequence.
He promised something infinitely greater:
“You will be with Me.”
Sometimes Christ changes your circumstances.
Sometimes He gives you grace to face the consequences of what you have done.
But forgiveness means your consequences no longer have the authority to define your eternal destination.
Your worst chapter does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat of everything we mean when we say:
Not that scandal becomes good.
Not that sin becomes irrelevant.
Not that accountability disappears.

But that Jesus Christ is able to take a genuinely guilty human being, bring that sinner to repentance, wash away guilt through His saving work, and write grace where condemnation appeared to have written the ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps you know someone who desperately needs to hear this.
Someone who thinks abortion put her beyond mercy.
Someone who thinks adultery became his permanent identity.
Someone in prison who thinks society's sentence must also be God's final sentence.
Someone recovering from addiction who cannot stop remembering who they were.
Someone who abandoned their family.
Someone who walked away from church.
Someone who has spent years pretending not to care about God because admitting how desperately they need Him feels too painful.
Someone who says, “You don't know what I've done.”
Send this to them.
And if this story exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending before God.
There may come a night when your past gets loud again.
Read it then.
Read Luke 23:39–43 again.
Remember the dying criminal.
Remember the dying Savior.
Remember that the guilty man had no achievements left to offer...
and remember who spoke the final word.

Your support helps us keep producing and sharing biblical content intended to point people toward Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformed lives. Supporting Gospel work should never replace giving to your local church, caring for your family, serving people in need, or obeying Christ personally.
Come to Jesus.
The merchandise cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
A church building cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your good works cannot erase your guilt.
Jesus Christ saves.
And that is why the man beside Him still speaks without having written a single book, preached a single sermon, built a single ministry, or lived one respectable Christian year after his conversion.
His final moments became a monument to grace.
He entered that day condemned by Rome.
He ended it promised paradise by Christ.
He began the scene with nothing in his hands.
He left it with Jesus' word over his eternity.
His reputation could not be repaired.
His crimes could not be undone.
His remaining minutes could not become decades of restitution.
But there was enough time to look toward Jesus.
Enough time to stop defending himself.
Enough time to confess the truth.
Enough time to recognize the King.
Enough time to ask for mercy.
And enough mercy in Jesus to save him.
So when your past whispers, “Look what you did,” look toward the cross and remember what He did.
When shame says, “You are disqualified,” remember the criminal beside Christ.
When the enemy tells you that your story is already finished, remember that there was once a dying man whose final chapter looked like absolute ruin...
until Jesus spoke.
And perhaps that is the sentence your heart needs to carry tonight:

When you have no time left to repair your reputation, no strength left to defend your record, and nothing left to offer God, you may finally discover that Jesus was never asking you to purchase mercy—He was calling you to receive it.
Because somewhere tonight, someone thinks they have gone too far.
Someone thinks Jesus would turn away if He knew everything.
Someone believes the ruins are the ending.
But the criminal beside Jesus leaves us with a different picture.
A cross.
A confession.
A King.
A promise.
Paradise.
The world may remember the scandal that brought you to the cross, but when a repentant sinner turns to Jesus, grace can write an ending shame never saw coming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU WANTED HEALING TO MEAN YOU NEVER HURT AGAIN. SOMETIMES HEALING MEANS THE WOUND NO LONGER GETS TO RULE YOU.
paragraphs: YOU WANTED HEALING TO MEAN YOU NEVER HURT AGAIN. SOMETIMES HEALING MEANS THE WOUND NO LONGER GETS TO RULE YOU.
Maybe the proof that Jesus is healing you isn't that you can no longer remember what happened. Maybe it's that what happened can no longer decide who you become.
You prayed for healing.
But if you're honest, you had a particular definition of healing in mind.
You thought healing meant forgetting.
You thought one morning you would wake up and their name wouldn't tighten something inside your chest anymore.
You thought the anniversary would eventually become just another square on the calendar.
You thought the betrayal would stop replaying in your mind.
You thought you would walk into that familiar place and feel absolutely nothing.
No shaking hands.
No memories.
No questions.
No tears.
You thought healing meant becoming the person you were before it happened.
And because you're still hurting sometimes, a frightening thought has begun whispering in the quiet:
Maybe God hasn't healed me.
Maybe you've even wondered whether something is wrong with your faith.
Because Christians sometimes know how to celebrate dramatic testimonies better than slow ones.
We understand, “I was broken, Jesus touched me, and everything changed.”
And praise God when that happens.
But what about the testimony that sounds like this?
“I still remember.”
“I still have difficult days.”
“I still cry sometimes.”
“But I don't live there anymore.”
What if that is also a testimony?
What if you have misunderstood what healing can look like?
Because Scripture gives us an image of God that is far more tender than the demand to “just get over it.”
Psalm 147:3 says:
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.”
The Hebrew is painfully beautiful:
הָרֹפֵא לִשְׁבוּרֵי לֵב וּמְחַבֵּשׁ לְעַצְּבוֹתָם
Hā-rōfē’ lishvurei lev, u-meḥabbēsh le‘atzevotam.
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.”
Don't rush past that picture.
God does not mock the wounded.
He does not stand across the room shouting, “Why aren't you over this yet?”
He comes near.
He heals.
He binds.
The Hebrew verb translated “heals” comes from רָפָא — rāfā’, meaning to heal, cure, or restore.
But then Scripture gives us another word.
וּמְחַבֵּשׁ — u-meḥabbēsh.
“And He binds up.”
It comes from חָבַשׁ — ḥābash, a word associated with binding or wrapping.
Do you see the tenderness in that?
A wound that is being bound is still a wound.
It hasn't been denied.
It hasn't been called imaginary.
It hasn't been erased from history.
It is being cared for.
Maybe someone needs to hear that tonight.
Being wounded and being abandoned are not the same thing.
And still feeling pain does not automatically mean God has stopped working.
Sometimes the deepest evidence of healing isn't that the wound disappeared.
It's that the wound lost its throne.
There was a time when what happened controlled everything.
It controlled how you trusted.
How you loved.
How you slept.
How you saw yourself.
How you interpreted silence.
How quickly you panicked when somebody's tone changed.
How terrified you became when someone you loved seemed distant.
Maybe someone betrayed you so deeply that now innocent people occasionally pay emotional debts they never created.
Maybe somebody walked away.
Maybe somebody died.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe a parent failed you.
Maybe someone you trusted in church wounded you.
Maybe somebody made promises before God and later behaved as though those promises had never existed.
Maybe what happened wasn't one dramatic event.
Maybe it was years.
Years of being ignored.
Years of manipulation.
Years of rejection.
Years of pretending everything was fine because explaining what was happening felt impossible.
And then you finally escaped the situation...
but discovered the situation had not completely escaped you.
That's the part nobody warned you about.
You can leave the room and still carry the room inside you.
You can delete the messages and still remember the words.
You can forgive someone and still grieve what their choices cost you.
You can genuinely love Jesus and still need time to learn how to trust again.
You can know Romans 8:28 and still cry.
You can believe in resurrection while standing beside a grave.
Even Jesus did.
John 11 records one of Scripture's shortest and most devastating sentences:
“Jesus wept.”
He knew Lazarus was about to rise.
Think about that.
Jesus knew resurrection was coming...
and still wept.
