So tears are not necessarily evidence that faith has failed.
Grief and hope can occupy the same heart.
Pain and faith can exist in the same prayer.
A person can be healing while still having tender places.
The Christian hope is not emotional numbness.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
And Jesus does something far greater than teaching wounded people how to pretend nothing happened.
He redeems.
He restores.
He transforms.
He takes what sin intended to destroy and refuses to allow it to have the final word.
That doesn't mean every relationship will be restored.
Some relationships should not return to what they were.
Forgiveness does not automatically require renewed access.
Reconciliation requires more than one person's willingness; trust can require repentance, truth, wisdom, changed behavior, and time.
You can forgive someone before God while still establishing wise boundaries.
You can release vengeance without volunteering for another betrayal.
Jesus told His disciples to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”
Grace is not stupidity.
Forgiveness is not pretending evil wasn't evil.
The cross itself proves that God takes sin too seriously to pretend it doesn't matter.
Our sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And God's grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly came to save sinners.
This is where healing becomes Gospel.
Because beneath every wound another problem eventually appears.
Our greatest problem is not merely what others have done to us.
It is also what sin has done within us.
Pain can become bitterness.
Betrayal can become hatred.
Fear can become control.
Grief can become despair.
Being sinned against can tempt us toward sin of our own.
And suddenly we discover that we need more than emotional recovery.
We need a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to make wounded people feel better.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He endured shame.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
The Gospel doesn't tell you your wound doesn't matter.
The Gospel tells you your wound does not get the final word because Jesus Christ does.
Maybe you have spent years asking Jesus to erase something He intends to redeem.
You keep praying:
“Lord, make me forget.”
And perhaps the deeper prayer eventually becomes:
“Lord, even if I remember, don't let this memory own me.”
That is a different prayer.
“Jesus, I still remember what they did...
but I refuse to become what they did.”
“I still remember being abandoned...
but abandonment will not become my identity.”
“I still remember being betrayed...
but betrayal will not teach me to hate.”
“I still remember the funeral...
but death will not convince me resurrection isn't coming.”
“I still have scars...
but my scars don't get to name me.”
Christ does.
That is healing without erasure.
And perhaps that's why scars are such a powerful Christian image.
After His resurrection, Jesus was unmistakably victorious, yet the Gospel of John records Him showing His disciples His hands and His side.
Victory did not require pretending crucifixion never happened.
The resurrection did not make Calvary unreal.
Calvary had happened.
The wounds had been real.
But death had lost authority over Him.
And there is something breathtaking in that.
Your story does not need to become unhappened for Jesus to redeem it.
God does not need to rewrite yesterday's historical facts in order to rewrite tomorrow.
He can take the chapter you would never have chosen and refuse to let that chapter become the ending.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters darkness carrying resurrection.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying a wound nobody around you knows exists.
You smile.
You work.
You worship.
You answer messages.
You tell everybody, “I'm okay.”
Then nighttime comes.
And something hurts again.
Please hear this carefully:
Don't measure God's faithfulness exclusively by how little pain you feel today.
Look also at what the pain can no longer make you do.
Maybe you still cry, but you don't run back to what destroyed you.
That's growth.
Maybe you still remember, but you don't fantasize about revenge anymore.
That's growth.
Maybe certain days still hurt, but you no longer believe your life ended there.
That's growth.
Maybe you still struggle to trust, but you're learning to place your deepest trust in Christ instead of another human being.
That's growth.
Maybe the wound occasionally speaks...
but it isn't preaching your identity anymore.
Jesus is.
And perhaps you haven't noticed how far God has already carried you because you have been measuring healing only by what remains instead of noticing what has changed.
Look again.
There was once a night you didn't think you would survive.
You survived it.
There was once a morning you couldn't imagine getting out of bed.
You got up.
There was once a betrayal you thought would destroy your ability to love forever.
Yet something inside you still wants goodness.
Still wants truth.
Still wants Jesus.
You are reading an article about healing because somewhere underneath the scar, hope is still breathing.
Don't worship your progress.
Don't make an idol out of becoming “strong.”
Look toward Christ.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of wounded people becoming impressive.
It is the story of helpless sinners being rescued by an astonishing Savior.
And maybe the next step in your healing isn't demanding that you never hurt again.
Maybe it is surrendering the hurt again.
“Jesus, this still hurts.”
That's a prayer.
“Jesus, I'm angry again.”
That's a prayer.
“Jesus, I thought I had forgiven them, but something came back today.”
Bring that too.
Repent wherever pain has produced sin in you.
Forgive as Christ commands you to forgive.
Seek wise, godly help where you need it.
Tell the truth.
Stop pretending.
Receive grace.
Keep walking.
Healing is not always a straight line.
And Scripture never tells us that every sorrow disappears in this present age.
In fact, Revelation points us toward a coming day when God Himself “will wipe away every tear,” and death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally be gone.
That means Christianity offers something much stronger than the promise of an easier week.
It offers resurrection.
A new creation.
Christ forever.
A world in which the last tear really will be the last tear.
Until then, we walk with scars.
We worship through tears.
We forgive while remembering what forgiveness cost.
We learn boundaries.
We repent.
We fall.
We get up.
We keep coming back to Jesus.
And little by little, wounds that once commanded us become places where God's mercy becomes visible.
One day you may sit beside someone who has just experienced what nearly destroyed you.
They will look at you with swollen eyes and say:
“I don't think I'm going to survive this.”
And suddenly you will understand something.
You won't give them a cliché.
You won't tell them to get over it.
You'll sit beside them.
Because you remember.
And perhaps you'll whisper:
“I know it doesn't feel possible right now. But stay close to Jesus. One day this pain may still be part of your story without being the ruler of your story.”
That's when scars become ministry.
Not because suffering was good.
But because God is so redemptive that He can bring good even from what was evil.
Joseph could eventually look back on devastating human betrayal and recognize God's sovereign hand bringing good from what others intended for evil.
The cross is the supreme demonstration.
Human beings committed history's greatest injustice against the sinless Son of God.
Yet through that very cross, God accomplished redemption for sinners.
From scandal...
to grace.
That is our story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling betrayal beautiful.
Not by calling abuse good.
Not by telling mourners they shouldn't mourn.
But by declaring that sin, shame, betrayal, suffering, Satan, and death do not possess the authority to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So perhaps today you need to stop condemning yourself because healing has taken longer than you expected.
Bring the wound back to Christ.
Again.
And tomorrow, if necessary...
again.
The same God who “heals the brokenhearted” is also the God who “binds up their wounds.”
Bandaging implies tenderness.
Attention.
Care.
And sometimes process.
God knows exactly where it hurts.
Psalm 147 moves almost immediately from God binding broken hearts to God numbering the stars and calling them by name.
The One whose attention reaches the heavens is not too occupied for your broken heart.
You have not disappeared from His sight.
And if you're reading this with tears in your eyes, don't rush away from this moment.
Talk to Jesus.
Not polished Christian language.
Truth.
Tell Him what still hurts.
Tell Him what you're angry about.
Confess where bitterness has taken root.
Confess where you have sinned because you were sinned against.
Ask Him for grace to forgive.
Ask for wisdom about boundaries.
Ask Him to restore what should be restored and give you courage to release what should not.
And above everything else, ask Him to make you more like Christ.
Because the greatest healing isn't merely becoming comfortable again.
It is belonging to Jesus and being transformed by Him.
And if you have spent months or years pretending you're completely fine, maybe today your confession is only three words:
“No more hiding.”
Someone reading those words may realize they aren't alone.
And if you know someone who has been discouraged because their healing is taking longer than they expected, send this article to them.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It doesn't.

If this ministry helps keep you close to Scripture, stay connected. Invite your family. Invite the friend struggling with faith. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the person who isn't even sure they believe yet.
Come to Jesus.
Not the stronger version of you.
Not the healed-enough version.
Not the version who finally stopped crying.
You.
Right now.
With the wound.
With the questions.
With the memory.
With the parts of your heart that still flinch.
Come to Christ.
Because perhaps healing was never supposed to mean that you could look backward and feel absolutely nothing.
Perhaps sometimes healing looks like looking backward and realizing:
“That happened to me...
but it does not own me.
It wounded me...
but it does not name me.
I remember it...
but I no longer worship at its grave.
Jesus found me there.
Jesus carried me from there.
Jesus is still healing me.
And Jesus—not my wound—gets the final word.”
And remember this when the scar aches again:
The wound may remain part of your testimony, but because of Jesus, it no longer has to remain the author of your identity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE STILL” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT YOU THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs:
“BE STILL” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT YOU THINK IT MEANS
You may have been reading Psalm 46:10 as a comforting whisper. In its original setting, it sounds much more like God walking onto a battlefield and telling the whole world to drop its weapons.
There are Bible verses we place on bedroom walls because they make us feel safe.
Verses we print on mugs.
Verses we put beneath photographs of mountains, quiet lakes, sunsets, and empty beaches.
And few verses have been wrapped in more peaceful imagery than this one:
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
Psalm 46:10.
Beautiful.
Comforting.
Familiar.
But what if I told you that when those words were first written, the picture surrounding them was not primarily a peaceful morning with a cup of coffee?
There was chaos.
There were nations raging.
There were kingdoms trembling.
There were weapons.
There was war.
The earth itself was pictured as giving way.
And right there—when everything seemed capable of collapsing—God spoke.
That changes the way you hear the verse.
Because perhaps you came here exhausted.
Maybe there is something happening in your life that you cannot fix.
A marriage you cannot force back together.
A child you cannot control.
A diagnosis you never expected.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
A financial burden quietly crushing you.
A temptation you thought you had defeated.
A secret nobody knows.
A grief you keep disguising as strength.
Or perhaps you are simply tired.
Not sleepy.
Soul tired.
The kind of tired where you still smile at people, still answer messages, still go to work, still attend church, still say “God is good”...
but somewhere underneath all of that, your heart has been whispering:
“God, I don't know how much longer I can carry this.”
Then Psalm 46 is for you.
But perhaps not for the reason you thought.
The Hebrew words behind the famous command are:
הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים
Harpû ûde‘û kî ’ānōkhî ’ĕlōhîm.
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
That first word matters.
הַרְפּוּ — harpû.
It comes from the Hebrew verb רפה (raphah), carrying the idea of slackening, letting go, ceasing, releasing, or desisting.
So “be still” should not be reduced to:
“Find somewhere quiet.”
“Clear your mind.”
“Relax for a few minutes.”
Those things may sometimes be helpful, but Psalm 46 is saying something much bigger.
In this context, the command carries the force of:
Cease.
Let go.
Stop.
Drop your resistance.
Recognize who God is.
That is why translations legitimately render the idea in ways such as “cease striving,” “stop striving,” or even “stop fighting.”
And suddenly the verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us are willing to believe in God...
as long as we can remain in control.
We pray, but then manipulate.
We surrender, but then grab everything back.
We tell God, “Your will be done,” while quietly adding, “as long as Your will looks reasonably similar to mine.”
We ask Him to lead while keeping both hands clenched around the steering wheel.
And sometimes what we call “faith” is actually anxiety wearing Christian vocabulary.
Read the whole psalm.
“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”
Therefore the psalmist says we will not fear—even if the earth changes, even if mountains fall into the sea, even if waters roar.
Then the scene widens.
“The nations rage, the kingdoms totter...”
And then something extraordinary happens.
God makes wars cease.
He breaks the bow.
He shatters the spear.
He burns the instruments of war.
Then comes the voice:
הַרְפּוּ
Harpû.
Enough.
Cease.
And know that I am God.
“I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.”
This is not the voice of a nervous God begging frightened people to calm down.
This is the declaration of the sovereign God before whom human power finally reaches its limit.
God is not panicking.
God is not improvising.
God is not pacing heaven wondering how He is going to survive what is happening on earth.
He is God.
And perhaps that is the part your exhausted heart desperately needs to remember.
You are not.
That sentence may sound harsh until you realize how liberating it is.
You do not have to be God.
You do not have to know everything.
You do not have to control every outcome.
You do not have to carry tomorrow before tomorrow arrives.
You do not have to understand every chapter while you are still living inside the middle of the story.
You do not have to make everybody love you.
You do not have to rescue everybody.
You do not have to force every door open.
You do not have to defend yourself before every person who misunderstands you.
You do not have to manufacture what only God can provide.
You do not have to pretend you are okay when you desperately need grace.
You can loosen your grip.
Not because your circumstances are trustworthy.
Because God is.
There is a difference.
Biblical stillness is not pretending the storm does not exist.
It is recognizing that the storm is not God.
The diagnosis is not God.
The bank account is not God.
Your employer is not God.
Your critics are not God.
Your past is not God.
Your addiction is not God.
Your fear is not God.
Your political leaders are not God.
Your enemies are not God.
Your own emotions are not God.
And Satan is certainly not God.
There is one God.
And the psalm does not merely command, “Be still.”
It continues:
וּדְעוּ — ûde‘û.
“And know.”
The verb comes from יָדַע (yada‘)—to know, recognize, perceive.
The command is not empty passivity.
It is recognition.
Stop acting as though everything depends upon you...
and recognize who God is.
That is why Psalm 46 begins and ends with confidence in His presence.
“The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.”
Notice that description carefully.
“The God of Jacob.”
Not the God of people who never failed.
Not the God of people with spotless histories.
Jacob was complicated.
Jacob knew deception.
Conflict.
Fear.
Consequences.
Wrestling.
And grace.
Yet God attached His name to Jacob's story.
That should give hope to every person reading this with a history they wish they could rewrite.
Because Scripture is filled with people whose worst chapters did not become their final chapters.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The thief beside Christ reached the final hours of a ruined life.
Again and again, human scandal collided with divine grace.
But nowhere is that collision more breathtaking than at the cross.
Because Christian stillness can never finally mean vague spirituality.
It must bring us to Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, humanity's deepest problem was exposed.
Our problem was not merely stress.
Not merely lack of confidence.
Not merely difficult circumstances.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We had rebelled against the God we were created to worship.
We had exchanged His authority for our own.
We had sinned in thought, desire, word, and deed.
And no amount of self-improvement could erase our guilt.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed a Savior.
And God did what we could never do for ourselves.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, went to the cross.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“Try harder until God likes you.”
Not:
“Become religious enough to erase your past.”
Not:
“Fix yourself and then approach Jesus.”
The Gospel announces that salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith in Christ.
Your surrender does not purchase His mercy.
Christ purchased redemption.
Your tears do not pay for your sins.
Christ's blood was shed.
Your good deeds cannot resurrect your dead heart.
Christ saves.
And perhaps this is where “be still” becomes painfully personal.
Because there may be something you need to stop fighting.
Maybe you have spent years fighting God Himself.
You know what He has been asking you to surrender.
You know the relationship.
You know the compromise.
You know the bitterness.
You know the hidden browser history.
You know the secret conversations.
You know the pride.
You know the unforgiveness.
You know the addiction you keep renaming a “struggle” because calling it sin would mean confronting it.
You know.
And God knows.
Maybe your problem is not that God has been silent.
Maybe everything around you has simply become so loud that surrender feels terrifying.
Because surrender means admitting:
“I cannot save myself.”
And that confession is precisely where grace becomes beautiful.
Jesus did not come for people who could save themselves.
He came for sinners.
He did not say the healthy need a physician.
He came calling sinners to repentance.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave.
It means turning.
Coming home.
Dropping the weapon.
Opening the clenched fist.
Stopping the exhausting attempt to justify what God is asking you to surrender.
And saying:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Maybe that prayer needs to happen right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become stronger.
Not when you finally feel spiritual.
Right now.

Jesus Christ, I have sinned. I cannot rescue myself. Forgive me. I turn from my sin and place my trust in You. Take what I keep trying to control. Teach me to obey You. Change my heart. Make my life Yours.
Not magic words.
Not a religious formula.
A surrendered cry to the Savior.
And if something inside you is breaking while you read this, don't hide behind silence.
There are seasons when those three words require more courage than a thousand polished Christian sentences.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Because “be still” does not mean Christians never act.
Scripture never teaches laziness disguised as trust.
Noah still built.
Abraham still went.
Moses still walked forward.
David still faced Goliath.
Nehemiah still rebuilt.
The apostles still preached.
Paul still endured.
Faith obeys.
Faith works.
Faith moves when God says move.
But faith refuses to pretend that the power belongs to us.
There are moments when obedience means walking.
There are moments when obedience means waiting.
There are moments when obedience means speaking.
There are moments when obedience means becoming silent.
There are moments when obedience means fighting the good fight of faith.
And there are moments when God must pry our fingers away from battles we were never commanded to control.
The question is not merely:
“Am I doing something?”
The question is:
“Am I trusting and obeying God?”
That distinction can change your life.
Because maybe you have been begging God to give you peace while refusing to release control.
Maybe you want resurrection while desperately clutching the tomb.
Maybe you want a new chapter while rereading the page God told you to turn.
Maybe you keep asking Jesus to heal what you keep reopening.
Maybe you keep praying for freedom while protecting the very chain He told you to break.
Maybe you keep asking Him to guide you while negotiating every command that makes you uncomfortable.
Harpû.
Let go.
Not of faith.
Not of obedience.
Not of prayer.
Not of responsibility.
Let go of the illusion that you are sovereign.
Let go of the belief that your life will collapse unless your hands control every detail.
Let go of the secret conviction that God needs your permission to be God.
And know.
Know that He is God when the answer comes.
Know that He is God while you are waiting.
Know that He is God when the door opens.
Know that He is God when the door stays closed.
Know that He is God when people understand you.
Know that He is God when they walk away misunderstanding you.
Know that He is God in abundance.
Know that He is God in uncertainty.
Know that He is God beside the hospital bed.
Know that He is God at the graveside.
Know that He is God when you are laughing.
Know that He is God when tears soak the pillow and nobody else knows you cried.
And please understand this carefully:
Knowing God does not mean every painful circumstance will end the way you want.
Psalm 46 does not promise believers a life without trouble.
It begins by calling God a very present help in trouble.
Christian hope is not built upon the promise that nothing painful will happen.
It is built upon the presence, character, promises, sovereignty, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
That means your confidence does not have to rise and fall with your circumstances.
Christ remains Christ.
The cross remains sufficient.
The tomb remains empty.
Grace remains available to the repentant sinner.
And God remains God.
This is why the Gospel changes the meaning of your worst chapter.
The world may identify you by what you did.
Jesus can call you by what His grace is making you.
The enemy whispers:
“Scandal.”
Grace says:
“Redeemed.”
The enemy says:
“Too dirty.”
Christ says:
“Come.”
The enemy says:
“Too late.”
Jesus still saves.
The enemy says:
“Your story is over.”
Then Christ walks toward graves.
That is what Jesus does.
He enters places everyone else has already declared hopeless.
He touches the unclean.
He receives the rejected.
He restores failures.
He forgives sinners.
He resurrects what death claimed.
He rewrites stories.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is more powerful than denial.
Grace looks directly at sin and says the cross was necessary.
Then grace looks directly at the repentant sinner and says the cross was enough.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
There may be a night when fear returns and you need to read these words again:
הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים
Harpû ûde‘û kî ’ānōkhî ’ĕlōhîm.
Cease.
Know.
He is God.
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor—it doesn't.
Christ alone saves, and grace cannot be bought.
Someone may be considering giving up.
Someone may be drowning in shame.
Someone may have stopped praying.
Someone may believe Jesus would never receive them again.
Someone may never walk through the doors of your church...

If you want to glorify God through the opportunities He has placed in your hands, use those opportunities to make Christ known. Sharing Gospel-centered truth is one simple way you can participate in that mission.
Send this privately to someone whose battle should not be exposed publicly.
Think of that support as partnership in the mission—not payment for God's favor.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Make Jesus known.
That distinction matters.
Algorithms disappear.
Platforms change.
Pages rise and fall.
Human applause evaporates.
But Jesus Christ is Lord.
Because perhaps the miracle you have been waiting for does not begin when everything around you finally becomes quiet.
Perhaps it begins when, in the middle of the noise, your clenched hands finally open...
and you realize the throne was never empty.
The storm may still be screaming—but it no longer gets to tell you who God is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HAVE CHURCHES BECOME TOO AFRAID OF OFFENDING PEOPLE?
paragraphs: HAVE CHURCHES BECOME TOO AFRAID OF OFFENDING PEOPLE?
When keeping people comfortable becomes more important than calling people to Christ, the church may still be crowded—but has it forgotten why Jesus came?
There is a sentence almost no pastor wants to hear anymore.
“I was offended by that sermon.”
Those words can trigger meetings.
They can produce angry messages, lost members, unfollows, complaints, awkward conversations, and sometimes financial consequences.
So, little by little, almost invisibly, a temptation can creep into Christian ministry.
Don’t say that too strongly.
Don’t mention sin too specifically.
Don’t talk about judgment too much.
Don’t call people to repentance too directly.
Don’t touch that subject.
Someone might leave.
Someone might get angry.
Someone might stop giving.
Someone might post about us.
Someone might be offended.
And eventually a frightening question emerges:
What happens when the church becomes more afraid of offending people than it is afraid of withholding truth from them?
Before we point fingers at pastors, churches, denominations, or ministries, though, we need enough humility to turn the question around.
Because maybe the problem is not only that some churches are afraid to preach difficult truth.
Maybe sometimes we are afraid to hear it.
Maybe we want sermons that comfort our wounds but never confront our idols.
Maybe we want Jesus as Savior while quietly resisting Jesus as Lord.
Maybe we want encouragement without correction, grace without repentance, resurrection without crucifixion.
And Scripture warned that this temptation would come.
Paul told Timothy:
“For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine…”
The Greek is piercing:
ἔσται γὰρ καιρὸς ὅτε τῆς ὑγιαινούσης διδασκαλίας οὐκ ἀνέξονται
Estai gar kairos hote tēs hygiainousēs didaskalias ouk anexontai.
The expression translated “sound doctrine” contains ὑγιαινούσης — hygiainousēs, carrying the idea of being sound, healthy, wholesome.
Paul’s picture is therefore bigger than merely winning theological arguments.
Truth is spiritually healthy.
And Paul continues by describing people accumulating teachers according to their own desires, with “itching ears” (2 Timothy 4:3).
That is uncomfortable because it exposes something profoundly human.
We naturally prefer voices that confirm us.
Tell me I’m doing fine.
Tell me God understands, but please don’t tell me I need to change.
Tell me about purpose.
Tell me about breakthrough.
Tell me about blessing.
Tell me God loves me.
But please…
don’t touch the thing I refuse to surrender.
And yet sometimes the most loving sentence God can send into your life is the sentence you desperately wish were not true.
Imagine a physician discovering something dangerous in your body.
You sit across the desk.
The doctor sees the results.
The doctor knows something is wrong.
But the doctor thinks:
This diagnosis may upset them.
So instead of telling you what the tests revealed, the doctor smiles.
“You’re doing amazing.”
You leave relieved.
The doctor remains popular.
Nobody feels uncomfortable.
And the disease keeps growing.
Would you call that compassion?
Of course not.
You would call it negligence.
Why, then, would spiritual truth operate differently?
A church that refuses to confront sin because confrontation may make people uncomfortable is not necessarily becoming more loving.
It may simply be becoming quieter about the very disease for which Christ came offering the cure.
But there is another danger on the opposite side.
And Christians must hear this too.
Being offensive is not the same thing as being faithful.
Cruelty is not courage.
Arrogance is not boldness.
Humiliating sinners is not preaching holiness.
Winning arguments is not the same thing as winning souls.
Jesus was not merely “truth.”
John says something breathtaking about Him:
πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας
plērēs charitos kai alētheias.
“Full of grace and truth.”
Not grace instead of truth.
Not truth without grace.
Grace and truth.
That matters enormously.
Jesus could look at sinners without pretending sin was harmless.
He could confront hypocrisy without becoming hypocritical.
He could call people to repentance while receiving the broken.
He could expose darkness while offering Himself as Light.
Christ never needed to dilute truth in order to demonstrate love.
And He never needed to abandon love in order to defend truth.
That is where parts of the modern Christian conversation sometimes break apart.
One side can become so afraid of offending people that repentance disappears.
The other can become so obsessed with “telling it like it is” that tenderness disappears.
Jesus gives us neither counterfeit.
He gives us Himself.
Grace and truth.
The Gospel itself proves this.
The cross is simultaneously devastating and beautiful.
It tells you something devastating:
Your sin is serious.

Serious enough that reconciliation with God could never be accomplished through self-improvement, religious performance, good intentions, charitable deeds, positive thinking, or comparison with people who seem worse than you.
But the cross also tells you something unimaginably beautiful:
You were loved enough that Christ came for sinners.
The Gospel does not flatter humanity.
It rescues humanity.
That distinction changes everything.
The Gospel says you cannot save yourself.
Then it announces that Jesus saves.
It exposes the wound…
and then reveals the Physician.
It announces guilt…
and then points toward forgiveness.
It calls for repentance…
and then opens the door to grace.
It brings us to the cross…
and then shows us an empty tomb.
That is why biblical preaching cannot simply become motivational speaking with occasional Bible verses sprinkled over it.
People do not merely need better self-esteem.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need regeneration.
We need Christ.
Paul’s words in Galatians become painfully relevant:
“Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men?”
Then comes the line that should sober every preacher, teacher, Christian creator, ministry leader—and every believer:
“If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.” — Galatians 1:10
That does not mean Christians should deliberately make people angry.
It means human approval cannot become the compass determining what Christians are willing to say.
Jesus Himself gave an unsettling warning:
“Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for their fathers treated the false prophets in the same way.” — Luke 6:26
Popularity has never been a reliable test of truth.
But neither is unpopularity.
The test is faithfulness to Christ and His Word.
Sometimes biblical truth will comfort you.
Sometimes it will confront you.
Sometimes it will reassure you.
Sometimes it will dismantle the excuse you have protected for years.
Sometimes Scripture feels like a blanket.
Sometimes it feels like a surgeon’s scalpel.
Both can be mercy.
Because God loves us too deeply to merely manage our feelings while leaving our souls untouched.
Think about the woman caught in adultery.
Think about Peter after denying Jesus.
Think about Zacchaeus.
Think about the thief beside Christ.
Think about Paul—the persecutor who became a preacher.
Again and again, Scripture gives us people with histories that should have buried them.
Failure.
Sexual sin.
Cowardice.
Greed.
Violence.
Pride.
Religious hypocrisy.
Public shame.
Private darkness.
And Jesus enters the story.
This is where Christianity becomes different from mere moralism.
Moralism says, “Clean yourself up and perhaps you will become worthy.”
The Gospel says Christ came for sinners, and those who belong to Him are called into a transformed life.
Grace does not tell the adulterer adultery is beautiful.
Grace says your adultery does not have to write your final chapter.
Grace does not tell the addict bondage is freedom.
Grace says your chains do not have to become your identity.
Grace does not tell the proud person pride is harmless.
Grace brings us low enough to discover that mercy was waiting there.
Grace does not rename darkness light.
Grace enters the darkness and leads people out.
This is why repentance is not an embarrassing doctrine Christians should hide from modern audiences.
Repentance is an invitation home.

The Greek New Testament commonly uses μετάνοια — metanoia, and the related verb μετανοέω — metanoeō, for repentance. The idea involves a genuine change of mind and turning, not merely feeling embarrassed because consequences arrived.
Biblical repentance says:
I cannot keep defending what Christ died to deliver me from.
I cannot keep calling bondage freedom simply because surrender hurts.
I cannot ask Jesus to rewrite my story while fighting Him for possession of the pen.
And maybe that is where this article stops being about “churches.”
Maybe now it becomes about you.
And me.
Because it is easy to complain that pastors have become afraid to preach hard truths.
But what happens when God sends one directly toward us?
What if the sermon touches our relationship?
Our pornography?
Our bitterness?
Our secret messages?
Our dishonesty?
Our pride?
Our greed?
Our unforgiveness?
Our gossip?
Our hidden addiction?
Our compromise?
Our lukewarmness?
Our obsession with approval?
Do we still want biblical truth when biblical truth begins reading us?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Maybe you have spent years sitting in church while carefully protecting one locked room inside your heart.
Everyone sees the Christian version of you.
You know when to smile.
You know the songs.
You know the verses.
You know when to say “Amen.”
But there is something you hope nobody ever discovers.
And perhaps you have confused God’s patience with God’s approval.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling you.
Not toward public humiliation.
Toward repentance.
Toward forgiveness.
Toward freedom.
Toward Himself.
You do not have to polish the scandal before bringing it to Christ.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the thing you cannot undo.
Bring Him the night you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the habit you keep promising to stop.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shattered marriage.
Bring Him the wandering heart.
Bring Him your hypocrisy.
Bring Him your religious performance.
Bring Him the exhausted version of you that has become tired of pretending.
Because the central message of Christianity is not that good people successfully climbed their way toward God.
It is that God came down to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose again.
And forgiveness is not offered because sin does not matter.
Forgiveness is offered because Christ paid a terrible price for sinners.
That is why churches cannot abandon either side.
Truth without grace can crush the wounded.
Grace without truth can leave the captive believing his chains are jewelry.
But Jesus Christ comes full of grace and truth.
He loves enough to receive us.
He loves enough to confront us.
He loves enough to forgive us.
And He loves enough not to leave His people unchanged.
So have churches become too afraid of offending people?
Some undoubtedly can fall into that temptation, just as others can fall into harshness, pride, sensationalism, or loveless confrontation.
The deeper question is whether we have become too afraid of biblical truth when it costs us comfort.
A faithful church should never measure success merely by whether everybody leaves smiling.
Sometimes people should leave encouraged.
Sometimes strengthened.
Sometimes comforted.
Sometimes convicted.
Sometimes with tears running down their faces because God finally touched the wound beneath the performance.
And sometimes someone should walk toward their car thinking:
Something has to change.
Not because a preacher manipulated them.
Because Scripture confronted them.
Because Christ became impossible to ignore.
Because the Holy Spirit brought what was hidden into the light.
And because, for the first time in years, repentance did not sound like condemnation.
It sounded like freedom.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess honestly.
Repent genuinely.
Trust Him.
Return to Scripture.
Seek mature believers who will walk with you.
Find a faithful local church where Christ and His Word matter more than trends, personalities, algorithms, applause, or outrage.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail.
But you can make one small declaration.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover they are not the only person fighting.
That is what Christian community can look like even here.
Not performance.
People pointing broken people toward Jesus.
You never know who has been silently asking God for a sign that it is time to come home.
There may be a night when you need these words again.
There is another way you can help this work continue.
Gospel ministry requires people willing to pray, serve, share, give, create, teach, encourage, and support the work according to their calling and ability.
Scripture must govern how we speak about that support.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia, mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs.
In essence: each person should give as he has determined in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So this is not a demand.
It is not a purchase of God’s favor.
It is not a substitute for obedience, repentance, generosity toward your local church, care for your family, or compassion toward people in need.

Your support helps us keep creating Christ-centered content, reaching people who may never enter a church building, encouraging wounded believers, confronting spiritual complacency, and pointing people back to Scripture and the Gospel.
Pray.
One share costs nothing.
But somewhere on the other side of that share may be a person sitting alone at 2:13 in the morning, ashamed of what they have become, wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them anymore.
Imagine this article reaching them because you pressed one button.
Imagine them discovering that conviction is not necessarily God pushing them away.
It may be mercy calling them home.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy is not that the church might offend someone with truth.
Perhaps the greater tragedy would be possessing the message of eternal life and becoming too frightened to speak it with courage, humility, tears, grace, and love.
The world does not need Christians who enjoy offending people.
The world needs Christians who love people enough not to lie to them.
Churches do not need manufactured outrage.
They need Christ.
Sinners do not need humiliation.
They need Christ.
The wounded do not need empty slogans.
They need Christ.
The self-righteous do not need applause.
They need Christ.
The ashamed do not need another hiding place.
They need Christ.
And when Christ enters a scandal, the scandal does not have to become the ending.
Peter denied Him.
Grace rewrote the story.
Paul persecuted His people.
Grace rewrote the story.
Broken men and women have walked toward Jesus carrying histories they could not erase…
and discovered that the cross was never frightened by their past.
Neither is Jesus frightened by yours.
So come into the light.
Tell Him the truth.
Drop the performance.
Stop negotiating with the thing destroying you.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Christ.
And then become courageous enough to give somebody else the truth that once rescued you.
Because the truth that wounds your pride may become the truth that saves your life.
And sometimes the sentence that offends the person you were is the very sentence Jesus uses to awaken the person He is calling you to become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE CAMEL WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO FIT
paragraphs:
THE CAMEL WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO FIT
What Jesus Really Meant by “It Is Easier for a Camel to Go Through the Eye of a Needle”—and Why the Next Words He Spoke May Be the Ones Your Soul Desperately Needs
There is a version of this story that makes Jesus easier to live with.
Maybe you have heard it.
A rich young man walks away from Jesus. Jesus turns to His disciples and says that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.
Then somebody explains that the “eye of the needle” was supposedly a tiny gate in Jerusalem. A camel could get through, they say, but only after its baggage was removed and it knelt down.
It preaches beautifully.
Lay down your baggage.
Humble yourself.
Get on your knees.
Squeeze through.
There is only one enormous problem.
That explanation can distract us from the terrifying beauty of what Jesus actually said.
Because Jesus was not giving the rich young ruler a difficult spiritual obstacle course.
He was describing an impossibility.
And once you understand why, the story stops being merely about a wealthy man who lived two thousand years ago.
It starts becoming about you.
And me.
And every respectable thing we have ever secretly trusted instead of Christ.
The story begins with a man running toward Jesus.
Not away from Him.
Toward Him.
He kneels.
He asks a spiritual question.
He appears moral, serious, respectful, successful.
If this happened outside one of our churches today, we might immediately think, “This man is ready.”
But Jesus sees what nobody else can see.
The man asks:
“Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
Listen carefully to the question.
What must I do?
There is the crack in the foundation.
The man has spent his life accomplishing things, possessing things, managing things, obeying things. Now eternal life itself has become another item he hopes to secure.
Tell me the requirement.
Tell me the price.
Tell me the achievement.
I can handle it.
Jesus begins exposing him through the commandments, and the man replies that he has kept these things from his youth.
Then Mark records one of the most beautiful details in the entire encounter:
“Jesus, looking at him, loved him.”
Do not rush past that.
Jesus was about to put His finger directly onto the man’s idol...
and Scripture calls it love.
Sometimes the love of Christ comforts you.
Sometimes the love of Christ confronts you.
Sometimes Jesus loves you too deeply to leave untouched the thing that is quietly destroying you.
Then comes the sentence that breaks the man open.
Jesus tells him that he lacks one thing: sell what he has, give to the poor, and he will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow Him.
The command is radical.
But notice where it ends.
“Follow Me.”
Jesus was not merely recruiting another philanthropist.
He was calling a man away from his functional god and toward Himself.

The issue was not that possessing money automatically condemns a person. Scripture contains faithful people who possessed significant wealth. Abraham had great possessions. Job was wealthy. Joseph of Arimathea is explicitly described as rich and became a disciple of Jesus.
Money itself was not the Savior standing before this man.
Jesus was.
The tragedy was that when Christ touched the place where this man’s security lived, the man discovered that he wanted eternal life...
but he did not want Jesus at the cost of his idol.
Mark says his face fell.
He went away sorrowful.
Because he had great possessions.
Read that slowly.
The possessions that appeared to make him powerful were powerful enough to make him walk away from Christ.
He owned them.
Until Jesus revealed that, in another sense, they owned him.
And suddenly this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps you are not rich.
Perhaps there is no mansion.
No luxury car.
No investment portfolio.
Maybe you are reading this while worrying about rent, debt, groceries, school fees, hospital bills, or tomorrow's meal.
And yet you can still understand the rich young ruler.
Because wealth was his idol.
It does not have to be yours.
Your “great possessions” may be reputation.
Control.
Career.
A relationship.
Sexual sin.
Approval.
A secret addiction.
Religious respectability.
Your plans for your children.
Your bitterness toward someone who hurt you.
The image you have spent years protecting.
Even ministry can become something we grip harder than Christ.
Anything we refuse to surrender when Jesus says, “Follow Me,” has begun revealing where our treasure really is.
Then Jesus looks around and says how difficult it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God.
The disciples are astonished.
Jesus presses the point again.
Then comes the camel.
Mark 10:25 preserves the statement in Greek:
“εὐκοπώτερόν ἐστιν κάμηλον διὰ τῆς τρυμαλιᾶς τῆς ῥαφίδος διελθεῖν ἢ πλούσιον εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰσελθεῖν.”
The crucial words matter.
κάμηλον — kamēlon — camel.
τρυμαλιᾶς — trymalias — opening, hole, or eye.
ῥαφίδος — rhaphidos — needle.
In straightforward English:
“It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”
Picture what Jesus is saying.
A camel.
An enormous animal by comparison.
Now picture the eye of an actual sewing needle.
Jesus deliberately places the absurdly large beside the impossibly small.
Try pushing the camel through.
Turn it sideways.
Unload it.
Push harder.
Try religion.
Try morality.
Try generosity.
Try reputation.
Try discipline.
Try harder.
The camel still does not fit.
That is precisely why the disciples’ reaction matters.
They do not respond:
“That sounds difficult.”
They respond with astonishment:
“Then who can be saved?”
And that question unlocks the passage.
Who can be saved?
If the point were simply that rich people needed to humble themselves enough to squeeze through a difficult entrance, Jesus’ answer could have been a lesson in humility.
Instead Jesus looks at them and says:
“παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἀδύνατον ἀλλ᾽ οὐ παρὰ θεῷ.”
With human beings...
ἀδύνατον.
Adynaton.
Impossible.
Not inconvenient.
Not unlikely.
Not reserved for unusually disciplined people.
Impossible.
Then Jesus continues:
“πάντα γὰρ δυνατὰ παρὰ τῷ θεῷ.”
For all things are possible with God.
There is the Gospel hiding in plain sight.
The camel cannot make itself smaller.
The needle cannot make itself larger.
The sinner cannot manufacture salvation.
The rich cannot purchase it.
The poor cannot earn it through poverty.
The moral cannot deserve it.
The religious cannot perform their way into it.
The broken cannot cry enough tears to purchase it.
The generous cannot donate enough money to buy it.
The disciplined cannot climb high enough.
The ashamed cannot punish themselves enough.
The churchgoer cannot attend enough services.
The preacher cannot preach enough sermons.
The theologian cannot know enough Greek.
The sinner cannot save the sinner.
“With man it is impossible.”
But Jesus does not stop there.
Thank God He does not stop there.
Because if the sentence ended with human impossibility, Christianity would be nothing but the announcement of our funeral.
Instead Jesus adds four words that turn despair into Gospel:
“But not with God.”
That changes everything.
The impossibility is ours.
The saving power is His.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of humanity climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue humanity.
The rich young ruler asked, essentially, “What can I do?”
Jesus eventually gives the disciples the answer:
You cannot save yourself.
God must do what you cannot.
And this is where the road leads toward a cross.
The Man speaking about impossible salvation would soon walk toward Jerusalem.
He would be betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The sinless Son of God would bear sin.
And what we could never accomplish through morality, money, religious performance, reputation, discipline, or effort, Christ would accomplish through His death and resurrection.
We could not reach God.
So in Christ, God came for us.
We could not pay our debt.
Christ paid it.
We could not cleanse ourselves.
Christ shed His blood for sinners.
We could not defeat death.
Christ walked out of the grave.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace that destroys boasting because nobody gets to stand at the gates of heaven and say:
“I made the camel fit.”
No.
The redeemed will have only one boast.
Jesus Christ saved me.
And perhaps that is why this passage makes us uncomfortable.
We like Christianity until Jesus touches the thing we use to feel safe without Him.
We like grace until grace tells us we cannot rescue ourselves.
We like surrender until Christ names what must be surrendered.
We like calling Jesus Savior while quietly negotiating whether He may also be Lord.
The rich young ruler did not walk away because Jesus hated him.
Remember the sentence.
Jesus looked at him...
and loved him.
Christ exposed his idol because Christ loved him.
Maybe He is doing something similar to you through these words.
What are you holding?
What could Jesus touch that would make your heart immediately tighten?
What possession, relationship, habit, ambition, identity, resentment, secret, bank account, dream, pleasure, applause, or reputation would make you say:
“Jesus, anything except that”?
That “except that” deserves your attention.
Because sometimes the thing standing between a person and surrender is not something obviously evil.
Sometimes it is something good that has been promoted into God's place.
Money is a gift until it becomes a master.
Career is a gift until it becomes identity.
Family is a gift until it becomes an idol.
Success is a gift until losing it feels like losing yourself.
Even religious activity can become camouflage for a heart that has never surrendered to Christ.
And Jesus still looks at people like that with love.
Not sentimental love.
Holy love.
Cross-shaped love.
The kind of love willing to tell you the truth before your idol carries you farther away.
Maybe you have spent years trying to push your camel through the needle.
Trying to become good enough.
Trying to undo what you did.
Trying to compensate for the affair.
The addiction.
The lies.
The greed.
The abortion.
The betrayal.
The pornography.
The years you wasted.
The people you wounded.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The church you abandoned.
The faith you pretended to have.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you are fine.
But at night, when everything gets quiet, you know there is a courtroom inside your chest.
And you keep trying to defend yourself.
One more good deed.
One more promise.
One more religious restart.
One more attempt to become the person you wish you had been.
Listen to Jesus.
“With man it is impossible.”
Those words are not cruelty.
They are liberation.
You can stop pretending you are your own savior.
The camel was never supposed to fit.
You were supposed to discover that you need God.
That is where grace begins.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin and false gods toward the living Christ.
Faith is not presenting Jesus with an impressive résumé.
Faith comes empty-handed.
Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself sufficiently, then approach Jesus.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus saves sinners, forgives the guilty, receives the repentant, and transforms those who belong to Him.
You come because you need mercy.
And mercy has a name.
Jesus.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps you are reading it defensively.
Perhaps there is one sentence you wish you could forget.
Do not run from the wound if Christ is using it to expose what needs healing.
The rich young ruler walked away sorrowful.
You do not have to.
You can stay.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can open the clenched fist.
You can tell Christ the truth He already knows.
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
That confession is not defeat.
It may be the beginning of freedom.
Someone scrolling silently tonight may need evidence that grace still reaches people in real life.
Do not make the comments a stage for pretending.
Make them a place where somebody discovers they are not fighting alone.
It belongs to Christ.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We should never turn ministry support into the very transaction this passage destroys.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ, not by purchasing spiritual approval.
But if this message has served you, sharing it can serve someone else.
That can be an act of love.
They may never open a Bible tonight.
They may never tell you they are considering giving up.
But they might stop for a sentence about a camel, a needle, and a Savior who specializes in what human beings cannot accomplish.
So share it.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical expression of generosity, but it must never be confused with earning God's blessing or salvation.
If you want to support the mission and go deeper with us:
Not because you need another saved Facebook post you will never read again.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who has questions.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Let them come close enough to hear the Gospel clearly.
Because the world does not need another Christianity built around impressive people proving how good they are.
It needs Christ.
The Christ who looked at an idol-bound man and loved him.
The Christ who told the truth even when the truth hurt.
The Christ who said human salvation was impossible and then became the Savior who accomplished the impossible.
Maybe you came into this article thinking the camel was the strange part.
It wasn't.
The truly astonishing part is grace.
That holy God would rescue sinners.
That Christ would receive the repentant.
That guilty people could be forgiven.
That dead hearts could live.
That captives could become free.
That people defined by yesterday could receive a new identity in Christ.
That a cross designed for shame could become the place where mercy and justice meet.
That a tomb could become empty.
That your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter when Jesus Christ becomes the Author of what comes next.
So stop trying to make the camel fit.
Bring Christ the truth.
Bring Him the sin.
Bring Him the idol.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the success you secretly worship.
Bring Him the reputation you are terrified to lose.
Bring Him the hands that cannot save themselves.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Jesus.
Because the sentence that first sounds like the death of hope—
“With man it is impossible”—
is immediately followed by the sentence that makes redemption possible:
“But not with God.”
And perhaps that is the line you were meant to carry away tonight:
The camel cannot pass through the needle—but Christ can carry a sinner all the way home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RIZPAH WAS SAUL’S CONCUBINE—Then Became Famous for Guarding Her Dead Sons’ Bodies
paragraphs: RIZPAH WAS SAUL’S CONCUBINE—Then Became Famous for Guarding Her Dead Sons’ Bodies

Two sons were dead. Their bodies were left exposed. And one grieving mother refused to walk away. But the most haunting thing about Rizpah’s story is not what she did beside the dead—it is what her vigil forces us to confront about sin, love, justice, and the only Savior who can do what no grieving human being ever could.
There are some stories in the Bible we love to frame.
David standing before Goliath.
Daniel surrounded by lions.
Moses before the Red Sea.
Mary kneeling near Jesus.
And then there is Rizpah.
No triumphant army.
No palace celebration.
No miraculous escape recorded for her sons.
Just a woman.
A rock.
Sackcloth.
Dead bodies.
Birds circling overhead.
Wild animals approaching in the darkness.
And a mother who would not leave.
If you have ever loved someone you could not save, keep reading.
If you have ever prayed for something that did not end the way you begged God for it to end, keep reading.

If you have ever sat beside the wreckage of something you could not repair—your marriage, your family, your reputation, your child, your past, your own terrible decisions—Rizpah’s lonely vigil may feel painfully familiar.
But do not stop halfway through this story.
Because 2 Samuel 21 is disturbing if we sanitize it, dangerous if we misread it, and breathtaking when we finally allow it to drive us beyond Rizpah, beyond David, beyond human grief...
to Jesus Christ.
Rizpah first appears in Scripture as a woman connected to a collapsing royal house.
She was the daughter of Aiah and a concubine of Saul.
That description matters.
She had been connected to a king, but she was not Israel’s queen.
She lived near power without possessing the security of the throne.
By 2 Samuel 21, Saul was dead.
Jonathan was dead.
The kingdom had passed to David.
And now a terrible unresolved matter from Saul’s reign returned to the surface.
Israel experienced famine for three successive years.
David sought the LORD, and the answer pointed backward to bloodguilt connected with Saul’s attempt to destroy the Gibeonites.
That background reaches even farther back.

In Joshua 9, Israel had sworn an oath concerning the Gibeonites. Whatever the complicated circumstances surrounding that covenant, Israel had sworn before the LORD. Saul later violated that obligation through bloodshed.
The Bible does not permit us to rename murderous zeal as righteousness simply because someone claims to be acting for God’s people.
Religious passion is not automatically holy.
Zeal without obedience can become destruction.
And eventually, buried blood cries louder than public appearances.
David asked the Gibeonites what could be done.
They did not ask for money.
They asked for seven male descendants of Saul to be handed over.
David spared Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth because of the oath between David and Jonathan, but seven others were handed over—including Rizpah’s two sons, Armoni and another man named Mephibosheth.
They were killed and their bodies exposed.
The text says this happened at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Then the camera of Scripture seems to move away from kings, national politics, famine, treaties and royal decisions...
and stops on one woman.
Rizpah.
Listen to the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:10:
וַתִּקַּח רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה אֶת־הַשַּׂק וַתַּטֵּהוּ לָהּ אֶל־הַצּוּר מִתְּחִלַּת קָצִיר עַד נִתַּךְ־מַיִם עֲלֵיהֶם מִן־הַשָּׁמָיִם
Vattiqqaḥ Riṣpāh bat-ʾAyyāh ʾet-haśśaq...
Rizpah daughter of Aiah took הַשַּׂק — haśśaq, the sackcloth, and spread it for herself upon the rock.
From the beginning of harvest until water came down from heaven, she remained associated with that terrible place.
Then Scripture gives us the detail that makes the scene almost unbearable.
She would not allow the birds of the heavens to rest upon the bodies by day...
or the beasts of the field by night.
Day.
Night.
Day.
Night.
Imagine the exhaustion without inventing details Scripture never gives us.
The Bible does not tell us every thought that passed through her mind.
It does not record a speech from Rizpah.
It does not tell us exactly how many days she remained there.
It does not give us permission to manufacture conversations between her and her sons.
It gives us something stronger.
It gives us what she did.
She stayed.
When the birds came, she drove them away.
When darkness came and animals approached, she guarded the dead.
Morning arrived.
She stayed.
Another sunset.
She stayed.
The bodies she protected could not thank her.
They could not embrace her.
They could not whisper, “Mother, go home.”
They could not reward her loyalty.
Her sons were dead.
And still she stayed.
There is a kind of love that becomes visible only when there is nothing left to receive in return.
Maybe that is why this woman, who could easily have disappeared into a footnote of royal history, became unforgettable.
Scripture later identifies her plainly as פִּלֶגֶשׁ שָׁאוּל — pilegesh Sha’ul, Saul’s concubine.
But notice what eventually reaches David.
Not merely what she was.
What she did.
David was told about Rizpah.
Somebody saw.
Somebody carried the story.
The king heard that this grieving woman was still there.
And David acted.

He retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead. The bones of those who had been killed were gathered as well. Saul and Jonathan were buried in the tomb of Kish, Saul’s father, and the chapter tells us that afterward God answered prayer for the land.
Rizpah could not reverse death.
But her devotion refused to let disgrace have the final visible word over those bodies.
And there is something here many wounded people need to hear.
Sometimes you cannot undo what happened.
You cannot travel backward.
You cannot unsay the sentence.
You cannot uncommit the sin.
You cannot recover every wasted year.
You cannot force another person to return.
You cannot resurrect yesterday.
Some of you know exactly what it feels like to stand beside something dead and keep asking:
“God... what am I supposed to do with this now?”
Rizpah teaches us something profoundly human.
There are moments when faithfulness looks less like conquering and more like refusing to abandon what love requires of you.
But we must be careful here.
Rizpah is not Jesus.
Her suffering did not atone for Israel.
Her vigil did not purchase salvation.
Her grief did not cleanse anyone from sin.
The Bible does not say that.
And if we turn Rizpah into the savior of this chapter, we will miss the greater ache her story awakens.
Because eventually every Rizpah reaches the limit of human love.
She could guard her sons.
She could not raise them.
She could drive away birds.
She could not drive away death.
She could protect their remains from beasts.
She could not put breath back into their lungs.
She could remain beside the dead...
but she could not command the grave to surrender them.
And suddenly this ancient mother sitting on sackcloth beside a rock leaves us longing for Someone greater.
Someone who does not merely mourn outside a tomb.
Someone who has authority over it.
Jesus said:
“I am the resurrection, and the life.”
That changes everything.
Christianity does not proclaim merely that Jesus teaches grieving people how to cope with death.
The Gospel declares that Jesus Christ entered death Himself.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Romans 5:8 announces the astonishing heart of the Gospel: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after the scandal disappeared.
Not after we had successfully hidden everything we were ashamed of.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And He did not remain dead.
Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:20 that Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have died.
Rizpah guarded bodies awaiting burial.
Jesus walked out of His own grave.
That is the difference between beautiful human devotion and divine redemption.
And maybe that is exactly where this story finds you.
Maybe you have been guarding dead things.
A dead version of yourself.
A relationship God has already exposed.
A secret sin you keep protecting.
An identity built from something somebody did to you twenty years ago.
A season you cannot release.
A failure you keep replaying.
A wound you have made into your permanent address.
Maybe everybody thinks you moved on.
But internally, you are still sitting beside the rock.
Still fighting the birds.
Still reliving the night.
Still asking why.
There are things worth faithfully protecting.
There are people worth loving through suffering.
There are wounds that require time to grieve.
The Bible never commands us to pretend pain does not hurt.
Jesus Himself wept.
But there is also a moment when grief must meet resurrection hope.
Because Christ did not die and rise again merely to make your prison more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive.
To reconcile us to God.
To break sin’s dominion.
To give new life.
And repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from the road that is killing you and returning to the God who gives life.
Maybe your scandal is sexual sin.
Maybe it is adultery.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
A secret addiction.
Dishonesty.
A double life.
Unforgiveness.
Religious hypocrisy.
Maybe your scandal is not something you committed but something somebody did to you, and you have allowed the wound to become the lens through which you see everything—including God.
Hear this carefully:
Jesus does not ask you to pretend sin is harmless.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is God doing for guilty and helpless sinners what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
At Calvary, justice was not treated as meaningless.
Sin was not shrugged away.
Christ gave Himself for sinners.
And in His resurrection, death did not get the last word.
This is why the Gospel is greater than motivational religion.
Motivation tells dead people to try harder.
The Gospel announces a living Christ.
Motivation says, “Rewrite yourself.”
The Gospel says Jesus saves, forgives, restores, and transforms those who come to Him.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have the authority to become your savior, your master, or your final identity.
Rizpah entered Scripture as Saul’s concubine.
But when word of her finally reached David in this chapter, it was because of extraordinary devotion in grief.
That should stop somebody.
Because people may introduce you by your lowest chapter.
God is not limited to the chapter where people learned your name.
They may remember your divorce.
Your addiction.
Your prison sentence.
Your breakdown.
Your bankruptcy.
Your affair.
Your rebellion.
Your failure.
Your humiliation.
Your years away from God.
Your worst decision.
But when Jesus Christ takes hold of a surrendered life, the scandal does not have to become the ending.
This does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Rizpah’s story certainly does not teach that.
Biblical grace is deeper than pretending consequences do not exist.
Grace can meet us in the wreckage.
Forgiveness can cleanse the repentant sinner.
Christ can transform what shame tried to permanently name.
That is why our message remains:
Not because scandal is imaginary.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because pain disappears when Christians quote a verse.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the graveyard of your past.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by falsifying what happened...
but by refusing to let what happened have greater authority than what He can redeem.
Maybe you have spent years chasing away the birds from memories you cannot bury.
Maybe you have exhausted yourself defending the remains of who you used to be.
Maybe tonight God is not asking you to become stronger.
Maybe He is calling you to surrender.
Come to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Stop performing.
Stop bargaining.
Stop hiding behind church attendance while protecting the sin destroying your soul.
Stop assuming you must clean yourself before approaching the One who came for sinners.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust Jesus Christ.
There is mercy for the guilty.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is forgiveness for sinners who come to Christ.
There is hope beyond the tomb because the tomb of Jesus Christ is empty.
Be honest before God.
You do not need to publish private details. God already knows them.
But sometimes the first crack in secrecy is simply admitting that you need prayer.
And somebody reading those comments may realize they are not the only believer fighting in the dark.
If this article brought someone to your mind, do not merely think about them.
Send it privately if their struggle is sensitive.
But do it for the right reason.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in love, obedience, generosity, truth, and the faithful use of what He has entrusted to us.
Not because sharing saves you.
Jesus saves.
Christ cannot be bought.
Support because the Gospel is worth spreading.
Share because somebody is sitting beside their own rock tonight.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is growing cold.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the wounded Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who says they no longer believe.
Let them encounter Scripture.
Let them wrestle with Jesus.
Let the Gospel do what clever marketing never can.
And never forget Rizpah.
A woman beside a rock.
A mother refusing to abandon the bodies of her sons.
A vigil so striking that word eventually reached a king.
But then look beyond Rizpah.
Look toward another scene of grief.
Another death.
Another body.
Another stone.
And then...
an empty tomb.
Rizpah could love the dead.
Jesus Christ conquered death.
Rizpah could remain beside those she could not rescue.
Jesus came specifically to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
So whatever lies behind you, do not build your home beside the tomb.
Grieve what must be grieved.
Confess what must be confessed.
Repent of what must be abandoned.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek help where you need help.
But keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the Gospel does not promise that your history will become painless.
It promises something infinitely greater:
in Christ, your history does not have to be your god.
Your shame does not have to be your name.
Your sin does not have to remain your master.
And death itself will not have the final word over those who belong to the risen Christ.
So when the birds circle...
when night comes...
when yesterday starts calling you by the name Jesus is teaching you to leave behind...
remember this:
You were never meant to spend the rest of your life guarding the grave of the person grace is calling you to stop being.
And before you leave, comment something real.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or simply:
“Jesus, I surrender.”
Because your story may contain chapters you wish had never been written.
But if you belong to Jesus, the grave does not hold the pen.
The scandal may explain how you arrived at the rock—but grace decides whether the rock becomes your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID THE PATRIARCHS FOLLOW GOD’S IDEAL—OR THEIR CULTURE?
paragraphs: DID THE PATRIARCHS FOLLOW GOD’S IDEAL—OR THEIR CULTURE?

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob had Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So here is the uncomfortable question many Christians quietly wonder but rarely dare to ask: If these were men of God, why did their homes sometimes look more like the surrounding culture than the garden God designed?
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible.
We can read everything a biblical hero did and assume that because Scripture records it, God approved it.
Abraham did it.
Jacob did it.
David did it.
Solomon did it.
So surely it could not have been that wrong.
Right?
But then Jesus says something that changes the entire conversation.
He does not point us back to Abraham.
He does not point us back to Jacob.
He does not point us back to David.
He goes farther back.
Back before kings.
Before patriarchs.
Before Israel.
Before human traditions had centuries to accumulate.
Jesus takes us all the way back to creation.
And suddenly the question is no longer, “What did the patriarchs practice?”
The question becomes...
“What did God intend from the beginning?”
That distinction changes everything.
Because the Bible is brutally honest about its heroes.
It does not airbrush them.
It does not hide their family disasters to protect their reputations.
It lets Abraham become afraid.
It lets Jacob deceive.
It lets Moses lose his temper.
It lets David commit terrible sin.
It lets Peter deny Jesus.
And that honesty is one of the reasons Scripture is so powerful.
The Bible is not primarily the story of extraordinary people who were good enough for God.
It is the story of a holy God who remains faithful while working through deeply flawed human beings.
That means something uncomfortable but liberating:
Being used by God does not mean everything a person does represents the will of God.
And perhaps someone reading this needs that sentence for reasons having nothing to do with ancient marriage.
Maybe you love Jesus, yet there are pieces of your life that still resemble the culture around you more than Christ.
Maybe you inherited patterns you never questioned.
Maybe everyone in your family did it.
Maybe everyone in your church circle accepts it.
Maybe everybody around you calls it normal.
But “normal” and “biblical” have never been synonyms.

The patriarchs lived inside real ancient cultures, with customs concerning marriage, inheritance, fertility, household survival, servants, concubines, tribal alliances, and descendants. Scripture describes those realities with remarkable honesty.
But description is not automatically prescription.
The Bible can tell us what happened without telling us to imitate everything that happened.
And nowhere is that clearer than in the tangled households of Genesis.
Before Abraham ever took Hagar...
before Jacob ever woke beside Leah...
before Rachel gave Bilhah to her husband...
before kings accumulated wives...
there was Eden.
And Eden gives us the starting point.
Genesis 2:24 says:
עַל־כֵּן֙ יַֽעֲזָב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzov-’îš ’et-’āvîw wə’et-’immō, wədāvaq bə’ištō, wəhāyû ləvāsār ’eḥād.
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Look closely at the final Hebrew words:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
And the verb דָּבַק — davaq carries the idea of clinging, holding fast, adhering closely.
This is covenant language expressed through intimacy, loyalty, and union.
One man.
His wife.
Holding fast.
One flesh.
This is the picture before sin begins distorting everything.
Then something changes.
By Genesis 4, humanity is already east of Eden.
Violence is growing.
Pride is growing.
Sin is multiplying.
And then we meet Lamech.
Scripture says:
וַיִּֽקַּֽח־ל֥וֹ לֶ֖מֶךְ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֑ים
Vayyiqqaḥ-lō Lemeḵ shətê nāšîm.
“Lamech took two wives.”

That is the Bible's first explicit description of a man taking two wives, and its literary setting matters: Genesis 4 is tracing humanity's movement into violence and disorder after the fall. The text reports Lamech's two wives; it does not present a command from God establishing polygamy as the creation ideal.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because years later, Abraham enters the story.
God promises him descendants.
But the promise seems impossible.
Sarah cannot conceive.
Years pass.
Hope becomes painful.
And eventually Sarah proposes a solution.
Hagar.
Genesis 16 records Sarah telling Abraham to go to her Egyptian servant so that perhaps she could build a family through her.
Then comes one of those painfully simple biblical sentences:
Abram listened.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham as a wife.
Hagar conceived.
And almost immediately...
the household began bleeding.
Contempt entered the relationship.
Sarah blamed Abraham.
Hagar was mistreated.
Hagar fled.

The arrangement produced a child whom God saw, heard, cared for, and blessed with promises concerning his descendants—but the narrative never requires us to pretend the human choices surrounding his conception were God's original marital design. God even meets Hagar in her affliction, and Ishmael's name itself is connected with the truth that the LORD heard her suffering.
That is breathtaking.
God's compassion toward people caught in the consequences of human decisions does not mean God endorses every decision that put them there.
And that is where some of us misunderstand grace.
We think:
“God blessed me afterward, therefore what I did must have been right.”
Not necessarily.
Sometimes God's blessing is not His endorsement of your mistake.
Sometimes it is evidence of His mercy despite it.
Read that again.
God can redeem what He never commanded.
That truth runs through Scripture.
And maybe it runs through your story too.
Maybe you made decisions God never told you to make.
Maybe impatience spoke louder than faith.
Maybe loneliness chose for you.
Maybe fear chose for you.
Maybe lust chose for you.
Maybe ambition chose for you.
Maybe family expectations chose for you.
Maybe culture chose for you.
And somehow God still met you afterward.
Do not mistake His mercy for approval of everything behind you.
But do not mistake your failure for the end of your story either.
Because grace knows how to enter places human beings have complicated.
Jacob's household makes that painfully clear.
Jacob loves Rachel.
But through Laban's deception he receives Leah.
Then Rachel.
Then Bilhah.
Then Zilpah.
Children are born inside an atmosphere repeatedly marked by rivalry, jealousy, longing, competition, and pain.
One woman aches because she is unloved.
Another aches because she is barren.
Servants become part of a struggle over children.
Sisters compete.
Eventually the children themselves become caught inside family favoritism, culminating in Joseph's brothers selling him into slavery.
Yet somehow...
through this fractured household...
God forms the twelve tribes of Israel.
Does that mean the dysfunction was God's ideal?
No.
It means God's sovereignty is greater than human dysfunction.
There is a difference.
And if you miss that difference, you may read the Bible backward.
You may begin using God's ability to redeem broken situations as permission to create them.
Grace does not make sin wise.
Grace means sin does not get the final word.
Even Israel's kings were warned.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says concerning the king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.”
The warning is explicit: multiplying wives could turn the king's heart away.
Then Solomon arrives.
