The Gospel is not the announcement that good people can repair themselves.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And those who come to Him in repentance and faith receive something infinitely greater than marriage advice.
Forgiveness.
A new identity.
A new Lord.
A new heart being transformed by His Spirit.
Grace does not merely repaint the ruins.
Jesus begins making people new.
And sometimes that transformation spills into a marriage everyone thought was finished.

Not every marriage story will end the way we desperately want it to. Scripture never promises that if one spouse prays hard enough, behaves perfectly enough, or follows the correct formula, the other person will necessarily repent or the marriage will necessarily be restored.
But nobody has to wait for their spouse to pursue Jesus.
You can surrender today.
You can repent today.
You can tell the truth today.
You can seek godly help today.
You can stop hiding today.
You can forgive without calling evil good.
You can become obedient even while the outcome remains uncertain.
Maybe that is the conversation this article was meant to start.
Not:
“Look what you did to our marriage.”
But:
“What would happen if both of us stopped defending ourselves long enough to ask what Jesus wants to change in us?”
If your spouse sent this to you, resist the temptation to read it as an accusation.
Maybe it was an invitation.
Sit together.
Put the phones away.
Pray.
Listen.
Tell the truth.
And if the wounds are too deep to navigate alone, asking a mature, biblically grounded pastor or qualified marriage counselor for help is not an admission that your faith failed.
Sometimes humility sounds like:
“We need help.”

And if Christ has already carried your marriage, or your own broken heart, through a season you thought would destroy you, tell part of that testimony. Someone reading the comments tonight may need proof that grace still walks into impossible rooms.
Better yet, send it privately and ask, “Can we read this together?”
And invite the married couple barely hanging on.
The believer becoming spiritually numb.
The friend carrying a secret.
The person ashamed to admit home does not look like the photographs.
Even the skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely religious people pretending to have perfect families.
Let them see what the Gospel actually says:
We are not saved because our lives were never scandalous.
We are saved by a Savior who entered our scandal and carried sinners toward grace.
Christ alone is Lord, and our obedience belongs first to Him.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somewhere behind somebody else’s smiling family photograph may be two people quietly falling apart.
Your share might become the conversation they have been avoiding.
Your tag might reach the friend who stopped believing restoration was possible.
Your comment might make another wounded believer realize they are not the only one struggling.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not merely admire the message.
Live the prayer.
Because perhaps the miracle you keep asking God to perform in your marriage begins with the surrender you keep postponing in your own heart.
And even when you cannot rewrite another person’s choices, you can place your own life into the hands of the One who still writes redemption across ruined pages.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD COULD HAVE GIVEN MOSES ANY NAME. WHY DID HE SAY, “I AM”?
paragraphs: GOD COULD HAVE GIVEN MOSES ANY NAME. WHY DID HE SAY, “I AM”?

The burning bush was not merely where Moses discovered God's name. It was where a broken fugitive discovered that the God who needs nothing had come looking for people who had nothing left—and thousands of years later, Jesus would speak words that make the fire of Exodus burn all over again.
There are moments when one sentence changes everything.
Moses had one.
But before we stand beside the burning bush, we need to remember what kind of man was standing in front of it.
He wasn't arriving from a victory.
He was arriving from a scandal.

Moses had once lived inside Pharaoh's world. Then blood was spilled. An Egyptian died. Moses fled. The man who had once moved through the corridors of power disappeared into Midian and became a shepherd.
Imagine the silence of those years.
The memories.
The questions.
The version of your life you thought you were going to live... gone.
Maybe that is why this story reaches places inside us that theology alone sometimes does not.
Because some people reading this know what it means to look at their life and quietly wonder:
How did I get here?
You once had plans.
Then came the failure.
The divorce.
The addiction.
The secret.
The betrayal.
The compromise nobody knows about.
The prayer that seemed unanswered.
The season when you disappointed yourself so badly that you stopped believing God could still use you.
And somewhere along the way, you started thinking your worst chapter had become your identity.
Moses could have believed that too.
But Exodus 3 opens with a shepherd walking through the wilderness.
And then...
fire.
A bush is burning, yet it is not consumed.
Moses turns aside.
God calls his name.
“Moses, Moses.”
And the fugitive answers.
“Here I am.”
Don't miss the irony.
A man who does not yet know what his future is stands before the God who simply is.
God tells Moses that He has seen the suffering of His people in Egypt. He has heard their cries. He knows their suffering. He has come down to deliver them.
Then comes the part Moses probably never expected.
God intends to send him.
The runaway.
The former prince.
The shepherd.
The man with blood in his history.
Moses responds essentially the way frightened people still respond when God calls them beyond the identity created by their failures:
“Who am I?”
That question is more revealing than it sounds.
Who am I to do this?
Who am I after what I've done?
Who am I after wasting all those years?
Who am I when somebody else is more gifted?
Who am I when my past can still testify against me?
God's answer is stunning because He does not spend the moment rebuilding Moses' self-esteem.
He gives Moses something infinitely stronger.
His presence.
God tells him, in Exodus 3:12:
כִּי־אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ
ki ʾehyeh ʿimmakh
The heart of the statement is:
“I will be with you.”
There is that word.
אֶהְיֶה — ʾehyeh.
Remember it.
Because only moments later Moses asks what he should tell Israel when they ask for the name of the God who sent him.
And God answers with one of the most famous and mysterious declarations in all Scripture:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
ʾEhyeh ʾAsher ʾEhyeh.
Traditionally:
“I AM WHO I AM.”
The Hebrew also allows the future-oriented sense:
“I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.”
And suddenly God's earlier promise becomes impossible to ignore.
ʾEhyeh with you.
ʾEhyeh ʾAsher ʾEhyeh.
This isn't God handing Moses a philosophical riddle to impress theologians thousands of years later.
This revelation occurs inside a rescue mission.
Israel is enslaved.
Moses is afraid.
Pharaoh is powerful.
The future looks impossible.
And God reveals Himself.
The point is not that Moses finally possesses a magical pronunciation capable of controlling God.
Quite the opposite.
God cannot be reduced to something Moses can control.
He is not one more tribal deity dependent upon a temple, territory, Pharaoh, human permission, or political empire.
He is God.
He will be who He will be.
He will accomplish what He purposes.
And Moses' weakness cannot cancel God's presence.
Then God gives the covenant name by which Israel is to remember Him:
יהוה
Commonly represented in English as YHWH, the four Hebrew consonants traditionally called the Tetragrammaton.
Its precise ancient pronunciation is uncertain, though “Yahweh” is a common scholarly reconstruction. English Bibles have traditionally represented YHWH as LORD in small capitals.
And this matters.
Because Scripture does not present God's name as an abstract vocabulary lesson.
His name is connected with His character, His covenant faithfulness, His presence, and His saving action.
The God speaking from the bush is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
He has not forgotten His promises.
He has not become indifferent to Israel's suffering.
Egypt may have believed Hebrew slaves were disposable.
Pharaoh may have believed himself untouchable.
Moses may have believed his useful years were behind him.
But God had not forgotten any of them.
That is what makes “I AM” terrifying to the proud and breathtaking to the broken.
Pharaoh's authority was temporary.
God is not.
Egypt's power had boundaries.
God does not.
Moses' failure belonged to his history.
God was already standing in his future.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that sentence more than they realize.
Your failure exists inside time. God does not become trapped inside the chapter that trapped you.
You keep introducing yourself by what happened.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Addicted.
Abandoned.
Ashamed.
Unworthy.
Failure.
Damaged.
Too late.
But those are descriptions of wounds, experiences, sins, consequences, or seasons.
They are not the name of God.
And they do not have the authority to become your final identity when Christ has claimed you.
There is a dangerous counterfeit version of Christian encouragement that says, “Believe in yourself.”
Exodus gives us something better.
Moses asks, “Who am I?”
God's decisive answer is not, “Moses, you are amazing.”
It is:
I will be with you.
That changes everything.
Your confidence does not ultimately rest in your ability to become impressive enough for God.
It rests in the God who remains faithful when you are painfully aware of how small you are.
And this is where the road from the burning bush begins moving toward something even greater.
Because centuries later, another scene unfolds.
Not in Midian.
In Jerusalem.
Jesus is speaking.
The conversation turns toward Abraham.
His opponents challenge Him.
And Jesus answers with words that have thundered through Christian history:
πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί.
prin Abraam genesthai, egō eimi.
“Before Abraham came to be...
I am.”
Not merely, “I was.”
ἐγὼ εἰμί — egō eimi.
I am.
John tells us what happened next.
They picked up stones.
This was not received as harmless religious poetry.
Jesus was making an astonishing claim about His identity.
And within the wider testimony of John's Gospel, the connection becomes breathtaking.
The eternal Word was with God and was God.
The Word became flesh.
The invisible God had drawn near.
The One through whom creation came into existence entered His creation.
And now the Gospel forces every reader to confront a question even more important than the question Moses asked beside the bush.
Not merely:
“Who am I?”
But:
Who is Jesus?
Because Christianity does not ultimately stand or fall on whether Jesus can improve your circumstances.
It stands on who Jesus Christ actually is.
If Jesus were merely a moral teacher, admire Him.
If He were merely a prophet, listen to Him.
If He were merely an inspirational figure, quote Him.
But if the New Testament is telling the truth about Him...
then fall at His feet.
The Gospel is not God shouting motivational advice from heaven.
God came near.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed sinners.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called people to repentance.
He forgave sins.
He carried the cross.
And at Calvary, the sinless Son of God was crucified.
Think about the scandal.
Human hands drove nails through the hands of the One through whom those hands ultimately existed.
The Creator entered creation and permitted His creatures to crucify Him.
The Holy One bore the judgment sinners deserved.
Then came the silence of the tomb.
Friday looked like defeat.
Saturday felt like absence.
But Sunday revealed that death had encountered Someone it could not hold.
Jesus Christ rose.
And that is why grace is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
Grace went through a cross.
Grace walked out of a grave.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and God's mercy is so astonishing that Christ willingly came to save sinners.
That means the answer to shame is not pretending you never sinned.
It is repentance.
The answer to guilt is not learning to love your darkness.
It is bringing your darkness into the light of Christ.
The answer to your scandal is not rewriting history until you look innocent.
It is discovering that Jesus can redeem a history you cannot erase.
Moses had a past.
David had a past.
Peter had a night he desperately wished he could take back.
Paul carried memories of persecuting the church.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a God whose grace does not merely locate spotless people.
He transforms sinners.
That does not make sin beautiful.
It makes grace astonishing.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe underneath everything you show people, there is something you have been carrying alone.
Something you hope nobody discovers.
Something you confessed but still cannot forgive yourself for.
Something you keep returning to.
Something that has made you wonder whether God finally became tired of you.
Listen carefully.
The God who called Moses from the wilderness is not asking you to save yourself.
Jesus already did what you could never do.
But grace is not permission to remain chained.
Christ calls you out.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop using grace as camouflage for something Jesus died to free you from.
Bring Him the real story.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the Facebook version.
The real one.
The lust.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The hidden bottle.
The private browser history.
The jealousy.
The unforgiveness.
The spiritual exhaustion.
The fear that everybody thinks you are stronger than you actually are.
Bring it into His light.
Because you cannot shock the One who already knew your entire story before calling you.
And you cannot earn the mercy Christ purchased by His blood.
You receive Him by faith.
You turn from sin.
You trust Christ.
And slowly, sometimes painfully, sometimes through tears and confession and consequences and rebuilding, He begins rewriting what you thought had to be the ending.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because Christians become perfect overnight.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He turns rebels into sons and daughters.
Enemies into family.
The condemned into the justified.
The wandering into the found.
The ashamed into people who can finally stop hiding.
The spiritually dead into people made alive in Him.
So perhaps the question tonight is not whether you know that God's name is “I AM.”
Perhaps the question is whether the God who revealed Himself to Moses has become merely information to you.
You can know Hebrew words and still refuse surrender.
You can explain the Tetragrammaton and still hide your sin.
You can defend the deity of Christ online and still refuse to let Christ rule your private life.
You can say “Jesus is Lord” publicly while protecting a locked room in your heart where you behave as though you are lord.
And maybe that is the room He is confronting right now.
Not because He delights in crushing you.
Because He loves you too much to bless the prison you keep calling freedom.
Be honest.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded person from giving up tonight.
Then think of one person.
Not an audience.
One person.
The friend whose faith is disappearing quietly.
The brother hiding an addiction.
The woman convinced her past disqualified her.
The Christian who has become numb.
The unbeliever who believes Christianity is only about religious people pretending to be good.

Not as a religious performance. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it absolutely does not. Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Christ, not a reward for supporting a ministry.
If this truth served you, save it too. There will probably come a night when you need to remember that your changing circumstances never changed the identity of God.
But understand the distinction clearly:
You do not glorify God by purchasing access to Him.
You do not buy His favor.
You do not purchase salvation.
Christ paid the price for salvation.
The free resources remain free.
The Gospel remains priceless.
And the purpose remains Jesus.
Moses stood before the fire and discovered that his weakness was not bigger than God's presence.
Israel stood before the sea and discovered that Pharaoh was not bigger than God's deliverance.
Humanity stood before the cross and discovered that our sin was not bigger than God's redeeming love.
And the empty tomb declared that even death does not get the final word when Jesus Christ enters the story.
So when your past whispers,
“You are finished”...
remember who God is.
When shame whispers,
“You can never come home”...
look toward the cross.
When fear whispers,
“You cannot survive what comes next”...
remember what God told the trembling Moses:
I will be with you.
And when the world asks why you still believe after everything you have been through, point beyond yourself.
Not “I am strong.”
Not “I figured everything out.”
Not “I saved myself.”
But:
He is faithful.
The God of Abraham.
The God of Isaac.
The God of Jacob.
The God who called Moses.
The God who hears the cry of the oppressed.
The God who keeps covenant.
The God revealed supremely to us in Jesus Christ.
The Savior who was crucified.
The King who rose.
The Lord who calls sinners to repent and promises eternal life to those who trust in Him.
Maybe your story really is a scandal.
Maybe there are pages you wish you could tear out forever.
But the glory of the Gospel is not that Jesus finds people who never needed rewriting.
He finds sinners whose stories looked finished—and writes grace where shame thought it had already written the final sentence.
Because when everything else in your life becomes uncertain, there remains One whose identity never trembles:
I AM.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about the God who said “I AM” is this:
He already knew every page you would be ashamed of—and He still walked into your wilderness calling your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES THE BIBLE TEACH KARMA?
paragraphs:
DOES THE BIBLE TEACH KARMA?
The Dangerous Lie That Sounds Almost Biblical—Until You See What Jesus Did on the Cross
Maybe you have said it.
Maybe you have thought it.
Maybe you watched someone hurt another person and whispered under your breath:
“Karma will get them.”
Or maybe you were the one who did the hurting.
And now every time something goes wrong, a terrifying thought crawls into your mind.
Is this God paying me back?
The relationship collapsed.
The opportunity disappeared.
Your child started struggling.
The diagnosis came.
The money ran out.
The consequences finally caught up with you.
And somewhere inside your heart, a voice began keeping score.
You did something bad.
Now something bad is happening.
This must be what you deserve.
It sounds logical.
It can even sound spiritual.
After all, doesn’t the Bible say that you reap what you sow?
Yes.
But that does not mean the Bible teaches karma.
And understanding the difference could completely change the way you see your sin, your suffering, your enemies, your forgiveness—and the cross of Jesus Christ.
Because karma says, in one form or another, that your actions carry consequences that eventually return to you according to a moral order.
The Gospel announces something far more shocking:
A guilty sinner can receive what he did not earn because Jesus Christ willingly received judgment in his place.
That is not karma.
That is grace.
And grace is scandalous.

The Bible certainly teaches that actions have consequences. Scripture repeatedly warns that sin destroys, righteousness matters, God judges justly, and human beings often harvest the consequences of what they cultivate.
Paul writes in Galatians 6:7:
The Greek is striking:
ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.
Ho gar ean speirē anthrōpos, touto kai therisei.
Essentially:
Whatever a person sows, this he will also reap.
But keep reading.
Paul is not teaching an impersonal cosmic mechanism called karma.
He is talking about living either according to the flesh or according to the Spirit:
“For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.”
That distinction matters enormously.
Biblical sowing and reaping takes place underneath the sovereignty of the personal, holy, merciful God.

Karma, particularly in its historic religious contexts, belongs to a very different theological framework involving moral causation and, in major traditions that teach it, cycles of rebirth or future existence.
The Bible does not teach reincarnation.
Hebrews 9:27 says:
“And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.”
Once to die.
Then judgment.
Christianity therefore cannot simply rename karma “sowing and reaping.”
They are not interchangeable doctrines.
Yes, choices matter.
Yes, consequences are real.
Yes, God is just.
But biblical Christianity introduces something karma cannot adequately explain:
the substitutionary cross of Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing before God with every hidden thing exposed.
Every lie.
Every lustful thought.
Every cruel word.
Every betrayal.
Every moment of pride.
Every secret compromise nobody discovered.
Every time you knew what was right and deliberately chose something else.
No excuses left.
No carefully edited Facebook version of yourself.
No reputation to hide behind.
Just you.
And truth.
If Christianity were merely a system saying, “Everybody eventually gets exactly what his deeds deserve,” there would be no good news for sinners.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
And Romans 6:23 begins with terrifying clarity:
“For the wages of sin is death...”
The Greek word translated “wages” is ὀψώνια — opsōnia.
It carries the idea of wages or compensation.
Something earned.
Sin has wages.
And those wages are death.
If the verse stopped there, we would have reason to tremble.
But it does not stop there.
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Look at the collision.
Wages.
Then...
Gift.
What you earned.
Then what God gives.
Justice.
Then grace.
Death.
Then life.
And standing between the sinner and eternal destruction is Jesus Christ.
This is where Christianity becomes gloriously offensive to the human instinct that insists everybody should simply “get what they deserve.”
Because the Gospel says God can forgive guilty people without pretending their evil never mattered.
How?
The cross.
Isaiah wrote centuries before the crucifixion:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities...”
The Hebrew of Isaiah 53:5 begins:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ
Vehu mecholal mippesha'einu.
“He was pierced/wounded because of our transgressions.”
Read that slowly.
Our transgressions.
His suffering.
Our guilt.
His wounds.
Our rebellion.
His cross.
And this is precisely why reducing Christianity to “good things happen to good people and bad things happen to bad people” completely collapses at Calvary.
Because look at Jesus.
Who sinned?
We did.
Who suffered there?
Christ.
Who deserved judgment?
We did.
Who bore the curse?
Christ.
Galatians 3:13 says:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.”
For us.
Those two words destroy every attempt to turn Christianity into a simplistic spiritual scoreboard.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The righteous One died for the unrighteous.
Peter says it unmistakably:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.”
That is the Gospel.
And maybe this is where this article stops being theological information and starts becoming personal.
Because perhaps you have secretly believed in a Christianized version of karma for years.
You sinned badly when you were younger.
Maybe nobody knows.
And now something painful has happened in your life.
So you have concluded:
God is finally getting me.
Please be careful.
The Bible absolutely teaches divine discipline, temporal consequences for sin, and final judgment. God is not indifferent to evil.
But Scripture does not give us permission to interpret every tragedy as God's direct repayment for a particular sin.
Jesus confronted exactly that kind of simplistic thinking.
In John 9, His disciples encountered a man who had been blind from birth.
They asked:
“Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Do you hear the assumption?
Someone must have done something.
Someone must be paying.
Jesus rejected their proposed explanation.
“Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.”
Jesus was not claiming that the man or his parents were sinless people. He was rejecting the idea that this blindness could simply be traced to the particular guilt assumed by the disciples.
That should make us extraordinarily cautious about looking at someone suffering and saying:
“That’s karma.”
You don't know that.
When someone loses a job, you don't know every purpose of God.
When someone's marriage collapses, you don't know every hidden circumstance.
When sickness enters someone's home, you don't possess heaven's confidential files.
When the person who wounded you begins suffering, Christianity does not invite you to sit comfortably in the corner whispering:
Good. They deserved it.
Something much harder is required of Christians.
Jesus said:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them...”
Karma has become culturally attractive partly because it can give resentment a spiritual vocabulary.
You don't have to say:
“I hope something terrible happens to them.”
You can simply say:
“Karma.”
And somehow vengeance sounds sophisticated.
But Jesus goes after the heart.
You want them punished.
Jesus tells you to pray.
You want humiliation.
Jesus commands love.
You want revenge.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Notice what Christianity does not say.
It does not say evil doesn't matter.
It says judgment belongs to God.
That is radically different.
You are allowed to pursue justice appropriately.
You are allowed to establish boundaries.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending abuse was acceptable.
Reconciliation and restored trust are not automatically identical to forgiveness, particularly when repentance and safety are involved.
But the Christian heart cannot nourish revenge as though hatred were holy.
Why?
Because Christians themselves live by mercy.
There is another uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes you really do reap what you sow.
Drink destructively for years and your body may suffer.
Destroy trust repeatedly and relationships may collapse.
Live dishonestly and eventually your lies may find you.
Spend recklessly and debt can consume you.
Feed pornography and it can distort your desires, damage intimacy, and enslave your imagination.
Plant bitterness every morning and don't be surprised when bitterness eventually grows roots.
Grace does not magically make every earthly consequence disappear.
David was forgiven, yet devastating consequences followed his sin.
The thief beside Jesus was promised paradise, yet he still died on his cross.
Forgiveness does not mean history is erased.
But here is the difference that changes everything:
For the person who belongs to Christ, consequences do not have to become the final chapter.
Your scandal does not have to receive the last word.
Your worst night does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your failure does not outrank the blood of Jesus.
Your shame does not possess greater authority than the Son of God.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Did you notice something astonishing?
John doesn't merely say God is merciful to forgive.
He says He is faithful and just to forgive.
How can forgiveness of guilty sinners be just?
Because Christian forgiveness is not God sweeping evil underneath a cosmic rug.
Christ paid the price.
At the cross, mercy and justice meet.
Sin is treated seriously enough that Christ dies.
Grace is powerful enough that sinners can live.
And this is where the person drowning in shame needs to listen carefully.
Repentance is not the same thing as spending the rest of your life punishing yourself.
Some people confess their sin to God but continue privately sentencing themselves.
God says forgiven.
They say, Not yet.
God says cleansed.
They say, Maybe after I suffer longer.
God says come home.
They remain outside rehearsing their crimes.
That is not humility.
The answer to sin is not self-atonement.
You cannot become your own savior.
You cannot bleed enough emotionally to improve the blood of Jesus.
You cannot hate yourself into holiness.
Biblical repentance turns away from sin and turns toward God through faith in Christ.
The Greek New Testament frequently uses μετάνοια — metanoia, “repentance,” carrying the idea of a changed mind and turning reflected in a changed direction.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel less guilty.
He came to reconcile sinners to God and transform them.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been waiting for karma to punish the person who destroyed something inside you.
You remember what they did.
You remember the message.
The betrayal.
The manipulation.
The humiliation.
The night you discovered everything.
You have replayed it so many times that anger has started feeling like companionship.
You tell yourself:
“One day they will get theirs.”
Maybe justice will come in this life.
Maybe consequences will arrive.
Maybe you will never personally witness them.
But your healing cannot depend on watching another human being collapse.
Bring the wound to Christ.
Release vengeance into God's hands.
That doesn't excuse what happened.
It means the person who wounded you no longer gets to occupy the throne of your emotional life.
And remember something humbling:
The Gospel that offers mercy to you is powerful enough to save the person you hate.
Yes.
Even them.
That is where grace becomes scandalous.
We love grace when it rescues us.
Grace becomes harder to celebrate when Jesus offers it to our enemies.
But look again at the cross.
The men crucifying Jesus did not hear Him whisper:
“Just wait until karma gets you.”
They heard:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
That is Jesus.
And that Jesus is still saving sinners.
So no—the Bible does not teach karma.
It teaches something infinitely more personal, more morally serious, and more beautiful.
It teaches a holy Creator.
Human rebellion.
Real consequences.
Divine justice.
Judgment.
Repentance.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
Forgiveness.
New birth.
And grace.
Karma cannot become your Savior.
Your good deeds cannot crawl backward through history and erase your sins.
Your suffering cannot purchase your redemption.
Being “better now” cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem you.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
Because His sacrifice was sufficient.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not because you needed another religious debate.
Maybe you needed someone to tell you that your past does not have to become your god.
Stop worshiping your shame.
Stop running.
Stop pretending.
Bring the truth into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust Jesus Christ.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing at the cross.
There is a new identity in Christ.
There is life after the scandal.
And there is grace for people who finally stop pretending they don't need it.

If God has already carried you through consequences you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another broken person desperately needs tonight.
And please don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ alone saves, entirely by grace through faith.
But if Gospel-centered truth has helped you, sharing it is one practical way you can place that truth in front of someone who may never search for it themselves.
Send this to the believer drowning in shame.
Share it with the person waiting for revenge.
Share it with the skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely another system of cosmic reward and punishment.
Supporting Gospel Warrior is not a condition of salvation, proof of salvation, or a payment to God. You can glorify God whether or not you ever give this ministry a cent.
Come to Jesus.
Not when you have repaired yourself.
Not after you have suffered enough.
Not after you have somehow balanced the spiritual scales.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Because Christianity's greatest announcement is not that the universe will eventually give you what you deserve.
It is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners who could never save themselves.
And maybe the sentence you have feared for years is:
One day my past will catch me.
But at the cross, there is another possibility.
Grace can meet you first.
Your sin may explain part of your story.
Your consequences may leave scars.
Your past may still have chapters you wish you could tear out.
But when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your life, the scandal no longer gets to write the ending.
The world says you eventually get what you deserve. The Gospel says Jesus took what repentant sinners deserved—and gives them what they could never earn.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: TAMAR’S SEXUAL SCANDAL MAKES MORE SENSE WHEN YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT JUDAH WITHHELD FROM HER
paragraphs: TAMAR’S SEXUAL SCANDAL MAKES MORE SENSE WHEN YOU UNDERSTAND WHAT JUDAH WITHHELD FROM HER

Everyone remembers the disguise. The roadside encounter. The pregnancy. The shocking confrontation. But Genesis 38 becomes far more disturbing—and far more beautiful—when you notice what happened before Tamar ever covered her face.
There is a moment in Tamar’s story that most people rush past.
And if you miss it, you can easily misunderstand almost everything that follows.
Because before Tamar disguised herself…
before Judah propositioned the woman he assumed was a prostitute…
before she became pregnant by her own father-in-law…
before Judah demanded that she be brought out for punishment…
something had already been withheld from her.
A promise.
A future.
A place in the family.
And the man withholding it was Judah.
That changes the way you read Genesis 38.
Not because everything Tamar did suddenly becomes simple.
It doesn’t.
The Bible does not need us to sanitize its uncomfortable stories. Scripture is remarkably willing to bring us into rooms we would rather keep locked.
But Genesis 38 is not merely a story about sexual scandal.

It is a story about human failure, hypocrisy, responsibility, exposure, confession—and a God whose redemptive purposes can move through a family history so broken that most of us would have tried to erase it.
And somehow…
Jesus Christ would eventually be named in the genealogy that came through this story.
Sit with that for a moment.
Because if you have ever believed that your history is too complicated for grace, Tamar’s story has something to say to you.
Tamar entered Judah’s household as the wife of his firstborn son, Er.
Genesis tells us that Er was wicked before the LORD, and he died.
Tamar became a widow.
Then Judah instructed his second son, Onan, to fulfill his responsibility toward his brother’s widow.
The Hebrew of Genesis 38:8 is revealing:
“בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ”
Bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehakem zera le’achikha.
In context: go to your brother’s wife, perform the duty of a brother-in-law toward her, and raise offspring for your brother.
The important word is connected to the Hebrew root יבם (y-b-m), the language of performing the duty of a brother-in-law.

The more formally codified levirate law appears later in Deuteronomy 25:5–10, so we should be careful not to pretend Genesis 38 is simply quoting legislation that had not yet been given at Sinai. But Genesis itself clearly presents a recognized family obligation: the dead brother’s line was not simply to disappear, and Tamar was not supposed to be abandoned without a future.
Onan knew this.
And he refused.
But notice how he refused.
He was willing to receive sexual access to Tamar while deliberately preventing the very offspring that his responsibility toward her and his dead brother was meant to provide.
Genesis does not portray his wrongdoing merely as a biological act isolated from its context.
The text explicitly tells us his motive.
He knew the offspring would not be reckoned as his.
So he repeatedly prevented conception “so that he would not give offspring to his brother.”
He wanted something from Tamar while withholding what he owed in the arrangement.
And God saw it.
Onan died.
Now Tamar had buried two husbands.
Imagine the silence after the second funeral.
Imagine being the woman everyone begins looking at strangely.
Two brothers.
Both dead.
And you are the widow left standing.
Then Judah spoke.
His third son, Shelah, was still young. Judah told Tamar to return to her father’s house and remain a widow until Shelah grew up.
It sounded like a promise.
But Genesis lets us hear what Judah was actually thinking.
He feared Shelah might die too.
Tamar did not hear that internal thought.
She heard the promise.
So she waited.
That detail matters.
She waited.
And waited.
Shelah grew.
Still Tamar waited.
Then Scripture gives us the sentence that unlocks what follows:
“וְהִוא לֹא־נִתְּנָה לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה”
Vehi lo-nittenah lo le’ishah.
“And she had not been given to him as a wife.”
That is the wound underneath the scandal.
Judah had withheld Shelah.
Tamar had been told to live as a widow waiting for a future Judah apparently never intended to give her.
She was caught in a devastating position.
Not fully restored to an ordinary life.
Not given the son she had been promised.
Waiting inside someone else’s fear.
And some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to have years of your life trapped inside somebody else’s broken promise.
Maybe nobody promised you Shelah.
But somebody promised they would stay.
Somebody promised they would change.
Somebody promised they would protect you.
Somebody told you, “Just wait.”
So you waited.
You kept believing.
You kept making excuses for them.
You kept staring at the door.
And eventually you realized the person who told you to wait had quietly moved on while you were still organizing your life around their words.
That kind of betrayal does something to a person.
Genesis does not tell us every emotion Tamar experienced, so we should not put invented thoughts into her mind.
What it does tell us is enough.
Shelah had grown.
She had not been given to him.
Then Tamar learned that Judah was traveling to Timnah for sheep shearing.
She removed her widow’s clothing.
She covered herself.
She sat where Judah would pass.
And Judah saw her.
He did not recognize his own daughter-in-law.
He assumed she was a prostitute.
Then came one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable encounters.
Judah approached her for sex.
Tamar asked what he would give her.
He promised a young goat.
She wanted collateral until the payment arrived.
His seal.
His cord.
His staff.
Do not miss those objects.
In that world, these were identifying possessions.
Judah was essentially handing a stranger evidence capable of identifying him.
He entered the encounter believing he could walk away afterward.
Tamar walked away carrying proof.
She conceived.
Then she disappeared from his view.
Judah later attempted to send the promised goat through his friend, but the woman could not be found.
And then, approximately three months later, word reached Judah.
Tamar was pregnant.
The widow who had supposedly been waiting for his son was carrying a child.
Judah’s response was immediate and severe.
“Bring her out…”
The man who had secretly participated in sexual immorality was suddenly ready to pronounce judgment when someone else’s sexual scandal became visible.
There is the mirror.
And it is uncomfortable because human beings have not changed much.
We can become ferocious toward sins that are visible in other people while becoming astonishingly patient with sins hidden in ourselves.
We condemn the evidence while protecting the secret.
We demand accountability from somebody else while negotiating exemptions for ourselves.
We know exactly which Bible verse applies to their behavior…
and somehow forget the verses that expose ours.
Judah saw a pregnant woman.
God knew the whole story.
And just before judgment fell, Tamar sent Judah a message.
She did not initially shout his name before everyone.
She sent the objects.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
Then essentially said:
Identify these.
Who owns them?
Suddenly Judah was no longer staring at Tamar’s scandal.
He was staring at himself.
And what he said next is one of the great moments of moral recognition in Genesis:
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי”
Tzadqah mimmeni.
The phrase is often translated:
“She is more righteous than I.”
And Judah immediately explains why:
“Because I did not give her to Shelah my son.”
There it is.
Judah himself identifies the withheld promise as central to what happened.
This does not require us to turn Tamar into a modern symbol for whatever cause we prefer.
It does not require pretending that deception and sexual irregularity are somehow God’s normal design.
It requires something harder.
Read what the text actually says.
Judah had failed her.
And when the truth came into the light, Judah finally acknowledged it.
“I did not give her to Shelah.”
The scandal exposed something deeper than Tamar’s pregnancy.
It exposed Judah.
And perhaps that is why this story can become so personal.
Because sometimes the thing we desperately want God to remove is the very thing He uses to reveal us.
Not because public humiliation saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
Not because scandal itself is holy.
It isn’t.
But God has an unsettling way of allowing truth to reach places our excuses have barricaded.
Judah had already participated in another terrible deception.
Earlier, he had joined his brothers in the events surrounding Joseph. Joseph was sold, his robe was used to deceive their father, and Jacob was left believing his beloved son was dead.
Judah knew what concealment looked like.
Now Judah himself was being confronted with identifying evidence.
The deceiver was being forced to recognize the truth.
And something in Judah begins to change.
Genesis does not give us a neat paragraph saying, “Judah repented and became a different man that afternoon.”
We should not claim more than Scripture says.
But keep reading Genesis.
Later, when Benjamin’s freedom and Jacob’s heart are on the line, Judah steps forward before Joseph.
The man who once helped surrender a brother now offers himself in another brother’s place.
“Please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers” (Genesis 44:33).
Something has happened to Judah.
The man is not standing where he once stood.
And that is where Tamar’s scandal begins pointing beyond Tamar.
Beyond Judah.
Beyond Genesis 38.
Because Tamar conceived twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez continued the family line.
Generations passed.
Perez’s line led to Boaz.
Then Obed.
Then Jesse.
Then David.
And when Matthew opens the New Testament and begins announcing the genealogy of Jesus Christ, Tamar is not edited out.
Matthew 1:3 deliberately remembers her:
Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.
Her name remains.
The uncomfortable story remains.
The family scandal remains.
And through that line eventually comes Jesus Christ.
Not because God approved every sinful action committed by everyone in that genealogy.
Far from it.
The genealogy is powerful precisely because God’s redemptive faithfulness is greater than human wreckage.
Jesus did not come from a sanitized human family history.
He entered ours.
Matthew’s genealogy contains stories of failure, outsiders, sexual brokenness, violence, compromised people, unexpected mercy, and astonishing providence.
Then comes Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Not humanity climbing high enough to reach God.
God coming down to rescue sinners.
Jesus did not come because our histories were clean.
He came because we needed redemption.
He did not die for an imaginary collection of respectable people who had never made a mess.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15).
And at the cross, He did something Judah could never do for himself.
He bore sin.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
He carried judgment.
He died.
And He rose again.
So when we say, “From Scandal to Grace,” we are not saying scandal becomes grace.
We are saying Jesus can meet sinners inside histories soaked with shame and write a redemptive future that sin could never produce.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth about evil—and then offers forgiveness to the guilty through Christ.
That distinction matters.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your “seal, cord, and staff” are still hidden somewhere metaphorically, and you live terrified that somebody will discover what happened.
Maybe you were the person who was betrayed.
Maybe you were the person who betrayed someone.
Maybe you were used.
Maybe you used someone.
Maybe someone withheld what they promised you.
Maybe you were the one who made promises you never intended to keep.
Maybe you have spent years pointing at Tamar because looking at Judah would bring you too close to yourself.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
Every room.
Every message.
Every compromise.
Every night.
Every secret.
Every wound.
Every excuse.
Every sin.
Every tear.
And the Gospel invitation is not “hide it better.”
It is:
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Bring the truth to Jesus.
Because there is a massive difference between being exposed without hope and being exposed before a Savior.
Judah said:
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי.”
He finally stopped defending himself.
There are moments when spiritual transformation begins with words painfully similar to these:
I was wrong.
I sinned.
I hurt them.
I lied.
I withheld what I promised.
I have been blaming everybody except myself.
Jesus, have mercy on me.
That is not the end of the story.
Sometimes it is where grace finally begins to be received.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
The blood of Jesus is not intimidated by the chapter you hope nobody reads.
And repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Christ.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One who alone can save you from it.
Maybe this article did not merely teach you something about Tamar.
Maybe somewhere between Judah’s promise and Judah’s confession, you recognized yourself.
Talk to God.
Tell Him the truth.
If you have never trusted Christ, come to Him.
If you belong to Christ but have been hiding, come back into the light.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging that you need grace is one small way of refusing to keep pretending.
And read the comments of others with mercy.
There may be someone underneath this article whose battle looks nothing like yours but who desperately needs to know another Christian will pray rather than throw stones.
You may need to read Genesis 38 differently again someday.
There are people starving for biblical truth who may never walk into a church this week—but they may stop long enough to read something you shared.
Supporting Gospel work does not earn favor with God. We are saved by grace through faith in Christ, not by financial support.
Come to Christ.
Because Tamar’s story ultimately matters for more than the scandal beside the road.
A woman was denied what had been promised.
A man’s hypocrisy was exposed.
The truth came into the light.
Judah confessed his failure.
Perez was born.
The generations continued.
David came.
And eventually, according to the flesh, from that astonishingly complicated family line came Jesus Christ.
The Lion of the tribe of Judah.
The King who does not hide our sin by pretending it never happened.
The King who deals with it at the cross.
Maybe you thought the ugliest chapter meant your story was over.
Look again at Tamar.
Look again at Judah.
Then look beyond both of them.
Look at Jesus.
Because the hands that were pierced for sinners are still capable of taking a story you thought could only end in shame and making its final testimony about grace.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity when your story is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jesus Said You Will Answer for Every Careless Word—and That Should Terrify the Part of Us That Says, “I Was Only Joking”
paragraphs: Jesus Said You Will Answer for Every Careless Word—and That Should Terrify the Part of Us That Says, “I Was Only Joking”

The words you deleted, whispered, posted, shouted, disguised as humor, or justified because you were angry may have been forgotten by everyone else. Jesus says they are not meaningless—and what He says next turns an uncomfortable warning about our mouths into a devastating examination of our hearts.
There are sentences you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
You know the ones.
The words you said when you were angry enough to stop caring.
The insult you disguised as a joke.
The gossip you introduced with, “I probably shouldn’t tell you this, but…”
The comment you typed because a screen made you forget there was a human soul on the other side.
The sarcastic remark that made everyone laugh while quietly humiliating somebody.
The argument where winning became more important than loving.
The conversation where someone trusted you with their weakness, and later you used that weakness as ammunition.
The words spoken about your spouse after the argument.
The things said about your parents.
Your children.
Your pastor.
Your church.
Your coworker.
Your enemy.
The person who wounded you.
Maybe even the cruel things you have repeatedly said about yourself.
And then there are the words that never felt serious enough to repent of.
That may be the category Jesus makes impossible to ignore.
Because tucked inside Matthew 12 is a statement from Christ that should make even the most talkative among us suddenly become quiet:
“But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.” — Matthew 12:36, KJV
Read it again.
Every.
Idle.
Word.
The Greek is painfully precise:
πᾶν ῥῆμα ἀργόν
pan rhēma argon
Every idle, ineffective, useless, careless utterance.

The word translated “idle” is ἀργόν — argon, carrying the sense of something idle, inactive, useless, or unproductive. Jesus is not merely warning about the spectacular verbal sins that destroy reputations and families. His words reach into that category we so easily excuse—the speech we treat as insignificant because we assume words disappear once the sound is gone.
Jesus says they matter.
And suddenly the sentence you dismissed with “I didn’t mean anything by it” does not feel quite so harmless.
But before fear turns this passage into something Jesus did not mean, we have to hear Him in context.
Christ was not giving anxious believers a new reason to obsess over every accidental syllable as though salvation depended upon maintaining a flawless vocabulary.
He was confronting something much deeper.
The verses surrounding the warning tell us exactly where Jesus was aiming.
“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.” — Matthew 12:34
There it is.
The mouth is revealing something.
Speech is fruit.
The heart is the tree.
Jesus had just spoken about a tree being known by its fruit. Then He moved directly to the human heart and the words flowing from it.
In other words, the terrifying question is not merely:
“What did I say?”
It is:
“What did those words reveal about what was happening inside me?”
That changes everything.
Because sometimes anger reveals an idol.
Sometimes gossip reveals pride.
Sometimes sarcasm reveals contempt.
Sometimes constant criticism reveals bitterness.
Sometimes exaggeration reveals insecurity.
Sometimes filthy speech reveals what we have allowed to feed our imagination.
Sometimes slander reveals hatred.
Sometimes boasting reveals our hunger to be admired.
Sometimes cruelty reveals wounds we never surrendered to Christ.
Sometimes our jokes reveal things about our hearts that our Sunday vocabulary carefully conceals.
And sometimes silence reveals something too.
We knew somebody was being destroyed by gossip, and we said nothing.
We watched a person being humiliated because joining the crowd was easier than defending them.
We had the opportunity to say, “I love you.”
We withheld it.
We needed to say, “I was wrong.”
Pride locked our mouth.
We should have said, “Forgive me.”
Instead we explained ourselves.
We should have spoken about Jesus.
Fear convinced us there would always be another opportunity.
Words matter.
And Christ refuses to let us pretend otherwise.
Perhaps that is uncomfortable because most of us have built an entire defense system around our speech.
“I was angry.”
“I was joking.”
“That’s just how I talk.”
“They deserved it.”
“Everybody says things like that.”
“You’re too sensitive.”
“I only said what was true.”
But truth can still be weaponized without love.
A technically accurate sentence can still come from a corrupt motive.
You can win an argument and wound a soul.
You can expose someone’s sin while secretly enjoying their humiliation.
You can quote Scripture and still speak without the heart of Christ.
That last possibility should sober every Christian with a platform, a comment section, a pulpit, a group chat, or simply another human being within hearing distance.
Because religious language does not automatically make speech holy.
The Pharisees knew religious language.
And Jesus was confronting them.
This is why Matthew 12:36 cannot honestly be reduced to etiquette.
Jesus is exposing the heart.
Imagine for a moment that every word you spoke during the last seven days appeared on a screen.
Not only church words.
Everything.
Every private conversation.
Every voice message.
Every comment.
Every whispered complaint.
Every joke.
Every angry response.
Every sentence spoken when you thought nobody important was listening.
Would you want your family to read the transcript?
Would you want your church to hear it?
Would you want Jesus standing beside you as it played?
That question hurts because somewhere inside us we already know the answer.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity does not announce that good people with clean mouths are welcomed by God while messy people are discarded.
Christianity announces that sinners need a Savior.
Including sinners whose tongues have done damage.
Peter knew something about words he desperately wished he could retrieve.
On the night Jesus was betrayed, Peter did not merely become quiet.
He denied Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again.
The disciple who had boldly confessed Jesus eventually spoke as though he did not even know Him.
Imagine living with that sentence inside your memory.
Imagine hearing your own voice denying the One who loved you.
Then the rooster crowed.
Peter remembered.
And he wept bitterly.
That could have been the end of Peter's story.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
Words he could never unsay.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ met the disciple who had failed Him.
Jesus did not pretend the failure never happened.
Grace is not amnesia.
Grace tells the truth about sin and then reveals that sin does not get the final word over the repentant sinner.
Three denials were not stronger than the mercy of the risen Christ.
Peter's mouth had denied Jesus.
Later that same mouth would proclaim Him.
The tongue that once said, in effect, “I don't know Him,” would preach Christ publicly.
That is redemption.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely teach dirty mouths to use cleaner vocabulary.
He transforms hearts.
And when Christ changes the heart, eventually the fruit begins changing too.
This is why merely policing vocabulary will never be enough.
You can train yourself not to swear while remaining vicious.
You can stop gossiping publicly while judging people privately.
You can replace obvious insults with sophisticated contempt.
You can learn Christian phrases while harboring an un-Christian heart.
Jesus wants deeper access.
He goes toward the source.
“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”
Maybe that is what God is exposing in you right now.
Not because Christ delights in humiliating you.
Because He loves you too much to leave poison undiscovered.
Maybe your mouth has been revealing bitterness you keep calling personality.
Maybe your sarcasm has become permission to be cruel.
Maybe gossip makes you feel important because knowing someone else's secrets gives you social currency.
Maybe your home receives the version of you that church people never see.
You sing about grace on Sunday and speak without grace on Monday.
You lift your hands in worship and use the same mouth to tear somebody apart afterward.
James saw the contradiction.

“With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God… My brothers, these things ought not to be so.” — James 3:9–10, translated closely from the Greek sense.
That is painfully contemporary.
We can say “God bless you” publicly and assassinate someone's character privately.
We can worship Jesus with our lips while refusing to apologize for what those lips have done.
Scripture does not permit that contradiction to become comfortable.
Paul gives us another stunning picture in Ephesians 4:29.
The Greek begins:
Πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς… μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω
Pas logos sapros… mē ekporeuesthō
The word σαπρός — sapros means rotten, corrupt, worthless, spoiled.

Paul's instruction is essentially that rotten speech must not be allowed to proceed from our mouths. But he does not stop with prohibition. Christian speech is supposed to become something entirely different—speech suitable for building people up according to their need, speech that gives χάριν — charin, grace, to those who hear.
Think about that.
Your mouth can become an instrument of grace.
The same tongue that once wounded can learn to heal.
The same voice that once gossiped can defend.
The same person who once screamed can learn gentleness.
The same mouth that lied can confess truth.
The same lips that cursed can bless.
The same person who said, “I'll never forgive you,” can eventually say, through the transforming power of Christ, “Because I have been forgiven, I am choosing forgiveness.”
That is not behavior modification.
That is Gospel transformation.
And perhaps the most Christian sentence some of us could speak today is only five words:
“I was wrong. Forgive me.”
No explanation.
No “but you also…”
No courtroom defense.
No rewriting history.
Just repentance.
Maybe someone still remembers what you said even though you forgot saying it.
That possibility is painful.
Some words leave bruises nobody photographs.
Children remember sentences parents considered insignificant.
Spouses remember words spoken during arguments years earlier.
People remember being mocked about their bodies.
Their intelligence.
Their failures.
Their past.
Their poverty.
Their weakness.
Sometimes a ten-second sentence becomes a ten-year wound.
That is why Jesus' warning is mercy.
He is teaching us not to treat lightly what can carry tremendous spiritual and emotional weight.
Yet if you are reading this and remembering your worst words, do not confuse conviction with a declaration that redemption is impossible.
Run toward Christ.
Repentance does not mean hiding from Jesus until you become worthy enough to return.
You will never become worthy through self-repair.
Come into the light.
Confess what your speech has revealed.
Where restitution or apology is appropriate, make it.
Ask forgiveness.
Stop defending what God is exposing.
And remember the center of Christianity:
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
The cross is where our excuses die and mercy speaks.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is not God pretending sin was harmless. Forgiveness was purchased at immeasurable cost.
The answer to Matthew 12:36 is therefore not, “I need to become verbally perfect so God will finally love me.”
The answer is:
“I need Christ.”
I need His forgiveness for yesterday.
His Spirit for today.
His wisdom before I speak tomorrow.
I need Jesus when somebody provokes me.
Jesus when gossip enters the room.
Jesus when my fingers hover over “Post.”
Jesus when anger rises.
Jesus when somebody wounds me.
Jesus when I am tempted to say the sentence that will hurt them exactly where I know they are weakest.
Jesus when my pride wants the final word.
Sometimes the most Spirit-controlled sentence is the one you never say.
And sometimes obedience means speaking when fear tells you to remain silent:
“I forgive you.”
“I love you.”
“I was wrong.”
“Can I pray for you?”
“Jesus changed my life.”
Words can destroy.
Words can also carry grace.
So before you speak, perhaps a new prayer needs to become instinctive:
Jesus, does this sound like You?
Not merely:
Is it true?
Not merely:
Will people agree?
Not merely:
Will this get likes?
Not merely:
Can I defend saying it?
But:
Does this sound like Jesus?
Will it build what should be built?
Will it confront what needs confronting without enjoying someone's destruction?
Will it give grace?
Does it come from love?
What does it reveal about my heart?
Sit with it.
Ask the Holy Spirit to search you.
Remember the conversation.
Remember the person.
Remember the sentence.
Then bring it to Jesus.
If necessary, go apologize.
If necessary, delete the post.
If necessary, leave the gossip circle.
If necessary, call the person you wounded.
If necessary, stop calling cruelty “just my personality.”
And if your spirit is whispering, “Lord, my mouth has not honored You,” you do not need to perform for anyone here.
But you can make your response tangible.
Somebody who believes they can never change may need to see evidence that sanctification is real.
Then think of one person who needs this—not somebody you want to shame, but somebody you love.
“Lord, start with me.”
It matters.
There is enough empty noise online.
Let's help put the Gospel into the stream.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you glorify God.
It does not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient lives, and financial support is only one voluntary way believers may help sustain Gospel ministry.
Give Jesus your heart.
Because eventually your mouth reveals what your heart treasures.
The goal is not simply becoming someone who says fewer bad things.
The goal is becoming someone increasingly transformed into the likeness of Christ.
A person whose truth has love in it.
Whose correction has humility in it.
Whose disagreement has dignity in it.
Whose confession has honesty in it.
Whose testimony has Jesus in it.
Whose words leave grace behind.
There may be things you have said that you cannot unsay.
There may be wounds you cannot rewind.
There may be sentences you would give anything to erase.
But your worst sentence does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Peter discovered that.
The cross proves it.
The empty tomb declares it.
Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still changes hearts.
Jesus still teaches wounded mouths to speak grace.
So share this if you believe our generation needs to rediscover the holiness of words.
Save it before your next difficult conversation.
And when you fail, do not hide behind excuses.
Run back to Jesus.
Repent.
Receive grace.
Make things right where you can.
Then let the Savior keep rewriting you.
Because one day we will answer for our words.
But today, mercy is still calling sinners home.
You cannot retrieve every word you have spoken—but you can surrender the heart that will speak the next one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD” — ONE TINY HEBREW WORD CHANGES HOW YOU READ PSALM 23
paragraphs:
“THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD” — ONE TINY HEBREW WORD CHANGES HOW YOU READ PSALM 23
You may have quoted this Psalm your entire life. But have you ever stopped long enough to realize what David was actually daring to say?
There are Bible verses we read.
And then there are Bible verses that read us.
Psalm 23 is one of them.
You have probably heard it beside hospital beds.
At funerals.
During sleepless nights.
In church sanctuaries.
Whispered through tears when someone had run out of explanations but had not completely run out of faith.
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
Beautiful.
Familiar.
Comforting.
Maybe dangerously familiar.
Because sometimes we repeat Scripture so often that the words stop surprising us.
We know what comes next before our hearts have even caught up with what we just said.
But go back.
Slow down.
Look at the opening words David originally wrote:
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
YHWH ro‘i, lo ’eḥsar.
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
And there is one small Hebrew word hiding in plain sight that can change the emotional weight of the entire Psalm.
רֹעִי — ro‘i.
“My shepherd.”
Not merely a shepherd.
Not merely the Shepherd.
My Shepherd.
That little possessive ending matters.
David did not merely make a theological statement about what God does.
He made a relational confession about who God was to him.
And maybe that is exactly where Psalm 23 becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to believe that God is the Shepherd...
without actually letting Him shepherd you.
It is possible to know Christian language, attend church, repost Bible verses, sing worship songs, defend biblical truth, and still quietly shepherd your own life.
“My money.”
“My plans.”
“My relationship.”
“My body.”
“My future.”
“My decisions.”
“My way.”
And then when everything collapses, we wonder why the Shepherd feels so far away.
But perhaps the question Psalm 23 places before us is not merely:
“Do you believe the LORD is a Shepherd?”
The deeper question is:
“Can you honestly call Him yours?”
Because sheep do not merely admire shepherds.
They follow them.
And that changes everything.
David knew something about shepherding.
Before palaces...
before armies...
before songs sung throughout generations...
before anyone called him king...
there were fields.
There were sheep.
There were lonely nights beneath the stars.
There were predators hiding beyond the firelight.
There were animals that wandered.
Animals that needed leading.
Animals that could not survive very long pretending they did not need anyone.
David knew what a shepherd did.
So when he wrote,
יְהוָה רֹעִי — YHWH ro‘i — “The LORD is my Shepherd,”
he was saying far more than, “God makes me feel safe.”
He was confessing dependence.
The Shepherd determines the direction.
The Shepherd knows where the water is.
The Shepherd sees dangers the sheep cannot see.
The Shepherd searches when one wanders.
The Shepherd protects.
The Shepherd leads.
And the sheep must learn the terrifying freedom of trusting someone wiser than themselves.
That is where Psalm 23 stops being decoration for your wall and becomes confrontation for your soul.
Because some of us want a Shepherd who comforts us...
but not one who leads us.
We want Him beside us in the valley but not ahead of us when He chooses the road.
We want His protection without His authority.
His promises without His commands.
His heaven without His holiness.
His forgiveness without repentance.
His cross without our surrender.
We want Jesus to rescue the life we designed instead of becoming Lord over the life He purchased.
And yet David says:
“My Shepherd.”
Those words contain surrender.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something nobody knows about.
You look fine.
You answer messages.
You go to work.
You take care of your family.
You laugh when you are supposed to laugh.
Maybe you even serve at church.
But there is another version of you that appears when the room gets quiet.
The frightened version.
The ashamed version.
The exhausted version.
The version replaying that mistake from years ago.
The version wondering whether God has finally become tired of forgiving you.
The version scrolling late at night because silence makes your thoughts too loud.
The version praying,
“Lord... I don't know how much longer I can keep doing this.”
Psalm 23 was written for valleys like that.
But notice something extraordinary.
David does not say the Shepherd prevents every valley.
He says the Shepherd accompanies him through it.
“Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil...”
Why?
Not because David suddenly becomes powerful.
Not because the valley disappears.
Not because the enemies apologize.
Not because circumstances become understandable.
The reason is astonishingly simple:
“For thou art with me.”
That is the heartbeat of the Psalm.
God's presence.
And there is something beautiful hidden in the movement of David's language.
Earlier, David speaks about God.
“He maketh me...”
“He leadeth me...”
“He restoreth my soul...”
“He leadeth me in the paths of righteousness...”
But when David enters the valley, his language becomes intimate.
“Thou art with me.”
Suddenly he is speaking to God.
Sometimes suffering does that.
Sometimes the valley turns theology into prayer.
Sometimes the place you begged God to remove becomes the place where you finally stop merely knowing things about Him and begin crying out directly to Him.
Maybe you know that valley.
The diagnosis.
The betrayal.
The divorce papers.
The child who walked away.
The ministry wound.
The addiction nobody knows you are fighting.
The financial disaster.
The grave you stood beside wishing heaven would give someone back.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The temptation you thought you had defeated.
The shame that keeps whispering:
“You call yourself a Christian after what you did?”
And then Psalm 23 walks into the darkness with you.
Not with shallow optimism.
Not with “everything happens for a reason.”
Not with religious clichés.
With a Shepherd.
“Thou art with me.”
But the story becomes even more breathtaking when we move from David's Psalm to the words of Jesus.
Centuries later, Christ stood before His listeners and said something unmistakable:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
Jesus did not merely teach people how to find the Shepherd.
He identified Himself as the Good Shepherd.
And then He explained what kind of Shepherd He is.
“The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Read that again.
The Shepherd dies...
for the sheep.
That is where Psalm 23 leads us toward the Gospel.
Because our greatest problem was never simply anxiety.
It was never merely loneliness.
It was never merely that life became difficult.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We wandered from God.
Scripture describes humanity like sheep that have gone astray.
We wanted our own direction.
Our own morality.
Our own throne.
Our own definition of good and evil.
We wandered.
And the scandal of grace is that the Shepherd came looking for sinners.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He loved the rejected.
Touched the unclean.
Welcomed repentant sinners.
Confronted hypocrisy.
Called people away from darkness.
And then the Good Shepherd willingly walked toward a Roman cross.
Not because He had lost control.
Not because evil had defeated Him.
But because, as He said, the Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
At Calvary, the Shepherd became the sacrifice.
Think about that.
The One we wandered from came looking for us.
The One we sinned against carried judgment for sinners.
The innocent Christ was crucified.
His hands were pierced.
His blood was shed.
His body was broken.
He died.
And on the third day...
the Shepherd walked out of the grave.
Alive.
Death did not keep Him.
The tomb did not own Him.
Sin did not defeat Him.
And suddenly Psalm 23's final confidence becomes even more magnificent:
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.”
Forever.
The Christian hope is not merely that God will make difficult weeks easier.
Our hope is Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Our Shepherd has walked through death itself.
And He came out the other side.
So when He leads His people through the valley of the shadow of death, He is not leading them somewhere He is afraid to go.
The Shepherd already knows the road.
Maybe now those two words sound different.
My Shepherd.
Because Christianity cannot remain someone else's testimony forever.
Your grandmother's faith cannot save you.
Your pastor's relationship with Christ cannot substitute for yours.
Your parents knowing Jesus cannot reconcile you to God.
Knowing Bible verses cannot replace repentance.
Eventually the question becomes personal.
Is He your Shepherd?
Have you trusted Christ?
Have you surrendered?
Have you repented of your sin and placed your faith in the One who died and rose again?
Or have you simply learned how to stand close enough to Christianity that everyone assumes you belong to the Shepherd while your heart keeps wandering?
That question hurts.
It should.
Grace becomes astonishing only when we stop pretending we never needed rescuing.
David himself would eventually become living evidence of this.
The shepherd became king.
The worshiper became adulterer.
The warrior became a man desperately needing mercy.
David's story contained glory and scandal.
Faith and failure.
Songs and consequences.
There were moments in his life he surely would have erased if history had handed him an eraser.
But his worst chapter did not become his final chapter.
When confronted with his sin, David eventually stopped hiding behind power and confessed.
That is grace.
Not God calling evil good.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God meeting repentant sinners in the wreckage and refusing to let sin write the ending.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs exactly that truth.
Your scandal does not have to be your final sentence.
Your affair does not have to write the ending.
Your addiction does not have to write the ending.
Your pornography does not have to write the ending.
Your anger does not have to write the ending.
Your pride does not have to write the ending.
Your years away from God do not have to write the ending.
Your secret does not have to write the ending.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives those who repent and come to Him.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
Jesus still receives wandering sheep.
This is not permission to remain in sin.
It is an invitation to come home.
Because grace does not simply say,
“You are forgiven. Keep wandering.”
Grace brings the wandering sheep back beneath the Shepherd's care.
Maybe you have spent years trying to shepherd yourself.
You planned everything.
Controlled everything.
Carried everyone.
Fixed everything.
Anticipated every disaster.
Protected yourself from disappointment.
And somewhere along the way you became exhausted.
Perhaps Psalm 23 is inviting you to finally admit something sheep have never been ashamed to admit:
You need a Shepherd.
There is no humiliation in needing Jesus.
The tragedy is spending your entire life pretending you don't.
You do not need to know what happens ten years from now.
You need to know who walks with you today.
You do not need enough strength for every valley you will ever face.
You need the Shepherd.
You do not need to manufacture peace.
You need to follow the Prince of Peace.
And maybe your prayer tonight does not need to be eloquent.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, I have wandered.”
“I have tried to control everything.”
“I have sinned.”
“I have hidden.”
“I have been afraid.”
“I need mercy.”
“Forgive me.”
“Lead me.”
“Be my Shepherd.”
Bring it into the light before Christ.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging what God is stirring privately becomes one small act of refusing to hide anymore.
Someone reading beneath you may discover they are not the only sheep walking through darkness.
There may come a night when you need these words more than you need them today.
And think of one person who has been wandering.
One.
Maybe they stopped going to church.
Maybe disappointment hardened them.
Maybe shame convinced them they could never come home.
Maybe they still smile while quietly falling apart.
Or send this privately.
Somebody may need to remember there is still a Shepherd.

We want this community to remain a place where Scripture is opened, Christ is proclaimed, sin is taken seriously, grace is treasured, wounded believers are encouraged, and wandering hearts are continually pointed home.
Not because financial support purchases spiritual favor.
And certainly not because anyone can buy God's grace.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
But one practical way to glorify God with what He has entrusted to us is to help truthful Gospel ministry reach more people.
Not to prove that you love God.
Not because an algorithm determines your faithfulness.
But because if Christ has given us good news, good news was never meant to die quietly in our hands.
Someone you know may be one share away from reading the words they desperately needed tonight.
And perhaps when they reach the first line of Psalm 23, they will finally notice what you noticed.
Not merely...
“The LORD is Shepherd.”
But:
יְהוָה רֹעִי
YHWH ro‘i.
The LORD is my Shepherd.
“My.”
One tiny word.
One enormous confession.
It means I do not belong to my fear.
I do not belong to my past.
I do not belong to my shame.
I do not belong to the valley.
I do not belong to the voices that told me I could never come home.
If I am in Christ...
I belong to the Shepherd.
And the Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep is alive.
So when the valley gets dark...
keep following.
When you cannot see tomorrow...
keep following.
When shame tells you to run...
run toward Christ instead.
When you fall...
repent and return.
When you hear the Shepherd calling you away from something you love but He calls sin...
trust Him enough to leave it behind.
And when death itself eventually casts its shadow across the path...
remember:
the Shepherd walking beside you has already conquered the grave.
Maybe Psalm 23 was never primarily promising that nothing frightening would happen.
Maybe its comfort is infinitely stronger.
The valley may come.
The enemies may remain.
The night may become darker than you imagined.
But the sheep are not abandoned.
Because the heart of Psalm 23 was never the green pasture.
It was never the still water.
It was never even the overflowing cup.
The treasure was always the Shepherd.
