And after everything you have survived, everything you regret, everything you lost, everything you wish you could rewrite...
there is still a voice calling wandering sheep home.
Your darkest valley does not get the final word when your Shepherd walked out of His grave.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WENT DOWN INTO THE PIT
paragraphs:
HE WENT DOWN INTO THE PIT
The Snow Was Falling. A Lion Was Waiting. And Benaiah Did the Unthinkable.
There are Bible stories you remember because they are famous.
David and Goliath.
Daniel and the lions.
Moses and the Red Sea.
Then there are verses hiding in plain sight that make you stop, read them again, and whisper:
Wait… he did what?
This is one of them.

Buried among the names and exploits of David’s mighty men is a sentence so strange, so violent, so cinematic, and so unexpectedly human that it almost sounds like somebody slipped an action scene into the Old Testament.
But it is there.
Benaiah.
Son of Jehoiada.
A warrior from Kabzeel.
Snow falling.
A pit.
A lion.
And instead of staying safely above it…
he went down.
The King James Version preserves the stark simplicity of the moment:
“And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada… went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow.” — 2 Samuel 23:20
The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 11:22 records the same extraordinary event.
Read those words carefully.
He went down.
The Hebrew behind the phrase is וְהוּא יָרַד — vehu yarad — essentially, “and he went down.”
Not “he accidentally fell.”
Not “he was pushed.”
Not “the lion dragged him in.”
The biblical text tells us that Benaiah went down.

We should also be careful not to make Scripture say more than Scripture actually says. You may have heard this preached as Benaiah “chasing” the lion into the pit or “jumping” after it. Those images are dramatic, but the Hebrew text itself simply tells us that he went down and struck the lion in the pit.
And somehow…
that makes the story even more haunting.
Because Scripture does not tell us what Benaiah was thinking.
It does not tell us why the lion was there.
It does not tell us whether Benaiah was terrified.
It does not describe the fight.
It gives us something far more unforgettable:
a man went down…
and came back out.
Maybe that is why this strange little verse has survived in the imagination of believers for generations.
Because sooner or later, everybody discovers a pit.
Maybe yours does not have snow around it.
Maybe yours does not have claws.
But you know what it feels like to stand at the edge of something you desperately wish God would remove.
The diagnosis you never expected.
The marriage that became painfully cold.
The temptation you promised Jesus you would never return to.
The secret browser history.
The addiction nobody at church knows about.
The child who stopped answering your calls.
The betrayal that changed the way you trust people.
The bills sitting unopened because looking at them makes your chest tighten.
The grief that waits until everybody goes home.
The ministry wound you smile through on Sunday.
The private shame underneath your public worship.
The night you whispered, “God, I don't know how much longer I can do this.”
We want Christianity to mean that lions disappear.
Sometimes they don't.
We want obedience to guarantee warm weather.
Sometimes snow falls.
We want faithfulness to mean there will never be pits.
Sometimes the road God permits us to walk passes directly beside one.
And this is where we must resist turning Benaiah into a motivational poster.
Because the Bible is not ultimately a book about discovering the warrior inside yourself.
It is the story of the God who saves sinners who cannot save themselves.
Benaiah's courage is real.
His exploit is extraordinary.
But Benaiah is not Jesus.
And neither are you.
That matters.
Because if you read this story merely as “be fearless like Benaiah,” eventually life will give you a lion bigger than your courage.
Eventually your strength runs out.
Eventually your hands shake.
Eventually there is something you cannot defeat.
Eventually every human being reaches the enemy no warrior can overcome by determination:
death.
And that is where the Gospel becomes infinitely greater than motivational Christianity.
Jesus did not come merely to teach frightened people how to become braver.
He came to rescue the guilty.
He came for sinners.
He came for rebels.
He came for hypocrites.
He came for people carrying histories they wish they could rewrite.
He came for people who have failed after promising God they would change.
He came for the ashamed.
The sexually broken.
The bitter.
The addicted.
The religious.
The self-righteous.
The exhausted.
The prodigal.
The person reading this right now who knows there is something underneath the surface that almost nobody knows.
Christ did not stand safely above our ruin shouting instructions.
He came down.
That is the greater descent.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He entered our suffering.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He ate with the despised.
He welcomed the broken.
And then He walked toward something infinitely darker than Benaiah's pit.
The cross.
Jesus knew what waited there.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Blood.
Nails.
Judgment.
Death.
And He went willingly.
Not because humanity deserved rescue.
Because grace moved toward people who could never rescue themselves.
At Calvary, Jesus bore sin.
Not His sin.
Ours.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant who would be “wounded for our transgressions.”
The apostle Peter would later write that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree.”
Paul would announce the scandalous exchange of the Gospel: the One who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
That is Christianity.
Not:
“Become strong enough and God will accept you.”
But:
Christ was strong where you were helpless.
Christ was righteous where you were guilty.
Christ paid what you could never pay.
Christ entered death…
and death could not keep Him.
The stone was rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly Benaiah walking out of a pit after facing a lion becomes a small earthly echo of something infinitely greater.
Because Jesus entered the grave itself…
and came out victorious.
Yet even here we must keep the biblical picture clear.
Benaiah's lion is not presented in 2 Samuel as a direct prophecy of Satan, nor does Scripture tell us that the pit symbolizes hell or that the snow carries some secret prophetic code.
We do not need to manufacture symbolism to make this passage powerful.
The history is powerful enough.
A real man faced a real danger on a real snowy day.
And within the larger story of Scripture, his courage reminds us that God's servants sometimes encounter terrifying circumstances rather than comfortable ones.
Faith is not pretending the lion isn't dangerous.
Faith is trusting God when danger is real.
Some of you have misunderstood courage because you thought courage meant you stopped feeling afraid.
It doesn't.
Sometimes courage is trembling while obeying.
Sometimes courage is praying while crying.
Sometimes courage is deleting the number.
Sometimes courage is finally confessing what you have hidden.
Sometimes courage is admitting, “I need help.”
Sometimes courage is opening your Bible again after months of spiritual numbness.
Sometimes courage is forgiving someone without pretending what they did was acceptable.
Sometimes courage is walking away from the relationship that keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Sometimes courage is returning to church after shame convinced you everybody would judge you.
Sometimes courage sounds less like a battle cry and more like:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And perhaps that is the sentence someone needed today.
You do not have to impress Jesus with your strength.
You need to surrender to His.
Because some lions cannot be conquered by trying harder.
Sin cannot be forgiven by trying harder.
Guilt cannot be erased by trying harder.
Eternal life cannot be earned by trying harder.
You need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe your greatest pit is not what happened to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
That changes the emotional weight of everything, doesn't it?
It is easier to talk about wounds than sins.
Easier to say, “I was hurt,” than:
“I lied.”
“I cheated.”
“I betrayed somebody.”
“I became bitter.”
“I watched things I should never have watched.”
“I abandoned someone who needed me.”
“I let pride destroy something beautiful.”
“I knew what God said and did the opposite.”
“I have been pretending.”
That is where the Gospel becomes scandalously beautiful.
Because Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending your past never happened.
Grace does something far more costly.
Christ meets you in the truth of what happened…
and offers forgiveness purchased with His blood.
Repentance is not pretending.
Repentance is turning.
The Greek New Testament commonly expresses repentance with the word μετάνοια — metanoia — carrying the idea of a changed mind that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Repentance turns toward God.
It stops defending darkness.
It stops negotiating with sin.
It stops calling chains freedom.
It comes into the light.
And the breathtaking promise of the Gospel is that the person who comes to Christ in repentance and faith does not meet a reluctant Savior.
Jesus said:
“him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37
Read that again if shame has been preaching to you.
I will in no wise cast out.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
It does not have authority to write the ending when Christ takes hold of your life.
Ask David.
The king whose mighty men included Benaiah was himself a complicated man.
David knew victory.
David also knew catastrophic moral failure.
Adultery.
Deception.
Bloodshed.
Consequences that tore through his household.
Scripture does not sanitize him.
That matters.
The Bible's heroes are not airbrushed.
Their sins are exposed because God's grace does not depend upon pretending human beings are better than they are.
When confronted, David eventually stopped hiding.
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a shattered man:
“Have mercy upon me, O God.”
That is where restoration begins.
Not reputation management.
Not excuses.
Mercy.
David's story did not teach that sin has no consequences. It had devastating consequences.
Grace is not permission to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy toward sinners that transforms those who receive it.
And this is why our message remains:
Not because Jesus edits history.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because Christians become perfect overnight.
Jesus rewrites everything because the sinner's identity, standing before God, direction, hope, and eternal future can be transformed through union with Christ.
Condemned becomes forgiven.
Lost becomes found.
Enemy becomes child.
Dead in sin becomes alive in Christ.
Ashamed becomes covered by grace.
Slave becomes free.
And sometimes the person who thought the pit would become his grave discovers that God was not finished with his story.
Benaiah survived that snowy pit.
But his story did not end there.

Scripture later shows him entrusted with significant responsibility. David placed Benaiah over his guard, and in the turbulent transition after David's reign, Benaiah remained aligned with Solomon and eventually became commander of the army.
The man remembered for going down into a pit eventually stood in places of tremendous responsibility.
Do not turn that into a prosperity formula.
The Bible never promises that facing your lion guarantees a promotion.
But it does remind us that one terrible season does not necessarily contain the final sentence of your life.
Your snowy day is not necessarily your last day.
Your pit is not necessarily your grave.
Your failure is not greater than Christ's mercy.
Your temptation is not permission to surrender.
Your wounds do not give darkness ownership of you.
And if you belong to Jesus, your story is moving toward something far greater than earthly success.
Resurrection.
There is coming a day when every believer in Christ will discover that the final lion has lost its teeth.
Death itself will die.
The grave will not keep God's children.
Christ will make all things new.
So maybe today you are standing above something frightening.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you're doing fine.
You smiled this morning.
Answered messages.
Went to work.
Posted something funny.
Said, “I'm okay.”
But your soul knows better.
There is a pit nearby.
And something inside it has been roaring for months.
Listen carefully.
You do not need to prove you are Benaiah.
You need Jesus.
You need the One who already entered the darkness you could never conquer and walked out of the tomb alive.
If there is hidden sin, confess it.
If there is bitterness, surrender it.
If there is someone you need to forgive, begin bringing that wound honestly before Christ.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, stop imagining that becoming “better” will eventually make you worthy.
You cannot clean yourself enough to need no Savior.
Come as a sinner.
Come believing.
Come repentant.
Come empty-handed.
Christ is enough.
Be honest.
There are moments when another believer needs to see that they are not the only person fighting quietly.
Your honesty may become someone else's permission to stop pretending.
Not to embarrass them.
Not because you know their secrets.
Because perhaps they need to remember that the pit is not necessarily the end of the story.
Not as a religious performance.
Someone may need the Gospel while everyone else is sending them entertainment.
Someone may need to hear that Jesus still receives sinners.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is still possible.
Someone may need to hear that grace is still available.
Someone may need to hear that Christ is still alive.
Salvation cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased.

If you want to glorify God through supporting this ministry, do it freely and cheerfully, not under compulsion. Scripture says, “whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should never be done “grudgingly, or of necessity.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Stay close to truth.
Stay hungry for Scripture.
Stay near believers who keep pointing you back to Jesus.
But before you leave, remember the image.
Snow falling.
A dark opening in the earth.
A lion below.
A man going down.
Thousands of years later, we still know his name.
Not because the day was easy.
Because he went down into the place most people would have spent their lives avoiding.
Yet there is a greater name than Benaiah.
A greater descent.
A greater enemy defeated.
A greater victory.
Jesus Christ entered our darkness.
He carried our sin.
He tasted death.
And He walked out of the grave.
So when your past tells you the story is finished…
when shame tells you to hide…
when temptation tells you surrender is inevitable…
when grief tells you morning will never come…
when the pit looks deeper than your faith…
look again at the empty tomb.
Because sometimes the place you were certain would become the grave of your story becomes the place where you discover that Jesus already holds the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: TAMAR’S DESPERATE DISGUISE: Why a Widow Risked Everything to Expose Judah
paragraphs: TAMAR’S DESPERATE DISGUISE: Why a Widow Risked Everything to Expose Judah

She dressed like a prostitute, became pregnant by her father-in-law, and was nearly condemned to death. But buried inside one of Genesis’ most scandalous stories is a terrifying confrontation with hypocrisy—and a bloodline that eventually leads straight to Jesus Christ.
There are Bible stories we like to put on children’s walls.
Noah and the rainbow.
David and Goliath.
Daniel surrounded by lions.
And then there is Genesis 38.
Nobody is painting this one above the nursery crib.

A twice-widowed woman changes her clothes, covers her face, waits beside a road, allows her father-in-law to mistake her for a prostitute, becomes pregnant by him, keeps his personal belongings as evidence, and months later finds herself facing his judgment.
Then she produces the evidence.
And with one sentence, Judah’s entire moral courtroom collapses.
But if you read Tamar’s story merely as ancient sexual scandal, you will miss what Scripture is doing.
Because Tamar’s disguise is not the greatest exposure in Genesis 38.
Judah is.
And somewhere inside his exposure, we may discover our own.
Tamar first entered Judah’s household as the wife of his firstborn son, Er. Genesis gives us a brutally short assessment of him: Er was wicked before the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.
Tamar became a widow.

Then Judah instructed his second son, Onan, to fulfill his familial obligation toward Tamar so that offspring might be raised for his dead brother. Onan, however, knew the offspring would not be reckoned as his own, and deliberately frustrated that responsibility. Scripture again tells us that what he did was evil in the LORD’s sight, and he also died.
Now Tamar had buried two husbands.
Imagine the silence after the second funeral.
Imagine being the woman people begin whispering about.
Imagine wondering whether every room becomes uncomfortable when you enter it.
Judah had one remaining son: Shelah.
He told Tamar to remain a widow in her father’s house until Shelah grew up.
So she waited.
And waited.
And waited.
Genesis eventually reveals the painful truth.
Shelah grew up.
Tamar was still not given to him.
The text itself gives the reason for her later action: she saw that Shelah had grown, yet she had not been given to him.
This matters.

The later law in Deuteronomy 25:5–10 describes what is commonly called levirate marriage: when a man died without an heir, his brother had a responsibility connected with preserving the deceased brother’s family line. Genesis 38 predates that later Mosaic formulation, and Tamar’s circumstances are not identical to the legal procedure later stated in Deuteronomy. Still, the stories clearly share the ancient concern for offspring, family continuity, and the vulnerable position of a childless widow.
Tamar had been promised a future inside Judah’s family.
That future was being withheld.
She was waiting for a promise Judah apparently had no intention of keeping.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because desperation can grow in the soil of somebody else’s broken promise.
Some people reading this know that feeling.
You did what you were told.
You waited.
You trusted.
You stayed quiet.
And eventually you realized the person who told you to wait had moved on with life while you remained trapped inside the consequences.
Genesis does not ask us to imitate every action Tamar takes. Narrative description is not automatically moral prescription.
But neither does Scripture allow Judah to hide behind Tamar’s shocking method.
That distinction is crucial.
Then Judah’s wife died.
After his mourning period, Judah traveled toward Timnah, where his sheep were being sheared.
Tamar heard about it.
And she made a decision that would change the history of her family.
She removed her widow’s clothing.
Covered herself with a veil.
Wrapped herself.
And sat along Judah’s route.
Judah saw her.
But Judah did not recognize her.
Genesis says he assumed she was a prostitute because her face was covered.
Think about that scene.
The man who had effectively left Tamar waiting in widowhood was walking directly toward the woman whose future he had withheld...
and he could not recognize her.
There are moments in Scripture when physical blindness becomes an uncomfortable picture of moral blindness.
Judah could see a woman he desired.
He could not see the woman he had wronged.
He approached her.
A negotiation followed.
He offered a young goat as payment.
Tamar asked for security until the payment arrived.
Judah asked what pledge she wanted.
Her answer was astonishingly specific.
The Hebrew of Genesis 38:18 reads:
חֹתָמְךָ וּפְתִילֶךָ וּמַטְּךָ אֲשֶׁר בְּיָדֶךָ
ḥotamkha u-fetilekha u-matkha asher beyadekha.
In straightforward English:
“Your seal, your cord, and your staff that is in your hand.”
Not random objects.
Personal objects.
Identifying objects.
The seal in particular functioned as an instrument of identity and authority. Tamar was not simply taking collateral with monetary value.
She was preserving evidence.
Judah handed them over.
The encounter occurred.
Tamar conceived.
Then she disappeared.
Judah later sent the promised goat through his friend to recover his pledge.
But the mysterious woman could not be found.
Eventually Judah essentially decided to let the matter disappear rather than risk public embarrassment.
And there is a frighteningly recognizable human instinct buried there.
Let it disappear.
Nobody needs to know.
Protect the reputation.
Move forward.
Forget the night.
Forget the compromise.
Forget what was handed over in the darkness.
But sin has an uncomfortable habit of leaving fingerprints.
About three months later, news reached Judah.
Tamar was pregnant.
Suddenly Judah became very interested in morality.
Read that again.
The man who had recently solicited the woman he believed to be a prostitute now heard that his widowed daughter-in-law was pregnant through sexual immorality...
and he erupted in judgment.
Genesis records his words with terrifying brevity:
“Bring her out, and let her be burned.”
There it is.
One of the ugliest tendencies of the human heart.
Mercy for me.
Judgment for you.
Context for my failure.
Condemnation for yours.
Excuses when my darkness is exposed.
Righteous outrage when yours becomes visible.
How quickly we become prosecutors when somebody else’s sin distracts everyone from our own.
We can condemn publicly what we secretly tolerate privately.
We can post Scripture while hiding compromise.
We can sing worship songs while refusing repentance.
We can know exactly what another person should have done differently while avoiding the question God is asking us:
What about you?
Tamar was being brought out.
Picture the moment.
People staring.
Whispers spreading.
Judah standing in judgment.
Tamar carrying Judah’s children inside her while Judah participates in condemning the woman carrying them.
And then Tamar sends something to him.
A seal.
A cord.
A staff.
No screaming defense is recorded.
No long accusation.
No public speech exposing every detail.
Just evidence.
Then came the sentence.
In Hebrew:
הַכֶּר־נָא לְמִי הַחֹתֶמֶת וְהַפְּתִילִים וְהַמַּטֶּה הָאֵלֶּה
Hakker-na lemi haḥotemet vehapetilim vehammatteh ha’elleh.
Essentially:
“Recognize, please, whose these are—the seal, the cords, and the staff.”
Recognize them, Judah.
Look carefully.
You wanted judgment?
Start here.
You wanted evidence?
Hold it.
You wanted somebody’s sin exposed?
Look at what belongs to you.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most important sentences in Judah’s life.
וַיַּכֵּר יְהוּדָה
Vayyaker Yehudah.
“Judah recognized them.”
He recognized more than three objects.
He recognized himself.
Then Judah said:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tzadqah mimmeni.
The expression can be rendered:
“She is more righteous than I.”
And Judah immediately explains why:
because he had not given Tamar to his son Shelah.
This does not transform every choice in the story into a command for believers to imitate.
It does something much more devastating.
It makes Judah stop looking at Tamar long enough to tell the truth about Judah.
That is repentance’s doorway.
Not “Look what they did.”
Not “You don't understand what happened to me.”
Not “Everybody does it.”
Not “At least I'm not as bad as them.”
Not “God knows my heart.”
But:
I was wrong.
Some of us have spent years asking Jesus to expose everyone except us.
We want Him to expose the person who betrayed us.
Expose the hypocrite.
Expose the corrupt leader.
Expose the cheating spouse.
Expose the fake Christian.
Expose the liar.
Expose the person who wounded us.
And sometimes truth absolutely must come into the light.
But what happens when Christ turns the light toward us?
What happens when the seal is ours?
The cord is ours?
The staff is ours?
The browser history is ours.
The secret messages are ours.
The bitterness is ours.
The hidden relationship is ours.
The pride is ours.
The unforgiveness is ours.
The hypocrisy is ours.
The compromise is ours.
The thing we hoped nobody would ever connect back to us...
is ours.
That is where this story stops being about an ancient widow beside a road.
Now it is about you and me.
Because the Gospel does not begin with pretending we have no evidence against us.
The Gospel begins with truth.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23 does not leave a special category for respectable sinners.
Neither religious activity nor public reputation can erase guilt before a holy God.
We do not need better disguises.
We need a Savior.
And this is where Tamar’s scandal becomes something breathtaking.
Tamar gave birth to twins: Perez and Zerah.
Perez’s name continued through Israel’s history.
Through generations.
Through failures.
Through kings.
Through exile.
Until centuries later, the Gospel of Matthew begins introducing Jesus Christ.
And Matthew does something remarkable.
He names Tamar.
The Greek of Matthew 1:3 reads:
Ἰούδας δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Φαρὲς καὶ τὸν Ζαρὰ ἐκ τῆς Θάμαρ
Ioudas de egennēsen ton Phares kai ton Zara ek tēs Thamar.
Judah fathered Perez and Zerah through Tamar.
There she is.
Matthew did not airbrush her out.
God did not need a sanitized family tree before sending the spotless Savior.
Do not misunderstand that.
The holiness of Jesus does not come from approving the sins, failures, injustices, or brokenness found among His human ancestors.
Christ is sinless.
The wonder is different.
God’s redemptive purpose was not defeated by human wreckage.
The Messiah entered a human family history containing scandal, grief, outsiders, moral collapse, broken people, and complicated stories.
Jesus did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
Jesus came because humanity could not save itself.
That is Christianity.
Not bad people pretending to be good.
Not religious people curating spotless reputations.
Not sinners learning how to hide the evidence.
It is guilty people meeting a holy Savior who died for sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did not disguise the seriousness of sin.
He bore its judgment.
He did not call darkness light.
He entered our darkness.
He did not tell us repentance was unnecessary.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
He does not merely improve our reputation.
He gives new life.
That is grace.
Grace is not God saying your sin did not matter.
Grace is God showing how much it mattered at Calvary—and how immeasurably He loved sinners when Christ gave Himself to save them.
Maybe your life has a chapter you wish could be removed from the genealogy.
Maybe your family carries a scandal nobody discusses.
Maybe you have been Tamar—forgotten, vulnerable, waiting for somebody to keep a promise.
Maybe you have been Judah—quick to recognize another person’s failure and painfully slow to recognize your own.
Maybe you have been both wounded and sinful.
Many of us have.
The Gospel has room for the entire truth.
You do not have to lie about what happened to you.
And you do not have to lie about what you have done.
Bring both to Jesus.
Because repentance is not God destroying the repentant sinner.
Repentance is surrendering the disguise.
It is finally saying:
“Jesus, this belongs to me.”
My pride.
My lust.
My deception.
My bitterness.
My secret.
My rebellion.
My sin.
No more blaming.
No more hiding.
No more religious costume.
No more pretending.
And the astonishing message of the Gospel is that the One before whom nothing is hidden is also the One who came to save.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
It was purchased by Christ.
That distinction matters.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to cancel your sin.
Salvation is the gift of God received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And when grace truly takes hold of someone, it does not leave that person untouched.
Grace produces gratitude.
Grace creates generosity.
Grace makes us want other people to hear the truth that rescued us.
Bring it to Christ.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores broken lives.
And think of one person who needs this story.
Not fifty strangers.
One person.
The friend hiding behind a smile.
The believer quietly drifting.
The family member convinced their past has disqualified them.
The person who thinks church is only for people with clean histories.
Save it too.
There may come a night when your own past starts whispering that God could never use someone with your history.
Come back and remember Tamar.
Come back and remember Judah.
Most of all, come back and remember Jesus.
God is glorified when Christ is treasured, His truth is proclaimed, believers serve faithfully, and the Gospel reaches people.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous.
Only Christ saves.
Share because somebody in your circle may be hiding behind a disguise right now.
Somebody may think their scandal is stronger than God's grace.
Somebody may believe their family history has already written the ending.
Somebody may be one Gospel encounter away from finally whispering:
“Jesus... I’m done hiding.”
Tamar walked into Genesis 38 wearing a disguise.
Judah walked through it wearing another kind of disguise—the disguise of a man who could identify sin everywhere except in himself.
But eventually the evidence was placed in his hands.
Recognize these.
And he did.
Perhaps that is the question following us out of this story.
What would happen if Jesus placed the evidence before us tonight?
Would we defend ourselves?
Condemn somebody else?
Hide again?
Or finally say:
“It is mine.”
Because the moment the disguise falls is not necessarily the moment your story ends.
In Christ, it may become the moment truth finally begins.
Tamar’s name survived the scandal.
Perez entered the lineage.
Matthew wrote her name.
And generations later came Jesus Christ—the sinless Son of God, not contaminated by the broken history into which He entered, but mighty enough to redeem sinners from theirs.
Your scandal does not become holy because God can redeem you.
Your sin does not become good because grace exists.
But your sin does not have to have the final word either.
Jesus does.
And when Jesus becomes the Author of what comes next, even the chapter you wanted torn from the book can become the place where people discover just how far His grace can reach.
The evidence may tell the truth about where you have been—but the scars in the hands of Jesus tell you who paid to give repentant sinners a new ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A CAPTIVE WOMAN WAS GIVEN TIME TO MOURN BEFORE MARRIAGE—Then the Law Forbade Selling Her
paragraphs: A CAPTIVE WOMAN WAS GIVEN TIME TO MOURN BEFORE MARRIAGE—Then the Law Forbade Selling Her

Deuteronomy 21 contains one of the Bible’s most uncomfortable laws. Read slowly, however, and something startling emerges: in a world of war, captivity, male power, and human desire, God placed restraints on the powerful man—and made him stop long enough for the powerless woman to grieve.
She had just lost her world.
Perhaps her father was dead.
Perhaps her mother was dead.
Perhaps they were alive somewhere she could never return to.
The text does not tell us.
And we should not romanticize what it does tell us.
She was a captive.
Not a woman strolling peacefully toward a wedding. Not the heroine of an ancient love story. Not someone Scripture describes as meeting an Israelite soldier and falling helplessly in love.
She was among the defeated.
He was among the victors.
He had military power.
She was extraordinarily vulnerable.
And that is precisely why this passage deserves to be read carefully rather than avoided, sanitized, or weaponized.
Because in Deuteronomy 21:10–14, the Torah looks directly into an ugly reality of the ancient world and begins placing boundaries around the man who possesses the power.
Listen to the Hebrew:
וְרָאִיתָ בַּשִּׁבְיָה אֵשֶׁת יְפַת־תֹּאַר וְחָשַׁקְתָּ בָהּ
Vera’ita bashivyah eshet yefat-to’ar, vechashaqta vah...
“You see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire her...”
The Bible does not pretend the desire is not there.
But neither does desire receive unlimited authority.
That distinction matters.
Especially now.
Because we live in a culture that has repeatedly taught human beings that wanting something is nearly synonymous with having a right to it.
“I want it.”
“I feel it.”
“I desire it.”
“I deserve it.”
But Scripture repeatedly confronts that logic.
Desire is real.
Desire can be powerful.
Desire can even feel overwhelming.
But desire is not God.
And here, in one of Scripture’s hardest passages, a victorious soldier encounters something between his desire and immediate gratification:
a command to wait.

He must bring the woman into his house. The passage describes the cutting or shaving of her hair, the treatment of her nails, and the removal of the clothing of her captivity. Interpreters have debated the precise significance of some of these actions, so we should resist pretending the text tells us more than it actually does.
But then comes something unmistakable.
וּבָכְתָה אֶת־אָבִיהָ וְאֶת־אִמָּהּ יֶרַח יָמִים
Uvakh’tah et-aviha ve’et-immah, yerach yamim.
“She shall mourn her father and her mother a month of days.”
A month.
Before the marriage described in the passage proceeds, her grief is given time.
Think about that.
The soldier sees beauty.
God's law makes room for mourning.
The soldier feels desire.
The law inserts delay.
The soldier has power.
The law gives him boundaries.
And the woman?
She cries.
For her father.
For her mother.
For an entire month.
Do not rush past those tears.
They may be the most human part of the passage.

We are not told what she said while she mourned. We are not given her private thoughts. We do not know whether every tear was for people she had lost, a homeland she might never see again, the terror of captivity, or all of it together.
So we should not invent her story.
But Scripture refuses to erase her grief.
That alone should confront something inside us.
Because human beings are remarkably good at seeing someone else's usefulness while overlooking their wounds.
We see the employee and forget the exhausted mother.
We see the attractive body and forget the soul.
We see the person who can help our plans and forget that they may be carrying a funeral inside them.
We see what we want.
God sees the mourner.
And then Deuteronomy says something even more arresting.
If the relationship later collapses—if the man no longer desires her—he does not get to turn yesterday's wife into tomorrow's merchandise.
The Hebrew becomes forceful:
וְשִׁלַּחְתָּהּ לְנַפְשָׁהּ וּמָכֹר לֹא־תִמְכְּרֶנָּה בַּכָּסֶף
Veshillachtah lenafshah, umakhor lo-timkerennah bakasef.
He must let her go.
And:
“You shall certainly not sell her for money.”
Then comes another prohibition:
לֹא־תִתְעַמֵּר בָּהּ
Lo tit’ammer bah.
She is not to be treated as merchandise or exploited as a slave.
Why?
The verse ends with difficult words:
תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר עִנִּיתָהּ
Tachat asher innitah.
Translations vary in how they render the force of עִנִּיתָהּ — innitah, a form of the Hebrew root ענה, which in this context carries the painful sense of having humbled, afflicted, or mistreated her.
That language matters.
The text does not simply tell the powerful man, “You changed your mind, so recover your investment.”
No.
She is not inventory.
She is not livestock.
She is not an unwanted object to be resold.
Whatever else we wrestle with in this ancient law—and there is much here that should make a modern reader uncomfortable—the restriction is unmistakable:
You may not sell her.
And that should stop us from making a shallow argument such as, “See? This passage is basically modern marriage.”
It isn't.
The power imbalance is severe. The woman is a war captive. The text does not explicitly narrate her consent. We should not manufacture consent where Scripture does not describe it.
Nor should we make the opposite mistake and pretend the restrictions in the law are meaningless.
We need enough courage to hold both realities at once.
This is an ancient wartime law addressing circumstances far removed from ordinary modern courtship.
And within those circumstances, the man's power is not allowed to remain absolute.
His desire is delayed.
Her mourning is recognized.
Marriage creates obligations.
And rejection does not grant him the right to sell her.
That does not make the situation beautiful.
It makes the restraint significant precisely because the situation is so broken.
Sometimes biblical law meets humanity not in Eden as it ought to be, but in the wreckage of the world as human sin has made it.

Jesus Himself gives us an important category for understanding laws operating within human hardness when, speaking about divorce, He explains that Moses permitted something “because of your hardness of heart,” while pointing His hearers back toward God's creational intention (Matthew 19:8).
That does not mean we can casually label every difficult Old Testament command a concession and walk away.
It means Scripture itself teaches us to distinguish between God's holy character, God's creational purposes, and laws regulating human life in a fallen world.
And suddenly Deuteronomy 21 becomes painfully personal.
Because you may never stand on an ancient battlefield.
You may never encounter this particular legal situation.
But you know what it means to live in a world where power can consume weakness.
Maybe you know what it is to be wanted for what someone could get from you.
Then discarded.
Maybe somebody loved your appearance but never learned your heart.
Maybe they wanted your body but had no patience for your wounds.
Maybe they loved what you provided.
Your loyalty.
Your money.
Your attention.
Your usefulness.
Your influence.
Your affection.
Your availability.
Until you stopped being convenient.
Then you discovered something devastating:
They didn't know how to love a person they could no longer use.
And perhaps that is why these ancient words hurt.
“You shall not sell her.”
Thousands of years later, the human heart still needs to hear the principle underneath that prohibition:
People are not merchandise.
People are not disposable.
People are not products whose worth expires when our desire changes.
And before we point at everyone who used us, perhaps Scripture asks us an even harder question.
Whom have we used?
Who became valuable to us because they could give us something?
Who became invisible when they couldn't?
Who have we reduced to a body?
A paycheck?
A connection?
A follower?
A customer?
A spouse who exists merely to satisfy us?
A church member who exists merely to serve our ministry?
A child who exists merely to make us proud?
A friend we contact only when we need something?
The Gospel does not merely expose the people who wounded us.
It exposes us.
That is where Christianity becomes dangerous to our pride.
Because Jesus did not come merely to confirm that everyone else is guilty.
He came announcing:

“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
—Matthew 4:17
Repentance means I stop using somebody else's sin as camouflage for mine.
It means I stop asking only, “Who hurt me?”
and begin asking,
“Lord, whom have I hurt?”
“Whom have I objectified?”
“Whom have I manipulated?”
“Whose tears did I ignore because my desires mattered more?”
“Where have I confused wanting with entitlement?”
“Where have I treated someone made in God's image as though they existed for me?”
That question can break you.
But if it breaks you at the feet of Jesus, it can also become the beginning of healing.
Because the Christian message does not end with exposure.
It ends at a cross.
And the cross changes everything.
Jesus Christ does not meet sinners merely with accusation. He calls us to repentance and offers forgiveness purchased at terrible cost.
Peter writes:
—1 Peter 2:24
Paul says:

“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
That is scandalous grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that pretends wounds never happened.
Not grace that gives predators permission to continue predation.
Not grace without repentance.
But grace that walks directly into the wreckage of human sin and declares that the sinner who turns to Christ does not have to remain what sin made him.
The exploiter can repent.
The objectifier can repent.
The selfish can repent.
The sexually broken can repent.
The person drowning in shame can repent.
The wounded can come to Christ.
The guilty can come to Christ.
The discarded can come to Christ.
The person who caused the damage can come to Christ.
And none of us comes because we have earned the right.
We come because Jesus died and rose again.
That is why the Gospel is not merely “be a better person.”
If human beings could rescue themselves through moral improvement, Calvary would be unnecessary.
The Gospel says something far more devastating and far more beautiful:
You are sinful enough that Christ had to die.
You are loved enough that Christ willingly did.
And if you belong to Him, your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not because scandal becomes harmless.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because victims owe abusers access to them.
Not because repentance is a magic phrase that erases justice.
But because Jesus Christ can take a human being imprisoned by sin and create something genuinely new.

“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
—2 Corinthians 5:17
Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps you are reading this carrying another kind of captivity.
You are not chained to an ancient conqueror.
But you are chained to pornography.
Bitterness.
Secret lust.
Adultery.
Approval.
Pride.
Resentment.
Shame.
The memory of what somebody did to you.
Or the memory of what you did to somebody else.
You smile in photographs.
You say “God bless.”
You attend church.
You know the worship songs.
But there is a locked room inside your soul that you hope Jesus never opens.
He already knows what is inside.
And He is still calling you.
Not to hide it better.
To bring it into the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write the details publicly.
And if Christ has already been rebuilding something people thought was permanently destroyed, leave a testimony:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Someone scrolling beneath your comment may desperately need proof that another Christian is fighting the same battle.
Someone may realize they are not the only one crying behind a smiling profile picture.
Someone may decide tonight to stop hiding.
And someone may finally pray:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That matters more than algorithms.
That is a soul.
And souls matter to God.
Come back when shame tries to convince you that grace is only for cleaner people.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Grace is grace.

But if this ministry is helping you know Scripture, confront sin, understand difficult passages, heal through biblical truth, and keep your eyes fixed on Christ, then supporting it is one practical way you can help this work reach another person.

If you want to glorify God through what you share online, let your support flow from gratitude rather than guilt. Help put Christ-centered truth where despair, temptation, confusion, shallow teaching, and spiritual loneliness are already reaching people every day.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer who is barely holding on.
Invite the person wrestling with doubt.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who knows something needs to change.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say to broken people.
But before you leave, go back to that unnamed woman in Deuteronomy.
We never learn her name.
We never hear her voice quoted.
We do not know what became of her.
But Scripture preserved the command that her powerful captor could not simply turn her into merchandise when he no longer wanted her.
Her grief mattered enough to be written into the law.
Her humanity mattered enough for boundaries to be placed around male power.
And her story still forces us to ask whether we see people as people—or merely as answers to our appetites.
Then the Gospel forces us to go deeper.
Because at the cross, Jesus does not merely expose what humanity does when desire becomes its god.
He bears sin.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives the undeserving.
He receives the ashamed.
He transforms those who surrender to Him.
And He teaches His people to look at human beings differently.
Not as bodies to consume.
Not as tools to exploit.
Not as possessions to control.
Not as merchandise to discard.
But as human beings who stand beneath the gaze of God.
So be honest before Christ tonight.
What owns you?
What desire have you been obeying?
Whose tears have you ignored?
Who have you treated as disposable?
What secret are you protecting from the light?
And what would happen if, instead of defending yourself one more time, you finally whispered:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That prayer has been spoken by sinners for generations.
And Jesus is still saving sinners.
And comment—not for performance, but with whatever honest words your heart can actually say:
“Jesus, rewrite my story.”
Because maybe the most frightening prison was never the one other people built around you.
Maybe it was the one sin built inside you.
And maybe the door you thought would never open already has a cross-shaped key.
Your worst chapter may explain some of your scars—but when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your story, your scars do not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THREE WARRIORS BROKE THROUGH AN ENEMY ARMY JUST TO BRING DAVID A DRINK OF WATER
paragraphs:
THREE WARRIORS BROKE THROUGH AN ENEMY ARMY JUST TO BRING DAVID A DRINK OF WATER
David asked for water. Three men risked their lives to bring it to him. Then he did something with that water nobody expected—and hidden inside that moment is a picture of worship that may expose what we have been calling “sacrifice.”
There was an enemy army between David and a drink of water.
Read that again.
Not between David and a throne.
Not between David and a chest of gold.
Not between David and some military secret that could change the war.
Water.
Just water.
And before this story is finished, three warriors will put their lives on the line to retrieve it, David will hold the water they nearly died to obtain...
and then pour every drop onto the ground.
If you had been one of those three men, what would you have felt watching it fall?
Because until you understand why David poured it out, this story can look almost wasteful.
Once you understand it, however, it becomes one of the most breathtaking pictures of costly devotion in the Old Testament.
And then it becomes uncomfortable.
Because eventually this story stops asking what David did with the water.
It starts asking what you are doing with your life.
The scene is recorded in 2 Samuel 23:13–17.

David is in a stronghold. The Philistines have established themselves in Bethlehem. The enemy occupies the place connected to David's childhood memories, and somewhere inside that occupied territory is a well near Bethlehem's gate.
Then David remembers the water.
Scripture says:
"וַיִּתְאַוֶּה דָוִד"
Vayyit'avveh David.
David longed.
David desired.
David yearned.
And out of that longing came a sentence:
“Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem which is by the gate!”
It sounds almost ordinary.
Perhaps David was remembering home.
Perhaps his mind traveled backward to younger days in Bethlehem—the shepherd boy before the crown, before national responsibility, before so many battles.
Scripture does not tell us everything moving through David's mind, so we should resist inventing details God did not give us.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
David longed for that water.
And three warriors heard him.
David does not appear in the passage to issue them a military command.
There is no recorded promise of money.
No promotion.
No medal.
No applause.
No bargain.
They heard the longing of their leader...
and moved.
Then Scripture gives us an extraordinary Hebrew expression:
"וַיִּבְקְעוּ שְׁלֹשֶׁת הַגִּבֹּרִים"
Vayyivqe'u sheloshet haggibborim.
“The three mighty men broke through.”
The word gibborim describes mighty men, warriors, men of valor.
And these three men went straight through the Philistine position.
Imagine the insanity of the mission from a purely practical perspective.
Three men.
Enemy territory.
For water.
They break through.
They reach Bethlehem.
They approach the well near the gate.
They draw the water.
But now remember something.
Getting into Bethlehem was only half the journey.
They still had to bring the water back.
That detail changes the picture.
They were not simply fighting their way toward something.
They were carrying something precious away from the enemy and back to David.
One wrong movement.
One spear.
One arrow.
One ambush.
One warrior falls.
Perhaps the water falls with him.
Yet somehow they return.
Dust on their bodies.
Danger behind them.
Water in their hands.
David had longed for it.
Now it was finally in front of him.
Imagine the moment.
The water from Bethlehem.
The very thing he wanted.
The thing three men had risked their lives to retrieve.
Surely David drinks now.
But he doesn't.
He pours it out.
Before the LORD.
And suddenly the story becomes holy.
David looks at that water and realizes that he cannot treat it like ordinary water anymore.
Why?
Because of what it cost.
He says, in essence, “Should I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?”
The Hebrew text uses language involving their lives—their nephesh, their very life or person.
The water had become inseparable in David's mind from the lives risked to obtain it.
So David refuses to consume casually what came to him at such extraordinary cost.
Instead, he pours it out before God.
What looked like wasted water became worship.
That is the part we need to feel.
David wasn't dishonoring their sacrifice by pouring it out.
He was treating their sacrifice as too precious merely to satisfy himself.
The gift was so costly that David turned it upward.
Toward God.
There are things whose value cannot adequately be measured by what they are.
Their value is measured by what they cost.
A glass of water is cheap.
A glass of water carried through an enemy army at the risk of three lives is another matter entirely.
And now the story comes dangerously close to us.
Because Christians can become so familiar with the language of the Gospel that we begin handling something infinitely costly as though it were ordinary.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
The cross.
The blood of Christ.
We say the words so often that they can stop making us tremble.
“Jesus died for me.”
Yes.
But do you hear what you just said?
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And He willingly gave His life for sinners.
Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, “but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Precious.
That word belongs in our hearts again.
Grace is free to the sinner.
But grace was not cheap.
We could never purchase reconciliation with God.
Christ accomplished what we could not accomplish.
We did not climb our way to God.
God came to rescue sinners.

And this is where David's water begins pointing beyond itself—not because 2 Samuel explicitly identifies the episode as a prophecy of Jesus, because it does not, but because its picture of costly devotion helps us understand something Christians must never forget:
Cost should change the way a gift is received.
David looked at water and remembered the lives risked for it.
The Christian looks at grace and remembers the Savior who died and rose again.
And suddenly Christianity cannot remain merely cultural.
Casual.
Decorative.
Something we visit on Sunday and abandon on Monday.
You were bought with a price.
Paul therefore says, “glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20).
Notice the movement.
Grace first.
Then response.
Christ's sacrifice first.
Then surrender.
We do not surrender ourselves so Christ will love us.
We surrender because in Christ we have encountered a love greater than anything we deserved.
This distinction matters.
Christian obedience is not payment for salvation.
You cannot repay Calvary.
You cannot reimburse Jesus for His blood.
You cannot place enough money in an offering, perform enough religious works, share enough Christian posts, or accumulate enough good deeds to purchase the forgiveness Christ gives by grace.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But grace does something to the person who truly sees it.
It changes what we consider valuable.
It changes what we are willing to release.
It changes the question from...
“How little can I give God and still call myself Christian?”
to...
“Jesus, after everything You have done for me, how could I keep pretending that my life belongs only to me?”
Maybe that is where this story finds you.
Perhaps nobody knows how exhausted you have become.
You still say “God is good.”
You still share verses.
You still know the worship songs.
But privately...
something has dried up.
Prayer became mechanical.
Sin became easier to excuse.
Compromise stopped frightening you.
The Bible stayed closed longer.
You learned how to appear spiritually alive while becoming spiritually thirsty.
And maybe there is something behind enemy lines that your heart keeps running toward.
Approval.
Pornography.
Money.
Bitterness.
Secret messages.
Pride.
Attention.
Control.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A hidden habit you promised God you would quit.
A wound you have turned into permission to sin.
Nobody else sees the battlefield.
But you do.
And God does.
This is where grace becomes scandalous.
Because Jesus does not wait for cleaned-up sinners to become impressive enough for Him.
The Gospel announces something far better.
Christ came for sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
The ashamed.
The guilty.
The compromised.
The religious hypocrite.
The prodigal.
The person who has prayed the same repentance prayer and then fallen again.
The person wondering whether God could possibly still want them.
Jesus does not minimize sin.
He went to the cross because sin is deadly serious.
But the cross also means your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Repentance is not God demanding that you repair yourself before approaching Him.
It is turning from sin and coming to the One who alone can save.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance means pretending nothing happened.
Jesus rewrites everything because the sinner's deepest identity and eternal future can be transformed through union with Christ.
Guilt can meet forgiveness.
Rebellion can meet mercy.
Bondage can meet freedom.
Death can meet resurrection.
A sinner can become a son or daughter welcomed by grace.
And perhaps the most powerful part of David's story is still sitting there on the ground.
The water.
Poured out.
David could have consumed it.
Instead, he consecrated the moment to God.
And perhaps some of us have been trying desperately to preserve what God has been asking us to surrender.
Our reputation.
Our comfort.
Our secret sin.
Our bitterness.
Our plans.
Our need to be admired.
Our insistence on controlling the future.
We keep asking, “How much do I have to give up?”
Maybe love asks a different question.
“What is Jesus worthy of?”
Not to earn salvation.
Because He already purchased what we could never purchase.
Not to manipulate God.
Not to impress other Christians.
But because when grace finally becomes real to you, surrender stops looking like God stealing your life.
It begins looking like worship.
The three warriors risked their lives because they loved their king.
David poured out their gift because he recognized its cost.
And Christians stand before a greater King.
David himself was flawed.
His story contains courage and worship, but also devastating sin and scandal.
Scripture does not airbrush him.
That matters.
The Bible's heroes keep reminding us that humanity needs more than another human hero.
We need Jesus.
The Son of David.
The righteous King.
The King who does not merely receive sacrifice from His people but first gives Himself for them.
David's warriors crossed enemy lines for their king.
Jesus crossed the distance to rescue His enemies.
Romans 5 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Think about that.
He did not die because you finally became lovable enough.
He loved and gave Himself while sinners were still sinners.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace that does not excuse sin but defeats its claim over those who belong to Christ.
Grace that finds people in caves.
Grace that finds people behind enemy lines.
Grace that finds people whose stories have chapters they wish could be burned.
Grace that says the worst thing you have done does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
So maybe tonight your response does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it needs to be honest.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I have treated Your grace casually.”
“Jesus, I keep trying to drink what should have been surrendered.”
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
That prayer is not weakness.
It is where pretending ends.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer sees and realizes...
“I am not the only one fighting.”
Do not turn vulnerability into performance.
But do not underestimate the power of honest testimony either.
Someone reading quietly may desperately need to know that Christians struggle, repent, get back up, cling to Christ, and keep walking.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Not because sharing a Facebook post proves somebody is a faithful Christian.
It doesn't.
and eventually encounter the message of Jesus Christ.
Think of one person.
Your brother.
Your daughter.
Your old friend.
The believer who disappeared.
The person whose smile has been hiding exhaustion.
The skeptic who thinks Christianity is only rules and condemnation.
The Christian who has become comfortable with compromise.
Send it privately if that would serve them better.
There is already enough noise competing for our attention.
We want to keep putting something different in front of people:
Scripture.
Jesus.
Repentance.
Grace.
Biblical truth.
Healing rooted in Christ.
Discipleship.
Hope.
It does not make you more spiritual.
It does not earn salvation.
Jesus cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people, and if you believe this ministry is worth sustaining, we would be deeply grateful to have you beside us.
do not leave this story without hearing its deepest challenge.
Three warriors crossed enemy territory for a cup of water.
David received it...
looked at what it had cost...
and realized he could no longer treat it as ordinary.
Christian...
look again at the cross.
Look again at the nails.
Look again at the Savior.
Look again at the empty tomb.
Look again at the grace you have grown accustomed to.
The question is not whether you can repay Jesus.
You cannot.
The question is whether seeing His mercy will change the way you live.
Perhaps the most tragic thing would not be having nothing to pour out.
Perhaps it would be standing before the One who gave everything...
while spending your entire life protecting everything from Him.
So bring Him the hidden thing.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the ambition.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the reputation.
Bring Him the future.
Bring Him the part of yourself you keep guarding.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy Christ purchased.
Then rise and follow Him.
And when the enemy whispers that your scandal is too ugly, your history too damaged, your failures too numerous, remember what the Gospel declares:
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Grace still reaches guilty people.
The cross still stands.
The tomb is still empty.
And no surrendered life poured out before Jesus is wasted.
What is the one thing you know you need to surrender to Jesus?
You don't need to tell the whole story.
Even two words are enough:
“No more hiding.”
Because sometimes the moment grace begins rewriting a story is the moment somebody finally stops pretending there is nothing to rewrite.
The water David would not drink became worship when he poured it out—and the life you are afraid to surrender may finally become worship when you place it completely in the hands of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CONTENTMENT DOES NOT MEAN YOU STOP WANTING THINGS. IT MEANS YOUR JOY STOPS BEING HELD HOSTAGE BY THEM.
paragraphs: CONTENTMENT DOES NOT MEAN YOU STOP WANTING THINGS. IT MEANS YOUR JOY STOPS BEING HELD HOSTAGE BY THEM.
You are allowed to want the door to open. You just cannot let your soul die in the hallway.
Maybe nobody ever explained contentment to you like this.
Maybe you thought being a “good Christian” meant pretending you did not want anything anymore.
So you learned the language.
“I’m fine.”
“Whatever God wants.”
“It doesn’t matter.”
“I’m content.”
But underneath those words, something still mattered.
You still wanted the marriage.
You still wanted the child.
You still wanted the breakthrough.
You still wanted the business to succeed.
You still wanted enough money to stop calculating every purchase before reaching the cashier.
You still wanted the diagnosis to change.
You still wanted your family restored.
You still wanted someone to choose you.
You still wanted the ministry to grow.
You still wanted the opportunity you prayed about while everyone else was asleep.
And somewhere along the way, you began feeling guilty because you wanted it.
As though wanting something deeply meant Jesus was no longer enough.
But what if that is not biblical contentment at all?
What if contentment is not the death of desire?
What if it is the death of desire’s dictatorship?
There is a difference.
A massive one.

And if you miss it, you can spend years performing a version of Christianity in which your mouth says, “God is enough,” while your heart quietly wonders whether it is sinful to hope for anything else.
Paul gives us something far more human.
Far more difficult.
And far more beautiful.
He writes from circumstances most people would desperately want changed:
“Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content.” — Philippians 4:11
The Greek deserves our attention.
Paul says:
ἐγὼ γὰρ ἔμαθον ἐν οἷς εἰμι αὐτάρκης εἶναι
A close, literal rendering is:
“For I learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be content.”
The word translated “content” is αὐτάρκης — autarkēs.
It carries the sense of being sufficient, content, not controlled by external circumstances.
But notice something that can change the way you read the entire passage.
Paul says:
ἔμαθον — emathon.
“I learned.”
Contentment was learned.
Paul did not emerge from the womb spiritually unbothered.
He learned it.
That means there were circumstances through which God taught him.
There were days when contentment had to become more than theology.
There were losses.
Delays.
Need.
Abundance.
Hunger.
Provision.
Uncertainty.
Pain.
Paul continues:
“I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound.”
Then comes another remarkable Greek expression:
ἐν παντὶ καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν μεμύημαι
A close rendering is:
“In everything and in all circumstances, I have learned the secret.”
The word μεμύημαι — memyēmai — carries the idea of having been initiated into or instructed in a secret.
Paul had discovered something circumstances could not teach from the outside.
He had learned it by walking through them with Christ.
He knew hunger.
He knew abundance.
Read that again.
Abundance.
Christian contentment is not merely learning how to survive when you have less.
It is also learning how not to worship what you have when you have more.
Paul knew what it was to have plenty, and he knew what it was to be hungry.
He knew abundance, and he knew need.
Then comes one of the most quoted sentences in the New Testament:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με
“I can do all things through Him who strengthens me.” — Philippians 4:13
But in context, Paul is not standing on a victory platform telling Christians that Jesus will enable them to accomplish anything they can imagine.
He is talking about contentment.
He is saying, in effect:
I can endure plenty without making plenty my god.
I can endure need without believing God has abandoned me.
I can walk through abundance.
I can walk through hunger.
I can survive the season I would never have chosen.
I can receive blessing without being possessed by blessing.
I can lose what I thought I needed and discover that Christ is still holding me.
Why?
Because my strength is coming from Someone my circumstances cannot remove.
That is Philippians 4:13.
And suddenly contentment stops sounding passive.
It becomes warfare.
Because there are things you desperately want.
And wanting them is not necessarily the problem.
The question is what happens when you do not get them.
That is where desire reveals whether it has become captivity.
You can want marriage without making marriage your messiah.
You can want financial stability without making money your savior.
You can want success without asking success to tell you who you are.
You can want your ministry to grow without turning numbers into proof that God loves you.
You can want healing while still trusting Jesus when healing has not yet come.
You can want reconciliation without allowing another person’s response to determine whether you have peace.
You can dream.
You can build.
You can pursue.
You can apply.
You can pray boldly.
You can knock on doors.
You can work hard.
You can ask God for things that matter deeply to you.
The Bible does not command you to become emotionally numb.
It commands you to become spiritually free.
Psalm 37:4 does not portray God as hostile toward desire:
“Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart.”
That verse is not a blank check promising that every desire will materialize exactly as imagined.
Something deeper is happening.
Your delight is being anchored in God Himself.
And when God becomes your deepest treasure, your desires are increasingly brought under His lordship.
You begin to pray differently.
“Father, I want this.”
Not:
“Father, You owe me this.”
“I desperately hope this happens.”
Not:
“If this does not happen, You cannot possibly love me.”
“Lord, please open this door.”
Not:
“If You keep it closed, my life is worthless.”
There is extraordinary freedom in being able to tell God what you want without threatening Him with your unbelief if He says no.
Jesus Himself shows us that surrender does not require pretending you have no preference.
In Gethsemane, facing the horror before Him, Jesus prayed:
“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” — Luke 22:42
Do not rush past that.
There was an expressed desire:
“Remove this cup from me.”
And there was perfect surrender:
“Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
Biblical surrender does not require lying about what you want.
It requires refusing to place what you want above the will of God.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because there is probably something you have been asking God for.
Something you rarely tell people about anymore.
You have prayed about it so many times that you are tired of hearing yourself say it.
Maybe you watched someone else receive exactly what you have been begging God for.
You congratulated them.
You smiled.
You meant it.
And then you went somewhere private and felt your heart collapse.
Their answered prayer somehow reminded you of your unanswered one.
And then came the guilt.
“I should be more grateful.”
“I shouldn’t feel this.”
“A real Christian would be content.”
But contentment does not mean disappointment stops hurting.
Contentment means disappointment does not become your god.
You can cry and still trust Jesus.
You can grieve and still trust Jesus.
You can admit, “Lord, I really wanted this,” and still trust Jesus.
You can stand outside a closed door with tears running down your face and still say:
“Christ is enough for me here.”
Not because the door does not matter.
But because the door is not Jesus.
That distinction can save your soul from years of captivity.
Some of us are not exhausted because we desire too much.
We are exhausted because we have handed our desires the authority to decide whether today is worth living.
“If I get it, I can finally have peace.”
“If she comes back, I can finally breathe.”
“If he chooses me, I can finally feel valuable.”
“If the money comes, I can finally feel secure.”
“If the numbers grow, I can finally believe my work matters.”
“If God answers this one prayer, then I will know He loves me.”
Do you see what happened?
A desire became a throne.
Something created began demanding what belongs to the Creator.
Your peace.
Your identity.
Your security.
Your hope.
Your joy.
Your sense of worth.
And eventually your worship.
That is captivity.
Contentment looks desire in the face and says:
“I may deeply want you, but you do not own me.”
“I may pray for you, but I will not worship you.”
“I may work toward you, but I will not sacrifice my soul to obtain you.”
“I may grieve if I lose you, but I will not lose Jesus with you.”
“I may celebrate if God gives you to me, but I will not confuse the gift with the Giver.”
This is why Paul can later tell Timothy:
“Godliness with contentment is great gain.” — 1 Timothy 6:6
And why Hebrews can call believers away from the love of money and toward contentment, grounding that command not merely in disciplined thinking but in the promise of God’s presence:
“I will never leave you nor forsake you.” — Hebrews 13:5
Do you see the foundation?
Christian contentment is not:
“I have everything I want.”
It is:
“I have Christ, and therefore what I lack cannot ultimately destroy me.”
That does not make ambition evil.
It purifies ambition.
Work.
Build.
Create.
Study.
Dream.
Write the book.
Start the business.
Apply for the position.
Develop your gift.
Save money.
Provide for your family.
Pursue excellence.
Pray for marriage.
Pray for children.
Pray for healing.
Pray for restoration.
Ask God to enlarge your usefulness for His kingdom.
But hold every dream with open hands.
Because a closed fist cannot receive differently from God.
And sometimes differently is exactly how grace arrives.
You asked God for a door.
He gave you endurance.
You asked Him to remove someone.
He taught you forgiveness.
You asked for immediate success.
He built character nobody could see.
You asked for certainty.
He taught you dependence.
You asked Him to change your circumstances.
And while you were watching the circumstances, Christ was changing you.
That does not mean every disappointment is secretly a guarantee of some bigger earthly reward.
Scripture gives us no right to promise that.
Sometimes loss is genuinely loss.
Sometimes believers suffer.
Sometimes faithful prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Sometimes the thorn remains.
Sometimes the prison door does not immediately open.
Sometimes obedience costs something.
Christianity is not the promise that every painful chapter will become comfortable before this earthly life ends.
Christianity is the proclamation that suffering, sin, death, disappointment, and even the grave do not get the final word because Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
That is our hope.
Not manifestation.
Not positive thinking.
Not pretending.
Resurrection.
And perhaps this is the scandal of grace:
Jesus does not always rewrite your story by giving you the ending you demanded.
Sometimes He rewrites you so completely that the ending no longer has the power to determine whether you worship.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Think about the thing you want most right now.
Name it.
Do not sanitize it.
Do not give God the church answer.
Tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, I want this.”
Then ask the harder question:
“If You do not give me this when I want it, will I still belong to You?”
That question exposes things.
Maybe it exposed something in you just now.
If it did, do not hide behind religious language.
There is no shame in admitting the battle.
Sometimes another believer needs to see your honesty before they find courage to become honest themselves.
And maybe someone reading your comment will whisper, “Me too.”
That is how community begins.
Not when everybody pretends to be strong.
But when people bring their real hearts into the light and keep pointing one another toward Christ.

Not because you need another saved post collecting dust on your phone, but because there may come a night when the thing you want feels so important that you begin confusing its absence with God’s absence.
Come back and remember:
The unanswered prayer is not proof of an absent Savior.
The closed door is not proof of a closed heaven.
The waiting season is not proof that your life has been forgotten.
And your desire does not have to become your master.
If someone immediately came to mind while you were reading this, send this to them.
Your share could place biblical truth in front of a person who would never have searched for it themselves.
That matters.
Supporting Gospel-centered work matters too.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is grace.
More importantly, stay close because discipleship cannot survive on occasional inspiration alone.
But before you leave, remember why you came this far.
Paul did not say he stopped wanting.
He said he learned contentment.
He learned how to have much without being owned by much.
He learned how to have little without believing he had lost everything.
He discovered a secret that circumstances could not confiscate.
Christ.
Christ in abundance.
Christ in hunger.
Christ when doors opened.
Christ when chains remained.
Christ when there was plenty.
Christ when there was need.
Christ when tomorrow made sense.
Christ when it did not.
And perhaps you are learning the same secret right now.
Maybe God is teaching your heart to say:
“I still want it, Jesus.
I am still praying for it.
I may still cry over it.
I may still work toward it.
I may still hope You give it to me.
But it will not be my god anymore.
If You give it, I will worship You.
If You withhold it, I will worship You.
If I have abundance, strengthen me.
If I walk through need, strengthen me.
Because my joy belongs to You before it belongs to my circumstances.”
That is not giving up.
That is freedom.
That is desire without captivity.
That is contentment.
And that kind of contentment cannot be manufactured by pretending you do not care.
It is learned at the feet of Jesus.
What is the thing you are learning to want without allowing it to own you?
Let somebody pray with you.
Let somebody know they are not the only believer still learning this.
Because someday you may finally hold the thing you have been praying for.
Or someday you may discover that God wrote the chapter differently.
Either way, do not surrender the deepest joy of your soul to something that can be gained today and lost tomorrow.
Hold your desires.
But let Jesus hold you.
And when your hands are empty, remember this:
You can lose the thing you wanted without losing the One your soul was made for.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “MY BELOVED IS TO ME A SACHET OF MYRRH BETWEEN MY BREASTS”: Yes, That Image Is in the Bible
paragraphs: “MY BELOVED IS TO ME A SACHET OF MYRRH BETWEEN MY BREASTS”: Yes, That Image Is in the Bible

Song of Songs 1:13 contains one of Scripture’s most intimate images—and beneath its startling beauty is a truth about love, longing, nearness, and ultimately the Savior who came close enough to carry our shame.
There are Bible verses people put on coffee mugs.
There are Bible verses stitched onto pillows.
There are verses quoted at graduations, printed beneath sunsets, and posted whenever somebody needs encouragement.
And then there is Song of Songs 1:13.
“My beloved is unto me as a bundle of myrrh, that lieth betwixt my breasts.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
And before somebody nervously turns the page, makes a joke, or wonders why God allowed language this intimate into Holy Scripture, perhaps we should do something increasingly rare.
Perhaps we should let the Bible speak without being embarrassed by it.

Because what appears at first to be a startling sentence about a woman, her beloved, perfume, and her breasts becomes something deeply beautiful when we slow down long enough to hear what the Hebrew is actually saying.
The Hebrew reads:
צְרוֹר הַמֹּר דּוֹדִי לִי בֵּין שָׁדַי יָלִין
Tseror hammor dodi li, bein shadai yalin.
Literally, the sense is something like:
“A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; between my breasts he spends the night.”
The language is intimate.
There is no honest reason to pretend otherwise.

The Song of Songs celebrates the powerful affection, desire, delight, exclusivity, beauty, and longing between a man and a woman. Scripture does not treat marital love as something filthy that God reluctantly tolerates. The God who created humanity male and female also created covenant intimacy, and within its God-given boundaries Scripture can speak about that intimacy with a poetic freedom that sometimes makes modern religious people more uncomfortable than the Bible itself seems to be.
But look more closely.
She is not describing a sexual act.
She is describing precious nearness.
Myrrh was aromatic and valuable. A small bundle or sachet of it could be worn close to the body, allowing its fragrance to remain with the wearer.
That changes the picture.
Her beloved is so precious to her that she compares him to fragrance kept against her heart.
Close.
Treasured.
Remembered.
Carried.
His presence remains with her.
Even when he is not physically there, the fragrance reminds her of the one she loves.
And suddenly an ancient love poem begins asking a painfully modern question:
What are you carrying closest to your heart?
Not what do you post about.
Not what Bible verse is in your bio.
Not what worship song is playing in your car.
What actually lives near your heart when nobody is watching?
Because everybody carries something there.
Some carry the memory of someone who wounded them.
Some carry the name of someone who left.
Some carry an addiction they have learned to hide beneath Christian vocabulary.
Some carry resentment.
Some carry pornography.
Some carry ambition.
Some carry the desperate need to be admired.
Some carry grief so quietly that even the people sitting beside them in church have no idea they are barely surviving.
Some carry shame.
Old shame.
The kind that learned your address years ago and never seemed to move out.
Maybe that is why this strange little verse can become so unsettling.
“My beloved…”
Not merely my doctrine.
