Don't turn that sentence into shallow self-esteem theology.
The Gospel is not simply, “You are valuable, so believe in yourself.”
The Gospel goes much deeper.
You and I are not merely wounded people needing affirmation.
We are sinners needing reconciliation with a holy God.
We have been sinned against...
and we have sinned.
We have wounds.
And we have guilt.
We have been victims in some chapters...
and painfully selfish in others.
That is why Jesus did not come merely to make us feel better about ourselves.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He came for the betrayed.
And the betrayer who repents.
The exploited.
And the exploiter who lays down his pride and cries for mercy.
The abandoned.
And the one who finally realizes how many people he abandoned.
The woman who believes she became worthless when someone chose another.
The man staring into the mirror realizing he became the kind of person he once swore he would never become.
The religious person hiding secret sin beneath respectable Christianity.
The exhausted believer wondering whether God is finished with them.
The prodigal.
The hypocrite.
The ashamed.
The guilty.
The broken.
People like us.
And at the cross, Jesus does something infinitely greater than merely modifying the conditions of our bondage.
He pays for sinners with His own blood.
Not because Satan had to be paid.
Not because God owed our captors anything.
But because divine justice against our sin had to be satisfied, and Christ willingly stood in the place of His people.
We had a debt we could never settle.
Christ bore our sin.
We deserved judgment.
Christ endured the curse.
We were powerless to make ourselves righteous.
Christ gives righteousness to those who trust Him.
And then resurrection morning announces that sin, death, and the grave do not get the final sentence.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous.
Grace does not say sin was harmless.
Grace says sin was so serious that the Son of God went to the cross...
and His mercy is so astonishing that sinners can come home.
Maybe you clicked this article because the headline sounded shocking.
Maybe you expected an argument about slavery.
Maybe you came prepared to defend the Bible.
Or attack it.
But somewhere along the way...
the passage started reading you.
Maybe you've been treating somebody as disposable.
Repent.
Maybe you're cheating emotionally and telling yourself it isn't adultery because nothing physical has happened.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe pornography has taught your heart to consume bodies instead of honoring people made in God's image.
Repent.
Maybe you're carrying bitterness toward the person who replaced you.
Give Christ the wound before the wound becomes your identity.
Maybe you've spent years pretending you're okay because Christians around you seem uncomfortable with broken people.
Stop pretending before God.
He already knows.
Maybe your marriage is bleeding.
Maybe your conscience is screaming.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you think the scandal permanently became your name.
Listen carefully.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Repentance is not pretending the chapter never happened.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Forgiveness is not God becoming indifferent toward justice.
The cross proves the opposite.
At Calvary, sin is exposed as deadly...
and mercy is revealed as breathtaking.
So come to Christ honestly.
No religious performance.
No edited testimony.
No pretending.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust the crucified and risen Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of respectable people earning God's approval.
It is the story of guilty people receiving a Savior they could never deserve.
And perhaps that is why this obscure law in Exodus hits so unexpectedly hard.
A woman whose world could have treated her as property was not beyond God's notice.
Her deprivation had consequences.
Her mistreatment mattered.
Her freedom mattered.

And thousands of years later, the same Scriptures lead us toward Jesus Christ—the One who sees people the world overlooks, confronts those who abuse power, calls sinners to repentance, welcomes the broken, and transforms those who come to Him in faith.
Be honest.
And if you are fighting quietly just to remain faithful...
Someone reading underneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only Christian struggling to hold on.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone scrolling tonight may be carrying betrayal they have told nobody about.
Someone may be angry with Scripture because nobody ever slowed down long enough to explain passages like this honestly.
Someone may be one conversation away from opening a Bible again.
It hasn't.
Not if Christ is rewriting the story.
But hear this carefully:
It cannot.
Do not give under spiritual compulsion.

Scripture says giving is to come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity,” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). At the same time, the New Testament plainly recognizes the legitimacy of believers materially supporting Gospel ministry; Paul speaks of churches sharing with him in “giving and receiving,” and describes such support as an offering pleasing to God, while 1 Corinthians 9:14 affirms support for those proclaiming the Gospel.
I would rather tell you the truth: give prayerfully, willingly, responsibly, and for the glory of God.
Pray.
Follow.
Save the teaching.
Share it publicly.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Because ultimately this isn't about building an audience.
It is about people encountering Christ.
It is about sinners repenting.
Prodigals returning.
Wounded believers discovering that suffering did not make God abandon them.
Proud hearts being humbled.
Hidden sins coming into the light.
Broken homes finding biblical truth.
And people discovering that grace is not God's permission to remain who they were.
Grace is God's invitation to come to Christ...
be forgiven...
and be changed.
Exodus 21 begins by taking us somewhere uncomfortable.
A vulnerable woman.
An ancient household.
A man holding enormous power.
Another woman enters the picture.
And God says the first woman cannot simply be deprived without consequence.
Her life matters.
Her treatment matters.
Her freedom matters.
Then the whole biblical story keeps moving.
Through wilderness.
Through judges.
Through kings.
Through prophets.
Through exile.
Until eventually...
outside Jerusalem...
another Person is treated as though He were disposable.
Rejected.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Nailed to wood.
Jesus Christ.
Except this time the One suffering is not powerless.
He willingly lays down His life.
And the cross becomes the place where justice and mercy meet...
where sinners discover that God did not ignore our guilt...
and where the guilty discover that guilt does not have to be the final word.
Three days later, the grave is empty.
And suddenly the deepest message running through Scripture becomes impossible to miss:
What human sin destroys, Jesus is able to redeem.
So whatever brought you here...
the betrayal...
the shame...
the secret...
the abandonment...
the addiction...
the hypocrisy...
the anger...
the years you wasted...
the person you hurt...
the person who hurt you...
don't give the scandal the pen.
Give it to Christ.
Because the chapter that made you think your story was over may become the very place where grace begins writing something you never imagined.
The scandal may explain how you arrived here—but only Jesus gets to decide what redemption can make of what remains.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS TELL MARY MAGDALENE NOT TO CLING TO HIM?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS TELL MARY MAGDALENE NOT TO CLING TO HIM?

She thought she had finally gotten Jesus back. But the risen Christ said something that has confused readers for centuries: “Do not cling to Me.” What happened in that garden was not rejection. It was resurrection teaching—and hidden inside His words is something every heart terrified of losing Jesus needs to hear.
There are moments when you have lost so much that, if God gave even one piece of it back, you would hold it so tightly your fingers would ache.
Mary Magdalene knew that feeling.
She had watched Jesus die.
Not metaphorically.
Not spiritually.
Die.
The voice that had spoken freedom into broken lives had gone silent.
The hands that touched lepers had been pierced.
The feet that walked dusty roads toward forgotten people had been nailed to wood.
The One Mary loved as Lord had been wrapped for burial and placed behind a stone.
Then Sunday came.
John tells us that Mary arrived at the tomb while it was still dark.
That detail almost feels like more than a description of the sky.
Because sometimes it is morning on the calendar while it is still midnight inside you.
Maybe you know something about that.
You still go to church.
Still whisper prayers.
Still tell people, “God is good.”
Still share Bible verses.
But somewhere underneath all of it, you are standing beside your own tomb asking why Jesus allowed something you loved to die.
Mary came looking for a corpse.
She was not expecting resurrection.
And perhaps that is the first scandal of grace in this story:
Jesus was already alive while Mary was still grieving as though everything was over.
Read that again.
The thing Mary believed was the ending had already been rewritten by God.
She just did not know it yet.
Peter and the other disciple came. They saw the empty tomb. They left.
Mary stayed.
Crying.
Then she looked inside and saw angels.
Even that did not stop her tears.
Then someone stood behind her.
She assumed He was the gardener.
Imagine the scene.
The risen Son of God is standing within speaking distance, and grief has made Him unrecognizable to her.
Jesus asks why she is weeping and whom she is seeking.
Mary, still believing someone has taken the body, essentially says: Tell me where you put Him, and I will take Him away.
Then Jesus says one word.
Her name.
“Mary.”
Everything changes.
She turns.
“Rabboni!”
Teacher.
Lord.
Jesus.
Alive.
The grave had lost.
Death had failed.
Rome had crucified Him, but Rome could not keep Him.
The stone had been sealed, but stones cannot imprison the Author of life.
Hell had thrown everything it had at the Son of God, and Sunday morning answered with an empty tomb.
Mary had come searching for Jesus among the dead.
Jesus found Mary among the living.
And then comes the sentence.
The strange sentence.
The sentence that can sound almost cold when removed from its context.
John 20:17 records the Greek:
“Μή μου ἅπτου, οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα…”
Mē mou haptou, oupō gar anabebēka pros ton patera…
Often rendered:
“Do not cling to Me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.”
The older English “Touch Me not” can create the wrong picture.
Jesus was not acting as though Mary were dirty.
He was not suddenly untouchable.
He was not ashamed of her.
And He was certainly not rejecting the woman standing before Him.
The Greek verb translated “cling” is related to haptomai—ἅπτομαι—and here John uses ἅπτου (haptou).
The expression can carry the sense of holding onto, grasping, attaching oneself to, or clinging.
That matters.

Because later in the same chapter Jesus does not establish some universal rule that His resurrected body cannot be touched. When Thomas struggles to believe, Jesus directs him toward the evidence of His wounds.
So the issue in the garden is not simply physical contact.
Something deeper is happening.
Mary has found the Jesus she thought she had lost.
And naturally, desperately, beautifully, she wants to hold on.
Can you blame her?
If you watched someone you loved tortured and crucified on Friday and found Him standing alive before you on Sunday, would you want to let go?
Mary's reaction makes perfect human sense.
But Jesus is showing her that resurrection does not mean everything is simply returning to the way it was before Calvary.
He did not rise merely to resume the old arrangement.
The cross changed everything.
The resurrection announced something new.
The ascension was coming.
The Spirit would be given.
The Gospel would go outward.
And Mary could not remain forever in the garden clutching yesterday's experience of Jesus.
She had somewhere to go.
Someone to tell.
A message to carry.
Listen to the movement in Jesus' words:
“Do not cling to Me…”
then…
“Go…”
That may be one of the most important movements in Christian discipleship.
We encounter Christ…
and then Christ sends us.
Grace does not merely comfort us.
Grace commissions us.
The Gospel does not simply give us something beautiful to hold.
It gives us Someone glorious to proclaim.
Jesus continues:
“Go to My brothers…”
Do not race past those words.
“My brothers.”
Who were these “brothers”?
The disciples.
The same men who had scattered when Jesus was arrested.
Peter had denied Him.
Others had fled.
Their courage had collapsed when the pressure became unbearable.
And what does the resurrected Jesus call them?
Failures?
Cowards?
Disappointments?
Traitors?
No.
“My brothers.”
That is grace.
They failed Jesus.
Jesus did not stop being faithful to them.
Their worst night did not cancel His redemptive purpose.
The resurrection did not merely defeat death.
It announced that grace could still reach frightened disciples hiding behind locked doors.
Maybe that is where this story stops being Mary's story and becomes yours.
Because perhaps you love Jesus…
but you know you have failed Him.
Perhaps there are things in your history you wish you could erase.
Maybe you promised God you would never go back to that sin.
Then you went back.
Maybe you were on fire for Christ once.
Then something happened.
A disappointment.
A betrayal.
An unanswered prayer.
A secret compromise.
A relationship you knew was pulling you away from God.
An addiction nobody knows about.
A season when prayer became rare, Scripture became distant, worship became mechanical, and conviction became easier to silence.
You still knew Christian language.
But your heart was drifting.
And perhaps somewhere inside you there is a fear you rarely admit:
“After everything I've done… does Jesus still want me?”
Look at Easter morning.
Look at the people Jesus calls “My brothers.”
Grace does not pretend their failure never happened.
Grace does something infinitely greater.
Jesus carries the judgment for sin at Calvary, rises victorious over death, and comes looking for sinners He intends to restore.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes the cross magnificent.
The Gospel is not God shrugging at your rebellion.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin so seriously that the Son of God bears judgment, and loving sinners so deeply that the Son willingly gives Himself to save them.
That is why repentance matters.
Biblical grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls you out of hiding.
Grace says you do not have to clean yourself enough to make Jesus willing to receive you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Trust Christ.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop pretending the secret sin is harmless simply because nobody has discovered it.
Jesus did not walk out of a grave so you could spend your life decorating yours.
He came to make dead people live.
And maybe the hardest part of Mary’s encounter is this:
Sometimes loving Jesus means releasing the version of life you thought Jesus was supposed to give you.
Mary wanted Him there.
Jesus was preparing her for mission.
Mary wanted to hold.
Jesus told her to go.
Mary wanted the familiar.
Jesus was unfolding something larger than she could yet understand.
Have you ever prayed for God to restore something while God was teaching you to trust Him without it?
Have you ever begged Him to return life to the way it used to be?
“Jesus, give me that relationship back.”
“Give me that opportunity back.”
“Give me that person back.”
“Give me my old life back.”
“Give me the feeling I used to have when I prayed.”
Sometimes we are not clinging to Jesus.
We are clinging to the version of our story we expected Jesus to preserve.
There is a difference.
Mary had to learn that she could release her grip without losing her Savior.
So do we.
Because Christian faith is not possessing God on our terms.
It is belonging to Christ on His.
And the risen Jesus was not disappearing into irrelevance.
He was moving His redemptive mission toward its appointed fulfillment.
He tells Mary:
“I am ascending to My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God.”
Do you hear the intimacy?
Your Father.
Your God.
The woman who arrived believing everything had been taken from her walked away carrying news that would change human history.
She came grieving a dead Christ.
She left proclaiming a risen Christ.
John tells us what happened next:
Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples,
“I have seen the Lord.”
Five words that changed everything.
She did not have every theological question answered.
She had encountered Jesus.
She had heard His voice.
And now she had a testimony.
“I have seen the Lord.”
That is what grace does.
It turns mourners into messengers.
It turns graves into testimonies.
It takes people whose stories look finished and puts resurrection language in their mouths.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your life has chapters you would never voluntarily read aloud.
Maybe there are pages stained with shame.
Divorce.
Sexual sin.
Addiction.
Pride.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Abortion.
Greed.
Unbelief.
Religious hypocrisy.
Broken promises.
Years wasted running from God.
Things done to you.
Things done by you.
Things nobody knows.
Jesus Christ is not intimidated by the chapter you wish had never been written.
The cross proves He knows exactly what sin costs.
The empty tomb proves sin and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Him.
Your scandal does not become beautiful because sin was beautiful.
Your story becomes beautiful because grace entered the wreckage.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
By redeeming what the past could never repair.
And maybe today you are Mary standing in the garden.
Crying over something God has already begun transforming.
Maybe you are one of the disciples hiding behind a locked door because shame keeps telling you Jesus must be finished with you.
Maybe you are Thomas saying, “I need evidence.”
Maybe you are simply exhausted.
Still believing.
Still trying.
Still fighting battles nobody sees.
Hear the risen Christ.
The answer is not “try harder until you become worthy.”
The answer is Jesus.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Lord over death.
Calling sinners to repentance.
Offering forgiveness.
Giving new life to those who trust Him.
And sending redeemed people into a broken world carrying good news.
Mary could not stay at the tomb.
Neither can we.
There are people who need to hear that Jesus still saves.
There are people on your Facebook friends list silently falling apart.
People posting jokes while fighting depression.
People posting family photographs while their marriage is bleeding behind closed doors.
People quoting Scripture while privately wondering whether God still hears them.
People who have not prayed sincerely in years.
People who think Christianity is merely religion because nobody has ever explained grace to them.
People convinced their past disqualifies them from coming home.
This is why sharing the Gospel matters.
Not because an algorithm deserves another post.
Because somebody behind a screen may be standing emotionally beside a tomb.
Not for applause.
For mission.
Send it privately to someone if tagging them publicly would embarrass them.
Be honest before God.
What are you still clinging to?
What are you afraid to surrender?
What hidden thing needs to come into Christ's light?
What disappointment have you allowed to become more authoritative than God's character?
What sin have you been excusing?
What grave have you mistaken for the ending?
Someone reading may desperately need proof that God still restores broken people.
But there is another way you can help this Gospel mission continue.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep putting Christ-centered Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, and Gospel hope in front of people who desperately need it.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or a better standing before God.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption with His blood.
And Christian generosity must never be manipulated out of people through guilt or pressure.
Scripture teaches giving from the heart rather than under compulsion.
So pray first.
Take care of the responsibilities God has entrusted to you.
Support your local church and faithful Gospel work as you are convicted and able.
Think of it as voluntary ministry support—an offering of partnership, not a substitute we can biblically declare to be your required tithe.
Your support helps us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep publishing.
Keep reaching.
Keep putting the name of Jesus into places where somebody may encounter the Gospel at the exact moment they were ready to give up.
And sharing costs nothing.
Pray.
Share.
One share can travel farther than you imagine.
One person you tag may return to Scripture.
One person you invite may hear the Gospel.
But merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The mission is.
The Gospel is.
And then do what Mary did.
Go tell somebody.
Mary Magdalene walked into the garden thinking she had lost Jesus.
She walked out knowing death had lost Him.
And perhaps that is the word your heart needed today.
You do not need to hold Jesus tightly enough to keep Him alive.
He is risen.
You do not need to manufacture resurrection.
You need to trust the resurrected Christ.
You do not need to pretend your scandal never happened.
Bring it to the Savior whose wounds prove that grace was purchased at an unimaginable price.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Release what He is asking you to release.
Then rise from the place where you have been weeping…
and go.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Because the most astonishing thing about that garden was not that Mary finally found Jesus.
It was that the Jesus she thought she had lost already knew her name.
And when Christ calls your name, even the grave is no longer allowed to write your ending.
The hands Mary could not keep clinging to were the scarred hands already holding a future death could never steal.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS SAY MOSES ALLOWED SOMETHING GOD NEVER INTENDED “FROM THE BEGINNING”?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS SAY MOSES ALLOWED SOMETHING GOD NEVER INTENDED “FROM THE BEGINNING”?
The disturbing words of Jesus about divorce, hardened hearts, and the difference between what God permits in a fallen world and what God designed before sin broke it.
There is a sentence from Jesus that can make a careful Bible reader stop.
Not because Jesus contradicts Scripture.
He doesn’t.
Not because Moses got God’s will wrong.
That is not what Jesus says either.
But because Jesus reveals something about the human heart that is uncomfortable enough to follow us home.
The Pharisees came to Jesus with a question about divorce.
On the surface, it sounded theological.
“Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?”
But Jesus did something remarkable.
They wanted to debate the boundary of what was permitted.
Jesus took them back to what God intended.
He answered:
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female...?”
Then Jesus brought them to Genesis—to creation, covenant, union, and the mysterious reality of two becoming one flesh.
And He concluded:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
That should have ended the conversation.
It didn’t.
Because they had another verse.
They asked Him, in essence:
Then why did Moses allow divorce?
And Jesus answered with words that still expose religious hearts today:
“Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read that again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
In Greek, Matthew records:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs
A natural rendering is:
“But from the beginning it has not been this way.”
There is the tension.
Moses permitted something.
Jesus says it was not so “from the beginning.”
So what happened?
Did God change His mind?
Did Moses lower God's standard without permission?
Was the Law of Moses flawed?

Or is Jesus showing us something much deeper about Scripture, sin, mercy, and the terrifying ability of human beings to become so hardened that divine legislation must sometimes address the devastation of a fallen world without pretending that devastation represents God's original design?
Because this conversation is about divorce.
But it is not only about divorce.
It is also about us.
We are remarkably skilled at asking:
“What am I allowed to do?”
when perhaps the more searching question is:
“What does the heart of God desire?”
And those are not always the same question.
The Pharisees appealed to Moses.
Jesus appealed to creation.
That distinction matters enormously.
Their question refers back to Deuteronomy 24:1–4, a passage involving a man who divorces his wife, gives her a certificate of divorce, and sends her away.
The Hebrew expression associated with that certificate is:
סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת
sefer keritut
Literally, a written document of cutting off or severance—a certificate of divorce.
But here is something crucial.
Deuteronomy 24 is often spoken about as though Moses were standing before Israel enthusiastically establishing divorce as God's beautiful ideal.
That misses the nature of the passage.
The text addresses an already broken situation.
A divorce has happened.
A certificate has been given.
A remarriage has occurred.
Then another separation takes place through divorce or death.
The legislation regulates what follows.
It does not present marital rupture as the creation ideal.
That is exactly why Jesus can acknowledge the Mosaic provision while simultaneously saying:
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Moses was dealing with humanity east of Eden.
Jesus takes His listeners back before Eden shattered.
Back before betrayal.
Back before domination.
Back before abandonment.
Back before lust.
Back before manipulation.
Back before men and women learned how to wound the people they once promised to cherish.
Back to Genesis.
“Male and female he created them.”
Then:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24 contains the Hebrew:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
One flesh.
Not disposable flesh.
Not temporary flesh.
Not “until someone more exciting comes along” flesh.
One flesh.
Jesus therefore refuses to allow a debate over legal permission to obscure the sacredness of God's design.
But then He identifies the disease underneath the concession.
Hardness of heart.
Matthew uses:
σκληροκαρδία
sklērokardia
The word combines the idea of hardness with the heart.
It is where we get the concept behind the English word “sclerocardia.”
Jesus says:
πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn
“Because of your hardness of heart...”
And suddenly this passage becomes frighteningly personal.
Because hardened hearts did not disappear when the Pharisees walked away.
We still know how to harden ours.
We know how to stop listening.
How to justify what once convicted us.
How to collect Bible verses that protect the decision we have already made.
How to ask how close we can walk to sin without technically crossing the line.
How to turn commandments into loopholes.
How to call bitterness “discernment.”
How to call lust “a weakness.”
How to call pride “standards.”
How to call unforgiveness “boundaries” when what we actually mean is that we secretly want someone to keep paying forever.
How to call compromise “freedom.”
How to ask God to approve what we have never truly surrendered to Him.
And this is where Jesus refuses to play our game.
We ask:
“How far can I go?”
Jesus asks:
“What happened to your heart?”
We ask:
“Is there a verse that permits this?”
Jesus asks:
“Does this reflect what God intended?”
We ask:
“Can I technically justify myself?”
Jesus reaches beneath the argument and touches the wound.
Hardness of heart.
That does not mean every divorce happens because one innocent person woke up with a hardened heart and decided to destroy a marriage.
Scripture is more sober than simplistic blame.

Marriage can become the scene of grievous sin, betrayal, abandonment, coercion, violence, and profound human suffering. Jesus Himself speaks further about sexual immorality in Matthew 19:9, and Paul addresses abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7:15. Christians have disagreed over some details of how these passages should be applied, and faithful interpretation should acknowledge those debates rather than pretending every difficult case is identical.
But none of that changes Jesus' central movement in Matthew 19.
He moves from permission to purpose.
From Deuteronomy back to Genesis.
From regulation in a fallen world back to creation before the fall.
From the certificate in someone's hand to the hardness inside someone's heart.
And perhaps that is why this passage reaches much farther than marriage.
Because sometimes God regulates human brokenness without calling brokenness good.
There is a profound difference between God's holy design and provisions given within a world already ravaged by sin.
Fail to understand that, and we may confuse concession with celebration.
Regulation with endorsement.
Permission with perfection.
And then we may begin constructing our Christianity around the lowest boundary we believe we can technically survive.
But Jesus did not die merely to make us experts at locating loopholes.
He came to make us new.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not fundamentally:
“How much of my old life can I keep while still getting into heaven?”
It is:
“Jesus Christ gave Himself for me. What remains that I have not surrendered?”
And maybe that sentence makes you uncomfortable.
Good.
Stay there for a moment.
Because there are places inside us where we desperately want Moses' certificate when Jesus is asking about our heart.
There are relationships where we would rather prove ourselves right than become Christlike.
There are private habits we keep negotiating.
Secret messages.
Hidden resentment.
Pornography erased from browser histories but not surrendered at the cross.
Emotional affairs renamed “friendship.”
Greed renamed ambition.
Gossip disguised as a prayer request.
A marriage slowly dying because two wounded people have become more committed to winning than forgiving.
A faith slowly dying because someone learned how to look Christian without remaining close to Christ.
Nobody else sees it.
But Jesus does.
And here comes the scandal.
He sees it...
and still calls you toward Himself.
That is grace.
Not grace that tells sin it doesn't matter.
Grace that says sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
Not grace that lowers God's holiness until our rebellion becomes comfortable.
Grace that meets guilty people where they actually are and refuses to leave them there.
At the cross, we discover something far greater than permission.
We discover redemption.
Jesus did not come merely to answer the Pharisees' legal puzzle.
He came ultimately to deal with the hardened human heart itself.
The prophets had already pointed toward God's answer.
Through Ezekiel, God promised:
“I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.”
A heart of stone.
That sounds painfully close to the problem Jesus exposed.
And the Gospel announces that our deepest need cannot be solved by becoming cleverer religious lawyers.
We need mercy.
We need cleansing.
We need regeneration.
We need Christ.
We need hearts that can love what God loves again.
Maybe you are reading this after a divorce.
Maybe you caused tremendous damage.
Maybe someone else's sin devastated you.
Maybe you fought for your marriage until you had nothing left.
Maybe your story contains adultery.
Maybe it contains abandonment.
Maybe you carry regret over decisions you would give almost anything to reverse.
Maybe you have remarried and still wonder whether God sees you primarily through the worst chapter of your life.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that your past was insignificant.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is greater than your past.
Repentance does not rewrite history by pretending nothing happened.
Jesus rewrites what history gets to become.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery was dragged publicly into shame.
Again and again, Scripture introduces us to people whose stories looked ruined.
Then Jesus entered them.
And whenever Christ enters a ruined story, sin does not suddenly become righteousness.
Something better happens.
Sinners can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The guilty can repent.
The wounded can begin healing.
The enslaved can become free.
The dead can live.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because grace is greater.
Not cheap grace.
Not sentimental grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Cross-shaped grace.
Grace that forgives and transforms.
Grace that can look directly at the wreckage and still say:
“This does not have to be your final chapter.”
And perhaps this is the question Jesus' words leave burning inside us:
Have I been searching Scripture to surrender to God... or searching Scripture for permission to avoid surrender?
That question can hurt.
Let it.
Sometimes conviction is mercy knocking before destruction kicks the door down.
Maybe your issue is not divorce.
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it is what happens on your phone after midnight.
Maybe it is the bitterness you rehearse every morning.
Maybe it is the apology you refuse to give.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe you have become spiritually numb.
You still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You can still quote Scripture.
You can still say “God is good.”
But privately, something has become hard.
And the frightening thing about a hardened heart is that eventually it can stop feeling hard.
Sin begins feeling normal.
Conviction begins feeling irritating.
Repentance begins sounding extreme.
Obedience begins looking unreasonable.
Then one day we find ourselves asking exactly the kind of question Jesus' opponents asked:
“But am I allowed?”
When the King who rescued us is asking:
“Will you trust Me?”
There is no loophole that can heal your soul.
But there is a Savior who can.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Be honest.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need Him is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building.
Let other believers know that behind the profile picture is a human being who needs grace.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
But sharing biblical truth can genuinely become one small way of pointing someone toward Jesus.
Someone quietly preparing to walk away.
Someone hiding an affair.
Someone drowning in shame after a divorce.
Someone convinced that the worst thing they ever did permanently disqualified them from grace.
Someone who will never search for a sermon...
but might stop for an article you shared.
Am I seeking God's heart—or merely seeking permission?
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who has questions Christians sometimes seem afraid to discuss.

Supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful act of generosity when it is freely given from love for God and neighbor. The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
And there is something else we want believers to know about.
But whether you ever give us a cent or not...
Do not leave Jesus standing at the edge of the one room in your heart you refuse to unlock.
Because Matthew 19 is not merely an ancient argument about Moses.
It is a mirror.
Moses dealt with what hardened hearts had produced.
Jesus pointed back to what God intended.
And through the Gospel, Christ does something even more astonishing:
He takes hardened hearts and makes them new.
So stop asking only:
“What can I get away with?”
Ask:
“Jesus, what would You have me become?”
Bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the divorce.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the certificate.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the consequences you cannot erase.
Bring Him the heart that does not feel anything anymore.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
Make restitution where it is possible and appropriate.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where circumstances require it.
And trust the crucified and risen Christ with the chapter you thought had permanently defined you.
Because the most astonishing thing about Jesus is not that He teaches us how things were “from the beginning.”
It is that through Him, broken people can receive something they could never manufacture for themselves:
a new beginning.
Because somewhere between “Moses allowed” and “from the beginning”, Jesus exposed the tragedy of the hardened human heart.
And somewhere between our scandal and His cross...
grace wrote another ending.
The chapter you are ashamed to reread may become the very page where someone else discovers that Jesus still rewrites lives.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “AS A MAN THINKS IN HIS HEART, SO IS HE” — THE FAMOUS BIBLE VERSE THAT DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MILLIONS THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs: “AS A MAN THINKS IN HIS HEART, SO IS HE” — THE FAMOUS BIBLE VERSE THAT DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MILLIONS THINK IT MEANS

Proverbs 23:7 has been printed on inspirational posters, preached from pulpits, quoted by motivational speakers, and used to tell millions of people that their thoughts determine who they become. There is only one problem.
That is not what Solomon was talking about.
You may have quoted this verse for years.
Maybe you highlighted it.

Maybe somebody preached it to you as proof that if you think positively enough, believe strongly enough, visualize faithfully enough, and remove negative thoughts from your mind, you can somehow construct a different life.
“For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he…”
It sounds powerful.
It sounds inspirational.
It even sounds biblical.
But something happens when you stop at verse 7.
You never meet the man Solomon was actually talking about.
And once you meet him, the verse becomes uncomfortable in an entirely different way.
Because Proverbs 23:7 is not sitting alone in Scripture as a motivational slogan about creating your reality with your thoughts.
It is sitting at a dinner table.
There is food on that table.
There is a host smiling across from you.
He is telling you to eat.
And according to Solomon…
he does not mean it.
Read the surrounding words.

“Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats: For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee. The morsel which thou hast eaten shalt thou vomit up, and lose thy sweet words.”
—Proverbs 23:6–8, KJV
Suddenly the famous sentence sounds different.
The subject is not a person sitting alone thinking himself into success.
The subject is a miserly, begrudging, calculating person offering hospitality outwardly while inwardly resenting what his hospitality costs him.
His mouth says:
“Eat.”
His heart says:
“I wish you wouldn't.”
His lips appear generous.
His inner life is keeping the bill.
That changes everything.
The Hebrew underneath this passage makes the picture even more revealing.
Proverbs 23:6 literally speaks about someone with an “evil eye”—רַע עָיִן (raʿ ʿayin)—an expression connected in this context with stinginess or selfishness.
Then comes the difficult but fascinating Hebrew expression behind verse 7:
כִּי כְּמוֹ שָׁעַר בְּנַפְשׁוֹ כֶּן־הוּא
Ki kemo shaʿar benafsho, ken-hu.
The traditional English wording made famous through the King James tradition reads:
“For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he.”
But the Hebrew verb שָׁעַר (shaʿar) here can carry the idea of calculating, estimating, or reckoning.
And בְּנַפְשׁוֹ (benafsho) literally points toward what is happening “in his soul,” or within himself.
That is why translations can legitimately render the thought along the lines of a man calculating inwardly.
The point is not:
“Imagine yourself successful and eventually you will become successful.”
The point is much closer to:
“Do not be fooled by what this man is saying. Look at what is really governing him inside.”
His words say generosity.
His inner calculation says resentment.
His invitation says welcome.
His heart says cost.
And now this ancient dinner table begins looking disturbingly modern.
Because haven't you met people like this?
Maybe worse…
haven't you sometimes been this person?
“Of course I forgive you.”
But inside:
I will never let you forget what you did.
“I’m happy for you.”
But inside:
Why did God give that to you instead of me?
“Anything you need, brother.”
But inside:
You owe me now.
“I’m praying for you.”
But inside:
I hope everyone eventually discovers what you did.
“I surrender everything to You, Jesus.”
But somewhere behind the worship song, behind the raised hands, behind the Christian language…
Everything except that.
That is where Proverbs 23:7 becomes far more piercing than the motivational quotation we turned it into.
Solomon is forcing us to confront the terrifying distance that can exist between what a human being says and what a human being actually treasures.
“Eat and drink,” the man says.
Then Scripture exposes him:
“but his heart is not with thee.”
There it is.
His mouth arrived.
His food arrived.
His manners arrived.
His heart never did.
And perhaps that sentence deserves to sit with us for a moment.
Because you can bring your body into church while your heart remains somewhere else.
You can sing about surrender while privately negotiating the terms.
You can give money while craving applause.
You can serve while secretly needing recognition.
You can forgive publicly while prosecuting someone privately in the courtroom of your imagination.
You can tell everyone that God is enough while building your identity on whether people notice you.
You can post Scripture while starving spiritually.
You can look alive while becoming exhausted inside.
You can know Christian vocabulary so well that eventually even you stop noticing when your lips and your heart have become strangers.
Jesus repeatedly went after this division.
He did not merely deal with polished appearances.
He went after hearts.
Speaking about religious hypocrisy, Jesus quoted Isaiah:
“This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.”
—Matthew 15:8, KJV
Read that slowly.
Their mouths knew where God was.
Their hearts didn't follow.
That is frightening because Christianity can be imitated externally.
You can learn when to say “Amen.”
You can learn the songs.
You can learn the language.
You can learn how Christians dress, post, pray, speak, debate, worship, and testify.
You can learn how to appear spiritually healthy.
But you cannot fool Christ.
People see the invitation.
Jesus sees the calculation.
People hear “Eat and drink.”
Jesus sees whether your heart is actually there.
And this is where the Gospel becomes infinitely better than motivational thinking.
Because Christianity does not say:
“Your biggest problem is that you have been thinking too negatively about yourself.”
Christianity goes deeper.
Jesus said:
“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts…”
—Mark 7:21, KJV
Notice the direction.
The biblical problem is not merely bad thoughts floating around outside us that we need to replace with successful thoughts.
Something inside humanity has gone wrong.
Sin reaches into our desires.
Our loves.
Our motives.
Our imaginations.
Our ambitions.
Our relationships.
Our worship.
Our generosity.
Our private thoughts.
Our hidden calculations.
That means you do not merely need a more positive mindset.
You need redemption.
You do not merely need better affirmations.
You need reconciliation with God.
You do not merely need to visualize a better version of yourself.
You need Christ.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because if “as a man thinks, so is he” becomes a formula for self-creation, eventually Jesus becomes unnecessary.
The hero becomes your mindset.
The savior becomes your thinking.
The gospel becomes self-improvement.
Faith becomes technique.
And Christianity quietly turns into motivational philosophy wearing Bible verses.
But the biblical Gospel does something radically different.
It tells you the truth about yourself…
and then introduces you to Someone who can save you.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people think more positively.
He came for sinners.
He came for hypocrites.
He came for the ashamed.
He came for the greedy.
He came for people whose mouths and hearts do not always agree.
He came for people hiding things.
He came for people who promised God they would stop and then returned to the same sin.
He came for people who worship on Sunday and wrestle with darkness on Monday.
He came for people who have discovered that knowing what is right does not automatically give them the power to become righteous.
He came for people exactly like us.
That is why the cross is so offensive to human pride and so beautiful to the broken sinner.
At Calvary, God does not congratulate humanity for discovering its hidden potential.
The cross announces that our condition was serious enough that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And forgiveness is not purchased by your positive thinking, spiritual performance, religious reputation, or ability to reinvent yourself.
It is grace.
Grace.
That word destroys both despair and pride.
Because grace tells the worst sinner:
“You are not beyond the reach of Christ.”
And grace tells the proudest religious person:
“You cannot save yourself.”
Maybe you have been pretending.
Maybe everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
Maybe it isn't.
Maybe everyone thinks your faith is strong.
Maybe you barely prayed this week.
Maybe people come to you for encouragement while you secretly wonder whether you have anything left yourself.
Maybe there is an addiction nobody knows about.
Maybe there is bitterness you keep baptizing as “discernment.”
Maybe there is envy underneath your criticism.
Maybe you have become very skilled at saying:
“Eat and drink.”
While your heart whispers something completely different.
Here is the Gospel invitation:
Stop hiding.
Not because exposure saves you.
Because Christ receives repentant sinners.
You do not need to clean yourself up enough to approach the cross.
You come because you cannot clean your own heart.
David understood this when he cried:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
—Psalm 51:10, KJV
Create.
Not decorate.
Not disguise.
Not manage.
Create.
That prayer understands something modern self-help often cannot tolerate:
sometimes the answer is not finding a better version of yourself.
Sometimes you need God to do what you cannot do.
And this is why biblical transformation cannot be reduced to “think better thoughts.”
Yes, Scripture absolutely cares about our minds.
Paul tells believers to be transformed by the renewing of their minds in Romans 12:2.
Philippians 4:8 deliberately directs believers toward what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and worthy of praise.
Christianity is not anti-thought.
It is deeply concerned with truth filling the mind.
But biblical renewal is not manifestation.
It is not “I think it, therefore the universe must give it to me.”
It is not “I imagine myself wealthy, therefore wealth becomes spiritually inevitable.”
It is not “my thoughts create reality.”
Biblical transformation is God conforming redeemed people to the character of Christ.
And Christ does not merely change what you say.
He changes what you love.
The miser in Proverbs says:
“Eat and drink.”
His heart says:
“Look what this is costing me.”
Jesus looks at undeserving sinners and gives Himself.
Do you see the contrast?
The begrudging host counts every morsel.
Christ gives Himself.
The begrudging host appears generous while resenting the cost.
Christ knows the cost and goes willingly toward the cross.
The host's table reveals hypocrisy.
Christ's table reveals grace.
And perhaps that is the deepest place this misunderstood proverb can finally take us.
Away from ourselves.
Toward Jesus.
Because the goal of Scripture was never to turn you into someone obsessed with constructing the perfect version of yourself.
The goal is Christ.
Knowing Him.
Trusting Him.
Following Him.
Being forgiven by Him.
Being transformed by Him.
Learning to love because He loved you first.
Learning generosity from the One who gave Himself.
Learning forgiveness from the One who forgave His enemies.
Learning truth from the One who called Himself the Truth.
Learning surrender from the One who prayed in Gethsemane:
“not my will, but thine, be done.”
Maybe you came into this article expecting a Bible-study correction.
Maybe somewhere along the way the verse started reading you instead.
That happens.
We open Scripture thinking we are examining a text…
and suddenly God's Word exposes the examiner.
So ask yourself something uncomfortable.
Where are your lips saying one thing while your heart is saying another?
Where have you become the smiling host?
Where are you performing what you no longer possess?
Where are you calling something “obedience” while secretly bargaining with God?
Where have you learned to appear healed instead of admitting you are hurting?
Where are you pretending?
Don't answer me.
Answer Christ.
Because Jesus already knows.
And strangely, that is incredibly good news.
The One before whom hiding is impossible is also the One before whom repentance is possible.
You don't have to manufacture a better image.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come back.
Let grace reach the room you keep locked.
Let Christ confront the thing your Christian vocabulary has learned to conceal.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Jesus…
and Jesus restored Peter.
Thomas doubted…
and Jesus met him.
Paul persecuted Christians…
and grace turned the persecutor into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The cross itself looked like the greatest scandal imaginable—the righteous Christ crucified between criminals.
Then came Sunday morning.
The stone moved.
The tomb emptied.
Death did not get the final sentence.
Jesus did.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your scandal never existed.
Not by calling sin harmless.
Not by replacing repentance with inspirational language.
He rewrites everything through truth, repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and grace.
Be honest.
Not for appearances.
Let it become a confession.
There are moments when three honest words are worth more than three paragraphs of pretending.
Then think about one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person who keeps quoting this verse as motivational advice.
The believer quietly confusing Christianity with manifestation.
The friend whose smile has become camouflage.
The person who serves everybody but is collapsing privately.
The person who needs to discover that Jesus is not asking them to become their own savior.
Save it too.
Because sooner or later, we all need the reminder that Scripture deserves context and our hearts deserve examination.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him—not through a transaction.
A share costs you seconds.
But God may use the truth someone encounters through it far beyond what either of us will ever see.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who walked away from church.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who doesn't believe yet.
Invite the Christian who desperately wants to understand the Bible rather than merely collect Bible quotes.
Follow. Save. Share. Join the conversation.
But above everything else…
follow Jesus.
Because Proverbs 23:7 was never a magic formula teaching you how to think yourself into the person you dream of becoming.
It was exposing the dangerous difference between appearances and the heart.
And the Gospel answers that exposure with something infinitely greater than positive thinking.
A crucified and risen Savior.
You don't need to become your own miracle.
You need Jesus.
You don't need another mask.
You need grace.
You don't need to convince Christ that your heart is clean.
You need to bring Him the heart that isn't.
And perhaps the verse we spent years using to tell ourselves what we could become was waiting all along to expose who we really are beneath the words.
Jesus does not merely hear the invitation coming from your lips. He sees the heart sitting behind the table.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY USED HER SEXUAL SIN AS A WEAPON—AND JESUS SAW THROUGH THEM
paragraphs: THEY USED HER SEXUAL SIN AS A WEAPON—AND JESUS SAW THROUGH THEM

They dragged her shame into public, quoted Scripture over her exposed life, and expected Jesus to help destroy her. Instead, He exposed something far more terrifying than her adultery: the hearts of people who could hate another person while convincing themselves they were defending God.
Imagine being remembered for the worst thing you ever did.
Not your childhood.
Not the nights you cried where nobody could hear you.
Not the prayers you whispered when you wanted to change.
Not the good you once did.
Not the person you hoped you would become.
Just your sin.
One moment.
One failure.
One scandal.
And suddenly that becomes your name.
That is how millions of people have met the woman in John 8.
We do not know her name.
We do not know where she grew up.
We do not know whether she had children.
We do not know how long she had been trapped in that sin.
We do not know what happened inside her heart before that morning.
Scripture simply brings us into the moment when religious leaders dragged a woman caught in adultery into the temple and placed her in the middle of a crowd.
And there she stood.
Exposed.
Humiliated.
Guilty.
Surrounded.
Waiting for stones.
But the most frightening thing in the scene may not be the woman’s sexual sin.
It may be how easily human beings can turn another person’s sin into a weapon.

Before going further, biblical honesty requires us to acknowledge something important. John 7:53–8:11 has a well-known textual history. The earliest Greek manuscripts of John do not contain this passage, and ancient manuscripts place it in different locations. Christians should never hide that fact. Faith does not need frightened scholarship or concealed evidence. At the same time, the account has a very ancient history within the Christian textual tradition and has been received and preached throughout much of the Church for centuries. So we should handle it with both reverence and honesty, refusing to pretend that the manuscript question does not exist.

And what this account portrays about Jesus harmonizes powerfully with truths unquestionably taught throughout the New Testament: Christ confronts hypocrisy, refuses to participate in self-righteous condemnation, calls sinners to repentance, and came not merely to expose sinners but to save them.
Now look again at the courtyard.
“They caught her.”
That matters.
This was not merely gossip.
The accusation presented in the narrative was adultery.
Jesus never responds by pretending sexual sin is harmless.
He never calls darkness light.
He never tells her morality is subjective.
He never says, “Just follow your heart.”
Jesus will eventually tell her to leave her life of sin.
Grace does not require God to rename sin.
Grace means God can rescue the sinner without becoming dishonest about the sin.
But there is something strange about the accusation.
Where is the man?
Adultery requires two people.
The Law itself did not merely condemn the woman. Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 explicitly held both the adulterer and adulteress accountable.
Yet only she is standing there.
We must be careful here.
Scripture does not tell us why the man was absent, so we should not invent a conspiracy and call it biblical truth.
But we are absolutely permitted to notice what the text itself makes impossible to ignore:
They brought the woman.
They did not bring the man.
And John explicitly tells us that their question was a trap intended to give them grounds for accusing Jesus.
Suddenly she was more than a sinner in their eyes.
She was useful.
Her humiliation had become ammunition.
Her brokenness had become leverage.
Her scandal had become a theological weapon.
And perhaps that is why this story still feels painfully modern.
Because people still do this.
We screenshot failures.
We circulate scandals.
We whisper prayer requests containing details that were never ours to distribute.
We turn somebody’s collapse into entertainment.
We expose people not because we desperately want restoration, but because outrage makes us feel morally taller.
Sometimes we even use Scripture while doing it.
And that should terrify every Christian reading this.
Because possessing a Bible does not automatically mean our hearts resemble Jesus.
The devil quoted Scripture in the wilderness.
Religious vocabulary can occupy a mouth while cruelty occupies the heart.
There is a difference between confronting sin because you love someone and exposing sin because you enjoy watching someone bleed.
Jesus knew the difference.
They said to Him, in effect, “Moses commanded judgment. What do You say?”
They thought they had constructed the perfect trap.
But Jesus bent down.
And wrote on the ground.
For centuries people have wondered what He wrote.
Names?
Commandments?
Their secret sins?
Jeremiah?
We do not know.
And perhaps humility requires us to stop pretending we do.
Scripture does not tell us.
What Scripture does tell us is far more powerful.
They kept pressing Him.
So Jesus stood and said:
“Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος… βαλέτω λίθον.”
Ho anamartētos hymōn prōtos… baletō lithon.
The force of the statement is:
“Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone.”
That word is devastating:
ἀναμάρτητος — anamartētos.
Without sin.
Free from sin.
And suddenly the trial changed.
A few seconds earlier everyone was looking at her.
Now everyone had to look inward.
That is what Jesus does.
We arrive carrying someone else’s evidence.
Jesus turns on the light inside us.
We arrive prepared to discuss their pornography.
Their affair.
Their abortion.
Their addiction.
Their divorce.
Their secret messages.
Their drunkenness.
Their hypocrisy.
Their past.
Their sexual failure.
Their scandal.
And somehow, standing before Jesus, the question changes from:
“What did they do?”
to:
“What is hiding inside me?”
That does not make their sin innocent.
It makes our self-righteousness impossible.
One by one...
they left.
Can you hear the stones hitting the ground?
One.
Then another.
Then another.
The older ones first.
Footsteps moving away.
Voices disappearing.
Dust settling.
Until the woman who had been surrounded by accusers discovered that she was standing before the only Person there who was actually without sin.
Think about that.
The only One morally qualified to condemn her was the One who refused to join their spectacle.
Jesus looked at her.
“Woman, where are they?”
Imagine lifting your head after expecting death.
“Has no one condemned you?”
“No one, Lord.”
Then come words that have carried broken people through centuries:
“οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω.”
Oude egō se katakrinō.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
But do not stop reading there.
Because modern culture desperately wants half of Jesus’ sentence.
We want:
“Neither do I condemn you.”
We are less enthusiastic about:
“Go, and sin no more.”
Yet Jesus said both.
That is the Gospel-shaped tension.
No condemnation does not mean no transformation.
Grace is not God telling you that your chains are jewelry.
Grace breaks the chains.
Jesus did not say:
“Your adultery does not matter.”
He essentially told her:
Your accusers do not own your future...
and neither does your sin.
Go.
Leave it.
There is another life now.
This is where the story stops being about a nameless woman standing in an ancient courtyard.
Because now it becomes about you.
What have you done that you hope nobody ever discovers?
What browser history would embarrass you?
What conversation would destroy the image people have of you?
Whose spouse have you been thinking about?
Who are you secretly messaging?
What relationship have you justified even though the Holy Spirit has been convicting you?
What pornography keeps returning after every promise that “this was the last time”?
What memory makes you wonder whether God could still want you?
Maybe your scandal was sexual.
Maybe it was not.
Maybe nobody caught you.
That can be worse.
Because when nobody catches us, we become skilled at appearing alive while something inside us slowly dies.
You can sing worship songs while hiding.
You can preach while hiding.
You can post Bible verses while hiding.
You can have a Christian profile picture and a secret life.
You can tell everyone “God is good” while desperately hoping nobody looks underneath the floorboards of your soul.
But Jesus already knows.
Every message.
Every fantasy.
Every compromise.
Every deleted photograph.
Every lie.
Every lonely night.
Every rationalization.
Every promise you broke.
He knows.
And still He calls you toward Himself.
Not toward denial.
Toward repentance.
There is an enormous difference.
Repentance is not paying God back for your sin.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who paid what you could never pay.
Jesus did not come because respectable people needed religious improvement.
He came because sinners needed resurrection.
The Gospel is not that sinful people learned how to polish themselves until God tolerated them.
The Gospel is that the spotless Son of God entered our ruin.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly toward the cross.
And there, the sinless One bore judgment for sinners.
The stones we deserved did not become irrelevant.
Judgment did not simply evaporate because God decided sin was no longer serious.
At Calvary we discover how serious sin actually is...
and how astonishing grace actually is.
Christ was crucified.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And because He lives, scandal does not have to write your final chapter.
That affair does not have to become your identity.
That pornography does not have to become your master.
That abortion does not have to become the only word you hear when you look into the mirror.
That divorce does not have to become your name.
That night does not have to own the rest of your life.
That secret does not outrank the blood of Jesus Christ.
But hear this carefully:
Grace is not permission to continue destroying yourself.
Jesus does not rescue us so that we can comfortably return to the same grave.
“Go... and sin no more.”
There is tenderness there.
And authority.
Mercy.
And holiness.
Forgiveness.
And transformation.
Jesus does not merely want you uncondemned.
He wants you free.
Somebody reading this has been asking God to forgive something you keep returning to.
You cry afterward.
You promise afterward.
You hate yourself afterward.
Then loneliness comes.
Temptation comes.
The phone lights up.
The memory returns.
The craving wakes up.
And suddenly you are back where you swore you would never be again.
Listen carefully.
Stop confusing shame with repentance.
Shame says, “Hide from Jesus until you become worthy.”
The Gospel says, “Run to Jesus because you never were.”
Bring the whole filthy truth.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the church version.
Not the version where you somehow remain the hero.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess.
Turn.
Ask for help.
Cut off access where necessary.
Bring trusted, mature believers into the battle.
Seek accountability.
Repair what can biblically and responsibly be repaired.
Stop protecting the sin that is killing you.
And receive the mercy Christ purchased.
Perhaps you are not the woman in this story.
Perhaps you are holding the stone.
That possibility should make us tremble.
Maybe somebody failed, and you secretly enjoy knowing it.
Maybe someone’s marriage collapsed and you forwarded the story.
Maybe somebody confessed sexual sin and instead of grieving for their soul, you became fascinated by the details.
Maybe you have been calling cruelty “discernment.”
Maybe you have been calling gossip “concern.”
Maybe you have been calling humiliation “accountability.”
Maybe you have been defending biblical morality with an unbiblical heart.
Put the stone down.
Truth does not need your hatred to remain true.
Holiness does not require humiliation.
Biblical correction aims toward repentance and restoration, not entertainment.
And if a brother or sister falls, remember that you are not standing above them because you were naturally better.
If you stand at all, you stand by grace.
The Church must become a place where sin can be confessed without sin being celebrated...
where holiness can be preached without wounded people being treated like garbage...
where sexual immorality is confronted...
where repentance is real...
where accountability matters...
where victims are protected...
where truth is not softened...
and where repentant sinners discover that Jesus Christ still receives people whose lives became scandals.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not pretending consequences never exist.
Not pretending repentance eliminates every earthly result of our choices.
But believing that Jesus Christ can take a human being whose story looks irredeemable and begin writing something new.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your sin. Protect appropriate privacy. But you can take one small step out of darkness.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And if you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray without demanding your private details:
“Pray for me.”
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of the end of years of hiding.
Someone scrolling beneath your comment may desperately need proof that Christians are not people who never became broken.
We are people who discovered a Savior inside the wreckage.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Not as religious decoration.
You may never know who reads it at 2:17 a.m.
You may never know whose hand stops before opening pornography again.
You may never know whose affair ends because conviction finally broke through.
You may never know who decides not to abandon Christ because this reminded them that Jesus receives repentant sinners.
And when you share, do not merely send this to the obvious person.
Send it privately to the believer who stopped attending church because shame convinced them everyone would judge them.
Send it to the Christian who is fighting temptation.
Send it to the seeker.
Even send it to the person who says they no longer believe.
You cannot save anybody.
Neither can Gospel Warrior.
Jesus saves.
Our responsibility is simply to keep carrying the message toward people who need to hear it.
Come to Christ.
Not to a page.
Not to merchandise.
Not to a personality.
Not to religion.
To Christ.
Because one day every human hiding place disappears.
And on that day your greatest need will not be a reputation clean enough to impress religious people.
You will need a Savior.
The woman entered that courtyard surrounded by people who knew what she had done.
She left having encountered Someone who knew what she could become by grace.
Perhaps that is why this story refuses to die.
Because somewhere inside almost every human heart is the fear that if people really knew us, they would reach for stones.
And somewhere deeper is the desperate hope that Jesus already knows...
and is still calling our name.
So put down the stone.
Come out of hiding.
Confess the sin.
Receive His mercy.
Leave the darkness.
Follow Jesus.
And remember this when your past begins screaming again:
The hands that could have condemned the sinner would soon be stretched upon a cross to save sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU’RE PROBABLY A GOOD PERSON. ROMANS 3:23 SAYS THAT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH.
paragraphs: YOU’RE PROBABLY A GOOD PERSON. ROMANS 3:23 SAYS THAT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH.
What “All Have Sinned and Fall Short” Really Says About Human Goodness—and Why the Verse That Humiliates Our Pride May Be One of the Most Hope-Filled Sentences Ever Written
There is a sentence almost nobody wants to hear.
Especially the person who has tried to live decently.
You worked for what you have.
You love your children.
You help people when you can.

You have never murdered anyone. You are not robbing houses. You are not deliberately destroying lives. Maybe you give to people who need help. Maybe you have stayed beside someone in a hospital room. Maybe you have forgiven things nobody knows you had to forgive.
And when you look at some of the darkness in this world, there is a thought that can quietly rise inside you:
I know I’m not perfect… but surely I’m a good person.
Then Romans 3 walks into the room.
And it refuses to flatter you.
But if you stay long enough, you discover something astonishing.
It refuses to flatter you because God intends to give you something infinitely better than flattery.
Grace.
Paul writes:
Pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou theou.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
The sentence is short.
Its implications are devastating.
And its next words are breathtaking.
Because Romans 3:23 was never meant to be ripped away from Romans 3:24.
Paul continues:
“δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι…”
Being justified freely—without payment, without earning it—by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That changes everything.
The scandal is not merely that sinners are worse than they think.
The greater scandal is that God’s grace is better than sinners could ever deserve.
Maybe you have heard Romans 3:23 used like a hammer.
“All have sinned.”
End of discussion.
But Paul was not writing a slogan. He was constructing an argument that systematically dismantles every human hiding place so that every sinner can see why Jesus Christ is not merely helpful.
He is necessary.
And that includes the respectable sinner.
The generous sinner.
The religious sinner.
The churchgoing sinner.
The sinner who volunteers.
The sinner who pays his bills.
The sinner everybody calls “a wonderful person.”
And yes…
the sinner writing these words.
The sinner reading them.
“All.”
The Greek begins with πάντες—pantes.
All.
Not merely notorious people.
Not merely criminals.
Not merely adulterers, addicts, abusers, hypocrites, liars, thieves, or people whose scandals became public.
All.
That word leaves no VIP entrance into the kingdom of God.
No résumé.
No family name.
No denomination.
No charitable record.
No amount of religious activity.
No secret folder marked, “But look at all the good things I did.”
And here is where Romans 3 is sometimes misunderstood.
Paul is not saying human beings are incapable of doing anything that appears genuinely kind or beneficial toward another person.
A non-Christian can feed someone who is hungry.
An unbelieving father can sacrifice for his children.
An atheist can return a lost wallet.
A person who does not know Christ can give money to the poor, care for a dying parent, rescue someone in danger, show patience to a child, or perform extraordinary acts of civic courage.
Christians do not need to deny obvious human kindness in order to defend biblical truth.
The question Romans 3 forces upon us is deeper.
Not:
Have you ever done something good?
But:
Are you righteous before a perfectly holy God?
Those are radically different questions.
Imagine standing beside an ocean holding a glass of clean water.
The water may really be clean.
But nobody would confuse your glass with the ocean.

In a similar way, human beings can perform acts that are good in a real, creaturely, social sense while still falling infinitely short of God's perfect holiness and having no goodness capable of cancelling our guilt.
Our mistake is comparing horizontally.
We look sideways.
We compare ourselves with the alcoholic.
The adulterer.
The corrupt politician.
The abusive father.
The woman who abandoned her children.
The man in prison.
The hypocrite exposed on television.
And suddenly we feel clean.
But Romans 3 turns our face upward.
The standard is not your neighbor.
The standard is not the worst person you know.
The standard is not whether society considers you respectable.
Paul says humanity falls short of the glory of God.
That is an entirely different measurement.
You can be taller than every person standing beside you and still be nowhere near touching the stars.
And that is why comparison is such a dangerous spiritual anesthetic.
It can make a dying person feel healthy simply because somebody nearby appears sicker.
You say:
“I have never cheated on my spouse.”
Good.
But have you loved God perfectly?
“I give to charity.”
Good.
But has every motive of your heart always been pure?
“I never killed anyone.”
Good.
But have hatred, bitterness, contempt, revenge, or cruelty ever found shelter inside you?
“I go to church.”
Good.
But have you ever worshiped while your heart was miles away?
“I help people.”
Good.
But have you never secretly wanted recognition for being the person who helps?
“I believe in God.”
Even then the question remains:
Have you loved Him with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength every moment of your life?
Suddenly the courtroom becomes quiet.
Because the Gospel does not merely examine the polished exterior.
God sees the heart.
He sees the generosity that secretly wanted applause.
The apology designed to end an argument rather than heal a wound.
The prayer spoken publicly while resentment remained privately protected.
The worship song sung while pride sat comfortably on the throne.
The kindness performed partly because we wanted to believe something good about ourselves.
And even our genuinely loving acts cannot travel backward through history and erase sins already committed.
You cannot hug enough people today to make yesterday’s lie become truth.
You cannot donate enough money tomorrow to make yesterday’s lust become purity.
You cannot serve enough meals to make yesterday’s hatred become love.
Good works are good.
But good works are terrible saviors.
They were never designed to carry the weight of your eternity.
This is where the Gospel becomes offensive to human pride.
We desperately want to contribute something to the verdict.
Surely God will place our sins on one side of a scale and our kindness on the other.
Surely He will notice that we tried.
Surely heaven contains some divine accounting department where our good deeds can compensate for our rebellion.
But Scripture destroys that fantasy.

Paul says salvation is by grace through faith, not from ourselves, not from works so that nobody can boast. And then—beautifully—he says those who belong to Christ are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
Not good works therefore Christ accepts us.
Christ saves us therefore a transformed life begins producing good works.
Good works are not the purchase price of salvation.
They are fruit growing from a life touched by grace.
The Gospel does not say:
“Become good enough and Jesus will take you.”
It says:
“You cannot make yourself righteous before God, so Jesus came for sinners.”
That is why Christ matters.
If human goodness could save us, Calvary becomes unnecessary.
If moral improvement could reconcile us to God, Jesus could have remained in heaven and sent us better instructions.
If salvation were simply “try harder,” humanity needed a coach.
If salvation were simply education, humanity needed a teacher.
If salvation were simply inspiration, humanity needed a motivational speaker.
But Scripture says we needed redemption.
We needed a Savior.
We needed Jesus.
The cross announces something simultaneously humiliating and glorious:
Your sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
God's grace was great enough that Christ willingly did.
And perhaps that is what hurts.
Because grace does something human pride hates.
Grace removes bragging rights.
At the foot of the cross, the respectable businessman kneels beside the recovering addict.
The pastor kneels beside the prisoner.
The lifelong church member kneels beside the prodigal who wasted twenty years.
The virgin kneels beside the former prostitute.
The person whose sins were hidden kneels beside the person whose sins became headlines.
Nobody arrives holding a trophy.
Nobody walks through heaven saying, “I knew I was better than them.”
We come empty-handed.
We come guilty.
We come needing mercy.
And somehow this is not bad news.
It is liberation.
Because if salvation depended upon you becoming good enough, when would you finally know that you had done enough?
How many prayers?
How many donations?
How many years of obedience?
How many tears?
How many Bible chapters?
How many people helped?
How many temptations resisted?
How much regret would finally pay the debt?
You would spend your entire life staring at yourself.
Was I sincere enough?
Did I repent enough?
Did I serve enough?
Did I sacrifice enough?
Am I finally enough?
The Gospel turns your eyes away from your résumé and toward a cross.
Toward Christ.
Toward blood shed for sinners.
Toward a Savior who does what human morality never could.
And maybe this is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needs:
You do not need to pretend you are better than you are when your hope rests in Someone infinitely better than you could ever be.
That is freedom.
You can finally confess.
You can finally stop hiding.
You can finally say:
“Yes. I sinned.”
“Yes. I hurt people.”
“Yes. There are things I regret.”
“Yes. Some of my motives were ugly.”
“Yes. I knew better.”
“Yes. I walked away.”
“Yes. I looked religious while hiding things.”
“Yes. I need mercy.”
Because Christianity does not begin when a bad person successfully convinces God that he is good.
Christianity begins when a sinner stops defending himself and runs to Christ.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
It is surrendering our excuses.
It is agreeing with God about sin and turning toward the Savior.
And there is another side we cannot miss.
Once grace finds you, grace does not give you permission to remain comfortably unchanged.
The Christ who forgives also transforms.
The Gospel is not:
“You sinned, but don't worry about it.”
It is:
“You sinned. Christ died and rose. Come to Him. Receive mercy. Follow Him. Let Him remake what sin distorted.”
