Jesus does not merely improve the public relations surrounding your scandal.
He begins rewriting the person.
Pride begins learning humility.
Greed begins learning generosity.
Lust begins learning purity.
Bitterness begins learning forgiveness.
Selfishness begins learning sacrifice.
A liar begins learning truth.
A taker begins becoming a giver.
A person who once lived entirely for himself begins whispering something that would once have sounded impossible:
“Jesus, my life belongs to You.”
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
Not without battles.
But genuinely.
That is why Christian good works matter enormously.
Not because they purchase heaven.
Because they reveal the transforming fingerprints of the One who saved us.
You are not saved because you performed enough good works.
You are saved by grace through faith in Christ—and the grace that saves begins teaching your life a different way to walk.
That means Romans 3:23 is not permission to shrug and say, “Everybody sins, so who cares?”
Quite the opposite.
Everybody sins.
Therefore everybody desperately needs Jesus.
Including your father.
Your daughter.
Your closest friend.
Your coworker.
Your spouse.
The person you cannot stand.
The person everyone admires.
The person secretly falling apart tonight.
And the person staring back at you from the mirror.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe there was never a viral post.
No police report.
No affair exposed.
No addiction discovered.
No dramatic testimony.
Maybe your scandal lived entirely behind your ribs.
Pride.
Envy.
Secret lust.
Coldness toward God.
Resentment.
Self-righteousness.
Years spent believing you were good because you had carefully chosen worse people as your measuring stick.
God saw it.
And still the Gospel came looking for you.
That is grace.
Not God pretending your sin never mattered.
God dealing with sin through Jesus Christ.
Not God lowering holiness until you could reach it.
Christ coming down to rescue those who could not climb high enough.
Not good people earning their way into God's family.
Sinners receiving what they could never purchase.
That is the scandal of grace.
And perhaps the greatest shock of Romans 3:23 is that verse 23 does not get the final word.
Verse 24 follows it.
Sin does not get the final word.
Grace speaks.
Your failure does not get the final word.
Christ speaks.
Your worst chapter does not automatically become the ending.
Jesus still writes.
So stop presenting God with your moral résumé.
Bring Him your surrender.
Stop saying, “At least I'm better than…”
Look at Jesus.
Stop asking whether you have accumulated enough goodness to deserve Him.
You haven't.
Neither have I.
That is precisely why grace is grace.
Come empty-handed.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come trusting not in your record, but in Christ.
Talk to Jesus.
Right there.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary required.
Confess what He already knows.
Ask Him for mercy.
Trust in Christ.
Someone reading the same comments may realize tonight that they are not the only person still fighting.
Your honesty may become another person's courage.
And please don't keep this article inside a private religious bubble.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” somehow proves your Christianity. It cannot.
It isn't.
Somebody may need to discover that Jesus did not come merely to make good people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
There will probably come a day when pride tells you, “You're doing pretty well.”
Or shame tells you, “You've done too much.”
Come back and remember:
Neither pride nor shame gets to define the Gospel.
Jesus does.
And there is much more waiting for believers who are serious about growing.
But remember what matters most.
Sharing this article cannot save you.
Owning Christian books cannot save you.
Being generous cannot save you.
Being religious cannot save you.
Being nicer than the person next door cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And once that truth reaches the deepest place in your heart, Romans 3:23 stops sounding merely like an accusation.
It becomes the doorway to astonishing hope.
“All have sinned.”
Yes.
You too.
Me too.
Every one of us.
But the sentence continues into grace.
The guilty can be justified.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The proud can finally put down their trophies.
The broken can stop pretending.
The sinner can come home.
Not because human goodness finally became impressive enough for God…
but because Jesus Christ was always enough for sinners.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you after everything else fades:
When your goodness runs out and your excuses finally fall silent, you may discover that Jesus was never waiting for your résumé—He was calling for your surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABOVE ALL ELSE, GUARD YOUR HEART—WHAT ARE YOU LETTING INSIDE?
paragraphs: ABOVE ALL ELSE, GUARD YOUR HEART—WHAT ARE YOU LETTING INSIDE?

You are guarding your passwords, your money, your reputation, and your home. But Scripture warns you to guard something even closer—because what enters there can quietly shape the direction of your entire life.
There are things you would never knowingly invite into your house.
You would not open the front door at midnight, step aside, and tell a thief, “Make yourself comfortable.”
You would not hand a stranger your bank password.
You would not knowingly pour poison into your drinking water and tell yourself, “It’s only a little.”
You understand boundaries when something valuable is at stake.
But what about your heart?
What have you been allowing through that door?
What have you been watching until it no longer bothers you?
What voices have been speaking into you so consistently that you have stopped asking whether they are telling you the truth?
What resentment have you rehearsed?
What fantasy have you fed?
What secret conversation have you justified?
What comparison has been slowly poisoning your gratitude?
What wound have you allowed to become your identity?
What sin have you renamed so you would not have to repent of it?
And what if the greatest danger to your spiritual life is not always something violently attacking you from the outside...
but something you have quietly given permission to live inside?
That is why one sentence in Proverbs feels less like decorative wisdom and more like an alarm:
“Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.”
Proverbs 4:23.
The Hebrew makes the warning even more vivid:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ כִּי־מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים
Mi-kol mishmar, netzor libbekha, ki mimmennu totze'ot chayyim.
A close rendering is:
“More than all guarding, guard your heart, for from it are the outgoings of life.”
Read that slowly.
Guard your heart.
Not because Scripture teaches that every emotion you feel should be trusted.
Not because Christianity is about following your heart.
Actually, Scripture repeatedly refuses that sentimental idea.

The biblical “heart”—לֵב (lev) or לֵבָב (levav)—is far richer than our modern use of the word. In Scripture, the heart can involve thought, desire, intention, affection, moral decision, and the inner orientation of a person. It is not merely where you “feel.”
It is the inner person from which your life is being directed.
That changes everything.
Proverbs is not merely saying, “Protect your feelings.”
It is saying:
Watch what is shaping the person you are becoming.
And the surrounding verses prove it.
“Put away from you crooked speech,” Proverbs says. “Let your eyes look directly forward.” Then it speaks about pondering the path of your feet and refusing to turn toward evil.
Mouth.
Eyes.
Feet.
Heart.
This is not mystical self-help.
This is wisdom for the whole life.
What fills and governs the inner person eventually shows itself in speech, attention, choices, habits, relationships, and direction.
Jesus takes us even deeper.
He says:
“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”
Matthew 12:34.
Then, in Mark 7, Jesus destroys one of humanity’s favorite excuses—the belief that our deepest problem is always somewhere outside us.
“For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery…”
Mark 7:21.
That is uncomfortable Christianity.
Because Jesus will not allow us to blame everything on culture, temptation, childhood, social media, our spouse, our enemies, our circumstances, or the devil.
Those things can influence us. Some can wound us terribly. Temptation is real. Spiritual warfare is real. Other people can genuinely sin against us.
But Jesus puts His finger somewhere we would rather He did not.
Within.
The heart.
And suddenly “guard your heart” becomes much more serious than avoiding people who hurt your feelings.
You are guarding the command center of your life while simultaneously recognizing that the command center itself needs redemption.
That is the tension.
And that is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because if your heart were naturally pure, you would only need protection.
But because the human heart has been corrupted by sin, you need something far greater.
You need transformation.
You need Jesus.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been letting inside.
Your family sees you functioning.
Your coworkers see you smiling.
Your church sees you worshiping.
Your Facebook friends see the photograph you chose to post.
But God sees what happens after everyone else goes to sleep.
He sees the messages.
The browser history.
The envy.
The private rage.
The fantasy.
The secret attachment.
The bitterness you keep replaying because somehow being angry feels safer than forgiving.
He sees the insecurity hiding underneath the confidence.
He sees the person who wounded you still occupying rooms inside your mind without paying rent.
He sees the endless scrolling that leaves your soul emptier.
He sees how badly you want someone to tell you that you matter.
He sees the temptation you have fought so many times that you are embarrassed to admit you are still fighting it.
And perhaps most frighteningly...
He sees the things that used to convict you but barely disturb you anymore.
Sin rarely walks into the heart announcing:
“I am here to destroy you.”
Sometimes it arrives disguised as relief.
Just one look.
Just one conversation.
Just one compromise.
Just one night.
Just one grudge.
Just one lie.
Just one more scroll.
Just one private indulgence because life has been difficult and you tell yourself you deserve something that makes you feel better.
Then one becomes ten.
Ten becomes normal.
Normal becomes defended.
Defended becomes identity.
And eventually you are protecting the very thing God is trying to rescue you from.
That is why guarding your heart requires more than asking, “Is this technically sinful?”
Sometimes wisdom asks a more penetrating question:
What is this doing to my love for Jesus?
Because something does not have to make you publicly abandon Christ to quietly cool your affection for Him.
Something can be lawful and still dominate you.
Something can entertain you while spiritually numbing you.
Something can make you laugh while teaching your conscience not to blush.
Something can be culturally normal while training your desires away from holiness.
Something can consume hours without ever appearing important enough to call an idol.
Paul understood this danger.
“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are helpful… I will not be dominated by anything.”
1 Corinthians 6:12.
That word should stop us.
Dominated.
What controls your attention?
What changes your mood when you cannot have it?
What occupies your imagination when the room becomes quiet?
What do you run toward when you are lonely?
What do you instinctively reach for when you are anxious?
What would be unusually painful to surrender if Jesus put His finger on it tonight?
Sometimes the thing sitting on the throne of your heart is revealed by the thing you cannot imagine living without.
And yes, that can include social media.
Entertainment.
Pornography.
Approval.
Money.
Success.
Romance.
Politics.
Anger.
Food.
Work.
Even ministry.
Even religious recognition.
The human heart can turn almost anything into something ultimate.
But here is where we must be careful.
“Guard your heart” does not mean “build walls around yourself so nobody can ever hurt you.”
Jesus was not emotionally unavailable.
He loved.
He wept.
He welcomed.
He touched lepers.
He ate with sinners.
He allowed betrayal close enough to kiss Him.
Biblical guarding is not the same thing as emotional isolation.
Some people have called their fear “discernment.”
Some have called unforgiveness “boundaries.”
Some have called suspicion “wisdom.”
Some have called emotional numbness “strength.”
But a guarded heart and a hardened heart are not the same thing.
A guarded heart remains surrendered to God.
A hardened heart resists Him.
And perhaps that distinction exposes something in us.
Because sometimes we are extraordinarily careful about keeping painful people out...
while being strangely careless about letting destructive things in.
We block the person who offended us but repeatedly consume content that feeds lust.
We avoid difficult conversations but entertain bitterness for years.
We protect ourselves from correction while opening ourselves endlessly to affirmation.
We say, “I’m protecting my peace,” when sometimes what we really mean is, “I do not want anyone challenging what I have decided to believe.”
But Jesus did not die merely to protect your comfort.
He died to redeem you.
There is a difference.
And this is where Proverbs 4:23 must eventually bring us to the Gospel.
Because you can unfollow every toxic account.
You can install every filter.
You can delete every app.
You can leave unhealthy relationships.
You can build better routines.
You can discipline your eyes.
You can clean your environment.
Those things may be wise.
But none of them can create a new heart.
David understood that.
After his devastating sin, he did not merely pray, “God, improve my habits.”
He cried:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”
Psalm 51:10.
The Hebrew verb translated “create” is בָּרָא (bara).
David understood that his problem went deeper than reputation management.
He needed God to do something in him that he could not accomplish by cosmetic spiritual improvement.
And centuries later, God promised through Ezekiel:
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.”
Ezekiel 36:26.
Then Jesus came.
Not simply to make bad people behave slightly better.
Not simply to give religious people better boundaries.
Not simply to provide motivational principles for protecting mental health.
Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Grace does not tell you your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we want to admit.
Grace tells you that your sin does not have to have the final word because Jesus paid for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
This is the scandal.
The lustful can be cleansed.
The bitter can forgive.
The adulterer can repent.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can bow.
The addicted can cry for mercy.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The wounded can learn not to become what wounded them.
The hypocrite can stop pretending.
The prodigal can come home.
Not because sin suddenly became insignificant...
but because Christ is greater.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere between the Hebrew words and these uncomfortable questions, something inside you became quiet.
Maybe a name came to mind.
An account.
A habit.
A relationship.
A website.
A conversation.
A memory.
A resentment.
A secret.
Maybe you already know what has been getting through the gate.
Do not merely feel guilty and keep scrolling.
Bring it to Christ.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
The New Testament word μετάνοια (metanoia) carries the idea of repentance—a decisive turning, a changed mind and orientation that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Christian repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning from sin toward God because His mercy has met you in Jesus Christ.
John writes:
1 John 1:9.
Notice the invitation.
Confess.
Not disguise.
Not rename.
Not curate.
Not manage appearances.
Confess.
The Gospel gives you permission to stop pretending.
Jesus already knows what is behind the door.
And He is still calling you.
So guard your heart—but do not try to become your own savior.
Guard what enters your eyes.
Guard what repeatedly enters your ears.
Guard the conversations feeding your desires.
Guard the bitterness you rehearse.
Guard the fantasies you entertain.
Guard the theology you absorb.
Guard the voices you trust.
Guard the private compromises nobody applauds or confronts.
But above all, keep bringing your heart under the lordship of Jesus Christ and filling your mind with what is true.
Paul writes:
Philippians 4:8.
You cannot control every thought that knocks.
You cannot prevent every temptation from appearing.
You cannot live in a world without ugliness.
But you do not have to give everything that knocks a bedroom and a key.
Some things need to be refused.
Some need to be confessed.
Some need to be deleted.
Some need to be unfollowed.
Some need accountability.
Some need forgiveness.
Some need professional help alongside faithful Christian community.
Some need you to stop negotiating and obey.
And some wounds need to be brought repeatedly before Jesus because healing does not always happen according to the timetable we wanted.
But hear this carefully:
Guarding your heart is not earning the love of God.
If you belong to Christ, obedience is the fruit of grace, not the price of grace.
You do not clean yourself enough to make Jesus willing to save you.
You come to Him because you cannot save yourself.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith,” Paul writes. “And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.”
Ephesians 2:8.
Then the same passage says we are created in Christ Jesus “for good works.”
Grace saves.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to walk differently.
That is why Christianity is neither “do whatever you want because God forgives” nor “be good enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better:
Christ saves sinners by grace, and the Christ who saves us begins changing the people He saves.
So perhaps tonight the question is not simply:
“Have I guarded my heart?”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, what have I been allowing inside that is teaching my heart to love something more than You?”
That prayer can become dangerous.
Because He may answer.
And you may need to delete something.
End something.
Confess something.
Forgive someone.
Call someone.
Ask for help.
Open your Bible again.
Return to church.
Get accountable.
Stop feeding the secret.
Stop defending the compromise.
Stop calling chains freedom.
And come home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. But you can make a simple declaration of surrender.
Come back to it the next time something is asking for access to your heart that has no business living there.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ alone saves, entirely by grace.

But if this message faithfully points people toward Christ, repentance, Scripture, forgiveness, and restoration, then helping put that truth in front of another person can be one simple way of using what you have to glorify God.
Someone losing a battle nobody knows exists.
Someone becoming numb to a sin that once terrified them.
Someone wondering whether Jesus would still receive them if the truth came out.
Let this article find them.
Because one day you may realize that the thing you kept calling “small” had been quietly asking for your whole heart.
And your heart was never created to belong to your chains.
It was created to bow before the King who breaks them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU HEARD EVERY WORD JESUS SAID—SO WHY DIDN’T IT CHANGE YOU?
paragraphs: YOU HEARD EVERY WORD JESUS SAID—SO WHY DIDN’T IT CHANGE YOU?
The terrifying meaning behind “He who has ears to hear, let him hear”—and why the greatest danger may not be rejecting Jesus openly, but hearing Him so often that His voice no longer disturbs you.
There is a frightening possibility almost nobody wants to consider.
You can sit in church and still not hear God.
You can own three Bibles.
You can underline verses.

You can know worship songs by heart, say “Amen” at exactly the right moment, share Christian posts, defend biblical doctrine, and even become known as the person everyone calls when they need prayer...
…and still become deaf to the very voice you claim to love.
Not physically deaf.
Something far more dangerous.
Spiritually unresponsive.
Jesus once stood before people who possessed perfectly functioning ears and said something so simple that we can easily miss how unsettling it really was:
“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”
In Greek, Mark 4:9 reads:
Ὃς ἔχει ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω.
Hos echei ōta akouein akouetō.
“Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”
The word translated “hear” comes from ἀκούω — akouō.
But Jesus was obviously not checking whether the crowd’s auditory nerves were functioning.
They had already heard the sound of His voice.
They heard the story.
They heard about the sower.
They heard about the seed.
They heard every syllable.
Yet Jesus still told them to hear.
Why?
Because there is a difference between sound entering your ear...
and truth entering your heart.
And maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
How many times has God already spoken to you through Scripture about the very thing you are still refusing to surrender?
That relationship.
That bitterness.
That secret habit.
That pride.
That hidden conversation.
That unforgiveness.
That compromise nobody at church knows about.
That private version of yourself you keep carefully separated from the Christian version everybody sees.
Maybe you have been asking God to speak.
But what if He already has?
What if the problem is not God's silence?
What if the problem is that you have learned how to hear Him without responding?
That is the danger Jesus was exposing.
And it did not begin in Mark.
Long before Jesus walked the roads of Galilee, God described His rebellious people through the prophet Jeremiah as people who possessed eyes but did not truly see and ears but did not truly hear.
Ezekiel used almost the same terrifying language.
Isaiah described people who kept hearing without understanding and seeing without perceiving.
So when Jesus spoke about ears that could hear, His Jewish listeners were standing inside a much older biblical warning.
The problem was never merely the ear.
It was the heart.

That is why Matthew's account of Jesus' teaching becomes even more uncomfortable. Jesus connects the people's inability to receive what they are hearing with Isaiah's prophecy and describes a heart that has grown dull.
Think about that phrase.
A dull heart.
Not necessarily an atheist heart.
Not necessarily a loudly rebellious heart.
A dull one.
A heart that used to tremble but now shrugs.
A conscience that used to hurt but now negotiates.
A person who once cried over sin but now explains it.
Someone who once ran from temptation but now sees how close they can stand without technically crossing the line.
Someone who once opened Scripture asking, “Lord, what must change in me?”
But now opens Scripture mainly looking for something comforting.
That is how spiritual deafness can become terrifying.
It usually does not announce itself.
Nobody wakes up one morning and says, “Today I am going to harden my heart against Jesus.”
It happens more quietly.
One ignored conviction.
Then another.
One compromise justified.
One apology postponed.
One sin renamed.
One warning dismissed.
One uncomfortable verse explained away.
One more Sunday hearing something you already know you have no intention of obeying.
Eventually the extraordinary becomes ordinary.
Grace becomes vocabulary.
The cross becomes jewelry.
Repentance becomes theology.
Jesus becomes content.
And somehow you can talk about a bleeding Savior without your heart breaking anymore.
That should scare us.
Because the most dangerous place spiritually may not always be where nobody has heard about Jesus.
Sometimes it is where people have heard about Him so many times that they assume hearing is the same thing as following.
It isn't.
Judas heard Jesus.
Think about that.
Judas did not receive secondhand Christianity.
He heard the Sermon on the Mount from the mouth that authored truth.
He watched blind eyes open.
He saw demons flee.
He witnessed mercy walking on two feet.
He ate beside Jesus.
Travelled beside Jesus.
Listened beside Jesus.
And eventually betrayed Jesus.
Proximity to holy things does not automatically produce a holy heart.
You can stand close enough to Jesus to hear His words and still refuse His lordship.
And before we point at Judas, we should examine ourselves.
Because perhaps you remember when the name of Jesus affected you differently.
There was a time you prayed because you wanted Him, not merely because you needed something.
There was a time certain sins bothered you immediately.
There was a time Scripture could expose you and you would not become defensive.
There was a time worship was not background noise.
There was a time you cared deeply whether your life pleased Christ.
Then life happened.
Disappointment happened.
Church hurt happened.
Temptation happened.
Success happened.
Failure happened.
You prayed for something that never came.
Someone you trusted betrayed you.
You watched hypocrites speak about God.
You became exhausted.
And somewhere along the road you did not exactly abandon Jesus...
you just stopped listening closely.
You learned how to survive around Christian language without allowing Christ into the locked rooms.
Maybe nobody noticed.
You still smiled.
Still posted verses.
Still said, “God is good.”
Still showed up.
But privately?
Something became quiet.
And perhaps that is why you are reading this now.
Not because you accidentally found another Christian article.
Maybe because somewhere beneath all the noise, your soul knows exactly what Jesus means:
“He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
Listen.
Not merely with your ears.
Listen with the room you keep locked.
Listen with the wound you refuse to discuss.
Listen with the resentment you have justified for years.
Listen with the sin you keep promising to quit “eventually.”
Listen with the shame that tells you God could never want you after what you did.
Because spiritual deafness has more than one voice.
Sometimes pride says, “I don't need to repent.”
But shame says something equally destructive:
“Repentance won't matter for someone like me.”
Both voices keep you from Jesus.
The Gospel destroys both lies.
You are more sinful than self-righteousness wants to admit...
and more loved in Christ than shame wants to believe.
Jesus did not come because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He came because sinners needed resurrection.
He came for people who could not save themselves.
He came for liars.
Adulterers.
Cowards.
Religious hypocrites.
Addicts.
The ashamed.
The angry.
The sexually broken.
The spiritually exhausted.
The person with a past nobody knows.
The person who has prayed the same apology a hundred times.
The person wondering whether God is finally tired of them.
Christ came into our scandal.
And He carried it to a cross.
There, the sinless Son of God was crucified.
Not as a mascot for self-improvement.
Not merely as an inspirational example.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
Our rebellion deserved judgment.
Christ bore judgment.
Our sin produced guilt.
Christ shed His blood.
Death held humanity.
Christ entered the grave.
And on the third day...
the grave lost.
Jesus rose.
That is Christianity.
Not “become a slightly nicer version of yourself.”
Not “try harder so God might tolerate you.”
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ calling sinners to repent and believe.
Grace does not pretend your scandal never happened.
Grace says your scandal does not get the final sentence when Jesus becomes Lord of your story.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave.
The Greek New Testament frequently uses μετάνοια — metanoia, “repentance,” and its related verb μετανοέω — metanoeō, carrying the idea of a changed mind that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns toward God.
It stops defending what Christ died to deliver us from.
And maybe the reason this article feels uncomfortable is because you already know where repentance needs to begin.
I don't know your secret.
But you do.
And God does.
That browser history.
That emotional affair.
That jealousy.
That hatred.
That addiction.
That dishonest money.
That hidden pride.
That person you refuse to forgive.
That double life.
That obsession with approval.
That relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
That private compromise you would panic to see projected on the screen at church.
Listen carefully.
The enemy wants you to hear conviction and translate it into condemnation.
Jesus calls you to bring darkness into light.
There is a difference.
Condemnation whispers, “Run from God. You're disgusting.”
The Gospel says, “Run to Christ. You need mercy.”
The enemy says, “Hide.”
Jesus says, “Come.”
The enemy reminds you what you did.
The cross reminds you what Jesus did.
And perhaps the saddest thing you could do now would be to feel something deeply...
Because emotion is not repentance.
Tears are not automatically surrender.
Feeling convicted is not the same thing as obeying conviction.
You can cry during worship and return to the same chains.
Jesus is after more than your reaction.
He wants you.
Your actual life.
Your habits.
Your sexuality.
Your money.
Your relationships.
Your wounds.
Your ambitions.
Your private thoughts.
Your Sunday morning.
Your Tuesday midnight.
All of you.
And here is the scandalous beauty of grace:
You may discover that the door you were terrified to open is the exact place where Christ has been waiting to begin restoration.
Peter knew something about scandal.
He swore loyalty to Jesus.
Then denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine hearing yourself say the words.
“I don't know Him.”
Imagine remembering afterward that Jesus had warned you.
Imagine realizing the Man you loved was going to the cross while your courage collapsed beside a fire.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
His failure was real.
Scripture does not sanitize it.
But Peter's failure did not write Peter's final chapter.
The risen Jesus came for him.
Restored him.
Commissioned him.
Used him.
That is grace.
Not pretending Peter never denied Jesus.
Jesus rewrote what Peter's failure meant for his future.
Peter's worst night did not become his final identity.
And yours does not have to either.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal was your own choice.
Maybe someone else's sin shattered you.
Maybe you are carrying consequences that cannot simply disappear.
The Gospel does not promise that following Christ magically erases every earthly consequence.
But it promises something greater.
In Christ, guilt can be forgiven.
The condemned can be justified.
The estranged can be reconciled.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The enslaved can begin walking in freedom.
The prodigal can come home.
And sinners can become sons and daughters of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
So why did Jesus say some people had ears but could not hear?
Because hearing God has never been merely about possessing ears.
It is possible to encounter truth while resisting truth.
It is possible to hear Scripture while hardening yourself against Scripture.
It is possible to become so practiced at postponing obedience that conviction begins to feel like background noise.
And that means perhaps the question is not:
“Does God still speak?”
The question may be:
“What have I done with what He has already said?”
That question reaches me too.
It reaches every preacher.
Every ministry leader.
Every person sharing Christian content.
Every lifelong believer.
Every new convert.
Nobody graduates from needing a responsive heart.
Even Jesus' disciples were once confronted with the question, “Having eyes do you not see, and having ears do you not hear?”
So this warning should not become ammunition for judging “those people.”
It should become a mirror.
Where am I not listening?
Where are you not listening?
Maybe today your prayer does not need to be complicated.
“Jesus, I hear You.
Forgive me.
I surrender.
Change me.”
If there is sin, confess it.
If restitution needs to be made, begin making it.
If someone needs forgiveness, bring that wound before Christ.
If you need mature Christian accountability, stop hiding and find it.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have never truly trusted Christ, stop confusing familiarity with Christianity.
You can know stories about Jesus without knowing Jesus.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
The Savior who warns us about hardened hearts is the same Savior who welcomed sinners, touched lepers, restored failures, forgave the guilty, carried a cross, and walked alive out of His grave.
His warning is severe precisely because what He offers is so precious.
Life.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Himself.
And if something inside you is whispering, “I've gone too far,” remember the kind of people Jesus came to save.
Grace has always looked scandalous when it reaches people everyone else had already written off.
Maybe people wrote you off.
Maybe you wrote yourself off.
Jesus gets the final word.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores broken people.
Don't let this become another article you felt and forgot.
Return to it on the day your heart starts becoming numb again.
And think of one person right now—not fifty random people, just one person—who has slowly become distant from God.
Send this to them.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you hear Scripture more clearly, you can help us keep putting Christ-centered biblical content in front of people who desperately need it.

It does not make God love you more. But if you have been asking, “How can I use what God has entrusted to me to help spread biblical truth?” supporting Gospel-centered ministry is one meaningful way you can choose to do that for the glory of God.
Not to make us famous.
Make Jesus known.
Because somewhere tonight someone will be holding a phone with perfectly functioning ears...
while their heart is quietly dying.
Someone will read about Jesus while wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want them.
Someone will recognize themselves in Peter.
Someone will realize they have been sitting near Christianity without surrendering to Christ.
Someone may finally stop running.
Maybe that someone is the person you share this with.
Maybe...
it is you.
Jesus is still calling.
The question was never whether you had ears.
The question is whether, after hearing His voice, you will finally come home.
Because the most heartbreaking kind of deafness is hearing Jesus call your name—and becoming so accustomed to His voice that you no longer turn around.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MIDIANITE WAR ENDED WITH AN ORDER MOST CHRISTIANS WOULD RATHER NOT READ ALOUD
paragraphs: THE MIDIANITE WAR ENDED WITH AN ORDER MOST CHRISTIANS WOULD RATHER NOT READ ALOUD

Numbers 31 contains words about women, children, judgment, and war that can make even a devoted Christian recoil. But perhaps the answer is not to hide the passage—or defend it carelessly. Perhaps we need to stand before the text long enough to discover what it actually says, what it does not say, and why the road from this terrible battlefield ultimately makes us desperate for Jesus Christ.
There are Bible passages we embroider on pillows.
Numbers 31 is not one of them.
There are verses we underline because they comfort us when the night is long. Verses we send to a grieving friend. Verses we whisper over our children before they sleep.
And then there are passages like this.
Passages that make the room uncomfortable.
Passages that make believers lower their voices and skeptics raise theirs.
Passages that do not seem interested in protecting our feelings.
Numbers 31 is one of those passages.
Israel goes to war against Midian.
Men die.
Cities and encampments burn.
Women and children are taken captive.
The soldiers return.
And then Moses discovers that the women have been spared.
His response is terrifying.
He reminds the commanders of what happened at Peor and of the role attributed to Balaam's counsel. Then comes the sentence many readers wish were not in their Bible.
The Hebrew of Numbers 31:17–18 reads in part:
“וְעַתָּה הִרְגוּ כָל־זָכָר בַּטָּף … וְכֹל הַטַּף בַּנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר הַחֲיוּ לָכֶם”
A close rendering is:
“Now therefore kill every male among the little ones … but all the female children who have not known a man’s bed, keep alive for yourselves.”
That is substantially what the Hebrew says.
Read it again.
Slowly.
Do not rush past it because you are afraid of what somebody might ask you.
Do not soften it into something it is not.
But do not make it more horrifying than the text itself says, either.
Because if we love Scripture, we owe Scripture more than defense.
We owe it honesty.
And here is where that honesty becomes crucial.

The Hebrew expression translated “have known a man” refers to sexual experience. The females spared in verse 18 are specifically described as those who had not “known a man’s bed”; translation notes identify them as girls or female children.
But Numbers 31:18 does not say that these girls were preserved for rape.
It does not explicitly say that they were preserved to become sexual slaves.
It does not describe soldiers being given permission to sexually abuse them.
Those conclusions are sometimes inserted into the passage as though the verse explicitly says them.
It does not.
That matters.
But so does this:
The text is still disturbing.
We do Christianity no favors when we pretend otherwise.

Even after removing sensational claims that go beyond the words on the page, we are still looking at warfare, killing, captivity, judgment, terrified survivors, dead children, and a command that collides violently with modern moral instincts.
There is no clever Hebrew word that makes all of that disappear.
There is no theological sentence that turns a battlefield into a greeting card.
There should not be.
The Bible is brutally honest about a world ruined by sin.
And perhaps before asking why Numbers 31 is so violent, we need to remember what happened before Numbers 31.
There was Peor.

Numbers 25 describes Israel being drawn into idolatry and sexual immorality connected with the worship of Baal of Peor. A plague followed. Twenty-four thousand Israelites died according to the narrative.
And the Midianite connection was not incidental.

Numbers 25:16–18 specifically identifies Midianite hostility and deceit in connection with Peor, while Numbers 31:16 looks backward and says that through Balaam's counsel the Israelites were caused to act unfaithfully against the LORD in that affair.
So Numbers 31 is not presented as Israel randomly waking up one morning and deciding to slaughter innocent neighbors for territory.
Within the narrative, it is presented as divine judgment connected to the catastrophe at Peor.
That context matters enormously.
It does not make the deaths emotionally easy.
It tells us what kind of claim the biblical writer is making.
This is judgment.
And that word makes modern people uncomfortable.
Sometimes Christians too.
Because we love hearing that God is merciful.
He is.
We love hearing that God forgives.
He does.
We love hearing that God restores sinners.
He absolutely does.
But the same Bible that says God is merciful refuses to tell us that evil is ultimately inconsequential.
Sin destroys things.
Sin destroys people.
Sin destroys families.
Sin destroys nations.
And sometimes we speak about sin so casually because we have never watched it finish eating somebody alive.
Peor shows us what temptation looks like when the music is still playing.
Numbers 31 shows us a world after the bill arrives.
That is terrifying.
Because we are usually fascinated by the beginning of sin.
Scripture keeps showing us the end.
At the beginning, temptation whispers.
At the end, somebody is crying.
At the beginning, compromise looks manageable.
At the end, generations can be carrying wounds nobody remembers how to explain.
At the beginning, Balaam could not curse Israel.
So according to Numbers 31:16, another avenue became devastatingly effective.
Seduction.
Compromise.
Unfaithfulness.
And perhaps that is where this ancient battlefield suddenly stops feeling so ancient.
Because some of the greatest battles for your soul will not arrive looking like battles.
They will arrive looking attractive.
Convenient.
Private.
Harmless.
Deserved.
Nobody needs to know.
Just once.
You're lonely.
You're angry.
God will forgive you anyway.
And somewhere between the first compromise and the hundredth excuse, something inside you begins dying.
Maybe that is why this chapter bothers us so deeply.
We want sin to be small and grace to be enormous.
Scripture says grace is enormous precisely because sin is not small.
But another question remains.
A harder one.
What about the children?
What about those who died who were not personally responsible for seducing Israel at Peor?
What about collective judgment?
What about the female children who survived and became captives?
Those questions should not be mocked.
They should not be silenced with “just have faith.”
Faith is not pretending a difficult verse is easy.
Christians have wrestled with texts of divine judgment for centuries because Scripture itself gives us a God who is perfectly just while also giving us narratives whose severity can overwhelm us.
Numbers 31 does not provide answers to every moral and emotional question a twenty-first-century reader will bring to it.
We should have the humility to admit that.
There is also something else in the chapter that deserves attention.
After the battle, those who killed or came into contact with the dead could not simply stroll back into Israel's camp celebrating.
They remained outside the camp and underwent purification.
Numbers 31:19 says:
“וְאַתֶּם חֲנוּ מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה שִׁבְעַת יָמִים”
“And you, encamp outside the camp seven days…”
Those who had killed or touched the slain had to undergo purification, and the captives were included in the purification instructions as well.
That detail does not erase the killing.
But it should stop us from reading biblical warfare as though bloodshed were casual entertainment.
Death contaminates.
Death belongs to the brokenness of this world.
Even after a battle the narrative presents as commanded judgment, contact with death requires purification.
The soldiers do not return from killing and immediately walk untouched into sacred space.
There is a boundary.
There is cleansing.
There is death outside.
There is holiness within.
And thousands of years later, another Man would stand outside.
Not carrying a sword.
Carrying a cross.
Jesus.
And suddenly the entire Bible begins pulling our eyes toward something Numbers 31 could never accomplish.
Because Numbers 31 can show judgment.
But Numbers 31 cannot become the final answer to the human problem.
Israel itself would sin again.
And again.
And again.
The people commissioned to execute judgment would themselves need mercy.
Moses needed mercy.
Israel needed mercy.
Midian needed mercy.
You need mercy.
I need mercy.
The scandal of Scripture is not merely that God judges sinners.
The scandal of grace is that God came to save them.
At the cross, God did not announce that sin never mattered.
He demonstrated just how much it mattered.
Christianity does not proclaim a God who simply shrugged at human wickedness and said, “Forget about it.”
The Gospel proclaims Christ crucified.
The Son of God entered our violent, corrupted, rebellious world.
He was betrayed.
Beaten.
Mocked.
Condemned.
Crucified.
And instead of calling His followers to imitate ancient Israel's national warfare, Jesus told His disciples to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them.
The kingdom was moving toward its appointed fulfillment through a crucified Messiah.
This distinction matters desperately.
The church is not ancient Israel camped beside the Jordan.
Christians have no mandate from Numbers 31 to conduct religious warfare against unbelievers.
The enemies Christ commands His followers to love are not targets for a Christian sword.
The Gospel advances through witness, truth, sacrificial love, holiness, proclamation, suffering, prayer, and the power of the Holy Spirit—not forced conversion and not holy war.
Look at Jesus.
When Peter reached for a sword at Christ's arrest, Jesus stopped him.
When Christ stood before Pilate, He declared that His kingdom was not of this world in the manner of earthly kingdoms; otherwise, His servants would fight.
Then the King allowed Himself to be crucified.
Think about that.
The One with the legitimate authority to judge the world chose, at His first coming, to endure judgment for sinners.
The Judge stepped beneath judgment.
The Holy One was treated like the guilty.
The Innocent One was condemned.
The King wore thorns.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by humanity.
And from the cross came not a warrior's scream for revenge, but words of forgiveness.
That does not mean judgment vanished.
The New Testament still speaks soberly about final judgment.
Jesus did not save us by declaring evil imaginary.
He saves sinners from something real.
And that means Numbers 31 should never make Christians bloodthirsty.
It should make us tremble.
Because if God's judgment against evil is real, then none of us should be standing around congratulating ourselves that we are not Midianites.
The question is not merely:
“What happened to them?”
The question eventually becomes:
“How can any sinner stand before a holy God?”
And Christianity gives an answer so astonishing that we sometimes become numb to it.
Jesus Christ.
Not your religious résumé.
Not the fact that you grew up Christian.
Not the verses in your bio.
Not the worship songs in your playlist.
Not the cross hanging around your neck.
Christ.
Your righteousness cannot save you.
Your excuses cannot save you.
Your secret goodness cannot cancel your secret sin.
But Jesus saves sinners.
This is where the battlefield reaches your bedroom.
Your browser history.
Your private messages.
Your bitterness.
Your addiction.
Your pride.
Your hidden affair.
Your unforgiveness.
Your double life.
Your carefully maintained Christian appearance.
Your secret anger at God.
Your compromise nobody has discovered yet.
You may never stand on the plains of Moab.
But you know Peor.
You know what it is to feel something pulling your heart away from God.
You know what it is to rename disobedience so you can sleep beside it.
And maybe you have been telling yourself:
It isn't that serious.
Numbers 31 whispers something frightening across the centuries:
Sin becomes serious long before we decide to call it serious.
But Calvary says something even louder:
There is mercy for the sinner who comes home.
Not cheap mercy.
Blood-bought mercy.
Not permission to continue hiding.
Grace that drags hidden things into the light and says:
You don't have to die here.
Repent.
Come home.
Christ still receives sinners.
Maybe that is the word somebody reading this needs tonight.
Come home.
Not when you have fixed yourself.
Not after you become worthy.
Not after you have successfully hidden the evidence.
Come to Christ honestly.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Let the Savior meet the person underneath the performance.
Because repentance is not God humiliating you for returning.
Repentance is the road by which the prodigal discovers the Father was worth coming home to.
And grace is not Jesus pretending your scandal never happened.
Grace is Jesus refusing to let your scandal have the final word.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because history can be erased.
Not because painful Bible passages become painless.
But because Jesus Christ enters stories filled with rebellion, shame, judgment, wreckage, captivity, and death—and writes redemption where human beings expected only an ending.
If this passage disturbed you, do not run from Scripture.
Dig deeper.
Ask harder questions.
Read context.
Learn the languages when you can.
Refuse sensational interpretations that say more than the text says.
And refuse shallow interpretations that say less than the text says.
Most importantly, keep walking until the whole counsel of Scripture leads your eyes to Christ.

And if grace has already pulled you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell your testimony. Somebody scrolling through those comments may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty, but because somebody in your circle may be wrestling with this exact passage—or with the God they think this passage portrays.
Let them see that biblical faith does not require intellectual dishonesty.
Numbers 31 is not a chapter most people understand after one hurried reading.
There is another practical way you can help this ministry continue.
It cannot buy salvation, increase Christ's love for you, or make you more righteous before God.

But voluntary, cheerful financial support can function as a genuine offering toward ministry work—helping Gospel Warrior continue creating, researching, publishing, and expanding Christ-centered resources for people around the world.
If you believe this work glorifies God, one meaningful way to participate in it is to help sustain it.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Point somebody toward Jesus.
Those things matter too.
If you want to become part of that support:
Give freely.
Give prayerfully.
Never from manipulation or fear.
Support the Gospel because Christ is worthy, not because anyone promised you that a monthly payment could purchase His blessing.
And whatever you do after reading Numbers 31, do not walk away merely fascinated by ancient violence.
Walk away asking whether there is anything inside you that still needs to surrender.
Because the most dangerous battlefield may not be somewhere in Midian.
It may be the hidden territory of the human heart.
And the greatest wonder of Scripture is not that sinners can hide from judgment forever.
It is that sinners can run directly to Jesus and find mercy.
The sword in Numbers 31 should make us tremble—but the scars in the hands of Jesus should make us run home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY CALLED HIM “CHRIST”—BUT MOST PEOPLE HAVE NEVER BEEN TOLD WHAT THAT WORD ACTUALLY MEANS
paragraphs:
THEY CALLED HIM “CHRIST”—BUT MOST PEOPLE HAVE NEVER BEEN TOLD WHAT THAT WORD ACTUALLY MEANS
“Messiah” is not Jesus’ last name. “Christ” is not merely a religious title. Behind both words is an ancient biblical reality of anointing, kingship, priesthood, suffering, victory, and a promise that reaches from Israel’s Scriptures all the way to the cross, the empty tomb, and the throne of God.
There is a moment in the Gospel of Matthew that is easy to read too quickly.
Jesus looks at His disciples and asks a question that eventually confronts every human heart:
“But whom say ye that I am?”
Peter answers:
“Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
—Matthew 16:15–16
We have heard those words so often that they can lose their force.
The Christ.
But what if you had been standing there in the first century?
What would you have heard?
Because Peter was not giving Jesus a surname.
He was making a staggering confession.
He was saying, in effect:
You are the One.
The promised King.
The Anointed One.
The One Israel has been waiting for.
The One upon whom everything ultimately turns.
And suddenly one of the most familiar words in Christianity becomes enormous.
“Christ” comes from the Greek word Χριστός—Christos—meaning “Anointed One.”
Behind that Greek title stands the Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ—māšîaḥ, commonly written “Messiah”—which likewise means “anointed one.”
That connection matters.
The English words “Messiah” and “Christ” may sound like two different religious concepts, but biblically they point to the same central idea.
The Messiah is the Christ.
The Christ is the Anointed One.
That is why John’s Gospel can say:
“We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ.”
—John 1:41
John even preserves the connection for his readers. The Greek text uses Μεσσίαν (Messian) and then explains it with Χριστός (Christos).
This was not decorative theology.
It was identity.
And to understand why that identity matters, you have to understand anointing.

In the Old Testament world, anointing could mark someone as specially appointed or consecrated for a God-given role. Kings were famously anointed. Priests were anointed. The language of anointing became inseparable from divine appointment, consecration, authority, and calling.
When Samuel anointed David, Scripture says:
“Then Samuel took the horn of oil, and anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward.”
—1 Samuel 16:13
Imagine that scene.
David was not sitting on a throne.
He was not wearing a crown.
He was not commanding armies.
He was the overlooked son who had been out tending sheep.
Yet oil ran over the head of a shepherd boy while heaven declared something that circumstances had not caught up with yet.
A king was standing in the room.
That is one of the strange patterns of Scripture.
God's purposes are often present before human eyes recognize them.
David was anointed before he was enthroned.
And generations later, Israel was still waiting for David's greater Son.
The prophets had created an expectation that God would act decisively through His promised ruler.
Isaiah spoke of a coming figure upon whom God's Spirit would rest:
“And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD.”
—Isaiah 11:2
Then Isaiah gives us another astonishing picture:
“The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek…”
—Isaiah 61:1
Centuries later, Jesus walked into a synagogue in Nazareth.
He was handed Isaiah.
He read:
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor…”
Then He sat down.
Every eye was fixed on Him.
And Jesus said:
“This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.”
Think about the weight of that sentence.
Jesus was not merely announcing that He had an inspirational message.
He was placing Himself inside the fulfillment of Israel's prophetic hope.
The Anointed One had come.
But then the story becomes stranger.
Because if you were expecting God's Messiah to arrive, you might expect immediate visible conquest.
A throne.
An army.
Political liberation.
Public vindication.
Instead, the Messiah touches lepers.
He eats with people carrying terrible reputations.
He receives sinners.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He washes feet.
He weeps.
He allows Himself to be betrayed.
He is mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
And crucified.
That is where the scandal begins.
How could the Anointed King end up on a Roman cross?
How could the Messiah appear defeated?
How could the One who came announcing God's kingdom be hanging beneath an accusation written over His dying body?
The cross seemed to say that everything had gone wrong.
But the apostles came to proclaim something breathtaking:
The cross was not the cancellation of God's plan.
It stood at the very heart of God's saving purpose.
After His resurrection, Jesus told His disciples:
“Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?”
—Luke 24:26
The Messiah who suffers before entering glory.
The King whose crown is preceded by thorns.
The victorious Christ whose triumph passes through death.
That changes the way we understand Jesus.
And it changes the way we understand grace.
Because Jesus was not anointed merely to become an inspirational figure you admire from a safe distance.
He came to save sinners.
That means people like us.
People with memories we wish we could erase.
People who have worshiped while hiding things.
People who promised God, “Never again,” and eventually did it again.
People who know the Bible but sometimes struggle to obey it.
People who have smiled at church while privately falling apart.
People who have carried guilt so long that shame started feeling like a name.
Maybe nobody knows your secret.
Maybe everyone thinks your faith is strong.
Maybe your Bible has highlighted verses while your heart has hidden rooms.
And perhaps the frightening question isn't whether other people would still love you if everything became visible.
Perhaps the question underneath it is:
Would Jesus still want me?
Look at the Gospel.
The answer is not that your sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
The answer is that His grace is greater than your ability to save yourself.
Christianity does not tell sinners to pretend the darkness is light.
It calls us to repentance.
To confession.
To surrender.
To Christ.
And repentance is not paying God enough tears to persuade Him to become merciful.
Repentance turns from sin toward the God whose mercy has been revealed in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel destroys both our excuses and our despair.
You cannot stand at the cross and honestly say sin is insignificant.
But neither can a repentant sinner stand at the cross and honestly say there is no mercy for sinners.
The blood says otherwise.
Jesus said:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
—Luke 19:10
Lost.
That word may be more personal than some of us want to admit.
You can know worship songs and still wander.
You can post Bible verses and still be starving spiritually.
You can look clean in photographs and feel filthy in private.
You can know Christian language while slowly learning how to hide from the Christ whose name you speak.
Yet the Gospel keeps bringing us back to Him.
Not merely “Jesus the teacher.”
Not merely “Jesus the miracle worker.”
Not merely “Jesus who helps me accomplish my plans.”
Jesus the Christ.
The Messiah.
God's Anointed King.
The crucified and risen Lord.
This is why Peter's confession matters so deeply.
“Thou art the Christ.”
It is not trivia for a theology examination.
It demands a response.
If Jesus really is the Christ, then He is not an accessory to the life we have already decided to live.
We do not recruit the King into our plans.
We surrender to Him.
And this is where the meaning of “anointing” can become distorted in modern Christian culture.
Sometimes people speak about “the anointing” as though it were spiritual celebrity.
A powerful personality.
A platform.
A microphone.
An atmosphere.
A particular emotional sensation.
Or even a religious shortcut to prosperity and prominence.
But Scripture does not give us permission to reduce biblical anointing to charisma, fame, wealth, or human impressiveness.
Jesus—the Christ, the Anointed One—walked directly toward a cross.
His glory cannot be reduced to applause.
His kingdom cannot be reduced to branding.
His authority does not depend upon followers, views, stages, algorithms, or public approval.
And this matters for every Christian who has secretly wondered:
“If God is really with me, why is this so hard?”
Look at Christ.
Difficulty by itself does not prove abandonment by God.
Obedience can be costly.
Faithfulness can hurt.
Love can involve sacrifice.
Jesus' road to resurrection passed through Golgotha.
But be careful here.
The Gospel is not telling us that suffering saves us.
Jesus saves us.
Your pain does not atone for your sin.
Your tears do not purchase forgiveness.
Your religious performance cannot resurrect your soul.
Christ is the Savior.
That distinction is everything.
We do not need a motivational coach to teach dead hearts how to behave more successfully.
We need the living Christ.
And that is why another passage carries such power.
Peter preached:
“God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.”
—Acts 10:38
Then Peter does not stop with Jesus' ministry.
He moves to His death and resurrection.
Jesus was killed.
God raised Him.
The Gospel cannot be separated from the crucified and risen Christ.
That is the center.
And perhaps that is why this truth can feel uncomfortable.
Because if Jesus is merely inspirational, you can admire Him.
If Jesus is merely useful, you can call Him when life hurts.
If Jesus is merely a teacher, you can quote the teachings you like and quietly ignore the ones you don't.
But if Jesus is the Christ…
the King…
the Lord…
then eventually you have to decide what to do with His authority.
There are places inside us where we still want the crown.
Our money.
Our relationships.
Our sexuality.
Our ambitions.
Our grudges.
Our habits.
Our screens.
Our private thoughts.
Our reputation.
Our future.
We want Jesus close enough to rescue us but sometimes not close enough to rule us.
And He loves us too much to cooperate with that illusion.
Grace does not merely soothe.
Grace transforms.
Paul writes:
—2 Corinthians 5:17
Notice those words.
“In Christ.”
Not merely impressed by Christ.
Not culturally associated with Christ.
Not occasionally inspired by Christ.
In Christ.
The Anointed One becomes the center of a new identity.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter himself is proof.
The man who declared, “Thou art the Christ,” later denied that he even knew Jesus.
Three times.
Think about the humiliation.
Peter had confessed the Messiah with his mouth and then, under pressure, denied Him with the same mouth.
If Peter's worst moment had been the final chapter, his story would have ended beside a charcoal fire with fear winning.
But Jesus writes endings differently.
After the resurrection, Peter encounters the risen Christ.
Failure is confronted.
Love is questioned.
Calling is restored.
“Feed my sheep.”
The man who denied Jesus became a witness to Jesus.
That is not permission to treat sin casually.
It is evidence that failure does not possess greater authority than the grace of the risen Christ.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needs tonight.
Your sin should bring you to repentance.
But your sin does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your shame does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your past does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your addiction does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your reputation does not deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
Your success does not deserve the throne either.
Jesus does.
He is the Christ.
And when that becomes more than vocabulary, Christianity stops being a religious decoration and becomes surrender.
Maybe you've spent years asking Jesus to bless a life you never actually surrendered to Him.
Maybe you know how to appear Christian.
Maybe nobody realizes how exhausted you are from maintaining the appearance.
You do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Seek trustworthy Christian help where you need help.
Stop calling chains “personality.”
Stop calling compromise “just who I am.”
Stop treating tomorrow like a promise.
And do not confuse repentance with hopelessness.
You are not being invited to stare endlessly at yourself.
You are being called to look to Christ.
The Messiah has come.
The King was crucified.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus lives.
And sinners who come to Him do not need to manufacture a cleaner past before asking for mercy.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not pretend grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that cleanses.
Grace that teaches us to leave the darkness.
Grace that takes scandals human beings would use as permanent labels and refuses to let those labels have the final word over a repentant life surrendered to Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished religious response.
Be honest.
If your spirit has felt dry and you need believers to stand with you in prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people in real life.
And if one particular person came into your mind while reading this, don't ignore that.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Because maybe they need to remember who Jesus really is.
Let your support become stewardship, not spiritual performance; gratitude, not guilt.
And whether or not you ever purchase anything, keep growing.
It means the Anointed One.
The promised King.
The Messiah.
But never confuse supporting Gospel Warrior with the Gospel itself.
We cannot sell grace.
No product can cleanse a conscience.
No ministry can replace Christ.
No platform died for you.
Jesus did.
Come to Christ.
The Messiah is not waiting for you to become impressive.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
The King who wore the crown of thorns is risen.
And perhaps the scandal you thought would become the title of your life is only the place where grace is about to write a sentence you never thought possible.
Your darkest chapter does not get to name the book when the risen Christ holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A KING DISGUISED HIMSELF FOR BATTLE—BUT A “RANDOM” ARROW STILL FOUND HIM
paragraphs: A KING DISGUISED HIMSELF FOR BATTLE—BUT A “RANDOM” ARROW STILL FOUND HIM

He changed his clothes so the enemy would not recognize him. He thought the disguise might protect him. Then an unnamed soldier pulled his bow without apparently aiming at anyone in particular—and the arrow entered the one opening in the king’s armor.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every hiding heart tremble.
Not because God is cruel.
Because God cannot be fooled.
King Ahab had already heard the warning.
He knew what the prophet had said.
He knew the battle would not end the way he wanted.
And somehow, instead of surrendering to the word of God, he apparently thought he could outmaneuver it.
So he disguised himself.
Then he went into battle.
And somewhere across that battlefield stood a man who did not know that a king was hiding among ordinary soldiers.
The man lifted his bow.
Pulled the string.
Released.
And Scripture gives us one of the most haunting descriptions of what happened next:
“וְאִישׁ מָשַׁךְ בַּקֶּשֶׁת לְתֻמּוֹ”
Ve’ish mashakh baqeshet letummo.
The key expression is לְתֻמּוֹ — letummo.
It carries the sense of acting innocently, without a particular target in mind, or at random from the archer’s human perspective.
That is why many English translations communicate the idea as an archer drawing his bow “at random.”
But the arrow was about to teach Ahab—and us—the terrifying difference between random to man and unknown to God.
The arrow flew.
Past soldiers.
Past shields.
Past armor.
Past everything that might have stopped it.
And it struck Ahab “between the scale armor and the breastplate” (1 Kings 22:34; compare 2 Chronicles 18:33).
One vulnerable opening.
One arrow.
One disguised king.
And the word God had spoken through His prophet was not defeated by a costume.
Read that again.
Ahab could disguise himself from soldiers.
He could not disguise himself from God.
And maybe that is why this ancient battlefield suddenly feels uncomfortably modern.
Because some of us have become very good at disguises.
Not literal ones.
Sunday disguises.
Facebook disguises.
Church disguises.
Marriage disguises.
Ministry disguises.
“I’m okay” disguises.
We know how to smile while something inside us is collapsing.
We know which Christian words to use.
We know when to say, “God is good.”
We know how to post the verse.
Raise the hands.
Say amen.
Serve.
Give.
Sing.
Encourage somebody else.
And still keep one locked room in the heart where we hope Jesus will not ask too many questions.
Ahab changed his clothes.
What did you change?
Your vocabulary?
Your public image?
Your browser history?
Your explanation?
Your story?
Maybe nobody knows what happened after midnight.
Maybe nobody knows how angry you really are.
Maybe nobody knows about the bitterness you keep feeding.
The compromise you keep renaming.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The secret conversation.
The addiction.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The money.
The unforgiveness.
The hidden life.
Maybe you have become so skilled at appearing spiritually alive that people come to you for prayer while your own soul is quietly starving.
And the frightening thing about Ahab’s story is that disguise did not change reality.
Neither does ours.
But before turning this passage into a simplistic slogan about “random arrows,” we need to hear the whole story.
Ahab was not an innocent man who accidentally wandered into judgment.
His life had been marked by persistent rebellion.
First Kings describes him as doing evil in the sight of the LORD and as surpassing the wickedness of the kings before him (1 Kings 16:30–33).
Under Ahab and Jezebel, Baal worship received royal support.
The prophets of the LORD were persecuted.
Naboth was falsely accused and killed so Ahab could possess his vineyard.
And God repeatedly confronted Ahab.
That matters.
Because God warned before judgment came.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Even more astonishingly, when Ahab humbled himself after Elijah announced judgment concerning Naboth, God noticed.
God said to Elijah:
“Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me?”
Read 1 Kings 21:27–29.
That moment destroys the caricature of a God eagerly waiting to crush anyone who fails.
Even Ahab’s temporary humiliation was noticed by God, and judgment upon his house was correspondingly delayed.
But temporary remorse is not the same thing as a transformed life.
By 1 Kings 22, another decision stood before Ahab.
He wanted Ramoth-gilead.
Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, asked that they first inquire for the word of the LORD.
Hundreds of prophets gave Ahab the answer he wanted.
Victory.
Success.
Go.
But Jehoshaphat sensed something was wrong.
“Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?”
There was.
Micaiah.
And Ahab’s response reveals the sickness beneath everything:
“I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil.”
That sentence is devastating.
Ahab did not primarily want truth.
He wanted affirmation.
And that disease never died with Ahab.
It can sit in a church pew.
It can hold a Bible.
It can follow Christian pages.
It can listen only to sermons that soothe it.
It can become angry at the person who tells the truth and strangely affectionate toward anyone who baptizes its desires in religious language.
Sometimes we say we want God to speak when what we really mean is:
“God, please agree with the decision I already made.”
Micaiah would not.
He foretold disaster and Ahab’s death.
Ahab responded by imprisoning the messenger.
Then he went to battle anyway.
Think about that.
The warning was heard.
The warning was rejected.
The prophet was punished.
And the king changed his clothes.
This was not ignorance.
This was rebellion dressed as strategy.
Ahab told Jehoshaphat, in effect, that he himself would disguise himself while Jehoshaphat wore his royal robes.
Then the battle began.
The Syrian commanders were looking specifically for the king of Israel.
They saw Jehoshaphat.
They assumed he was Ahab.
They pursued him.
Jehoshaphat cried out.
They realized he was not their target and turned away.
Ahab’s plan appeared to be working.
Can you imagine the temptation in that moment?
Micaiah was wrong.
I escaped.
The disguise worked.
Maybe the warning wasn’t really from God.
Then an unnamed archer drew his bow letummo.
And everything changed.
This does not mean the Bible teaches that every accident, tragedy, illness, or painful event in your life is a secret arrow of divine punishment.
Do not weaponize this passage against suffering people.
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic assumptions that particular sufferers must have been worse sinners than everyone else; see Luke 13:1–5 and John 9:1–3.
The lesson here is specific and sobering.
Ahab had received a prophetic word of judgment, rejected it, and attempted to proceed anyway.
The apparently unaimed arrow became the means by which that announced judgment came to pass.
From the archer’s perspective, there was no carefully selected royal target.
From the perspective of the biblical narrative, God’s word had not failed.
And there is something else we must not miss.
The arrow did not need to destroy all the armor.
It only needed the gap.
That thought has followed me.
Because sometimes the place we defend least is the place we excuse most.
“It’s only one habit.”
“It’s only flirting.”
“It’s only bitterness.”
“It’s only when I’m lonely.”
“It’s only online.”
“It’s only a little dishonesty.”
“It’s nobody else’s business.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“It isn’t hurting anybody.”
That tiny opening may become the place through which enormous destruction enters.
Scripture repeatedly warns us not to make peace with sin.
Not because God wants to rob us of joy.
Because sin lies about where it is taking us.
James describes desire conceiving and giving birth to sin, and sin, when fully grown, bringing forth death (James 1:14–15).
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying:
“Hello. I have come to destroy you.”
It usually whispers:
“Just this once.”
Ahab’s battlefield therefore asks a question we would rather avoid:
What are you disguising instead of surrendering?
There is something almost unbearable about imagining him standing wounded in his chariot.
The battle continued.
His blood flowed into the bottom of the chariot.
By evening, he was dead.
The disguise that seemed clever that morning could not save him by sunset.
And somewhere inside this story is a warning for every person who keeps postponing repentance because judgment has not arrived yet.
Delay is not approval.
Silence is not permission.
Getting away with something today does not make it safe tomorrow.
But if we stop here, we have not yet reached the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not merely the announcement that you cannot hide from God.
That would leave every one of us terrified.
The Gospel announces something far more astonishing:
The God from whom you cannot hide is the God who came looking for sinners.
Ahab disguised himself in an attempt to escape judgment.
Jesus Christ did something infinitely different.
He knew exactly what awaited Him in Jerusalem.
He did not disguise Himself.
He did not run.
He did not manipulate someone else into taking His place.
He set His face toward the cross.
At Gethsemane, when armed men arrived to arrest Him, Jesus did not disappear into the crowd.
He stepped forward.
“Whom do you seek?”
“Jesus of Nazareth.”
“I am he.”
See John 18:4–8.
Do you see the contrast?
A guilty king disguised himself and sent another king into battle wearing royal robes.
The sinless King revealed Himself and willingly gave Himself for guilty people.
Ahab tried to avoid the consequences announced against him.
Jesus willingly bore the judgment our sins deserved—not because He was trapped by circumstances, but because He loved us and gave Himself for us.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the Servant who would be “pierced for our transgressions” and “crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
At Calvary, Jesus was not dying for His own rebellion.
He had none.
He was the spotless Lamb.
The righteous for the unrighteous, “that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
And suddenly Ahab’s story becomes more than a warning about a king who could not escape.
It becomes a mirror showing why we desperately need a King who came to rescue.
Because you and I have disguises too.
We have sinned.
We have hidden.
We have blamed.
We have performed.
We have promised God things and broken those promises.
We have wanted His blessings while resisting His authority.
We have asked Him to forgive what we secretly intended to repeat.
And yet—
Jesus still calls sinners to come into the light.
Not so He can humiliate them.
So He can save them.
The cross means you do not have to keep pretending.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can come home.
First John 1:9 does not tell us to perfect ourselves before approaching God. It tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about yourself.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a genuine turning of mind and heart toward God that bears fruit in life.
Jesus did not come merely to make hidden sinners feel slightly better while they continue hiding.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Restore.
Transform.
So maybe the most important moment in this article is not the arrow.
Maybe it is this one.
Right now.
You.
God.
No audience.
No performance.
No disguise.
What have you been hiding?
You do not need to type the details publicly.
But you do need to stop lying to God about something He already sees.
Maybe your prayer needs to become painfully simple:
“Jesus, I have been hiding. Forgive me. Change me. I surrender.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
Not because public engagement earns forgiveness.
Forgiveness is grace.
Someone reading may stop and pray for you.
Somebody still hiding in the darkness may need to discover that repentance does not have to be the end of their story.
It can be the doorway home.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article is a biblical requirement for glorifying God—it is not.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But sharing biblical truth can be one practical way of serving someone else.
A cousin quietly losing faith.
A friend trapped in secret sin.
A husband who feels spiritually numb.
A wife who cries when nobody sees.
A teenager questioning whether God could possibly forgive what they have done.
A believer who has mastered the disguise.
Because temptation has a way of making us forget what conviction made painfully clear.
Come back when the disguise starts feeling comfortable again.
It cannot earn salvation.
It cannot make God love you more.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But financial support can help Gospel-centered work continue reaching people with Scripture, discipleship resources, encouragement, and the message of Christ.
The invitation of this story is not ultimately:
“Support a page.”
It is:
Stop hiding from Jesus.
Because one day every disguise falls.
Every reputation ends.
Every secret becomes irrelevant before the God who has always known the truth.
And the miracle of grace is that you do not have to wait until that day to be exposed.
You can come willingly now.
You can repent now.
You can confess now.
You can surrender now.
