Genesis 30:1 says:
“When Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister; and said unto Jacob, Give me children, or else I die.”
The Hebrew is even more emotionally striking:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, ve’im-ayin, metah anokhi.
Literally, the sense is:
“Give me sons/children—and if not, I am dying.”
Listen to the desperation.
Rachel was not simply requesting motherhood.
She was unraveling.
And to understand why, you have to remember the house she lived in.
Rachel was loved deeply by Jacob.

Genesis 29:18 tells us that Jacob loved Rachel. He worked seven years for the right to marry her, only to be deceived by Laban and given Leah instead. He then married Rachel as well and served another seven years.
Rachel had the love Leah desperately wanted.
Leah had the children Rachel desperately wanted.
What a painfully broken household.
One sister went to sleep knowing her husband loved another woman more.
The other went to sleep knowing the sister she envied could conceive while she could not.
Leah wanted to be loved.
Rachel wanted to be fruitful.
And both women lived close enough to watch the other possess what they themselves were aching for.
That is one of comparison’s cruelest tricks.
It makes you stare at somebody else’s blessing until you can no longer see your own.
Rachel had Jacob’s affection, but eventually even that was not enough.
Genesis says:
“Rachel envied her sister.”
The Hebrew verb is connected with קנא — qana, carrying the sense of jealousy or envy.
Pain had become comparison.
Comparison had become envy.
Envy became desperation.
And desperation was about to become a decision.
Rachel turned toward Jacob and demanded:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Jacob responded angrily:
“Am I in God’s stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?”
There is something important here that we cannot miss.
Jacob understood something Rachel, in that agonizing moment, was struggling to accept:
Jacob was not God.
He could not command conception.
He could not manufacture the blessing Rachel wanted.
He could not take the throne that belonged to God.
But Rachel had a plan.
She said:
“Behold my maid Bilhah, go in unto her; and she shall bear upon my knees, that I may also have children by her.”
The Hebrew includes these striking words:
וְתֵלֵד עַל־בִּרְכַּי וְאִבָּנֶה גַם־אָנֹכִי מִמֶּנָּה
Veteled al-birkai, ve’ibbaneh gam-anokhi mimmennah.
The sense is:
“She shall bear upon my knees, and I also may be built up through her.”
Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob as a wife/concubine, and Jacob “went in unto her”—biblical language meaning that he had sexual relations with her.
Bilhah conceived.
She bore Jacob a son.
Rachel named him Dan, connecting his birth with her conviction that God had judged or vindicated her cause and heard her voice.
Then Bilhah conceived again.
Another son was born.
Rachel called him Naphtali, speaking of her great wrestlings with her sister.
And suddenly this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Scripture is not giving us a polished family devotional.
It is giving us jealousy.
Sex.
Infertility.
Rivalry.
Power imbalance.
Surrogacy according to ancient household customs.
A husband caught in a destructive family competition.
Two sisters wrestling for significance.
And a servant woman whose body becomes part of their struggle.
This is exactly where careful Bible reading matters.
The Bible describing something does not mean the Bible is commanding or approving everything being described.
Genesis faithfully records human beings as they actually were.
Abraham had Hagar.
Jacob had a deeply fractured polygamous household.
Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob.
Leah later gave Zilpah to Jacob.
None of this overturns the creation pattern Jesus Himself pointed back to when speaking about marriage: God’s design of the man and woman becoming “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6).
Scripture does not hide the consequences when human desire, cultural practice, favoritism, rivalry, and impatience collide.
And that may be precisely why Rachel’s story matters so much.
Because Rachel’s deepest problem was not that she wanted a child.
Wanting children was not sinful.
Her grief was real.
Infertility can carry profound sorrow, and Scripture never requires us to mock or minimize that sorrow.
The danger came when her longing began consuming her identity.
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Have you ever silently said your own version of that?
“God, if this relationship does not work, I’m finished.”
“If You don’t heal me, I can’t keep going.”
“If I don’t get this opportunity, my life is worthless.”
“If I cannot have what they have, something must be wrong with me.”
“If You really loved me, You would have answered already.”
Different words.
Same human heart.
We can become so consumed with one gift that we begin treating the absence of that gift as evidence that God has abandoned us.
And then comparison enters.
You open Facebook.
Another engagement.
Another pregnancy announcement.
Another ministry growing.
Another promotion.
Another testimony.
Another family photograph.
Another answered prayer.
You tap “like.”
You type, “Congratulations!”
Then you put the phone down.
And something inside you whispers:
Why not me?
That whisper can become dangerous when we feed it.
Because comparison rarely begins by telling us to rebel against God.
It simply keeps showing us what somebody else has.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until gratitude begins suffocating.
Until another person’s blessing starts feeling like our rejection.
Until we begin trying to force tomorrow because we cannot tolerate today.
Rachel looked at Leah and saw children.
Leah looked at Rachel and saw love.
Neither woman could find peace by possessing what belonged to the other.
And there is a warning here for us:
You can spend so much time staring at somebody else’s blessing that you completely misunderstand the story God is writing through your own life.
But Rachel’s story did not end in Genesis 30:8.
That matters.
Keep reading.
Genesis 30:22 contains words Rachel could never manufacture:
“And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.”
God remembered Rachel.
Not because God had literally forgotten she existed and suddenly recalled her name.
Biblical language about God “remembering” often signals God turning His covenant attention toward someone in order to act.
Rachel conceived.
And she gave birth to Joseph.
The woman who once screamed, “Give me children, or else I die,” eventually held her own son.
But even here, Scripture refuses to become a simplistic formula.
This passage does not promise that every person struggling with infertility will eventually conceive biologically if they pray hard enough.
That would place a promise into the text that God did not put there.
Rachel’s particular outcome belonged to Rachel’s particular story in redemptive history.
Our confidence is not that God must give every believer the earthly outcome they request.
Our confidence is that God remains God when the answer is yes, when the answer is no, and when heaven seems painfully silent.
And eventually, the tangled family of Jacob became part of something far greater than any of them could have understood.
God was forming Israel.
Even through an astonishingly dysfunctional household.
Dan mattered.
Naphtali mattered.
Joseph mattered.
Leah’s sons mattered.
Bilhah’s sons mattered.
Zilpah’s sons mattered.
God was moving His covenant purposes through people whose family history looked nothing like the sanitized religious stories we sometimes imagine.
And then comes one of the most breathtaking details.
The ultimate Redeemer would not arrive because this family finally became perfect.
He would come because God remained faithful.
Jesus Christ entered a human genealogy containing broken marriages, sexual scandal, outsiders, deceivers, kings, failures, sinners, and wounded people.
The Messiah came into our mess.
And He did not come merely to make dysfunctional people slightly better behaved.
He came to save sinners.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not stand at the edge of your wreckage waiting for you to make yourself presentable enough for Him.
He enters the story.
He bears sin.
He carries shame.
He goes to the cross.
He sheds His blood.
He dies.
He rises.
And He calls sinners to repent and believe.
The scandal of human sin meets the greater scandal of divine grace.
At the cross, Jesus took what we deserved so that those who trust in Him could receive what they could never earn: forgiveness, reconciliation, righteousness, adoption, and eternal life.
Maybe your Bilhah moment looks different.
Maybe you forced a relationship because you were terrified of being alone.
Maybe you compromised sexually because you wanted to feel wanted.
Maybe you manipulated circumstances because waiting frightened you.
Maybe jealousy has quietly poisoned the way you look at somebody you love.
Maybe somebody else’s blessing has secretly made you angry with God.
Maybe you have smiled publicly while privately asking:
“Why them, Lord? Why not me?”
Or perhaps you were the person caught inside somebody else’s desperate choices.
Used.
Overlooked.
Compared.
Treated as useful instead of precious.
The Gospel speaks there too.
Your value is not determined by another human being’s willingness to recognize it.
Your deepest identity cannot safely rest in marriage, fertility, beauty, money, ministry success, status, sexuality, popularity, possessions, or the approval of another person.
Those things make terrible gods.
Christ alone can carry the weight of your soul.
And maybe that is what somebody reading this needs to hear before doing something desperation will make them regret:
Do not let the pain of waiting convince you that disobedience is the only door left open.
God’s silence is not permission to manufacture your own savior.
Bring the disappointment to Him.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the anger.
Bring the questions you are embarrassed to say aloud.
Bring the secret resentment.
Bring the comparison.
Bring the thing you wanted so badly that it started owning you.
Jesus already knows.
Repentance does not mean pretending the wound never hurt.
It means refusing to let the wound become your god.
Grace does not tell you that your choices never mattered.
Grace tells you that your failures do not have to write the final sentence.
That is why we keep returning to this truth:
From scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing consequences.
He rewrites everything by redeeming sinners who could never redeem themselves.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
Someone reading quietly may discover through your testimony that they are not the only believer who has wrestled with jealousy, infertility, loneliness, unanswered prayer, regret, or waiting.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
We are saved by grace, not transactions.

But if Gospel-centered teaching has strengthened you and you want to help Gospel Warrior keep putting biblical truth in front of people who desperately need Jesus, sharing and financially supporting the work are practical, voluntary ways to help that mission continue.
There may come a night when somebody else’s answered prayer makes your unanswered prayer hurt again.
Come back and remember Rachel.
Remember that desperation does not have to become your master.
Remember that another person’s blessing is not proof of your abandonment.
Remember that God cannot be reduced to the timetable you wanted Him to follow.
And above everything else, remember Jesus.
It is never a substitute for belonging to a faithful local church.
It is never a way to buy God’s favor.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity when you believe that work is helping people encounter biblical truth.
Let Rachel’s painful story reach the woman crying because another pregnancy announcement appeared on her screen.
Let it reach the man quietly wondering why God has not answered him.
Let it reach the believer who is about to make a permanent decision because temporary desperation has convinced them they cannot wait another day.
Let it reach the person who thinks the Bible has nothing to say about messy families.
Let it reach someone who believes their scandal has made them unusable.
Because Scripture never needed perfect people in order to tell the truth about a perfect Savior.
Rachel was desperate.
Jacob was flawed.
Their household was fractured.
Their decisions carried consequences.
Yet God’s redemptive purpose kept moving.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ stepped into our fallen world.
The spotless One entered the story of sinners.
The innocent One carried the guilt of the guilty.
The rejected Savior opened the way for rebels to become children of God.
The crucified King rose from the grave.
And now the person who believes their worst chapter has already determined the ending can hear the Gospel say:

Your sin may explain chapters of your story, your wounds may have shaped chapters of your story, and your failures may have scarred chapters of your story—but none of them possesses the authority that belongs to Jesus Christ.
So stop asking your idols to give you what only Christ can give.
Stop asking another person’s life to tell you whether God loves you.
Stop letting comparison preach to you.
Bring the envy into the light.
Bring the desperation to Jesus.
Bring the scandal.
Bring the regret.
Bring the broken pieces.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Wait when God calls you to wait.
Trust Him when you cannot understand Him.
And receive the grace you could never manufacture for yourself.
Because perhaps the sentence haunting you right now is:
“Give me this… or I cannot go on.”
But Jesus is inviting you into something deeper:
“Give Me your heart—even here.”
And when everything you desperately wanted seems delayed, remember the truth Rachel had to learn through tears:
The thing you are waiting for was never meant to become the god you worship while you wait.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I AM MY BELOVED’S, AND HIS DESIRE IS FOR ME”: What Does Biblical Desire Really Look Like?
paragraphs: “I AM MY BELOVED’S, AND HIS DESIRE IS FOR ME”: What Does Biblical Desire Really Look Like?
We have been taught to ask whether somebody wants us. Scripture asks a more dangerous question: What kind of desire is worthy of the person God created you to be?
There is a sentence buried inside one of the most intimate books of the Bible that can stop a wounded heart in its tracks.
Not because it promises that everyone will eventually find romance.
Not because it turns God into a divine matchmaker.
And certainly not because it gives religious language to lust.
It stops us because it describes something many people spend their entire lives trying to find:
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me.” — Song of Solomon 7:10, KJV
In Hebrew:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani le-dodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved’s, and toward me is his desire.”
Read it again.
Slowly.
I am my beloved’s.
Not his possession to abuse.
Not her body to consume.
Not someone’s emotional emergency room.
Not the secret relationship hidden behind deleted messages.
Not the person kept around because somebody is terrified of loneliness.
Not an option.
Not a backup plan.
Not a body being mistaken for a soul.
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me.”
Maybe that sentence hurts more than you expected.
Because some of us know what it feels like to be wanted without ever being loved.
There is a difference.
Someone can desire your body and disregard your soul.
Someone can crave your attention and refuse responsibility for your heart.
Someone can become jealous when you leave while remaining careless while you stay.
Someone can say, “I need you,” when what they actually mean is, “I need what you give me.”
And sometimes we call that love because loneliness has lowered our definition.
That is where this ancient Hebrew sentence becomes painfully relevant.
The word translated “desire” is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.

It is an unusually rare Hebrew word. It appears only three times in the Hebrew Old Testament: Genesis 3:16, Genesis 4:7, and here in Song of Songs 7:10. Lexically, it carries the idea of desire, longing, or a powerful reaching toward something. The exact nuance in Genesis has generated real interpretive debate, which means we should resist building elaborate doctrines on a definition more precise than the evidence allows.
But here, in the Song, the context is unmistakably intimate.
The woman can say something extraordinary:
His longing is directed toward me.
And notice what she does not sound like.
Terrified.
Used.
Manipulated.
Reduced.
She is not begging, “Please choose me.”
She is not stalking his affection for evidence that she matters.
She is not trying to become beautiful enough to earn desire.
She speaks from the security of mutual belonging.
“I am my beloved’s…”
There is reciprocity here.
There is delight.
There is intimacy without erasure.
There is desire without dehumanization.
And that distinction may expose some things we would rather leave hidden.
Because desire itself is not the enemy.
God created human beings embodied.
God created attraction.
God created marriage.
God created sexuality to have a holy place within His design.
The Bible does not solve lust by pretending bodies are ugly. It confronts lust because bodies are precious.
Lust says, “How can I use you?”
Love asks, “How can I honor you?”
Lust isolates the body from the person.
Biblical love refuses to separate them.
Lust wants access without covenant.
Love accepts responsibility.
Lust says, “Satisfy me.”
Love learns sacrifice.
Lust becomes impatient with boundaries because boundaries interfere with consumption.
Love can honor boundaries because the beloved matters more than immediate gratification.
And suddenly the question changes.
The question is no longer merely, “Does this person desire me?”
The question becomes:
“What does their desire want to do with me?”
Does it draw you toward holiness or teach you to hide?
Does it honor your conscience or repeatedly pressure you to violate it?
Does it make truth easier or secrecy necessary?
Does it see your body as sacred before God, or merely available?
Does it celebrate your relationship with Christ, or slowly compete with Christ for the throne of your heart?
Because not everything intense is holy.
Not everything that gives you butterflies came from God.
Not everything you cannot stop thinking about should be pursued.
And not every person who says “I love you” understands biblical love.
Sometimes what we call chemistry is simply two wounds recognizing familiar dysfunction.
Sometimes what feels irresistible is not intimacy but dependency.
Sometimes we keep returning because rejection has made being chosen feel more important than being cherished rightly.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is stop calling bondage “love.”
That may be difficult to hear.
Especially if you have already given somebody years.
Especially if you compromised things you once promised God you would protect.
Especially if the relationship became physical and now shame whispers that you are permanently tied to your worst decisions.
Especially if you knew better.
That sentence can be brutal:
I knew better.
Peter knew better when he denied Jesus.
David knew better when desire crossed into devastating sin.
The prodigal son knew he had a father and still walked toward the far country.
Human beings have an extraordinary ability to know truth and still choose the thing that wounds us.
But this is where Christianity becomes more than moral advice.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to tell ruined people that they should have made better choices.
He came to save sinners.
That changes everything.
The Gospel does not say your sexual history is your identity.
It does not say your divorce is your identity.
Your affair is not your identity.
Your pornography addiction is not your identity.
Your unwantedness is not your identity.
Your rejection is not your identity.
Your loneliness is not your identity.
Your abuse is not your identity.
Your past is not powerful enough to overrule the blood of Jesus Christ.
Sin is real.
Consequences can be real.
Repentance is necessary.
But grace is also real.
And biblical repentance is not pretending the wound never happened. It is turning from sin toward the Savior who was crucified for sinners and rose again.
This is why Jesus is not an accessory to this conversation.
He is the center of it.
Without Christ, an article about biblical desire can easily become another relationship manual: find somebody healthier, establish better boundaries, communicate properly, wait for marriage.
Those things can matter.
But Christianity goes deeper.
The deepest disorder in human desire is not merely that we sometimes want the wrong person.
It is that sinful humanity wants created things more than the Creator.
We ask another human being to tell us we are enough.
We ask romance to cure our loneliness.
We ask sex to prove our worth.
We ask marriage to give us identity.
We ask another wounded human being to occupy a throne that belongs to Jesus Christ.
And then we are devastated when they collapse beneath the weight of being our god.
No husband can be your Savior.
No wife can be your Savior.
No boyfriend can be your Savior.
No girlfriend can be your Savior.
No wedding ring can resurrect a dead heart.
Jesus can.
The astonishing heart of Christianity is not that you finally become desirable enough for God.
It is that God moved toward sinners who could never rescue themselves.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV.
While we were sinners.
Not after the makeover.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after the relationship became respectable.
Not after we cleaned the search history.
Not after we learned Christian vocabulary.
Christ died for sinners.
And He does not save us so that we can remain enslaved to the desires that were destroying us.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Jesus does not merely cover yesterday.
He claims tomorrow.
That means the person who has lived through sexual sin can become holy.
The person who has confused attention with love can learn security in Christ.
The person addicted to pornography can seek help, confess, repent, establish radical boundaries, and walk toward freedom.
The person who has used others can repent.
The person who has been used does not have to believe that what someone did to them determines their value.
The adulterer can repent.
The bitter spouse can repent.
The secretly lustful churchgoer can repent.
The lonely believer about to compromise can turn around before tonight becomes tomorrow's regret.
There is grace at the cross.
But grace is not permission to keep walking toward the grave.
Grace is Christ meeting us there and saying, in effect:
Come out.
There is another way to live.
And this is where Song of Songs becomes beautiful again.
We should respect what the book actually is before turning every romantic line into an allegory. Song of Songs celebrates human love and marital desire in poetic form. Its immediate context matters.
Yet the whole Christian canon also teaches us something even greater: human marriage is not ultimate.
Paul describes marriage in Ephesians 5:31–32 and then points beyond it to Christ and His church.
So the married Christian can read Song of Songs and thank God for the goodness of covenant love.
The single Christian can read it without believing life is incomplete until another human being arrives.
The widowed Christian can read it without believing the best part of existence died with a spouse.
And the believer who has been betrayed can read it without concluding that another person's unfaithfulness has made faithful love impossible.
Every good human love is a gift.
Jesus remains Lord.
There is a dangerous freedom in finally understanding that.
You do not need to seduce someone into staying.
You do not need to surrender your convictions to avoid being abandoned.
You do not need to become sexually available to prove you are lovable.
You do not need to chase someone who repeatedly makes you question whether you matter.
You do not need a relationship status to prove that God has not forgotten you.
And if you are married, biblical desire does not give you permission to demand another person's body as though covenant erased tenderness, dignity, patience, or sacrificial love.
Christ-shaped love does not ask, “What am I entitled to take?”
It learns to give.
Jesus Himself becomes the pattern.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV.
Gave Himself.
There is the shape of Christian love.
Not consumption.
Self-giving.
Not exploitation.
Sacrifice.
Not manipulation disguised as passion.
Love shaped by Christ.
And maybe this is where you need to become painfully honest.
Not with the person sitting beside you.
Not with Facebook.
Not even with us.
With God.
What have you been calling love that you already know is destroying your obedience?
Whose attention have you made necessary for your identity?
What secret desire are you feeding that you would be ashamed to place openly before Jesus?
What relationship are you protecting more fiercely than your communion with Christ?
What fantasy keeps getting fed while your marriage starves?
What wound makes you run toward anyone who makes you feel temporarily wanted?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because typing words saves anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when hiding finally ends, and somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only Christian struggling in silence.
That is why this message should not end with you.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list smiling publicly while privately negotiating with temptation.
Someone staying in a relationship because they believe loneliness would be worse.
Someone married but starving for tenderness.
Someone ashamed of what happened last night.
Someone convinced God could forgive everybody except them.
Not as religious decoration.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
There is another way you can help this work continue.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone should manipulate you into giving by suggesting God will love you more if you pay.
Scripture says the opposite of coercion: giving is to come from a heart that has freely decided to give, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).

At the same time, Scripture openly recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting Gospel labor. Paul writes that “the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14, KJV).
If you have been wondering how you can help, this is one practical way.
And if monthly financial support is not possible, please do not carry shame.
Share.
Pray.
Save the articles.
Faithful Gospel partnership is bigger than a transaction.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation has already been purchased at a price none of us could pay—the precious blood of Christ.
The call of the Gospel is not “pay.”
It is:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
And when Christ captures the heart, even our desires begin learning a new language.
We begin wanting holiness more than the thrill of secrecy.
Truth more than appearances.
Covenant more than consumption.
Faithfulness more than fantasy.
Christ more than the temporary relief of being wanted by somebody who cannot save us.
Maybe that is what you needed tonight.
Not another person to desire you.
Not another notification.
Not another flirtation.
Not another message saying, “I miss you,” from the same person whose presence keeps pulling you away from God.
Maybe you needed to remember whose voice matters most.
The world will tell you that your greatest victory is becoming irresistible.
Jesus offers something infinitely greater:
redemption.
He takes people who have been used and teaches them dignity.
People who have used others and leads them to repentance.
People buried beneath sexual shame and clothes them in grace.
People addicted to counterfeit intimacy and teaches them communion.
People who thought their scandal was the final chapter and begins writing something they never believed possible.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin was insignificant.
The cross proves sin was devastatingly serious.
But the empty tomb declares that sin does not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
So if you remember only one thing after this article disappears from your screen, remember this:

You do not need to be desired by everyone when your entire life has been summoned into the redeeming love and lordship of Jesus Christ—and whatever sin has written across your past, Christ is still able to write grace across your future.
Because perhaps the greatest transformation of desire is not finally getting everything your heart once demanded.
Perhaps it is reaching the place where your heart can finally say:
Jesus, I want You more.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: FIERY SERPENTS ENTERED ISRAEL’S CAMP—THEN GOD TOLD MOSES TO RAISE A BRONZE SERPENT
paragraphs: FIERY SERPENTS ENTERED ISRAEL’S CAMP—THEN GOD TOLD MOSES TO RAISE A BRONZE SERPENT
They were dying from the bite. God did not tell them to pretend the venom wasn't there. He told them to look at something lifted up—and centuries later, Jesus said their story was pointing to Him.
Imagine hearing the screaming before you understand what is happening.
A child cries out.
Someone tears open a tent flap.
Another person falls into the sand.
Then another.
And suddenly the camp realizes something terrifying is moving among them.
Serpents.
Not somewhere beyond the tents.
Inside the camp.

Israel had survived Egypt. They had watched the Red Sea open. They had eaten bread that appeared with the morning dew. They had seen water come from a rock. They had witnessed a mountain tremble beneath the presence of God.
And still...
they complained.
That is what makes Numbers 21 so uncomfortable.
Because the people in this story are not people who had never seen God move.
They are people who had seen Him move repeatedly...
and still allowed unbelief to poison their hearts.
Maybe that is why this story feels frighteningly close to home.
You can have answered prayers in your history and complaints in your mouth today.
You can remember what God delivered you from and still resent where He is leading you.
You can know Scripture and still struggle to trust the Author.
You can sing on Sunday and privately ask on Monday,
“God, why have You brought me here?”
Israel was traveling around Edom, and Numbers tells us that “the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way.”
Then frustration became accusation.
They spoke against God and Moses.
Why had they been brought out of Egypt?
Why were they in the wilderness?
Why was there no ordinary food and water?
Why did they despise the provision God had given them?
Then the wilderness changed.
Numbers 21:6 says:
“And the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.”
The Hebrew is chilling:
הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים
hanneḥāšîm haśśərāfîm
Literally, “the serpents, the burning ones” or “fiery serpents.”
The word connected with “serpent” is נָחָשׁ — nāḥāš.
The word translated “fiery” comes from שָׂרָף — śārāf, associated with burning.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us whether “fiery” describes their appearance, their venom's burning effect, or another characteristic. We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
What Scripture does reveal is enough.
They bit.
People died.
Judgment had entered the camp.
And suddenly the complaints stopped.
Funny how quickly the things we thought were unbearable can become small when we finally see the condition of our souls.
The people ran to Moses.
“We have sinned.”
Not...
“We've been misunderstood.”
Not...
“We were merely expressing ourselves.”
Not...
“Everybody complains.”
“We have sinned.”
There are three words pride hates saying:
I have sinned.
Yet those words can become the doorway through which repentance begins.
Some of us have spent years renaming what God has already named.
We call bitterness “protecting my peace.”
We call lust “just looking.”
We call pride “knowing my worth.”
We call gossip “venting.”
We call unforgiveness “having boundaries,” even when the boundary has quietly become hatred.
We call spiritual apathy “being busy.”
We call compromise “being realistic.”
And sometimes we spend so much energy explaining our wounds that we never confess the ways we have wounded others.
Israel finally stopped explaining.
“We have sinned.”
Moses prayed.
Then God gave him one of the strangest instructions in the Old Testament.
Make a fiery serpent.
Put it on a pole.
Anyone who has been bitten may look at it and live.
So Moses made a serpent of bronze.
The Hebrew expression is:
נְחַשׁ נְחֹשֶׁת
neḥaš neḥōšet
A serpent of bronze.
The similarity between the Hebrew sounds for serpent and bronze makes the expression memorable.
But think about how strange the command must have sounded.
The people had been bitten by serpents...
and God told Moses to raise the likeness of a serpent before them.
No medicine is mentioned.
No antidote is described.
No elaborate pilgrimage.
No price.
No achievement.
No heroic act.
Look.
And live.
Imagine being bitten.
Your body is burning.
Your strength is disappearing.
You are lying in the dust.
Someone shouts,
“Look!”
And perhaps everything inside you wants something more complicated.
Surely there must be something I can do.
Surely I must earn this.
Surely looking cannot be enough.
But the dying Israelite did not need to understand every mystery surrounding the bronze serpent.
He needed to trust the word God had spoken.
He looked.
He lived.
And this is where the story becomes much bigger than Numbers 21.
Because centuries later, Jesus Christ reached back into Israel's wilderness and told us where the deepest meaning of that lifted serpent was ultimately pointing.
Jesus was speaking to Nicodemus.
A religious man.
A teacher.
A man with knowledge, reputation, theology, and questions.
And Jesus told him that he needed something he could never accomplish through religious credentials.
He needed to be born again.
Then Jesus said:
Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ...
Kai kathōs Mōysēs hypsōsen ton ophin en tē erēmō...
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness...”
Then came the words that transform the wilderness story:
“...even so must the Son of man be lifted up.”
Jesus was talking about Himself.
The Greek verb ὑψόω — hypsoō — means to lift up or raise up.
The serpent was lifted.
Christ would be lifted.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus is not saying that He is evil.
He is not saying the serpent was secretly divine.
He is not telling us to worship the bronze object.
The comparison centers upon the God-appointed lifting up and the life received by those who believe.
The Israelites were dying and could not save themselves.
Humanity is dying in sin and cannot save itself.
God provided the means.
The dying person looked in faith.
And Jesus declares that the Son of Man would likewise be lifted up so that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life.
Now the wilderness becomes a mirror.
Because the serpent's venom was killing bodies.
Sin is killing something far deeper.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
That includes the preacher.
The church member.
The skeptic.
The addict.
The respectable businessman.
The exhausted mother.
The teenager hiding browser history.
The person reading Christian articles while secretly drifting from Christ.
The person everybody thinks is strong.
The person who knows exactly how to raise their hands during worship while carrying a private life they desperately hope nobody discovers.
All.
Have.
Sinned.
The Gospel begins where our excuses end.
But please hear this:
Christianity is not the announcement that bad people should try harder to become respectable.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who cannot rescue themselves have been offered salvation through Jesus Christ.
Look at the cross.
Not sentimentally.
Look at what happened there.
The eternal Son of God took upon Himself true humanity.
He lived without sin.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Lifted up.
And the One who knew no sin bore our sin.
The cross exposes something devastating about us:
Our condition was so serious that moral improvement could never cure it.
But the cross reveals something breathtaking about God:
His love was so great that He gave His Son to save sinners.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
The scandal is your sin.
The scandal is mine.
The scandal is that creatures made by God rebel against their Creator and then convince themselves that we are basically fine.
The scandal is that humanity crucified the sinless Son of God.
But grace...
Grace is that the cross where humanity displayed its rebellion became the place where Christ accomplished redemption.
Grace is Jesus praying for His enemies.
Grace is blood shed for sinners.
Grace is forgiveness offered to the guilty.
Grace is the condemned thief hearing hope while dying beside the King.
Grace is Peter being restored after denying Jesus.
Grace is Saul the persecutor becoming Paul the apostle.
Grace is God taking people whose stories should have ended in judgment and giving them a new ending through Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But there is another warning hidden inside the bronze-serpent story that many people never mention.
The bronze serpent survived.
Generations passed.
And eventually something God had once used became something Israel worshiped.
During the reign of Hezekiah, Scripture says the Israelites were burning incense to that bronze serpent.
Hezekiah destroyed it.
Think about that.
Something once associated with God's deliverance had become an idol.
And that should frighten every religious heart.
Because we can begin worshiping what God used instead of worshiping God.
A ministry can become an idol.
A pastor can become an idol.
A church tradition can become an idol.
A worship style can become an idol.
A theological tribe can become an idol.
A Christian page can become an idol.
Even memories of yesterday's encounter with God can become substitutes for walking with God today.
The bronze serpent could not save anyone independently of God's word.
It was never the Savior.
And eventually, when people treated it like an object of worship, it had to be smashed.
Jesus alone is Savior.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a preacher.
Not a denomination.
Not a Christian influencer.
Not a book.
Not a relic.
Not a religious object.
Jesus.
If Gospel Warrior ever helps you, let it help you look beyond Gospel Warrior toward Christ.
If an article convicts you, do not worship the messenger.
Run to Jesus.
If a devotional strengthens you, do not merely admire the devotional.
Open your Bible.
Pray.
Repent.
Believe.
Obey Christ.
Because the purpose of Christian ministry is not to gather spectators around a bronze object.
It is to point dying people toward the living Christ.
Maybe you have been bitten by things nobody sees.
Bitterness.
Pornography.
Secret adultery.
Envy.
Alcohol.
Drugs.
Pride.
Religious hypocrisy.
A temper your family fears.
A wound you turned into permission to wound others.
A private addiction beneath a public smile.
Maybe you keep telling yourself,
“I'm managing it.”
But the venom is moving.
Maybe your marriage feels colder.
Your prayer life is disappearing.
Scripture feels distant.
Sin that once disturbed you now feels normal.
You still know Christian vocabulary...
but somewhere inside, you know something is dying.
Hear the Gospel.
You do not need to clean yourself up enough to become worthy of looking to Jesus.
Look to Jesus because you are not worthy—and because He is merciful.
Repentance does not mean pretending you never sinned.
Repentance means turning from sin toward the Savior.
Faith is not pretending the venom is harmless.
Faith admits,
“I cannot save myself.”
Then it looks to Christ.
Maybe you think you have gone too far.
Look.
Maybe you failed again last night.
Look.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually healthy while you know you are barely breathing.
Look.
Maybe shame whispers that Jesus wants everyone except you.
Look.
Not to yourself.
Not to your record.
Not to your promises that “this time I'll do better.”
Look to Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
The serpent was raised in a wilderness full of dying people.
Jesus was raised on a cross for a world full of sinners.
And unlike the bronze serpent, Jesus did not remain an object hanging on a pole.
The crucified Christ was buried.
And on the third day...
the tomb was empty.
Death did not keep Him.
Sin did not defeat Him.
The grave did not write the final sentence.
Jesus rose.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is reconciliation with God in Christ.
There is a new heart in Christ.
There is power to fight sin in Christ.
There is resurrection hope in Christ.
There is grace for repentant sinners in Christ.
And maybe right now your greatest need is not another inspirational quote.
Maybe you need to stop hiding.
Confess your sin to God.
Call it what He calls it.
Turn from it.
Trust Jesus.
And where your sin has harmed someone, seek biblical reconciliation and make things right where possible.
You may have spent years trying to manage venom.
Christ offers something infinitely greater.
Life.
Be honest before God.
If you genuinely need His mercy, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if Christ has already pulled you from a place you thought would destroy you, tell your testimony. Someone reading the comments may be standing where you once stood.
Do not turn vulnerability into theater.
Let it become fellowship.
“Don't stop looking to Jesus.”
and suddenly encounter the Gospel.
That share could become an invitation to open Scripture.
To repent.
To pray.
To return to church.
To call someone for help.
To look toward Christ.

If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, don't let that support become empty religious consumerism. Worship belongs to God alone. But generosity, sharing biblical truth, encouraging Gospel ministry, and helping others encounter Scripture can be genuine acts of Christian stewardship when they flow from love for Christ rather than pressure or self-glory.
Grace cannot be bought.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
The gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession, testimony, encouragement, and prayer begin when one believer finally stops pretending.
Then close Facebook for a moment.
Open your Bible.
Read Numbers 21:4–9.
Then read John 3:1–21.
And when you reach the words about Moses lifting up the serpent in the wilderness, remember:
Jesus knew exactly where humanity's story was going.
Toward a hill.
Toward a cross.
Toward nails.
Toward blood.
Toward a tomb.
And then...
toward resurrection.
The Israelites looked upward because death was already working inside them.
Perhaps that is the image you need to carry with you tonight.
Not people pretending they were never bitten.
Not people boasting about how little venom they had.
Not people comparing wounds.
Dying people looking toward the provision God had given.
And now Christ calls sinners to something greater.
Look to Him.
Your sin may explain how you reached this wilderness.
Your scars may testify to battles you wish you had never fought.
Your consequences may not disappear overnight.
But for the person who turns to Jesus Christ in repentant faith, sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Your addiction does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
The grave does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
The venom may explain why you fell—but the cross announces why your story does not have to end in the dust.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CHRISTIAN MARRIAGE DOES NOT MEAN UNLIMITED SEXUAL ENTITLEMENT
paragraphs:
CHRISTIAN MARRIAGE DOES NOT MEAN UNLIMITED SEXUAL ENTITLEMENT
A Wedding Ring Is Not a Lifetime Permission Slip to Ignore Your Spouse’s Pain — and the Gospel Never Turns Covenant Love Into a License to Take
There are wounds that happen outside marriage.
And then there are wounds that happen in the very place where someone believed they would finally be safe.
That second kind can be harder to explain.
Because what do you say when the person hurting you is the person who prayed beside you at the altar?
What do you call it when Scripture is hanging on the bedroom wall, wedding photographs are smiling from the hallway, everyone at church thinks you have a beautiful Christian marriage...

but behind the closed door, one spouse has learned that saying “not tonight,” “I’m hurting,” “I’m exhausted,” “I’m frightened,” or simply “please stop” may bring anger, accusations, manipulation, spiritual pressure, sulking, threats, or punishment?
What happens when someone begins using the Bible not as a lamp...
but as leverage?
This is where Christians must have enough courage to say something clearly:
Marriage creates a profound covenant of sexual faithfulness and mutual belonging.
It does not create unlimited sexual entitlement.
And Scripture itself will not allow us to pretend otherwise.
Go all the way back to the beginning.
Genesis describes marriage with breathtaking language:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vedavaq be'ishto vehayu levasar echad.
A man “clings” or “holds fast” to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
Basar echad.
One flesh.
Not one human being swallowing another.
Not one will erasing another.
Not one body becoming property to be used regardless of suffering.
Two persons enter a covenantal union so intimate that Scripture describes them as one flesh.
That is sacred.
That is why adultery is devastating.
That is why sexual faithfulness matters.
That is why Christian sexuality cannot be reduced to personal appetite.
And that is precisely why sexual selfishness inside marriage should disturb us too.
Because “one flesh” is not permission to stop seeing the other person.
It is a reason to see them more deeply.
Paul develops this startling mutuality in 1 Corinthians 7.
And this is one of those passages that can become dangerous when someone quotes half of it.
Paul says that a wife does not exercise exclusive authority over her own body, but her husband does.
Someone looking for ammunition might stop there.
But Paul does not.
The Greek continues:
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ...
“Likewise also...”
And then Paul turns the statement directly around.
The husband does not exercise exclusive authority over his own body either, but his wife does.
Read the symmetry.
Feel the weight of it.
Paul does not write:
He gives neither spouse unilateral bodily sovereignty over the other while preserving unilateral sovereignty for themselves.
The language is reciprocal.
The Greek verb is ἐξουσιάζει — exousiazei — relating to exercising authority.
And Paul deliberately places husband and wife under corresponding obligations.
Then, when he discusses abstaining from sexual relations, he says it should occur:
ἐκ συμφώνου
ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
By mutual consent.
The very passage sometimes dragged into marriages to demand sex actually contains reciprocity and mutual agreement.

Yes, Scripture teaches that husbands and wives should not selfishly weaponize sexual deprivation against each other. Sexual intimacy is a real and important part of marriage. Persistent rejection, manipulation, infidelity, pornography, selfishness, emotional abandonment, and sexual indifference can deeply injure a marriage and should not simply be ignored.
But there is an enormous moral difference between teaching spouses to lovingly give themselves to one another...
and teaching someone that marriage gives them unrestricted access to another human body.
Christian marital intimacy is supposed to be giving.
Not taking.
That difference matters.
Especially to the spouse reading this with tears already forming because nobody ever told them they were allowed to say:
“That hurt.”
“I am afraid.”
“I need you to stop.”
“Something is wrong between us.”
“I need help.”
Maybe you have spent years wondering whether acknowledging your pain somehow makes you a rebellious husband or wife.
Maybe every conversation eventually became the same accusation.
“But the Bible says your body belongs to me.”
Please keep reading.
Because the Bible says something else too.
When Paul describes Christian marriage in Ephesians 5, he does not hand husbands a blank check for selfish domination.
He hands them a cross.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
The Greek is devastatingly beautiful:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
Christ loved the church...
and gave Himself up for her.
ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν.
He gave Himself.
That is the pattern.
Jesus does not stand before His bride asking, “How much can I extract?”
He gives Himself.
Christian marriage therefore cannot faithfully imitate Christ while making selfish acquisition its governing principle.
A husband is told to love his wife as Christ loved His church. Paul goes even further and tells husbands to love their wives as their own bodies, nourishing and cherishing them.
Think about that.
If she trembles when you touch her, something matters more in that moment than satisfying your desire.
Her trembling matters.
If he is emotionally shattered, his condition matters.
If your spouse is sick, recovering from childbirth, grieving, traumatized, frightened, physically hurting, emotionally overwhelmed, or desperately trying to explain that something feels wrong...
love listens.
Love notices.
Love does not hear “please stop” and begin searching for a Bible verse powerful enough to silence it.
And we need to say something uncomfortable here.
A marriage certificate cannot transform cruelty into Christlikeness.
A wedding ceremony does not baptize selfishness.
Putting the word “biblical” in front of domination does not make domination holy.
And quoting Scripture while disregarding the suffering of the person beside you is not spiritual maturity.
Jesus repeatedly confronted people who knew religious language while missing mercy, justice, faithfulness, and the heart of God.
So perhaps the question Christian spouses should ask in the bedroom is not merely:
“What am I allowed to receive?”
Perhaps there is a much more Christlike question:
“How can I love you?”
That changes everything.
Because Christian sexuality is not supposed to be two people negotiating how much they can take from each other.
It is two covenant partners learning to give themselves faithfully, tenderly, joyfully, truthfully, and sacrificially.
Sometimes that giving looks like passionate intimacy.
Sometimes it looks like waiting.
Sometimes it looks like asking, “Are you okay?”
Sometimes it looks like holding someone without expecting sex afterward.
Sometimes it means confessing selfishness.
Sometimes it means confronting persistent rejection rather than pretending everything is fine.
Sometimes it means counseling.
Sometimes it means medical care.
Sometimes it means exposing abuse that has been hidden beneath religious language.
And sometimes the most Christian sentence spoken in a bedroom may simply be:
“I love you more than I love getting what I want tonight.”
That sounds remarkably close to the shape of the cross.
This truth also cuts both ways.
A wife should not manipulate her husband sexually.
A husband should not manipulate his wife sexually.
Neither spouse should use affection as currency.
Neither should deliberately humiliate the other.
Neither should weaponize Scripture.
Neither should treat the other's body as an appliance for personal gratification.
Neither should use prolonged withholding as revenge or coercion.
Neither should assume that being married eliminates the need for tenderness, communication, patience, repentance, and mutual care.
Biblical mutuality does not mean sexual demands become irrelevant.
It means those needs are handled inside love rather than domination.
There may be someone reading this who has been the hurting spouse.
But there may also be someone reading this who suddenly realizes:
I have been the one doing the hurting.
Don't run from that realization.
Run to Christ with it.
Maybe you never considered yourself abusive.
Maybe you thought pressure was normal.
Maybe you confused leadership with control.
Maybe you believed marriage meant your spouse could never refuse you.
Maybe you became angry when intimacy did not happen.
Maybe you punished your spouse emotionally afterward.
Maybe you quoted 1 Corinthians 7 while conveniently forgetting that the same chapter speaks reciprocally.
Maybe your spouse eventually stopped arguing.
And you called the silence peace.
But silence is not always peace.
Sometimes silence is what happens when somebody has given up believing they will be heard.
If that realization cuts you...
do not waste the wound.
Repent.
Not the cheap repentance that says, “I'm sorry you felt that way.”
Real repentance.
“I sinned against you.”
“I used pressure where I should have shown love.”
“I cared more about getting what I wanted than understanding what you were experiencing.”
“I used Scripture selfishly.”
“I frightened you.”
“Will you forgive me?”
And then accept that forgiveness cannot be demanded on your timetable either.
Repentance bears fruit.
It changes behavior.
It welcomes accountability.
It stops hiding.
It stops defending what Christ is exposing.
Because this is where the Gospel enters the room.
Not as decoration.
Not as a religious excuse.
As rescue.
Christianity is not the story of righteous people successfully hiding their scandals.
It is the story of sinners being exposed by holiness and then offered mercy through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for sexual sinners.
Christ died for selfish spouses.
Christ died for adulterers.
Christ died for people drowning in pornography.
Christ died for manipulators.
Christ died for the ashamed.
Christ died for the wounded.
Christ died for those who have committed sins they desperately wish they could erase.
And Christ is able to transform people who truly come to Him in repentance and faith.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace brings darkness into the light and refuses to leave us there.
That is why repentance and grace belong together.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
Truth without grace becomes condemnation.
But at Calvary we see both.
Our sin was serious enough that Christ died.
His mercy was great enough that Christ willingly died for sinners.
That is scandalous grace.
And perhaps that is why this subject matters so much.
Because the bedroom is one of the places where Christians can become extraordinarily skilled at pretending.
Nobody at church sees it.
Nobody in the Bible study knows.
Nobody watching the smiling family photograph understands what happened fifteen minutes before it was taken.
But Jesus sees.
He sees the spouse crying quietly in the bathroom.
He sees the husband terrified to admit that something in his marriage is broken.
He sees the wife who has confused endurance with holiness.
He sees the spouse whose selfishness has been protected by theology.
He sees the shame.
He sees the secrets.
He sees the wounds.
And He also sees what redemption could become.

If you are experiencing sexual coercion, violence, threats, or abuse, seeking safety and trustworthy help is not a betrayal of Scripture. Serious harm should not be hidden merely to preserve appearances. Reach out to appropriate local emergency services when immediate danger exists and to trustworthy pastoral, professional, legal, medical, or domestic-abuse support as appropriate to your situation.
And if you are the spouse causing fear...
stop.
Do not demand another chance while continuing the behavior.
Do not demand secrecy.
Do not demand instant forgiveness.
Bring what you have done into the light.
Seek serious pastoral and professional accountability.
Repent before God.
Accept consequences.
Learn what Christlike love actually looks like.
Because Jesus did not save us so we could become more sophisticated at defending our sin.
He saves sinners to transform them.
This is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a slogan.
Your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Your wound does not have to become your identity.
Your worst sin does not have to become the last sentence written over your life.
Your marriage may need help.
Your theology may need correction.
Your heart may need repentance.
Your wounds may need years of healing.
Your situation may require difficult decisions and wise counsel rather than simplistic internet advice.
But Jesus Christ still specializes in resurrection.
Dead things are not intimidating to the One who walked out of a grave.
So bring Him the truth.
Not the Instagram marriage.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the cleaned-up testimony.
The truth.
“Jesus, this is what happened.”
“Jesus, this is what I did.”
“Jesus, this is what was done to me.”
“Jesus, this is what I became.”
“Jesus, I need mercy.”
There is grace at the cross.
Not permission to continue hurting people.
Grace to become different.
Grace to confess.
Grace to forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Grace to establish truth.
Grace to pursue safety.
Grace to rebuild what can faithfully be rebuilt.
Grace to stop pretending.
Grace to repent.
Grace to heal.
Grace to become more like Jesus.
And maybe this article needs to travel farther than your screen.
There is probably a husband who needs to read it before selfishness destroys tenderness in his marriage.
There may be a wife who has spent years believing God requires her to silently endure what God never called holy.
There may be a newlywed couple who need to understand this before harmful patterns become normal.

There may be a pastor, counselor, father, mother, son, daughter, friend, struggling believer, seeker, lukewarm Christian, or even an unbeliever who needs to discover that biblical Christianity is not a license for sexual selfishness.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient love, truth, mercy, holiness, generosity, and service.

But if this truth can protect a marriage, expose hidden sin, comfort somebody suffering in silence, or lead one person toward repentance and Jesus Christ, sharing it can become one small act of putting useful truth into someone else's path.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become evidence that Christians can tell the truth without pretending to have perfect lives.
Not because money purchases spiritual blessing.
And never because the Gospel is for sale.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But Gospel work can be supported.
Because somebody in your circle may never tell you what is happening behind their bedroom door.
Somebody may read silently.
Somebody may cry.
Somebody may finally ask for help.
Somebody may finally repent.
Somebody may discover that the Bible they thought condemned them actually points them toward the crucified and risen Christ.
And somebody may finally understand that Christian marriage was never meant to make one spouse the possession of another.
It was meant to become a living witness to covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, truth, holiness, tenderness, forgiveness, and the astonishing love of Jesus Christ.
A ring can tell the world that you are married.
But only the way you love when nobody is watching reveals what you believe marriage is for.
And when selfishness, shame, wounds, and hidden sins have already written pages you wish could disappear, remember this:
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read. Give Him the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY BEAT THEM UNTIL THEY BLED. AT MIDNIGHT, THEY STARTED SINGING—THEN THE PRISON BEGAN TO SHAKE
paragraphs: THEY BEAT THEM UNTIL THEY BLED. AT MIDNIGHT, THEY STARTED SINGING—THEN THE PRISON BEGAN TO SHAKE

Paul and Silas had no reason to sing if worship depended on circumstances. Their backs were wounded. Their feet were locked in stocks. Their future was uncertain. But somewhere around midnight, two suffering men began praising God—and before the night was over, doors were open, chains were loose, a suicidal jailer was alive, and an entire household had heard about Jesus.
There is a kind of worship you sing because life is beautiful.
And then there is the song that crawls out of you when life has beaten you bloody.
That second song is different.
It costs something.
Maybe that is why somebody else needs to hear it.
Acts 16 takes us into one of the most unforgettable nights in the New Testament.

Paul and Silas had been publicly attacked. Their clothes were torn from them. They were beaten repeatedly with rods. Then, without being given the comfort we might expect servants of God to receive, they were thrown into prison.
Not merely prison.
The jailer put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in stocks.
Imagine the darkness.
Imagine trying to find a position that does not hurt when your back has been struck again and again.
Imagine dried blood against skin.
Imagine the questions that could have entered their minds.
God, we obeyed You.
God, we preached Christ.
God, we were serving You.
How did obedience lead us here?
That question may be closer to your life than you want to admit.
You prayed, but the marriage still fractured.
You served, but somebody betrayed you.
You tried to obey God, yet the door still closed.
You asked for healing, but the report still frightened you.
You raised your child to know Christ, and now you barely recognize the direction of his or her life.
You told everybody that God was faithful...
and then midnight came.
That is where some people quietly lose their song.
Not because they stopped believing God exists.
Because they cannot understand why the God they trusted allowed the prison they are sitting in.
And this is where Acts 16 becomes almost painfully beautiful.
Luke writes in the original Greek:
Kata de to mesonyktion Paulos kai Silas proseuchomenoi hymnoun ton Theon…
“About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God…”
Acts 16:25.
Look carefully.
The text does not say they were singing because the prison doors had opened.
They were singing while the doors were still shut.
They were praising while their feet were still restrained.
They worshiped before they knew what God would do next.
That matters.
The Greek word translated “were singing hymns” is ὕμνουν — hymnoun, from the verb hymneō: to sing praise, to hymn, to celebrate in song.
They were not pretending the beating did not hurt.
Biblical faith is not denial.
Christian worship does not require you to call pain pleasure, tragedy good, abuse acceptable, or heartbreak imaginary.
They could acknowledge the wounds and still acknowledge God.
And sometimes that is one of the purest forms of worship:
“Lord, I do not understand You right now...
but I still belong to You.”
“I don't know why You permitted this...
but Jesus is still Lord.”
“My circumstances are screaming at me to despair...
but my circumstances are not my Savior.”
That is faith with scars on it.
And there is another detail in the verse that is easy to rush past.
The prisoners were listening.
The Greek says:
ἐπηκροῶντο — epēkroōnto.
They were listening to Paul and Silas.
Think about that.
Two wounded Christians believed they were singing to God.
But prisoners were listening.
Someone is always listening to the song you sing in your midnight.
People may admire your faith when everything is working.
They examine it when everything falls apart.
Your children are listening.
Your spouse is listening.
Your unbelieving friend is listening.
The coworker who knows you follow Jesus is listening.
The person who secretly wonders whether Christianity is real is watching what happens when your prayers seem unanswered.
And perhaps that is why some of our most powerful testimony is not produced on a stage.
It is produced in a prison.
Not when we tell people, “Look how successful Christianity made me.”
But when suffering strips away the things we leaned upon and somehow Jesus remains precious.
Then suddenly...
the ground moved.
Acts 16:26 begins:
ἄφνω δὲ σεισμὸς ἐγένετο μέγας…
Aphnō de seismos egeneto megas…
“Suddenly there was a great earthquake…”
The foundations of the prison shook.
The doors opened.
The bonds came loose.
It is a breathtaking moment.
But be careful here, because this passage is sometimes turned into something Scripture itself never promises.
“Praise God and your earthquake will come.”
“Sing hard enough and every prison door will open.”
“Worship and God will immediately remove your problem.”
That sounds exciting.
But that is not the whole Gospel.

Paul himself would later endure other imprisonments. Christians throughout Scripture suffered faithfully. Some believers experienced miraculous deliverance; others glorified Christ by remaining faithful through suffering.
Jesus never promised His followers a life without prisons.
He gave us something infinitely greater.
Himself.
So Paul and Silas were not manipulating God through music.
Praise was not a key inserted into heaven's vending machine.
They worshiped because God was worthy before the earthquake ever came.
And if you only worship God when He opens the door, perhaps what you actually love most is the open door.
But worship says:
“Even here, Jesus.”
Even here.
Even bleeding.
Even confused.
Even waiting.
Even when I cannot see tomorrow.
You are still Lord.
Then the story takes a turn many people miss.
The earthquake opened the prison.
But the real miracle was about to happen inside a man.
The jailer woke.
He saw the doors standing open and assumed the prisoners had escaped.
He drew his sword.
He was preparing to end his own life.
Pause there.
Because while everybody remembers the earthquake...
heaven's attention seems to move toward one desperate man standing in the darkness with a weapon.
Paul could have run.
Silas could have disappeared.
They had been beaten unjustly.
The doors were open.
Freedom was physically in front of them.
Yet Paul shouted:
“Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.”
Think about the scandal of that grace.
The prisoner became concerned about the jailer.
The wounded man tried to save the man who had guarded his wounds.
The victim refused to treat another human life as disposable.
That is what grace does.
The world says, “He hurt you. Let him suffer.”
Jesus teaches His people another kingdom.
A kingdom where mercy can interrupt revenge.
A kingdom where wounded people can become instruments of healing.
A kingdom where the person you assumed was your enemy may actually be standing one encounter away from becoming your brother.
The jailer called for lights.
He rushed inside.
He fell trembling before Paul and Silas.

Then came the question every human being eventually has to face, whether whispered in a hospital room, buried beneath success, screamed through addiction, concealed behind religion, or finally admitted when life falls apart:
“What must I do to be saved?”
And Paul did not answer:
“Become a better person.”
He did not say:
“Earn God's acceptance.”
He did not give the jailer a religious performance plan.
He pointed him to a Person.
“Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved…”
Acts 16:31.
There is the center of the story.
Not Paul.
Not Silas.
Not music.
Not an earthquake.
Not supernatural doors.
Jesus Christ.
The jailer needed more than escape from a frightening night.
He needed salvation.
So do we.
Because the deepest prison in Acts 16 was never made of stone.
And the deepest chains in your life may not be the circumstances you desperately want God to change.
Sin is a deeper captivity.
Guilt.
Shame.
Pride.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Self-righteousness.
Secret compromise.
The exhausting attempt to appear holy while something inside you is dying.
You can walk through every open door this world offers and remain imprisoned in your soul.
You can have money and be chained.
You can have followers and be chained.
You can smile in church and be chained.
You can quote Scripture and still hide sin.
You can know Christian language while your heart remains far from Christ.
That is why Jesus did not come merely to improve our circumstances.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God bore sin and shame. He died and was buried. He rose again.
The Gospel is not that good people climb high enough to reach God.
The Gospel is that God came down in Christ to rescue people who could never save themselves.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up so Jesus might tolerate you.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can rescue you.
Grace does not tell you your sin does not matter.
Grace tells you that your sin mattered so terribly that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishing that sinners who trust Him can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
Maybe you have been waiting for an earthquake.
God, change my spouse.
Change my finances.
Change my body.
Change my job.
Change my circumstances.
Open this door.
Break this chain.
And yes, bring those requests to Him.
Pray.
Cry.
Ask.
But what if tonight the question is deeper?
What if the door God most urgently wants opened is your heart?
What if you have spent years asking Jesus to change everything around you while resisting His authority over what is inside you?
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because midnight still comes.
Not always at 12:00 a.m.
Sometimes midnight is a diagnosis.
Sometimes midnight has divorce papers.
Sometimes midnight is an empty bedroom after someone dies.
Sometimes midnight is the relapse nobody knows about.
Sometimes midnight is staring into a mirror and realizing you have become someone you never intended to become.
Sometimes midnight is lying beside somebody you love and feeling completely alone.
Sometimes midnight is knowing exactly what Scripture says and realizing you have been running from it.
And sometimes...
midnight is where God exposes what daylight allowed us to hide.
So if you are in your midnight right now, hear this carefully:
You do not have to fake a song.
You do not have to manufacture happiness.
You do not have to pretend your wounds do not hurt.
Bring the real you to Jesus.
The frightened you.
The angry you.
The ashamed you.
The exhausted you.
The version of you nobody sees when the church clothes come off and the bedroom door closes.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Because the Savior who met sinners in Scripture is still the Savior proclaimed by the Gospel.
And maybe someone reading this has been standing spiritually where that jailer stood.
You are tired.
You have carried things nobody knows.
Perhaps you have wondered whether your life can ever become different.
Hear Paul's cry across the centuries:
Do not destroy yourself.
There is hope beyond this moment.
And His name is Jesus.
If you are in immediate danger of hurting yourself, move toward another person now and contact emergency or crisis support where you live. Do not remain alone with that moment.
Your story does not need to end in the prison.
The jailer's didn't.
That same night, the man who had been guarding wounded prisoners began washing their wounds.
Read that slowly.
The jailer washed the wounds of the prisoners.

Then he and his household heard the word of the Lord. They responded in faith, and baptism followed. Before the night ended, there was food on a table and rejoicing in a household that had come to believe in God.
Look at what Jesus can do with one night.
A prison became a sanctuary.
A jailer became a brother.
Wounds were washed.
The Word was preached.
People believed.
Baptism followed.
A household rejoiced.
That is our heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not always by erasing the chapter you wish had never happened.
Sometimes He demonstrates His grace by refusing to let that chapter have the final word.
Your scars may remain part of your testimony.
But they do not have to remain the definition of your identity.
Your failure may explain something about yesterday.
It does not have authority to be your savior—or your master—today.
Your sin may be darker than anyone knows.
Christ's grace is not permission to remain there.
It is a call to come into the light, repent, believe, and follow Him.
And your midnight?
It may not end tonight with an earthquake.
I will not promise you that.
Scripture does not give me permission to.
But I can tell you something far more dependable:
Jesus Christ is still worthy at midnight.
He is worthy before the answer.
Worthy before the healing.
Worthy before reconciliation.
Worthy before the door opens.
Worthy while tears are still falling.

And if the door never opens in the way you expected, Christ has already opened through His death and resurrection the only door that ultimately matters: reconciliation with God and eternal life for those who belong to Him.
So perhaps your prayer tonight is not complicated.
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I believe. Help my unbelief.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
“Jesus, teach me to worship You even here.”
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your struggle. But sometimes three honest words are the beginning of admitting that you cannot keep carrying everything alone.
And if you know someone living through midnight right now, send this to them.
They may never tell you.
Share it anyway.
It does not.
Not because financial support earns favor with God. It cannot.
Christ alone saves, and grace cannot be bought.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help biblical encouragement and discipleship resources continue reaching people. If you want to glorify God through your support, let the motive be love for Christ and love for people—not pressure, superstition, or the expectation that God owes you something in return.
Not so people will notice you.
So perhaps one hurting person will notice Jesus.

Invite your family. Invite the friend drifting from faith. Invite the believer who is exhausted. Invite the seeker with questions. Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening. Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
And keep coming back to the Word.
Because eventually every believer discovers this:
Faith is not proven only by how loudly you celebrate when the prison opens.
Sometimes faith sounds like two wounded men singing while the door is still locked.
And somewhere in the darkness...
someone is listening.
Your midnight may remember your tears, but it does not get to write the last sentence—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE HID THEM UNDER THE FLAX—BUT GOD WAS HIDING SOMETHING BIGGER
paragraphs:
SHE HID THEM UNDER THE FLAX—BUT GOD WAS HIDING SOMETHING BIGGER
Rahab thought she was hiding two hunted men on her roof. She could not have known that, in that terrifying night, God was writing a former prostitute into the story that would eventually lead to Jesus Christ.
There were footsteps outside her door.
Not friendly footsteps.
Not neighbors coming to borrow something. Not customers wandering through the night. These were the king’s men.
They knew.
Somebody had seen the strangers enter Rahab’s house.
And somewhere above them, on the flat roof of a house built into Jericho’s defenses, two Israelite spies were lying beneath stalks of flax.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine Rahab hearing the voices below while knowing that the men they wanted were only a short distance away.
One wrong movement.
One frightened cough.
One stalk shifting beneath a nervous hand.
And everything could have ended differently.
Joshua 2:6 preserves the scene in Hebrew:
"וְהִיא הֶעֱלָתַם הַגָּגָה וַתִּטְמְנֵם בְּפִשְׁתֵּי הָעֵץ"
Vehi he‘elatam haggagah, vattitmenem bepishtei ha‘etz...
The sense is strikingly ordinary:
She had taken them up to the roof and hidden them among the stalks of flax.
Flax.
Not armor.
Not a fortress.
Not soldiers.
Flax.
And underneath it were two men carrying information connected with Israel’s entrance into the land God had promised.
But the most extraordinary thing happening on that roof was not that two spies were hidden.
It was what was happening inside Rahab.
Because Rahab had heard.
She had heard what Israel's God had done.
She had heard about the sea.
She had heard about the kings who had fallen.
Jericho had heard too.
That matters.
The entire city had information.
But Rahab did something with it.
She tells the spies:
"יָדַעְתִּי כִּי־נָתַן יְהוָה לָכֶם אֶת־הָאָרֶץ"
Yada‘ti ki-natan YHWH lakhem et-ha’aretz.
“I know that the LORD has given you the land.”
Then comes one of the most astonishing confessions in the chapter:
"כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת"
Ki YHWH Eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma‘al ve‘al-ha’aretz mittakhat.
The LORD your God—He is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath.
Read that again.
Not from Joshua.
Not from a priest.
Not from someone raised inside Israel’s covenant community.
Rahab.
The woman Scripture introduced as a prostitute.
That is where this story stops being merely ancient history and starts getting uncomfortably close to us.
Because some of us know what it feels like to have one word attached to our identity.
Divorced.
Addict.
Adulterer.
Failure.
Liar.
Abandoned.
Abuser.
Abused.
Prisoner.
Backslider.
Unwanted.
Dirty.
Hypocrite.
Maybe nobody says the word anymore.
You still hear it.
Maybe people have forgotten what you did.
You haven't.
Maybe you learned how to smile in church while privately remembering a version of yourself you desperately wish had never existed.
And Rahab’s story whispers something dangerous to shame:
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your final chapter.
God does.
Scripture does not sanitize Rahab.
That is part of what makes her story so powerful.
Joshua 2 introduces her plainly. She is Rahab, the prostitute.
The Bible does not need to pretend her past never happened in order to demonstrate what grace can do with a human life.
And Christianity does not proclaim that sinners save themselves by becoming respectable enough for God.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He rose.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something shame could never manufacture:
forgiveness.
Rahab's story is not the Gospel itself.
But her story points beautifully toward the kind of God revealed fully in the Gospel—a God whose grace reaches people whom respectable society might have already reduced to their history.
And here is something easy to miss.
Everybody in Jericho had heard.
Rahab herself says that they had heard what the LORD had done.
Their hearts melted.
They were afraid.
But hearing about God is not the same thing as trusting God.
Fear alone did not save Rahab.
Information alone did not save Rahab.
