Her action finally becomes the center of the sentence.
And David responds.
He retrieves the bones of Saul and Jonathan and gathers the remains of those who had been executed. They are buried in the tomb of Kish, Saul’s father.
The woman who once seemed almost voiceless had performed an act that reached the ears of a king.
Do you see it?
Her first appearance was wrapped in scandal.
Her later appearance was marked by costly devotion.
The Bible did not erase the painful chapter.
God simply did not allow that chapter to be the only chapter containing her name.
And that is where Rizpah’s story reaches across thousands of years and grabs some of us by the heart.
Because maybe you have been trying to erase your past when Jesus is offering something greater than erasure.
Redemption.
Christianity does not teach that God pretends evil never happened.
The cross proves the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
Grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly went there for sinners.
This is why the Gospel is not positive thinking.
It is not “believe in yourself.”
It is not “your past does not matter.”
Your sin matters.
My sin matters.
Justice matters.
Truth matters.
Repentance matters.
But grace matters too.
And at the center of Christianity stands Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, bearing the judgment sinners could never escape by reinventing themselves.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23
That includes religious people.
Broken people.
Respectable people.
Secretly addicted people.
People sitting in church while carrying sins nobody around them knows exist.
People who have been sinned against.
People who have sinned terribly against others.
All of us need more than reputation management.
We need reconciliation with God.
And the answer is Jesus.
The New Testament word often translated “grace” is χάρις—charis.
Grace.
Gift.
Favor that cannot be purchased by pretending you deserve it.
Paul writes:
—Romans 3:24
Freely.
By His grace.
Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
There is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin should be excused.
Not because consequences magically disappear.

But because Jesus Christ is greater than the worst thing a repentant sinner has ever done, greater than the ugliest thing somebody has done to you, and greater than the label people tried to nail permanently over your life.
Christ was nailed to a cross.
And He rose.
That changes everything.
Maybe your story does not look like Rizpah’s.
But maybe you know her rock.
Maybe your rock is the hospital chair where you watched somebody you loved slowly disappear.
Maybe it is the bedroom floor where you cried quietly because nobody knew your marriage was dying.
Maybe it is the addiction you keep fighting after everybody assumes you have recovered.
Maybe it is the child you keep praying for while watching him run farther from God.
Maybe it is grief.
Maybe betrayal.
Maybe shame.
Maybe you are exhausted from chasing away the “birds” that keep returning to feed upon your wounds.
And nobody seems to notice.
Rizpah reminds us that hidden faithfulness is not necessarily invisible forever.
But Jesus gives us an even stronger promise.
Your hope is not that an earthly king eventually hears about you.
Your hope is that your heavenly Father already knows.
Jesus said:
“Your Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.”
—Matthew 6:4
He sees.
That changes the darkness.
He sees the temptation you resisted that nobody applauded.
He sees the prayer you prayed through tears.
He sees the repentance nobody posted online.
He sees you trying to rebuild what your sin damaged.
He sees you forgiving somebody who never understood what forgiveness cost you.
He sees the mother praying at 2:00 a.m.
He sees the father wondering where he failed.
He sees the believer whispering, “Jesus, help me,” because those are the only words left.
And if this is exposing something you have been hiding from God, stop hiding.
Not from people indiscriminately.
From God.
Bring it into His light.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Come to Christ.
Do not confuse shame with repentance.
Shame says, “Hide because you are beyond hope.”
The Gospel says, “Come into the light because Christ saves sinners.”
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Maybe right now your prayer is only:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Pray it honestly.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Christ saves.
Let the comment simply become your public reminder that you are finished pretending darkness is safer than grace.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Then think of one person whose name came into your mind while reading this.
You know who they are.
The friend quietly collapsing.
The mother grieving.
The believer drifting.
The person drowning in shame.
The Christian who has become spiritually numb.
The unbeliever who believes Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that Jesus still receives broken people.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him, not through social-media metrics.
But if biblical truth has helped you, sharing it can be one simple way of putting that truth where another person might encounter it.
There are nights when strong believers become tired believers.
There are mornings when yesterday’s confidence becomes today’s battle.
Come back when you need to remember:
The chapter that wounded you does not have authority to become the final chapter Christ writes through your life.
It cannot.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But ministry does require people willing to help carry biblical teaching farther.
Because somewhere tonight there may be a Rizpah sitting on a rock.
Someone exhausted.
Someone grieving.
Someone whose name has become associated with the worst thing that ever happened to them.
Someone convinced that their story has already been decided.
Let them hear the truth.
Rizpah entered the biblical narrative surrounded by accusation and political scandal.
But that was not the last time Scripture spoke her name.
And your worst chapter does not possess the authority to define your eternity either.
Jesus does.
Repentance is still possible.
Forgiveness is still offered.
Grace is still astonishing.
The cross is still enough.
The tomb is still empty.
Christ is still saving sinners.
Christ is still restoring the broken.
Christ is still calling prodigals home.
Christ is still transforming people whose stories looked impossible to redeem.
So do not hand your identity to the people who remember only your scandal.
Hand your life to Jesus Christ.
Because perhaps the most beautiful thing about grace is not that God pretends the broken pages were never written.
It is that He can take a story stained by sin, grief, failure, injustice, and tears...
and make the next pages testify to the mercy of Christ.
The world may remember the chapter where your name became attached to scandal—but Jesus is still writing after the sentence where everyone else thought your story ended.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, ‘I have done no wrong.’”
paragraphs: “Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, ‘I have done no wrong.’”
Read it again.
Slowly.
She eats.
She wipes.
She denies.
The picture is almost shockingly ordinary.
Someone finishes a meal, wipes away the evidence, gets up from the table, and continues with life.
Nothing to see here.
Nothing happened.
And that is precisely the horror of the image.
Sin has become ordinary enough to consume without trembling and convenient enough to erase without repentance.
The Hebrew calls her אִשָּׁה מְנָאָפֶת — ishah mena’afet, an adulterous woman.
And after the act she says:
לֹא־פָעַלְתִּי אָוֶן — lo-fa’alti aven.
“I have done no wrong.”
That sentence may be more dangerous than the scandal itself.
Because there is hope for the sinner who falls to the floor crying, “God, be merciful to me.”
There is hope for the prodigal who finally realizes the pigpen is not home.
There is hope for Peter weeping bitterly after denying Jesus.
There is hope for the person whose hands are dirty but whose heart finally stops pretending they are clean.
But what happens when we become so comfortable with darkness that we stop calling it darkness?
What happens when conviction arrives and we immediately wipe our mouth?
“I deserve to be happy.”
“God understands.”
“Everybody does it.”
“It wasn't technically adultery.”
“We never slept together.”
“It was just messaging.”
“My marriage was already dead.”
“I only looked.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“At least I'm not as bad as them.”
“Nobody knows.”
“No one got hurt.”
“I prayed about it.”
And perhaps the most dangerous one:
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
He does.
That should sober us more than comfort us when we are using grace to protect something Jesus is calling us to surrender.
Because God sees what the spouse does not see.
God sees the deleted conversation.
God sees the second account.
God sees what happens when the browser history disappears.
God sees the emotional affair nobody has named an affair.
God sees the bitterness rehearsed privately.
God sees the secret appetite.
God sees the money nobody knows about.
God sees the private compromise behind the public ministry.
God sees what we keep explaining away.
And this passage is not permission for men to point self-righteously at women.
If you read Proverbs 30:20 merely thinking, “What a terrible woman,” you may have missed the mirror.
The image concerns an adulterous woman, but the spiritual pathology of committing wrong and then denying, minimizing, concealing, or normalizing it belongs to humanity.
Men wipe their mouths too.
Pastors can wipe their mouths.
Church members can wipe their mouths.
Husbands can.
Wives can.
Single people can.
Religious people can become frighteningly skilled at it.
You can sing worship songs on Sunday with lips that spent Saturday destroying somebody in private.
You can post Scripture publicly while feeding an addiction privately.
You can say “God first” in your biography while knowingly placing Him last in your decisions.
You can learn Christian vocabulary without developing Christian repentance.
You can even learn how to use grace as a napkin.
Sin.
Wipe.
Smile.
Repeat.
Until conviction becomes quieter.
But there is something we must make absolutely clear.
The adulterous woman of Proverbs 30:20 should not simply be identified with the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
They are different passages making different points.
Proverbs gives us the chilling picture of someone who says, essentially, “I have done nothing wrong.”
The woman standing before Jesus in John 8 does not say that.
She is standing exposed.
Accused.
Humiliated.
Her sin has become public spectacle.
And there, in one of the Gospel’s most famous scenes, religious men bring a woman caught in adultery before Jesus.
Imagine the sound.
Feet scraping across the ground.
Voices rising.
People staring.
No carefully written testimony.
No polished Sunday clothes capable of hiding what has happened.
Her shame has a crowd.
The accusers have a question.
And Jesus has the final word.
Eventually the accusers leave.
Then comes the exchange that generations of broken people have clung to.
Jesus asks whether anyone has condemned her.
She answers:
Οὐδείς, κύριε — Oudeis, kyrie.
“No one, Lord.”
Then Jesus says:
Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου … μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.
“Neither do I condemn you. Go … sin no more.”
Do not tear that sentence in half.
Our generation desperately needs both sides.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
And:
“Sin no more.”
Grace does not say sin never happened.
Grace says sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Jesus does not stand beside the woman and announce, “Adultery isn't really a problem.”
He does not redefine holiness to protect her feelings.
He does not call evil good.
Yet neither does He join a bloodthirsty crowd eager to reduce a human being to the worst thing associated with her life.
That is what makes Jesus so breathtaking.
Perfect holiness stands in front of human failure...
and holiness does not become compromise.
Mercy does not become permission.
Truth does not become cruelty.
Grace does not become denial.
The Savior neither celebrates sin nor abandons the sinner.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
Grace.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Transformation.
This is where some of us have misunderstood the Gospel.
We thought Jesus came merely to make us feel better about the person we refuse to stop becoming.
But Jesus did not die merely to make sin more emotionally comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
Forgive sinners.
Cleanse sinners.
Reconcile sinners to God.
Give sinners new hearts.
Call sinners out of darkness.
And ultimately transform those who belong to Him.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing beside your chains saying, “Don't feel ashamed about these.”
The Gospel is Jesus paying an unimaginable price to break your chains and then calling you to walk with Him in freedom.
That means there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“You sinned, therefore there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel says:
“You sinned, therefore you desperately need the Savior—and the Savior came for sinners.”
Condemnation tells you to run away from Christ.
Conviction drives you toward Him.
Condemnation says, “Hide.”
Grace says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Your scandal is your identity.”
Jesus says something far greater:
Your sin may explain why you need saving.
It does not possess the authority to overrule what Christ can make of a surrendered life.
And maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody dragged you into the middle of a crowd.
Maybe your husband doesn't know.
Maybe your wife doesn't know.
Maybe your parents don't know.
Maybe your pastor doesn't know.
Maybe the people who follow you online would be shocked.
Maybe you have become so practiced at wiping your mouth that even you barely feel the stain anymore.
But you know.
And God knows.
So here is the question Proverbs 30:20 quietly forces upon us:
What have you been wiping from your mouth while telling yourself you did nothing wrong?
Don't answer quickly.
What have you renamed so you would not have to repent of it?
What have you called “a weakness” that God calls you to put to death?
What relationship have you defended because surrendering it would hurt?
What habit have you hidden because bringing it into the light would cost you something?
What apology have you refused because pride matters more than reconciliation?
What secret have you protected more fiercely than your intimacy with Jesus?
What if the greatest danger facing your soul right now is not that God refuses to forgive you...
but that you have become determined to insist there is nothing requiring forgiveness?
Scripture says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
Then immediately comes hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice the difference.
One person says:
Nothing is wrong.
The other says:
God, I have sinned.
One wipes the mouth.
The other opens the heart.
One protects the image.
The other seeks cleansing.
Christianity does not begin with pretending you are clean.
It begins with admitting you cannot cleanse yourself.
That is why the cross matters.
If human beings were basically fine and simply needed encouragement, Calvary would make no sense.
If sin could be removed by self-improvement, the Son of God did not need to shed His blood.
If our deepest problem were low self-esteem, we would need inspiration.
But if our deepest problem is sin separating rebellious humanity from a holy God, we need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need Jesus Christ.
At the cross, God does something far greater than pretend our sins never mattered.
Christ bears sin.
Justice is not mocked.
Grace is not cheapened.
Forgiveness is purchased at terrible cost.
The innocent One suffers for the guilty.
And then comes resurrection morning.
The stone moves.
Death loses its claim.
The crucified Christ rises.
And suddenly the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Your sin can be confessed without becoming your final identity because Jesus Christ is alive.
Peter's denial was not his final chapter.
The thief's criminal past was not his final chapter.
The persecutor Saul's violence was not his final chapter.
And your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter either.
But grace is not pretending the chapter was beautiful.
Grace is allowing Jesus to rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not from scandal to denial.
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to carefully managed appearances.
From scandal...
to repentance...
to mercy...
to restoration...
to transformation...
through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years believing repentance means God is waiting to humiliate you.
Look again at Christ.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not earning forgiveness.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy you could never deserve and whose Son accomplished what you could never accomplish for yourself.
The Greek word so often associated with repentance in the New Testament, μετάνοια — metanoia, speaks of a change of mind, a turning that reaches into the direction of life.
Biblical repentance is deeper than saying, “Sorry I got caught.”
It is deeper than crying while secretly planning to return.
It is deeper than deleting evidence while preserving desire.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, I agree with You about my sin.”
“No more excuses.”
“No more hiding.”
“No more calling darkness light.”
“I cannot save myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
“Change me.”
And perhaps someone reading this is thinking:
You don't know what I've done.
You're right.
I don't.
But Jesus does.
Maybe you betrayed someone who trusted you.
Maybe pornography has been consuming years of your life.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once swore you never would.
Maybe your marriage is bleeding because of choices nobody else understands.
Maybe you have lied so many times that you no longer remember which version of yourself people believe.
Maybe you abandoned God and now feel hypocritical even whispering His name.
Maybe you are reading an article about an adulterous woman while carrying your own secret scandal.
Hear this carefully.
The answer is not:
“I have done nothing wrong.”
And the answer is not:
“I have done too much wrong for Jesus.”
Both statements keep you from grace.
One denies the disease.
The other denies the Physician.
The Gospel destroys both lies.
Yes, sin is real.
Yes, judgment is real.
Yes, repentance matters.
And yes...
Jesus saves sinners.
That includes the ashamed.
The compromised.
The sexually broken.
The religious hypocrite who finally stops pretending.
The prodigal who smells like the far country.
The believer who wandered.
The person who thought they would never fall this far.
Christ's invitation is not permission to remain there.
It is an invitation to come home.
Maybe today is the day you stop wiping your mouth.
Maybe today is the day the secret finally becomes a confession before God.
Maybe today you contact the mature believer or pastor you have been avoiding and say, “I need help.”
Maybe today you remove access to what keeps dragging you backward.
Maybe today you stop negotiating with the thing Christ is telling you to surrender.
Not because surrender purchases God's love.
But because the grace that saves us also teaches us that sin is no longer our master.
And please don't turn this article into ammunition against somebody else's scandal.
Before you share it thinking about “that adulterer,” “that hypocrite,” “that backslider,” or “that person who needs to read this,” allow Scripture to search you.
Where are you wiping your mouth?
Where am I tempted to excuse what God wants brought into the light?
The ground beneath the cross destroys boasting.
There are no superior sinners standing there.
Only needy people and a sufficient Savior.
So if this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of your sin in a Facebook comment.
But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Or simply write:
Let those words become more than engagement.
Let them become a line in the sand.
And then actually seek prayer.
Actually confess where appropriate.
Actually pursue accountability.
Actually return to Christ.
If somebody came to your mind while reading this—not someone you want to embarrass, but someone you genuinely love—send this to them privately.
He does.
And He calls them out of darkness.
Go to Jesus.
The point is not Gospel Warrior.
The point is Christ.
The One who sees the stain you tried to wipe away.
The One before whom excuses collapse.
The One who knows the chapter you wish had never been written.
The One who calls sin what it is...
and still stretches wounded hands toward sinners who repent and believe.
You do not need another napkin.
You need cleansing.
You do not need a better excuse.
You need mercy.
You do not need to convince God that nothing happened.
You need to discover that Jesus already knows what happened—and the Gospel is powerful enough to meet repentant sinners there.
So stop wiping your mouth.
Stop rehearsing the defense.
Stop running.
Bring the scandal into the light of Christ.
Because the most unforgettable thing about grace is not that Jesus helps us pretend the stain was never there.
It is that He can take the very life sin tried to ruin and make it a testimony to the mercy of God.
And maybe the sentence you have been afraid to speak—
“Jesus, I sinned. Please forgive me.”
—is the sentence that finally opens the door to the chapter you thought could never be written.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at Jesus' feet, but it does not get to decide who rises from them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL HAD TO TELL A CHURCH TO STOP DEPRIVING THEIR SPOUSES SEXUALLY
paragraphs: PAUL HAD TO TELL A CHURCH TO STOP DEPRIVING THEIR SPOUSES SEXUALLY

The passage many Christians whisper about may expose something far deeper than a lack of sex: the quiet distance, rejection, resentment, selfishness, and spiritual warfare slowly entering marriages behind closed doors.
There are Bible verses people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses we underline in church.
There are verses we quote when life falls apart.
And then there are verses we almost never hear preached because everybody suddenly becomes uncomfortable.
First Corinthians 7 contains some of those verses.
Paul is writing to believers in Corinth about marriage, holiness, temptation, singleness, sexuality, and devotion to God when he says something startlingly direct.
In the Greek text:
“μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους”
Mē apostereite allēlous.
In context:
Do not deprive one another.

Those words are found in 1 Corinthians 7:5. The verb translated “deprive” is apostereō—language of withholding or depriving someone of something. Paul is addressing husbands and wives who apparently needed to understand that marriage was not supposed to become a battlefield where sexual intimacy could simply be withheld unilaterally.
But before somebody weaponizes that verse against a husband or wife tonight, keep reading.
Because Paul’s message is far more beautiful—and far more demanding—than “my spouse owes me sex.”
In fact, read carefully enough and Paul destroys that selfish interpretation.
He begins this section by answering matters the Corinthians themselves had written to him about: “Περὶ δὲ ὧν ἐγράψατε”—“Now concerning the matters about which you wrote.”
Something was happening in Corinth.

Paul had already confronted sexual immorality elsewhere in the letter, but apparently another danger had emerged at the opposite extreme. Some believers seem to have been wrestling with the idea that abstaining from sexual relations was spiritually superior. Paul therefore has to explain that holiness inside marriage does not require spouses to become strangers to one another.
Then he says something extraordinary.
“The husband should give to his wife what is due her and likewise the wife to her husband.”
Notice who receives responsibility.
Both.
Notice who receives dignity.
Both.
Notice who matters.
Both.
Then Paul goes further.

He says the wife does not exercise exclusive authority over her body but her husband does—and then, in a strikingly reciprocal statement, says the husband does not exercise exclusive authority over his body but his wife does.
In Greek, the repeated word is ἐξουσιάζει—exousiazei, from the language of authority.
And Paul applies the principle in both directions.
That matters enormously.
Paul is not handing husbands a divine permission slip for sexual domination. He is confronting selfishness in both spouses with radical mutuality.
Christian marriage is not:
“Your body belongs to me, so give me what I want.”
It is closer to:
“I no longer live as though my desires, comfort, affection, vulnerability, and body concern only me. I have entered covenant with you, and therefore your good matters deeply to me.”
That changes everything.
Because biblical intimacy cannot be reduced to taking.
It involves giving.
Listening.
Tenderness.
Patience.
Faithfulness.
Vulnerability.
Mutual care.
And love.
This is why 1 Corinthians 7:5 must never become ammunition for coercion, intimidation, manipulation, marital rape, or ignoring a spouse’s pain, trauma, illness, exhaustion, fear, or safety.
Those things are not justified by Paul’s words.
The passage itself says temporary abstinence should happen “ἐκ συμφώνου”—ek symphōnou—by agreement.
Mutual agreement.
The idea behind symphōnos is agreement or harmony; it is related to the word from which English gets “symphony.”
Think about that.
Paul’s picture is not one spouse overpowering the other.
It is two lives learning harmony.
Two people listening.
Two people caring.
Two people belonging to Christ and therefore refusing to treat one another as objects.
And suddenly this uncomfortable passage becomes painfully relevant.
Because sometimes the deepest problem in a marriage is not what happens in the bedroom.
It is everything that happened before the bedroom door closed.
It was the argument nobody resolved.
The apology nobody gave.
The affection that slowly disappeared.
The phone that became more interesting than the person sitting beside you.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The flirtation dismissed as harmless.
The resentment quietly accumulating.
The exhaustion nobody noticed.
The rejection nobody talked about.
The harsh words that never really left the room.
The husband who feels unwanted but is ashamed to admit it.
The wife who feels used rather than cherished but does not know how to say it.
Two people sleeping inches apart while emotionally living miles away.
Same house.
Same bed.
Same wedding photographs hanging on the wall.
But something has gone cold.
And perhaps nobody knows except them.
And God.
That is why reducing Paul's teaching to “have more sex” misses his point.
Sex can reveal problems.
But sex cannot save a marriage.
Jesus can transform people.
The Gospel reaches deeper than physical intimacy because the Gospel confronts the selfish heart that damages intimacy in the first place.
Scripture tells husbands elsewhere to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Think about the standard.
Christ did not exploit His bride.
Christ sacrificed Himself for His bride.
He did not say, “What can I take from you?”
He gave Himself.
That is the shadow of the cross hanging over Christian marriage.
A husband cannot appeal to biblical authority while ignoring Christlike sacrifice.
A wife cannot appeal to her husband's duty while refusing Christlike love.
Neither spouse gets permission to use intimacy as punishment.
Neither spouse gets permission to demand intimacy without tenderness.
Neither spouse gets permission to cultivate secret sexual sin and expect the marriage to remain untouched.
Neither spouse gets permission to stop caring about the heart of the person they promised to love.
Paul calls husband and wife away from selfish possession and toward mutual self-giving.
And then comes the warning.
Paul says not to deprive one another except by mutual agreement “for a time,” for devotion to prayer, and afterward to come together again so Satan does not exploit their lack of self-control.
Paul is realistic.
He knows temptation exists.
He knows sexual desire exists.
He knows marriage does not magically eliminate temptation.
And he refuses to pretend otherwise.
But notice something else.
Paul does not say temptation excuses adultery.
He does not say a spouse’s rejection makes pornography acceptable.
He does not say sexual frustration gives anyone permission to cheat.
Sin remains sin.
The answer to temptation is not blame.
It is faithfulness.
Self-control.
Communication.
Prayer.
Repentance.
Grace.
And when necessary, wise pastoral or professional help.
Maybe this article hurts because your marriage has been cold for months.
Maybe years.
Maybe you stopped touching because every touch started feeling like a request.
Maybe your spouse stopped initiating because rejection became too painful.
Maybe childbirth changed everything.
Maybe illness did.
Maybe hormones did.
Maybe betrayal did.
Maybe pornography shattered trust.
Maybe trauma made physical closeness complicated.
Maybe resentment entered quietly and unpacked its bags.
Maybe you cannot even remember when you stopped laughing together.
And now you are reading Paul's words thinking:
Where did we go?
Listen carefully.
This passage was not written so wounded spouses could beat each other with Scripture.
It was written to call Christian marriages back toward covenant faithfulness.
If intimacy has become painful, frightening, coercive, medically difficult, emotionally unsafe, or tangled in trauma, the answer is not to force the verse harder.
Love listens.
Love protects.
Love seeks help.
Love is patient.
Love does not dishonor another person.
Love does not insist on selfish gratification while ignoring another person's suffering.
And where there is abuse or sexual coercion, getting to safety and seeking qualified help is not rebellion against Scripture. Biblical submission to Christ never requires silently permitting abuse.
But for other marriages, the conviction may land differently.
Maybe there is no abuse.
No illness.
No trauma.
No genuine obstacle.
Maybe intimacy has become a weapon.
“If you make me angry, I will reject you.”
“If you do not do what I want, I will punish you with distance.”
“You hurt me, so now I will make you hurt.”
That is not reconciliation.
That is retaliation wearing pajamas.
And resentment can become incredibly sophisticated.
It learns Christian vocabulary.
It still goes to church.
It still smiles in photographs.
It still says, “Everything is fine.”
But behind the bedroom door, two hearts are keeping score.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully practical.
Jesus did not save us merely so we could sing louder on Sunday.
He came to make dead hearts alive.
He came to confront pride.
He came to expose hidden sin.
He came to teach selfish people how to love.
He came to forgive the guilty and transform the forgiven.
Maybe the prayer your marriage needs tonight is not:
“God, change my spouse.”
Maybe it begins:
“Jesus... show me where I have stopped loving.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because He might answer it.
He might expose the pornography.
The bitterness.
The selfishness.
The manipulation.
The emotional absence.
The contempt.
The laziness.
The entitlement.
The refusal to forgive.
The years of avoiding the conversation.
But exposure in the hands of Jesus is not the end of the story.
That is where grace enters.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners do not have to remain what sin has made them.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners and rose again.
At the cross, our deepest scandal met a deeper grace.
Our lust.
Our selfishness.
Our adultery.
Our pornography.
Our bitterness.
Our manipulation.
Our hidden fantasies.
Our emotional cruelty.
Our failures as husbands.
Our failures as wives.
Our secret shame.
None of those things are stronger than the blood of Christ.
Repentance does not mean pretending the damage never happened.
Grace does not mean consequences disappear overnight.
Forgiveness does not mean trust must instantly return.
Restoration may require confession, boundaries, counseling, accountability, patience, and a long road of rebuilding what sin destroyed.
But Jesus specializes in resurrection.
And resurrection means the grave does not get the final sentence.
Maybe your marriage will not heal because somebody finally wins the argument.
Maybe healing begins when somebody finally puts down the weapon.
When someone says:
“I was wrong.”
“I have been selfish.”
“I stopped seeing you.”
“I used rejection to punish you.”
“I pressured you instead of loving you.”
“I hid things from you.”
“I hurt you.”
“Please forgive me.”
“I need help.”
“Jesus, change me.”
That is where scandal can begin turning into grace.
Not because sex fixes everything.
Not because Christians pretend everything is fine.
But because Jesus rewrites people.
And rewritten people can begin rewriting patterns.
The cold room can become a place of conversation again.
The hand that stopped reaching can learn tenderness again.
The confession can finally happen.
The counseling appointment can finally be made.
The secret addiction can finally be dragged into the light.
The apology can finally be spoken without excuses.
The marriage that has been surviving on appearances can finally tell the truth.
And sometimes the first miracle is simply this:
Two people stop asking, “What am I owed?”
and begin asking,
“How can I love you like Christ?”
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not rush past the conviction.
Sit with Jesus.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is necessary.
Talk honestly with your spouse where it is wise and safe.

And if your marriage needs help beyond what the two of you can repair alone, seek mature, biblically grounded pastoral counsel and qualified professional care. There is no spiritual trophy for letting serious wounds become deeper because you were too ashamed to ask for help.
It does.
Marriage will not cure selfishness.
Sex will not cure lust.
Another human being cannot become your savior.
Christ must occupy that throne.

Paul himself immediately recognizes singleness as a gift from God. Scripture does not teach that everyone must marry, nor that sexual fulfillment is necessary for a meaningful Christian life. Jesus Himself shows us that perfect humanity does not require marriage or sexual activity.
So whether married or single, the center remains the same.
Jesus Christ.
If you are married, love your spouse under the lordship of Christ.
If you are single, honor Christ with your body.
If you have sexually sinned, repent and run toward Christ rather than hiding from Him.
If you have been sexually wounded, know that Scripture does not give another person permission to exploit you.
If your marriage is struggling, stop protecting the image while the covenant bleeds.
Bring what is hidden into the light.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about 1 Corinthians 7 is not that Paul talked openly about sex.
Perhaps it is that God cares about what happens in the parts of our lives we thought were too private for discipleship.
Jesus wants the Sunday version of you.
And the Monday version.
The public version.
The private version.
Your worship.
Your marriage.
Your sexuality.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your secrets.
Your entire life.
He is Lord of all of it.
So be honest.
Did this hit somewhere you did not expect?
And if Christ is restoring something you once thought was beyond repair, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the hope another husband or wife desperately needed tonight.
Come back to it when resentment starts speaking louder than covenant.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture faithfully, sharing it is one practical way you can help put biblical truth in front of someone who might never search for it themselves.
And stay close.
Because this ministry was never supposed to terminate on a screen.
The goal is transformation.
More Scripture opened.
More truth understood.
More sin brought into the light.
More wounded people pointed toward Christ.
More marriages learning grace.
More prodigals coming home.
More believers becoming disciples rather than spectators.
More people discovering that their worst chapter does not have authority to write their final one.
Because maybe tonight there is a husband staring at the ceiling beside the woman he loves, wondering when they became strangers.
Maybe there is a wife reading this with tears she does not want anyone to notice.
Maybe there is someone carrying sexual shame from years ago.
Maybe there is a marriage barely breathing beneath years of unresolved hurt.
And maybe somebody needs to hear one final truth before closing this article.
Jesus is not frightened by the room you have been afraid to let Him enter.
Open the door.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the sexual brokenness.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him yourself.
The same Savior who carried scandal to a cross walked out of a grave—and no chapter surrendered to Him has to remain exactly as sin wrote it.
Your marriage may have pages stained by rejection, failure, tears, and shame... but never mistake a stained page for the end of the story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR PRIVATE LIFE IS PREACHING A SERMON NO ONE HEARS—EXCEPT GOD
paragraphs: YOUR PRIVATE LIFE IS PREACHING A SERMON NO ONE HEARS—EXCEPT GOD
Understanding Why Your Hidden Life Matters More Than Your Christian Image
There is a version of you that people know.
And then there is the version of you that only God sees.
The first one walks into church.
The second one walks into an empty room.
The first one knows when to say, “God is good.”
The second one knows what you search when nobody is watching.
The first one can raise its hands during worship, quote Scripture, share Christian posts, encourage hurting people, serve faithfully, and look completely surrendered.
The second one appears when the door closes.
When the browser opens.
When the conversation becomes private.
When nobody would ever know.
When you are angry enough to say what you would never say publicly.
When temptation whispers, “This stays between us.”
When bitterness starts rehearsing somebody’s failures again.
When loneliness makes compromise look like comfort.
When your public Christianity has gone to sleep...
but your secret appetites are still awake.
And here is the uncomfortable question:
If everyone saw the Christianity you live when nobody is watching, would they recognize the Jesus you proclaim when everybody is watching?
Don’t run from that question.
Stay here.
Because this is not an article about exposing hypocrites.
It is about exposing the place where hypocrisy can quietly begin in any of us.
Including me.
Including you.
And strangely enough, that hidden place may also become the very place where grace does some of its deepest work.
Jesus repeatedly confronted a religious culture obsessed with appearances.
In Matthew 6, He spoke about giving, praying, and fasting—three practices that could look extraordinarily spiritual while secretly becoming performances for human approval.
Again and again, Jesus used a striking expression:
ὁ Πατήρ σου ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ
ho Patēr sou ho blepōn en tō kryptō
“Your Father who sees in secret.”
That word κρυπτῷ — kryptō carries the idea of what is hidden, concealed, private.
Jesus was reminding His hearers of something both terrifying and beautiful:
There is no such thing as a truly private life before God.
People see the post.
God sees the motive behind the post.
People hear the prayer.
God knows whether prayer continues when there is no audience.
People see generosity.
God sees whether generosity came from love, guilt, pride, compassion, obedience, or the hunger to be admired.
People see the Bible in your hand.
God sees what happens when His Word confronts something in your heart that you do not want to surrender.
People can measure reputation.
God searches hearts.
That is why the hidden life matters so much.
Not because God is crouching in heaven waiting to catch you doing something wrong.
But because the hidden life reveals what applause can conceal.
Long before Jesus addressed religious performance, God told Samuel something humanity continually forgets.
Samuel was looking at Jesse’s sons, trying to discern whom God had chosen as Israel’s next king. Eliab looked impressive enough that Samuel assumed he must be the one.
God corrected him.
“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
The Hebrew reaches even deeper.
כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַיהוָה יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב
ki ha’adam yir’eh la‘einayim, vaYHWH yir’eh lalevav.
Human beings look toward what the eyes can see.
The LORD looks toward the לֵבָב — levav.
The heart.
The inner person.
The place beneath presentation.
And this changes everything.
Because Christianity can become frighteningly easy to perform.
You can learn the vocabulary.
You can learn when to say “Amen.”
You can discover which posts receive Christian engagement.
You can know the songs.
You can know the theology.
You can defend biblical morality.
You can even tell other people how they should live.
And somewhere along the way, without deliberately planning it, you can become highly skilled at looking spiritually alive while privately starving.
That is one of the great dangers of Christian image.
An image does not necessarily have to be false.
The danger begins when maintaining the image becomes more important than becoming like Christ.
Then confession feels dangerous because confession threatens the image.
Accountability feels invasive because accountability enters the hidden room.
Correction feels offensive because correction damages the identity we have constructed.
Repentance becomes increasingly difficult because repentance requires admitting that the person everyone admires still desperately needs mercy.
So we hide.
Adam hid.
David hid.
Peter tried to distance himself from the Man he loved.
Human beings have been hiding ever since sin entered the world.
Maybe your hiding looks more sophisticated.
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you really are.
Maybe people call you strong because they have never seen you crying in the car before walking inside.
Maybe you encourage everyone else while privately wondering why God feels distant.
Maybe there is pornography in your history that you have buried beneath ministry.
Maybe envy is eating you alive while you publicly celebrate the people you secretly resent.
Maybe your spouse gets a version of you your church would barely recognize.
Maybe you preach forgiveness while refusing to forgive.
Maybe your private messages contain conversations you would panic to see projected onto the church wall.
Maybe you have become addicted to being perceived as spiritual.
Or maybe your secret is not some dramatic scandal.
Maybe it is simply this:
You barely know God anymore.
You know Christianity.
You know Christian culture.
You know Christian content.
But somewhere beneath all the noise, your actual relationship with Jesus has become painfully thin.
And nobody knows.
That sentence can hurt.
Nobody knows.
But Someone does.
Your Father sees in secret.
And that truth is not merely a warning.
It is an invitation.
Because the God who sees what is hidden is also the God before whom you no longer have to pretend.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come to rescue carefully maintained reputations.
He came to save sinners.
The Christian message is not that good people become impressive enough for God.
The Christian message is that guilty people who could never save themselves are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Grace does not say your hidden sin does not matter.
Grace says your hidden sin mattered so much that Christ carried sin to the cross—and His mercy is so great that sinners who turn to Him do not have to remain imprisoned by what they have done.
There is an enormous difference between concealment and repentance.
Concealment says:
“I need to make sure nobody finds out.”
Repentance says:
“Jesus, I cannot keep becoming this person.”
Concealment protects the image.
Repentance brings the real person into the light.
The apostle John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice that Christianity does not require pretending there is nothing to confess.
It gives sinners somewhere to bring what must be confessed.
Jesus.
That is why you should never confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The voice telling you, “Hide forever. God could never want you now,” is not the message of the Gospel.
The Gospel says come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Walk differently.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Jesus is sufficient.
And perhaps someone reading this is thinking:
But you don't know what I did.
No.
I don't.
But Christ knew the full weight of human sin when He went to Calvary.
Peter knew what it meant to fail publicly and painfully.
On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had declared his loyalty eventually declared that he did not know Jesus.
Imagine the shame afterward.
Imagine hearing the rooster.
Imagine remembering Jesus’ words.
Imagine watching the image you had of yourself collapse.
Peter thought he was the man who would die beside Jesus.
Then pressure revealed something hidden inside him.
Fear.
Self-preservation.
Weakness.
And sometimes God allows the collapse of the person we thought we were so that grace can begin rebuilding the person we actually are.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
He did not pretend Peter’s failure never happened.
But neither did He discard Peter.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Then:
“Feed my sheep.”
The failure was real.
The grace was real.
The restoration was real.
And the man who denied Christ would eventually stand publicly and proclaim Christ.
That is our theme in its most beautiful form.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by renaming rebellion as authenticity.
Not by giving us permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus rewrites everything by forgiving sinners, restoring the broken, exposing darkness, creating new hearts, and teaching redeemed people to walk in the light.
Maybe the scandal nobody knows about is yours.
Maybe there is no dramatic scandal at all—just years of quiet compromise.
Either way, your story does not have to end where your sin took you.
But you must stop treating your Christian image as something more valuable than your Christian integrity.
Your reputation cannot forgive you.
Your followers cannot cleanse you.
Your ministry cannot justify you.
Your theological knowledge cannot substitute for obedience.
Your church attendance cannot crucify your flesh.
Your Christian posts cannot repent for you.
Only Jesus saves.
And when Jesus saves, He does not merely polish the outside.
He begins transforming the person underneath.
This is why hidden obedience is so powerful.
There is something beautiful about praying when nobody will ever compliment your prayer.
Closing the page when nobody would have caught you.
Refusing the flirtation nobody else would have discovered.
Returning money nobody knew you took.
Apologizing when pride desperately wants to win.
Forgiving without announcing your forgiveness to the world.
Opening Scripture when there is no camera nearby.
Worshiping when there is no music.
Serving somebody who cannot increase your status.
Choosing purity in a room where compromise would have remained completely secret.
That kind of obedience may never go viral.
Heaven sees it.
Your Father sees in secret.
And perhaps that is the Christianity we desperately need again.
Not merely Christians who look holy under church lights.
Christians who belong to Jesus when the lights are off.
Men who fear God when the phone is unlocked.
Women who trust Christ when comparison begins whispering.
Teenagers who choose Jesus when their friends would applaud compromise.
Pastors who are the same men outside the pulpit.
Parents whose children encounter the same Christianity at home that everyone else sees at church.
Believers whose private prayers are deeper than their public captions.
Not perfection.
Integrity.
Not sinlessness.
Repentance.
Not performance.
Abiding.
Because the goal is not to manufacture a spotless Christian image.
The goal is to become increasingly conformed to Christ.
And when we fail, we run toward Him rather than building another hiding place.
So tonight, when the noise disappears, ask yourself something.
Not:
“What do people think about my faith?”
Ask:
“Jesus, what do You see in me that I have been afraid to bring into Your light?”
Then be quiet.
Maybe a name comes to mind.
Maybe an addiction.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe dishonesty.
Maybe pride.
Maybe secret ambition.
Maybe spiritual emptiness.
Maybe a relationship.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe nothing dramatic at all.
Whatever God exposes through His Word and Spirit, do not immediately reach for shame.
Reach for Christ.
Confess specifically.
Repent genuinely.
Where another person has been harmed, seek wise and appropriate steps toward making things right.
Where temptation repeatedly defeats you, stop relying on secrecy and willpower alone. Seek mature Christian accountability and pastoral help.
Where your habits keep feeding sin, change your habits.
Where you have fallen, get up in grace.
Sanctification is not pretending you never struggle.
It is refusing to make peace with the sin Christ is calling you away from.
And maybe that is why you encountered these words today.
Not so you can think of the hypocritical Christian who “really needs to read this.”
You.
Me.
Us.
Before you share this with somebody else, allow God to search you.
David prayed:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
In Hebrew, that heart is again לֵבָב — levav.
Search the interior.
Search what nobody applauds.
Search what nobody suspects.
Search what I excuse.
Search what I protect.
Search what I have renamed.
Search the room inside me where I keep telling You not to enter.
And then David asks God to lead him “in the everlasting way.”
That is the destination.
Not exposure for exposure’s sake.
Transformation.
Maybe you have spent years protecting an image that Jesus never asked you to maintain.
You can put it down now.
You do not need to impress the Savior who already knows everything.
You need to surrender to Him.

And if Christ has already been restoring areas of your hidden life, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer finally believes restoration is possible.
Not because every article deserves saving.
Because there may come a night when the old temptation returns and you need to remember:
Your Father sees in secret.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through Christ, not something purchased by supporting a ministry.

But if you sincerely want to glorify God with your resources, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one voluntary expression of generosity alongside giving, serving, sharing truth, helping people in need, and faithfully stewarding what God has entrusted to you.
Not because sharing a post makes you righteous.
It doesn't.
Somebody may read the first few lines and finally confess.
Somebody may call a pastor.
Somebody may delete what has been destroying them.
Somebody may return to Scripture.
Somebody may finally tell their spouse the truth.
Somebody may whisper a prayer after months of silence.
Somebody may come home to Jesus.
You may never know.
But God sees in secret.
And perhaps the greatest evidence of your faith will never be the Christianity everyone saw.
Perhaps it will be all those small, unseen moments when temptation offered you secrecy...
and you chose Jesus anyway.
When nobody would have known...
but you remembered that your Father was there.
When your image could have survived the compromise...
but your heart wanted Christ more.
That is where integrity grows.
That is where idols lose oxygen.
That is where repentance becomes freedom.
That is where the person on the platform and the person behind the closed door slowly become the same person.
And when you stumble, remember Peter.
The rooster was not the final sound of his story.
Jesus was.
Your worst hidden chapter does not have to become your final chapter when it is surrendered to Christ.
One day the Christian image you worked so hard to protect will disappear—but the person you became with Jesus when nobody was watching will have mattered all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: NOT EVERYONE WHO SAYS “GOD TOLD ME” ACTUALLY HEARD FROM GOD
paragraphs: NOT EVERYONE WHO SAYS “GOD TOLD ME” ACTUALLY HEARD FROM GOD
The four words that can silence discernment, manipulate a wounded heart, and put God's signature on something He never said.
There are four words that can make a Christian stop asking questions.
Four words that can turn somebody’s private opinion into what sounds like a command from heaven.

Four words that have started relationships, ended marriages, launched ministries, justified reckless decisions, wounded churches, frightened vulnerable believers, and left sincere people wondering why God supposedly promised something that never happened.
“God told me.”
Maybe you have heard those words spoken over you.
Maybe someone looked directly into your eyes and said, “God told me you are supposed to do this.”
Maybe somebody told you whom you were going to marry.
Maybe someone said God had revealed your future.
Maybe a person told you that if you walked away from them, you were walking away from God.
Maybe a preacher announced that God had guaranteed something Scripture never guaranteed.
Or perhaps this article is uncomfortable for a different reason.
Maybe you have said those words yourself.
And maybe, if you are painfully honest, you are no longer certain that God actually said what you claimed He said.
Stay with me.
Because this is not an attack on the Holy Spirit.

This is not an argument that God is distant, silent, powerless, or unable to guide His children. Scripture teaches the reality and activity of the Holy Spirit. Jesus said His sheep hear His voice and follow Him. The Spirit glorifies Christ and guides believers in truth.
The danger is not believing that God speaks.
The danger is believing that everything presented as God's voice must therefore be God's voice.
Those are not the same thing.
And the Bible itself commands us to know the difference.
John writes:
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits…”
—1 John 4:1
That Greek expression is devastatingly clear.
Μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε — mē panti pneumati pisteuete.
Do not believe every spirit.
Then comes the command:
δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα — dokimazete ta pneumata.
Test the spirits.
The verb dokimazō carries the idea of examining or testing something to determine its genuineness.
Notice what John does not say.
He does not say, “If someone sounds spiritual, believe them.”
He does not say, “If they are confident, believe them.”
He does not say, “If they have a large ministry, believe them.”
He does not say, “If they cry while saying it, believe them.”
He does not say, “If you get goosebumps, believe them.”
He says:
Test.
That means biblical discernment is not unbelief.
Discernment is obedience.
You are not dishonoring the Holy Spirit when you test something by the truth God has already revealed. You are obeying the Holy Spirit-inspired Scriptures when you do.
And this problem did not begin with social media prophets.
Long before microphones, livestreams, conference stages, viral reels, and charismatic personalities existed, God confronted people who were putting His name behind their own words.
Jeremiah records one of Scripture's most sobering rebukes of false prophetic claims.
God describes prophets proclaiming lies in His name and crying:
“חָלַמְתִּי חָלָמְתִּי”
ḥālamtî, ḥālamtî.
“I have dreamed! I have dreamed!”
—Jeremiah 23:25
Then God exposes something terrifying.
Their messages were coming from what Jeremiah describes as the deceit of their own hearts.
Think about that.
A person can be deeply convinced…
emotionally stirred…
religiously sincere…
and still mistake what is arising from within themselves for something God has spoken.
That should humble every one of us.
Because sometimes what we call “God told me” may actually mean:
“I desperately want this.”
“I am afraid of losing this.”
“This makes sense to me.”
“I had a powerful emotional experience.”
“I had a dream.”
“I felt strongly about it.”
“I heard somebody else say something similar.”
“I cannot explain this feeling.”
None of those things automatically means God did not lead you.
But none of them automatically means He did.

There is an enormous difference between saying, “I sense the Lord may be leading me here, and I want to test this biblically,” and declaring, “God told me,” as though your interpretation carries the authority of Scripture.
One posture is humble.
The other can become spiritually dangerous.
Because once someone places the words “God told me” in front of a personal opinion, disagreement suddenly feels like rebellion against God.
Imagine a young woman hearing:
“God told me you're supposed to marry me.”
What happens if she does not want to?
Now she is not merely rejecting a man's proposal.
She has been made to feel as though she is rejecting God's will.
Imagine a church member hearing:
“God told me you need to give this amount.”
Imagine a wounded spouse hearing:
“God told me our marriage is finished,” when the speaker is using divine language to bypass biblical responsibility.
Imagine someone terrified because a stranger confidently predicted tragedy over their family.
Imagine a believer being told:
“If you leave this ministry, you're leaving God's covering.”
This is why claiming divine authority is serious.
God's name is not punctuation for our preferences.

And Scripture shows just how seriously God takes people speaking presumptuously in His name. Deuteronomy 18 warns against the prophet who speaks a word God did not command. It also tells Israel that when a supposed prediction spoken in God's name fails, they are not to fear the speaker.
That last part matters.
You do not have to live imprisoned by failed prophecies.
You do not have to spend ten years terrified because somebody told you God said something would happen.
You do not have to force circumstances to fulfill another person's prediction.
You do not have to marry somebody because they said God selected you.
You do not have to remain under spiritual manipulation because someone attached God's name to their demands.
You belong to Jesus Christ.
And Jesus did not rescue you from darkness so another human being could control your conscience by pretending to possess unquestionable access to God's private instructions for your life.
But there is another side to this.
And it may hurt more.
Sometimes the person misusing “God told me” is not a manipulative preacher.
Sometimes it is us.
Sometimes we want something so badly that we baptize desire as revelation.
We want the relationship.
God told me.
We want the job.
God told me.
We want to leave.
God told me.
We want to stay.
God told me.
We want the ministry.
God told me.
We dislike somebody's correction.
God told me they're jealous.
We do not want accountability.
God told me I don't need anyone's approval.
And suddenly God seems to agree with everything we already wanted.
That should make us tremble.
Not because Christians must live paralyzed, terrified of making decisions.
But because humility before God is safer than pretending certainty we do not possess.
Sometimes one of the most spiritually mature sentences you can say is:
“I believe God may be leading me, but I could be wrong.”
There is no shame in that sentence.
There is humility in it.
The apostles themselves commended examination.
When Paul preached in Berea, Acts 17:11 tells us that the Bereans received the message eagerly while “examining the Scriptures daily” to determine whether what they were hearing was true.
Think about who they were checking.
Paul.
The apostle Paul.
They did not say, “He's an apostle, so asking questions would dishonor him.”
They searched the Scriptures.
And Scripture praises them for it.
The Greek describes them as:
ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς — anakrinontes tas graphas.
Examining the Scriptures.
Christian faith was never intended to require shutting down your mind whenever a religious person speaks confidently.
Open your Bible.
Examine.
Pray.
Seek wise counsel.
Look at the fruit.
Look at the context.
Ask whether what you are hearing agrees with God's revealed character and Word.
And above everything else…
look at Jesus.
Because the Holy Spirit does not exist to make human personalities impressive.
Jesus said concerning the Spirit:
“He will glorify Me.”
—John 16:14
That gives us a beautiful center of gravity.
The Spirit's ministry exalts Christ.
So when supposed revelation consistently produces obsession with a messenger rather than worship of Jesus, something has gone terribly wrong.
When the personality becomes untouchable…
when questioning the leader becomes equivalent to questioning God…
when every disagreement receives a convenient “God told me”…
when failed predictions disappear without repentance…
when fear keeps people loyal…
when Scripture is twisted to protect the speaker…
when Jesus becomes almost secondary to revelations, personalities, experiences, money, power, and spectacle…
do not surrender your discernment.
Test.
Because spectacular does not automatically mean spiritual.
Paul's warning in Galatians goes even further.
He essentially tells the church that even if an angel from heaven proclaimed a gospel contrary to the one already received, that messenger was to be rejected.
Let that settle into your heart.
Even an extraordinary supernatural claim does not outrank the Gospel.
Not a dream.
Not a vision.
Not an angelic claim.
Not a prophecy.
Not a famous preacher.
Not your favorite Christian creator.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not me.
Jesus Christ and the truth He has revealed must remain above every human messenger.
That is why you should never believe something merely because we publish it.
Open your Bible.
Check the context.
Test what we say.
If we ever point you away from Jesus Christ, reject what we say.
If we ever teach a gospel contrary to the apostolic Gospel, reject what we say.
If we ever ask you to treat our voice as though it carries the authority of Scripture, reject that demand.
A Christian ministry should never be afraid of an open Bible.
And there is something else we desperately need to recover.
Repentance when we get it wrong.
Perhaps you once told somebody, “God told me,” and later realized it may have been your own desire.
You do not need to hide.
You can repent.
Maybe you frightened somebody with a prediction.
You can apologize.
Maybe you manipulated someone by attaching God's authority to what you wanted.
Confess it.
Maybe you were deceived by someone else's supposed word from God and now feel foolish.
Come back to Christ.
Grace is waiting.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not go to the cross only for respectable sins.
He died for our religious pride too.
He died for our manipulation.
Our presumption.
Our dishonesty.
Our hunger to appear spiritually important.
Our desperate need to be right.
Our secret craving to be seen as somebody who has a special connection with heaven.
At Calvary, the masks come off.
There is no celebrity prophet at the foot of the cross.
No impressive Christian.
No spiritual superstar.
Only sinners who need mercy.
And Christ gives mercy.
The Gospel does not say, “Pretend you never got anything wrong.”
The Gospel says repent and believe.
Bring your mistakes into the light.
Bring your false certainty.
Bring the words you should never have spoken in God's name.
Bring the decisions you made from fear.
Bring the wounds left by spiritual manipulation.
Bring your confusion.
Bring your embarrassment.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
Because Jesus specializes in taking the places where sin wrote shame and rewriting them with grace.
That is our heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps somebody reading this right now is carrying a wound nobody sees.
Somebody once told you, “God said…”
And you obeyed because you were afraid not to.
Then everything collapsed.
Now you do not know whom to trust.
Maybe you do not even trust yourself anymore.
Hear this carefully:
A human being misrepresenting God does not mean God misrepresented Himself.
People can fail you.
Leaders can fail you.
Christ does not.
Someone can misuse Scripture.
Scripture is not therefore false.
Someone can lie in God's name.
God does not therefore become a liar.
Do not let somebody else's counterfeit voice steal your hunger for the real Shepherd.
Return to Jesus.
Return to His Word.
Learn His character.
Become so rooted in Scripture that spiritual-sounding manipulation becomes harder to sell to you.
And when you do believe the Lord is leading you personally, hold that conviction with reverence and humility.
You do not need to make God your accomplice to win an argument.
You do not need “God told me” to make your opinion impressive.
Sometimes “I believe…”
“I sense…”
“I am praying…”
“I think wisdom is leading me…”
“I could be mistaken…”
are profoundly Christian sentences.
Humility does not weaken genuine faith.
It protects us from confusing ourselves with God.
Stay here for a moment.
Ask Jesus:
“Lord, have I ever used Your name to strengthen something You never said?”
And listen.
Maybe there is someone you need to apologize to.
Maybe there is a prediction you need to stop fearing.
Maybe there is a relationship where spiritual language has been used to control you.
Maybe there is a teacher you have been treating as unquestionable.
Maybe there is simply a deeper hunger rising in you:
“Jesus, teach me to recognize truth.”
Not because typing a phrase saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light is where honesty begins.
And please do not turn this article into ammunition for attacking every Christian who says they believe God led them.
That would miss the point completely.
The goal is not cynicism.
The goal is discernment.
The goal is not mocking spiritual gifts.
The goal is biblical faithfulness.
The goal is not becoming suspicious of everyone.
The goal is becoming deeply anchored in Christ.
Strong feelings are real feelings.
But strong feelings are not Scripture.
Send it privately to the person recovering from spiritual manipulation.
Share it with the young believer who needs to understand that discernment is not rebellion.
Grace cannot be bought.
But generosity and practical support can help Christian ministry continue.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with following the Messiah.
Ministries are servants.
Jesus is Lord.
And the safest place for your soul will never be beneath the unquestionable voice of a human personality.
It will be at the feet of Jesus, with your Bible open, your heart humble, your sins confessed, your discernment awake, and your eyes fixed on Christ.
Because someday you may discover that the most dangerous spiritual sentence was not spoken by an obvious enemy.
It came from someone you trusted.
Perhaps even from your own lips.
“God told me.”
So test it.
Bring it beneath Scripture.
Bring it before Jesus.
And never be afraid to discover that God did not say what a human being claimed He said.
Because God's truth does not need our exaggeration.
His Word does not need our manipulation.
And Jesus does not need counterfeit authority to change a human heart.
Never let someone else's “God told me” become louder in your soul than what God has actually revealed in His Word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES GOD REALLY NEED ANOTHER ANGEL IN HEAVEN?
paragraphs:
DOES GOD REALLY NEED ANOTHER ANGEL IN HEAVEN?
The comforting words we whisper at funerals may sound beautiful—but the truth Scripture gives grieving hearts is far more powerful: God did not take your loved one because heaven was short an angel. And if they belonged to Jesus Christ, their story did not end in a cemetery.
There are sentences people say when they do not know what else to say.
“Heaven gained another angel.”
“God needed another angel in heaven.”
“They got their wings.”
Usually, nobody saying these things is trying to teach theology.
They are trying to survive a funeral.
They are standing beside a coffin looking at a face they would give almost anything to see smile again.
They are scrolling through photographs at two in the morning.
They are staring at an empty chair.
An untouched coffee cup.
A name still saved in their phone.
A conversation they never knew would be the last one.
And when grief becomes too large for ordinary vocabulary, people reach for words that somehow make death hurt less.
So this is not an article written to shame grieving people.
If you have ever whispered, “God needed another angel,” because your heart was shattered and you needed something—anything—to hold onto, these words are not coming after you.
They are coming to sit beside you.
Because there is something Scripture says that is even better than the comforting phrase we invented.
God does not need another angel.
And human beings do not become angels when they die.
The biblical hope is far greater than that.
You were never created to become an angel.
You were created to belong to God.
And through Jesus Christ, the final destination of the redeemed is not becoming a different species of heavenly being, floating forever with wings and a harp.
It is resurrection.
Restoration.
Life with God.
A redeemed humanity in a renewed creation under the reign of Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
In Scripture, angels and human beings are not interchangeable.

Hebrews describes angels as “ministering spirits” sent to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). Human beings, meanwhile, bear the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27), fell into sin, stand in need of redemption, and are offered reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Even the biblical languages preserve this distinction.
The Hebrew word often translated “angel” is מַלְאָךְ — mal’akh — fundamentally meaning a messenger.
The Greek word is ἄγγελος — angelos — likewise meaning messenger.

The words can sometimes refer to human messengers depending on context, but when Scripture speaks of heavenly angels, it speaks of spiritual servants of God—not dead human beings who have transformed into angels.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not become an angel to save us.
The eternal Son truly entered humanity.
John 1:14 says:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Not angel.
Flesh.
Humanity mattered enough to God that the Son entered our condition.
Hebrews says Christ shared in “flesh and blood” so that through death He might destroy the one holding the power of death and deliver those enslaved by the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).
Think about that the next time death whispers that it has won.
Christianity does not ask you to pretend death is beautiful.
The Bible calls death an enemy.
“The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26).
An enemy.
That means your grief is not necessarily evidence that your faith is weak.
Jesus Himself stood outside the tomb of Lazarus and wept.
The shortest verse many Christians memorized as children contains one of the deepest revelations of the heart of Christ:
“Jesus wept.” (John 11:35)
He knew Lazarus would shortly walk out of that tomb.
And still…
Jesus wept.
So Christianity does not tell the grieving mother, “Stop crying.”
It does not tell the widower, “If you trusted God more, this wouldn't hurt.”
It does not tell the child missing a parent, “Just get over it.”
Jesus shows us that faith and tears can occupy the same face.
You can trust God and still ache.
You can believe in resurrection and still hate the silence of an empty bedroom.
You can worship with tears running down your cheeks.
But Scripture refuses to leave us at the graveside.
Because before Jesus wept, He said something astonishing.
In John 11:25, Jesus declared:
Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή.
Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē.
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
“I know where resurrection is.”
“I can explain resurrection.”
“I can show you resurrection.”
He said:
I AM.
The Christian hope is ultimately not an idea.
It is a Person.
Jesus Christ.
That changes everything about the question, “Does God need another angel in heaven?”
God is not sitting helplessly in heaven with vacant angelic positions that must be filled by human deaths.
The sovereign Creator does not suffer from staffing shortages.
Acts 17:25 says God is not served by human hands “as though he needed anything,” because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything.
God does not need us in the sense that His existence, power, or glory depends upon us.
He loves us.
There is an enormous difference.
And that difference matters when someone dies.

Because saying “God needed another angel” can unintentionally paint a frightening picture of God—as though He saw somebody's father, mother, husband, wife, son, daughter, brother, sister, or friend and decided heaven needed that person more than the family did.
Scripture gives us something deeper than that picture.
It gives us a God who enters suffering.
A Savior who cries beside a tomb.
A Christ who carries a cross.
A Messiah who experiences death.
And a risen King who defeats the grave.
This is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
The One through whom all things were made allowed nails to pierce His hands.
The sinless One was crucified among criminals.
The Lord of life entered death.
Then death discovered it had swallowed Someone it could not hold.
The tomb could not keep Him.
Jesus rose.
And because Christ rose, Christians do not merely believe that souls somehow “go somewhere better.”
Our hope is anchored in something even greater.
Resurrection.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15 that Christ has been raised from the dead as the “firstfruits” of those who have fallen asleep.
Later he declares:
ἐγερθήσονται ἄφθαρτοι
egerthēsontai aphthartoi
“the dead will be raised imperishable.”
That is Christian hope.
Not becoming angels.
Being raised.
Paul develops the same hope in 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18. He does not want believers to grieve “as others do who have no hope.” Notice carefully: he does not say Christians never grieve.
We grieve.
But not without hope.
Because Jesus died and rose again.
And Revelation carries that hope toward its breathtaking conclusion.
“Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.” (Revelation 21:3)
Then comes one of Scripture's most tender promises:
“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more.” (Revelation 21:4)
Read that slowly.
Death shall be no more.
Not managed.
Not renamed.
Not romanticized.
Gone.
There is coming a day when cemeteries will become obsolete.
A day when nobody receives the phone call.
Nobody sits beside the hospital bed watching the monitor go silent.
Nobody has to explain death to a child.
Nobody kisses a forehead goodbye knowing it will be the last time in this age.
Nobody stands over fresh soil wondering how the world can keep moving when their world has stopped.
Death shall be no more.
But there is another side of this truth that cannot be softened away.
The Christian hope is not simply, “Everybody dies and everything automatically turns out fine.”
Jesus repeatedly called people to repentance and faith.
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Separation from God is real.
And salvation is not found in sentimental sayings about heaven.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
Romans 6:23 tells us the wages of sin is death—but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
The cross exists because our problem was far deeper than sadness.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed rescue.
And we could not purchase it.
We could not behave our way into it.
We could not donate our way into it.
We could not become religious enough to deserve it.
Then came grace.
Jesus took upon Himself what sinners could never overcome.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
That is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Look through Scripture.
Peter denied Jesus.
Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to build an impressive religious résumé.
He had only a guilty past, a dying body, and enough faith to turn toward the crucified King.
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” (Luke 23:42)
And Jesus answered him:
“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43)
That is scandalous grace.
A dying criminal could not climb down from his cross and repair his reputation.
He could not undo his crimes.
He could not spend thirty years proving that his repentance was sincere.
He could only turn toward Jesus.
And Jesus was enough.
Maybe that is why you found yourself reading this far.
Perhaps death has been closer to you than people realize.
Maybe you have lost someone.
Maybe you are terrified of losing someone.
Maybe you have attended enough funerals to realize that someday people will attend yours.
Or maybe the person you are grieving is actually yourself.
Not physically.
Spiritually.
You remember who you used to be.
You remember when prayer felt alive.
You remember when worship was not just music playing while your mind wandered somewhere else.
You remember when sin bothered you more quickly.
You remember when Jesus was not merely part of your life.
He was the center.
But something happened.
Disappointment.
Secret sin.
Pornography.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Success.
Failure.
Church hurt.
A relationship.
An addiction.
Exhaustion.
Grief.
Slow compromise.
And nobody noticed the funeral happening inside you.
You still knew the songs.
Still knew when to say amen.
Still posted the verse.
Still smiled at church.
But somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary was a soul whispering:
“God… where did I go?”
Hear this carefully.
Jesus still raises dead things.
The same Christ who called Lazarus from the tomb is not intimidated by the darkness you have been hiding.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to approach Him.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Confess.
Believe.
Surrender.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved to sin.
