Grace is God's power bringing sinners home and teaching redeemed people to live differently.
Maybe your scandal is known by everybody.
Maybe nobody knows it except God.
Either way, Jesus already knows the unedited version of your story.
And He still calls sinners to Himself.
That is why we should be careful about making angels the center of our language about death.
Angels are magnificent servants of God.
But angels are not the Gospel.
Jesus is.
Your hope is not that someday you will earn wings.
Your hope is that Christ died for sinners and rose victorious over death.
Your hope is that those who belong to Christ belong to the One whom death could not conquer.
And if someone you love died trusting in Jesus, you do not need to imagine them becoming something Scripture never promised.
You can hold onto what Scripture actually promises.
Christ.
Presence with the Lord.
Resurrection.
Restoration.
A future where death is destroyed.
A new creation where God dwells with His people.
And tears wiped away by God Himself.
Perhaps someone you know needs those words tonight.
Not another argument.
Not another cliché.
Hope.
If you thought about a father quietly carrying loss, send it to him.
Otherwise, send it privately.
And if this corrected something you have believed for years, there is no shame in learning.
But please do not leave this article merely thinking differently about angels.
Ask the harder question.
Do I belong to Jesus?
Not:
“Am I religious?”
Not:
“Was I baptized once?”
Not:
“Does my family believe?”
Not:
“Do I post Christian things?”
Not even:
“Do I believe God exists?”
Do you belong to Christ?
Have you turned from trusting yourself and placed your hope in Jesus Christ?
Are you willing to bring your sin into His light?
Because eventually the question will not be whether God needed another angel.
The question will be whether you were ready to meet God.
And you do not need to wait until a hospital room to settle that question.
You can turn toward Jesus now.

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. I believe You died and rose again. I surrender myself to You. Change me. Teach me to follow You. Let my life belong to You.”
Those words are not a magical formula.
Christ is the Savior.
Come to Him.
And if something inside you has been breaking while reading this, do not hide behind silence.
Sometimes another believer needs to see that they are not the only person fighting through tears to keep trusting Jesus.
Somebody reading quietly may desperately need evidence that grief can wound a Christian without destroying their faith.
Not because God needs your money.
He doesn't.
We should never manipulate people by pretending otherwise.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God by helping biblical Gospel-centered teaching reach more people, supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership.
And there is much you can access without paying anything.
If this ministry strengthens you, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the Christian who is tired of pretending.
Invite the seeker who has questions.
Invite the lukewarm believer who needs awakening.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about death.
Follow so you can continue growing with us.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because honest testimony can become somebody else's lifeline.
Before you leave, remember this.
Your loved one did not need to become an angel for death to lose the final word—and neither do you need wings to have hope.
You need Jesus.
Because the greatest comfort Christianity offers is not that heaven gained another angel.
It is that the grave lost its claim to final victory when Jesus Christ walked out alive.
And one day, for everyone who belongs to Him, the last goodbye will have already been spoken.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Revenge Feels Like Justice When You’re the One Who Was Hurt
paragraphs: Revenge Feels Like Justice When You’re the One Who Was Hurt
The Bible never asks you to pretend the wound was acceptable. It asks you to surrender the right to become the judge, jury, and executioner of the person who caused it.
There is a kind of anger that does not feel sinful.
It feels reasonable.
Almost righteous.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone lied about you.
Someone humiliated you in front of people whose respect mattered to you.

Someone took advantage of your kindness, damaged your reputation, abandoned you when you needed them, cheated you, manipulated you, abused your trust, destroyed something you spent years building—or walked away smiling while you were left carrying consequences they created.
And somewhere inside you, a sentence began forming.
I just want them to know what this feels like.
Not murder.
Not violence.
Maybe not even anything you would publicly call revenge.
You simply want life to hurt them back.
You want the truth exposed.
You want their comfortable little world interrupted.
You want the person who made you cry to finally lose some sleep.
You want the one who embarrassed you to be embarrassed.
You want the person who replaced you to discover what they threw away.
You want the liar caught.
The betrayer betrayed.
The manipulator manipulated.
The person who broke your heart to someday sit alone with the pieces of their own.
And because what happened to you really was wrong, revenge can begin disguising itself as justice.
That is what makes this so dangerous.
Because revenge rarely walks into a wounded heart announcing,
“Hello. I am sin.”
Sometimes it enters whispering,
“I just want what is fair.”
Paul writes to Christians in Rome:
—Romans 12:19
The Greek is painfully direct.
Μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες, ἀγαπητοί
Mē heautous ekdikountes, agapētoi.
“Do not avenge yourselves, beloved.”
That word ἐκδικοῦντες (ekdikountes) comes from the idea of exacting justice or vindication.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say evil does not matter.
He does not tell wounded people that injustice is imaginary.
He does not command Christians to call abuse love, betrayal acceptable, exploitation harmless, or criminal behavior something that should simply be ignored.
Biblical forgiveness is not pretending evil was good.

And refusing personal vengeance does not mean refusing lawful justice, appropriate consequences, wise boundaries, church discipline, protection of victims, reporting crimes, or truthful accountability.
Romans 13, immediately following this passage, even describes governing authority as having a legitimate role in responding to wrongdoing.
So Romans 12 is not abolishing justice.
It is confronting something far more personal.
The desire to become the one who personally makes the offender pay.
And perhaps that is exactly where this finds you.
You don't merely want justice anymore.
You want them to hurt.
There is a difference.
Justice asks:
What is right?
Revenge asks:
How can I make you feel what you made me feel?
Justice can seek protection.
Revenge seeks satisfaction.
Justice can establish boundaries.
Revenge wants emotional repayment.
Justice can tell the truth.
Revenge wants the truth to become a weapon.
Justice may sometimes require consequences.
Revenge needs suffering to feel complete.
And Jesus knows the difference even when nobody else does.
That is uncomfortable because wounded people can become extremely creative at baptizing revenge.
We call it “closure.”
We call it “matching their energy.”
We call it “teaching them a lesson.”
We call it “giving them what they deserve.”
We post something carefully vague enough to deny who it is about but specific enough that they know.
We tell their story to people who never needed to hear it.
We rehearse imaginary conversations in the shower.
We check their profile hoping their life has fallen apart.
We fantasize about the day they come crawling back.

We imagine ourselves finally successful, healed, married, prosperous, admired, or happy—not merely because those things are beautiful gifts, but because we desperately want them to see us having them.
Sometimes even our dream of healing secretly contains an audience.
We don't merely want to recover.
We want our recovery to punish whoever wounded us.
That is when pain has begun demanding worship.
And Scripture loves us too much to leave us there.
Paul continues:
“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink…”
Then comes the command that destroys the entire revenge fantasy:
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”
—Romans 12:20–21
The Greek carries the confrontation beautifully:
Μὴ νικῶ ὑπὸ τοῦ κακοῦ, ἀλλὰ νίκα ἐν τῷ ἀγαθῷ τὸ κακόν.
Mē nikō hypo tou kakou, alla nika en tō agathō to kakon.
Do not be conquered by evil.
Conquer evil with good.
Think about what that means.
The person who hurt you does not have to destroy your life to defeat you.
If their cruelty teaches you cruelty, evil has gained territory.
If their dishonesty turns you dishonest, evil has gained territory.
If their bitterness becomes your bitterness, evil has gained territory.
If their betrayal transforms you into someone incapable of trusting, loving, forgiving, or obeying Christ, then what they did is continuing to wound you long after the original moment ended.
They hurt you once.
Hatred can make you carry them for years.
You wake up with them.
Drive with them.
Eat with them.
Pray with them.
Go to church with them.
Go on dates with them.
Lie beside your spouse thinking about them.
Open Facebook and look for them.
Hear their name and your nervous system remembers everything.
They may not even be in the room anymore.
But somehow they are still controlling the temperature of your heart.
That is one of revenge's cruelest secrets.
You think revenge keeps the offender imprisoned.
Often it keeps you chained to the offense.
But now comes the sentence wounded people sometimes misunderstand:
“Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.”
Paul is drawing from Deuteronomy 32:35, where the Hebrew begins:
לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם
Li naqam veshillem.
“Vengeance is Mine, and recompense.”
God is not saying injustice does not matter.
He is saying judgment belongs ultimately to Him.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity does not ask you to release vengeance because evil is insignificant.
Christianity asks you to release vengeance because God is Judge and you are not.
You are not surrendering justice into emptiness.
You are surrendering judgment to the One who sees what you never saw.
He heard the conversations you never heard.
He knows the motives you cannot prove.
He saw what happened behind the closed door.
He knows which apology was sincere and which one was manipulation.
He knows the full measure of your offender's guilt.
And He knows yours.
That last sentence changes the room.
Because eventually Christianity forces every wounded person to stand somewhere uncomfortable.
At the foot of a cross.
There, you cannot divide humanity neatly into innocent people like you and sinful people like them.
At Calvary, there is one perfectly innocent Man.
And it isn't us.
Jesus Christ was betrayed by someone close enough to kiss Him.
Abandoned by friends who promised loyalty.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Publicly humiliated.
Spat upon.
Nailed to wood.
And while His enemies were participating in His execution, Jesus prayed:
“Father, forgive them…”
—Luke 23:34
Do not sentimentalize that sentence.
Those words came from a crucified Man.
Forgiveness was spoken through blood.
Jesus was not teaching that evil has no consequences.
The cross itself proves the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the self-giving sacrifice of the Son of God.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace is God dealing with sin through Christ and offering mercy to sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And suddenly Romans 12 becomes much more personal.
Because the Gospel does not merely tell you to stop seeking revenge.
It reminds you that you yourself live because mercy triumphed over the judgment you deserved.
Every Christian is somebody who needed grace.
Maybe your sins looked different.
Maybe nobody screenshotted yours.
Maybe yours never became public.
Maybe nobody whispered about them after church.
Maybe your worst moments never reached Facebook.
But Christ did not save you because you had never been guilty.
He saved you because He is merciful.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
And those who trust Christ are “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 3:23–24
That doesn't make what happened to you smaller.
It makes grace bigger.
Perhaps someone reading this has spent months imagining revenge against a former spouse.
Perhaps somebody was cheated on.
Perhaps your family betrayed you over money.
Perhaps someone destroyed your name with a lie and never corrected it.
Perhaps a parent wounded you in ways you are still trying to understand.
Perhaps someone from church—the very place where you expected safety—became the reason walking through church doors now feels difficult.
Perhaps you were used.
Discarded.
Ghosted.
Scammed.
Manipulated.
Abandoned.
Maybe the person never apologized.
And that is the part that burns.
Because forgiveness feels almost offensive when the guilty person seems perfectly fine.
You may be thinking:
So they just get away with it?
No.
Forgiveness does not mean declaring them innocent.
Forgiveness means refusing to make yourself God.
You can forgive and still tell the truth.
Forgive and maintain boundaries.
Forgive and never restore the same level of access.
Forgive and report criminal conduct.
Forgive and cooperate with lawful authorities.
Forgive and seek protection.
Forgive without pretending trust has automatically been rebuilt.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical. Reconciliation ordinarily requires truth, repentance, and the rebuilding of trust between people.
Sometimes the godliest thing you can do is forgive someone from a distance while refusing to return to an unsafe situation.
But revenge?
That belongs somewhere else.
Put it into the hands of God.
Even if your hands shake while releasing it.
Tell Him exactly what happened.
The Psalms prove that God is not frightened by brutally honest prayers.
Tell Him you are angry.
Tell Him you want them exposed.
Tell Him part of you wants them to suffer.
Tell Him you don't know how to forgive.
Tell Him you keep replaying it.
Tell Him you hate what this wound is turning you into.
Prayer does not require pretending.
Bring the ugly truth into the presence of God.
Then surrender it.
Again tomorrow if necessary.
And again the day after that.
Forgiveness is sometimes a decisive act followed by a long war against returning resentment.
You may have to surrender the same offense repeatedly as memories resurface.
That does not necessarily mean the first surrender was fake.
It may simply mean the wound is deep.
But do not feed it.
Do not build your identity around what someone did to you.
You are more than the person who was betrayed.
More than the divorce.
More than the rumor.
More than the rejection.
More than the childhood wound.
More than the scandal.
More than the thing they did when nobody defended you.
If you belong to Christ, the deepest truth about you is not what someone did to you.
It is what Jesus did for you.
He died.
He rose.
He forgives.
He redeems.
He restores.
And He is still rewriting stories human beings thought were finished.
That is why our message will always be:
Not because scandal never happened.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because justice no longer matters.
But because Jesus Christ can take what should have become the graveyard of your soul and make it the place where grace begins growing.
Maybe the greatest victory over the person who wounded you isn't watching their life collapse.
Maybe it is discovering that what they did no longer controls yours.
Imagine being able to hear their name without hatred poisoning your afternoon.
Imagine praying without secretly asking God to destroy them.
Imagine no longer checking whether karma found them.
Imagine no longer needing them to regret losing you before you can believe you have value.
Imagine becoming so rooted in Christ that their opinion can no longer determine your identity.
That is freedom.
And sometimes freedom begins with one trembling prayer:
Jesus, I give You my right to revenge.
Not because they deserve mercy.
Because you belong to Christ.
And because the cross has already shown you what God can do with guilty people who receive His mercy.
There is no prize for pretending the wound doesn't hurt.
Bring it to Jesus.
Someone scrolling tonight may be one betrayal away from making a decision they will regret.
Your share could put Romans 12 in front of them before revenge gets the final word.
Because forgiveness often needs to be remembered more than once.
There may come another night when the memory returns, anger rises, and everything inside you wants repayment.
Come back.
Read Romans 12:19–21 again.
Remember who the Judge is.
Remember who you are.
Remember the cross.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Jesus, follow this ministry and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. We want this community to remain a place of daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, repentance, grace, and spiritual nourishment centered unapologetically on Jesus Christ.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical resources into the hands of people who need them.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be treated as purchasing God's favor, proving your faith, or earning spiritual merit. We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of loving obedience to Him. But one legitimate way believers can glorify God is through generous, willing support of Gospel work and by helping biblical truth reach others.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.

It is helping build a community where wounded people are pointed toward Christ instead of revenge, sinners toward repentance instead of hiding, exhausted believers toward grace instead of despair, and broken stories toward the Savior who still rewrites them.
Not as pressure.
As mission.
They may never tell you.
But they might read this.
And tonight they might finally unclench their fist.
Not because what happened suddenly became okay.
Not because justice stopped mattering.
But because they remembered that final judgment belongs to God—and their wounded heart belongs in the hands of Jesus.
You do not have to watch the person who hurt you suffer before you finally give yourself permission to heal.
Let God be Judge.
Let truth remain truth.
Let lawful justice do its proper work where necessary.
Let wise boundaries remain.
But give Jesus the poison you were never created to carry.

The cross has already proved that God can confront evil without becoming evil, uphold justice while extending mercy, and take humanity's darkest scandal and turn it into the doorway of redeeming grace.
And if Christ can rewrite the story of a sinner…
He can rewrite yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE TOOK WHAT WAS PRECIOUS—AND GOD SAID HE COULD NOT WALK AWAY
paragraphs: HE TOOK WHAT WAS PRECIOUS—AND GOD SAID HE COULD NOT WALK AWAY

The shocking command hidden in Exodus 22 reveals something our disposable culture desperately needs to hear: intimacy creates responsibility, desire does not erase accountability, and even after sexual sin has written a scandal into your story, Jesus Christ can still write grace across the ending.
There is a verse in Exodus that almost nobody puts on a coffee mug.
It is not the kind of passage people quote when they need encouragement before work.
It is uncomfortable.
Ancient.
Easy to misunderstand.
And painfully relevant.
Because buried inside Israel’s covenant law is a scene that still happens in different forms today.
A man wants a woman.
He persuades her.
Desire becomes intimacy.
Something happens that cannot simply be treated as though nothing happened.
And then God speaks.
Not because God is embarrassed by sexuality.
Not because Scripture believes women are merchandise.
Not because marriage can magically erase sexual wrongdoing.
God speaks because human beings are not disposable.
Listen carefully to the Hebrew of Exodus 22:16:
“וְכִי־יְפַתֶּה אִישׁ בְּתוּלָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא־אֹרָשָׂה וְשָׁכַב עִמָּהּ מָהֹר יִמְהָרֶנָּה לּוֹ לְאִשָּׁה”
Ve-khi yefatteh ish betulah asher lo-orasah, ve-shakhav immah, mahor yimharennah lo le-ishah.
The opening verb matters.
יְפַתֶּה — yefatteh
It comes from the Hebrew root פתה — p-t-h, carrying the idea of enticing, persuading, alluring, or seducing.
The woman is described as:
בְּתוּלָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא־אֹרָשָׂה
betulah asher lo-orasah
—a virgin who was not betrothed.
Then comes the consequence.
מָהֹר יִמְהָרֶנָּה
mahor yimharennah.
The word מֹהַר — mohar refers to the bride-price associated with marriage.
In other words, the man could not treat sexual intimacy as an inexpensive moment of pleasure and then disappear as though another person's future did not matter.
There was accountability.
There was responsibility.
There was cost.
But there is something else in the passage that is absolutely essential—and missing it can turn the text into something God never said.
The next verse declares that if her father absolutely refuses to give her to him, the man must nevertheless pay the amount corresponding to the bride-price for virgins.
Marriage was therefore not automatic.
The man did not acquire an unconditional right to the woman because he had slept with her.
The Hebrew intensifies the refusal:
אִם־מָאֵן יְמָאֵן אָבִיהָ
im ma'en yema'en aviha
“If her father utterly refuses…”
The construction emphasizes refusal.
He could say no.
And the financial accountability remained.
That changes the picture considerably.
This passage should therefore not be casually reduced to, “A man slept with a woman, so God forced her to marry him.”
That is not what Exodus 22:16–17 says.

Nor should this passage automatically be described as Israel’s law concerning rape. The Hebrew verb used here centers on enticement or persuasion. Other biblical legal texts address sexual violence with different circumstances and language.
Exodus 22 is dealing with sexual intimacy outside the recognized protection and obligations of marriage—and refusing to allow the man to pretend his actions carried no consequences.
And suddenly this ancient command begins sounding painfully modern.
Because we live in a world that has become extraordinarily skilled at separating desire from responsibility.
“I love you.”
Then...
“I’m not ready for commitment.”
“You mean everything to me.”
Then...
“I need space.”
“We don't need a piece of paper to prove our love.”
Then somebody gets pregnant.
Somebody gets abandoned.
Somebody discovers another person.
Somebody stops answering messages.
Somebody lies awake at 2:13 in the morning staring at a phone that is never going to light up with the name they desperately want to see.
And somebody whispers through tears:
“How could I mean so little to someone who once told me I meant everything?”
That is where Exodus 22 suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because underneath the bride-price and the ancient social structure is a truth modern humanity keeps trying to escape:
Intimacy is not meaningless.
Bodies matter.
Promises matter.
Sex matters.
People matter.
And what we do with another person's vulnerability matters before God.
Our culture can rename things.
Casual.
No strings attached.
Situationship.
Friends with benefits.
Just having fun.
But changing the vocabulary cannot change the human soul.
You can call something casual while crying over it for six months.
You can say there were “no strings attached” while discovering that your memories have strings.
Your emotions have strings.
Your conscience has strings.
Your body remembers.
Your heart remembers.
And sometimes the person who walked away barely remembers at all.
Perhaps that is why this passage feels almost offensive to modern ears.
God places responsibility where our culture often places excuses.
The man cannot simply say:
“But she agreed.”
“But I never promised forever.”
“But we were both adults.”
“But things changed.”
“But it was only one night.”
Exodus interrupts the excuses.
You touched a human life.
You do not get to pretend nothing happened.
And before anyone uses that truth merely to condemn somebody else, there is another uncomfortable question waiting for us.
What about you?
Maybe you were the one who walked away.
Maybe you made promises because you wanted access to somebody's heart—or body—and afterward discovered that your promises were much easier to make than to keep.
Maybe you knew exactly what to say.
Maybe you said, “I love you,” when what you really meant was, “I want you.”
Maybe somebody trusted you.
And you used that trust.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your church does not know.
Maybe the person sitting beside you on Sunday hears you sing about holiness while you remember the things you did in darkness.
Be honest.
This may be hitting harder than you expected.
Or perhaps you are on the other side of the story.
You were persuaded.
You trusted.
You thought it was love.
You gave somebody something deeply personal because you genuinely believed they were staying.
Then they left.
And eventually you began blaming yourself.
You wondered whether God looked at you differently.
You wondered whether purity lost meant worth lost.
You wondered whether your future marriage had somehow been permanently ruined.
You wondered whether you were now the scandal in somebody else's testimony.
Hear this carefully:
Your sexual history is not your identity.
Your worst night is not your name.
What somebody did with your vulnerability does not determine your value before God.
And your own sexual sin—real as it may be—is not stronger than the blood of Jesus Christ.
This is where the story moves from scandal to grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that says sin does not matter.
Biblical grace says something far more breathtaking.
Sin matters so much that Christ died for it.
And grace is so powerful that Christ can forgive it.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend our guilt was imaginary.
He carried it.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant who would bear our iniquities.
John the Baptist pointed at Jesus and cried, “Behold the Lamb of God.”
Paul declared that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Peter wrote that Christ Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.
This is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for being cleaner than bad people.
It is guilty people discovering that the Son of God came looking for sinners.
Jesus repeatedly walked directly into human scandal.
A Samaritan woman with a shattered relational history met Him beside a well.
A woman caught in adultery was dragged into public humiliation and found herself standing before the only truly sinless Man present.
A prostitute could weep at His feet.
A thief could hang dying beside Him.
Peter could deny Him.
Thomas could doubt Him.
Saul could persecute His church.
And still...
Grace came looking.
Grace did not call evil good.
Grace called sinners home.
That distinction matters.
Jesus never needed to redefine sin in order to love sinners.
He loved sinners enough to rescue them from sin.
“Neither do I condemn you” was never permission to remain unchanged.
It was followed by a call to leave sin.
That is the Gospel.
Forgiveness and transformation.
Mercy and repentance.
Grace and truth.
Maybe you have been using grace as permission.
Come home.
Maybe you have been drowning in shame even after repentance.
Come home.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to consume people rather than love them.
Come home.
Maybe you keep entering relationships because loneliness terrifies you more than disobedience.
Come home.
Maybe you are sleeping with someone you know is not your spouse and have been asking God to bless what He has called you to surrender.
Come home.
Maybe you destroyed somebody's trust.
Come home—and where possible and appropriate, accept responsibility rather than hiding behind religious language.
Maybe you were exploited, abandoned, manipulated, or deceived, and you have carried somebody else's actions like they were your identity.
Come to Jesus.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, “This must come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “You can never come into the light.”
Jesus calls us out of darkness precisely because darkness does not get the final word.
And this is where Exodus 22 reaches beyond ancient economics.
The bride-price is not the Gospel.
Israel’s civil law is not a secret formula for modern dating.
But the passage reveals something about God's moral world that modern hearts desperately need to recover:
People must never become disposable objects for our appetites.
Sexual desire does not cancel responsibility.
Persuasion does not eliminate consequences.
Intimacy must not become exploitation.
And sin should never be treated casually simply because society has learned to normalize it.
But then comes Jesus.
And Jesus takes us somewhere Exodus 22 by itself could never take us.
Because ultimately all of us owe something we cannot pay.
Not a bride-price.
A debt of sin.
We have sinned against God.
Some sexually.
Some secretly.
Some proudly.
Some religiously.
Some through lust.
Some through deception.
Some through bitterness.
Some through adultery.
Some through self-righteousness.
Some through years of pretending.
“For all have sinned.”
All.
The religious person.
The sexually broken person.
The adulterer.
The virgin.
The addict.
The pastor.
The prostitute.
The person reading this with tears forming in their eyes.
All.
And none of us can purchase our own redemption.
Then Christ enters the story.
Jesus does not merely tell us to pay our debt.
He gives Himself.
The Judge steps down.
The innocent One stands where the guilty should have stood.
The sinless Son bears judgment.
The cross becomes the place where justice and mercy meet without either being destroyed.
And three days later, the grave loses.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a story about damaged people becoming respectable.
It is the story of dead people being made alive in Christ.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Jesus can rewrite it.
Maybe your story contains betrayal.
Jesus can rewrite it.
Maybe your story contains abortion, adultery, pornography, secret messages, broken vows, exploitation, shame, or years you wish you could erase.
Jesus can rewrite it.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Grace does not always remove consequences.
Sometimes repentance means apologizing.
Sometimes it means confession.
Sometimes it means ending a sinful relationship.
Sometimes it means rebuilding trust slowly.
Sometimes it means accepting that somebody you wounded does not owe you immediate reconciliation.
Sometimes repentance costs something.
Exodus 22 understood that actions have consequences.
The cross proves something even greater:
Consequences do not have to become your identity.
Jesus Christ can take a scandal that Satan intended to use as your permanent name and turn it into the place where grace became real to you.
Not because your sin was small.
Because His mercy is greater.
Somebody is being seduced by promises they desperately want to believe.
Somebody is considering walking away from a person they used.
Somebody is hiding sexual sin.
Somebody believes they are too dirty for Jesus.
Somebody has been abandoned and thinks their value left when that person walked out the door.
Not for an algorithm.
For a soul.
Send it privately to someone if publicly tagging them would expose something that should remain private.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own heart, do not hide behind silence.
You do not owe strangers the details of your wounds.
But sometimes four honest words become the first crack through which light enters.
Not because every sentence is easy.
We want this ministry to remain a place where Scripture is not softened to protect our comfort and grace is not weakened by religious condemnation.
It does not.
Not because salvation can be purchased.
It cannot.
Not because giving to Gospel Warrior is a substitute for obedience, generosity, caring for your family, serving your local church, or helping people in need.
It is not.
And we will not tell you that God requires you to pay this ministry in order to prove your faith.
Scripture teaches Christian generosity from the heart, not giving manufactured through pressure.
But voluntary financial support can help Gospel Warrior continue creating, publishing, expanding, and distributing Christ-centered resources to people around the world.
If you have been asking, “How can I help this continue?” this is one practical way.
Share.
Pray.
Save these messages.
Invite others to follow.
Put biblical truth where somebody who would never search for it might suddenly encounter it while scrolling alone at midnight.
Because behind every screen is a human being.
Behind every profile picture is a story.
Behind some smiles is secret shame.
Behind some marriages is betrayal.
Behind some church clothes is addiction.
Behind some angry comments is pain.
Behind some unbelief is a person wondering whether God could possibly want someone like them.
And the answer of the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up and perhaps Jesus will consider you.”
The Gospel says Christ came for sinners.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
Receive the mercy you could never purchase.
And then let grace change the way you live.
Exodus 22 tells us that intimacy carried responsibility.
Calvary tells us that sin carried a debt.
And Jesus tells us something neither lust nor shame wants us to believe:
Your story does not have to end where your scandal happened.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still repentance.
There is still restoration.
There is still Jesus.
So when your past whispers, “Look what you did,” point to the cross and remember what He did.
When shame says, “This is who you are,” remember whose you can become in Christ.
When temptation says, “It won't cost anything,” remember that sin always sends an invoice somewhere.
And when grace whispers, “Come home,” stop running.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable thing about your scandal will not ultimately be how badly you fell.
Perhaps it will be how far Jesus came to bring you home.
The scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but only Jesus gets to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Asked God to Heal the Wound. He Never Asked You to Pretend It Didn’t Hurt.
paragraphs: You Asked God to Heal the Wound. He Never Asked You to Pretend It Didn’t Hurt.
Maybe faith was never supposed to make you pretend the wound wasn’t real. Maybe the God you have been trying to look strong for has been standing closer to your broken heart than you realized.
There is a particular kind of pain Christians sometimes become very good at hiding.
You know how to worship while carrying it.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know which verse to quote.
You know how to smile when someone asks how you are doing.
You know how to lift your hands in church while part of your heart is quietly asking a question you are almost ashamed to admit:
“Jesus… why does this still hurt?”
You prayed.
You forgave—or you are trying to.
You opened your Bible.
You asked God to heal you.
Months passed.
Maybe years.
And somehow the wound still knows your name.
A song can find it.
A photograph can find it.
An empty chair can find it.
A familiar street can find it.
A date on the calendar can find it.
Sometimes one innocent sentence from another person touches the place you thought had finally stopped bleeding, and suddenly you are fighting tears nobody else understands.
Then comes another pain on top of the original pain.
Guilt.
Shouldn't I be over this by now?
If I really trusted God, wouldn't I be stronger?
If I truly forgave, why can I still remember?
Why am I grieving when everyone else seems to have moved on?
And perhaps somewhere along the way, you began confusing healing with pretending.
But Scripture never asks you to call a wound painless when it hurts.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב
Qārōv YHWH lenishberê-lēv.
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted.”
That word translated “brokenhearted” comes from the Hebrew root שָׁבַר — shāvar, carrying the idea of breaking, shattering, or crushing.
Notice what David does not say.
He does not say the brokenhearted are embarrassing to God.
He does not say God stands at a distance until they become emotionally presentable.
He does not say, “Stop crying and prove your faith.”
He says:
קָרוֹב — qārōv.
Near.
That changes everything.
God does not merely tolerate the brokenhearted.
He draws near.
And the context matters.

Psalm 34 is traditionally connected with one of David's humiliating escapes from danger. The superscription recalls David altering his behavior before Abimelech, being driven away, and escaping—an episode corresponding to the account involving Achish in 1 Samuel 21.
This is not poetry floating above real life.
It was praise written in the shadow of fear, danger, humiliation, and deliverance.
David knew what it meant to be afraid.
In Psalm 34:4 he says that he sought the LORD and was delivered from his fears.
Later he speaks of the righteous having many afflictions.
Many.
Biblical faith does not require us to erase that word.
Scripture does not teach that belonging to God means never being wounded. It teaches us where the wounded can go.
And sometimes that is precisely where religious pretending becomes dangerous.
Because you can become so committed to appearing healed that you stop bringing the actual wound to the Healer.
You tell everyone, “I'm fine.”
But you're not.
You say, “It doesn't bother me anymore.”
But it does.
You insist, “I've moved on.”
Then you lie awake at 2:13 in the morning replaying the conversation.
You post the verse.
You encourage everybody else.
You answer prayer requests.
You serve.
You worship.
You laugh.
And then you go somewhere nobody can see you…
and fall apart.
Listen carefully.
Falling apart in the presence of God is not the same thing as abandoning faith.
Sometimes lament is faith refusing to run anywhere else.
The Bible contains an entire vocabulary for suffering because God apparently never intended His people to become strangers to honest grief.
“Why, O LORD, do you stand far away?” cries Psalm 10:1.
“How long, O LORD?” asks Psalm 13:1.
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” begins Psalm 22:1.
These words are not preserved in Scripture so we can shame hurting people for feeling them.
They are Scripture.
God gave His people language for the nights when ordinary language fails.
And then something staggering happens in the Gospel.
Jesus Himself takes the opening cry of Psalm 22 upon His lips at the cross.
Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί
Ēli Ēli lema sabachthani?
Matthew 27:46 records the anguished cry and explains it:
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Jesus was not sinning by expressing anguish.
He was suffering.
The sinless Son of God did not turn agony into a performance of emotional cheerfulness.
And before Calvary, standing at the tomb of Lazarus, Scripture gives us one of its shortest and most devastating sentences:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.

“Jesus wept.”
John 11:35.
Think about that.
Jesus knew resurrection was coming.
He knew Lazarus would walk out of that tomb.
And Jesus still wept.
Hope did not make tears unnecessary.
Knowledge of what God would do next did not make present grief unreal.
That means your tears are not automatically evidence that your faith has failed.
Grief and hope can occupy the same heart.
A Christian can know that Christ is risen and still miss someone who died.
A believer can forgive and still need time for damaged trust to be rebuilt wisely.
A person can believe God is good while grieving something terrible that happened.
A wounded Christian can seek prayer, pastoral care, mature friendship, and when appropriate professional support without betraying dependence upon God.
Scripture itself repeatedly pictures God's people carrying burdens together.
“Bear one another's burdens,” Paul tells believers in Galatians 6:2.
James tells suffering believers to pray.
Romans tells Christians to “weep with those who weep.”
Not lecture them into smiling.
Not rush them through grief.
Not turn their suffering into a theological examination they must pass before receiving compassion.
Weep.
With.
Them.
Maybe someone needed to do that for you.
Maybe instead they told you to get over it.
Maybe somebody spiritualized the wound because sitting beside your pain made them uncomfortable.
Maybe they handed you Romans 8:28 before they gave you permission to cry.
Romans 8:28 is gloriously true.
But truth is not meant to be used as a weapon against grief.
The same Paul who wrote about God working all things together for good also described creation as groaning.
He described believers as groaning.
He spoke of weakness.
He spoke of suffering.
And Romans 8 does not end by pretending suffering is imaginary.
It ends by proclaiming that suffering cannot separate God's people from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
That is a far stronger hope.
Christianity does not say:
“Nothing hurts.”
Christianity says:
Nothing—not even what hurts—can separate those who are in Christ from His love.
There is a difference.
And perhaps that is why you have been exhausted.
You haven't only been carrying the wound.
You have been carrying the performance.
Trying to convince everybody that what happened didn't change you.
Trying to prove that you forgave.
Trying to look victorious.
Trying not to make anybody uncomfortable.
Trying to be the “strong Christian.”
But Jesus never asked you to become your own savior.
He already took that position.
There is a strange freedom in finally praying:
“Lord, this hurt me.”
Not accusing God.
Not worshiping the wound.
Not making pain your identity.
Just telling the truth in His presence.
“Jesus, I still miss them.”
“Jesus, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I don't understand.”
“Jesus, I forgave them, but I am still rebuilding.”
“Jesus, I thought I would be farther along by now.”
“Jesus, I'm tired.”
“Jesus, help me.”
That last prayer may be more faithful than a thousand counterfeit smiles.
Because grace begins where pretending ends.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve your mood.
He came to save sinners.
Our deepest problem is greater than emotional pain: sin has alienated humanity from our holy God, and no amount of self-improvement can reconcile us to Him.
Yet God did what we could never do for ourselves.
Christ entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Christian message is not that sufficiently wounded people can rescue themselves.
It is that a crucified and risen Savior rescues sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
So bring Him more than your wound.
Bring Him your sin.
Bring the bitterness you have secretly fed.
Bring the hatred.
Bring the unbelief.
Bring the compromises you justified because somebody hurt you first.
Bring the secret habits you used to numb what you didn't want to feel.
Bring the pride that keeps saying, “I can handle this myself.”
Bring everything into the light.
Repentance is not God humiliating wounded people.
It is His call to turn from sin and come home to Him.
And forgiveness is not God announcing that sin never mattered.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
Grace is not denial.
Grace tells the truth about our sin and then points us to the Savior whose mercy is greater.
That is why the cross can hold truths we often tear apart.
You were genuinely hurt.
And you may also genuinely need repentance.
Someone may have sinned against you.
And your response to that sin may have grown sinful too.
What happened to you may not have been your choice.
What you do with your heart before God still matters.
Jesus can confront the sinner and comfort the wounded person without confusing either one.
Sometimes He is doing both in the same human heart.
Maybe yours.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because Jesus rewrites history as though evil never happened.
He does something far greater.
He redeems people evil tried to destroy.
Joseph could eventually say of those who betrayed him, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
Joseph did not call evil good.
He called it evil.
Then he confessed that evil did not have the final word.
That is biblical redemption.
Your scars may remain part of your story without remaining the author of your story.
The betrayal does not get the last sentence.
The divorce does not get the last sentence.
The abandonment does not get the last sentence.
The funeral does not get the last sentence.
The abuse does not get the last sentence.
The failure does not get the last sentence.
The years you lost do not get the last sentence.
Your own worst sin does not have to get the last sentence if you come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Jesus does.
And resurrection means God specializes in endings human beings could never have written.
But please hear this carefully:
Healing is not always instant.
The Bible does not give us permission to promise that every emotional wound disappears on our preferred timetable.
Sometimes God delivers dramatically.
Sometimes restoration unfolds slowly through prayer, Scripture, wise community, boundaries, forgiveness, counsel, repeated surrender, and years of learning to walk in truth.
Sometimes consequences remain even where forgiveness is real.
Sometimes reconciliation is possible.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
Forgiveness and unrestricted access are not identical.
Trust can require rebuilding.
And lament may visit again without meaning you have returned to the beginning.
A scar aching does not mean the wound is still controlling you.
Sometimes it simply reminds you that something happened there.
So when the memory returns, you don't have to panic.
You can say:
“Yes, Lord. That still hurts.
And You are still here.”
קָרוֹב יְהוָה.
Qārōv YHWH.
The LORD is near.
Near when you cannot explain yourself.
Near when worship comes through tears.
Near when you need somebody trustworthy to sit beside you.
Near when yesterday unexpectedly enters today.
Near when healing feels painfully slow.
Near when you finally stop saying, “I'm okay,” and whisper what heaven already knows:
“I'm hurting.”
Perhaps this article found you because you have spent too long apologizing for being human.
So don't perform for God tonight.
Pray.
Tell Him what hurts.
Confess what is sinful.
Ask for wisdom about what needs boundaries.
Ask for courage where forgiveness is required.
Ask for trustworthy believers who will carry the burden with you.
Seek appropriate pastoral or professional help when the weight is more than you know how to carry alone.
Open the Psalms and discover that Scripture is not frightened by tears.
Then look toward Jesus.
Not merely as an example of suffering.
As Savior.
The Man of Sorrows who went through death and emerged victorious.
The Lamb who was slain.
The risen King.

The One who does not merely make wounded people feel temporarily better but reconciles sinners to God and promises His people a future in which death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally be no more.
That day is coming.
Until then, Christianity gives us something stronger than pretending.
Presence.
Hope.
Truth.
Grace.
Christ.
They post normally.
They laugh.
They go to work.
They attend church.
Nobody knows that after everyone goes to sleep, the wound starts talking again.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
But glorifying God includes making His truth known, serving others, supporting faithful Gospel work according to our ability, and refusing to hide the hope we have received.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks continuing pain means God is disappointed in them.
Tell the truth.
Someone reading beneath this article may need evidence that wounded people can keep walking with Jesus.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become a place where believers bear one another's burdens.
Where somebody discovers they aren't the only one still grieving.
Where somebody who has been hiding finally asks for prayer.
Where somebody who wandered remembers that Jesus is still calling sinners home.
Because perhaps the most painful mistake you made was believing God would only come near after you stopped looking broken.
Psalm 34 says the opposite.
He is near to the brokenhearted.
So stop handing Jesus the edited version of your heart.
Give Him the bleeding one.
Give Him the frightened one.
Give Him the angry one.
Give Him the ashamed one.
Give Him the exhausted one.
Give Him the sinful one in repentance.
Give Him the heart that still doesn't understand why it happened.
And let the Savior meet you in truth.
You asked God to heal the wound.
He never asked you to pretend it didn't hurt.
The wound may explain some of your tears—but because of Jesus, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LUST KEEPS PROMISING INTIMACY AND LEAVING YOU MORE ALONE
paragraphs: LUST KEEPS PROMISING INTIMACY AND LEAVING YOU MORE ALONE
You thought you were looking for pleasure. Maybe what your heart has been screaming for all along is something lust can imitate for a moment—but can never actually give you.
There is a particular kind of loneliness nobody notices.
You can carry it into church.
You can carry it into marriage.
You can carry it into a room full of friends.
You can carry it while laughing, serving, worshiping, posting Bible verses, raising children, leading people, or telling everyone, “I’m doing fine.”
And sometimes it becomes loudest when the room gets quiet.
The phone is in your hand.
Nobody else is watching.
And something inside you whispers...
Just look.
Just imagine.
Just one more time.
You need this.
Maybe for a few minutes, the loneliness disappears.
Someone wants you in the fantasy.
Someone notices you.
Someone's body is available to your imagination.
You don't have to risk rejection. You don't have to expose your insecurities. You don't have to wait. You don't have to serve. You don't have to be known.
You only have to consume.
And for a moment, counterfeit intimacy feels almost convincing.
Then the screen goes dark.
The fantasy ends.
The conversation stops.
The person leaves.
The secret encounter is over.
And somehow...
you're still alone.
Sometimes more alone than before.
That is one of lust's cruelest deceptions.
Lust keeps promising intimacy while quietly training your heart for isolation.
It says, “This will satisfy you.”
Then asks you to come back tomorrow.
It says, “This will make you feel wanted.”
Then leaves you wondering why being wanted never made you feel known.
It says, “This is freedom.”
Yet slowly you discover how difficult it has become to say no.
It says, “Nobody gets hurt.”
But something is happening inside you.
Your eyes are learning something.
Your imagination is learning something.
Your desires are learning something.
Your heart is learning how to look at another human being and ask, consciously or unconsciously:
What can you give me?
And that is precisely where lust begins separating itself from love.
Love asks, “How can I honor you?”
Lust asks, “How can I consume you?”
Love sees a person.
Lust can reduce a person to a body, an experience, an image, an emotional drug, a fantasy, or a means of satisfying desire.
Love is willing to sacrifice itself for another.
Lust is tempted to sacrifice another for itself.
And Scripture does not treat that distinction casually.
Paul writes to the Thessalonian believers:
Touto gar estin thelēma tou Theou, ho hagiasmos hymōn, apechesthai hymas apo tēs porneias...
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality...” — 1 Thessalonians 4:3
Then Paul continues:
“μη εν παθει επιθυμιας”
mē en pathei epithymias
Not in what can be rendered the “passion of lust” or “lustful passion.”
That phrase is devastatingly revealing.
Paul is not merely giving Christians an arbitrary list of sexual restrictions.
He is describing two profoundly different ways of inhabiting your own body and relating to other human beings.
One is characterized by hagiasmos—holiness, sanctification.
The other allows desire to become ruling passion.
And notice where Paul takes the argument.
He speaks of living “in holiness and honor.”
Honor.
That word matters.
Because biblical sexual holiness is not merely about what you refuse to do with somebody else's body.
It is about learning to honor God, to honor another person, and to honor the body God entrusted to you.
Christian purity was never supposed to mean, “Sex is dirty.”
God created sexuality.
God created the human body.
God created covenant marriage.
God created the mysterious union Scripture describes when husband and wife become “one flesh.”
The enemy does not need to invent sexuality in order to corrupt it.
He only needs to separate God's gift from God's design.
Take desire away from covenant.
Take pleasure away from responsibility.
Take bodies away from personhood.
Take intimacy away from faithfulness.
Take sexuality away from holiness.
Then offer the fragments back to us and call them freedom.
And an entire generation can become sexually stimulated while relationally starving.
Maybe that sentence explains more of your story than you want to admit.
Because perhaps pornography was never only about pornography.
Perhaps the fantasy was never only about sex.
Perhaps the inappropriate messages weren't only about attraction.
Perhaps that person you keep imagining wasn't merely somebody you desired.
Maybe underneath the sexual hunger there was another hunger you couldn't name.
You wanted to be chosen.
You wanted to feel desirable.
You wanted someone to stay.
You wanted comfort.
You wanted tenderness.
You wanted escape.
You wanted reassurance that you still mattered.
You wanted relief from stress.
You wanted somewhere to run when life hurt.
You wanted intimacy.
And lust offered you an imitation.
That does not excuse sin.
It helps expose the lie beneath it.
Because repentance becomes deeper when you stop merely asking, “How do I stop doing this?” and begin bringing another question before Jesus:
“Lord... what am I asking this sin to give me that I should be seeking in You and receiving according to Your design?”
That question can hurt.
Because sometimes the answer is loneliness.
Sometimes rejection.
Sometimes boredom.
Sometimes resentment toward your spouse.
Sometimes wounds from your childhood.
Sometimes insecurity.
Sometimes entitlement.
Sometimes curiosity that became habit, habit that became bondage, and bondage that eventually became something you thought you could never confess.
Sometimes you don't even know anymore.
You just know that when the ache arrives, your hand reaches for the same escape.
And afterward comes that familiar silence.
You delete the history.
Close the tab.
Erase the messages.
Promise yourself this was the last time.
Maybe whisper a prayer.
Then wake up tomorrow still carrying the thing nobody knows about.
If that is you, hear this carefully:
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross merely to make your secret behavior slightly more respectable.
He came to redeem you.
All of you.
Your body.
Your imagination.
Your desires.
Your wounds.
Your sexuality.
Your relationships.
Your future.
Even the rooms inside your heart you have been terrified to let Him enter.
The Gospel does not say sexual sin is harmless.
But neither does the Gospel say sexual sinners are hopeless.
Look at the people Jesus came to save.
Look at the scandal surrounding His ministry.
Broken people.
Sexually sinful people.
Religious hypocrites.
Adulterers.
The ashamed.
The exploited.
The self-righteous.
The morally shattered.
People whose reputations could not save them.
People whose secrets could have destroyed them.
And into the middle of humanity's disgrace walked the spotless Son of God.
Jesus did not become contaminated by touching sinners.
Sinners became clean by coming to Jesus.
That is grace.
Not pretending sin doesn't matter.
Grace matters precisely because sin does.
Grace does not rename darkness.
Grace brings you out of it.
The cross tells you simultaneously that your sin was more serious than you wanted to believe and that God's mercy is greater than you dared to hope.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And forgiveness is not offered because you finally became worthy enough to deserve another chance.
Forgiveness is offered through the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
That means repentance is not you crawling toward a Savior who wishes you would disappear.
Repentance is turning away from the thing killing you and returning to the One who gives life.
Maybe you have failed sexually more times than you can count.
Come back.
Maybe pornography has been part of your life for years.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe you're married and your imagination has wandered into places your spouse knows nothing about.
Repent.
Maybe you're single and tired of hearing people talk about purity as though loneliness isn't real.
Bring the loneliness to Christ too.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you swore you never would.
Come back.
Maybe somebody used you, and now sexuality is tangled together with wounds you never chose.

Please understand the difference between what was done to you and the sins you yourself choose. Do not carry guilt for another person's evil. Bring the wound to Christ and seek wise, trustworthy help.
Maybe you are reading this immediately after falling again.
Then don't spend tonight negotiating with shame.
Confess.
Repent.
Get honest.
Remove access where necessary.
Stop protecting the secret that keeps destroying you.
Tell a mature, trustworthy believer who will care about your soul more than your reputation.
And come to Jesus.
Because there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, “Come out of hiding.”
Condemnation whispers, “Stay there. God doesn't want someone like you.”
The Gospel answers:
He already knew what kind of sinner He was dying for.
You did not surprise the cross.
But grace is not permission to keep making peace with what nailed Christ there.
Grace teaches us to belong to Him.
And perhaps this is where the loneliness begins to heal.
Because lust says:
Take.
Jesus says:
“Follow Me.”
Lust says:
Use.
Jesus teaches us to love.
Lust says:
Hide.
Jesus calls us into the light.
Lust says:
Consume another person.
Jesus demonstrates love by giving Himself.
The pattern of Christ is the exact opposite of lust.
At the cross, Jesus did not ask, “What can these people give Me?”
He gave Himself for sinners.
That is why Christian love can never be reduced to strong feelings.
Love has the shape of a cross.
Self-giving.
Faithful.
Truthful.
Holy.
Sacrificial.
Patient.
And when Christ begins transforming a person's sexuality, He is doing something much bigger than helping that person stop looking at forbidden images.
He is retraining the heart to love.
To see people instead of bodies.
To see image-bearers instead of opportunities.
To recognize that the attractive stranger on your screen is not content.
That woman has a soul.
That man has a soul.
That person you keep fantasizing about belongs to God's creation and is not yours to mentally consume.
Suddenly purity becomes something far more beautiful than rule keeping.
Purity becomes learning to see human beings the way lust refuses to see them.
With dignity.
With honor.
With eternity in view.
And yes, sometimes obedience hurts.
Sometimes you'll put the phone down while every appetite inside you screams to pick it back up.
Sometimes you'll have to delete something.
End something.
Block something.
Confess something.
Walk away from something.
Sometimes you'll sit alone in a room and discover that you don't know what to do with the loneliness now that you aren't anesthetizing it.
Stay there with Jesus.
Don't run back simply because healing feels unfamiliar.
The ache you finally feel may have been underneath the addiction for years.
Bring it to Him.
Pray when you don't feel spiritual.
Open Scripture when your imagination is screaming louder than your faith.
Call somebody before the temptation becomes a decision.
Flee what Scripture tells you to flee.
And when you fall, do not turn one failure into an excuse for a week of surrender.
Run back to Christ.
Again.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because Jesus does.
Sanctification is not pretending temptation disappeared.
It is increasingly learning that temptation is no longer your master.
Your impulses are not your lord.
Your hormones are not your lord.
Your loneliness is not your lord.
Your browser history is not your lord.
Your past is not your lord.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And perhaps tonight, for the first time, you understand why lust never actually satisfied you.
You were asking consumption to give you communion.
You were asking fantasy to give you covenant.
You were asking stimulation to give you love.
You were asking another human body to carry a weight it was never created to carry.
And after every encounter, every fantasy, every image, every secret conversation, every imaginary relationship...
your soul remained hungry.
Because lust can imitate closeness without giving you the vulnerability of being known.
It can imitate affection without faithfulness.
It can imitate passion without covenant.
It can imitate intimacy without love.
It can give your body a sensation while leaving your heart untouched.
Counterfeit intimacy always charges more than the advertised price.
Eventually it asks for your peace.
Your attention.
Your integrity.
Your ability to see others clearly.
Sometimes your marriage.
Sometimes your testimony.
Sometimes years of your life.
And still it whispers:
One more time.
No.
You were created for something better.
Not merely less sexual desire.
Redeemed desire.
Not merely behavioral management.
Holiness.
Not merely shame avoidance.
Honor.
Not merely isolation from temptation.
Communion with Christ and healthy fellowship with His people.
Not merely trying harder.
Transformation.
This is why the Gospel Warrior message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not because your scandal was imaginary.
Because grace can write a future your sin never could.
Maybe your story has chapters you would burn if anyone could read them.
Jesus already knows every word.
And He is still calling sinners to repent, believe, follow Him, and walk in the light.
Do something with the conviction.
Your honesty may become the permission somebody else needed to stop pretending.
And there is something deeper behind this work than another social-media page.
If you believe this kind of biblical discipleship should keep reaching people, don't only read it. Help carry it.
Not because Gospel Warrior deserves glory.
Jesus does.

And if supporting this ministry enables more people to encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ, then let your support become part of sending the message farther than you could carry it alone.
But before you leave, remember this when temptation comes back.
Because it probably will.
Lust will tell you that you are lonely.
It will tell you that nobody sees.
It will tell you that one image, one fantasy, one message, one secret encounter will finally quiet the ache.
Remember what happened last time.
Then remember the cross.
You do not need another counterfeit version of intimacy.
You need the One who already knows the ugliest truth about you and still calls you out of darkness—not so you can remain what you were, but so He can teach you what love was supposed to be.
Jesus is not asking you to trade pleasure for emptiness.
He is calling you to trade counterfeit intimacy for holiness, honor, truth, covenant faithfulness, genuine human love, and ultimately communion with Him.
So come out of hiding.
Repent where you have sinned.
Receive the mercy Christ purchased.
Bring the wound underneath the craving into His light.
Learn to see people as souls again.
And when lust whispers, “Take what you need so you won't feel alone,” remember the Savior whose scarred hands answer:
You were never created to consume your way into being loved.
The screen can know what you desire. Only love allows you to be truly known—and Christ already knows you completely and is still calling you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HE WILL MAKE YOUR PATHS STRAIGHT” — BUT GOD NEVER SAID THE ROAD WOULDN’T HURT
paragraphs: “HE WILL MAKE YOUR PATHS STRAIGHT” — BUT GOD NEVER SAID THE ROAD WOULDN’T HURT
Proverbs 3:6 is not God promising you a painless journey. It is God promising something infinitely better: when you surrender the road to Him, you will never have to walk it without His direction.
There is a version of Proverbs 3:6 that many of us desperately want to believe.
Give your life to God...
and everything will finally start making sense.
Pray enough, obey enough, trust enough...
and the doors will open.
The relationship will survive.
The diagnosis will change.
The money will come.
The child will return.
The depression will lift.
The betrayal will somehow be undone.
The prayer you have whispered until you have almost run out of tears will finally receive the answer you wanted.
Because Scripture says:
“In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.”
Proverbs 3:6.
So somewhere along the way, we quietly translated “direct thy paths” into something the verse never actually says:
God will make your life easy.
And then life happened.
The person you prayed for died anyway.
The marriage you begged God to restore still collapsed.
The door you were certain God would open slammed shut.
The ministry struggled.
The business failed.
Your family misunderstood you.
You obeyed...
and still lost something.
You prayed...
and heaven seemed silent.
You trusted...
and the road became harder.
And perhaps somewhere inside you, a frightening question began forming.
God... I thought You said You would make my path straight.
Maybe that question is why you are reading this right now.
Because there is something hidden inside Proverbs 3:6 that changes everything.
Not because somebody discovered a secret code in the Bible.
Not because the verse promises that your suffering is about to disappear.
But because when we return to what the Hebrew actually says, we discover that God made a promise far deeper than the one many of us accidentally invented.
The Hebrew reads:
בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ
Bəkhol-derakhekha da'ehu, wəhu yəyashsher orkhotekha.
“In all your ways know Him, and He will make straight your paths.”
Look carefully at the center of that sentence.
דָעֵהוּ
Da'ehu.
It comes from the Hebrew verb yada — “to know.”
Not merely...
“Remember God exists.”
Not...
“Mention God occasionally.”
Not...
“Put a Bible verse in your bio.”
The command carries the idea of knowing, recognizing, acknowledging Him.
“In all your ways...
know Him.”
Your career.
Know Him there.
Your marriage.
Know Him there.
Your money.
Know Him there.
Your sexuality.
Know Him there.
Your secret thoughts.
Know Him there.
Your ambitions.
Know Him there.
Your disappointment.
Know Him there.
Your unanswered questions.
Know Him there.
Your suffering.
Know Him even there.
Then comes the promise:
יְיַשֵּׁר
Yəyashsher.
From yashar — to make straight, right, level, or directed.
And suddenly the verse becomes far more demanding—and far more beautiful—than the motivational slogan we sometimes make it.
God is not promising that every road will be comfortable.
He is promising to straighten the path of the person who refuses to walk independently of Him.
There is a difference.
A massive difference.
A straight path can still climb a mountain.
A straight path can still pass through a valley.
A straight path can still run through territory you never wanted to enter.
Straight does not mean painless.
Straight does not mean prosperous by the world's definition.
Straight does not mean predictable.
Straight does not mean there will never be tears running down your face while you whisper...
“Jesus, I don't understand this.”
Sometimes the straightest road God can lead you down passes directly through the place you would have avoided.
Ask Joseph.
God gave him dreams...
and then Joseph found himself inside a pit.
Then slavery.
Then false accusation.
Then prison.
If Joseph had interpreted God's faithfulness as an easy road, he could have concluded that God had abandoned him.
But God was still writing.
The pit wasn't the final paragraph.
The prison wasn't the ending.
The betrayal wasn't the conclusion.
God was moving Joseph through suffering toward something Joseph could not yet see.
Ask Moses.
Obedience did not lead him directly from the burning bush into a comfortable retirement.
It led him straight toward Pharaoh.
Ask David.
Anointing did not immediately produce a throne.
For a season it produced caves.
Ask Paul.
Following Jesus did not protect him from beatings, imprisonment, rejection, danger, hunger, and suffering.
And then...
look at Jesus.
If anyone perfectly acknowledged the Father in all His ways, it was Christ.
Yet the Father's will led Him toward Gethsemane.
Toward betrayal.
Toward nails.
Toward a cross.
That alone destroys the idea that walking in God's will guarantees an easy life.
Jesus was perfectly inside the Father's will...
and still suffered.
In Gethsemane, Christ prayed:
“Not my will, but thine, be done.”
That is what Proverbs 3:5–6 ultimately confronts inside us.
Not merely our confusion.
Our control.
Because the verse immediately before Proverbs 3:6 says:
“Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.”
There it is.
The battle underneath the battle.
We want God to direct our paths...
as long as He chooses the path we already selected.
We want guidance without surrender.
Lord, direct my career...
but please don't close that door.
Lord, direct my relationship...
but please don't tell me this person isn't right for me.
Lord, use my life...
but please don't make me uncomfortable.
Lord, transform me...
but don't touch the habit I secretly love.
Lord, lead me...
but let me hold the map.
And perhaps that is exactly where some of us are exhausted.
We have been asking God to bless directions He never gave us.
We keep begging Him to straighten a road He may be trying to rescue us from.
Some doors aren't opening because you need another motivational sermon.
Some doors may remain closed because God sees what you cannot.
Sometimes His direction feels like disappointment before it looks like mercy.
Sometimes the answer is no.
Sometimes it is wait.
Sometimes it is leave.
Sometimes it is stay.
Sometimes it is forgive.
Sometimes it is repent.
Sometimes it is...
“Trust Me even though I am not explaining everything yet.”
And that last one hurts.
Because faith becomes painfully real when explanations disappear.
Anyone can say “God is good” when the bank account is full, the family is healthy, the prayers are being answered, and tomorrow looks promising.
But there is another kind of worship.
The worship whispered from a hospital hallway.
The worship offered beside an empty chair.
The worship spoken through trembling lips after betrayal.
The worship that says...
“I don't understand You right now, God...
but I still trust You.”
That kind of faith doesn't pretend suffering isn't painful.
Christianity never asks us to pretend.
Jesus Himself wept.
Jesus experienced anguish.
Jesus knew rejection.
Jesus knew betrayal.
Jesus knew what it meant to suffer.
The Gospel is not the announcement that Christians will avoid suffering.
The Gospel is the announcement that God entered our suffering.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we could never live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The darkest road in human history became the road through which redemption came.
Think about that.
On Friday, the disciples could see only catastrophe.
Their Messiah was dead.
Their hope appeared buried.
Their future looked destroyed.
If they had judged God's faithfulness only by what they could see that evening, everything would have looked hopeless.
But Sunday was already inside God's story.
The tomb they thought represented God's absence became evidence of Christ's victory.
And maybe somebody reading this is living somewhere between Friday and Sunday.
You are looking at something that feels finished.
A dream.
A relationship.
A season.
Your reputation.
Your confidence.
Maybe even your faith.
And you cannot see resurrection from where you are standing.
Please hear this carefully:
Proverbs 3:6 does not give us permission to promise that every earthly tragedy will reverse itself.
Some losses remain losses in this life.
Some wounds leave scars.
Some prayers receive answers different from what we desperately wanted.
The Christian hope is bigger than “everything will work out exactly the way I want.”
Our hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
And because Christ rose from the dead, suffering does not receive the final word.
Sin does not receive the final word.
Shame does not receive the final word.
Death does not receive the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe your path feels crooked tonight.
Maybe you have been staring at your life thinking...
How did I end up here?
Maybe nobody knows how tired you actually are.
You still attend church.
Still smile.
Still say “God is good.”
Still share encouraging verses.
But privately?
You have questions you are almost afraid to say aloud.
Why did God allow this?
Why hasn't He answered?
Why did that person walk away?
Why did obedience cost so much?
Why am I still struggling with something I thought I would have defeated years ago?
There is no shame in bringing those questions to Christ.
Bring them.
But bring yourself with them.
Not merely the polished version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version everybody else thinks you are.
You.
The angry you.
The confused you.
The ashamed you.
The exhausted you.
The you who made terrible decisions.
The you carrying consequences.
The you who wandered farther than you ever intended.
The you who wonders whether Jesus could possibly want you after everything you have done.
Because this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to give decent people better directions.
He came to save sinners.
Maybe your crooked path wasn't something that simply happened to you.
Maybe some of it was your own doing.
Your choices.
Your pride.
Your addiction.
Your affair.
Your dishonesty.
Your anger.
Your compromise.
Your secret sin.
And now you are standing inside consequences you helped create.
Grace does not require you to rewrite history before coming home.
Grace tells the truth about your sin...
and then points you toward a Savior whose blood is greater than it.
Repentance isn't pretending the road wasn't crooked.
Repentance is turning around because you finally realize Christ is better than the road you chose.
You may not be able to undo yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem what yesterday did to you.
Peter could not unsay:
“I do not know the man.”
Three times.
But Jesus wasn't finished with Peter.
The cross looked like scandal.
Peter's denial looked like scandal.
Human failure looked like the end of the story.
Then grace walked out of a tomb.
And the risen Christ restored a broken disciple.
That is why we keep saying it:
From Scandal to Grace...
because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin acceptable.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking sinners who deserve judgment, washing them through His grace, calling them to repentance, and making something new out of lives surrendered to Him.
Maybe the miracle you need tonight isn't an easier road.
Maybe it is finally surrendering the map.
Maybe your prayer needs to change from...
“Jesus, make my plan work”
to...
“Jesus, make me Yours.”
From...
“Lord, remove every difficult road”
to...
“Lord, don't let any road take me away from You.”
From...
“Explain everything”
to...
“Teach me to trust You when I cannot see.”
That is a dangerous prayer.
Because surrender means Jesus becomes Lord rather than consultant.
He gets your yes before you know where obedience leads.
But there is freedom there.
You no longer have to know everything.
You only need to know the One leading you.
So if your road is painful right now, do not automatically conclude that God has abandoned you.
Difficulty is not proof that you missed God.
Ease is not proof that you found Him.
The question is deeper:
Are you acknowledging Him in this road?
Are you knowing Him here?
Are you trusting Christ here?
Are you obeying what Scripture has already made clear?
Are you willing to repent where He exposes sin?
Are you willing to wait where He has not yet opened the door?
Are you willing to follow even when the road doesn't resemble the life you imagined?
Maybe you needed Proverbs 3:6 tonight...
not because God is about to make everything easy...
but because you were about to mistake difficulty for abandonment.
Don't.
The Shepherd has not ceased being the Shepherd because the path entered a valley.
Psalm 23 never says there will be no valley.
It says He is with you inside it.
And perhaps those four words are more precious than an easy life could ever be.
Thou art with me.
Somebody reading beneath this article may be standing where you once stood. Your story may remind them that darkness is not necessarily the final chapter.
Not because every sentence will feel necessary today.

There may be somebody scrolling quietly tonight who looks perfectly fine in photographs and is privately wondering whether God abandoned them. One share can put truth in front of someone you may never know needed it.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters to us:
It does not purchase favor from Jesus.
It does not replace repentance, faith, obedience, generosity to those in need, or faithful participation in your local church.
Scripture teaches something more beautiful than religious pressure.
Paul writes that giving should come from what a person has purposed in the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That means genuine Christian generosity is not supposed to be manipulated out of you.
It should flow from grace.
But the merchandise is not the mission.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
Souls matter.
Truth matters.
Discipleship matters.
Pray.
Share.
Never underestimate what God can do with something as ordinary as one faithful share.
And tonight, before you leave this article, return once more to those ancient Hebrew words:
בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ
In all your ways, know Him...
That is where the promise begins.
Not with understanding everything.
Not with controlling everything.
Not with avoiding every valley.
With knowing Him.
So perhaps you still cannot see where this road ends.
Perhaps tomorrow remains uncertain.
Perhaps the prayer is still unanswered.
Perhaps tears are still falling.
But if Christ has you...
