Look normal.
Produce the testimony everybody understands.
And for many people, marriage and family are extraordinary gifts from God.
Scripture honors them.
Jesus Himself reaches back to creation in this very chapter:
“Male and female He created them.”
He speaks of a man leaving father and mother and being joined to his wife, and He treats that covenant with tremendous seriousness.
So this passage is not Jesus dismantling marriage.
It is Jesus refusing to make marriage the definition of a complete human life.
That distinction is enormous.
Because standing in front of the disciples was the most complete human being who ever lived.
And Jesus never married.
Think about that.
Christianity worships a celibate Savior.
The Son of God never needed sexual experience to become fully human.
He never needed marriage to establish His worth.
He never needed biological children to leave an eternal legacy.
His identity was rooted in the Father.
His mission was the Kingdom.
His love was not smaller because it was not expressed through marriage.
His life was not incomplete because it did not follow the expected domestic script.
Jesus Christ was—and remains—perfectly whole.
That should destroy one of the cruelest lies many people quietly carry:
“If my life doesn't look like everyone else's, something must be fundamentally wrong with me.”
Maybe you have felt it.
Maybe you sit in church while another wedding is announced and everybody celebrates, while something inside you aches.
Maybe your body carries circumstances nobody around you understands.
Maybe marriage never happened.
Maybe children never came.
Maybe your sexual desires have become an arena of painful conflict between what you feel and what you believe obedience to Christ requires.
Maybe you have questions you are terrified to say aloud because you already know how quickly Christians can reach for labels.
Maybe your story is so complicated that you stopped telling it.
You learned Christian vocabulary.
You learned when to smile.
You learned which questions were safe.
You learned how to say, “I'm doing fine.”
But God knows what happens after everybody goes home.
He knows the questions.
He knows the loneliness.
He knows the desires.
He knows the shame.
He knows the history.
He knows the body you inhabit.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows what you chose.
He knows what you regret.
And He knows the difference.
You do not have to lie to Jesus.
That is one of the most beautiful things about Him.
People may demand a polished testimony.
Jesus asks for truth.
People may be frightened by complexity.
Jesus walked directly into it.
People may reduce you to one part of your story.
Jesus sees the soul.
But there is another mistake we must avoid.
Compassion does not mean pretending Jesus never calls anyone to repentance.
He does.
Every one of us.
The Gospel is not, “Come to Jesus and He will affirm everything you already believe about yourself.”
The Gospel is infinitely better.
It is:
Come to Jesus and die.
Then discover what it means to truly live.
Jesus said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
That invitation does not single out one category of sinner.
It reaches the sexually immoral and the self-righteous.
The adulterer and the gossip.
The person consumed by lust and the person consumed by greed.
The person whose private browser history would humiliate them and the religious person secretly delighted to condemn them.
Nobody walks into the Kingdom carrying a certificate that says:
“No repentance required.”
Not you.
Not me.
Nobody.
The scandal of Christianity is not that certain people are sinners.
The scandal is that all of us are.
And the greater scandal is what God did about it.
The Gospel does not begin with our ability to repair ourselves.
It begins with a cross.
There hangs Jesus.
Rejected.
Humiliated.
Wounded.
Bloodied.
Mocked.
Stripped before the world.
The innocent One bearing the judgment of the guilty.
Why?
Because sin is more serious than modern culture wants to admit.
And grace is more astonishing than religious people sometimes allow themselves to believe.
At Calvary, Jesus does not tell sinners to clean themselves up enough to become lovable.
He gives Himself for sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after the pornography stopped.
Not after the affair was confessed.
Not after the bitterness disappeared.
Not after the secret relationship ended.
Not after the identity questions were resolved.
Not after the religious hypocrisy was exposed.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
But grace does not leave us where it found us.
The same Jesus who forgives says:
“Follow Me.”
And following Jesus eventually puts every identity, every desire, every relationship, every ambition, every wound, every appetite, every dream, and every future at His feet.
Christianity is not ultimately about discovering the perfect label for yourself.
It is about belonging to Christ.
Paul says something breathtaking in Galatians 2:20:
“Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι.”
“I have been crucified with Christ.”
Then:
“ζῇ δὲ ἐν ἐμοὶ Χριστός.”
“Christ lives in me.”
That is Christian identity at its deepest level.
Not “I finally explained myself.”
But:
“I belong to Jesus.”
And perhaps that is why Matthew 19 becomes even more beautiful when we remember another eunuch later in the New Testament.
Acts 8 takes us onto a desert road.
There is an Ethiopian official.
A eunuch.
A powerful man entrusted with the treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.
He is returning from Jerusalem.
And he is reading Isaiah.
Think about the scene.
A man whose embodied and social existence placed him outside the ordinary reproductive future is sitting in a chariot reading about a suffering Servant.
Philip approaches him.
The eunuch asks the question that changes everything:
“About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this?”
And Acts tells us:
“Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.”
Jesus.
Not a political ideology.
Not a modern identity manifesto.
Not a religious purity performance.
Jesus.
And while traveling down the road, they encounter water.
The eunuch asks:
“What prevents me from being baptized?”
That question almost hurts when you understand it.
What prevents me?
My body?
My past?
My status?
My difference?
My inability to fit the expected future?
What prevents me?
The story answers with water.
He is baptized.
And then Scripture says he “went on his way rejoicing.”
That is Gospel.
A person who might have been defined by what had happened to his body becomes defined by his relationship to Jesus Christ.
A person whose future did not look ordinary discovers that God's Kingdom is larger than ordinary human expectations.
And there is an even deeper biblical echo behind his story.
Isaiah had spoken directly to eunuchs centuries earlier.
Isaiah 56 records God's promise to those who keep His covenant:
“I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters.”
A name better than sons and daughters.
For someone unable to produce the descendants ancient societies considered essential to legacy, those words must have sounded almost impossible.
God was saying:
Your story does not end where human expectation ends.
You can belong to Me.
You can have a name in My house.
Your life can carry eternal significance even when it cannot produce the future society expected from you.
And then, generations later, an Ethiopian eunuch sits on a road reading Isaiah.
Philip tells him about Jesus.
Water appears.
He is baptized.
He goes home rejoicing.
Tell me Scripture is not beautiful.
The Bible's answer to human difference is not that every difference automatically becomes holy.
Neither is its answer that everyone who differs from the social norm should be treated as spiritually disposable.
The answer is Jesus.
Jesus receives sinners.
Jesus tells the truth.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus commands repentance.
Jesus restores dignity.
Jesus creates a new people.
Jesus gives people a name no human circumstance can finally erase.
Jesus does not save us because our desires are perfect.
He saves us because His mercy is.
And He does not merely forgive us so we can return unchanged to whatever enslaved us.
He gives us His Spirit.
He teaches us obedience.
He sanctifies us.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes through battles nobody else sees.
Sometimes through prayers that sound less like victory speeches and more like:
“Jesus, please help me make it through tonight.”
Maybe that is you.
You love Christ.
But there is something you are still fighting.
Something about your desires, body, loneliness, sexuality, marriage, singleness, history, or future that does not fit into an easy church testimony.
Listen carefully.
Do not run from Jesus because Christians have sometimes failed to represent Him well.
And do not remake Jesus simply because obedience hurts.
Come to the real Christ.
The Christ who is full of grace and truth.
Bring Him everything.
Your body.
Your sexuality.
Your shame.
Your desires.
Your wounds.
Your questions.
Your loneliness.
Your failures.
Your secret habits.
Your future.
Your entire identity.
Put all of it before Him and say:
“Jesus, I would rather belong to You than belong to the version of myself I am afraid to surrender.”
That prayer may cost you something.
Following Jesus always does.
But the One asking for your life is the One who first gave His life for you.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
The scandal may be what happened to you.
The scandal may be what you did.
The scandal may be what you desire.
The scandal may be the secret you buried.
The scandal may even be the cruelty of religious people who convinced you that Jesus wanted nothing to do with you.
But none of those things gets the final sentence.
Jesus does.
At the cross, guilty people find forgiveness.
In the resurrection, dead things discover that death is not the end.
In Christ, the person everybody else reduced to a category receives a new name:
Beloved.
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Disciple.
Brother.
Sister.
Child of God.
Not because sin stopped mattering.
Because the blood of Jesus mattered more.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“Do I fit ordinary expectations?”
Perhaps the question is:
“Does my life belong to Jesus?”
Because one day nobody will stand before Christ and boast about how convincingly normal they appeared.
We will stand before the King.
And what will matter is whether we knew Him.
Whether we trusted Him.
Whether His grace became more precious than our excuses.
Whether repentance became more precious than hiding.
Whether Christ became more precious than the identity we constructed without Him.
If something in these words exposed a place you have been hiding, don't perform for anyone.
Just be honest.
Someone silently reading may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people in complicated places.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if this truth can help one frightened person stop running from Christ, sharing it becomes a simple way of using the platform God has placed in your hands to point somebody toward Him.
Salvation cannot be bought.
But generosity can be worship when it flows from love for Christ.
And there is more available to help you grow.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is convinced that the complicated truth about their body, desires, past, or future has made them unreachable.
They need to know something.
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter of your story you are afraid to let anybody read—and when you surrender the pen to Him, your worst chapter does not have to become your final one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ADAM AND EVE WERE NAKED TOGETHER AND FELT NO SHAME—WHAT CHANGED AFTER SIN?
paragraphs: ADAM AND EVE WERE NAKED TOGETHER AND FELT NO SHAME—WHAT CHANGED AFTER SIN?

They were naked before sin entered the world. They were still naked afterward. Yet suddenly they were hiding from each other, covering themselves, and running from God. The human body had not suddenly become evil. Something far deeper had happened.
There is a sentence in Genesis that sounds almost impossible to people living in the world we know now.
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” — Genesis 2:25
The Hebrew is striking:
וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ
Vayyihyu sheneihem ‘arummim, ha’adam ve’ishto, velo yitboshashu.
They were both naked—the man and his wife—and they were not ashamed.
Read those final words again.
וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ — velo yitboshashu.
And they were not ashamed.
No masks.
No carefully edited version of themselves.
No wondering whether the other person was comparing them with somebody else.
No fear that vulnerability would someday become ammunition.
No secret browser history.
No lust poisoning the way one human being looked at another.
No betrayal hiding behind a password.
No insecurity whispering, “You are not enough.”
No desperate need to impress.
No terror of being completely known.
Nothing to conceal.
Nothing to manipulate.
Nothing to prove.
They were naked, and there was no shame.
Then Genesis 3 happens.
And everything fractures.
The serpent speaks. Eve listens. Adam participates. God's command is violated. The forbidden fruit is eaten.
And then Scripture records one of the saddest awakenings in human history:
“Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves coverings.” — Genesis 3:7
The Hebrew says:
וַתִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם וַיֵּדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם הֵם
Vattippaqachnah ‘einei sheneihem, vayyede‘u ki ‘eirummim hem.
The eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked.
But wait.
They had already been naked.
Their bodies had not suddenly changed.
Adam did not look down after eating and discover something physically present that had not been there five minutes earlier.
Eve did not suddenly receive a human body.
What changed was not their nakedness.
What changed was the condition of the human heart.
That is where this story stops being merely about Adam and Eve.
Because somewhere between Genesis 2 and Genesis 3...
you will find yourself.
Maybe you are wearing clothes right now, but emotionally you have been sewing fig leaves together for years.
Maybe nobody knows what is underneath your smile.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
Your church thinks you are doing well.
Your friends see the pictures you post.
People see the Bible verses you share.
They hear you say, “God is good.”
But there is something you desperately hope nobody discovers.
A habit.
A wound.
A relationship.
An addiction.
A resentment.
A private compromise.
A secret failure.
A memory you cannot forgive yourself for.
A version of you that exists when nobody else is watching.
And somewhere deep inside, you have wondered:
If people really knew me, would they still love me?
That question is ancient.
It was born among the fig leaves.
Before sin, Adam and Eve could be fully seen without being ashamed.
After sin, exposure became terrifying.
And human beings have been hiding ever since.
We simply became better at making fig leaves.
Some people use success.
Some use religion.
Some use humor.
Some use money.
Some use beauty.
Some use anger.
Some use ministry.
Some use relationships.
Some use pornography.
Some use alcohol.
Some bury themselves in work.
Some constantly post happiness because silence might force them to admit they are miserable.
And some people know enough Christian language to hide behind Christianity itself.
We can even turn religious activity into camouflage.
Everyone sees what we are doing for God.
Nobody sees what is happening inside us.
But the Gospel begins to become breathtaking when you notice something in Genesis that is easy to miss.
After Adam sinned...
God came looking for him.
The man was hiding.
God was approaching.
The man was afraid.
God called.
The man had covered himself.
God still wanted him to come out.
Then comes the question:
“Where are you?” — Genesis 3:9
God was not asking because the Creator had misplaced Adam somewhere among the trees.
The omniscient God did not suddenly need directions.
The question confronted the hiding man.
Adam, where are you?
And perhaps those words have traveled farther than Eden.
Perhaps they have reached you.
Where are you?
Not where does everybody think you are.
Where are you?
Not what did you post this morning.
Where are you?
Not what position do you hold at church.
Not how many Bible verses can you quote.
Not whether everybody thinks you have your life together.
Where are you?
Because sin does something devastating.
It does not merely make us guilty.
It makes guilty people want to hide from the very God they desperately need.
Adam eventually answers:
“I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; and I hid myself.” — Genesis 3:10
There it is.
Fear.
Nakedness.
Hiding.
The vocabulary of fallen humanity.
And we still speak it fluently.
We hide because we fear exposure.
We fear exposure because we expect condemnation.
We construct coverings because somewhere inside us we know something has gone terribly wrong.
But fig leaves have one enormous problem.
They cannot remove guilt.
They can cover skin.
They cannot cleanse conscience.
Humanity has spent thousands of years trying to solve an internal problem with external coverings.
Look successful enough.
Become attractive enough.
Earn enough.
Achieve enough.
Be religious enough.
Distract yourself enough.
Convince everyone that you are okay.
But when the room gets quiet...
the leaves begin to fall.
And this is why the Gospel is not merely advice about becoming a nicer person.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve your fig leaves.
He came to deal with the sin underneath them.
This is where Eden begins pointing us toward something much greater.
Genesis 3:21 tells us:
“Also for Adam and his wife the LORD God made tunics of skin, and clothed them.”
Do not force more into that verse than Scripture explicitly says. Genesis does not directly call this the first sacrifice, nor does the verse explain every detail of how the skins were obtained.
But the theological movement of Scripture is unmistakable:
Human beings cannot finally rescue themselves from sin.
God must provide what sinners cannot provide for themselves.
And as the biblical story unfolds, sacrifice, atonement, covering, cleansing, forgiveness, and eventually the cross come increasingly into view.
Until one day...
outside Jerusalem...
another human body would be exposed in shame.
Jesus Christ would be mocked.
Stripped.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
The One who had no sin entered the place of sinners.
The New Testament says of Christ:
“He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
Do you see the reversal?
Adam sins...
and hides.
Christ bears our sin...
and is publicly exposed.
Adam reaches for leaves.
Christ stretches out His hands.
Adam blames.
Christ bears.
Adam's rebellion brings condemnation and death into humanity's story.
Christ comes bringing righteousness and life to those who belong to Him.
Paul develops this Adam-Christ contrast powerfully in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15.
“For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ all shall be made alive.” — 1 Corinthians 15:22
This is bigger than nakedness.
Bigger than sexuality.
Bigger than embarrassment about the human body.
Genesis 2:25 and Genesis 3:7 reveal something profound about what sin did to human existence.
Sin ruptured innocence.
Sin corrupted relationships.
Sin introduced alienation.
Sin brought guilt.
Sin produced fear.
Sin sent humanity running for cover.
And we have been running ever since.
But Jesus came for people who are tired of running.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe underneath all your questions about Adam and Eve, there is another question you have been afraid to ask:
What happens if God sees everything in me?
Everything?
The thought you never admitted.
The thing you watched.
The lie you told.
The person you betrayed.
The bitterness you nurtured.
The promises you broke.
The years you wasted.
The compromises nobody caught.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The faith you pretended was stronger than it really was.
What happens when Jesus sees that?
Here is what makes grace so shocking:
He already knows.
You are not confessing your sin to inform an uninformed God.
You are bringing into the light what He already sees.
And the Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
It says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty sinners could never provide for themselves.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
But Scripture continues with justification by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
The scandal is not that sinners need forgiveness.
The scandal is that forgiveness was purchased at such a cost.
Jesus.
The sinless One.
The Lamb of God.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
And now the invitation is not:
“Hide better.”
It is:
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop defending what Jesus died to forgive.
Stop decorating the chains He came to break.
Stop calling darkness something harmless simply because you have learned how to function inside it.
Bring your sin into the light.
Not because you can save yourself by confession.
Not because tears purchase forgiveness.
Not because religious effort cancels yesterday.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The apostle John writes:
Notice the word.
Cleanse.
Not merely conceal.
Not cosmetically improve.
Cleanse.
The Gospel offers something fig leaves never could.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new identity.
A cleansed conscience.
Peace with God through Jesus Christ.

This does not mean Christians never experience embarrassment, insecurity, temptation, painful memories, or struggles with shame. We still live in a fallen world, and sanctification is real growth rather than instant emotional perfection.
But shame no longer gets the final word over the person who belongs to Christ.
Your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
Your past does not sit on God's throne.
Your failure is not your savior.
Your reputation is not your righteousness.
Your ability to appear holy cannot justify you.
Jesus Christ does.
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one truth:
Not because Jesus edits history until sin becomes acceptable.
He does something infinitely better.
He redeems sinners.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The woman caught in adultery stood exposed before accusers, yet Jesus refused both self-righteous condemnation and permission to continue in sin.
Again and again Scripture shows us that grace does not say, “Your sin never mattered.”
Grace says:
Your sin does not have to own you anymore.
Maybe your fig leaves are falling right now.
Good.
Not because exposure is pleasant.
But because sometimes the collapse of our disguises becomes the place where we finally stop pretending we can save ourselves.
You do not need another mask.
You need Jesus.
You do not need a better hiding place.
You need Jesus.
You do not need enough religious performance to make God owe you mercy.
You need Jesus.
Talk to God.
Confess honestly.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek reconciliation where Scripture requires it and where doing so is wise and safe.
Ask mature believers for help when you need accountability.
And come again to the cross.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But perhaps those words can mark an honest moment when you stop pretending that everything is fine.
And if God has been healing places in you that once seemed beyond restoration, tell somebody what Christ has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Then think of one person who has mastered the art of appearing okay.
You know who came to mind.
Send this article to them.
Not accusingly.
Not saying, “This is about you.”
Just send it.
the Christian answer to shame is not better hiding. It is Christ.
But hear this carefully.
It does not buy salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
And it should not be confused with a biblical command that every Christian must financially support this particular ministry.
Christian generosity must never be manipulated.

Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Paul also describes believers financially partnering in Gospel ministry (Philippians 4:15–18), while Jesus teaches that giving must never become religious theater (Matthew 6:1–4).
Think of it as partnership in the mission, not payment for God's blessing.
And there is another way you can help without spending anything:
One share can travel farther than you imagine.
One person reads it.
That person sends it to someone hiding.
That person finally talks to God.
That person opens a Bible.
That person walks back into church.
That person asks for help.
That person hears the Gospel clearly.
We may never know on this side of eternity how far one faithful act of sharing traveled.
But merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The mission is not building a collection of consumers.
It is making disciples.
It is putting Scripture in front of people whose Bibles have gathered dust.
It is calling wandering hearts toward repentance.
It is reminding ashamed believers about grace.
It is confronting comfortable Christianity with the words of Christ.
It is telling a generation drowning in carefully manufactured identities that they do not need another filter.
They need a Savior.
Share intentionally.
Tag personally.
Because Genesis began this story with two people who were completely exposed and felt no shame.
Sin entered...
and humanity started hiding.
We learned to sew leaves.
We learned to blame.
We learned to pretend.
We learned to run.
And then Jesus entered our fallen story.
He did not come to teach sinners how to manufacture better coverings.
He came to save them.
So maybe the most important question is no longer:
Why did Adam and Eve suddenly realize they were naked?
Maybe the question is:
What are you still using to hide from God?
He already knows what is underneath the leaves.
The question is whether you will keep running...
or finally come to Christ.
Because the hands you are afraid will expose you are the hands that were pierced to save repentant sinners.
Eden taught us to fear being uncovered; Calvary shows us where guilty people can finally stop hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY PROPHESIED, CAST OUT DEMONS, AND DID MIRACLES—SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?
paragraphs: THEY PROPHESIED, CAST OUT DEMONS, AND DID MIRACLES—SO WHY DID JESUS SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU”?

The most terrifying words in Matthew 7 were not spoken to atheists who wanted nothing to do with Jesus. They were spoken about people who called Him “Lord,” performed extraordinary works in His name, and apparently expected heaven—only to discover that knowing about the power of Jesus is not the same thing as belonging to Jesus.
There is a sentence in the Bible that should make every person who calls himself a Christian go quiet.
Not because Jesus whispers it to someone who hated Him.
Not because He says it to someone who spent his entire life mocking Christianity.
Not because the people standing before Him had never heard His name.
Quite the opposite.
They knew His name.
They called Him Lord.
They spoke in His name.
They claimed supernatural works in His name.
And apparently, right up until the moment Jesus answered them, they believed their spiritual résumé meant something.
Then Christ said:
“I never knew you.”
Read that again.
Not, “I knew you once.”
Not, “I knew you until you made too many mistakes.”
Not, “You weren't impressive enough.”
“I never knew you.”
And suddenly Matthew 7:21–23 becomes more than a warning about “those fake Christians out there.”
It becomes a mirror.
Jesus says:
“Οὐ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι· Κύριε κύριε…”
Ou pas ho legōn moi, Kyrie kyrie…
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord’…”
The Greek Κύριε, κύριε — Kyrie, kyrie is emphatic. These people are addressing Jesus as Lord. Their mouths contain orthodox-sounding language. Their defense is not, “Jesus, we rejected You.”
Their defense is essentially:
Jesus, look at everything we did for You.
That is what makes the passage so disturbing.
Because the people Jesus describes are not spiritually indifferent.
They are spiritually impressive.
“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name?”
“Did we not cast out demons in Your name?”
“Did we not do many mighty works in Your name?”
Imagine hearing those words without knowing what comes next.
You might expect Jesus to say:
“Well done.”
Instead, the Judge of humanity answers:
“καὶ τότε ὁμολογήσω αὐτοῖς ὅτι Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς…”
Kai tote homologēsō autois hoti oudepote egnōn hymas…
“And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you.’”
The word translated “never” is οὐδέποτε — oudepote.
Never.
At no time.
And the verb translated “knew” is ἔγνων — egnōn, from γινώσκω — ginōskō, “to know.”
Jesus' point is not that He lacked information about these people. The One presented in this very passage as the final Judge obviously isn't saying, “I don't recognize your face.”
This is relational language.
They could use His name while never truly belonging to Him.
They could speak about Him while remaining strangers to Him.
They could build a public identity around Jesus while their hearts remained unsubmitted to Jesus.
And perhaps that is the question this passage forces into places we would rather keep locked:
What if people know you as a Christian, but Christ does not know you as His?
You can know worship songs.
You can know Christian vocabulary.
You can repost sermons.
You can argue theology.
You can own six Bibles.
You can serve at church.
You can cry during worship.
You can say “God told me.”
You can have thousands of followers listening to you talk about Jesus.
You can preach.
You can lead.
You can build ministries.
You can become known for Christianity…
…and still need Christ.
That is not meant to drive the genuine believer into endless neurotic terror, forever wondering whether one more failure has erased the grace of God.
It is meant to destroy something far more dangerous:
false assurance.
Because Jesus does not tell us to place our confidence in religious performance.
In fact, look carefully at the defense of these people.
“Did we not prophesy?”
“Did we not cast out demons?”
“Did we not perform many mighty works?”
Their final argument is a list of accomplishments.
But no sinner will enter the Kingdom because his résumé impressed the King.
The Gospel has never been:
“Look what I did for Jesus.”
The Gospel begins with:
Look what Jesus did for sinners.

The Son of God came for people who could never rescue themselves. He lived without sin. He gave Himself for sinners. He bore sin at the cross. He died and rose again. Forgiveness is not wages paid to impressive religious people; it is grace received through faith in Christ.
So Matthew 7 cannot mean, “Perform enough good works and Jesus will finally accept you.”
That would contradict the Gospel.
Jesus is exposing something else.
He says in Matthew 7:21 that the person who enters the Kingdom is the one who does “τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου” — to thelēma tou patros mou — “the will of My Father.”
Then in verse 23 He describes those He rejects as:
“οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν”
hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian
“those practicing lawlessness.”
The word ἀνομία — anomia carries the sense of lawlessness, disregard for God's righteous rule.
Notice the contrast.
Jesus does not contrast “people who perform miracles” with “people who perform even bigger miracles.”
He contrasts outward claims with obedience.
Profession with reality.
Spectacle with fruit.
A mouth saying “Lord” with a life refusing His lordship.
And that makes even more sense when you refuse to rip verses 21–23 away from their context.
Just before these words, Jesus warns about false prophets who come appearing harmless but are inwardly ravenous.
Then He says:
“You will recognize them by their fruits.”
Fruit.
Not fame.
Fruit.
Not followers.
Fruit.
Not supernatural stories.
Fruit.
Not platform size.
Fruit.
Not how loudly someone says “Jesus.”
Fruit.
Jesus' warning is devastating precisely because spectacular gifts are not the same thing as godly character.
A person may attract attention without displaying holiness.
A person may know how to move a crowd without knowing how to kneel privately before God.
A person may preach repentance publicly while protecting secret sin privately.
A person may become skilled at looking anointed while becoming comfortable with what crucified Christ.
And this is where the article must stop being about somebody else.
Because it is easy to read Matthew 7 and immediately think of the preacher you distrust.
The celebrity pastor who fell.
The hypocrite who hurt you.
The religious relative who lives differently on Monday.
The person online whose Christianity seems fake.
But Jesus did not give us this passage so we could comfortably use it as binoculars.
Sometimes Scripture is a mirror.
So forget everybody else for a moment.
What happens when nobody is watching you?
What are you protecting that you would be ashamed to bring into the light?
What sin have you renamed so you don't have to repent of it?
What bitterness have you baptized as “discernment”?
What lust have you excused as weakness while refusing to fight it?
What dishonesty have you called survival?
What pride have you disguised as confidence?
What unforgiveness have you defended because the person really did hurt you?
What secret life exists underneath your public Christianity?
And before shame convinces you to run away from God, hear this carefully:
Jesus exposes darkness because He calls sinners into light.
Conviction is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come.
That is why the answer to Matthew 7 is not pretending harder.
It is not performing harder.
It is not panicking until you have accumulated enough spiritual accomplishments to feel safe again.
It is coming honestly to Jesus Christ.
Repenting.
Believing.
Surrendering.
Receiving mercy you could never earn.
Because the same Christ whose words terrify the hypocrite is the Christ who welcomes the repentant sinner.
That distinction matters.
Peter failed Jesus spectacularly.
Peter denied that he even knew Him.
Three times.
Yet Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
Why?
Because Christianity is not the story of flawless people maintaining flawless records.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a flawless Savior.
Judas could stand near Jesus and remain hardened.
Peter could collapse in failure and be restored.
The difference was not that Peter's sin was cute.
It wasn't.
The difference was that grace brought a broken sinner back to Christ.
That is what Jesus does.
He rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by lowering God's holiness until sin becomes harmless.
He rewrites the story by taking guilty people who deserve judgment and giving forgiveness to those who come to Him in repentant faith.
And Scripture gives us another chilling scene that prevents us from treating the name of Jesus like a religious formula.
In Acts 19, some itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of Jesus over evil spirits. The sons of Sceva were among those doing this.
They had heard the Name.
They tried to use the Name.
But they did not possess a magical formula.
The evil spirit answered:
“Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?”
The attempt ended disastrously.
And when Ephesus heard what happened, something remarkable followed.
The name of Jesus was not diminished.
It was magnified.
People came confessing their practices. Those involved in magic brought their books and publicly burned them.
In other words, genuine encounter with the authority of Christ produced something counterfeit spirituality does not want:
repentance.
The name of Jesus is not an incantation.
Christianity is not spiritual magic.
Jesus is not a tool for getting power, money, influence, healing, attention, success, followers, miracles, or a better life.
He is Lord.
And perhaps one of the greatest dangers in modern Christianity is wanting everything Jesus can give while resisting Jesus Himself.
We want peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Heaven without holiness.
Promises without obedience.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A Savior who rescues us from consequences but never confronts our idols.
But biblical grace does not merely pardon.
Grace transforms.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without battles.
Not without falls, tears, confession, discipline, and desperate prayers.
But genuinely.
A person rescued by Christ does not become sinless in this life, but he cannot make peace with sin as though Christ died merely to make rebellion comfortable.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and settling down with it.
One says:
“Jesus, I hate that I keep falling. Have mercy on me. Change me. Help me fight.”
The other says:
“I know what God says. I simply intend to keep doing what I want.”
One falls while facing toward Christ.
The other wants Christ's benefits while reserving the throne.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you know you have failed Him, don't misunderstand the warning.
Your tears do not disqualify you from grace.
Your past does not place you beyond the blood of Christ.
Your secret is not stronger than His mercy.
Your scandal is not bigger than His cross.
The question is not whether you have ever sinned.
We all have.
The question is what you will do when Christ brings your sin into the light.
Hide?
Excuse it?
Defend it?
Rename it?
Blame somebody else?
Or fall before Jesus and say:
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
There is mercy there.
Real mercy.
Not cheap mercy.
Blood-bought mercy.
The kind purchased at a Roman cross where the innocent Son of God suffered for guilty sinners.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride dies because you cannot save yourself.
Despair dies because Christ saves sinners.
You cannot boast:
“Look what I have done.”
But you also do not have to whisper:
“I have gone too far.”
At Calvary, the answer to both is Jesus.
Jesus.
Jesus.
That is why the most important question of your life is not:
“Do people think I'm Christian?”
Not:
“Have I had spiritual experiences?”
Not:
“Did I grow up in church?”
Not:
“Was I baptized?”
Not:
“Can I quote Scripture?”
Not even:
“Have I done ministry?”
The question beneath all of those questions is terrifyingly personal:
Do I belong to Jesus Christ?
You may forget this article.
You may forget the person who shared it.
You may forget half the sentences you just read.
But please do not forget:
“I never knew you.”
Those words are too serious to gamble eternity on appearances.
Examine yourself honestly.
Run to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Abandon what needs abandoning.
Forgive where you need to forgive.
Make restitution where repentance requires it.
Open the locked room.
Bring the secret into the light.
And trust Christ rather than your religious résumé.
If you are exhausted from fighting sin and afraid your repeated failures mean Jesus wants nothing more to do with you, remember: the answer is not to run from Him.
Run to Him.
The Savior who warned us in Matthew 7 is the Savior who went to the cross for sinners.
Maybe your prayer tonight doesn't need impressive words.
Maybe it is simply:

“Jesus, I don't want to perform Christianity anymore. Search me. Expose what is false in me. Forgive me. Save me. Change me. Teach me to obey You because I belong to You. I have nothing to boast about except Your mercy.”
And if that is where your heart is right now, don't make this another emotional moment that disappears tomorrow morning.
Stay near Scripture.
Stay near Christ.
Find a faithful Bible-teaching church.
Pray when nobody applauds.
Repent when nobody knows.
Obey when obedience costs something.
Love people who cannot increase your platform.
Serve when nobody records it.
Give when nobody praises it.
Forgive when your flesh wants revenge.
And when you fail, confess it instead of constructing another mask.
That quiet life may never look spectacular on social media.
But the Kingdom of God was never built around looking spectacular.
Somebody hiding in the same darkness you once knew may need to discover that Jesus still restores sinners.
Don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Not because clicking “share” proves you are saved. It doesn't.
But if this truth has helped you, sharing it is one simple way you can glorify God by putting His Word in front of someone who may desperately need to hear it.
Send it privately to someone if publicly tagging them would embarrass them.
Because one day, the applause stops.
The platforms disappear.
The titles mean nothing.
The crowds are gone.
There is no microphone.
No follower count.
No reputation to hide behind.
No ministry résumé to hand Jesus.
Only you…
and the King.
And on that day, the greatest miracle will not be that your name was known by thousands of people.
It will be that the sinner who had every reason to hide finally ran to Jesus—and discovered that grace had been calling them home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM MARRIED AGAIN AFTER SARAH DIED—AND HAD SIX MORE SONS
paragraphs: ABRAHAM MARRIED AGAIN AFTER SARAH DIED—AND HAD SIX MORE SONS

Sarah was gone. The woman who had walked beside Abraham through promises, failures, laughter, tears, barrenness, miracles, and nearly a lifetime of waiting was buried in a cave. You might expect Abraham’s story to quietly fade after that. Instead, Scripture records something many Christians barely remember: another woman entered his story, six more sons were born, and the old man whom God had once called out of Ur was still watching the promise of God unfold. But there is something even greater hiding beneath these names—and it points beyond Abraham, beyond Keturah, and beyond every human attempt to repair a broken story. It points to Jesus Christ.
There is a strange silence that enters a home after someone dies.
The chair is still there.
Their belongings remain.
Memories seem to live in ordinary objects.
And sometimes the hardest part of grief is discovering that morning keeps coming even when someone you loved no longer wakes up with you.
Abraham knew something about that silence.

Genesis 23 records the death of Sarah at 127 years old. Abraham mourned and wept for her. He then purchased the cave of Machpelah as a burial place and laid the woman who had shared his extraordinary pilgrimage to rest.
Sarah was not merely a passing character in Abraham’s biography.
She had left home with him.
She had wandered with him.
She had endured his failures.
She had carried the ache of barrenness.
She had heard an impossible promise.
She had laughed.
And eventually, when human possibility had nearly disappeared, she held Isaac in her arms.
Then she died.
But Abraham did not.
And this is where Scripture gives us one of those quiet passages that can be read in seconds and forgotten just as quickly.
Genesis 25 opens with these Hebrew words:
וַיֹּסֶף אַבְרָהָם וַיִּקַּח אִשָּׁה וּשְׁמָהּ קְטוּרָה
Vayyosef Avraham vayyiqqach ishah, ushemah Qeturah.
In straightforward English:
“And Abraham again took a wife, and her name was Keturah.”
That first Hebrew expression matters.
וַיֹּסֶף — vayyosef
It carries the sense of adding, continuing, or doing again.
Abraham’s life was not finished.
Grief had entered his story, but grief was not permitted to write the final sentence.
Then comes her name.
קְטוּרָה — Qeturah.
Keturah.

Genesis calls her Abraham’s אִשָּׁה — ishah, “woman” or “wife,” in Genesis 25:1. Yet Scripture gives us another important detail. In 1 Chronicles 1:32, Keturah is described as Abraham’s concubine. Genesis 25:6 also refers to Abraham’s concubines. So we should resist inventing details the Bible does not give us. Scripture clearly associates Keturah with Abraham and records the children she bore him, while using both wife and concubine terminology in the biblical record.
And what happened through Keturah is astonishing.
She bore Abraham six sons:
Zimran.
Jokshan.
Medan.
Midian.
Ishbak.
Shuah.
Six sons.
Think about that.
This is Abraham.
The man who once looked at his aging body and Sarah’s barrenness and wondered how the promise of descendants could possibly happen.
The man who had spent years waiting for one promised son.
The man whose wife laughed at the thought of giving birth in old age.
The man who had tried to solve God’s promise through Hagar and Ishmael.
The man who finally watched God do what human strength could never accomplish when Isaac was born.
Now, near the closing chapters of Abraham’s life, Scripture suddenly surrounds him with descendants.
There is something painfully beautiful about that.
Because some of you reading this believe the most meaningful chapter of your life has already happened.
You lost someone.
You lost a marriage.
You lost years.
You lost opportunities.
You buried a dream.
Maybe you buried a person.
Maybe nobody died physically, but something inside you did.
And somewhere along the way you quietly concluded:
“God probably doesn’t have much left for me.”
Abraham’s story whispers something different.
Loss is real.
Grief is real.
Death is real.
But God is still God after the funeral.
That does not mean every bereaved person will remarry.
It does not mean everyone will have children.
It does not mean Christians should turn Abraham’s experience into a formula promising another spouse, another family, another business, another house, or another earthly success.
The Bible promises none of that.
And we must never manipulate grieving people with promises God did not make.
The deeper truth is better.
Your circumstances can change without God changing.
A chapter can close without God surrendering authorship.
You can weep and still worship.
You can grieve and still obey.
You can carry scars into tomorrow without believing tomorrow belongs to your scars.
Abraham continued walking.
And God continued being faithful.
But there is another detail we cannot ignore.
Keturah’s sons were Abraham’s sons…
but they were not Isaac.
That distinction matters enormously.
Genesis tells us:
“Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.”
He also gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them eastward, away from Isaac.
Why?
Because the covenant line was not determined merely by biology.
God had already declared concerning Isaac:
“In Isaac shall thy seed be called.”
Isaac occupied a unique place in the covenant promise.
This is where the story becomes much bigger than a surprising piece of biblical family history.
Abraham had other sons.
Ishmael was his son.
Keturah bore him six more sons.
Yet God had specifically established His covenant promise through Isaac.
And generations later, the New Testament would force us to look even farther down that line.
Not merely toward Isaac.
Not merely toward Jacob.
Not merely toward Israel.
But toward Christ.
Paul writes in Galatians 3:16 that the promises were spoken to Abraham and his “seed,” and he ultimately identifies that promised Seed with Christ.
Suddenly Abraham’s story is no longer merely about an elderly patriarch having more children.
The camera pulls back.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Generations rising and falling.
Kings.
Failures.
Exile.
Return.
Silence.
Then…
Bethlehem.
A Child.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God entering the wreckage of human history.
And that is where Abraham’s story touches yours.
Because the greatest thing God eventually brought through Abraham’s covenant story was not Abraham’s comfort.
It was Christ.
That distinction can change the way you read your entire Bible.
We often approach God asking:
“What are You going to give me?”
God’s redemptive story keeps asking:
“Do you see My Son?”
We want another opportunity.
Another relationship.
Another breakthrough.
Another financial miracle.
Another open door.
Another chapter.
And God may graciously give many earthly blessings.
But every earthly blessing eventually ends.
Abraham eventually died.
Keturah eventually disappeared from the biblical narrative.
His sons became generations.
Generations became history.
And history kept moving.
But Jesus Christ remains.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally the promise that God will replace everything you lose with something bigger.
Christianity announces something infinitely greater:
God has given sinners His Son.
And sinners desperately need Him.
Abraham knew something about failure too.
We sometimes polish biblical heroes until they no longer resemble human beings.

But Abraham’s life contains fear, impatience, questionable decisions, family complications, and moments when he tried to navigate circumstances through human reasoning instead of resting confidently in God.
He lied about Sarah being his wife.
More than once.
He listened when Sarah proposed using Hagar to obtain the child they desperately wanted.
That decision produced anguish inside Abraham’s own household.
This was not a spotless man earning the favor of God through flawless behavior.
That is precisely why Genesis contains another sentence so central that the New Testament repeatedly returns to it:
“And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.”
Abraham needed grace.
So do you.
Maybe that is why this story is hitting somewhere uncomfortable.
You have been trying to make yourself presentable before God.
You cleaned up the language.
You learned Christian vocabulary.
You post verses.
You attend church.
You know when to say “Amen.”
People may even come to you for spiritual advice.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know where the bodies are buried.
Not literal bodies.
Secrets.
Compromises.
Bitterness.
Pornography.
Pride.
Jealousy.
Lust.
Unforgiveness.
Religious hypocrisy.
Private addictions.
The conversation you deleted.
The person you still hate.
The money nobody knows about.
The secret life hidden behind a worship playlist.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is pretending none of it exists.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you to become better at hiding.
It tells you to come into the light.
Jesus did not die so you could construct a more respectable mask.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with consequences.
People who cannot rewrite yesterday.
People who finally stop defending themselves long enough to say:
“God, have mercy on me.”
Repentance is not pretending sin was harmless.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Forgiveness is not Jesus shrugging at rebellion.
At Calvary we discover exactly how serious sin is.
The Son of God was crucified.
And at Calvary we simultaneously discover how astonishing divine mercy is.
The Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
This is the scandal.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The unclean can be washed.
The rebellious can be reconciled.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
Not because we successfully rewrote our past…
but because Jesus Christ entered our story.
Abraham could not undo every mistake he made.
Neither can you.
You cannot crawl backward through time.
You cannot unsay the sentence.
You cannot unclick the button.
You cannot unbetray the trust.
You cannot restore your virginity.
You cannot recover every wasted year.
You cannot erase every consequence.
You cannot resurrect the person you lost.
You cannot make yesterday happen differently.
But hear this carefully:
Your inability to rewrite yesterday does not mean Jesus is powerless over what your life becomes from here.
That is the heartbeat of grace.
Not denial.
Redemption.
Not pretending the wound never happened.
Healing.
Not calling darkness light.
Rescue from darkness.
Not polishing sinners.
Making them new.
This is why Jesus must remain at the center.
Abraham cannot save you.
Sarah cannot save you.
Isaac cannot save you.
Keturah cannot save you.
Your pastor cannot save you.
Religion cannot save you.
Christian merchandise cannot save you.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He died for sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the Gospel calls us not merely to admire Him but to repent and believe.
Maybe you have been reading this thinking about Abraham.
Now I want you to think about yourself.
If tonight were your final night…
what are you trusting?
Your morality?
Your church attendance?
Your baptism?
Your generosity?
Your theology?
Your family’s Christianity?
The fact that you are “not as bad as other people”?
None of those can bear the weight of your soul.
You need Christ.
And maybe the most courageous prayer you can pray tonight is not impressive at all.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change me. I surrender.”
Not magic words.
Not a religious transaction.
A heart turning toward the Savior.
Be honest.
And when you see someone else write those words, do not mock them.
Do not interrogate them.
Pray for them.
Because behind usernames are human beings.
Behind profile pictures are battles.
Behind smiling photographs can be people desperately trying not to collapse.
The Church should be one of the safest places on earth to confess that we desperately need Jesus.
And perhaps someone on your Facebook friends list needs this truth tonight.
Not another argument.
Not another outrage post.
Not another piece of gossip.
Jesus.
Send it privately to the person who would never publicly admit they are struggling.
Save it too.
There may come a night when you need to read these words again—not because this article has power in itself, but because you need to be pointed again toward the Scriptures and toward Christ.
Salvation is the gift of God, not something bought through financial support.
Support Christian work because you freely want to help sound biblical truth travel farther.
But never confuse supporting the messenger with following the Savior.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the reason.
Jesus is the One who saves.
Abraham eventually reached the end of his earthly pilgrimage.
Genesis says he died at 175 years old, “in a good old age,” and his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah.
Imagine that final scene.
The man who once left his homeland because God said, “Go.”
The man who stared into a night sky while God spoke about descendants.
The man who waited.
Failed.
Believed.
Feared.
Obeyed.
Wandered.
Wept.
Laughed.
Buried Sarah.
Took Keturah.
Fathered more sons.
And finally breathed his last.
Abraham died.
But the promise of God did not.
Generation followed generation until, in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
And perhaps that is the truth you needed before leaving this page.
Something in your life may have died.
Something may have ended.
Something may never return.
And Christianity does not require you to pretend that does not hurt.
Abraham wept for Sarah.
Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus’s tomb.
Tears are not unbelief.
But neither are tears the end of the Gospel.
Because Christians worship a crucified Savior whose grave is empty.
The Gospel takes us directly through death…
and then shows us resurrection.
So bring Him the chapter you cannot repair.
Bring Him the shame you cannot erase.
Bring Him the grief you cannot explain.
Bring Him the addiction you are tired of hiding.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the heart that feels too dirty to pray.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Christ.
And discover that grace does not mean your past never happened.
Grace means your past does not get to be your savior, your master, or the final author of your identity.
Jesus Christ gets the final word.
And comment before you leave.
Not for appearances.
Not because everyone needs to know your private details.
Just enough honesty to remind another struggling believer that they are not the only person still learning to surrender.
“Christ is still rewriting me.”
Because maybe somebody scrolling beneath you needs to see those words.
Maybe they thought Christians never struggled.
Maybe they thought grace was only for people whose scandals were smaller than theirs.
Maybe they thought Jesus wanted the edited version of their testimony.
He already knows the unedited one.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
The God who remained faithful through Abraham’s unfinished, complicated human story has not changed.
And the Savior who died for sinners is risen.
Your darkest chapter may explain where you have been—but only Jesus has the authority to say who you become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE RECORD INCEST WITHOUT TRYING TO HIDE IT?
paragraphs:
WHY DOES THE BIBLE RECORD INCEST WITHOUT TRYING TO HIDE IT?
Genesis 19:30–38 is not permission. It is not pornography. It is a terrifying portrait of what happens when human beings carry the darkness they escaped from into the place where they thought they were finally safe.
There are stories in the Bible we love to underline.
And then there are stories we almost wish were not there.
Genesis 19:30–38 belongs to the second kind.
It is uncomfortable.
Disturbing.
Morally horrifying.
And Scripture does not hide it.
Lot has escaped the destruction of Sodom. Fire has fallen. His wife is gone. His home is gone. The life he knew has collapsed behind him.
Now he is living in a cave with his two daughters.
You might expect the story to become quieter here.
They survived.
Surely the worst is over.
But sometimes escaping the place of destruction does not mean the destruction has finished working inside the people who escaped.
And that may be one of the most frightening truths hidden inside this passage.
Because Genesis does not merely show us a ruined city.
It shows us a ruined family.
The Hebrew text begins with an almost painfully simple description:
וַיַּעַל לוֹט מִצּוֹעַר וַיֵּשֶׁב בָּהָר וּשְׁתֵּי בְנֹתָיו עִמּוֹ
Vayyaʿal Lot mi-Tzoʿar, vayyeshev bahar, ushtei venotav ʿimmo.
“Lot went up from Zoar and settled in the hill country, and his two daughters with him.”
Then comes the detail that changes the atmosphere:
וַיֵּשֶׁב בַּמְּעָרָה הוּא וּשְׁתֵּי בְנֹתָיו
“He lived in a cave, he and his two daughters.”
A cave.
Three survivors.
No mother.
No husbands.
No ordinary future they can see.
And fear begins talking.
The older daughter tells the younger:
אָבִינוּ זָקֵן וְאִישׁ אֵין בָּאָרֶץ לָבוֹא עָלֵינוּ כְּדֶרֶךְ כָּל־הָאָרֶץ
“Our father is old, and there is not a man in the land to come in to us according to the way of all the earth.”
Whatever exactly they believed about the world beyond that cave, their reasoning is presented as desperate and catastrophically wrong.
Then comes the plan.
They will make their father drunk.
They will lie with him.
They will preserve offspring through him.
And the Bible records it.
That is precisely where many readers become uncomfortable enough to ask the question:
Why?
Why would a holy God allow something this ugly to remain in His holy Scriptures?
Why not skip the cave?
Why not protect the reputation of the family?
Why preserve a story involving intoxication, incest, deception, fear, and generations of consequences?
Because the Bible is not propaganda for human goodness.
It is revelation about a holy God dealing with desperately fallen human beings.
That difference matters.
Scripture does not airbrush its characters.
Noah survives the flood and later becomes drunk.
Abraham believes God and also fails through fear.
Jacob deceives.
Judah enters one of the most scandalous episodes in Genesis.
David becomes an adulterer and arranges a man's death.
Peter swears that he does not know Jesus.
And Lot's family survives Sodom only for Genesis to take us into a cave where another tragedy unfolds.
The Bible could have hidden these things.
It did not.
And that should tell us something about the kind of book we are reading.
The heroes of Scripture are not presented to convince us that human beings can save themselves.
Again and again, Scripture destroys that illusion.
Genesis 19 does not tell you, “Look how admirable these people are.”
It leaves you staring at what sin, fear, moral confusion, isolation, and human desperation can produce.
There is also an important distinction every serious reader of Scripture must make:
Description is not prescription.
The Bible recording an act does not mean God approves of the act.
Genesis does not insert a sentence after every evil action saying, “This was wrong.”
Often the narrative itself, together with the wider moral teaching of Scripture, makes the judgment unmistakable.
Later biblical law explicitly prohibits sexual relations between close relatives. Leviticus 18:6 commands:
אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה
“None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness.”
So Genesis 19 cannot responsibly be used as biblical approval of incest.
It is recording something broken.
And notice something else.
Lot is intoxicated.
The text repeatedly emphasizes that he does not know when his daughters lie down or when they rise.

That does not transform Lot into a flawless character—Genesis has already shown us enough about Lot's compromised decisions to prevent that reading—but it does mean the text itself presents the sexual acts as something carried out while his awareness is profoundly impaired.
There is no romance here.
No celebration.
No command to imitate it.
There is only tragedy.
But the story becomes even more unsettling when you remember where this family has just come from.
Sodom.
Lot had once looked toward the Jordan Valley and seen prosperity.
Genesis 13 says it was well watered.
It looked good.
So Lot moved his tents toward Sodom.
Eventually, we find him living there.
Then, in Genesis 19, he is sitting at the city's gate.
That progression should disturb us.
Sometimes compromise does not announce itself by saying, “Today I will destroy my family.”
Sometimes it begins with what looks profitable.
Convenient.
Beautiful.
Close enough to danger that we still believe we are in control.
Lot's daughters had lived in that environment.
Then suddenly everything was gone.
Their city.
Their security.
Their mother.
Their imagined future.
And now, inside a cave, fear appears to become their counselor.
That does not excuse their sin.
Trauma does not turn evil into righteousness.
But context helps us understand the terrible human logic of the narrative.
They apparently believe their future is disappearing.
So they decide they must manufacture one themselves.
And that temptation is much closer to us than we would like to admit.
Maybe you have never stood in Lot's cave.
But perhaps you know what it means to become so frightened that obedience begins to feel impractical.
You prayed.
Nothing seemed to happen.
You waited.
Nothing changed.
The relationship collapsed.
The money disappeared.
The diagnosis came.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone died.
The future you expected vanished.
And somewhere inside you came the whisper:
“If I don't take control now, everything is over.”
That whisper has destroyed more lives than we realize.
Fear says:
God is taking too long.
Fear says:
God has forgotten you.
Fear says:
His boundaries are beautiful until you are desperate.
Fear says:
Do whatever you have to do.
And when fear becomes lord, things we once called unthinkable can slowly become reasonable.
That cave is not merely ancient geography.
There are caves inside human hearts.
Places where disappointment has been sitting for years.
Places where shame lives without sunlight.
Places where we make decisions nobody knows about.
Places where we say, “God, I know what You said, but You don't understand how desperate I am.”
And perhaps this is one reason God allowed Genesis 19:30–38 to remain exactly as uncomfortable as it is.
God does not need edited family histories.
We do.
We hide the addiction.
We hide the affair.
We hide what happened in the family.
We hide what we watched last night.
We hide the anger.
We hide the abuse.
We hide the compromise.
We hide behind church attendance.
We hide behind Bible verses.
We hide behind ministry.
We hide behind smiles.
We hide because we are terrified that if anyone sees the unedited version of us, grace will disappear.
Then you open Scripture...
and discover that God wrote a redemption story filled with people whose scandals were not deleted.
Not because scandal is good.
Because grace is greater.
And Genesis 19 has consequences.
The older daughter bears a son named Moab.
The younger bears Ben-ammi, associated with the Ammonites.
Those names become nationally significant later in the biblical story.
But here is where the story becomes astonishing.
Because Moab does not disappear from Scripture.
Generations later, a Moabite widow walks into another biblical story.
Her name is Ruth.
Ruth the Moabite.
A descendant of a people whose origin Genesis connects to this horrifying cave episode.
If human beings were writing a respectable religious pedigree, that detail might have been removed.
God did not remove it.
Ruth turns toward the God of Israel.
She tells Naomi:
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
Then Ruth becomes part of the family line of David.
And Matthew begins his Gospel by tracing the genealogy that leads to Jesus Christ.
Matthew names Ruth.
Do you see what Scripture is doing?
Genesis gives us the cave.
Ruth gives us the field.
Matthew gives us the genealogy.
And the Gospel gives us Christ.
The Bible does not pretend the cave never happened.
God brings redemption through history without calling the darkness light.
That is grace.
Grace is not God pretending sin is harmless.
Grace is God confronting sin so completely that the Son of God goes to a cross because sin is not harmless.
Jesus does not save us by rewriting evil into goodness.
He saves sinners by bearing judgment, offering forgiveness, defeating death, and creating something new in those who come to Him.
That distinction matters.
Because “From Scandal to Grace” does not mean:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
It means:
Your sin matters so much that Christ died—and Christ's mercy is so great that your sin does not have to have the final word.
At the cross, nobody gets to boast.
The religious person cannot boast.
The sexually broken person cannot boast.
The respectable family cannot boast.
The ruined family cannot boast.
The pastor cannot boast.
The prisoner cannot boast.
The person with the polished testimony cannot boast.
The person who can barely speak about what happened cannot boast.
We come the same way.
Empty-handed.
Repentant.
Dependent upon Jesus Christ.
And perhaps you have spent years believing your story contains a chapter God cannot touch.
Something happened.
Maybe something you did.
Maybe something someone did to you.
Maybe both.
And you have been living as though that chapter disqualified the rest of the book.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ does not need you to lie about the chapter.
He calls you into the light.
The Gospel is not an invitation to rename darkness.
It is an invitation to leave it.
Repentance means we stop defending what God calls sin.
Faith means we stop trying to become our own savior.
Grace means Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
Forgiveness means guilt does not have to remain your permanent identity.
Transformation means Jesus does not merely offer a cleaner reputation.
He gives new life.
That is why the Bible can afford to tell the truth about Lot's cave.
God is not threatened by the truth.
We are.
God does not have to manipulate the evidence to make redemption look impressive.
Redemption is impressive precisely because the evidence is so terrible.
The Bible shows us how deep the wound goes...
then shows us a Savior whose grace goes deeper still.
Maybe your cave has a different name.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Adultery.
Pride.
Secret drinking.
Greed.
Resentment.
Religious hypocrisy.
A relationship you know dishonors Christ.
A wound you have turned into permission to wound others.
Something hidden behind a password.
Something hidden behind “I'm fine.”
Something hidden behind “God understands.”
He does understand.
But His understanding is not permission to remain enslaved.
It is an invitation to come out.
Into truth.
Into repentance.
Into mercy.
Into Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to confess the details publicly. But you can make one small declaration that you are finished pretending.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is where pretending finally begins to die.
And please hear this too:
If someone else's sin wounded you, Genesis 19 must never be weaponized to tell you that abuse is acceptable because “it's in the Bible.”
No.
Scripture's honesty about human evil is not Scripture's endorsement of human evil.
The Gospel does not demand that victims call evil good.
Jesus brings truth into darkness.
And the same Christ who commands repentance from sinners shows compassion toward the wounded.
Maybe someone you love needs to understand that.
Send this article to them.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand difficult passages of Scripture without hiding the hard parts, follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too.
Not so we can build an audience around ourselves.
So we can keep pointing people toward Jesus.

You are helping Gospel Warrior continue producing Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, discipleship resources, and Gospel content that can reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. You cannot buy grace. You cannot purchase forgiveness.
Salvation is God's gift in Jesus Christ.
But Christians have always had opportunities to voluntarily support the spread of Gospel ministry and biblical teaching.
So if this ministry strengthens your walk with Christ and you want to help Gospel Warrior continue creating and sharing these resources, we would be grateful to have you alongside us.
Genesis 19 was never given to us so we could stare at Lot's family from a safe distance and whisper:
“How could they?”
Scripture eventually turns the mirror toward us.
Not necessarily toward their particular sin.
Toward the same human disease.
The same instinct to distrust God.
The same impulse to seize control.
The same capacity to justify what fear desires.
The same desperate need for mercy.
And then Scripture points beyond Lot.
Beyond Abraham.
Beyond Judah.
Beyond David.
Beyond Ruth.
Beyond every compromised human being in the biblical story.
To Jesus.
The One who did not need His scandal erased because He had none.
The One who entered a human family tree filled with scandal without participating in its sin.
The One who touched the unclean.
Ate with sinners.
Called hypocrites to repentance.
Received the broken.
Carried the cross.
Shed His blood.
Rose from the grave.
And still calls sinners out of hiding.
That is why Genesis can tell the truth.
Because the Bible's final hope was never Lot.
It was never his daughters.
It was never Abraham.
It was never David.
It was never you.
And it was never me.
The hope has always been Jesus Christ.
So share this if somebody you know has mistaken biblical honesty for biblical approval.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable thing about Genesis 19 is not that God allowed the cave to remain in the Bible.
It is that the cave was never powerful enough to stop the story of redemption.
Your darkest chapter does not become holy by being renamed—but when it is brought to Jesus, it no longer gets to pretend it is the author of your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BATHSHEBA BOWED BEFORE THE DYING KING—BUT WHAT SHE WAS FIGHTING FOR WOULD REACH ALL THE WAY TO JESUS
paragraphs: BATHSHEBA BOWED BEFORE THE DYING KING—BUT WHAT SHE WAS FIGHTING FOR WOULD REACH ALL THE WAY TO JESUS

Near the end of David’s life, a woman carrying one of the Bible’s most painful histories walked into the king’s chamber, lowered her face toward the ground, and fought for the future of her son. But behind Solomon’s threatened throne was something even greater: the unfolding story of a God who does not erase scandal—He redeems sinners and carries His promises forward until they lead us to Christ.
Imagine the room.
David is no longer the young shepherd running toward Goliath.
No sling in his hand.
No songs echoing across the hills of Bethlehem.
No armies waiting for his command.
No triumphant entrance into Jerusalem.
The warrior king is old now.
Very old.
His body is failing. His kingdom is restless. His sons are positioning themselves around a throne that will soon be empty.
And somewhere outside that aging king’s chamber, another man is already celebrating as though the throne belongs to him.
Adonijah.
David’s son.
He has gathered supporters. Sacrifices have been offered. Important men have been invited. People are already crying out in celebration of “King Adonijah.”
There is only one problem.
David is still alive.
And Solomon is the son David had sworn would reign after him.

Nathan the prophet realizes the danger immediately. He goes to Bathsheba and warns her that Adonijah has effectively begun presenting himself as king without David’s knowledge. Nathan’s words are frighteningly direct: Bathsheba must act if she hopes to preserve both her own life and Solomon’s.
So Bathsheba walks toward David’s chamber.
And if you know her history, you understand why this scene carries so much emotional weight.
Because this is not the first time Scripture has brought Bathsheba into David’s story.
Years earlier, she had been the wife of Uriah.
David saw her.
David sent for her.
David slept with her.
She became pregnant.
Then David tried to conceal what he had done.
When his attempts failed, Uriah was placed where battle would consume him.
Uriah died.
David took Bathsheba as his wife.
Their first child died after Nathan confronted David over his sin.
There is nothing romantic about the beginning of this story.
It is a story stained by lust, abuse of royal power, deception, bloodshed, grief, judgment, and consequences.
Scripture does not sanitize David merely because David was Israel’s celebrated king.
And neither should we.
Yet Scripture also refuses to allow David’s sin to become the final sentence.
David eventually repented. Grace did not make his sin harmless, and forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence. But God did not abandon His redemptive purposes.
Bathsheba later gave birth to Solomon.
And then Scripture says something astonishingly simple:
“The LORD loved him.”
That is the testimony of 2 Samuel 12:24.
Read that slowly.
The LORD loved him.
A child born into a family carrying terrible scars was not outside the reach of God’s love.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that sentence more than you realize.
Because maybe you have spent years believing that where you came from determines where God can take you.
Maybe your family history is messy.
Maybe your parents failed.
Maybe your marriage has scars.
Maybe your own decisions produced consequences you wish you could reverse.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you would delete immediately if God handed you the pen.
But the Bible repeatedly confronts our instinct to believe that human wreckage is stronger than divine grace.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace does something far more astonishing.
Grace enters places where evil has done real damage and begins creating something evil never intended.
Years pass.
Solomon grows.
David grows old.
And now Bathsheba hears that the future promised to her son is in danger.
Nathan tells her to go to David.
So she goes.
First Kings 1:16 describes the moment:
“Bathsheba bowed and paid homage to the king.”
The Hebrew behind the scene is vivid:
וַתִּקֹּד בַּת־שֶׁבַע וַתִּשְׁתַּחוּ לַמֶּלֶךְ
Vattiqqod Bat-Sheva vattishtachu la-melekh.
Bathsheba bowed and prostrated herself before the king.
That wording deserves careful handling.

The Hebrew verb שָׁחָה — shachah can describe bowing down or prostrating oneself. Context determines whether that bowing is worship offered to God or homage shown before a human superior. Here the object is explicitly לַמֶּלֶךְ — la-melekh — “to/before the king.”
Bathsheba is not worshiping David as God.
She is approaching Israel’s king with the courtly humility appropriate to her position and the seriousness of the moment.
And then David asks her one piercing question:
“What do you desire?”
Imagine everything behind her answer.
Years of memories.
A dead husband.
A dead child.
A marriage born from catastrophe.
A son now threatened by a rival claimant.
An aging king.
A kingdom waiting.
And Bathsheba reminds David of his oath.
Solomon was supposed to reign.
Yet Adonijah had moved ahead.

Bathsheba tells David that Israel is watching him. If David dies without settling the succession, she warns that she and Solomon may be treated as offenders. Nathan then enters and confirms the crisis.
Bathsheba did not burst into that room screaming.
She bowed.
Then she spoke.
There is something deeply human in that.
Sometimes courage does not look like standing on a battlefield with a sword.
Sometimes courage looks like walking into a room you would rather avoid and saying what must be said.
Sometimes faithfulness whispers before it roars.
Sometimes the bravest thing you can do is refuse to remain silent when something entrusted to you is being threatened.
David listens.
And the dying king awakens to the responsibility still resting upon him.
He swears that Solomon will indeed reign after him and declares that he will act that very day.
Then Bathsheba bows again.
This time the Hebrew becomes even more visually powerful:
וַתִּקֹּד בַּת־שֶׁבַע אַפַּיִם אֶרֶץ וַתִּשְׁתַּחוּ לַמֶּלֶךְ
Vattiqqod Bat-Sheva appayim eretz vattishtachu la-melekh.
Bathsheba bows with her face toward the earth and pays homage before the king.
Then she says:
“May my lord King David live forever!”
Think about the irony.
The king is dying.
Yet Bathsheba says, “May the king live forever.”
David would not.
Solomon would not.
No earthly son of David would.
Every throne built by human hands eventually meets a grave.
David died.
Solomon died.
Kings came.
Kings disappeared.
Kingdoms rose.
Kingdoms collapsed.
And that is where this story becomes much larger than Bathsheba fighting for Solomon’s succession.
Because Solomon was not the final King.
God had already spoken of Solomon as a son of peace who would build a house for His name. First Chronicles records the promise concerning Solomon and the establishment of his royal line.
But even Solomon—with his wisdom, wealth, temple, and glory—could not become the flawless king humanity needed.
Solomon himself would fail.
The kingdom would fracture.
Jerusalem would eventually fall.
The temple would be destroyed.
Israel would experience exile.
And still God’s promise would keep moving.
Generation after generation.
Through righteous kings.
Through wicked kings.
Through war.
Through exile.
Through silence.
