A pregnancy exposes what happened.
A powerful man demands punishment for sexual immorality while apparently remaining blind to his own.
Then three ordinary objects are produced in public...
A seal.
A cord.
A staff.
And suddenly the accuser realizes:
They belong to him.
The scandal is his.
The child is his.
The woman he is prepared to condemn is carrying his offspring.
And she is his daughter-in-law.
But if you stop reading Genesis 38 at the scandal, you will miss something astonishing about Scripture.
The Bible does not hide the ugliness of the people through whom God works.
And ultimately, this disturbing story becomes part of the family history leading to Jesus Christ.
That should make every person carrying a past they are ashamed of keep reading.
Genesis 38 begins with Judah leaving his brothers and eventually marrying a Canaanite woman. They have three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah.
Judah arranges for his firstborn, Er, to marry a woman named Tamar.
Then the text becomes brutally concise:
“But Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; and the LORD slew him.”
Genesis 38:7, KJV.
Tamar becomes a widow.

Under the family obligations reflected in this ancient setting—and later formally addressed in Israelite law in Deuteronomy 25:5–10—the continuation of the deceased brother’s family line carried enormous importance.
Judah therefore tells Onan to fulfill his responsibility toward Tamar and provide offspring for his dead brother.
Onan refuses in a particularly calculated way.

He is willing to use Tamar sexually while deliberately preventing the offspring that would preserve his brother's line. Genesis explicitly says that what he did displeased the LORD, and Onan also dies under divine judgment.
Now Tamar has buried two husbands.
Judah still has another son, Shelah.
But Judah is afraid.
He tells Tamar to remain a widow in her father's house until Shelah grows up.
She waits.
Shelah grows.
And Tamar realizes that Judah has not given him to her.
Think about the human experience underneath those few sentences.
Waiting.
Depending upon someone else's promise.
Watching time move while your future does not.
Being told, in effect, “Later.”
And then discovering that “later” apparently meant never.

Scripture does not present Tamar's subsequent deception as a moral template Christians should imitate. Description is not automatically endorsement. The Bible frequently records sinful, broken, and morally complicated human actions without commanding believers to repeat them.
But Scripture does make Judah's failure impossible to ignore.
Tamar eventually hears that Judah is traveling to Timnah.
She removes her widow's garments, covers herself with a veil, and positions herself where Judah will see her.
Genesis tells us:
“When Judah saw her, he thought her to be an harlot; because she had covered her face.”
Genesis 38:15, KJV.
He does not recognize his own daughter-in-law.
He propositions her.
She asks what he will give her.
Judah promises a young goat.
Tamar asks for something as security until payment arrives.
“What pledge shall I give thee?”
She asks for his signet, his bracelets or cord, depending on translation, and his staff.
This matters.
These are not random souvenirs.
His seal or signet was connected with personal identity and authority. His staff was likewise personally identifiable.
Judah hands over the evidence of his identity.
Then he sleeps with her.
She conceives.
Afterward Tamar leaves, removes the veil, and returns to her widow's clothing.
Judah later sends the promised goat through his friend, intending to retrieve his pledge.
But the woman cannot be found.
The men of the area say there was no prostitute there.
Judah eventually decides to let the objects go rather than risk public embarrassment.
He thinks the incident is finished.
That is one of the most haunting illusions sin can create.
Finished.
Hidden.
Buried.
Nobody knows.
Life moves forward.
Until approximately three months later.
Word reaches Judah:
“Tamar thy daughter in law hath played the harlot; and also, behold, she is with child by whoredom.”
And Judah responds:
“Bring her forth, and let her be burnt.”
Genesis 38:24, KJV.
Read that slowly.
The man who recently solicited someone he believed to be a prostitute is outraged when he hears that Tamar has become pregnant through sexual immorality.
He wants judgment.
He wants consequences.
He wants the shame exposed.
Just not his shame.
How terrifyingly human.
We can become experts at identifying in someone else the sin we have learned to excuse in ourselves.
We notice their lust.
Their dishonesty.
Their compromise.
Their hypocrisy.
Their secret messages.
Their addiction.
Their pride.
Their failure.
Their broken marriage.
Their terrible decision.
And somewhere inside us, we whisper:
At least I'm not like them.
Jesus would later expose this spiritual blindness when He warned about noticing the speck in another person's eye while ignoring the beam in our own.
Judah is about to learn that lesson centuries before Jesus speaks those words.
Tamar is brought out.
She does not begin screaming accusations.
She sends Judah the objects he had left behind.
And then comes one of the most devastating sentences in Genesis:
“By the man, whose these are, am I with child.”
Then:
“Discern, I pray thee, whose are these, the signet, and bracelets, and staff.”
Genesis 38:25, KJV.
Imagine Judah looking down.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
His.
There are moments when conviction does not need a sermon.
It just places the evidence in front of you.
Maybe yours is not a signet and a staff.
Maybe it is a message you hope nobody finds.
A browser history you keep deleting.
A relationship you keep justifying.
Money nobody knows about.
Bitterness hidden beneath Christian vocabulary.
A habit you promised God you would stop.
A secret version of yourself that looks nothing like the person people see at church.
Maybe you have become very good at hiding.
But Scripture says:
“Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight.”
Hebrews 4:13, KJV.
Nothing is hidden from God.
And strangely enough, that truth is not merely terrifying.
For the person who comes to Christ, it can become liberating.
Because grace does not require you to successfully deceive God.
He already knows.
Judah recognizes his belongings.
Then he says something extraordinary:
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי”
Tzadqah mimmeni.
Genesis 38:26.
The Hebrew is commonly translated:
“She hath been more righteous than I.”
Judah immediately explains why:
“because that I gave her not to Shelah my son.”
This does not mean Tamar was being declared absolutely sinless.

The statement concerns the moral comparison within this particular crisis. Judah finally acknowledges his own culpability. He recognizes that his failure toward Tamar helped create the situation he is now condemning.
Notice what Judah does not say.
He does not say:
“But you don't understand what I was going through.”
He does not say:
“Everybody makes mistakes.”
He does not say:
“Technically, she deceived me.”
He does not launch a campaign to destroy Tamar's reputation so that his own looks better.
He admits the truth.
She is more righteous than I.
That is where scandal begins moving toward grace.
Not when sin is renamed.
Not when consequences disappear.
Not when wrongdoing becomes acceptable.
But when the hiding stops.
Repentance begins where excuses end.
And somebody reading this has been exhausted by hiding.
You love Jesus, perhaps.
You know Scripture.
You may even serve in ministry.
But there is a locked room inside your life that you desperately hope nobody enters.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not an invitation to become better at hiding your scandal.
It is an invitation to bring your sin into the light and run to the Savior who already knows everything.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is connected with the Greek μετανοέω—metanoeō—carrying the sense of changing one's mind or turning in response to truth.
Biblical repentance is more than embarrassment because you were exposed.
It is not merely feeling horrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Confessing.
Forsaking the lie.
Returning to God.
And the Christian message is not that repentant sinners must somehow scrub themselves clean enough for Jesus to accept them.
The message is that Jesus Christ came precisely because sinners cannot save themselves.
The apostle Paul writes:
Romans 5:8, KJV.
While we were sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we became respectable.
Not after everyone forgot what happened.
Christ died for sinners.
That is why Genesis 38 becomes even more astonishing when you turn to the first chapter of Matthew.
Matthew begins the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Then Judah.
And Matthew could have quietly moved on.
Instead:
“Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar...”
Matthew 1:3, KJV.
Tamar.
Her name is there.
Perez is there.
Judah is there.
The scandal was not deleted from the genealogy.
And through Perez's line eventually came David.
Then, generations later, according to His human ancestry, Jesus the Messiah.
Do not misunderstand this.
God did not need Judah's sin in order to accomplish redemption, and Genesis 38 does not transform sexual immorality or deception into virtues.
Something far greater is being revealed.
Human sin cannot outmaneuver God's redemptive purpose.
God can work through catastrophically broken human histories without approving the evil within them.
That is grace.
The Bible's genealogy of Christ is not a carefully airbrushed family portrait filled exclusively with respectable people.
It contains brokenness.
Sexual scandal.
Outsiders.
Violence.
Failure.
Shame.
And sinners desperately needing mercy.
Then Jesus enters the story.
Holy.
Sinless.
The One who does not inherit their guilt, imitate their rebellion, or participate in their corruption.
He comes to save sinners.
The Greek New Testament says of Him:
“αὐτὸς γὰρ σώσει τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν.”
“For he shall save his people from their sins.”
Matthew 1:21.
From their sins.
Not merely from embarrassment about their sins.
Not merely from the social consequences of their sins.
Jesus came to save His people from sin itself.
That means grace is not God pretending your darkness was light.
Grace is God confronting the darkness and providing the Savior.
At Calvary, Christ bears sin's judgment.
He dies.
He is buried.
He rises again.
And now forgiveness is offered to those who come to Him in repentant faith.
This is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But hear the other side of that truth.
Grace is not permission to keep writing the same rebellion forever.
Jesus does not rescue us so that we can comfortably return to the chains He came to break.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
The same Gospel that says, “Come as you are,” refuses to leave you enslaved to what was destroying you.
Maybe Genesis 38 bothers you because Judah looks uncomfortably familiar.
Not because you committed his exact sin.
But because you know what hypocrisy feels like.
You know what it is to condemn publicly what you struggle with privately.
You know how quickly religious people can reach for stones while carefully hiding their own evidence.
Or perhaps Tamar's waiting feels familiar.
You were promised something.
You trusted someone.
You were forgotten.
Used.
Marginalized.
You watched other people's lives move while yours seemed frozen.
Maybe someone else's sin left consequences inside your story that you never chose.
Genesis 38 does not give us permission to call every human response righteous simply because we were wounded.
But it does show us a God who sees people others overlook.
And the Gospel reveals a Savior who enters broken human stories rather than remaining distant from them.
Jesus knows the entire genealogy.
He knows every chapter.
And He still came.
Perhaps that is what somebody needs to hear tonight.
Jesus knows.
Not the edited version.
Not your Sunday version.
Not the version you upload.
Not the version your family believes.
The whole thing.
And He is still calling sinners to repentance, faith, forgiveness, cleansing, and new life.
So stop running from the evidence.
Bring it into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent where repentance is necessary.
Seek forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Get accountable.
Ask mature believers for help.

And where another person's wrongdoing has wounded you, remember that forgiveness does not require pretending evil was good, nor does reconciliation always mean immediately restoring trust or remaining in an unsafe situation.
Grace tells the truth.
That is why grace can heal what pretending never will.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish your private sin for strangers to inspect. But you can make one honest confession before God today.
Your comment might become the sentence another ashamed believer reads before finally asking Jesus for help.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media engagement, financial support, purchases, or religious performance.
Not to prove that you glorify God.
Share because the Gospel is worth carrying beyond ourselves.
Someone you know may recognize themselves in Judah's hypocrisy.
Someone may recognize themselves in Tamar's pain.
Someone may believe their family history is too ugly.
Someone may be sitting alone thinking Jesus could never want them after what they have done.
Let this article find them.
Because Genesis 38 does not ultimately leave us staring at Judah's bed.
It leads us forward through Perez.
Through generations of deeply imperfect human beings.
Toward Bethlehem.
Toward Christ.
Toward a cross where the spotless Son of God would bear the judgment sinners deserved.
Toward an empty tomb announcing that sin and death do not receive the final word.
And toward the breathtaking promise that in Christ, a human life can become something more than the sum of its worst decisions.
Judah looked at the evidence and finally admitted the truth.
Perhaps today, the evidence is sitting in front of you.
Do not hide it again.
Take it to Jesus.
Because the most unforgettable thing about your scandal may someday be that it became the place where you finally stopped running—and discovered that Christ was calling you home.
Your shame may know the opening sentence of your story, but Jesus Christ still holds the pen over the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: REUBEN SLEPT WITH BILHAH—AND JACOB MENTIONED IT AGAIN ON HIS DEATHBED
paragraphs: REUBEN SLEPT WITH BILHAH—AND JACOB MENTIONED IT AGAIN ON HIS DEATHBED

One sentence in Genesis records the scandal. Years later, an old father spoke of it again. Reuben discovered something every believer needs to understand: forgiven people can still live with consequences—but even a ruined legacy does not place a sinner beyond the reach of the grace that would ultimately come through Jesus Christ.
There are sins you desperately hope will never be mentioned again.
You wish you could bury them beneath enough years.
Enough church services.
Enough good deeds.
Enough Bible verses posted online.
Enough smiles when somebody asks, “How are you doing?”
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe somebody does.
Maybe the person you hurt never forgot.
And perhaps the most frightening thought is not that people remember.
It is that God knows.
Reuben knew something about that kind of memory.
His story contains one of the most abrupt sexual scandals in Genesis. There is no elaborate introduction. No long explanation of his motives. No attempt to soften what happened.
Scripture simply tells us:
“Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father’s concubine: and Israel heard it.” — Genesis 35:22, KJV
Then the narrative moves on.
Almost brutally.
But Jacob had heard.
Remember those words.
Israel heard it.
Because years later, when Jacob was preparing to die, Reuben would discover that what seemed like an old chapter had never become an irrelevant one.
To understand the weight of the scandal, you have to understand who Reuben was.
He was not simply another son.
He was Jacob’s firstborn.
When Jacob eventually addressed him in Genesis 49, he began with extraordinary language:
“Reuben, thou art my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength...” — Genesis 49:3, KJV
The Hebrew begins:

רְאוּבֵן בְּכֹרִי אַתָּה
Re’uven, bekhori attah.
“Reuben, you are my firstborn.”
That word בְּכֹרִי — bekhori comes from the language of the firstborn. Reuben entered life carrying position, expectation, dignity, and responsibility.
Jacob even described him as possessing excellence of dignity and power.
Imagine hearing that from your dying father.
Imagine standing among your brothers while the patriarch who had wrestled with God looked toward you and essentially said:
You were first.
You had dignity.
You had strength.
You had privilege.
You had so much in your hands.
And then came the sentence Reuben could never outrun.
“Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel...”
The Hebrew of Genesis 49:4 opens with the striking expression:
פַּחַז כַּמַּיִם — pachaz kamayim.
The rare Hebrew word pachaz carries the idea of turbulence, recklessness, or instability; translations differ somewhat because the word is unusual. The image is unmistakable, however.
Water that will not remain contained.
Power without restraint.
Impulse without government.
Desire without boundaries.
Jacob was not telling Reuben that he lacked potential.
He had just described how much potential Reuben possessed.
That is precisely what makes the story painful.
Reuben's tragedy was not the absence of strength.
It was strength without self-control.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You can love God and still have an area you have not surrendered.
You can know Scripture and still entertain temptation.
You can have gifts people admire while secretly feeding desires that could eventually destroy what those gifts were supposed to build.
You can be respected publicly and reckless privately.
And sin has an ugly ability to make a few minutes feel more important than decades.
One night.
One decision.
One secret message.
One compromise.
One click.
One meeting nobody was supposed to know about.
One return to the thing God had already convicted you to leave.
Then suddenly you are standing in the aftermath asking:
What have I done?
Reuben slept with Bilhah.
Bilhah was not a random woman. Genesis identifies her as his father’s concubine. She had been Rachel’s servant and had borne Jacob sons.
The biblical text does not tell us exactly why Reuben did it.
That matters.

Some interpreters have understood his action not merely as sexual immorality but also as a challenge to his father’s household authority; biblical parallels show that taking a ruler or father’s concubines could carry political or authority-related significance. Genesis itself, however, does not explicitly tell us Reuben’s motive, so we should not pretend certainty where Scripture remains silent.
What Scripture makes unmistakably clear is the offense.
Reuben had violated his father’s bed.
And Jacob knew.
Years passed.
Families grew.
Joseph disappeared and was eventually found alive in Egypt.
Famine came.
The family moved.
Reuben grew older.
Jacob grew old.
Perhaps Reuben wondered whether that terrible moment had disappeared into history.
Then Genesis 49 arrives.
Jacob gathers his sons.
Death is approaching.
These are not casual words spoken over breakfast. Jacob is speaking into the future of the tribes descending from his sons.
Then his eyes reach Reuben.
“Reuben, thou art my firstborn...”
For one heartbeat, perhaps Reuben remembered everything he had once been expected to become.
Then Jacob continued:
“Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father’s bed; then defiledst thou it...” — Genesis 49:4, KJV
There it was.
After all those years.
The bed.
The scandal.
The thing Reuben might have wished everyone would forget.
Jacob mentioned it on his deathbed.
And Scripture later confirms that the consequences were not merely emotional.
First Chronicles says Reuben was indeed Israel’s firstborn, but because he defiled his father’s bed, his birthright was given to Joseph’s sons.
Read that slowly.
Reuben did not cease being Jacob’s biological firstborn.
But he lost privileges associated with that position.
That distinction matters enormously for Christians.
Because sometimes we talk about grace as though grace means consequences disappear.
Scripture does not teach that.
Grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
The cross itself proves how seriously sin matters.
Sin is so serious that our reconciliation required what we could never provide for ourselves—the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You can be forgiven and still need to rebuild trust.
You can repent and still face consequences.
You can receive mercy and still have wounds to repair.
You can be restored to fellowship with God while discovering that certain earthly opportunities do not automatically return.
David was forgiven, yet his sin produced devastating consequences.
Peter was restored, but he still had to face the shame of having denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ received paradise, but he was not removed from his cross.
Grace does not always rewrite history by erasing what happened.
Sometimes grace rewrites what happens after what happened.
And that may be exactly what somebody needed to hear today.
Because perhaps your deepest fear is:
“If people knew what I did, would God still want me?”
Listen carefully.
The Bible never requires us to call darkness light.
Reuben's sin was sin.
Your sin is sin.
My sin is sin.
We do not honor Jesus by minimizing what required His blood.
But neither do we honor Jesus by acting as though our sin possesses greater saving power than His grace.
That is where this story becomes far bigger than Reuben.
Because Genesis does not end at Genesis 49.
The Bible keeps moving.
And eventually another Firstborn appears.
Not Reuben.
Jesus.

The New Testament calls Christ “the firstborn of every creature” in Colossians 1:15 and “the firstborn from the dead” in Colossians 1:18. The Greek word is πρωτότοκος — prōtotokos, language of firstborn status and supremacy in context.
Reuben was the firstborn who failed beneath the weight of privilege.
Christ is the Son who remained perfectly obedient.
Reuben entered a bed that was forbidden.
Jesus entered a cross He did not deserve.
Reuben dishonored his father.
Jesus could say that He always did what pleased His Father.
Reuben's uncontrolled desire cost him.
Jesus, in perfect obedience, surrendered Himself to save sinners whose desires have cost them everything.
That is the Gospel.
Not that your scandal never happened.
Not that consequences are imaginary.
Not that holiness is optional because God is gracious.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ came for guilty people.
Real ones.
Not sanitized church people.
Not imaginary Christians with spotless histories.
Sinners.
Liars.
Adulterers.
Porn addicts.
Proud people.
Bitter people.
Hypocrites.
People carrying secrets.
People who crossed lines they once swore they never would.
People who cannot believe they became capable of the thing they did.
People sitting in churches while privately wondering whether God has already finished with them.
Christ came for sinners.
And the response of faith is not hiding.
It is repentance.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning. Biblical repentance is not merely feeling horrible because you were exposed.
Judas felt remorse.
Repentance goes deeper.
It stops defending the darkness.
It stops negotiating with the sin.
It brings what is hidden into the light before God.
It turns toward Christ.
And this is where Reuben's story should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because maybe your Bilhah is not sexual sin.
Maybe it is resentment.
Maybe jealousy.
Maybe greed.
Maybe secret pornography.
Maybe gossip dressed up as “concern.”
Maybe you are emotionally involved with somebody who is not your spouse and keep telling yourself nothing physical has happened yet.
Maybe it is alcohol controlling more of your life than you admit.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe you have mastered Christian vocabulary while your prayer life is dying.
Maybe you look alive spiritually online and feel almost nothing toward Christ when the screen turns off.
The question is not whether your scandal resembles Reuben's.
The question is whether there is something in your life that you keep hoping God will simply stop mentioning.
Something the Holy Spirit keeps touching.
Something you keep burying.
Something you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would force you to make a decision.
Reuben teaches us that time does not transform sin into righteousness.
Ten years cannot make rebellion holy.
Silence cannot turn darkness into light.
But Jesus can forgive repentant sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice Scripture does not say God is faithful to excuse us while we cling to sin.
It says confess.
Bring it into agreement with God.
Stop editing the story.
Stop presenting evidence for the defense.
Call it what He calls it.
Then run toward the Savior rather than away from Him.
Because the devil loves two lies.
Before sin, he whispers:
It won't cost you that much.
After sin, he whispers:
You have gone too far to come home.
Both are lies.
Sin can cost far more than you imagined.
And Christ can save far more completely than you imagined.
That tension is where biblical grace lives.
Consequences are real.
Grace is real.
Judgment is real.
Mercy is real.
Repentance is necessary.
Forgiveness is available.
And the cross refuses to let us cheapen either side.
Maybe that is why Reuben's story feels so painfully human.
He was more than his worst moment, but his worst moment mattered.
Scripture does not erase his name.
Reuben remains a son of Jacob. His descendants remain part of Israel's story.
But Scripture also refuses to pretend his actions had no consequences.
This is not cancellation.
It is truth.
And truth is where genuine restoration begins.
You do not heal by inventing a cleaner past.
You heal by bringing the real past to a real Savior.
So perhaps tonight you do not need another inspirational sentence telling you how amazing you are.
Perhaps you need to get alone with God.
Put the phone down.
Close the door.
Stop performing.
And tell Jesus the truth.
“Lord, this is what I did.”
“This is what I keep wanting.”
“This is what I have hidden.”
“This is who I hurt.”
“This is where I compromised.”
“This is what I cannot repair by myself.”
Then remember why Jesus came.
He did not walk toward Calvary because humanity needed motivational advice.
He went because sinners needed redemption.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And the same Christ who exposes sin calls sinners out of darkness and into life.
You may not be able to recover every opportunity sin cost you.
You may have apologies to make.
Boundaries to establish.
Relationships to repair where possible.
Habits to kill.
Accountability to seek.
Consequences to accept.
But do not confuse consequences with abandonment by God.
The cross still stands.
The tomb is still empty.
Christ still receives those who come to Him.
And your worst chapter does not possess authority to write the final sentence over a life surrendered to Jesus.
That belongs to Him.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make a simple declaration:
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer in a battle.

Not because Reuben's scandal deserves to be remembered for entertainment, but because the next time temptation tells you that one decision does not matter, you may need to remember the dying words of Jacob.
And the next time shame tells you that failure means you should run from God, you may need to remember the cross of Christ.
Not to expose them.
To remind them where exposed sinners can run.
To Jesus.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach more people—but it is never a payment to God, proof of salvation, or substitute for obedience. We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him; when we freely use our resources to help sound Gospel ministry reach others, that support can become part of our service.
Invite your family. Invite the struggling believer. Invite the lukewarm Christian. Invite the seeker. Even invite the unbelieving friend who has questions about Jesus.
Think about Christ.
Reuben reminds us how quickly uncontrolled desire can damage a legacy.
Jesus reminds us that grace can reach people standing in the wreckage.
Reuben's father remembered the bed he defiled.
At Calvary, Jesus willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved so that everyone who truly turns to Him in faith can receive something scandalous in an entirely different sense:
Mercy.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new life.
So bring Him the chapter you wish had never been written.
Bring Him the night you regret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the consequences you cannot reverse.
Bring Him the broken pieces without pretending they were never broken.
Because Jesus does not need a fictional version of your story in order to redeem the real one.
Your sin may explain a chapter of your past, but when you belong to Christ, it does not get to be the author of your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU BE DEPRESSED AND STILL TRUST JESUS?
paragraphs:
CAN YOU BE DEPRESSED AND STILL TRUST JESUS?
What if the darkness in your mind is not proof that you have lost your faith—but the very place where you are discovering what it actually means to need a Savior?
There are Christians reading this who know exactly how to look okay.
You know when to smile.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know which Bible verse to post.
You know how to worship while people are watching.
And maybe nobody knows that when the room becomes quiet, something inside you collapses.
You love Jesus.
But you are tired.
You believe God is real.
But some mornings you do not want to get out of bed.
You know the promises.
But your emotions seem incapable of feeling them.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps somebody gave you another burden to carry.
“If you really trusted God, you wouldn’t feel like this.”
So now you are carrying two pains.
The darkness itself...
and the shame of wondering whether the darkness means you are disappointing Jesus.
Please hear this carefully:
The Bible does not teach that genuine faith means never experiencing profound emotional anguish.
In fact, Scripture is far more emotionally honest than many Christians allow themselves to be.
Listen to the psalmist:
מַה־תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי וַתֶּהֱמִי עָלָי הוֹחִילִי לֵאלֹהִים
“Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God...” — Psalm 42:5
Notice what happens here.
The psalmist does not pretend his soul is fine.
The Hebrew says, “מַה־תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי... נַפְשִׁי” — “Why are you cast down, my soul?”
נַפְשִׁי, nafshi, means “my soul,” “my life,” “my self.”
And then comes the command:
הוֹחִילִי לֵאלֹהִים
Hochili l’Elohim.
“Hope in God.”
That is breathtaking.
His soul is cast down...
and he tells that same soul to hope in God.
The anguish and the faith are present in the same person.
That matters.
Because perhaps you have been measuring faith by how emotionally strong you feel when Scripture sometimes shows faith as what you cling to precisely when you do not feel strong.
Faith is not always shouting from a mountaintop.
Sometimes faith is whispering the name “Jesus” from the floor.
Sometimes faith is opening your Bible with trembling hands.
Sometimes faith is praying when the only prayer you can produce is:
“Lord, help me.”
Sometimes faith is simply refusing to walk away from Christ while everything inside you is screaming that you cannot continue.
And if you think real servants of God never reached places like that, listen to Paul.
This is an apostle.
A missionary.
A preacher.
A man who suffered for Christ and proclaimed the risen Jesus across the ancient world.
Yet Paul wrote:
“Οὐ γὰρ θέλομεν ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν... ὥστε ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῆν.”
He explains that the affliction he and his companions experienced was so overwhelming that they “despaired even of life.” — 2 Corinthians 1:8.
The Greek word is devastating:
ἐξαπορηθῆναι — exaporēthēnai.
To despair. To be utterly at a loss.
Paul did not write, “Nothing bothered me because I had enough faith.”
He said they were burdened beyond their strength and despaired even of life.
And then Paul tells us where that terrible experience drove them.
Not away from God.
Deeper into dependence upon God.
He continues by explaining that they felt they had received the sentence of death so that they would not rely upon themselves, “but on God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9).
There it is.
Christian faith does not always mean:
“I feel strong because God is with me.”
Sometimes it means:
“I have discovered that I am not strong enough, so my entire weight is falling upon the God who raises the dead.”
Maybe that is where you are.
You are not asking Jesus to make you impressive anymore.
You are asking Him to keep you alive inside.
And Scripture knows that territory.
Look at Elijah.
Be careful here: the Bible does not give Elijah a modern psychiatric diagnosis, so we should not pretend Scripture says something it does not say.
But 1 Kings 19 unquestionably describes a servant of God experiencing extraordinary fear, exhaustion, isolation and despair.
This is the same Elijah who had just stood at Mount Carmel.
Fire fell.
God answered.
The prophets of Baal were defeated.
You might expect Elijah to become spiritually untouchable after witnessing something like that.
Instead, Jezebel threatens his life.
And Elijah runs.
Eventually he sits beneath a broom tree.
Alone.
Exhausted.
And he says:
“It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life...” — 1 Kings 19:4.
Read that again.
A prophet who had seen fire fall from heaven reached a moment when he did not want to continue living.
Yesterday’s spiritual victory did not make him immune to tomorrow’s emotional collapse.
And look at what God does next.
God does not stand over Elijah screaming:
“Where is your faith?”
God lets him sleep.
God provides food.
God provides water.
Elijah sleeps again.
God feeds him again.
Only afterward does the journey continue.
There is something profoundly tender about this scene.
The God who could send fire from heaven also cared about an exhausted man needing food and sleep.
Sometimes we make spirituality so abstract that we forget God created bodies too.
You are not merely a floating soul.
You are an embodied human being.
Sleep matters.
Food matters.
Trauma matters.
Grief matters.
Relationships matter.
Your nervous system is not an enemy of Christianity.
And receiving appropriate help is not automatically evidence that you have abandoned God.
If you broke your leg, seeking medical care would not necessarily mean you had stopped trusting Jesus.
Likewise, seeking qualified help for serious mental or emotional suffering does not automatically mean you have replaced Jesus.
Christ remains Lord.
Christ remains Savior.
Christ remains our ultimate hope.
But the Lord routinely works through means.
He works through pastors.
Friends.
Family.
Doctors.
Counselors.
Medicine.
Rest.
Community.
Prayer.
Scripture.
And sometimes through the person who notices you have become unusually quiet and refuses to leave you alone.
Please do not turn suffering into a competition between prayer and appropriate care.
Pray.
And ask for help.
Read Scripture.
And tell somebody the truth.
Seek Christ.
And if you are experiencing persistent depression, speak with an appropriately qualified healthcare professional.
You do not glorify God by hiding dangerous suffering simply because you are afraid someone will question your faith.
There is another Man in Scripture we must talk about.
Jesus.
No, Jesus was not sinful.
No, we should not casually impose modern diagnoses upon Him.
But the Son of God was not emotionally numb.
At Lazarus’ tomb:
“Jesus wept.” — John 11:35.
And in Gethsemane, Jesus said:
“Περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου.”
“My soul is deeply sorrowful, even to death.” — Matthew 26:38.
Περίλυπος — perilypos.
Deeply grieved.
Overwhelmed with sorrow.
The sinless Son of God experienced crushing sorrow without that sorrow making Him sinful.
Jesus knows what tears taste like.
He knows betrayal.
He knows abandonment.
He knows anguish.
He knows what it means to cry out.
Christianity does not give you a Savior standing far away from human suffering.
It gives you Jesus Christ.
God the Son who entered our suffering.
The Word became flesh.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And from the cross came that haunting cry:
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Jesus was invoking Psalm 22—the prayer of the righteous sufferer.
And here is where Christianity refuses to end the story where despair wants to end it.
The cross was not the last page.
The tomb was not the last page.
Friday was not the last page.
Jesus rose.
That changes everything.
Christian hope is not the claim that believers never enter darkness.
Christian hope is that darkness does not get the final word.
Depression may speak.
Grief may speak.
Trauma may speak.
Your past may speak.
Your exhaustion may speak.
Your own mind may sometimes accuse you.
But none of them gets to be your Savior.
Jesus does.
And perhaps the deepest question is not merely, “Can a Christian be depressed?”
Perhaps it is:
“Will Jesus still receive me when I am?”
Look at Him.
The Jesus who welcomed failures.
The Jesus who touched lepers.
The Jesus who restored Peter after Peter publicly denied Him.
The Jesus who ate with sinners.
The Jesus who carried a cross for guilty people.
The Jesus who prayed for His executioners.
The Jesus who told a dying criminal beside Him that paradise was coming.
Do you really think your tears frighten Him?
Do you think your exhausted prayers surprise Him?
Do you think He discovered your weakness this morning?
He already knew.
And still He went to the cross.
That is grace.
Grace is not God discovering that you are stronger than you thought.
Grace is discovering that Christ is sufficient when you finally admit you are not.
Maybe you have sins that need repentance.
Bring them into the light.
Maybe depression has become tangled together with isolation, bitterness, destructive habits, addiction, shame or secret sin.
Do not hide those things behind a diagnosis.
Repent where repentance is needed.
But do not call every symptom of suffering a sin either.
We need enough biblical wisdom to distinguish guilt from grief.
Both need Jesus.
But not in exactly the same way.
Sin needs forgiveness.
Wounds need healing.
Falsehood needs truth.
Isolation needs community.
Exhaustion may need rest.
Illness may need treatment.
And every human heart ultimately needs reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is bigger than “cheer up.”
The Gospel says something infinitely stronger.
You were separated from God by sin, and you could not rescue yourself.
Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He died for sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives forgiveness and life.
Your deepest hope is therefore not that tomorrow morning you will suddenly feel amazing.
Your deepest hope has a name.
Jesus.
Feelings rise.
Feelings fall.
Christ remains.
There will be mornings when you feel the truth.
There may be mornings when you have to believe the truth while feeling almost none of its comfort.
Jesus remains Lord in both mornings.
So perhaps trust looks different tonight.
Maybe trust means calling somebody and saying:
“I’m not okay.”
Maybe trust means making the appointment you have been postponing.
Maybe trust means asking your church family for prayer.
Maybe trust means getting out of isolation.
Maybe trust means eating something, sleeping, stepping outside and allowing your body to breathe.
Maybe trust means opening Psalm 42 and borrowing somebody else’s words because you cannot find your own.
Maybe trust means whispering:
“Jesus, I cannot carry myself anymore.”
Good.
Christianity never required you to save yourself.
There is already a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.

If thoughts of suicide or self-harm are part of what you are experiencing, please do not treat that as a private spiritual test you have to survive alone. Tell someone you trust immediately and contact emergency services or a crisis service where you live. Stay with another person and put distance between yourself and anything you could use to hurt yourself. Asking for immediate help is not spiritual failure. Your life matters, and you should not face that moment alone.
And to the Christian reading this who is not depressed...
please remember this article when somebody you love is.
Do not hand them a cliché and disappear.
Sit down.
Listen.
Bring food.
Call tomorrow.
Pray with them.
Help them find qualified care when needed.
Walk with them.
Bear one another’s burdens.
Sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is remain beside someone long enough for them to realize their suffering did not make them untouchable.
And maybe that is why this article needs to leave your screen.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
We are saved by grace, not social-media engagement.
Send it privately to the person whose silence has been worrying you.
Because there may come a night when you need these truths yourself.
If you are exhausted but still holding onto Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Someone reading underneath this article may desperately need evidence that another believer has walked through a dark valley and discovered that Christ was still there.

If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, let that support flow from grace, not guilt. Pray. Share biblical truth. Tell people about Jesus. Serve your church. Care for suffering people. Give generously where God leads you.
Following keeps this kind of biblical encouragement near you.
Sharing carries it beyond you.
Tagging can put it directly in front of someone you love.
Commenting reminds another hurting believer that they are not the only one fighting.
Saving gives you something to return to when the night becomes heavy again.
If you want to support that mission and go deeper with us:
But before you leave, remember the person underneath the broom tree.
Elijah thought he was finished.
God was not finished.
Remember the psalmist talking to his own downcast soul.
“Hope in God.”
Remember Paul, crushed beyond his own strength, learning not to rely upon himself but upon the God who raises the dead.
And above all...
remember Jesus.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
Your darkness is real.
But it is not Lord.
Your feelings are real.
But they are not your Savior.
Your suffering may become part of your story.
But through Jesus Christ, suffering does not have authority to write the ending.
Maybe you came to this article asking:
“Can I be depressed and still trust Jesus?”
Yes.
You can weep and trust Jesus.
You can tremble and trust Jesus.
You can receive treatment and trust Jesus.
You can tell someone you are struggling and trust Jesus.
You can have questions and still bring those questions to Jesus.
You can be exhausted and keep reaching toward Jesus.
Sometimes trust does not look like standing triumphantly above the darkness.
Sometimes trust looks like collapsing into the arms of Christ and discovering that when you could no longer hold onto Him with strength...
He was still holding you.
And perhaps tonight you do not need enough strength to see the entire road ahead.
Perhaps you only need enough strength for one prayer.
“Jesus, keep me.”
And if that is all you have...
give Him that.
Because the Savior who walked out of a sealed tomb is not intimidated by the darkness you cannot yet walk out of.
The night inside you may be louder than your faith right now—but the risen Christ is louder than the grave.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: NOAH GOT DRUNK AND LAY NAKED IN HIS TENT—THEN HIS FAMILY WAS NEVER THE SAME
paragraphs:
NOAH GOT DRUNK AND LAY NAKED IN HIS TENT—THEN HIS FAMILY WAS NEVER THE SAME
He survived the judgment of the entire world. He walked out of the ark carrying humanity’s future. Then Genesis records something painfully human: Noah planted a vineyard, drank its wine, became drunk, and lay exposed inside his tent. What happened next reveals something terrifying about sin, shame, families—and the kind of covering only Jesus Christ can ultimately provide.
There are some Bible stories we clean up before we tell them.
This is not one of them.
Noah had heard the rain hammer against the ark while the world he knew disappeared beneath the water.
He had survived the Flood.
He had watched the waters recede.
He had stepped onto dry ground and built an altar to the LORD.
He had received God’s covenant and seen the rainbow stretched across the sky.
If anybody looked like a man who had already survived his darkest chapter, it was Noah.
But then came the vineyard.
And the wine.
And the tent.
And the shame.
And a family that would never look quite the same again.
Maybe that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual danger does not arrive while the storm is raging.
Sometimes it arrives after the storm is over.
When everybody thinks you are fine.
When the crisis has passed.
When the testimony has already been told.
When people know what God brought you through...
but nobody knows what is happening inside your tent.
Genesis does not airbrush its heroes. It tells the truth.
The Hebrew of Genesis 9:21 is painfully direct:
וַיֵּשְׁתְּ מִן־הַיַּיִן וַיִּשְׁכָּר וַיִּתְגַּל בְּתוֹךְ אָהֳלֹה
Vayyesht min-hayyayin, vayishkar, vayitgal betokh oholoh.
He drank from the wine.
He became drunk.
He became uncovered inside his tent.
No excuse.
No polished religious language.
No attempt to protect Noah’s reputation.
The man Scripture had earlier described as righteous is now lying exposed in drunkenness.
That should destroy one dangerous illusion many Christians quietly carry:
Being used by God does not make a person incapable of falling.
Yesterday’s obedience does not give us immunity from today’s temptation.
Noah had obeyed God when virtually an entire world would not.
And Noah still needed grace.
So do you.
So do I.
The Bible is not a museum filled with statues of flawless people.
It is the history of a holy God dealing with painfully fallen human beings.
And that is precisely why the Bible can tell the truth about Noah without destroying the entire story.
God already knew what Noah was capable of when He called him.
Think about that.
God did not discover Noah's weakness inside that tent.
The God who commanded him to build the ark already knew every chapter that would follow.
That does not excuse Noah's drunkenness.
It magnifies God's grace.
Somebody reading this needs that distinction desperately.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God meeting sinners who could never save themselves.
And perhaps you understand Noah's tent more than you would ever admit publicly.
Maybe your tent is not alcohol.
Maybe nobody has ever found you drunk.
But perhaps there is something else you keep behind canvas walls.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
An affair nobody knows about.
Secret messages you keep deleting.
A temper your church friends never see.
Jealousy.
Greed.
An addiction.
A private compromise.
A prayer life that disappeared months ago while you kept posting Bible verses as though everything were fine.
Maybe everybody sees your ark...
but God sees your tent.
That sentence may hurt.
Let it.
Not because Christ wants to humiliate you.
Because He loves you too much to let darkness convince you that hiding is healing.
Then somebody entered Noah's story.
Ham saw his father's nakedness.
The Hebrew says:
וַיַּרְא חָם... אֵת עֶרְוַת אָבִיו
Ham “saw the nakedness of his father.”
Then he went outside and told his brothers.

Scripture does not explicitly explain every detail of Ham's offense, and interpreters have debated whether something more than seeing occurred. We should therefore resist pretending certainty where the biblical text itself does not give us certainty.
What Scripture makes unmistakable is the contrast.
Ham saw.
Ham went out.
Ham told.
Shem and Japheth responded differently.
Genesis says they took a garment and placed it across their shoulders.
Then something extraordinary happened.
They walked backward.
Imagine the scene.
Two grown sons slowly stepping backward toward the exposed body of their father.
Their faces turned away.
A garment stretched between them.
Step...
after step...
after step.
Until they could lower the covering over Noah.
The Hebrew deliberately emphasizes what they did:
וַיְכַסּוּ אֵת עֶרְוַת אֲבִיהֶם
Vaykhasu et ervat avihem.
They covered the nakedness of their father.
And Scripture immediately emphasizes that their faces were turned backward and they did not look upon their father's nakedness.
One son encountered another person's shame and carried the story outward.
Two sons encountered that same shame and carried a covering inward.
Read that again slowly.
Because sooner or later, somebody else's weakness will become visible to you.
And what you do next will reveal something about your own heart.
There is a difference between confronting sin and enjoying somebody's humiliation.
There is a difference between protecting someone and enabling someone.
There is a difference between bringing darkness into the light for repentance and carrying somebody's failure from person to person because scandal tastes delicious when it belongs to somebody else.
Our generation has turned exposure into entertainment.
Someone falls.
Screenshots spread.
Messages get forwarded.
Private agony becomes public content.
People gather around somebody's collapse and call their curiosity “discernment.”
Christians can do it too.
We can disguise gossip as prayer requests.
We can disguise cruelty as “speaking truth.”
We can become fascinated with who fell, how badly they fell, and exactly what happened.
Yet Shem and Japheth remind us that holiness does not need to feast on another person's nakedness.
They did not pretend Noah was clothed.
They covered him.
There is a difference.
Biblical grace never requires calling evil good.
Biblical grace tells the truth while refusing to make another person's humiliation our entertainment.
And then Noah woke up.
Imagine that moment.
The pounding head.
The fragments of memory.
The garment over him.
The realization.
Genesis says:
וַיִּיקֶץ נֹחַ מִיֵּינוֹ
“Noah awoke from his wine.”
Some awakenings are brutal.
Maybe you know.
The morning after.
The conversation after.
The discovery after.
The consequences after.
The moment when whatever numbed you wears off and reality is still sitting beside the bed.
Sin promises escape.
Then eventually you wake up.
You wake up to the damaged marriage.
You wake up to the frightened children.
You wake up to the bank account.
You wake up to the messages.
You wake up to the person in the mirror.
You wake up and realize that what happened privately did not necessarily remain private.
That is one of the sobering truths of Noah's story.
Our choices can spill into our families.
Genesis records that after Noah learned what had happened, he pronounced words concerning Canaan, Ham's son, as well as blessings involving Shem and Japheth.
The consequences now echo beyond one drunken night.
And here we must be careful with Scripture.

The text says Canaan was cursed; it does not say that an entire race of people was cursed because of skin color. This passage has been grotesquely abused in history to rationalize racial slavery. That distortion should be rejected. The biblical text names Canaan, and faithful reading must not turn the passage into permission for racial hatred.
But the family consequences are still sobering.
One man's private collapse became a family crisis.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because children often live downstream from choices they did not make.
Families can inherit wounds.
A father's uncontrolled anger becomes the atmosphere of a home.
A mother's bitterness can become a daughter's language.
Addiction can echo through generations.
Patterns can become traditions.
Pain can teach pain.
And sometimes somebody eventually has to stand before God and say:
This may have reached me, but by the grace of Jesus Christ, it will not rule me.
Maybe that somebody is you.
Maybe your father drank.
Maybe your mother disappeared emotionally.
Maybe your childhood taught you survival before it ever taught you safety.
Maybe your family knew church language but not repentance.
Maybe secrets were protected while wounded people were silenced.
Maybe everybody learned to pretend.
And now you are grown...
but part of you is still standing outside somebody else's tent wondering what to do with what you saw.
Hear this carefully.
You are not required to call abuse acceptable.
You are not required to protect dangerous behavior from legitimate accountability.
You are not required to remain silent about crimes, exploitation, or situations where someone is unsafe.
Shem and Japheth covering Noah's nakedness is not permission to conceal abuse.
Truth and grace are not enemies.
Jesus embodies both.
And that brings us to the deepest part of this story.
Because Genesis begins with another nakedness.
Adam and Eve sinned.
Their eyes were opened.
They realized they were naked.
And they hid.
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
Different gardens.
Different tents.
Different centuries.
Same shame.
We sew fig leaves.
We build reputations.
We manufacture appearances.
We learn Christian vocabulary.
We smile for photographs.
We say, “God is good,” while secretly wondering whether God could possibly still want us if everyone knew everything.
But the Gospel is not the story of human beings becoming good enough to stand uncovered before God.
It is the story of God coming for sinners.
And eventually another Man would be exposed in shame.
Jesus Christ.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Humiliated.
Crucified publicly.
The sinless One stood where guilty humanity deserved to stand.
Noah lay naked because of his own drunkenness.
Christ was stripped while bearing shame that was not His.
At Calvary, the innocent Son of God carried the judgment of sinners.
Isaiah had prophesied that the Servant would be wounded for our transgressions.
The New Testament declares that Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree.
And here the Gospel becomes almost unbearable in its beauty:
We spend our lives trying to cover ourselves.
God offers us Christ.
Not denial.
Not pretending.
Not religious makeup over spiritual infection.
Christ.
His righteousness instead of ours.
His blood for our guilt.
His mercy for our rebellion.
His resurrection for our death.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that redemption cost the blood of the Son of God—and His love was so great that He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
That is grace.
Scandal does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Noah's story should therefore make us afraid of sin without making repentant sinners afraid of Christ.
There is a difference.
If you are hiding something tonight, Jesus already knows.
You are not informing Him when you confess.
You are surrendering.
Repentance means turning from sin toward God.
Stop defending what Christ died to save you from.
Stop calling bondage a personality.
Stop renaming compromise.
Stop waiting until your private tent becomes somebody else's public tragedy.
Come into the light.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is cleansing in Jesus Christ.
There is restoration in Jesus Christ.
There is power to begin again in Jesus Christ.
And if consequences remain, Christ can walk with you through those consequences too.
Grace does not always erase earthly consequences.
Grace does something even deeper.
It reconciles guilty sinners to God and begins transforming them from the inside out.
Perhaps that is why you were meant to read Noah's story today.
Not so you could stare at Noah.
So you could recognize yourself.
Where are you exposed?
Where are you hiding?
Whose failure have you been enjoying instead of grieving?
Whose shame have you been broadcasting when love required discretion?
What generational pattern have you accepted as inevitable?
What vineyard have you planted that is slowly becoming your master?
What would happen if today you finally stopped hiding?
Maybe your prayer does not need sophisticated words.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That may be enough to begin.
Not because typing words saves anyone. Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes a small public confession becomes the moment we stop pretending.
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not interrogate them.
Pray for them.
This is what the Church should look like.
Not a crowd standing outside the tent laughing.
A family carrying coverings toward wounded people while still calling them toward truth.
If somebody came into your mind while reading this, send this article to them.
Not with judgment.
With love.
Save it too.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.
It does not.
Not because financially supporting a ministry proves that you love God. It does not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, truth, worship, and lives surrendered to Him.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing Scripture, reaching hurting people, and building resources designed to point people toward Jesus.
Sometimes evangelism begins with something as simple as pressing “share.”
Not because an algorithm can save a soul.
It cannot.
But because behind every screen is a human being.
And behind some of those screens tonight is somebody sitting alone with a secret.
Somebody ashamed.
Somebody addicted.
Somebody convinced they have gone too far.
Somebody wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want them.
Let them hear the answer.
Yes, sin destroys.
Yes, choices have consequences.
Yes, Noah got drunk.
Yes, Noah lay exposed.
Yes, his family was shaken by what followed.
But Noah's tent is not where the biblical story ends.
Humanity's story keeps moving...
through Abraham...
through Israel...
through kings and prophets...
through failure after failure...
until eventually the story reaches Bethlehem.
Then Golgotha.
Then an empty tomb.
And suddenly we understand why Scripture can afford to tell us the ugliest truth about its people.
Because the Bible was never ultimately about how impressive its human characters were.
It was always moving toward the One who could save them.
Jesus Christ.
So come out of hiding.
Put down the bottle.
Close the secret conversation.
Confess the bitterness.
End the affair.
Tell the truth.
Ask for help.
Return to Scripture.
Find mature believers who will walk with you.
Repent.
And run toward Christ.
Because the most shocking thing about your story may not ultimately be what you did in your darkest moment.
It may be what Jesus did after you finally brought it into His light.
Your shame may explain a chapter of your story—but when Jesus takes hold of the pen, shame does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID GOD APPROVE OF CONCUBINES?
paragraphs: DID GOD APPROVE OF CONCUBINES?
The Bible Records Men Having Them. But Does That Mean God Wanted Them?
There is a question hiding inside some of the Bible’s most uncomfortable stories.
Abraham had Hagar.
Jacob had Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had concubines.
Solomon had hundreds.
And because the Bible does not erase these men from its pages—because some of them were even used mightily by God—an unsettling question eventually rises:
Did God actually approve of concubines?
Be careful with the answer.
Because if we read the Bible as though everything it records is something it recommends, we can make Scripture endorse almost anything.
The Bible records murder.
It records incest.
It records adultery.
It records drunkenness, betrayal, polygamy, rape, slavery, idolatry, political corruption, family dysfunction, and horrifying violence.
But recording something truthfully is not the same thing as approving it morally.
Sometimes Scripture tells you, “Thus says the LORD.”
Sometimes Scripture tells you, in effect, “This is what fallen human beings did.”
And knowing the difference changes everything.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh.

It refers to a woman in a recognized relationship with a man that possessed marital or quasi-marital characteristics but generally did not carry the same social standing as a primary wife. The exact legal and social circumstances varied across the ancient world and across individual biblical narratives, so we should resist forcing every concubine mentioned in Scripture into one modern category.
But one thing becomes painfully clear as the biblical story unfolds:
God did not introduce concubinage in Eden.
Human beings did.
Go back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings, armies, palaces, or dynasties.
Go back to the beginning.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew speaks of אִישׁ — ish, “man,” and אִשָּׁה — ishshah, “woman/wife,” moving into the covenantal reality Scripture describes as בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad:
“one flesh.”
That is the picture at creation.
Not one man accumulating women according to wealth, power, fertility, politics, or desire.
One-flesh covenant.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something extraordinarily important.
He went back to creation.
Jesus said:

“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female… Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh?”
Then He declared:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
The Greek expression is οἱ δύο — hoi duo:
“the two.”
Jesus did not point His hearers toward the complicated households of Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon as the definition of marriage.
He pointed them backward.
To Eden.
To God’s intention before sin had twisted human relationships.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because someone can ask, “But didn’t God allow these arrangements?”
Yes—in the sense that Scripture describes a fallen world in which practices existed that God regulated without thereby establishing them as His original ideal.
Regulation is not necessarily endorsement.
Jesus Himself gives us the principle.
Speaking about divorce, He said Moses permitted divorce “because of your hardness of heart,” but then added:
“from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read that again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
There are things God addressed within fallen human societies because sinful people were already doing them.
That does not mean those things represented Eden.
That does not mean brokenness became holiness merely because God placed boundaries around human behavior.
And suddenly the stories of concubinage begin looking very different.
Consider Abraham.
God promised Abraham descendants.
But the promise seemed impossible.
Sarah was barren.
Years passed.
Bodies aged.
Hope became painful.
And Genesis 16 records Sarah giving Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham in an attempt to obtain children through her.
Genesis does not present this as a glorious demonstration of faith.
The household fractures almost immediately.
Hagar conceives.
Tension erupts.
Sarah becomes bitter.
Hagar suffers.
Hagar flees.
A child is eventually born into a conflict he did not create.
And yet here is where the Gospel-shaped beauty of Scripture begins appearing even in the wreckage.
God sees Hagar.
The woman caught inside somebody else’s desperate attempt to control the promise discovers that heaven has not forgotten her.
She calls the LORD:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Roi.
“The God who sees me.”
Genesis 16:13.
That should stop us.
Because Scripture is not merely telling the stories of powerful patriarchs.
God sees the wounded people standing in the shadows of their decisions too.
Maybe that is why this subject matters more than we think.
Concubinage is not merely an ancient theological puzzle.
It exposes something painfully modern.
Human beings still try to rewrite God’s boundaries whenever obedience becomes inconvenient.
We still rename compromise.
We still justify what benefits us.
We still point toward somebody else’s failure and say, “See? They did it.”
We still confuse God’s patience with God’s approval.
We still want biblical characters to give us permission for things the biblical story itself is warning us about.
Jacob’s household becomes another painful example.
Through Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah, Jacob fathers the sons who become the foundation of Israel’s tribes.
And yes, God sovereignly works through that family.
But sovereignty is not endorsement.
God accomplishing His purpose through human dysfunction does not make the dysfunction righteous.
Look at the household.
Jealousy.
Competition.
Women desperately fighting for affection.
Children becoming entangled in rivalry.
Brothers eventually selling Joseph into slavery.
The family through whom God would bring covenant blessing is simultaneously a family desperately in need of grace.
That is one of Scripture’s recurring messages:
God can accomplish holy purposes through deeply broken people without calling their brokenness holy.
Then comes David.
The man after God’s own heart.
The psalmist.
The warrior.
The king.
And a man whose sexual and family failures eventually brought catastrophic pain into his household.
Deuteronomy had already warned Israel’s future king:
“He shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Deuteronomy 17:17.
That command existed before David occupied Jerusalem.
And long before Solomon filled his palace.
So when Scripture later tells us that David acquired additional wives and concubines, the mere fact that the historical narrative records it cannot erase the standard God had already revealed.
Some readers raise 2 Samuel 12:8, where through Nathan God describes giving David Saul’s house and Saul’s wives “into your arms” or “into your bosom.”
Does that prove God morally commanded David to practice polygamy or concubinage?
That conclusion goes beyond what the passage requires.

The context is Nathan confronting David after David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged Uriah’s death. The language emphasizes everything associated with Saul’s royal house and kingdom being placed under David’s authority. It magnifies the enormity of David’s ingratitude: God had given him abundance, yet David seized what belonged to another man.
Whatever complexities surround the ancient royal-household language, 2 Samuel 12 cannot reasonably be used to cancel Deuteronomy 17:17 or the creation pattern to which Jesus Himself later appeals.
And then there is Solomon.
If sheer biblical description meant divine approval, Solomon would be the strongest case imaginable.
First Kings 11:3 tells us:
“He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines.”
A thousand women.
Power beyond imagination.
Political alliances.
Royal prestige.
Everything an ancient king could use to convince himself that excess meant blessing.
Then Scripture gives the verdict.
“His wives turned away his heart.”
1 Kings 11:3.
There it is.
The very danger Deuteronomy warned about became Solomon’s tragedy.
The wisest king alive became foolish enough to allow divided affection to produce divided worship.
The issue was not simply that Solomon had “too much love.”
His heart moved away from exclusive loyalty to the LORD.
That is where sin eventually takes us.
It promises expansion.
Then produces fragmentation.
It promises freedom.
Then demands allegiance.
It tells us God will understand.
Then slowly teaches our hearts to live without asking what God actually desires.
And perhaps nowhere is the ugliness surrounding concubinage more emotionally devastating than Judges 19.
There, a concubine becomes the victim of horrific sexual violence and dies.
The chapter is supposed to disturb you.
Judges is showing a society collapsing under sin.
Its recurring diagnosis is chilling:
“Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
Judges 21:25.
That is not a celebration of Israelite morality.
It is an indictment of it.
The Bible refuses to airbrush what human rebellion does to people.
Especially vulnerable people.
Especially women.
Especially those whose suffering powerful people would rather forget.
That is one reason the Bible can be so uncomfortable.
It tells the truth.
It does not manufacture flawless heroes.
Abraham needs grace.
Jacob needs grace.
Judah needs grace.
David needs grace.
Solomon needs grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And perhaps this is where the question changes.
We began by asking:
“Did God approve of concubines?”
But underneath that question may be another one.
“What has God tolerated in my life that I have mistaken for His approval?”
That question gets closer.
Maybe nothing catastrophic happened after your compromise.
Maybe the relationship survived.
Maybe nobody discovered the messages.
Maybe the addiction remains hidden.
Maybe the bitterness has become so familiar that you call it personality.
Maybe you keep saying, “God understands,” when deep inside you know the Holy Spirit has been calling you to surrender.
God’s patience should never be confused with permission.
Romans 2:4 says that God’s kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
Not deeper into hiding.
Repentance.
The Greek word is μετάνοια — metanoia.
It carries the idea of a changed mind, a turning—a transformation of how we understand our sin before God that produces a changed direction.
Christian repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns toward God.
It brings the hidden thing into the light.
It stops negotiating.
It stops asking how close to the edge we can live while still calling ourselves faithful.
And this is where Jesus becomes more than the conclusion to an argument about ancient marriage.
Jesus becomes our only hope.
Because if the Bible were merely a record of good people earning God’s approval, its pages would be remarkably empty.
Instead, Scripture is filled with scandal.
Broken families.
Sexual failure.
Deception.
Violence.
Pride.
Betrayal.
People making promises they cannot keep.
People receiving mercy they do not deserve.
And through all that wreckage, God keeps moving history toward Christ.
Jesus does not enter the story because humanity finally became respectable.
He enters because humanity needs redemption.
At the cross, Jesus does not call evil good.
He bears sin’s judgment.
He does not redefine rebellion until it becomes acceptable.
He offers forgiveness to rebels.
He does not tell sinners to clean themselves perfectly before approaching Him.
He calls them to repent and believe.
And the blood of Christ reaches places shame told you God would never touch.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Power to become new.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
2 Corinthians 5:21.
Christianity is not the announcement that your past never mattered.
It is the announcement that your past does not have to be your master anymore.
Maybe your scandal does not involve concubines.
Maybe it was adultery.
Pornography.
A secret relationship.
A divorce filled with wounds nobody understands.
Sex outside marriage.
A pregnancy surrounded by shame.
Years of manipulation.
A marriage you damaged.
Someone you betrayed.
Someone who betrayed you.
Or maybe your scandal has nothing to do with sexuality at all.
Maybe it is pride.
Greed.
Hatred.
Religious hypocrisy.
A hidden addiction.
A double life.
You know the sentence you are terrified someone will someday say about you.
Jesus already knows it.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Let Him change you.
This is why the Bible’s broken characters should never become excuses for our sin.
They should become evidence that God is astonishingly capable of redeeming sinners.
The scandal is real.
But grace gets the final word for everyone who comes to Christ.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Simply comment, “No more hiding,” if today you are choosing surrender over excuses.
Or comment, “Jesus, forgive me,” if your heart knows exactly what needs to be brought before Him.
And if you are exhausted from fighting, comment, “Pray for me.”
There are moments when another believer needs to know that the person sitting silently beside them is fighting too.
Not because saving a post makes anyone righteous, but because there may come a night when compromise starts sounding reasonable again and you need to remember:
God’s patience is not permission.
His grace is calling you home.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in worship, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and lives surrendered to Him.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical truth reach another person.
Jesus is calling sinners home.
The God who saw Hagar still sees the forgotten.
The God who disciplined David still forgives the repentant.
The God who warned Solomon still calls divided hearts back to Himself.
And the Savior who spoke about marriage by pointing humanity back to the beginning is also the Savior who went to a cross to redeem people who have wandered far from God’s design.
So do not use Abraham to excuse what God is asking you to surrender.
Do not use David to baptize compromise.
Do not use Solomon to make excess look harmless.
Do not mistake what Scripture records for what God recommends.
Look instead at Jesus.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
There is your standard.
There is your mercy.
There is your hope.
There is your way home.
Someone needs your testimony.
Someone needs to discover that repentance did not destroy you.
It brought you home.
Someone needs to hear that grace did not make your sin acceptable.
Grace made redemption possible.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing in all these scandalous biblical stories is not that human beings could fall so terribly.
We already know they can.
The shocking thing is that God kept pursuing sinners.
Until eventually He came Himself.
And when the nails went through the hands of Jesus, God proved once and for all that He was not interested in pretending our scandal did not exist.
He intended to redeem us from it.
Never confuse God’s patience with His approval—but never confuse the depth of your failure with the limit of His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD LOVES A CHEERFUL GIVER—BUT WHAT IF PAUL WAS TALKING ABOUT MORE THAN YOUR MONEY?
paragraphs: GOD LOVES A CHEERFUL GIVER—BUT WHAT IF PAUL WAS TALKING ABOUT MORE THAN YOUR MONEY?

We turned one of the most beautiful passages about grace, willingness, generosity, and Christlike love into a sentence about the offering plate. Paul’s actual message goes much deeper—and it may expose the one thing you have been withholding from God.
There is a sentence Christians know so well that sometimes we stop hearing it.
“God loves a cheerful giver.”
You have heard it before an offering.
You have seen it printed on envelopes.
You may have heard it quoted while someone was raising funds for a church building, a ministry project, a missionary, or a person in need.
And yes—the passage absolutely involves money.
We should not pretend otherwise.
But if all we hear is money, we can quote Paul correctly while missing the breathtaking Gospel reality surrounding his words.
Because when Paul wrote:
“God loves a cheerful giver,”
he was not handing the Church a clever fundraising slogan.
He was describing what grace can do to a human heart.
And that changes everything.
The words appear in 2 Corinthians 9:7. In Greek, the crucial portion reads:
“ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.”
Hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos.
“For God loves a cheerful giver.”
The word translated “cheerful” is ἱλαρόν — hilaron, from hilaros.
It carries the sense of cheerful, glad, willing, gracious giving—not giving dragged painfully out of someone by pressure.
But notice what Paul says immediately before it:
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion…”
That matters.
The Greek expression translated “under compulsion” is ἐξ ἀνάγκης — ex anankēs.
Out of necessity.
Under constraint.
Because you feel forced.
Paul is drawing a line between generosity flowing freely from the heart and giving extracted through pressure.
That means this verse should never become a weapon for manipulating people.
“God loves a cheerful giver” does not mean:
“Give me money if you really love God.”
It does not mean:
“Prove your faith by giving beyond wisdom.”
It does not mean:
“God will love you more if your offering is bigger.”
And it certainly does not mean that salvation, favor, healing, forgiveness, or blessing can be purchased.
The Gospel destroys that idea.
Grace cannot be bought.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Forgiveness cannot be bought.
Eternal life cannot be bought.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith…”
That is Ephesians 2:8.
But here is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Sometimes we defend ourselves against manipulative teaching so aggressively that we quietly create another error.
We hear, “God does not need my money,” and somehow turn it into:
“Therefore God has no claim upon anything I possess.”
My money.
My schedule.
My home.
My gifts.
My attention.
My influence.
My reputation.
My comfort.
My plans.
My voice.
My opportunities.
My life.
Mine.
Mine.
Mine.
And perhaps that little word reveals more about our hearts than we realize.
Because Scripture’s vision of generosity is bigger than an offering envelope.

Paul’s immediate subject in 2 Corinthians 8–9 really is a financial collection for needy believers. We must preserve that context. He is encouraging the Corinthians to complete the gift they had previously desired to give.
But Paul places that financial generosity inside something much larger.
Grace.
Again and again, grace surrounds the discussion.
And at the center of Paul’s appeal stands Jesus Christ.
“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 8:9, “that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.”
There it is.
The deepest Christian reason for giving is not guilt.
It is Christ.
Before Paul asks believers to look at their possessions, he makes them look at Jesus.
Look at Him.
The eternal Son did not cling selfishly to privilege.
He came.
He humbled Himself.
He served.
He touched people others avoided.
He welcomed sinners.
He gave Himself.
And ultimately, He went to the cross.
Christian generosity begins there.
Not with your wallet.
With His wounds.
Not with what someone can pressure out of you.
With what Christ freely gave for you.
