And if you have never trusted Christ, Christianity is not an invitation to become impressive enough for God.
It is an invitation to admit that you aren't.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Christ died for sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
The Savior Abraham's story ultimately anticipated has come.
And the question is no longer whether you can make yourself worthy of Him.
You cannot.
The question is whether you will stop hiding and entrust yourself to the One who saves sinners.
Talk to God.
Tell Him the truth.
Somebody hiding in shame may need to see evidence that repentance is not the end of the story.
Not because every sentence will be needed today.
Because old fears have a habit of returning in new locations.
And when yours does, come back to Genesis 20 and remember:
Abraham's repeated weakness did not make God unfaithful.
Let them meet Abraham in Genesis 20.
Then let them meet Jesus.
If you want to glorify God through what He has entrusted to you, prayerfully consider whether supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work can be one expression of your stewardship.
“No more hiding.”
Abraham did it again.
God knew.
God intervened.
God confronted.
God preserved.
God restored.
And generations later, God sent the One Abraham could never be—the perfectly obedient Son who carried our sin to a cross and walked out of a grave.
So when the enemy points at the chapter you wish could be deleted, point him toward the empty tomb.
Your worst chapter may explain some of your scars—but when you belong to Christ, it does not get to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOB MADE A COVENANT WITH HIS EYES—Was He Saying He Never NOTICED an Attractive Woman?
paragraphs: JOB MADE A COVENANT WITH HIS EYES—Was He Saying He Never NOTICED an Attractive Woman?
Job 31:1 is not telling you to become blind to beauty. It is exposing what can happen in the terrifying distance between what your eyes notice…and what your heart decides to do next.
There is a difference between seeing someone beautiful…
and deciding to keep looking.
That difference may last only a few seconds.
But sometimes those few seconds reveal a war happening inside the soul.

Job said something thousands of years ago that still confronts a man holding a smartphone at midnight, a woman scrolling through somebody else's life, a married person lingering over someone who is not their spouse, and a Christian quietly wondering whether simply noticing that another human being is attractive means they have already sinned.
“I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?” — Job 31:1, KJV
But read it in the language in which Job comes down to us in the Hebrew Scriptures:
בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי וּמָה אֶתְבּוֹנֵן עַל־בְּתוּלָה
Berit karati le'enai; umah etbonen al-betulah.
A close sense of the words is:
“I made a covenant with my eyes; why then should I gaze intently upon a maiden?”
That matters.
A lot.
Because Job was not claiming that his eyes had somehow stopped functioning.
He wasn't saying he had lost the ability to recognize beauty.
He wasn't claiming that an attractive woman could walk past him and his brain would somehow fail to register that she was attractive.
The issue runs deeper.

The Hebrew verb behind “think upon” in the KJV is related to bin, a word associated with considering, discerning, attending to, or contemplating. Here the form אֶתְבּוֹנֵן — etbonen carries the idea of directing one's attention toward something, not merely having an involuntary visual encounter.
Some translations therefore render Job's statement with the language of “gazing.”
That distinction is enormously important.
Because there is a difference between the first look that tells you someone is there…
and the second kind of look that begins asking the heart to stay.
There is a difference between recognition and fixation.
Between seeing and feeding.
Between noticing beauty and mentally undressing the person carrying it.
Between an image entering your field of vision and you inviting that image to build a bedroom inside your imagination.
And Job knew the difference.
The rest of Job 31 proves it.
A few verses later, Job says something remarkably revealing:
“If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes…” — Job 31:7.
Read those words again.
“My heart walked after mine eyes.”
There is the danger.
The eyes see.
Then the heart can begin to follow.
Job's concern wasn't merely that his eyes possessed the ability to see. His concern was what his heart might do with what his eyes had seen.
And then he becomes even more explicit:
“If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour's door…” — Job 31:9.
Now the picture becomes clearer.
This chapter isn't fundamentally about pretending physical attraction doesn't exist.
It is about integrity.
Desire.
Faithfulness.
Intentionality.
Sexual purity.
And the refusal to cultivate desire that dishonors another person, another marriage, your own marriage, or God.
Job understood something our generation desperately needs to rediscover:
You cannot always control what enters your eyes.
But you can begin learning, by the grace of God, what you permit your heart to do with it.
And that is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because some of us haven't merely noticed.
We returned.
We zoomed in.
We searched the name.
We opened the profile.
We watched another video.
We told ourselves it was innocent.
We deleted the history.
We waited until everyone was asleep.
We learned exactly how long to stare without getting caught.
We followed accounts we would be embarrassed to open beside our spouse.
We entertained conversations we would never want read aloud.
And somewhere along the way, something that began with the eyes started walking toward the heart.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your wife doesn't know.
Your husband doesn't know.
Your parents don't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your small group doesn't know.
The people who see your Bible verses online certainly don't know.
But God does.
And Job knew that too.
Immediately after speaking about his covenant with his eyes, he asks what his portion would be from God above, and then says:
“Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?” — Job 31:4.
That is the deeper foundation beneath Job's covenant.
Job lived with the consciousness that God saw him.
Not merely his public behavior.
His ways.
His steps.
His heart.
His private integrity.
And before you interpret that as nothing but terrifying surveillance, remember where the Gospel eventually takes this story of human sin.
Because Christianity does not announce merely:
“God saw what you did.”
Christianity announces something infinitely more astonishing:
God saw what you did…
and Christ came for sinners anyway.
That does not make sin smaller.
It makes grace bigger.
Jesus takes the battle of Job 31 and drives it even deeper into the human heart.
“You have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you…”
And then Jesus moves from the external act to the internal intention.
“Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.” — Matthew 5:27–28.
The Greek is piercing.
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
The construction points toward looking with lustful desire—with the looking directed toward desire.
Again, the issue is not the biological ability to recognize that another human being is attractive.
Jesus is exposing the heart that turns looking into lusting.
He refuses to let us hide behind the defense:
“But I never touched anybody.”
Because your hands can remain technically innocent while your imagination becomes a secret adulterer.
You can remain physically faithful while repeatedly rehearsing unfaithfulness in your mind.
You can sit beside the person you promised to love while feeding desire for somebody on a screen who doesn't even know your name.
And pornography has industrialized this tragedy.
It takes human beings made in the image of God and trains the consumer to experience them as products.
Swipe.
Watch.
Discard.
Another.
Another.
Another.
Bodies without covenant.
Pleasure without responsibility.
Desire without sacrifice.
Intimacy without being known.
And then real marriage can begin feeling painfully ordinary because fantasy has trained the mind to demand endless novelty.
But listen carefully.
This article was not written to crush the person who is already ashamed.
It was written to expose the hiding place so Jesus can meet you there.
Maybe you have failed your covenant with your eyes.
Maybe badly.
Maybe repeatedly.
Maybe last night.
Maybe five minutes before you found this article.
Your failure is serious.
But your failure does not have the authority to write the final chapter of your life.
Jesus does.
This is where scandal meets grace.
The scandal is not merely that human beings lust.
The deeper scandal is that people created to worship God repeatedly exchange His glory for desires that cannot satisfy them.
Yet the breathtaking scandal of grace is that the holy Son of God willingly moved toward sinners.
Jesus did not die because our sins were insignificant.
He died because sin was so serious that reconciliation cost blood.
At the cross, Christ did not excuse darkness.
He entered it.
He carried sin.
He bore judgment.
And He opened the door to forgiveness for people who finally stop pretending they do not need it.
The Gospel does not say:
Clean yourself completely, then come to Jesus.
It says:
Come to Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Repentance is not negotiating with God.
It is surrender.

It is bringing the hidden browser history, the fantasy, the emotional affair, the wandering eyes, the secret messages, the pornography, the shame, the excuses, and the double life into the light and saying:
“Jesus, I cannot keep calling this freedom when it is making me a slave.”
And perhaps that is the covenant some people reading this need to make tonight.
Not:
“I promise I will never notice another beautiful human being again.”
That is neither realistic nor what Job 31:1 requires us to pretend.
Instead:
“My eyes do not get to command my heart.”
“I will not deliberately feed what Christ is calling me to starve.”
“I will not turn another person made in God's image into material for my private imagination.”
“I will stop protecting the very thing that is destroying me.”
“I will flee what I have been trying to manage.”
“I will confess what I have been trying to hide.”
“I will bring my sexuality under the lordship of Jesus Christ.”
And when you fail?
Do not turn grace into permission to keep sinning.
But do not turn failure into permission to run away from Christ either.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Get back up.
Remove access where necessary.
Stop pretending unlimited access is spiritual maturity.
Sometimes wisdom looks like unfollowing.
Deleting.
Blocking.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Ending the conversation.
Installing accountability.
Confessing to a mature believer.
Telling the truth to your spouse where appropriate and seeking wise pastoral or professional help for how to navigate the consequences faithfully.

Jesus spoke with startling seriousness about dealing radically with what leads us into sin in the very context of lust in Matthew 5:29–30. His language is deliberately severe because sin is not a pet to domesticate.
Some temptations are not meant to be stared down.
They are meant to be fled.
Joseph did not stand beside Potiphar's wife trying to demonstrate how spiritually mature he was.
He ran.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is leave the room.
And please understand something else.
Biblical purity is not hatred of women.
It is not fear of women.
It is not treating every attractive woman as a dangerous object responsible for a man's thoughts.
Women are not temptations wearing skin.
They are image-bearers.
Men are image-bearers too.
Biblical purity teaches us to see people as people rather than reducing them to what their bodies can make us feel.
That changes everything.
You can acknowledge beauty without claiming it.
You can appreciate another human being without consuming them in your imagination.
You can see without possessing.
You can notice without nurturing lust.
And through the transforming work of Christ, your eyes can gradually learn to serve love rather than appetite.
That is far more beautiful than simply trying not to look.
Job made a covenant with his eyes because Job understood that eyes can become doors.
But Jesus wants more than guarded doors.
He wants the house.
Your heart.
Your imagination.
Your desires.
Your wounds.
Your sexuality.
Your memories.
Even the parts of you that embarrass you.
Especially the parts you've been hiding.
Because Christianity is not behavior modification wrapped in religious vocabulary.
The Gospel is resurrection.
Dead people made alive in Christ.
Slaves becoming sons and daughters.
The guilty being justified.
The unclean being washed.
The ashamed learning to stand in grace.
And sinners discovering that holiness is not payment for God's love.
It becomes the fruit of having been loved by God.
Maybe you came into this article wondering whether Job ever noticed an attractive woman.
Maybe the better question is:
What happens inside you after you notice?
Where do your eyes take your heart?
And where has your heart been taking you?
Be honest.
Not with me.
With God.
Because perhaps beneath the polished Christian image there is a tired person saying:
“I don't want to live divided anymore.”
Then don't hide behind shame tonight.
Bring it to Jesus.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9.
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
That doesn't mean consequences instantly disappear.
It doesn't mean temptation never returns.
It means your sin does not have to remain your secret master.
Christ can forgive you.
Christ can cleanse you.
Christ can teach you another way to see.
Christ can rebuild what lust damaged.
Christ can restore integrity where compromise hollowed you out.
Christ can teach a wandering heart to come home.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished religious answer.
There is no trophy for pretending.
Grace meets truth.
And somebody reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle nobody can see.
Not because every sentence feels comfortable.
Seeing is not the same as surrendering.
Temptation is not permission.
Failure is not final.
And Jesus is still worth obeying.
You don't have to know who they are.
Just share it.
Sometimes the person who needs a message most desperately will never click “like.”
They will never comment.
They may never tell you.
But at 1:37 in the morning, when everyone else is asleep and their secret battle is screaming again, they may remember the article you shared.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you grow closer to Christ, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support earns salvation.
It never could.
Scripture says, “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through guilt.
Your support helps us keep writing, publishing, expanding, and placing Christ-centered truth in front of people who may be scrolling through Facebook carrying battles nobody else knows about.
And sharing costs nothing.

One share can put the Gospel in front of a friend you didn't know was searching. One tag can reach someone who has been quietly drifting. One saved article can return to somebody at exactly the moment they are ready to stop hiding.
But the greatest reason to stay connected isn't merchandise.
It is Jesus.
Give because you want Christ proclaimed.
Share because someone else may need what helped you.
Tag because sometimes love means refusing to let someone fight alone.
Save because truth forgotten in daylight may be desperately needed in the darkness.
Follow because your soul needs more than whatever the algorithm happens to feed it.
Job made a covenant with his eyes.
Jesus goes deeper.
He wants the heart behind them.
And maybe tonight the greatest miracle isn't that you finally stop seeing temptation.
Maybe the miracle is that, little by little, Jesus becomes more beautiful to you than the thing that has been stealing your eyes.
Your eyes may have wandered through a thousand secret places—but grace still knows the road that leads your heart home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SOLOMON MARRIED PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER—AND BUILT HER A SEPARATE HOUSE
paragraphs: SOLOMON MARRIED PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER—AND BUILT HER A SEPARATE HOUSE
The wisest man alive could build a house for the woman he loved—but he could not build a wall strong enough to protect a heart that slowly stopped listening to God.
There is a sentence buried in the story of Solomon that is easy to read too quickly.
It sounds political.
Almost harmless.
Until you know how the story ends.
“Solomon made also an house for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had taken to wife…” — 1 Kings 7:8, KJV.
Read that again.
Pharaoh’s daughter.
Egyptian royalty.
Married to the king of Israel.
And Solomon built her a house.

This was not gossip invented centuries later. First Kings explicitly tells us that Solomon entered a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt and took Pharaoh’s daughter as his wife. The Hebrew of 1 Kings 3:1 opens:
וַיִּתְחַתֵּן שְׁלֹמֹה אֶת־פַּרְעֹה מֶלֶךְ מִצְרָיִם
Vayyitchatten Shelomoh et-Par‘oh melekh Mitsrayim…
In context, Solomon formed a marriage alliance with Pharaoh, king of Egypt, took Pharaoh’s daughter, and brought her into the City of David while his great building projects were still underway.
Then 1 Kings 7:8 quietly tells us that Solomon constructed a residence for her.
Later, 1 Kings 9:24 records Pharaoh’s daughter moving up from the City of David to the house Solomon had built for her.
There is something haunting about that progression.
A marriage.
A palace.
A kingdom flourishing.
A king renowned for wisdom.
And eventually…
a heart wandering from God.
But be careful here.

We must not accuse Pharaoh’s daughter of things Scripture does not accuse her of. The Bible does not tell us that Solomon built her separate residence because she personally demanded it. It does not tell us that this particular palace caused Solomon’s apostasy. It does not give us permission to invent private conversations between them.
Scripture is powerful enough without our embellishment.
And the truth Scripture actually gives us is far more disturbing.
Because Solomon’s greatest danger was never simply that an Egyptian princess entered his palace.
The greatest danger was that compromise eventually entered Solomon’s heart.
And that should frighten anyone who has ever whispered:
“I know what God says…but I can handle this.”
Solomon could have said something very few human beings could ever say.
God had appeared to him.
He had received extraordinary wisdom.
Kings listened to him.
Nations knew his reputation.
His wealth was staggering.
His kingdom was magnificent.
He built the temple.
He prayed publicly.
He offered sacrifices.
He spoke wisdom that generations would remember.
And yet none of those things made him immune to spiritual drift.
That may be the first wound this story opens in us:
Knowing truth is not the same thing as surrendering to truth.
You can know Scripture and still negotiate with it.
You can give somebody else excellent advice while secretly refusing God’s counsel in your own life.
You can recognize foolishness instantly when another person commits it and somehow rename the same foolishness “complicated” when it becomes yours.
You can worship publicly while compromising privately.
You can build beautiful things for God while allowing something dangerous to be built inside your own heart.
And Solomon?
Solomon was warned before his palace ever existed.
Long before his reign, Israel’s law had already spoken about its future kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim, ve-lo yasur levavo…
In straightforward sense:
He must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
The Hebrew words strike painfully when placed beside Solomon’s biography.
יַרְבֶּה — yarbeh: to multiply, increase, make numerous.
נָשִׁים — nashim: women/wives.
לְבָבוֹ — levavo: his heart.
יָסוּר — yasur: turn aside, depart.
God’s warning involved the heart.
And when Kings later describes Solomon’s collapse, what does the narrator emphasize?
His heart.

First Kings 11 tells us Solomon loved many foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter, and says his wives turned his heart toward other gods. By his old age, his heart was no longer wholly devoted to the LORD.
Do you see the tragedy?
The warning came first.
The fulfillment came later.
And between those two moments was enough time for compromise to feel normal.
That is how spiritual drift often works.
Not with thunder.
Not with someone waking one morning and announcing, “Today I will destroy my relationship with God.”
It happens quietly.
One justification.
One affection we refuse to surrender.
One command we reinterpret because obedience would cost too much.
One boundary moved.
Then another.
One compromise that seems survivable because judgment does not fall immediately.
And after enough time, the thing that once troubled your conscience can start living comfortably inside your life.
Maybe that is why Solomon’s story feels uncomfortably modern.
Because you do not need 700 wives and 300 concubines to understand a divided heart.
You just need one thing you love more than obedience.
One relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
One hidden habit you keep defending.
One appetite you feed while starving your prayer life.
One resentment you refuse to release.
One private browser history nobody knows about.
One secret conversation you would panic to see projected on a church wall.
One ambition for which you would quietly compromise conviction.
One idol with a respectable Christian name taped over it.
And perhaps you keep telling yourself:
“I’m still close to God.”
“I still go to church.”
“I still pray.”
“I still post Bible verses.”
“I still believe.”
“I’m not like those people.”
Neither did Solomon begin as the old king described in 1 Kings 11.
That is the terrifying part.
Spiritual collapse can begin while everything still looks successful.
The temple can still be standing.
The palace can still be beautiful.
The bank account can still be full.
The reputation can still be intact.
People can still admire you.
And your heart can already be moving.
Slowly.
Quietly.
Away.
Solomon’s story destroys the illusion that wisdom alone will save us from sin.
Education cannot crucify the flesh.
Intelligence cannot replace obedience.
Biblical knowledge cannot substitute for a surrendered heart.
A person can understand consequences intellectually and still walk directly toward them spiritually.
There are people reading this right now who know exactly what God has been confronting them about.
Not somebody else.
You.
There is a door you know you should close.
A relationship requiring truth.
A secret requiring confession.
A habit requiring repentance.
A bitterness requiring forgiveness.
A compromise requiring surrender.
And perhaps you have become extremely intelligent at explaining why today is not the day.
Solomon knew wisdom.
But knowing what is wise and choosing what is holy are not identical.
Eventually 1 Kings stops describing merely what Solomon possessed and begins describing what Solomon worshiped.
That is where the story becomes devastating.

The king who built the temple of the LORD eventually built high places connected with the gods of his foreign wives. First Kings 11 says Solomon went after other gods and built a high place for Chemosh and for Molech; the chapter explicitly concludes that Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow Him.
Think about the symbolism.
Hands capable of building something magnificent for the worship of Yahweh were also capable of building what dishonored Yahweh.
Same hands.
Same king.
Different allegiance emerging from a divided heart.
And suddenly this stops being ancient history.
Because what are your hands building?
What is your money building?
What are your clicks building?
What are your relationships building?
What is your attention building?
What is your private life building?
You can build a Christian image while constructing an altar to approval.
You can build a career while sacrificing your family.
You can build followers while losing intimacy with Christ.
You can build theological knowledge while becoming proud.
You can build financial security until money becomes the god you would never call a god.
You can build a ministry while secretly craving applause more than the presence of Jesus.
The question is not merely:
“What have I accomplished?”
The deeper question is:
What is my heart becoming while I accomplish it?
Because Solomon’s tragedy was not that he lacked wisdom.
It was that his heart eventually refused to remain wholly surrendered to the God who gave him wisdom.
And here the story could leave us crushed.
Except the Bible is not ultimately the story of Solomon.
It is the story that leads us beyond Solomon.
To Jesus.
Centuries later, Jesus spoke astonishing words about Himself:
“Behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” — Matthew 12:42.
Greater than Solomon.
Solomon was a son of David.
Jesus is the promised Son of David.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom.
Christ is greater.
Solomon ruled a kingdom whose glory faded.
Christ reigns with a kingdom that will not pass away.
Solomon’s heart turned.
Christ remained obedient.
Solomon accumulated glory and eventually compromised.
Jesus possessed divine glory and humbled Himself.
Solomon built a temple.
Jesus spoke of His own body in temple language and, through His death and resurrection, accomplished what stone buildings never could: reconciliation between sinful people and the holy God.
Solomon shows us what even the wisest fallen king cannot do.
Jesus shows us the King we actually need.
Because your deepest problem is not that you need better advice.
You need redemption.
You do not merely need someone to tell you which road is wrong.
You need a Savior who can forgive you for all the times you knowingly walked down it.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who successfully kept every room of their lives clean.
He came for sinners.
For adulterers.
For liars.
For hypocrites.
For addicts.
For the proud.
For the sexually broken.
For the religious performer.
For the person whose public life and private life no longer recognize each other.
For people who knew better and did it anyway.
For people ashamed of what they became.
For people who thought they had gone too far.
Christ came.
Christ obeyed.
Christ was crucified.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
And forgiveness is not purchased by pretending your sin was small.
Grace becomes breathtaking when you finally admit that your sin was real.
Repentance is not saying, “I made a few unfortunate choices.”
Repentance says:
“Lord, I have sinned. I have defended what You condemned. I have loved things more than I loved obedience. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me because of Jesus Christ.”
And the Gospel answers the repentant sinner not with a self-improvement program but with a Person.
Jesus.
The greater Solomon.
The faithful King.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
Maybe you have built your own version of Solomon’s palace.
Something beautiful enough to hide what is happening underneath.
Everyone thinks you are okay.
You laugh.
You work.
You post.
You serve.
You worship.
You tell people, “God is good.”
And He is.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know.
Something has been pulling your heart away.
Listen carefully:
Do not wait until a compromise becomes an altar.
Do not wait until an appetite becomes a master.
Do not wait until secrecy becomes captivity.
Do not wait until the thing you once controlled begins controlling you.
Bring it to Christ now.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Repentance does not mean God finally discovers what you have done.
He already knows.
Repentance means you stop running from the One who already knows and still calls sinners to come.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is forgiveness for the guilty.
There is cleansing for the defiled.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is freedom for the captive.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the blood of Jesus does.
Maybe this exposed something you have been hiding even from yourself.
Then do not turn this moment into another piece of Christian content you consume, react to, and forget.
Talk to God.
Confess specifically.
Turn specifically.
Ask for help specifically.
Bring another mature believer into the battle if secrecy has been feeding your bondage.
You do not have to publish the details of your struggle. God does not require you to expose private wounds to strangers online.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years constructing.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer still fighting.
Not because an algorithm needs another save, but because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday’s convictions feel distant tomorrow.
Come back when compromise starts sounding reasonable again.
Come back when you begin believing that wisdom makes you invulnerable.
Come back and remember Solomon.
Then remember the greater Solomon.
Jesus Christ.
Protect your heart.
Stay close to Jesus.
Do not let a small compromise negotiate for permanent residence.
And send this privately to the person who would never comment publicly but may read every word alone tonight.
That is what sharing Christian truth should be about.
Not numbers.
Not vanity.
Not making Gospel Warrior famous.
People.
Souls.
Christ.
Truth traveling farther than we could carry it ourselves.
It does not.
It does not.
Not because you must support Gospel Warrior in order to glorify God.
Scripture never gives any ministry the right to make that claim.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and Christian giving is to be willing rather than coerced.
It is to surrender.
Solomon had wealth.
Palaces.
Wisdom.
Influence.
Recognition.
A magnificent temple.
And still his heart could wander.
So perhaps the prayer we need is much simpler than we imagined:
Jesus, keep my heart.
When success comes, keep my heart.
When temptation whispers, keep my heart.
When compromise looks harmless, keep my heart.
When everyone applauds me, keep my heart.
When nobody sees me, keep my heart.
When I am old and tired and tempted to loosen convictions I once defended, keep my heart.
And when I fail, lead me quickly—not into hiding—but back to the cross.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that Solomon built Pharaoh’s daughter a house.
The deeper warning is that a man can build extraordinary things while his own heart slowly moves away from God.
And the greatest hope is not that we can become wiser than Solomon.
It is that One greater than Solomon has come.
His name is Jesus.
And when a sinner turns to Him, the final word does not have to be scandal.
It can be grace.
Because one day the palace will be gone.
The applause will be gone.
The achievements will be gone.
The things we fought so desperately to possess will belong to somebody else.
And when everything we built has finally become dust, one question will still matter:
Who had your heart?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PROVERBS WARNS ABOUT A MARRIED WOMAN WHO SAYS HER HUSBAND IS AWAY—THEN INVITES A YOUNG MAN TO HER BED
paragraphs: PROVERBS WARNS ABOUT A MARRIED WOMAN WHO SAYS HER HUSBAND IS AWAY—THEN INVITES A YOUNG MAN TO HER BED

He thought he was walking toward pleasure. Scripture says he was walking toward slaughter. And the most terrifying part of Proverbs 7 is that the trap did not begin in the bedroom—it began long before he reached the door.
There is a moment in Proverbs 7 that feels almost uncomfortably modern.
Night has fallen.
A young man is walking through the city.
He knows where he is going.
A married woman meets him.
She is persuasive. Bold. Prepared.
Her bed has already been arranged. The room is perfumed. Her words are carefully chosen.
Then comes the sentence designed to remove the final obstacle from his conscience:
Her husband is away.
Nobody will know.
There is time.
There is opportunity.
Come inside.
And somewhere between temptation and consequence, this young man makes a decision that Proverbs describes with one of the most frightening images in the entire chapter:
He follows her like an ox walking toward slaughter.
That is Proverbs 7.
But before anyone turns this chapter into nothing more than a warning about “dangerous women,” we need to read what Scripture actually says.
Because God is exposing something much deeper.
He is showing us what temptation does to the human heart.
And whether you are male or female, married or single, young or old, there may be something in this ancient nighttime scene that knows your address.
The chapter begins before the woman ever appears.
A father is pleading with his son to treasure wisdom.
Keep my words.
Guard my commands.
Write them upon your heart.
Make wisdom so intimate to you that it becomes like family.
Why?
Because eventually there will come a moment when obedience will cost you something.
Eventually there will be a night when desire starts arguing with truth.
Eventually something forbidden may become available.
And in that moment, you probably will not have time to build convictions you never developed.
That is why Proverbs 7 begins with wisdom before it introduces temptation.
The battle is often decided before the temptation arrives.
Then the father looks through his window.
He sees young men outside, but one catches his attention.
The Hebrew describes him as:
נַעַר חֲסַר־לֵב — naʿar ḥasar-lēv
A young man “lacking heart.”

In biblical Hebrew, this does not simply mean he is unintelligent. The “heart” is associated with the inner center of judgment, understanding, desire, and moral discernment. The picture is of a young man lacking the wisdom necessary to recognize where his choices are taking him. Proverbs identifies him among the peta’im—the naïve or inexperienced.
And notice something uncomfortable.
He is not simply standing innocently somewhere when temptation kidnaps him.
He is moving.
Toward her corner.
Toward her street.
Toward her house.
The Hebrew verb in the passage conveys his movement in that direction. The NET textual notes observe that the wording portrays the youth intentionally making his way toward her house.
That matters.
Because sometimes we ask God to deliver us from temptations toward which we keep deliberately walking.
We pray for purity while keeping the conversation alive.
We pray for freedom while reopening the private message.
We ask God to remove feelings we continue feeding.
We say, “Nothing has happened.”
But we keep walking down the street.
We keep getting closer to the corner.
We keep telling ourselves we know our limits.
Maybe that is where this chapter becomes personal.
Because adultery rarely begins in a bed.
It can begin with attention.
A conversation.
A secret.
A message deleted before your spouse sees it.
A friendship you would struggle to explain honestly.
An emotional connection that becomes more intimate than it should.
A second glance that becomes a fantasy.
A fantasy that becomes a conversation.
A conversation that becomes an arrangement.
And somewhere along the way, the heart begins manufacturing permission for what conscience once called wrong.
Then she appears.

Proverbs describes the woman as married and sexually unfaithful. The language translated in various English versions as the “strange,” “foreign,” “wayward,” or adulterous woman should not automatically be understood as an ethnic description. In this context, scholars and translation notes recognize the terminology as describing a woman morally outside covenant faithfulness—an adulterous or sexually unfaithful woman.
And she knows how to speak.
That detail matters enormously.
Proverbs 7 repeatedly focuses on words.
Smooth words.
Persuasive words.
Flattering words.
The Hebrew behind this imagery is connected with making something smooth or slippery—the language becomes an instrument of seduction.
Temptation rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I have come to destroy your marriage.”
It says:
“You deserve to feel wanted.”
It does not say:
“I want to damage your children.”
It says:
“Nobody understands you like I do.”
It does not say:
“I want to weaken your relationship with God.”
It says:
“It is only one conversation.”
It does not say:
“This secret will eventually own you.”
It whispers:
“Nobody needs to know.”
Sin has always been talented at renaming itself.
Lust becomes “chemistry.”
Emotional adultery becomes “connection.”
Compromise becomes “complicated.”
Secrecy becomes “privacy.”
And rebellion becomes “following your heart.”
Then Proverbs takes us into the room.
She tells him that her bed has been prepared.
Perfumed.
Ready.
Then comes the invitation.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 7:18 reads:
לְכָה נִרְוֶה דֹדִים עַד־הַבֹּקֶר
Lekhah nirveh dodim ʿad-ha-boqer.
In context, the sense is:
Come, let us drink deeply of lovemaking until morning.
This is not an innocent invitation.
It is sexual.
Intentional.
And adulterous.
Then comes the reassurance:
כִּי אֵין הָאִישׁ בְּבֵיתוֹ
Ki ein ha-ish beveito.
“For the man is not in his house.”
The next line explains that he has gone on a distant journey.
In other words:
He is gone.
We have time.
We will not be discovered.
And perhaps that is one of the oldest lies temptation has ever told:
You can sin safely if nobody sees you.
But the husband being absent does not make God absent.
Darkness does not make God blind.
A deleted message is not deleted from heaven.
An incognito browser cannot hide a heart from the One who searches hearts.
A locked phone cannot lock God outside.
And the tragedy is that the young man seems to think the danger is getting caught.
God knows the greater danger is what sin is doing to him.
Then Scripture gives us the horrifying picture.
The persuasion works.
He follows.

And Proverbs compares him to an ox going to slaughter and a bird rushing toward a trap without realizing that its life is at stake. The chapter concludes by warning that this road leads downward toward death.
Read that again.
The ox does not understand the destination.
The bird sees bait.
The hunter sees a trap.
That is what unchecked desire can do.
It shrinks your field of vision until you can see pleasure but not consequences.
The young man sees a woman.
Wisdom sees a funeral procession.
He sees a bed.
Wisdom sees a slaughterhouse.
He sees tonight.
Wisdom sees tomorrow morning.
And suddenly Proverbs 7 is no longer an ancient story.
Because some of us know exactly what it means to discover that what promised pleasure came carrying chains.
Maybe your story was adultery.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe an emotional affair.
Maybe secret messages.
Maybe fornication.
Maybe fantasy.
Maybe you crossed a boundary you once promised yourself you would never cross.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe the marriage survived.
Maybe it did not.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying the shame of something that happened twenty years ago.
Or maybe—and this matters—you are standing near the corner right now.
Nothing physical has happened yet.
But your heart knows.
You wait for that message.
You hide the conversation.
You enjoy being desired.
You know the relationship is becoming something you would never comfortably place before your spouse and Jesus Christ.
Do not wait for the slaughterhouse before admitting you are on the wrong road.
Turn around at the corner.
There is still time.
And please understand this: Proverbs 7 is not permission for men to blame women for male sin.
The woman is guilty of adultery and deliberate seduction.
The young man is also responsible for where he walks and what he chooses.
Scripture does not erase either person's moral agency.
And the Bible's sexual ethic applies to men and women alike.
The New Testament does not tell Christian men merely to “watch out for seductive women.”
It commands believers:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — pheugete tēn porneian.
Flee sexual immorality.
The Greek verb pheugete carries the straightforward force of fleeing—getting away.
Not negotiate.
Not see how close you can stand.
Not prove how spiritually strong you are.
Flee.

Paul then grounds sexual holiness in something astonishing: believers belong to God, their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, they were bought at a price, and therefore they are to glorify God with their bodies.
That changes everything.
Christian purity is not God trying to prevent you from enjoying life.
It is the God who purchased you through Christ telling you:
You are too precious to keep walking toward slaughter.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become better at hiding our chains.
He came to set captives free.
And this is where the Gospel enters Proverbs 7.
Because perhaps you did not stop at the corner.
Perhaps you entered the house.
Perhaps you crossed the line.
Perhaps you became the adulterer.
Perhaps you became the adulteress.
Perhaps you shattered someone's trust.
Perhaps you have lived with secret sexual sin so long that hearing a message about holiness immediately makes you want to hide.
Then hear this carefully.
The Gospel does not call your darkness light.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He calls sinners out of darkness.
Christian grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin matters so profoundly that Christ bore judgment for sinners.
And grace is not permission to continue walking toward destruction.
Grace brings us home.
Scripture says that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Confession means the hiding can stop.
Repentance means you do not merely feel terrible about the road.
You turn around.
Maybe that means ending the relationship.
Deleting the number.
Closing the account.
Confessing what has been hidden.
Inviting mature Christian accountability into your life.
Getting pastoral help.
Seeking appropriate professional counseling where a marriage has been deeply wounded.
Removing access to what repeatedly pulls you back.
Whatever genuine repentance requires, do not call the cage “grace” simply because leaving it hurts.
Jesus is worth the turning.
Your soul is worth the turning.
Your marriage is worth fighting for.
Your future obedience is worth fighting for.
And if your past already contains a scandal, remember the heart of the Gospel:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church contained people whose pasts included serious sexual sin—and Paul could speak of what some of them had been, because in Christ they had been washed, sanctified, and justified.
That is Christianity.
Not sin becoming harmless.
Sinners becoming new.
Not scandal being renamed.
Scandal meeting grace.
Not a God who shrugs at our rebellion.
A Savior who entered history, carried sin to a Roman cross, died, was buried, rose again, and now calls sinners to repentance, faith, forgiveness, and new life.
That means Proverbs 7 should frighten us.
But it should not leave the repentant sinner hopeless.
Maybe the most important sentence you can say tonight is not:
“I can handle this.”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, I need You to rescue me.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
But you can make one small declaration of surrender.
Someone reading the comments may need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars keep pointing us toward the wounded hands of Jesus.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.

But if this ministry is helping you know Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, and point people toward Jesus, then supporting and sharing this work can be one practical way you participate in putting biblical truth in front of someone who desperately needs it.
Someone may be one message away from destroying something precious.
Someone may already have fallen and believes Jesus could never want them again.
Someone may be smiling publicly while privately drowning in shame.
You may never know which person stops scrolling because you shared it.
Send it privately to someone you love if public tagging would embarrass them.
It does not buy salvation.
It does not replace your local church, prayer, Scripture, repentance, or obedience.
But it does help support the continued work of creating and distributing Christ-centered biblical content so more people can encounter truth in the places where they are already scrolling.
Proverbs 7 is standing at the window.
It sees the young man walking.
It sees the corner.
It sees the woman waiting.
It sees the decorated bed.
It hears the persuasive words.
It hears, “My husband is away.”
And wisdom screams what desire refuses to see:
You are not walking toward freedom.
Turn around.
If you have not entered the house yet, turn around.
If you are already inside, come out.
If you fell yesterday, repent today.
If your marriage has been wounded, bring the wound into truth.
If pornography has colonized your imagination, stop protecting the secret that is destroying you.
If another person's attention has become more precious than your covenant, confess what is happening before fantasy becomes history.
If shame tells you there is no road home, look again at Jesus Christ.
The cross is proof that God takes sin more seriously than we imagine.
The empty tomb is proof that sin and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
So flee what is killing you.
Run toward the One who died to save you.
And when grace finds you covered in the wreckage of decisions you wish you could erase, do not confuse forgiveness with permission to return to the same road.
Get up.
Repent.
Follow Jesus.
Walk differently.
Tell someone what Christ has done.
Save these words for the night when temptation starts sounding reasonable again.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is hearing the ancient lie:
Nobody will know.
But the better truth is this:
Jesus already knows—and He is still calling you to come out of the darkness and follow Him home.
The scandal may explain where you have been. Grace can change where you go from here.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOHN THE BAPTIST WOULD RATHER LOSE HIS HEAD THAN REWRITE GOD’S STANDARD
paragraphs: JOHN THE BAPTIST WOULD RATHER LOSE HIS HEAD THAN REWRITE GOD’S STANDARD

They could imprison the preacher. They could silence his voice. They could even separate his head from his body. But they could not make John call sin holy—and the question haunting the Church today is whether we still have that kind of courage.
There was a head on a platter.
But before there was a platter, there was a prison.
Before there was a prison, there was an offended ruler.
And before there was an offended ruler, there was one sentence John the Baptist refused to soften.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
That sentence cost him everything.
Read it slowly, because this is not merely an ancient story about a strange prophet, a corrupt palace, an angry woman, and a weak ruler.
This story walks uncomfortably close to us.
Because somewhere between John’s prison cell and Herod’s banquet hall is a question every generation of Christians eventually has to answer:
What happens when obedience to God starts costing you something?
Not when Christianity gets you encouragement.
Not when quoting Scripture earns applause.
Not when your convictions happen to agree with the people around you.
What happens when biblical truth costs you approval?
A friendship?
A relationship?
An opportunity?
Followers?
Income?
Reputation?
Comfort?
What happens when telling the truth could put something you love on the chopping block?
John had already answered.
Mark tells us that Herod Antipas had John arrested and imprisoned because of Herodias, whom Herod had married. John had confronted him concerning that relationship.
The Greek preserves the force of John’s words:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.
Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gynaika tou adelphou sou.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
Notice what John did not say.
He did not say, “Personally, I would have made a different choice.”
He did not say, “This lifestyle simply isn’t for me.”
He did not say, “We all interpret these things differently.”
He did not survey the palace to determine which version of truth would offend the fewest people.
He said:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν.
“It is not lawful.”
Why?
Because John did not believe he possessed the authority to rewrite what God had spoken.
The background reaches into the Torah. Leviticus 18:16 says:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
‘ervat eshet-achikha lo tegalleh.
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife.”
John was not inventing morality according to his personality.
He was standing beneath a Word greater than himself.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Biblical courage is not shouting your personal opinions more aggressively than everybody else.
Biblical courage is submitting yourself to God’s Word first—and then refusing to pretend God said something different simply because obedience has become expensive.
John was not the author of the standard.
He was its messenger.
That is why the title of this story must never become an excuse for cruelty.
John’s courage does not authorize Christians to become arrogant, vicious, self-righteous, or obsessed with condemning everybody else.

The same Bible that calls sin sin commands us to speak truth in love. The same Jesus who preached repentance welcomed sinners who came to Him. The same Gospel that exposes rebellion announces forgiveness to rebels.
Truth without love becomes a weapon in the hands of proud people.
But love without truth becomes permission to continue walking toward destruction.
Jesus gives us something better.
Grace and truth.
And John understood something our age desperately needs to recover:
You do not love someone by lying to them about what God has said.
Imagine that prison cell.
Stone walls.
Chains.
Darkness.
Perhaps footsteps occasionally approaching through the corridor.
John—the wilderness preacher who once stood beside the Jordan with crowds gathering around him—is now confined.
The voice that cried in the wilderness is behind bars.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because John could have changed his situation with something remarkably simple.
He did not necessarily need an army.
He did not need to overpower the guards.
He only needed to change his message.
Imagine how easy compromise could have sounded.
“Maybe I was too harsh.”
“Maybe I should have kept that part private.”
“Maybe Herod’s situation is complicated.”
“Maybe truth needs updating when powerful people dislike it.”
“Maybe survival matters more than faithfulness.”
Haven’t we heard versions of those whispers ourselves?
Maybe nobody needs to know.
Maybe Scripture doesn’t really mean that.
Maybe God understands.
Maybe repentance can wait.
Maybe obedience is too costly right now.
Maybe everybody does it.
Maybe if I call it something different, it will stop being sin.
But changing the vocabulary does not change reality before God.
And John refused to purchase freedom by selling truth.
Yet there is something even more disturbing in Mark’s account.
Herod listened to him.
Scripture says Herod feared John because he knew him to be righteous and holy. Herod was perplexed by him, yet he still liked listening to him.
Think about that.
A man can enjoy hearing a preacher he refuses to obey.
A person can admire holiness while refusing repentance.
You can listen to sermons.
Watch Christian videos.
Share Bible verses.
Cry during worship.
Follow Christian pages.
Feel convicted.
Even enjoy being convicted...
and still protect the very thing God is telling you to surrender.
Herod proves that fascination with truth is not the same thing as submission to truth.
And suddenly this is no longer merely Herod’s story.
It is ours.
There are people who want Jesus close enough to comfort them but never close enough to contradict them.
We want Christ as Savior but resist Him as Lord.
We want grace without repentance.
Forgiveness without surrender.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without a cross.
But Jesus never came merely to decorate the life we already chose.
He came to save us from sin and make us new.
That means the Gospel will eventually confront something in us.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our dishonesty.
Our unforgiveness.
Our greed.
Our secret habits.
Our relationships.
Our idols.
Our desperate hunger for human approval.
And when Christ puts His finger on the thing we have been defending, we discover whether we really want Jesus—or merely the parts of Jesus that make us comfortable.
Then came the banquet.
Power gathered around tables.
Officials.
Commanders.
Influential men.
Food.
Entertainment.
Status.
Applause.
Herodias’s daughter danced, and Herod made a reckless promise before his guests.
Then came the request.
John’s head.
The Gospel tells us Herod became deeply distressed.
That detail matters.
His conscience was not completely silent.
He knew something was terribly wrong.
But he had made promises in front of important people.
And now Herod faced his own moment of decision.
John had already chosen God’s approval over a king’s approval.
Herod chose the approval of the room over obedience to what he knew was right.
Do you see the tragedy?
John was physically imprisoned...
but Herod was the greater prisoner.
John was chained to a wall.
Herod was chained to public opinion.
John could lose his head.
Herod could not bear losing face.
And there are prisons without bars.
The fear of being mocked.
The fear of being unfollowed.
The fear of losing friends.
The fear of being called intolerant.
The fear that family will misunderstand.
The fear that someone will leave if you finally obey God.
The fear of standing alone.
Some people will surrender their convictions before they surrender their reputation.
Herod shows us where that road can lead.
The executioner entered the prison.
There was no miraculous escape recorded.
No angel opened the door.
No earthquake shattered the chains.
John died.
That can trouble us because we sometimes confuse faithfulness with earthly success.
We imagine that if God is pleased with us, every faithful decision must produce an immediate happy ending.
But Scripture never promises that obedience will always preserve your comfort.
Sometimes obedience costs.
Sometimes righteousness is mocked.
Sometimes faithful witnesses suffer.
And eventually every disciple is confronted with Jesus’ words about denying self, taking up the cross, and following Him.
John’s death was not evidence that God had lost control.
Nor was John the Savior.
John himself had made that clear.
He was the voice preparing the way.
Jesus was the Lamb.
John said of Christ:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
And here is where this story must ultimately take us.
Not merely to John’s courage.
To Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of brave people trying harder to obey rules.
It is the story of guilty people who desperately need a Savior.
John confronted Herod’s sin.
But the Gospel confronts ours too.
If we finish this article thinking only, Yes, somebody needs to tell the world to repent, we may have missed the blade pointed toward our own hearts.
What does Jesus need to confront in you?
What have you renamed because repentance would hurt?
What relationship have you placed above Christ?
What hidden compromise survives because nobody knows?
What bitterness have you justified?
What secret appetite are you feeding?
What truth have you stopped saying because you desperately need people to like you?
What Scripture have you been negotiating with instead of obeying?
Do not answer quickly.
There are moments when God’s Word stops being information and becomes a mirror.
This may be one of them.
And if you see something ugly in that mirror, do not run away from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Because the center of Christianity is not a severed head on Herod’s platter.
It is the crucified and risen Christ.
Jesus did what John could never do.
John could announce repentance.
Jesus could purchase redemption.
John could identify sin.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
John could point toward the Lamb.
Jesus was the Lamb.

At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore judgment for sinners. He died and rose again, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something Herod desperately needed and every one of us desperately needs:
Mercy.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new life.
This is why biblical repentance is not God standing over broken people saying, “Clean yourself up before you approach Me.”
It is the sinner finally dropping the weapons of rebellion and coming empty-handed to Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem a surrendered life.
You cannot make your sins disappear by renaming them.
But Christ can forgive them.
You cannot save yourself by becoming religious enough.
But Jesus saves sinners who come to Him.
That is the scandal of grace.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.

Grace says your sin mattered so terribly that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishingly great that the repentant sinner can be washed, forgiven, restored, adopted, and transformed.
From scandal to grace... because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting God’s standard.
By rewriting the sinner’s story.
That difference is everything.
Jesus does not need to redefine darkness to rescue someone from it.
He brings them into light.
He does not rename chains.
He breaks them.
He does not tell the guilty that guilt is imaginary.
He bears their guilt and offers righteousness they could never manufacture themselves.
So maybe the question is no longer whether John would lose his head rather than rewrite God’s standard.
We know his answer.
The question is:
What are you willing to lose rather than lose your faithfulness to Christ?
And perhaps an even deeper question:
What are you finally willing to surrender so Christ can have all of you?
Maybe your prayer is only three words.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Not for performance.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
Only Jesus saves.
Let your comment simply become an honest confession that you do not want to hide anymore.
And then look through those comments.
You may discover someone else fighting a battle you understand.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Christ.
This is what Christian community should look like—not perfect people displaying polished lives, but redeemed sinners pointing one another toward a perfect Savior.
And please do not keep this message trapped on this page.
Somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly negotiating with a sin that is destroying them.
Somebody may be terrified to obey God because obedience could cost a relationship.
Somebody may be living for the approval of the room like Herod.
Somebody may believe they have sinned too badly to return to Jesus.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
There may come a day when compromise sounds reasonable and obedience feels painfully expensive.
Come back and remember the prisoner who would not rewrite the message just to escape the prison.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or serving the people God has placed around you.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Truth.
Accountability.
Encouragement.
Spiritual nourishment.
A place continually calling us away from compromise and back toward Jesus Christ.

Because perhaps glorifying God today looks less like making a grand speech and more like refusing to be ashamed of Christ when one click could place biblical truth in front of someone who desperately needs it.
No livestream.
No microphone.
No algorithm.
He had a voice.
And when speaking cost him everything, he still refused to make God’s truth more convenient.
We have been given voices too.
May we use them with humility.
May we use them with compassion.
May we use them without self-righteousness.
May we use them without fear.
And above everything, may we use them to point people—not toward ourselves—but toward the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
Because one day every applause will fade.
Every follower count will become meaningless.
Every human opinion will fall silent.
Herod’s banquet ended.
The powerful men went home.
The platter disappeared.
Herod’s kingdom passed into history.
But the truth John refused to sell is still being preached.
And the Christ to whom John pointed is still saving sinners.
So when culture offers you applause in exchange for silence...
when compromise promises comfort...
when obedience becomes expensive...
when you are tempted to edit Scripture until it stops confronting you...
remember the prison.
Remember the banquet.
Remember the platter.
Remember John.
Then look beyond John to Jesus.
Repent where you have compromised.
Receive the grace Christ purchased.
Stand again.
Speak truth with love.
And follow the Lamb wherever He leads.
They could take John’s head, but they could never make him bow his conscience—and two thousand years later, his silence after death is still louder than Herod’s entire banquet.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LEVITICUS HAD TO TELL ISRAEL NOT TO SLEEP WITH A BROTHER’S WIFE
paragraphs: LEVITICUS HAD TO TELL ISRAEL NOT TO SLEEP WITH A BROTHER’S WIFE

And thousands of years later, one fearless preacher confronted a king over the same command—and lost his head. But beneath this disturbing law is something far more personal: what happens when desire starts demanding permission to cross a boundary God has already drawn?
There are verses in the Bible we underline.
There are verses we put on coffee mugs.
There are verses we whisper beside hospital beds, print on T-shirts, frame above fireplaces, and send to friends when life is falling apart.
And then there is Leviticus 18:16.
A verse almost nobody puts on a coffee mug.
In Hebrew it reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָחִיךָ הִוא
ʿErwat ʾeshet-ʾaḥikha lo tegalleh; ʿerwat ʾaḥikha hi.
Literally, with the Hebrew idiom preserved:
“The nakedness of your brother’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your brother’s nakedness.”
That language sounds strange to modern ears.
But “uncover nakedness” is a recurring Hebrew expression in Leviticus 18 describing prohibited sexual relations.
So strip away the distance of three thousand years and hear what God was actually telling Israel:
There are sexual boundaries you do not cross.
Including this one.
Your brother’s wife is not yours to take.
And perhaps the uncomfortable question is not merely, “Why did God have to command this?”
Perhaps the more frightening question is:
Why does God have to command human beings not to do so many things that should already feel unthinkable?
Because Scripture does not flatter us.
The Bible does not present humanity as basically pure people occasionally making unfortunate mistakes.
It tells a much darker story.
And then it tells a much better one.
We are creatures capable of taking something beautiful that God created and twisting it around ourselves.
Love.
Sex.
Marriage.
Power.
Family.
Desire.
Even religion.
Give the human heart something good, and sin will eventually whisper:
What if you used it your way instead of God's?
That is why Leviticus 18 matters far beyond one ancient prohibition.
It is holding up a mirror.
God had delivered Israel from Egypt, and now He was teaching a redeemed people that deliverance was supposed to change how they lived.
They were not to imitate the sexual practices of the nations around them.
They belonged to Yahweh.
And belonging to God meant that even their most private desires were not beyond His authority.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because we love a Jesus who enters our suffering.
We are less comfortable with a Jesus who enters our bedroom.
We love a God who heals our wounds.
We become nervous when that same God challenges our appetites.
We celebrate grace when grace means forgiveness.
We sometimes resist grace when grace means transformation.
But biblical grace never says:
“Keep whatever is destroying you.”
Grace says:
“Come out of the grave.”
Leviticus returns to the brother’s-wife prohibition later with even stronger language:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִקַּח אֶת־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו נִדָּה הִוא
Weʾish ʾasher-yiqqaḥ ʾet-ʾeshet ʾaḥiw, niddah hi...
Leviticus 20:21 condemns a man taking his brother’s wife and describes the act as a violation of his brother’s nakedness.
But careful Bible reading matters here.
This should not be carelessly turned into the claim that Scripture prohibited every possible union between a man and his brother’s widow under every circumstance.

Deuteronomy 25:5–10 gives Israel a specific provision commonly called levirate marriage: when brothers lived together and one died without a son, the surviving brother had a covenant responsibility concerning his deceased brother’s widow and family line.
That is not a contradiction we need to hide.
Context matters.
Leviticus is prohibiting illicit sexual appropriation.
Deuteronomy addresses a particular situation involving a deceased brother, preservation of his family line, and responsibility toward his widow.
Scripture deserves more than slogans.
It deserves to be read carefully enough that we do not make God say something He did not say.
And then centuries passed.
Empires rose.
Empires collapsed.
Israel's kings became dust.
The prophets died.
And eventually another ruler decided he wanted his brother’s wife.
His name was Herod Antipas.
Her name was Herodias.
And standing between royal desire and biblical truth was a wilderness preacher who apparently had not learned the modern art of making conviction marketable.
John the Baptist.
Imagine the scene.
Herod had political authority.
John had camel's hair.
Herod had soldiers.
John had a voice.
Herod could imprison John.
John could tell Herod the truth.
And he did.
The Gospel records the accusation with terrifying simplicity:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.
Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gynaika tou adelphou sou.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
No sophisticated rebranding.
No attempt to make sin sound respectable because the sinner was powerful.
John looked toward a ruler who could destroy him and essentially said:
God's boundary still stands.
And eventually John's head was carried into a banquet.
Think about that.
A command from Leviticus became part of the reason a prophet lost his life.
John could have remained silent.
He could have preached something safer.
He could have told Herod that God loved him without ever explaining that the love of God called him to repentance.
He could have protected his platform.
Protected his influence.
Protected his neck.
But John understood something much of modern Christianity desperately needs to recover:
Love does not become more loving by hiding the truth that could lead someone to repentance.
Yet there is another danger here.
A religious person can read an article about sexual sin and immediately begin thinking about everybody else's bedroom.
Herod.
Herodias.
That relative.
That celebrity.
That friend.
That person at church.
Anybody...
except the person reading.
So before you use Leviticus as binoculars to inspect somebody else's sin, use it as a mirror.
Maybe you have never touched your brother's wife.
But perhaps you have crossed another boundary while telling yourself it was different because your feelings were sincere.
Perhaps nobody knows what is on your phone after midnight.
Perhaps your spouse believes you are faithful because you have carefully narrowed the definition of unfaithfulness.
Perhaps there is a conversation you delete.
A relationship you keep hidden.
A fantasy you repeatedly feed.
A pornography history nobody sees.
A flirtation you call harmless.
An emotional affair you insist is only friendship.
A secret account.
A second life.
Or perhaps sexual sin is not your battlefield at all.
Perhaps your hidden room contains bitterness.
Envy.
Pride.
Greed.
Dishonesty.
Resentment.
Self-righteousness.
A wound you have turned into permission to wound others.
The details change.
The ancient whisper does not.
Did God really say you cannot have this?
That whisper is older than Leviticus.
Older than Israel.
Older than Egypt.
It was already crawling through Eden.
The serpent did not begin by forcing Eve to eat.
He began by making God's boundary seem suspicious.
That is still how temptation works.
First the boundary feels restrictive.
Then crossing it feels reasonable.
Then repeating it feels normal.
Then hiding it feels necessary.
Then defending it feels personal.
Eventually repentance feels like an attack on your identity because you have lived beside the sin so long that you no longer know where it ends and you begin.
And that is exactly where Jesus becomes more beautiful than we expected.
Because Christ did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came looking for sinners.
People with histories.
People with stains.
People with appetites they could not control.
People who had crossed boundaries.
People who had been sexually broken.
People who had broken others.
Religious hypocrites.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Thieves.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The ruined.
Us.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God went to Calvary.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that sinners are beyond recovery.
Look at the cross again.
God loved sinners so deeply that Christ went there willingly.
That tension is Christianity.
Your sin is worse than your excuses have admitted, and Christ's mercy is greater than your shame has imagined.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by entering the scandal with nail-scarred hands.
He does not rename darkness as light.
He brings light into darkness.
He does not call bondage freedom.
He breaks chains.
He does not tell the guilty person, “There was never anything to forgive.”
He offers something infinitely better:
real forgiveness.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the doorway through which the person who is finished hiding finally walks toward home.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It speaks of turning, reconsidering, changing one's mind in a way that redirects life toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns.
Toward Christ.
Toward truth.
Toward obedience.
Toward the Father.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years believing that if Christians knew what happened, they would never look at you the same way.
Maybe you crossed sexual boundaries.
Maybe somebody crossed yours.
Those are not morally identical things, and they should never be treated as though they are.
If you were sexually abused, coerced, exploited, or violated, another person's sin against you is not transformed into your guilt simply because it involved your body.
Hear that clearly.
But if you willingly sinned...
hear this just as clearly:
You do not have to spend the rest of your life hiding either.
Confession may be painful.
Consequences may remain.
Trust may take time to rebuild.
Repentance may require difficult changes.
Grace does not magically erase every earthly consequence of our choices.
But Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
The blood shed at Calvary was not reserved for people with presentable testimonies.
There are no presentable testimonies.
There are only different versions of:
I needed mercy.
Maybe that is why this obscure command in Leviticus can hit so hard.
It begins with another man's wife.
It ends with your heart.
What boundary have you been negotiating with God about?
What have you renamed so you would not have to repent of it?
What would terrify you if it appeared publicly tonight?
What relationship are you protecting more fiercely than your obedience to Christ?
What secret has begun demanding more and more of you?
And how long are you planning to hide?
Because sin makes extraordinary promises.
Then sends devastating invoices.
It promises pleasure and collects peace.
Promises intimacy and collects integrity.
Promises freedom and collects your ability to look people in the eyes.
Promises secrecy and slowly builds a prison.
Then Jesus stands outside the cell.
Not pretending there are no bars.
Not pretending you did not walk inside.
But holding the key.
There is a reason 1 John 1:9 has rescued so many trembling believers: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive and cleanse.
Not because confession purchases mercy.
Because Christ already purchased redemption.
And there is a reason Romans 8:1 sounds almost impossible to people who finally understand their guilt:
There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not reduced condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
Not condemnation waiting until God gets tired of you.
No condemnation.
For whom?
Those in Christ Jesus.
That is the center.
Not moral self-improvement.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Christ.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who told the truth about sin without becoming cruel to sinners.
The One who carried a cross through Jerusalem.
The One whose hands were pierced.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who still saves.
Maybe you clicked because the title sounded scandalous.
Good.
Now let the scandal lead you to grace.
Because the greatest scandal in this story is not that ancient Israel needed laws governing sexual boundaries.
The greatest scandal is that a holy God knew exactly what humanity would become...
and still chose redemption.
He knew Peter would deny.
He knew Thomas would doubt.
He knew His disciples would scatter.
He knew what you would do.
He knew what I would do.
And Christ still walked toward Golgotha.
That does not give us permission to sin.
It destroys the excuse that says repentance is pointless because we have sinned too much.
So stop bargaining.
Stop editing the story.
Stop calling chains jewelry.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
If restitution is needed, pursue it wisely.
If accountability is needed, seek it.
If a relationship must end because maintaining it requires continuing sin, obedience may hurt—but Christ is worth more than the thing you are afraid to surrender.
If you have fallen again after promising God you never would, do not turn another failure into an excuse for another year of hiding.
Run to Christ.
Not away from Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Get up.
Walk again.
And when Satan whispers, “Look what you did,” learn to answer by looking at the cross and saying:
Look what Jesus did.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your private life in a Facebook comment section. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone scrolling beneath you may need to discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescue.
We are people who know the Rescuer.
Not because every sentence will be easy to revisit, but because someday temptation may begin making an old boundary look negotiable again.
Not as proof that you are better than the Herods of the world.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of using what God has entrusted to you for the spread of biblical truth. Jesus already paid the price of redemption in full.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend whose faith is barely breathing.
Invite the believer who has become lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Invite the person who thinks their past has disqualified them forever.
Because perhaps they do not need another polished religious performance.
Perhaps they need someone brave enough to tell them:
Yes, sin is real.
Yes, God's boundaries matter.
Yes, repentance may cost you something.
But no...
your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still mercy for the repentant.
There is still cleansing for the stained.
There is still restoration for the broken.
There is still Jesus.
And maybe the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades is this:
The secret you thought would become the last sentence of your life may become the very place where Jesus begins writing grace in the margins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Sarah Told Abraham to Sleep With Hagar—Then Everything Changed
paragraphs:
Sarah Told Abraham to Sleep With Hagar—Then Everything Changed
One desperate decision. One wounded woman running into the wilderness. One God who saw what everyone else had overlooked. And a warning for every believer who has ever become tired of waiting for God.
There are moments when waiting on God begins to hurt.
Not because you stopped believing in Him.
Not because you suddenly became an atheist.
Not because you wanted to rebel.
But because you prayed.
And prayed.
And prayed.
And nothing seemed to happen.

The promise still looked impossible. The calendar kept moving. Your body kept aging. Other people received what you had begged God for. You tried to remain faithful, but somewhere between the promise and its fulfillment, disappointment started whispering something dangerous:
Maybe I need to help God.
That whisper is where Genesis 16 becomes painfully personal.

And before we go any further, there is an important detail worth getting right. Genesis 16 occurs before God changes Abram's name to Abraham and Sarai's name to Sarah in Genesis 17. So although we know them best as Abraham and Sarah, in this chapter they are still Abram and Sarai.
God had already made staggering promises to Abram.

He had called him out of his homeland. He had promised to make him a great nation. He had promised offspring. Genesis 15 had brought Abram outside beneath the night sky, where God told him to look toward heaven and count the stars, if he could count them.
That was the promise.
But Genesis 16 opens with something painfully different.
Barrenness.
The Hebrew text says of Sarai:
וְשָׂרַי אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם לֹא יָלְדָה לוֹ
Ve-Sarai eshet Avram lo yaldah lo.
In context: “Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children.”
That sentence is devastating precisely because of what God had promised.
There was a promise in the heavens.
But there was still emptiness in Sarai's arms.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that tension feels like.
God said one thing.
Your circumstances seem to say another.
You believe God is faithful, but your life currently looks like evidence against everything you thought He was doing.
That is where impatience becomes dangerous.
Sarai had an Egyptian servant named Hagar. And Sarai said something that would change all of their lives.
She told Abram that because she had not borne children, he should go in to Hagar, hoping that through Hagar she might obtain children.
