This was not simply the crude impulsiveness it can sound like to modern ears. Surrogacy-like arrangements involving enslaved or servant women existed in the ancient Near Eastern world. But cultural availability does not mean divine command.
That distinction matters.
Something can be socially understandable and still not be what God instructed.
Something can appear practical and still create devastation.
Something can even look like the solution to your prayer while quietly being an attempt to seize control of what you were supposed to entrust to God.
Then Genesis records a haunting line:
וַיִּשְׁמַע אַבְרָם לְקוֹל שָׂרָי
Vayishma Avram leqol Sarai.
“And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.”
Abram did not merely stand nearby while everything happened.
He participated.
Sarai proposed the arrangement.
Abram accepted it.
Hagar was placed inside a situation shaped by the decisions and power of other people.
And suddenly the household that was supposed to be waiting for God's promise became a house full of jealousy, humiliation, anger, pain, and blame.
Hagar conceived.
Then the relationships began to fracture.
Sarai felt dishonored. Conflict erupted between Sarai and Abram. Sarai dealt harshly with Hagar, and Hagar fled.
Read that slowly.
She fled.
A pregnant servant woman ran into the wilderness.
Whatever hopes anyone had attached to this human solution, the result was now a wounded woman alone in a dangerous place.
This is what sin and unbelief so often do.
They do not remain contained inside the moment in which we choose them.
They spill.
Into marriages.
Into children.
Into friendships.
Into families.
Into years we cannot rewind.
We make decisions because we are hurting, and then discover that hurting people can create new wounds while desperately trying to escape their own.
Maybe that is why this chapter hurts so much.
Because perhaps you have been Sarai—so disappointed that you tried to control the outcome.
Perhaps you have been Abram—passive when you should have exercised faithful responsibility.
Perhaps you have been Hagar—caught inside consequences you did not entirely create, carrying wounds caused by people who had more power than you did.
Or perhaps, painfully, you recognize yourself in all three.
But then Genesis 16 turns.
Hagar is in the wilderness.
And God finds her.
וַיִּמְצָאָהּ מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה
Vayimtza'ah mal'akh YHWH.
“And the angel of the LORD found her.”
Do not rush past that.
Hagar ran away from Abram's household.
But she did not run beyond the sight of God.
The woman treated as expendable by human beings was not invisible to heaven.
The Lord's messenger addressed her personally:
“Hagar, servant of Sarai…”
Hagar had a name.
God knew it.
God knew where she had come from.
God knew where she was going.
God knew she was pregnant.
God knew the suffering behind her flight.
And God heard.
The name of her son would testify to it.
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma'el — Ishmael.
The name is connected to the Hebrew root שׁמע — shamaʿ, “to hear.”
Genesis explains the name because the LORD had heard her affliction.
The God of Abraham was also listening to the cry of an Egyptian servant woman in the wilderness.
And Hagar responded with one of the most extraordinary declarations in Genesis.
She called the LORD who spoke to her:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i
commonly rendered in the sense of “God who sees me” or “the God who sees.”
Think about who is saying this.
Not Abram.
Not Sarai.
Hagar.
The wounded outsider.
The woman running through the wilderness.
She discovered something about God in the place where human beings had failed her:
He saw her.
And perhaps this is the sentence someone desperately needed today.
God sees you.
Not the polished version you put on Facebook.
Not the version that smiles at church.
Not the version that tells everyone, “I'm okay.”
You.
The exhausted you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The you who made decisions you wish you could undo.
The you carrying consequences that were never entirely your choice.
The you who has wondered whether God noticed what happened behind closed doors.
He sees.
And Scripture never requires us to pretend that seeing means approving everything we have done.
That is what makes biblical grace so powerful.
God can see us completely without calling darkness light.
He can expose sin and still pursue sinners.
He can confront us without abandoning us.
He can meet human beings in the wreckage without pretending the wreckage is beautiful.
That pattern reaches its fullest clarity in Jesus Christ.

Genesis 16 should not be forced into saying something it does not explicitly say. The chapter itself is about Abram, Sarai, Hagar, Ishmael, human impatience, suffering, and the God who sees and hears.
But Genesis does not stand alone.
The biblical story keeps moving.
God's covenant promise continues.
Isaac will eventually be born to Sarah.
And generations later, through the covenant line Scripture traces through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the story ultimately moves toward Jesus Christ.

The New Testament even returns explicitly to Hagar and Sarah. In Galatians 4, Paul uses them allegorically in an argument about slavery and freedom, contrasting reliance on the flesh with God's promise. We should respect Paul's specific argument rather than inventing our own symbolism, but his central warning reaches straight into the human heart:
You cannot manufacture by the flesh what ultimately depends upon God's promise.
And that is where Genesis 16 stops being ancient family history and begins looking uncomfortably like us.
How many “Hagars” have we created because we could not wait?
Not people—substitutes.
Counterfeits.
Shortcuts.
We prayed for companionship, became tired of loneliness, and accepted a relationship that pulled us farther from Christ.
We prayed for provision, panicked, and compromised our integrity.
We prayed for restoration, became impatient, and tried to manipulate people into producing the ending we wanted.
We prayed for ministry growth and began measuring success by attention instead of faithfulness.
We prayed for God to open a door and eventually decided to kick one down.
We told ourselves we were pursuing the promise.
But somewhere along the way, we stopped trusting the Promiser.
That is the terrifying temptation of waiting.
Eventually, your greatest temptation may not be to stop believing God's promise.
It may be to achieve it without depending on God.
And some of us are living with the consequences right now.
You cannot go backward.
You cannot unsend the message.
You cannot undo the affair.
You cannot unspend the money.
You cannot recover every year.
You cannot erase every sentence spoken in anger.
You cannot make everyone you wounded forget.
And Christianity does not offer us a time machine.
It offers us something greater.
A Redeemer.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve the reputations of people who already had their lives together.
He came for sinners.
He came proclaiming repentance and the kingdom of God.
He came touching the unclean, receiving the rejected, confronting hypocrites, calling sinners to leave their sin, forgiving the guilty, carrying our sin to the cross, dying, and rising again.
Grace does not mean your choices never mattered.
Grace means your worst choices do not have to become your final identity.
That is the difference.
The Gospel does not say, “Nothing happened.”
The Gospel says, “Something happened at Calvary that is greater than what happened in your past.”
Your sin is real.
Christ's blood is sufficient.
Your guilt is real.
His mercy is greater.
Repentance is necessary.
Forgiveness is available.
Your history cannot be rewritten by pretending it never happened.
But your future can belong to Jesus.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you tried to force what God told you to trust Him with.
Repent.
Maybe your impatience hurt someone.
Do not merely call it a mistake. Where reconciliation is possible and appropriate, confess what was yours, seek forgiveness, and make what you can right.
Maybe you are Hagar in this story.
You were wounded by somebody else's fear, selfishness, weakness, or sin.
Please hear what Genesis refuses to let you forget:
God sees people other people overlook.
God hears cries other people ignore.
And if you belong to Christ, your wounds do not possess the authority to write the last sentence of your life.
Jesus does.
There is also something sobering here for those who have been Christians for years.
Abram was not a pagan stranger to God's promises when Genesis 16 happened.
He was a man who had already encountered God.
Which means spiritual history does not make us immune to present unbelief.
Yesterday's faith cannot replace today's obedience.
Knowing Bible verses does not make impatience harmless.
Having experienced God before does not mean every decision we make afterward automatically carries His approval.
We still need Him.
Every morning.
Every temptation.
Every waiting season.
Every wilderness.
Every time fear whispers, Take control.
Maybe the holiest thing you can do today is stop trying to manufacture an answer.
Stop forcing the relationship.
Stop manipulating the outcome.
Stop pretending the compromise is God's provision simply because it appeared when you were desperate.
Bring it into the light.
Bring the mess.
Bring the shame.
Bring the anger.
Bring the consequences.
Bring the secret you have been hiding.
Bring it to Jesus.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the door opening while you are still standing in the burning house.
Run toward Christ.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Now.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your life. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Not for performance.
Not so people think you are spiritual.
Because sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, worship, and lives surrendered to Him.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
An Abram who has compromised.
A Hagar who believes nobody sees her.
A believer hiding consequences they cannot undo.
A skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
Or a person sitting alone tonight who desperately needs to discover that the Bible is not merely populated by polished saints.
It is filled with deeply flawed human beings encountered by a relentlessly faithful God.
Genesis 16 is not a pretty story.
It contains barrenness.
Impatience.
Sexual and household power imbalance.
Conflict.
Harsh treatment.
Flight.
Fear.
Consequences.
A wilderness.
Yet standing inside that wilderness is a truth no human failure can erase:
God sees.
And the larger biblical story reveals something even greater.
The God who sees did not remain distant from our brokenness.
The Word became flesh.
Jesus entered our world.
He walked among sinners.
He carried the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose.
And He still calls sinners to repent, believe, receive mercy, and follow Him.
So maybe your story contains a chapter you wish had never been written.
Maybe there is a Genesis 16 in your life.
A decision made because you were afraid.
A shortcut taken because you were tired.
A person you wounded.
A wilderness you ran into.
A consequence you still carry.
Do not confuse a terrible chapter with the final page.
Turn to Christ.
Because the most unforgettable truth in this story is not merely that human beings made a mess while waiting for God's promise.
It is that God was still God after they made it.
He was still faithful.
Still seeing.
Still hearing.
Still working.
And thousands of years later, the Gospel announces that sinners do not have to be imprisoned forever by the worst thing they have done—or forever defined by the worst thing done to them.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is grace in Jesus.
There is a new life in Jesus.
There is a cross for your guilt.
There is an empty tomb for your hopelessness.
There is a Savior for your scandal.

So when you are tempted to believe that the chapter you ruined has ruined the entire story, remember the woman standing beside a spring in the wilderness who discovered that heaven had never taken its eyes off her.
You may be standing in the chapter you wish you could erase, while God is already calling you toward the grace that will keep it from becoming your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DO NOT AWAKEN LOVE UNTIL IT PLEASES”: Is the Bible Warning Us About Sexual Timing?
paragraphs: “DO NOT AWAKEN LOVE UNTIL IT PLEASES”: Is the Bible Warning Us About Sexual Timing?
We were taught to fear sexual desire. Scripture does something far more beautiful: it teaches us why something this powerful must not be awakened carelessly.
There are some fires you do not extinguish because the fire is evil.
You guard them because the fire is powerful.
And there are some doors you do not refuse to open because what waits behind them is shameful.
You wait because some doors lead into rooms your heart was never meant to enter casually.
That may be one of the most forgotten truths in modern Christianity.
We live in a culture that has learned how to awaken desire before it has learned how to carry covenant.
We know how to flirt before we know how to remain faithful.
We know how to create chemistry before we know how to build character.
We know how to expose bodies before we know how to expose souls.
And sometimes Christians respond by going to the opposite extreme.
We speak about sexual desire as though the desire itself were filthy.
As though attraction were automatically lust.
As though holiness meant becoming emotionally numb.
As though God created the human body, looked at sexuality, became embarrassed by His own design, and then spent the rest of Scripture trying to keep people away from it.
But then you open the Bible...
and you find the Song of Songs.
And suddenly Scripture is speaking about longing.
Beauty.
Desire.
Bodies.
Kisses.
Fragrance.
Touch.
Marriage.
Delight.
Not with pornography’s exploitation.
Not with hookup culture’s disposability.
Not with lust’s selfish hunger.
But with poetry.
Tenderness.
Exclusivity.
Longing.
And astonishing dignity.
Then, right in the middle of all that desire, Scripture repeatedly whispers a warning that sounds almost as though it were written directly to our generation:
“Do not awaken or arouse love until it pleases.”
The Hebrew of Song of Songs 2:7 reads:
הִשְׁבַּ֨עְתִּי אֶתְכֶ֜ם בְּנ֤וֹת יְרוּשָׁלַ֙͏ִם֙ בִּצְבָא֔וֹת א֖וֹ בְּאַיְל֣וֹת הַשָּׂדֶ֑ה אִם־תָּעִ֧ירוּ וְֽאִם־תְּע֥וֹרְר֛וּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָ֖ה עַ֥ד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּֽץ
Hishba‘ti etkhem benot Yerushalayim... im-ta‘iru ve’im-te‘oreru et-ha’ahavah ‘ad sheteḥpatz.
In a fairly literal sense:
“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem... do not awaken, and do not arouse, love until it desires.”
That refrain does not appear only once.
It returns in Song of Songs 3:5.
And again, with slightly different wording, in 8:4.
Almost as though the Song keeps returning to the same warning:
Love is beautiful.
Desire is powerful.
So do not play with its awakening.
The Hebrew makes the warning especially striking.

The verbs תָּעִירוּ (ta‘iru) and תְּעוֹרְרוּ (te‘oreru) come from the root עוּר (‘ur), associated with waking, stirring, or rousing. The NET translators note that the repeated root gives rhetorical force to the command and that interpreters have understood the image in several related ways—including prematurely forcing romantic love, interfering with passionate love, or stirring sexual passion. In this context, אַהֲבָה (’ahavah, “love”) can carry the force of passionate or sexual desire.
That matters.
Because the Bible is not saying:
“Never awaken love.”
It says:
Do not awaken it until.
There is an until.
And that one word changes everything.
God is not necessarily standing against the fire.
He is teaching His children when the fire belongs in the fireplace.

Sexual desire is not presented throughout Scripture as inherently dirty. Within God’s design, marital intimacy is treated as something honorable; Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage honorable and its bed undefiled. Proverbs 5 even speaks unapologetically about a husband delighting in his wife.
The Song itself eventually gives us one of Scripture’s fiercest descriptions of love:
“For love is strong as death... Many waters cannot quench love.”
That is precisely why love should not be treated like a toy.
You do not hand something “strong as death” to your impulses and say, “Let’s see what happens.”
And perhaps somebody reading this already knows what happens.
You said it was only texting.
Then the conversations moved later into the night.
You said you were only friends.
Then emotional intimacy started creating expectations neither of you had promised to fulfill.
You said it was only flirting.
Only touching.
Only pictures.
Only one night.
Only this once.
And then one morning you discovered that “only” had somehow become attachment.
Now you are trying to forget someone your body remembers.
Trying to stop checking a profile you promised yourself you would stop checking.
Trying not to replay conversations.
Trying to understand why losing someone you were “never technically with” feels strangely like divorce.
Trying to worship while memories you wish you could erase walk through your mind.
Trying to convince yourself that because nobody saw what happened, nothing happened.
But your soul knows.
Your body knows.
Your memories know.
And God knows.
This is where Christians must be careful.

Song of Songs 2:7 is poetry, not a technical manual establishing a precise dating timeline. Faithful interpreters differ over some details of the refrain. We should therefore resist building an entire doctrine of premarital sexuality from this verse alone.
But when the refrain is read alongside the rest of Scripture, a larger biblical sexual ethic becomes unmistakable.
Jesus does not merely address adultery as an outward act; He takes His hearers into the heart and confronts lustful looking in Matthew 5:27–28.
Paul tells believers in 1 Corinthians 6:18 to flee sexual immorality, grounding sexual holiness in the astonishing reality that our bodies belong to Christ.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5, sanctification includes learning to govern sexual desire in holiness and honor rather than being governed by passion.
And Jesus points back to creation when speaking about marriage: male and female, joined together, becoming one flesh.
The Christian vision is therefore much larger than:
“How far can I go before God gets angry?”
That question has already misunderstood holiness.
The better question is:
“How can I love another human being without awakening something I am unwilling or unable to honor?”
Read that again.
Because some of us were not trying to love somebody.
We were trying to use somebody to medicate loneliness.
And we called it love.
We wanted attention.
We wanted reassurance.
We wanted somebody to make us feel attractive again.
We wanted the notifications.
The late-night messages.
The secret conversations.
The feeling of being wanted.
We wanted another human being to silence wounds that should have been brought to Jesus.
And when two wounded people begin asking each other to become saviors, desire can become extraordinarily confusing.
You can feel intensely connected to someone who is profoundly unhealthy for you.
Intensity is not covenant.
Chemistry is not character.
Attention is not faithfulness.
Being desired is not the same thing as being loved.
And sexual access is certainly not proof that someone intends to cherish you.
That distinction is almost revolutionary in a culture where bodies can be exchanged before last names are remembered.
The Gospel says your body has meaning.
Your sexuality has meaning.
The person you desire has meaning.
And because people bear the image of God, nobody should be reduced to a temporary source of pleasure.
This also means Christian sexual boundaries are not supposed to be arbitrary fences erected by frightened religious people.
At their best, boundaries say:
“I refuse to awaken in you what I am not prepared to honor.”
“I refuse to use your loneliness to satisfy mine.”
“I refuse to demand husband privileges while avoiding husband responsibility.”
“I refuse to demand wife privileges while avoiding wife responsibility.”
“I refuse to let tonight create wounds tomorrow will have to carry.”
That is not repression.
That can be love.
Real love does not ask only:
“What do I want from you right now?”
Real love asks:
“What will help you stand before Jesus with greater freedom, greater holiness, and greater joy?”
And suddenly restraint begins looking less like rejection and more like protection.
But perhaps this article has become painful for another reason.
Maybe you did awaken it.
Maybe the warning arrived years too late.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Maybe you gave yourself to somebody who disappeared.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe pornography rewired years of your desires.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once swore you never would.
Maybe there was an affair.
Maybe there was a secret relationship.
Maybe your sexual history feels less like Song of Songs and more like a crime scene.
And every time Christians talk about purity, you feel yourself shrinking.
Because somewhere along the way you started believing the cruelest counterfeit gospel imaginable:
God forgives clean people who made small mistakes.
But not people like me.
Listen carefully.
That is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come for people with spotless histories.
He came for sinners.
The cross was not constructed for respectable mistakes.
It was constructed because sin is devastating enough that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
Paul reminded the Corinthians of people whose pasts included sexual immorality, adultery, greed, drunkenness and other sins, and then wrote some of the most breathtaking words in the New Testament:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they rewrote their own history.
Because Christ gave them a new identity.
Paul continues: they had been washed, sanctified and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not celebrating what Christ died to save us from.
But neither is Christianity sentencing forgiven people to lifelong spiritual humiliation.
Repentance says:
“What I did was sin.”
Grace says:
“Sin does not get the final word.”
Repentance brings the darkness into the light.
Grace meets us there.
Repentance stops defending the chains.
Grace breaks them.
And Jesus begins rewriting what shame insisted was already finished.
Maybe your virginity cannot be physically restored.
Maybe certain memories cannot simply be deleted.
Maybe consequences remain.
Maybe somebody broke your heart.
Maybe you broke theirs.
But hear this:
Jesus does not need an untouched past to create a holy future.
The Gospel does not give you a time machine.
It gives you resurrection.
And resurrection is greater.
This is where our theme becomes more than a slogan.
He does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely better.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He teaches.
He transforms.
And He takes people who thought their worst chapter had become the title of their entire life and begins writing something new.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
“Is the Bible warning us about sexual timing?”

Yes, there is genuine wisdom here about refusing to prematurely awaken powerful romantic and sexual desire, and the wider witness of Scripture clearly calls Christians to sexual holiness. But the deeper question is:
Who is controlling what has already been awakened in you?
Your hormones?
Your loneliness?
Pornography?
Your boyfriend?
Your girlfriend?
Your trauma?
Your need to be wanted?
Your fear of losing someone?
Or Jesus?
Because Christianity is not merely about delaying sex.
A person can remain technically abstinent while feeding lust every night.
You can avoid intercourse and still manipulate somebody emotionally.
You can maintain a public image of purity while privately consuming people through a screen.
Biblical holiness reaches deeper.
Jesus wants the heart.
He wants the imagination.
He wants the body.
He wants the secret messages.
He wants the search history.
He wants the wounds beneath the appetite.
He wants the loneliness beneath the compromise.
He wants the shame underneath the hiding.
Not because He is eager to destroy you.
Because He came to make you free.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need impressive language.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, I awakened something I could not control.”
“Jesus, I crossed lines.”
“Jesus, I have been using desire to numb loneliness.”
“Jesus, I still miss someone I know I should release.”
“Jesus, my mind has become polluted.”
“Jesus, I keep returning to pornography.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
That prayer may be more beautiful in heaven than a thousand religious performances.
Because grace begins where pretending ends.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your story. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Sometimes somebody else needs to see that they are not the only Christian still fighting.
And if one particular person came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore that.
Send this privately if their story should remain private.
Save it too.
Because temptation has an interesting way of making us forget in the night what we believed clearly in the morning.
Come back when loneliness starts negotiating.
Come back when an old relationship calls.
Come back when temptation tells you, “Just once.”
Come back and remember:
You are not protecting yourself because desire is worthless.
You guard it because God created sexuality with extraordinary meaning.
But I want to say this carefully because words matter.

Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity—not pressured giving. Paul writes that each person should give as he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Let it be an offering of support, not a transaction with God.
And if you already faithfully set aside giving according to your biblical convictions, do not let us manipulate your conscience into redirecting what you believe belongs elsewhere.
Pray.
Save.
Sometimes supporting the spread of the Gospel costs money.
Sometimes it costs thirty seconds and the courage to let your friends see what you believe.
Neither action purchases God’s approval.
Christ already paid the price we never could.
We serve because we have been loved.
We give because we have received.
We share because somebody else is still hiding in the darkness we once knew.
And perhaps that is the final lesson buried inside those ancient Hebrew words:
אִם־תָּעִירוּ וְאִם־תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ
Do not carelessly awaken what was designed to carry enormous power.
Do not treat holy things casually.
Do not confuse desire with destiny.
Do not confuse chemistry with covenant.
Do not let loneliness choose what wisdom would refuse.
But if you already awakened it...
if you already crossed the boundary...
if you already carry the memories...
if the scandal already happened...
then look at the cross.
Because the warning is not the end of the Bible.
Jesus is.
And your sexual past does not possess authority greater than His blood.
Your shame does not outrank His grace.
Your worst night does not get to veto His redemption.
Your scars may explain part of your story.
They do not have to write its ending.
The fire you awakened too soon may have burned pages of your story—but it cannot burn the pen out of the hand of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN SEARCHED THE CITY AT NIGHT FOR THE MAN SHE LOVED
paragraphs: THE WOMAN SEARCHED THE CITY AT NIGHT FOR THE MAN SHE LOVED

She left her bed, walked into the darkness, questioned the watchmen, and refused to stop searching. But beneath this ancient love story is a question that may expose what your own heart has been chasing in the dark.
There is something almost haunting about the scene.
A woman is lying awake at night.
The city is dark.
The streets are quiet.
The man she loves is nowhere beside her.
And eventually, staying in bed becomes more painful than getting up and searching for him.
Song of Songs 3 opens with words that still carry the ache of longing thousands of years later:
עַל־מִשְׁכָּבִי בַּלֵּילוֹת בִּקַּשְׁתִּי אֵת שֶׁאָהֲבָה נַפְשִׁי
ʿal-mishkavi balleilot biqqashti et she’ahavah nafshi...
A close rendering is:
“Upon my bed in the nights, I sought the one whom my soul loves.”
Then comes the painful confession:
בִּקַּשְׁתִּיו וְלֹא מְצָאתִיו
biqqashtiv velo metzativ.
“I sought him, but I did not find him.”
Song of Songs 3:1.
Read that again slowly.
“I sought him, but I did not find him.”
Some of you know exactly what those words feel like.
Not because you have wandered through an ancient city looking for a lover...
but because you know what it is to reach for something you desperately wanted and touch nothing.
You prayed.
Nothing seemed to happen.
You loved.
They left.
You trusted.
You were betrayed.
You built something.
It collapsed.
You thought marriage would heal the loneliness.
It didn’t.
You thought money would quiet the fear.
It didn’t.
You thought success would finally make you feel significant.
It didn’t.
You thought another relationship would erase the memory of the last one.
It didn’t.
You thought if enough people admired you, followed you, needed you, praised you, or wanted you, the ache inside your chest would finally become quiet.
And then night came.
And when everything became silent...
the ache was still there.
That is what makes this woman unforgettable.
She does not pretend she does not long.
She gets up.
אָקוּמָה נָּא וַאֲסוֹבְבָה בָעִיר
Aqumah na va’asovevah vaʿir.
“I will arise now and go about the city...”
She searches the streets.
She searches the squares.
She looks for “the one whom my soul loves.”
And again:
בִּקַּשְׁתִּיו וְלֹא מְצָאתִיו
“I sought him, but I did not find him.”
Song of Songs 3:2.
There is desperation here.
Movement.
Longing.
Vulnerability.
This is not a woman casually wondering where somebody went.
Something inside her refuses to remain still.
Then she encounters the watchmen who patrol the city.
She asks them:
אֵת שֶׁאָהֲבָה נַפְשִׁי רְאִיתֶם
Et she’ahavah nafshi re’item?
“Have you seen the one whom my soul loves?”
Song of Songs 3:3.
What a question.
Have you seen the one my soul loves?
Not merely the one I find attractive.
Not merely the one who makes life convenient.
Not merely the one who can give me something.
“The one whom my soul loves.”
And then...
after the bed...
after the darkness...
after the streets...
after the searching...
after the watchmen...
she finds him.
Song of Songs says:
כִּמְעַט שֶׁעָבַרְתִּי מֵהֶם עַד שֶׁמָּצָאתִי אֵת שֶׁאָהֲבָה נַפְשִׁי
“Scarcely had I passed them when I found the one whom my soul loves.”
And what does she do?
אֲחַזְתִּיו וְלֹא אַרְפֶּנּוּ
Ahaztiv velo arpen-nu.
“I held him and would not let him go.”
Song of Songs 3:4.
That sentence changes the atmosphere.
She searched.
She found.
She held.
She would not let go.
But before we turn this into something it was never meant to say, we need to respect Scripture enough to let Scripture speak.
Song of Songs is poetry celebrating love, desire, beauty, longing, and covenantal intimacy between a man and a woman. In its immediate literary context, this woman is searching for the man she loves.
We do not need to pretend that every street, watchman, bedroom, embrace, or detail is secretly a coded reference to Jesus.
Christ does not need us to distort Scripture in order to preach Christ.
But when this woman's longing is allowed to remain what it is, something deeply human begins to surface.
We were made capable of longing.
We attach ourselves to what we treasure.
We pursue what we believe will satisfy us.
And that raises a far more uncomfortable question:
What does your heart search for when nobody is watching?
That may be where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because everybody is searching.
Some search bedrooms.
Some search bars.
Some search churches.
Some search bank accounts.
Some search careers.
Some search pornography.
Some search relationships.
Some search applause.
Some search achievements.
Some search social media at two in the morning because silence forces them to feel things scrolling helps them avoid.
Some keep returning to the person God has already shown them they need to release.
Some keep pursuing validation from people who cannot heal the wound that created the hunger for validation.
Some are not looking for love anymore.
They are looking for anesthesia.
Anything to make the loneliness stop.
Anything to make the shame quiet.
Anything to make them feel wanted again.
And sometimes the most dangerous moment is not when you realize you are lost.
It is when you become comfortable searching in the wrong city for something that city can never give you.
There are desires that are good.
Marriage is good.
Love is good.
Intimacy is good.
Being known is good.
Companionship is good.
Song of Songs itself refuses the idea that godly love must be cold, emotionless, or embarrassed by affection.
But even the greatest human love cannot bear the weight of being God.
Your husband cannot be your savior.
Your wife cannot be your savior.
Your boyfriend cannot be your savior.
Your girlfriend cannot be your savior.
Your children cannot be your savior.
Your pastor cannot be your savior.
Your career cannot be your savior.
And the person whose absence broke your heart cannot become the god around whom the rest of your existence revolves.
Human love can be breathtaking.
But human beings are finite.
We cannot ask another person to heal what ultimately requires the grace of God.
And this is where the story begins touching a wound much deeper than romance.
Because Scripture tells another story about searching.
Only this time...
we are not the hero.
Jesus said:
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
Luke 19:10.
Think about the reversal.
We spend our lives imagining ourselves searching for God.
Yet the Gospel confronts us with something far more astonishing.
God moved toward sinners.
Christ came seeking the lost.
The scandal of Christianity is not that morally impressive people successfully climbed their way toward God.
The scandal is that holy God showed mercy toward guilty people who could never save themselves.
We wandered.
He came.
We sinned.
He remained holy.
We hid.
He called.
We accumulated guilt we could not erase.
And Christ went to the cross.
The Bible does not say our deepest problem is simply loneliness.
Our deepest problem is sin.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Sin is not merely having a bad day or making an unfortunate mistake.
Sin places us in rebellion against the God who made us.
That is why no relationship can ultimately rescue us.
We do not merely need somebody to hold us.
We need reconciliation with God.
And that is exactly why Jesus Christ matters.
He did not come merely to make sad people feel better about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin and its judgment so that those who turn to Him in repentance and faith can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Bring us to God.
That is the destination.
Not merely a better mood.
Not merely a better relationship.
Not merely religious inspiration.
God.
And maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps you have spent years asking God to give you the thing you thought would complete you...
while God has been exposing how desperately you need Him.
Maybe you have been searching the city at night.
Not literally.
But spiritually.
Looking through old messages.
Returning to old sins.
Reopening old wounds.
Replaying old conversations.
Checking whether somebody noticed you.
Wondering why somebody abandoned you.
Trying to become attractive enough, successful enough, spiritual enough, useful enough, impressive enough...
so that nobody will ever leave you again.
And Jesus is not standing at the end of that road offering another temporary distraction.
He offers forgiveness.
Grace.
Reconciliation.
A new identity.
A new heart.
A new direction.
Life in Him.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace restored him.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Grace met him at a cross.
Paul carried a history of persecuting Christians.
Grace transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
Jesus knew it.
He still spoke to her.
He still offered living water.
He still revealed truth.
And her story did not end at the well.
That is the Gospel Warrior message:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because grace means God pretends sin does not matter.
Grace is costly precisely because sin is serious.
The cross proves both.
At Calvary, God did not call evil good.
Christ bore judgment.
And the empty tomb declares that sin, death, and the grave do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So maybe the question tonight is no longer:
“Have you seen the one whom my soul loves?”
Maybe the question is:
What has my soul been loving more than Jesus?
That question can hurt.
Let it.
What do you protect even when obedience to Christ threatens it?
Whose approval controls you?
What secret sin keeps receiving the affection that belongs to God?
What relationship have you turned into an idol?
What are you terrified of losing because somewhere inside you, you believe you cannot survive without it?
What do you run toward when your heart hurts?
Your answer may reveal what your heart has been worshiping.
And if this exposes something hidden, do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning away from sin and returning to the One who is worthy.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
For those who come to Christ, grace does not say, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Grace says, “Come.”
And then Christ begins changing you.
Maybe somebody reading this has been hiding for years.
Everybody thinks you are strong.
Everybody thinks your faith is fine.
Everybody thinks your marriage is fine.
Everybody thinks your mind is fine.
Everybody thinks your private life matches your public Christianity.
But you know.
God knows.
And perhaps you are exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
One people applaud.
And one you desperately hope nobody discovers.
You do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Bring what is hidden into His light.
Receive the mercy God offers through Jesus Christ.
And where your sin has harmed others, repentance should begin producing truth, humility, restitution where appropriate, changed behavior, and obedience.
Grace is not permission to keep running into darkness.
Grace is the reason you can finally come out of it.
And perhaps tonight your prayer does not need impressive language.
Maybe it simply needs honesty:

“Jesus, I have been searching everywhere except where I needed to look. I have loved things more than You. I have sinned. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change me. Teach my heart to treasure You above everything else.”
If that is where you are, do not merely feel emotional and keep scrolling.
Respond.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray.
Repent.
Seek mature Christian community.
Return to Christ.
Somebody else may be reading silently who needs to know that Christ still saves, restores, forgives, and transforms sinners.
Do not underestimate what sharing truth can do.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, and salvation is the gift of God, not the result of our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But if Gospel-centered truth has strengthened you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone who desperately needs to encounter it.
Your support is not a payment to God.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus cannot be bought.
But generosity can support ministry, and sharing biblical truth can help carry the message beyond the person who first received it.
There will be nights when feelings become louder than truth.
Come back and remember what is true.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the Christian who has become lukewarm.
Invite the person quietly fighting temptation.
Invite the person recovering from failure.
Invite the seeker who is not even sure what they believe yet.
And yes...
invite the person who does not believe.
Because the Gospel was never meant to remain locked inside the lives of people who already know it.
The woman in Song of Songs walked into the night searching for the one her soul loved.
She searched until she found him.
And when she found him...
she held on.
But the greater story of Scripture leaves us with something even more staggering.
While sinners were wandering, God acted in love.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
The Shepherd came looking for the lost.
The Savior carried a cross.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The grave received Him.
And the grave could not keep Him.
So when the night becomes dark...
when loneliness whispers...
when shame resurrects old names...
when temptation tells you to return to what Christ called you out of...
when your past tries to convince you that you will always be the person you used to be...
remember this:
Your scandal does not have greater authority than the grace of Jesus Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
And once you discover that Jesus is not merely another object for your restless heart to consume, but the risen Lord worthy of your whole life...
stop searching for salvation in places that were never strong enough to save you.
Because one day you may discover that the darkest night of your searching became the very place where Christ showed you what your heart had been searching for all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EZEKIEL SAID JERUSALEM PAID HER LOVERS INSTEAD OF BEING PAID LIKE A PROSTITUTE
paragraphs: EZEKIEL SAID JERUSALEM PAID HER LOVERS INSTEAD OF BEING PAID LIKE A PROSTITUTE
And the most terrifying part of Ezekiel 16 is realizing how easily we can spend what God gave us chasing what can never love us back.
There are Bible chapters people underline because they comfort them.
There are chapters people quote because they inspire them.
And then there is Ezekiel 16.
A chapter so disturbing, so graphic, so emotionally violent in its imagery that many Christians quietly move past it.
But perhaps we should not.
Because buried inside its shocking language is one of the most devastating pictures of sin in Scripture...
and one of the most astonishing pictures of grace.
God tells Jerusalem something almost unbelievable.
You were not merely unfaithful.
You were paying your lovers.
Read that again.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:33 says:
לְכָל־זֹנוֹת יִתְּנוּ־נֵדֶה וְאַתְּ נָתַתְּ אֶת־נְדָנַיִךְ לְכָל־מְאַהֲבַיִךְ
L'khol-zonot yittenu-nedeh, ve'att natat et-nedanayikh l'khol-me'ahavayikh...
The sense is devastating:
Other prostitutes were given gifts.
Jerusalem gave gifts to her lovers.
Then Ezekiel makes the reversal unmistakable:
וּבְתִתֵּךְ אֶתְנָן וְאֶתְנַן לֹא נִתַּן־לָךְ
U'vetittekh etnan, ve'etnan lo nittan-lakh...
You gave the payment.
Payment was not given to you.
That is actually what the Hebrew says.

Jerusalem was so desperate after her false lovers that instead of being pursued, she spent her own treasure to pursue them. Ezekiel 16:33 says she effectively bribed them to come to her. Verse 34 emphasizes that this made her the reverse of the ordinary pattern Ezekiel was invoking.
But if we turn this chapter into nothing more than a shocking story about prostitution, we completely miss Ezekiel's point.
God is not giving Israel a lesson about the economics of the sex trade.
He is exposing covenant betrayal.
And before pointing our finger at ancient Jerusalem, we need to hear what this chapter is capable of exposing inside us.
Because some of us are still paying our lovers.
Not with coins.
With years.
With attention.
With purity.
With peace.
With marriages.
With families.
With convictions.
With sleep.
With money.
With calling.
With hours we will never get back.
With pieces of ourselves that belonged to God.
And the frightening thing about an idol is that it will keep accepting sacrifices without ever becoming a Savior.
That is where Ezekiel 16 becomes painfully personal.
The chapter does not begin with prostitution.
It begins with rescue.
That matters.
God portrays Jerusalem as an abandoned infant, unwanted and helpless, lying in the open field. No one had cared enough to properly tend the child.
Then God passed by.
And God said:
“Live.”
That is where the story begins.
Not with Jerusalem's goodness.
God's mercy.
Not Jerusalem finding God.
God finding Jerusalem.
Not Jerusalem cleaning herself first.
God rescuing her when she could not rescue herself.
Later the imagery changes. Jerusalem matures, and God describes entering covenant with her. Ezekiel 16:8 says, in part:
וָאָבוֹא בִבְרִית אֹתָךְ
Va'avo bivrit otakh.
“I entered into a covenant with you.”
And then:
וַתִּהְיִי לִי
Vattihyi li.
“You became Mine.”
God clothed her.
God adorned her.
God provided for her.
God gave her beauty.
God gave her dignity.
God gave her abundance.
And then comes one of the most tragic turns in the entire chapter.
“But you trusted in your beauty...”
Ezekiel 16:15.
There it is.
The gift replaced the Giver.
What God gave became the very thing Jerusalem used to forget the God who gave it.
Her beauty was from Him.
Her clothing was from Him.
Her gold was from Him.
Her silver was from Him.
Her food was from Him.
Yet Ezekiel describes Jerusalem taking those very gifts and devoting them to idols. The text specifically says that the gold and silver she used had been given to her by God.
Do you see why this chapter hurts?
Because idolatry is not merely loving something evil.
Sometimes idolatry is taking something good God gave you and allowing it to occupy the place only God deserves.
A career can become an altar.
A relationship can become an altar.
Beauty can become an altar.
Success can become an altar.
Money can become an altar.
Ministry can become an altar.
Even the approval of people who call themselves Christians can become an altar.
And eventually we can find ourselves sacrificing God's gifts to maintain something that cannot save us.
That is when Ezekiel's disturbing image becomes a mirror.
Jerusalem paid her lovers.
And maybe you have too.
Maybe you have paid for someone's acceptance by becoming someone you never wanted to become.
Maybe you kept lowering your convictions because you were terrified they would leave.
Maybe you surrendered your peace trying to keep someone interested.
Maybe you compromised privately because being wanted temporarily felt better than feeling lonely.
Maybe you have spent money you did not have maintaining an image for people who would disappear the moment the image collapsed.
Maybe you have sacrificed your family for success.
Maybe you have sacrificed prayer for entertainment.
Maybe you have sacrificed truth for applause.
Maybe you have sacrificed obedience for a relationship.
Maybe you have sacrificed your secret life to pornography and discovered that pornography never says, “Enough.”
Maybe you have fed bitterness for years and bitterness has never once healed the wound that created it.
Maybe you keep returning to the same sin expecting it to finally give you what it promised the first time.
And every time...
it charges you again.
That is one of sin's oldest lies.
Sin advertises pleasure while concealing the invoice.
It says, “Take this.”
It does not tell you what taking it may eventually take from you.
Jerusalem discovered this brutally.
Her lovers did not become her salvation.
They became part of her humiliation and judgment.

The very alliances and idols she pursued could not provide covenant security. Ezekiel's metaphor deliberately connects spiritual unfaithfulness with Jerusalem's pursuit of idols and foreign powers rather than trusting the LORD.
That historical context matters.
This passage should never be weaponized against women, sex workers, people with painful sexual histories, or anyone carrying sexual shame.
Ezekiel's target is Jerusalem's covenant infidelity.
Jerusalem is personified as an adulterous wife because covenant betrayal is the theological center of the metaphor.
And there is something else we must not sanitize.
Ezekiel 16 does not present sin as cute.
Modern culture often turns rebellion into personality.
Scripture treats rebellion as deadly.
We say, “Nobody is perfect.”
True.
But sometimes we use a true sentence to avoid an uncomfortable word:
Repent.
Jesus did not die so we could rename chains and continue wearing them.
Grace does not mean God stopped caring about holiness.
Grace means sinners who could never cleanse themselves can be forgiven, reconciled, transformed, and brought home through what God has done.
And this is where Ezekiel 16 does something extraordinary.
If the chapter ended with Jerusalem exposed, judged, and humiliated, it would already be terrifying.
But it doesn't end there.
After all the betrayal...
after all the idolatry...
after everything God has exposed...
God says:
“Nevertheless...”
That word changes the atmosphere.
Ezekiel 16:60 declares:
וְזָכַרְתִּי אֲנִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי אֹתָךְ בִּימֵי נְעוּרָיִךְ
Vezakharti ani et-beriti otakh bimei ne'urayikh...
“I will remember My covenant with you in the days of your youth...”
And God speaks of establishing an everlasting covenant.
Think about the emotional weight of that.
Jerusalem forgot.
God remembered.
Jerusalem broke covenant.
God spoke of covenant restoration.
Jerusalem had spent God's gifts pursuing lovers.
Yet the final movement of the chapter is not Jerusalem boasting about how she repaired herself.
It is Jerusalem being silenced by shame as God acts in mercy.
Then comes Ezekiel 16:63.
One of the most breathtaking lines in the chapter.
God speaks of making atonement for what she had done.
The Hebrew uses the verb:
כַפְּרִי — kapperi
from the Hebrew root כפר — k-p-r, associated with atonement.
That does not erase the judgment Ezekiel has just pronounced.
It means judgment is not the final word in the chapter.
God's covenant mercy is.
And for Christians reading the whole biblical story, we cannot encounter the themes of covenant, guilt, atonement, forgiveness, and restoration without eventually arriving at Jesus Christ.
Not because Ezekiel 16:63 should be ripped from its historical context and treated as though Ezekiel were simply narrating Calvary in advance.
He wasn't.
Ezekiel was speaking God's word concerning Jerusalem.
But the trajectory of Scripture carries us toward God's ultimate answer to human guilt.
Jesus.
At the Last Supper, Jesus took the cup and declared:
“This cup is the new covenant in my blood...”
Luke 22:20.
At the cross, Jesus did something our idols could never do.
Our idols consume sacrifices.
Christ became the sacrifice.
Our idols demand that we keep paying.
Christ declared:
“It is finished.”
Our idols tell us to destroy ourselves to keep them.
Jesus gave Himself to rescue sinners.
Our idols expose us and abandon us.
Christ knows us completely and calls sinners to repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
And perhaps that is why Ezekiel 16 is more than a shocking chapter.
It is a warning about what happens when the human heart searches everywhere except God for what only God can ultimately provide.
You can keep paying your lovers.
Or you can come home.
And I am not merely talking about sexual sin.
What owns your heart?
What gets the first claim on your attention?
Whose approval controls your obedience?
What loss frightens you so deeply that you would compromise God's Word to prevent it?
What do you repeatedly feed while your relationship with Christ starves?
What are you afraid to surrender because somewhere inside you, you suspect you need it more than you need God?
That may be where your altar is.
Be honest.
Because God already knows.
Repentance is not informing God of something He failed to discover.
Repentance is finally agreeing with God about what He has already exposed.
Maybe somebody reading this feels filthy right now.
Maybe Ezekiel's language touched something you desperately wanted to keep buried.
Maybe you have committed adultery.
Maybe you have betrayed someone.
Maybe addiction has eaten years of your life.
Maybe nobody at church knows what happens when your door closes.
Maybe you have promised God, “Never again,” more times than you can remember.
And now shame whispers:
“You've gone too far.”
Look at the scandal of Scripture.
David fell terribly.
Peter denied Christ.
The prodigal went into the far country.
Paul once persecuted believers.
And the Gospel does not tell us sin does not matter.
The Gospel tells us sin matters so much that the Son of God went to the cross.
And grace is so astonishing that the cross can become the place where condemned sinners find forgiveness.
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
Not after we became impressive.
While sinners.
That is grace.
But grace calls us out of hiding.
If this exposed something you have been protecting, do not merely react to an article.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Bring it into the light.
Seek mature Christian help where necessary.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Stop financing the thing that is destroying you.
Stop paying lovers that cannot save you.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to be painfully simple:

“Jesus, forgive me. I have taken things You gave me and used them to run from You. I have loved gifts more than the Giver. I have looked for life in things that are killing me. Have mercy on me. Cleanse me. Teach me to love You again.”
If that prayer is yours, don't hide behind a reaction button.
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you, simply write:

You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Some things belong in confidential conversation with trusted pastors, counselors, mature believers, or appropriate professionals rather than a public comment section.
But you do not have to pretend you have no struggle at all.
And if Christ has already been restoring an area of your life you thought was beyond repair, tell somebody what His grace has done.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading the comments may be one testimony away from believing that repentance is still possible.
Not because Gospel Warrior needs another meaningless number on a screen.
They may never tell you.
They may laugh publicly and collapse privately.
They may need to discover that conviction is not God's invitation to despair.
It can become an invitation to come home.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.

But voluntary financial support of Gospel ministry is thoroughly compatible with the New Testament pattern of believers generously helping gospel work according to their means and convictions. Paul spoke appreciatively of believers who partnered with him in “giving and receiving” (Philippians 4:15–18), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 makes the principle equally important: Christian giving is not to be extracted through compulsion.
Think of it as partnership in the mission—not payment for grace.
But whether or not you ever send one cent, hear the greater invitation.
Give yourself to Christ.
Money without surrender is not discipleship.
Sharing Christian content while secretly worshiping another master will not heal your soul.
Jesus does not merely want space on your timeline.
He is Lord.
So before you leave this article...
ask yourself one final question.
What have I been paying to keep something in my life that Jesus has been asking me to surrender?
Maybe tonight is the night the payments stop.
Maybe tonight the secret gets confessed.
Maybe tonight the idol loses its altar.
Maybe tonight somebody returns to prayer.
Maybe tonight a husband tells the truth.
A wife forgives.
A prodigal comes home.
An addict asks for help.
A lukewarm Christian stops pretending.
A wounded believer whispers the name of Jesus again.
A sinner finally understands that being exposed by God's Word does not mean being invited to run farther from God.
It means there is still time to repent.
Ezekiel's Jerusalem paid her lovers.
But the Gospel announces something infinitely greater:
You cannot purchase redemption.
You cannot seduce God into loving you.
You cannot perform enough religion to erase your past.
You cannot pay the debt of sin with promises to “do better.”
Our hope is Jesus Christ—crucified and risen.
So stop paying what cannot save you.
Come to the One who can.
Because perhaps the most haunting tragedy in Ezekiel 16 was never simply that Jerusalem had lovers.
It was that she kept spending what God had given her to purchase what God had already offered her in covenant love.
Don't spend another piece of your life trying to buy from idols what can only be found in Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS FOLD THE LINEN CLOTH?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS FOLD THE LINEN CLOTH?
The Tiny Detail in the Empty Tomb We Were Never Supposed to Ignore—and the Truth Is More Powerful Than the Story You May Have Heard
There is a detail inside the empty tomb that takes only a few words to describe.
No angel explains it.
No disciple gives a sermon about it.
Jesus never tells us why it was there.
And yet John remembered it.

Decades after that morning, when he wrote about running toward the tomb, bending down, stepping into the place where the murdered body of Jesus Christ had been laid, John deliberately told us about a piece of cloth.
Not the stone.
Not only the angels.
Not merely the empty place where Jesus had been.
A cloth.
And once you understand what John actually wrote—not what internet legends have added to it—that little detail becomes even more powerful.
Because sometimes the most breathtaking evidence of what God has done is sitting quietly in the place where you expected to find death.
Mary Magdalene arrived while it was still dark.
That detail feels almost painfully human.
Because some of the most important moments of faith happen while it is still dark.
Before you understand.
Before the answer arrives.
Before grief loosens its grip.
Before the diagnosis changes.
Before the marriage heals.
Before the child comes home.
Before the addiction loses its hold.
Before you can explain what God is doing.
Mary came to a tomb.
She wasn't expecting resurrection.
She was expecting a corpse.
She saw the stone moved and immediately assumed something terrible had happened: “They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him” (John 20:2, KJV).
Think about that.
The greatest victory in human history had already happened...
and Mary thought something had gone terribly wrong.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Maybe God has been working in a place you have already pronounced dead.
Maybe you looked at the stone being moved and thought, “This is getting worse.”
Maybe heaven was writing resurrection while you were still reading tragedy.
Peter and John ran.
John arrived first, looked inside, and saw the linen cloths.
Peter arrived behind him and, characteristically, went straight into the tomb.
Then John records the detail that has fascinated generations:
“And the napkin, that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.” — John 20:7, KJV
The Greek deserves our attention.
John writes:
Transliterated:
kai to soudarion, ho ēn epi tēs kephalēs autou, ou meta tōn othoniōn keimenon alla chōris entetyligmenon eis hena topon.
In straightforward English:
“And the face cloth, which had been upon His head, not lying with the linen cloths, but separately, having been wrapped or rolled up, in one place.”
That matters.
The word John uses is σουδάριον — soudarion.
It refers to a small cloth, here the cloth associated with Jesus' head or face. John uses the same word earlier when Lazarus comes out of his tomb with his face wrapped in a cloth.
Then there is the word that creates so much discussion:
ἐντετυλιγμένον — entetyligmenon.
It comes from entylissō, meaning to wrap, roll, or fold up.
Some English translations therefore say “folded up.” Others say “rolled up.” The central observation is clear even where translators differ over the precise English wording:
The head cloth was separate from the other burial linens.
And here we need to protect something sacred.
The truth.
Perhaps you have heard the famous sermon illustration that says a folded napkin at a Jewish meal was a secret cultural signal from a master to his servant meaning:
“I am coming back.”
It is a beautiful story.
It preaches wonderfully.
There is only one serious problem.
Scripture does not say that.
John does not explain such a custom.
The Greek text does not contain the message “I am coming back.”
And reliable evidence for the popular table-napkin custom as it is often preached is lacking.
Christians should never be afraid when a favorite illustration turns out to be weaker than we thought.
Jesus does not need legends to make Him glorious.
The resurrection is powerful enough without embellishment.
Our faith does not become stronger when we force Scripture to say something it never said. Our faith becomes stronger when we love the Word of God enough to let it speak for itself.
So why mention the cloth?
John's emphasis is not a coded restaurant message.
It is the scene inside an empty tomb.
The linen wrappings are there.
The head cloth is there, separately.
Jesus is not.
Something has happened that does not look like the aftermath of frantic grave robbery.
Imagine the scene.
If someone had simply stolen the body, why leave the burial wrappings behind?
Why remove them from a corpse at all?
And why does John slow the story down enough for us to notice their condition and the separate head cloth?
The Gospel does not give us permission to reconstruct every physical movement that occurred during the resurrection. We should be humble where Scripture is silent.
But John absolutely wants us looking inside that tomb.
Because immediately after describing what was there, he tells us what happened to him.
“Then went in also that other disciple, which came first to the sepulchre, and he saw, and believed.” — John 20:8, KJV
He saw.
And believed.
Those words are enormous.
The cloth was not the resurrection.
The arrangement of the burial garments was not the Gospel.
The empty tomb by itself was not the whole Christian message.
Jesus Christ—crucified, buried, bodily risen and alive—is the center.
But the things left behind mattered.
They were part of what John saw in the place where death was supposed to have won.
And maybe that is where this story reaches through two thousand years and touches us.
Because all of us have grave clothes.
Things attached to versions of ourselves that Jesus came to put to death.
Shame.
Secret sin.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness we have renamed “discernment.”
Pride disguised as strength.
Church attendance without surrender.
Religious vocabulary without intimacy with Christ.
The affair.
The lie.
The bottle hidden where nobody looks.
The private messages.
The resentment toward the person who wounded you.
The guilt from something you did ten years ago that still whispers your name at 2:00 in the morning.
The smile you wear at church while your soul quietly bleeds underneath it.
We know what it means to carry evidence of death.
And some reading this have become so accustomed to their grave clothes that they have started calling them their identity.
“This is just who I am.”
“I'll always struggle with this.”
“God could forgive other people, but not after what I've done.”
“My family has always been this way.”
“I've already ruined too much.”
“I'll come back to Jesus when I get myself together.”
Listen carefully.
You do not clean yourself up so Jesus can resurrect you.
Dead people cannot resurrect themselves.
That is precisely why we need Christ.
Christianity is not the story of bad people becoming respectable.
It is the announcement that sinners who were spiritually dead can receive life through the crucified and risen Son of God.
Jesus did not walk out of that tomb because humanity finally deserved another chance.
He walked out because death could not hold the Author of life.
The cross had looked like scandal.
The Messiah stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Spat upon.
Nailed between criminals.
A crown of thorns pressed into His head.
His disciples scattered.
Peter denying Him.
His body placed inside another man's tomb.
If you had frozen history on Friday evening, Christianity would have looked like a failed movement surrounding a dead Teacher.
But God was not finished writing.
Friday's scandal was not the final sentence.
Sunday came.
And Jesus rewrote everything.
Not by pretending sin did not matter.
The cross proves sin matters more terribly than we often want to admit.

Our rebellion against a holy God is not a minor personality flaw. Scripture calls us sinners. We have violated God's commands, loved created things more than the Creator, and tried to rule lives that belong to Him.
The Gospel is not “God thinks you're wonderful, so don't worry.”
The Gospel is infinitely better.
God knew exactly how guilty we were...
and Christ came anyway.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus endured judgment.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And Jesus rose.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace says the price has been paid by Someone else.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the tomb.
Maybe the real question isn't merely, “Why was the cloth folded?”
Maybe the question is:
What are you still doing among the grave clothes when Jesus is calling you into life?
You can know every resurrection fact and still refuse the risen Christ.
You can debate Greek verbs and remain spiritually dead.
You can attend Easter services every year and never surrender.
You can repost Christian quotes while protecting the very sin Jesus is confronting.
You can wear a cross around your neck while refusing to carry one.
John entered.
He saw.
He believed.
Eventually he would understand much more.
And somewhere right now, somebody reading this knows this stopped being an article several paragraphs ago.
God has put His finger on something.
You know exactly what it is.
That hidden relationship.
That habit.
That unforgiveness.
That secret compromise.
That spiritual exhaustion.
That carefully maintained Christian appearance.
That voice saying you have gone too far to come home.
You haven't out-sinned the sufficiency of Christ's blood.
But grace is not permission to remain in rebellion.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Run to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become worthy.
Not after you repair your reputation.
Come filthy.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with the scandal.
Come with the wreckage.
Come with the truth.
Jesus is in the business of resurrection.
Peter's story itself proves it.
Only days before that empty tomb, Peter had denied even knowing Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory toward the tomb.
Imagine running toward the grave of the Man you swore you would never abandon—the Man you abandoned anyway.
Peter had every reason to believe his story ended in disgrace.
But the risen Jesus would meet him again.
Restore him.
Commission him.
Use him.
That is scandal becoming grace.
And perhaps somebody needs those words more than an explanation about ancient cloth.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter when surrendered to Jesus Christ.
That doesn't mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
It doesn't mean wounds become imaginary.
It doesn't mean repentance is unnecessary.
It means failure does not possess greater authority than the risen Christ.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your shame is not stronger than His blood.
Your chains are not stronger than His resurrection.
Your past does not get to sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
So when you picture that tomb again, don't build your faith on a sentimental legend about a dinner napkin.
Build it on something infinitely stronger.
Christ is risen.
The tomb was empty.
The burial cloths remained.
The head cloth lay separately.
John saw.
John believed.
And soon the disciples would encounter the risen Lord Himself.
Christian faith ultimately stands or falls not on whether a cloth was neatly folded, but on Jesus Christ crucified and risen from the dead.
That is our hope.
And if Christ rose, then everything changes.
Sin does not have the final word.
Shame does not have the final word.
Death does not have the final word.
Your past does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God, don't manufacture a religious response. Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. God already knows them. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who has been quietly disappearing.
The believer who thinks his failure disqualified him.
The daughter carrying shame.
The father nobody realizes is exhausted.
The person who stopped going to church.
The person who thinks Christianity is nothing but myths and religious manipulation.
The person who desperately needs to discover that biblical Christianity does not require us to defend made-up stories. Truth is powerful enough.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't. We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if this ministry is faithfully pointing people toward Jesus Christ, then supporting and sharing that work can be one practical way to glorify God by helping biblical truth travel farther.
They may never open the Bible you offered them.
But they might stop for an article you shared at exactly the moment their world is collapsing.
There may come a night when shame tries to convince you that your story cannot be redeemed, and you will need to remember the empty tomb again.
It is not an offering that buys grace.
It is not proof that you are a better Christian.

It is simply a practical way to stand behind the work—to help Gospel-centered content reach people who may be one article, one Scripture, one moment of conviction away from turning back toward Christ.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
To glorify God.
Because somewhere beyond your screen may be a person still standing outside a tomb, convinced that everything is over.
Let them see what John saw.
The grave clothes remained.
But Jesus didn't.
And perhaps the most unforgettable thing about that linen cloth is not that Jesus left us a secret message by folding it.
It is that He no longer needed it.
Death had lost its claim.
The tomb had lost its prisoner.
And the scandal of the cross was becoming the announcement of grace to the world.
So bring Jesus the chapter you thought ruined the whole story.
Bring Him the denial.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the grave clothes.
Because the risen Christ is still doing what human beings could never do for themselves.
He makes dead things live.
He forgives sinners.
He restores failures.
He breaks chains.
He calls wanderers home.
He turns graves into testimonies.
And He takes stories stained by scandal and writes grace across pages we thought were already finished.
The cloth was left in the tomb because the One who wore it had walked into resurrection—and whatever Jesus brings out of the grave never has to belong to death again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PROVERBS DOESN’T JUST SAY “DON’T COMMIT ADULTERY”—IT SHOWS YOU HOW SEDUCTION WORKS
paragraphs: PROVERBS DOESN’T JUST SAY “DON’T COMMIT ADULTERY”—IT SHOWS YOU HOW SEDUCTION WORKS

The Bible exposes what happens long before the bedroom—the flattering words, the private conversation, the emotional hunger, the seemingly innocent steps toward the door…and the devastating moment when someone realizes the affair did not begin when two bodies touched. It began when a heart stopped guarding the distance.
There is a terrifying sentence buried inside Proverbs that many people read too quickly.
Not because it is complicated.
Because it is painfully simple.
“Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house.”
Proverbs 5:8.
Not merely…
“Don’t sleep with her.”
Not…
“Be careful once you get inside.”
Not even…
“Stand at the doorway and prove how spiritually strong you are.”
Stay away from the door.
That is how seriously biblical wisdom treats seduction.
And maybe someone reading this already knows why.
Because adultery rarely introduces itself by saying:
Hello. I am here to destroy your marriage.
It usually arrives much more politely.
A conversation.
A compliment.
A notification.
A message you probably should not answer.
Someone noticing something your spouse has stopped noticing.
Someone laughing at your jokes.
Someone listening.
Someone saying, “You deserve better.”
Someone telling you how attractive you still are.
Someone who seems to understand the lonely parts of you.
Nothing has happened yet.
That is what you tell yourself.
Nothing happened.
We only talked.
We only had coffee.
I only replied.
I was only being friendly.
She understands me.
He listens to me.
My marriage has been difficult.
Nobody needs to know.
I can stop whenever I want.

And thousands of years before private messages, disappearing chats, smartphones, secret accounts, dating apps, workplace messaging, and late-night texting existed, Scripture described the anatomy of this trap with disturbing accuracy.
Proverbs does not merely condemn adultery.
It takes you inside the seduction.
Listen to the Hebrew imagery of Proverbs 5:3:
כִּי נֹפֶת תִּטֹּפְנָה שִׂפְתֵי זָרָה וְחָלָק מִשֶּׁמֶן חִכָּהּ
Ki nofet tittof'nah siftei zarah, vechalaq mishemen chikkah.
The imagery is vivid:
The lips of the forbidden woman drip honey.
Her speech is smoother than oil.
That is important.
Because temptation is not described as ugly at the beginning.
It is sweet.
Smooth.
Attractive.
Pleasant.
That is precisely why it is dangerous.
If every temptation looked like the devastation it eventually produced, very few people would choose it.
Imagine if the first flirtatious message arrived carrying photographs of the children crying six months later.
Imagine if that secret conversation immediately showed you the courtroom.
The custody arrangement.
The shattered trust.
The spouse sitting alone asking:
Was any of our marriage real?
Imagine if pornography immediately showed the years of distorted desire it might cultivate.
Imagine if emotional infidelity immediately displayed the face of the husband or wife who would eventually discover those messages.
Imagine if lust introduced itself by its destination instead of its sensation.
But temptation rarely shows you the ending.
It shows you the honey.
Proverbs shows you both.
The next verse turns the camera around.
“But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword.”
The Hebrew begins:
וְאַחֲרִיתָהּ מָרָה
Ve'acharîtah marah.
Her end is bitter.
Notice the contrast.
Beginning: honey.
Ending: bitterness.
Beginning: smooth.
Ending: sharp.
That is one of sin's oldest deceptions.
It advertises the beginning and hides the ending.
Satan did something similar in Eden.
The fruit was desirable.
The consequences were obscured.
And human beings have been reaching for beautiful beginnings while ignoring terrible endings ever since.
But Proverbs goes even deeper.
Chapter 7 gives us what almost feels like a cinematic reconstruction.
A young man appears.
Scripture describes him as lacking sense.
He is walking through the street.
Evening comes.
Darkness gathers.
And then comes one of the most important details in the entire account.
He passes near her corner.
Read that carefully.
He was not suddenly transported into adultery.
He was walking somewhere.
He took a route.
He approached a place.
He entered an environment.
He placed himself within reach of something wisdom had already told him to avoid.
That means the collapse did not begin with the sexual act.
There were footsteps before there was a fall.
And that may be the sentence somebody needs tonight:
There are always footsteps before the fall.
The affair may begin before the hotel room.
Before the kiss.
Before the touching.
Before anyone removes a wedding ring.
Sometimes adultery begins in the imagination.
Sometimes with resentment you refuse to surrender to Christ.
Sometimes with comparison.
Sometimes when you begin telling another person things that rightly belong inside your marriage.
Sometimes when you begin dressing for one particular person's attention.
Sometimes when you repeatedly check whether they viewed your story.
Sometimes when you delete a conversation—not because anything explicitly sexual happened, but because deep inside you already know why you do not want your spouse to see it.
That delete button can become a doorway.
The hidden password can become a doorway.
The lunch nobody knows about can become a doorway.
The emotional dependence can become a doorway.
The private joke can become a doorway.
The message after midnight can become a doorway.
And Proverbs says:
Don't stand there admiring the architecture.
Get away from the door.
Then Proverbs 7 reveals another mechanism of seduction.
Words.
“With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.”
Seduction works on the imagination before it captures the body.
It creates a story.
You deserve this.
Your spouse doesn't understand you.
This isn't really cheating.
God wants you happy.
You're only talking.
Nobody will ever know.
You can repent afterward.
Your marriage was already dead.
This person is your soulmate.
And perhaps the most dangerous lie:
I can get close without falling.
But biblical wisdom does not tell you to discover how close you can stand to destruction.
It tells you to flee.
That is why Joseph's response to Potiphar's wife is so powerful.
When she grabbed him, Joseph did not remain in the room to demonstrate superior willpower.
He ran.
He left his garment behind.
His reputation would temporarily suffer for it.
He would be falsely accused.
He would be imprisoned.
But he kept something more valuable than the garment she held in her hands.
His integrity before God.
Sometimes holiness looks remarkably undramatic.
Sometimes holiness is blocking the number.
Deleting the conversation.
Changing the route.
Ending the private lunches.
Confessing the emotional attachment.
Installing accountability.
Handing your phone to your spouse.
Leaving the room.
Running.
Not because you are weak.
Because you finally understand that you are not invincible.
Paul later gives Christians essentially the same battle strategy:
“Flee fornication.”
And again:
“Flee also youthful lusts.”
There are battles Scripture tells us to stand and fight.
Sexual temptation is repeatedly treated differently.
Create distance.
Because wisdom knows something pride refuses to admit:
You can genuinely love Jesus and still make catastrophic decisions when you repeatedly place yourself near temptation.
David knew God.
David worshiped.
David wrote psalms.
