You are protecting your secret from His lordship.
He knows.
He knows what happened.
He knows what you did.
He knows what they did to you.
He knows why you reach for it.
He knows how long it has been happening.
He knows the relapse.
He knows the resentment.
He knows the fantasy.
He knows the fear.
He knows the thing you have never said aloud.
And still the cross stands.
That is why repentance is possible.
You are not walking toward a Savior who discovers your scandal halfway through the conversation.
You are coming to the Savior who knew the full debt before He went to Calvary.
This is grace.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Power to stop hiding.
Maybe today your prayer does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe it needs honesty.

“Jesus, I have called You Lord while keeping this from You. I have wanted Your comfort without Your authority here. I have defended what You are asking me to surrender. Forgive me. I cannot transform myself. Have mercy on me. Renew my mind. Teach me obedience. Give me strength to do whatever repentance requires. This room is Yours too.”
Then open the door.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more compromise.
Not when you finally feel spiritual enough.
Bring it into His light now.
And if this exposed the room you have been protecting, don't turn the conviction into another passing emotional moment.
You do not owe strangers the private details of your struggle. But there is something powerful about refusing to pretend you have no struggle at all.
And read the comments beneath this article.
Someone may need to discover that Christians are not people who never fight battles.
We are people learning to bring our battles under the lordship and mercy of Jesus Christ.
Not as proof that you have mastered surrender.
Your share may place the message of repentance, mercy, and the lordship of Christ in front of someone who would never have searched for it themselves.
Because the frightening thing about living sacrifices is that tomorrow we wake up alive again.
There will be another morning.
Another temptation.
Another decision.
Another opportunity to crawl away from yesterday's surrender.
Come back and remember:
Because of His mercies...
present yourself again.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you follow Jesus, stay close.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ. But if this work helps you and you want to participate in helping it reach others, your support allows us to keep sowing.
And there is more waiting for those who are serious about growing deeper.
But before you leave...
go back to the room.
You know the one.
Maybe nobody else knows it exists.
Maybe you have become so skilled at Christian language that everyone assumes every door is open.
Jesus is not asking for your polished performance.
He wants you.
And the astonishing news of the gospel is that the Savior standing outside that room is not unfamiliar with scandal.
He carried ours.
He was pierced for sinners.
He walked into death carrying guilt that was not His.
And He walked out of the grave victorious.
So you can stop hiding.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can surrender.
You can come home.
You can hand Him the key.
And when your fingers are trembling because you are afraid of what obedience will cost, remember the nail-scarred hands receiving it.
The One asking for everything is the One who first gave Himself for you.
Perhaps the last room you surrender will become the place where you finally discover how deep His mercy reaches.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SARAH LOOKED AT HAGAR’S SON AND SAID, “SEND THEM AWAY”—BUT WHAT GOD DID IN THE DESERT CHANGES HOW YOU READ THE ENTIRE STORY
paragraphs: SARAH LOOKED AT HAGAR’S SON AND SAID, “SEND THEM AWAY”—BUT WHAT GOD DID IN THE DESERT CHANGES HOW YOU READ THE ENTIRE STORY

The heartbreaking story of Sarah, Abraham, Hagar, Ishmael, and Isaac is not merely about a broken household. It exposes what happens when human beings try to manufacture what God promised—and reveals the astonishing mercy of the God who still hears people crying in the wilderness.
There are sentences in the Bible that are difficult to read slowly.
This is one of them.
Sarah looked at Abraham—the man who had waited decades with her for the promised child—and demanded that another woman and Abraham’s own son be sent away.
Not relocated.
Not given another room.
Sent away.
The Hebrew of Genesis 21:10 is painfully direct:
גָּרֵשׁ הָאָמָה הַזֹּאת וְאֶת־בְּנָהּ
Gāresh hā’āmāh hazzō’t we’et-benāh.
“Drive out this servant woman and her son.”
Then Sarah gives the reason.
כִּי לֹא יִירַשׁ בֶּן־הָאָמָה הַזֹּאת עִם־בְּנִי עִם־יִצְחָק
“For the son of this servant woman shall not inherit with my son, with Isaac.”
Those words tore through Abraham.
Scripture does not portray him as emotionally untouched.
Genesis says:
וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר מְאֹד בְּעֵינֵי אַבְרָהָם עַל אוֹדֹת בְּנוֹ
The matter was exceedingly grievous in Abraham’s eyes...
because of his son.
That last phrase matters.
Ishmael was not an inconvenience to Abraham.
He was his son.
Before Isaac ever laughed inside Abraham’s tent, Ishmael had called Abraham father.
Before Isaac took his first steps, Abraham had watched Ishmael grow.
Abraham had held him.
Loved him.
Circumcised him in obedience to God.
And when God previously told Abraham that Sarah would bear the covenant son, Abraham himself cried:
“Oh that Ishmael might live before You!”
There was a father underneath the patriarch.
And now that father was being torn apart.
But to understand why this family reached such a devastating morning, you have to go backward.
Because Hagar did not simply appear in Abraham’s story.
She entered the story when faith became tired of waiting.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
And eventually the silence between promise and fulfillment became unbearable.
So Sarah devised another way.
Genesis 16 records that Sarah gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham so that a child might be obtained through her.
And Abraham agreed.
That decision is one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable mirrors because we still do the same thing.
God speaks.
We believe Him.
Then nothing seems to happen.
Days become months.
Months become years.
Prayer begins to feel like talking into an empty room.
And somewhere between “God promised” and “God fulfilled,” we become tempted to help God accomplish what only God can accomplish.
We manufacture.
Manipulate.
Force doors.
Compromise convictions.
Choose relationships God never gave us.
Create shortcuts.
Call impatience “wisdom.”
Call fear “being realistic.”
And sometimes we even attach God’s name to decisions that were born from our inability to wait for Him.
Abraham and Sarah had received a promise.
But Hagar became entangled in their attempt to produce through human strength what God intended to accomplish through divine faithfulness.
Then Hagar conceived Ishmael.
And suddenly what looked like a solution became a household wound.
There was resentment.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
Hagar fled.
And this is where something astonishing happened.
The woman caught inside Abraham and Sarah’s broken decision ran into the wilderness...
and God went looking for her.
Genesis 16 says the Angel of the LORD found her near a spring.
Think about that.
Hagar was an Egyptian servant.
Socially vulnerable.
Pregnant.
Running.
Hurting.
Probably wondering whether anyone in the world cared what happened to her.
But heaven knew her location.
God called her by name.
“Hagar.”
And God told her that the child inside her would be named:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma‘el.
Ishmael.
The name is built around the Hebrew verb שָׁמַע — shāma‘, “to hear.”
His name carried a message:
God hears.
The biblical explanation is explicit: the LORD had heard Hagar’s affliction.
Imagine carrying that name through life.
Every time Hagar called her son—
“Ishmael!”
—she was repeating the testimony of the wilderness.
God hears.
Dinner is ready, God-hears.
Come home, God-hears.
Stay close to me, God-hears.
My son...
God heard me.
And Hagar responded to this encounter with one of the most moving confessions in Genesis.
She spoke of the God who saw her.
The invisible servant had discovered that she was not invisible to heaven.
Remember that when you feel overlooked.
Remember Hagar when everyone seems to have continued living while you are barely surviving.
Remember her when your prayers seem trapped beneath the ceiling.
Remember her when someone else's decisions created wounds you never asked to carry.
Human beings may overlook you.
People may use you.
Families may fail you.
Someone may put you in a situation you never chose and then leave you carrying the consequences.
But you have never disappeared from God's sight.
Years passed.
Then God did what human strength could never do.
Sarah conceived.
Isaac was born.
The impossible child arrived.
The promised son laughed inside Abraham’s house.
And eventually Sarah saw Ishmael מְצַחֵק — metzaḥeq.

The Hebrew word comes from the same root associated with laughter and Isaac’s name. English translations render the scene differently, including ideas such as laughing, playing, or mocking; the precise nuance has been debated. The New Testament later interprets the conflict in Galatians 4:29 in terms of the son born according to the flesh persecuting the son associated with God’s promise.
Sarah responded:
Send the servant woman away.
Send her son away.
And Abraham was devastated.
Then God spoke.
This is where careless readings of the story can become dangerous.
God did not tell Abraham that Ishmael was worthless.
God did not say Hagar was invisible.
God did not suddenly forget the woman He had previously found beside the spring.
Instead, God reaffirmed that His covenant line would be reckoned through Isaac while simultaneously promising concerning Ishmael:
“I will make a nation of the son of the servant woman also, because he is your offspring.”
Isaac had a particular covenant role.
Ishmael still remained under God's providential care.
Those truths must not be confused.
God's election of Isaac for the covenant promise was not a declaration that Ishmael possessed no human worth.
Then morning came.
Abraham rose early.
There was bread.
There was water.
There was Hagar.
There was Ishmael.
And there was goodbye.
Try not to rush through that scene.
Scripture gives us no sentimental soundtrack.
No lengthy recorded farewell speech.
Just Abraham preparing provisions...
and sending them away.
Hagar entered the wilderness of Beersheba.
Then the water ran out.
That sentence becomes terrifying when you are a mother in a wilderness.
No convenience store.
No emergency vehicle.
No hospital.
No phone.
No visible rescue.
Just heat.
Dust.
Thirst.
And your child dying in front of you.
Eventually Hagar could no longer bear watching.
She placed the boy beneath a shrub.
Then she walked away and sat at a distance.
Her reasoning was devastating:
Do not let me see the boy die.
Then she wept.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of prayer.
Not polished prayer.
Not church prayer.
Not the prayer where every theological phrase is perfectly arranged.
The prayer that sounds more like sobbing.
The prayer where you have run out of explanations.
The prayer whispered from a hospital corridor.
The prayer prayed beside divorce papers.
The prayer after the funeral.
The prayer when your child has wandered from God.
The prayer when the money is gone.
The prayer when addiction has returned.
The prayer when nobody knows how exhausted you actually are.
The prayer where all you have left is:
And tears.
Then Genesis says something breathtaking.
וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־קוֹל הַנַּעַר
Vayyishma Elohim et-qol hanna‘ar.
“God heard the voice of the boy.”
Do you see it?
His name was Ishmael.
God hears.
Years earlier, God had heard Hagar’s affliction.
Now in the wilderness, God heard the boy.
The name had become the story.
And the story had become testimony.
God hears.
When the water disappears...
God hears.
When the family breaks...
God hears.
When the future looks buried underneath a desert shrub...
God hears.
When your strength cannot produce another sentence...
God hears.
God called to Hagar and told her not to fear.
Then Scripture says:
“God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.”
Read that again.
The wilderness had convinced Hagar that death was the only ending available.
God opened her eyes...
and there was water.
Sometimes despair does that to us.
It narrows our vision until pain becomes the only thing we can see.
We begin believing the chapter we are living must be the final chapter.
The marriage failed, therefore everything is over.
The child wandered, therefore nothing can change.
I sinned, therefore God cannot use me.
I wasted years, therefore redemption has passed me by.
I ruined something beautiful, therefore grace has finally reached its limit.
But the Gospel announces something radically different.
Your worst chapter does not possess authorship over your final chapter.
Jesus does.
And this is where Sarah, Hagar, Isaac, and Ishmael ultimately confront something inside every one of us.
We want to save ourselves.
We want to produce the promise.
We want righteousness we can manufacture.
We want enough morality, enough religion, enough effort, enough reputation, enough church attendance, enough spiritual achievement to make ourselves acceptable before God.
But Scripture keeps destroying that illusion.
Paul eventually reaches back into this very family tragedy in Galatians 4.
He speaks of Abraham's two sons and uses their story allegorically in his argument about slavery and freedom, flesh and promise.
Paul's point is not permission to despise Hagar or Ishmael.
Nor is it a justification for ethnic hostility.
His argument is theological.
Human effort cannot manufacture the freedom God gives by promise.
And that brings us directly to Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people finally tried hard enough to reach God.
It is the announcement that God came for people who could not rescue themselves.
Jesus entered our wilderness.
He stepped into human rejection.
He knew betrayal.
He knew abandonment.
He knew what it meant to be despised.
And at the cross, the sinless Son of God carried sins that were not His.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our secret compromises.
Our religious hypocrisy.
Our manipulation.
Our impatience.
Our attempts to control what should have been surrendered.
Our hidden browser history.
Our private hatred.
Our unforgiveness.
Our self-righteousness.
Our rebellion.
Our shame.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
And there He died.
Not as a tragic victim trapped by history...
but as the Lamb of God giving Himself for sinners.
Then the grave received Him.
And the grave could not keep Him.
Jesus Christ rose.
That changes everything.
Because perhaps the deepest wilderness is not Hagar's desert.
It is the distance sin created between humanity and God.
And we cannot manufacture enough water to escape it.
We cannot perform our way out.
We cannot religiously decorate our chains and call ourselves free.
We need grace.
We need forgiveness.
We need Christ.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so much.
There is a little Abraham in us—trying to control what God promised.
There is something of Sarah's impatience in us—hurting people while trying to protect what we fear losing.
There is something of Hagar's wilderness in us—wondering whether anybody sees.
There is something of Ishmael's cry in us—needing God to hear.
And there is only one Savior standing above all of it.
Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years blaming everyone else for the wilderness while refusing to confront the decisions that helped bring you there.
Maybe you were the wounded person.
Maybe you were the person who caused the wound.
Maybe somehow you have been both.
The Gospel has room for that confession.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ who died and rose to redeem sinners.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth about evil...
then reveals a Savior greater than our sin.
That is why you do not need to hide anymore.
Bring Christ the resentment.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the secret addiction.
Bring Him the marriage you damaged.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the bitterness you have carefully justified.
Bring Him the religious mask.
Bring Him the wilderness.
Bring Him the empty water skin.
Bring Him the thing underneath the shrub that you have already decided cannot survive.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Someone reading silently tonight may need to discover that deserts are not always graves.
Not because every sentence is easy.
God hears.
Not as religious decoration.
Even send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that Jesus still receives sinners.
Supporting Gospel ministry is never a purchase of God's favor. We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, service, and lives surrendered to Him.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and go deeper with us:
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because perhaps someone in your world is currently sitting beside an empty water skin.
Someone is crying where nobody can hear them.
Someone thinks their scandal became their identity.
Someone believes the mistake they made fifteen years ago wrote the ending.
Someone thinks the wilderness proves God abandoned them.
Someone needs to hear the ancient name again:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל.
Yishma‘el.
God hears.
And someone needs to hear an even greater name:
Jesus.
The One who saves His people from their sins.
Sarah could demand that Hagar leave.
Abraham could send her into the wilderness.
The water could run out.
Hagar could lose sight of hope.
But none of them could send Hagar beyond the reach of God.
And neither can your past send you beyond the reach of Christ.
Not your scandal.
Not your shame.
Not your failure.
Not the wilderness.
Not the years you lost.
Not the chapter you wish you could tear out of your life.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the mercy you could never manufacture for yourself.
And when Christ has rewritten what sin tried to make permanent, do not hide the testimony.
Follow and stay close to the Word.
Support the mission if God has given you the desire and means to do so.
Then go tell another thirsty soul where the living water is found.
Because perhaps the most beautiful truth buried inside this painful family story is this:
When human failure sends someone into the wilderness, God can still meet them there—and the desert does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE WARNS AGAINST ADULTERY—Then Immediately Celebrates Sexual Delight in Marriage
paragraphs: THE BIBLE WARNS AGAINST ADULTERY—Then Immediately Celebrates Sexual Delight in Marriage
Proverbs 5 does something many Christians are almost afraid to do: it warns you about the bed that can destroy your life… then tells a husband to rejoice deeply in the wife God has given him.
Because the Bible does not merely say, “Do not commit adultery.”
It does something far more confronting.
It takes you to the edge of forbidden desire.
It shows you the sweetness.
It shows you the seduction.
It shows you the aftermath.
And then—almost without warning—it turns around and celebrates passionate delight inside marriage.
That matters.

Because perhaps one of the great tragedies in Christian conversations about sexuality is that we have sometimes spoken loudly about what God forbids while whispering about what God created to be good.
Proverbs 5 does neither.
It does not blush at marital desire.
And it does not romanticize adultery.
It tells the truth about both.
Listen carefully to the opening warning:
“For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil: But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword.”
That is Proverbs 5:3–4 in the King James Version.
The Hebrew makes the contrast even more vivid.
The forbidden woman’s lips are described as dripping נֹפֶת — nōp̄eṯ, honey or sweetness.
Her speech is smoother than שֶׁמֶן — shemen, oil.
But her end is מָרָה — mārāh.
Bitter.
That is temptation in one devastating picture.
Sweet at the entrance.
Bitter at the end.
And somebody reading this already knows exactly what that feels like.
Maybe your temptation did not begin in a bedroom.
Maybe it began with a message.
A notification.
A conversation you knew was becoming too personal.
A coworker who seemed to understand you in ways your spouse no longer seemed to.
An old relationship you searched for “just to see how they were doing.”
A private browser.
A second account.
A friendship you kept defending because technically, technically, technically…
“Nothing happened.”
But something was happening inside you.
Your heart had begun traveling somewhere your body had not yet gone.
And that is why Proverbs is so mercifully ruthless.
God does not merely warn us about the moment of adultery.
He warns us about the road leading there.
“Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house.”
Not merely her bed.
Her door.
There are doors you do not prove your strength by standing beside.
There are conversations you do not continue to demonstrate your maturity.
There are temptations you do not negotiate with.
There are messages you do not need to answer.
There are relationships you do not need to “manage.”
Sometimes wisdom looks remarkably unheroic.
You leave.
You block.
You confess.
You tell your spouse.
You call somebody mature enough to hold you accountable.
You stop pretending that secrecy is harmless simply because nobody has caught you yet.
Because sin almost always makes promises about the beginning while hiding the ending.
Proverbs shows you the ending.
Years lost.
Honor given away.
Strength consumed.
Regret arriving when consequences can no longer be undone.
Until the person finally cries:
“How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof…”
That may be one of the saddest moments in the chapter.
Not because the sinner lacked warnings.
Because the sinner had warnings and kept walking.
Imagine realizing that the voice you called restrictive was actually trying to rescue you.
Imagine discovering that the boundary you resented was a guardrail beside a cliff.
That is biblical sexual holiness.
God is not standing between you and joy.
He is standing between you and the counterfeit that promises joy while quietly sharpening a knife.
But then Proverbs 5 does something extraordinary.
After warning against illicit sexual desire, Scripture does not conclude:
“Therefore, desire itself is dirty.”
It turns toward marriage.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Then comes the line:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
The Hebrew word translated “rejoice” is שָׂמַח — śāmaḥ.
Rejoice.
Be glad.
Take joy.
This is not reluctant tolerance.
This is not cold obligation.
This is delight under covenant.
And then Scripture becomes even more intimate:
“Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
And no, Proverbs does not apologize for it.
The Hebrew behind “be thou ravished” is related to שָׁגָה — shāgāh, a word that can convey being captivated, enraptured, even overwhelmed.
Read the contrast carefully.
The chapter is not contrasting sexuality with holiness.
It is contrasting covenant delight with covenant-breaking desire.
That changes everything.
God is not anti-sex.
God created human beings male and female.
God created marriage.
God created the body.
And within the covenant of marriage, Scripture can speak of sexual delight without treating it as filthy.
The problem is not that desire exists.
The question is where desire is taking you.
Toward covenant?
Or away from it?
Toward faithfulness?
Or secrecy?
Toward giving yourself faithfully to your spouse?
Or consuming another person in your imagination?
Toward gratitude?
Or endless appetite?
Because Proverbs 5 asks a haunting question:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
In other words:
Why abandon the fountain God has given you to chase water that cannot satisfy?
And then comes the verse that destroys the illusion of secret sin:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.”
Before the eyes of the LORD.
The Hebrew name there is יְהוָה — YHWH, the covenant name of God.
The hidden messages.
Before Him.
The deleted history.
Before Him.
The fantasies nobody knows about.
Before Him.
The emotional affair you keep renaming “friendship.”
Before Him.
The loneliness inside your marriage.
Before Him.
The wounds that made forbidden attention feel intoxicating.
Before Him.
The temptation you have resisted for months and never told anybody about.
Before Him too.
And that last part matters.
Because God does not merely see the person falling.
He sees the person fighting.
He sees the husband turning his eyes away.
He sees the wife refusing emotional intimacy that belongs inside her covenant.
He sees the believer deleting what needs to be deleted.
He sees the trembling confession.
He sees the tears.
He sees the marriage trying to heal after betrayal.
He sees the spouse wondering whether trust can ever live again.
He sees the person ashamed of what they have become.
And perhaps that person is you.
So what happens if Proverbs 5 did not reach you before the fall?
What happens when the warning comes after the affair?
After the pornography?
After the messages?
After the secret relationship?
After the betrayal?
After you became the person you once swore you would never become?
This is where we must read Proverbs 5 inside the larger story of Scripture.
The Bible does not minimize sexual sin.
But neither does the Gospel declare sexual sinners beyond redemption.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who successfully kept every stain off their history.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin—not imaginary sin, sanitized sin, socially acceptable sin, but real sin.
Ugly sin.
Secret sin.
Sexual sin.
Pride.
Deception.
Lust.
Adultery.
Hypocrisy.
The sins we confess publicly and the sins we would rather die than have projected onto a screen.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says it was so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
And the resurrection says your sin does not get the final word.
Repentance is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Forgiveness is not permission to return to the same chains.
Jesus forgives—and Jesus calls people out of darkness.
That is why grace is so much greater than religious image management.
You can protect an image while your soul is dying.
You can sing worship songs while hiding messages.
You can quote Scripture while feeding an addiction.
You can sit beside your spouse in church while emotionally belonging to somebody else.
You can convince everybody.
Except God.
And strangely, that may be the beginning of hope.
Because the God who already knows everything is still calling you into the light.
You do not have to manufacture innocence.
You need mercy.
You need repentance.
You need Christ.
If you have never crossed the physical line but you know your heart is getting dangerously close, do not wait for catastrophe to make you serious.
Move away from the door.
If your marriage has become cold, do not use its pain as permission to build another relationship in secret.
Seek help.
Speak truth.
Pray.
Listen.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Relearn tenderness.
Pursue your spouse.
Protect your covenant.
And where serious betrayal, abuse, coercion, or danger exists, seeking wise pastoral and qualified professional help is not faithlessness. Safety and truth matter.
If you have already fallen, stop building your future around hiding your past.
Bring sin into the light.
Confess to God.
Turn away from it.
Seek wise accountability.
Where you have harmed others, take responsibility without demanding instant trust or cheap forgiveness.
Repentance has fruit.
Restoration may take time.
Consequences do not always disappear.
But shame does not have to become your permanent identity.
Because there is a difference between being exposed by sin and being defined by sin.
Peter failed.
David fell terribly and suffered consequences.
The Corinthian church included people with deeply broken sexual histories, yet Paul could write:
Were.
Then:
“But ye are washed…”
“But ye are sanctified…”
“But ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is 1 Corinthians 6:11.
Do not turn grace into an excuse to keep sinning.
But do not turn your past into a throne more powerful than the cross either.
Jesus Christ is greater.
Maybe you are reading this beside someone you love while knowing there is something on your phone they have never seen.
Maybe your spouse is asleep.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is fine.
Maybe you have not touched another person, but your imagination has been living somewhere else for months.
Maybe you are the betrayed one, and every sentence in this article hurts because you did not choose the scandal that entered your home.
Maybe you are single and wondering whether any of this applies to you.
It does.
Proverbs is teaching all of us what desire becomes when wisdom no longer governs it.
Sexual integrity begins long before marriage and matters long after the wedding photographs have faded.
And if you are married, hear what Proverbs 5 refuses to let religious shame erase:
Faithfulness is not merely refusing everybody else.
It is learning again to delight in the covenant God has entrusted to you.
See your spouse.
Talk.
Touch with tenderness.
Listen.
Flirt with your spouse instead of feeding attention somewhere else.
Protect time together.
Pray together.
Forgive.
Get help when you need it.
Remember that marriage is made of two imperfect people who need grace every morning.

And never confuse marital sexual delight with entitlement. Biblical intimacy is not coercion. Love does not use another person's body. Christian marriage calls husband and wife to faithful, self-giving love, honor, tenderness, and mutual care.
The world often tells us that freedom means removing boundaries.
Proverbs gives another picture.
Some boundaries protect the very thing you hope will remain beautiful.
A fireplace is warm because the fire has a place to burn.
Outside that place, the same fire can consume the house.
Desire needs covenant.
Passion needs faithfulness.
Pleasure needs wisdom.
And sinners need grace.
That is why Proverbs 5 is not merely a warning about adultery.
It is an invitation to stop drinking poison while calling it honey.
It is an invitation to come home.
And perhaps somebody needs to come home tonight.
Not merely to a spouse.
To God.
No more hiding.
No more rehearsing excuses.
No more waiting until consequences force the confession your conscience has been begging you to make.
Jesus already knows.
Come into the light.
One wife may need courage to speak.
One young person may need to understand that God's boundaries are not hatred of pleasure.
One secret sinner may finally confess.
One shattered spouse may discover that Christ has not abandoned them.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever you have been praying for to follow too. Sometimes sharing truth is one of the simplest ways we can place a light where someone in darkness might see it.
It does not.
Not because giving money can purchase forgiveness or blessing.
It cannot.

Rather, Scripture teaches willing, generous support for Gospel work. Paul wrote that giving should be purposeful and not coerced—“not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7)—and he also taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for that work (1 Corinthians 9:14).
So pray about it.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, reaching, creating, and putting Christ-centered resources into the hands of people who need them.
Send it privately to someone you love.
Pray for the ministry.
Keep pointing people toward Jesus.
The mission is Christ.
The sinner coming home.
The marriage being protected.
The hidden sin being confessed.
The wounded heart discovering grace.
The tempted believer choosing the narrow road.
The ashamed person discovering that the cross is not frightened by their history.
The lost hearing that Jesus still saves.
Proverbs 5 begins with a father pleading with his son to listen.
Thousands of years later, the warning still reaches us.
Honey can become bitter.
Secret roads can become chains.
A moment can become a wound that lasts for years.
But you do not have to keep walking toward the door.
Turn around.
And if you already walked through it…
turn around anyway.
There is still a Savior.
There is still repentance.
There is still grace.
There is still a cross where guilty people can kneel.
There is still an empty tomb declaring that death, shame, and sin do not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needs to carry with them after everything else here fades:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when you surrender the pen to Jesus, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LOT OFFERED HIS VIRGIN DAUGHTERS TO A VIOLENT MOB—WHY IS THIS HORRIFYING STORY IN SCRIPTURE?
paragraphs:
LOT OFFERED HIS VIRGIN DAUGHTERS TO A VIOLENT MOB—WHY IS THIS HORRIFYING STORY IN SCRIPTURE?
Genesis 19 is not asking you to admire Lot’s decision. It is showing you what happens when sin becomes normal, human judgment becomes distorted, and even the people being rescued desperately need grace.
There are Bible stories we teach children.
David facing Goliath.
Daniel in the lions’ den.
Jesus calming the storm.
And then there are passages we almost hope nobody asks about.
Genesis 19 is one of them.
Because there is a moment in this chapter so disturbing that even people who have read the Bible for years can reach it and think:
Why is this here?
A violent crowd surrounds Lot’s house in Sodom.
Two visitors have entered his home.
The men of the city demand that Lot bring them outside so they can sexually violate them.
And then Lot walks out and says something horrifying.
“Behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man…”
He offers his own daughters instead.
Read that again.
His daughters.
Not strangers.
Not soldiers.
Not himself.
His daughters.
And suddenly the Bible does something uncomfortable.
It refuses to protect one of its own characters from our disgust.
It does not airbrush him.
It does not quietly delete the sentence.
It leaves the scandal on the page.
Why?
Because Scripture is not propaganda for supposedly perfect religious people.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing deeply fallen human beings.
And sometimes the darkness Scripture exposes is not outside the house.
Sometimes it is standing in the doorway.

Genesis 19 begins with two angels arriving in Sodom in the evening. Lot is sitting at the city gate. He urges them strongly not to remain in the public square and persuades them to stay under his roof.
Then the atmosphere changes.
Before they lie down, men from the city surround the house.
Genesis describes the breadth of the gathering with chilling language: “both old and young, all the people from every quarter.”
Their demand is brutal.
“Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out unto us, that we may know them.”
The Hebrew verb translated “know” is יָדַע — yādaʿ.
Normally, yādaʿ simply means “to know.” Context determines its sense. In Genesis it can also describe sexual relations, as when Genesis 4:1 says Adam “knew” Eve.
But Genesis 19 removes any reasonable ambiguity about what this mob intends.
Lot goes outside.
He shuts the door behind him.
He begs them not to act wickedly.
And then comes the sentence we wish had never been spoken:
“Behold now, I have two daughters which have not known man; let me, I pray you, bring them out unto you…”
There is no responsible way to make that beautiful.
There is no Christ-centered reason to pretend it was noble.

Hospitality was enormously important in the ancient world. Protecting guests who had entered one’s household carried serious social obligations. Understanding that cultural background helps us understand the situation.
It does not require us to call Lot’s proposed solution righteous.
Explanation is not justification.
The Bible reports many human actions it does not endorse.
Scripture tells us Cain murdered Abel.
It does not endorse murder.
Scripture tells us David committed adultery and arranged Uriah’s death.
It does not endorse adultery or murder.
Scripture records Peter denying Jesus.
It does not endorse denying Christ.
And Genesis records Lot offering his daughters to the mob.
Narration is not approval.
That distinction matters enormously.

In fact, the surrounding biblical witness makes the value of those daughters impossible to dismiss. They bear God’s image just as men do. Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image, “male and female created he them.”
Lot's daughters were not disposable objects.
They were human beings bearing the image of God.
The horror of Lot’s offer therefore should not be softened merely because Lot occupies a complicated place in the biblical story.
And complicated he certainly is.
Years later, the New Testament gives us another uncomfortable detail.
Second Peter 2 calls him “righteous Lot” and says he was distressed by the immoral conduct surrounding him.
The Greek expression includes δίκαιον Λώτ — dikaion Lōt, “righteous Lot.”
That can surprise us.
How could Scripture use such language about a man capable of saying what Lot said?
Because biblical righteousness never means that every recorded decision made by a believer was righteous.
Abraham believed God, yet Abraham also failed terribly.
David belonged to God, yet David committed devastating sins.
Peter belonged to Christ, yet Peter denied Him.
Lot could be a man whom God distinguished from Sodom while still being a deeply compromised man capable of a morally horrifying decision.
That distinction is essential.
And perhaps that is where Genesis 19 begins getting dangerously close to us.
Because Lot had spent years living near Sodom.
Then in Sodom.
And eventually Sodom was not merely outside his window.
Something about the moral confusion of that world appears to have entered his thinking.
Genesis does not explicitly tell us every motive behind his offer, so we should resist pretending to know what Scripture does not say.
But the narrative certainly shows us a man attempting to prevent one evil by proposing another terrible evil.
That should frighten every believer.
Because compromise rarely introduces itself by saying:
Hello. I have come to destroy your conscience.
It usually arrives more quietly.
You tolerate something.
Then accommodate it.
Then explain it.
Then defend it.
Then one day you discover that something which once would have horrified you no longer shocks you the same way.
That is one of the terrifying possibilities Genesis 19 puts before us:
You can hate the darkness around you while still allowing some of its assumptions to reshape you.
You can recognize evil in somebody else and remain frighteningly blind to the distortion developing inside yourself.
Lot looked at the mob and essentially said, “Do not do this wicked thing.”
He correctly recognized their wickedness.
Then almost immediately proposed something horrifying himself.
That contradiction is painfully human.
We are remarkably skilled at seeing everybody else's Sodom.
Their compromise.
Their addiction.
Their hypocrisy.
Their sexual sin.
Their anger.
Their greed.
Their pride.
Their deception.
Their secret life.
And all the while Jesus asks a much more frightening question:
What is happening inside you?
That does not mean all sins are identical in severity, consequences, or circumstances.
It means none of us should use another person's darkness as camouflage for our own.
Because the Gospel begins destroying our masks.
And Genesis 19 destroys another mask too.
The myth that the Bible is filled with sanitized heroes who earned God's rescue because they were better than everybody else.
Look closely at the chapter.
Lot does not engineer his own deliverance.
The angels intervene.
They pull him back inside.
They strike the threatening men with blindness.
They warn Lot to flee.
And then something extraordinary happens.
Lot hesitates.
Sodom is about to be judged…
and Lot lingers.
Genesis 19:16 says:
“While he lingered…”
The Hebrew is וַיִּתְמַהְמָהּ — vayitmahmah.
He delayed.
He hesitated.
Then Scripture says the men seized his hand, his wife’s hand, and the hands of his daughters and brought them outside the city.
Why?
This is the sentence that changes the emotional center of the story:
“…the LORD being merciful unto him.”
Merciful.
Lot is not pictured sprinting heroically from destruction while angels applaud his spiritual maturity.
He hesitates.
God's messengers have to take him by the hand.
That is grace in an uncomfortable form.
Not grace saying sin does not matter.
Judgment is coming precisely because evil matters.
Rather, grace reaches into the place of judgment and pulls undeserving people toward safety.
And if we are reading the whole Bible through the fulfillment found in Jesus Christ, that should sound familiar.
Because eventually humanity would need a rescue far greater than escape from Sodom.
We needed rescue from sin.
From condemnation.
From the rebellion inside us.
From the guilt we could never wash away ourselves.
And God did not stand at a safe distance shouting instructions toward sinners.
The eternal Son entered our world.
Jesus Christ came near.
The sinless One walked among sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He confronted hypocrites.
He received the broken.
He called sinners to repentance.
And then He went to a cross.
Here the contrast with Genesis 19 becomes breathtaking.
Lot was willing to sacrifice others to protect his house.
Jesus willingly gave Himself to save His people.
Christ does not throw the vulnerable outside so He can remain safe.
The Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
Jesus says in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
And when Christ cries from the cross, “It is finished,” John's Gospel records the Greek word:
Τετέλεσται — Tetelestai.
“It has been completed.”
“It has been accomplished.”
Jesus did not merely expose humanity's scandal.
He bore sin's judgment for those who trust Him.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally the announcement that good people should try harder.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The cross tells us two things simultaneously:
Your sin is more serious than your excuses want you to believe.
And God's grace in Christ is greater than your shame wants you to believe.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is coming into the light.
It is stopping the exhausting performance.
It is finally agreeing with God about what sin is and turning toward the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
Maybe people at church think you are doing wonderfully.
Maybe your Facebook feed looks blessed while your private life feels spiritually hollow.
Maybe you know exactly how to speak Christian while quietly becoming comfortable with something that once convicted you.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Secret messages.
Dishonesty.
Pride.
Unforgiveness.
A hidden relationship.
Greed.
Religious hypocrisy.
A slowly cooling love for Christ.
And maybe the hardest sentence you could say tonight is simply:
“Jesus, I have compromised.”
Say it.
Not to us.
To Him.
Because the point of seeing darkness is not to become fascinated with darkness.
It is to run toward the Light.
Jesus did not come merely to make scandalous people more respectable.
He came to make dead people alive.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He teaches compromised hearts to love holiness again.
This is why Genesis 19 remains in Scripture.
Not because God wants us to imitate Lot's horrifying offer.
Not because the vulnerable are expendable.
Not because every action of a biblical character carries divine approval.
It remains because the Bible tells the truth about evil.
The evil of cities.
The evil of crowds.
The evil of cultures.
And the frightening capacity for moral confusion inside individual human hearts.
The Bible does not need fake heroes because it has a perfect Savior.
That may be one of the most important truths you ever learn about reading Scripture.
Abraham cannot save you.
Moses cannot save you.
David cannot save you.
Peter cannot save you.
Lot certainly cannot save you.
They are not Jesus.
There is only one spotless Lamb.
Only one sinless Son.
Only one crucified and risen Savior.
Only one name by which sinners are reconciled to God.
Jesus Christ.
So when you reach a disturbing passage like Genesis 19, do not run from the Bible because its characters are uglier than you expected.
Notice what kind of Book you are holding.
A Book honest enough to expose its people.
A Book holy enough to call evil evil.
A Book compassionate enough to show mercy.
A Book whose long story keeps moving beyond broken human beings toward Jesus Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing the opposite.
You think your worst chapter disqualifies you from ever coming home.
You think if Christians knew what happened, they would never look at you the same way.
Maybe you did something you cannot undo.
Maybe somebody did something terrible to you.
Maybe you carry shame that was never yours to carry.
Hear this carefully:
The Gospel does not call evil good.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending wounds never happened.
Jesus does something greater.
He enters the history.
He confronts sin.
He forgives repentant sinners.
He restores the broken.
He brings light into darkness.
And He begins writing a future that shame could never produce.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your private life. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Not as an algorithmic ritual.
As a confession.
As a prayer.
As one small public reminder that grace is for people who know they need it.

Sharing Christian content is not itself what glorifies God; Scripture calls us to glorify Him with our whole lives. But sharing biblical truth can become one simple way of pointing someone beyond us toward Christ.
Because there may come a night when somebody asks you why Scripture contains stories this dark.
You will want to remember:
The Bible records human depravity without requiring us to approve it.
And the darkness of its human characters makes the holiness of Jesus shine even brighter.
And there is more waiting for those who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown tired.
Invite the seeker with uncomfortable questions.
Invite the Christian who has drifted.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Scripture is afraid of scrutiny.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them repentance is still possible.
Tell them forgiveness is real.
Tell them grace does not pretend darkness is light.
Tell them Christ walked into humanity's darkness and came out of the grave alive.
Because the most shocking thing in Genesis 19 may not finally be how dark humanity can become.
It may be that a holy God still reaches into darkness to rescue sinners.
And perhaps that is why this disturbing story was never erased.
Because God knew people like us would eventually read it.
People with contradictions.
People with regrets.
People who have hesitated.
People who compromised.
People carrying stories they wish could be deleted.
People desperately needing Someone to take them by the hand and lead them out.
Your darkest chapter does not become beautiful because the darkness was acceptable; it becomes a testimony when Jesus meets you there and leads you into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Esau Married Judith and Basemath—and They Made Life Bitter for Isaac and Rebekah
paragraphs: Esau Married Judith and Basemath—and They Made Life Bitter for Isaac and Rebekah
Two verses. One marriage decision. A Hebrew expression filled with pain. And a warning to every family that discovering grace does not mean pretending our choices have no consequences.
There are Bible stories we remember because somebody killed a giant.
There are stories we remember because the sea opened.
And then there are two quiet verses tucked into Genesis that almost disappear between much larger events.
No miracle.
No thunder.
No angel.
Just a son getting married.
But the final words are devastating.
“When Esau was forty years old, he took as wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite; and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.”
Genesis 26:34–35.
Read that last sentence again.
They made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
The Hebrew is even more piercing.
וַתִּהְיֶיןָ מֹרַת רוּחַ לְיִצְחָק וּלְרִבְקָה
Vattihyena morat ruach le-Yitzchaq ule-Rivqah.
Literally, the expression centers on something like “bitterness of spirit” for Isaac and Rebekah.
Not merely inconvenience.
Not simply, “Our parents don't approve of our relationship.”
The biblical writer reaches for רוּחַ — ruach—a word that can mean spirit, breath, or wind—and joins it to the language of bitterness.
Something had entered the home that weighed upon the spirit of an aging father and mother.
And perhaps that is why these two verses hurt so much.
Because some of you know exactly what “bitterness of spirit” feels like.
You know what it is to love someone you cannot control.
You know what it is to lie awake because somebody you raised is making decisions you cannot make for them.
You know the strange grief of watching a person you love walk willingly toward something you fear will wound them.
Maybe it is your child.
Maybe your spouse.
Maybe your brother.
Maybe your sister.
Or perhaps the person making everyone grieve has been you.
That possibility is harder to admit.
Esau was forty years old.
He was not a little boy.
He was responsible for his choices.
Genesis tells us that he married Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon the Hittite. The text specifically identifies both women as Hittites.
That matters in the story of Genesis.
Abraham had been deeply concerned that Isaac not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites. He made his servant swear concerning Isaac:
“You will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell.”
That is Genesis 24:3.
Later, Rebekah herself would say:
“I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife of the daughters of Heth like these, of the daughters of the land, what good will my life be to me?”
Genesis 27:46.
Then Isaac sent Jacob away with an explicit command not to marry a Canaanite woman (Genesis 28:1–2).
So Genesis 26:34–35 is not floating in isolation.
Esau's marriages sit inside a larger covenant-family story.
But we must be careful here.
The point is not permission for Christians to turn ethnicity into righteousness.
It is not.
The Bible itself destroys that interpretation.

Rahab was a Canaanite woman, yet by faith she entered the people of God and eventually appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 11:31). Ruth was a Moabite, yet her faithfulness to the God of Israel became one of Scripture's great testimonies of covenant devotion, and she too stands in the Messiah's genealogy.
God's saving grace is not restricted by ethnicity.
The deeper issue running through Genesis is covenant faithfulness—whether the family through whom God had promised blessing to the nations would live in faithfulness to the God who called them.
And that makes Esau's story much more uncomfortable.
Because the real danger is always easier to see when it belongs to someone else.
We can read about Esau and shake our heads.
But Scripture has an uncomfortable way of turning the mirror around.
How many times have we known what God desired and still chosen what we desired?
How many decisions looked harmless because they felt good immediately?
How many believers have prayed, “Lord, bless this,” after already deciding they were unwilling to hear Him say no?
How many parents are carrying morat ruach because someone they love is drifting?
And how many sons and daughters have never stopped to consider how their rebellion has wounded the people praying for them?
Be honest.
Maybe this story is no longer ancient.
Maybe it just walked into your house.
Esau's marriage choices also belong to a larger portrait Scripture gives us of him.
Earlier, hunger had reduced his perspective to the immediate moment.
Jacob offered him food in exchange for his birthright, and Esau answered:
“I am about to die; so what is this birthright to me?”
Genesis 25:32.
Then comes one of Scripture's saddest little sentences:
“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
Genesis 25:34.
A bowl in front of him seemed more urgent than an inheritance beyond him.
That is how spiritual compromise often works.
It rarely introduces itself by saying, “I am here to destroy something sacred.”
It says:
You need this now.
You deserve this now.
Everybody else does it.
It isn't that serious.
God will understand.
Tomorrow you can deal with the consequences.
And sometimes tomorrow arrives carrying morat ruach.
Bitterness of spirit.

This does not mean every painful family situation can be reduced to a simple formula in which suffering proves somebody sinned. Scripture never gives us permission to make that cruel assumption. Job suffered without the explanation his friends tried to force upon him. Jesus rejected simplistic attempts to connect every tragedy directly to an individual's particular sin.
But Scripture does teach something modern culture desperately wants us to forget:
Choices have consequences.
Grace does not make consequences imaginary.
Forgiveness does not make wisdom unnecessary.
And love does not require calling destructive decisions harmless.
There is another detail responsible readers should know.

When Genesis later lists Esau's wives and descendants in Genesis 36, the names and family details are presented differently from Genesis 26. Genesis 36 mentions Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael. Various explanations have been proposed for how the names and traditions correspond, including the possibility of alternate names, but Scripture does not explicitly give us an explanation that allows us to settle every identification with certainty.
So we should not pretend it does.
Genesis 26:34–35 itself is clear about the point it wants us to see:
Esau took Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite, and the result was morat ruach for Isaac and Rebekah.
Bitterness of spirit.
And maybe somebody reading this has been carrying that bitterness for years.
You still love them.
That is what makes it hurt.
If you did not care, you could walk away emotionally.
But you remember when they were small.
You remember their voice.
Their laugh.
Their questions.
Maybe you taught them to pray.
Maybe you carried them into church.
Maybe you opened a Bible beside their bed.
And now you watch them making decisions you cannot stop.
You have discovered one of the most painful truths about love:
Love cannot force surrender.
Even God does not need your manipulation to accomplish His purposes.
So what do you do when somebody you love is living in a way that breaks your heart?
You keep loving without pretending darkness is light.
You pray without trying to become the Holy Spirit.
You speak truth without making cruelty sound like courage.
You examine your own heart.
You repent where you have sinned.
You forgive where forgiveness is needed.
You refuse to let another person's rebellion become permission for your own bitterness to rule you.
And you remember that as long as there is breath, you do not know the final chapter.
Because this is where the Gospel changes how we read painful family stories.
The Bible is not a museum filled with perfect families.
Abraham's household was complicated.
Isaac's household was fractured by favoritism.
Jacob's family became a battlefield of jealousy, deception, rivalry, and grief.
Judah's story contained sexual scandal.
David's family carried devastating consequences.
The genealogy of Jesus contains stories that polite religious people might have preferred to edit out.
Yet God did not abandon His redemptive purpose.
Generation after generation, through human weakness, failure, scandal, betrayal, and sin, the promise kept moving forward until the story arrived at Jesus Christ.
Not because those families were flawless.
Because God is faithful.
That is the heartbeat of grace.
Grace does not say sin did not matter.
Grace says sin will not have the final word over the person who comes to Christ.
Jesus did not go to the cross because our choices were insignificant.
He went because sin was so serious that reconciliation required a price we could never pay.
At Calvary, Jesus bore sin.
He bore shame.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood for sinners.
And He rose again.
The Christian message is not “try harder until your family looks respectable.”
It is:
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the family history you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the decision you cannot undo.
Bring Him the child you cannot control.
Bring Him the marriage you damaged.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the shame you buried.
Bring Him your morat ruach.
Because Jesus specializes in meeting people where the consequences are real.
Maybe you are Isaac or Rebekah in this story, grieving over someone else's choices.
But maybe you are Esau.
Maybe you have spent years choosing what was immediate over what was sacred.
Maybe people who loved you warned you.
Maybe you called conviction “judgment” because you did not want to change.
Maybe you have wounded your parents.
Your spouse.
Your children.
Your church.
Your own soul.
And somewhere underneath all your explanations, you know.
You know.
Do not use grace as another excuse to run.
Grace is not God's permission to remain unchanged.
Paul asks in Romans 6:1–2 whether believers should continue in sin so grace may increase.
His answer is emphatic:
“By no means!”
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace trains us.
Titus 2:11–12 says the grace of God teaches us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
The grace that forgives you is the grace that begins transforming you.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the sinner finally stopping the exhausting attempt to call darkness light.
It is coming home.
It is saying:
Jesus, I was wrong.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, I cannot repair myself.
Jesus, take what I have become and make me Yours.
And Christ does not receive repentant sinners reluctantly.
He told of a father who saw his returning son while that son was still far away, felt compassion, ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him.
The son came home carrying a scandal.
The father met him with mercy.
That does not make rebellion beautiful.
It makes grace breathtaking.
Maybe that is what somebody in your family still needs.
Not your approval of their sin.
Not your endless condemnation.
Jesus.
Truth and grace.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A Savior powerful enough to rewrite what sin has written.
And maybe that somebody is you.
Be honest.

And if you have lived through a family season of morat ruach and have seen God restore what looked impossible, share as much of your testimony as wisdom allows. Somebody reading quietly may desperately need evidence that another chapter can still be written.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The mother quietly grieving a child.
The father wondering where everything changed.
The son making decisions he knows are destroying him.
The daughter carrying shame she has never confessed.
The believer slowly becoming numb to compromise.
The person who thinks their scandal has disqualified them from ever coming home.
Send this privately if their pain should remain private.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
Christ purchased salvation; social-media engagement cannot.
Share because truth worth hearing is truth worth carrying.
It may describe your house.
And when that night comes, remember:
You can grieve and still trust God.
You can tell the truth and still love.
You can repent after terrible choices.
You can forgive without pretending nothing happened.
You can surrender what you cannot control.
And you can believe that Jesus is still Jesus in families that do not have neat endings yet.

Supporting Gospel ministry is never a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, caring for your family, or serving people in need. But when a ministry genuinely feeds your faith and you freely choose to support it, that support can help the work continue and help biblical truth travel farther.
We want it to become part of a deeper rhythm of discipleship—Scripture, biblical nourishment, conviction, encouragement, healing, accountability, and spiritual sharpening centered on Jesus Christ.
Not to prove that you love God.
Love for God is not measured by a Facebook share.
Perhaps a mother has been crying where nobody sees.
Perhaps a father has stopped knowing what to pray.
Perhaps someone thinks the worst chapter of their life has already determined the ending.
They need to know it has not.
Genesis does not hide the bitterness.
The Gospel does not deny the scandal.
The cross does not pretend sin is harmless.
But Jesus Christ walked directly into humanity's ruin, carried our sin to Calvary, died, was buried, rose victorious, and now calls sinners to repent, believe, and follow Him.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is why the prodigal can still come home.
That is why the ashamed can still kneel.
That is why wounded families can still pray.
That is why sinners can still become sons and daughters of God through faith in Christ.
Esau's choices brought bitterness into Isaac and Rebekah's home.
Scripture refuses to hide it.
But Scripture also refuses to let broken human families become the end of God's story.
Eventually the promised line leads us beyond Isaac.
Beyond Jacob.
Beyond every dysfunctional household.
Beyond every scandal.
To Jesus.
And when Jesus enters the story, grace does not erase yesterday.
It does something greater.
It gives the repentant sinner a tomorrow yesterday could never have produced.
The chapter that made your family weep does not have to be the chapter that gets the final word—because the pen is safest in the scarred hands of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU WERE TOLD, “GIVE AND GOD WILL GIVE YOU MORE”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS WAS TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING FAR DEEPER?
paragraphs: YOU WERE TOLD, “GIVE AND GOD WILL GIVE YOU MORE”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS WAS TALKING ABOUT SOMETHING FAR DEEPER?
Understanding “Give and It Will Be Given to You” Without Turning God Into an Investment Plan—and discovering the scandalous grace hidden inside one of Christianity’s most misunderstood promises.
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible that can make God sound less like a Father and more like an investment opportunity.
Put something in.
Wait for the return.
Give $100.
Believe for $1,000.
Plant a “seed.”
Expect a financial harvest.
And somewhere along the way, a breathtaking statement from the lips of Jesus can be reduced to something resembling a heavenly transaction:
“Give, and it will be given to you.”
It sounds convincing when those words are isolated.
It sounds even more convincing when the rest of the verse is quoted:
“Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be put into your bosom.”
Luke 6:38.
That sounds like abundance.
Overflow.
Multiplication.
And it is.
But there is a question we desperately need to ask before building a theology of money around it:
What was Jesus actually talking about?
Because if we love Jesus, we cannot merely ask what a verse can be made to say.
We must ask what Jesus meant.
And what happens when we put Luke 6:38 back where Jesus put it may surprise you.
It may even expose something in us.
Because immediately before saying, “Give, and it will be given to you,” Jesus says:
“Judge not, and you shall not be judged. Condemn not, and you shall not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
Then comes:
“Give, and it will be given to you.”
Read that slowly.
Jesus has been talking about mercy.
Judgment.
Condemnation.
Forgiveness.
Generosity.
The way human beings treat one another.
And the larger sermon makes His point even more uncomfortable.
Jesus says:
“Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who spitefully use you.”
Then:
“Love your enemies, do good, and lend, hoping for nothing in return.”
Luke 6:35.
And then He gives the reason:
“Therefore be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.”
Luke 6:36.
That changes everything.
Jesus is not standing behind a heavenly cash register saying, “Give Me enough money and I will make you rich.”
He is revealing what people transformed by the mercy of God begin to look like.
They give.
They forgive.
They show mercy.
They release condemnation.
They love people who cannot repay them.
They lend without making repayment the center of their kindness.
They become generous because their Father is generous.
The Greek makes the statement beautifully direct:
δίδοτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν
didote, kai dothēsetai hymin
“Give, and it will be given to you.”
The first word, δίδοτε — didote, comes from didōmi, “to give.”
It is an imperative.
Jesus really is commanding generosity.
We should not weaken that.
Christianity is not permission to clutch everything God places in our hands.
But notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not provide an investment percentage.
He does not promise that every dollar donated will return as multiple dollars.
He does not turn generosity into a technique for controlling Providence.
In fact, only a few sentences earlier He tells His disciples to lend while “hoping for nothing in return.”
That is devastating to transactional Christianity.
Jesus is teaching generosity that can survive even when there is nothing in it for you.
And perhaps that is exactly where this teaching begins to hurt.
Because many of us are willing to give...
as long as God pays us back the way we want.
We will obey if the marriage improves.
Serve if somebody notices.
Forgive if they apologize.
Give if our finances increase.
Pray if the breakthrough arrives.
Remain faithful if life starts making sense.
But what happens when you give and the bank account does not suddenly overflow?
What happens when you forgive and the person never says sorry?
What happens when you serve and nobody applauds?
What happens when you obey God and your circumstances become harder?
What happens when the “return” you expected never arrives?
Does God still deserve your obedience?
That question reaches much deeper than money.
It reaches the hidden contract many of us have attempted to write with God.
“Lord, I will give You this...
if You give me that.”
And Jesus quietly tears up the contract.
Because grace was never a business transaction.
The Gospel itself proves it.
God did not look down at humanity and find spiritually wealthy customers worthy of an investment.
He found sinners.
Rebels.
The guilty.
The ashamed.
The self-righteous.
The sexually broken.
The greedy.
The bitter.
The religious hypocrite hiding behind respectable clothes.
The person who promised God, “Never again,” and returned to the same sin three days later.
People like us.
And Scripture says:
“But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
Before you could repay Him.
Before you could impress Him.
Before you cleaned yourself up.
Before you had anything worthy to place on the table...
Christ came.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
Jesus Christ carried sin to the cross, suffered, died, and rose again so that sinners who repent and trust in Him could be forgiven and reconciled to God.
Christian generosity begins there.
Not with:
“How much can I get?”
But:
“How much have I already received in Christ?”
Forgiveness you could never purchase.
Mercy you could never earn.
Adoption you could never deserve.
A Savior you could never repay.
Eternal life you could never afford.
And suddenly giving changes.
You are no longer putting coins into heaven hoping God’s machine spits out prosperity.
You are opening hands that were already filled by grace.
This does not mean Scripture separates God from material provision.
It does not.
Jesus taught us to pray:
“Give us day by day our daily bread.”
Luke 11:3.
Paul tells us that God is able to provide sufficiently so believers can abound in good works, and he connects generosity with thanksgiving to God in 2 Corinthians 9:6–11.
Philippians 4:19 declares:
“And my God shall supply all your need according to His riches in glory by Christ Jesus.”
God provides.
God cares.
God owns everything.
God can bless materially.
God can open doors nobody else can open.
God can provide through work, generosity, community, circumstances, and means we never anticipated.
But biblical provision is not the same thing as turning God into an investment plan.
There is an enormous difference between trusting the Father to provide and attempting to manipulate the Father through giving.
One says:
“Father, everything I possess belongs to You.”
The other says:
“God, I gave You something. Now You owe me.”
One is worship.
The other is leverage wearing religious clothing.
And God will not be reduced to leverage.
There is another beautiful detail in Luke 6:38.
Jesus describes the measure as:
μέτρον καλὸν πεπιεσμένον σεσαλευμένον ὑπερεκχυννόμενον
A good measure—pressed down, shaken together, running over.
The picture is vivid.
Imagine dry goods being measured into a container. The contents are pressed and shaken so empty spaces disappear, then more is poured until the measure overflows.
Jesus gives His listeners a picture they could feel.
Abundance.
Generosity without stinginess.
Then comes the principle:
“For with the same measure that you use, it will be measured back to you.”
But even here, we must resist forcing Jesus into a simplistic formula.
This is not a divine vending machine.
The Bible itself refuses that interpretation.
Consider the apostle Paul.
If faithfulness automatically produced material prosperity, Paul should have been extraordinarily wealthy.
Instead, he describes hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, beatings, imprisonment, danger, and hardship.
Consider Jesus Himself.
He lived without the luxurious earthly prosperity some modern preaching implies every faithful believer should expect.
The cross alone destroys the idea that obedience always produces immediate comfort.
Sometimes obedience costs you.
Sometimes faithfulness empties the room.
Sometimes telling the truth loses the opportunity.
Sometimes refusing corruption costs money.
Sometimes generosity means you possess less afterward.
Sometimes following Jesus leads through suffering before resurrection.
And still...
He is worthy.
This is where “give and it will be given to you” becomes far more beautiful than a promise of easy money.
Jesus is forming a people whose lives reflect their Father.
People who do not merely calculate what others deserve.
People who know how much mercy they themselves needed.
People whose hands stay open because grace opened their hearts.
Maybe you know what it feels like to need that kind of mercy.
Maybe there is something you have never told anybody.
A failure buried beneath church clothes.
A private addiction.
A relationship you destroyed.
Money you mishandled.
A betrayal.
A secret habit.
A season when you ran from God so aggressively that you wondered whether there was any road back.
Maybe people remember your scandal.
Maybe you remember it every morning.
And shame keeps whispering:
“You cannot become what God wanted anymore.”
But shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Peter denied Him.
A thief was dying beside Him.
Paul once persecuted His church.
The Corinthian believers had histories Scripture itself describes with shocking honesty.
Yet the Gospel repeatedly shows God taking ruined stories and writing redemption across them.
Not because sin does not matter.
Sin matters enough that Christ went to the cross.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
Truth matters.
But grace means your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your story.
That is why we say:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
He does something greater.
He redeems sinners.
He forgives the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He transforms people from the inside out.
He takes hands that once grabbed...
and teaches them to give.
He takes hearts that once condemned...
and teaches them mercy.
He takes people drowning in unforgiveness...
and reminds them of the cross where their own impossible debt was answered by grace.
Perhaps the greatest evidence that you understand “give and it will be given to you” is not the size of your bank account.
Perhaps it is what grace has done to your heart.
Can you give when nobody applauds?
Can you serve when nobody posts your name?
Can you help someone who cannot advance your career?
Can you forgive without pretending the wound was acceptable?
Can you bless someone without secretly calculating what you will receive?
Can you give because Christ has already become your treasure?
That is freedom.
Money stops being your master.
Possessions stop being your identity.
Giving stops being gambling with God.
Generosity becomes worship.
And yes, faithful Christian ministries need support.
Books need to be written.
Resources need to be created.
The Gospel needs to be proclaimed.
Believers need discipleship.
People drowning in darkness need someone willing to carry the light into places where despair has become normal.
But hear this carefully:
Do not give because somebody frightened you into believing your blessing depends on paying us.
Do not support any Christian ministry because you believe your money purchases favor from God.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot bribe God into blessing you.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support Gospel Warrior because you believe Christ should be proclaimed.
Support because biblical truth should travel farther than deception.
Support because somebody scrolling Facebook at 2:13 in the morning, exhausted, ashamed, spiritually numb, and seconds away from giving up may encounter words that point them back to Jesus.
But the discount is not the reason to stand with us.
Christ is.
And there is another way you can help that costs nothing.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
They need to know:
God's grace is not for sale.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own relationship with God, do not hide behind silence.
Someone else reading the comments may realize they are not the only person learning this.
Because eventually you will hear Luke 6:38 quoted again.
And when you do, come back.
Read the verses around it.
Remember the mercy.
Remember the enemies Jesus told us to love.
Remember the forgiveness.
Remember the command to lend expecting nothing in return.
Remember the Father whose generosity His children are called to imitate.
Because the world does not merely need Christians who know how to quote Bible verses.
It needs Christians willing to let the Bible correct them.
Christians whose generosity cannot be purchased by applause.
Christians whose mercy confuses a cruel world.
Christians who give without turning God into a debtor.
Christians who understand that the greatest gift they ever received did not arrive because they planted enough money.
It arrived while they were sinners.
At a cross.
Outside Jerusalem.
Where the Son of God stretched out His hands.
Empty.
Wounded.
Pierced.
Giving Himself.
And perhaps that is the image we should remember whenever someone asks what Christian giving ultimately looks like.
Not a clenched fist demanding return.
Open hands.
A surrendered life.
A crucified Savior.
Jesus did not die so we could discover a religious technique for becoming rich.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
He rose so death would not have the final word.
And when His grace captures a human heart, something astonishing begins to happen.
The person who once asked,
“What can I get?”
slowly begins asking,
“Lord, what can I give?”
Not to purchase His love.
Because His love has already changed them.
Not to earn salvation.
Because salvation is by grace.
Not to manipulate tomorrow.
Because tomorrow belongs to Him.
But because once you understand what happened at Calvary...
you stop treating God like an investment.
You start treating Him like your King.
So give.
Give generously.
Give wisely.
Give joyfully.
Give to those in need.
Give toward faithful Gospel work.
Give your time.
Give encouragement.
Give forgiveness.
Give mercy.
Give without worshiping the return.
And above everything else...
give yourself to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the One who gave Himself for sinners.
Because eventually every earthly account closes.
Every possession changes hands.
Every investment stays behind.
Every human body returns to dust.
And on that day, the question will not be how cleverly you turned religion into profit.
The question that matters eternally is whether you belong to Christ.
And maybe that is what your heart needed to hear today.
You were never meant to use Jesus to obtain your treasure—Jesus Himself is the Treasure.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD CALL SOME ANIMALS CLEAN—AND OTHERS UNCLEAN?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CALL SOME ANIMALS CLEAN—AND OTHERS UNCLEAN?

The strange food laws of Leviticus were never merely about what was on Israel’s plate. They were teaching a holy people how to recognize the difference between what God sets apart and what He does not—and they ultimately drive us toward a much deeper question: What can actually make an unclean sinner clean?
There is something unsettling about Leviticus 11.
Not because it is difficult to read.
Because it is strangely specific.
A cow?
Clean.
A pig?
Unclean.
Certain fish could be eaten. Others could not.
Some birds belonged on Israel’s table. Others were forbidden.
Even creatures that crawled along the ground were classified.
And somewhere between the divided hoof, the chewing of the cud, fins, scales, birds, insects, and creeping things, a modern reader can understandably stop and ask:
Why?
Why would the God who created every animal call some “clean” and others “unclean”?
Was God saying pigs were evil?
Were certain animals spiritually corrupt?
Was this merely an ancient health code disguised as religion?
