And perhaps the question underneath all the others is even more important:
If God cared so much about these distinctions then, why do Christians today eat foods that Israel was commanded not to eat?
Stay with that question.
Because what begins with animals eventually reaches the human heart.
And when it does, Leviticus stops feeling like an ancient dietary manual.
It starts feeling like a mirror.
Long before Moses stood before Israel, Scripture already used the distinction between clean and unclean animals.
Before Sinai.
Before Leviticus.
Before the Mosaic covenant was formally given.
When Noah entered the ark, Genesis 7:2 distinguishes between animals described in Hebrew as הַבְּהֵמָה הַטְּהוֹרָה—ha-behemah ha-tehorah, “the clean animal”—and animals “that are not clean.”
So the concept did not suddenly appear in Leviticus.
But at Sinai, God incorporated these distinctions into Israel’s covenant life with extraordinary detail.

Leviticus 11 describes land animals Israel could eat as those possessing particular characteristics, including divided hooves and chewing the cud. Aquatic creatures needed fins and scales. The chapter also identifies prohibited birds and distinguishes among insects and other creatures.
But if we stop at the menu, we miss the sermon.
Near the end of the chapter, God reveals something much deeper:
כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אָנִי
Ki ani YHWH Eloheikhem, vehitqaddishtem vihyitem qedoshim, ki qadosh ani.
In essence:
“For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves and be holy, because I am holy.”
That is Leviticus 11:44.
There is the heartbeat.
Holiness.
The Hebrew word קָדוֹשׁ—qadosh—carries the idea of holiness, of being set apart.
God was forming Israel into a people who belonged uniquely to Him.
Their worship would be different.
Their sacrifices would be different.
Their calendar would be different.
Their covenant signs would be different.
Their relationship with the nations would be different.
Even ordinary moments around a dinner table could remind them:
You belong to God.
Imagine that.
You wake up in the morning.
God matters.
You worship.
God matters.
You work.
God matters.
You prepare dinner.
Even there...
God matters.
Israel could not conveniently confine the LORD to a religious ceremony and then live the remainder of life as though He did not exist.
The covenant reached into ordinary existence.
That was part of the point.
And Scripture itself explicitly connects Israel’s animal distinctions with Israel’s own distinction from the nations.
Leviticus 20 tells Israel to distinguish between clean and unclean animals and then immediately reminds them that God had set Israel apart from other peoples to belong to Him.
Do you see it?
God separated His people.
Then He taught His separated people to live with separation woven into the rhythms of everyday life.
Not because creation itself was somehow evil.
Genesis had already declared God’s creation good.
Rather, within Israel’s covenant, God designated creatures differently for particular purposes and taught His people to recognize His distinctions.
Leviticus 11:47 gives the purpose with remarkable clarity:
לְהַבְדִּיל בֵּין הַטָּמֵא וּבֵין הַטָּהֹר
Lehavdil bein ha-tamei uvein ha-tahor.
“To distinguish between the unclean and the clean.”
The Hebrew verb lehavdil carries the idea of separating or distinguishing.
Tamei means unclean.
Tahor means clean.
God was teaching discernment.
There is a difference.
There are boundaries.
God defines holiness.
Human preference does not overrule divine revelation.
That lesson reaches far beyond dinner.
And this is where we should be careful with explanations that sound convincing but go beyond Scripture.
You may have heard that the forbidden animals were prohibited simply because they were unhealthy, carried more disease, were scavengers, or were medically dangerous.
Some proposed explanations may contain observations worth discussing.
But the Bible itself does not tell us that disease prevention was the comprehensive reason for the classifications.
So we should not pretend God explained something He did not explain.
Scripture gives us firmer ground.

These regulations belonged to Israel’s covenant life and were explicitly associated with holiness, distinction, obedience, and Israel’s identity as a people belonging to God. Deuteronomy similarly places dietary instructions alongside the declaration that Israel was a holy people chosen as God’s treasured possession.
And suddenly the dinner table becomes a classroom.
Day after day.
Meal after meal.
Generation after generation.
Clean.
Unclean.
Set apart.
Belonging to God.
Distinguish.
Obey.
Remember who you are.
But then Jesus arrives.
And everything moves toward something deeper.
In Mark 7, Jesus is confronting a controversy concerning defilement.
And He moves the conversation from the outside...
to the inside.
From hands.
To heart.
From what enters a person.
To what comes out of a person.
The Greek text of Mark 7:19 contains the striking expression:
καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα
katharizōn panta ta brōmata
“cleansing/declaring clean all foods,” reflected in many modern translations as Jesus declaring all foods clean.
But then Jesus says something considerably more frightening than anything about pork.
What truly defiles a human being comes from within.
Evil thoughts.
Sexual immorality.
Theft.
Murder.
Adultery.
Greed.
Wickedness.
Deceit.
Sensuality.
Envy.
Slander.
Pride.
Foolishness.
And now the knife turns toward us.
Because it is easy to stand over Leviticus 11 asking:
“Why was that animal unclean?”
It is considerably harder to stand before Mark 7 asking:
“What is unclean inside me?”
We like external religion because external religion can sometimes be managed.
Eat this.
Avoid that.
Wear this.
Attend that.
Post the verse.
Say the Christian words.
Know when to raise your hands.
Know when to say “Amen.”
Know how to look clean.
But Jesus walks past appearances and goes straight into the room we hoped nobody would enter.
The heart.
That resentment you have been feeding.
That pornography nobody knows about.
That bitterness you have renamed “discernment.”
That affair beginning inside your imagination.
That secret message you keep deleting.
That jealousy hiding behind congratulations.
That pride disguised as spiritual maturity.
That hatred you justify because the other person hurt you first.
That double life.
That addiction.
That lie.
That hidden version of you that appears when the church people are gone.
We can wash hands.
We can change diets.
We can clean appearances.
But who cleans the heart?
That is the question.
And suddenly the ancient language of clean and unclean becomes painfully personal.
Because humanity’s deepest problem has never been that we accidentally touched the wrong animal.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have not merely violated dietary boundaries.
We have violated the holiness of God.
We have sinned in thought.
In desire.
In word.
In action.
In things we committed.
And things we should have done but refused to do.
The scandal is not simply that something outside us might be unclean.
The scandal is that sin has come from within us.
And no amount of religious cosmetics can wash it away.
But this is exactly where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make bad people slightly more respectable.
He came to save sinners.
The Holy One walked among the unclean.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed sinners.
He ate with people respectable religion preferred to keep at a distance.
Yet He did not become morally contaminated by their sin.
Instead, holiness moved toward the unclean.
Grace moved toward the guilty.
Mercy moved toward the ashamed.
And eventually Jesus walked toward a cross.
The One without sin was treated as condemned.
The innocent Christ bore judgment.
The spotless Lamb shed His blood.
Not because our sin was insignificant.
Because it was so serious that redemption cost blood.
The Gospel is not God pretending you were always clean.
The Gospel is God confronting the full horror of our sin and providing cleansing through Christ.
That is grace.
Not denial.
Not religious makeup.
Not spiritual public relations.
Grace.
You do not cleanse yourself and then approach Jesus.
You approach Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
You have been hiding because you believe Jesus only welcomes the already-clean.
So you keep saying:
“When I fix myself...”
“When I stop struggling...”
“When I finally become disciplined...”
“When I get my life together...”
“Then I’ll come back to God.”
But if sinners could make themselves clean enough to deserve God, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
You do not need a better disguise.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Then Acts 10 gives us one of the most dramatic moments in this entire biblical storyline.
Peter sees a vision.
A sheet descends containing various animals.
A voice tells him to rise, kill, and eat.
Peter protests that he has never eaten anything koinon kai akatharton—“common and unclean.”
Then comes the response:
Ἃ ὁ Θεὸς ἐκαθάρισεν σὺ μὴ κοίνου
Ha ho Theos ekatharisen, sy mē koinou.
“What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”
But we must not rip the vision away from its own inspired interpretation.
Peter later explains what God showed him:
κἀμοὶ ὁ θεὸς ἔδειξεν μηδένα κοινὸν ἢ ἀκάθαρτον λέγειν ἄνθρωπον
God had shown him not to call any person common or unclean.
Cornelius was a Gentile.
The Gospel was breaking through barriers.
The good news of Jesus Christ was not a private possession for one ethnicity.
Christ's kingdom would gather people from the nations.
Think about Peter standing there.
A Jewish man shaped by a lifetime of boundaries.
Then God sends him through the doorway of a Gentile home.
And the Gospel walks in with him.
This was bigger than dinner.
People whom Peter might once have regarded as outside were hearing the Gospel.
Grace was crossing the threshold.
And this is why Christians must be cautious about turning food into a basis for spiritual superiority.
Paul writes in Romans 14:14:
οὐδὲν κοινὸν δι’ ἑαυτοῦ
Nothing is “common” or unclean in itself, while he also commands believers to take conscience and love for one another seriously.
Paul likewise warns Christians not to allow others to judge them regarding food and drink in Colossians 2:16.
And 1 Timothy 4:4 says:
ὅτι πᾶν κτίσμα θεοῦ καλόν
hoti pan ktisma Theou kalon
“For every creation of God is good...”
and is to be received with thanksgiving.
That does not mean Christians should become careless about health, gluttony, conscience, stewardship, or loving fellow believers.
Christian freedom is never permission for selfishness.
But the New Testament does not place Gentile believers under Israel’s Levitical dietary code as the means by which they become holy before God.
Our standing before God is not produced by the contents of our refrigerator.
It is found in Christ.
And maybe now we can finally see why this seemingly strange chapter matters so much.
Leviticus taught Israel:
God is holy.
God determines what is clean and unclean.
God's people belong to Him.
God's people must learn distinction.
Sin and impurity cannot simply be shrugged away.
And the Gospel eventually reveals the astonishing answer to the problem those categories force us to confront:
How can the unclean become clean?
Jesus.
Not your reputation.
Jesus.
Not your religious performance.
Jesus.
Not your denomination.
Jesus.
Not your ability to hide what happened.
Jesus.
Not your promise that you will “do better this time.”
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
The blood of Christ reaches places human religion cannot reach.
And perhaps you have spent years trying to appear clean while quietly bleeding inside.
People see the Sunday version of you.
God sees Tuesday night.
People see your Bible verses.
God sees your browser history.
People hear your worship songs.
God hears what you tell yourself when the room is empty.
People see your smile.
God sees the wound beneath it.
And still...
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
Still...
mercy is offered.
Still...
the cross stands.
Still...
the tomb is empty.
Still...
Jesus saves.
Repentance does not mean pretending the stain never happened.
It means bringing the truth into the light and turning toward Christ.
Grace does not tell you sin was acceptable.
Grace tells you sin does not have to have the final word.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Just be honest.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Send this privately to the person who thinks they have become too dirty for Jesus.
you will want more than a one-sentence answer.
Jesus Christ.
Scripture explicitly teaches Christian generosity without coercion: giving is to come from a willing heart rather than compulsion.
But voluntary financial support can still become a meaningful way of participating in Gospel ministry.
One share can put Scripture in front of someone we could never personally reach.
One tag can begin a conversation.
One saved article can be rediscovered on the night somebody desperately needs it.
One honest comment can give another struggling believer permission to stop pretending.
whether you purchase anything or never do...
never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So give freely if God has put generosity in your heart.
Share freely if this truth could help someone.
Save what strengthens your faith.
Follow if you want to keep growing.
And above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because perhaps the most haunting lesson hidden inside the ancient distinction between clean and unclean is not that God once cared deeply about what Israel placed on the table.
It is that the holy God has always had the right to define holiness.
And when we discovered that we could never make ourselves clean enough to stand before Him...
the Holy One came looking for the unclean.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Life You Keep Postponing Until “Things Calm Down” Is the Life You Are Already Living
paragraphs: The Life You Keep Postponing Until “Things Calm Down” Is the Life You Are Already Living

You keep telling yourself you will pray more, love better, forgive sooner, give more freely, and finally become serious about Jesus when life settles down. James asks a terrifying question: What if “later” was never yours to begin with?
There is a sentence many of us have been quietly repeating for years.
“When things calm down…”
When things calm down, I’ll pray again.
When things calm down, I’ll spend real time with my children.
When things calm down, I’ll open my Bible instead of merely carrying it to church.
When things calm down, I’ll deal with what is happening in my marriage.
When things calm down, I’ll forgive them.
When things calm down, I’ll serve.
I’ll give.
I’ll call my mother.
I’ll apologize to my father.
I’ll stop hiding.
I’ll finally surrender that secret sin.
I’ll become the man God has been calling me to become.
I’ll become the woman I know I should be.
Soon.
Just not today.
Because today is complicated.
Today there are bills.
Deadlines.
Children who need something every five minutes.
Messages you forgot to answer.
People disappointing you.
A body that gets tired.
A house that never stays clean.
A job that consumes more of you than you intended to give it.
A relationship that somehow became distant while both of you were busy surviving.
So you make a quiet agreement with tomorrow.
You promise tomorrow that you will become spiritually intentional once today stops being so difficult.
And tomorrow keeps accepting promises it never intends to collect.
Months pass.
Then years.
And one day something deeply uncomfortable becomes clear:
The interruption was your life.
The exhausting season was your life.
The ordinary Tuesday you were trying to get through was your life.
The children making noise in the next room were your life.
The spouse you kept saying you would reconnect with “soon” was your life.
The Bible gathering dust while you waited to become less busy was your life.
The person you kept meaning to forgive was part of your life.
The opportunity to love somebody while they were still here was your life.
You were waiting for life to begin.
But it had already begun.
And this is exactly where James walks into our carefully organized plans and says something almost painfully simple.
“Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a city and spend a year there and trade and make a profit’—yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring.”
Then comes the question:
“What is your life?”
Not, “What is your five-year plan?”
Not, “How secure is your career?”
Not, “How much money have you accumulated?”
Not even, “What are your intentions?”
“What is your life?”
In Greek, the question is arrestingly compact:
ποία γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν;
poia gar hē zōē hymōn?
“What is your life?”
James answers his own question:
ἀτμὶς γάρ ἐστε ἡ πρὸς ὀλίγον φαινομένη, ἔπειτα καὶ ἀφανιζομένη.
atmis gar este hē pros oligon phainomenē, epeita kai aphanizomenē.
“You are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes.”
James 4:14.
A mist.
Think about that.
You walk outside early in the morning and see vapor hanging above the earth.
For a moment it is there.
Beautiful.
Visible.
Real.
Then the sun rises.
And it disappears.
James does not say your life is meaningless.
Scripture teaches precisely the opposite. Human beings bear God’s image. Christ considered sinners worth pursuing at the cost of His own blood. Our lives matter profoundly before God.
James is confronting something else:
our illusion of control.
We speak about tomorrow as though tomorrow belongs to us.
Next month.
Next year.
After retirement.
After graduation.
After the promotion.
After the children grow up.
After the debt disappears.
After the grief becomes manageable.
After the anxiety settles.
After the church situation improves.
After we finally get ourselves together.
Then I’ll obey.
Then I’ll become generous.
Then I’ll be present.
Then I’ll take holiness seriously.
Then I’ll make things right.
But Scripture never gives us ownership of tomorrow.
James continues:
“Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.’”
James 4:15.
The Greek phrase is:
ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ
ean ho kyrios thelēsē
“If the Lord wills.”
That is not fatalism.
It is surrender.
It is the confession that God is God and we are not.

Planning itself is not the sin James condemns. Scripture contains examples of wise preparation and commends prudence. The problem is planning that quietly removes God from the center and treats tomorrow as personal property.
James exposes the arrogance beneath that illusion:
“As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil.”
James 4:16.
And then James lands the blow many of us would rather skip:
“So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.”
James 4:17.
Read that again slowly.
There are sins committed by doing what God forbids.
But James also confronts the tragedy of knowing the good and continually postponing it.
You knew you needed to apologize.
But you waited.
You knew someone needed encouragement.
But you assumed there would be another opportunity.
You knew your prayer life had become almost nonexistent.
But you kept saying, “When things calm down.”
You knew your family was getting the exhausted leftovers of you while everybody else received your attention.
You knew resentment had been growing inside you.
You knew that habit was dragging your heart farther from Christ.
You knew somebody was lonely.
You knew you had enough to share.
You knew God had been pressing something upon your conscience through His Word.
But you kept negotiating with obedience.
Soon, Lord.
Soon.
There is a strange kind of spiritual procrastination that can disguise itself as good intentions.
You are not rejecting God outright.
You are simply delaying Him.
And because “later” sounds less rebellious than “no,” we convince ourselves that postponement is harmless.
But delayed obedience can quietly become lifelong disobedience.
That is what makes James 4 so unsettling.
Nobody in the passage announces, “There is no God.”
They simply make their plans as though God is irrelevant.
Nobody says, “Tomorrow definitely does not belong to God.”
They simply live as though it belongs to them.
And perhaps that is where this gets personal.
Because some of us are not running away from Jesus dramatically.
We are postponing Him politely.
We still believe.
We still attend.
We still know the verses.
We still say grace before meals.
We still share Christian posts occasionally.
But somewhere between surviving life and planning the future, intimacy with Christ became something we keep scheduling for later.
And maybe you are tired of hearing yourself say it.
“I need to get back to God.”
How long have you been saying that?
Three weeks?
Six months?
Five years?
Maybe you remember a version of yourself that prayed differently.
There was tenderness then.
Conviction.
Hunger.
You could read Scripture and suddenly realize thirty minutes had disappeared.
You worshiped without wondering who was watching.
Sin bothered you before it became familiar.
You talked to Jesus throughout the day.
Then life became busy.
Or painful.
Or disappointing.
Maybe somebody hurt you in church.
Maybe you prayed for something that never happened.
Maybe grief entered your house.
Maybe success entered your house—and somehow distracted you just as effectively as suffering could have.
You did not wake up one morning and decide to become distant from God.
Distance rarely announces itself.
It happens through a thousand tiny postponements.
Not tonight.
Tomorrow.
Not now.
Soon.
And “soon” slowly becomes years.
But here is where the Gospel interrupts the story.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make you feel guilty about wasted time.
He came to redeem sinners.
The Christian message is not “Try harder before your mist disappears.”
It is that the eternal Son of God entered our fragile human history.
Jesus stepped into time.
He took on flesh.
He walked among people whose lives were mist.
He touched lepers.
Ate with sinners.
Welcomed children.
Confronted hypocrisy.
Wept beside a tomb.
Called wanderers home.
And then He went willingly to a cross.
There, the One without sin bore the judgment sinners deserved.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
2 Corinthians 5:21.
Your procrastination cannot be erased by becoming more productive.
Your neglected obedience cannot be cleansed by filling out a better planner.
Your secret sins cannot be redeemed by promising God that next year will be different.
You need grace.
You need forgiveness.
You need Jesus.
And at the cross, grace is not theoretical.
Blood was shed.
Sin was judged.
A debt was paid.
Then the tomb was opened.
Jesus rose.
That means your story does not have to end with all the years you wasted.
This is the scandal of grace:
God can meet you in the very life you wish you had lived differently.
Peter knew something about that.
He had promised Jesus loyalty.
Then, under pressure, he denied even knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
Imagine remembering the sound of your own voice saying, “I do not know the man.”
Imagine watching Jesus die after you had abandoned Him.
Peter could not undo that night.
But resurrection morning changed what Peter's failure meant for his future.
Jesus restored him.
Grace did not pretend Peter never failed.
Grace refused to let failure write the final chapter.
That is what Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your scandal is simply the quiet realization that you have been present for everyone except the people who needed your heart.
Maybe it is how many mornings you reached for your phone before reaching for God.
Maybe it is a marriage living on logistical conversations.
Maybe it is a child who stopped asking you to play because you said “later” too many times.
Maybe it is a parent whose number you keep meaning to call.
Maybe it is generosity you keep postponing until you feel financially invincible.
Maybe it is forgiveness you have withheld because resentment makes you feel protected.
Maybe it is repentance you keep delaying because you are terrified of what surrender might cost.
Maybe you have spent years telling yourself:
“When things calm down.”
But what if they never do?
What if the goal was never to construct a life with no interruptions?
What if following Jesus happens precisely here?
In traffic.
In dishes.
In deadlines.
In diapers.
In hospital rooms.
In grief.
In ordinary conversations.
In small acts of generosity nobody applauds.
In turning the phone off and listening to your child.
In praying when you do not feel spiritual.
In forgiving while the wound is still tender.
In opening Scripture when you only have fifteen minutes.
In confessing what you have been hiding.
In saying “I was wrong” before pride has time to prepare another defense.
In loving the person sitting across from you before they become somebody you can only remember.
This is your life.
Not the imaginary version beginning next year.
This one.
Today.
Right here.
With all its unfinished rooms and unpaid bills and unanswered questions and messy relationships and exhausted prayers.
Jesus is not standing somewhere in your perfect future waiting for a more impressive version of you.
He calls you today.
Hebrews says:
“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
Hebrews 3:15.
Today.
There is something wonderfully merciful about that word.
Because if you are reading this, your story is still being written.
You cannot relive yesterday.
You cannot guarantee tomorrow.
But by God's mercy, you have this moment.
So pray now.
Not beautifully.
Honestly.
“Jesus, I have been postponing You.”
That is enough to begin.
Put the phone down and look at the person you love.
Make the call.
Send the apology.
Forgive.
Give.
Open the Bible.
Sit quietly before God.
Confess the sin.
Ask for help.
Tell somebody you love them.
Hold your children a little longer.
Listen instead of preparing your response.
Stop waiting to become the person who obeys Jesus.
Obey Jesus in the life you actually have.
And understand this carefully:
Doing these things does not purchase salvation.
Christian obedience is not payment for grace.

We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8–9). Yet the very next verse says believers are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared for us to walk in (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace saves.
And saving grace changes the direction of a life.
So perhaps the question is not:
“When will things finally calm down?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What good has God already placed in front of me that I keep postponing?”
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed to read tonight.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore that.
But Gospel work does require people willing to carry truth beyond themselves.
Not because every sentence must be remembered.
“When things calm down…”
And when you do, come back.
Remember James.
Remember the mist.
Remember that tomorrow is God's territory.
Remember that grace is available today.
Because somebody you love may be waiting for a better time to seek God.
And none of us were promised a better time.
We were given today.
Maybe the most painful thing about wasted years is realizing how ordinary they looked while we were wasting them.
But perhaps the most beautiful thing about grace is this:
Jesus can take an ordinary day—the kind you were trying to hurry through—and turn it into the day you finally came home.
So stop waiting for your real life to begin.
The noisy kitchen is part of it.
The difficult marriage is part of it.
The unanswered prayer is part of it.
The workday is part of it.
The children growing faster than you realize are part of it.
The opportunity to forgive is part of it.
The chance to repent is part of it.
The person sitting beside you is part of it.
And this moment...
this fragile, unrepeatable moment...
is part of it too.
You kept waiting for life to calm down before giving yourself fully to Jesus—only to discover that Jesus had been calling your name in the middle of the noise all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD DOUBLE THE PURIFICATION TIME AFTER THE BIRTH OF A DAUGHTER?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD DOUBLE THE PURIFICATION TIME AFTER THE BIRTH OF A DAUGHTER?

Leviticus says forty days after a son, eighty after a daughter. Was God saying women were less valuable? Was childbirth sinful? Or have we been reading an ancient holiness law through modern eyes—and missing the road that eventually leads straight to Jesus?
There is a verse in the Bible that can make a modern reader stop cold.
Not because it is difficult to translate.
Because it seems difficult to understand.
A woman gives birth to a son.
Forty days.
A woman gives birth to a daughter.
Eighty days.
Double.
And immediately the questions begin.
Why?
Was a baby girl somehow considered more unclean than a baby boy?
Was God placing less value on daughters?
Was childbirth itself sinful?
And if none of those things is true, why would the God who created male and female establish two different periods?
Stay with this question.
Because buried inside one of the Bible's least-discussed chapters is something many Christians have never noticed.
And before we reach the end, we are going to walk from a bleeding mother in Leviticus...
to a poor young mother standing in Jerusalem with two birds in her hands...
to the blood of Jesus Christ.
But first, we have to let Scripture say what Scripture actually says.
Leviticus 12 opens:
"אִשָּׁה כִּי תַזְרִיעַ וְיָלְדָה זָכָר"
Ishah ki tazria veyaldah zakhar...
Literally, the Hebrew speaks of a woman who conceives or “brings forth seed” and gives birth to a male.

The text continues that she becomes ritually unclean—Hebrew טָמֵא, tameʾ—for seven days. On the eighth day the boy is circumcised. Then the mother continues for another thirty-three days in what the Hebrew calls:
"דְּמֵי טָהֳרָה"
demei tohorah—
literally, something like “bloods of purification” or “bloods of purity.”
Seven days plus thirty-three.
Forty days.
Then comes the sentence that has troubled readers for centuries:
"וְאִם־נְקֵבָה תֵלֵד וְטָמְאָה שְׁבֻעַיִם כְּנִדָּתָהּ וְשִׁשִּׁים יוֹם וְשֵׁשֶׁת יָמִים תֵּשֵׁב עַל־דְּמֵי טָהֳרָה"
Ve'im neqevah teled...
“But if she bears a female...”
The first period becomes fourteen days.
The second becomes sixty-six.
Eighty days altogether.

The Hebrew text really does make the distinction. It is not a mistranslation or something inserted by later Christianity. Leviticus gives seven plus thirty-three days following the birth of a son and fourteen plus sixty-six following the birth of a daughter.
But here is where responsible Bible reading becomes absolutely essential.
God tells Israel what the periods are. Leviticus does not explicitly tell us why the period is doubled for a daughter.
That sentence may save us from a mountain of bad theology.
Because people hate unanswered questions.
So when Scripture leaves something unexplained, we are tempted to fill the silence ourselves.
And eventually somebody's theory gets repeated so many times that Christians begin calling it “what the Bible says.”
It isn't.

Various explanations have been proposed across Jewish interpretation and modern scholarship. Some ancient interpreters connected the periods symbolically with Adam and Eve. Some scholars have explored connections with circumcision, noting that the boy's eighth-day circumcision appears directly between the seven-day and thirty-three-day instructions. Others have compared ancient Near Eastern birth rituals and proposed that the doubled period marked or ritually signaled the sex of the newborn. Still others have examined the language in relation to postpartum bleeding and ancient concepts of ritual purity. These are attempts to explain the law; none should be confused with an explanation explicitly supplied by Leviticus itself.
That distinction matters.
Deeply.
Because one of the easiest conclusions to make is also one of the conclusions the passage never makes:
A daughter was not worth half as much as a son.
Leviticus 12 never says that.
It never calls the baby girl sinful.
It never calls the baby boy morally superior.
It never says God loves sons more.
And it never says that giving birth is itself a moral transgression.
That last point is especially important because English readers often see words such as “unclean,” “sin offering,” and “atonement” and automatically imagine personal wrongdoing.
But the ritual-purity system of Leviticus is not simply a chart dividing “good people” from “bad people.”

A person could become ritually unclean through bodily conditions that were not acts of moral rebellion. Leviticus 15, for example, treats bodily discharges and menstruation within the purity system. The categories of tahor and tameʾ—clean and unclean—cannot simply be collapsed into our categories of “righteous person” and “wicked sinner.”
That means a mother holding her newborn was not being declared evil because she had given birth.
Think about that.
She had just participated in something God Himself commanded humanity to do:
“Be fruitful and multiply.”
Life had entered the world.
A tiny chest was rising and falling.
Small fingers were curling around hers.
She was exhausted.
Bleeding.
Recovering.
Holding a human being who had never existed before.
And God's law recognized that something profound had happened.
There was blood.
There was bodily vulnerability.
There was separation from sacred space.
There was waiting.
Then restoration.

The first stage following childbirth was compared with menstrual impurity, while the following thirty-three or sixty-six days had a different status: the woman was restricted from contact with consecrated things and entrance into the sanctuary until the purification period was completed. In other words, even Leviticus itself presents more nuance than the simple statement, “She was dirty for forty or eighty days.”
And perhaps that word—dirty—is exactly where many of us begin misunderstanding the story.
Because we know what it feels like to feel dirty.
Not ceremonially.
Personally.
You know the feeling.
You prayed, promised God you would change, and then returned to the same secret.
You smiled at church while something inside you was collapsing.
You raised your hands during worship with memories you desperately hoped nobody in the room knew.
Maybe you have wondered whether God still wants you near Him.
Maybe you have thought:
If they knew everything about me, they wouldn't look at me the same.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
But heaven saw it.
The hidden addiction.
The bitterness.
The affair.
The pornography.
The pride.
The lie.
The years wasted running from God.
The prayerlessness.
The coldness.
The secret compromise.
The wound you turned into anger.
The shame you learned to disguise as confidence.
And suddenly this strange chapter in Leviticus does something unexpected.
It forces us to confront an ancient reality:
There was once a boundary around sacred space.
You could not simply stroll into the sanctuary on your own terms.
God is holy.
Human beings do not define holiness.
God does.
And throughout the Torah, approaching His sacred presence was not casual.
There were boundaries.
There were sacrifices.
There was blood.
There was cleansing.
There was waiting.
There was a priest.
And then...
centuries later...
a young Jewish mother started counting days.
Her name was Mary.
Her Son's name was Jesus.
Do not miss this.
The Gospel of Luke tells us that when the required purification time was completed according to the Law of Moses, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to Jerusalem. Luke then records their offering:
“A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.”
Those words point directly back into the world of Leviticus 12.
Read Leviticus 12:8 and something breathtaking appears.
The normal instruction involved a lamb and a bird, but if the mother could not afford the lamb, the law permitted two turtledoves or two young pigeons.
And that is the offering Luke records when Mary and Joseph arrive.
Two birds.
The mother of Jesus walked into the story governed by the very purification law we are reading.
The One through whom all things were made entered a household that obeyed the law given to Israel.
The Son of God did not arrive surrounded by earthly luxury.
And here is the image I cannot get out of my mind:
Mary could not bring a lamb.
She brought birds.
But she was carrying the Lamb.
The law asked for sacrifice.
And sleeping in her arms was the One toward whom the entire sacrificial story was moving.
Jesus.
The Lamb of God.
The One who would not merely restore someone to ceremonial access for another season.
The One who would deal with sin at its deepest level.
This is where Leviticus stops being an obscure book people skip in their Bible-reading plan.
This is where the shadows begin pointing toward a Person.

Hebrews tells us that the law possessed “a shadow of the good things to come” and that repeated sacrifices could not bring final perfection to those drawing near. Then Hebrews turns our eyes toward the offering of Jesus Christ “once for all.”
Once.
For.
All.
Under the old covenant, purification had days attached to it.
Wait.
Seven.
Thirty-three.
Fourteen.
Sixty-six.
Then bring the offering.
Approach according to what God commanded.
But at Calvary, something greater happened.
Jesus did not enter our uncleanness because He needed cleansing.
He entered our world because we did.
He touched the rejected.
He welcomed sinners.
He moved toward people respectable religion preferred to avoid.
And ultimately He carried our sin to the cross.
Not ceremonially.
Actually.
Not symbolically.
Redemptively.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
So the deepest question raised by Leviticus 12 is ultimately not merely:
“Why forty days for a boy and eighty for a girl?”
That is a legitimate historical and interpretive question, and humility requires us to admit that Scripture does not explicitly reveal the reason for the doubling.
But there is another question Scripture answers with thunderous clarity:
How can unclean, guilty, sinful human beings ever come near a holy God?
Jesus Christ.
That is the answer.
Not your record.
Not your religious résumé.
Not pretending.
Not hiding.
Not performing Christianity convincingly enough that nobody discovers the truth.
Jesus.
And maybe that is why this obscure chapter can hurt in the most beautiful way.
Because some of us have been living as though our purification period never ended.
God forgave you...
but you sentenced yourself to another year.
Jesus washed you...
but you keep returning to the courtroom to prosecute yourself.
You repented...
but every time your past whispers your name, you put the chains back on.
You know the Gospel intellectually.
But emotionally?
You are still standing outside.
Still waiting.
Still wondering whether Jesus really wants somebody with your history.
Listen carefully.
Repentance is real.
Sin is serious.
Grace is not permission to remain in rebellion.
Jesus did not die so that we could decorate our chains with Christian language and keep serving the same master.
He calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, die to self, and walk in newness of life.
But the Gospel is equally clear about this:
Christ does not merely expose sinners. He saves sinners.
He does not merely uncover scandal.
He rewrites what scandal thought it owned.
Peter had denial.
Jesus wrote restoration.
Paul had persecution.
Jesus wrote apostleship.
The thief had a criminal sentence.
Jesus spoke paradise.
And maybe your story has a chapter you wish you could tear out.
Jesus already knows.
The question is not whether He has seen it.
The question is whether you will finally bring it into His light.
No more pretending.
No more negotiating.
No more telling Jesus, “You can have everything except this.”
Repent.
Come home.
The blood of Christ is stronger than the stain you keep staring at.
And suddenly the strange waiting periods of Leviticus become a doorway into something enormous.
Under that covenantal system, the worshiper learned that holiness mattered.
Blood mattered.
Cleansing mattered.
Approaching God mattered.
Then Christ came.
And He did not announce that holiness no longer mattered.
He made a way for sinners to be reconciled to the Holy One.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost to Himself.
So why was the purification period different after the birth of a son or daughter?
The most biblically responsible answer is:
Leviticus clearly establishes the difference, but Scripture does not explicitly tell us why God doubled the period after the birth of a daughter.
We can examine the Hebrew.
We can study circumcision.
We can compare ancient interpretations.
We can investigate historical context.
We can consider scholarly proposals.
But where God has not explicitly explained His reason, humility should stop us from pretending He did.
And perhaps there is a lesson even there.
We do not need to invent an answer to defend God.
Sometimes faithfulness means saying:
“This is what Scripture says.”
“This is what Scripture does not say.”
“This is what interpreters have proposed.”
And then refusing to confuse the three.
That kind of Bible reading may not produce sensational answers.
But it produces trustworthy disciples.
And we desperately need those.
If this changed the way you have understood Leviticus 12, don't let the conversation die in your head.
Or did you grow up hearing another explanation?
If you need prayer because your faith has been exhausted lately, simply write:
There is no trophy for pretending to be strong.
Sometimes confession begins with four words typed beneath an article.
And somebody reading your comment may discover that they are not the only person still fighting their way back toward Jesus.
Come back to the text.
Test everything.
And yes—even send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity cannot survive hard questions.
Truth does not need us to be afraid of questions.
It doesn't.
It can't.
And not because Christians should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from a willing heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
More importantly, your support helps us keep putting Scripture-centered material in front of people who desperately need Jesus.
Not to build an audience around us.
To keep pointing an audience beyond us.
To Christ.
But whether you ever give a cent or not, hear this before you leave.
The woman in Leviticus waited outside sacred space.
Mary eventually walked toward the Temple carrying two birds...
and the Savior of the world.
And years later, outside Jerusalem, that Child stretched out His hands on a cross so guilty people like us could be brought near.
Maybe you came here wondering why one mother waited forty days and another eighty.
Maybe the question you needed answered was something else entirely:
“After everything I've done...can I still come near?”
Look at the cross.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Jesus.
Because the Gospel was never the story of clean people congratulating themselves for staying clean.
It is the story of a holy Savior rescuing people who could never cleanse themselves.
And when your past whispers, “Look what you did,” point to the empty tomb and answer, “Look what Jesus did.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jesus Looked Around the Table and Said, “One of You Will Betray Me.” Suddenly Everyone Started Asking the Same Question.
paragraphs: Jesus Looked Around the Table and Said, “One of You Will Betray Me.” Suddenly Everyone Started Asking the Same Question.
The Betrayer Revealed — and the terrifying question the disciples asked before anyone dared accuse somebody else.
There was bread on the table.
A cup.
Men who had walked dusty roads together.
Men who had watched demons flee, storms become still, blind eyes open, crippled bodies rise, and grieving families receive their dead back alive.
And somewhere at that table sat a traitor.
He did not look like one.
That may be the most disturbing part.
Judas Iscariot was not standing outside the room wearing the face of an enemy. He was reclining near Jesus with the others.
Close enough to eat with Him.
Close enough to hear His voice.
Close enough to receive bread from His hand.
And yet his heart was already moving toward betrayal.
Then Jesus spoke.
Matthew records His words in Greek:
“Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι εἷς ἐξ ὑμῶν παραδώσει με.”
Literally:
“Truly I tell you, one of you will hand Me over.”
One of you.
Imagine what happened to that room.
Conversations died.
Hands stopped moving.
Eyes lifted from the table.
The men who had been eating beside Jesus suddenly realized that the greatest threat in the room was not outside the door.
It was sitting among them.
But then something happened that should haunt every Christian who has ever become more skilled at detecting another person's sin than examining his own heart.
The disciples did not immediately begin pointing fingers.
They began asking questions.
About themselves.
Matthew 26:22 preserves the question:
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, κύριε;”
“Mēti egō eimi, Kyrie?”
“Surely it is not I, Lord?”
Read that again.
Not:
“Lord, is it Peter?”
Not:
“Is it Matthew?”
“Is it Thomas?”
“I always suspected Judas.”
No.
“Surely it is not I, Lord?”
Suddenly every man at the table was forced to look somewhere most of us desperately try to avoid.
Inside.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being about Judas for a moment and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because it is easy to read the Bible already knowing who the villain is.
We know Judas betrays Jesus.
We know the silver.
We know the kiss.
We know Gethsemane.
We know how the story ends.
So we can sit safely on the other side of two thousand years, point toward Judas, and whisper:
“How could you?”
But Scripture does not give us that luxury.
Before the betrayer is fully exposed, the question echoes around the table.
“Is it I?”
And maybe before asking how Judas could betray Jesus, we need enough courage to ask where our own hearts have betrayed Him.
Have I confessed Christ with my mouth while negotiating with sin in private?
Have I worshiped on Sunday and deliberately ignored Him on Monday?
Have I wanted Jesus as Savior but resisted Him as Lord?
Have I learned Christian vocabulary while slowly losing Christian tenderness?
Have I condemned sins I can see in other people while protecting the ones nobody can see in me?
Have I become comfortable sitting near Jesus while refusing to surrender something to Jesus?
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because proximity to holy things is not the same thing as surrender to Christ.
Judas had extraordinary proximity.
He heard teachings from Jesus Himself.
He witnessed miracles.
He traveled with the Twelve.
He participated in their shared ministry.
He occupied a trusted position involving the common money bag, according to John’s Gospel.
He sat at the final meal.
And still...
his heart was not right.
That should destroy one of Christianity's most dangerous illusions:
“I am around Christian things, therefore everything between God and me must be fine.”
You can know worship songs and still need repentance.
You can quote Scripture and still conceal bitterness.
You can post verses and still harbor secret compromise.
You can serve in ministry and still need your heart searched.
You can know what Christians say without truly surrendering what Christ asks.
None of those observations means every struggling believer is another Judas.
Far from it.
Peter failed catastrophically too.
Before sunrise, Peter would deny Jesus three times.
Yet Peter's story would not end in denial.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Gospel is not teaching that one failure automatically makes someone Judas.
It is showing us something much deeper about the human heart, sin, repentance, and grace.
Judas betrayed.
Peter denied.
Both sinned terribly.
But Peter would eventually be broken, restored, recommissioned, and sent to feed Christ's sheep.
Failure does not have to become your final chapter.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a warning about betrayal.
It is an invitation to come out of hiding.
Maybe you have betrayed your own confession more times than you want to remember.
Maybe there are things on your phone you would panic if someone discovered.
Maybe bitterness has lived in you so long that you have renamed it “discernment.”
Maybe your marriage sees a version of you your church never sees.
Maybe you have been pretending to be spiritually alive while privately wondering when your heart became this cold.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
And that truth can either terrify you...
or become the beginning of your freedom.
Because the Jesus at this table is not confused.
He is not discovering Judas's betrayal in real time.
He knows.
Matthew records Jesus saying that the Son of Man goes “as it is written of Him,” while also pronouncing a dreadful warning concerning the betrayer.
Human evil is real.
Human responsibility is real.
And yet human betrayal does not overthrow the sovereign redemptive purpose of God.
Judas is not stronger than Jesus.
The conspiracy is not stronger than Jesus.
The soldiers will not be stronger than Jesus.
Pilate will not be stronger than Jesus.
The nails will not be stronger than Jesus.
The tomb will not be stronger than Jesus.
The scandal will not have the last word.
Grace will.
But we need to be precise about how the betrayer is revealed, because the Gospel accounts give us details that become even more powerful when we do not flatten them into one scene.
In Matthew 26, after the disciples ask, “Surely it is not I, Lord?” Jesus speaks about the one dipping his hand with Him in the dish.
Then Judas asks a question of his own.
His wording is striking.
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, ῥαββί;”
“Surely it is not I, Rabbi?”
Notice the difference Matthew records.
The other disciples had addressed Jesus as “Lord.”
Judas says, “Rabbi.”
Teacher.
Jesus answers him:
“Σὺ εἶπας.”
“You have said it.”
But John's Gospel takes us even closer.
John 13 says Jesus became troubled in spirit and testified that one of them would betray Him.
The disciples looked at one another, uncertain whom He meant.
Peter motioned to the disciple whom Jesus loved to ask Jesus who it was.
Jesus answered that it was the one for whom He would dip the morsel and give it to him.
Then Jesus dipped the morsel.
And gave it to Judas.
Do not rush past that.
The hand Judas would betray was still extending something toward him.
The Lord knew what Judas was about to do.
And Judas was still close enough to receive from His hand.
Then comes one of the darkest sentences in the New Testament.
John 13:27:
“καὶ μετὰ τὸ ψωμίον τότε εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ὁ Σατανᾶς.”
“And after the morsel, then Satan entered into him.”
Jesus tells Judas:
“What you are doing, do quickly.”
And Judas leaves.
John adds a tiny sentence.
Three Greek words:
“ἦν δὲ νύξ.”
“Now it was night.”
Of course it was.
Night outside.
Night inside.
A man walked away from the Light of the world and disappeared into darkness.
Yet even here we should resist adding something Scripture does not say.

John tells us that Jesus gave the identifying sign concerning the morsel, but the other disciples still did not understand why Judas left. Some thought Jesus had instructed him, because Judas kept the money bag, to buy what was needed for the feast or give something to the poor.
Think about that.
Even when Judas walked out, they apparently did not all comprehend what was happening.
The betrayer had hidden well.
Sin often does.
It learns vocabulary.
It learns appearances.
It learns when to smile.
It learns how to survive around holy people without surrendering to a holy God.
And that is why the question at the table matters so much.
“Is it I?”
There are moments when mature faith stops saying, “God, show me what is wrong with everybody else,” and begins praying something closer to David's prayer in Psalm 139:
Search me.
Know me.
Test me.
See whether there is a grievous way in me.
Lead me.
That prayer is dangerous because God may answer it.
He may expose the resentment you have justified.
The secret habit you have minimized.
The pride you disguised as confidence.
The envy you called ambition.
The unforgiveness you renamed boundaries.
The lukewarmness you blamed entirely on exhaustion.
The compromise you promised yourself was temporary.
But when Jesus exposes something, the answer is not to run deeper into darkness.
Bring it into His light.
This is where Judas's story should drive us not toward hopelessness, but toward Christ.
Because somewhere reading this is a person thinking:
“If people knew what I have done, they would never look at me the same.”
Maybe.
People are people.
But salvation was never built upon people knowing the polished version of you.
It was built upon Jesus Christ knowing the worst truth about sinners and going to the cross anyway.
The Gospel does not say your sin is small.
It says Christ is sufficient.
It does not say rebellion does not matter.
It says there is forgiveness for those who turn to Christ.
It does not tell you to decorate your chains.
It calls you out of them.
Repentance is not pretending the darkness never happened.
Repentance is turning from darkness toward the One who is Light.
Grace is not God announcing that sin never mattered.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that the sinless Son of God suffered for sinners.
Grace means that Christ bore what guilty people could never erase by religious performance.
He was betrayed.
Arrested.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Scourged.
Crucified.
And He rose.
The cross appeared to be scandal.
God turned it into the proclamation of grace.
What looked like the triumph of darkness became the place where Christ bore sin.
What looked like the end became the road toward resurrection morning.
That is why your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter either.
Not because you can rewrite yourself.
Because Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Because Jesus restores the repentant.
Because Jesus still calls people out of darkness.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe the most important question you can ask tonight is not:
“Who is Judas in my life?”
Maybe it is:
“Lord... is there something in me that I have been refusing to surrender?”
Do not answer quickly.
Sit there for a moment.
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, κύριε;”
“Surely it is not I, Lord?”
If your conscience immediately brought something to mind, do not scroll fast enough to silence it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Ask for mercy.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is biblically possible.
Ask another mature believer for help if you need accountability.
There is no spiritual prize for becoming excellent at hiding.
Christ did not call you to manage darkness.
He called you into light.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every private detail. But you can make one honest declaration.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer fighting a private battle.
Someone may finally ask for prayer.
Someone may finally repent.
Someone may finally come home.
And if you know a Christian who has slowly become cold, send this to them without condemnation.
Sharing the Gospel cannot save us.
Jesus saves us.
But saved people have beautiful reasons to tell others about the Savior.

So if you want your Facebook presence to glorify God, consider using it deliberately for Christ. Let truth travel farther than gossip. Let grace travel farther than scandal. Let the name of Jesus appear in places where despair has been getting all the attention.
There may come a night when the question is no longer theoretical.
When temptation is loud.
When your heart is cold.
When you need to remember three words:
“Is it I?”
And then three more:
“Come to Jesus.”
It does not.
It cannot.
Not because you must give money to earn grace.
You cannot.
Grace cannot be bought.
More importantly, your support helps us keep pointing people beyond merchandise, beyond personalities, beyond algorithms, and back toward Jesus Christ.
Not for guilt.
Not for applause.
Not to prove your Christianity.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them repentance is still possible while there is breath to turn to Him.
Tell them grace is not permission to remain in darkness.
Tell them forgiveness was purchased at an immeasurable price.
Tell them the cross is stronger than their shame.
Tell them the empty tomb means darkness does not get the final sentence.
And before you leave this table...
ask the question.
Not about your spouse.
Not about your pastor.
Not about the politician you cannot stand.
Not about the Christian who disappointed you.
Not about Judas.
About you.
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, κύριε;”
“Lord... is it I?”
And when Jesus puts His finger on the place you hoped He would overlook, do not run into the night.
Run toward Christ.
Because the most frightening thing about Judas was not merely that he fell.
It was that he walked away from Jesus into the darkness.
You do not have to.
Come into the light.
Come with the failure.
Come with the shame.
Come with the secret.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Come to the crucified and risen Christ.
And when grace has found you there, do not keep the story to yourself.
Follow.
Invite someone else closer to the truth.
Support Gospel work if God has given you the desire and means to do so.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because one day nobody will care how convincing your Christian appearance was.
Only whether you truly belonged to Christ.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
Do not become so comfortable sitting at the table with Jesus that you stop asking whether your heart still belongs to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You can delete the platform in seconds. You can silence the notifications. You can disappear from the feed. But what happens when the screen goes dark…and the hunger to be noticed is still alive?
paragraphs: You can delete the platform in seconds. You can silence the notifications. You can disappear from the feed. But what happens when the screen goes dark…and the hunger to be noticed is still alive?
You deleted the app.
Maybe you finally got tired of it.
Tired of checking.
Tired of scrolling.
Tired of watching people you barely know live lives that somehow made your own feel smaller.
Tired of posting something and pretending you did not care whether anyone reacted to it…while quietly checking five minutes later.
Then ten.
Then twenty.
Maybe you hated what social media was doing to you.
So you deleted it.
And for a moment, it felt like freedom.
No notifications.
No follower counts.

No endless parade of vacations, engagements, promotions, perfect marriages, transformed bodies, expensive dinners, successful ministries, smiling children, beautiful houses, and carefully edited lives.
Silence.
Finally.
But then something uncomfortable happened.
The app disappeared…
and the ache didn't.
You still noticed who complimented you.
You still replayed conversations wondering what people thought about you.
You still felt strangely wounded when somebody else received the attention you secretly wanted.
You still wanted to be impressive.
Still wanted to be admired.
Still wanted somebody to notice how hard you were trying.
Still wanted to walk into a room and matter.
And perhaps that is when the real question begins.
What if the app was never the deepest problem?
What if it was merely a mirror?
What if deleting Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, or whatever platform consumed you removed one outlet for the hunger…but never confronted the hunger itself?
Because an appetite for human approval does not need Wi-Fi to survive.
It can migrate.
From followers to coworkers.
From likes to compliments.
From comments to applause.
From strangers online to people at church.
From posting photographs to displaying spirituality.
From wanting people to admire your appearance to wanting Christians to admire your holiness.
You can leave social media and still perform.
You can put the phone down and still compare.
You can stop posting selfies and start posting righteousness.
You can stop chasing followers and begin chasing the approval of religious people.
And suddenly an ancient sentence written by the apostle Paul becomes painfully modern.
“For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.”
Galatians 1:10, KJV.
The Greek presses even closer.
“Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν Θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν; εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην.”
There is a word in that sentence worth sitting with: “ἀρέσκειν” — areskein — from areskō, carrying the sense of pleasing, satisfying, or seeking to please.
Paul is not saying that kindness is sinful.
He is not commanding Christians to become abrasive, insensitive, or deliberately offensive.

Scripture itself tells believers, “Let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification” (Romans 15:2, KJV). Paul elsewhere says that he seeks the good of others so that they may be saved (1 Corinthians 10:33).
So Galatians 1:10 cannot honestly mean, “I should never care how my actions affect another person.”
The issue is deeper.
Who sits on the throne of your obedience?
Whose approval becomes decisive when pleasing people and obeying Christ collide?
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because some of us do not merely enjoy approval.
We feed on it.
A compliment can carry us for hours.
Criticism can ruin an entire day.
Being overlooked can feel like rejection.
Watching somebody else succeed can awaken something ugly that we immediately try to rename.
“I’m just discouraged.”
Maybe.
But sometimes discouragement is wounded pride wearing respectable clothes.
Sometimes we are not devastated because God was dishonored.
We are devastated because somebody else was noticed.
Sometimes we call it loneliness when what we desperately want is an audience.
Sometimes we call it “sharing our journey” when underneath the sharing is a trembling question:
Do you see me?
Do I matter?
Am I attractive enough?
Successful enough?
Spiritual enough?
Interesting enough?
Loved enough?
Please…
somebody tell me I am enough.
And that is where the Gospel walks into the room.
Not carrying another self-esteem slogan.
Not telling you to stare into a mirror and convince yourself that everybody else is wrong.
The Gospel gives you something infinitely stronger than the applause of strangers.
It gives you Christ.
There is a reason human approval makes such a cruel master.
It changes constantly.
Yesterday they celebrated you.
Today they forgot you.
Yesterday the post performed well.
Today nobody seems interested.
Yesterday somebody called you inspiring.
Tomorrow the same person may misunderstand you.
Build your identity on applause and you will eventually become terrified of silence.
Build it on admiration and criticism will feel like death.
Build it on being seen and being overlooked will feel unbearable.
But Jesus offers an identity that does not rise and fall with an algorithm.
Consider the scandal of the Gospel.
The Son of God was rejected.
“He is despised and rejected of men” (Isaiah 53:3, KJV).
The One whose approval actually matters entered a world obsessed with status and willingly walked toward humiliation.
Jesus was mocked.
Spat upon.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Crucified.
Crowds that could gather around Him could also turn against Him.
Yet Christ did not need public approval to tell Him who He was.
At His baptism, before the public ministry that would make His name known throughout the region, the Father declared:
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
Matthew 3:17, KJV.
Before the miracles multiplied.
Before the crowds swelled.
Before Calvary.
Beloved.
There is something here our approval-starved generation desperately needs to understand.
Jesus did not go to the cross so you could become impressive.
He went to the cross to save sinners.
You do not need a better personal brand nearly as much as you need reconciliation with God.
And reconciliation does not come through followers.
It comes through Christ.
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
1 Timothy 2:5, KJV.
Your deepest problem is not low engagement.
It is sin.
And your greatest hope is not greater visibility.
It is grace.
That changes everything.
Because now you can finally admit the embarrassing things.
You can admit that sometimes you wanted the photograph to make somebody jealous.
You can admit that you checked who viewed the story.
You can admit that somebody else's success bothered you.
You can admit that you exaggerated because the ordinary truth did not seem impressive enough.
You can admit that you have occasionally performed happiness while privately falling apart.
You can even admit something more frightening.
Sometimes you wanted people to think you were close to God more than you actually wanted to be close to God.
That one hurts.
Because religious approval can become just as intoxicating as worldly approval.
Jesus warned about people who did righteous acts “to be seen of men” (Matthew 6:1).
Think about those words.
“To be seen.”
Two thousand years before social media, Jesus was already exposing the heart behind spiritual performance.
He spoke about charitable giving that could become theater.
Prayer that could become theater.
Fasting that could become theater.
The technology changed.
The human heart did not.
You can turn even Christianity into content designed primarily to make people admire you.
You can know when to say “Amen.”
Know which verse to post.
Know how to sound broken without actually repenting.
Know how to look surrendered while secretly being addicted to recognition.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave that hidden.
Grace does not merely comfort.
Grace exposes before it heals.
Not to humiliate you for entertainment.
To free you.
Because imagine the freedom of no longer needing every room to notice you.
Imagine being able to celebrate someone else's blessing without secretly wondering why God passed over you.
Imagine obeying Jesus when nobody applauds.
Giving when nobody knows.
Praying when nobody hears.
Serving when nobody posts a photograph.
Forgiving when nobody congratulates you.
Remaining faithful when obedience makes you less popular rather than more popular.
That is freedom.
Not becoming indifferent to people.
Becoming liberated from needing people to function as your god.
Proverbs 29:25 says, “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.”
A snare.
That is such an accurate word.
Approval promises belonging and quietly builds a cage.
Soon you edit yourself before speaking.
You hide convictions because somebody might unfollow you.
You soften truths Christ has made clear because obedience could cost social acceptance.
Or you swing in the opposite direction and become needlessly provocative because outrage gives you another kind of attention.
Either way, people are still controlling you.
That is why the answer is not merely deleting an app.
Sometimes deleting the app may be wise.
Jesus taught radical seriousness about removing occasions of sin (Matthew 5:29–30). Scripture repeatedly calls believers to wisdom, self-control, and vigilance.
Set the boundary.
Turn off the notifications.
Unfollow what repeatedly drags your heart toward envy.
Take the break.
Put the phone outside the bedroom.
Do whatever wise boundary helps you walk faithfully.
But do not confuse pruning the branch with healing the root.
You can delete the app tonight and reinstall approval addiction tomorrow under another name.
The deeper prayer sounds more like this:
Jesus, why do I need them to notice me?
Why does their silence hurt this much?
Why am I threatened when somebody else shines?
Why do I keep rehearsing what people might think about me?
Why am I more frightened of disappointing them than disobeying You?
Why do I want to be seen?
And then comes the question many of us would rather avoid.
What am I trying to get from strangers that I should be receiving from God?
Maybe you have been carrying rejection for years.
Maybe somebody important made you feel invisible.
Maybe affection in your childhood had to be earned.
Maybe praise became proof that you were safe.
Maybe popularity became medicine for an old wound.
Those experiences can help explain why approval feels powerful.
But they cannot become your savior.
Jesus can meet you deeper than applause ever will.
He knows the version of you nobody follows.
The version without the lighting.
Without the filters.
Without the clever captions.
Without the Sunday smile.
Without the accomplishments.
Without the performance.
He sees the envy.
The vanity.
The insecurity.
The secret competition.
The desperation.
The shame.
And the astonishing message of Christianity is not that Jesus discovered the real you and walked away.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8, KJV.
While we were yet sinners.
Not once we became impressive.
Not once our image was repaired.
Not once everybody approved.
Christ died for sinners.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of healing.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who receives repentant sinners by grace.
You do not have to protect your image before Jesus.
There is nothing behind your carefully managed curtain that surprises Him.
Bring it into the light.
“God, I wanted their praise.”
Bring it.
“God, I was jealous.”
Bring it.
“God, I wanted to be admired.”
Bring it.
“God, I have been pretending.”
Bring it.
“God, I cared more about their opinion than Your Word.”
Bring it.
“God, forgive me.”
Bring that too.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9, KJV.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Because grace is greater.
Jesus does not merely rewrite your public reputation.
He begins transforming the heart underneath it.
And perhaps someday you will open social media again.
Perhaps you will not.
That is not ultimately the measure of victory.
The greater question is whether the platform remains on the throne after the app is gone.
Can you post without needing worship?
Can you disappear without feeling worthless?
Can you be corrected without collapsing?
Can somebody else receive applause while you sincerely rejoice?
Can you tell the truth even when truth costs approval?
Can you obey Jesus when the room becomes quiet?
Can you serve when nobody knows your name?
Because heaven is not measuring your worth in likes.
The cross has already exposed how worthless our self-made righteousness is—and how immeasurably costly the grace of God is.
So perhaps the next time your hand reaches instinctively toward your phone, stop for a moment.
Not because phones are inherently evil.
Because sometimes our reflexes reveal our hungers.
Ask yourself:
What am I looking for right now?
Connection?
Distraction?
Escape?
Comparison?
Validation?
Someone to tell me that I matter?
Then remember whose eyes matter eternally.
You are standing before God.
And if you are in Christ, your hope is not that you successfully convinced the world you were worthy.
Your hope is Jesus Christ—crucified for sinners, risen from the dead, reigning as Lord, and sufficient for everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
Maybe this article made you uncomfortable.
Good questions often do.
Sit with Galatians 1:10.
Ask the Holy Spirit to expose where human approval has quietly begun competing with obedience to Christ.
And if something hidden was exposed, be honest.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting this battle.
Save it too.

Approval addiction rarely dies after one moment of conviction. Come back when comparison returns. Come back when criticism stings. Come back when somebody else's success awakens jealousy. Come back when you are tempted to measure your value by attention again.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, and Jesus Christ, follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Let your sharing become mission rather than performance.
Come to Christ.
Because eventually every notification becomes silent.
Every trend disappears.
Every follower count stops increasing.
Every photograph ages.
Every platform changes.
Every human audience eventually looks somewhere else.
But the question of Galatians 1:10 remains.
Whose approval rules your heart?
You deleted the app.
Now bring Jesus the hunger that made you need the applause.
Because perhaps the freedom you were searching for was never hiding behind the delete button.
Perhaps it begins when you finally stop asking strangers to give you what only Christ can ultimately secure.
You were never created to spend your life auditioning for people who cannot save you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “INTOXICATED WITH HER LOVE”: THE BIBLE IS MORE POSITIVE ABOUT MARITAL DESIRE THAN MANY CHRISTIANS REALIZE
paragraphs: “INTOXICATED WITH HER LOVE”: THE BIBLE IS MORE POSITIVE ABOUT MARITAL DESIRE THAN MANY CHRISTIANS REALIZE
What if some Christians have spent years feeling ashamed of something God Himself told a husband and wife to enjoy?
There is a sentence in the Bible so intimate that, if you heard it quoted without knowing where it came from, you might wonder whether it belonged in Scripture at all.
But it does.
Not hidden in some obscure manuscript.
Not smuggled into the text by a modern culture obsessed with sex.
It sits in the wisdom literature of the Old Testament, surrounded by warnings against adultery, spoken precisely because God cares about holiness.
The Hebrew says:
“אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד”
“A loving doe, a graceful mountain goat. Let her breasts satisfy you at all times; be infatuated with her love always.” — Proverbs 5:19
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because generations of Christians have sometimes spoken about marital sexuality with embarrassment while Scripture itself can speak about it with remarkable warmth.
The final Hebrew words are especially striking:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
“With her love, be continually captivated.”

The verb שָׁגָה — shagah — can carry the idea of wandering, reeling, being intoxicated or overwhelmed. In Proverbs 5:19, the imagery is deliberately intense: the husband is being told not merely to tolerate his wife's affection, but to remain deeply captivated by her love.
That matters.
Because the surrounding context makes the contrast unmistakable.
The same chapter warns a man about sexual unfaithfulness. Proverbs does not answer forbidden desire by declaring all desire filthy. It redirects desire toward covenant faithfulness.
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.” — Proverbs 5:18
Then comes the language of satisfaction, delight and intoxication.
Then immediately:
“Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman?”
Do you see what Scripture is doing?
It does not say, “Stop desiring.”
It essentially says:
Desire faithfully.
Desire covenantally.
Rejoice in the person to whom you have given yourself.
There is an enormous difference between lust that consumes another person and marital desire that delights in a beloved spouse.
One says, “Your body exists for my appetite.”
The other says, “You are my beloved, and I delight in the gift of belonging faithfully to one another.”
One takes.
The other gives.
One objectifies.
The other knows, cherishes, protects and remains.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that because you grew up believing holiness meant becoming almost embarrassed by the body God created.
Maybe nobody ever explained this to you.
Maybe sex was discussed only when somebody sinned.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Fornication.
Pregnancy outside marriage.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
So somewhere along the way, without anyone deliberately teaching it, you absorbed an assumption:
Sex must be dirty because Christians only talk about it when something goes wrong.
Then you got married.
And suddenly you were expected to flip a switch.
Yesterday, desire was something you were terrified of.
Today, somehow, you were supposed to understand how to receive it as a gift.
Nobody told your nervous system that marriage had happened.
Nobody explained that biblical holiness is not hatred of the body.
And maybe the shame followed you into the bedroom.
That is where this gets painfully personal.
Because there are Christian husbands who love Jesus but have never learned tenderness.
There are Christian wives who love Jesus but quietly wonder whether enjoying their husband's desire makes them less spiritual.
There are spouses who share a bed but have stopped sharing their hearts.
There are couples who can pray together in church yet cannot talk honestly about loneliness, affection, rejection, fear or intimacy.
And there are wounded people carrying experiences of coercion, betrayal, pornography, abuse, infidelity or years of emotional neglect.
So this subject cannot be handled carelessly.
Biblical marital desire is never permission for selfishness.
It is never permission for coercion.
It is never permission to weaponize Scripture against a spouse.

And 1 Corinthians 7 is particularly important here because Paul describes marital responsibility with startling mutuality. The husband has obligations toward his wife, and the wife toward her husband. Paul then deliberately mirrors his language: neither spouse is presented as an autonomous consumer of the other's body. His instruction concerning temporary abstinence explicitly includes mutual agreement.
That means biblical intimacy cannot honestly be reduced to:
“You owe me.”
Christian marriage moves toward:
“I give myself to you.”
Those sentences may sound similar to selfish ears.
They are worlds apart.
Jesus Himself gives us the pattern for Christian love—not domination, but self-giving love.
Christ does not teach His people to ask, “How much can I extract from someone who belongs to me?”
The Gospel teaches us to ask, “How can I love faithfully, sacrificially and truthfully?”
This is why marital intimacy, at its healthiest, is larger than physical release.
It becomes another language through which covenant says:
I still choose you.
I see the years on your face.
I know what childbirth did to your body.
I know what age has changed.
I know the insecurities you hide when the lights go out.
I know where you have been wounded.
I know we have argued.
I know we have disappointed each other.
And I am still here.
Still faithful.
Still learning you.
Still choosing you.
Still thankful that God entrusted your heart to my care.
There is something profoundly beautiful about that.
