Scripture's celebration of romantic love becomes even more unmistakable in the Song of Songs.

There, husband and wife—or the lovers moving toward and within covenantal union, depending on how particular passages are interpreted—speak with extraordinary delight about one another's appearance, presence, fragrance, touch and desire.
The woman is not portrayed as an emotionless object.
She speaks.
She desires.
She seeks.
She delights.
She is delighted in.
At one breathtaking moment she says:
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.” — Song of Songs 7:10
The Hebrew word for “desire” there is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.
That word is rare in the Hebrew Bible.
And here, in this poetry of love, desire is not treated as something inherently degrading. Within the biblical vision of faithful love, it can be received as something beautiful.
This is important because Christianity is not ultimately a religion teaching us that physical creation is evil.
Genesis begins somewhere very different.
God made humanity embodied.
Male and female.
And before sin corrupted anything, Scripture says God's creation was “very good.”
Sin did not invent the body.
God did.
Sin did not invent marriage.
God did.
Sin did not invent the capacity for marital union.
God did.
What sin does is twist gifts away from their Giver and their purpose.
Desire becomes lust.
Attraction becomes exploitation.
Pleasure becomes addiction.
Intimacy becomes manipulation.
Bodies become commodities.
People become images on screens.
Covenant becomes convenience.
And suddenly something created for faithful union becomes another place where human beings hide, use, betray and destroy one another.
That is the scandal.
But the Gospel never ends at the scandal.
Jesus enters the wreckage.
This is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a slogan.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He meets adulterers.
He meets the sexually broken.
He meets the ashamed.
He meets people whose histories cannot be posted publicly.
He meets people carrying memories they wish could be erased.
And Christ does not save us by pretending sin was harmless.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin was so serious that redemption cost blood.
But grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly shed His own.
Jesus did not die so we could rename bondage freedom.
He died to actually free us.
He does not merely cover scandal with religious language.
He transforms sinners.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He teaches us how to love again.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Maybe pornography followed you for years.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe you gave yourself away searching for love and discovered that being wanted is not the same thing as being cherished.
Maybe your marriage looks healthy in photographs but feels painfully distant after everyone goes home.
Maybe you cannot remember the last time your spouse looked at you with tenderness instead of exhaustion.
Maybe desire disappeared under diapers, bills, grief, arguments, medication, insecurity, work, menopause, illness, resentment or years of unresolved hurt.
This article is not telling you to fake passion.
It is telling you something more hopeful.
Your marriage does not have to be discipled by shame.
Bring the truth into the light.
Talk.
Listen.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where wounds are deep.
If there has been abuse or coercion, safety and accountability matter; biblical teaching about marriage must never be used to trap someone in harm.
And if the problem is simply that two people who once adored each other slowly became roommates...
begin again.
Not necessarily with sex.
Begin with seeing.
Put down the phone.
Ask the question you stopped asking.
Touch without demanding.
Listen without fixing.
Apologize without defending yourself.
Tell your wife she is beautiful without making it a transaction.
Tell your husband what you still admire about him before another year disappears.
Pray together even if the first prayer feels awkward.
Laugh again.
Date again.
Flirt again.
Hold hands again.
Learn one another again.
Because covenant love is not merely remembering who someone was when you married them.
It is discovering who they are becoming and choosing to love that person too.
And when marital desire grows inside that soil—trust, tenderness, safety, faithfulness, laughter, forgiveness and covenant—it need not be treated as Christianity's embarrassing relative.
Scripture does not.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
“Be captivated by her love.”
Those words are in your Bible.
Perhaps the church should stop being more embarrassed about God's design than God appears to be.
But we must also refuse the opposite error.
Our culture often treats sexual desire as sovereign.
If you desire it, pursue it.
If attraction changes, leave.
If fulfillment fades, replace the person.
If boundaries frustrate you, boundaries must be oppressive.
The Bible offers something radically different.
Desire is good.
But desire is not God.
Pleasure is good.
But pleasure is not God.
Marriage is good.
But marriage is not God.
Your spouse is precious.
But your spouse cannot be your Savior.
Every human love eventually reveals its limitations.
Bodies age.
Libido changes.
Illness comes.
Beauty changes.
Death separates.
No husband can carry the infinite weight of his wife's soul.
No wife can carry the infinite weight of her husband's soul.
There is a hunger beneath every human hunger that another human being cannot finally satisfy.
That hunger leads us to Christ.
Marriage can whisper something about covenant.
But Jesus is the Bridegroom who never breaks covenant.
Human love can say, “I choose you.”
At Calvary, Christ showed what covenant love ultimately costs.
Human spouses sometimes fail.
Jesus remains faithful.
Human beings sometimes hide when their shame is exposed.
Jesus walked toward the cross carrying ours.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
You may have a past.
Christ has grace.
You may have scars.
Christ has wounds.
You may have secrets.
Christ already knows.
You may have failed sexually, relationally, emotionally or spiritually.
Repentance does not lead you away from Jesus.
It brings you running toward the One who already knew the worst chapter and still went to the cross.
The Christian message is not:
“Good people never become scandals.”
The Christian message is:
Christ saves sinners.
He forgives the guilty.
He restores the broken.
He teaches selfish hearts how to love.
He takes what sin distorted and begins the long work of redemption.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe that is the sentence your marriage needs tonight.
Not another performance.
Not another accusation.
Not another comparison with somebody else's marriage online.
Grace.
Truth.
Repentance.
Tenderness.
Jesus.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded Christian reads at 2:00 in the morning and realizes, “I am not the only one fighting for healing.”
Not because every marriage problem can be solved by rereading a Facebook post, but because shame has a way of making us forget what is true.

Send it privately to the couple who may be struggling behind smiling photographs. Share it with the single Christian who needs to know that biblical sexual ethics are not rooted in hatred of desire, but in God's purpose for covenant, holiness and human flourishing.
We glorify God through Christ-centered obedience in every area of life.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somewhere in your circle is a husband ashamed to admit his marriage feels cold.
A wife wondering whether God cares about the loneliness beside her in bed.
A believer fighting pornography in secret.
A wounded spouse trying to believe intimacy can ever feel safe again.
A young Christian being taught by culture that biblical holiness means repression.
A married couple who desperately need to remember that covenant is worth fighting for.
And maybe they will never search for an article like this.
Maybe it has to find them through you.
Because Christianity does not teach us to worship desire.
And it does not require married believers to be ashamed of desire either.
It teaches us something far more beautiful.
Let desire bow before Christ.
Let passion live inside covenant.
Let pleasure remain a gift rather than becoming a god.
Let husbands cherish rather than consume.
Let wives be cherished rather than objectified.
Let both spouses give rather than demand.
Let repentance enter the places shame locked shut.
Let grace enter the bedroom.
Let Jesus enter the marriage.
And when He does, do not be surprised if He begins rewriting things you thought were already over.
The marriage you thought was merely surviving.
The affection you assumed had died.
The body you learned to hate.
The past you believed disqualified you.
The shame you carried into marriage.
The secret you finally confessed.
The wound that still needs time.
The love that needs rebuilding.
The sinner who needs forgiving.
The heart that needs returning home.
Maybe the most shocking thing about Proverbs 5:19 is not that the Bible tells a husband to be intoxicated with his wife's love.
Maybe the shocking thing is that the God who knows how badly humanity has distorted love still believes love is worth redeeming.
And perhaps that is what grace has been whispering through this entire story:
What sin distorted, Jesus is not afraid to enter—and what shame told you to bury, Christ may yet redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WAS LOVED LESS—AND GOD SAW EVERY SECOND OF IT
paragraphs:
SHE WAS LOVED LESS—AND GOD SAW EVERY SECOND OF IT
What Leah and Rachel Teach Us About Favoritism, Rejection, Comparison, and the God Who Refuses to Measure Your Worth by Someone Else’s Preference
There is a particular kind of pain that does not leave bruises.
No one sees it on your skin.
No one calls an ambulance.
No one knows you went home carrying it.
It is the pain of watching someone else receive what you desperately wanted.
The affection.
The attention.
The invitation.
The promotion.
The praise.
The marriage you prayed for.
The child you longed for.
The family approval you never received.
The tenderness someone seemed capable of giving everybody except you.
And sometimes the deepest wound is not that you were never loved.
It is that you were loved less.
That is where Leah’s story begins to hurt.
Genesis 29 introduces two sisters, Leah and Rachel, daughters of Laban. Rachel catches Jacob’s attention, and Jacob agrees to work seven years for the privilege of marrying her.
Scripture says those seven years “seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her” (Genesis 29:20, KJV).
It sounds romantic.
Until you remember there is another woman standing inside this story.
Leah.
Jacob works for Rachel, but Laban deceives him and gives Leah to Jacob instead. After the wedding is consummated, Jacob discovers what has happened.
Imagine being Leah.
We often read the passage concentrating on Jacob being deceived—and he certainly was.
But imagine waking up as the woman whose husband realizes that you are not the woman he wanted.
Imagine discovering that your marriage began with another woman occupying your husband’s heart.
Imagine living beside your sister while knowing that when your husband looks at her, he sees the woman he chose.
And when he looks at you...
perhaps he remembers the deception.
The Bible does not give us permission to invent Leah’s private thoughts, so we should not pretend Scripture tells us everything she felt.
But Scripture tells us enough.
Genesis 29:30 says Jacob “loved also Rachel more than Leah.”
Then comes one of the most devastating—and beautiful—sentences in the chapter:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren” (Genesis 29:31, KJV).
Look closely at the Hebrew.
The word translated “hated” is שְׂנוּאָה — senu’ah, from the Hebrew root שָׂנֵא (sane’), “to hate.”
But context matters.
Genesis has just told us that Jacob loved Rachel “more than Leah.” For that reason, many translations appropriately communicate the relational contrast with language such as “unloved.”
This does not make Leah’s suffering smaller.
It makes the tragedy more recognizable.
She was living beneath another person’s preference.
And God saw her.
That may be the sentence someone reading this desperately needs tonight.
God saw her.
Not merely the beautiful sister.
Not merely the desired sister.
Not merely the woman Jacob had worked seven years to marry.
God saw Leah.
The overlooked woman.
The less-loved wife.
The person standing in somebody else’s shadow.
God saw her.
And He sees you.

Earlier, Genesis 29:17 describes the sisters with words that have generated considerable discussion. The Hebrew says Leah’s eyes were רַכּוֹת — rakkot—a word associated with softness, tenderness, delicateness, or weakness depending on context and interpretation. Rachel, meanwhile, is described as יְפַת־תֹּאַר וִיפַת מַרְאֶה — yefat-to'ar vifat mar'eh—beautiful in form and beautiful in appearance.
We should be careful here.
Scripture does not plainly say, “Leah was ugly.”
That conclusion goes beyond the text.
The passage contrasts Leah’s eyes with Rachel’s striking physical beauty, but precisely what rakkot communicates in this verse has long been debated.
What is not debatable is what follows.
Jacob wanted Rachel.
Rachel received his greater affection.
Leah lived with the consequences.
And favoritism began poisoning the house.
That is what favoritism does.
It rarely wounds only the person who receives less.
Eventually everybody begins bleeding.
Leah wanted Jacob’s love.
Rachel wanted children.
Jacob wanted Rachel.
The sisters wanted what the other possessed.
And suddenly a family became a battlefield of longing.
Leah conceived and gave birth to Reuben.
Listen to what she says:
“Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me” (Genesis 29:32, KJV).
There it is.
The ache beneath the pregnancy.
Maybe now he will love me.
Not merely, “God gave me a son.”
But...
Maybe now I will finally be enough.
Have you ever lived like that?
Maybe if I lose the weight, they will notice me.
Maybe if I make more money, my family will respect me.
Maybe if I become successful, the person who rejected me will regret leaving.
Maybe if my ministry grows, people will finally recognize my calling.
Maybe if I become prettier...
stronger...
more spiritual...
more accomplished...
less complicated...
less emotional...
more useful...
then somebody will choose me.
Leah had a son.
But apparently the hole remained.
She conceived again.
She named him Simeon, saying:
“Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated, he hath therefore given me this son also” (Genesis 29:33, KJV).
Do you hear the progression?
First:
God has seen.
Then:
God has heard.
She has another child, Levi, and says:
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me” (Genesis 29:34, KJV).
Still reaching.
Still hoping.
Still trying to turn blessing into leverage for affection.
Three sons.
Three hopes.
Three attempts to reach a heart she could not control.
Then Judah is born.
And something changes in Leah’s words.
“This time will I praise the LORD.”
Genesis 29:35.
Not:
This time my husband will love me.
Not:
This time he will choose me.
Not:
This time I will finally beat my sister.
This time...
I will praise the LORD.
She names him Judah—יְהוּדָה, Yehudah—a name connected in the narrative with praise or thanksgiving.
Something has shifted.
Her circumstances have not magically become perfect.
Jacob has not suddenly become the husband she desperately wanted him to be.
Rachel has not disappeared.
The complicated family has not become uncomplicated.
But for this moment, Leah’s attention moves away from the man whose affection she cannot command...
toward the God who has never stopped seeing her.
And this is where her story begins pointing beyond Leah.
Because Judah matters.
Much later, Scripture identifies Jesus Christ as coming from the tribe of Judah.
Matthew’s genealogy traces the royal Messianic line through Judah.
Hebrews calls Jesus “our Lord” who “sprang out of Juda” (Hebrews 7:14, KJV).
Revelation calls Christ “the Lion of the tribe of Juda” (Revelation 5:5, KJV).
Think about that.
The woman living with the humiliation of being loved less became the mother of Judah, and through Judah’s line, according to the flesh, came the Messiah.
Jesus.
The rejected stone who became the cornerstone.
The Savior who was “despised and rejected of men” (Isaiah 53:3, KJV).
The King who entered human rejection so rejected people could be reconciled to God.
Leah could not have understood the fullness of what God was doing through her life.
She saw a household.
God was moving redemptive history.
She saw rejection.
God saw generations.
She wanted Jacob to choose her.
God was weaving her into a story that would ultimately lead to Christ.
That does not mean suffering is automatically evidence that something spectacular is about to happen.
The Bible never promises that every rejection will produce earthly success, marriage, wealth, influence, or public vindication.
Sometimes rejection simply hurts.
Sometimes people really do choose somebody else.
Sometimes families play favorites.
Sometimes parents compare their children.
Sometimes husbands and wives make devastating comparisons.
Sometimes churches celebrate visible gifts while quiet servants wonder whether anybody notices.
Sometimes social media makes another person's highlight reel feel like evidence that God forgot your address.
But Leah's story confronts one of favoritism's greatest lies:
Someone else's preference does not determine your value before God.
And Rachel’s side of the story matters too.
Because it would be easy to turn Leah into the suffering hero and Rachel into the privileged villain.
Scripture will not let us do that.
Rachel was deeply loved...
and deeply hurting.
Genesis 30:1 says that when Rachel saw she was not bearing children, she envied her sister and cried to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
The favored woman was miserable too.
That is the trap of comparison.
Leah looked at Rachel and saw what she lacked.
Rachel looked at Leah and saw what she lacked.
Leah had children and wanted Rachel’s affection from Jacob.
Rachel had Jacob’s affection and wanted Leah’s fertility.
Each woman could look across the room and think:
If I had what she has, I would finally be happy.
Does that sound familiar?
You are looking at somebody else's marriage.
They may be looking at your freedom.
You are looking at somebody else's children.
They may be carrying struggles you know nothing about.
You are looking at somebody else's body.
They may hate what they see in the mirror.
You are looking at somebody else's ministry.
They may be exhausted behind the platform.
You are looking at somebody else's money.
They may be terrified of losing everything.
You are looking at somebody else's life...
while somebody may be looking at yours.
Comparison keeps whispering:
God gave the better story to somebody else.
Favoritism reinforces the lie by ranking human beings according to preference.
But the Gospel destroys the scoreboard.
James 2 explicitly warns believers against partiality. Christians cannot confess faith in “our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory” while practicing sinful favoritism based on status and appearance.
The kingdom of Christ is not supposed to reproduce the world's obsession with ranking people.
Jesus repeatedly moved toward people society pushed toward the edges.
The unclean.
The ashamed.
The socially despised.
The morally ruined who repented.
The forgotten.
The people religious respectability would rather avoid.
And then the cross exposes something even deeper.
Before God, our greatest problem is not that somebody failed to choose us.
Our greatest problem is sin.
We have all sinned.
We have all fallen short of God's glory.
We have not merely been wounded by broken people; we ourselves are broken sinners who need reconciliation with a holy God.
That is why Jesus did not come merely to improve our self-esteem.
He came to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He died for sins.
He rose from the dead.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives something infinitely greater than winning somebody else's approval:
forgiveness.
Grace.
Reconciliation.
New life.
A new identity in Christ.
Maybe favoritism wounded you.
Maybe you were the sibling who could never compete.
Maybe Mom always defended the other child.
Maybe Dad celebrated your brother's achievements while barely noticing yours.
Maybe a pastor made you feel invisible.
Maybe your spouse compared you with somebody else.
Maybe you have spent years trying to become worthy of affection.
Or maybe this story is exposing something more uncomfortable.
Maybe you are Jacob.
Maybe you have been playing favorites.
Maybe one child gets your patience while another gets your irritation.
Maybe you treat attractive people differently.
Maybe you honor wealthy people more quickly.
Maybe you have made someone feel that they must perform to deserve tenderness from you.
Maybe there is a Leah in your life who has been quietly bleeding because of the way you distribute affection.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing sin, do not hide behind excuses.
Repent.
Favoritism is not healed by pretending nobody was hurt.
Where appropriate and safe, confess it.
Ask forgiveness.
Change how you treat people.
And receive the grace of Christ yourself.
Because Christianity is not the story of flawless people finally becoming good enough for God.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a flawless Savior.
And perhaps that is why the story of Leah and Rachel still reaches into us thousands of years later.
Because somewhere inside most human beings is a wounded sentence:
Why wasn't I enough?
But the Gospel asks a better question.
What if your life no longer had to revolve around being enough for somebody else because your hope was anchored in Christ?
Human love matters.
Rejection matters.
Favoritism can cause real damage.
Christian faith does not require pretending those wounds do not hurt.
But no human being should be forced to carry the impossible weight of becoming your savior.
Jacob could not save Leah.
Rachel's beauty could not save Rachel.
Children could not save either sister.
And getting what the other woman possessed could not heal the deepest problem of the human heart.
Only God can occupy God's place.
Only Christ saves.
Maybe you have spent years standing at the emotional doorway asking somebody to choose you.
Tonight, stop building your identity at that door.
Bring the wound to Jesus.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the rejection.
Bring Him the bitterness you have been disguising as strength.
Bring Him the resentment toward your sibling.
Bring Him the anger toward your parents.
Bring Him the secret obsession with proving everyone wrong.
Bring Him even the ugly parts you do not want Christians to know exist.
Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek wise help where wounds run deep.
And stop asking human favoritism to pronounce the final verdict over a life that belongs to God.
And if you have been the one showing favoritism, perhaps your response needs to be even simpler:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Not for performance.
Not for an algorithm.
Because confession can be the beginning of an honest conversation, and someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only person fighting this battle.

Not because every sentence will feel equally urgent tonight, but because there may come a day when rejection whispers your name again and you need to remember that another person's preference is not God's verdict.
Send it privately to the person who thinks being overlooked means being worthless.

Sharing biblical truth can be one practical way to serve others and glorify God—but never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor. Grace cannot be bought. Jesus has already paid the price His people could never pay.
Your support helps us keep putting Scripture-centered encouragement, conviction, discipleship, and Gospel truth in front of people who may desperately need it.
But remember what Leah's story leaves echoing long after Genesis 29 ends:
You may have spent years grieving because someone chose another person over you—but the hands of God can still write redemption across pages human rejection tried to ruin.
The story did not end with the unwanted bride.
Judah came.
Generations passed.
And eventually...
Jesus.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TRIBE THAT ALMOST VANISHED: THE HORROR AT GIBEAH AND THE TERRIFYING COST OF DEFENDING WHAT GOD CONDEMNS
paragraphs: THE TRIBE THAT ALMOST VANISHED: THE HORROR AT GIBEAH AND THE TERRIFYING COST OF DEFENDING WHAT GOD CONDEMNS

Benjamin survived by only a remnant. But the darkest part of the story is not merely what happened in Gibeah—it is how an entire people nearly destroyed themselves after refusing to confront evil among their own.
There are stories in the Bible that comfort you.
There are stories that strengthen you.

And then there are stories that make you close the Bible for a moment, stare into the silence, and realize just how far human beings can fall when everyone begins doing what seems right in their own eyes.
Judges 19–21 is one of those stories.

It contains sexual violence, cowardice, murder, tribal loyalty, civil war, grief, rash vows, and further exploitation of women. Scripture does not invite us to admire these events. It forces us to look at them.
And perhaps that is why this story still matters.
Because Gibeah did not collapse in a single night.
The horror exposed something that had already been rotting.
The book of Judges repeatedly gives us the diagnosis:
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
That refrain reaches its terrible conclusion in Judges 21:25.
The Hebrew is chilling:
בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Bayyamim hahem ein melekh beYisra’el; ish hayashar be‘einav ya‘aseh.
“In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
Everyone did what was obviously evil in his own eyes.
It says people did what was right in their own eyes.
That is more frightening.
Because human beings rarely need to convince themselves that evil is evil before committing it.
We rename it.
We defend it.
We justify it.
We surround ourselves with people who approve of it.
Eventually, what God calls darkness can begin looking reasonable to eyes that have become accustomed to the dark.
That is the world into which Judges 19 takes us.
A Levite was traveling with his concubine. The Hebrew word is פִּילֶגֶשׁ, pilegesh, referring to a woman in a recognized but secondary marital relationship in that ancient social setting.
Their journey eventually brought them toward Gibeah, a town belonging to Benjamin.
There is bitter irony here.
The travelers had passed near Jebus, inhabited by non-Israelites, but the Levite preferred Gibeah because it belonged to Israel.
He expected greater safety among the covenant people.
Instead, Gibeah became a nightmare.
At first, no one offered them hospitality. Eventually an elderly man took them into his home.
Then wicked men surrounded the house.
What followed is among the most horrifying episodes recorded in Scripture. The woman was subjected to brutal sexual violence and died.
We should not sanitize that.
But neither should we sensationalize her suffering.
She was not a prop for a sermon.
She was a human being.
And one disturbing feature of the narrative is precisely how people repeatedly treat women as objects to be exchanged, sacrificed, seized, or used to solve the problems created by men.
The Bible records these actions.
Recording is not approving.
That distinction is essential when reading Judges.
Much of Judges is showing us what humanity looks like when covenant faithfulness collapses.
After the woman's death, the Levite performed an appalling act: he divided her body and sent the pieces throughout Israel, provoking national outrage.
Israel assembled.
The crime at Gibeah had become impossible to ignore.
And then comes the moment where the tragedy could have taken another direction.
Israel demanded that Benjamin surrender the perpetrators.
Benjamin refused.
Read that slowly.
The entire tribe was not originally accused of personally committing the atrocity.
Men of Gibeah were.
But when accountability came knocking, Benjamin rallied around Gibeah instead of handing over the guilty men.
That decision transformed a local atrocity into a national catastrophe.
There is a warning here that reaches painfully beyond ancient Israel.
You do not have to commit another person's sin to become entangled in it.
Sometimes you only have to decide that protecting “our people” matters more than confronting what is wrong.
Family can do this.
Churches can do this.
Friend groups can do this.
Ministries can do this.
Communities can do this.
Someone hurts people, and suddenly the first question becomes not, “What is true?”
but...
“How do we protect our reputation?”
Someone sins, and instead of bringing darkness into the light, everyone starts calculating what exposure might cost.
Someone with influence is confronted, and people defend the person because admitting the truth feels like betraying the group.
Benjamin's tragedy warns us what tribal loyalty becomes when loyalty separates itself from righteousness.
There are moments when protecting someone from legitimate accountability is not love.
It is participation in the darkness that is destroying them.
Benjamin gathered for war.
Judges 20 describes twenty-six thousand Benjaminite swordsmen from the towns, together with seven hundred selected men from Gibeah.
Among them were seven hundred elite left-handed warriors, extraordinarily skilled with the sling.
Benjamin was small.
Benjamin was dangerous.
Benjamin was confident.
And initially Benjamin won.
Israel lost twenty-two thousand men in the first battle.
Then another eighteen thousand in the second.
Think about that.
Forty thousand Israelites fell before Benjamin's decisive defeat.
This is not a simplistic story in which one side is presented as morally spotless and effortlessly destroys the villains.
Judges will not give us that comfort.
The entire nation is bleeding.
Israel weeps.
They fast.
They offer sacrifices.
They inquire of the LORD.
And on the third engagement, the battle turns.
Benjamin is devastated.
Judges 20:46 says approximately twenty-five thousand Benjaminite fighting men fell that day.
Then comes one of the most haunting images in the story.
Six hundred men escape to the rock of Rimmon.
Six hundred.
A tribe that had entered battle with tens of thousands of warriors is reduced to a tiny surviving male remnant.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine those men sitting among the rocks.
No cheering.
No military pride.
No swagger.
Just survivors.
Behind them were dead brothers, devastated cities, destroyed families, and a tribe standing frighteningly close to disappearance.
All because sin had spread farther than anyone imagined it would.
That is one of sin's oldest lies.
“This will stay here.”
It almost never does.
The hidden affair does not stay inside the hotel room.
The addiction does not remain behind the locked screen.
The bitterness does not stay inside the heart.
The lie does not remain one sentence.
The secret does not remain one secret.
The compromise does not remain one compromise.
Sin grows roots.
Then branches.
Then fruit.
Then somebody who never planted the original seed ends up eating the harvest.
Perhaps that is why this story feels uncomfortably modern.
We are remarkably skilled at condemning Gibeah while hiding our own rooms.
We can become furious about another person's corruption while negotiating with our own.
We can demand repentance publicly while avoiding it privately.
We can quote Scripture about someone else's darkness and then quickly swipe past the verse that exposes ours.
And Jesus will not allow us to live forever behind that mask.
Christ does not merely expose the obvious sinner.
He exposes the religious pretender.
The respectable hypocrite.
The person who knows Christian vocabulary but has learned to protect the very thing God keeps asking them to surrender.
Maybe your Gibeah is not something anyone can see.
Maybe it is resentment.
Pornography.
An affair.
Dishonesty.
Secret messages.
Pride.
Greed.
Unforgiveness.
A double life.
A habit you keep promising God you will stop.
A wound that has hardened into hatred.
Maybe nobody knows.
But you know.
And God knows.
This is where the story must become personal.
Not because Benjamin's historical judgment can simply be mapped one-for-one onto every private struggle. It cannot.
But because the spiritual principle remains terrifyingly clear throughout Scripture:
Sin should never be protected merely because it belongs to us.
Jesus said:
“For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved.”
But He continued:
“He that doeth truth cometh to the light.”
That is John 3:20–21.
And this is where Gibeah begins pointing us beyond Gibeah.
Toward Christ.
Because if this story ended with human beings receiving everything their sins deserved, none of us could read it comfortably.
Romans declares:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον
pantes gar hēmarton.
“For all have sinned.”
Not Benjamin alone.
Not Gibeah alone.
Not the person whose secret scandal became public.
All.
You.
Me.
Every human heart eventually arrives at the same courtroom.
And the Gospel does not announce that our sin was insignificant.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Our sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross...
and His grace is so astonishing that He went willingly.
At Calvary, God did not pretend evil was harmless.
Jesus bore judgment.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.”
Christian grace is not God shrugging at Gibeah.

Grace is God dealing with sin so seriously that the Son of God bears the curse for sinners—and dealing with sinners so mercifully that everyone who comes to Christ in repentance and faith can be forgiven.
This is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is coming home.
It is opening the locked room.
It is dropping the defense.
It is finally saying:
“Jesus, I cannot keep protecting the thing that is killing me.”
And maybe someone reading this has spent years believing that their scandal has already written the final chapter.
Listen carefully.
Benjamin nearly disappeared.
But Benjamin did not disappear.
The tribe survived.
Generations passed.
And Scripture gives us an extraordinary detail.
Centuries later, another Benjaminite walked onto the pages of the New Testament.
His name was Saul.
He was fiercely zealous.
He persecuted Christians.
He participated in the violent suppression of the early church.
Then Jesus Christ met him.
And Saul of Tarsus eventually wrote:
“I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”
Benjamin.
The tribe nearly extinguished in Judges.
The tribe stained by Gibeah.
The tribe reduced to six hundred surviving men.
And centuries later, from Benjamin comes the apostle Paul—the man whose letters would proclaim the grace of Jesus Christ across nations and generations.
Do you see it?
Gibeah was not Benjamin's final sentence.
Failure was not the final word.
Scandal was not the final chapter.
Grace kept writing.
That does not make the horror insignificant.
Grace never requires us to call evil good.
The Gospel does something greater.
It tells the truth about evil...
and then demonstrates that Jesus Christ is capable of redeeming people whose history would make redemption seem impossible.
Paul himself became living evidence.
The persecutor became the preacher.
The destroyer became the disciple.
The man who once dragged believers away became the man willing to suffer so others could know Christ.
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending your past never happened.
Not rewriting history so you look innocent.
Not hiding Gibeah.
Jesus does something far more beautiful.
He takes guilty, ruined, repentant people and gives them a future their past could never have produced.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
What am I defending that God is asking me to surrender?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has already brought something to mind.
Do not protect it.
Bring it into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Where you have wronged someone, pursue repentance and appropriate restitution rather than hiding behind religious words.
Where you need mature pastoral help or professional help, seek it.
Where another person is being harmed or abused, protecting the victim and pursuing appropriate accountability is not betrayal.
And if shame is whispering that Jesus would never receive someone like you, remember the cross.
Christ did not die for imaginary sinners.
He died for real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People with consequences.
People who finally stop running and come to Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise does not belong to people who successfully hid everything.
It belongs to people who come into the light.
If this exposed something you have been protecting, you do not need to tell strangers the details. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus is still changing lives.
Do not let this article disappear into another scroll.

Return to Judges 19–21 yourself. Read the uncomfortable chapters. Wrestle with them. Let Scripture correct you where you have unconsciously confused God's description of human wickedness with His approval of it.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
Salvation is by grace.

But if this ministry is helping proclaim Christ, teach Scripture, call people toward repentance, and put biblical resources into people's hands, supporting that work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in the Gospel.
If you want to glorify God through what you share online, let your timeline carry something that points beyond outrage and toward Jesus.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but whom you know is hurting.
It is support for the ministry and an invitation into deeper discipleship, biblical nourishment, accountability, spiritual sharpening, and Christ-centered resources.
If this ministry has helped you, supporting it allows Gospel-centered material to keep reaching people who may be sitting alone tonight with a Bible, a secret, and one desperate question:
“Can Jesus still do something with my life?”
Yes.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves that it does.
And not because we deserve another chapter.
Because Christ is merciful.
Benjamin once sat among the rocks with only six hundred surviving men.
Yet Benjamin's story continued.
And centuries later, a son of Benjamin would write words that sound almost impossible after reading Judges:
“Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.”
That does not mean grace makes peace with sin.
It means sin does not get the final word over the person who belongs to Jesus Christ.
So bring Him the chapter you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the consequences.
Bring Him the shattered pieces.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Trust Christ.
And discover what the Gospel has been declaring all along:
The place where your story became scandal does not have to be the place where your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Before Delilah, There Was a Nameless Woman in Gaza — And Samson Walked Out Carrying the Gates
paragraphs:
Before Delilah, There Was a Nameless Woman in Gaza — And Samson Walked Out Carrying the Gates
Everyone remembers Delilah. Almost nobody remembers the unnamed prostitute who appears just verses before her—and the terrifying night in Gaza that showed how a man could carry a city’s gates on his shoulders while still being unable to master the desires inside his own heart.
There is something unsettling about the way Scripture tells the truth.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not protect their reputations.
It does not quietly remove the chapters that would make religious people uncomfortable.
And Samson’s story is one of the clearest examples.
Long before Delilah became the name almost everyone associates with his downfall, Scripture takes us into Gaza.
Not into a synagogue.
Not onto a battlefield.
Not into a moment of glorious worship.
Into Gaza.
And into the presence of a prostitute.
Judges 16:1 says:
“Then went Samson to Gaza, and saw there an harlot, and went in unto her.”
The Hebrew is painfully direct:
וַיֵּלֶךְ שִׁמְשׁוֹן עַזָּתָה וַיַּרְא־שָׁם אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה וַיָּבֹא אֵלֶיהָ
Vayyelekh Shimshon ‘Azzatah, vayar-sham ishah zonah, vayavo eleha.
Samson went to Gaza. He saw there an אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishah zonah, a woman who was a prostitute, and he went in to her.
No name is given.
No romantic explanation is offered.
No excuse is inserted.
And we should not invent one.

The Bible does not tell us that this woman rescued Samson. It does not say she betrayed him. It does not say she converted, repented, believed, or became his ally. Scripture simply places her inside the scene immediately before the men of Gaza surround the place, wait at the city gate, and plan to kill Samson in the morning.
That silence matters.
Because sometimes what Scripture refuses to embellish is as important as what it reveals.
Samson had been set apart before birth.

Judges 13 records the angelic announcement concerning him. His mother was told that the child would be a Nazirite to God from the womb and that he would begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.
Think about the contradiction.
A man consecrated before birth…
walking into Gaza looking at a prostitute.
A man empowered by the Spirit of the LORD…
repeatedly moving toward desires capable of destroying him.
A man strong enough to tear a lion apart…
yet increasingly vulnerable to what his eyes wanted.
Maybe that contradiction is why his story still feels frighteningly modern.
Because some of us know what it is to love God and still walk toward something we know can wound us.
We know what it is to have been used by God and still have secret places.
We know what it is to carry Scripture in our mouths while carrying temptation in our phones.
To worship publicly and struggle privately.
To encourage everyone else while quietly returning to the thing we promised God we were finished with.
That is what makes Samson uncomfortable.
He destroys the illusion that gifting automatically equals maturity.
Strength is not the same thing as holiness.
Calling is not the same thing as character.
Being used by God does not mean every decision you are making is approved by God.
And surviving the consequences of one dangerous decision does not mean you have permission to repeat it.
That last truth may be the one somebody reading this desperately needs.
Because Samson survived Gaza.
And surviving Gaza may have made Delilah seem less dangerous.
The Gazites learned that Samson was there.
Judges 16 says they surrounded him and waited all night at the gate of the city. Their plan was simple:
Wait until morning.
Then kill him.
Imagine the scene.
Dark streets.
Closed gates.
Armed men waiting.
Samson apparently trapped inside enemy territory.
The city believed morning would bring his death.
But midnight came first.

Scripture says Samson arose around midnight, seized the doors of the city gate along with the two posts, pulled them up—bar and all—put them on his shoulders, and carried them away toward the hill facing Hebron.
Read that slowly.
He did not merely open the gate.
He took it.
The very structure meant to keep him trapped became something he carried away on his shoulders.
What an image.
His enemies were waiting for daylight to kill him, and before daylight arrived, the entrance they trusted to contain him was gone.
Yet this is where we must resist turning Samson into something Scripture does not.
This is not ultimately a motivational story about discovering the “Samson inside you.”
The Bible is not telling us that if we believe strongly enough, we can rip the gates off whatever city has trapped us.
Samson’s extraordinary strength belonged to his unique calling within Israel’s history, and Judges repeatedly identifies the LORD as the true source behind his empowerment.
And even Samson’s spectacular escape does not turn his sexual choices into righteousness.
Deliverance is not endorsement.
Mercy is not permission.
Escape is not innocence.
Sometimes God is merciful to us in circumstances where we were foolish enough to put ourselves.
And one of the most dangerous things we can do afterward is confuse His mercy with His approval.
Maybe you survived something that should have broken you.
Maybe nobody discovered what you were doing.
Maybe the relationship ended before everything collapsed.
Maybe the addiction has not yet cost you your marriage.
Maybe the secret has not become public.
Maybe you walked away from the wreckage thinking, “I got away with it.”
Samson walked away from Gaza too.
But his story was not finished.
Judges 16:4 begins with words that should make anyone who knows the ending tremble:
“Afterward it came to pass, that he loved a woman in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.”
Afterward.
That word carries enormous weight.
After Gaza.
After the prostitute.
After the ambush.
After the gates.
After another escape.
Delilah entered the narrative.
This time Scripture gives us her name.
And eventually the man who could not be held behind Gaza’s gates would be bound.
His hair would be shaved.
His strength would leave him.
His eyes would be gouged out.
The man who had spent so much of his story seeing what he wanted would eventually lose his sight.
Judges 16:21 says the Philistines seized him, put out his eyes, brought him down to Gaza, bound him with bronze shackles, and forced him to grind grain in prison.
Back to Gaza.
Do you see the terrible circle?
Earlier, Samson walked into Gaza by his own choice and walked out carrying its gates.
Later, Samson was dragged into Gaza blind and bound.
The city he once escaped became the city of his humiliation.
That should destroy the casual way we sometimes speak about recurring sin.
Sin does not always collect its entire payment the first time.
Sometimes there is an interval.
Sometimes you escape.
Sometimes you still feel strong.
Sometimes you still preach.
Still sing.
Still work.
Still laugh.
Still post Bible verses.
Still serve.
Still look completely fine.
And because nothing immediately collapsed, you begin believing the thing you are entertaining cannot destroy you.
But Scripture warns:
“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” — Galatians 6:7
The terrifying lesson of Samson is not merely that strong people can fall.
It is that repeated compromise can make a strong person increasingly blind long before anyone physically removes his eyes.
But if Samson’s story ended with blindness, chains, humiliation, and failure, it would only be tragedy.
Scripture gives us something else.
Judges 16:22 contains one of the quietest sentences in the chapter:
“Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven.”
His hair…
began…
to grow…
again.

That verse is not teaching that Samson’s hair itself possessed magical power. The narrative has already shown that his strength ultimately depended upon God, while his uncut hair belonged to the Nazirite sign associated with his consecration.
But the image is almost unbearably powerful.
The Philistines could shave his head.
They could destroy his eyes.
They could put chains on his wrists.
They could laugh at the fallen judge.
But while they were celebrating what they believed was the end of Samson…
something was growing again.
And this is where Samson’s broken story begins pointing beyond Samson.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that strong people can repair themselves.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Samson carried the gates of Gaza on his shoulders.
Jesus Christ carried a cross.
Samson escaped death that night.
Jesus willingly went into death.
Samson’s enemies planned to kill him and failed in Gaza.
Christ’s enemies crucified Him outside Jerusalem—but His death became the very means through which God accomplished redemption.
And then the grave itself could not hold Him.
This is the center.
Not Samson.
Not his strength.
Not Gaza.
Not Delilah.
Jesus.
The Gospel does not say, “Become strong enough that you never need mercy.”
The Gospel says you were never strong enough to save yourself.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were sinners.
Not after we repaired our image.
Not after we defeated every addiction.
Not after we became impressive Christians.
Not after we successfully hid the scandal.
Christ died for sinners.
That is why grace is so offensive to pride and so beautiful to the broken.
Grace does not pretend sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we often understand.
But the cross also proves that the mercy of God reaches further than our self-righteousness ever could.
Repentance, then, is not cosmetic religious embarrassment.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia carries the sense of repentance, a turning of mind and direction toward God.
Jesus did not come merely to make you feel less guilty while you continue walking toward the same destruction.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Reconcile.
Transform.
And call you to follow Him.
Perhaps your Gaza has a different name.
Nobody else may know it.
A conversation you keep deleting.
A browser history you keep clearing.
A relationship you keep rationalizing.
A resentment you secretly feed.
A substance you keep returning to.
A hunger for attention.
Pornography.
Pride.
Greed.
Bitterness.
Sexual compromise.
Secret dishonesty.
A double life.
Maybe you have carried the gates away so many times that you have convinced yourself nothing can trap you.
Please hear the warning inside Samson’s story:
Do not mistake another escape for proof that your chains are harmless.
But also hear the Gospel:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Samson eventually prayed.
“Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once…” — Judges 16:28
There is heartbreak in that prayer.
The swagger is gone.
The eyes are gone.
The illusion of invincibility is gone.
A broken man calls upon God.
Hebrews 11 later does something astonishing.
When recounting people associated with faith, Hebrews 11:32 actually names Samson.
Samson.
The compromised judge.
The reckless man.
The fallen strongman.
Samson appears in Scripture’s testimony concerning faith.
Not because his sins suddenly became virtues.
Not because Scripture rewrote evil into good.
But because failure did not erase the reality that God was still sovereignly working through this deeply flawed man.
And that is precisely why we must understand our theme correctly:
From Scandal to Grace does not mean God calls the scandal good.
It means grace can write beyond the scandal.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending your past never happened.
He rewrites everything by giving repentant sinners something their past could never manufacture:
forgiveness.
A new identity.
A new direction.
A new Master.
A new heart.
A future anchored not in personal perfection but in His finished work.
Maybe you came into this article fascinated by a prostitute in Gaza.
But perhaps the person God wanted you to notice was you.
The unnamed woman is there.
Samson is there.
The assassins are there.
The gates are there.
Delilah is coming.
But behind the entire broken landscape stands the uncomfortable reality of human sin and the astonishing patience of God.
So do not leave this story merely saying, “Samson should have known better.”
Ask the harder question.
Where should I know better?
What am I calling harmless because judgment has not arrived?
What am I calling freedom simply because I have escaped consequences so far?
What relationship with sin am I protecting that Christ is calling me to surrender?

And if that question exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to confess your private details publicly. Bring them honestly before God. Seek trusted, biblically mature help where needed. But you can make one simple declaration here:
Not for performance.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
Salvation is found in Christ, not in a comment section.
But sometimes a small public acknowledgment can become the moment somebody stops pretending there is no battle.
And somebody else reading your words may realize they are not the only Christian still fighting.
We glorify God through lives of faith, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and worship in Christ.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach further.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior. Send it to the believer who is exhausted from fighting.
But never confuse the library with the Treasure.
The Treasure is Christ.
Never confuse Christian content with Christ.
Never confuse engagement with repentance.
And never confuse surviving Gaza with being safe from Delilah.
Samson once walked out of Gaza carrying gates.
Later he returned blind and chained.
Yet even there, in the wreckage of everything his compromises had cost him, his story had not slipped beyond the sovereignty of God.
So if you are reading this with your own wreckage behind you, do not run farther into darkness.
Run to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the forgiveness purchased through His blood.
And follow the One who does something Samson could never do for himself—and something you cannot do for yourself either.
Jesus saves sinners.
Jesus restores what sin has devastated according to His wisdom and grace.
Jesus gives new life.
Jesus makes captives free.
And when Jesus becomes the center of the story, your scandal no longer gets the privilege of writing the final sentence.
The gates you once escaped may warn you about where you have been—but the scars of Christ tell you Who can bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE FRUITFUL AND MULTIPLY”: Was Sex Part of God’s Design BEFORE Sin Entered the World?
paragraphs: “BE FRUITFUL AND MULTIPLY”: Was Sex Part of God’s Design BEFORE Sin Entered the World?

Before there was lust, adultery, pornography, shame, abuse, or a single broken marriage, there was a man, a woman, a garden—and a command from God that forces us to rethink what we were taught about sex.
There is something almost shocking about the timing.
Not because God said it.
Because of when He said it.
No serpent had whispered yet.
No forbidden fruit had been eaten.
No human being had ever lusted.
No marriage had ever been betrayed.
No body had ever been exploited.
No one had hidden behind a screen.
No one had awakened with regret.
No one had whispered, “What have I done?”
There was no sexual shame because there was no sin.
And into that untouched world, God created humanity male and female, blessed them, and spoke these words:
“Be fruitful, and multiply.”
The Hebrew of Genesis 1:28 begins:
פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ — pərû ûrəḇû
“Be fruitful and multiply.”
Read that again.
This command did not come after Genesis 3.
It came before it.
Before shame.
Before the curse.
Before humanity fell.
And that means we need to confront a misconception that has quietly wounded generations of Christians:
Sex did not enter the human story because sin entered the human story.
Sexual sin did.
Lust did.
Exploitation did.
Adultery did.
Sexual violence did.
Pornography did.
The twisting of desire did.
But the male-and-female reality from which marital union and human reproduction arise?
That appears on the pages of Scripture while creation is still unfallen.
Genesis 1:27 says:
וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ... זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha’adam betsalmo... zakhar uneqevah bara otam.
In straightforward English:
God created humankind in His image... male and female He created them.
Then comes the blessing.
Then comes the command.
פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ
Be fruitful.
Multiply.
Fill the earth.
Genesis is not embarrassed by the human body.
God created it.
Genesis is not embarrassed that humanity exists as male and female.
God designed humanity that way.
And Genesis certainly does not introduce reproduction as some unfortunate emergency measure God invented after Adam sinned.
The command to multiply was already there.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because some believers have unconsciously inherited the idea that holiness means pretending sexuality itself is dirty.
It does not.
Biblical holiness does not require us to call God's creation evil.
It requires us to distinguish God's creation from what sin has done to it.
And those are two very different things.
Perhaps you know the confusion personally.
Maybe nobody ever gave you a biblical theology of sexuality.
Maybe you were only told what not to do.
Don't look.
Don't touch.
Don't think about it.
Don't talk about it.
And certainly don't ask questions.
So somewhere along the way, you began confusing temptation with embodiment.
You began feeling guilty merely for experiencing desire.
Or perhaps your story went the opposite direction.
Maybe culture told you desire itself is sovereign—that whatever the body wants, the body should receive.
One voice taught you to fear the body.
Another taught you to worship it.
Scripture does neither.
Scripture says the body has a Creator.
And therefore our bodies have meaning.
But we have to be careful here, because biblical faithfulness requires us to say both what Genesis says and what Genesis does not say.
Genesis never gives us a sentence reading, “Adam and Eve had sexual intercourse before the Fall.”
That event is not explicitly narrated.
So we should not manufacture a verse God did not give us.
But the question, “Was sexual union part of God's design before sin?” is different from the question, “Does Genesis explicitly tell us Adam and Eve had intercourse before sin?”
The first can be answered from the creation account.
The second cannot be established from an explicit narrated event.
And that distinction protects us from sensationalism while allowing Scripture to speak with extraordinary clarity.
Because Genesis 2 takes us deeper.
God says:
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
Notice the words.
For chapter after chapter, creation has been called good.
Light—good.
Land and sea—good.
Vegetation—good.
Sun, moon, and stars—good.
Living creatures—good.
Then suddenly:
Not good.
The man is alone.
God forms the woman.
Adam sees her.
And Scripture gives us something astonishing:
“This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.”
Then Genesis gives the theological explanation:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Al-ken ya‘azav-ish et-aviv ve’et-immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
A man leaves his father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and they become:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
One flesh.
And where are we?
Still before the serpent.
Still before the fruit.
Still before the Fall.
Still before shame.
Marriage is not God's repair job after sin.
It is there in Eden.
One-flesh union is not introduced as punishment.
It is there before judgment.
And the next verse may be one of the most tender descriptions of unfallen human intimacy ever written:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25.
Naked.
And not ashamed.
Then Genesis 3 happens.
And suddenly the same human beings hide.
That contrast is devastating.
Before sin:
Naked and unashamed.
After sin:
Afraid and hiding.
Maybe that is where this stops being an ancient theological discussion and starts becoming your story.
Because some of us are still hiding.
Different garden.
Different leaves.
Same instinct.
We hide browser histories.
We hide addictions.
We hide affairs.
We hide fantasies.
We hide wounds.
We hide what someone did to us.
We hide what we did to someone else.
We hide dissatisfaction inside marriages that look perfect in photographs.
We hide years of sexual shame beneath church clothes and worship songs.
We know how to lift our hands on Sunday while carrying secrets we pray nobody ever discovers.
And suddenly Genesis does not feel ancient anymore.
Because sin still makes people hide.
But here is what we must understand:
The enemy did not create sexuality. He corrupts what God created.
That pattern runs throughout Scripture.
Food is good.
Gluttony distorts it.
Rest is good.
Laziness distorts it.
Authority can serve good purposes.
Abuse corrupts it.
Money can accomplish good.
Greed enslaves through it.
Sexual union within God's covenant design is not made sinful simply because sinners have horribly distorted sexuality.
The distortion does not define the design.
Go back before the distortion.
Go back to Eden.
Male and female.
Blessing.
Fruitfulness.
Marriage.
One flesh.
Naked and unashamed.
And then listen to the verdict of Genesis 1:31:
God saw what He had made, and it was very good.
Not barely acceptable.
Not spiritually suspicious.
Very good.
Centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something enormously important.
He pointed backward.
Back beyond Moses' concessions to fallen human hardness.
Back beyond Israel.
Back beyond Abraham.
Back to creation.

Jesus said that the Creator made them “male and female” from the beginning and then appealed to Genesis 2:24: a man leaves father and mother, is joined to his wife, and the two become one flesh. Then Christ concludes that what God has joined together should not be separated.
Jesus treated Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 as foundational for understanding marriage.
Think about what that means.
When Christ explained marriage, He pointed toward Eden.
He did not treat embodied marital union as an embarrassing relic of humanity's fall.
He grounded marriage in the Creator's intention “from the beginning.”

And the apostle Paul later speaks with striking mutuality about marital intimacy: husband and wife each owe marital faithfulness to the other, and neither is given unilateral permission to use intimacy selfishly or weaponize deprivation. His language places obligations on both spouses.
Biblical sexuality, therefore, cannot rightly be reduced to appetite.
It involves covenant.
Faithfulness.
Mutual responsibility.
Love.
Embodiment.
And, in Genesis, the extraordinary calling of participating in the multiplication of human life.
That does not mean every sexual act produces children.
It does not mean a marriage without children is somehow counterfeit.
It does not mean infertile couples have failed God's purpose.
And it certainly does not mean every Christian must marry.
The New Testament explicitly recognizes singleness as a genuine gift and calling. Paul himself speaks of different gifts from God in this very context.
So “be fruitful and multiply” must never become a weapon against the infertile, the unmarried, the widowed, or those carrying private grief around children they desperately wanted but never received.
God sees those tears too.
But none of those pastoral qualifications change the startling reality of Genesis:
Human sexuality did not originate in the Fall.
Its corruption did.
And perhaps that changes how we understand redemption.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel less guilty.
He came to save sinners.
To reconcile rebels to God.
To forgive what we cannot undo.
To cleanse what we cannot cleanse ourselves.
To bring what has been dragged through darkness into His light.
Maybe sexuality is where your deepest shame lives.
Maybe you crossed lines you swore you never would.
Maybe pornography trained your imagination before Scripture ever shaped it.
Maybe someone treated your body as though it existed for their gratification.
Maybe you entered marriage carrying wounds you never knew how to explain.
Maybe you were unfaithful.
Maybe someone was unfaithful to you.
Maybe your marriage feels cold.
Maybe your secret life looks nothing like the person everyone sees at church.
Maybe you have spent years thinking:
If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.
Perhaps.
But Jesus already knows.
That is the terrifying part.
And the beautiful part.
You do not shock the One who went willingly to a cross for sinners.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation cost the blood of Christ.
Yet grace is so astonishing that the sinner who comes to Christ in repentance and faith is not told to clean himself first and return later.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
The answer to sexual brokenness is neither pretending sexuality is evil nor pretending sexual sin does not matter.
The answer is redemption.
The answer is Jesus.
Because Christ does something shame cannot do.
Shame tells you:
Hide.
Jesus calls you:
Come.
Shame says:
You are only the worst thing you have ever done.
The Gospel says that in Christ there is forgiveness, cleansing, adoption, sanctification, and a new identity that sin does not have the authority to write.
Shame whispers:
If God really knew...
The cross answers:
He knew.
And He came anyway.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace opens the prison door.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace does not rename darkness so we can comfortably remain inside it.
Grace takes us by the hand and leads us toward the light.
That is why the story begins in a garden where humanity was naked without shame...
and the biblical story eventually leads us to Christ, publicly stripped and crucified while bearing the shame of sinners.
Do not miss the terrible beauty of that.
Human beings sinned and covered themselves.
Christ came and allowed Himself to be stripped.
Human beings hid among trees.
Christ was nailed to a tree.
Human beings ran from God.
The Son of God came searching for the lost.
This is bigger than a debate about sex.
This is the Gospel.
Maybe you began reading because the title made you curious.
Maybe you expected an argument.
But perhaps somewhere between Eden and the cross, the question changed.
It is no longer merely:
“Was sex part of God's design before sin?”
Perhaps now the question is:
“What has sin done to me—and will Jesus still receive me?”
Yes.
But He loves you too much to leave you hiding.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the marriage that feels like it is dying.
Bring Him the memories you cannot erase.
Bring Him the part of your story you carefully omitted when everyone else heard your testimony.
Not because merely naming these things magically fixes them.
But because repentance begins by coming out of hiding and turning toward God.

And where another person's sin has wounded you, hear this carefully: being sinned against is not the same thing as committing that sin. Another person's abuse or exploitation of you does not make you morally guilty for what they chose to do.
Christ receives wounded people too.
The Garden teaches us what humanity was created for.
The Fall shows us what sin has done.
The cross shows us what our rescue cost.
And the resurrection announces that sin and death do not get the final sentence.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Not scandal celebrated.
Not scandal hidden.
Not scandal excused.
Scandal brought into the light...
met by truth...
called to repentance...
and carried to the feet of Jesus.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly.
Someone reading the comments may realize for the first time that they are not the only believer fighting a battle nobody sees.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because someone in your circle may be silently carrying shame.
Someone may have confused God's design with sin's distortion.
Someone may believe they are too dirty for Jesus.
Someone may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from finally coming out of hiding.
Give willingly.
Support willingly.
Share willingly.
As Scripture teaches, Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted reluctantly or under compulsion.
Let them encounter Scripture.
Let them wrestle with truth.
Let them hear about repentance.
Let them discover grace.
Let them meet Jesus.
Because this entire conversation ultimately comes back to something far greater than sexuality.
We were made by God.
Sin distorted us.
We cannot redeem ourselves.
Christ came for sinners.
He died.
He rose.
He forgives.
He restores.
And He is still calling hiding people out from behind their leaves.
Adam and Eve discovered shame and hid.
Maybe you have been hiding too.
But the Gospel leaves us with a truth worth carrying long after this article disappears from your screen:
The sin that taught you to hide does not have to write the final chapter of the life you surrender to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “NEITHER DO I CONDEMN YOU” WAS NEVER JESUS SAYING, “KEEP LIVING THIS WAY”
paragraphs:
“NEITHER DO I CONDEMN YOU” WAS NEVER JESUS SAYING, “KEEP LIVING THIS WAY”
We love the sentence that removes the shame. But Jesus did not stop speaking there. The same Savior who refused to crush the woman caught in adultery looked at her with mercy and said the words our generation desperately needs to hear again: “Go, and sin no more.”
There is a version of Jesus many people are comfortable with.
He forgives.
He welcomes.
He refuses to throw the stone.
He sits with sinners.
He gives another chance.
And every one of those things is beautifully true.
But sometimes we stop the story exactly where it stops confronting us.
We quote:
“Neither do I condemn you.”
Then quietly close the Bible before Jesus finishes the sentence.
Because what comes next is harder.
What comes next reaches into the secret relationship.
The hidden browser history.
The bitterness nobody knows about.
The addiction we renamed a “struggle” years ago because calling it sin became too uncomfortable.
The compromise we keep asking God to forgive while making plans to return to it.
The private life that looks nothing like the Christian identity displayed publicly.
Jesus looked at the woman standing before Him and said:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” — John 8:11
In Greek:
Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.
Oude egō se katakrinō; poreuou, kai apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
“Neither do I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because there are two cliffs here, and Jesus refuses to let us fall from either one.
Neither do I condemn you.
And:
Sin no more.
Grace.
And transformation.
Mercy.
And repentance.
Forgiveness.
And a changed direction.
Jesus does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
He does not say, “What you did was actually fine.”
He does not redefine adultery so the woman can remain comfortable.
But neither does He become another executioner standing over a humiliated sinner.
That is what makes this scene so devastatingly beautiful.
She is standing in the place where her worst moment has become public.
Imagine that.
Not your Sunday clothes.
Not your favorite Bible verse.
Not the version of yourself everybody respects.
Imagine being dragged into public view by the thing you hoped nobody would ever discover.
The accusation was adultery.
The shame was public.
Her accusers were ready.
And according to John, they were using her as part of a trap against Jesus.
“This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him.” — John 8:6
She was not merely a person to them anymore.
She had become evidence.
A theological trap.
A scandal with a heartbeat.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows what that feels like.
Maybe nobody dragged you physically through the street.
But somebody found out.
The marriage collapsed.
The screenshots surfaced.
The addiction was discovered.
The secret debt became impossible to hide.
The affair came into the light.
The child learned what happened.
The church found out.
Your spouse found out.
Your parents found out.
Or perhaps nobody knows.
And that is almost worse.
Because every Sunday you carry your own courtroom inside your chest.
You worship while remembering.
You smile while remembering.
You tell people, “God is good,” while another voice whispers:
“If they knew who you really were…”
Maybe that is why these words of Jesus have survived inside so many wounded hearts:
“Neither do I condemn you.”
The Greek verb translated “condemn” is κατακρίνω — katakrinō, carrying the sense of condemning or pronouncing judgment against.
But notice something crucial.
Jesus' refusal to condemn her does not become permission to continue destroying herself.
Mercy speaks first.
Then mercy tells her where to walk.
πορεύου — poreuou.
Go.
Move forward.
Do not build your home in this moment.
Do not make your failure your permanent address.
And then:
μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε — mēketi hamartane.
Sin no more.
The word μηκέτι — mēketi means “no longer,” “no more.”
Jesus is not merely rescuing her from something.
He is calling her toward something.
A different life.
That is the Gospel pattern we desperately need to recover.
Jesus does not save us because we successfully cleaned ourselves up before approaching Him.
But the Jesus who saves us does not call us to make peace with the chains from which He came to deliver us.
Grace is not God pretending sin is harmless.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And this is where Christianity becomes either breathtakingly beautiful or unbearably offensive.
Because the Gospel tells us two things about ourselves that human pride struggles to hold simultaneously.
Our sin is worse than we want to admit.
And God's grace is greater than we dared to hope.
At the cross, God did not shrug at evil.
Sin was treated with such seriousness that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
Yet sinners were loved with such astonishing mercy that Christ willingly gave Himself for them.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Romans 5:6
Not the impressive.
Not the cleaned-up.
Not people who finally became worthy.
The ungodly.
Romans 5:8 presses the truth even deeper:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
There is grace.
But Paul refuses to let anyone twist that grace into permission to remain enslaved.
He anticipates the argument in Romans 6:
“What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?”
And his answer is explosive:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
“By no means!”
Absolutely not.
Grace does not mean sin became acceptable.
Grace means the sinner can finally come home.
This distinction matters because some Christians have been crushed by condemnation while others have become comfortable with compromise.
Jesus offers neither.
To the broken person who thinks, “God could never want me after what I've done,” Christ points toward grace.
To the comfortable person who thinks, “God forgives me anyway, so why change?” Christ calls for repentance.
And sometimes…
we are both people.
We want mercy for our favorite sin and judgment for somebody else's.
We want Jesus to put down the stone aimed at us while secretly wishing He would pick one up for them.
The adulterer.
The gossip.
The hypocrite.
The addict.
The sexually immoral.
The arrogant church member.
The liar.
The person who betrayed us.
The person whose political opinions make us furious.
The person whose sin happens to be different from ours.
But Scripture demolishes the fantasy that some of us arrive before God as morally superior rescuers while others arrive as uniquely disgusting sinners.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23.
All.
That word leaves very little room for boasting.
The ground beneath the cross is crowded with people who need mercy.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe yours wears respectable clothing.
Pride can wear a suit.
Greed can have a retirement account.
Lust can carry a Bible.
Bitterness can sing worship songs.
Self-righteousness can memorize Scripture.
And rebellion can learn Christian vocabulary so well that nobody notices it anymore.
But Jesus sees.
That sounds terrifying until you understand who is doing the seeing.
The One who sees everything is also the One who went to the cross.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows what you keep hiding.
He knows what you promised Him you would never do again.
He knows how many times you returned.
He knows how exhausted you are from fighting yourself.
He knows the part of your testimony you carefully edit when telling it publicly.
And still the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come.
Not because sin does not matter.
Come because Christ is the only Savior sufficient for sinners.
The apostle John writes:
Notice again what grace does.
Forgives.
And cleanses.
The Gospel is not merely:
“You are forgiven, now return to the mud.”
It is:
“You are forgiven. Come out of the grave.”
This is why repentance must never be treated as the enemy of grace.

The New Testament word often translated “repentance,” μετάνοια — metanoia, speaks of repentance involving a changed mind and turning toward God. Biblical repentance is not purchasing forgiveness by becoming good enough.
You cannot.
Christ already paid what you could never pay.
Repentance is the sinner turning from rebellion toward the God whose mercy has confronted him.
It is not perfection overnight.
That matters.
Because someone reading this may already be discouraged.
You love Jesus.
You really do.
And yet you still struggle.
You still stumble.
You have prayed through tears about the same temptation more times than you can count.
So when you hear “go and sin no more,” you may hear:
“Become flawless immediately or Jesus wants nothing to do with you.”
That is not the Gospel.
The New Testament plainly recognizes the continuing battle with sin in believers. John writes to Christians:
But he immediately continues:
“But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” — 1 John 2:1
Do you see the tension?
So that you may not sin.
And:
If anyone does sin, we have an advocate.
Christianity is neither casual surrender to sin nor hopeless despair when a believer stumbles.
The difference is not that genuine Christians never fall.
The difference is that grace teaches us not to call the ground our home.
You confess.
You get up.
You run toward Christ.
You bring darkness into light.
You seek help.
You cut off what keeps feeding the temptation.
You forgive when your flesh wants revenge.
You leave what keeps pulling you from God.
You return again and again to Scripture.
You pray when you feel strong.
