You pray when you feel absolutely nothing.
And when you fall, you do not say:
“Well, apparently holiness doesn't matter.”
You say:
“Jesus, have mercy on me. I need You again.”
Because you do.
So do I.
So does every person reading this.
Maybe the deepest scandal of Christianity is not that sinners exist.
We already knew that.
The scandal is that a holy God loves sinners enough to rescue them without pretending their rebellion is righteousness.
He does not rewrite evil into good.
Jesus rewrites the sinner.
That is the miracle.
From scandal…
to grace.
From exposure…
to forgiveness.
From slavery…
to freedom.
From hiding…
to confession.
From death…
to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But please hear this carefully.
Jesus is not asking you merely to become a more disciplined version of yourself.
Christianity is not self-improvement with Bible verses attached.
You need more than behavior modification.
You need Christ.
You need the Savior who died and rose again.
You need the Holy Spirit.
You need grace when your strength runs out.
You need forgiveness for yesterday and power to obey today.
And perhaps you need to stop negotiating with the thing God has already been asking you to surrender.
You know what it is.
Nobody else reading this needs to know.
But you know.
That relationship.
That resentment.
That secret habit.
That deception.
That double life.
That unforgiveness.
That compromise you keep defending because surrender will cost you something.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has been putting His finger on it for months.
And you keep saying:
“Later.”
One day.
After this season.
After one more time.
After I feel stronger.
But what if grace is meeting you here?
Not tomorrow.
Here.
Not when you become worthy.
Now.
What if the words that frightened you are actually words of freedom?
Go.
You don't have to stay here.
Sin no more.
You don't have to keep handing your chains back to the jailer.
And when the enemy says, “Look at what you did,” point him toward what Christ has done.
When shame says, “Your story is over,” remember the empty tomb.
When temptation says, “You will always belong to me,” remember whom Christ purchased.
When pride says, “You don't need repentance,” look again at the cross.
When despair says, “You are beyond grace,” look again at the cross.
The cross destroys both pride and hopelessness.
You were sinful enough that Christ had to die.
You were loved enough that He willingly did.
That is why we cannot separate:
“Neither do I condemn you”
from:
“Go and sin no more.”
Remove the first, and Christianity becomes crushing legalism.
Remove the second, and grace becomes a caricature that leaves people chained to the very things destroying them.
Jesus gives us something infinitely better.
Grace that forgives.
Truth that confronts.
Mercy that restores.
Love that refuses to leave us unchanged.
Be real.

And if Christ has already rescued you from something you once thought would own you forever, tell somebody what Jesus did. Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed person finally believes there is still a road home.
Not because every sentence is easy to hear.
Not as religious decoration.
Somebody may believe Jesus wants nothing to do with them.
Somebody else may have mistaken forgiveness for permission to remain enslaved.
Let them encounter the whole sentence.
And yes—even invite the skeptic, the seeker, the lukewarm Christian, and the person who hasn't entered a church in years.
Not so Gospel Warrior gets another statistic.
So another human being encounters the truth about Jesus Christ.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor.
You do not purchase grace.
You cannot buy God's approval.
Christ alone saves.
Use them.
Share them.
Give them to the new believer who doesn't know where to begin.
Send them to the exhausted Christian who needs nourishment.
Put biblical resources into the hands of someone hungry to know Christ.
Give them Scripture.
Give them truth.
Give them the Gospel.
Give them Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight, another person will sit alone believing the worst thing they ever did has become the final sentence over their life.
And maybe God will use something as simple as your share to place these words in front of them:
“Neither do I condemn you.”
But don't stop there.
Let them hear Jesus finish.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Grace does not hand you a pillow so you can sleep comfortably inside the prison.
Grace opens the cell door and calls you by name into the light.
And when Jesus Christ takes hold of a scandalous, shattered, guilty human story, the final chapter no longer belongs to the sin that almost destroyed it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re Not Just Raising a Child Who Behaves. You’re Showing Them What God Is Like—or Isn’t.
paragraphs: You’re Not Just Raising a Child Who Behaves. You’re Showing Them What God Is Like—or Isn’t.

Your child may obey every rule in your house and still grow up with the wrong picture of God. Christian parenting was never meant to produce children who merely behave—it is meant to point human hearts toward the Father revealed in Jesus Christ.
There is a kind of silence in a house that can fool a parent.
The children are quiet.
Nobody is arguing.
Nobody is talking back.
The room is clean.
The rules are being followed.
And for a moment, everything looks successful.
But sometimes that silence is not peace.
Sometimes it is fear.
Sometimes the child sitting quietly at the table is not thinking, “I understand why Mom corrected me.”
He is thinking, “I better not make Dad angry.”
Sometimes the daughter who immediately says, “Yes, Mom,” is not learning wisdom.
She is learning how to avoid punishment.
Sometimes what adults celebrate as obedience is actually a frightened little heart becoming extremely skilled at reading the emotional temperature of the room.
And that should make every Christian parent uncomfortable.
Because you are not merely teaching your child how to behave around you.

Day after day, through correction, affection, patience, anger, confession, forgiveness, consistency, inconsistency, tenderness, discipline, and grace, you are helping shape their earliest understanding of authority.
And somewhere inside that experience, they are beginning to form ideas about God.
That is why one sentence from Paul should stop Christian parents in their tracks:
“Καὶ οἱ πατέρες, μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ Κυρίου.”
Ephesians 6:4.
Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children to anger, but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Notice what Christianity does not say.
It does not say:
Make them scared enough to obey.
Embarrass them until they change.
Control them until they become manageable.
Demand perfection so the family looks spiritual.
Win every argument.
Make sure everyone at church thinks you have wonderful children.
Paul reaches deeper.
The Greek word translated “provoke to anger” is παροργίζετε — parorgizete, carrying the idea of provoking or stirring someone toward anger.
Then comes ἐκτρέφετε — ektrephete: nourish, bring up, rear, care for.
Think about that contrast.
Do not continually provoke them.
Bring them up.
Nourish them.
And how?
“In the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”
The word παιδείᾳ — paideia can refer to training, education, upbringing, or discipline. νουθεσίᾳ — nouthesia carries the sense of instruction, admonition, or corrective counsel.
This is far richer than making children behave.
Christian parenting is formative.
It reaches toward the heart.
It teaches.
Corrects.
Warns.
Models.
Nourishes.
Disciplines.
Forgives.
And continually points beyond the parent toward Christ.
That means the question after your child misbehaves cannot always be merely:
“How do I stop this behavior?”
Sometimes the more important question is:
“What does my child need to understand?”
Because behavior matters.
Scripture never teaches otherwise.

Children are called to obey their parents in the Lord. Parents are responsible to teach, correct, and discipline. Biblical grace is not parental passivity, and love is not pretending rebellion does not matter.
But outward obedience and inward discipleship are not identical.
A child can learn to say the right words while resentment grows underneath them.
A teenager can learn how to perform Christianity while secretly counting the days until leaving home.
A child can memorize Scripture and simultaneously believe that admitting failure is dangerous.
A family can look beautifully Christian in a Sunday photograph while everyone inside the house knows which subjects must never be mentioned because Dad might explode.
That is the scandal nobody wants posted on Facebook.
Sometimes our children meet our Christian reputation before they experience our Christian character.
We tell them God is patient...
then lose control when milk spills.
We tell them God forgives...
then resurrect something they did six months ago.
We tell them God welcomes confession...
then make honesty so frightening that lying feels safer.
We tell them Jesus is gentle...
then use humiliation as discipline.
We tell them their identity is found in Christ...
then act as though their grades determine their worth.
We tell them grace cannot be earned...
then withdraw affection when they disappoint us.
And children notice contradictions adults think they have successfully hidden.
This does not mean a parent must become perfect.
If perfection were required to raise children faithfully, no human being would qualify.
The Gospel begins with something far more hopeful:
You are a sinner raising sinners who desperately need the same Savior.
That changes everything.
Because one of the greatest gifts Christian parents can give their children is not the illusion of flawless parents.
It is the experience of repentant ones.
Imagine a father standing outside his child's bedroom after losing his temper.
Everything inside him wants to justify himself.
“He shouldn't have talked back.”
“I already told her three times.”
“They know better.”
“I've had a terrible day.”
Maybe every sentence contains some truth.
But none of those truths erase his sin.
So he opens the door.
He sits beside his child.
And instead of delivering another lecture, he says something that child may remember thirty years later:
“I was right to correct what you did. But the way I spoke to you was wrong. I sinned against you. Will you forgive me?”
Something enormous happens in that moment.
Authority does not disappear.
Discipline has not been abandoned.
The parent has not surrendered leadership.
The Gospel has entered the room.
The child is discovering that Christianity has somewhere to put failure.
At the cross.
This is what separates Gospel-centered parenting from image-centered parenting.
Image-centered parenting asks:
“What will people think of my child?”
Gospel-centered parenting asks:
“What is happening in my child's heart?”
Image-centered parenting is terrified of embarrassment.
Gospel-centered parenting is concerned with formation.
Image-centered parenting needs the child to make the parent look successful.
Gospel-centered parenting remembers that the child belongs ultimately to God.
And perhaps most importantly, Gospel-centered parenting allows children to watch their parents need Jesus too.
Your child should not grow up believing Christianity is a religion for people who never fail.
Let them discover that Christianity is about a Savior who came precisely because we do.
Jesus did not come for polished families with immaculate reputations.
He came for sinners.
He came for exhausted mothers.
Impatient fathers.
Angry teenagers.
Defiant children.
Broken marriages.
Wounded families.
People carrying things nobody else knows about.
People who have said things they wish they could pull back into their mouths.
People who have slammed doors.
People who have cried behind locked bathroom doors.
People who love God and still discover frightening amounts of selfishness inside themselves.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good families can become slightly better.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ bore our sins.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ offers forgiveness.
Christ gives new life.
And when that Gospel begins saturating a home, discipline changes.
Not because consequences disappear.
Because redemption becomes the destination.
The goal is no longer merely:
“You broke the rule.”
It becomes:
“Something happening in your heart produced this behavior, and I love you too much to ignore it.”
Now correction becomes an opportunity for discipleship.
Why did you lie?
Were you afraid?
Why did you hit your brother?
What were you wanting so badly that anger took control?
Why did you hide what happened?
Did you think telling me the truth would cost you my love?
Those conversations take longer than shouting.
They require patience.
They interrupt schedules.
They expose the parent's heart too.
But hearts are rarely discipled efficiently.
Children need truth repeated.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Much like adults do.
And there will be nights when you get it wrong.
You will become impatient.
You will speak before thinking.
You will discipline from irritation rather than wisdom.
You may discover patterns inherited from your own childhood coming out of your mouth.
Perhaps that is where this article becomes painful.
Because some parents reading this are suddenly remembering another house.
Another voice.
Another childhood.
Maybe you were raised where obedience was everything.
You learned early that mistakes brought humiliation.
Maybe affection disappeared when you failed.
Maybe Scripture itself was sometimes used like a weapon.
Maybe nobody apologized because adults were always right.
And now, years later, you hear yourself saying things you swore you would never say.
That realization can feel devastating.
But listen carefully.
Your family's story does not have to end where it began.
This is exactly where grace becomes more than a theological word.
Jesus Christ redeems sinners.
The cross means your worst parenting moment does not have to become the final chapter of your family.
Repentance can interrupt generations.
Grace can enter patterns that seemed permanent.
A father can learn tenderness.
A mother can learn patience.
A wounded adult can discover that biblical authority does not require cruelty.
A family can learn confession.
Children can witness restoration.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
This is our theme for a reason:
Not because consequences magically vanish.
Not because wounds never leave scars.
Not because repentance erases history.
But because Jesus can take sinners who finally stop defending themselves and begin transforming them by His grace.
Parents, your children do not need you to pretend you are Jesus.
They need you to keep pointing them to Jesus.
When you discipline them, point them toward Jesus.
When they fail, point them toward Jesus.
When they succeed, point them toward Jesus.
When you fail them, repent and point them toward Jesus.
When they ask questions you cannot answer, search Scripture with them and point them toward Jesus.
When their faith struggles, resist the temptation to panic over appearances. Listen. Pray. Speak truth. Stay present. Point them toward Jesus.
Your authority has limits.
His does not.
Your patience has limits.
His does not.
Your wisdom has limits.
His does not.
You cannot regenerate your child's heart.
You cannot manufacture saving faith.
You cannot yell someone into loving God.
You cannot control a soul into surrendering to Christ.
You can teach.
You can discipline.
You can pray.
You can model repentance.
You can confess.
You can forgive.
You can open Scripture.
You can proclaim Christ.
You can create a home where truth and grace are not enemies.
And then you entrust the heart of your child to God.
Maybe tonight your child does not need another sermon about what they did wrong.
Maybe they need a conversation.
Maybe you need to knock on a bedroom door.
Maybe there is an apology you have delayed because you thought apologizing would weaken your authority.
It won't.
Hypocrisy weakens Christian witness far more than repentance does.
Maybe the sentence your child needs tonight is:
“I love you too much to pretend what you did was okay. But nothing you did tonight makes me stop loving you. We are going to deal with this truthfully, and we are going to walk through it together.”
What a small glimpse of the Gospel that can become.
Truth without abandonment.
Correction without rejection.
Discipline surrounded by love.
Not perfect parenting.
Christian parenting.
And if reading this exposed something uncomfortable in you, do not run from it.
Bring it to Christ.
If you have wounded your children, repent before God and, where appropriate, seek their forgiveness.
If your discipline has become rage, do not rename it “biblical authority.”
If your desire for obedience has become a desire for control, confess it.
If you have cared more about how your children make you look than who they are becoming before God, confess that too.
There is mercy at the cross.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Mercy that calls sinners out of hiding and into transformation.
Maybe your children will someday forget many of the rules you made.
They may forget which chores happened on Tuesdays.
They may forget the lectures.
They may forget the consequences.
But they may remember something much deeper.
What happened when they told you the truth.
What your face looked like when they failed.
Whether correction felt like guidance or humiliation.
Whether home was a place where sin was confronted but confession was safe.
Whether Dad could say, “Forgive me.”
Whether Mom could admit, “I was wrong.”
Whether Jesus seemed like Someone the family actually needed—or merely Someone whose name appeared on decorations and Sunday schedules.
So ask yourself the difficult question:
What picture of God is my parenting helping my child imagine?
Not because you perfectly represent God. You don't.
No parent does.
But because Christian parents have been entrusted with the extraordinary responsibility of raising children “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”
That responsibility should humble us.
And send us running toward grace.
And don't keep this conversation inside your own house.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Financial support is never a substitute for obedience to Christ, but voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership.
Not to prove that you love God.
Not to purchase His blessing.
Not because an algorithm measures faithfulness.
But because somewhere behind another screen may be a tired mother crying after losing her temper...
a father terrified that he is becoming the man who wounded him...
a parent who thinks the damage is already too deep...
or a grown child who needs to discover that what happened in their childhood was not an accurate picture of the heart of Jesus.
Send truth into their story.
And tonight, before correcting your child's behavior again, remember what is standing in front of you.
Not an inconvenience.
Not an embarrassment.
Not a reputation-management problem.
A soul.
A human being entrusted to your care for a little while.
Teach them truth.
Give wise discipline.
Set boundaries.
Require obedience.
But let them also witness mercy.
Let them hear repentance.
Let them experience forgiveness.
Let them discover that authority does not have to mean humiliation.
And above everything else, let them see a mother or father who keeps returning to Jesus.
Because one day your child may walk out of your house carrying far more than memories of your rules.
They may carry an image of what authority, forgiveness, confession, discipline, mercy, and love feel like.
Make sure that when your parenting fails to show them the Father clearly, your repentance points them back to the Son.
Your child does not need a parent who never falls; they need to see where a Christian goes after the fall—and watch you walk back to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT WOULD JESUS SAY TO SOMEONE TRAPPED IN PORN TODAY?
paragraphs: WHAT WOULD JESUS SAY TO SOMEONE TRAPPED IN PORN TODAY?

If Jesus were standing beside you after you closed that private tab, He would not pretend your sin was harmless. But the Savior who exposes what is killing you is also the Savior who went to the cross to set captives free.
There is a moment after the screen goes dark when the room becomes painfully quiet.
You know that moment.
Maybe nobody else knows.
Your spouse may be sleeping beside you.
Your parents may think you are asleep.
Your friends at church may think you are doing well.
You may have worshiped on Sunday, lifted your hands, quoted Scripture, encouraged somebody else, posted something about Jesus...
and then, when nobody was watching, you went back.
Again.
The screen lit your face in the darkness.
For a few minutes, you escaped.
Then it ended.
And the shame came home.
You promised God last time was the last time.
You meant it.
You really did.
But now you are sitting there wondering whether God is disgusted with you.
Whether you have gone too far.
Whether you are even a real Christian.
Whether Jesus could possibly still want someone who keeps crawling back to something he knows is destroying him.
And underneath all those questions is another one you may be afraid to ask:
If Jesus were sitting beside me right now... what would He say?
Not what would the internet say.
Not what would an angry preacher say.
Not what would a permissive culture say.
What would Jesus Christ say?
We do not have to invent His answer.
Jesus already spoke about the heart behind sexual lust.

His words are uncomfortable because Jesus refuses to perform the strange surgery we perform on ourselves—the surgery where we separate what our eyes deliberately consume from what our hearts are becoming.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text records:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν...
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn...

Jesus is speaking of looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her, and He says that such a person has already committed adultery with her ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ — en tē kardia autou — “in his heart.”
That matters.
Because pornography desperately wants you to believe that what happens on a screen stays on a screen.
Jesus says it reaches the heart.
Porn says, “Nobody touched anybody.”
Jesus looks deeper.
Porn says, “It is only fantasy.”
Jesus looks deeper.
Porn says, “Everybody does it.”
Jesus looks deeper.
Porn says, “At least I haven't actually cheated.”
Jesus looks deeper.
Because Jesus is not merely interested in whether your body crossed a geographical boundary.
He cares about what your heart is learning to desire.
And that means Jesus would not look at pornography addiction and say:
“It doesn't matter.”
He would love you too much to say that.
But hear this carefully...
Neither would He simply stand over your failure screaming:
“Filthy.”
“Disgusting.”
“Hopeless.”
“Get away from Me.”
Some people have confused condemnation with holiness for so long that they can barely imagine Jesus confronting sexual sin without imagining hatred in His eyes.
But look at the Gospel.
Jesus tells the truth about sin because He came to rescue sinners from it.
He does not rename chains so that prisoners can feel comfortable wearing them.
He breaks chains.
And sometimes the first sound freedom makes is the painful sound of truth.
Jesus continues in Matthew 5 with shocking language about tearing out an offending eye and throwing it away.
He was not commanding His followers to mutilate themselves. Removing an eye cannot remove lust from the heart.
His language communicates the terrifying seriousness with which His disciples should deal with sin.
In other words:
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
That may be exactly what somebody reading this needs to hear.
Because perhaps you have been praying for deliverance while keeping unrestricted access to the very thing feeding your bondage.
You ask God to rescue you...
but keep the secret account.
You cry afterward...
but refuse accountability beforehand.
You delete something...
then reinstall it.
You confess vaguely...
because specific confession feels too dangerous.
You tell yourself you are fighting pornography while quietly protecting the doorway pornography uses to reach you.
Jesus' words tear through that compromise.
If something repeatedly becomes your pathway into sin, radical obedience may require radical removal.
Delete it.
Block it.
Move the device.
Change the routine.
Stop taking the phone into the place where you repeatedly fall.
Ask someone trustworthy to hold you accountable.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Not because deleting an app can save your soul.
It cannot.
Jesus saves.
But genuine repentance does not merely say, “Lord, forgive me,” while carefully preserving every convenient route back to the sin.
Repentance turns.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because the person trapped in pornography often thinks Christianity's message is:
Clean yourself up, and maybe Jesus will take you back.
That is not the Gospel.
You cannot scrub your heart clean enough to purchase mercy.
You cannot produce enough guilt to atone for yesterday.
You cannot punish yourself into holiness.
You cannot hate yourself into purity.
Jesus did not climb Calvary because relatively decent people needed motivational advice.
Christ died for sinners.
At the cross, Jesus carried judgment that guilty people could never exhaust through self-punishment.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because your sin was insignificant...
but because His sacrifice is sufficient.
This is why Romans 8:1 contains words some ashamed believers desperately need to read slowly:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
Ouden ara nyn katakrima tois en Christō Iēsou.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Οὐδὲν — ouden.
No condemnation.
That does not mean no conviction.
Conviction and condemnation are not identical.
Conviction says, “This sin is killing something precious. Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “You are beyond mercy. Hide.”
Conviction drives you toward Christ.
Condemnation tells you to run from Him.
Conviction produces repentance.
Condemnation produces despair.
The Gospel does not say your pornography use is harmless.
The Gospel says your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die—and His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not have to remain your master.
Imagine Jesus looking directly into the part of your life you have worked hardest to hide.
No filters.
No deleted history.
No excuses.
No Christian vocabulary.
He sees the first time.
The hundredth time.
The promises you broke.
The images you wish you could erase from your mind.
The people you reduced to objects in your imagination.
The loneliness underneath some of it.
The entitlement underneath some of it.
The wounds you tried to medicate with it.
The rebellion underneath some of it.
The shame afterward.
He sees everything.
And still the Gospel invitation is:
Come to Me.
Not:
“Come when you have seven clean days.”
Not:
“Come when you finally deserve Me.”
Not:
“Come after you have punished yourself sufficiently.”
Come.
But do not confuse coming to Jesus with asking Jesus to become your assistant while pornography remains your master.
Jesus came to be Lord.
Grace does not merely forgive the prisoner.
Grace opens the cell and says:
Walk out.
Paul writes with equally uncompromising urgency in 1 Corinthians 6:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Flee.
Not study how close you can stand to it.
Not negotiate.
Not flirt with it.
Not see how much temptation you can tolerate before falling.
Flee.
And then Paul gives one of Christianity's most beautiful reasons for sexual holiness.
Your body is not worthless.
Your body matters to God.
For the believer, Paul describes the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit and says:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς...
ēgorasthēte gar timēs...
“You were bought with a price.”
Then comes the command:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
Do you see the difference?
Christian purity is not ultimately:
“My body is disgusting, so I must hate it.”
It is:
“I belong to Christ, therefore my body has become territory on which I want God glorified.”
Pornography tells you bodies exist for consumption.
Jesus teaches you to see people as image-bearers, neighbors, souls—not products for private gratification.
Porn trains the eyes to consume.
Jesus teaches the heart to love.
Porn says:
“Take.”
Jesus says:
“Love.”
Porn says:
“Use.”
Jesus says:
“Serve.”
Pornography turns a human being into pixels arranged for appetite.
The Gospel teaches you to remember there is a person behind the image.
Someone's daughter.
Someone's son.
Someone God created.
Someone with fears, memories, wounds, dignity, and an eternal soul.
And suddenly the battle is bigger than “How do I stop looking at porn?”
The deeper question becomes:
What kind of person is Jesus transforming me into?
Because Christianity is not merely behavior modification.
It is resurrection.
Maybe pornography became your anesthetic.
Maybe you discovered it when you were young and did not understand what it would eventually do to you.
Maybe it became the place you ran when you felt rejected.
Lonely.
Stressed.
Angry.
Bored.
Unwanted.
Maybe pornography became a counterfeit sanctuary.
A place where you could experience stimulation without vulnerability.
Desire without relationship.
Pleasure without covenant.
Intimacy without being known.
And that may be why simply saying “stop watching” has never reached deep enough.
Because sometimes underneath the sexual habit is a hurting human heart trying to make pain disappear.
But pornography cannot heal loneliness.
It rents you relief and sends you the bill afterward.
Jesus offers something radically different.
He offers Himself.
Not merely cleaner browsing history.
A new heart.
Not merely stronger willpower.
A new identity.
Not merely another streak on an accountability calendar.
Communion with God.
And perhaps tonight your breakthrough begins with something painfully ordinary.
You tell somebody.
Not everybody.
Somebody trustworthy.
A mature Christian.
A pastor.
A mentor.
A spouse where appropriate.
A qualified counselor if the pattern has become compulsive or is tied to deeper wounds.
You stop calling secrecy “privacy.”
You stop measuring repentance by how terrible you feel afterward and begin measuring seriousness by what you are willing to change beforehand.
You stop saying:
“I'll beat this alone.”
Because isolation has been pornography's favorite room in your house.
Bring another believer into the room.
Pray.
Confess.
Install barriers.
Change habits.
Learn your triggers.
Replace secrecy with fellowship.
Fill your mind with Scripture.
Pursue Christ rather than merely pursuing an impressive number of porn-free days.
And when you stumble, do not turn one failure into permission for fifty more.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Continue fighting.
Because there is a difference between falling in battle and making peace with the enemy.
If you hate this sin because you increasingly love Christ, keep fighting.
If you fell yesterday, keep fighting.
If you feel embarrassed to admit how long this has controlled you, keep fighting.
If somebody else's testimony makes freedom look effortless while your battle feels brutal, keep fighting.
Your hope is not that your grip on Jesus will always feel strong.
Your hope is that Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
Maybe you need to say something publicly—not details that expose you unnecessarily, but enough truth to stop pretending.
And if you cannot even find strong words tonight, simply write:
There is no trophy for pretending.
Sometimes another believer needs to discover that he is not the only person in the church fighting in silence.
Sometimes confession breaks the illusion that everybody else is effortlessly holy.
And sometimes somebody reading the comments realizes:
Not because saving a post makes you holy, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget everything we believed five minutes earlier.
Come back when the night gets quiet.
Come back before opening the tab.
Come back when shame tells you God wants nothing to do with you.
Read the Scriptures again.
Then open the Bible itself.
Pray.
Call somebody.
Run toward Christ.
Not as a badge announcing that you have mastered the subject.
A husband.
A wife.
A teenager.
A ministry leader.
A lonely believer.
A skeptic who assumes Christianity offers nothing but shame.
Someone may never tell you that your share reached them at 1:17 in the morning when they were seconds away from going back.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns forgiveness.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption at a price none of us could pay.
But Scripture does call believers to glorify God with what He has entrusted to them, and voluntary support can help Gospel-centered truth reach people who desperately need it.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
But before you leave this article, hear the question again.
What would Jesus say to someone trapped in porn today?
He would tell the truth.
Your sin is not harmless.
Your heart matters.
What you repeatedly feed matters.
The people on that screen possess human dignity.
Sexual holiness matters.
Repentance matters.
Your body matters.
Eternity matters.
So stop making treaties with the thing crucifying your intimacy with God.
Flee.
Bring it into the light.
Cut off the pathway.
Ask for help.
Repent.
But then hear the other half of the Gospel.
Your shame is not greater than His cross.
Your history is not stronger than His blood.
Your chains are not more powerful than the risen Christ.
You are not being invited merely to become a person who “doesn't watch porn anymore.”
You are being invited into something infinitely greater.
To know Christ.
To love Christ.
To belong to Christ.
To learn to see people through eyes being purified by Christ.
To glorify God in your body.
To become the kind of person who no longer needs darkness because he has discovered something better than secrecy:
the presence of Jesus.
So when the screen goes dark tonight and the silence returns...
do not hide from Him.
Run toward Him.
The same Jesus who exposes the chain is the Jesus who gave His life to redeem the captive.
And perhaps the most scandalous thing about grace is not that Jesus pretends your sin never mattered.
It is that He knows exactly how much it mattered...
and went to the cross anyway.
Follow so that truth remains closer than the voices pulling you backward.
And never forget this:
The screen may remember your history, but the risen Christ is writing your future—and the scars in His hands prove your darkest chapter does not have to be your final one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WAS RAHAB’S HOUSE BUILT INTO JERICHO’S WALL?
paragraphs:
WHY WAS RAHAB’S HOUSE BUILT INTO JERICHO’S WALL?
She lived in the place everyone trusted for protection. Then the wall fell—and the woman everyone could have condemned became the one God refused to forget.
There is one detail in the story of Rahab that is so easy to read past that most people never stop long enough to feel its weight.
Her house was in the wall.
Not simply near Jericho’s wall.
Not merely somewhere inside the city.
Scripture says:
וַתּוֹרִדֵם בַּחֶבֶל בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן כִּי בֵיתָהּ בְּקִיר הַחוֹמָה וּבַחוֹמָה הִיא יוֹשָׁבֶת
Vattoridem baḥevel be'ad haḥallon, ki veitah beqir haḥomah, uvaḥomah hi yoshevet.
“Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was in the wall of the fortification, and she was dwelling in the wall.”
—Joshua 2:15
The Hebrew is striking.
בְּקִיר הַחוֹמָה — beqir haḥomah
Literally, “in the wall of the fortification.”
Then Scripture emphasizes it again:
וּבַחוֹמָה הִיא יוֹשָׁבֶת — uvaḥomah hi yoshevet
“And in the wall she was dwelling.”

The text wants you to notice where Rahab lived. Ancient Jewish interpreters noticed it too; Joshua 2:15 became the basis of discussion precisely because her dwelling was understood as being associated with, or actually within, the city wall.
And once you notice it, the story becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because the wall that should have made Rahab vulnerable became the location from which salvation entered her house.
Think about that.
Jericho was facing judgment.
Israel was coming.
Rahab knew it.
The city knew it.
Fear was already spreading before a single wall collapsed.
She told the spies:
יָדַעְתִּי כִּי־נָתַן יְהוָה לָכֶם אֶת־הָאָרֶץ
Yada'ti ki-natan YHWH lakhem et-ha'aretz.
“I know that the LORD has given you the land.”
—Joshua 2:9
Not “I wonder.”
Not “I have heard rumors.”
Yada'ti.
“I know.”
Something had happened inside this woman before anything happened to Jericho’s walls.
Faith had entered.
And that changes everything.
Rahab is introduced in Joshua 2:1 with an uncomfortable word:
זוֹנָה — zonah.
The ordinary Hebrew meaning is a prostitute.

Some later traditions have associated Rahab with an inn or innkeeping, but we should not erase the scandal Scripture itself allows to stand. The Greek New Testament is even more explicit. Hebrews 11:31 calls her Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē, “Rahab the prostitute,” and James 2:25 similarly identifies her as Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη.
The Bible does not sanitize her résumé before telling us what grace did with her.
That matters.
Because some of us have spent years trying to edit the parts of our story we are afraid other Christians might discover.
We know how to smile in church.
We know what to post.
We know which Bible verse belongs in the caption.
We know when to say, “God is good.”
But somewhere behind the smile is a room we hope nobody enters.
An addiction.
An affair.
A secret.
A compromise.
A season of rebellion.
A body carrying memories nobody knows about.
A marriage barely surviving.
A private habit contradicting a public testimony.
A past you wish could be deleted.
Rahab’s story begins with Scripture refusing to delete hers.
“Rahab the prostitute.”
And strangely, that is part of what makes the Gospel-shaped trajectory of her life so beautiful.
God is not glorified because Rahab had no scandal.
God is glorified because her scandal did not get the final word.
But there is another question.
Why was her house in Jericho’s wall?
Scripture never directly tells us why Rahab personally came to occupy that particular dwelling. We should be careful not to invent an explanation and call it biblical truth.
What Scripture does tell us is that her house’s position made the events of Joshua 2 possible.
Her house had a window opening through the wall.
That meant two Israelite spies trapped inside an enemy city had an escape route.
Rahab lowered them through that window by a rope.
The place where she lived suddenly became strategically important in God’s unfolding purpose.

Archaeology confirms that ancient Jericho was a heavily fortified Canaanite settlement during portions of the Bronze Age. Excavations have revealed substantial fortification systems involving stone retaining structures, mudbrick defenses, ramparts, and multiple phases of construction. Scholars continue to debate the chronology and how particular archaeological destruction levels should be correlated with the biblical account, so archaeology should not be stretched beyond what it can establish. No responsible reading requires us to pretend that archaeologists have discovered a house and proven, “This was Rahab’s bedroom.”
The inspired text gives us what we actually need.
Her dwelling was associated so intimately with Jericho’s fortification that she could lower the spies through its window to the outside.
And suddenly her address becomes part of the story.
The woman on the edge of the city...
was positioned at the edge of a miracle.
Imagine that night.
Two men disappear through her window.
A rope rubs against the wall.
Rahab watches them descend into darkness.
These men belong to the people whose God is coming against her city.
Everything Rahab has known is behind her.
Everything she has chosen to believe is disappearing into the night in front of her.
And she has been given a command.
Put a scarlet cord in the window.
The Hebrew expression in Joshua 2:18 is:
תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי — tiqvat ḥut hashani
A cord—or line—of scarlet.
The word תִּקְוָה — tiqvah can carry the sense of a cord in this context and elsewhere means “hope” or “expectation.”
We should be careful here.
Joshua does not explicitly tell us that the author intends the scarlet cord as a direct prophecy of Christ’s blood.
The New Testament does not explicitly make that identification either.
So we should not declare a symbolism Scripture itself does not declare.
But a Christian reader can hardly miss the larger biblical pattern without feeling its resonance.
Judgment is approaching.
A household has received a promise of deliverance.
A visible sign marks the place where those trusting the promise have gathered.
And those who remain within are spared.
It inevitably reminds us of Passover.
Blood on a doorway.
Judgment passing through.
A household sheltered because God had provided the terms of deliverance.
And both stories eventually point our eyes toward the greater deliverance accomplished not through a cord in a window or blood on an Egyptian doorway, but through Jesus Christ Himself.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that good people can escape judgment.
It is the announcement that guilty people can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus.
That is Rahab territory.
That is Gospel territory.
That is where some of us are standing right now.
Between what we have been...
and what grace is calling us to become.
Then Jericho falls.
Joshua 6 says Israel circles the city according to God’s command.
Trumpets sound.
The people shout.
And the wall collapses.
Now think again about where Rahab lives.
In the wall.
The very thing that gave her house its location was the thing under divine judgment.
Yet before Jericho fell, Rahab had already made her choice.
She had chosen the God of Israel over the gods of Jericho.
Listen to her confession:
כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת
“For the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
—Joshua 2:11
Do you see what happened?
Before Rahab ever left Jericho...
Jericho had begun leaving Rahab.
Her address was still Canaanite.
Her past was still Canaanite.
Her neighbors were still Canaanite.
Her house was physically attached to Jericho’s defenses.
But her faith had changed allegiance.
And perhaps that is exactly where someone reading this is living.
You have not escaped everything yet.
Your circumstances have not changed yet.
The addiction is still calling.
The divorce papers are still sitting there.
The grief is still in the room.
Your family still remembers who you used to be.
Your consequences have not magically disappeared.
Your reputation may not have recovered.
You may still be physically surrounded by the world you are trying to leave spiritually.
Rahab understands.
She trusted God while she was still living in Jericho.
Faith began before relocation.
Then judgment came.
Joshua commanded the two spies:
“Go into the prostitute’s house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her.”
They went in.
They brought Rahab out.
Her father.
Her mother.
Her brothers.
Everything belonging to her.
Her family.
The woman whose house had once stood as part of Jericho’s wall crossed from the condemned city into the company of God’s covenant people. Joshua 6:25 says Rahab lived among Israel afterward.
But God was not finished.
Centuries pass.
Kings rise.
Kingdoms fall.
Prophets speak.
Generations are born and buried.
Then Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
And there...
inside a genealogy most people rush through...
a familiar name appears.
Ῥαχὰβ — Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 places Rahab in the genealogy leading to David and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
Stop there.
The woman introduced in Joshua as a prostitute appears in Matthew in the ancestral line through which the Messiah enters history.
The woman in the wall became a woman in the genealogy.
Jericho knew her by her occupation.
Scripture remembers her by her faith.
Hebrews 11 places her among examples of faith:
“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had received the spies with peace.”
James remembers her too, presenting her actions as evidence of living faith.
Her past remained part of the testimony.
But it was no longer the conclusion.
That is grace.
Grace does not pretend the old chapter was never written.
Grace gives the story a new ending.
And that is why Rahab’s story must ultimately bring us to Jesus.
Because Jesus does not merely make embarrassing people respectable.
He saves sinners.
The cross tells the truth about us more brutally than our shame ever could.
Our sin is not a minor defect requiring improvement.
It separates us from a holy God.
We cannot rescue ourselves by becoming religious enough, moral enough, charitable enough, or publicly respectable enough.
We need mercy.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we could never perfectly live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something Rahab discovered long before Bethlehem:
God's mercy can reach a person standing inside a condemned city.
Maybe you have been living inside your own Jericho.
Building walls.
Protecting secrets.
Telling everyone you are fine.
Perhaps you have become so skilled at hiding that nobody knows you are exhausted.
But you know.
And God knows.
Maybe the question is no longer whether God can forgive someone like Rahab.
The question is whether you believe He can forgive someone like you.
He can.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves that it does.
And not because repentance is unnecessary.
Rahab’s faith changed her allegiance.
Saving faith does not say, “Jesus, bless the Jericho I refuse to leave.”
It says, “Jesus, I surrender.”
Repentance is not paying God back.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save.
Maybe your scarlet cord moment is now.
Not because repeating a sentence saves you.
Not because commenting on a Facebook post saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But perhaps you need to stop hiding.
And believers who see those words—do not judge them.
Pray for them.
Because the church should be one of the safest places on earth for a Rahab to encounter the truth that leads to repentance and the grace that leads to restoration.
Not merely because sharing helps a page.
It does not.
Not because supporting a ministry earns salvation. It cannot.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.
But believers have always used their resources to help truthful Gospel ministry continue.
Not out of guilt.
Out of mission.
Because somewhere behind somebody's carefully constructed wall is a person convinced that God would never want them if everyone knew what they had done.
Rahab destroys that lie.
Her story does not teach us that sin is harmless.
It teaches us that grace is greater.
Her story does not tell us everyone automatically escapes judgment.
It tells us that faith takes God seriously enough to change allegiance.
Her story does not end with a prostitute hiding spies in Jericho.
It reaches forward into Hebrews.
Into James.
Into Matthew.
Into the genealogy of Jesus Christ.

And ultimately toward the Savior whose Gospel announces that sinners can become sons and daughters, outsiders can be brought near, shame does not have to become identity, and yesterday does not have authority to write tomorrow.
Maybe that is why the location of Rahab’s house feels so unforgettable.
She lived in a wall everyone thought was strong enough to protect a city.
Then the wall failed.
But the God she trusted did not.
Jericho's wall could not save Rahab.
Her reputation could not save Rahab.
Her courage could not ultimately save Rahab.
Her works demonstrated the reality of her faith, but salvation belonged to the God in whom she placed that faith.
And the same truth reaches us through the completed Gospel today.
Your church attendance cannot save you.
Your Christian posts cannot save you.
Your charitable giving cannot save you.
Your good intentions cannot save you.
Your ability to hide your scandal cannot save you.
Jesus can.
So come out from behind the wall.
Bring the shame.
Bring the memories.
Bring the consequences.
Bring the years you wish you could recover.
Bring the secret nobody knows.
Bring the heart you thought God could never want.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of spotless people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of a holy God coming down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Rahab had a window in a wall.
God turned it into an escape route.
Rahab had a past stained by sin.
God turned it into a testimony of faith.
Rahab belonged to a condemned city.
God brought her among His people.
Rahab carried a name associated with scandal.
God placed that name inside the earthly family line leading to Christ.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about Rahab is that Scripture never needed to pretend she had always been someone else.
Grace was powerful enough to tell the truth.
The wall carrying Rahab's old life fell—but the mercy carrying her future never did.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY PAUL SAID RUN INSTEAD OF NEGOTIATE
paragraphs: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY PAUL SAID RUN INSTEAD OF NEGOTIATE

The temptation you keep trying to manage may be the very thing God is telling you to escape—and what waits on the other side of obedience is not merely a cleaner record, but a heart learning again that it belongs to Jesus.
There is a moment in temptation when you already know.
Before the click.
Before the message.
Before the second look.
Before you tell yourself, We’re only talking.
Before you reopen the conversation you deleted last night.
Before you search the name.
Before you close the bedroom door.
Before you convince yourself that pornography is harmless because nobody else is physically in the room.
Before you start explaining to yourself why this relationship is somehow different from what Scripture plainly says.
You know.
Something inside you is already sounding the alarm.
And perhaps that is exactly why these words from Paul feel so startlingly severe:
“Flee fornication.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18, KJV
Not analyze it.
Not flirt with it.
Not discover how close you can get without technically crossing the line.
Not prove how spiritually mature you are by standing beside the fire.
Flee.
The original Greek is even harder to soften:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”

The verb φεύγετε — pheugete carries the sense of fleeing, escaping, getting away. Paul does not present sexual temptation as a debate Christians should become skilled enough to win while remaining comfortably inside the room. His command demands movement.
Get away.
Why?
Because Paul understands something about sexual sin that modern culture desperately wants us to forget.
Your body is not meaningless.
Sex is not meaningless.
Desire is not meaningless.
And most importantly...
you are not your own.
That is where Paul's argument actually goes.
Read the command in its context rather than isolating it:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν...”
Then only a few lines later:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς”
ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“For ye are bought with a price.” — 1 Corinthians 6:20, KJV
There is the Gospel underneath the command.
Paul does not simply say, “Run because sex is dirty.”
Christianity does not teach that.

God created human beings male and female. Marriage and the one-flesh union did not originate in pornography, Hollywood, hookup culture, or human invention. Scripture places the one-flesh reality within God's design for marriage.
The problem is not that God hates sexuality.
The problem is that sin takes God's gifts and tries to enjoy them while removing God's authority.
And Paul tells believers to flee because something infinitely greater than temporary gratification is at stake.
You were bought.
Think about those words.
Bought with a price.
What price?
Not money.
Not religious performance.
Not church attendance.
Not promises that you will “do better next time.”
Blood.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
Suddenly sexual holiness is not merely about avoiding scandal.
It is about remembering ownership.
Your body belongs to the One who was crucified for you.
Your eyes belong to Jesus.
Your hands belong to Jesus.
Your imagination belongs to Jesus.
Your sexuality belongs to Jesus.
Your phone belongs under the lordship of Jesus.
Your private messages belong under the lordship of Jesus.
Your hotel room belongs under the lordship of Jesus.
Your dating relationship belongs under the lordship of Jesus.
Your loneliness belongs in the hands of Jesus.
Even the parts of your life nobody else sees belong to Jesus.

Paul says immediately before his command that believers' bodies are members of Christ, and immediately afterward he describes the believer's body as a temple of the Holy Spirit. His conclusion is breathtaking:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
Glorify God in your body.
That changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“How far can I go before this becomes sin?”
The better question becomes:
“How can Christ be glorified in my body?”
And sometimes the most God-glorifying thing your feet can do...
is run.
Joseph understood that centuries before Paul wrote to Corinth.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly tried to seduce him.
Joseph refused.
He understood that yielding would not merely violate his master's trust. He called it wickedness and sin against God.
But then came the day when discussion was over.
She grabbed his garment.
The opportunity was immediate.
Nobody needed to know.
Joseph was far from home.
There was no accountability partner standing beside him.
No pastor watching.
No parent checking his phone.
No church congregation looking through the window.
Just Joseph...
a woman who wanted him...
an opportunity...
and God.
Genesis says Joseph left his garment in her hand and fled out of the house.
He lost his coat.
Then he lost his reputation.
Then, because of her false accusation, he lost his freedom.
But he did not surrender his faithfulness to God.
There are moments when running will make you look foolish to people who do not understand what you are protecting.
Run anyway.
Delete the conversation.
Block the number.
Leave the room.
End the secret relationship.
Stop arranging “accidental” encounters.
Move the computer.
Put accountability on the device.
Tell a mature believer what has been happening.
Stop taking your phone into the place where you repeatedly fall.
Stop calling secrecy “privacy” when secrecy is feeding your bondage.
You do not have to demonstrate spiritual strength by remaining unnecessarily close to temptation.
Sometimes maturity looks like leaving.
Sometimes courage looks like blocking.
Sometimes worship looks like shutting the laptop.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks surprisingly ordinary:
You get up.
You walk away.
You call someone.
You confess.
You pray.
You refuse to return.
Paul later gives Timothy remarkably similar counsel:
“Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace...” — 2 Timothy 2:22, KJV.
Notice what biblical fleeing is not.
It is not simply running from something.
It is running toward Someone.
Flee youthful passions...
and pursue righteousness.
Pursue faith.
Pursue love.
Pursue peace.
Pursue these things with others who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
That last part matters more than many Christians realize.
You were never meant to fight every battle alone.
Sexual sin thrives in darkness.
It loves passwords nobody knows.
Browser histories nobody sees.
Relationships nobody can question.
Conversations nobody is allowed to read.
Rooms where nobody asks what happened.
Shame whispers:
Don't tell anyone.
They'll think differently about you.
Fix yourself first.
Then you can come back.
But the Gospel says something radically different.
Come into the light.
Not because sin does not matter...
but precisely because Jesus is greater than your sin.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you are reading this after failing again.
You promised God last time was the last time.
You cried.
You deleted everything.
You prayed.
Maybe you even felt clean for several weeks.
Then loneliness arrived.
Or stress.
Or rejection.
Or boredom.
Or anger.
Or late-night scrolling.
And suddenly the old doorway appeared again.
You walked through it.
Now you feel disgusting.
You cannot understand why God would still want you.
So hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not permission to keep sinning.
Grace is not God pretending sexual immorality does not matter.
Jesus did not endure the cross so that we could become comfortable with the sins from which He came to save us.
But neither is the Gospel the announcement that sexually broken people are beyond redemption.
Look at the Christians to whom Paul was writing.
Immediately before this discussion, Paul lists patterns of unrighteousness, including sexual sins, and then says something astonishing:
“And such were some of you...”
Were.
Then:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus...” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV.
That might be one of the most beautiful words a sexually broken person could ever hear.
Were.
Your sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have to own the ending.
Your pornography addiction does not get the final word.
Your adultery does not get the final word.
Your secret messages do not get the final word.
Your sexual past does not get the final word.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
This is why repentance is so much more beautiful than religious shame.
Shame says:
Hide from God.
Repentance says:
Run to God.
Shame says:
You have gone too far.
The Gospel says Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
Shame says:
Clean yourself before approaching Jesus.
The Gospel says you need Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after sin.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns.
It agrees with God about sin, abandons the attempt to justify it, and turns toward Christ in faith.
And that means some readers cannot finish this article merely feeling inspired.
Something has to change.
Perhaps there is a person you need to stop contacting.
Perhaps there is an app you need to remove.
Perhaps there is an affair you need to end.
Perhaps pornography has been discipling your imagination longer than Scripture has.
Perhaps you have been calling something “love” that requires disobedience to God in order to survive.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Yet.
And perhaps the sentence frightening you most is:
I need to tell someone.
Then tell someone trustworthy.
Bring it into the light.
Seek mature pastoral help and wise accountability. If another person is being exploited, coerced, abused, or placed in danger, getting appropriate professional or legal help may also be necessary.
Do not protect darkness merely because exposure is uncomfortable.
Your soul is worth more than your image.
And if you are married and your sexual sin has wounded your spouse, repentance cannot mean demanding immediate trust simply because you apologized.
Forgiveness and rebuilding trust are not identical.
Repentance accepts truth.
Repentance accepts accountability.
Repentance stops blaming the spouse.
Repentance stops blaming loneliness.
Repentance stops blaming alcohol.
Repentance stops blaming the internet.
Repentance says:
I sinned.
And then repentance looks toward Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of humans becoming disciplined enough to rescue themselves.
It is the story of a Savior rescuing sinners.
Christ was tempted, yet without sin.
Christ went willingly toward the cross.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And the same Jesus who commands holiness also offers mercy to repentant sinners.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls darkness light.
Not grace that leaves chains untouched.
Grace that forgives...
then begins transforming the forgiven.
Grace that finds someone on the bathroom floor whispering, “God, I did it again,” and calls them out of hiding.
Grace that enters the wreckage.
Grace that tells the adulterer to repent.
Grace that tells the pornography addict there is a battle worth fighting.
Grace that tells the sexually compromised Christian, “Do not make peace with what Christ died to free you from.”
Grace that does not merely cover yesterday...
but teaches us to walk differently tomorrow.
Maybe you have been waiting for the temptation to disappear before you become serious about holiness.
Do not wait.
Paul never promised Timothy that youthful passions would politely vanish.
He said:
Flee them. Pursue righteousness.
There will be nights when obedience feels expensive.
There will be moments when your body wants what your spirit knows you should refuse.
There will be times when nobody would discover what you did.
And in those moments, holiness becomes worship.
Not because resisting temptation earns salvation.
It cannot.
Christ saves.
But because the person purchased by Christ begins to understand:
I belong to Him.
That is Paul's argument.
Not:
“Your body is filthy.”
But:
Your body belongs to Christ.
Not:
“Sexual sinners can never come home.”
But:
Some of you were this—and you were washed.
Not:
“Become pure enough for Jesus to purchase you.”
But:
You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.
The order matters.
Grace first.
Then grateful obedience.
Christ's purchase.
Then our surrender.
Identity.
Then conduct.
The cross.
Then the transformed life.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years trying to reverse that order.
You thought:
If I can stay clean long enough, maybe Jesus will love me again.
No.
You fight from the reality of His grace, not toward the possibility of earning it.
You confess because Christ is merciful.
You flee because Christ is worthy.
You pursue holiness because you belong to Him.
And when you fall, you do not build a house in the mud.
You repent.
You get up.
You return to Christ.
You seek help.
You learn where the trap was.
You remove access.
You rebuild boundaries.
And you keep walking.
No more negotiating with the thing trying to enslave you.
No more asking temptation what terms it will accept.
No more standing beside the doorway pretending you are strong enough.
Run.
Run toward Scripture.
Run toward prayer.
Run toward trustworthy Christian community.
Run toward confession.
Run toward accountability.
Run toward the cross.
Run toward Jesus.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to know that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.

Not every act of sharing glorifies God merely because Christian content is involved. But when you sincerely spread biblical truth because you want Christ known, believers strengthened, and struggling people called toward repentance and grace, even something as ordinary as sharing a message can become an act offered to God's glory.
Following keeps these messages near you.
Saving keeps truth available when the battle returns.
Commenting reminds struggling believers that they are not fighting alone.
Tagging puts truth in front of someone you personally care about.
Sharing carries the message beyond the people we could ever reach ourselves.
But before you leave this article...
remember the command.
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Flee sexual immorality.
Paul did not say run because there is no hope for you.
He told you to run because you belong to Someone worth running for.
You were bought with a price.
You are not fighting for permission to approach the cross.
You are running from the chains because the crucified and risen Christ has called you His.
So when temptation whispers tonight...
when the screen lights up...
when the message arrives...
when loneliness starts rewriting your convictions...
when your flesh says, Just once...
when secrecy says, Nobody will ever know...
remember who paid for you.
Then run.
Not merely away from sin.
Run toward the Savior whose scars prove that your soul was worth pursuing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: TWO DESPERATE MOTHERS MADE A HORRIFYING AGREEMENT DURING THE SIEGE OF SAMARIA
paragraphs: TWO DESPERATE MOTHERS MADE A HORRIFYING AGREEMENT DURING THE SIEGE OF SAMARIA

One mother kept her terrible promise. The other hid her son. But buried inside one of the Bible’s darkest stories is a warning about what happens when desperation replaces trust in God—and a breathtaking picture of the God who can bring abundance to a city that has reached the end of itself.
There are Bible stories we love to put on walls.
David facing Goliath.
Daniel among the lions.
Moses before the Red Sea.
Jesus calming the storm.
And then there are passages like this one.
Passages we read once...
and wish we had not seen.
Because 2 Kings 6 takes us inside a starving city and introduces us to two mothers who had become so desperate that they made an agreement almost impossible to comprehend.
One of their children would die today.
The other would die tomorrow.
They would eat them.
And one mother actually kept her side of the agreement.
Read that again slowly.
Not because the horror should entertain us.
Because Scripture refuses to lie about how far human suffering and rebellion can descend.
Samaria was under siege.
Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had surrounded the city. Nothing was getting through. Food disappeared. Prices became grotesque. Hunger began stripping away the normal rhythms of civilization.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיְהִי רָעָב גָּדוֹל בְּשֹׁמְרוֹן
Vayehi ra'av gadol beShomron.
“And there was a great famine in Samaria.”
That word רָעָב — ra'av means famine, hunger.
But by the time the biblical narrator brings us to these two women, “hunger” almost feels too small a word.
A donkey's head had become extraordinarily expensive. Even something translated as “dove's dung”—whose precise identification has been debated—was being sold at a desperate price.
This wasn't skipping dinner.
This wasn't an empty refrigerator.
This was civilization collapsing one stomach at a time.
Then the king of Israel was walking along the city wall when a woman screamed to him for help.
“Help me, my lord the king!”
Imagine her voice.
Maybe cracked from dehydration.
Maybe trembling.
Maybe furious.
Maybe carrying a grief so deep she didn't even know how to cry anymore.
The king's response was revealing:
“If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you?”
He had no grain.
No wine.
No solution.
A king was standing above a starving woman wearing a crown that could not save her.
And there is something painfully familiar about that.
We keep discovering things we thought could save us...
until the siege comes.
Money feels powerful until money cannot fix what is broken.
Influence feels powerful until influence cannot quiet your conscience.
Pleasure feels powerful until you are alone after midnight and the emptiness returns.
People feel powerful until the person you built your identity around walks away.
Religion can even become something we hide behind until suffering tears open the costume and reveals whether we actually know God.
The king asked the woman what was wrong.
And then came the sentence that must have frozen him where he stood.
She explained that another woman had proposed an agreement:
אֶת־בְּנֵךְ וְנֹאכְלֶנּוּ הַיּוֹם וְאֶת־בְּנִי נֹאכַל מָחָר
In context:
“Your son... we will eat him today, and my son we will eat tomorrow.”
Then she continued.
וַנְּבַשֵּׁל אֶת־בְּנִי וַנֹּאכְלֵהוּ
Vannevashel et-beni vannokhelehu.
“We boiled my son and ate him.”
There are sentences in Scripture that should never become ordinary to us.
This is one of them.
A mother had once carried that little boy inside her.
She had felt him move.
She had given birth to him.
Perhaps she had held him through fever.
Perhaps she knew exactly how he sounded when he laughed.
Perhaps she had watched him sleep.
And somehow starvation had brought her to a place where the child she once fed from her own body became food for hers.
Then came the next day.
She went to the other mother.
It was time for the second woman to fulfill her promise.
But the text says:
וַתַּחְבִּא אֶת־בְּנָהּ
Vattachbi et-benah.
“She hid her son.”
And suddenly the first mother was standing before the king demanding justice.
Think about how broken everything had become.
The complaint wasn't simply, “My child is dead.”
Her grievance was essentially:
“I kept the agreement. She didn't.”
That is how distorted suffering can make the human heart.
And before we stand safely outside this story and condemn these women as monsters, we should notice what Scripture is doing.
The Bible had warned Israel that covenant rebellion could eventually bring siege conditions of precisely this horrifying kind.
Deuteronomy 28:53 warned of a time when, under siege and distress, people would eat “the fruit of your womb.”
The Hebrew is devastating:
וְאָכַלְתָּ פְרִי־בִטְנְךָ
Ve'akhaltā peri-vitnekha.
“You shall eat the fruit of your womb.”
Leviticus 26:29 likewise warned:
וַאֲכַלְתֶּם בְּשַׂר בְּנֵיכֶם וּבְשַׂר בְּנֹתֵיכֶם
“You shall eat the flesh of your sons and the flesh of your daughters.”
This does not make the women's actions morally good.
It makes the scene even more terrifying.
The covenant warnings were no longer distant words.
The warning had walked into Samaria.
The warning had entered someone's kitchen.
The warning had become a mother's testimony before the king.
Sin always promises freedom before revealing the chains.
That is still how it works.
Nobody wakes up planning to destroy everything precious.
Compromise usually arrives quietly.
Just this once.
Nobody will know.
You deserve this.
You can stop whenever you want.
God understands.
Tomorrow you'll repent.
And tomorrow becomes next month.
Next month becomes next year.
The secret becomes a habit.
The habit becomes a master.
And eventually you look around at the wreckage and wonder:
“How did I get here?”
Maybe your siege doesn't look like Samaria.
Maybe nobody sees yours at all.
Maybe your siege happens when the bedroom door closes.
Maybe it's pornography you promised Jesus you would stop watching.
Maybe bitterness toward somebody has lived inside you so long that hatred now feels justified.
Maybe you smile at church while privately wondering whether you still believe anything you sing.
Maybe your marriage looks alive publicly and feels dead privately.
Maybe success has become your god.
Maybe you're exhausted from pretending.
Maybe there is something hidden on your phone, in your relationship, in your bank statements, in your thoughts, or inside your heart that you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
And somewhere along the way, you started making agreements with desperation.
“I'll compromise this once.”
“I'll hide this.”
“I'll become this person just to survive.”
“I'll deal with God later.”
Listen carefully.
The terrifying lesson of Samaria is not merely that desperate people can do unimaginable things.
It is that when humanity moves farther and farther from God, things we once thought impossible can eventually become negotiable.
But the story does not end with the mothers.
Thank God.
Because while Samaria was collapsing, God was not absent.
The king tore his clothes when he heard the woman's story.
Underneath his royal garments was sackcloth.
He was grieving.
But grief is not necessarily repentance.
Instead of humbling himself before God, the king turned his rage toward Elisha.
He wanted the prophet dead.
That is another frightening possibility.
Sometimes when God's Word exposes us, we would rather attack the messenger than surrender to the message.
We blame the church.
We blame our spouse.
We blame our childhood.
We blame Christians who disappointed us.
We blame circumstances.
Sometimes we even blame God.
Anything except saying the words that heaven is waiting to hear:
“Lord... I have sinned.”
Yet right there, when everything looked irrecoverable, Elisha announced something outrageous.
“Listen to the word of the LORD.”
Tomorrow...
food.
Tomorrow...
abundance.
Tomorrow...
the market that had been destroyed by famine would change.
Not eventually.
Not after a military campaign lasting six months.
Tomorrow.
One royal officer essentially laughed at the possibility.
Even if God opened windows in heaven, could something like that happen?
He could see the siege.
He could calculate the food shortage.
He could measure the impossibility.
What he could not calculate was God.
And while Samaria slept hungry, something was happening outside the walls.
Four marginalized men went toward the Aramean camp expecting that they might die.
Instead, they discovered something unbelievable.
The camp was abandoned.
Scripture tells us that the Lord had caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army.
They panicked.
They fled.
They left food behind.
They left possessions behind.
They left everything.
Samaria thought salvation required an army.
God used a sound.
The starving city thought the enemy was still surrounding them.
The enemy had already run away.
Don't miss that.
There were people inside Samaria starving beside a provision they did not yet know existed.
And perhaps somebody reading this feels exactly like that spiritually.
You think your sin has the final word.
You think what you did is too ugly.
You think your addiction has owned you too long.
You think your marriage has gone too far.
You think God is tired of hearing you repent.
You think the years you wasted have permanently disqualified you.
You think the scandal became your identity.
But the Gospel announces something greater than self-improvement.
Jesus Christ entered our famine.
He entered our broken world.
He came to sinners who could not rescue themselves.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And on the third day...
the tomb was empty.
Christianity is not the announcement that bad people can polish themselves until God tolerates them.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required what we could never provide for ourselves.
Yet God's love is so astonishing that Christ came willingly.
That is why the Gospel can look directly at your worst chapter without looking away.
The cross has already seen scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
A thief died beside Him.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The woman caught in adultery was dragged into public shame.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
Again and again, Jesus met people at places they probably wished could be erased from their stories.
And He did not call darkness light.
He called sinners to repentance...
and offered grace.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not Jesus saying, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace is Jesus calling us out of the grave.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
We could never pay.
It is the turning of the sinner toward the Savior who alone can save.
The mothers of Samaria show us where human desperation can descend.
The empty Aramean camp shows us how quickly God can overturn circumstances.
But the cross shows us something infinitely greater:
what God has done about humanity's deepest siege.
Sin.
Guilt.
Judgment.
Death.
The Gospel does not promise that following Jesus means every earthly famine disappears tomorrow.
Christians suffer.
Christians grieve.
Christians bury people they love.
Christians walk through seasons when heaven seems painfully quiet.
So don't turn 2 Kings 7 into a formula saying every crisis will disappear within twenty-four hours.
That isn't what the text promises us.
What Scripture gives us is better than a formula.
It gives us God.
A God whose Word remains true when circumstances scream otherwise.
A God who is not defeated by impossible situations.
And ultimately, a Savior whose resurrection guarantees that sin and death will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Maybe that is why this disturbing story has found you today.
Not so you can stare at two desperate mothers from thousands of years ago.
But so you will ask what desperation has been doing inside you.
What have you been feeding that is slowly consuming what you love?
What compromise have you renamed “survival”?
What sin have you protected because surrender feels too expensive?
What have you hidden?
Who have you blamed?
How long have you been standing behind the walls of your own Samaria, starving spiritually while refusing to come home to God?
You do not need another disguise.
You need Jesus.
Not religious performance.
Jesus.
Not another promise that you'll fix yourself next Monday.
Jesus.
Not another carefully edited Christian image.
Jesus.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is mercy for the ashamed.
There is cleansing for the guilty.
There is restoration for the broken.
There is a new identity stronger than the worst thing you have ever done.
Your scandal does not become good.
Grace does something better.
Grace refuses to let the scandal have the final sentence.
That is why we keep saying it:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the ugly pages never happened.
But by taking ruined people and making them trophies of mercy.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a spiritual speech. Just be honest.
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may desperately need evidence that God still restores broken lives.
Don't underestimate what your testimony can do in another person's midnight.
And don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not as a superstition. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. Salvation is by grace; a Facebook share cannot purchase it.
Supporting a ministry does not make God love you more.
Sharing does not earn heaven.
Jesus purchased salvation—not us.
But when Christ has given us good news, we can gladly help carry that good news to others.
If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, stay close.
Because there may come a night when you need to remember that the situation screaming “finished” is not sovereign.
God is.
And before you leave, remember the two mothers.
Remember the starving city.
Remember the abandoned enemy camp.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Samaria's darkest night was not proof that God had ceased to be God.
And your darkest chapter does not possess the authority to write the ending of your story.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Bring the guilt.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the anger.
Bring the shame.
Bring the shattered marriage.
Bring the questions.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the secret you wish you could erase.
Bring yourself.
Not to an algorithm.
Not to a ministry.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
