Bring yourself to Jesus Christ.
It is pointing another human soul toward the Savior.
The chapter that makes you ashamed to tell your story may become the very place where people someday see how fiercely Christ's grace pursued you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE CROSSED THE EARTH WITH QUESTIONS—THEN JESUS REVEALED WHY HER JOURNEY STILL MATTERS
paragraphs: SHE CROSSED THE EARTH WITH QUESTIONS—THEN JESUS REVEALED WHY HER JOURNEY STILL MATTERS

The Queen of Sheba came carrying gold, spices, and questions. But what took her breath away was something money could never purchase—and centuries later, Jesus Christ used her journey to confront every soul that keeps asking questions while refusing to come to the Truth.
She had everything powerful people are supposed to have.
Wealth.
Influence.
An entourage large enough to announce her importance before she ever spoke a word.

Camels moved toward Jerusalem carrying spices, enormous quantities of gold, and precious stones. Servants traveled with her. Resources surrounded her. Somewhere behind the royal appearance stood a woman accustomed to entering rooms where other people lowered their heads.
But she was traveling because there was something all her wealth could not give her.
Answers.
And perhaps that is where her story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because you can have money and still lie awake wondering why your heart feels empty.
You can have people admiring you and secretly wonder whether anybody actually knows you.
You can smile in church while carrying questions you are afraid to say aloud.
You can quote Scripture while privately wrestling with disappointment.
You can believe God exists and still whisper in the darkness:
“Lord... where are You?”
“Why did You allow this?”
“Why didn't You answer me?”
“Why am I still fighting the same temptation?”
“Why did they leave?”
“Why did I lose what I prayed so desperately to keep?”
“Can You forgive what I have done?”
“Can someone like me really begin again?”
The Bible does not introduce the Queen of Sheba as a woman without questions.
It introduces her as a woman willing to travel with them.
And that changes everything.
The Hebrew text of 1 Kings 10:1 says:
“וּמַלְכַּת־שְׁבָא שֹׁמַעַת אֶת־שֵׁמַע שְׁלֹמֹה לְשֵׁם יְהוָה וַתָּבֹא לְנַסֹּתוֹ בְּחִידוֹת”
U-malkat Sheva shoma'at et-shema Shelomoh... vattavo lenassoto beḥidot.
The final word matters:
בְּחִידוֹת — beḥidot.
It is the plural of ḥidah and can refer to riddles, enigmas, difficult or perplexing questions.
She did not travel all that distance for small talk.
She came to test Solomon.
She had heard about his extraordinary wisdom in connection with the name of the LORD, and she wanted to discover whether what she had heard could survive examination.
That is important because biblical faith is not presented here as terror of sincere questions.
The woman came questioning.
She came testing.
She came searching.
And Scripture does not hide it.
But then 1 Kings 10:2 gives us a sentence that may be even more beautiful:
She spoke to Solomon about all that was in her heart.
Not merely politics.
Not merely philosophy.
Not merely royal trivia.
Her heart entered the conversation.
That is where some of us stop.
We will bring God our church vocabulary.
We will bring Him our Sunday clothes.
We will bring Him carefully edited prayers.
We will bring Him the version of ourselves we think Christians are supposed to display.
But we are terrified to bring Him what is actually in our hearts.
The resentment.
The lust.
The envy.
The doubt.
The grief.
The secret habit.
The anger toward someone who hurt us.
The disappointment with God that we would never dare admit publicly.
The shame attached to something we did years ago.
The question we think a “good Christian” should have stopped asking by now.
So we polish the outside while something inside us is bleeding.
The Queen of Sheba arrived with treasure...
but she also arrived with questions.
Maybe you need to hear this today:
Stop pretending before God.
He already knows.
The God who sees your public worship also sees the private war.
The God who hears the prayer you speak aloud also knows the sentence you were too ashamed to finish.
You do not shock an omniscient God by finally telling Him the truth.
Bring Him what is in your heart.
But there is another side to this story, and we must not miss it.
The Queen did not merely want her skepticism protected.
She was willing to have her assumptions overturned.
That is the difference between searching for truth and merely searching for arguments that protect what we already want to believe.
She traveled.
She listened.
She observed.
She tested.
Then she allowed the evidence before her to change what she believed.
Solomon answered her questions. She saw his wisdom, his house, his table, his servants, their order and attire, and his relationship to the worship of the LORD.
Then Scripture gives us an extraordinary Hebrew expression:
וְלֹא־הָיָה בָהּ עוֹד רוּחַ
ve-lo hayah vah od ruaḥ.
Literally, there was no more ruaḥ—breath, wind, spirit—in her.
She was overwhelmed.
Breathless.
The woman who arrived prepared to examine Solomon found herself stunned by what she encountered.
Then something beautiful happened.
Her amazement did not terminate on Solomon.
She said:
“Blessed be the LORD your God.”
That matters.
Because Solomon's wisdom was never supposed to make Solomon the ultimate object of worship.
The gift was supposed to point beyond the gifted man to the Giver.

She recognized that Solomon's throne and wisdom existed within the LORD's purposes for Israel, and 1 Kings 10:9 connects his kingship with God's enduring love for Israel and with the responsibility to practice justice and righteousness.
And here the story could end beautifully.
A foreign queen hears.
She travels.
She questions.
She sees.
She becomes overwhelmed.
She blesses the LORD.
But Jesus refused to let the story remain safely buried in Israel's history.
Centuries passed.
Solomon died.
His magnificent kingdom fractured.
The gold lost its shine.
The palace could not preserve him.
And Solomon himself, despite extraordinary God-given wisdom, was still a fallen man. Scripture later records the tragedy of his heart being turned away through his loves and compromises.
Human wisdom had shown its limit.
Human kingship had shown its limit.
Human glory had shown its limit.
Then Jesus came.
And suddenly the Queen of Sheba's journey became far more than an ancient royal visit.
Jesus Himself reached back into this story.
In Matthew 12:42 He spoke about the Queen of the South coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom.
Then He said words that completely change how Christians must read this story:
“καὶ ἰδοὺ πλεῖον Σολομῶνος ὧδε.”
Kai idou pleion Solomōnos hōde.
“And behold, something greater than Solomon is here.”
Greater than Solomon.
Jesus did not point His hearers backward and say, “If only Solomon were still here.”
He pointed to Himself.
Solomon possessed wisdom given by God.
Christ is greater than Solomon.
Solomon sat upon Israel's throne for a season.
Christ is the promised Son of David whose kingdom reaches beyond the temporary splendor of an earthly palace.
Solomon could answer extraordinary questions.
Jesus answers humanity's deepest catastrophe.
Sin.
Guilt.
Alienation from God.
Judgment.
Death.
Solomon could tell a queen what she did not know.
Jesus came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And this is where the story stops being comfortable.
Because Jesus' reference to the Queen of the South was not merely admiration.
It was a warning.
She traveled from far away because she heard there was wisdom in Jerusalem.
Yet the people standing before Jesus had Someone greater than Solomon in their midst.
She moved toward the light she had received.
They were in danger of rejecting greater light standing directly before them.
Think about that.
She traveled an enormous distance to hear Solomon.
Some of us will not cross the distance between our pride and repentance to come to Christ.
She brought difficult questions.
We sometimes use difficult questions as barricades.
She investigated what she heard.
She admitted that what she had heard was not even half of what she discovered.
We sometimes encounter Christ repeatedly and remain determined to keep Him at a safe religious distance.
That is the knife-edge of this story.
Your questions are not necessarily the greatest danger to your soul.
Sometimes the greater danger is deciding beforehand that no answer will ever be allowed to change you.
There is a difference between saying, “Jesus, I don't understand—teach me,” and saying, “Jesus, I will only follow You if You agree with everything I have already decided.”
One is the posture of a disciple.
The other tries to put God on trial while refusing to let God examine us.
And eventually the questions turn around.
You came asking whether Christianity is true.
But sooner or later Christ confronts you with another question:
What will you do with Me?
You came asking why the world is broken.
Christ begins exposing the brokenness inside your own heart.
You came asking why people are hypocrites.
Christ asks what you have been hiding.
You came asking why God allows evil.
Then His holiness forces you to confront the evil you have excused when it benefited you.
You came looking for an argument.
You discovered a mirror.
And suddenly...
there is no more breath in you.
Because the Gospel does something human pride hates.
It tells us that our deepest problem is not merely ignorance.
We are sinners in need of reconciliation with a holy God.
We cannot purchase our innocence.
We cannot outperform our guilt.
We cannot decorate our way into heaven.
We cannot carry enough gold into Jerusalem to ransom our own souls.
But this is exactly where scandal becomes grace.
Because the King greater than Solomon did something Solomon never could.
Jesus did not merely sit upon a throne waiting for broken people to make the journey to Him.
He came for us.
The eternal Son entered our humanity.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He received the rejected.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called sinners to repentance.
And then the innocent Christ went to the cross.
The King wore thorns.
The righteous One was treated as condemned.
The sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
The One greater than Solomon did not simply answer our difficult questions.
He carried our guilt.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was insignificant.
And grace did not mean that holiness disappeared.
Christ bore sin's judgment so that forgiveness could be offered to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
Then death itself received a question it could not answer.
The tomb received Jesus...
and could not keep Him.
He rose.
That is Christianity's staggering announcement.
Not “become slightly more religious.”
Not “clean yourself up enough for God to tolerate you.”
Not “hide your scandal carefully so church people never discover it.”
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Receive grace.
Be forgiven.
Be made new.
The Queen of Sheba brought Solomon what was in her heart.
What would happen if tonight you finally brought Jesus what is in yours?
Not the edited version.
Everything.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I have doubts.”
“Jesus, I am addicted.”
“Jesus, I have been pretending.”
“Jesus, I don't know how to repair what I destroyed.”
“Jesus, I am tired of hiding.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There are people reading these words who have mastered appearing fine.
Your family thinks you're fine.
Your Facebook friends think you're fine.
People at church think you're fine.
Maybe even your spouse thinks you're fine.
But you know what happens when the room gets quiet.
You know the memory.
You know the browser history.
You know the bitterness.
You know the compromise.
You know the prayer you stopped praying because hope became painful.
And Christ knows too.
Yet the Gospel invitation remains.
Come.
Not because your sin does not matter.
Come because Christ is sufficient for sinners who repent and trust Him.
Maybe your hardest question was never, “Can God explain everything to me?”
Maybe it was:
“After everything I have done, would Jesus still receive me?”
Look toward the cross.
That is where Christianity tells you to search for the answer.
The Gospel is not the story of impressive people climbing high enough to reach God.
It is the announcement that God acted in Christ to save sinners who could never save themselves.
So bring your questions.
But bring your heart too.
Bring your doubts.
But bring your willingness to surrender when truth confronts you.
Bring your wounds.
Bring your failures.
Bring your secret history.
Bring the chapter you wish could be ripped from your story.
Jesus is greater than Solomon.
And He is not merely offering you information.
He calls you to Himself.
We glorify God through lives of faith, obedience, love, worship, generosity, and witness.
Do not keep every Gospel resource inside the walls of people who already agree with you.
Let the searching person see it.
Let the exhausted believer see it.
Let the person who hasn't entered a church for years see it.
Let the person carrying shame see it.
Let the skeptic with difficult questions see it.
Let the lukewarm Christian see it.
Let someone discover that Christianity is not frightened by honest questions—and that ultimately the Christian hope is not found in Solomon's wisdom, but in Jesus Christ.
It is simply a practical way to support Gospel Warrior's continued work while receiving deeper discipleship content, biblical nourishment, spiritual sharpening, encouragement, and accountability.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous before God.
Perhaps they have gold in their hands but emptiness in their heart.
Perhaps they look successful while privately falling apart.
Perhaps they have spent years testing Christianity from a distance.
Perhaps they are waiting for permission to bring everything in their heart before Jesus.
The Queen of Sheba traveled from the ends of the earth because she heard about the wisdom of Solomon.
You do not need a caravan.
You do not need camels carrying gold.
You do not need precious stones.
You do not need to become respectable enough to approach Christ.
You need to come.
And when you come, remember the words of Jesus:
Someone greater than Solomon is here.
Your questions may have started the journey.
But Jesus is the destination.
And maybe the greatest surprise awaiting you is not that Christ can answer every question you carry...
but that while you were searching for answers, the Savior was exposing the deeper question of your heart:
Will you trust Me?
Bring Him what is in your heart.
Even the scandal.
Especially the scandal.
Because the cross declares that your darkest chapter does not have to be the final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.

You may have come carrying a thousand questions—but when you truly encounter the King greater than Solomon, the question that follows you home is whether you can ever again live as though you never met Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHERE YOUR MONEY GOES WHEN NOBODY IS WATCHING MAY BE REVEALING WHERE YOUR HEART HAS ALREADY GONE
paragraphs:
WHERE YOUR MONEY GOES WHEN NOBODY IS WATCHING MAY BE REVEALING WHERE YOUR HEART HAS ALREADY GONE
Jesus Wasn’t Merely Talking About Money When He Said, “Where Your Treasure Is, There Your Heart Will Be Also.” He Was Exposing the Invisible Direction of the Human Heart.
There is a frightening possibility that most of us would rather not consider.
Your heart may already be living somewhere your mouth would never admit.
You can say Jesus is first.
You can sing that Jesus is enough.
You can post Scripture, attend church, pray before meals, call yourself blessed, and tell everyone that God is the center of your life...
while quietly arranging your entire existence around something else.
And Jesus knew that.
That is why He said something so simple that we can read it in seconds...
and spend the rest of our lives trying to escape what it exposes.
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
— Matthew 6:21, KJV
In the Greek text:
ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου.
hopou gar estin ho thēsauros sou, ekei estai kai hē kardia sou.
A straightforward rendering is:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not merely say, “Where your heart is, there your treasure will go.”
He said your heart will be where your treasure is.
That should make us uncomfortable.
Because suddenly this verse is not just something beautiful to print on a coffee mug.
It is diagnostic.
It is a mirror.
It asks a question many Christians spend years avoiding:
Where is your treasure actually going?
Because Jesus says your heart is going there too.
Maybe that is why this passage can hurt so deeply when we stop quoting it and actually allow it to examine us.
Look at what receives your best energy.
Look at what receives your money.
Look at what receives your attention.
Look at what occupies your imagination when the room gets quiet.
Look at what you are terrified of losing.
Look at what makes you jealous when somebody else has it.
Look at what you continually sacrifice for.
Look at what you cannot imagine being happy without.
Look at what you protect when obedience to Jesus threatens it.
And somewhere in those answers...
you may find your treasure.
And somewhere near your treasure...
Jesus says you will find your heart.

That does not mean spending money on a house, clothing, food, recreation, a business, your family, or ordinary earthly responsibilities is automatically sinful. Scripture does not teach that material possessions themselves are evil.
The danger is deeper.
The danger begins when a gift becomes a god.
When something God created becomes something we cannot live without.
When provision becomes identity.
When stewardship becomes possession.
When enjoyment becomes worship.
When “I have this” quietly becomes...
“I need this to be okay.”
That is why we have to hear Matthew 6:21 inside the sermon Jesus was actually preaching.
Just before these words, Christ says:
“Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal.”
— Matthew 6:19–20, KJV
Then comes the sentence that exposes us:
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
Jesus contrasts treasure that can disappear with treasure that cannot.
Earthly treasure is vulnerable.
Heavenly treasure is secure.
And that truth has not become less relevant with time.
We simply have different moths now.
Different thieves.
Different ways of losing what we thought would make us whole.
The account balance can change.
The business can collapse.
The career can disappear.
The body you worked so hard to perfect will age.
The applause can stop.
The person whose approval became your oxygen can leave.
The possessions can break.
The followers can unfollow.
The algorithm can forget your name.
The house eventually belongs to somebody else.
The clothes wear out.
The trophies gather dust.
And eventually...
someone else will clean out the room containing the things you once believed you could not live without.
That is not pessimism.
That is mortality.
And Jesus loves us too much to allow us to build our identity on something death can take away.
Perhaps that is why some losses hurt far beyond the value of what was lost.
Sometimes we are not merely grieving the thing.
We are discovering how much of our heart had been stored inside it.
The relationship ended...
and you did not know who you were anymore.
The money disappeared...
and your peace disappeared with it.
Someone criticized you...
and suddenly your entire sense of worth collapsed.
You were overlooked...
and bitterness began eating you alive.
Someone else succeeded...
and instead of celebrating them, something inside you whispered:
Why wasn’t that me?
That moment can reveal something.
Not necessarily that you are uniquely wicked.
But that the human heart is extraordinarily capable of turning good things into ultimate things.
And Scripture has been warning us about this from the beginning.
The problem is not merely that we possess treasures.
The problem is that treasures can possess us.
Jesus continues:
“The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness.”
— Matthew 6:22–23, KJV
And then He brings the confrontation home:
“No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon.”
— Matthew 6:24, KJV
There it is.
This was never merely financial advice.
It was about worship.
It was about mastery.
It was about allegiance.
It was about what sits on the throne of the heart.
And this is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Because idolatry does not always look like someone bowing before a statue.
Sometimes it looks like a Christian who cannot obey Jesus because obedience might cost too much.
Sometimes it looks like refusing generosity because security has become sacred.
Sometimes it looks like compromising truth because acceptance has become treasure.
Sometimes it looks like abandoning conviction because a relationship has become treasure.
Sometimes it looks like working yourself into spiritual emptiness because achievement has become treasure.
Sometimes it looks like needing strangers online to validate you because attention has become treasure.
Sometimes it even wears religious clothing.
Ministry can become treasure.
Recognition can become treasure.
Being considered “anointed” can become treasure.
Being right can become treasure.
A platform can become treasure.
Even serving God can become twisted into a way of making ourselves important.
And perhaps one of the hardest prayers a believer can pray is:
Jesus, show me what I would struggle to surrender if You asked for it.
Do not pray that casually.
Because the answer may reveal your treasure.
Imagine Christ standing beside everything you have spent years accumulating.
Your money.
Your plans.
Your reputation.
Your relationship.
Your career.
Your dreams.
Your possessions.
Your platform.
Your achievements.
Your future.
Then imagine Him asking:
“If following Me cost you this, would I still be enough?”
Something inside us wants to negotiate.
“Jesus, You know how hard I worked for this.”
“Jesus, You know how badly I need this.”
“Jesus, You know what I went through.”
“Jesus, surely You wouldn’t ask me to surrender that.”
And maybe He will not.
But the question remains:
Could He?
Does Jesus have permission to be Lord over the thing you treasure most?
Because Christianity is not adding Jesus to the collection of things we already worship.
Jesus does not come to become another ornament in our lives.
He comes as Lord.
And here is where this message could easily become cruel if we stop before the Gospel.
We could simply say:
“You love money too much.”
“You love approval too much.”
“You love possessions too much.”
“You love yourself too much.”
“Try harder.”
“Give more.”
“Be better.”
But that is not the good news.
The Gospel is not God standing over guilty people shouting, “Become worthy enough for Me.”
The Gospel announces that the One who exposes our disordered hearts came to rescue them.
The astonishing truth of Christianity is not merely that Jesus asks us where our treasure is.
It is that Jesus Christ became the treasure sinners did not deserve.
Paul writes:
— 2 Corinthians 8:9, KJV
Read that slowly.
For your sakes.
The eternal Son did not cling to earthly comfort.
Christ entered our poverty.
He entered suffering.
He entered rejection.
He entered humiliation.
He walked toward a cross.
Not because suffering itself was treasure...
but because He came in obedience to the Father to save sinners.
At Calvary, Jesus was stripped.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The world looked at Him and saw scandal.
God was accomplishing redemption.
Jesus carried our sins in His body on the tree.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The righteous One for the unrighteous.
The Savior died...
and rose again.
That changes everything.
Because now the question is no longer merely:
“What must I give up for God?”
The Gospel first confronts us with:
“Look at what God has given for sinners in Christ.”
Grace changes the economy of the heart.
We do not surrender earthly treasure so that Jesus will finally love us.
We surrender our idols because in Christ we have discovered Someone infinitely better.
We do not purchase forgiveness through generosity.
We do not buy salvation through donations.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
— Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
That distinction matters enormously.
Supporting Christian work can be an act of worship.
Generosity can glorify God.
Sharing biblical truth can serve others.
Helping ministries continue their work can be beautiful.
But none of those things purchases the favor of God.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So if you want to examine your treasure today, do not begin by asking how much money you should send somewhere.
Begin here:
Does Jesus have my heart?
Not my Christian vocabulary.
Not my Sunday morning.
Not my public image.
My heart.
The hidden one.
The frightened one.
The ambitious one.
The wounded one.
The jealous one.
The one that still wants people to notice.
The one that still wants control.
The one that sometimes trusts a bank balance more easily than a promise from God.
The one that sometimes says, “Jesus is enough,” while secretly whispering...
“Jesus plus this.”
Maybe that is what this article has exposed.
Your sentence has an extra word.
Jesus plus money.
Jesus plus success.
Jesus plus romance.
Jesus plus popularity.
Jesus plus comfort.
Jesus plus recognition.
Jesus plus the dream you refuse to surrender.
And Christ is gently but relentlessly bringing you back to the question:
If everything after the word “plus” disappeared, would Jesus still be your treasure?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because typing those words saves you.
It does not.
But because sometimes confession begins when we finally stop hiding.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer struggling to put Jesus above the thing their heart keeps running toward.
Not to perform spirituality.
Not to earn favor with God.
Sometimes glorifying God looks like refusing to keep life-giving biblical truth to ourselves and using what we have—including our voice, resources, and influence—to point someone toward Christ.
Because the treasure test is not something we take once.
Success may require you to take it again.
Loss may require you to take it again.
Temptation may require you to take it again.
And one day, when something created begins demanding the devotion that belongs to the Creator, you may need to return to the words:
“Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
But remember why this matters.
Buying something does not make God love you more.
Supporting Gospel Warrior does not purchase spiritual blessing.
Christ alone saves.
Where is your treasure?
Not where should it be.
Not where do you tell people it is.
Where is it?
Follow the trail.
Follow your attention.
Follow your sacrifices.
Follow your anxieties.
Follow your deepest fear of loss.
Follow what you protect at almost any cost.
Eventually...
you may find your heart standing there.
And if what you discover embarrasses you, do not run away from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Repentance is not the end of your story.
Peter failed.
The thief on the cross had nothing left to offer.
Paul carried a history he could never erase.
The Gospel is filled with people whose stories should have ended in shame.
Then Jesus entered them.
Scandal met grace.
Guilt met forgiveness.
Bondage met freedom.
Death met resurrection.
And sinners discovered that Christ does not merely rearrange priorities.
He gives new hearts.
Maybe your treasure has been misplaced.
Maybe your heart has wandered.
Maybe something temporary has occupied a throne it was never created to hold.
Then bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Repent.
Trust Christ.
Ask Him to teach you to hold temporary things with open hands and eternal things with a tighter grip.
And then live like someone whose greatest treasure cannot be stolen.
Because if Christ is your treasure, bankruptcy cannot take Him.
Rejection cannot take Him.
Cancer cannot take Him.
A broken relationship cannot take Him.
A collapsing career cannot take Him.
Age cannot take Him.
The grave itself cannot take Him.
Paul could therefore write:
— Philippians 1:21, KJV
Only someone with an indestructible treasure can speak like that.
That is the freedom Jesus is calling us toward.
Not poverty for poverty’s sake.
Not shame over every possession.
Not performative generosity.
Freedom.
Freedom to own without being owned.
Freedom to give without terror.
Freedom to lose without losing yourself.
Freedom to celebrate another person’s blessing.
Freedom to stop performing.
Freedom to stop proving.
Freedom to say:
Everything I have belongs to God, but nothing I have is God.
Then send this to somebody you love.
Share it publicly if you believe your Facebook friends need this reminder.
But above everything else...
Treasure Christ.
Because one day your hands will release everything they are currently holding.
And when that day comes, the greatest question will not be how much treasure you managed to leave behind...
but whether your heart had already found the Treasure death could never take away.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why Sin Keeps Paying You Even When It Looks Harmless
paragraphs: THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why Sin Keeps Paying You Even When It Looks Harmless

Romans 6:23 is one of the most quoted verses in Christianity—and one of the most terrifyingly misunderstood. Because sin rarely hands you its bill when you first say yes. It lets you enjoy the purchase first.
There are some things you would never have done if you had known what they were going to cost you.
If you had known that one secret conversation would eventually fracture your marriage…
If you had known that one “harmless” habit would become something you could no longer control…
If you had known that bitterness would keep the person who hurt you living inside your mind rent-free for years…
If you had known that the private compromise nobody could see would slowly change the person looking back at you in the mirror…
Maybe you would have walked away.
But that is one of sin’s oldest strategies.
It rarely shows you the funeral while it is inviting you to the party.
It shows you the pleasure.
It hides the paycheck.
And then Paul writes one sentence that tears the disguise off the entire system:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Romans 6:23, KJV.
Read it again.
Not merely the “consequences.”
Not merely the “possibilities.”
The wages.
The Greek text begins:
Τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος
Ta gar opsōnia tēs hamartias thanatos.
“For the wages of sin [is] death.”
That word translated “wages” is ὀψώνια — opsōnia.
It could refer to pay, compensation, provisions, or wages, and it was associated especially with what was due for service, including a soldier’s pay.
Paul’s choice of language is devastating.
Because a wage is not a random gift.
A wage is something paid.
Something earned.
Something due in connection with service.
And that matters because Romans 6 is not merely discussing isolated bad decisions. Paul has been describing two competing masters—sin and obedience, slavery and freedom, death and righteousness.
Earlier he asks:
“Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey…?”
Romans 6:16.
That changes how Romans 6:23 lands.
Sin is not merely something you occasionally “do.”
Paul personifies sin as a cruel master.
And the master pays.
That is the hook buried inside the verse that should make every human heart uncomfortable:
Everybody gets paid by the master they serve.
The problem is that sin’s paycheck often arrives long after the pleasure.
That is why sin can look harmless.
The first drink does not show you the addiction.
The first flirtation does not show you the divorce papers.
The first lie does not show you the life you will eventually have to construct to protect it.
The first pornographic image does not show you distorted intimacy.
The first act of revenge does not show you the bitterness that may eventually consume your peace.
The first compromise does not introduce itself by saying, “Hello. I have come to harden your heart.”
It says…
“It’s only once.”
“Nobody knows.”
“You deserve this.”
“You can stop whenever you want.”
“Everybody does it.”
“It isn’t hurting anybody.”
And perhaps the most dangerous:
“God will forgive you anyway.”
Grace is real.
But using grace as permission to embrace the very slavery Christ died to free us from is not freedom.
Paul confronted that distortion at the beginning of Romans 6:
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Romans 6:1–2.
The Greek is even more forceful in its brevity:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
May it never be.
Paul will not allow grace to become an excuse for bondage.
Because Jesus did not bleed so that we could become comfortable prisoners.
He came to set captives free.
And maybe this is where the article stops being about “those people.”
Maybe this is where it finds you.
Because some sins do not look scandalous.
Some wear respectable clothes.
Nobody knows about the jealousy you feed.
Nobody sees what you watch after midnight.
Nobody hears the conversations you replay because you still fantasize about proving somebody wrong.
Nobody knows how much approval controls you.
Nobody sees the pride underneath your ministry.
Nobody knows that you have learned how to lift your hands in worship while refusing to forgive someone in your heart.
Nobody knows what you delete.
What you hide.
What you justify.
What you keep promising God you will surrender “eventually.”
You can fool your spouse.
You can fool your church.
You can fool your followers.
You can even become frighteningly skilled at fooling yourself.
But sin is still paying wages.
Sometimes the payment begins showing up before physical death.
A damaged conscience.
Broken trust.
Spiritual numbness.
Enslaving habits.
Destroyed relationships.
Shame.
Fear.
Isolation.
A heart increasingly comfortable living far from God.

We should be careful here, because Romans 6:23 should not be reduced merely to earthly psychological consequences. Paul’s word is θάνατος — thanatos: death. Within the argument of Romans, sin ultimately leads to death in contrast with the eternal life God gives in Christ.
The deepest problem with sin is not merely that it can ruin your circumstances.
Sin separates rebellious humanity from the holy God who is our life.
That is why the Gospel is infinitely greater than self-improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people nicer.
We needed resurrection.
And now comes perhaps the most beautiful word in the entire verse.
Paul could have written:
“The wages of sin is death, and the wages of righteousness is eternal life.”
But he did not.
Look at the contrast:
Τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος, τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.
Ta gar opsōnia tēs hamartias thanatos, to de charisma tou theou zōē aiōnios en Christō Iēsou tō kyriō hēmōn.
“For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Do you see the contrast?
ὀψώνια — wages.
Then:
χάρισμα — gift.
Sin pays wages.
God gives a gift.
Death is what sin earns.
Eternal life is not a salary God owes us for behaving well.
It is χάρισμα — charisma: a gracious gift.
And where is that life found?
Paul does not say it is found in becoming religious enough.
Not in cleaning yourself up enough.
Not in donating enough.
Not in having Christian parents.
Not in church attendance.
Not in knowing theological vocabulary.
Not even in promising God that this time you really mean it.
It is:
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — en Christō Iēsou.
“In Christ Jesus.”
That is Christianity.
Not “try harder and maybe God will love you.”
Christ.
Not “hide your scandal until everyone thinks you are holy.”
Christ.
Not “pay God back.”
Christ.
Jesus Christ stepped into the wreckage sinners created.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore our sins in His body.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not pretend your sin was harmless.
The cross proves it was deadly serious.
But the cross also proves something else.
Your sin is not greater than the Savior.
That secret you are ashamed to name?
Christ already knows.
That chapter you wish you could tear from your history?
He knows.
That night?
He knows.
That betrayal?
He knows.
That addiction?
He knows.
That hypocrisy?
He knows.
That thing you did after telling God you would never do it again?
He knows.
And still the Gospel calls sinners to come.
Not to celebrate the chains.
To be freed from them.
Not to rename darkness.
To step into the Light.
Not merely to feel guilty.
To repent and believe.
Repentance is not God standing over you saying, “Become worthy enough for Me.”
Repentance is turning from the master who is killing you toward the King who died to save sinners.
Somebody reading this has been confusing conviction with rejection.
They are not the same thing.
When Scripture exposes your sin, the answer is not to run farther into hiding.
Run to Christ.
Remember Adam and Eve.
Sin entered.
Shame followed.
Then hiding.
That pattern is still painfully familiar.
We sin.
We become ashamed.
We hide.
And while hiding, we often sin again because the very place we run for relief becomes another prison.
But Jesus has always had a way of walking toward scandals everybody else wanted to whisper about.
A Samaritan woman with a complicated relationship history.
A tax collector despised by his community.
A woman caught in adultery.
Peter after denying Him.
A persecutor named Saul with blood on his reputation.
Christ did not redefine their darkness as light.
He did something far more beautiful.
He met sinners with truth and grace—and rewrote what their lives could become.
This is why our heartbeat remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners.
Peter's denial was real.
So was his restoration.
Paul's persecution of Christians was real.
So was the grace that transformed the persecutor into an apostle who would suffer for the Name he once tried to destroy.
The cross does not erase truth.
It changes what truth gets to say about your future when you belong to Christ.
Maybe your past says adulterer.
Maybe addict.
Maybe liar.
Maybe hypocrite.
Maybe angry.
Maybe sexually broken.
Maybe greedy.
Maybe self-righteous.
Maybe religious but spiritually empty.
Maybe you cannot even say the word for what happened.
Jesus is not intimidated by the chapter you are ashamed to read aloud.
But He loves you too much to tell you that the chains around your wrists are jewelry.
Sin still pays wages.
And the wage is still death.
Which means the loving thing is not to make peace with the prison.
The loving thing is to tell you where the door is.
Jesus.
Perhaps you have spent years asking God to remove consequences while secretly protecting the sin creating them.
“Lord, save my marriage…”
but you will not end the affair.
“Lord, give me peace…”
but you keep feeding the bitterness.
“Lord, restore my mind…”
but you continue returning to what poisons it.
“Lord, bring me closer…”
but you keep negotiating over the one thing He has already convicted you to surrender.
There comes a moment when prayer must become surrender.
Not because surrender purchases salvation.
It does not.
Christ purchased redemption.
But genuine faith does not make a treaty with the master Jesus came to overthrow.
So be honest right now.
What is sin paying you?
What looked harmless six months ago?
A year ago?
Ten years ago?
What has it already taken?
Your peace?
Your tenderness toward God?
Your marriage?
Your integrity?
Your ability to pray without immediately remembering what you are hiding?
What are you terrified it might take next?
And here is the question that may hurt most:
If the thing you keep defending is slowly destroying you, why are you still calling it freedom?
Do not answer publicly just to impress somebody.
But do answer God.
And if this exposed something you have kept buried, you do not need to write the details for strangers to inspect.
Let those words become more than engagement.
Let them become the beginning of an honest conversation with God.
Somebody still sitting inside the prison you escaped may need evidence that the door really opens.
But hear this carefully.
A comment cannot save you.
A share cannot save you.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. Salvation is by grace. Eternal life is God's gift in Christ.
But grace creates gratitude.
And gratitude moves.
If this truth helped you see Christ more clearly, do not let it die on your screen.
Not because sharing earns points with God.
Send it privately to the person you know is ashamed.
Share it with the believer who has grown numb.
Share it with the seeker who thinks Christianity is merely about behaving better.
Share it even with the person who does not yet believe, because perhaps Romans 6:23 will finally help them understand why Christians keep talking about sin, grace, the cross, and Jesus.
You never know which person scrolling alone tonight is one sentence away from finally admitting:
“I need Christ.”
Not for the algorithm.
For the night temptation comes back.
For the morning shame tells you there is no point praying anymore.
For the day your old life begins whispering that slavery was easier.
Come back and remember:
Sin pays.
Grace gives.
And Christ saves.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to prove your faith.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior is a requirement for glorifying God.
But because one practical way believers can glorify God is by willingly supporting faithful Gospel work and helping biblical truth reach people who may never walk through a church door.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
That library exists because discipleship should not stop when the post ends.
Who is your master?
Because every master has a destination.
Sin offers freedom and produces slavery.
It advertises pleasure and conceals death.
It gives you the experience first and sends the invoice later.
But Jesus does something completely different.
He tells you the truth about the cost.
Then He bears a cost you could never bear yourself.
And instead of handing you the wage your rebellion deserves, God offers eternal life as His gift in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is grace.
Scandal does not become grace because sin stops being scandalous.
Scandal becomes a story of grace when a sinner meets the Savior.
So stop negotiating with what is killing you.
Stop decorating the chains.
Stop calling the prison home.
Bring the secret into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Return.
And when shame whispers, “After everything you've done, how could Jesus possibly want you?”
Look toward the cross.
Then look toward the empty tomb.
The answer is not that your sin was small.
The answer is that your Savior is greater.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“No more hiding.”
And if Christ has already rewritten a chapter of your story, tell us what He did. Your testimony may become the hand that points another wounded person toward the Savior.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is enjoying what sin promised them…
and they still have not seen the paycheck coming.
May they meet Jesus before it arrives.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE STRUCK THE RIVER WITH A DEAD MAN’S MANTLE—THEN THE JORDAN SPLIT OPEN
paragraphs: HE STRUCK THE RIVER WITH A DEAD MAN’S MANTLE—THEN THE JORDAN SPLIT OPEN

Elisha stood where his mentor was gone, his future was terrifyingly real, and the same river that had opened for Elijah now stood in front of him. Then he picked up what had fallen, struck the water, and asked one question every wounded believer eventually asks: “Where is the LORD?” — 2 Kings 2:13–14
There are moments when God removes what you thought you could not live without.
And then leaves you standing in front of a river.
That may be one of the most painful details in the story of Elisha.
Because before the Jordan divided, something else had already been torn apart.
Elisha’s world.
He had followed Elijah.
Walked with Elijah.
Learned beneath Elijah.
Refused repeatedly to abandon Elijah.
And then, suddenly, the man he called “my father” was gone.
No long goodbye.
No comfortable transition.
No opportunity to ask one final question.
Elisha watched Elijah disappear in the whirlwind, cried out, tore his own clothes in grief—and then found himself standing there with something lying on the ground.
A mantle.
Elijah’s mantle.
Scripture says:
“וַיָּרֶם אֶת־אַדֶּרֶת אֵלִיָּהוּ אֲשֶׁר נָפְלָה מֵעָלָיו”
Vayyarem et-adderet Eliyyahu asher nafelah me‘alav.
“He picked up Elijah’s mantle, which had fallen from him.”
—2 Kings 2:13
The Hebrew word אַדֶּרֶת — ’adderet refers to the mantle or cloak.
But do not miss what Scripture is actually showing us.
The power was never in the cloth.
The mantle was not a magical relic.
Elisha was not practicing superstition.
The God who had worked through Elijah was still God when Elijah was gone.
That distinction matters.

Because sometimes we become so attached to the person, ministry, season, relationship, church, mentor, opportunity, or method God once used that we quietly begin trusting the instrument more than the One who held it.
And God loves us too much to allow an instrument to become our god.
Elisha walked back toward the Jordan carrying the mantle of the man he could no longer see.
Imagine that walk.
Every step toward the river was another step into a future without Elijah beside him.
Maybe you know something about that walk.
Maybe somebody you thought would always be there is gone.
Maybe the marriage changed.
The friendship ended.
The person died.
The ministry collapsed.
The door closed.
The job disappeared.
The diagnosis arrived.
The child grew distant.
The dream you prayed over for years somehow ended differently than you imagined.
Or maybe nothing dramatic happened at all.
Maybe you simply woke up one morning and realized that the spiritual season you once enjoyed was over.
Prayer feels different now.
Worship feels different.
You read Scripture and remember when the words seemed to burn inside your chest.
Now you are standing at your own Jordan wondering whether God is still there.
That is why what Elisha says next is so painfully human.
He reaches the river.
He takes Elijah’s mantle.
He strikes the water.
And he cries:
“אַיֵּה יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ”
’Ayyeh YHWH, ’Elohei Eliyyahu?
“Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?”
—2 Kings 2:14
Where is the LORD?
Read that again.
This is a prophet asking.
A man who had witnessed the supernatural.
A man who had walked beside Elijah.
A man who had just watched his master taken away in extraordinary glory.
And standing at the Jordan, Elisha still asks:
“Where is the LORD?”
Perhaps faith is not always pretending you never have questions.
Sometimes faith carries the question directly to God.
Where are You, Lord?
Where were You when everything collapsed?
Where are You in this house that used to be filled with laughter?
Where are You when I pray and hear silence?
Where are You while my child is wandering?
Where are You while temptation keeps returning?
Where are You when everybody thinks I am strong but I am barely holding myself together?
Where are You when I know the verses but cannot stop crying?
Where are You when I have served You and still feel empty?
There are Christians reading this who love Jesus and are frightened by how tired their souls have become.
You smile at church.
You answer, “I’m blessed.”
You post the verse.
You encourage everybody else.
Then the room becomes quiet.
And inside you is a question you are almost ashamed to admit.
“God… where are You?”
Elisha’s story does not shame that question.
It shows us what he did with it.
He brought it to the river.
And then he struck the water.
Scripture says:
“וַיֵּחָצוּ הֵנָּה וָהֵנָּה”
Vayyechatzu hennah vahennah.
The waters “divided here and there”—to one side and to the other.
And Elisha crossed over.
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not say Elisha discovered secret power inside Elijah’s clothing.
It does not say Elijah had become the source of Elisha’s authority.
The narrative points beyond Elijah to the LORD Himself.
Earlier, Elijah had struck this same Jordan with his mantle, and the waters divided so that Elijah and Elisha crossed on dry ground.
Now Elijah was gone.
The mantle remained.
The river remained.
Elisha remained.
But the decisive reality was this:
The LORD remained.
That is the heartbeat of this story.
Elijah could leave.
God did not.
And somebody needs those four words tonight.
God did not leave.
People can leave.
Strength can leave.
Money can leave.
Youth can leave.
Opportunities can leave.
Applause can leave.
A season can leave.
Even faithful servants of God eventually leave this earth.
But the faithfulness of God does not expire when the person through whom you first encountered Him is no longer beside you.
The Jordan divided because the living God was still at work.
And there is something even deeper happening.

Elisha had asked Elijah for a “double portion” of his spirit. In the biblical setting, that language evokes the inheritance of the firstborn. Elisha was not simply begging to become twice as spectacular as Elijah. The scene concerns succession—being enabled to carry forward the prophetic calling that God had placed before him.
And after Elisha crossed the Jordan, the sons of the prophets recognized that “the spirit of Elijah” rested upon Elisha.
The mantle had fallen.
The calling had not.
But Christians must read even this magnificent Old Testament moment within the larger story of Scripture.
Elisha is not the Savior.
Elijah is not the Savior.
The mantle is not the Savior.
Every prophet eventually forces us to confront the fact that humanity needs Someone greater than another prophet.
And the biblical story moves relentlessly toward Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not merely inherit another prophet’s ministry.
He is the Son.
He did not come merely to amaze crowds with miracles.
He came to save sinners.
Our deepest Jordan was never simply unemployment, heartbreak, loneliness, sickness, disappointment, or a closed door.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We had rebelled against a holy God.
We could not cleanse ourselves.
Religion could not rescue us.
Good intentions could not erase guilt.
Christian merchandise could not save us.
Church attendance could not purchase forgiveness.
A mantle could not reconcile sinners to God.
We needed a Redeemer.
And Jesus came.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.

This is where every story of biblical power must eventually lead the Christian heart—not into obsession with objects, personalities, “anointings,” or spectacular experiences, but into worship of the living God revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest miracle is not that water once moved out of a prophet’s way.
The greater wonder is that through Christ, guilty sinners can be forgiven.
The scandal of the Gospel is that people with histories they cannot rewrite can be given futures they could never earn.
The liar can repent.
The adulterer can repent.
The addict can repent.
The bitter can repent.
The hypocrite can repent.
The religious performer can repent.
The secret sinner scrolling through Christian content while hiding another life can repent.
The person who has fallen again after promising God, “Never again,” can come honestly to Christ.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves exactly how seriously God takes sin.
And not because grace is cheap.
Grace cost the blood of Christ.
Maybe that is your river.
Not something outside you.
Something inside you.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness you have learned to justify.
The affair living inside your messages.
The envy disguised as ambition.
The pride hiding behind ministry.
The prayerlessness hidden beneath Christian vocabulary.
The unforgiveness you keep feeding.
The secret habit you delete from your history but cannot delete from your conscience.
You have become skilled at looking alive spiritually while something inside you is drowning.
And maybe you have been asking:
“Where is the God of Elijah?”
When another question desperately needs to be asked:
“Lord, what in me needs to die?”
Because Christianity is not about borrowing somebody else’s mantle while refusing your own cross.
Jesus said that anyone who would come after Him must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Him.
The Gospel does not invite you to decorate your old life with Christian language.
Jesus calls you into a new life.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave you have been decorating.
Grace does not whisper, “Your sin doesn’t matter.”
Grace says, “Your sin mattered enough for Christ to die—and His mercy is greater than the ruin you brought to Him.”
This is why Elisha standing beside the Jordan is such a powerful image.
He could not remain on that bank forever.
Eventually faith had to move.
The water divided.
Then Scripture says:
“וַיַּעֲבֹר אֱלִישָׁע”
Vayya‘avor Elisha.
“And Elisha crossed over.”
He crossed.
There comes a moment when yesterday cannot be recovered and tomorrow cannot be entered by nostalgia.
Elisha could honor Elijah without becoming Elijah.
He could remember yesterday without living there.
He could grieve what was gone without abandoning what God was calling him to become.
Some of you have spent years standing emotionally beside something God already brought to an end.
You keep replaying the conversation.
Reopening the wound.
Checking the profile.
Remembering the betrayal.
Rehearsing the failure.
Punishing yourself for the person you used to be.
You have mistaken perpetual self-condemnation for repentance.
But if you are in Christ, your identity is not “the scandal.”
Your identity is not the worst thing you did.
Your identity is not what somebody did to you.
Your identity is not your relapse, divorce, bankruptcy, rejection, addiction, humiliation, or failure.
The Gospel does not pretend those things never happened.
It announces that they do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is what we mean when we say:
He does not rewrite history by pretending your sin never existed.
He rewrites everything by redeeming sinners inside real history.
The scars may remain.
Consequences may remain.
Restitution may be necessary.
Relationships may require years of rebuilding.
Some earthly losses may never be recovered.
Biblical grace is not fantasy.
But neither is your failure sovereign.
Jesus is.
Your scandal does not outrank His cross.
Your shame does not outrank His mercy.
Your past does not outrank His resurrection.
And your river does not outrank the God who stands beyond it.
So perhaps you are standing there now.
The mantle is in your hand.
The water is in front of you.
Yesterday is behind you.
And you are terrified.
Good.
Not because fear is good—but because this may finally be the place where you discover that your confidence was never supposed to rest in your own strength.
Elisha’s question was answered not by Elijah returning but by God remaining faithful.
Maybe you keep asking God to bring something back when He is calling you to discover that He is enough even when it does not come back.
That person may not return.
That season may not return.
That opportunity may not return.
The old version of your life may never return.
But Christ is not standing behind you demanding that you resurrect yesterday.
He calls you to follow Him today.
And if this is exposing something you have been hiding, do not hide behind another religious sentence.
Be honest.
Somebody reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that broken people can keep walking with Jesus.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose faith has been collapsing quietly.
The friend grieving someone they cannot replace.
The believer trapped in shame.
The prodigal who thinks Christians only know how to condemn.
The person who still follows you on Facebook but has stopped following Jesus.
Send this to them.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God. It does not.
But if something points truthfully toward Christ, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.
You never know who is scrolling at 2:17 in the morning asking, “God, where are You?”
Your share may place the message in front of them.
There may come a night when you are the one standing at the river again.
We want this ministry to keep putting the Gospel where wounded people can find it.

We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of faithful obedience. But voluntary generosity and practical support can be genuine ways believers participate in Gospel work when they give freely and with biblical motives.
If God has used this ministry to strengthen you, you can support the work and go deeper with us here:
Jesus is still the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a mantle.
Not a preacher.
Not a ministry.
Jesus.
If you have Him, you possess something money could never buy.
And if you have wandered from Him, come home.
Repent.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is killing your intimacy with God.
Stop waiting until you become clean enough to approach the One who cleanses sinners.
Come honestly.
Come empty-handed.
Come with the confession you have been terrified to speak.
Come to the crucified and risen Christ.
Elisha once stood beside the Jordan holding something that belonged to yesterday.
Then he discovered that the God of yesterday was already waiting in tomorrow.
The river opened.
Elisha crossed.
And his story continued.
Maybe yours can too.
Not because you found Elijah’s mantle.
Because Jesus Christ is still alive.
So when you reach the river and everything familiar has disappeared, remember this:
What fell from your hands may belong to yesterday—but the Christ who redeemed you is already Lord over the other side.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES LEVITICUS FORBID SEX WITH YOUR GRANDDAUGHTER?
paragraphs: WHY DOES LEVITICUS FORBID SEX WITH YOUR GRANDDAUGHTER?

Leviticus 18:10 sounds disturbing to modern ears. But once you understand why God said it, this uncomfortable verse becomes a window into something breathtaking about His character: God draws boundaries around the vulnerable because love does not exploit what it was entrusted to protect.
There are verses in the Bible we underline.
There are verses we frame.
There are verses we quote when life falls apart.
And then there are verses we quietly read... blink twice... and wonder why they are even there.
Leviticus 18:10 is one of those verses.
Why would God need to tell a grandfather not to have sexual relations with his granddaughter?
Why would something that seems so obviously wrong need to be written into the Law?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
What does a command written thousands of years ago have to do with you?
More than you might think.

Because beneath this disturbing prohibition is a truth about God, family, sexuality, power, holiness, human corruption, and grace that reaches all the way from ancient Israel to the secret rooms of the human heart.
And before this is over, Leviticus 18:10 may stop feeling like one of those strange verses you hurry past.
It may become one of the verses that helps you understand why God's boundaries are sometimes among His greatest mercies.
Listen to the Hebrew:
עֶרְוַת בַּת־בִּנְךָ אוֹ בַת־בִּתְּךָ לֹא תְגַלֶּה עֶרְוָתָן כִּי עֶרְוָתְךָ הֵנָּה
‘Ervat bat-binkha o bat-bittekha lo tegalleh ‘ervatan, ki ‘ervatekha hennah.
A close translation is:
“The nakedness of your son’s daughter or your daughter’s daughter you shall not uncover their nakedness, for their nakedness is your own.”
That final expression is striking.
כִּי עֶרְוָתְךָ הֵנָּה — ki ‘ervatekha hennah.
“For their nakedness is yours.”

The Hebrew expression “uncover nakedness” is not merely talking about accidentally seeing someone without clothing. Within Leviticus 18, it functions as sexual language. The chapter establishes boundaries around sexual relations within close kinship and other prohibited relationships.
So Scripture is not being mysterious here.
God is drawing a line.
A grandfather must never turn the granddaughter entrusted to his family into an object of sexual possession.
But why state something so obvious?
Because Scripture was not written about imaginary people living in sanitized religious worlds.
The Bible knows what humanity is capable of.
That is one reason the Bible can sometimes make us uncomfortable.
It refuses to pretend.
We often want a Bible filled only with shepherds, sunsets, promises, miracles, angels, worship songs, and reassuring words.
God gives us something more honest.
He gives us a Bible that walks directly into the wreckage human sin can create.
Abuse.
Incest.
Adultery.
Betrayal.
Violence.
Exploitation.
Family dysfunction.
Sexual corruption.
Power misused against the vulnerable.
The Bible does not introduce those realities because God delights in darkness.
It exposes darkness because darkness grows where nobody is willing to name it.
And Leviticus 18 names it.

The chapter begins with God telling Israel not to imitate the practices surrounding them. Then comes the governing boundary in verse 6: a person must not approach a close relative to “uncover nakedness.”
What follows is not a collection of random sexual taboos.
It is a fence around the family.
Mother.
Father's wife.
Sister.
Granddaughter.
Half-sister.
Aunt.
Daughter-in-law.
Sister-in-law.
The pattern keeps moving through relationships where family identity and sexual access must never be confused.
And suddenly Leviticus 18:10 begins to look different.
This isn't God being strangely obsessed with sex.
This is God saying:
There are people in your life you were given to love without consuming.
Read that again.
There are people you were given to love without consuming.
Some relationships are sacred precisely because sexual access is forbidden.
A granddaughter should be able to approach her grandfather without wondering what he wants from her.
A daughter should be able to trust her father.
A sister should be able to trust her brother.
A child should be able to sleep beneath the roof of her family without fearing that someone entrusted with protecting her will become the person she needs protection from.
That is what sin does at its ugliest.
It takes something entrusted to us...
and asks how we can use it for ourselves.
God says no.
Family is not your hunting ground.
Authority is not permission.
Access is not consent.
Closeness is not ownership.
And love is never a license to exploit.
The prohibition of Leviticus 18:10 therefore preserves something essential: the distinction between familial love and sexual possession.
The older generation has responsibility toward the younger generation.
Protection.
Wisdom.
Provision.
Example.
Blessing.
Not sexual entitlement.
And that exposes something much bigger than incest.
Because you may read Leviticus 18:10 and think:
“I would never do that.”
Perhaps you never would.
Thank God.
But don't close the Bible yet.
Because the deeper spiritual question has already entered the room.
Have you ever turned something God gave you to protect into something you used for yourself?
A relationship?
Someone's trust?
A position of authority?
Someone's vulnerability?
A marriage?
A ministry?
A friendship?
Someone's admiration?
A secret somebody trusted you with?
A person who needed guidance from you?
Sin does not always begin with hatred.
Sometimes sin begins when love quietly becomes appetite.
When service becomes control.
When leadership becomes domination.
When affection becomes possession.
When desire begins rewriting boundaries that God established.
And perhaps that is why biblical holiness can feel offensive to us.
Holiness tells desire:
You are not God.
Our culture often treats strong desire as though desire itself creates moral permission.
“I want it.”
“I feel it.”
“This is who I am.”
“It makes me happy.”
“No one can tell me otherwise.”
But Scripture asks a more frightening question:
What if something you deeply desire is something you must surrender?
Jesus never taught that discipleship meant baptizing every appetite.
He said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
Christianity is not the announcement that every desire inside us is sacred.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus is Lord.
And sometimes the most worshipful word a believer can say to his own flesh is:
No.
No, because Christ is worth more.
No, because another human being bears God's image.
No, because love refuses to turn people into objects.
No, because holiness matters.
No, because obedience matters.
No, because my appetite does not sit on the throne.
But there is another side to this passage that must be handled carefully.
Some people reading these words are not thinking academically.
Your hands may have become cold before you reached this sentence.
Because you know what it is like when someone crosses a boundary that should never have been crossed.
Maybe it happened in your family.
Maybe the person who was supposed to protect you became the person who wounded you.
Maybe nobody believed you.
Maybe everyone protected the family reputation instead of protecting you.
Maybe somebody used religion to silence you.
Maybe you carried shame for something someone else did.
And now you are reading a command like Leviticus 18:10 differently.
Please hear what the command itself reveals.
God does not call exploitation love.
He names boundaries.
He holds people morally responsible for crossing them.
The existence of the command means the boundary matters to Him.
What happened in darkness is not made holy simply because someone powerful demanded silence.
Jesus Himself repeatedly dignified people others discarded, confronted hypocrisy, welcomed the wounded, and reserved severe warnings for those who caused vulnerable people to stumble.
God is not honored by covering abuse in order to preserve somebody's reputation.
Truth matters.
Protection matters.
Justice matters.
And if abuse is happening now, seeking immediate safety and appropriate help is not rebellion against God.
But maybe your story is different.
Maybe you were not only wounded.
Maybe you have wounded someone.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe you manipulated trust.
Maybe there is something in your history you have spent years hiding.
And suddenly this article doesn't feel like theology anymore.
It feels like a mirror.
Then don't run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
But understand what running to Jesus means.
Grace is not God pretending sin was harmless.
Grace is not permission to keep destroying people.
Grace does not rename darkness so that repentance becomes unnecessary.
Jesus Christ came precisely because sin is so serious that human beings could never rescue themselves from its guilt and power.
At the cross, we discover two truths simultaneously.
Our sin is worse than our excuses admit.
And God's mercy is greater than our shame can imagine.
Jesus did not bleed because sin was insignificant.
He bled because redemption is costly.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that God shrugs at evil.
The scandal is that the Holy One came looking for sinners.
Christ bore sin.
Christ conquered death.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
Christ forgives.
Christ cleanses.
Christ transforms.
Christ teaches people who once lived by appetite to walk by the Spirit.
And that means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repentance may require confession.
It may require accepting consequences.
It may require making restitution where appropriate and possible.
It may require surrendering access to people you have harmed.
It may require professional and pastoral accountability.
It may mean finally bringing into the light what you spent years protecting in darkness.
Grace does not eliminate truth.
Grace gives us somewhere to go when truth finally catches us.
That somewhere is Jesus.
This is why the Gospel is not merely “God loves you.”
The Gospel is far more breathtaking.
The Gospel says that the God who knows the parts of you that you desperately hope nobody discovers still calls you out of darkness and toward His Son.
Not so you can remain unchanged.
So you can become new.
There is a cross for your guilt.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is healing for the wounded.
There is truth for the deceived.
There is strength for the tempted.
There is holiness for people who once thought they could never become clean.
There is a Savior.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Leviticus draws the boundary.
Humanity crosses boundaries.
The Law exposes sin.
And the Gospel announces the One who came to save sinners without ever calling sin good.
That is why Scripture's uncomfortable passages matter.
If we only read verses that make us comfortable, we may accidentally create a god who never confronts us.
But the God of Scripture loves us enough to say:
Don't touch what isn't yours.
Don't exploit the vulnerable.
Don't confuse desire with righteousness.
Don't turn family into a place of sexual predation.
Don't call darkness freedom.
Don't hide forever.
Come into the light.
And perhaps that is the word somebody reading this desperately needed.
Come into the light.
You don't have to tell strangers every detail of your life.
But stop lying to yourself.
Stop protecting the secret that is destroying you.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need help, seek help.
If someone is currently being endangered, protect them and involve appropriate authorities and qualified support.
If you have been wounded, don't let another person's sin convince you that Jesus has abandoned you.
And if temptation is fighting for control of your mind, don't negotiate with it.
Bring it to Christ.
There is no shame in needing rescue.
There is tragedy in refusing the Rescuer.
Maybe this article exposed something you have hidden even from yourself.
If so, you don't need to describe private details publicly.
And if conviction brought you face-to-face with something you need to confess to God, let your first response be to Him. Jesus does not need a social-media comment to hear repentance.
He wants your heart.
Send it to the friend who loves Scripture.
Send it privately to someone who needs to know that God's boundaries are not evidence of His cruelty but can be expressions of His holiness, order, and protection.
One day you may meet someone who needs these words more desperately than you do today.
I want to be careful here because Scripture deserves honesty.
Scripture does not say that.
Christian giving is worship, but it must not be manipulated.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
The heart of 2 Corinthians 9:7 is that each person should give according to what he has resolved in his heart, not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
So pray about your giving. Honor your responsibilities before God and the local church where you worship and receive pastoral care. Care for people in need.
If this ministry glorifies Christ and bears good fruit in your life, consider becoming one of the people who helps keep it moving.
Not because God can be purchased.
Not because salvation can be bought.
You cannot buy grace.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
Support because you freely want the Gospel proclaimed.
Support because you want Scripture taught.
Support because you want hurting people reached.
Support because generosity can help good Gospel work continue.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help.
That costs nothing.
Yet one share can place the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
One tag can become someone's invitation back to Scripture.
One saved article can become tomorrow's conversation.
One honest comment can remind another struggling believer that they are not the only person fighting.
And one person encountering Jesus can matter more than numbers on a screen ever will.
Because this was never supposed to end with Leviticus 18:10.
It ends where all Scripture ultimately drives the Christian heart:
toward the holiness of God...
the reality of sin...
the necessity of repentance...
the wonder of grace...
and Jesus Christ.
The God who says, “Do not cross this boundary,” is not trying to destroy love.
He is teaching fallen humanity what love must never become.
And when fallen humanity crosses the boundaries anyway, the answer is not to rewrite God's holiness.
It is to run to the Savior who rewrites sinners.
Maybe your family has a scandal.
Maybe you are the scandal.
Maybe somebody else's sin wrote chapters into your life you never asked to live.
Maybe shame has been holding the pen for years.
Give Jesus the pen.
Because the Gospel does not say your past never happened.
It says your past does not get to be your lord.
Somebody may have written darkness into your story—but darkness does not get the final sentence when Jesus Christ is holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOW MUCH WAS JUDAS PAID IN TODAY’S MONEY?
paragraphs:
HOW MUCH WAS JUDAS PAID IN TODAY’S MONEY?
Thirty pieces of silver bought a betrayal. But before you ask what those coins would be worth today, there is a far more terrifying question: What would it take for you to put a price on Jesus?
Thirty pieces.
That was the number.
Not thirty bags of gold.
Not a palace.
Not enough money to become one of the wealthiest men in Jerusalem.
Thirty pieces of silver.

For centuries, Christians have read those words so often that they can lose their ability to shock us. Judas betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. We know the story. We know the kiss. We know the garden. We know the rope.
And because we know how it ends, we can read straight past the moment when something almost incomprehensible happened:
A man who had walked with Jesus began negotiating His price.
Think about that.
Judas had heard the voice that commanded storms.
He had watched sick bodies restored.
He had seen demons flee.
He had eaten beside Christ.
Walked beside Christ.
Listened while Christ taught.
He had been close enough to hear Jesus pray.
Close enough to watch Him weep.
Close enough to receive bread from His hand.
And somehow, eventually, Judas looked at the Son of God and asked another group of men:
What will you give me for Him?
Matthew records the question in Greek:
“Τί θέλετέ μοι δοῦναι κἀγὼ ὑμῖν παραδώσω αὐτόν;”
Tí théleté moi doûnai kagṑ hymîn paradṓsō autón?
In straightforward English:
“What are you willing to give me, and I will hand Him over to you?”
Then comes the sentence that has echoed through history:
“οἱ δὲ ἔστησαν αὐτῷ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια.”
hoi de éstēsan autō triákonta argýria.
“They set/weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver.”
Matthew 26:15.
The Greek expression τριάκοντα ἀργύρια — triákonta argýria literally gives us “thirty silver pieces” or “thirty pieces of silver.”
And here we need to be careful.
The Bible does not tell us the precise coin type Judas received.
That matters because you will find confident articles and videos claiming, “Judas was paid exactly $___ in today's money.”
Scripture does not give us enough information to make that claim with certainty.

Many historical reconstructions identify the payment with shekel-weight silver coinage circulating in the region, often proposing Tyrian shekels. That is plausible, but Matthew himself simply says thirty silver pieces.
So if somebody gives you one precise modern number and tells you, “This is exactly what Judas received,” they are claiming more precision than Matthew gives us.
But we can make an illustrative calculation.
If we model the thirty pieces as roughly thirty shekel-weight silver coins of about 14 grams each, we arrive at approximately 420 grams of silver, or around 13.5 troy ounces.
At a recent September 2026 silver price of roughly $66 per troy ounce, the raw metal would come to somewhere around $890.
Approximately.
Not exactly.
And that distinction matters.

Because ancient purchasing power cannot responsibly be translated into modern money simply by multiplying ancient silver weight by today's commodity price. The economic worlds are radically different. Wages, food, land, taxation, coinage, scarcity, and standards of living do not map neatly onto one another.
So was Judas paid “about $900”?
In raw silver value under that particular reconstruction and using current silver prices, roughly.
Was the payment economically equivalent to having only $900 in his ancient world?
We cannot responsibly say that.
And strangely enough, once you stop forcing the Bible into a modern currency calculator, the real meaning becomes far more devastating.
Because Matthew wants you looking somewhere else.
Long before Judas walked into the presence of the chief priests, the Hebrew Scriptures had already made the number thirty unsettling.
Exodus 21:32 says:
“כֶּסֶף שְׁלֹשִׁים שְׁקָלִים”
kesef sheloshim sheqalim.
“Thirty shekels of silver.”
The context?
Compensation involving a slave killed by an ox.
Thirty shekels.
Now listen to the prophet Zechariah.
Zechariah 11:12 contains the haunting words:
“וַיִּשְׁקְלוּ אֶת־שְׂכָרִי שְׁלֹשִׁים כָּסֶף”
Vayyishqelu et-sekhari sheloshim kasef.
“So they weighed out my wages, thirty pieces/shekels of silver.”
And in the next verse, that insulting valuation is thrown into the house of the LORD.
Then Matthew tells us Judas received...
Thirty pieces of silver.
This is why the deepest answer to “How much was Judas paid?” is not found on a commodity exchange.
The number carries biblical meaning.
Matthew's Gospel later explicitly connects Judas's returned silver with the prophetic imagery associated with Jeremiah and Zechariah in Matthew 27:9–10.
The tragedy is not merely that Judas received silver.
The tragedy is the valuation.
Human beings looked at Jesus Christ...
and put a price on Him.
Let that sit there for a moment.
Because this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
It is easy to hate Judas when Judas remains safely two thousand years away from us.
It is harder when we realize that Judas's question can still live inside the human heart.
“What will you give me?”
What will you give me if obedience costs too much?
What will you give me if following Jesus threatens my relationship?
What will you give me if biblical truth damages my reputation?
What will you give me if compromise makes my life easier?
What will you give me if nobody finds out?
What will you give me if I can keep Christianity publicly while negotiating with sin privately?
Suddenly the thirty pieces of silver are no longer lying on an ancient table.
They are sitting in front of us.
Maybe yours isn't silver.
Maybe yours is approval.
Maybe it is pornography.
