He takes the guilty who come to Him in faith and gives them forgiveness they could never earn.
He takes stories that seemed destined to end in darkness...
and writes grace across the final pages.
Maybe your story is not finished.
Maybe this is the paragraph where you stop hiding.

If something in this exposed an area you have been protecting from God, be honest. You do not need to publish the details of your private sin for strangers to inspect. But you can make a simple confession of need.
Someone reading the comments may need to know that restoration is possible.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
Someone who has been listening to truth but struggling to surrender.
Someone drifting.
Someone hiding.
Someone exhausted from pretending.
Someone convinced that what they have done has disqualified them forever.
Or send this article privately with compassion.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
Not to earn favor with God.
Not because sharing a post saves anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sharing truth can put the message in front of someone who desperately needs to hear it.
We are saved by grace, not by transactions. Your support helps this ministry keep putting Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement and the message of Jesus before more people.
If this ministry feeds your faith, consider helping keep the message moving.
But before you leave...
go back to that prison cell one final time.
Imagine John sitting in the darkness.
Footsteps approaching.
A door opening.
The executioner entering.
John does not know that generations will remember his courage.
He does not know that you will be reading his story thousands of years later.
He simply knows that truth is still truth...
Jesus is still worthy...
and obedience is worth more than survival.
Then look upstairs.
Herod has everything John does not.
A throne.
A banquet.
Influence.
Applause.
Freedom.
And yet John is the freer man.
Maybe the question you should carry away from this story is not:
Would I die like John?
Maybe it is much closer.
What would I have to stop protecting today if I actually believed Jesus was worth obeying?
Do not merely admire the prophet.
Do not become another Herod who loves hearing truth while postponing surrender.
Come to Christ.
Bring the scandal.
Bring the shame.
Bring the compromise.
Bring the secret.
Bring the years you cannot recover.
Bring the pieces.
Repent and believe.
Because the Savior John announced is still receiving sinners.
The cross is still sufficient.
The tomb is still empty.
Grace is still available.
And Jesus Christ is still rewriting lives.
You do not have to silence the truth when you can surrender to the Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR BODY IS NOT DISPOSABLE JUST BECAUSE YOUR SOUL IS ETERNAL
paragraphs: YOUR BODY IS NOT DISPOSABLE JUST BECAUSE YOUR SOUL IS ETERNAL
You may be preparing your soul for heaven while treating the body God entrusted to you as though it does not matter—and Scripture refuses to let us separate the two so easily.
There is a strange contradiction hiding inside the lives of many sincere Christians.
We pray for healing...
while sometimes refusing stewardship.
We ask God for strength...
while repeatedly ignoring the ordinary things within our responsibility.
We pray, “Lord, use me.”

But sometimes we treat the very body through which we serve, work, worship, embrace our children, help our neighbors, preach the Gospel, care for our families, and carry out our calling as though it were disposable.
And because Christians know that eternal life is real, we can accidentally begin thinking as though the physical life God gave us is spiritually insignificant.
After all...
This body will die.
Christ will raise His people.
Eternity is coming.
So why should this temporary body matter very much?
Because it matters to God.
And perhaps one of the most uncomfortable questions a believer can ask is not simply:
“Do I believe God can heal me?”
But:
“Am I honoring God with the body I keep asking Him to heal?”
That question must be handled carefully.
Very carefully.
Because somewhere reading this is a faithful Christian living with cancer.
Someone has an autoimmune disease.
Someone was born with a disability.
Someone has chronic pain despite years of prayer.
Someone eats carefully, exercises faithfully, attends medical appointments, and still received devastating news.
Someone buried a health-conscious husband.
Someone watched a godly mother die younger than anyone expected.
So hear this before anything else:
Illness is not proof that you failed God.
Health is not proof that you pleased Him.
A long life is not God's guaranteed reward for eating correctly, exercising regularly, sleeping enough, or maintaining the “right” weight.
And Christianity is not a baptized wellness program promising that sufficient discipline will prevent disease.
We live in a fallen creation where even faithful believers suffer, weaken, age, become sick, and eventually die unless Christ returns first.
The Gospel gives us something infinitely greater than a guarantee of physical longevity.
It gives us resurrection.
But resurrection does not make your present body meaningless.
In fact, the Christian hope of resurrection tells us something astonishing:
God does not despise embodied human existence.
Jesus Christ did not save some invisible spiritual fragment of you while dismissing everything physical as worthless.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He walked.
He became tired.
He ate.
He slept.
He touched lepers.
He bled.
He suffered.
He died bodily.
And He rose bodily.
Christianity is not the story of human beings escaping God's mistake called “the body.”
It is the story of the Creator redeeming fallen human beings through the incarnate, crucified, and risen Christ.
Which makes Paul's words to Corinth impossible to shrug off.
He writes:
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV
The Greek brings Paul's language into even sharper focus:
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν... καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν; ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς· δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
The heart of Paul's declaration is devastating to the illusion of Christian self-ownership:
οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν — ouk este heautōn.
“You are not your own.”
Then:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς — ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“You were bought with a price.”
And therefore:
δοξάσατε... τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν — doxasate... ton theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
“Glorify God in your body.”
We need to be honest about the context.
Paul was not writing a first-century fitness manual.

He was confronting sexual immorality and correcting a disastrous view of the body. Earlier in the passage he declares that “the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body” (1 Corinthians 6:13, KJV).
So we should not rip verses 19–20 out of their context and pretend Paul was directly prescribing exercise routines, calorie limits, medical screenings, sleep schedules, or nutritional plans.
He wasn't.
But the theological principle underneath his argument reaches far deeper than our modern categories.
Your body belongs to the Lord.
That changes everything.
Your body is not God.
But neither is it garbage.
It is not worthy of worship.
But neither is it worthy of careless contempt.
You are not commanded to become obsessed with preserving youth.
You are not commanded to chase an impossible physique.
You are not commanded to measure your spiritual worth by a scale, a mirror, a blood test, a diagnosis, a clothing size, or the number of years you live.
But you are called to recognize ownership.
You belong to Christ.
That means Christian stewardship can reach places we sometimes prefer to keep outside discipleship.
What we eat.
How we rest.
How we work.
Whether we repeatedly push ourselves beyond reasonable limits.
Whether we seek appropriate medical help when something is wrong.
Whether we knowingly feed destructive habits.
Whether vanity controls us.
Whether laziness controls us.
Whether anxiety about health has become its own idol.
Whether we neglect our bodies because caring for them feels inconvenient.
And yes...
whether we keep asking God to change circumstances while refusing to examine choices He has actually placed within our responsibility.
Not because disciplined Christians never get sick.
They do.
Not because stewardship guarantees tomorrow.
It doesn't.
Not because every illness can be prevented.
It cannot.
But because obedience does not become meaningless simply because outcomes remain in God's hands.
A farmer cannot command rain.
He still plants.
A parent cannot guarantee what an adult child will become.
She still loves, teaches, corrects, and prays.
A Christian cannot guarantee another heartbeat.
We still steward the life God has entrusted to us.
Maybe that is where this becomes personal.
You have prayed:
“Lord, give me strength.”
But perhaps your body has been whispering exhaustion for months and you keep treating rest like weakness.
You have prayed:
“Lord, help me serve my family.”
But perhaps you have accepted patterns you already know are harming you because changing them feels difficult.
You have prayed:
“Lord, heal me.”
And perhaps there is absolutely nothing you could have done to prevent what happened.
If that is your story, this article is not an accusation.
Christ does not stand over suffering believers with folded arms saying, “You caused this.”
Remember the man born blind.
The disciples wanted an explanation they could neatly attach to personal sin:
“Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?”
Jesus rejected their simplistic conclusion.
“Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents...” (John 9:2–3, KJV).
The Bible gives us no permission to look at a sick person and automatically diagnose a moral failure.
Job should have cured us of that arrogance a long time ago.
Sometimes suffering arrives without giving us an explanation that fits neatly inside our theology.
Sometimes faithful people hurt.
Sometimes children become sick.
Sometimes people do nearly everything “right” and still die young.
Sometimes the strongest believer in the hospital room is the person lying in the bed.
And sometimes the deepest worship a human body will ever offer God is not running another mile.
It is whispering...
“Jesus is Lord.”
through exhausted lungs.
That matters.
Because bodily stewardship is not bodily worship.
There is another ditch on the opposite side of neglect, and Christians fall into it too.
Health can become an idol.
Fitness can become an idol.
Youth can become an idol.
Food can become an idol.
Appearance can become an idol.
Longevity can become an idol.
The mirror can become an altar.
The gym can become a sanctuary.
Fear of sickness can become a master.
And suddenly someone who began wanting to “honor God” spends more emotional energy trying to preserve the body than preparing the heart to meet Christ.
That is not stewardship either.
The goal is not to make your body immortal.
You can't.
The goal is not to make yourself beautiful enough to feel valuable.
Christ already settled your value somewhere far more terrible and beautiful than a mirror.
At a cross.
“Ye are bought with a price.”
There is the center.
There is the Gospel.
There is the reason Christian stewardship can never merely become self-improvement.
The deepest reason your body matters is not because you can optimize it.
It is because Christ purchased you.
Not with money.
Not with accomplishments.
Not because you finally became disciplined enough to deserve Him.
Scripture tells believers that they were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Think about that.
The hands you criticize.
The face you compare.
The body you sometimes hate.
The aging skin you wish you could reverse.
The scarred body carrying memories nobody knows about.
The disabled body someone once made you feel ashamed of.
The chronically ill body that frustrates you.
The healthy body you have taken for granted.

The exhausted body that carried children, worked night shifts, buried parents, survived trauma, served churches, cleaned houses, drove long roads, held crying people, and somehow got you through nights you thought would break you...
Christ's claim over you is deeper than your feelings about yourself.
You are His.
And that means stewardship is not punishment.
It is worship.
Maybe the change you need does not begin with:
“I hate what I have become.”
Maybe it begins with:
“Jesus, this belongs to You.”
My eyes belong to You.
My hands belong to You.
My sexuality belongs to You.
My appetite belongs to You.
My strength belongs to You.
My limitations belong to You.
My work belongs to You.
My rest belongs to You.
My remaining years belong to You.
Even my weakness belongs to You.
Teach me to glorify You here.
That prayer is different.
Because shame says:
“Fix yourself so God will accept you.”
The Gospel says:
“In Christ you have been bought at immeasurable cost. Now live like someone who belongs to Him.”
Grace does not say stewardship is irrelevant.
Grace changes the reason we steward.
We are not trying to earn God's love.
We respond because in Christ we have encountered a love we could never earn.
That is the difference between legalism and worship.
Maybe you have neglected yourself for years.
Maybe food became comfort because nobody knew how badly you were hurting.
Maybe exhaustion became normal because everybody needed something from you.
Maybe you stopped caring after the divorce.
Maybe grief hollowed you out.
Maybe depression made ordinary care feel impossibly heavy.
Maybe trauma changed your relationship with your body.
Maybe you spent years serving everyone except the person staring back from your mirror.
Maybe nobody ever taught you that stewardship could be gentle.
Perhaps repentance for you does not look dramatic tonight.
Perhaps it looks like admitting:
“Lord, I have not handled well what You entrusted to me.”
No excuses.
No self-hatred.
No promises that tomorrow you will become a completely different human being.
Just surrender.
Because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God today.
And there is grace here.
So much grace.
The Gospel is filled with ruined people discovering that Jesus does not merely expose what sin has done.
He redeems what sin has touched.
Peter failed.
Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him.
The thief reached the final hours of a wasted life and discovered that grace was still standing beside him on a cross.
That is why your neglected years do not have to become your identity.
You may not be able to reverse every consequence.
You may never recover everything lost.
You cannot bargain your way into another forty years.
But you can place whatever remains into the hands of Christ.
One year.
Twenty years.
Six months.
Tomorrow.
This afternoon.
This breath.
Whatever remains can become worship.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not repainting our failures with religious language.
Not hiding our neglect behind “God is in control” while refusing responsibility.
And not pretending our obedience gives us control over outcomes that belong to God.
It is bringing the whole complicated story to Jesus...
the neglect...
the fear...
the sickness...
the shame...
the habits...
the regrets...
the scars...
the diagnosis...
the years we cannot recover...
and discovering that Christ still knows how to write redemption into pages we thought we had ruined.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So perhaps today you do not need another extreme resolution.
Maybe you need surrender.
Eat with gratitude.
Move according to your ability.
Rest without treating yourself like a machine.
Receive appropriate medical care without shame.
Listen when your body is signaling that something may be wrong.
Reject sexual immorality because your body belongs to Christ.
Reject vanity because your body is not your god.
Reject despair because weakness does not erase your worth.
Reject judgment toward the sick because you do not know their story.
Reject the fantasy that healthy choices make you sovereign over tomorrow.
And reject the lie that because your soul is eternal, your body is disposable.
Your body will not last forever in its present mortal condition.
But what you do with it can glorify the One who will.
Be honest.

And if God has been teaching you the difference between caring for your body and worshiping it, share your testimony. Someone scrolling silently may desperately need to know that faithful stewardship can begin again without shame.
If this truth can help another believer move from neglect, shame, fear, or idolatry toward Christ-centered stewardship, let your share become an act of service.
Send it to the believer who needs conviction without condemnation.
Send it to the suffering Christian who needs to hear that sickness is not proof God is disappointed in them.
Send it to the person who has confused bodily neglect with spirituality.
And send it to someone who needs to remember that Christianity's ultimate hope is not perfect health now, but Jesus Christ and resurrection life with Him.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to biblical truth.
It is helping sustain content centered on repentance, grace, forgiveness, restoration, Scripture, and Jesus Christ.
And if you are ready to go deeper and support the mission:
But before you leave this page, remember this:
One day you will lay this mortal body down—but until that day, let every breath still entrusted to you become an answer to the blood that purchased you: “Jesus, what remains of me is Yours.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU BE FREE FROM LUST WITHOUT BEING FREE FROM MASTURBATION?
paragraphs:
CAN YOU BE FREE FROM LUST WITHOUT BEING FREE FROM MASTURBATION?
The question most Christians whisper about—but Jesus may be using it to expose a much deeper question: Who actually owns your desires?
There are sins Christians confess out loud.
And then there are battles they delete from their browser history.
Battles hidden behind locked doors, cleared screens, long showers, late nights, private fantasies, and promises whispered to God that nobody else ever hears.
“Lord, this was the last time.”
Then it happens again.
You repent.
You feel ashamed.
You make another promise.
You stay clean for a while.
Then loneliness comes.
Stress comes.
Rejection comes.
A suggestive image appears.
An old memory resurfaces.
Your body remembers a pattern your mouth already told God you wanted to leave behind.
And suddenly you are standing in the wreckage of another promise, wondering whether you are a hypocrite, wondering whether God is disgusted with you, wondering whether you have ever really changed.
But perhaps you have been asking the wrong question.
Maybe the deepest question is not merely:
“Is masturbation a sin?”
Maybe the question underneath the question is:
Can I honestly say I am becoming free from lust while still protecting the behavior that repeatedly takes me back to it?
That question is harder.
Because it refuses to let us hide behind terminology.
And Jesus has always been more interested in the heart than in our ability to find loopholes.
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
The Greek of Matthew 5:28 contains a devastating little expression:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn

The key verb, ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, speaks of desire, craving, longing. Context determines whether that desire is good or evil. Here the context is deliberately cultivating sexual desire toward someone who is not yours to possess.
Jesus takes the conversation beneath behavior.
Into desire.
Into imagination.
Into intention.
Into the secret theater of the heart where nobody sees what you are watching except God.
And that matters enormously when Christians talk about masturbation.
Because we need enough courage to say something that may surprise people on both sides of this debate:
The Bible never explicitly mentions masturbation by name.
That matters.
Biblical faithfulness means we should never pretend God wrote a verse He did not write.

The story of Onan in Genesis 38 is sometimes used as though it were a direct prohibition of masturbation, but that is not what the passage describes. Onan deliberately refused his obligation to provide offspring for his deceased brother while exploiting the sexual relationship for himself. His judgment cannot responsibly be reduced to a universal proof-text about masturbation.
So we should not manufacture Scripture.
But neither should we use Scripture's silence about the word masturbation as permission to ignore everything Scripture says about the heart surrounding our sexual behavior.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.

Because masturbation may occur in dramatically different moral circumstances, but for many people it has become deeply connected to pornography, fantasy, objectification, compulsive desire, escapism, and the deliberate stimulation of lust.
And once that is true, arguing about whether the physical mechanism itself appears in a Bible verse can become a sophisticated way of avoiding the condition of the heart.
Paul gives us another question.
“‘All things are lawful for me,’ but not all things are helpful. ‘All things are lawful for me,’ but I will not be dominated by anything.”
That final idea in 1 Corinthians 6:12 is powerful.
οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος — ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos
“I will not be mastered by anything.”
Not mastered.
Not controlled.
Not owned.
And suddenly the question becomes intensely personal.
Can you stop?
Not theoretically.
Actually.
Can you walk away when the urge arrives?
Can you experience loneliness without immediately needing sexual release?
Can you feel anxiety without escaping into fantasy?
Can you encounter an attractive person without mentally undressing them later?
Can you go to bed frustrated and remain frustrated without believing your body must receive whatever it demands?
Can you pray when temptation comes instead of negotiating with it?
Can you surrender even the behavior you insist is technically permissible if you discover that, for you, it has become a doorway back into bondage?
Because Christian freedom is not merely being allowed to do something.
Christian freedom includes being able not to do it.
That is where some of us discover something frightening.
We thought we had a habit.
The habit had us.
And perhaps that explains why you keep returning.
Sometimes what appears to be sexual hunger is carrying something else underneath it.
Loneliness.
Rejection.
Boredom.
Stress.
Fear.
A craving to feel wanted.
A desire to shut your mind off for a few minutes.
The wound may not be sexual even though the medication has become sexual.
And temporary relief can quietly become a counterfeit refuge.
You feel pressure.
You escape.
Relief comes.
Then conviction.
Then shame.
Then another promise.
Then pressure returns.
And the cycle begins again.
But shame is a terrible savior.
It can tell you what you did without giving you the power to become someone new.
That is why Christianity is not ultimately a story about people becoming strong enough to clean themselves before approaching God.
It is the story of a Savior walking directly into humanity's scandal.
Jesus did not come for people who successfully concealed their darkness.
He came for sinners.
He ate with them.
He touched the unclean.
He defended the humiliated without pretending sin did not matter.
He called people to repentance while simultaneously offering the grace that made repentance possible.
The Gospel does not say:
“Fix your lust, defeat every compulsive behavior, purify your imagination, and then perhaps Jesus will receive you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν — eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn
“While we were still sinners.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after thirty clean days.
Not after the browser history disappeared.
Not after temptation stopped.
Christ died for sinners.
But grace is not permission to remain chained.
The Jesus who forgives also transforms.
Paul writes in Romans 6:14:
The Greek word translated “have dominion” is related to κυριεύω — kyrieuō: to rule, exercise lordship, be master.
Read that again slowly.
Sin does not get to be your lord.
Because Jesus is.
That changes the entire conversation.
The goal is not merely to stop touching your body.
The goal is for Jesus Christ to become Lord over your body, imagination, sexuality, loneliness, wounds, desires, habits, screens, memories, and secret places.
And this is where we must be careful.

Some Christians will need to stop masturbating because they have discovered that, in their actual lives, it is practically inseparable from lust, pornography, fantasy, compulsivity, or spiritual compromise.

Others may insist they can separate the physical act from lust. Scripture does not give us permission to pronounce an explicit universal prohibition where it does not explicitly state one. But Scripture does give every believer demanding tests to apply.
Does this cultivate purity?
Does this require fantasy about someone who is not your spouse?
Does this awaken desires you are then feeding rather than governing?
Does it undermine self-control?
Does it master you?
Can you sincerely thank God while doing it?
Can you bring it into the light?
Can you surrender it without resentment if the Spirit convicts your conscience?
Does it help you honor God with your body?
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
Paul continues in 1 Thessalonians 4 by calling believers to learn how to possess or control their own bodies in holiness and honor rather than in the passion of lust.
Christian sexuality is therefore not primarily about asking:
“How close can I get to the boundary without technically crossing it?”
It asks:
“How completely can this part of me belong to Christ?”
That is sanctification.
Not mutilating desire.
Redeeming it.
Sexual desire itself is not dirty.
God created human beings as embodied creatures.
Marriage is not dirty.
Sex within God's design is not dirty.
Desire is not automatically lust.
Temptation is not automatically sin.
And experiencing sexual arousal does not make you spiritually defective.
The battle begins when desire becomes disordered, deliberately cultivated toward what God has forbidden, or elevated into a master we obey.
That distinction matters because some Christians have spent years hating their bodies when what Jesus wants is not self-hatred but holiness.
You do not defeat lust by becoming disgusted with being human.
You learn to bring your humanity under the lordship of Christ.
And sometimes that means doing something terrifyingly simple.
Bringing the secret into the light.
James says:
“Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.”
Not announce everything publicly.
Not humiliate yourself online.
Not expose intimate details indiscriminately.
But stop fighting entirely alone.
Find a mature, trustworthy believer.
A pastor.
A mentor.
An accountability partner.
Someone who will neither excuse sin nor weaponize your confession against you.
Pornography thrives in secrecy.
Compulsion thrives in secrecy.
Fantasy thrives in secrecy.
Shame thrives in secrecy.
But healing loves light.
You may also need practical boundaries that feel almost embarrassingly ordinary.
The phone may need to stay outside the bedroom.
Certain accounts may need to disappear.
Certain websites may need to be blocked.
Certain conversations may need boundaries.
You may need to recognize that what you call “temptation at midnight” often began with what you willingly watched at 7:30.
You may need sleep.
Exercise.
Community.
Prayer before the urge becomes overwhelming rather than only after you fall.
You may need to stop measuring victory solely by how many consecutive days you have gone without failure and begin measuring whether your reflexes are increasingly turning toward Christ.
And if you fall?
Run toward Him.
Not away.
Repentance is not saying, “God, I am worthless.”
Repentance is saying, “God, this cannot remain my master because You are.”
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia carries the idea of repentance, a changed mind and turning that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Real repentance does not merely mourn consequences.
It turns.
Sometimes trembling.
Sometimes crawling.
Sometimes after the hundredth battle.
But it turns toward Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this has already failed today.
You almost closed this article because shame whispered:
“People like you don't belong in Christian conversations about holiness.”
But listen carefully.
Peter denied Jesus.
David carried devastating sexual sin in his story.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply broken sexual histories.
And after listing serious sins from which some of them had come, Paul wrote one of the most breathtaking sentences in Scripture:
“And such were some of you.”
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε — kai tauta tines ēte
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Your sin can describe where Christ found you.
It does not have authority to decide where Christ is taking you.
So can you be free from lust without being free from masturbation?
The most biblically responsible answer cannot be reduced to a slogan.
Scripture does not explicitly identify masturbation by name, so Christians should be cautious about declaring an explicit biblical prohibition that the text itself does not state.

But if masturbation in your life depends upon lustful fantasy, pornography, objectification, compulsive sexual stimulation, or a pattern that masters you rather than being mastered by you, then claiming freedom from lust while deliberately preserving its feeding system is not freedom.
You cannot sincerely ask Jesus to burn down the prison while keeping a private key because you still enjoy visiting the cell.
And maybe that sentence hurt.
Good questions sometimes do.
Not because Christ is trying to crush you.
Because He loves you too much to negotiate with the chains you have learned to decorate.
Jesus did not endure the cross merely to make your captivity slightly more comfortable.
He came to redeem you.
Your sexuality too.
Your imagination too.
Your private life too.
Your midnight battles too.
Your loneliness too.
Your body too.
All of you.
So tonight, instead of making another dramatic promise that you will never struggle again, make a smaller and perhaps more honest prayer:
“Jesus, show me what owns me.”
Then do not run from the answer.
If pornography owns part of you, bring it into the light.
If fantasy owns part of you, surrender it.
If masturbation has become compulsive, stop defending what you already know is controlling you.
If loneliness is underneath the behavior, let Christ lead you toward real community instead of another temporary anesthetic.
If shame has convinced you that Jesus is finished with you, return to the cross and remember who died there.
And if you need help, ask for it.
You were never commanded to become holy without Christ.
You were invited to abide in Him.
Maybe somebody you know is fighting this exact battle while pretending everything is fine.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Send it privately to the believer who has been fighting in silence.
Someone reading your five words may realize they are not the only person fighting.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to prove your faith.
If this ministry is feeding your faith, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is drifting.
Invite the believer nobody realizes is struggling.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to the secret wounds people carry.
Come to Jesus.
Not tomorrow when you feel cleaner.
Now.
Come with the browser history.
Come with the fantasies.
Come with the shame.
Come with the relapse.
Come with the questions.
Come with the part of your story you desperately wish could be erased.
Bring it into His light.
Confess what is sin.
Surrender what has become your master.
Receive the grace you could never earn.
And then get up and follow Him again.
Because perhaps freedom is not the day you never feel temptation again.
Perhaps freedom begins the day temptation knocks...
and discovers that someone else now owns the house.
Your secret may explain the scandal in your story—but it does not get to write the ending. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID PAUL WORK WHILE PREACHING?
paragraphs: WHY DID PAUL WORK WHILE PREACHING?

He could have asked the churches to support him. Scripture says he had that right. Yet sometimes Paul deliberately worked with his own hands—and the reason exposes something painfully relevant about ministry, money, sacrifice, and the Gospel today.
There is a detail about the apostle Paul that is easy to read past.
He preached Christ.
He planted churches.
He reasoned in synagogues.
He endured beatings, imprisonment, rejection, hunger, sleepless nights, persecution, and eventually death for the name of Jesus.
But somewhere between proclaiming the risen Christ and strengthening exhausted believers…
Paul went to work.
Not metaphorically.
Physically.
Acts tells us that when Paul came to Corinth, he met Aquila and Priscilla, and because they shared the same trade, he stayed and worked with them.
The Greek text says:
ἦσαν γὰρ σκηνοποιοὶ τῇ τέχνῃ
ēsan gar skēnopoioi tē technē
“For by trade they were tentmakers.”
—Acts 18:3
Imagine that scene.

The man whose letters would one day be read across continents, translated into thousands of languages, preached from pulpits, whispered beside hospital beds, studied in seminaries, carried into prisons, and memorized by children…
was working with his hands.
Paul could preach Christ and still labor.
He could carry revelation and still carry the ordinary burdens of life.
He could be an apostle and still know what tired hands felt like.
And perhaps that is exactly where this story begins touching us.
Because some of you know what it feels like to love God while still having bills.
You know what it is to pray before your shift begins.
To open Scripture exhausted.
To serve people while wondering whether anyone notices what serving is costing you.
To worship while carrying financial pressure nobody at church knows about.
To encourage somebody else while your own heart is tired.
And sometimes you wonder:
“If God really called me, why is life still this hard?”
Paul's hands give us an answer we desperately need.
Hard work was not necessarily evidence that Paul had missed his calling.
Sometimes it was part of how he protected it.
Paul explains his reasoning with startling clarity in 1 Corinthians 9.

He argues that those who proclaim the Gospel legitimately possess a right to receive material support from Gospel ministry. He even reaches back into the Law and then points directly to Christ's instruction concerning those who proclaim the Gospel.
Then he says something remarkable:
ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐχρησάμεθα τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ ταύτῃ
all’ ouk echrēsametha tē exousia tautē
“But we have not used this right.”
Then comes the reason:
ἵνα μή τινα ἐγκοπὴν δῶμεν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ
hina mē tina enkopēn dōmen tō euangeliō tou Christou
“…lest we should hinder the gospel of Christ.”
—1 Corinthians 9:12
There it is.
Paul was not ashamed of receiving support.
He explicitly defended the right of Gospel workers to receive it.
But in circumstances where exercising that legitimate right might become an obstacle to people hearing Christ, Paul was willing to surrender the right.
That distinction matters.
Paul did not say money was evil.
He did not say ministers must always work another job.
He did not teach that receiving financial support makes someone less spiritual.
In fact, Philippians tells us that believers supported Paul materially, and Paul received their gifts with gratitude.
His principle was deeper:
The Gospel mattered more to Paul than his entitlement.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because we live in a culture obsessed with rights.
My platform.
My recognition.
My compensation.
My comfort.
My opportunity.
My reputation.
My audience.
Paul looked at something he could legitimately claim and asked a radically different question:
“Will using this right help or hinder someone from hearing about Jesus?”
That question can rearrange a life.
Paul was willing to lose something legitimate rather than risk obscuring something eternal.
He could have demanded.
Instead, sometimes, he worked.
He could have insisted.
Instead, sometimes, he sacrificed.
Not because poverty made him holy.
Not because employment saved him.
Not because Christians earn grace through exhaustion.
But because Paul had already been conquered by something greater than comfort.
He had been conquered by Christ.
And remember who this man used to be.
Before people called him Apostle Paul, Scripture introduces him as Saul.
A persecutor.
A man terrifying Christians.
A man approving Stephen's death.
A man entering houses and dragging believers away.
A man breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord.
Then Jesus met him.
That changes everything about the hands working in Acts 18.
Those hands had once participated in persecution.
Now they were working so that nothing unnecessary would obstruct the message of Christ.
Those feet had once traveled toward Damascus carrying authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
Now those feet traveled from city to city proclaiming the Jesus he once opposed.
That mouth had once threatened Christians.
Now it proclaimed:
Χριστὸν ἐσταυρωμένον
Christon estaurōmenon
“Christ crucified.”
See the scandal.
Then see the grace.
Saul did not repair Saul.
Jesus rewrote him.
And maybe that is why Paul's story still reaches into our carefully hidden places.
Because most of us have chapters we wish nobody had read.
Things we said.
Things we did.
People we hurt.
Promises we broke.
Secret compromises.
Private addictions.
Years we wasted.
Moments when we knew better and did it anyway.
We become experts at editing our public image while secretly believing God must be disappointed with the unedited version.
But the Gospel does not say, “Make yourself respectable enough for Jesus.”
The Gospel announces that the holy Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus Christ lived the righteousness we could never perfectly live, died for sins, and rose again in victory.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
Grace confronts sin so deeply that Christ went to the cross because of it.
But grace also declares that your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
Paul understood that personally.
He later wrote:
Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς ἦλθεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἁμαρτωλοὺς σῶσαι
Christos Iēsous ēlthen eis ton kosmon hamartōlous sōsai
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.”
—1 Timothy 1:15
Paul wasn't discussing sinners from a safe theological distance.
He immediately included himself.
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for being better than bad people.
Sinners rescued by a Savior.
And when grace truly captures someone, it changes the question from:
“What can I get?”
to:
“What can I give?”
From:
“What do people owe me?”
to:
“How can my life make Christ clearer?”
That helps explain Paul's work ethic.
In Thessalonica, he reminded believers:
νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας ἐργαζόμενοι
nyktos kai hēmeras ergazomenoi
“working night and day.”
He explained that he did this so he would not become an unnecessary burden, while also giving believers an example to imitate.
—2 Thessalonians 3:8–9
Again, context matters.
Paul was not creating a universal rule that every pastor, missionary, evangelist, or Christian teacher must refuse financial support.
That would contradict Paul's own teaching elsewhere.
He was demonstrating something much harder:
Christian freedom can voluntarily surrender legitimate privileges for the sake of love and Gospel witness.
That sounds suspiciously like Jesus.
Christ possessed infinitely more than Paul ever surrendered.
Yet Philippians 2 tells us that Christ humbled Himself.
The eternal Son did not cease being God. Rather, He took the form of a servant and humbled Himself in obedience even to death on a cross.
The King became the servant.
The righteous One suffered for sinners.
The innocent One was condemned.
The One who deserved worship received mockery.
The hands worthy of heaven's praise were pierced.
And He did it to rescue people who could never repay Him.
So when Paul surrendered a right for the Gospel, he was following the pattern of his Lord.
That is why Christian generosity cannot ultimately be reduced to fundraising.
It begins at Calvary.
We give because Christ first gave Himself.
Maybe this article found you while you are tired.
Maybe you're working a job you never imagined having.
Maybe you're building something that nobody seems to notice.
Maybe you're serving at church while fighting battles you haven't told anyone about.
Maybe you're a parent trying to raise children faithfully while barely keeping yourself together.
Maybe you wonder whether your ordinary work matters because nobody applauds it.
Remember Paul's hands.
The kingdom of God is not measured by visibility.
There is dignity in honest work.
There is worship in faithfulness.

There can be holiness in showing up, doing what is right, providing for those entrusted to you, serving people well, refusing dishonesty, and quietly carrying Christ into places where nobody will ever hand you a microphone.
Your workplace can become mission territory.
Your desk can become an altar of obedience.
Your workshop can become a place of witness.
Your classroom.
Your kitchen.
Your hospital ward.
Your construction site.
Your taxi.
Your store.
Your office.
Your farm.
Your night shift.
You do not become spiritually significant only when somebody gives you a platform.
Jesus spent years working in ordinary obscurity before His public ministry.
Never confuse obscurity with uselessness.
But there is another side to Paul's teaching we should not avoid.
The same apostle who sometimes worked so he would not burden a church also taught Christians to materially support legitimate Gospel ministry.
Paul wrote:
οὕτως καὶ ὁ κύριος διέταξεν τοῖς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον καταγγέλλουσιν ἐκ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου ζῆν
houtōs kai ho kyrios dietaxen tois to euangelion katangellousin ek tou euangeliou zēn
“In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.”
—1 Corinthians 9:14
So Scripture gives us both truths.
Gospel workers may legitimately receive support.
And Gospel workers should be willing to surrender legitimate rights when necessary for the Gospel.
Christian generosity supports Gospel work.
Christian integrity ensures the Gospel never becomes merely a product.
That balance matters deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
It does not.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot buy salvation.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
If you repent and trust in Christ, salvation rests in Him—not in your financial contribution.

But if Gospel Warrior has helped you encounter Scripture, return to Christ, understand biblical truth, repent, heal, grow, or encourage someone else, there is a practical way you can help this ministry keep reaching people.
Support the work.

Not because supporting Gospel Warrior is the only way to glorify God—Scripture gives believers countless ways to glorify Him—but because voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work can itself become one expression of generosity, partnership, and mission.
Send it privately to the friend who would never admit publicly that he is drifting.
And comment honestly.
No polished testimony required.
No pretending.
Just truth.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting quietly.
Your testimony might become somebody else's reason to seek Jesus again.
But the deepest reason to stay connected isn't merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who isn't even sure they believe.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is scrolling through Facebook carrying a secret.
A marriage cracking behind smiling photographs.
A believer returning to an addiction they swore they had defeated.
A father wondering how he will provide.
A mother crying where her children cannot see.
A teenager questioning whether God hears them.
A Christian ashamed because everybody thinks they are spiritually strong.
A person contemplating walking away from church.
Someone who believes their scandal has finally become too ugly for grace.
Maybe they will never search for a sermon.
Maybe they will never walk voluntarily into a church tomorrow.
Maybe they will never type, “How can Jesus forgive me?”
But they might see what you share.
That changes the meaning of a share button.
It can become more than distribution.
It can become an invitation.
“Come and see.”
And perhaps that is one modern way we can understand the heart behind Paul's worn-out hands.
Whatever it took.
Whatever could be surrendered.
Whatever honest labor was necessary.
Whatever legitimate sacrifice could remove an unnecessary obstacle.
Just don't hide Christ.
Paul worked.
Paul preached.
Paul received support at times.
Paul surrendered support at other times.
Paul suffered.
Paul kept going.
Not because Paul was extraordinary enough to save the world.
Because Paul knew the One who could.
Jesus.
The Jesus who stopped a persecutor on the Damascus road.
The Jesus who transformed an enemy into an apostle.
The Jesus who took hands associated with persecution and turned them into hands serving the Gospel.
The Jesus who takes shame and writes redemption across it.
The Jesus who still calls sinners to repentance.
The Jesus who still forgives.
The Jesus who still restores.
The Jesus who still makes dead hearts alive.
So perhaps the most important question isn't merely:
“Why did Paul work while preaching?”
Perhaps the question underneath it is:
What am I willing to surrender so someone else can see Jesus more clearly?
Comfort?
Pride?
Time?
Money?
Reputation?
A grudge?
A secret sin?
The need to always be right?
The fear of telling somebody what Christ has done for you?
Paul's working hands still preach.
They remind us that calling does not always look glamorous.
Sometimes calling looks like tired hands that refuse to quit.
Sometimes worship looks like honest work.
Sometimes evangelism looks like refusing to exploit people.
Sometimes generosity looks like financially supporting someone else who is carrying the Gospel farther than you personally can.
Sometimes mission looks like sharing one article because one name suddenly entered your mind while you were reading it.
You know the name.
Don't ignore it.
Send this to them.
But above everything else…
Follow Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
Paul cannot save you.
Your work cannot save you.
Your generosity cannot save you.
Your religious history cannot save you.
Your good intentions cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
So bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the exhausted faith.
Bring Him the chapter you wish you could tear out of your story.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
And discover what Paul discovered on the road to Damascus:
Jesus is not intimidated by the chapter you're ashamed of.
He knows how to write what comes next.
And maybe that is the line you need to carry with you tonight:
The hands that once carried your shame do not have to carry it forever when those hands surrender everything to the scarred hands of Jesus.
It isn't.
Not when Jesus enters the story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PEOPLE-PLEASING LOOKS LIKE KINDNESS—UNTIL TELLING THE TRUTH MIGHT COST YOU THEIR APPROVAL
paragraphs: PEOPLE-PLEASING LOOKS LIKE KINDNESS—UNTIL TELLING THE TRUTH MIGHT COST YOU THEIR APPROVAL

You can spend years calling it kindness when, underneath the smiles, apologies, swallowed convictions, and exhausted yeses, you are terrified that someone will stop loving you the moment you finally tell the truth.
There is a kind of “nice” that looks almost Christian.
It smiles.
It avoids arguments.
It says yes when it desperately wants to say no.
It apologizes just to make tension disappear.
It stays silent when something is wrong because speaking might make the room uncomfortable.
It keeps answering messages when the soul is exhausted.
It lets boundaries be crossed and then crossed again.
It laughs at things that grieve the Spirit.
It softens convictions until nobody feels challenged.
It knows what should be said...
but also knows what saying it might cost.
And because everyone calls you kind, patient, easygoing, understanding, and loving, you may never stop long enough to ask the terrifying question:
Am I actually loving people... or am I terrified of losing their approval?
Because those are not always the same thing.
Sometimes what we call kindness is fear wearing church clothes.
Sometimes what we call keeping the peace is simply avoiding obedience.
Sometimes what we call being understanding is an unwillingness to establish a necessary boundary.
Sometimes silence isn't love.
Sometimes silence is self-protection.
And sometimes the person you are desperately trying not to disappoint has quietly occupied a place in your heart that belongs only to God.
That is where Galatians 1:10 becomes painfully personal.
Paul writes:
The sense of Paul's words is piercing:
Am I seeking the approval of people, or of God? Am I trying to please people? If pleasing people were still governing me, I could not be Christ's servant.
Notice where Paul ends.
Χριστοῦ δοῦλος — Christou doulos.
A servant—indeed, one belonging to Christ.
That is the battlefield.
Not kindness versus cruelty.
Not compassion versus courage.
Not whether Christians should care about people's feelings.
We absolutely should.
The question is deeper:
Who owns your obedience?
Because you can love people deeply without belonging to their opinions.
You can listen compassionately without surrendering conviction.
You can be gentle without becoming controlled.
You can forgive someone without granting unlimited access to wound you again.
You can say no without hatred.
You can establish a boundary without bitterness.
You can speak truth without becoming arrogant.
And you can disappoint someone without sinning against them.
Somebody needed that last sentence.
Maybe you grew up learning that love meant keeping everybody happy.
Maybe disagreement brought punishment.
Maybe affection disappeared when you disappointed someone.
Maybe you learned to study faces before you learned to study Scripture.
A changed tone could ruin your entire day.
A delayed reply could make you wonder what you had done wrong.
Someone saying, “I'm disappointed in you,” could send you into an emotional spiral.
So you became skilled.
Skilled at reading rooms.
Skilled at becoming whatever people needed.
Skilled at saying, “It's okay,” when it wasn't.
Skilled at laughing when something hurt.
Skilled at apologizing for things that weren't yours to carry.
Skilled at shrinking.
And eventually people began calling you “the nice one.”
But nobody saw what happened afterward.
Nobody saw the resentment.
Nobody saw you replaying conversations at midnight.
Nobody saw how exhausted you became from managing everybody else's emotions.
Nobody saw how often you betrayed your own conscience just to keep somebody from being upset with you.
And perhaps the hardest thing to admit is this:
You weren't always giving from love.
Sometimes you were giving because you were afraid.
Afraid they would leave.
Afraid they would misunderstand.
Afraid they would talk about you.
Afraid they would call you selfish.
Afraid they would think you had changed.
Afraid they would stop inviting you.
Afraid they would unfollow you.
Afraid they wouldn't need you anymore.
Afraid that if you finally became honest, you might discover that some relationships survived only because you never had boundaries.
That realization hurts.
But Jesus does not expose our chains to humiliate us.
He exposes them because He intends to free us.
And freedom from people-pleasing does not mean becoming insensitive.
It means becoming surrendered.
There is an important biblical distinction here.
Scripture does not teach us to become unnecessarily offensive people who proudly say, “I don't care what anybody thinks.”
That isn't spiritual maturity.
Jesus calls us to love.

Paul himself could speak about seeking another person's good rather than his own. He could become “all things to all people” for the sake of the Gospel. Christian freedom is never permission to become harsh, selfish, or indifferent.
So Galatians 1:10 cannot honestly mean:
“Never care whether your actions affect anyone.”
The context is far more serious.
Immediately before verse 10, Paul is defending the Gospel against distortion. He has warned the Galatians about accepting a different gospel. Then comes his question about human approval.
In other words, there are moments when maintaining people's approval would require compromising something God has made clear.
And at that moment...
approval becomes too expensive.
If keeping them happy requires hiding Christ, the price is too high.
If keeping the relationship requires calling sin righteousness, the price is too high.
If avoiding conflict requires violating conscience, the price is too high.
If belonging requires becoming someone God never called you to be, the price is too high.
If being loved requires disobedience to Jesus...
the price is too high.
Jesus Himself embodied perfect love without becoming controlled by human approval.
Think about Him.
He touched people society rejected.
He ate with people religious elites despised.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He spoke tenderly to the broken.
He told uncomfortable truth.
He showed mercy to sinners without redefining sin.
He washed feet.
He wept.
He forgave.
He welcomed children.
He restored failures.
And He also allowed people to walk away.
That last part unsettles people-pleasers.
Jesus loved people enough to let them reject Him rather than manipulate them into staying.
When the rich young ruler walked away sorrowful, Jesus did not chase him down and renegotiate the cost of discipleship.
When truth offended crowds, Christ did not redesign truth around audience retention.
When Peter resisted the road toward the cross, Jesus did not abandon the Father's will to preserve Peter's comfort.
And eventually...
the crowd turned.
The same human appetite that can shout praise can later shout condemnation.
Christ knew something every recovering people-pleaser eventually has to learn:
Human approval makes a terrible savior.
It cannot hold you.
It cannot cleanse you.
It cannot justify you.
It cannot resurrect you.
It cannot tell you who you are.
And it certainly cannot die for your sins.
Only Jesus did that.
This is where people-pleasing becomes more than a personality issue.
It can become worship.
Whatever possesses the authority to determine your obedience is functioning dangerously close to a god.
If someone's disappointment can consistently make you disobey Jesus, their approval has gained spiritual power it was never meant to possess.
That doesn't mean you stop honoring people.
It means you stop worshiping their acceptance.
There is only one throne.
And perhaps your freedom begins with admitting who has been sitting on it.
Your parents?
Your spouse?
Your friends?
Your pastor?
Your coworkers?
Your audience?
Your followers?
Your critics?
That one person whose approval you have spent half your life trying to earn?
Be honest.
Whose disappointment scares you more than God's displeasure?
That question may hurt.
Let it.
Not every pain is an enemy.
Sometimes conviction is the mercy of God putting His finger on the chain you've learned to decorate.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying resentment toward people you keep saying yes to.
You tell yourself, “They keep taking advantage of me.”
Maybe they do.
But there may also be another difficult truth:
You keep giving them a yes that your heart secretly means as no.
Then you punish them internally for believing the answer you gave them externally.
That is not freedom.
A truthful boundary can sometimes be more loving than a resentful sacrifice.
Jesus taught that our “Yes” should mean yes and our “No” should mean no.
There is remarkable freedom in becoming the same person internally and externally.
No performance.
No secret scorekeeping.
No manipulation.
No “yes” designed to purchase affection.
Just truth spoken with love.
Sometimes that sounds like:
“I love you, but I cannot participate in this.”
Sometimes:
“I forgive you, but trust needs to be rebuilt.”
Sometimes:
“I understand you're disappointed, but I cannot violate my conscience to make this easier.”
Sometimes:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Because freedom from people-pleasing also means becoming willing to disappoint your own pride.
Sometimes you aren't the courageous truth-teller in the story.
Sometimes you're simply wrong.
Following Christ means being free enough from human approval to admit that too.
This is not about becoming harder.
It is about becoming truer.
More humble.
More courageous.
More loving.
More surrendered.
And that transformation happens at the cross.
Because underneath people-pleasing is often an aching question:
Will I still be loved if they reject me?
The Gospel answers with blood-stained certainty.
Your deepest acceptance was never supposed to come from them.
In Christ, the repentant sinner does not stand before God desperately performing for a place at His table.
Jesus purchased what you could never earn.
At the cross, Christ carried sin and shame.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Condemned.
Crucified.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not say, “Become impressive enough and perhaps God will approve of you.”
The Gospel announces that salvation is God's gift through Christ, received by faith—not a trophy for people who finally become impressive enough.
That means the approval addiction can finally begin to loosen its grip.
You do not need everybody to choose you when Christ has called you His.
You do not need everybody to understand you before you obey Him.
You do not need universal applause.
You need grace.
You need truth.
You need Jesus.
And yes, obedience may cost you something.
Some people preferred the version of you who had no boundaries.
Some preferred you exhausted.
Some preferred you silent.
Some preferred the version of you who could be guilted into anything.
When you become healthier, truthful, and more obedient to Christ, somebody may accuse you of changing.
Maybe you have.
The question is:
Who are you becoming more like?
If you are becoming arrogant, repent.
If you are becoming cold, repent.
If you are using “boundaries” as an excuse for unforgiveness, repent.
If you are using “truth” as permission to be cruel, repent.
But if you are learning to obey Jesus without requiring everyone's permission...
keep walking.
If your hands shake when you finally tell the truth, keep walking.
If someone misunderstands your boundary, keep walking.
If obedience costs applause, keep walking.
If following Christ exposes how addicted you were to being needed, keep walking.
Grace is teaching you how to live free.
Not free from loving people.
Free to actually love them.
Because genuine love does not merely ask:
“How do I keep you happy with me?”
Love asks:
“What is true?”
“What honors Christ?”
“What genuinely serves your good?”
“What can I say without pretending?”
“What does faithfulness require here?”
And sometimes love hugs.
Sometimes love listens.
Sometimes love stays.
Sometimes love gives.
Sometimes love sacrifices.
Sometimes love says, “I'm sorry.”
And sometimes love looks someone in the eyes, with tears instead of anger, and says:
“I love you too much to lie to you.”
That may cost approval.
But Christianity was never built on the promise that everyone would approve of transformed people.
It was built around a rejected Savior carrying a cross.
So maybe this article found you because you're exhausted.
Exhausted from being everybody's peace while having none yourself.
Exhausted from checking whether everybody is okay with you.
Exhausted from apologizing for existing.
Exhausted from carrying relationships you are terrified to examine.
Exhausted from editing your convictions according to the temperature of the room.
Bring that exhaustion to Jesus.
And repent where fear has become lord.
Not with self-hatred.
With surrender.

“Jesus, forgive me for craving human approval more than Your approval. Forgive me for the times I compromised truth because rejection frightened me. Forgive me for calling fear kindness and avoidance peace. Teach me to love people without worshiping their opinions. Make me gentle without making me cowardly. Make me courageous without making me cruel. Teach me to speak truth in love. Teach me when to remain silent and when silence would become disobedience. I belong to You.”
Maybe your first courageous act is not confronting somebody else.
Maybe it is confessing something to God.
Not because typing words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes putting an honest confession into words is the moment we stop pretending the battle isn't there.
And if you're still fighting the fear of rejection, you can simply comment, “I'm still fighting.”
Someone else reading those words may realize they aren't fighting alone.
Then think of one person who constantly exhausts themselves trying to keep everybody happy.
Not somebody you want to indirectly attack.
Somebody you genuinely love.
Not as a performance. Not to earn anything from God. Not because sharing a post somehow proves your faith.
Supporting Gospel work financially does not purchase God's favor, salvation, blessing, or spiritual status. Christ cannot be bought.
But generosity can be an act of worship when it flows freely from a heart that wants God glorified.
Because the next time someone's disappointment makes you question an obedient decision, you may need these words again.
And comment because somebody else needs to know Christians can be honest about this battle.
But above everything...
come back to Jesus.
Because the goal was never to become a person who doesn't care what anybody thinks.
The goal is to become a person who loves people deeply...
without asking them for permission to belong completely to Christ.
Maybe they reject you.
Maybe they misunderstand you.
Maybe somebody walks away.
Maybe the room becomes uncomfortable when you finally stop pretending.
But when your identity is anchored in the crucified and risen Christ, rejection no longer gets the final word.
Grace does.
You may have spent years changing yourself so people wouldn't leave.
Jesus is inviting you into something better:
to let Him change you even if some people do.
And remember this when the fear rises again:
You don't have to lose your kindness when you stop people-pleasing—you only have to lose the fear that taught you to call slavery love.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FAITH CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS”—BUT WHAT MOUNTAIN WAS JESUS ACTUALLY TALKING ABOUT?
paragraphs: “FAITH CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS”—BUT WHAT MOUNTAIN WAS JESUS ACTUALLY TALKING ABOUT?
Jesus never told you to pretend your mountain isn’t real. He told you where to look when the mountain becomes bigger than you.
There are some Bible verses we know so well that we stop hearing them.
“Faith can move mountains.”
We put it on mugs.
We print it on shirts.
We write it beneath photographs of sunsets.
We whisper it when the diagnosis comes back.
We repeat it when the marriage is trembling.
We post it when the bills are piling up.
We tell it to the mother praying for a child who no longer wants anything to do with God.
We say it to the man sitting alone at 2:13 in the morning, staring into the darkness because nobody knows how close he is to giving up.
Faith can move mountains.
But what if Jesus was saying something far deeper than the slogan we have made from His words?
What if we have spent years asking God to move our mountains without first hearing the command Jesus gave immediately before He spoke about them?
Because in Mark 11, Jesus did not begin with the mountain.
He began with God.
Ἔχετε πίστιν θεοῦ.
Echete pistin Theou.
“Have faith in God.”
Not faith in your ability to believe hard enough.
Not faith in positive thinking.
Not faith in religious formulas.
Not faith in your declarations.
Not faith in your emotions.
Not even faith in faith.
Faith in God.
And maybe somebody reading this desperately needs that distinction, because you have secretly blamed yourself for years.
You prayed.
Nothing happened.
You believed.
The door stayed closed.
You fasted.
The sickness remained.
You begged God to restore something that still fell apart.
Then somewhere inside you came the terrible accusation:
Maybe my faith just wasn't strong enough.
But listen carefully to Jesus.
He was never teaching His disciples how to manipulate God.
He was teaching frightened, limited human beings where confidence belongs when they encounter something human strength cannot move.
And the setting makes His words breathtaking.
Mark places this teaching during the final days before the cross.
Jesus has entered Jerusalem.
He has confronted corruption in the temple.
He has overturned tables.
A fig tree has withered after His word of judgment.
The religious establishment is moving against Him.
The shadow of Calvary is getting longer.
And somewhere along the road between Jerusalem and Bethany, surrounded by the geography of mountains, Jesus says:
“Have faith in God.”
Then comes the sentence Christians have repeated for centuries.
In Greek:
ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ὃς ἂν εἴπῃ τῷ ὄρει τούτῳ...
Amēn legō hymin... hos an eipē tō orei toutō...
“Truly I say to you... whoever says to this mountain...”
Notice those words.
Not merely “a mountain.”
τῷ ὄρει τούτῳ.
This mountain.
That matters.

Scholars have debated precisely which mountain Jesus intended His hearers to envision. Some identify the Mount of Olives, which dominated the landscape along the Bethany-Jerusalem route. Others see a deliberate reference to the Temple Mount, especially because Mark surrounds this saying with Jesus' judgment upon fruitless worship and His confrontation at the temple.
We should be humble where Scripture does not explicitly identify the mountain.
But we should not miss what Scripture makes unmistakable.
Jesus took something enormous, immovable and humanly impossible and placed it beside the power of God.
He continued:
“Be taken up and thrown into the sea.”
Picture the disciples hearing that.
A mountain.
Not a pebble.
Not a chair.
Not something twelve men could push if they worked together.
A mountain.
Something that silently tells you:
I was here before you arrived.
I will still be here after you leave.
You cannot move me.
Maybe now you understand why this teaching has survived inside wounded hearts for two thousand years.
Because everyone eventually meets a mountain.
Sometimes your mountain has a medical name.
Sometimes it has your last name.
Sometimes it sleeps beside you.
Sometimes it left you.
Sometimes it is buried in a cemetery.
Sometimes it appears on a bank statement.
Sometimes it lives inside your memories.
Sometimes nobody else can see it.
Addiction can become a mountain.
Shame can become a mountain.
Bitterness can become a mountain.
Pornography can become a mountain.
Debt can become a mountain.
Grief can become a mountain.
An unbelieving child can feel like a mountain.
A broken marriage can feel like a mountain.
Years of secret sin can become a mountain.
And sometimes the most terrifying mountain is the person looking back at you from the mirror.
You have promised God before.
You cried before.
You deleted the number before.
You threw it away before.
You went back to church before.
You said, “This is the last time,” before.
And somehow...
here you are again.
Standing at the foot of something you cannot move.
That is exactly where cheap Christianity tells you to become stronger.
Jesus tells you to trust God.
There is an enormous difference.
Biblical faith is not pretending the mountain is small.
Biblical faith knows God is greater.
That is why the mustard seed matters.
Matthew records another occasion when Jesus told His disciples:
“If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed...”
The Greek expression is:
πίστιν ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως
pistin hōs kokkon sinapeōs.
Faith like a mustard seed.
We often hear that and immediately begin measuring ourselves.
How much faith do I have?
But the beauty of the image is precisely its smallness.
Jesus does not glorify enormous human confidence.
He directs weak human beings toward an enormous God.
A mustard seed does not boast.
It simply possesses life.
And living faith, however trembling, reaches outside itself toward the One who is faithful.
That means the prayer of a shattered believer can still be faith.
“Jesus... help me.”
Faith.
“Lord... I believe; help my unbelief.”
Faith.
“Father... I don't understand this.”
Faith.
“Jesus... I cannot carry this anymore.”
Faith.
Faith is not always shouting.
Sometimes faith crawls.
Sometimes faith weeps.
Sometimes faith has no beautiful speech left.
Sometimes faith is simply a bruised soul whispering the name of Jesus one more time.
And here is where the Gospel becomes far more beautiful than motivational Christianity.
Because Jesus did not come merely to teach you how to conquer difficult circumstances.
He came to rescue sinners.
Our greatest mountain was never merely sickness, poverty, rejection, disappointment or adversity.
Our greatest problem was sin.
Sin separated humanity from a holy God.
We could not climb our way back.
Religion could not erase our guilt.
Good behavior could not rewrite yesterday.
Our tears could not purchase forgiveness.
Our promises could not resurrect a spiritually dead heart.
We needed something only God could do.
And God did it.
Not by telling sinners to climb the mountain to Him...
but by coming down to us.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
The sinless Son of God walked toward Jerusalem knowing exactly what waited there.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Nails.
Blood.
A cross.
And notice the breathtaking irony.
The One who told mountains to move did not use His power to escape Calvary.
He surrendered to the Father's will.
At Gethsemane, He prayed.
At Golgotha, He was crucified.
And there, the greatest obstacle between sinful humanity and holy God was dealt with through the blood of Christ.
Our guilt.
Our condemnation.
Our rebellion.
Our impossible debt.
Jesus carried it.
Then they placed Him inside a tomb.
For one horrifying Sabbath, it looked as though the mountain had won.
Hope was sealed behind stone.
The disciples scattered.
Dreams died.
Silence fell.
Then Sunday came.
The stone moved.
The tomb opened.
And Jesus Christ walked out alive.
That is Christianity.
Not “believe in yourself.”
Not “manifest your future.”
Not “speak whatever you want into existence.”
Christ crucified.
Christ buried.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
And suddenly “faith can move mountains” becomes infinitely more beautiful.
Because Christian faith is not confidence that God must give me whatever outcome I demand.
It is confidence that the God revealed in Jesus Christ is trustworthy even when I cannot understand what He is doing.
Sometimes God moves the mountain.
Sometimes God leads you over it.
Sometimes He takes you around it.
Sometimes He makes a road straight through it.
And sometimes He allows the mountain to remain while transforming the person standing before it.
Paul begged for his thorn to leave.
It remained.
But grace arrived.
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
So unanswered prayer does not automatically mean absent faith.
A mountain remaining does not automatically mean God abandoned you.
The cross itself proves that apparent defeat can become the doorway through which God accomplishes redemption.
Friday looked like catastrophe.
Sunday revealed victory.
Maybe you are living somewhere between Friday and Sunday right now.
You prayed, but nothing changed.
You forgave, but it still hurts.
You obeyed, but the door still closed.
You trusted God, but the person still died.
You came back to Jesus, but temptation did not magically disappear.
You expected resurrection...
and all you can see is a stone.
Do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
The disciples once stood before a sealed tomb believing the story was finished.
God was writing the sentence they could not yet see.
And perhaps this is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a phrase.
Peter knew scandal.
He swore he would never abandon Jesus.
Then fear entered the courtyard.
One accusation.
One denial.
Another accusation.
Another denial.
Then another.
“I don't know Him.”
And somewhere in the darkness...
a rooster crowed.
Imagine Peter's mountain then.
Shame.
Failure.
Cowardice.
The memory of Jesus looking at him.
How do you move that mountain?
You don't.
Grace does.
After the resurrection, Jesus did not discard Peter.
He restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
Again.
Again.
Three denials met by three invitations back into love and calling.
That is what Jesus does with surrendered ruins.
He does not call evil good.
He forgives evil and transforms sinners.
He doesn't pretend the scandal never happened.
He writes grace through it.
Maybe your mountain is something you caused.
That hurts differently, doesn't it?
It is easier to ask God to deliver us from what someone did to us than to face what we did ourselves.
Maybe you wrecked the relationship.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you betrayed someone's trust.
Maybe your family knows the church version of you while God knows what happens when the door closes.
Maybe you have learned how to raise your hands during worship while hiding chains beneath them.
And you are terrified that if anyone knew everything...
they would never look at you the same way again.
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every deleted message.
Every hidden tab.
Every secret conversation.
Every compromise.
Every rationalization.
Every night you said you would stop.
And still the Gospel invitation remains:
Repent.
Come home.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the cross proves exactly how much it matters.
Grace is not God shrugging at your sin.
Grace is the holy Son of God bleeding to save you from it.
Repentance is not paying God back.
It is finally dropping your weapons.
It is saying:
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
And perhaps that is the mountain that must move first.
Pride.
The mountain that keeps saying:
I can fix myself.
I don't need anybody.
I'll come to God when I'm better.
No.
Come broken.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with mustard-seed faith.
Come with shaking hands.
Come with tears.
Come without excuses.
But come to Jesus.
Because salvation has never depended upon sinners becoming impressive enough for Christ.
It depends upon Christ being sufficient for sinners.
And He is.
Not because typing words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let believers who see it pray instead of judge.

If God has already carried you through something you once believed would destroy you, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the flashlight another wounded person needs while walking through their own midnight.
And send this article to the person whose mountain immediately entered your mind while reading.
You know who they are.
Don't merely click “like” and keep scrolling.
You may never know what God does with one faithful share.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support purchases blessing.
It cannot.
Christ purchased our redemption, and grace cannot be bought.
Support Christian ministry because you freely want to participate in spreading biblical truth and glorifying God through generosity—not because anyone frightened or pressured you into giving.
And beyond products, the deeper reason to stay connected is discipleship.
Not because you need another saved post.
Because eventually another mountain may appear.
And when it does, you may need to remember:
Jesus never told you to have faith in your faith.
He said:
“Have faith in God.”
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the seeker who has questions.
Even invite the person who does not yet believe.
Let them encounter Scripture.
Let them wrestle with Jesus.
Let them see that Christianity is not the story of flawless people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of a holy Savior coming for sinners.
Because perhaps the greatest miracle is not that faith can throw a mountain into the sea.
Perhaps the miracle you desperately need to remember tonight is that Jesus can take a heart buried beneath shame and make it alive again.
He can forgive the unforgivable sinner who truly comes to Him.
He can restore what sin shattered according to His wisdom.
He can break chains.
He can resurrect hope.
He can turn persecutors into apostles.
Cowards into witnesses.
Prodigals into sons and daughters who finally came home.
Scandal into testimony.
Graves into beginnings.
And sinners into saints—not because we became powerful enough...
but because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
So stand before your mountain.
Acknowledge how enormous it is.
Stop pretending.
Stop bargaining.
Stop trying to impress God.
Then look beyond the mountain.
There is a cross.
Beyond the cross...
an empty tomb.
And seated above every mountain, every kingdom, every power, every fear, every failure and every impossible circumstance is the risen Jesus Christ.
Your mountain may be enormous.
Your faith may feel microscopic.
But your Savior is neither.
Remember that when the mountain whispers that your story is over:
The stone that looks like the end of your story may be standing at the entrance to a resurrection only Jesus can write.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Adam Had a Garden Full of Food. Jesus Had Forty Days of Hunger. One Reached for the Fruit. The Other Reached for the Word.
paragraphs: Adam Had a Garden Full of Food. Jesus Had Forty Days of Hunger. One Reached for the Fruit. The Other Reached for the Word.

The first Adam stood among trees overflowing with food and fell when the serpent questioned God’s Word. Jesus stood starving in a wilderness and refused to turn stones into bread. Between those two moments lies the story of humanity—and the breathtaking reason your worst failure does not have to become your final chapter.
There was food everywhere.
That is what makes the story so uncomfortable.
Adam was not wandering through a wasteland desperately searching for something to eat. He was not starving. He was not abandoned in some barren wilderness with his body screaming for survival.
He was in Eden.
A garden planted by God.
Genesis says that the LORD God caused to grow from the ground “every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food” (Genesis 2:9).
Think about that.
Abundance.
Beauty.
Provision.
Trees everywhere.
Food everywhere.
Permission everywhere except one place.
God told the man that he could freely eat from every tree of the garden, but not from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Genesis 2:16–17).
The Hebrew intensifies the generosity of that permission:
אָכֹל תֹּאכֵל
akhol tokhel.
