Literally, it carries the force of “you may surely/freely eat.”
Before there was a prohibition, there was generosity.
Before God said, “Do not eat from that tree,” He had effectively said, “Look at everything I have given you.”
That matters.
Because temptation has always had a way of making one forbidden thing appear larger than a thousand gifts from God.
And maybe that is where this story stops being ancient history.
Maybe Eden is closer than we think.
You can have blessings surrounding you and still obsess over what God has withheld.
You can have a spouse who loves you and still stare too long at someone who is not yours.
You can have enough and still envy somebody else’s life.
You can have Scripture available on your phone, sermons playing through your headphones, people praying for you, mercy waking you up every morning—and still hear the ancient whisper:
“Did God really say?”
That was the serpent’s strategy.
Not merely fruit.
Distrust.
Genesis 3:1 records the question:
אַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים
’aph ki-amar Elohim...
“Did God actually say...?”
The attack began with the Word of God.
Before the hand reached toward the fruit, confidence in God’s Word was being dismantled.
The serpent did not begin by saying, “Reject God.”
He began by making God questionable.
Is God really good?
Is His command really necessary?
Is obedience really worth it?
Is He keeping something from you?
Will one compromise really matter?
And thousands of years later, the voice of temptation still knows the same language.
Nobody usually wakes up and says, “Today I want to destroy my relationship with God.”
It happens more quietly.
Just this once.
Nobody will know.
You deserve this.
God will forgive you anyway.
Everybody struggles with it.
You can repent later.
And suddenly the forbidden tree does not look like rebellion.
It looks reasonable.
Eve ate.
Then she gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate (Genesis 3:6).
And Scripture places particular covenantal significance upon Adam’s transgression. Paul would later write, “sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin” (Romans 5:12).
Paradise had become the scene of humanity’s catastrophe.
Then Scripture takes us somewhere very different.
Not another garden.
A wilderness.
Not abundance.
Hunger.
Not Adam surrounded by food.
Jesus after fasting forty days and forty nights.
Matthew tells us plainly:
ὕστερον ἐπείνασεν
hysteron epeinasen.
“Afterward, He was hungry” (Matthew 4:2).
Do not race past those words because you already know the story.
He was hungry.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son who had truly taken human flesh, experienced real physical hunger.
Forty days.
Then the tempter came.
Notice the timing.
The devil came when Jesus was hungry.
There are moments when temptation does not attack your theology first.
It attacks your exhaustion.
Your loneliness.
Your disappointment.
Your unmet desire.
Your anger.
Your grief.
Your appetite.
Your need to feel seen.
Your need to escape.
Your need to make the pain stop for five minutes.
Some of your most dangerous spiritual moments will arrive when something legitimate inside you is screaming for relief.
Food was not evil.
Hunger was not sinful.
Bread was not sinful.
That is what makes the temptation so revealing.
The tempter said:
“Εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ...”
Ei huios ei tou Theou...
“If You are the Son of God...”
“...command these stones to become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3).
Jesus could make bread.
Later He would multiply bread for thousands.
The issue was not whether bread was evil.
The issue was whether the Son would abandon obedient trust in the Father and answer the tempter on the tempter’s terms.
And Jesus answered with Scripture.
Γέγραπται.
Gegraptai.
“It is written.”
Then He quoted Deuteronomy 8:3:
“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).
Do you see the breathtaking contrast?
In Eden, the serpent questioned God’s Word.
In the wilderness, Jesus answered with God’s Word.
Adam stood in abundance and disobeyed.
Christ stood in deprivation and remained obedient.
Adam was surrounded by food and reached beyond God’s command.
Jesus was starving and refused to satisfy Himself outside obedient trust in His Father.
The contrast is almost painful.
But it was never meant merely to make you admire Jesus from a distance.
It was meant to make you understand why you desperately need Him.
Because if you are honest, you have been Adam.
So have I.
Maybe not beside a literal tree.
But we know what it is to receive a thousand gifts from God and become consumed by the one thing we want that He has forbidden.
We know what it is to exchange obedience for a moment.
We know what it is to believe the lie that sin will give us something God cannot.
We know what happens afterward too.
The hiding.
That may be one of the saddest sentences in Genesis.
After they sinned, Adam and Eve hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden (Genesis 3:8).
The trees that once testified to God’s generosity became hiding places from His presence.
Isn't that what shame still does?
You fall...
then hide.
You relapse...
then hide.
You lose your temper...
then hide.
You open the website again...
then hide.
You return to the secret conversation...
then hide.
You compromise what you promised God you would surrender...
then hide.
You smile at church.
You answer, “I’m good.”
You post something encouraging.
You tell everybody God is faithful.
But somewhere underneath all of it is a terrified heart sewing fig leaves together, hoping nobody discovers what happened beside your tree.
And perhaps the hardest person to face is not your pastor.
Not your spouse.
Not your parents.
Not your friends.
God.
Because you knew better.
You had His Word.
You had warnings.
You had opportunities to walk away.
And you still reached.
This is where Christianity becomes infinitely more beautiful than religious self-improvement.
The Gospel does not announce that another Adam finally learned how to behave better.
The Gospel announces that Another Adam came.
Paul deliberately places Adam and Christ beside one another.
“For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one Man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).
One man’s disobedience.
One Man’s obedience.
One trespass bringing condemnation.
One righteous act opening the way of justification and life (Romans 5:18).
Paul goes even further in 1 Corinthians 15:45:
“The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.
Jesus did not come merely to give fallen sons and daughters inspirational advice about resisting temptation.
He came to accomplish what Adam failed to accomplish.
He came in obedience.
He remained without sin.
He resisted the tempter.
He trusted the Father.
He walked toward the cross.
And there He carried something infinitely heavier than wilderness hunger.
Our sin.
Our shame.
Our rebellion.
Our guilt.
Our hiding.
The story moves from a tree where humanity rebelled against God to a cross where the obedient Son gave Himself for sinners.
This does not mean the cross was God pretending sin did not matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin mattered enough that redemption cost blood.
Grace is free to us because it was unimaginably costly to Christ.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And He willingly laid down His life.
Then the grave that appeared to have swallowed the hope of humanity could not keep Him.
Christ rose.
That changes everything.
Your Christian hope is not that you will eventually become strong enough never to need grace.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Your salvation is not built upon the impressive consistency of your obedience.
It rests upon Christ—His righteousness, His atoning death, His resurrection, His grace received through faith.
And grace does something far greater than excuse your sin.
Grace calls you out of hiding.
Grace teaches you to say no to ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
Grace brings repentance.
Grace restores.
Grace transforms.
Grace takes people whose stories smell like scandal and begins writing redemption across pages they thought were ruined forever.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you are reading this after losing another battle.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you promised God that last time really was the last time.
Then it happened again.
And now shame is preaching a sermon to you:
“Look at you.”
“You will never change.”
“God must be tired of you.”
“Stay hidden.”
But listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation do not lead in the same direction.
The Gospel does not tell you to make peace with your sin.
It tells you to bring it into the light.
Repent.
Confess.
Turn.
Run toward Christ rather than using your failure as another reason to run away from Him.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
The answer to your failure is not pretending the forbidden fruit never entered your mouth.
The answer is coming honestly to the Savior whose blood is sufficient for sinners.
And the next time temptation whispers, remember the wilderness.
Jesus answered:
Γέγραπται.
Gegraptai.
“It is written.”
There is something worth noticing here.
Jesus knew Scripture before the temptation arrived.
He did not wait until the wilderness to decide whether the Father could be trusted.
That should confront those of us trying to survive spiritual warfare on scraps of biblical truth.
You cannot feed your mind endlessly on lust, outrage, envy, entertainment, fear, comparison, and noise, then wonder why your soul feels weak when temptation arrives.
You need the Word.
Not inspirational fragments detached from context.
Not merely somebody else’s relationship with Scripture.
You need to know God through His revealed Word.
Read it when you feel powerful.
Read it when you feel nothing.
Read it when obedience feels beautiful.
Read it when your flesh hates what it says.
Store truth before the wilderness comes.
Because the wilderness comes.
And perhaps someone you love is already standing in one.
Someone may be smiling publicly while hiding privately.
Someone may need to remember tonight that temptation does not have the final word.
Send this to the person who thinks failure has permanently disqualified them.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not turn the comments into a performance.
Be honest.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “I need someone to stand with me.”
Not because you need another post buried in a collection, but because there may be a night when the forbidden thing suddenly looks beautiful again.
Come back.
Remember Eden.
Remember the wilderness.
Remember:
Γέγραπται.
It is written.
And remember that Christianity is not the story of strong people proving they deserve God.
It is the story of sinners being rescued by a strong Savior.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's favor, prove your salvation, or make you more righteous before Him. Jesus has already accomplished what money could never accomplish.
But generosity and willing support can help biblical resources travel farther.
And the support is about more than merchandise.
Not as a religious badge.
As a doorway.
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
They may never admit how close they came to giving up.
But God can use a Scripture-filled message placed in front of them at the right moment.
Invite your family.
Send it to the struggling believer.
Send it to the lukewarm Christian.
Send it to the person questioning everything.
Even send it to the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only about good people trying harder.
Let them discover Jesus.
Save what you may need when another wilderness comes.
And share because somebody else's battle may be happening silently on the other side of your screen.
Adam had a garden full of food.
Jesus had a wilderness full of stones.
Adam had abundance and reached for what God forbade.
Jesus had hunger and remained obedient to His Father.
But here is the part you must never forget:
Jesus did not overcome merely so you could stare at His victory and feel worse about your failures.
He overcame as the faithful Son.
He went to the cross for sinners.
He rose from the grave.
And He calls fallen people out from behind their trees.
So stop sewing fig leaves.
Stop pretending.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop allowing shame to convince you that hiding is safer than repentance.
Come into the light.
The God who confronted sin in Eden is the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Your sin is serious.
Christ is sufficient.
Repentance matters.
Grace is real.
Forgiveness is available in Him.
And transformation is possible because the Gospel does not leave surrendered sinners where it found them.
The serpent's oldest strategy was to make humanity doubt what God had said.
So when the whisper comes again...
when the screen is glowing...
when nobody is watching...
when loneliness starts negotiating...
when hunger becomes an excuse...
when the forbidden thing begins looking beautiful...
remember the starving Savior in the wilderness.
Γέγραπται.
It is written.
And remember this:
The tree you reached for may explain your scandal, but the cross Jesus carried can become the place where grace begins rewriting your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID SEX DURING MENSTRUATION?
paragraphs:
WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID SEX DURING MENSTRUATION?
The Command Almost Everyone Misunderstands—and What It Reveals About Holiness, Intimacy, Blood, and the Grace of Jesus Christ
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people frame.
There are verses people quote when they are afraid, grieving, confused, or desperately trying to hold onto faith.
And then there are verses people quietly hurry past.
Leviticus 18:19 is one of them.
It speaks about menstruation.
It speaks about sex.
It speaks about something so private that many Christians have probably never heard a sermon about it.
And yet God put it in Scripture.
That alone should make us stop.
Because if we believe that “all Scripture is breathed out by God” (2 Timothy 3:16), then we cannot treat uncomfortable passages as embarrassing leftovers from an ancient religion.
We have to ask the uncomfortable question.
Why?
Why would the God who created marriage, sexuality, the female body, fertility, blood, desire, and intimacy tell Israel that sexual intercourse was forbidden during menstruation?
Was menstruation sinful?
Was God shaming women?
Was this merely an ancient health regulation?
Does the command apply directly to Christians today?
And perhaps the question underneath all those questions is this:
What does any of this have to do with Jesus?
Stay with this until the end.
Because what begins with a command concerning blood eventually forces us to confront something much closer to home:
the difference between being physically unclean under Israel's covenant and being morally guilty before a holy God...
and the breathtaking reason Christians can never read Leviticus correctly without eventually looking toward Christ.
The Hebrew of Leviticus 18:19 says:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el-ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ervatah.
A careful rendering is:
“You shall not approach a woman in her menstrual impurity to uncover her nakedness.”
Three expressions deserve attention.
נִדָּה — niddah
The word is associated here with menstruation and the condition of menstrual impurity.
טֻמְאָה — tum’ah
This means impurity or uncleanness.
And then:
לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ — legalot ervatah
Literally, “to uncover her nakedness,” an expression used in the sexual laws of Leviticus.
So we should begin by refusing to soften what the passage actually says.
Leviticus 18:19 prohibits sexual relations during menstrual impurity.
Leviticus 20:18 makes the prohibition even more explicit:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה וְגִלָּה אֶת־עֶרְוָתָהּ אֶת־מְקֹרָהּ הֶעֱרָה וְהִיא גִּלְּתָה אֶת־מְקוֹר דָּמֶיהָ וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם׃
The text describes a man lying sexually with a menstruating woman, exposing the source of her blood, and declares that both are to be “cut off” from among their people.
This was not presented to Israel as optional advice.
But now we have to notice something that changes the conversation.
Menstruation itself was not a moral sin.
That distinction matters enormously.

Leviticus 15 places menstruation inside a much larger system of ritual purity and impurity. Male bodily discharges appear there too. Sexual emission could result in temporary uncleanness. Childbirth also involved ritual impurity elsewhere in Leviticus.
None of those realities means that the body itself was evil.
None means that being female was sinful.
None means that a menstruating woman had committed some moral offense simply because her body was functioning normally.
This is where careless teaching can wound people.
Biblical “uncleanness” is not automatically identical with personal moral guilt.
A person could become ritually unclean without committing a sin.
That distinction is essential for understanding Leviticus.
God was teaching Israel to live within categories of holy and common, clean and unclean, permitted and forbidden.
Israel was not merely another ancient nation with a religious decoration attached to its culture.
They belonged to Yahweh.
Their worship belonged to Him.
Their food belonged under His authority.
Their calendar belonged under His authority.
Their bodies belonged under His authority.
And yes...
their sexuality belonged under His authority too.
That may be one of the most confronting lessons in the entire passage.
Because modern culture often treats sexual desire as virtually sovereign.
“If I desire it, why should anyone tell me no?”
“If two people want it, what business does God have interfering?”
But Scripture begins somewhere radically different.
The body belongs to its Creator.
Sex is not outside God's jurisdiction.
Marriage is not outside God's jurisdiction.
Desire is not outside God's jurisdiction.
Even the most private room in the house is not a place where God suddenly stops being Lord.
And perhaps that is where this ancient command begins reaching into our modern lives.
Not because every ritual boundary given to Israel is automatically a command imposed unchanged upon the church...
but because the God revealed in Scripture has never surrendered His authority over human sexuality.
There is another important detail.
Blood occupies an extraordinary place in Leviticus.
Later, Leviticus 17:11 declares:
כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הַבָּשָׂר בַּדָּם הִוא
Ki nefesh habbasar badam hi.
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood.”
But we need to be careful here.
It is tempting to build an elaborate explanation and say, “Therefore this is exactly why intercourse during menstruation was prohibited.”
The Bible itself does not explicitly give that explanation in Leviticus 18:19.
So we should not pretend God said something He did not say.
Various explanations have been proposed across Jewish and Christian history—ritual, theological, symbolic, social, and even medical.
Some may contain useful observations.
But faithful interpretation requires humility.
We can confidently say what God commanded.
We can understand that command within Leviticus' larger concern for holiness, purity, blood, sexuality, and Israel's covenant identity.
But where Scripture does not explicitly say, “This is the sole reason why,” we should resist turning an inference into revelation.
Sometimes reverence means refusing to make the Bible say more than it says.
And this is where another question becomes unavoidable.
What does this mean for Christians?
This is where Jesus must become central rather than being attached to the end of the discussion as a religious afterthought.
Christians do not approach Leviticus as though Jesus never came.
The New Testament presents Jesus as the fulfillment toward which the law and sacrificial system point.
Jesus said:
“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets... I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17).
Hebrews tells us that the old covenant contained shadows pointing toward realities fulfilled in Christ.
And something remarkable happens when Jesus enters the world of ritual impurity.
He touches people others feared touching.
A leper comes to Him.
Jesus touches him.
A woman suffering from a flow of blood for twelve years reaches through a crowd and touches His garment.
Think about that scene.
Twelve years.
Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years of suffering.
Twelve years of doctors.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Mark tells us she “had suffered much under many physicians” and had spent everything she possessed, yet instead of improving she became worse.
Then she heard about Jesus.
She pushed through the crowd.
Perhaps terrified.
Perhaps ashamed.
Perhaps desperate enough that embarrassment no longer mattered.
And she touched His garment.
Immediately, the bleeding stopped.
Jesus turned.
“Who touched my garments?”
The disciples were confused because everyone was pressing against Him.
But Jesus knew.
The woman came trembling.
She fell before Him.
And told Him the whole truth.
Imagine how exposed she must have felt.
Then Jesus called her something beautiful.
“Daughter.”
Not contamination.
Not embarrassment.
Not inconvenience.
Daughter.
“Your faith has made you well; go in peace.”
That is Jesus.
Under ordinary purity logic, uncleanness spreads through contact.
But when the unclean encounter Christ, something astonishing happens.
His holiness is not defeated by their uncleanness.
His purity overwhelms what defiles.
The sick encounter Him and healing flows outward.
The rejected encounter Him and dignity returns.
The guilty encounter Him and discover mercy.
The spiritually dead encounter Him and life walks out of the tomb.

And suddenly Leviticus begins sounding less like an irrelevant collection of strange ancient restrictions and more like the vocabulary of a world desperately waiting for Someone holy enough to deal with uncleanness once and for all.
But there is an even deeper problem than ritual impurity.
Sin.
Because you and I may never have violated Leviticus 18:19...
and still desperately need a Savior.
Maybe your uncleanness has nothing to do with menstrual blood.
Maybe it is hidden in your browser history.
Maybe it is the message thread you keep deleting.
Maybe it is the affair nobody discovered.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Maybe it is pride disguised as spirituality.
Maybe it is envy that smiles in public.
Maybe you know exactly how to raise your hands during worship while refusing to surrender the one room in your heart you have locked against God.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually strong.
But you know.
You know what happens when nobody is watching.
You know what thought keeps returning.
You know what relationship crossed a boundary.
You know what compromise you renamed so you would not have to call it sin.
You know what God has been asking you to surrender.
And perhaps this is why Leviticus makes us uncomfortable.
Because holiness always becomes uncomfortable when we have grown comfortable with compromise.
We want a Jesus who comforts us.
Scripture gives us that Jesus.
But Scripture also gives us the Jesus who says:
“Repent.”
We want grace.
Thank God, grace is real.
But biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost to Himself.
The cross is where nobody can honestly say sin is trivial.
Look at Jesus.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
Bleeding.
And there is the scandal at the center of Christianity:
the Holy One taking the place of the guilty.
Peter writes:
Paul says:
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
The blood imagery that runs through Scripture reaches its climactic Christian meaning not in menstruation, but in the sacrificial death of Christ.
Hebrews declares:
“Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.”
And then it points beyond repeated sacrifices toward Jesus.
Christ does what bulls and goats could never finally accomplish.
He offers Himself.
Once for all.
That changes how Christians read passages about purity.
We do not mock them.
We do not erase them.
We do not pretend they were meaningless.
We read them through the fulfillment accomplished by Jesus Christ.

The Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 did not place the entire Mosaic ritual system upon Gentile believers. Paul likewise warns against treating old-covenant calendar and food regulations as the basis of justification before God.
Christians therefore need wisdom when moving from an old-covenant command to new-covenant practice.
We should neither casually impose every Israelite purity regulation unchanged upon Christians nor throw Leviticus away as though holiness no longer matters.
The covenantal administration has changed.
The holiness of God has not.
And maybe that is the word somebody reading this desperately needs.
Grace did not make holiness irrelevant.
Grace made holiness possible in people who could never make themselves clean.
Jesus did not die so that we could become comfortable with the sins destroying us.
He died to save us from them.
Maybe you have spent years hiding.
Maybe your secret has become so familiar that you no longer remember who you were before it.
Maybe shame has convinced you that if people knew everything about you, they would leave.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every deleted message.
Every night.
Every compromise.
Every relapse.
Every rationalization.
Every wound beneath the behavior.
He knows what happened to you.
And He knows what you chose afterward.
Yet the Gospel invitation still stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to approach Christ.
You approach Christ because you cannot clean yourself.
That bleeding woman did not wait until she was healed before reaching for Jesus.
She reached because she needed healing.
And maybe spiritually, that is you.
Still bleeding somewhere nobody sees.
Still smiling.
Still working.
Still posting.
Still going to church.
Still telling people, “I'm okay.”
But exhausted.
Jesus is not asking you to become impressive.
He is calling you to come into the light.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let other believers see it.
Let somebody pray.
Let somebody realize they are not fighting alone.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become another person's reason not to give up tonight.
Because the Gospel is not the story of good people proving how clean they are.
It is the story of sinners discovering that Jesus Christ can do what they could never do for themselves.
From impurity...
to cleansing.
From guilt...
to forgiveness.
From bondage...
to freedom.
From hiding...
to confession.
From death...
to life.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this article helped you see a difficult passage of Scripture differently, don't let it disappear into your feed.
There will be a day when someone asks you why Christians still bother reading Leviticus.
Come back to this.
Study the passages yourself.
Test what you read against Scripture.
Not as a performance.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
God's grace cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid that price.
Open your Bible.
Look at Leviticus again.
Then keep reading until you reach Matthew.
Keep reading until the woman with the flow of blood touches Jesus.
Keep reading until Jesus carries the cross.
Keep reading until blood runs from the body of the spotless Lamb.
Keep reading until the stone is rolled away.
Keep reading until you understand:
The Bible's story was never about humanity climbing high enough to reach a holy God.
It is about the Holy God coming down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
So share the truth.
Save what strengthens your faith.
And then do not leave it as a comment.
Take it to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Walk differently.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you are unclean.
The greatest tragedy would be standing within reach of the One who cleanses sinners...
and choosing to keep hiding.
The hands you are afraid to approach are the very hands that were pierced to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A GARDEN LOCKED, A SPRING SEALED: Is Song of Songs Talking About Sexual Exclusivity?
paragraphs: A GARDEN LOCKED, A SPRING SEALED: Is Song of Songs Talking About Sexual Exclusivity?
There is a reason Scripture describes intimacy as a garden—and there is a reason not everyone is given the gate.
Some verses whisper.
Some verses thunder.
And then there are verses that seem almost too intimate to read aloud in church.
Song of Songs 4:12 is one of them.
In Hebrew, the words are striking:
גַּן נָעוּל אֲחֹתִי כַלָּה גַּל נָעוּל מַעְיָן חָתוּם
Gan na‘ul, achoti kallah; gal na‘ul, ma‘yan chatum.
“A locked garden is my sister, my bride; an enclosed spring, a sealed fountain.”
Read that again.
A garden.
Locked.
A spring.
Enclosed.
A fountain.
Sealed.
And the man speaking these words is addressing “my bride.”
Not merchandise.
Not an object.
Not a possession without a will.
A beloved woman.
And suddenly an ancient love poem begins asking a painfully modern question:
Does God intend sexual intimacy to be exclusive?
Because we live in a world that has spent decades telling us that freedom means access.
Give your body if you want.
Take someone else's if they consent.
Experiment.
Explore.
Collect experiences.
Do what feels right.
And if your heart breaks afterward, pretend the body had nothing to do with it.
But Scripture speaks differently.
It does not begin with shame.
It begins with a garden.
That matters.

The Hebrew expression גַּן נָעוּל — gan na‘ul means a locked or enclosed garden. The same Hebrew participle na‘ul carries the idea of something shut, barred, or secured. The verse then intensifies the picture with מַעְיָן חָתוּם — ma‘yan chatum: a spring or fountain that is sealed.
The poetry is deliberate. The NET Bible's textual note even observes the wordplay created by the repeated imagery of the locked garden and enclosed spring.
But we need to be careful here.
We should not force the Bible to say more than it says.

Song of Songs 4:12 is poetry, not a dictionary definition of virginity. The Hebrew words themselves do not constitute a technical theological formula saying, “This phrase means virginity and nothing else.”
Yet neither should we drain the poetry of its obvious intimacy.
Look at what happens around the verse.

The woman is described through the imagery of an extraordinary garden filled with pomegranates, choice fruits, henna, nard, saffron, cinnamon, myrrh, aloes, spices, fresh water, and streams from Lebanon. Then she responds:
“Awake, O north wind; come, O south wind!”
She invites the wind to spread the fragrance of her garden, and then invites her beloved into it.
“May my beloved come into his garden and eat its delightful fruit!”
And immediately afterward, in Song of Songs 5:1, the beloved answers the invitation.
The movement of the poetry is difficult to miss.
Closed.
Desired.
Invited.
Entered.
Enjoyed.
The garden is not portrayed as evil because it is sexual.
It is portrayed as precious because intimacy is precious.
Biblical holiness is not God standing outside human sexuality shouting, “Dirty!”
The God who created the human body also created covenant intimacy.
Genesis tells us that before sin entered the world, a husband and wife could stand naked before each other without shame.
Think about that.
Sexuality existed before pornography.
Desire existed before adultery.
Nakedness existed before exploitation.
Marriage existed before shame.
Sin did not invent sexuality.
God did.
Sin distorted what God made beautiful.
And perhaps that is why the image of a locked garden matters so deeply.
A garden has a boundary not because everything inside it is shameful.
A garden has a boundary because something inside it is valuable.
You do not put walls around garbage.
You protect treasure.
You guard what can be violated.
You preserve what is meant to flourish.
And this is where Scripture's vision collides violently with ours.
Our culture often treats sexual access as liberation.
Scripture repeatedly treats sexual union as profoundly consequential.
Genesis 2:24 says the man and woman become one flesh.
Jesus Himself returns to those words when teaching about marriage:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Jesus did not treat marriage as a disposable social invention.
He pointed backward.
Back beyond modern culture.
Back beyond Rome.
Back beyond Moses.
Back to creation.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two bodies experiencing chemistry.
Something joins.
Something is shared.
Something covenant-shaped is happening.
That is why Paul can warn the Corinthians about sexual immorality with startling seriousness. In 1 Corinthians 6 he argues that the believer's body belongs to the Lord and ultimately declares:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
Notice what Christianity does not say.
It does not say your body is worthless.
It says your body matters so much that Christ redeemed you wholly.
Your soul belongs to Jesus.
Your mind belongs to Jesus.
Your future belongs to Jesus.
And yes—
your sexuality belongs under the lordship of Jesus too.
But now somebody reading this feels their stomach tightening.
Because your garden wasn't locked.
Or maybe somebody broke into it.
Maybe you gave yourself to someone who promised forever and disappeared six months later.
Maybe you slept with somebody because you desperately wanted to feel wanted.
Maybe you confused being desired with being loved.
Maybe pornography taught you intimacy before Scripture did.
Maybe you have crossed boundaries you swore you never would.
Maybe you are married now, but memories of people from your past still walk through rooms in your mind where your spouse has never been.
Maybe your story contains adultery.
Maybe secret messages.
Maybe hookups.
Maybe years of sexual compromise.
Or maybe what happened to you was not chosen at all.
Perhaps somebody violated your boundaries.
Perhaps somebody took what you never freely offered.
If that is your story, hear this carefully:
Another person's sin against you is not your sexual sin.
Scripture's call to sexual holiness must never be twisted into blaming victims of abuse, assault, coercion, or exploitation.
And for those carrying guilt over choices you did make, there is something else you desperately need to hear.
The Gospel is not the announcement that ruined gardens must remain ruined.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ makes sinners new.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because Jesus does not merely save people with clean histories.
He saves sinners.
The sexually broken.
The adulterer.
The porn-addicted.
The promiscuous.
The hypocrite.
The person who crossed the line once.
The person who crossed it a thousand times.
The person everybody knows failed.
And the person whose browser history knows what nobody else does.
The cross was not built for people who never needed forgiveness.
Christ died for sinners.
And when Jesus encountered sexual brokenness, He demonstrated something our world still struggles to hold together:
grace without pretending sin isn't sin.
He could say:
“Neither do I condemn you.”
And He could also say:
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Grace did not erase holiness.
Holiness did not erase grace.
Jesus carried both.
Perfectly.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this has been missing.
You thought Christianity was asking you to pretend you had never fallen.
No.
Christianity announces something far more astonishing:
your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter.
Jesus does.
Perhaps your garden has been entered by people who never should have been there.
Perhaps you opened gates because you were lonely.
Perhaps somebody climbed a wall by force.
Perhaps weeds have grown where flowers once lived.
Perhaps the water became muddy.
Perhaps shame convinced you that nothing sacred could ever grow there again.
But listen—
Jesus Christ is not frightened by damaged gardens.
He walked out of a garden tomb carrying resurrection.
He specializes in places everybody else assumes are finished.
And repentance is not God humiliating you for what happened yesterday.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One who can give you a different tomorrow.
The Greek New Testament often uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance, from the idea of a changed mind, a turning of one's inner orientation toward God.
Real repentance is deeper than regret.
Regret says, “I hate what this cost me.”
Repentance says, “Jesus, I want You more than I want the sin.”
That changes everything.
Sexual purity is therefore not merely about saying no.
It is about knowing Who owns the yes.
For the unmarried Christian, sexual boundaries are not a declaration that desire is disgusting. They are a confession that desire is powerful enough to surrender to Christ.
For the married Christian, exclusivity is not merely avoiding adultery.
It is cultivating a garden where one covenant partner is uniquely welcomed.
There is something breathtaking about that.
One person sees what the world does not see.
One person receives what strangers cannot demand.
One person is invited behind walls others must respect.
Not because marriage creates ownership over another human being, but because husband and wife freely give themselves to one another in covenant faithfulness.
And perhaps this is why Proverbs uses remarkably similar imagery.
Speaking about marital faithfulness, Proverbs 5 tells a husband to drink water from his own cistern and flowing water from his own well, then tells him to rejoice in the wife of his youth.
Water.
Fountain.
Exclusivity.
Delight.
Marriage.
The biblical pattern is not difficult to recognize.
Song of Songs does not portray marital desire as embarrassing.
It celebrates it.
The lovers notice one another.
Long for one another.
Praise one another.
Seek one another.
And delight in one another.
Biblical sexuality is not less passionate because it has boundaries.
Its boundaries help give the passion its covenant meaning.
A river without banks eventually becomes a flood.
Fire without a fireplace can destroy a house.
And intimacy without faithfulness can leave people carrying wounds long after the moment itself has disappeared.
But perhaps the deepest question isn't whether Song of Songs 4:12 refers to sexual exclusivity.
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Who has access to the garden of your heart now?
Because you can be physically abstinent and emotionally unfaithful.
You can be married and secretly cultivate another relationship.
You can never touch another person and still feed fantasies that are consuming your covenant.
You can delete messages while keeping desires.
You can clear browser history without cleansing your heart.
You can look holy in church while hiding an entire second life behind a locked phone.
Jesus does not merely want edited behavior.
He wants you.
The secret you.
The midnight you.
The lonely you.
The tempted you.
The version of you nobody at church knows.
And if these words have uncovered something hidden, do not run from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Confess it.
Bring it into light.
Ask for help.
Establish boundaries.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
If another person is involved, stop feeding what must die.
If pornography owns a room in your life, stop calling captivity “a struggle” while continuing to furnish the room.
Bring the darkness into light.
Not because confession earns salvation.
Jesus already paid for salvation at the cross.
But because people who have been brought into the light should no longer make peace with darkness.
And maybe tonight your prayer does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be honest.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Maybe those three words are where the gate begins closing again.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need mercy breaks the pride that kept us hiding.
Someone else reading the comments may discover they are not fighting alone.
And if Christ has already begun restoring areas of your life you once believed were permanently destroyed, tell somebody what grace has done.
Your testimony might become another person's doorway back to Jesus.
Send it privately to the believer who has disappeared because shame convinced them they could never come home.
There is also another practical way to stand with this ministry.
Scripture never gives us permission to sell grace.
But voluntary generosity toward Gospel ministry is thoroughly biblical.

Paul describes believers partnering in Gospel work through giving. Christian ministry has historically depended upon believers who freely decide that something worth spreading is also worth supporting.
But whether you ever give a cent or not, do not miss the greater invitation.
Give yourself to Christ.
Money cannot replace obedience.
Sharing a Christian article cannot replace following Jesus.
Religious activity cannot cleanse sin.
Only Christ saves.
Only His blood atones.
Only His grace can take a human story stained by sin and begin writing something holy.
And perhaps that is why this strange little image from an ancient Hebrew love poem refuses to leave us alone.
גַּן נָעוּל — gan na‘ul.
A garden locked.
מַעְיָן חָתוּם — ma‘yan chatum.
A fountain sealed.
Maybe you cannot change who entered yesterday.
Maybe you cannot erase every memory.
Maybe you cannot recover years you gave away.
Maybe you cannot return to the innocence you once possessed.
But in Jesus Christ, your future does not have to become a hostage to your past.
Grace does not give you a time machine.
It gives you something better.
A new direction.
You can close doors today.
You can end the affair.
Delete the number.
Confess the secret.
Seek help.
Rebuild trust.
Wait faithfully.
Honor your spouse.
Honor your future spouse.
Honor your body.
Honor another person's body.
And above everything else—
honor Christ.
Because purity was never ultimately about convincing people that you had a spotless history.
It is about surrendering your present and future to the One whose righteousness truly is spotless.
Jesus.
The Bridegroom who loved His people enough to bleed for them.
The Savior who does not excuse our sin but paid its terrible price.
The King who receives repentant sinners rather than throwing their broken stories away.
So guard the garden.
Not because sexuality is dirty.
Because covenant intimacy is precious.
Guard the spring.
Not because your body should become an idol.
Because your body belongs to the Lord.
And if the garden has already been wounded...
bring it to Jesus.
There is still grace.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still repentance.
There is still restoration.
There is still a Savior.
Not to buy God's favor.
Not to purchase grace.
But freely, gratefully, and prayerfully—to help more wounded people discover the message you just read.
Because somewhere tonight, someone believes what they did—or what was done to them—has permanently written their identity.
But scars may tell you where the story broke; only Jesus gets to decide where redemption writes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID RACHEL STEAL HER FATHER’S HOUSEHOLD GODS?
paragraphs:
WHY DID RACHEL STEAL HER FATHER’S HOUSEHOLD GODS?
She had Jacob. She had children. She had witnessed the God of Abraham provide for her family. So why, while fleeing her father’s house, did Rachel secretly reach for the idols of the very world she was leaving behind?
There are moments in Scripture that make you stop because the person in the story does something you do not expect.
Rachel’s is one of them.
Jacob is running.
Laban is behind him.
The household is moving.
Children. Servants. Livestock. Possessions. Tension.
And somewhere inside that hurried escape, while one chapter of Rachel’s life is closing behind her, she does something almost painfully human.
She steals her father’s gods.
Genesis 31:19 records it with startling simplicity:
“Rachel had stolen the images that were her father’s.”
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
וְרָחֵל גָּנְבָה אֶת־הַתְּרָפִים אֲשֶׁר לְאָבִיהָ
Ve-Rachel ganvah et-ha-teraphim asher le-aviha.
“And Rachel stole the teraphim that belonged to her father.”
The word translated “images,” “household gods,” or sometimes “idols” is תְּרָפִים — teraphim.
And suddenly this is no longer merely a strange family story.
It becomes a mirror.
Because Rachel was leaving Laban’s house…
but something from Laban’s house was still traveling with Rachel.
Read that again.
She was leaving the place.
But she carried something from the place with her.
And maybe that is why this ancient story still knows how to find us.
Because you can leave Egypt and still crave Egypt.
You can escape the relationship and still carry the wounds.
You can walk away from the addiction while still secretly romanticizing what it did for you.
You can stop living the old life while keeping pieces of the old life hidden underneath you.
You can say, “I belong to God,” while your trembling fingers are still reaching beneath the saddle for something familiar.
And that is where Rachel’s story becomes uncomfortable.
What exactly was she reaching for?
Genesis does not explicitly tell us Rachel’s motive.
That matters.
Scripture tells us what she did, but it does not directly tell us why she did it.
So we should be careful not to preach speculation as revelation.
Several explanations have been proposed across centuries of interpretation.
Perhaps Rachel believed the teraphim offered protection or blessing.
Perhaps they represented inheritance or household authority.
Perhaps she wanted to deprive Laban of objects associated with divination.
Perhaps she was attempting to sever something from her father’s religious world.
Perhaps there was some combination of family, property, religion, fear, and cultural expectation involved.
But Genesis does not settle the question for us.
And perhaps the silence itself forces us to notice something more important than solving Rachel psychologically.
Whatever her motive was…
she took the gods.
That is the fact the text gives us.
And Laban cared enough about those gods to pursue Jacob’s company and demand:
“Why did you steal my gods?”
There is almost something tragic in that sentence.
“My gods.”
Gods that could be stolen.
Gods that could disappear.
Gods that had to be searched for.
Gods that could be hidden underneath a woman sitting on a camel saddle.
Think about the irony.
The living God had spoken to Jacob.
The living God had protected Jacob.
The living God had prospered Jacob.
The living God warned Laban in a dream not to harm Jacob.
And while the sovereign God of heaven was actively governing the situation…
Laban was desperately searching tents for gods that could not even rescue themselves.
That contrast is devastating.
One God speaks.
The others must be carried.
One God protects His people.
The others need people to protect them.
One God sees what happens in darkness.
The others cannot reveal where they have been hidden.
One God directs history.
The others are luggage.
And yet Rachel stole them.
That is the frightening part.
Because false gods do not have to be powerful to become powerful over us.
They only have to become precious.
Sometimes an idol is not something you bow before in a temple.
Sometimes it is whatever you cannot imagine losing.
Approval.
Money.
Control.
Beauty.
Sex.
Status.
Success.
A relationship.
A career.
Your reputation.
Your secret.
Your bitterness.
Your political identity.
Your image of yourself.
Even ministry can become an idol when being seen serving Jesus becomes more important than actually knowing Jesus.
And some idols are especially difficult to recognize because they do not look evil.
They look necessary.
That is how idols survive.
We rename them.
We justify them.
We hide them.
We sit on them.
Rachel hid the teraphim.
And when Laban entered the tent searching for them, she remained seated.
The thing her father desperately wanted was underneath her.
Hidden.
Close.
Unseen.
And maybe somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Everybody thinks you have moved on.
Everybody thinks you are free.
Everybody thinks you surrendered everything.
You worship.
You pray.
You post Scripture.
You tell people God is good.
And He is.
But there is something underneath the saddle.
Something hidden.
Something you have learned to sit on so nobody notices.
Maybe nobody knows what you watch when you are alone.
Nobody knows about the messages.
Nobody knows about the bitterness.
Nobody knows about the secret account.
Nobody knows how badly you need validation.
Nobody knows about the compromise.
Nobody knows how angry you still are.
Nobody knows that you forgive people publicly while replaying the offense privately.
Nobody knows how exhausted your faith has become.
Nobody knows that underneath the Christian language, underneath the church attendance, underneath the smiling profile picture…
you are afraid.
Afraid that God will not be enough.
And perhaps that is one of the deepest roots beneath every idol.
“What if God is not enough?”
What if God does not provide?
What if God does not heal?
What if God does not restore the relationship?
What if obedience costs me something I cannot replace?
What if I surrender this and end up empty?
So we keep Jesus…
and keep a teraphim.
We want the God of Abraham for eternity and the little household god for emergencies.
We want Christ to save our souls, but we still want control to calm our nerves.
We want grace, but keep shame because somehow punishing ourselves feels safer than believing we have actually been forgiven.
We want freedom, but keep the chains nearby.
Just in case.
That is the insanity of idolatry.
It promises security while making you its servant.
But Rachel’s story does not end underneath that saddle.
Later, something changes.
Genesis 35 records Jacob receiving a command from God to return to Bethel and build an altar.
Bethel.
The place where Jacob had encountered God when he had almost nothing.
And before the household went there, Jacob said:
“Put away the strange gods that are among you, and be clean, and change your garments.”
Then something extraordinary happened.
They gave Jacob the foreign gods they possessed.
Jacob buried them.
That image is powerful.
What had traveled with the family could not travel with them into the next act of consecration.
Some things had to be buried.
Genesis does not explicitly say that Rachel’s stolen teraphim were among the objects surrendered in Genesis 35, so we should not claim that the text says they were.
But the theological movement is impossible to miss.
Foreign gods had existed among Jacob’s household.
Then came the call:
Put them away.
Purify yourselves.
Get up.
Go to Bethel.
Return to the place of encounter.
Return to the God who met you when you were running.
Return to the God who kept you when you could not keep yourself.
And somebody reading this needs Bethel.
Not another motivational speech.
Not another Christian slogan.
Bethel.
The place where pretending ends.
The place where idols get buried.
The place where God becomes more than something you discuss.
The place where you finally say:
“Jesus, I do not want to hide this anymore.”
Because there is something even greater than Rachel’s story happening throughout Scripture.
Human beings keep reaching for idols.
And God keeps reaching for human beings.
We exchange His glory.
He pursues us.
We hide.
He calls.
We wander.
He seeks.
We sin.
And ultimately, God does something no household god could ever do.
He comes for us.
Not as an object made by human hands…
but as the eternal Son who took on flesh.
Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is not the story of humanity finally climbing high enough to reach God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And at the cross, Jesus did not merely expose our idols.
He carried our guilt.
He carried our shame.
He carried the judgment our sin deserved.
The hands that never stole were nailed to wood for thieves.
The mouth that never lied was struck for liars.
The heart that never worshiped another was pierced for idolaters.
The spotless Lamb stood where guilty people belonged.
And when Jesus cried,
Τετέλεσται.
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
He was not offering humanity another household god to add to the collection.
He was announcing a finished work that no idol could accomplish.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ victorious.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately about hiding your idols better.
It is about repentance.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a turning of mind and direction toward God.
Not cosmetic Christianity.
Not religious reputation management.
Not learning how to look clean while sitting on something hidden.
Turn.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Believe.
Surrender.
Because Jesus already knows what is underneath the saddle.
And still He calls you.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Grace does not tell you the idol is acceptable.
Grace gives you somewhere to go when the idol has exposed how desperately you need a Savior.
Maybe your scandal is not Rachel’s scandal.
Maybe yours has a different name.
Pornography.
Pride.
Greed.
Envy.
Adultery.
Fear.
Self-righteousness.
Resentment.
Dishonesty.
An obsession with being admired.
An inability to forgive.
A secret you are terrified somebody will discover.
Maybe you have spent years wondering what Jesus would do if the whole truth about you were dragged into the light.
Look at the cross.
That is what He did.
He died for sinners.
And He rose.
Your deepest hope is not that your scandal was small.
Your hope is that Christ is greater.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because grace means pretending evil was good.

Jesus rewrites everything because the Gospel can take guilty people, wash them, forgive them, reconcile them to God, and begin transforming them into people who no longer need to live beneath the tyranny of what once owned them.
So maybe today is burial day.
Maybe you need to name the thing.
Maybe you need to confess it to God instead of explaining it away.
Maybe you need to seek appropriate accountability.
Maybe you need to apologize.
Maybe you need to delete something.
Maybe you need to walk away from something.
Maybe you need to stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Whatever repentance requires, do not confuse conviction with rejection.
The Christ who exposes darkness is the Christ who invites sinners into light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise does not say He forgives the person who successfully convinces everyone else that nothing is wrong.
It says:
confess.
There is freedom in finally agreeing with God.
No more hiding.
No more pretending.
No more protecting the little god that has never once been able to save you.
Let believers reading the comments become believers who pray instead of believers who merely scroll.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another wounded person believe that coming home is still possible.
Not because every sentence is easy to hear.
Because some truths need to find us twice.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow with you.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you glorify God.
It does not.
We glorify God through lives of faith, worship, obedience, love, generosity, and faithful stewardship made possible by His grace.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity when you freely choose to help that work continue reaching people.
Not as a transaction with God.
As mission.
Because somewhere behind another smiling profile picture may be a Rachel running toward a new life while secretly carrying something from the old one.
Maybe they have never told anyone.
Maybe they are ashamed.
Maybe they think Jesus is disgusted with them.
Maybe they believe they have gone too far.
Let this article find them.
Let the Gospel interrupt them.
Let them discover that repentance is not the doorway into humiliation but the road back into fellowship with the God they were created to know.
Rachel stole gods that had to be carried.
But the God of Scripture carries His people.
And centuries after Rachel ran from her father’s house, Jesus Christ walked toward a cross carrying something infinitely heavier than household idols.
Our sin.
Our guilt.
Our judgment.
He carried it all the way to Calvary.
Then He rose from the grave.
So stop asking your idols to do what only Jesus can do.
Your money cannot forgive you.
Your reputation cannot cleanse you.
Your pleasure cannot resurrect you.
Your achievements cannot reconcile you to God.
Your secrets cannot protect you forever.
Your shame cannot pay for your sins.
Jesus can save.
And perhaps the most unforgettable question in Rachel’s story is no longer:
“Why did Rachel steal her father’s household gods?”
Perhaps it is this:
What are you still carrying that Jesus is asking you to bury?
Do not hide beneath the saddle another night.
Come into the light.
There is a cross for your guilt.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is resurrection after ruin.
There is a Savior for sinners.
And sometimes the thing you are terrified to surrender is the very thing keeping your hands too full to receive what grace has been offering you all along.
The idol has to be carried. Jesus carries you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Call It “Just Porn.” Your Heart Knows It Is Teaching You to Consume People.
paragraphs: You Call It “Just Porn.” Your Heart Knows It Is Teaching You to Consume People.

The screen may be private. The habit may be hidden. Nobody may know what you watched last night. But Jesus cares about what your secret gaze is teaching your heart to do with another human being—and He does not expose sexual sin to convince you that you are beyond redemption. He exposes it because He intends to lead sinners out of darkness and into freedom.
There is a moment after the screen goes dark when the room becomes painfully quiet.
No music.
No images.
No movement.
Just you.
Maybe you know that silence.
You close the browser. Delete the history. Put the phone facedown. Promise yourself that this was the last time.
Again.

And somewhere underneath the excuses, underneath the adrenaline, underneath the shame, underneath the carefully constructed sentence “It’s just porn,” something inside you knows this has become more than something you watch.
It is teaching you how to look.
How to desire.
How to consume.
How to separate another person’s body from another person’s soul.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that you can become accustomed to it.

Someone created in the image of God appears on a screen, and instead of asking who that person is, what wounds they carry, what fears they hide, what dignity God gave them, or what eternity means for them, the heart learns another question:
What can I get from this body?
That is why this conversation cannot stop at browser history.
Jesus takes us deeper.
He takes us into the heart.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus recalls the commandment against adultery and then penetrates beneath outward respectability to the interior life:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
The crucial idea is not that accidentally noticing an attractive person makes someone an adulterer.
Jesus is confronting the cultivated gaze—the looking that is directed toward lust.

The phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι carries the sense of looking toward the purpose of desiring lustfully. Jesus moves the moral battlefield from merely “Did you physically commit adultery?” to something far more searching:
What are you choosing to do with another person inside your heart?
Then comes Christ’s devastating conclusion:
“ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
He has already committed adultery with her “in his heart.”
Not because temptation itself is identical to sin.
Not because noticing beauty is evil.
Not because sexual desire, within God’s design, is dirty.
Scripture does not teach those things.
The problem is the deliberate cultivation of lust—the inward appropriation of another person for sexual gratification.
And pornography industrializes that gaze.
It gives the consuming heart an almost endless procession of bodies while whispering that nobody is really being touched because everything is happening behind glass.
But Jesus refuses to let distance erase the condition of the heart.
The person on that screen is not pixels before they are a person.
Male or female, famous or anonymous, willing or exploited, known to you or completely unknown—the human being you are looking at bears a dignity pornography trains you to ignore.
Genesis 1:27 says humanity was created in the image of God.
That changes everything.
The body you are consuming belongs to an image-bearer.
And pornography trains desire to say:
Your body exists for my experience.
The Gospel teaches us something radically different:
People are not products.
They are neighbors.
They are image-bearers.
They are souls for whom we should desire holiness, mercy, justice, healing, and ultimately reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
That is why porn is never merely about nakedness on a screen.
It is also about what repeated lust can teach the heart to believe about human beings.
Maybe that makes you uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because shame is the destination.
Because awakening sometimes hurts.
There are people reading this who have been carrying this secret for years.
Some started when they were children and did not even understand what they had discovered.
Some were exposed accidentally.
Some went looking.
Some became curious.
Some became dependent.
Some have stopped for months only to return during loneliness, stress, rejection, boredom, anger, exhaustion, or disappointment.
Some love Jesus sincerely.
And still fall.
Sunday morning, hands raised.
Monday night, history erased.
Bible beside the bed.
Pornography in the phone.
Worship playlist in the headphones.
Secret tabs in the browser.
And eventually the contradiction becomes exhausting.
You begin wondering whether you are a hypocrite.
Whether God is disgusted with you.
Whether you have ruined yourself.
Whether you should simply stop trying.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin is insignificant.
And the Gospel does not tell you that your sin is stronger than Jesus.
Both lies must die.
Grace is not God pretending pornography does not matter.
Grace is God meeting guilty people with a crucified and risen Savior powerful enough to forgive them, cleanse them, transform them, and teach them how to walk differently.
That is why Jesus’ next words in Matthew 5 are so severe.
“If your right eye causes you to sin…”
“If your right hand causes you to sin…”
Christ speaks of tearing out and cutting off.
These words are intentionally shocking. They are not instructions for bodily mutilation. Removing an eye would not remove lust from the heart, and removing a hand would not purify desire.
Jesus is demanding radical action against sin.
In other words:
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Stop keeping convenient access to the thing you keep begging God to deliver you from.
Stop calling surrender “legalism” because surrender inconveniences you.
If the app repeatedly becomes the doorway, remove it.
If being alone with unrestricted internet at midnight repeatedly becomes the battlefield where you collapse, change the battlefield.
If secrecy protects the addiction, bring the secret into the light with a mature, trustworthy believer.
If your phone has become your private doorway into sexual sin, establish restrictions you cannot casually bypass.
If certain accounts awaken lust, unfollow them.
If certain entertainment continually feeds fantasies you are trying to starve, stop consuming it.
Not because deleting an app saves you.
Jesus saves you.
But people who genuinely want freedom stop lovingly decorating the prison cell.
Repentance has feet.
And this is where some people misunderstand grace.
They think grace means Jesus whispers, “Don’t worry about it.”
Biblical grace says something infinitely better.
Jesus says, in effect:
Come out.
Come out of hiding.
Come out of the cycle.
Come out of the double life.
Come out of the lie that because you failed yesterday, you are required to surrender tomorrow.
Pornography promises intimacy without covenant, pleasure without self-giving love, bodies without biographies, sexuality without responsibility, and consumption without communion.
Jesus offers something entirely different.
He teaches us to see people instead of products.
To love instead of consume.
To honor instead of use.
To confess instead of hide.
To surrender instead of rationalize.
To become holy rather than merely appear religious.
And perhaps right now you are thinking:
But you don’t know how many times I have failed.
No.
But Christ does.
You may hide browser history from your spouse.
You may hide it from your parents.
You may hide it from your pastor.
You may hide it from your friends.
You may hide it from everyone who thinks you have your Christian life together.
You have never hidden it from Jesus.
And yet here is the scandal of grace:
The One who already knows the truth is the One calling you toward Himself.
Romans 5:8 does not say Christ waited until sinners repaired themselves before loving them.
God demonstrates His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
The cross destroys two excuses at once.
You cannot look at Calvary and say sin does not matter.
And you cannot look at Calvary and say repentant sinners cannot be forgiven.
Your sin was serious enough that redemption cost blood.
His grace is powerful enough that His blood was not wasted.
First John 1:9 gives hiding Christians somewhere to go: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Confession is not informing God.
He already knows.
Confession is where you stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop renaming bondage.
You stop saying “just porn.”
You stop promising vaguely that someday you will get serious.
You come into the light.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need eloquence.
Maybe it needs truth.
Jesus, I have sinned.
I have used people in my imagination.
I have fed desires I should have resisted.
I have hidden.
I have made promises and broken them.
I cannot cleanse myself.
Have mercy on me.
Teach me to see people the way You see them.
Teach me to desire holiness more than secrecy.
Give me courage to destroy the pathways I keep using to return.
Forgive me.
Change me.
That prayer is not magic.
The Savior to whom you are praying is the hope.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your browsing habits.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He died for sins.
He rose from the grave.
He reigns.
And the Christian response is not merely “I should watch less pornography.”
It is repentance and faith.
A turning from sin toward Christ.
A surrender of the hidden room.
A refusal to keep calling darkness harmless because admitting its darkness hurts.
And then comes the practical work of discipleship.
You may need accountability.
You may need pastoral help.
You may need professional counseling, especially where trauma, compulsion, abuse, or deeply entrenched patterns are involved.
You may need to confess to someone trustworthy.
You may need safeguards.
You may need to stop carrying a smartphone into the bedroom.
You may need to accept inconvenience.
You may need to become radically boring about protecting your soul.
Do it.
Freedom is worth being inconvenienced.
And if you fall?
Do not convert failure into permission.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Return to Christ.
Strengthen the boundaries that failed.
Tell the truth to the person keeping you accountable.
Learn what preceded the fall.
Keep walking.
Sanctification is not permission to become casual about recurring sin. Neither is recurring struggle proof that Christ has abandoned every person who is still fighting.
The answer is neither complacency nor despair.
The answer is Christ.
Again.
Christ when temptation comes.
Christ when shame screams.
Christ when the screen glows.
Christ when loneliness aches.
Christ when confession costs you pride.
Christ when obedience feels inconvenient.
Christ when yesterday was ugly.
Christ when tomorrow feels uncertain.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe somebody sent you this article privately.
Maybe they did not know how to confront you.
Maybe they were afraid you would feel attacked.
Maybe they recognized something because they have fought the same war.
Do not become angry with the messenger before you have listened to the warning.
Perhaps this was sent because somebody believes your soul is worth an uncomfortable conversation.
And perhaps you know someone who needs the same conversation.
Not as a declaration that “those people” need fixing.
Somebody may read it at 1:13 in the morning with tears in their eyes.
Somebody may finally confess.
Somebody may finally install the boundary.
Somebody may finally call the friend.
Somebody may finally stop hiding.
Send it privately to the person who came to mind while you were reading.
Sexual bondage thrives in secrecy, but bringing sin into the light should never become an excuse to publicly shame another person.
You do not need to tell strangers every detail of your life.
Let somebody discover that the Church is not supposed to be a museum of people pretending they were never tempted.
We are people desperately dependent upon the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Not because saving a post changes a heart.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday’s convictions feel distant.
Come back when the excuses begin sounding reasonable again.
Come back when “just once” begins negotiating with you.
Come back when you need to remember that the person on the screen is not an object.
And neither are you.
You were not created to spend your life being discipled by an algorithm of endless appetite.
You were created for God.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, confront hidden sin, understand grace, or keep walking with Jesus, follow and stay close.
Salvation cannot be bought, and grace is never merchandise.
But generosity, sharing truth, and helping sound Gospel-centered work reach people are meaningful ways believers can choose to serve others and honor Christ.
Send it privately.
Tag wisely.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that merely admires Christian content.
The goal is that people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
That sinners repent.
That hidden things come into the light.
That wounded people discover grace.
That enslaved hearts learn obedience.
That believers stop treating other image-bearers as consumable bodies.
That marriages are guarded.
That consciences become tender again.

That people who thought they were too dirty to return discover the Savior who ate with sinners, touched the unclean, forgave the guilty, confronted hypocrisy, carried our sins to the cross, conquered death, and still calls people out of darkness.
Maybe pornography has written chapters of your story you wish you could erase.
Maybe lust has taken more from you than you ever intended to give.
Maybe you cannot recover yesterday.
But yesterday does not get to be your savior.
And yesterday does not get to be your lord.
Jesus Christ does.
Repentance may hurt.
Confession may embarrass you.
Boundaries may inconvenience you.
Healing may take time.
Discipleship may expose places in your heart you would rather leave untouched.
But do not confuse the pain of coming into the light with the hopelessness of remaining in darkness.
Christ did not shed His blood so that you could make peace with chains.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the appetite.
Bring Him the failures.
Bring Him the phone.
Bring Him the fantasies.
Bring Him the excuses.
Bring Him the version of yourself nobody else sees.
Not because your surrender earns His cross.
Because His cross is the reason guilty people can finally stop running.
And remember this when the screen goes dark and that terrible silence returns:
Jesus already knows what you watched in the darkness—and He is still calling you into the light, not so your scandal gets the final word, but so His grace does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DRAW ME AFTER YOU; LET US RUN”: The Woman in Scripture Who Wasn’t Ashamed to Express Desire
paragraphs: “DRAW ME AFTER YOU; LET US RUN”: The Woman in Scripture Who Wasn’t Ashamed to Express Desire

Song of Songs 1:4 is more daring than many Christians realize—and beneath its poetry is a truth about desire, intimacy, shame, and the God who does not redeem us by making us less human, but by making us holy.
“Draw me after you; let us run.”
Read that again.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
Because it is almost startling that it is in the Bible.
A woman is speaking.
She is not emotionless. She is not embarrassed. She is not pretending she has no longing. She does not hide behind religious language or apologize for wanting to be near the man she loves.
She wants him.
She says it.
And Scripture does not censor her.
The Hebrew is even more vivid:
מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה
Māshkēnî ʾaḥăreykā nārûṣāh.
“Draw me after you; let us run.”
Then comes the rest of the verse:
הֱבִיאַנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲדָרָיו
Hĕbîʾanî hammelekh ḥădārāyw.
“The king has brought me into his chambers.”
There it is.
Desire.
Longing.
Pursuit.
Intimacy.
Joy.
And not in some forbidden manuscript hidden from respectable Christians.
It is Holy Scripture.
Maybe that makes some of us uncomfortable.
And maybe our discomfort reveals something.
Because some Christians have unknowingly learned to treat holiness as though it means becoming less human.
We know how to talk about temptation.
We know how to warn people about lust.
We know how to say, “Flee sexual immorality.”
And Scripture absolutely does.
But sometimes we have been far less comfortable saying something else Scripture also says:
God created human beings capable of desire.
And desire itself is not the enemy.
Sin corrupts desire.
Sin disorders desire.
Sin can turn another human being into an object, turn affection into possession, turn longing into lust, and turn intimacy into exploitation.
But Christianity does not teach that the human body is evil.
It teaches something infinitely more beautiful.
The body belongs to God.
Love belongs to God.
Marriage belongs to God.
Faithfulness belongs to God.
And even our desires must ultimately come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because Song of Songs 1:4 is not a frightened woman trying to erase her femininity.
She speaks.
She longs.
She desires closeness.
And the biblical text lets her voice remain.
The Hebrew verb behind “draw me” is מָשַׁךְ — māshakh.
It can carry the sense of drawing, pulling, or leading.
In this verse the form מָשְׁכֵנִי — māshkēnî — is intensely personal:
“Draw me.”
Then suddenly her language expands:
נָּרוּצָה — nārûṣāh.
“Let us run.”
There is movement in this love.
Not indifference.
Not coldness.
Not detached admiration from a safe distance.
Run.
The woman of the Song does not merely want to analyze love.
She wants to experience the presence of the one she loves.
And perhaps that is where this ancient love song begins exposing something much deeper in us.
Because we are creatures of desire.
Every one of us is running after something.
Some run after affection.
Some run after validation.
Some run after money because poverty once terrified them.
Some run after applause because silence makes them feel invisible.
Some run from relationship to relationship because being wanted for one night feels temporarily better than feeling unwanted for a lifetime.
Some scroll through photographs hoping someone else's life will distract them from their own loneliness.
Some keep returning to pornography because counterfeit intimacy seems easier than vulnerability.
Some stay in destructive relationships because crumbs of affection feel better than an empty table.
Some pretend they do not need anyone.
Some hide behind ministry.
Some hide behind marriage.
Some hide behind jokes.
Some even hide behind theology.
But eventually, when the room becomes quiet enough, the heart asks the question we have been avoiding:
What am I really longing for?
That is where Song of Songs becomes dangerous in the best possible way.
It refuses to pretend desire does not exist.
The woman does not say, “I have transcended longing.”
She essentially says:
Draw me.
I want to come closer.
And Scripture is not ashamed of her.
But we must also be careful here.

Song of Songs is poetry celebrating human love and desire. We should not erase its plain literary meaning by pretending every kiss, fragrance, chamber, or embrace is secretly a coded reference to Christ.
The lovers are lovers.
The poetry is romantic.
The desire is real.
And that is part of its biblical beauty.
Yet when the whole canon of Scripture is opened before us, this celebration of rightly ordered human longing can also become a mirror.
Not because the woman in Song 1:4 is secretly saying the name of Jesus.
She isn't.
But because every good created love ultimately reminds Christians that no created person can carry the full weight of the human soul.
Your husband cannot be your Savior.
Your wife cannot be your Savior.
Your boyfriend cannot be your Savior.
Your girlfriend cannot be your Savior.
Sex cannot save you.
Marriage cannot save you.
Being desired cannot save you.
Being beautiful cannot save you.
Being wanted cannot save you.
And being alone cannot condemn you.
There is a hunger underneath all our hungers that creation was never designed to satisfy completely.
We were made for God.
And this is where the words begin to sound different in the heart of a Christian:
“Draw me after you; let us run.”
Because Jesus Christ does not merely tell sinners to find their way home.
He comes looking for them.
Think about the scandal of the Gospel.
God did not wait until you became desirable.
Christ did not die for a polished version of you.
He did not climb Calvary for the person you pretend to be on Sunday.
He knew.
The secret browser history.
The affair nobody discovered.
The fantasies.
The jealousy.
The hunger for attention.
The compromises.
The relationship you knew was pulling you away from God.
The nights you promised, “Never again,” only to fall again.
The shame beneath the smile.
The prayer life that disappeared.
The Bible collecting dust while your phone knew exactly what could keep you awake until 2:00 in the morning.
He knew.
And still—
the cross.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
