Sometimes three honest words are where healing conversations begin.
And think of one person who needs this tonight.
Not fifty strangers.
One person.
The friend quietly drifting from Christ.
The believer fighting an addiction nobody sees.
The brother who thinks failure has disqualified him forever.
The woman carrying shame from a chapter she cannot rewrite.
Send this to them privately if their struggle is sensitive.
Because one day the temptation may return disguised as “one small request,” and you may need to remember:
Do not negotiate with what God called you to surrender.
It doesn't.
Not because sharing saves you.
It cannot.
Jesus saves.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting the spread of biblical truth, one practical way you can participate is by supporting, sharing, and helping Gospel-centered resources reach farther than they could otherwise reach.
Not as a religious badge.
As a seed.
Because somebody scrolling tonight may be smiling publicly while privately reaching again for the very thing that nearly destroyed them.
Somebody needs to discover that repentance is still possible.
Somebody needs to hear that grace has not run out.
Somebody needs to know that Jesus receives people who finally stop defending their rebellion and come home.
Adonijah's story ends with death.
But yours does not have to end where your rebellion began.
There is another King.
A greater Son of David.
A King wiser than Solomon.
A King whose throne cannot be stolen.
A King who died beneath a sign declaring His kingship and rose with death defeated beneath His feet.
His name is Jesus.
And maybe the most important question left by Adonijah's story is not whether you understand why Solomon considered Abishag politically dangerous.
Maybe the question is much closer.
What are you still reaching for after God told you to surrender it?
What old throne are you still circling?
What “small request” is secretly carrying a much larger rebellion?
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
There is mercy at His feet.
There is forgiveness in His blood.
There is resurrection after ruin.
There is grace after scandal.
And when Jesus takes the pen, your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence.
The throne you keep fighting to control may be the very thing keeping you from discovering the freedom of finally kneeling before the King who died to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DISEASE WAS IN HIS FEET—BUT THE DEEPER SICKNESS WAS SOMEWHERE ELSE
paragraphs: THE DISEASE WAS IN HIS FEET—BUT THE DEEPER SICKNESS WAS SOMEWHERE ELSE

King Asa once cried to God when an army overwhelmed him. Years later, when disease overwhelmed his own body, Scripture records one devastating sentence: he sought the physicians—but did not seek the LORD. What happened between those two moments may be one of the most frightening warnings ever written for people who have walked with God for years.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are verses that seem to quietly follow you out of the room.
Second Chronicles 16:12 is one of them.
“In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa became diseased in his feet, and his malady was severe; yet in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but the physicians.”
Read that slowly.
Because the tragedy is not simply that a king became sick.
The tragedy is that a man who once knew where to run...
apparently forgot.
And perhaps that is why Asa's story can become painfully personal.
Because some of us have not stopped believing in God.
We have simply stopped seeking Him first.
We know Christian language. We know worship songs. We know what verses to post when someone else is hurting. We know how to say, “God is faithful.”
But when our own world begins collapsing, something else reveals what we actually trust.
The bank account.
The specialist.
The relationship.
The influential friend.
The strategy.
The medication.
The career.
Our own intelligence.
None of those things is necessarily sinful.
That distinction matters enormously.

Second Chronicles 16:12 should not be twisted into an argument that Christians should reject physicians, medicine, or legitimate medical treatment. Scripture itself does not say that Asa sinned merely because physicians were involved. The accusation is much more precise—and far more uncomfortable:
“he did not seek the LORD.”
That is the wound beneath the wound.
The Hebrew text makes the contrast striking:
וְגַם־בָּחֳלְיוֹ לֹא־דָרַשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה כִּי בָּרֹפְאִים
vegam-baḥolyō lo-darash et-YHWH, ki barofe'im
The crucial expression is לֹא־דָרַשׁ אֶת־יְהוָה — lo-darash et-YHWH:
“He did not seek the LORD.”
The verb darash carries the sense of seeking, inquiring, resorting to, turning toward.
And that word matters because Asa's story is fundamentally a story about where a human heart turns when pressure comes.
Not merely where his feet hurt.
Where his heart turned.
That makes the story frightening because Asa was not some lifelong pagan king who had never experienced God's faithfulness.
He knew better.
Long before diseased feet confined him, Asa had stood before something far more terrifying.
An enormous enemy force came against Judah.
And the younger Asa did something beautiful.
He prayed.
“O LORD, there is none beside thee to help, between the mighty and him that hath no strength: help us, O LORD our God; for we rely on thee...” — 2 Chronicles 14:11
There it is.
The heartbeat of the younger Asa:
“We rely on You.”
He looked at an enemy he could not defeat and essentially said,
God, if You do not help us, we are finished.
And God delivered them.
Asa had lived the testimony people dream about having.
He had watched helplessness become the stage upon which God's power was displayed.
Later, Azariah came with another message:
“The LORD is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you...” — 2 Chronicles 15:2
There is our word again.
Seek.
Asa responded.
He removed idols.
He repaired the altar.
He gathered the people.
They entered covenant together to seek the LORD.
There was rejoicing.
There was reform.
There was rest.
There was evidence everywhere that God had been faithful.
And that is precisely what makes the ending hurt.
Because years passed.
Success accumulated.
Experience accumulated.
Power accumulated.
And somewhere along the road, the man who once knew how desperately he needed God began behaving as though he could manage without Him.
Maybe you know that road.
Not rebellion with flashing lights.
Not waking up one morning and declaring that Jesus is no longer Lord.
Something quieter.
You used to pray before making decisions.
Now you make them and ask God to bless them afterward.
You used to open Scripture because you were hungry.
Now you mostly encounter verses while scrolling.
You used to confess quickly.
Now you explain yourself.
You used to tremble at conviction.
Now conviction irritates you.
You used to say, “Lord, what do You want?”
Now the first question is, “What do I want?”
Nothing dramatic happened.
You just slowly learned how to live while depending less consciously upon God.
Then came Ramah.
Baasha king of Israel threatened Judah.
And Asa faced another crisis.
Years earlier, an overwhelming army had made Asa pray.
This time, Asa calculated.
He took silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, seeking an alliance.
Strategically?
It worked.
Baasha withdrew.
The immediate problem disappeared.
And this may be one of the most dangerous moments in the entire story.
Because sometimes something can work and still reveal that your heart is moving away from God.
Success is not always proof that our spiritual condition is healthy.
Hanani the seer confronted Asa:
“Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God...” — 2 Chronicles 16:7
There it is again.
Reliance.
The issue that had once been Asa's strength was becoming his downfall.
Then Hanani reminded him of the past.
God had delivered Asa before.
God had already proved Himself.
And then came one of Scripture's magnificent declarations:
“For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him...” — 2 Chronicles 16:9
God was not reluctant to help Asa.
Think about that.
The Lord was looking to show Himself strong.
Asa's tragedy was not that God's arm had suddenly become too short.
Asa had changed where he placed his confidence.
And when confronted...
he did not repent.
He became angry.
He imprisoned the messenger.
He oppressed people.
This is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
The young Asa cried to God because he knew he was weak.
The older Asa became furious when someone reminded him that he was weak.
Have you ever wondered whether this is happening to you?
There was a time when correction brought you to your knees.
Now correction makes you defensive.
There was a time when Scripture exposed something and you whispered,
“Lord... change me.”
Now your instinct is,
“That doesn't apply to me.”
That is dangerous ground.
Because one of the most frightening spiritual conditions is not weakness.
It is becoming unable to admit weakness.
Then three years after the confrontation with Hanani, Scripture tells us about Asa's feet.
His disease became severe.
The Bible does not give us enough information to diagnose the precise illness, and responsible interpretation should resist pretending otherwise.
We know what Scripture wants us to know.
It was serious.
It affected his feet.
And in the midst of it, Asa still did not seek the LORD.
Do you see the tragedy now?
The feet are almost the final scene of a much longer spiritual story.
Asa had already stopped relying upon God during national crisis.
He had already rejected prophetic correction.
He had already hardened himself.
The physical disease did not create the deeper problem.
It exposed it.
And this is where we must be careful.
The lesson is not:
“Never go to a doctor.”
Please do not turn this passage into something Scripture itself does not say.
God can work through physicians.
God can work through medicine.
God can work through surgery, therapy, treatment, wise counselors, skilled professionals, friends, employers, and ordinary human means.
The issue is not whether you use means.
The question is whether the means have replaced the God upon whom your soul ultimately depends.
You can pray on the way to the hospital.
You can seek the LORD while receiving chemotherapy.
You can trust God while taking prescribed medicine.
You can ask God for wisdom while sitting across from a physician.
Faith and appropriate medical care do not have to be enemies.
The problem begins when created help becomes our functional god.
When we seek everybody...
except Him.
When we Google before we pray.
Panic before we pray.
Call everyone before we pray.
Strategize before we pray.
Spend before we pray.
Post before we pray.
And sometimes we do eventually pray...
after every other door has failed.
As though Jesus were the emergency exit instead of Lord.
Maybe your “physicians” are not physicians at all.
Maybe yours is a person you cannot imagine living without.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe alcohol.
Maybe constant entertainment because silence forces you to confront what is happening inside you.
Maybe it is approval.
Maybe you need people to tell you that you matter because somewhere along the way you stopped resting in what Christ says about you.
Maybe you have become extraordinarily skilled at managing symptoms while refusing to bring the disease of your heart into the light.
And perhaps nobody knows.
You still smile.
Still attend church.
Still share Bible verses.
Still tell everyone God is good.
But privately?
You are exhausted.
Something hurts.
Something has been hurting for a long time.
And instead of running toward Jesus, you have become very good at surviving around the pain.
Please hear the Gospel here.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to teach damaged people better coping strategies.
He came to save sinners.
He came for people whose deepest disease could never be cured by human effort.
Sin has gone deeper than our habits.
Deeper than our image.
Deeper than the things other people can see.
And we cannot heal ourselves.
That is why the Gospel is not “try harder.”
The Gospel is Christ.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He suffered under judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people can improve enough for God to accept them.
It is that guilty people can be forgiven because Jesus Christ took the place of sinners.
Grace does not pretend your sin is small.
Grace says the cross was sufficient.
And this is where Asa's story reaches through centuries and puts a hand on our shoulder.
You may have drifted.
You may have trusted other things.
You may have resisted correction.
You may have wasted years.
You may have known God faithfully in another season and barely recognize your heart now.
But while you are breathing, the invitation of the Gospel is still:
Come.
Not after you fix yourself.
Come now.
Repentance means you stop defending what God is exposing.
You turn.
You confess.
You come back to Christ.
And 1 John 1:9 gives sinners extraordinary hope: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Maybe your prayer does not need impressive language tonight.
Maybe it simply needs honesty.
Jesus...
I have been seeking everything except You.
Forgive me.
I have trusted things You created more than I trusted You.
Forgive me.
I have become defensive when You tried to correct me.
Forgive me.
I have learned how to look spiritually alive while becoming dry inside.
Forgive me.
I need You.
Not merely Your blessings.
Not merely Your rescue.
Not merely Your healing.
You.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this has been avoiding for years.
“I need You.”
There is no shame in needing Christ.
That is Christianity.
The strongest believer in the room is still breathing borrowed breath.
The mature Christian has not graduated from dependence upon Jesus.
We never outgrow grace.
We never become too experienced for prayer.
We never become too knowledgeable for Scripture.
We never become too successful to kneel.
And we never become so spiritually mature that Jesus becomes optional.
Asa's beginning warns us not to trust ourselves.
Asa's ending warns us not to assume yesterday's faithfulness guarantees today's dependence.
But the Gospel directs our eyes beyond Asa.
To a better King.
Asa faltered.
Jesus did not.
Asa's heart wandered.
Christ remained perfectly obedient to the Father.
Asa could not save himself.
Jesus saves completely those who come to God through Him.
That is why our hope is ultimately not that we will become strong enough never to stumble.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
The King who does not fail.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Shepherd who searches for wandering sheep.
The Advocate for those who confess.
The Redeemer who can take chapters we are ashamed of and make them evidence of His mercy.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
There may come a day when the diagnosis arrives, the relationship breaks, the money disappears, the plan fails, or fear starts whispering at 2:00 in the morning.
On that day, remember Asa.
Then remember Jesus.

Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not. We are saved by grace, not by social-media activity—but because sharing biblical truth can place the Gospel in front of someone you may never know is struggling. Our glory belongs to God alone; our support of Gospel work should flow from gratitude to Him, never from an attempt to purchase His approval.
But whatever you do after reading this, never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Savior.
You need Jesus.
No purchase can save you.
No share can cleanse you.
No comment can reconcile you to God.
No ministry membership can substitute for repentance and faith.
Only Christ saves.
So seek the doctor when you need the doctor.
Take wise counsel when you need wise counsel.
Receive legitimate help without shame.
But underneath every appointment, every treatment, every strategy, every relationship, every resource, every unanswered question and every frightening night...
seek the LORD.
Because the saddest sentence in Asa's story was not that his feet became diseased.
It was that when suffering came, the man who once knew how to seek God no longer sought Him.
Do not let that become the final sentence of your story.
Your deepest tragedy would not be discovering that your feet could no longer carry you—it would be forgetting the Savior who carried you all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RIZPAH: FROM SAUL’S CONCUBINE TO ONE OF THE BIBLE’S FIERCEST GRIEVING MOTHERS
paragraphs:
RIZPAH: FROM SAUL’S CONCUBINE TO ONE OF THE BIBLE’S FIERCEST GRIEVING MOTHERS
They took her sons. They left their bodies exposed. But they underestimated what a grieving mother would do when love refused to walk away.
There are women in Scripture whose names became sermons.
Sarah. Ruth. Esther. Mary.
And then there is Rizpah.
A woman many Christians have read past without realizing they had just walked by one of the most haunting scenes in the Old Testament.
Her story does not begin with a crown.
It begins with a label.
“Concubine.”
It moves through political violence, public death, unbearable grief, and a lonely vigil beside the dead.
And somehow, in the middle of one of the Bible’s darkest narratives, Rizpah becomes unforgettable.
Not because she stopped the tragedy.
She didn’t.
Not because she brought her sons back to life.
She couldn’t.
Not because Scripture records some magnificent speech from her lips.
It doesn’t.
Rizpah becomes unforgettable because when almost everything had been taken from her, love remained.
And sometimes the most devastating faith stories are not about people who escaped the fire.
Sometimes they are about people who stayed when everyone else had gone home.
Maybe that is why her story hurts.
Because some of you know what it is like to remain beside something you cannot repair.
A marriage you prayed over.
A child you cried over.
A family you tried to hold together.
A funeral that divided your life into “before” and “after.”
A prayer that seemed to disappear into heaven without an answer.
A version of yourself that no longer exists.
You kept waiting for God to change the circumstances.
But the circumstances changed you instead.
If that is you, do not rush through Rizpah.
Sit beside her for a while.

Her story begins in the violent aftermath of Saul’s reign. Israel suffered a famine for three successive years, and David sought the LORD concerning it. According to 2 Samuel 21, the answer connected the crisis with Saul’s bloodguilt against the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn to protect.
David asked the Gibeonites what restitution they required.
Their answer was terrible.
They requested seven male descendants of Saul to be handed over.
David agreed, while sparing Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, because of the oath between David and Jonathan.
Among the seven handed over were two sons of Rizpah.
Their names mattered.
Armoni.
Mephibosheth—the son of Saul and Rizpah, distinct from Jonathan’s better-known son of the same name.
The Hebrew text identifies her as:
רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה
Ritspah bat-Ayyah.
“Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.”
Do not miss that.
Before Scripture tells us what she did, it tells us who she was.
She had a name.
She was somebody’s daughter.
And she was the mother of two sons who were about to die.
Second Samuel 21:9 says the seven were put to death and that they fell together. The passage places this at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Then comes verse 10.
And suddenly the political narrative becomes painfully personal.
“Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth…”
The Hebrew says:
וַתִּקַּח רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה אֶת־הַשַּׂק
Vattiqqach Ritspah bat-Ayyah et-hassaq.
Rizpah took the sackcloth.
Sackcloth.
The rough fabric associated throughout Scripture with mourning, humiliation, calamity, and grief.
She spread it for herself upon the rock.
And she stayed.
The text says she remained from the beginning of harvest until rain fell upon them from heaven.
Then Scripture gives us an image almost too painful to picture.
She did not allow the birds of the heavens to settle upon the bodies by day.
She did not allow the beasts of the field to come near by night.
Day.
Night.
Sun.
Darkness.
Birds circling overhead.
Animals moving beyond the edge of visibility.
A mother on a rock.
Watching.
Guarding.
Waiting.
Scripture does not tell us everything she thought during those days.
So we should not pretend it does.
We are not told every prayer she prayed, whether she screamed, whether she sat in silence, or what memories passed through her mind.
But Scripture tells us enough.
She stayed.
That is what makes Rizpah so difficult to forget.
She could not reverse what had happened.
But she could refuse to abandon those she loved to dishonor.
There are seasons when faith looks triumphant.
David standing before Goliath.
Moses lifting his staff.
Elijah calling down fire.
Peter preaching at Pentecost.
But there are other moments when faithfulness looks much quieter.
It looks like showing up again.
Praying again.
Holding on again.
Refusing to let bitterness have the final word.
Remaining tender when suffering has given you every excuse to become hard.
Rizpah could not control the king.
She could not control the Gibeonites.
She could not control death.
She could not command heaven to rain.
But she could remain.
And she did.
Maybe you understand that kind of helplessness.
You cannot make someone love Jesus.
You cannot repent for another person.
You cannot undo yesterday.
You cannot force reconciliation.
You cannot make a prodigal come home.
You cannot resurrect a relationship God has allowed to end.
You cannot rewrite your childhood.
You cannot return to the hospital room and change what happened.
There are limits to human power.
And admitting those limits can break something inside us.
But Rizpah reminds us that powerlessness does not make love meaningless.
Then something happens.
The king hears about her.
Second Samuel 21:11 says that David was told what Rizpah had done.
Think about that.
She had no army.
No recorded public speech.
No throne.
No political office.
She simply refused to abandon her vigil.
And eventually the king heard.
David then retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan and gathered the remains of those who had been executed. They were buried in the tomb of Kish, Saul’s father, in Benjamin.
Only after this does the chapter say:
God responded to the plea for the land.
Rizpah did not resurrect her sons.
But her actions became part of the chain of events that led to their honorable burial.
Her grief was seen.
Her devotion became known.
Her sons would not remain exposed indefinitely.
The story did not end on the rock.
And neither does the biblical story of grief.
Because centuries later, another grieving mother would stand near another publicly exposed Son.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Rome meant the cross to humiliate.
To strip.
To shame.
To announce that the condemned person had been defeated.
John tells us that near the cross of Jesus stood His mother.
Mary could not stop the nails.
She could not order Rome away.
She could not prevent the spear.
She stood near her Son while the world did its worst.
But here the similarities must give way to the greater Gospel reality.
Rizpah guarded the bodies of sons who could not rise.
Mary watched the death of the Son who would.
Jesus was buried.
The stone was sealed.
The disciples grieved.
Hope appeared dead.
But death was not writing the final chapter.
On the third day, Jesus Christ rose.
That is where Christianity becomes more than advice for coping with pain.
The Gospel does not merely say, “Be strong while you grieve.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ entered death itself and conquered it.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:54–55:
Then he reaches back into the prophets and cries:
“Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?”
The Greek word translated “victory” is:
νῖκος
nikos.
Victory.
Conquest.
Triumph.
Christian hope is not that faithful people never cry.
Jesus Himself wept.
Christian hope is that because Christ is risen, death does not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
That changes how we read Rizpah.
Her story is not the Gospel itself, and we should not force every detail into an allegory Scripture never makes.
But her grief creates an ache that the Gospel ultimately answers.
A mother guards the dead.
Human beings cannot defeat death.
Kings cannot defeat death.
Governments cannot defeat death.
Money cannot defeat death.
Medicine can postpone death but cannot abolish it.
And then Jesus walks out of a tomb.
This is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
Maybe people know you by what happened to you.
Divorced.
Abandoned.
Widowed.
Rejected.
Addicted.
Betrayed.
Bankrupt.
Brokenhearted.
Disgraced.
Maybe you even introduced yourself inwardly by your wounds for so long that you forgot God still calls you by name.
Rizpah entered the biblical record carrying a socially vulnerable title associated with Saul’s household.
But she did not disappear into that title.
Scripture remembers her name.
And the Gospel goes further.
In Christ, your deepest identity is not the scandal behind you.
It is not the sin you have repented of.
It is not what someone did to you.
It is not what you lost.
It is not even the worst thing you ever did.
For those who are in Christ, Paul says:
εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις
ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis.
“If anyone is in Christ, [there is] a new creation.”
Second Corinthians 5:17.
New.
Not cosmetically repaired.
Not religiously decorated.
New.
That does not mean Jesus pretends your past never happened.
Grace is more powerful than denial.
Jesus can take the chapter you wish had never been written and refuse to let it become the ending.
That is the heartbeat of everything we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing historical facts.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending consequences do not exist.

Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming what sin tried to destroy, forgiving those who repent and believe, restoring what can be restored, transforming sinners, healing wounded hearts, and giving eternal life where death once appeared to have the final word.
Perhaps your rock is not a literal rock.
Perhaps it is a hospital chair.
An empty side of the bed.
A divorce decree.
A child’s bedroom.
A rehabilitation center.
A grave.
A silent phone.
A Bible stained by tears.
Perhaps nobody understands how exhausting it has been to keep believing while protecting the last fragile pieces of your heart.
God sees what human beings overlook.
But hear this carefully.
You were never meant to build your permanent home beside the grave.
Rizpah’s story moved toward burial.
The Gospel moves beyond burial toward resurrection.
There is a difference between honoring what you lost and allowing your loss to become your god.
There is a difference between grieving and surrendering your identity to grief.
There is a difference between remembering yesterday and refusing to follow Jesus into tomorrow.
Some of us have guarded our pain longer than we have guarded our relationship with Christ.
We replay the betrayal.
Feed the resentment.
Visit the wound.
Rehearse the offense.
Imagine conversations that will never happen.
And somewhere along the way, pain becomes familiar enough to feel like home.
Jesus did not die and rise again merely to make your prison more comfortable.
He came to set captives free.
Maybe this is the moment to stop pretending.
Maybe you love Jesus, but you are exhausted.
Maybe you are angry with God and ashamed to admit it.
Maybe grief has hollowed you out.
Maybe you have smiled at church while quietly wondering whether heaven remembers your address.
Maybe there is sin underneath the grief too—something you have hidden, justified, fed, protected, and refused to surrender.
Bring that into the light.
Not because Jesus is waiting to humiliate you.
Because the crucified and risen Christ already knows the truth.
Repentance is not running away from Jesus in shame.
It is turning toward Him because you finally understand that hiding cannot heal you.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια—metanoia—for repentance, carrying the idea of a changed mind and turning of life toward God.
Grace does not tell you your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters terribly.
Grace tells you Jesus was willing to bear the judgment sinners could never remove themselves.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
And the risen Christ still receives sinners.
Pray.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Confess your sin.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him your anger.
Bring Him the person you cannot forgive.
Bring Him the loss you cannot understand.
Bring Him the secret nobody knows.
You do not need to explain everything publicly.
Two words are enough.
Pray for me.
And believers reading those words—do not merely react to them.
Pray for that person.
Let the comments beneath this article become more than engagement.
Let them become reminders that wounded people are not walking toward Jesus alone.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because someone on your Facebook friends list may be sitting beside their own invisible rock tonight.
There may come a night when you need to read Rizpah’s name again and remember:
God sees people the world passes over.
We want this space to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ.

If you have been blessed by this ministry and want to glorify God through generosity, one practical way you can choose to do that is by helping Gospel Warrior continue putting the Gospel in front of people who desperately need it.
Not as payment for God’s favor.
Never that.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.

But Christians can glorify God by generously supporting faithful Gospel work, just as they can glorify Him through prayer, service, hospitality, sharing truth, and countless other acts of obedience and love.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Because Rizpah’s story eventually forces us to confront a question far larger than Rizpah.
What do we do when everything we love seems to have been carried to a place we cannot follow?
For the Christian, we look beyond the rock.
Beyond the cross.
Beyond the grave.
Toward an empty tomb.
Rizpah stayed beside death because love would not abandon her sons.
Jesus entered death because love would not abandon sinners.
And unlike Rizpah, He possessed the power to defeat the grave.
So when your story reaches a chapter that feels irreversible, remember this:
The Author is not standing helplessly outside the tomb.
He walked out of one.
And perhaps that is the line your wounded heart needs to carry with it tonight:
When grief tells you that you have reached the final page, look again—the hands holding your story still carry the scars of the One who walked out of the grave.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Man Was Sleeping With His Father’s Wife—and the Corinthian Church Was Proud
paragraphs:
A Man Was Sleeping With His Father’s Wife—and the Corinthian Church Was Proud
The scandal in Corinth was horrifying. But what should terrify us even more is that Paul was not only confronting the man in sin—he was confronting a church that had learned how to tolerate what should have broken its heart.
There are Bible passages we love to underline.
And then there are Bible passages we quietly wish were not there.
First Corinthians 5 is one of them.
It does not begin with a miracle.
It does not begin with an inspirational promise.
It begins with a scandal.
A sexual scandal.
Inside a church.
And somehow, the most disturbing part of the story is not simply what one man was doing behind closed doors.
It is what the church was doing in public.
They were proud.
Paul had heard what was happening in Corinth, and when he addressed it, he did not soften the language to protect anyone's comfort:
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife.”
—1 Corinthians 5:1, ESV
The Greek is even more revealing.
“Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία…”
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
Literally, the opening carries the force of something like:
“Sexual immorality is actually being reported among you…”
The word Paul uses is πορνεία — porneia.
It refers broadly to sexual immorality—sexual behavior outside the boundaries established by God.
Paul was not describing gossip.
He was not talking about a misunderstanding.
He was confronting an ongoing sexual relationship so scandalous that he says even the surrounding Gentile culture did not ordinarily tolerate it.
A man had his father’s wife.

Most interpreters understand Paul to mean the man's stepmother rather than his biological mother, particularly because Paul says “his father’s wife.” The language also echoes the Old Testament prohibition against uncovering one's father's nakedness by taking his wife.
Leviticus 18:8 says:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife; it is your father’s nakedness.”
This was not merely socially awkward.
It was rebellion against God's revealed sexual boundaries.
But then Paul says something that should stop every Christian who has ever learned to become comfortable around unrepentant sin.
“And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?”
—1 Corinthians 5:2, ESV
The Greek is devastating:
καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ
Kai hymeis pephysiōmenoi este.
“And you are puffed up.”
Inflated.
Swollen with pride.
Paul expected grief.
He found arrogance.
He expected mourning.
He found boasting.
He expected a church brokenhearted that someone bearing the name of Christ was openly living contrary to Christ.
Instead, something had happened to their conscience.
They had apparently learned how to coexist with scandal without mourning it.
And suddenly this ancient Corinthian church does not feel quite so ancient anymore.
Because there is a terrifying stage in spiritual decline when sin no longer shocks us.
Then comes another stage when it no longer grieves us.
And eventually, if we are not careful, we begin finding sophisticated reasons to defend what Scripture tells us to repent of.
That is when Corinth stops being merely a city on an ancient map.
Corinth becomes a mirror.
And perhaps that is why this chapter makes us uncomfortable.
It is easier to stare at the unnamed man than to let Scripture stare back at us.
We can read about his sexual immorality and think:
How could he?
But Paul turns toward the congregation and essentially asks:
How could you become comfortable with it?
That question reaches beyond sexual sin.
How did bitterness become normal in your heart?
How did secret pornography become something you manage instead of something you bring into the light?
How did dishonesty become “just business”?
How did hatred become “discernment”?
How did gossip become “concern”?
How did unforgiveness become “boundaries” when, deep down, you know you are feeding resentment?
How did pride become confidence?
How did greed become ambition?
How did prayerlessness become busyness?
How did months pass without opening your Bible while you continued telling everyone that you were “just going through a season”?
How did you become able to sing about holiness on Sunday while protecting the very thing Jesus has been asking you to surrender?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your family does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe the person sitting beside you at church would never imagine it.
But God knows.
And strangely enough, that should not merely terrify you.
For the repentant sinner, it should give you hope.
Because the God who sees what you are hiding is also the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Paul's response in Corinth was severe because sin is severe.
He instructed the church to remove this persistently immoral professing believer from their fellowship.
That sounds harsh to modern ears until we understand the purpose.
Paul writes that such a person was to be handed over “for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.”
The goal was not cruelty.
The goal was restoration.
The discipline was meant to destroy the illusion that someone could cling defiantly to sin while enjoying all the assurances of Christian fellowship as though nothing were wrong.
Biblical love does not smile while someone walks toward destruction.
Biblical love tells the truth.
But biblical truth does not end with condemnation either.
This is where the story becomes astonishing.
Because when many Christians hear “church discipline,” they imagine permanent exile.
God's purpose is different.
Correction aims toward repentance.
Repentance opens the door toward restoration.
And there is a fascinating connection many interpreters have seen between 1 Corinthians and Paul's later words in 2 Corinthians.

We should be careful here: Scripture does not explicitly identify the repentant person in 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 as the same man from 1 Corinthians 5. Many interpreters have proposed that connection, while others believe Paul was referring to a different offender.
But regardless of the man's exact identity, Paul's theology of restoration could not be clearer.
When discipline has produced repentance, Paul does not tell Christians to keep crushing the sinner.
He says:
“You should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.”
—2 Corinthians 2:7, ESV
Read that again.
Forgive him.
Comfort him.
Then Paul says:
“So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.”
—2 Corinthians 2:8, ESV
This is Christianity.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not redefining rebellion until repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not humiliating broken people forever because their worst chapter became public.
Truth confronts.
Grace restores.
The cross explains why both are necessary.
Jesus did not die because sin was insignificant.
Jesus died because sin was deadly.
And Jesus did not rise because sinners were beyond redemption.
He rose because death itself would not have the final word over everyone united to Him.
That changes how we read Corinth.
The Gospel is not:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
The Gospel is not:
“Try harder so God will finally tolerate you.”
The Gospel is that the holy God against whom we have sinned came near to sinners in Jesus Christ.
Christ lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose bodily from the grave.
Forgiveness therefore is not God pretending your rebellion never happened.
Forgiveness was purchased at terrible cost.
Grace is free to us because it was costly to Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years misunderstanding grace.
You thought grace meant God would leave you alone.
But grace loves you too much for that.
Paul later asks the Corinthians:
“Do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God?”
Then he names sins.
Sexual immorality.
Idolatry.
Adultery.
Theft.
Greed.
Drunkenness.
Reviling.
Swindling.
And then comes one of the most beautiful sentences ever written to a scandal-filled church:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Not because they had never committed those sins.
They had.
Not because their histories had somehow become respectable.
They had not.
But something happened.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11, ESV
That is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needed.
Such were some of you.
Your past can describe where Christ found you without determining where Christ is taking you.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Liar.
Pornography-bound.
Greedy.
Bitter.
Proud.
Drunk.
Sexually broken.
Religiously hypocritical.
Secretly exhausted.
Spiritually numb.
Ashamed.
The Gospel does not require you to manufacture a cleaner history.
Jesus specializes in resurrecting people who finally stop pretending they are alive.
But do not confuse grace with permission.
Jesus does not merely forgive us in our sin.
He begins freeing us from its dominion.
Repentance is not payment for salvation.
You cannot purchase the blood of Christ with tears.
You cannot earn justification by cleaning yourself up.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But genuine grace changes direction.
The New Testament word often translated “repentance,” μετάνοια — metanoia, speaks of a change of mind that involves a transformed orientation toward God and sin.
Repentance says:
“I cannot keep calling good what God calls evil.”
“I cannot keep hiding.”
“I cannot keep blaming everyone else.”
“I cannot keep asking Jesus to save me while demanding that my favorite idol remain untouched.”
Maybe your Corinth is a browser history.
Maybe it is an affair nobody has discovered.
Maybe it is the person you cannot forgive.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe it is the image you maintain online.
Maybe it is your private messages.
Maybe it is envy.
Maybe it is a relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe your scandal has never appeared publicly.
But heaven does not need screenshots.
God already sees it.
And still—
Christ calls you.
That is what makes grace almost unbearable in its beauty.
Jesus already knew the ugliest truth about you when He called sinners to Himself.
You cannot shock an omniscient Savior.
You cannot reveal something in confession that God only discovered when you finally admitted it.
Repentance is not informing God.
It is agreeing with Him.
And confession is not crawling toward a reluctant Christ who must somehow be persuaded to show mercy.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, ESV
Maybe this article is your moment.
Not because these words are magical.
They are not.
But perhaps the Word of God has put its finger on something you have been protecting.
There is a kind of pain that destroys you.
And there is a kind of pain that finally makes you stop touching the thing that has been destroying you.
Bring it to Jesus.
Name it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
If another person is being harmed, stop the harm.
If accountability is needed, seek it.
If you need your pastor or mature believers around you, tell them.
If your situation involves abuse, coercion, exploitation, or danger, seek appropriate professional and lawful help rather than treating the matter as merely a private spiritual struggle.
Come into the light.
Not because Christians never fall.
But because people being transformed by Christ cannot make peace with darkness forever.
And Christian, when another believer genuinely repents, remember Corinth from the other direction too.
Do not become the person who loves exposing sin more than seeing sinners restored.
Some Christians know how to discipline but have forgotten how to forgive.
They know someone's scandal from ten years ago better than they know the evidence of God's grace in that person's life today.
But if heaven rejoices over repentance, why would we resent restoration?
The cross leaves no room for moral superiority.
Every redeemed person stands at Calvary with empty hands.
There are no VIP sections beneath the blood of Jesus.
Only sinners.
Only grace.
Only a Savior worthy of all the glory.
Maybe that is why the Corinthian scandal still matters.
It forces us to hold two truths together that our culture constantly tries to separate.
Sin is worse than we want to admit.
And Jesus is more merciful than we dared to hope.
Take away the first truth and grace becomes cheap sentimentality.
Take away the second and Christianity becomes hopeless condemnation.
At the cross, both truths meet.
Your sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
His grace is powerful enough to rewrite what sin tried to make your final chapter.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this message:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner.
Not by renaming darkness.
By bringing us into light.
Not by telling guilty people that holiness no longer matters.
By washing, sanctifying, justifying, restoring, and transforming people through the Gospel.
So be honest.
What did this expose?
If there is something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your sin for strangers to inspect. But you can stop pretending.
You do not have to explain everything.
Sometimes three words are enough to say, I don't want to fight alone anymore.
Then look around the comments.
Remember that behind those names are real human beings fighting battles you may know nothing about.
Pray for one another.
Encourage repentance rather than humiliation.
Point one another toward Jesus.
And if one person came to mind while you were reading this, send this article to them personally.
Not as an accusation.
Not with, “This is about you.”
Send it with love.
It hasn't.

Supporting Gospel work financially is not what saves you, proves your salvation, or purchases God's blessing. Christ alone saves, and Christians glorify God in many forms of faithful obedience. But voluntary generosity can be one meaningful way believers participate in Gospel ministry.
More importantly, your support helps us keep creating and sharing Scripture-centered resources designed to call people away from darkness and toward Jesus Christ.
Not to prove anything to God.
Not because clicking “Share” makes anyone righteous.
And before you leave, remember this:
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the feet of Jesus—but once grace takes hold of you, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: God Grew a Plant Over Jonah—Then Sent a Worm to Destroy It
paragraphs:
God Grew a Plant Over Jonah—Then Sent a Worm to Destroy It
Jonah wanted relief from the heat. God wanted to expose what was happening inside his heart. And sometimes the thing God allows to wither is the very thing revealing what we have learned to love more than the people He wants to save.
There is something almost uncomfortable about the ending of Jonah.
No triumphant closing scene.
No celebration.
No neat little sentence telling us Jonah finally understood.
Instead, there is a plant.
A worm.
A scorching wind.
An angry prophet sitting outside a city that God has just spared.
And then God asks a question.
The book ends.
That is what makes Jonah 4:6–11 so haunting.
Because perhaps the unanswered question was never meant to remain with Jonah.
Perhaps it was meant to follow us home.
Jonah had already lived through the kind of testimony people would have talked about for generations.
He ran from God.
God pursued him.
A storm erupted.
Jonah was thrown into the sea.
A great fish swallowed him.
He prayed from a place that should have become his grave.
God heard him.
God commanded the fish.
Jonah was vomited onto dry land.
Then the runaway prophet finally went to Nineveh and proclaimed the warning God had given him.
And Nineveh responded.
The people turned from their evil ways.
God saw their response and did not bring upon them the destruction He had threatened.
You would expect Jonah to rejoice.
He did not.
Jonah 4:1 says that what God did displeased Jonah exceedingly, and Jonah became angry.
Think about that.
A preacher preached.
People repented.
Judgment was withheld.
Lives were spared.
And the preacher was furious.
Jonah had received mercy when he was drowning, but he struggled with mercy when God gave it to people he did not want forgiven.
That is where this story stops being merely ancient.
Because it is possible to love grace when grace is rescuing us…
and resent grace when it is rescuing them.
It is possible to sing about forgiveness while quietly maintaining a list of people we hope God makes pay.
It is possible to know Scripture, speak about God, serve God, and still have corners of the heart that have not surrendered to the heart of God.
Then something strangely beautiful happens.
Jonah leaves the city and sits east of Nineveh. He makes himself a shelter and waits to see what will happen.
And God appoints a plant.
The Hebrew wording is striking.
וַיְמַן יְהוָה־אֱלֹהִים קִיקָיוֹן
Vayman YHWH Elohim qiqayon.
“And the LORD God appointed a plant…”
The Hebrew verb וַיְמַן (vayman, from מנה, manah) carries the idea of appointing, preparing, or assigning.
That matters because the plant is not the only thing God “appoints” in Jonah.
God appoints the great fish.
God appoints the plant.
God appoints the worm.
God appoints the scorching east wind.
Jonah thinks his story is about circumstances.
God is working on Jonah.
The fish was not random.
The plant was not random.
The worm was not random.
The wind was not random.
They become instruments inside the lesson God is teaching His prophet.
And perhaps that is worth sitting with for a moment.
Some of us immediately interpret comfort as God’s approval and discomfort as God’s absence.
But Jonah received both a plant and a worm under the sovereignty of the same God.
One gave shade.
One destroyed the shade.
And God was present in both moments.
Scripture says God appointed the plant “to save him from his discomfort.”
Then comes one of the most revealing sentences in the entire book.
Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant.
Finally, Jonah is happy.
Nineveh repents?
Angry.
Thousands receive mercy?
Angry.
A plant gives him shade?
Exceedingly glad.
That plant exposed him.
Not because enjoying shade was sinful.
It was not.
The problem was the contrast.
Jonah could experience extraordinary joy over something that improved his personal comfort while remaining deeply disturbed that God had shown compassion to human beings.
And that is where Jonah becomes a mirror.
What makes us rejoice?
What makes us angry?
What devastates us when we lose it?
What receives our emotional energy?
A promotion?
Recognition?
Comfort?
Money?
A relationship?
Our reputation?
Our plans?
Our political tribe?
Our preferred lifestyle?
Our convenience?
Our ability to control what happens next?
None of those things automatically represents Jonah’s plant.
But anything temporary can expose a disordered heart when losing it troubles us more deeply than lost people living far from God.
Then morning comes.
And God sends the worm.
Jonah 4:7 says:
וַיְמַן הָאֱלֹהִים תּוֹלַעַת
Vayman ha-Elohim tola‘at.
“God appointed a worm…”
The same God who appointed the plant appointed what struck the plant.
And the plant withered.
Imagine Jonah watching the leaves collapse.
Yesterday there was shade.
Today there is nothing.
Then God appoints a scorching east wind.
The sun beats down upon Jonah’s head.
His comfort disappears.
His frustration intensifies.
Jonah becomes so miserable that he says it would be better for him to die than to live.
Then God asks him:
“Do you do well to be angry for the plant?”
Jonah answers:
“Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die.”
It is almost shocking.
Jonah is arguing with the God who rescued him.
But God does not crush Jonah.
He teaches him.
The LORD points to Jonah's compassion for the plant.
The Hebrew of Jonah 4:10 uses the verb חוּס (ḥus), conveying pity, concern, or compassion.
Jonah cared about a plant he did not labor for.
He did not make it grow.
It appeared in a night and perished in a night.
Then God turns Jonah’s own concern back toward Nineveh.
If Jonah could care so deeply about a temporary plant…
should God not have compassion on a great city filled with human beings?
That question is the blade hidden inside the story.
Jonah cared about what gave him shade.
God cared about people.
Jonah mourned a plant.
God saw a city.
Jonah was occupied with his comfort.
God was concerned with human lives.
And before we condemn Jonah too quickly, we should ask whether we recognize him.
Because there are things we can lose today that would consume our thoughts for weeks.
But someone we know can spend years walking without Christ and barely appear in our prayers.
We can become furious over something posted online…
yet remain strangely unmoved by a friend who is spiritually dying.
We can spend hours protecting our image and minutes seeking God.
We can grieve when our plans collapse while scarcely grieving that someone we love does not know the Savior.
The worm did not merely destroy Jonah’s plant.
It revealed Jonah’s priorities.
And sometimes God allows our temporary shade to disappear because there are truths about our hearts that comfort was helping us avoid.

That does not mean every loss, disappointment, sickness, financial struggle, broken relationship, or hardship is God punishing you or deliberately “sending a worm.” Scripture does not give us permission to make that assumption about every painful circumstance.
But Jonah does teach something we dare not miss:
God loves His people enough to confront what is distorted inside them.
He does not merely want to change our circumstances.
He wants to transform our hearts.
And this is where Jonah begins pointing beyond Jonah.
Because centuries later, another Man would speak about the “sign of Jonah.”
Jesus Christ.
Jonah went outside the city angry that sinners had been spared.
Jesus went outside the city to suffer so sinners could be saved.
Jonah wanted judgment to fall upon his enemies.
Jesus bore judgment for His enemies.
Jonah sat under temporary shade concerned about himself.
Jesus carried a cross toward Golgotha, giving Himself for others.
Jonah descended into the depths because of his own rebellion.
Jesus descended into death though He had committed no sin.
Jonah emerged and preached judgment to Nineveh.
Jesus rose from the grave and commissioned His people to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins to the nations.
Do not miss the Gospel hiding behind the discomfort of Jonah.
You and I are not standing over Nineveh deciding whether sinners deserve mercy.
Apart from Christ, we are the sinners who need mercy.
We are not merely Jonah under the plant.
We are people who have rebelled against God.
We have loved created things more than the Creator.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Envied.
Hated.
Judged.
Hidden.
Compromised.
Worshiped comfort.
Protected pride.
Excused sins in ourselves that we condemned in other people.
And God would be perfectly righteous to judge sin.
Yet the Gospel announces something scandalous.
God did not save us because our sins were insignificant.
He saves through Christ because His grace is greater than the guilt we bring to Him.
At the cross, God did not pretend sin did not matter.
Jesus bore sin.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree,” Peter writes.
Justice was not discarded.
Christ took the judgment sinners deserved, and the risen Christ now offers forgiveness and reconciliation to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That is grace.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that does not tell you to remain exactly as you are.
Grace that calls you out of hiding.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that can take the scandalous chapters of a human life and write redemption across them.
Maybe your plant is withering right now.
Something you thought would remain has disappeared.
Something that made life comfortable is gone.
Something you leaned on cannot hold you anymore.
And you keep staring at the dead leaves asking:
“God, why did You let this happen?”
I cannot tell you why every painful thing has happened to you.
Jonah does not authorize anyone to make simplistic claims about another person’s suffering.
But I can ask you the question Jonah forces us to confront:
What is your heart revealing while the shade is gone?
Has the loss exposed an idol?
Has disappointment uncovered resentment?
Has discomfort exposed how much your peace depended upon circumstances rather than Christ?
Has someone else receiving mercy revealed bitterness you thought you had buried?
Has God been trying to turn your eyes from the plant toward the city?
Toward people?
Toward eternity?
Toward Jesus?
Maybe the deepest tragedy would not be losing the plant.
Maybe it would be getting another plant and never realizing why your heart was so devastated when the first one died.
Because everything under the sun eventually withers.
Money withers.
Beauty withers.
Popularity withers.
Influence withers.
Applause withers.
Possessions break.
Careers end.
Bodies age.
Platforms disappear.
People disappoint us.
Even the best gifts in this world were never designed to become our gods.
But Jesus Christ remains.
And perhaps you have been running.
Perhaps you have been hiding behind Christian language while privately knowing your heart is far from God.
Perhaps resentment has been eating you alive.
Perhaps there is a Nineveh in your life—a person you cannot imagine forgiving, a person whose repentance you would secretly distrust, a person you would rather see humiliated than restored.
Remember the mercy that found you.
The Gospel destroys our right to stand proudly over another sinner.
At the foot of the cross, nobody boasts.
We come empty-handed.
We come guilty.
We come needing mercy.
And Christ receives repentant sinners.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess it.
Repent.
Ask Him to change what you cannot change by pretending.
If you need words, let them be simple:
“Jesus, have mercy on me. Forgive my sin. Tear down what I have loved more than You. Teach me to love what You love. Change my heart. I trust in You.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when we finally stop pretending.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only person struggling.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally confess what they have been hiding because you had the courage to stop hiding first.
And please do not keep this article imprisoned on your screen.
Send it to someone whose “plant” has just withered.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, caring for the poor, or sharing Christ personally.

But when you freely support Gospel Warrior, you help us continue producing and distributing Christ-centered resources designed to point people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation in Jesus.

If glorifying God is genuinely your desire, do not let the truth He gives you stop with you. Put it into practice. Tell someone about Christ. Share biblical truth. Support faithful Gospel work where you prayerfully believe God is using it.
Not from guilt.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
Someone angry with God.
Someone confused.
Someone grieving.
Someone whose comfort has disappeared.
Someone staring at the worm while God is trying to turn their eyes toward something eternal.
Maybe they need to discover that the end of their shade is not the end of their story.
Maybe they need to hear that Jesus still receives sinners.
Maybe they need to remember that repentance is still possible.
Forgiveness is still offered.
Grace is still astonishing.
The tomb is still empty.
Christ is still Lord.
And God is still in the business of transforming hearts.
Jonah ends with a question because perhaps God wanted every generation afterward to answer it.
What matters more to you…
the plant…
or the people?
Temporary comfort…
or eternal souls?
Being proven right…
or seeing sinners restored?
Your little kingdom…
or His?
One day every plant we fought to preserve will be gone.
But the people standing around us will step into eternity.
So love them.
Pray for them.
Forgive as you have been forgiven.
Tell them about Jesus.
And when God exposes something ugly inside your own heart, do not run from Him like Jonah did.
Run toward the cross.

Because the God who exposed Jonah’s heart is also the God whose mercy pursued Jonah through a storm, through the sea, through the belly of a fish, through his anger, through a plant, through a worm, and all the way to one final question.
And the Gospel tells us something even greater:
Jesus did not merely come to expose sinners.
He came to save them.
Sometimes the worm that breaks your heart reveals the plant that quietly took its place—and Jesus loves you too much to let temporary shade become your savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DO ALGORITHMS KEEP FEEDING TEMPTATION?
paragraphs:
WHY DO ALGORITHMS KEEP FEEDING TEMPTATION?
When Your Screen Learns What Your Flesh Wants — and Jesus Still Offers a Way Out
There is something terrifying about realizing that your phone may know which temptation makes you hesitate.
Not because your phone has a soul.
Not because an algorithm is a demon.
Not because technology somehow invented sin.
But because you stopped scrolling for half a second.
Then you looked again.
You watched a little longer.
You clicked.
You searched.
Maybe you went back.
And somewhere inside an enormous mathematical system that does not know your name the way God knows your name, a pattern became useful:
This keeps this person looking.
So it showed you something similar.
Then something slightly stronger.
Then another.
And before long, what began as a moment of curiosity started becoming an environment.
That is what makes temptation in the digital age feel so strange.
Previous generations had to go looking for many of the things that tempt us.
Now temptation can come looking for us.
You can be sitting alone after midnight, tired, disappointed, lonely, angry with your spouse, frustrated with your life, spiritually dry, or simply bored...
and your thumb moves.
Scroll.
Scroll.
Scroll.
Then suddenly...
there it is.
The image.
The body.
The lifestyle.
The outrage.
The gossip.
The fantasy.
The person you envy.
The thing you cannot afford.
The relationship you wish you had.
The face that awakens something you thought you had surrendered.
And perhaps the most dangerous thought arrives next:
I didn't search for this.
Maybe you didn't.
But now you have a decision to make.
Because an algorithm can place something before your eyes.
It cannot make your heart worship it.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because Christians can spend so much time blaming the darkness around us that we never allow Scripture to expose the desires within us.
James does.
He writes:
James 1:14.
The language is painfully personal.
ἰδίας — idias.
His own.
ἐπιθυμίας — epithymias.
Desire. Craving. Longing.
ἐξελκόμενος — exelkomenos.
Being drawn away.
δελεαζόμενος — deleazomenos.
Being enticed.
James refuses to let us pretend that temptation is only an external problem.
Something outside us may present the bait.
Something inside us recognizes it.
That distinction matters.
Because your algorithm did not create the fallen human heart.
Sin existed before smartphones.
Lust existed before Instagram.
Envy existed before Facebook.
Greed existed before online shopping.
Pride existed before likes.
Gossip existed before comment sections.
Pornography did not invent lust.
Social media did not invent vanity.
Technology did not invent idolatry.
The serpent did not need Wi-Fi in Eden.
The human heart has been vulnerable to distorted desire since humanity's rebellion against God.
And yet...
something genuinely different has happened.
The bait can now follow us.
The temptation can be personalized.
The door can remain in our pocket.
And what you repeatedly give your attention to can influence what is placed in front of you again.
That means there are moments when your feed becomes something disturbingly close to a mirror.
Not a perfect mirror.
Not a morally conscious mirror.
But sometimes a mirror of repeated attention.
And maybe that is why this article is uncomfortable.
Because perhaps you have blamed the algorithm for something you have also been quietly training.
You paused.
You clicked.
You watched.
You returned.
You told yourself you hated it.
Then you fed it another second of attention.
And the system learned.
But underneath that technological loop, something much older was happening.
Your heart was being invited to desire something other than God.
That is where the real war is.
Jesus said:
“The lamp of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.”
Matthew 6:22.
Christ was not teaching twenty-first-century media theory.
We should not force modern technology into a text that was written long before algorithms existed.
But His teaching exposes something timeless:
What receives our gaze matters.
What fills our attention matters.
What we treasure matters.
Because Jesus had already said only a few verses earlier:
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
Matthew 6:21.
Your attention is not identical to worship.
But attention can reveal desire.
And repeated attention can nourish desire.
That should make every Christian ask a harder question than, “Why does my feed keep showing me this?”
Ask:
Why do I keep wanting to look?
That question hurts.
Especially when the answer has a name.
Loneliness.
Lust.
Validation.
Envy.
Bitterness.
Anger.
Comparison.
Greed.
Curiosity.
Escapism.
Maybe you don't actually want the woman on the screen.
Maybe you want to feel desired.
Maybe you don't really want the luxury car.
Maybe you desperately want to feel successful.
Maybe you don't actually enjoy watching someone else's downfall.
Maybe seeing another person fall temporarily makes you feel better about yourself.
Maybe you aren't addicted merely to outrage.
Maybe anger makes you feel powerful when the rest of your life makes you feel helpless.
Maybe your endless scrolling isn't really entertainment anymore.
Maybe you're trying not to be alone with your thoughts.
And suddenly the problem becomes deeper than software.
Because you can delete an app without healing a heart.
You can install a filter while still craving the thing behind the filter.
You can unfollow every seductive account and still carry lust into tomorrow.
You can throw away your phone and still be a sinner.
Which means Christianity cannot merely offer you digital discipline.
You need redemption.
You need a Savior.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your browsing habits.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
The compromised.
The double-minded.
The secretive.
The person who sings worship songs publicly and loses battles privately.
The person whose search history would devastate them if projected onto the church wall.
The woman drowning in comparison.
The husband hiding pornography.
The teenager desperate for approval.
The believer who keeps deleting something...
then reinstalling it.
Deleting.
Reinstalling.
Repenting.
Returning.
Crying.
Promising.
Failing.
Hiding.
And eventually wondering:
Does Jesus still want me?
Look at the cross.
That is your answer.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not cheap grace.
Not “God understands, so don't worry about repentance.”
No.
The cross tells you something infinitely better.
Your sin is serious enough that Christ died.
And His grace is powerful enough that sinners can be forgiven.
Paul writes:
Romans 5:8.
Not after you cleaned your history.
Not after you conquered every temptation.
Not after you became spiritually impressive.
“While we were yet sinners.”
Christ died for sinners.
And the Christ who forgives also calls sinners out of darkness.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that you could make peace with the chains He came to break.
Grace does not teach us to comfortably coexist with sin.
Grace teaches us to come into the light.
That may mean doing something painfully practical tonight.
Unfollow the account.
Block the page.
Delete the secret folder.
Turn off the recommendation.
Stop taking the phone into bed.
Move the device out of the bedroom.
Tell your spouse.
Tell a mature believer.
Ask for accountability.
Stop calling bondage “privacy.”
Stop treating repeated compromise like an unfortunate personality trait.
Jesus spoke with shocking seriousness about dealing with occasions of sin.
“If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee.”
Matthew 5:29.
Christ is not commanding self-mutilation. His language communicates the radical seriousness with which His disciples should deal with sin.
In modern language:
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
If an app repeatedly becomes the doorway, removing it is not legalism.
It may be wisdom.
If an account continually awakens lust, unfollowing it is not weakness.
It may be obedience.
If scrolling at 1:00 a.m. repeatedly ends in compromise, stop pretending that midnight is spiritually neutral territory for you.
Know your weakness.
And then hear something beautiful.
Paul says:
“πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος· πιστὸς δὲ ὁ Θεός...”
“No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to humanity...”
And then come the words exhausted believers desperately need:
“πιστὸς δὲ ὁ Θεός.”
Pistos de ho Theos.
But God is faithful.
Read that again.
The center of your hope is not:
I am strong.
It is:
God is faithful.
Paul continues that God will provide “τὴν ἔκβασιν” — tēn ekbasin.
The escape.
The way out.
The exit.
Sometimes the escape is spectacular.
Often it looks painfully ordinary.
Close the app.
Put down the phone.
Leave the room.
Call someone.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Go to sleep.
Confess.
Walk away.
Run.
We sometimes ask God for supernatural deliverance while ignoring the ordinary exit door He has already placed three feet away.
And there may be someone reading this whose escape is literally one tap away.
Close it.
Right now.
You do not have to finish watching.
You do not have to click the profile.
You do not have to see where the conversation goes.
You do not have to answer that message.
You do not have to prove how close you can stand to the fire without burning.
Run toward Christ.
Because temptation makes you believe you are about to lose something wonderful by obeying God.
The Gospel tells you that Christ Himself is better.
Better than the fantasy.
Better than the validation.
Better than the secret relationship.
Better than the applause.
Better than the rage.
Better than the body.
Better than the money.
Better than being admired.
Better than being envied.
Better than whatever glowing rectangle has promised to give your soul for thirty seconds before demanding another thirty.
Jesus said:
“What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
Mark 8:36.
Imagine gaining the whole feed...
and starving your soul.
Imagine knowing everybody's life...
but barely knowing Scripture.
Imagine watching thousands of strangers...
while slowly becoming a stranger to prayer.
Imagine feeding your eyes for hours...
while your spirit survives on crumbs.
Maybe the greatest danger is not that technology suddenly turns Christians into atheists.
Maybe for many of us the danger is quieter.
Distracted Christianity.
Prayerless Christianity.
Comparison-soaked Christianity.
Secretly compromised Christianity.
A Christianity that still believes everything correctly but rarely becomes still enough to adore Christ.
You open your Bible...
then reach for your phone.
You begin praying...
then hear the notification.
You worship...
then check who viewed your story.
You say Jesus is enough...
while your nervous system waits for another digital reward.
And Christ remains where He has always been.
Calling.
Not with an algorithm engineered around your attention.
But with grace.
“Come unto me...”
Matthew 11:28.
Come.
Not scroll.
Come.
Not hide.
Come.
Not perform.
Come.
Not pretend.
Come.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs tonight.
Come back.
You have wandered far enough.
You have hidden long enough.
You have promised yourself “last time” enough times.
Bring the whole ugly thing into the light.
Jesus already knows.
Your shame is not shocking Him.
Your browsing history did not surprise heaven.
Your failure did not overturn the Gospel.
But do not confuse His mercy with indifference toward the sin that is eating you alive.
Repentance means turning.
Grace means there is somewhere—and Someone—to turn toward.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Merciful.
Holy.
Alive.
And still rewriting stories.
Peter denied Him.
Grace was not finished.
Paul persecuted His church.
Grace was not finished.
The thief beside Jesus had a ruined past and almost no future left on earth.
Grace was not finished.
And if you belong to Christ, your worst digital moment does not have to become the final sentence of your story either.
That is Gospel Warrior's heartbeat:
The scandal may be secret.
The grace is not.
The Gospel announces publicly that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
So stop giving the algorithm authority it does not possess.
It can recommend.
It cannot reign.
It can predict patterns.
It cannot predestine your next sin.
It can place bait before you.
It cannot force you to bite.
And it certainly cannot forgive you when you do.
Only Christ can do that.
The algorithm knows patterns.
Jesus knows you.
It may know what makes you pause.
Jesus knows why you are hurting.
It may know what you clicked yesterday.
Jesus knows every day you have ever lived.
It may keep resurfacing your appetite.
Jesus can transform your desires.
It can keep feeding your past.
Jesus can rewrite your future.
That is the difference.
So perhaps tonight you need to stop asking only:
“Why does the algorithm keep feeding my temptation?”
And begin asking:
“Jesus, what am I feeding?”
What are you feeding with your eyes?
What are you feeding with your time?
What are you feeding with your imagination?
What are you feeding when nobody else is watching?
And what might happen if you began feeding your soul with Scripture as consistently as you have fed your appetite with scrolling?
Not to earn salvation.
Jesus purchased salvation with His blood.
Not to make God love you.
For those in Christ, His love is not a wage you earn by maintaining a clean screen.
But because you have been loved...
because you have been bought...
because you have been called out of darkness...
you can stop decorating the prison cell.
Walk toward the exit.
ἔκβασις.
There is a way out.
And beyond that exit is not merely better digital hygiene.
There is Christ.
Be honest.
Someone who thinks freedom is impossible may need to discover that another believer has been where they are.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a substitute for giving faithfully, serving your local church, caring for the poor, or obeying Christ.
Send it privately to someone fighting temptation.
Because somewhere tonight...
someone is scrolling.
Someone is hiding.
Someone is one click away from repeating the thing they begged God to forgive yesterday.
Someone thinks their secret has disqualified them from grace.
Someone believes the temptation is stronger than the Savior.
And maybe God will use something as ordinary as your share to place a different message in front of them:
There is a way out.
Not because the algorithm became merciful.
Because God is faithful.
The screen may remember what once held your attention—but the blood of Jesus speaks a better word over everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
The algorithm can keep recommending your old appetite. Jesus Christ can give you a new heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES DEUTERONOMY HAVE A LAW ABOUT A WOMAN GRABBING A MAN’S GENITALS DURING A FIGHT?
paragraphs: WHY DOES DEUTERONOMY HAVE A LAW ABOUT A WOMAN GRABBING A MAN’S GENITALS DURING A FIGHT?

One of the strangest laws in the Bible sounds almost too shocking to preach—but beneath the uncomfortable words of Deuteronomy 25:11–12 is a sobering lesson about human violence, justice, the seriousness of bodily harm, and why sinners desperately need the grace revealed in Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses people underline.
There are Bible verses people frame.
There are Bible verses people memorize when life falls apart.
And then there are verses like this one.

You are reading Deuteronomy, perhaps expecting another command about worship, justice, marriage, property, or Israel’s covenant life, when suddenly Scripture gives you a scene so strangely specific that you almost wonder whether you read it correctly.
Two men are fighting.
One man's wife sees her husband being struck.
She rushes in to rescue him.
Then she reaches for the other man's genitals.
And the Torah says:
“You shall cut off her hand. Your eye shall have no pity.”
Wait.
What?
Why is that in the Bible?
Why would God preserve a law about something this graphic?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question:
What are Christians supposed to do with it?
Don't skip the verse because it embarrasses you.
Don't soften it because it makes you uncomfortable.
And don't turn it into sensational Christian clickbait either.
Because sometimes the passages we are most tempted to avoid are precisely the passages that force us to stop reading Scripture superficially.
The actual Hebrew of Deuteronomy 25:11–12 reads:

כִּי־יִנָּצוּ אֲנָשִׁים יַחְדָּו אִישׁ וְאָחִיו וְקָרְבָה אֵשֶׁת הָאֶחָד לְהַצִּיל אֶת־אִישָׁהּ מִיַּד מַכֵּהוּ וְשָׁלְחָה יָדָהּ וְהֶחֱזִיקָה בִּמְבֻשָׁיו׃ וְקַצֹּתָה אֶת־כַּפָּהּ לֹא תָחוֹס עֵינֶךָ׃
Ki-yinnatsu anashim yachdav… v’shalchah yadah v’hechezikah bimvushav. V’katsotah et-kappah; lo tachos einekha.
In straightforward English:

When men are fighting and the wife of one approaches to rescue her husband from the man striking him, reaches out her hand and takes hold of his private parts, the text commands that her hand be cut off and that no pity be shown.
Yes.
The passage really does say that.

The unusual Hebrew word מְבֻשָׁיו — mevushav is associated with “shame” and functions here as a euphemistic expression for the man's private parts. The Torah is not describing an innocent touch or accidental contact. It describes deliberately seizing a man's genital area during violent conflict.
And the word כַּפָּהּ — kappah refers to her palm or hand.
So we should resist an easy escape hatch.
The difficult language is actually there.
But understanding a verse requires more than proving that its words exist.
It requires context.
And this is where the passage becomes far more interesting than the shock value usually attached to it.
The woman's motive is explicitly given.
She is attempting “to rescue her husband.”
That matters.
The Torah does not introduce her as a sexually immoral woman prowling around looking for a man to violate. She enters an existing physical confrontation because her husband is being attacked.
Yet her desire to protect him does not automatically justify every method she might use.
That principle reaches far beyond this ancient fight.
Because human beings have an extraordinary ability to excuse sinful or destructive behavior whenever we believe our motives are good.
“I only lied because I wanted to protect my family.”
“I destroyed that person's reputation because they hurt someone I love.”
“I became cruel because I was defending myself.”
“I humiliated them because they deserved it.”
“I crossed the boundary because I was trying to help.”
Good intentions do not magically transform every action into righteousness.
But there is another dimension to this strange law that modern readers can easily miss.
