Maybe there are chapters of your childhood you rarely discuss because every time you revisit them, something inside you becomes that frightened child again.
Or maybe your scandal was not inherited.
Maybe you created it yourself.
The affair.
The addiction.
The prison sentence.
The abortion.
The betrayal.
The secret browser history.
The drunken years.
The divorce.
The lies.
The years you wandered away from God while everybody thought you were doing fine.
And somewhere inside you is a question you have never quite been able to silence:
Can God still do something holy with a life connected to something this broken?
Keep reading.
Because Jephthah’s story is not going where his brothers thought it was going.
His father, Gilead, had other sons by his wife. Those sons grew up.
And apparently, so did their contempt.
Judges 11:2 says:
וַיְגָרְשׁוּ אֶת־יִפְתָּח
Vayegareshu et-Yiftach.
“They drove Jephthah out.”
The Hebrew verb carries the force of expelling or driving someone away.
Imagine the moment.
This was not Jephthah leaving home because he wanted adventure.
His own brothers forced him out.
And then they gave him the reason:
“You shall not inherit in our father’s house; for you are the son of another woman.”
Think about how cruel that sentence was.
Jephthah had not chosen his mother.
He had not chosen the circumstances surrounding his birth.
He had not created the situation into which he was born.
Yet other people turned something outside his control into a verdict against his worth.
“You don't belong here.”
“You don't get what we get.”
“You are different.”
“You are the son of another woman.”
Some wounds do not bleed where anyone can see them.
They bleed in identity.
Maybe nobody literally expelled you from your home.
But perhaps you have known another kind of exile.
The family that made you feel like the disappointment.
The church people who remembered your worst season longer than they remembered the grace of God.
The relatives who compared you with the successful sibling.
The marriage where you slowly became invisible.
The friendship circle where everyone was welcome until your life became inconvenient.
The people who knew what you had done and decided that your worst chapter should become your permanent name.
Rejection has a strange way of continuing to speak long after the people who rejected us have left the room.
You can be forty years old and still hear something said when you were fourteen.
You can become successful and still secretly be trying to prove yourself to people who stopped watching years ago.
You can lead.
Preach.
Serve.
Build.
Achieve.
Smile.
Post Scriptures.
Encourage everybody else.
And still carry one hidden sentence:
“Maybe they were right about me.”
Jephthah ran.
Scripture says he fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob.
The rejected son became an exile.
Then something unexpected happened.
Other marginalized men began gathering around him.
The discarded man became a leader among discarded men.
The one who had been pushed outside began developing strength outside the place that had rejected him.
And then history turned.
The Ammonites went to war against Israel.
Suddenly Gilead had a problem.
A serious one.
And the elders needed a warrior.
Guess whose name came back into the conversation?
Jephthah.
The man who had once been inconvenient suddenly became necessary.
The rejected brother became the sought-after warrior.
The people of Gilead traveled to Tob and said:
“Come, and be our captain, that we may fight with the children of Ammon.”
You can almost feel the old wound opening.
Jephthah answered them:
“Did not ye hate me, and expel me out of my father's house? and why are ye come unto me now when ye are in distress?”
That question has centuries inside it.
Why are you coming to me now?
Where were you when I was being thrown away?
Where were you when I needed someone to defend me?
Why is my value suddenly visible because you need what I carry?
Somebody reading this understands that question.
People can overlook you until your gift becomes useful.
They can ignore your struggle and celebrate your success.
They can disappear during your wilderness and return when they see fruit.
But here is where we must be careful.
Because the Gospel is not a motivational slogan telling rejected people, “One day everyone will regret how they treated you.”
Jesus offers something infinitely deeper than revenge disguised as success.
The goal of redemption is not to become so powerful that the people who hurt you finally envy you.
The goal is Christ.
Freedom.
Forgiveness.
Holiness.
A new identity.
A heart no longer controlled by the people who wounded it.
Jephthah eventually became Gilead's leader, and Judges tells us that “the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah” before the battle.
God used the man others rejected.
But this is exactly where Jephthah's story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Judges does not give us a polished hero.
It gives us a complicated man.
A courageous man.
A rejected man.
A man used in Israel's deliverance.
And a man capable of making a horrifyingly reckless vow.

Before battle, Jephthah vowed that if God delivered the Ammonites into his hands, whatever came from the doors of his house to meet him upon his return would belong to the LORD, and he spoke of offering it as a burnt offering.
God gave Israel victory.
Then Jephthah returned home.
And the door opened.
His daughter came out.
His only child.
With tambourines.
With dancing.
She was celebrating her father's victory.
And suddenly the victorious warrior tore his clothes.
This is one of the darkest moments in Judges.

Interpreters have long debated whether Judges 11:39 describes Jephthah literally sacrificing his daughter or consigning her to lifelong dedication and virginity. The text says he “did with her according to his vow,” and many interpreters understand this as an actual human sacrifice; others have argued for perpetual dedication. What should never be confused, however, is God's revealed will: the Law explicitly condemned human sacrifice.
God did not need Jephthah to bargain for victory.
The Spirit of the LORD had already come upon him before the vow.
That should terrify us in a spiritually healthy way.
Because you can be gifted and still wounded.
You can experience God's mercy and still need transformation.
You can know biblical language and still make terrible decisions.
You can survive rejection without allowing Christ to heal what rejection planted inside you.
Jephthah's tragedy warns us not merely about reckless vows.
It warns us about what can happen when broken people gain power without surrendering every chamber of the heart to God.
Pain does not automatically produce wisdom.
Sometimes pain produces compassion.
Sometimes it produces pride.
Sometimes vigilance.
Sometimes rage.
Sometimes ambition.
Sometimes an obsessive need to prove ourselves.
That is why we need more than a changed situation.
We need a changed heart.
And this is where Jephthah's story begins pointing beyond Jephthah.
Because centuries later another rejected Man would appear.
Jesus Christ.
He too was despised and rejected.
He too knew what it was for His own not to receive Him.
He was mocked.
Accused.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Cast outside.
Crucified.
But there is an immeasurable difference.
Jesus was not another flawed deliverer in the cycle of Judges.
He was the sinless Son of God.
Jephthah was a deliverer who desperately needed redemption himself.
Jesus is the Redeemer.
Jephthah's story contains human brokenness tangled with divine mercy.
Jesus entered human brokenness to conquer sin and death.
And at the cross, Christ did something no motivational speech can accomplish.
He dealt with our guilt.
Not merely our embarrassment.
Not merely our rejection.
Not merely our trauma.
Our sin.
Because the deepest problem in our lives is not only what people have done to us.
It is also what sin has done within us—and what we ourselves have done before a holy God.
This is why the Gospel is better than self-esteem.
Jesus does not stand over broken sinners shouting, “Believe in yourself.”
He calls:
Repent.
Come to Me.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Me.
Be made new.
Maybe people gave you a name.
Dirty.
Illegitimate.
Failure.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Hypocrite.
Unwanted.
Ruined.
Too far gone.
But when a sinner comes to Christ in repentance and faith, shame does not get the final word.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
Read those words slowly.
In Christ Jesus.
That is where identity changes.
Not because your history disappears.
Not because consequences magically vanish.
Not because everything people said about your past was false.
But because the cross declares that your sin does not possess greater authority than the blood of Christ.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewrites what the scandal gets to mean.
Peter really denied Jesus.
Paul really persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman's complicated history was real.
The thief on the cross really was condemned.
The people in Corinth really had histories of sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, theft, greed, drunkenness and more.
Then Paul wrote:
“And such were some of you...”
Were.
What a word.
The Gospel gives sinners a were.
That was me.
That was my bondage.
That was my rebellion.
That was my identity apart from Christ.
That was where sin took me.
But Jesus Christ met me there.
Washed me.
Forgave me.
Claimed me.
And began making me new.
Maybe that is why you needed Jephthah's story today.
Not so you could pretend he was a flawless hero.
He wasn't.
Not so you could turn his painful life into a prosperity slogan.
You shouldn't.
But so you could see something Scripture repeatedly refuses to let us forget:
God is not intimidated by ugly beginnings.
And your painful beginning does not give you permission to remain spiritually broken forever.
Bring it to Christ.
The father wound.
The mother wound.
The rejection.
The humiliation.
The secret resentment.
The craving to prove yourself.
The memory that still makes your chest tighten.
The person you have supposedly forgiven but still rehearse imaginary arguments with at night.
Bring the whole thing.
Jesus did not die so you could decorate your chains with Christian language.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile us to God.
To transform us.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life auditioning for people who already rejected you.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, you have already been invited somewhere infinitely greater.
To the Father's table.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer:
“What did they call me?”
The question is:
“Who is Jesus Christ calling me to become?”
Pray.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is commanded.
Seek wise Christian help where wounds run deep.
You do not have to publish the details.
God knows them.
Somebody reading beneath this article may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Not because Jephthah's story is comfortable.
Because someday rejection may whisper your old name again, and you may need to remember that the people who rejected you do not possess the authority to define your standing before God.
Not as an algorithm trick.
As ministry.
Somewhere in your circle may be a person smiling publicly while privately wondering whether God could possibly want someone with their history.
Let the Gospel find them through your share.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for giving to your local church, obeying Christ, serving others, or living generously.
If these resources strengthen you, help us place them in front of someone else.
Share.
Save what you need to revisit.
Follow so you can keep growing with us.
Not because clicking a button glorifies God automatically.
But because when our choices are made in faith, love, generosity, truth, and a genuine desire to help others encounter Christ, even ordinary tools can become instruments of Gospel ministry.
Jephthah entered Scripture carrying a scandal he did not choose.
He became a mighty warrior.
He experienced God's empowering presence.
Yet his story also became a warning that outward victory cannot replace inward surrender.
That is why we need someone greater than Jephthah.
We need Jesus.
Maybe your story started in scandal.
Maybe parts of it became scandal because of your own choices.
Maybe people drove you away.
Maybe you drove yourself into places you never imagined going.
But if you can still hear the Gospel, there is still an invitation before you.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Jesus Christ still receives sinners.
Grace is still greater than shame.
The cross is still sufficient.
The tomb is still empty.
And Christ is still making people new.
Your past may explain some of your wounds—but only Jesus should be allowed to write the final sentence over your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID PAUL SAY SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE BODY”?
paragraphs:
WHY DID PAUL SAY SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE BODY”?
Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 6 is far more disturbing—and far more hopeful—than “Christians shouldn’t have sex outside marriage.” He was exposing what happens when a body that belongs to Christ is carried into an intimacy it was never created to treat as meaningless.
There are sins people confess quickly.
And then there are sins they rename.
A temper becomes “just how I am.”
Greed becomes “ambition.”
Pornography becomes “stress relief.”
Sex without covenant becomes “just two consenting adults.”
And somewhere along the way, something God designed to communicate profound bodily union gets reduced to recreation.
No promises.
No permanence.
No covenant.
No consequences.
Just bodies.
At least, that is what we tell ourselves.
But then the apostle Paul says something so startling that, nearly two thousand years later, it can still stop a reader cold:
“Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, ‘The two will become one flesh.’”
—1 Corinthians 6:16
Read that again.
Paul does not say merely that prostitution is immoral.
He reaches all the way back to Genesis.
Back before Corinth.
Back before prostitution.
Back before sexual brokenness entered the human story.
Back to Eden.
“For the two,” Paul says, “will become one flesh.”
Why?
Why would Paul take words associated with the union of man and woman in Genesis and apply them to a man having sex with a prostitute?
Does sex automatically make two people married?
Does “one flesh” mean every sexual partner becomes your spouse?
Does this teach that people mysteriously exchange fragments of their souls?
And if someone has already crossed sexual boundaries—once, repeatedly, willingly, desperately, secretly—are they permanently attached to everyone with whom they have slept?
The answer matters.
Because bad theology can make wounded people believe Jesus can forgive their sin but somehow cannot untangle their past.
And Paul’s message is actually much more Christ-centered than that.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:16 is striking:
“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν;”
Ē ouk oidate hoti ho kollōmenos tē pornē hen sōma estin?
“Or do you not know that the one joining himself to the prostitute is one body [with her]?”
The word that deserves attention is κολλώμενος—kollōmenos—from κολλάω, kollaō.
It carries the idea of joining, attaching, or clinging.
Then Paul explains his statement by quoting Genesis:
“Ἔσονται γάρ, φησίν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.”
“For, He says, the two will become one flesh.”
Paul is drawing from the creation language of Genesis 2:24.
The Hebrew text says:
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
vehayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
This is where we need to be careful.
Paul is not saying that visiting a prostitute creates a biblical marriage covenant.

If intercourse itself automatically constituted marriage, Paul’s argument would become strangely self-defeating: he would effectively be telling the Corinthians that the sexually immoral man had become married through the very act Paul commands him to flee.
That is not his point.
Nor does Scripture teach the popular modern idea that sexual partners literally exchange pieces of their souls that must later be retrieved through special rituals.
The Bible takes sexual union seriously enough without our needing to invent mystical mechanisms Scripture itself does not teach.
Paul’s argument is more concrete.
More embodied.
And, in some ways, more confronting.
Sex can occur outside covenant.
But it cannot therefore be made meaningless.
That distinction matters.
The sexual act participates in the “one flesh” reality for which human sexuality was created, even when human beings tear the act away from the covenantal faithfulness that should surround it.
That is part of the tragedy of sexual immorality.
We attempt to make the body say something while insisting it means nothing.
The body joins.
The heart says, “Don’t get attached.”
The body gives itself.
The mind says, “This is casual.”
The body enters extraordinary vulnerability.
The culture says, “It’s only sex.”
Paul refuses the word “only.”
Because Christianity does not teach that your body is an accessory hanging beneath your brain.
You are not a soul temporarily driving around inside disposable flesh.
Your body matters to God.
And this becomes unmistakable when you read Paul’s entire argument instead of isolating one provocative verse.
Just before speaking about the prostitute, Paul says:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
—1 Corinthians 6:15
That changes everything.
Paul’s deepest question is not simply:
“How could you sleep with that person?”
It is:
“Have you forgotten whose you are?”
The scandal is not merely that a Christian has violated a sexual rule.
The scandal is that someone united to Christ is taking a body belonging to Christ and using it as though Jesus had no claim over it.
Paul continues:
“Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!”
Then comes verse 16.
Then another astonishing statement:
“But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.”
—1 Corinthians 6:17
Notice Paul’s movement.
Joined to a prostitute: one body.
Joined to the Lord: one spirit.
Then:
“Flee from sexual immorality.”
Then:
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you.”
Then:
“You are not your own.”
Then:
“You were bought with a price.”
Then, finally:
“So glorify God in your body.”
This passage is not ultimately about how dirty sexually broken people are.
It is about how sacred redeemed people have become.
That is the part shame rarely tells you.
Shame says:
“Look what you did with your body.”
The Gospel says:
“Look what Christ paid to redeem you—body and soul.”
Shame whispers:
“You gave yourself away.”
Jesus says:
“You were bought with a price.”
Shame says:
“You are permanently contaminated.”
Paul says:
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.”
Do you see the reversal?
Paul does not lower the seriousness of sexual sin.
He raises the dignity of the sinner whom Christ has redeemed.
And maybe that is why this passage hurts.
Because some people reading this remember a hotel room.
A boyfriend.
A girlfriend.
A stranger.
An affair.
A screen.
A secret relationship.
A night you wish you could erase.
Maybe you were looking for affection.
Maybe you wanted validation.
Maybe loneliness became louder than conviction.
Maybe you knew exactly what Scripture said and did it anyway.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody thinks you are spiritually strong.
You still worship.
Still quote Scripture.
Still say, “God is good.”
But there is a room inside your memory you rarely open because you are afraid of what you will find there.
Listen carefully.
Paul does not write 1 Corinthians 6 so that forgiven people will spend the rest of their lives psychologically crawling back into that room.
He writes because grace teaches us that our bodies belong somewhere better.
And Paul knew exactly what kind of church he was addressing.
Immediately before this discussion, he lists patterns of sin that included sexual immorality, adultery, greed, drunkenness and other forms of rebellion.
Then come three of the most beautiful words in the New Testament:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because the Corinthians had immaculate histories.
Not because their memories disappeared.
Not because their consequences necessarily vanished.
But because Christ had intervened.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
This is why Christianity can tell the truth about sexual sin without surrendering people to sexual shame.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin was harmless.
He saves us precisely because it was not.
At the cross, forgiveness is not God shrugging His shoulders at what destroyed us.
The cross is God taking sin so seriously that redemption cost the blood of His Son.
And taking sinners so lovingly that He willingly paid it.
Maybe you have heard people say, “Your body count defines your value.”
It does not.
Maybe you have heard the opposite extreme: “Your sexual choices do not matter at all.”
That is not biblical either.
The Gospel destroys both lies.
Your sin matters.
And your sin is not greater than Christ.
Your history matters.
And your history does not possess greater authority over your identity than the risen Jesus.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
What you do with your body matters.
But for the person who turns to Christ, yesterday does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why “flee sexual immorality” is not merely a frightened religious command.
It is the language of rescue.
Run because you were purchased.
Run because you belong to Christ.
Run because your body is not cheap.
Run because grace has given you something worth protecting.
Run because freedom sometimes looks less like standing heroically in front of temptation and more like getting out of the room.
Joseph ran.
Sometimes holiness has feet.
Delete the conversation.
Leave the bedroom.
Cancel the meeting.
End the affair.
Install the accountability.
Tell the truth.
Confess.
Ask for help.
Stop calling bondage “complicated.”
Stop negotiating with what Christ told you to flee.
Not because Jesus will love you more if you become clean enough.
But because in Christ you have been loved at a price so staggering that continuing to hand yourself back to slavery no longer makes sense.
And if you fall?
Do not turn grace into permission.
But do not turn failure into a throne either.
Repent.
Come home.
Again.
Confess your sin.
Bring it into the light.
Receive the forgiveness Scripture promises to those who come to God through Christ.
And begin walking differently.
Some readers need to hear something else too.
If your sexual history includes something done to you without your consent, another person's sin against you is not the same as your voluntary sexual sin.
Do not carry another person's guilt as though it belonged to you.
Christ's compassion is not confused about the difference.
He sees truth completely.
He sees wounds nobody else understands.
And He is not disgusted by the wounded who come to Him.
For everyone else who knows, painfully, “I chose it”...
Grace is still grace.
Repentance does not require pretending you were innocent.
It requires admitting you were not—and discovering that Jesus saves guilty people.
That is the miracle.
The Christian testimony is not:
“I never became dirty.”
It is:
“I could not wash myself, so Christ washed me.”
“And such were some of you.”
Maybe those words need to become personal today.
Such was I.
Addicted.
Such was I.
Unfaithful.
Such was I.
Secretly consuming pornography while pretending everything was fine.
Such was I.
Looking for intimacy in people who could never heal what was aching inside me.
Such was I.
Running from God while using His gifts against His purposes.
Such was I.
But Jesus Christ did not meet me merely to improve my behavior.
He came to make me His.
That is the center of Paul's argument.
You are not your own.
For the modern ear, that can initially sound restrictive.
Until you realize who owns you.
Not pornography.
Not lust.
Not the person who abandoned you.
Not the person who used you.
Not your ex.
Not your appetite.
Not your hormones.
Not your worst night.
Not your sexual history.
Not the accusation repeating inside your head.
If you belong to Christ, you belong to the One who was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
“You were bought with a price.”
The price was not silver.
Not religious achievement.
Not years of punishment.
Christ gave Himself.
So Paul reaches his conclusion:
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
Not someday when you have a cleaner history.
Now.
With this body.
The body with scars.
The body carrying memories.
The body that has sinned.
The body that has been sinned against.
The body Christ claims.
The body in which the Holy Spirit dwells.
Glorify God with it.
Your sexuality can become worship.
Your boundaries can become worship.
Your faithfulness in marriage can become worship.
Your chastity while single can become worship.
Your decision to turn away from pornography tonight can become worship.
Your confession can become worship.
Your repentance can become worship.
Your restored obedience can become worship.
And perhaps glorifying God with what you have also means refusing to keep life-giving truth trapped on your own screen.
If this exposed a hidden battle, comment, “Jesus, lead me into holiness.”
If shame has kept you hiding, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
If you are fighting sexual temptation and need believers to pray with you, comment, “Pray for me.”
Somebody may need proof tonight that Christians still struggle.
And somebody else may desperately need proof that Christ still restores.
We never want to imply that giving money earns God's favor or proves someone's salvation. The Gospel is a gift of grace.
But generosity can be an act of worship when it flows from a heart that wants God's truth to reach others.
Not because clicking “Share” makes you more righteous.
Not because God needs an algorithm.
But because somewhere behind another glowing screen may be a man convinced his sexual past has disqualified him forever.
A woman certain she can never become clean again.
A husband hiding an addiction.
A teenager being discipled by pornography.
A believer who fell last night and is wondering whether there is any point getting back up.
Let the truth reach them.
Sex was never meaningless.
Sin is never harmless.
Your body matters.
Holiness matters.
Repentance matters.
But the blood of Jesus still speaks a better word over every sinner who comes to Him.
You may have joined your body to what God told you to flee.
You may have tried to turn intimacy into anesthesia.
You may have spent years calling chains freedom.
But if you are hearing the voice of Christ calling you home, your story does not have to end where your shame says it does.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is repentance.
There is restoration.
There is a new way to live.
There is Jesus.
And perhaps the sentence you will remember long after closing this article is this:
Your body may remember where you have been, but in Christ, your past does not get to decide whose you are.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “COME, MY BELOVED, LET US GO OUT”: The Woman in Scripture Who Openly Expressed Romantic Desire
paragraphs: “COME, MY BELOVED, LET US GO OUT”: The Woman in Scripture Who Openly Expressed Romantic Desire

The Bible did not silence her desire. It preserved her words in Scripture—and what she says may completely change the way you think about love, marriage, intimacy, shame, and the God who created the human heart.
There is a woman in the Bible who says something so intimate, so confident, and so startlingly human that many Christians can read past it without realizing what just happened.
She does not merely wait to be admired.
She speaks.
She desires.
She invites.
And the Holy Spirit allowed her words to remain in Scripture.
Listen to the Hebrew:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
Then she continues:
לְכָה דוֹדִי נֵצֵא הַשָּׂדֶה
Lekhah dodi, netze hasadeh.
“Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field.”
And then comes the line many people were never prepared to hear a woman in Scripture say:
שָׁם אֶתֵּן אֶת־דֹּדַי לָךְ
Sham etten et-dodai lakh.
“There I will give my love to you.”
Song of Songs 7:11–13.
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because whatever else we do with this passage, we should not make it less human than God allowed it to be.
This is not pornography.
It is not vulgarity.
It is not a woman being shamed for having affection.
It is biblical poetry celebrating love.
And the woman is not voiceless inside it.
She knows she is desired.
She desires in return.
She speaks openly to the man she loves.
“Come, my beloved…”

There is something almost shocking about that when you have spent years around versions of Christianity that sometimes treated every discussion of romantic desire as though holiness required pretending human beings had no bodies.
Some people were taught to fear desire more than they were taught to understand it.
Some women learned that modesty meant becoming emotionally invisible.
Some men learned that attraction itself was dirty rather than something requiring holiness, wisdom, self-control, and covenant faithfulness.

Some young Christians became terrified by normal feelings because nobody taught them the difference between temptation and sin, between desire and exploitation, between covenant intimacy and lust that consumes another person.
So they hid.
They prayed desperately for God to remove feelings He never said were inherently sinful.
They carried shame into marriage.
And some discovered something painful.
A wedding ceremony can change your marital status overnight.
It cannot automatically heal years of shame.
Then Song of Songs opens its mouth.
And suddenly there is fragrance.
Vineyards.
Pomegranates.
Longing.
Beauty.
Mutual affection.
A woman speaking.
A man responding.
Two people delighting in one another without Scripture apologizing for their humanity.
That matters.
The Hebrew word in Song of Songs 7:11 translated “desire” is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.
Her beloved’s desire is directed toward her.
Then she answers that desire not with embarrassed silence but with invitation:
“Come, my beloved…”
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not teach that every desire is holy.
It does not authorize adultery.
It does not erase sexual boundaries.
It does not make lust harmless.
And it certainly does not teach that another human being exists for our consumption.
The wider witness of Scripture refuses all of those conclusions.

Jesus takes sexual sin seriously enough to address lust at the level of the heart (Matthew 5:27–30). Paul commands believers to flee sexual immorality and reminds Christians that their bodies belong to God (1 Corinthians 6:18–20). Hebrews tells believers to honor marriage and keep the marriage bed undefiled (Hebrews 13:4).
Christian holiness is not permission to use another person.
But neither is holiness hatred of the body.
That distinction is enormous.
Because the God who says “flee sexual immorality” is also the God whose Scriptures contain the Song of Songs.
Maybe some of us have spent so much time running from what sexuality can become when corrupted that we have forgotten who created human beings in the first place.
Before there was pornography, there was Eden.
Before there was adultery, there was covenant.
Before there was sexual exploitation, there was the declaration:
“male and female he created them.”
Genesis 1:27.
And after creating humanity embodied as male and female, God looked upon what He had made and called His creation “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
Sin did not invent the human body.
God did.
Sin corrupts.
God creates.
That difference changes everything.
Song of Songs does not invite us to worship desire.
It teaches us that desire does not have to become a god in order to be acknowledged as human.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe your story with desire is not beautiful.
Maybe yours became secret.
Maybe somebody used you.
Maybe you used somebody.
Maybe pornography rewired the way you learned to look at people.
Maybe an affair destroyed trust.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once swore you never would.
Maybe you gave your body hoping somebody would finally give you love.
Maybe you confused being wanted with being valued.
Maybe you stayed in a relationship because loneliness frightened you more than compromise.
Maybe you have been married for years, yet shame still follows you into the bedroom.
Maybe nobody violated you.
Nobody abandoned you.
Nothing dramatic happened.
You simply learned somewhere along the way that being deeply human made God disappointed in you.
And so you became very good at hiding.
Church clothes.
Bible open.
Worship music playing.
Hands raised.
Search history deleted.
Messages erased.
Memories buried.
Questions unanswered.
Smiling when someone asks how you are doing.
But God sees the whole person standing behind the Christian vocabulary.
And this is where Song of Songs cannot save you.
Romance cannot save you.
Marriage cannot save you.
Sex cannot save you.
Being desired cannot save you.
Being married to the person of your dreams cannot save you.
There is a deeper hunger underneath every human hunger.
And eventually every created thing collapses beneath the weight of being asked to become a Savior.
That is where Jesus Christ enters the story.
Not as the destroyer of humanity.
As its Redeemer.
The Christian Gospel is not the announcement that respectable people have finally learned to suppress themselves well enough for God to tolerate them.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never cleanse themselves have been offered reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Christ came into our scandal.
Our lust.
Our pride.
Our adultery.
Our secret fantasies.
Our broken marriages.
Our loneliness.
Our self-righteousness.
Our wounds.
Our shame.
Our attempts to find in another body what only God can ultimately give.
And He did something scandalous with scandal.
He carried sin to a cross.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
2 Corinthians 5:21.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending you never sinned.
Not renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not drowning in shame as though Christ's blood were insufficient.
Repentance and grace meet at the cross.
Jesus does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how much it matters.
But the cross also declares that your sin does not have to write the final sentence of your life.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needed tonight.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your title.
The affair does not have to become your identity.
The addiction does not have to become your name.
The abuse committed against you does not determine your worth.
The thing you did does not become righteous merely because God loves you—but neither is the repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ because the thing was terrible.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is transformation.
There is a new way to live.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 8:1.
Do not turn that verse into permission to remain chained.
It is an invitation to come out of the prison.
Grace does not merely whisper, “You are forgiven.”
Grace begins teaching the forgiven person how to walk free.

And suddenly the woman saying, “Come, my beloved,” can teach us something deeper—not because Song of Songs should be flattened into an allegory in which every romantic sentence secretly means Jesus, but because its celebration of rightly ordered human love reminds us that redemption does not make us less human.
Christ restores us toward what holiness was always meant to be.
Not numbness.
Not shame.
Not exploitation.
Not uncontrolled appetite.
Wholeness.
A heart learning to love without possessing.
Eyes learning to see people rather than objects.
A body surrendered to God rather than ruled by appetite.
A marriage where tenderness does not need to apologize.
A single life where holiness does not mean worthlessness.
A wounded life where healing is possible.
A fallen life where repentance can become the doorway to restoration.
And there is another beautiful detail in the woman's words.
She says:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי
Ani ledodi.
“I am my beloved’s.”
There is belonging here.
Not consumption.
Not anonymous bodies.
Not scrolling.
Not swiping through human beings as though souls were products.
Belonging.
And that should confront our generation.
We have never had greater technological access to bodies while remaining capable of extraordinary loneliness.
We can see almost anything and know almost nobody.
We can collect attention and still ache to be known.
We can receive hundreds of reactions and wonder whether one person would remain after seeing everything.
Because lust says:
“What can I take from you?”
Love asks:
“How can I seek your good?”
Lust reduces.
Love recognizes.
Lust consumes the image.
Covenant remains when the image changes.
And the Gospel goes deeper still.
Jesus knew what was inside us before we cleaned anything up.
He knew the browser history.
The memory.
The betrayal.
The craving.
The hypocrisy.
The secret.
And He still called sinners to repentance and offered mercy.
That does not make sin small.
It makes grace astonishing.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to punish themselves for something Jesus is calling them to bring into the light.
You cannot repent of the person you keep pretending does not exist.
Stop hiding.
Bring the truth to Christ.
If necessary, confess to the person you have sinned against and seek wise pastoral or professional help where appropriate.
Install the boundaries.
End the affair.
Delete the secret account.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Tell someone trustworthy.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is safe and appropriate.
And where another person's sin wounded you, hear this carefully:
Their sin does not make you dirty.
You are not required to call evil good in order to forgive.
You are not required to return yourself to an unsafe person to prove you love Jesus.
Healing can be slow.
But Christ is not frightened by wounds.
Look at the risen Jesus.
He conquered death, yet His resurrected body still bore scars.
Scars were not the evidence that death won.
They became witnesses that death had lost.
Maybe yours can become witnesses too.
Not because everything that happened was good.
It wasn't.
But because Jesus Christ can write redemption into places sin intended to destroy.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because repentance magically repairs every relationship.
Not because Christians never struggle again.
But because the Gospel means your story no longer has to end where sin left you.
Be human.
Be honest.
You do not owe strangers the details of your story.
Sometimes those three words are enough.
The married couple silently struggling with intimacy.
The teenager drowning in shame.
The believer secretly battling pornography.
The woman who thinks her past destroyed her worth.
The man who has never told anyone what he is fighting.
The Christian who confused holiness with hating their own humanity.
The person who does not even believe in Jesus yet but desperately needs to discover that Christianity is not about polishing sinners until they look respectable.
It is about a Savior who raises the dead.
Better yet, send this privately when privacy is kinder.
Save it too.
Because shame has a strange way of returning after conviction fades, and you may need these words again:
Desire is not your god.
Shame is not your master.
Sin is not your identity.
Jesus Christ is still calling people out of darkness.
And grace is still stronger than the chapter you wish you could erase.
If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, you can also help this ministry continue.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.
Scripture says that giving should come from a willing heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
A Facebook share can travel farther than you imagine.
The discount is a thank-you.
It is not the reason to give.
Jesus is not for sale.
Grace is not merchandise.
Support simply helps the work continue.
Follow Jesus.
Open your Bible.
Pray when nobody is watching.
Repent quickly.
Forgive deeply.
Love faithfully.
Fight secret sin.
Protect the vulnerable.
Honor your marriage.
Honor your singleness.
Refuse to turn another human being into an object.
And when you fall, do not build a house in the mud.
Run back to Christ.
Because thousands of years ago, Scripture preserved the voice of a woman who was not ashamed to say:
“Come, my beloved…”
Her desire was not erased from the Bible.
It was written into it.
And perhaps the deeper shock for some of us is not that Scripture can speak honestly about desire.
Perhaps the shock is discovering that God has never needed our pretending.
He wants truth in the inward being.
He wants the hidden person.
The wounded person.
The tempted person.
The ashamed person.
The person behind the Sunday face.
He calls sinners to repentance not so He can humiliate them, but because Christ came to save sinners.
So share this if somebody needs freedom.
But above everything else—
come to Christ.
Because one day every romance ends at the edge of eternity.
Every beautiful body grows old.
Every human embrace eventually has to loosen.
Every earthly beloved is mortal.
And when everything temporary falls from your hands, only One can carry you through death itself.
His name is Jesus.
The chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read may become the very page where someone finally sees what the grace of Jesus Christ can do.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PRISONER PAUL REFUSED TO RUN AWAY FROM
paragraphs:
THE PRISONER PAUL REFUSED TO RUN AWAY FROM
The prison doors were open. The chains were gone. Paul could finally escape. But somewhere in the darkness, a man was about to die—and suddenly Paul understood that his freedom was not the greatest miracle God was working that night.
There are moments in Scripture that become almost too familiar.
We know the earthquake.
We know the prison doors opened.
We know Paul and Silas sang at midnight.
We know the jailer eventually asked the question that has echoed across centuries:
“What must I do to be saved?”
But there is something buried in this story that is easy to rush past.
Something almost frightening when you really see it.
Paul had every reason to leave.
And he stayed.
Not because the door was locked.
The door was open.
Not because the chains still held him.
The chains were loose.
Not because the authorities had suddenly treated him fairly.
They had not.
Paul and Silas had been seized, dragged before the authorities, beaten with rods, struck repeatedly, thrown into the inner prison, and fastened in stocks.
Then midnight came.
Their backs were wounded.
Their bodies hurt.
Their feet were restrained.
And somewhere between the blood, darkness, humiliation, and pain, two beaten Christians did something the prison probably wasn't prepared to hear.
They worshiped.
Luke writes:
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God…
Acts 16:25
And then Luke adds something beautiful:
“…ἐπηκροῶντο δὲ αὐτῶν οἱ δέσμιοι.”
The prisoners were listening.
That detail matters.
Paul did not know who was listening while he worshiped wounded.
Neither do you.
Someone may be watching how you follow Jesus when the prayer has not yet been answered.
Someone may be listening to your faith while your own heart is hurting.
Someone may eventually believe that Christ is real because they watched you discover that Jesus was still enough when everything else was stripped away.
Then suddenly—
the earth moved.
Luke says:
“ἄφνω δὲ σεισμὸς ἐγένετο μέγας…”
Suddenly there was a great earthquake.
The foundations shook.
The doors opened.
The bonds came loose.
Imagine being Paul.
You were beaten unjustly.
Now the door is open.
You were imprisoned.
Now the chains are gone.
You were trapped.
Now there is a way out.
Most of us would have called that answered prayer.
We would have said, “God opened the door!”
We would have run through it and testified about the miracle later.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because an open door is not always God's permission to walk through it.
Sometimes God opens the door to reveal what matters more to you than your own escape.
The jailer woke.
He saw the doors.
He assumed the prisoners had escaped.
And he drew his sword.
Luke's Greek is painfully direct:
“…ἤμελλεν ἑαυτὸν ἀναιρεῖν…”
He was about to kill himself.
Paul could have remained silent.
Think about that.
This man was part of the prison system holding Paul captive.
Paul was bleeding.
Paul had been humiliated.
Paul had been treated unjustly.
And now the man responsible for guarding the prison was standing in the darkness believing everything was over.
Paul could have run.
Paul could have decided, “His problem is not my problem.”
He could have interpreted the earthquake entirely through the lens of his own suffering.
God opened my prison.
God broke my chains.
God gave me an escape.
But Paul saw a man.
And suddenly the prisoner became concerned about the freedom of his jailer.
“Μηδὲν πράξῃς σεαυτῷ κακόν…”
“Do not harm yourself…”
Then came the words that changed the entire night:
“ἅπαντες γάρ ἐσμεν ἐνθάδε.”
“We are all here.”
Acts 16:28.
We are all here.
Paul stayed.
Silas stayed.
The prisoners were still there.
The door had opened, but Paul had discovered something more important on the other side of his suffering than escape.
A soul.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needs:
Your open door may not be the biggest miracle in the room.
Maybe you have spent months praying, “Lord, get me out.”
Get me out of this season.
Get me out of this pain.
Get me out of this disappointment.
Get me out of this place where nobody understands me.
And sometimes God does open the door.
But what if the Gospel has trained us to ask a deeper question?
Not merely:
“How quickly can I escape?”
But:
“Jesus, is there someone here You still want to reach?”
Paul had been wronged, yet he refused to allow another man's destruction to become payment for his pain.
That is what grace does.
The flesh says, “After what they did to me, they deserve whatever happens.”
Grace remembers:
So did I.
The flesh keeps score.
Grace remembers the cross.
The flesh asks whether someone deserves mercy.
The Gospel reminds us that mercy would cease to be mercy if it were earned.

This does not mean Christians must remain in abusive or dangerous situations. Scripture does not command us to manufacture suffering or refuse legitimate protection. Paul himself later insisted on his rights as a Roman citizen when the magistrates attempted to release him quietly after having beaten and imprisoned him without proper process.
Paul was not addicted to suffering.
He was surrendered to Christ.
There is a difference.
He could defend his rights without surrendering his mercy.
He could demand justice without craving another man's destruction.
That is Christ-shaped strength.
The jailer called for lights.
He rushed inside.
The man who had possessed the keys moments earlier was now trembling before the prisoners.
And then he asked:
“Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
Notice what Paul did not say.
He did not say:
Become religious enough.
Repair yourself first.
Punish yourself for what you have done.
Earn God's attention.
Promise never to fail again.
Paul and Silas answered:
“Πίστευσον ἐπὶ τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν…”
“Believe in the Lord Jesus…”
Acts 16:31.
There is the center of the story.
Not Paul.
Not the earthquake.
Not the singing.
Not the prison.
Jesus.
The earthquake could open a prison.
Only Christ could open a heart.
Broken chains could change the jailer's circumstances.
Only the Gospel could change the jailer.
And this is where Christianity becomes scandalously beautiful.
The Gospel is not God rewarding respectable people for behaving well.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who cannot save themselves can be reconciled to the holy God through Jesus Christ.
Jesus entered our darkness.
Jesus bore sin on the cross.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And forgiveness is offered not because we finally became worthy of Him, but because Christ is sufficient to save those who turn to Him in faith.
Repentance is not polishing yourself so Jesus will accept you.
It is turning from sin and self-rule toward the Savior who alone can rescue you.
Faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is entrusting yourself to the Lord Jesus Christ.
And grace does not leave us unchanged.
Watch what happens next.
Paul and Silas spoke “the word of the Lord” to the jailer and those in his house.
Then something quietly breathtaking happened.
The jailer washed their wounds.
And he and his household were baptized.
Later, food was placed before them.
Do you see the reversal?
The keeper of the prison becomes the washer of wounds.
The man associated with confinement begins serving the men he guarded.
The house that might have awakened to tragedy instead fills with rejoicing.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely improve behavior.
He changes allegiance.
He turns enemies into family.
He turns shame into testimony.
He turns wounded people into worshipers.
He turns those who once participated in pain into people capable of washing wounds.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe you have been reading this thinking about the jailer.
But perhaps you are Paul.
You have been hurt so deeply that you secretly want permission to stop caring.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone humiliated you.
Someone used you.
Someone abandoned you.
Someone wounded you and continued living as though nothing happened.
There is anger underneath your worship.
You love Jesus.
But there is still one name you struggle to place into His hands.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
It does not mean pretending nothing happened.
It does not automatically mean restoring trust, removing boundaries, avoiding justice, or returning to unsafe relationships.
But forgiveness does mean refusing to become the final judge of another human soul.
Paul would not let his wounds decide whether the jailer was worth saving.
Jesus had already taught Paul what undeserved mercy looked like.
Remember who Paul had been.
Before he became the imprisoned missionary singing hymns, Saul had persecuted the church.
He had once been the terrifying man in somebody else's story.
Then Jesus met him.
That changes the way you look at your enemies.
Paul knew what it meant for Christ to interrupt a man's destruction.
So when another man stood on the edge of destruction, Paul shouted into the darkness.
Do not harm yourself.
We are here.
Perhaps one of the greatest evidences that grace has reached your heart is that you begin wanting grace to reach people you once believed deserved only judgment.
That does not make sin less serious.
The cross proves exactly how serious sin is.
Our redemption required the blood of Christ.
But the cross also destroys our illusion that some sinners are beyond the reach of mercy.
The persecutor became an apostle.
The jailer became a brother.
And if Jesus could rewrite their stories, perhaps you should stop assuming He has finished writing yours.
Maybe your prison is not made of stone.
Maybe your prison is shame.
Addiction.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness you disguise as discernment.
A marriage quietly collapsing.
A prayer life that disappeared months ago.
Church attendance without intimacy with Christ.
A smile everyone believes.
A private life you hope nobody discovers.
You know how to say “God is good” while secretly wondering why you feel so empty.
You know the worship songs.
You know the verses.
You know how Christians are supposed to sound.
But somewhere inside you is a person sitting at midnight wondering whether God still wants you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not telling you to become impressive.
It is telling you to come to Christ.
Bring the scandal.
Bring the secret.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the religious performance.
Bring the failure you keep replaying.
Bring the part of your story you would delete if you could.
Jesus already knows.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is no sin so small that you do not need His cross, and no repentant sinner so ruined that Christ's grace is insufficient.
And perhaps the strangest thing will happen.
One day the place where you thought your story ended may become the place from which somebody else hears the Gospel.
Your scars may become evidence that Jesus restores.
Your midnight may teach somebody how to worship.
Your testimony may reach the person standing beside a sword you cannot see.
That is why your story cannot remain only yours.
There are people scrolling tonight who are silently exhausted.
People in your family who would never walk into a church but might read something you shared.
Friends carrying secret shame.
Believers drifting from Jesus.
People smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Seekers wondering whether God could possibly want them.
Even someone who claims not to believe may be closer to asking “What must I do to be saved?” than you realize.
Somebody reading beneath you may need evidence that midnight does not last forever.
Not because every sentence will matter today.
Because there may come a midnight when you need to remember that an open door is not the only evidence God is working.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Send it privately to the person you have been worried about.
Not because paying for something earns God's favor.
It absolutely does not.
The Gospel cannot be purchased, salvation cannot be bought, and giving money does not make anyone more righteous before God.
The goal is not to build an audience that merely admires Christian content.
The goal is disciples.
People who know Scripture.
People who repent.
People who forgive.
People who endure midnight.
People who refuse to make an idol of comfort.
People who love Jesus when the chains remain and still love people when the chains fall.
People willing to shout into somebody else's darkness:
Do not destroy yourself.
There is still hope.
There is still grace.
There is still a Savior.
Not because clicking “share” automatically glorifies God. Scripture never teaches that.
But sharing truth about Christ can be an act done for God's glory when the heart behind it sincerely desires that another person encounter the Gospel.
You may never know who reads it at midnight.
You may never know whose chains are invisible.
You may never know who has already drawn the emotional equivalent of a sword and decided that hope is over.
Paul did not know that when the prison doors opened, the greatest rescue of the night had not happened yet.
His chains were already loose.
But another man was still bound.
And Paul refused to make his freedom more important than that man's soul.
That is the part I cannot forget.
The miracle was not merely that God opened the prison.
The miracle was that grace had changed Paul enough that when the prison opened, he was willing to stay for somebody else.
Maybe that is what Jesus wants to rewrite in us.
Not merely our circumstances.
Us.
Until wounded people become merciful people.
Until forgiven people become forgiving people.
Until rescued people start looking for somebody else to rescue with the Gospel.
Until our first question stops being:
“How do I get out?”
And becomes:
“Jesus, who are You trying to reach while I am here?”
Because someday your chains may fall.
The door may open.
Your midnight may finally break.
And standing somewhere between your pain and your freedom may be one human soul desperately needing to discover why you did not run.
Sometimes the greatest proof that Jesus has set you free is not that you can finally leave the prison—but that you are free enough to stay long enough to help someone else find Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOST DANGEROUS SEDUCTION IN SCRIPTURE ISN’T ALWAYS SEXUAL
paragraphs:
THE MOST DANGEROUS SEDUCTION IN SCRIPTURE ISN’T ALWAYS SEXUAL
Some temptations want your body. The most dangerous ones want your worship—and they are patient enough to make you think you are still following Jesus while your heart quietly learns to live without Him.
There is a kind of seduction Christians know how to fear.
The secret message.
The lingering glance.
The relationship nobody is supposed to know about.
The browser history erased before anyone sees it.
The emotional affair disguised as “just talking.”
We know what that temptation looks like.
We preach about it.
We warn our children about it.
We install accountability software because of it.
We pray against it.
And we should.
But what if some of the most dangerous seductions in Scripture never begin in a bedroom?
What if they begin with an idea?
A desire.
An opportunity.
A little compromise.
A hunger to be admired.
A fear of being left behind.
A dream of becoming successful enough that you will never have to depend on anyone again.
What if the enemy does not always need to tempt you into obvious immorality?
What if he can simply persuade you to want something more than you want Christ?
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because you can refuse sexual immorality and still be seduced.
You can remain physically faithful to your spouse while becoming spiritually unfaithful to God.
You can attend church every Sunday and slowly fall in love with applause.
You can quote Scripture while secretly worshiping money.
You can lead worship while craving recognition.
You can preach about surrender while being addicted to control.
You can post verses about trusting God while your entire sense of security rests on your bank account.
You can look like a faithful Christian to everyone around you while something else has quietly become the thing you cannot imagine living without.
And Scripture has a frightening word for that kind of relationship.
Adultery.
James writes:
Moichalides…
“Adulteresses…”
Then comes the question:
Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?
James 4:4 is not primarily describing a secret sexual affair.
He is using the language of marital betrayal to expose spiritual betrayal.
That should stop us.
Because apparently God takes the allegiance of the human heart far more seriously than many of us do.
We tend to measure faithfulness by the scandals we have avoided.
“I never cheated.”
“I never got drunk.”
“I never abandoned my family.”
“I never stole.”
“I never had an affair.”
“I never walked away from church.”
But God sees something deeper.
He sees what owns the imagination when the room becomes quiet.
He sees what loss would make you believe life is no longer worth living.
He sees whose approval controls you.
He sees what you secretly envy.
He sees the compromise you keep renaming “wisdom.”
He sees what you chase when nobody is applauding your Christianity.
He sees the throne.
And He sees what is sitting on it.
That is why the most dangerous seduction may not be the temptation that says, “Abandon God.”
Sometimes it whispers:
“You can have God too.”
Just put this beside Him.
Success.
Money.
Romance.
Influence.
Comfort.
Political power.
Beauty.
Status.
Sex.
Career.
Recognition.
Your children.
Your ministry.
Even your reputation for being godly.
The seduction becomes deadly when a gift begins demanding the devotion that belongs to the Giver.
And this strategy is ancient.
Paul reaches all the way back to Eden when he tells the Corinthian believers:
“ὡς ὁ ὄφις ἐξηπάτησεν Εὕαν…”
“As the serpent deceived Eve…”
The verb translated “deceived” is ἐξαπατάω — exapataō, carrying the idea of thoroughly deceiving or beguiling.
But notice Paul’s fear.
He is not warning the Corinthian church that a literal serpent is about to hand them literal fruit.
He fears that their minds will be corrupted and drawn away from sincere devotion to Christ.
That is terrifying because it reveals the battlefield.
The serpent wants the mind because eventually the feet follow what the mind has learned to desire.
Eden was not merely about fruit.
The fruit was hanging from a deeper question.
Can God really be trusted?
Is His Word really good?
Is His boundary actually protecting you—or restricting you?
Could there be something better on the other side of obedience?
That is how seduction works.
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying:
“Hello. I am here to destroy your marriage, numb your conscience, hollow out your prayer life, damage your children, corrupt your worship, and slowly pull your heart away from Jesus.”
No.
Sin is a salesman.
It shows you the pleasure.
It hides the invoice.
It shows you the fruit.
It hides the exile.
It shows you thirty pieces of silver.
It hides the rope.
It shows you Bathsheba.
It hides Uriah's funeral.
It shows you Egypt's food.
It hides Egypt's chains.
It shows you the applause.
It hides the slavery required to keep receiving it.
And sometimes the bait is not even inherently evil.
That is what makes this so dangerous.
Money is not inherently evil.
Success is not inherently evil.
Marriage is not inherently evil.
Influence is not inherently evil.
A beautiful home is not inherently evil.
Growing a business is not inherently evil.
Wanting to provide for your children is not inherently evil.
Having a platform is not inherently evil.
But good things become cruel masters when they occupy the place reserved for God.
Paul gives us one of Scripture's clearest examples:
“ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία…”
The crucial word is φιλαργυρία — philargyria.
Love of money.
Not money itself.

Paul's warning in 1 Timothy 6:10 is commonly paraphrased in modern English as “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.” The underlying Greek literally speaks of the “love of money” in relation to “all evils,” and translators and commentators differ over the best way to express the construction in English.
But Paul's pastoral warning is unmistakable.
Some people reached for money…
and wandered from the faith.
Read that again.
They did not necessarily wake up one morning and announce:
“I reject Jesus Christ.”
They wandered.
That word should frighten every comfortable Christian.
Because wandering usually happens one step at a time.
One compromise.
One excuse.
One prayer skipped because you're busy.
One Sunday sacrificed because there is money to make.
One lie because the deal is too valuable to lose.
One relationship neglected because ambition feels more urgent.
One conviction silenced because obedience would cost too much.
One more purchase to prove you have finally become somebody.
One more achievement.
One more promotion.
One more zero.
One more follower.
One more compliment.
One more person noticing you.
Until one day you realize something horrifying.
You never officially left Jesus.
But somehow Jesus stopped being enough.
That may be one of the most dangerous places a believer can reach.
Not screaming rebellion.
Quiet replacement.
And perhaps that is why some people reading this feel strangely exposed right now.
Maybe your seduction isn't sexual.
Maybe yours is approval.
You tell yourself you don't care what people think.
But one criticism ruins your entire day.
One unfollow feels personal.
One person overlooking you feels unbearable.
You replay conversations because you desperately need to know whether people were impressed.
Maybe yours is money.
Not because you are wealthy.
Poor people can worship money too.
You think about it constantly.
Fear losing it.
Dream about having more of it.
Measure God's goodness by how much of it you receive.
Maybe yours is romance.
You say Jesus is enough, but deep inside you have made an agreement with yourself:
“I will believe God is good when He finally gives me someone.”
Maybe yours is ministry.
This one hurts.
You started because you loved Jesus.
Then people started listening.
The numbers grew.
The compliments came.
And somewhere between serving Christ and building the platform, you began checking whether people noticed you more often than you checked whether God was pleased.
Now imagine something even more uncomfortable.
What if God took the platform away?
Would you still worship Him?
If the business failed?
Would He still be good?
If nobody applauded?
Would obedience still be worth it?
If the relationship ended?
Would Christ still be enough?
If the prayer you have prayed for ten years remained unanswered?
Would Jesus still deserve your life?
Those questions reveal things success can hide.
Because idols often remain invisible until God touches them.
Then suddenly we discover how tightly we were holding them.
And here is where this article could become nothing more than condemnation.
But that would miss the Gospel completely.
Because Jesus did not come merely to expose adulterous hearts.
He came to rescue them.
Think about Peter.
A man who swore he would never abandon Jesus.
Then pressure arrived.
Fear entered the courtyard.
And Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The rooster crowed.
And Peter broke.
Imagine carrying that memory.
The sound of your own voice saying:
“I don't know Him.”
The face of the Savior you failed.
The unbearable knowledge that when your moment came…
you folded.
Some of you know that feeling.
Maybe not Peter's exact sin.
But you know what it feels like to disappoint yourself spiritually.
You promised God you were finished with it.
Then you returned.
You deleted the number.
Then contacted them again.
You confessed.
Then hid again.
You surrendered.
Then grabbed it back.
You cried during worship Sunday…
and compromised Monday.
And somewhere inside you began wondering whether Jesus eventually gets tired of rewriting the same broken story.
Then comes John 21.
The risen Christ meets Peter.
Not with a sword.
Not with public humiliation.
Not with, “I told you so.”
Jesus asks him a devastatingly tender question:
“Do you love Me?”
There it is again.
Love.
Because beneath so many sins is a war of loves.
What do you love?
Whom do you love?
What has your heart?
Jesus does not merely want behavioral modification.
He wants Peter.
And Peter, the man whose failure could have become the final chapter of his life, becomes a living picture of restoration.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not pretend sin is harmless.
The cross proves the exact opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly went there for sinners.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
So repentance is not crawling back toward a Savior reluctantly tolerating you.
Repentance is turning from the thing that promised life but produced chains and running toward the One who died to make sinners His own.
Maybe your hidden seduction has finally been named.
Approval.
Money.
Lust.
Power.
Comfort.
Bitterness.
Control.
Recognition.
A relationship.
A secret habit.
Your own image.
Maybe nobody else knows.
But Christ does.
And still the invitation stands.
Come.
Not when you have cleaned yourself enough.
Come now.
Bring the idol into the light.
Bring the compromise.
Bring the double life.
Bring the appetite you have been terrified to confess.
Bring the shame.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the thing you thought would satisfy you.
Bring the broken pieces.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the mercy you could never purchase.
And follow Jesus again.
This is why grace is scandalous.
Because the world expects ruined people to remain ruined.
Jesus makes dead people alive.
The world remembers Peter's denial.
Jesus writes Pentecost.
The world remembers the thief's crimes.
Jesus speaks of paradise.
The world sees a sinner.
Jesus can create a testimony.
The world sees the chapter you wish you could erase.
Christ sees a place where grace can write what sin never could.
That does not make consequences imaginary.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Repentance is not pretending damage never happened.
The Gospel is better than denial.
Jesus enters the truth of what we have done and offers forgiveness purchased by His blood, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life under His lordship.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe the sentence you need to remember tonight is this:

The most dangerous seduction is not always the sin that makes you look rebellious. Sometimes it is the thing that makes you feel successful while quietly teaching your heart that Jesus is no longer enough.
So be honest before God.
What has been seducing your heart?
Not somebody else's heart.
Yours.
What do you fear losing more than you fear losing intimacy with Christ?
What do you daydream about becoming?
What compromise have you been defending?
What blessing have you turned into an idol?
What would devastate you so completely that you would question whether God was still worth worshiping?
Don't hide behind Christian vocabulary.
Jesus already knows.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light begins with finally refusing to pretend.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't merely think about them.
Return to it when the thing God exposed starts looking attractive again.

The Gospel cannot be bought. But Christians can glorify God through willing generosity, sharing truth, and supporting ministry when those acts flow from faith, love, wisdom, and a free heart rather than pressure.
Your support helps us keep creating Christ-centered biblical content and sharing resources meant to call people toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, discipleship, and deeper life in Jesus.
And don't keep Gospel Warrior to yourself.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has been drifting.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who has questions about Jesus.
Invite the Christian who needs conviction instead of another motivational slogan.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks grace could never possibly be for someone like them.
Come back to Jesus.
Because someday the money will stay behind.
The followers will stop counting.
The applause will become silent.
Beauty will fade.
Positions will be filled by somebody else.
Platforms will disappear.
Possessions will belong to another generation.
Everything this world used to seduce you will eventually loosen its grip because you will eventually loosen your grip on everything.
And when all the glitter falls away…
Christ will still be Christ.
The question was never merely whether you could resist temptation.
The deeper question was always:
When every rival lover has been exposed, will Jesus still have your heart?
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ONAN WANTED TAMAR’S BODY—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH HER
paragraphs:
ONAN WANTED TAMAR’S BODY—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH HER
He kept going into his brother’s widow while secretly making sure she could never receive what he had been commanded to give her. Genesis 38 is not merely an ancient sexual scandal. It is a terrifying portrait of what happens when someone wants the privilege of intimacy while rejecting the responsibility of covenant—and hidden inside this disturbing family story is a road that eventually leads all the way to Jesus Christ.
There is a sentence in Genesis that becomes more disturbing the longer you sit with it.
Not because Scripture is trying to be graphic.
Not because God delights in exposing sexual scandal.
But because one man found a way to appear obedient while privately arranging things so that obedience would never cost him what he wanted to keep.
His name was Onan.
And Tamar was the woman caught in the consequences.
Read the Hebrew carefully:
"וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוּדָה לְאוֹנָן בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ"
Vayyomer Yehudah le-Onan, bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehaqem zera le-achikha.
Judah tells Onan, in essence:
“Go in to your brother’s wife, perform the duty of a brother-in-law toward her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Genesis 38:8.
The Hebrew expression וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ — vehaqem zera le-achikha means to “raise up offspring for your brother.”
That is crucial.
Er, Tamar’s husband, had died without a child. Judah therefore commanded his surviving son Onan to fulfill the family obligation toward Tamar and his deceased brother.

Later Mosaic legislation would formally describe the related institution in Deuteronomy 25:5–10: when a brother died without a son under the circumstances described there, his surviving brother was to take responsibility for the widow, and the firstborn son would preserve the dead brother’s name in Israel.
Genesis 38 predates the giving of that Mosaic legislation, so we should not carelessly pretend that every later legal detail had already been formally enacted in exactly the same form.
But the underlying purpose in Genesis 38 is unmistakable because the narrator tells us directly.
Onan understood exactly what was expected of him.
And he did not want it.
Here is where the story becomes painfully uncomfortable.
Onan did not simply refuse Tamar.
Had the story merely said, “Onan would not take her,” we would be reading a different story.
Instead:
"וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע"
Vayyeda Onan ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
Genesis 38:9.
There is his motive.
Scripture opens the locked room of his heart.
He knew.
The issue was not ignorance.
It was not confusion.
It was not an accident.
He knew the child would not be counted as his.
And because the benefit would belong to his dead brother’s line rather than ultimately serving his own interests, Onan deliberately prevented Tamar from conceiving.
The Hebrew continues:
"וְהָיָה אִם־בָּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו"
Whenever he went in to his brother’s wife, he deliberately wasted his seed on the ground “so as not to give offspring to his brother.”
Do not rush past those words.
Whenever.
The Hebrew construction describes repeated behavior.
This was not one moment of weakness.
Not one frightened decision.
Not one impulsive failure followed by remorse.
Onan continued taking Tamar sexually while deliberately ensuring that the very purpose for which he had been given responsibility toward her would never be fulfilled.
He wanted access without obligation.
Intimacy without sacrifice.
The woman without the responsibility.
The privilege without the covenantal cost.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that, from the outside, he could appear to be fulfilling his duty.
He went to Tamar.
But God saw what happened when nobody else was watching.
That is where this ancient story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because Onan’s temptation did not die with Onan.
We have simply learned how to dress it differently.
How many people want the comfort of another person without carrying responsibility for that person?
How many want sex without covenant?
Marriage without sacrifice?
Family without faithfulness?
Church without surrender?
Grace without repentance?
Jesus as Savior while quietly resisting Jesus as Lord?
How many of us have discovered sophisticated ways of looking obedient publicly while arranging our private lives so obedience never interferes with what we really want?
That is the nerve Genesis 38 touches.
And before we use Onan’s story as a weapon against somebody else, we should allow Scripture to turn the light toward us.
Because you do not have to be Onan to possess an Onan-shaped corner of the heart.
A place where you say yes with your mouth while your choices quietly say no.
A place where you want what God gives but resist what God asks.
A place where you want the pleasure, comfort, reputation, relationship, ministry, blessing, forgiveness, platform, marriage, influence, or security—but not the surrender attached to it.
People can be fooled by religious appearances.
God cannot.
Genesis says:
"וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה"
Vayyera be'enei YHWH asher asah.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
Genesis 38:10.
Notice the language.
What he did was evil before God.

The passage does not permit us to reduce Onan’s sin to a slogan about one isolated sexual act. The narrator has already supplied the motive: Onan knew the offspring would not belong to him, and he intentionally acted “so as not to give offspring to his brother.”
His sexual behavior was inseparable from his selfish refusal of responsibility.
He was exploiting the arrangement while sabotaging its purpose.
And Tamar paid the price.
That matters because Tamar can disappear when this passage is discussed only as a debate about male sexuality.
But Genesis does not allow her to disappear.
She had already buried a husband.
Now the man charged with helping preserve her deceased husband’s family line repeatedly came to her while secretly making sure she remained childless.
Then Onan died.
And Tamar was left waiting again.
Judah promised that when his younger son Shelah grew up, Tamar would be given to him.
But Judah became afraid.
So Tamar waited.
And waited.
Shelah grew.
The promise did not.
Imagine what that waiting meant in her world.

She could not simply reinvent her life according to twenty-first-century expectations. Her future, household security, motherhood, and place within the family structure were entangled with decisions being made by men around her.
Er failed.
Onan failed.
Then Judah failed to give her Shelah as promised.
Three times, Tamar's future was affected by men who possessed more social power than she did.
Then Genesis 38 becomes even more scandalous.
Tamar disguises herself.
Judah sees her, fails to recognize her, assumes she is a prostitute, and sleeps with her.
She conceives.
Months later, Judah hears that Tamar is pregnant.
His reaction is horrifyingly swift.
He calls for judgment.
But Tamar possesses Judah’s seal, cord, and staff—the identifying objects he had given as a pledge.
She sends them to him.
No screaming.
No public speech.
Just evidence.
“Recognize, please, whose these are.”
And suddenly Judah is standing face-to-face with himself.
Then comes one of the great confession moments in Genesis:
"צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי"
Tzadqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Genesis 38:26.
And Judah explains why:
Because he had not given her to Shelah his son.
The man who was prepared to condemn Tamar was forced to recognize his own failure.
That sentence should frighten every religious person who finds it easier to identify somebody else’s scandal than his own sin.
Sometimes we are furious about the visible evidence of someone else's brokenness while remaining strangely merciful toward the hidden compromises that helped create it.
Judah looked at Tamar and saw disgrace.
God was forcing Judah to look at Judah.
And something changed.
Genesis 38 does not leave Judah as the same man.
Earlier, in Genesis 37, Judah was the brother who proposed selling Joseph.
Later, when Benjamin’s freedom and his father Jacob’s heart are at stake, Judah becomes the brother willing to offer himself in Benjamin’s place.
“Please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord.”
Genesis 44:33.
