The man who once surrendered a brother to save himself becomes a man willing to surrender himself to save a brother.
That is transformation.
Not perfection.
Transformation.
And now the story becomes breathtaking.
Because Tamar became pregnant with twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez became part of the line that eventually produced David.
And centuries later, when Matthew opens his Gospel and records the genealogy of Jesus Christ, he does something ancient genealogies could easily have avoided.
He mentions Tamar.
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar…”
Matthew 1:3.
There she is.
The scandal was not erased.
The complicated history was not airbrushed.
Tamar's name stands in the genealogy that leads toward Christ.
Not because sin became righteous.
Not because deception became God's ideal.
Not because sexual brokenness ceased to matter.
But because human sin cannot outmaneuver the redemptive purposes of God.
Read that again if your past embarrasses you.
Human sin cannot outmaneuver the redemptive purposes of God.
The family line was messy.
God was faithful.
Judah had failed.
God was faithful.
Tamar had been wronged.
God was faithful.
Onan acted selfishly.
God was faithful.
Generations passed.
Kings rose and fell.
And eventually another Son of Judah appeared.
Jesus Christ.
But unlike Onan, Jesus did not take while refusing to give.
Jesus gave Himself.
Onan protected his own interests at another person's expense.
Christ surrendered His own life for sinners.
Onan refused a costly responsibility because the resulting legacy would not be his.
Jesus willingly embraced the cross to bring people who had nothing to offer Him into the family of God.
Onan's story is curved inward toward self.
The Gospel opens outward in sacrificial love.
Jesus said:
“The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
Mark 10:45.
There is the greater Man.
There is the faithful Bridegroom.
There is the One who does not use His bride.
He dies for her.
Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25.
That is why Genesis 38 must eventually lead us beyond outrage at Onan.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of bad people over there being exposed.
It is the story of sinners being brought into the light and offered mercy through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Maybe your hidden sin is sexual.
Maybe it is not.
Maybe nobody knows what you keep deleting.
Maybe nobody knows what happens when the door closes.
Maybe people at church know one version of you while your phone knows another.
Maybe you keep taking emotionally from someone you have no intention of loving faithfully.
Maybe you want someone’s body but not their heart.
Maybe you keep another person close enough to satisfy your loneliness while knowing you will never give them honest commitment.
Maybe your hidden compromise has nothing to do with sexuality at all.
Maybe you want God's provision but not God's commands.
His forgiveness but not repentance.
His heaven but not His holiness.
His promises but not His authority.
And perhaps you have become very good at making partial obedience look complete.
Onan reminds us that God sees the difference.
But if conviction is rising inside you right now, do not mistake conviction for an invitation to despair.
The Bible did not preserve Genesis 38 merely to tell us that God sees hidden evil.
It preserved a story in which disgrace, failure, selfishness, injustice, confession, and a deeply broken family history somehow become part of the road toward Bethlehem.
That is grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that enters where evil has done its damage and begins rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
Maybe that is why you needed this story today.
You thought your chapter disqualified the whole book.
Jesus is still writing.
You thought the things done to you had permanently named you.
Jesus is still writing.
You thought the things you did in secret meant God could never use what remained.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn away from it.
And come to Christ.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23.
But Scripture does not stop there.
We are “justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 3:24.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending.
Not hiding.
Not performing.
Not finding somebody whose scandal looks worse than yours so you can temporarily feel clean.
Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Grace offered freely.
Repentance demanded honestly.
Forgiveness purchased completely.
A new life made possible through Him.
Where are you taking while refusing to give?
Where are you enjoying privilege while avoiding responsibility?
Where have you learned to imitate obedience while secretly protecting rebellion?
And what would happen if tonight you stopped hiding it from Jesus?
He already knows.
The question is whether you will bring it into the light.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can make one honest declaration.
And believers—do not turn that comment section into a courtroom.
Make it somewhere wounded people encounter truth and grace.
Pray for one another.
Point one another toward Christ.
Supporting Gospel-centered teaching can itself be one practical way to help truthful Christian content reach more people. Scripture calls us to glorify God with our whole lives.
Jesus Christ.
The One who walked willingly into humanity's scandal.
The One who carried sin He never committed.
The One who was stripped, mocked, crucified, and buried.
The One who rose.
The One who still receives repentant sinners.
Tamar's story survived.
Judah's failure was exposed.
Onan's secret was seen.
And through a family history no public-relations department would ever have chosen, the genealogy kept moving until Matthew could write:
That is the Gospel's strange beauty.
God does not need a spotless family history to accomplish a holy purpose.
He creates redeemed people through a spotless Savior.
So when Satan points at the chapter you wish had never been written, point him toward the cross.
Because the chapter that looks like the end of your story may become the very place where grace teaches you that Jesus still holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Can Leave the World Behind and Still Bring Your Self-Righteousness Into the Church
paragraphs: You Can Leave the World Behind and Still Bring Your Self-Righteousness Into the Church

You can stop drinking, stop partying, clean up your language, carry a Bible, serve in church, give faithfully, pray every morning—and still walk into the presence of God carrying something more dangerous than the sins you left behind: confidence in your own righteousness.
There is a frightening kind of lostness that does not look lost.
It knows the songs.
It knows when to raise its hands.
It knows the verses.
It knows Christian vocabulary.
It can recognize false doctrine, rebuke compromise, defend biblical morality, and tell you exactly what is wrong with the culture.
It may have a testimony about everything it no longer does.
And somewhere along the road from scandal to respectability, it can quietly begin looking at broken people and thinking:
Thank God I’m not like them.
That sentence should make every serious Christian uncomfortable.
Because Jesus once told a story about two men who entered the same place of worship.
One looked righteous.
The other knew he wasn't.
And according to Jesus, only one of them walked home justified.
Luke introduces the parable with words so precise that we should not rush past them. In the Greek text, Jesus speaks to people described as:
τοὺς πεποιθότας ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῖς ὅτι εἰσὶν δίκαιοι
Tous pepoithotas eph’ heautois hoti eisin dikaioi.
They had become confident—trusting in themselves—that they were righteous.
But Luke adds something else:
καὶ ἐξουθενοῦντας τοὺς λοιπούς
...kai exouthenountas tous loipous.
And they treated the others with contempt.
That connection is devastating.
Confidence in personal righteousness had begun producing contempt for other people.
Jesus was not confronting atheists who mocked holiness.
He was confronting religious confidence.
Two men went to the temple to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
The other was a tax collector.
If you already know the story, resist the temptation to immediately make the Pharisee the villain.
That can become another form of the very sin Jesus is exposing.
“Thank God I am not like that Pharisee.”
Do you see how quickly the trap closes?
The Pharisee begins praying:
Ὁ θεός, εὐχαριστῶ σοι...
Ho Theos, eucharistō soi...
“God, I thank You...”
It sounds beautiful at first.
He addresses God.
He gives thanks.
Then comes the poison.
He is thankful that he is not like other people.
Not extortioners.
Not unjust people.
Not adulterers.
Then his eyes apparently find the man standing farther away.
“...or even like this tax collector.”
There it is.
A man standing before a holy God somehow manages to make another sinner the measuring stick of his righteousness.
And we still do it.
Maybe you no longer get drunk.
But now you despise the alcoholic.
Maybe God delivered you from sexual immorality.
But now you speak about sexually broken people as though disgust were a fruit of the Spirit.
Maybe your marriage survived.
But somewhere inside, you feel superior to the divorced believer sitting three rows behind you.

Maybe your children are walking with God, and instead of falling on your knees thanking Him for mercy, you quietly conclude that another parent's struggling child proves something about their parenting.
Maybe you know Scripture.
Maybe you understand doctrine.
Maybe you can spot theological error in thirty seconds.
But knowledge that should have driven you to worship has instead become ammunition for winning arguments and humiliating people.
Maybe you tithe.
Maybe you fast.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you never miss Sunday worship.
Maybe you have been a Christian for thirty years.
And none of those things are evil.
That is precisely what makes self-righteousness so deceptive.
The Pharisee was not boasting about committing adultery.
He was boasting about religious obedience.
“I fast twice a week.”
“I give tithes of all that I get.”
The problem was not that fasting was evil.
The problem was not generosity.
The problem was not obedience.
The problem was where his confidence had landed.
His obedience had stopped being evidence of dependence upon God and had become evidence in the courtroom of his own imagination that he was better than somebody else.
This is one of the most dangerous transformations that can happen in a Christian life.
God rescues us from obvious sin...
and eventually we begin admiring the person He rescued.
We forget the pit.
We forget the chains.
We forget the nights when nobody knew what was happening inside us.
We forget how many prayers God answered that we did not deserve.
We forget how many temptations He prevented us from encountering.
We forget how many times grace restrained us.
We forget that if there is anything genuinely beautiful growing in our lives, God deserves the glory.
Then slowly...
mercy becomes résumé.
Testimony becomes trophy.
Conviction becomes comparison.
Holiness becomes hierarchy.
And the rescued sinner begins looking down into the pit at people who have not climbed out yet.
But perhaps the most frightening detail in Jesus' story is this:
The Pharisee was standing in the temple.
You can leave the nightclub and bring pride into the sanctuary.
You can throw away the bottle and keep the arrogance.
You can abandon pornography and become addicted to superiority.
You can stop swearing and begin murdering people with contempt.
You can leave worldly rebellion behind while carrying your self-righteousness straight through the church doors.
You can change your clothes without changing your confidence.
You can change your habits without changing your heart.
You can become respectable without becoming humble.
Then Jesus turns our attention toward the other man.
The tax collector stands far away.
He will not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beats his chest.
No spiritual résumé.
No comparison.
No list of accomplishments.
No attempt to explain why somebody else is worse.
Just this:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
What a prayer.
He has stopped negotiating.
He has stopped comparing.
He has stopped pretending.
He brings God the one thing the Pharisee refuses to bring:
his need for mercy.
And Jesus says something that must have stunned His listeners.
The tax collector went home δεδικαιωμένος — dedikaiōmenos.
Justified.
Declared righteous before God.
Not because tax collecting made him righteous.
Not because sin suddenly became harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because God lowered His standard.
He went home justified because he came before God without pretending that his righteousness could save him.
This is where the parable points us toward the beating heart of the Gospel.
Because the Christian message is not:
“Bad people should try harder until God likes them.”
It is not:
“Become slightly better than the person beside you.”
It is not:
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps heaven will be impressed.”
The Gospel announces that sinners need a righteousness they cannot manufacture.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The sinless Son of God lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
At the cross, He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And those who turn from sin and trust in Christ do not stand before God boasting, “Look what I achieved.”
We stand amazed and confess:
“Look what Jesus has done.”
That changes everything.
Because when the cross becomes enormous in your vision, superiority becomes absurd.
How can I kneel beneath a blood-stained cross where the innocent Son of God died for sinners...
and brag that my particular collection of sins looks more respectable than yours?
How can I sing about amazing grace on Sunday and treat someone as beneath me on Monday?
How can I rejoice that Christ did not reject me at my ugliest and then decide somebody else is too ugly for my compassion?
The cross does not tell me my sin was small.
The cross tells me my sin was so serious that Christ had to die—and His grace is so astonishing that He willingly came to save sinners.
That destroys both despair and pride.
The broken sinner cannot say, “I am beyond mercy.”
The religious sinner cannot say, “I am beyond needing mercy.”
Both must come to Jesus.
Perhaps this article is uncomfortable because you have genuinely changed.
You really did leave things behind.
You really did stop sleeping around.
You really did become sober.
You really did become faithful.
You really did begin reading Scripture.
You really did become disciplined.
Praise God.
Do not return to the chains Christ broke.
Do not romanticize your old bondage.
Do not confuse humility with pretending obedience does not matter.
Jesus calls us to repentance, holiness, faithfulness, love, obedience, and transformed lives.
But never forget Who gets the glory.
Christian maturity is not reaching a point where you need grace less.
Christian maturity is seeing more clearly how completely dependent upon Christ you have always been.
Maybe somebody entered church this morning smelling like cigarettes while you smelled like expensive perfume.
Maybe someone's marriage is collapsing while yours appears strong.
Maybe somebody has relapsed.
Maybe someone's teenager is rebelling.
Maybe somebody walked through the doors after committing a sin last night that would horrify you.
Maybe someone is sitting quietly while fighting an addiction nobody knows exists.
Maybe the person scrolling through Christian posts and never commenting is secretly wondering whether Jesus would still receive them if everyone knew the truth.
And perhaps the question heaven is pressing upon us is not merely:
“What did they do?”
Perhaps it is:
“Have you forgotten what mercy did for you?”
There is a difference between discernment and contempt.
Biblical Christianity does not require us to call evil good.
Jesus never needed to redefine sin in order to love sinners.
Truth and mercy met perfectly in Him.
We can call people to repentance without treating ourselves as their savior.
We can oppose sin without despising sinners.
We can pursue holiness without converting holiness into a pedestal.
We can defend truth without forgetting that truth revealed our own guilt before it ever became something we used to correct somebody else.
And perhaps one of the clearest signs that grace has gone deep is that obedience makes us more grateful, not more arrogant.
The closer we walk with Jesus, the less impressive our spiritual résumé begins to look beside His holiness.
Suddenly the prayer changes.
Not:
“God, thank You that I am better than them.”
But:
“Jesus, thank You that You did not abandon me.”
“Jesus, keep my heart tender.”
“Jesus, expose whatever pride is hiding beneath my obedience.”
“Jesus, teach me to hate sin without learning to hate sinners.”
“Jesus, if I become more holy, make me more humble too.”
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to become “the good Christian.”
You have become dependable.
Disciplined.
Respected.
People ask you for advice.
People assume your spiritual life is strong.
And perhaps somewhere underneath all of that goodness is an exhausted soul constantly measuring itself against everyone else.
Better than him.
More faithful than her.
More biblical than them.
More disciplined.
More conservative.
More generous.
More committed.
More spiritual.
And Jesus is offering you freedom from that prison too.
You do not have to be the best person in the room.
You need Christ.
You do not have to prove somebody else is worse in order to believe God loves you.
You need Christ.
You do not need another person's failure to validate your obedience.
You need Christ.
You do not need to hide your weakness beneath religious achievement.
You need Christ.
And when Christ becomes your righteousness rather than merely the mascot attached to your righteousness, something beautiful happens.
You can finally look at the struggling sinner without needing to stand above them.
You can kneel beside them.
You can say:
“I know where mercy is.”
That is Christianity.
Not one beggar bragging to another beggar about having cleaner clothes.
It is one rescued sinner pointing another toward the Savior.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.

Not to create an audience of Christians who congratulate themselves for knowing more than everyone else, but to keep pointing wounded, growing, repenting people back toward Jesus Christ, Scripture, grace, truth, holiness, restoration, and the Gospel.
If this exposed something uncomfortable in you, don't rush past it.
Be honest before God.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove spirituality.
Let it be a small public confession that none of us graduates from needing grace.
There may be another believer reading those words who needs to know they are not the only one still being sanctified.
Then think of one person you love.
Not somebody you want to insult.
Not somebody you want to “teach a lesson.”
Someone you genuinely love.
Come back to it the next time another person's failure begins making you feel spiritually tall.
It doesn't.
Not because financial support proves you are a better Christian.
It doesn't.
And certainly not because grace can be purchased.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased redemption at a price none of us could pay.
But Christians can freely choose to glorify God through generosity, stewardship, sharing biblical truth, and helping sound Gospel ministry reach more people.
Think about Jesus.
Think about the temple.
Think about those two men.
One had an impressive résumé.
The other had a desperate prayer.
One looked across the room and saw someone beneath him.
The other looked toward heaven and knew mercy was his only hope.
And Jesus said the second man went home justified.
So tonight, before you tell God everything you have done right...
before you remember everything somebody else has done wrong...
before you congratulate yourself for how far you have come...
remember the tax collector standing far away.
Remember his lowered eyes.
Remember his hand striking his chest.
Remember his prayer.
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
God...
have mercy on me,
the sinner.
Perhaps the greatest evidence that Jesus has changed you is not that you can finally see how sinful everyone else is.
Perhaps it is that after everything He has changed in you, you are still astonished that He had mercy on you.
And here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
Be careful that the sins you conquered do not become the throne from which you judge the sinners Jesus died to save.
Because the scandal was never too ugly for His grace.
The sinner was never too dirty for His mercy.
And the religious heart was never too respectable to need repentance.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES THE BIBLE ACTUALLY FORBID MASTURBATION?
paragraphs:
DOES THE BIBLE ACTUALLY FORBID MASTURBATION?
What Scripture Says—and What It Never Says

Millions of Christians have asked this question in private. Some have cried after doing it. Some have promised God they would never do it again. Some have been trapped in the cycle for years. But before we call something a sin—or excuse something God wants to confront—we need the courage to ask a more dangerous question: What does the Bible actually say?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe nobody would ever guess.
You worship.
You pray.
You open your Bible.
You love Jesus.
And yet there is this private part of your life that almost never enters the conversation.
It happens behind a locked door.
Under a blanket.
In the shower.
After everyone else has gone to sleep.
Sometimes after pornography.
Sometimes after scrolling too long.
Sometimes after loneliness.
Sometimes after rejection.
Sometimes without another person's image at all.
Then comes the silence.
And for many Christians, the silence is followed by shame.
You stare at the ceiling afterward and wonder...
Did I just sin against God?
Then another question follows.
Where does the Bible actually say that?
That question deserves more than a slogan.
It deserves more than somebody shouting, “Of course it is!”
It also deserves more than somebody shrugging, “The Bible never mentions it, so do whatever you want.”
Neither response is careful enough.
Because here is the uncomfortable truth:
There is no verse in Scripture that explicitly says, “You shall not masturbate.”
The Bible never directly names masturbation as a distinct sexual act and then gives a command specifically prohibiting it.
That matters.
Christians should never manufacture commandments and then put God's signature underneath them.
But don't close this article yet.
Because the absence of an explicit sentence does not mean Scripture has nothing to say about what happens in your bedroom, imagination, desires, habits, body, conscience, or heart.
And that is where this becomes much more personal.
The question may not simply be:
“Is masturbation forbidden?”
The deeper question may be:
“What is happening inside me when I do it—and is that part of me being surrendered to Jesus Christ?”
That question is harder to escape.
People sometimes bring up Onan in Genesis 38 and claim that God killed him for masturbation.
But read the story carefully.

Onan's sin was not described as masturbation. He was obligated within the family structure of his time to provide offspring for his deceased brother, yet he deliberately frustrated that responsibility because he knew the resulting offspring would not be counted as his own.
Genesis 38:9 describes him spilling his seed on the ground.
But turning that passage into a direct biblical prohibition of masturbation goes beyond what the text actually says.
God judged Onan for the wickedness described in the narrative—his selfish refusal and exploitation—not because Scripture suddenly inserted a universal command about masturbation.
We must allow Scripture to say what Scripture says.
Nothing less.
Nothing more.
But then Jesus takes us somewhere far more uncomfortable than Genesis 38.
He takes us into the heart.
Jesus says in Matthew 5:28 that the person who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
The Greek is striking.
The expression involves ἐπιθυμῆσαι — epithymēsai, from epithymeō: to desire, long for, covet, lust after.
Jesus does not merely police the physical boundary.
He walks straight past the locked bedroom door and enters the imagination.
He confronts what we deliberately cultivate within ourselves.
And suddenly the question changes.
If masturbation is being fueled by pornography...
If you are mentally undressing someone...
If you are replaying sexual images...
If you are imagining somebody else's spouse...
If you are deliberately turning another human being into material for your private sexual gratification...
then saying, “But the Bible doesn't use the word masturbation,” misses what Jesus is exposing.
The hands may be hidden.
The browser history may be erased.
Nobody at church may know.
But Jesus keeps pointing toward the heart.
And perhaps that is why this subject hurts so much.
Because some people reading this aren't really asking whether masturbation appears in a concordance.
They're asking whether the secret world they have built around it can survive under the lordship of Christ.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is πορνεία — porneia.
The New Testament uses this broad sexual-ethical category repeatedly when addressing sexual conduct contrary to God's purposes.
But even here we need honesty.
Paul does not write, “Masturbation equals porneia.”
That sentence isn't in the text.
So Christians should be careful about claiming more precision than Scripture gives us.
Yet Paul gives another principle that reaches even deeper.
In 1 Corinthians 6:12, he refuses to be dominated by anything.
Then, later in the chapter, he reminds believers that their bodies belong to Christ and have been bought with a price.
That means there is another question worth asking:
Can you stop?
Not for one afternoon.
Not because you're busy.
Can you genuinely surrender it?
Because something can begin as pleasure and slowly become a master.
“I need it to sleep.”
“I need it when I'm stressed.”
“I need it when I'm lonely.”
“I need it when I'm rejected.”
“I need it when I'm anxious.”
“I'll stop tomorrow.”
Then tomorrow becomes next week.
Next week becomes another month.
And somewhere along the way, what you said you controlled begins controlling you.
This is bigger than masturbation.
It is the ancient battle of the human heart:
Who is Lord here?
Paul speaks elsewhere of ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia: self-control.
That word matters because Christianity is not merely a religion of avoiding prohibited behaviors.
Jesus is forming a new kind of person.
A person whose appetites no longer sit on the throne.
Sexual desire itself is not evil.
Your body is not dirty.
Being sexually tempted does not mean God is disgusted with you.
Scripture does not teach that holiness means becoming incapable of sexual desire.
God created human beings as embodied creatures, and Scripture celebrates marital sexual intimacy rather than treating sexuality itself as contamination.
The problem is not that your body can experience desire.
The question is what you do with desire.
Does desire become worship?
Does desire become fantasy?
Does desire turn another person into an object?
Does desire drag you toward pornography?
Does desire command you?
Does desire make you hide?
Does desire repeatedly override your conscience?
Does it move you toward love, faithfulness and self-control—or deeper into isolation and secrecy?
Those questions are much more biblically useful than pretending there is a verse saying something Scripture never actually says.
And there is another distinction Christians desperately need.
Temptation is not identical to sin.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin.
Feeling sexual arousal is therefore not automatically the same thing as committing sexual sin.
An unwanted thought entering your mind is not identical to deliberately feeding that thought.
A temptation appearing is not identical to inviting it inside, giving it dinner, locking the door and asking it to stay.
Some believers have tortured themselves because they were taught to treat every involuntary bodily sensation as moral failure.
That can produce something Christianity was never supposed to produce:
obsession without transformation.
Fear without freedom.
Rule keeping without intimacy with Christ.
But the opposite error is just as dangerous.
“It's natural” is not the final Christian standard.
Anger can feel natural.
Greed can feel natural.
Pride can feel natural.
Revenge can feel natural.
Christian discipleship does not ask merely, “Does this impulse occur naturally?”
It asks:
“Can I bring this desire beneath the lordship of Jesus?”
Imagine someone alone tonight.
Phone glowing.
Door locked.
Nobody watching.
He knows exactly which website he wants.
She knows exactly whose profile she wants to revisit.
The temptation is already building.
And perhaps the real spiritual battle begins several minutes before the physical act.
One more image.
One more fantasy.
One more search.
One more promise:
After tonight I'll stop.
That is where grace needs to enter.
Not after you have cleaned yourself up.
Not after you've maintained a perfect streak.
Not after you have become worthy enough to pray.
Right there.
In the temptation.
In the loneliness.
In the mess.
In the bathroom.
In the bedroom.
In the shame.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross because humanity had successfully conquered its appetites.
He went because sinners needed redemption.
That distinction changes everything.
The Gospel is not:
“Become sexually flawless and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel is that sinners are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ, and the Christ who forgives also transforms those who belong to Him.
Grace does not tell sin that it doesn't matter.
Grace tells the sinner that sin does not get the final word.
Maybe you failed last night.
Maybe five minutes ago.
Maybe you've been fighting pornography and masturbation together for ten years.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse doesn't know.
Maybe your pastor doesn't know.
Maybe everyone sees the Bible you carry but nobody sees the browser you clear.
Listen carefully.
Do not turn conviction into hiding.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring what is hidden into the light.
Where pornography is involved, cut off access instead of negotiating with it.
Where fantasy about another person is deliberately cultivated, call it what Jesus calls it and surrender it.
Where masturbation has become compulsive, don't romanticize bondage by calling it freedom.
Where loneliness is underneath the behavior, deal with the loneliness too.
Where trauma, anxiety, depression, compulsive behavior, or deep emotional distress is tangled into the pattern, getting appropriate pastoral and professional help is not spiritual failure.
And where Scripture has not explicitly spoken, be careful not to create a new verse God never wrote.
This means Christians discussing masturbation need something rarer than outrage.
We need biblical precision.
The Bible does not explicitly name masturbation and declare every instance sinful in a standalone command.
That should be admitted plainly.

But Scripture does directly confront lust, sexual immorality, impurity, lack of self-control, enslavement to appetite, violation of conscience, exploitation of others, and what we choose to cultivate in our hearts.
So masturbation cannot responsibly be evaluated in isolation from those things.
For many people, pornography alone settles a major part of the issue.
For others, deliberate lustful fantasy does.
For others, compulsive enslavement does.
For others, the issue becomes conscience and whether they can genuinely bring the behavior before Christ with faith and thanksgiving rather than secrecy, rationalization, or rebellion.
And this is precisely where simplistic answers fail people.
Because someone can technically avoid one behavior while remaining consumed by lust.
And someone else can become so obsessed with whether a bodily response “counts” as sin that Christ disappears behind a scoreboard of streaks, failures, promises and shame.
Jesus wants more than behavioral cosmetics.
He wants the heart.
Your sexuality.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your wounds.
Your habits.
Your body.
Your future marriage, if He gives you one.
Your singleness, if that is where you are now.
Your desires.
Your secrets.
Everything.
There may be somebody reading this whose deepest problem isn't even masturbation anymore.
It's despair.
You've failed so many times that you've begun believing repentance is pointless.
You apologize to God and hear your own mind whisper:
He must be tired of you.
But look again at the Gospel.
Peter denied Christ.
David's sexual sin produced devastation.
Paul once persecuted believers.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated sexual and relational history.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply broken pasts.
Christianity is filled with people whose stories should have ended in scandal.
Then Jesus entered the story.
Not to rename darkness as light.
Not to tell sinners that holiness doesn't matter.
But to forgive, cleanse, redeem and transform.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal has never appeared publicly.
Maybe it exists only between you and a glowing screen.
Maybe nobody has caught you.
But perhaps you don't need to be caught.
Perhaps you need to come home.
You don't need another promise whispered at 2:00 a.m.
You need Christ.
You need grace powerful enough to forgive you and truth powerful enough to change you.
You need to stop asking only:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
and begin asking:
“Jesus, how completely can I belong to You?”
That prayer changes the battlefield.
Because Christianity was never primarily about discovering the maximum amount of pleasure you can keep while remaining technically innocent.
It is about Jesus becoming Lord.
Be honest.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a private battle.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drowning in shame.

Supporting Gospel ministry can be one practical way of participating in getting biblical resources before more people, but it must never be confused with purchasing God's favor. Salvation cannot be bought. Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Jesus is not for sale.
Forgiveness is not merchandise.
The Gospel is not a loyalty program.
And sharing this article will not save you.
Jesus saves.
So tonight, when nobody else can see the battle...
when the screen begins glowing...
when the familiar urge returns...
when shame whispers that you've already gone too far...
remember this:
The ultimate question is not whether you can hide your hands.
It is whether you will surrender your heart.
Bring the desire.
Bring the loneliness.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the fantasies.
Bring the relapse.
Bring the shame.
Bring the questions Scripture does not answer with the precision you wish it did.
Bring everything into the presence of Christ.
Repent where Scripture exposes sin.
Receive grace where shame tries to condemn what Christ has forgiven.
Seek accountability where secrecy has become a prison.
Practice self-control where appetite has become master.
And refuse both legalism that invents commandments and permissiveness that ignores the commands God actually gave.
You may have entered this article asking:
“Does the Bible forbid masturbation?”
Perhaps you are leaving with a more important question:
“Does Jesus have this part of me too?”
Because the secret you keep protecting may be the very room where Christ is asking you to open the door.
And when Jesus enters the room you were most ashamed to show Him, your scandal does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DINAH’S BROTHERS LOOTED THE CITY—AND TOOK ITS WOMEN AND CHILDREN
paragraphs: DINAH’S BROTHERS LOOTED THE CITY—AND TOOK ITS WOMEN AND CHILDREN
What happened after Dinah was violated is one of Genesis’ darkest family scandals—and buried inside the bloodshed is a warning about what happens when wounded people try to become their own judges.
There are Bible stories we teach children.
And then there are Bible stories we barely know how to talk about.
Genesis 34 is one of them.
It begins with a young woman named Dinah.

Before the chapter ends, a woman has been violated, an entire city’s men have been killed, houses have been plundered, children and women have been carried away as captives, a father is terrified, brothers are defiant...
and a family chosen to carry God’s covenant is standing in the wreckage of its own scandal.
But here is what makes this chapter so uncomfortable.
The people who committed the massacre were not pagans attacking Jacob’s family.
They were Jacob’s sons.
They were Abraham’s great-grandsons.
They belonged to the covenant family.
They knew the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
And still...
they became capable of terrible violence.
That should make every religious person uncomfortable.
Because Genesis 34 destroys one of our favorite illusions:
Being near holy things does not automatically make the human heart holy.
You can know the language of faith and still be ruled by rage.
You can defend something righteous through unrighteous means.
You can be genuinely wounded and still wound others.
You can begin by demanding justice...
and end by becoming something justice never required you to become.
Dinah, the daughter of Jacob and Leah, went out to see the women of the land.
Then Shechem, son of Hamor, saw her.
Genesis describes what followed in disturbing terms. He took her and violated her.
Whatever else we say about Genesis 34, we must never make Dinah disappear from her own story.
Something grievous happened to her.
Her brothers had reason to be outraged.
Genesis itself says they were grieved and very angry because a disgraceful thing had been done in Israel.
Their anger did not appear out of nowhere.
There had been real evil.
Real violation.
Real dishonor.
And that matters, because Christianity does not require us to pretend evil is harmless.
Biblical forgiveness is not calling darkness light.
Grace does not mean abuse was acceptable.
Forgiveness does not require calling injustice justice.
But then something happens inside Dinah’s brothers.
Their outrage begins to mutate.
Justice becomes revenge.
Pain becomes permission.
And wounded brothers become dangerous men.
Shechem wanted Dinah as his wife. Hamor came to negotiate with Jacob’s family. But Jacob’s sons answered deceitfully.
They demanded that every male in Shechem’s community be circumcised.
Circumcision was the covenant sign God had given Abraham.
Think about how disturbing that is.
Something associated with God’s covenant was now being incorporated into a deception.
The men agreed.
Then came the third day.
The men of the city were in pain.
Simeon and Levi picked up their swords.
They entered the city.
And they killed the males.
They killed Hamor.
They killed Shechem.
They removed Dinah from Shechem’s house.
But the violence did not stop there.
The other sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city.
They took the sheep.
The cattle.
The donkeys.
What was inside the city.
What was in the fields.
And then Genesis gives us one of those verses we can read too quickly because we already know how the story ends.
The Hebrew of Genesis 34:29 reads:
וְאֶת־כָּל־חֵילָם וְאֶת־כָּל־טַפָּם וְאֶת־נְשֵׁיהֶם שָׁבוּ וַיָּבֹזּוּ וְאֵת כָּל־אֲשֶׁר בַּבָּיִת
Ve’et-kol cheilam, ve’et-kol tappam, ve’et-nesheihem shavu vayavozzu, ve’et kol-asher babbayit.
In straightforward sense:
They took their wealth, their little ones, and their women captive, and they plundered what was in the houses.
The Hebrew makes the horror difficult to sanitize.
טַפָּם — tappam refers to their little ones, children or dependents.
נְשֵׁיהֶם — nesheihem means their women or wives.
שָׁבוּ — shavu, from the Hebrew root shavah, means they took captive.
And וַיָּבֹזּוּ — vayavozzu, from bazaz, means they plundered or looted.
Read that again.
Children.
Women.
Captivity.
Plunder.
This was no longer simply two brothers confronting the man who had violated their sister.
The circle of suffering had widened.
People who had not committed Shechem’s act were now caught inside the consequences of vengeance.
That is what uncontrolled revenge does.
It keeps expanding the list of victims.
Pain whispers:
“Make them hurt like you hurt.”
Then anger whispers:
“A little more.”
Then vengeance whispers:
“They deserve everything coming to them.”
And eventually you can become so convinced of your righteousness that you stop noticing the innocent people bleeding around your anger.
Maybe you have never held a sword.
But perhaps you know something about this kind of revenge.
Someone betrayed you...
so now everyone gets your suspicion.
Someone abandoned you...
so now the next person has to pay for what the previous person did.
Someone humiliated you...
so you replay imaginary arguments at night, dreaming of the moment they finally feel what they made you feel.
Someone in church wounded you...
and now you cannot hear the word “Christian” without feeling your defenses rise.
Your father failed you.
Your mother wounded you.
Your spouse betrayed you.
Your friend exposed you.
Someone abused your trust.
Someone destroyed something inside you that they had no right to touch.
And the dangerous question is not merely:
“Were you wronged?”
Maybe you absolutely were.
The deeper question is:
What is your wound turning you into?
Because being sinned against does not make everything we do afterward righteous.
Dinah’s violation was evil.
That does not automatically sanctify everything her brothers did afterward.
And Scripture eventually removes any doubt that we should romanticize Simeon and Levi’s violence.
Years later, when Jacob was nearing death, Genesis 49 returned to what happened.
Jacob remembered Simeon and Levi.
He remembered their weapons.
He remembered their anger.
And he did not bless their cruelty.
He condemned their fierce anger and cruel wrath.
That later biblical judgment matters.
Genesis 34 tells us what happened.
Genesis 49 helps us understand that their violent rage was not something Scripture asks us to celebrate.
This is one of the most important rules for reading difficult Bible stories:
Description is not always prescription.
The Bible can truthfully report what someone did without telling you to imitate it.
Scripture does not airbrush its families.
No public-relations department cleaned up Jacob’s household before Genesis was published.
Abraham had failures.
Isaac’s household fractured.
Jacob deceived and was deceived.
His sons lied.
Judah would later fall into sexual scandal.
Joseph would be sold by his own brothers.
The covenant family could look shockingly dysfunctional.
And yet...
God did not abandon His redemptive purpose.
That does not mean God approved their sin.
It means human sin was not powerful enough to cancel divine grace.
And now the story begins pointing beyond itself.
Because the Bible gives us another Son who would one day encounter violence.
Another Son of Israel.
But this Son would be unlike Simeon and Levi.
Jesus Christ.
Simeon and Levi responded to evil with swords.
Jesus would tell Peter to put his sword away.
Dinah’s brothers entered a city and spilled the blood of others.
Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing His own blood would be spilled.
Human vengeance says:
“You hurt me, so you must bleed.”
At Calvary we see something radically different.
Christ, the sinless One, willingly gives Himself for sinners.
He does not pretend sin does not matter.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption costs blood.
But instead of demanding that guilty sinners somehow save themselves, Jesus bears judgment as the sacrificial Lamb and opens the way for forgiveness to those who repent and believe.
This is why the Gospel is not sentimental.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace is costly.
Grace has scars.
Grace has a cross.
And maybe that is why Genesis 34 still reaches into places we would rather keep hidden.
Some of us are carrying swords nobody can see.
Not steel swords.
Memories.
Resentments.
Names.
Screenshots.
Old conversations.
Family wounds.
Betrayals we keep rehearsing because anger has become the only connection we still have to what happened.
We say we want healing...
but secretly we still want them to suffer.
We say we surrendered it to God...
but every few nights we reopen the courtroom inside our minds.
We prosecute them again.
Convict them again.
Sentence them again.
And for a few seconds, revenge feels powerful.
But it never resurrects what was lost.
It cannot return your childhood.
It cannot undo betrayal.
It cannot erase what happened behind that closed door.
It cannot force someone to become sorry.
And it cannot heal your soul.
Only Christ can enter the places revenge cannot reach.
This does not mean abandoning lawful justice.
It does not mean protecting abusers.
It does not mean remaining in dangerous situations.
It does not mean refusing appropriate authorities, accountability, boundaries, or consequences.
It means refusing to make personal vengeance your god.
The New Testament says:
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Justice belongs ultimately to God.
That means you can tell the truth about what happened.
You can call evil evil.
You can pursue proper justice.
You can establish boundaries.
You can grieve.
You can weep.
You can seek help.
And still refuse to let hatred become your identity.
Because Jesus did not save you merely from what other people did to you.
He came to save you from what sin is doing inside you too.
That is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Maybe your greatest spiritual danger is not the wound everybody knows about.
Maybe it is what you have been feeding because of the wound.
The bitterness.
The fantasy of revenge.
The coldness.
The refusal to forgive.
The secret satisfaction when the person who hurt you suffers.
The hatred you have learned to justify because your original pain was legitimate.
Listen carefully:
Your pain may explain your anger.
It does not have to become your master.
Jesus can meet you there.
Not with shallow religious clichés.
Not by pretending nothing happened.
With truth.
With justice.
With wounds in His own hands.
With grace strong enough to confront your sin without abandoning you.
With mercy strong enough to loosen your fingers from the sword you have been gripping for years.
Perhaps you need to pray something frighteningly honest tonight:
“Jesus, what happened to me was wrong.
But I do not want what happened to me to decide who I become.
Judge what needs judging.
Heal what needs healing.
Expose what needs confessing.
Teach me to forgive without calling evil good.
Take this hatred before it consumes me.
I surrender my right to personal vengeance.
Have mercy on me.
Rewrite this part of my story.”
That prayer may hurt.
Pray it anyway.
Because the Gospel is filled with stories God entered after humans had already made a mess.
And perhaps that is the astonishing thread running through Genesis.
Scandal does not get the final word.
Grace does.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that celebrates sin.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that takes broken people and begins making them new.
Even the tribe of Levi carries an extraordinary later story.
The violence of Levi in Genesis 34 was not called good. Jacob later condemned the brothers’ cruel anger.
Yet Levi’s name was not erased from Israel.
In later generations, the Levites would be set apart for sacred service.
That does not retroactively make Simeon and Levi’s massacre righteous.
It shows something different and far more beautiful:
God is able to write redemption into a family history without rewriting evil as good.
And that is hope for somebody reading this with a past you cannot erase.
Maybe your scandal really happened.
Maybe you were the wounded one.
Maybe you became the one doing the wounding.
Maybe you have been both.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you desperately wish had never been written.
The Gospel does not ask you to edit the evidence.
Bring the real story to Jesus.
The shame.
The rage.
The abuse you suffered.
The harm you caused.
The resentment.
The years you wasted.
The people you wounded.
The things you cannot undo.
Bring all of it.
Repent where you sinned.
Seek justice without worshiping revenge.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
And trust the crucified and risen Christ with the chapters you cannot repair yourself.
Because Jesus specializes in meeting people where scandal appears to have destroyed everything.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The cross looked like defeat.
The tomb looked final.
Then Sunday came.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending Friday never happened.
Resurrection.
Be honest before God.
Someone else reading the comments may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable today, but because there may come a night when the old wound opens again and you need to remember that vengeance is not your healer.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone must pay money to glorify God.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can be one genuine way Christians support Gospel work they believe is bearing fruit.
And there is much more here than individual articles.
Come for Scripture.
Stay for truth.
Grow through discipleship.
One share may put the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
One comment may make a wounded believer realize they are not alone.
Jesus Christ is not for sale. Grace is not behind a paywall. The invitation to repent, believe, be forgiven, and follow Him remains free.
Dinah’s brothers walked away from Shechem carrying plunder.
But the family still carried wounds.
That is the haunting lesson.
You can win your revenge...
and still lose your peace.
So put down the sword.
Bring the wound to Jesus.
Let Him judge what you cannot judge perfectly.
Let Him heal what revenge could never heal.
Let Him expose what bitterness has been hiding.
Let Him forgive what repentance finally brings into the light.
And let the Savior who walked out of His own grave prove that even the darkest chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
The wound may explain a chapter of your life—but only Jesus deserves to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EZEKIEL PACKED HIS BELONGINGS AND DUG THROUGH A WALL WHILE EVERYONE WATCHED
paragraphs: EZEKIEL PACKED HIS BELONGINGS AND DUG THROUGH A WALL WHILE EVERYONE WATCHED

They thought they were watching a prophet do something strange. They were actually watching God turn one man's body into a warning—and the most frightening part of Ezekiel 12 may be how easily we can recognize ourselves in the people who watched him.
Imagine opening your door and seeing Ezekiel packing.
Not for vacation.
Not because he had found somewhere better to live.
He was gathering the kind of belongings a person would carry when home was about to become a memory.
People were watching.
That was the point.
Then evening came.
Ezekiel walked toward a wall.
And started digging through it.
With his hands.
No explanation first. No polished sermon. No comfortable religious language to soften what God was saying.
Just a prophet, some belongings, a wall, and the eyes of a rebellious people fixed on him.
And somewhere inside this unsettling scene is a question that refuses to leave us alone:
What if God has been trying to get your attention too... and you have become so accustomed to seeing that you no longer truly see?
Ezekiel 12 begins with words that should make every religious person uncomfortable.
God says of the people:

עֵינַיִם לָהֶם לִרְאוֹת וְלֹא רָאוּ
אָזְנַיִם לָהֶם לִשְׁמֹעַ וְלֹא שָׁמֵעוּ
Einayim lahem lir'ot velo ra'u; oznayim lahem lishmoa velo shame'u.
They had eyes to see, but they did not see; ears to hear, but they did not hear.
The problem was not blindness.
They had eyes.
The problem was not deafness.
They had ears.
Their tragedy was that functioning eyes had stopped perceiving and functioning ears had stopped listening.
God calls them:
בֵּית־הַמֶּרִי — beit-hammeri
A rebellious house.
That is what makes this passage terrifyingly relevant.
Because rebellion does not always scream.
Sometimes rebellion sits quietly in a church.
Sometimes it knows worship songs.
Sometimes it posts Bible verses.
Sometimes it says, “Amen,” while privately protecting the very thing God has been confronting.
Sometimes rebellion looks like hearing the same truth so many times that truth no longer makes you tremble.
You know Jesus died for sinners.
You know repentance matters.
You know bitterness is poisoning you.
You know pornography is not harmless.
You know pride is destroying relationships.
You know the secret messages need to stop.
You know the apology needs to be made.
You know the relationship is pulling you away from Christ.
You know you cannot keep worshiping God publicly while deliberately feeding what He calls sin privately.
You know.
And perhaps that is the frightening part.
Because sometimes our greatest spiritual danger is not ignorance.
It is knowing... and refusing to move.
So God told Ezekiel to make the message impossible to ignore.
עֲשֵׂה לְךָ כְּלֵי גוֹלָה
“Prepare for yourself baggage for exile.”
The Hebrew expression כְּלֵי גוֹלָה — keli golah carries the idea of equipment or belongings associated with exile.
Pack what an exile would pack.
Carry it out.
Do it during the day.
Do it—
לְעֵינֵיהֶם — le'eineihem
“before their eyes.”
That expression keeps returning.
Before their eyes.
Before their eyes.
Before their eyes.
God wanted them watching.
Ezekiel was not performing for applause. He was embodying a warning.
Then came the command that must have looked almost absurd:
לְעֵינֵיהֶם חֲתָר־לְךָ בַקִּיר
“Before their eyes, dig through the wall.”
Picture it.
Dust falling.
Hands working.
People staring.
Perhaps somebody laughed.
Perhaps somebody whispered.
Perhaps someone shook his head at the strange prophet.
But Ezekiel kept digging.
Because obedience sometimes looks foolish to people who cannot yet see what God sees.
Verse 7 is almost painfully simple:
וָאַעַשׂ כֵּן כַּאֲשֶׁר צֻוֵּיתִי
Va'as ken ka'asher tzuvveiti.
“I did so, just as I was commanded.”
There is an entire sermon in that sentence.
God commanded.
Ezekiel obeyed.
He did not need everybody to understand before he obeyed.
He did not need everybody to approve before he obeyed.
He did not rewrite God's command until it became socially comfortable.
He obeyed.
And perhaps somebody reading this already knows exactly where that lands.
There is something God has made clear through His Word that you keep negotiating with.
You keep calling delay “discernment.”
You keep calling compromise “complexity.”
You keep calling bondage “just something I struggle with.”
You keep waiting for obedience to become convenient.
But there are moments when faith sounds remarkably simple:
God spoke.
I obeyed.

That does not mean every strange impulse in our minds is a command from God. Ezekiel was a prophet receiving a specific divine revelation, and Christians must not use this passage to baptize personal impulses with “God told me.”
But where Scripture has already spoken clearly, endless negotiation can become disguised disobedience.
Forgive.
Flee sexual immorality.
Tell the truth.
Love your enemy.
Care for the vulnerable.
Turn from idols.
Confess Christ.
Repent.
Follow Jesus.
Some things do not require another sign.
They require surrender.
And Ezekiel's performance was about something very specific.
This was not originally a motivational metaphor about “breaking through your walls.”
That would flatten the passage.
God Himself explains the sign after verse 7.

Ezekiel was acting out coming judgment and exile. The people of Jerusalem would be driven away, and the ruler in their midst would attempt to leave under darkness. Ezekiel declares, אֲנִי מוֹפֶתְכֶם — ani mofetkhem, essentially, “I am your sign/portent.”
The prophet was carrying tomorrow's catastrophe on his shoulder while people were still living as though tomorrow would never arrive.
And history made the warning horrifyingly concrete.
Jerusalem did fall.
King Zedekiah attempted to flee. He was captured. His sons were killed before him, his eyes were put out, and he was taken to Babylon.
The man who tried to escape under darkness ended up unable to see.
Ezekiel's strange sign had not been religious theater.
God had warned them.
And that is where this ancient scene reaches across the centuries and puts its hand on our shoulder.
Because we are extraordinarily talented at assuming there will always be more time.
More time to repent.
More time to forgive.
More time to come back to church.
More time to take Jesus seriously.
More time to tell our children about Christ.
More time to reconcile with someone.
More time to surrender the addiction.
More time to stop pretending.
More time.
Tomorrow becomes one of the easiest places to hide from God.
But Scripture never gives us tomorrow as property.
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15).
Notice that word.
Today.
The Gospel is not God telling you to clean yourself up enough to deserve Him.
You cannot.
Neither can I.
The Gospel is the announcement that the holy God against whom we have sinned came near to sinners in Jesus Christ.
And this is where Ezekiel's wall eventually forces Christian readers to look beyond Ezekiel.
Not because Ezekiel 12 secretly predicts Jesus digging through a wall—it does not.
But because the judgment against rebellion that Ezekiel announces belongs to the larger biblical story of human sin, divine holiness, judgment, mercy, and ultimately God's saving work in Christ.
Ezekiel carried the belongings of an exile.
Jesus carried a cross.
Ezekiel acted out judgment that guilty people could not indefinitely escape.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God willingly entered suffering for sinners.
“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Christ was not dragged to Calvary because Rome had finally outmaneuvered Him.
He gave Himself.
The hands that could have summoned deliverance were stretched out.
The One without sin stood where sinners deserved to stand.
The righteous for the unrighteous, that He might bring us to God.
And when Jesus cried, “It is finished,” grace did not announce that sin had never mattered.
The cross announced the opposite.
Sin mattered so much that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
Grace is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do to rescue sinners from what their rebellion deserves.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance runs toward grace.
You do not confess because Jesus is reluctant to forgive.
You confess because in Jesus there is forgiveness.
You do not come into the light because you have finally become presentable.
You come because hiding cannot heal you.
Maybe you have spent years carrying something nobody knows about.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your children see the Christian version of you.
Your Facebook friends see the verses.
People see the smile.
But somewhere behind the wall is another room.
And you are exhausted from guarding the entrance.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows what is behind it.
Every compromise.
Every relapse.
Every lie.
Every bitter thought.
Every secret search.
Every night you cried afterward.
Every promise you made to God and broke three days later.
Every moment you wondered whether you had finally gone too far.
He knows.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not, “Hide it better.”
It is:
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation says, “Hide from God because you are filthy.”
The Gospel says, “Run to Christ because He alone can wash sinners clean.”
This is why some walls need to come down.
Not because Ezekiel 12 promises a mystical “breakthrough.”
But because the same human heart capable of watching Ezekiel and refusing to see is alive in every generation.
We build walls between what God says and what we want.
Walls of excuses.
Walls of religious performance.
Walls of “everybody does it.”
Walls of “God understands.”
Yes, God understands more completely than anyone.
Which means He also understands exactly what our sin is doing to us.
The surgeon who loves you does not call the tumor harmless.
And the Savior who died for you loves you far too deeply to rename your chains freedom.
Maybe this article is your moment at the wall.
Not because these words are magical.
Not because Gospel Warrior can save you.
We cannot.
Only Jesus saves.
But perhaps Scripture has exposed something you have been carefully avoiding.
Put the phone down for a moment.
Talk to Jesus.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary required.
Tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I sinned.”
“Lord, I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I am addicted.”
“Lord, I have become cold.”
“Lord, I don't know how to come back.”
“Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.”
And then remember the promise of Scripture: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are words for people who have dirt on them.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace strong enough to tell the truth about your sin without abandoning you in it.
Grace that does not merely improve your image.
Grace that begins rewriting your life.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your name has been dragged through conversations you were not in.
Maybe the divorce happened.
Maybe the ministry collapsed.
Maybe the addiction became visible.
Maybe your child discovered what you were hiding.
Maybe you lost years you cannot recover.
Consequences are real, and following Christ does not guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears.
But consequences do not get the final word over the person who belongs to Jesus.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted His people.

The Corinthian church contained people with histories Scripture does not sanitize, yet Paul could write that they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is why our message remains:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Because Jesus is.
Not because sin deserves celebration.
Because redemption deserves proclamation.
Not because your past becomes imaginary.
Because in Christ your past no longer has authority to name your future.
Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this exposed something hidden, do not make the comment section another stage where everybody pretends to be okay.
And believers—when somebody writes those words, do not judge them.
Pray for them.
Let the comments beneath this article become less like an audience and more like people carrying one another toward Jesus.
Then think of one person.
Just one.
The person whose smile has not looked quite right lately.
The friend who stopped attending church.
The believer quietly drifting.
The person carrying shame.
The family member who thinks God could never want them again.
I haven't forgotten you.”
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
If Christ has given you truth, letting someone else encounter that truth can be an act of love.
Save this too.
There may be a night when the feelings return.
When shame starts speaking.
When temptation starts bargaining.
When you need to remember the prophet digging through a wall while everybody watched—and the terrifying danger of seeing without seeing.
Come back.
Read the Scripture again.
Christ alone is our righteousness.
Do it only if you genuinely want to support the mission.
Pray.
Save the article.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.

Because glorifying God is bigger than supporting any particular ministry. But when a ministry faithfully proclaims Christ, those who believe in its mission can glorify God by helping that truth travel farther—through prayer, generosity, encouragement, sharing, and faithful participation.
Somewhere tonight, another person is staring at a wall.
Behind it is the secret.
The shame.
The compromise.
The memory.
The thing they believe has disqualified them forever.
Maybe that person is someone who will see this because you shared it.
Maybe that person...
is you.
Ezekiel dug through a wall because judgment was coming and God's people refused to see.
Centuries later, the Gospel tells us something we dare not refuse to see:
Judgment is real.
Sin is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is forgiveness.
So is repentance.
So is restoration.
So is Jesus.
The question is no longer whether God has spoken.
The question is whether we will keep watching...
or finally see.
Because the wall you are desperately using to hide your scandal may be the very place where grace is calling you into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN THE MAN BEHIND THE PULPIT HAS MORE THAN ONE WIFE
paragraphs: WHEN THE MAN BEHIND THE PULPIT HAS MORE THAN ONE WIFE
Some Preachers Call Multiple Wives a “Reward From God.” But What Does Scripture Actually Say—and What Should You Do If This Is Your Church?
Imagine sitting in church one Sunday.
The worship is powerful. People are lifting their hands. The preacher opens his Bible. He speaks confidently about holiness, obedience, blessing, marriage, family, and the favor of God.
Then you discover something that makes your stomach tighten.
Your pastor has more than one wife.
Not a complicated past before coming to Christ. Not a deceased wife followed by remarriage. Not merely a rumor circulating among disgruntled members.
Multiple living wives at the same time.
And when someone questions it, the answer is not repentance.
It is celebration.
“God blessed me with these women.”
“Look at Abraham.”
“Look at Jacob.”
“Look at David.”
“Having several wives proves God has favored me.”
Perhaps you have heard something like this.
And now you are confused because the man saying it can preach.
He knows Scripture.
People respect him.
Maybe people call him “Papa,” “Prophet,” “Apostle,” or “Man of God.”
Perhaps miracles are attributed to his ministry. Maybe the church is growing. Maybe thousands follow him.
So you quietly wonder something you are almost afraid to say aloud:
What if he is right?
And if he is wrong...
what am I supposed to do?
Before answering, we need to establish something that can save Christians from enormous spiritual confusion:
The Bible recording something is not the same thing as the Bible recommending it.
Scripture records murder.
That does not make murder holy.
Scripture records adultery.
That does not sanctify adultery.
Scripture records drunkenness, betrayal, incest, idolatry, deception, violence, and catastrophic human failure.
The Bible is brutally honest about fallen humanity.
And yes—the Old Testament records men having multiple wives.
Abraham had relationships with Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel, along with Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon's marriages multiplied on an extraordinary scale.
But there is a dangerous way of reading Scripture that says:
“A biblical character did it, therefore God approves of it.”
Follow that method consistently and the Bible becomes a weapon for justifying almost anything.
The better question is not merely, “Did someone in the Bible do this?”
The question is:
“What does the whole counsel of Scripture reveal about God's design?”
Go backward.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Back to Eden.
Genesis 2:24 describes the foundational pattern: a man leaves father and mother, is joined to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Then something remarkable happens centuries later.
Jesus Himself reaches back to that creation account when teaching about marriage.
He does not point His listeners to Solomon's household as the model.
He points them back to the beginning.
Christ speaks of the Creator making humanity male and female, and of a man being joined to his wife so that “the two” become one flesh.
The emphasis matters.
Jesus directs the conversation toward God's creational design rather than using the broken marital histories of Old Testament figures as the standard.
And even Israel's kings were specifically warned:
“He shall not multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.”
Deuteronomy 17:17.
That warning becomes painfully visible in Solomon's story. The accumulation of wives is not presented as a trophy proving spiritual maturity.
It becomes part of his tragedy.
But now we come even closer to the question you are actually asking.
Because your question is not simply:
“Did anyone in the Old Testament practice polygamy?”
Your question is:
“Can a Christian pastor have multiple wives and call them God's reward?”
That question brings us directly into the New Testament qualifications for church leadership.
Paul writes concerning an overseer in 1 Timothy 3:2 that he must be above reproach and describes him with the Greek expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, the expression carries the sense of “a man of one woman,” commonly rendered “the husband of one wife.” Some translations express the ethical force as being “faithful to his wife.”

Paul uses substantially the same qualification when discussing elders in Titus 1:6. The text again presents the elder as ἑνὸς? No—the relevant construction is again the “one-woman man” idea reflected in translations such as “husband of one wife,” while some translations render its force as faithfulness to his wife.
Christians have debated some details of this phrase.
Does it exclude remarriage after widowhood?
What about a man divorced before conversion?
How should churches evaluate complicated histories after genuine repentance?
Faithful Christians do not agree on every one of those pastoral questions.
But those debates should not be used to erase what is unmistakable about Paul's picture of an overseer.
The pastor is supposed to demonstrate sexual and marital faithfulness.
He is supposed to be above reproach.
His household is supposed to reinforce rather than contradict his ministry.
He is not given a special sexual privilege because he has a pulpit.
Pastoral authority does not lower God's standard.
It intensifies accountability.
And that is why describing the accumulation of wives as a spiritual “reward from God” creates such a serious problem.
Where does the New Testament promise pastors additional wives as a reward for obedience?
It doesn't.
Where does Jesus tell faithful ministers that multiple wives are evidence of divine favor?
He doesn't.
Where do the apostolic qualifications for elders celebrate multiplying wives?
They don't.
Instead, the New Testament presents marriage through a breathtakingly Christ-centered picture.
Paul tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Notice the direction.
Biblical marriage is not supposed to display a man's appetite.
It is supposed to display Christ's sacrifice.
Jesus does not exploit His bride.
He dies for her.
He does not use spiritual authority to satisfy Himself.
He gives Himself.
The cross therefore destroys one of the ugliest distortions of spiritual leadership:
the idea that greater authority gives a man greater permission to indulge himself.
Jesus reveals the opposite.
Greater authority means greater service.
The King wears a crown of thorns.
The Lord kneels to wash feet.
The Bridegroom gives His body for His bride.
That is the Man standing behind every Christian pastor.
Jesus Christ.
And every preacher eventually has to answer to Him.
Maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps you are reading this while attending exactly this kind of church.
Maybe you love the people there.
Maybe your children have friends there.
Maybe that church helped you when nobody else did.
Maybe you came to Christ there.
Maybe the pastor prayed with you during one of the darkest nights of your life.
Maybe leaving feels like betrayal.
Maybe questioning him feels like questioning God.
Listen carefully.
A pastor can teach you something true and still later require biblical correction.
A church can contain genuine believers while its leadership embraces serious error.
And acknowledging something wrong does not require pretending everything you ever experienced there was fake.
Your ultimate loyalty was never supposed to belong to a preacher.
It belongs to Jesus.
There is only one Christ.
Your pastor did not die for your sins.
Your denomination did not carry your cross.
Your church founder was not raised from the dead for your justification.
Jesus was.
That means the question is not simply:
“Do I like this pastor?”
Nor:
“Has this ministry helped me?”
Nor:
“Is the church growing?”
Nor even:
“Can this man preach powerfully?”
The question becomes:
Is what is being taught consistent with Scripture, and is the leadership willing to submit to Scripture when challenged?
That last question is crucial.
Do not leave a church merely because somebody posted an accusation on social media.
Do not destroy someone's reputation because of gossip.
Verify what is actually true.
Listen carefully.
Examine the teaching in context.
Look at the man's actual marital situation.
Ask whether responsible elders know about it.
If appropriate and safe, seek clarification through mature church leadership.
Bring Scripture—not rumors.
And watch what happens when Scripture confronts power.
That response can reveal a great deal.
If a pastor is discovered in serious sin and responds with brokenness, repentance, accountability, and submission to biblical discipline, that is one situation.
Repentance does not automatically erase every consequence or restore someone immediately to pastoral office. Leadership qualifications still matter.
But repentance matters enormously because Christianity is built around grace for sinners who turn to Christ.
The Gospel Warrior message cannot become:
“Bad people are beyond hope.”
If that were the Gospel, every one of us would be finished.
The message is:
Christ saves sinners.
Christ forgives sinners.
Christ changes sinners.
Christ restores broken people.
But grace never requires us to rename darkness as light.
Repentance means turning.

That is why an openly polygamous pastor who teaches that multiplying wives is a divine reward presents a very different situation from a broken man confessing sin and submitting himself to correction.

When leadership openly celebrates what Scripture's pastoral qualifications contradict, refuses meaningful accountability, and teaches the congregation to accept that contradiction as God's will, remaining under that teaching deserves serious reconsideration.

Paul did not tell churches that sexual conduct becomes irrelevant when the guilty person is influential. In 1 Corinthians 5, he rebuked a congregation for tolerating serious sexual immorality and even condemned their pride about the situation.
So should you leave?
Do not make the decision from panic.
Do not make it from gossip.
Do not make it because someone online told you to become suspicious of every pastor.
But neither should fear of a charismatic leader imprison your conscience.
Test what you are being taught by Scripture.
Seek counsel from mature, biblically trustworthy Christians outside the leader's immediate circle if necessary.
Look for genuine accountability.
Look for repentance.
Look at whether Scripture is allowed to correct the pastor—or whether the pastor has become the person who is allowed to correct Scripture.

And if the leadership knowingly persists in teaching serious error, protects it from biblical correction, celebrates it rather than repenting of it, and demands that members violate their conscience in order to defend the leader, then finding a biblically faithful congregation where Christ and His Word stand above personalities can be a wise and responsible course.
Leaving an unhealthy church does not mean leaving Jesus.
Sometimes following Jesus requires refusing to make an idol out of the person who introduced you to Him.
But there is another danger here.
Do not read this article merely to collect ammunition against somebody else's pastor.
Because the Word of God has an uncomfortable habit.
While we are pointing it at somebody else...
it turns around and searches us.
Maybe your scandal is not polygamy.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe yours lives in browser history.
Maybe it sleeps inside bitterness.
Maybe it hides inside secret messages.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe greed.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe spiritual hypocrisy.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are doing wonderfully while inside you know you are slowly drifting away from Jesus.
Then hear the Gospel before you hear another word of judgment.
Jesus did not come only for respectable sinners.
He came for real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People whose lives became complicated because of choices they desperately wish they could undo.
People who ruined things.
People who were ruined by others.
People who have stood in church smiling while their souls were bleeding.
People who know what it feels like to whisper:
“Jesus... if You still want me, I need You.”
He still calls sinners to repentance.
And His grace is not permission to continue hiding.
His grace is the open door home.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps saying:
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to theological gymnastics.
Not from scandal to pretending sin never happened.
From scandal...
to grace.
And grace takes us through repentance.
Through confession.
Through truth.
Through the cross.
Until the person who once defended darkness can finally stand in the light and say:
“I was wrong. Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That sentence may contain more spiritual power than a thousand sermons preached by a man determined to protect his reputation.
If this exposed something in your own heart—not merely somebody else's—be honest.

And if Christ has rescued you from spiritual manipulation, sexual sin, false teaching, or a season when you confused loyalty to a leader with loyalty to Jesus, your testimony may become somebody else's lifeline. Tell it carefully. Tell it truthfully. Tell it without unnecessary gossip—but tell people what Christ has done.
Not because every church controversy requires departure, but because confusion becomes dangerous when emotions are high and Scripture becomes distant.
It doesn't.
Scripture itself commends examining teaching.
And please do not weaponize this article to harass a particular pastor, denomination, family, or congregation. The purpose is not a digital mob.
The purpose is truth, repentance, protection, restoration, and Jesus Christ.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, consider following and supporting this ministry.
