It does not make you more spiritual. It does not earn blessing, salvation, or a higher place in God's kingdom.
Christ cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is free.
Sometimes glorifying God looks like putting truth where another wounded person can find it.
Gospel Warrior is not your Savior.
Your pastor is not your Savior.
Your church is not your Savior.
Jesus Christ is.
Follow Him.
Test teaching by His Word.
Refuse to confuse charisma with character.
Refuse to call something God's reward merely because a powerful religious personality says it is.
And when you discover sin—whether behind a famous pulpit or buried inside your own heart—do not run away from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Because the final hope of Christianity is not that pastors never fall.
It is not that Christians never become confused.
It is not that churches never become corrupted.
Our hope is that there is still a throne above every pulpit...
a Shepherd above every pastor...
a Word above every human opinion...
and a Savior whose blood is still sufficient for every sinner who truly comes home.
Remember this when the preacher disappoints you:
Never let the failure of a man behind a pulpit make you walk away from the Man who carried a cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The woman Genesis never names, the question skeptics keep asking, and the uncomfortable truth hiding in plain sight in the Hebrew text.
paragraphs: The woman Genesis never names, the question skeptics keep asking, and the uncomfortable truth hiding in plain sight in the Hebrew text.
There is a woman standing almost invisibly on one of the most controversial pages of the Bible.
We never hear her speak.
We are never told her name.
We are not told when she was born.
Genesis does not describe her childhood, her appearance, her personality, or the moment she first met Cain.
And yet one sentence about her has generated a question that has followed Christians for centuries:
If Adam and Eve were the first human couple...
where did Cain get his wife?
Some people ask it sincerely.
Some whisper it because they are afraid the answer might shake their faith.
Others throw it at Christians like a grenade.
“Cain had a wife? Where did she come from?”
“Was there another civilization?”
“Were there other humans God never mentioned?”
“Did Cain marry someone who wasn't descended from Adam and Eve?”
And sometimes believers panic.
They shouldn't.
Because Genesis never says Cain traveled into some mysterious foreign land and suddenly discovered a completely unrelated woman waiting for him.
That idea is being imported into the story.
Read what the text actually says.
Genesis 4:17 begins:
וַיֵּדַע קַיִן אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ
Vayyeda Qayin et-ishto.
Literally, in the normal biblical idiom:
“And Cain knew his wife.”

The Hebrew word יָדַע — yadaʿ — “to know” can describe intimate marital relations in this context. The same expression appears at the beginning of the chapter when Adam “knew” Eve and she conceived Cain.
Genesis 4:17 continues that Cain's wife conceived and gave birth to Enoch. The Hebrew text does not stop to introduce her ancestry. It simply calls her אִשְׁתּוֹ — ishto — “his wife.”
That distinction matters.
The Bible tells us that Cain had a wife.
It does not tell us her name.
And it does not explicitly say, “Cain married his sister.”
So biblical faithfulness requires us to resist two opposite mistakes.
We should not pretend Scripture gives information it never gives.
But neither should we pretend Scripture gives us no information from which the situation can reasonably be understood.
Because only a few verses later, Genesis gives us the detail people often overlook.
Adam did not have only three children.
Cain, Abel, and Seth are the children emphasized by name in the narrative, but Genesis 5:4 says:
וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת
Vayyoled banim uvanot.
“And he fathered sons and daughters.”
בָּנִים — banim — sons.
בָּנוֹת — banot — daughters.
Not merely Cain.
Not merely Abel.
Not merely Seth.
Sons and daughters.
Genesis says Adam lived hundreds of years after Seth's birth and fathered additional children. The text does not give their names or tell us how many there were. It simply tells us they existed.
Suddenly the supposedly impossible wife is not so impossible.

If Genesis is read according to its own presentation of humanity's beginnings, Cain's wife would have belonged to Adam and Eve's expanding family line. The most straightforward traditional inference is that she was a sister—or potentially another close female relative depending on the chronology assumed.
Notice the wording carefully.
Inference.
Not an explicitly named identification.
Anyone who tells you, “The Bible says Cain's wife was named ______,” has gone beyond Genesis.
Genesis does not give her name.
Anyone who says Genesis 4:17 itself explicitly calls her Cain's sister has also gone beyond the verse.
It doesn't.
What Scripture does tell us is that Adam fathered sons and daughters, and within the Genesis account Adam and Eve stand at the fountainhead of the human family.
That leads naturally to the uncomfortable question.
“Then are you saying members of the first human family married close relatives?”
Within the traditional reading of Genesis, some form of close-relative marriage would have been unavoidable in the earliest generations.
And yes...
to modern ears, that sounds disturbing.
It should.
Because we live on the other side of biblical laws that explicitly prohibit certain close-kin sexual relationships.
Leviticus 18 later establishes boundaries concerning close relatives.
But here is where people can accidentally commit a serious interpretive mistake:
They take a law revealed much later in biblical history and assume that the identical social and legal situation must already have existed at humanity's beginning.
Genesis itself does not say that.

Indeed, later Genesis narratives contain marriages within extended family networks that would sound unusually close to many modern readers. Abraham describes Sarah as his half-sister in Genesis 20:12. Whatever questions these passages raise, they demonstrate why we must allow the biblical text to speak within its own historical storyline rather than silently inserting modern assumptions into every ancient scene.
There is another argument Christians sometimes make: that humanity's earliest genetic condition was sufficiently different that close-relative reproduction initially carried fewer biological risks.
That is possible within some creationist models.
But honesty matters.
Genesis does not explicitly explain Cain's marriage genetically.
The Bible never says, “Cain could marry a close relative because the human genome was nearly perfect.”
That may be offered as a scientific or theological model, but it should not be preached as though Moses wrote it into Genesis 4.
Sometimes defending Scripture requires enough humility to say:
“The Bible doesn't tell us.”
Those five words do not weaken Scripture.
Sometimes they protect us from putting our own ideas into God's mouth.
And perhaps that is where this strange question begins reaching much deeper than Cain's family tree.
Because Cain's wife is not actually the darkest mystery in Genesis 4.
Cain is.
Think about the man standing beside this unnamed woman.
He had already murdered his brother.
Abel's blood had soaked into the ground.
God confronted Cain:
“Where is Abel your brother?”
And Cain answered with words that still expose the human heart:
“I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?”
The first recorded murder in Scripture came not from a stranger attacking another stranger...
but from brother against brother.
Family against family.
Blood spilling blood.
Sin had entered through Adam and Eve's rebellion in Genesis 3, and by Genesis 4 the poison had already reached the next generation.
Jealousy.
Anger.
Murder.
Lying.
Alienation.
Fear.
Exile.
This is the real scandal.
Not merely, “Where did Cain find a wife?”
But:
What happened to the human family after humanity walked away from God?
Genesis answers with terrifying speed.
The first couple hides.
Their son kills.
A brother lies dead.
A mother grieves.
A father buries what no father was created to bury.
And Cain walks eastward carrying the consequences of what he has done.
Then comes one of the strangest transitions imaginable.
Cain has a son.
Cain builds a city.
He names it after Enoch.
The murderer becomes a father.
The wanderer builds.
Human civilization begins moving forward while human sin moves forward with it.
Generations appear.
Technology develops.
Music appears.
Metalworking appears.
Cities rise.
Culture grows.
And yet the human heart remains wounded.
By the time the narrative reaches Lamech, violence has not disappeared.
It has become something to boast about.
Cain's story is therefore not merely an ancient curiosity.
It is a mirror.
We build more sophisticated cities.
We create better machines.
We develop astonishing technology.
We accumulate knowledge.
We produce music, art, wealth, institutions, and empires.
Yet none of those things can perform heart surgery on humanity.
We can put a computer in someone's hand that would have looked like supernatural power to an ancient king...
and that same hand can still destroy another human being.
Cain's deepest problem wasn't that he lacked civilization.
Cain's deepest problem was Cain.
And ours is us.
That is why the Bible does not end in Genesis 4.
Another line continues.
Seth comes.
Generations pass.
Abraham comes.
Israel comes.
David comes.
Prophets cry out.
Promises accumulate.
Human beings continue failing.
Until eventually another Son enters the story.
Jesus Christ.
And suddenly Cain's question becomes part of something infinitely larger.
Cain asks, in effect:
“Am I my brother's keeper?”
Jesus comes and does what fallen humanity continually refuses to do.
He loves.
He serves.
He seeks the lost.
He touches the unclean.
He welcomes sinners.
He gives Himself.
Cain's hands become associated with his brother's blood.
Christ's hands are pierced and His own blood is poured out for sinners.
Abel's blood cried from the ground.
The New Testament deliberately remembers Abel when speaking about Jesus.
Hebrews 12:24 speaks of Jesus and “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.”
Do not rush past that.
Abel's blood testified that something terrible had happened.
A righteous man's blood had been spilled.
Justice cried out.
Then Christ came.
And at Calvary, the truly righteous One willingly shed His blood for the guilty.
Cain deserved judgment.
So do we.
Yet the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
God's answer to guilty sinners is not that sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we ever imagined.
God's answer is that Christ bore judgment so that sinners who repent and trust Him can receive forgiveness they could never purchase for themselves.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the blood on our hands isn't there.
Grace is God cleansing what we could never wash away.
Maybe you clicked this article because you wanted an answer about Cain's wife.
Maybe you expected archaeology.
Genealogy.
Hebrew.
An argument.
Instead, Genesis quietly dragged all of us into the crime scene.
Because Cain's story forces a more personal question.
What is hiding inside you?
Maybe you've never murdered anyone.
But Jesus goes beneath the visible act and confronts the heart.
Anger.
Hatred.
Contempt.
Jealousy.
Bitterness.
The secret pleasure you feel when someone who hurt you finally suffers.
The resentment you have rehearsed for years.
The apology you refuse to give.
The person you cannot forgive.
The private sin nobody at church knows exists.
The browser history.
The hidden relationship.
The addiction.
The pride.
The double life.
The smile everyone sees...
and the war nobody sees.
We are very good at asking questions about Cain because questions about ancient people feel safe.
But Scripture has a frightening habit of turning the question around.
You came asking:
“Who was Cain's wife?”
And somewhere along the way God may be asking:
“What is happening inside your heart?”
That question matters infinitely more.
You can correctly explain Genesis 4 and still be far from Christ.
You can know Hebrew words and never know the Savior.
You can win an argument with a skeptic and lose the battle happening inside your own soul.
You can defend the Bible publicly while disobeying its Author privately.
And if that sentence hurt...
don't run from it.
Run to Jesus.
Cain tried to live east of Eden carrying what he had become.
You do not have to spend your life running from God.
Christ calls sinners home.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the moment you finally stop defending the prison that is killing you.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the religious pride.
Bring Him the wounds you turned into weapons.
Bring Him the thing you desperately hope nobody discovers.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus can rewrite what yesterday does to tomorrow.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
From scandal...
to grace.
From guilt...
to forgiveness.
From hiding...
to confession.
From death...
to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
but because someone may click because of Cain and unexpectedly encounter Christ.
Difficult questions return, and when they do, you should be able to return to Scripture rather than fear.
Your giving before God is a matter of faithful stewardship, conscience, worship, and the teaching of Scripture.
But voluntarily supporting Gospel work can be a genuine act of generosity.
And sharing costs you nothing.
A share can travel farther than you can.
One person shares.
Another person stops scrolling.
A skeptic starts reading because the title irritates him.
A wounded Christian keeps reading because something feels painfully familiar.
A hidden sinner encounters the Gospel.
A conversation begins.
A Bible opens.
A prayer happens.
You may never know what God does with something as simple as pressing Share.
You cannot buy God's favor.
You cannot purchase salvation.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support the work because you freely believe the work is worth supporting.
Share because someone needs truth.
Give because you want the Gospel carried farther.
Pray because no ministry can manufacture what only the Holy Spirit can do.
And when you encounter difficult questions about Scripture, don't panic.
Open the Bible.
Read what it actually says.
Look carefully at the words.
Distinguish revelation from assumption.
Be courageous enough to say what Scripture says...
and humble enough to stop where Scripture stops.
So...
who was Cain's wife?
Genesis never gives us her name.

Genesis 4 simply identifies her as Cain's wife, while Genesis 5 explicitly tells us Adam fathered sons and daughters. Within the traditional reading in which Adam and Eve stand at the beginning of the human family, the natural conclusion is that Cain married within that first expanding family—most likely a sister or other close female relative. Anything more specific than that should be identified as interpretation or tradition rather than an explicit statement of Genesis.
But perhaps the unnamed woman was never the most important mystery on the page.
Perhaps the greater mystery is how quickly sin shattered the first family...
and how relentlessly God continued moving history toward redemption.
From Adam's rebellion...
through Cain's bloodstained field...
through generations of sinners...
through prophets and promises...
until outside Jerusalem another innocent Man's blood touched the earth.
Except this time...
the blood did not merely cry out concerning the guilty.
It was poured out for the guilty.
For Cain-like hearts.
For jealous hearts.
For angry hearts.
For sexually broken hearts.
For religious hearts.
For skeptical hearts.
For hypocritical hearts.
For your heart.
For mine.
And perhaps that is what you should remember when you close this article:
The Bible's greatest wonder is not where Cain found his wife—it is that after everything humanity became, God still came looking for us.
Because somewhere tonight, another person is hiding east of Eden...
and they need to know there is still a road home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN ENJOY SEX? The Bible’s Answer Is More Surprising Than Shame-Based Religion Suggests
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN ENJOY SEX? The Bible’s Answer Is More Surprising Than Shame-Based Religion Suggests

Some Christians learned how to feel guilty about sex before they ever learned what God actually said about it. And what Scripture says may force us to confront both our secret lust and our unnecessary shame.
There are questions Christians ask out loud.
Then there are questions they type into a search bar when nobody is watching.
Questions they would never ask during Bible study.
Questions they would be terrified to ask their pastor.
Questions married Christians sometimes carry silently for years because somewhere along the way they absorbed the idea that holiness means pretending sexuality barely exists.
And one of those questions is painfully simple:
Can a Christian actually enjoy sex?
Not merely tolerate it.
Not reluctantly participate because married people are “supposed to.”
Enjoy it.
Desire your husband.
Desire your wife.
Laugh together.
Long for each other.
Experience pleasure without feeling as though God must be standing somewhere in heaven disappointed that you enjoyed something physical.
For some believers, even reading those sentences produces discomfort.
And that discomfort tells a story.
Because many Christians were taught something Scripture itself never teaches:
that sex is basically dirty, marriage simply makes it permissible, and truly spiritual Christians should avoid talking about it.
But open your Bible.
Really open it.
Not through the filter of pornography.
Not through the filter of hookup culture.
Not through the filter of religious embarrassment either.
Let Scripture speak.
And something astonishing appears.
The God who says no to sexual immorality is also the God who created sexual intimacy.
The God who establishes boundaries around sexuality is the same God who placed desire inside covenant.
Biblical holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is the redemption of the whole person—including our desires—under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Before there was pornography, adultery, prostitution, exploitation, lust, sexual trauma, broken marriages, secret browser histories, or bedrooms filled with resentment, there was a garden.
And Scripture says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24.
The Hebrew expression translated “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
Not two people using each other.
Not one person taking while another submits unwillingly.
Not strangers consuming bodies.
A covenant union in which two lives are joined.
And notice when this happens.
Before Genesis 3.
Before humanity falls.
Before sin enters the human story.
That matters enormously.
Sexual union was not invented by Satan.
Satan corrupts what God creates.
Sexuality does not originate in pornography.
Pornography parasitically distorts something God made.
Desire itself is not evidence that you are spiritually defective.
The question is what governs that desire.
Is it ruled by Christ—or does it rule you?
Is it covenantal—or consuming?
Does it love—or merely take?
Does it honor another image-bearer—or turn that person into an object?
That distinction changes everything.
Because Christianity does not teach, “Your body is evil.”
Christianity teaches something far more demanding and far more beautiful:
Your body belongs to God.
Paul writes, “your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost” and then reaches his conclusion:
“therefore glorify God in your body.”
That means Jesus does not merely want Sunday morning.
He wants Monday night.
He wants your thoughts.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your browser history.
Your dating life.
Your marriage.
Your bedroom.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your secrets.
Everything.
And that may sound frightening until you understand the character of the One asking for it.
Jesus does not expose darkness because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He brings darkness into the light because darkness is where chains survive.
Some of you know exactly what those chains feel like.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your church friends would never imagine it.
Maybe you learned sexuality through pornography before anyone ever taught you biblical intimacy.
Maybe what should have been associated with covenant became associated with secrecy.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe someone crossed yours.
Maybe sex became performance.
Maybe it became leverage.
Maybe it became something demanded from you.
Maybe years of rejection made you feel undesirable.
Maybe betrayal destroyed your ability to trust.
Maybe religious shame convinced you that even healthy desire inside marriage somehow makes you less spiritual.
Maybe you love Jesus deeply...
but there is an entire room inside your heart you have never allowed Him to enter.
Keep reading.
Because the Gospel was made for locked rooms.
Consider the Song of Songs.
Entire generations of Christians have sometimes seemed almost embarrassed that this book is in the Bible.
Yet there it remains.
A biblical poem filled with attraction, longing, beauty, anticipation, affection, delight, and marital love.
The woman declares:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me.”
Song of Songs 7:10.
Read that slowly.
Desire.
In Scripture.
The Bible is not embarrassed by covenant love.
We are.
And sometimes Christians have confused embarrassment with holiness.
They are not the same thing.
Biblical sexuality has boundaries precisely because sexuality has enormous power.
Fire inside a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire released through the house can destroy it.
The existence of boundaries does not prove that fire is evil.
It proves that fire matters.
That is why Scripture can celebrate marital intimacy and condemn sexual immorality without contradiction.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept undefiled, while warning that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
The biblical answer therefore is not:
“Sex is dirty.”
Nor is it:
“Anything consensual must therefore be holy.”
Scripture gives us something richer.

Sexual intimacy belongs inside the covenant of marriage, where faithfulness, exclusivity, love, honor, responsibility, and mutual self-giving surround something powerful enough to join bodies and touch souls.
Then Paul says something in 1 Corinthians 7 that would have been remarkable in his world.
He does not speak only about what a wife owes her husband.
He immediately makes the responsibility reciprocal.
The husband owes his wife marital affection too.
Then Paul says something even more striking.
The husband does not possess absolute autonomous authority over his own body in marriage—and neither does the wife.
Paul deliberately mirrors the language.
The Greek text uses the verb ἐξουσιάζει — exousiazei, from exousiazō, carrying the idea of exercising authority.
His argument moves in both directions.
Wife toward husband.
Husband toward wife.
Mutuality.
Self-giving.
Belonging.
This is profoundly different from using Scripture to justify sexual entitlement.
First Corinthians 7 must never be weaponized to tell an abused, frightened, sick, traumatized, or unwilling spouse that Christianity requires sexual coercion.
Paul himself speaks of abstaining temporarily ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou—by agreement, by mutual consent.
Christian intimacy cannot be separated from Christian love.
And Christian love “seeketh not her own.”
Love does not say:
“You owe me your body, therefore your fear does not matter.”
Love asks:
“How can I cherish you?”
Love listens.
Love protects.
Love is patient.
Love refuses humiliation.
Love refuses coercion.
Love cares whether the other person feels safe.
Love is not merely interested in experiencing pleasure.
Love wants to give.
And perhaps this is where some marriages need healing more than another argument about frequency.
Sometimes the real problem is not sex.
It is everything that enters the bedroom before the couple does.
Resentment enters.
Exhaustion enters.
Unforgiveness enters.
Body insecurity enters.
Past trauma enters.
Pornography enters.
Comparison enters.
Years of criticism enter.
Children screaming outside the door enter.
Financial stress enters.
Betrayal enters.
Silence enters.
Then two people wonder why intimacy feels complicated.
Sometimes healing begins outside the bedroom.
With repentance.
With listening.
With forgiveness.
With counseling.
With patience.
With rebuilding trust.
With learning to see your spouse as a person to cherish rather than a need to satisfy.
And sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is stop asking, “Why am I not getting what I want?” and begin asking, “What is happening inside the heart of the person I promised to love?”
That is where Jesus enters the conversation.
Because Christianity is not ultimately a sexual-improvement program.
It is a redemption story.
And all of us need redemption.
The sexually immoral need Jesus.
The self-righteous need Jesus.
The porn-addicted need Jesus.
The sexually ashamed need Jesus.
The adulterer needs Jesus.
The betrayed spouse needs Jesus.
The virgin needs Jesus.
The married couple needs Jesus.
The single Christian needs Jesus.
The person carrying sexual trauma needs Jesus.
The person secretly fantasizing about someone else's spouse needs Jesus.
The person who has failed repeatedly needs Jesus.
Every road eventually arrives at the same cross.
And here comes the scandal.
Jesus already knows.
That thing you desperately hope nobody discovers?
He knows.
The memories.
The websites.
The fantasies.
The affair.
The compromise.
The shame.
The confusion.
The night you wish you could erase.
The thing done to you that you still struggle to speak about.
He knows.
And still Christ went to the cross.
Not to tell us sin does not matter.
The cross proves sin matters more than we imagined.
But the cross also proves grace reaches farther than we imagined.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could rename bondage “freedom.”
He shed His blood to actually set captives free.
Grace does not merely forgive us while leaving us chained.
Grace teaches us to walk differently.
This is why the Gospel speaks to sexuality so powerfully.
Jesus does not say:
“Hide better.”
He says:
“Come.”
Jesus does not say:
“Clean yourself sufficiently and perhaps I will receive you.”
He calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning around because you finally realize the road you are walking is killing something precious.
Maybe that road is pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe lust.
Maybe sexual selfishness inside marriage.
Maybe using sex as manipulation.
Maybe withholding affection as punishment.
Maybe shame so deep that you cannot believe God could restore what has been wounded.
Bring it to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become respectable.
Now.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people can become slightly better.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is transformation.
And there is no category of sexual sin that somehow places a repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ's blood.
Read 1 Corinthians 6.
Paul lists people marked by serious sin, including sexual sin.
Then come some of the most beautiful words in the New Testament:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
That word should make somebody cry.
Your sin can describe where Christ found you without being permitted to dictate where Christ is taking you.
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified…”
That is Christianity.
Not pretending you were never dirty.
Washed.
Not pretending you never wandered.
Brought home.
Not pretending you never broke anything.
Redeemed.
So can Christians enjoy sex?
Within biblical marriage, yes.
Not guiltily tolerating God's supposedly embarrassing concession.
Enjoying a good gift under the lordship of the Giver.
A husband can delight in his wife.
A wife can delight in her husband.
They can desire one another.
They can communicate.
They can laugh.
They can be affectionate.
They can learn each other patiently.
They can pursue mutually loving intimacy without believing pleasure itself makes them unholy.
But Christian freedom is never permission to detach sexuality from holiness.
The same Bible that celebrates marital desire also commands believers to flee sexual immorality.
The same God who created pleasure also commands faithfulness.
And maybe that combination is exactly what our generation desperately needs.
Because the world often offers desire without covenant.
Religion sometimes offers covenant without delight.
Scripture refuses both distortions.
It gives us covenant and delight.
Holiness and tenderness.
Boundaries and beauty.
Truth and grace.
And Jesus at the center of all of it.
If this article uncovered something you have kept buried, you do not need to describe private sexual details publicly. But you do not have to keep pretending spiritually either.
Let those words become a confession of hope.
No explanation required.
Then make that comment mean something when the screen goes dark.
Pray.
Repent.
Open Scripture.
Seek trustworthy pastoral help or professional counseling where wounds, trauma, addiction, betrayal, or marital breakdown require deeper care.
Tell the truth to the people who appropriately need to know it.
Bring darkness into light.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
We glorify God through faith, obedience, love, worship, generosity, truth, and lives surrendered to Christ—not by financially supporting a particular page.
Someone may believe sexual failure has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone's marriage may be bleeding behind smiling photographs.
Someone may have spent twenty years believing that what was done to them made them dirty.
Someone may desperately need to discover that Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners and heals wounded hearts.
If you want to support that mission and continue walking with this community:
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Jesus.
If supporting this ministry enables more people to hear about Him, we are grateful.
But the mission is not building customers.
The mission is pointing sinners toward Christ.
Because maybe the deepest question underneath “Can a Christian enjoy sex?” was never really about sex.
Maybe the question underneath it was:
“Can Jesus have this part of me too?”
Your desire.
Your marriage.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your failures.
Your sexuality.
Your loneliness.
Your body.
Your shame.
Your future.
Yes.
Especially that part.
Bring it under His lordship.
Bring the sin that needs repentance.
Bring the wound that needs healing.
Bring the marriage that needs restoration.
Bring the shame that keeps whispering you are permanently contaminated.
Bring the desires that need to be reordered.
Bring the whole story.
Because Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to read aloud.
And when surrendered to Him, the ugliest chapter does not have to become the final chapter.
The place where shame told you to hide may become the very place where grace teaches you to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Keep Saying, “We Just Fell Out of Love”—But Love Was Never Meant to Be Only Something You Fall Into
paragraphs: You Keep Saying, “We Just Fell Out of Love”—But Love Was Never Meant to Be Only Something You Fall Into
Maybe the most dangerous moment in a marriage isn't when the butterflies disappear. Maybe it's when two people mistake their disappearance for proof that love has died.
“We just fell out of love.”
There it is.
Five words that can carry years of disappointment.
Five words spoken across kitchen tables, inside parked cars, in counseling rooms, through tears, sometimes with anger, sometimes with frightening calm.
“We don't hate each other.”
“We're just different now.”
“The feeling isn't there anymore.”
“I care about them. I'm just not in love anymore.”
And sometimes behind those words is something terribly serious.
Betrayal.
Abuse.
Coercion.
Addiction.
Repeated adultery.
Manipulation.
Fear.
A home where someone no longer feels safe.

Those realities should never be minimized with a sentimental Christian slogan. Scripture does not give anyone permission to use “covenant” as a weapon for keeping another person silent while evil continues unchecked. Biblical love “does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). Jesus Himself addressed sexual immorality when teaching about divorce, and Paul addressed abandonment and said that God has called His people to peace (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15).
So this article is not telling an abused spouse to endure violence.
It is not telling someone in danger to remain in danger.
It is not pretending every broken marriage has the same story.
Wisdom, truthful pastoral care, appropriate professional help, lawful protection, accountability, and immediate safety can be necessary when serious harm is present.
But there is another marriage story happening quietly all around us.
No bruises.
No terror.
No secret second family.
No catastrophic betrayal.
Just distance.
Two people who once couldn't stop talking now struggle to find anything to say.
The person whose name once made your heart race walks through the front door, and you barely look up.
The hand you once reached for automatically now feels unfamiliar.
You remember staying awake until two in the morning because neither of you wanted to hang up.
Now you lie inches apart in the same bed...
scrolling separate screens...
living separate emotional lives...
wondering where “us” went.
And eventually someone whispers the sentence:
“We fell out of love.”
But what if part of the problem is hidden inside the sentence itself?
We fell in love.
We fell out of love.
As though love were a hole in the ground.
As though nobody chose anything.
As though love simply happened to us, and then one morning stopped happening.
But when Paul describes love in 1 Corinthians 13, something startling appears in the original Greek.
He writes:
Hē agapē makrothymei, chrēsteuetai hē agapē…
“Love is patient and kind…”
Then Paul continues:
“πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστεύει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει.”
Panta stegei, panta pisteuei, panta elpizei, panta hypomenei.
Love bears.
Love believes.
Love hopes.
Love endures.
Notice what Scripture is doing.
Love isn't merely being described as something you feel.
Love is doing things.
It is acting.
Patient.
Kind.
Refusing envy.
Refusing arrogance.
Refusing selfishness.
Refusing to celebrate wrongdoing.
Rejoicing when truth wins.
Bearing.
Believing.
Hoping.
Enduring.
That doesn't mean emotion is irrelevant.
Romantic affection is beautiful.
Desire matters.
Tenderness matters.
Enjoying your spouse matters.
Missing them matters.
Laughing together matters.
Holding hands matters.
The butterflies were never evil.
They just weren't strong enough to carry a covenant by themselves.
Because feelings are extraordinary servants...
and terrible gods.
Feelings change when you're tired.
Feelings change when the baby hasn't slept.
Feelings change when bills arrive.
Feelings change after disappointment.
Feelings change when your body changes.
Feelings change when work becomes crushing.
Feelings change through grief.
Feelings change when two imperfect people spend years discovering exactly how imperfect the other person really is.
The wedding photographs don't show that part.
They capture the dress.
The suit.
The flowers.
The smiling families.
The trembling hands.
The vows.
The kiss.
Nobody photographs the argument six years later at 11:47 p.m.
Nobody frames the month when intimacy becomes difficult.
Nobody puts the mortgage crisis in the wedding album.
Nobody posts the silence after somebody says something cruel and immediately wishes they could pull the words back into their mouth.
Nobody warns you that sometimes the person you promised to love will become difficult to love.
And neither did they realize that sometimes...
so would you.
That is where the Gospel begins getting painfully close.
Because Christianity does not begin with the announcement that lovable people deserved to be loved.
It begins with grace.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
Read that slowly.
Christ did not wait for humanity to become attractive enough for Calvary.
He loved sinners.
He moved toward rebels.
He gave Himself for people who could never repay Him.
And that does not mean a spouse becomes another spouse's savior.
Jesus alone is Savior.
Your marriage cannot bear the weight of being your gospel.
Your husband is not Jesus.
Your wife is not Jesus.
And you are not Jesus either.
But Christian marriage is called to look toward Him.
That is why Paul's command in Ephesians is so breathtaking:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Not merely...
Love her while she thrills you.
Love her while everything is easy.
Love her while she looks exactly as she did at twenty-five.
Love her while she never disappoints you.
Love her while your emotional chemistry remains permanently electrifying.
No.
Look at Christ.
And that changes the question.
The question stops being only:
“Do I still feel what I felt?”
And becomes:
“What does faithfulness to Jesus require of me here?”
Sometimes the answer may involve repentance.
Sometimes confession.
Sometimes forgiveness.
Sometimes boundaries.
Sometimes counseling.
Sometimes confronting serious sin rather than pretending it isn't happening.
Sometimes rebuilding trust one agonizing brick at a time.
Sometimes seeking safety because what is happening is genuinely dangerous.
And sometimes...
sometimes the answer is painfully ordinary.
Put the phone down.
Look at your spouse.
Listen again.
Apologize without adding “but.”
Stop keeping score.
Stop weaponizing mistakes from eight years ago.
Ask what has been hurting them.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Remember that neglect can become a habit long before anybody calls it a crisis.
Do something kind without calculating whether they deserve it.
Because perhaps you haven't entirely “fallen out of love.”
Perhaps love has been buried beneath exhaustion.
Beneath resentment.
Beneath familiarity.
Beneath untreated wounds.
Beneath pride.
Beneath years of small moments when both people waited for the other one to move first.
“I'll be affectionate when she changes.”
“I'll respect him when he earns it.”
“I'll apologize when they apologize.”
“I'll try when they start trying.”
And two people sit across from one another...
starving beside a table where neither is willing to serve first.
Then Jesus walks into the story.
Not as decoration.
Not as a religious slogan pasted over marital dysfunction.
As Lord.
As the crucified Christ who destroys our illusion that love must always wait to receive before it gives.
The Gospel exposes both of us.
Maybe your spouse has sinned against you.
Maybe you have sinned against your spouse.
Maybe both statements are painfully true.
Grace does not call evil good.
Forgiveness does not rename abuse “love.”
Reconciliation does not mean trust magically returns without repentance, truth, accountability, or change.
And biblical endurance does not require pretending everything is fine when everything is bleeding.
Remember Paul's words.
Love “rejoices with the truth.”
Truth matters.
Repentance matters.
Safety matters.
Justice matters.
Accountability matters.
But so does grace.
And grace asks an uncomfortable question of the person staring into the mirror:
Have I become more committed to documenting my spouse's failures than confronting my own?
Because 1 Corinthians 13 says love “does not count up wrongdoing.”
The Greek expression is:
“οὐ λογίζεται τὸ κακόν”
ou logizetai to kakon.
It carries the picture of not reckoning or keeping an account of the wrong.
That doesn't mean pretending the wrong never happened.
It doesn't mean removing necessary consequences.
It doesn't mean destroying boundaries.
It means love refuses to make resentment its permanent bookkeeping system.
Some marriages have become emotional accounting departments.
You hurt me Tuesday.
I ignored you Wednesday.
You embarrassed me in 2022.
I withheld affection because of what happened in 2023.
You owe me.
I owe you.
Nobody forgives.
Nobody forgets the ledger.
Nobody knows how to come home anymore.
And suddenly the Cross stands between two accountants carrying books full of debt.
Because that is precisely what the Gospel confronts in us.
We owed a debt we could not pay.
Jesus did not excuse our sin.
He bore judgment for sin.
At Calvary, grace was not God announcing that sin didn't matter.
The Cross proves exactly how much it mattered.
And resurrection proves sin does not get the final word.
That is why Christian hope for a wounded marriage is not naïve optimism.
It isn't:
“Pretend nothing happened.”
It is:
Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
Dead dreams.
Dead tenderness.
Dead honesty.
Dead trust.
Dead places inside human beings.
None of these intimidate the One who walked out of a grave.
Does that mean every marriage will be restored?
Scripture never gives us permission to promise that.
Human beings can refuse repentance.
Hearts can remain hardened.
Consequences can become profound.
Some situations involve realities far more complicated than an article could responsibly address.
But we can say this:
Never declare Jesus powerless merely because your feelings changed.
Maybe what died was not love.
Maybe what died was infatuation.
Maybe what died was novelty.
Maybe what died was the fantasy that another human being could continuously make you feel complete.
And maybe...
just maybe...
God is inviting you into something deeper than the love story you imagined.
A love with scars.
A love that learned repentance.
A love that survived truth.
A love that discovered forgiveness isn't weakness.
A love that stopped asking, “What am I getting?” long enough to ask, “Jesus, who are You calling me to become?”
Maybe tonight you need to sit beside the person you've been emotionally avoiding.
Maybe you need to say:
“I've been blaming you for everything, and that isn't true.”
Maybe:
“I have neglected you.”
Maybe:
“I need help.”
Maybe:
“I forgive you, but rebuilding trust will take time.”
Maybe:
“What happened to us?”
Maybe simply:
“Can we pray?”
And perhaps the first prayer doesn't sound impressive.
Maybe it's barely audible.
“Jesus...
we don't know how to fix this.
But we need You.”
That prayer may contain more hope than another thousand accusations.
Because the center of Christianity has never been human beings becoming impressive enough to save themselves.
It is Christ coming for people who cannot save themselves.
This is why the phrase “we fell out of love” deserves deeper examination.
You can fall out of emotional intensity.
You can lose attraction.
You can become distant.
You can become exhausted.
You can become disappointed.
You can become wounded.
Those experiences are real.
But biblical love cannot be reduced to emotional weather.
Love has hands.
Love has knees that bend in prayer.
Love has a mouth that says, “I was wrong.”
Love has ears that listen.
Love tells the truth.
Love refuses wrongdoing.
Love seeks another's good.
Love forgives without calling evil harmless.
Love hopes without becoming foolish.
Love endures without making an idol of suffering.
And Christian love keeps looking toward Jesus.
So if this article exposed something you have been hiding behind the sentence “we just fell out of love,” don't turn conviction into shame.
Take it to Christ.
Maybe you need to repent.
Maybe you need to forgive.
Maybe you need wise counseling.
Maybe you need to confess something you've hidden.
Maybe you need to pursue safety and serious outside help because your situation involves abuse or danger.
Maybe you need to stop waiting for an emotion and begin practicing the kind of love Scripture describes.
Whatever the truth is...
bring the truth to Jesus.
He already knows.
And grace is still available.
Not because a comment magically repairs a marriage.
But because sometimes honesty begins when someone finally stops pretending.
Somebody reading silently tonight may desperately need evidence that difficult chapters don't always become final chapters.

Not because every sentence applies to every marriage, but because there may come a night when emotion is screaming louder than covenant and you need to return to Scripture before making decisions from pain alone.
Someone in your circle may be smiling in photographs while privately wondering whether their marriage is already dead.
Don't share it to shame them.
Share it so they remember where hope ultimately lives.
In Jesus Christ.

Supporting Gospel work should never replace giving faithfully, serving your local church, caring for your family, or helping people in genuine need. And no one purchases God's favor by supporting a ministry.
But if God has used this work to strengthen you, voluntary support is one practical way you can help Gospel Warrior continue putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who need it.
If these messages strengthen your walk with Christ, stay close.
Invite your husband or wife.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend whose marriage is struggling.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the seeker who isn't even sure what they believe yet.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the greatest love story in Scripture isn't about two flawless people who never stopped feeling butterflies.
It is about a holy Savior pursuing sinners, paying their debt at a cross, rising from a grave, forgiving those who repent and believe, and making broken people new.
Maybe your marriage story contains chapters you wish you could tear out.
Maybe there are sentences written in anger.
Pages stained by tears.
Paragraphs of silence.
Years you cannot recover.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But you can surrender today to Christ.
And sometimes grace begins with two trembling words:
“Jesus, help.”
Because when the feeling fades, covenant asks what emotion alone never had the strength to answer:
Will I let Jesus teach me what love becomes when falling is over and faithful loving begins?
The chapter that feels like the end may become the very page where grace teaches you how deeply Jesus can rewrite a surrendered story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID THE EVIL YOU FEAR IS CLOSER THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs:
JESUS SAID THE EVIL YOU FEAR IS CLOSER THAN YOU THINK
What Christ Meant When He Said Evil Comes From Within the Heart—and Why the Most Frightening Sinner You Will Ever Have to Face May Be the One Looking Back at You in the Mirror
There is something Jesus said that destroys one of the most comforting lies we tell ourselves.
It is the lie that evil is mostly “out there.”
In corrupt people.
In terrible families.
In violent criminals.
In politicians we despise.
In celebrities who scandalize us.
In people whose sins happen to be more visible than ours.
We look at someone who destroyed a marriage and think, I would never do that.
We hear about someone caught stealing and think, What kind of person does something like that?
We watch another Christian fall publicly and quietly wonder how someone who claimed to love God could become capable of such hypocrisy.
And somewhere beneath all that disappointment can hide a dangerous little assumption:
I am different.
Then Jesus speaks.
And suddenly there is nowhere left to hide.
Because Christ does not merely point toward the darkness surrounding humanity.
He points toward something inside humanity.
“From within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts…”
Mark 7:21.
The Greek is even more arresting:
ἔσωθεν γὰρ ἐκ τῆς καρδίας τῶν ἀνθρώπων
esōthen gar ek tēs kardias tōn anthrōpōn
“For from within, out of the heart of human beings…”
That word ἔσωθεν — esōthen means “from within,” “from the inside.”
And καρδία — kardia, “heart,” is not merely the organ beating inside your chest, nor is it simply the modern idea of your emotions.
In biblical thought, the heart describes the inner person—the center from which desires, intentions, thoughts, commitments, and moral decisions emerge.
Jesus was performing spiritual surgery.
And He did not allow us to remain spectators.
He put every human heart on the operating table.
Including yours.
Including mine.
That is what makes Mark 7 so uncomfortable.
Jesus had been confronted over ritual purity. His disciples were being criticized because they ate without following the traditional ceremonial handwashing practices of the elders.
The controversy looked external.
Hands.
Food.
Purity.
Tradition.
But Jesus drove the conversation somewhere much deeper.
He essentially forced His hearers to confront a question far more frightening than, “What touched me?”
The question became:
What is living inside me?
Jesus said what enters a person from outside does not enter the heart but the stomach. Then He delivered the diagnosis:
“What comes out of a person is what defiles him.”
And then comes the list.
Not a comfortable list.
Not a list designed to make religious people feel superior.
A mirror.
διαλογισμοὶ οἱ κακοί — dialogismoi hoi kakoi
Evil thoughts.
Then sexual immorality.
Theft.
Murder.
Adultery.
Coveting.
Wickedness.
Deceit.
Sensuality.
Envy.
Slander.
Pride.
Foolishness.
And Jesus concludes:
“All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.”
Mark 7:23.
Read that slowly.
Jesus did not say every person commits every conceivable evil act.
He did not say temptation itself is identical to committing sin.
He did not teach that every intrusive or unwanted thought makes someone guilty of carrying out the evil it depicts.
And He certainly was not giving Christians permission to look at suffering people and accuse them of secretly wanting every darkness that crosses their minds.
His point is deeper.
Humanity's fundamental moral problem cannot be solved merely by controlling the environment around us because sin is not merely an environmental contamination.
Something has gone wrong within us.
And that changes everything.
Because we are remarkably talented at blaming what is outside.
“I became angry because of what she said.”
“I lied because I was under pressure.”
“I looked because it appeared on my screen.”
“I became bitter because they hurt me.”
“I cheated because my marriage was already falling apart.”
“I gossip because what I said was true.”
“I became obsessed with money because I need security.”
“I haven't forgiven because they don't deserve forgiveness.”
And sometimes the wounds behind those sentences are painfully real.
People really betray us.
People really abuse trust.
People really abandon families.
People really manipulate.
People really traumatize others.
Jesus never requires us to call evil good.
But there is a difference between explaining the circumstances in which sin surfaced and identifying the source from which sin came.
Pressure can reveal something without creating it.
Imagine squeezing a bottle.
What comes out?
Whatever was inside.
The pressure explains why the contents appeared at that moment.
But the pressure did not manufacture the contents.
That is why some of the most revealing moments of your spiritual life may be the moments you wish everyone would forget.
The argument when something vicious came out of your mouth.
The private browser history nobody knows exists.
The jealousy you felt when your friend's prayer was answered before yours.
The strange satisfaction when someone who hurt you finally suffered.
The lie that escaped almost effortlessly.
The resentment you rehearse while smiling politely.
The secret fantasy.
The hidden greed.
The spiritual pride that whispers, At least I'm not like them.
Those moments can be terrifying because sometimes what shocks us most is not what somebody did to us.
It is what came out of us afterward.
Have you ever said something in anger and five minutes later wondered:
Where did that come from?
Jesus answered that question two thousand years ago.
From within.
That does not mean circumstances are irrelevant.
It means circumstances are insufficient as an explanation for our moral condition.
And here is where Christianity becomes radically different from mere behavior management.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave better.
He came because sinners need something far deeper than improved appearances.
We need reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
A new heart.
A new life.
We need grace.
The Old Testament had already prepared us for this diagnosis.
Jeremiah declared:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?”
Jeremiah 17:9.
The Hebrew word translated “heart” is לֵב — lev, a word frequently referring to the inner person—the seat of thought, will, desire, and moral orientation.
Centuries before Jesus stood before that crowd, God had already promised through Ezekiel something astonishing:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you…”
Ezekiel 36:26.
Notice the location of God's promised work.
Within.
Human rebellion comes from within.
God promises renewal within.
And then Jesus comes.
This is where the story becomes breathtaking.
Because the One exposing the human heart is the very One who came to save human beings.
The Physician giving the diagnosis came carrying the cure.
Christianity does not say, “Your heart has darkness in it, so make yourself worthy enough for God.”
That would leave every one of us condemned.
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
God knows exactly what is inside you.
And Christ came anyway.
He knows the thought you would be horrified to have projected onto a screen.
He knows the bitterness underneath your worship songs.
He knows how much of your generosity secretly wants recognition.
He knows the jealousy beneath the congratulations.
He knows the pride hidden inside your theology.
He knows the difference between the person everyone applauds and the person who exists when nobody is watching.
There has never been a moment when Jesus was deceived about you.
And still He went to the cross.
That is scandalous grace.
We spend enormous energy editing ourselves for human approval.
Jesus walked straight past the edited version.
Straight into the heart.
And rather than pretending our corruption wasn't serious, He went to Calvary because it was.
The cross simultaneously destroys two lies.
The first is:
My sin isn't really that bad.
Look at the cross.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required the saving work of Christ.
But the cross destroys another lie too:
My sin is so bad that Jesus could never want me.
Look again at the cross.
He already knew.
And He came.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is finally agreeing with God about what has been killing you.
It is laying down the exhausting defense.
No more blaming everyone else.
No more polishing the outside while starving the inside.
No more carefully managed Christianity.
No more pretending the pornography is harmless.
No more baptizing greed as ambition.
No more calling gossip “concern.”
No more disguising unforgiveness as discernment.
No more calling pride “strong convictions.”
No more performing holiness while secretly feeding what crucified your Savior.
Just truth.
Jesus, this is in me.
And that confession can feel terrifying.
Until you remember who is standing in front of you.
Jesus Christ.
The friend of sinners.
The Lamb of God.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One who did not merely come to expose sinners but to redeem them.
Scripture says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Not conceal.
Confess.
Not perform.
Come.
Not repair yourself enough to deserve mercy.
Receive mercy through Christ.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace did not pretend the denial never happened.
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
Grace did not rename persecution as an innocent mistake.
Christ transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The Gospel never needs to make sin smaller in order to make grace beautiful.
Grace is beautiful precisely because our sin is real and Christ is sufficient.
Maybe that is why this teaching of Jesus feels so personal.
Because somewhere inside you there may be a room you keep locked.
You pray.
You worship.
You post verses.
You encourage people.
You tell everyone you are okay.
But there is a door inside your heart you hope Jesus never opens.
Maybe bitterness lives there.
Maybe lust.
Maybe envy.
Maybe pride.
Maybe hatred.
Maybe secret compromise.
Maybe shame over something you already did.
Maybe you have spent years blaming your darkness on the people who wounded you because admitting what has grown inside your own heart feels unbearable.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already sees the room.
The Gospel is not Jesus discovering your secret and walking away disgusted.
The Gospel is Jesus knowing the truth and calling you out of hiding.
You cannot shock the Savior who carried the sins of His people to Calvary.
But neither can you follow Him faithfully while demanding permission to keep cherishing what He calls you to surrender.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace brings us to the One who forgives and transforms.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
Maybe it needs honesty.
Jesus, search me.
Show me what I keep blaming on everybody else.
Expose what I have learned to excuse.
Forgive me.
Cleanse me.
Change my desires.
Teach me to hate what destroys communion with You and love what pleases You.
Create in me a clean heart.
I cannot save myself.
I need You.
That is not weakness.
That is where surrender begins.
And perhaps someone reading this has never truly trusted Christ at all.
You have known Christian language.
Maybe Christian culture.
Maybe church attendance.
Maybe religious habits.
But Christianity is not ultimately the project of making your exterior religious enough to compensate for what is inside.
You need Jesus.
The crucified and risen Christ calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the real you.
Not the Instagram version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version your family thinks exists.
The real one.
Turn from sin.
Trust Christ.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And follow Him.
Then something extraordinary begins.
God does not merely address what comes out of us.
He transforms us from within.
The Spirit produces new fruit.
Old desires are confronted.
New affections grow.
Repentance becomes a way of life.
Forgiveness replaces vengeance.
Generosity attacks greed.
Humility begins suffocating pride.
Truth replaces deception.
Purity goes to war against lust.
Love begins occupying territory hatred once controlled.
Not instant perfection.
Real transformation.
Sometimes slow.
Sometimes painful.
Sometimes involving tears, confession, accountability, restitution, and getting back up after another battle.
But Christ does not merely repaint tombs.
He raises the dead.
Stay in front of the mirror.
What has been coming out of your heart lately?
When you are ignored?
When somebody corrects you?
When another person succeeds?
When nobody can see your screen?
When someone wounds your pride?
When God says wait?
When money gets tight?
When your spouse disappoints you?
When someone disagrees with you?
When you are exhausted?
What comes out?
Don't run from the answer.
Run with the answer to Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every private detail. But perhaps you need to stop pretending.
Sometimes two honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Someone quietly drowning beneath religious appearances may encounter it because you refused to keep the Gospel to yourself.
Save it too.
Not because an article can change your heart.
Only God can do that.
We want this community to remain a place where sinners are not entertained into spiritual sleep but lovingly pointed toward Jesus Christ.
Not to purchase God's favor.
Never.
You cannot buy grace. You cannot purchase salvation.

But if this ministry genuinely glorifies Christ, strengthens believers, reaches people with biblical truth, and places Gospel-centered resources into hands that need them, financial support is one practical way believers can participate in keeping that work moving.
Do not hide from Jesus.
Share His truth.
Tell somebody about Christ.
Open your Bible.
Repent quickly.
Forgive freely.
Confess honestly.
Pray desperately.
Follow faithfully.
Because Jesus was right.
The deepest human problem was never merely what surrounded us.
It was what lived within us.
And the breathtaking hope of the Gospel is that Jesus did not stand outside our darkness shouting instructions about how to escape.
He entered our world.
He bore sin at the cross.
He conquered death.
And He calls sinners out of hiding and into grace.
The heart you are most afraid for Jesus to see may become the very place where His grace writes its most beautiful testimony.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Sapphira Walked Into the Room Not Knowing Her Husband Had Just Died. Peter Asked Her One Question.
paragraphs: Sapphira Walked Into the Room Not Knowing Her Husband Had Just Died. Peter Asked Her One Question.

She thought she was walking into a room where a lie was still alive. She did not know her husband was already in a grave. What happened next is one of the most terrifying moments in Acts—and underneath the judgment is a warning every Christian who has ever been tempted to look more surrendered than they really are needs to hear.
She walked through the door approximately three hours too late.
Sapphira did not know.
That detail matters.

Her husband had already fallen to the ground dead. Young men had already wrapped his body. They had already carried him outside. The earth had already received Ananias, and somewhere beyond that doorway there was now a grave Sapphira did not know existed.
And then she entered.
Luke records the moment with chilling simplicity:
“ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ μὴ εἰδυῖα τὸ γεγονὸς εἰσῆλθεν.”
His wife entered, not knowing what had happened.
Acts 5:7.
No dramatic soundtrack.
No warning from someone outside.
No final conversation with her husband.
She simply walked into the room carrying the same secret she and Ananias had agreed to carry together.
Peter looked at her.
Then he asked one question.
“Εἰπέ μοι, εἰ τοσούτου τὸ χωρίον ἀπέδοσθε;”
“Tell me, did you sell the land for this amount?”
She answered:
“Ναί, τοσούτου.”
“Yes, for that amount.”
And with those words, the lie that could have ended at the doorway crossed her lips.
This story is frightening because Sapphira was not dragged into the room and forced to confess something Peter had already publicly announced.
She was asked.
She was given an opportunity to tell the truth.
And she chose the agreement she had made with her husband over truth before God.
But before we turn Sapphira into a distant villain, there is something uncomfortable we need to admit.
We understand the temptation more than we want to.
Maybe we have never sold property and laid money at an apostle's feet.
But we know what it is like to manage appearances.
We know how to say, “I'm fine,” when our soul is starving.
We know how to raise our hands in worship while secretly refusing to surrender the thing God keeps touching.
We know how to post Scripture publicly and neglect prayer privately.
We know how to speak about forgiveness while nurturing bitterness.
We know how to appear generous while craving recognition.
We know how to tell people, “God has everything,” while quietly placing certain rooms of our lives behind locked doors.
And that is why Acts 5 should not merely make us ask, “How could Sapphira do that?”
It should make us whisper:
Where am I doing the same thing in another form?
Because the central problem in this passage was not that Ananias and Sapphira failed to donate enough money.
Peter explicitly removes that misunderstanding.
Before the property was sold, it belonged to them. After it was sold, the proceeds remained at their disposal.
There was no apostolic tax demanding one hundred percent.
They could have sold the property and given half.
They could have given a quarter.
They could have kept it.
The horror was not merely in the amount withheld.
It was in presenting a partial sacrifice as though it were total surrender.
Ananias brought part of the proceeds while apparently representing the gift in a way that constituted a lie to the Holy Spirit. Sapphira knew about the arrangement and later confirmed the deception.
Luke uses an especially revealing word when describing what Ananias did:
“ἐνοσφίσατο” — enosphisato.
He “kept back” part of the proceeds.

The same verb appears in the Greek Old Testament account of Achan in Joshua 7, where something devoted to God was secretly appropriated. That does not make the two stories identical, but the echo is difficult to miss: at crucial moments in the life of God's covenant people, hidden deception is exposed as anything but harmless.
And suddenly Acts 5 becomes painfully contemporary.
You can put something at God's feet while still keeping something hidden in your heart.
You can give Jesus your Sunday and keep your Monday.
You can give Him your vocabulary and keep your fantasies.
You can give Him your public testimony and keep your private addiction.
You can give Him your reputation and keep your resentment.
You can give Him the version of yourself everybody applauds while desperately protecting the version nobody sees.
That is the danger.
Not imperfection.
Hypocrisy.
There is a difference.
The Gospel has never required you to pretend that you are already perfect.
It calls you to come into the light because you are not.
Jesus did not go to the cross for polished people who successfully convinced everyone they were righteous.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
Peter himself should make that impossible to forget.
The man questioning Sapphira was not a man with a spotless history.
This was Peter.
Peter knew what it meant to fail publicly.
He knew what it meant to make confident promises and collapse under pressure.
He had told Jesus that even if everyone else fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then, in the courtyard, fear took hold of him.
Once.
Twice.
Three times.
“I do not know the man.”
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine Peter's shame when Jesus looked at him.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Yet Peter's story did not end beside that fire.
After the resurrection, Jesus came for him.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to call darkness light.
Not to tell Peter that sin did not matter.
Jesus restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Three denials.
Three questions.
Then:
“Feed My sheep.”
That is grace.
Grace does not say your sin is insignificant.
Grace says your sin was so serious that Christ went to a cross—and His blood is so sufficient that the repentant sinner does not have to remain buried beneath the shame of it.
Peter was not standing in Acts 5 because he had never failed.
He was standing there because Jesus had rewritten the story of a man who had.
And perhaps that is where this passage cuts deepest.
Ananias and Sapphira wanted the appearance of something they were unwilling to live truthfully.
Peter had once failed terribly too—but Peter's failure was dragged into the light and met by the restoring Christ.
One story shows us the horror of protecting deception.
The other shows us what Jesus can do with a sinner who no longer has anything left to pretend.
Maybe you need that distinction tonight.
Because perhaps you have been hiding.
Not from God—you cannot actually hide from Him.
From people.
From accountability.
Perhaps even from yourself.
Maybe there is a browser history you keep deleting.
A relationship nobody knows about.
Money you obtained dishonestly.
Bitterness you have baptized as “discernment.”
Pride disguised as ministry.
A secret conversation.
An addiction.
A compromise.
A double life.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are spiritually strong because you learned how to speak Christian fluently.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know the worship songs.
You know the verses.
You know when to lift your hands.
You know what photographs to post.
You know what testimony people expect.
But when the room becomes quiet...
you know.
And God knows.
That sentence may feel frightening.
God knows.
But for the person willing to repent, it can become one of the most beautiful sentences imaginable.
God knows...
and Jesus still calls sinners to come.
God knows...
and the cross still stands.
God knows...
and the blood of Christ was shed for real guilt, not imaginary guilt.
God knows...
and you do not have to manufacture a cleaner version of yourself before approaching Him.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Fix yourself well enough and perhaps I will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
And forgiveness is not purchased by our performance but received through faith in the crucified and risen Christ—a faith that turns us from darkness toward Him.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance runs toward grace.
The enemy whispers:
“Hide it.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
The enemy says:
“If people knew, everything would be over.”
Jesus says:
“Whoever comes to Me I will never cast out.”
The enemy says:
“Protect the image.”
Jesus says:
“Walk in the light.”
The enemy says:
“Pretend.”
Jesus says:
“Truth will set you free.”
Sapphira walked into that room without knowing what had happened.
But you know what happened.
You have Acts 5.
You have been given the warning she did not have when she crossed that doorway.
And Peter's question reaches through nearly two thousand years and lands somewhere far deeper than a property transaction:
Will you keep agreeing with the lie?
Sapphira answered Peter.
Then Peter answered her.
“Why have you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord?”
The Greek is striking:
“Τί ὅτι συνεφωνήθη ὑμῖν πειράσαι τὸ πνεῦμα κυρίου;”
The word behind “agreed together,” symphōneō, carries the idea of agreeing or being in accord.
They were united.
But united around deception.
That matters because not every agreement is holy merely because two people made it together.
Some relationships strengthen obedience.
Others normalize compromise.
Sometimes the person holding your hand is also helping you walk away from God.
Love does not require you to participate in somebody else's lie.
Marriage does not make sin righteous.
Friendship does not make compromise faithful.
Loyalty to another human being must never become disloyalty to Christ.
There are moments when love must say:
“No. I cannot agree with this.”
“No. We need to tell the truth.”
“No. We cannot keep hiding.”
“No. I love you too much to help you destroy yourself.”
Maybe somebody reading this is trapped inside an agreement that should never have been made.
Break agreement with the lie.
Not tomorrow.
Not when it becomes convenient.
Now.
Tell the truth.
Seek forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Ask for help.
Bring trusted, mature believers into the darkness you have been guarding.
Most importantly, run to Jesus.
Because Acts says that after Sapphira fell, “great fear” came upon the whole church and everyone who heard about these events.
“φόβος μέγας” — phobos megas.
Great fear.

Modern Christianity can sometimes become uncomfortable with passages like this because we prefer a God who comforts but never confronts, embraces but never judges, forgives but never calls sin what it is.
But Scripture will not permit us to manufacture that God.
The God revealed in Scripture is holy.
And the astonishing beauty of Christianity is not that God's holiness somehow disappeared when Jesus arrived.
It is that at the cross, divine holiness and divine mercy meet in a way sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
Grace is astonishing enough that Christ willingly did.
That is why the cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride cannot survive because you could not save yourself.
Despair does not have to survive because Jesus came to save sinners.
So perhaps the most important question is not whether you have something hidden.
Most of us know exactly where the locked room is.
The question is what you will do now that Christ has brought you to the door.
Will you defend it?
Rename it?
Minimize it?
Blame someone else for it?
Promise yourself you will deal with it eventually?
Or will you finally place the key in Jesus' scarred hand?
You do not need another religious performance.
You need Christ.
You do not need to look surrendered.
You need to surrender.
You do not need people to think you are clean.
You need Jesus to wash you.
You do not need applause for appearing holy.
You need mercy.
And mercy has a name.
Jesus.
Maybe this article exposed something you have carefully kept beneath the surface.
Pray.
Confess.
Repent.
Come into the light.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once believed would destroy your life, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer needs to read tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
We are sinners.
Christ is Savior.
Grace is real.
And Jesus still rewrites stories.
Scripture does not teach that, and we will not place that burden on your conscience.
Glorifying God belongs to the whole life of faith and obedience.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is done freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and for the right reason.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot donate enough to erase one sin.
Someone already paid the price you could never pay.
Jesus Christ.
That is the center of everything.
And perhaps that is the final irony of Sapphira's story.
The story begins with money.
But ultimately, it was never really about money.
It was about truth before God.
It was about the terrifying danger of wanting the reputation of surrender without surrender itself.
So before you leave this article, imagine the doorway one final time.
Sapphira enters.
She does not know there is already fresh earth over her husband's body.
Peter looks at her.
One question.
One opportunity to abandon the lie.
And suddenly the ancient room becomes uncomfortably close.
Because today you are the one who knows the story.
You are the one standing before the question.
You are the one who can stop pretending.
You are the one who can bring the hidden thing into the light.
And unlike Sapphira walking unknowingly into that room, you are reading these words while there is still time to respond.
So come to Christ honestly.
Come guilty.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come without the mask.
Come without the carefully edited testimony.
Come without pretending that your partial surrender is complete.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Because Jesus has never needed the fake version of you.
He came to redeem the real one.
Because the most frightening thing about Sapphira's final doorway was not that God saw what was hidden.
It was that she was still protecting the lie when the truth was standing right in front of her.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JEALOUSY WITHOUT EVIDENCE WAS SERIOUS ENOUGH TO HAVE ITS OWN TORAH PROCEDURE
paragraphs: JEALOUSY WITHOUT EVIDENCE WAS SERIOUS ENOUGH TO HAVE ITS OWN TORAH PROCEDURE
Before you destroy someone over what you suspect, remember this: God wrote an entire procedure into the Torah for a marriage trapped between suspicion and proof.
There is a kind of pain that begins without a photograph.
Without a confession.
Without a witness standing in the doorway.
Without the text message you can screenshot and send to everybody.
Just a thought.
A change in behavior.
A conversation that felt a little too comfortable.
A name that suddenly comes up too often.
A silence that feels different.
A phone turned facedown.
A delayed reply.
A look you cannot explain.
And then something starts moving inside you.
What if?
What if there is someone else?
What if I am being lied to?
What if everybody knows except me?
What if the person sleeping beside me has already given part of their heart—or their body—to somebody else?
And once jealousy enters the room, it can become terrifyingly good at collecting “evidence.”
A late arrival becomes evidence.
A smile becomes evidence.
A deleted message becomes evidence.
A bad mood becomes evidence.
Even an attempt to explain yourself can become evidence.
“You’re defensive.”
Silence?
“See? You have something to hide.”
Suddenly the person you love is standing trial inside a courtroom that exists entirely in your mind.
And thousands of years ago, the Torah described a situation disturbingly close to this.

Numbers 5 contains one of the strangest, hardest, and most frequently misunderstood passages in Scripture: the procedure traditionally associated with the sotah, the woman suspected of marital unfaithfulness.
Read carefully before deciding what the passage means.
The text describes a situation in which suspected sexual unfaithfulness is hidden and “there is no witness against her.”
Then comes this extraordinary sentence:
וְעָבַר עָלָיו רוּחַ־קִנְאָה
Ve'avar alav ruaḥ-qin'ah.
Literally, something like:
“And a spirit of jealousy passes over him.”
The Hebrew word קִנְאָה — qin'ah can carry the sense of jealousy or zeal.
But then the Torah does something we cannot afford to miss.
It explicitly allows for two possibilities.
The husband is jealous...
וְהִוא נִטְמָאָה
vehi nitma'ah—
and she has been defiled.
Or the husband is jealous...
וְהִיא לֹא נִטְמָאָה
vehi lo nitma'ah—
and she has NOT been defiled.
Read that again.
Because it changes the emotional landscape of the passage.
The Torah recognizes the possibility that jealousy is present...
while guilt is not.
The suspicion may correspond to reality.
Or it may not.
That means jealousy itself is not proof.
Suspicion is not omniscience.
A husband's anguish does not automatically establish his wife's guilt.
Feeling betrayed and proving betrayal are two different things.

And instead of allowing unresolved suspicion simply to become private vengeance, the matter is brought out of the husband's hands and before the priest—ultimately, in the theological world of the text, before the LORD.
That does not make Numbers 5 an easy passage.
It isn't.
Modern readers should not pretend otherwise.

The ritual belongs to ancient Israel's covenantal, priestly, and patriarchal social world. It is gender-asymmetrical, and Christians are not commanded to reproduce this ritual today. Nor should anyone weaponize Numbers 5 to justify controlling, humiliating, threatening, or abusing a spouse.
But neither should we miss what the text itself refuses to let jealousy do.
