Every eye was fixed on Him.
And Jesus declared:
“Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
Luke 4:21
Think about the weight of that moment.
The Scriptures they had heard for years were standing before them in flesh.
The promise had entered their synagogue.
The Messiah was not merely being discussed.
He was speaking.
And some of the people in that room probably remembered Him when He was younger.
That was the problem.
They could remember His past.
But they could not comprehend His identity.
Mark records their astonishment at His teaching. They recognized extraordinary wisdom. They had heard about His mighty works.
Yet their questions quickly became personal.
“Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary…?”
Mark 6:3
The Greek is brutally revealing:
οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ τέκτων
ouch houtos estin ho tektōn
“Is this not the craftsman/carpenter?”
The word τέκτων — tektōn refers to a craftsman or builder, traditionally rendered “carpenter.”
Do you hear what familiarity was doing?
They were trying to fit divine revelation into an old category.
We know Him.
We know where He came from.
We know His family.
We know what He used to do.
We remember Him.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because you can know facts about Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
You can recognize His name without recognizing His authority.
You can grow up around Christianity and never truly bow before Christ.
You can own three Bibles and still resist the One the Bible reveals.
You can quote Scripture while secretly refusing to let Scripture confront you.
You can sing about surrender with both hands raised while protecting one locked room of your heart from God.
Nazareth's tragedy was not lack of exposure.
It was exposure without surrender.
They had become so occupied with the Jesus they thought they knew that they stumbled over the Jesus standing before them.
Mark uses a powerful expression:
καὶ ἐσκανδαλίζοντο ἐν αὐτῷ
kai eskandalizonto en autō
“And they were taking offense at Him.”
That verb, σκανδαλίζω — skandalizō, carries the idea of stumbling, being caused to fall, or taking offense.
Jesus became their stumbling point.
The One who came to save them offended the categories they had built for Him.
They wanted a Messiah.
Just apparently not this Messiah.
Not the carpenter they remembered.
Not Mary's son.
Not someone whose relatives they knew.
God had come too close.
Too ordinary-looking.
Too familiar.
And they stumbled over Him.
That should frighten every person who has been around Christianity long enough to stop being amazed.
Because familiarity can quietly produce a counterfeit confidence.
“I already know this.”
I know John 3:16.
I know Jesus loves me.
I know He died for my sins.
I know Easter.
I know grace.
I know repentance.
I know the Gospel.
But the question is not merely:
Do you know the Gospel?
The question is:
Has the Gospel brought you to repentance and faith in Jesus Christ?
There is a difference.
A terrifying one.
Demons knew who Jesus was.
Religious leaders knew Scripture.
Crowds witnessed miracles.
Judas walked beside Christ.
Knowledge alone has never been the same thing as saving faith.
And maybe somebody reading this has been mistaking proximity for relationship.
Your parents believed.
Your grandmother prayed.
You grew up in church.
You were baptized.
You learned the songs.
You served.
You posted verses.
People assume you are spiritually strong.
But late at night, when nobody is watching…
you know.
Something has become cold.
Prayer became occasional.
Scripture became content instead of bread.
Sin became something to manage instead of something to confess.
Jesus became Someone you agree with rather than the Lord you obey.
And slowly, almost invisibly, familiarity replaced wonder.
You did not necessarily walk away from Christianity.
You simply stopped trembling.
Nazareth shows us where that road can lead.
Mark says Jesus responded:
“Prophets are not without honor, except in their hometown and among their own kin and in their own house.”
Then comes one of Scripture's most sobering descriptions.
Jesus did only a few healings there, and Mark says:
“And he was amazed at their unbelief.”
Mark 6:6
Imagine that.
Throughout the Gospels, people are amazed at Jesus.
Nazareth gives us Jesus amazed at them.
Not at their intelligence.
Not at their achievements.
Not at their religious heritage.
At their unbelief.
But we must be careful here.
The passage does not teach that Jesus somehow lost divine power because the people failed to generate enough positive faith.
Jesus was not helpless in Nazareth.
Mark explicitly says He laid His hands upon a few sick people and healed them.
The tragedy is not that unbelief drained Christ of power.
The tragedy is that the people rejected the One standing among them.
And rejection has consequences.
Luke's account becomes even more disturbing.
At first, they marvel at His gracious words.
Then Jesus exposes something deeper.
He reminds them of Elijah and the widow of Zarephath.
He reminds them of Elisha and Naaman the Syrian.
Grace was never something Nazareth could possess as though God owed it to them.
God's mercy reaches outsiders.
The needy.
The unlikely.
The foreigner.
The person who knows he has nothing with which to bargain.
And suddenly admiration became rage.
The congregation that had been listening to Scripture rose against the One who fulfilled it.
Luke says they drove Jesus out of town and brought Him toward the brow of the hill intending to throw Him down.
Think about that progression.
They heard Him.
They marveled at Him.
They questioned Him.
They became offended by Him.
They became furious with Him.
Then they wanted Him gone.
That is what the human heart can do when Jesus refuses to remain inside the version of Him we prefer.
We love a Jesus who comforts.
But what happens when He confronts?
We love Jesus the healer.
But what happens when He exposes the disease?
We love Jesus the Savior.
But do we receive Jesus the Lord?
We love grace.
But what happens when grace tells us we must repent?
We love forgiveness.
But what happens when forgiveness requires admitting we were guilty?
We love hearing that Christ receives sinners.
But what happens when Christ tells us to leave our sin and follow Him?
This is where Nazareth stops being an ancient village.
Nazareth becomes a mirror.
Because there is a little Nazareth hiding inside the human heart.
A place where we say:
Jesus, You may come this far.
But not there.
You can have Sunday.
Not my sexuality.
You can have worship.
Not my bitterness.
You can have my public testimony.
Not my private browser history.
You can have my prayers.
Not my money.
You can have my Christian vocabulary.
Not my secret relationship.
You can have my tears.
Not my pride.
You can have the parts of me people already see.
But that locked room?
Please stay outside.
And Jesus will not accept the role of religious decoration.
He is Lord.
The Gospel is not an invitation to add Jesus to your existing life.
It is the announcement that the crucified and risen Christ is King—and sinners are called to repent, believe, receive mercy, and follow Him.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some of us have become more comfortable talking about Jesus than actually obeying Him.
We have made Him familiar enough to discuss…
but not holy enough to fear.
Familiar enough to quote…
but not sovereign enough to surrender to.
Familiar enough to post…
but not precious enough to abandon sin for.
And still—
look at Jesus.
Nazareth rejects Him.
Jesus continues His mission.
People misunderstand Him.
Jesus keeps walking.
They despise the carpenter.
He continues toward the cross.
Because the scandal of Nazareth would eventually become the scandal of Calvary.
The carpenter would be nailed to wood.
The hands that had built things would be pierced.
The One rejected by His hometown would be rejected outside Jerusalem.
The innocent One would be condemned.
The sinless One would bear sin.
The King would wear thorns.
The Author of life would enter death.
And humanity would look at the Son of God and say, in effect:
We don't want You.
Yet the cross reveals something almost impossible to comprehend.
The Christ we rejected came to rescue rebels like us.
The Gospel does not say you were good enough for Jesus.
It says Jesus was gracious enough for you.
It does not say your sin was small.
The cross says your sin was so serious that redemption required the death of the Son of God—and God's love so astonishing that He gave His Son for sinners.
Jesus was crucified.
Buried.
And on the third day He rose.
Death did not keep Him.
The grave did not defeat Him.
The rejected carpenter of Nazareth is the risen Lord.
And that means your story does not have to end where Nazareth's unbelief began.
Maybe you have treated Christ casually.
Come back.
Maybe religion became routine.
Come back.
Maybe you wandered.
Come back.
Maybe you have been hiding sin for years.
Bring it into His light.
Maybe shame has whispered that after everything you have done, Jesus could never receive you.
Look at the cross.
Grace was made for guilty people.
Repentance is not pretending you never sinned.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who died for sinners.
And if you come to Christ, you do not come because you deserve another chance.
You come because Jesus Christ is merciful.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by renaming sin.

Jesus rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth, calling them to repentance, cleansing those who trust Him, forgiving what they could never erase, and creating something new where shame once claimed the final word.
Have I become so familiar with Jesus that I have stopped actually following Him?
Don't answer quickly.
Sit with it.
When was the last time His Word changed your plans?
When was the last time conviction produced repentance?
When was the last time you confessed something instead of defending it?
When was the last time you opened Scripture because you were hungry for Christ rather than merely looking for something inspirational?
When was the last time the cross broke your pride?
Maybe today is your Nazareth moment.
Jesus is closer than you expected.
And you must decide whether familiarity will make you stumble…
or whether you will finally fall at His feet.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already rescued you from a season of coldness, compromise, or unbelief, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to remind another struggling person that restoration is possible.
Not because every article deserves saving.
Because there may come a night when Jesus feels ordinary again, sin feels strangely harmless, prayer feels unnecessary, and your heart needs to remember Nazareth.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to earn God's favor.
Not because sharing a post makes anyone righteous before God.
We are saved by God's grace, not by social-media activity.
Send it privately to the person you cannot stop praying for.
And the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is nourishment.
And if you want to go deeper and help this Gospel-centered work continue:
Come to Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy in Nazareth was not that they failed to recognize a successful hometown carpenter.
They stood near the Savior…
heard the Savior…
marveled at the Savior…
and still stumbled over the Savior.
Do not let familiarity do that to you.
You may have known His name since childhood.
Today, bow to the King behind the name.
You may know His stories.
Know Him.
You may know Christian language.
Follow Christ.
You may know what repentance means.
Repent.
You may know that Jesus forgives sinners.
Come receive His mercy.

Because one day every familiar Bible verse, every sermon you heard, every conviction you postponed, every invitation you ignored, and every moment Christ was presented before you will make one question unbearably personal:
What did you do with Jesus?
And perhaps the saddest words that could ever describe a human life would be:
I was around Him so long that I stopped seeing Him.
But that does not have to be your ending.
The carpenter they underestimated became the Savior who carried a cross.
The One they rejected became the cornerstone.
The One they wanted outside their town opened His arms outside Jerusalem for sinners.
And the risen Jesus is still calling people out of unbelief, shame, compromise, religious familiarity, and death into repentance, forgiveness, grace, and life.
Never become so familiar with Jesus that you forget you are standing before the One who can rewrite your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SPEAK THOSE THINGS THAT ARE NOT AS THOUGH THEY WERE” — ROMANS 4:17 IS NOT TELLING YOU TO MANIFEST YOUR REALITY
paragraphs: “SPEAK THOSE THINGS THAT ARE NOT AS THOUGH THEY WERE” — ROMANS 4:17 IS NOT TELLING YOU TO MANIFEST YOUR REALITY
You were never commanded to create reality with your words. You were invited to trust the God who can create life where there is nothing but death.
There is a Bible verse being passed around like a spiritual blank check.
You may have heard it after losing a job.
“Speak your new job into existence.”
After receiving bad news.
“Don’t say what you see. Speak what you want.”
When money is disappearing faster than it comes in.
“Declare abundance.”
When the relationship is broken.
“Call it restored.”
When the dream seems impossible.
“Speak those things that are not as though they were.”
And then Romans 4:17 gets attached to it.
It sounds biblical.
It sounds powerful.
It sounds like faith.
There is only one problem.
That is not what Romans 4:17 says.
And once you see what Paul actually wrote, the verse becomes far more beautiful than manifestation could ever make it.
Because Romans 4 is not teaching you how to become the creator of your reality.
It is teaching you how to trust the Creator when your reality looks impossible.
Read Paul's words carefully:

“As it is written, ‘I have made you the father of many nations’—in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.” — Romans 4:17, ESV
Now look at the crucial words in Greek:
θεοῦ τοῦ ζῳοποιοῦντος τοὺς νεκροὺς καὶ καλοῦντος τὰ μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα
theou tou zōopoiountos tous nekrous kai kalountos ta mē onta hōs onta
The heart of the sentence is staggering.
God is the One “giving life to the dead” and “calling the things that are not as though they are.”
Notice who is doing the calling.
God.
Not Abraham.
Not Sarah.
Not you.
Not me.
God.
That one observation changes everything.
Romans 4:17 does not say, “Abraham called things that were not as though they were.”
Paul describes God as the One who does this.

The popular expression “speak those things that are not as though they were” can therefore become seriously misleading when it is presented as a command for Christians to verbally manufacture desired circumstances.
The verse is not giving humanity God's creative authority.
It is revealing the character of the God Abraham trusted.
And maybe that disappoints part of you.
Because manifestation offers something incredibly attractive.
Control.
Say the correct words.
Think the correct thoughts.
Maintain the correct energy.
Refuse negative confessions.
Visualize hard enough.
Declare consistently enough.
And eventually reality supposedly has to cooperate.
But biblical faith is different.
Biblical faith does not put reality under your authority.
Biblical faith puts you under God's authority while teaching you to trust Him in the middle of reality.
That is harder.
And infinitely safer.
Because sometimes you can speak faithfully and still walk through suffering.
Sometimes you can pray desperately and the answer is not the answer you wanted.
Sometimes the diagnosis remains.
Sometimes the person leaves.
Sometimes the business fails.
Sometimes the door stays closed.
Sometimes you bury someone you begged God to heal.
And if Christianity has been reduced to “your words create your world,” what happens then?
You begin blaming yourself.
Maybe I spoke negatively.
Maybe I doubted.
Maybe my faith wasn't strong enough.
Maybe I ruined my miracle.
And now suffering has acquired another wound:
shame.
But look at Abraham.
Paul is not describing a man pretending reality didn't exist.
He is describing a man staring directly at an impossible reality while trusting a God greater than it.
Romans 4:19 says Abraham considered the condition of his own body, which was “as good as dead,” since he was about a hundred years old, and he considered Sarah's barrenness.
Abraham knew what his body was telling him.
He knew Sarah's history.
He knew the mathematics.
He knew the biology.
Faith did not require him to become delusional.
Faith required him to decide whether God's promise was more trustworthy than his circumstances were powerful.
That distinction matters.
Christian faith is not denying facts.
It is refusing to make facts greater than God.
There are facts.
And then there is God.
Cancer can be a fact.
Debt can be a fact.
Infertility can be a fact.
Grief can be a fact.
Betrayal can be a fact.
A shattered marriage can be a fact.
Your own terrible decisions can be facts.
The Gospel never requires you to rename darkness “light” just to prove you have faith.
Scripture repeatedly teaches God's people to tell the truth.
The Psalms are filled with people crying, grieving, questioning, confessing, pleading, and lamenting before God.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane:
“My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” — Matthew 26:39, ESV
Think about that prayer.
Jesus did not “manifest” another outcome.
He surrendered Himself to the Father.
“Not as I will, but as You will.”
That sentence demolishes the idea that mature spirituality means forcing reality to conform to personal desire.
The center of Christianity is not the sovereignty of your desires.
It is the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the message becomes uncomfortable.
Because manifestation spirituality can dress itself in Christian vocabulary while quietly moving the center of faith.
God becomes the mechanism.
Your dream becomes the destination.
Faith becomes the technique.
Words become the instrument.
And you remain at the center.
But Christianity begins with something radically different:
Jesus is Lord.
Not my vision.
Not my preferred future.
Not my timetable.
Not my declaration.
Jesus.
Biblical confession certainly matters.
Words matter.
Prayer matters.
Hope matters.
Faith matters.
Scripture even teaches believers to ask God boldly.
But asking God boldly is not the same thing as commanding reality independently.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray:
“Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” — Matthew 6:10, ESV
There it is again.
Your will.
Christian prayer is bold without becoming sovereign.
Confident without becoming controlling.
Expectant without pretending God owes us our preferred outcome.
We can pray for healing.
We can pray for provision.
We can pray for reconciliation.
We can ask God to open doors no human being could open.
We can believe that God still does what appears impossible.
Romans 4 absolutely encourages that kind of faith.
But our confidence rests in God, not in some supposed metaphysical power hidden inside our vocabulary.
Abraham's greatness in Romans 4 was not that he discovered how to manipulate the universe.
It was that he believed God.
Romans 4:20–21 says:
“No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.” — ESV
Read the last part again.
God was able to do what God had promised.
That is the engine of Abraham's faith.
Not:
“I am able to create whatever I repeatedly declare.”
But:
“God is able to do what He has promised.”
That is an enormous difference.
Biblical faith does not begin by asking, “What reality do I want to create?”
It asks, “What has God actually promised?”
Because God has never promised to obey every dream we attach His name to.
Sometimes the thing you desperately want is not what He has promised.
And sometimes His mercy appears in the very door you begged Him to open remaining shut.
You may not understand that immediately.
Joseph probably did not understand the pit.
David probably did not understand years of running from Saul.
Paul asked for his thorn to leave and instead heard:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, ESV
Paul did not fail manifestation.
He encountered sufficient grace.
There is a world of difference.
Perhaps you have been exhausting yourself trying to control tomorrow with today's declarations.
Perhaps you are afraid that admitting fear will create something bad.
Perhaps somebody convinced you that acknowledging pain is a “negative confession.”
So you learned to smile while bleeding.
You learned to call yourself victorious while privately collapsing.
You learned Christian vocabulary without Christian surrender.
And somewhere beneath all those declarations is a frightened human being whispering:
“What if I can't make this happen?”
Here is the freedom Romans 4 gives you.
You don't have to.
You were never God.
You were never supposed to carry God's job.
You cannot speak creation into existence the way the Creator can.
You cannot guarantee tomorrow.
You cannot control every outcome.
You cannot manipulate Providence by arranging sentences correctly.
But you can know the One who holds tomorrow.
And that is better.
Abraham's story ultimately leads beyond Abraham.
Paul's argument does not end with Isaac.
It moves toward Jesus.
Romans 4:23–25 explains that the righteousness credited to Abraham was written also for those who believe in the God who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.
Suddenly Romans 4:17 becomes even more breathtaking.
The God “who gives life to the dead” is the God who raised Jesus Christ.
Christianity is built upon resurrection.
Not manifestation.
Resurrection.
Manifestation says, in effect, “Use your inner power to bring your desired future into reality.”
The Gospel announces something altogether different:
You were spiritually helpless, and God acted to save.
Jesus entered our scandal.
Our rebellion.
Our guilt.
Our shame.
Our death.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And God raised Him from the dead.
We didn't manifest salvation.
We needed rescue.
We didn't declare ourselves righteous until heaven accepted the vocabulary.
Christ became our righteousness.
We didn't speak our sins out of existence.
Jesus shed His blood for sinners.
That is why grace is so offensive to human pride.
Grace means you cannot save yourself.
But grace is also breathtakingly beautiful for exactly the same reason.
You don't have to.
Maybe your life right now doesn't resemble the testimony you imagined you would have.
Maybe your marriage has scars.
Maybe your children have wandered.
Maybe addiction left wreckage behind.
Maybe pornography has become the secret room nobody knows exists.
Maybe you smile at church while wondering whether God could possibly still want you.
Maybe your bank account terrifies you.
Maybe your prayers seem to hit the ceiling.
Maybe you keep declaring victory because you're terrified to admit:
“God, I'm tired.”
Say it.
He already knows.
Biblical faith can survive honesty.
David's did.
Job's did.
Jeremiah's did.
Peter's did.
Because faith is not pretending everything is okay.
Faith is bringing everything that is not okay to the God who remains faithful.
And perhaps the greatest “thing that is not” in your story is not the house you want, the promotion you want, the relationship you want, or the money you want.
Maybe what looks impossible is you.
The person you have become.
The years you wasted.
The sins nobody knows about.
The marriage you damaged.
The promises you broke.
The secret habits.
The bitterness.
The shame.
The version of yourself you cannot seem to escape.
And now Romans 4:17 suddenly sounds different:
He gives life to the dead.
That is your hope.
Not that you can manifest a better version of yourself.
That Jesus Christ raises dead people.
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians and became an apostle of Christ.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer—no lifetime to repair, no ministry résumé to build, no reputation to recover—and Christ still promised him paradise.
Scandal.
Then grace.
Failure.
Then mercy.
Death.
Then resurrection.
This is what Jesus does.
He does not pretend the scandal never happened.
He writes grace through it.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears. Grace is not permission to continue sinning, nor does forgiveness erase every temporal result of our choices.
But in Christ, sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Death itself does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
So stop trying to become the god of your own universe.
You can finally put that burden down.
You don't need to manifest.
You need to trust.
You don't need magical words.
You need Christ.
You don't need to deny your circumstances.
You need to know that circumstances cannot dethrone your Savior.
You don't need to declare yourself powerful.
You can confess your weakness and discover that His grace is sufficient.
And if you have wandered into spirituality where Jesus became little more than a tool for getting the life you wanted, come home.
Repentance is not humiliation designed to crush you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the lie and back toward Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Follow Him.
Let His Word correct you even when the correction hurts.
Because sometimes the verse you thought promised you control was actually offering you something better:
God Himself.
When it is, remember the subject of the sentence.
God.
It cannot. Christ cannot be bought, and grace is not merchandise.

Support can, however, help this ministry continue creating and distributing Christ-centered teaching, Gospel encouragement, discipleship resources, and biblical content. One practical way to glorify God is to use what He has entrusted to you to help truthful Gospel ministry reach other people.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting your salvation.
Jesus already paid for that.
And He did not pay fifty percent.
He gave Himself.
So the next time someone tells you Romans 4:17 means you can speak whatever future you desire into existence, remember Abraham standing before an impossible situation.
His hope was never the power of Abraham's mouth.
His hope was the faithfulness of Abraham's God.
And maybe that is exactly what your exhausted soul needed to hear.
You do not have to control tomorrow with your words.
You can entrust tomorrow to the One who walked out of a grave.
You were never given the burden of speaking your reality into existence—you were given the breathtaking privilege of trusting the God who raises the dead.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOMER IS MORE THAN A SERMON ILLUSTRATION ABOUT AN “UNFAITHFUL WOMAN”
paragraphs:
GOMER IS MORE THAN A SERMON ILLUSTRATION ABOUT AN “UNFAITHFUL WOMAN”
We Have Spent Centuries Looking at Her Shame. Hosea Was Written to Make Us Recognize Ours.
There is something dangerously comfortable about preaching Gomer as though she were somebody else.
The immoral woman.
The adulteress.
The scandal.
The woman who wandered while a faithful man kept loving her.
We hear her name and instinctively stand beside Hosea.
We imagine ourselves among the faithful.
We look across the sanctuary at Gomer.
And perhaps that is exactly where the book of Hosea begins dismantling us.
Because Gomer was never placed in Scripture merely so respectable people could shake their heads at an unfaithful woman.
She became part of a prophetic sign aimed directly at the covenant people of God.
At worshipers.
At people who knew God's name.
At people who could still participate in religion while their hearts belonged somewhere else.
And if you read Hosea long enough, an uncomfortable realization begins crawling beneath your skin:
You were never supposed to watch Gomer from a safe distance.
You were supposed to recognize yourself.
The opening command is shocking even in Hebrew.
God tells Hosea:
“לֵךְ קַח־לְךָ אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים”
Lekh, qach-lekha eshet zenunim.
“Go, take for yourself a wife of whoredom.”

The expression eshet zenunim is severe. The noun zenunim belongs to the Hebrew vocabulary of sexual unfaithfulness or prostitution. But the verse immediately tells us why this marriage is being used prophetically:
“כִּי־זָנֹה תִזְנֶה הָאָרֶץ מֵאַחֲרֵי יְהוָה”
“For the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD.”
—Hosea 1:2
That final clause changes how we must read everything.
The deepest scandal in the opening chapter is not merely the sexual history of a woman.
It is the spiritual adultery of a people.
Israel belonged to Yahweh and pursued other gods.
The nation received His provision and attributed His gifts elsewhere. Later God says of Israel, “She did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil” (Hosea 2:8).
Read that slowly.
God gave.
Someone else received the credit.
And suddenly Hosea stops feeling ancient.
Because idolatry does not always look like bowing before a carved statue.
Sometimes it looks like needing human approval more than God's approval.
Sometimes it is the relationship you know is dragging you from Christ but refuse to surrender.
Sometimes it is money.
Sometimes pornography.
Sometimes status.
Sometimes resentment.
Sometimes ministry itself.
Sometimes we want God's gifts while quietly resenting God's authority.
We pray when frightened, praise when blessed, disappear when comfortable, return when shattered—and somehow still imagine Gomer is the shocking character in this story.
But Hosea will not let us remain spectators.
Gomer is named in Hosea 1:3:
“וַיֵּלֶךְ וַיִּקַּח אֶת־גֹּמֶר בַּת־דִּבְלָיִם”
“So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim.”
She becomes Hosea's wife.
Children are born.
And their names become sermons walking through Israel.
Jezreel.
Lo-Ruhamah.
Lo-Ammi.
The final two are particularly devastating.
Lo-Ruhamah carries the sense of “No Mercy” or “Not Pitied.”
Lo-Ammi means “Not My People.”
Imagine hearing a mother calling those names home at sunset.
Imagine children carrying the judgment of a nation in their introductions.
“What is your name?”
“Not My People.”
Yet this is where Hosea becomes astonishing.
Judgment does not get the last word.
Almost immediately after “Not My People,” God announces a future reversal:
“In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it shall be said to them, ‘Children of the living God.’”
—Hosea 1:10
That is the heartbeat beneath the wreckage.
God exposes sin because sin destroys what He loves.
Biblical grace does not pretend betrayal never happened.
Grace tells the truth about the wound...
and then does something human beings rarely expect.
God begins speaking restoration over the guilty.
Hosea 2 moves through accusation, judgment, discipline and then into one of Scripture's most breathtaking turns.
God says:
“לָכֵן הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מְפַתֶּיהָ”
“Therefore, behold, I will allure her...”
And He says He will bring her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her.
—Hosea 2:14
Did you notice the word?
Therefore.
We expect:
Therefore, I will destroy her.
Therefore, I will humiliate her.
Therefore, I will never speak her name again.
Instead...
God pursues.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because covenant love does.
Then comes language so beautiful that it almost sounds impossible after everything preceding it:
“וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי לְעוֹלָם”
Ve'erastikh li le'olam.
“I will betroth you to Me forever.”
And again:
“וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי בֶּאֱמוּנָה”
“I will betroth you to Me in faithfulness.”
Not merely tolerate you.
Not merely keep you around as permanent evidence of your worst season.
Betroth you.
The language moves toward renewed covenant relationship.
Righteousness.
Justice.
Steadfast love.
Mercy.
Faithfulness.
This does not make sin small.
It makes grace enormous.
And then Hosea 3 opens with another disturbing command.
“Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress...”
—Hosea 3:1
Here we need to be careful with Scripture.

Hosea 3 does not explicitly call this woman Gomer by name. She has traditionally been understood by many interpreters to be Gomer, and that reading naturally connects chapters 1 and 3, but we should not present an inference as though the verse itself names her.
What the text makes unmistakable is the meaning of Hosea's commanded love.
The verse continues by comparing it with the LORD's love for Israel even while Israel turns toward other gods.
Then Hosea says:
“וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי בַּחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר כָּסֶף”
“So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver...”
—Hosea 3:2
The exact circumstances behind that transaction are not explained.
Scripture does not tell us enough to reconstruct every detail of what happened to the woman.
Was this payment connected with slavery, debt, marital arrangements, or another ancient economic circumstance?
The text does not fully tell us.
And we should resist the temptation to manufacture cinematic details Scripture never gives.
The Bible's actual words are powerful enough.
Hosea pays a price.
He brings the woman into a renewed relationship.
And the prophetic meaning points beyond their household toward God and His covenant people.
But for Christians reading Hosea within the whole canon of Scripture, something even greater comes into view.
Because centuries later, another Bridegroom would come for an unfaithful people.
Jesus Christ.
And unlike Hosea, Christ would not purchase His people with silver.
The apostle Peter writes:
Now the story becomes painfully personal.
Because Christianity does not say Jesus died for impressive people who occasionally needed spiritual improvement.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
Before grace rescued us, sin was not merely around us.
It was in us.
We were not standing safely beside the Redeemer analyzing everybody else's scandal.
We needed redemption.
Every one of us.
That changes how we read Gomer.
It should destroy spiritual superiority.
The church should be the last place on earth where redeemed sinners compete over whose past is least embarrassing.
The Cross has already exposed the truth about us.
Our sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
And God's mercy is magnificent enough that Christ willingly did.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not redeem us so we can return comfortably to the idols that enslaved us.
Grace is not permission to keep running.
Grace calls us home.
Jesus began His public proclamation with a command that modern Christianity sometimes whispers when Scripture says it plainly:
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
—Mark 1:15
Repentance is not paying God back.
It is turning.
Coming into the light.
Dropping the disguise.
Leaving the idol.
Confessing the sin.
Trusting the Savior.
You may have learned how to look Christian while your heart has been wandering for years.
You can raise your hands and still hide something.
You can quote Scripture and still nurture bitterness.
You can serve in ministry while secretly starving for applause.
You can be married and emotionally belong to someone else.
You can tell everybody God is enough while spending every night desperately trying to make something else fill the emptiness.
You can know worship songs without truly worshiping.
And perhaps the most terrifying form of wandering is the kind nobody notices.
Except God.
But listen carefully:
The God who sees what is hidden is also the God who calls sinners home.
Not through denial.
Not through cheap grace.
Through repentance and redemption.
The Cross proves both realities simultaneously.
Your sin is worse than your excuses say.
God's grace in Christ is greater than your shame says.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Some people reading this have spent years believing their worst chapter became their permanent name.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Abandoned.
Abuser.
Used.
Lukewarm.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Too dirty.
Too late.
But Scripture contains a startling pattern of renamed futures.
“Not My People” does not remain the final declaration.
Hosea announces restoration.
And the New Testament later reaches back into Hosea's language when describing God's astonishing mercy and the calling of His people (Romans 9:25–26; 1 Peter 2:10).
That does not mean everybody is automatically reconciled to God regardless of Christ.
The New Testament is relentlessly Christ-centered.
Forgiveness is found in Him.
Reconciliation is through Him.
New life is in Him.
The Gospel does not tell you to rename yourself.
It tells you to come to Jesus.
There is a difference.
Self-reinvention says, “I can become somebody better.”
The Gospel says, “I need a Savior.”
And maybe somebody reading this has reached the end of pretending.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your browser history knows.
Maybe your deleted messages know.
Maybe your spouse suspects.
Maybe your pillow has absorbed prayers you were too ashamed to speak aloud.
Maybe church people know the polished version of you while Jesus knows the exhausted one.
Then stop running.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Come to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Seek forgiveness where forgiveness needs to be sought.
Bring hidden sin into appropriate, trustworthy Christian accountability.
And believe what the Gospel announces about the crucified and risen Jesus:
There is mercy for repentant sinners.
There is cleansing.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is a new life that cannot be manufactured by pretending harder.
You do not have to make your scandal disappear before approaching Jesus.
You approach Jesus because only He can deal truthfully and finally with your sin.
And perhaps that is the detail we have missed while turning Gomer into a sermon illustration.
The book was never asking us merely:
“How could she do that?”
It was forcing God's people to confront another question:
“How have we?”
Where have I taken God's gifts and forgotten the Giver?
Where have I called Jesus Lord while negotiating privately with an idol?
Where have I demanded grace without repentance?
Where have I judged someone else's visible wreckage while protecting my invisible rebellion?
Where have I mistaken religious activity for covenant faithfulness?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Pray.
Repent.
Talk to Jesus.
And if you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
You do not need to publish the details of your private struggle.
God knows them.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years constructing.
“Pray for me.”
And if Christ is restoring something you thought was beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescuing.
We are people whose hope is Jesus Christ.
Not because forwarding an article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought, and salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith, not a reward for financial support.
Send it privately to the believer who is tired of pretending.
Send it to the person everybody else has already written off.
Send it even to the skeptic who believes Christianity is only a gathering of respectable people condemning broken ones.
Let them see the Cross.

Saving this article may also matter more than you think. There may come a night when shame begins preaching again, when an old temptation calls your name, or when someone you love confesses something that leaves you unsure how grace and truth can possibly coexist.
Come back to Hosea.
Then go from Hosea to Jesus.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not as proof that you love Jesus.
But as a voluntary way of helping this ministry continue producing and sharing Christ-centered biblical content with people who desperately need it.
If these resources strengthen your walk, consider helping us keep putting biblical truth in front of people who might otherwise never stop long enough to hear it.
Do not merely admire the Gospel.
Respond to Christ.

Because the greatest tragedy would be reading all the way through Gomer's story, feeling emotional about relentless love, sharing the article, commenting on it, saving it, even supporting the ministry...
and still refusing the Savior to whom the story ultimately points.
Jesus is not asking you to become impressive enough to deserve redemption.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
The Cross is where our excuses die.
The empty tomb is where hopelessness loses its authority.
And grace is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never accomplish for themselves through Jesus Christ.
So the next time someone says “Gomer,” do not immediately picture somebody else's worst mistake.
Remember Israel.
Remember yourself.
Remember the holiness of God that refuses to call evil good.
Remember the mercy of God that pursues the undeserving.
Remember the blood of Christ.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the Gospel is not the announcement that your past was harmless.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is mighty enough to redeem sinners from it.
And comment one sentence if it is genuinely your prayer:
“Jesus, bring my wandering heart home.”
Because perhaps Gomer's most uncomfortable legacy is this:
We kept calling her the scandal until the Gospel showed us that we were the wanderers too—and Christ was the One who came to redeem.
Your worst chapter does not deserve the final word; bring it to the Savior whose scars prove that grace has already written in blood.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET GO AND LET GOD” — The Christian Phrase That Sounds Biblical… Until Life Starts Bleeding
paragraphs: “LET GO AND LET GOD” — The Christian Phrase That Sounds Biblical… Until Life Starts Bleeding
What if God never told you to stop fighting—but told you to stop fighting without Him?
“Let go and let God.”
You have probably heard it whispered over hospital beds.
Posted beneath pictures of sunsets.
Spoken to the mother who cannot sleep because her child is walking away from God.
Given to the husband whose marriage is collapsing.
Repeated to the woman staring at bills she cannot pay.
Offered to the believer who has prayed the same prayer for three years and is beginning to wonder whether heaven has gone silent.
“Just let go and let God.”
It sounds peaceful.
It sounds spiritual.
It even sounds biblical.
But there is a problem.
Those exact words are not a verse in Scripture.
And depending on what we mean by them, “let go and let God” can either point us toward a profoundly biblical surrender...
or toward a dangerously incomplete Christianity.
Because sometimes what we call surrender is actually avoidance.
Sometimes what we call faith is fear wearing church clothes.
Sometimes “I’m waiting on God” really means, “I’m terrified of doing the difficult thing God already told me to do.”
And sometimes we are exhausting ourselves trying to control something that was never ours to control in the first place.
That is where this becomes personal.
Maybe there is something in your life right now that you desperately want God to fix.
A marriage.
A child.
A diagnosis.
A financial crisis.
An addiction nobody knows about.
A wound you thought you had forgiven.
A door that refuses to open.
A prayer that seems to have disappeared into the ceiling.
You have tried harder.
Prayed harder.
Worried harder.
Controlled harder.
And now you are tired.
So somebody tells you:
“Let go.”
But what exactly are you supposed to let go of?
Your responsibility?
Your obedience?
Your effort?
Your anxiety?
Your plans?
Your sin?
Your desire for control?
The Bible gives an answer far richer than the slogan.
Psalm 46:10 is often quoted as though God were gently whispering to an anxious believer beside a quiet lake:
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
Beautiful words.
But listen to the Hebrew.
הַרְפּוּ וּדְעוּ כִּי־אָנֹכִי אֱלֹהִים
Harpū u-də‘ū kî ’ānōḵî ’ĕlōhîm.
“Be still”—הַרְפּוּ, harpū—comes from the Hebrew root רפה (rāphāh), carrying ideas such as letting slacken, ceasing, desisting, or letting drop.
And the context is not primarily a peaceful morning devotional.
The earth is shaking.
Nations are raging.
Kingdoms are tottering.
Wars are raging.
Bows are being broken.
Spears are being shattered.
Then God speaks.
Cease.
Know that I am God.
“I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.”
That changes the picture.
God is not merely saying, “Relax.”
He is declaring:
Stop pretending you are sovereign.
Stop fighting as though history rests upon your shoulders.
Stop behaving as though chaos has somehow removed Me from My throne.
I am God.
You are not.
And strangely...
that is wonderful news.
Because some of us are carrying responsibilities that belong only to God.
You cannot control another person's heart.
You cannot manipulate someone into repentance.
You cannot guarantee tomorrow.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot make everybody understand you.
You cannot force somebody to love you.
You cannot manufacture the answer to prayer.
You cannot save yourself.
And you certainly cannot carry the universe.
There is a throne.
You are not sitting on it.
God is.
That is the part of “let go and let God” that desperately needs to be recovered.
Let go of your illusion of sovereignty.
Let go of the belief that enough anxiety will somehow produce control.
Let go of the secret conviction that everything depends upon you.
Let go of the future you keep rehearsing at 2:17 in the morning.
Let go of the conversations you keep replaying.
Let go of the need to know exactly how God will work everything out before you obey Him.
Peter writes:
πᾶσαν τὴν μέριμναν ὑμῶν ἐπιρίψαντες ἐπ’ αὐτόν, ὅτι αὐτῷ μέλει περὶ ὑμῶν.
Pasan tēn merimnan hymōn epiripsantes ep’ auton, hoti autō melei peri hymōn.
“Casting all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.”
That word translated “casting”—ἐπιρίψαντες (epiripsantes)—carries the concrete picture of throwing or casting something upon another.
Peter does not tell suffering Christians to pretend their burden is light.
He tells them where to put it.
On God.
And notice why.
Not because your problem is imaginary.
Not because Christians never hurt.
Not because faithful people never cry.
Not because everything will unfold according to your preferred timetable.
But...
“because He cares for you.”
That may be one of the most intimate truths in the New Testament.
The God who holds galaxies together cares about you.
Not humanity merely.
You.
Your trembling prayer.
Your exhausted mind.
Your private grief.
Your temptation.
Your disappointment.
Your fear about tomorrow.
Your tears nobody saw.
Christian surrender is therefore not throwing your pain into emptiness.
It is throwing your weight onto Someone.
Jesus Christ.
But here is where the popular slogan can become dangerous.
Biblical surrender does not mean biblical passivity.
Jesus never said, “Do absolutely nothing and call it faith.”
When Christ called Peter and Andrew, He said:
“Follow me.”
They left their nets and followed.
When Jesus encountered the man with the withered hand, He told him:
“Stretch out your hand.”
When He spoke about discipleship, He said:
“Take up your cross... and follow me.”
James warns us that faith without works is dead.
Paul describes the Christian life using images of running, fighting, training, pressing forward, standing firm and putting on armor.
Then Philippians gives us one of the clearest corrections to lazy spirituality:
“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you...”
Read that carefully.
You work...
because God works in you.
Not:
You work instead of God.
And not:
God works so you never have to obey.
Grace creates obedience.
God's power does not make faithful action unnecessary.
God's power makes faithful action possible.
That is Christianity.
Not self-salvation.
Not passive fatalism.
Dependent obedience.
You pray...
and then forgive.
You trust God...
and tell the truth.
You surrender the outcome...
and make the phone call.
You cast your anxiety upon Christ...
and take the next obedient step.
You ask God to heal your marriage...
and repent when you have sinned against your spouse.
You pray for financial provision...
and practice wisdom and stewardship.
You pray for freedom from temptation...
and flee the circumstances feeding it.
You ask Christ to restore you...
and stop protecting the secret that is destroying you.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do after praying is stand up and obey.
Remember Gethsemane.
Jesus knew suffering was coming.
He prayed:
“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.”
That is surrender.
But Jesus did not pray those words...
and run away.
He surrendered His will to the Father...
then walked toward the cross.
Think about that.
Biblical surrender did not remove the road of obedience.
It empowered Christ's obedient journey through suffering.
And at Calvary we discover something infinitely greater than a motivational slogan.
Jesus did not merely come to make overwhelmed people calmer.
He came to save sinners.
Our deepest problem is not that life feels uncontrollable.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have rebelled against the God who made us.
We have wanted His gifts while resisting His authority.
We have tried to sit upon a throne that belongs to Him.
We have sinned in thought, desire, word and deed.
And no amount of “letting go” can erase our guilt.
We needed a Savior.
So Christ came.
The sinless Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived the righteousness we could never produce.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The Gospel is not:
“Try harder until God accepts you.”
Nor is it:
“Do nothing because God does everything.”
The Gospel announces something far more glorious.
Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Salvation is received by grace through faith.
And the grace that saves us begins transforming us.
This is why repentance matters.
Maybe what you need to “let go” of is not merely anxiety.
Maybe it is sin.
The affair.
The pornography.
The bitterness.
The pride.
The hidden messages.
The addiction.
The dishonesty.
The resentment.
The secret life.
The identity built around people's approval.
The grudge you keep polishing because being angry feels safer than forgiving.
The version of Christianity where Jesus may comfort you but never command you.
Some things should not be “managed.”
They should be brought to the cross.
Maybe you have been asking God to remove consequences while protecting the very sin producing them.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit is pressing one uncomfortable question into your heart:
What are you calling “surrender” that is actually disobedience?
Be honest.
Nobody reading your answer needs to know everything.
But God already does.
And astonishingly...
He still invites you to come.
That is grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Not privately.
Not accidentally.
Three times.
The man who had sworn loyalty collapsed under pressure and denied even knowing Christ.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster.
Imagine remembering Jesus' words.
Imagine believing your worst moment had just become your permanent identity.
Scandal.
Failure.
Cowardice.
Then resurrection morning came.
And eventually, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus met Peter again.
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never failed.
He restored him.
“Do you love me?”
Then:
“Feed my sheep.”
Failure was not given the final word.
Jesus was.
Peter's story moved from scandal...
to grace.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because Christ's mercy was greater.
That is why you cannot reduce Christianity to “let go and let God.”
Christianity is about dying and rising.
Repentance and grace.
Surrender and obedience.
Weakness and divine strength.
The cross and the empty tomb.
Maybe the better sentence is:
Let go of what God never commanded you to carry...
and take hold of what Christ has commanded you to obey.
Let go of control.
Hold onto Christ.
Let go of condemnation when you have truly come to Him.
Hold onto grace.
Let go of secret sin.
Hold onto holiness.
Let go of revenge.
Hold onto forgiveness.
Let go of self-salvation.
Hold onto the finished work of Jesus.
Let go of tomorrow.
Obey Christ today.
And when you cannot see the road ahead?
Take the next faithful step.
You do not need enough light for the next twenty years.
You need enough grace for today.
Somebody reading this has been exhausted because you thought surrender meant understanding.
It doesn't.
You can trust God without understanding God.
Job never received an explanation proportionate to his suffering.
Abraham obeyed without possessing the whole map.
Joseph spent years between the dream and its fulfillment.
Paul prayed repeatedly for his thorn to leave and received sustaining grace instead.
Even Jesus, in His true humanity in Gethsemane, walked through anguish while submitting perfectly to the Father.
Faith does not always receive an explanation.
Sometimes faith receives a hand to hold in the darkness.
And His name is Jesus.
So cry if you need to cry.
Grieve what needs grieving.
Confess what needs confessing.
Apologize where repentance requires an apology.
Seek wise help where help is needed.
Make the difficult decision Scripture already makes clear.
Then release the outcome to God.
That is not weakness.
That is surrender with a backbone.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it needs to be painfully simple:
“Jesus, I cannot carry this anymore.”
“I surrender what I cannot control.”
“Forgive what I have tried to hide.”
“Give me courage to obey what You have already shown me.”
“I trust You with what happens next.”
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn this moment into another piece of Christian content you consume and forget.
Respond.
You do not have to publish the details.
Sometimes two honest words are enough to tell another believer, “I need someone standing with me.”
And read the comments too.
You may discover that the person sitting in another country with a completely different life has been fighting the same invisible battle.
That is part of why the body of Christ matters.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.
But generosity, encouragement, sharing biblical truth, and supporting faithful Gospel work can become practical ways believers participate in spreading truth.
But the deepest value we want to give you is not merchandise.
It is truth.
Discipleship.
Scripture.
Encouragement when faith feels weak.
Conviction when compromise feels comfortable.
And constant reminders that Jesus Christ remains the center.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because eventually every slogan fails.
Every inspirational quote reaches its limit.
Every human voice becomes insufficient.
There will be nights when “let go and let God” sounds painfully small compared with what you are carrying.
And on those nights, remember:
Christianity does not ultimately give you a slogan.
It gives you a Savior.
A Savior with scars.
A Savior acquainted with grief.
A Savior who carried a cross.
A Savior who entered death.
A Savior who walked out of a tomb.
A Savior who restores failures.
A Savior who forgives sinners.
A Savior who receives the exhausted.
A Savior who tells the guilty to repent and then offers cleansing no human being could manufacture.
A Savior who does not merely rewrite circumstances.
He rewrites people.
So perhaps you do need to let go.
But do not let go into nothing.
Let go of the illusion that you are God.
Let go of the sin Christ commands you to abandon.
Let go of the condemnation Christ already carried for everyone who truly belongs to Him.
Let go of your demand to control tomorrow.
Then fall with all your weight upon Jesus Christ...
and get back up to obey Him.
Because surrender was never supposed to mean that you stopped walking.
It means you finally stopped pretending you were walking alone.
You were never asked to carry the throne—only to trust the One who sits upon it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HANNAH’S HUSBAND ASKED, ‘AM I NOT MORE TO YOU THAN TEN SONS?’”
paragraphs: “HANNAH’S HUSBAND ASKED, ‘AM I NOT MORE TO YOU THAN TEN SONS?’”
He loved her. He gave her more. He tried to comfort her. And still Hannah cried—because sometimes being deeply loved does not make the thing you lost hurt any less.
There is a sentence in the Bible that sounds tender until you realize it was spoken to a woman who could barely eat.
A husband looked across the table at the woman he loved.
She was crying again.
Food sat in front of her, untouched.
Around her were the sounds of a family she desperately wanted to have for herself. Children. Voices. Movement. Life.
And somewhere nearby was Peninnah—the woman who possessed the very thing Hannah had prayed for and who knew exactly how to press that wound until it bled.
Then Elkanah asked Hannah:
“Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?”
—1 Samuel 1:8, KJV
In Hebrew, the final question reads:
הֲלוֹא אָנֹכִי טוֹב לָךְ מֵעֲשָׂרָה בָּנִים
Halo anokhi tov lakh me'asarah banim?
Literally, the thought is essentially:
“Am I not better/good to you than ten sons?”
The Hebrew word טוֹב — tov carries the ordinary sense of “good” or “better” in this comparison.
But perhaps the most heartbreaking thing about the question is that Elkanah was not Hannah's enemy.
He loved her.
That matters.
Scripture tells us so.
He gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her. He saw her tears. He noticed she was not eating. He recognized that something inside his wife was breaking.
He cared.
And yet...
he could not become the answer to every ache inside her.
Maybe that is why this ancient scene feels painfully modern.
Because perhaps you have had someone love you and still not understand why you hurt.
Maybe someone has told you:
“But you have so much to be thankful for.”
“You have a good family.”
“You have a husband.”
“You have a wife.”
“You have a job.”
“You have a roof over your head.”
“Other people have it worse.”
“Why are you still sad?”
And everything they said may have been true...
except for the conclusion they expected you to reach.
Because gratitude and grief can live in the same heart.
You can love what God has given you and still grieve what you do not have.
You can worship God and still cry.
You can believe God is good while admitting that something hurts terribly.
You can be surrounded by blessings and still carry one empty room inside your soul that nobody else seems able to enter.
Hannah did.
And Scripture does not mock her for it.
The Bible does not flatten her into a motivational slogan.
It lets her weep.
That matters more than some Christians realize.
Hannah's suffering was not merely that she had no child.
Her pain had acquired a voice.
Peninnah.
Scripture says her rival provoked her severely because of her barrenness.
And then Scripture adds three devastating words:
“year by year.”
Not one terrible afternoon.
Not one insensitive comment.
Year.
After year.
After year.
Imagine arriving at worship already knowing what is coming.
Imagine preparing to seek God while carrying the dread that someone is going to remind you of the prayer God has not answered.
Imagine watching Peninnah's children growing while your own arms remain empty.
Another year.
Another journey to Shiloh.
Another sacrifice.
Another prayer.
Another reminder.
Another tear.
There are wounds that hurt once.
Then there are wounds that wake up every morning with you.
Maybe yours is infertility.
Maybe miscarriage.
Maybe the child you buried.
Maybe the marriage that collapsed.
Maybe the person who promised forever and disappeared.
Maybe the son who no longer calls.
Maybe the daughter who walked away from God.
Maybe the diagnosis you never expected.
Maybe the ministry that failed.
Maybe the addiction you thought you had conquered.
Maybe the financial pressure nobody knows about.
Maybe you smile in church because explaining the truth would take too long.
Maybe you have learned how to worship while bleeding.
Hannah would understand.
And here is something astonishing.
Elkanah asks:
“Am I not better to thee than ten sons?”
But Hannah does not answer him in the recorded text.
She gets up.
And she goes to God.
That may be one of the most important movements in the entire chapter.
Because there comes a moment when human comfort reaches its boundary.
A husband can love you without being able to heal you.
A wife can hold you without being able to rescue you.
A friend can listen without possessing the answer.
A pastor can pray with you without controlling tomorrow.
People can sit beside your wound.
Only God can be God.
Hannah rises and goes before the LORD.
And then Scripture gives us words almost too raw to read casually:
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.”
—1 Samuel 1:10, KJV
The Hebrew describes her as:
מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — marat nephesh
A woman bitterly distressed in her very being.
This was not polished prayer.
This was not religious performance.
This was not Hannah trying to impress the people standing nearby.
She was shattered.
So she prayed shattered.
Her lips moved.
Her voice could not be heard.
Tears were saying what sentences could not.
And then, as though Peninnah's cruelty were not enough, even the priest misunderstood her.
Eli watched her mouth moving and concluded she was drunk.
Think about that.
She came into the presence of God wounded...
and was misjudged by a religious leader while she was praying.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You finally tried to reach for God, and somebody misunderstood you.
You were struggling, and people called you rebellious.
You were exhausted, and somebody called you lazy.
You were grieving, and somebody told you your faith was weak.
You were trying to survive, and someone judged the way survival looked on you.
Hannah finally answered Eli:
“I... have poured out my soul before the LORD.”
That is the line.
That is where hiding ends.
She poured it out.
Not part of it.
Not the church-safe version.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the sentence that makes everybody comfortable.
Her soul.
Before the LORD.
And perhaps that is what somebody needs to hear today:
God is not frightened by the prayer you are afraid to pray.
You do not need to clean up your tears before bringing them to Him.
You do not need to pretend disappointment is victory.
You do not need to call pain “peace” to prove you have faith.
Bring Him the real thing.
The jealousy.
The confusion.
The exhaustion.
The anger you are ashamed to admit.
The question you keep swallowing.
The prayer you stopped praying because another unanswered year felt unbearable.
Pour it out.
Not because God owes us whatever we request.
Hannah's story must never be twisted into a formula that says, “Cry hard enough and God will give you exactly what you want.”
Scripture does not teach that.
Faithful believers sometimes receive the thing they begged God for.
Faithful believers sometimes do not.
Paul pleaded about his thorn and received sustaining grace rather than removal.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane, “not my will, but thine, be done.”
Biblical faith is not forcing God's hand.
Biblical faith places our trembling hand into His.
Hannah asked specifically.
Boldly.
Desperately.
But notice what happened next.
Before Samuel entered her arms...
something happened to Hannah's face.
After Eli spoke peace over her, Scripture says:
“So the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad.”
—1 Samuel 1:18, KJV
Do not rush past that.
Samuel had not been born.
Hannah was not pregnant yet.
Her circumstances had not visibly changed.
Peninnah had not vanished.
There was no positive pregnancy test waiting at home.
There was no baby crying in her arms.
Yet Hannah got up...
ate...
and her face was no longer as it had been.
Something changed before the circumstance changed.
She had poured out what she could no longer carry alone.
That does not mean every grieving believer will immediately feel emotionally better after praying. Scripture never turns prayer into a mechanical switch for human emotion.
But Hannah's story shows us something beautiful:
there can be surrender before there is an answer.
There can be worship before there is evidence.
There can be peace while the womb is still empty.
And then came morning.
Do you know what Hannah and Elkanah did before going home?
They worshiped.
That might be one of the most beautiful acts in the chapter.
Hannah worshiped the God who had not yet placed Samuel in her arms.
That is faith.
Not pretending.
Not bargaining.
Not denying reality.
Worship.
Then Scripture says something that echoes throughout the Bible:
“the LORD remembered her.”
This does not mean God had forgotten Hannah and suddenly recovered the memory.
When Scripture speaks this way, God's “remembering” points to His turning toward someone according to His covenant purpose and acting on their behalf.
The God who seemed silent had never been absent.
And in time Hannah conceived.
A boy was born.
Samuel.
The child she had cried for became the child she would surrender back to God.
That is where Hannah's story becomes even more challenging.
Because many of us want God to give us something.
Hannah received what she asked for...
and then released Samuel into God's service according to her vow.
The gift did not replace the Giver.
Her answered prayer became an offering.
And perhaps that is where this story reaches beyond infertility and reaches every one of us.
What if the thing you are asking God for eventually arrives?
Will it become your god?
Or will it become something you can place back into God's hands?
The relationship.
The healing.
The opportunity.
The business.
The platform.
The child.
The ministry.
The money.
The restored life.
Hannah teaches us to pray for the gift without worshiping the gift.
And centuries later, another promised Son would enter the story of humanity.
Not Samuel.
Jesus Christ.
Samuel would become a prophet used mightily by God.
But Samuel could not carry the sin of the world.
Jesus could.
Hannah's empty arms eventually held a son.
But humanity's deeper emptiness required the Son.
Jesus Christ entered our grief, our shame, our rebellion, our death.
He was misunderstood.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Crucified.
And on that cross He bore sin—not because humanity had finally become worthy, but because God is rich in mercy.
This is where every human scandal meets grace.
Our scandal is deeper than what others did to us.
It includes what sin has done within us.
We have sinned.
We have hidden.
We have worshiped created things.
We have wounded others.
We have tried to become our own gods.
And Christianity's answer is not:
“Try harder.”
It is Christ.
The sinless Son of God crucified for sinners and risen from the dead.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves how seriously He takes it.
Grace is God offering forgiveness and reconciliation through Jesus Christ to sinners who could never rescue themselves.
So perhaps your deepest need today is not for God to give you your “Samuel.”
Perhaps your deepest need is Jesus.
And even if the prayer you desperately want answered remains unanswered tonight...
Christ is still enough to save you.
Christ is still worthy.
Christ is still risen.
Christ is still merciful.
Christ still receives sinners who come to Him.
Your unanswered prayer does not cancel the cross.
Your tears do not frighten Him.
Your past does not surprise Him.
Your shame is not stronger than His grace.
Your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Maybe you have spent years trying to appear strong.
Stop performing before God.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent where you need to repent.
Confess what you have hidden.
Bring Him what hurts.
Trust Christ with what you cannot repair.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Someone who cries after everybody sleeps.
Someone whose prayer seems unanswered.
Someone who thinks God has forgotten their name.
Put this on your profile where they might find it.
It does not.
Not because money buys salvation, spiritual favor, answered prayer, or a place in God's family.
It never could.
Give freely, prayerfully, and without compulsion.

But if you believe this ministry is bearing Gospel fruit, voluntarily supporting it is one practical way you can help us keep creating, publishing, expanding, and placing Christ-centered resources before people who desperately need them.
It helps us write.
Publish.
Reach.
Teach.
Encourage.
And continue building resources for believers who are hungry to go deeper into Scripture.
You can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone hurting.
Because ministry is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
And perhaps somewhere tonight...
there is another Hannah sitting silently in a crowded room.
Loved...
but hurting.
Blessed...
but grieving.
Surrounded...
but lonely.
Trying to understand why God seems to be answering everybody else's prayer.
Maybe nobody around her understands.
Maybe even the person who loves her most keeps asking why she cannot simply be happy with what she already has.
But Heaven is not intimidated by the prayer she cannot say aloud.
God sees the moving lips.
God sees the untouched food.
God sees the years.
God sees the provocation.
God sees the private tears.
And whether His answer comes in the form she desperately hopes for or through sustaining grace she never expected, she can entrust herself to the God revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
So pour out your soul.
Then place it in His hands.
You may not know what God will write on the next page.
But because of Jesus, you can know that sin, shame, suffering, and death do not get the final word.
Sometimes the prayer that begins with an empty heart becomes the place where you discover that Christ was holding you before your answer ever arrived.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RELIGIOUS PEOPLE WERE FURIOUS BECAUSE JESUS WAS EATING WITH SINNERS. HIS ANSWER REVEALED WHY HE CAME.
paragraphs: RELIGIOUS PEOPLE WERE FURIOUS BECAUSE JESUS WAS EATING WITH SINNERS. HIS ANSWER REVEALED WHY HE CAME.
Jesus sat at a table respectable religion wanted Him to avoid—and what He said next still exposes the difference between looking righteous and desperately needing a Savior.
There was food on the table.
There were sinners in the room.
And Jesus stayed.
That may be one of the most uncomfortable pictures of Christ in the Gospels for anyone who has learned to associate holiness with keeping a safe distance from people whose lives are visibly messy.
Because Jesus was not accidentally caught in the wrong house.
He was not passing through.
He was eating with them.
Tax collectors.
Sinners.
People carrying reputations.
People religious society knew how to categorize.
People whose names may have been spoken differently when they entered the room.
And there, reclining at the table among them, was Jesus Christ.
Mark records the scene:
“Καὶ γίνεται κατακεῖσθαι αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ αὐτοῦ…”
Kaì gínetai katakeîsthai autón en tē̂i oikíāi autoû…
In plain English, Jesus was reclining at the table in the house.
That Greek verb, κατάκειμαι (katakeimai), matters because this was not the picture of Jesus standing outside the doorway shouting religious instructions at broken people.
He was at the table.
Mark continues by telling us that many tax collectors and sinners were reclining together with Jesus and His disciples.
And then the atmosphere changed.
Not because the sinners complained.
Because the religious observers did.
The scribes associated with the Pharisees saw Jesus eating with these people and asked His disciples the question that exposed everything:
Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?
Think about that.
They were looking at the same Jesus.
The sinners saw someone willing to sit near them.
The religious critics saw someone they believed should have stayed away from them.
One room.
One Christ.
Two completely different reactions.
And perhaps that room is much closer to us than we would like to admit.
Because some of us know what it feels like to be the person at that table.
You know what it is to carry something you desperately hope nobody discovers.
You know what it is to smile at church while privately fighting thoughts you would never put into a prayer request.
You know what it is to worship with your hands raised while your heart whispers:
“If they really knew me…”
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe it was adultery.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Greed.
A secret relationship.
A destroyed marriage.
Years away from God.
A lie that became another lie and then another.
Maybe you did not destroy your reputation.
Maybe you simply became spiritually numb.
You still know the songs.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You can still quote Scripture.
But somewhere inside, the fire became ashes.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that other people discovered your sin.
Perhaps it is that you became so accustomed to it that you stopped being disturbed by it yourself.
Then Jesus walks into Levi's house.
And suddenly the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Because before this meal, Jesus had encountered Levi sitting at the tax booth.

Tax collectors in the Roman world could become deeply despised among their own people because their work was tied to the occupying system and could be associated with exploitation. Levi was not introduced polishing his religious résumé.
He was sitting at the place associated with the life he had been living.
And Jesus said:
“Follow Me.”
Not because Levi had already repaired himself.
Not because his reputation had suddenly become respectable.
Not because he had completed enough religious exercises to become worthy of Christ.
Jesus called him.
And Levi followed.
Then somehow the man who had been sitting at a tax booth became the man with Jesus sitting at his table.
Do not rush past that.
Grace had entered the house.
But grace did not enter to tell darkness that darkness was acceptable.
Jesus eating with sinners was never Jesus approving sin.
The same Christ who welcomed sinners called people to repentance.
He forgave sins.
He commanded transformed lives.
He spoke of denying ourselves, taking up the cross, and following Him.
He warned about judgment.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called evil what it was.
And ultimately He went to the cross because sin was so devastating that our rescue would cost the blood of the Son of God.
Christian grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
That distinction changes everything.
Jesus did not become contaminated by sitting near sinners.
He came to rescue them.
The physician does not prove compassion by avoiding the hospital.
And that is exactly the picture Jesus gave His critics.
When He heard their question, He answered:
“Οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ ἀλλ᾽ οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες…”
Ou chreían échousin hoi ischýontes iatroû, all’ hoi kakō̂s échontes…
Those who are strong or well do not need a physician, but those who are sick.
Then came the sentence that explained the table.
“οὐκ ἦλθον καλέσαι δικαίους ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλούς.”
Ouk ē̂lthon kalésai dikaíous allà hamartōloús.
“I did not come to call righteous people, but sinners.”
There it is.
Why was Jesus at that table?
Because this is why He came.
The question was essentially:
“Jesus, why are You with people like these?”
His answer was:
Because sick people need a physician.
And suddenly the scandal was no longer merely about who was sitting beside Jesus.
It was about who understood that they needed Him.
That is where this story turns toward us.
Because there are two dangerous places you can occupy spiritually.
You can know you are sick and run from the Physician.
Or you can be sick and convince yourself that you are healthy.
The second may be far more difficult to cure.
The tax collectors had obvious reputations.
The religious critics had respectable appearances.
But every human being at that house needed grace.
So do we.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The openly rebellious.
The secretly addicted.
The respected church member.
The skeptic.
The pastor.
The person reading this with tears beginning to form.
The person reading this while feeling absolutely nothing.
All.
This is why Christianity cannot ultimately be reduced to good people versus bad people.
The Gospel is about guilty people and a gracious Savior.
Dead people receiving life.
Lost people being found.
Enemies being reconciled.
Sinners being forgiven.
And forgiven sinners becoming followers of Jesus.
There is no room at the foot of the cross for boasting.
Only surrender.
Perhaps you have spent years thinking you needed to clean yourself up before coming back to God.
“One day.”
“When I stop this.”
“When my marriage improves.”
“When I overcome the addiction.”
“When I feel worthy again.”
“When I can pray without feeling like a hypocrite.”
Listen carefully.
You do not take a bath before taking a bath.
You do not cure yourself before visiting the physician.
And you cannot become your own savior before approaching Jesus.
Come honestly.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come without pretending.
But come ready to surrender.
Because Christ does not merely invite you to feel better about remaining exactly as you are.
He calls you to Himself.
And when Jesus truly takes hold of a life, grace begins rewriting things.
That does not mean every consequence disappears overnight.
It does not mean temptation vanishes.
It does not mean Christians become instantly flawless.
It means the sinner no longer belongs to the sin that once claimed him.
There is a new Master.
A new direction.
A new identity.
A new war against the flesh.
A new hunger for holiness.
A new reason to get back up after falling.
This is repentance.
The Greek noun often translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), carrying the idea of a changed mind that expresses itself in a changed direction toward God.
There is an important textual detail worth knowing here.

Many familiar English Bibles influenced by later manuscript traditions render Mark 2:17 as Jesus calling “sinners to repentance.” The wording “to repentance” is absent from the earlier critical Greek text of Mark at this point, which simply reads that Jesus came to call sinners. But the theology of repentance is not remotely absent from Jesus’ ministry. Mark begins Jesus’ proclamation with the command to repent and believe the Gospel, and the parallel account in Luke 5:32 explicitly records Jesus saying that He came to call sinners “to repentance.”
So the biblical picture remains beautifully whole:
Jesus receives sinners.
Jesus calls sinners.
Jesus forgives sinners.
Jesus calls sinners to repent.
Jesus transforms sinners.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain chained.
Power to come home.
And maybe that is exactly why this story hurts.
Because perhaps you have been hiding.
Not from people.
