From Jesus.
You have assumed that because you failed again, He wants nothing to do with you.
Perhaps you promised God you would stop.
Then returned.
You cried.
Then returned.
Deleted it.
Downloaded it again.
Walked away.
Went back.
Prayed.
Compromised.
Repented.
Fell.
And somewhere along the way shame began preaching its own gospel:
“You have gone too far.”
“You knew better.”
“God must be tired of you.”
“People like you don't belong near Jesus.”
But look again at the table.
Who is sitting there?
Sinners.
And who intentionally came near them?
Jesus.
Your sin is serious.
Your shame is not your savior.
Jesus is.
The answer is not to rename your sin so you can live comfortably inside it.
The answer is not to hide your sin until it destroys you.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Forsake it.
Seek help where help is needed.
Turn toward Christ.
Trust the One who carried sin to the cross.
Because the Physician came for sick people.
And if you can finally admit, “Lord, I am sick,” that confession is not the end of your story.
It may be the moment you finally stop refusing treatment.
Jesus Christ did more than eat with sinners.
He died for sinners.
The table points forward to a cross.
There, the sinless Son of God would be treated like the guilty one.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Crucified.
Jesus “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Paul says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we became useful.
While we were sinners.
And the crucified Christ rose.
The grave did not keep Him.
Sin does not have the final word.
Death does not have the final word.
Your worst chapter does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Grace is.
Not because sin deserves celebration.
The Savior deserves celebration.
Not because our past does not matter.
Because Christ can redeem people whose past seemed capable of destroying their future.
Maybe you are Levi today.
Jesus is calling you away from the booth.
Maybe you are one of the nameless sinners at the table, wondering whether there could possibly be room near Christ for someone carrying your history.
There is.

Maybe, more uncomfortably, you resemble the religious observers standing outside the beauty of the moment because you are too busy questioning why Jesus would welcome someone whose sins look worse than yours.
Then you need the Physician too.
We all do.
The church should never become a museum where polished Christians display how respectable they have become.
It is a redeemed family gathered around a crucified and risen Savior, filled with people who can say:
I was lost.
Jesus found me.
I was guilty.
Jesus forgave me.
I was enslaved.
Jesus began setting me free.
I was dead.
Christ gave me life.
And I am still following Him.
So be honest.
Which person are you in this story?
The sinner afraid to approach Jesus?
The believer who fell again?
The religious person who has become better at identifying other people's sins than grieving your own?
The wounded Christian wondering whether grace still has your name on it?
The skeptic quietly hoping Jesus might actually be who Christians say He is?
Do not hide behind a reaction button.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to give another wounded person courage to come home.
Then think of one person who needs this table.
One.
That brother who disappeared from church.
That daughter who thinks God could never want her.
That friend trapped in addiction.
That believer smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
That person everybody else gave up on.
Send this privately if their struggle should remain private.
If Christ has given us good news, we should not be ashamed to carry it.
There may come a night when shame tries to convince you that Jesus only wants cleaned-up people.
Come back and remember the table.

Gospel Warrior exists to keep placing Scripture, biblical conviction, Gospel hope, discipleship, and Christ-centered encouragement in front of people who are hungry for more than shallow inspiration. Someone you love may be one Scripture away from finally asking the question they have been afraid to ask.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a way to purchase God's favor, earn salvation, or prove that you love Jesus. Salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith in Christ.
But generosity, sharing truth, encouraging others, and helping faithful Gospel work continue can become meaningful expressions of gratitude to God.

So if you believe this work should keep reaching the person scrolling alone at midnight…the ashamed believer…the wandering son…the wounded daughter…the Christian barely holding onto faith…you can help carry it farther.
The Physician is still calling sick people.
The Savior is still receiving repentant sinners.
Grace is still greater than the scandal you thought would define you forever.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing about Levi's table was never that sinners were sitting near Jesus.
It was that Jesus knew exactly who they were…
and came for them anyway.
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you, but His grace gets to decide what happens after He calls your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EZEKIEL DESCRIBED JERUSALEM AS AN ABANDONED BABY—THEN AS AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE
paragraphs: EZEKIEL DESCRIBED JERUSALEM AS AN ABANDONED BABY—THEN AS AN UNFAITHFUL WIFE

She was thrown away, covered in blood, and left to die. God walked past her and said one word that changed everything: “LIVE.” Then the child He rescued grew beautiful... and eventually used His gifts to betray Him. But the most shocking part of Ezekiel 16 is not Jerusalem’s scandal. It is what God says after He exposes it.
There are chapters in the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that encourage you.
And then there are chapters that seem to grab you by the shoulders, turn your face toward the mirror, and refuse to let you look away.
Ezekiel 16 is one of those chapters.
It is uncomfortable.
Graphic.
Heartbreaking.
At times almost unbearable.
Yet underneath its disturbing imagery lies one of Scripture’s most devastating portraits of human sin—and one of its most astonishing pictures of covenant mercy.
Because Ezekiel 16 is not merely the story of a wicked city.
It is the story of what happens when people forget who found them.
And perhaps that is why this chapter still hurts.
Because some of us have forgotten too.
God tells Ezekiel:
בֶּן־אָדָם הוֹדַע אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלַם אֶת־תּוֹעֲבֹתֶיהָ
Ben-adam, hoda et-Yerushalayim et-to'avoteha.
“Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations.”

God is speaking about Jerusalem through an extended allegory. The city becomes a woman whose entire life is placed before us—from unwanted infant, to rescued child, to beloved bride, to unfaithful wife, to disgraced sinner, and finally to the astonishing possibility of covenant restoration.
And it begins in a field.
Not a palace.
Not a temple.
Not surrounded by priests.
A field.
A newborn baby lies there.
Her umbilical cord has not been properly cut.
She has not been washed.
She has not been salted according to the customs described in the passage.
She has not been wrapped.
Nobody wants her.
Nobody even pities her.
Ezekiel says she was thrown into the open field because she was despised on the day she was born.
Then God passes by.
Imagine the scene.
No mother running toward the crying child.
No father searching desperately.
No hands reaching down.
No human voice saying, “I want you.”
Only blood.
Dirt.
Exposure.
Helplessness.
And death approaching.
Then—
God.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:6 is unforgettable:
וָאֶעֱבֹר עָלַיִךְ וָאֶרְאֵךְ מִתְבּוֹסֶסֶת בְּדָמָיִךְ
“I passed by you and saw you wallowing in your blood.”
Then come the words that change the entire story:
בְּדָמַיִךְ חֲיִי
Bedamayikh chayi.
“In your blood—live.”
And God says it again.
בְּדָמַיִךְ חֲיִי
“Live.”
Before she could clean herself—
Live.
Before she could prove herself—
Live.
Before she could repay anything—
Live.
Before she possessed beauty, status, influence, wealth, reputation, or anything she could offer—
God saw her.
That matters.
Because we have become very skilled at presenting the cleaned-up version of ourselves.
We know what photograph to upload.
We know what testimony to tell.
We know which parts of our history are safe enough to reveal.
We know how to say “God is good” while hiding the room inside our heart that we are terrified to let Him enter.
But God did not meet Jerusalem after she cleaned the blood away.
He found her in it.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to understand what grace actually means.
Grace is not God discovering that you were secretly worthy all along.
Grace is God showing mercy to the undeserving.
The Gospel does not begin with humanity climbing toward God.
It begins with God coming toward sinners.
That truth eventually reaches its blazing center in Jesus Christ.
“For while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
Not once we became impressive.
Not after we repaired everything.
While we were sinners.
That is scandalous grace.
But Ezekiel 16 does not end in the field.
The abandoned child grows.
God provides for her.
She reaches maturity.
Then the imagery changes.
God describes entering covenant with her.
Ezekiel 16:8 says:
וָאָבוֹא בִבְרִית אֹתָךְ
Va'avo bivrit otakh.
“I entered into a covenant with you.”
That word matters:
בְּרִית — berit
Covenant.
This is not merely romantic imagery. The chapter is describing Jerusalem’s relationship to the LORD in covenant terms.
God covers her nakedness.
Washes her.
Anoints her.
Clothes her.
Adorns her.
Feeds her.
Raises her from abandonment into splendor.
The child nobody wanted becomes like royalty.
And then comes one of the most important sentences in the chapter.
God tells Jerusalem that her beauty became perfect because of His splendor that He had placed upon her.
Do not miss that.
Her glory was borrowed glory.
Her beauty was given beauty.
Her abundance was received abundance.
Everything she became rested upon what God had given.
Then everything changes.
וַתִּבְטְחִי בְיָפְיֵךְ
Vattivtechi veyofyekh.
“But you trusted in your beauty.”
There is the fracture.
She began trusting the gift instead of the Giver.
The rescued forgot the Rescuer.
The blessed forgot the Blesser.
The woman who once possessed nothing began behaving as though everything had always belonged to her.
And suddenly Ezekiel 16 stops feeling ancient.
Because haven't we done this?
God gives someone intelligence, and eventually intelligence becomes the reason they believe they no longer need God.
God gives someone success, and success quietly becomes their identity.
God gives someone a relationship, and that person becomes more important than obedience.
God gives money, and money becomes security.
God gives influence, and applause becomes oxygen.
God gives beauty, and the mirror becomes an altar.
God gives ministry, and eventually the ministry itself can become an idol.
Even spiritual gifts can become dangerous when we begin loving what God placed in our hands more than the God whose hands gave it.
Jerusalem took what God had given and used it in idolatry.
The chapter deliberately uses the language of marital unfaithfulness to expose covenant betrayal.
It becomes darker still.
Jerusalem sacrifices her children to idols.
She pursues foreign powers.
She multiplies her unfaithfulness.
God says something devastating:
לֹא זָכַרְתְּ אֶת־יְמֵי נְעוּרָיִךְ
Lo zakhart et-yemei ne'urayikh.
“You did not remember the days of your youth.”
You forgot.
That may be one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions imaginable.
Not simply suffering.
Forgetting.
Forgetting what the pit felt like.
Forgetting the prayer you prayed when nobody else could help you.
Forgetting how desperately you once needed mercy.
Forgetting the addiction Christ began breaking.
Forgetting the night you cried until there were no tears left.
Forgetting the hospital room.
Forgetting the betrayal.
Forgetting the loneliness.
Forgetting how empty your life was when sin promised everything and delivered chains.
Forgetting what it was like before grace found you.
And eventually forgetting the One who found you.
Some people do not walk away from God because life became terrible.
Sometimes they drift because life became comfortable.
The prayer that once sounded like “Jesus, please save me” quietly becomes “I can handle this.”
The Bible stays closed a little longer.
Prayer gets shorter.
Conviction becomes irritating.
Worship becomes routine.
Secret compromises begin receiving respectable names.
And slowly...
almost invisibly...
the rescued heart begins trusting its own beauty.
That is why Ezekiel's language is so severe.
God refuses to flatter Jerusalem while she is destroying herself.
Biblical love does not pretend rebellion is harmless.
Grace never requires God to lie about sin.
Jesus Himself came preaching:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15).
Repentance is not God humiliating you for entertainment.
It is the mercy of God calling you away from the thing that is killing you.
Ezekiel exposes Jerusalem's idolatry, injustice, pride, bloodshed, covenant breaking, and spiritual adultery.
And then he makes an observation many readers overlook.
When Jerusalem is compared with Sodom, Ezekiel 16:49 identifies among Sodom's sins pride, abundance, complacent ease, and failure to strengthen the poor and needy.
That should disturb comfortable religion.
God notices what we do with abundance.
God notices the person everyone else ignores.
God notices when religious people possess enough to help but train themselves not to see suffering.
God notices.
Yet even after everything Jerusalem has done, Ezekiel 16 takes another breathtaking turn.
Judgment is real.
Shame is real.
Consequences are real.
God does not erase the moral seriousness of what happened.
But then...
after rebellion...
after idolatry...
after betrayal...
after judgment...
God says:
וְזָכַרְתִּי אֲנִי אֶת־בְּרִיתִי
Vezakharti ani et-beriti.
“I will remember My covenant.”
Jerusalem forgot.
God remembered.
Sit with that.
She forgot the field.
She forgot the blood.
She forgot the voice saying “Live.”
She forgot the washing.
She forgot the covering.
She forgot the covenant.
But God says:
“I will remember.”
And in Ezekiel 16:60 He speaks of establishing an everlasting covenant.
Then the final verse reaches a word that Christians should recognize as extraordinarily significant.
בְּכַפְּרִי־לָךְ לְכָל־אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂית
The expression comes from the Hebrew root כפר — k-p-r, associated with making atonement.
The chapter closes with God speaking of making atonement for what Jerusalem has done.
That does not mean sin never mattered.
It means mercy has not spoken its final word yet.
And for Christians reading the whole biblical story, our eyes are drawn toward Jesus.
Toward a hill outside Jerusalem.
Toward another scene involving blood.
Toward the Lamb of God.
Toward the One who did not merely tell dying sinners to rescue themselves, but gave Himself for them.
At the cross, God's holiness is not discarded so that grace can exist.
Sin is taken with terrible seriousness.
Christ bears sin.
Redemption comes at a cost we could never pay.
And resurrection announces that death does not get the final sentence.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally a self-improvement program.
You do not need Jesus merely to make a reasonably decent person slightly nicer.
We needed rescue.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
New life.
We needed Christ.
Perhaps the hardest question in Ezekiel 16, then, is not:
“How could Jerusalem betray God after everything He did?”
Perhaps the harder question is:
Where have I done the same thing?
What gift have you begun loving more than the Giver?
What secret compromise have you renamed so you no longer have to call it sin?
What did Jesus rescue you from that you are slowly walking back toward?
What prayer did you stop praying because life became comfortable?
What conviction have you been silencing?
What part of yourself are you hiding behind Christian language?
Be honest.
Not with Facebook.
Not with me.
With God.
Because the God who saw Jerusalem bleeding in the field is not intimidated by what He sees when He looks into the places you hide.
You cannot shock an omniscient God with a confession.
He already knows.
The question is whether you will keep running—or finally come into the light.
Maybe you have fallen farther than you ever imagined.
Maybe you once worshiped passionately, but now your heart feels numb.
Maybe you know Scripture but secretly feel miles from God.
Maybe your browser history and your Sunday worship tell two different stories.
Maybe bitterness has been living inside you so long that you have started calling it discernment.
Maybe pride learned how to quote Bible verses.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong, but spiritually you are exhausted.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something you have never told anyone.
Hear the Gospel again.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
There is forgiveness in Him.
There is cleansing in Him.
There is restoration in Him.
There is no sin so small that you do not need His grace, and no repentant sinner needs to conclude that Christ's mercy is too small for them.
Come home.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become worthy.
Come honestly.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Return to Christ.
Just be real.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward Jesus.
That matters.
And think of one person who needs Ezekiel 16 today.
Not twenty random people.
One.
The friend who is drifting.
The brother who thinks his past disqualifies him.
The woman silently carrying shame.
The believer who has become comfortable.
The person who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to have perfect lives.
Sometimes sharing the Gospel begins with one ordinary click that places truth in front of someone you may never have known was struggling.
Not because you need another saved post.
A night when shame tells you to run from God.
A night when temptation whispers that nothing has changed.
A night when success tempts you to believe you no longer need Him.
Come back and remember:
בְּדָמַיִךְ חֲיִי
Live.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, understand difficult passages, confront sin honestly, and keep your eyes on Jesus, stay close to this ministry.

Scripture teaches that Christian giving should come from a willing heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Your local church and your own biblical convictions about tithes, offerings, generosity, and stewardship should be honored.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Help put the truth of Jesus in front of one more wounded person.
Because Ezekiel 16 begins with a baby nobody wanted...
but it does not end with abandonment.
It begins with blood...
but it does not end with death.
It travels through beauty, pride, betrayal, idolatry, exposure, judgment, shame, remembrance, covenant, and atonement.
And that is why this chapter is so difficult to forget.
The deepest scandal is not merely that Jerusalem became unfaithful.
The wonder is that after exposing the betrayal, God was still speaking about covenant and atonement.
And the Gospel takes us farther still—to Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, calling sinners to repentance and offering forgiveness to everyone who comes to Him in faith.
Maybe you came to this article thinking about ancient Jerusalem.
Maybe God used it to make you think about yourself.
Remember the field.
Remember the blood.
Remember the voice.
Remember who found you.
Remember who carried you.
Remember who forgave you.
Remember the cross.
And when shame whispers, “Look what you have done,” look toward Christ and remember what He has done.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life has been surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID HAD MANY WOMEN—YET SCRIPTURE MAKES A POINT OF SAYING HE DIDN’T SLEEP WITH ABISHAG
paragraphs:
DAVID HAD MANY WOMEN—YET SCRIPTURE MAKES A POINT OF SAYING HE DIDN’T SLEEP WITH ABISHAG
The man who once took another man’s wife was eventually placed beside an exceedingly beautiful woman—and Scripture stopped to tell us what did not happen.
There is one sentence near the end of David’s life that is incredibly easy to read past.
Four Hebrew words.
Quiet words.
No battlefield. No giant. No adultery exposed by a prophet. No murdered husband. No dead child. No rebellious son. No public humiliation.
Just an old king lying in a cold room with a beautiful young woman beside him.
And then Scripture says:
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ
Veha-melekh lo yeda‘ah.
“And the king did not know her.”
—1 Kings 1:4
In biblical Hebrew, yada‘—“to know”—can describe ordinary knowledge, but in this kind of context it is a recognized biblical way of referring to sexual relations.
In other words:
David did not sleep with Abishag.
And that sentence becomes astonishing when you remember who David was.
This was not a man whose history with women was spotless.
This was David.
David had wives.
David had concubines.
David had known sexual desire.
David had also catastrophically abused power in connection with Bathsheba.
He saw her.
He wanted her.
He sent for her.
He took her.
And when her pregnancy threatened to expose what he had done, David eventually arranged circumstances that resulted in Uriah's death.
The Bible does not airbrush that scandal.
That matters.
Scripture refuses to turn its heroes into plastic saints.
David could write psalms and still sin terribly.
He could defeat Goliath and still be defeated by his own desires.
He could be courageous before armies and dangerously weak in private.
He could genuinely love God and still commit sins that brought devastating consequences upon himself and others.
That should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because we prefer testimonies where the darkness is far enough in the past that we can safely applaud the ending.
But David’s story does something more painful.
It shows us what sin can destroy.
Then it shows us what repentance looks like when excuses finally die.
And years later, when David is old and physically failing, Scripture places another woman beside him.
Not merely a woman.
The narrator deliberately tells us:
וְהַנַּעֲרָה יָפָה עַד־מְאֹד
Veha-na‘arah yafah ‘ad-me’od.
“The young woman was exceedingly beautiful.”
Her name was Abishag the Shunammite.

David had become so old that clothing could no longer keep him warm. His servants therefore searched for a young virgin who could attend him and lie close to him so that her body warmth might warm the aging king.
They searched throughout Israel.
They found Abishag.
She entered David’s chamber.
She served him.
She remained physically close to him.
She was exceedingly beautiful.
Then Scripture gives us that strange, deliberate sentence:
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ
“But the king did not know her.”
Why tell us?
Why does the narrator care that we know what did not happen?
We should be careful here.
The Bible does not explicitly say, “God placed Abishag there as David’s final temptation.”
It does not tell us that this scene was a divinely arranged test designed to prove David’s repentance.
We should not claim more than Scripture claims.
Nor should we romanticize David's earlier sexual history. The biblical narratives surrounding his household contain enormous dysfunction, grief, violence, rivalry, and consequences.
But the narrator unquestionably wants us to know one particular fact about Abishag:
David did not have sexual relations with her.
That fact becomes especially striking because readers already know David’s history.
Once, David stood on a rooftop and saw a beautiful woman.
Later, David lay in a bed with another beautiful woman close enough to warm his failing body.
Once, desire became taking.
Here, proximity did not become intercourse.
And somewhere between those two scenes lies a lifetime of scars.
Bathsheba.
Uriah.
Nathan.
A dead child.
A fractured household.
Amnon.
Tamar.
Absalom.
Rebellion.
Grief.
David learned something many of us learn far too late:
Sin can be forgiven without becoming harmless.
Grace does not mean consequences were imaginary.
David's repentance did not resurrect Uriah.
It did not erase Bathsheba’s suffering.
It did not magically repair every fracture in his family.
Forgiveness is not God pretending evil was acceptable.
Forgiveness is God refusing to let evil have the final word over the repentant sinner.
And that is where David's story begins reaching through the centuries and touching ours.
Because perhaps your name is not David.
Perhaps your scandal never became public.
Perhaps nobody confronted you with the words Nathan spoke to David:
“You are the man.”
Maybe your battlefield is a phone screen nobody else sees.
A private conversation.
A relationship you know is crossing boundaries.
Pornography you keep deleting and returning to.
Bitterness you have learned to disguise as discernment.
Money you should not be touching.
Attention you secretly crave.
An emotional affair you insist is “just friendship.”
A habit you keep renaming because calling it sin would require repentance.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing well spiritually.
You worship.
You post Scripture.
You encourage people.
You know Christian vocabulary.
But there is a room inside your life where you keep telling Jesus:
“Not this one.”
David's story will not let us comfortably divide humanity into good people and scandalous people.
The Gospel gives us a more devastating diagnosis.
We are sinners who need a Savior.
David needed one.
You need one.
I need one.
And Christianity's answer is not simply, “Try harder than David did.”
Its answer is Jesus Christ.
David was Israel's king.
But David was never Israel's final King.
He was a shepherd, but another Shepherd was coming.
He defeated enemies, but another Son of David would defeat the enemies David could never conquer for us: sin and death.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus came to purchase it.
David's hands were stained.
Christ's hands were pierced.
David sometimes used royal power for himself.
Jesus Christ, the rightful King, humbled Himself and gave Himself for sinners.
At the cross, God does not tell us that our sins do not matter.
The cross tells us they matter so much that redemption cost blood.
And yet it also tells us something almost impossible to believe when shame has been whispering in your ear for years:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That does not make your sin small.
It makes Christ's grace enormous.
David understood something of this long before Calvary when, after Nathan confronted him, he stopped constructing defenses and cried to God.
Psalm 51 preserves the language of a shattered man:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Notice what David wanted.
Not merely a cleaner reputation.
A clean heart.
Not better public relations.
Transformation.
Not “Help everyone forget.”
“God, change me.”
That is repentance.
Repentance is more than being embarrassed because someone discovered what you did.
It is more than regretting consequences.
It is coming into agreement with God about your sin and turning toward Him for mercy and transformation.
And perhaps that is why the Abishag sentence can hit so hard.
The Bible remembered David's Bathsheba chapter.
But David was not frozen forever at the worst thing he had done.
Read that again.
David was not frozen forever at the worst thing he had done.
Neither does Scripture pretend the worst thing never happened.
That balance is the beauty of biblical grace.
Grace tells the truth about yesterday without surrendering tomorrow to yesterday.
Some people live as though repentance cannot possibly change anything because they have already failed too badly.
Others talk about grace as though repentance changes nothing because forgiveness means continuing exactly as before.
The Gospel permits neither lie.
Jesus receives sinners.
Jesus forgives sinners.
And Jesus transforms sinners.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
The question becomes whether you are willing to walk out.
There may eventually come a moment when the old temptation stands close again.
Same smell.
Same opportunity.
Same loneliness.
Same secret access.
Same type of person.
Same trigger.
Same late-night vulnerability.
And suddenly you discover whether you merely regretted the consequences...
or whether God has been changing your heart.
Sometimes one of the most beautiful testimonies is not what somebody finally does.
It is what, by God's grace, they no longer do.
Nobody applauds because you closed the browser.
Nobody sees that you deleted the number.
Nobody knows you walked away.
Nobody realizes you could have taken the money and didn't.
Nobody hears the message you decided not to send.
Nobody knows what was available behind the closed door.
Nobody celebrates the temptation you refused.
But heaven does not need an audience before obedience matters.
There are victories that make no noise.
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ.
The king did not know her.
Four Hebrew words.
Yet for someone reading this while fighting an old version of themselves, they can sound like thunder.
Your past may explain why temptation recognizes your address.
It does not have the authority to own the house forever.
You may have been the adulterer.
The liar.
The addict.
The hypocrite.
The angry father.
The unfaithful spouse.
The compromised believer.
The person who knew better and still did it.
Repentance does not require pretending otherwise.
But if you belong to Christ, neither should you build your permanent identity around the sin from which Christ came to redeem you.
Paul wrote that if anyone is in Christ, there is new creation.
Not reputation management.
Not religious cosmetics.
New creation.
And that means perhaps someone reading this needs to stop saying:
“This is simply who I am.”
No.
Maybe it is what you have repeatedly done.
Maybe it has been your pattern for fifteen years.
Maybe you have failed so often that freedom sounds naïve.
But Jesus Christ did not walk out of a tomb so that your favorite sin could write your biography forever.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Repent.
Seek accountability where necessary.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Put boundaries around the places where you repeatedly fall.
Stop protecting what is killing you.
And run toward Christ.
Not after you become clean.
Run to Him because you cannot cleanse yourself.
That is the Gospel.
We do not wash ourselves sufficiently and then approach Jesus.
We approach Jesus because sinners need washing.
There is another important reason Abishag matters.
Immediately after Scripture tells us David did not know her sexually, the story turns toward succession and the throne.
David is dying.
Adonijah begins positioning himself as king.
Eventually Abishag herself becomes entangled in the royal succession crisis when Adonijah asks to receive her as his wife.
So 1 Kings 1:4 is not merely an inspirational sentence about sexual restraint. It also helps establish Abishag's relationship to David as the narrative moves into a dangerous struggle over kingship.
That context protects us from turning the passage into a motivational slogan.
But it does not make the contrast with David's history disappear.
The Bible wants us to remember the whole David.
Giant killer.
Psalmist.
King.
Adulterer.
Repentant sinner.
Broken father.
Worshiper.
Old man.
A deeply flawed servant of God whose life kept pointing beyond himself toward the King humanity actually needed.
Jesus.
Because David cannot save you.
David cannot save David.
Only Christ can save sinners.
And perhaps this article found you at precisely the uncomfortable moment when you are tired of performing Christianity while privately negotiating with something Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Then do not merely admire David's restraint with Abishag.
Go deeper.
Remember David on the floor of repentance.
Remember Psalm 51.
Remember the Son of David carrying a cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing toward God.
It is the story of the holy God coming for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Maybe today your prayer needs to become painfully simple:
Jesus, no more hiding.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, create a clean heart in me.
Jesus, teach me to hate what is destroying me and love what pleases You.
Jesus, rewrite what sin tried to make permanent.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers the private details. But you can make a small public declaration that you are finished pretending.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
Not to expose them.
To remind them that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
and a Savior who is greater than all of it.
Save it as well.
Because old temptations have a strange habit of returning after powerful moments of conviction have faded.
You may need these words again on a weaker night.
Gospel Warrior exists because biblical truth should not merely fill timelines.
It should make disciples.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor.
But generosity, partnership, and willingly helping sound Gospel ministry reach more people can genuinely be acts through which believers seek to glorify God.
It is mission.
It is helping truth travel.
It is helping another exhausted believer find Scripture at midnight.
Another ashamed sinner discover that repentance is still possible.
Another wandering Christian remember the cross.
Another person encounter Jesus.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Christ alone is our righteousness.
Share because somebody else may desperately need the truth you almost scrolled past.
Tag because sometimes one name placed beneath one message becomes the doorway to one necessary conversation.
Save because conviction should survive longer than a moment.
Follow because discipleship requires more than occasional inspiration.
And above everything else...
Come to Christ.
David's story is not ultimately beautiful because David eventually behaved better around Abishag.
It is beautiful because Scripture tells the truth about sinners while continually directing our hope toward the God who redeems them.
The Bible did not erase David's scandal.
God's grace did something greater.
It refused to let scandal have the last word.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody needs to carry away from this today:
The chapter you are most ashamed to remember may still become the place from which you spend the rest of your life remembering how desperately you needed Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Keep Asking Why God Hasn’t Sent Someone. Singleness Is Not Proof He Forgot Your Address.
paragraphs: You Keep Asking Why God Hasn’t Sent Someone. Singleness Is Not Proof He Forgot Your Address.
Maybe the hardest part of being single isn't sleeping alone. Maybe it's watching everyone else receive what you've been asking God for—and wondering why heaven seems to keep passing your address.
There is a particular kind of silence that happens after midnight.
The wedding photos have stopped scrolling.
The congratulations have stopped appearing.
The phone is face-down beside you.
And suddenly there is nobody left in the room except you, God, and the question you have tried very hard not to ask again.
“Lord… what about me?”
You love Him.
At least you're trying to.
You've prayed.
You've waited.
You've watched people who seemed less serious about God meet someone, fall in love, get engaged, get married, have children.
Meanwhile, you keep hearing the same Christian sentences.
“Your person is coming.”
“God is preparing somebody for you.”
“When you stop looking, that's when God will send them.”
“Just enjoy your season.”
“You'll understand when you meet the one.”
Sometimes those words are spoken by kind people who genuinely want to encourage you.
But when another birthday comes...
another wedding invitation arrives...
another relationship ends before it really begins...
another person asks why you're “still single”...
those sentences can start sounding less like encouragement and more like promises God Himself never actually made.
So perhaps somebody needs to tell you something more difficult.
And more compassionate.
And more biblical.
Your desire for marriage is not shameful.
Your loneliness is not imaginary.
Wanting somebody to come home to does not make you spiritually immature.
And singleness is not proof that God forgot your address.
But Scripture also does not promise every Christian a spouse.
That may sting.
Stay with me.
Because what sounds painful at first may actually rescue you from spending years measuring God's love by something He never promised.
Paul writes something remarkable in 1 Corinthians 7:32:
“Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀμερίμνους εἶναι.”
Thelō de hymas amerimnous einai.
In context, the sense is: “I want you to be free from concern.”
Then Paul speaks directly about the unmarried believer:
“ὁ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου”
ho agamos merimna ta tou kyriou
“The unmarried person is concerned about the things of the Lord.”
And then comes Paul's destination:
“εὐπάρεδρον τῷ κυρίῳ ἀπερισπάστως”
The language points toward faithful, undistracted devotion to the Lord.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not look at unmarried Christians and say, “Don't worry. God is preparing your spouse.”
He does not call them incomplete Christians.
He does not describe them as people stuck in God's waiting room until their “real life” begins.
He gives singleness dignity.
He looks at a life without a spouse and sees something our relationship-obsessed culture often cannot imagine:
a life that can belong profoundly, fruitfully, beautifully to Christ.
And before somebody misunderstands Paul, he is not attacking marriage.
The same chapter makes clear that marrying is not sin. Marriage has God-given goodness, responsibilities, intimacy, sacrifice, and beauty.
Paul's point is not that marriage is dirty and singleness is holy.
His point is that marriage changes the distribution of your legitimate responsibilities.
The married believer has a spouse to love.
A household to consider.
Promises to keep.
Another human being whose needs cannot simply be ignored because ministry called.
Paul describes this reality with the Greek word μεμέρισται—memeristai—“is divided.”
Not divided between God and evil.
Divided among legitimate responsibilities.
That matters.
Because Paul is not describing singleness as an empty space where marriage should have been.
He sees it as a condition in which attention can be offered to Christ in ways that married believers may not have available to them.
And maybe that changes the question.
Maybe instead of only asking...
“God, when will You send somebody?”
there is another question worth trembling over:
“Jesus, what can I give You while my life is still arranged like this?”
That does not mean you have to stop wanting marriage.
You can want marriage deeply and still worship Jesus faithfully.
You can pray for a husband.
You can pray for a wife.
You can hope.
You can date wisely.
You can feel the ache of an empty passenger seat.
You can wish someone were sitting across from you at dinner.
You can cry when another relationship falls apart.
You can admit that sometimes the loneliness hurts so badly you don't want another sermon about “using your singleness.”
God does not require you to pretend pain isn't painful before He will call you faithful.
Jesus Himself knew loneliness.
He knew misunderstanding.
He knew rejection.
He knew what it meant to be surrounded by people and still carry something nobody around Him fully understood.
And most importantly for this conversation...
Jesus never married.
Think about what that means.
If marriage were necessary for a fully meaningful human life, then Christians would be forced into an impossible conclusion about the most complete human life ever lived.
Christ was not incomplete.
Christ was not waiting for romance to validate His existence.
Christ was not less human because He had no wife.
His identity was rooted in the Father.
His mission was obedience.
His love was poured out sacrificially.
His life was full.
And if you belong to Him, your deepest identity cannot finally be “single.”
It cannot finally be “married,” either.
It is in Christ.
Before somebody calls you husband...
before somebody calls you wife...
before somebody chooses you at an altar...
there was a Savior who chose to set His love upon sinners at immeasurable cost.
The Gospel is not the story of God finally sending you your soulmate.
The Gospel is the story of God sending His Son.
Jesus entered our brokenness.
He carried our sin.
He went willingly toward the cross.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the grave.
And He calls men and women everywhere to repent, believe, follow Him, and receive a life that no relationship status can manufacture.
That is where the deepest scandal becomes grace.
We were not merely lonely.
We were separated from God by sin.
And Christ came for us.
Maybe you've been asking God to send somebody because, underneath the request, another belief has quietly taken root:
“If somebody finally chooses me, I'll know I'm worth choosing.”
That is too much weight to put on another human being.
No husband can carry it.
No wife can carry it.
Marriage cannot be your resurrection.
Romance cannot be your gospel.
Another person's affection cannot cleanse your conscience, reconcile you to God, conquer death, or tell you who you ultimately are.
Only Jesus can occupy that throne without destroying you.
And this is where singleness can expose things we would rather leave hidden.
Sometimes we don't merely desire marriage.
Sometimes we have begun worshiping the future we imagine marriage will give us.
We picture the photos.
The house.
The children.
The anniversary.
The person reaching for our hand in church.
And without realizing it, we begin bargaining with God.
“I've stayed pure.”
“I've served You.”
“I've waited.”
“I didn't settle.”
“So where is my reward?”
But Jesus is not a vending machine into which we insert obedience until a spouse falls out.
Obedience is not currency used to purchase your preferred future.
We obey because He is Lord.
We love because He first loved us.
And grace means God owes us nothing...
yet in Christ He has given us what we could never deserve.
This is why unwanted singleness can become spiritually dangerous when disappointment turns into accusation.
“God must not love me.”
“Something must be wrong with me.”
“Maybe I'm being punished.”
“Maybe everyone else is more worthy.”
No.
Your relationship status cannot tell you whether God loves you.
Look somewhere else.
Look at the cross.
If you want to know how seriously God takes sin, look at the cross.
If you want to know how costly grace is, look at the cross.
If you want to know whether Jesus is willing to pursue the undeserving, look at the cross.
And if you want to know whether suffering means God has abandoned His children...
look at the cross again.
The beloved Son suffered.
Pain is not automatic evidence of divine rejection.
Waiting is not automatic evidence of divine neglect.
And marriage is not automatic evidence of divine approval.
Some married people are desperately lonely.
Some single people are profoundly fruitful.
Some marriages beautifully display Christ and His church.
Some singleness beautifully displays that Christ Himself is enough to build a meaningful life around.
Neither relationship status saves anybody.
Jesus does.
Perhaps the hardest possibility to surrender is this:
You may marry someday.
You may not.
Scripture gives us permission to desire marriage.
It gives us wisdom for marriage.
It celebrates marriage.
But it does not authorize us to turn a desire into a prophecy.
There is enormous freedom in refusing to make God sign promises He never wrote.
You don't need another viral Christian post guaranteeing, “Your spouse is closer than you think.”
Maybe they are.
Maybe they aren't.
We don't know.
What we do know is better.
Christ is yours now.
Not someday.
Not after the wedding.
Not when somebody finally recognizes your worth.
Now.
Your life is happening now.
Your calling is happening now.
Your sanctification is happening now.
There are people you can love now.
There are wounds Christ can heal now.
There is Scripture to know now.
There are lonely people you can notice now.
There are unbelievers who need the Gospel now.
There are younger believers who need somebody steady enough to disciple them now.
There are prayers nobody else will pray exactly like you can.
There are acts of generosity you can perform.
There are places you can serve.
There are sins to put to death.
There is holiness to pursue.
There is joy to receive.
There is a Savior to know.
Now.
Do not spend the entire life God has actually given you grieving the imaginary life you thought He was required to give you.
Grieve honestly.
Absolutely.
But don't disappear into the grief.
Bring it to Jesus.
Tell Him when you're lonely.
Tell Him when seeing another engagement hurts.
Tell Him when you're jealous.
Tell Him when you're tired of being the third wheel.
Tell Him when sexual temptation feels unbearable.
Tell Him when you wonder whether anybody will ever know you deeply.
Tell Him the ugly parts too.
He already knows.
Repent where longing has become idolatry.
Receive grace where shame has become your identity.
Ask for wisdom.
Ask for community.
Ask for courage.
Ask for contentment—not the fake contentment that says, “I don't want marriage anymore,” when you still do.
Ask for Christian contentment.
The kind that says:
“Jesus, I still want this. But I want You more. And if I cannot have both today, I will not call You cruel because You have not given me everything I desire.”
That prayer costs something.
But there is freedom on the other side of it.
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7:35 that he is speaking for the believer's benefit, not to throw a βρόχον—brochon, a restraint or snare—over them.
That detail is beautiful.
Biblical teaching about singleness is not supposed to become another rope around your neck.
Paul isn't trying to imprison single Christians.
He's trying to free their attention for Jesus.
So if church culture has made you feel defective because you're unmarried, Scripture gives you permission to reject that verdict.
If somebody told you that greater faith would guarantee a spouse, reject that promise too.
If somebody made you feel that wanting marriage means Jesus isn't enough, reject that false choice.
You can ache and worship.
You can hope and surrender.
You can desire marriage and refuse to idolize it.
You can ask God boldly and still trust Him when the answer has not arrived.
And you can build a life so deeply rooted in Christ that whether marriage comes next year, ten years from now, or never, Jesus will not have been merely the Person you used to survive the waiting.
He will have been the Treasure.
Maybe that's what someone reading this needs tonight.
Not another prediction.
Not another “God told me your spouse is coming.”
Not another shallow promise designed to make lonely Christians click.
Maybe you need permission to cry...
and then permission to live.
Your singleness is not proof God forgot your address.
He knows where you are.
But the greater miracle of Christianity is not that God knows your street.
It is that through Christ, God knows your name.
And maybe you know someone who has been quietly hurting under the weight of unwanted singleness.
Send this to them.
Not as a hint.
Not as correction.
As companionship.
Someone younger in the faith may need evidence that a meaningful Christian life does not begin at the altar.
Because loneliness has a strange way of making us forget truths we were certain about yesterday.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased.
But supporting faithful Christian work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement reach more people.
Then invite someone with you.
A family member.
A struggling believer.
A seeker.
The friend drifting from church.
The Christian whose faith has grown cold.
Even the unbelieving friend who keeps asking difficult questions.
Because maybe the greatest testimony of your single years will not eventually be...
“Then God finally sent me somebody.”
Maybe it will be...
“Jesus became so precious to me that I finally stopped treating the life He had already given me as the hallway to the life I actually wanted.”
And if marriage eventually comes, receive it gratefully.
Love that person sacrificially.
Build something holy together.
But never ask another human being to become what only Christ can be.
And if marriage has not come...
you have not been forgotten.
You have not been demoted.
You have not been sentenced to a meaningless life.
Your story is not waiting for romance before Jesus can write something beautiful with it.
Sometimes the miracle isn't that God finally sends someone. Sometimes the miracle is discovering that while you were staring at the empty chair beside you, Jesus had never left His place beside you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “I AM A WALL, AND MY BREASTS ARE LIKE TOWERS”: One of Scripture’s Strangest Statements About Maturity
paragraphs: “I AM A WALL, AND MY BREASTS ARE LIKE TOWERS”: One of Scripture’s Strangest Statements About Maturity

Song of Songs 8:10 sounds almost embarrassingly strange to modern ears. But underneath those ancient words is a breathtaking declaration about boundaries, maturity, love, dignity—and the kind of person grace is forming you to become.
There are verses people underline.
There are verses people frame.
There are verses people quote when life is falling apart.
And then...
there is Song of Songs 8:10.
“I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers.”
You probably will not find that embroidered on a throw pillow.
Most Christians have probably never heard anyone preach an entire sermon about it. Some readers race past it because they do not know what to do with language that feels this intimate.
But perhaps we have been moving too quickly.
Because hidden inside this strange sentence is the voice of someone who has grown up.
And if you have ever regretted giving too much of yourself to someone who did not deserve access to you...
if you have ever confused attention with love...
if you have ever compromised because you were terrified of being alone...
if you have ever looked backward and wished you could recover the person you were before somebody used your vulnerability against you...
stay here.
This verse may be stranger than you expected.
But it may also be far closer to your story than you imagined.
The Hebrew reads:
אֲנִי חוֹמָה וְשָׁדַי כַּמִּגְדָּלוֹת אָז הָיִיתִי בְעֵינָיו כְּמוֹצְאֵת שָׁלוֹם
Ani chomah, veshadai kammigdalot; az hayiti ve'enav kemotzet shalom.
Literally, the imagery is approximately:
“I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers; then I became in his eyes like one finding peace.”
That last Hebrew word matters:
שָׁלוֹם.
Shalom.
Peace.
Wholeness.
Well-being.
The verse begins with a wall.
It ends with peace.
And everything between those two images tells a story about maturity.
But you cannot understand verse 10 if you rip it away from verses 8 and 9.
The scene begins with other people talking about a younger girl:
“We have a little sister, whose breasts are not yet formed. What shall we do for our sister when she is spoken for?”
Then comes the strange proposal:
“If she be a wall, we will build upon it a silver battlement; if she be a door, we will panel it in cedar.”
Then suddenly another voice answers:
“I am a wall, my breasts are like towers.”
The contrast is deliberate.
Earlier she is the “little sister.”
Others are discussing her future.
Others are asking what should be done with her.
Others are wondering what kind of woman she will become.
But eventually...
she speaks for herself.
“I am a wall.”
אֲנִי חוֹמָה.
Ani chomah.
Not:
“I hope someday I become a wall.”
Not:
“Please make me a wall.”
Not:
“Tell me who I am.”
“I am a wall.”
The girl once described in terms of immaturity now describes herself with the architecture of strength.

The image of her breasts being “like towers” also connects directly with the earlier observation that the little sister's breasts had not yet developed. The imagery therefore includes physical maturation. In context, however, the wall-and-door metaphor also concerns how she responds to romantic and sexual access. Major commentators accordingly understand the passage as involving maturity, sexual integrity, and readiness for covenant love—not merely anatomy.
A wall has boundaries.
A door permits entrance.

That does not mean doors are evil and walls are holy. The poetry is not teaching that intimacy itself is dirty. Song of Songs would be an extraordinarily strange book from which to make that argument.
The Song celebrates marital desire with astonishing freedom.
The issue is not whether love should ever enter.
The issue is whether everyone gets access.
There is a difference.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why that difference matters.
You let someone through because they said the right things.
You ignored what your conscience was whispering because loneliness was screaming louder.
You called attachment “love.”
You called obsession “commitment.”
You called compromise “understanding.”
You kept opening the door because you thought being wanted meant being valued.
Then one day you discovered that someone can desire your body without honoring your soul.
Someone can enjoy your presence without intending to protect your heart.
Someone can say “I love you” while slowly teaching you to betray everything you once believed.
That is why maturity sometimes sounds like:
“I am a wall.”
Not because your heart has turned to stone.
Because you finally understand that love and access are not synonyms.
This woman is not ashamed of becoming mature.
She is not ashamed of her sexuality.
She is not presented as less beautiful because she possesses boundaries.
Her maturity and her integrity belong in the same sentence.
That matters enormously in a culture that often offers two equally destructive lies.
One says your body is shameful.
The other says your body is meaningless.
Scripture says neither.
Your body matters.
Your choices matter.
Desire matters.
Love matters.
Faithfulness matters.
And because these things matter, boundaries matter too.
But here is where we need to be careful.
Song of Songs 8:10 is first a poem about human love. We should not pretend every breast, tower, vineyard, spice, kiss, wall, and doorway secretly represents something else.
The safest Christian reading begins by allowing the text to say what it actually says.
This is biblical wisdom about embodied love, maturity, desire, faithfulness, and appropriate boundaries.
Only then can we ask how those truths sit inside the larger story of Scripture.
And eventually that larger story brings us to Jesus Christ.
Not because Jesus is a secret code hidden behind the word “tower.”
But because every Christian understanding of holiness eventually confronts an uncomfortable reality:
none of us has been a perfect wall.
Maybe your failure was sexual.
Maybe it was emotional.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you protected your body but surrendered your heart to bitterness.
Maybe you maintained an impressive Christian appearance while privately feeding an addiction.
Maybe your browser history tells one story and your Sunday worship tells another.
Maybe you crossed boundaries willingly.
Maybe boundaries were crossed against your will—and if so, another person's sin against you must never be confused with your guilt.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
But you know.
God knows.
And suddenly “I am a wall” can feel less like your testimony and more like the testimony you wish you had.
That is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that good people successfully protected themselves from becoming scandalous.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Christ did not wait at a safe distance until damaged people repaired themselves.
He entered our ruin.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable religion despised.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And grace does something shame never can.
Grace does not merely tell you that what happened does not matter.
Grace tells the truth about sin...
and then refuses to let sin have the final word over the repentant sinner.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning around because grace has shown you there is somewhere better to go.
Jesus does not save us so we can continue calling bondage freedom.
He forgives us and begins transforming us.
The Gospel does not say:
“Your boundaries failed, therefore you are worthless.”
It says:
“Come to Christ.”
The Gospel does not say:
“You made yourself dirty, therefore stay away.”
It says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.”
The Gospel does not say:
“Pretend nothing happened.”
It says something infinitely stronger:
You can be redeemed.
Some of you need that distinction desperately.
Because you have been punishing yourself for something Jesus is calling you to bring into the light.
You have mistaken endless self-hatred for repentance.
But staring endlessly at your failure does not make Christ larger.
Bring it to Him.
Confess what was sin.
Grieve what was lost.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make restitution where restitution is appropriate.
Establish boundaries that should have existed years ago.
Walk away from what keeps dragging you backward.
And receive the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
Then learn to say again:
“I am a wall.”
Not arrogantly.
Not self-righteously.
Not because you believe you could never fall.
Because grace is teaching you that you do not have to remain who you were.
Maybe maturity for you means finally telling someone, “No.”
Maybe it means deleting the number.
Maybe it means ending the secret relationship.
Maybe it means refusing to flirt with someone else's spouse.
Maybe it means admitting that pornography has been discipling your imagination more consistently than Scripture.
Maybe it means refusing to return to an abusive situation simply because someone has weaponized Christian language about forgiveness against you.
Maybe it means confessing to your spouse.
Maybe it means asking your pastor or a mature believer for help.
Maybe it means stopping tonight and whispering:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living like this.”
Walls are not always rejection.
Sometimes walls are stewardship.
Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls because something valuable needed guarding.
Proverbs warns about the person without self-control being like a city broken into and left without walls.
And Song of Songs gives us this remarkable woman saying:
“I am a wall.”
There are things in your life worth guarding.
Your marriage.
Your mind.
Your integrity.
Your children.
Your testimony.
Your attention.
Your private life.
Your worship.
Your sexuality.
Your relationship with Christ.
Not because guarding them earns God's love.
Because grace teaches us to treasure what sin once taught us to waste.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of Song of Songs 8:10 is where the sentence lands.
שָׁלוֹם.
Shalom.
Peace.
The Hebrew can carry the sense of finding peace or favor in the beloved's eyes, and commentators note the deliberate literary wordplay around shalom in this closing section of the Song.
Think about the movement.
Immaturity.
Uncertainty.
Boundaries.
Maturity.
Love.
Peace.
Not exploitation.
Not frantic validation.
Not “What must I surrender so you won't leave me?”
Peace.
That may be what some readers have never experienced.
You have experienced chemistry.
Intensity.
Jealousy.
Possession.
Manipulation.
Butterflies.
Breakups.
Reconciliation.
Another breakup.
Midnight messages.
Deleted messages.
Secret messages.
But peace?
You barely know what that feels like.
Biblical love is not necessarily emotionless or easy—the Song itself burns with passion—but godly love does not require you to destroy yourself in order to keep it alive.
And here the Christian heart sees something even greater.
Our deepest shalom does not finally come from finding the perfect human relationship.
It comes through reconciliation with God.
Paul says that because we have been justified by faith, “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Peace with God.
Imagine that.
The Judge becomes Father.
The guilty are justified.
The wandering are brought home.
The ashamed are clothed in grace.
The sinner does not rewrite the scandal.
Jesus does.
That is our message.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by changing evil into good.
Not by calling sin holiness.
He rewrites everything because the cross means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter.
Peter denied Him.
Grace was not finished.
The woman caught in adultery stood exposed before accusers.
Grace was not finished.
The thief was dying beside Jesus with no lifetime left to repair.
Grace was not finished.
Paul had blood attached to his reputation.
Grace was not finished.
And maybe your name belongs somewhere in that sentence too.
Grace is not finished.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private struggle publicly.
But you can make one small confession of dependence:
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer needs tonight.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Somebody's daughter.
Somebody's husband.
Somebody's teenager.
Somebody sitting in church tomorrow while carrying a secret they believe disqualifies them from grace.
There may come a night when temptation gets loud again.
You may need to remember:
“I am a wall.”

We want this ministry to remain a place where people encounter Scripture rather than empty motivational religion; where conviction leads toward Christ rather than despair; where wounded believers find biblical nourishment; and where sinners hear that repentance and grace still meet at the feet of Jesus.
Not under compulsion.
Not because money earns blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or a higher place in God's kingdom.

Scripture explicitly says giving should come from what a believer has decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” while also teaching that generous Christian service can result in thanksgiving and glory to God.
If you want to glorify God through supporting this particular work, do it freely, prayerfully, and joyfully—not as though God were sending you an invoice.
Your local church and your responsibilities before God should not be neglected.
It is simply an opportunity to stand with this ministry.
If you want to become part of that support:
Invite someone closer to Jesus.
Because sometimes evangelism begins with something as ordinary as pressing “Share” and trusting God with the person who sees it next.
And before you leave, go back to that strange verse one final time.
“I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers.”
Perhaps it does not sound quite as strange anymore.
It sounds like someone who grew.
Someone who learned.
Someone who discovered that maturity is not becoming incapable of love.
It is becoming capable of loving without surrendering what should be sacred.
And for the Christian, there is an even deeper hope.
Maybe yesterday you were a door when you should have been a wall.
Maybe yesterday you failed.
Maybe yesterday is the scandal.
Jesus Christ is still Lord today.
Repent.
Come home.
Receive grace.
And let Christ begin rebuilding what sin tore down.
Because the most unforgettable thing about a ruined wall is not that it once fell.
It is what happens when grace begins laying stones in the rubble.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: NAKED AND UNASHAMED: What Adam and Eve Had Before Sin Entered the Bedroom
paragraphs: NAKED AND UNASHAMED: What Adam and Eve Had Before Sin Entered the Bedroom

Before pornography. Before comparison. Before betrayal. Before insecurity. Before bodies became weapons, bargaining chips, objects, or sources of shame—there was a husband, a wife, and a sentence so breathtakingly simple that our wounded world barely knows what to do with it.
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” — Genesis 2:25
Read that again.
Not because you missed the words.
Because we may have forgotten the world those words describe.
There was once a marriage where nobody needed to hide.
No deleted messages.
No secret browser history.
No comparing a spouse’s body to somebody else's.
No fear of being rejected after being completely known.
No manipulation disguised as affection.
No using intimacy to control.
No wondering, If you really saw all of me, would you still want me?
No shame.
That may be one of the saddest things about Genesis 2:25.
We recognize the nakedness.
But many of us hardly recognize the absence of shame.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ
Wayyihyu shenehem ‘arummim ha’adam we’ishto welo yitboshashu.
The man and his wife were both עֲרוּמִּים — ‘arummim — naked, and they were not יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ — yitboshashu — ashamed.
Genesis is not embarrassed by the human body.
God created it.
And Genesis 2 does not present the first husband and wife as two dirty people who somehow had not yet discovered modesty.
They were innocent.
There was nothing corrupt in their seeing.
Nothing predatory in their desire.
Nothing deceptive in their hearts.
Nothing to conceal from God.
Nothing to conceal from one another.
Their nakedness was physical, certainly, but the beauty of the verse reaches further than skin.
They were exposed without being exploited.
Known without being humiliated.
Vulnerable without being weaponized.
Close without pretending.
They had something many marriages spend years desperately trying to recover:
safety in being fully known.
And then came the serpent.
Then came the lie.
Then came sin.
And almost immediately, something changed between human beings and their own nakedness.
Genesis 3:7 says:
וַתִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם וַיֵּדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם הֵם
Their eyes were opened, and they knew they were naked.
Then they sewed fig leaves together.
Notice the tragedy.
God had created them naked.
Sin taught them to hide.
Before sin, nakedness existed without shame.
After sin, nakedness suddenly demanded covering.
But the deepest problem was never fabric.
It was alienation.
Something had entered the human heart.
Fear.
Accusation.
Self-consciousness.
Blame.
Hiding.
The man who once looked at the woman and erupted into poetry—“bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”—would soon point toward her while answering God:
“The woman whom You gave to be with me…”
Sin did not merely make humanity guilty before God.
Sin began turning lovers into accusers.
That is what sin still does.
It enters bedrooms long before anyone physically commits adultery.
It enters through resentment nobody confesses.
Through pornography nobody knows about.
Through fantasies protected like private property.
Through bitterness carried under the blankets.
Through cruel jokes about a spouse’s body.
Through rejection used as punishment.
Through selfishness disguised as “needs.”
Through comparison.
Through coercion.
Through emotional withdrawal.
Through wounds that were never healed because both people became better at pretending than confessing.
Two people can sleep inches apart and be miles away.
They can share a bed without sharing their hearts.
They can know one another’s bodies while becoming strangers to one another’s souls.
That is why “naked and unashamed” is so much bigger than sex.
It is a picture of intimacy before sin fractured intimacy.
And perhaps that is why this passage hurts.
Because some people reading this remember when marriage felt safer.
Some remember the betrayal.
Some remember discovering what was on the phone.
Some remember being compared to somebody else.
Some remember hearing words about their body that they still cannot forget.

Some have never been betrayed by a spouse but arrived in marriage already carrying shame from abuse, pornography, promiscuity, rejection, abandonment, or years of believing their worth depended on being desirable.
Some love Jesus deeply and still tense when the lights go off.
Some pray together but struggle to talk honestly.
Some have forgiven, but the scar still aches.
Some are single and already carrying into a future marriage wounds they hope a wedding ceremony will magically erase.
And somebody reading this has become so accustomed to hiding that you no longer know where the mask ends and you begin.
Please hear this carefully:
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside your shame shouting at you to clean yourself up.
The Gospel is God coming after hiding sinners.
Listen to the question echoing through Eden:
“Where are you?”
God was not confused about Adam’s GPS coordinates.
Adam was hiding.
And God came looking.
That pattern runs like blood through Scripture.
We sin.
We hide.
God calls.
We manufacture fig leaves.
God provides what we cannot provide for ourselves.
Genesis 3:21 says:
וַיַּעַשׂ יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם
The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife and clothed them.
Do not force more into that verse than Scripture explicitly says. Genesis does not directly call this event a sacrifice or state that these garments were a prophetic symbol of Christ.
But do not miss what the text plainly shows either.
Their homemade covering was not the end of the story.
God clothed them.
And as Scripture unfolds, the problem of human guilt and shame eventually leads us far beyond Eden—to Jesus Christ.
At the cross, humanity does something almost unbearably cruel.
We strip the One who never needed to hide.
We shame the One in whom there was no sin.
We mock the innocent One.
We expose Him publicly.
We crucify Him.
And He remains obedient unto death.
Jesus does not save us because our fig leaves became impressive enough.
He saves sinners by grace.
He bears sin.
He bears judgment.
He conquers death.
He rises.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives something Adam's leaves could never manufacture:
forgiveness.
This is where the bedroom meets the Gospel.
Christian marriage was never meant to be a sanitized version of the world's selfishness.
It was meant to be shaped by Christ.
When Paul speaks to husbands in Ephesians 5, the Greek text says:
Οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That destroys selfish masculinity.

Biblical headship cannot honestly be used as an excuse for domination, intimidation, selfish sexual demands, or cruelty when the model placed before the husband is a crucified Savior giving Himself for His bride.
Christlike love does not ask, “How much can I take?”
It asks, “How faithfully can I give?”
And when Paul addresses marital intimacy in 1 Corinthians 7, something remarkable appears.
Mutuality.

The wife’s body is not presented as property for male consumption while the husband remains autonomous. Paul immediately places husband and wife under corresponding obligations to one another. Neither spouse is given biblical permission to turn the other person into an object.
This is covenant.
Not consumption.
Not coercion.
Not pornography with wedding rings.
Not selfishness baptized with Bible verses.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is to be held in honor and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
The Greek word translated “bed” is κοίτη — koitē.
Scripture is capable of speaking positively about marital intimacy while simultaneously condemning sexual immorality and adultery.
The Bible is not anti-sex.
The Bible is against the corruption of what God created good.
That distinction matters.
Because somewhere along the way, some Christians learned to speak about sex as though holiness meant embarrassment.
And the world responded by speaking about sex as though freedom meant having no boundaries.
Scripture gives us neither shame-filled prudishness nor boundaryless appetite.
It gives us something holier.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Honor.
Sacrificial love.
Mutual responsibility.
Purity.
Tenderness.
Truth.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Maybe the serpent never physically crawled into your bedroom.
But his old vocabulary did.
“Did God really say?”
“You deserve something else.”
“Nobody will know.”
“Your spouse isn't enough.”
“It's only fantasy.”
“It's only flirting.”
“It's only one message.”
“It's your body.”
“It's your secret.”
“You can repent later.”
“You need this.”
And eventually…
fig leaves.
Delete the history.
Turn over the phone.
Change the password.
Hide the purchase.
Lie about the conversation.
Pretend you are fine.
Blame your spouse.
Blame stress.
Blame loneliness.
Blame anything except the sin slowly teaching your heart how to hide from the person you promised to love.
That is the scandal.
But scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Grace can enter the room.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls adultery harmless.
Not grace that tells an abused spouse to tolerate danger.
Not grace that uses forgiveness to eliminate accountability.
Not grace that pretends betrayal has no consequences.
Biblical grace tells the truth precisely because Jesus paid too high a price for us to keep pretending darkness is light.
Grace says:
Come out of hiding.
Confess.
Repent.
Tell the truth.
Get help.
Destroy the secret access.
End the affair.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Seek wise pastoral care.
Seek qualified professional help where wounds, trauma, addiction, abuse, or serious marital breakdown require it.
And where there is abuse or coercion, biblical submission is not a command to remain silently available for someone else's violence. Evil should be brought into the light, and safety matters.
Grace is not permission for darkness to remain comfortable.
Grace brings sinners into the light and begins making them new.
Maybe your marriage will never look exactly like Eden.
None of us can crawl backward through Genesis 3.
But Christians are not people desperately trying to reverse history.
We are people following a Redeemer who is moving history toward restoration.
Jesus Christ is not merely repairing Adam's old world.
He is making all things new.
And that means your deepest hope is not finally becoming attractive enough.
Not finally having the perfect marriage.
Not finally becoming sexually confident enough.
Not finally erasing every painful memory.
Your deepest hope is Christ.
Because one day, everyone who belongs to Him will stand completely known by God and completely covered by the righteousness and grace of Christ.
No secret sin left hidden.
No accusation left unanswered.
No shame left reigning.
No betrayal.
No pornography.
No adultery.
No exploitation.
No insecurity.
No abuse.
No death.
The story that began with nakedness without shame and descended into hiding does not end behind fig leaves.
It ends in redemption.
So maybe tonight the bravest thing you can do is not become more desirable.
Maybe it is become more truthful.
Maybe you need to tell your husband, “I have been hiding.”
Maybe you need to tell your wife, “I wounded you.”
Maybe you need to kneel beside the bed where resentment has slept between you for years and finally pray together.
Maybe you need to confess the pornography.
Maybe you need to stop blaming your spouse for sin you chose.
Maybe you need to forgive—not by pretending nothing happened, but by surrendering vengeance to God while walking wisely through whatever restoration requires.
Maybe you are unmarried, and Christ is calling you to stop treating your future spouse as an imaginary cure for lust, loneliness, insecurity, or shame.
Maybe there is no spouse at all in your story.
Maybe this article found you because the person you cannot stand being naked before is yourself.
You look into the mirror and hear every insult.
Every comparison.
Every rejection.
Every memory.
And somewhere underneath all of it is the fear:
If somebody truly knew me, would they still love me?
The Gospel answers with something far deeper than romantic affirmation.
God already knows.
And in Christ, sinners who repent and believe are invited near.
You do not shock an omniscient Savior with the chapter you are afraid to tell Him.
He knew what He was purchasing when He went to the cross.
So stop sewing leaves.
Come into the light.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because consequences disappear.
Because condemnation does not have the final word over those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because every marriage will survive every betrayal.
Because even when human relationships break, Christ remains a faithful Redeemer.
Be honest.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
That matters.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable, but because there may come a night when the old shame returns and you need to remember that Jesus did not die merely to improve your hiding place.
Not as a performance of righteousness.
Somebody may be one secret message away from destroying a covenant.
Somebody may believe pornography has already ruined them beyond redemption.
Somebody may be carrying sexual shame from something done to them and mistakenly believing another person's sin made them worthless.
Somebody needs to hear that Jesus still calls sinners out of hiding.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases spiritual blessing. It cannot.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
Your support helps Gospel-centered truth keep moving beyond the people who already know where to find it.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Not so Gospel Warrior becomes famous.
So Jesus becomes known.

Because beneath our polished photos, carefully edited marriages, church clothes, private browser histories, old wounds, secret temptations, and frightened hearts, humanity is still repeating the ancient story.
We sin.
We notice our nakedness.
We become ashamed.
We sew leaves.
We hide.
And God still calls:
“Where are you?”
Maybe today is the day you stop answering Him from behind the trees.
Come out.
Jesus already knows what you are hiding.
And the hands calling you into the light are the same hands that were pierced to save sinners.
The serpent taught humanity to hide—but Jesus walked into our shame so we would not have to live there forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS TALK ABOUT PEOPLE WHO “MADE THEMSELVES EUNUCHS” FOR THE KINGDOM?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS TALK ABOUT PEOPLE WHO “MADE THEMSELVES EUNUCHS” FOR THE KINGDOM?
One of Jesus’ Most Shocking Statements Was Never Permission to Mutilate Your Body—It Was a Radical Declaration That Christ Can Become More Precious Than Marriage, Sex, Romance, and Every Dream You Thought You Needed to Be Whole
There are verses people underline.
There are verses people put on coffee mugs.
And then there are verses people quietly hope nobody asks them to explain.
Matthew 19:12 is one of those verses.
Jesus says:
