He forgives.
He restores.
He teaches.
He disciplines.
He calls.
He changes what we love.
And sometimes that transformation creates painful moments when loyalty to Christ clashes with loyalty to people we deeply love.
But notice something crucial.
Supreme love for Christ does not authorize cruelty toward family.
Jesus affirmed the command to honor father and mother.
He condemned using religious excuses to avoid caring for parents in Mark 7.
Even while hanging on the cross, Jesus made provision for His mother, entrusting her to the beloved disciple in John 19:26–27.
Think about that.
The same Jesus who said that disciples must “hate” father and mother, in the comparative and allegiance-demanding sense of Luke 14, cared for His own mother while dying.
So if someone uses Luke 14:26 to justify abusing parents, despising a spouse, neglecting children, or behaving hatefully toward relatives, that person has missed Jesus’ meaning.
Christ is not commanding sinful hatred.
He is demanding unrivaled allegiance.
In fact, loving Jesus above your family should ultimately teach you how to love your family more faithfully.
You stop making people into gods.
You stop demanding that your spouse become your savior.
You stop making your children responsible for your identity.
You stop obeying parents when they demand what God forbids.
You stop worshiping human approval.
And because Christ occupies the place only Christ should occupy, you can love people as people rather than idols.
Sometimes loving Jesus first will make you more patient with your family.
Sometimes it will make you apologize.
Sometimes it will make you forgive.
Sometimes it will make you finally establish a righteous boundary.
Sometimes it will make you care for an aging parent when it is inconvenient.
Sometimes it will make you remain faithful when culture tells you faithfulness is foolish.
Sometimes it will make you tell someone you love:
“I love you deeply. But I cannot disobey Christ for you.”
And that sentence can hurt.
Because discipleship is beautiful.
But Jesus never advertised it as painless.
Perhaps that is why Luke 14:26 bothers us.
Maybe the deepest problem is not that we cannot understand the word “hate.”
Maybe we understand the demand behind it far too well.
Jesus will not share His throne.
And somewhere inside us, we know exactly which rival we do not want Him to touch.
So forget everyone else for a moment.
Forget the theological argument.
Forget the comment section.
Forget the person you wish would read this.
Ask yourself the question.
Who—or what—could make me walk away from Jesus?
A relationship?
Money?
Sex?
Success?
Family approval?
Fear of loneliness?
Political identity?
Social acceptance?
A hidden addiction?
Resentment toward God because He did not answer the prayer the way you wanted?
What would have to be threatened before you told Christ:
“You can have everything except that”?
Because whatever completes that sentence may reveal something you have placed dangerously close to His throne.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop pretending.
You have been near Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
Close enough to hear Christian language.
Close enough to share Christian posts.
Close enough to know the songs.
Close enough to look faithful.
But there is a locked room inside you.
And you know what is inside.
Jesus knows too.
Yet notice what He does with sinners who come to Him.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
The disciple who swore he would never abandon Jesus collapsed under fear and insisted that he did not know Him.
What a scandal.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
The risen Christ met him again.
Restored him.
Commissioned him.
Grace rewrote the story.
That does not mean Peter's denial did not matter.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
Grace confronts sin, forgives the repentant sinner, and begins writing something new.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe people think you are strong.
Maybe you have learned how to smile while your spiritual life quietly bleeds.
Maybe you love Jesus, but you are exhausted.
Maybe you have fallen again.
Maybe shame keeps whispering that after everything you have done, God must be finished with you.
Look at the cross.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally managed to reach God.
It is the announcement that God came for sinners.
Repentance means we stop defending the darkness and turn toward Christ.
Faith means we stop trusting ourselves and entrust ourselves to Him.
Grace means forgiveness cannot be bought.
And discipleship means the Jesus who rescued us now has the right to lead us.
So no—Jesus was not commanding you to cultivate malicious hatred toward your mother, father, spouse, children, brothers, or sisters.
He was saying something that may be even harder:
Love Me above them all.
And above yourself.
Not because family is worthless.
Because Jesus is Lord.
Not because human love is evil.
Because even the best human love becomes destructive when asked to occupy God's throne.
Christ first.
Then let your love for everyone else flow from Him.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not perform for strangers.
Be honest before God.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
And perhaps your honesty will become the reason another wounded Christian finally stops hiding.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture, follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen. Let them encounter daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and above all, the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Jesus is not asking merely for your attention.
He is calling for you.
Your allegiance.
Your heart.
Your sin brought into the light.
Your idols removed from the throne.
Your life surrendered beneath His lordship.
The question is no longer, “Did Jesus really tell me to hate my family?”
The question underneath His shocking words is much more personal:
When every other love asks you to choose, will Jesus still be first?
Because one day you may discover that the hardest thing Christ asked you to surrender was the very thing keeping you from discovering how completely His grace could rewrite your story.
Some things Jesus asks you to release not because He wants your heart empty—but because His throne was never meant to be shared.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES GOD IGNORE SMALL SINS?
paragraphs:
DOES GOD IGNORE SMALL SINS?
The compromise you keep calling “nothing” may be revealing something much bigger—and the good news is that Jesus did not come merely to expose your darkness. He came to bring you out of it.
It was only a little lie.
Nobody got hurt.
At least, that is what you told yourself.

It was only one private message you should not have sent. One glance that lasted too long. One expense you quietly misrepresented. One piece of gossip disguised as concern. One grudge you kept feeding because admitting you were bitter would have been uncomfortable.
One click.
One drink too many.
One secret.
One exaggeration.
One compromise.
One thought entertained instead of resisted.
One moment when you knew what was right...
and chose something else.
Nothing dramatic happened afterward.
No lightning came through the ceiling.
Your family did not suddenly disappear.
Your church did not discover your secret.
Your friends still respected you.
You woke up the next morning, checked your phone, went to work, made coffee, smiled at people, perhaps even prayed.
So somewhere deep inside, a dangerous conclusion began forming:
Maybe God does not care that much about the little things.
But what if the greatest danger of a “small” sin is not that God immediately punishes you?
What if the greatest danger is that you become comfortable carrying something Jesus died to free you from?
That question reaches deeper than behavior.
It reaches the heart.

Because Scripture never teaches that every sin produces identical earthly consequences. Murder and an angry thought do not necessarily produce the same temporal damage. Adultery and temptation are not identical acts. Stealing millions and coveting someone else's possessions do not create identical consequences for other people.

The Bible recognizes degrees of accountability and consequences. Jesus Himself spoke of some receiving “many stripes” and others “few” in Luke 12:47–48. In John 19:11, Jesus told Pilate that the one who delivered Him over had “the greater sin.”
So biblical Christianity does not require us to pretend every sinful act is identical in severity, consequence, knowledge, or responsibility.
But Scripture gives us absolutely no permission to conclude from this that some sins simply do not matter to God.
That distinction could save someone reading this from years of spiritual compromise.
There may be sins with smaller earthly consequences.
There are no sins that become holy because we decided they were small.
James writes:
James 2:10.

James is not saying that every violation causes precisely the same earthly harm. His point is about our relationship to God's law and the God who gave it. Breaking one command still makes us lawbreakers.
And then James says something devastatingly practical:
“But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed. Then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, brings forth death.”
The Greek is painfully vivid.
The word translated “desire” is ἐπιθυμία—epithymia—a strong desire or craving which, depending on context, can become wrongful desire.
Then James says desire “conceives.”
συλλαβοῦσα—syllabousa.
The imagery is reproductive.
Something begins inside before everybody else can see what is growing.
Desire conceives.
Sin is born.
Sin grows.
And eventually...
death comes.
Notice what James does not say.
He does not say every temptation immediately becomes catastrophic public destruction.
He describes a process.
And that is why the sin you consider “small” deserves your attention.
Not because every stumble means you are beyond hope.
Not because Christians must live terrified that one imperfect moment has erased the grace of Christ.
But because sin rarely introduces itself by saying:
“Hello. I am here to destroy everything you love.”
It usually whispers:
Just this once.
Nobody knows.
You deserve this.
You're stressed.
You're lonely.
Everyone does it.
It's not technically that bad.
You can repent later.
And perhaps the most dangerous one:
At least you're not doing what they are doing.
That is how comparison becomes anesthesia.
We look at someone else's scandal so we do not have to confront our compromise.
We point toward somebody else's adultery while feeding lust.
We condemn somebody else's dishonesty while exaggerating our own stories.
We criticize another person's greed while secretly worshiping money.
We recoil at someone else's cruelty while murdering people with words behind closed doors.
We can become experts at measuring other people's darkness while keeping our own favorite shadows.
Jesus destroyed that illusion in the Sermon on the Mount.
“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder’... But I say to you that whoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment.”
Matthew 5:21–22.
Then He goes further.

“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that whoever looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28.
Jesus was not saying inward lust and the physical act of adultery create identical consequences.
He was doing something far more uncomfortable.
He was refusing to let respectable people hide behind respectable appearances.
He took the spotlight off the public scandal...
and aimed it toward the heart.
Because God sees what nobody else applauds or condemns.
The private resentment.
The hidden fantasy.
The secret jealousy.
The pride behind the prayer.
The manipulation hidden inside kindness.
The unforgiveness beneath the Christian smile.
The hunger to be admired.
The resentment when someone else succeeds.
The conversation you keep deleting.
The habit you keep renaming.
The compromise you keep defending.
The thing you would desperately hope nobody finds if your phone, thoughts, browser history, finances, motives, and private conversations suddenly became visible.
And maybe right now something came to mind.
Do not run from that moment.
But do not run toward despair either.
Run to Jesus.
Because this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people need to become slightly better.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Paul writes:
Romans 3:23.
The Greek word translated “sinned” comes from ἁμαρτάνω—hamartanō—to sin, to fail in relation to what is right.
But Romans does not leave us standing beneath the verdict.
The sentence continues.
We are “justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 3:24.
Read those words again.
Freely.
Grace.
Redemption.
Christ Jesus.
The answer to sin is not pretending it is smaller.
The answer is discovering that Christ is greater.
Some people minimize sin because they are afraid that admitting its seriousness will crush them.
But the Gospel gives us permission to stop pretending.
You can call sin what God calls it because your hope does not depend upon convincing God that you are innocent.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
This is why 1 John 1:9 is precious:
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The Greek verb translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν—homologōmen, from ὁμολογέω—homologeō.
At its core, it means to confess, acknowledge, or agree.
Biblical confession is not negotiation.
It is not:
“God, technically it wasn't that serious because...”
It is:
“God, You are right about this.
I was wrong.
I need mercy.”
And mercy is exactly what Christ offers.
That is why repentance is not God screaming, “Stay away from Me.”
Repentance is God's summons to turn.
The New Testament word μετάνοια—metanoia—speaks of repentance, a change of mind that expresses itself in turning toward God.
Real grace does not merely make us feel better about remaining unchanged.
Paul asks the question directly:
“Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound?”
And answers:
“Certainly not!”
Romans 6:1–2.
Grace is not permission to make peace with chains.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace does not whisper, “Your sin does not matter.”
Grace announces, “Your sin mattered so much that Christ bore sin at the cross—and His love is so great that He willingly came to save sinners.”
Look at the cross.
There is your answer to the question, “Does God care about sin?”
Look again.
There is your answer to the question, “Does God still love sinners?”
At Calvary, holiness and mercy are not enemies.
Justice is not erased.
Love is not sentimentalized.
Jesus, the sinless Son of God, gives Himself for sinners.
Peter says:
“who Himself bore our sins in His own body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness.”
1 Peter 2:24.
Not merely that we might be forgiven and then lovingly escorted back into our cages.
That we might live for righteousness.
That changes everything.
Maybe your battle seems small today.
Deal with it while it is small.
Bring it into the light.
Tell God the truth.
If another person has been harmed, seek to make things right where biblically and wisely possible.
If you need accountability, find a mature believer who loves Christ more than your reputation.
Delete what needs deleting.
Leave what needs leaving.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive whom you need to forgive.
Stop feeding what you keep begging God to starve.
Do not confuse struggling against sin with surrendering to sin.
A Christian may stumble.
A Christian may experience fierce temptation.
A Christian may find himself or herself crying before God over the same weakness more times than expected.
But there is a profound difference between falling while fighting and decorating the prison cell because you have decided to live there.
Micah 7:8 contains one of Scripture's beautiful declarations of hope:
“Do not rejoice over me, my enemy; when I fall, I will arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.”
The Hebrew behind “I will arise” is אָקוּם—ʾāqûm.
I will rise.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needed tonight.
Not permission to stay down.
Not condemnation telling you there is no way home.
A call to rise.
You fell?
Rise in Christ.
You compromised?
Confess it.
You wandered?
Come home.
You became numb?
Ask God to soften your heart again.
You have been hiding?
Step into the light.
You have sinned?
Look toward the Savior.
Because the central story of Christianity is not the greatness of your failure.
It is the greatness of Jesus.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted His church.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime remaining to repair his reputation.
Yet throughout Scripture, grace keeps invading places where human beings expected the story to be over.
This is our heartbeat:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin should be celebrated.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
But because Jesus Christ can rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
He does not rewrite the past by pretending it never happened.
He rewrites the story through forgiveness, redemption, sanctification, restoration, and a new direction.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe five thousand people will never know.
Maybe five people will never know.
Maybe nobody knows except you and God.
It still matters.
And you still matter to Him.
The shepherd in Jesus' parable did not shrug because only one sheep wandered.
He went after the one.
The woman did not ignore one lost coin because she still possessed nine.
She searched.
Heaven does not treat repentance casually.
Jesus says:
“There is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”
Luke 15:10.
One sinner.
One turning.
One homecoming.
And perhaps tonight...
one reader.
You.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not merely react to the article and continue scrolling.
Talk to God.
Right now.
No performance.
No polished religious vocabulary.
Tell Him the truth.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that God is dealing with your heart becomes a small line in the sand: I am finished pretending.
And if grace has already pulled you out of something you thought would own you forever, tell your testimony. Someone reading the comments may desperately need evidence that God still restores people.
Not as a religious performance. Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.
Someone may be quietly drowning while looking completely normal online.
Someone may have convinced themselves that because their secret is small, their soul is safe.
Someone may need to discover tonight that repentance is not the end of hope.
It can be the doorway home.
It does not.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift.
But if you desire to glorify God by helping biblical resources reach more people, supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one voluntary expression of stewardship and partnership.
Come to Jesus.
Because someday your merchandise will be gone.
Your social-media account will be gone.
Your reputation will be gone.
Your possessions will belong to somebody else.
And what will matter infinitely more than whether people knew your name is whether you knew Christ.
So no...
God does not simply ignore the sins we prefer to classify as small.
But neither does He turn away the repentant sinner who comes to Christ for mercy.
That is the part shame never wants you to discover.
The enemy wants you in one of two prisons.
Either:
“It isn't serious enough to repent of.”
Or:
“It's too terrible to be forgiven.”
The Gospel demolishes both lies.
Sin is serious.
Grace is greater.
Repentance matters.
Mercy is real.
Jesus saves.
So bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the dishonesty.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the thing you keep minimizing.
Bring Him the scandal nobody knows.
And stop asking whether your sin is small enough to keep.
Start asking whether Jesus is precious enough to follow.
Because the smallest compromise you refuse to surrender can become a hiding place—but the smallest honest prayer of repentance can become the moment you finally step into the light.
The sin you keep calling “small” may be the very place where Jesus is calling you to stop hiding and discover how enormous His grace really is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TRUST IN THE LORD WITH ALL YOUR HEART” — THE NEXT WORDS ARE THE HARD PART
paragraphs: “TRUST IN THE LORD WITH ALL YOUR HEART” — THE NEXT WORDS ARE THE HARD PART

You may have quoted this verse for years. You may have written it in journals, posted it on walls, highlighted it in your Bible, and whispered it through tears. But there are six words hiding in the verse that expose whether we actually trust God—or simply trust Him when His plans make sense.
There is a strange kind of silence that happens when the prayer you were certain God would answer...
isn't answered the way you expected.
You prayed.
You waited.
You tried to be faithful.
You told yourself, “God has a plan.”
But then the door closed anyway.
The relationship still ended.
The opportunity disappeared.
The money still wasn't enough.
The diagnosis still came.
The person you begged God to change remained the same.
The future you had already pictured suddenly collapsed.
And somewhere between what you prayed for and what actually happened, a frightening question entered your heart:
“Lord... what are You doing?”
That is where Proverbs 3:5 becomes more than something beautiful to print on a coffee mug.
It becomes surgery.
The familiar English words say:
“Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.” — Proverbs 3:5, KJV
But listen to the Hebrew:
בְּטַח אֶל־יְהוָה בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ וְאֶל־בִּינָתְךָ אַל־תִּשָּׁעֵן
Bəṭaḥ el-YHWH bəḵol-libbeḵā; wə'el-bīnāṯəḵā 'al-tiššāʿēn.
“Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.”
We love the first command.
Trust in the LORD.
It sounds courageous.
Faithful.
Strong.
But then comes the part that hurts:
“And do not lean on your own understanding.”
That is the hard part.
Because many of us want to trust God...
while still understanding everything first.
We want God to explain why.
We want Him to show us the timeline.
We want Him to justify the delay.
We want Him to tell us why that person walked away.
Why the opportunity disappeared.
Why obedience cost so much.
Why someone else received what we had been praying for.
Why He allowed something we desperately wanted Him to prevent.
We say, “I trust You, Lord.”
But quietly, underneath the prayer, there is often another sentence:
“Just make it make sense.”
And sometimes...
He doesn't.
Not yet.

That doesn't mean Christianity celebrates irrationality or that believers should reject wisdom, evidence, counsel, planning, medicine, learning, or careful thought. Scripture repeatedly commends wisdom and discernment.
The warning is against making our own understanding the thing upon which our souls finally rest.
The Hebrew verb translated “lean,” תִּשָּׁעֵן — tiššāʿēn, comes from a verb associated with leaning upon or supporting oneself on something.
Picture someone placing his entire weight upon a staff.
That staff had better hold.
And Proverbs is asking a devastatingly personal question:
What are you putting the weight of your life on?
God?
Or your ability to understand God?
Those are not the same thing.
You can believe God exists while still demanding that His decisions pass through the courtroom of your understanding before you will trust Him.
You can worship on Sunday and spend Monday terrified because circumstances stopped matching your expectations.
You can know Bible verses and still secretly believe:
“If I cannot see how God will fix this, maybe He cannot fix it.”
That is where faith gets exposed.
Because genuine trust becomes most visible when the map disappears.
Abraham knew something about that.
God called him to leave his country and go to a land God would show him. Hebrews 11:8 says Abraham obeyed and went out, “not knowing whither he went.”
Not knowing.
Those words are terrifying.
We prefer:
Knowing, then obeying.
Understanding, then surrendering.
Seeing, then trusting.
Receiving confirmation, then moving.
But sometimes God says:
Follow Me.
And the explanation doesn't come first.
Abraham had a promise but not the entire map.
Israel had a pillar of cloud and fire but not a detailed itinerary.
Peter heard Jesus say, “Come,” while there was still a storm beneath his feet.
And perhaps that is where some of us are tonight.
We don't need another motivational quote.
We need enough faith to take the next step without possessing the entire explanation.
Because maybe your greatest battle right now isn't that God has abandoned you.
Maybe it is that God isn't explaining Himself according to your timetable.
And those are very different things.
Read the next verse.
“In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.” — Proverbs 3:6, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ
Bəḵol-dərāḵeḵā ḏāʿēhū.
“In all your ways know Him” or, as traditionally rendered, “acknowledge Him.”
Not merely when life is collapsing.
Not merely when you need a miracle.
Not merely when there is nowhere else to go.
In all your ways.
Your relationships.
Your money.
Your ambitions.
Your private habits.
Your sexuality.
Your resentment.
Your career.
Your secret browser history.
Your plans.
Your wounds.
Your success.
Your disappointment.
Your future.
Your entire life.
This is where the verse becomes uncomfortable.
We often want God to direct paths we have never actually surrendered to Him.
We ask Him to bless relationships we never asked Him to govern.
We ask Him to prosper ambitions we never placed at His feet.
We ask Him for peace while protecting the very sin disturbing our fellowship with Him.
We want Jesus as Savior while resisting Jesus as Lord.
But biblical trust isn't giving God a small religious compartment of your life.
It is surrender.
And surrender becomes frightening precisely because surrender means I am no longer pretending that I am sovereign.
Maybe that is why this verse hits differently when life falls apart.
When everything works, we can accidentally mistake favorable circumstances for strong faith.
Then something breaks.
Suddenly the thing we were leaning on cannot carry us anymore.
The relationship cannot carry us.
Money cannot carry us.
Achievement cannot carry us.
Our reputation cannot carry us.
Our plans cannot carry us.
Even our own understanding cannot carry us.
And there, underneath the wreckage of everything we thought would hold...
Christ remains.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Christianity does not ultimately say, “Try harder to trust.”
It points us to Someone trustworthy.
Jesus Christ.
And if you ever wonder whether God can be trusted when you cannot understand what He is doing, look at the cross.
Imagine standing near Golgotha without knowing Sunday is coming.
Jesus has been betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Condemned.
Crucified.
His followers scatter.
Their hopes appear buried behind a stone.
If you froze the story on Friday afternoon, everything would look like defeat.
The Messiah is dead.
The disciples are devastated.
The enemies appear victorious.
The future appears impossible.
And yet the darkest moment in the story becomes the very place where God's redemptive purpose is being accomplished.
The cross teaches us something our pain desperately needs to remember:
God can be working when everything looks wrong.
That does not mean every tragedy is secretly pleasant.
It does not mean suffering should be minimized.
It does not mean evil becomes good.
The crucifixion itself shows how seriously Scripture takes evil and suffering.
But it means appearances do not have the final word.
God does.
The disciples saw a tomb.
God was writing resurrection.
They saw humiliation.
God was accomplishing redemption.
They saw blood.
God was providing atonement.
They thought the story was ending.
Jesus was rewriting everything.
And maybe you need to hear this before you close this article:
Do not confuse the chapter you cannot understand with the ending God has not yet revealed.
Your pain is real.
Your disappointment is real.
Your questions are real.
But your inability to see the entire story does not mean God has stopped being God.
And trusting Him does not mean pretending you aren't hurting.
Jesus Himself wept.
Biblical faith has room for tears.
It has room for lament.
It has room for questions.
The Psalms are full of people crying, “How long?”
Trust isn't smiling while your heart is bleeding and pretending everything feels wonderful.
Sometimes trust sounds like:
“God, I don't understand this.”
Sometimes:
“God, this hurts.”
Sometimes:
“God, I wanted something different.”
Sometimes:
“God, I am angry, confused, exhausted, and afraid.”
And then comes the sentence hell desperately wants you never to say:
“But Jesus, I am still Yours.”
That is trust.
Not the absence of questions.
Not emotional numbness.
Not pretending suffering doesn't matter.
Trust is refusing to make your limited understanding the final authority over God's character.
And perhaps you have not merely struggled with circumstances.
Perhaps you have wandered.
Maybe disappointment became bitterness.
Bitterness became distance.
Distance became compromise.
Compromise became secrecy.
And secrecy became a life you never imagined yourself living.
Maybe you still know how to look Christian.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You still know the songs.
You know the vocabulary.
But God knows what happens when nobody is watching.
And so do you.
Please hear this carefully:
Jesus is not inviting you to become better at hiding.
He is calling you into the light.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is turning from sin and returning to the God whose mercy you desperately need.
You do not clean yourself sufficiently and then approach Christ.
You come because you need Christ.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to climb their way to God.
It is the announcement that while sinners were helpless, Christ came for us.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He died for sins.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered through Him.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe the scandal isn't what you did.
Maybe it is what was done to you, and you have carried the shame as though someone else's sin became your identity.
Maybe your story contains divorce.
Addiction.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Pride.
Greed.
Abuse.
Church hurt.
A secret failure.
Years of pretending.
A prodigal season.
A prayer you stopped praying because disappointment became too painful.
Whatever brought you here, the Gospel does not tell you that sin does not matter.
The Gospel tells you sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross—and grace is powerful enough that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is why our heartbeat is:
Not because scandal is glamorous.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still restores broken people.
Jesus still receives prodigals.
Jesus still forgives those who repent and come to Him.
Jesus still transforms lives.
Jesus still writes resurrection into places that smelled like death.
And maybe the path back begins tonight with one prayer:
“Jesus, I don't understand everything anymore.
But I trust You.
Forgive my sin.
Break what needs to be broken in me.
Heal what needs to be healed.
Expose what I keep hiding.
Teach me to obey You even when obedience costs me.
I surrender what I cannot control.
My plans.
My fear.
My future.
My shame.
My questions.
My entire heart.
I am Yours.”
If something inside you cracked while reading this, don't rush past it.
Be honest.
If you are exhausted and need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you:
You don't have to explain everything publicly.
God already knows the whole story.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, don't ignore that either.
Send it to the prodigal.
Send it to the exhausted mother.
Send it to the man quietly fighting temptation.
Send it to the believer whose prayers seem unanswered.
Send it even to the person who isn't sure what they believe anymore.
Not for numbers.
For people.
One share can place the Gospel in front of someone you may never know was struggling.
Because there may come a night when Proverbs 3:5 no longer feels inspirational.
There may come a night when trusting God costs something.
And on that night, come back and remember:
You were never commanded to understand everything before you trusted the One who sees everything.
Scripture says giving should not be “grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So there is no spiritual price tag attached to grace.
Jesus cannot be bought.
God's blessing cannot be purchased.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing:
A share helps carry the message.
A comment helps create a visible community where hurting people realize they are not struggling alone.
A tag can reach the one person who desperately needed these words tonight.
A save keeps truth close for the day you need to read it again.
And a follow keeps daily Scripture, biblical encouragement, conviction, healing, and discipleship appearing in your journey.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, keep following Jesus.
Open your Bible.
Pray when you don't feel eloquent.
Repent quickly.
Forgive.
Stay close to faithful believers.
Serve.
Give as God leads you.
Tell somebody what Christ has done.
And when life stops making sense, return to those ancient words:
בְּטַח אֶל־יְהוָה בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ
Trust in the LORD with all your heart.
Then remember the hard part:
וְאֶל־בִּינָתְךָ אַל־תִּשָּׁעֵן
And do not lean on your own understanding.
You don't know everything happening behind the page you are living.
You cannot see tomorrow.
You cannot see every consequence God is restraining, every door He is preparing, every lesson He is forming, or every way He may redeem what you thought was wasted.
But you can look backward toward a bloodstained cross and an empty tomb.
And there you find the reason Christian trust ultimately rests not in circumstances...
but in Christ.
So when you cannot understand the road, remember the Savior who walked all the way to Calvary for you.
When you cannot see what God is doing, remember what God has already done in Jesus.
When Friday convinces you the story is finished...
remember Sunday.
Because sometimes the chapter that makes you wonder whether God has forgotten you becomes the chapter from which you will one day testify that He never let you go.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU BE ADDICTED TO SEXUAL FANTASIES WITHOUT WATCHING PORN?
paragraphs:
CAN YOU BE ADDICTED TO SEXUAL FANTASIES WITHOUT WATCHING PORN?
You Deleted the Videos. You Blocked the Websites. But What If the Screen You Cannot Turn Off Is Inside Your Mind?
There is a kind of sexual bondage nobody can find in your browser history.
No hidden website.
No deleted app.
No secret folder.
No explicit video playing behind a locked door.
Just you.
Your imagination.
And a scene you keep returning to when nobody else is watching.
Maybe that is why you have been telling yourself you are okay.
“I don't watch porn anymore.”
And perhaps that is true.
But there is another question that may be harder to answer:
What are you watching in your mind?
Because some battles survive after the browser closes.
Some images no longer need a screen.
Some fantasies have been rehearsed so many times that all it takes is loneliness, rejection, stress, boredom, anger, an attractive face, a memory, a name, or a quiet room...
and the theater opens again.
Nobody knows.
Your spouse may not know.
Your pastor may not know.
Your friends at church may never suspect it.
Your phone could survive the strictest accountability check imaginable.
Yet somewhere behind your eyes, you have built a room you keep visiting.
And Jesus cares about that room.
Not because He is waiting to humiliate you.
Because He loves you too much to leave any part of you enslaved.

Before going further, something must be said carefully. “Addiction” is a clinical word and should not casually be attached to every strong desire or recurring sexual thought. Sexual attraction itself is not sinful. An unwanted sexual thought appearing in your mind is not identical to deliberately cultivating lust. Temptation is not the same thing as surrendering to temptation. Even Jesus “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

Modern clinical language also tends to speak more precisely about compulsive sexual behavior rather than simply labeling every difficult sexual pattern an addiction. The World Health Organization's ICD-11 recognizes compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, but merely experiencing sexual thoughts or fantasies does not automatically mean someone has a psychiatric disorder.
That distinction matters.
Because Christians should never manufacture guilt where Scripture does not.
But we should not manufacture innocence where Scripture confronts us either.
Jesus takes the interior life seriously.
In Matthew 5:28 He says:
“Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek makes His words especially piercing:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
The key verb is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō.
It can describe longing, desiring, coveting, setting one's desire upon something.
Jesus is not teaching that accidentally noticing someone attractive makes you an adulterer.
He is going deeper.
He is exposing the intentional cultivation of lust.
The look that becomes dwelling.
The noticing that becomes possessing in imagination.
The temptation that is welcomed, fed, developed, replayed.
Jesus moves the battlefield from merely the bedroom...
to the heart.
And suddenly this becomes uncomfortable.
Because pornography can exist on a screen.
But lust can exist without one.
You can delete every explicit photograph from your phone while preserving an entire archive in your imagination.
You can stop searching for pornography while mentally replaying previous sexual experiences.
You can fantasize about someone else's spouse.
A coworker.
An ex.
A stranger.
A fictional person.
Someone you follow online.
Someone sitting three rows ahead of you at church.
And because nobody can inspect your imagination, you may begin calling secrecy freedom.
But secrecy and freedom are not the same thing.
Paul gives us an extraordinary test in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
“All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient... I will not be brought under the power of any.”
The Greek expression translated around this idea of being mastered is striking:
ἐξουσιασθήσομαι — exousiasthēsomai
It carries the idea of being brought under another's authority or control.
That means one revealing question is not merely:
“Do I watch pornography?”
It is:
“What has power over me?”
Can you walk away from the fantasy?
Can you refuse to feed it?
Or does your mind begin bargaining with you?
“Just for a minute.”
“Nobody will know.”
“At least I'm not watching porn.”
“I'm not actually touching anybody.”
“This is better than what I used to do.”
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence:
“It's only in my head.”
Only?
Your worship happens there.
Your prayers happen there.
Your decisions begin there.
Hatred can grow there.
Faith can grow there.
Covetousness can grow there.
Love can grow there.
And Jesus said adultery can begin there.
The heart is not “only” anything.
James describes temptation with frightening psychological accuracy:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.” — James 1:14
The Greek word translated “desire” or “lust” is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia, meaning desire or longing, and in this context desire that entices away from obedience.
Then James describes a progression:
“Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin...” — James 1:15.
Notice that Scripture does not say the mere arrival of temptation equals completed sin.
Desire is pictured as conceiving.
Something is being entertained.
Something is being joined.
Something is being allowed to develop.
And that may describe the difference between an intrusive thought and a cultivated fantasy better than many Christians realize.
A thought knocks.
You did not invite it.
That is temptation.
But then you open the door.
You pull up a chair.
You dim the lights.
You give the thought a storyline.
You decide what happens next.
You return tomorrow and continue where you stopped.
Now something different is happening.
The imagination has stopped being merely attacked.
It has begun cooperating.
And repeated cooperation can become a pattern.
Perhaps you know that pattern.
You get stressed...
you fantasize.
You feel rejected...
you fantasize.
Your marriage feels cold...
you fantasize.
You cannot sleep...
you fantasize.
You feel lonely...
you fantasize.
You feel worthless...
you fantasize.
For a few moments, the fantasy becomes medication.
Nobody rejects you there.
Nobody disappoints you there.
Nobody tells you no there.
Nobody sees your insecurities there.
Everything happens according to your script.
And suddenly you may discover that this battle was never exclusively about sex.
Sometimes lust becomes anesthesia.
You thought you were chasing pleasure.
Maybe you were also running from pain.
Maybe sexual fantasy became the place where you escaped loneliness.
Or rejection.
Or disappointment.
Or insecurity.
Or resentment toward your spouse.
Or wounds you never processed.
Or memories you never surrendered.
And that realization changes the prayer.
Instead of merely saying,
“God, make me stop thinking sexual thoughts,”
you may finally begin asking,
“Jesus... what am I trying not to feel?”
That question can hurt.
But sometimes healing begins precisely where excuses end.
There is another painful truth.
Sexual fantasy can quietly turn another human being into raw material for your private gratification.
The person in your imagination bears God's image.
They have fears.
A childhood.
A soul.
A future.
Perhaps a spouse.
Perhaps children.
Perhaps wounds you know nothing about.
Yet lust can reduce an entire human being into a body existing for your imaginary consumption.
Jesus calls us toward something radically different.
Love.
Honor.
Purity.
Seeing people as people rather than objects.
This is why biblical sexual purity is much more beautiful than merely “don't watch porn.”
God is reclaiming the way you see human beings.
And perhaps right now shame is beginning to speak.
“You're disgusting.”
“You're fake.”
“You've prayed about this before.”
“You promised God you would stop.”
“You failed again.”
“Maybe you aren't really saved.”
Listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same voice.
Conviction exposes your sin so you will run toward Christ.
Condemnation weaponizes your sin so you will hide from Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin is harmless.
The Gospel tells you that your sin was serious enough for Jesus Christ to die for...
and His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not get the final word.
Remember what Paul tells sexually broken people in Corinth.
After naming serious sins, he says:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus...” — 1 Corinthians 6:11.
Were.
That word is thunder.
Your temptation does not have to become your identity.
Your history does not have to become your destiny.
Your worst night does not get to name you.
Porn does not own you.
Lust does not own you.
Fantasy does not own you.
Your past does not own you.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, you have been purchased by Someone else.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than religious advice.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your behavior.
He came to redeem you.
At the cross, Christ carried real guilt for real sinners.
Not polished sinners.
Not respectable sinners.
Sinners.
Liars.
Adulterers.
The sexually immoral.
The proud.
The greedy.
The religious hypocrite.
The secret sinner.
People like us.
He was crucified, buried, and raised again.
And forgiveness is offered not because you finally become clean enough to approach Him, but because His blood is sufficient to cleanse those who repent and trust Him.
So what do you do when the fantasy returns?
Do not negotiate with it.
Do not romanticize it.
Do not panic because temptation appeared.
Bring it into the light.
Name what is happening before God.
Redirect your attention.
Remove triggers you knowingly keep feeding.
Stop protecting the little doors through which the old pattern keeps returning.
If social media repeatedly becomes fuel, change how you use it.
If certain conversations awaken fantasies you deliberately cultivate, establish boundaries.
If loneliness is underneath the pattern, pursue real Christian community instead of imaginary intimacy.
If your marriage is wounded, pursue honest communication and godly help rather than building a secret alternative relationship in your mind.

If the pattern feels genuinely compulsive or is causing serious distress or impairment, seek help from an appropriately qualified mental-health professional, ideally someone who can respect and understand your Christian convictions, alongside mature pastoral support.
And find someone trustworthy who can ask you questions you cannot answer with church language.
Not someone who will crush you.
Someone who will refuse to help you hide.
Because sin grows extraordinarily well in secrecy.
James 5:16 tells believers to confess faults to one another and pray for one another.
There is tremendous freedom in finally saying:
“I need help.”
Maybe that is your sentence today.
Not another dramatic promise.
Not “I swear I'll never struggle again.”
Just:
“Jesus, I cannot keep hiding this.”
That is repentance.
Not merely feeling terrible.
Turning.
Bringing darkness into light.
Agreeing with God.
And then walking toward Christ again and again and again.
Some victories happen instantly.
Others become wars in which grace teaches you how to fight.
But do not mistake a long battle for permission to surrender.
Romans 6:12 says:
“Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof.”
Notice the language.
Reign.
Sin wants a throne.
Jesus already has one.
And perhaps that is the deepest question underneath this entire article.
Not:
“Am I technically addicted?”
Not even:
“How frequently do I fantasize?”
But:
Who rules this room inside me?
You may have spent years trying to destroy lust while secretly believing lust was stronger than Christ.
It isn't.
The goal is not becoming a person incapable of experiencing temptation.
The goal is becoming a person increasingly captivated by Someone greater.
Jesus.
Not merely Jesus as emergency relief after sexual failure.
Jesus as treasure.
Jesus as Lord.
Jesus when nobody is watching.
Jesus when desire screams.
Jesus when loneliness aches.
Jesus when the old mental movie starts playing.
Jesus when shame says hide.
Jesus when you fall.
Jesus when you stand again.
Jesus when obedience costs something.
Jesus when holiness feels harder than fantasy.
Because eventually you discover something astonishing.
You were asking God to remove something from your heart...
while God was inviting you to give Him the heart itself.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to describe your private sexual struggle publicly. But you can make one honest declaration.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only Christian fighting quietly.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, do not weaponize this article against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
Then send it privately if appropriate.
Invite your family, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too.
We glorify God because we belong to Christ, and Christian generosity must never be manipulated.
If this ministry has strengthened you, help strengthen the person who has not discovered it yet.
The greatest invitation in this article is not an invitation to support Gospel Warrior.
It is an invitation to surrender to Jesus Christ.
Maybe your browser history is clean.
Maybe nobody suspects anything.
Maybe you have become very good at appearing victorious.
But you know about the room.
The room behind your eyes.
The room where memories become fantasies.
Where loneliness becomes lust.
Where temptation becomes rehearsal.
Where nobody enters except you.
Tonight, when that door opens again...
remember:
Jesus is not standing outside because He is afraid of what He will find.
He already knows.
He knew before Calvary.
And He went to the cross anyway.
Open the door.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the craving.
Bring Him the loneliness underneath it.
Bring Him the version of yourself you have worked hardest to keep hidden.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His grace.
Then get up and learn to walk in the freedom He purchased.
Because the most powerful evidence of grace is not that your past suddenly becomes beautiful.
It is that Jesus can enter what sin tried to destroy...
and write something redemption-shaped over it.
The screen may exist only inside your mind—but the Savior who came to set captives free is more real than anything playing on it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Keep Calling It a Habit Because “Bondage” Sounds Too Serious.
paragraphs: You Keep Calling It a Habit Because “Bondage” Sounds Too Serious.
The most dangerous chain may be the one you keep renaming so you never have to admit that it is holding you.
You keep calling it a habit.
Maybe because “bondage” sounds too dramatic.
Too religious.
Too uncomfortable.
A habit sounds manageable.
A habit is something you will eventually get around to changing.
A habit lets you say, “I should probably stop.”
Bondage forces a much harder question:
“Why do I keep returning to something I say I want freedom from?”
And maybe that question just made your stomach tighten.
Because you know exactly what “it” is.
Maybe nobody else does.
Maybe your spouse doesn't know.
Your parents don't know.
Your children don't know.
Your church friends certainly don't know.
Maybe people see you worship, laugh, work, serve, post Bible verses, encourage everybody else...
but they don't see the moment when the door closes.
The screen lights up.
The craving returns.
The bottle opens.
The bet gets placed.
The purchase gets made.
The message gets sent.
The food becomes anesthesia.
The scrolling becomes escape.
The fantasy begins again.
The anger explodes again.
The substance promises relief again.
The secret relationship pulls you back again.
Or whatever your particular hiding place happens to be.
You told yourself it would only happen once.
Then once became occasionally.
Occasionally became regularly.
Regularly became secretly.
Secretly became desperately.
And somewhere along the way, you stopped asking whether you were free and started becoming very good at explaining why what controls you isn't really controlling you.
That is why Paul's words are so unsettling.
He writes:
1 Corinthians 6:12.
The thought can be rendered:
“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anything.”
Read that last line again.
I will not be mastered by anything.
The Greek verb is devastatingly appropriate:
ἐξουσιασθήσομαι — exousiasthēsomai.
It carries the idea of being brought under another's authority or mastery.
Paul's concern isn't merely, “Can I do this?”
He pushes deeper.
“What is this doing to me?”
Not merely...
“Is this technically permissible?”
But...
“Is this becoming my master?”
And that changes the conversation.
Because perhaps the question isn't whether you can stop.
Perhaps the question is why you keep needing to prove that you can.
“I can quit whenever I want.”
Then quit.
“I don't really need it.”
Then walk away.
“It's not controlling me.”
Then why does the thought of losing it make you uncomfortable?
Why do you keep protecting it?
Why do you become defensive when somebody questions it?
Why have you hidden how often you do it?
Why have you deleted the evidence?
Why have you promised God you would stop...
and then found yourself standing in the same place again?
This isn't written to diagnose every repeated behavior as clinical addiction. Human struggles are complex, and not every bad habit is an addiction.
But Scripture gives us no permission to make peace with something simply because we found a softer name for it.
There is a difference between struggling against something and quietly arranging your life so that you can keep surrendering to it.
And some of us have become experts at vocabulary.
We call drunkenness “taking the edge off.”
We call lust “just looking.”
We call pornography “a private struggle.”
We call greed “ambition.”
We call compulsive spending “retail therapy.”
We call rage “just how I am.”
We call gluttonous excess “comfort.”
We call obsession “passion.”
We call constant digital escape “unwinding.”
We call sinful relationships “complicated.”
We call compromise “balance.”
We call chains...
habits.
Because if we call them chains, we might finally have to admit that we need freedom.
And freedom can be frightening because freedom requires truth.
Jesus said that those who continue in His word will know the truth, and the truth will set them free.
Notice what Christ connects with freedom.
Truth.
Not pretending.
Not image management.
Not religious performance.
Truth.
And truth sometimes begins with an embarrassingly simple sentence:
“Jesus, this has more power over me than I want anyone to know.”
There.
No polished church language.
No excuses.
No pretending.
Just truth.
Maybe you love Jesus deeply and still recognize yourself here.
Then hear this carefully.
Your struggle does not make the Gospel irrelevant.
It reveals how desperately you need everything the Gospel actually promises.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people can improve themselves.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners can be rescued by a Savior.
And the context surrounding 1 Corinthians 6:12 matters enormously.
Immediately before Paul's warning about being mastered, he reminds the Corinthians of what some of them once were.
Then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in the chapter:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then Paul points to what God had done.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you see it?
Paul does not confront sin by removing grace.
He confronts sin because grace has created a new identity.
The Gospel doesn't say:
“Clean yourself up sufficiently, and perhaps Jesus will receive you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Christ came for sinners.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds forgiveness that cannot be purchased, manufactured, performed, or deserved.
But grace does not teach us to decorate our chains.
Grace teaches us that chains no longer have the right to define us.
That is why this article isn't saying, “Try harder.”
You have probably tried harder.
You cried harder.
Promised harder.
Swore this was the last time harder.
Deleted everything harder.
Reinstalled everything harder.
Made resolutions harder.
Felt disgusted with yourself harder.
Then failed...
and wondered whether Jesus finally became disgusted too.
Listen.
The answer to bondage isn't simply stronger disgust toward yourself.
It is deeper surrender to Christ accompanied by honest, concrete steps into the light.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks remarkably practical.
It looks like confessing what you have hidden.
It looks like calling a mature believer and saying, “I need help.”
It looks like accountability.
It looks like removing access.
It looks like changing routines.
It looks like refusing the environment where you repeatedly fall.
It may look like counseling.
For substance dependence or another serious addiction, it may mean seeking qualified medical or professional treatment rather than trying to survive withdrawal or recovery alone.
Getting appropriate help is not evidence that prayer failed.
You can pray while making the phone call.
You can trust Jesus while entering treatment.
You can believe Scripture while sitting across from a counselor.
You can depend upon the Holy Spirit while giving trusted believers permission to ask questions you would rather avoid.
God's grace and responsible action are not enemies.
Sometimes one of the bravest prayers a Christian can pray is:
“Lord, give me enough humility to stop hiding.”
Because secrecy feeds what confession exposes.
James tells believers to confess sins to one another and pray for one another.
Not because another human being replaces Christ.
Never.
Jesus alone saves.
Jesus alone paid the debt of sin.
Jesus alone is our Mediator.
But Christ never designed His people to fight every battle in isolation.
Maybe that is where this article found you.
Not at rock bottom.
Maybe nobody has discovered anything.
Maybe your marriage hasn't collapsed.
Maybe your finances haven't disappeared.
Maybe your health hasn't broken.
Maybe your ministry hasn't been exposed.
Maybe your children still believe everything is okay.
Maybe your secret hasn't become a scandal.
Yet.
And perhaps grace is reaching you before consequences have to scream what conviction has already been whispering.
Don't wait for devastation to become honest.
Don't wait until somebody catches you.
Don't wait until the doctor gives you frightening news.
Don't wait until your spouse finds the messages.
Don't wait until the debt becomes impossible.
Don't wait until the secret becomes public.
Don't wait until something you could have confronted in the light has consumed years in darkness.
There is no trophy for reaching rock bottom.
You are allowed to reach for Christ before everything collapses.
And if everything already has collapsed...
reach for Him anyway.
Because this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus is not merely Lord of the person you should have been.
He is Redeemer of the person standing in the wreckage.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The Corinthian church itself was filled with people whose former lives Paul could describe in painfully explicit terms.
Yet Scripture contains that astonishing phrase:
“such were some of you.”
Your past can become past tense.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write the ending.
Your secret does not sit on the throne.
Your craving does not sit on the throne.
Your shame does not sit on the throne.
Your addiction does not sit on the throne.
Your failure does not sit on the throne.
Jesus Christ does.
And perhaps repentance begins tonight without fireworks.
Maybe nobody applauds.
Maybe there is no dramatic music.
Maybe you're simply sitting alone with a phone in your hand and tears forming in your eyes.
And for once you stop saying...
“It's nothing.”
You whisper:
“Lord Jesus... it has become something.”
That may be one of the most important sentences you ever pray.
“Forgive me.”
“Help me.”
“Expose what needs exposing.”
“Remove what needs removing.”
“Give me courage to tell someone.”
“I cannot keep calling slavery freedom.”
“I want You more than I want this.”
And tomorrow the craving may still speak.
Repentance does not mean temptation instantly ceases to exist.
Recovery can involve setbacks, difficult days, accountability, rebuilding damaged trust, professional treatment, changed routines, boundaries, and repeated dependence upon God.
But now something is different.
You stopped protecting the chain.
You stopped negotiating with the prison.
You stopped confusing secrecy with safety.
You finally called the thing what it was.
And you brought it toward the light.
That is why Paul's statement becomes more powerful when we continue reading the chapter.
He doesn't merely say, “Don't be mastered.”
He tells believers whose they are.
Your body belongs to the Lord.
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore...
glorify God in your body.
That is Christianity's answer to bondage.
Not merely:
“Stop doing bad things.”
But:
“You belong to Someone.”
You were purchased at immeasurable cost.
Not silver.
Not gold.
Blood.
Christ's blood.
The hands stretched across the cross were pierced for sinners who could not rescue themselves.
The Savior who knew every filthy secret humanity would ever hide still walked toward Calvary.
He did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was deadly.
And He did not rise because redemption was impossible.
He rose because death itself could not keep the Son of God in the grave.
So when Jesus calls you out of darkness, He isn't trying to steal your pleasure.
He is calling you away from masters that cannot love you.
The bottle cannot love you.
Pornography cannot love you.
The drug cannot love you.
The screen cannot love you.
The applause cannot love you.
The affair cannot love you.
The casino cannot love you.
Money cannot love you.
Food cannot love you.
Your secret cannot love you.
They can demand.
They can consume.
They can promise.
They can numb.
They can briefly satisfy.
But they cannot bleed for you.
Jesus did.
And maybe that's the sentence someone you know desperately needs tonight.
Not another lecture.
Not another condemnation.
A reminder that there is a Savior stronger than the thing they are afraid to name.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't. We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
Someone you love may have spent years calling bondage a habit because “bondage” sounded too serious.
Maybe your share becomes the interruption.
Maybe your message becomes the doorway to confession.
Maybe someone finally whispers:
“I need help.”
And if this exposed something in you, don't disappear quietly.
Be honest.

Or, if Christ has already carried you through a season of bondage, leave a testimony that gives somebody else courage. You don't need to publish details that should remain private. Simply tell another wounded person that Jesus still redeems.
There may be a night when temptation becomes loud again and you need to remember the question:
“Am I choosing this—or has this begun choosing for me?”
It doesn't.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is a gift.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting the spread of biblical, Christ-centered content, one practical way you can participate is by supporting the work that produces and distributes it.
before you share...
before you comment...
before you tag anyone...
do the thing that matters infinitely more.
Go to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become respectable.
Not after thirty clean days.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Now.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the craving.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the bottle.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the receipts.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the promises you broke.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are terrified anyone else might see.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
And then take whatever wise, concrete steps obedience requires to stop feeding what has been mastering you.
Because perhaps the scandal isn't simply that you became chained to something you once thought you controlled.
Perhaps the greater scandal is grace itself:
that Jesus already knew the ugliest chapter...
and still went to the cross.
He knew.
He came.
He died.
He rose.
And He still calls sinners out of darkness by name.
So stop giving your chains harmless names.
There is no shame in admitting that you need rescue when the One reaching toward you has scars in His hands.
The chain wants you to keep calling it a habit. Jesus is calling you into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MALACHI SAYS GOD WAS WITNESS BETWEEN YOU AND THE WIFE YOU BETRAYED
paragraphs: MALACHI SAYS GOD WAS WITNESS BETWEEN YOU AND THE WIFE YOU BETRAYED
You may have deleted the messages. You may have buried the secret. You may have convinced everyone that nothing happened. But there was one Witness you could never remove from the room.
There is a terrifying moment in the book of Malachi when men come before God with worship in their hands and confusion in their hearts.
They are crying.
They are bringing offerings.
They are standing at the altar.
And yet something is wrong.
God is not receiving what they are bringing as though everything between them and Him is fine.
They want to know why.
And God's answer reaches through thousands of years and lands painfully close to home:
“Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.”
Malachi 2:14.
Read that again slowly.
Not because it is comfortable.
Because it isn't.
The Hebrew is even more arresting:
“עַל כִּי־יְהוָה הֵעִיד בֵּינְךָ וּבֵין אֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה בָּגַדְתָּה בָּהּ וְהִיא חֲבֶרְתְּךָ וְאֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ”
The heart of the accusation is impossible to miss.
YHWH Himself had been witness between the man and “the wife of your youth.”
And then comes the word that should make every covenant-breaking heart tremble:
בָּגַדְתָּה — bagadta.
You dealt treacherously.
You acted faithlessly.
You betrayed.
Malachi does not dress betrayal in softer clothing so the guilty person can remain comfortable.
He does not call treachery “finding yourself.”
He does not call covenant-breaking “following your heart.”
He does not make the betrayed spouse responsible for sanitizing the betrayer's sin.
God calls it what it is.
Treachery.
But notice something else.
God saw it.
That changes everything.
Because some betrayals happen where nobody else is watching.
A second phone.
A conversation that became too intimate.
A message deleted before coming home.
A relationship called “just friendship” even though your heart knew it had crossed a line.
A hotel room.
A secret account.
A hidden addiction.
A spouse lying awake wondering why the person beside them suddenly feels a thousand miles away.
Maybe nobody at church knew.
Maybe your pastor shook your hand Sunday morning.
Maybe you lifted your hands during worship.
Maybe your children thought everything was normal.
Maybe your spouse suspected something but could never prove it.
Maybe you became frighteningly good at living two lives.
But Malachi introduces Someone who cannot be removed from the story.
God.
“The LORD hath been witness.”
Not merely a spectator.
A witness.
The God before whom the covenant was lived knew what happened when nobody else knew.
He saw the promises.
He saw the beginning.
He saw the young couple who once looked at each other with hope.
He saw the years nobody applauded.
He saw the sacrifices.
He saw the arguments.
He saw the disappointments.
He saw the moments when love required something more difficult than emotion: faithfulness.
And He saw the betrayal.
This is why biblical marriage cannot be reduced merely to a contract between two people.
Malachi calls her:
“אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ”
eshet beritekha.
The wife of your covenant.
That word בְּרִית — berit — means covenant.
She was not merely someone sharing your address.
Not merely someone who carried your surname.
Not merely someone who cooked meals, raised children, paid bills, shared a bed, endured difficult seasons, or stood beside you while you built a life.
She was your covenant companion.
And Malachi uses another beautiful word:
חֲבֶרְתְּךָ — chavertekha.
Your companion.
Think about that.
Before the betrayal became theological, it became painfully personal.
Your companion.
The person who knew how you took your coffee.
The person who recognized your footsteps.
The person who saw you without the public version of yourself.
The person who knew when “I'm fine” meant you weren't.
The person who may have believed you when believing you eventually became expensive.
And perhaps that is why betrayal hurts differently from almost every other wound.
An enemy can hurt you.
But betrayal requires access.
Betrayal says, “You trusted me enough to let me close, and I used that closeness to wound you.”
That is why Scripture refuses to treat marital faithlessness casually.
And this passage should never be weaponized to humiliate someone who has already been betrayed.
Malachi's rebuke is pointed in the opposite direction.
God confronts the one acting treacherously.
He identifies with the seriousness of the violated covenant.
He refuses to pretend that religious activity can erase unrepented injustice at home.
That is sobering.
Because human beings are extraordinarily skilled at compartmentalizing.
We can sing while hiding.
We can preach while hiding.
We can post Bible verses while hiding.
We can serve in ministry while hiding.
We can say “God knows my heart” as though God's knowledge of our hearts should always comfort us.
Sometimes it should terrify us.
Because He really does know.
He knows whether the apology was repentance or damage control.
He knows whether you ended the affair or merely learned to hide it better.
He knows whether you confessed because your heart broke over your sin or because you were caught.
He knows whether you are trying to rebuild what you shattered or demanding that the wounded person “get over it.”
He knows.
And yet...
Here is where the Gospel walks into the wreckage.
Because if the story ended with “God saw what you did,” none of us could stand.
The same Bible that exposes covenant-breaking sinners reveals a Savior who came for sinners.
Jesus Christ did not come because respectable people needed polishing.
He came because guilty people needed redemption.
The cross does not tell us our sin was small.
The cross tells us our sin was so serious that redemption cost the blood of the Son of God.
Grace is not God pretending betrayal never happened.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do for themselves.
Christ bears judgment.
Christ offers forgiveness.
Christ calls sinners out of darkness.
Christ makes repentance possible.
Christ begins making ruined people new.
That means there is hope for the betrayed.
And there is hope for the betrayer who truly repents.
But biblical grace must never become cheap permission to continue destroying people.
Jesus did not die so we could rename darkness.
He died to rescue us from it.
Repentance is not saying, “I'm sorry you were hurt.”
Repentance says, “What I did was sin.”
Repentance stops defending what God condemns.
Repentance stops blaming the wounded person for the wound you created.
Repentance brings darkness into the light.
Repentance accepts consequences.
Repentance seeks accountability.
Repentance tells the truth even when the truth costs something.
Repentance does not demand instant trust.
Trust may take a long time to rebuild.
Some consequences may remain.
Some relationships may carry scars.
And Scripture does not promise that every betrayed marriage will automatically return to what it once was simply because someone finally confessed.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, restored trust, and removal of consequences are related concepts, but they are not identical.
Real repentance does not manipulate the injured person with Bible verses.
It bows before Christ and says:
“Lord, I have sinned.”
No excuses.
No editing.
No carefully constructed version where everyone else shares enough blame that you never have to face yourself.
Just truth.
And perhaps someone reading this right now knows exactly why these words feel uncomfortable.
You haven't physically committed adultery.
But someone else has your emotional intimacy.
Someone else receives the conversations your spouse should be receiving.
Someone else's notification makes your heart race.
Someone else has become the secret place you run to.
And you keep telling yourself:
“Nothing has happened.”
Be careful.
Most catastrophic betrayals do not begin in a bedroom.
They begin with permission.
One conversation you knew should have ended.
One boundary moved.
One secret protected.
One lie justified.
One attraction entertained.
One little door left unlocked.
Until one day you look behind you and wonder how you traveled so far from the person you promised you would be.
Come back.
Not merely to your marriage.
Come back to Christ.
Because ultimately every sin is first against God.

David understood this after his own horrifying sexual sin and the devastation surrounding it. His repentance in Psalm 51 did not deny the people he had harmed; it recognized that his rebellion had ultimately risen against God Himself.
That is where restoration begins.
Not image management.
Not religious performance.
Truth.
Brokenness.
Repentance.
Grace.
Jesus.
And if you are the betrayed spouse reading this with tears gathering in your eyes, hear something equally important:
God saw you too.
He saw the night you discovered it.
He saw your hands shaking.
He saw the message.
The photograph.
The confession.
The bank statement.
The lie that finally collapsed.
He saw you sitting alone wondering which memories were real.
He saw you looking into a mirror asking what was wrong with you.
He saw the humiliation.
He saw the anger.
He saw the strange grief of mourning someone who was still alive.
He saw you trying to function for your children while your private world was collapsing.
He saw.
Malachi's words mean the betrayer did not sin in an empty room.
God was witness.
That does not magically remove your pain.
But it means your pain was never invisible to Him.
And please hear this carefully:
Someone else's treachery does not determine your worth.
Christ does.
You do not have to pretend the wound is small in order to prove that your faith is strong.
You can grieve.
You can seek wise pastoral counsel.
You can seek appropriate professional help.
You can establish necessary boundaries.
You can tell the truth.
And you can bring the ugliest parts of your grief before Jesus without frightening Him away.
He already knows.
Perhaps you are reading from the other side.
You were the one who betrayed.
And shame is whispering:
“There is no coming back from this.”
Do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Hopelessness says, “Stay in the darkness because you are beyond redemption.”
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
It says Jesus is greater.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The woman in John 8 stood publicly accused of adultery.
The Bible is filled with human scandal.
And over and over again, God demonstrates something astonishing:
Scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Grace can.
Not grace without repentance.
Not grace that baptizes rebellion.
Not grace that makes victims return immediately to unsafe situations.
Not grace as religious makeup smeared over an infected wound.
Grace that tells the truth.
Grace that leads us to repentance.
Grace that brings sinners to the cross.
Grace that teaches us to walk differently.
Grace purchased by Jesus Christ.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal is marital betrayal.
Maybe yours has another name.
Pornography.
Lying.
Pride.
Secret addiction.
Bitterness.
Greed.
Religious hypocrisy.
Sexual sin.
A hidden relationship.
A hardened heart.
A private life that looks nothing like your public Christianity.
Whatever it is, stop running.
There is nowhere you can hide where Christ cannot find you.
And there is no darkness so deep that the light of Christ is afraid to enter it.
But you must stop calling darkness light.
Bring it to Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Turn.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness must be asked.
Make restitution where restitution is possible.
Accept accountability.
Stop protecting the version of yourself that Jesus came to crucify.
And begin walking in the light.
Maybe tonight the most spiritual thing you can do is not post another Bible verse.
Maybe it is telling the truth.
Maybe it is handing over the phone.
Maybe it is ending the secret relationship.
Maybe it is confessing to your spouse.
Maybe it is calling a mature pastor or trusted Christian counselor and saying, “I need help.”
Maybe it is falling on your knees after everyone else is asleep and finally saying the sentence heaven has been waiting to hear:
“Jesus, I have sinned. Have mercy on me.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing even a small confession into the light is the moment someone stops pretending.
Let believers pray instead of letting shame isolate you.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person still walking through the wreckage.
Share it not as an accusation.
Share it as a warning wrapped in hope.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions feel negotiable tomorrow.
Come back and read Malachi's words again when you need to remember:
God is witness.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, face uncomfortable truth, understand the Gospel more deeply, or keep walking with Jesus during a difficult season, stay close.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ purchased salvation, and grace cannot be bought.
Share because somebody may need the warning you almost ignored.
Follow because truth is worth keeping close.
And comment because your testimony, confession, or simple “pray for me” may become the doorway through which another hurting person realizes they are not suffering alone.
Malachi leaves us with a God who sees covenant treachery.
The Gospel brings us to a cross where that same holy God offers mercy to repentant sinners through Jesus Christ.
That is the tension we cannot soften.
God saw.
God knows.
God calls sin what it is.
And God still calls sinners home.
So if you have betrayed someone, stop hiding.
If you have been betrayed, stop believing you were invisible.
If your marriage is drifting, wake up before distance becomes destruction.
If your secret life is swallowing your soul, drag it into the light.
And wherever you are standing in the wreckage, look toward Christ.
Because the final word over a repentant sinner does not have to be the worst thing they ever did.
The Witness who saw the betrayal is also the God who sent the Savior—and when everything hidden finally comes into the light, the scars do not have to become the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS STILL SPEAK IN TONGUES TODAY?
paragraphs:
SHOULD CHRISTIANS STILL SPEAK IN TONGUES TODAY?
What If Both Sides Have Been Asking the Wrong Question?
There is a sentence in the New Testament that should make both the skeptic and the enthusiast uncomfortable.
Not because it is confusing.
Because it is painfully clear.
