“Do not forbid speaking in tongues.”
Those words did not come from a modern Pentecostal preacher. They were not written by someone trying to manufacture an emotional church service. They came from the apostle Paul.
And yet the same Paul who wrote those words also spent an extraordinary amount of time correcting the way spiritual gifts were being used.
That tension matters.

Because somewhere between the Christian who says, “Tongues are fake,” and the Christian who implies, “If you do not speak in tongues, you do not really have the Holy Spirit,” Scripture stands in the middle and refuses to surrender to either extreme.
So before defending your tradition, your denomination, your experience, your lack of experience, or the church culture that formed you, there is a more uncomfortable question:
What does the Bible actually say?
And even deeper than that...
Are we willing to obey Scripture if its answer unsettles our camp?
The New Testament word translated “tongue” is γλῶσσα — glōssa. Literally, it can refer to the physical tongue, but it can also mean a language. That matters immediately when we arrive at Pentecost.
Acts 2:4 reads:
“καὶ ἐπλήσθησαν πάντες Πνεύματος Ἁγίου, καὶ ἤρξαντο λαλεῖν ἑτέραις γλώσσαις...”
Kai eplēsthēsan pantes Pneumatos Hagiou, kai ērxanto lalein heterais glōssais...
“And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues...”
The phrase ἑτέραις γλώσσαις — heterais glōssais — means “other tongues” or “other languages.”
And Luke does not leave us guessing about what happened.
People from different regions heard the disciples speaking in their own languages.
The miracle was not meaningless noise.
God was making Himself known.
Men and women heard “the mighty works of God.”
Think about that.
Humanity had languages, borders, ethnic divisions, histories, rivalries, and wounds. Then the Spirit came, and suddenly the mighty works of God were being proclaimed across linguistic boundaries.
Pentecost was never primarily about making Christians look spiritually impressive.
It was about making Christ known.
That single truth already exposes something in us.
Because whenever a spiritual gift becomes more useful for displaying the spirituality of the believer than displaying the glory of Jesus, something has gone terribly wrong.
Paul later addresses tongues extensively in 1 Corinthians 12–14. And Corinth was not exactly the picture of spiritual maturity.
They had gifts.
They also had division.
They had knowledge.
They also had pride.
They had manifestations.
They also had disorder.
They could be spiritually impressive and spiritually immature at the same time.
That should terrify anyone who believes supernatural experiences automatically prove spiritual maturity.
They do not.
Jesus Christ is not impressed by our ability to appear spiritual.
The question is what the Spirit is producing in us.
Are we becoming more loving?
More holy?
More humble?
More obedient?
More forgiving?
More Christlike?
Because Paul deliberately places one of the most famous passages about love right in the middle of his discussion of spiritual gifts.
We often pull 1 Corinthians 13 out for weddings.
Paul wrote it to a church fighting over spirituality.
“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.”
Imagine possessing extraordinary spiritual gifts...
and heaven hearing nothing but noise.
That is sobering.
You could impress a room and still grieve God with your pride.
You could defend the gifts of the Spirit while displaying very little fruit of the Spirit.
You could speak mysteriously in worship and then use the same mouth to destroy someone through gossip.
You could raise your hands on Sunday and refuse to forgive on Monday.
You could argue passionately that supernatural gifts still exist while quietly tolerating sin Jesus died to deliver you from.
And you could stand on the opposite side too.
You could know theology.
You could explain Greek grammar.
You could expose counterfeit manifestations.
You could mock emotional Christianity.
You could pride yourself on discernment...
and still have a heart frozen toward God.
Neither emotionalism nor intellectualism can save you.
Jesus saves.
That is why this discussion must never become a contest between charismatic Christians and cessationist Christians.
It must become a journey back to Scripture.

Some Christians believe miraculous sign gifts such as tongues belonged especially to the apostolic foundation of the early church and therefore ceased as that foundational era came to completion. Others believe the New Testament gives no explicit statement that tongues would cease before Christ's return and therefore understand the gift as potentially continuing until then.
Both positions have been defended by Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture.
But sometimes one verse becomes the battlefield.
First Corinthians 13:8 says:
“Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε πίπτει... εἴτε γλῶσσαι, παύσονται...”
Hē agapē oudepote piptei... eite glōssai, pausontai...
“Love never fails... as for tongues, they will cease...”
The word παύσονται — pausontai — means they “will cease.”
So yes.
Scripture explicitly says tongues will cease.
The disagreement is not really over whether they cease.
The disagreement concerns when.
Paul continues:
“For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.”

Some cessationist interpretations have associated “the perfect” with the completion or maturity of the church’s revelatory foundation. Many continuationist interpreters understand it as the consummation associated with Christ’s return, especially because Paul soon says:
“For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face.”
Whatever position you adopt, humility is necessary because Paul’s central point is larger than winning an argument about spiritual gifts.
Gifts are temporary.
Love belongs to eternity.
There will come a day when nobody needs prophecy.
Nobody needs tongues.
Nobody needs partial knowledge.
Because faith will become sight.
The wounded hands of Jesus will be before us.
And suddenly many arguments that consumed Christians on earth will look very small beside the Lamb who was slain.
But until that day, what should Christians do?
Here is where another Greek sentence refuses to disappear.
Paul concludes his extended discussion in 1 Corinthians 14:39:
“ζηλοῦτε τὸ προφητεύειν, καὶ τὸ λαλεῖν μὴ κωλύετε γλώσσαις.”
Zēloute to prophēteuein, kai to lalein mē kōlyete glōssais.
“Earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.”
Do not forbid it.
But keep reading.
Because Paul does not say, “Therefore anything that happens in a worship service and is called spiritual must be accepted.”
Quite the opposite.
He regulates it.
He insists that corporate worship should build up the church.
He distinguishes private edification from intelligible congregational edification.
He says that if someone speaks publicly in a tongue, interpretation is necessary.
He limits how many should speak.
He says they should speak one at a time.
And if there is no interpreter?
Silence.
That does not sound like uncontrolled spiritual chaos.
It sounds like Spirit-governed order.
Paul eventually says:
“Let all things be done decently and in order.”
That means “the Holy Spirit made me do it” cannot become an excuse for disobeying instructions the Holy Spirit Himself inspired.
Think about that carefully.
The Spirit who gives gifts is the same Spirit who gave Scripture.
The Holy Spirit will never need you to violate the Word He inspired in order to prove that He is present.
So should Christians speak in tongues today?
Scripture gives us several boundaries that cannot honestly be ignored.
Tongues were genuinely present in the New Testament church.
They were a gift of the Holy Spirit.
Not every believer possessed the same gift.
Paul refused to forbid tongues.
Public use required order and, in the circumstances Paul describes, interpretation.
Spiritual gifts were intended to build others up rather than elevate the person possessing them.
And no spiritual gift can replace love, holiness, truth, repentance, or allegiance to Jesus Christ.
Those boundaries matter because there are painful abuses associated with this subject.
Some believers have been told that unless they speak in tongues, they do not have the Holy Spirit.
Paul's own teaching about the diversity of gifts makes that claim difficult to sustain.
In 1 Corinthians 12 Paul asks a sequence of rhetorical questions:
“Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues?”
The expected answer is no.
The body has many members.
The Spirit distributes gifts according to His will.
Your salvation does not rest upon whether you have spoken in tongues.
Your salvation rests upon Jesus Christ.
His incarnation.
His sinless life.
His cross.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His grace.
His promise.
If you belong to Christ, you do not need to manufacture an experience to make yourself acceptable to God.
You need Jesus.
Maybe somebody pressured you.
Maybe everyone around you seemed to experience something you did not.
Maybe you stood in a church service while people prayed over you and whispered inside:
“God... what is wrong with me?”
Listen carefully.
Do not fake something to impress Christians.
God already knows what is real.
You do not need borrowed syllables.
You do not need spiritual theater.
You need truth.
And if God gives a gift, you do not need to manufacture what God is perfectly capable of giving.
But perhaps your story is the opposite.
Maybe you have experienced something you sincerely believe was from the Holy Spirit, and somebody mocked you for it.
Your responsibility is not to retaliate.
Your responsibility is to test everything by Scripture.
Experiences do not interpret the Bible.
The Bible judges our experiences.
If something is genuinely from God, it does not need dishonesty to defend it.
And if something is false, calling it “spiritual” will not make it holy.
This is where the question about tongues becomes something much deeper.
Because maybe your greatest spiritual problem has nothing to do with tongues.
Maybe you speak beautifully in church but brutally to your spouse.
Maybe you can debate spiritual gifts but cannot remember the last time you wept over your sin.
Maybe you know exactly why another denomination is wrong but have become almost completely blind to the pride growing inside your own heart.
Maybe you want supernatural power without supernatural holiness.
Maybe you want manifestations without mortification of sin.
Maybe you want gifts without the Giver.
And Jesus is standing at the center of this entire conversation saying:
Come back to Me.
Because Christianity was never about tongues.
Christianity was never about cessationism.
Christianity was never about continuationism.
Christianity is about Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Buried.
Risen.
Reigning.
Returning.
The Holy Spirit was not sent to create celebrities out of Christians.
Jesus said the Spirit would glorify Him.
That becomes one of the safest questions we can ask about anything claiming to be spiritual:
Does this magnify Jesus?
Does it agree with Scripture?
Does it build up His people?
Does it produce humility?
Does it move sinners toward repentance?
Does it produce love?
Does it make Christ precious?
Or does it make the person with the microphone impressive?
Because there is something far more frightening than never speaking in tongues.
It is speaking Christian language your entire life while never truly knowing Christ.
You can learn the vocabulary.
You can learn when to raise your hands.
You can learn how Christians talk.
You can learn theology.
You can learn worship culture.
You can learn charismatic culture.
You can learn Reformed culture.
You can learn Baptist culture.
You can learn Pentecostal culture.
And still hide from Jesus.
That is the scandal beneath the argument.
We keep asking which gifts we possess while Jesus keeps confronting who possesses our hearts.
The Gospel begins by stripping away our performance.
All have sinned.
All fall short.
The charismatic needs grace.
The cessationist needs grace.
The preacher needs grace.
The theologian needs grace.
The person praying quietly in the last pew needs grace.
And the Savior gives grace to sinners who could never earn it.
Jesus took our guilt to the cross.
He carried the judgment our sin deserved.
He died.
And the grave could not keep Him.
That is where every spiritual gift must ultimately point.
Not to us.
To Him.
So if God has genuinely given you a spiritual gift, use it humbly.
If you believe certain gifts have ceased, hold that conviction from Scripture rather than contempt for Christians who disagree.
If you are unsure, keep studying.
Do not be frightened by the question.
Open the Bible.
Read Acts.
Read 1 Corinthians 12, 13, and 14 together rather than building your theology from isolated verses.
Pray.
Ask God for wisdom.
Test claims.
Reject manipulation.
Reject counterfeit spirituality.
Reject spiritual pride.
And above everything...
cling to Jesus.
Because someday tongues will cease.
Prophecies will end.
Our partial knowledge will give way to something infinitely greater.
But love never fails.
And when you finally see Jesus face to face, you will not regret one moment spent pursuing truth with humility.
Maybe this article exposed something in you.
Pride.
Fear.
Confusion.
A wound from church.
A counterfeit experience you have been afraid to question.
Or perhaps an arrogance that made you dismiss brothers and sisters before genuinely hearing them.
Do not hide behind another theological argument.
Bring it to Christ.
Someone reading quietly may need your testimony more than you realize.
And do not keep Gospel truth trapped behind your screen.
Come to Jesus.
Not merely to an experience.
Not to a denomination.
Not to a manifestation.
Not to an argument.
To Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Let Christ forgive what shame keeps replaying.
Let Him expose what religion taught you to hide.
Let Him rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
Because the greatest evidence that God has touched your life will never be how mysterious your words sound.
It will be that your life increasingly sounds like Jesus.
And long after every tongue has fallen silent, the voice that will matter most is the voice of the Savior who called you by name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD TELL A NEWLY MARRIED MAN TO STAY HOME FOR AN ENTIRE YEAR?
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD TELL A NEWLY MARRIED MAN TO STAY HOME FOR AN ENTIRE YEAR?
Buried inside an ancient law about war is a breathtaking glimpse of what God thinks a marriage is worth—and what happens when we become too busy fighting battles to love the people He entrusted to us.
There is a strange command hiding in Deuteronomy that most Christians have probably read right past.
A man gets married.
Then God says, in effect:
Don’t send him away.
Don’t send him to war.
Give him a year at home.
At first, it sounds almost unbelievable.
Israel was not living in a comfortable world. These were people who understood enemies, armies, survival, land, responsibility, sacrifice, and war. Every able man mattered.
And yet, right in the middle of laws governing Israel’s national life, God placed a newly formed marriage behind a protective wall.
The Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 24:5 says:
“כִּֽי־יִקַּ֥ח אִישׁ֙ אִשָּׁ֣ה חֲדָשָׁ֔ה לֹ֤א יֵצֵא֙ בַּצָּבָ֔א וְלֹא־יַעֲבֹ֥ר עָלָ֖יו לְכׇל־דָּבָ֑ר נָקִ֞י יִהְיֶ֤ה לְבֵיתוֹ֙ שָׁנָ֣ה אֶחָ֔ת וְשִׂמַּ֖ח אֶת־אִשְׁתּ֥וֹ אֲשֶׁר־לָקָֽח׃”
The heart of it is this:
“נָקִי יִהְיֶה לְבֵיתוֹ שָׁנָה אֶחָת”
Nāqî yihyeh ləvêto shānāh eḥāt.
He was to be free for his household for one year.
Then comes the phrase that makes the command remarkably tender:
“וְשִׂמַּח אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ”
Wəśimmaḥ ’et-ishtô.
Literally, the verb carries the idea of causing gladness—bringing joy to his wife.
This matters because the command is sometimes exaggerated into something Scripture does not actually say.

Deuteronomy does not say a newly married Israelite man was forbidden to perform every kind of work for twelve months. The specific protection concerns military service and being assigned away for other obligations of that sort. The point was not twelve months of laziness.
It was twelve months of protected presence.
And suddenly this ancient command begins sounding painfully modern.
Because we have become very good at being physically married while emotionally deployed.
You can sleep beside someone and still be absent.
You can pay the bills and never ask what is happening inside your spouse’s heart.
You can provide a house while starving the relationship living inside it.
You can build a career.
Build a ministry.
Build a reputation.
Build a business.
Build a following.
Build everybody else’s dreams...
and slowly lose the person who once looked into your eyes and believed you would build a life together.
Maybe that is why this little verse feels so uncomfortable.
God was teaching Israel that some things are important enough to protect from interruption.
A marriage was one of them.
And notice something else.
This protection was given in a culture that knew war.
Earlier, Deuteronomy 20:7 had already instructed that a man who had become betrothed but had not yet taken his wife should return home rather than risk dying in battle before beginning married life.
Think about that.
There is an army assembling.
There is an enemy ahead.
There are weapons being prepared.
Men are going to battle.
And somewhere among those soldiers is a man whose heart belongs to a woman waiting at home.
Human logic might say:
“We need every soldier.”
God's law says:
“Send that man home.”
Not because marriage was more important than every national responsibility in every circumstance.
Not because Israel could ignore danger.
But because God was building something larger than an army.
He was building a covenant people.
And covenant faithfulness had to reach all the way into the home.
That should challenge us.
Because our culture often celebrates sacrifice without asking what is being sacrificed.
We praise the man who never stops working.
We admire the woman who carries everyone.
We applaud packed schedules.
We romanticize exhaustion.
We call emotional absence “providing.”
We call neglect “being busy.”
Sometimes we even spiritualize it.
“I’m doing this for God.”
“I’m doing this for my family.”
“I’m doing this for our future.”
And sometimes those words are completely true.
But sometimes...
they become beautiful sentences we use to avoid an ugly reality:
The people closest to us are receiving whatever remains after everyone else has taken their portion.
Deuteronomy 24:5 refuses to treat marriage like leftovers.
God gave the new husband something enormously valuable.
Time.
Presence.
Attention.
A protected beginning.
The verse does not present marriage merely as a wedding ceremony that happened yesterday.
Marriage had to become a shared life.
The husband was not simply told, “You have acquired a wife.”
He was directed toward her joy.
“וְשִׂמַּח אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ”
Bring gladness to the wife you have taken.
That is astonishingly personal language inside ancient legislation.
She mattered.
Her experience of this new covenant mattered.
The home they were establishing mattered.
Their relationship was not an inconvenience squeezed between supposedly more important responsibilities.
God made room for it.

And before anyone turns this verse into a simplistic formula—“Every Christian husband must therefore take exactly one year away from his job”—we need to respect Scripture enough not to make it say what it does not say.
This command belonged to Israel's covenant legislation.

Christians are not ancient Israel under the Mosaic civil order, and the New Testament does not reproduce Deuteronomy 24:5 as a command requiring every Christian newlywed man to stop ordinary employment for twelve months.
But the God revealed through the command has not suddenly become indifferent to covenant faithfulness.
The principle resonates throughout Scripture.
Marriage matters to God.
Faithfulness matters.
Sacrificial love matters.
Presence matters.
And when we arrive at the New Testament, marriage becomes the setting for an even more breathtaking picture.
Paul writes that a husband should love his wife “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).
There is the center.
Jesus.
Christian marriage ultimately cannot be understood merely as romance.
It points beyond itself.
Christ loved His people sacrificially.
He did not love from a safe distance.
He gave Himself.
He entered our ruin.
He carried our sin.
He endured the cross.
He rose from the grave.
And this is where an ancient command about a newly married Israelite becomes a mirror held painfully close to our hearts.
Because maybe your problem is not that you went to war.
Maybe you simply stopped coming home emotionally.
Maybe your spouse has been trying to tell you something for months.
Maybe the conversations became shorter.
The phones became louder.
The tenderness disappeared.
The prayers together stopped.
The affection became mechanical.
The resentment became normal.
And somewhere along the way, two people who promised they would never leave each other became strangers sharing responsibilities.
Maybe your marriage is not collapsing dramatically.
Maybe it is disappearing quietly.
Those can be the frightening ones.
No affair.
No screaming.
No packed suitcase.
Just distance.
A little more every month.
Until one day someone whispers:
“I don't know you anymore.”
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Maybe you are the spouse waiting.
Waiting for the person you married to notice you again.
Waiting for them to put the phone down.
Waiting for them to ask something deeper than, “What are we having for dinner?”
Waiting for affection that doesn't immediately ask for something.
Waiting to feel chosen again.
Or maybe...
you are the one who drifted.
And reading this hurts because you know it.
Don't run from that conviction.
Run to Christ with it.
The Gospel does not exist merely to make guilty people feel worse.
The Gospel announces that guilty people can be forgiven.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
For selfish husbands.
For bitter wives.
For distracted fathers.
For wounded mothers.
For people who broke promises.
For people who were broken by somebody else's broken promises.
For people who cannot rewind the years.
That is what grace means.
Grace does not pretend the wound never happened.
Grace meets us in the wound and begins writing something sin could never write by itself:
redemption.
Maybe you cannot recover the first year of your marriage.
Maybe you wasted it.
Maybe ten years disappeared.
Maybe twenty.
Maybe you wish you could go back to the day you stood before God and said your vows with trembling hands.
You cannot go back.
But Jesus Christ is Lord of what comes next.
That is the scandal of grace.
God takes people with histories they cannot erase and gives them futures their failures could never earn.
Repentance does not mean pretending everything is fine.
It means turning.
Turning from pride.
Turning from secrecy.
Turning from emotional laziness.
Turning from pornography.
Turning from adultery.
Turning from bitterness.
Turning from selfishness.
Turning from the endless obsession with work, status, money, ministry, recognition, entertainment, or anything else that has occupied the throne that belongs to Christ.
And turning toward Jesus.
Because your spouse cannot be your savior.
Your marriage cannot save you.
A perfect home cannot save you.
Only Christ can.
The husband who reads Deuteronomy 24:5 and concludes merely, “I should spend more time with my wife,” has seen something true—but not yet everything.
The deeper question is:
What kind of man am I becoming before God?
And the wife reading this should not hear, “Your happiness is entirely your husband's responsibility.”
Scripture does not teach that either.
No human being can carry the weight of another person's ultimate joy.
That throne belongs to God.
But marriage does create covenant responsibilities.
And love does cost something.
Sometimes the cost is not dying heroically.
Sometimes the cost is putting down your phone.
Listening when you are tired.
Apologizing without defending yourself.
Praying when conversation feels awkward.
Coming home when your ego wants to escape.
Seeking help when pride says, “We can handle this ourselves.”
Forgiving as you have been forgiven.
Being faithful when nobody is applauding.
Choosing tenderness after disappointment.
Maybe the great battle for your marriage will never happen on a battlefield.
Maybe it is happening tonight at your dinner table.
Maybe the enemy does not need to destroy your home with one spectacular scandal if he can slowly teach you to stop caring.
And maybe God brought this ancient verse in front of you today because something in your home needs attention.
Not tomorrow.
Not when work slows down.
Not after the next promotion.
Not when the children grow up.
Not after one more project.
Today.
Ask your spouse:
“Have I been present?”
Then have enough humility not to interrupt the answer.
Ask:
“Where have you felt alone?”
Ask:
“What have I stopped doing that once made you feel loved?”
And if the answer hurts...
listen anyway.
Marriage is not saved by winning every argument.
Sometimes healing begins when someone finally stops trying to win.
And perhaps this reaches beyond marriage.
Maybe you are single.
Widowed.
Divorced.
Separated.
Abandoned.
Maybe reading about marriage touches a wound rather than a romance.
The Gospel still has something for you here.
Your deepest identity is not “married.”
It is not “single.”
It is not “divorced.”
It is not “wanted.”
It is not “rejected.”
For those who belong to Jesus Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
Human covenant can fail.
Christ does not.
People can abandon.
Christ remains faithful.
People can break promises.
Jesus carried His covenant love all the way to a cross.
And if you have failed...
there is grace.
If you have been betrayed...
there is grace.
If your home feels cold...
there is grace.
If reconciliation is possible and safe, pursue truth, repentance, wisdom, counsel, forgiveness, and restoration.

And where another person's continued abuse or destructive behavior makes simplistic advice dangerous, remember this: biblical faithfulness never requires pretending evil is good. Seek wise pastoral, professional, and appropriate practical help.
Grace is not denial.
Grace brings darkness into the light.
That is what Jesus does.
He exposes what is killing us not because He delights in humiliation, but because He came to save sinners from the things destroying them.
So perhaps Deuteronomy 24:5 is not strange after all.
Perhaps what is strange is us.
We live in a world where people will spend years building careers and weeks planning weddings...
then assume marriages will somehow build themselves.
They won't.
Covenants must be tended.
Love must become action.
Repentance must become change.
Forgiveness must become practice.
Christ must remain at the center.
The ancient Israelite groom was given a protected year in which the claims of military service were not permitted to immediately pull him away from the household he had just formed.
Thousands of years later, the details of our world are different.
But the question underneath that command can still follow us home:
What are you protecting?
Because whatever gets your first attention, your deepest energy, your constant sacrifice, and your guarded time eventually reveals something about what you treasure.
Maybe tonight your greatest act of spiritual maturity is not posting another Bible verse.
Maybe it is walking into the next room.
Sitting beside your spouse.
Looking into their eyes.
And saying:
“I think I've been away even when I was here.”
Then listen.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness can be given.
Get help where help is needed.
And invite Jesus into the rooms you have kept locked.
Be honest.
Someone else reading your words may realize they are not fighting alone.
You may need to read it again on a night when pride returns.
Not as proof that your marriage is perfect, but as a quiet declaration that covenant still matters, repentance still matters, families still matter, and Jesus Christ still restores broken people.
Above all, glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and a life surrendered to Him.
And please don't keep truth that helped you locked inside your own screen.
Because perhaps the most haunting truth hidden inside this ancient command is this:
Sometimes the battle God wants you to stop fighting long enough to notice is the heart waiting for you at home.
And when we discover how badly we have loved, how far we have wandered, or how much we have broken, the answer is not to hide from Christ.
Run toward Him.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is a cross.
There is an empty tomb.
There is grace.
And where Jesus Christ is welcomed as Lord, failure does not have to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HAGAR BECAME PREGNANT BY SARAH’S HUSBAND—And Their Household Exploded
paragraphs:
HAGAR BECAME PREGNANT BY SARAH’S HUSBAND—And Their Household Exploded
One desperate decision. One pregnant servant. One wounded wife. One silent husband. And a God who walked into the wilderness after the woman everybody else had used.
There are Bible stories we sanitize because the truth makes us uncomfortable.
This is not one of them.

Genesis 16 opens the door of Abraham’s household and lets us hear what happens when waiting becomes unbearable, pain begins making decisions, and human beings try to manufacture what God has promised.
Before she was Sarah, she was Sarai.
Before he was Abraham, he was Abram.
And before Isaac ever laughed inside their tent, another woman became pregnant by Sarai’s husband.
Her name was Hagar.
Read slowly, because Genesis does not hide the scandal:
“וְשָׂרַי אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָם לֹא יָלְדָה לוֹ”
VeSarai eshet Avram lo yaldah lo.
“Sarai, Abram’s wife, had borne him no children.” — Genesis 16:1
That sentence looks simple until you remember what came before it.
God had already called Abram.
God had already made promises.
God had already spoken about offspring.
Yet Sarai remained childless.
And waiting has a way of exposing what is buried inside us.
You can believe God and still become exhausted.
You can know His promise and still hate His timing.
You can pray faithfully for years and eventually begin wondering whether heaven has forgotten your address.
Maybe that is why this story feels painfully modern.
Somebody reading this knows what it means to wait while everybody else seems to receive what you have been begging God for.
A marriage.
A child.
Healing.
Restoration.
A breakthrough.
A door opening.
An answer.
You celebrated other people while quietly asking God, “When will it be me?”
And eventually the temptation changes.
At first you ask God to fulfill His promise.
Later you begin trying to fulfill it for Him.
That is where Sarai stood.
She told Abram:
“בֹּא־נָא אֶל־שִׁפְחָתִי אוּלַי אִבָּנֶה מִמֶּנָּה”
Bo-na el-shifchati, ulai ibbaneh mimmennah.
The thought is essentially: “Go in to my maidservant; perhaps I may be built up through her.”
That expression “אִבָּנֶה” (ibbaneh) comes from the language of being built up. Sarai was trying to build the family she could not produce herself.
And there is the wound.
She wanted something God had promised.
But pain convinced her that she needed to engineer the outcome.
That is one of the most dangerous spiritual places a believer can enter:
when the destination may look right, but we no longer trust God with the road.
Genesis says Abram listened to Sarai.
Then comes a detail we should not rush past.
They had been in Canaan ten years.
Ten years of waiting.
Ten years can make compromise sound reasonable.
Ten years can make desperation sound like wisdom.
Ten years can make something culturally understandable feel spiritually necessary.
So Sarai took Hagar, her Egyptian servant, and gave her to Abram.
Scripture records what happened. That does not mean Scripture is presenting every human action in the story as God's ideal.
Hagar was not merely a convenient plot device.
She was a woman living with drastically less power than Abram and Sarai.
Then Abram went in to Hagar.
And she conceived.
Four Hebrew words change the emotional temperature of the entire household:
“וַיָּבֹא אֶל־הָגָר וַתַּהַר”
Vayyavo el-Hagar vattahar.
“He went in to Hagar, and she conceived.”
Suddenly the plan worked.
And everything started falling apart.
That is frightening.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing about a flesh-driven decision is that it appears to work.
The relationship happened.
The pregnancy happened.
The solution seemed successful.
But success is not always evidence that God authorized the method.
Some doors open because we kicked them down.
Some relationships continue because we refuse to surrender them.
Some plans produce results while simultaneously producing wounds.
Hagar became pregnant, and Genesis tells us that Sarai became diminished in Hagar’s eyes.
The woman who could conceive was now looking differently at the woman who could not.
Imagine that tent.
Imagine the glances.
Imagine Sarai seeing Hagar's body beginning to carry the evidence of everything Sarai desperately wanted.
Imagine Hagar carrying Abram's child while still living under Sarai's authority.
The solution had become a daily reminder of the wound.
Jealousy entered.
Contempt entered.
Blame entered.
Power entered.
Bitterness entered.
And Sarai exploded at Abram.
“The wrong done to me is on you.”
That line should make every married person uncomfortable.
Because Abram had agreed to the plan.
But now that the consequences were bleeding through the household, everybody was hurting.
Isn't that what sin does?
It promises an escape from pain and often multiplies the pain.
It tells us, “This will fix it.”
Then we wake up surrounded by consequences we never imagined.
Sarai blamed Abram.
Hagar despised Sarai.
Abram withdrew from responsibility.
And eventually Sarai treated Hagar so harshly that Hagar ran away.
Pregnant.
Alone.
Into the wilderness.
Think about that.
The woman carrying Abram's child was running through the desert because remaining in the household had become unbearable.
And this is where Genesis 16 turns from household scandal into something breathtaking.
God went looking for Hagar.
The text says:
“וַיִּמְצָאָהּ מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה”
Vayyimtza'ah mal'akh YHWH.
“The angel of the LORD found her.”
Found her.
Do not miss that word.
Abram let her go.
Sarai drove her away.
But heaven knew where she was.
God found the woman in the wilderness.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needed tonight.
God knows where you are.
Not the version of you everybody sees on Facebook.
You.
The exhausted you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The person sitting in the car because you do not want to walk inside the house yet.
The person smiling in church while privately wondering whether your faith is dying.
The person who made decisions you cannot undo.
The person carrying consequences that keep reminding you of yesterday.
The person who feels used.
Forgotten.
Unwanted.
Invisible.
God knew Hagar's location.
And God knew her name.
“Hagar.”
Then came the question:
Where have you come from, and where are you going?
She could answer the first.
She was fleeing from Sarai.
But the second question hung over the wilderness.
Where are you going?
That question still follows wounded people.
You know what you are running from.
But do you know where you are running to?
Pain can make almost anywhere look like freedom.
Sometimes we are so desperate to escape yesterday that we never ask what tomorrow will become if we keep running without God.

The Lord's messenger instructed Hagar to return and submit to her mistress, while also giving her promises concerning her descendants. This difficult passage must never be twisted into a blanket command telling abused people today to remain in dangerous situations. Genesis is describing a specific divine encounter in Hagar's particular covenant-historical circumstances, not handing abusers a verse with which to imprison victims.
Then God spoke about the child inside her.
His name would be Ishmael.
In Hebrew:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל
Yishma'el.
The name carries the idea that “God hears.”
Genesis explicitly connects his name with the LORD hearing Hagar's affliction.
Think about that.
Every time she called her son's name, she would be reminded:
God heard me.
“Ishmael!”
God heard me.
Come home, Ishmael.
God heard me.
Eat, Ishmael.
God heard me.
Sleep, Ishmael.
The child conceived inside a shattered household would carry a name reminding his mother that heaven had heard her suffering.
But Hagar did something equally extraordinary.
She spoke of the God who had spoken to her as:
“אֵל רֳאִי”
El Ro'i.
Often rendered, “God who sees me.”
The servant nobody asked what she wanted had encountered the God who saw her.
The woman caught inside somebody else's attempt to solve a problem had discovered that she was not invisible to heaven.
The household saw a servant.
God saw Hagar.
The household saw a pregnancy.
God saw a person.
The household saw a complication.
God saw a woman in affliction.
And perhaps that is why Genesis 16 refuses to become merely ancient family drama.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to become somebody else's “problem.”
You were the embarrassing chapter.
The divorced one.
The addicted one.
The betrayed one.
The one who failed publicly.
The one whose child walked away.
The one whose marriage collapsed.
The one who got pregnant before the wedding.
The one who cheated.
The one who was cheated on.
The one who came back to church after years away and wondered whether everybody was looking.
The one carrying consequences nobody knows about.
People may reduce your entire life to the worst thing connected with your name.
God does not.
And here we must go deeper than Hagar.
Because Genesis 16 is not the end of Scripture.
The Bible keeps moving.
Abram becomes Abraham.
Sarai becomes Sarah.
Isaac eventually comes according to God's promise.
Generations pass.
Kings rise.
Prophets speak.
Human beings continue failing.
And ultimately the biblical story brings us to Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
He came into humanity's wreckage.
The Gospel is not God standing far away from scandal shouting instructions.
It is the Son of God entering our fallen world to rescue sinners.
Jesus touched people others avoided.
He ate with sinners.
He welcomed the disgraced.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people to repentance.
And then He went to a cross carrying something far deeper than social embarrassment.
Our sin.
“For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to die.
Not that consequences disappear.
Scripture never promises that.
Not that everybody in Genesis 16 was secretly innocent.
They were not.
The beauty is that human failure cannot overthrow God's redemptive purposes.
That changes how we read our own lives.
Maybe you made your Hagar decision.
You became tired of waiting.
You forced something.
You manipulated something.
You entered something God never told you to enter.
Maybe you compromised because you were lonely.
Maybe bitterness made you cruel.
Maybe fear made you controlling.
Maybe you blamed somebody else for a decision you helped make.
Maybe you have been Abram—passive when courage was required.
Maybe you have been Sarai—so wounded that your pain wounded somebody else.
Maybe you have felt like Hagar—caught inside decisions made by people more powerful than you, running toward a wilderness because anywhere seemed safer than where you had been.
Genesis 16 will not allow us to flatten these people into cartoon villains and heroes.
Human beings are messier than that.
So are we.
And grace is more astonishing because of it.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth and still opens a door home.
Grace does not say, “Nothing happened.”
Grace says, “Something terrible happened, sin is real, wounds are real, consequences are real—and God is still God.”
That is why Jesus matters.
Christianity is not self-improvement for respectable people.
It is resurrection for people who cannot save themselves.
You cannot repent deeply enough to become your own Savior.
You cannot serve enough.
Donate enough.
Post enough Christian content.
Attend enough services.
Cry enough tears.
Or repair enough of your history to purchase forgiveness.
Christ saves by grace.
Our response is repentance and faith.
And when grace reaches us, obedience begins flowing from gratitude rather than an attempt to buy God's love.
Maybe you need to stop pretending tonight.
Maybe your prayer does not need impressive words.
Maybe it needs to sound like:
“Jesus, I sinned.”
“Jesus, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I am tired.”
“Jesus, I tried to control everything.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
He already sees the wilderness.
Bring Him the truth.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need grace becomes the first crack in the wall we have spent years building.
And read the other comments.
You may discover you were never as alone as shame told you.
There may come a night when your wilderness gets loud again and you need to remember two Hebrew words:
El Ro'i.
The God who sees me.
Then send this to the person whose smile has been convincing everybody except you.

Supporting Gospel work is never a purchase of God's blessing and never a condition of glorifying Him; salvation and God's favor cannot be bought. But believers can glorify God through willing generosity, faithful stewardship, and helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it.
And there is something larger behind this mission.
And before you leave, remember the pregnant woman standing beside that wilderness spring.
Her circumstances were complicated.
Her future was uncertain.
Her household was fractured.
She could not rewrite what had happened.
But God saw her.
God heard her.
And the same Bible that refuses to hide the scandal also refuses to let the scandal have the final word.
That is the heartbeat running through Scripture.
Sin speaks.
Grace speaks louder.
Failure leaves scars.
Christ bears scars too.
Your history may explain some of your wounds, but for everyone who belongs to Jesus, your history does not get to become your savior, your master, or your final identity.
So repent where you sinned.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek help where you have been wounded.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
Stop trying to manufacture tomorrow because you are terrified of waiting today.
Trust the God who sees the wilderness.
Trust the Christ who entered our broken world.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable truth inside this scandal is this:
When everyone else saw Hagar as the problem inside Abraham's house, God saw a person worth finding in the wilderness.
And if Jesus Christ can take sinners from guilt to forgiveness, from rebellion to repentance, from death to life, then your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
And never forget:
The chapter you wish you could erase may become the very place where you discover that God never stopped seeing you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE DEVIL ATTACK THROUGH SEXUAL SIN SO OFTEN?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE DEVIL ATTACK THROUGH SEXUAL SIN SO OFTEN?
Because sexual sin rarely stops at the body. It reaches for your worship, your identity, your relationships, your secrecy—and the very place Christ purchased for His glory.
There is a reason some temptations seem to know exactly when you are lonely.
Late at night.
After the argument.
After the rejection.
After everybody else has gone to sleep.
After you promised God you would never do it again.
The room is quiet. The screen is glowing. Nobody appears to be watching.
And somewhere inside you, a familiar voice begins negotiating.
Just once.
You've been doing so well.
You deserve some relief.
Nobody will know.
Then afterward comes another voice.
Look at you.
You call yourself a Christian?
After everything God has done for you?
Don't even pray. You're disgusting.
And this is where many Christians misunderstand the battle.
Temptation says, “Come closer.”
Shame says, “Stay away from God.”
One pulls you toward sin.
The other tries to keep you from the Savior after you fall.
And if you don't understand that pattern, you can spend years trapped between craving and condemnation—sinning because you feel empty, then hiding from the only One who can actually make you whole.
So why does sexual sin appear so frequently in spiritual warfare?
Scripture gives us an answer far deeper than “because sex is bad.”
Sex is not bad.
God created sexuality.

Before pornography existed, before adultery existed, before prostitution existed, before lust corrupted what God designed, the Creator made humanity male and female and established the covenant union of husband and wife.
The enemy did not invent sexuality.
He corrupts what God created.
That distinction matters.

Satan's strategy throughout Scripture is often not simply to persuade humanity that evil is good. He distorts something God made good until we attempt to enjoy God's gift while rejecting God's authority.
That pattern is ancient.
In Eden, the serpent's attack revolved around God's Word:
“Yea, hath God said...?” (Genesis 3:1, KJV)
That question still echoes through temptation.
Did God really say?
Is this really wrong?
Would a loving God actually deny you this?
Does it matter what you watch if nobody gets hurt?
Does it matter what you fantasize about?
Does it matter what happens between consenting adults?
Does God really care what you do with your body?
Then Paul answers with words almost violently direct:
“Flee fornication.”
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:18 begins:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — Pheugete tēn porneian.
The command φεύγετε (pheugete) comes from pheugō—to flee, escape, run away.
And πορνεία (porneia) is the broad New Testament term associated with sexual immorality.
Notice what Paul does not say.
Manage it.
Study how close you can get.
Prove how spiritually mature you are by standing beside it.
Negotiate with it.
He says:
Run.
There are battles where courage means standing your ground.
Sexual temptation is one of those battles where courage sometimes looks like running for your life.
Joseph understood this centuries before Paul wrote those words.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly attempted to seduce him. Then one day she grabbed his garment and demanded that he sleep with her.
Joseph did not stay to conduct a theological seminar.
He fled.
He lost his garment...
but kept his integrity.
And sometimes that is exactly what obedience costs.
You may lose a relationship.
You may have to delete an app.
You may need to end conversations that secretly feed something you keep calling harmless.
You may need to stop carrying your phone into the room where you repeatedly fall.
You may need accountability.
You may need to confess what darkness has convinced you must remain secret.
You may have to look foolish to somebody else in order to remain faithful before God.
Better to leave the coat behind than leave your character behind.
But we also need to correct something Christians sometimes say too casually.
Not every sexual temptation means Satan personally attacked you.
Scripture will not allow us to blame the devil for everything happening inside us.
James writes:
The Greek word translated “desire” or traditionally “lust” is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia. Depending on context, it refers to desire or craving; in James 1 it is desire functioning in a sinful direction.
James continues with terrifying imagery:
“Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.” (James 1:15, KJV)
Read that slowly.
Desire.
Conception.
Birth.
Growth.
Death.
Sin promises an experience.
Then produces a master.
That is why the biblical picture of temptation is more serious—and more useful—than saying, “The devil made me do it.”
Scripture speaks of the devil and his schemes. Scripture speaks of a fallen world. Scripture also speaks about desires arising within fallen human beings.
The Christian battle therefore isn't merely “me versus Satan.”
There is an enemy outside.
There is a fallen world around us.
And there remain disordered desires within us that must be brought under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
But why can sexual sin become such devastating territory?
Because biblical sexuality involves more than physical sensation.
Paul asks:
“Know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:15, KJV)
Then comes one of Scripture's strongest statements concerning sexual immorality:
“Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.” (1 Corinthians 6:18, KJV)
And then Paul takes the argument somewhere astonishing.
Your body is not disposable.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
Your body does not belong to pornography.
It does not belong to your boyfriend.
It does not belong to your girlfriend.
It does not belong to an affair.
It does not belong to your impulses.
It does not ultimately belong even to you.
“Ye are not your own... For ye are bought with a price.” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV)
That changes everything.
Christian purity is not fundamentally God shouting:
Don't touch.
It is Christ declaring:
You were bought at a price.
The gospel doesn't merely tell you what to run from.
It tells you whom you belong to.
This is why reducing Christian sexual ethics to shame is such a catastrophic mistake.
Jesus is not recruiting sexually flawless people.
There aren't any.
He is redeeming sinners.
Some carry histories nobody knows.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Fornication.
Secret messages.
Fantasy.
Same-sex sexual behavior.
Sexual compromise.
Emotional affairs.
Years of hidden habits.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying memories you desperately wish could be erased.
Maybe people at church know the polished version of you.
They know your worship songs.
Your Bible verses.
Your Christian posts.
Your smile.
But they don't know what happens when loneliness enters the room.
They don't know your browser history.
They don't know the messages you deleted.
They don't know about the relationship you keep returning to even though conviction keeps telling you to leave.
They don't know how many times you have whispered:
“God, please forgive me. This is the last time.”
Only it wasn't.
And now perhaps the worst part isn't even the temptation anymore.
It's the exhaustion.
You are tired of disappointing yourself.
Tired of confessing the same thing.
Tired of wondering whether repentance is real when you keep stumbling.
Tired of hiding.
And maybe you have begun believing that Jesus must be tired of you too.
Listen carefully.
The gospel does not minimize your sin.
It does something infinitely better.
It provides a Savior powerful enough to deal with it.
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth after describing forms of serious sexual and other sin:
“And such were some of you.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
Were.
That word carries thunder.
Their sins were real.
Their histories were real.
Their guilt was real.
But their histories were not sovereign.
Paul continues:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus...” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewriting what the scandal thought would be the final chapter.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity needed motivational advice.
He went because sin produces real guilt before a holy God and sinners cannot rescue themselves.
At Calvary, Christ bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not God's reluctant decision to pretend your sin wasn't serious.
Forgiveness was purchased at unimaginable cost.
That means grace is not permission to keep sleeping with sin.
Grace is the power and mercy that calls you out of its bed.
Jesus does not say:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
He says, in effect:
“It mattered enough for Me to die for sinners. Now follow Me.”
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance isn't merely feeling horrible afterward.
Shame can make you feel horrible.
Fear can make you feel horrible.
Consequences can make you feel horrible.
Biblical repentance turns toward God.
It brings darkness into light.
It stops defending what Christ died to save us from.
It stops asking, “How much can I get away with?”
And begins asking:
“How completely can I belong to Jesus?”
Perhaps that is the deeper reason sexual sin becomes such strategic ground.
Because it can distort intimacy while promising intimacy.
It can offer pleasure while cultivating slavery.
It can train us to consume people instead of loving them.
It can make secrecy feel safer than confession.
It can separate physical desire from covenant faithfulness.
It can leave people simultaneously stimulated and starving.
And after enough repetition, what once shocked the conscience can begin feeling normal.
That is how bondage often works.
Not all at once.
One compromise.
Then another.
Then secrecy.
Then rationalization.
Then repetition.
Then identity.
Eventually someone stops saying:
“I am struggling with this.”
And begins believing:
“This is simply who I am.”
That lie must die at the feet of Jesus.
Your temptation is not your identity.
Your worst night is not your identity.
Your pornography history is not your identity.
Your adultery is not your identity.
Your virginity is not your identity either.
Your sexual past does not possess the authority to name you forever.
Jesus does.
But grace must never be twisted into cheap reassurance.
If you are deliberately maintaining sexual sin while expecting Jesus merely to keep forgiving what you have no intention of forsaking, Scripture calls you toward repentance, not comfort in rebellion.
Jesus is Savior.
And Jesus is Lord.
The same grace that welcomes the sinner begins transforming the sinner.
Sometimes transformation is dramatic.
Sometimes it is warfare measured one obedient day at a time.
Sometimes victory looks like walking away.
Sometimes it looks like calling someone before you fall.
Sometimes it looks like confessing to your spouse.
Sometimes it means seeking mature pastoral accountability or qualified professional help where compulsive behavior, trauma, or other serious issues are involved.
Sometimes it means installing barriers because you have finally stopped confusing access with freedom.
Sometimes it means sitting alone before God, shaking, ashamed, with nothing impressive left to say except:
“Jesus... have mercy on me.”
And that prayer is closer to freedom than a thousand excuses.
Because the Christian's hope was never:
I became strong enough.
Our hope is Christ.
You will never defeat sexual sin merely by hating yourself more.
Self-hatred cannot sanctify you.
You need truth.
You need repentance.
You need the Holy Spirit.
You need Scripture.
You need the body of Christ.
You need wise boundaries.
You need to learn to run before temptation becomes negotiation.
Above all, you need your heart increasingly captivated by Someone better than the counterfeit.
Because ultimately Christianity does not merely offer better behavior.
It offers Christ Himself.
Maybe you already fell.
Maybe it happened last night.
Maybe ten minutes before you found this article.
Maybe you feel filthy reading these words.
Then hear this without turning it into an excuse to sin again:
Run to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you've managed seven clean days.
Not when you feel worthy enough to pray.
Come now.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off what keeps dragging you backward.
Ask for help.
Bring the secret into appropriate, trustworthy light.
There is no spiritual prize for maintaining the appearance of holiness while privately bleeding to death.
And if you are thinking, But you don't understand what I've done...
Perhaps not.
But the cross was built for sinners, not people with impressive résumés.
Peter denied Jesus.
David's sexual sin shattered lives and brought devastating consequences.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
The Corinthian church contained people with histories Paul did not sanitize.
The Bible is scandalously unwilling to airbrush its people.
Yet Scripture is equally unwilling to let sin have the final word over everyone who comes to God through Christ.
That is our story.
Not because scandal becomes acceptable.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites condemned into justified.
Unclean into washed.
Far away into brought near.
Slave into free.
Enemy into reconciled.
Orphaned into adopted.
Dead into alive.
Not through positive thinking.
Not through pretending.
Through His blood.
Through His resurrection.
Through grace received by faith—a grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness and live under His lordship.
So when temptation comes again—and it may—remember what is actually at stake.
You are not merely deciding whether to click something.
You are practicing what you believe will satisfy you.
You are practicing whom you will obey.
You are practicing where you run when your soul aches.
And every time you run toward Christ instead of the counterfeit, even trembling, even tempted, even exhausted, you are declaring:
Jesus is better.

And if Christ has already begun healing a part of your life you once thought could never change, tell someone. Your testimony may become another wounded person's reason to believe that grace still reaches people like us.
Send it privately to the person who has been struggling in silence.

If you choose to support Gospel Warrior, you help us keep creating and sharing Christ-centered Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and Gospel resources with people who desperately need them.
But before you leave, remember this:
The sin that whispers your story is over has never held the pen—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE BIBLE’S GREATEST MARRIAGE STORY ISN’T REALLY ABOUT MARRIAGE?
paragraphs:
WHAT IF THE BIBLE’S GREATEST MARRIAGE STORY ISN’T REALLY ABOUT MARRIAGE?
From the loneliness of Eden to the wedding feast of the Lamb, Scripture tells one breathtaking story: a faithful Bridegroom pursuing a broken people—and a God who refuses to let sin write the final chapter.
There is a wedding at the beginning of the Bible.
And there is a wedding at the end.
That is not something to rush past.
Genesis opens with a man, a woman, a garden, and God.
Revelation moves toward a Bridegroom, a bride, a restored creation, and God dwelling with His people forever.
But between those two scenes?
Betrayal.
Shame.
Adultery.
Broken promises.
Nakedness.
Hiding.
Judgment.
Blood.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
And finally...
a wedding.
Once you see that thread running through Scripture, marriage becomes more than a subject Christians occasionally discuss.
It becomes one of the Bible’s most powerful pictures of covenant, faithfulness, human rebellion, sacrificial love, and the Gospel itself.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
The marriage story of Scripture does not merely reveal what God intended marriage to be.
It reveals what we have done to covenant—and what God has done about covenant-breakers like us.
The story begins before there is a church building, a pastor, a wedding ceremony, or even human sin.
God forms the man from the dust.
Then comes a sentence that should stop us because everything God has made until this moment has been declared good.
But suddenly God says:
לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ
Lo-tov heyot ha’adam levado.
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
—Genesis 2:18
God then creates the woman, and Adam responds with something resembling humanity’s first recorded love poem:
זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי
Zot happa‘am, etsem me‘atsamai uvasar mibbesari.
“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
—Genesis 2:23
Then Scripture gives us the pattern:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife...”
—Genesis 2:24
The Hebrew verb דָבַק — davaq carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, sticking closely.
Leave.
Cling.
Become one flesh.
And before shame enters the human story, Genesis gives us one final breathtaking picture:
“The man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.”
—Genesis 2:25
No hiding.
No masks.
No fear of being known.
No carefully edited version of themselves offered to the other.
Known...
and unashamed.
Then Genesis 3 happens.
And suddenly the people who were naked without shame are covering themselves.
The people created for fellowship are hiding from God.
The man blames the woman.
The woman points toward the serpent.
Sin does not merely break rules.
Sin fractures relationships.
With God.
With one another.
Even within ourselves.
And maybe that is why this story feels painfully modern.
We have become experts at covering ourselves.
Not with fig leaves.
With smiles.
Church attendance.
Carefully written captions.
Success.
Humor.
Busyness.
Relationships.
Ministry.
Money.
Religious vocabulary.
Some of us know exactly how to look spiritually alive while something inside us is starving.
You can sit beside your spouse and feel a thousand miles away.
You can worship with both hands raised while secretly carrying something you hope nobody discovers.
You can know Bible verses and still be terrified of being truly known.
You can tell everybody, “God is good,” while privately wondering why your heart feels so empty.
We inherited the instinct of Eden:
Hide.
But the astonishing thing about Genesis 3 is not simply that humanity hides.
It is that God comes looking.
“Where are you?”
—Genesis 3:9
God was not geographically confused.
The question exposes the tragedy.
Adam...
where have you gone?
And humanity has been running ever since.
That is where the Bible's marriage story becomes uncomfortable.
Because later, God repeatedly uses marriage and marital unfaithfulness as covenant imagery to describe His relationship with His people.
Israel receives covenant love...
and repeatedly runs toward other gods.
The prophets sometimes describe idolatry in deliberately shocking marital language.
Jeremiah speaks of covenant betrayal.
Ezekiel 16 uses severe imagery to expose Jerusalem’s unfaithfulness.
Hosea turns the metaphor into a heartbreaking lived sign.
God tells Hosea to marry Gomer.
Their household becomes a prophetic picture of Israel’s spiritual unfaithfulness.
And then comes one of the most astonishing promises in Hosea.
God speaks of restoring His people:
וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי לְעוֹלָם
Ve’erastikh li le‘olam.
“I will betroth you to me forever.”
Then:
וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי בֶּאֱמוּנָה
Ve’erastikh li be’emunah.
“I will betroth you to me in faithfulness.”
Read that again.
The scandal is not merely that God's people were unfaithful.
The scandal is the faithfulness of God toward people who had repeatedly betrayed covenant.
This does not mean Scripture trivializes betrayal, excuses abuse, eliminates consequences, or commands people to remain in dangerous situations.
It means something much larger in the prophetic story:
Human unfaithfulness does not make God unfaithful.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because eventually the marriage imagery moves toward Jesus.
John the Baptist speaks of Christ as the bridegroom in John 3:29.
Jesus uses bridegroom imagery of Himself in the Gospel tradition.
Then Paul says something extraordinary when teaching about Christian marriage.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25
The Greek word translated “love” is:
ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate
It is a form of ἀγαπάω — agapaō, “to love.”
But Paul does not leave that love undefined.
He immediately shows us what Christ-shaped love looks like:
ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς
“He gave himself up for her.”
Christian marital love therefore cannot legitimately be reduced to domination, entitlement, sentimentality, sexual attraction, or getting another human being to fulfill your desires.
Paul points to Jesus.
And Jesus gives Himself.
That changes everything.
Biblical marriage is not ultimately a stage upon which one person proves superiority over another.
In Ephesians 5, Christian marriage is pulled underneath the shadow of a cross.
Sacrifice.
Holiness.
Love.
Faithfulness.
Self-giving.
Christ.
Then Paul reaches Genesis itself:
“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”
—Ephesians 5:31
But the next sentence is staggering:
τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν
To mystērion touto mega estin.
“This mystery is profound...”
And then:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“...and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
—Ephesians 5:32
There it is.
Paul reaches all the way back to Genesis...
and then points forward to Christ.
Marriage matters deeply.
But marriage is not God.
Your spouse is not your savior.
Romance cannot carry the weight of redemption.
Marriage cannot forgive your sins.
Marriage cannot resurrect your dead heart.
Marriage cannot reconcile you to God.
And this also means an unmarried Christian is not living a spiritually incomplete version of Christianity.
Jesus Himself was unmarried.
Paul could speak positively about singleness in 1 Corinthians 7.
Our ultimate hope is therefore not “find the right person and live happily ever after.”
Our ultimate hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe you desperately wanted marriage and never received it.
Maybe you married and discovered that two wounded people do not magically become whole because they exchanged vows.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful.
Maybe it is strained.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe you were the one who betrayed someone.
Maybe divorce is part of your story.
Maybe widowhood left an empty chair nobody else understands.
Maybe you grew up watching a marriage collapse and quietly promised yourself you would never become your parents.
Maybe you carry sexual shame.
Maybe you have spent years trying to make another person satisfy a hunger that was deeper than romance from the beginning.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend those wounds are small.
But neither does the Gospel permit your wounds—or your sins—to become your final identity.
Because the Bible's marriage story keeps moving.
Jesus goes to a cross.
And this is where sentimental Christianity fails us.
The Bridegroom does not rescue His people with flowers.
He rescues them with His blood.
Paul writes:
Jesus does not merely tell sinners to clean themselves until they become worthy of Him.
He gives Himself.
At the cross, the sinless Christ bears sin.
The innocent One suffers for the guilty.
The One we rejected becomes the One through whom reconciliation with God is offered.
This is grace.
Not God pretending sin never mattered.
Grace is costly because sin mattered so much that redemption led to Calvary.
And if you have spent years hiding, perhaps this is the part you need to hear.
Jesus already knows.
The pornography.
The affair.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The bitterness.
The fantasies.
The coldness.
The lies.
The compromises nobody sees.
The spiritual numbness behind your worship songs.
He knows.
And the Gospel invitation is not:
Hide better.
It is:
Repent and come home.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance,” speaks of a changed mind and turning reflected in a changed direction of life.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Repentance turns toward God.
It stops defending darkness.
It brings sin into the light.
It agrees with God about what sin is.
It abandons the illusion that we can save ourselves.
And it runs toward the mercy offered in Jesus Christ.
This is why 1 John 1:9 remains such good news:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice the foundation.
He is faithful.
Our hope rests finally not upon the perfection of our grip on God...
but upon the faithfulness of the God who saves.
And then Scripture takes us somewhere breathtaking.
The Bible began with a marriage.
It approaches its conclusion with another.
Revelation 19 announces:
ἦλθεν ὁ γάμος τοῦ ἀρνίου
Ēlthen ho gamos tou arniou.
“The marriage of the Lamb has come.”
—Revelation 19:7
The Lamb.
That matters.
The Bridegroom at the wedding feast is the Lamb who was slain.
The scars of redemption stand behind the celebration.
And Revelation 21 speaks of the holy city prepared “as a bride adorned for her husband.”
Then comes the destination toward which the whole biblical story has been moving:
“Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.”
—Revelation 21:3
Do you see it?
Genesis:
God with humanity.
Sin:
humanity hiding from God.
The prophets:
a covenant people repeatedly wandering from God.
The Gospel:
God comes to us in Jesus Christ.
The cross:
Christ gives Himself for His people.
Resurrection:
death does not win.
Revelation:
God dwells with His redeemed people forever.
The Bible's marriage story reveals something enormous about God.
He is faithful.
Human beings break covenant.
God remains faithful to His character.
Human beings hide.
God calls.
Human beings wander.
God pursues according to His covenant mercy.
Human beings sin.
Christ saves sinners who turn to Him.
Human beings create scandals.
Grace writes endings nobody deserved.
And maybe now you understand why the phrase matters so much:
Because Scripture is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Adam fell.
Abraham failed.
Jacob deceived.
Judah sinned scandalously.
David committed terrible evil.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet grace did not mean their sins suddenly became righteous.
Grace meant sin did not have to possess the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why the deepest question this article asks is not:
“How healthy is your marriage?”
It is not even:
“Will you ever get married?”
The deeper question is:
Are you reconciled to the Bridegroom?
You can have a beautiful wedding and an empty soul.
You can stay married for fifty years and never surrender your heart to Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
You can defend biblical marriage publicly while privately resisting the Lord to whom marriage ultimately points.
And you can be unmarried, widowed, divorced, abandoned, or carrying a relational history you wish you could erase...
and still belong completely to Jesus Christ through faith.
Your relationship status is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
So stop hiding.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Not after you fix yourself.
Come honestly.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Where reconciliation with people is biblically appropriate and safe, pursue truth, repentance, forgiveness, accountability, and restoration.
But above everything else...
come to Christ.
Because the greatest love story in Scripture is not about flawless human beings finally learning how to love perfectly.
It is about the faithful Christ giving Himself for people who desperately needed grace.
Bring it to Jesus.
There may be someone reading the comments tonight who thought they were the only one still fighting.
Your honesty may remind another wounded believer that repentance is not the end of hope.
It may be where restoration begins.

And if you know somebody whose marriage is struggling, somebody who feels disqualified because of their past, somebody drowning in shame, somebody afraid they have wandered too far from God, or somebody who has mistaken romance for salvation...
send them this.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor, proving that you glorify God, or earning spiritual blessing. Salvation is God's gift of grace, not something anyone buys.
But generosity and voluntary support can genuinely help Christian teaching and Gospel-centered resources reach more people.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has stopped going to church.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person rebuilding after failure.
Invite the person who doesn't believe yet but is willing to listen.
to Jesus.
And before you leave, remember this:

The enemy wants your scandal to become your name. Jesus calls repentant sinners out of hiding, washes what shame could never clean, and proves that your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
The Bible begins with a marriage.
It ends looking toward a wedding.
And standing at the center of everything is Jesus Christ—
the crucified Lamb,
the risen Lord,
the faithful Bridegroom,
and the Savior of sinners.
Come out of hiding.
The story is not over.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WAS INCEST HAPPENING INSIDE THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH?
paragraphs:
WHY WAS INCEST HAPPENING INSIDE THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH?
The scandal was horrifying. But what Paul confronted next may be even more frightening—because the greatest danger was not simply what one man was doing in secret, but what an entire church had learned to tolerate in the name of belonging.
Imagine walking into church on Sunday.
People are talking.
Someone is praying.
Someone is quoting Scripture.
Someone is probably convinced that this congregation understands grace better than everybody else.
And somewhere in that gathering sits a man whose relationship has become so scandalous that Paul says even the surrounding pagan culture would recognize something was terribly wrong.
Yet the church is still functioning.
People are still gathering.
People are still talking about spiritual things.
And apparently, somehow, they have learned to live with it.
Then a letter arrives.
Paul has heard.
And the opening words of 1 Corinthians 5 land like a thunderclap:
“Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία…”
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you…”
Then Paul becomes painfully specific.
“…ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.”
…hōste gynaika tina tou patros echein.
Literally, the horrifying situation involved a man “having” his father’s wife.
Paul does not say “his mother.”
He says “his father’s wife.”
That distinction matters.

The wording most naturally suggests that the woman was the man’s stepmother, although Paul does not give us enough information to reconstruct every detail of the relationship. We are not told whether the father was dead, divorced, separated, or otherwise absent from the situation. Scripture does not tell us, so we should not pretend that it does.
But Scripture tells us enough.
This relationship violated a boundary God had already made unmistakably clear.

Leviticus 18:8 forbade uncovering the nakedness of one’s father’s wife. Leviticus 20:11 condemns sexual relations with one’s father’s wife. Deuteronomy 27:20 pronounces a curse upon the one who lies with his father’s wife because he has dishonored his father’s bed.
Paul was not inventing a new Christian sexual ethic because Corinth made him uncomfortable.
He was confronting behavior that stood against the moral boundaries already revealed in Scripture.
And there is something else we need to understand before turning Corinth into a convenient story about “those terrible ancient people.”
Paul's Greek word is πορνεία—porneia.
Sexual immorality.
But Paul's outrage is not directed only toward the man committing it.
Read the next sentence and suddenly the spotlight moves.
“And you are proud!”
That is where this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because Paul does not merely ask:
How could this man do this?
Paul effectively asks:
How could the church become comfortable while this was happening?
That question survived Corinth.
It walked through twenty centuries of church history.
And now it is standing in front of us.
Because the terrifying lesson of Corinth is not simply that terrible sin can enter a church.
We already know that.
Churches are filled with sinners because there is no other kind of human being available.
The terrifying lesson is that people can become so confused about grace, freedom, love, acceptance, status, spirituality, or tolerance that they stop grieving over what is destroying someone.
There is a difference between welcoming sinners and celebrating bondage.
There is a difference between showing mercy and renaming darkness.
There is a difference between refusing self-righteous condemnation and refusing biblical discernment.
Jesus ate with sinners.
Jesus loved sinners.
Jesus touched people religious society avoided.
Jesus defended the broken.
Jesus received the ashamed.
And Jesus called people to repentance.
Those truths do not fight each other.
They meet at the cross.
That is where Corinth had to be brought.
And that is where we have to be brought too.
Because perhaps the question beneath the scandal is not merely, “Why was incest happening inside the Corinthian church?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
Why had the church stopped mourning?
Paul tells them they should have grieved.
That word changes the atmosphere completely.
Christian holiness is not supposed to sound like a mob celebrating the destruction of somebody caught in sin.
It sounds like mourning.
It sounds like a family watching someone they love walk toward a cliff.
It sounds like tears.
It sounds like, “Brother, this is killing you.”
It sounds like, “Sister, Jesus has something better than this.”
It sounds like someone loving you enough to refuse to applaud while chains are wrapping themselves around your soul.
Biblical correction without love becomes cruelty.
But what our generation desperately needs to understand is that love without truth can become cruelty too.
If someone is walking toward destruction, silence is not always kindness.
Sometimes silence is abandonment wearing a smile.
And Corinth had apparently become dangerously comfortable.
Paul writes:
Then he gives them an image almost anybody in the ancient world could understand.
A little leaven works through the whole lump.
Sin rarely stays politely inside the boundaries we assign to it.
What we excuse begins teaching us.
What we repeatedly tolerate begins reshaping our conscience.
What once made us tremble eventually becomes ordinary.
The first compromise feels enormous.
The fiftieth barely registers.
That is how spiritual numbness works.
Nobody usually wakes up one morning and announces, “Today I will destroy my conscience.”
It happens slowly.
One justification.
One hidden browser window.
One secret conversation.
One flirtation.
One dishonest transaction.
One bitterness we refuse to surrender.
One addiction we keep renaming.
One relationship we know dishonors Christ but cannot imagine releasing.
One compromise followed by another.
And eventually we become capable of sitting peacefully beside something that once would have driven us to our knees.
Maybe that is why this chapter makes us uncomfortable.
We want to stare at Corinth's scandal.
Paul wants us to examine our own tolerance.
You may never commit the particular sin described in 1 Corinthians 5.
But you can still become Corinthian in the way you protect the thing Jesus is asking you to surrender.
