We all know how to rename our favorite sins.
Greed becomes ambition.
Gossip becomes concern.
Lust becomes loneliness.
Bitterness becomes discernment.
Pride becomes confidence.
Cowardice becomes keeping the peace.
Materialism becomes “God's blessing.”
Unforgiveness becomes boundaries even when what we actually mean is revenge.
Compromise becomes complexity.
And sometimes rebellion simply becomes, “God understands.”
Yes.
God understands.
Far more deeply than we do.
He understands the wound beneath the behavior.
He understands the loneliness.
He understands the childhood.
He understands the trauma.
He understands the temptation.
He understands the nights nobody saw.
He understands why you reached for something that promised relief.
He understands every tear.
Every failure.
Every rationalization.
Every relapse.
Every secret.
And because He understands completely, He also understands exactly what that sin is doing to you.
Grace does not mean God finally decides sin does not matter.
Grace means sin mattered so much that Jesus Christ carried its judgment upon Himself so sinners could be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and transformed.
That is why Paul's response to Corinth sounds severe.
He commands the church to remove the unrepentant man from their fellowship.
But even here, the purpose is not merely humiliation.
Paul's stated horizon is ultimately redemptive: “…so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”
Do not miss that.
Even discipline has salvation in view.
Even confrontation has restoration in view.
Even the painful removal of false security is meant to awaken someone before destruction becomes permanent.
Biblical church discipline is not supposed to be revenge.
It is not entertainment.
It is not gossip dressed like discernment.
It is not an opportunity for spiritually proud people to feel cleaner because somebody else's sin became public.
It is a desperate refusal to tell someone that everything is fine when everything is not fine.
Because Jesus loves sinners too much to make peace with the thing enslaving them.
And then Paul does something breathtaking.
In the middle of a chapter about sexual scandal, discipline, corruption, and judgment, he suddenly points toward a Lamb.
“For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”
There.
That is the center.
Not Corinth.
Not incest.
Not scandal.
Christ.
The answer to human corruption is not merely stronger embarrassment.
The answer is Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
Our Passover Lamb has been sacrificed.
The blood has been shed.
The price has been paid.
The door of mercy is open.
And that means the person reading this with a secret does not need to run farther into darkness.
You can come home.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been doing.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
Maybe you lead.
Maybe you preach.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe you post Bible verses while fighting something privately that would shock the people who follow you.
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
But heaven does not need screenshots.
God already knows.
And strangely enough, that may be the most comforting sentence you read today.
God already knows.
And He is still calling you.
Not toward excuses.
Toward repentance.
Not toward hiding.
Toward light.
Not toward pretending.
Toward confession.
Not toward self-destruction.
Toward Christ.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside your locked room waiting for you to clean everything before He enters.
The Gospel is Jesus coming for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
But when grace finds us, grace does not leave us chained to the same grave.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace finally convinces us that coming home is better than staying hidden.
Maybe this article stopped being about an unnamed man in ancient Corinth several paragraphs ago.
Maybe now it is about you.
The affair nobody knows about.
The pornography.
The secret messages.
The hatred.
The money.
The dishonesty.
The double life.
The addiction.
The relationship.
The compromise.
The pride.
The resentment you feed whenever their name appears.
The private version of yourself you desperately hope never becomes public.
Listen carefully.
Your greatest danger may not be that somebody discovers your scandal.
Your greatest danger may be becoming comfortable enough with it that you no longer want freedom.
That is what makes Corinth frightening.
They had apparently learned to coexist with what should have made them mourn.
Do not wait until your chains feel normal.
Bring them to Jesus.
Not because you are beyond grace.
Because grace is exactly why you can stop hiding.
There is no repentance so deep that Christ's mercy becomes shallow.
There is no confession that surprises the One who already carried our sins to Calvary.
There is no stain that becomes stronger than the blood of Christ.
But grace must never become permission to protect what nailed our Savior to the cross.
Grace opens the prison door.
Repentance walks out.
And Jesus calls us into freedom.
So perhaps you need to do something after reading this.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you feel more spiritual.
Today.
Tell God the truth.
If another person needs to know, seek wise, biblically faithful help and bring what has been hidden into appropriate light.
If someone has been harmed, repentance includes taking responsibility rather than manipulating them into instant reconciliation.
If you need pastoral accountability, pursue it.
If you are trapped in habitual sexual sin, stop treating isolation as strength.

And if what happened to you involved abuse, coercion, exploitation, or victimization, understand this clearly: being sinned against is not the same thing as committing the sin described in 1 Corinthians 5. Do not carry another person's guilt as though it were yours.
The cross exposes evil without confusing the wounded with the one who wounded them.
And the cross offers mercy to sinners who truly turn to Christ.
That is the strange beauty hidden inside this horrifying chapter.
Scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Peter's denial did not write his final sentence.
The Samaritan woman's past did not write hers.
The thief's crimes did not get the last word beside the cross.
Paul's persecution of Christians did not become the final chapter of his life.
And your worst chapter does not have authority to finish your story if your story is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
From scandal...
to confession.
From confession...
to repentance.
From repentance...
to grace.
From grace...
to restoration.
From restoration...
to a life that becomes evidence that Jesus still rewrites people.
Maybe someone you know is hiding right now.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks failure means Jesus no longer wants them.
And if this exposed something hidden, you do not owe strangers the intimate details of your life. But you can simply comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There are people reading who need to discover that they are not the only ones fighting.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture outrage.
Not to build a platform around other people's failures.
But to keep bringing wounded, wandering, compromised, hungry people back to Scripture...
back to repentance...
back to grace...
back to the cross...
back to Jesus Christ.
We glorify God ultimately through lives surrendered to Christ.

If you want deeper biblical nourishment, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, accountability, and Christ-centered teaching that refuses both loveless condemnation and comfortable compromise, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
Invite the person whose life looks perfect online and is collapsing behind the screen.
Because somewhere tonight, someone may be staring at a secret and wondering whether their story is already over.
Tell them it isn't.
Tell them Corinth was scandalous.
Tell them the church had failed.
Tell them sin was confronted.
Tell them repentance mattered.
Tell them grace was not cheap.
Tell them Christ had been sacrificed.
Tell them there is still a road home.
And before you leave this page, remember the sentence the enemy desperately hopes you will forget:
Your scandal may explain the chapter you are standing in, but surrendered to Christ, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A JEALOUS HUSBAND, A SUSPECTED AFFAIR, AND BITTER WATER: Numbers 5 Explained
paragraphs:
A JEALOUS HUSBAND, A SUSPECTED AFFAIR, AND BITTER WATER: Numbers 5 Explained
She stood before the priest accused of a secret nobody could prove. Then came the dust, the oath, and the bitter water. But what Numbers 5 actually says may be far more unsettling—and far more revealing—than the version you have heard.
Imagine being accused of something that happened where nobody could see.
No eyewitness.
No courtroom evidence.
No confession.
Only suspicion.
Your husband believes something happened.
Maybe he is right.
Maybe he is terribly wrong.
And now the accusation has entered your marriage like smoke under a locked door.
You cannot simply wave it away.
He cannot prove it.
You cannot make him unknow his suspicion.
Trust is bleeding out, and nobody knows how to stop it.
Then you are brought before the priest.
Not merely before your husband.
Not before neighborhood gossip.
Not before a furious mob.
Before the LORD.
That is where one of the strangest passages in the Bible begins.

Numbers 5:11–31 has disturbed readers for centuries. Some have called it barbaric. Some claim it describes an abortion ritual. Others race through the passage so quickly that they never allow themselves to feel how frightening the scene actually is.
But if we are going to defend Scripture, we must not defend something Scripture never said.
And if we are going to understand Scripture, we cannot sanitize something merely because it makes us uncomfortable.
We have to stand inside the tension.
The Hebrew text introduces a situation in which a wife may have been sexually unfaithful, but there is no witness and she has not been caught.
Then comes this expression:
רוּחַ־קִנְאָה — ruaḥ qin'ah
Literally, a “spirit of jealousy.”

Numbers 5:14 deliberately presents two possibilities: the husband's jealousy arises and his wife has been defiled—or his jealousy arises and she has not been defiled. In other words, his suspicion itself is not treated as proof.
That matters.
A jealous husband does not automatically become judge, jury, and executioner.
His feelings do not establish reality.
His suspicion does not become truth merely because he feels it intensely.
The unresolved case is taken out of his hands and brought into a prescribed ritual before God.

The priest takes holy water in an earthen vessel and places dust from the floor of the tabernacle into it. The woman is placed before the LORD. An offering is involved. An oath is spoken. The written curses are washed into what Scripture calls:
מֵי הַמָּרִים הַמְאָרֲרִים — mei hammārîm ham'ārărîm
The bitter waters that bring the curse.
The woman answers:
אָמֵן אָמֵן — amen, amen.
Then she drinks.
It is one of those biblical scenes that refuses to become comfortable.
But notice something easily missed.
The water is not presented as an ordinary poison whose chemistry exposes adultery.
Holy water.
Dust.
Written words washed into the water.
None of those ingredients naturally possesses the ability to determine whether someone secretly committed adultery.
The outcome is placed in God's judgment.

That is crucial to understanding the ordeal. Scholarly discussion of the passage commonly recognizes it as a trial or ordeal intended to resolve a charge for which ordinary evidence was unavailable. The text itself repeatedly places the woman “before the LORD.”
And then we reach the words that have generated enormous controversy.
Numbers 5:21–22 contains the Hebrew:
בְּתֵת יְהוָה אֶת־יְרֵכֵךְ נֹפֶלֶת וְאֶת־בִּטְנֵךְ צָבָה
And shortly afterward:
לַצְבּוֹת בֶּטֶן וְלַנְפִּל יָרֵךְ
The difficulty is that the anatomical language is unusual.
בֶּטֶן — beten refers to the belly, abdomen, or womb region depending upon context.
יָרֵךְ — yarekh literally means “thigh,” but biblical Hebrew can also use the term in connection with the reproductive or genital region.
The passage therefore describes a severe bodily judgment involving the abdomen and “thigh,” but exactly what medical condition the ancient language denotes is debated.

Traditional translations speak of the belly swelling and the thigh falling or wasting away. Some modern interpretations understand the expressions as reproductive catastrophe; proposals have included miscarriage, infertility, uterine prolapse, or other gynecological consequences. Scholarly literature itself reflects that uncertainty. One Society of Biblical Literature discussion, for example, notes both a possible miscarriage interpretation and an argument for uterine prolapse.
That means Christians should be careful with a popular internet claim:
“Numbers 5 is obviously instructions for performing an abortion.”
That statement goes beyond what the Hebrew securely establishes.
The passage never says that the woman is pregnant.
It never identifies a fetus.
It never commands the priest to terminate a pregnancy.
And Numbers 5:28 says that if the woman is innocent:
וְנִקְּתָה וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע — weniqqetah wenizre'ah zara'
She will be free from the curse and “shall conceive seed,” or, more literally, “shall be sown with seed.”
The Hebrew therefore places fertility directly within the contrast between judgment and vindication.
Could the judgment described in the preceding verses have involved reproductive devastation? Quite possibly.
Can we responsibly pretend every linguistic question has been solved? No.
Biblical faithfulness does not require pretending difficult Hebrew is easy.
Sometimes honoring God's Word means saying, “The text clearly tells us this much—and beyond this point interpreters disagree.”
But perhaps an even bigger question is waiting underneath all of this.
Why is this disturbing ritual here at all?
Because secret sin creates a human problem.
What happens when something may have happened...
but nobody can prove it?
Think about the alternatives in an ancient society.
Private vengeance.
Violence.
Endless accusation.
Public humiliation based solely upon suspicion.
A husband taking punishment into his own hands.
Instead, the Torah establishes boundaries around the accusation and transfers ultimate judgment away from the jealous husband.
The woman is not simply condemned because he suspects her.
The text explicitly allows for the possibility that she is innocent.
“If the woman has not defiled herself and is clean,” Numbers 5:28 says, she escapes the curse.
Her husband's jealousy does not determine her guilt.
God does.
That does not make every feature of this ancient ritual emotionally comfortable to modern readers. Nor should we pretend the social world behind Numbers was identical to ours.
But understanding a difficult text requires asking what it actually did within its own covenantal world before importing twenty-first-century categories into it.
And then something happens when Christians keep reading the Bible.
The scene begins to echo.
A woman.
Accusation.
Sexual sin.
Public exposure.
Judgment hanging in the air.
And eventually, centuries later, another woman would stand exposed before Jesus.
John 8 describes a woman caught in adultery being brought publicly before Christ.
This time there were accusers everywhere.
They wanted judgment.
They wanted Jesus trapped.
And Jesus did something astonishing.
He did not announce that adultery was harmless.
He did not rename sin so nobody would feel uncomfortable.
He did not say holiness no longer mattered.
After her accusers departed, He told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Grace...
and repentance.
Mercy...
and holiness.
No condemnation from Christ...
and no permission to continue living in sin.
That is the Gospel pattern so many of us desperately need.
Because maybe you have never stood before a priest holding bitter water.
But you know what it is like to stand before God carrying something bitter.
Maybe the secret was yours.
Maybe the betrayal was yours.
Maybe you crossed a line nobody knows about.
Maybe your spouse still doesn't know.
Maybe your church friends would never imagine it.
Maybe your browser history knows a version of you that your Sunday clothes conceal.
Maybe there are messages you deleted because you knew exactly what they meant.
Maybe you keep calling it friendship because admitting emotional adultery would force you to confront what your heart has already done.
Maybe nothing physical happened.
But you wanted it to.
And Jesus said that lust is not spiritually insignificant simply because nobody touched anybody.
Or perhaps you are standing on the other side.
You were betrayed.
Someone made promises before God and shattered them in secret.
Now every late reply feels suspicious.
Every unfamiliar name becomes a threat.
Every unexplained absence reopens the wound.
You hate what jealousy is turning you into, but betrayal taught your nervous system to expect another knife.
Numbers 5 understands something modern people sometimes pretend not to understand:
Hidden sexual betrayal can poison a covenant.
But suspicion can poison one too.
That is why truth matters.
That is why God refuses to call guilt innocence.
And why human suspicion must never masquerade as omniscience.
Only God sees the room nobody else entered.
Only God heard the conversation nobody recorded.
Only God knows whether “nothing happened” really means nothing happened.
Only God sees what was deleted.
Only God knows whether your heart is clean.
And that realization should frighten the hypocrite...
but strangely comfort the falsely accused.
Because the God who sees hidden guilt also sees hidden innocence.
People may misunderstand you.
Rumors may survive your explanations.
Someone may construct an entire story about you from fragments.
You may never persuade everybody.
But human suspicion does not become divine knowledge simply because it is repeated loudly.
God knows.
There is another truth, though.
If you actually are guilty, God knows that too.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
We love the idea of an all-seeing God when we have been falsely accused.
We become much less comfortable with an all-seeing God when we are hiding something.
We want Him to see their betrayal...
and overlook ours.
See their lies...
but not ours.
Expose their hypocrisy...
while protecting our reputation.
But the Gospel does not offer reputation management.
It offers resurrection.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people appear innocent.
He came to save sinners.
There is an enormous difference.
At the cross, God does not shrug at sin.
He demonstrates just how serious sin is.
Christ bears judgment.
The innocent One suffers for the guilty.
The sinless Son of God takes what sinners could never remove from themselves.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:21 that God made the One who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Peter says Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Do you see it?
Numbers 5 brings an unresolved accusation before God because human beings cannot see the hidden truth.
The Gospel announces that God has seen the hidden truth about all of us...
and Christ came anyway.
He saw the affair.
He saw the fantasy.
He saw the lie.
He saw the pornography.
He saw the secret conversation.
He saw the resentment.
He saw the self-righteousness.
He saw the jealousy.
He saw what happened behind the closed door.
He saw what happened only inside your heart.
And still the Son of God went to the cross.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because it mattered enough to require blood.
And because you mattered enough for Christ willingly to shed His.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the scandal never happened.
God writing redemption where scandal appeared to have written the final sentence.
Maybe that is why this strange chapter can reach deeper than arguments about ancient ritual.
Eventually the bitter water asks something of us.
Not literally.
Spiritually.
What truth about yourself are you terrified to place before God?
What would happen if you stopped defending yourself long enough to confess?
What if repentance is not God waiting to humiliate you...
but Christ calling you out of the prison you have exhausted yourself trying to decorate?
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
That does not erase earthly consequences.
Forgiveness does not magically rebuild trust overnight.
A betrayed marriage may need years of truth, counsel, accountability, patience, boundaries, and healing.
Repentance is not merely crying because you were caught.
It is turning.
Grace is free, but grace is not permission to keep returning to the darkness Christ died to rescue you from.
So if this article exposed something you have hidden, don't merely feel emotional for thirty seconds and keep scrolling.
Talk to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows it.
Repent.
Come into the light.
And if you have trusted Christ, remember what the cross means: your ugliest chapter does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is not a slogan about pretending scandals are beautiful.
Scandal destroys.
Sin wounds.
Adultery devastates.
Jealousy can consume.
False accusations can crush innocent people.
But Jesus Christ is still in the business of taking human stories that appear irredeemable and writing something sin could never write on its own:
Redemption.
If you are reading this with tears you did not expect, be honest.
And if you are not ready to explain everything publicly, even three words can become your confession:
“No more hiding.”
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only Christian still fighting for healing.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Not as a performance of spirituality.
He redeems broken ones.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the person who does not yet believe—to follow too.

Supporting Gospel work is one practical way you can help truth travel farther, but supporting this particular ministry is not a biblical requirement for glorifying God. Scripture calls believers to glorify God with their whole lives, including generosity, service, witness, obedience, and love.
Because somewhere behind another glowing screen may be a husband consumed by suspicion.
A wife carrying betrayal.
A believer hiding sexual sin.
A falsely accused person wondering whether God knows the truth.
A Christian convinced their worst chapter disqualified them forever.
Or a sinner who has never understood why Jesus had to die.
Send it to them.
Not because an article can save anybody.
It cannot.
Jesus can.
And perhaps the sentence they cannot escape tonight will be this:
The God who knows what happened behind the closed door is the same God who opened the door of grace through the blood of Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DANIEL REFUSED THE KING’S FOOD BEFORE HE EVER ENTERED THE LIONS’ DEN
paragraphs: DANIEL REFUSED THE KING’S FOOD BEFORE HE EVER ENTERED THE LIONS’ DEN
Everyone remembers the lions. Almost nobody remembers the dinner table where Daniel first learned how to say no.
There is something terrifying about a room full of lions.
But there is something spiritually dangerous about a table where nothing looks dangerous at all.
No roaring.
No claws.
No execution order.
Just food.
Comfort.
Opportunity.
A seat at the table of the most powerful empire on earth.
And a quiet decision nobody would have blamed Daniel for making.
That may be why the beginning of Daniel’s story deserves another look.
Because long before Daniel stood above a den filled with lions, he sat before the food of a king.
And before he ever had to decide whether God was worth dying for, he had already begun deciding whether God was worth living differently for.
That changes the story.
We love Daniel 6 because it is dramatic.
A jealous conspiracy. An irreversible decree. An open window. A praying man. An angry king. A sealed stone. Hungry lions. An angel. Morning light.
But Daniel did not suddenly become Daniel when somebody threatened him with lions.
By Daniel 6, Scripture says that when he learned the decree had been signed, he went home, knelt three times a day, prayed, and gave thanks to God “as he did aforetime” (Daniel 6:10, KJV).
Those words matter.
“As he did aforetime.”
Daniel did not manufacture courage for the crisis.
The crisis revealed the man his private choices had already formed.
And if you trace that faithfulness backward through his life, eventually you arrive somewhere much less spectacular.
A table.
Daniel was probably still a young man when Babylon tore his world apart.
Jerusalem had been attacked. Sacred vessels from the house of God were carried into the land of Shinar. Daniel and other young Judeans were taken into the machinery of Babylonian imperial life.
Then came something subtler than chains.
Reeducation.
New literature.
A new language.
Royal service.
Even new names.
Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah were given Babylonian names (Daniel 1:6–7).
Babylon was not merely changing where these young men lived.
It was attempting to reshape the world in which they understood themselves.
Then the king assigned provisions from his own food and wine.
And here Scripture slows down.
Daniel 1:8 begins in Hebrew:
וַיָּשֶׂם דָּנִיֵּאל עַל־לִבּוֹ אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יִתְגָּאַל
Vayyāśem Dāniyyēl ʿal-libbo ʾăšer lō-yitgaʾal...
The sense is:
Daniel set it upon his heart that he would not defile himself.
Read that again.
He set it upon his heart.
The Hebrew verb associated here with defilement is from גָּאַל (ga'al), carrying the idea in this context of becoming defiled or polluted.
The text does not present Daniel stumbling accidentally into conviction.
Something had already been settled inside him.
Before the confrontation came, the heart had decided whom it belonged to.

Scripture does not explicitly tell us every reason Daniel regarded the royal provisions as defiling. Interpreters have proposed concerns involving Israel’s dietary laws, food associated with pagan worship, the wine, or identification with the king’s table. We should not pretend the text specifies what it does not specify.
What Scripture does tell us is enough:
“Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself” (Daniel 1:8).
And perhaps that is exactly where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because most of us will never be lowered into a literal lions’ den.
But almost everybody eventually sits at a Babylonian table.
It may be a relationship you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
A private browser window.
A compromise at work.
Money nobody would know you took.
A conversation where joining the gossip would make you belong.
A secret addiction protected by a respectable public life.
A bitterness you have fed so long that you have begun calling it discernment.
A sexual compromise everybody around you says is normal.
A dishonest number you could change and probably never get caught changing.
A prayer life that disappeared gradually because scrolling became easier than seeking God.
Nobody is threatening to kill you.
Nobody is demanding that you renounce Jesus publicly.
There are no lions.
Just a table.
And that is precisely why the table can be so dangerous.
Some compromises arrive screaming.
Others arrive beautifully plated.
Daniel's first recorded stand in Babylon was not spectacular.
He simply refused to let Babylon decide what faithfulness meant.
And notice something else.
Daniel was not obnoxious about it.
He did not confuse holiness with hostility.
Daniel 1:8 says he requested permission from the chief official not to defile himself.
Conviction did not make him arrogant.
Faithfulness did not require cruelty.
Holiness did not become an excuse for self-righteousness.
Daniel could resist Babylon without becoming Babylonian in spirit.
There is a lesson there for Christians who believe that courage must always sound angry.
Sometimes courage sounds like a respectful no.
Sometimes holiness whispers.
Sometimes the strongest person in the room is the one who does not need everybody else to know how strong he is.

Daniel asked for a test involving vegetables and water. After the appointed period, Daniel and his companions appeared healthy, and Scripture ultimately credits God—not a magical diet—with giving these young men knowledge and understanding (Daniel 1:12–17).
That distinction matters.
Daniel 1 is not primarily a biblical weight-loss program.
It is a story about allegiance.
And behind Daniel's faithfulness stands something even greater:
God's faithfulness.
Daniel had lost Jerusalem.
But he had not lost God.
He had lost the familiar structures of home.
But God had not lost him.
Babylon could change Daniel's address.
Babylon could change his curriculum.
Babylon could give him another name.
Babylon could place royal food in front of him.
But Babylon could not own the heart Daniel had entrusted to God.
Years passed.
Kings changed.
Empires shifted.
Daniel grew older.
And eventually the table became a den.

By Daniel 6, enemies who wanted to destroy Daniel encountered an irritating problem: they could not find corruption in his administration. Scripture describes him as faithful and says they could find no error or fault in him concerning his work (Daniel 6:4).
Think about the continuity.
Daniel 1:
A private conviction about defilement.
Daniel 6:
A public reputation for faithfulness.
That does not happen accidentally.
Then Daniel's enemies discovered the one place where they knew he would never negotiate.
His God.
They persuaded King Darius to establish a decree forbidding petitions to any god or man except the king for thirty days.
Daniel knew the decree had been signed.
He knew what violation meant.
And then he went home.
No theatrical rebellion.
No manufactured spectacle.
No social-media announcement about how persecuted he was.
He opened his windows toward Jerusalem.
He knelt.
He prayed.
He gave thanks.
Just as he had done before.
That may be one of the most devastating details in the entire account.
The government changed the law.
Daniel did not change his prayer life.
The threat became extraordinary.
Daniel remained ordinary.
He simply continued being faithful.
Because when you have practiced surrender in places where nobody applauds, you do not have to invent faith when everybody is watching.
The lions' den did not create Daniel's faithfulness.
It exposed it.
The decree did not create his prayer life.
It revealed it.
The danger did not create his convictions.
It tested convictions formed long before the danger arrived.
The young man who could say no to the king's food became the older man who could say no to the king's decree.
There is a frightening question hiding here for every one of us:
What are your small decisions turning you into?
Not what do you claim to believe.
Not what does your Facebook bio say.
Not what Christian content do you repost.
Not what church do you attend.
What are your repeated private decisions turning you into?
Because there may come a day when you desperately want Daniel's courage in the lions' den...
while having spent years refusing Daniel's discipline at the table.
We want lion-den faith with banquet-table compromise.
We want public courage without private surrender.
We want to stand when persecution comes while repeatedly kneeling before temptations that come with no consequences at all.
But faithfulness is usually built in ordinary rooms.
When nobody is watching.
When nobody will praise you.
When compromising would make life easier.
When obedience costs something small enough that you can easily convince yourself it does not matter.
That is where character is being formed.
And maybe this article is reaching you at your table.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been wrestling with.
Maybe your spiritual life looks healthier from the outside than it feels from inside your own heart.
Maybe you love Jesus, but something has slowly occupied territory in you that belongs to Him.
And perhaps you keep telling yourself:
It's only this once.
It's not hurting anybody.
God understands.
Everybody struggles.
I'll stop eventually.
I'll repent later.
But hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people successfully resist every temptation.
If that were Christianity, none of us would survive it.
Daniel's faithfulness should convict us, but Daniel is not our Savior.
Jesus is.
And this is where the story must travel beyond Babylon.
Because eventually another faithful Man stood before earthly power.
Jesus Christ.
He too was tempted.
He too refused to exchange obedience for comfort.
He too faced political and religious powers.
He too remained faithful unto death.
But unlike Daniel, Jesus was not rescued from death.
He entered it.
The innocent Christ was condemned.
Mocked.
Struck.
Crucified.
His body was laid in a tomb.
A stone was placed at its entrance.
And then came the morning when death discovered that it could not keep the Son of God.
Daniel came out of the lions' den alive.
Jesus came out of the grave victorious.
That is not a minor connection.
That is where Christian hope ultimately rests.
Your salvation does not depend upon becoming courageous enough to impress God.
It depends upon Christ.
The One who obeyed where we have failed.
The One who bore sin at the cross.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls sinners not merely to admire holiness but to repent, believe, receive mercy, and follow Him.
Maybe you failed at the table.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe you knew better and did it anyway.
Maybe the secret is not theoretical.
Maybe while reading this, a name came into your mind.
A website.
A habit.
A bottle.
A conversation.
A lie.
A hidden relationship.
A grudge.
A compromise.
And suddenly this is not an article about Daniel anymore.
It is about you.
Listen.
Your failure does not have to become the final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
The prodigal walked home and found the father running toward him.
Paul carried a history of persecuting Christians and became a servant of the Christ he once opposed.
The cross exists because sin is serious.
And the cross proves that grace is greater than the scandal of the repentant sinner who comes to Christ.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not renaming sin so nobody feels uncomfortable.
Not hiding what darkness did.
But bringing the truth into the light and discovering that Jesus Christ is still in the business of redeeming people.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your next lions' den is years away.
Maybe it never comes.
But your table may already be in front of you.
And the question is not whether vegetables are holier than royal food.
The question is:
Who owns your heart?
There are decisions you make today that nobody will remember tomorrow but that may quietly shape the person you become ten years from now.
Every private prayer matters.
Every temptation resisted by the grace of God matters.
Every confession matters.
Every act of repentance matters.
Every time you close the door on sin and turn toward Christ, something is happening inside you.
Not earning salvation.
Not purchasing God's love.
But learning obedience as someone who belongs to Jesus.
So do not wait for lions before deciding what you believe.
Settle some things at the table.
Settle who your King is.
Settle where your identity comes from.
Settle whether Scripture or culture gets the final word.
Settle whether applause is worth disobedience.
Settle whether temporary pleasure is worth starving your soul.
And when you fail—and every Christian still needs grace—do not run farther into hiding.
Run to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Get back up.
Follow Him again.
Somebody reading this may be exhausted from pretending.
But you also do not have to keep hiding.
And if Christ has already brought you through a season you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reminder not to quit.
Then think of one person sitting at a table of compromise right now.
You know who they are.
Maybe they are smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Maybe they stopped attending church.
Maybe they still attend but their heart has wandered miles away.
Maybe they do not even believe in Jesus yet.
Send this privately if that would serve them better.
Because someday the temptation may not look dangerous.
Someday Babylon may offer you something beautiful.
And you may need to remember:
Daniel refused the king's food before he ever faced the king's lions.
If Gospel Warrior is helping you know Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, and grow closer to Jesus Christ, follow and stay connected.
Supporting a ministry does not earn God's favor.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical way to help that work continue.
Not because sharing a post proves your faith.
It doesn't.
And tonight, before you worry about whether you could survive a lions' den, ask a quieter question.
What is sitting on the table in front of me that Jesus is asking me to surrender?
Because the faith people someday admire in the lions' den may be forming right now in the quiet place where nobody sees you say no.
The lions only revealed what the table had already decided.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOHN THE BAPTIST WORE CAMEL HAIR AND ATE LOCUSTS AND WILD HONEY—BUT THE STRANGEST THING ABOUT HIM WASN’T WHAT HE ATE
paragraphs: JOHN THE BAPTIST WORE CAMEL HAIR AND ATE LOCUSTS AND WILD HONEY—BUT THE STRANGEST THING ABOUT HIM WASN’T WHAT HE ATE

The wilderness prophet looked nothing like the kind of man the world would follow. Yet entire crowds walked into the desert to hear him—and what he said there still confronts every comfortable Christian today.
There is something almost unsettling about John the Baptist.
Not because he was evil.
Because he was free.
Free from the desperate need to impress people.
Free from the addiction to comfort.
Free from the exhausting performance of trying to look important.
Free enough to stand in a wilderness wearing camel hair, eating locusts and wild honey, and tell religious people something they desperately did not want to hear:
Repent.
Then, when the crowds began gathering around him, John did something even stranger.
He refused to make himself the center of the story.
Think about that.
People were leaving Jerusalem.
They were walking into the wilderness.
They were listening.
Confessing.
Being baptized.
John finally had what so many human hearts secretly crave—attention.
Influence.
A platform.
A following.
And instead of building a kingdom around his own name, John pointed beyond himself toward Someone coming after him.
Toward Jesus.
That may be the most uncomfortable part of his story.
Because camel hair is easier to talk about than surrender.
Locusts are easier to debate than repentance.
Wild honey is easier to study than asking whether Jesus Christ truly has first place in our lives.
Matthew gives us one of Scripture’s most unforgettable descriptions:
“And the same John had his raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins; and his meat was locusts and wild honey.”
Matthew 3:4, KJV.
The Greek is even more vivid:
“Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Ἰωάννης εἶχεν τὸ ἔνδυμα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τριχῶν καμήλου καὶ ζώνην δερματίνην περὶ τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτοῦ· ἡ δὲ τροφὴ ἦν αὐτοῦ ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι ἄγριον.”
The key words are wonderfully ordinary.
“τριχῶν καμήλου” — trichōn kamēlou — hair of a camel.
“ἀκρίδες” — akrides — locusts.
“μέλι ἄγριον” — meli agrion — wild honey.
Matthew is not trying to make John sound fashionable.
He is painting a prophet.
And suddenly an older biblical figure begins appearing in the shadows.
Elijah.
Centuries earlier, Elijah was recognized by a striking description involving a hairy garment and a leather belt around his waist.
John appears in the wilderness dressed in a way that deliberately echoes that prophetic world.
This matters because John was not merely an eccentric man who happened to enjoy wilderness cuisine.
His entire life had become a signpost.
His clothes preached.
His location preached.
His simplicity preached.
His voice preached.
But none of those things were the destination.
Jesus was.

Even John's food has sometimes been softened by modern readers because eating insects sounds strange to many cultures today. Some have suggested that the “locusts” were something plant-based, sometimes associated with carob.
But the straightforward reading of the Greek is exactly what generations of translators have understood it to mean:
Locusts.
And this was not contrary to the Torah.
Leviticus 11:22 explicitly permits certain kinds of locusts and related insects as food.
John was not violating God's Law by eating them.
He was living simply in the wilderness.
Locusts.
Wild honey.
Camel hair.
A leather belt.
No palace.
No luxury wardrobe.
No banquet table.
And yet Jerusalem came looking for him.
There is something painfully beautiful about that.
Because we live in a world constantly teaching us that before anyone will listen, we must become impressive.
Look successful.
Build the image.
Polish the appearance.
Gain followers.
Become desirable.
Protect the brand.
John walked into history looking like a man who had forgotten the entire rulebook of human approval.
And people came.
Why?
Not because camel hair possesses spiritual power.
Not because poverty automatically makes someone holy.
Not because eating unusual food brings a person closer to God.
Christianity is not a costume.
You could dress exactly like John and remain desperately far from John's God.
You could eat locusts every morning and never repent of one sin.
The power was never in the wardrobe.
The power was never in the diet.
The power was in the message God entrusted to him.
“Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because John is suddenly standing in front of us.
And his question is no longer, “Would you eat locusts?”
The question becomes:
What owns you?
What would become of your faith if nobody applauded it?
Would you still follow Christ if obedience cost you popularity?
Would you still tell the truth if truth made you inconvenient?
Would you still worship if God stripped away the comforts you quietly began confusing with His goodness?
Would Jesus still be enough?
That question hurts.
Especially when faith has slowly become comfortable.
There is a version of Christianity that can learn how to look alive while becoming spiritually numb.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know which verse to post.
We know which worship song makes us emotional.
We know how to appear strong when somebody asks how we are doing.
Meanwhile, behind the polished profile picture, there may be anger we refuse to surrender.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness we have renamed “boundaries.”
Pride disguised as discernment.
Greed disguised as ambition.
Gossip disguised as concern.
Secret compromise.
A prayer life that has almost disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust while our phones receive hours of our attention.
And perhaps most frightening of all…
we can become comfortable with it.
Then John walks out of the wilderness.
Camel hair rubbing against his skin.
Leather around his waist.
The taste of wild honey lingering in his mouth.
And he does not tell us to improve our image.
He says:
Repent.
The Greek word Matthew uses is “μετανοεῖτε” — metanoeite.
It carries the call to change one's mind, to turn, to undergo a fundamental reorientation.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is not self-hatred.
It is not theatrical guilt.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And John was preparing people for Someone infinitely greater than himself.
This is where the wilderness begins pointing toward grace.
John knew he was not the Savior.
He never claimed to be.
When Jesus came toward him, John eventually gave us one of the clearest summaries of his entire ministry:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
John 3:30.
Read that slowly.
“He must increase.”
Not my reputation.
Not my platform.
Not my comfort.
Not my applause.
Christ.
And that may be the sentence our generation desperately needs.
Because many of us have spent years asking Jesus to increase our plans while John was calling us to decrease before His glory.
We ask God to bless our kingdoms.
John points to God's King.
We ask Jesus to make our names known.
John spends his ministry making Jesus known.
We obsess over who notices us.
John essentially says:
Stop looking at me.
Look at Him.
Then comes the moment everything in John's life has been preparing for.
Jesus approaches.
And John sees Him.
The wilderness preacher who has spent his life telling people to prepare suddenly looks at Christ and declares:
“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.”
John 1:29.
There.
That is the heart of everything.
Not camel hair.
Not locusts.
Not honey.
Not John.
The Lamb.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God.
The One John was preparing people to receive.
The One who would go to the cross.
The One who would bear sin.
The One who would rise from the grave.
The One whose sandals John considered himself unworthy to carry.
John could call people to repentance.
But John could not die for their sins.
John could baptize them in the Jordan.
But John could not cleanse the human heart by his own blood.
John could expose sin.
Only Jesus could save sinners.
And maybe that is exactly why this strange wilderness story matters so much.
Because some people reading this are carrying things nobody knows about.
You love Jesus…
but something has been eating away at you.
Maybe you failed again.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
Maybe people think your marriage is fine.
It isn't.
Maybe everyone sees you serving at church, but nobody sees you crying alone.
Maybe your children think you are strong.
Maybe your parents think you are okay.
Maybe your friends believe your laughter.
God knows what happens after everybody goes home.
And somewhere along the way, shame whispered:
“You cannot come back now.”
“You knew better.”
“You've gone too far.”
“God must be tired of you.”
Listen carefully.
John's message was repentance because Jesus was coming.
Repentance and grace are not enemies.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves how seriously God takes sin.
But the cross also proves something else:
God's mercy reaches sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Jesus did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
He came because we couldn't.
That is the scandal.
Holy God.
Guilty sinners.
And between them stands a blood-stained cross where the sinless Son of God gives Himself for people who could never earn Him.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the story of the ashamed.
He rewrites the story of the addict who finally stops hiding.
He rewrites the story of the bitter heart that learns forgiveness.
He rewrites the story of the religious person who discovers that knowing Christian language is not the same thing as knowing Christ.
He rewrites the story of the prodigal who smells like the far country.
He rewrites the story of Peter after denial.
He rewrites the story of persecutors like Saul.
He rewrites sinners like us.
Not by pretending the old pages never happened.
But by redeeming people through His grace and making them new.
Maybe you have spent years trying to edit your own story.
Delete this memory.
Hide that failure.
Crop this part.
Filter that part.
Make sure nobody sees the real version.
Jesus does something infinitely greater than image management.
He redeems.
And suddenly John's camel-hair garment begins saying something unexpectedly beautiful.
You do not have to impress the world to belong to God.
You do not need a palace.
You do not need applause.
You do not need everybody to understand your obedience.
You need Christ.
John's wilderness life was not an advertisement for misery.
It was evidence that a human life can become radically centered on a mission greater than comfort.
And yet John's story also protects us from another mistake.
Asceticism itself does not save.
John's unusual lifestyle did not make him the Messiah.
John knew that.
That is why genuine Christian discipleship can never terminate in admiration for John the Baptist.
John points away from himself.
Follow his finger.
It points to Jesus.
That is the entire purpose of the messenger.
The greatest tragedy would be to become fascinated with the man wearing camel hair while missing the Lamb of God standing in front of him.
So perhaps the question tonight is not whether you could survive John's wilderness diet.
Perhaps the question is whether there is anything Jesus has been asking you to surrender that you keep protecting.
A relationship?
A secret habit?
An unforgiving heart?
A double life?
Your pride?
Your obsession with approval?
Your need to control everything?
Your refusal to forgive?
Your fear of being completely known by God?
You already are completely known.
And still Christ calls sinners to come.
Not to remain unchanged.
To repent.
To believe.
To follow.
Grace does not merely comfort us in the prison.
Grace opens the door and calls us out.
Maybe you need to stop pretending tonight.
No speech.
No performance.
Just honesty before God.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
“Jesus, change me.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is where honesty begins.

And if grace has already pulled you out of places you once thought would destroy you, tell someone what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to remind another wounded believer that the story is not over.
Not as religious decoration.
Someone may need to hear the word John thundered into the wilderness:
Repent.
And someone desperately needs to hear what John said when Jesus appeared:
Behold the Lamb of God.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. Grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased. God's blessing is not merchandise.
But Christians can freely choose to support ministry and help biblical content reach more people.
Use them.
Share them.
Give them to the believer who is struggling.
Send them to the person asking questions about Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is standing in a wilderness nobody else can see.
Maybe that somebody is you.
And perhaps you thought the wilderness meant God had abandoned your story.
John reminds us that sometimes the wilderness is precisely where the noise becomes quiet enough for the most important announcement in human history to be heard.
Prepare the way.
The King is coming.
And when John finally saw Him, he did not point toward himself.
He pointed toward Jesus.
So when people remember your life, may they not merely remember what you owned, what you achieved, what you wore, how many people followed you, or whether the world considered you successful.
May they remember where you pointed.
Toward Christ.
Camel hair eventually decays.
Wild honey disappears.
Crowds go home.
Platforms vanish.
Human applause becomes silence.
But Jesus Christ remains.
And perhaps the greatest life is not the life that convinces the most people to look at us.
Perhaps it is the life that leaves people unable to forget the One we pointed them toward.
When everything else in your story has been stripped away, may the last thing people can still see be your finger pointing toward Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS MASTURBATION A SIN? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS WHISPER BUT JESUS REFUSES TO ANSWER WITH SHAME
paragraphs:
IS MASTURBATION A SIN? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS WHISPER BUT JESUS REFUSES TO ANSWER WITH SHAME
The Bible never actually uses the word “masturbation.” So why do so many Christians feel condemned afterward—and what does Scripture really say?
There are questions Christians ask in Bible study.
And then there are questions they erase from the search bar.
This is one of them.
You promised God you would stop.
Maybe it happened after midnight.
Maybe loneliness was louder than your convictions.
Maybe pornography was involved. Maybe it wasn’t.
Maybe there was only an imagination you knew you should not have entertained.
Then came the silence afterward.
The screen went dark.
The pleasure disappeared almost as quickly as it came.
And suddenly you were alone with your thoughts.
Again.
You whispered, “God, forgive me.”
Again.
You promised, “This was the last time.”
Again.
Then somewhere inside you came the question you were almost afraid to ask:
Is masturbation actually a sin according to the Bible—or have Christians simply told me that it is?
That question deserves more than embarrassment.
It deserves Scripture.
And before going any further, something needs to be said that may surprise people on both sides of this debate:
The Bible never explicitly mentions masturbation by name.
There is no Hebrew word in the Old Testament or Greek word in the New Testament that simply translates, “masturbation is a sin.”
That matters.
Christians should never claim that God explicitly said something Scripture does not explicitly say.
But that is not the end of the discussion.
Because the Christian question is not merely:
“Can I find a verse containing the name of this behavior?”
The deeper question is:
What happens when I bring my desires, fantasies, habits, body, conscience, and sexuality beneath the lordship of Jesus Christ?
And that changes everything.
Some people immediately point to Onan in Genesis 38.
Onan had sexual relations with Tamar and “spilled” his semen rather than providing offspring for his deceased brother. God judged him.
For generations, this story has sometimes been used as though Onan were punished for masturbation.
But read the passage carefully.
That is not what happened.

Onan was having intercourse with Tamar. His offense involved deliberately refusing the familial obligation expected of him while exploiting the sexual relationship for himself. Genesis 38 is therefore not an explicit biblical prohibition of masturbation.
We should not make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
But we should not make it say less either.
Because then Jesus takes us somewhere much deeper than merely asking what our hands are doing.
He goes after the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text includes the words:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial verb is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō.
It means to desire, long for, or covet; context determines whether that desire is good or sinful.
Jesus is speaking specifically about looking at another person with sexually covetous intent.
He does not merely confront physical adultery.
He exposes the desire that begins rehearsing adultery internally.
That matters enormously to this conversation.
Because masturbation cannot be evaluated biblically merely as a mechanical bodily action detached from everything happening inside the person.
What are you imagining?
Whom are you mentally using?
What are you watching?
What desire are you deliberately feeding?
Would you willingly bring that fantasy into the presence of Christ?
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we ask, “Is masturbation technically forbidden?”
when the Holy Spirit may be confronting a much deeper question:
“Why are you fighting so hard to protect something that repeatedly pulls your heart away from Me?”
Pornography makes the issue considerably clearer.
Pornography trains the eyes and imagination to consume another person's body for sexual gratification. It cultivates precisely the kind of sexually possessive looking that Jesus takes seriously.
The person on your screen has a soul.
The person in your fantasy bears the image of God.
Christian sexuality cannot reduce another human being into material for private consumption.
But suppose pornography is not involved.
Suppose you say:
“I don't watch anything.”
Then the question deserves more care.
It would be biblically irresponsible to invent a verse saying that the physical act itself is explicitly condemned when Scripture never directly names it.
At the same time, absence of an explicit verse does not automatically mean unrestricted moral permission.
Paul gives believers a startling principle in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
“I will not be dominated by anything.”
The Greek verb behind the idea of being dominated is related to ἐξουσιάζω — exousiazō, carrying the sense of exercising authority or mastery.
Now ask yourself something harder than, “Can I do this?”
Can I stop?
That question has exposed more hearts than a hundred arguments.
Can you go without it?
Or does your body begin negotiating with your convictions?
Do you repeatedly say, “Never again,” only to return?
Do stress, boredom, loneliness, rejection, anger, insomnia, or anxiety automatically send you toward sexual release?
Have you started needing increasingly intense fantasies?
Has it become medication for emotions you do not know how to bring before God?
Because there is an enormous difference between experiencing sexual desire and becoming enslaved to a sexual habit.
Sexual desire itself is not dirty.
God created human beings as embodied sexual creatures.
The existence of sexual desire does not make you disgusting.
Temptation itself is not identical to sin.
Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
But desire can be cultivated, entertained, directed, and fed in sinful ways.
And this is where Paul becomes devastatingly relevant.
In 1 Corinthians 6, Paul refuses to treat the human body as spiritually irrelevant.
He says:
“The body is...for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.”
Then:
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.”
And finally:
“You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.”
Think about that.
Christianity does not say your body is worthless.
Christianity says your body is so valuable that Christ purchased you at the price of His blood.
Your body is not the enemy.
Your sexuality is not something Jesus is embarrassed to discuss.
Your desires are not beyond His authority.
And holiness is not God standing over sexually struggling people screaming, “Filthy!”
Holiness is Christ saying:
“You belong to Me now.”
That is an entirely different kind of conviction.
There is a difference between shame and conviction.
Shame says:
“Hide from God.”
Conviction says:
“Run to God.”
Shame says:
“You are disgusting.”
Conviction says:
“This is destroying something I love.”
Shame says:
“God doesn't want you anymore.”
The Gospel says:
Jesus already knew the worst thing about you when He went to the cross.
Do you understand how scandalous grace really is?
Christ did not die for the edited version of you.
He did not shed His blood only for the version of you who remembers to pray, reads the Bible every morning, controls every appetite, and never searches for anything embarrassing.
Romans 5:8 says Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Before.
At Calvary, Jesus was not surprised by your browser history.
He was not surprised by the fantasy.
He was not surprised by the relapse.
He was not surprised by the secret nobody knows.
And still...
He stayed on the cross.
But grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace does not say, “Keep feeding whatever is killing you because Jesus forgives.”
Paul anticipated that distortion.
Grace forgives us and transforms us.
The Jesus who refuses to condemn the repentant sinner is also the Jesus who calls sinners into a different life.
So, is masturbation a sin?
Here is the most biblically responsible answer:

Scripture does not explicitly identify masturbation by name as a sinful act, so Christians should be cautious about claiming an explicit prohibition where the biblical text gives none. But masturbation can clearly become sinful through lust, pornography, covetous fantasy, lack of self-control, enslavement, violation of conscience, or its place within a broader pattern of sexual immorality and self-centered sexuality.
And for many people, that distinction is not an escape hatch.
It is actually more confronting.
Because now you cannot merely ask:
“Where does the Bible say I can't?”
You have to ask:
“Can I honestly do this before Jesus and say, ‘Lord, this glorifies You with my body’?”
And maybe that question just changed the atmosphere.
Because perhaps this was never only about masturbation.
Maybe this is about what you do when you are lonely.
Maybe this is about pornography.
Maybe this is about someone you cannot stop fantasizing about.
Maybe this is about the marriage that has grown cold.
Maybe this is about wounds you have never confronted.
Maybe sexual release became the anesthetic you use whenever life hurts.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your parents don't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your friends at church definitely don't know.
People see you worship.
They see you share Bible verses.
They see the Christian posts.
They see the smiling profile picture.
But they don't see 1:17 a.m.
God does.
And strangely...
He has not walked away.
That may be the part somebody desperately needed to hear.
Not because your sin does not matter.
But because Jesus is greater than what has mastered you.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after doing something.
Biblical repentance involves turning.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and orientation that expresses itself in a changed direction.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, I don't want merely to feel guilty anymore. I want You to change what I love.”
That prayer is terrifying.
Because sometimes we don't actually want freedom.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
We want God to silence our guilt while leaving our habits untouched.
We want enough Jesus to calm our conscience but not enough Jesus to interrupt our appetites.
And Jesus loves us too much for that arrangement.
Maybe your next act of repentance means deleting pornography.
Maybe it means putting the phone outside the bedroom.
Maybe it means confessing the struggle to a mature believer you trust.
Maybe it means refusing to isolate yourself when temptation becomes strongest.
Maybe it means finally admitting that what you called “a little habit” has been controlling you for years.
Maybe it means learning that sexual temptation is sometimes easier to resist when you address the loneliness, anxiety, exhaustion, resentment, or emotional pain underneath it.
And when you fail?
Do not turn failure into permission.
But do not turn failure into despair either.
Confess.
Get up.
Return to Christ.
Fight again.
First John 1:9 says that when believers confess their sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Notice that.
Faithful.
Not reluctant.
Not irritated that you came back.
Faithful.
Somebody reading this has repented of the same sexual sin so many times that you are embarrassed to pray anymore.
You think heaven must be tired of hearing your voice.
So instead of running toward Jesus after falling, you hide for three days.
Then five days.
Then two weeks.
You stop reading Scripture because Scripture makes you uncomfortable.
You stop praying because prayer feels hypocritical.
You withdraw from God until you somehow feel spiritually clean enough to approach Him again.
But listen carefully.
You do not wash yourself before coming to the One who washes sinners.
Come exposed.
Come ashamed.
Come trembling.
Come having failed for the hundredth time if necessary.
But come repentant.
Come wanting Christ more than the darkness.
Because the Gospel is not the story of disciplined people rescuing themselves.
It is the story of dead people being made alive by Jesus Christ.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
You cannot boast, because you needed a Savior.
But you cannot despair, because you have a Savior.
Maybe tonight will be different.
Not because you suddenly became stronger.
But because instead of merely saying, “I need to stop masturbating,” you finally pray:
“Jesus, teach me what my body is for.”
And Scripture answers:
For the Lord.
Your eyes?
For the Lord.
Your imagination?
For the Lord.
Your sexuality?
For the Lord.
Your singleness?
For the Lord.
Your marriage?
For the Lord.
Your private life?
For the Lord.
Even the room where nobody else can see you?
For the Lord.
This is bigger than behavior modification.
This is worship.
Be honest.
Somebody scrolling silently may need evidence that freedom is possible.
Not because reading an article can sanctify you, but because there may be a night when temptation starts rewriting your theology and you need to remember what is true.
Send it privately to the friend who has been fighting alone.
There are people in churches everywhere silently asking this exact question while being too ashamed to say it aloud.
Because Christianity was never the announcement that good people finally became good enough.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
And perhaps that is what makes this entire conversation so important.
The question began:
“Is masturbation a sin?”
But perhaps the question you needed to leave with was different.
Who owns my body?
Paul's answer is breathtaking.
You were bought with a price.
There are nail scars behind that sentence.
Blood behind that sentence.
A cross behind that sentence.
An empty tomb behind that sentence.
Jesus did not purchase you so you could spend the rest of your life terrified that one more failure will make Him abandon you.
And He did not purchase you so you could comfortably remain enslaved to what He died to redeem.
He purchased you to make you His.
So when temptation comes tonight...
remember whose you are.
When shame whispers tomorrow...
remember whose you are.
When you fall...
remember whose you are, repent, and run home.
When you stand again...
remember who lifted you.
And when the enemy tries to define you by the secret chapter you wish you could tear out of your story, point him toward the cross and remember:
Jesus has always done some of His most beautiful rewriting in the chapters we were most ashamed to let anyone read.
Because your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD ASKED, “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” ONE MAN ANSWERED BEFORE HE EVEN KNEW WHERE GOD WOULD SEND HIM.
paragraphs:
GOD ASKED, “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” ONE MAN ANSWERED BEFORE HE EVEN KNEW WHERE GOD WOULD SEND HIM.
Isaiah did not ask where. He did not ask how difficult it would be. He did not ask whether people would listen. He simply said, “Here I am. Send me.” But what happened immediately before those words changes everything about what surrender really means.
There are prayers we whisper because we want God to change our circumstances.
And then there are prayers that give God permission to change us.
Those prayers are dangerous.
Not because God is cruel.
Because surrender means handing Him the blank page before you know what He intends to write on it.
Isaiah prayed one of those prayers.
But perhaps you have heard his famous words so many times that they no longer frighten you.
“Here am I; send me.”
Beautiful words.
Missionary words.
Words printed across shirts, journals, church banners, and social media graphics.
But put Isaiah 6:8 back where Scripture placed it, and suddenly those words stop sounding decorative.
They become terrifying.
Because Isaiah did not receive an itinerary first.
God did not show him the audience.
God did not promise him applause.
God did not tell him that obedience would make him popular.
Isaiah heard a question.
And surrendered before knowing what his yes would cost.
The Hebrew preserves the moment with breathtaking simplicity:
וָאֶשְׁמַע אֶת־קוֹל אֲדֹנָי אֹמֵר אֶת־מִי אֶשְׁלַח וּמִי יֵלֶךְ־לָנוּ וָאֹמַר הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Va’eshma et-qol Adonai omer, et-mi eshlah, umi yelekh-lanu? Va’omar: hinnēnî, šəlāḥēnî.
“I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here am I; send me.’”
הִנְנִי — hinnēnî.
“Here I am.”
שְׁלָחֵנִי — šəlāḥēnî.
“Send me.”
Not…
“Where?”
Not…
“How much will this cost me?”
Not…
“Will they appreciate me?”
Not…
“Will this become successful?”
Not even…
“What exactly do You want me to do?”
Here I am.
Send me.
But there is something many of us miss when we rush straight to verse 8.
Isaiah did not begin the chapter saying, “Send me.”
He began by falling apart.
Before there was commission, there was conviction.
Before there was mission, there was cleansing.
Before Isaiah volunteered his mouth for God, Isaiah became painfully aware that his mouth was unclean.
That matters.
Isaiah sees the Lord “high and lifted up.”
The seraphim cry:
“Holy, holy, holy.”
The foundations shake.
The house fills with smoke.
And Isaiah does not look upon the holiness of God and congratulate himself for being spiritual enough to witness it.
He collapses beneath the contrast.
“Woe is me!”
He realizes something horrifying.
The closer he comes to the holiness of God, the less impressive his own righteousness appears.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes yours.
Because it is possible to spend years around Christian things without truly seeing yourself before a holy God.
You can know worship songs.
You can quote verses.
You can post Christian content.
You can attend church.
You can defend biblical truth online.
You can tell everybody else what they need to repent of…
while quietly protecting the one room inside your own heart where you do not want Jesus turning on the light.
Then God gets close.
And suddenly the excuses sound different.
The secret addiction looks different.
The bitterness looks different.
The pride looks different.
The hidden messages look different.
The resentment toward your spouse looks different.
The private fantasy looks different.
The dishonest business decision looks different.
The unforgiveness you renamed “boundaries” looks different.
The gossip you renamed “concern” looks different.
The spiritual laziness you renamed “being busy” looks different.
The compromise you promised yourself you could control looks different.
Isaiah saw the King.
And Isaiah saw Isaiah.
“Woe is me.”
That is the scandal.
A sinful human being standing before unbearable holiness with absolutely nothing impressive enough to make himself clean.
But then something moves through the smoke.
A seraph flies toward Isaiah carrying a burning coal taken from the altar.
The coal touches the very place Isaiah confessed as unclean.
His lips.
And Isaiah is told that his guilt has been taken away and his sin atoned for.
Do not race past this.
Isaiah did not cleanse himself.
He confessed.
God provided the cleansing.
Isaiah did not repair his impurity and then approach God with an improved résumé.
Grace came to the place of his uncleanness.
That is why Isaiah 6 is more than a motivational speech about volunteering.
It reveals a biblical pattern that reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
God is holy.
We are sinful.
Our sin must actually be dealt with.
And what Isaiah experiences symbolically through the altar points our eyes toward the greater reality proclaimed throughout the Gospel: sinners cannot save themselves.
We need atonement.
We need mercy.
We need a Savior.
And God did not leave humanity searching for one.
Jesus Christ came.
The sinless Son of God entered our fallen world, lived the righteousness we could never manufacture, gave Himself for sinners at the cross, was buried, and rose again.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
The Gospel is that your sin mattered so terribly that redemption required a cost you could never pay—and Jesus willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved.
At Calvary, scandal collided with grace.
Our rebellion.
His obedience.
Our guilt.
His righteousness.
Our condemnation.
His mercy.
Our death.
His resurrection.
And because Jesus rewrites everything, the person who comes to Him in repentance and faith does not have to remain imprisoned by the chapter that once defined them.
The adulterer does not have to die merely “the adulterer.”
The addict does not have to remain merely “the addict.”
The liar does not have to remain “the liar.”
The bitter believer does not have to remain bitter.
The ashamed woman does not have to spend the rest of her life hiding.
The broken man does not have to pretend he was never broken.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace does something infinitely better.
Grace forgives the guilty and begins transforming the forgiven.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now we finally understand why Isaiah could say:
הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Hinnēnî. Šəlāḥēnî.
Here I am.
Send me.
The man answering God in verse 8 is the man who cried “Woe is me” in verse 5.
Something happened between those sentences.
Grace.
That changes the entire meaning of Christian service.
We do not surrender so God will forgive us.
In Christ, we surrender because His grace has captured us.
We do not serve to purchase redemption.
We serve because redemption cannot leave a surrendered heart untouched.
And here comes the uncomfortable part.
Isaiah said yes before hearing the assignment.
Read what follows.
His ministry would not be an easy road of instant visible success.
He would speak to people resistant to the message.
Isaiah eventually asks:
“How long?”
That may be one of the most painfully human questions in the chapter.
How long, Lord?
Maybe you know that prayer.
How long do I keep praying for this child?
How long do I remain faithful when nobody notices?
How long do I forgive?
How long do I fight this temptation?
How long do I keep serving when I feel invisible?
How long do I speak truth when people would rather hear something comfortable?
How long do I trust You when nothing looks the way I thought obedience would look?
How long?
Somewhere along the way, many of us absorbed a version of Christianity in which obedience was supposed to produce immediate visible rewards.
Follow God and everything falls into place.
Say yes and doors open.
Serve faithfully and people appreciate you.
Speak truth and people listen.
Give generously and prosperity follows.
Pray faithfully and the answer arrives according to schedule.
But Isaiah's calling destroys that illusion.
Sometimes obedience sends you directly into difficulty.
Sometimes faithfulness costs you something.
Sometimes you speak and people reject you.
Sometimes you obey God without getting the outcome you hoped obedience would produce.
Sometimes your assignment is not to be impressive.
It is simply to be faithful.
That is why hinnēnî is so costly.
“Here I am.”
Not merely my Sunday morning.
Here I am.
Not merely the parts of my life I am comfortable giving You.
Here I am.
My reputation.
My future.
My plans.
My money.
My wounds.
My gifts.
My disappointments.
My relationships.
My ambitions.
My secret places.
My remaining years.
Here I am.
And maybe that is the sentence God has been waiting to hear from you.
Not because God lacks power without you.
He does not.
God is not pacing heaven desperately hoping somebody will rescue His plans.
The sovereign Lord who filled Isaiah's vision does not need human beings in the way human beings need Him.
The wonder is that He calls people at all.
He allows redeemed sinners to participate in His purposes.
Think about that.
The God before whom seraphim cover themselves chooses to send forgiven human beings into the world carrying His truth.
And centuries after Isaiah, Jesus would speak again about sending.
After His resurrection, Christ told His disciples that as the Father had sent Him, He was sending them.
The risen Christ would commission His followers to make disciples of the nations.
Christianity was never intended to terminate with us.
Someone carried the Gospel until it reached you.
Someone preached.
Someone prayed.
Someone translated Scripture.
Someone taught a child.
Someone planted a church.
Someone crossed a border.
Someone endured ridicule.
Someone opened a Bible at a kitchen table.
Someone shared the truth when staying silent would have been easier.
And eventually…
you heard.
Now the question travels across centuries and lands uncomfortably close to your own heart.
Whom shall I send?
Perhaps you have been waiting for God to give you the whole map before you surrender.
God, show me exactly what happens, and then I will trust You.
Show me who will stay.
Show me what I will earn.
Show me whether this succeeds.
Show me whether they will accept me.
Show me whether I will get hurt.
Show me how everything ends.
Then I will say yes.
But that is not surrender.
That is negotiation.
Isaiah's answer came before the explanation.
Here I am.
Send me.
And before you turn that sentence into an emotional promise, remember where Isaiah's surrender began.
At the altar.
With sin exposed.
With grace given.
So perhaps your first hinnēnî today is not “Send me to another country.”
Perhaps it is:
Jesus, here is the sin I have been hiding.
Here is my pride.
Here is my pornography.
Here is my bitterness.
Here is my jealousy.
Here is my hypocrisy.
Here is the relationship I know dishonors You.
Here is the grudge I keep feeding.
Here is the secret version of me nobody at church knows exists.
Here is my exhausted faith.
Here is my fear.
Here is my shame.
Here I am.
All of me.
Have mercy on me.
Cleanse me.
Change me.
Lead me.
And when Christ forgives you, do not mistake grace for permission to return comfortably to the chains from which He came to rescue you.
Grace calls us out.
Grace changes allegiance.
Grace teaches surrendered people to say yes.
Maybe your “send me” means finally sharing the Gospel with your family.
Maybe it means apologizing.
Maybe it means forgiving.
Maybe it means opening your home.
Maybe it means discipling your children instead of outsourcing their spiritual formation.
Maybe it means returning to church after shame convinced you to disappear.
Maybe it means refusing the compromise everybody else calls normal.
Maybe it means using your business, your voice, your resources, your social media, your influence, your suffering, your testimony, or your remaining years for the glory of Jesus Christ.
You may never stand behind a pulpit.
You may never have a platform.
Your name may never become famous.
Good.
The question was never:
“Who wants to become known?”
It was:
“Whom shall I send?”
And there is a world of difference.
Be honest.
There are other believers reading who need to discover that they are not fighting alone.
Your honesty may become somebody else's permission to finally ask for prayer.
Not merely because an algorithm rewards sharing.
Send this privately to the person you cannot stop thinking about while reading.
Save it too.
Because one day the cost of your own “yes” may become heavier than the emotion you feel right now, and you may need to come back and remember:
Isaiah did not know everything when he volunteered.
He knew the One calling him.
Not because paying for something earns God's favor.
It never could.
It does not.
Christ purchased salvation; we cannot buy it.
