But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement, discipleship resources, and Gospel proclamation continue reaching people.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to prove your faith.
Not because sharing a post somehow makes you righteous.
Jesus alone saves.
Share because the Gospel is worth carrying.
Support faithful Christian work because generosity can serve the spread of truth.
But above everything else…
Yourself.
Maybe heaven's question is closer than you thought.
Maybe God has already placed someone within reach of your testimony.
Maybe somebody needs the Gospel you have been too afraid to share.
Maybe your children need to see what surrendered Christianity actually looks like.
Maybe the person God intends to use is not a more talented person, a less wounded person, a more educated person, or a person with a cleaner history.
Maybe grace has brought you all the way to this sentence.
הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Hinnēnî. Šəlāḥēnî.
Here I am.
Send me.
You do not need to know every mile of the road before entrusting yourself to the One who already knows where it ends.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
The man who once cried, “Woe is me,” became the man who could say, “Send me”—because grace touched the very place where shame told him he was unusable.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY “MY CUP OVERFLOWS” IS MORE POWERFUL THAN MOST CHRISTIANS REALIZE
paragraphs: WHY “MY CUP OVERFLOWS” IS MORE POWERFUL THAN MOST CHRISTIANS REALIZE
You may have quoted Psalm 23 for years. But hidden inside one familiar sentence is a picture of God’s goodness that becomes breathtaking when you realize where David is sitting when he says it.
There is a sentence Christians whisper in hospital rooms.
They print it on mugs.
They underline it in Bibles.
They quote it when life is going well.
“My cup overflows.”
Beautiful words.
But perhaps we have made them so familiar that we have stopped feeling their weight.
Because David does not say these words while standing on a mountain celebrating a trouble-free life.
He says them at a table.
And according to the psalm, something disturbing is nearby.
Enemies.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.”
Then comes the oil.
“You anoint my head with oil.”
And then:
“My cup overflows.”
Psalm 23:5.
Read that sequence again slowly.
A table.
Enemies.
Oil.
An overflowing cup.
David is not describing a life from which every threat has disappeared.
He is describing what it is like to belong to a Shepherd whose goodness is greater than the danger surrounding His sheep.
That changes everything.
The Hebrew behind the famous phrase is wonderfully compact:
כּוֹסִי רְוָיָה
kōsî rəwāyāh
“My cup is abundance.”
Or, naturally expressed in English:
“My cup overflows.”
The Hebrew word כּוֹסִי (kōsî) means “my cup.” The final -î carries the sense of “my.”
Then comes רְוָיָה (rəwāyāh), a word communicating abundance or saturation—something richly filled.
David gives us an image of sufficiency that has crossed into abundance.
But we need to understand what he is—and is not—promising.
Psalm 23 is not a divine guarantee that every Christian will become wealthy.
It is not a secret formula for financial prosperity.
It does not mean faithful believers will never experience cancer, grief, persecution, unemployment, betrayal, depression, loneliness, or death.
David himself knew suffering.
He knew what it was to be hunted.
He knew betrayal.
He knew warfare.
He knew family devastation.
He knew the consequences of his own terrible sin.
Yet this same man could look toward God and say:
“My cup overflows.”
Maybe that is why the sentence carries so much power.
Overflow does not necessarily mean you have everything you wanted.
Sometimes overflow means you discovered that God Himself was enough when almost everything else disappeared.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have smiled for photographs while quietly falling apart.
You have answered, “I’m okay,” because explaining the truth would have taken too long.
You have encouraged everyone else while wondering who would encourage you.
You have worshiped while carrying questions you were afraid to say aloud.
Maybe you prayed for something that never happened.
Maybe somebody left.
Maybe somebody died.
Maybe you failed.
Maybe the person who wounded you claimed to love God.
Maybe the deepest scandal in your story is not what somebody did to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
And perhaps that is the part nobody knows.
The browser history.
The secret messages.
The bitterness.
The affair.
The addiction.
The compromise.
The resentment.
The pride.
The money.
The lie.
The hidden habit.
The version of yourself that appears at church and the version that exists when nobody is watching.
You know the vocabulary of Christianity.
But lately your soul has felt empty.
And here comes David saying something almost offensive to exhausted people:
“My cup overflows.”
How?
Look again at the verse.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.”
God does not wait until every enemy leaves before preparing the table.
That matters.
We often tell God:
“Remove this, and then I will have peace.”
“Fix them, and then I will worship.”
“Answer this prayer, and then I will trust You.”
“Change my circumstances, and then I will know You are good.”
But Psalm 23 gives us another picture.
The enemies remain present.
And God prepares the table anyway.
The threat is real.
But so is the Host.
The valley was real earlier in the psalm too:
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death…”
David never pretends darkness is imaginary.
Biblical faith is not denial.
Christianity does not ask you to look at a grave and pretend it does not hurt.
It does not ask a betrayed spouse to call betrayal good.
It does not ask the persecuted believer to pretend persecution is pleasant.
It does not ask the grieving mother to stop crying.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Gospel does something infinitely greater than teaching us to pretend darkness is light.
It announces that darkness does not get the final word.
That is why Psalm 23 ultimately becomes even more beautiful when read in the light of Jesus Christ.
David begins:
“The LORD is my shepherd.”
Centuries later Jesus says:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
John 10:11.
Do not miss what Christianity is claiming.
The Shepherd does not merely point frightened sheep toward safety.
The Shepherd gives Himself for them.
And this is where the overflowing cup becomes painfully beautiful.
Because before resurrection morning…
before the empty tomb…
before victory was announced…
Jesus entered suffering.
In Gethsemane He prayed concerning the “cup” before Him.
“My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”
Matthew 26:39.

The Bible uses the imagery of a cup in different ways depending on context, including blessing and judgment. We should not carelessly collapse every biblical reference to a cup into one identical symbol.
But the contrast should still humble us.
David speaks of a cup characterized by abundance.
Christ willingly goes toward the suffering appointed for Him.
At the cross, Jesus bears sin and gives His life for sinners.
Not because humanity deserved rescue.
Because grace is grace precisely because we did not.
That is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
The innocent One condemned.
The guilty offered forgiveness.
The Holy One surrounded by sinners.
The King wearing thorns.
The Shepherd dying for sheep who wandered away.
Jesus Christ crucified.
And then—
the grave loses.
Christ rises.
Suddenly “my cup overflows” becomes more than a decorative sentence for comfortable days.
For the Christian, our deepest abundance is not measured by what is parked in the driveway.
It is measured by what happened at an empty tomb.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Adopted.
Redeemed.
Given hope beyond death.
Invited to the table of a King we once rebelled against.
That is overflow.
You can lose money and still possess Christ.
You can lose popularity and still possess Christ.
You can lose the approval of people and still possess Christ.
You can walk through grief while being held by Christ.
You can stand beside a grave and still possess a hope death cannot ultimately destroy.
This does not make suffering small.
It makes Jesus greater.
And perhaps somebody needs that distinction today.
God's goodness is not proven by the absence of valleys.
Psalm 23 itself destroys that idea.
The Shepherd is good even while the sheep walk through the valley.
The Shepherd is present even while enemies watch.
The Shepherd provides even before circumstances become comfortable.
And David does not merely say the cup is full.
It overflows.
There is something deeply convicting about overflow because overflow was never meant merely to terminate on us.
Grace received begins reshaping the person who receives it.
The forgiven learn forgiveness.
The comforted begin comforting.
The rescued begin telling other prisoners where freedom can be found.
The person who has tasted mercy begins saying:
“You need to meet the One who met me.”
Maybe this is why your scars survived.
Not because God enjoyed your pain.
But because healed scars can sometimes become signposts pointing wounded people toward the Healer.
Peter failed spectacularly.
He denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering your own voice saying you did not know Him.
Peter's failure became public Scripture.
His worst night has been read for centuries.
Talk about scandal.
Yet Jesus did not throw Peter away.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him and commissioned him to care for His people.
Failure was not Peter's final chapter.
Grace rewrote what shame wanted to make permanent.
That does not mean sin did not matter.
It mattered enormously.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace is why repentance becomes possible without despair.
We confess because sin is serious.
We run to Christ because His mercy is greater.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Maybe you have spent years trying to hide the empty places in your cup.
Jesus already sees them.
Maybe you have spent years trying to fill them with attention.
Relationships.
Pornography.
Money.
Success.
Food.
Approval.
Ministry recognition.
Alcohol.
Achievement.
Endless scrolling.
Another purchase.
Another person.
Another promise to yourself that tomorrow you will finally become different.
Yet the soul remains thirsty.
Because some thirsts cannot be satisfied by putting more of the world into them.
Jesus said:
“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.”
John 7:37.
Come to Me.
Not perform for Me.
Not impress Me.
Not repair yourself sufficiently and then approach Me.
Come.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself enough to deserve Jesus.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because you finally understand that sin cannot give you what it promised.
The Gospel says Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
It does not have to write the ending.
Jesus does that better.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps right now your cup does not feel overflowing.
Perhaps it feels cracked.
Perhaps you feel like you have poured yourself into everyone until there is almost nothing left.
Then hear this carefully:
You do not have to manufacture overflow.
A cup cannot fill itself.
The Shepherd provides.
The Shepherd leads.
The Shepherd restores.
“He restores my soul.”
Psalm 23:3.
There may be someone reading these words with tears beginning to form because you have been trying to restore yourself.
You cannot.
But Christ can redeem what you surrender to Him.
Not necessarily by restoring every circumstance to the exact shape you wanted.
Sometimes His work is deeper than that.
He changes us.
He forgives.
He sanctifies.
He teaches us to trust.
He carries us through valleys.
He transforms wounds into compassion.
He exposes idols we thought we needed.
He teaches us that the greatest gift at God's table is ultimately God Himself.
And someday every believer in Christ will discover just how temporary the valley really was.
Psalm 23 ends:
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.”
Forever.
That is the word suffering cannot defeat.
Forever.
Cancer does not get forever.
Grief does not get forever.
Temptation does not get forever.
The cemetery does not get forever.
Your enemies do not get forever.
Your shame does not get forever.
Jesus does.
And if you belong to Christ, your story is moving toward Him.
Maybe now you understand why “my cup overflows” is far more powerful than many Christians realize.
It is not the boast of someone who finally acquired enough possessions.
It is the testimony of someone who discovered the goodness of the Shepherd even with enemies nearby.
The table is prepared.
The Shepherd is present.
The cup is abundant.
And grace keeps spilling over the edges.
So do not keep this truth trapped on your screen.
If someone came to your mind while reading this, send it to them.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be brave enough to comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but still refusing to abandon your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Someone else may recognize their valley inside the story of how Christ carried you through yours.
It cannot.
Not because financial support earns salvation.
It never will.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
If you want another practical way to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel ministry and sharing biblical truth can be part of that stewardship.
Not for applause.
Not to prove your spirituality.
Not because an algorithm can measure faithfulness.
One person hiding a scandal.
One marriage barely surviving.
One exhausted believer thinking about walking away.
One prodigal wondering whether Jesus would still receive them.
One person silently asking whether grace could possibly reach this far.
You may never know who reads because you shared.
But you can make sure they have the opportunity.
Share. Comment. Save the article. Pray for the ministry. Invite someone into Scripture.
Because the goal was never merely to build an audience.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus.
The Shepherd.
The Savior.
The crucified and risen King.
The One who meets sinners in their scandal and does not leave repentant sinners where He found them.
So tonight, when you whisper those familiar words again—
“My cup overflows”—
do not picture only money.
Do not picture only success.
Do not picture a painless life.
Picture a table surrounded by enemies.
Picture a Shepherd who has not abandoned His sheep.
Picture grace you could never purchase.
Picture forgiveness you could never earn.
Picture a cross where your Savior gave Himself.
Picture an empty tomb announcing that death does not have the last word.
Picture every undeserved mercy that carried you to this moment.
Then look at the cracks in your story.
Maybe they are not proof that the cup is useless.
Maybe they are places where people can finally see what has been filling it.
And remember this:
The world may remember the scandal that emptied you, but Jesus is still writing the grace that will overflow from you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SLEPT THROUGH A STORM VIOLENT ENOUGH TO TERRIFY EXPERIENCED FISHERMEN
paragraphs: JESUS SLEPT THROUGH A STORM VIOLENT ENOUGH TO TERRIFY EXPERIENCED FISHERMEN
They thought the sleeping Jesus did not care that they were dying. Then He stood up—and the storm discovered Who had been sleeping in the boat.
There is something deeply unsettling about Jesus sleeping while terrified men are trying to keep a boat from sinking.
Read that again.
Jesus was asleep.
Not after the storm.
During it.

The wind was screaming across the water. Waves were crashing into the boat. Water was accumulating inside it. Men who knew boats, nets, wind, waves, and the unpredictable temperament of the Sea of Galilee were frightened enough to believe they were about to die.
And Jesus...
slept.
If you have ever prayed while your life seemed to be falling apart and wondered why heaven felt strangely quiet, do not rush past this story.
Because maybe the most frightening part of your storm is not the storm.
Maybe it is the silence of the One you know could stop it.
Mark tells us:
“καὶ γίνεται λαῖλαψ μεγάλη ἀνέμου...”
Kai ginetai lailaps megalē anemou...
“And there arises a great storm of wind...” — Mark 4:37.

The expression λαῖλαψ μεγάλη—lailaps megalē—describes no gentle inconvenience. Mark is describing a great, violent windstorm. Then he says the waves were breaking into the boat until the boat was already filling.
This was not nervous disciples overreacting to a little bad weather.
The boat was taking on water.
And some of the men inside that boat were fishermen.
Peter and Andrew had made their living with nets. James and John had worked the water with their father. Boats were not foreign territory to them.
Yet something happened that night that brought these men to the edge of themselves.
And sometimes that is exactly where we finally discover who Jesus is.
Because you can know how to handle boats and still meet a storm your experience cannot handle.
You can know how to manage money and still receive a bill you cannot pay.
You can understand relationships and still watch your marriage fracture.
You can raise children faithfully and still cry over a son or daughter walking away.
You can know Scripture and still experience nights when your hands shake.
You can love Jesus and still become afraid.
Faith does not mean pretending the waves are small.
Biblical faith looks directly at the waves and discovers that Christ is greater.
But there is another detail Mark refuses to let us miss.
“καὶ αὐτὸς ἦν ἐν τῇ πρύμνῃ... καθεύδων.”
Jesus was in the stern...
sleeping.
There He was.
The boat filling.
The disciples panicking.
The wind roaring.
Jesus sleeping on a cushion.
And eventually the disciples could not endure the silence anymore.
They woke Him.
But listen carefully to what came out of their mouths, because this is where an ancient storm suddenly becomes painfully modern.
“Διδάσκαλε, οὐ μέλει σοι ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα;”
Didaskale, ou melei soi hoti apollymetha?
“Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?”
Do You not care?
There it is.
The question beneath so many questions.
God, do You care?
Maybe you have never spoken those exact words.
Maybe you were too afraid to.
But perhaps you have felt them.
When the diagnosis came.
When somebody you trusted betrayed you.
When the person you begged God to heal died anyway.
When your marriage became cold.
When your child stopped believing.
When the job disappeared.
When the loneliness became unbearable.
When temptation returned after you promised God it never would.
When you prayed sincerely...
and nothing seemed to move.
“Jesus...
do You not care?”
Notice what the disciples assumed.
Jesus was silent, therefore Jesus was indifferent.
Jesus was sleeping, therefore Jesus was unconcerned.
Jesus had not stopped the storm, therefore perhaps Jesus did not care about them.
We still make that mistake.
We interpret God through the weather.
When circumstances are peaceful, God must be near.
When circumstances become violent, God must have abandoned us.
But the Gospel refuses that equation.
Because Jesus was in the boat.
The storm was real.
And His presence was real at the same time.
That matters.
Following Jesus never came with a promise that storms would avoid you.
In fact, this storm occurred after the disciples obeyed Him.
Jesus Himself had said, “Let us go across to the other side.”
They were not in that water because they had rebelled against Christ.
They were there because they followed Him.
Some storms are consequences of foolishness.
Some storms expose sin.
Some storms result from living in a fallen world.
And sometimes obedience itself carries you into circumstances you never would have chosen.
So do not automatically interpret difficulty as proof that you missed God.
The disciples were exactly where Jesus had led them...
and waves were still entering the boat.
Then Jesus awakened.
Mark says He rebuked the wind and spoke to the sea:
“Σιώπα, πεφίμωσο.”
Siōpa, pephimōso.
“Silence. Be still.”
The second command carries the force of being restrained or muzzled.
And creation obeyed its Creator.
The wind stopped.
The waves settled.
And Mark writes:
Kai egeneto galēnē megalē.
“And there was a great calm.”
Do you see what Mark has done?
A great storm.
Then a great calm.
But the story is not finished.
Because something greater than both was standing inside the boat.
Jesus.
The disciples had been terrified of the storm.
Now they looked at Jesus with another kind of fear and asked:
“Τίς ἄρα οὗτός ἐστιν...?”
“Who then is this...?”
Because even the wind and the sea obey Him.
That is the question Mark wants echoing inside us.
Who is this?
Not merely, “How can I survive my storm?”
Not merely, “How can Jesus improve my circumstances?”
Not merely, “How quickly can God make my life comfortable again?”
Who...
is...
this?
The miracle points beyond itself to the identity of Christ.
The Scriptures of Israel repeatedly portray the LORD as sovereign over the waters. Psalm 107 describes sailors caught in a storm, crying to the LORD in their distress, and God stilling the storm.
Then Mark shows Jesus standing in a boat and commanding wind and sea.
And they obey Him.
This story is not ultimately telling you to discover the sleeping giant within yourself.
It is not teaching that positive thinking can silence your storms.
It is not promising Christians that every cancer will disappear, every marriage will be restored, every financial crisis will vanish, or every prayer will receive the answer we demand.
That would turn Jesus into a technique.
The Gospel gives us something infinitely greater.
Jesus Himself.
The One in the boat is Lord.
And this becomes even more breathtaking when you realize that the same Jesus who commanded the sea would later refuse to escape another storm.
There would come another darkness.
Another terrifying hour.
Another moment when His followers would scatter.
But this time Jesus would not rebuke the violence directed toward Him.
He would be betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crowned with thorns.
Nailed to a Roman cross.
And while He possessed authority to escape, He remained.
Why?
Because there was a storm deeper than weather threatening humanity.
Sin.
Guilt.
Judgment.
Death.
Our greatest problem was never merely what was happening around us.
It was what sin had done within us and between us and our holy God.
We needed more than calmer circumstances.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed redemption.
We needed a Savior.
And Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The hands that commanded the sea would be pierced.
The voice that silenced the wind would cry from the cross.
The One whom creation obeyed would willingly humble Himself unto death.
Not because He was powerless.
Because He loved.
And the cross answers the accusation hidden inside the disciples’ frightened question:
“Do You not care?”
Look at Calvary.
There is your answer.
He cares enough to bleed.
He cares enough to bear sin.
He cares enough to enter death.
He cares enough to save people who could never save themselves.
Then came the morning that changed everything.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
Sin did not win.
Death did not win.
The grave did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “Jesus will calm every storm.”
Sometimes He does.
Sometimes the storm continues longer than we understand.
Sometimes God delivers us from suffering.
Sometimes He sustains us through suffering.
And every Christian eventually encounters the final storm of death unless Christ returns first.
Our hope is not that believers never encounter storms.
Our hope is that nothing—not suffering, not Satan, not sin, not death itself—can overthrow the risen Christ.
Maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needed tonight.
You have been measuring God's love by the waves.
Stop for a moment.
Look again at the boat.
Jesus was sleeping...
but He had not left.
His silence was not His absence.
His sleep was not indifference.

And although we should be careful not to force every detail of this historical account into an allegory about our individual circumstances, the identity revealed in that boat remains the foundation of Christian hope:
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Maybe your storm right now is something nobody knows about.
Everyone sees your profile picture.
Nobody sees what happens after you put your phone down.
They see you at church.
They do not see you sitting alone afterward.
They hear you say, “God is good.”
They do not hear the questions you whisper at 2:17 in the morning.
Maybe you have become very good at appearing spiritually strong while quietly drowning.
Maybe the water has been entering your boat for months.
Pornography you keep deleting and returning to.
Bitterness you have learned to justify.
A marriage you no longer know how to repair.
A secret relationship.
An addiction.
Fear.
Grief.
Debt.
Shame.
A private compromise nobody knows about.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
Or maybe something even more frightening:
You still know Christian language...
but your heart has slowly become cold toward Christ.
Listen.
Do not waste your storm by merely asking Jesus to make your circumstances easier.
Ask the deeper question.
“Who then is this?”
And when Scripture answers...
respond.
Repent.
Come home.
Stop hiding.
Jesus did not die so that you could decorate your chains with religious language.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace brings sinners to the Savior who forgives, restores, and transforms.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Christ who paid what you could never pay.
Maybe your scandal is known by everybody.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe the scandal is not something you did but something done to you, and you have been carrying wounds that were never yours to deserve.
Either way, Jesus is not intimidated by ruined stories.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The disciples panicked in a boat with the Lord of creation only a few feet away.
Yet grace kept writing.
That is the heartbeat of everything we proclaim at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by removing repentance from the Gospel.
Jesus rewrites everything by entering the truth of our sin and brokenness with a cross, an empty tomb, forgiveness, reconciliation, and resurrection power.
Maybe you came to this article because the title sounded dramatic.
Maybe you stayed because somewhere between that boat and your own life, you recognized yourself.
Then do not leave unchanged.
If there is hidden sin, bring it into the light before Christ.
If you have wandered, return.
If you are exhausted, cry out to Him.

If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, understand what Christianity is actually announcing: you cannot rescue yourself from sin, but Christ died for sinners and rose again. Turn to Him. Trust Him. Follow Him.
And if your faith feels battered tonight, perhaps your prayer does not need impressive language.
Maybe all you can say is:
“Jesus, I need You.”
He is worthy of that surrender.
Your comment might become the sentence another struggling believer reads and realizes, “I am not the only one.”
And please do not keep this article trapped on your screen.

Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not. Salvation is by God's grace, not social-media activity. But if this truth can point one frightened person toward Jesus, one wandering believer toward repentance, one exhausted Christian toward Scripture, or one unbelieving friend toward the Gospel, sharing becomes a simple opportunity to glorify God by making Christ known.
The friend who stopped talking about what hurts.
The brother who is quietly drifting.
The woman who keeps saying she is okay when you know she is not.
The believer who needs to remember that a violent storm does not dethrone Jesus.
Because someday the water may rise again, and you may need to remember what frightened fishermen learned in the darkness:
The storm can be terrifying...
and Jesus can still be Lord.
Your support can help this message travel farther.
Because somewhere tonight...
someone is sitting inside a storm.
Someone believes God's silence means God does not care.
Someone is watching the water rise.
Someone is seconds away from giving up.
And perhaps the truth they desperately need is the truth frightened fishermen discovered two thousand years ago:
The greatest revelation in the boat was not that the storm could stop.
It was that Jesus was in the boat.
And the greatest hope of the Gospel is not that Jesus will make every chapter painless.
It is that sin does not get to write the ending.
Shame does not get to write the ending.
Failure does not get to write the ending.
Your worst night does not get to write the ending.
The grave does not get to write the ending.
Jesus does.
And when Jesus holds the final word, even a story drowning in darkness can still end in grace.
The storm was loud enough to make them believe they were dying—but it was never loud enough to make Jesus stop being Lord.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON’S MOTHER WAS TOLD NOT TO DRINK WINE WHILE CARRYING THE CHILD GOD HAD CHOSEN
paragraphs: SAMSON’S MOTHER WAS TOLD NOT TO DRINK WINE WHILE CARRYING THE CHILD GOD HAD CHOSEN

Before Samson ever tore apart a lion, carried the gates of Gaza, loved Delilah, lost his hair, lost his eyes, or brought a Philistine temple crashing down… God was already speaking about his life while he was still in his mother’s womb.
There is something haunting about the beginning of Samson’s story.
Most people remember the muscles.
The lion.
The jawbone.
The gates ripped from the ground.
Delilah.
The haircut.
The betrayal.
The blindness.
The final prayer.
The collapsing temple.
But Scripture begins Samson’s story somewhere far quieter.
Before Samson became strong enough to terrify armies, there was a woman carrying the weight of years of disappointment.
She was barren.
Scripture does not even give us her name.
It introduces her simply as Manoah’s wife.
No child.
No pregnancy.
No little feet running through the house.
No son to carry the family forward.
Then God interrupted the silence.
An angel of the LORD appeared to her and announced that the woman who had been unable to conceive was going to bear a son.
And then came an instruction that is easy to rush past:
“Now therefore beware, I pray thee, and drink not wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing.” — Judges 13:4, KJV
The Hebrew is even more striking:
וְעַתָּה֙ הִשָּׁ֣מְרִי נָ֔א וְאַל־תִּשְׁתִּ֖י יַ֣יִן וְשֵׁכָ֑ר וְאַל־תֹּאכְלִ֖י כָּל־טָמֵֽא
Ve'attah hishameri na, ve'al-tishti yayin vesheikhar, ve'al-tokhli kol-tame.
“Now therefore, please be careful: do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.”
The word יַיִן — yayin means wine.
שֵׁכָר — shekhar refers to strong or intoxicating drink.
But perhaps the word that deserves our attention first is הִשָּׁמְרִי — hishameri.
Be careful.
Guard yourself.
Watch yourself.
Why?
Because something had changed.
She was about to carry something consecrated to God.
The angel continued:

“For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.” — Judges 13:5, KJV
Read that again slowly.
From the womb.
Before Samson could understand his calling, God had already spoken over it.
Before he could make a decision, before he could fight a battle, before anyone could applaud his strength or condemn his failures, his life had been touched by divine purpose.
The Hebrew says:
כִּֽי־נְזִ֧יר אֱלֹהִ֛ים יִֽהְיֶ֥ה הַנַּ֖עַר מִן־הַבָּ֑טֶן
Ki-nezir Elohim yihyeh hana'ar min-habaten.
“For the boy shall be a Nazirite of God from the womb.”
נְזִיר — nazir.
One separated.
Consecrated.
Set apart.

This connects Samson’s story with the Nazirite idea described in Numbers 6, although Samson’s unusual lifelong calling in Judges 13 has its own particular features. We should therefore be careful not to force every detail of Numbers 6 onto Samson’s story.
And notice something especially important.
Judges 13 specifically records the command concerning wine and strong drink being given to Samson’s mother while she was carrying him.
That detail matters.
God was not merely announcing what Samson would someday do.
God was preparing the environment into which Samson would be born.
And suddenly this ancient story begins to feel uncomfortable.
Because we love talking about destiny.
We love promises.
We love hearing that God has a purpose.
We love Jeremiah 29:11 printed on coffee mugs.
We love declarations about calling.
But Judges 13 whispers something our generation does not always want to hear:
Sometimes purpose comes with boundaries.
Sometimes calling requires surrender.
Sometimes God says, “I am going to do something through this life,” and then immediately begins rearranging what surrounds that life.
Not because every restriction found in Samson’s story is a universal command for every Christian.
It is not.
Judges 13 is describing a specific divine calling in a specific redemptive-historical situation.
But the principle underneath it should still make us examine ourselves.
What are we unwilling to surrender even when God is calling us closer?
That question goes much deeper than alcohol.
This passage should not be twisted into saying that every Christian must follow Samson’s mother’s dietary instructions.
That would go beyond Scripture.
The deeper confrontation is this:
What happens when the God we call “Lord” touches something we wanted to keep under our own control?
Our habits.
Our relationships.
Our entertainment.
Our secret conversations.
Our appetites.
Our bitterness.
Our pride.
Our money.
Our sexuality.
Our screens.
Our ambitions.
Our hidden compromises.
We sometimes want God’s purpose without God’s authority.
We want anointing without surrender.
Calling without consecration.
Deliverance without discipline.
Resurrection without a cross.
But Jesus never invited people merely to admire Him.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” — Matthew 16:24, KJV
And here is where Samson’s story becomes painfully human.
Because Samson was chosen…
but Samson was not flawless.
Far from it.
The child announced by an angel eventually became a man repeatedly pulled by appetite.
He possessed astonishing physical strength while displaying devastating moral weakness.
He could tear a lion apart.
But some desires inside himself were harder to conquer.
He could defeat enemies surrounding him.
But he struggled with the enemy within him.
And maybe that is why his story still reaches across thousands of years and grabs us by the chest.
Because some of us know exactly what that feels like.
You love God…
but there is something you keep returning to.
You know Scripture…
but there is a private battle nobody sees.
People think you are strong.
They call you faithful.
They come to you for encouragement.
You smile.
You worship.
You post verses.
You tell everyone else, “God is faithful.”
And somewhere behind the screen there is a part of you whispering:
“If they knew what I was fighting, would they still think I was strong?”
Samson knew what it was to carry calling and contradiction in the same body.
And eventually the contradiction became catastrophe.
Delilah entered the story.
The secret was exposed.
The hair was cut.
The Philistines seized him.
His eyes were gouged out.
The mighty Samson became a prisoner.
The man who had once carried city gates on his shoulders was now being led around by others.
Imagine the darkness.
No applause.
No victories.
No crowds celebrating his strength.
Only chains.
Regret.
Memory.
And blindness.
Perhaps he remembered the things his parents had told him.
The angel.
The promise.
The calling.
The consecration.
Perhaps he remembered what his life was supposed to have been.
And there are people reading this who know that kind of grief.
Not blindness.
Not Philistine chains.
Something quieter.
You remember who you used to be with God.
You remember praying differently.
You remember when worship made you cry.
You remember when sin bothered you faster.
You remember when opening the Bible was not an obligation.
You remember when you could feel conviction and respond immediately.
Then something happened.
Maybe slowly.
Maybe secretly.
Maybe repeatedly.
And now you sometimes look at your spiritual life and wonder:
“How did I get here?”
But there is a sentence buried inside Samson’s darkest chapter that sounds almost like God whispering through the ruins.
“But the hair of his head began to grow again after it was shaven.” — Judges 16:22, KJV
The hair began to grow again.
What a sentence.
The consequences had not disappeared.
His eyes did not suddenly return.
His captivity was real.
His failures were real.
His suffering was real.
Scripture does not pretend otherwise.
But the story was not finished.
And neither is yours simply because you have failed.
Samson eventually prayed:
“O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once…” — Judges 16:28, KJV
Listen to that prayer.
Not the voice of the swaggering warrior.
Not the confident champion.
A broken man calling upon God.
“Remember me.”
And God heard him.
This does not make Samson’s sins insignificant.
Grace never requires us to pretend sin was harmless.
Biblical grace is far more powerful than denial.
Grace looks directly at the wreckage and says that sin does not get the final word when a sinner turns toward God.
And that brings us beyond Samson.
Because Samson can point us toward our need for a greater Deliverer.
Samson began to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
Jesus came to save His people from their sins.
Samson’s calling was announced before his birth.
Christ’s coming fulfilled promises God had been unfolding across generations.
Samson stretched out his arms in death and killed his enemies.
Jesus stretched out His arms on a Roman cross and prayed for His enemies.
Samson's death brought destruction upon the Philistines gathered around him.
Christ's death accomplished redemption for sinners, and His resurrection proclaimed that death itself would not have the final word.
Samson was a deeply flawed deliverer.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Savior.
That distinction changes everything.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings becoming strong enough to rescue themselves.
It is the story of sinners who could not rescue themselves being pursued by a Savior who could.
Maybe your scandal is not Samson’s scandal.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe it lives in browser history.
Maybe it lives in a bottle.
Maybe in bitterness.
Maybe in an affair nobody discovered.
Maybe in pornography.
Maybe in pride dressed like spirituality.
Maybe in resentment toward somebody you have smiled at every Sunday.
Maybe you have been pretending for so long that you almost forgot you were pretending.
Jesus already knows.
And still the Gospel calls you.
Not to hide better.
To come into the light.
Not to excuse sin.
To repent.
Not to punish yourself until you feel worthy again.
To trust the One who bore judgment for sinners at the cross.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will take you back.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Christ and calls sinners to repent and believe.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, failure does not have to become your identity.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to rename you.
Your shame does not sit on the throne.
Your addiction does not own the final sentence.
Your past cannot overrule the blood of Christ.
Your scandal does not outrank His grace.
This is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation’s sake.
Repentance is coming home to truth.
It is finally dropping the mask.
Finally opening the locked room.
Finally saying:
“Jesus, this is what I have become. This is what I did. This is what I keep fighting. I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me.”
And there is mercy in Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But do not keep running from Jesus.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another wounded person realize there is still hope.
Not for an algorithm.
For the person.
The quiet person.
The ashamed person.
The believer who still attends church but feels spiritually numb.
The father carrying a secret battle.
The mother crying after everyone goes to sleep.
The young person convinced one terrible decision ruined everything.
The Christian who thinks God could never use them again.
Because there may come a night when the person who needs to reread it is you.
There is another way you can stand with this ministry as well.
It does not.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It cannot.
Scripture gives us no right to say that.
The New Testament teaches generosity that comes from the heart rather than coercion: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful way to use what God has entrusted to us for ministry.
Whether you support financially or not, please pray.
Share Scripture.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
And never confuse supporting a ministry with belonging to Christ.
Your hope is not Gospel Warrior.
Your hope is Jesus.
Jesus can.
A donation cannot reconcile you to God.
Jesus can.
Religious activity cannot resurrect a dead heart.
Jesus can.
And perhaps that is the most important thing Samson’s story leaves echoing inside us.
A person can be called and still stumble.
Gifted and still vulnerable.
Strong in public and bleeding in private.
Consecrated and still desperately dependent upon God.
So do not build your identity around how strong you think you are.
Build your life upon Christ.
If you are standing, depend on Him.
If you are slipping, call upon Him.
If you have fallen, repent and turn toward Him.
If shame has blinded you to hope, remember the cross.
And if the enemy keeps whispering that your story ended at the moment of your greatest failure…
remember Samson sitting in the darkness.
Remember the chains.
Remember the regret.
Then remember one quiet sentence:
The hair began to grow again.
Not because Samson deserved another moment of strength.
Because God was not finished accomplishing His purposes.

And for everyone who belongs to Jesus, your confidence is greater still—not in hair growing back, not in human strength returning, but in a crucified and risen Savior whose grace is greater than your ability to destroy yourself.
So come back.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
There is blood enough at Calvary for sinners.
There is grace enough in Christ for the ashamed.
There is forgiveness for those who repent and believe.
There is a Savior whose scars declare that sin is serious, judgment is real, mercy is costly, and redemption was purchased.
And when Jesus takes hold of a ruined story, the scandal may remain part of the testimony…
but it no longer gets to write the ending.
Your darkest chapter may explain where you have been, but only Jesus has the authority to write what grace makes possible next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Yes, the Bible Talks About Mutual Sexual Responsibility in Marriage
paragraphs:
Yes, the Bible Talks About Mutual Sexual Responsibility in Marriage
What Paul Said Was Shockingly Mutual in a World Where Marriage Could Easily Become One-Sided
There is a verse in the Bible that some husbands have quoted loudly.
And some wives have heard painfully.
But sometimes the tragedy is not that Scripture said something cruel.
The tragedy is that someone stopped reading halfway through the sentence.
Because when Paul spoke about sexual responsibility inside marriage, he did something remarkably important.
He made it mutual.
Not merely the wife toward the husband.
The husband toward the wife.
Not one body demanding access to another.
Two people belonging to one another in a covenant where selfishness is supposed to keep dying.
And once you see what Paul actually wrote, it becomes much harder to use this passage as a weapon.
Listen carefully:
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
Then Paul continues:
“For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
—1 Corinthians 7:3–4
That word “likewise” matters.
In Greek, Paul repeatedly uses language of reciprocity.
The phrase ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ (homoiōs de kai) carries the force of “likewise also.”
He does not establish one rule for women and another convenient rule for men.
He turns the responsibility around and places it on both.
And that matters more than many Christians realize.
Because biblical marriage was never supposed to become a sanctuary for sanctified selfishness.
Your wedding vows did not give you permission to stop caring about the heart of the person whose hand you held at the altar.
Marriage does not magically make selfishness holy.
A marriage certificate cannot baptize manipulation.
And Scripture should never be twisted into permission to pressure, intimidate, humiliate, threaten, punish, or force a spouse sexually.
Paul's words about mutual responsibility are precisely that:
mutual.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 7:3 is striking:
τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί
A close rendering is:
“Let the husband render to the wife what is due, and likewise also the wife to the husband.”
Notice who Paul addresses first.
The husband.
Before telling the wife what she owes her husband, Paul tells the husband that he has a responsibility toward his wife.

That alone should make us reconsider every version of Christian marriage where the husband's desires matter enormously while the wife's emotional, relational, and sexual well-being barely enters the conversation.
But Paul goes even further.
In verse 4, he writes:
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή
The startling part comes again:
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνήρ
“Likewise also the husband.”
Whatever responsibility Paul describes for the wife, he immediately places a corresponding responsibility upon the husband.
That destroys the interpretation in which the woman exists merely to satisfy the man.
But it also challenges the opposite extreme in which either spouse treats physical intimacy as irrelevant to the marriage.
Christian marriage is neither sexual entitlement nor sexual indifference.
It is covenantal self-giving.
And then Paul says something else that must not be conveniently forgotten:
“Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time…”
—1 Corinthians 7:5
By agreement.
The Greek word is:
συμφώνου — symphōnou
It carries the idea of mutual agreement or consent.
It is related to the word from which English gets “symphony.”
Think about that.
Paul's picture is not one spouse conducting while the other is treated like an instrument.
There is mutuality.
Agreement.
A shared life.

This does not mean every desire must always be fulfilled immediately. Human beings are not machines. Illness is real. Exhaustion is real. Trauma is real. Pregnancy and postpartum recovery are real. Disability is real. Hormonal changes are real. Medication effects are real. Grief is real. Emotional wounds are real. Seasons of extraordinary stress are real.
And love notices.
Love listens.
Love does not stare at a hurting spouse and say, “But you owe me.”
That is not how Christ loves His people.
The same New Testament that speaks about marital responsibility commands husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25
Read those words again.
Gave himself up for her.
Christian headship can never biblically mean, “How much can I extract from you?”
Its model is Jesus Christ.
And Jesus went to a cross.
The pattern is sacrifice.
Self-giving.
Tenderness.
Holiness.
Love.
Paul later tells husbands to love their wives “as their own bodies” and reminds them that nobody normally hates his own flesh but nourishes and cherishes it.
Peter commands husbands to live with their wives “in an understanding way” and to show honor to them as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
The Bible's vision is therefore far richer than:
“You owe me sex.”
That reduction is not biblical maturity.
It is biblical amputation.
You cannot cut 1 Corinthians 7 away from the character of Christ and then claim that whatever remains represents Christian marriage.
Jesus changes the atmosphere of the entire conversation.
Maybe that exposes something uncomfortable.
Perhaps you have been the spouse who felt rejected so many times that resentment quietly moved into the bedroom.
Perhaps you stopped asking what your husband or wife was experiencing and started keeping score.
Three days.
Two weeks.
A month.
Maybe every rejection began sounding like:
“You're undesirable.”
“You're unwanted.”
“You don't matter anymore.”
And eventually you became angry.
Or cold.
Or tempted.
Or distant.
Those feelings should not automatically be mocked.

Persistent sexual rejection can deeply wound a marriage. Scripture does take marital intimacy seriously. A spouse should not casually weaponize affection or sexual intimacy as punishment, leverage, manipulation, or control.
But pain does not give us permission to become cruel.
Your wound does not authorize another wound.
Maybe you are standing on the other side of this story.
You are the spouse who keeps withdrawing.
Not because you stopped caring.
Because something happened.
Maybe nobody has asked why.
Maybe intimacy became another obligation in an already exhausting life.
Maybe resentment accumulated beneath conversations that never happened.
Maybe harsh words during the day made tenderness at night feel impossible.
Maybe trust was damaged.
Maybe pornography entered the marriage.
Maybe comparison entered.
Maybe infidelity entered.
Maybe childbirth changed your body.
Maybe illness changed everything.
Maybe you have been silently carrying memories you do not know how to explain.
And the person beside you keeps seeing the symptom without asking about the wound.
This is where Christian marriage has to become more than rule enforcement.
It has to become discipleship.
Two sinners learning to love each other underneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing a husband can do is stop demanding an explanation and start listening.
Sometimes the most loving thing a wife can do is stop pretending nothing is wrong and finally speak.
Sometimes repentance sounds like:
“I have been selfish.”
Sometimes:
“I have been withholding affection to punish you.”
Sometimes:
“I pressured you.”
Sometimes:
“I ignored your loneliness.”
Sometimes:
“I stopped pursuing you emotionally and expected physical intimacy anyway.”
Sometimes:
“I have been comparing you to pornography.”
Sometimes:
“I let resentment grow instead of telling you that I was hurting.”
Sometimes:
“I made you feel undesirable.”
Sometimes:
“I used Scripture to win instead of using Scripture to become like Jesus.”
And sometimes the holiest moment in a bedroom has nothing immediately to do with sex.
It is two people crying.
Confessing.
Forgiving.
Finally telling the truth.
Because before God restores intimacy, He may expose what has been poisoning it.
That is grace.
Not grace that pretends sin never happened.
Grace that brings sin into the light so Jesus can begin rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
This is why Paul's teaching cannot responsibly be summarized as unlimited sexual access.
His actual language emphasizes reciprocal obligation and mutuality.
Neither can the passage responsibly be erased because modern ears find the idea of marital obligation uncomfortable.
Scripture challenges both selfish entitlement and selfish neglect.
The husband matters.
The wife matters.
His loneliness matters.
Her pain matters.
Her desires matter.
His desires matter.
His body is not merely his own.
Her body is not merely her own.

Yet neither statement gives Christians permission to abandon the rest of Christian ethics—love, patience, gentleness, honor, understanding, self-control, sacrificial care, and the imitation of Christ.
And there is another truth we desperately need.
Sex cannot save a marriage.
Jesus can transform the people inside one.
More frequent intimacy cannot cleanse adultery.
It cannot cure pornography addiction.
It cannot substitute for repentance.
It cannot repair cruelty without confession.
It cannot manufacture trust where lies remain hidden.
It cannot replace tenderness.
It cannot resurrect spiritual intimacy when two people refuse to surrender themselves to Christ.
The Gospel goes deeper than behavior modification.
Jesus does not merely rearrange the furniture in broken houses.
He resurrects dead things.
The husband who has sinned sexually does not primarily need better techniques.
He needs repentance.
The wife drowning in bitterness does not merely need motivational advice.
She needs grace.
The couple who have become strangers sleeping inches apart need more than another argument over frequency.
They need truth.
They need forgiveness.
They need wisdom.
Sometimes they need qualified pastoral counsel.
Sometimes they need professional medical or therapeutic help.
And above everything else, they need Jesus Christ at the center rather than merely invoked as ammunition during arguments.
Because marriage was never meant to become two people screaming:
“Give me what I deserve.”
At the center of Christianity stands Someone who gave Himself for people who could never deserve Him.
Jesus.
Betrayed.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Crucified.
Bearing sin.
Offering mercy.
Calling sinners to repentance.
Rising from the grave.
And saying that our old lives do not have to write the final chapter.
That changes marriage.
When Christ enters the room, the question slowly changes from:
“What am I entitled to receive?”
to:
“How can I love you faithfully before God?”
And the other spouse has to ask the same question.
That is mutual responsibility.
Not one person disappearing.
Not one person dominating.
Two people learning to surrender selfishness to Christ.
Maybe this article found you because your marriage looks beautiful on Facebook and painfully different when the phone screen goes dark.
Nobody knows.
Church sees the smiles.
Family sees the anniversary pictures.
Friends see the vacation.
God sees the bedroom door close.
He sees the rejection.
He sees the pressure.
He sees the resentment.
He sees the tears nobody posts.
He sees the browser history.
He sees the conversations you deleted.
He sees the loneliness beside someone who once promised never to leave.
And still—
grace is standing at the door.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that tells you to continue destroying each other.
Grace that calls you into the light.
Grace that says repent.
Grace that says forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Grace that says get help.
Grace that says stop hiding.
Grace that says your worst chapter does not have to become your last chapter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers the details.
But you can take one small step toward honesty.
And if repentance is what God is pressing into your heart, you can simply write:
Not “change my spouse first.”
Me.
That prayer can become dangerous to selfishness.
Not because every marriage problem can be solved by rereading a Facebook post, but because there may come a night when anger returns and you need to remember that your spouse is not your enemy.
Send it privately to the couple nobody realizes is struggling.
And even send it to the believer who has heard 1 Corinthians 7 quoted before but has never stopped long enough to notice Paul's repeated:
“likewise.”

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to Jesus, confront sin, or keep fighting for your faith, following and supporting this ministry helps that message continue reaching people who may never walk voluntarily through the doors of a church.
And if you genuinely want to glorify God through what you have received here, don't let conviction terminate with you.
Pass truth forward.
Sharing costs nothing, but somebody on your Facebook feed may desperately need the message you almost scrolled past.
Invite your husband.
Invite your wife.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who has questions nobody at church has been willing to answer honestly.
Go look at your spouse.
Not as an obligation.
Not as an opponent.
Not as a body that exists to satisfy you.
Look at the person whose weaknesses you know better than almost anybody else's.
Then remember:
Christ knows yours even better.
And He still calls you toward grace.
Maybe tonight does not need another argument.
Maybe it needs confession.
Maybe it needs listening.
Maybe it needs an apology.
Maybe it needs a doctor's appointment.
Maybe it needs counseling.
Maybe it needs forgiveness that will take time.
Maybe it needs boundaries and safety where harm has occurred.
Maybe it needs two trembling hands reaching across a bed that has felt like an ocean.
And maybe the first words do not have to be impressive.
Maybe they can simply be:
“I don't want us to keep living like this.”
Then pray.
Tell the truth.
Seek help where needed.
Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive without pretending wounds were insignificant.
Learn your spouse again.
And let Jesus enter the places embarrassment taught you to keep locked.
Because the scandal is that sinners can hurt the people they promised to cherish.
But the grace is that Christ still transforms sinners who come into the light.
The marriage you are fighting over may be waiting for both of you to stop asking who owes more—and start asking who is willing to look more like Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WILL THERE BE NO MORE SEA IN THE NEW EARTH?
paragraphs:
WHY WILL THERE BE NO MORE SEA IN THE NEW EARTH?
The Strange Promise in Revelation That Is Far More Personal Than You Think
Imagine opening your eyes in a world where nobody is dying.
No hospital rooms.
No graves.
No cancer diagnosis whispered across a desk.
No child standing beside a coffin trying to understand why someone they loved is not coming home.
No betrayal waiting in your messages.
No war.
No funeral clothes.
No nightmares from something that happened twenty years ago.
No temptation stalking you when nobody else is watching.
No Satan.
No curse.
No hiding.
No goodbye.
And then John tells us something unexpected.
There is no sea.
Of all the things God could have shown him about the New Earth, why mention that?
Why would the Holy Spirit make sure this strange little detail survived almost two thousand years so that you would eventually read it?
Because perhaps the sentence is carrying far more weight than we first realize.
John writes in Revelation 21:1:
Kai eidon ouranon kainon kai gēn kainēn … kai hē thalassa ouk estin eti.
In straightforward English:
“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth … and the sea was no more.”
The crucial Greek words are hauntingly simple:
ἡ θάλασσα — hē thalassa — “the sea.”
οὐκ ἔστιν ἔτι — ouk estin eti — “is no longer,” or “is not anymore.”
John does not say the sea became cleaner.
He does not say it became calmer.
He says it will be no more.
Before we race toward symbolism, we need enough humility to let Scripture say exactly what Scripture says.

Revelation 21:1 presents the absence of the sea as part of John's vision of the new creation. Christians have debated how literally various details of Revelation should be understood, and Scripture never gives us a sentence saying, “God removes the sea for this one specific reason.”
So we should not pretend God explained something He did not explicitly explain.
But Scripture does give us a remarkable biblical backdrop.
And once you see it, Revelation 21:1 begins to feel less like an obscure geographical detail and more like the final note of a song that began near the opening pages of the Bible.
Go back to Genesis.

Before human rebellion enters the story, before Cain spills Abel's blood, before kingdoms rise and armies march, Genesis 1:2 presents the earth as unformed and empty, with darkness over the face of תְּהוֹם — tehom — “the deep.”
Then God speaks.
Order emerges.
Light breaks through darkness.
Creation responds to its Creator.
The waters are not another god competing against Yahweh. Scripture leaves no room for that pagan idea. The waters are under God's sovereign authority.
And throughout the biblical story, the sea repeatedly appears at moments involving danger, judgment, hostile powers, death, or forces human beings cannot control.
Think about Noah.
Water becomes the instrument through which judgment sweeps across a violently corrupted world.
Think about Israel trapped between Pharaoh and the sea.
There is death behind them.
There appears to be death before them.
Then God makes a road where human beings could never make one.
Israel walks through.
Pharaoh's forces do not.
The sea that looked like Israel's grave becomes the stage upon which God reveals His power to save.
Then Scripture gives us another startling image.
Daniel sees four great beasts emerging from the sea in Daniel 7.
Later, John himself stands in the imagery of Revelation 13 and sees a beast rising out of the sea.
That matters.
The Bible does not teach that oceans themselves are morally evil. God created the seas, rules them, and displays His glory through creation.

But within biblical imagery—especially prophetic and apocalyptic imagery—the turbulent sea can carry associations of chaos, rebellion, hostile kingdoms, danger, death, and everything that seems violently opposed to God's ordered kingdom.
Isaiah 57:20 says the wicked are “like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest.”
The picture is restlessness.
Churning.
Mud.
Filth.
Something that will not become still.
Does that sound strangely familiar?
Because some people reading this have an ocean like that inside them.
Nobody knows.
Your Facebook pictures look fine.
You still answer, “I'm good.”
You still laugh when you're supposed to laugh.
You still go to work.
You may still sit in church.
You may still lift your hands during worship.
But underneath everything…
the water will not stop moving.
Regret comes in waves.
Shame comes in waves.
Temptation comes in waves.
Grief comes in waves.
Memories come in waves.
You think you have finally escaped what happened, and suddenly, at 2:17 in the morning, your mind drags you straight back into it.
Another wave.
Maybe your sea has a name.
Addiction.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Adultery.
Fear.
Pride.
Secret resentment.
The person you lost.
The marriage that collapsed.
The child who walked away.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The sin you promised God you would never commit again.
And you did.
Another wave.
Another failure.
Another apology.
Another night wondering whether God could possibly still want somebody like you.
Now hear something you desperately need to hear.
The Gospel does not begin with you becoming strong enough to swim back to God.
It begins with God coming for people who cannot save themselves.
This is why Jesus Christ must remain at the center of every Christian conversation about the New Earth.
Revelation is not ultimately giving us Christian trivia about future geography.
It is revealing the triumph of the Lamb.
The same Jesus who walked beside the Sea of Galilee.
The same Jesus who stepped into a boat with frightened disciples.
The same Jesus who slept while seasoned fishermen thought they were going to die.
Then He stood.
He rebuked the wind.
He spoke to the sea.
And creation obeyed Him.
The disciples asked the right question:
“What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41).
They were beginning to discover who was standing in their boat.
Not merely another teacher.
Not merely a miracle worker.
Not merely someone who could give inspirational advice for difficult seasons.
The Lord of creation was standing among them.
And then came another storm.
Much darker.
This time Jesus would not merely stand over threatening waters.
He would enter death itself.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserved.
The hands that had calmed storms were nailed open.
The voice that commanded creation cried out from a cross.
The One through whom all things were made allowed sinful men to crucify Him.
And for a moment, scandal seemed to have won.
Jesus was dead.
His body was placed in a tomb.
A stone was rolled across the entrance.
Hope appeared buried.
But Sunday came.
The stone moved.
Christ rose bodily from the dead.
Death discovered that it had swallowed Someone it could not keep.
And that resurrection changes how Christians read the final chapters of Revelation.
Because the New Earth is not God's desperate Plan B after creation failed.
It is the consummation of His redemptive purpose in Christ.
Revelation 21 does not simply tell us what disappears.
It tells us Who arrives.
John hears:
“Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men.”
That is the heartbeat.
God with His people.
Then come words that have carried grieving Christians through cemeteries for centuries:
God will wipe away every tear.
Death will be no more.
Neither will mourning, crying, nor pain remain.
Why?
Because “the former things are passed away.”
Notice the pattern.
The sea is no more.
Death is no more.
Mourning is no more.
Crying is no more.
Pain is no more.
Later in Revelation 22, the curse itself is no more.
This is not merely God redecorating the universe.
This is creation finally liberated from everything that has scarred it.
The Bible begins with humanity living in God's good creation.
Sin enters.
Exile follows.
Death follows.
Thorns follow.
Blood follows.
Graves follow.
And the biblical story moves toward something astonishing:
God does not abandon His creation.
He redeems.
Revelation does not end with redeemed humanity floating forever as disembodied spirits somewhere in the clouds.
John sees the holy city coming down.
God dwells with humanity.
Creation is made new.
And at the center is the Lamb.
Jesus Christ.
That changes the question.
Perhaps instead of only asking, “Will there literally be oceans on the New Earth?” we should also ask what John desperately wants us to see through the entire vision.
Everything opposed to God's final kingdom is finished.
Every enemy of Christ is defeated.
Every source of death is removed.
Every barrier between God and His redeemed people is gone.
Nothing remains that can threaten the everlasting peace of God's kingdom.
The beast does not rise again.
Babylon does not rebuild.
Death does not escape.
Satan does not get another attempt.
There will never be another Genesis 3.
Think about that.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, there is coming a morning after which you will never sin again.
You will never disappoint your Savior again.
You will never bury someone again.
You will never receive another phone call that makes your knees collapse.
You will never stand beside another hospital bed begging God for one more day.
You will never fight another lustful thought.
You will never feel shame crawling through your chest.
You will never wonder whether you are enough.
You will never watch evil prosper and ask God, “How long?”
You will never say goodbye to another redeemed brother or sister.
Never.
Not because humanity finally learned to fix itself.
Not because politics saved us.
Not because technology defeated mortality.
Not because we became enlightened enough.
Because the Lamb who was slain reigns.
That is Christian hope.
And suddenly “no more sea” becomes part of something breathtaking.
Whatever the full physical configuration of the New Earth will be—and we should resist claiming details God has not revealed—the theological message surrounding John's vision is unmistakable:
God wins.
Christ reigns.
The curse ends.
Death dies.
God dwells with His people.
And everything is made new.
But there is another side to Revelation 21 that our culture does not like discussing.
Not everyone automatically inherits this kingdom.
Grace is free.
Grace is astonishing.

Grace reaches adulterers, liars, addicts, hypocrites, criminals, religious frauds, sexually broken people, angry people, proud people, frightened people, and people whose past would scandalize everyone around them.
But biblical grace never means sin does not matter.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could comfortably make peace with the thing that nailed Him to the cross.
The Gospel calls us to repent and believe.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Perhaps you thought you clicked an article about oceans.
And somewhere along the way, the article started talking about you.
About your hidden sea.
About what keeps churning when everybody thinks you're okay.
You know what it is.
God knows too.
And still Christ calls sinners to Himself.
You do not have to clean yourself before coming to Jesus.
You come because you cannot clean yourself.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the unbelief.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
Repent.
Stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Stop calling darkness harmless because admitting the truth hurts.
Come into the light.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
Because the most beautiful part of Christianity is not that good people eventually earn paradise.
Christianity announces something infinitely better:
Sinners can be forgiven.
Enemies can become children.
The guilty can be justified.
The filthy can be washed.
The dead can live.
The scandal can become a testimony of grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If something in you broke while reading this, don't rush past it.
Be honest.
Your testimony may become the rope God uses to encourage another exhausted believer to keep holding onto Christ.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.

But if biblical truth has strengthened you, supporting its spread can be one practical expression of stewardship. If you genuinely want to glorify God by helping put Christ-centered biblical content in front of people who may never walk voluntarily through a church door, help us carry it farther.
Send it to the person grieving.
Send it to the believer drifting from Christ.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about death.
But before you leave, return once more to John's vision.
One day the last funeral will have already happened.
The last tear will have already fallen.
The last temptation will have already been resisted.
The last believer will have already suffered.
The last grave will have already surrendered its dead.
The last accusation against God's redeemed people will have already been silenced.
The last rebellion will be over.
And the Lamb will still be standing.
Jesus will not merely have brought you through the storm.
He will bring His redeemed people into a creation where the old storm can never return.
So when Revelation whispers those strange words—
ἡ θάλασσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἔτι.
“The sea is no more.”
Do not hear merely the disappearance of water.
Hear the thunderous announcement surrounding the whole vision:
What terrified you does not reign.
What wounded you does not reign.
Your shame does not reign.
Your past does not reign.
The grave does not reign.
Satan does not reign.
Jesus Christ reigns.
And for everyone who is His, the story does not end beneath the waves.
It ends with God dwelling with His redeemed people, tears wiped away, death defeated, the curse gone, and the Lamb reigning forever.
So keep following Christ.
Keep repenting.
Keep believing.
Keep fighting the good fight.
Keep telling people what Jesus has done.
And when the waves rise again tomorrow, remember where the story is going.
The sea may be roaring tonight—but it does not exist on the final page of your redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: God’s Silence Is Not Permission to Rewrite What He Already Said
paragraphs: God’s Silence Is Not Permission to Rewrite What He Already Said
When heaven feels quiet, the most dangerous temptation may not be giving up on God—it may be quietly changing what obedience means so the waiting hurts less.
There is a particular kind of silence that can make even a sincere believer question everything.
You prayed.
Nothing happened.
You waited.
Nothing changed.
You opened your Bible looking for some unmistakable confirmation, some sentence that seemed written specifically for that morning, some sudden peace that would settle the war inside you.
Still… silence.
And eventually a dangerous thought begins whispering:
Maybe God doesn’t expect me to keep obeying when obedience hurts this much.
That thought rarely arrives looking like rebellion.
It usually sounds reasonable.
Compassionate, even.
Maybe the Bible doesn’t really mean that.
Maybe my circumstances are different.
Maybe God understands why I need to compromise here.
Maybe this door opening is His way of telling me the old boundary no longer applies.
Maybe His silence means I am free to decide.
And this is where some of the most consequential spiritual battles happen.
Not when someone stands up and announces, “I reject God.”
But when someone still loves God, still talks about God, still calls Jesus Lord—and slowly begins renegotiating what God has already made clear because waiting has become painful.
Psalm 119:105 gives us a picture that is both beautiful and uncomfortable:
“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.”
The Hebrew reads:
נֵר־לְרַגְלִי דְבָרֶךָ וְאוֹר לִנְתִיבָתִי
Ner-l’ragli devarekha, ve’or lintivati.
Literally, the imagery is striking: God’s word is a נֵר — ner, a lamp, for the psalmist’s feet, and an אוֹר — ’or, a light, for his path.
Notice what the verse does not promise.
It does not say God’s Word is a floodlight illuminating the next twenty years.
It does not promise that you will understand why the road bends.
It does not promise advance explanations for every disappointment.
It does not promise that every prayer will receive an immediate answer.
It gives you something else.
Light enough to walk faithfully.
And maybe that is exactly where this article finds you.
You want the whole map.
God has given you enough light for the next obedient step.
You want an explanation.
Scripture has already given you a command.
You want God to tell you whether His standards still apply in this unusually painful situation.
And somewhere underneath all the questions, you may already know the answer.
You are just exhausted by what that answer costs.
That is different from sincere biblical uncertainty.
There really are questions on which faithful Christians must study carefully, pray humbly, seek wise counsel, examine context, and admit where Scripture does not give us exhaustive detail.
But there are also moments when “I’m still trying to understand” becomes camouflage for “I don’t like what obedience will cost me.”
That distinction matters.
Because God’s silence is not permission to rewrite what God has already said.
Think about Abraham.
God promised him descendants, yet years passed.
His body aged.
Sarah aged.
The promise remained.
The circumstances screamed impossibility.
Then Genesis 16 records one of Scripture’s painfully human moments.
Sarah proposed that Abraham have a child through Hagar.
It made cultural sense.
It solved an obvious biological problem.
It created a path where apparently there was none.
But human urgency attempted to accomplish by human arrangement what God had promised according to His own purpose.
Waiting had become painful enough that an alternative started looking reasonable.
That ancient story still happens in modern clothes.
God says to tell the truth.
But telling the truth might cost you the opportunity.
So you edit it.
God calls His people toward sexual holiness.
But loneliness has lasted longer than you expected.
So you redefine the boundary.
God calls you to forgive.
But the wound still burns.
So bitterness gets renamed “protecting my peace.”
God calls you away from greed.
But everyone around you is chasing more.
So covetousness gets baptized as ambition.
God calls you to integrity.
But integrity threatens the promotion.
So compromise gets renamed wisdom.
God tells us not to repay evil for evil.
But revenge feels satisfying.
So vengeance gets renamed justice.
Do you see how subtle this can become?
Sin rarely walks through the front door introducing itself as sin.
Sometimes it arrives carrying explanations.
Sometimes compromise knows Christian vocabulary.
Sometimes disobedience can even be dressed in the language of peace, opportunity, authenticity, blessing, self-care, destiny, or an “open door.”
But an open door is not automatically God’s door.
A strong feeling is not automatically God’s voice.
A convenient opportunity is not automatically God’s approval.
And silence is not consent.
That sentence may sting because there is something you have been asking God about when, deep down, the question is no longer whether Scripture speaks.
The question is whether you are willing to obey what it says.
Maybe you have been praying:
“God, show me what to do.”
And perhaps the painful reality is that He already has.
Not through a mysterious sign.
Not through a viral prophecy.
Not through circumstances aligning perfectly.
Through His Word.
And you were hoping His silence would eventually become permission to choose something easier.
There is a heartbreaking moment in 1 Samuel 13 that exposes what pressure can do to obedience.
Saul was waiting for Samuel.
The people were scattering.
The enemy threat was real.
Samuel did not arrive when Saul expected.
The pressure increased.
So Saul acted.
He offered the burnt offering.
Then Samuel arrived.
Saul immediately explained himself.
The people were scattering.
Samuel had not arrived at the expected time.
The Philistines were gathering.
Saul felt compelled.
Read the logic carefully.
It sounds painfully familiar.
I was under pressure.
Things weren’t happening quickly enough.
I thought I had to do something.
And Samuel’s response cuts through every excuse.
Saul had not kept the command of the Lord.
Pressure explained Saul’s decision.
It did not transform disobedience into obedience.
That distinction could save someone reading this from a decision they will regret for years.
Your loneliness may explain your vulnerability.
It does not rewrite holiness.
Your financial pressure may explain your temptation.
It does not rewrite honesty.
Your wounds may explain your anger.
They do not automatically sanctify bitterness.
