Your disappointment may explain your doubts.
It does not make God unfaithful.
Your waiting may explain why compromise suddenly looks attractive.
It does not make compromise righteous.
And please hear the Gospel here, because Christianity is not the story of terrified people earning God’s acceptance through flawless performance.
If that were the message, every one of us would be finished.
We have all crossed lines.
We have all rationalized.
We have all known something was wrong and found language sophisticated enough to make ourselves feel better about doing it.
We have all needed mercy.
That is why Jesus Christ is not a footnote to this message.
He is the center of it.
Jesus did what Adam failed to do.
Where humanity rebelled, Christ obeyed.
Where we have compromised, Christ remained faithful.
Where we deserve judgment, Christ willingly went to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God pretending your rebellion never mattered.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin so completely through Jesus Christ that sinners who repent and trust in Him can be forgiven, reconciled, cleansed, and transformed.
Grace does not give us permission to rewrite sin.
Grace gives sinners somewhere to run when sin has already written chapters we wish we could erase.
That is why repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is coming home.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Nobody knows.
Your family does not know.
Your church does not know.
The people who follow you online certainly do not know.
You learned how to smile while carrying it.
You learned which Bible verses to post.
You learned how to answer, “How are you?”
You learned how to look spiritually alive while privately negotiating with something God told you to surrender.
And perhaps the silence has been unbearable because you expected God to make obedience easier.
But what if He is teaching you to trust Him without receiving the explanation first?
Psalm 119 does not describe a believer floating above suffering.
The psalm repeatedly speaks from affliction, opposition, longing, persecution, and distress.
Yet the writer keeps returning to God’s Word.
That changes how Psalm 119:105 lands.
“Your word is a lamp to my feet…”
A lamp matters most when it is dark.
Maybe you are angry because God has only illuminated your next step.
But the next step may be enough.
You do not need to know who you will marry ten years from now to remain faithful tonight.
You do not need to know whether the business will survive to refuse dishonesty today.
You do not need to know when reconciliation will happen to refuse revenge.
You do not need to understand why God allowed the season to choose holiness inside it.
You do not need tomorrow’s explanation to obey today’s light.
And sometimes obedience will feel terribly ordinary.
Delete the conversation.
Tell the truth.
Return what is not yours.
Confess what you have hidden.
Stop feeding the secret relationship.
Apologize without defending yourself.
Forgive without pretending the wound was acceptable.
Walk away from the opportunity that requires you to violate conscience and Scripture.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Go back to church.
Ask mature believers for help.
Keep waiting.
Keep trusting.
Keep walking.
One illuminated step at a time.
And when you fail—and believers still fail—do not turn failure into a new theology that makes repentance unnecessary.
Run to Christ.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
There is forgiveness.
Real forgiveness.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Christ is sufficient.
Maybe that is the word someone desperately needs tonight.
You compromised.
But Jesus has not stopped being Savior.
You wandered.
But the road home is still open.
You made a mess.
But grace can reach into places shame told you were permanently ruined.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
The voice.
The courtyard.
The accusation.
The denial.
Then the rooster.
Luke tells us Jesus looked at Peter.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
It could have been the final scene of Peter’s story.
Scandal.
Failure.
Cowardice.
Shame.
But Jesus was not finished.
After the resurrection, John 21 records Christ restoring Peter and entrusting him again with responsibility toward His sheep.
Peter’s failure was real.
So was Christ’s grace.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Not because Jesus rewrites God’s moral truth to accommodate our scandal.
Because Jesus rewrites the sinner’s future through redemption.
There is a world of difference.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace walks into darkness and rescues people from it.
Jesus does not need to redefine your chains to free you from them.
He breaks chains.
He forgives sinners.
He restores the fallen.
He receives the repentant.
He transforms hearts.
And sometimes the first sound of freedom is a believer finally whispering:
“Lord… I knew.”
“I knew what Your Word said.”
“I was just tired.”
“I was lonely.”
“I was afraid.”
“I wanted the relationship.”
“I wanted the money.”
“I wanted revenge.”
“I wanted control.”
“I wanted the answer now.”
“I wanted my way more than I wanted obedience.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Be honest.
Pray for them.
There is a human soul behind that screen.
Maybe someone needs to discover that Christians can still confess weakness without being devoured by one another.
Maybe someone needs to see a community where grace does not erase truth and truth does not erase compassion.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that their faith is struggling.
Not because following a page saves anybody.
Jesus saves.

But if a page can keep putting Scripture, biblical conviction, encouragement, repentance, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel in front of people who desperately need Christ, helping that message travel is worthwhile.
Scripture calls Christian giving willing rather than coerced; 2 Corinthians 9:7 explicitly rejects giving “under compulsion.”
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
Christ purchased what your works never could.
Share because truth travels through people willing to carry it.
Share because somebody’s smiling profile picture may be hiding a collapsing faith.
Share because somebody is interpreting heaven’s silence as permission.
Share because somebody is about to exchange a clear command for a convenient explanation.
And maybe God will use the Scripture they encounter through something you shared to turn them back before they take another step.
There will be seasons when God seems painfully quiet.
There will be prayers whose answers do not arrive according to your timetable.
There will be doors that remain shut.
There will be relationships you thought God would restore.
There will be opportunities you thought He would provide.
There will be nights when you ask why.
There will be moments when the darkness makes the old boundaries look unreasonable.
When that moment comes, remember the lamp.
נֵר־לְרַגְלִי דְבָרֶךָ וְאוֹר לִנְתִיבָתִי
Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
You may not have the map.
You have the lamp.
You may not have the explanation.
You have His Word.
You may not know when morning comes.
You know who Christ is.
And when you discover that you have wandered outside the light, do not run farther because you are ashamed of how far you went.
Turn around.
Repent.
Come to Jesus.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is forgiveness for the guilty.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is mercy for the prodigal.
There is a cross for sinners.
There is an empty tomb declaring that death does not get the final word.
And there is still enough light for your next step home.
When heaven feels silent, do not rewrite the Word—let the Word rewrite the direction of your feet.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Promotion Didn’t Make You Proud. It Just Gave Your Pride a Bigger Office.
paragraphs: The Promotion Didn’t Make You Proud. It Just Gave Your Pride a Bigger Office.
Success doesn’t always corrupt the heart. Sometimes it simply turns on the lights—and reveals what was already sitting behind the desk.
The email came.
The promotion was yours.

Maybe it wasn’t an office. Maybe it was a title beside your name. A larger salary. More employees answering to you. More people asking for your opinion. A growing ministry. A thriving business. A bigger platform. More followers. More invitations. More influence.
You thanked God.
And perhaps you genuinely meant it.
But somewhere between “Lord, I couldn’t have done this without You” and everyone beginning to treat you like somebody important, something almost invisible started happening.
You became easier to offend.
Correction began sounding like disrespect.
Questions started feeling like challenges to your authority.
People who once felt like friends slowly became people beneath your position.
You still prayed, but sometimes your prayers became strangely concerned with maintaining what you had achieved.
You still served, but only when serving didn’t make you look small.
You still talked about humility, but secretly expected recognition for being humble.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that nobody noticed.
Maybe you didn’t either.
Because pride rarely walks into the room announcing, “I am pride.”
Sometimes it wears a suit.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it has a corner office.
Sometimes it stands behind a pulpit.
Sometimes it says, “After everything I’ve accomplished, I deserve better than this.”
Sometimes it sounds almost reasonable.
That is why success can become such a revealing test of the soul.
Success did not necessarily manufacture the pride.
It may have simply given your pride a bigger office.
Jesus spoke directly into this temptation.

In Mark 10, James and John approached Him with an extraordinary request. They wanted places of prominence in His glory. They were following the Messiah, but ambition was still alive inside their discipleship.
The other disciples became angry when they heard about it.
And then Jesus gathered them together.
What He said should still make every Christian leader, executive, pastor, entrepreneur, manager, creator, parent, ministry worker, and person with influence uncomfortable.
“You know that those who are considered rulers over the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you.”
Then Jesus overturned the entire human definition of greatness:
“But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.”
And then came the sentence that destroys every Christian attempt to baptize ego as leadership:
“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
The Greek underneath this passage makes the confrontation even sharper.
When Jesus describes earthly rulers who “lord it over” people, Mark uses the verb κατακυριεύουσιν — katakyrieuousin, from katakyrieuō: to exercise dominion or mastery over another.
Then Jesus says:
οὐχ οὕτως δέ ἐστιν ἐν ὑμῖν
ouch houtōs de estin en hymin
“But it is not so among you.”
Those words deserve to follow every Christian into every room where power is exercised.
Not so among you.
The world may teach you that reaching the top means finally getting people to serve you.
Not so among you.
Corporate culture may tempt you to measure importance by how many people need your approval.
Not so among you.
Success may whisper that your accomplishments have earned you exemption from ordinary kindness.
Not so among you.

Even religious culture can tempt leaders into believing that because God entrusted them with influence, everyone else exists to protect their comfort, defend their reputation, carry their burdens, and celebrate their importance.
Not so among you.
Jesus gives another definition.
διάκονος — diakonos.
Servant.
Then He goes lower.
δοῦλος — doulos.
Slave. Bondservant.

Jesus is not romanticizing abusive human systems. He is radically reversing the disciples’ hunger for rank. In Christ’s kingdom, greatness is not measured by how successfully you position yourself above people.
It is revealed by what you are willing to become for their good.
And Jesus did not merely teach this.
He became the pattern.
“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve…”
Read that again slowly.
The Son of Man.
The One deserving all glory.
The One before whom every human title eventually becomes meaningless.
He came not to be served.
That sentence should terrify our pride.
Because if Jesus Christ did not consider Himself too important to serve, what promotion could possibly make you too important?
What salary?
What title?
What ministry?
What degree?
What audience?
What accomplishment?
What office door with your name printed across it could ever place you above the posture of your King?
And this is where the article stops being about “prideful leaders.”
Because that category is wonderfully convenient.
It lets us picture somebody else.
Your boss.
Your pastor.
That arrogant executive.
That successful relative.
That person who changed after making money.
But Scripture has an uncomfortable habit of turning the mirror around.
What happens inside you when someone younger corrects you?
What happens when somebody you trained becomes more successful than you?
What happens when another person receives the recognition you thought belonged to you?
What happens when your idea is rejected?
When your employee disagrees?
When nobody thanks you?
When you walk into a room where nobody knows your accomplishments?
When someone fails to use your title?
When another believer receives the opportunity you prayed for?
That reaction inside you may reveal more about your heart than the Christian words coming out of your mouth.
Pride is not merely thinking, “I am amazing.”
Sometimes pride says:
“How dare they treat me like this?”
“Do they know who I am?”
“I shouldn’t have to do that anymore.”
“They should be grateful I’m even here.”
“I deserve recognition.”
“Why wasn’t I mentioned?”
“Why did they promote him?”
“Why is her ministry growing faster?”
“Why does nobody appreciate everything I do?”
And suddenly the promotion becomes a spiritual X-ray.
It exposes something.
Success often reveals character more than it creates character.
When you had little influence, your pride had fewer tools.
Give it money, and now it can compare lifestyles.
Give it authority, and now it can demand obedience.
Give it followers, and now it can become addicted to applause.
Give it ministry influence, and now it can disguise itself as “protecting the calling.”
Give it knowledge, and now it can humiliate people who know less.
Give it success, and now it can rewrite your history until somehow everybody who helped you disappears from the story.
Eventually even God can become a footnote.
“I worked for this.”
“I built this.”
“I earned this.”
“My discipline.”
“My intelligence.”
“My leadership.”
My.
My.
My.
Until the person who once cried, “God, please open a door,” begins walking through opened doors as though God should feel fortunate to have them inside the building.
That is a dangerous place.
Not because success is sinful.
It isn’t.
Scripture contains people entrusted with wealth, responsibility, influence, governmental authority, and leadership.
The danger is not having influence.
The danger is influence having you.
There is nothing inherently holy about being unsuccessful, and nothing inherently sinful about advancement. The question is what your advancement is doing to your heart.
Are you becoming harder to correct?
Or easier?
More entitled?
Or more grateful?
More obsessed with being seen?
Or increasingly willing to serve where nobody applauds?
Do the people beneath your authority experience your success as a blessing—or as something they must survive?
That question hurts.
It should.
Because Christian leadership cannot merely be evaluated from the stage.
Ask the assistant.
Ask the receptionist.
Ask the employee who made the mistake.
Ask the waiter who brought the wrong order.
Ask the cleaner.
Ask the spouse who sees the successful Christian when nobody else is watching.
Ask the children.
Ask the people who cannot advance your career.
How do you treat people who can do absolutely nothing for you?
There is often the truest résumé of your soul.
And then look at Jesus.
The Gospel does not give us a Messiah climbing over people to reach a throne.
It gives us the eternal Son moving toward a cross.

Philippians 2 describes Christ Jesus, who did not exploit His divine status for selfish advantage but humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
The Greek word there is again:
δοῦλος — doulos.
Servant.
Slave.
The King stooped.
The Lord served.
The sinless One suffered.
The One who deserved worship accepted humiliation.
The hands worthy of holding the universe were pierced.
And He did it for sinners.
For proud people.
For ambitious people.
For people addicted to recognition.
For people who secretly need everyone to know how important they are.
For people like us.
That is why Christianity is not simply a command to “be more humble.”
If humility were merely another achievement, pride would eventually boast about accomplishing it.
The Gospel does something deeper.
It brings us to the cross where boasting dies.
At Calvary, you discover simultaneously that your sin is worse than your ego wanted to admit and that Christ's grace is greater than your shame dared to believe.
You were sinful enough that Christ had to die.
You were loved enough that Christ willingly did.
There is no room left for superiority.
And there is no need left for despair.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Maybe success exposed something ugly in you.
Maybe your family has noticed.
Maybe your employees have felt it.
Maybe your spouse has watched you become someone different.
Maybe you have used authority to control instead of serve.
Maybe you have confused intimidation with leadership.
Maybe you have demanded honor you were unwilling to give.
Maybe you have secretly loved being needed because being needed made you feel important.
Maybe ministry became your identity.
Maybe the applause became oxygen.
Maybe you cannot remember the last time you served someone who could never repay you.
Do not hide behind your title.
Bring it into the light.
Repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is coming home.
Jesus Christ does not merely expose pride so He can shame proud people.
He exposes what is killing us so grace can reach what we keep hiding.
Confess it.
Not vaguely.
Not, “Lord, forgive me if I've ever been prideful.”
Name it.
“Jesus, I have wanted recognition more than service.”
“Jesus, I have treated people as beneath me.”
“Jesus, I have resented correction.”
“Jesus, I have taken credit for gifts You gave me.”
“Jesus, I have wanted the seat more than the towel.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And then remember what Christ came to do.
Mark 10:45 says the Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many.”
The Greek word translated “ransom” is λύτρον — lytron: the price paid to secure release.
Jesus was moving the disciples beyond leadership advice toward the heart of the Gospel.
The ultimate Servant would give His own life.
The cross would become the place where sinners who could never purchase their own redemption would be redeemed through Christ.
So you do not conquer pride by pretending you are worthless.
You conquer pride by remembering whose you are.
Everything good in you is grace.
Every ability is stewardship.
Every open door is stewardship.
Every dollar is stewardship.
Every employee is a human being bearing God's image, not a prop in your success story.
Every follower is a soul, not a statistic.
Every position eventually expires.
Every title eventually disappears.
Every office eventually belongs to somebody else.
And one day the question will not be how impressive your name looked underneath your job title.
The question will be what you did with what God placed in your hands.
So perhaps tomorrow you walk into that office differently.
Perhaps you listen before speaking.
Perhaps you apologize to someone you wounded.
Perhaps you thank the employee nobody notices.
Perhaps you stop taking credit for somebody else's work.
Perhaps you allow correction without immediately defending yourself.
Perhaps you serve.
Not perform service.
Serve.
Quietly.
Joyfully.
Without posting about it.
Without needing somebody to notice.
Because your King sees.
And maybe that is enough.

Not because typing words earns forgiveness. It does not. Salvation and forgiveness are gifts of God's grace received through faith in Jesus Christ. But sometimes publicly admitting that God is dealing with us becomes a small act of honesty in a world built around appearances.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It cannot.

But if this message is faithful to Scripture and you believe more people need to encounter Christ-centered truth like this, then supporting and sharing the work can be one practical way to help put that truth in front of another human being.
Someone may need this mirror tonight.
Someone may need to discover that Jesus is not asking them to abandon excellence—He is asking them to surrender the throne.
Come back when the next promotion arrives.
Come back when the applause gets louder.
Come back when people begin treating your opinion as important.
Come back when correction starts irritating you.
And ask yourself:
Did God give me a larger platform to make me larger…
or to give me more people to serve?
It is simply a tangible way for those who value this ministry to help sustain and extend the work.
Follow Jesus.
Repent where pride has taken root.
Receive His grace.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Serve because your King served you.
Use whatever influence God entrusts to you so that people leave your presence seeing more of Christ—not merely more of you.
Because perhaps the greatest evidence that God can trust you with a bigger office is that you are still willing to pick up the towel.
The promotion may have changed the name on your door. Never let it replace the name written across your life: Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Satan Quoted Scripture to Jesus. That Should Make Every Christian Pay Attention.
paragraphs: Satan Quoted Scripture to Jesus. That Should Make Every Christian Pay Attention.
The wilderness temptation of Jesus exposes one of Satan’s most dangerous strategies: sometimes the lie does not arrive looking like a lie. Sometimes it arrives carrying a Bible verse.
There is a moment in the Gospel of Matthew that should unsettle every Christian who has ever assumed that hearing Scripture quoted automatically means hearing truth.
Jesus is standing in the wilderness.
Hungry.
Physically weakened after forty days of fasting.
Alone beneath a merciless sky.
And Satan begins talking to Him about the Bible.
Not atheism.
Not paganism.
Not some obvious invitation to abandon God.
Scripture.
That is what makes this encounter so disturbing.
The devil who tempted Eve with distorted words now stands before the incarnate Son of God and reaches for words God Himself inspired.
And if Satan was willing to quote Scripture to Jesus Christ, Christians should never assume that a Bible verse—merely because it has been quoted—is therefore being used faithfully.
Read that again.
The enemy does not always need to convince you that the Bible is false.
Sometimes he only needs to convince you that the Bible means something God never intended it to mean.
Matthew tells us that after Jesus had fasted forty days and forty nights, He was hungry. Then the tempter approached Him.
The Greek gives him a revealing name:
ὁ πειράζων — ho peirazōn
“The one who tempts,” or “the tempter.”
And his opening words are calculated:
Εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ...
“If You are the Son of God...”
Then comes the challenge:
Command these stones to become bread.
Think about the cruelty hidden inside that temptation.
Jesus really is hungry.
Bread is not evil.
Eating is not sinful.
Jesus possesses divine authority.
So where is the trap?
The temptation is not merely about bread.
It is about whether the Son will trust the Father or seize satisfaction on the tempter’s terms.
Jesus answers from Deuteronomy:
Οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος...
“Man shall not live by bread alone...”
The Hebrew text behind Jesus’ quotation says:
לֹא עַל־הַלֶּחֶם לְבַדּוֹ יִחְיֶה הָאָדָם
Lo al-halechem levado yichyeh ha-adam.
Human beings do not live by bread alone.

Jesus reaches back to Israel’s wilderness experience in Deuteronomy 8:3. Israel had been hungry in the wilderness too. God was teaching His people that their existence ultimately depended not upon what they could grasp for themselves, but upon Him.
And where Israel repeatedly failed in the wilderness, Jesus remains faithful.
But Satan is not finished.
Then something happens that should make every Bible-reading Christian sit upright.
The devil takes Jesus to Jerusalem, places Him at the pinnacle of the temple, and essentially says:
If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down.
And then Satan quotes Scripture.
Psalm 91.
Yes.
Satan quotes a psalm.
He tells Jesus that Scripture says God will command His angels concerning Him and that they will bear Him up.
Imagine hearing Psalm 91 coming from the mouth of the devil.
The words themselves came from Scripture.
The application came from hell.
That distinction can save your spiritual life.
Because a verse can be accurately recited while being dangerously applied.
Satan did not need to manufacture a fake Bible verse.
He needed to weaponize a real one.
He took the language of God’s protection and attempted to turn trust into presumption.
Psalm 91 celebrates the security of the person who takes refuge in God. Satan twists that beautiful promise into a dare: force the Father to prove Himself.
But Jesus knows something many people forget.
Scripture interprets Scripture.
A verse ripped away from the character of God, the broader teaching of Scripture, and its proper context can become a weapon in the hands of someone determined to manipulate.
So Jesus answers:
Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου.
“You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”
Again, Jesus answers from Deuteronomy.
He does not deny Psalm 91.
He refuses Satan’s interpretation of Psalm 91.
That difference is enormous.
Jesus will trust His Father.
He will not manipulate His Father.
Faith says, “God is trustworthy.”
Presumption says, “God must prove Himself on my terms.”
Those two things can sound frighteningly similar when wrapped in religious language.
And that is why this story belongs much closer to your everyday life than you may think.
Because most believers will never hear an audible voice telling them to jump from a temple.
But you may hear:
“God wants you happy.”
And perhaps that sentence becomes permission to abandon holiness.
You may hear:
“Do not judge.”
And perhaps those words are used to silence every loving call to repentance.
You may hear:
“Ask and it will be given to you.”
And suddenly Jesus is treated like a mechanism for acquiring everything your flesh desires.
You may hear:
“I can do all things through Christ.”
And a verse originally spoken from a context of contentment in hardship becomes a slogan promising limitless personal achievement.
You may even hear biblical language used by someone controlling, exploiting, frightening, or spiritually manipulating another person.
The vocabulary can sound Christian.
That does not automatically make the message Christlike.
This is where discernment becomes painfully personal.
Some of the most dangerous lies you will encounter will not begin with:
“Reject Jesus.”
They may begin with:
“Surely God understands.”
“You deserve this.”
“Everybody struggles with it.”
“You can repent afterward.”
“You don't need the church.”
“You don't need accountability.”
“God knows your heart.”
And individually, some of those statements may contain an element of truth.
That is precisely why distortion works.
A counterfeit is most convincing when it resembles what is real.
Perhaps you know this battle.
You know the verse.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say “Amen.”
Your Bible may be highlighted from Genesis to Revelation.
But there is one relationship you keep defending that continually pulls you away from Christ.
One habit you keep renaming so you do not have to call it sin.
One private browser history nobody sees.
One resentment you have baptized as “discernment.”
One appetite that keeps demanding to be fed.
One compromise you keep explaining.
One wound that has slowly become permission to disobey.
And every time conviction gets close, your mind suddenly becomes a defense attorney.
That word has protected many hidden rooms.
But God understands.
But they hurt me first.
But everybody does it.
But I prayed about it.
But I still believe in Jesus.
Maybe you do.
That is why this matters.
The wilderness is not merely a story about obviously wicked people doing obviously wicked things.
It is a confrontation between truth and distorted truth.
And then comes the third temptation.
Satan shows Jesus the kingdoms of the world and their glory and offers them in exchange for worship.
Now the mask comes off.
The destination of temptation is finally exposed.
Worship.
That is where the battle was heading.
Satan offers a kingdom without the road of obedient suffering.
Glory without the cross.
A crown without Calvary.
Possession without submission to the Father.
And Jesus answers:
Ὕπαγε, Σατανᾶ.
“Go away, Satan.”
Then:
Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου προσκυνήσεις καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις.
“You shall worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.”
Only.
There is the line Satan cannot cross.
Jesus belongs wholly to the Father.
And here the wilderness begins pointing us toward something far greater than a lesson about memorizing Bible verses.
Because if all you take from this story is “Jesus used Scripture, so I should memorize Scripture,” you have learned something true—but you have not yet reached the center.
The center is Jesus.
He is the faithful Son.
Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness and repeatedly failed.
Jesus enters the wilderness for forty days and remains obedient.
Adam stood in a garden surrounded by food and fell.
Jesus stands hungry in a wilderness and remains faithful.
And eventually, the obedient Son walks toward another place of suffering.
Not the wilderness.
Golgotha.
There, mockery again circles around His identity as the Son of God.
There, He does not call angels to rescue Him.
There, He does not escape suffering merely because He possesses the power to do so.
There, the faithful Son completes His obedience all the way to death on a cross.
Why?
For sinners like us.
For people who have fallen to temptations far smaller than the ones Jesus resisted.
For people who knew the verse and still clicked.
Knew the command and still crossed the line.
Knew the warning and still returned.
Knew better and did it anyway.
For the hypocrite.
The addict.
The angry believer.
The secret sinner.
The exhausted Christian.
The prodigal who remembers what home smelled like but is ashamed to knock on the door.
For you.
For me.
This is where scandal meets grace.
The scandal is that our sin is worse than the excuses we have created for it.
The grace is that Christ is greater than the sin we finally stop hiding.
Jesus did not overcome temptation so He could stand at a distance and mock everyone who failed.
Hebrews tells us that we have a High Priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses, One who has been tempted yet without sin.
He knows the battlefield.
But unlike us, He never surrendered to the enemy.
And because the sinless Christ went to the cross for sinners and rose again, failure does not have to write the final chapter of your life.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave before you decorate it and call it home.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere between Satan quoting Psalm 91 and Jesus answering from Deuteronomy, something uncomfortable happened inside you.
You remembered something.
A compromise.
A conversation.
A teaching you accepted because it sounded biblical.
A sin you have been justifying with religious language.
A voice you trusted because it knew how to quote verses.
Or perhaps you realized something even more frightening:
You can know Scripture and still use Scripture to protect yourself from surrendering to the God of Scripture.
So ask the harder question.
Not merely:
“Can I find a verse that seems to support what I want?”
Ask:
“Am I actually following Jesus?”
Does this interpretation honor the context of Scripture?
Does it agree with the broader witness of God’s Word?
Does it reflect the character and teaching of Christ?
Does it lead toward holiness, truth, love, humility, repentance, obedience, and worship of God?
Or am I searching the Bible for permission to keep something Jesus is asking me to surrender?
There is a difference between bringing your desires under Scripture and bringing Scripture under your desires.
One creates disciples.
The other creates religious excuses.
And Satan is perfectly comfortable with Bible vocabulary if Bible vocabulary keeps you from biblical obedience.
That should make every Christian pay attention.
Do not merely ask whether someone quoted Scripture.
Ask whether Scripture was handled truthfully.
Do not merely ask whether a preacher sounded powerful.
Ask whether what was preached actually points you toward the biblical Christ.
Do not merely ask whether a message made you feel encouraged.
Sometimes the Holy Spirit comforts.
Sometimes the Word cuts.
Sometimes grace embraces you.
Sometimes grace overturns the tables you built inside your heart.
Real grace does not merely make sinning people comfortable.
Grace saves us and begins transforming us.
And if something has been hiding in you, bring it into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You do not need a polished speech.
You do not need religious theatrics.
You need Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess what you have done.
Stop negotiating with the thing that is destroying you.
Turn toward Jesus.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose victorious.
Not for performance.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
Forgiveness is found in Christ, received by grace through faith.
But sometimes publicly admitting, “I need Jesus,” becomes the moment we finally stop pretending we have everything together.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover they are not the only believer fighting a war nobody else can see.
And send this article to someone you love.
Not as an accusation.
As a warning wrapped in love.
Even share it where a seeker or unbelieving friend may encounter the Christ who refused Satan’s shortcuts and later gave Himself for sinners.
Because temptation rarely schedules an appointment.
There may come a night when you need these words again.
If this ministry genuinely feeds you, consider helping us feed others.
And there is much more available beyond paid products.
If you have been reading quietly for months, perhaps today is the day to stop being only a reader and become part of helping this truth travel farther.
One share can reach the person we never could.
One tag can reach the friend who would never search for an article about temptation.
One honest comment can give another struggling Christian courage to confess.
One saved article can become a lifeline on a difficult night.
And one believer who encounters the real Jesus through the truth of Scripture matters more than numbers on a screen ever will.
Satan quoted Scripture to Jesus.
Jesus answered with Scripture rightly understood, trusted His Father, refused the shortcut, rejected false worship, and walked the road of obedience that would ultimately lead Him toward the cross.
So know your Bible.
But more than collecting verses, learn to read them faithfully.
Know their context.
Test what you hear.
Know the Gospel.
Know the character of God revealed through His Word.
And above everything else, know Christ.
Because the enemy may know how to quote a verse.
But Satan cannot offer you what Jesus purchased at Calvary.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Freedom.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new life.
Grace.
And when your own wilderness exposes chapters you wish had never been written, remember this:
The devil may quote your failures back to you, but he does not get to write your ending—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Did Rebekah Cover Jacob’s Hands With Goat Skins?
paragraphs: Why Did Rebekah Cover Jacob’s Hands With Goat Skins?

The disturbing detail in Genesis 27 wasn’t random. Jacob was about to walk into his blind father’s tent wearing his brother’s clothes, carrying his brother’s smell, and hiding beneath the skin of something that had just died—and what happened next exposes something painfully familiar about the human heart.
There is a moment in Genesis that becomes more unsettling the longer you sit with it.
An old father can barely see.
A mother is moving quickly.
A younger son is wearing clothes that do not belong to him.
Food is being prepared to imitate another son’s cooking.
And then Rebekah does something strangely specific.
She takes the skins of young goats and puts them on Jacob’s hands and around the smooth part of his neck.
The Hebrew of Genesis 27:16 reads:
“וְאֵת עֹרֹת גְּדָיֵי הָעִזִּים הִלְבִּישָׁה עַל־יָדָיו וְעַל חֶלְקַת צַוָּארָיו”
Ve’et ‘orot gedaye ha‘izzim hilbishah ‘al-yadav ve‘al chelqat tzavvarav.
In straightforward English:
“And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.”
That wording matters.

The Hebrew ‘orot means “skins” or “hides.” Gedaye refers to young goats or kids. Hilbishah comes from a verb associated with clothing or putting something on. And chelqat describes the smooth part of Jacob’s neck.
Rebekah was, quite literally, clothing Jacob’s smoothness with another creature’s skin.
Why?
Because Jacob had a problem.
He was trying to receive something while pretending to be someone he was not.
And his father knew the difference between the two sons.
Earlier, Genesis describes Esau as unusually hairy. Jacob himself understands the danger immediately when Rebekah proposes the deception:
“Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.” — Genesis 27:11
Jacob knows Isaac may touch him.
And if Isaac touches him, the lie may collapse.
Notice something uncomfortable about Jacob’s objection.
His first recorded concern is not simply, “Mother, this would be wrong.”
His concern is that he might get caught.
He tells Rebekah that if his father feels him, he may appear to be a deceiver and bring a curse upon himself instead of a blessing.
That is frighteningly human.
Sometimes we are more afraid of being exposed than we are grieved over being false.
More afraid somebody will discover the secret than we are concerned that God already sees it.
More concerned about consequences than repentance.
More concerned about protecting the image than healing the heart.
And perhaps that is why this ancient scene can feel so painfully modern.
Rebekah’s goatskins were practical camouflage.
Genesis does not leave us guessing about the immediate purpose.

Rebekah takes Esau’s best garments and puts them on Jacob. Then she places the goatskins over his hands and the smooth area of his neck. Jacob enters Isaac’s presence carrying the food Rebekah prepared.
Isaac becomes suspicious almost immediately.
“The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” — Genesis 27:22
Read that again.
The voice said Jacob.
The hands said Esau.
Something was wrong.
Isaac could hear one identity while touching another.
So he reached out.
And the disguise worked.

The goatskins were there because Rebekah anticipated the possibility that Isaac would test Jacob by touch. Isaac’s eyesight was failing, so the deception had to survive his remaining senses. Esau’s clothing supplied the familiar smell. The prepared meal imitated what Isaac expected from Esau. The goatskins imitated Esau’s hairiness.
This was not a spontaneous little lie.
It became an elaborate impersonation.
And that is where the story becomes more uncomfortable than a Sunday-school retelling sometimes allows.
Jacob was not merely telling a lie.
He was wearing one.
He was standing before his father covered in a manufactured identity.
And some of us know exactly what that feels like.
Not because we have ever wrapped goatskins around our hands.
But because we know what it is to wear something.
The church smile.
The “I’m blessed” response.
The Bible verse posted publicly while privately drowning.
The marriage everyone thinks is fine.
The secret addiction nobody knows about.
The resentment hidden beneath worship songs.
The pornography deleted before anyone checks the phone.
The jealousy disguised as discernment.
The pride disguised as spiritual maturity.
The exhaustion disguised as strength.
The doubt we are terrified to admit.
The sin we keep renaming because calling it what God calls it would require repentance.
Different century.
Different disguise.
Same terrifying instinct.
“Please don’t touch the place where you might discover who I really am.”
But there is another layer to Genesis 27 that must be handled carefully, because it is easy to turn this story into something Scripture itself never says.
God had already spoken concerning Jacob.
Before Jacob and Esau were born, before either brother had performed the events recorded in Genesis 27, the LORD told Rebekah:
“Two nations are in your womb… and the older shall serve the younger.” — Genesis 25:23
God’s sovereign purpose did not originate with Rebekah’s scheme.
That is crucial.
Rebekah did not need to manipulate God into choosing Jacob.
Jacob did not need to deceive Isaac to make God remember His word.
Human beings were trying to secure through manipulation what ultimately depended upon the purposes of God.
That does not make their deception righteous.
It makes the story even more sobering.
Because sometimes our greatest mistakes happen when we believe God’s promise but refuse to trust God’s way.
We pray…
then manipulate.
We say we trust God…
then control everyone around us.
We believe He has a plan…
but panic because His timetable frightens us.
We want the blessing so desperately that we begin justifying whatever appears necessary to obtain it.
And when fear joins faith, we can start doing sinful things while convincing ourselves we are protecting a holy outcome.
God does not need our deception to accomplish His purposes.
He does not need your compromise.
He does not need your manipulation.
He does not need you to become somebody else.
That is one of the great tensions running through Jacob’s life.
Jacob spends much of his early story grasping.
Even his name becomes associated in the narrative with the complicated history of grasping and supplanting.
He wants blessing.
He wants security.
He wants a future.
And in Genesis 27 he walks into his father’s presence dressed like another man to obtain what he desperately desires.
But God is not finished with Jacob.
That may be the most beautiful truth in this entire scandal.
Jacob’s sin has consequences.
This story does not end with Jacob stealing a blessing and riding happily into the sunset.
The family fractures.
Esau is devastated.
Esau plans to kill Jacob.
Jacob flees.
Rebekah sends away the son she was trying so desperately to advance.
Jacob eventually enters the household of Laban, where the deceiver discovers what it feels like to be deceived.
The man who used disguise inside his father’s tent enters years of painful formation.
Sin can be forgiven, but that does not mean sin is harmless.
Grace is not God pretending the wreckage never happened.
Grace is God refusing to let the wreckage have the final word.
And this is where Jacob’s story becomes breathtaking.
Because eventually God meets the deceiver.
Not the costume.
Not Esau’s clothes.
Not the goatskins.
Jacob.
Years later, in Genesis 32, Jacob wrestles through the night and receives a new name.
Israel.
The man who once entered his father’s presence pretending to be somebody else eventually encounters God with nowhere left to hide.
There is something profoundly Gospel-shaped about that movement, even while we must be careful not to claim that every object in Genesis 27 is a direct prophecy.
Genesis never explicitly says, “The goatskins represent Jesus.”
We should not pretend it does.
But the larger biblical story gives Christians something infinitely greater to behold.
Jacob tried to obtain blessing through disguise.
The Gospel announces that sinners are received by God through Christ.
Not because we successfully fool the Father.
Not because we learn to imitate somebody righteous.
Not because we hide our sinful condition well enough.
The exact opposite.
We come into the light.
We confess.
We repent.
We stop pretending.
And we discover that Jesus Christ has done what no disguise could ever accomplish.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
That is not camouflage.
That is redemption.
The New Testament speaks of believers being “in Christ.” Paul can even speak of having “put on Christ” in Galatians 3:27.
But do not miss the difference.
Jacob put on Esau’s clothing in order to deceive his father about who was standing before him.
We are united to Christ not to deceive God, but because God Himself graciously saves sinners through His Son.
God knows exactly who you are.
That is what makes grace astonishing.
He knows.
He knows what happened.
He knows what you watched.
He knows what you said.
He knows what you deleted.
He knows why you did it.
He knows the bitterness.
He knows the envy.
He knows the secret habit.
He knows the nights when your faith felt almost dead.
He knows how much of your public Christianity has sometimes been stronger than your private obedience.
He knows the version of you nobody follows online.
And still the Gospel calls you out of hiding.
Not so that Christ can humiliate the repentant sinner.
So that Christ can save.
That is the scandal of grace.
We spend years stitching together goatskins, while Jesus keeps calling us to come uncovered.
We polish appearances.
Jesus searches hearts.
We manage reputations.
Jesus offers resurrection.
We hide sin.
Jesus shed His blood for sinners.
We attempt to manufacture blessing.
Jesus became the source of eternal salvation for those who belong to Him.
We keep asking, “How can I make myself acceptable?”
And the cross answers, “You cannot save yourself. Come to Christ.”
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because eventually every goatskin becomes exhausting to wear.
Pretending is exhausting.
Hiding is exhausting.
Trying to convince everybody you are spiritually healthy while starving inside is exhausting.
Maintaining the reputation of a strong Christian while secretly wondering whether you are becoming cold toward God is exhausting.
And Jesus did not die so you could become better at pretending.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He transforms people from the inside out.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive theology.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, I’m tired of hiding.”
Maybe repentance begins when your hands stop pretending to belong to somebody else.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years believing, “If people knew the real me, they would never look at me the same way.”
Perhaps they would not.
But Jesus already knows the real you.
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
The cross proves sin is deadly serious.
But the cross also proves something else.
God’s mercy is greater than the identity you manufactured to survive without Him.
Christ did not come for imaginary righteous people.
He came to save sinners.
That means you can stop negotiating with the truth.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can ask forgiveness.
You can make things right where possible.
You can seek accountability.
You can bring hidden darkness into godly light.
And you can trust Jesus rather than the costume.
Someone reading beneath you may need to know they are not the only person fighting to come back into the light.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It is not.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives increasingly surrendered to Him.

But if this ministry is helping you grow in Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, and point people toward Jesus, then supporting and sharing Gospel-centered work can become one practical way of helping truth travel farther.
They look fine.
They post normally.
They laugh.
They work.
They attend church.
And nobody knows how desperately tired they are of pretending.
God does not need the person you pretend to be.
He is calling the person you actually are to Jesus.
But the greatest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be mission.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase God’s blessing.
Not because clicking “share” makes anyone more righteous.
There may be a Rebekah trying to control what she should have entrusted to God.
There may be an Esau carrying wounds nobody has allowed him to talk about.
There may be someone who believes their scandal disqualified them forever.
Send this story into their darkness.
Because Genesis 27 is not merely a strange ancient story about a mother, two brothers, a blind father, a stolen blessing, and goat skins.
It is a mirror.
It asks what we are wearing.
It asks what we are hiding.
It asks whether we trust God enough to obey Him without manipulating the outcome.
And ultimately, the larger story of Scripture leads us beyond Jacob, beyond Isaac, beyond Esau, beyond Rebekah, beyond every human failure and every human disguise…
to Jesus Christ.
The One who does not need to be deceived into blessing sinners.
The One who already knows the worst chapter.
The One who calls us to repentance rather than performance.
The One whose blood actually cleanses.
The One whose grace does not excuse sin but breaks its dominion.
The One who takes people with scandalous histories and begins writing stories of redemption.
So take off the goatskins.
Come into the light.
Tell Jesus the truth He already knows.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive grace.
And let Christ begin transforming the person you kept trying to hide.
Because one day you may discover that the part of your story you were most desperate to conceal became the very place where people could most clearly see the mercy of Jesus.
You do not have to die wearing the disguise you once believed you needed to survive.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID WALKED TOWARD GOLIATH WITH FIVE STONES—AND REFUSED SAUL’S ARMOR
paragraphs: DAVID WALKED TOWARD GOLIATH WITH FIVE STONES—AND REFUSED SAUL’S ARMOR
The giant was covered in bronze. David carried a sling. But the most dangerous thing on that battlefield was not what David held in his hand—it was Who David knew was fighting the battle.
There is a moment in the story of David and Goliath that we often rush past.
We remember the stone.
We remember the sling.
We remember the giant crashing to the earth.
But before David ever picked up those five smooth stones, something quieter happened.
Something deeply uncomfortable.
David took off the armor.
King Saul had dressed him for battle.
Helmet.
Armor.
Sword.
Everything a warrior was supposed to wear.
Everything that looked responsible.
Everything that made sense to frightened human eyes.
And David tried to walk.
Then he stopped.
Because sometimes the first act of faith is not picking something up.
Sometimes it is finally having the courage to take something off.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 17:39 preserves David’s words:
“לֹא אוּכַל לָלֶכֶת בָּאֵלֶּה כִּי לֹא נִסִּיתִי”
Lo ukhal lalekhet ba'elleh, ki lo nissiti.
In context:
“I cannot go with these, because I have not tested them.”
Then Scripture says:
“וַיְסִרֵם דָּוִד מֵעָלָיו”
Vayesirem David me'alav.
David removed them from himself.
That sentence is easy to read.
Living it is harder.
Because Saul's armor was not necessarily bad armor.
It simply was not David's tested equipment.
And there are things in your life that may not be sinful in themselves, yet they become dangerous when you begin trusting them more than you trust God.
Someone else's image.
Someone else's calling.
Someone else's personality.
Someone else's success.
Someone else's way of praying.
Someone else's ministry.
Someone else's approval.
Someone else's definition of what a victorious Christian is supposed to look like.
You can spend years trying to walk in armor God never trained you to wear.
And perhaps that is why you are exhausted.
Not because God abandoned you.
Maybe you have been trying to fight tomorrow's battle dressed in somebody else's expectations.
David took Saul's armor off.
Then he walked toward the water.
Scripture says:
“וַיִּבְחַר־לוֹ חֲמִשָּׁה חַלֻּקֵי־אֲבָנִים מִן־הַנַּחַל”
He chose for himself five smooth stones from the brook.
Five.
Not because Scripture secretly assigns each stone a mystical meaning.
The Bible does not tell us that one stone represented faith, another courage, another prayer, another obedience, and another grace.
Those can make memorable sermon illustrations, but they should not be confused with what the biblical text actually says.
Scripture simply tells us David chose five smooth stones.
And there is something even more beautiful than inventing symbolism.
David came carrying ordinary things into an impossible situation while trusting an extraordinary God.
A shepherd's staff.
A pouch.
A sling.
Five stones.
That was what people could see.
What they could not see was everything God had already done in the wilderness.
David had been keeping sheep when nobody thought he mattered.
He had faced the lion.
He had faced the bear.
He had learned what deliverance felt like before there was an audience to applaud him.
That matters.
Because sometimes God prepares His servants where nobody is watching.
The private battle.
The lonely prayer.
The night you cried and still opened your Bible the next morning.
The temptation nobody knew you resisted.
The season when nobody congratulated you for remaining faithful.
The forgiveness you gave while your heart was still bleeding.
The worship whispered from a room where you felt forgotten.
You called it obscurity.
God may have been calling it training.
David had already told Saul that the LORD who delivered him from the lion and the bear would deliver him from the Philistine.
David's confidence was not positive thinking.
It had history behind it.
He remembered God.
And then the shepherd walked into the valley.
Try to see it.
Goliath is approaching with a shield-bearer ahead of him.
The Philistine warrior sees David and despises him.
He sees youth.
He sees vulnerability.
He sees a staff.
He does not see what David sees.
And perhaps that is where some of us have been losing battles before they even begin.
We have been staring at what the giant has instead of remembering Who God is.
Goliath has armor.
God is still God.
Goliath has a spear.
God is still God.
Goliath has experience.
God is still God.
Goliath is terrifying.
God is still God.
Your diagnosis may frighten you.
God is still God.
Your marriage may be hurting.
God is still God.
Your child may be wandering.
God is still God.
Your past may still whisper your name.
God is still God.
Your bank account may make you afraid to look.
God is still God.
Your addiction may have knocked you down again.
God is still God.
Your grief may make getting out of bed feel like warfare.
God is still God.
That does not mean every earthly story ends exactly the way we demand.
Biblical faith is not manipulating God into giving us our preferred outcome.
It means that even when the valley is real, the enemy is real, the pain is real, and tomorrow is uncertain, God remains God.
Then David speaks.
And suddenly the entire story changes.
Goliath had been talking about weapons.
David starts talking about God.
“You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin…”
Then comes the sentence that reveals why this shepherd boy is standing while trained soldiers are hiding.
David says he comes in the name of the LORD of hosts—the God of the armies of Israel.
And then:
“כִּי לַיהוָה הַמִּלְחָמָה”
Ki laYHWH hammilchamah.
For the battle belongs to the LORD.
There it is.
Not:
“The battle belongs to David.”
Not:
“I am stronger than you think.”
Not:
“Believe in yourself.”
Not:
“Manifest your victory.”
Not:
“You have a giant-killer hidden inside you.”
No.
The battle belongs to the LORD.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because the story of David and Goliath is not ultimately a motivational speech about discovering your inner champion.
It is a testimony to the living God who saves.
David explicitly says the coming victory will show the earth that there is a God in Israel and that the LORD does not save by sword and spear.
David's objective was larger than personal success.
He wanted God to be known.
And that exposes something in us.
How many times have we asked God for victory because we wanted to look victorious?
How many prayers were secretly asking:
“Lord, make them regret doubting me.”
“Lord, prove that I was right.”
“Lord, embarrass the people who embarrassed me.”
“Lord, make me successful enough that everyone who rejected me has to watch.”
But David's heart points somewhere higher.
Let the earth know there is a God.
That is different.
Faith does not merely ask, “How can I win?”
Faith asks:
“How can Christ be glorified through me?”
And then something happens that should change the way we picture David forever.
First Samuel 17:48 says that when Goliath moved forward, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him.
He ran.
Toward him.
The boy everybody underestimated ran toward the thing everybody feared.
Not because David believed stones were magical.
Not because David was incapable of fear.
Not because David had suddenly become physically greater than Goliath.
David had already settled the deepest question.
Who owns this battle?
The LORD.
And some of you reading this have spent years running in the opposite direction.
Running from confession.
Running from repentance.
Running from accountability.
Running from the conversation you know you need to have.
Running from church because somebody wounded you.
Running from Scripture because conviction became uncomfortable.
Running from prayer because silence made you wonder whether God was listening.
Running from Jesus because you are terrified of what surrender might cost.
You have changed relationships.
Changed churches.
Changed jobs.
Changed cities.
Changed passwords.
Changed appearances.
Changed your explanation.
But the wound came with you.
The shame came with you.
The secret came with you.
And eventually you discover something terrifying:
You can outrun people.
You cannot outrun your own soul.
Maybe your Goliath is not standing across a literal battlefield.
Maybe he is staring back from your mirror.
Maybe the giant has your voice.
Maybe it says:
“You'll never change.”
“You already ruined everything.”
“If people knew the real you, they would leave.”
“God must be tired of forgiving you.”
“You're too dirty now.”
“You're too compromised.”
“You knew better.”
“You promised God you would stop, and you went back.”
And this is where David's story must lead us beyond David.
Because David himself would eventually need grace.
The young shepherd who defeated Goliath would not live a spotless life.
Years later, King David would commit devastating sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah.
The giant-killer would become the man desperately crying for mercy.
And suddenly the Bible refuses to let us worship its human heroes.
David could defeat Goliath.
David could not become his own Savior.
Neither can you.
That is why this story ultimately leaves us hungry for someone greater than David.
Jesus Christ.
David entered a valley representing God's people against an enemy they feared.
But generations later, the Son of David entered a far deeper battle.
Christ did not merely confront a Philistine warrior.
He confronted sin.
Death.
Judgment.
The powers of darkness.
And unlike David, Jesus was without sin.
He did not need Saul's armor.
He did not need five stones.
He did not need an army to rescue Him.
He willingly went toward the cross.
People mocked Him.
Stripped Him.
Beat Him.
Rejected Him.
A crown of thorns was pressed onto His head.
Nails went through His hands and feet.
And to everyone watching, it looked like the enemy had won.
But Golgotha was not the collapse of God's rescue plan.
It was at the center of it.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And Jesus rose.
The grave did not get the final word.
Sin did not get the final word.
Satan did not get the final word.
Death did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
And this is where your story can change.
Not because you found the right five stones.
Not because you finally became strong enough.
Not because you learned how to imitate somebody else's armor.
But because the Gospel announces that sinners can be forgiven through Jesus Christ.
You do not need to pretend anymore.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the unbelief.
Bring Him the secret nobody knows.
Bring Him the religious performance.
Bring Him the nights you wish you could erase.
Repentance does not mean pretending your sin was small.
Grace means Christ is greater.
The cross does not tell you sin does not matter.
The cross tells you sin mattered so terribly that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners—and that His mercy reaches people who could never save themselves.
Maybe this article was supposed to be about David's five stones.
But perhaps God is pressing something else into your heart.
What armor are you still wearing?
What have you been trusting instead of Christ?
What identity are you terrified to remove?
What sin are you protecting because surrender feels too expensive?
What giant have you allowed to preach to you every morning?
And whose voice will have the final word?
Goliath's?
Your past's?
Your shame's?
The world's?
Or Jesus Christ's?
Be honest.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Send it to the believer who feels defeated.
Send it to the person who has wandered from God.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is simply about good people becoming better.
Send it to someone who needs to hear that Christianity is about sinners who need a Savior—and a Savior who is mighty to save.
Because there may come a morning when the giant sounds louder than your faith, and you will need to remember again:
כִּי לַיהוָה הַמִּלְחָמָה
Ki laYHWH hammilchamah.
The battle belongs to the LORD.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, helping you return to Scripture, confronting you when you need conviction, or reminding you of Jesus when life becomes unbearably loud, stay close.
It is simply another way you can help Gospel Warrior keep putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who desperately need it.
It is discipleship.
It is helping truth keep moving.
It is helping another exhausted believer encounter the Gospel at 2:00 in the morning.
It is helping another prodigal remember the Father's mercy.
It is helping another person hear the name of Jesus.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Do it because Jesus Christ is worthy of being known.
Do it because somebody's giant has been talking long enough.
Do it because somebody you know may be standing in a valley right now, convinced that the story is over.
David walked toward Goliath.
But David's greatest legacy was never a stone embedded in a giant's forehead.
David's story pointed beyond himself toward the greater Son of David.
Jesus.
The King who does not merely help broken people manage their scandals.
The King who forgives repentant sinners.
The King who restores.
The King who redeems.
The King who transforms.
The King who walked toward death itself—and walked out of the grave alive.
So take off the borrowed armor.
Stop pretending.
Stop letting shame write theology for you.
Turn from sin.
Come to Christ.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
And when the giant speaks again tomorrow, remember what David knew before the stone ever left the sling:
The size of the giant was never the final truth of the valley. The presence of God was.
And perhaps the thing you are most ashamed to place at the feet of Jesus will one day become the place where people see most clearly what His grace can rewrite.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY LOWERED JEREMIAH INTO THE MUD TO SILENCE HIM—BUT GOD HAD NOT FINISHED WRITING HIS STORY
paragraphs: THEY LOWERED JEREMIAH INTO THE MUD TO SILENCE HIM—BUT GOD HAD NOT FINISHED WRITING HIS STORY

He told the truth God gave him. They hated him for it. Then the ropes lowered him into darkness, his feet disappeared into the mud, and the prophet discovered something every wounded believer eventually has to learn: being abandoned by people does not mean you have been abandoned by God.
There is a particular kind of pain that comes when you suffer not because you betrayed God...
but because you obeyed Him.
Jeremiah knew that pain.
Imagine the moment.
Jerusalem is dying.

Babylon is closing in. Hunger is tightening its hands around the city. Political leaders are desperate. Fear is everywhere. And in the middle of that collapsing world stands one inconvenient prophet with an inconvenient message.
Jeremiah.
He does not tell the rulers what they want to hear.
He tells them what God has said.
And sometimes truth becomes most offensive when people have built their lives around avoiding it.
The officials hear Jeremiah's words and decide that the problem is not their rebellion.
The problem, apparently, is Jeremiah.
That is one of sin's oldest tricks.
When truth exposes us, we can repent...
or we can attack the messenger.
They chose the messenger.
King Zedekiah, weak and frightened, effectively surrendered Jeremiah into their hands.
Then came the ropes.
Jeremiah 38:6 preserves the scene with almost unbearable simplicity:
"וּבַבּוֹר אֵין־מַיִם כִּי אִם־טִיט וַיִּטְבַּע יִרְמְיָהוּ בַּטִּיט"
Uvabbor ein-mayim ki im-tit, wayyiṭbaʿ Yirmeyahu baṭṭit.
A close rendering is:
"In the cistern there was no water, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud."
Do not rush past that last word.
טִיט — ṭit.
Mud. Mire.
And the verb וַיִּטְבַּע — wayyiṭbaʿ — means that Jeremiah sank.
They did not merely put him into a comfortable underground prison.
They lowered him by ropes into a cistern where there was no water, only mire.
Then they left him there.
Try to feel the story before turning it into a sermon.
Feel the rope against his body.
Feel his feet touch the bottom.
Then sink.
Ankles.
Calves.
Perhaps deeper.
Cold mud gripping his legs.
Walls rising around him.
Daylight somewhere above.
No staircase.
No escape.
No crowd applauding the prophet for being faithful.
No visible miracle yet.
Just mud.
And perhaps that is where this story stops feeling ancient.
Because some of you know exactly what it means to obey God and still end up in something that feels like a pit.
You prayed...
and the marriage still broke.
You forgave...
and they still walked away.
You tried to live clean...
and temptation still followed you home.
You told the truth...
and somehow you became the villain.
You served people who disappeared when you needed them.
You poured yourself into a family that barely notices how tired you are.
You kept smiling at church while privately wondering how much longer your soul could carry what nobody else could see.
You thought obedience would keep you out of the mud.
Jeremiah teaches us otherwise.
Faithfulness does not guarantee a painless life.
Sometimes faithfulness is exactly what puts you in conflict with a world that does not want God's truth.
But listen carefully:
The cistern was not proof that God had abandoned Jeremiah.
And your pit is not automatically proof that God has abandoned you.
There are seasons when God's presence is not demonstrated by immediate escape.
Sometimes His faithfulness is revealed by the fact that the pit does not get the final sentence.
Jeremiah could not climb out.
That matters.
We live in a culture obsessed with telling wounded people to rescue themselves.
Believe in yourself.
Find your strength.
Manifest your future.
Become your own salvation.
But Jeremiah had mud beneath him and walls around him.
He needed someone from above to intervene.
And that is where an unexpected man enters the story.
Not one of Jerusalem's powerful officials.
Not one of the men who had protected Jeremiah's reputation.
A Cushite named Ebed-melech.
When Ebed-melech hears what has happened, he goes to the king and calls the act what it is: evil.
Then the king authorizes a rescue.
And suddenly ropes descend into the darkness again.
Think about that.
The first ropes lowered Jeremiah toward death.
The next ropes were coming to lift him toward life.
Same prophet.
Same pit.
Different purpose.
And Scripture records a strangely tender detail.
Ebed-melech does not simply throw down ropes and shout, "Grab on."
He brings old rags and worn-out cloths and tells Jeremiah to place them under his armpits beneath the ropes.
Why?
Because rescue did not have to become another wound.
There is something beautiful here.
God's providence can arrive through ordinary things.
Old cloth.
Ropes.
A courageous servant.
Hands willing to pull.
No thunder.
No fire falling from heaven.
No angel visibly splitting the sky.
Just mercy entering the pit through someone willing to act.

Some of us keep waiting for God to rescue us spectacularly while overlooking the people, Scripture, conviction, church community, unexpected phone call, quiet provision, or ordinary act of compassion He has already placed above the cistern.
And sometimes...
you are Ebed-melech.
Someone you know is sinking.
They still post pictures.
Still answer, "I'm okay."
Still attend church.
Still go to work.
Still laugh.
But underneath everything, they are exhausted.
Their faith is hanging by threads.
Their marriage is hurting.
Their secret sin is consuming them.
Their grief is suffocating them.
Their prayers have become shorter because they no longer know what to say.
Maybe they do not need another person standing above the pit explaining why they should have avoided it.
Maybe they need someone willing to lower a rope.
This is why sharing the Gospel matters.
This is why telling someone about Jesus matters.
This is why checking on the person God suddenly puts on your heart matters.
Someone is sitting in darkness wondering whether anybody knows they are there.
Your obedience may become the rope God uses.
But Jeremiah's cistern points beyond Jeremiah.
Because centuries later, another righteous sufferer would be rejected for speaking truth.
Jesus Christ.
Jeremiah was hated by leaders who did not want his message.
Jesus "came unto his own, and his own received him not" (John 1:11).
Jeremiah was handed over by a compromised ruler.
Jesus stood before Pontius Pilate while political pressure and human fear surrounded His condemnation.
Jeremiah descended into a place from which he could not rescue himself.
Jesus willingly descended all the way into death.
But here the comparison must remain careful.
Jeremiah was a prophet who needed rescue.
Jesus is the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
Jeremiah suffered because he faithfully proclaimed God's word.
Christ did something infinitely greater: He bore our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
The Gospel is not that Jesus came merely to inspire wounded people.
He came to save sinners.
Our deepest cistern is not depression, betrayal, poverty, rejection, addiction, loneliness, or failure—terrible as those things can be.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Sin separates.
Sin deceives.
Sin hardens.
Sin makes us hide from God while convincing us that hiding is freedom.
And eventually sin pays its terrible wage: death.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to "God will get you through difficult times."
The Gospel is far more glorious.
Christ came because we needed forgiveness.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed redemption.
We needed Someone to do for us what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely sympathize with sinners trapped in the pit.
He gave Himself for them.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
The stone did not keep Him.
Death did not keep Him.
The grave did not write the ending.
Jesus did.
That is why grace can reach you wherever you are reading this.
Even if your life feels muddy.
Even if you made the decisions that brought you there.
Even if your pit was not caused by faithfulness like Jeremiah's but by your own rebellion.
That distinction matters.
Sometimes we suffer because we obeyed God.
Sometimes we suffer because we ignored Him.
Sometimes we suffer simply because we live in a fallen world.
But none of those realities places a repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ.
Maybe your mud has a name.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Secret messages.
An affair nobody knows about.
Jealousy.
Greed.
Religious hypocrisy.
Unforgiveness.
A double life.
Maybe you have become frighteningly good at appearing spiritually alive while something inside you is slowly sinking.
You know the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say "Amen."
You know which verse to post.
You know how to lift your hands.
But when the room becomes quiet and there is nobody left to impress...
you know.
You know where the mud is.
And Jesus knows too.
Yet the shocking message of the Gospel is not that Christ waits above the pit laughing at filthy people.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers mercy.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He makes new.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from the mud because you finally believe Jesus is better.
Grace does not tell you the mud is clean.
Grace tells you that you do not have to die there.
That is the scandal.
Holy God receiving guilty people.
The spotless Christ dying for sinners.
The condemned being forgiven.
The ashamed being clothed in righteousness they could never earn.
The rebel becoming a child of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The person everyone else wrote off becoming living evidence that God is still writing.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the seriousness of sin.
He rewrites everything by redeeming what sin meant to destroy.
Look at Jeremiah again.
The men who lowered him apparently expected the cistern to silence him.
Yet thousands of years later, we are still reading his words.
The mud could not erase the message.
The pit could not cancel the calling.
The people who wanted Jeremiah forgotten are remembered largely because Scripture records what they did to Jeremiah.
And the prophet they tried to silence still speaks.
That should make somebody reading this reconsider the chapter you thought destroyed your story.
Your betrayal may not be the final chapter.
Your relapse does not have to be the final chapter.
Your divorce does not have to be the final chapter.
Your shame does not have to be the final chapter.
Your grief does not have to be the final chapter.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Your past does not possess authorship rights over your future.
Jesus does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears when we come to Him.
He promises something greater than cosmetic repair.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
New life.
His presence.
A new identity rooted not in what we have done but in what Christ has done for those who trust Him.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing about a pit is that after enough time in darkness, you begin believing darkness is where you belong.
No.
Hear the Gospel.
You may have fallen.
You may have failed.
You may have sinned horribly.
You may have wounds nobody understands.
But if you can still hear Christ calling you to repent and come to Him, the story is not over.
Stop decorating the cistern.
Stop defending the mud.
Stop calling bondage personality.
Stop calling compromise freedom.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy enough to approach Jesus.
You will never climb high enough to deserve Calvary.
Come because He is merciful.
Come because His blood is sufficient.
Come because sinners are exactly the people He came to save.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come empty-handed.
Be honest.
And if God has already brought you out of a pit you thought would bury you, tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Your testimony might become another person's rope.
Send it privately to the person who has gone unusually silent.

Supporting Gospel work financially or through sharing is one way believers may freely participate in ministry, but it should never be confused with earning God's approval or proving that you glorify Him. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ; when you freely support sound Gospel ministry, you help that ministry place biblical resources before more people.
Jesus Christ.
Not the platform.
Not the merchandise.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Jesus.
Because Jeremiah's story is not ultimately an advertisement for positive thinking.
It is a witness that human beings do not possess the final word over what God purposes to do.
And the Gospel takes that truth to its blazing center.
They rejected Christ.
Mocked Him.
Stripped Him.
Nailed Him to a cross.
Watched Him die.
Sealed His tomb.
And human history seemed to place a period where God had written a comma.
Then came Sunday.
The grave opened.
Christ rose.
And ever since, every sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith can know that shame does not have to write the ending.
Maybe tonight you feel the mud around your feet.
Maybe you cannot see the rope yet.
Maybe you cannot imagine how God could possibly redeem what has happened.
Jeremiah could not see through the walls of his cistern either.
But above him, while he was still in the mud, God was already moving through a man named Ebed-melech.
You do not have to see everything God is doing to trust the God who sees you.
So cry if you need to.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Ask for help.
Reach for the rope.
And above everything else...
reach for Christ.
Because sometimes the chapter that looks most like your burial becomes the chapter you later point to and whisper:
"That was where I discovered He had not abandoned me."
The mud may explain where you have been—but because of Jesus, it does not get to decide who you become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Man Cursed King David to His Face—and David Refused to Let His Soldiers Kill Him
paragraphs:
A Man Cursed King David to His Face—and David Refused to Let His Soldiers Kill Him
He threw stones at the king, called him a murderer, and humiliated him in front of everyone. David had enough armed men to silence him in seconds. Instead, the fallen king said something that exposes what may be hiding inside all of us.
There are moments when you discover who you really are.
Not when people applaud you.
Not when everything is working.
Not when your prayers seem answered, your family is peaceful, your reputation is intact, and everyone around you agrees that God is blessing your life.
