You discover something much deeper about yourself when you are wounded...
and someone decides to throw another stone.
That is where David was.
Not sitting securely on the throne.
Not standing over Goliath with Israel shouting his name.
Not carrying the giant’s severed head while people celebrated the shepherd boy who trusted God.
This David was running.
His own son Absalom had turned against him.
The conspiracy had grown.
Jerusalem was slipping from his hands.
Men who once honored him were choosing sides.
David—the king, warrior, psalmist, giant-killer—was leaving Jerusalem in humiliation.
And then came Shimei.
Sometimes the cruelest voices do not arrive when you are strong.
They wait until you are bleeding.
Second Samuel 16:5 tells us that as David approached Bahurim, Shimei son of Gera came out from the family of Saul and began cursing him.
He did not merely mutter under his breath.
He followed David and his men.
He cursed.
He threw stones.
He kicked dust into the air.
Imagine the scene.
David is surrounded by warriors, mighty men who have spilled blood on battlefields. Yet this man walks along the hillside hurling insults and stones at Israel’s king.
And Shimei knows exactly where to strike.
He attacks David’s past.
He essentially calls him a man of blood.
A worthless man.
He interprets David’s catastrophe as divine judgment and tells him that his kingdom has collapsed because God is paying him back.
There is something especially painful about being attacked with a version of your own history.
Because David really did have blood in his past.
Uriah was dead.
Bathsheba had been taken.
David had committed adultery.
He had manipulated circumstances surrounding Uriah’s death.
The prophet Nathan had confronted him.
David had confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13).
And although God forgave David, forgiveness did not mean that every earthly consequence disappeared.
That is what makes Shimei’s accusations so psychologically brutal.
They were not entirely disconnected from David’s shame.
Have you ever been forgiven by God...
but someone still knew where the grave was buried?
Have you ever repented of something, yet a person kept resurrecting the version of you that Christ was changing?
Have you ever heard words that hurt so badly because somewhere inside you whispered:
“What if I deserve this?”
Then you understand something about that road to Bahurim.
Shimei kept cursing.
And one of David’s warriors had heard enough.
Abishai, son of Zeruiah, said to the king:
“Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head.”
That was not metaphorical.
Abishai wanted Shimei dead.
One command from David...
and the cursing would stop.
One nod.
One sword.
Silence.
And here is where the story becomes dangerous for anyone who has ever fantasized about making somebody pay.
David refused.
The Hebrew of his response deserves attention.
David says:
כִּי יְקַלֵּל וְכִי יְהוָה אָמַר לוֹ קַלֵּל אֶת־דָּוִד
Ki yeqallel, vekhi YHWH amar lo, qallel et-David...
The sense is:
“If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, ‘Curse David’...”
Then David asks, in effect:
Who can demand, “Why have you done this?”
David was not declaring that every accusation Shimei made was true.
He was not establishing a doctrine that every abusive voice speaks for God.
He was not telling victims that cruelty should always be tolerated.
And he certainly was not declaring Shimei morally innocent.
David was doing something far more searching.
He was acknowledging the sovereignty of God even while he was being humiliated.
He refused to seize vengeance merely because vengeance was within reach.
That distinction matters.
Biblical surrender is not pretending evil is good.
Biblical forgiveness is not calling abuse holy.
Biblical humility is not saying lies are true.
And trusting God with justice does not mean justice ceases to matter.
It means you refuse to become your own god in order to obtain it.
David could have killed Shimei.
Instead, David looked beyond Shimei.
That is extraordinary.
Most of us stare at the stone.
David looked toward God.
Most of us obsess over the person throwing dirt.
David wondered what God might be doing in the dust.
Then David said something heartbreaking.
His own son was trying to kill him.
Why, then, should he be shocked that a Benjaminite cursed him?
And then comes the sentence that changes the emotional temperature of the entire scene:
אוּלַי יִרְאֶה יְהוָה בְּעֵינִי
Ulay yir’eh YHWH be‘eini...
“Perhaps the LORD will look upon my affliction...”
David does not know how this ends.
Read that again.
He does not know.
There is no triumphant soundtrack playing behind him.
No prophet steps out and announces that everything will be restored by sunset.
David is walking through humiliation while Shimei continues cursing him.
And all David has is...
perhaps.
“Perhaps the LORD will look upon my affliction...”
Perhaps God sees.
Perhaps God has not abandoned me.
Perhaps God can bring good even out of this.
Perhaps mercy is still possible.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what it feels like to live inside that word.
Perhaps.
Perhaps my marriage can still heal.
Perhaps my child will come home.
Perhaps God can restore what my sin damaged.
Perhaps Jesus can still use me after what I did.
Perhaps I am not beyond redemption.
Perhaps the chapter everybody thinks destroyed me is not the chapter where God stops writing.
And this is where David’s road points beyond David.
Because centuries later, another King would be rejected.
Another Son of David would walk a road of humiliation.
Another King would be mocked.
Another King would be falsely accused.
Another King would have insults thrown at Him.
Another King would possess the power to destroy His enemies...
and refuse to use that power to escape the suffering before Him.
Jesus Christ.
At His arrest, Jesus said that He could appeal to His Father and receive more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53).
Think about that.
Calvary did not happen because Jesus lacked power.
The cross happened while infinite power was being restrained by infinite love.
They mocked Him.
He stayed.
They struck Him.
He stayed.
They drove nails through Him.
He stayed.
And while hanging between heaven and earth, Jesus prayed:
“Father, forgive them...”
David spared the man who cursed him.
Jesus went infinitely further.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners who had rebelled against God.
That includes us.
The scandal of the Gospel is not merely that wicked people can be forgiven.
The scandal is that forgiveness came at the cost of the blood of the innocent Son of God.
You and I are not merely David in this story.
Sometimes we are Shimei.
We have thrown our own rebellion toward the King.
Maybe not with literal stones.
But with sin.
Pride.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Secret compromise.
Self-righteousness.
Gossip.
Hatred.
Religious performance without surrender.
We wanted God’s gifts while resisting His authority.
We wanted grace without repentance.
Heaven without holiness.
A Savior without a Lord.
And yet Jesus did not come merely to crush rebels.
He came to save sinners.
The King we offended became the sacrifice for our sin.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we like to admit.
Grace means the judgment our sin deserved was borne by Christ for everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
Jesus does not simply improve your public image.
He raises spiritually dead people to life.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
He rewrites stories.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But there is another uncomfortable question hiding on that dusty road.
Who is your Shimei?
Whose name immediately entered your mind?
Who embarrassed you?
Who betrayed you?
Who keeps reminding people of what you did?
Who misunderstood you?
Who posted something about you?
Who walked away?
Who said the thing you still replay at 2:00 in the morning?
Who made you want to reach for your own version of Abishai’s sword?
Maybe your sword is not steel.
Maybe it is a Facebook post.
A screenshot.
A rumor.
A perfectly crafted message designed to wound them exactly where you know they are vulnerable.
Maybe your sword is silence used as punishment.
Maybe it is public humiliation.
Maybe it is telling everybody your side until their reputation is buried beneath it.
Maybe you keep saying, “I just want the truth known.”
But somewhere beneath the truth...
you want blood.
David’s restraint asks a terrifying question:
What if victory is not getting the last word?
What if sometimes victory is having the power to retaliate...
and placing the sword back into its sheath?
That does not mean refusing appropriate boundaries.
It does not mean remaining in danger.
It does not mean concealing crimes, protecting abusers, rejecting lawful justice, or pretending wrongdoing never happened.
Scripture does not require us to call darkness light.
But there is a difference between pursuing what is right and feeding revenge.
Romans 12:19 tells believers not to avenge themselves, but to leave room for the judgment of God.
Why?
Because vengeance makes a terrible god out of a wounded human heart.
And wounded hearts are rarely satisfied with “enough.”
We want the other person to feel what we felt.
Then a little more.
And another little more.
Until somewhere along the road, while punishing the person who wounded us...
we become someone we never intended to become.
David refused that road.
But do not romanticize him.
This is the same David who had failed catastrophically.
That is part of the beauty.
The man showing restraint here is not a flawless saint.
He is a broken man.
A disciplined man.
A forgiven man living amid consequences.
A man who has learned that possessing power does not mean you have permission to use it however your emotions demand.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Some lessons can only be learned after we have been shattered.
Sometimes the person who once abused power becomes the person who finally understands restraint.
Sometimes the person who desperately needed mercy becomes slower to deny mercy to somebody else.
And maybe you are standing somewhere on that road right now.
Stones are flying.
Dust is in your eyes.
Your reputation feels bruised.
Your past is screaming.
And the sword is within reach.
Before you swing...
look toward Jesus.
Not because what happened to you was insignificant.
Not because the person who wounded you was necessarily right.
Not because justice does not matter.
Look toward Jesus because bitterness cannot resurrect you.
Revenge cannot cleanse you.
Winning the argument cannot heal the deepest wound in you.
Only Christ can reach that far.
Maybe the real battle is not between you and the person throwing stones.
Maybe the battle is over what their stones are turning you into.
Do not let somebody else’s sin disciple your heart.
Do not let their cruelty teach you cruelty.
Do not let their hatred decide who you become.
Bring the wound to Christ.
Bring the rage.
Bring the humiliation.
Bring the fantasies of revenge you would never admit in church.
Bring the screenshots.
Bring the memory.
Bring the name.
Jesus already knows.
Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek justice where justice is appropriate.
Establish wise boundaries where they are necessary.
But do not worship vengeance.
And if you have been Shimei...
if you have been the one throwing stones...
repent.
Stop defending it.
Stop dressing cruelty in spiritual language.
Stop calling gossip “discernment.”
Stop calling hatred “truth.”
Stop using another person’s genuine failures as permission to enjoy destroying them.
Jesus did not die so we could become religious experts at throwing stones.
He died to reconcile sinners to God and create a people transformed by grace.
Maybe this exposed something you have been hiding.
Be honest.
There may be another believer reading your words who needs to discover they are not the only Christian still fighting this battle.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, do not weaponize the article against them.
Pray first.
Then, if sharing it would genuinely help rather than shame them, send it with love.
We do not purchase favor with Him. Grace cannot be bought.
You need Jesus.
Not merchandise.
Not an inspirational quote.
Not religious appearance.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen King.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Lord who can take the ugliest chapter of your life and refuse to let it become the title of your story.
David walked while Shimei cursed.
Stone after stone.
Insult after insult.
Dust rising around him.
And David refused to answer every stone with a sword.
Maybe that is the word someone desperately needs tonight.
You do not have to destroy everyone who reminds you of your wounds.
You do not have to win every battle your pride volunteers you for.
You do not have to rewrite your past by yourself.
There is already a King who walked through humiliation.
A King who endured the cross.
A King who entered the grave.
A King who rose again.
And when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, even the chapters covered in dust, blood, regret, betrayal, and shame are no longer beyond redemption.
So when the stones start flying again...
remember who is holding the pen.
Your wound may explain why you reached for the sword—but Jesus can teach your scarred hand how to let it go.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON SPENT THE NIGHT WITH A PROSTITUTE—THEN WALKED AWAY CARRYING THE CITY GATES
paragraphs: SAMSON SPENT THE NIGHT WITH A PROSTITUTE—THEN WALKED AWAY CARRYING THE CITY GATES
He was strong enough to rip Gaza’s gates from the ground—but there was something inside Samson that brute strength could never conquer.
There is a terrifying kind of Christianity where you can still look strong while something inside you is quietly collapsing.
You can still pray.
Still quote Scripture.
Still serve.
Still worship.
Still post about God.
Still have people admire your strength.
And still be losing a private war nobody knows exists.
Samson knew what that felt like.
His story does not begin with Delilah.
It does not even begin with a haircut.
Long before the scissors touched his hair, Samson had already been playing dangerously close to the edge.
Then Judges 16 opens with a sentence so abrupt that it almost feels scandalous to read aloud:
“Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her.”
The Hebrew is equally stark:
וַיֵּלֶךְ שִׁמְשׁוֹן עַזָּתָה וַיַּרְא־שָׁם אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה וַיָּבֹא אֵלֶיהָ
Vayyēlekh Shimshon ‘Azzatah, vayar-sham ishah zonah, vayavo eleha.
The key expression is אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishah zonah: a woman who was a prostitute.
Scripture does not sanitize Samson.
It does not protect the reputation of its heroes by airbrushing their failures.
It tells the truth.
That matters because some of us have spent years believing God could only deal with the edited version of us.
So we bring Him the Sunday version.
The worship version.
The smiling profile-picture version.
The “I’m blessed” version.
Meanwhile, somewhere behind the screen, behind the ministry, behind the marriage, behind the laughter, behind the Bible verses we repost…
there is a Gaza.
A place we know we should not be.
A habit we keep returning to.
A conversation we keep deleting.
A browser history we would hate to explain.
A relationship we keep justifying.
An appetite we keep feeding.
A wound we keep medicating with something that can never heal it.
And perhaps the most frightening part of Samson’s night in Gaza is what happened next.
His enemies heard he was there.
The men of Gaza surrounded the place and waited at the city gate through the night. They thought they had him trapped.
They planned to kill him in the morning.
Samson, however, got up around midnight.
Then he walked toward the gate.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine the darkness.
Imagine the men waiting for sunrise, convinced the mighty Samson had finally cornered himself.
Then Samson seized the doors of the city gate, together with the two posts.
Judges tells us he pulled them up—bar and all—put them on his shoulders, and carried them toward the hill facing Hebron.
He did not merely break a lock.
He carried the gate away.
The very thing his enemies expected to use to imprison him became something he carried on his shoulders.
It is one of the most visually staggering scenes in the Old Testament.
But do not misunderstand it.
Samson carrying Gaza’s gates does not mean God approved of what Samson had just done.
Extraordinary strength was not proof of extraordinary holiness.
Giftedness is not the same thing as godliness.
And that distinction may be one of the most uncomfortable lessons in Samson’s entire life.
You can be gifted and compromised.
You can be useful and wounded.
You can experience astonishing mercy while still making disastrous choices.
You can carry gates on your shoulders while carrying chains in your heart.
That is what makes Samson frighteningly relatable.
Because eventually we discover that the enemy outside us is not always the most dangerous enemy.
Sometimes the gate is easier to tear down than the appetite.
Sometimes defeating a thousand men is easier than telling your flesh “no.”
Sometimes public victories hide private defeats.
Samson could overpower lions.
He could strike down enemies.
He could snap restraints.
He could uproot gates.
But Samson repeatedly struggled to govern Samson.
And maybe that sentence just found you.
Because there are battles you know how to win in public.
You know how to work.
You know how to provide.
You know how to lead.
You know how to encourage everybody else.
You know how to look composed when your world is shaking.
But there is one room in your soul where you keep losing.
One temptation.
One memory.
One resentment.
One secret.
One hunger.
One compromise.
One thing you promised God you would never return to.
And somehow…
you returned.
Again.
This is where Samson’s story stops being ancient history and starts feeling like a mirror.
Because sin rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I have come to destroy you.”
It usually whispers:
“Just this once.”
“You deserve this.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You can stop whenever you want.”
“God understands.”
“You’re still doing good things, so how bad can this really be?”
That last lie is particularly dangerous.
Samson still possessed remarkable strength after Gaza.
And a person can mistake continued ability for divine approval.
We can mistake God’s patience for permission.
We can mistake delayed consequences for nonexistent consequences.
We can mistake spiritual gifts for spiritual health.
But Scripture will not let us make that mistake with Samson.
The trajectory continues.
After Gaza comes Delilah.
After repeated compromise comes exposure.
After Samson repeatedly plays with the secret of his consecration, Judges 16 reaches one of the saddest sentences in his story.
Delilah calls out that the Philistines are upon him.
Samson wakes and thinks he will escape as before.
Then Scripture says:
“וְהוּא לֹא יָדַע כִּי יְהוָה סָר מֵעָלָיו”
Vehu lo yada ki YHWH sar me‘alav.
“But he did not know that the LORD had left him.”
Judges 16:20.
Read that slowly.
He did not know.
That is terrifying.
Samson had become so accustomed to getting away with compromise that he expected yesterday’s strength to rescue him from today’s rebellion.
But this time he rose…
and discovered that something had changed.
The Philistines seized him.
They gouged out his eyes.
They took him to Gaza—the same Gaza whose gates he had once carried away.
The man who once walked out of that city carrying its gates was eventually dragged back into it blind and bound.
Sin has a cruel sense of irony.
What begins as pleasure can end as slavery.
What begins as “freedom” can become a chain.
What begins with you controlling the habit can end with the habit controlling you.
And this is precisely where somebody reading this may want to close the article.
Because now it feels too personal.
Don’t.
Stay.
Because Samson’s story does not end in the prostitute’s room.
It does not end with Delilah.
It does not end with blindness.
It does not end with chains.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, neither does your story have to end at the worst thing you have done.
There is a tiny sentence in Judges 16 that carries enormous hope:
“But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.”
Hair was not magical.
Samson’s power ultimately came from God, not keratin growing from his scalp.
But narratively, that quiet regrowth appears like a whisper in the darkness.
Something was not finished.
Samson was blind.
But something was growing.
He was imprisoned.
But something was growing.
He had failed catastrophically.
But something was growing.
Nobody applauded it.
Nobody posted it.
Nobody celebrated the first millimeter.
But something was growing.
And perhaps that is where you are.
You cannot undo what happened.
You cannot return to yesterday and make a different decision.
You cannot unsend the message.
You cannot unwatch what you watched.
You cannot unsay what you said.
You cannot erase the affair, addiction, bitterness, pride, dishonesty, compromise, or years you wasted running from God.
But repentance is not pretending yesterday never happened.
Repentance turns toward God today.
And the Gospel gives us something even greater than Samson’s final restoration.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
Samson was a deeply flawed deliverer in Israel’s history.
Jesus is the sinless Savior.
Samson repeatedly surrendered to temptation.
Jesus was tempted and remained without sin.
Samson’s failures helped bring suffering upon himself.
Jesus willingly suffered for sins that were not His own.
Samson died while destroying his enemies.
Jesus died praying forgiveness over His enemies.
Samson’s death brought a temporal victory over Philistine oppressors.
Christ’s death and resurrection accomplished something infinitely greater: redemption for sinners and victory over sin and death.

And suddenly the image of a mighty man carrying something enormous on his shoulders points our hearts beyond Samson—not as though every detail were a direct prophecy, but as a contrast that makes the Gospel shine brighter.
Because Jesus carried something Samson never could.
Our sin.
Our guilt.
Our shame.
Our judgment.
Peter writes that Christ “himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
The Greek expression is breathtaking:
ὃς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν
hos tas hamartias hēmōn autos anēnenken
“He himself bore our sins.”
He Himself.
Not the cleaned-up you.
Not the religious you.
Not your good works.
Not your promises that this time you will do better.
Jesus Christ.
And He did not bear our sins so we could become comfortable living inside them.
Peter continues: Christ bore our sins so that, having died to sins, we might live to righteousness.
That is grace.
Grace is not God shrugging at the thing destroying you.
Grace is God meeting sinners who cannot save themselves, forgiving those who come to Him through Christ, and calling them into a new life.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace becomes more beautiful to you than the chains you were defending.
Maybe you have been carrying your own Gaza for years.
Nobody knows.
You have mastered smiling while bleeding.
You have mastered worshipping while hiding.
You have mastered saying “God is good” while secretly wondering whether God could possibly still want you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not an invitation to hide better.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Not some unrighteousness.
Not only respectable failures.
Not only sins that happened before you became a Christian.
“All unrighteousness.”
But confession is not bargaining.
Repentance is not saying, “Jesus, forgive me so I can comfortably return to the same darkness.”
It is surrender.
It is finally saying:
“Jesus, I cannot keep calling this freedom when it has become my prison.”
“Forgive me.”
“Change me.”
“Teach me to hate what is destroying me.”
“Give me the strength to walk in the light.”
“Take the secret rooms too.”
Maybe you are reading this with tears nobody can see.
Maybe your sin is sexual.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe dishonesty.
Maybe alcohol or another dependency.
Maybe rage.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe pride.
Maybe you have not stepped inside a church in years because you are convinced everybody there would reject you if they knew.
People may disappoint you.
Jesus already knows.
And still the invitation of the Gospel stands.
Not an invitation to remain unchanged.
An invitation to come and be made new.
Jesus said:
“The one who comes to me I will certainly not cast out.”
John 6:37.
That is where scandal meets grace.
Not because the scandal suddenly becomes good.
Not because sin stops being sin.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
But because Jesus Christ receives sinners, forgives those who come to Him, and transforms lives that seemed beyond recovery.
This is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior:
Talk to God.
Tell Him the truth.
Not because typing three words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let believers reading your words know there is a real person behind that screen who needs prayer.
Somebody trapped in the place you escaped may need to know that Jesus still restores people.
Then think of one person.
Not your entire friends list.
One person.
The friend who has become distant from God.
The brother who jokes about everything because he does not know how to talk about his pain.
The woman carrying shame she has never told anyone about.
The believer quietly drifting.
The person who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have themselves together.

There may come a night when temptation starts negotiating with you again, when shame starts preaching to you again, or when you need to remember that giftedness cannot replace holiness and failure does not have to become your final chapter.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel-centered work should never be merchandise.
It should be mission.
It does not make someone more spiritual.
It does not earn blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or a place in heaven.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is free.
But Gospel ministry has always been strengthened by believers who voluntarily support the spread of God’s Word.
And please do not disappear silently if God used this to confront your heart.
Because somewhere beneath Samson’s astonishing strength is a warning every generation needs:
You can carry a city gate and still be unable to carry the weight of your own sin.
But that is why we need more than Samson.
We need Jesus.
The One who did not merely escape the place of death.
He conquered death.
The One who does not simply make sinners look stronger.
He makes them new.
So bring Him the part you keep editing out of your testimony.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the appetite.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the wreckage.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk into the light.
And remember this when your past whispers that your story has already been written:
The chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read may become the very place where the grace of Jesus Christ becomes impossible to forget.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY THE HIGH PRIEST WORE BELLS ON HIS GARMENT
paragraphs:
WHY THE HIGH PRIEST WORE BELLS ON HIS GARMENT
The Sound That Said a Sinner Was Still Standing Before a Holy God
Imagine hearing him before you could see him.
A faint sound of gold striking gold.
Movement.
Silence.
Then another sound.
He was walking toward a place where ordinary men did not casually walk.
Toward holiness.
Toward the presence of the LORD.
And hanging from the hem of his robe were little golden bells.
Not decoration for decoration’s sake.
Not religious jewelry designed merely to make Aaron impressive.
God commanded them.
And hidden inside that strange command is a truth modern Christianity desperately needs to recover:
God is loving beyond anything we can comprehend—but His love has never made His holiness less holy.
Listen to the command itself.
In Exodus 28, God gives instructions concerning the robe of the high priest. Around its hem were to be representations of pomegranates, with golden bells placed among them.
The Hebrew calls a bell פַּעֲמֹן — paʿamon.
Exodus later describes the pattern with an almost audible rhythm:
פַּעֲמֹן וְרִמֹּן פַּעֲמֹן וְרִמֹּן
paʿamon ve-rimmon, paʿamon ve-rimmon.
“A bell and a pomegranate, a bell and a pomegranate.”
Around the hem.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Then comes the sentence that changes the atmosphere completely.
Aaron was to wear the robe when he ministered, and the sound was to be heard when he entered the sanctuary before the LORD and when he came out—
“so that he will not die.”
Read that slowly.
Not because God was theatrical.
Because God is holy.

The bells were part of a larger priestly system God Himself prescribed. Exodus does not invite us to reduce them to a cute inspirational symbol. Their sound accompanied Aaron's movement as he approached and departed from sacred space before the LORD.
And Scripture connects that sound with life and death.
That should disturb something in us.
Because we have become remarkably comfortable talking about approaching God.
We say we are going into His presence.
We sing about His presence.
We post about His presence.
We ask God to manifest His presence.
But ancient Israel understood something we often forget:
The presence we desire is the presence of the Holy One.
This is not merely emotional atmosphere.
This is not spiritual entertainment.
This is not a religious feeling produced by music.
This is God.
The One before whom Isaiah cried,
“Woe is me!”
The One whose holiness exposes every hidden thing.
The One whom sinful humanity cannot approach on its own terms.
Aaron did not simply decide one morning, “I feel close to God today,” and stroll into sacred space wearing whatever seemed comfortable.
God determined how the priest approached.
The garments mattered.
The sacrifices mattered.
The blood mattered.
The priesthood mattered.
The holiness of God mattered.
Even the sound mattered.
And perhaps that is where this ancient robe begins speaking painfully into our modern hearts.
Because some of us want access to God without surrender to God.
We want comfort without repentance.
Grace without confession.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We want God close enough to rescue us but not close enough to expose us.
We want Christianity to soothe our anxiety while leaving our secret idols untouched.
But the bells whisper from Exodus:
You are approaching the Holy One.
And suddenly this is no longer a story about Aaron's clothes.
It is about you.
About me.
About every hidden browser history.
Every private bitterness.
Every compromise nobody discovered.
Every conversation deleted before someone could read it.
Every addiction dressed up as “struggling.”
Every grudge renamed “discernment.”
Every act of pride disguised as ministry.
Every Sunday smile hiding a heart that has been drifting from Jesus for months.
God sees what people don't.
That truth is terrifying...
until you understand the Gospel.
Because the same Bible that teaches us to tremble before God's holiness reveals something almost unbelievable:
The Holy God made a way for guilty people to come near.
That story runs through the priesthood, the sacrifices, the blood, the tabernacle, the Day of Atonement...
and ultimately reaches Jesus Christ.
The Old Testament priesthood was never the final destination.
Hebrews points us beyond Aaron.
Beyond repeated sacrifices.
Beyond priests who themselves were mortal sinners.
Toward Christ.
Jesus is not merely another priest standing in a long line of priests.
Hebrews presents Him as our great High Priest.
And this High Priest is different.
He does not first need cleansing for His own sin.
He is holy.
He is innocent.
He is undefiled.
And He does not enter God's presence carrying the blood of an animal as though another sacrifice must continually be offered for human guilt.
Christ gives Himself.
This is where the bells become more than an interesting Bible-study detail.
They make us feel the distance.
The Gospel shows us who crossed it.
Under the old covenant, the priest approached according to God's commands.
In Christ, sinners are given something astonishing:
access.
Not casual access.
Not arrogant access.
Not access because sin suddenly stopped mattering.
Access purchased at an unimaginable price.
Blood.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
That is why biblical grace should never make sin seem small.
Grace proves how catastrophic sin actually was.
If our rebellion could have been solved through moral improvement, motivational speeches, religious rituals, or positive thinking, Calvary would have been unnecessary.
But Christ was crucified.
The Son of God bore our sins.
The innocent suffered for the guilty.
The righteous One stood where rebels deserved to stand.
The cross tells you simultaneously:
Your sin is worse than you wanted to believe.
And God's mercy is greater than you dared to hope.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending you were never scandalous.
Not pretending you never fell.
Not rewriting your past so you appear respectable.
The Gospel does something infinitely better.
Jesus meets sinners in the wreckage and redeems them.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still serve.
Still attend church.
Still say “God bless you.”
Still post verses.
But underneath all of it there is something you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
And you wonder sometimes:
“If people knew the real me, would they still love me?”
There is an even more important question.
What happens when God knows the real you?
He already does.
Every chapter.
Every thought.
Every motive.
Every night you regret.
Every promise you broke.
Every temptation you entertained.
Every person you wounded.
Every time you knew what was right and chose something else.
He knows.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that God discovered you were secretly better than everyone thought.
The Gospel is the announcement that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus does not save the fictional version of you.
He saves sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People with shame.
People who have ruined things.
People who cannot travel backward and undo what happened.
People who finally stop defending themselves and cry for mercy.
Maybe that is you tonight.
Maybe your heart has been exhausted from pretending.
Then stop running.
Not toward religion.
Toward Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave you have been decorating.
Bring the sin into the light.
Call it what God calls it.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Confess.
Turn.
Come to Jesus.
Because the One who exposes sin is also the One who offers cleansing.
And perhaps you need to hear this clearly:
You do not clean yourself sufficiently and then come to Christ.
You come because you need Christ.
The thief on the cross had no years remaining to rebuild his reputation.
No ministry résumé.
No opportunity to repay everything.
No impressive spiritual performance.
He had a dying body, a guilty history, and faith turned toward Jesus.
And grace met him there.
That is scandalous.
That is beautiful.
That is the Gospel.
The bells on Aaron's robe remind us that sinful humanity does not stroll thoughtlessly into divine holiness.
But Jesus reveals something even greater:
God Himself has provided the Mediator we could never provide for ourselves.
So when Hebrews speaks of believers approaching the throne of grace with confidence, that confidence is not confidence in ourselves.
It is confidence in Christ.
There is a universe of difference.
Christian confidence does not say:
“I deserve to be here.”
It says:
“Jesus brought me here.”
Not my morality.
Not my church attendance.
Not my theological vocabulary.
Not my reputation.
Not my followers.
Not my ministry.
Not the fact that people think I am a good Christian.
Jesus.
Only Jesus.
And someday everything else you used to define yourself will become strangely small.
The applause.
The money.
The house.
The position.
The argument you were determined to win.
The person whose approval controlled you.
The secret sin you kept promising to quit “later.”
All of it will eventually collide with eternity.
So perhaps the question isn't merely,
“Why did the high priest wear bells?”
Perhaps the question beneath the question is:
If I stood before the holiness of God tonight, what am I trusting in?
Your goodness?
Your denomination?
Your baptism?
Your parents' faith?
Your Christian posts?
Your charitable giving?
Your religious knowledge?
Or Jesus Christ?
Be honest.
Not with me.
With God.
Some people reading this are tired.
Not physically.
Spiritually.
You have been fighting the same battle so long that you have started wondering whether God is finished with you.
You fall.
Repent.
Fight.
Fall.
Cry.
Try again.
And somewhere along the way shame started whispering,
“Stop coming back. God must be tired of you.”
Listen carefully.
Shame wants you hiding.
Jesus calls you into the light.
Repentance does not mean treating sin casually. It means refusing to let sin have the final word.
Not because typing a sentence saves you.
Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Let that comment become a moment of honesty rather than performance.
Maybe somebody else will see it and realize they are not the only person fighting.
Maybe someone will pray for you.
Maybe your honesty becomes the reason another exhausted believer stops hiding.
That is what the body of Christ should look like.
Not a museum filled with people pretending they were never broken.
A redeemed people pointing one another toward the One who heals.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose them.
Not because sharing earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But if this truth has helped you, sharing it can place Scripture and the message of Christ in front of someone who might never have searched for it themselves.
That can be an act of Christian witness.
Someone scrolling alone at two in the morning might need what you just read.
Someone who has almost abandoned the faith.
Someone hiding an addiction.
Someone convinced Jesus could never want them back.
Someone who has never understood why Christians keep talking about blood, priests, holiness, grace, and the cross.
Let the truth travel farther than you.
There are truths we understand differently when the next temptation comes.
When shame returns.
When you fail.
When somebody discovers something about you.
When you begin believing you must somehow earn your way back into God's love.
Come back and remember:
Our hope was never that sinners could become impressive enough to enter God's presence. Our hope is that Jesus Christ became the perfect Mediator sinners desperately needed.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Do it not as though money could glorify God automatically, because Scripture never allows us to purchase spiritual favor. Give freely, prayerfully, and willingly.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people.
Don't leave Jesus at the bottom of an article.
Look at Him.
The priesthood pointed beyond itself.
The sacrifices pointed beyond themselves.
The blood pointed beyond itself.
The sanctuary pointed beyond itself.
Humanity needed a Mediator.
And Christ came.
The One without sin walked willingly toward a cross carrying the judgment sinners deserved.
His hands were pierced.
His blood was shed.
His body was broken.
He died.
And death did not keep Him.
Jesus Christ rose.
So your deepest need is not becoming a slightly improved version of yourself.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need forgiveness.
You need new life.
You need Christ.
Maybe you arrived here because you were curious about some tiny golden bells hanging from an ancient priestly garment.
And somehow, thousands of years later, those bells have brought you face-to-face with a question about your own soul.
That is the strange beauty of Scripture.
A garment becomes a doorway.
A bell becomes a warning.
A priest becomes a shadow.
And the shadow leads us toward Christ.
So listen one final time.
A bell.
A pomegranate.
A bell.
A pomegranate.
A priest moving before the Holy One.
And then look toward Calvary.
There hangs the greater answer to humanity's problem.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen in victory.
Calling the guilty to repent.
Calling the ashamed out of hiding.
Calling the exhausted home.
Calling the religious to stop trusting religion.
Calling the broken to stop believing brokenness is their identity.
Calling you.
Then read the other comments.
Pray for somebody.
Encourage somebody.
Remind somebody that Jesus is still worthy.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because one day the question will not be how much Christian content we consumed, how many posts we shared, how many books we owned, or whether people thought we looked religious.
The question beneath everything is whether our hope rests in Christ.
Aaron's bells once sounded as a priest moved through sacred space before the LORD.
But the Gospel announces something infinitely greater:
because of Jesus, repentant sinners do not have to spend their lives running away from the God who already knows everything about them.
They can come home.
And perhaps that is the sound your soul has been waiting to hear.
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you—but His grace gets the final word over the person He is making you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ONAN’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN THE PHYSICAL ACT EVERYONE FIXATES ON
paragraphs: ONAN’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN THE PHYSICAL ACT EVERYONE FIXATES ON
Everyone remembers what Onan did with his body. Almost nobody slows down long enough to ask what was happening in his heart.
And that changes the way you read the entire story.

Because Genesis 38 is not merely preserving an ancient account about a sexual act. It is exposing something frighteningly familiar: the human ability to receive the benefits of a relationship while deliberately refusing the responsibility that comes with it.
That is where this story gets uncomfortably close to us.
Onan wanted something from Tamar.
He simply did not want to give Tamar what his responsibility required.
And somewhere between those two realities, Scripture gives us one of the Bible’s shortest and most sobering portraits of calculated selfishness.
The story begins in a broken household.

Judah’s firstborn son, Er, married a woman named Tamar. Scripture tells us that Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death. We are not told precisely what Er did. The Bible refuses to satisfy our curiosity.
Then Judah turned to his second son, Onan.
Genesis 38:8 records Judah telling him to fulfill his responsibility toward his deceased brother’s wife and raise offspring for his brother.
The Hebrew becomes especially important here.
וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ
wəyabbēm ʾōtāh
The key verb is יָבַם — yābam.
It refers to performing the duty of a brother-in-law toward the widow of a deceased brother.
Judah continues:
וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ
wəhāqēm zeraʿ ləʾāḥîkā
“Raise up offspring for your brother.”
The word זֶרַע — zeraʿ — can mean seed, offspring, or descendants depending on context.
This matters enormously.
The passage itself tells us what Onan understood.
Genesis 38:9 says:
וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע
Wayyēdaʿ ʾÔnān kî lō lô yihyeh hazzāraʿ.
“And Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
There it is.
The narrator takes us inside his reasoning.
Onan knew.
That may be the most terrifying phrase in the story.
He was not confused.
He was not ignorant of what was expected.
He knew.

And because he knew that the resulting offspring would be reckoned to his dead brother rather than to himself, Genesis tells us that whenever he went in to Tamar, he deliberately prevented conception.
Read that carefully.
He did not simply refuse the arrangement openly.
He participated in the part that benefited him while sabotaging the part that benefited someone else.
That is why reducing the entire account to one isolated physical action can cause us to miss a major emphasis of the narrator.
The text explicitly gives Onan’s motive.
He knew the offspring would not be his, and therefore he acted “so that he would not give offspring to his brother.”
That final purpose clause matters.
His body was carrying out a decision his heart had already made.

This does not mean Christians throughout history have agreed on every moral question people later associated with this passage. They have not. Different Christian traditions have drawn different conclusions concerning sexual ethics and contraception from Genesis 38.
We should be careful not to force the passage to answer every later debate by itself.
But we should be equally careful not to erase what Genesis explicitly says.
Onan knowingly took what he wanted while deliberately withholding what he owed.
He treated Tamar as though her body could serve his desires while her future could remain somebody else’s problem.
And suddenly this ancient story does not feel ancient anymore.
Because Onan’s pattern did not die with Onan.
We can do the same thing without ever standing anywhere near Genesis 38.
We want the comfort of marriage without sacrificial love.
The benefits of church without serving anyone.
The promises of God without surrender to God.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Christian community without accountability.
A platform without responsibility.
Influence without integrity.
Grace without transformation.
We want Jesus as Savior while quietly negotiating whether He may also be Lord.
Take what benefits me.
Withhold what costs me.
That is the heartbeat beneath so much human rebellion.
And God sees it.
Genesis 38:10 says that what Onan did was evil “in the eyes of the LORD.”
The Hebrew reads:
וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
Wayyēraʿ bəʿênê YHWH ʾăšer ʿāśāh.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of YHWH.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not merely tell us that ancient society disapproved.
It does not say Judah found it embarrassing.
It does not say Tamar complained.
The narrator takes us directly into the courtroom that ultimately matters.
The eyes of the LORD.
People saw an ordinary family arrangement.
God saw the heart behind it.
People could see Onan entering Tamar’s life.
God could see why.
And there are few truths more comforting—or more terrifying—than this:
God sees motives that human beings cannot.
You can look obedient while resisting God internally.
You can stand in church with your hands raised while keeping entire rooms of your life locked.
You can know the worship songs.
Know the Bible verses.
Know Christian language.
Know exactly when to say “Amen.”
And still quietly tell Jesus:
“You can have everything except this.”
Maybe that is why Onan’s story makes us uncomfortable when we stop arguing about the physical mechanics long enough to listen.
Because suddenly Onan is not merely “that man in Genesis.”
Suddenly the question becomes:
What am I withholding from God because obedience would cost me something?
That question reaches deeper than sexual ethics.
Maybe you know you need to forgive someone, but resentment feels too valuable to surrender.
Maybe you know you need to confess something, but your reputation feels too valuable to risk.
Maybe there is a relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ, but loneliness terrifies you.
Maybe money has quietly become your security.
Maybe pornography has become your hidden refuge.
Maybe pride has made apology almost impossible.
Maybe you serve publicly while starving spiritually.
Maybe you keep asking God to bless a life you have never fully surrendered to Him.
And perhaps nobody knows.
That is the frightening part.
Nobody knew everything happening inside Onan either.
But God did.
The Gospel never gives us permission to hide behind outward appearances.
Jesus repeatedly confronted precisely that kind of religion.

People could clean the outside while corruption remained within. People could honor God with their lips while their hearts remained far from Him. People could appear righteous before others while God saw beneath the performance.
Christ has never been interested merely in managing appearances.
He came for the heart.
And this is where Genesis 38 becomes even more astonishing.
Because if the chapter ended with judgment, it would already be sobering.
But Genesis does not end there.
The story keeps moving.
Judah fails Tamar too.
Tamar eventually takes desperate and morally complicated action.
Judah is exposed.
A pregnancy follows.
Twins are born.
One of them is Perez.
And generations later, another genealogy appears.
Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
And then Matthew does something remarkable.
He names Tamar.
“Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.”
The scandal was not erased from the family history of the Messiah.
God put it in the genealogy.
Not because sin does not matter.
Genesis 38 makes painfully clear that it does.
But because human failure cannot prevent God from accomplishing His redemptive purpose.
Perez enters the line that eventually leads to David.
And through David’s royal line, according to the flesh, comes Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A chapter containing death, selfishness, sexual brokenness, deception, exploitation, shame, family dysfunction, and public exposure becomes part of the road toward Bethlehem.
Only God writes stories like that.
We would have edited Genesis 38 out.
God preserved it.
We would have hidden Tamar.
Matthew named her.
We would have cleaned up the Messiah’s genealogy before publishing it.
God displayed the broken family tree and then placed Jesus at its culmination.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people managed to produce a Savior.
Christianity is the announcement that a Savior entered the wreckage of humanity to rescue sinners.
That Savior is Jesus.
He did what Onan would not.
Onan acted according to what served himself.
Christ came not to be served, but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Onan withheld what would cost him.
Jesus withheld nothing necessary for our redemption.
Onan’s story exposes the instinct to protect ourselves at another person’s expense.
Jesus willingly gave Himself for people who had nothing with which to repay Him.
At Calvary, Christ did not exploit the vulnerable.
He became vulnerable.
He was mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Pierced.
Crucified.
And He remained obedient to the Father even unto death.
There is the contrast our hearts desperately need.
Not merely Onan versus better behavior.
Onan versus Christ.
Self-protection versus self-giving love.
Calculated selfishness versus holy obedience.
Taking versus giving.
Sin versus righteousness.
Death versus resurrection.
And here is where the Gospel becomes personal.
You do not overcome the Onan inside the human heart merely by trying harder.
Sin runs deeper than behavior.
Jesus said evil proceeds from within the human heart.
We need more than external restraint.
We need a new heart.
That is why Christ did not come merely to make immoral people more respectable.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He bore sin on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
And repentance is not God humiliating you for finally admitting what He already knows.
Repentance is dropping the disguise.
It is coming into the light.
It is saying:
“Jesus, I have taken what I wanted and withheld what You asked.”
“I have used people.”
“I have protected my idols.”
“I have excused what I should have confessed.”
“I have looked obedient while negotiating with You privately.”
“I have sinned.”
And then grace does what shame never could.
Grace does not tell you the sin was harmless.
Grace tells you the blood of Christ is sufficient.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings you out of darkness.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Grace says, “Come to Jesus exactly as you are—and He will not leave you exactly as you are.”
This is why our message has always been:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
He does something greater.
He redeems sinners.
Peter still denied Him.
Paul still persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well still had her history.
The thief still reached the cross guilty.
Tamar’s name still appears in a complicated story.
Judah’s failure is still written in Genesis.
Yet failure did not receive the final word.
Jesus did.
And maybe you needed that tonight.
Maybe you have been reading this thinking about someone else.
Someone selfish.
Someone sexually broken.
Someone hypocritical.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone who used you.
But perhaps somewhere along the way the Holy Spirit turned the mirror around.
And now you are thinking about you.
Do not run from that moment.
Run to Christ.
There is no freedom in defending the darkness Jesus came to forgive.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask for help.
Seek accountability where needed.
If you have sinned against someone, pursue biblical reconciliation where it is safe and appropriate.
If a hidden habit has mastered you, stop protecting it.
If you have been performing Christianity while starving inside, tell Jesus the truth.
He already knows.
The wonder of the Gospel is that the One who knows you most completely is the One whose grace is sufficient for every sinner who comes to Him in faith.
So be honest.
Did this hit harder than you expected?
If God exposed something you have been hiding, you can comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but refuse to walk away from Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if you are watching Jesus patiently rebuild areas of your life you once thought were beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Sometimes somebody scrolling through those comments needs to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a battle behind a smile.
Your honesty may become someone else’s invitation into the light.
And if one person came to mind while reading this, do not merely think about them.
Send it privately to the believer who has grown cold.
Share it with the person who thinks their past has permanently disqualified them from grace.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Not to a brand.
Not to a personality.
Not to merchandise.
Not to religious performance.
Jesus.
The One who knows what you did.
The One who knows why you did it.
The One who sees the secret compromises nobody else sees.
The One who calls sin what it is.
And the One who went to the cross so sinners could be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled to God, and transformed.
Onan’s tragedy was bigger than the physical act everyone remembers.
His outward action revealed an inward refusal.
And perhaps that is the warning Genesis 38 still whispers across thousands of years:
God is not merely watching what our hands do.
He sees what our hearts refuse to surrender.
So do not give Jesus the appearance of obedience while secretly reserving the throne for yourself.
Give Him the hidden room.
Give Him the wound.
Give Him the appetite.
Give Him the resentment.
Give Him the relationship.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the secret.
Give Him the future.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy purchased at the cross.
Then rise and walk differently—not because your obedience purchases grace, but because grace has found you.
And remember this when your past starts whispering that God could never make anything beautiful from what happened:
There was scandal in the family tree that led to Bethlehem, but scandal did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
And He still does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF YOU ASK ANYTHING IN MY NAME, I WILL DO IT” — IS THAT A BLANK CHECK FROM JESUS?
paragraphs: “IF YOU ASK ANYTHING IN MY NAME, I WILL DO IT” — IS THAT A BLANK CHECK FROM JESUS?

What if one of the most comforting promises Jesus ever gave has also become one of the most painfully misunderstood—and what if understanding what He actually meant could change the way you pray forever?
You prayed.
You really prayed.
Not the casual kind. Not the half-awake prayer before falling asleep. Not the polite words people say because Christians are supposed to pray.
You begged.
Maybe your face was wet with tears.
Maybe your hands were shaking.
Maybe you whispered the same sentence so many times that eventually there were no sentences left.
“Jesus, please…”
Please heal her.
Please bring him home.
Please save this marriage.
Please give me this job.
Please take this pain away.
Please let the test come back negative.
Please fix what I destroyed.
Please don’t let my child walk away from You.
Please…
And somewhere in the middle of that desperation, perhaps you remembered something Jesus said:
“If you ask Me anything in My name, I will do it.”
John 14:14.
Anything.
That word can feel enormous when your heart is breaking.
So you asked.
You even ended the prayer correctly.
“In Jesus’ name, amen.”
And then…
nothing happened the way you expected.
The relationship still ended.
The opportunity disappeared.
The sickness remained.
The door stayed closed.
The person died.
The prodigal did not immediately come home.
The answer you desperately wanted never arrived.
And suddenly the promise that once comforted you began quietly accusing you.
Maybe I didn’t have enough faith.
Maybe God didn’t hear me.
Maybe I prayed incorrectly.
Maybe there is something wrong with me.
Or perhaps the question became darker:
Can I really trust what Jesus said?
That is where many believers suffer silently.
Because nobody wants to admit that sometimes unanswered prayer hurts.
Nobody wants to say out loud that there are moments when heaven seems unbearably quiet.
But Jesus is not frightened by that question.
And the answer is not found by weakening His promise.
It is found by listening carefully to what He actually promised.
The New Testament was written primarily in Koine Greek, and John records Jesus’ words this way:
“καὶ ὅ τι ἂν αἰτήσητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου, τοῦτο ποιήσω, ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ Πατὴρ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ.”
Kai ho ti an aitēsēte en tō onomati mou, touto poiēsō, hina doxasthē ho Patēr en tō Huiō.
“Whatever you ask in My name, this I will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”
Then Jesus says:
“ἐάν τι αἰτήσητέ με ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου, ἐγὼ ποιήσω.”
“If you ask Me anything in My name, I will do it.”
The breathtaking word is certainly “whatever.”
But there is another phrase we cannot afford to ignore:
“ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου.”
En tō onomati mou.
“In My name.”
That changes everything.
Because Jesus was not teaching His disciples to attach a sacred password to whatever they already wanted.
“In Jesus’ name” is not a magical formula.
It is not heaven’s PIN number.
It is not a spiritual loophole that forces God to approve our preferred outcome.
And prayer is not a blank check on which we write our desires and require Jesus to sign His name at the bottom.
To act in someone’s name carries the idea of acting under that person’s authority and in relation to who that person is.
Imagine someone arriving at a bank saying, “I am here in the king’s name,” while carrying instructions the king never authorized.
Using the king’s name would not create the king’s approval.
It would expose the fraud.
And perhaps that is where this verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we do something remarkably similar with Jesus.
We decide what we want.
We build the dream.
We choose the outcome.
We determine the timeline.
Then we approach God and ask Him to bless the plan.
And at the end we say:
“In Jesus’ name.”
But what if praying in Jesus’ name means something far deeper than adding Jesus’ name to my desires?
What if it means bringing my desires underneath Jesus?
Look again at the sentence immediately surrounding the promise.
Jesus does not merely say He will answer.
He tells us why:
“ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ Πατὴρ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ.”
Hina doxasthē ho Patēr en tō Huiō.
“So that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”
There is the heartbeat.
The purpose of the promise is the glory of the Father through the Son.
Jesus is not handing His disciples a mechanism for obtaining everything their fallen hearts can imagine.
He is preparing them for mission.
Read the room.
This is John 14.
Jesus is speaking to His disciples shortly before the cross.
Betrayal is coming.
Fear is coming.
Confusion is coming.
Jesus has been preparing them for His departure.
And immediately before this promise He tells them that whoever believes in Him will continue His works, even speaking of “greater works,” because He is going to the Father.
Immediately afterward He speaks about loving Him, keeping His commandments, and the coming Holy Spirit.
This is not a prosperity seminar.
This is a farewell discourse.
These men are about to lose the physical presence of their Teacher, watch Him crucified, encounter Him risen, receive the Holy Spirit, proclaim the Gospel and suffer for His name.
And Jesus tells them they will not be abandoned.
They can ask in His name.
They will continue His mission under His authority.
The Father will be glorified through the Son.
Suddenly the promise looks different.
Not smaller.
Bigger.
Because Jesus is promising something infinitely better than becoming the servant of our wishes.
He is inviting ordinary human beings into the purposes of God.
This understanding also fits the rest of Scripture.
John later writes:
1 John 5:14.
There it is again.
Confidence in prayer does not mean sovereignty over God.
It means confidence in God.
Jesus Himself demonstrates this in Gethsemane.
He knows agony is coming.
His soul is overwhelmed.
He falls before the Father and prays about the cup before Him.
Yet His surrender remains absolute:
“Nevertheless, not My will, but Yours, be done.”
Luke 22:42.
Think about that.
The perfect Son prayed with complete faith…
and complete surrender.
So surrender is not weak faith.
Sometimes surrender is faith at its purest.
Faith does not say, “God must do what I tell Him.”
Faith says, “Father, I trust You enough to tell You exactly what I desire, and I trust You enough to surrender the outcome.”
That is much harder.
Because most of us love the first half of prayer.
“Ask.”
We struggle with the second half.
“Your will be done.”
We want resurrection without Gethsemane.
Provision without dependence.
Promise without surrender.
Crown without cross.
But Jesus does not merely want to change your circumstances.
Jesus came to redeem you.
And sometimes the greatest miracle happening during prayer is not that God changes what is around you.
It is that God changes what is inside you.
Perhaps you prayed for a door to open.
It closed.
Years later you realized that door would have destroyed you.
Perhaps you begged God to preserve a relationship.
It ended.
And eventually you discovered how much of your identity had been wrapped around another human being instead of Christ.
Perhaps you prayed for immediate deliverance from a struggle.
The battle continued.
And through that battle you learned dependence, humility, endurance and compassion for wounded people that effortless victory might never have taught you.
But we also need to be careful here.
We should never look at someone grieving and casually announce, “God did that to teach you a lesson.”
We do not know all of God’s hidden purposes.
The Bible does not give us permission to invent explanations for another person’s suffering.
Sometimes we simply weep with those who weep.
Sometimes the most faithful sentence we can speak is:
“I don’t know why.”
Christian faith does not require pretending pain is painless.
At Lazarus’ tomb, Jesus knew resurrection was moments away.
And still:
“Jesus wept.”
John 11:35.
He knew the ending…
and He entered the grief.
So if you have been wounded by unanswered prayer, Jesus is not standing far away demanding that you stop hurting.
Bring the hurt to Him.
Bring the confusion.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the prayer you are almost afraid to pray again.
But bring your interpretation of His promise back to Scripture too.
Because there is another dangerous extreme.
Some people have been disappointed so often that they stop asking boldly altogether.
They protect themselves by expecting nothing.
They call it surrender.
Sometimes it is simply fear wearing religious clothing.
Jesus really did say:
Ask.
Scripture really does call believers to pray.
We really can approach God.
We really should bring requests before Him.
God really does answer prayer.
The correction is not to stop asking boldly.
The correction is to stop confusing boldness with control.
Pray for healing.
Pray boldly.
Pray for reconciliation.
Pray boldly.
Pray for provision.
Pray boldly.
Pray for your wandering child.
Pray boldly.
Pray for freedom from addiction.
Pray boldly.
Pray for impossible doors to open.
Pray boldly.
Ask the Father for things so enormous that only His power could accomplish them.
But somewhere inside every genuine prayer in Jesus’ name lives this surrendered heartbeat:
“Jesus, I want what You want more than I want what I want.”
Read that again.
Because that sentence may expose us.
“Jesus, I want what You want more than I want what I want.”
Can you say that about the prayer you have been praying?
That promotion?
That relationship?
That person?
That healing?
That dream?
That opportunity?
That future?
Could you place it into the scarred hands of Christ and say:
“If giving this to me glorifies You, give it.
If withholding it glorifies You, sustain me.
If I must wait, teach me.
If I need correction, correct me.
If there is sin in what I desire, expose it.
If my motives are selfish, purify them.
If there is another road, lead me.
But whatever happens…
do not let me have my desire at the cost of losing intimacy with You.”
That is dangerous prayer.
Because now Jesus is no longer merely being invited into your plans.
You are being surrendered into His.
And perhaps this is the scandal hidden inside grace:
We often come to Jesus wanting Him to rewrite our circumstances.
Jesus begins rewriting us.
We ask Him for something.
He gives us Himself.
We ask for escape.
Sometimes He gives endurance.
We ask for explanation.
Sometimes He gives presence.
We ask for immediate relief.
Sometimes He gives grace sufficient for today.
And sometimes—beautifully, unexpectedly, unmistakably—He gives exactly what we asked.
The door opens.
The diagnosis changes.
The prodigal comes home.
The marriage begins healing.
Provision arrives from somewhere nobody expected.
And when it happens, we do not say, “Look how powerful my prayer was.”
We say:
“Look how merciful my God is.”
Because answered prayer was never designed to glorify the person praying.
Jesus said the purpose Himself:
“That the Father may be glorified in the Son.”
Maybe you needed to read this because you have quietly been angry with God.
Maybe you thought Jesus broke His promise.
Maybe somebody taught you that enough faith could force the outcome.
Maybe you have carried shame because someone told you your loved one was not healed because you did not believe strongly enough.
Do not carry a burden Scripture never placed on your shoulders.
Biblical faith is not the ability to manipulate God.
Biblical faith trusts God.
Even through tears.
Even in waiting.
Even when the answer is different from what we begged for.
And ultimately, Christianity rests upon the greatest apparent unanswered prayer becoming the doorway to the greatest act of redemption.
Gethsemane led to Calvary.
Calvary looked like defeat.
The Messiah was mocked.
Stripped.
Nailed to wood.
Blood ran down the body of the One through whom the universe was made.
The disciples watched their expectations collapse.
Then came the tomb.
Silence.
A stone.
Saturday.
Imagine judging God's faithfulness on Saturday.
Imagine deciding the story was finished because heaven appeared silent.
But Sunday was coming.
The stone moved.
Christ rose.
Sin's debt was answered.
Death was defeated.
And what looked like the darkest scandal became the announcement of grace.
That is the Gospel.
Not that God gives sinners everything they request.
But that God gave sinners the Son they desperately needed.
Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again.
Repentance is not negotiating with God for a better life.
It is turning from sin toward the living Christ.
Grace is not God becoming useful to our ambitions.
Grace is God rescuing people who could never rescue themselves.
And maybe your greatest prayer today should not be:
“Jesus, give me what I want.”
Maybe it should become:
“Jesus, make me Yours.”

Supporting a Christian ministry is not a requirement for earning God's favor, proving your faith, or glorifying Him—as though grace could be purchased. But voluntary generosity can help biblical teaching reach people who need it.
But before you leave, there is one prayer worth carrying with you.
Not because it guarantees an easy tomorrow.
Not because it guarantees the answer you imagined.
But because it places your life where prayer was always meant to place it—in the hands of Jesus.

“Lord Jesus, I will ask boldly because You told me to ask. I will trust deeply because You are worthy of trust. I will surrender completely because You are Lord. Purify what I desire. Correct what is selfish. Strengthen me when Your answer is wait. Hold me when Your answer hurts. Humble me when Your answer is yes. And whatever You do, let the Father be glorified through the Son. I do not merely want Your gifts. I want You. Amen.”
Maybe the silence you called abandonment was never the end of the story.
Maybe you are standing in Saturday…
and Jesus is still writing Sunday.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Paul Said Widows Were Free to Remarry—but Added Four Important Words: “Only in the Lord”
paragraphs: Paul Said Widows Were Free to Remarry—but Added Four Important Words: “Only in the Lord”

She had already buried one love. Paul did not tell her she could never love again. He said she was free. But then he placed four words beside that freedom—words powerful enough to change whom you marry, how you date, and what you believe Christian marriage is actually for.
There are sentences in Scripture that feel almost painfully personal when you have lived long enough.
You can read them when you are twenty and barely notice them.
Then grief happens.
A chair becomes empty.
A side of the bed becomes untouched.
A familiar voice disappears from the house.
A wedding ring that once represented beginnings suddenly becomes a reminder that something ended.
And then one day you come across something Paul wrote nearly two thousand years ago:
“A wife is bound for so long time as her husband liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is free to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord.”
—1 Corinthians 7:39, ASV
Read the sentence slowly.
Because there is both tenderness and thunder inside it.
“She is free…”
Those words matter.
Christianity does not teach that a widow who loved her husband deeply somehow betrays him by eventually loving again.
Paul does not sentence the widow to permanent loneliness.
He does not say that remarriage after the death of a spouse is adultery.
He says she is free.
Romans 7:2–3 makes the same basic point: death ends the marriage bond, and the surviving spouse is therefore free from that marital obligation.
And elsewhere Paul can even counsel younger widows to marry, raise families, and manage their households.
So Scripture does not treat remarriage after widowhood as some dirty secret requiring embarrassment.
Grief does not cancel the possibility of another chapter.
The grave may close one marriage without closing the surviving spouse’s entire earthly story.
Maybe somebody reading this needs permission to hear that without guilt.
You loved your spouse.
You still miss your spouse.
There may still be photographs you cannot look at without feeling something tighten inside your chest.
There may be songs you avoid.
Restaurants you stopped visiting.
Anniversaries you survive rather than celebrate.
You may even wonder whether smiling beside another person someday would somehow dishonor the person whose hand you once held beside a hospital bed.
Paul does not mock that grief.
But neither does Scripture turn grief into a prison.
“She is free…”
And yet Paul does not put a period there.
That is where this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because after giving freedom, Paul gives a boundary.
The Greek is strikingly compact:
μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ
monon en Kyriō
Literally:
“only in the Lord.”
Four English words.
An entire theology of Christian marriage hiding inside them.
Paul essentially says: You may marry whom you desire…
only in the Lord.
Your heart matters.
Your desire matters.
Your freedom matters.
But Jesus still matters more.
And that changes everything.
Because modern culture often asks only one question about relationships:
“Does this person make you happy?”
Scripture asks something deeper:
Can this relationship be lived faithfully under the lordship of Jesus Christ?
That is not the same question.
Someone can make your heart race and still pull your heart away from Christ.
Someone can make you laugh and still slowly make prayer disappear from your life.
Someone can be attractive, successful, attentive, financially stable, emotionally fascinating, and socially impressive…
and still not share the One who sits on the throne of your life.
This is where “only in the Lord” stops being merely a rule for widows and exposes something much larger about Christian marriage.
Marriage for a Christian is never merely two people agreeing that they love each other.
Jesus is Lord.
Not Cupid.
Not chemistry.
Not loneliness.
Not sexual attraction.
Not financial security.
Not the fear of growing old alone.
Not the desperate thought:
“At least somebody wants me.”
Christ is Lord.
And when Christ is Lord, even our deepest desires come underneath His authority.
That does not mean desire is evil.
Notice Paul says the widow is free to marry whom she wishes.
There is genuine human choice here.
Scripture is not describing some mechanical system where Christians must somehow discover one secret soulmate hidden by God among billions of people.
There is freedom.
There is desire.
There is choice.
But Christian freedom is never freedom from Christ.
It is freedom in Christ.
That little phrase changes the entire atmosphere of the verse.
μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ.
Only in the Lord.
Paul is not telling a grieving woman, “You have suffered enough, so now God does not care whom you choose.”
He is saying something far more beautiful.
Your suffering did not remove you from the lordship of Jesus.
Your loneliness did not remove you from the lordship of Jesus.
Your longing did not remove you from the lordship of Jesus.
Your second chapter still belongs to Jesus.
That matters because loneliness can become a dangerous counselor.
Loneliness whispers:
“Take whatever love you can get.”
Loneliness says:
“You're getting older.”
“Your opportunities are disappearing.”
“Nobody else will come.”
“Maybe this is your last chance.”
“Sure, they don't really follow Jesus, but they're a good person.”
“They respect your faith.”
“They said they don't mind you going to church.”
And sometimes we rename desperation as providence because we are terrified of another empty night.
But there is an enormous difference between someone who merely tolerates your Christianity and someone whose life belongs to Christ.
“Only in the Lord” is not asking whether someone will allow you to own a Bible.
It points toward shared allegiance to Jesus.
Imagine trying to build one life when the deepest centers of two lives are moving toward different thrones.
When suffering comes—and it will—where do you run?
When money becomes tight, what governs your decisions?
When forgiveness feels impossible, who defines forgiveness?
When sexuality becomes difficult, who defines holiness?
When children arrive, whose truth shapes them?
When ambition calls, who decides what success means?
When one of you is wounded, bitter, exhausted, tempted, depressed, angry, frightened, or spiritually dry, what authority stands above both of you?
For the Christian, marriage cannot ultimately survive on the sentence:
“We love each other.”
Eventually another question arrives:
Whom do we worship?
This is why biblical boundaries are not God trying to ruin human happiness.
They come from the God who sees what infatuation cannot see.
We usually see the next date.
God sees the direction of a life.
We see the wedding.
God sees year fourteen.
We see photographs.
God sees arguments nobody photographs.
We see chemistry.
God sees discipleship.
We see somebody holding our hand.
God sees where that person may help lead our heart.
And sometimes grace sounds like permission.
Sometimes grace sounds like warning.
Sometimes grace opens a door.
Sometimes grace says:
Not that door.
That may be especially difficult for someone who has already lost a spouse.
Because grief creates hunger.
Not merely sexual hunger.
Human hunger.
Someone to talk to after everyone else has gone home.
Someone who notices when you're tired.
Someone who asks whether you ate.
Someone beside you at church.
Someone whose name appears on your phone.
Someone to laugh with.
Someone to pray beside.
Someone who makes the house feel alive again.
There is nothing shameful about wanting companionship.
God Himself said in Genesis that it was not good for the man to be alone.
But a legitimate hunger can still tempt us toward an illegitimate compromise.
Esau was genuinely hungry when he traded something precious for immediate relief.
And many believers have discovered that loneliness can make a bowl of stew look like destiny.
That is why those four words matter.
Only in the Lord.
Not because God hates romance.
Because God loves you beyond the romance.
Not because God wants widows miserable.
Because the widow still belongs to Christ.
Not because remarriage is forbidden.
Paul explicitly says the opposite.
She is free.
That freedom is real.
But it is Christian freedom.
Freedom underneath the gracious reign of Jesus.
And maybe this article is no longer speaking only to widows.
Maybe it found you while you are dating somebody you already know is pulling you away from Jesus.
Maybe you have been explaining away what your conscience keeps bringing back.
Maybe you keep saying:
“They're spiritual.”
But you know spiritual is not the same thing as surrendered to Christ.
Maybe you say:
“They believe in God.”
James reminds us that mere belief that God exists is hardly the definition of saving allegiance.
Maybe you say:
“I can change them.”
But you are slowly becoming more like them.
You pray less.
You compromise more.
Conviction has become inconvenient.
Church attendance became negotiable.
Sexual boundaries moved.
Things that once troubled your conscience barely trouble you now.
And somewhere underneath all your explanations is one frightening possibility:
You are not leading them closer to Jesus.
They are helping you become comfortable farther away from Him.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
