The text describes honey on the ground, yet the soldiers refuse to eat because they fear the oath.
Jonathan does not know.
He reaches out the end of his staff, dips it into the honeycomb, brings the honey to his mouth...
and Scripture says:
“his eyes were enlightened.”
—1 Samuel 14:27, KJV
The Hebrew is vivid.
וַתָּאֹרְנָה עֵינָיו
vatta'ornah einav
Literally, his eyes became bright.
His strength revived.
Then somebody tells him about Saul's oath.
Jonathan's response is devastating:
“My father hath troubled the land.”
—1 Samuel 14:29, KJV
The Hebrew verb behind “troubled” is עָכַר — ʿakhar, carrying the sense of bringing trouble or calamity.
Jonathan sees what Saul apparently cannot.
The oath has not strengthened God's people.
It has weakened them.
The men are exhausted.
Victory could have been greater.
And when starving soldiers finally obtain food, they become so desperate that they begin eating meat with the blood still in it, violating God's revealed command concerning blood.
Think about the tragedy.
A humanly imposed restriction contributed to circumstances in which the people rushed into actual sin.
That should make every believer uncomfortable.
Because religious intensity is not automatically spiritual maturity.
A rule can sound holy and still be foolishly applied.
A tradition can be defended passionately and still need to be tested by Scripture.
A leader can speak with tremendous confidence and still be wrong.
And obedience to God must never be replaced by unquestioning loyalty to human authority.
That does not mean biblical authority is meaningless.
It means the opposite.
God's Word is so authoritative that every human command must remain beneath it.
Parents are not God.
Pastors are not God.
Church traditions are not God.
Denominations are not God.
Influencers are not God.
Your favorite preacher is not God.
Gospel Warrior is not God.
Only God is God.
And every voice—including ours—must ultimately bow before the written Word and point people toward Jesus Christ.
But the story becomes darker.
Saul seeks further direction concerning the battle and receives no answer.
He concludes that sin must be present among the people.
Then Saul makes another terrifying declaration.
“For, as the LORD liveth, which saveth Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.”
—1 Samuel 14:39, KJV
Read that again.
“Though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.”
The man God had used so powerfully that day is now standing beneath a death sentence from his own father.
The investigation eventually identifies Jonathan.
Saul asks what he has done.
Jonathan answers:
“I did but taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in mine hand, and, lo, I must die.”
—1 Samuel 14:43, KJV
And Saul answers:
“God do so and more also: for thou shalt surely die, Jonathan.”
—1 Samuel 14:44, KJV
This is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Saul is prepared to kill his own son.
Not because Jonathan betrayed Israel.
Not because Jonathan worshiped the Philistine gods.
Not because Jonathan abandoned the battle.
Jonathan had courageously entered the battle.
He trusted God's power.
He helped bring deliverance to Israel.
He ate some honey because he had never heard the oath.
And now his father is prepared to let an ill-conceived oath become a death sentence.
There is a warning here for anyone who has ever loved being right more than being righteous.
For anyone who has defended a decision because admitting it was wrong felt more humiliating than watching somebody else suffer from it.
For parents who confuse control with discipleship.
For leaders who begin protecting their authority instead of protecting the people entrusted to them.
For believers who can quote their standards faster than they can demonstrate mercy.
For churches where maintaining appearances becomes more important than restoring wounded people.
And for every one of us who has ever secretly thought:
“I already said it, so I cannot back down now.”
Sometimes repentance sounds like:
I was wrong.
Sometimes humility sounds like:
I should never have demanded that.
Sometimes spiritual maturity means admitting that what you called conviction was actually pride.
But Saul does not rescue Jonathan.
The people do.
They answer Saul:
“Shall Jonathan die, who hath wrought this great salvation in Israel? God forbid: as the LORD liveth, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he hath wrought with God this day.”
—1 Samuel 14:45, KJV
And then Scripture says:
“So the people rescued Jonathan, that he died not.”
Jonathan lives.
But something about this story leaves a wound.
Because you begin wondering how a father reaches the place where keeping his word becomes more important than keeping his son alive.
And then the Gospel turns the question around.
Because centuries later...
another Son would stand beneath a sentence of death.
But this time the Father was not defending a foolish oath.
And this Son was not an accidental offender.
Jesus Christ willingly came for sinners.
The New Testament announces the astonishing heart of the Gospel:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because God had made a reckless human promise and needed to protect His pride.
Christ's death was the fulfillment of God's redemptive purpose.
Jesus said:
“Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.
No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.”
—John 10:17–18, KJV
Jonathan nearly died because of another man's words.
Jesus willingly laid down His life because of divine love and the saving purpose of God.
Jonathan needed the people to intervene so that he would not die.
Jesus became the One who intervened for us.
We were the guilty ones.
We were the sinners.
We were the rebels.
We were the ones who had actually broken God's commands.
And Christ stepped into history not merely to improve us...
but to save us.
The Greek word used repeatedly in the New Testament for grace is χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Favor given rather than earned.
And Ephesians declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
—Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
That is where scandal becomes grace.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
It tells you that your sin was so serious that redemption required what you could never provide for yourself—and that God's love was so astonishing that Christ came willingly to save sinners.
Maybe your story has rules in it too.
Rules you broke.
Rules somebody imposed upon you.
Standards you could never reach.
Promises you failed to keep.
Secret sins nobody knows about.
Maybe you have spent years believing that God is merely waiting for one more failure before He finally gives up on you.
Hear the Gospel clearly.
Grace is not permission to remain in sin.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could make peace with the very darkness from which He came to rescue us.
Grace calls us to repentance.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a turning of heart and mind that results in a changed direction.
Jesus does not merely cover the scandal while leaving you chained to it.
He calls you out.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He teaches you to walk differently.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing you could do after reading Jonathan's story would be to spend all your time judging Saul without asking where Saul might be hiding inside you.
What rule have you made more important than mercy?
What grudge are you defending because surrendering it would require admitting you were wrong?
Whom have you wounded while convincing yourself that your intentions justified it?
What religious performance are you using to avoid repentance?
What secret compromise have you renamed so that you do not have to surrender it?
What would happen if tonight you stopped defending yourself before God?
No speech.
No excuses.
No pretending.
Just:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing an honest confession into the light is the first outward sign that we are finished pretending.
Be honest.
This story may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because every sentence is unforgettable, but because Scripture deserves to be returned to when pride begins sounding like conviction and control begins disguising itself as faithfulness.
And yes, supporting Gospel-centered work matters—but do it for the right reason.
You do not earn favor with God by sharing an article.
You do not purchase blessing by supporting a ministry.
The Gospel will never be for sale.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior's work, help us keep putting biblical truth in front of people who may never walk voluntarily through a church door.
do not leave this story merely remembering Saul.
Remember Jonathan's faith.
Remember the honey.
Remember the exhausted army.
Remember how quickly human pride can dress itself in religious language.
And above everything else...
remember Jesus.
Because your salvation does not rest upon your ability to construct the perfect religious record.
It rests upon the crucified and risen Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come out of hiding.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Then let that grace transform the way you speak, lead, parent, forgive, worship, and treat the people God has placed in your hands.
Saul almost let his own words become Jonathan's grave.
Do not let your pride become somebody else's.
And never forget this:
The rule Jonathan never heard almost became his death sentence—but at the Cross, Jesus willingly entered ours so grace could rewrite the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Vanity Is Exhausting Because the Mirror Never Says, “Enough.”
paragraphs: Vanity Is Exhausting Because the Mirror Never Says, “Enough.”
You can spend years trying to become beautiful enough for people who will eventually grow old beside you—while forgetting that God has been looking at something the mirror could never show.
There is something the mirror has never said to you.
Enough.
It has never looked back and whispered, “You can stop now. You have nothing left to prove.”
It never will.
Because a mirror can show you a face.
It cannot tell you what that face is worth.
And when you ask something incapable of measuring your value to determine your value, you enter a race with no finish line.
Maybe you know that race.
You take the photograph.
You look at it.
Everyone else sees you.
But you see the wrinkle.
The weight.
The skin.
The hair.
The nose.
The scar.
The part of your body you wish were different.
The evidence that you're getting older.
Someone tells you, “You look beautiful.”
And somehow one unflattering photograph speaks louder than ten compliments.
So you take another.
Then another.
Different angle.
Better lighting.
Hold your stomach.
Lift your chin.
Fix your hair.
Delete.
Retake.
Filter.
Post.
Then wait.
And sometimes what looks like confidence on somebody's screen is actually a frightened human being quietly asking the world:
Am I still enough?
That question doesn't belong only to teenage girls staring at social media.
It belongs to men watching their hairlines disappear.
Women discovering another wrinkle beneath bathroom lighting.
Mothers trying to recognize the bodies pregnancy changed.
Teenagers comparing themselves with edited faces.
Men comparing their physiques with bodies built under perfect lighting and carefully selected angles.
Women entering rooms where they quietly calculate whether they are still attractive enough to be noticed.
People approaching forty, fifty, sixty, seventy and realizing that the culture which once celebrated their youth has already begun looking toward someone younger.
Different generations.
Different mirrors.
Same ache.
Am I still visually worthy?
And that is why vanity is exhausting.
Not because caring about your appearance is automatically sinful.
Not because washing your face is vanity.
Not because wearing beautiful clothes is rebellion.
Not because makeup, jewelry, grooming, fitness, style, or wanting to look presentable automatically means your heart is far from God.
First Peter 3:3–4 is sometimes handled as though Peter were simply issuing a divine prohibition against looking attractive.
But listen carefully to the contrast in the Greek:
“ὧν ἔστω οὐχ ὁ ἔξωθεν … κόσμος … ἀλλ’ ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος…”
The thought is essentially this:
Do not let your defining adornment be merely external…but let it be the hidden person of the heart.
Peter mentions braided hair, gold, and clothing, then deliberately moves our attention inward.
And there is a fascinating word sitting inside the passage.
κόσμος — kosmos.
Here it refers to adornment or ornament.
Something arranged.
Something presented outwardly.
Something seen.
But then Peter points toward something the crowd cannot photograph.
“ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος”
The hidden person of the heart.
Hidden.
That word almost hurts in a generation obsessed with being seen.
Because God places extraordinary value on something that may never receive a single like.
Something that cannot be filtered.
Something no cosmetic procedure can manufacture.
Something no expensive wardrobe can purchase.
Something an algorithm cannot rank.
Character.
The heart.
The person you are when nobody is applauding.
Peter continues:
“ἐν τῷ ἀφθάρτῳ…”
In the imperishable.
There it is.
The word our mirrors hate.
Imperishable.
Because almost everything appearance-based worth depends upon is perishable.
Youth is perishable.
Smooth skin is perishable.
Physical strength is perishable.
Fashion is perishable.
Trends are perishable.
Bodies change.
Hair changes.
Faces change.
The photograph you once hated may someday become the photograph you look at and whisper, “I was so young.”
And perhaps that is one of vanity's cruelest tricks.
It can convince you to hate today's body until tomorrow makes you miss it.
Read that again.
You may be criticizing a face right now that twenty years from now you would give anything to see looking back from the mirror.
How much of your life will you sacrifice trying to stop yourself from looking human?
How many dinners will you attend while thinking about your stomach?
How many photographs with your children will you avoid because you don't like your body?
How many beaches?
How many celebrations?
How many ordinary Tuesdays?
How many moments with people who love you?
How much joy will you surrender because you were busy inspecting the container instead of inhabiting the life God placed inside it?
And one day, your children may not care whether you looked ten pounds lighter.
They may simply wish there were more photographs with you in them.
That thought changes something.
Because suddenly this isn't really about mirrors anymore.
It's about worship.
Anything can become an altar when we ask it to give us what only God can ultimately give.
Beauty can become one.
Approval can become one.
Attention can become one.
Desirability can become one.
And the frightening thing about idols is that they never finally say:
Enough.
Feed them another compliment.
Another purchase.
Another procedure.
Another photograph.
Another person's attention.
Another number on the scale.
Another approving glance.
Another hundred likes.
Another year of trying not to age.
Still they whisper:
More.
Because an idol survives by keeping you hungry.
Jesus does something radically different.
He meets hungry people and offers Himself.
He doesn't tell sinners to become visually impressive enough to approach Him.
He doesn't wait for the ashamed to become socially desirable.
Look at the people surrounding Christ in the Gospels.
Lepers.
Beggar Bartimaeus.
The bleeding woman.
Tax collectors.
A woman known publicly as a sinner.
The demonized.
The diseased.
The rejected.
The grieving.
The morally disgraced.
The socially inconvenient.
Jesus repeatedly moved toward people others moved away from.
And then came the cross.

Isaiah's prophecy of the suffering Servant gives us a Messiah who was not presented according to humanity's obsession with impressive appearance. Christ's glory was revealed through sacrificial love, obedience, holiness, mercy, suffering, and redemption.
The most beautiful event in history looked like a scandal.
God incarnate.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Bloodied.
Crucified between criminals.
The world looked at Calvary and saw humiliation.
Heaven saw redemption being accomplished.
The world saw weakness.
God was reconciling sinners to Himself.
The world saw a condemned man.
Faith sees the Lamb of God.
And three days later, the stone moved.
Jesus rose.
That changes what the mirror gets to say about you.
Because if you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is no longer negotiated every morning between your face and your reflection.
Your worth is not determined by whether strangers find you attractive.
Your identity is not hanging from somebody else's opinion.
Your soul does not depreciate when your skin wrinkles.
Your usefulness to God's kingdom does not expire when youth does.
And your salvation certainly does not depend upon remaining desirable.
Christ did not shed His blood to make you photogenic.
He died and rose to reconcile sinners to God.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not another self-esteem program whispering, “Actually, you're perfect just the way you are.”
The Gospel says something far deeper.
We are sinners who need grace.
Our problem is not merely that we think too little of ourselves.
Sometimes we worship ourselves.
Sometimes we worship people's opinions of ourselves.
Sometimes we turn beauty into currency and attention into oxygen.
Sometimes vanity isn't self-love at all.
Sometimes vanity is self-obsession wearing insecurity's clothes.
And Jesus does not merely soothe that bondage.
He calls us out of it.
Repent.
Come home.
Stop asking the creation to give you what belongs to the Creator.
Stop making strangers your judges.
Stop allowing photographs to become courtrooms.
Stop allowing wrinkles to become verdicts.
Stop treating aging as though it were moral failure.
Stop letting comparison disciple you.
There is another way to live.
Peter calls attention to what is ἀφθάρτῳ — imperishable.
And then he describes a gentle and quiet spirit as something precious before God.
The final word in the verse lands with enormous weight:
πολυτελές — polyteles.
Precious.
Costly.
Of great value.
Notice whose evaluation ultimately matters.
“ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ”
Before God.
Maybe that's the sentence somebody reading this desperately needed.
There is a beauty God sees when nobody else notices.
The prayer whispered when everybody is asleep.
The temptation resisted without applause.
The forgiveness extended when revenge would have felt easier.
The kindness nobody photographed.
The purity nobody rewarded.
The repentance nobody posted.
The humility that surrendered the need to be noticed.
The faithfulness of an aging believer whose hands have wrinkled while her heart has grown tender toward Jesus.
The grandfather whose body has weakened but whose prayers have become stronger.
The mother whose stomach carries evidence that she carried life.
The cancer survivor looking at scars.
The teenager who doesn't resemble the faces dominating her feed.
The man whose body will never look like the fitness advertisement.
The woman whose hair is turning gray.
God sees farther than skin.
And perhaps you have spent years trying to make people admire something God already told you would fade while neglecting the person He calls precious.
That realization can sting.
Let it.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation says, “Hide from God.”
Grace says, “Come into the light.”
Maybe you have worshiped appearance.
Tell Him.
Maybe you have silently believed being attractive makes you more valuable than somebody else.
Confess it.
Maybe aging terrifies you because attention has become part of your identity.
Bring that fear to Jesus.
Maybe somebody's rejection made you hate your body.
Bring the wound.
Maybe you've stared into the mirror and spoken words over yourself you would never speak over another human being.
Bring those words too.
Jesus already knows.
No filter required.
No flattering angle.
No pretending.
Just you.
And Him.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because Jesus has always been extraordinarily good at meeting people in places they would rather hide.
Your insecurity doesn't shock Him.
Your vanity doesn't frighten Him.
Your jealousy isn't hidden from Him.
Your aging isn't disappointing Him.
Your scars aren't embarrassing Him.
Your sin isn't beyond the reach of His cross.
Come honestly.
Repent honestly.
Receive grace honestly.
And begin learning how to inhabit your body without worshiping it.
Care for it.
Steward it.
Dress it.
Wash it.
Exercise it.
Rest it.
Treat it with dignity.
But don't ask it to become your god.
Your body was never designed to carry the unbearable weight of proving your worth every morning.
And your mirror was never qualified to pronounce judgment over your soul.
Some mornings you will look wonderful.
Some mornings you won't.
Some photographs will flatter you.
Some will betray every angle you hoped nobody would discover.
Age will eventually alter what youth convinced you would remain.
But there is something time cannot wrinkle.
A life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
A heart becoming gentler.
Faith becoming deeper.
Love becoming less selfish.
Holiness becoming more precious.
Pride dying.
Mercy growing.
The hidden person of the heart being formed under the hands of God.
That is not an argument for neglecting yourself.
It is an invitation to stop worshiping yourself.
There is freedom there.
Imagine walking into a room without needing to be the prettiest person in it.
Imagine seeing somebody beautiful without feeling diminished.
Imagine complimenting another woman without secretly comparing bodies.
Imagine seeing a younger person without interpreting their youth as evidence that your own life is disappearing.
Imagine growing older without believing you're becoming invisible to God.
Imagine taking the photograph.
Smiling.
And keeping it.
Because someday somebody who loves you may treasure the face you're criticizing today.
And imagine looking into the mirror tomorrow morning and refusing to ask:
“Am I beautiful enough?”
Instead:
“Jesus, am I becoming more like You?”
Now the mirror has lost its throne.
Be honest.
And read the other comments.
You may discover that the person you assumed was confident has been fighting the same war.
That matters.
Because shame grows beautifully in secrecy and begins losing oxygen when brought honestly into the light.
Send this to the person who never believes your compliments.
Your share could place truth in front of someone whose mirror has been cruel all week.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one practical way you may choose to serve is by helping sound biblical encouragement reach someone who otherwise may never encounter it.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
Stay because conviction matters.
Stay because encouragement matters.
Stay because we need more than inspirational fragments—we need Scripture, repentance, grace, discipleship, accountability, healing, spiritual sharpening, and Jesus Christ at the center.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not because clicking “share” makes anyone righteous.
Jesus alone saves.
And tonight, before you walk away from this article, stand in front of your mirror for a moment.
Look carefully.
Not because the reflection is everything.
Because it isn't.
That face will change.
Those eyes will age.
That skin will crease.
Time will keep moving.
Then remember Peter's words.
ἀφθάρτῳ.
Imperishable.
There is something more important being formed than the face looking back at you.
And when the mirror whispers tomorrow,
“Not enough…”
remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember whose judgment ultimately matters.
Remember that Jesus Christ did not come to make fading things last forever.
He came to give eternal life to dying people.
So let the mirror grow old.
Let the photographs change.
Let youth pass without turning its departure into a funeral for your worth.
Follow Christ.
Become beautiful where heaven is looking.
Because someday the mirror will show a face you barely recognize…
but if you have spent those years becoming more like Jesus, heaven will have watched something far more beautiful appearing all along.
The mirror will keep changing its verdict. The cross already gave you somewhere better to stand.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON CAUGHT 300 FOXES, TIED TORCHES TO THEM, AND RELEASED THEM INTO THE FIELDS
paragraphs:
SAMSON CAUGHT 300 FOXES, TIED TORCHES TO THEM, AND RELEASED THEM INTO THE FIELDS
But the strangest part of this story isn’t the fire. It’s what happens when a man chosen by God lets the fire outside him become a picture of the fire consuming him inside.
Imagine standing at the edge of a Philistine field just before harvest.
The grain is heavy.
Months of labor are standing beneath the afternoon sky. Families are depending on that harvest. Olive trees have taken years to mature. Somewhere, workers are thinking about tomorrow.
Then something moves between the stalks.
Not one animal.
Not ten.
Hundreds.
And then you see the fire.
Judges records one of the strangest scenes in the entire Old Testament:
“וַיֵּלֶךְ שִׁמְשׁוֹן וַיִּלְכֹּד שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵאוֹת שׁוּעָלִים”
Vayyelekh Shimshon vayilkod shelosh-me’ot shu‘alim...
“And Samson went and caught three hundred foxes...”
Then Scripture says:
“וַיַּבְעֶר־אֵשׁ בַּלַּפִּידִים וַיְשַׁלַּח בְּקָמוֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּים”
Vayyav‘er esh ballappidim vayeshallach beqamoth Pelishtim...
He set fire to the torches and released them into the standing grain of the Philistines.
Judges 15:4–5.
Three hundred shu‘alim.
Torches.
Fire.
Standing grain.
Harvest.
Vineyards.
Olive trees.
And within moments, what had taken months—or years—to grow was burning.
But if all you see in this passage is a bizarre ancient act of warfare, you may miss something hauntingly human hiding inside it.
Because Samson did not arrive at that field emotionally untouched.
He arrived wounded.
He had gone back to the woman he regarded as his wife only to discover that her father had given her to another man—Samson’s companion.
Read that slowly.
The warrior who could tear apart a lion could not control what people did with his heart.
The man capable of extraordinary physical strength was still vulnerable to rejection, betrayal, humiliation, anger, and desire.
And that is where Samson becomes uncomfortable.
Because Samson is not the polished Bible hero many of us would prefer him to be.
His story is messy.
Painful.
At times disturbing.
He was chosen by God before birth for a purpose connected with Israel’s deliverance from Philistine oppression.
Yet the man God used was also deeply flawed.
Samson could defeat enemies around him while struggling terribly with what was happening inside him.
And maybe that is why his story still gets underneath our skin.
Because some of us know exactly what it means to appear strong while privately bleeding.
You know how to work.
You know how to smile.
You know how to worship.
You know what verse to quote.
You know how to tell everybody, “God is good.”
But somewhere inside you there is still a field burning.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone walked away.
Someone lied about you.
Someone chose somebody else.
Someone humiliated you.
Someone took something from you that you believed belonged in your future.
And although years may have passed, part of you is still standing beside the flames.
That is why we must be careful with Samson.
Judges 15 is not permission for Christians to baptize revenge.
Jesus does not call His disciples to find their own metaphorical foxes whenever somebody wounds them.
Quite the opposite.
Jesus says:
“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.”
Matthew 5:44.
Paul later writes:
Romans 12:19.
So we cannot rip Samson’s actions out of the period of the judges, ignore Israel’s conflict with Philistine oppression, and turn his behavior into a Christian instruction manual for retaliation.
The Bible is more honest than that.
Scripture frequently tells us truthfully what people did without commanding us to imitate everything they did.
And Samson’s story becomes even more powerful when we allow Samson to remain what Scripture presents him as:
a real deliverer...
used by a real God...
possessing extraordinary gifts...
and carrying devastating weaknesses.
That combination should terrify every gifted believer.
Because gifting is not the same thing as maturity.
Calling is not the same thing as character.
Being used by God does not mean every desire inside us has surrendered to God.
You can be strong enough to carry something publicly and still be weak enough to be destroyed by something privately.
Samson knew how to fight Philistines.
But Samson repeatedly struggled with Samson.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows that battle.
Your greatest enemy may not be the person who hurt you.
It may be what their hurt awakened inside you.
Bitterness.
Lust.
Pride.
Hatred.
The need to prove yourself.
The fantasy of making somebody regret losing you.
The secret desire to watch somebody who wounded you finally suffer.
Nobody sees it.
But God does.
And here is the uncomfortable question:
How many fields have you burned because you refused to let Jesus heal the wound?
Maybe you never set anything physically on fire.
But you sent the message.
You posted the indirect attack.
You destroyed the friendship.
You poisoned somebody else’s reputation.
You stopped speaking to people who had nothing to do with what happened.
You carried the anger into your marriage.
You brought childhood wounds into adulthood.
You punished someone new for something someone old did.
You kept replaying the betrayal until the person who hurt you was living rent-free inside your mind.
That is what unresolved pain can do.
It spreads.
One wounded moment becomes another wounded relationship.
Then another.
Then another.
Until eventually you look behind you and wonder:
How did so much of my life catch fire?
Samson’s literal flames moved through Philistine agriculture.
Our fires often move through people.
Children inherit anger they did not create.
Spouses receive punishment for betrayals they never committed.
Friends get pushed away because someone else abandoned us first.
Churches become places where wounded people wound wounded people while everybody keeps saying they are “fine.”
And Jesus stands before all of our pretending and refuses to merely decorate the surface.
He wants the heart.
This is where Samson’s story ultimately makes us hunger for a better Deliverer.
Because Samson was never the final Savior.
Jesus is.
Samson was a deliverer with weaknesses.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Deliverer.
Samson’s story contains retaliation against enemies.
Jesus looked at the people crucifying Him and prayed:
“Father, forgive them.”
Samson’s strength was associated with an extraordinary calling that eventually culminated in his death among his enemies.
Jesus willingly laid down His life and then shattered death itself through resurrection.
Samson killed enemies in his death.
Jesus died for His enemies.
Including us.
That changes everything.
Because Romans 5:8 does not say Christ waited until we became respectable.
It says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
You were not rescued because you cleaned yourself up beautifully enough.
You were rescued because Jesus is merciful enough.
You were not forgiven because your scandal disappeared.
You were forgiven because the blood of Christ is greater than your scandal.
That secret you hope nobody discovers?
Jesus already knows.
That relapse?
He knows.
That rage?
He knows.
That pornography history?
He knows.
That affair?
He knows.
That bitterness?
He knows.
That hypocrisy?
He knows.
That season when you looked Christian publicly and lived completely differently privately?
He knows.
And knowing does not mean He approves of your sin.
Grace never calls darkness light.
Jesus calls us to repent.
He confronts what is killing us precisely because He loves us too much to leave us enslaved to it.
The Gospel is not God whispering, “Your sin doesn’t matter.”

The Gospel declares that our sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishing that the sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and made new.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain chained.
Power to come home.
Maybe your life currently feels more like Judges than Psalms.
Messy.
Violent inside.
Confusing.
One bad decision colliding with another.
You love God, but you are ashamed of yourself.
You have prayed the same prayer a hundred times.
You promised you would stop.
Then you returned.
You told God you surrendered it.
Then secretly picked it back up.
And now there is a voice telling you:
“You have failed too many times.”
Listen carefully.
That voice does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Peter had a scandal.
Jesus restored him.
The woman caught in adultery had a scandal.
Jesus met her with mercy and a call to leave sin.
Paul carried the history of persecuting the church.
Grace rewrote his future.
And Samson?
Even after catastrophic failure later in his story, blinded and humiliated, he called upon the LORD again.
“Lord GOD, remember me...”
Judges 16:28.
What a prayer.
Not impressive.
Not polished.
Desperate.
“Remember me.”
Somebody reading this may need only those words tonight.
Lord...
remember me.
I made a mess.
Remember me.
I knew better.
Remember me.
I have been hiding.
Remember me.
I am tired of pretending.
Remember me.
I cannot undo yesterday.
Remember me.
And the Gospel answers our desperation with something even greater:
In Jesus Christ, God does not merely offer you a chance to pretend yesterday never happened.
He offers forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new direction.
A new identity.
Not because you deserve a rewrite.
Because Jesus purchased redemption with His blood.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the sinner finally dropping the torch.
It is admitting:
“I cannot keep burning my life down and calling it freedom.”
“I cannot keep feeding this bitterness.”
“I cannot keep sleeping with this secret.”
“I cannot keep blaming everybody else.”
“I cannot keep pretending.”
“I need Christ.”
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not because you needed another strange Bible fact about 300 foxes.
Maybe you needed God to use an ancient burning field to show you something burning inside your own heart.
So be honest.
What are you still carrying?
Who are you still trying to punish?
What wound became an identity?
What secret sin have you learned to manage instead of confess?
What are you terrified Jesus will ask you to surrender?
Your soul matters more than your image.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes bringing what has been hidden into honest confession is the moment we stop pretending we do not need mercy.
If you are exhausted but you have not abandoned your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you cannot explain publicly what you are going through but desperately need believers to pray for you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if you have already watched Jesus begin rebuilding something sin, grief, betrayal, addiction, shame, or failure nearly destroyed, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
That matters.
And think of one person who needs this story.
Not everybody.
One person.
The friend whose smile has become too convincing.
The brother quietly drifting.
The daughter who thinks her mistake became her identity.
The husband carrying anger he cannot explain.
The believer who stopped attending church because shame convinced them God no longer wanted them.
The unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is about good people congratulating themselves for being good.
Send this to them.
Save it too.
There may come a night when the fire inside you starts talking again.
Come back and remember:
You do not have to obey every emotion you feel.
You do not have to avenge every wound you receive.
You do not have to become the worst thing somebody did to you.
You can bring the wound to Christ.
We want this community to be somewhere people encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
Absolutely not.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But one practical way believers can glorify God is by willingly supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work that is helping people hear His truth.
Not as a transaction with God.
As a testimony.
As mission.
As a way of saying, “Jesus Christ is worth talking about.”
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
They may look perfectly okay.
But tonight they may be asking whether God can possibly do anything beautiful with what remains of their life.
Let your share reach them.
Let Scripture reach them.
Let the Gospel reach them.
Let them discover that Christianity is not the story of flawless people successfully impressing God.
It is the story of sinners who desperately need a Savior—and a Savior who actually came.
Samson’s story reminds us that extraordinary strength cannot save the human heart.
Talent cannot.
Popularity cannot.
Religious activity cannot.
Willpower cannot.
Only Christ can reconcile sinners to God.
So bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the humiliation.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the pieces you cannot put back together.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Then get up and walk with Jesus.
Because the most important fire in Judges 15 is not ultimately the one we should carry away in our hearts.
There is another scene in Scripture.
Another hill.
Another Deliverer.
And instead of releasing destruction upon His enemies, He stretched out His hands and allowed His enemies to nail Him to wood.
Jesus Christ took the judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
So your deepest story does not have to end at the place where everything burned.
There can be grace after scandal.
Forgiveness after failure.
Restoration after ruin.
Life after death.
Not because Samson rewrites everything.
Not because you rewrite everything.
Because Jesus does.
And perhaps years from now, when you look back at the chapter you thought destroyed your entire story, you will finally understand:
The ashes were never strong enough to cancel what Christ could redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN HAVE CONCUBINES?
paragraphs:
CAN A CHRISTIAN HAVE CONCUBINES?
The Bible’s Answer Is More Uncomfortable Than Many Want to Admit
David had them.
Solomon had hundreds of women.
Abraham had Hagar.
Jacob had Bilhah and Zilpah.
And all of them appear in the Bible.
So here is the question that makes some Christians uncomfortable:
If men in Scripture had concubines, can a Christian have concubines today?
Before you answer too quickly, there is something you need to understand about the Bible.
The Bible is brutally honest about human beings.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not hide Abraham's failures.
It does not erase Jacob's dysfunctional household.
It does not protect David's reputation.
It does not rewrite Solomon's compromises to make him look more spiritual.
Scripture often tells you what happened without telling you to imitate what happened.
And confusing biblical description with biblical permission can lead a person into devastating error.
That distinction matters enormously here.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “concubine” is פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh.

A concubine in the ancient world was not simply identical to the modern idea of a secret girlfriend or casual sexual partner. The precise legal and social arrangements varied, but generally she occupied a recognized relationship of lower status than a primary wife. Scripture records such relationships in the patriarchal and monarchical worlds.
But recording something is not the same thing as calling it God's ideal.
The Bible records drunkenness.
The Bible records incest.
The Bible records polygamy.
The Bible records adultery.
The Bible records murder.
The Bible records kings doing horrific things.
Nobody reads those accounts and concludes, “It happened to someone in the Bible, therefore God approves of it.”
So when someone says, “But Abraham had Hagar,” the real question is not whether Abraham did it.
He did.
The real question is:
Was Abraham's household arrangement the pattern Jesus gave His followers for marriage?
That changes everything.
Go back before Abraham.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings.
Go all the way back to creation.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression for “one flesh” is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
Not merely two people occupying the same household.
Not a powerful man collecting women around himself.
Not a husband keeping one woman as his official wife while maintaining additional sexual partners.
There is covenantal union.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something enormously important.
He went back to Genesis.
Jesus said:
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
— Matthew 19:4–6
Jesus did not point His hearers to Solomon's household.
He pointed them to creation.
That should stop us.
Because sometimes we search the Bible looking for the lowest arrangement we can defend when Jesus is calling us back to the highest design God revealed.
There is a difference between asking:
“What did fallen people sometimes do?”
and asking:
“What does Christ call me to do?”
Those are not the same question.
And this is where the issue becomes personal.
Because maybe you are not really asking about an ancient concubine.
Maybe the word is different in your life.
Maybe it is “side relationship.”
Maybe it is “second woman.”
Maybe it is “friends with benefits.”
Maybe it is someone you sleep with while insisting that technically you are not committing adultery.
Maybe it is a relationship hidden from your spouse.
Maybe it is a person you keep emotionally and sexually available while refusing covenant faithfulness.
Maybe nobody calls her a concubine.
But you know she is occupying a place in your life that does not belong to her.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is this:
Changing the vocabulary does not change what God sees.
The New Testament brings Christian sexual ethics into even sharper focus.
Paul writes:
— 1 Corinthians 7:2
The Greek is striking:
ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω
hekastos tēn heautou gynaika echetō, kai hekastē ton idion andra echetō.
In context, Paul directs each man toward his own wife and each woman toward her own husband.
Christian sexuality is not built around accumulating sexual access.
It is shaped by covenant faithfulness, holiness, self-giving love, and belonging to Christ.
Paul tells the Thessalonian believers:
“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication.”
— 1 Thessalonians 4:3
The Greek word translated “fornication” is πορνεία — porneia, a broad term for sexual immorality.
Then Paul says something our sexually saturated culture desperately needs to hear:
“For God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness.”
— 1 Thessalonians 4:7
Holiness.
Not technical loopholes.
Not, “How many relationships can I justify?”
Not, “Which Old Testament man can I use as precedent?”
The Christian question is:
“How can my body, marriage, sexuality, and relationships belong completely to Jesus Christ?”

Even the qualifications given for Christian overseers reflect marital fidelity. Paul speaks of being μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra — commonly rendered “the husband of one wife” in 1 Timothy 3:2.

Scholars discuss the precise scope of that expression—whether its emphasis is specifically monogamy, marital faithfulness, or being a “one-woman man.” We should not pretend an interpretive discussion does not exist.
But none of the credible possibilities turns the phrase into permission for maintaining concubines.
The direction is toward fidelity.
That direction becomes even clearer when marriage is placed beside Christ Himself.
Ephesians 5 does not present marriage merely as a convenient human contract.
Christian marriage points beyond itself.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
— Ephesians 5:25
Think about that.
Christ does not teach husbands to use women.
Christ teaches husbands to imitate a Savior who gives Himself.
Christ does not turn marriage into a monument to male appetite.
He turns it into a picture of sacrificial love.
This is why the biblical stories involving multiple wives and concubines should sober us rather than provide excuses.
Look at the fruit.
Abraham's decision involving Hagar produced anguish within his household. Genesis 16 records jealousy, conflict, harsh treatment, and Hagar fleeing into the wilderness.
Jacob's household became consumed by rivalry between Leah and Rachel, with their servants Bilhah and Zilpah drawn into the struggle for children and affection.
David's family became a landscape of sexual sin, violence, rivalry, betrayal, and grief.
And Solomon?
Scripture could hardly be clearer:
“But king Solomon loved many strange women…”
— 1 Kings 11:1
Then:
“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods…”
— 1 Kings 11:4
The man famous for wisdom still discovered that possessing wisdom is not the same as obeying it.
That should terrify anyone using Solomon's relationships as permission.
His women were not presented at the end of his story as proof that God approved of multiplying partners.
They became part of the account of his heart turning away.
God had already warned Israel's kings:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away…”
— Deuteronomy 17:17
So can a Christian have concubines?

If by “concubine” we mean maintaining additional women as sexual partners alongside or outside the covenantal faithfulness of marriage, that practice cannot be reconciled with the sexual ethic Jesus and the apostles give Christ's followers.
The existence of concubines in biblical history does not establish concubinage as Christian discipleship.
But please don't stop reading here.
Because if you already crossed that line, the Gospel has something to say to you too.
And it is not merely:
“Disgusting. Leave.”
It is:
“Repent. Come home.”
There is a world of difference.
Maybe this article found you while you are already living a double life.
Maybe there is a wife who trusts you and another woman whose messages you delete.
Maybe there is a husband who does not know.
Maybe there are relationships you have carefully renamed because calling them what they really are would force you to confront them.
Maybe you have been using Abraham, David, or Solomon as theological camouflage for something your conscience has already been warning you about.
You do not need a better excuse.
You need Jesus.
And that is not condemnation without hope.
That is precisely where hope begins.
Because Christianity is not the story of morally spotless people congratulating themselves.
It is the story of sinners being rescued by a spotless Savior.
Jesus did not die because our sin was insignificant.
He died because our sin was so serious that reconciliation with God required what we could never provide for ourselves.
At the cross, Christ carried sin.
At the empty tomb, death lost its claim.
And now the invitation is not to hide more intelligently.
It is to repent.
The Greek word so closely associated with repentance is μετάνοια — metanoia.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because you were exposed.
It is a genuine turning—a changed mind that bears fruit in a changed direction.
You stop defending what Christ calls you to surrender.
You stop making peace with what is destroying your soul.
You stop asking Scripture to approve the life you already chose and begin allowing Scripture to confront, correct, and reshape you.
And yes, repentance can hurt.
Truth often does before healing begins.
A relationship may have to end.
A confession may have to happen.
Trust may need years of rebuilding.
Pastoral help may be necessary.
Accountability may become uncomfortable.
Consequences do not magically disappear simply because someone says, “God forgive me.”
But grace means your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Look at David.
His sin brought devastating consequences, and Scripture never pretends otherwise.
Yet Psalm 51 records the cry of a shattered man:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
David did not need God to help him justify his desires.
He needed God to make his heart clean.
Maybe that is what you need to pray tonight.
Not:
“God, show me how this relationship might technically be allowed.”
But:
“God, create in me a clean heart.”
There are people reading this who have spent years asking how close they can stand to sin without technically stepping into it.
Jesus offers something better.
Freedom.
Purity.
A clean conscience.
A restored heart.
A life where you no longer need secret passwords, disappearing messages, hidden hotel receipts, carefully constructed lies, or theological excuses.
Imagine sleeping without hiding.
Imagine praying without defending your secret life.
Imagine looking at your spouse without carrying another person in the shadows.
Imagine worshiping God without simultaneously negotiating with the sin you refuse to surrender.
That freedom has a name.
Jesus Christ.
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
— John 8:36
So no, the biblical presence of concubines is not a license for Christians to maintain them.
The Bible is showing us something far greater than permission to repeat the broken patterns of ancient men.
It is showing us why broken people need redemption.
And perhaps that is why their scandals were never edited out.
Because if Scripture contained only flawless people, you might think there was no room in it for you.
Abraham failed.
Jacob's household fractured.
David fell spectacularly.
Solomon compromised despite extraordinary wisdom.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul once persecuted the church.
Yet the Bible keeps pointing beyond flawed human beings to the One who never sinned.
Jesus.
That is where your eyes belong.
Not on David to excuse your lust.
Not on Solomon to defend your relationships.
Not on Abraham to rationalize your choices.
On Christ.
The question was never simply, “What could ancient men get away with?”
The deeper question is:
“Now that I belong to Jesus, what must I surrender so that my life looks more like Him?”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the conviction into shame and run farther from God.
Bring it into the light.
There is no trophy for pretending.

And if Christ has already rescued you from sexual sin, adultery, secret relationships, pornography, betrayal, or a life you thought could never change, your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable, but because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions difficult to remember tomorrow.
Someone may be one secret relationship away from losing a marriage. Someone may already believe they have sinned too badly to return.
Send this to them.
Christ alone is our Savior, and obedience to Him is far bigger than supporting any particular ministry.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because clicking “share” makes anyone righteous.
Save what you need to remember.
Share what somebody else desperately needs to read.
And comment if God is dealing with your heart.
Because maybe the most dangerous secret is not the one everybody eventually discovers.
Maybe it is the one you successfully hide long enough to convince yourself that God no longer sees it.
But He sees you.
And astonishingly, in Jesus Christ, the God who sees your scandal is still calling you toward grace.
Not grace that blesses the chains.
Grace that breaks them.
Not grace that gives sin a new name.
Grace that gives the sinner a new life.
Not grace that tells you to remain exactly where you are.
Grace that takes your trembling hand and leads you home.
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you—but it does not get to decide who you become after He does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM SENT HAGAR AND HIS SON INTO THE WILDERNESS WITH BREAD AND WATER
paragraphs:
ABRAHAM SENT HAGAR AND HIS SON INTO THE WILDERNESS WITH BREAD AND WATER
She walked away carrying bread, water, and a breaking heart—but the God who seemed silent had already heard the cry that nobody else could hear.
There are Bible stories we read too quickly because slowing down would make them hurt.
Genesis 21 is one of them.
Abraham rises early in the morning.
He takes bread.
He takes a skin of water.
He gives them to Hagar.
Then he sends her away.
Not into another comfortable household.
Not into a carefully prepared future.
Into the wilderness.
And beside her is her son.
Read that slowly.
A mother.
A child.
Bread that will eventually disappear.
Water that will eventually run dry.
And behind them, the household that had once represented security growing smaller with every step.
Genesis does not invite us to pretend this scene is painless.
It is painful.
It is complicated.
And it began long before Hagar stepped into that wilderness.
It began when human beings tried to accomplish through human strategy what God had promised to accomplish by His power.
God had promised Abraham an heir. But as the years passed and Sarah remained childless, waiting became unbearable.
So Sarah gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham in an attempt to obtain children through her.
Hagar conceived.
Ishmael was born.
And what looked like a solution became a household filled with wounds.
That is one of the frightening things about unbelief.
Sometimes it does not look like rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like problem-solving.
Sometimes it sounds reasonable.
Sometimes it even appears successful for a while.
But whenever we attempt to manufacture what God has asked us to trust Him for, the consequences can reach people we never intended to hurt.
Years passed.
Then God did what He had promised.
Sarah conceived.
Isaac was born.
The impossible child arrived because the God who makes promises is not limited by aging bodies, impossible circumstances, or exhausted human hope.
But the arrival of Isaac did not erase the consequences of what had happened before him.
At the feast celebrating Isaac's weaning, Sarah saw Ishmael behaving toward Isaac in a way that Genesis describes with the Hebrew participle מְצַחֵק — məṣaḥēq.

The word comes from the root צחק (ṣ-ḥ-q), associated with laughter. English translations render the expression differently, and the later apostolic interpretation in Galatians 4:29 describes the son born according to the flesh as persecuting the son born according to the Spirit.
Sarah demanded that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away.
Abraham was deeply distressed.
Genesis 21:11 says the matter was very grievous in Abraham's sight because Ishmael was his son.
His son.
That matters.
Ishmael was not an inconvenience to Abraham.
He was his child.
God then told Abraham not to be distressed concerning the boy and Hagar, affirming that the covenant line would be reckoned through Isaac while also promising concerning Ishmael:
כִּי־זַרְעֲךָ הוּא
ki-zar‘akha hu
“Because he is your offspring.”
God had not confused Ishmael with Isaac.
Isaac was the son through whom the covenant promise would continue.
But Ishmael was not invisible to God.
That distinction is crucial.
Election of Isaac for the covenant line did not mean divine indifference toward Ishmael.
So morning came.
Abraham took bread and water and gave them to Hagar.
Then she departed.
The Hebrew text says:
וַתֵּלֶךְ וַתֵּתַע בְּמִדְבַּר בְּאֵר שָׁבַע
vattelekh vattēta‘ bemidbar Be’er Shava
She went and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
Wandered.
There is something painfully human in that word.
Maybe you know what it feels like.
You still wake up.
Still go to work.
Still answer messages.
Still smile when somebody asks whether you are okay.
Still post photographs.
Still tell people, “God is good.”
But inside?
You are wandering.
You know how to keep moving.
You just do not know where you are going anymore.
Maybe something happened that you never imagined would become part of your testimony.
A marriage broke.
Someone betrayed you.
Your child walked away.
A ministry disappointed you.
A door closed.
Someone you prayed for died anyway.
The money disappeared.
The diagnosis came.
The person who promised to stay left.
Or maybe the wilderness was partly created by your own decisions.
That can hurt even more.
Because now you are not only suffering.
You are remembering.
“If only I had listened.”
“If only I had waited.”
“If only I had not sent that message.”
“If only I had walked away.”
“If only I had trusted God.”
Regret has a cruel way of making the wilderness feel deserved.
But Genesis 21 gives us a picture we desperately need.
The water eventually ran out.
Hagar placed her son beneath one of the shrubs.
Then she moved away.
Why?
Because she could not bear to watch him die.
The woman who had survived conflict, displacement, rejection, and wandering finally reached the place where she had nothing left to fix.
No water.
No plan.
No visible rescue.
She sat at a distance and wept.
Perhaps you have been there.
Not physically beneath a desert shrub.
But spiritually?
Absolutely.
There are moments when the strongest prayer you can produce is crying.
Moments when you have explained yourself enough.
Fought enough.
Pretended enough.
Held everybody together enough.
And now there is nothing left except tears.
Then comes one of the most beautiful sentences in this entire account.
וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־קוֹל הַנַּעַר
Vayyishma Elohim et-qol hanna‘ar.
“God heard the voice of the boy.”
God heard.
Before Hagar saw provision, God heard.
Before circumstances changed, God heard.
Before she knew how the story would end, God heard.
The wilderness was silent to Hagar.
But heaven was not deaf.
And there is something even deeper here.
The name Ishmael, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishma‘el), carries the idea “God hears.”
The boy whose name testified that God hears was crying in a wilderness where it looked as though God had forgotten him.
But God heard him.
His circumstances had not cancelled the truth carried in his own name.
And your wilderness has not cancelled the character of God either.
You may not understand what He is doing.
You may not know why He permitted something.
You may be living with consequences that cannot simply be reversed.
But silence is not proof of absence.
Pain is not proof that God has stopped seeing.
And exhaustion is not evidence that His promises have failed.
The angel of God called to Hagar from heaven:
“What troubles you, Hagar?”
Then came the words a terrified mother desperately needed:
“Fear not.”
Why?
Because God had heard.
Then Scripture says:
וַיִּפְקַח אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עֵינֶיהָ
Vayyifqach Elohim et-‘eineha.
“God opened her eyes.”
And she saw a well of water.
Do not miss that.
The text does not say that Hagar created the well.
It says God opened her eyes and she saw it.
Sometimes grace does not arrive by giving us the future we imagined.
Sometimes grace opens our eyes to the provision of God in the middle of the future we never wanted.
Hagar filled the skin with water.
She gave the boy a drink.
And then Genesis says something astonishingly simple:
וַיְהִי אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הַנַּעַר
Vayehi Elohim et-hanna‘ar.
“God was with the boy.”
The household was gone.
Abraham was no longer beside him.
The water had failed.
The wilderness surrounded him.
But God was with the boy.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needed tonight.
People can leave you and God can still be with you.
A chapter can close and God can still be with you.
Your plans can collapse and God can still be with you.
You can carry scars from other people's decisions and God can still be with you.
You can carry consequences from your own decisions and discover that repentance and grace are still real.
But we must be careful here.
Genesis 21 is not teaching that every painful separation is automatically God's will.
It is not permission to abandon responsibilities and then call the consequences “God's plan.”
And Hagar's story is not a sentimental slogan telling wounded people that suffering does not matter.
Scripture is much more honest than that.
Sin has consequences.
Human impatience has consequences.
Family dysfunction has consequences.
Trying to accomplish God's purposes by sinful or faithless shortcuts has consequences.
Yet human failure does not place people beyond the reach of divine mercy.
And that brings us somewhere even greater than Abraham's wilderness.
It brings us to Jesus Christ.
Because the Bible's great story is not about wounded people eventually becoming strong enough to rescue themselves.
It is about a holy God rescuing sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
Abraham could not save humanity.
Isaac could not save humanity.
Israel could not save humanity.
You cannot save yourself.
Neither can I.
The deepest wilderness is not financial difficulty, loneliness, betrayal, rejection, or heartbreak.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have sinned against the God who made us.
And no amount of religious performance can purchase our reconciliation with Him.
But God did not leave humanity beneath the shrub waiting to die.
He came for us.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He touched the rejected.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He carried the cross.
And on that cross, He bore sin.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
Then He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is the Gospel.
Not “try harder.”
Not “become religious enough.”
Not “hide your scandal well enough that Christians will accept you.”
Jesus saves sinners.
Grace does not pretend your past never happened.
Grace declares that your past does not have to possess the final word.
Repentance is not pretending the wilderness was beautiful.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy is greater than your rebellion.
Faith is not trusting your ability to repair yourself.
Faith is trusting Jesus Christ.
This is why the Gospel reaches so deeply into stories like Hagar's.
The Bible is full of messy families.
Broken people.
Shameful decisions.
Betrayals.
Failures.
Outcasts.
Sinners.
People who ran.
People who doubted.
People who fell.
People who discovered that God was still writing when they thought their story had ended.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe everybody thinks you are okay.
But you know about the wilderness.
You know about that thing you never discuss.
You know about the nights when the room becomes quiet and your memories become loud.
You know what you did.
You know what they did to you.
You know what you lost.
You know what you are afraid might never return.
And perhaps you have wondered:
“Could Jesus possibly want somebody with a story like mine?”
Look at the cross.
Christ did not die for imaginary people with spotless histories.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15).
Bring Him the real story.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
The real one.
Confess your sin.
Stop defending what God is asking you to surrender.
Stop hiding what Christ already knows.
Turn to Him.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is mercy in Jesus.
There is reconciliation with God in Jesus.
There is a new life in Jesus.
And there are people reading this right now who need permission to stop pretending.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around our hearts.
Someone reading your two words may stop and pray.
Someone else may realize they are not alone.
And perhaps the wilderness that convinced you nobody could understand will become the place where somebody else finally finds courage to seek Jesus.
That is why this message should not stop with you.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that they are seen.
God hears.

We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ—through faith, obedience, love, generosity, service, witness, and worship. Supporting Gospel ministry can be one expression of that devotion when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for the sake of Christ rather than human recognition.
But the greater invitation is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is feeding your soul instead of endlessly feeding your distractions.
Share Christ.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Send this to the person who thinks their scandal has disqualified them from grace.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling Christians.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Because somewhere tonight, another Hagar is crying.
Somewhere, another person believes the water is gone and therefore hope must be gone too.
Somewhere, someone has mistaken a wilderness chapter for the final page.
But Genesis 21 whispers across thousands of years:
God heard.
God opened her eyes.
God provided.
God was with the boy.
And the whole testimony of Scripture ultimately leads us beyond a well in Beersheba to the Savior who said:
“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).
Bread runs out.
Water skins become empty.
Human strength collapses.
People disappoint us.
Earthly security disappears.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So when your wilderness tells you, “This is where your story dies,” remember the God who hears.
When shame tells you, “Nobody could love you if they knew everything,” remember the cross.
When sin tells you, “You have gone too far,” remember the Savior who calls sinners to repent and come home.
When yesterday tells you, “Your scandal is your identity,” remember grace.
And when you cannot see the next chapter, remember this:
The wilderness may expose everything you have lost, but it can never erase the God who hears your cry—and in Jesus Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence.
Somewhere between the empty water skin and the opened well, despair discovered that God had been listening all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MICHAL PUT AN IDOL IN DAVID’S BED—AND WHAT HAPPENED THAT NIGHT EXPOSES THE THINGS WE HIDE
paragraphs: MICHAL PUT AN IDOL IN DAVID’S BED—AND WHAT HAPPENED THAT NIGHT EXPOSES THE THINGS WE HIDE

Saul’s assassins were outside. David had only hours to live. His wife lowered him through a window—and then placed something disturbing beneath the covers. But the strangest object in David’s bedroom may point us toward a question far closer to home: What is lying beneath the covers of our own hearts?
There were men outside the house waiting for morning.
Not visitors.
Not friends.
Killers.
King Saul had sent them.

Inside was David—the shepherd who had killed Goliath, the musician who had played before the king, the warrior Israel celebrated, the man whom God had already chosen for a future David himself could not yet see.
And beside him was Michal.
Saul’s daughter.
David’s wife.
A woman trapped between the father who wanted David dead and the husband whose life was running out of time.
Imagine the silence inside that house.
Imagine looking through the darkness and realizing armed men are watching the exits.
Imagine knowing that sunrise may become a death sentence.
Then Michal tells David something terrifying:
If you do not escape tonight, tomorrow you will be killed.
There is no dramatic army coming to rescue him.
No throne.
No royal guard defending the future king.
There is only a window.
So Michal lowers David through it.
David runs.
He flees into the darkness.
He escapes.
Then Michal turns back toward the bed.
And this is where the story becomes strange.
Very strange.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 19:13 says:
"וַתִּקַּח מִיכַל אֶת־הַתְּרָפִים וַתָּשֶׂם אֶל־הַמִּטָּה"
Vattiqqaḥ Mikhal et-hatteraphim vattasem el-hammittah.
In straightforward English:
“Michal took the teraphim and put it in the bed.”
The crucial Hebrew word is הַתְּרָפִים — hatteraphim.
Teraphim.
Household images or household idols.
Michal puts the teraphim in David’s bed, arranges goat hair at its head, and covers it with a garment.
From outside the room, beneath the covering, there appears to be someone lying there.
David is gone.
But something that looks enough like David is still beneath the covers.
When Saul sends men to seize him, Michal says:
“He is sick.”
Saul is not moved by compassion.
He essentially orders them to bring David to him in the bed so he can kill him.
Think about that.
Not even supposed sickness would satisfy Saul’s murderous determination.
The messengers return.
They approach the bed.
They pull back the deception.
And there is no David.
There is the teraphim.
The hunted man has escaped.
The idol remained behind.
And there is something almost painfully symbolic about that image, even though we must be careful not to pretend the biblical writer explicitly gives it the symbolism we may see in it.
A bed.
A covering.
An image pretending to be something it is not.
A room filled with deception.
And the real man already gone.
Maybe that is why this obscure scene can feel unexpectedly modern.
Because some of us know what it means to keep something beneath the covers.
Not a literal teraphim.
Something else.
Something hidden.
Something carefully arranged so that people looking from the outside see what we want them to see.
They see the Christian posts.
They see the Bible verses.
They see the worship songs.
They see Sunday clothes.
They hear “God is good.”
They hear “I’m blessed.”
They see the smile.
But beneath the covering...
there may be something we desperately hope nobody discovers.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Secret messages.
An affair that began emotionally before it ever became physical.
Jealousy.
Greed.
Alcohol hidden where nobody looks.
A private addiction.
Unforgiveness toward someone whose name still changes your heartbeat.
An obsession with money.
A hunger for attention.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Religious pride.
A secret habit you keep promising God you will stop.
Or perhaps nothing scandalous enough to shock anybody.
Maybe your hidden idol is simply approval.
You need people to like you.
You need to be noticed.
You need someone to tell you that you matter.
And without realizing it, their approval has begun occupying a place in your heart that belongs to God.
That is what makes idolatry so dangerous.
An idol does not need a carved face.
It only needs God's place.

Anything can become spiritually disordered when we begin looking to it for what ultimately belongs to God—to define us, save us, rule us, satisfy us, or become the treasure around which everything else revolves.
Money can become an idol.
Romance can become an idol.
Success can become an idol.
Family can become an idol.
Ministry can become an idol.
Even the desire to appear righteous can become an idol.
And sometimes the most dangerous idols are not sitting on shelves.
They are lying quietly inside hearts.
But we should also resist turning Michal herself into a simplistic villain.

The Bible does not stop in this passage to explain why the teraphim was available in the house, who regarded it as belonging to whom, or precisely what religious significance Michal attached to it. We should not invent details God did not give us.
What Scripture does tell us is dramatic enough.
Saul wanted David dead.
Michal warned David.
Michal helped him escape.
Michal used the teraphim in the bed as part of the deception.
And David lived.
The irony is breathtaking.
Saul thinks he can eliminate the man God has chosen.
He surrounds the house.
He controls the soldiers.
He has royal authority.
David appears cornered.
Yet David escapes through a window.
This is one of Scripture’s recurring humiliations of human pride:
Power looks enormous until it collides with the purposes of God.
Saul had a palace.
David had a window.
Saul had messengers.
David had nowhere secure to sleep.
Saul wore the crown.
David was running for his life.
Yet the future did not belong to Saul merely because Saul appeared stronger that night.
God’s purposes were not trapped inside that bedroom.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that truth.
Your present circumstances are not the final authority over your future.
But be careful.
That does not mean every dream you have is guaranteed because “God has a plan.”
Christian hope is deeper than motivational optimism.
Our confidence is not that God must fulfill every personal ambition.
Our confidence is that God is faithful to His purposes, His promises, and ultimately His saving work in Jesus Christ.
David escaped that window.
But David’s story would still contain caves, betrayal, grief, warfare, terrible personal sin, consequences, family anguish, and repentance.
Grace did not make David’s life painless.
And grace never meant David was sinless.
That matters because Christianity does not present David as the Savior.
David needed one.
We need one too.
David would later commit sins far darker than anything happening in this bedroom.
The man running from another man's murderous violence would eventually become responsible for arranging Uriah's death after committing adultery with Bathsheba.
That is uncomfortable.
It is supposed to be.
The Bible does not airbrush its heroes.
Scripture has an astonishing willingness to tell us the truth about human beings.
Kings fail.
Families fracture.
Desire becomes corruption.
Fear produces deception.
Power becomes dangerous.
People whom God has used can still sin catastrophically.
And suddenly the Bible stops feeling like a museum filled with polished religious statues.
It starts feeling like our family.
Our marriages.
Our phones.
Our histories.
Our secrets.
Our failures.
Our hearts.
Maybe that is one reason some people stay away from Jesus.
They think Christianity is for people who have managed to clean themselves up.
They imagine church as a room full of respectable people pretending they never needed mercy.
But open the Bible.
Look closely.
You will find scandal everywhere.
Adam hiding.
Jacob deceiving.
Judah disgraced.
Moses failing.
Samson collapsing.
David sinning.
Peter denying Christ.
Thomas doubting.
Paul remembering that he once persecuted the church.
And over all of it stands a message no sinner could have invented:
Grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that tells us repentance is unnecessary.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then points guilty people toward a Savior.
This is where the story must eventually lead us.
Not merely to Michal.
Not merely to David.
Not merely to Saul.
To Jesus Christ.
Because centuries after David escaped through a window, another Son of David would be hunted.
Religious leaders would conspire against Him.
Authorities would arrest Him.
False testimony would surround Him.
Soldiers would mock Him.
His clothing would be taken.
His body would be wounded.
And unlike David that night...
Jesus would not escape.
He would go to the cross.
Not because His enemies had somehow defeated God's plan.
The cross was at the heart of God's redemptive purpose.
Jesus Christ, the righteous One, gave Himself for sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is where every hidden idol eventually meets its greatest threat.
Not in religious shame.
At the cross.
Because Jesus did not die merely to improve the decorations around our idols.
He came to save sinners and make us new.
He does not merely straighten the covering over the bed.
He exposes what is underneath.
Then He calls us to Himself.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
Somebody reading this has become exhausted from hiding.
You know exactly what that means.
You delete the history.
You erase the messages.
You rehearse the explanation.
You manage the appearances.
You promise yourself, “That was the last time.”
Then comes another night.
Another temptation.
Another fall.
Another morning filled with regret.
And somewhere deep inside you is the fear that if people knew everything about you, they would walk away.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that your sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to die.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that you should continue hiding.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is a road home.
Not because you can rewrite yesterday.
Because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners.
Maybe your scandal is known.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your marriage broke.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe your children know the person you used to be.
Maybe your church knows.
Maybe your family still remembers.
Maybe you are carrying consequences that forgiveness will not magically erase.
Grace is not pretending consequences are imaginary.
Grace means your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than Jesus Christ.
That is why our message is:
Not because Jesus rewrites Scripture.
Not because He rewrites truth.
Not because He calls darkness light.
Jesus rewrites everything because He changes the destiny of people who come to Him.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The enslaved can become free.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
The prodigal can come home.
The sinner can become a child of God.
The past can remain historically true without remaining spiritually sovereign.
And maybe the strangest detail in Michal’s bedroom is speaking to your heart right now.
There was something beneath the covering pretending to be what it was not.
What is beneath yours?
What have you been protecting?
What would you panic about if someone uncovered it tonight?
What has quietly taken God's place?
What do you run toward when you are afraid?
What controls your decisions?
What could you not imagine surrendering even if Christ asked for it?
Don't answer publicly unless you should.
But answer God.
Be honest.
Because the frightening thing about hiding from people is that eventually we can begin behaving as though we are hiding from God.
We are not.
Psalm 139 asks where we could go from His Spirit.
Nowhere.
Darkness cannot conceal us from Him.
Yet for the person who turns to Christ, that truth does not have to end in terror.
