The God who sees is also the God who saves.
He already knows.
And still the invitation of the Gospel goes out.
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
There is no idol worth losing your soul over.
There is no secret pleasure worth being mastered by.
There is no human applause worth replacing the approval that matters eternally.
There is no sin Jesus needs you to disguise before you approach Him.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are terrified anybody else might see.
You do not heal by making the bed look convincing.
You begin healing when you stop hiding what is underneath it.
Not to perform repentance for strangers.
Let it be a marker—a simple public confession that you are tired of pretending everything is fine and you want Christ to search your heart.
And believers, when you see someone write those words, don't attack them.
Don't interrogate them.
Pray.
We have enough spectators.
The wounded need brothers and sisters.
And if you have wandered farther than you ever thought you would, remember this:
David escaped through a window that night.
But the greater escape humanity needed would eventually come through a cross and an empty tomb.
The deepest question is no longer what Michal placed in David's bed.
It is what we have placed where only God belongs.
Pull back the covering.
Bring it into the light.
Give it to Christ.
Because the thing you are most afraid for Jesus to uncover may become the very place where you finally discover how desperately you needed His grace.
Your secret does not frighten the Savior—but loving your darkness more than His light can keep you hiding from the freedom He calls you into.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD USE SHOCKING SEXUAL LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE ISRAEL’S IDOLATRY?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD USE SHOCKING SEXUAL LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE ISRAEL’S IDOLATRY?

The disturbing words of Ezekiel weren’t written to entertain dirty minds. They were meant to expose wandering hearts—and once you understand what God was saying, you may never look at idolatry the same way again.
There are passages in the Bible that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading and stare at the page.
Ezekiel 16 and Ezekiel 23 are among them.
The language becomes so sexually graphic, so emotionally violent, so uncomfortable that a modern reader may instinctively wonder:
Why is this even in the Bible?
Why would the holy God speak about His covenant people using imagery of prostitution, adultery, nakedness, lust, lovers, breasts, sexual desire, and marital betrayal?
And Ezekiel 23 goes further still.
Far further.
The Hebrew becomes deliberately disturbing.
There is a line many churches would probably never read aloud on Sunday morning.
Yet God permitted it to remain in Scripture.
Why?
Because sometimes we sanitize the very sins that are destroying us.
We call idolatry a “distraction.”
God called it betrayal.
We call compromise a “season.”
God showed Israel an unfaithful marriage.
We say, “I’ve just been distant from God lately.”
Scripture sometimes describes that distance with the vocabulary of adultery.
That difference should make us uncomfortable.
Because perhaps one reason Ezekiel shocks us is that God takes spiritual unfaithfulness more seriously than we do.
And before going any further, something must be made absolutely clear.

These chapters should never become an excuse for vulgar preaching, sexual humiliation, hatred toward women, or treating victims of sexual violence as morally responsible for what was done to them. Modern scholars have rightly pointed out how troubling the gendered violence and sexual rhetoric of Ezekiel 16 and 23 can be, and interpreters have disagreed over how some elements of these metaphors should be understood. The sexual imagery must therefore be handled carefully rather than sensationalized.
The woman in Ezekiel's metaphor is not “women” as a class.
The prophetic target is covenant-breaking Israel and Judah.
Ezekiel himself tells us who the characters represent.
In Ezekiel 23, two sisters appear: Oholah and Oholibah.
The Hebrew names are אָהֳלָה (Oholah) and אָהֳלִיבָה (Oholibah).
Then Scripture removes the mystery:
“Samaria is Oholah and Jerusalem Oholibah.”
These are personified cities and kingdoms.
This is prophetic metaphor.
And once that is understood, the disturbing language begins revealing something terrifyingly beautiful about the heart of God.
Because adultery hurts only where covenant exists.
Betrayal hurts only where love existed first.
You cannot betray someone who never loved you.
And that is where Ezekiel 16 begins.
Not with prostitution.
Not with judgment.
Not with sexual scandal.
With grace.
Jerusalem is pictured as an abandoned infant.
Unwanted.
Unwashed.
Unprotected.
Lying helplessly in blood.
Nobody has compassion.
Nobody rescues her.
Then God comes.
He gives life.
He cleanses her.
He clothes her.
He adorns her.
He provides for her.
And eventually the imagery becomes covenantal and marital.
God says that He entered into covenant with her and she became His.
The Hebrew word underneath this covenant idea is בְּרִית — berit.
Covenant.
That matters enormously.
Israel did not rescue herself and then impress God enough to become His people.
God found her.
God chose her.
God covered her.
God provided for her.
God beautified her.
Grace came first.
And then comes one of the most devastating turns in prophetic literature:
“But you trusted in your beauty…”
There it is.
The tragedy of the human heart in a sentence.
She began admiring the gifts until she forgot the Giver.
The beauty God gave became the beauty she trusted.
The resources God supplied became resources she used against Him.
The blessings that should have produced worship became instruments of rebellion.
Then Ezekiel uses the Hebrew vocabulary of prostitution.
The important root is זנה — zanah.
Depending on grammatical form and context, it carries the idea of engaging in prostitution or acting promiscuously.
But in Ezekiel's prophetic metaphor, we cannot simply flatten that word into literal sexual behavior.
Ezekiel explicitly connects this “prostitution” with idols, pagan worship, and relationships with foreign powers.
That is why the language is so fierce.
Israel wasn't merely violating regulations.
She was violating relationship.
Imagine a husband giving his wife a beautiful necklace because he loves her.
Then imagine her wearing that necklace while pursuing another lover.
The problem isn't the necklace.
The horror is that a gift of love has become an accessory to betrayal.
That is essentially the accusation of Ezekiel 16.
God had given Israel gold, silver, clothing, food, beauty, security and covenant privilege.
Then Israel took what God had provided and devoted it to idols.
And suddenly the ancient prophecy becomes frighteningly modern.
Because we can do exactly the same thing.
God gives someone intelligence.
They build a life in which they no longer need Him.
God gives someone influence.
They become addicted to applause.
God gives someone money.
Money becomes their security.
God gives someone beauty.
Beauty becomes their identity.
God gives someone a relationship.
The relationship becomes more important than obedience.
God gives someone ministry.
And eventually the ministry becomes more important than God.
God gives someone a platform supposedly built for Jesus.
Then slowly...
quietly...
almost invisibly...
Jesus becomes a tool for building the platform.
That is idolatry wearing church clothes.
And this is why Ezekiel's language cannot safely remain locked in ancient Jerusalem.
The idols change.
The human heart doesn't.
We may never bow before Baal.
We can still bow before approval.
We may never burn incense to Asherah.
We can still sacrifice our integrity for success.
We may never construct a pagan shrine.

We can still build an altar inside ourselves where money, sex, romance, politics, reputation, career, comfort, entertainment, influence, family—or even ministry—receives the trust that belongs to God.
An idol is not merely a statue.
It is something created that begins receiving what belongs ultimately to the Creator.
Your deepest trust.
Your obedience.
Your identity.
Your hope.
Your fear.
Your devotion.
Your functional worship.
And sometimes you don't discover your idol by asking what you love.
You discover it by asking what you cannot imagine losing.
That question may hurt.
Let it.
Ezekiel was supposed to hurt.
But now we arrive at the passage that has made generations of readers recoil.
Ezekiel 23 intensifies the imagery dramatically.

The prophet describes Israel's attraction toward foreign powers through explicitly sexual imagery. In verse 20, the Hebrew text uses startling bodily language, including בְּשַׂר — basar, literally “flesh,” which in context functions as a sexual reference.
The comparison that follows is intentionally crude.
Modern translations differ in how explicitly they render it.
But the shock is there in Hebrew.
We should neither pretend otherwise nor linger over it voyeuristically.
The question is not:
“How graphic can we make this?”
The better question is:
“Why would prophetic Scripture speak this way?”
Because Israel had made rebellion attractive.
God's rhetoric tears the perfume off the idol.
Israel looked toward powerful nations and saw strength, security and desirability.
God exposes the lust underneath that political and spiritual dependence.
What Israel romanticized, Ezekiel makes grotesque.
That is one of idolatry's greatest tricks.
It makes slavery look beautiful before the chains close.
Pornography promises intimacy and produces isolation.
Greed promises security and produces endless hunger.
Human approval promises belonging and produces anxiety.
Pride promises greatness and makes repentance unbearable.
Bitterness promises justice while quietly chaining you to the person who wounded you.
Secret sin promises relief.
Then demands secrecy.
Then demands repetition.
Then demands more.
And eventually the thing you thought you controlled begins controlling you.
This is why biblical idolatry is not merely about statues.
It is about misplaced desire.
Misplaced trust.
Misplaced dependence.
Misplaced worship.
Israel sought from other gods and nations what she was supposed to receive ultimately from Yahweh.
And here is the part that should break something open inside us:
God's jealousy in covenant Scripture is not the insecurity of a needy deity desperate for attention.
God does not need us to complete Him.
Rather, covenant jealousy reflects the exclusive relationship to which His people belong.
The tragedy of idolatry is therefore not simply that God is denied something.
The worshiper is giving himself to something that cannot save him.
That is why idols are cruel masters.
They take sacrifices.
But they cannot resurrect anyone.
They demand devotion.
But they cannot forgive sin.
They promise identity.
But they cannot tell you who you were created to be.
They can consume your life.
They cannot give you eternal life.
And maybe your idol isn't something obviously wicked.
Maybe it is the person whose approval determines whether you feel valuable.
Maybe it is the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ but you're terrified to surrender.
Maybe it is the secret browser history nobody knows about.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe attention.
Maybe your image.
Maybe achievement.
Maybe your children.
Maybe your ministry.
Maybe being right.
Maybe being wanted.
Maybe being noticed.
Maybe being admired.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something you have repeatedly promised God you would surrender.
Then you went back.
Again.
And again.
And again.
You deleted it.
Reinstalled it.
Confessed it.
Returned to it.
Cried about it.
Hid it.
Promised God.
Broke the promise.
And now shame whispers:
After everything you've done, why would God still want you?
This is where the Gospel enters the scandal.
Because Ezekiel 16 does not end where many people assume it should.
Judgment is real.
Sin is not minimized.
Covenant betrayal has consequences.
Yet near the end, God speaks again about covenant.
He declares that He will remember His covenant.
That does not make the rebellion insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
The Bible's answer to human unfaithfulness is not that human beings eventually become good enough to deserve another chance.
The story moves toward something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ.
The One who does not merely expose adulterous hearts.
He comes to redeem sinners.
At the cross, God does not pretend our spiritual betrayal never happened.
Sin is dealt with.
Judgment is not waved away as though holiness doesn't matter.
Christ bears sin.
And resurrection announces that sin, death, guilt and condemnation do not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Him.
This is why the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up and maybe God will take you back.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Christ and calls sinners to repent and believe.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance.
It is not cosmetic Christianity.
Not religious damage control.
Not learning how to hide your idols better.
Repentance is a turning.
A changed mind that results in changed direction.
You stop defending the thing separating you from God.
You bring it into the light.
You call it what God calls it.
You turn toward Christ.
And here is where scandal becomes grace.
Jesus does not merely rewrite reputations.
He transforms people.
The sexually broken can be redeemed.
The proud can be humbled.
The addicted can begin walking in freedom.
The hypocrite can confess.
The bitter can forgive.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The wanderer can return.
The sinner can be washed.
Not because sin wasn't serious.
Because the blood of Christ is sufficient.
There is another Greek word worth remembering:
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Not divine permission to continue worshiping idols.
Grace rescues us from them.
Grace does not say, “Your betrayal doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Christ paid what you could never pay, so stop running from the One who came to save you.”
Maybe that is why you needed to encounter Ezekiel's uncomfortable language today.
Not because God wanted to disgust you.
Because He wanted to wake you.
Some sins survive because we keep giving them polite names.
We call greed ambition.
Lust loneliness.
Pride confidence.
Cowardice wisdom.
Bitterness discernment.
Compromise complexity.
Idolatry priorities.
And spiritual coldness “being busy.”
But there comes a moment when grace loves you enough to stop flattering you.
So be honest before God.
What has your heart?
Not your Sunday vocabulary.
Your heart.
What do you run toward when you hurt?
What do you fear losing most?
Whose approval controls you?
What determines whether you feel valuable?
What do you repeatedly choose even when obedience to Jesus requires surrendering it?
What occupies your imagination when everything becomes quiet?
What has become so important that you would rather compromise with God than lose it?
Don't answer publicly unless you should.
But answer God.
And if this article exposed something hidden, you don't need to tell strangers every detail.
Your comment might become the sentence another struggling believer sees at midnight and realizes:
I'm not the only one fighting.
That matters.
So does sharing this.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly losing a war nobody knows they're fighting.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.
It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be bought.
Your support helps us keep creating and sharing Scripture-centered resources designed to point people toward Jesus, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation.
If these words convicted you, don't merely admire the conviction.
Respond to it.
But above everything else—
come back to Jesus.
Because the deepest message of Ezekiel's shocking imagery is not that sinners are too filthy to return.
It is that sin is far uglier than we imagined...
and covenant grace is far more astonishing than we deserved.
The idol you keep running toward will eventually ask you to sacrifice something it can never give back.
Jesus gave Himself to rescue people who had nothing worthy to offer Him.
So when your scandal tells you the story is finished, remember the empty tomb.
Grace still knows how to write on pages shame thought were already ruined.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY IS AN ENTIRE BOOK OF ROMANTIC DESIRE SITTING BETWEEN ECCLESIASTES AND ISAIAH?
paragraphs: WHY IS AN ENTIRE BOOK OF ROMANTIC DESIRE SITTING BETWEEN ECCLESIASTES AND ISAIAH?

The Bible could have moved from Solomon’s search for meaning straight into Isaiah’s thunderous visions of holiness. Instead, right in the middle, God preserved a song filled with kisses, perfume, longing, beauty, bodies, absence, desire, marriage, and a love so fierce it is compared with death. Why? Maybe because God refuses to surrender one of the deepest parts of being human to the enemy.
There is a moment when an honest Bible reader reaches the Song of Songs and quietly wonders what nobody in church taught them to ask.
What is this doing here?
You have just walked through Ecclesiastes.
“Vanity of vanities.”
Death.
Time.
Work.
Regret.
Meaning.
The aching realization that everything under the sun eventually slips through our fingers.
Then you turn the page...
And suddenly someone wants to be kissed.
The Hebrew does not soften it.
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth...” — Song of Songs 1:2.
That is not a mistranslation.
That is Scripture.
The book opens with שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים — Shir haShirim — “Song of Songs.” The construction functions like a superlative: not merely a song, but the supreme song, the song among songs.
And immediately, it begins with desire.
No apology.
No embarrassment.
No attempt to pretend human beings do not have bodies.
No nervous religious cough before changing the subject.
Then, after this astonishing collection of longing and delight, the Bible moves into Isaiah:
“Holy, holy, holy.”
So why is a book of romantic desire sitting there?
Why would God preserve poetry about attraction, longing, beauty, exclusivity, marriage, absence, reunion and desire inside Holy Scripture?
Perhaps the question underneath the question is even more uncomfortable:
What if God is not embarrassed by something the church has sometimes been embarrassed to discuss?
And what if the enemy has been extraordinarily successful at corrupting precisely what God intended to be received with holiness, covenant, gratitude and joy?
Because sexuality was not invented by pornography.
Desire was not invented by Hollywood.
The human body was not invented by lust.
Marriage was not invented by culture.

Long before sin distorted desire, God created humanity male and female. Long before pornography commercialized bodies, Genesis declared the naked husband and wife unashamed. Long before adultery fractured homes, God established covenant. Long before lust whispered, “Take what does not belong to you,” God created a love capable of saying, “I belong to my beloved.”
That sentence appears in the Song itself:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְדוֹדִי לִי
Ani le-dodi ve-dodi li.
“I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.” — Song of Songs 6:3.
Read it again.
Not consumption.
Belonging.
Not exploitation.
Mutuality.
Not anonymous bodies using each other for temporary relief.
Covenantal language of giving and receiving.
This matters because many people reading this know what it feels like when desire stops feeling beautiful.
Some know what it is to have pornography sitting in browser history while a Bible sits on the nightstand.
Some know what it is to be married and lonely.
Some know what it is to have given their body to someone who promised permanence and disappeared.
Some know what it is to wake up beside somebody and somehow feel more alone than when the bed was empty.
Some have confused attention with love.
Some have accepted manipulation because they were starving to feel wanted.
Some learned sexuality from screens before anyone taught them holiness.
Some were wounded by somebody else's sinful desire.
Some carry memories they desperately wish they could erase.
Some have repented repeatedly and still wonder whether Jesus is disgusted with them.
And some became so ashamed of desire itself that they quietly began believing holiness meant becoming less human.
Then Song of Songs sits in the Bible like a protest.
God does not redeem us by teaching us to hate His creation.
He redeems what sin has distorted.
That distinction changes everything.

The Song should not be reduced to an ancient Christian code in which every vineyard, breast, fragrance, kiss and garden secretly means something else. Its plain literary surface celebrates the passionate love of a man and woman. Christian tradition has also long read the Song spiritually, while the New Testament itself uses marriage and bridegroom imagery for Christ and His people. The responsible Christ-centered reading therefore does not have to erase human love in order to see where the whole biblical story eventually leads.
The Bible can celebrate covenant love between husband and wife...
and then show us that marriage itself ultimately points beyond itself.
Paul does exactly that in Ephesians 5.
He speaks about husband and wife, then suddenly opens a window into something infinitely larger:
Christ and His Church.
Human marriage is real.
Human desire within its God-given covenant is real.
But even the most faithful marriage cannot carry the weight of being somebody's savior.
Your husband cannot redeem your soul.
Your wife cannot cleanse your sin.
Romance cannot resurrect you.
Sex cannot give you eternal life.
Being desired cannot finally tell you who you are.
There is a hunger underneath our hungers that another human being cannot permanently satisfy.
And that is where the love story becomes breathtaking.
Because the Gospel does not announce that humanity climbed its way back to God.
It announces that God came looking for humanity.
Jesus Christ entered our shame.
He touched people respectable religion avoided.
He ate with sinners.
He received the broken.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people to repentance.
He carried our sin to a Roman cross.
And there, the One who had no scandal of His own was publicly crucified beneath ours.
Our lust.
Our adultery.
Our pornography.
Our secret messages.
Our betrayal.
Our pride.
Our religious pretending.
Our selfishness.
Our attempts to turn people into objects.
Our desperate search for love in places that could never love us back.
He bore sin—not so we could rename darkness and remain inside it, but so sinners could be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled and transformed.
That is grace.
Grace is not Jesus looking at sin and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace is Jesus looking at a sinner and saying, in effect, “Your sin mattered enough for Me to bleed for it, and I love you enough not to leave you enslaved to it.”
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the moment you finally stop defending the prison whose door Christ has opened.
Maybe that is why this book feels so dangerous.
Because beneath all its perfume and poetry is a truth our generation desperately needs:
Love is not casual.
Love has weight.
Song of Songs eventually erupts with one of Scripture's most staggering descriptions of it:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-azzah khamavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death...” — Song of Songs 8:6.
Then comes an extraordinary expression:
שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה
shalhevetyah.

A blazing flame—an expression traditionally understood as “a flame of Yah,” or an intensely mighty flame. The Hebrew imagery refuses to describe love as harmless sentimentality. It burns. It claims. It costs. It cannot simply be purchased like merchandise.
And suddenly our culture's version of “love” begins looking painfully thin.
Swipe.
Use.
Hide.
Delete.
Replace.
Repeat.
But biblical love keeps moving toward covenant.
Toward faithfulness.
Toward giving.
Toward belonging.
Toward sacrifice.
And when Scripture reaches its fullest revelation of sacrificial love, we do not find perfume.
We smell blood.
We do not find a garden of romantic celebration.
We first find another garden where Jesus sweats in anguish and says yes to the Father's will.
Then we find a cross.
The Bridegroom loves His people at unimaginable cost.
Christ does not merely desire a beautiful bride.
He gives Himself to make His people holy.
That is why the Gospel is not the story of beautiful people finally becoming worthy enough for Jesus.
It is the story of Jesus giving Himself for sinners and making a people His own.
Scandal becomes grace.
Shame meets mercy.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
The wandering are called home.
The unclean are washed.
The spiritually dead are offered life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have been calling yourself by the name of your worst chapter.
Cheater.
Addict.
Used.
Dirty.
Rejected.
Divorced.
Unwanted.
Porn addict.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Too far gone.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not save you by pretending your past never happened.
He does something greater.
He refuses to let your past have the final word.
At the cross, sin is exposed as terrible enough to require the death of the Son of God.
At the resurrection, grace is revealed as powerful enough that death itself cannot keep the final word.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Redemption.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace writing an ending the scandal could never produce.
And perhaps now we begin understanding why Song of Songs belongs in the Bible.
Because God cares about what we love.
God cares about how we desire.
God cares about how husbands and wives treat each other.
God cares about bodies because He created bodies.
God cares about fidelity because He is faithful.
God cares about covenant.
God cares about wounded hearts.
God cares about the person who feels unwanted.
God cares about the person fighting sexual temptation at 2:17 in the morning when nobody else knows.
God cares about the marriage that has become cold.
God cares about the single Christian who wonders whether waiting is worth it.
God cares about the person whose boundaries were violated and whose understanding of intimacy was wounded by someone else's sin.
God cares about the believer ashamed to admit that this battle is still a battle.
And Jesus is not calling you merely to behavior modification.
He wants your heart.
That is where Christianity becomes painfully personal.
You can delete the app and still crave validation.
You can install the filter and still worship desire.
You can stop sleeping with someone and still secretly make that person your god.
You can be technically sexually pure and remain consumed by pride.
You can wear a wedding ring and be emotionally unfaithful.
You can quote Scripture while starving your spouse of tenderness.
You can condemn the sexual sins everybody can see while carefully protecting the lust nobody can.
Jesus did not come merely to polish the outside of religious people.
He came to make dead hearts alive.
So be honest.
What are you actually hungry for?
To be touched?
To be chosen?
To be noticed?
To be wanted?
To be told you are beautiful?
To know someone will stay?
Those longings can become disordered, but their existence may reveal something painfully human.
We ache to be known without being abandoned.
And here the Gospel reaches deeper than romance ever can.
God already knows.
The secret.
The browser history.
The fantasy.
The betrayal.
The loneliness.
The night you never told anybody about.
The thing done to you.
The thing you did.
The prayer you stopped praying.
The marriage nobody knows is struggling.
The addiction hidden beneath Christian language.
The tears after everyone went to sleep.
He knows.
And the invitation of Christ is not, “Clean yourself until I can tolerate you.”
It is:
Repent.
Come.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Me.
Be made new.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already carried you out of a place you thought would destroy you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed to survive tonight.
This is why Gospel truth must keep traveling.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Save this too.
Because temptation has a way of returning after conviction fades.
Loneliness returns.
Shame starts talking again.
Old names come knocking.
And you may need to remember:
your hunger is not your master.
your history is not your savior.
your sexuality is not your identity.
your shame does not own you.
Jesus Christ is Lord.

Scripture allows those who proclaim the Gospel to receive material support for Gospel work, while also teaching that Christian giving must never be extracted through pressure or compulsion; it should come willingly from the heart. Salvation cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel ministry continue.
It should be the mission.
If this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life and you want to help that Gospel-centered work reach farther, prayerfully consider becoming one of the people who helps carry it.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Save it so you can return to it.
Share it publicly so the Gospel can travel farther than our own reach.
Follow and invite others to follow so they can continue receiving Scripture-centered encouragement.
Because perhaps that is the final surprise hidden inside the Song of Songs.
The Bible contains a song of desire because the God who created us is not interested only in the polished religious pieces of us.
He claims the whole person.
Mind.
Body.
History.
Desire.
Wounds.
Relationships.
Failures.
Future.
He enters places shame told us to hide.
He confronts what sin distorted.
He forgives what repentance brings into the light.
He restores what can be restored.
He teaches us to love without consuming.
To desire without worshiping desire.
To belong without possessing another person as an idol.
To see bodies without turning people into objects.
To understand marriage without making marriage a savior.
And finally...
to discover that beneath every lesser longing is the question eternity keeps asking:
What happens when the thing you have been searching for in human arms can finally be found only in the pierced hands of Christ?
Maybe your story has scandal in it.
Maybe more than anybody knows.
But if you bring that story to Jesus, the scandal does not get to write the final sentence.
Grace does.
The chapter you are most ashamed to reread may become the very page where someone else discovers what Jesus can redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Want a Godly Spouse. Are You Becoming the Kind of Person Who Knows How to Love One?
paragraphs: You Want a Godly Spouse. Are You Becoming the Kind of Person Who Knows How to Love One?

Maybe God is doing something deeper in your waiting season than preparing someone for you. Maybe He is teaching you how to become someone who can love another human being without asking them to become what only Jesus can be.
You have prayed for them.
Maybe more times than you would admit.
“Lord, send me someone who loves You.”
Someone faithful.
Someone emotionally mature.
Someone who will pray with me.
Someone who understands commitment.
Someone who won’t play games with my heart.
Someone who will stay.
Someone who knows Scripture.
Someone who wants marriage, not situationships.
Someone who is serious about Jesus.
And there is nothing shameful about desiring that.
Marriage is not a dirty desire. Scripture presents marriage as honorable, and the longing to share your life with another person can be beautiful.

But somewhere between another wedding invitation, another engagement announcement on your screen, another “So, are you seeing anyone?” from a relative, and another night lying alone with your phone glowing beside you...
the desire can quietly become something else.
You stop merely wanting marriage.
You start believing marriage will finally make you whole.
And that is where a good desire can begin carrying a weight God never designed it to carry.
Because you can spend years asking God,
“Where is the right person?”
while God is confronting you with another question:
Are you becoming the kind of person who knows how to love one?
That question hurts differently.
Because it is easier to create a checklist for somebody else than to let Jesus examine us.
Faithful.
Kind.
Patient.
Pure.
Prayerful.
Emotionally available.
Humble.
Forgiving.
Gentle.
Spiritually mature.
We know what we want.
But imagine placing your own name at the top of the list.
Not theirs.
Yours.
Am I faithful?
Am I kind when I am disappointed?
Am I patient when I don't get what I want?
Can I apologize without defending myself?
Can I hear correction without turning cold?
Do I know how to forgive?
Can I disagree without humiliating someone?
Do I manipulate affection when I feel insecure?
Do I punish people with silence?
Do I demand reassurance because I have made another human being responsible for wounds I refuse to bring before Christ?
Do I know how to serve when nobody applauds me?
Do I know how to love someone when loving them costs me something?
Suddenly the prayer changes.
“God, send me the right person” becomes...
“Jesus, make me faithful.”
And maybe that is one of the holiest things that can happen in your waiting season.
Paul wrote to believers in Colossae:
“Put on therefore, as God’s elect, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;
Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye.
And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.”
— Colossians 3:12–14, KJV
The original Greek makes Paul's language even more striking.
He begins with:
Ἐνδύσασθε οὖν — endýsasthe oun
“Therefore, clothe yourselves.”
The verb ἐνδύω — endýō carries the idea of putting on clothing.
Paul is describing something believers are called to intentionally wear because of who they already are in Christ.
Compassion.
Kindness.
Humility.
Gentleness.
Patience.
These are not merely traits you should search for on somebody's dating profile.
They are garments Christ calls you to put on.
Then comes a phrase that destroys romantic fantasy:
ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων — anechómenoi allḗlōn
“bearing with one another.”
That isn't particularly cinematic.
Nobody puts that on a Valentine's card.
Nobody posts engagement photographs with the caption:
“I finally found someone I will occasionally have to bear with.”
But Scripture understands something romantic culture often hides.
You will marry a sinner.
And if you marry, your spouse will marry one too.
You.
Marriage does not bring together two flawless Christians who have finally completed God's compatibility assessment.
It brings together two human beings who desperately need grace.
There will be mornings when neither person looks particularly spiritual.
There will be misunderstandings.
Stress.
Exhaustion.
Financial pressure.
Unspoken expectations.
Bad moods.
Old wounds.
Disappointments.
There may be moments when the person who once made your heart race becomes the person who tests your patience before breakfast.
That is why biblical love requires something deeper than chemistry.
Paul continues:
χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς — charizómenoi heautoîs
“forgiving one another.”
The verb χαρίζομαι — charízomai is related to χάρις — cháris:
grace.
Paul does not merely tell Christians to tolerate each other's imperfections.
He points them toward grace.
And then he gives the standard:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Κύριος ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν
“as the Lord forgave you.”
There it is.
Jesus.
Christian relationships cannot ultimately be understood by staring endlessly at ourselves or our romantic expectations.
We look at Christ.
You want someone forgiving?
Look at Jesus.
You want someone patient?
Look at Jesus.
You want someone sacrificial?
Look at Jesus.
You want someone faithful?
Look at Jesus.
And then comes the uncomfortable part:
Follow Him.
Because Christianity is not primarily about finding somebody who resembles your ideal spouse.
It is about being transformed into the likeness of Christ.
This means singleness is not God's waiting room where your real life has not started yet.
Read that again.
Your life with Jesus is happening now.
You are not spiritually parked until somebody proposes.
You are not half a person waiting for your missing half.
Marriage is precious, but marriage is not your Messiah.
A husband cannot bear the weight of being your savior.
A wife cannot carry the burden of becoming your ultimate source of identity.
No spouse can heal every wound, silence every insecurity, fulfill every longing, remove every loneliness, and make your soul complete.
Eventually, the pedestal collapses.
Not necessarily because they were terrible.
But because they were human.
There is only One who can occupy the throne of your heart without being crushed by the weight of your expectations.
Jesus Christ.
Somebody reading this has been praying desperately for a relationship because loneliness has begun whispering:
“If somebody chooses you, then you'll finally know you're worth loving.”
But the Gospel tells a different story.
Before your future spouse knows your name, Christ knew you.
Before anyone chooses you at an altar, Christ demonstrated His love toward sinners.
Before someone puts a ring on your finger, there was a Savior whose hands were pierced.
Your deepest identity cannot begin with:
“Someone wants me.”
It begins with belonging to Jesus.
That changes dating.
That changes waiting.
That changes rejection.
That changes heartbreak.
Because rejection can still hurt without becoming your identity.
Loneliness can still ache without becoming your master.
You can desire marriage without worshiping marriage.
You can pray for a spouse without treating God like a divine matchmaking service.
You can grieve another relationship that didn't work without concluding that God has forgotten you.
And you can finally stop asking another human being to prove what the cross has already declared:
Christ's love is not something you earned by becoming desirable enough.
It is grace.
Maybe you have made mistakes romantically.
Maybe your story is already messy.
Maybe you gave your heart away recklessly.
Maybe you ignored warning signs because loneliness frightened you more than compromise.
Maybe you stayed because you were terrified nobody else would want you.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you never would.
Maybe you manipulated.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you were cheated on.
Maybe you used someone.
Maybe someone used you.
Maybe you are carrying sexual sin, resentment, shame, bitterness, pornography, emotional dependency, jealousy, or memories you desperately wish you could erase.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not pretending none of it mattered.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace tells the truth about sin...
and then points sinners toward a Savior.
Jesus Christ did not come for people with spotless romantic histories.
He came to save sinners.
Repentance means we stop defending what Christ calls sin and turn toward Him.
And forgiveness does not mean your choices suddenly have no consequences.
It means your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
That is the scandal of grace.
Your sin can be real.
Your consequences can be real.
Your wounds can be real.
Your regrets can be real.
And the mercy of Christ can still be greater.
From scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners through His blood and teaching redeemed people how to live differently.
Maybe that is what God wants to do in your waiting.
Not simply hand you somebody.
Transform you.
Teach you how to tell the truth.
Teach you boundaries.
Teach you purity.
Teach you patience.
Teach you how to communicate instead of manipulate.
Teach you how to apologize.
Teach you how to forgive.
Teach you to recognize unhealthy attachment.
Teach you how to serve.
Teach you how to be alone without believing you are abandoned.
Teach you that “no” can sometimes be mercy.
Teach you that attraction is not discernment.
Teach you that chemistry is not character.
Teach you that somebody quoting Bible verses does not automatically mean they live under the authority of Scripture.
And teach you to stop asking only:
“Do they love God?”
while refusing to ask:
“Does the way they live consistently bear evidence of that confession?”
But turn the question around too.
Does yours?
Because it is dangerously easy to demand spiritual maturity from the person you hope to marry while excusing immaturity in yourself.
“I need someone who communicates.”
Do you?
“I need someone humble.”
Are you?
“I need someone loyal.”
Are you faithful when nobody is watching?
“I need someone emotionally mature.”
Can you receive correction without retaliation?
“I need someone who puts Christ first.”
Does Jesus actually have first place in your own life?
Not your Christian aesthetic.
Not your church attendance.
Not the verse in your bio.
Jesus.
Paul reaches the climax of Colossians 3:14:
ἐπὶ πᾶσιν δὲ τούτοις τὴν ἀγάπην
“And above all these things, love.”
The word is ἀγάπη — agápē.
And Paul calls this love:
σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος — sýndesmos tēs teleiótētos
the bond of completeness, maturity, or perfect unity.
Biblical love is not merely finding someone who gives you butterflies.
Sometimes love is extraordinarily unglamorous.
It listens.
It tells the truth.
It repents.
It forgives.
It serves.
It remains gentle during disagreement.
It refuses manipulation.
It celebrates another person's growth.
It carries burdens.
It chooses faithfulness when feelings fluctuate.
And Christian love ultimately takes its shape from Jesus.

This does not mean you should stay in an abusive or dangerous relationship because you are supposed to “bear with” somebody. Scripture's commands toward patience and forgiveness should never be twisted into permission for abuse, coercion, violence, exploitation, or unrepentant destructive behavior.
Nor does forgiveness automatically mean restored trust.
Trust can require repentance, truth, wisdom, boundaries, and time.
But for ordinary imperfect relationships between imperfect believers, Colossians gives us something our romantic culture desperately needs.
Stop searching for someone who will never inconvenience you.
That person does not exist.
Instead, become deeply rooted in the Christ who can teach two imperfect people to practice compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience, forgiveness, and love.
And here is perhaps the question worth carrying into prayer tonight:
If God gave you the kind of spouse you have been praying for tomorrow, would the person receiving them know how to love them in a Christlike way?
Don't answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Maybe you would.
Maybe there are places where Jesus has already done beautiful work in you.
Thank Him for that.
But maybe the question exposed something.
Pride.
Impatience.
Entitlement.
Fear.
Lust.
Control.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
A desperate need to be chosen.
Don't hide it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Christian conviction is not an invitation to self-hatred.
It is an invitation to repentance and transformation.
The Gospel does not merely say, “Try harder to become marriage material.”
The Gospel says you need Christ.
We cannot manufacture Christlike character merely by becoming more disciplined daters.
We need the grace of God.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need Scripture.
We need repentance.
We need Christian community.
We need Jesus continually reshaping desires that have become disordered.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be:
“Jesus, where is my spouse?”
Maybe it needs to become:
“Jesus, make me more like You.
Teach me compassion when selfishness feels easier.
Teach me kindness when irritation rises.
Teach me humility when my pride wants to win.
Teach me gentleness when my words could wound.
Teach me patience when waiting hurts.
Teach me forgiveness because You have forgiven me.
Teach me to love without turning another person into an idol.
And whether marriage comes soon, years from now, or not according to the story I imagined...
do not let me waste this season.
Make me Yours.”
That prayer may not produce an engagement announcement tomorrow.
But it can produce something far more important today:
discipleship.
And if marriage eventually comes, you may discover that the waiting season was never empty.
Jesus was there.
Building things nobody could see.
Removing things nobody else knew were there.
Healing wounds you once expected another person to heal.
Teaching you that being alone and being abandoned are not the same thing.
Teaching you that your relationship status never determined your worth.
Teaching you that marriage is a gift...
but Christ is the treasure.
It does not.
Not because financially supporting a Christian ministry somehow proves that you glorify God. Salvation and God's acceptance cannot be purchased.
But before you leave, remember this:
Maybe the greatest love story being written in your waiting season isn't about the person you're hoping God sends—maybe it is the story of Jesus teaching your heart how to love like His.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “YOU ARE GODS” — The Verse People Keep Using to Make Themselves Bigger… When Jesus Was Revealing Someone Greater
paragraphs: “YOU ARE GODS” — The Verse People Keep Using to Make Themselves Bigger… When Jesus Was Revealing Someone Greater

What Jesus Really Meant in John 10:34—and why one of the Bible’s most misunderstood statements was never permission to make yourself divine, but part of a breathtaking confrontation pointing us toward the unique Son of God.
There are four words in the Bible that can become dangerous when they are ripped away from the words surrounding them.
“You are gods.”
Jesus said them.
That is exactly why they can sound so convincing when someone isolates them.
Maybe you have heard someone quote John 10:34 as though Jesus finally revealed humanity’s hidden secret:
“You don’t know how powerful you are.”
“You have divinity inside you.”
“You are a little god.”
“You can create your own reality.”
“You just need to awaken to who you really are.”
And because the words appear in red letters in many Bibles, the argument can feel almost impossible to challenge.
After all…
Jesus said it.
But what if those four words were never meant to exalt you?
What if Jesus was quoting a judgment passage?
What if the original text actually destroys human pride instead of feeding it?
And what if the most astonishing truth in this passage is not that you are a god…
…but that the true Son of God came into a world full of people trying to take God's place—and still chose to save them?
Stay with the passage.
Because context changes everything.
Jesus is standing in Jerusalem during the Feast of Dedication.
The tension around Him has become unbearable.
His opponents surround Him and demand an answer.
If He is the Messiah, they want Him to say it plainly.
Jesus points them toward His works. He speaks about His sheep. He says that no one can snatch them from His hand. Then He says that no one can snatch them from His Father's hand.
And then comes the sentence that detonates the conversation:
“I and the Father are one.”
The Greek is striking:
ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν
Egō kai ho Patēr hen esmen.
“I and the Father are one.”
Notice something important.
Jesus does not say, “Everyone is God.”
He does not say, “You are one with God in exactly the same way I am.”
He speaks about Himself and the Father.
His opponents understand His words as an extraordinary claim, because they immediately pick up stones.
Jesus asks them why.
They answer that it is not because of His good works but because, in their accusation, He—a man—was making Himself God.
And that is where Jesus says the words so often pulled out of context:
“Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’?”
In Greek:
ἐγὼ εἶπα· θεοί ἐστε
Egō eipa: theoi este.
“I said, you are gods.”
But Jesus did not invent that sentence during this confrontation.
He was quoting Scripture.
Specifically, Psalm 82:6.
And once you go back to the psalm Jesus quoted, something fascinating happens.
The Hebrew reads:
אֲנִי־אָמַרְתִּי אֱלֹהִים אַתֶּם
Ani amarti, elohim attem.
“I said, you are elohim.”
The word that immediately demands our attention is:
אֱלֹהִים — elohim.
Yes, elohim is the familiar Hebrew word frequently used for God.
But words receive their precise sense from context.
The mere appearance of elohim does not automatically mean that everyone described with the term possesses the unique, uncreated being of Yahweh.
And Psalm 82 certainly does not suddenly announce the existence of multiple Almighty Gods competing with the LORD.
Read what happens next.
The beings addressed as elohim are condemned.
They have failed in justice.
The weak have suffered.
The needy have been neglected.
The wicked have received favor.
And then comes the line that almost never appears on the motivational quote:
“Nevertheless, like man you shall die.”
That changes the atmosphere completely.
“You are gods” is followed by death and judgment.
Whatever precisely elohim identifies in Psalm 82, the passage is not a coronation ceremony teaching ordinary people to discover that they are independent deities.
It is a courtroom.
And God is Judge.
There is an important interpretive question here, and Christians should be honest enough not to pretend it does not exist.

For centuries, many interpreters have understood the elohim of Psalm 82 as human rulers or judges exercising delegated authority under God. Other scholars understand Psalm 82 against the ancient biblical picture of a heavenly or divine council and therefore identify these elohim as created spiritual beings under Yahweh's absolute authority.
The disagreement is real.
But notice what neither interpretation requires:
That every human being is an autonomous god possessing the same divine nature as the LORD.
That idea simply is not what Jesus is teaching here.
In fact, Jesus continues His argument immediately:

“If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”
Read that slowly.
Jesus does not quote Psalm 82 and then announce:
“See? Everybody is God.”
He draws attention back to Himself.
To the One whom the Father sanctified.
To the One whom the Father sent into the world.
To the Son.
His argument moves from the lesser case toward the greater.

If Scripture can employ such extraordinary terminology for beings subordinate to God without Scripture becoming guilty of blasphemy, His opponents cannot simply hear the title “Son of God,” scream “blasphemy,” and refuse to examine the identity, works, and mission of the One standing before them.
Jesus tells them, in effect, to examine His works.
And then John records another staggering statement:
“the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”
The center of the passage is still Christ.
That matters.
Because human beings have been reaching for God's throne since Eden.
The serpent's temptation was not merely about forbidden fruit.
It attacked trust in God.
“God is withholding something.”
“You could have more.”
“You could determine good and evil for yourself.”
“You could be like God.”
Humanity reached upward.
And fell.
That ancient temptation still knows how to dress itself for every generation.
Sometimes it wears religious clothing.
Sometimes spiritual clothing.
Sometimes self-help clothing.
Sometimes it sounds almost Christian.
“You have limitless power within yourself.”
“You create reality with your words.”
“You don't really need rescue; you need awakening.”
“You aren't a sinner needing reconciliation—you've simply forgotten your divinity.”
Then somebody discovers John 10:34.
“You are gods.”
Four words.
A whole theology built upon them.
But Jesus never came to awaken us to our supposed independent deity.
Jesus came to save sinners.
That distinction is enormous.
Christianity does proclaim something breathtaking about human beings.
We are created in God's image.
We may become children of God through faith in Christ.
Believers are united with Christ.
The Holy Spirit dwells in God's people.
Christians are being transformed into Christ's likeness.
Peter can even speak of believers becoming “partakers of the divine nature” in 2 Peter 1:4—a text that Christian theology has discussed deeply across the centuries.
But participation in God's life by grace is not the same thing as becoming God by nature.
The Creator remains Creator.
We remain creatures.
Redeemed creatures can be brought unimaginably close to God without becoming another Almighty God.
That is not an insult to humanity.
It is something far more beautiful.
You don't have to be God to be loved by God.
You don't have to possess omnipotence to matter.
You don't have to manufacture your own salvation.
You don't have to speak universes into existence.
You don't have to pretend you are limitless.
You are allowed to be a creature held by your Creator.
You are allowed to say:
“I need You.”
And perhaps that is where this passage becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us would rather discover secret power inside ourselves than admit desperate need before Jesus.
Power sounds attractive.
Repentance does not.
Self-deification strokes the ego.
The cross crucifies it.
“Discover the god within you” asks very little of your pride.
“Deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Me” asks for everything.
And yet the cross is where grace begins doing what pride could never accomplish.
Because the Gospel is not the story of humans finally realizing they were gods.
It is the story of the Son of God entering the ruin humans created by trying to live without God.
Think about that.
The One through whom all things were made entered His creation.
The Holy One walked among sinners.
The innocent Christ was condemned.
The King wore thorns.
Hands that healed were pierced.
The One who deserved worship received mockery.
Jesus carried sin to the cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
Not because humanity needed a motivational speech about its hidden greatness.
Because humanity needed a Savior.
Maybe that is what makes grace so difficult for proud hearts to receive.
Grace requires you to admit that you cannot rescue yourself.
You cannot outgrow sin.
You cannot manifest away guilt.
You cannot rename rebellion enlightenment.
You cannot save yourself by discovering some hidden spark of deity.
You need forgiveness.
So do I.
We need Christ.
And the beautiful scandal of Christianity is that when sinners finally stop pretending to be their own gods, they discover that the true God is more merciful than they imagined.
Maybe you have been running.
Maybe nobody knows what is happening inside you.
Church people see the smile.
Family sees the version of you that you know how to perform.
Facebook sees the photographs.
Friends hear “I'm okay.”
But God sees the secret.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The affair nobody knows about.
The anger.
The envy.
The pride.
The private messages.
The compromises.
The prayerlessness.
The doubts you are afraid to say aloud.
The nights when you wonder whether you have wandered too far to come home.
And here is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Jesus did not come for a fictional, polished version of you.
Christ died for sinners.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide your scandal until you become worthy of grace.
Grace meets sinners in the scandal and calls them into repentance, forgiveness, holiness, and new life.
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves sin is more serious than we want to believe.
But the same cross proves something else.
God's grace in Christ reaches deeper than the grave.
This is why Jesus must remain at the center of John 10.
Not us.
Not our supposed divinity.
Jesus.
The Son whom the Father sent.
The Shepherd whose sheep hear His voice.
The One who gives eternal life.
The One whose works bear witness to Him.
The One who is in the Father and the Father in Him.
The One standing before people holding stones…
while knowing He would soon surrender Himself to nails.
And perhaps the question John 10 ultimately presses into your heart is not:
“Am I a god?”
Perhaps the real question is:
What will I do with the Son of God?
You can study the Greek and still avoid Him.
You can debate elohim and never surrender.
You can win an argument about Psalm 82 while losing sight of the Shepherd calling you.
Biblical knowledge is precious.
But the Scriptures were never given merely so that we could become cleverer sinners.
They lead us toward truth.
And truth brings us face-to-face with Jesus Christ.
So if you have used “you are gods” to build yourself a throne, come down.
If someone taught you that Christianity is ultimately about discovering that you possess God's unique deity, come back to the text.
If pride has convinced you that you don't need repentance, come back to the cross.
And if shame has convinced you that Jesus would never receive someone like you…
come back to the cross too.
Pride says, “I don't need saving.”
Shame says, “I can't be saved.”
The Gospel destroys both lies.
Jesus says to repent and believe the good news.
The answer to your sin is not pretending you are divine.
The answer is the crucified and risen Christ.
Don't turn the comments into a place for theological performance.
Let them become a place where somebody realizes they are not the only person fighting to come home.
And think of one person who needs this article.
Not twenty random names.
One.

Maybe a friend has encountered teaching about “little gods.” Maybe someone you love is being pulled toward spirituality that borrows Christian vocabulary while quietly removing Christ from the center. Maybe someone believes his scandal has already written the final chapter of his life.
Stay because you want more Scripture.
Stay because you want your theology tested against the Word instead of whatever happens to be trending.
Stay because following Jesus is worth taking seriously.
Read them.
Save them.
Study them.
Share them.
Send them to the struggling believer.
Send them to the seeker.
Send them to the lukewarm Christian.
Even send them to the unbelieving friend willing to investigate who Jesus really is.
remember Jesus.
Scripture does not need us to make ourselves bigger.
It reveals a Christ greater than we imagined.
And maybe tonight the most freeing prayer you could pray is not:
“God, show me how powerful I am.”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, show me who You are. Show me who I really am before You. Forgive what must be forgiven. Break what must be broken. Heal what must be healed. And teach me to follow You.”
Because the greatest miracle in this passage was never that sinful humanity could steal God's title.
It is that the true Son of God would come looking for sinners anyway.
Your scandal does not have to write your final sentence.
Put down the crown you were never meant to carry—and receive the grace only the King could give.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE GUARDED HER DEAD SONS UNTIL THE RAIN CAME
paragraphs: SHE GUARDED HER DEAD SONS UNTIL THE RAIN CAME

Rizpah could not bring her children back. She could not undo the judgment, stop the execution, or force a king to notice her grief. But when everyone else walked away from the bodies, one grieving mother stayed—and her terrible vigil still whispers something about love, justice, dignity, and the Savior who entered our shame to redeem what sin had ruined.
There are Bible stories we love to put on coffee mugs.
This is not one of them.
There are passages we teach children with bright pictures of lions, rainbows, slingshots, shepherds, and boats.
This is not one of them either.
This story begins with famine.
It moves through an old sin nobody had adequately dealt with.
Then there are seven dead men.
Exposed bodies.
Birds circling overhead.
Wild animals prowling after dark.
And beneath them...
a mother.
Her name was Rizpah.
And once you understand what she did, it becomes very difficult to forget her.

Second Samuel 21 records a famine during David's reign that lasted three successive years. David sought the LORD, and the answer reached backward into the reign of Saul. Saul had attempted to destroy the Gibeonites despite Israel's covenant obligation toward them.
The past was not as dead as everybody imagined.
That alone should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because human beings are remarkably skilled at burying things without actually dealing with them.
We rename bitterness "boundaries."
We rename greed "ambition."
We rename lust "a private struggle."
We rename unforgiveness "protecting my peace."
We rename compromise "being realistic."
And sometimes we become so accustomed to what is wrong that we stop asking whether God calls it wrong.
But Scripture repeatedly confronts us with a God of truth and justice.
What people hide does not become holy simply because enough time passes.

Yet 2 Samuel 21 is also a difficult passage, and we should resist turning its tragedy into a simplistic formula. This is an account from Israel's covenant history, not permission for Christians to punish children for their parents' sins or to imitate ancient executions. Scripture elsewhere explicitly rejects ordinary human courts putting children to death for their fathers' sins. The point is not, "Go and do what happened here."
The point is to stand trembling before what Scripture actually records.
The Gibeonites requested seven male descendants of Saul.
David handed them over.
Among them were Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth.
And they died.
Try not to race past that sentence.
They died.
Rizpah had carried those boys.
She had probably remembered their first cries.
Perhaps she remembered tiny hands wrapping around her fingers.
Perhaps there had once been laughter inside rooms that would later become unbearably quiet.
The Bible does not give us those details, so we should not pretend to know them.
But it tells us enough.
She was their mother.
And now they were dead.
Then comes one of the most haunting verses in the Old Testament.
The Hebrew begins:
"וַתִּקַּח רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה אֶת־הַשַּׂק"
Vattiqqach Ritzpah bat-Ayyah et-haśśaq...
"Then Rizpah daughter of Aiah took the sackcloth..."
Sackcloth.
The clothing of grief.
The fabric of mourning.
She spread it upon the rock.
And she stayed.
Scripture says her vigil lasted "מִתְּחִלַּת קָצִיר"—mittəchillat qatsir—from the beginning of harvest, until water came down from heaven.

We often say Rizpah guarded the bodies "for months," and that is a reasonable description of the extended seasonal vigil implied by the text, but Scripture itself does not give us an exact number of days.
That distinction matters.
Because God's Word is powerful enough without our exaggerating it.
The truth is already devastating.
Day after day...
she stayed.
Night after night...
she stayed.
When birds descended, she drove them away.
When animals approached in darkness, she refused them.
Imagine the exhaustion.
Imagine sleeping lightly because every sound in the night might mean something was approaching.
Imagine sunrise no longer meaning a fresh beginning.
It only meant seeing the bodies again.
Imagine sunset no longer meaning rest.
It meant another night of guarding them.
She could not resurrect her sons.
She could not reverse what had happened.
She could not negotiate with death.
But she could refuse to abandon their remains to scavengers.
So Rizpah stayed.
And maybe that is why this story reaches into places that polished Christianity sometimes avoids.
Because some of you know what it means to stay beside something you cannot fix.
You have prayed over a marriage that still feels cold.
You have whispered the name of a child who has wandered far from God.
You have watched somebody you love disappear into addiction.
You have buried someone and discovered that grief does not obey calendars.
You have asked God for an answer and received another sunrise instead.
You have gone to church smiling while something inside you was screaming.
People told you to "move on."
But grief does not always move on.
Sometimes grief sits on a rock.
Sometimes grief keeps watch.
Sometimes faith does not look like shouting in victory.
Sometimes faith looks like surviving another night.
But we must be careful here.
Rizpah's vigil is moving, yet the Bible does not say that her endurance earned salvation, purchased God's favor, or atoned for sin.
Only Christ can bear that weight.
Rizpah can show us the fierce persistence of love.
She cannot save us.
And this is where the story begins turning our eyes toward Someone greater.
Because eventually...
someone noticed.
Second Samuel says:
"וַיֻּגַּד לְדָוִד"
Vayyuggad leDavid.
"And it was told David..."
Somebody told the king.
Think about that.
The woman who possessed almost no political power did something that reached the palace.
She apparently delivered no recorded speech.
She commanded no army.
She issued no royal decree.
She simply refused to leave.
And eventually the king heard about Rizpah.
David then acted.
He retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead and gathered the remains of those who had been exposed. They were buried in the tomb of Kish, Saul's father.
What had been left exposed was finally given burial.
What had been hanging in public disgrace was gathered.
Rizpah's grief had become impossible to ignore.
But there is something even deeper here.
Because the Christian Gospel tells us about another public death.
Another place of shame.
Another body exposed before watching crowds.
Another execution outside the comfort of ordinary life.
Jesus Christ.
And we need to say immediately what we do not mean.
Rizpah's sons were not Jesus.
Their deaths did not atone for the world.
Their execution should not be forced into an artificial one-to-one allegory of Calvary.
Jesus stands alone.
He willingly gave Himself according to the Father's redemptive purpose.
He was the sinless Son of God.
He bore our sins.
He accomplished what no ordinary human suffering could ever accomplish.
Yet reading Rizpah's terrible scene as Christians can make the scandal of crucifixion feel painfully physical again.
We have made the cross so beautiful in jewelry that we can forget how horrifying crucifixion was.
The cross was an instrument of public execution.
Humiliation.
Exposure.
Blood.
Mockery.
Death.
Jesus did not save us from a comfortable distance.
He entered our world of death.
Our guilt.
Our curse.
Our disgrace.
Our graves.
The apostle Paul writes in Greek:
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law."
How?
"γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα"
genomenos hyper hēmōn katara.
By "becoming a curse for us."
That is Galatians 3:13.
Do not sanitize those words.
The Gospel is not that decent people needed a little spiritual encouragement.
The Gospel is that sinners needed redemption.
We had something worse than vultures circling our mistakes.
We had guilt.
Something worse than public embarrassment.
Sin against a holy God.
Something worse than physical death.
Judgment.
And Jesus came for us.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because God pretends sin does not matter.
Calvary proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
Yet God's love is so astonishing that the Son willingly came to save sinners.
"He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree," Peter writes.
Our sins.
Mine.
Yours.
The secret one.
The repeated one.
The one nobody knows.
The one you promised God you would never do again.
The thing behind the browser history.
The resentment behind the smile.
The pride beneath the ministry.
The jealousy you disguise as discernment.
The unforgiveness you have rehearsed so long that it now feels justified.
The double life.
The spiritual numbness.
The version of you everybody applauds...
and the version of you only God sees.
Jesus already sees both.
And still the Gospel says:
Come.
Not "clean yourself up enough to deserve Me."
Come.
Not "hide the scandal until respectable Christians approve of you."
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Because grace does not mean Jesus helps us hide our sin more comfortably.
Grace brings us out of hiding.
Grace forgives.
Grace cleanses.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace takes people with histories they cannot rewrite and gives them futures only Christ could have authored.
That is why our theme is not "From Scandal to Denial."
It is not "From Scandal to Reputation Management."
It is not "From Scandal to Pretending It Never Happened."
It is...
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something dead inside you.
A dream.
A relationship.
Your confidence.
Your innocence.
Years you cannot recover.
Maybe you keep returning emotionally to the place where everything collapsed.
And perhaps you have secretly wondered...
"Does God see me here?"
Rizpah's story does not promise that every earthly loss will be reversed.
Christianity does not ask us to lie about graves.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Gospel gives us something infinitely stronger than denial.
Resurrection.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
And Jesus Christ rose.
Death did not write the final sentence.
The tomb did not get the final word.
And because Christ lives, those who belong to Him possess a hope that suffering cannot manufacture and death cannot ultimately destroy.
Maybe the sentence you need tonight is simply this:
Your darkest chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life belongs to Jesus Christ.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
David's own story proves that grace does not magically erase every earthly consequence of sin.
It means something greater.
Your sin does not have to remain your master.
Your shame does not have to remain your identity.
Your failure does not have to remain your name.
Your grave will not remain your permanent address if you are in Christ.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never existed.
By overwhelming the scandal with grace.
And perhaps Rizpah's vigil carries one final challenge.
She guarded what she loved.
So what are we doing with the Gospel we claim to love?
If Christ really rescued you, why should His name remain hidden on your timeline?
If the Gospel really is good news, somebody you know desperately needs to hear it.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
But gratitude does something.
Love moves.
Witness speaks.
Generosity supports ministry.
And people who have received good news naturally want someone else to hear it.
Think about one person whose faith has been exhausted.
Think about the mother praying for a wandering child.
The believer secretly fighting temptation.
The friend who stopped going to church.
The person carrying grief nobody understands.
The unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely religion for respectable people.
Send this to them.
One share may place the truth about Jesus in front of someone who would never walk into a church today.
And don't disappear silently after reading.
Someone scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that Christ is still restoring broken people.
There may come a night when you need to remember the woman on the rock...
the rain finally falling...
the bodies finally being gathered...
and the God whose redemptive story ultimately leads us beyond every human king to Jesus Christ.
Not to purchase God's favor.
Not to prove that you love Jesus.
But because supporting Gospel-centered work can help more Scripture, discipleship resources, and Christ-centered messages reach people who need them.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Grace is not for sale.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Salvation belongs to Christ.
Repent and believe in Him.
And if Gospel Warrior helps keep your eyes fixed on Jesus, then help us keep placing that truth in front of others. Follow for what comes next.
Rizpah could not raise her sons.
But she refused to abandon them to the darkness.
And centuries later, when humanity lay beneath something far worse than the shadow of circling birds, God did what Rizpah never could.
He sent His Son into our death.
Christ bore sin.
Christ entered the grave.
Christ rose victorious.
And now sinners who thought their story ended in shame can discover that the blood of Jesus has written another ending.
So when the enemy points at your past, remember the cross.
When shame whispers your old name, remember who calls sinners to repentance and gives His people a new identity.
When grief tells you the darkness will last forever, remember the empty tomb.
When you think God has forgotten the place where you have been weeping...
remember the rain.
Remember the rock.
Remember the grieving woman who stayed.
And then look beyond Rizpah.
Look to Jesus.
Because the deepest hope of this story is not that a grieving mother refused to abandon the dead.
It is that God did not abandon sinners to death.
And that is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
Rizpah stayed beside the dead until the rain came—but Jesus entered death itself so that everyone who belongs to Him can one day rise.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE HUSBAND WHO FOLLOWED HIS WIFE CRYING: Paltiel’s Heartbreaking Bible Story
paragraphs:
THE HUSBAND WHO FOLLOWED HIS WIFE CRYING: Paltiel’s Heartbreaking Bible Story
He Followed Her Down the Road Weeping—Until One Command Forced Him to Turn Around
There is a man in the Bible whose heartbreak takes only a few words to describe.
No psalm bears his name.
No great sermon of his survives.
No miracle is credited to him.
He does not kill a giant. He does not command an army. He does not sit on Israel’s throne.
He simply walks behind a woman...
and cries.
Then someone tells him to go home.
And he does.
That is almost everything Scripture tells us about Paltiel son of Laish.
Yet buried inside that painfully brief scene in 2 Samuel is one of the most haunting pictures of human attachment in the Old Testament.
Read it slowly.
Not because the Bible tells us everything about this man.
It does not.
Read it slowly because sometimes Scripture can break your heart without explaining every detail.
David had demanded the return of Michal, Saul’s daughter. Years earlier Michal had become David’s wife, but Saul subsequently gave her to another man, Palti—called Paltiel in 2 Samuel.
Then the political world shifted.
Saul was dead.
David was rising.
And Michal was demanded back.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 3:16 says:
“וַיֵּלֶךְ אִתָּהּ אִישָׁהּ הָלוֹךְ וּבָכֹה אַחֲרֶיהָ”
Vayyelekh ittah ishah, halokh uvakho achareha...
The sense is devastatingly simple:
Her husband went with her, following behind her, weeping.
The Hebrew construction הָלוֹךְ וּבָכֹה—halokh uvakho—carries the movement of continuing action.
Going...
and weeping.
Walking...
and crying.
Following...
and losing.
Until Bahurim.
Then Abner spoke.
“לֵךְ שׁוּב”
Lekh, shuv.
“Go. Return.”
And Paltiel returned.
That is it.
The Bible does not record his protest.
It does not record Michal turning around.
It does not tell us whether she cried.
It does not tell us whether she wanted to stay with Paltiel or return to David.
It does not tell us whether Paltiel ever saw her again.
And we should resist the temptation to invent what God chose not to reveal.
But Scripture does tell us this:
The man walked behind her crying.
And sometimes two Hebrew words are enough to make thousands of years disappear.
Because maybe you know something about walking behind what you cannot keep.
Maybe you have watched somebody leave.
Maybe you have stood beside a hospital bed knowing that love could not command another heartbeat.
Maybe you have watched a marriage collapse despite prayers whispered when everyone else was asleep.
Maybe your child stopped calling.
Maybe somebody chose somebody else.
Maybe death took the person whose name was woven into your everyday life.
Maybe you buried a dream you genuinely believed God had given you.
Maybe you watched the door close and discovered that faith does not always prevent tears.
Sometimes faith has to walk while crying.
And that is where Paltiel becomes painfully recognizable.
But we must understand his story carefully.
Michal originally loved David.
Scripture explicitly tells us that in 1 Samuel 18:20.

Saul offered her to David, and David fulfilled the required bride-price. Yet while David was later fleeing Saul, 1 Samuel 25:44 records that Saul gave Michal—whom the text still identifies as David’s wife—to Palti son of Laish of Gallim.
Years pass between those scenes.
The Bible gives us almost nothing about what happened inside the household of Michal and Paltiel during those years.
That silence matters.
We cannot honestly preach that theirs was certainly a beautiful marriage.
We cannot honestly claim Michal loved Paltiel.
We cannot honestly claim she hated him.
We cannot turn biblical silence into revelation merely because it makes a more dramatic story.
What we can say is that when she was taken from him, Paltiel followed her crying.
That is what God allowed us to see.
And perhaps the restraint of Scripture makes the scene even more powerful.
There are no speeches.
No soundtrack.
No explanation.
Just footsteps and tears.
Imagine the road—not as additional Scripture, but simply as the human reality the inspired words force us to confront.
One person is being taken away.
Another keeps following.
How far do you follow someone you know you are losing?
Another hundred steps?
Another bend in the road?
Until someone finally turns toward you and says:
Enough.
Go home.
There is something brutal about those words.
Lekh, shuv.
Go.
Return.
Because returning means admitting the road will continue without you.
Returning means walking back through the same landscape where, minutes earlier, you still had hope.
Returning means eventually reaching a house containing reminders of someone who is no longer there.
And perhaps that is why this tiny biblical scene reaches beyond Paltiel.
Because almost everyone eventually encounters a road where love cannot make someone stay.
But there is an important Gospel truth here.
Paltiel is not Jesus.
And Jesus is not merely another character in Paltiel’s tragedy.
The Bible’s ultimate message is not that every person or relationship we lose will be returned to us exactly as we want.
Christianity offers something infinitely deeper than that.
It offers Christ Himself.
There are losses God may not reverse in this life.
There are graves that remain occupied until resurrection.
There are relationships that repentance cannot reconstruct exactly as they once were.
There are consequences grace forgives without pretending they never happened.
There are prayers answered differently from the answer we begged for.
The Gospel does not promise that following Jesus means never reaching Bahurim.
It promises that when everything earthly proves unable to save us, Jesus Christ still can.
And this is where the road becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us are not merely grieving what was taken from us.
