Because there may come a night when anger is burning again and you need to remember:
Cain had a moment before the field.
You do too.
Send it privately to the friend whose faith has become exhausted.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
Look at your own door.
Listen for the warning.
And look to Christ.
Because somewhere between the anger and the field, between temptation and consequence, between conviction and catastrophe…
there is still a moment when you can turn around.
Cain heard God before Abel’s blood touched the ground. Whatever God is warning you about today, do not wait until something precious is bleeding to finally listen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WHO CUT GOD’S WORD WITH A KNIFE AND BURNED IT
paragraphs: THE KING WHO CUT GOD’S WORD WITH A KNIFE AND BURNED IT
He thought destroying the scroll would silence the warning. Instead, God rewrote the words—and history remembered the man who tried to burn them.
There is something terrifying about watching a man hold the Word of God in his hands…
and reach for a knife.
Not because he misunderstood it.
Not because he could not read it.
Not because nobody had warned him.
But because he understood enough to know that he did not want to hear it.
His name was Jehoiakim.
He was king of Judah.
He had a palace, servants, authority, wealth, political power, and a throne inherited from a dynasty whose story stretched back to David.
But one winter day, while sitting comfortably beside a fire, this king was confronted by something more powerful than his throne.
The Word of God.
And when the Word began exposing what he did not want exposed, Jehoiakim did something almost unimaginable.
He took a knife to it.
Then he threw it into the fire.
And perhaps that is why his story is so uncomfortable.
Because most of us have never physically burned a Bible.
But some of us have become very skilled at cutting out the parts we do not want to obey.
Stay with this story.
Because before it is over, the knife in Jehoiakim’s hand may begin to look disturbingly familiar.
The account is found in Jeremiah 36.
Judah was living under the shadow of judgment. The nation had repeatedly rebelled against God, and Jeremiah had spent years proclaiming warnings that were anything but comfortable.
Then the LORD commanded Jeremiah to take a scroll and write upon it the words He had spoken concerning Israel, Judah, and the nations.
And God revealed something beautiful about the purpose behind the warning.
Jeremiah 36:3 records:
“Perhaps the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
That matters.
God was not warning them because He delighted in destruction.
The warning itself was mercy.
Behind the announcement of judgment stood an invitation to repentance.
Behind the frightening words stood the possibility of forgiveness.
In the Hebrew text, the heart of the invitation is:
וְיָשֻׁבוּ אִישׁ מִדַּרְכּוֹ הָרָעָה
veyashuvu ish middarko hara'ah
“…that each man may turn from his evil way…”
Then comes the breathtaking purpose:
וְסָלַחְתִּי לַעֲוֹנָם וּלְחַטָּאתָם
vesalachtî la'avonam ulechatatam
“…and I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
The Hebrew verb behind “turn,” שׁוּב — shuv, carries the basic idea of turning or returning.
That is the heartbeat of biblical repentance.
Turn.
Come back.
Stop running toward destruction.
Return to the God you abandoned.
And notice what waits on the other side.
Forgiveness.
The God who exposes sin is also the God who offers mercy to sinners who turn to Him.
So Jeremiah dictated the message to Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote the words upon a scroll.
Eventually that scroll reached the royal court.
Jehudi began reading it aloud before King Jehoiakim.
Picture the room.
It was winter.
The king was sitting in his winter apartment.
A fire burned before him.
The scroll was being read.
The words of God were entering the room sentence by sentence.
Then Jeremiah 36:23 tells us what happened:
“When Jehudi had read three or four columns, the king cut them off with a scribe’s knife and threw them into the fire in the brazier, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire.”
Three or four columns.
Slice.
Fire.
More words.
Slice.
Fire.
Again.
Again.
Again.
The image is almost unbearable.
God speaks.
The king cuts.
God warns.
The king burns.
God calls for repentance.
The king feeds the warning to the flames.
And Scripture records an even darker detail.
Jeremiah 36:24 says:
“Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.”
No trembling.
No mourning.
No repentance.
No brokenness.
The scroll burned…
and apparently the king felt safer when the words disappeared.
But destroying the page did not destroy the truth.
And that is where Jehoiakim’s story walks out of an ancient palace and directly into our lives.
Because you do not need a knife to cut the Bible.
You can do it quietly.
You can love:
“God is love.”
And cut:
“Repent.”
You can treasure:
“Judge not.”
While ignoring Christ’s command:
“Go, and sin no more.”
You can celebrate grace while resisting holiness.
You can sing about surrender while secretly protecting the one thing you refuse to surrender.
You can want Jesus as Savior while resisting Jesus as Lord.
And suddenly Jehoiakim’s knife does not feel quite so ancient anymore.
Sometimes our knife is preference.
Sometimes it is culture.
Sometimes it is politics.
Sometimes it is lust.
Sometimes it is bitterness.
Sometimes it is a relationship we know is pulling us away from Christ.
Sometimes it is money.
Sometimes it is pride.
Sometimes it is simply this:
“I know what Scripture says…
but I do not want God telling me what to do.”
That sentence can live inside a church pew.
It can sing worship songs.
It can quote Scripture.
It can even run a Christian social-media page.
Religious appearance has never been the same thing as surrender.
And this story becomes even more sobering when you compare Jehoiakim with his father, Josiah.
Years earlier, another book connected with God’s law had been read before King Josiah.
Josiah heard the words…
and tore his clothes.
Jehoiakim heard the words…
and tore the scroll.
One king allowed the Word to break him.
The other tried to break the Word.
That may be one of the most important spiritual questions you ever ask yourself:
When Scripture contradicts me, which one gets cut?
My desires?
Or God’s Word?
When Jesus confronts my pride, do I repent—or reinterpret?
When Scripture exposes my relationship, do I surrender—or search until I find someone willing to tell me what I want to hear?
When the Gospel exposes my secret sin, do I confess it—or defend it?
When Christ commands forgiveness, do I obey—or keep rehearsing why my bitterness is justified?
Because eventually every disciple reaches the place where Jesus says something the flesh does not want to hear.
And that moment reveals whether we merely admire Christ…
or actually follow Him.
Jehoiakim had another problem.
He apparently believed fire could accomplish what rebellion never can:
make God's Word disappear.
It could not.
After the scroll was burned, the LORD spoke again to Jeremiah.
Jeremiah 36:28 records:
“Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.”
Read that slowly.
Take another scroll.
The king had a knife.
God had another scroll.
The king had a fire.
God still had His Word.
Jehoiakim could destroy parchment.
He could not overthrow the One who spoke through His prophet.
Then Jeremiah 36:32 tells us Jeremiah took another scroll, Baruch wrote the words again, and:
“many similar words were added to them.”
What a reversal.
Jehoiakim tried subtraction.
God answered with addition.
The king tried to silence the message.
The message survived the king.
And centuries later, almost nobody remembers Jehoiakim because of the magnificence of his throne.
Millions remember him because Scripture records the day he tried to burn what God had spoken.
The fire went out.
The king died.
The Word remained.
But there is something deeper here than a warning about respecting the Bible.
This story points toward the desperate condition of the human heart.
Because humanity's deepest problem is not merely that we sometimes dislike particular commandments.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We do not merely need better habits.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need rescue.
We need a new heart.
And that is why the Bible does not end with Jeremiah's burning scroll.
The story keeps moving.
Through exile.
Through promises.
Through prophets.
Through generations waiting for redemption.
Until eventually the Word was not merely written on a scroll.
John opens his Gospel with words that still shake the soul:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος
En archē ēn ho Logos.
“In the beginning was the Word…”
Then John 1:14 declares:
Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Jesus Christ came.
Not merely another prophet.
Not merely another moral teacher.
The eternal Son entered human history.
And humanity did something even more horrifying than Jehoiakim did to the scroll.
We rejected Him.
Jehoiakim used a knife.
Human beings used nails.
Jehoiakim threw God's written warning into a fire.
Human beings nailed the incarnate Son of God to a cross.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And placed in a tomb.
For a moment, it looked as though sinful humanity had silenced Him too.
But you cannot bury the Author of life and expect the grave to keep Him.
Jesus rose.
That is the Gospel.
Not that good people finally learned to behave.
Not that broken people repaired themselves.
Not that sinners climbed high enough to reach God.
God came to us.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
The scandal of the cross became the place where grace was displayed.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come home.
The rebellious can repent.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The person who has spent years cutting God's commands out of his life can finally drop the knife.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe there is a verse you avoid because it gets too close.
Maybe there is a conviction you keep drowning beneath entertainment.
Maybe there is a secret browser history nobody knows about.
Maybe there is an affair hidden behind deleted messages.
Maybe there is bitterness you have carried so long that it feels like part of your personality.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are strong while you know your prayer life has almost disappeared.
Maybe you preach holiness publicly while negotiating with sin privately.
Maybe you still call yourself Christian, but if you are painfully truthful, Jesus has been standing outside rooms in your heart that you refuse to unlock.
And perhaps this article did not find you because you needed another inspirational Christian post.
Perhaps you needed the uncomfortable mercy of being confronted.
Remember Jeremiah 36.
The warning was not given because God had no interest in forgiving them.
The warning came so they might turn…
and God might forgive.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction calls you out of darkness.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide from Jesus until you become worthy.
You will never become worthy enough to purchase grace.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Confess what you have been defending.
Bring into the light what you have been hiding.
Stop cutting away every truth that hurts.
Sometimes the verse that wounds your pride is the very verse God uses to rescue your life.
And if you have fallen badly, remember our theme:
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
Not because repentance is optional.
Jesus Himself called sinners to repentance.
Not because grace gives us permission to continue worshiping our chains.
Paul rejected that distortion of grace.
Grace saves us and begins transforming us.
Your scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Your addiction does not have to write the ending.
Your adultery does not have to write the ending.
Your pornography does not have to write the ending.
Your pride does not have to write the ending.
Your bitterness does not have to write the ending.
Your religious hypocrisy does not have to write the ending.
Your years of running do not have to write the ending.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your past never happened…
but by redeeming sinners who could never redeem themselves.
What have you been cutting out?
What truth do you hope God will stop mentioning?
What command makes your hand reach for the knife?
What sin are you asking Jesus to tolerate instead of forgive and transform?
Do not burn the warning.
Receive the mercy hidden inside it.
Put down the knife.
Open the Word.
And surrender.
Be real.
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not judge them.
Pray for them.
We need fewer Christians pretending they have never struggled and more believers pointing struggling people toward Jesus.
It does not.
Not because giving money makes anyone more spiritual. It does not.
Salvation cannot be bought, and the Gospel must never be sold as though grace had a price tag.
Because Jehoiakim teaches us something we cannot afford to forget.
You can cut the page.
You can burn the scroll.
You can silence the preacher.
You can close the Bible.
You can unfollow the account.
You can drown conviction beneath another night of distraction.
But none of those things changes what God has spoken.
The fire eventually dies.
The knife eventually falls from the hand.
Kings eventually become dust.
But the Word of our God stands forever.
And perhaps the most beautiful possibility is this:
You do not have to become another Jehoiakim.
The hand holding the knife can open in surrender.
The heart resisting correction can break in repentance.
The sinner running from God can turn around.
And because Jesus Christ was crucified and risen for sinners, the story that looked destined to end in judgment can become a testimony of grace.
So put down the knife.
Jesus is still calling you home.
The king burned the scroll because he wanted the warning to disappear—but maybe God preserved the story because He never wanted you to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES PAUL SAY A WIFE HAS AUTHORITY OVER HER HUSBAND’S BODY TOO?
paragraphs: WHY DOES PAUL SAY A WIFE HAS AUTHORITY OVER HER HUSBAND’S BODY TOO?
The verse that sounds shocking until you notice what Paul did to male privilege—and how the Gospel turns marriage from possession into mutual self-giving love.
There is a sentence in the Bible that many husbands have heard quoted.
Far fewer have heard the other half.
And leaving out that other half can turn something beautiful into something dangerous.
Paul writes:
Some people stop there.
Conveniently.
But Paul does not.
He immediately turns the sentence around:
“Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
—1 Corinthians 7:4
Read that again.
The husband does not have authority over his own body.
The wife does.
For readers accustomed to hearing Christianity portrayed as though biblical marriage simply gives a husband power while requiring a wife to surrender hers, Paul’s actual words can be startling.
But the Greek is even more revealing.
Paul writes:
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.
A careful translation is:
“The wife does not exercise authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise also the husband does not exercise authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
That word translated “has authority” or “exercises authority” comes from ἐξουσιάζω (exousiazō), a verb connected with authority or having rights over something.
But perhaps the most important word for understanding Paul’s point is much smaller:
ὁμοίως.
Homoiōs.
“Likewise.”
“In the same way.”
Paul refuses to make the principle travel in only one direction.
Whatever responsibility he places upon the wife, he places reciprocally upon the husband.
And that matters enormously.
Because 1 Corinthians 7 is not a biblical permission slip for a husband to demand sexual access to his wife.
It is not divine authorization for coercion.
It is not Scripture telling a frightened spouse that “no” is rebellion against God.
It is certainly not permission for abuse.
Paul is describing the astonishing mutuality of the marriage covenant.
And to understand why, we need to hear what was happening before verse 4.

The Corinthian Christians had questions about sex, marriage, celibacy, and holiness. Some apparently regarded sexual abstinence—even within marriage—as spiritually desirable. Paul responds not by portraying marital intimacy as dirty, but by affirming the reciprocal responsibilities of husband and wife.
Listen to the symmetry:
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
—1 Corinthians 7:3
Again:
Likewise.
Then comes verse 4. Her body belongs covenantally to him—and his body belongs covenantally to her.
Then Paul continues:
“Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again…”
—1 Corinthians 7:5
And there is the detail that must never disappear from this conversation:
“by agreement.”
The Greek word is συμφώνου—related to symphōnos, meaning agreement or mutual consent.
It is the idea behind our word “symphony.”
Not one instrument crushing another.
Agreement.
Harmony.
Together.
Paul could hardly have constructed the paragraph more reciprocally.
The husband gives.
The wife gives.
The wife does not treat her body as though marriage has no claim upon her.
The husband does not treat his body as though marriage has no claim upon him.
Neither should deprive the other selfishly.
And periods of abstinence are approached by agreement.
Paul is not handing one spouse a weapon.
He is taking selfishness away from both.
That distinction changes everything.
Because sinful humanity hears “authority” and immediately asks:
“What can I demand?”
Jesus teaches us to ask:
“What can I give?”
That is the heartbeat of Christian marriage.
Not possession.
Self-giving.
Not domination.
Sacrificial love.
Not “Your body exists for my gratification.”
But:
“I am no longer living as though my desires are the only desires that matter.”
And husbands especially cannot separate 1 Corinthians 7 from the wider New Testament picture of Christlike love.
Paul tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25
Notice the direction of Christ’s love.
He gave Himself.
The model placed before the Christian husband is not a king sitting comfortably on a throne demanding service.
It is Jesus Christ laying Himself down.
A cross.
Sacrifice.
Tenderness.
Holiness.
Love willing to bleed for the good of another.
So imagine the tragedy when someone takes 1 Corinthians 7:4—a verse built around mutual self-giving—and uses it to justify selfish taking.
The text has been turned upside down.
A husband cannot faithfully say, “Your body belongs to me,” while conveniently forgetting that Paul says his body belongs to her too.
And neither spouse should turn Paul’s language into ammunition.
Marriage is not two people standing across the bedroom shouting biblical claims of ownership at one another.
It is two people learning, imperfectly, to say:
“I belong to Christ, and because I have covenanted myself to you, I will not live as though only my comfort, appetite, schedule, fear, exhaustion, pleasure, or preference matters.”
That does not eliminate bodily dignity.
It deepens covenant responsibility.
There may be illness.
Pain.
Trauma.
Pregnancy.
Postpartum recovery.
Medication.
Disability.
Hormonal changes.
Emotional wounds.
Exhaustion.
A spouse may need patience, safety, conversation, medical care, counseling, repentance, restoration, or simply tenderness.
Biblical love does not bulldoze those realities with a verse.
Love listens.
Love does not dishonor.
Love “does not insist on its own way” (1 Corinthians 13:5).
That sentence alone should make us tremble before using Scripture selfishly.
Because the same apostle who writes that spouses have marital claims upon one another’s bodies also writes that love does not insist upon its own way.
There is no contradiction.
There is covenant.
There is the difference between demanding and giving.
Between entitlement and devotion.
Between using another person and becoming one flesh with another person.
And perhaps this passage is exposing something much deeper than what happens in a bedroom.
Maybe the uncomfortable question is not:
“Does my spouse owe me?”
Maybe it is:
“How much of myself am I still refusing to surrender?”
Because selfishness rarely stays in one room.
It appears when you stop listening.
When affection becomes conditional.
When resentment becomes punishment.
When silence becomes a weapon.
When pornography secretly rewrites your expectations.
When flirtation outside the marriage begins feeding an appetite you promised to guard.
When a husband expects tenderness he refuses to give.
When a wife uses distance to punish rather than communicate.
When either spouse begins keeping an invisible ledger:
I did this.
So you owe me that.
Then marriage slowly stops looking like covenant and starts looking like commerce.
And Jesus did not save us so that we could become expert accountants of what other people owe us.
The Gospel destroys the illusion that love is merely a transaction.
At the cross, Christ does not merely tell sinners to love.
He shows us what holy love costs.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
There is the center.
Jesus.
Not sex.
Not marital power.
Not winning an argument.
Jesus.
Because even the healthiest Christian marriage is not the Gospel.
Marriage points beyond itself to something greater.
Christ and His people.
A Savior who pursues sinners not to exploit them but to redeem them.
A Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
A Lord whose authority is perfectly holy and whose sacrifice reaches all the way to Calvary.
And suddenly Paul's words become more uncomfortable in the right way.
The question is no longer:
“How much authority do I have over my spouse?”
The question becomes:
“Has Jesus transformed the way I use whatever power, strength, influence, sexuality, affection, and freedom I possess?”
That question can expose a marriage.
It can expose a husband who knows Bible verses but has forgotten tenderness.
It can expose a wife carrying years of resentment she has never brought honestly into the light.
It can expose hidden pornography.
Secret messages.
Emotional affairs.
Manipulation.
Bitterness.
Coldness.
Shame.
Fear.
Past wounds.
It can expose two people sleeping inches apart while their souls feel miles away.
Maybe nobody knows.
Sunday comes.
You dress nicely.
You smile.
You sit beside each other.
Someone asks how the family is doing.
“Good.”
But God knows what “good” is hiding.
He sees the silence on the drive home.
He sees the screen you quickly close.
He sees the nights one of you quietly cries.
He sees the rejection that became bitterness and the bitterness that became distance.
He sees the apologies that never came.
He sees the words you wish you could take back.
He sees the loneliness nobody at church notices.
And He does not expose darkness because He delights in humiliating you.
He calls darkness into the light because Jesus came to save sinners.
That is where scandal can become grace.
Not when we pretend the scandal never happened.
When we bring it to Christ.
Christian repentance is not saying, “Nobody is perfect.”
It is saying:
“Lord, this is sin. I have no excuse. Forgive me. Change me.”
Grace is not God pretending our sin does not matter.
Grace cost the blood of Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, Christ bore sin so sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed.
That means the controlling husband can repent.
The bitter wife can repent.
The pornography-addicted spouse can repent.
The emotionally absent spouse can repent.
The person who weaponized Scripture can repent.
The person who withheld affection to punish can repent.
The person carrying shame from what was done to them can discover that another person's sin does not place them beyond Christ's compassion.

And where there has been abuse or coercion, repentance must never be reduced to religious language that pressures the harmed spouse into immediate trust or unsafe reconciliation. Serious wrongdoing requires truth, accountability, protection, and appropriate pastoral, professional, and when necessary legal help. Forgiveness does not require pretending danger is safe.
Jesus does not need us to hide evil in order to protect Christianity.
He is the Light.
Bring it into the light.
That may be the word someone reading this has avoided for years.
Light.
No more hiding.
No more performing.
No more carefully edited Christianity.
Maybe your marriage needs a conversation tonight.
Maybe you need to say:
“I have been selfish.”
“I have not listened to you.”
“I used Scripture to win instead of allowing Scripture to change me.”
“I have made you feel unwanted.”
“I have made you feel unsafe.”
“I have been hiding something.”
“I need help.”
“I was wrong.”
“Will you forgive me?”
Those sentences can feel terrifying.
But sometimes resurrection begins where pretending finally dies.
Not because strangers need the details of your private life.
They do not.
But sometimes three words become a line in the sand between the person who keeps pretending and the person who finally admits:
Jesus, I need You to change me.
Let believers pray without demanding your private story.
Someone else may desperately need to know that restoration is possible.
Not as a performance.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But if Christ has given you truth that may rescue another person from distortion, shame, selfishness, or despair, sharing that truth can become an act of love.
“Is this really what the Bible teaches?”
Someone may have had Scripture weaponized against them.
Someone may be destroying a marriage through selfishness while calling it biblical authority.
Someone may believe what they have done is too ugly for Jesus to forgive.
Let this reach them.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too.
Supporting Gospel Warrior should never be confused with earning God's favor. You cannot purchase grace, and God is not glorified by manipulation.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not miss Paul’s point.
He was never teaching husbands how to take more.
He was teaching husbands and wives that covenant love means selfishness no longer gets the final word.
Your spouse is not an object.
Not an entitlement.
Not a reward.
Not a servant assigned to satisfy your desires.
They are a person made in the image of God.
And Christian marriage calls two redeemed sinners to learn something the flesh desperately resists:
mutual self-giving love.
You will fail at it sometimes.
So will your spouse.
There will be misunderstandings.
There may be tears.
There may be seasons when intimacy feels effortless and seasons when loving one another requires extraordinary patience.
But Christ remains.
And where sin has written chapters of selfishness, shame, betrayal, resentment, or broken trust, Jesus is still able to write repentance.
Forgiveness.
Truth.
Holiness.
Healing.
Grace.
Maybe that is why this difficult verse is more beautiful than we realized.
Paul did not merely tell a wife:
“You are not your own.”
He looked at the husband and said:
Neither are you.
Likewise.
ὁμοίως.
One small Greek word.
One devastating blow to selfish entitlement.
One reminder that beneath the cross, Christian marriage cannot faithfully become a kingdom where one sinner exists for the comfort of another.
Both belong first to Christ.
Both are called to love.
Both are called away from selfishness.
Both need grace.
And both must remember that the Savior at the center of their covenant did not conquer His bride by exploiting her.
He loved her.
He gave Himself for her.
He died.
And He rose again.
So before you ask what your spouse owes you, stand beneath the cross long enough to remember what Jesus gave for you.
Because sometimes the marriage Jesus begins restoring is the one where two people finally stop asking, “What am I owed?” and kneel before Christ asking, “Lord, what in me still needs to die?”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JEZEBEL PAINTED HER EYES, FIXED HER HAIR, AND WAITED AT THE WINDOW
paragraphs: JEZEBEL PAINTED HER EYES, FIXED HER HAIR, AND WAITED AT THE WINDOW

She knew judgment was coming. Yet instead of humbling herself before God, she prepared her appearance. The terrifying question is not what Jezebel did at that window—but how many of us are still decorating what Jesus is calling us to surrender.
There is something haunting about a woman fixing her appearance while judgment is approaching the city.
Not because makeup is sinful.
It isn't.
Not because fixing your hair is evil.
It isn't.
And not because Scripture gives us permission to turn every woman wearing cosmetics into some modern caricature of “Jezebel.”
It doesn't.
The horror of 2 Kings 9:30 is much deeper than cosmetics.
Jezebel had heard.
That is where the verse becomes frightening.
She knew something was happening.
Jehu was coming.
Her son Joram was dead.
The dynasty around which she had built her power was collapsing.
And the judgment God had spoken years earlier through Elijah was moving toward its fulfillment.
Then Scripture gives us this unforgettable picture:
“Now when Jehu arrived in Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it. So she painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.”
—2 Kings 9:30
The Hebrew is even more visually striking:
וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ וַתֵּיטֶב אֶת־רֹאשָׁהּ וַתַּשְׁקֵף בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן
Vattasem bappukh eineha, vatteitev et-roshah, vattashqef be'ad hachallon.
Literally, the language describes Jezebel putting her eyes “in” or “with” paint, beautifying or adorning her head, and looking down through the window.
Pause there.
Because Scripture does not explicitly tell us exactly what was going through Jezebel's mind.

Some interpreters have understood her appearance as an attempt at seduction or manipulation. Others have seen the actions as royal defiance—a queen determined to face death looking like a queen. The biblical writer does not settle that question for us.
So we shouldn't pretend he does.
But Scripture makes something else unmistakably clear.
Jezebel heard.
And still there is no recorded repentance.
No tearing of garments.
No ashes.
No confession.
No cry for mercy.
No turning from Baal.
No acknowledgment of the LORD she had opposed.
She heard judgment approaching...
and prepared herself to meet Jehu.
That should disturb us.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition isn't ignorance.
It's hearing God...
and refusing to bow.
You can know the sermon was for you and still scroll to the next video.
You can feel conviction during worship and still return to the same secret sin.
You can know you need to apologize and still protect your pride.
You can know the relationship is pulling you away from Christ and still call it love.
You can know bitterness is poisoning your heart and still rehearse what they did to you every night.
You can know your private life is contradicting your public Christianity and still learn how to look spiritual enough that nobody notices.
You can hear.
And still paint the eyes.
You can hear.
And still fix the hair.
You can hear.
And still stand at the window as though everything is under control.
That is what makes this story more than ancient history.
There is a little window in every human heart where image and truth eventually meet.
And some of us have become frighteningly good at standing there.
The church clothes look right.
The Bible verse gets posted.
The worship song plays in the car.
“God is good” rolls easily from the mouth.
Everybody thinks you're strong.
But behind the window...
you're exhausted.
You're hiding something.
You're angry with God.
You're addicted.
You're carrying unforgiveness.
You're flirting with compromise.
You're secretly jealous.
You're spiritually numb.
You're performing Christianity while privately starving for Christ.
And perhaps nobody knows.
But Jesus does.
That isn't written to crush you.
It is written because being exposed by Christ can become the beginning of being healed by Christ.
Jezebel's story did not begin at the window.

Long before 2 Kings 9, Scripture introduces her as the Sidonian princess who became the wife of Ahab. First Kings 16 says Ahab served Baal and worshiped him. Jezebel became deeply associated with the promotion of Baal worship in Israel. First Kings 18 tells us that prophets of the LORD were being killed and that Jezebel supported hundreds of prophets of Baal and Asherah.
Then came Naboth.
And this is where the story becomes painfully human.
Naboth owned a vineyard beside Ahab's palace.
Ahab wanted it.
Naboth refused because the land was his ancestral inheritance.
Ahab went home resentful.
Jezebel stepped in.
Letters were written in Ahab's name.
False witnesses were arranged.
Naboth was accused.
Naboth was killed.
Then Jezebel essentially told Ahab:
Get up.
Take the vineyard.
The man who wouldn't sell it to you is dead.
Imagine that.
A man dies because powerful people wanted what belonged to him.
A family loses someone.
Blood enters the soil.
And the palace gets its vineyard.
But heaven saw the transaction.
God sent Elijah.
Judgment was pronounced against Ahab's house, and concerning Jezebel came the dreadful prophecy that dogs would devour her in Jezreel.
Years passed.
That matters.
Because delayed judgment can deceive a rebellious heart into believing judgment has disappeared.
Nothing happened today.
So perhaps God didn't see.
Nothing happened this month.
Perhaps God doesn't care.
You sinned and woke up the next morning.
The sun still rose.
Your job remained.
People still respected you.
Your ministry continued.
Your secret stayed secret.
So slowly, dangerously, mercy begins to feel like permission.
But Scripture says God's patience has a purpose.
Romans 2:4 asks whether we presume upon the riches of His kindness, not realizing that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
Mercy is not God's approval of your rebellion.
Mercy is God giving the rebel time to come home.
And that changes how we should read Jezebel at the window.
The tragedy is not merely that judgment finally arrived.
The tragedy is all the opportunities to turn before it did.
How many warnings had passed through her world?
How many demonstrations of God's power?
How many moments in which pride could have broken?
How many opportunities to recognize that Baal was not God?
Yet when the final scene arrives, Scripture records no repentance.
Just a woman at a window.
Painted eyes.
An adorned head.
And footsteps approaching.
There are moments when the Bible stops feeling like something you are reading...
and starts reading you.
Maybe this is one of them.
What are you decorating that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What are you managing instead of confessing?
What are you explaining instead of repenting of?
What are you keeping alive because admitting the truth would cost you your image?
Maybe your “painted eyes” aren't cosmetics.
Maybe they're success.
Maybe they're ministry.
Maybe they're humor.
Maybe they're theological knowledge.
Maybe they're money.
Maybe they're busyness.
Maybe they're the carefully edited version of your life everyone else gets to see.
Anything can become camouflage when the heart learns to hide behind it.
And Jesus has never been interested merely in improving camouflage.
He came to resurrect dead people.
That is where Jezebel's window eventually points us beyond Jezebel.
Because if this article ended with Jezebel's death, we could walk away saying, “What a terrible woman.”
And miss ourselves completely.
The Bible will not allow that.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23 does not say some.
All.
Jezebel needed mercy.
Ahab needed mercy.
Jehu needed mercy.
You need mercy.
I need mercy.
The religious person needs mercy.
The addict needs mercy.
The pastor needs mercy.
The prostitute needs mercy.
The person reading Scripture every morning needs mercy.
The person who hasn't opened a Bible in twenty years needs mercy.
Different scandals.
Same disease.
Sin.
And there is only one Savior.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the window at Jezreel eventually gives way to a hill outside Jerusalem.
Because the Gospel does not announce that good people managed to make themselves presentable enough for God.
The Gospel announces that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus did not wait for you to fix yourself.
He came for sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with tax collectors.
He received the disgraced.
He confronted hypocrites.
He forgave the repentant.
He welcomed the broken.
And then He carried a cross.
At Calvary, Jesus wasn't covering sin with religious cosmetics.
He was paying for it.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the Servant who would be pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities.
At the cross, the holy Son of God bore sin's judgment.
Then He was buried.
And on the third day...
the tomb was empty.
This is Christianity.
Not behavior modification.
Not image management.
Not “try harder.”
Not “look religious.”
Christ crucified.
Christ buried.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ calling sinners to repent and believe.
And that means your story does not have to end at the window.
Read that again.
Your story does not have to end at the window.
You may have betrayed someone.
You may have destroyed trust.
You may have wasted years.
You may have slept with someone you shouldn't have.
You may have watched things you would be terrified for your family to discover.
You may have lied.
You may have cheated.
You may have become addicted.
You may have walked away from God.
You may have mocked Christianity.
You may have used religion to hide a heart far from Jesus.
You may have built such a convincing exterior that everyone thinks you're fine.
But while there is breath in your lungs, the call of the Gospel is not:
“Fix your hair.”
It is:
Come to Christ.
Stop painting over what needs forgiveness.
Stop defending what Jesus died to deliver you from.
Stop hiding wounds He already sees.
Stop confusing shame with repentance.
Repentance does not mean making yourself worthy enough for Jesus.
You cannot.
Repentance means turning from sin toward the Savior who is worthy.
Bring Him the real thing.
The ugly thing.
The embarrassing thing.
The thing you keep deleting from your browser history.
The resentment you've justified for eleven years.
The affair nobody knows about.
The pride hidden beneath ministry.
The secret drinking.
The greed.
The envy.
The double life.
The cold marriage.
The unbelief.
The exhaustion.
The anger.
Bring Him you.
Because grace is not God pretending your sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves that sin matters terribly.
Grace is God doing in Christ what you could never do for yourself.
And this is why “From Scandal to Grace” is more than a phrase.
It is the heartbeat of redemption.
Peter denied Jesus and became a preacher of the risen Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians and became an apostle proclaiming the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward Christ and heard words of paradise.
Again and again Scripture shows us that God is capable of entering ruined stories.
Not approving the ruin.
Redeeming the sinner.
That distinction matters.
Grace doesn't call evil good.
Grace takes guilty people and, through Christ, makes forgiveness possible.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the first chapters never happened...
but by refusing to let sin have the final word over everyone who comes to Him.
So I want to ask you something more personal than whether you enjoyed this article.
What is happening behind your window?
Not your spouse's.
Not your pastor's.
Not the politician you hate.
Not the celebrity whose scandal everybody is discussing.
Yours.
What would happen if Jesus stripped away every filter tonight?
Would He find surrender...
or performance?
Would He find repentance...
or excuses?
Would He find someone fighting sin...
or someone learning to live comfortably beside it?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess it.
Ask for mercy.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer reads at 2:13 in the morning and realizes, “I'm not the only one fighting.”
And please don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.
But if you genuinely want your digital life to glorify God, one practical way to do that is to help put biblical truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door.
Even send it privately to the person you know would never respond publicly.
There may come a night when the person who needs to read it again is you.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not replace supporting your local church, caring for your family, giving to people in need, or obeying however God directs your stewardship.
But it can be a practical way of standing behind work you believe is helping proclaim Christ.
Not as an algorithm trick.
As mission.
Someone may be fixing the outside while their soul is begging for rescue.
Someone may believe they've sinned too badly to come home.
Someone may need to discover tonight that Christianity isn't the story of sinners successfully hiding their stains.
It is the story of a Savior whose blood washes sinners clean.
Jezebel heard judgment approaching and stood at her window.
But you are still reading.
You are still breathing.
And right now, through the Gospel, mercy is still calling.
Don't paint over what Jesus is asking you to bring into the light.
Don't decorate the prison when Christ is offering freedom.
Don't spend another year protecting an image while your soul starves behind it.
Come to Jesus.
The window does not have to be the final scene.
Because the most beautiful thing about grace is that Jesus can meet you in the chapter you are ashamed of—and make sure it isn't the chapter that gets the last word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re Waiting to Feel Sorry Enough Before You Come Back to God
paragraphs: You’re Waiting to Feel Sorry Enough Before You Come Back to God
You keep thinking you need to hurt a little longer before God will let you come home. But Jesus told a story about a Father who started running while His filthy, ashamed son was still on the road.
There is a strange punishment some Christians give themselves that God never asked them to carry.
They sin.
They know they sinned.
Conviction comes.
And somewhere between conviction and repentance, shame whispers something that sounds almost holy:
Not yet.
You cannot pray yet.
You cannot worship yet.
You cannot open your Bible yet.
You cannot lift your hands yet.
You cannot call yourself close to God yet.
You need to feel worse first.
You need to prove that you really regret it.
Maybe after several miserable days...
Maybe after enough tears...
Maybe after you have punished yourself emotionally...
Maybe after you have finally become disgusted enough with what you did...
then you can come back.
And because shame can disguise itself as humility, you believe it.
So you stay away from the very Father you need most.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
You have opened your Bible and felt like a hypocrite.
You have tried to pray and heard the memory of what you did louder than your own words.
You have watched other believers worship while thinking, If they knew what I did...
You have promised God things before.
You have cried before.
You have repented before.
And somehow you ended up here again.
Same temptation.
Same secret.
Same collapse.
Same sick feeling afterward.
So this time you decide you are not going to run immediately to grace.
That would feel too easy.
You think you should suffer first.
But what if the delay you are calling repentance is actually shame keeping you away from repentance?
Because biblical repentance is not convincing God to take you back.
It is turning back to the God who calls sinners to Himself.
Jesus painted this truth with devastating beauty in Luke 15.
A younger son demanded his inheritance from his father and left home. He traveled into a distant country and squandered what he had in reckless living.
Eventually everything collapsed.
The money disappeared.
A famine came.
The friends apparently disappeared with the money.
And the son who once had a place at his father's table found himself feeding pigs.
For Jesus' Jewish audience, that detail would have made the degradation especially vivid. Pigs were unclean animals under the Mosaic law.
Then Jesus gives us one of the great turning points in the parable.
Luke 15:17 begins:
“εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν...”
Eis heauton de elthōn...
Literally, the expression carries the sense of “coming to himself.”
Something broke through the madness.
The son saw where his rebellion had taken him.
He remembered his father.
He remembered home.
He decided to rise and return.
Listen carefully, because this is where many wounded believers misunderstand repentance.
The son did not sit beside the pigs waiting until he could manufacture a sufficient quantity of shame.
He got up.
That matters.
Luke 15:18 records his decision:
“ἀναστὰς πορεύσομαι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα μου...”
Anastas poreusomai pros ton patera mou...
“I will arise and go to my father.”
That is the movement shame desperately wants to prevent.
I will arise.
I will go.
Not because the far country did not matter.
Not because rebellion was harmless.
Not because sin suddenly stopped being sin.
He knew he had sinned.
He planned to confess it plainly:
“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.”
There is no excuse there.
No blame-shifting.
No pretending.
No theological vocabulary designed to make rebellion sound respectable.
He calls sin what it is.
This is not cheap grace.
This is confession.
This is repentance.
This is a sinner turning toward home.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of the story is what happens before the son can finish the speech he has rehearsed.
Jesus says:
“ἔτι δὲ αὐτοῦ μακρὰν ἀπέχοντος...”
Eti de autou makran apechontos...
“While he was still a long way off...”
His father saw him.
Please do not hurry past that.
He was still far away.
Still carrying the evidence of the far country.
Still returning from the pigs.
Still carrying his confession.
Still unable to repair everything he had destroyed.
And his father saw him.
Jesus says the father was moved with compassion.
The Greek word is powerful:
“ἐσπλαγχνίσθη”
esplanchnisthē.
It describes deep, inward compassion—a mercy felt profoundly within.
Then the father ran.
He ran toward the son.
Embraced him.
Kissed him.
And suddenly the speech the son had practiced collided with a mercy larger than the shame he had carried home.
The son confessed:
“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.”
Notice something extraordinary.
Earlier, while rehearsing what he would say, the son planned to add:
“Make me like one of your hired servants.”
But in Jesus' telling, once the father reaches him, the recorded confession stops before that proposed bargain is completed.
Then the father starts giving orders.
Not instructions for punishment.
Instructions for restoration.
Bring the best robe.
Put a ring on his hand.
Put shoes on his feet.
Prepare the feast.
Celebrate.
Why?
“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”
Do you see what Jesus is exposing?
The son came home knowing he was unworthy.
The father did not disagree by pretending the rebellion never happened.
Instead, the father's compassion answered the returning sinner with restoration.
This does not mean every earthly consequence of sin magically disappears.

Scripture never promises that repentance eliminates every temporal consequence. Forgiveness does not always restore lost money, repair every damaged relationship overnight, erase legal consequences, or instantly rebuild broken trust.
Grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Grace is God's mercy meeting guilty people who turn to Him.
And this is where the Gospel becomes even greater than the parable.
Because our forgiveness is not based upon God simply deciding that sin does not matter.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine.
He died for sinners.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).
And Romans 5:8 goes further:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we cleaned ourselves.
Not after we generated enough shame.
Not after we became emotionally impressive penitents.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is why repentance can never mean purchasing God's mercy with emotional suffering.
You cannot buy with tears what Jesus purchased with His blood.
Tears may accompany repentance.
Grief may accompany repentance.
In fact, Scripture speaks about godly grief producing repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10).
But grief is not currency.
Feeling terrible enough does not make the cross finally become effective.
Jesus Christ is sufficient.
That is why 1 John 1:9 does not say, “If we punish ourselves long enough...”
It says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Maybe those words are difficult for you to receive because you have confused self-hatred with holiness.
You think beating yourself emotionally proves that you take sin seriously.
But there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says:
This is sin. Bring it into the light. Turn from it. Come to Christ.
Shame says:
You are disgusting. Hide. Stay away until you deserve to return.
One leads toward God.
The other drives you deeper into the far country.
And some of you have been living spiritually beside the pigs because you think staying miserable honors the Father more than getting up and going home.
It does not.
Your shame is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
Read that again.
Your shame is not your Savior. Jesus is.
Maybe you fell sexually.
Maybe pornography has become the secret you keep promising God you will defeat.
Maybe bitterness has been eating your heart alive.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe your marriage is carrying wounds you helped create.
Maybe you betrayed someone's trust.
Maybe alcohol, drugs, gambling, greed, envy, anger, pride, or another bondage has pulled you farther than you ever imagined you would go.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe the scandal is public.
Maybe the scandal lives only between you, God, and the browser history you keep deleting.
Maybe you have become incredibly skilled at looking spiritually alive while quietly starving inside.
And every time God draws your heart toward repentance, another voice tells you:
You have done this too many times.
God must be tired of you.
You need to prove yourself first.
Stay away.
But hear Jesus' words.
The son arose.
The son went to his father.
You do not repent by running away from God until you become worthy of God.
You repent by turning from sin and returning to God because you know you are not worthy—and trusting His mercy.
That does not minimize sin.
It destroys the illusion that you can save yourself from it.
Real repentance is not saying, “What I did doesn't matter.”
Real repentance says, “What I did matters so much that I will stop defending it, stop hiding it, confess it, turn from it, and throw myself upon the mercy of God in Jesus Christ.”
That is a completely different posture.
And if your sin involves another person, repentance may require more than private tears.
You may need to tell the truth.
You may need to apologize without excuses.
You may need to make restitution where possible.
You may need accountability.
You may need to cut off access to whatever keeps pulling you back.
You may need pastoral help.
You may need to rebuild trust slowly instead of demanding that someone trust you immediately because you said sorry.
Grace does not make repentance shallow.
Grace makes repentance possible.
Because now you are no longer crawling toward God trying to negotiate the price of admission.
Christ has already paid what you could never pay.
The cross leaves no room for boasting.
And it leaves no room for despairing as though your sin were somehow more powerful than the blood of Christ.
This is the scandal of grace.
The guilty are invited home.
The unclean can be washed.
The lost can be found.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The prodigal does not rewrite his own ending.
The Father receives him.
And ultimately, the Gospel tells us that God accomplished our redemption through His Son.
Jesus Christ took the place of sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith discovers that grace is not God's reluctant tolerance of sinners who finally became impressive enough.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward people who could never rescue themselves.
So what are you waiting for?
Another night of hating yourself?
Another week avoiding prayer?
Another Sunday standing in worship while believing everyone else is allowed near Jesus except you?
How much shame would finally be enough?
Ten tears?
A hundred?
A thousand?
How many sleepless nights would purchase forgiveness?
How many days of self-loathing would equal one drop of the blood shed at Calvary?
None.
You cannot punish yourself into being forgiven.
And you do not need to crucify yourself beside Jesus as though His sacrifice needs your suffering added to it.
Repent.
Turn.
Come home.
Not tomorrow when you feel spiritual.
Now.
Confess what needs confessing.
Abandon what needs abandoning.
Repair what can be repaired.
Ask for help where you need help.
And put your confidence not in the intensity of your remorse but in the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But maybe you need to stop pretending you are okay.
Your testimony might become the sentence another wounded believer needs to read tonight.
Someone on your Facebook feed may be silently convinced that they have to become worthy before God will receive them.
They may never tell you.
They may still attend church.
They may still post Bible verses.
They may still smile in photographs.
But inside, they are standing a long way from home.
There may come a night when your own heart needs these words again.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. The Gospel is too precious to keep inside the walls of people who already know it.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus. It does not.
And not because God needs a transaction from you before He will bless or forgive you.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Come to Christ.
Because someday the shirts will fade.
The mugs will break.
The books will gather dust.
Facebook itself will eventually become another forgotten chapter of human technology.
But Jesus Christ remains.
And perhaps tonight, after all your running, all your hiding, all your rehearsed speeches about why you are no longer worthy...
you finally need to hear the sound Jesus placed in this story.
Footsteps.
Not yours.
The Father's.
Running toward the repentant son while he was still a long way off.
You thought you needed enough shame to begin the journey.
But shame was never the road home.
Repentance turns around. Grace meets you on the road. And Jesus is the reason home is possible.
Because maybe the most dangerous lie shame ever told you was not that you sinned.
You did.
It was that because you sinned, you should stay away from the only One who can bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY JONATHAN ATE THE HONEY WHEN AN ENTIRE ARMY WAS FASTING
paragraphs:
WHY JONATHAN ATE THE HONEY WHEN AN ENTIRE ARMY WAS FASTING
One Taste Opened His Eyes—and Exposed Something Terrifying About the Kind of Religion That Can Exhaust People While God Is Trying to Give Them Victory
There was honey on the ground.
Imagine that scene.
Thousands of exhausted men. Weapons in their hands. Dust on their faces. Adrenaline draining from their bodies. Stomachs empty. Legs weakening.
And honey was right in front of them.
Not hidden.
Not locked away.
Not across enemy lines.
Right there.
Yet no one touched it.
Men who were brave enough to charge armed Philistines were afraid to put food into their mouths.
Then Jonathan walked into the forest.
He saw the honey.
He extended his staff.
He dipped its end into the honey.
He tasted it.
And something happened that Scripture describes with a remarkably vivid Hebrew expression:
"וַתָּאֹרְנָה עֵינָיו"
vatta'ornah einav.
“And his eyes brightened.”
—1 Samuel 14:27
That tiny moment raises an enormous question.
Why was Jonathan eating when the entire army was fasting?
Was he rebellious?
Was he disrespecting authority?
Was this some mysterious biblical endorsement of breaking a fast?
No.
And if we rip this scene away from its context, we can make it say things God never said.
Jonathan was not secretly sneaking food because he disagreed with his father.
Scripture explicitly tells us:
"וְיוֹנָתָן לֹא־שָׁמַע בְּהַשְׁבִּיעַ אָבִיו אֶת־הָעָם"
VeYonatan lo-shama behashbia aviv et-ha'am.
“Jonathan had not heard when his father made the people swear.”
—1 Samuel 14:27
Jonathan ate because he did not know about Saul's oath.
That detail matters.
But what happened after he ate reveals something even deeper.
Because this story is not primarily about honey.
It is about what happens when human zeal begins masquerading as spiritual wisdom.
It is about leadership that can sound religious while crushing the people underneath it.
And eventually, it points us toward our desperate need for a better King.
Go backward a few verses.
Before Saul ever commanded the army not to eat, Jonathan had already done something astonishing.
Israel was facing the Philistines.
Jonathan looked at his armor-bearer and essentially said: Let's go.
Two men.
Against an enemy outpost.
His confidence was not in numbers.
Listen carefully to his theology:
"כִּי אֵין לַיהוָה מַעְצוֹר לְהוֹשִׁיעַ בְּרַב אוֹ בִמְעָט"
“For nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.”
—1 Samuel 14:6
There is Jonathan.
Then there is Saul.
Jonathan moves because God is powerful.
Saul imposes an oath because Saul wants revenge.
That difference is easy to miss.
Saul said:
“Cursed be the man who eats food until evening, before I have avenged myself on my enemies.”
Notice the language.
“My enemies.”
“My revenge.”
The battle belonged to the LORD, but Saul's language was becoming painfully centered on Saul.
And while Saul was trying to intensify Israel's pursuit through an oath, the result was the opposite.
The soldiers became weak.
The Hebrew text later describes them as:
"וַיָּעַף הָעָם מְאֹד"
Vayya'af ha'am me'od.
The people were exceedingly faint, exhausted, famished.
The king demanded more.
The soldiers had less strength to give.
Then Jonathan tasted a little honey.
His eyes brightened.
Suddenly he understood what the exhausted army could not say.
“My father has troubled the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.”
Then Jonathan makes the painfully practical observation that if the soldiers had been permitted to eat from the enemy's spoil, Israel's victory could have been even greater.
Think about that.
Saul's command was apparently intended to strengthen the pursuit.
Instead, it weakened the pursuers.
And then things became worse.
The starving soldiers eventually became so ravenous that they rushed upon the spoil and ate meat improperly with the blood, violating God's command.
Do not miss the irony.
A man-made restriction intended to intensify religious commitment helped create circumstances in which exhausted people rushed into actual disobedience.
That does not mean biblical fasting is wrong.
Far from it.
Scripture presents genuine fasting as a meaningful expression of humility, repentance, mourning, prayer, and seeking God.
Jesus Himself fasted.
Jesus taught about fasting.
The early church fasted.
The problem in 1 Samuel 14 was not simply “fasting.”
This was Saul's oath imposed upon soldiers in the middle of battle, under threat of a curse, tied explicitly to Saul's desire for vengeance before evening.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because sometimes people read this story and conclude:
“Jonathan teaches us to break religious rules.”
No.
That is not what happened.
Jonathan had not heard the oath.
And there is another dangerous interpretation we should reject.
The honey was not some magical substance that spiritually enlightened Jonathan.
The phrase “his eyes brightened” describes the reviving effect of nourishment on an exhausted man.
Jonathan ate.
His strength returned.
His condition visibly changed.
But there is something haunting about the image nevertheless.
An entire army walked past provision because they were terrified of a curse spoken by their king.
Jonathan tasted what they feared to touch...
and his eyes brightened.
Maybe that image feels uncomfortably familiar.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to become exhausted in the name of religion.
You prayed.
Served.
Gave.
Volunteered.
Stayed quiet.
Tried harder.
Smiled at church.
Quoted Scripture.
Told everyone you were blessed.
But somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary, you became spiritually exhausted.
Not because Jesus was cruel.
Not because God's Word failed.
But because somewhere along the road, human expectations became tangled together with God's commands.
And eventually you could no longer tell the difference.
Someone told you that being tired meant you lacked faith.
Someone made their personal conviction sound like God's universal command.
Someone used fear where Scripture offered grace.
Someone demanded performance but rarely spoke of the finished work of Christ.
Maybe that person was a leader.
Maybe it was your family.
Maybe it was an entire religious culture.
Or maybe...
it was you.
Maybe the harshest Saul in your life has sometimes been the voice inside your own head.
“Do more.”
“God must be disappointed.”
“Try harder.”
“You haven't prayed enough.”
“You haven't sacrificed enough.”
“You aren't spiritual enough.”
“You failed again.”
And slowly Christianity stops feeling like knowing Christ and starts feeling like desperately trying to convince Christ not to reject you.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say, “Exhaust yourself until God finally loves you.”
The Gospel says God loved sinners so profoundly that He gave His Son.
The Gospel does not say, “Perform well enough and perhaps your debt will disappear.”
Jesus said from the cross:
“Τετέλεσται.”
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
—John 19:30
Finished.
Not “almost finished if you can complete the rest.”
Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
This is where Jonathan's story must ultimately drive the Christian heart—not toward Jonathan as our savior, but toward Jesus Christ as the King Jonathan could never be and Saul tragically was not.
Because Scripture gives us another King.
Saul burdened exhausted men for the sake of his victory.
Jesus carried the burden Himself for the sake of His people.
Saul pronounced a curse that endangered his own son.
Christ willingly bore the curse to rescue His enemies.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
—Galatians 3:13
Saul was prepared to let his son die because of a rash oath.
The Father gave His Son according to His eternal saving purpose so sinners could live.
That difference is everything.
Jesus does not lower God's holiness.
He fulfills righteousness.
Jesus does not pretend sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves how terribly sin matters.
Grace is not God shrugging at your rebellion.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty sinners could never provide for themselves.
And that means repentance is not an enemy of grace.
Repentance runs toward grace.
You don't repent so Jesus will become merciful.
You repent because the crucified and risen Jesus is the only refuge sinners have.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness you've learned to justify.
An affair happening mostly through messages—but you know where your heart has gone.
Pride dressed like discernment.
Greed disguised as ambition.
Gossip renamed “concern.”
A prayer life disappearing behind endless scrolling.
A Bible collecting dust while your phone knows every movement of your thumb.
Maybe you're not running from church.
You attend every Sunday.
You're just running from surrender.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that nobody around you knows.
You know the songs.
You know when to raise your hands.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know Christian language well enough to hide inside it.
But Jesus does not want the edited version of you.
He already knows the unedited one.
And still the invitation of the Gospel stands.
Repent.
Come home.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Stop hiding behind your performance and bring your actual sin to the actual Savior.
There is another detail in Jonathan's story that becomes almost unbearable.
Saul eventually discovered that Jonathan had eaten.
He was prepared to kill him.
Jonathan—the man whose faith had helped ignite Israel's victory—stood under a death sentence because of an oath he had never even heard.
Then the people intervened.
They refused to let Jonathan die.
But every human rescue in Scripture leaves us longing for the rescue only Christ can accomplish.
Because unlike Jonathan, we cannot stand before God and say:
“I didn't know.”
We have sinned knowingly too.
We have crossed lines with our eyes open.
We have ignored convictions.
Broken promises.
Returned to sins we swore we would abandon.
Loved things God told us to leave.
Failed people who trusted us.
And if our only hope were our innocence...
we would have no hope.
But Christianity announces something far better than the innocence of the sinner.
It announces the righteousness of Christ.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Grace that finds guilty people and changes them.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that disciplines.
Grace that restores.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace that can take the chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read and refuse to let that chapter become the final sentence of your life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your scandal never happened.
But by taking repentant sinners and writing redemption where condemnation once seemed inevitable.
Perhaps that's why the honey in Jonathan's hand still speaks so vividly thousands of years later.
One exhausted man tasted provision...
and his eyes brightened.
But there is a sweetness infinitely greater than honey.
The psalmist said of God's words:
“How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!”
And the Gospel tells us those words ultimately lead us to a Person.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe your soul isn't starving because God abandoned you.
Maybe you've been trying to survive spiritually on everything except Christ.
Approval.
Religious performance.
Entertainment.
Relationships.
Money.
Sex.
Recognition.
Ministry.
Even theology can become a hiding place if knowing information about Jesus replaces actually walking with Jesus.
Your soul was never designed to live on applause.
It was never designed to live on dopamine.
It was never designed to live on people's approval.
You were created for God.
And no amount of earthly honey can satisfy a heart that was created to know its Creator.
What is starving inside you?
What have you been pretending isn't there?
What are you afraid Jesus will expose if you finally become completely honest with Him?
Bring that thing into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You do not need prettier religious language.
You need Christ.
You need repentance.
You need grace.
You need the cross.
You need the empty tomb.
You need the Holy Spirit changing what willpower alone could never transform.
And if this exposed something you've been hiding, don't write an impressive comment.
Write an honest one.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer struggling.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally stop pretending because you stopped pretending first.
And if this article made you think of one particular person, don't just think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Not merely because an algorithm rewards sharing.
Someone smiling in their profile picture may be barely holding onto faith.
Someone who would never walk into a church might read something a friend shared at 2:00 in the morning.
It isn't.

You glorify God through Jesus Christ by loving Him, obeying His Word, loving your neighbor, living faithfully, proclaiming the Gospel, serving others, giving generously as God leads, and using what He has entrusted to you for His purposes.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the King.
Jonathan tasted honey and his eyes brightened.
But when a sinner truly sees the grace of God in the face of Jesus Christ, something far greater begins.
The hiding can end.
The striving for acceptance can end.
The excuses can end.
The old master can lose its grip.
A sinner can repent.
A prodigal can come home.
A wounded believer can rise again.
A scandal can become a testimony of grace.
So share this if someone needs it.
Because perhaps the most dangerous kind of starvation is having provision in front of you while believing you are forbidden to receive it.
And perhaps someone reading this tonight needs to discover that the arms of the crucified and risen Christ are still open to repentant sinners.

You may remember Jonathan for the honey—but never forget the Savior whose grace is sweeter, whose cross went deeper, and whose mercy can still rewrite the chapter you thought had ruined your story forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS WAIT EIGHT DAYS BEFORE APPEARING TO THOMAS?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS WAIT EIGHT DAYS BEFORE APPEARING TO THOMAS?
Thomas asked for wounds he could touch. Jesus gave him eight days of silence—and then walked through a locked door.
There are eight days in the Bible that we almost never talk about.
Eight days between a man's doubt and the moment Jesus stood in front of him.
Eight days between, “Unless I see…” and “My Lord and my God!”
Eight days when Thomas had to live with everybody else’s testimony while carrying questions of his own.
And if you have ever watched other people celebrate what God was doing while secretly wondering why Jesus had not met you yet…
Thomas may be more familiar than you think.
John tells us that on the evening of the resurrection, Jesus appeared to His disciples behind locked doors.
He showed them His hands and His side.
They saw Him.
They rejoiced.
But one disciple was missing.
“Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came.” — John 20:24
We are not told why Thomas was absent.
That matters.

Scripture does not say he had abandoned the faith. It does not tell us he was angry, rebellious, lazy, or deliberately avoiding the disciples. Any confident explanation of his absence goes beyond the text.
John simply gives us the painful fact:
Thomas was not there.
Imagine returning afterward.
Imagine seeing their faces.
“We have seen the Lord.”
In Greek, John records their announcement:
Ἑωράκαμεν τὸν κύριον — Heōrakamen ton kyrion.
“We have seen the Lord.”
They were not discussing a theory.
They were claiming an encounter.
Peter had seen Him.
John had seen Him.
The others had seen Him.
Thomas had not.
And sometimes that is where faith becomes painfully personal.
Everybody around you seems to have a testimony.
Someone says God answered the prayer.
Someone says the door opened.
Someone says Christ restored their marriage, rescued their child, broke an addiction, provided what they needed, or carried them through the darkest season of their life.
And you are standing there thinking…
But what about me?
You still believe enough to remain near believers, yet something inside you hurts too much to borrow somebody else’s certainty.
Thomas answered:
“Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.” — John 20:25
The Greek is even more forceful.
οὐ μὴ πιστεύσω — ou mē pisteusō.
The construction is emphatic.
“I certainly will not believe.”
Thomas draws a line.
Not because crucifixion was theoretical to him.
Because it was horrifyingly real.
He had followed Jesus.
He had heard Him.
He had loved Him.
He had once said, when Jesus was heading toward danger, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16).
This was not a man who had never cared.
This was a wounded disciple whose world had collapsed.
And wounded people sometimes build walls where hope used to live.
Then John writes one little phrase that changes everything:
Καὶ μεθ’ ἡμέρας ὀκτὼ…
Kai meth’ hēmeras oktō…
“And after eight days…”
Eight days.
Why?
Why did Jesus wait?
Why not appear immediately?
Why not walk through the door five minutes after Thomas made his demand?
Why let him sleep that night without an answer?
And another?
And another?
We need to be careful here, because the Bible never gives us a sentence saying, “Jesus waited eight days because…”
So we should never manufacture an explanation and call it Scripture.
There is also an important cultural detail.

Ancient Jewish counting commonly used inclusive reckoning, counting the starting and ending days. John 20:19 places the first appearance on “the first day of the week,” and John 20:26 describes the next scene as “after eight days.” In context, this naturally points to the following first day of the week—approximately one week later by modern counting.
So this is not necessarily eight complete twenty-four-hour periods of Jesus deliberately refusing Thomas.
But the interval remains.
Thomas had to wait.
And what happened during that interval tells us something beautiful.
Thomas stayed close enough to be there when Jesus came again.
Read that slowly.
He doubted…
but he stayed.
He questioned…
but he stayed.
He could not yet say what the others were saying…
but he stayed.
Eight days later, the disciples were inside again.
And this time Thomas was with them.
Maybe somebody reading this needs precisely that sentence.
Stay in the room.
You may have questions.
Stay.
You may be disappointed.
Stay.
You may be carrying wounds you cannot explain to the people celebrating beside you.
Stay.
Do not confuse unanswered questions with an absent Savior.
Do not walk away from Christ because you cannot yet understand what Christ is doing.
Thomas did not have all his questions resolved.
He simply remained where Jesus’ people gathered.
Then…
Jesus came.
The doors were shut.
And suddenly Christ stood among them.
“Peace be unto you.”
In Greek:
Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν — Eirēnē hymin.
“Peace to you.”
Then Jesus turned toward Thomas.
And what He said next should stop us.
“Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing.” — John 20:27
Do you see it?
Jesus answered the very terms Thomas had spoken when Jesus was not visibly standing in the room.
Thomas had said he needed to see the nail marks.
Jesus mentioned them.
Thomas had said he needed to put his hand near Christ’s wounded side.
Jesus invited him.
Jesus did not arrive confused about Thomas’s struggle.
He knew.
And Christ did not humiliate him before answering him.
He confronted his unbelief, yes.
But He confronted it by revealing Himself.
“Do not become unbelieving, but believing.”
The Greek contrast is piercing:
μὴ γίνου ἄπιστος ἀλλὰ πιστός
mē ginou apistos alla pistos
Do not be unbelieving, but believing.
Jesus was not merely trying to win an argument.
He was calling a disciple back to faith.
And Thomas breaks.
There is no recorded speech about how unfair the previous week felt.
No list of objections.
No attempt to defend himself.
He looks at the risen Christ and says five Greek words:
Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου.
Ho Kyrios mou kai ho Theos mou.
“My Lord and my God.”
That is where the story was heading.
Not merely from doubt to evidence.
From doubt to worship.
Thomas wanted proof.
He encountered a Person.
Thomas wanted wounds.
The wounds led him to worship.
Thomas wanted certainty.
He ended up confessing the deity and lordship of Jesus Christ.
“My Lord…”
Not merely the Lord.
My Lord.
“My God…”
Not merely a teacher.
Not merely a prophet.
Not merely a crucified martyr whose followers refused to let His memory die.
Thomas stands before the risen Jesus and confesses:
My Lord and my God.
And Jesus receives that confession.
Maybe this is why Thomas's story still reaches people who feel ashamed of their questions.
The Gospel does not need us to pretend.
Christian faith is not built upon pretending that suffering does not hurt.
It does not require you to call confusion clarity.
It does not command you to manufacture emotions you do not possess.
But neither does Jesus leave Thomas comfortably enthroned inside his unbelief.
Grace meets him…
and calls him forward.
That is biblical grace.
Grace does not say unbelief does not matter.
Grace brings us to the One who can overcome it.
Jesus says:
“Thomas, because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.” — John 20:29
And suddenly Thomas’s story reaches through the centuries and finds us.
Because we were not standing in that room.
We did not physically inspect the wounds.
We did not hear Thomas gasp.
We did not watch Jesus enter despite the closed doors.
Yet John immediately explains why these signs were recorded:
“These are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.” — John 20:31
There it is.
John did not preserve this story merely so we could analyze Thomas.
He wrote so that we might believe.
The text moves from Thomas’s confession to your heart.
His encounter becomes testimony.
The testimony becomes written Scripture.
And through that apostolic witness, people who never stood inside that locked room are summoned to believe in the same risen Christ.
Maybe you are living inside your own “eight days” right now.
You prayed.
Nothing happened the way you expected.
You begged God to intervene.
The phone still rang with terrible news.
The relationship still collapsed.
The person still left.
The diagnosis still came.
The opportunity disappeared.
The grief did not magically lift.
