You watched other Christians testify while heaven seemed painfully quiet around you.
And somewhere inside, a sentence began forming:
Unless God does this…
Unless Jesus proves Himself this way…
Unless He fixes this…
Unless He answers me according to my conditions…
I will not believe.
Be careful.
Pain can quietly turn a prayer into an ultimatum.
Thomas had essentially told Jesus what evidence Jesus would need to provide.
But when Christ arrived, Thomas discovered something greater than getting his conditions fulfilled.
Christ Himself.
And that is where some of us need to surrender again.
Jesus is not merely the means by which we get the life we wanted.
Jesus is Lord.
Jesus is God.
Jesus is the crucified and risen Savior.
The Gospel is not the promise that believers will never experience an agonizing week.
The Gospel is that the One who was crucified for sinners has risen from the dead.
The scars remained visible on His resurrected body.
Think about that.
The scandal of Friday was not erased from the story.
It was transformed into testimony.
The wounds that looked like proof of defeat became evidence that the crucified Jesus standing before Thomas was alive.
That is the heartbeat of everything we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the nails never happened.
Not by pretending betrayal never happened.
Not by pretending the tomb never happened.
Jesus rewrites the story by walking alive out of the grave.
Christianity does not proclaim a Savior untouched by suffering.
It proclaims a Savior who entered suffering, bore sin, died, was buried, and rose victorious.
Your scars are not the Savior.
Your pain is not the Gospel.
Your trauma does not automatically become holy merely because you survived it.
Jesus is the Savior.
And only Jesus can take what sin, shame, grief, failure, and brokenness tried to use as the final chapter and write grace where you thought only ruin remained.
Perhaps your greatest scandal is something nobody knows.
Maybe you are the Christian who knows exactly how to smile at church while quietly wondering whether God has finally become tired of you.
Maybe you fell again.
Maybe the addiction came back.
Maybe your prayer life disappeared.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong while privately you are exhausted from pretending.
Then hear what Thomas’s story does not say.
It does not say, “Thomas doubted, so Jesus discarded him.”
Jesus came back into the room.
And Thomas was there.
That does not make unbelief harmless.
It makes Christ merciful.
So come into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Stop bargaining with Jesus.
Stop demanding that He become the Savior you designed before you will bow to the Savior who actually rose.
Look again at Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the grave.
Worthy of Thomas’s confession.
Worthy of yours.
My Lord and my God.
If something hidden in you has been exposed while reading this, do not hide behind religious language.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting where your heart really is becomes the moment you stop pretending you have no struggle.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting through questions.
Not as a transaction with God. Not because a share button earns favor with Him.
The person who still attends but does not talk much anymore.
The one whose faith was wounded by grief.
The one who thinks having questions means Jesus no longer wants them.
Send it privately if tagging them publicly would embarrass them.
Because eventually, almost every believer encounters a season when someone else's testimony arrives before their own answer does.
When that day comes, remember Thomas.
He did not understand everything.
But he stayed close.
And Jesus knew exactly where to find him.
Not because an algorithm is Lord.
Jesus is.
But algorithms carry messages into human eyes, and behind those eyes are real people carrying real wounds, real questions, real sin, real loneliness, and real need for Christ.
One share can place the testimony of the risen Jesus in front of somebody you may never know was struggling.
One tag can say, “I remembered you.”
One saved article can become something you return to on the night doubt becomes loud again.
One honest comment can remind another wounded believer that Christians do not have to pretend.
Thomas’s words will still matter.
Ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου.
My Lord and my God.
Because the deepest question in John 20 was never merely why Thomas waited approximately a week.
The deepest question is what Thomas finally saw when Jesus stood before him.
He saw that the cross had not won.
The grave had not won.
His doubt would not have the final word.
Jesus did.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth hidden inside those eight days is this:
The silence between your question and Christ’s answer is not proof that He has forgotten your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “YOUR LIPS DRIP NECTAR”: Why Does Scripture Describe Romantic Attraction This Sensually?
paragraphs: “YOUR LIPS DRIP NECTAR”: Why Does Scripture Describe Romantic Attraction This Sensually?
Song of Songs 4:11 is the kind of Bible verse people rarely read from the pulpit—and perhaps that says more about us than it does about God.
“Your lips drip nectar…”
Wait.
That is in the Bible?
Not tucked away in some forbidden ancient love poem.
Not smuggled into Scripture by mistake.
Not a sentence God somehow forgot to edit out.
It is there.
Right in the Song of Songs.
And the Hebrew is arguably even more vivid than some English translations allow you to feel:

נֹפֶת תִּטֹּפְנָה שִׂפְתוֹתַיִךְ כַּלָּה
דְּבַשׁ וְחָלָב תַּחַת לְשׁוֹנֵךְ
Nōp̄eṯ tiṭṭōp̄ənāh śip̄ṯōṯayiḵ, kallāh; dəḇaš wəḥālāḇ taḥaṯ ləšōnēḵ.
In straightforward English:
“Your lips, my bride, drip nectar; honey and milk are under your tongue…”
—Song of Songs 4:11
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because if you grew up believing that holiness required Christians to become embarrassed whenever romantic attraction entered the conversation, this verse can feel almost scandalous.
Her lips.
Her tongue.
Her fragrance.
His delight in her.
And God allowed all of it into Holy Scripture.
Why?
That question takes us somewhere much deeper than romance.
It takes us into the wreckage of what sin has done to human desire—and into the astonishing beauty of what God intended desire to be before we corrupted it.
Because perhaps the scandal is not that Scripture can speak this sensually.
Perhaps the scandal is that sin has distorted sexuality so thoroughly that we struggle to imagine sensuality without impurity.
There is a difference.
A massive one.
And if we miss it, we may spend our lives calling something dirty that God created beautiful while simultaneously tolerating versions of desire that God calls destructive.
Look closely at the Hebrew.
The word נֹפֶת — nōp̄eṯ refers to flowing or dripping honey, sweetness associated with the honeycomb.
Then comes תִּטֹּפְנָה — tiṭṭōp̄ənāh, from the Hebrew root נטף — nāṭap̄, carrying the idea of dripping, dropping, or distilling.
This is not sterile language.
The poet could have said, “You are attractive.”
He does not.
He describes sweetness that drips.
Honey.
Milk.
Lips.
Tongue.
Fragrance.
And the surrounding passage becomes even more sensory.
The beloved is compared with a garden, fruit, spices, perfume, flowing water, pomegranates, nard, saffron, cinnamon, myrrh, aloes, and Lebanon.
You can almost smell the poetry.
Almost taste it.
Almost walk through it.
Biblical Hebrew poetry does not merely inform the intellect here.
It awakens the senses.
And that matters.
Because God created human beings with senses.
God created the eye that notices beauty.
God created the nose that recognizes fragrance.
God created taste.
Touch.
Longing.
Affection.
The capacity to look at another human being within the covenantal goodness God designed and say, in effect…
You are beautiful to me.
I desire you.
I delight in you.
There is nothing inherently unholy about those words.
The tragedy is what humanity has done with them.
Go all the way back to Genesis.
Before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before exploitation.
Before lust became an industry.
Before bodies became commodities.
Before people learned to swipe past one another as though human beings were disposable merchandise.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
There was covenant.
There was nakedness.
And there was no shame.
Genesis 2:25 tells us that the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
Then Genesis 3 happened.
Sin entered.
And almost immediately, nakedness became entangled with hiding.
That should break something inside us.
Because one of sin's earliest achievements was taking what had existed without shame and surrounding it with fear.
Human beings have been hiding ever since.
Sometimes behind clothes.
Sometimes behind screens.
Sometimes behind pornography.
Sometimes behind religious performance.
Sometimes behind jokes.
Sometimes behind secret browser histories.
Sometimes behind marriages where two people sleep inches apart but have not felt emotionally known in years.
Sometimes behind the sentence…
“I’m fine.”
And maybe that is why Song of Songs can make religious people uncomfortable.
It refuses to pretend that embodied human love does not exist.
But it also refuses to treat desire the way our culture often treats it.
The Song does not reduce the beloved to a body for consumption.
Again and again, attraction exists alongside admiration, exclusivity, tenderness, delight, longing, belonging, and covenant-shaped language.
Notice the word immediately following the description of her lips:
כַּלָּה — kallāh.
Bride.
That word matters.
The sensuality is not floating in moral emptiness.
It exists inside relational belonging.
A few verses earlier the man says, “You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride” (Song of Songs 4:9).
Then, immediately after the nectar, honey, milk, and fragrance imagery, comes another striking picture:
גַּן נָעוּל אֲחֹתִי כַלָּה… מַעְיָן חָתוּם
Gan nāʿūl, ʾaḥōṯî kallāh… maʿyān ḥāṯūm.
“A garden locked…a spring sealed.”
—Song of Songs 4:12
Whatever interpretive questions surround every detail of this extraordinary poem, one thing should be impossible to miss:
Biblical desire is not presented as indiscriminate consumption.
There is beauty.
There is longing.
There is restraint.
There is belonging.
There is exclusivity.
And that is almost the opposite of what lust teaches.
Lust says:
I want your body without carrying the weight of your soul.
Love says:
You are not an object.
Lust asks:
What can I take?
Godly love asks:
How can I honor?
Lust consumes and moves on.
Covenant stays.
That distinction may expose something uncomfortable.
Because you can technically avoid adultery while allowing lust to colonize your imagination.
You can attend church on Sunday and spend Monday feeding desires you would be terrified for anyone to discover.
You can know worship songs by heart and still secretly use people in your imagination.
You can preach purity publicly while privately starving for images that slowly teach your brain to treat human beings as products.
And perhaps the most frightening part is how normal it can begin to feel.
One click.
One look.
One fantasy.
One conversation you know has crossed a boundary.
One secret relationship.
One private habit.
One compromise followed by another.
Until eventually the person in the mirror knows exactly where to hide.
But Jesus does not merely address what our bodies do.
He goes after the heart.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Christ takes the command against adultery and drives it beneath external behavior into lustful intention.
That is devastating.
Because suddenly the question is no longer simply:
“Have I physically cheated?”
The question becomes:
“What have I been teaching my heart to desire?”
And now Song of Songs becomes even more remarkable.
Because Christianity's answer to corrupted desire is not that beauty must become ugly.
The answer is redemption.
God does not need to apologize for creating attraction.
We need forgiveness for corrupting it.
There are people reading this who know exactly what that means.
Maybe your sexuality carries memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe someone used you.
Maybe you used someone.
Maybe pornography has followed you for years.
Maybe your marriage is bleeding.
Maybe you crossed a line.
Maybe you became the person you once promised yourself you would never become.
Maybe nobody knows.
You sing.
You pray.
You post Bible verses.
You smile when people see you at church.
But there is another version of your life behind the locked door.
And when everything becomes quiet, shame starts preaching.
It tells you:
Dirty.
Ruined.
Hypocrite.
Disqualified.
Too far gone.
And this is where the Gospel becomes infinitely greater than religious embarrassment.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to teach sexually broken people better behavior.
He came to save sinners.
Completely.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for an edited version of you.
He knew.
The secret.
The image.
The affair.
The fantasy.
The abuse you suffered.
The abuse you inflicted.
The years you wasted.
The thing you have never said aloud.
He knew the entire record before the nails entered His hands.
And He went to the cross anyway.
That does not make sin small.
It reveals how enormous grace is.
The cross is not God saying your sin never mattered.
The cross is God demonstrating exactly how seriously sin mattered—and how far His redeeming love was willing to go.
Jesus was crucified.
Buried.
And He rose again.
So repentance is not crawling toward a Savior who would rather you stayed away.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One whose mercy sinners could never purchase.
You do not repent because Christ hates you.
You repent because sin is killing what Christ came to restore.
That means the person trapped in pornography does not have to make peace with chains.
The adulterer does not have to make adultery an identity.
The sexually wounded do not have to believe what happened to them determines their worth.
The ashamed do not have to spend the rest of their lives hiding from God.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is cleansing.
There is a new heart.
There is transformation.
Not cheap grace that whispers, “Keep doing whatever you want.”
Real grace.
Grace that finds you in the mud and loves you too much to leave you there.
Maybe that is what makes Song of Songs 4:11 so unexpectedly beautiful.
“Your lips drip nectar.”
Those words do not belong to pornography.
Pornography stole something.
Lust stole something.
Sin stole something.
God created beauty before Satan ever learned to counterfeit it.
God created intimacy before humanity learned to exploit it.
God created desire before sin taught us to worship it.
God created marriage before culture learned to trivialize it.
And Scripture is not embarrassed about the goodness of what God made.
Neither should we be.
But neither should we confuse God's design with every desire our fallen hearts happen to produce.
Christian holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is the surrender of the whole person—body included—to God.
Your eyes belong to Christ.
Your imagination belongs to Christ.
Your sexuality belongs to Christ.
Your singleness belongs to Christ.
Your marriage belongs to Christ.
Your loneliness belongs to Christ.
Your wounds belong before Christ.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Christ.
Even the parts you are ashamed to name.
Especially those.
Because Jesus does not redeem us by pretending our scandals never happened.
He redeems us by entering the story and writing an ending sin could never produce.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Then stop performing for one moment.
Be honest.
Did this expose something?
Did a sentence land somewhere you hoped nobody would touch?
Then perhaps your response does not need to be sophisticated.
Maybe it needs to be surrender.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
Christ purchased redemption, not your comment.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop protecting the darkness.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only believer fighting a battle behind a smile.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Someone's marriage may be hanging by a thread.
Someone may have pornography open in another tab.
Someone may believe sexual failure has placed them permanently outside the reach of Christ.
Someone may need to discover tonight that conviction is not the same thing as condemnation—and that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Some truths need to be read again when temptation gets loud.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow as well.
That support matters.
But hear this carefully, because truth matters more than fundraising:
Scripture gives us a better foundation than pressure.
Paul writes that giving should be “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
The Greek phrase is striking:
μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης — mē ex anankēs
Not from compulsion.
Not because somebody manipulated your guilt.
Not because somebody frightened you into believing God's favor has a monthly price.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is not behind a paywall.
But believers can freely choose to support Gospel work they believe is bearing good fruit.
And whether or not you can financially support the ministry, you can still help.
Send it privately to someone fighting temptation.
Send it to the single Christian trying to understand desire without being ruled by it.
Send it to the believer drowning in pornography who thinks God is finished with them.
Send it to the wounded person who has confused what someone did to them with who they are.
And tell them:
Come back to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Because the final message of Christianity is not that good people successfully avoided scandal.
The message is that sinners can be redeemed by a crucified and risen Savior.
The Bible can describe a bride's lips dripping nectar without embarrassment because God is not embarrassed by the goodness of His creation.
He is opposed to what sin does to it.
And Jesus Christ came not merely to cover our shame with religious language, but to reconcile sinners to God and begin making broken people new.
So bring Him your desire.
Bring Him your marriage.
Bring Him your singleness.
Bring Him your memories.
Bring Him your secret habits.
Bring Him your wounded sexuality.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot seem to control.
Bring Him the part of your story you are convinced would make everybody leave.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk in the light.
And discover that the Savior who knows the ugliest chapter is still capable of writing holiness into the pages that remain.
Because perhaps the most scandalous thing in this entire story was never that Scripture said, “Your lips drip nectar.”
Perhaps the greater scandal is that Jesus looked at sinners covered in shame…
and still chose the cross.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but once Jesus takes the pen, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JUDAH’S WIFE DIED—And After His Mourning, He Went Where He Mistook Tamar for a Prostitute
paragraphs: JUDAH’S WIFE DIED—And After His Mourning, He Went Where He Mistook Tamar for a Prostitute

Genesis 38 contains grief, deception, sexual failure, hypocrisy, public exposure, confession—and one of the most astonishing reminders in Scripture that God can carry His redemptive purpose through a family story people would rather erase.
There are Bible stories we put on nursery walls.
And then there is Genesis 38.
No pastel colors.
No peaceful animals walking two by two.
No shepherd boy holding a sling beneath a beautiful sunset.
Just a grieving widower walking down a road...
a forgotten widow waiting beside it...
a hidden face...
a terrible decision...
and a family secret that would eventually appear in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Yes.
Jesus.
Because before this story is finished, Judah will sleep with the woman he believes is a prostitute.
He will later discover she is Tamar—his own daughter-in-law.
And somehow, when Matthew opens the New Testament and begins recording the earthly genealogy of Jesus Christ, God does not erase her name.
He leaves Tamar there.
Maybe that should tell us something before we go any further.
Maybe God is not as frightened by the chapters of your life that embarrass you as you are.
Genesis 38:12 begins quietly:
וַיִּרְבּוּ הַיָּמִים וַתָּמָת בַּת־שׁוּעַ אֵשֶׁת־יְהוּדָה
Vayyirbu hayyamim... vattamot bat-Shua eshet-Yehudah.
Many days passed, and the daughter of Shua—Judah's wife—died.
Then comes a small Hebrew expression carrying enormous human weight:
וַיִּנָּחֶם יְהוּדָה
Vayyinachem Yehudah.
Judah was comforted.
The sense is that his period of mourning had passed. He had grieved his wife. Life was beginning to move again.
Then Judah went toward Timnah, where his sheep were being sheared.
And somewhere along that road...
Tamar was waiting.
But to understand why, we have to understand what happened to her before Judah ever saw that veiled woman beside the road.
Tamar had married Judah's son Er.
Er died under God's judgment.
According to the family obligation described in the narrative, Judah then directed his second son, Onan, to provide offspring for his deceased brother through Tamar.
Onan exploited the situation.
He took what he wanted while deliberately refusing the responsibility attached to it.
God judged him too.
Now Tamar had lost two husbands.
Judah still had another son: Shelah.
Judah told Tamar to remain a widow until Shelah grew up.
So she waited.
Imagine that.
Waiting while everyone else's life continues.
Waiting while years quietly disappear.
Waiting because somebody gave you their word.
Waiting because you believed there would eventually be justice.
Then Shelah grew up.
And Tamar was still waiting.
Genesis does not hide the reason Judah hesitated. He feared that Shelah might die too.
So Tamar remained trapped inside somebody else's fear.
That detail matters.
Because it is easy to read Genesis 38 and reduce Tamar to the disguise she eventually wore.
Scripture forces us to look deeper.
Before Tamar covered her face, Judah had failed to fulfill what he had led her to expect.
Genesis 38:14 explicitly gives the reason behind what happened next: Tamar saw that Shelah had grown, yet she had not been given to him as wife.
She removed her widow's garments.
She covered herself with a veil.
She sat near the road to Timnah.
Then Judah saw her.
And Genesis 38:15 says:
וַיִּרְאֶהָ יְהוּדָה וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ לְזוֹנָה
Vayir'eha Yehudah vayachsheveha lezonah.
Judah saw her and thought her to be a prostitute.
Notice the wording carefully.
The Bible does not say Tamar was a prostitute.
It says Judah thought she was one.
There is a difference.
A huge one.
The Hebrew word זוֹנָה — zonah refers to a prostitute or sexually immoral woman in this context.
Judah sees a covered woman beside the road and makes an assumption.
He does not recognize Tamar.
Then he approaches her for sex.
This is one of those moments where Scripture refuses to protect the reputation of its characters.
The Bible could have edited this.
It doesn't.
Judah's grief did not make his choice righteous.
His loneliness did not make sin holy.
His loss did not turn temptation into permission.
Pain can explain vulnerability.
It cannot transform sin into obedience.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual moments arrive after suffering.
You buried something.
Lost someone.
Watched a marriage collapse.
Lost your job.
Were betrayed.
Got rejected.
Spent months feeling invisible.
And somewhere inside that pain, you started giving yourself permission to become somebody you never intended to become.
Nobody knew.
You still went to church.
Still posted the verse.
Still said, "God is good."
But late at night...
when loneliness started speaking...
when the phone was in your hand...
when nobody was watching...
you went looking for anesthesia.
Pornography.
An affair.
Alcohol.
Secret conversations.
Attention from somebody who was not your spouse.
Bitterness.
Compulsive spending.
Anything that could make the ache disappear for five minutes.
Judah had mourned.
Then Judah walked down a road.
And somewhere on that road grief collided with temptation.
Be careful where your wounds take you.
Not every place that makes you temporarily forget your pain is a place of healing.
Some doors numb you while quietly destroying you.
Judah negotiated with the woman he did not recognize.
She asked what he would give her.
He promised a young goat.
But Tamar wanted collateral until payment arrived.
His seal.
His cord.
His staff.
Personal objects.
Identifying objects.
Judah handed them over.
Think about that.
Sin has always demanded collateral.
It promises a moment...
then asks for pieces of you.
Your peace.
Your integrity.
Your marriage.
Your credibility.
Your prayer life.
Your ability to look somebody in the eyes.
Your confidence before God.
Sometimes you do not realize what you surrendered until the moment is already over.
Judah went on.
Tamar disappeared.
Life appeared to return to normal.
And isn't that often the most deceptive stage of hidden sin?
Nothing happens immediately.
No thunder.
No lightning.
Nobody calls.
Nobody exposes you.
So you begin thinking...
Maybe I got away with it.
But months later, Judah received news.
Tamar was pregnant.
And suddenly Judah became furious over another person's apparent sexual sin.
Read that again.
The man who had secretly slept with someone he believed was a prostitute was now outraged because Tamar appeared sexually immoral.
That mirror is uncomfortable.
Because religious hypocrisy is not merely committing sin.
It is becoming merciless toward people whose visible failures remind us of the hidden failures we have excused in ourselves.
Judah demanded judgment.
Then Tamar produced the evidence.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
And she sent a message to Judah.
Essentially:
Recognize whose these are.
Imagine the silence.
Judah looking at the objects.
His objects.
The things he had handed over when he thought nobody important was watching.
And suddenly the scandal was no longer about Tamar.
The evidence pointed back at him.
There are moments when God allows us to meet ourselves.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the version everybody applauds.
The real one.
The person behind the password.
Behind the deleted messages.
Behind the private browser.
Behind the resentment.
Behind the excuses.
Behind the smile.
And when that moment arrives, there are usually two roads.
Defend yourself.
Or confess.
Judah chose confession.
Genesis 38:26 gives us one of the most important sentences in the entire story:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tzadqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Judah recognized that he had failed Tamar by not giving her to Shelah.
He stopped hiding behind his authority.
He stopped making Tamar carry all the blame.
He acknowledged his own failure.
That sentence is where something changes.
Not because Judah suddenly becomes sinless.
But because Judah finally becomes truthful.
And repentance always begins where excuses end.
Maybe your breakthrough does not begin when everybody else finally understands what they did to you.
Maybe it begins when you become willing to say before God:
"I did this."
"I became this."
"I lied."
"I betrayed them."
"I kept returning to it."
"I blamed everybody else."
"I knew it was wrong."
"I need mercy."
That confession will feel like death to your pride.
But it may become the doorway to life.
Because the Gospel is not good news for people who successfully convince everyone they are righteous.
The Gospel is good news for sinners who finally stop pretending they do not need a Savior.
And now comes the part that makes Genesis 38 almost impossible to forget.
Tamar became pregnant with twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez.
Remember that name.
Because centuries later Matthew begins telling us about Jesus Christ.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
And then Scripture says that Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar.
Her name survived.
The scandal survived in the genealogy.
God did not airbrush the family tree of the Messiah.
Tamar's name is there.
Perez is there.
Judah is there.
And generations later that line leads toward David...
and ultimately, in Matthew's genealogy, toward Jesus Christ.
Do not misunderstand this.
God's ability to redeem a broken story does not mean He approves of every action inside that story.
Grace does not rename evil "good."
Redemption does not mean sin never mattered.
The cross itself proves how seriously God takes sin.
Jesus did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was deadly.
But the cross also announces something breathtaking:
Your sin does not have to write the final sentence.
Jesus can.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We sinned.
Christ came.
We were guilty.
Christ bore judgment.
We were separated.
Christ reconciles.
We could not clean ourselves enough to climb our way to God, so the Son of God came down to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because we have a spotless history, but through the grace of God received through faith in Christ.
That means you can stop pretending.
You can repent.
You can bring the thing you hate remembering into the light.
You can confess what you have hidden.
You can surrender the addiction.
End the affair.
Delete the secret connection.
Ask forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Seek help.
Come home.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance erases every earthly wound.
But because Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Maybe that is why this chapter feels so painfully human.
A dead wife.
A grieving husband.
A forgotten widow.
Broken promises.
Sexual sin.
Disguise.
Hypocrisy.
Exposure.
Confession.
Then...
a child named Perez.
And generations later...
Jesus.
Not because scandal becomes beautiful.
But because grace is powerful enough to enter what sin shattered and begin writing something new.
So what is the chapter you keep trying to tear out of your story?
The divorce?
The abortion?
The addiction?
The betrayal?
The years you wasted?
The person you slept with?
The marriage you damaged?
The child you abandoned?
The secret habit nobody knows about?
The season when you walked away from God?
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not ask you to pretend it never happened.
He calls you to repent.
Bring it into His light.
Call sin what God calls it.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Receive His mercy.
Then follow Him.
That is far more beautiful than pretending you were never broken.
Maybe somebody reading this right now has been running from God because you believe Christians would reject you if they knew everything.
People might disappoint you.
Jesus already knows.
And He still calls sinners to Himself.
That does not make sin cheap.
It makes grace astonishing.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your private sin. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Somebody reading the comments may desperately need to know they are not the only person who has needed mercy.
And please...
send this to the person who believes their worst chapter disqualified them forever.
Not merely because sharing helps this ministry reach more people—although it genuinely does—but because somewhere in your circle may be a person smiling publicly while privately drowning in shame.
It doesn't.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving. Scripture teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not compulsion.
Every share can place the Gospel in front of another human being.
Every tag can become a personal invitation.
Every meaningful comment can help create a place where people realize Christians still struggle, repent, heal, testify, and desperately need Jesus.
do not leave Genesis 38 merely shocked by Judah.
See yourself.
And then look beyond yourself.
Look at Christ.
Because perhaps the most astonishing thing about Judah's story is not that his sin was exposed.
It is that exposure was not the end.
There was confession.
There was a future.
There was Perez.
There was a lineage.
And eventually Matthew opened his Gospel and refused to hide Tamar's name.
The family history of Jesus Christ contains names connected with deeply complicated human stories.
That should humble every self-righteous person.
And give hope to every repentant sinner.
God is not asking you to rewrite yesterday.
You cannot.
He is calling you to give Him today.
So repent where you need to repent.
Confess what you need to confess.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where it is wise and possible.
Stop feeding the secret that is consuming you.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the enemy wants your worst chapter to become your identity.
Jesus calls sinners into something greater.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Transformed.
His.
And maybe one day you will look back at the chapter you once wished you could erase and realize something you could not see while you were living through it:
The page you thought proved your story was over became the place where grace taught you that Jesus still held the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Sometimes “I’m Just Being Honest” Means “I Never Learned to Control My Tongue.”
paragraphs:
Sometimes “I’m Just Being Honest” Means “I Never Learned to Control My Tongue.”
You can tell the truth and still sin with the way you tell it. Sometimes the sentence we call “honesty” is simply cruelty wearing a respectable Christian name.
“I’m just being honest.”
Four words.

Four words that have ended friendships, humiliated spouses, wounded children, divided churches, embarrassed people in public, and left wounds that lasted far longer than the conversation that caused them.
Maybe you have heard them.
Maybe you have said them.
Maybe someone looked directly at the part of you that was already bleeding, pressed their finger into it, and then defended themselves with those four words:
“I’m just being honest.”
And perhaps the most uncomfortable possibility is this...
Sometimes we really were telling the truth.
But we were not speaking like Jesus.
That distinction matters more than many Christians realize.
Because Scripture never gives us permission to baptize cruelty simply because the information coming out of our mouth happens to be factually correct.
A statement can be technically true and spiritually reckless.
You can have the right facts and the wrong heart.
You can expose something real and still expose it for the wrong reason.
You can win the argument and wound the person.
You can say, “But I didn’t lie,” while completely missing the question God may actually be asking:
Why did you need to say it like that?
Proverbs gives us an image so violent that we should never again think careless speech is a small spiritual issue.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 12:18 reads:
יֵשׁ בּוֹטֶה כְּמַדְקְרוֹת חָרֶב וּלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים מַרְפֵּא
Yesh boteh kemadqerot charev, uleshon chachamim marpe.
The King James Version renders it:
“There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.”
Modern translations commonly capture the first image as reckless or rash speech being like the thrusts of a sword.
Do not rush past that picture.
A sword.
God could have compared careless words to rain.
He could have compared them to dust.
He could have described them merely as annoying or unpleasant.
Instead, wisdom gives us the picture of something penetrating flesh.
The Hebrew expression behind the reckless speaker carries the idea of blurting or speaking rashly. The image that follows is madqerot cherev—the piercings or thrusts of a sword.
Then comes the breathtaking contrast:
uleshon chachamim marpe.
“But the tongue of the wise is healing.”
Marpe carries the sense of healing, health, cure, or remedy.
Two tongues.
Two possibilities.
One pierces.
One heals.
And here is what should disturb us:
Both mouths may be saying something true.
The dividing line in this proverb is not simply truth versus falsehood.
It is reckless speech versus wise speech.
That means biblical wisdom asks a question our culture often refuses to ask:
Not only, “Is it true?”
But also...
“Why am I saying it?”
“Does this need to be said?”
“Does it need to be said now?”
“Does it need to be said publicly?”
“Am I trying to restore this person—or punish them?”
“Am I speaking because I love them—or because hurting them will make me feel powerful for thirty seconds?”
That last question is painful.
Because sometimes “honesty” is revenge with clean hands.
We were angry.
We wanted them to feel what they made us feel.
We knew exactly which insecurity to touch.
Exactly which failure to mention.
Exactly which old wound to reopen.
Exactly which sentence would silence the room.
And then we said it.
The face changed.
The eyes dropped.
The room became quiet.
Something inside the other person collapsed.
And because what we said was technically accurate, we told ourselves we had done nothing wrong.
“I only told the truth.”
But truth was never given to us as a weapon for satisfying our flesh.
The New Testament refuses to separate truth from love.
Paul tells believers to be “speaking the truth in love” in Ephesians 4:15.
Notice what Christianity does not require us to choose between.
Truth or love.
Biblical love does not require lying.
Biblical truth does not require cruelty.
Jesus embodies both perfectly.
John describes Him as “full of grace and truth.”
Not fifty percent grace and fifty percent truth.
Not grace when people behaved and truth when they irritated Him.
Grace and truth dwelling perfectly together in one Person.
Jesus could confront sin with terrifying clarity.
He could expose hypocrisy.
He could call people to repentance.
He never needed to dilute holiness to appear compassionate.
Yet look at what happened when broken people encountered Him.
A woman caught in adultery was brought before Him publicly.
Her sin was real.
Jesus did not rename adultery.
He did not declare sin harmless.
But neither did He join the crowd eager to destroy her.
After her accusers disappeared, He told her that He did not condemn her and commanded her to leave her life of sin.
Grace did not erase truth.
Truth did not erase grace.
Grace rescued her from condemnation.
Truth called her into transformation.
That is Jesus.
And some of us need to admit that what we have called “boldness” looks very little like Him.
We have confused having no filter with having courage.
We have confused sarcasm with discernment.
We have confused public embarrassment with correction.
We have confused saying everything we think with spiritual maturity.
But self-control is fruit of the Spirit.
Read that again.
Self-control.
That includes what happens between the thought entering your mind and the words leaving your mouth.
Not every true thought deserves a microphone.
Not every observation deserves a comment.
Not every disagreement requires a response.
Not every failure needs to be announced.
Not every correction belongs in public.
Not every piece of truth belongs in every moment.
Sometimes holiness looks like opening your mouth.
Sometimes holiness looks like keeping it closed.
And perhaps nowhere is this more painful than inside families.
A child remembers being called stupid twenty years after the parent forgot saying it.
A wife remembers the joke her husband made about her body while everyone laughed.
A husband remembers the comparison his wife made between him and another man during an argument.
A teenager remembers being told, “You’ll never amount to anything.”
A church member remembers being publicly corrected for something that could have been handled privately.
A struggling believer remembers finally admitting what they were fighting—and wishing afterward they had never trusted anyone enough to confess it.
The speaker moved on.
The hearer carried the sentence home.
That is the terrifying thing about words.
You can finish speaking before they finish bleeding.
James understood this.
He compares the tongue to something tiny capable of setting an enormous forest ablaze.
A small flame.
A huge destruction.
Anyone who has lived long enough has watched this happen.
One text message.
One comment.
One accusation.
One rumor.
One sentence spoken while angry.
One humiliating joke.
One “I’m just saying what everybody else is thinking.”
And suddenly a relationship that took fifteen years to build is burning.
We often think the solution is simply to become nicer.
It is deeper than that.
Jesus teaches that words reveal the heart.
Our mouths are not independent machines malfunctioning above our shoulders.
Eventually the mouth exposes what has been living underneath it.
Pride speaks.
Jealousy speaks.
Bitterness speaks.
Fear speaks.
Unforgiveness speaks.
Insecurity speaks.
Self-righteousness speaks.
The tongue eventually gives the heart away.
So if you repeatedly destroy people with your words, the Gospel calls you to something deeper than learning better communication techniques.
It calls you to repentance.
Not shame without hope.
Repentance.
The beautiful, devastating mercy of God that allows us to stop defending what Christ wants to transform.
Maybe you have said things you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Maybe you watched someone’s expression change the moment the words landed.
Maybe years have passed and you still remember what you said.
Maybe your child remembers too.
Maybe your spouse does.
Maybe your mother does.
Maybe the friend you lost does.
And perhaps you have spent years protecting yourself with one sentence:
“But it was true.”
Today, Jesus may be asking you to surrender that defense.
Because repentance does not begin when we explain ourselves better.
It begins when we stop explaining away what God is exposing.
You may need to say:
“I was wrong.”
Not...
“I’m sorry you were offended.”
Not...
“I’m sorry, but you know what I said was true.”
Not...
“I apologize if you misunderstood me.”
Just:
“I was wrong. What I said was cruel. I should not have spoken to you that way. Please forgive me.”
There is enormous spiritual power in an apology without an escape hatch.
And if you are reading this from the other side—if you were the person cut by somebody else’s words—hear this carefully:
What someone said about you is not automatically what God says about you.
People speak from anger.
People speak from wounds.
People speak from jealousy.
People speak from immaturity.
People speak from distorted perceptions.
Sometimes people even take a real weakness and turn it into your entire identity.
“You failed” becomes “You are a failure.”
“You made a foolish decision” becomes “You are stupid.”
“You sinned” becomes “You are worthless.”
“You disappointed me” becomes “Nobody could ever love you.”
That is not how the Gospel speaks.
The Gospel tells the truth about sin more seriously than our culture ever will.
We have sinned.
We cannot save ourselves.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
But then comes the scandal of grace.
Christ came for sinners.
Christ bore sin at the cross.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ calls sinners to repent and believe.
And those who belong to Him are not sentenced to remain forever imprisoned inside the worst thing they have ever done.
That is why Gospel speech should sound different.
We can confront sin without erasing the sinner's humanity.
We can correct without humiliating.
We can disagree without dehumanizing.
We can warn without enjoying the fear in somebody’s eyes.
We can tell hard truths while tears are in our own eyes because we genuinely want the other person restored.
That is completely different from cruelty.
Ask yourself one question before your next difficult conversation:
Do I want this person healed—or do I want this person hurt?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Because sometimes we call it correction when what we really want is retaliation.
Sometimes we say, “Someone needs to tell them,” when what we secretly mean is, “I want to be the one who finally puts them in their place.”
Sometimes we disguise bitterness as discernment.
Sometimes we disguise gossip as concern.
Sometimes we disguise humiliation as accountability.
Sometimes we disguise cruelty as honesty.
Jesus sees through every disguise.
And yet...
He still offers grace.
That may be the most beautiful part of this entire conversation.
The same Jesus who exposes the sin of our speech is willing to forgive the sinner speaking.
Peter once used his mouth to deny that he even knew Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine carrying those sentences after the crucifixion.
Imagine remembering your own voice.
“I do not know the man.”
But Peter's worst words did not become the final chapter of his story.
The risen Christ restored him.
Then the mouth that once denied Jesus became a mouth proclaiming Him.
That is Gospel transformation.
Jesus does not merely forgive what your tongue has done.
He can transform what your tongue becomes.
The mouth that once gossiped can begin protecting reputations.
The mouth that once cursed can begin blessing.
The mouth that once humiliated can begin encouraging.
The mouth that once lied can begin speaking truth.
The mouth that once tore a spouse down can begin building them up.
The parent who spoke death can begin speaking life.
The believer known for cruelty can become known for wisdom.
The tongue that once pierced like a sword can become, by God's transforming grace, an instrument of healing.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe that rewriting begins today with one sentence you refuse to say.
One apology you finally make.
One conversation you choose to have privately instead of publicly.
One piece of gossip you refuse to repeat.
One comment you delete before posting.
One person you stop humiliating.
One moment when the Holy Spirit whispers, “Don't say it,” and for once...
you listen.
If this exposed something in you, do not hide behind embarrassment. Bring it into the light before Christ.
You do not have to explain the wound publicly.
But you also do not have to pretend words never hurt.
Read it yourself first. Pray over your own heart first. Then, if you believe it may genuinely help them, send it with humility.
Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can itself be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory.
Jesus wants more than your support.
He wants your heart.
He wants the bitterness you have justified.
The anger you have rehearsed.
The wounds you have weaponized.
The words you wish you could retrieve.
The shame you have carried because of what someone said about you.
Bring all of it to Him.
Repent where you have wounded.
Forgive as Christ gives you grace to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where it is wise and possible.
And surrender your tongue to the One who surrendered His life for you.
Because one day you may forget the argument.
You may forget what started it.
You may forget what room you were standing in.
But someone may remember your sentence for the rest of their life.
So before you say, “I’m just being honest”...
remember the sword.
Remember the healing.
And remember Jesus.
The tongue surrendered to Christ does not have to stop telling the truth—it learns to stop using truth as a knife.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Know Everybody Else’s Theology. When Did Knowing Jesus Become Secondary?
paragraphs:
You Know Everybody Else’s Theology. When Did Knowing Jesus Become Secondary?
You can identify bad doctrine in seconds, defend the faith for hours, and explain what everybody else gets wrong. But when knowledge makes us easier to impress with ourselves and harder to recognize as people who have been with Jesus, something sacred has gone terribly wrong.
There is a frightening way to be right about God…
and slowly become unlike Him.
You know the verses.
You know the doctrines.
You know the debates.

You know which preacher mishandled the text, which denomination you disagree with, which theological system has holes in it, which translation you prefer, which interpretation you reject, which church movement concerns you, and which Greek word everybody on Facebook apparently misunderstood.
Someone posts a theological statement, and before you finish reading it, your mind is already preparing the correction.
You know everybody else’s theology.
But here is the question that may hurt more than any doctrinal argument:
When did knowing Jesus become secondary?
Not knowing about Jesus.
Knowing Him.
Loving Him.
Worshiping Him.
Obeying Him when obedience costs something.
Sitting before His Word without needing to prove that you already understand it.
Repenting when Scripture exposes you instead of immediately thinking about somebody else who needs to read it.
Becoming gentler because Christ has been gentle with you.
Becoming slower to condemn because you remember how much mercy it took to rescue you.
Becoming holy because the One you study has become the One you treasure.
Paul confronted something painfully similar in Corinth.

The immediate controversy involved food sacrificed to idols. Some Corinthian Christians possessed legitimate theological knowledge. They understood truths about idols and about God that mattered. Paul did not solve the problem by declaring theology irrelevant.
Instead, he exposed what knowledge can become when the heart holding it is no longer governed by love.
In 1 Corinthians 8:1, Paul writes:
ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ, ἡ δὲ ἀγάπη οἰκοδομεῖ.
Hē gnōsis physioi, hē de agapē oikodomei.
In context, the sense is:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
Look at those words.
γνῶσις — gnōsis — knowledge.
φυσιοῖ — physioi — puffs up, inflates.
ἀγάπη — agapē — love.
οἰκοδομεῖ — oikodomei — builds up, edifies.
Paul is not saying knowledge is evil.
He is showing us what knowledge can do when it becomes disconnected from love.
It can inflate.
That image should disturb every serious student of Scripture.
Because inflation creates the appearance of enlargement without necessarily creating corresponding substance.
And that means you can become larger in your own eyes while becoming smaller in love.
You can increase your theological vocabulary while decreasing your patience.
You can memorize more Scripture while becoming less merciful toward people who are still learning it.
You can understand justification and still secretly justify your arrogance.
You can defend sovereign grace while behaving as though your superior intelligence saved you.
You can explain sanctification while refusing to repent.
You can study the humility of Christ and become proud of how accurately you understand His humility.
That last one should frighten us.
Because spiritual pride can feed on almost anything.
Even truth.
Especially truth, when we forget that truth is something we received before it was something we mastered.
Somewhere along the journey, Bible study can quietly stop being a place where we meet God and become a place where we collect ammunition.
The Scriptures become weapons for winning arguments rather than a sword first permitted to pierce our own hearts.
We begin reading with other people in mind.
“This verse is exactly what they need.”
“This destroys their position.”
“This proves our side.”
“This pastor needs to hear this.”
“This denomination needs to repent.”
“This person clearly hasn't studied enough.”
Maybe sometimes those concerns are legitimate.
False teaching is real.
Doctrine matters profoundly.
The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to discern truth, guard the Gospel, resist deception, teach faithfully, and grow in understanding.
Christian love is not intellectual laziness.
And biblical humility does not require pretending every interpretation is equally faithful to Scripture.
But there is another danger that serious Christians sometimes find harder to detect:
You can become skilled at discovering error everywhere except in yourself.
Paul continues:
εἴ τις δοκεῖ ἐγνωκέναι τι, οὔπω ἔγνω καθὼς δεῖ γνῶναι.
Ei tis dokei egnōkenai ti, oupō egnō kathōs dei gnōnai.
The thought of 1 Corinthians 8:2 is devastating:
If someone imagines that he knows something, he has not yet known as he ought to know.
Read that slowly.
Paul is confronting the arrogance that says,
“I know.”
Not humble confidence in revealed truth.
Not conviction.
Not careful doctrine.
But the posture that has stopped being teachable because it has become impressed with itself.
And then Paul turns the entire conversation toward something deeper:
εἰ δέ τις ἀγαπᾷ τὸν θεόν, οὗτος ἔγνωσται ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ.
Ei de tis agapa ton theon, houtos egnōstai hyp’ autou.
“But if anyone loves God, he is known by Him.”
Suddenly the center of gravity changes.
The ultimate wonder of Christianity is not that you have accumulated information about God.
It is that, by grace, God knows you.
You belong to Him.
You have been called into fellowship with His Son.
Christianity was never supposed to terminate in your ability to explain Christianity.
Theology is meant to lead somewhere.
To wonder.
To worship.
To obedience.
To love.
To holiness.
To communion with the living Christ.
The goal is not to know less theology.
The goal is to know God so truly that what you know begins transforming the person who knows it.
That distinction matters.
Because sound doctrine is precious.
We desperately need it.
A church without truth becomes vulnerable to every spiritual counterfeit wearing Christian vocabulary.
But doctrine was never given to us as a throne from which we could look down upon everyone who knows less.
It was given as light leading sinners toward the glory of God revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to become painfully honest.
When was the last time studying Scripture made you weep?
Not because the interpretation was fascinating.
Because Jesus became beautiful again.
When was the last time you closed your Bible and needed to repent?
When was the last time you discovered something true about God and your first impulse was worship rather than posting?
When was the last time your theology made you more patient with the immature believer?
More compassionate toward the struggling Christian?
More burdened for the unbeliever?
More forgiving toward the person who wounded you?
More willing to serve where nobody applauds?
More aware of your dependence upon grace?
When was the last time knowing more made you feel smaller before the majesty of God rather than larger beside other Christians?
Because there is a difference between theological maturity and theological accumulation.
Accumulation can fill notebooks.
Maturity changes people.
Accumulation can win debates.
Maturity knows when winning the person matters more than displaying the argument.
Accumulation can quote Christ.
Maturity increasingly resembles Him.
And then we come to Jesus Himself.
The One about whom all our Christology speaks.
The One whose nature we debate.
The One whose atonement we defend.
The One whose resurrection we proclaim.
The One whose return we await.
Look at Him.
Jesus knew every Scripture perfectly.
He never misunderstood the Father.
He never held an incorrect doctrine.
He never needed correction.
Absolute truth stood in human flesh.
And what did perfect knowledge look like when it walked among sinners?
It touched lepers.
It welcomed children.
It confronted hypocrisy.
It defended truth.
It wept.
It served.
It washed feet.
It called sinners to repentance.
It showed compassion to the broken.
And then…
it carried a cross.
There is your theology with skin on it.
Jesus Christ did not become less truthful in order to become loving.
And He did not become less loving in order to remain truthful.
In Him, grace and truth are not enemies.
At Calvary, the holiness of God was not discarded.
Sin was not renamed.
Judgment was not treated as imaginary.
The cross tells us sin is far worse than our culture wants to believe.
But it also tells us grace is far greater than religious pride wants to admit.
The Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Not people who had finally accumulated enough theological precision to deserve Him.
Sinners.
Rebels.
The guilty.
People with ruined histories.
People who misunderstood.
People who failed.
People who hid.
People who promised loyalty and then collapsed under pressure.
People like Peter.
People like the Corinthians.
People like us.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
Jesus takes people whose sin should have been the final chapter and begins writing something new.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
This is why the Gospel destroys both intellectual arrogance and intellectual laziness.
We cannot say truth does not matter, because Christ is the truth.
But we cannot boast as though understanding truth makes us superior, because everything we possess is grace.
The cross leaves no room for swagger.
You did not save yourself.
Your systematic theology did not bleed for you.
Your favorite teacher did not rise from the grave for you.
Your denomination cannot wash away your sin.
Your apologetics cannot reconcile you to God.
Your knowledge cannot justify you.
Jesus saves.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And when that truth moves from the edges back to the center, something happens.
The Bible student becomes a worshiper again.
The debater remembers that the person on the other side of the screen has a soul.
The teacher trembles before teaching.
The mature believer remembers how patient somebody once had to be with them.
Correction becomes less about humiliation and more about restoration.
Conviction becomes less performative.
Repentance becomes personal.
Truth remains truth.
But pride starts losing oxygen.
Maybe that is why this article feels uncomfortable.
Perhaps you have not abandoned Jesus.
Perhaps something subtler happened.
You became fascinated with everything surrounding Him…
and stopped being fascinated with Him.
You know the controversies.
You know the camps.
You know the terminology.
You know everybody who is supposedly wrong.
But somewhere beneath all that knowledge is a heart that remembers when simply hearing the name Jesus could undo you.
When grace amazed you.
When the cross felt personal.
When salvation was not merely a doctrine you could define but a miracle you could barely believe had happened to you.
When you opened Scripture hungry rather than armed.
Maybe you miss that person.
Maybe Christ is calling you away from the exhausting need to prove that you belong among the knowledgeable and back into the joy of simply belonging to Him.
That does not mean throwing away serious theology.
It means putting theology back where it belongs:
At the feet of Jesus.
Study harder.
Read carefully.
Learn biblical languages if you can.
Understand church history.
Test teachings against Scripture.
Know why you believe what you believe.
Protect the Gospel.
Teach sound doctrine.
Refuse counterfeit Christianity.
But never become so impressed with knowing things about God that you forget the terrifying, beautiful privilege of actually knowing Him.

And whenever knowledge begins making you cruel, suspiciously proud, contemptuous, unteachable, addicted to controversy, or incapable of loving the people for whom Christ died, do not congratulate yourself for being discerning.
Bring your heart back under the Word.
Let Scripture examine the examiner.
Let truth correct the person correcting everybody else.
Repent.
Because repentance is not intellectual defeat.
Repentance is one of grace's greatest victories.
Maybe your scandal was never the kind people whisper about.
Maybe yours was quieter.
Nobody saw it.
You became proud.
You started needing to be the smartest Christian in the room.
You began measuring spiritual maturity by how much somebody agreed with you.
You forgot that knowledge is stewardship.
You forgot that the person you corrected was a person.
You forgot your own rescue.
And perhaps Jesus is rewriting that story too.
From pride to humility.
From argument to worship.
From merely knowing propositions about Christ to walking closely with Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
Someone reading may pray for you instead of judging you.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought, and salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
But if Gospel-centered teaching has genuinely strengthened you, supporting work that spreads biblical truth can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
Your share may place the Gospel in front of the person who would never walk into a church but will quietly read something a friend posted at 2:00 in the morning.
Your tag may reach the Christian who has become exhausted by religious performance.
Your comment may give another believer permission to stop hiding.
Your support can help Gospel-centered material keep moving.

It is an opportunity to help sustain and expand Gospel-centered discipleship while receiving deeper biblical nourishment, encouragement, accountability, and resources designed to keep pointing you toward Christ.
Jesus is not for sale.
The blood of Christ cannot be purchased.
Come to Him empty-handed.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Then spend the rest of your life learning the truth—not so you can stand taller than other sinners, but so you can bow lower before the Savior.
Because one day, nobody will be impressed that you won every theological argument.
The question underneath all the questions will remain:
Did all that truth lead you deeper into Christ?
Did knowing more make you love Him more?
Did it make you obey Him?
Did it make you worship?
Did it make you love the people He loves?
Did it make you look more like Jesus?
Never become so knowledgeable about the Light that you forget to stand in it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SOLOMON BUILT GOD’S TEMPLE IN MAGNIFICENT GLORY—THEN HIS OWN HEART BECAME DIVIDED
paragraphs: SOLOMON BUILT GOD’S TEMPLE IN MAGNIFICENT GLORY—THEN HIS OWN HEART BECAME DIVIDED

The man who once knelt before God with lifted hands eventually gave pieces of his heart to other gods. Solomon’s decline is not merely the tragedy of an ancient king. It is a warning to every believer who thinks yesterday’s devotion can protect today’s compromise.
There is something terrifying about Solomon’s story.
Not because he began badly.
Because he began so well.

He was the son of David. The king entrusted with an extraordinary calling. The man associated with wisdom, wealth, influence, international renown, and one of the most magnificent acts of worship in Israel’s history.
He built the Temple.
Think about that.
Stone upon stone.
Gold upon gold.
Craftsmen worked. Priests prepared. Sacrifices were offered. The ark of the covenant was brought into the Most Holy Place.
And then came a moment Solomon could never manufacture with money, architecture, political power, or human brilliance.
The glory of God filled the house.
Scripture says:

“And it came to pass, when the priests were come out of the holy place, that the cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud: for the glory of the LORD had filled the house of the LORD.”
—1 Kings 8:10–11, KJV
Imagine standing there.
The king who commissioned the Temple watches the priests retreat because the manifestation of God’s glory is overwhelming the house.
Then Solomon stands before the altar of the LORD.
He spreads his hands toward heaven.
And he prays.
This powerful king acknowledges something breathtakingly humble:
“But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?”
—1 Kings 8:27, KJV
Solomon understood something many people still miss.
God was greater than the building.
Greater than the gold.
Greater than the ceremony.
Greater than Solomon.
And yet the man who understood that truth would eventually allow his heart to wander toward gods that could neither speak nor save.
That is what makes Solomon’s decline so disturbing.
Because spiritual collapse does not always begin with someone screaming, “I reject God.”
Sometimes it begins with something much quieter.
A tolerated affection.
A rationalized relationship.
A command we decide is inconvenient.
A compromise nobody notices.
A desire we refuse to surrender.
A small corner of the heart where Jesus is welcomed—but not permitted to rule.
And slowly…
almost invisibly…
the heart that once belonged wholly to God becomes divided.
The Hebrew language of 1 Kings gives us a particularly important window into Solomon’s tragedy.
Scripture says:
וַיְהִי לְעֵת זִקְנַת שְׁלֹמֹה נָשָׁיו הִטּוּ אֶת־לְבָבוֹ אַחֲרֵי אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים
In transliteration:
Vayehi le'et ziknat Shelomoh, nashav hittu et-levavo acharei elohim acherim…
The sense is:
“When Solomon was old, his wives turned away his heart after other gods…”
Then comes the devastating diagnosis:
וְלֹא־הָיָה לְבָבוֹ שָׁלֵם עִם־יְהוָה אֱלֹהָיו
Velo-hayah levavo shalem im-YHWH Elohav.
“And his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God…”
—1 Kings 11:4, ESV
That word deserves attention.
Shalem.
שָׁלֵם
It carries the idea of being whole, complete, sound, undivided.
Solomon’s great catastrophe was not that he suddenly forgot everything he knew about God.
His heart was no longer whole toward God.
Divided.
That is frightening because you can still know biblical truth with a divided heart.
You can remember what God has done and still compromise.
You can have spiritual history and still drift.
You can have influence and still drift.
You can have knowledge and still drift.
You can have helped other people encounter truth…
and still drift yourself.
Solomon had built something breathtaking for God while eventually failing to guard something God cared deeply about:
his heart.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being about Solomon.
Perhaps it becomes about us.
Because you may never build a temple.
You may never sit on a throne.
You may never possess Solomon’s wealth.
But you have a heart.
And something is always competing for it.
Jesus later said:
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
—Matthew 6:21, KJV
So the uncomfortable question is not simply:
“Do I believe in God?”
The deeper question is:
“What has my heart?”
Because we have become very skilled at looking spiritually healthy while privately becoming spiritually divided.
A person can sing worship songs while feeding a secret addiction.
Read Scripture while refusing to forgive.
Post Bible verses while living another life when nobody is watching.
Serve in church while starving spiritually.
Talk about holiness while protecting one cherished compromise.
Say, “Jesus is Lord,” while quietly adding:
“Except here.”
Except this relationship.
Except this habit.
Except my money.
Except my sexuality.
Except my ambition.
Except my bitterness.
Except my entertainment.
Except my reputation.
Except the thing I desperately want God to leave alone.
And that is where division begins.
Solomon’s decline did not occur because God had failed him.
God had warned him.
In fact, long before Solomon’s reign, Israel’s kings had been commanded not to multiply wives for themselves, “that his heart turn not away” (Deuteronomy 17:17).
The warning was already written.
Solomon was wise enough to understand warnings.
But wisdom known is not the same thing as obedience practiced.
That distinction can destroy a life.
You can know the verse and ignore the Voice behind it.
You can explain temptation while surrendering to it.
You can teach boundaries you refuse to keep.
You can recognize somebody else’s compromise while carefully renaming your own.
And perhaps one of the most dangerous moments in the Christian life comes when familiarity with Scripture begins masquerading as submission to Scripture.
Solomon knew much.
But knowledge did not make disobedience safe.
Neither does ours.
The Bible says Solomon loved many foreign women, and his wives turned his heart toward other gods. He followed Ashtoreth, Milcom, and built high places connected with Chemosh and Molech.
The king who built the Temple of the LORD…
built high places for idols.
Read that slowly.
The same life.
The same man.
The same hands.
Once building for the glory of God.
Later accommodating what dishonored Him.
How does somebody get there?
Usually not in one dramatic leap.
One compromise becomes normal.
Then another.
What once troubled the conscience becomes familiar.
What was once unthinkable becomes explainable.
Then defensible.
Then habitual.
And eventually the person who once said, “I would never,” cannot remember when “never” became “sometimes,” and when “sometimes” became a way of life.
That is why this story should disturb comfortable Christianity.
Your greatest spiritual danger may not be the temptation you hate.
It may be the compromise you have learned to live with.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Maybe your children think everything is fine.
Maybe the people at church see the polished version.
Maybe you still say grace before dinner.
Maybe you still know exactly when to lift your hands during worship.
But somewhere beneath all of that…
your heart knows.
God knows.
And perhaps while reading this, one particular thing has already entered your mind.
Do not rush past it.
Because conviction is not God amusing Himself with your shame.
Conviction is mercy knocking before destruction finishes what compromise started.
Solomon’s story is a warning, but the Bible does not leave us staring hopelessly at Solomon.
Someone greater than Solomon came.
Jesus said of Himself:
“Behold, a greater than Solomon is here.”
—Matthew 12:42, KJV
That sentence changes everything.
Solomon was a son of David.
Jesus Christ is the promised Son of David and Messiah.
Solomon possessed remarkable wisdom.
Christ is the One in whom are hidden “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).
Solomon built a glorious temple.
Jesus spoke of His own body as the temple that would be destroyed and raised again (John 2:19–21).
Solomon’s heart became divided.
Jesus remained perfectly obedient to the Father, even unto death.
Solomon’s kingdom fractured after him.
Christ’s kingdom will never end.
Solomon demonstrates how even extraordinary human wisdom cannot rescue a sinful heart.
Jesus came to save sinners.
And this is where scandal becomes grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that smiles at idolatry.
Not grace that whispers, “Keep your idols. God understands.”
Biblical grace does something far more beautiful.
It calls the sinner out of hiding.
It tells the truth about sin.
Then it points toward a crucified and risen Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the public appearance of divided people.
He came to redeem them.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He suffered for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God pretending our rebellion was insignificant.
The Gospel is God demonstrating just how serious sin is—and just how astonishing His saving grace truly is.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…”
—1 Peter 3:18, KJV
Did you catch those final words?
“That he might bring us to God.”
Maybe you wandered.
Maybe your heart became divided.
Maybe you built a beautiful Christian exterior while something underneath began collapsing.
Maybe you have compromised for so long that returning feels hypocritical.
Come anyway.
Not because your sin does not matter.
Because Christ is sufficient for sinners who repent and trust Him.
Repentance is not performing enough sorrow to persuade God to love you.
It is turning from sin toward the God you have sinned against, trusting in Christ.
The New Testament commonly uses the Greek word μετάνοια—metanoia—for repentance, carrying the sense of a change of mind that involves a genuine turning.
And perhaps that is exactly what somebody reading this needs.
Not another religious performance.
Not another inspirational quote.
Not another promise that tomorrow you will somehow become stronger.
Turn.
Come back.
Bring the secret into the light.
Delete what needs deleting.
End what needs ending.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive whom you need to forgive.
Ask for help where you need help.
Stop negotiating with the thing that has been slowly stealing your heart.
And run to Christ.
Not after you become clean enough.
Run to Christ because you cannot cleanse yourself.
There is a prayer hidden inside Scripture that feels almost painfully appropriate after reading Solomon’s story.
David prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
—Psalm 51:10, KJV
The Hebrew opening is unforgettable:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Maybe that should become your prayer tonight.
Not:
“God, make everybody think I am okay.”
Not:
“God, let me keep everything while avoiding the consequences.”
But:
“Create in me a clean heart.”
Because the greatest tragedy would not be losing the image you built.
It would be protecting the image while losing your heart.
So be honest.
Has something been dividing your heart lately?
Has success?
Money?
Lust?
Pornography?
Approval?
Resentment?
A relationship?
Pride?
Comfort?
Politics?
Ministry itself?
Has something become so precious that obedience to Jesus now feels like a threat to it?
Then you already know where the battle is.
You do not need to confess your private details publicly, but do not hide from God.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer reads and realizes:
“I’m not the only person fighting to come home.”
And please do not consume this message and immediately scroll into another distraction.
There may come a night when compromise starts sounding reasonable again, and you will need the warning.
Send it privately to the believer who has disappeared.
Send it to the successful person everyone admires but nobody asks, “How is your soul?”
Send it to your children.
Your parents.
Your spouse.
Your church family.
Even send it to the person who does not yet believe.

If this truth glorifies God, do not bury it where only you can see it. Let sharing become part of your witness—not a performance, not a transaction with God, but a simple act of putting Gospel truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to truth in a world constantly competing for your heart.
But before you leave, remember Solomon.
Remember the Temple.
Remember the cloud.
Remember the king standing before the altar with his hands stretched toward heaven.
And remember that years later, the same man allowed his heart to become divided.
His story asks every generation a question:
What good is magnificent devotion yesterday if I am quietly surrendering my heart today?
Do not merely protect what you have built.
Guard your heart.
Do not assume yesterday’s encounter guarantees today’s obedience.
Do not confuse biblical knowledge with faithfulness.
Do not wait until compromise has constructed its own altar inside you.
Bring it to Jesus now.
The Savior who exposed Peter’s failure restored Peter.
The Christ who received sinners still calls sinners to repentance.
The blood shed at Calvary is sufficient.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is alive.
And your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
Grace for the guilty.
Restoration for the broken.
Hope for the wandering.
And a Savior greater than Solomon for every divided heart willing to come home.
And comment something honest.
Even if all you can write is:
Because perhaps the most dangerous heart is not the one that knows it has wandered.
It is the one that has wandered so gradually it no longer realizes how far it has gone.
You can build something magnificent for God and still lose the battle inside your own heart—so before you ask God to bless what your hands are building, ask Him to keep your heart wholly His.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BEFORE YOU JUDGE THE COLOR OF THEIR SKIN, REMEMBER WHO PUT HIS IMAGE BENEATH IT
paragraphs: BEFORE YOU JUDGE THE COLOR OF THEIR SKIN, REMEMBER WHO PUT HIS IMAGE BENEATH IT
You can know Bible verses, sing worship songs, defend Christian doctrine—and still need Jesus to confront the way you see another human being.
There is a terrifying possibility that nobody likes talking about.
You can hold a Bible in your hand...
and prejudice in your heart.
You can sing about the blood of Jesus on Sunday and look down on somebody because of the color of their skin on Monday.
You can say, “God loves everyone,” and still feel uncomfortable when your child befriends someone from another ethnicity.
You can post Scripture.
You can wear a cross.
You can know Christian language.
You can even tell people how long you have been saved.

And still, somewhere beneath the religious vocabulary, there can be a corner of the heart where another person has been reduced to a color, an accent, a nationality, a tribe, a surname, or a stereotype.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve the language coming out of our mouths.
He came to transform the heart producing it.
And before this article is finished, perhaps the question will no longer be, “Are other people racist?”
Perhaps the question will become much closer.
“Lord... is there something in me You still need to crucify?”
Go all the way back to the beginning.
Before nations.
Before borders.
Before flags.
Before the labels humanity would eventually use to divide itself.
Genesis says:
“וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ”
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha’adam betsalmo...
“And God created humankind in His image...”
Genesis 1:27.
The Hebrew expression בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — betselem Elohim means “in the image of God.”
Stop there.
Before Scripture tells you a person’s nationality, social status, accomplishments, education, wealth, or appearance, Scripture gives humanity an astonishing dignity:
Image-bearer.
The person you were taught to distrust bears the image of God.
The person whose skin is darker than yours bears the image of God.
The person whose skin is lighter than yours bears the image of God.
The person whose accent sounds strange to you bears the image of God.
The immigrant.
The foreigner.
The neighbor.
The stranger.
The person from the ethnic group your family mocked when you were growing up.
The person whose people have historically hurt your people.
None of this means every culture, belief, action, ideology, or behavior is morally equivalent. Scripture never teaches that.
It means something deeper.
Human worth is not distributed according to pigmentation.
God never gave us permission to measure human dignity with a color chart.

And racism becomes especially grotesque when it enters the heart of someone claiming allegiance to Jesus, because the Christian is supposed to look at another human being through the revelation of God—not through inherited contempt.
Sometimes prejudice arrives loudly.
Sometimes it wears a hood.
Sometimes it screams slurs.
Sometimes it commits violence.
But sometimes it is much quieter.
Sometimes it sounds like a joke everyone in the family laughs at.
Sometimes it is the hesitation before sitting beside someone.
Sometimes it is the assumption that “those people” are all the same.
