Sometimes it is the person you would happily evangelize but would never want your daughter to marry simply because of ethnicity.
Sometimes it is treating one group’s failures as individual failures while treating another group’s failures as proof of what “they” are all like.
Sometimes nobody else can see it.
But God can.
That is what makes Scripture dangerous to our pride.
The Bible does not merely give us ammunition for confronting everybody else.
It turns the blade toward us.
James wrote:
“Ἀδελφοί μου, μὴ ἐν προσωπολημψίαις ἔχετε τὴν πίστιν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ...”
“My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ... with partiality.”
James 2:1.
The Greek word is striking: προσωπολημψίαις — prosōpolēmpsiais.
It speaks of partiality—showing favoritism based on outward status or appearance.
James was addressing favoritism toward rich and poor, not writing a modern essay about race. We should respect that context.
But then James drives the principle deeper.
“If you show partiality, you commit sin.”
James 2:9.
Not merely bad manners.
Not merely cultural insensitivity.
Sin.
That should disturb us.
Because Christianity gives us no safe category where contempt for another image-bearer becomes acceptable simply because everybody around us learned the same contempt.
Maybe your grandfather said it.
Maybe your parents believed it.
Maybe your neighborhood normalized it.
Maybe your friends laughed about it.
Maybe your culture handed it to you before you were old enough to examine it.
But inherited sin does not become holiness simply because it has been in the family for generations.
At some point Jesus stands in front of every inherited darkness and says:
Follow Me.
Not your prejudice.
Not your tribe.
Not your pride.
Me.
Paul stood in Athens among people separated by geography, history, religion, and culture and declared something extraordinary about humanity:
“ἐποίησέν τε ἐξ ἑνὸς πᾶν ἔθνος ἀνθρώπων...”
Acts 17:26.
Literally, the crucial phrase ἐξ ἑνὸς — ex henos means “from one.”
From one, God made every nation of humanity.

There is an important manuscript detail worth knowing rather than hiding: some later Greek manuscripts add αἵματος — haimatos, “blood,” which is why older English translations such as the KJV famously say God “hath made of one blood all nations of men.” The critical Greek text simply has “from one.”
Either way, Paul’s argument destroys racial boasting.
Humanity does not consist of separate classes of human worth.
We share a common human origin under one Creator.
Different nations?
Yes.
Different peoples?
Yes.
Different languages?
Absolutely.
Different histories, traditions, foods, music, clothing, experiences, and cultures?
Of course.
Scripture does not erase human diversity.
It refuses to turn diversity into a hierarchy of human value.
And then something even greater happens at the cross.
Jesus does not merely tell hostile human beings to tolerate one another.
He creates a redeemed people.
Paul writes:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek... for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”
Galatians 3:28.
Read that carefully.
Paul is not claiming Jewish people stopped being Jewish or Greeks stopped being Greek.
The New Testament continues recognizing ethnic and cultural identities.
He is declaring that those distinctions cannot determine someone’s standing before God or superiority within Christ.
εἷς ἐστε — heis este.
“You are one.”
Not identical.
One.
The Gospel does not produce a colorless humanity.
It produces a reconciled humanity whose deepest identity is found in Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes people try to defeat racism by pretending differences do not exist.
Scripture gives us something more beautiful.
God sees nations.
God sees peoples.
God sees languages.
God sees tribes.
And He redeems people from among them.
John was permitted to see where history is going.
He looked toward the throne and saw:
“ἐκ παντὸς ἔθνους καὶ φυλῶν καὶ λαῶν καὶ γλωσσῶν...”
“from every nation and tribes and peoples and languages...”
Revelation 7:9.
Do you see it?
Heaven is not embarrassed by human diversity.
The redeemed multitude does not appear as one earthly ethnicity that defeated all the others.
Every nation.
Every tribe.
Every people.
Every language.
Standing before one throne.
Worshiping one Lamb.
Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing there someday.
Imagine seeing faces from peoples you never encountered on earth.
Languages you never understood.
Cultures you never experienced.
People your ancestors may once have called enemies.
People history separated.
People politics divided.
People wars taught to hate each other.
And there they are.
Redeemed.
White robes.
One Savior.
One song.
One Lamb.
Then imagine having to remember that while you were on earth, you once believed your skin somehow made you better than theirs.
How small our prejudice will look before the throne of God.
How embarrassing our superiority will become beneath the glory of the Lamb.
And here is where the Gospel refuses to leave us merely ashamed.
Because Christianity is not simply the announcement that racism is wrong.
If that were the whole message, we would leave convicted but unchanged.
The Gospel goes further.
It says the racist can repent.
The hateful can be forgiven.
The wounded can begin healing.
The proud can be humbled.
The bitter can surrender their bitterness.
The person who spent decades despising another group can receive a new heart.
Because Jesus Christ did not die only for respectable sins.
He died for sinners.
There may be someone reading this who has carried racial hatred for years.
Maybe you know exactly where it began.
Somebody hurt you.
Somebody humiliated you.
Someone from another ethnicity betrayed your family.
Perhaps history itself wounded your people.
And slowly pain became generalization.
Generalization became suspicion.
Suspicion became resentment.
Resentment became hatred.
Eventually you stopped seeing individuals.
You saw categories.
But listen carefully.
What happened to you may have been evil.
The Gospel never requires us to pretend injustice did not happen.
Forgiveness does not rename evil as good.
But another person's sin does not give us permission to surrender our heart to hatred.
Jesus can heal what hatred has occupied.
Maybe your story is different.
Nobody traumatized you.
You simply inherited prejudice.
You heard the jokes at the dinner table.
You heard the comments in the car.
You watched adults recoil from certain people.
Nobody sat you down and taught you a doctrine of racial superiority.
They didn't have to.
Children learn what adults repeatedly communicate.
And years later you became an adult carrying assumptions you never consciously chose.
Now Christ is exposing them.
Do not run from that moment.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction can be mercy knocking on a locked room.
Open it.
Let Jesus inside.
Say it plainly.
“Lord Jesus, I have judged people You created.”
“I have carried contempt.”
“I have laughed when I should have spoken.”
“I have stereotyped people I never even knew.”
“I have allowed bitterness to become prejudice.”
“Forgive me.”
That prayer is not weakness.
That is where freedom begins.
The Hebrew Scriptures gave Israel this command:
“וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ”
Ve’ahavta lere’akha kamokha.
“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Leviticus 19:18.
Jesus later identified love for neighbor as one of the great commandments.
Not tolerate your neighbor.
Not merely avoid attacking your neighbor.
Love.
And Christian love is not sentimental blindness.
It seeks another person's good because that person matters before God.
So perhaps the next step after reading this is not posting an angry argument.
Perhaps it is repentance.
Perhaps it is calling somebody.
Perhaps it is listening.
Perhaps it is apologizing for the joke you thought was harmless.
Perhaps it is teaching your children something healthier than what you inherited.
Perhaps it is refusing to forward the degrading meme.
Perhaps it is defending someone when everybody else expects you to laugh.
Perhaps it is looking into the face of someone you were conditioned to distrust and remembering:
Image-bearer.
And perhaps the hardest person to confront today is not “the racist people out there.”
Perhaps it is the person in the mirror.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't perform for anybody.
Be honest before Christ.
Someone who thinks people never change may need to see evidence of grace.
There should be no shame in admitting that healing is still happening.
Grace works in real people with real scars.
Not because sharing a Facebook article makes somebody righteous.
It doesn't.
Someone may have been wounded by racism and quietly wondering whether Christianity has anything better to offer.
Someone may need to discover that Jesus does not belong to one race.
Not merely because you agree with it today, but because prejudice has a way of hiding behind new language. Return to the Scriptures. Test your heart again.
But I also want to ask something deeper of those who believe this work should continue.
Gospel ministry requires people willing to carry it.
Some preach.
Some write.
Some pray.
Some share.
Some give.
Some quietly help make it possible for the message to reach the next person.
But please understand this biblically.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Christian generosity is supposed to come from a willing heart. Paul wrote:
“μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs
“not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
2 Corinthians 9:7.
So if you support Gospel Warrior, do it freely.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you believe spreading Scripture, Gospel-centered discipleship, Christian resources, and the message of Jesus is worth supporting.

Financially supporting faithful Gospel work can be one way we use what God has entrusted to us for His glory—but giving must never become a transaction in which we imagine we are purchasing God's favor.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Let truth travel farther than hatred.
Let Scripture speak louder than stereotypes.
Let the Gospel go where prejudice has lived for generations.
Because racism will never finally be defeated merely by teaching people which words they are forbidden to say.
The heart itself must change.
And only Jesus Christ can take a heart filled with pride, hatred, bitterness, fear, tribal superiority, and inherited darkness...
and make it new.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast about the color of the skin covering their body.
We boast in Christ.
At the throne, redeemed humanity will not be celebrating which race conquered the others.
Every nation, tribe, people, and language will be looking toward the same Lamb.
So the next time you are tempted to judge someone because their skin does not look like yours, remember something eternity will make impossible to forget:
The skin you almost used as a reason to despise them is wrapped around a human being God commanded you to love—and a soul for whom Christ is mighty to save.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A SINGLE CHRISTIAN HAVE MANY BOYFRIENDS OR GIRLFRIENDS?
paragraphs:
CAN A SINGLE CHRISTIAN HAVE MANY BOYFRIENDS OR GIRLFRIENDS?
You may call it “keeping your options open.” But what happens when several hearts are being held by promises you were never prepared to keep?
There is a kind of heartbreak nobody talks about in church.
It happens before marriage.
Sometimes before an official relationship even exists.
Two people talk every night.
They pray together.
They share things they have never told anyone else.
“Good morning” becomes expected.
“Good night” becomes intimate.
There are pet names. Jealousy. Flirting. Emotional dependence. Private promises. Future plans disguised as jokes.
One person says, “We’re not technically together.”
But the other person’s heart has already started living as though they are.
Then comes the revelation.
There is someone else.
Maybe two.
Maybe three.
And suddenly the sentence appears:
“But I’m single. I’m allowed to talk to whoever I want.”
Legally? Perhaps.
Technically? Perhaps.
But the Christian life has never been merely about asking:
“How much can I technically get away with before it becomes sin?”
Jesus calls us to something much deeper.
The question is not merely, “Am I officially single?”
The question is:
“Am I loving these people in a way that looks like Jesus?”
And that changes everything.
Because Scripture does not contain a verse saying, “Thou shalt not have three people you are casually dating.”
The modern boyfriend-girlfriend system did not exist in exactly the form we know today.
So we have to be careful.
We must not manufacture commandments God did not give.
But neither should we pretend Scripture has nothing to say simply because the Bible does not use our modern dating vocabulary.
Scripture gives us something far more penetrating than a dating rulebook.
It gives us the character of Christ.
And once His character enters the conversation, our excuses begin losing oxygen.
Paul writes:
The Greek is painfully direct:
ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται
Hē agapē tō plēsion kakon ouk ergazetai.
In context, the idea is that love does not work evil or harm toward one’s neighbor.
Notice what Paul does not say.
Love does no harm only after engagement.
Love does no harm only after becoming Facebook official.
Love does no harm only after exclusivity has been verbally established.
No.
Christian love asks what our behavior is doing to another human being.

That means a single Christian may certainly meet people, develop friendships, discern compatibility, and—in cultures where this is normal—even go on early dates with more than one person before exclusivity has been established.
That fact by itself is not automatically sexual immorality or adultery.
We should not call something sin merely because we personally dislike it.
But there is an enormous difference between honest non-exclusive discernment and collecting romantic attachments.
There is a difference between:
“I’m getting to know people, and everyone understands that I have not entered an exclusive relationship,”
and:
“I am making several people feel chosen because I enjoy being desired by all of them.”
One can involve transparent discernment.
The other can become deception dressed in the language of freedom.
And maybe that is where this article just touched a nerve.
Because perhaps you do not have several boyfriends.
You just have several people who think they might eventually become your boyfriend.
Perhaps you do not call them girlfriends.
You simply give multiple women enough emotional intimacy to keep them hoping.
One gets your late-night vulnerability.
One gets your flirting.
One gets your physical affection.
One gets your spiritual conversations.
One gets your “maybe someday.”
And whenever somebody asks what this actually is, you retreat behind the safest sentence available:
“We’re just friends.”
But are you treating them like friends?
That is the harder question.
Because you can remain technically single while becoming emotionally dishonest.
You can avoid the word “relationship” while enjoying nearly every emotional privilege of one.
You can keep someone close enough to feed your loneliness but far enough away that you never have to become responsible for what you are awakening in their heart.
And Christians are not called merely to avoid technical adultery.
We are called to walk in truth.
Paul says in Ephesians 4:25:
“Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor.”
The Greek phrase includes:
λαλεῖτε ἀλήθειαν
laleite alētheian—
speak truth.
Truthfulness is bigger than avoiding explicit lies.
You can deceive someone without saying the sentence, “I am lying to you.”
Sometimes deception happens through carefully maintained ambiguity.
You know they think they are special.
You know they believe this is heading somewhere.
You know they would be devastated if they saw how you speak to somebody else.
Yet you keep receiving their affection because it feels good to be wanted.
That deserves examination before God.
Not because attraction is evil.
Not because singleness is shameful.
Not because dating is dirty.
But because people are not emotional vending machines created to dispense affirmation whenever loneliness hits.
They bear the image of God.
And if you are serious about following Jesus, you cannot ask only:
“What am I allowed to take from this relationship?”
You eventually have to ask:
“How can I honor this person before Christ?”
Paul gives another astonishingly practical command:
“Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.” — Romans 12:10
The Greek word translated “honor” is:
τιμή — timē
It carries the sense of honor, value, esteem.
Imagine what Christian dating would become if that became the question.
Not:
“How many options can I maintain?”
Not:
“How many people find me attractive?”
Not:
“How long can I keep this undefined?”
But:
“Am I treating this person as someone of value before God?”
That question reaches the man secretly maintaining five flirtatious conversations.
It reaches the woman keeping three men emotionally attached because she fears choosing the wrong one.
It reaches the person who says, “I never promised anything,” while knowing perfectly well that their behavior communicated something their mouth carefully avoided saying.
It also reaches the wounded Christian doing this because somebody once did it to them.
Maybe you were abandoned.
Maybe you were cheated on.
Maybe someone promised forever and disappeared.
Maybe now you keep several people around because having options feels safer than vulnerability.
If one leaves, there is another.
If one rejects you, somebody else still wants you.
If one stops texting, another notification protects you from silence.
It feels like power.
But sometimes what looks like romantic freedom is actually fear wearing expensive perfume.
You are not choosing several people because you love deeply.
You are keeping several doors open because you are terrified of standing in one doorway long enough to be rejected.
Jesus sees that wound too.
And His answer is not humiliation.
His answer is truth and grace.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not the story of morally impressive people learning better dating etiquette.
It is the story of sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have played with hearts.
Maybe you have lied.
Maybe you have used somebody physically.
Maybe you have kept someone emotionally attached while secretly pursuing someone else.
Maybe you crossed sexual boundaries and then used “we aren’t married” as permission.
Scripture does speak clearly about sexual holiness.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is:
πορνεία — porneia
In New Testament usage, it refers broadly to sexual immorality.
Then Paul continues with something our culture desperately needs to hear:
“that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter.” — 1 Thessalonians 4:6
Sexual holiness is therefore not merely about rules concerning your own body.
It also concerns how your desires affect another person.
God cares about bodies.
God cares about hearts.
God cares about truth.
God cares about the person you are touching.
God cares about the person you are promising yourself to.
God cares about the person whose affection you are receiving.
And God cares about you.
That is why biblical boundaries are not evidence that God hates romance.
They are evidence that God understands its power.
Sexual and romantic intimacy can bind memories to people.
It can awaken expectations.
It can produce profound vulnerability.
It can leave wounds that continue speaking years after a relationship ends.
So should single Christians date several people?
Here is the careful biblical answer:

Scripture does not explicitly prohibit a single Christian from initially getting to know more than one potential spouse when there has been no commitment to exclusivity and everyone involved understands the situation honestly.
But Scripture absolutely confronts deception, selfishness, sexual immorality, exploitation, dishonesty, manipulation, and failure to love our neighbor.

Therefore, if “having many boyfriends or girlfriends” means maintaining multiple simultaneous committed romantic relationships while each person reasonably believes they have your exclusive devotion, deception has entered the picture.
If it means keeping several people romantically attached without honest disclosure because you enjoy the attention, you need to examine your heart.
If it means sexual involvement outside marriage, Scripture calls you toward sexual holiness.

And if it simply means transparently meeting different people while prayerfully discerning marriage before making an exclusive commitment, Christians should be careful not to create a commandment where Scripture itself does not give one.
But there is still another question.
A more uncomfortable one.
Why do you need so many people wanting you?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit there for a moment.
Why does losing romantic attention frighten you so much?
Why does an unanswered message make you feel invisible?
Why does being desired make you feel valuable?
Why does being alone make you wonder whether something is wrong with you?
Maybe the deepest issue was never how many people you are allowed to date.
Maybe the deepest issue is that you have been asking human affection to tell you something only God can finally settle.
“Am I worth loving?”
And into that ache comes Jesus Christ.
Not another match.
Not another notification.
Not another admirer.
Jesus.
The One who knew the worst chapter before He called your name.
The One who does not discover your hidden history after falling in love with a polished version of you.
He already knows.
And still the Gospel says:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
While we were still sinners.
Not after the profile was cleaned.
Not after the secret conversations were deleted.
Not after the lust disappeared.
Not after you finally became marriage material.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not excuse sin.
It destroys our excuse for remaining in it.
Grace is not Jesus whispering, “Keep using people. It doesn’t matter.”
Grace is Jesus saying:
“Come out of hiding. I paid too much for you to keep calling your chains freedom.”
Repentance is not self-hatred.
The New Testament word is:
μετάνοια — metanoia
It speaks of repentance, a turning of mind and heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Real grace can produce real change.
So perhaps today your repentance looks painfully practical.
You stop maintaining romantic backups.
You tell somebody the truth.
You apologize without demanding forgiveness.
You end the sexual relationship you know dishonors Christ.
You stop flirting with someone you have no intention of pursuing.
You stop calling manipulation “being friendly.”
You stop demanding relationship privileges from someone you refuse to commit to.
You stop treating people like insurance policies against loneliness.
And perhaps, for the first time in years, you become single in the deepest sense.
Not abandoned.
Not unwanted.
Not forgotten.
Simply no longer using another human being to prove that you matter.
Then you discover something terrifyingly beautiful:
Jesus is still there.
Maybe you recognize yourself in these words.
Do not hide.
There is no trophy for pretending.
The Church should be a place where sinners can step into the light and discover that Jesus still saves sinners.
And maybe someone on your Facebook friends list desperately needs this truth.
Because loneliness has a strange ability to make yesterday’s convictions negotiable tomorrow night.
And there is more than content behind this mission.
If you are tired of shallow Christianity...
If you want Scripture that confronts you and grace that brings you home...
If you want biblical nourishment, accountability, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual sharpening centered on Jesus Christ...
Stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the person who says they do not believe.
But before you leave, remember the question with which we began.
Can a single Christian have many boyfriends or girlfriends?
Maybe the better question is no longer:
“How many hearts can I hold without technically sinning?”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, how do I hold another person's heart without forgetting that it belongs first to You?”
Because someday, the person whose attention you are enjoying today may become somebody else's husband.
Somebody else's wife.
Somebody else's answered prayer.
Treat them accordingly.
Love does not need ambiguity to survive.
Truth does not need manipulation to keep someone interested.
And you do not need a collection of human hearts to prove that yours has value.
At the cross, Jesus already settled the question of how far divine love was willing to go to rescue sinners.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Tell the truth where truth has been avoided.
Release the people you have been keeping as options.
Forgive where you have been wounded.
Receive grace where shame has been screaming.
And let Christ teach you how to love without using, desire without possessing, discern without deceiving, and walk away without destroying.
Your romantic history does not have to become the final name of your story.
The chapter you are ashamed to reread may become the very page where Jesus begins writing redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Herodias Wanted the Preacher Silenced Because He Wouldn’t Bless Her Relationship
paragraphs: Herodias Wanted the Preacher Silenced Because He Wouldn’t Bless Her Relationship
She didn’t hate John because he was cruel. She hated what his words forced everyone to confront: some relationships can feel worth defending and still stand condemned by the Word of God.
There are sermons people applaud.
And then there are sermons people want buried.
John the Baptist preached one of the shortest sermons imaginable to a powerful man.
No stage lights.
No carefully engineered introduction.
No attempt to protect his influence.
No rebranding of sin so nobody important would become uncomfortable.
Just a prophet, a king, a forbidden relationship—and one sentence that eventually helped put John’s head on a platter.
Mark records his confrontation with Herod Antipas:
“For John had said unto Herod, It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother’s wife.” — Mark 6:18, KJV
Matthew preserves essentially the same confrontation:
“For John said unto him, It is not lawful for thee to have her.” — Matthew 14:4, KJV
The Greek is brutally direct:
Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.
Ouk exestin soi echein tēn gynaika tou adelphou sou.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
That matters.
John was not merely saying, “I personally disagree with your relationship.”
He was not offering a competing lifestyle preference.
He was declaring that Herod did not possess moral permission to continue as though God approved what God’s law condemned.
And Herodias hated him for it.
Mark 6:19 says:
“Therefore Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him; but she could not.”
The Greek is even more vivid:
Ἡ δὲ Ἡρῳδιὰς ἐνεῖχεν αὐτῷ
The verb ἐνέχω — enechō carries the sense of holding something against someone, bearing hostility, nursing a grievance.
John had become a living reminder of something Herodias desperately wanted treated as acceptable.
So understand the headline correctly.
Scripture does not record Herodias walking up to John and literally saying, “Bless my relationship.”
It tells us something more serious.
John publicly declared that the relationship was unlawful before God, and Herodias wanted the man making that declaration destroyed.
She could imprison the preacher.
But she could not make his message become false.
And that is where this ancient scandal becomes frighteningly modern.
Because sometimes we do not actually want God to tell us whether something is holy.
We have already decided we want it.
We simply want God to approve the decision afterward.
We want heaven’s signature beneath a contract we wrote without Him.
We want Scripture to comfort us without correcting us.
We want Jesus as Savior while quietly negotiating whether He must also be Lord.
And when the Word touches the one thing we refuse to surrender…
something inside us starts looking for ways to silence the preacher.
Maybe you have never imprisoned a prophet.
Maybe you have never demanded anyone’s execution.
But perhaps you stopped listening to the Christian friend who challenged you.
Perhaps you unfollowed the pastor who preached the verse you did not want to hear.
Perhaps you found another teacher who told you exactly what you hoped God would say.
Perhaps you learned to call conviction “judgment” whenever conviction came too close to the thing you loved.
Or maybe your battlefield is not a relationship at all.
Maybe it is money.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Adultery.
Gossip.
An unforgiving heart.
Secret messages your spouse would be devastated to discover.
A business practice you know is dishonest.
An addiction hidden behind a respectable Christian face.
A relationship with God maintained publicly while privately you are becoming someone you barely recognize.
This is where Herodias stops being merely a notorious woman in an ancient palace.
Her story becomes a mirror.
Because the terrifying question is not merely, “How could Herodias hate John so much?”
The terrifying question is:
What truth about my own life am I tempted to silence because obedience would cost me something I do not want to surrender?
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because there may be something you have been asking God to bless that He has actually been asking you to surrender.
John understood something much of modern Christianity is tempted to forget:
Love does not require lying to people about sin.
The same Bible that declares that “all have sinned” also declares that God loved the world enough to give His Son.
Biblical truth and biblical love are not enemies.
They meet perfectly at the cross.
The cross does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross says your sin mattered so much that Christ died—and that God loved sinners so deeply that Christ willingly came to save them.
This is why genuine Christian preaching cannot merely tell people, “Follow your heart.”
Scripture warns:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9, KJV
And Jesus does not merely decorate the desires we already possess.
He calls us to Himself.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” — Matthew 16:24, KJV
That word “deny” comes from the Greek ἀπαρνέομαι — aparneomai.
This is not Jesus asking for a minor adjustment.
Following Christ involves surrendering our claim to ultimate self-rule.
That is offensive to the flesh.
Because we want a Jesus who saves us without contradicting us.
A Jesus who forgives but never commands.
A Jesus who comforts but never confronts.
A Jesus who carries the cross so we never have to carry ours.
But that Jesus is not the Jesus of Scripture.
The biblical Jesus could look at a woman caught in devastating sexual sin without joining the crowd determined to destroy her—and still tell her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Look at those words.
Grace did not throw the stone.
Truth did not call the sin righteousness.
Jesus did neither of the cruel things human beings so often do.
He did not crush the sinner.
And He did not redefine the sin.
He offered mercy and called for transformation.
That is Gospel grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved.
Power to come home.
And maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear tonight.
Your scandal does not have to become your identity.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sexual history is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
Your affair is not beyond His forgiveness.
Your divorce is not beyond His compassion.
Your addiction is not beyond His power.
Your secret is not too filthy for His mercy.
Your hypocrisy is not too complicated for repentance.
Your years of running have not exhausted the invitation of Christ.
But grace is not God pretending darkness is light.
Grace is God entering our darkness to rescue us from it.
That is why Jesus began His public proclamation with a word modern ears sometimes resist:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite.
“Repent.”
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness by becoming good enough.
You cannot.
Neither can I.
Repentance is turning toward the God whose grace meets sinners precisely because they cannot save themselves.
The Gospel is not:
Clean yourself up, and perhaps Jesus will accept you.
The Gospel is:
You could never cleanse yourself from sin, so Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
John the Baptist could expose Herod’s sin.
But John could not die as Herod’s Savior.
Jesus could.
John could point at darkness.
Jesus came as Light.
John could announce repentance.
Jesus could purchase redemption.
And here lies one of the saddest possibilities inside Herod’s story.
Mark tells us that Herod actually feared John, recognized him as righteous and holy, protected him for a time, and even listened to him.
Think about that.
Herod listened.
He was disturbed.
He was fascinated.
He knew something about John was different.
And still the moment came when protecting his pride mattered more than responding rightly to truth.
At his birthday banquet, Herod made a reckless oath after Herodias’s daughter danced before the guests.
She consulted her mother.
The request returned:
“The head of John the Baptist.”
And eventually the voice Herod had been listening to was carried into the room on a platter.
What a terrifying picture.
A man can listen to truth repeatedly and still never surrender to it.
You can enjoy sermons and remain unchanged.
You can save Christian videos and remain unrepentant.
You can know worship songs by heart while protecting the very sin Christ keeps touching.
You can cry during an altar call and still walk home clutching the chains Jesus told you to release.
You can admire the preacher…
and still silence the message.
That is why this article cannot end with Herodias.
It has to come to you.
And me.
What have we been protecting from God?
What relationship?
What habit?
What resentment?
What secret?
What ambition?
What version of ourselves?
What would happen if instead of asking, “How can I make Scripture agree with me?” we finally whispered:
“Lord Jesus, make me agree with You.”
That prayer can hurt.
Because surrender often feels like death before it feels like freedom.
But Christ never calls us away from sin because He wants less life for us.
Sin promises life and eventually produces slavery.
Jesus calls slaves into freedom.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming because you already know what God has been confronting.
You do not need another argument.
You need courage to surrender.
Then surrender.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one more secret meeting.
Not after one more night.
Not after you clean yourself up enough to feel worthy.
Come to Christ now.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess what you have done.
Stop defending what He has exposed.
Ask for mercy.
Trust Christ.
Seek godly help where necessary.
Make restitution where biblical wisdom requires it.
Walk away from what must be abandoned.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the mud.
Run back to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of flawless people proving how righteous they are.
It is the story of guilty people discovering that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Peter had scandal.
The Samaritan woman had scandal.
The Corinthian church had scandal.
Paul carried a past stained with persecution and blood.
Yet the Gospel kept doing what the Gospel does.
Grace entered stories sin seemed to have ruined.
And Jesus rewrote everything.
That does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
It means sin no longer gets the final word over the person who belongs to Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction draws us toward repentance.
Condemnation tells us to hide from God.
The Gospel tells us to come into the light because Christ has already done what sinners could never do for themselves.
Do not merely admire John’s courage.
Ask whether you have been behaving like Herodias toward the truth.
Do not merely condemn Herod’s compromise.
Ask where compromise has been growing inside you.
Do not merely praise Jesus for saving sinners.
Ask whether you have actually surrendered to Him.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest enough to say it.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that repentance is not the end of a person’s story.
It can be the beginning of coming home.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Let sharing become ministry rather than performance.
We glorify God fundamentally through Christ-centered faith and obedience.
You are helping truth travel.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior by following the page for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend quietly losing faith.
Invite the Christian who has become spiritually numb.
Invite the person ashamed to return to church.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who thinks their scandal has disqualified them forever.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical resources into the hands of people who need them.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is trying desperately to silence the voice telling them to repent.
But perhaps what feels like an interruption is actually mercy.
Perhaps conviction is not God abandoning you.
Perhaps it is evidence that you are still being called home.
Herodias wanted the preacher silenced because his message threatened what she wanted to keep.
Herod listened to the preacher but ultimately surrendered to something else.
And John lost his head without changing his message.
But even John was never the hero of the Gospel.
Jesus is.
The Lamb of God John had pointed toward eventually walked toward His own execution.
John's head was placed on a platter because powerful sinners wanted his voice silenced.
Jesus was nailed to a cross according to God's redemptive purpose, bearing sin for sinners.
And death could not silence Him.
The tomb could not hold Him.
The scandal of your past cannot overpower His grace.
So stop asking Jesus merely to bless the story you have already written.
Give Him the pen.
Give Him the relationship.
Give Him the addiction.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the hidden room.
Give Him the reputation you have exhausted yourself protecting.
Give Him the future.
Give Him you.
Because there is something infinitely better than getting God to approve everything we want.
There is being forgiven, redeemed, transformed, and finally learning to want Him.
The truth you are most tempted to silence may be the very mercy Jesus is using to call you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: If God Hates Evil, Why Is He Still Letting Tomorrow Come?
paragraphs: If God Hates Evil, Why Is He Still Letting Tomorrow Come?

The terrifying answer to “Why doesn’t God end evil today?” is that the moment God finally removes every trace of rebellion from His creation, none of us gets to stand before Him pretending evil was only something other people did.
There is a question people whisper beside hospital beds.
They scream it over graves.
They ask it after watching another child suffer, another family collapse, another innocent person become somebody else’s victim.
Sometimes they ask it while staring at a ceiling at 3:17 in the morning because the person who hurt them is sleeping peacefully while they are still carrying what that person did.
And sometimes the question is much simpler.
“If God is good… why doesn’t He just end evil today?”
Not someday.
Not after another sermon.

Not after another generation of funerals, wars, abuse, trafficking, betrayal, cancer, murder, corruption, addiction, exploitation, and children learning far too young how cruel human beings can become.
Today.
If God is really God, why not stop it all before the sun rises tomorrow?
It sounds like an accusation.
But underneath it is often something else.
Pain.
And Scripture never requires wounded people to pretend that evil does not hurt.
The Bible contains people crying, “How long?”
The prophets grieved over injustice. The psalmists asked why wicked people seemed to prosper. Habakkuk looked at violence and demanded an answer from God.
And Jesus Himself stood outside the tomb of Lazarus and wept.
Christianity does not ask you to call evil good.
It tells you something far more astonishing:
God hates evil more than you do.
But that creates an uncomfortable question.
Why is it still here?
Maybe the answer begins with something most of us would rather not admit.
When we imagine God “ending evil,” we normally imagine Him ending the evil out there.
Stop the murderer.
Stop the abuser.
Stop the dictator.
Stop the trafficker.
Stop the corrupt official.
Stop the person who destroyed my family.
Stop the person who betrayed me.
Stop them.
And certainly, Scripture teaches that God will judge wickedness. Biblical Christianity offers no final universe in which cruelty simply gets away with everything.
But there is a problem.
Where exactly should God draw the line?
At murder?
Jesus took us deeper and confronted hatred.
At adultery?
Jesus confronted lust within the heart.
At theft?
What about greed?
At deception?
Then what happens to our lies?
At cruelty?
What about the words we used deliberately because we knew exactly where they would hurt?
At pride?
At envy?
At unforgiveness?
At selfishness?
At the secret sin nobody knows exists because we became very good at looking Christian in public?
Suddenly the question changes.
“God, why don't You destroy evil?”
becomes…
“God, when You destroy evil, what happens to the evil in me?”
That is where the question becomes frighteningly personal.
Scripture does not divide humanity into innocent people over here and evil people over there.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The religious.
The rebellious.
The respected.
The disgraced.
The person in prison and the person preaching behind a pulpit.
Sin differs terribly in its earthly consequences. Saying everyone is sinful does not mean every sin causes equal damage or that victims and perpetrators are morally interchangeable.
They are not.
Justice matters.
Victims matter.
Accountability matters.
But before the holiness of God, none of us can say, “There is absolutely no rebellion in me. Judge everyone else.”
And now we are getting dangerously close to the answer.
Peter wrote about people wondering why God's promised judgment seemed delayed.
His words in Greek are striking:
οὐ βραδύνει κύριος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας… ἀλλὰ μακροθυμεῖ εἰς ὑμᾶς
“The Lord is not slow concerning the promise… but is patient toward you.”
That word matters:
μακροθυμεῖ — makrothymei.
It carries the idea of patience, longsuffering, restraint.
God's apparent delay is not evidence that He has failed to notice evil.
Peter continues:
μὴ βουλόμενός τινας ἀπολέσθαι ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετάνοιαν χωρῆσαι
“…not wishing any to perish, but all to come to repentance.” — 2 Peter 3:9.
Read that again.
What looks like delay can be mercy.
Tomorrow exists because repentance is still being offered.
That does not answer every philosophical question surrounding suffering. Christianity never gives us permission to explain every individual tragedy by casually announcing why God allowed it.
We often do not know.
But Scripture does tell us something about the apparent delay of final judgment.
God has appointed judgment.
And until that day, mercy is still calling sinners home.
Which means the frightening possibility is this:
You may have asked God why He hasn't judged the wicked yet…
while living inside the very mercy that has delayed judgment for you.
Think about Saul of Tarsus.
There was a time when Christians might reasonably have prayed for God to stop him.
Saul persecuted followers of Jesus. Acts tells us he approved of Stephen's death and ravaged the church.
Imagine being a Christian mother hearing that Saul was approaching your city.
You would not know Romans was coming.
You would not know Galatians was coming.
You would not know Philippians was coming.
You would not know that the persecutor would become the persecuted apostle proclaiming the Christ he once opposed.
You would only know that Saul was dangerous.
Then Jesus met him.
Grace interrupted his story.
The enemy became a brother.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The man Christians feared became a man willing to suffer for the name he once tried to silence.
What if God had answered someone's prayer for Saul by simply destroying Saul?
There would have been justice.
But there would not have been Paul's redemption.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly why that matters.
Because you have a past too.
Maybe yours was never public.
Maybe nobody made a documentary about your worst decisions.
Maybe your scandal never became gossip.
But you know.
You remember the version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever meets.
The addiction.
The affair.
The pornography.
The rage.
The dishonesty.
The years wasted.
The person you wounded.
The marriage you almost destroyed.
The secret double life.
The faith you abandoned.
The promises you made to God and broke before the week was over.
And perhaps you are still carrying something you cannot undo.
Listen carefully.
God's answer to evil was never pretending evil did not matter.
Look at the cross.
Christianity places at its center an innocent Man publicly tortured and executed.
Jesus does not minimize evil.
He enters the world where evil is happening.
He is betrayed.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
And from the darkness of Golgotha comes the staggering announcement of the Gospel:
God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
The cross tells us sin is worse than we imagined because redemption required the blood of Christ.
And the cross tells us God's love is greater than we imagined because Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
This is why Christianity cannot answer suffering with a cold sentence like, “Everything happens for a reason,” and then walk away.
The center of Christianity is not an explanation written on a chalkboard.
It is Jesus Christ hanging on a cross.
God entered suffering.
And then something happened on the third day.
The tomb opened.
Jesus rose.
And resurrection changed the ending.
That matters enormously when asking why evil continues today, because Christianity does not teach that evil continues forever.
God's patience has an expiration known to God.
Peter's very next words after describing God's patience warn that the Day of the Lord will come.
Justice delayed is not justice cancelled.
Scripture moves toward a day when Christ returns, evil is judged, death is defeated, and creation is made new.
Revelation gives us one of Scripture's most breathtaking promises: God will dwell with His people, wipe away their tears, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
Not managed.
Not temporarily reduced.
Gone.
The Bible's ending is not humanity escaping creation while evil wins.
It is God making all things new.
That means the Christian answer to evil has two words that must never be separated:
judgment and mercy.
If there were no final judgment, victims could reasonably ask whether evil ultimately mattered.
If there were no mercy, sinners like us would have no hope.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
And suddenly another thought becomes almost unbearable.
Every morning you wake up in a world where evil still exists is also a morning when the door of repentance has not yet closed.
The breath entering your lungs is mercy.
The heartbeat you barely notice is mercy.
Another opportunity to confess is mercy.
Another chance to forgive is mercy.
Another opportunity to make restitution where possible is mercy.
Another moment to turn from secret sin is mercy.
Another opportunity to surrender to Jesus Christ is mercy.
We keep asking:
“God, when will You finally do something about evil?”
And from Calvary comes the answer:
“I already have.”
And from the empty tomb:
“I am not finished.”
And from the promise of Christ's return:
“I will.”
Past.
Present.
Future.
At the cross, Jesus broke sin's claim upon everyone who belongs to Him.
Through His Spirit, He is transforming His people now.
At His return, evil and death will not have the final word.
So why doesn't God end evil today?
Part of the biblical answer is terrifyingly beautiful:
Because today is still a day of mercy.
Today another Saul can become Paul.
Today another prodigal can come home.
Today another addict can cry out for freedom.
Today another hypocrite can stop pretending.
Today another wounded believer can discover that suffering did not make Jesus abandon them.
Today another person who thought they were too dirty for God can discover what grace actually means.
Today…
maybe you.
And this is where this article stops being theology about somebody else.
What if God is giving you another day?
Not another day to hide.
Another day to come home.
You can fool followers.
You can fool family.
You can fool church people.
You can even learn enough Christian vocabulary to fool yourself.
But you cannot fool Jesus.
And strangely enough, that may be the best news you have heard all day.
Because the Christ who sees everything is still calling you.
Repentance in the New Testament is captured by the word μετάνοια — metanoia: repentance, a turning of mind and life toward God.
Not religious performance.
Not cleaning yourself up sufficiently so Jesus will finally tolerate you.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
Receive grace you could never purchase.
And then let that grace begin changing the places you once protected from God.
Maybe you have been furious because God has not ended the evil that wounded you.
Your wound matters.
Seeking justice is not a failure of faith.
Getting safe from an abusive situation is not rebellion against God.
Forgiveness does not require calling evil good, and reconciliation is not identical to forgiveness; trust may require genuine repentance, truth, safety, and time.
Jesus does not ask victims to pretend they were never wounded.
The risen Christ still carried scars.
Scars and resurrection occupied the same body.
Think about that.
Healing does not require pretending the wound never happened.
Jesus can redeem a story without rewriting history into something painless.
He does something greater.
He refuses to let evil write the final sentence.
That is Gospel Warrior's heartbeat:
Not because scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin didn't matter.
Not because suffering wasn't devastating.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He turns persecutors into apostles.
Prodigals into sons and daughters coming home.
Shame into testimony.
Bondage into freedom.
Condemnation into forgiveness.
Graves into resurrection ground.
And sinners into saints—not because they finally became impressive enough for God, but because Jesus saves.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished religious response.
Be honest.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another hurting person reading.
Then think of one person who has asked, “If God is real, why is there so much evil?”
Not for an algorithm.
For a person.
Send it privately to someone whose faith is hanging by a thread.
I want to say this carefully because biblical truth matters more than fundraising:
Salvation is by grace. Christian giving is to be willing rather than coerced; Paul says it should not be given “reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary financial generosity can genuinely be an act through which Christians honor God and help Gospel ministry continue.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Leave a meaningful comment.
Pray for the people who will read it.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is asking:
“Why hasn't God ended evil?”
Maybe what they do not yet realize is that the same God who promises to end evil is holding open the door of mercy right now.
And one day that door will no longer be called today.
So while it is today…
come home.
Not to religion.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Come to Jesus Christ.
The cross says your evil is serious.
The blood says forgiveness was costly.
The empty tomb says death is defeated.
God's patience says repentance is still possible.
And Christ's promised return says evil does not get the last word.
Maybe God hasn't ended the story yet because grace is still writing names into its final chapters.
And maybe tonight…
He is calling yours.
The world is waiting for God to end evil, while heaven is giving sinners one more day to run into the arms of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Sin You Keep Calling a Struggle May Have Become Something You’ve Decided to Protect
paragraphs: The Sin You Keep Calling a Struggle May Have Become Something You’ve Decided to Protect
There is a terrifying difference between falling while you are fighting sin… and quietly arranging your life so the sin you say you hate never has to die.
There is a question most of us would rather never be asked.
Not because we do not know the answer.
Because somewhere underneath the worship songs, the Bible verses, the church attendance, the Christian posts, the promises to God, and the repeated prayers for freedom…
we may already know.
What if the sin you keep calling your “struggle” is no longer merely something you are struggling against?
What if, somewhere along the way, you started protecting it?
Read that slowly.
Because there is a difference between a wounded Christian crawling away from temptation and a Christian secretly leaving the door unlocked so temptation can come back tonight.
There is a difference between falling into a pit and furnishing it.
There is a difference between being ambushed and keeping the enemy’s phone number.
There is a difference between saying, “God, please deliver me,” while removing access to sin…
and saying, “God, please deliver me,” while carefully preserving every pathway that takes you back to it.
And perhaps that is why Paul’s words in Romans 13 are so painfully direct.
He does not speak as though darkness is something Christians should negotiate with.
He writes:
“The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near.”
Then comes the response:
“ἀποβαλώμεθα οὖν τὰ ἔργα τοῦ σκότους…”
Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness.
Not rename them.
Not domesticate them.
Not explain them until they stop frightening us.
Cast them off.
And then Paul reaches the devastating conclusion of Romans 13:14:
“ἀλλὰ ἐνδύσασθε τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν μὴ ποιεῖσθε εἰς ἐπιθυμίας.”
Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh with respect to its desires.
That word deserves our attention.
“πρόνοιαν” — pronoian.
Provision.
Forethought.
Planning ahead.
Paul is not merely confronting the sinful act after it happens.
He reaches backward into the architecture surrounding the sin.
The planning.
The access.
The environment.
The little arrangements that make tomorrow night’s failure easier.
In other words, Scripture does not merely ask, “Did you sin?”
It forces us to confront another question:
“What have you been arranging so that this sin can survive?”
That question hurts.
Because sometimes what we call weakness is accompanied by preparation.
You deleted the conversation…
but memorized the number.
You confessed the pornography…
but kept the private browser, hidden account, unfiltered device, and late-night isolation that continually lead you back.
You said the relationship was pulling you away from Christ…
but kept enough emotional access to reopen it whenever loneliness became stronger than conviction.
You told God you were finished with the gossip…
but still sit eagerly in conversations where another person’s reputation becomes entertainment.
You asked Jesus to heal your bitterness…
while replaying the offense every night because anger has begun to feel strangely comforting.
You prayed for freedom from envy…
then continued feeding yourself an endless stream of other people’s lives until gratitude became almost impossible.
You asked God to free you from sexual immorality…
but kept flirting with the very boundary you begged Him to strengthen.
You said you wanted sobriety…
but preserved the relationships, locations, routines, or secret supply that made relapse conveniently available.
Different sins.
Same frightening possibility.
We can ask God to kill what we keep feeding.
And then wonder why it refuses to die.
Please understand something important before shame twists this message into something Scripture does not say.
The existence of temptation does not mean you are fake.
Being tempted is not the same thing as consenting to sin.
A Christian can genuinely hate a sin and still fall terribly.
A Christian can relapse.
A Christian can stumble repeatedly.
A Christian can cry after doing the very thing he promised God he would never do again.
The Bible is brutally realistic about human weakness.
Peter denied Jesus after insisting he would die for Him.
David committed horrifying sins.
The disciples repeatedly misunderstood Christ.
And Paul himself describes the agonizing conflict with sin in Romans 7.
Christian maturity is not sinless perfection.
Our hope has never been that we become morally impressive enough for God to tolerate us.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
But grace must never be twisted into permission to preserve what crucified our Savior.
The frightening question is not simply whether you have fallen.
The question is what you do with the road that led you there.
Do you barricade it?
Or maintain it?
Do you expose the secret?
Or improve the hiding place?
Do you remove the opportunity?
Or merely promise yourself you will be stronger next time?
Do you confess because you want forgiveness while secretly hoping nothing actually has to change?
There is a difference between someone who falls while fleeing temptation…
and someone who continually redesigns life so temptation remains comfortably accessible.
Jesus Himself spoke with shocking seriousness about dealing radically with sin.
In Matthew 5, when speaking about lust, He used the severe imagery of tearing out an eye and cutting off a hand rather than allowing sin to rule us.
Christ was not commanding bodily mutilation.
A removed eye cannot cure a sinful heart.
His language exposes something far deeper:
Do not treat casually what is destroying you.
That is why repentance sometimes looks painfully practical.
Block the number.
Delete the account.
Move the computer.
Stop going there.
Tell somebody.
Confess what secrecy has protected.
Put accountability where privacy became dangerous.
Leave the relationship that continually requires disobedience to sustain it.
Stop calling “discernment” what is actually gossip.
Stop calling lust “just looking.”
Stop calling emotional adultery “just friendship.”
Stop calling unforgiveness “having boundaries” when what you are actually preserving is hatred.
Stop calling greed “ambition.”
Stop calling pride “knowing your worth.”
Stop calling compromise “being human” when you have already decided you will not surrender it.
Not every boundary will look identical for every person.
But repentance eventually becomes visible.
Because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God today.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel guilty enough to behave better.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
For the exposed.
For the person reading this with a secret nobody knows.
For the believer who has prayed the same embarrassed prayer at 2:13 in the morning more times than they can count.
For the person who whispers,
“Jesus… I did it again.”
There is something you need to know.
Christ already knows the room you keep locked.
He knows the search history.
He knows the messages.
He knows what happened on the trip.
He knows the money.
He knows the addiction.
He knows what you watched.
He knows who you touched.
He knows who you hate.
He knows the fantasy you replay.
He knows what happened when everyone thought you were asleep.
He knows the version of you nobody at church has ever met.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is enormous.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He went because sin brings guilt, corruption, slavery, separation, and death.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore judgment for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something human effort could never purchase:
forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new standing before God.
A new heart.
A new Master.
A new direction.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past can be forgiven.”
Grace also teaches us that our old master no longer owns us.
That is why Romans 13 does not end with “try harder.”
Paul says:
“ἐνδύσασθε τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.”
Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
That is the center.
Christ.
Not behavior modification without Christ.
Not shame.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Jesus Christ.
You do not defeat darkness merely by staring harder at darkness.
You come into the light.
You put on Christ.
You fill the spaces previously designed for sin with the things of God.
Prayer where there was secrecy.
Scripture where there was fantasy.
Fellowship where there was isolation.
Confession where there was hiding.
Worship where there was self-indulgence.
Accountability where there was convenient privacy.
Obedience where there was negotiation.
And when you fall?
Run toward Jesus, not away from Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Return.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because Christ does.
First John 1:9 gives believers extraordinary hope: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Notice the Gospel beauty of that.
The answer to hidden sin is not better hiding.
It is coming into the light.
Maybe that is what God is confronting in you right now.
Not merely the sin.
The provision.
The backup plan.
The doorway.
The relationship.
The password.
The bottle.
The app.
The private conversation.
The resentment.
The convenient excuse.
The environment you know makes obedience nearly impossible.
Maybe you have spent months praying:
“Lord, take this away.”
And perhaps tonight another prayer needs to follow:
“Lord, show me what I have been protecting.”
That prayer can become expensive.
Because God may put His finger on something you desperately want to keep.
And suddenly you understand why you kept calling it a struggle.
Calling it a struggle allowed you to mourn it without necessarily surrendering it.
But repentance eventually reaches the keys.
The passwords.
The schedule.
The relationships.
The money.
The habits.
The private room.
The places nobody else can see.
Because Jesus does not merely want the Sunday version of you.
He is Lord over Monday night too.
He is Lord over your phone.
Your body.
Your sexuality.
Your thoughts.
Your finances.
Your anger.
Your relationships.
Your loneliness.
Your browser history.
Your ambitions.
Your wounds.
Your secret life.
Everything.
And surrender may feel like death because, in a very real biblical sense, something is dying.
The old way.
The protected darkness.
The fantasy of belonging to Christ while keeping one private throne for yourself.
But what waits beyond surrender is not emptiness.
It is freedom.
Maybe imperfect freedom at first.
Maybe trembling freedom.
Maybe freedom that still requires accountability, counseling, discipleship, boundaries, tears, difficult conversations, and daily dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
But freedom nonetheless.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
If Scripture is exposing something in you right now, do not waste the moment defending yourself.
Run to Christ.
There is no need to impress the One who already knows everything.
Tell Him the truth.
Maybe your prayer tonight is embarrassingly simple:
“Jesus, I don't just want forgiveness for touching this again. I want to stop protecting the road that keeps taking me back.”
That may be where the war changes.
Not when temptation disappears.
But when you stop helping it find you.
And when you see someone else saying those words, do not interrogate them.
Pray for them.
There are battles people cannot safely explain in a Facebook comment.
Let the Church remember how to carry wounded people toward Jesus instead of turning confession into spectacle.
Not because these words are magical.
Do not make provision for the flesh.
And there may be someone in your life who keeps begging God for freedom while unknowingly—or perhaps knowingly—preserving access to the very thing enslaving them.
Send this privately if that would protect their dignity.
Someone scrolling quietly tonight may be losing a battle nobody knows exists.
Your share may place a biblical warning—and the hope of Jesus Christ—in front of someone who would never admit they went searching for it.

If Gospel Warrior has helped point you toward Christ, consider following and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Stay close for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot donate your way into forgiveness.
You cannot merchandise your way into righteousness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
The call is to repent and believe the Gospel.
So tonight, before another promise…
before another apology…
before another deleted history…
before another tearful “God, this is the last time”…
look around.
What are you still protecting?
What door have you deliberately left unlocked?
What provision have you made for the flesh while praying for the Spirit to give you victory over it?
Bring it into the light.
Destroy the provision.
Run to Jesus.
Because perhaps the greatest evidence that you truly want freedom is not that you never stumble again.
It is that you stop building comfortable places for your chains to live.
And if you fell yesterday, hear the Gospel one more time:
your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Peter's denial did not write his final chapter.
The shame of sinners does not intimidate Christ.
The cross still speaks.
The tomb is still empty.
Grace still calls sinners out of darkness.
Jesus still receives the repentant.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
And Jesus is still worthy of whatever you have been afraid to surrender.
So bring Him the secret.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the version you can explain away.
The real one.
Because the thing you drag into Christ's light no longer has to control you from the darkness.
You keep asking Jesus to break the chain. Tonight, ask Him to show you whether your own hands are still protecting the key.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID VASHTI REFUSE TO COME WHEN THE KING SUMMONED HER?
paragraphs:
WHY DID VASHTI REFUSE TO COME WHEN THE KING SUMMONED HER?
One woman said no. An empire panicked. Another woman would eventually wear her crown. But hidden inside this scandal is a warning about power, pride, fear—and the mysterious providence of God that prepares the way before anyone realizes what He is doing.
There are moments in Scripture that make you wish the Bible had given us one more sentence.
Just one.
One sentence explaining what she was thinking.
One sentence telling us what happened behind those palace doors.
One sentence answering the question people have debated for generations:
Why did Queen Vashti refuse to come?
The banquet had already lasted for days.
Wine was flowing.
Power was on display.
King Ahasuerus had surrounded himself with officials, nobles, servants, luxury, and the visible evidence of an enormous kingdom.
Then, on the seventh day, Scripture tells us that the king's heart was “merry with wine.”
And he gave an order.
Bring the queen.
Not because he needed her counsel.
Not because the empire faced a crisis.
Not because he wanted her opinion.
The text itself gives the stated purpose:
“to show the peoples and the princes her beauty; for she was fair to look on.”
Then comes one of the most explosive sentences in the opening chapter of Esther:
וַתְּמָאֵן הַמַּלְכָּה וַשְׁתִּי לָבוֹא
Vatte-ma'en hammalkah Vashti lavo.
“But Queen Vashti refused to come.”
Esther 1:12.
The Hebrew verb מָאֵן — ma'en carries the straightforward sense of refusing.
She refused.
That is what Scripture says.
And this is where we must be careful, because sometimes people become so hungry to know what the Bible does not reveal that they accidentally turn speculation into revelation.
The biblical text never explicitly tells us why Vashti refused.
It does not tell us that she refused because she was modest.
It does not explicitly say she was being ordered to appear naked.
It does not say she refused because she hated the king.
It does not tell us that she was frightened, sick, angry, humiliated, rebellious, courageous, or making a statement about women's dignity.
Those explanations may appear in interpretations or later traditions, but they should not be preached as though Esther 1 itself says them.
It doesn't.
And sometimes the silence of Scripture is part of the lesson.
Because what Scripture does tell us is already devastating enough.
The king wanted to display her beauty.
Vashti refused.
The king became furious.
And suddenly a private conflict inside a marriage became a political emergency throughout an empire.
Read that again.
One woman refused one command...
and powerful men started worrying about what every other woman might do.

Memucan tells the king that Vashti has not merely wronged the king. He argues that her action will become known among women throughout the kingdom and that wives will begin looking upon their husbands with contempt.
The fear spreads through the room.
“If the queen can refuse the king...
what happens when our wives hear about it?”
And there is something painfully human about that scene.
Power often looks enormous until somebody says no.
Then you discover how frightened power can become.
The king who ruled provinces could not command the response of one woman.
The palace was filled with gold.
The wine was abundant.
The servants obeyed.
The officials bowed.
The empire listened.
But Vashti did not come.
And the man who possessed almost everything discovered that possessing authority does not mean possessing another person's will.
Perhaps that is why this ancient scene still feels strangely modern.
Some of us know what it feels like to be valued more for what people can display than for who we actually are.
Maybe nobody has summoned you into a Persian banquet hall.
But perhaps somebody has treated your appearance as your greatest value.
Perhaps you were useful while you made someone look successful.
Perhaps you were celebrated when you complied.
Perhaps you discovered that certain people loved your agreement more than they loved you.
And perhaps the moment you finally said, “I cannot do this anymore,” everything changed.
But we must also resist turning Vashti into whatever modern symbol we want her to become.
The Bible does not give us enough information to pronounce her either the flawless heroine of the chapter or its unquestionable villain.
It gives us her refusal.
It gives us the king's anger.
It gives us the advisers' fear.
It gives us the decree.
And then...
Vashti disappears from the story.
That silence is haunting.
Because while everyone inside that palace thought the story was about a queen refusing a king, God was moving history toward something none of them could yet see.
Vashti's removal created an empty place.
That empty place would eventually be occupied by Esther.
And Esther would eventually stand at the center of a crisis involving the survival of her people.
Notice the difference.
Vashti was summoned and refused to come.
Later Esther would approach the king when she had not been summoned.
That contrast should stop us.
Vashti risks everything by not appearing.
Esther later risks everything by appearing.
Two queens.
Two dangerous moments.
Two decisions involving the presence of a king.
Yet the biblical story does not invite us merely to compare two women.
It invites us to watch providence unfold.
God's name is famously absent from the Hebrew text of Esther, yet His providential fingerprints seem to surround the entire story.
A banquet.
A refusal.
An angry king.
A royal decree.
A search for another queen.
A Jewish orphan named Hadassah—Esther—entering the palace.
A forgotten act of loyalty recorded in royal chronicles.
A sleepless night.
A murderous conspiracy.
A courageous queen.
An enemy exposed.
A people preserved.
What looked like disconnected human decisions became pieces inside a story larger than any person in the palace understood.
That should speak to somebody reading this with a broken heart.
Because you may be standing inside a chapter that makes absolutely no sense.
Something ended.
Someone left.
A door closed.
A relationship collapsed.
A plan disappeared.
You prayed...
and heaven seemed silent.
You looked at the wreckage and asked God,
“What are You doing?”
Esther reminds us that God's apparent silence is not evidence of God's absence.
But be careful here.
This does not mean every painful thing is good.
It does not mean every rejection was righteous.
It does not mean every loss was directly caused by God.
It does not mean Christians should romanticize abuse, betrayal, injustice, or suffering.
It means the sovereign God is not defeated by human sin, human pride, human failure, human decisions, or circumstances we cannot understand.
He can accomplish His purposes even through a world filled with broken people making broken decisions.
And that truth reaches far beyond Persia.
It reaches all the way to Calvary.
Because if you want to see the ultimate example of God bringing redemption through what looked like catastrophe, look at Jesus Christ.
The cross looked like defeat.
The Messiah was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
His enemies believed they had silenced Him.
His followers watched their hope bleed beneath a Roman sky.
Then came Sunday.
The tomb was empty.
What appeared to be the greatest scandal became the place where God's redemptive purpose was revealed in breathtaking glory.
Human wickedness did not overthrow God's plan.
God brought salvation through the crucified and risen Christ.
And suddenly Esther's world feels much closer to ours.
Because maybe your deepest question is not really,
“Why did Vashti refuse?”
Maybe the question beneath your question is:
“Where is God when something happens that I cannot explain?”
Where was God when the marriage failed?
Where was God when you were betrayed?
Where was God when somebody humiliated you?
Where was God when you lost the opportunity?
Where was God when your child wandered?
Where was God when you prayed and nothing changed?
Where was God when your own decisions destroyed something precious?
Where was God when you became ashamed of the person you saw in the mirror?
The book of Esther whispers something powerful without even placing God's name in the narrative:
He was not absent.
And neither is He absent from your story.
But there is another danger here.
Sometimes we want God to rewrite our circumstances while refusing to let Him rewrite us.
We want restoration without repentance.
Peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without confession.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without a cross.
We want Jesus to repair the consequences while leaving the rebellion untouched.
But that is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make broken people feel better about remaining broken.
He came to save sinners.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile us to God.
To give new life.
To make us His.
Grace does not tell you that sin never mattered.
Grace tells you that your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is greater than the sin you bring to Him in repentance and faith.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your family thinks you're strong.
Your friends think you're okay.
You smile at church.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say “Amen.”
But somewhere behind the polished version of you is a room you don't want anyone entering.
A secret.
An addiction.
Bitterness.
Lust.
Pride.
Unforgiveness.
A compromise you keep renaming so you don't have to repent of it.
A wound you have allowed to become an identity.
A prayer life that quietly disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust while your soul starves.
And Jesus is not standing outside that room because He wants to humiliate you.
He calls sinners into the light because darkness is killing us.
Christ already knows what is behind the door.
And still He calls.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not the cheap grace that says, “Nothing needs to change.”
The costly grace that says:
Come home.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Me.
Let Me make you new.
Vashti's story reminds us that one decision can change the direction of a story.
But the Gospel announces something infinitely greater:
Jesus Christ can change the direction of a life.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to become your final chapter.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your divorce does not get the last word.
Your betrayal does not get the last word.
Your failure does not get the last word.
Your past does not get the last word.
Death itself does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
That is why the theme we repeat here is more than a slogan:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because Christianity teaches us to edit ugly chapters out of our testimony.
Jesus rewrites everything because redemption can transform what shame wanted to use as your grave into a testimony of the mercy of God.
Peter denied Christ and was restored.
Paul persecuted believers and became a servant of the Gospel.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer—and found mercy in his dying hours.
The cross itself appeared to be scandal and defeat, yet through Christ's death and resurrection came the proclamation of forgiveness and eternal life for everyone who believes.
So maybe you opened this article wanting to know why Vashti refused.
Scripture does not tell us.
And perhaps there is humility in admitting that.
But Scripture does show us what happened afterward.
A throne became vacant.
Esther entered the story.
Danger came.
Courage was required.
Providence unfolded.
Deliverance came.
And generations later, we are still reading the story.
