There may be things in your own life whose “why” you will not understand today.
Do not manufacture an answer God has not given.
Do not call speculation revelation.
Do not pretend every tragedy makes sense.
Instead, cling to what God has revealed.
Christ is Lord.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose again.
Repentance is not the end of hope; it is the turning of a sinner toward the One in whom hope is found.
Grace is real.
Forgiveness is real.
Redemption is real.
And nobody is too stained to come honestly to Jesus Christ.
Bring it to Christ.
You don't need to explain everything publicly.
Just stop pretending you don't need grace.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer fighting a battle in silence.
Not because every sentence is easy, but because there may come a night when you need to remember that God's silence does not mean His absence.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, or keep your eyes on Jesus, follow and stay connected.

Supporting Gospel-centered work is one practical way believers can help truthful Christian resources continue reaching people. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ. But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one voluntary expression of generosity that helps that work continue reaching others.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the friend carrying shame.
Invite the person asking questions about Christianity.
Invite the one who stopped going to church.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks their past has made them unreachable.
Because you never know which ordinary share God may use to place truth in front of somebody at exactly the moment they are finally ready to hear it.
We may never know why Vashti refused to walk into that room.
But we know what happened when Jesus walked out of the tomb.
And because He lives, your story does not have to end where your shame says it should.
The chapter you cannot explain may still become the place where, years from now, you look back and realize God had not abandoned the story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When the Drink Becomes the Place You Go to Escape Your Life, Something Deeper Is Asking for Help
paragraphs: When the Drink Becomes the Place You Go to Escape Your Life, Something Deeper Is Asking for Help

You may never call yourself an alcoholic. You may still go to work, pay the bills, love your family, laugh with friends, and sit in church on Sunday. But if alcohol has quietly become the place you run when being fully present in your own life hurts too much, the deepest question may not be how much you drink—but what you are trying so desperately not to feel.
There is a moment nobody sees.
The bottle opens.
The glass fills.
The first swallow goes down.
And for a little while, everything gets quieter.
Not fixed.
Just quieter.

The argument is still real. The marriage is still strained. The loneliness is still waiting. The bills did not disappear. The memory still happened. The grief still has your address. The shame still knows your name.
But for a few hours, maybe you do not have to feel all of it.
And that is precisely why this conversation is harder than simply saying, “Drinking is bad.”
Because sometimes the drink is not really about the drink.
Sometimes it is about escape.
Maybe nobody would look at you and think you have a problem.
You are functioning.
You show up.
You provide.
You answer messages.
You make people laugh.
Maybe you even serve at church.
And you certainly do not identify with the word “alcoholic.”
So when somebody starts talking about alcohol abuse, you immediately think, That isn't me.
Maybe it isn't.
Not everyone who drinks has alcohol use disorder, and Scripture does not teach that every use of wine is inherently sinful.
But there is another question worth asking.
When life hurts, where do you go?
When the house becomes quiet and your thoughts become loud, where do you go?
When disappointment sits on your chest...
when resentment begins boiling...
when you feel like a failure...
when the marriage feels cold...
when nobody knows how exhausted you really are...
when memories you thought you buried begin climbing out of their graves...
where do you go?
Because you can spend years debating whether you deserve a label while completely missing the refuge your heart has chosen.
And perhaps that is why Paul's words in Ephesians feel so piercing.
The Greek text says:
“καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία, ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι”
“And do not get drunk with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit.”
— Ephesians 5:18
Look closely at the contrast.
Paul does not merely say, “Stop.”
He says, in effect, do not be filled this way; be filled another way.
Do not surrender yourself to intoxication.
Be filled with the Spirit.
That distinction matters.
The Greek verb translated “get drunk” is μεθύσκεσθε — methyskesthe, referring to becoming intoxicated or drunk.
Then Paul uses πληροῦσθε — plērousthe: “be filled.”
One influence increasingly takes possession of the person through intoxication.
Paul points believers toward another filling altogether: the Holy Spirit.
And between those two commands appears a sobering word:
ἀσωτία — asōtia.
It carries the sense of dissipation, reckless or wasteful living.
This same word family appears in the New Testament's description of the prodigal son's reckless life.
That makes Paul's contrast painfully relevant.
Because intoxication promises something it cannot finally deliver.
It says:
Come here. I'll make tonight easier.
Come here. You won't have to think about her.
Come here. You won't have to remember him.
Come here. You won't have to feel like a failure.
Come here. You can finally relax.
And perhaps, temporarily, you do.
That temporary relief is part of what makes escape so powerful.

Modern research on alcohol dependence recognizes something Scripture's wisdom should make Christians take seriously: people can use alcohol to cope with stress or emotional discomfort, and although drinking may provide temporary relief, that pattern can become part of a destructive cycle in which negative emotions and further drinking reinforce one another.
In other words, sometimes you are not chasing pleasure anymore.
You are running from pain.
And there is an enormous difference.
Maybe the question you need tonight is not:
“Am I an alcoholic?”
Maybe the question is:
“Why do I keep needing to leave myself?”
Read that again.
Why does sober reality sometimes feel like somewhere you cannot bear to stay?
What are you anesthetizing?
What are you trying not to remember?
Whose rejection still hurts?
What disappointment have you never grieved?
What secret shame follows you home?
What anger do you refuse to name?
What happened to you that you keep insisting “wasn't that bad”?
What are you afraid would happen if you sat completely sober before God and finally told Him the truth?
Because sometimes we keep trying to kill a thirst without asking what created it.
You pour another drink because sleep will not come.
But maybe sleep is not the deepest problem.
You drink because your nerves will not settle.
But maybe anxiety is knocking on a door you have kept locked for years.
You drink because your relationship is unbearable.
But perhaps alcohol has become easier than the conversation you know needs to happen.
You drink because you feel alone.
But eventually the thing you use to escape loneliness can begin isolating you even further.
You drink because you hate who you have become.
And then tomorrow morning, you hate yourself for drinking again.
So you promise:
Tonight will be different.
And sometimes it is.
Until another terrible day arrives.
Until another fight.
Another memory.
Another disappointment.
Another lonely night.
Then the old refuge whispers your name again.
This is where shame usually enters the story.
“You call yourself a Christian?”
“You prayed about this already.”
“You promised God you would stop.”
“Look at you.”
“Don't tell anyone.”
“They'll think you're a hypocrite.”
So you hide.
And hiding makes the darkness stronger.
But listen carefully:
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross so broken people could become better actors.
He came to save sinners.
The Gospel does not begin with pretending you are strong enough.
It begins with admitting that you are not.
Christian repentance is not theatrical self-hatred.
It is turning.
It is bringing what has been hidden into the light and agreeing with God about it.
Where drunkenness, deception, neglect, cruelty, irresponsibility, idolatry, or other sin has accompanied your drinking, repentance means refusing to rename darkness as harmless.
But biblical wisdom also refuses a shallow answer to a complicated human struggle.
Not every painful pattern is solved by shouting, “Try harder.”

Alcohol misuse can involve deeply established behavioral, emotional, social, and physical patterns. Some people need pastoral care. Some need Christian community. Some need counseling. Some need medical evaluation or professional addiction treatment. Some need all of these working together.
Seeking appropriate help is not a betrayal of faith.
Truth is not the enemy of faith.
Wisdom is not the enemy of faith.
And asking someone trustworthy to walk with you is not the opposite of depending on God.
Sometimes one of the most spiritually honest prayers a person can pray is:
Jesus, I cannot keep hiding this. Please help me tell somebody.

And if you have become physically dependent on alcohol, do not assume that abruptly stopping on your own is always safe. Alcohol withdrawal can become medically serious. Getting qualified medical guidance can be an act of wisdom, not weakness.
But even when treatment addresses the drinking, another question remains:
Where will your soul run now?
Because removing the bottle without discovering a deeper refuge can leave a frightening emptiness.
Paul's words do not end with:
“Do not get drunk.”
They continue:
“...but be filled with the Spirit.”
Christianity is not merely subtraction.
It is replacement.
Not merely stop running there.
Come here.
Not merely put down the counterfeit refuge.
Meet the real Refuge.
Jesus does not simply want to remove something from your hand while leaving your heart abandoned.
He calls you to Himself.
And no, that does not mean every craving instantly disappears when someone prays.
It does not mean recovery never includes relapse, counseling, accountability, treatment, tears, difficult conversations, changed routines, or painful consequences.
Grace is not magic language for pretending consequences do not exist.
Grace means your failure does not get the final word.
The cross does.
Think about Peter.
He swore that he would remain faithful.
Then pressure came.
Fear came.
And Peter denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame after the rooster crowed.
Peter had failed publicly and spiritually.
Yet the risen Jesus went looking for him.
Christ did not pretend Peter's denial did not matter.
He restored him.
He recommissioned him.
He transformed the site of failure into a testimony of grace.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not call evil good.
He overcomes evil with redemption.
He does not erase repentance.
He makes repentance a road home.
Maybe your scandal is hidden inside bottles nobody counts.
Maybe your family knows.
Maybe they have begged you.
Maybe your children have learned to recognize the difference between sober you and drinking you.
Maybe somebody you love has stopped believing your promises.

Maybe you have awakened with messages you regret sending, words you cannot retrieve, money you should not have spent, memories blurred around the edges, or apologies that are beginning to sound painfully familiar.
Or perhaps none of that has happened.
Perhaps nobody suspects anything.
Perhaps this struggle lives quietly behind a respectable life.
But God sees deeper than appearances.
And astonishingly, the One who sees everything is still calling you closer.
Not deeper into hiding.
Closer.
The Gospel says your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one truth:
Not because your past was imaginary.
Not because consequences vanish.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because at Calvary, Jesus Christ took the guilt of sinners upon Himself, died, and rose again so that those who turn to Him in faith do not have to remain prisoners of who they were.
There is forgiveness.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is a new identity in Christ.
There is power to walk differently.
There is community.
There is wisdom.
There is help.
There is another way home.
Maybe tonight your first act of courage is not making a dramatic promise that you will never struggle again.
Maybe it is telling the truth.
Jesus, I have been using this to escape.
Jesus, I don't know how to face what I feel.
Jesus, I need help.
Jesus, forgive what is sinful in me.
Jesus, show me what I have been running from.
Jesus, lead me to people who can help me walk in the light.
That prayer may not feel spectacular.
But heaven has never required theatrical language from a repentant heart.
Come honestly.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come confused.
Come with questions.
Come needing professional help.
Come needing accountability.
Come knowing that you have failed again.
Just stop believing the lie that you must become clean enough to approach the One who came precisely to rescue sinners.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to give strangers your entire story.
But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting for another day.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who will never click an article titled “How to Know If You're an Alcoholic.”
They reject the label.
They insist they are fine.
But they know exactly what it means to pour a drink because they cannot bear another evening alone with their thoughts.
Send it privately to the person whose struggle should not become public conversation.
If this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ, there is also a practical way to stand behind the mission.
It helps us keep reaching the person scrolling at midnight.
The ashamed believer.
The exhausted parent.
The recovering addict.
The skeptic.
The prodigal.
The person who would never walk into a church today but might stop long enough to read about Jesus on a screen.
He is the point.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Jesus Christ.
If you are drinking because you are trying to escape your life, perhaps the deepest invitation tonight is not merely to put down a glass.
It is to stop running alone.
Tell the truth to God.
Tell the truth to someone safe.
Seek appropriate professional help when it is needed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where shame tells you there can be none.
And begin learning what it means to take refuge in Christ rather than disappearing from your pain.
Because the bottle can make you forget for a night.
Jesus can teach you how to live in the light.
The bottle may temporarily numb what hurts.
Jesus can meet you inside what hurts.
The bottle offers escape.
Christ offers Himself.
And when morning comes, escape eventually asks you to pay for what it promised you last night.
Christ already paid at the cross for the sinner He came to redeem.
So tonight, before you reach automatically for whatever helps you disappear, ask yourself one question:
What am I actually trying to escape?
Then ask another:
What would happen if, instead of escaping, I brought it to Jesus and finally let someone help me carry it?
And comment.
Not for an algorithm alone.
“No more hiding.”
Maybe that is where your next chapter starts.
And remember this when the old refuge whispers again:
You do not need another place to disappear; in Jesus Christ, you have finally been given Someone to whom you can come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “REJOICE IN THE WIFE OF YOUR YOUTH”: BIBLICAL FAITHFULNESS WAS NEVER MEANT TO BE COLD
paragraphs: “REJOICE IN THE WIFE OF YOUR YOUTH”: BIBLICAL FAITHFULNESS WAS NEVER MEANT TO BE COLD

Proverbs 5:18 does not merely tell a husband to stay. It calls him to rediscover joy in the woman he once chose—and exposes the quiet distance that can grow inside a marriage long before anyone walks away.
There is a kind of adultery that happens before a body ever enters another bed.
It begins with distance.
A conversation you stopped having.
A touch you stopped giving.
A tenderness you assumed would always be there.
Two people can still wear their wedding rings, still sleep beneath the same roof, still sit beside each other at church, still smile for family photographs…
and slowly become strangers.
No affair.
No divorce papers.
No public scandal.
Just a marriage quietly starving while everybody thinks it is still alive.
And into that uncomfortable silence, Scripture says something startling:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
—Proverbs 5:18
The Hebrew is even more vivid.
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorkha varukh, usmach me'eshet ne'urekha.
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
That word translated “rejoice” comes from the Hebrew שָׂמַח — samach.
It carries the sense of rejoicing, being glad, taking joy.
God did not merely say:
Tolerate her.
Provide for her.
Stay legally married to her.
Avoid committing adultery.
He said:
Rejoice.
That changes everything.
Because biblical faithfulness was never supposed to mean cold coexistence.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to admit something painful:
You have remained physically present…
but your heart has been slowly checking out.
Maybe there was no catastrophic moment.
Maybe there was simply exhaustion.
Children came.
Bills came.
Responsibilities came.
Disappointments came.
Arguments accumulated.
Apologies became shorter.
Kisses became routine.
Date nights disappeared.
The person you once could not wait to see became the person you barely look at across the dinner table.
And somewhere between surviving Monday and paying Friday's bills, marriage became administration.
Schedules.
Groceries.
School.
Work.
Laundry.
Money.
Sleep.
Repeat.
Then Proverbs 5 walks directly into that ordinary exhaustion and reminds a husband:
She is not merely your roommate.
She is not merely the mother of your children.
She is not merely the woman helping you manage your household.
She is “the wife of your youth.”
There is memory in those words.
History.
Covenant.
A younger version of you once looked at this woman differently.
You noticed her laugh.
You remembered tiny details.
You wanted another five minutes beside her.
You looked forward to hearing her voice.
You found reasons to touch her hand.
You probably did things then that would embarrass you now.
And perhaps that is precisely the tragedy.
Not that you grew older.
But that somewhere along the way, familiarity convinced you to stop seeing the miracle standing beside you.
Proverbs 5 is not sentimental poetry floating above real life.
Its context is intensely serious.

The father is warning his son about sexual temptation and the destructive seduction of adultery. Rather than merely commanding him to run away from forbidden intimacy, Scripture redirects his desire toward covenant intimacy.
The next verse becomes remarkably intimate:
“Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
—Proverbs 5:19
Scripture is not embarrassed by marital desire.
God created marriage.
God created covenant affection.
God created the capacity for a husband and wife to delight in one another.
Sin did not invent intimacy.
God did.
And within the covenant of marriage, Scripture does not treat affection as dirty.
It protects it.
That matters in a world where sexual desire is constantly detached from covenant.
The culture says desire needs novelty.
Scripture points desire home.
The culture says excitement requires someone different.
Proverbs says, in effect:
Look again at the covenant you already made.
Remember.
Return.
Rejoice.
This does not mean pretending every marriage is healthy.
It does not mean ignoring abuse, coercion, betrayal, addiction, manipulation, or serious danger.

Biblical covenant faithfulness never requires calling evil good. Scripture repeatedly condemns oppression and wrongdoing, and someone facing abuse should seek safety, wise pastoral counsel, and appropriate professional or legal help.
Nor does Proverbs 5 mean that every struggling marriage can be repaired by arranging a romantic dinner and buying flowers.
Some wounds are deep.
Some trust has been shattered.
Some conversations require counseling.
Some marriages are carrying years of unresolved grief.
But there is still a question worth asking:
When did you stop pursuing the person you promised to love?
Not when did you stop paying the bills.
Not when did you stop coming home.
Not when did you stop wearing the ring.
When did you stop pursuing?
Because there is a difference between remaining married…
and nurturing a marriage.
There is a difference between occupying the same house…
and sharing a life.
There is a difference between faithfulness that merely says, “I didn't cheat”…
and covenant love that says,
“I am still choosing you.”
And before husbands turn this article into ammunition against their wives, remember where Proverbs places the responsibility.
The command confronts the man.
You rejoice.
It does not say:
“Rejoice if she never disappoints you.”
“Rejoice if she still looks twenty-five.”
“Rejoice if she always understands you.”
“Rejoice if she meets every emotional need perfectly.”
Marriage joins two sinners.
That means covenant love eventually discovers something infatuation never had to face:
the person you love is imperfect.
And so are you.
That is where marriage begins teaching us something much deeper than romance.
It begins teaching us about grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses sin.
Not fake peace that buries wounds.
Grace that looks truth in the face and still seeks redemption.
And suddenly marriage starts pointing beyond marriage.
Toward Christ.
Paul writes:
—Ephesians 5:25
Read that slowly.
Christ did not love His people because His people were flawless.
He loved sacrificially.
He gave Himself.
Christian marriage therefore cannot ultimately be sustained by butterflies.
Butterflies are wonderful.
But butterflies cannot carry a covenant through cancer.
They cannot carry it through unemployment.
They cannot carry it through sleepless nights with babies.
They cannot carry it through grief.
They cannot carry it through aging.
They cannot carry it through seasons when two exhausted people look at each other and realize they have almost forgotten how to talk.
Covenant needs something stronger.
It needs grace.
It needs forgiveness.
It needs repentance.
It needs Christ.
Maybe your marriage does not need another inspirational quote tonight.
Maybe it needs one person courageous enough to say:
“I've been distant.”
“I've taken you for granted.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I became defensive.”
“I have been physically here but emotionally somewhere else.”
“I've expected you to change while refusing to examine myself.”
“I am sorry.”
There are three words pride hates:
I was wrong.
And three words wounded marriages desperately need:
Please forgive me.
Repentance is not humiliation.
For the Christian, repentance is the doorway through which grace enters places pride has kept locked.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because some people reading this are carrying more than marital regret.
You are carrying secret sin.
Pornography.
Fantasy.
Emotional attachment to somebody who is not your spouse.
Messages you would panic if your husband or wife saw.
A relationship you keep calling “innocent” because admitting what it has become would require you to change.
Perhaps nobody knows.
But God does.
Proverbs 5:21 says:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.”
That sentence should sober us.
But it should not drive the repentant sinner away from Christ.
It should drive us to Him.
Because Christianity is not the story of respectable people successfully hiding their scandals.
It is the story of sinners being brought into the light…
and meeting a Savior there.
Jesus does not call sin harmless.
He died because sin is deadly.
But the cross also declares something astonishing:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
That does not mean there are no consequences.
It means condemnation does not have the final word over the one who belongs to Christ.
So if you have crossed boundaries…
repent.
If you are approaching boundaries…
run.
If something needs to be confessed…
bring it into the light with wisdom and appropriate support.
If you have stopped pursuing your spouse…
begin again.
If your marriage is wounded…
seek help.
If you have become cold…
ask God to soften what disappointment hardened.
And if you have failed spectacularly, do not confuse shame with repentance.
Shame whispers:
Hide.
Jesus calls:
Come.
Shame says:
You are permanently defined by what you did.
The Gospel says that in Christ there is forgiveness, cleansing, a new identity, and a new way to walk.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
That is why our message will always return here:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Not because betrayal is painless.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes sinners who thought hiding would save them and teaches them to walk in light.
He takes proud hearts and teaches them repentance.
He takes wounded people and teaches them forgiveness without pretending the wound never happened.
He takes lust and calls us toward holiness.
He takes selfishness and teaches sacrificial love.
He takes dead places and, according to His wisdom and will, can breathe life where people thought nothing beautiful could grow again.
Maybe tonight your first act of obedience is surprisingly small.
Put the phone down.
Look at your wife.
Look at your husband.
Really look.
Remember the person behind the responsibilities.
Remember the story.
Remember what you have survived.
Remember the prayers God answered.
Remember the laughter.
Remember the tears.
Remember that covenant should never become an excuse to stop cherishing the person you promised to love.
And husbands…
hear Proverbs again.
וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Usmach me'eshet ne'urekha.
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Not merely endure.
Not merely coexist.
Not merely avoid divorce.
Rejoice.
Perhaps you cannot manufacture feelings on command.
But you can begin cultivating what neglect has been starving.
You can listen.
You can confess.
You can pray.
You can put boundaries around temptation.
You can become curious about your spouse again.
You can speak tenderness instead of assuming they already know.
You can seek biblical counseling when the wounds are beyond what the two of you know how to repair alone.
You can ask Christ to teach you how to love when your natural resources feel exhausted.
And wives reading this, the Gospel does not reduce you to an object responsible for keeping your husband's attention.
You bear God's image.

Marriage calls both husband and wife into covenant faithfulness, honor, love, and mutual marital responsibility. First Corinthians 7 speaks with striking reciprocity about husband and wife belonging faithfully to one another, while Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage honorable and the marriage bed undefiled.
The Christian vision is not one spouse consuming the other.
It is covenant.
Faithfulness.
Holiness.
Sacrifice.
Joy.
And ultimately…
Christ.
Maybe this article exposed something you have been avoiding.
Pray.
Then, where appropriate, talk to your spouse.
And if your heart is saying, God, I have allowed something precious to become cold, be honest before Him.
Someone quietly losing hope may need to hear that restoration can require time, truth, repentance, boundaries, forgiveness, counseling, and above all the grace of God.
Not because you need another post sitting forgotten in a folder…
but because there may come a night when resentment is louder than remembrance.
Come back and read Proverbs 5 again.
Send it privately to somebody fighting for a marriage nobody else knows is hurting.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, you can help us continue producing and expanding Christ-centered resources.

Scripture teaches voluntary generosity, not spiritual coercion: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Your responsibility to honor God with your resources extends far beyond any online ministry, including faithful generosity through your local church and care for people in need.
Think of it as more than paying for content.
Think of what your support can help make possible:
another exhausted believer encountering Scripture at 2:00 in the morning…
another marriage being confronted before temptation becomes catastrophe…
another prodigal remembering Jesus…
another wounded Christian opening the Bible again…
another person discovering that grace is not permission to remain in sin but the power of Christ calling sinners out of darkness.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you believe Gospel-centered discipleship is worth helping continue.
A share costs nothing, yet it may place biblical truth in front of the exact person who was never going to search for it themselves.
Because eventually every marriage discovers this:
You did not marry someone who would never need grace.
You married someone who would.
And they married someone who would need it too.
You.
So go home to the covenant.
Go back to the conversation.
Go back to prayer.
Go back to truth.
Go back to tenderness.
Go back to repentance where repentance is needed.
Go back to forgiveness where forgiveness can rightly begin.
And above everything else…
go back to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most dangerous moment in a marriage is not when two people finally admit something is broken.
Perhaps it is when they stop believing anything is worth fighting to restore.
The ring may tell the world whom you married—but the way you love when nobody is watching reveals whether covenant is still alive in your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY MANNA FELL EVERY MORNING—EXCEPT ON THE SABBATH
paragraphs:
WHY MANNA FELL EVERY MORNING—EXCEPT ON THE SABBATH
God Wasn’t Just Feeding Israel. He Was Teaching Them Something About Trust That Many of Us Still Haven’t Learned.
Imagine waking up tomorrow morning with nothing left.
No pantry full of food.
No paycheck coming.
No backup plan.
No field to harvest. No grocery store down the road. No refrigerator humming quietly in the kitchen.
Just wilderness.
And mouths to feed.
Your children look at you as if you have the answer.
You don’t.
Then you step outside.
And the ground is covered with something you have never seen before.
Small.
Fine.
Flake-like.
Resting beneath the morning light.
The Israelites stare at it and ask one another:
מָן הוּא — man hu?
“What is it?”
That bewildered question is connected with the biblical name “manna.”
They didn’t know what it was.
But God did.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes the thing keeping you alive doesn’t look like the thing you asked God for.
Sometimes provision arrives disguised as confusion.
Sometimes heaven answers while you are still asking, “What is this?”
And sometimes God gives you exactly enough for today because He loves you too much to let tomorrow become your god.
The story begins in Exodus 16.
Israel had escaped Egypt, but Egypt had not completely escaped Israel.
They had witnessed the sea open.
They had walked between walls of water.
They had watched Pharaoh’s power collapse behind them.
They had sung about deliverance.
And then they became hungry.
Suddenly slavery started looking better in their memories than freedom looked in their circumstances.
That is one of the frightening things suffering can do to the human heart.
Pain can romanticize the chains God already broke.
Israel began murmuring.
They remembered Egypt’s food while conveniently forgetting Egypt’s whips.
They remembered the pots of meat while forgetting the bricks.
They remembered being fed while forgetting they had been enslaved.
And before we condemn them too quickly...
we should recognize ourselves.
How many times have you asked God to deliver you from something, only to miss it when obedience became uncomfortable?
The relationship you begged Him to free you from.
The addiction you swore you were finished with.
The compromise that almost destroyed you.
The old life.
The old habits.
The old secret.
The old version of yourself.
God leads you out...
then the wilderness gets hard...
and suddenly Egypt starts whispering your name again.
That is where manna appeared.
Not after Israel had demonstrated flawless faith.
Not after they had earned God's kindness.
Not after they had stopped complaining.
God fed people who were grumbling against Him.
That does not make grumbling righteous.
It makes grace astonishing.
The Lord told Moses:
הִנְנִי מַמְטִיר לָכֶם לֶחֶם מִן־הַשָּׁמָיִם
Hineni mamtir lakhem lechem min-hashamayim.
“Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you.”
That is the language of Exodus 16:4.
Bread.
From heaven.
But notice what God says next.
The people were to go out and gather a day’s portion each day so that God might test whether they would walk according to His instruction.
The miracle was not merely about feeding Israel.
The provision itself became a classroom.
Every sunrise asked a question:
Will you trust Me today?
They could gather what they needed.
But ordinarily, they could not hoard tomorrow’s security.
Some tried.
They kept manna overnight.
By morning, it bred worms and stank.
Imagine the lesson.
Yesterday’s provision could not become a substitute for today’s dependence.
God was teaching former slaves how to live as His covenant people.
Egypt had trained them to understand life through Pharaoh.
God was teaching them to understand life through Him.
Then something extraordinary happened.
On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much.
Moses told them:
שַׁבָּתוֹן שַׁבַּת־קֹדֶשׁ לַיהוָה מָחָר
Shabbaton shabbat-qodesh laYHWH machar.
“Tomorrow is a solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD.”
The manna they normally could not preserve overnight?
This time it remained good.
No stench.
No worms.
And when Sabbath morning arrived...
there was no manna on the ground.
Nothing.
The God who had made bread appear could have made it appear seven mornings a week.
He chose not to.
Why?
Because the absence was part of the miracle.
Read that again.
The absence was part of the miracle.
God was not failing to provide on the seventh day.
He had already provided for it on the sixth.
What looked like an empty field was actually evidence of yesterday’s faithfulness.
And somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Because you have been staring at an empty field and assuming God abandoned you.
You prayed.
Nothing seemed to happen.
You waited.
Nothing appeared.
You looked where yesterday’s blessing had been...
and the ground seemed empty.
But what if emptiness does not always mean abandonment?
What if there are moments when God is saying:
“You don’t need to scramble today. I already provided what this day requires.”
The Sabbath manna exposed something deep inside the human heart.
We find it difficult to stop.
Because stopping requires trust.
We work.
Push.
Build.
Accumulate.
Refresh.
Check.
Compare.
Worry.
Calculate.
We tell ourselves we are simply being responsible.
Sometimes we are.
But sometimes underneath our relentless activity is a frightened confession:
“If I stop holding everything together, everything will fall apart.”
Israel had to learn that the universe did not depend on Israel gathering manna seven mornings a week.
And neither does the universe depend on you.
That does not glorify laziness. Scripture repeatedly honors diligent labor.
It destroys the illusion that human striving is sovereign.
God told Israel not to go gathering on the seventh day.
Yet some still went out.
Exodus says they found none.
Think about that scene.
Someone wakes early.
Grabs a basket.
Walks outside.
Starts searching.
Nothing.
Maybe farther away.
Nothing.
Maybe beyond that hill.
Still nothing.
God had already told them there would be none.
But anxiety has a strange ability to make obedience feel irresponsible.
That sentence might expose more of us than we would like.
Sometimes we disobey God not because we openly hate Him...
but because we secretly believe our anxiety is wiser than His instruction.
The Sabbath taught Israel that God could sustain them while their hands were empty.
And this pattern becomes even more significant when Deuteronomy looks back on the wilderness.
Moses explains that God humbled Israel, allowed them to hunger, and fed them with manna so they would understand:
כִּי לֹא עַל־הַלֶּחֶם לְבַדּוֹ יִחְיֶה הָאָדָם
Ki lo al-halechem levado yichyeh ha-adam.
“Man does not live by bread alone.”
Human beings need bread.
But bread is not God.
Money is useful.
But money is not God.
Work matters.
But work is not God.
Planning is wise.
But planning is not God.
Your job is not your ultimate provider.
Your business is not your ultimate provider.
Your followers are not your ultimate provider.
Your bank balance is not your ultimate provider.
Israel could hold manna in their hands while God was teaching them to place their lives in His.
And then, centuries later...
Jesus entered a wilderness.
Hungry.
Tempted.
The devil challenged Him to turn stones into bread.
And Jesus answered from Israel’s wilderness lesson:
“Man shall not live by bread alone.”
Where Israel repeatedly struggled to trust God in the wilderness, Jesus remained faithful.
But the connection goes deeper.
In John 6, after Jesus fed the multitude, people came searching for Him.
They wanted more bread.
Jesus confronted their motives and redirected them beyond temporary food.
Then He said something breathtaking:
“I am the bread of life.”
And later:
“I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”
The manna was real provision.
But it was not the final Bread.
Israel ate manna and eventually died.
Christ offers eternal life.
Manna temporarily satisfied physical hunger.
Jesus came to deal with the deeper famine inside humanity.
Sin.
Alienation from God.
Guilt.
Condemnation.
Death.
We do not merely need improved circumstances.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And this is where the wilderness story becomes the Gospel.
You and I have our own Egypt.
Sin enslaves.
We have our own wilderness.
Human strength cannot save us.
We have our own hunger.
The soul reaches for things that cannot finally satisfy it.
Success.
Sex.
Approval.
Money.
Attention.
Religion without relationship.
Achievement.
Pleasure.
Control.
We consume...
and eventually become hungry again.
Then Jesus stands before starving humanity and says:
“I am the bread of life.”
Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that hungry people should try harder.
It is the announcement that Bread came down.
Grace came down.
The Son of God came down.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we have failed to live, gave Himself for sinners at the cross, and rose from the dead.
Our salvation is not purchased by religious performance.
It is received through repentance and faith in Christ.
That is scandalous grace.
You cannot hoard enough goodness to erase your guilt.
You cannot work enough religious hours to purchase forgiveness.
You cannot manufacture resurrection.
You need Jesus.
Maybe that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
Because manna confronts our obsession with control.
Every morning Israel had to receive.
And receiving is humbling.
We would rather achieve.
We would rather deserve.
We would rather tell God, “Look what I brought You.”
The Gospel empties our hands.
Then grace fills them.
Perhaps you have been carrying shame for years.
People know the polished version of you.
They know your church smile.
Your inspirational posts.
Your “God is good” comments.
But they do not know what happens when the screen goes dark.
They do not know what you keep replaying.
They do not know what you did.
They do not know what was done to you.
They do not know what you cannot forgive yourself for.
You wonder whether God could still want you.
Look again at the wilderness.
Manna fell among complainers.
Grace appeared among people still learning trust.
Then look beyond the manna.
Look at the cross.
Christ did not wait for sinners to become worthy before giving Himself.
Scripture says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That does not make sin insignificant.
The cross proves how serious sin actually is.
But the same cross reveals how astonishing God's mercy is toward repentant sinners who come to Christ.
Your scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Your failure does not have to write the last sentence.
Your addiction does not get the final word.
Your adultery does not get the final word.
Your pornography does not get the final word.
Your pride does not get the final word.
Your hypocrisy does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Repentance is not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is Christ meeting guilty people with a salvation they could never purchase, then beginning the work of transforming them.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe today your field looks empty.
Maybe you are exhausted from gathering.
Maybe you have been trying to create security by collecting enough manna for ten tomorrows.
Maybe God is confronting the fear beneath all that striving.
You know the fear.
“What if there isn't enough?”
“What if God doesn't come through?”
“What if I lose everything?”
“What if tomorrow is worse?”
Israel's manna answered that fear one morning at a time.
And the Sabbath answered it with silence.
Six mornings said:
“God provides.”
The seventh said:
“God is still providing even when you cannot see something falling.”
That is unforgettable once you see it.
Sometimes faith gathers.
Sometimes faith rests.
Both can be obedience.
And ultimately Christian hope is not faith in a predictable life.
It is faith in a faithful Christ.
Maybe you need to stop asking God merely for another handful of temporary bread and surrender yourself to the Bread of Life.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are hiding, step into His light.
If you have never trusted Christ, do not confuse knowing Christian language with knowing Jesus.
Turn to Him.
Confess your sin.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace opens the prison door.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't perform spirituality here.
Be honest.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not fighting alone.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, don't merely think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Because perhaps they have been silently carrying an empty basket into an empty field every morning, wondering whether God has forgotten their name.
Not as a transaction with God, and not because sharing a post earns His favor—Christ alone is our Savior.

If Gospel-centered words have strengthened you here, consider helping Gospel Warrior keep placing biblical encouragement, conviction, discipleship, and the message of Jesus Christ before people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
It is practical support for the work of creating and distributing Christ-centered resources.
Because one day the field may look empty again.
And when it does, you may need to remember what Israel learned in the wilderness:
The morning when manna did not fall was not the morning God stopped being faithful.
It was the morning His people were supposed to discover that His faithfulness had already gone ahead of them.
And above every temporary provision stands Jesus Christ—the true Bread from heaven—still calling hungry sinners away from the food that perishes and toward the life only He can give.
Sometimes the empty ground beneath your feet is where you finally discover that the hands of God were never empty.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ONAN’S SIN: Was God Really Judging Masturbation—or Something Else?
paragraphs:
ONAN’S SIN: Was God Really Judging Masturbation—or Something Else?
One of the Bible’s Most Misquoted Sexual Stories Is More Disturbing Than You Think—Because Onan’s Real Sin Wasn’t Simply What Happened to His Seed. It Was What Was Happening in His Heart.
There are Bible stories people think they know because they have heard one interpretation repeated for years.
Then one day, they actually read the text.
Slowly.
In context.
And suddenly the story becomes far more uncomfortable.
Genesis 38 contains one of those moments.
For generations, the name “Onan” has become so closely associated with masturbation that the English word onanism eventually came to be associated with masturbation and related sexual practices.
So many Christians approach Genesis 38 already believing they know what happens.
Onan spills his seed.
God kills Onan.
Therefore, the argument goes, God killed Onan for masturbating.
Simple.
Except there is a serious problem.
That is not actually what Genesis says happened.
And once you see what the Hebrew text emphasizes, the story becomes much deeper than a debate about one sexual act.
It becomes a story about a man who wanted intimacy without responsibility.
Pleasure without sacrifice.
A woman without accepting the obligation he owed her.
The privileges of his position without the cost of faithfulness.
And perhaps that is why this ancient story can still make modern hearts uncomfortable.
Because Onan is easier to condemn when we reduce his story to something he did with his body.
It becomes much harder when Scripture forces us to look at what he was doing with another human being.
The story begins with death.
Judah's firstborn son, Er, had married a woman named Tamar. Genesis tells us that Er was wicked before the LORD, and he died.
Tamar was left a widow.
Then Judah told his second son, Onan, to fulfill his obligation toward her:
"וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ"
veyabbēm ʾōtāh vehāqēm zeraʿ leʾāḥîkā
In context: perform the duty of a brother-in-law toward her and “raise up offspring for your brother.”
That word matters.
זֶרַע — zeraʿ
It can mean “seed,” but in this context it means offspring or descendants.
And Scripture immediately tells us exactly what Onan understood.
"וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע"
Vayyēdaʿ ʾÔnān kî lō-lô yihyeh hazzāraʿ.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
That sentence unlocks the passage.
Onan understood the responsibility.
He understood what was expected.
He understood that a child resulting from this union would preserve his dead brother's line.
And he did not want that.
Yet notice something extraordinarily important.
Onan did not simply refuse Tamar.
He continued going to her.
Genesis 38:9 describes what happened when he had sexual relations with his brother's wife:
"וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה"
veshiḥēt ʾartṣāh
Literally, he “destroyed” or “wasted” it toward the ground.
But Scripture then supplies the purpose behind his action:
"לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו"
leviltî netan-zeraʿ leʾāḥîw
“So as not to give offspring to his brother.”
Do not rush past those words.
So as not to.
The narrator does not leave us guessing about Onan's motive.
This was deliberate.
Repeated.
Calculated.

Genesis describes him having intercourse with Tamar and deliberately preventing conception because he did not want to produce offspring for his dead brother. The text therefore does not describe masturbation as such. It describes interrupted intercourse performed specifically to frustrate the obligation Judah had commanded him to fulfill.
And then comes the terrifying sentence:
"וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה"
Vayyēraʿ beʿênê YHWH ʾăšer ʿāśāh.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
And God put him to death.
But here is where responsible Bible reading matters.
Genesis does not say:
“Onan masturbated, and therefore God killed him.”
Nor should we rewrite the verse to make it say that.
Onan was actually having intercourse with Tamar.
The text explicitly tells us why he spilled his semen: he intended to prevent the offspring from being reckoned to his deceased brother.

Later Mosaic legislation helps us understand the cultural world behind this obligation. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 describes the duty of a surviving brother toward the childless widow of his deceased brother. The purpose included preserving the deceased brother's name in Israel. A man who refused could publicly decline, but that refusal brought a formal procedure and public disgrace.
Genesis 38 occurs before that Mosaic legislation was given, so we should not carelessly pretend Onan was violating the later written statute word-for-word.
But the family obligation behind what would later be called levirate marriage is plainly present.
Judah tells him what he must do.
Onan understands.
Then Onan deliberately frustrates it.
And that makes what happened to Tamar particularly disturbing.
She had already buried her husband.
Her future was precarious.
Her place within Judah's family depended heavily upon the very household that was now failing her.
Onan apparently accepted sexual access to Tamar while deliberately refusing the offspring-producing responsibility attached to that relationship.
Think about that.
He wanted what Tamar's body could give him while refusing what faithfulness required of him.
He participated physically while withholding covenantal responsibility.
This was not merely uncontrolled desire.
There was calculation in it.
And suddenly Genesis 38 stops sounding like an obscure ancient argument about semen.
It starts sounding frighteningly modern.
Because humanity still wants pleasure without responsibility.
We still want intimacy without covenant.
Sex without holiness.
Promises without sacrifice.
Christianity without repentance.
Grace without surrender.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We want the benefits of belonging to Christ while secretly negotiating which rooms of our lives He is permitted to enter.
And sometimes we become experts at appearing obedient while quietly engineering outcomes that serve ourselves.
Onan looked as though he was fulfilling the obligation.
He went to Tamar.
But behind the visible act was an invisible refusal.
Other people could see his body participating.
God could see his motive resisting.
That should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because you can look obedient while your heart is saying no.
You can sing worship songs while protecting a secret addiction.
You can post Scripture while refusing to forgive someone.
You can attend church while feeding lust all week.
You can speak about purity while treating another person's body as something existing for your gratification.
You can preach grace while refusing repentance.
You can call Jesus “Lord” while continually telling Him:
“Everything except this.”
And eventually Christianity reaches that locked door.
Not because Christ is cruel.
Because Christ loves us too much to pretend slavery is freedom.
Now someone will immediately ask the obvious question.
“So does that mean masturbation is fine?”
No.
It means Genesis 38 should not be made to say something it does not explicitly say.
That is different.
A Christian sexual ethic cannot be built honestly by taking Onan's story out of context.
But neither can Christian sexual ethics be reduced to the question, “Where does the Bible explicitly mention this exact modern behavior?”
Jesus takes us deeper than technical loopholes.
He goes after the heart.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus moves beyond merely avoiding the physical act of adultery and confronts lustful intention.
That changes the question.
The Christian cannot merely ask:
“Can I technically get away with this?”
The disciple of Jesus asks:
“What is forming my heart?”
“Where is my imagination going?”
“Am I learning self-control or becoming controlled?”
“Am I reducing another human being—real or imagined—to an instrument for my gratification?”
“Can I bring this before Christ without hiding?”
“Is this helping me love God and people more faithfully, or teaching me to consume people privately?”
Those questions are harder.
But holiness has never been about discovering the largest amount of darkness we can retain while still calling ourselves Christians.
Holiness is learning to love the Light.
And maybe this is where someone reading needs to stop pretending.
Maybe your struggle isn't Onan's struggle.
Maybe yours is pornography.
Maybe it is compulsive masturbation bound tightly to pornography and fantasy.
Maybe it is adultery.
Maybe sexting.
Maybe an emotional affair nobody knows about.
Maybe you have spent years feeding fantasies involving people who would be devastated if they knew how you were imagining them.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your Sunday worship.
Maybe you have promised God twenty times:
“Never again.”
And then you fell again.
Now shame whispers:
“Don't go back to Jesus this time.”
Listen carefully.
That voice is lying to you.
The Gospel is not the announcement that clean people can approach Christ.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can.
Jesus Christ did not shed His blood because your sin was small.
He shed His blood because your need for mercy was enormous.
Scripture does not tell sinners to hide until they become worthy.
It tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Confession is not telling God something He doesn't know.
It is finally refusing to hide what He already sees.
That is where grace becomes breathtaking.
God sees the thing you desperately hope nobody discovers.
He sees what happened at 2:13 in the morning.
He sees the deleted history.
The second account.
The fantasy.
The relapse.
The compromise.
The secret relationship.
The hypocrisy.
He sees everything.
And the same Christ who exposes darkness stretches scarred hands toward sinners.
Not to baptize our chains.
To break them.
Not to tell us sin doesn't matter.
To forgive us and transform us.
This is where Christian grace differs radically from cheap permission.
Grace does not say:
“Stay exactly where sin left you.”
Grace says:
“Come out of the grave.”
Repentance is not purchasing God's forgiveness by becoming good enough.
Repentance is turning toward the Savior because you finally realize your sin cannot save you.
You may fall while learning to walk.
You may need accountability.
You may need to remove access.
You may need to confess to a mature believer.
You may need to stop calling something “a struggle” when you have quietly arranged your life so that you can keep feeding it.
But do not confuse warfare with abandonment.
A believer fighting sin may have scars.
The question is whether you are making peace with the enemy or running again toward Christ.
And there is another extraordinary twist in Genesis 38.
Onan's failure is not the end of Tamar's story.
Judah also fails her.
Tamar's story becomes messy, painful, morally complicated, and scandalous.
Yet God is not finished.
Read Matthew's genealogy of Jesus Christ.
There she is.
Tamar.
Matthew 1:3 names Perez and Zerah by Tamar in the genealogy that ultimately leads to Jesus.
Let that sink in.
The woman standing inside one of Genesis' most uncomfortable family scandals appears in the lineage through which Scripture traces the Messiah.
Human failure did not derail God's redemptive purpose.
The scandal did not get the final word.
Grace did.
And that does not mean God approved everything everyone did in Genesis 38.
It means human sin could not prevent God from carrying His redemptive plan forward.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Human beings bring sin.
God brings redemption.
We bring ruins.
Christ raises the dead.
We bring shame into hiding.
Christ brings sinners into the light.
We bring stories we wish could be erased.
Jesus writes resurrection across pages we thought were permanently ruined.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why you needed this story today.
You came wondering whether Onan was killed for masturbation.
But perhaps Scripture has brought you somewhere more personal.
Not:
“What exactly was Onan allowed to do?”
But:
“What am I hiding from Jesus?”
That question may matter far more.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
Let those words become a confession instead of another performance.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting battles nobody sees.
And if you are exhausted and need believers to pray for you, simply write:
No details required.
No pretending required.
Just honesty.
Send it privately to the believer who has been struggling.
But Christians can glorify God through generous, willing support of faithful Gospel work when that support flows freely from love rather than spiritual pressure.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the person who hasn't opened a Bible in years.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing to say except condemnation.
Because the Christian message is not merely:
“Look how terrible sin is.”
It is:
Look how magnificent the Savior is.
Onan's story warns us that God sees beyond religious appearances into motives, selfishness, exploitation, and hidden rebellion.
Tamar's story reminds us that scandal does not have sovereign authority over the future.
And Jesus Christ shows us what redemption ultimately looks like.
Not sin excused.
Sin carried to a cross.
Not sinners abandoned.
Sinners called home.
Not darkness renamed as light.
Darkness invaded by Light Himself.
So tonight, when shame tells you to hide...
remember Eden.
Humanity hid.
God came looking.
Remember Peter.
He failed spectacularly.
Jesus restored him.
Remember the cross.
A criminal dying beside Jesus had nothing left to offer Him except desperate faith.
And Christ still opened Paradise.
Your darkest chapter does not have greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive His mercy.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Onan's story is not that God saw what happened on the ground.
It is that God saw what happened in the heart.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is this:
Jesus sees what is hiding in your heart too—and He is still calling you out of the darkness and into His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A RAPIST WAS ORDERED TO PAY: What Deuteronomy’s Difficult Marriage Laws Actually Mean
paragraphs:
A RAPIST WAS ORDERED TO PAY: What Deuteronomy’s Difficult Marriage Laws Actually Mean
The Bible did not call the violated woman guilty. It compared rape to murder, condemned the attacker, and forced men to bear consequences in a world where women could be left carrying them for life. But one disturbing passage still remains—and Christians should be courageous enough to read every word.
There are Bible verses people frame on walls.
This is not one of them.
Deuteronomy 22:28–29 is the kind of passage somebody screenshots, drops into a comment section, and asks:
And suddenly the Christian who was confidently defending Scripture five minutes earlier starts searching desperately for an explanation.
Maybe you have wondered about it too.
Maybe you were afraid to admit that.
Or perhaps this subject is not merely theological to you.
Perhaps somebody violated you.
Perhaps someone used your body, ignored your “no,” exploited your vulnerability, or left you carrying memories you never volunteered to carry.
If that is your story, this passage should never be thrown at you casually.
Because sexual violence is not an intellectual game.
And Scripture itself does not treat it like one.
So before we rush toward an answer, we need enough courage to hear the question.
Does the Bible really command a rape victim to spend the rest of her life married to the man who assaulted her?
Read the passage.
Read the Hebrew.
Read what comes immediately before it.
And something much more complicated—and much more revealing—begins to emerge.
Deuteronomy 22:28 opens:
“כִּי־יִמְצָא אִישׁ נַעֲרָ בְתוּלָה אֲשֶׁר לֹא־אֹרָשָׂה וּתְפָשָׂהּ וְשָׁכַב עִמָּהּ וְנִמְצָאוּ”
Ki-yimtza ish na'arah betulah asher lo-orasah, utefasah, veshakhav immah, venimtza'u.
In straightforward English:
If a man encounters an unbetrothed virgin, seizes her, lies with her, and they are discovered...
The crucial verb is וּתְפָשָׂהּ — utefasah, from the Hebrew root תפשׂ — taphas, carrying the sense of taking hold of, grasping, or seizing.
Then comes the consequence.
The man who slept with her must give her father fifty shekels of silver, and the text says she is to become his wife because:
תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר עִנָּהּ — tachat asher innah
Because he violated, afflicted, or humiliated her.
And then comes a restriction placed not upon the woman, but upon the man:
לֹא־יוּכַל שַׁלְּחָהּ כָּל־יָמָיו
Lo-yukhal shallechah kol-yamav.
He is not permitted to send her away all his days.
That is uncomfortable.
It should be.
The intellectually responsible Christian response is not to pretend an ancient Israelite law sounds exactly like twenty-first-century criminal law.
It does not.

The Torah arose within an ancient Near Eastern social world in which marriage, virginity, bride-price, inheritance, household economics, and a woman's future security were interconnected in ways profoundly different from most modern societies.
That historical distance matters.
But context does not make the passage disappear.
It helps us understand what the law was doing in its own world.
And the verses immediately before it are essential.
Just three verses earlier, Deuteronomy describes a man overpowering a betrothed woman.
The Hebrew uses another forceful expression:
וְהֶחֱזִיק־בָּהּ — vehecheziq-bah
The man takes hold of her and lies with her.
What does God's law say about the woman?
Not that she tempted him.
Not that she should have dressed differently.
Not that she should have fought harder.
Not that her violation made her guilty.
Deuteronomy 22:26 says:
וְלַנַּעֲרָ לֹא־תַעֲשֶׂה דָבָר
“Do nothing to the young woman.”
And then:
אֵין לַנַּעֲרָ חֵטְא מָוֶת
“There is in the young woman no sin deserving death.”
Then Scripture makes an astonishing comparison.
Her assault is compared to a man rising against his neighbor and murdering him.
Think about that.

In the very context people sometimes cite to portray Scripture as indifferent toward sexual violence, the text explicitly recognizes the assaulted woman as innocent and compares the offense against her to lethal violence.
The guilty man in that case dies.
The woman does not.
The law refuses to transfer his guilt onto her.
That matters.
Then verses 28–29 address a different legal status: an unbetrothed virgin.
And this is where modern readers encounter the provision involving fifty shekels and marriage.

Scholars have debated precisely how the case should be characterized and how Deuteronomy relates to the similar law in Exodus 22:16–17. Some interpreters have tried to read Deuteronomy 22:28–29 as consensual seduction. Others understand the language—especially taphas and the statement that he innah her—as describing coercion or rape. Serious scholarship recognizes the latter reading as a substantial, and often compelling, interpretation.
We should therefore resist the convenient Christian escape hatch of simply declaring, “It definitely wasn't rape.”
The Hebrew does not give us permission to dismiss the difficulty that easily.
But neither does the text say what the popular accusation often claims.
It never says:
“The victim must choose her rapist.”
It never describes the assault as acceptable.
It never declares the woman guilty.
And the marriage provision is not presented as a romantic reward for the attacker.
Quite the opposite.
The man has created devastation for which ancient Israelite society could easily have forced the woman to carry the consequences alone.
The law makes him pay.
He cannot violate her, destroy her prospects in that society, walk away, find another woman, and leave her economically exposed.
Fifty shekels of silver were imposed.
Permanent responsibility was imposed.
And the right of divorce was removed from him.
That final detail is especially important.
לֹא־יוּכַל שַׁלְּחָהּ כָּל־יָמָיו
He cannot simply send her away.
In an ancient society where a man could otherwise abandon a woman after taking advantage of her, the law closes an escape route for the offender.
That does not transform the arrangement into something a modern survivor would necessarily desire.
Nor should Christians romanticize it.
The Bible is describing law operating within an ancient patriarchal society, not handing twenty-first-century governments a ready-made sexual-assault statute.
And there is another piece of Torah that must remain in the conversation.
Exodus 22:16–17 addresses an unbetrothed virgin in a seduction case and explicitly allows the woman's father to refuse the marriage while financial payment remains required.

How exactly Exodus and Deuteronomy should be harmonized has been debated by Jewish and Christian interpreters and modern scholars. We should therefore be cautious about claiming Deuteronomy 22:28–29 explicitly gives the woman a veto when those verses themselves do not say that.
Biblical faithfulness does not require us to invent words God did not put on the page.
It requires us to tell the truth about the words that are there.
And what is there is not a celebration of rape.
It is consequence.
A man has done something that has harmed a woman.
He does not get to treat her like disposable flesh.
He does not get to take what he wanted and vanish.
He pays.
He loses privileges.
He acquires obligations.
The woman is not sentenced as the criminal.
The man is held responsible for what he has done.
Still...
perhaps something inside you is saying:
“But why did the law operate this way at all?”
That is a fair question.
And perhaps the deeper answer begins when we stop pretending the Old Testament was written in our century.
God's revelation entered an actual human world.
A brutal one.
A patriarchal one.
A world containing slavery, warfare, poverty, blood vengeance, sexual exploitation, economic dependence, and enormous power imbalances.
The Torah repeatedly places boundaries, responsibilities, protections, and consequences into that world.
That does not mean every social structure regulated by Mosaic law represents God's ultimate picture of human flourishing.
Jesus Himself teaches us something crucial about reading Mosaic legislation.
When questioned about divorce, Christ says Moses permitted certain arrangements “because of your hardness of heart,” before pointing His hearers back toward God's creational intention (Matthew 19:8).
That sentence should humble every simplistic reading of biblical law.
Law sometimes restrains what human hardness has broken.
Redemption aims deeper.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because Christianity does not end at Deuteronomy 22.
It moves through prophets and promises...
through Bethlehem...
through Galilee...
through a Savior who repeatedly restored dignity to women whom society shamed...
through a cross where human evil did its worst...
and through an empty tomb announcing that evil does not receive the final word.
Jesus never treated vulnerable women as disposable.
He defended the publicly humiliated.
He welcomed the socially rejected.
He exposed predatory hypocrisy.
He treated women as moral persons capable of faith, discipleship, testimony, courage, and devotion.
And ultimately He gave Himself for sinners.
Not because sin was small.
Because sin was so deadly that redemption required blood.
The Gospel never tells the wounded that evil did not matter.
The cross says precisely the opposite.
Sin matters so much that Christ bore judgment to redeem sinners from it.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace is God confronting evil and rescuing people who could never rescue themselves.
And this is where an ancient disturbing law suddenly starts asking modern questions.
Maybe you have never sexually assaulted anyone.
But have you used somebody?
Manipulated someone?
Taken affection you had no intention of honoring?
Used pornography while forgetting that the people on the screen bear God's image?
Pressured somebody sexually?
Hidden betrayal behind religious language?
Damaged somebody and quietly moved on because apologizing would cost too much?
We are frighteningly talented at wanting pleasure without responsibility.
We want the moment...
without the consequences.
Sin whispers:
Take what you want.
Grace says:
Look at what your taking has done.
Sin hides.
Repentance comes into the light.
Sin excuses.
Repentance confesses.
Sin asks, “How quickly can I escape the consequences?”
Jesus asks us to die to ourselves.
That is why this strange ancient law can still expose something painfully modern.
God cares what happens after somebody has been used.
He cares about responsibility.
He cares about the vulnerable.
He cares about guilt being placed where guilt belongs.
And for the person reading this who was the victim rather than the perpetrator, hear this carefully:
What somebody did to you does not make you dirty in the eyes of Christ.
Another person's sin is not your identity.
Your worth was never located in another person's ability to respect it.
Human beings may have treated you like an object.
Jesus does not.
You bear the image of God.
And if you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not “damaged,” “used,” “ruined,” or “discarded.”
You are someone for whom Jesus Christ shed His blood.
Healing may take time.
Trauma may require wise pastoral care, trusted community, and professional help.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending a crime was harmless.
It does not mean refusing justice.
It does not require returning to an unsafe person.
And reconciliation is not identical to forgiveness.
The Gospel does not demand that victims call evil good.
Christ calls evil what it is...
and then proves that evil does not get to write the final chapter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by deleting the wound.
Not by renaming darkness “light.”
Jesus walks directly into human wreckage and does what only the Redeemer can do.
He takes sinners toward repentance.
He takes shame toward grace.
He takes condemnation toward forgiveness.
He takes broken stories toward redemption.
He takes graves toward resurrection.
Maybe that is why this passage bothers us so deeply.
We want evil answered.
God does too.
But Scripture's answer becomes bigger than fifty shekels.
Bigger than an ancient courtroom.
Bigger than Deuteronomy.
At Calvary, we discover the staggering cost of human sin.
There the innocent Christ bears judgment for the guilty.
Not because perpetrators deserve cheap escape...
but because none of us can purchase our own cleansing before a holy God.
Jesus paid what silver never could.
And the same Gospel that offers forgiveness to the repentant sinner fiercely refuses the lie that sin does not matter.
Grace is free to us.
It was unimaginably costly to Him.
So if this article exposed something you have hidden, do not merely feel emotional and keep scrolling.
Bring it to Christ.

If you have harmed someone, repentance may require more than private tears. It may require confession, accountability, changed behavior, restitution where appropriate, and accepting legitimate consequences.
If you have been harmed, do not confuse somebody else's crime with your worth.
Come to the One who sees you completely.
Christ is not disgusted by wounds inflicted upon you.
He is near to the brokenhearted.
And if you are exhausted from pretending you are okay, you do not have to manufacture a polished Christian answer tonight.
You can simply pray:
“Jesus, meet me here.”
And He already knows where “here” is.
Someone silently reading beneath you may desperately need proof that another chapter can still be written.
Send it privately to the person who has been quietly wrestling with whether Scripture actually cares about victims.

If you want to glorify God through what you read, let that desire move beyond consuming Christian content into helping biblical truth travel—through prayer, sharing, discipleship, generosity, and support for faithful Gospel work. Salvation cannot be bought.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because perhaps one person behind one screen is asking whether God sees what happened to them.
Perhaps one skeptic thinks Christians are afraid of this verse.
Perhaps one survivor believes Scripture has already condemned them.
Perhaps one guilty person has spent years running from repentance.
And perhaps your share becomes the doorway through which somebody finally hears:
The victim is not the villain.
Sin is not harmless.
Grace is not cheap.
Jesus still saves.
And no human being who comes to Him has reached a chapter too ruined for redemption.
The wound may explain part of your story, but it does not own the pen—Jesus Christ still writes resurrection into places everyone else thought were finished.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAUL PROMISED HIS DAUGHTER TO DAVID—THEN GAVE HER TO ANOTHER MAN
paragraphs:
SAUL PROMISED HIS DAUGHTER TO DAVID—THEN GAVE HER TO ANOTHER MAN
David thought he was hearing a promise from a king. What he could not hear was the murder hiding behind the promise. And if you have ever been promised something, remained faithful, and then watched it go to somebody else… you need to read what happened next.
There are betrayals that announce themselves with shouting.
And then there are betrayals that smile at you first.
They shake your hand.
They praise your faithfulness.
They speak as though they are opening a door for you.
They make a promise.
And while you are trying to honor God with what they placed before you, you discover that what sounded like favor was never as innocent as it appeared.
David knew something about that kind of pain.
He had already faced Goliath.
He had already risked his life for Israel.
He had already served Saul.
He had played the harp when Saul was tormented.
He had gone where Saul sent him.
He had fought Israel’s enemies.
He had succeeded.
And the people loved him.
That should have been a beautiful story.
Instead, David’s success awakened something dark inside Saul.
Jealousy.
Fear.
A desperate need to preserve what Saul felt slipping from his hands.
Then Saul made David an extraordinary offer.
His daughter.
Merab.
Listen carefully to the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 18:17:
“הִנֵּה֩ בִתִּ֨י הַגְּדוֹלָ֤ה מֵרַב֙ אֹתָהּ֙ אֶתֶּן־לְךָ֣ לְאִשָּׁ֔ה”
Hinnēh bittî haggĕdōlāh Mērab, ʾōtāh ʾetten-lĕkā lĕʾiššāh.
“Behold, my older daughter Merab—I will give her to you as a wife.”
“I will give her to you.”
That sounds like favor.
That sounds like elevation.
That sounds like the shepherd boy from Bethlehem is about to become the king’s son-in-law.
But keep reading.
Because Scripture allows us to hear something David could not hear.
Saul’s private thoughts.
Saul told David:
“Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD’s battles.”
Religious language.
Noble language.
Even holy-sounding language.
Fight the LORD’s battles.
But underneath Saul’s words was another intention.
The Hebrew continues:
“אַל־תְּהִ֤י יָדִי֙ בּ֔וֹ וּתְהִי־ב֖וֹ יַד־פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים”
ʾAl-tĕhî yādî bô, ûtĕhî-bô yad-Pĕlištîm.
In essence:
“Let not my hand be against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.”
There it is.
The promise had a trap hiding behind it.
Saul wanted David fighting because Saul hoped somebody else would kill the man he was afraid to kill himself.
Think about how chilling that is.
David was being told to fight “the LORD’s battles,” while Saul was secretly hoping those battles would become David’s grave.
And maybe this is where the story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because some of the deepest wounds in life come from discovering that somebody’s words and somebody’s intentions were not the same thing.
Maybe someone promised to stay.
They left.
Maybe somebody told you they believed in you.
Later, you discovered they were undermining you.
Maybe someone made you believe the position was yours.
It went to somebody else.
Maybe you sacrificed years for something that disappeared in a conversation you were not even invited into.
Maybe you were faithful to somebody who was quietly using your faithfulness.
Maybe you kept wondering why the situation hurt so badly.
It wasn't merely what you lost.
It was what you had been led to believe.
David was promised Merab.
And David’s response is remarkable.
He did not swagger into the palace acting entitled.
He said:
“Who am I… that I should become the king’s son-in-law?”
There is humility here.
The young man Israel was celebrating was still capable of asking:
Who am I?
And then comes one of those verses in Scripture that can almost feel brutally short compared with the emotional weight inside it.
1 Samuel 18:19 says:
“וַיְהִ֗י בְּעֵ֥ת תֵּ֛ת אֶת־מֵרַ֥ב בַּת־שָׁא֖וּל לְדָוִ֑ד וְהִ֧יא נִתְּנָ֛ה לְעַדְרִיאֵ֥ל הַמְּחֹלָתִ֖י לְאִשָּֽׁה”
Vayhî bĕʿēt tēt ʾet-Mērab bat-Šāʾûl lĕDāwid, vĕhî nitĕnāh lĕʿAdrîʾēl hammĕḥōlātî lĕʾiššāh.
When the time came for Merab, Saul’s daughter, to be given to David…
she was given to Adriel the Meholathite instead.
Read that again.
When the time came.
Not when David first heard the promise.
When the expected moment finally arrived.
Merab was given to another man.

Scripture does not tell us everything we might want to know about that decision. It does not explicitly tell us what Merab herself thought about it, nor does this verse directly explain Saul’s motive for giving her to Adriel. We should not invent details God did not reveal.
But Scripture makes the broken promise unmistakable.
David was told one thing.
Something else happened.
And perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
You prayed over it.
Waited for it.
Prepared for it.
You thought, “Maybe this is finally happening.”
Then someone else got it.
Someone else married the person.
Someone else received the promotion.
Someone else walked through the door.
Someone else received the opportunity.
And you were left staring at a reality that did not match what you thought had been promised.
Those moments can do dangerous things to the soul.
They can make you question your worth.
They can make you replay conversations at 2:00 in the morning.
They can make you compare yourself with the person who received what you thought would be yours.
“What did they have that I didn't?”
“Was I not enough?”
“Did God forget me?”
“Why did God allow me to get this close?”
And perhaps the hardest question:
“Lord, if You are with me, why did You let this happen?”
But here is something easy to miss in David’s story.
The loss of Merab was not the loss of David’s calling.
Saul could manipulate circumstances.
Saul could break his word.
Saul could give Merab to another man.
Saul could send David into dangerous battles.
Saul could throw spears.
Saul could eventually drive David into the wilderness.
But Saul could not rewrite what God had spoken over David.
That distinction matters.
