Human beings can interfere with your plans without overthrowing the sovereignty of God.
A closed door does not automatically mean God abandoned you.
A broken human promise does not mean God broke His promises.
Someone choosing somebody else does not mean heaven rejected you.
Someone mistreating you does not determine your value.
David's security ultimately could not rest in Saul keeping his word.
It had to rest in God keeping His.
And that is where this story begins reaching beyond David.
Because the Bible is not ultimately a collection of inspirational stories telling you that if you endure long enough, you will eventually get everything people took from you.
The Gospel offers something infinitely greater.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
David would eventually become king, but even David was not the final King.
Another King would come through David’s line.
Jesus.
And Jesus would know betrayal far more deeply than David ever did.
One of His own disciples would betray Him.
Religious leaders would conspire against Him.
False testimony would surround Him.
Soldiers would mock Him.
A crowd would choose Barabbas.
His garments would be divided.
His hands and feet would be pierced.
And there on the cross, what appeared to be the triumph of human wickedness became the very place where God accomplished redemption.
That is the scandal of grace.
The cross looked like defeat.
God made it the doorway of salvation.
The grave looked final.
Jesus walked out.
Sin demanded judgment.
Christ bore judgment for sinners.
We deserved condemnation.
Christ offers forgiveness.
We ran from God.
God came after us.
We were guilty.
Jesus did not merely give us advice for becoming better people.
He gave Himself.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “God will give you something better.”
Sometimes He does restore what was lost.
Sometimes He opens another door.
Sometimes He does not give us an explanation in this life.
The Gospel gives us something deeper than a guarantee of improved circumstances.
It gives us Christ Himself.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs desperately to hear.
You have spent years allowing somebody else's treatment of you to become the definition of you.
They rejected you, so you decided you were unwanted.
They betrayed you, so you decided nobody could be trusted.
They replaced you, so you decided you were disposable.
They broke their promise, so you began assuming God would break His too.
But Saul was never God.
Neither is the person who hurt you.
Neither is the person who left you.
Neither is the person who chose somebody else.
Neither is the person who promised something and then changed their mind.
Stop giving human beings authority over parts of your identity that belong to Jesus Christ.
Your deepest identity is not “the one who got rejected.”
Not “the one who got cheated.”
Not “the one whose marriage failed.”
Not “the one who was abandoned.”
Not “the one who wasn't chosen.”
For those who are in Christ, the defining word is grace.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Adopted.
Loved.
Made new.
And maybe there is another side to this story that hurts even more.
Maybe you are not David in this story.
Maybe you have been Saul.
Maybe you made promises you knew you did not intend to keep.
Maybe you used somebody.
Maybe jealousy has been eating you alive while everybody around you thinks you are fine.
Maybe you secretly resent somebody simply because God seems to be blessing them.
Maybe you have smiled publicly while hoping privately that they would fail.
Saul’s jealousy did not stay a feeling.
It began shaping his decisions.
That is what unchecked sin does.
We entertain it privately until it begins controlling us publicly.
Jealousy whispers.
Then jealousy schemes.
Bitterness whispers.
Then bitterness speaks.
Lust whispers.
Then lust acts.
Pride whispers.
Then pride destroys relationships.
Sin rarely walks into your life announcing the final destination.
It simply asks you to take one more step.
And this is why the answer is not merely “try harder.”
Repent.
Bring it to Jesus.
Name the sin without dressing it in religious vocabulary.
Stop calling jealousy “discernment.”
Stop calling bitterness “boundaries” when what you really want is revenge.
Stop calling pride “standards.”
Stop hiding behind what people think of you.
Christ already knows.
And astonishingly, He still calls sinners to come.
That is grace.
Not pretending your sin is harmless.
Not telling you that you are wonderful exactly as you are and therefore never need to change.
Grace looks directly at our guilt and says there is forgiveness through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is turning from the road that is destroying you and running toward the Savior who died for sinners.
Maybe this article found you because something is still bleeding underneath your smile.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending the betrayal did not hurt.
Maybe everybody thinks you moved on.
But you remember.
The conversation.
The promise.
The day everything changed.
The moment somebody else received what you believed was coming to you.
Bring that wound to Christ.
Not because Christians are forbidden to grieve.
David grieved many times.
Bring it to Christ because bitterness makes a terrible savior.
Revenge cannot resurrect you.
Human validation cannot heal your soul.
Getting the last word will not cleanse your heart.
Jesus can meet you where the promise was broken.
Jesus can forgive what you have done.
Jesus can heal what was done to you.
Jesus can teach you to release what you cannot change.
And Jesus can transform even chapters you would never have chosen into places where His grace becomes unmistakable.
That is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by promising that every earthly loss will be returned exactly as we imagined.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming sinners, defeating death, forgiving guilt, restoring us to God, and ensuring that evil will not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So be honest for a moment.
What broken promise are you still carrying?
What name still changes the atmosphere inside you?
What disappointment have you never surrendered to Jesus?
What jealousy have you been hiding?
What wound has slowly become bitterness?
You do not have to tell strangers every detail. But maybe today is the day you stop pretending before God.
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that pain does not get the final sentence.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
But before you leave, remember David.
A king made him a promise.
The promise was broken.
The daughter promised to him was given to another man.
Yet the story God was writing over David's life did not end in 1 Samuel 18.
And neither does the Gospel end at betrayal.
Judas had his coins.
The soldiers had their nails.
The authorities had their sentence.
The tomb had its stone.
For one terrible moment, it looked as though darkness had written the ending.
Then Sunday morning came.
The stone moved.
Christ rose.
And every wounded believer was given a truth stronger than every broken human promise:
People may change what they promised you, but they cannot cancel what God is accomplishing in Christ.
That is the line I hope follows you after you close this article.
That is the line I hope you remember when an old betrayal wakes you at night.
That is the line I hope you share with somebody who thinks rejection has become the title of their life.
Because when Jesus Christ enters the story, even the grave does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “GOD IS WITHIN HER, SHE WILL NOT FALL”—BUT WHO IS “SHE”? THE TRUTH BEHIND THE VERSE MAY BE MORE POWERFUL THAN THE QUOTE
paragraphs:
“GOD IS WITHIN HER, SHE WILL NOT FALL”—BUT WHO IS “SHE”? THE TRUTH BEHIND THE VERSE MAY BE MORE POWERFUL THAN THE QUOTE
Psalm 46:5 was never written as a promise that a strong woman will never stumble. Its original picture is far bigger: a city surrounded by chaos, sustained by the presence of God—and that changes how we understand the verse, our suffering, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
“God is within her, she will not fall.”
You have probably seen those words before.
Printed beneath a photograph of a woman standing on a mountain.
Written across a journal.
Posted after heartbreak.
Shared after betrayal.
Placed beside a testimony about surviving something that almost destroyed a person.
And perhaps those words became personal to you.
Maybe you whispered them while trying to convince yourself that you were going to survive.
Maybe you held onto them when your marriage was trembling.
When the diagnosis came.
When someone walked away.
When money disappeared faster than hope.
When you were smiling publicly and quietly falling apart privately.
“God is within her, she will not fall.”
Beautiful words.
But there is something about Psalm 46:5 that many inspirational posts never tell you.
And strangely, discovering it does not make the verse less beautiful.
It makes it breathtaking.
Because when the psalmist wrote about “her,” he was not originally describing an individual woman.
He was describing the city of God.

And once you see the city surrounded by chaos, hear the waters roaring around it, and understand why it remains standing, Psalm 46 stops sounding like motivational self-confidence and starts sounding like what it really is:
a declaration about the terrifyingly dependable presence of God.
The Hebrew reads:
“אֱלֹהִים בְּקִרְבָּהּ בַּל־תִּמּוֹט”
Elohim bəqirbah, bal-timmot.
Literally, the thought is:
“God is in her midst; she shall not be moved.”
That word matters.
בְּקִרְבָּהּ — bəqirbah — means “in her midst,” or “within her.”
But who is “her”?
Read what comes immediately before it.
Psalm 46:4 speaks of:
“the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High.”
The feminine pronoun in verse 5 points naturally back to that city.
So Psalm 46:5 is not originally saying, “God lives inside a Christian woman, therefore nothing bad will happen to her.”
It is saying something larger.
Something ancient.
Something thunderous.
The city of God cannot ultimately be overthrown because God is in her midst.
That distinction matters because Christians do not honor Scripture by making it say what we wish it said.
We honor God by listening to what He actually said.
And what He actually said here is astonishing.
Look at the world surrounding the verse.
Psalm 46 does not begin peacefully.
“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”
Then the earth gives way.
Mountains fall into the sea.
Waters roar.
Nations rage.
Kingdoms totter.
This is not the landscape of a comfortable life.
This is creation coming apart at the seams.
And right there—in the middle of everything shaking—stands the city of God.
Not because the city is powerful enough.
Not because its people mastered positive thinking.
Not because faithful people never experience fear.
Not because believers are guaranteed painless lives.
The city stands because God is there.
“God is in the midst of her.”
That is the heartbeat of the verse.
The strength is not ultimately in “her.”
The strength is in Him.
And perhaps that is precisely what someone reading this needs to hear.
Because you have spent months trying to be “her.”
The woman who does not fall.
The mother who keeps everybody together.
The daughter who never admits she is exhausted.
The wife who keeps swallowing the pain.
The single woman who pretends loneliness never touches her.
The believer who thinks tears are evidence of weak faith.
The Christian who posts encouraging verses while wondering privately whether God still sees what is happening behind the screen.
You thought faithfulness meant never trembling.
But Psalm 46 never says nothing trembles.
Everything trembles.
That is the point.
Mountains tremble.
Waters roar.
Nations rage.
Kingdoms collapse.
Yet God remains.
Maybe you did fall.
Maybe that is the part you have been ashamed to admit.
You fell emotionally.
You fell financially.
You fell into temptation.
You fell back into something you promised God you would never touch again.
You trusted somebody you should not have trusted.
You ignored warnings.
You compromised.
You became bitter.
You stopped praying.
You stopped opening your Bible.
You began hiding from people who loved you because hiding felt easier than explaining what happened.
And now that beautiful quote—“she will not fall”—almost feels like an accusation.
Because you did.
So what now?
Now we remember that Christianity was never the story of impressive people saving themselves.
It is the story of a Savior rescuing sinners.
This is where motivational Christianity reaches its limit and the Gospel begins to shine.
Jesus did not come merely to tell fallen people to stand stronger.
He came to save them.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people receive trophies.
It is that guilty people can receive mercy because the righteous Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserved.
Jesus Christ entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He carried sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Christian hope therefore is not:
“I am too strong to fall.”
It is:
“Christ is strong enough to save.”
There is an enormous difference.
One makes you stare at yourself.
The other makes you look to Jesus.
And Scripture relentlessly moves our eyes toward Him.
There is even a profound biblical trajectory behind the imagery of God's dwelling.
In Psalm 46, God is in the midst of His city.
Then John tells us something staggering about Jesus:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
The Greek uses the verb:
ἐσκήνωσεν — eskēnōsen.
It carries the idea of dwelling or pitching a tent among us, language that powerfully echoes the biblical theme of God's dwelling with His people.
God did not remain distant from human misery.
The Word became flesh.
Jesus walked into it.
Touched lepers.
Received sinners.
Wept beside a grave.
Ate with people respectable religion despised.
Called the guilty to repentance.
Forgave sinners.
Carried a cross.
And Revelation eventually brings the biblical story toward its magnificent conclusion: God dwelling with His redeemed people.
That is why the deepest beauty of Psalm 46:5 is not feminine self-empowerment.
It is divine presence.
God with His people.
And for the Christian, that truth becomes intensely personal without requiring us to distort Psalm 46.
The New Testament teaches believers that the Spirit of God dwells in them.
Paul asks in 1 Corinthians 6:19:
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...?”
So yes, a Christian woman can rejoice that God dwells in her by His Spirit.
A Christian man can rejoice in that truth too.
But that doctrine comes from passages that actually teach it.
Psalm 46:5 should be allowed to say what Psalm 46:5 says.
And perhaps its actual message is exactly what we needed.
Because the Bible does not promise Christian women that they will never stumble.
Peter stumbled.
David fell catastrophically into sin.
Elijah became deeply discouraged.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples scattered.
Paul described pressures severe enough that he wrote of despairing even of life.
Faithful people bleed.
Faithful people grieve.
Faithful people can become exhausted.
Faithful people sometimes stumble.
The miracle is not that God's people possess some mystical immunity to human weakness.
The miracle is grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
“I do not know the man.”
Then the rooster.
Then the realization.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
If Christianity were merely a religion for people who never fall, Peter's story should have ended there.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him.
“Feed my sheep.”
Failure was real.
Sin was real.
Peter's denial was not renamed as strength.
But neither was his failure given the final word.
Jesus was.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin acceptable.
Not by turning repentance into self-esteem.
Jesus rewrites everything through truth, repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and grace.
Maybe your story has a chapter you desperately wish you could tear out.
Jesus already knows it exists.
Maybe you have spent years editing your testimony so nobody discovers what happened in the pages you refuse to read aloud.
Jesus has read every page.
And He still calls sinners to come.
Not to remain unchanged.
To repent.
To believe.
To be forgiven.
To be made new.
There is therefore another danger hidden inside the popular treatment of “God is within her, she will not fall.”
We can accidentally make ourselves the hero.
She is strong.
She is unstoppable.
She cannot be shaken.
She rises.
She conquers.
She wins.
But Psalm 46 keeps whispering:
Look again.
The hero is God.
“God is our refuge.”
“God is in the midst of her.”
“The LORD of hosts is with us.”
“The God of Jacob is our fortress.”
And finally:
“Be still, and know that I am God.”
Not:
Be still and remember how powerful you are.
Not:
Be still and manifest the future you deserve.
Not:
Be still because nothing painful can touch you.
“I am God.”
There is the anchor.
And notice something else.
Psalm 46 calls Him “the God of Jacob.”
Jacob.
The deceiver.
The schemer.
The complicated man with the complicated family and the complicated past.
Yet Scripture says:
“The God of Jacob is our fortress.”
There is grace hiding even in the name.
God is not ashamed to identify Himself as the God of deeply flawed people whom He has chosen to redeem.
That does not excuse their sin.
It magnifies His mercy.
Perhaps your life is shaking tonight.
Then do not turn Psalm 46:5 into pressure to perform strength.
Read the whole Psalm.
Let the mountains fall.
Let the waters roar.
Let the nations rage.
Let the kingdoms totter.
And then notice who never moves.
God.
Your security was never supposed to rest in your ability to maintain perfect emotional composure.
Christians are not saved because we hold onto God with flawless strength.
Our confidence rests in the God who faithfully keeps His people.
That does not mean every circumstance will end the way you want.
It does not mean the relationship will return.
It does not mean the illness will disappear tomorrow.
It does not mean Christians cannot experience tragedy.
And it certainly does not mean believers never die.
Psalm 46 points us toward something stronger than temporary comfort:
God remains God when the earth itself gives way.
And the Gospel reveals how far His saving love has gone.
All the way to a cross.
Then through a sealed tomb.
Then out the other side.
Resurrection.
So perhaps you came here because you loved the sentence:
“God is within her, she will not fall.”
Keep loving the Scripture.
But love it enough to hear it in context.
“She” is the city of God.
Her confidence is God's presence.
The surrounding world is collapsing.
And God is enough.
Then carry that truth to Christ.
Because your ultimate hope is not becoming a woman who never falls.
Your hope is belonging to the Savior who conquered sin and death.
And if you have fallen into sin, do not use grace as permission to remain there.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Cut off what is dragging you away from Christ.
Seek godly help where you need it.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship.
But above everything:
Return to Jesus.
The cross proves that sin is far more serious than our culture wants to admit.
The cross also proves that God's grace is more astonishing than ashamed sinners dare to believe.
You can simply write, “Jesus, bring me back.”
If you are exhausted but still clinging to Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”

And if God has already carried you through a season where everything seemed to collapse, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needs tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Send it privately to the person whose smile has been hiding a war.
Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can itself be an act offered for God's glory when it flows from love rather than pressure. Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And there is more waiting for those who genuinely want to grow.
Not because sharing proves you love God.
They may never tell you.
They may never post about it.
They may simply be scrolling at 2:17 in the morning wondering whether God has left.
And perhaps this is what they need to discover:
The Bible never promised that everything around God's people would remain standing.
Psalm 46 actually imagines the opposite.
The earth moves.
Mountains collapse.
Waters roar.
Nations rage.
Kingdoms fall.
Yet in the center of the chaos stands one magnificent reality:
God is there.
So when your world shakes, do not build your hope around the sentence:
“I will never fall.”
Build it around Someone infinitely stronger:
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
Jesus Christ rose from the grave.
Jesus Christ receives the repentant.
Jesus Christ restores the broken.
Jesus Christ remains faithful.
And when your trembling hands can barely hold another promise, remember this:
The greatest security in Psalm 46 is not that “she” is unshakable—it is that God is in the midst of what is shaking.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS AND WIVES NOT TO SEXUALLY DEPRIVE EACH OTHER—BUT THAT VERSE HAS BEEN ABUSED
paragraphs: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS AND WIVES NOT TO SEXUALLY DEPRIVE EACH OTHER—BUT THAT VERSE HAS BEEN ABUSED

1 Corinthians 7 was never permission to demand someone’s body in the name of God. Read Paul’s actual words carefully, and something far more beautiful—and far more challenging—emerges: mutual belonging, mutual responsibility, mutual tenderness, and a marriage transformed by the self-giving love of Christ.
There is a sentence from the Bible that has followed some husbands and wives into their bedrooms like a threat.
“Do not deprive one another.”

For some married couples, those words have been life-giving. They have reminded two tired, distracted people that intimacy matters. That marriage should not slowly become two roommates sharing bills, children, responsibilities, and a surname while their hearts live miles apart.
But for others, those same words have been weaponized.
“You cannot tell me no.”
“The Bible says your body belongs to me.”
“You are sinning if you refuse.”
“You owe me.”

And somewhere in a bedroom where Scripture should have brought light, a husband or wife has lain awake wondering whether God Himself was demanding something from them that felt frightening, humiliating, painful, coercive, or emotionally devastating.
But what if Paul never said what they were told he said?
What if we have sometimes taken a passage about mutual marital self-giving and twisted it into unilateral entitlement?
Because when you actually slow down and read 1 Corinthians 7, something remarkable happens.
Paul destroys the very argument used by someone who wants to turn this passage into a weapon.
He does it with one word repeated through the passage:
Likewise.

Paul is answering questions from believers in Corinth concerning marriage, sexuality, singleness, and abstinence. He begins the chapter by referring to matters about which the Corinthians had written to him. The surrounding discussion shows that sexual abstinence itself was part of the controversy. Paul responds by affirming marriage and mutual marital responsibility.
Then comes the passage so often quoted:
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
Then Paul says something extraordinarily countercultural:
“For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does.”
Someone determined to dominate could stop reading right there.
And tragically, some people effectively have.
But Paul does not stop.
“Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
That second sentence changes everything.
The Greek makes the symmetry unmistakable:
“ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.”
The crucial word is ὁμοίως — homoiōs.
Likewise.
In the same way.
Paul does not tell the wife that her body exists for her husband's desires while allowing the husband to remain sovereign over himself.
He places them both beneath the same radical principle.
Her body is not something she uses selfishly against him.
His body is not something he uses selfishly against her.
Marriage is not one person possessing another.
It is two people learning covenantal self-giving.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because there is a universe of difference between saying, “Because I love you, I give myself to you,” and hearing, “Because you married me, I can take what I want from you.”
One sounds like covenant.
The other sounds like ownership.
And Jesus did not teach His people to love by domination.
Christian love reaches its highest definition at a cross.
Christ gives Himself.
He does not exploit.
He does not manipulate.
He does not use another person's vulnerability for selfish gratification.
The pattern of Christlike love is sacrificial: “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” That is the atmosphere Christian marriage is meant to breathe.
Then Paul continues:
“Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again…”
Now look carefully at the Greek behind “by agreement”:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou.
It carries the idea of agreement together—mutual consent.
The word is related to the idea from which English gets “symphony”: voices sounding together.
Not one voice overpowering another.
Together.
Paul therefore does not picture one spouse announcing, “We are abstaining whether you like it or not.”
Nor does he picture another spouse saying, “You must give me sex whenever I demand it because verse 5 says not to deprive me.”
The temporary abstinence Paul describes is ἐκ συμφώνου—mutually agreed upon—and πρὸς καιρόν, for a limited time.
Even abstinence is treated relationally.
Even here, Paul sees two people who should talk, listen, care, agree, and eventually return to one another.
That means this passage confronts more than one kind of selfishness.
It confronts the spouse who deliberately weaponizes sex.
And it confronts the spouse who weaponizes Scripture to obtain sex.
Both can turn intimacy into power.
One says, “I will withhold myself until you suffer.”
The other says, “I will quote God until you surrender.”
Neither sounds like Jesus.
Sexual intimacy within marriage is not meant to become currency.
Not payment for good behavior.
Not punishment for bad behavior.
Not leverage.
Not revenge.
Not proof of masculinity.
Not proof of femininity.
Not a bargaining chip.
Not something extracted through guilt.
It is meant to belong within covenant love.
And that is precisely why this conversation requires tenderness.
Because behind the word “deprivation” there may be stories nobody sees.
Maybe she is not trying to punish him.
Maybe she is exhausted.
Maybe pregnancy changed her body.
Maybe childbirth left pain nobody prepared her for.
Maybe she spends all day being touched by children and reaches nighttime with nothing emotionally left.
Maybe she feels invisible everywhere except when someone wants something from her body.
Maybe he is not rejecting her.
Maybe he is ashamed.
Maybe stress has crushed his desire.
Maybe medication, illness, hormones, grief, depression, age, sexual dysfunction, relational wounds, or unresolved conflict have entered a marriage neither spouse expected.
Maybe there is betrayal that has never actually healed.
Maybe pornography shattered trust.
Maybe harsh words outside the bedroom made tenderness inside the bedroom feel impossible.
Maybe one spouse carries trauma from long before the wedding.
Maybe sex physically hurts.
Maybe somebody learned to smile while quietly dissociating.
And maybe the sentence “The Bible says you can't deprive me” did not heal any of it.
It only made the wound deeper.
Scripture should never be used to silence suffering that love should be willing to hear.
At the same time, another painful truth must also be spoken.
Sometimes intimacy really is withheld deliberately.
Sometimes affection becomes punishment.
Sometimes sex becomes a reward system.
Sometimes one spouse knows the other is lonely and uses that loneliness as leverage.
Sometimes months become years, communication dies, resentment grows, and nobody wants to say what is happening.
Paul's words confront that too.
Biblical correction cuts in both directions.
The spouse who says, “Your needs never matter to me,” should hear Paul's call to mutual care.
The spouse who says, “Your boundaries never matter to me,” should hear it too.
Marriage does not give Christians permission to become selfish in opposite directions.
It calls them into something harder.
Love.
Patient love.
Truthful love.
Listening love.
Repentant love.
Love that asks instead of assumes.
Love that notices tears.
Love that cares whether the other person feels safe.
Love that refuses to punish.
Love that refuses to manipulate.
Love willing to say, “Something between us is hurting. Can we talk about it?”
And sometimes love says, “We need help.”

There is no shame in a married couple seeking wise pastoral counsel, qualified marriage counseling, or appropriate medical care when pain, trauma, dysfunction, medication effects, hormonal changes, disability, illness, or deep relational wounds are affecting intimacy.
Prayer matters.
Scripture matters.
And getting appropriate help does not compete with faithfulness to God.
Sometimes seeking help is one of the ways we stop hiding.
But there is something even deeper in Paul's language that modern readers can easily miss.
In a world where sexual double standards were hardly unusual, Paul deliberately gives husband and wife corresponding responsibilities.
“The husband…”
“Likewise the wife…”
“The wife…”
“Likewise the husband…”
“Do not deprive one another…”
This is reciprocity.
Not entitlement.
The bedroom becomes one more place where the Christian learns the death of selfishness.
And suddenly the passage becomes much more uncomfortable than the weaponized version.
Because the weaponized version lets me ask:
“What am I owed?”
The Gospel-shaped version makes me ask:
“How am I loving?”
That question reaches farther than sex.
Have I become emotionally unavailable?
Have I stopped being affectionate except when I want intercourse?
Have I treated my spouse like a sexual vending machine—attention inserted, sex expected?
Have I rejected my spouse repeatedly without caring enough to explain what is happening?
Have I used spiritual language to avoid an honest conversation?
Have I made my spouse afraid to tell me no?
Have I punished vulnerability?
Have I ignored pain?
Have I allowed resentment to become a wall and then pretended the wall appeared by itself?
Have I demanded tenderness while refusing to be tender?
And perhaps the hardest question:
Have I ever used God's Word to win against the person I vowed to love?
That question should make every Christian tremble.
Because the Bible was never given to us as ammunition for controlling other people.
The Word exposes us too.
Before you quote 1 Corinthians 7:5 at your husband or wife, stand beneath it yourself.
Before asking what your spouse owes you, ask what Christ is changing in you.
Your selfishness.
Your pride.
Your resentment.
Your lust.
Your coldness.
Your impatience.
Your manipulation.
Your refusal to communicate.
Your unwillingness to forgive.
Your unwillingness to repent.
This is where the scandal meets grace.
Because perhaps you have failed here.
Maybe badly.
Maybe you pressured someone you claimed to love.
Maybe you withheld affection to hurt them.
Maybe you mocked your spouse's body.
Maybe pornography taught your mind to consume instead of cherish.
Maybe rejection became bitterness.
Maybe bitterness became cruelty.
Maybe years of silence now sit between you in bed.
Maybe you are reading this and realizing that something you called “biblical authority” was actually selfishness wearing a Bible verse.
What now?
Jesus.
Not hiding.
Not pretending.
Jesus.
The Gospel does not tell sinners to manufacture innocence.
It tells sinners where forgiveness can be found.
Christ went to the cross for real sin.
Sexual sin.
Marital sin.
Secret sin.
Religious hypocrisy.
Manipulation.
Lust.
Pride.
Cruelty.
Bitterness.
All the ugly things we would rather rename than confess.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for the imaginary version of you that never wounded anyone.
He died for sinners.
And repentance means we stop defending what He is calling us to surrender.
Sometimes repentance sounds like this:
“I was wrong.”
No excuse afterward.
No “but you…”
Just truth.
“I pressured you.”
“I ignored your pain.”
“I punished you with rejection.”
“I used Scripture against you.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I let pornography corrupt the way I looked at you.”
“I made intimacy about myself.”
“I need forgiveness.”
That may not instantly repair everything.
Forgiveness does not magically erase consequences, restore trust overnight, or eliminate the need for safety, counsel, accountability, medical treatment, or patient rebuilding.
But repentance opens the door that pride keeps locked.
And grace walks through doors like that.
This is what Jesus does.
He enters places shame told us to hide.
He exposes what darkness told us to protect.
Then He does something scandalous.
He offers mercy.
Not cheap mercy that calls evil good.
Grace tells the truth about sin and then announces that sin does not have to write the final chapter.
The cross proves both things simultaneously.
Sin is serious enough that Christ died.
Grace is powerful enough that Christ rose.
So perhaps your marriage does not need another argument over who owes whom sex.
Perhaps it needs two people kneeling before Jesus again.
Perhaps it needs confession.
Perhaps it needs forgiveness.
Perhaps it needs a difficult conversation.
Perhaps it needs months of rebuilding trust.
Perhaps it needs professional help.
Perhaps it needs tenderness without expectation.
Perhaps it needs intimacy rediscovered slowly, patiently, prayerfully.
Perhaps it needs husband and wife looking at each other not as competitors keeping score, but as two redeemed sinners learning how to love because Christ first loved them.
Paul was not handing husbands a weapon.
He was not handing wives one either.
He was calling married Christians away from selfish isolation and toward mutuality.
And if somebody ever quotes, “Do not deprive one another,” while conveniently forgetting ἐκ συμφώνου, mutual agreement, and ὁμοίως, likewise, read the whole passage.
Context matters.
Words matter.
Your spouse matters.
And Christ matters most.
If this exposed something you have hidden even from yourself, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your marriage. But you can take one honest step into the light.
No explanations required.
Someone reading those words may realize tonight that they are not the only Christian struggling behind a smiling family photograph.

Someone in your circle may have spent years believing that God endorsed the very coercion that wounded them. Someone else may need to realize that deliberately weaponizing rejection is not loving either.
And whether you ever spend a cent or not, keep pursuing Christ.
Because your marriage was never meant to become a courtroom where two people argue over their rights.
At its most Christlike, it becomes a place where two redeemed people keep learning how to give, listen, repent, forgive, protect, cherish, and love.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needs tonight:
Jesus can enter even the room where love became a weapon—and teach wounded hearts how to become tender again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: One of Judah’s Most Wicked Kings Finally Cried Out to God From Captivity. What Happened Next Is Almost Never Preached.
paragraphs: One of Judah’s Most Wicked Kings Finally Cried Out to God From Captivity. What Happened Next Is Almost Never Preached.
Manasseh’s story is terrifying because it shows how far a human heart can fall. It is breathtaking because it shows how far the mercy of God can reach when that heart finally breaks.
There are some people we secretly believe are too far gone.
We would never say it in church.
We know the correct theology. We know the verses about grace. We sing about mercy. We tell people that Jesus saves.
But then somebody hurts our family.
Somebody destroys innocent lives.
Somebody spends years mocking everything holy.
Somebody becomes so corrupt, so cruel, so spiritually dark that when we hear what they have done, something inside us quietly decides:
Not that person.
Maybe God forgives liars.
Maybe God restores addicts.
Maybe God receives prodigals.
But him?
Surely not him.
Then the Bible introduces us to Manasseh.
And if you think you understand grace, his story may disturb you before it comforts you.
Manasseh was the son of Hezekiah, one of Judah’s most celebrated reforming kings. Yet when Manasseh became king, he did not merely wander from his father’s faith.
He tore in the opposite direction.

Second Kings 21 and Second Chronicles 33 describe a reign saturated with idolatry and rebellion. He rebuilt pagan high places his father had destroyed. He erected altars to the Baals. He made Asherah poles. He worshiped the host of heaven. He placed pagan altars within the precincts associated with the house of the LORD.
Then the story gets darker.
He practiced sorcery, divination, and occultism. He consulted mediums and spiritists. He led Judah into evil.
And Scripture says he made his own sons pass through the fire.
Second Kings goes further still, saying Manasseh shed “very much innocent blood” until he had filled Jerusalem “from one end to another” (2 Kings 21:16).
Stop there for a moment.
Do not sanitize him because you already know there is repentance coming.
Do not turn him into a harmless Sunday-school character who simply “made some mistakes.”
The Bible does not.
Manasseh used power to normalize rebellion against God. His sin was personal, public, religious, cultural, and devastating. He did not simply fall into darkness.
He helped lead a nation into it.
Second Chronicles 33:9 gives a chilling summary: Manasseh led Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem astray so that they did greater evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed before Israel.
Then comes one of the saddest sentences in the account:
God spoke.
They would not listen.
That sentence should frighten us more than we usually allow it to.
Because Manasseh’s greatest danger was not simply that he had sinned.
It was that God was speaking while he continued refusing to hear.
And perhaps that is where his ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Maybe you have never built an altar to Baal.
Maybe you have never consulted a medium.
Maybe nobody would describe you as a wicked king.
But how many times has God confronted something in you that you kept protecting?
The secret relationship.
The pornography you keep deleting and returning to.
The bitterness you have renamed “discernment.”
The pride you call confidence.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The money you cannot surrender.
The apology you know you owe.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The religious appearance covering a private life that would terrify you if it were projected onto the church wall.
God speaks.
And sometimes we become experts at hearing sermons without hearing Him.
Manasseh would not listen.
So eventually, consequences came knocking.
Second Chronicles tells us that the LORD brought against Judah the commanders of the army of the king of Assyria. They captured Manasseh, bound him, and took him to Babylon.
The Hebrew description is striking.
Second Chronicles 33:11 says they bound him:
בַּנְחֻשְׁתַּיִם — banĕḥushtayim
The word refers to bronze fetters or shackles.
The king who had lived with power was now restrained.
The man who had commanded others was now being commanded.
The ruler who would not bow before God had been brought terrifyingly low.

Scripture does not specifically tell us that Manasseh sat inside what we would call a “prison cell,” so we should not pretend it does. What it does tell us is more than enough: he was captured, bound in bronze fetters, and carried away to Babylon.
And somewhere inside that humiliation, something happened that military force could never manufacture.
Manasseh broke.
Not merely politically.
Not merely emotionally.
Spiritually.
Second Chronicles 33:12 says:
וּכְהָצֵר לוֹ חִלָּה אֶת־פְּנֵי יְהוָה אֱלֹהָיו וַיִּכָּנַע מְאֹד
Ukhĕhatsēr lo, ḥillāh et-pĕnē YHWH Elohav, vayikkānaʿ mĕ’od...
In context, the sense is that when he was in distress, he sought or entreated the favor of the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly.
That last movement matters.
וַיִּכָּנַע מְאֹד — vayikkānaʿ mĕ’od.
He humbled himself greatly.
The man who had exalted himself against God finally came low before God.
And here is where the story becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because God listened.
Think about who was praying.
A man associated with idolatry.
A man who practiced occultism.
A king who had led others into rebellion.
A man under whose reign Jerusalem was filled with innocent blood.
A father who had participated in horrific pagan practices involving his own children.
Manasseh prayed.
And God did not say, “You had your chance.”
God did not say, “Your record is too long.”
God did not say, “Mercy is available for respectable sinners, not people like you.”
Second Chronicles 33:13 tells us that Manasseh prayed to Him, and God was moved by his entreaty.
Then comes the sentence that can dismantle years of hopelessness:
וַיִּשְׁמַע תְּחִנָּתוֹ
Vayyishmaʿ tĕḥinnato.
“He heard his supplication.”
God heard him.
After everything.
God heard him.
And the LORD brought Manasseh back to Jerusalem and restored him to his kingdom.
Then Scripture says:
וַיֵּדַע מְנַשֶּׁה כִּי יְהוָה הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים
Vayyēdaʿ Mĕnashsheh ki YHWH hu ha’Elohim.
“Then Manasseh knew that the LORD, He is God.”
Read that slowly.
The throne did not teach him what the chains finally did.
His power could not save him.
His idols could not save him.
His occult practices could not save him.
His royal status could not save him.
His past certainly could not save him.
He needed mercy.
And so do we.
This does not mean Manasseh’s evil suddenly became insignificant.
Grace never requires us to pretend evil was not evil.
Forgiveness does not rename wickedness.
Repentance does not erase every earthly consequence.

In fact, Scripture refuses to give us a shallow ending. Manasseh attempted reforms after his return. He removed foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, tore down altars he had built, restored the LORD’s altar, offered sacrifices, and commanded Judah to serve the LORD.
Something had changed.
His repentance began producing visible fruit.
Yet the damage of his earlier influence did not simply disappear.

The people still sacrificed at the high places, though Chronicles says they did so to the LORD their God. Later biblical history also continues to remember the catastrophic evil associated with Manasseh’s reign.
That tension matters.
Grace is free.
Sin is not cheap.
Forgiveness is real.
Consequences can also be real.
And repentance is more than feeling terrible because your life finally became painful.
Biblical repentance turns.
It bows.
It comes home.
It begins tearing down the altars it once built.
That is why Manasseh’s story is not permission to postpone repentance.
It is a warning against doing exactly that.
Someone reading this may be thinking, Then I can keep living however I want. Manasseh came back at the end.
No.
You are not promised Manasseh’s tomorrow.
The miracle of his repentance should never become an excuse for ours to wait.
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15).
Today.
Not after one more affair.
Not after one more secret night.
Not after you finally destroy your marriage.
Not after your children inherit what you refused to confront.
Not when addiction has taken everything.
Not when consequences finally put chains around your wrists.
Today.
And this is where Manasseh’s story points beyond Manasseh.
Because the ultimate hope of Scripture is not that terrible people can become slightly better people.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Manasseh could humble himself and cry for mercy, but he could not pay the infinite moral debt of humanity.
Christ came to do what no repentant king could accomplish.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend sin was small.
He showed us how serious it truly is.
And He showed us how astonishing the love of God truly is.
The sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not that your past does not matter.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ is greater than your past.
It is not that judgment is imaginary.
It is that Christ bore sin and offers forgiveness and reconciliation to those who turn to Him in faith.
It is not that repentance earns grace.
Repentance comes empty-handed.
Grace is grace precisely because you cannot purchase it.
Maybe that is why Manasseh makes some religious people uncomfortable.
We like grace when we are the recipients.
We struggle with grace when God gives it to someone we believe deserves destruction.
But that is the scandal.
If mercy were only available to people who deserved mercy, it would no longer be mercy.
And before we stand over Manasseh congratulating ourselves because our sins look cleaner than his, the Gospel brings every one of us down from our little thrones.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Different histories.
Different wounds.
Different sins.
The same desperate need for a Savior.
You may not be Manasseh.
But you need Manasseh’s God.
And you need the Savior to whom the whole biblical story ultimately points.
Jesus.
Maybe your chains are invisible.
Nobody at church knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your followers certainly do not know.
You have learned how to smile while spiritually bleeding.
You know how to say, “God is good,” while privately wondering whether God could possibly want you after what you have done.
Listen carefully.
Manasseh’s story does not tell you that sin is harmless.
It tells you that hiding is useless.
It tells you that pride can break.
It tells you that repentance is possible.
It tells you that God hears the humbled sinner who turns toward Him.
And the New Testament gives us the breathtaking fullness of that hope:
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
You do not need to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Bring Him the truth.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the Christian vocabulary.
Not the version you would comfortably tell your small group.
The truth.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
“Jesus, I cannot fix what I have become.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the moment into mere emotion and keep scrolling.
Turn toward Christ.
There is no magic in the words. A comment cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing what was hidden into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
And perhaps somebody else scrolling silently through the comments needs to discover that they are not the only Christian still fighting, still repenting, still healing, still learning to surrender.
You may never know who reads because you shared.
We glorify God through Christ-centered faith and obedience.

Invite your family. Invite your friends. Invite struggling believers. Invite seekers. Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years. Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only a religion for people with clean histories.
Let them meet Manasseh.
Then let them meet Jesus.
This story is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about a King greater than Manasseh.
A King who never practiced evil.
A King who never needed repentance.
A King who willingly entered suffering for sinners.
A King whose crown was surrounded by thorns.
A King who was nailed to a cross.
A King who walked out of the grave.
A King before whom every other king will bow.
Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the question is no longer whether God could have mercy on Manasseh.
Scripture has already answered that.
The question is what you will do now that God has confronted you.
Will you keep defending the altar?
Or will you tear it down?
Will you keep hiding?
Or will you confess?
Will you keep running?
Or will you come home?
Because the same Bible that refuses to minimize Manasseh’s wickedness also refuses to hide the breathtaking reality of his repentance.
He humbled himself greatly.
He prayed.
God heard.
And the man who had spent years dishonoring the LORD finally knew:
כִּי יְהוָה הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים
Ki YHWH hu ha’Elohim.
The LORD—He is God.
Maybe your story contains pages you wish you could burn.
Maybe there are chapters you would give anything to rewrite.
You cannot go backward.
But in Jesus Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And follow the Savior who still transforms sinners into testimonies of grace.
Sometimes God allows the throne beneath us to collapse so we can finally discover that His mercy was waiting beneath our knees.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS ASKED THE DEMON ONE QUESTION. THE ANSWER WAS CHILLING: “LEGION.”
paragraphs:
JESUS ASKED THE DEMON ONE QUESTION. THE ANSWER WAS CHILLING: “LEGION.”
He lived among graves, screamed through the night, mutilated his own body, and could no longer be restrained. Everyone else had learned to fear him, bind him, or avoid him. Then Jesus stepped out of a boat—and everything occupying that ruined life discovered that Someone stronger had arrived.
There are places most people would rather Jesus never take them.
Places where the smell of death hangs in the air.
Places where respectable people do not linger.
Places where somebody's son has become the person everyone whispers about.
Mark 5 takes us to one of those places.
Jesus has just crossed the sea with His disciples. Behind Him is a storm He silenced with a word. Ahead of Him is something even darker.
A man is coming out of the tombs.
Not a metaphorical tomb.
Not merely a difficult season.
Tombs.
This man is living among the dead.
Mark describes him as a man “with an unclean spirit.” He had repeatedly been restrained with chains and shackles, but he tore them apart. Nobody was strong enough to subdue him.
Then comes one of the saddest sentences in the passage.
Night and day he wandered among the tombs and mountains, crying out and injuring himself with stones.
Imagine what his family had already endured.
Imagine remembering the boy he used to be.
Maybe somebody once held him as a baby.
Maybe somebody once knew the sound of his ordinary laughter.
Maybe there had been dinners, conversations, friendships, dreams.
But now?
The town knew him by his condition.
Dangerous.
Unclean.
Uncontrollable.
The man in the tombs.
And that is one of the cruelties of darkness: eventually, what has happened to you can begin to sound like who you are.
Addict.
Failure.
Adulterer.
Drunk.
Rejected.
Abused.
Angry.
Pornographer.
Liar.
Backslider.
Broken.
Unwanted.
Too far gone.
Maybe nobody calls you those things aloud.
Maybe you call yourself those things when the room gets quiet.
You can wear clean clothes, go to work, raise children, answer messages, smile for photographs, post Scripture on Facebook—and still have places inside you that feel like tombs.
Hidden shame.
Secret bondage.
Memories you cannot erase.
A recurring sin you promised God you would never commit again.
A private war nobody knows you are losing.
And before going any further, we need to be biblically careful.

Not every psychological struggle is demon possession. Not every illness, temptation, addiction, intrusive thought, depression, trauma, or emotional wound should automatically be attributed to demons. Scripture recognizes physical sickness, human sin, suffering, temptation, and demonic oppression without carelessly collapsing them into one category.
Mark 5, however, explicitly presents a genuine confrontation with unclean spirits.
And what happens next is terrifying—not because of how powerful the demons appear, but because of how powerless they suddenly become when Jesus arrives.
The man sees Him from a distance.
He runs.
Then he falls before Jesus.
Think about that.
People could not control him.
Chains could not hold him.
Human strength could not subdue him.
Yet Jesus does not wrestle him to the ground.
Christ simply arrives.
The unclean spirit cries out through the man:
“What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?”
The darkness knows who just stepped onto the shore.
Jesus had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man.
Then Christ asks the question that has echoed through centuries:
“What is your name?”
The Greek of Mark 5:9 preserves the chilling answer:
Λεγιὼν ὄνομά μοι, ὅτι πολλοί ἐσμεν.
Legiōn onoma moi, hoti polloi esmen.
Literally, in natural English:
“My name is Legion, because we are many.”
One word changes the atmosphere.
Λεγιών — Legiōn.
Legion.

The term comes from the Roman military world. A Roman legion was a massive military formation numbering thousands of soldiers. But Scripture does not give us permission to turn this into an exact demon headcount. Mark explains the point himself:
ὅτι πολλοί ἐσμεν — hoti polloi esmen
“because we are many.”
Luke makes the meaning even more explicit: the answer was “Legion” because many demons had entered the man.
Many.
Not one.
Many.
And suddenly the chains make sense.
The violence.
The isolation.
The tombs.
The screaming.
The destruction.
The man before Jesus is horribly overwhelmed.
But do not miss what the demons themselves have already revealed.
They are begging.
That changes everything.
A legion is speaking...
but the legion is pleading.
They recognize Jesus.
They fear His authority.
They cannot dictate terms to Him.
They cannot simply remain where He commands them to leave.
The story is not fundamentally about the impressive strength of demons.
It is about the incomparable authority of Jesus Christ.
And somebody reading this needs to understand the difference.
Christianity does not invite you to become fascinated with darkness.
It calls you to behold Christ.
The center of Mark 5 is not Legion.
The center is Jesus.
Darkness may be numerous.
Jesus is Lord.
Darkness may have occupied territory for years.
Jesus is Lord.
Darkness may have convinced a human being that freedom is impossible.
Jesus is Lord.
The demons plead to be sent into a nearby herd of pigs.
Jesus permits it.
They leave the man, enter the animals, and the herd—about two thousand pigs—rushes down the steep bank into the sea.
The scene is violent.
Chaotic.
Disturbing.
But then Mark turns our eyes away from the water.
Back toward the man.
And this may be one of the most beautiful pictures of restoration in the Gospel of Mark.
The townspeople arrive.
They know what they expect to find.
They know this man.
They know the screams.
They know the violence.
They know nobody could restrain him.
But there he is.
Sitting.
Clothed.
In his right mind.
Read those words slowly.
Sitting.
The man who could not rest.
Clothed.
The man whose dignity had been devastated.
In his right mind.
The man everyone had considered beyond control.
Jesus did not merely silence a disturbance.
He restored a person.
Behind the frightening description “Legion” was still a human being made in the image of God.
Jesus saw the man everyone else had learned to fear.
And perhaps that is where this story reaches through the page and finds us.
Because people often identify us by the worst chapter they know about us.
Jesus sees farther.
People remember what you did.
Jesus knows what grace can make of you.
People remember the breakdown.
Jesus sees the testimony that can rise from the wreckage.
People see the tombs.
Jesus sees someone who can go home again.
This is Gospel territory.
This is scandal becoming grace.
Because the Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Christ is greater.
It does not pretend darkness is imaginary.
It declares that darkness does not have the final word.
It does not tell sinners to save themselves.
It announces a Savior.
And ultimately, Jesus would confront something even greater than the tombs of the Gerasenes.
He would go toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward humiliation.
Toward a Roman cross.
The sinless Son of God would give Himself for sinners.
He would bear sin's judgment, shedding His blood for our redemption.
He would die.
He would be buried.
And on the third day, the tomb that appeared to have swallowed Jesus would become evidence that death itself could not hold Him.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a message of self-improvement.
It is good news about Jesus Christ.
His death.
His resurrection.
His lordship.
His grace.
His call to repentance and faith.
The answer to our deepest problem is not “try harder until you become worthy of God.”
You cannot.
Neither can I.
The Gospel says that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Forgiveness is not purchased by our goodness.
Redemption is found in Christ.
Repentance is not pretending your chains never existed. It is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can forgive, cleanse, reconcile, and transform.
And there is another disturbing part of Mark 5 that is easy to overlook.
When the townspeople see the restored man, they become afraid.
Then they ask Jesus to leave.
Imagine that.
A man has been delivered.
A destroyed life has been restored.
Someone who lived among graves is sitting clothed and sane.
And they ask Jesus to go away.
Why?
Mark tells us they were afraid, but he does not reduce their response to one simplistic motive.
Whatever all their reasons were, the tragedy is unmistakable:
Jesus was standing among them...
and they wanted distance.
That may be the most frightening moment in the entire story.
Not “Legion.”
“Leave.”
Because demons are not the only ones who can recognize something about Jesus while refusing joyful fellowship with Him.
You can know Bible verses and still resist Him.
You can attend church and still protect a secret sin from Him.
You can sing worship songs while quietly telling Christ, “You can have everything except this.”
My money.
My sexuality.
My resentment.
My relationship.
My ambition.
My addiction.
My pride.
My unforgiveness.
My reputation.
My private browser history.
My plans.
My whole life.
We sometimes want enough Jesus to comfort us...
but not enough Jesus to overthrow us.
Enough Jesus to bless the house.
Not enough to become Lord of every room.
So this story eventually forces a question upon us.
Not merely, “Do you believe demons exist?”
Something far more personal.
What are you asking Jesus to leave untouched?
Be honest.
Maybe this article has found you in a season when you have become exhausted from hiding.
You love Jesus—or desperately want to—but there is something underneath the surface.
Something keeps dragging you back toward places Christ is calling you out of.
Then hear this carefully:
Do not build your identity around your bondage.
Do not make peace with sin.
Do not romanticize darkness.
Do not assume that because the struggle has been long, Christ has become weak.
Bring your sin into the light.
Repent.
Seek Christ.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Confess where Scripture commands confession.
Seek mature Christian help.

And when mental illness, trauma, self-harm, addiction, or other serious health concerns are involved, seeking qualified medical or mental-health care is not a denial of faith. Human suffering should never be reduced carelessly to demonization.
Jesus is not glorified by pretending.
He is glorified when truth comes into the light.
And look at what happens to the restored man.
As Jesus prepares to leave, the man begs to go with Him.
Who could blame him?
Jesus had given him his life back.
But Jesus gives him a mission instead.
Go home.
Go to your own people.
Tell them what the Lord has done for you.
Tell them about His mercy.
And the man goes throughout the Decapolis proclaiming what Jesus had done for him.
Do you see the transformation?
At the beginning of the story, his voice echoes through graveyards.
At the end, his voice carries a testimony.
The mouth that screamed in torment now tells people about mercy.
The man who frightened a region becomes a witness to a region.
The one who lived among tombs goes home carrying good news.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming what the scandal tried to destroy.
Maybe that is why you are still here.
Maybe grace has already pulled you through things that should have destroyed you.
Maybe somebody needs the testimony you keep calling embarrassing.
You survived the addiction.
Tell them who carried you.
You wandered from God and came home.
Tell them about mercy.
Your marriage nearly collapsed.
Tell them what Christ taught you through repentance and forgiveness.
You spent years pretending.
Tell them what happened when you finally stopped hiding.
You thought your past disqualified you.
Tell them about the cross.
Your testimony does not need to make you the hero.
Jesus is the Hero.
That is what makes a Christian testimony powerful.
Not “Look how strong I became.”
But:
Look what the Lord has done for me.
And read the other comments too.
You may discover you were never the only person fighting.
But if Gospel Warrior is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent honestly, and remain close to biblical truth, you can help this work reach others.
If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel-centered ministry, one practical way is to help put biblical truth in front of people who might never search for it themselves.
Come to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy would be to read about a delivered man while refusing the Deliverer.
The demons knew His identity.
Knowing facts about Jesus was not salvation.
The townspeople witnessed His power.
Witnessing something extraordinary was not salvation.
The restored man wanted Jesus.
And Jesus sent him out carrying a testimony of mercy.
That is where this story leaves us.
A boat departing.
A restored man standing on the shore.
A region about to hear his story.
And perhaps somewhere in that crowd was somebody who remembered what he had been.
“What happened to you?”
He had an answer.
Jesus.
The man once identified by his bondage now had something greater to say than the name of what held him.
He could speak the name of the One who set him free.
So share this if Christ has shown you mercy.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but as an honest response before God:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Because maybe the most unforgettable truth in the story is not that the darkness called itself Legion.
It is that Legion met Jesus—and Legion had to beg.
Whatever once named your darkest chapter does not deserve the final sentence of your story. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Keep Asking God to Change Them—What If the Prayer He Wants to Answer First Is You?
paragraphs: You Keep Asking God to Change Them—What If the Prayer He Wants to Answer First Is You?
You have prayed about their attitude, their failures, their words, their coldness, their stubbornness. But what happens when Jesus quietly turns the prayer around—and asks you to look in the mirror?
There is a prayer that can sound deeply spiritual while keeping us safely hidden.
“God, change them.”
Change my husband.
Change my wife.
Change my parents.
Change my child.
Change my friend.
Change that person who betrayed me.
Change the person who refuses to apologize.
Change the person who keeps hurting me.
Change the person who cannot seem to see what everyone else can see.
And sometimes that prayer is completely appropriate.
People really do sin against us.

People really can be selfish, cruel, manipulative, dishonest, neglectful, proud, or destructive. Scripture never commands us to pretend evil is good simply because admitting we have our own sins feels more “humble.” Biblical self-examination is not denial of another person’s wrongdoing.
But there is an uncomfortable moment that can happen in prayer.
You begin talking to God about everything wrong with them...
and somehow God begins dealing with you.
You came carrying evidence.
He brings a mirror.
You came ready to explain what they did.
He begins touching your pride.
You came asking Him to expose their selfishness.
He begins exposing your bitterness.
You wanted Him to confront their words.
He reminds you of yours.
You wanted justice for the way they wounded you.
He begins asking what you have been feeding in your heart since the wound happened.
And suddenly the prayer you thought was about them becomes frighteningly personal.
Jesus spoke directly into this instinct:

“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye.”
Matthew 7:3–5
The Greek makes the image almost impossible to soften.
Jesus speaks of the κάρφος — karphos, the speck or small bit of material in your brother’s eye.
Then He speaks of the δοκός — dokos in your own.
A beam.
A large piece of timber.
The contrast is deliberately startling.
There you are, leaning toward someone else’s face, carefully diagnosing the tiny object obstructing their vision...
while somehow ignoring the timber obstructing yours.
It is almost comedic.
Until you realize Jesus is describing us.
We can become extraordinarily observant when someone else is wrong.
We remember dates.
Words.
Screenshots.
Tone of voice.
Promises they broke.
Things they should have noticed.
Things they should have said.
Things they should never have said.
We can reconstruct the entire argument while washing dishes.
We can retry the case while driving.
We can deliver imaginary closing arguments in the shower.
And somehow, in every reenactment, we remain remarkably reasonable.
They remain remarkably guilty.
That is the unwanted mirror of Matthew 7.
Jesus is not merely asking, “Did they sin?”
He is asking:
Can you still see yourself clearly?
That question can hurt more than the argument.
Because there are seasons when another person truly has behaved badly, yet their wrongdoing has slowly become permission for ours.
“They made me angry.”
“They pushed me this far.”
“If they respected me, I wouldn’t talk like this.”
“If they apologized, I wouldn’t be bitter.”
“If they changed, I could finally become peaceful again.”
Listen carefully to what has happened.
Your spiritual condition has been placed into somebody else’s hands.
Your obedience is waiting for their obedience.
Your repentance is waiting for their repentance.
Your peace is waiting for their behavior.
Your tenderness is waiting for their apology.
Your holiness is waiting for them to become easier to love.
And Jesus loves you too much to leave you there.
He does not say the speck does not exist.
This matters.
Matthew 7:5 does not end with Jesus saying, “Forget your brother’s eye.”
He says first remove the log from your own eye, “and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye.”
The goal is not moral blindness.
It is clear sight.
The Greek verb translated “you will see clearly” is διαβλέψεις — diablepseis.
The issue is vision.
Jesus is confronting the kind of hypocrisy that can recognize another person’s problem without recognizing how badly our own sin has distorted our sight.
That means Matthew 7 is not teaching, “Nobody may ever correct anybody.”

Jesus Himself confronted sin. The apostles confronted sin. The New Testament teaches believers to restore those caught in transgression—but to do so with gentleness while watching ourselves lest we also be tempted (Galatians 6:1).
Christian correction begins differently from self-righteous accusation.
It begins before God.
It begins with the terrifying possibility:
“Lord, show me where I am wrong too.”
That is a dangerous prayer for your ego.
But it may save your soul from becoming hardened.
Because pride wants a courtroom.
Grace brings you to a cross.
Pride wants evidence against somebody else.
Grace asks what needs crucifying in you.
Pride says, “Look what they did.”
Repentance says, “Jesus, search me too.”
And maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe you are reading this while thinking about one specific person.
You know exactly who they are.
Perhaps you have prayed for months that God would change them.
Maybe years.
And perhaps they genuinely need to change.
So keep praying for them.
But tonight, add another prayer.
“Jesus... what about me?”
Not because everything is your fault.
Not because their sin suddenly becomes acceptable.
Not because forgiveness requires you to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation.
Not because biblical humility means surrendering boundaries or pretending betrayal never happened.
But because someone else’s sin cannot become your permission to resist Christ.
Ask Him:
Where has hurt become bitterness?
Where has disappointment become contempt?
Where has discernment become superiority?
Where has correction become punishment?
Where has silence become manipulation?
Where has “protecting myself” become refusing to forgive?
Where have I exaggerated their faults and minimized mine?
Where am I demanding from them a repentance I am unwilling to practice myself?
That prayer changes things.
Sometimes it changes the relationship.
Sometimes it does not.
Sometimes the other person still refuses responsibility.
Sometimes reconciliation is possible.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
Sometimes forgiveness happens without restored trust because repentance and trustworthy fruit have not followed.
Christian grace does not require pretending consequences are unnecessary.
But something profound happens when you stop making another person's transformation a prerequisite for your own obedience.
You become free to obey Jesus now.
You can repent now.
You can forgive before you receive the apology you imagined.
You can refuse revenge now.
You can stop rehearsing hatred now.
You can confess your words now.
You can make restitution where necessary now.
You can become more like Christ even while another person is still resisting Him.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is this:
You may have been right about what they did and still be wrong about what you became because of it.
Read that again.
Because being wounded does not automatically make every response righteous.
The cross destroys our favorite categories.
At Calvary, nobody gets to stand before Jesus boasting, “At least I wasn't as bad as them.”
Scripture says:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Romans 3:23
All.
Your enemy.
Your spouse.
Your parents.
Your children.
Your pastor.
Your friend.
The person who wounded you.
And you.
And me.
But the Gospel does not stop with exposure.
Thank God it does not stop there.
Because if Christianity were only a mirror showing us how sinful we are, eventually every honest person would despair.
The mirror prepares us to see our need for the Savior.
Jesus does not expose the beam in your eye because He enjoys humiliating you.
He exposes what is destroying your sight because He came to save sinners.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God took upon Himself the judgment sinners deserved.
Jesus did not die because we successfully proved somebody else was worse.
He died because we needed mercy.
He rose again because death would not have the final word.
And now the invitation is not:
“Fix yourself so Jesus will accept you.”
It is:
“Come to Jesus. Repent. Believe. Receive mercy. Then let His grace begin transforming the places you have spent years defending.”
The Greek word so often translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It carries the idea of changing one’s mind, turning from the old way, reorienting oneself toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling guilty.
Judas felt anguish.
Pharaoh regretted consequences.
Repentance turns.
Repentance stops negotiating with the sin.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, You are right about me.”
And grace answers:
“Come.”
Maybe that is the word you needed.
Not condemnation.
Come.
Come out from behind the evidence.
Come out from behind the screenshots.
Come out from behind what they did five years ago.
Come out from behind the sentence, “But they started it.”
Bring the anger.
Bring the disappointment.
Bring the betrayal.
Bring the marriage that does not look like you imagined.
Bring the friendship that broke.
Bring the family wound nobody understands.
Bring the apology you never received.
Bring the things you wish you had never said.
Bring the version of yourself you hardly recognize anymore.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
There is enough mercy at the cross for what they did.
And there is enough mercy for what you did too.
That is the scandal of grace.
Nobody arrives righteous.
Nobody purchases forgiveness.
Nobody earns resurrection.
We come empty-handed.
And Christ rewrites everything.
Perhaps the miracle you have been asking God for really does begin with the other person changing.
God can do that.
Pray for it.
But perhaps the first miracle He wants to perform is quieter.
The miracle of making you tender again.
The miracle of teaching you to apologize without adding “but you...”
The miracle of letting you hear correction without immediately building a defense.
The miracle of giving you enough security in Christ that admitting you were wrong no longer feels like death.
The miracle of forgiving somebody who may never understand what their actions cost you.
The miracle of boundaries without hatred.
Truth without cruelty.
Correction without superiority.
Discernment without contempt.
Conviction without despair.
Grace without pretending sin does not matter.
Maybe the prayer changes tonight.
“Lord, change them.”
Pause.
“And Jesus...
change me too.”
Search what I defend.
Expose what I excuse.
Show me the beam I cannot see because I have spent too long staring at their speck.
Make me quick to repent.
Slow to accuse.
Faithful to truth.
Generous with mercy.
And unwilling to call bitterness “discernment” simply because somebody really did hurt me.
Make me look like You.
That prayer may not instantly repair your relationship.
But it can begin transforming you.
And transformation is exactly what grace does.
If this article put a name to something you have been hiding, don't rush past the discomfort.
Stay there with Jesus.
Open Matthew 7 again.
Read verses 1–5 slowly.
Then pray without mentioning the other person for a few minutes.
That may be harder than you expect.
Ask only:
“Jesus, what are You showing me about me?”
And listen.
Not as a performance.
Not because typing a sentence earns grace.
But as an honest confession that you no longer want everybody else's sin to distract you from the transforming work Christ wants to do in your own heart.
There are moments when believers do not need another argument.
They need brothers and sisters willing to carry them before God.
Please do not send Matthew 7 to somebody as another way of saying, “See? Jesus agrees that you're the problem.”
That would be an almost painfully ironic way to use this passage.
They may desperately need to discover that repentance is not humiliation.
In Christ, repentance is a doorway home.
It cannot.
Scripture makes no such claim.

But if you want another practical way to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, you can help Gospel-centered truth reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church but will stop for a story on their screen.
Your support helps us keep writing, sharing Scripture, encouraging struggling believers, reaching seekers, and pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
Send it privately to the person who keeps blaming everyone because looking inward feels unbearable.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person quietly losing faith.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the Christian who knows all the right language but has forgotten how to repent.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is about religious people pretending they are better than everybody else.
Let them discover the opposite.
Christianity begins with sinners admitting we cannot save ourselves.
Then Jesus steps into the scandal.
With truth.
With wounds in His hands.
With mercy we could never purchase.
With grace we could never deserve.
And He begins rewriting people.
Maybe even the person you have spent months asking Him to change.
But tonight...
before you say their name again...
stand before the mirror.
Look at the cross.
And whisper:
“Jesus, start with me.”
Because sometimes the answer to “Lord, why won't You change them?” begins when grace whispers back:
“Will you let Me change you?”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING HAD THE CROWN—BUT GOD PUT THE MESSAGE IN HULDAH’S MOUTH
paragraphs: THE KING HAD THE CROWN—BUT GOD PUT THE MESSAGE IN HULDAH’S MOUTH

When Josiah’s officials needed to know what God was saying, they walked past power, position, and prestige and went to a prophetess in Jerusalem. What she told them was terrifying. What happened next reveals something every believer desperately needs to remember: when the Word of God exposes you, the condition of your heart determines what happens next.
There are moments when God does not whisper what we want to hear.
He tells us what we need to hear.
And sometimes the person carrying that truth is someone we never would have expected.
King Josiah had a problem.
Not a political problem.
Not a financial problem.
Not an enemy gathering outside Jerusalem's walls.
Something far more dangerous had happened.
The Word of God had been found.
Think about the tragedy hidden inside that sentence.
The temple was still standing.
Priests were still serving.
Religious activity still existed.
Yet the Book of the Law had become so neglected that its discovery became an event.
You can have a temple and lose the Word.
You can preserve religious activity and lose obedience.

You can know Christian vocabulary, attend church, post Bible verses, sing worship songs, wear a cross around your neck—and still discover that somewhere along the way the living Word of God stopped governing the hidden rooms of your life.
That is where Josiah's story becomes uncomfortable.
During repairs to the temple, Hilkiah the high priest found the Book of the Law and gave it to Shaphan the secretary. Shaphan read it, then carried it before the king.
And when Josiah heard what was written, he tore his clothes.
He did not argue with Scripture.
He did not edit Scripture.
He did not accuse Scripture of being too severe.
