He did not search for someone who would reinterpret God's commands until his disobedience felt comfortable.
The king broke.
That may be one of the most important details in the entire story.
Because God's Word had exposed a scandal much bigger than Josiah himself.
Judah had forsaken the LORD.
Generations had wandered.
Idolatry had penetrated the nation.
Judgment was no longer an abstract theological concept. Josiah realized that his people stood guilty before a holy God.
So he commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah to inquire of the LORD.
And then Scripture gives us a detail too important to rush past.
These powerful royal officials went to a woman named Huldah.
The Hebrew text identifies her as:
חֻלְדָּה הַנְּבִיאָה
Ḥuldāh han-nevī'āh.
Huldah the prophetess.
The word הַנְּבִיאָה — han-nevī'āh is the feminine form identifying her as a prophetess.
This was not a title modern readers placed upon her.
This is how the biblical text presents her.

Huldah was the wife of Shallum, who was associated with the royal wardrobe, and she lived in Jerusalem's Second Quarter. When the king's delegation needed an authoritative prophetic response concerning the rediscovered Book of the Law, they went to her. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 34 preserves the same essential episode.
Pause there.
The king had the crown.
Hilkiah had the priesthood.
Shaphan had access to the palace.
But Huldah had been entrusted with a word from God.
And when these men arrived, she did not flatter them.
She did not appear intimidated by their titles.
She did not ask what message would be most acceptable to the king.
She spoke.
Her declaration begins with the unmistakable prophetic formula:
כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה
Koh amar YHWH.
“Thus says the LORD.”
Those words change everything.
Because Huldah was not offering a motivational opinion.
She was delivering a divine indictment.
Judah had forsaken God and turned toward other gods. The consequences announced in the covenant were coming upon them.
Imagine standing in that room.
These men represented the king.
One softened sentence could have protected Huldah socially.
One convenient reinterpretation could have made everyone more comfortable.
Instead, she delivered the message faithfully.
God's judgment was coming.
That is something Christianity cannot erase without eventually erasing the Cross itself.
We love saying God is love.
And He is.
We love saying God forgives.
And He does.
We love talking about grace.
We should.
But grace becomes sentimental nonsense if there is no real sin from which we need saving.
The Cross is not proof that sin does not matter.
The Cross is proof of how terribly sin matters—and how unimaginably far God's saving love was willing to go.
Huldah's message reminds us that the God of Scripture is holy.
Idolatry matters.
Rebellion matters.
Forsaking God matters.
The things we secretly worship matter.
And idols do not always have statues anymore.
Sometimes an idol fits inside your pocket.
Sometimes it looks like approval.
Sometimes it sounds like applause.
Sometimes it is money.
Sometimes it is lust.
Sometimes it is bitterness you refuse to surrender because hatred has begun feeling safer than forgiveness.
Sometimes it is a relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
Sometimes it is ministry itself—when being seen serving Jesus becomes more important than actually knowing Jesus.
Sometimes the idol staring back at us from the throne is ourselves.
That is why Huldah's story cannot remain an interesting account about an ancient prophetess.
The Book has been opened again.
And now it is reading us.
But Huldah's message did not end with judgment.
There was another message specifically for Josiah.
And this is where the story becomes painfully beautiful.
God said that because Josiah's heart was tender and because he humbled himself when he heard God's words—because he tore his clothes and wept before God—the LORD had heard him.
One Hebrew expression in 2 Kings 22:19 is especially striking:
יַעַן רַךְ־לְבָבְךָ
ya'an rakh-levavkha.
“Because your heart was tender…”
A tender heart.
Not a perfect résumé.
Not flawless ancestry.
Not political power.
A heart that could still be pierced by the Word of God.
That may be the question following you through this article.
Is your heart still tender enough for God to correct you?
Not, “Do you go to church?”
Not, “Do you believe Christian doctrine?”
Not, “Do people think you are spiritual?”
Can God's Word still break through your defenses?
When Scripture confronts something you love that God calls sin, what happens inside you?
Do you surrender?
Or negotiate?
Do you repent?
Or rationalize?
Do you weep?
Some of us have become frighteningly skilled at hearing sermons without hearing God.
We know when to say amen.
We know which worship songs make us emotional.
We know how to appear spiritually alive.
But when Scripture touches the one room we have locked…
the secret addiction…
the hidden messages…
the resentment…
the dishonesty…
the pornography…
the pride…
the relationship we have placed above Christ…
the unforgiveness we have rehearsed for years…
suddenly we become theologians looking for loopholes.
Josiah did something radically different.
He tore his clothes.
In his culture, that outward act expressed profound grief and distress.
But God looked deeper than torn fabric.
God saw the heart underneath it.
“Your heart was tender.”
There it is again.
That sentence should haunt us in the best possible way.
Because perhaps the greatest spiritual danger is not discovering that you have sinned.
The greater danger is reaching the point where discovering your sin no longer bothers you.
When conviction disappears, we should not automatically congratulate ourselves for finding peace.
Sometimes peace is surrender to God.
Sometimes what we call peace is simply a conscience we have repeatedly trained ourselves to ignore.
Josiah heard the Word and trembled.
And God heard Josiah.
What an extraordinary exchange.
Josiah heard God.
God heard Josiah.
This is where the road begins turning toward the Gospel.
Because Josiah's humility mattered, but Josiah could not ultimately carry Judah's guilt away.
His reforms were significant, but he was not the final Savior.
Another King had to come.
A greater Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
Josiah tore his garments because he heard judgment.
Jesus would allow His own body to be torn as He bore our sins on the Cross.
Josiah humbled himself before the Word of God.
Jesus, though without sin, humbled Himself in obedience to the Father, even unto death.
Josiah's reforms could confront idols.
Jesus came to transform idol-making hearts.
And at Calvary, judgment and mercy met in a way Huldah's generation could only anticipate within the unfolding story of redemption.
Jesus did not come to tell sinners that rebellion never mattered.
He came because it mattered eternally.
The Gospel is not God shrugging at your sin.
The Gospel is the holy God doing what you could never do to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
Grace does not mean God pretends the scandal never happened.
Grace means Jesus can rewrite what the scandal was going to become.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean repentance magically erases every wound we caused.
It means sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Shame does not have to write it.
Addiction does not have to write it.
Your past does not have to write it.
The worst thing you have ever done does not possess sovereign authority over the rest of your story.
Jesus does.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere beneath the polished Christian version of yourself there is something you are exhausted from hiding.
You have smiled while breaking.
Served while struggling.
Prayed publicly while privately wondering how you wandered this far.
Perhaps you are afraid that if people really knew what happened, they would look at you differently.
Perhaps they would.
But Jesus already knows.
He knows the chapter you keep trying to tear out.
He knows what happened behind the closed door.
He knows what you searched.
What you said.
What you touched.
What you took.
Who you hurt.
What you concealed.
He knows.
And still the Gospel calls you to come into the light.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Christ is sufficient.
Repentance is not God's attempt to humiliate you.
It is His call to stop running toward death.
The same Word that exposes our rebellion points us toward the Savior.
So perhaps your response today should resemble Josiah's—not necessarily torn clothing, but a torn-open heart.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary.
No pretending.
Just:
“Jesus, I have sinned. Have mercy on me. Change me. I don't want to keep hiding.”
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
Your testimony may remind a stranger that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend slowly drifting from Christ.
The believer hiding an addiction.
The person carrying unbearable shame.
The Christian who still attends church but whose heart has quietly grown cold.
There may come a night when you need to remember that conviction is not the end of the story.
There may come a morning when somebody you love finally admits, “I need help.”
Come back to this.
Send it to them.
Sit beside them.
Pray with them.
Point them to Jesus.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase your sins.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
Supporting Gospel work should flow from gratitude and willing generosity—not fear, pressure, or the idea that God owes us something because we gave.
That distinction matters.
Huldah did not manipulate the king.
She delivered God's Word.
Josiah did not bargain with God.
He humbled himself.
And the Gospel does not invite us to manipulate God either.
It invites us to repent and believe.
So before you leave this article, imagine that ancient scene one more time.
A king waits in Jerusalem.
Five officials stand before a prophetess.
A forgotten Book has been opened.
A nation has been exposed.
Huldah speaks.
Judgment is real.
Sin is real.
But somewhere inside the palace, a king's heart is breaking before God.
And heaven notices.
Thousands of years later, the question is no longer what Josiah will do.
It is what you will do when the Word finds you.
Will you defend the idol?
Or destroy it?
Will you hide the wound?
Or bring it to Christ?
Will you explain away your sin?
Or confess it?
Will you merely admire Josiah's tender heart?
Or ask God for one?
The King who ultimately matters is not Josiah.
His name is Jesus.
And when Jesus rewrites a life, He does not merely improve the old story.
He makes the sinner His own.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He teaches rebels to become disciples.
He takes people whose stories should have ended in darkness and makes their lives testimonies to undeserved grace.
So share this if someone needs to remember that conviction can become the doorway to repentance.
And comment.
Don't disappear silently if God has put His finger on something.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Whatever is true.
Because maybe the most important thing Huldah's story teaches us is not merely that God can place His message in an unexpected messenger.
It is that when God finally puts His finger on the chapter we desperately wanted to hide, He is not asking us to rewrite it ourselves.
He is calling us to surrender the pen to Christ.
The Word may expose the scandal—but in the hands of Jesus, the scandal does not have to become the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY COULDN’T ISRAEL’S HIGH PRIEST MARRY JUST ANY WOMAN?
paragraphs: WHY COULDN’T ISRAEL’S HIGH PRIEST MARRY JUST ANY WOMAN?

Leviticus 21 contains a marriage command that can sound painfully harsh—until you see the holiness behind it, the High Priest it ultimately makes us long for, and the Bride Jesus is preparing for Himself.
There is a sentence buried in Leviticus that most Christians have probably read too quickly.
Maybe you did too.
A few lines about priests. A few restrictions. Ancient Israel. Strange rules. Keep reading.
But then God says something that makes you stop.

Israel’s ordinary priests already lived under unusual restrictions because they ministered before the LORD. But when Scripture turns to the man occupying the highest priestly office, the boundaries become even narrower.
The high priest could not marry just anyone.
And once you understand why, Leviticus 21 stops feeling like an obscure chapter about somebody else’s religion thousands of years ago.
It begins asking uncomfortable questions about holiness.
About worship.
About what it means to belong to God.
And eventually...
about Jesus.
Listen to the Hebrew.
וְהוּא אִשָּׁה בִבְתוּלֶיהָ יִקָּח
Vehu ishah bivtuleha yiqqach.
Literally, with Hebrew word order smoothed into English:
“He shall take a woman in her virginity.”
The key expression is בִבְתוּלֶיהָ — bivtuleha, referring to her virginity or maidenhood.
Then comes the restriction:
אַלְמָנָה וּגְרוּשָׁה וַחֲלָלָה זֹנָה אֶת־אֵלֶּה לֹא יִקָּח
Almanah ugerushah vachalalah zonah... lo yiqqach.
A widow.
A divorced woman.
A woman described in the priestly holiness language as chalalah—profaned or disqualified.
A prostitute.
“These he shall not take.”

Instead, the text repeats that he must marry a בְּתוּלָה — betulah, a virgin from among his people. That is the straightforward requirement of Leviticus 21:13–14. The Hebrew text itself preserves these categories explicitly.
And right here we need to be careful.
Because careless preaching can wound people God never intended this passage to condemn.
Leviticus is not teaching that every widow was immoral.
Ruth was a widow.
It is not teaching that widowhood itself made a woman wicked.
It is not giving Christians permission to look at a divorced person and announce that he or she is beyond grace.
And it certainly is not saying that people with sexually sinful histories cannot be redeemed.
The Bible itself destroys that interpretation.
This command concerned the unique consecration of Israel’s high priest.
His life was not entirely his own.
His clothing was regulated.
His mourning was regulated.
His approach to death was regulated.
His marriage was regulated.
Why?
Because he occupied an office set apart for the service of the Holy One.
Then verse 15 gives us the theological heartbeat:
וְלֹא־יְחַלֵּל זַרְעוֹ בְּעַמָּיו כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה מְקַדְּשׁוֹ
Velo yechallel zar'o be'ammav, ki ani YHWH meqaddesho.
“And he shall not profane his offspring among his people, for I am YHWH who sanctifies him.”
That final word matters.
מְקַדְּשׁוֹ — meqaddesho.
“The One sanctifying him.”
“The One setting him apart as holy.”
The high priest's marriage restriction was therefore not an isolated piece of marital advice. It belonged to an entire system of priestly consecration.
God had separated this man for sacred service. His public ministry, household, descendants, and covenant responsibilities could not simply be detached from that calling.
And perhaps this is where the passage becomes uncomfortable for us.
We live in a world obsessed with asking:
“How much can I get away with?”
God keeps asking:
“Do you understand what it means to belong to Me?”
We ask how close we can walk to the edge.
God speaks about consecration.
We ask whether something is technically permissible.
God asks whether our lives display that we have been set apart.
And suddenly Leviticus does not feel quite so ancient anymore.
Because perhaps you know what it is like to want Jesus without surrender.
You want forgiveness...
but there is one room in your heart whose door remains locked.
You want peace...
but not repentance.
You want God to bless the relationship you already know is pulling you away from Him.
You want Jesus to heal the wound while protecting the habit that keeps reopening it.
You want the cross to remove guilt without allowing the Crucified One to become Lord.
And sooner or later every serious follower of Christ discovers something frightening and beautiful:
Grace is free.
But grace was never given to leave us unchanged.
Jesus does not rescue sinners because they have made themselves clean enough for Him.
He rescues sinners who cannot clean themselves.
But the Savior who receives us in our ruin loves us far too deeply to make peace with the ruin that is destroying us.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Leviticus 21 can easily be abused if we turn holiness into human worth.
The widow was not worthless.
The divorced woman was not subhuman.
A woman carrying a shattered history was not outside God's compassion.
The issue was the sanctity attached to a particular priestly office under the Mosaic covenant.
And Christians must never weaponize an ancient high-priestly marriage law against wounded people Jesus calls us to love.
But neither should we run so quickly from difficult biblical holiness that we miss what the chapter is teaching.
God is holy.
Approaching Him was never casual.
The priesthood was holy.
Sacrifice was holy.
The sanctuary was holy.
The high priest was set apart.
And all of it creates a tension no descendant of Aaron could finally resolve.
Because however carefully Israel's high priest married...
he was still a sinner.
However sacred his garments...
there was still sin underneath them.
However elaborate the purification...
he himself still needed atonement.
However distinguished his office...
death would eventually remove him from it.
The regulations could set apart a priest.
They could not create a sinless man.
And that is where the road through Leviticus eventually brings the Christian reader face-to-face with Jesus Christ.
Not because we are free to invent symbolism for every detail.
We are not.
Scripture deserves better than imaginative claims presented as biblical certainty.
But the New Testament itself deliberately presents Jesus in the language of high priesthood.
Hebrews says of Christ:
“Such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.”
Hebrews 7:26.
Holy.
Undefiled.
Exalted.
Here is the High Priest no Levitical regulation could ever manufacture.
Jesus did not merely satisfy ceremonial qualifications.
He possesses actual moral perfection.
He did not need sacrifices for His own sins.
He had none.
He did not enter God's presence carrying animal blood as though an animal could finally erase human rebellion.
He gave Himself.
The priesthood of Aaron kept producing priests who eventually died.
Jesus lives.
The old sacrifices kept being offered.
Jesus offered Himself.
The old system continually reminded worshipers that sin remained a deadly problem.
Jesus accomplished what those repeated sacrifices could never accomplish by their own power.
And here is where the story becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
The perfect High Priest came looking for people who were anything but perfect.
People like us.
The scandalous.
The ashamed.
The religious hypocrite who knows exactly how to look holy while dying privately.
The person carrying sexual regret.
The marriage that fell apart.
The believer who promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
The addict deleting the history before anyone sees.
The Christian smiling in church while secretly wondering whether God has finally become tired of forgiving them.
The person who knows Scripture but has grown cold toward the Savior Scripture reveals.
The one who worships publicly and compromises privately.
The one who has spent years believing:
“If everybody knew the real story, nobody would want me.”
Maybe nobody knows yours.
But Jesus does.
Every chapter.
Every deleted message.
Every night you wish you could erase.
Every secret compromise.
Every prayer you were embarrassed to pray.
Every promise you broke.
Every moment when conviction came and you pushed it away.
He knows.
And this is the astonishing center of the Gospel:
Christ did not discover your scandal after He went to the cross.
He went knowing exactly whom He had come to save.
But do not confuse His mercy with indifference toward sin.
The Jesus who refuses to abandon sinners also refuses to call the chains around their wrists freedom.
He says repent.
Come into the light.
Stop hiding.
Bring Him the truth.
Confess the sin.
Turn around.
Not so that repentance can purchase grace...
but because grace has opened the door home.
And then another biblical image appears.
The High Priest is also the Bridegroom.
Paul writes that Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her so that He might sanctify and cleanse her, ultimately presenting her holy and without blemish.
Notice what the Gospel does not say.
It does not say Jesus found a community of naturally spotless people and decided they were worthy enough to become His church.
He loved.
He gave Himself.
He sanctifies.
He cleanses.
He presents.
The glory belongs to Him.
That means the church's holiness is never permission for Christians to boast about being better than broken people.
We are the broken people Christ came to save.
Our testimony is not:
“Look how clean I was when Jesus found me.”
Our testimony is:
“Look what Jesus Christ can do with someone who finally stops hiding.”
That is Christianity.
Not cosmetic religion.
Resurrection.
Not reputation management.
Redemption.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace rewriting what the scandal tried to make final.
Perhaps that is why this ancient command can reach so deeply into a modern heart.
Leviticus shows us that holiness matters more than we thought.
The Gospel shows us that grace reaches farther than we imagined.
At the cross, neither truth disappears.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God gives Himself.
Grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly gives Himself for sinners.
Your sin is not small.
His mercy is not smaller.
Your past is real.
His blood is not imaginary.
Your wounds matter.
Your failures have consequences.
Repentance can hurt.
Restoration can take time.
Some earthly consequences may remain.
But none of those things have authority to rewrite the verdict God gives to the person who is in Christ.
Maybe you needed to hear that today.
Not because you are innocent.
But because Jesus is enough.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
But because the Holy One is the One saving you and transforming you.
Not because God shrugged at your sin.
But because Christ bore judgment at the cross and rose victorious from the grave.
So stop trying to edit your history before bringing it to Him.
Stop waiting until you feel clean enough to pray.
Stop confusing shame with repentance.
Shame whispers, “Hide from God.”
The Gospel calls, “Come into the light.”
Repentance says:
“Jesus, this is what I did.
This is what I became.
This is what I have been hiding.
I have sinned.
Have mercy on me.
Change me.
I don't want to protect what nailed You to the cross anymore.”
And grace answers with a Savior.
Not an excuse.
A Savior.
Talk to Christ.
You can simply write “Jesus, forgive me” if conviction has found you today.
And if you have watched Jesus restore pieces of your life you once thought were permanently destroyed, tell somebody what He has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because every sentence is unforgettable, but because tomorrow temptation may try to make you forget what Scripture reminded you today:
You were not called merely to appear religious.
You were called to belong to Jesus.
It is about sinners meeting a perfect Savior.
We glorify God through faith, obedience, love, generosity, worship, and lives surrendered to Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help biblical content continue reaching people.
But please remember the difference.
Do not share because you think an algorithm can make you righteous.
Do not comment because public emotion can replace private repentance.
Do not buy something because merchandise can make you holy.
Only Jesus saves.
Only Christ's righteousness can cover the guilty.
Only His sacrifice can reconcile sinners to God.
Only the Holy Spirit can transform a human heart.
Everything else is simply a tool we can place at His feet.
And now perhaps we can return to that strange ancient command and understand why it matters.
Why couldn't Israel's high priest marry just any woman?
Because the high priest did not belong merely to himself.
He had been consecrated to the LORD, and even his household stood within the boundaries attached to that sacred office.
But the deepest Christian hope is not that we finally become good enough to imitate every regulation given to Aaron.
Our hope is that a greater High Priest has come.
Jesus Christ.
Holy.
Undefiled.
Sinless.
Merciful.
Crucified.
Risen.
And He is still receiving sinners.
Still calling hypocrites into the light.
Still restoring the fallen.
Still cleansing the ashamed.
Still breaking chains.
Still teaching compromised hearts to become holy.
Still taking stories people thought were finished...
and writing grace across the final page.
So if you walked into this article carrying a scandal, do not walk away merely carrying information about an ancient priest.
Walk toward Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Because the most shocking thing in Leviticus 21 is not simply that God demanded holiness from the high priest.
The most shocking thing in the Gospel is that when none of us could become holy enough to climb our way to God...
the Holy One came down to rescue us.
And remember this when your past starts shouting again:
Your scandal may explain where Jesus found you—but it does not get to write where His grace is taking you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS MARITAL SEX ONLY FOR MAKING BABIES? Proverbs and Song of Songs Complicate That Answer
paragraphs: IS MARITAL SEX ONLY FOR MAKING BABIES? Proverbs and Song of Songs Complicate That Answer
If you were taught that a husband and wife should only come together to produce children, there are passages in your Bible that may make you uncomfortable—and perhaps they are supposed to.
There are subjects Christians can discuss over coffee without lowering their voices.
Grace.
Prayer.
Faith.
Heaven.
Marriage.
Then someone says the word “sex,” and suddenly the room changes.
Eyes move.
People become careful.
Some become embarrassed.
Some become defensive.
And some quietly carry wounds nobody in the room knows exist.
Because for many Christians, sexuality was never actually discipled.
It was merely warned about.
“Don’t.”
“Wait.”
“Stay pure.”
“Flee temptation.”
Those warnings matter. Scripture takes sexual holiness seriously.
But then a Christian gets married.
And sometimes the message they have absorbed for years does not magically disappear at the altar.
The person who spent years hearing that sexual desire was dangerous may now be expected to believe that marital desire is beautiful.
The person who learned to associate the body with shame may suddenly be told to receive the body of a spouse as a gift.
And somewhere beneath all of this sits a question Christians have wrestled with for centuries:
Is sex within marriage ultimately only for having children?
Children are unquestionably one of God's great gifts.
The Bible opens with God's blessing over humanity:
“Be fruitful, and multiply” (Genesis 1:28, KJV).
The Hebrew behind “be fruitful” is פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ — peru urevu — “be fruitful and multiply.”
Human fertility is not treated as an embarrassment in Scripture.
Children are not accidents interrupting the “real” purpose of marriage. Psalm 127 calls children a heritage from the LORD.

So any Christian understanding of marriage that despises fertility, treats children as inherently undesirable, or disconnects sexuality completely from the life-giving design of our bodies has missed something important.
But something else is equally important.
Genesis does not stop at reproduction.
Before sin enters the world, before shame enters the human experience, before broken desire and exploitation appear, Genesis says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad.
“They shall become one flesh.”
Not merely producers of offspring.
One flesh.
A covenant union involving the whole person.
Then you turn several hundred pages.
And Proverbs says something startling.
Not because it is vulgar.
Because it is holy.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Scripture becomes even more direct:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read it again.
Slowly.
God did not accidentally leave those words in the Bible.
The Hebrew is striking.
The final thought includes:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The imagery carries the sense of continually being captivated, exhilarated, even intoxicated by her love.
The passage is not instructing a husband merely to tolerate intimacy long enough to produce an heir.
It tells him to rejoice in his wife.
To delight in her.
To remain captivated by her love.
And notice the context.
Proverbs 5 is a warning against adultery.
The answer to forbidden sexuality is not the destruction of sexuality.
It is covenant faithfulness.
Scripture does not say, “Stop desiring.”
It redirects desire home.
There is something profoundly beautiful about that.
God's answer to lust is not lovelessness.
His answer to adultery is not marital coldness.
His answer to counterfeit intimacy includes the recovery of covenant intimacy.
And then you reach the Song of Songs.
If Proverbs makes some Christians uncomfortable, Song of Songs can make them wonder how the book ever survived a church committee.
It is poetry.
It is sophisticated.
Its imagery requires interpretation with humility.
Christians throughout history have also seen theological symbolism in its love poetry.
But whatever additional theological applications one recognizes, the text itself unmistakably celebrates the longing, beauty, exclusivity, and delight of human love.
The lovers notice one another.
They miss one another.
They praise one another's bodies.
They desire closeness.
They speak with an intensity that would sound almost scandalous if people had forgotten that God created marriage.
The bride says:
“Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits.”
Song of Songs 4:16.
And here is what cannot honestly be ignored:
The immediate poetic scene is not discussing conception.
There is no command in that verse to produce a child.
There is delight.
Invitation.
Mutual desire.
Belonging.
Love.
That does not erase the procreative dimension of marital sexuality.
It proves something more nuanced.
The Bible is capable of celebrating marital intimacy without making procreation the explicit subject of every embrace.
That matters.
Because some couples are infertile.
Some are elderly.
Some desperately want children and cannot conceive.
Some have endured miscarriage.
Some carry medical limitations.
Some have experienced sexual trauma.
Some marriages have spent years trying to recover tenderness after betrayal, pornography, resentment, exhaustion, childbirth, illness, grief, or emotional distance.
Imagine telling an infertile husband and wife that their sexual union has somehow lost its meaning because conception is impossible.
Scripture does not speak that way.
Imagine Abraham and Sarah in old age.
Imagine an elderly covenant couple whose childbearing years are gone.
Does tenderness suddenly become pointless?
Does affection expire when fertility does?
Proverbs answers with language that refuses to reduce marital love to reproduction:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
There is something breathtaking hidden in those words.
She is the wife of your youth.
But Proverbs is envisioning a love that continues.
Bodies change.
Faces change.
Hair changes.
Strength changes.
Pregnancy may come.
Infertility may come.
Children may fill the house.
Eventually children may leave it.
And two people who once stood trembling before an altar may one day look across a quiet room at faces marked by decades.
Still yours.
Still mine.
Still covenant.
Still beloved.
That is far more beautiful than a theology that treats a spouse like reproductive machinery.
And then Paul walks into the conversation.
First Corinthians 7:3–5 is sometimes quoted badly, especially when someone wants to demand sex from a spouse.
But read Paul's actual symmetry.
The husband has obligations toward the wife.
The wife has obligations toward the husband.
Then Paul makes a remarkably reciprocal statement concerning authority over their bodies.
And when he speaks of temporary abstinence, he uses the Greek expression:
ἐκ συμφώνου
ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
By mutual consent.
The word is related to the idea of being in harmony—“sounding together.”
Paul does not describe unilateral domination.
He describes reciprocity.
Then he tells married believers who temporarily abstain for prayer to come together again.
Think about the implication.
Paul does not say:
“Resume relations only when you intend to conceive.”
He recognizes sexual union as an ongoing dimension of marriage.
That does not mean a spouse can weaponize 1 Corinthians 7.
Never.
Biblical mutuality cannot legitimately be turned into permission for coercion, intimidation, manipulation, marital rape, or abuse.
A body entrusted in covenant is not a body available for cruelty.
Christian marriage should make a person safer, not more afraid.
The same Christ who calls husbands and wives into profound union calls His people to sacrificial love.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Ephesians 5:25).
Look at Jesus.
His model of authority is self-giving.
Not exploitation.
Not selfish appetite.
Not “You owe me.”
The cross destroys that kind of entitlement.
Christ gives Himself.
And suddenly the question becomes deeper than:
“What am I allowed to do?”
Christian marriage asks:
“How can I love this person entrusted to me in a way that reflects Christ?”
That changes everything.
Sex becomes neither god nor garbage.
Neither an idol to worship nor dirt to despise.
It becomes something that belongs beneath the lordship of Jesus.
And perhaps this is where some of us need healing.
Because you may have entered this article expecting a theological argument.
Instead, something personal surfaced.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Maybe you sleep inches apart physically and miles apart emotionally.
Maybe pornography taught you to consume bodies instead of cherish a person.
Maybe betrayal shattered something you thought would never break.
Maybe you have been rejected so many times that you stopped reaching.
Maybe you were pressured so often that tenderness now feels dangerous.
Maybe infertility made every intimate moment feel like a medical appointment.
Maybe years of trying to conceive turned something once tender into calendars, tests, disappointment, and tears behind a locked bathroom door.
Maybe someone used Scripture against you.
Maybe nobody ever told you that God cares about what happened to you.
And perhaps you need to hear this:
Jesus Christ did not come merely to regulate behavior.
He came to redeem people.
Shame says, “Hide.”
Jesus keeps calling people into the light.
Sin says, “Use.”
Jesus teaches us to love.
Lust says, “Take.”
Christ says, “Give yourself.”
Adultery says, “Break covenant for desire.”
Jesus can teach wounded people how to bring desire back beneath covenant.
Pornography says, “This body exists for your consumption.”
The Gospel says the person before you bears the image of God.
And grace says something scandalous to every sinner who has failed sexually:
Your sin can be forgiven.
Not excused.
Forgiven.
There is a difference.
The Gospel does not rename darkness as light.
It brings sinners out of darkness.
At the cross, Jesus carried real guilt.
Real sexual sin.
Real adultery.
Real lust.
Real pornography.
Real secret histories.
Real impurity.
Real selfishness.
Real shame.
And when a sinner comes to Christ in repentance and faith, grace does not merely cover the scandal like someone throwing a sheet over a crime scene.
Christ begins rewriting the person.
That is why our message has never been that scandal does not matter.
Our message is that scandal does not get the final word when Jesus enters the story.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you crossed lines before marriage.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe you became addicted to pornography.
Maybe your imagination became a place you would be terrified for anyone else to see.
Repent.
But do not confuse repentance with despair.
The blood of Jesus is stronger than the chapter you are ashamed to reread.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Cleanse.
Not merely tolerate.
Cleanse.
This is Christianity.
Not pretending the stain was never there.
Being washed by Christ.
And perhaps the church needs to recover the courage to say two truths at the same time:
Sexual immorality is serious.
And marital sexuality is not dirty.
Pornography is not Song of Songs.
Adultery is not Proverbs 5.
Lust is not covenant delight.
Coercion is not 1 Corinthians 7.
God's boundaries do not exist because sex is evil.
Boundaries protect something powerful enough to wound people deeply when severed from faithfulness, truth, covenant, and love.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the house destroys it.
The answer is not to hate fire.
The answer is to honor where it belongs.
So...
Is marital sex only for making babies?
The whole biblical witness makes that reduction difficult to sustain.
Procreation is profoundly important in Scripture.
“One flesh” union is also important.
Faithfulness is important.
Mutual care is important.
Marital delight is important.
Tenderness is important.
And Scripture itself can celebrate a husband delighting in his wife and lovers longing for one another without mentioning conception in every scene.
Proverbs does not blush.
Song of Songs does not apologize.
Paul does not describe marriage as a reproductive transaction.
And Jesus brings every dimension of our lives—including sexuality—under His redeeming lordship.
Maybe what needs to be rescued is not sexual license.
Maybe what needs rescuing is holy intimacy itself.
Rescued from pornography.
Rescued from selfishness.
Rescued from coercion.
Rescued from shame.
Rescued from adultery.
Rescued from performance.
Rescued from the idea that a spouse is either a temptation to fear or an object to use.
Back to covenant.
Back to tenderness.
Back to truth.
Back to Christ.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't pretend it didn't.
No details required.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “Please stand with me.”
And yes, even send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
One share can place biblical truth in front of someone we may never have been able to reach ourselves.
It cannot.
It does not.
Scripture tells believers to give willingly rather than under compulsion.
Your support helps keep the mission moving.
And there is another way you can help without spending anything:
Share.
A Facebook share costs you nothing, but it can carry the Gospel farther than you know.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help where wounds are deep.
Love your spouse as a person, not an object.
Bring hidden sin into the light.
Bring wounded intimacy before Jesus.
And never forget that Christianity is not the story of clean people avoiding dirty people.
It is the story of a holy Savior rescuing sinners.
Maybe even you.
Maybe especially the part of you nobody sees.
Because the most scandalous thing in your story may not be what you did, what was done to you, or what nearly destroyed your marriage.
The most unforgettable part may be discovering that Jesus was willing to enter the chapter you wanted to tear out—and begin writing redemption there.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE “BIBLE VERSE” JESUS NEVER SAID: Why “God Helps Those Who Help Themselves” Can Quietly Turn Grace Into Self-Salvation
paragraphs: THE “BIBLE VERSE” JESUS NEVER SAID: Why “God Helps Those Who Help Themselves” Can Quietly Turn Grace Into Self-Salvation

It sounds responsible. It sounds spiritual. It may even sound biblical. But when your strength finally disappears, this popular sentence leaves you standing exactly where the Gospel was meant to find you.
There is a sentence people repeat when someone is struggling.
Sometimes it is spoken gently.
Sometimes impatiently.
Sometimes by Christians trying to encourage another Christian.
“God helps those who help themselves.”
It sounds wise.
Get up. Try harder. Stop waiting. Take responsibility. Do something.
And there is enough truth near the sentence to make the sentence dangerous.

Because the Bible absolutely condemns laziness. Scripture calls people to work, obey, persevere, repent, pursue holiness, care for their responsibilities, make wise decisions, and act courageously. Biblical faith is never an excuse for passivity.
But here is the problem.
“God helps those who help themselves” is not a Bible verse.
Jesus never said it.
Paul never wrote it.
Moses never taught it.
And when that slogan is turned into a description of how God’s grace works—especially how sinners are rescued—it does not merely miss the Gospel by a few inches.
It reverses the direction of the rescue.
Because Christianity does not begin with a capable person climbing toward God.
It begins with God coming down to people who cannot save themselves.
And perhaps that difference matters more than you realize.
Because somewhere reading this is a person who has spent years “helping themselves.”
You fixed the mess.
Then another mess came.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you returned to it.
You told yourself this would be the year you became disciplined, holy, emotionally healthy, financially responsible, sexually pure, spiritually consistent.
You tried.
Failed.
Tried harder.
Failed more quietly.
And eventually you learned something religious people are very good at learning.
How to look okay while bleeding somewhere nobody can see.
So imagine hearing:
“God helps those who help themselves.”
What happens when you cannot?
What happens when the addiction has outgrown your promises?
When depression has drained your energy?
When grief has taken the strength from your knees?
When your marriage is collapsing?
When the consequences of your own sin are standing at your door?
When you have prayed the same apology so many times that even you are tired of hearing yourself say it?
What happens when there is nothing impressive left to offer God?
That is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Paul writes:
“While we were still weak…”
Romans 5:6.
That word matters.
ἀσθενῶν — asthenōn.
Weak.
Without strength.
Powerless.
And notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say:
“When we finally became strong enough, Christ came.”
“When we repaired ourselves, Christ accepted us.”
“When we demonstrated sufficient effort, Christ rewarded us.”
No.
Paul continues:
“…ὑπὲρ ἀσεβῶν ἀπέθανεν.”
Christ died “for the ungodly.”
Not the impressive.
Not the spiritually polished.
Not people who finally managed to make themselves worthy.
The ungodly.
That is scandalous grace.
The cross does not congratulate humanity for climbing high enough.
The cross announces that we could never climb high enough, so the Son of God came down.
And this is where the popular slogan can become spiritually poisonous if we make it a theology of grace.
Because the Gospel is not:
“Help yourself enough, and God will finish the job.”
The Gospel is:
You could not save yourself.
So Jesus came for you.
Paul makes the point even sharper in Ephesians:
“τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως…”
“For by grace you have been saved through faith…”
And then come four words every self-made savior needs to hear:
“οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν”
ouk ex hymōn.
“Not from yourselves.”
Then:
“θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον”
God’s gift.
Ephesians 2:8.
Read that again slowly.
Not.
From.
Yourselves.
There is the funeral of human boasting.
There is the collapse of spiritual pride.
There is the end of pretending that God looked down from heaven, saw something sufficiently impressive in us, and decided we were finally worth rescuing.
Grace is not wages for spiritual performance.
Grace is gift.
And gifts cannot be earned without ceasing to be gifts.
Yet someone may object:
“But doesn't the Bible teach personal responsibility?”
Absolutely.
And this is where we need precision rather than slogans.
The Bible does not teach helplessness as an excuse for laziness.
It teaches dependence on God as the foundation for faithful action.
There is an enormous difference.
Consider Nehemiah.
When enemies threatened Jerusalem, Nehemiah and the people did not say, “God will protect us, therefore we will do nothing.”
They prayed.
And they posted a guard.
Faith prayed.
Faith acted.
Or consider Paul, who could say that he worked intensely while simultaneously attributing what he accomplished to the grace of God working with him.
Biblical grace does not produce passivity.
Grace produces obedience.
But obedience is the fruit of grace, not the purchase price of grace.
You do not obey so that Christ will finally become willing to rescue you.
You obey because in Christ you have encountered the Savior who rescues sinners.
You do not work instead of depending on God.
You work because you depend on God.
You do not say, “Jesus, watch what I can accomplish without You.”
Jesus Himself destroys that fantasy:
“χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν.”
“Apart from Me you can do nothing.”
John 15:5.
Nothing.
That sentence is offensive to the self-made heart.
We want Jesus as an assistant.
Jesus presents Himself as the vine.
We want divine encouragement for our independent plans.
Jesus tells us branches cannot bear fruit disconnected from Him.
We want God to strengthen our self-sufficiency.
Jesus calls us into dependence.
And perhaps that is why this subject reaches much deeper than correcting a misquotation.
This is about the lie underneath it.
The lie that says:
“I should be able to fix myself.”
Maybe you have lived underneath that sentence for years.
You should be stronger by now.
You should pray more.
You should have conquered this already.
You should not still struggle with temptation.
You should not still remember what happened.
You should not need help.
You should not be this tired.
You should not have failed again.
So you hide.
Because self-reliance has an ugly twin.
Shame.
If everything depends upon your ability to rescue yourself, every failure becomes evidence that you are beyond rescue.
But Jesus walked directly toward people whose lives had become scandals.
Tax collectors.
Sexually broken people.
Religious hypocrites.
Social outsiders.
Doubters.
Failures.
Sinners.
People carrying histories they could not erase.
And when religious leaders complained about the company He kept, Jesus answered with the language of a physician.
“The healthy do not need a physician, but the sick do.”
Then He explained why He had come:
not to call the righteous, but sinners.
That changes everything.
A doctor is not offended because the patient arrives sick.
Sickness is why the patient needs the physician.
And sin is why you need the Savior.
Please do not misunderstand that.
Grace never tells you that sin does not matter.
The cross proves exactly how seriously God takes sin.
Jesus did not suffer because sin was insignificant.
He suffered because redemption was costly.
Grace does not tell the alcoholic to cherish the bottle.
Grace calls him out of slavery.
Grace does not tell the adulterer to celebrate betrayal.
Grace calls the sinner to repentance.
Grace does not tell the proud person to remain proud.
Grace exposes pride.
Grace does not leave us where it found us.
But grace does something self-help can never do.
It gives dead people life.
Christianity is not primarily a program for making bad people slightly better.
It is the announcement that through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, made new, and brought from death into life.
That is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not helping yourself enough to deserve Jesus.
Repentance is abandoning the throne you were never capable of occupying.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is finally admitting:
“I cannot be my own savior.”
And faith says:
“Jesus, You must be.”
Maybe this article found you during a season when your strength is disappearing.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well.
But you know.
There is something behind the smile.
Something behind the church attendance.
Something behind the Bible verses you post.
Something behind the “God is good” responses.
Maybe there is an addiction.
A secret relationship.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
A private compromise.
An unforgiven wound.
A prayer life that has almost disappeared.
A marriage nobody knows is breaking.
A heart becoming colder toward Christ while your public Christianity continues looking perfectly alive.
And perhaps you have been waiting to become “good enough” before coming back to God.
Listen carefully.
You have misunderstood the direction of grace.
You do not clean yourself before coming to the One who cleanses sinners.
You come.
You confess.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender.
You stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
You stop bargaining.
You stop pretending.
You bring Him the truth.
Not the Instagram version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version your family believes.
The truth.
And perhaps your prayer tonight needs to be embarrassingly simple:

“Jesus Christ, I cannot save myself. I have sinned. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change me. I surrender what I keep trying to control. Teach me to obey You. I trust what You accomplished through Your death and resurrection, not what I can accomplish for myself.”
That is not weakness masquerading as Christianity.
That is Christianity.
The strange glory of the Gospel is that admitting your inability to save yourself is not the end of hope.
It is where hope finally stops depending upon you.
And once grace has found you there, grace teaches you to stand.
To work.
To forgive.
To confess.
To seek help.
To flee temptation.
To repair what can be repaired.
To make restitution where appropriate.
To pursue holiness.
To serve.
To endure.
To get back up after falling.
Not because “God helps those who help themselves.”
But because God’s grace creates people who can now walk in the good works He prepared for them.
Ephesians 2 does not stop at verses 8–9.
Verse 10 speaks of believers as God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
Grace.
Salvation.
New creation.
Then works.
Not:
works → worthiness → salvation.
But:
grace → salvation → transformed life.
That order protects the Gospel.
And it protects exhausted sinners from believing their failures are stronger than Christ.
Your works cannot purchase salvation.
Your failures cannot improve the cross.
Your religious résumé cannot add anything to the blood of Jesus.
And your worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence when Christ becomes the Author of your redemption.
That is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by lowering God's holiness until sin becomes harmless.

Jesus rewrites everything by entering the sinner's real story with a real cross, bearing real judgment against sin, offering real forgiveness, producing real repentance, and beginning real transformation.
The scars may remain.
Consequences sometimes remain.
Memories may remain.
Some relationships may take years to rebuild.
Grace is not pretending yesterday never happened.
Grace means yesterday no longer gets to be your god.
Jesus does.
And maybe somebody you know desperately needs to hear this.
Not another motivational quote.
Not another command to “be stronger.”
They need Christ.
Send it privately to the believer who disappeared.
Send it to the friend who thinks Christianity is only for people who have their lives together.
Send it to the person who keeps saying, “I need to fix myself before I come back to God.”
They need to know:
You come to Christ because you cannot fix yourself.
And if this exposed something hidden in your own heart, do not disappear silently.
Your testimony may become another person's reason to believe there is still hope.
Because one day the voice of shame may return and tell you that God will love you once you finally get yourself together.
Come back and remember:
“οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν.”
Not from yourselves.
Grace.
Gift.
Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Jesus wants nothing to do with people like them.
It does not.
Not because financial support purchases blessing.
It cannot.
And not because anyone must give money to prove that they love Jesus.
The Gospel must never be turned into a transaction.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God by helping sound, Christ-centered Gospel content reach more people, supporting the work is one practical way you can participate alongside praying, sharing, serving, giving faithfully, and personally telling others about Christ.
Then do something that costs nothing.
They may never tell you they are struggling.
They may never comment.
They may never admit that they cried while reading.
But your share could place one sentence in front of them at exactly the moment they are ready to hear it:
Jesus did not wait for helpless sinners to become their own rescuers.
He came to rescue them.
And maybe that person is you.
So stop trying to audition for grace.
Come empty-handed.
Come guilty.
Come tired.
Come ashamed.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Come to Jesus.
Because the hands that cannot save themselves are finally free to reach toward the Savior who can.
You were never asked to become your own rescue story—the Gospel begins when Jesus becomes your Rescuer.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TWO MEN WHO REFUSED TO FEAR THE GIANTS
paragraphs:
THE TWO MEN WHO REFUSED TO FEAR THE GIANTS
Twelve men saw the same giants. Ten came back terrified. Two came back believing. And the difference was never the size of the giants—it was the size of the God they believed was standing with them.
There are moments when fear does not knock politely.
It kicks the door open.
The diagnosis comes back.
The marriage starts breaking.
The bills pile higher than the money.
Someone you trusted becomes someone you barely recognize.
The temptation you thought you defeated returns.
The prayer you have prayed for months seems to disappear into silence.
And suddenly there is a giant standing between you and everything you thought God promised.
That is where Numbers 13 takes us.
Not into a comfortable Bible story.
Into a crisis of faith.
Israel had already watched God humiliate Egypt's idols, split the sea, drown Pharaoh's army, provide bread in the wilderness, and reveal His presence among His people.
They had evidence.
They had history.
They had promises.
And still, when twelve spies entered Canaan and returned forty days later, ten men essentially said:
We cannot do this.
The people are too strong.
The cities are too fortified.
The giants are too big.
And tragically, they were not lying about what they saw.
That is what makes this story so painfully relevant.
Faith is not pretending the giants are small.
Biblical faith does not require you to lie about your cancer.
It does not require you to pretend betrayal did not hurt.
It does not demand that you call financial devastation "nothing."
It does not tell a grieving mother to stop crying.
It does not ask the exhausted Christian to pretend everything is wonderful.
The ten spies saw real obstacles.
Joshua and Caleb saw them too.
The difference was not eyesight.
The difference was interpretation.
Ten interpreted the giants without adequately accounting for God.
Two interpreted the giants in light of God.
And somebody reading this needs to understand the difference.
Numbers 13:30 tells us that Caleb quieted the people before Moses and declared:
“Let us go up at once and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.”
The Hebrew carries an intensity that English can easily flatten:
עָלֹה נַעֲלֶה
ʿālōh naʿăleh
The construction intensifies the verbal idea.
We can capture its force approximately as:
“We should absolutely go up.”
Then Caleb says:
יָכוֹל נוּכַל לָהּ
yākhol nūkhal lāh
Again, the Hebrew intensifies the declaration:
“We are certainly able to overcome it.”
Caleb was not practicing positive thinking.
He was not standing in front of a mirror repeating affirmations about his own greatness.
His confidence was rooted in something infinitely greater than self-confidence.
God had spoken.
That changes everything.
But the other spies looked at the same land and said:
“We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.”
Then came one of Scripture's most haunting descriptions of fear.
They said they saw the Nephilim, and then confessed:
וַנְּהִי בְעֵינֵינוּ כַּחֲגָבִים
vannehi veʿeineinu kaḥagavim
“We were in our own eyes like grasshoppers.”
Read those words again.
“In our own eyes.”
Before the giants defeated Israel on a battlefield, fear had already reduced these men inside their own minds.
They had become grasshoppers to themselves.
And fear still does this.
It whispers:
You are too damaged.
Too ordinary.
Too weak.
Too late.
Too sinful.
Too far gone.
Your family will never change.
Your addiction will always own you.
Your past will always define you.
Your failure is bigger than your future.
Your shame has the final word.
And sometimes the most dangerous giant is not standing in front of you.
It is speaking inside you.
The ten spies spread their fear through the camp.
That is another uncomfortable truth.
Fear is contagious.
One frightened voice became ten.
Ten frightened voices became a nation crying through the night.
People began wishing they had died in Egypt.
Some even wanted another leader who would take them back.
Back.
To Egypt.
Back to bondage.
Back to the place God had delivered them from.
Fear can make slavery look safer than obedience.
Sit with that.
Because some of us have done the same thing.
God begins pulling us out of something destructive, but when obedience becomes frightening, suddenly the old chains begin looking familiar.
You start missing the relationship God rescued you from.
You romanticize the addiction that was destroying you.
You reconsider the compromise you once begged God to break.
You return mentally to Egypt because Canaan contains giants.
But Joshua and Caleb refused to join the panic.
Numbers 14 tells us that Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh tore their clothes.
They pleaded with the people.
The land was exceedingly good.
If the LORD delighted in them, He would bring them into it.
Then they said:
“Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land.”
And then comes an astonishing declaration:
יְהוָה אִתָּנוּ אַל־תִּירָאֻם
YHWH ʾittānu, ʾal-tirāʾum.
“The LORD is with us. Do not fear them.”
There it is.
The entire battle compressed into one sentence.
The LORD is with us.
Joshua and Caleb were not fearless because the giants had disappeared.
They refused to be ruled by fear because God's presence mattered more than the giants' size.
That is biblical courage.
Courage is not the absence of trembling.
Courage is obedience when trembling has not stopped.
Faith is not saying, “There is no giant.”
Faith says, “There is a giant—and there is God.”
And God is not the smaller reality.
But we must be careful here.
This passage is not a blank check promising Christians that every personal dream will succeed if they simply believe hard enough.
Canaan was connected to a specific covenant promise God had given Israel.
So we should not turn Joshua and Caleb into mascots for self-help spirituality.
“Believe in yourself and conquer your dreams” is not the Gospel.
The deeper biblical principle is far more demanding:
Trust God enough to obey Him even when obedience frightens you.
And that brings us somewhere even deeper.
Because Joshua's name matters.
In Hebrew, Joshua is יְהוֹשֻׁעַ — Yehoshua.
The Greek form associated with that name is Ἰησοῦς — Iēsous.
Jesus bears that name.
And while Joshua son of Nun is not Jesus Christ, the biblical storyline ultimately carries us beyond Joshua and beyond Canaan toward the greater Deliverer.
Joshua led Israel toward earthly inheritance.
Jesus came to rescue sinners from enemies no human warrior could conquer.
Sin.
Condemnation.
Death.
We spend so much time talking about the giants around us that we can miss the monster within us.
The greatest human problem is not that life is difficult.
It is that humanity is alienated from a holy God by sin.
We do not merely need improved circumstances.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need new hearts.
We need Jesus.
And this is where the Gospel becomes scandalously beautiful.
Jesus did not come for people who had successfully defeated every giant.
He came for sinners.
For failures.
For deniers.
For doubters.
For people carrying histories they wish they could erase.
For people who promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
For people who know exactly how Peter must have felt when the rooster crowed.
For people who cannot believe God would still want them after everything they have done.
The cross answers that fear.
Christ did not die because humanity had finally become worthy of Him.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Grace walked toward the guilty.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That means your sin is serious—but for everyone who comes to Christ in repentance and faith, your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Your shame does not own the pen.
Your worst night does not own the pen.
Your addiction does not own the pen.
Your divorce does not own the pen.
Your betrayal does not own the pen.
Your failure does not own the pen.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your giant tonight has a name.
Maybe nobody knows it.
You smile at church.
You post encouraging verses.
You tell people you are blessed.
But behind the closed door, you are tired.
You have been fighting thoughts you are ashamed to admit.
You have wondered whether God has become tired of you.
You have asked whether you have failed too many times.
Maybe you have been staring at your giant so long that you have started seeing yourself as a grasshopper.
Small.
Powerless.
Finished.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not discovering that you are secretly powerful enough.
The answer is discovering again who Christ is.
Paul did not say, “I can survive because I finally discovered how impressive I am.”
His confidence was in Christ.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of strong people accomplishing impossible things for God.
It is the story of weak people discovering that God's grace is sufficient.
That changes the way we face giants.
Sometimes God removes the giant.
Sometimes He takes you through the battle.
Sometimes the prayer is answered differently than you desperately hoped.
Some believers are healed.
Others glorify Christ while suffering.
Some doors open.
Others remain closed.
Some storms stop.
In others, Christ keeps His people while the storm continues.
Faith does not dictate to God how the story must unfold.
Faith trusts the Author when we cannot understand the chapter.
Joshua and Caleb did not control the outcome.
They trusted the One who did.
And perhaps that is where this story has found you.
Standing between promise and fear.
Between yesterday's evidence of God's faithfulness and tomorrow's terrifying uncertainty.
You know what Scripture says.
You know what Christ has done.
But the giant still looks enormous.
Then do what Joshua and Caleb did.
Look again.
Not away from reality.
Look beyond it.
There is something bigger than the giant.
There is Someone.
Jesus Christ.
The One who touched lepers when others backed away.
The One who welcomed sinners when religious people wanted distance.
The One who forgave the undeserving.
The One who stood before death itself.
The One who entered a grave.
The One who walked out.
And because He lives, hopelessness does not get automatic authority over your story.
Maybe you have spent years running.
Come home.
Maybe you have hidden your sin beneath religious language.
Repent.
Maybe you have confused church attendance with knowing Christ.
Seek Him.
Maybe you have fallen again.
Get up and turn toward Jesus.
Maybe shame keeps telling you that God could never forgive someone like you.
Look at the cross.
Grace is not permission to remain in sin.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness that leads us away from the grave and into a transformed life with Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of what is killing you.
And perhaps your first courageous act today is not conquering some visible giant.
Perhaps it is finally becoming honest before God.
“No more pretending.”
“No more hiding.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If that is where your heart is right now, let your response become more than emotion.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer sees at midnight and realizes:
I am not fighting alone.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if the Gospel has strengthened you, sharing biblical truth can become one simple way of serving someone else. Someone scrolling through Facebook tonight may be silently standing before a giant nobody else can see.
Let them encounter hope.
Because giants have an irritating habit of returning after inspirational moments are over.
Save it so you can return to the words Joshua and Caleb carried into a terrified generation:
“The LORD is with us. Do not fear them.”
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is growing cold.
Invite the person who is questioning everything.
Invite the friend who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Invite even the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Supporting Gospel work is a meaningful act of generosity when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory—not as a transaction for divine favor.
And there is more.
Deeper than a comment.
Deeper than a share.
He is calling you to Himself.
Because eventually every Facebook post disappears down a feed.
Every shirt wears out.
Every mug breaks.
Every book grows old.
Every human platform eventually disappears.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So when the giants rise tomorrow, remember Joshua.
Remember Caleb.
Remember the ten men who allowed what they saw to become greater in their hearts than what God had said.
And remember those devastating words:
“We were in our own eyes like grasshoppers.”
Do not let fear become your identity.
You may feel weak.
You may be wounded.
You may have failed.
You may still be trembling.
But if you belong to Christ, trembling does not mean abandoned.
The giant can be real.
The tears can be real.
The battle can be real.
And God can still be faithful.
So share this with the person facing something enormous.
Because perhaps somewhere tonight there is another frightened person staring at another impossible giant.
And perhaps the truth God used to strengthen you is exactly what they need to encounter next.
The giant may be standing in front of you—but it does not get to sit on God's throne.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MARY MAGDALENE WAS NOT CALLED A PROSTITUTE: How Did That Story Become So Popular?
paragraphs:
MARY MAGDALENE WAS NOT CALLED A PROSTITUTE: How Did That Story Become So Popular?
For centuries, millions have pictured Mary Magdalene as the Bible’s redeemed prostitute. There is only one problem: the Gospels never call her one. And what Scripture actually says about Mary may be far more powerful than the story many of us inherited.
There are some things you can hear so many times that eventually you stop asking whether they are actually written in the Bible.
Mary Magdalene was a prostitute.
You may have heard it in a sermon.
Seen it in a painting.
Watched it portrayed in a movie.
Perhaps you remember the familiar image: a sexually immoral woman with a scandalous past encounters Jesus, falls at His feet, and becomes one of His devoted followers.
It is certainly a dramatic story of redemption.
There is just one serious problem.
The Bible never tells that story about Mary Magdalene.
Read that again.
Not once in Matthew.
Not once in Mark.
Not once in Luke.
Not once in John.
The New Testament never calls Mary Magdalene a prostitute.
It never says she sold her body.
It never identifies sexual immorality as her particular past.
It never even explicitly identifies her as the unnamed “sinful woman” who anointed Jesus in Luke 7.
What Scripture actually tells us is simultaneously more restrained and more extraordinary.
Luke introduces her immediately after the account of that unnamed woman, but he introduces Mary as a named person among the women accompanying Jesus:
“Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils.”
—Luke 8:2, KJV
The Greek is striking:
Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει
Maria hē kaloumenē Magdalēnē, aph’ hēs daimonia hepta exelēlythei.
In straightforward English:
“Mary, the one called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.”
That is what Luke tells us.
Seven demons.
Not seven sexual sins.
Not prostitution.
Not adultery.
Not a career in sexual immorality.
Seven demons had gone out from her.
And we need to resist the temptation to make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
Because when God gives us a person’s story, we do not have permission to rewrite the scandal.
And perhaps there is something deeply personal hiding inside that truth.
Because maybe somebody once rewrote yours.
Maybe something happened to you...
and eventually what people said about you became bigger than what actually happened.
A failure became your identity.
A divorce became your identity.
An addiction became your identity.
A season of rebellion became your identity.
A pregnancy became your identity.
A prison sentence became your identity.
A breakdown became your identity.
A rumor became your identity.
Something you did became the permanent headline above your life.
Or perhaps something done to you became the name people quietly attached to you.
And suddenly Mary Magdalene’s story is no longer merely an interesting historical correction.
It becomes painfully familiar.
Because human beings have always been good at turning somebody’s darkest chapter into their permanent biography.
Jesus does something different.
The Gospels do not introduce Mary by giving us lurid details about her bondage.
They introduce us to a woman who had been delivered.
That distinction matters.
Mary Magdalene had known darkness.
Whatever the precise nature and experience of her demonic oppression was—and Scripture does not give us enough information to reconstruct it safely—Luke wants us to know something unmistakable:
Jesus Christ had set her free.
Seven demons had gone out.
And after deliverance came discipleship.
Luke continues by naming Joanna, Susanna, and “many others,” women who accompanied Jesus and the Twelve and helped support the ministry from their resources.
Mary was not merely standing somewhere in the background of Christianity’s story.
She followed Christ.
She served.
She remained.
And when the story became unbearable, she was still there.
Think about that.
When Jesus was crucified, Mary Magdalene appears among the women associated with the crucifixion accounts.
When His body was laid in the tomb, she was there.
When Sabbath darkness gave way to resurrection morning, she went to the tomb.
And then comes one of the most breathtaking encounters in the New Testament.
John 20 places Mary outside the tomb...
weeping.
The Greek verb is κλαίω — klaiō.
She is grieving.
The One who had transformed her life was dead—or so she believed.
Then she sees someone.
She thinks He is the gardener.
Jesus asks why she is crying.
She still does not recognize Him.
And then...
one word.
Her name.
Μαριάμ — Mariam.
“Mary.”
Imagine hearing your name spoken by the Man you watched die.
Imagine grief colliding with impossible hope.
Imagine believing everything was over...
and suddenly discovering that Death itself had lost.
Mary turns toward Him.
“Rabboni!”
Teacher.
The tomb is empty.
Christ is alive.
And Jesus gives this woman a message.
“Go to my brethren...”
Then John records:
“Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord.”
—John 20:18, KJV
Do not race past that sentence.
She had seen the Lord.

The woman later generations would so often remember primarily through a sexualized story the Gospels never actually assign to her is presented in John as a witness proclaiming the risen Christ to His disciples.
The center of Mary Magdalene’s biblical identity is not prostitution.
It is Jesus.
Deliverance.
Discipleship.
The cross.
The empty tomb.
And resurrection testimony.
So how did the prostitute story become so deeply embedded in Christian imagination?
Part of the answer comes from something that happened centuries after the New Testament was written.
Luke 7 tells the story of an unnamed woman described as a sinner who enters the home of Simon the Pharisee. She weeps at Jesus’ feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them.
Luke does not call that woman Mary Magdalene.
Then Luke 8 introduces Mary Magdalene by name.
Elsewhere, John identifies Mary of Bethany—the sister of Martha and Lazarus—in an anointing account.
Over time, these women became intertwined in parts of Western Christian interpretation.

The association became especially influential through Pope Gregory I, Gregory the Great, in the late sixth century, when he treated Mary Magdalene, Mary of Bethany, and Luke’s unnamed sinful woman as the same person.
That interpretive fusion helped shape centuries of Western preaching, painting, literature, and popular imagination.
Eventually, the picture became so familiar that many Christians assumed they had read it directly in Scripture.
But familiarity is not the same thing as biblical accuracy.
And there is another important correction.
Even Luke 7 does not explicitly say that its unnamed “sinful woman” was a prostitute.
The Greek description is:
γυνὴ... ἁμαρτωλός
gynē... hamartōlos
A “woman... who was a sinner.”
The text tells us she had a sinful reputation.
It does not identify prostitution as her occupation.
That conclusion goes beyond what Luke actually says.
And this is where the story should make every Bible-reading Christian uncomfortable in the best possible way.
Because it is possible to defend a story for centuries...
and still need to open the Bible again.
Tradition can be valuable.
Teachers can help us.
Church history matters.
But Christians ultimately must allow Scripture to correct our assumptions.
Even cherished assumptions.
Especially cherished assumptions.
And correcting this misunderstanding does not weaken the Gospel of grace.
It strengthens it.
Because someone might hear that Mary Magdalene was not called a prostitute and wonder:
“But doesn't that ruin the beautiful redemption story?”
No.
Grace does not need an invented sin to become amazing.
Mary needed Jesus.
So do you.
So do I.
The Gospel does not require us to make Mary more sinful so that Christ can appear more merciful.
Scripture has already settled the condition of humanity:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
Mary needed grace.
Peter needed grace.
The unnamed woman of Luke 7 needed grace.
The thief on the cross needed grace.
The apostle Paul needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
Not because every person has committed the same sins...
but because every sinner needs the same Savior.
And perhaps that is why this correction can reach somewhere deeper than historical curiosity.
Somebody reading this has spent years believing that your worst moment is your truest name.
You believe God looks at you and sees the affair.
The addiction.
The abortion.
The pornography.
The lies.
The betrayal.
The bitterness.
The secret nobody knows.
The years you wasted.
The faith you abandoned.
The marriage you damaged.
The person you hurt.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
And shame keeps whispering:
That is who you are.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel never teaches that repentance means pretending sin never happened.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He forgives sinners.
He cleanses sinners.
He reconciles sinners to God.
He gives new life.
He transforms.
He restores.
He makes people His own.
This is why Paul could write:
—2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean sin becomes insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
And grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly went there for sinners.
That is Christianity.
Not self-improvement.
Not reputation management.
Not pretending darkness never existed.
Death...
then resurrection.
Guilt...
then forgiveness.
Bondage...
then freedom.
Lost...
then found.
Enemy...
then reconciled.
Sinner...
saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Mary Magdalene understood something about deliverance that comfortable religion can easily forget.
When you know what Christ rescued you from, following Him stops feeling like an accessory to your life.
It becomes your life.
And look where Mary eventually stands.
Near the cross.
Near the tomb.
Then before the risen Christ.
That sequence almost preaches by itself.
The cross.
The tomb.
The risen Jesus.
That is where every Christian story ultimately has to go.
Not merely toward Mary.
Toward Christ.
Mary Magdalene matters precisely because Jesus matters infinitely more.
She does not save us.
Her story does not save us.
Correcting misconceptions about her does not save us.
Jesus Christ saves.
The crucified and risen Son of God is the center.
And maybe the most beautiful thing about correcting Mary Magdalene’s story is discovering that the biblical version does not diminish grace at all.
It reveals something about grace we desperately need to remember.
Jesus does not need human beings to exaggerate your darkness in order to demonstrate His light.
He knows exactly what happened.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows what was bondage.
He knows what was sin.
He knows what was suffering.
He knows what was rumor.
He knows what was true.
He knows the parts everybody misunderstood.
And He knows the parts nobody knows at all.
There is nowhere to hide from Him.
And there is no reason to manufacture a cleaner biography before coming to Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come empty-handed.
Come to Christ.
