Maybe your story really is scandalous.
Maybe nobody had to invent anything.
Maybe if everything were projected onto a screen in church next Sunday, you would want the ground to swallow you.
The Gospel is still for sinners.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose.
And forgiveness is not purchased by your ability to repair your reputation.
It was purchased by His blood.
So repent.
Believe.
Stop negotiating with the sin Christ is calling you to abandon.
Stop making peace with chains He came to break.
Stop assuming that because you have failed repeatedly you are beyond the reach of mercy.
Run to Jesus.
The woman standing outside the empty tomb reminds us that Christ can take a human life that has known profound darkness and make that life a witness to resurrection.
That is the heartbeat behind From Scandal to Grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not inventing scandals Scripture never recorded.
Not celebrating sin.
But declaring that Jesus Christ has the final word over every sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
Send it to the person who has always believed Mary Magdalene was a prostitute.
Send it to the person drowning in shame.
Send it to the believer who thinks their past disqualified them forever.
And perhaps send it to someone who does not yet believe at all.
Let them encounter not merely an interesting correction about Mary Magdalene...
but the Jesus who stood outside a tomb alive.
Come back to the Scriptures in it. Test what you have read against the Word of God. Christians should never fear careful examination of Scripture.

Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's favor and is not a condition of glorifying Him—Christians glorify God through lives of faith, love, obedience, worship, generosity, and service—but if this particular ministry is feeding you spiritually and you want to help it reach others, your support can become part of making that work possible.
Leave looking at Jesus.
The Jesus who delivers.
The Jesus who receives repentant sinners.
The Jesus who went willingly to the cross.
The Jesus whose body was placed inside a tomb.
The Jesus who walked out alive.
The Jesus who called Mary by name.
And the Jesus who still calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Mary Magdalene's story was never powerful because later generations could attach a sensational past to her.
It was powerful because Jesus Christ had changed her future.
And perhaps that is the sentence you need to carry with you tonight:
People may keep introducing you by a chapter Jesus has already turned—but when Christ writes the ending, the tomb does not get the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A NEWLY MARRIED MAN COULD STAY HOME FROM WAR FOR A YEAR—Just to Bring Happiness to His Wife
paragraphs: A NEWLY MARRIED MAN COULD STAY HOME FROM WAR FOR A YEAR—Just to Bring Happiness to His Wife
Buried inside Deuteronomy is a command so tender that it can completely change the way you see marriage, responsibility, and the heart of God.
Imagine hearing the sound of war preparations outside your home.
Men are being summoned.

Families know what it means when husbands and sons disappear beyond the horizon. There are no guarantees. No text messages from the battlefield. No video calls before bed. No flight home for the weekend.
You have only recently married.
Your wife is still learning what it feels like to wake up beside you. You are still learning the strange, beautiful reality of saying “our home” instead of “my home.”
And then the nation goes to war.
Surely duty calls.
Surely marriage must wait.
Surely the battlefield matters more than tenderness.
Then God says something astonishing.
“Not him.”
Hidden in a chapter many Christians hurry past is one of Scripture’s most unexpectedly tender laws:
“כִּי־יִקַּח אִישׁ אִשָּׁה חֲדָשָׁה לֹא יֵצֵא בַּצָּבָא וְלֹא־יַעֲבֹר עָלָיו לְכָל־דָּבָר נָקִי יִהְיֶה לְבֵיתוֹ שָׁנָה אֶחָת וְשִׂמַּח אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר־לָקָח.”

“When a man has newly taken a wife, he shall not go out with the army or be assigned to it for any purpose; he shall be exempt one year for the sake of his household, to give happiness to the woman he has taken.”
—Deuteronomy 24:5
Read those Hebrew words again:
נָקִי יִהְיֶה לְבֵיתוֹ שָׁנָה אֶחָת
Nāqî yihyeh ləvêto shānāh ʾeḥāt.
He was to be free for his household for one year.
And then comes the phrase that can be easy to flatten when we read it too quickly:
וְשִׂמַּח אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ
Veśimmaḥ ʾet-ʾishtô.
He was to bring joy to his wife.
That wording matters.

The Hebrew does not simply picture a man being permitted to spend a happy year enjoying married life for himself. The verb is expressed in a form carrying the sense of causing or bringing gladness. His attention turns toward the woman he has married.
Even the ancient Aramaic tradition reflected this:
וְיַחְדֵּי יָת אִתְּתֵיהּ
He is to gladden the wife he has taken.
Think about that.
In a world where war could demand a man's strength, God wrote into Israel's law a protection for a newly formed household.
Before the battlefield could take him away, the marriage was given room to begin.
A year.
A year in which the newly married man was not to be sent out with the army or burdened with its duties.
A year for home.
A year for his bride.
A year in which one of his God-given responsibilities was remarkably tender:
Bring her joy.

And maybe that feels almost shocking because some of us have unconsciously learned a version of faith where God seems interested only in sacrifice, duty, productivity, suffering, ministry, and endurance.
Work harder.
Serve more.
Carry more.
Sacrifice more.
Prove yourself.
But then you encounter Deuteronomy 24:5 and discover that the God who commanded courage on battlefields also cared about tenderness inside a home.
God cared about what happened after the wedding celebration ended.
He cared about the beginning of a marriage.
He cared about a wife receiving the presence of the man who had covenanted himself to her.

That does not mean Deuteronomy 24:5 establishes a universal modern rule that every newlywed husband in every nation must receive twelve months away from employment or every form of public responsibility. This command belonged to the covenant legislation given to ancient Israel, and we should not rip it from its historical setting.
But neither should Christians rush past what it reveals.
Because Scripture repeatedly refuses to treat marriage casually.
From Genesis onward, marriage is covenantal rather than disposable.
“A man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
—Genesis 2:24
Jesus Himself reached back to this creation text when teaching about marriage:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
—Matthew 19:6
And later, Paul reaches for something even more breathtaking.
He describes the relationship between husband and wife and then points beyond marriage itself:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
—Ephesians 5:32
Suddenly that little law in Deuteronomy does not feel so little.
Marriage matters to God.
Presence matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Tenderness matters.
The person sleeping beside you is not supposed to become collateral damage in your pursuit of everything else.
And that may be where this verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because you do not need to be carrying a sword to abandon your home.
Some people leave without ever packing a suitcase.
A husband can be sitting three feet from his wife and be a thousand miles away.
A wife can lie beside her husband every night while resentment quietly builds a wall between them.
You can provide money and withhold affection.
You can post anniversary photographs while barely speaking when the camera disappears.
You can know exactly what strangers online are doing and have no idea what your spouse has been crying about.
You can serve at church while neglecting the person waiting at home.
You can win arguments and lose tenderness.
You can build a career and slowly dismantle a marriage.
You can even use “ministry” as an excuse for emotional absence.
And perhaps one of the most painful sentences a spouse can silently carry is this:
“I know you love me...
I just don't feel like you still see me.”
Deuteronomy 24:5 confronts that kind of disappearance.
The newly married Israelite was not merely told what he could avoid.
He was given someone toward whom his freedom was directed.
His wife.
Her joy mattered.
Her adjustment mattered.
Their newly established household mattered.
God was protecting something that had only just begun to grow.
There is wisdom there for every generation.
The strongest marriages are not sustained merely by one spectacular wedding day.
They are built in ordinary rooms.
At kitchen tables.
During exhausted conversations.
Through apologies nobody sees.
Through forgiveness after disappointment.
Through choosing to listen when you would rather defend yourself.
Through affection when life becomes repetitive.
Through praying together when neither person has impressive words.
Through turning the phone over.
Through asking, “Are you really okay?”
And waiting long enough to hear the real answer.
Sometimes love looks dramatic.
Sometimes love looks like staying.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is give your undivided attention to the person God entrusted to your care.
But there is something even deeper here.
Because eventually every human marriage exposes something uncomfortable about us.
We are sinners trying to love other sinners.
The honeymoon cannot cure selfishness.
Romance cannot crucify pride.
A wedding ring cannot regenerate a heart.
Eventually impatience appears.
Old wounds surface.
Expectations collide.
Words are spoken that cannot be pulled back into the mouth.
One person fails.
Then the other does.
And suddenly the fairy tale meets two fallen human beings.
That is where we desperately need something greater than marriage advice.
We need the Gospel.
We need Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity does not say, “Try harder until you become lovable.”
It tells us that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
The Son of God did not wait until His people became impressive enough to deserve redemption.
He came for sinners.
He carried our guilt.
He bore judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That changes how Christians understand love.
We forgive because we have been forgiven.
We confess because grace gives us somewhere to bring the truth.
We repent because Christ does not call us merely to feel guilty; He calls us to turn around.
We serve because the King Himself took the posture of a servant.
We love because He first loved us.

This does not mean remaining silent about abuse, tolerating violence, or pretending serious wrongdoing does not matter. Biblical forgiveness does not transform evil into good or eliminate the need for truth, safety, justice, wise boundaries, pastoral care, or appropriate civil intervention.
Grace is not pretending the wound never happened.
Grace tells the truth about the wound and still declares that sin does not get the final word.
That is why our message has always been:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your marriage started beautifully and now you barely recognize it.
Maybe there has been betrayal.
Maybe years of small disappointments became a mountain.
Maybe your spouse does not know how lonely you have become.
Maybe you are the one who stopped trying.
Maybe you have spent years blaming the other person while the Holy Spirit has been quietly putting His finger on something inside you.
Your pride.
Your temper.
Your secrecy.
Your pornography.
Your emotional affair.
Your dishonesty.
Your neglect.
Your unforgiveness.
Your refusal to apologize.
Your obsession with being right.
And perhaps the hardest prayer you could pray tonight is not:
“God, change my spouse.”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus...
show me what needs to change in me.”
That prayer can hurt.
Because repentance usually begins where excuses end.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
If you belong to Christ, your failure does not have to become the final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
The prodigal came home filthy and was embraced.
The woman caught in adultery encountered both mercy and a call to leave sin.
The cross itself stands at the center of history declaring that God does not minimize sin...
He deals with it.
And then grace does what shame never could.
Grace makes transformation possible.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs tonight.
Not another polished Christian quote.
Not another picture-perfect marriage pretending Christians never struggle.
You need permission to finally tell the truth.
“I am hurting.”
“I have failed.”
“I don't know how to fix what I damaged.”
“I still love them, but I am exhausted.”
“I need help.”
“I need forgiveness.”
“I need Jesus.”
If that is you, stop hiding.
Bring the truth into the light.
Talk to your spouse if it is safe and appropriate.
Seek wise biblical counsel.
Ask mature believers to walk with you.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
And above everything else, run toward Jesus rather than away from Him.
You do not clean yourself before coming to the cross.
You come because you cannot clean yourself.
Maybe your story has become scandalous.
Maybe people know what happened.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe the scandal is happening silently inside your own heart.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling sinners to repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and new life.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not that Christians never fall.
Not that Christian marriages never hurt.
Not that believers never make catastrophic mistakes.
But that Jesus Christ remains mighty to save.
So tonight, husbands, consider something ancient Israel was forced to remember:
Your home is not an interruption to your calling.
Your wife is not an accessory to your ambition.
And providing financially, while important, is not the entirety of loving her.
See her.
Hear her.
Pray for her.
Honor her.
Learn what weighs on her heart.
Bring tenderness back into places where familiarity has made you careless.
And wives, the same Gospel calls you toward Christ-shaped faithfulness, truth, honor, forgiveness, wisdom, and love toward your husband.
Marriage is not ultimately about two people extracting enough happiness from one another to survive.
It is two imperfect people desperately needing the grace of a perfect Savior.
And if you are single, widowed, divorced, separated, or carrying a story that does not fit neatly inside an article about marriage, do not assume this passage has nothing to say to you.
Look at the heart behind the command.
People are not machines.
Relationships are not disposable.
Covenants matter.
Presence matters.
Love costs time.
And God notices what the world considers small.
Perhaps that is why one obscure verse can stop us cold thousands of years later.
There was a war to fight...
and God still made room for a bride to be cherished.
Be honest.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that broken chapters do not always have to become final chapters.

Not because every sentence will be needed today, but because there may come a night when pride is loud, tenderness feels far away, and you need to remember what Scripture says about covenant, presence, repentance, and grace.
One share can put biblical truth in front of someone who would never search for it themselves.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ—through faith, obedience, worship, love, generosity, holiness, service, and making His truth known.
But before you leave this article, look once more at that ancient home.
Outside, there is a nation preparing for war.
Inside, there are two newlyweds learning how to become one household.
The world hears marching feet.
God hears the heartbeat of a marriage.
And He says:
Give it time.
Give her your presence.
Bring her joy.
Maybe tonight your battlefield is not somewhere beyond your front door.
Maybe it is the distance that has quietly grown across your own bed.

And maybe the bravest battle you will fight this week is the battle against your own pride—the battle that finally makes you put down the phone, look into the eyes of the person you promised to love, tell the truth, ask forgiveness, and invite Jesus back into the rooms where resentment has been living.
Because sometimes the greatest victory is not conquering something outside your home.
Sometimes it is refusing to let the war inside you destroy the person you once prayed God would give you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS BEING SEXUALLY ATTRACTED TO SOMEONE THE SAME THING AS LUSTING AFTER THEM?
paragraphs: IS BEING SEXUALLY ATTRACTED TO SOMEONE THE SAME THING AS LUSTING AFTER THEM?
What if the thought you have been condemning yourself for is not actually the sin Jesus condemned—but what you choose to do with that thought could lead you straight into it?
There is a moment almost nobody talks about honestly.
You see someone.
Something registers.
They are beautiful.
Handsome.
Attractive.
Your body notices before you have finished forming a theological explanation for what just happened.
And suddenly, especially if you are a Christian who genuinely wants to be pure, another voice enters the room.
I sinned.
I lusted.
God must be disappointed in me.
Maybe you immediately looked away.
Maybe nothing sexual was imagined.
Maybe you did not entertain a fantasy.
Maybe you simply recognized that another human being was sexually attractive—and then spent the next hour feeling filthy for noticing.
So we need to ask the question Christians sometimes answer far too quickly:
Is sexual attraction itself the same thing as lust?
Because if we get this wrong, we can make people feel guilty for experiencing something Scripture never identifies as sin.
But if we swing too far in the opposite direction, we can rename lust “attraction,” protect our fantasies with Christian vocabulary, and excuse the very thing Jesus warned us about.
Jesus leaves room for neither shame-driven legalism nor convenient compromise.
He goes somewhere much deeper.
Into the heart.
Matthew 5:27–28 records:
Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις. ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Those words are devastating.
But notice carefully what Jesus actually says.
The Greek phrase at the center of the passage is:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pros to epithymēsai autēn.
The construction carries the idea of looking with a view toward desiring her, or looking in order to desire her.
And the verb is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō.

It can mean to desire, long for, covet, or set one’s desire upon something. The word itself is not automatically sexual or sinful in every New Testament occurrence; its moral character depends upon its object and context.
That matters enormously.
Jesus is not teaching that merely possessing eyes capable of recognizing beauty is adultery.
He is confronting something deeper.
The gaze that becomes intentional desire.
The look that doesn't merely notice but begins to consume.
The imagination that takes another person somewhere they never consented to go.
The heart that turns a human being created in God's image into material for private sexual gratification.
There is a difference between recognition and cultivation.
Between noticing and feeding.
Between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside.
You may not control every initial awareness that flashes through your mind.
But what happens next matters.
A person walks past you.
“They're attractive.”
That recognition can happen almost instantly.
Then comes the crossroads.
Will you honor them as a person?
Or will you mentally undress them?
Will you release the thought?
Or replay it?
Will you recognize beauty?
Or begin constructing a fantasy?
Will you see a human being with a soul...
or convert that human being into something to consume?
That is where this gets painfully personal.
Because some of us have become very skilled at changing the vocabulary without changing the heart.
“I was only looking.”
But you kept looking.
“I just think she's beautiful.”
But you deliberately revisit her pictures because of what happens inside your imagination.
“I just think he's attractive.”
But the fantasy has already become a secret room you keep returning to.
Nobody else sees it.
No messages were sent.
No physical affair happened.
No one touched anyone.
Your spouse may never know.
Your church may never know.
Your browser history might even look clean.
But Jesus walks past the locked door of outward appearances and puts His finger on the heart.
ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν... ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
Already committed adultery...
in his heart.
That is why Christ's teaching is so uncomfortable.
He does not merely ask:
“What did your body do?”
He asks:
“What did your heart want to do?”
And suddenly respectable people need grace too.
Suddenly the person who never physically cheated cannot boast.
Suddenly purity is bigger than virginity.
Faithfulness is bigger than avoiding an affair.
Holiness is bigger than maintaining a clean public reputation.
Jesus is exposing the inner world.
And perhaps that scares you because your inner world has not always been beautiful.
Maybe nobody knows what you have imagined.
Maybe you love Jesus—and still fight sexual thoughts.
Maybe you are married and sometimes notice someone other than your spouse is attractive, and the realization terrifies you.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from wondering whether every experience of sexual attraction means you have disappointed God.
Maybe pornography trained your mind for years to turn bodies into commodities, and even after repentance you sometimes feel the old pathways trying to wake up.
Maybe you have prayed...
cried...
deleted things...
installed filters...
confessed...
promised God you would never struggle again...
and then struggled again.
Hear this carefully.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
Jesus Himself “has been tempted in every way, just as we are—yet he did not sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
The existence of temptation therefore cannot itself equal sin, because Christ was truly tempted and remained completely without sin.
And recognizing that someone is attractive does not automatically mean you have committed the heart-adultery Jesus describes in Matthew 5.
But neither should that truth become permission to play games with desire.
There is a moment when noticing becomes nurturing.
When awareness becomes intention.
When attraction becomes possession in the imagination.
When you stop resisting the thought and start feeding it.
You know that moment.
It is the second look you wanted because the first was not enough.
The profile you searched for again.
The image you allowed yourself to enlarge.
The fantasy you deliberately rewound.
The conversation you kept emotionally charging because you liked how it made you feel.
The person you began imagining belonging to you sexually even though they did not.
Sometimes lust never touches skin.
It survives perfectly well inside imagination.
And Jesus loves us too much to pretend that what happens there does not matter.
But here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not expose the heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He exposes what is hidden because He came to save sinners all the way down.
Not merely our public behavior.
Our hearts.
This is the same Jesus who would go to the cross.
The same Jesus who knew exactly how corrupted human desire could become.
The same Jesus who knew every secret thought humanity would ever hide—and still stretched out His hands.
The Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself enough sexually, and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel is that sinners who could never cleanse themselves are called to repent and come to Christ, and in Him there is forgiveness, cleansing, reconciliation, and new life.
You do not defeat lust by pretending attraction does not exist.
You learn to bring your desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
You begin seeing people differently.
That woman is not a body placed in your path for consumption.
She bears the image of God.
That man is not a character for your private fantasy.
He bears the image of God.
That person on your screen has a history.
A family.
Pain.
Fears.
A soul.
An eternity.
And once you begin seeing people as Christ calls you to see them, lust starts losing one of its favorite weapons:
dehumanization.
Lust says, “What can I take from this person in my imagination?”
Love asks, “How can I honor this person before God?”
Lust reduces.
Love recognizes.
Lust consumes.
Love protects dignity.
Lust wants the body without responsibility for the soul.
Christ teaches us to see the whole person.
That does not mean attraction magically disappears.
Christian holiness is not becoming incapable of recognizing physical beauty.
It is learning what to do with desire when beauty awakens it.
You can notice beauty and refuse to worship it.
You can experience attraction and refuse to cultivate forbidden fantasy.
You can be tempted and run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
And sometimes the most holy prayer you can pray in that instant is remarkably simple:
“Jesus, that person is beautiful. They belong to You, not to my imagination. Teach me to see them with honor.”
Then move on.
No theatrical shame.
No self-hatred.
No pretending you didn't notice.
Just surrender.
Because shame often says, “Hide from God until you become clean.”
Grace says, “Run to Christ because you cannot make yourself clean.”
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that distinction tonight.
You have spent years believing every involuntary moment of attraction meant you were spiritually disgusting.
So every temptation became a courtroom.
Every attractive face became evidence against you.
Every bodily response became another reason to wonder whether God had finally become tired of you.
But conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Biblical conviction brings darkness into the light and calls us toward repentance and Christ.
Condemnation whispers that hiding is safer.
It isn't.
Jesus already knows.
He knew before you confessed it.
He knew before you clicked it.
He knew before you fantasized about it.
He knew before you failed again.
And the astonishing scandal of grace is not that Jesus discovered your darkness and reluctantly decided to tolerate you.
It is that the Son of God came knowing exactly what kind of sinners He was coming to rescue.
That does not make sin small.
It makes the cross enormous.
Grace is not permission to lust.
Grace teaches us that when we have lusted, failure does not have to become our permanent identity.
Repentance is still possible.
Forgiveness is still real.
Transformation is still possible.
Jesus is still Lord.
Maybe you crossed the line long ago.
Maybe this article stopped being theoretical several paragraphs back.
Maybe you know exactly what account you need to unfollow.
Exactly which conversation needs boundaries.
Exactly which secret folder needs to disappear.
Exactly which relationship needs honesty.
Exactly what you keep calling “harmless attraction” even though you know you have been deliberately feeding it.
Then don't waste conviction.
Bring it into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Where appropriate, seek trustworthy Christian accountability.
Remove the provision you keep making for temptation.
And when you stumble, do not turn repentance into self-punishment as though your misery could add something to the blood of Christ.
Come back to Jesus.
Again.
And again.
Not casually.
Not presumptuously.
But desperately believing that the Savior who commands holiness is also the Savior who gives mercy to repentant sinners.
Some battles are won dramatically.
Others are won quietly...
one surrendered glance at a time.
One closed tab.
One honest confession.
One deleted message.
One prayer whispered while nobody else knows there is a war happening.
One decision to remember:
That person is not mine to consume.
And perhaps that is the question beneath the question.
Not simply:
“Am I attracted?”
But:
“What am I doing with my attraction?”
Am I surrendering it?
Feeding it?
Protecting it?
Fantasizing?
Coveting?
Or allowing Jesus to teach my eyes, imagination, body, and heart how to love people without consuming them?
That is a much harder question.
But it can also become a doorway to freedom.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to give details publicly.
But you don't have to pretend either.
And if Christ has already been healing your mind, restoring your marriage, freeing you from pornography, or teaching you how to see people differently, tell someone what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Don't excuse lust.
And don't mistake temptation for abandonment by God.
Not because giving money makes anyone more saved.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces biblical generosity through your local church or other faithful Christian giving.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from a willing heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Come to Jesus.
Not after you conquer every sexual temptation.
Not after your thoughts become spotless.
Not after you prove yourself worthy.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Bring Him the attraction.
Bring Him the temptation.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the pornography history.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret nobody else knows.
Bring Him the part of your heart you wish you could erase.
Because Christianity is not the story of spotless people climbing high enough to reach a holy God.
It is the story of a holy Savior coming down to rescue sinners.
And maybe tonight the greatest victory will not be that you never felt temptation.
Maybe it will be that when temptation came...
you chose Jesus.
When shame said hide...
you chose Jesus.
When lust said consume...
you chose Jesus.
When failure said stay down...
you chose Jesus.
And when the enemy tried to make your worst chapter the title of your entire life...
Jesus picked up the pen.

Your temptation does not have to become your master, your failure does not have to become your identity, and your hidden chapter does not have to become your ending—because the hands holding the pen still bear the scars.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID NUMBERS 5 DESCRIBE AN ABORTION?
paragraphs:
DID NUMBERS 5 DESCRIBE AN ABORTION?
Why Christians Fiercely Disagree About This Passage—and Why One Difficult Hebrew Sentence Changes the Conversation
There is a passage in the Bible that can make Christians on opposite sides of a room reach for the same Bible…and walk away convinced they have read two completely different things.
Numbers 5:11–31.
One person reads it and says, “This is obviously an abortion.”
Another reads exactly the same passage and says, “Absolutely not.”
And somewhere between those two voices sits an uncomfortable question many believers would rather avoid:
What does the Hebrew actually say?
Not what a meme says.
Not what a political slogan says.
Not what somebody’s favorite preacher said.
Not even what we desperately need the passage to say so that an argument becomes easier.
What did Moses actually write?
Because if we really believe Scripture is the Word of God, then Christians should never be frightened by examining Scripture more closely.
Truth does not become weaker when you look at it.
So stay with me.

Because buried inside this disturbing ancient ritual is a Hebrew expression so difficult that respected Bible translations render it very differently—and understanding that difference may completely change the way you have heard Numbers 5 used.
The scene itself is uncomfortable.
A husband suspects his wife has been sexually unfaithful, but there are no witnesses and she has not been caught in the act.
Under Israel's covenant law, the matter is brought before the LORD.
The woman stands before the priest.

Holy water is placed in an earthen vessel. Dust from the floor of the tabernacle is placed into the water. The woman is placed under oath. The words of the curse are written down and washed into the water.
Then she drinks.
If she is innocent, the curse does not condemn her.
If she is guilty, judgment follows.
That much is relatively straightforward.
Then we reach the words that started the modern controversy.
Numbers 5:27 contains this Hebrew expression:
וְצָבְתָה בִטְנָהּ וְנָפְלָה יְרֵכָהּ
Wəṣāḇəṯāh ḇiṭnāh wənāp̄əlāh yərēḵāh.
Very woodenly, the wording is something like:
“Her belly will swell, and her thigh will fall.”
And immediately we have a problem.
That does not sound like ordinary English because the Hebrew itself is difficult.
The word בֶּטֶן — beten can refer to the belly, abdomen, or bodily interior.
The word יָרֵךְ — yarekh ordinarily means thigh, hip, or loin, although in certain contexts it can function euphemistically in connection with the reproductive region.
The verb connected with צבה — tsabah is especially difficult because its occurrence here is unusual.
And נפל — naphal ordinarily carries the basic idea of falling.
So translators have to make interpretive decisions.
That is why one Bible can sound startlingly different from another.
The ESV renders the curse in terms of the woman’s body swelling and her thigh falling away.
The NRSVue uses the language of the womb discharging and uterus dropping.
The NIV makes the interpretation much more explicit and speaks of the womb miscarrying.
That difference is not imaginary.
It is sitting right there in our English Bibles.
And this is exactly where Christians need intellectual humility.

The NIV’s “miscarry” is an interpretive rendering of a difficult Hebrew expression. It should not be treated as though the Hebrew text simply contains the ordinary equivalent of the English sentence, “God causes an abortion.”
It does not.
But the opposite mistake is also possible.
Christians should not pretend that reproductive loss is linguistically impossible simply because that interpretation makes us uncomfortable.

The Hebrew is difficult enough that interpreters have understood the physical judgment in different ways, including reproductive catastrophe, infertility, bodily wasting, genital injury, uterine prolapse, miscarriage, or some combination of these ideas.

Ancient Jewish interpretation also demonstrates that the passage was understood as describing supernatural bodily judgment associated with sexual guilt; it was not simply read as an ordinary medical recipe for terminating pregnancy.
And there is another enormous detail that frequently disappears from online arguments:
Numbers 5 never explicitly tells us that the woman is pregnant.
Read that again.
The accusation is adultery.
Pregnancy is not stated as the prerequisite for the ritual.
There is no command saying, “If a woman becomes pregnant through adultery, terminate the pregnancy.”
There is no identified unborn child in the narrative.
There is no stated gestational stage.
There is no recipe for an abortifacient.
There is holy water, sanctuary dust, an oath, written curses, a grain offering, priestly administration, and judgment explicitly attributed to the covenant curse.

In other words, whatever physical judgment Numbers 5 describes, the text presents its effectiveness as an act of divine judgment—not as a repeatable medical procedure whose natural ingredients reliably cause an abortion.
Dust and water are not presented as the biological mechanism.
God is Judge.
That distinction changes the question.

Because saying, “Numbers 5 may describe pregnancy loss as one possible consequence of divine judgment,” is not the same claim as saying, “Numbers 5 establishes abortion as an Israelite medical practice.”
Those sentences are not interchangeable.
Even if one accepts “miscarriage” as the correct interpretation of the disputed Hebrew, another question remains:
Was there necessarily a pregnancy to miscarry?
Verse 28 makes the issue even more interesting.
If the woman has not defiled herself, she is vindicated and the Hebrew says:
וְנִזְרְעָה זָרַע
Wənizrāʿā zāraʿ.
Literally, something close to:
“She shall be sown with seed.”
The expression points toward fertility—the ability to conceive.
That is one reason many interpreters understand the curse as involving the woman’s reproductive capacity.
But once again, reproductive judgment is not automatically identical to induced abortion.
That distinction is essential.
And yet there is something else Christians should not run away from.
This passage is disturbing.
It comes from an ancient patriarchal society.
A jealous husband initiates the process.
The accused wife undergoes the ordeal.
Modern readers naturally ask difficult questions about power, vulnerability, marriage, sexuality, and justice.
Those questions deserve more than a dismissive sentence.
But there is a detail easily missed when we read the passage only through modern eyes.
The husband does not get to execute his own private judgment.
Suspicion alone does not establish guilt.
He cannot simply declare her guilty because jealousy burns inside him.
The unresolved accusation is brought out of his hands and before the covenant court, ultimately before God.
And if the woman is innocent, the curse does not condemn her.
Her husband’s suspicion does not magically become truth.
That does not remove every difficulty modern readers experience with the passage.
It does, however, prevent us from reducing the ritual to “a husband gets to punish his wife.”
The text places judgment beyond his personal power.
And that should make every Christian stop before turning Numbers 5 into ammunition.
Because sometimes we approach Scripture already carrying the conclusion we want.
Then we search the Bible for sentences that can be recruited into our argument.
We do this with abortion.
We do it with sexuality.
We do it with money.
We do it with politics.
We do it with divorce.
We do it with judgment.
We do it with grace.
And if we are not careful, we stop allowing Scripture to examine us because we are too busy using Scripture to examine everybody else.
Jesus confronted that kind of religious heart.
People could become experts at finding another person’s sin while remaining strangely blind to their own.
That is why the deeper danger surrounding Numbers 5 is not merely mistranslating one Hebrew phrase.
It is approaching God's Word with a verdict already written.
Sometimes we want the Bible to agree with us more than we want Jesus to correct us.
That is a terrifying place for a disciple to live.
Because the Christian confession is not that Scripture belongs to our tribe.
We belong to Christ.
And Christ is not a mascot for an ideology.
He is Lord.
The same Jesus who spoke uncompromisingly about sin moved toward sinners with astonishing mercy.
The same Jesus who called people to repentance welcomed people religious society considered ruined.
The same Jesus who refused to redefine holiness also refused to treat broken human beings as disposable.
Then He went to a cross.
And there the argument becomes personal.
Because eventually every one of us discovers that we are not standing before God as the attorney.
We are standing before God as the accused.
Maybe your scandal was never public.
Maybe nobody discovered the messages.
Maybe nobody knows what happened in that hotel room.
Maybe your church thinks you are strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe the addiction is hidden behind deleted browser history.
Maybe the bitterness is hidden behind worship songs.
Maybe the affair ended years ago, but you still wake up remembering it.
Maybe you were the one betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you carry a decision from your past that nobody around you knows about.
Maybe the word “abortion” itself opens a room inside your heart that you have kept locked for years.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sin does not matter.
The Gospel is the announcement that sin mattered so much that Christ bore judgment to rescue sinners.
At the cross, holiness and mercy do not cancel one another.
They meet.
Jesus does not save us by pretending we are innocent.
He saves guilty people through His own righteousness, His sacrificial death, and His resurrection.
That is why Christianity has something infinitely greater to offer than another shouting match.
Repentance.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Redemption.
A new life.
You may have done something you cannot undo.
But you are not beyond the reach of the crucified and risen Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
Jesus can redeem what yesterday did to you.
That does not mean consequences disappear.
It does not mean wounds become imaginary.
It does not mean repentance becomes optional.
Grace is not God calling darkness light.
Grace is God entering our darkness and bringing sinners into His light.
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Peter knew scandal.
David knew scandal.
The Samaritan woman knew scandal.
The woman caught in adultery knew public shame.
Paul carried the memory of persecuting Christians.
The early church was not assembled from people who had spotless histories.
It was assembled around a spotless Savior.
And perhaps that is why this strange passage in Numbers can ultimately send Christians somewhere more important than an internet argument.
It can remind us that God sees what human beings cannot see.
He knows innocence when people accuse.
He knows guilt when people hide.
He cannot be manipulated by appearances.
And none of us survives His judgment by being better at accusing someone else.
We need mercy.
We need Christ.
So, did Numbers 5 describe an abortion?
The most responsible answer is more careful than either viral slogan.

The disputed Hebrew describes severe bodily and apparently reproductive judgment, but its precise physiological meaning is genuinely debated. Some modern translations understand it as miscarriage; others translate the language more literally or understand a different reproductive catastrophe. The passage never explicitly says the accused woman is pregnant, never commands abortion as a general practice, and presents the outcome as supernatural covenant judgment administered by God rather than as an ordinary human medical procedure.
Therefore Numbers 5 should not be casually flattened into “the Bible gives instructions for abortion.”
But Christians should be equally careful not to claim that miscarriage is an impossible translation of the disputed language.
Faithfulness does not require pretending ambiguity does not exist.
Faithfulness requires refusing to make Scripture say more—or less—than Scripture says.
And maybe somebody reading this needed more than an answer about Hebrew.
Maybe you needed permission to stop hiding.
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every secret.
Every compromise.
Every wound.
Every night you wish you could erase.
Every person you hurt.
Every person who hurt you.
Every prayer you were ashamed to pray.
And still the Gospel calls:
Come to Christ.
Not because your past is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop defending the thing that is destroying you.
Stop believing shame when it tells you that hiding is safer than surrender.
Bring the scandal into the light of Christ.
There is forgiveness at His cross.
There is cleansing in His blood.
There is resurrection beyond the grave.
There is a new name beyond the accusation.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can take one small step out of the darkness.
It is grace.

Numbers 5 is one of those passages people repeatedly encounter stripped of its language and context. Come back when the argument appears again, open the text yourself, and refuse to let slogans do your Bible reading for you.
Supporting Gospel-centered work matters too.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be bought.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And if this article accomplishes anything worthwhile, may it not merely leave you knowing more about an obscure Hebrew phrase.
May it leave you wanting to know Him.
Because someday the arguments will stop.
The comment sections will disappear.
The platforms will be forgotten.
And every one of us will stand before the God who knows exactly what happened when nobody else was watching.
On that day, your greatest hope will not be that you won the argument.
Your greatest hope will be Jesus.
Your scandal may explain where you have been—but when you surrender it to Christ, it does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “ASK AND YOU SHALL RECEIVE” — DID JESUS REALLY PROMISE TO GIVE US ANYTHING WE WANT?
paragraphs:
“ASK AND YOU SHALL RECEIVE” — DID JESUS REALLY PROMISE TO GIVE US ANYTHING WE WANT?
What if one of Jesus’ most comforting promises has also become one of the most painfully misunderstood—and what if the prayers God did not answer the way you wanted were never proof that He stopped listening?
“Ask, and it will be given to you.”
You have probably heard those words before.
Maybe you whispered them beside a hospital bed.
Maybe you held onto them while your marriage was falling apart.
Maybe you repeated them while staring at bills you could not pay.
Maybe you prayed them over a child who was walking away from God.
Maybe you asked for healing.
For reconciliation.
For a job.
For a spouse.
For a miracle.
For one more chance.
And maybe...
nothing happened the way you expected.
That is where this verse can begin to hurt.
Because if Jesus really meant, “Ask Me for anything you want, and I guarantee you will receive exactly what you requested,” then unanswered prayer leaves us with terrifying questions.
Did I not believe hard enough?
Was my faith too weak?
Did God ignore me?
Did I use the wrong words?
Was there some secret spiritual formula I failed to discover?
Or worse...
Did Jesus make a promise He did not keep?
Before you answer that question, stay with His actual words.
Because Jesus did make an astonishing promise about prayer.
But He never handed humanity a blank check for its desires.
And understanding the difference may rescue someone who has quietly begun to wonder whether God abandoned them.
In Matthew 7:7, the Greek text reads:
Αἰτεῖτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν· ζητεῖτε, καὶ εὑρήσετε· κρούετε, καὶ ἀνοιγήσεται ὑμῖν.
Aiteite, kai dothēsetai hymin; zēteite, kai heurēsete; krouete, kai anoigēsetai hymin.
“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”
Ask.
Seek.
Knock.
Those are breathtaking words.
But notice what Jesus does next.
He does not begin describing mansions, promotions, luxury, perfect health, effortless relationships, or every earthly desire becoming reality.
He talks about a Father.
“For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.”
Then Jesus brings the promise into the intimacy of a family.
Which father, He asks, would give his son a stone when the child asks for bread? Or give him a serpent when he asks for a fish?
Then comes the key:
“If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11)
There it is.
The promise is not that God becomes the servant of every human desire.
The promise is that those who belong to God are approaching a good Father.
And a good father does not prove his love by saying yes to everything his child requests.
Sometimes love gives.
Sometimes love withholds.
Sometimes love says, “Not yet.”
Sometimes love gives something different.
Sometimes love protects the child from the very thing the child is begging to receive.
If a five-year-old asks his father for the keys to the family car, the father does not demonstrate love by handing them over.
The child sees a refusal.
The father sees a funeral avoided.
And perhaps that is where some of us have misunderstood prayer.
We interpreted God’s “no” as absence.
We interpreted His delay as indifference.
We interpreted His silence as rejection.
We thought faith meant convincing God to endorse our plans.
Jesus teaches us something much deeper.
Prayer is not about dragging God into our will.
Prayer progressively draws us into His.
That becomes even clearer when Scripture interprets Scripture.
John writes:
The Greek phrase is:
κατὰ τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ
kata to thelēma autou
“according to His will.”
Those words matter.
Biblical prayer is not “according to whatever I happen to desire.”
It is prayer under the wisdom, goodness, sovereignty, and will of God.
James becomes even more uncomfortable.
“You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.” (James 4:3)
Read that slowly.
Scripture itself says people can ask and not receive because their motives are wrong.
So “ask and you shall receive” cannot honestly mean, “God has obligated Himself to give Christians anything they request.”
The Bible will not allow us to interpret it that way.
And neither will Jesus.
Because on the darkest night before the cross, Jesus Himself prayed a prayer that destroys the idea that faith means demanding our preferred outcome.
Gethsemane.
Jesus knew what was coming.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Scourging.
Nails.
The cross.
The bearing of sin.
And He prayed:
“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)
Do not rush past that.
The perfect Son prayed.
The perfect Son asked.
The perfect Son surrendered.
And the cup was not removed.
The Father’s refusal was not evidence that the Father did not love the Son.
The unanswered request became part of the greatest act of redemption in human history.
Had the cup passed...
there would be no Calvary.
No blood shed for sinners.
No atoning sacrifice.
No empty tomb following the cross.
No Gospel announcement that guilty people can be reconciled to God through Christ.
What looked like a prayer unanswered was woven into the answer humanity desperately needed.
And that should make us tremble before declaring that every unanswered prayer means insufficient faith.
Paul knew this pain too.
He pleaded with the Lord three times concerning what he called his “thorn in the flesh.”
He wanted it gone.
God did not remove it.
Instead, Christ answered:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)
Paul asked for removal.
Christ gave sustaining grace.
Was Paul rejected?
No.
He received something different from what he requested because Christ was accomplishing something deeper than immediate relief.
That distinction matters when someone is suffering.
Please do not walk into the room of a grieving mother and tell her that her child died because she did not have enough faith.
Do not tell the cancer patient that healing would be guaranteed if only they believed harder.
Do not tell the financially desperate believer that a particular donation will force God to multiply their money.
Do not turn prayer into a transaction.
And do not turn the Gospel into a vending machine where faith is the coin and God is required to dispense the product.
That is not Christianity.
The center of Christianity is not getting everything we want from God.
The center of Christianity is getting God through Jesus Christ—being reconciled to the Father by grace through the crucified and risen Son.
This changes prayer.
It does not make prayer weaker.
It makes prayer breathtakingly deeper.
Because Christianity does not teach us to stop asking boldly.
Jesus explicitly tells us to ask.
Bring Him the diagnosis.
Bring Him the unpaid bills.
Bring Him your marriage.
Bring Him the prodigal child.
Bring Him your loneliness.
Bring Him your desire for healing.
Bring Him the impossible situation.
Bring Him the dream.
Bring Him the fear you have never admitted publicly.
Bring Him everything.
Ask boldly.
Ask repeatedly.
Ask believing that God is able.
But trust Him enough to let Him remain God after you have asked.
That is the part we often do not want.
We want His power without His sovereignty.
His gifts without His wisdom.
His promises without His lordship.
We want Jesus to sign the bottom of plans we already wrote.
But sometimes the greatest transformation happens when prayer stops sounding like...
“God, make my will happen.”
...and starts sounding like...
“Father, here is what I desperately desire. You already know. I am asking You for it. But I trust Your wisdom more than my limited sight. Your will be done.”
That is not weak faith.
Look at Gethsemane.
That is Christ-shaped faith.
And perhaps someone reading this is angry with God right now.
You asked.
You cried.
You fasted.
You believed.
You waited.
And what you feared still happened.
You have smiled at church while privately carrying one question:
“Why didn’t You answer me?”
I will not insult your pain with an easy explanation.
Scripture does not promise that we will understand every providence in this life.
Some wounds remain mysteries.
Some graves still hurt.
Some doors stay closed.
Some prayers seem to disappear into years of silence.
Christian faith does not require us to pretend those things do not hurt.
Jesus Himself wept.
The Psalms are filled with believers crying, “How long?”
Biblical faith can lament.
Biblical faith can ask why.
Biblical faith can weep until there are no elegant sentences left.
But biblical faith refuses to measure the goodness of God solely by whether today's circumstances matched yesterday's request.
Because there is one place where the Christian ultimately measures the love of God.
The cross.
When your circumstances make you wonder whether God loves you, look again at Christ crucified.
The Gospel does not say God loved you because He gave you everything you requested.
The Gospel says:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
That is scandalous grace.
We were not negotiating from a position of innocence.
We were sinners in need of reconciliation.
And Christ came for us.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The ashamed can come out of hiding.
The rebellious can repent.
The broken can be restored.
The sinner who has spent years running can turn around and discover that the invitation of Christ is still real.
Maybe the greatest thing you need to ask God for today is not the thing you originally thought you needed.
Maybe it is mercy.
“God, forgive me.”
“Jesus, save me.”
“Change my heart.”
“Break what is destroying me.”
“Teach me to want what You want.”
“Give me strength to obey when obedience hurts.”
“Make Christ more precious to me than the answer I have been demanding.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because God may begin rewriting things you thought would never change.
Your pride.
Your secret sin.
Your bitterness.
Your appetite for approval.
Your resentment toward someone who wounded you.
Your obsession with controlling outcomes.
Your carefully protected image.
Grace does not merely improve the old story.
In Christ, grace begins writing a new one.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because Christians never suffer.
Not because every prayer receives the outcome we requested.
Not because following Jesus guarantees earthly comfort.
But because the crucified and risen Christ can take sinners with histories we wish we could erase and write redemption where shame thought it had written the final sentence.
So ask.
Ask God for healing.
Ask for provision.
Ask for restoration.
Ask Him to save your family.
Ask Him to open doors no human being can open.
Ask Him for wisdom.
Ask Him for courage.
Ask Him for daily bread.
Ask Him for deliverance.
But above everything else...
ask for Him.
And when His answer is yes, worship Him.
When His answer is no, cling to Him.
When His answer is wait, remain near Him.
When you cannot understand what He is doing, remember the cross.
Because the God who did not spare His own Son for our redemption has already shown us that His love cannot be measured merely by comfortable circumstances.
And if this exposed something you have secretly carried against God, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to know that silence is not always abandonment and delay is not always denial.

Not because every painful question can be solved by rereading a post, but because there may come a night when disappointment whispers that God has forgotten you. Return to the Scriptures. Return to Gethsemane. Return to the cross.
Someone may have been manipulated by teaching that promised health, wealth, or miracles if they could only produce enough faith.
Someone may be blaming themselves for a tragedy.
Someone may be one prayer away from turning back toward Jesus.
Not to embarrass them. Not to preach at them. Simply to remind them:
God is still worth seeking even when we cannot understand His answer.

We want this ministry to remain a place where people are not merely emotionally moved for a few minutes, but continually pointed toward Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, biblical truth, and transformed lives.
Supporting a ministry is not a payment for God's favor. We are saved by grace through faith in Christ, not by financially supporting a page.
Invite someone else to follow.

And keep asking, seeking, and knocking—not as a customer demanding that heaven fulfill an order, but as a child approaching a Father whose wisdom reaches farther than yours and whose goodness was written in blood at Calvary.
Maybe one day you will understand why God said no.
Maybe you will understand why He said wait.
Maybe in this life you never will.
But the deepest promise of prayer was never that you could control God.
It was that through Christ, you could come to Him.
And sometimes the miracle is not that God finally gives you the thing you were begging for.
Sometimes the miracle is that after everything you lost...
you discover that Jesus is still enough—and your unanswered prayer did not become the grave of your faith, but the place where grace began rewriting your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RAHAB WAS A PROSTITUTE IN JERICHO—YET HER NAME ENTERED THE LINE OF CHRIST
paragraphs:
RAHAB WAS A PROSTITUTE IN JERICHO—YET HER NAME ENTERED THE LINE OF CHRIST
The woman a city could have remembered by her scandal became the woman Scripture remembers by her faith—and generations later, her name appeared in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
There are names people whisper.
Names attached to mistakes.
Names followed by a story nobody lets you forget.
Names that enter a room before the person does.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe nobody calls you by your old sin anymore, but you can still hear the accusation in your own head.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Abused.
Promiscuous.
Drunk.
Liar.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Backslider.
Too dirty.
Too late.
Too far gone.
And sometimes the cruelest voice isn't coming from another person.
It is coming from inside you.
You can sit in church, sing about grace, hear sermons about forgiveness, and still secretly wonder whether Jesus really wants someone with your history.
Then you meet Rahab.
And suddenly the excuses begin to collapse.
Because Scripture does not introduce Rahab by hiding the uncomfortable part.
Joshua 2:1 describes her as אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishshah zonah — a woman who was a prostitute.
The Greek New Testament is equally direct.
Hebrews 11:31 calls her Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē — “Rahab the prostitute.”
James 2:25 uses the same identifying word, πόρνη (pornē).
The Bible does not airbrush her past.
But neither does God allow her past to have the final word.
And that difference is everything.
Rahab lived in Jericho.
Not outside the coming judgment.
Inside it.

Israel had crossed into the land, and Jericho stood in their path. Joshua sent two men to spy out the city. They entered Rahab's house, and soon the king of Jericho learned that Israelite spies had arrived.
Rahab was suddenly standing at a terrifying crossroads.
Protect the men of Israel and risk everything.
Or surrender them and remain aligned with the city in which she had built her life.
She hid them.
But what makes her story extraordinary is not merely that she hid two spies.
It is what came out of her mouth afterward.
She told them:
“I know that the LORD has given you the land.”
Then Rahab revealed something even deeper.
She had heard.
She had heard what the LORD had done at the Red Sea.
She had heard what had happened to the kings east of the Jordan.
Jericho had heard about Israel's God.
The city was terrified.
But Rahab did something with what she heard.
She believed.
And then she confessed:
“For the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
That confession appears in Joshua 2:11.
Do not race past it.
A Canaanite woman.
A prostitute.
A woman living inside a city facing divine judgment.
And from her mouth comes a confession recognizing the supremacy of the God of Israel.
This is where Rahab's story stops being merely ancient history and begins getting dangerously personal.
Because many people hear about God.
Fewer entrust themselves to Him.
Jericho heard.
Rahab responded.
That is the difference.
You can know Christian language and still never surrender.
You can own a Bible and still resist its Author.
You can know worship songs and still protect the sin destroying you.
You can sit beneath preaching for years while continually telling Jesus, “You can have everything except this.”
Rahab's faith moved.
Hebrews 11:31 later declares:
“By faith the prostitute Rahab did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.”
There it is.
Two words that destroy the lie that your past automatically disqualifies you from God's mercy:
By faith.
Not because Rahab had a spotless history.
Not because she came from the correct nation.
Not because her reputation was respectable.
Not because she could rewrite yesterday.
By faith.

James later points to Rahab when explaining that genuine faith is demonstrated through action. Her actions did not erase her history by human effort; they revealed that what she professed to believe had become real enough to affect what she did.
Faith had crossed the distance between her mouth and her life.
And somewhere, somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Because perhaps you have been saying you believe in Jesus while refusing to let that belief touch the locked rooms of your life.
Your secret messages.
Your bitterness.
Your hidden relationship.
Your pornography.
Your dishonesty.
Your pride.
Your resentment.
Your unforgiveness.
Your double life.
Your private compromise.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping us become more comfortable while remaining enslaved to the very things He came to save us from.
Jesus calls sinners to Himself.
And when sinners truly come to Christ, grace does not merely excuse us so that we can comfortably remain where He found us.
Grace begins changing us.
Repentance is not purchasing God's mercy with improved behavior.
It is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy we desperately need.
Rahab could not undo yesterday.
Neither can you.
But yesterday did not prevent her from believing God today.
Read that again.
Yesterday did not prevent her from believing God today.
The spies gave Rahab instructions concerning a scarlet cord.
The Hebrew of Joshua 2:18 calls it תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי — tiqvat chut hashani, referring to the cord/thread of scarlet.
She was to tie it in the window.
Her family was to gather inside the house.
When judgment came upon Jericho, that house was to be spared according to the oath made to her.
There is something visually unforgettable about the scene.
Jericho waiting.
Walls towering.
An army approaching.
And hanging from the window of one house...
scarlet.

Christians naturally feel the Gospel resonance of that image. Scarlet can remind us of blood, sacrifice, Passover, and ultimately Christ. But we should be careful not to claim more than Scripture itself claims: Joshua does not explicitly tell us that the scarlet cord was a prophetic symbol of Jesus' blood.
We do not need to force the text to make Rahab's story point toward Christ.
The Bible itself takes us there.
Because Jericho fell.
Rahab survived.
Joshua 6 tells us that Rahab, her father, her mother, her brothers, and those belonging to her household were brought out.
The woman living in a condemned city was delivered.
But God was not finished.
Rahab did not simply escape Jericho.
She became part of Israel's story.
And then Matthew opens his Gospel.
Generation after generation appears.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Names move toward David.
Then eventually toward Joseph and Mary.
Toward Bethlehem.
Toward Christ.
And buried inside that genealogy is a name nobody expecting a polished religious family tree would have chosen.
Matthew 1:5 says:
“Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab...”
Ῥαχάβ.
Rahab.
Stop there.
The prostitute of Jericho is named in the genealogy recorded by Matthew that leads to Jesus Christ.
Her former occupation did not become holy.
Her sin was not romanticized.
God did not call evil good.
Grace is far more beautiful than pretending sin never mattered.
Grace says sin matters so much that sinners need saving—and God's mercy is so astonishing that sinners who turn to Him do not have to remain imprisoned by what they were.
Rahab's story did not end at the window.
It did not end beneath Jericho's rubble.
It did not even end with her rescue.
Her name entered a family line that Matthew traces to Jesus.
And here is where the story reaches across thousands of years and finds you.
What name has your shame given you?
What chapter are you convinced ruined the whole book?
What did you do that you hope nobody discovers?
What happened to you that still makes you feel dirty even though you were the one wounded?
What season keeps replaying at two in the morning?
What would people think if they knew everything?
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not save imaginary sinners.
He saves real ones.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People who have lied.
People who have lusted.
People who have betrayed.
People who have been betrayed.
People who wasted years.
People who knew better.
People who walked away.
People who crawled back.
That does not mean every person automatically receives salvation simply because God is merciful.
The Gospel calls us to repent and believe.
Jesus Himself proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite.
It carries the idea of repentance, a turning of mind and direction toward God.
Not cosmetic Christianity.
Not adding “Jesus” to a biography while refusing His lordship.
Not using grace as permission to protect sin.
Come to Christ.
Turn.
Believe.
Confess.
Surrender.
Because Rahab's story is not ultimately a motivational slogan telling you that you are secretly amazing.
It is something infinitely better.
It is evidence that the mercy of God reaches people respectable religion might have written off.
And the center of that mercy is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend sin was harmless.
He bore sin.
The sinless Son of God died and rose again.
The Gospel announces forgiveness not because our rebellion is insignificant, but because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for those who belong to Him.
Your salvation is not found in becoming another Rahab.
Your salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
Rahab needed Him too.
Every person in Matthew's genealogy needed Him.
Abraham needed grace.
Judah needed grace.
David needed grace.
Rahab needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
The genealogy does not ultimately display the greatness of human bloodlines.
It leads us to Christ.
That is why the scandal cannot be the ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by changing God's definition of holiness so we can remain comfortable.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The Gospel says, “Your sin does not have to be your master.”
The Gospel does not say, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
And following Him means some things have to die.
Some relationships may need to end.
Some habits must be confessed.
Some secret doors need to close.
Some apologies need to be made.
Some bitterness must be surrendered.
Some hidden sins need to come into the light.
Some people need to stop negotiating with the very thing Christ is calling them to leave behind.
Maybe this article found you while you are still inside your Jericho.
Everybody around you has normalized what is killing you.
You know something needs to change.
You have felt conviction before.
But you keep telling yourself:
Tomorrow.
When I'm stronger.
When life settles down.
When I stop struggling.
When I become worthy enough to come back to God.
No.
You do not clean yourself sufficiently enough to earn permission to approach the Savior.
You come because you need the Savior.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Come with the ruins.
Come with the confession.
Come with the history you cannot change.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe your prayer tonight is not eloquent.
Maybe it is only:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
He already knows the uncensored version of your story.
You are not informing Him when you confess.
You are finally agreeing with Him about what you have tried to hide.
And perhaps that is where your Jericho begins to fall.
Somebody reading quietly may need evidence that Jesus is still restoring lives.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not as a performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
There may be a night when the old accusations return and you need to remember the prostitute from Jericho whose name appears in Matthew's genealogy.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider staying close to this ministry.
Jesus alone saves.
But Christian ministry requires people willing to carry biblical truth farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend struggling secretly.
Invite the lukewarm believer who needs awakening.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Let them come close enough to hear the Gospel.
Rahab once looked out of a window in a city awaiting judgment.
A scarlet cord hung there.
Behind that window was a woman with a past.
Ahead of her was a future she could never have written for herself.
Centuries later, Matthew wrote her name.
Not because prostitution was beautiful.
Not because sin did not matter.
But because God's grace had entered her story.
And eventually the genealogy moved beyond Rahab.
Beyond Boaz.
Beyond David.
Generation after generation...
until Matthew brought us to Jesus.
That is the name your story ultimately needs.
Jesus.
Not self-improvement.
Not reputation management.
Not pretending.
Jesus Christ.
So when shame tells you, “Look at what you were,” remember Rahab.
When Satan tempts you to believe repentance is pointless because you have gone too far, remember Rahab.
When religious pride tempts you to look at another broken person and decide God could never use someone like that, remember Rahab.
And when your own past begins demanding the right to write your final chapter, take the pen out of shame's hand and run to Christ.
Because the most astonishing thing about Rahab is not simply that a prostitute appears in a genealogy.
It is where that genealogy leads.
To Jesus.
And maybe that is what your life needs more than anything else.
Not a cleaner past.
A redeemed future in Christ.
Your worst chapter may explain where you have been—but only Jesus has the authority to decide what grace can make of a surrendered life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: One Day Your Children Will Remember What Made You Put the Phone Down
paragraphs:
One Day Your Children Will Remember What Made You Put the Phone Down
They may forget the toys you bought, the places you took them, and a thousand ordinary afternoons. But they may remember what repeatedly received your eyes when they were standing right in front of you.
One day, there may be an empty chair where your child used to sit.
Not because something terrible happened.
Because childhood did what childhood always does.
It left.

The little shoes disappeared from the doorway. The toys stopped appearing under the couch. The voice calling “Mom!” or “Dad!” from another room changed. The child who once climbed into your lap eventually became too big for it.
And somewhere inside that grown son or daughter will live a collection of memories you cannot edit.
That is the frightening thing about memory.
You rarely know when you are making one.
Maybe your child will remember Saturday pancakes.
Maybe the way you prayed beside the bed.
Maybe the ridiculous voices you used while reading stories.
Maybe the nights you stayed awake when fever made sleep impossible.
Maybe the hugs after failure.
Maybe the apologies after arguments.
Maybe the sound of you worshiping when you thought nobody was listening.
But there is another possibility worth considering.
They may remember the phone.
Not the model.
Not the apps.
Not what you were looking at.
They may simply remember how often they had to compete with it for your eyes.
“Daddy, look.”
“One second.”
“Mommy, watch this.”
“Hold on.”
“Can I tell you something?”
“Just a minute.”
And sometimes that minute became five.
Sometimes five became twenty.
Sometimes the story was never told.
Nothing dramatic happened.
Nobody screamed.
Nobody abandoned anybody.
You were physically there.
That is what makes this kind of absence so difficult to recognize.
You were there.
Just somewhere else.

And before this becomes another guilt-soaked attack on parents who are already exhausted, overwhelmed, working, serving, cooking, cleaning, paying bills, answering necessary messages, managing businesses, caring for relatives, and trying desperately to hold life together, hear this carefully:
The phone is not the villain.
Technology is not automatically sinful.
Work is not sinful.
Answering a message is not sinful.
Taking a moment for yourself is not sinful.
And faithful parenting does not mean staring lovingly into your children's eyes every waking second.
The deeper question is not whether you own a phone.
The question is whether anything has quietly trained your attention away from the people God entrusted to you.
Because attention communicates value.
Again and again, without words, our habits tell the people around us:
“This matters right now.”
And Scripture has something piercing to say about the way Christians handle the moments placed into their hands.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:15–16:
The Greek is worth seeing:
“Βλέπετε οὖν ἀκριβῶς πῶς περιπατεῖτε, μὴ ὡς ἄσοφοι ἀλλ’ ὡς σοφοί, ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν, ὅτι αἱ ἡμέραι πονηραί εἰσιν.”
Paul was not writing about smartphones.
We should never pretend he was.
He was calling believers to careful, wise Christian living in a fallen age.
But that command reaches directly into the way we steward our lives now.
Look carefully at how you walk.
Not carelessly.
Not foolishly.
Wisely.
And then comes this extraordinary expression:
“ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν.”
Exagorazomenoi ton kairon.
The idea carries the sense of buying up, seizing, or making full use of the opportunity.
Kairos is especially important.
Paul is not merely telling Christians to become productivity machines who squeeze another seventeen tasks into Tuesday.
He is talking about opportunity.
The moment placed before you.
The opportunity that can be used wisely or allowed to pass.
And parent...
some opportunities do not come back.
Your daughter will not always ask you to sit beside her.
Your son will not always think showing you his drawing is the most important event of the afternoon.
They will not always want to tell you every detail about something that, to an adult, seems painfully unimportant.
They will not always ask you to watch them jump.
Again.
And again.
And again.
They will not always believe you can fix everything.
They will not always reach automatically for your hand.
One day you may reach for theirs...
and realize how long it has been since they reached first.
That is why distracted parenting is not merely a conversation about screens.
It is a conversation about kairos.
Opportunity.
The tiny windows that look ordinary while they are open and priceless after they close.
Imagine a little boy standing beside his father.
He has constructed something magnificent out of plastic blocks.
To everybody else, it is crooked.
Half the pieces do not match.
One tower appears structurally incapable of surviving another thirty seconds.
But to him?
It is a kingdom.
And he wants one person in the universe to see it.
“Dad, look.”
His father is holding a phone.
“Hang on.”
The boy waits.
“Dad.”
“One second, buddy.”
The father is not looking at pornography.
He is not gambling.
He is not committing some scandalous public sin.
Maybe he is reading the news.
Maybe answering work.
Maybe watching something harmless.
Maybe even reading Christian content.
The boy eventually walks away.
His father finishes what he was doing.
Nothing catastrophic happens.
Except...
the kingdom was demolished before Dad ever saw it.
That moment will probably never appear in a testimony.
Nobody will mention it at church.
There will be no family intervention.
But multiply that moment.
Three times a week.
Five times.
Ten.
For years.
Now reverse the scene.
“Dad, look.”
The phone goes facedown.
Dad looks up.
Not because plastic blocks are important.
Because the boy is.
That tiny movement may preach something to a child's heart before the child has words for theology:
You are worth my attention.
And suddenly putting down a phone can become something larger than digital discipline.
It can become love made visible.
This is where the Gospel must enter the conversation, because Christianity cannot end with “Try harder and become a better parent.”
If that is all we say, exhausted parents will leave carrying another stone.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve our parenting techniques.
He came to save sinners.
Maybe this article hurts because you already know.
You remember the little voice saying your name while you kept scrolling.
You remember snapping, “Not now.”
You remember sitting beside your family while mentally living somewhere else.
Maybe your screen-time report embarrassed you.
Maybe you have told your children, “Get off that thing,” while your own hand automatically reaches for yours every few minutes.
Maybe conviction is arriving right now.
Do not run from it.
But do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Conviction says, “Bring this into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Hide because you have already ruined everything.”
The Gospel says something far more beautiful.
Come to Christ.
There is grace here.
Real grace.
Not grace that pretends wasted moments were not wasted.
Not grace that calls distraction harmless.
Grace that tells the truth and still opens the door home.
Jesus Christ receives sinners who repent.
He forgives.
He restores.
He changes us.
