At the cross, we discover that our deepest problem is larger than technology.
The human heart is endlessly capable of turning toward created things instead of the Creator.
We can make idols out of approval.
Work.
Entertainment.
Achievement.
Comfort.
Even ministry.
And yes, sometimes a glowing rectangle can expose what already lives inside us: restlessness, escapism, comparison, loneliness, pride, boredom, or the desperate need to feel noticed.
But Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could merely exchange one behavioral addiction for a cleaner-looking life.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
He gives us something infinitely better than a digital detox.
He gives us Himself.
And when Christ becomes our treasure, repentance stops being merely “I need to use my phone less.”
It becomes:
“Jesus, teach me to love what You have given me.”
“Teach me to see people again.”
“Teach me to be present.”
“Teach me to recognize the opportunities I keep calling interruptions.”
Perhaps your child interrupting you is sometimes exactly that—an interruption.
Children need boundaries too.
Parents have responsibilities.
There are calls that must be answered, deadlines that must be met, and moments when “not now” is completely appropriate.
Biblical wisdom is not simplistic.
But perhaps there are also times when what you call an interruption is actually kairos.
An opportunity.
A little human being asking:
“Am I worth stopping for?”
Parents, we will fail here.
That needs to be said.
You will miss moments.
I will miss moments.
There is no flawless father except our Father in heaven.
There is no flawless mother.
There is no perfectly attentive Christian household.
Your children do not need the performance of perfection.
Sometimes one of the most powerful things they can witness is repentance.
Imagine looking your child in the eyes and saying:
“I haven't been listening well lately. I've been distracted. You matter more than I have made you feel. Will you forgive me?”
Do you realize what that teaches?
It teaches them that Christians repent.
It teaches them that authority does not eliminate humility.
It teaches them that saying “I'm sorry” is not weakness.
It teaches them that the Gospel is not something Mom and Dad merely talk about on Sunday.
Grace lives in the house.
Maybe that is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because failure becomes beautiful.
But because Jesus can enter failure and write something failure could never write by itself.
Redemption.
The parent who was distracted can become present.
The parent who was harsh can learn gentleness.
The parent who wasted years cannot retrieve yesterday...
but can surrender today.
And perhaps that is one of the most important truths in this entire article:
You cannot redeem yesterday by staring at it.
But you can surrender today to Christ.
The enemy would love for conviction about your past to consume the very present you still possess.
Don't give him another afternoon.
Put the phone down when wisdom says to put it down.
Look across the room.
There they are.
Maybe your toddler is making a disaster.
Maybe your teenager barely talks anymore.
Maybe your adult child has become distant.
Maybe your relationship is already wounded.
Start where you are.
Listen.
Ask questions.
Pray.
Apologize.
Play.
Sit at the table.
Open Scripture together.
Take the walk.
Make the call.
And when they speak, sometimes give them something increasingly rare in this distracted world:
your undivided eyes.
Because one day your children will remember what made you put the phone down.
Was it a notification that seemed more important?
Your boss?
Breaking news?
A celebrity?
A sale?
A battery warning?
Or did you put it down...
because they walked into the room?
There is something haunting about realizing that we carefully photograph childhood while sometimes failing to inhabit it.
Thousands of pictures.
Hundreds of videos.
Clouds filled with memories.
But were we there when they happened?
Perhaps we have become so determined to preserve moments that we sometimes forget to live them.
Take the photograph.
Absolutely.
Then maybe put the phone away.
Look with your own eyes.
Listen with your own ears.
Let the memory belong first to your heart.
Because your child does not primarily need documentation that you loved them.
They need to experience your love.
And if this is exposing something hidden in you, don't defend yourself.
Bring it to Jesus.
There is no need to pretend.
Christ already knows.
And He is still calling you closer.
Not because saving a post changes a family.
It doesn't.
ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν.
Make the most of the opportunity.
Not as a badge announcing that you are a wonderful parent.
But it can be a tangible way to help Gospel Warrior keep creating and distributing Christ-centered resources.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually numb.
Invite the parent quietly carrying regret.
Invite the person who does not yet know Jesus.
Because ultimately this was never merely an article about phones.
It is about what has our attention.
And beneath that is an even deeper question:
What has our heart?
Your children will grow.
The toys will disappear.
The bedrooms will change.
The little hands will become adult hands.
And one day you may sit across a table from the person who used to beg you to watch them jump from the third stair.
You will look at that grown face and realize something simultaneously heartbreaking and beautiful:
The ordinary days were the days.
The interruptions were part of the gift.
The minutes were the treasure.
The opportunity was standing right in front of you.
So when the little voice calls tonight...
when your teenager unexpectedly starts talking...
when your spouse begins telling you something you have heard before...
when somebody you love walks into the room...
remember Paul's words.
Walk carefully.
Walk wisely.
Buy up the opportunity.
Because the days pass.
Childhood passes.
Life passes.
But because of Jesus Christ, your failures do not have to write the final sentence.
Repentance can begin tonight.
Grace can enter the room tonight.
The phone can go facedown tonight.
Your eyes can come back up tonight.
And perhaps years from now, when your children remember what made you put the phone down, they will remember something beautifully ordinary:
It was them.
And maybe, through a thousand small acts of presence, they will have seen something even greater—that Mom or Dad kept learning to look up because Jesus Christ had captured their heart.
You cannot hold childhood still—but by the grace of Christ, you can still be present while it is passing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON KILLED 1,000 MEN WITH A DONKEY’S JAWBONE—BUT THE MOST DANGEROUS ENEMY WAS STILL INSIDE HIM
paragraphs: SAMSON KILLED 1,000 MEN WITH A DONKEY’S JAWBONE—BUT THE MOST DANGEROUS ENEMY WAS STILL INSIDE HIM

He walked away from a battlefield covered with a thousand fallen enemies. Yet the story of Samson reveals something terrifying: you can defeat what is standing against you while remaining vulnerable to what is living inside you.
There are Bible stories we have heard so many times that we stop feeling how shocking they actually are.
Samson and the jawbone of a donkey is one of them.
We picture the strong man. The impossible weapon. The overwhelming enemy. The astonishing victory.
One man.
One jawbone.
One thousand Philistines.
But slow the scene down.
Because Judges 15 is not a superhero movie.

It is the story of a deeply complicated man living in a deeply broken generation, empowered by the Spirit of God for a divine purpose while repeatedly displaying impulses that would eventually contribute to his destruction.
And somewhere inside Samson’s scandalous story is a warning for every person who has ever mistaken spiritual usefulness for spiritual health.
You can be gifted and still be wounded.
You can experience victory and still have dangerous appetites.
You can be used by God and still desperately need God.
You can defeat a thousand enemies in public...
and still lose battles nobody sees.
That is why Samson’s story matters.
And that is why you should not rush past the jawbone.

The moment begins after Samson has been bound and delivered into the hands of the Philistines. His own countrymen from Judah have tied him with new ropes because they fear the Philistines ruling over them.
Imagine that humiliation.
The man appointed to begin delivering Israel is handed over by Israelites themselves.
Then the Philistines see him.
They come shouting.
The ropes are around his arms.
The enemy believes the fight is already over.
And then Scripture says something far more important than the size of Samson’s muscles.
Judges 15:14 says:
“The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him.”
The Hebrew expression is:
וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה
Vattitzlach alav Ruach YHWH.
The verb commonly transliterated tsalach carries the sense here of rushing upon, coming powerfully upon, or empowering.
That changes the entire scene.
The theological center of the story is not:
“Look how strong Samson was.”
It is:
Look what happened when the Spirit of the LORD empowered the deliverer God had chosen.
The ropes on Samson’s arms become like burned flax. His restraints fall away.
Then he sees something lying nearby.
Not a sword.
Not a spear.
Not military armor.
Not the weapon anyone would choose before confronting an army.
A donkey’s jawbone.
Judges 15:15 records:
וַיִּמְצָא לְחִי־חֲמוֹר טְרִיָּה וַיִּשְׁלַח יָדוֹ וַיִּקָּחֶהָ וַיַּךְ־בָּהּ אֶלֶף אִישׁ
Vayyimtsa lechi-chamor teriyyah, vayyishlach yado vayyiqqacheha, vayyakh-bah elef ish.
In context:
“He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it, and struck down a thousand men with it.”
A thousand men.
With the jawbone of a donkey.
And Samson celebrates the victory with Hebrew wordplay preserved in Judges 15:16:

בִּלְחִי הַחֲמוֹר חֲמוֹר חֲמֹרָתָיִם
בִּלְחִי הַחֲמוֹר הִכֵּיתִי אֶלֶף אִישׁ
The line plays on the similar sounds of chamor, “donkey,” and chamor/chamorathayim, language associated with heaps or piled heaps.
English translations render the wordplay somewhat differently because its sound and force cannot be reproduced perfectly in English.
The basic sense is unmistakable:
“With the jawbone of a donkey... I have struck down a thousand men.”
It is brutal.
It is astonishing.
And it is easy to make Samson the hero.
But Judges refuses to give us such a simple character.
Samson is a deliverer, yes.
He was set apart from the womb.
God truly empowered him.
God truly used him against the Philistines.
But Samson is not Jesus.
That distinction matters enormously.
Samson is morally complicated.
Impulsive.
Often driven by personal desire.
Capable of tremendous acts under divine empowerment while simultaneously demonstrating catastrophic weaknesses of character.
And perhaps that is why his story gets uncomfortably close to us.
Because some of us know what it is like to look strong while something inside us is starving.
People see your victories.
God sees your thirst.
People see the ministry.
God sees the secret.
People see the marriage photos.
God sees the distance between you.
People see the Bible verses you post.
God sees what you search for when nobody is watching.
People hear you say, “God is good.”
God hears the thoughts you are afraid to say out loud.
People see someone who survived.
God sees someone exhausted from surviving.
And perhaps you have become incredibly skilled at killing the enemies everyone can see while feeding the enemy nobody can see.
Samson could stand against an army.
But Samson struggled to govern Samson.
Read that again.
A man powerful enough to leave a thousand enemies defeated could still be endangered by his own desires.
That should humble every Christian with a platform.
Every pastor.
Every leader.
Every parent.
Every husband.
Every wife.
Every worshiper.
Every person who knows how to look spiritually strong.
Giftedness is not the same thing as godliness.
A spiritual experience is not permission to stop pursuing holiness.
Yesterday’s victory does not make today’s temptation harmless.
And being used by God does not mean there are no areas of your life that desperately need repentance.
But something happens immediately after Samson’s astonishing victory that exposes another side of him.
He becomes desperately thirsty.
The warrior who just defeated a thousand men suddenly realizes he cannot even provide himself with water.
That detail is breathtaking.
Samson cries to the LORD in Judges 15:18:
“You have given your servant this great victory. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?”
There it is.
The strong man is thirsty.
The victorious man is desperate.
The man who just held a jawbone now has to pray.
And perhaps that is one of the most important images in Samson’s entire story.
Because eventually every strong person discovers something.
There are needs strength cannot satisfy.
There are wounds success cannot heal.
There are sins discipline alone cannot erase.
There is guilt achievement cannot silence.
There is a thirst this world cannot quench.
You can win the promotion and still be thirsty.
Build the business and still be thirsty.
Grow the platform and still be thirsty.
Get married and still be thirsty.
Become admired and still be thirsty.
Have thousands of followers and still go to bed feeling completely unknown.
You can even serve in church...
and still be thirsty.
The answer is not another jawbone.
The answer is not another victory.
The answer is not becoming more impressive.
You need living water.
And this is where Samson’s story begins pointing beyond Samson.
Centuries later, another Deliverer would come.
But He would be nothing like Samson.
Samson repeatedly moved through cycles of retaliation.
Jesus Christ willingly absorbed violence and injustice and went to the cross.
Samson killed his enemies.
Jesus prayed for His executioners.
Samson needed deliverance himself.
Jesus is the sinless Deliverer.
Samson stretched out his arms and brought death to his enemies.
Jesus stretched out His arms on a cross and willingly gave His life so His enemies could become His family.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel does not announce that good people can improve themselves enough for God.
The Gospel announces that sinners who could never rescue themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
We have sinned.
Not merely “made mistakes.”
Sinned.
We have loved things God hates.
Hidden things.
Excused things.
Worshiped ourselves.
Used people.
Fed pride.
Carried bitterness.
Entertained lust.
Clung to unforgiveness.
Pretended.
And no amount of religious performance can erase our guilt.
But Jesus came.
The eternal Son of God entered our brokenness, lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose again.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Sin is not treated as insignificant.
It is so serious that Christ bears its judgment.
Yet sinners are not declared unreachable.
Grace reaches them through Christ.
That means your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your life.
Your worst night does not have to own your eternity.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your pornography does not get the last word.
Your adultery does not get the last word.
Your bitterness does not get the last word.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your failure does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
But grace is not permission to continue comfortably in rebellion.
Grace calls us out of hiding.
Jesus does not merely forgive us so we can remain chained to the things destroying us.
He calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, and walk in newness of life.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with good behavior.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior because God’s grace has confronted us with the truth.
And maybe this is where the story stopped being about Samson.
Maybe it became about you.
What is your jawbone?
What is the visible victory you keep pointing toward because you do not want anyone examining the invisible battle?
What have you conquered publicly while secretly refusing to surrender privately?
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
But you are thirsty.
Maybe everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
But you know something is dying.
Maybe people call you faithful.
But your private browser history tells another story.
Maybe you sing worship songs with tears in your eyes while carrying resentment you refuse to release.
Maybe you preach grace to everybody except yourself.
Maybe you have spent years running from God because you believe what you did was simply too ugly.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to become a better Samson.
The answer is Jesus.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Stop negotiating with the thing crucifying your intimacy with God.
Stop protecting the secret that is poisoning you.
You do not need another performance.
You need surrender.
Be honest.
And believers reading those words—do not attack the wounded.
Pray.
Encourage.
Point people toward Jesus.
Let the comment section become something rarer than another internet argument.
Let it become a place where people remember they are not the only ones fighting.
Because somebody reading this tonight may be one prayer away from finally admitting, “I need help.”
Somebody may need your testimony.
Somebody may need to know Christ is still restoring people.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And please understand something else.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not a transaction with a ministry.
But if Christ has given you truth worth proclaiming, you can use what God has placed in your hands to point someone else toward Him.
It can carry the Gospel into the feed of someone who would never walk into a church.
Send it privately to the person you know is struggling.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about pretending to have everything together.
Scripture never gives us permission to make such claims.
But voluntary generosity, Gospel partnership, sharing biblical truth, and helping sound Christian resources reach others can genuinely be ways believers choose to glorify God.
Your support helps this kind of Christ-centered content continue reaching people who are scrolling through pain, temptation, doubt, loneliness, shame, and spiritual exhaustion.
Not as spiritual advertising.
As an invitation.
Because somewhere in your circle is a Samson.
Strong enough to fool everybody.
Successful enough to hide behind victories.
Smiling in photographs.
Functioning at work.
Showing up at church.
Answering, “I’m fine.”
And dying of thirst.
You may never know what God does with one article you were willing to share.
You may never know who reads it at 2:13 in the morning.
Who finally confesses.
Who finally calls someone for help.
Who opens a Bible again.
Who returns to church.
Who forgives.
Who repents.
Who falls to their knees.
Who realizes that Christianity was never about proving how strong they were.
It was about discovering how desperately they needed Christ.
Samson held the jawbone.
But the power was never ultimately in the jawbone.
And the deepest hope of Scripture was never Samson.
It was always moving toward Someone greater.
Jesus Christ.
The Deliverer who does not merely rescue us from enemies around us, but addresses the sin within us.
The Savior who knows every hidden chapter and still calls sinners to repentance.
The King who does not excuse our darkness but enters it with truth and grace.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Lord who rose.
The Christ who still saves.
So put down the performance.
Bring Him the thirst.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the appetite you cannot control.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the exhausted faith.
Bring Him the version of you nobody else knows exists.
And repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
Because the greatest miracle in Samson’s story was never meant to teach us that human beings can become strong enough to defeat everything.
It reminds us how desperately even the strongest among us need the power and mercy of God.
A thousand enemies may fall around you, but if your heart remains unsurrendered, the battle is not over.
And here is the line I hope follows you long after you close this article:
The strongest man in the room may still be the thirstiest soul in the room—and Jesus is still calling the thirsty to come to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MOSES MET HIS WIFE AFTER HE STOOD UP FOR WOMEN BEING DRIVEN AWAY AT A WELL
paragraphs:
MOSES MET HIS WIFE AFTER HE STOOD UP FOR WOMEN BEING DRIVEN AWAY AT A WELL
He arrived in Midian as a fugitive with a shattered past. He had no throne, no reputation, and no idea that an ordinary act of courage beside a desert well was about to become part of the story God would use to rebuild his life.
There are moments when your entire life seems to collapse so quickly that you cannot imagine God could possibly be writing anything beautiful with what remains.
Moses knew that feeling.
Before there was a burning bush…
before Pharaoh heard the words, “Let My people go”…
before the Red Sea opened…
before Sinai trembled…
before Moses became one of the most recognizable figures in Scripture…
there was a frightened man sitting alone beside a well.
And that detail matters.
Because Exodus does not introduce Moses to Zipporah while Moses is powerful.
It introduces them while Moses is displaced.
He had gone from the palace of Egypt to the wilderness of Midian.
From privilege to exile.
From being somebody in Egypt to being a stranger in somebody else’s land.
And he got there carrying a scandal.
Moses had seen an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. He looked around, killed the Egyptian, and hid the body in the sand. When Pharaoh learned what happened, he sought to kill Moses.
So Moses fled.
That is where Exodus 2 takes us.
Not to a victorious Moses.
Not yet.
To a fugitive.
“Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to slay Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian: and he sat down by a well.”
Exodus 2:15.
Read those final words again.
“He sat down by a well.”
He could not have known what was coming.
Maybe you understand that kind of place.
You made decisions you wish you could reverse.
Something collapsed.
A relationship ended.
Your reputation changed.
You lost something.
You ran from something.
Maybe nobody knows the whole story except you and God.
And now you are sitting emotionally in your own Midian wondering whether the most meaningful chapters of your life are already behind you.
But Moses did not know something.
The well where he sat exhausted was not the end of his story.
God was not finished.
Then seven women approached.
Scripture says they were daughters of the priest of Midian. They came to draw water and fill the troughs for their father’s flock.
Then the shepherds arrived.
And the Hebrew text gives us a detail worth slowing down for.
Exodus 2:17 says:
וַיָּבֹאוּ הָרֹעִים וַיְגָרְשׁוּם
Vayyavo’u haro‘im vaygareshum.
In context:
“The shepherds came and drove them away.”
That word translated “drove them away” comes from the Hebrew root גָּרַשׁ — garash — carrying the sense of driving out, expelling, or forcing away.
So describing the women as being harassed at the well captures the hostile character of the scene, but the precise biblical wording is even more concrete:
The shepherds drove them away.
Imagine the frustration.
The women had done the work.
They had drawn the water.
They had filled the troughs.
Then other shepherds came and pushed them away.
We are not told every detail of the confrontation, so we should not invent what Scripture does not reveal.
But Scripture tells us enough.
They were being wrongfully driven from the water they had prepared.
And Moses saw it.
Here is what is remarkable.
Moses was already carrying his own problems.
He was homeless.
He was displaced.
Pharaoh wanted him dead.
He had no visible future.
Nobody would have blamed him for thinking:
I have enough problems of my own.
But something happened when Moses watched vulnerable people being mistreated.
He stood up.
The Hebrew continues:
וַיָּקָם מֹשֶׁה וַיּוֹשִׁעָן
Vayyaqam Moshe vayoshi‘an.
“Moses rose up and helped them…”
The verb behind “helped” is especially striking.
וַיּוֹשִׁעָן — vayoshi‘an — comes from the Hebrew root יָשַׁע (yasha‘), associated with saving, delivering, or rescuing.
Moses rose.
Moses intervened.
Moses delivered them from the situation.
And then he did something wonderfully practical.
He watered their flock.
That matters.
Biblical compassion does not merely feel sorry.
It moves.
Moses did not know these women.
They could not advance his career.
He had no career.
He was not performing for an audience.
There was no crowd applauding.
No Israelite nation knew his name as deliverer yet.
No one was recording the moment for his reputation.
A broken man simply saw people being mistreated…
and stood up.
That should confront something in us.
Character is often revealed when doing the right thing offers us absolutely nothing in return.
Would you still defend someone if nobody knew?
Would you still help someone if there were no photograph?
Would you still show kindness if there were no applause?
Would you still speak when remaining silent would be easier?
Would you still serve when nobody could repay you?
Moses could not have known that the women walking toward that well were connected to the household that would become his home.
When they returned unusually early, their father asked:
“Why is it that ye are come so soon to day?”
Their answer was simple:
“An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and also drew water enough for us, and watered the flock.”
They did not even know the whole story of the man who had helped them.
To them, he appeared to be an Egyptian.
They did not know about the body in the sand.
They did not know Pharaoh wanted him dead.
They did not know he was running.
They did not know that the stranger beside the well had a history complicated enough to make many people uncomfortable.
They simply knew what he had done in front of them.
He helped.
Their father responded:
“And where is he? why is it that ye have left the man? call him, that he may eat bread.”
What a sentence.
Moses had fled Egypt.
Now someone was saying:
Call him.
Bring him inside.
Feed him.
There is something profoundly human about that transition.
One moment Moses is a fugitive sitting beside a well.
Soon he is sitting at a table.
Exodus continues:
“And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter. And she bare him a son, and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land.”
Exodus 2:21–22.
This is where Zipporah enters Moses’ life.
Not at Pharaoh’s palace.
Not during Moses’ years of prestige.
Not after Moses had become Israel’s great leader.
She enters his story in Midian.
In exile.
In obscurity.
After failure.
After flight.
After scandal.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to understand what that means without turning the passage into a promise Scripture never makes.
The lesson is not that if you defend somebody at a well, God owes you a spouse.
The Bible does not teach that.
The lesson is deeper.
Your worst chapter does not place you beyond the reach of God’s providence.
Moses’ sin had consequences.
His exile was real.
His loneliness was real.
God did not pretend the past had never happened.
Yet Moses’ failure was not powerful enough to prevent God from continuing His purposes.
That is where this ancient story begins reaching directly into our lives.
Some people believe their usefulness to God ended when everybody discovered what they did.
Others believe it ended when the marriage failed.
When the addiction returned.
When they lost control.
When they compromised.
When they became ashamed of themselves.
When they ran.
When their carefully constructed image collapsed.
And Christianity does not answer those realities by pretending sin does not matter.
The Gospel does something infinitely better.
It tells the truth about sin…
and then tells us about a Savior greater than our sin.
Moses can point us toward themes that ultimately become glorious in Jesus Christ, but Moses himself was not Jesus.
Moses was flawed.
Jesus was sinless.
Moses needed grace.
Jesus is the One through whom grace and truth came.
Moses delivered those women from shepherds at a well.
Jesus came to accomplish a deliverance infinitely greater.
The angel announced concerning Christ:
“Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
Matthew 1:21.
The Greek word translated “save” is σώσει — sōsei — from σώζω, sōzō: to save, rescue, deliver.
And here the Gospel stops being merely an interesting comparison.
Because your deepest problem is not simply what other people have done to you.
Nor is it merely the circumstances that have driven you into your personal wilderness.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have sinned against a holy God.
We cannot erase our guilt by becoming more religious.
We cannot bury sin deeply enough.
Moses buried the Egyptian in sand.
Human beings have been burying things ever since.
Secret habits.
Hidden messages.
Private bitterness.
Pornography.
Pride.
Jealousy.
Dishonesty.
Unforgiveness.
Religious hypocrisy.
Things deleted from phones but not from hearts.
Things hidden from spouses.
Things hidden from pastors.
Things hidden from friends.
Things we desperately hope nobody ever uncovers.
But there is no sand deep enough to hide a human heart from God.
And strangely, terrifyingly, beautifully…
that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because the God who completely knows you is the God who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not die for the imaginary version of you that never failed.
Christ died for sinners.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8.
That does not make sin insignificant.
The cross proves exactly how serious sin is.
Forgiveness was not purchased cheaply.
Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel is not God saying your rebellion never mattered.
The Gospel is God declaring that forgiveness has been made possible through the blood of His Son.
Repentance therefore is not polishing your image.
It is turning toward God.
It is dropping the disguise.
It is admitting:
Lord, I sinned.
Lord, I cannot save myself.
Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.
And maybe that is why Moses sitting beside that well feels so familiar.
Sometimes God meets people in places they never wanted to enter.
Not because every disaster is secretly pleasant.
Not because every painful circumstance was good.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because no wilderness is beyond God's reach.
Moses thought he was a stranger.
God knew his name.
Moses thought he had escaped into obscurity.
God was still writing.
Moses saw Midian.
God saw chapters Moses had not lived yet.
There would still be sheep.
Years of silence.
A burning bush.
A confrontation with Pharaoh.
A Passover night.
A sea opening.
A nation walking toward freedom.
But Moses knew none of that while sitting beside the well.
He only had the moment in front of him.
And maybe that is where faithfulness begins for you too.
You do not need to see the next twenty years.
You need to respond faithfully to Christ today.
Maybe your next act of obedience will not look spectacular.
Apologize.
Tell the truth.
Delete what keeps pulling you into sin.
Forgive.
Ask for help.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Return to church.
Serve somebody who cannot repay you.
Stand beside someone being mistreated.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Come home.
And above everything else, come to Jesus.
Because Moses can inspire us…
but Moses cannot save us.
Only Christ can.
Maybe you have been carrying a private scandal so long that you have started confusing what you did with who you must always be.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending your sin never happened.
Grace rewrites your future because Jesus Christ can forgive, redeem, restore, and transform sinners who turn to Him in faith.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not scandal to pretending.
Not scandal to self-justification.
Not scandal to religious performance.
Scandal to repentance.
Scandal to mercy.
Scandal to forgiveness.
Scandal to transformation.
Scandal to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
There are moments when another believer needs to know they are not the only person fighting their way through Midian.
Even send it to the skeptic or unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely about good people pretending they never made terrible mistakes.
You may need these words on a night when the wilderness feels longer than you expected.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and grace cannot be bought.
And there is far more than one article waiting for you.
Not because clicking “Share” makes someone more spiritual.
Because somewhere in your circle may be a Moses sitting beside a well.
Someone ashamed.
Someone running.
Someone convinced the story is over.
Someone who desperately needs to hear that Christianity does not offer them permission to hide their sin.
It offers them something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ.
A Savior.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A call to repentance.
And grace powerful enough to begin making a sinner new.
Moses arrived at that well carrying yesterday's disaster.
He walked away from it toward a future he could not yet see.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you when this article is over:

You may be sitting beside the well staring at everything you lost, while God already sees the chapters you have not lived yet—so do not make your wilderness your identity; turn your face toward Jesus and let grace have the next word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “RENDER UNTO CAESAR” — JESUS WAS SAYING MORE THAN “PAY YOUR TAXES”
paragraphs:
“RENDER UNTO CAESAR” — JESUS WAS SAYING MORE THAN “PAY YOUR TAXES”
We remember the coin. We remember Caesar. But we may have missed the devastating question hidden inside Jesus’ answer: If Caesar’s image tells you what belongs to Caesar… whose image is on you?
There is a moment in the Gospel of Matthew that most Christians have heard so many times that we can almost finish Jesus’ sentence before He says it.
“Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.”
Matthew 22:21.
Pay your taxes.
Obey the government.
Be a responsible citizen.

Those applications are not meaningless. Scripture elsewhere does address governing authorities and taxes. Paul explicitly tells believers to pay what is owed, including taxes and revenue, in Romans 13:6–7.
But if we reduce Matthew 22 to a lesson about paying taxes, we may walk away staring at Caesar’s coin while completely missing the far more terrifying question Jesus placed before the human soul.
Because Jesus did not merely ask them about money.
He asked them about an image.
And once you see what happens in that conversation, His words become difficult to forget.
The Pharisees wanted Jesus trapped.

Matthew tells us they deliberately plotted to “entangle him in his talk.” Then they sent their disciples together with the Herodians—a striking combination because these groups did not naturally represent the same interests.
They approached Jesus with compliments.
“Teacher, we know that thou art true…”
It sounded respectful.
It wasn’t.
Sometimes the most dangerous words spoken to you are the ones designed to make you comfortable enough to destroy yourself.
Then came the question.
“Is it lawful to give tribute unto Caesar, or not?”
The tax in view was the imperial poll tax imposed upon subject peoples.
The trap was brilliant.
Say yes, and Jesus could appear to side with the occupying imperial system in the eyes of people who resented Roman domination.
Say no, and His opponents could potentially portray Him as opposing Roman authority.
Either direction appeared dangerous.
But they had forgotten something.
They were trying to trap the One who knew what was inside the trapper.
Jesus saw through them.
“Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites?”
Then He said something almost painfully simple.
“Show me the tribute money.”
Someone reached into his possessions.
A coin appeared.
A denarius.
And suddenly the entire conversation changed.
Jesus did not produce the coin.
They did.
That detail deserves to sit with us for a moment.
The people attempting to trap Jesus over the legitimacy of Caesar’s tax were carrying Caesar’s currency.
The denarius circulated within Rome’s economic world, and the coin involved would have borne the image of the emperor; the NET Bible’s notes identify the figure as Tiberius Caesar.
Jesus looked at it.
Then He asked:
“Whose is this image and superscription?”
In the Greek text, the crucial word is:
εἰκών — eikōn.
Image.
Likeness.
Representation.
And the other word is:
ἐπιγραφή — epigraphē.
Inscription.
What is stamped on this thing?
Whose likeness does it carry?
Whose name does it bear?
They answered:
“Caesar’s.”
And Jesus replied:
“Ἀπόδοτε οὖν τὰ Καίσαρος Καίσαρι καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ τῷ Θεῷ.”
“Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
That first Greek word matters.
Ἀπόδοτε — apodote.
It carries the sense of giving back, paying, or rendering what is due. That is why translations legitimately render the statement as “render,” “give back,” or “pay.”
Caesar’s image was stamped on the coin.
Fine.
Give Caesar what belongs to Caesar.
But Jesus did not stop there.
“…and to God the things that are God’s.”
And now the question becomes infinitely larger.
What belongs to God?
Think carefully.
Jesus had just directed their attention to an image.
Whose image is this?
Caesar’s.
Therefore give it to Caesar.
But where else had Israel heard language about an “image”?
They had heard it at the beginning of everything.
Genesis 1:26–27.
“Let us make man in our image, after our likeness…”
Human beings were created in the image of God.

The Greek Septuagint—the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament—uses the same key noun, εἰκών, in Genesis 1:26 for “image.” The lexical connection between Matthew’s εἰκών and Genesis is real; the NET Bible notes specifically identify this Genesis-image resonance as an important way of understanding Jesus’ contrast.
And suddenly the coin in Jesus’ hand becomes a mirror.
Caesar stamped his image on silver.
God stamped His image upon humanity.
Caesar may have a claim upon the coin.
God has a claim upon you.
Your hands.
Your mind.
Your ambitions.
Your sexuality.
Your relationships.
Your money.
Your hidden life.
Your public life.
Your wounds.
Your future.
Your worship.
Your entire existence.
And this is where the passage stops being an argument from two thousand years ago and begins looking directly at us.
Because we are very good at giving God things.
An hour on Sunday.
A prayer before sleeping.
A verse shared online.
A worship song while driving.
A little money when we have enough.
A promise after we have sinned again.
A tear when life finally becomes unbearable.
We hand God pieces.
Jesus asks for the person.
Maybe that is why this passage can be so uncomfortable.
The question is no longer merely, “Did you pay what you owe?”
The deeper question becomes:
Have you given God what bears His image?
Have you given Him yourself?
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that question hurts.
You love Jesus.
At least you believe you do.
But there is a locked room inside your life where you have quietly hung a sign that says:
Not this, Lord.
You can have my church attendance.
Just not this relationship.
You can have my worship.
Just not this addiction.
You can have my Sunday.
Just not my private messages.
You can have my public Christianity.
Just don’t touch the bitterness I have protected for ten years.
You can have my theology.
Just don’t ask me to forgive them.
You can have my future.
As long as Your future looks like mine.
And somehow we have learned how to sing “I surrender all” while negotiating the definition of “all.”
But Jesus sees the inscription.
He sees what nobody else sees.
He knows where Caesar ends.
He knows where your excuses begin.
And He knows what belongs to God.
That should frighten us.
But if we stop there, we have not yet reached the Gospel.
Because the One demanding that we give ourselves to God is the same One who was preparing to give Himself for sinners.
Matthew 22 happens during the final stretch toward the cross.
The traps are tightening.
Opposition is growing.
Calvary is approaching.
Soon the hands holding that coin would be pierced.
The Teacher they attempted to trap would be arrested.
The innocent One would be treated like the guilty.
The sinless Christ would be mocked, beaten, crucified and killed.
And above His head another inscription would appear.
“This is Jesus the King of the Jews.”
The world put a title over the dying Christ.
But heaven knew what was really happening beneath it.
The Son of God was giving Himself for sinners.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not the story of good people successfully rendering enough goodness to God until God accepts them.
It is the story of sinners who could never repay their debt being rescued by a Savior who paid what they could not pay.
Jesus Christ “gave himself for our sins” according to Galatians 1:4.
Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” in 1 Peter 3:18.
Paul says that in Christ “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” in Ephesians 1:7.
That is grace.
Not God pretending your sin did not matter.
God dealing with sin at the cross.
Not Jesus helping decent people become slightly better.
Jesus rescuing sinners who could not rescue themselves.
Not self-improvement.
Resurrection.
Not image management.
Transformation.
Not hiding the scandal.
Grace rewriting the story.
Maybe your life does not look like something God would want right now.
Maybe you have spent years giving yourself away to things that never loved you back.
Pornography.
Approval.
Money.
Alcohol.
Anger.
Pride.
Secret conversations.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Religion without repentance.
Ministry without intimacy.
A carefully maintained Christian reputation covering a starving soul.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
And still He calls you.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not tell you the chains are imaginary.
Grace breaks them.
Grace does not rename darkness so you can remain comfortable inside it.
Grace calls you into the light.
Grace does not say, “Continue exactly as you are.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Repentance is not God stealing your life.
It is returning to the One your life belonged to from the beginning.
The coin belonged to Caesar because Caesar’s image was stamped upon it.
You belong to God because you bear the image of your Creator.
And through the Gospel something even more astonishing happens: those who belong to Christ are being renewed according to the image of the One who created them, as Colossians 3:10 teaches.
Sin has scarred us.
It has not made God surrender His redemptive purpose.
The Gospel is Christ taking people whose stories look ruined and making them new.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace found him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace stopped him on the road.
The thief beside Jesus reached the final hours of a wasted life.
Grace met him on a cross.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated history.
Jesus sat beside her well.
The prodigal smelled like the country he had wasted himself in.
The father still ran.
Again and again Scripture tells the same impossible story.
Scandal.
Then grace.
Failure.
Then mercy.
Death.
Then resurrection.
A past that appears to have written the final chapter…
until Jesus enters the story.
And maybe tonight the coin is in your hand.
Maybe Jesus is asking you the question you have spent months avoiding.
Whose image do you bear?
Not your addiction’s.
Not your ex’s.
Not your failure’s.
Not your trauma’s.
Not your bank account’s.
Not your political tribe’s.
Not the opinion of the people who abandoned you.
Not the label somebody placed on you during the worst season of your life.
You were made in the image of God.
And if you are in Christ, your deepest identity is not the scandal behind you but the Savior who redeemed you.
So yes—render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar.
Jesus really said it.
We should not erase the straightforward civic dimension of His answer.
But please do not walk away after handing Caesar his coin.
Jesus finished the sentence.
“…and unto God the things that are God’s.”
That part costs infinitely more.
Because the coin may leave your hand.
But God asks for the hand holding it.
He wants you.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
You.
The exhausted you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The secretly struggling you.
The person who promised God last time would be the last time.
The person wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want someone who knew better and sinned anyway.
Bring that person to the cross.
Stop hiding.
Repent.
Confess.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
Then get up and follow Him.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
If you need prayer, simply comment, “Pray for me.”

If Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another exhausted believer realizes there is still hope.
Save it too.
There may come a night when you need these words again.
If these resources are feeding you spiritually, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer quietly fighting an addiction.
Invite the person angry with God.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who thinks Jesus could never want them again.
Jesus Christ.
We are not the Gospel.
He is the center of it.
We cannot save anyone.
Jesus saves.
We cannot wash away sin.
His blood does.
We cannot resurrect a dead heart.
God can.
So share this because somebody needs Christ, not because an algorithm needs another post.
Follow because your soul needs more than endless noise.
And support Gospel work freely and prayerfully wherever God leads you, because the message is too precious to become merely another piece of content we consume and forget.
Caesar's coin eventually disappears.
Empires fall.
Currencies change.
Rulers become names in history books.
But the image God placed upon humanity points to something no empire can own.
And the Savior who held that denarius eventually stretched those same hands upon a cross to redeem sinners.
So the next time you hear, “Render unto Caesar,” remember the question behind the coin.
Whose image is on you?
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be failing to give Caesar his coin.
It would be spending your entire life giving everything else pieces of yourself…
and never surrendering yourself to the God whose image you carried all along.
The coin bore Caesar’s face—but your life bears the fingerprints of God, and Jesus did not go to the cross merely to improve your story; He came to redeem it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DRINK WATER FROM YOUR OWN CISTERN”: WAS PROVERBS REALLY TALKING ABOUT SEXUAL FAITHFULNESS?
paragraphs: “DRINK WATER FROM YOUR OWN CISTERN”: WAS PROVERBS REALLY TALKING ABOUT SEXUAL FAITHFULNESS?

Proverbs 5:15 sounds almost innocent—until you discover what the “water,” the “cistern,” and the “fountain” are doing in the rest of the chapter. Then one ancient sentence becomes an alarmingly intimate message about desire, marriage, temptation, adultery…and the God who refuses to let lust have the final word.
There are Bible verses we read quickly because we think we already understand them.
Then there are verses that stop looking innocent when you read what comes before and after them.
Proverbs 5:15 is one of those verses.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Beautiful.
Poetic.
Almost peaceful.
But Solomon was not giving his son advice about staying hydrated.
He was talking about sex.
More specifically, he was teaching something our generation desperately needs to hear:
Your desires are powerful, but they were never meant to become your master.
And if you keep reading, Proverbs does something surprising.
It does not merely tell a married man, “Don’t commit adultery.”
It tells him where his desire belongs.
The original Hebrew reads:
שְׁתֵה־מַיִם מִבּוֹרֶךָ וְנֹזְלִים מִתּוֹךְ בְּאֵרֶךָ
Sheteh-mayim miborekha, wenozelim mittokh be’erekha.
Literally, the imagery is straightforward:
“Drink water from your own cistern, and flowing water from your own well.”
The Hebrew verb שְׁתֵה — sheteh means “drink.”
מַיִם — mayim means “water.”
בּוֹר — bor refers to a pit or cistern, a place where water was gathered and preserved.
And בְּאֵר — be’er means a well.
But here is where everything changes.
You cannot correctly interpret verse 15 by ripping it away from Proverbs 5.
Because this entire chapter is a father warning his son about sexual temptation.
Earlier, he warns about the “strange woman” or forbidden woman.
Her lips drip sweetness.
Her speech is seductive.
Everything about temptation initially promises pleasure.
Then Scripture pulls back the curtain.
What tastes like honey eventually becomes bitter.
What looks like freedom can become slavery.
What promises excitement can leave destruction behind.
And suddenly that ancient warning does not feel ancient anymore.
Because maybe your temptation does not stand on a street corner.
Maybe it lives behind a screen.
Maybe it arrives through a private message.
Maybe it has a profile picture.
Maybe it begins with a conversation you know you should end.
Maybe it is pornography nobody knows you watch.
Maybe it is the coworker whose attention feels dangerously good.
Maybe it is the former relationship you keep checking.
Maybe it is the emotional affair you keep calling “friendship.”
Maybe nothing physical has happened.
Yet.
But somewhere inside, you already know why you keep returning.
And Scripture whispers across thousands of years:
Drink from your own cistern.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because God understands its power.
That distinction matters.
Christian teaching about sexuality is sometimes reduced to a giant list of prohibitions.
Don’t do this.
Don’t look there.
Don’t touch that.
Don’t desire this.
But Proverbs 5 does something far richer.
It warns against forbidden sexuality, yes.
Then it turns toward marital delight.
A few verses later we read:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi-meqorekha barukh, usemach me’eshet ne’urekha.
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth.”
There it is.
The metaphor opens.
The cistern.
The well.
The fountain.
The wife.
The covenant.
The rejoicing.
This is not a picture of sexuality as dirty.
It is a picture of sexuality as powerful enough to require covenant.
God is not embarrassed by marital desire.
He created the human body.
He created attraction.
He created intimacy.
He created marriage.
And Proverbs does not merely tolerate marital affection—it tells the husband to rejoice in his wife.
That Hebrew word, שְׂמַח — semach, carries the idea of rejoicing, being glad, taking delight.
That changes the conversation.
Biblical faithfulness is not merely refusing everyone else.
It is learning to treasure the covenant God has entrusted to you.
And perhaps that is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because adultery usually begins long before a bedroom.
Sometimes it begins with comparison.
A husband stops noticing his wife but notices everybody else.
A wife stops speaking honestly to her husband but begins emotionally confiding in another man.
Someone feels unseen.
Someone feels lonely.
Someone enjoys being desired again.
A notification arrives.
A conversation becomes private.
Private becomes secret.
Secret becomes intimate.
And eventually the heart starts drinking from somebody else’s well.
Nobody wakes up one morning planning to destroy everything they love.
Compromise usually comes quietly.
One look.
One conversation.
One rationalization.
One deleted message.
One secret.
One more night telling yourself:
“I can control this.”
That may be why Proverbs speaks so urgently.
Because sin rarely introduces itself by announcing where it intends to take you.
It shows you the entrance.
God shows you the destination.
And sexual sin has consequences that reach far beyond a moment of pleasure.
Trust can shatter.
Children can be wounded.
Marriages can collapse.
Consciences can become numb.
Friendships can be destroyed.
Church communities can be shaken.
A person can spend years trying to rebuild what took minutes to betray.
But if you have already fallen, keep reading.
Because this is where some Christians stop the story.
Jesus does not.
Maybe you are reading this carrying something nobody knows.
Maybe you have committed adultery.
Maybe you are trapped in pornography.
Maybe your marriage is barely alive.
Maybe you crossed boundaries emotionally.
Maybe you gave your body to people who never gave you covenant.
Maybe you have been sexually sinned against and now intimacy itself feels complicated.
Maybe your history is messy enough that words like “purity” make you want to leave the room.
Please hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sexually spotless people get Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can come to Jesus and be made clean.
That does not make sin harmless.
Grace never calls darkness light.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He enters our darkness and calls us out of it.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“You did this. Therefore this is who you are.”
The Gospel says:
“You sinned. Bring it into the light. Come to Christ.”
Because Jesus did not go to the cross for the imaginary version of you.
He died for sinners.
Real sinners.
Sexually broken sinners.
Adulterers.
The lustful.
The ashamed.
The secretive.
The wounded.
The people who promised God they would never do it again…and did.
The people who cannot believe how far they wandered.
The people who look fine in church while carrying wars nobody sees.
Christ came for people who need mercy.
At the cross, sin is not excused.
It is judged.

And the astonishing message of Christianity is that the judgment our sin deserves falls upon the willing, sinless Son of God, and those who turn to Him in faith receive forgiveness they could never purchase for themselves.
That is why grace is not permission to keep drinking from poisoned wells.
Grace gives you a reason to put the cup down.
Jesus does not merely forgive you so you can return unchanged.
He forgives.
Cleanses.
Restores.
Transforms.
Calls you to walk differently.
And sometimes repentance becomes painfully practical.
Delete the number.
End the secret conversation.
Stop protecting access to the thing destroying you.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Find mature Christian accountability.
Put boundaries around your phone.
Stop calling emotional adultery innocent because clothing never came off.
Stop feeding fantasies about somebody who does not belong to you.
If you are married, turn toward your spouse.
Talk.
Listen.
Repent where necessary.
Forgive where biblically possible.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where the wounds run deep.
Rebuild slowly.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Remember that covenant love is not maintained by emotion alone.
It is guarded by thousands of choices nobody applauds.
And if you are single, Proverbs 5 still speaks powerfully to you.
The principle is not, “Find somebody quickly so you can satisfy every desire.”
Your body does not become sovereign simply because you are unmarried.
Christian sexuality ultimately belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your desires may speak loudly.
They do not get the throne.
Jesus does.
There will be moments when obedience feels expensive.
There will be moments when temptation tells you that God is withholding something wonderful.
That lie is older than civilization.
“Did God actually say…?”
The serpent has always tried to convince human beings that God’s boundaries are evidence of God's stinginess.
But biblical boundaries are not prison bars around human flourishing.
They are guardrails around things powerful enough to destroy us when misused.
Fire belongs somewhere.
Water belongs somewhere.
Sexual desire belongs somewhere.
Proverbs calls the married person back to the covenant well.
Drink from your own cistern.
There is something almost heartbreaking about those words.
Your own.
Not somebody else’s spouse.
Not somebody on a screen.
Not the fantasy you have constructed.
Not the person sending you messages your husband or wife would be devastated to read.
Your own.
There is dignity in belonging.
There is holiness in fidelity.
There is worship in saying, when nobody would ever discover otherwise:
“No.
I belong to Christ.
And because I belong to Christ, my body does not get to make promises my soul has no right to make.”
Perhaps somebody reading this is seconds away from returning to something hidden.
This may be your interruption.
Close it.
Walk away.
Call somebody.
Pray.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
And perhaps somebody else is reading this after the damage has already happened.
Then your word is different.
Come home.
Not to pretending.
Not to image management.
Not to religious performance.
Come home to Jesus.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the screenshots.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish you could erase.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ is still Lord over what happens next.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal does not matter.
Because grace is greater.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that baptizes rebellion.
Grace that brings sinners to their knees and then raises them into newness of life.
Grace that teaches us to say no.
Grace that rebuilds ruined people.
Grace that turns confession into freedom.
Grace that takes the sentence you thought ended your story and places a cross where you thought there could only be a period.
Maybe Proverbs 5:15 was never merely about adultery.
Maybe beneath the warning is a much larger question:
Where are you drinking?
Where are you looking for satisfaction?
Where do you run when you feel empty?
Whose attention makes you feel valuable?
What secret desire has slowly become your refuge?
Because you can be sexually faithful outwardly while your heart is dying of thirst inwardly.
And no husband or wife can ultimately carry the weight of being your savior.
Marriage is sacred.
Sexual faithfulness matters.
But even the purest marriage cannot satisfy the deepest thirst of the human soul.
Only Christ can bear that weight.
Eventually every earthly cistern reminds us that human beings were created for something greater than pleasure.
We were created for God.
Jesus said that whoever drinks the water He gives will never thirst in the same ultimate way again.
That does not erase ordinary human longing.
It tells us where longing finally has to kneel.
So guard your marriage.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your messages.
Guard your imagination.
Guard your covenant.
But above everything else, give your heart completely to Jesus Christ.
Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of your struggle. But sometimes two honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.

And if God has already brought you through sexual brokenness, betrayal, addiction, shame, or a season when your marriage nearly collapsed, your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to surrender.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Let somebody reading know that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not somebody you want to shame.
Somebody you love.
Temptation has a strange way of making us forget convictions we were certain about yesterday.
You may need these words again.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity should come from a willing heart, not compulsion, while also affirming the legitimacy of supporting those laboring to spread the Gospel.
You can still help.
Pray.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is sitting alone with a glowing screen.
A message is waiting.
A temptation is whispering.
A marriage is hanging by a thread.
A Christian is wondering whether one secret decision really matters.
Maybe your share reaches them five minutes before a decision they cannot easily undo.
Maybe your testimony reminds them to close the door.
Maybe your comment makes another believer realize they are not the only one fighting.
Maybe Scripture reaches somebody through you.
And maybe they finally understand:
God's command was never simply,
“Do not drink.”
It was:
Do not destroy yourself drinking from a well that was never yours.
And when you discover that you already have…
there is still a Savior standing beside the ruins.
There is still repentance.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still grace.
There is still Jesus.
The well you drank from may explain your scandal—but it does not have the authority to write your ending. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID ABRAHAM’S DECISION ABOUT HAGAR HAVE LASTING CONSEQUENCES?
paragraphs: WHY DID ABRAHAM’S DECISION ABOUT HAGAR HAVE LASTING CONSEQUENCES?
The frightening story of what happens when faithful people grow tired of waiting on God—and the breathtaking grace of the God who still enters the wreckage.
There are decisions that end when the moment ends.
And then there are decisions that keep walking long after we thought we left them behind.
A conversation.
A compromise.
A relationship.
A secret.
A shortcut taken because waiting became unbearable.
Something you prayed about for years…until one exhausted day you stopped waiting for God to answer and decided to manufacture an answer yourself.
Abraham knew something about that kind of moment.
And perhaps that is why the story of Abraham, Sarah, Hagar, Ishmael, and Isaac can feel disturbingly familiar thousands of years later.
Because Genesis does not give us polished saints whose faith never trembled.
It gives us human beings.
People who believed God…and became impatient.
People who received promises…and still became afraid.
People capable of extraordinary faith who could also make decisions with heartbreaking consequences.
And standing inside one of the most painful episodes in Abraham’s household is a woman whose name should never be reduced to a theological footnote.
Hagar.
A servant.
A foreigner.
A woman caught inside someone else’s attempt to make God’s promise happen faster.
And then something extraordinary happened.
God saw her.
But before we reach the God who sees, we have to walk into the house where everything began to fracture.
God had already called Abram and promised to make of him a great nation. The problem was painfully obvious: years were passing, and Sarai remained childless.
That gap between promise and fulfillment became unbearable.
Genesis 16:2 preserves Sarai’s words in Hebrew:
“הִנֵּה־נָא עֲצָרַנִי יְהוָה מִלֶּדֶת”
Hinnēh-nā ʿăṣāranî YHWH milledet.
In context: “Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing.”
Then came the proposal.
“Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her.”
And then Scripture gives us a painfully simple sentence:
Abram listened to Sarai.
There is something haunting about how ordinary the beginning sounds.
No thunder.
No idol erected.
No dramatic announcement that Abraham was abandoning God.
Just a weary family looking at an impossible situation and choosing a human solution.
That is often how compromise begins.
Not with someone saying, “I no longer believe God.”
But with someone quietly thinking:
“I still believe God. I just think He needs my help.”
That thought can become dangerous.

To understand the ancient setting fairly, we should not pretend that Sarai invented an arrangement unheard of in her world. Surrogacy-like arrangements involving enslaved or servant women existed in the ancient Near East.
But something being culturally recognizable does not mean Scripture presents everything that follows as morally beautiful.
Genesis lets the consequences speak.
Hagar conceived.
Then contempt entered the household.
Sarai became afflicted by the situation.
Abram failed to resolve it justly.
Sarai dealt harshly with Hagar.
And Hagar ran.
Pause there.
Because it is easy to read this story so quickly that Hagar becomes merely “the woman who had Ishmael.”
But Hagar was a person.
She was an Egyptian servant living under the authority of people far more powerful than she was. Decisions were being made around her that would permanently change her body, future, and family.
Then she found herself pregnant and fleeing into the wilderness.
And there—in the wilderness—the story takes one of its most beautiful turns.
The angel of the LORD found her.
Not Abraham.
Not Sarah.
Hagar.
The runaway servant.
The wounded foreign woman.
The person seemingly standing at the edge of someone else’s promise.
God found her.
And after encountering Him, Hagar used astonishing language about the LORD:
“אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי”
Attah El Ro’i.
“You are a God who sees me.”
Imagine what those words meant coming from her mouth.
People had seen a servant.
God saw Hagar.
People had seen a solution to infertility.
God saw Hagar.
People had seen usefulness.
God saw a woman.
People may have treated her like a means to an end.
Heaven knew her name.
And maybe somebody reading this needs those words tonight.
God sees you.
Not the version of you smiling in photographs.
You.
The person underneath the performance.
The exhausted parent.
The husband silently losing hope.
The wife crying where nobody notices.
The believer who still goes to church but secretly wonders why God has remained silent.
The person living with consequences from decisions you wish you could reverse.
The person wounded by somebody else’s decision.
The person wondering whether your story has wandered too far from grace.
El Ro’i.
The God who sees.
But God seeing Hagar did not mean Abraham’s shortcut suddenly became harmless.
Ishmael was born.
Years passed.
Then God returned to the promise.
Sarah herself would bear Abraham a son.
Isaac was born exactly as God had promised.
And eventually tension erupted again.
Genesis 21 records the painful separation of Hagar and Ishmael from Abraham’s household.
Once again Hagar entered the wilderness.
Once again suffering followed.
And once again God heard.
This matters because Scripture does not teach that Ishmael was somehow invisible or worthless to God because the covenant line would continue through Isaac.
God explicitly promised to make a nation of Ishmael because he was Abraham’s offspring.
The covenant promise concerning the promised son remained with Isaac.
And God still showed mercy toward Ishmael.
Both truths belong in the story.
That distinction matters enormously.

We should therefore be cautious about turning Genesis into simplistic claims about every later political, ethnic, or religious conflict. The text certainly presents lasting family and covenant consequences, but Scripture does not authorize Christians to treat entire modern populations as personally guilty for Abraham and Sarah’s ancient choices.
The deepest warning is closer to home.
Abraham’s household demonstrates what can happen when we attempt to obtain through human control what God has asked us to receive through faith.
That is where this ancient story suddenly becomes uncomfortable.
Because Abraham’s temptation is still ours.
God says wait.
We say, “But nothing is happening.”
God says trust Me.
We say, “But time is running out.”
God gives a promise.
Circumstances contradict it.
Fear starts whispering.
Then impatience begins negotiating.
And eventually we convince ourselves that the shortcut is simply wisdom.
Maybe your “Hagar decision” does not involve anything resembling Abraham’s situation.
Maybe it is the relationship you know you should leave but keep trying to baptize with excuses.
Maybe it is dishonest money because you became terrified God would not provide.
Maybe it is pornography because loneliness became louder than conviction.
Maybe it is bitterness because forgiveness feels too expensive.
Maybe it is manipulation because trusting God with another person feels impossible.
Maybe it is compromising truth because obedience threatens your reputation.
Maybe it is simply controlling everything because surrender terrifies you.
The frightening thing about shortcuts is that they frequently offer immediate relief.
And immediate relief can disguise long-term consequences.
Sin sends invoices later.
But that is not the most important sentence in this story.
This is:
God’s grace entered the consequences.
Abraham failed.
Sarah failed.
Hagar was wounded.
A household fractured.
Yet God did not lose control of His redemptive purpose.
That does not make the sin good.
Grace never needs evil to become good in order to redeem what evil has damaged.
God remained faithful.
Isaac came.
The promise continued.
Generations passed.
And eventually another promised Son arrived.
Jesus Christ.
This is where Abraham’s story becomes bigger than Abraham.

Paul later reaches back to Abraham’s household in Galatians 4 and uses Hagar and Sarah allegorically to illustrate slavery and freedom in his argument about law, promise, and inheritance. His point is ultimately directed toward the freedom believers possess through God’s promise rather than justification through human effort.
And the Gospel takes us deeper still.
Humanity has been doing what Abraham did ever since Eden.
Trying to fix what only God can fix.
Trying to cover our nakedness.
Trying to justify ourselves.
Trying to become righteous enough.
Religious enough.
Successful enough.
Moral enough.
Useful enough.
Trying to construct ladders tall enough to reach heaven.
But Christianity announces something completely different.
God came down.
Jesus did not come merely to improve people who had almost managed to save themselves.
He came for sinners.
Christ lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He bore sin upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because sinners finally repair themselves, but because Jesus Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
This is why the answer to your worst decision is not another desperate attempt to manufacture redemption.
The answer is Christ.
Repentance does not mean pretending consequences disappear.
Sometimes forgiveness comes immediately while earthly consequences remain for years.
Sometimes relationships take time to heal.
Sometimes trust must be rebuilt.
Sometimes scars remain.
Abraham’s story proves that faith does not mean consequences magically evaporate.
But scars are not sovereign.
Jesus is.
Your worst chapter does not possess more authority than the Author of redemption.
Perhaps you made decisions while frightened.
Perhaps impatience cost you something precious.
Perhaps you knew better and did it anyway.
Perhaps there are names, memories, conversations, or consequences you wish you could erase.
The Gospel does not ask you to rewrite yesterday.
It calls you to surrender today.
Bring the wreckage into the light.
Confess the sin.
Stop defending what God is asking you to surrender.
Where reconciliation is biblically possible, pursue it.
Where restitution is necessary, make it.
Where consequences remain, walk through them with Christ.
But stop believing that because you cannot change the beginning, Jesus cannot redeem what comes next.
That is precisely where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by deleting every consequence.
He rewrites everything by taking sinners who deserve judgment and giving them mercy, forgiveness, adoption, restoration, and a new identity through Himself.
Maybe that is why this story survived thousands of years.
Maybe we needed Abraham to remain human on the page.
We needed to know that giants of faith sometimes stumbled.
We needed Hagar’s tears preserved.
We needed to hear that God sees people overlooked by powerful people.
We needed Ishmael’s cry remembered.
We needed Isaac’s impossible birth.
We needed to discover that human failure does not cancel divine faithfulness.
And maybe you needed this story today because you have spent years believing one terrible decision became the final definition of your life.
It did not.
Your sin matters.
Your choices matter.
Consequences matter.
Repentance matters.
But Jesus is greater.
Be honest.
If you are walking through consequences but refusing to abandon Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you are exhausted and need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need evidence that God still restores broken people.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not twenty random names.
One person.
The friend waiting too long and growing impatient.
The Christian quietly compromising.
The person drowning in regret.
The brother or sister who thinks yesterday has disqualified tomorrow.
“Can God still do something with the mess I made?”
Save it too.
There may come a night when the consequences feel louder than grace, and you will need to remember the God who saw Hagar in the wilderness and the Savior who still receives repentant sinners.
Our desire is to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and Christ-centered spiritual nourishment in front of people who desperately need Jesus.
But hear this carefully.
Scripture teaches voluntary generosity, not spiritual coercion. Paul writes:
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia… mē… ex anankēs.
In context: each person gives as he has purposed in his heart—not from compulsion.
“For God loves a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7
So pray about your giving and support your local church and faithful Christian ministry according to biblical conviction.
You can still help.
Pray.
Save these messages.
Invite somebody into Scripture.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Because the goal was never merely to build an audience.
The goal is that Christ would be known.
That sinners would repent.
That wounded people would encounter biblical hope.
That believers would grow.
That Scripture would be opened.
That the Gospel would travel farther than we could carry it alone.
Abraham’s story leaves us with a sobering warning: impatience can produce consequences that outlive the moment.
Hagar’s story leaves us with another truth: God sees people crying in wildernesses created by human brokenness.
Isaac’s story reminds us that God does not need sinful shortcuts to fulfill His promises.
And the Gospel gives us the greatest truth of all:
When our human solutions fail, God’s saving purpose has not failed.
Jesus Christ still saves.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
Jesus still walks into stories stained by choices we cannot undo and declares that the final word belongs neither to shame nor failure nor yesterday.
It belongs to Him.
So before you leave this page, ask yourself the question Abraham’s story forces every generation to confront:
Where am I trying to manufacture what God is asking me to trust Him for?
Do not answer quickly.
Let it hurt if it needs to hurt.
Then bring the answer to Jesus.
Because sometimes the wilderness created by our worst decision becomes the very place where we finally discover that grace has been looking for us all along.
Your failure may have written a chapter—but it never received permission to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU SAID YES TO JESUS—SO WHY DO YOU KEEP LOOKING BACK?
paragraphs:
YOU SAID YES TO JESUS—SO WHY DO YOU KEEP LOOKING BACK?
Understanding Luke 9:62 — The Terrifying Mercy Behind One of Jesus’ Hardest Warnings About Following Him
There are things you left behind when you came to Jesus.
And then there are things you left behind physically...
but never stopped missing secretly.
That distinction may be where Luke 9:62 becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to your walk with Christ is not something standing in front of you trying to stop you.
Sometimes it is something behind you...
still calling your name.
An old relationship.
An old addiction.
An old identity.
An old ambition.
An old bitterness.
The approval of people who liked the version of you that existed before Jesus began changing you.
Maybe you stopped going there, but part of you still misses being there.
Maybe you stopped doing it, but occasionally you romanticize how it made you feel.
Maybe your hands are following Christ...
while your heart keeps turning around.
And Jesus said something about that.
Something uncomfortable.
Something sharp enough that we should resist the temptation to soften it.
“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”
Luke 9:62.
The Greek is even worth seeing with your own eyes:
“Οὐδεὶς ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα ἐπ’ ἄροτρον καὶ βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω εὔθετός ἐστιν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ.”
Oudeis epibalōn tēn cheira ep’ arotron kai blepōn eis ta opisō euthetos estin tē basileia tou Theou.
In plain sense:
“No one, having laid the hand upon the plow and looking toward the things behind, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say you can never remember your past.
He does not say that feeling temptation means you have already abandoned Him.
He does not say that a believer who struggles, stumbles, weeps, repents, and runs back to Christ is beyond grace.
Peter would make that impossible to believe.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
And Jesus restored him.
So Luke 9:62 cannot honestly mean, “If you ever fail after deciding to follow Jesus, God is finished with you.”
Thank God.
Because if that were the meaning, who among us could stand?
The warning is deeper.
Jesus is exposing the divided heart that says:
“I will follow You, Lord...
but first.”
And those two words are hiding immediately before Luke 9:62.
A man had said to Jesus, in essence, “I will follow You, Lord, but first let me say goodbye to those at my home.”
At first hearing, that sounds reasonable.
Even loving.
Why would Jesus answer so severely?
Because this entire scene is about the cost and priority of discipleship.
Earlier in the chapter, Luke tells us that Jesus had resolutely set His course toward Jerusalem.
Think about that.
Jesus is moving toward Jerusalem.
Toward rejection.
Toward suffering.
Toward the cross.
And while Christ has His face set forward toward the place where He will give His life for sinners, would-be disciples are surrounding Him with qualifications.
Conditions.
Delays.
“I will follow You... but.”
Then comes the plow.
Anyone trying to plow a straight furrow while continually turning backward has a problem.
Your hands may still be holding the plow.
