Change me.
Teach me generosity that does not need cameras.
Teach me stewardship that remembers eternity.
Teach me to enjoy Your gifts without worshiping them.
Teach me to hold possessions with open hands because my life is already held securely in Yours.
That is a dangerous prayer.
Because God may not merely change your budget.
He may change your definition of wealth.
You may begin discovering that some of the richest moments of your life happen when nobody knows what you gave.
When a hungry person eats.
When a struggling family breathes again.
When a missionary receives support.
When Scripture reaches somebody searching for truth.
When a believer gets the discipleship resource they desperately needed.
When someone encounters the Gospel because another Christian decided the kingdom mattered more than keeping everything for themselves.
And before this becomes another emotional article you agree with and forget tomorrow, ask yourself one question:
What will change because I read this?
Not what did I feel.
What will change?
Maybe there is something you need to give.
Someone you need to help.
A purchase you need to reconsider.
A habit you need to confront.
A hidden idol you need to confess.
Or perhaps you simply need to stop measuring God's goodness by how many things He allows you to accumulate.
If this exposed something in you, do not hide behind religious language.
Not as a performance.
As honesty.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer wrestling with this.
Not because you need another saved post buried in a folder, but because comfort has a short memory. Return to 1 Timothy 6:17–19 when “more” starts whispering again.
Not to shame wealthy people.
Not to condemn people for owning things.
Send it privately to the person who has been wrestling with money, ambition, generosity, success, or contentment.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, think more seriously about Christ, confront hidden compromise, heal through biblical truth, and grow deeper in the Gospel, stay close.
God's grace cannot be bought.
Because perhaps one of the greatest tests of abundance is not whether you thanked God when you received more.
It is whether receiving more made you look more like Jesus.
One day, every house belongs to somebody else.
Every car stops running.
Every device becomes obsolete.
Every fashionable thing becomes old.
Every account we controlled passes beyond our control.
Every possession eventually slips from our hands.
But what Christ has done in a surrendered life reaches beyond the grave.
So enjoy what God gives you with gratitude.
Provide responsibly for those entrusted to you.
Save wisely.
Work diligently.
Do not manufacture guilt where Scripture does not.
But never confuse having more with being more blessed spiritually.
Never let God's gifts become competitors for God's throne.
Never allow comfort to convince you that you have arrived.
And never forget that the greatest treasure Christianity offers was never something God placed inside your hands.
It was Someone who allowed His own hands to be pierced for you.
Maybe the question was never how much God placed in your hands—but whether, after receiving it, your hands still looked like His: open.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What If Your Standards Aren’t High? What If Your Pride Just Learned Better Vocabulary?
paragraphs: What If Your Standards Aren’t High? What If Your Pride Just Learned Better Vocabulary?

There is a kind of pride that no longer brags, shouts, or demands attention. It calls itself discernment. It calls itself standards. It calls itself maturity. And sometimes, while we are congratulating ourselves for having “grown,” Jesus is exposing something far less flattering beneath the vocabulary.
What if the thing you have been calling “standards” is sometimes just a respectable way of deciding who is beneath you?
That question is uncomfortable.
Especially because standards are not inherently wrong.

Discernment is biblical. Wisdom matters. Character matters. Boundaries can be necessary. Scripture never commands you to trust everybody, date everybody, marry everybody, employ everybody, remain close friends with everybody, or give unlimited access to people who repeatedly demonstrate destructive behavior.
Jesus Himself said, “Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment” (John 7:24).
So this is not an argument for becoming naïve.
It is an invitation to ask a much more dangerous question:
Can I recognize what is wrong in someone without beginning to believe I am worth more than they are?
Because somewhere between discernment and disgust, between wisdom and superiority, between recognizing sin and despising the sinner...
pride can quietly change clothes.
And respectable pride is especially dangerous because it rarely introduces itself as pride.
It says:
“I just know my worth.”
“I protect my peace.”
“I have standards now.”
“I can read people.”
“I don't associate with people like that anymore.”
“They're not on my level.”
“I've outgrown them.”
Some of those sentences can describe legitimate boundaries.
But they can also hide something ugly.
Contempt.
And contempt can wear very clean clothes.
It can carry a Bible.
It can know theology.
It can quote sermons.
It can talk about “discernment.”
It can post about protecting its peace while secretly enjoying the feeling of being morally, intellectually, financially, socially, or spiritually above somebody else.
Then Philippians 2 walks into the room.
And suddenly there is nowhere comfortable for our ego to sit.
Paul writes:
“Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves.”
Philippians 2:3.
One Greek word deserves to stop us:
κενοδοξίαν — kenodoxian.
It carries the idea of empty glory, vain conceit, an inflated concern with one's own importance.
Empty glory.
That is terrifying because pride does not require you to stand in front of a mirror saying, “I am amazing.”
Sometimes pride only needs you to look at another person and quietly think:
“At least I'm not like them.”
Jesus already told a story about somebody who prayed like that.
A Pharisee stood before God and thanked Him that he was not like other people.
A tax collector, meanwhile, could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
His prayer was essentially:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
Jesus said it was the broken man who went home justified rather than the self-satisfied religious man.
That is Luke 18:9–14.
And notice how Luke introduces the parable.
Jesus told it to people who “trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt.”
There it is.
Not merely righteousness.
Not merely standards.
Contempt.
That is where the heart gets exposed.
Because biblical discernment can say, “What you're doing is wrong,” without saying, “Therefore, I am better than you.”
Biblical wisdom can establish a boundary without requiring hatred.
Biblical holiness can refuse participation in sin without forgetting that the sinner is still an image-bearer desperately needing the same Savior we desperately need.
You can walk away without looking down.
You can say no without sneering.
You can recognize someone's immaturity without worshiping your own maturity.
You can refuse a relationship without dehumanizing the person you refused.
You can identify false teaching without secretly enjoying the destruction of the false teacher.
You can confront sin while remembering the frightening sentence:
“But for the grace of God...”
Maybe that is where some of us have drifted.
We remember what people did to us, but forget what Christ forgave in us.
We remember their weakness, but forget ours.
We notice how far they still have to go while conveniently forgetting how far Jesus carried us.
And grace becomes something we celebrate when describing our own story...
but ration when describing somebody else's.
Read the next words of Philippians.
“Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.”
Then Paul does something devastating.
He does not merely tell us to become nicer.
He points us to Jesus.
“τοῦτο φρονεῖτε ἐν ὑμῖν ὃ καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.”
“Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus.”
Philippians 2:5.
Τοῦτο φρονεῖτε — touto phroneite.
Think this way.
Adopt this disposition.
Let this mindset shape you.
And whose mindset?
Not the mindset of the person with the strongest boundaries.
Not the person with the most impressive accomplishments.
Not the person with the cleanest reputation.
Not the person who has finally “leveled up.”
Jesus Christ.
And what does Paul immediately tell us about Him?

Christ, though existing in the form of God, did not exploit His equality with God for His own advantage, but emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.
The One who actually had every reason to be above us...
came down.
Think about that.
We spend so much energy climbing imaginary ladders above other sinners while the Lord of glory descended toward them.
We build status.
Jesus took the servant's place.
We protect our image.
Jesus accepted public shame.
We want to be recognized.
Jesus washed feet.
We want everybody to know our value.
Jesus allowed Himself to be mocked, stripped, beaten, rejected, and crucified.
The sinless One moved toward sinners.
The Holy One touched lepers.
The King ate with people respectable religion avoided.
And when Jesus encountered broken people, He never confused compassion with approval.
He could forgive without pretending sin was harmless.
He could love without lying.
He could say to the woman caught in adultery, “Neither do I condemn you,” and also, “go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11).
Grace and truth.
Mercy and holiness.
Compassion and repentance.
Jesus never needed contempt to maintain conviction.
Neither do we.
And maybe that is the line we desperately need to recover.
Standards determine what you permit. Superiority determines how you perceive.
Those are not the same thing.
You may have a standard that prevents someone from becoming your spouse.
That does not make that person worthless.
You may establish boundaries with a manipulative family member.
That does not give you permission to nurture hatred.
You may recognize serious theological error.
That does not make cruelty a fruit of the Spirit.
You may have grown beyond behaviors that once controlled you.
That does not mean the people still trapped there are beneath you.
Remember where Jesus found you.
Maybe your chains looked different.
Maybe your scandal was hidden.
Maybe nobody saw what happened in your mind.
Maybe your addiction never became public.
Maybe your bitterness looked respectable.
Maybe your lust stayed behind a screen.
Maybe your jealousy learned to smile.
Maybe your insecurity became ambition.
Maybe your need for validation became “excellence.”
Maybe your pride learned Christian vocabulary.
But Jesus knew.
Every thought.
Every motive.
Every secret.
Every compromise.
Every night you would never want projected onto a church screen.
Every failure buried beneath your reputation.
He knew the entire unedited story.
And still...
the cross.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus did not wait until sinners became impressive enough to deserve rescue.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not once we had our lives together.
Not once we became respectable.
Not once we reached His level.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
So how strange would it be to stand beneath a bloodstained cross, forgiven entirely by mercy, and begin sorting other sinners according to how far beneath us we think they are?
There are no self-made people at Calvary.
Only sinners and a Savior.
And this does not erase wisdom.
Please understand that.
Humility does not mean returning to an abusive relationship.
Forgiveness does not automatically mean restored trust.
Love does not mean enabling destructive behavior.
Christian compassion does not require abandoning biblical convictions.
Discernment matters.
Boundaries matter.
Truth matters.
Holiness matters.
But none of those things requires contempt.
You can have standards without having a throne.
Maybe that sentence needs to stay with you.
You can have standards without having a throne.
Because the throne was never yours.
Perhaps the person irritating you today is standing in a chapter you once occupied.
Perhaps the believer you consider immature is learning lessons God patiently taught you over years.
Perhaps the person whose failures embarrass you is living publicly through the kind of battle you were fortunate enough to fight privately.
Perhaps they really are wrong.
Perhaps your discernment is completely accurate.
And perhaps your heart toward them is still sinful.
Both things can be true.
That is what makes respectable pride so difficult to detect.
You can be correct about somebody...
and wrong before God in the way you hold your correctness.
Truth without humility can become a weapon for feeding the ego.
Paul understood this.

Galatians 6:1 tells believers that when someone is caught in transgression, those who are spiritual should restore that person “in a spirit of gentleness,” while watching themselves lest they too be tempted.
Not mock them.
Not publicly enjoy their collapse.
Not use their failure to demonstrate our superiority.
Restore them.
Gently.
While remembering:
I can fall too.
That sounds very different from the culture of public humiliation we have learned to consume.
Somebody falls, and everyone gathers.
Screenshots.
Reactions.
Comments.
Memes.
Whispers disguised as prayer requests.
And sometimes Christians participate while calling it “discernment.”
But imagine Jesus standing beside you while you talk about that person.
Would your tone change?
Would the joke still be funny?
Would you still share the screenshot?
Would you still enjoy exposing them?
Would you pray differently if you remembered that the blood you are depending upon for eternity is the same blood capable of cleansing the person you cannot stand?
This is where Christianity stops being branding and becomes crucifixion.
Not His crucifixion alone.
The death of our ego.
The death of our need to be above somebody.
The death of our addiction to comparison.
The death of that secret pleasure we experience when somebody else's failure makes our own life look cleaner.
And perhaps somebody reading this is realizing:
“I thought I was discerning. But somewhere along the way, I became proud.”
Then don't run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to repentance.
The Gospel does not say, “Discover how ugly your heart can be and then fix yourself.”
The Gospel says there is a Savior for proud people too.
Confess it.
Name it.
“Jesus, I have looked down on people You died to save.”
“Jesus, I have confused wisdom with superiority.”
“Jesus, I have enjoyed being right more than I have desired restoration.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And He is faithful.
First John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Grace reaches even here.
Even into respectable pride.
Even into religious pride.
Even into the heart that learned how to hide arrogance beneath sophisticated language.
That is what Jesus does.
He rewrites people.
Scandal becomes testimony.
Condemnation meets mercy.
Pride bows.
Shame loses its final word.
The sinner discovers grace.
And the forgiven learn to look at other sinners differently.
Not because sin suddenly stops mattering.
But because the cross reminds us that we needed rescue too.
So before you say someone is beneath your standards, ask yourself something harder:
Do my standards protect obedience to God...
or protect my sense of superiority?
When I establish boundaries, do I grieve for the person...
or secretly enjoy feeling above them?
When somebody falls, do I pray for restoration...
or become energized by the scandal?
When I notice someone's weakness, does it move me toward compassion...
or comparison?
When I say, “I know my worth,” do I mean my worth in Christ...
or have I begun using human beings as measuring sticks for my ego?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If God exposed something while you were reading this, don't turn the moment into shame. Turn it into surrender.
Somebody quietly fighting the same battle may need to know transformation is possible.
Not as a badge saying, “I know somebody who needs this.”
Share it first as a confession:
“I need this too.”
Leave changed.
Go back to Philippians 2.
Look again at Jesus.
The highest One descended.
The Holy One served.
The innocent One carried the cross.
The King humbled Himself.
And the Savior who had every right to condemn us chose to rescue everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
So keep your biblical convictions.
Keep wise boundaries.
Exercise discernment.
Pursue holiness.
But surrender the throne.
Because when grace has truly brought you to your knees at the foot of the cross, it becomes increasingly difficult to look down on somebody else.
You may have every reason to walk away from someone's behavior—but never forget that Jesus once walked toward a sinner like you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What If the Door You’re Begging God to Close Is the One You Keep Unlocking?
paragraphs: What If the Door You’re Begging God to Close Is the One You Keep Unlocking?
You keep asking God to deliver you from the temptation—but what if part of your deliverance requires finally surrendering the key?
There is a kind of prayer that can become painfully familiar.
“God, please take this away.”
You pray it after midnight.
You pray it after the relapse.
You pray it after deleting the messages.
After clearing the history.
After another argument.
After another compromise.
After another morning when you wake up carrying the sickening weight of something you promised Jesus—and yourself—you would never return to again.
“Lord, close this door.”
And maybe you mean it.
Maybe there are tears running down your face when you say it.
Maybe you hate what this pattern has done to you.
Maybe you genuinely love Jesus.
Maybe you are not playing games with God at all.
But there is a frightening question we sometimes avoid asking:
What if the door you are begging God to close is the same door you keep unlocking?
What if you are asking God to remove a temptation while quietly preserving your easiest route back to it?
That question is uncomfortable because it takes temptation out of the realm of vague spiritual warfare and brings it painfully close to our choices.
The contact is still saved.
The private account still exists.
The app is still installed.
The relationship still has secret access to you.
The bottle is still within reach.
The website is still bookmarked.
The conversation you know always crosses the line keeps restarting.
The place that weakens you remains part of your routine.
The person who pulls you away from Christ still gets the version of you nobody else sees.
The resentment is still being rehearsed.
The fantasy is still being fed.
The excuse is still available.
And somewhere between “God, deliver me” and “just one more time,” we can find ourselves standing at a door Jesus is teaching us to flee from while our own hand is still wrapped around the handle.
Paul's words to Timothy are startlingly practical:
“τὰς δὲ νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας φεῦγε, δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην, πίστιν, ἀγάπην, εἰρήνην…”
“Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace…” — 2 Timothy 2:22
Look carefully at those two commands.
φεῦγε — pheuge.
Flee.
And then:
δίωκε — diōke.
Pursue.
Paul does not tell Timothy merely to stand beside temptation and prove how spiritually strong he is.
He tells him to flee one direction and pursue another.

The Greek text places these ideas in striking contrast: flee youthful desires; pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace. Both φεῦγε and δίωκε are imperative verbs—commands. The Christian response to temptation therefore isn't merely saying “no” to something destructive. It involves actively running toward what is holy.
That changes the question.
Maybe victory does not always look like standing three inches away from your old bondage and demonstrating that you can resist it.
Sometimes victory looks like running.
Sometimes holiness looks embarrassingly practical.
Block the number.
Delete the account.
Leave the room.
End the secret conversation.
Change the route.
Tell somebody.
Stop calling the relationship “complicated” when you know it continually pulls you away from obedience to Christ.
Stop keeping souvenirs from a life you keep asking Jesus to rescue you from.
Not because deleting an app can save your soul.
Not because blocking a person makes you righteous.
Not because Christianity is behavior modification.
Jesus saves.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus transforms.
But grace was never permission to construct a comfortable pathway back toward the chains Christ is calling us to leave.
There is an important distinction here.
Being tempted is not identical to sinning.
Jesus Himself “has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
So do not condemn yourself merely because temptation knocks.
The issue is what happens when you begin preparing a room for it.

James describes desire progressing toward sin when desire is allowed to conceive, and sin eventually bringing forth death (James 1:14–15). Scripture therefore gives us something far wiser than the modern fantasy that mature believers should be able to expose themselves indefinitely to temptation without consequences.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray:
“Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”
And Paul told Timothy:
Flee.
There are battles God never commanded you to fight while standing in the enemy's bedroom.
There are fires you do not conquer by repeatedly putting your hand near the flame.
There are temptations you do not defeat by studying how close you can get without technically falling.
You flee.
Joseph understood this before Timothy ever read Paul's letter.
When Potiphar's wife grabbed his garment and demanded that he sleep with her, Joseph did not stay for a theological debate.
Genesis 39 says he left his garment in her hand and fled.
He lost the coat.
But he kept his integrity.
Somebody reading this has been trying desperately to keep both.
You want purity without losing the relationship.
You want freedom without deleting the access.
You want peace without surrendering the habit.
You want Jesus without disappointing the crowd.
You want healing without exposing the secret.
You want the Promised Land while keeping Egypt's phone number.
And perhaps that is why this hurts.
Because deep down, you already know which door this article is talking about.
You knew before you reached this sentence.
There is probably a name attached to it.
A face.
A website.
A substance.
A memory.
A conversation.
A hidden folder.
A private account.
An environment.
An emotional attachment.
A recurring hour of the night when your convictions become negotiable.
You keep calling it your weakness.
But perhaps part of the problem is that you have also kept it accessible.
And if that exposes something hidden in you, don't run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Not because a comment earns forgiveness.
It doesn't.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light begins with finally refusing to disguise it.
And please understand this before shame twists everything I am saying.
The Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up so Jesus will finally love you.”
The Gospel is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
The cross was not God's reward for people who successfully defeated all their temptations.
The cross was God's rescue for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Jesus did not bleed because you were impressive.
He bled because you were lost.
He did not rise from the grave merely to make badly behaved people more respectable.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
Repentance, therefore, is not purchasing God's mercy.
It is the turning of a heart that has encountered mercy.
Grace does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your sin mattered so much that Christ bore judgment for sinners—and His mercy is so great that your sin does not have to remain your master.”
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Not privately in his imagination.
Publicly.
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine carrying that memory.
Imagine hearing your own voice denying the One you once promised you would never abandon.
Imagine seeing Jesus again after the resurrection.
Peter's failure was real.
But Peter's failure did not become the final sentence of Peter's story.
Jesus restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
And the man who had collapsed under fear was recommissioned to care for Christ's sheep.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not call darkness light.
He does something infinitely better.
He enters the darkness and brings sinners into light.
So if you fell again last night, hear this carefully:
Do not use grace as an excuse to remain there.
But do not use your failure as an excuse to stay away from Christ either.
Come back.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Then get up and flee.
Maybe you have prayed, “Jesus, forgive me,” a hundred times over the same sin.
Come again.
First John 1:9 anchors our hope in God's faithfulness and righteousness to forgive those who confess their sins and to cleanse them from unrighteousness.
But confession and repentance should not become a ritual that protects the very arrangement repeatedly leading you toward compromise.
If you know the bridge keeps carrying you back toward destruction, eventually you have to ask why you keep repairing the bridge.
And there is another part of 2 Timothy 2:22 we often overlook.
Paul does not merely say flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace.
He continues:
“…μετὰ τῶν ἐπικαλουμένων τὸν κύριον ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας.”
“…along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.”
Along with.
Christian holiness was never designed as solitary warfare.
Paul doesn't picture Timothy running alone.
He tells him what to flee, what to pursue, and whom to pursue it with.
Maybe that is the missing piece.
You have been fighting privately.
Falling privately.
Crying privately.
Repenting privately.
Promising privately.
Then repeating privately.
Nobody knows.
Nobody asks.
Nobody can call you at 11:47 p.m. and say, “Don't go back.”
Nobody knows the password.
Nobody knows the relationship exists.
Nobody knows why you suddenly disappear.
Nobody knows what “I'm fine” is hiding.
And secrecy has become the greenhouse where temptation keeps growing.
You may need another believer.
A mature Christian friend.
A pastor.
A spouse, where appropriate.
An accountability partner.
Someone who loves Jesus enough to care more about your holiness than your ability to appear impressive.
Someone who can help you pursue righteousness when every part of your flesh wants to turn around.
Because sometimes the sentence “I need help” is one of the bravest sentences a Christian can speak.
And maybe you are not the person trapped in the cycle.
Maybe you are watching somebody you love keep returning.
Your son.
Your daughter.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your friend.
Your brother.
Your sister.
Someone who keeps crying over the same thing and then walking back toward it.
You don't know what else to say.
You are exhausted from watching.
Send them this article.
Not as an accusation.
Not with “SEE? I TOLD YOU.”
Send it with tenderness.
Say:
“I love you too much to watch this keep destroying you. I will walk with you toward Jesus.”
They may never tell you that this reached them.
Share it anyway.
That share may become somebody else's interruption.
Because temptation has a strange ability to make yesterday's convictions feel distant.
Save it so you can remember:
God didn't call you merely to admire freedom.
He called you to flee what enslaves and pursue what is righteous.
And if you fell again?
Come home.
The prodigal son rehearsed his speech while returning from the far country, but the father saw him while he was still far away and ran toward him.
That parable does not make rebellion harmless.
The far country cost the son dearly.
But the father's compassion tells us something breathtaking about the heart of God toward the repentant.
You may smell like the place you just escaped.
Come home.
You may be embarrassed that this is the seventh time.
Come home.
You may feel unworthy even to pray.
Come home.
You may have shattered promises you once made with tears.
Come home.
But this time, don't pack the key to the far country in your pocket.
Bring it to Jesus.
Lay down the access.
Lay down the excuses.
Lay down the backup plan.
Lay down the secret.
Lay down the fantasy that someday you will become so spiritually powerful that you can safely play with the thing that keeps devouring you.
Flee.
Then pursue.
Not emptiness.
Not mere restriction.
Pursue Christ.
Pursue righteousness.
Pursue faith.
Pursue love.
Pursue peace.
Pursue fellowship with believers who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.
Christianity is not ultimately about spending your life staring backward at everything you are forbidden to touch.
There is Someone ahead of you worth running toward.
Jesus Christ.
The One who was tempted yet without sin.
The One who welcomed sinners without blessing their sin.
The One who carried our guilt to Calvary.
The One who was crucified.
Buried.
Raised.
The One who still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness that cannot be purchased.
The One who can take the chapter you are ashamed of and refuse to let it become the title of your entire life.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
But by redeeming people who could never rewrite themselves.
Your testimony may become hope for the person convinced that change is impossible.
Stay close to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment that keeps pointing us back to Jesus Christ.

Supporting Gospel-centered ministry should never be treated as buying God's favor, earning spiritual merit, or proving that you love Him. Salvation is God's gift of grace in Christ, not a transaction.
But believers can glorify God through generous, willing support of Gospel work and through sharing truth with others.
Do something about the door.
And then examine your own hand.
Because perhaps you have spent months asking God why the door keeps opening...
when somewhere deep inside, you already know where you hid the key.
Give Jesus the key.
Run from what keeps dragging you backward.
Run toward the Savior whose grace is greater than the chapter you wish you could erase.
The door back to bondage may still remember your name—but you don't have to answer when it calls.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TORAH FORBADE SEX WITH YOUR FATHER’S WIFE—Why Did Scripture Need to Say This?
paragraphs: THE TORAH FORBADE SEX WITH YOUR FATHER’S WIFE—Why Did Scripture Need to Say This?
One disturbing sentence in Leviticus exposes something terrifying about human desire—and something breathtaking about the God who refuses to leave sinners in darkness.
There are Bible verses we underline.
There are verses we frame.
There are verses we whisper over hospital beds and repeat when life is falling apart.
And then there are verses like this one.
You read it.
You stop.
You read it again.
And somewhere inside you, an uncomfortable question forms:
Why did God even have to say that?
Leviticus 18:8 reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא
‘Erwat eshet-avikha lo tegalleh; ‘erwat avikha hi.
Literally, the Hebrew says:
“The nakedness of your father’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your father’s nakedness.”
Not a comfortable sentence.
Not a verse likely to appear on a coffee mug.
But perhaps that discomfort is exactly why we need to hear it.
Because buried inside this prohibition is a devastating truth about humanity:
God gives commands in a world where human beings are capable of crossing boundaries we sometimes imagine nobody would ever cross.
And Scripture refuses to pretend otherwise.
That may be one reason Leviticus can feel so painfully modern.
It does not write about humanity as we wish humanity were.
It speaks into humanity as humanity actually is.
Broken.
Desiring.
Self-justifying.
Capable of tenderness one moment and betrayal the next.
Capable of protecting a family—and capable of destroying one.

Leviticus 18 does not emerge from a fantasy world populated by morally uncomplicated people. God was forming Israel as His covenant people among nations whose practices Israel was explicitly commanded not to imitate. The chapter repeatedly establishes boundaries around sexual relationships and family relationships.
And then comes verse 8.
Your father’s wife is forbidden to you.
Notice the wording carefully.
The Hebrew says אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ — eshet avikha: “your father’s wife.”

The wording matters because the previous verse has already addressed the nakedness of one’s father and mother. Verse 8 specifically addresses the wife of one’s father, naturally encompassing the situation of a stepmother or another woman occupying that marital relationship to the father.
Then comes the startling explanation:
עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא — ‘erwat avikha hi.
“It is your father’s nakedness.”
In other words, sexual boundaries in Scripture are not merely about two bodies wanting something.
Relationships exist inside relationships.
Sex is never as isolated as sinful desire wants us to believe.
That is where this ancient command suddenly walks into the twenty-first century and sits beside us.
Because our culture loves one particular question:
“Do they both want it?”
Scripture asks deeper questions.
What covenant is being violated?
Whose trust is being betrayed?
What family is being wounded?
What boundary established by God is being crossed?
What does this desire do to another person?
And ultimately:
What does God say?
Sin has always tried to reduce morality to appetite.
“I want this.”
“I need this.”
“This makes me happy.”
“Nobody understands our relationship.”
“We love each other.”
“It’s complicated.”
But one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable revelations is that desire does not become holy simply because desire feels powerful.
You can desperately want something God has forbidden.
That sentence may hurt.
It may also save somebody.
Because some of the most destructive decisions of our lives begin when we quietly rename desire as destiny.
We feel something intensely, therefore we assume it must be authentic.
We experience attraction, therefore we assume pursuing it must be right.
We discover an opportunity, therefore we interpret the opportunity as permission.
But temptation often arrives carrying a counterfeit permission slip.
The existence of desire is not proof of divine approval.
And Leviticus 18 refuses to negotiate with desire when desire demands what belongs beyond God's boundary.
But here is where the passage becomes even more disturbing.
God apparently considered the warning necessary.
Think about that.
Why command people not to do something unless fallen human beings are capable of doing it?
The Bible understands us better than our carefully edited public lives suggest.
Scripture knows what human beings can become when desire is allowed to dethrone God.
And biblical history proves it.
Reuben went into Bilhah, his father Jacob’s concubine. Genesis records the act with painful brevity. Later, Jacob remembered it as the defiling of his bed.
Generations later, Absalom publicly went in to his father David’s concubines in an act loaded not merely with sexuality but humiliation, rebellion, and political domination.
Then we arrive in the New Testament.
And suddenly Leviticus 18:8 no longer feels ancient.
Paul writes to the church at Corinth that sexual immorality is being reported among them—specifically that a man has his father’s wife.
Read that again.
This wasn't happening in a pagan temple somewhere outside the church.
It was happening among people associated with the Christian community.
The scandal of Leviticus had walked straight into Corinth.
And perhaps the most frightening part of 1 Corinthians 5 is not merely that the sexual sin existed.
The church had apparently learned to coexist with it.
Paul expected grief.
Instead, there was pride.
That should frighten every generation of Christians.
Because there is something worse than falling into sin.
It is becoming comfortable enough with sin that repentance begins sounding offensive.
There is something worse than having darkness inside us.
It is redecorating the darkness and calling it freedom.
We rename lust “authenticity.”
We rename compromise “complexity.”
We rename cowardice “tolerance.”
We rename rebellion “being true to myself.”
And eventually we can become so skilled at changing vocabulary that we forget changing the name of a sin cannot change its nature before God.
Yet before you point toward somebody else’s scandal...
wait.
Because Leviticus 18 is holding a mirror, not handing you binoculars.
Maybe you have never touched your father’s wife.
Maybe the thought horrifies you.
But have you ever crossed a boundary you once swore you would never cross?
Have you ever deleted a conversation because you knew somebody should not see it?
Have you ever entertained an attraction you knew needed to die?
Have you ever kept returning mentally to something you knew dishonored Christ?
Have you ever called something “harmless” because admitting what it really was would require repentance?
Have you ever hidden behind “God knows my heart” while deliberately ignoring something God had already said?
Have you ever discovered that the person you thought you could never become was not as far away as you imagined?
That is where the self-righteous reader suddenly becomes quiet.
Because the Gospel does not divide humanity into scandalous sinners and respectable people.
It tells us that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Different histories.
Different temptations.
Different consequences.
Different scars.
Same desperate need for a Savior.
And this is where we must be careful.
Grace does not mean God suddenly stops caring about holiness.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could make peace with the very sin from which He came to save us.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace is God doing something unimaginably costly about evil.
The cross proves simultaneously that our sin is worse than we wanted to admit...
and God's mercy is greater than we dared to hope.
Look at Jesus.
The One who never crossed the Father's boundary.
The One who never surrendered to temptation.
The One who never used another person's body for selfish gratification.
The One who never betrayed covenant faithfulness.
The One who remained perfectly obedient...
walked willingly toward a cross occupied by sinners.
There the Holy One was stripped.
Mocked.
Shamed.
Crucified.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of the spotless Lamb of God.
And that changes the way we read Leviticus.
The commandments reveal God's holiness.
They expose human rebellion.
But the biblical story does not end with the sinner standing exposed.
It moves toward Christ.
Toward Calvary.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward forgiveness offered to people whose stories cannot be cleaned up with public relations.
That includes sexual sinners.
Adulterers.
The sexually immoral.
The secretly addicted.
The ashamed.
The hypocrite who finally admits he has been pretending.
The woman carrying memories she cannot erase.
The man who wishes he could travel backward ten years and make one different decision.
The person reading this article while thinking:
“If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.”
Jesus already knows.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the Sunday version.
Everything.
And the Gospel invitation still stands:
Repent.
Come into the light.
Turn from sin.
Come to Christ.
Receive mercy.
This does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every wound we created, restore every relationship we shattered, or remove every responsibility created by our actions.
But in Jesus Christ, guilt does not have to become your eternal identity.
Your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire story.
That is the heartbeat behind these words:
Not because scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes people who were hiding and teaches them to walk in light.
He takes people enslaved by desire and teaches them obedience.
He takes people drowning in shame and clothes them in grace.
He takes people who spent years saying, “This is just who I am,” and begins transforming them into people who can finally say, “That is who I was—but Christ met me there.”
This is why biblical boundaries are not the enemy of love.
God does not establish sexual boundaries because He hates human flourishing.
The God who designed covenant, family, sexuality, faithfulness, and the human body knows what happens when desire consumes everything in its path.
A guardrail beside a cliff is not hatred.
Sometimes the boundary is there precisely because somebody knows how far the fall goes.
Maybe that is the answer to our original question.
Why did Scripture need to say this?
Because human beings need boundaries.
Because desire can become destructive.
Because families can be violated.
Because sin can persuade us to cross lines we once thought unthinkable.
Because God's people are not immune to scandal.
Because holiness must be taught.
Because repentance must remain possible.
And because God loves human beings enough to tell us no when our desires are leading us toward destruction.
But there is another reason this verse matters.
Someone reading this is not identifying with the sinner in the story.
You are identifying with the wounded family.
Somebody crossed a boundary against you.
Somebody else's appetite became your trauma.
Somebody who should have protected your home shattered it.
Maybe the scandal wasn't yours.
Maybe the scar was.
Hear this carefully:
What happened in your family does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's restoration.
The Gospel never requires us to pretend evil was good.
Forgiveness is not calling darkness light.
Grace does not require rewriting evil as innocence.
Jesus can meet people inside histories they never chose.
He can restore what shame tried to steal.
He can teach the wounded that another person's sin does not have authority to define their worth.

And if this subject touches abuse, coercion, exploitation, or criminal behavior, spiritual language should never be used to silence victims or obstruct appropriate protection, reporting, accountability, or justice.
Biblical grace and truthful accountability are not enemies.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners also brings darkness into light.
So perhaps tonight the question is no longer:
“Why did God have to command something so obvious?”
Perhaps the question has become:
What boundary of God have I been slowly teaching myself to ignore?
That is a much harder question.
Don't answer publicly if doing so would expose private details or endanger you.
But answer God.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary.
No excuses.
Just truth.
“Jesus, this is where I have been hiding.”
That prayer may become the beginning of a completely different story.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people learning where to bring them.
And please don't turn this article into ammunition for humiliating someone whose scandal is more visible than yours.
Not as a purchase of God's favor. Never.
Grace cannot be bought.
But one practical way believers can help Gospel-centered work continue is by willingly supporting the work and sharing biblical teaching with others.
You cannot buy forgiveness.
You cannot merchandise your way into holiness.
You cannot financially support enough Christian work to erase one sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Come to Him.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what darkness has been protecting.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make restitution where restitution is possible and appropriate.
Walk away from what Christ is calling you to leave.
And receive the grace you could never earn.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing about Leviticus 18 is not that human beings were capable of crossing horrifying boundaries.
We already know what humanity can do.
The greater wonder is that the God who knew exactly how deep human corruption could descend still chose to pursue sinners with redemption.
The Bible knows our scandals.
Calvary proves God did too.
And still...
Jesus came.
The boundary you crossed may explain the scar—but it does not have to write the ending when your story is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOUR NAME BE BLOTTED OUT OF THE BOOK OF LIFE?
paragraphs: CAN YOUR NAME BE BLOTTED OUT OF THE BOOK OF LIFE?
The terrifying question behind Revelation 3:5—and the promise of Jesus that should make every pretending Christian examine what they are trusting before eternity arrives.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can make a Christian stop breathing for a moment.
Not because it says hell exists.
Not because it says judgment is coming.
But because Jesus speaks about a name…
a book…
and the possibility of being blotted out.
Maybe you have read the verse before and hurried past it because you did not know what to do with it.
Maybe someone used it to frighten you.
Maybe someone else assured you there was absolutely nothing to think about.
But perhaps the question has followed you into quieter places:
Can someone's name actually be blotted out of the Book of Life?
And beneath that theological question may be a much more personal one.
Could it happen to me?
If you have failed God after promising Him you would change…
if you have fallen into the same sin you once wept over…
if your prayer life has become almost nonexistent…
if nobody at church knows what you have been doing privately…
if you still call yourself a Christian but somewhere inside you know your heart has grown cold…
then this is not merely an interesting question about Revelation.
It feels like your name is being discussed.
And that is why we cannot answer it with slogans.
We have to open the Scriptures.
Jesus says to the church in Sardis:
“Ὁ νικῶν… καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐξαλείψω τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἐκ τῆς βίβλου τῆς ζωῆς…”
Ho nikōn… kai ou mē exaleipsō to onoma autou ek tēs biblou tēs zōēs…
“The one who conquers… I will never blot his name out of the book of life…”
—Revelation 3:5
Look closely.
The Greek verb translated “blot out” is ἐξαλείψω — exaleipsō, from exaleiphō.
It carries the idea of wiping away, erasing, obliterating.
But something incredibly important appears immediately before it:
οὐ μὴ — ou mē.
Greek can express negation in several ways, but this combination gives the statement emphatic force.
Jesus is not casually saying, “I probably won't erase his name.”
He gives the conqueror a promise:
I will certainly not blot out his name.
And He does not stop there.
He says He will confess that person's name before His Father and before His angels.
Think about that.
The Christian's ultimate hope is not merely that your name survives some heavenly administrative process.
Your hope is Jesus Christ Himself.
The One who knows everything about you is the One promising to acknowledge His people before heaven.
But before turning that promise into a theological slogan, we need to hear the entire message Jesus gave Sardis.
Because Sardis had a frightening problem.
They had a reputation for being alive.
Jesus said they were dead.
Imagine that church.
People knew the songs.
They knew when to stand.
They knew Christian vocabulary.
Their reputation looked healthy enough that other people thought spiritual life was present.
But Christ saw underneath the reputation.
That means it is possible to convince people that you are spiritually alive while Jesus sees something entirely different.
And suddenly Revelation 3 is no longer about somebody else.
People who say “God is good” publicly while secretly becoming comfortable with what nailed Christ to the cross.
People who learned how to look Christian before they learned how desperately they need Christ.
Maybe nobody suspects you.
But Jesus does not examine profiles.
He examines hearts.
And His words to Sardis were not:
“Try harder to protect your image.”
They were:
Wake up.
Remember.
Keep what you received.
Repent.
That word still cuts through two thousand years of religious camouflage:
Repent.
Not perform.
Not pretend.
Not hide.
Repent.
Yet Revelation 3 is not the first place Scripture speaks about a divine book.
Centuries earlier, Israel committed catastrophic rebellion at Sinai. While Moses was with God, the people made a golden calf.
Moses then interceded for them with astonishing language:
“וְאִם־אַיִן מְחֵנִי נָא מִסִּפְרְךָ אֲשֶׁר כָּתָבְתָּ”
Ve'im-ayin, mecheni na misifrecha asher katavta.
In context:
“If not, please blot me out of your book that you have written.”
—Exodus 32:32
The Hebrew expression מְחֵנִי — mecheni comes from the verb machah, meaning to wipe out or blot out.
God answers Moses:
“Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book.”
—Exodus 32:33
So yes—the language of blotting someone from God's book really is biblical.
But we must not carelessly assume that every biblical reference to God's “book” describes precisely the same theological concept in precisely the same way.
Scripture uses book imagery in several contexts: divine remembrance, earthly life, judgment, and eternal life.
That distinction matters.
Psalm 69:28 speaks of names being blotted out of “the book of the living.”
Daniel 12:1 speaks of God's people being delivered, everyone found written in the book.
Jesus tells His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
Paul speaks about fellow workers “whose names are in the book of life.”
And Revelation brings the imagery to its terrifying final horizon.
John sees the dead standing before God's throne.
Books are opened.
Then another book.
The Book of Life.
And Revelation 20:15 gives one of the most sobering sentences ever written:
Anyone whose name was not found written in the Book of Life was thrown into the lake of fire.
So we must not turn this subject into theological entertainment.
Eternity is involved.
But here we need humility, because faithful Christians have historically understood some of these passages differently.

Some understand Revelation 3:5 primarily as a promise of preservation: Christ is assuring genuine believers that their names will never be removed. On this reading, the verse is meant to comfort the persevering saints rather than describe genuine believers losing salvation.
Others understand the warning passages as indicating that apostasy is a genuine danger and that believers must continue in persevering faith rather than abandon Christ.
Still others distinguish between various biblical “book” passages, arguing that some refer to physical life or covenant membership while Revelation's Book of Life concerns final salvation.
We should not pretend those differences do not exist.
But something far more important can get lost while Christians fight over theological systems.
Every orthodox reading leaves you facing the same Christ.
Do not play games with Jesus.
The Bible never teaches you to stare at the Book of Life trying to discover invisible heavenly handwriting.
It tells you where to look.
Look to Christ.
Jesus said:
Notice the relationship.
They hear Him.
He knows them.
They follow Him.
He gives them eternal life.
Christian assurance is not found by saying:
“I prayed something once, therefore I can now live however I want.”
Neither is assurance found by endlessly inspecting yourself until anxiety destroys every trace of joy.

Assurance rests finally in Jesus Christ—His finished work, His promise, His grace—and genuine faith does not make peace with rebellion. The Spirit produces perseverance, repentance, obedience, and fruit in the lives of Christ's people.
Not sinless perfection.
But a new direction.
There is an enormous difference.
Peter denied Jesus.
Judas betrayed Jesus.
From a distance, both men catastrophically failed.
But their stories did not end the same way.
Peter wept.
Peter returned.
Peter was restored.
Peter discovered something every wounded believer needs to remember:
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when Jesus Christ holds the pen.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin is insignificant.
Sin was so serious that the Son of God was crucified.
Not that judgment is imaginary.
Christ Himself warned about judgment.
Not that repentance earns salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
The Gospel is that guilty sinners who could never cleanse themselves are reconciled to God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Christ carried sin.
Christ satisfied judgment.
Christ conquered death.
Christ rose.
And sinners who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive what they could never purchase:
forgiveness.
righteousness.
reconciliation.
life.
Maybe this is where the article stops being about “someone.”
Because you know why you clicked.
You were not merely curious about the Book of Life.
Something inside you has been afraid.
Maybe you have been wondering whether you wandered too far.
Maybe you returned to pornography after begging God to deliver you.
Maybe bitterness has been living inside you so long that it almost feels normal.
Maybe your marriage is collapsing.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe addiction came back.
Maybe you stopped praying because every prayer felt hypocritical.
Maybe you have spent years convincing everyone else that you are okay.
And now you are wondering whether Jesus could possibly still want you.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
The invitation of Christ is not:
“Clean yourself enough to become worthy of Me.”
It is:
Come.
Come exposed.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come without excuses.
Come without pretending.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
The same Jesus who confronted deadness in Sardis also commanded that church to wake up.
Why?
Because warning itself can be mercy.
When a smoke alarm screams in the middle of the night, you do not curse it for destroying your peace.
You thank God it woke you before the fire consumed the house.
Maybe this article is an alarm.
Not condemnation telling you there is no hope.
Mercy telling you:
Wake up.
You are still hearing His Word.
Stop hiding.
Confess what you have been protecting.
Turn from what is killing you.
Run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
Because the Gospel does something scandalous.
It takes people with histories they would erase if they could…
and gives them futures they could never deserve.
The adulterer can be forgiven.
The addict can be restored.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can be humbled.
The sexually broken can be made holy.
The religious hypocrite can finally stop performing.
The prodigal can come home.
Not because grace says sin does not matter.
Because Jesus paid a price sinners could never pay.
This is why our theme remains:
Your scandal does not shock Him.
Your hidden chapter does not surprise Him.
Your failure was not discovered by Jesus this morning.
He knew exactly what kind of sinner He was calling when He called you.
But grace is not permission to remain where He found you.
Grace rescues.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace takes us toward holiness because the Savior who forgives us also becomes our Lord.
So can someone's name be blotted out of the Book of Life?
Scripture undeniably uses blotting language, and we should never erase the Bible's warnings in an attempt to make Christianity comfortable.
But Revelation 3:5 itself places a magnificent promise on the lips of Jesus:
The conqueror will not be blotted out.
The verse does not invite faithful Christians to spend their lives terrified that Jesus is standing over heaven's ledger with an eraser waiting for one bad day.
It calls the church to wake up, repent, hold fast, and overcome.
And Revelation itself tells us how God's people overcome:
through the Lamb.
Christian victory ultimately belongs to people who cling to the victorious Christ.
So perhaps the question you need tonight is not:
“Can I calculate exactly when a name could be erased?”
Perhaps it is:
Do I belong to Jesus Christ?
Not:
“Does my family think I'm Christian?”
Not:
“Was I baptized?”
Not:
Not:
“Did I once walk down an aisle?”
But:
Am I trusting Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord?
Is there repentance?
Is there faith?
When you fall, do you run toward Christ or make peace with your chains?
Do you want Jesus Himself—or merely enough religion to quiet your fear of hell?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
Let them be.
Some discomfort saves us from much greater destruction.
And if your heart is breaking because you know you have wandered, do not interpret conviction as proof that you should run farther away.
Run home.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
There is mercy at the feet of Jesus.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is restoration for prodigals.
There is grace for the ashamed.
There is a cross for sinners.
There is an empty tomb for people who thought their story was already over.
And there is a Savior whose final word over His redeemed people is greater than the darkest word in their past.
There may be somebody scrolling tonight who would never walk into a church.
Somebody hiding an addiction.
Somebody thinking God could never forgive them.
Somebody one decision away from walking away from the faith.
But after all the Greek words…
after all the theological arguments…
after all the debates about whether a name can be blotted out…
there is something I do not want you to miss.
One day your Facebook account will disappear.
Your photographs will eventually fade.
Your possessions will belong to somebody else.
People who knew your name will themselves pass into eternity.
And when every earthly reputation has vanished, the question will not be whether people knew you as a Christian.
The question will be whether you belong to Christ.
So do not spend your life protecting a reputation while neglecting your soul.
Wake up.
Repent.
Come to Jesus.
And when shame whispers that your scandal has written the final sentence of your life, remember this:
The ink of your darkest chapter is not stronger than the blood of the Lamb.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PEREZ AND ZERAH WERE BORN FROM ONE OF GENESIS’ MOST SCANDALOUS SEXUAL ENCOUNTERS—THEN PEREZ ENTERED JESUS’ GENEALOGY
paragraphs: PEREZ AND ZERAH WERE BORN FROM ONE OF GENESIS’ MOST SCANDALOUS SEXUAL ENCOUNTERS—THEN PEREZ ENTERED JESUS’ GENEALOGY

There is a woman disguised beside a road. A grieving widower carrying his own failures. A sexual encounter neither of them will ever forget. A pregnancy. A public accusation. A death sentence. A scarlet thread tied around a tiny wrist. And generations later, one of the children conceived in that shattered story appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
There are chapters of the Bible we love to frame.
Genesis 38 is usually not one of them.
It is uncomfortable.
Complicated.
Painfully human.
And if we are honest, it contains exactly the kind of family history most people would rather delete before anyone else discovered it.
Yet when Matthew opens his Gospel and begins recording the human ancestry of Jesus Christ, he does something astonishing.
He does not hide this family.
He names it.
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar...” (Matthew 1:3).
Tamar.
Perez.
Zerah.
There they are.
Not erased.
Not sanitized.
Not buried underneath generations of respectable names.
Right there on the opening page of the New Testament.
And once you understand what happened in Genesis 38, those few words in Matthew can stop you cold.
Because Perez did not come from a neat story.
He came through a scandal.
And somehow...
the story kept moving toward Jesus.
That does not mean God approved of everything that happened.
Grace never requires us to rename sin as righteousness.
It means something far more beautiful:
human sin and human wreckage were not powerful enough to derail the redemptive purpose of God.
Maybe that is why this story feels so personal.
Because some of us have things in our history we desperately wish we could rewrite.
A relationship.
A night.
A betrayal.
A secret.
A divorce.
A pregnancy.
An addiction.
A lie.
Something done to us.
Something done by us.
Something carrying consequences long after everybody stopped talking about it.
You can smile in church while still wondering whether your worst chapter has quietly disqualified you from ever becoming useful to God again.
Then Matthew whispers a name.
Perez.
And suddenly an ancient genealogy starts sounding like good news.
Tamar's story begins in grief.

She married Judah's son Er, but Genesis says Er was wicked before the LORD and died. According to the family obligation operating in the narrative, Judah's next son, Onan, was expected to preserve his deceased brother's line through Tamar. Instead, Onan deliberately prevented the offspring from being raised for his brother. Genesis condemns his conduct, and he also died.
Tamar had now lost two husbands.
Judah then told her to remain a widow until his younger son Shelah grew up.
She waited.
And waited.
Shelah grew.
But Judah did not give him to Tamar.
That detail matters because Genesis itself later gives Judah's confession.
After everything exploded into the open, Judah said of Tamar:
“She is more righteous than I.”
The Hebrew is even more striking:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי — tsadqah mimmeni
In context, the sense is that Tamar was more in the right than Judah concerning what had happened. Judah himself explains why: he had failed to give her his son Shelah.
This does not turn every action in Genesis 38 into a model Christians should imitate.
It does something more honest.
It exposes Judah.
The man who would soon be ready to condemn Tamar had failed in his own responsibility toward her.
Then Judah's wife died.
After his mourning, Judah traveled toward Timnah for the shearing of his sheep.
Tamar heard he was coming.
She removed her widow's clothing, covered herself with a veil, and positioned herself where Judah would pass.
Judah saw her.
He did not recognize his own daughter-in-law.
He believed her to be a prostitute and propositioned her.
Tamar asked what he would give her.
A young goat, Judah promised.
But Tamar wanted a pledge until payment arrived.
His seal.
His cord.
His staff.
Personal objects.
Identifying objects.
Evidence.
Then the encounter happened.
Tamar conceived.
And Judah walked away without realizing that the woman with whom he had just slept was the daughter-in-law whom he had failed.
The story could almost disappear there.
Except sin and secrecy have a way of colliding with daylight.
About three months later, word reached Judah.
Tamar was pregnant.
And Judah's response was terrifying.
He demanded that she be brought out for judgment.
Imagine the scene.
A pregnant woman accused publicly.
The same man who had participated in the act did not yet know he was condemning the woman carrying his children.
And this is where Genesis 38 becomes almost unbearably human.
Because hypocrisy is often most confident before it recognizes itself in the evidence.
Tamar did not deliver a long speech.
She produced the objects.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
Then came essentially one devastating question:
Whose are these?
Judah looked.
And the courtroom inside his own heart collapsed.
He recognized them.
His property.
His evidence.
His sin.
His failure.
The man pointing outward suddenly had nowhere left to point.
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי.”
She is more in the right than I.
There is something here every believer needs to hear.
Repentance begins when we stop editing the evidence.
When we stop explaining why our sin was understandable.
When we stop measuring ourselves against somebody who looks worse.
When we stop asking, “What did they do?”
and finally ask,
“Lord... what have I done?”
Judah's confession did not erase the past.
But the story did not end with his exposure.
Tamar was carrying twins.
During childbirth, one baby stretched out his hand. The midwife tied a scarlet thread around his wrist to mark him as the one who appeared to be emerging first.
That child was Zerah.
The Hebrew text says:
וַתִּקְשֹׁר עַל־יָדוֹ שָׁנִי
The midwife tied shani—scarlet/crimson—upon his hand.
There was the little hand.
There was the scarlet marker.
There was the apparent firstborn.
Except the birth suddenly changed.
The hand withdrew.
His brother broke through first.
Genesis preserves the midwife's startled words:
מַה־פָּרַצְתָּ עָלֶיךָ פָּרֶץ
The wording plays directly on the Hebrew root פרץ — p-r-ts, associated with breaking or bursting through.
And the child was called:
פָּרֶץ — Peretz/Perez.
A breach.
A breaking through.
A child breaking unexpectedly into the world from a story already fractured by death, deception, sexual sin, neglect, hypocrisy, grief, and public shame.
Perez came first.
Then Zerah emerged with the scarlet thread still on his hand.
If Genesis 38 were merely a human scandal, perhaps we would expect the Bible to leave these people there.
But Scripture does something extraordinary.
It keeps following Perez.
Perez fathered Hezron.
The generations continued.
Eventually the line reached David.
Then centuries passed.
Kings rose.
Kings fell.
Jerusalem burned.
Exile came.
Generations lived and died.
Then Matthew opened the story of Jesus Christ.
And there it was:
Judah.
Tamar.
Perez.
Matthew could have simply written Judah and Perez.
Instead, Tamar is explicitly remembered.
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar...”
The scandal is not airbrushed out of the Messiah's genealogy.
It is remembered inside the story that leads to Him.
Do not misunderstand what this means.
Jesus did not come because sin was harmless.
Jesus came because sin is devastating.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The cross declares exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the spotless Lamb of God.
Yet grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly came into a human history filled with sinners to save sinners.
He entered our world without becoming corrupted by our sin.
Jesus Christ remained holy.
He did not inherit Tamar's guilt.
He did not inherit Judah's guilt.
He did not participate in their sin.
He came to save His people from their sins.
That is the shock of Matthew 1.
Before Matthew tells us about Christ's public ministry, before the Sermon on the Mount, before the miracles, before Calvary, he gives us names.
Names carrying stories.
Some beautiful.
Some broken.
Some embarrassing.
Some soaked in failure.
Then the genealogy arrives at Jesus.
As though Scripture were telling every ashamed person reading:
Look where God was taking the story.
Maybe your family tree has names nobody mentions.
Maybe your childhood contained things you still cannot comfortably explain.
Maybe you were born into circumstances that made you feel unwanted.
Maybe your parents' decisions became wounds you had to carry.
Maybe you made the decision.
Maybe the scandal has your fingerprints on it.
Maybe you knew better.
Maybe you promised God you would never do it again...
and did.
And somewhere along the way, shame taught you a theology Jesus never preached:
God can forgive other people, but He probably cannot do much with me now.
Look again at Perez.
Your origin is not your Savior.
Your family history is not your Savior.
Your reputation is not your Savior.
Your worst decision is not your Savior.
Your ability to repair yourself is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
And this is where cheap grace must be rejected.
Perez appearing in Christ's genealogy is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Grace does not say, “Stay where you are.”
Jesus saves sinners from sin.
The same Gospel that announces forgiveness calls us to repentance.
Bring the secret into His light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Stop defending what Scripture calls sin.
Stop pretending the wound does not hurt.
Stop using yesterday as permission for tomorrow's rebellion.
Come to Christ.
Not when you have cleaned yourself enough.
Come because you cannot cleanse your own soul.
The blood of Jesus does what reputation management never can.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He restores.
He makes new.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years trying to keep the scarlet thread hidden.
The evidence.
The memory.
The thing attached to your story.
But Christianity was never the announcement that respectable people can save themselves.
It is the announcement that a Savior has come.
His name is Jesus.
And He specializes in resurrection.
Dead hearts.
Dead hopes.
Dead consciences.
Dead dreams.
People who thought their story had already reached the final sentence.
This is why the Gospel is greater than inspirational self-improvement.
Jesus does not merely help you feel better about the old person.
In Him there is forgiveness and new life.
The cross deals with guilt.
The resurrection announces victory.
Grace does not simply repaint ruins.
Christ makes people new.
So maybe the question is no longer:
“How could God possibly use someone with my history?”
Maybe the better question is:
“What could Jesus write with a life completely surrendered to Him?”
Perez could not choose the circumstances of his conception.
Neither can you choose every chapter that brought you here.
But you can hear the Gospel today.
You can repent.
You can believe.
You can surrender.
You can stop hiding.

And if grace has already rewritten chapters you once thought were beyond redemption, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs to read tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody you know may be silently convinced that their scandal has placed them beyond the reach of Christ.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
It cannot.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never will.
Not because anyone should pressure you into giving. Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But supporting Gospel work can be an act of willing generosity offered for God's glory.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Invite even the unbeliever who has questions.
Let them encounter Scripture.
Let them encounter truth.
Most of all, pray that through everything Gospel Warrior publishes, they encounter the message of Jesus Christ crucified and risen for sinners.
Because Genesis 38 does not finally leave us staring at sexual scandal.
Matthew will not let it.
Matthew takes us from Tamar...
to Perez...
through generations...
to David...
through more broken generations...
until the genealogy arrives at Jesus.
And Jesus is where every story of redemption must ultimately lead.
Your scandal may explain part of your past.
It does not have the authority to become your god.
Your shame may speak loudly.
It does not get the final word.
Your wounds may be real.
Your consequences may be real.
Repentance may be costly.
Restoration may take time.
Some earthly consequences may remain.
But none of those truths make Jesus less powerful to forgive the repentant sinner and transform a surrendered life.
Perez was born into a story people might have wanted erased.
God did not erase his name.
Generations later, Matthew wrote it down.
And immediately beyond all those generations stands the name above every name:
Jesus Christ.
So when the enemy opens the file marked scandal, remember where the Gospel takes the story.
Not into denial.
Not into excuses.
Not into pretending sin never happened.
Through repentance.
Through grace.
Through redemption.
To Christ.
Because perhaps the detail you thought made your story unusable...
is the very place where, one day, people will look and marvel at what the grace of Jesus Christ has done.
The scarlet thread was visible. The scandal was real. But neither one got the final word. Jesus did.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY ONLY ONE MAN COULD ENTER THE MOST HOLY PLACE ONCE A YEAR
paragraphs:
WHY ONLY ONE MAN COULD ENTER THE MOST HOLY PLACE ONCE A YEAR
Behind that forbidden curtain was a terrifying message about your sin—and a breathtaking prophecy about the day Jesus would open the way home.
There was a room almost nobody on earth was allowed to enter.
Not the king.
Not the strongest warrior in Israel.
Not the wealthiest man.
Not the most respected elder.
Not even an ordinary priest.
One man.
One day.
Once a year.
And even he could not walk in casually.
He entered with blood.
Imagine standing outside that curtain.
You know what is behind it.
The ark of the covenant.
The place associated with the manifest presence of the Holy God.
The Most Holy Place.
And between you and that place hangs a veil that seems to preach without speaking:
You cannot simply walk into the presence of God on your own terms.
That sentence may feel uncomfortable in a generation accustomed to hearing that God should accept us however we choose to approach Him.
But Scripture does not begin the story of salvation by telling us how impressive humanity is.
It shows us how holy God is.
And how desperately we need mercy.
Leviticus 16 opens under the shadow of death.
“The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron who died when they approached the LORD.”
Nadab and Abihu had died after approaching God contrary to His command.
Then God spoke concerning Aaron.
The Hebrew warning of Leviticus 16:2 contains these words:
וְאַל־יָבֹא בְכָל־עֵת אֶל־הַקֹּדֶשׁ
Ve’al-yavo vekhol-et el-haqodesh.
In context:
He must not come “at every time” or whenever he wishes into the holy place.
Why?
Because the God on the other side of that curtain was not a religious accessory.
He was holy.
Utterly holy.
The problem was not that God was cruel.
The problem was that sinful humanity was attempting to stand before perfect holiness.
We sometimes speak about sin as though it were merely a collection of unfortunate mistakes.
God speaks about sin far more seriously.
Sin alienates.
Sin corrupts.
Sin enslaves.
Sin produces guilt.
Sin leads to death.
And perhaps one reason we struggle to understand the Gospel is that we have spent so much time making sin small that the cross no longer looks enormous.
If sin is merely a mistake, Jesus becomes merely an inspirational teacher.
But if sin has separated guilty human beings from a holy God, then suddenly Calvary becomes something breathtaking.
The Day of Atonement was preparing Israel to understand that.
Once each year, on Yom Kippur—the Day of Atonement—the high priest entered the Most Holy Place.
But before representing the people, the priest had a problem of his own.
He was sinful too.
Aaron could not stand before God and pretend he was different from everybody waiting outside.
He needed atonement himself.
That detail matters more than we sometimes realize.
The man representing sinners was himself a sinner.
The priest needed sacrifice.
The mediator needed mercy.
The one carrying blood for others needed blood offered for himself.
Hebrews later explains the scene with extraordinary precision:
εἰς δὲ τὴν δευτέραν ἅπαξ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ μόνος ὁ ἀρχιερεύς
The heart of the statement is unmistakable:
hapax tou eniautou—
“once in the year.”
Only the high priest entered the inner sanctuary, once each year, and not without blood.
Stop there.
Not without blood.
Because forgiveness is not God shrugging His shoulders at evil and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
It matters.
The lies mattered.
The lust mattered.
The hatred mattered.
The pride mattered.
The betrayal mattered.
The secret addiction mattered.
The cruelty nobody else saw mattered.
The words you wish you could pull back into your mouth mattered.
The nights when you knew exactly what God commanded and deliberately chose something else mattered.
Your sin matters.
Mine does too.
Yet this is where the story begins turning from terror toward grace.
Because the blood carried through that curtain was saying something.
Sin deserves judgment.
But God was providing a way of atonement.
The Hebrew language of Leviticus repeatedly uses the idea represented by כפר (k-p-r), commonly expressed in this context as “make atonement.”
The Day of Atonement was not humanity inventing a ladder high enough to reach God.
God Himself prescribed the way His covenant people were to approach.
The priest entered.
Atonement was made.
The people waited.
Then another year came.
And it happened again.
Another sacrifice.
Another Day of Atonement.
Another priest.
Another year.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Can you feel the incompleteness built into the repetition?
If the old sacrificial system had brought final perfection, why did the sacrifices continue?
Hebrews forces us to confront that question.
Those sacrifices pointed beyond themselves.
The earthly sanctuary was not the final destination.
The high priest was not the final Priest.
Animal blood was not the final sacrifice.
The curtain was not going to have the final word.
Someone greater was coming.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where the ancient ceremony suddenly reaches through thousands of years and grabs you personally.
Because Jesus did not arrive merely to make bad people slightly nicer.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
The old high priest entered with blood belonging to another creature.
Jesus offered Himself.
The old high priest first needed sacrifice for his own sin.
Jesus was sinless.
The old high priest entered an earthly sanctuary.
Christ entered the greater reality to which the earthly sanctuary pointed.
The old priest's ministry had to be repeated.
Jesus offered the decisive sacrifice once for all.
Hebrews says Christ appeared “once for all” to deal with sin through His sacrifice.
Once.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
Because His sacrifice was sufficient.
That changes everything.
You may have spent years believing God will finally receive you after you become clean enough.
So you hide.
You perform.
You promise.
You fail.
You cry.
You try again.
You delete the evidence.
You clean up your public image.
You learn Christian vocabulary.
You sit in church while carrying things inside you that nobody in the room knows.
People call you strong.
God knows you are exhausted.
People see your Sunday clothes.
God sees what happened Thursday night.
People hear your worship.
God hears the thoughts you never say aloud.
And somewhere underneath all that religious activity is a frightened question:
“If God really knew everything about me, would He still let me come near?”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not that God discovered your secrets and decided they were not serious.
The Gospel is that God knew the full horror of human sin and sent His Son anyway.
Jesus did not die for the edited version of you.
He died for sinners.
That is why repentance is not cleaning yourself before approaching Christ.
Repentance is turning from sin and coming to the Christ who alone can save you.
Grace does not tell you to keep loving what crucified your Savior.
