Grace calls you out of darkness.
Grace forgives.
Grace cleanses.
Grace changes allegiance.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace takes people with histories they are ashamed to remember and gives them a future centered on Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps you need that sentence more than you want anyone to know.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody discovered the affair.
Nobody knows about the pornography.
Nobody knows how bitter you have become.
Nobody knows about the money.
Nobody knows about the secret messages.
Nobody knows how far your prayer life has collapsed.
Nobody knows that you can encourage everybody else while privately wondering whether God is tired of you.
But Jesus knows.
And remarkably, His invitation to repent is still standing.
Not an invitation to excuse your sin.
An invitation to leave it.
Not an invitation to pretend judgment is unreal.
An invitation to run to the One who bore judgment for sinners.
The ancient high priest walked behind the curtain carrying sacrificial blood.
Jesus walked toward a cross carrying Himself.
Think about that.
The hands that fashioned humanity were pierced by human hands.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
The spotless Lamb was sacrificed.
And when Christ died, the Gospel accounts tell us that the temple curtain was torn.
What generations had known as restricted access suddenly became an unforgettable sign.
But do not misunderstand it.
The torn veil does not mean holiness stopped mattering.
It means Jesus accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
We do not stroll into God's presence because we finally became worthy.
We draw near because Christ is worthy.
Hebrews therefore does something astonishing.
After explaining priesthood, sacrifice, blood, sanctuary and the once-for-all work of Jesus, it tells believers to draw near.
Draw near.
Those words should almost make you tremble after reading Leviticus.
Once, the warning was:
Do not come whenever you wish.
Now, because of Christ:
Draw near.
Once, one representative priest entered.
Now those who belong to Jesus have access to God through their great High Priest.
Once, sacrificial blood testified year after year that atonement was necessary.
Now the Church looks back to the finished sacrifice of the Lamb of God.
This is Christianity.
Not “be good enough and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
Not “follow your heart.”
Not “invent your own truth.”
Not “compare yourself with somebody worse and hope heaven grades on a curve.”
Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Our great High Priest.
Our only sufficient Savior.
Our righteousness is not enough.
His is.
Our payment is not enough.
His blood is.
Our religious performance cannot reconcile us to God.
Jesus can.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is not that you have committed too many sins to be saved.
It is that you could become so comfortable around Christian things that you never actually surrender yourself to Christ.
You can know worship songs and still hide.
You can repost Bible verses and still refuse repentance.
You can know church language and still love darkness.
You can defend Christianity online while Christ remains outside the locked rooms of your heart.
The high priest could not enter the Most Holy Place carrying confidence in himself.
Neither can you.
Come empty-handed.
Come guilty.
Come confessing.
Come believing.
Come because Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
There is grace for the person reading this with tears forming in their eyes.
There is grace for the prodigal.
Grace for the hypocrite who is finally tired of pretending.
Grace for the addict ready to drag the hidden chains into the light.
Grace for the husband who failed.
Grace for the wife carrying secret shame.
Grace for the believer whose faith has become cold.
Grace for the person who thinks, “After everything I've done, surely God doesn't want me anymore.”
Do not confuse grace with permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives also calls you to follow Him.
The Christ who receives sinners transforms sinners.
He does not merely rewrite where your story ends.
He begins rewriting who you are.
So repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding.
Bring the secret thing into His light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Make restitution where Scripture requires it and where it can rightly be made.
Seek help where you are enslaved.
Return to prayer.
Return to Scripture.
Return to fellowship.
But above everything else...
return to Jesus.
Maybe somebody you love needs to read this tonight.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Because you remember what it felt like when somebody cared enough to bring truth into your darkness.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know there is still mercy in Christ.
If you have been hiding from God, comment, “No more hiding.”
If your faith has been exhausted but you refuse to walk away from Jesus, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If conviction is breaking through something you have kept secret, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
Somebody reading silently may need to see evidence that Christ still restores broken people.

And if you believe Gospel-centered truth like this should keep reaching believers, prodigals, seekers, struggling Christians, and people who may never voluntarily walk into a church, following and supporting Gospel Warrior is one practical way to help that mission continue.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
You cannot purchase grace.
Sharing an article cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus saves.
It is surrendering to Christ.
Because thousands of years ago, one man walked behind a curtain once a year carrying blood that could never be his final answer.
Then Jesus came.
And the temporary shadows gave way to the substance.
The repeated sacrifices pointed toward the sufficient sacrifice.
The sinful priests pointed toward the sinless High Priest.
The restricted sanctuary pointed toward access through Christ.
The blood pointed toward the Lamb.
And the curtain could not remain forever.
Maybe your whole life has felt like standing outside that curtain.
Too dirty.
Too ashamed.
Too far gone.
Too late.
But if you belong to Jesus, your hope is not that you finally became good enough to enter.
Your hope is that the perfect High Priest went before you.
So stop trying to save yourself.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is killing you.
Stop decorating the chains Christ is calling you to leave behind.
Turn around.
Look at the cross.
And come home.
The curtain said, “You cannot come this way alone.” The cross answered, “You don't have to—Jesus has made the way.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER: Did God Really Tell a Prophet to Marry a Sexually Unfaithful Woman?
paragraphs: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER: Did God Really Tell a Prophet to Marry a Sexually Unfaithful Woman?
The disturbing command behind one of Scripture’s most painful marriages—and why the real scandal is not Gomer’s unfaithfulness, but the relentless love of the God she represents.
There are Bible stories we put on nursery walls.
Noah and the rainbow.
David and Goliath.
Daniel surrounded by lions.
And then there is Hosea.
Nobody decorates a baby’s room with this story.
Because Hosea begins with a command so uncomfortable that, if you actually slow down and read it, you may wonder whether you understood it correctly.
God tells a prophet to marry a woman associated with sexual unfaithfulness.
Not merely preach about her.
Not simply counsel her.
Marry her.
Love her.
Build a home with her.
And eventually experience in his own heart something resembling the betrayal God’s covenant people had committed against Him.
The Hebrew of Hosea 1:2 refuses to make the moment comfortable:
לֵךְ קַח־לְךָ אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים
Lekh, qach-lekha eshet zenunim.
“Go, take for yourself a wife of whoredoms.”

The expression אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים — ’eshet zenunim carries the language of sexual immorality, prostitution, or promiscuous unfaithfulness. The ancient Greek translation of Hosea uses similarly forceful language:
γυναῖκα πορνείας — gynaika porneias
A woman—a wife—associated with porneia, sexual immorality.
But here we need to be careful.

The Bible does not give us enough information to reconstruct every detail of Gomer’s sexual history before her marriage. Christians and scholars have therefore understood the expression in different ways. Some understand Hosea 1:2 to mean that Gomer was already sexually promiscuous when Hosea married her. Others understand the language prospectively—that Hosea married the woman who would become unfaithful. Others emphasize that the marriage itself functions prophetically as a living picture of Israel’s covenant unfaithfulness.
Scripture leaves some questions unanswered.
But it leaves the central meaning painfully clear.
God explains His own metaphor:
“for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD.”
Hosea 1:2.
That is the wound underneath the story.
This was never merely a scandal about one woman.
It was an indictment of an entire people.
And if we read Hosea only thinking about Gomer’s sin, we may completely miss the terrifying mirror Scripture is holding in front of us.
Because somewhere in this story...
we are Gomer.
That sentence may sting.
It should.
Not because everyone has committed Gomer’s particular sins. Scripture never teaches that all sins are identical in their earthly consequences.
But spiritually, humanity has something devastating in common with her story.
We were made for God.
We receive life from God.
We breathe air God provides.
We live inside a universe held together by His power.
And still we wander.
We take gifts from the Giver and sometimes use those very gifts to run from Him.
Israel had done exactly that.
God had loved His people, provided for them, protected them, entered covenant with them—and they repeatedly pursued other gods.
Hosea later records the Lord saying of Israel:
“For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold.”
Hosea 2:8.
Read that slowly.
“I gave her.”
There is heartbreak in those words.
God gave.
Israel forgot.
God provided.
Israel credited another.
God remained God.
Israel wandered.
And suddenly Hosea stops being an ancient scandal and becomes painfully modern.
Because how many times have we prayed desperately when everything was falling apart...
then slowly forgotten God when everything became comfortable again?
How many people have cried, “Jesus, get me through this,” only to disappear from prayer once the crisis passed?
How often have we wanted God's peace without His lordship?
His protection without His correction?
His heaven without His holiness?
His forgiveness without repentance?
His gifts without His presence?
That is why Hosea is so uncomfortable.
It exposes the respectable version of spiritual adultery.
You can sit inside a church and still give your deepest affection to something else.
You can sing worship songs while secretly worshiping approval.
You can quote Scripture while being controlled by money.
You can post about Jesus while feeding an addiction nobody knows about.
You can know Christian language and still keep one locked room in your heart where Christ is not allowed to enter.
You can look faithful publicly while drifting privately.
And perhaps that is why this story hurts.
Because eventually we realize we have been standing at a safe distance judging Gomer...
while God has been asking us to examine ourselves.
But Hosea does not end where betrayal begins.
That is where grace becomes almost unbearable.
By Hosea 3, the prophet receives another command.
The wording is astonishing:
“Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel.”
Hosea 3:1.
Go.
Again.
Love.
Again.
Not because betrayal suddenly became acceptable.
Not because sin ceased to matter.
Not because covenant unfaithfulness was renamed freedom.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace goes after sinners while still calling sin what it is.
Hosea then says:
“So I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley.”
Hosea 3:2.
Whatever the precise historical circumstances behind that transaction—and interpreters debate the details—the text intentionally presents costly reclamation.
Hosea pays.
He brings her back.
And suddenly the story begins pointing beyond Hosea.
Beyond Gomer.
Beyond Israel.
Toward a greater Bridegroom.
Jesus Christ.
We must be careful here not to pretend every detail in Hosea is a direct prediction of Calvary. Hosea is first addressing Israel's covenant unfaithfulness and God's judgment and restoring love.
But within the whole biblical story, the pattern becomes breathtaking.
A people wander from God.
God confronts their sin.
God does not pretend their rebellion is harmless.
Yet God moves toward sinners in redeeming love.
And when the New Testament reveals the fullness of that redemption, we discover that our rescue costs infinitely more than silver and barley.
Peter writes:
There it is.
The Gospel.
Not humanity climbing toward God.
God coming for humanity.
Not sinners cleaning themselves enough to deserve Christ.
Christ dying for sinners who could never purchase their own redemption.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
At the cross, Jesus did not shrug at sin.
He bore its judgment.
The Son of God was betrayed, mocked, beaten, crucified and buried.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not say your sin never mattered.
The cross proves that it mattered more than we could imagine.
The Gospel says that God's mercy is greater than the sinner who comes to Christ in repentance and faith could ever deserve.
Maybe you need to hear that because you have been carrying something.
Something nobody at church knows.
Something buried beneath photographs, smiles, ministry, work, marriage, jokes, accomplishments, Bible verses and “I'm fine.”
Maybe you have wondered:
Would Jesus still want me if everybody knew?
Look at the cross.
That is not the death of a Savior who discovered your sins too late.
Jesus knew what He came to save.
He knew about the addiction.
He knew about the affair.
He knew about the lies.
He knew about the pornography.
He knew about the bitterness.
He knew about the secret messages.
He knew about the drunken nights.
He knew about the hypocrisy.
He knew about the pride.
He knew about the years you wasted.
He knew about the thing you desperately wish you could undo.
And still Christ came.
But do not confuse His love with permission to remain where you are.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us to repentance.
Grace is not God helping us become comfortable inside our chains.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace does not merely cover yesterday.
Grace begins transforming tomorrow.
The Gospel says that in Christ you can be forgiven...
and changed.
Perhaps the most astonishing movement in Hosea comes through the names attached to judgment.
Hosea's children become living prophetic signs.
One daughter receives the name Lo-Ruhamah—“No Mercy” or “Not Pitied.”
Another child is called Lo-Ammi:
לֹא עַמִּי — Lo ‘Ammi
“Not My People.”
Imagine carrying that name.
Imagine hearing it every time someone calls you.
Not mine.
Then comes one of the great reversals in the book.
Hosea 2:23 declares:
“I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people.”
Judgment does not receive the final sentence.
Mercy speaks.
Alienation is answered with restoration.

And centuries later, the apostles use Hosea's language when explaining the astonishing reach of God's saving mercy. Paul invokes Hosea in Romans 9:25–26, and Peter echoes the same reversal when speaking to believers:
“Which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God: which had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.”
1 Peter 2:10.
That is why Hosea matters so deeply.
The story is bigger than a shocking marriage.
It reveals the horror of spiritual unfaithfulness...
and the astonishing heart of the God who restores.
God does not romanticize rebellion.
He confronts it.
He judges it.
He calls His people away from it.
And yet His heart reaches toward restoration.
Later in Hosea, God cries:
“O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity.”
Hosea 14:1.
Return.
That may be the word somebody reading this has been avoiding.
Return.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Not when you have successfully repaired yourself.
Return to Christ.
Confess what you have hidden.
Stop defending what Scripture calls sin.
Stop making peace with what is killing your intimacy with God.
Bring your shame into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come home.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would be reading the story of Hosea and Gomer, becoming fascinated by their scandal, and never recognizing our own need for grace.
Gomer is not presented so we can stand above her.
Hosea's marriage becomes a mirror through which God's covenant people are confronted with their own wandering.
And through that brokenness comes a message that eventually shines with extraordinary clarity in Jesus Christ:
God saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with wounds.
People who have betrayed others.
People who have been betrayed.
People who made promises and broke them.
People who know exactly what they did.
People who still wake up remembering.
People who think they wandered too far.
The Gospel announces that the final word over the repentant believer does not have to be the worst thing they ever did.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is cleansing in Jesus.
There is reconciliation to God in Jesus.
There is a new identity in Jesus.
There is resurrection life in Jesus.
There is grace.
And maybe now the title of this story sounds different.
“Did God really tell Hosea to marry a sexually unfaithful woman?”

Hosea 1 unquestionably presents God commanding Hosea to take an eshet zenunim, a woman characterized by the language of sexual unfaithfulness, as a prophetic sign of Israel's spiritual infidelity. Scripture does not answer every question we might ask about Gomer's previous history or exactly when every act of unfaithfulness occurred.
But Scripture tells us exactly why Hosea's painful marriage mattered:
“for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD.”
The scandal was Israel's unfaithfulness.
The greater wonder was God's pursuing love.
And that story ultimately prepares our hearts to understand something even greater.
At Calvary, redemption was not purchased with barley.
It was purchased with blood.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He died for sinners.
He rose victorious.
And He still calls sinners to repent, believe, follow Him and come home.
Where have you been unfaithful to the God who has been faithful to you?
Don't answer with somebody else's name.
Don't think about your spouse.
Your pastor.
Your ex.
Your parents.
Your church.
Your enemy.
You.
Where is Jesus calling you to return?
And if Christ has already carried you from shame into restoration, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Let them encounter Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship and the Gospel of Jesus Christ day after day.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money proves that you love God.
It doesn't.
But one practical way believers can help Gospel-centered work reach more people is by voluntarily supporting the work that produces and distributes it.
Not because a share makes you more spiritual.
Not because an algorithm can measure devotion to God.
But because if biblical truth has helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.

We glorify God by belonging to Christ and living faithfully before Him. And when we freely use our voices, resources and influence to make Christ known, those ordinary acts can become instruments through which others hear the Gospel.
Hosea's story began with a marriage people could have called scandalous.
But Scripture would not allow scandal to have the last word.
Neither should you.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to overrule the blood of Jesus Christ.
Your shame does not outrank His mercy.
Your past is not stronger than His cross.
And when a sinner truly comes home to Christ, grace does something scandal never could:
Jesus does not merely erase the old headline—He gives the surrendered life a new ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID DEMANDED MICHAL BACK—BUT WAS IT LOVE, COVENANT, POLITICS… OR ALL THREE?
paragraphs:
DAVID DEMANDED MICHAL BACK—BUT WAS IT LOVE, COVENANT, POLITICS… OR ALL THREE?
She once risked her life to save him. Another man later walked behind her weeping when David took her back. And buried inside this disturbing love story is a warning about what happens when human hearts, broken promises, power, and God’s purposes collide.
There is one detail in David’s story that is almost impossible to read slowly without feeling uncomfortable.
David wanted his wife back.
Not merely requested.
Not merely remembered.
He made her return a condition.
Before he would complete an agreement with Abner, David declared:
לֹא־תִרְאֶה אֶת־פָּנַי כִּי אִם־לִפְנֵי הֱבִיאֲךָ אֵת מִיכַל בַּת־שָׁאוּל
Lo tir’eh et-panai ki im-lifnei havi’akha et-Mikhal bat-Sha’ul.
In context:
“You shall not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, when you come to see me.”
Then David sent another demand:
תְּנָה אֶת־אִשְׁתִּי אֶת־מִיכַל
Tenah et-ishti et-Mikhal.
“Give me my wife Michal.”
—2 Samuel 3:13–14
Notice the language.
My wife.
Not merely Saul’s daughter.
Not merely the princess.
Not merely a political asset.
אִשְׁתִּי — ishti — “my wife.”
And suddenly one of Scripture’s saddest relationships comes roaring back into view.
Because there was a time when Michal loved David.
The Bible actually says it.
“Michal Saul’s daughter loved David.”
—1 Samuel 18:20
That is significant because Scripture does not constantly stop to tell us who romantically loved whom.
But here it does.
Michal loved him.
And her father noticed.
Saul did not see his daughter’s love primarily as something beautiful.
He saw an opportunity.
“I will give her to him, that she may be a snare to him.”
—1 Samuel 18:21
Imagine that.
A young woman loves a man.
Her father discovers it.
And instead of protecting her heart, he weaponizes it.
Michal’s affection becomes political ammunition in Saul’s war against David.
Saul demands a deadly bride-price, hoping David will die trying to obtain her. David survives and fulfills the demand beyond what Saul required, and Michal becomes his wife.
The marriage begins under a shadow.
Love is there.
But so are ambition, violence, royal politics, jealousy, manipulation, and a father trying to murder his own son-in-law.
And it gets worse.
When Saul later tries to kill David, Michal helps David escape.
She lowers him through a window.
She deceives the messengers sent to seize him.
Whatever complexities eventually consumed their marriage, we should not erase this moment.
Michal once placed herself between David and death.
She chose her husband over her father’s murderous intentions.
Then David fled.
And somewhere in the chaos, Michal lost him.
David continued running.
David survived.
David fought.
David gathered men.
David eventually married other women.
And Saul gave Michal to another man.
1 Samuel 25:44 identifies him as Palti, son of Laish. In 2 Samuel 3 he is called Paltiel.
Years pass.
Saul dies.
The kingdom fractures.
David rules Judah while Saul’s surviving house struggles to retain Israel.
Then Abner, once the military power behind Saul’s house, decides to negotiate with David.
This could change everything.
Israel could be consolidated under David.
And David places a condition on the meeting.
Bring Michal.
Now here is where we must be careful.
We can preach things into Scripture that Scripture never actually says.
The Bible tells us plainly that Michal loved David.
It does not plainly tell us, “David demanded Michal because he still loved her.”
Neither does it plainly say, “David wanted her only for political reasons.”
So we should not pretend to know David’s private thoughts when God did not reveal them.
What we can see are several realities existing at once.
She was genuinely David’s wife.
Saul had given her to him after David fulfilled the demanded bride-price.
David had been violently driven away by Saul.
Michal had subsequently been given to another man.
And now David was moving toward kingship over the very nation once ruled by Michal’s father.
So was this covenant?
There is certainly a marital claim in David’s own words.
“Give me my wife Michal.”
Was it politics?
It is difficult to ignore the political significance.
Michal was not just any woman.
She was Michal daughter of Saul.
And strikingly, when David tells Abner she must be brought to him, the text identifies her exactly that way.
The daughter of the previous king would now be restored to the man becoming king over a reunited Israel.
That mattered in an ancient royal world.
Was there wounded affection buried somewhere underneath it?
Perhaps.
But Scripture does not tell us.
And sometimes biblical faithfulness means refusing to turn a possibility into a fact.
Yet what happens next is devastating enough without embellishment.
Michal is taken away from Paltiel.
And he follows her.
Crying.
The biblical narrator does not give us a speech from him.
No dramatic monologue.
No explanation of everything he felt.
Just this haunting image.
A woman being taken away…
and a man walking behind her,
weeping.
He follows until Abner finally tells him:
“Go. Return.”
And Paltiel turns back.
That scene hurts because Scripture does not sanitize the human cost of political history.
Kings are moving.
Dynasties are shifting.
A nation is being reunited.
David’s throne is strengthening.
But somewhere on the road is a crying man going home without the woman who had shared his life.
The Bible is remarkably honest like that.
It can show you history moving toward God’s sovereign purposes while simultaneously allowing you to hear the sound of broken human hearts underneath it.
And maybe that is where this story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because some of us know what it is like to become collateral damage in somebody else’s war.
Maybe nobody marched you down a road.
Maybe no king demanded you back.
But somebody made decisions around you that altered your life.
A parent’s dysfunction.
A spouse’s betrayal.
A leader’s ambition.
A family conflict.
A relationship where you were loved one day and treated like leverage the next.
You survived something other people reduced to “what happened.”
But to you, it was not merely what happened.
It became something you carried.
And there is another heartbreaking layer.
The Michal who returns to David is not introduced to us later as the young woman who once risked herself to save him.
When we meet their relationship again in 2 Samuel 6, something has changed.
David is bringing the ark of the LORD into Jerusalem.
He is celebrating before God.
Michal looks through a window.
A window.
Do you see the painful echo?
Once, a window was part of how she saved David.
Now she looks through one and despises him.
The Hebrew says:
וַתִּבֶז לוֹ בְּלִבָּהּ
vativez lo belibbah.
She despised him in her heart.
—2 Samuel 6:16
What happened between those two windows?
Scripture does not give us every conversation.
It does not tell us every wound.
We should resist inventing them.
But it does show us the destination.
Love has become contempt.
Whatever tenderness once existed has deteriorated into hostility.
Michal confronts David sarcastically.
David responds sharply, invoking the LORD’s choice of him over her father and his household.
And the chapter ends with one of the coldest sentences in their story:
Michal had no child until the day of her death.
The woman who once loved David.
The woman who once saved David.
The woman David later demanded back.
Ends her biblical story in barrenness and alienation.
This is not a fairy tale.
And David is not Jesus.
That distinction matters.
David was the LORD’s anointed king, a man through whose line God was unfolding His covenant purposes, but David was still a fallen man.
Scripture refuses to airbrush him.
He could worship passionately and still make devastating decisions.
He could write psalms that have carried broken believers for thousands of years and still become responsible for terrible sin.
Later he would take Bathsheba and arrange Uriah’s death.
David needed grace too.
David needed forgiveness too.
David needed a greater King.
And that is where this ancient royal scandal finally turns our eyes toward Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus is the Son of David…
but He is not another David.
Where earthly kings can use power in ways that leave people bleeding, Jesus uses His authority to save sinners.
Where human beings grasp, Christ gives.
Where sinful men sacrifice others to protect themselves, Jesus Christ sacrifices Himself to rescue others.
At the cross, Jesus did not make somebody else pay for His kingdom.
He paid for His people with His own blood.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where the story stops being merely about David and Michal.
It becomes a mirror.
Because you and I have complicated motives too.
We have called possession “love.”
We have called pride “conviction.”
We have called control “protection.”
We have called revenge “justice.”
We have sometimes wanted people back not because we were ready to love them rightly, but because losing them wounded our ego.
We have sometimes wanted God to restore something without asking Him to transform the person who broke it.
Us.
And perhaps you have been on the other side.
Used.
Discarded.
Manipulated.
Passed around emotionally by people who were supposed to protect you.
Maybe you still look through the windows of your past and feel something bitter rising in your heart.
Please hear this carefully.
Jesus does not ask you to pretend the wound never happened.
The Gospel is not denial.
The Gospel says sin is so real that the Son of God had to bleed for it.
But grace is so powerful that sin does not get the final word over everyone who comes to Christ.
The cross exposes us before it comforts us.
We are not merely people who have been wounded.
We are sinners who have wounded others too.
That realization destroys self-righteousness.
And then grace does something astonishing.
Christ receives repentant sinners.
Not because our record is clean.
Because His blood is sufficient.
The scandal of David’s family ultimately sits inside a much larger biblical story—a story moving toward Jesus Christ, the true King.
A King who does not merely reclaim what belongs to Him through royal command.
He comes seeking sinners who rebelled against Him.
He bears judgment.
He offers forgiveness.
He calls us to repent and believe.
He gives a new heart.
And He begins rewriting people the world had already written off.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Perhaps this stopped being a story about Michal several paragraphs ago.
Maybe God has put His finger on something you keep defending.
A relationship.
A resentment.
A secret.
A wound that became an identity.
A sin you renamed so you could keep it.
A person you have never forgiven.
A person you need to ask forgiveness from.
You can keep hiding it.
But hiding has never healed anyone.
Bring it to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Grieve where grief is needed.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek wise help where restoration requires time and safety.
But do not make a throne out of your wound.
And do not make an idol out of your past.
Jesus Christ is still King.
Maybe your story has scandal in it.
Maybe your family history has chapters you wish could be ripped out.
Maybe people know the worst thing you did.
Maybe they know the worst thing done to you.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Maybe your children watched you fall apart.
Maybe the person in the mirror remembers things nobody else knows.
The Gospel does not say those chapters were imaginary.
It says they do not have authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
That is why our message remains:
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because every earthly relationship gets restored exactly as we want.
But because at Calvary, Jesus proved that God can take the darkest reality of human sin and bring redemption through Christ.
There is no trophy for pretending you are fine.
Sometimes one honest sentence is where surrender begins.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, send this to them.
Not to shame them.
Not to win an argument.
Send it because perhaps they need to remember that Jesus is greater than the ugliest chapter in their story.
Save it too.
Some truths are not only for the moment when you first read them. You may need this again when an old wound begins talking louder than God’s promises.

If you sincerely want to glorify God, one practical way you can participate in Gospel work is to help biblical truth travel farther—through your prayers, your sharing, and, if you are able, your financial support.
But ministry does require people willing to help carry the message.
And before you leave, remember the road behind Michal.
Remember the man walking behind her crying.
Remember the window through which she once helped David escape.
Remember the window through which she later watched him with contempt.
Remember how quickly love, power, pain, pride, and unresolved wounds can become tangled inside the human heart.
Then remember the cross.
Because there stands a King infinitely greater than David.
A King without corruption.
A Bridegroom who does not exploit His bride.
A Savior who knew the full price of rescuing sinners and willingly paid it Himself.
And perhaps the most frightening tragedy is not that your story contains broken chapters—but that you might refuse the nail-scarred hands of the One who can redeem what sin has shattered.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jeremiah Was Told Not to Marry or Have Children — The Terrifying Reason God Asked a Prophet to Live Without the Family He Could Have Loved
paragraphs: Jeremiah Was Told Not to Marry or Have Children — The Terrifying Reason God Asked a Prophet to Live Without the Family He Could Have Loved

Jeremiah 16 contains one of the Bible’s most painful commands: God told His prophet not to take a wife and not to have sons or daughters. But hidden inside that lonely command is a warning about judgment, a lesson about obedience, and ultimately a breathtaking reminder that even after sin has written what looks like the final chapter, God can still write redemption.
Imagine meeting the person you could have loved for the rest of your life.
Imagine the wedding that could have happened.
Imagine hearing children running through your house.
A little boy reaching for your hand.
A daughter falling asleep against your chest.
Imagine birthdays, meals around the table, ordinary evenings, laughter from another room, growing old beside someone who knows your scars and still chooses you.
Now imagine God saying:
No.
Not because marriage is sinful.
Not because children are a burden.
Not because love is beneath the calling of a prophet.
But because something terrible is coming.
That is where Jeremiah found himself.
And if you read this story too quickly, you may miss just how much it cost him.
The Hebrew text of Jeremiah 16:2 is painfully direct:
“לֹא־תִקַּח לְךָ אִשָּׁה וְלֹא־יִהְיוּ לְךָ בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה”
Lo-tiqqach lekha ishshah, velo-yihyu lekha banim uvanot bammaqom hazzeh.
In context:
“You shall not take a wife for yourself, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place.”
There is no elaborate introduction.
No long explanation before the command.
Just a sentence that could alter the entire shape of a man's earthly life.
Do not take a wife.
Do not have sons or daughters.
Here.
Notice those final words:
“בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה — bammaqom hazzeh — in this place.”
That matters.
God was not declaring marriage evil.
He was not establishing celibacy as spiritually superior to marriage.
He was not commanding every prophet, pastor, missionary, or serious Christian to remain unmarried.
Scripture elsewhere describes marriage with honor, and the biblical story repeatedly treats children as gifts from God.
This was a specific prophetic command given to Jeremiah in a specific historical crisis.
Jeremiah's very life was becoming a sermon.
And the sermon was terrifying.
God immediately explained why.

The sons and daughters who would be born in that land, and the fathers and mothers who brought them into the world, were facing catastrophic judgment. Jeremiah 16:4 describes disease, sword, famine, death, and bodies left without ordinary burial.
The language is intentionally horrifying.
Because Judah's spiritual condition was horrifying.
This was not God throwing a tantrum because imperfect people made a few mistakes.
Jeremiah's generation stood within a long history of covenant rebellion. The book repeatedly confronts idolatry, injustice, bloodshed, stubbornness, and the abandonment of the LORD.
Later in this same chapter, God explains the heart of the problem: their fathers had forsaken Him and pursued other gods, and the present generation had acted even more corruptly.
They had walked away from the One who gave them life.
And eventually judgment was coming through national catastrophe.
Jeremiah therefore became more than a man delivering God's message.
Jeremiah became part of the message.
His empty house preached.
The wife who was not there preached.
The children who would never run through his doorway preached.
The family photographs that would never exist preached.
Every evening he returned to silence, his life announced something Judah desperately needed to understand:
You are living as though tomorrow is guaranteed.
That sentence should make us uncomfortable.
Because thousands of years later, human beings still do exactly that.
We make plans.
Next year.
When the children grow up.
When the business improves.
When the debt is paid.
When life settles down.
Someday I'll come back to God.
Someday I'll forgive.
Someday I'll confess what nobody knows.
Someday I'll stop watching that.
Someday I'll leave that relationship.
Someday I'll open the Bible again.
Someday I'll pray seriously.
Someday I'll surrender.
Someday.
Jeremiah stood before people who apparently assumed ordinary life would simply continue.
Weddings.
Children.
Funerals.
Celebrations.
Tomorrow.
But God knew what they did not know.
Their world was approaching catastrophe.
And Jeremiah's loneliness became a living alarm clock.
That is what makes this passage so unsettling.
Because sometimes we think God's greatest kindness is giving us what we want.
Scripture shows something deeper.
Sometimes mercy sounds like a warning.
Sometimes love interrupts.
Sometimes grace confronts.
Sometimes God refuses to flatter us while we are walking toward destruction.
We want a God who says, “Everything is fine.”
The God of Scripture loves too deeply to lie.
Think about Jeremiah.
People often talk about obedience as though it always produces immediate happiness.
Obey God and everything will work out.
Obey God and doors will open.
Obey God and you'll get the spouse.
The promotion.
The breakthrough.
The dream.
Jeremiah destroys that shallow theology.
Sometimes obedience costs something you genuinely wanted.
Sometimes faithfulness means walking a road nobody around you understands.
Sometimes obedience does not immediately fill your hands.
Sometimes obedience empties them.
And still...
God is worthy.
That is difficult Christianity.
Not the Christianity of inspirational captions.
Not the Christianity that treats Jesus as a machine for producing comfortable circumstances.
This is the faith that says:
“Even if obedience costs me something precious, Christ is still precious.”
Maybe that sentence touched something in you.
Maybe you wanted marriage and it never happened.
Maybe you wanted children and life unfolded differently.
Maybe the family you dreamed about collapsed.
Maybe you buried someone you thought would grow old beside you.
Maybe obedience to Christ cost you a relationship.
Maybe people walked away when you stopped compromising.
Maybe following Jesus has sometimes felt lonelier than anyone warned you it could feel.
Hear this carefully:
Jeremiah 16 does not mean your singleness, infertility, grief, or loneliness is proof that God is judging you.
Do not place that burden on yourself.
Jeremiah received a unique prophetic command tied to Judah's coming catastrophe.
Your suffering should not automatically be interpreted as God's punishment.
But Jeremiah does teach us something that reaches directly into our lives:
Faithfulness cannot be measured merely by how comfortable our circumstances become.
Jeremiah was obedient...
and lonely.
Faithful...
and misunderstood.
Chosen...
and wounded.
Used by God...
and acquainted with tears.
Sometimes those realities can exist in the same person.
Maybe they exist in you.
And there is another danger hidden in this story.
We can become so fascinated with Jeremiah's sacrifice that we miss why the sacrifice was necessary.
Sin had consequences.
That truth has become uncomfortable in many corners of modern Christianity.
We love talking about grace.
We should.
We love talking about forgiveness.
We should.
We love saying Jesus receives sinners.
He does.
But grace becomes cheap when we refuse to talk honestly about what grace rescues us from.
Sin destroys.
Sin deceives.
Sin hardens.
Sin promises freedom while quietly manufacturing chains.
The secret pornography.
The affair nobody discovered.
The bitterness you've justified for ten years.
The dishonesty that became normal.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The pride hidden beneath religious language.
The private addiction behind the public worship.
The resentment you feed every night.
The compromise you keep promising to quit.
The version of Christianity where Jesus is Savior but never Lord.
Sin always tells you:
“One more time.”
Then one more becomes ten.
Ten becomes a habit.
A habit becomes bondage.
And bondage eventually begins telling you who you are.
That is why biblical warnings are mercy.
God warns because God sees where roads end.
Jeremiah could see disaster approaching while many around him continued living as though nothing were wrong.
And perhaps somebody reading this is doing the same spiritually.
You still smile.
Still work.
Still post.
Still laugh.
Maybe you still attend church.
People assume you're okay.
But you know.
Something has been dying quietly inside you.
Prayer became occasional.
Scripture became distant.
Conviction became irritating.
Compromise became easier.
Jesus slowly moved from the center of your life toward the edge.
Nobody noticed.
But you did.
And God did.
If that is you, do not hear Jeremiah merely as condemnation.
Hear the alarm.
Wake up.
Come home.
Repent.
Not because Jesus is waiting to humiliate you.
Because Jesus died to save sinners.
This is where Jeremiah's story begins opening a door beyond judgment.
Even Jeremiah 16 does not end with destruction.
Later in the chapter, after announcing exile, God speaks of bringing His people back.
Judgment would not erase God's purposes.
Human rebellion would not have the final word.
And that pattern grows brighter across Scripture until we reach Jesus Christ.
Jeremiah lived the sign of approaching judgment.
Jesus stepped into the judgment sinners deserved.
Jeremiah was told not to build a household in a land facing devastation.
Jesus came to bring lost sons and daughters into the household of God.
Jeremiah wept over rebellious people.
Jesus wept over Jerusalem.
Jeremiah warned people that sin had consequences.
Jesus carried sin's curse to the cross.
And at Calvary, the scandal becomes grace.
The innocent One stands where the guilty should stand.
Christ is mocked.
Christ is wounded.
Christ is rejected.
Christ is crucified.
The One without sin bears sin.
And three days later, the grave discovers that it cannot keep its prisoner.
Jesus rises.
That is the Gospel.
Not that decent people learn to become slightly better.
Not that religious people finally earn God's approval.
The Gospel is that sinners who could never rescue themselves can be forgiven, reconciled, cleansed, adopted, and made new through Jesus Christ.
Your sin may explain chapters of your story.
It does not have to write the ending.
Your addiction may have written chapters.
Your divorce may have written chapters.
Your betrayal may have written chapters.
Your pride may have written chapters.
Your secret may have written chapters.
Your failure may have written chapters.
Your grief may have written chapters.
Your years away from God may have written chapters.
But if you come to Christ...
the pen is not finished.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin harmless.
Not by erasing accountability.
Grace does something infinitely greater.
Grace meets guilty people at the cross.
Grace tells the truth about our rebellion and then points toward the blood that was shed for rebels.
Grace does not say, “You never sinned.”
Grace says, “Christ died for sinners.”
Grace does not say, “There is nothing to repent of.”
Grace says, “Turn around. The Father's house is still open.”
Maybe this article found you during a season nobody understands.
Maybe your house feels too quiet.
Maybe your marriage feels broken.
Maybe your children are far from God.
Maybe your faith has become exhausted.
Maybe you have spent months pretending you're stronger than you actually are.
Then stop pretending for a moment.
You don't have to confess your entire private story publicly.
But you can take one small step toward honesty.
God isn't finished with me yet.
Someone reading those words may realize they aren't fighting alone.
Not to embarrass them.
Not because you assume you know their sins.
Tomorrow should never be presumed upon, and grace should never be postponed.
There are truths you understand differently when you return to them during a darker night.
Not as a religious performance. Not as a way of earning God's favor.
But if this message is faithful to Scripture and you believe someone in your circle needs to encounter it, sharing becomes a simple act of witness.
A cousin.
An old classmate.
A coworker silently losing faith.
A friend trapped in something they cannot admit.
A believer who has not prayed honestly in months.
Even someone who does not yet believe in Jesus.
One share can place the Gospel in front of a person who would never intentionally search for a sermon.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually numb.
Invite the seeker with difficult questions.
Invite the Christian who feels ashamed to come home.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending to have perfect lives.
Because Christianity is not the story of perfect people congratulating themselves.
It is the story of sinners meeting a perfect Savior.
Jeremiah's empty house once warned a generation that judgment was approaching.
Thousands of years later, his silence still speaks.
Life is shorter than we imagine.
Sin is more destructive than we admit.
Obedience can cost more than we expected.
Judgment is too serious to trivialize.
Grace is too costly to cheapen.
And Jesus is too glorious to keep at the edge of our lives.
If God interrupted the future you have planned, would Jesus still be enough?
If obedience cost something you desperately wanted, would He still be worthy?
If every hidden room of your heart suddenly stood open before Christ tonight, what would you desperately want Him to forgive?
Bring that thing to Him.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
There is mercy at the feet of Jesus.
There is forgiveness through His blood.
There is resurrection after ruin.
There is restoration after rebellion.
There is grace after scandal.
And there is still a Savior who specializes in writing endings sin never saw coming.
Your worst chapter does not deserve the final sentence when the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID SOMEONE WHO TOUCHED A MENSTRUATING WOMAN’S BED HAVE TO WASH?
paragraphs: WHY DID SOMEONE WHO TOUCHED A MENSTRUATING WOMAN’S BED HAVE TO WASH?

Leviticus 15 sounds disturbing until you understand what “unclean” actually meant. Then a bleeding woman reaches for Jesus—and suddenly an ancient command becomes part of one of the most beautiful pictures of the Gospel.
There is a verse in Leviticus that many Christians quietly skip.
Not because they hate Scripture.
Because they do not know what to do with it.
It talks about menstruation.
A bed.
Someone touching that bed.
Washing clothes.
Bathing.
And being “unclean until evening.”
And if we are honest, to modern ears it can sound almost insulting.
Was God saying a menstruating woman was dirty?
Was her body somehow sinful?
Why would simply touching the place where she slept require someone to wash?
And perhaps the uncomfortable question beneath all the others is this:
What kind of God makes rules like that?
Stay with the text.
Because if you stop at the word “unclean,” you may walk away with a picture of God that the passage itself does not require.
And if you keep reading the biblical story until a desperate, bleeding woman pushes through a crowd and touches Jesus...
everything changes.
Leviticus 15:19 begins in Hebrew:
וְאִשָּׁה כִּי־תִהְיֶה זָבָה דָּם
Ve’ishah ki-tihyeh zavah dam...
In straightforward English:
“When a woman has a discharge, and her discharge is blood...”
The passage says she enters a condition described with the Hebrew word נִדָּה — niddah, associated here with her menstrual state or separation.
Then comes another important Hebrew word:
טָמֵא — tamei.
It is often translated “unclean.”
That English word can mislead us if we automatically hear:
filthy.
disgusting.
immoral.
sinful.
That is not an adequate way to understand what Leviticus is describing.
This is the world of ritual purity and impurity.
And that distinction changes everything.
The woman was not being accused of committing a sin simply because she menstruated.
Think about what surrounds this passage.
Just a few verses earlier, Leviticus says that when a man has an emission of semen, he must bathe his body and remains tamei until evening.
Clothing or leather touched by semen must be washed.
After sexual relations involving an emission, both the man and woman bathe and remain tamei until evening.
Then the text turns to menstruation.
In other words, the chapter is not singling women out as uniquely dirty.
It is dealing with bodily discharges and the ritual categories governing Israel's life before God.
That matters.
Because sometimes people have used passages like this to place shame on women that the passage itself never placed there.
God did not look at a woman experiencing the ordinary functioning of the body He created and say:
“You have sinned by being a woman.”
The text does not say that.
Now read what happens to the bed.
Leviticus 15:20 says:
וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר תִּשְׁכַּב עָלָיו בְּנִדָּתָהּ יִטְמָא
Anything on which she lies during this condition becomes tamei.
Then verse 21 says:
וְכָל־הַנֹּגֵעַ בְּמִשְׁכָּבָהּ יְכַבֵּס בְּגָדָיו וְרָחַץ בַּמַּיִם וְטָמֵא עַד־הָעָרֶב
The person touching her bedding was to wash his clothes, bathe in water, and remain tamei until evening.
Notice something easily missed.
There is no punishment here.
No beating.
No fine.
No declaration that the person has become evil.
No statement that touching the bed was itself a moral transgression.
Instead:
Wash.
Bathe.
Wait.
Evening comes.
The temporary condition ends.
That is enormously important.
The washing was part of Israel's God-given system for dealing with ritual impurity.
Israel was being taught that approaching the holy God was not casual.
Life and death mattered.
Blood mattered.
The body mattered.
Purity mattered.
Boundaries mattered.
And the presence of God in the midst of His people mattered.
Leviticus 15 eventually gives the theological concern behind these regulations: Israel was not to defile God's dwelling place in their midst.
This was not merely an ancient hygiene manual.
And we should be careful not to reduce it to one.
Washing certainly involves actual water and physical cleansing, but the chapter itself places these washings within Israel's system of ritual purity.
The purpose was larger than “God was teaching them to kill germs.”
The text is concerned with holiness.
With access.
With sacred space.
With the astonishing reality that the holy God had chosen to dwell among human beings.
And that makes what happens centuries later almost breathtaking.
Because another woman begins to bleed.
Not seven days.
Not fourteen.
Not a month.
Twelve years.
Mark tells us about her.
She had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.
She had endured much.
She had sought help.
She had spent what she had.
And instead of becoming better, she had become worse.
Try not to read that clinically.
Imagine twelve years.
Twelve years of waking up hoping this might finally be over.
Twelve years of seeing the blood again.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Twelve years of explaining.
Twelve years of exhaustion.
Twelve years of wondering whether tomorrow will look exactly like yesterday.
And then she hears about Jesus.
A crowd surrounds Him.
People are pressing against Him.
And somewhere inside that crowd is a woman carrying twelve years of pain.
She tells herself that if she can only touch His garment, she will be healed.
Then she reaches.
Her fingers touch His clothing.
And immediately...
the bleeding stops.
But something even more beautiful happens.
Jesus stops too.
“Who touched My garments?”
The disciples are confused.
Everyone is touching You.
The crowd is pressing against You.
What do You mean, “Who touched Me?”
But Jesus keeps looking.
Until she comes trembling.
And tells Him the truth.
Imagine that moment.
She may have expected rebuke.
She may have expected exposure.
She may have expected to disappear back into the crowd as anonymously as she entered it.
Jesus would not let her leave merely knowing that her body had changed.
He wanted her to know how He saw her.
And the word He gives her is devastatingly tender:
“Daughter.”
Not nuisance.
Not contaminant.
Not embarrassment.
Not problem.
Daughter.
Then He sends her away in peace.
Do not flatten this story by pretending Mark explicitly says, “Jesus is now abolishing Leviticus 15.” Mark does not make that sentence.
But the biblical contrast is still extraordinary.
Under the Levitical purity system, bodily impurity could be transmitted through contact.
In this Gospel scene, the suffering woman touches Jesus...
and Jesus is not portrayed as becoming polluted.
Instead, healing goes from Him to her.
She reaches toward holiness...
and holiness restores her.
That is Jesus.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely:
“Why did somebody have to wash after touching a menstruating woman's bed?”
A deeper question begins to emerge:
How can unclean human beings ever draw near to a perfectly holy God?
That question reaches far beyond menstruation.
Because you may never have touched that ancient Israelite bed.
But you know what it is to need cleansing.
You know what it is to have something you wish nobody knew.
The browser history.
The affair.
The addiction.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The lies.
The pride.
The years spent pretending.
The prayer life that quietly disappeared.
The compromise everyone else calls harmless.
The shame you learned to hide behind church language.
Some stains cannot be removed in a shower.
Some guilt survives every attempt at self-improvement.
Some nights you can wash your face, change your clothes, climb into a clean bed...
and still feel dirty inside.
That is where this ancient language begins pointing us toward something greater.
The New Testament book of Hebrews looks back at the old covenant system of purification and then asks, in effect:
If those rites dealt with ceremonial purification, how much more can the blood of Christ cleanse the conscience?
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave more respectably.
He came for people who cannot cleanse themselves.
People like us.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people finally became good enough for God.
The scandal is grace.
The innocent One took the place of the guilty.
The Holy One welcomed sinners.
The spotless Lamb carried sin.
The One who had no sin went to a cross surrounded by sinners and died for sinners.
Then He rose.
And now the invitation is not:
“Clean yourself enough and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
It is:
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
Bring Him what you keep trying to conceal.
The Gospel does not tell you that sin is imaginary.
It tells you something infinitely better:
sin is real...
and Christ's grace is greater.
This is where we must make another distinction.
Menstruation was not moral sin.
Ritual impurity was not identical to wickedness.
We should never use Leviticus 15 to shame women for the bodies God gave them.

But the entire biblical drama of holiness, cleansing, sacrifice, priesthood, access, blood, and sanctuary prepares us to understand how astonishing it is that sinful humanity can finally approach God through Jesus Christ.
Hebrews says believers have confidence to enter God's presence by the blood of Jesus.
Think about that.
Leviticus teaches you not to treat holiness casually.
The Gospel does not make God less holy.
The Gospel reveals the staggering cost by which sinners are brought near to that holiness.
Jesus did not lower God's standard until we could crawl over it.
He fulfilled what we could never fulfill and gave Himself for us.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a self-cleaning program.
You do not scrub your soul until God loves you.
You come to Christ because while you could never rescue yourself, mercy came looking for you.
Maybe that is why the woman in Mark 5 feels so painfully familiar.
She had tried.
And tried.
And tried.
And eventually she reached the place where her hope was no longer:
“I can fix myself.”
Her hope became:
“If I can just get to Jesus.”
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have promised God you would stop.
Then did it again.
You told everybody you were okay.
You weren't.
You posted Scripture while privately falling apart.
You smiled in church while fighting something nobody in the room could see.
Maybe you have even begun wondering whether Jesus would still want you if everything hidden became visible.
Look again at the trembling woman.
Jesus already knew.
And He called her daughter.
That does not mean Jesus excuses sin.
The same Christ who forgives calls us to repentance, obedience, holiness, and a transformed life.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace tells the truth about our condition and then refuses to leave us there.
So maybe tonight your prayer does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be honest.
“Jesus, I need You.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, cleanse what I cannot cleanse.”
“Jesus, bring me home.”
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail.
But you can take one small step out of secrecy.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person still fighting.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally confess to God because your honesty gave them courage to become honest too.
And if you know someone who has been wounded by the idea that the Bible teaches women are inherently dirty because of menstruation, share this with them.
Not to win an argument.
To remove a burden Scripture never asked them to carry.
Because eventually someone will ask you why Leviticus calls menstruation “unclean,” and you will want to remember the difference between ritual impurity and moral guilt.
But please remember something even more important.
The point of understanding Scripture is not merely becoming the person in the room who knows the Hebrew word.
Knowledge that never leads us toward Christ can simply make us proud in another language.
The goal is Jesus.
Always Jesus.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to Christ, repent, heal, grow, or put difficult passages back into their biblical context, you can also help this work continue.
We are not selling God's favor.
Biblical giving must never be manipulated.
But voluntary financial support can absolutely be an act of Christian generosity and stewardship when it is given freely, prayerfully, and for the advancement of Gospel work.
And sometimes glorifying God looks remarkably ordinary.
Someone writes.
Someone studies.
Someone gives.
Someone shares.
Someone prays.
And God uses all of it.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.

One share may put this truth in front of the woman who has carried unnecessary religious shame for twenty years. One tag may reach the believer quietly losing faith because nobody ever explained the difficult passages. One comment may encourage someone who thought they were fighting alone.
Because after all the Hebrew...
after the washing...
after the bed...
after the blood...
after twelve years of suffering...
after the trembling woman reached through the crowd...
we arrive at the truth we needed from the beginning.
The God who taught Israel that holiness must never be treated casually is the same God who, in Christ, made a way for sinners to draw near.
The woman reached for Jesus because she believed touching Him could change everything.
She was right.
And maybe that is the part you need to remember tonight.
Your deepest stain is not stronger than the Savior who still calls broken people closer.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ONAN HAD SEX WITH TAMAR—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH IT
paragraphs:
ONAN HAD SEX WITH TAMAR—BUT REFUSED THE RESPONSIBILITY THAT CAME WITH IT
He wanted the intimacy without the obligation. He took what satisfied him while deliberately withholding what the relationship required. And buried inside one of Genesis’ most uncomfortable scandals is a warning about the terrifying difference between getting close to something sacred and actually surrendering to God.
There are Bible stories we sanitize because the details make us uncomfortable.
Genesis 38 refuses to let us do that.
There is a widow.
There is a dead husband.
There is a brother who knows what is expected of him.
There is sex.
There is deliberate refusal.
There is exploitation tangled inside family obligation.
And there is a God who sees what happens when someone accepts the privilege of a relationship while secretly rejecting the responsibility attached to it.
His name was Onan.
And perhaps the most disturbing thing about his story is not how foreign it feels.
It is how familiar the human heart behind it can become.
Because Onan did not simply walk away.
He went in.
That distinction matters.
After Tamar's husband Er died, Judah told his second son Onan:
“בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ”
Bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehaqem zera le'achikha.
In context, the command means essentially:
Go to your brother's wife, fulfill the brother-in-law's duty toward her, and raise up offspring for your brother.
Genesis 38:8.
The Hebrew word וְיַבֵּם (veyabbem) comes from the root יבם (y-b-m), associated with performing the duty of a brother-in-law toward a childless brother's widow.

This family obligation appears before the Mosaic Law was given, so we should not anachronistically claim that Onan was violating the later written command of Deuteronomy 25. But when the Torah later formally regulates this institution, the same Hebrew root appears.
Deuteronomy 25:5 says:
“יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ ... וְיִבְּמָהּ”
Her brother-in-law was to take responsibility for the widow and perform the brother-in-law's duty.
And Deuteronomy explains part of what was at stake: the continuation of the deceased brother's name and household.
That takes us directly into Onan's heart.
Because Genesis does not leave us guessing about his motive.
“וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע”
Vayyeda Onan ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
Genesis 38:9.
There it is.
He knew.
This was not ignorance.
Not an accident.
Not confusion.
He understood the responsibility.
And he did not want its cost.
Yet he still went to Tamar.
Genesis describes his behavior with uncomfortable directness. Whenever he had relations with his brother's wife, he deliberately spilled his semen on the ground.
But do not stop reading there.
Because if you stop there, you can miss the explanation Scripture itself gives for what he was doing.
The Hebrew says:
“לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו”
Levilti netan-zera le'achiv.
“So as not to give offspring to his brother.”
That final phrase is devastating.
Onan wanted what he could receive from the arrangement while deliberately sabotaging what he was supposed to give through it.
He accepted access.
Rejected obligation.
Participated physically.
Withheld intentionally.
And Tamar was left carrying the consequences.
She had already buried a husband.

Her future in that ancient household depended heavily upon family, offspring, protection, and the continuation of the line. Yet the man who had been called to help preserve that future repeatedly entered her bed while intentionally ensuring that the purpose entrusted to him would never be fulfilled.
Then Genesis says:
“וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה”
Vayyera be'enei YHWH asher asah.
“What he did was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
Genesis 38:10.
Notice the wording.
What he did.
God saw not merely the outward act but the rebellion expressed through it.

This passage has often been reduced to a single debate about contraception or a particular sexual act. Christians have historically disagreed about some of the broader ethical implications drawn from Onan's behavior, and we should be careful not to make Genesis say less—or more—than it actually says.
What Genesis explicitly tells us is this:

Onan knew the offspring would not be counted as his brother's, and because of that, he deliberately prevented Tamar from conceiving whenever he went to her, specifically so that he would not provide offspring for his brother.
His selfish motive is written into the sentence.
And that makes this story far bigger than the mechanics of sex.
It is about a heart willing to receive what it wants while refusing what faithfulness requires.
And suddenly Onan's ancient bedroom becomes an uncomfortable mirror.
Because how many of us want the benefits of covenant without the responsibilities of covenant?
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Comfort without obedience.
Promises without surrender.
Resurrection without a cross.
A Savior who rescues us from hell, but not necessarily a Lord who tells us what to do with our bodies, money, relationships, ambitions, secrets, habits, sexuality, bitterness, pride, and future.
We want Jesus close enough to comfort us...
but sometimes not close enough to command us.
That is where this ancient scandal starts walking into our modern lives.
You can attend church and still resist Christ.
You can sing worship songs while protecting a secret addiction.
You can post Bible verses while refusing to forgive someone.
You can say, “God knows my heart,” while knowing perfectly well that your heart is precisely the battlefield you refuse to surrender.
You can love Christian encouragement while hating Christian correction.
You can want God's peace while resisting God's authority.
You can even want Jesus for what He gives without wanting Jesus for who He is.
And that is where grace must be understood correctly.
Grace is not God's permission to keep exploiting His mercy.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy toward sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside your rebellion saying, “Nothing needs to change.”
The Gospel is Jesus Christ entering the catastrophe of human sin, bearing judgment in the sinner's place, rising from the dead, forgiving those who come to Him, and giving them a new life.
Not purchased by our obedience.
Purchased by His blood.
And the grace that saves us does not leave us untouched.
This is why Jesus said:
“If you love me, keep my commandments.”
John 14:15.
Not:
“Keep My commandments so I might finally love you.”
That would turn grace into wages.
The order matters.
We love because He first loved us.
We obey because we belong to Him.
Repentance does not purchase salvation.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has finally stopped defending its rebellion and runs toward the mercy of God.
And maybe this is where the story becomes painful.
Because perhaps you recognize something of Onan in yourself.
Not necessarily his particular sexual sin.
Something deeper.
Taking while withholding.
Receiving while resisting.
Wanting the blessing while refusing the burden of faithfulness.
Maybe you have been asking God to restore your marriage while secretly feeding the very behavior destroying it.
Maybe you have been praying for freedom while keeping private access to the thing enslaving you.
Maybe you want God to heal your heart, but you refuse to release the person you hate.
Maybe you want a godly relationship while repeatedly using people to soothe your loneliness.
Maybe you want financial blessing while refusing integrity when nobody is looking.
Maybe you want influence for Christ but cannot tolerate being unseen.
Maybe you want the crown...
but keep negotiating with the cross.
And here is where Genesis 38 becomes even more astonishing.
Because Tamar's story does not disappear into the scandal.
The family does not disappear.
Judah does not disappear.
The brokenness does not somehow prevent God from moving redemptive history forward.
Genesis 38 eventually records the birth of Perez through Tamar and Judah.
Then generations pass.
Names become genealogies.
Scandal becomes family history.
And when Matthew opens the New Testament and begins tracing the human ancestry of Jesus Christ, he does something remarkable.
He names Tamar.
“Tamar” appears in Matthew 1:3.
Think about that.
The Gospel of Matthew could have introduced Jesus with a polished genealogy that concealed every uncomfortable chapter.
Instead, Scripture carries Tamar's name forward.
Not because sin ceased to matter.
Not because everything that happened in Genesis 38 was righteous.
But because human scandal could not derail God's redemptive purpose.
Perez enters the line.
The generations continue.
David comes.
And ultimately, according to the flesh, the genealogy reaches Jesus Christ.

The Messiah enters a human family tree containing grief, sexual scandal, deception, failure, outsiders, kings, broken people, and stories most religious public-relations departments would probably prefer to hide.
God did not need a sanitized genealogy to send a spotless Savior.
Jesus was spotless.
The family history was not.
That is grace.
And maybe you need to hear that more than you realize.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sin should not be renamed, excused, celebrated, or hidden.
It can be confessed.
It can be brought into the light.
It can be carried to Christ.
Because Jesus does not redeem us by pretending our sin was harmless.
He redeems sinners at enormous cost to Himself.
At the cross, mercy did not become cheap.
The Son of God paid.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And the same Christ who forgives sinners also calls them out of darkness and into life.
So if this story exposed something hidden inside you, do not waste the conviction by turning it into temporary emotion.
Come to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary designed to make rebellion sound respectable.
No excuses.
“Jesus, I have wanted Your gifts while resisting Your rule.”
“Jesus, I have taken what I wanted and ignored whom I was hurting.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Change me.”
That prayer is not magic words.
But the Christ to whom a repentant sinner cries is mighty to save.
And if you have trusted Him, remember this too: conviction is not an invitation to despair. The answer to discovered sin is not to hide farther from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Walk differently.
And when you fall, do not make peace with the ground.
Get up and return to Christ.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years believing that what happened in their family permanently disqualified them.
Look at Tamar's name in Matthew.
Maybe somebody thinks their sexual history has made them unusable.
Look toward Christ.
Maybe somebody has exploited another person's vulnerability and knows this article is describing more of their heart than they wanted exposed.
Do not defend it.
Repent.
Where restitution and confession to people you have harmed can rightly and safely be made, seek godly wisdom and take responsibility.
Grace is not hiding from responsibility.
Grace gives sinners somewhere to go when responsibility finally crushes their excuses.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when someone finally stops pretending.
If your spirit is exhausted and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
And if God has been restoring places in you that you once thought were beyond repair, tell somebody what Christ has done.
Your testimony may become another wounded person's reason to look toward Jesus tonight.
Not because financial support proves that you love Jesus.
And certainly not because anyone can purchase favor with God.
The Gospel forbids that kind of manipulation.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, one legitimate expression of stewardship is voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work so that biblical teaching can continue reaching people who desperately need Christ.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not miss the greater invitation.
You can share an article and still need Jesus.
You can own every Christian book ever printed and still need Jesus.
The product is not the point.
The page is not the point.
Gospel Warrior is not the point.
Jesus Christ is.
Onan's tragedy was that he knew what was required and still chose himself.
The Gospel announces something infinitely greater:
Christ knew exactly what our redemption would cost...
and still chose the cross.
Where selfish humanity says, “I will take, but I will not give,” Jesus says of His own life:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.”
John 10:18.
Onan withheld.
Christ gave Himself.
We rebelled.
Christ obeyed.
We accumulated guilt.
Christ bore sin.
We deserved judgment.
Christ opened the door of mercy.
And death did not get the final word.
The tomb is empty.
The King is alive.
So the question left hanging over this ancient scandal is no longer merely what Onan did.
It is what you will do now that the light has reached you.
Will you keep negotiating?
Keep hiding?
Keep taking from God while resisting God?
Or will you finally open your hands and say:
“Jesus Christ, all of me belongs to You.”
Because the most dangerous place is not always far away from sacred things.
Sometimes it is close enough to touch them...
while the heart remains unsurrendered.
And the most beautiful truth is that even there, Christ still calls sinners to come home.
The scandal may explain where you have been—but when you surrender to Jesus, it does not get to decide where your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?” — THE CRY FROM THE CROSS THAT WAS REALLY ABOUT YOU
paragraphs:
“MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?” — THE CRY FROM THE CROSS THAT WAS REALLY ABOUT YOU
Jesus was not losing His faith. He was carrying sinners through the darkest hour of the Gospel—and the Psalm behind His cry changes how you hear Calvary forever.
There are words Jesus spoke from the cross that almost everyone recognizes.
But there are four words hiding inside them that many people have never really allowed themselves to feel:
Why have You forsaken Me?
Think about that.
This is Jesus.
The One who touched lepers when everyone else backed away.
The One who forgave adulterers, welcomed sinners, confronted hypocrites, opened blind eyes, and called dead men out of graves.
The One who taught His disciples to trust the Father.
Now He is hanging between earth and sky...
bleeding.
mocked.
rejected.
surrounded by people waiting for Him to die.
And suddenly, out of the darkness, comes a scream.
Matthew records the words this way:
“Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί”
Ēli, Ēli, lema sabachthani?
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Matthew 27:46.
Mark preserves the opening slightly differently:
“Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ λεμὰ σαβαχθανί”
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
The cry preserves Semitic wording in the Greek Gospel text. And it points directly backward to words Israel had already been praying for centuries.
Psalm 22.
That matters enormously.
Because Jesus was not inventing a sentence in His agony.
He was reaching into Scripture.
Psalm 22 begins in Hebrew:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
Eli, Eli, lamah azavtani?
“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”
Psalm 22:1.
Jesus was dying with Scripture on His lips.
But don't move past that too quickly.
Because knowing that Jesus was quoting Psalm 22 does not make His suffering pretend.
This was not Jesus performing religious theater for the crowd.
The nails were real.
The thirst was real.
The humiliation was real.
The darkness was real.
The death was real.
And His cry was real.
This is where Calvary becomes almost unbearable to look at.
The sinless Son of God had willingly stepped into the place of sinners.
Paul writes:
2 Corinthians 5:21.
Peter says Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
1 Peter 3:18.
Isaiah had seen the shadow of this suffering centuries earlier:
“He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities.”
Isaiah 53:5.
Do you see what is happening?
Jesus did not die because He had sinned.
He died for sinners.
He did not stand condemned because evil had finally defeated Him.
He willingly gave Himself as the spotless sacrifice through whom guilty people could be reconciled to God.
That means the question of the cross eventually reaches your name.
And mine.
Because sin becomes easy to tolerate when we only call it a “mistake.”
We hide pride behind personality.
We rename lust as weakness.
We disguise bitterness as boundaries.
We call greed ambition.
We call gossip concern.
We call compromise complexity.
We learn Christian vocabulary while quietly protecting the very things Jesus calls us to surrender.
We can sing worship songs on Sunday and feed secret addictions on Monday.
We can post Bible verses while refusing to forgive someone.
We can tell everybody that God is good while privately wondering why He allowed our lives to hurt this badly.
Some people reading this know exactly what hiding feels like.
You smile in photographs.
You answer, “I’m fine.”
You keep serving.
Keep working.
Keep posting.
Keep laughing.
Keep showing up.
