But somewhere behind the version of you everybody sees is another person whispering:
“God... where are You?”
Maybe someone abandoned you.
Maybe your marriage shattered.
Maybe the person you prayed for still died.
Maybe the child you raised walked away from God.
Maybe you begged for healing and the diagnosis remained.
Maybe you promised Jesus you would never return to that sin...
and then you did.
Again.
And now shame has convinced you that God must be tired of you.
That is why the cry from Calvary reaches so deeply into wounded people.
Jesus entered suffering so completely that Christianity cannot dismiss human anguish with shallow slogans.
At the cross, we do not meet a Savior unfamiliar with pain.
We meet the Man of Sorrows.
But something even greater is happening.
Jesus' words open Psalm 22.
And when you read the Psalm beside the crucifixion accounts, the parallels are striking.
The sufferer is mocked.
People ridicule his trust in God.
His suffering becomes physically devastating.
His garments are divided.
Lots are cast for his clothing.
Then look at Calvary.
Jesus is mocked.
His trust in God becomes part of the mockery.
His garments are divided.
Lots are cast.
Matthew's passion narrative repeatedly echoes the language and imagery of Psalm 22.
The crucified Jesus stands inside the story that Psalm 22 had already given God's people.
Yet Psalm 22 does something many people miss.
It does not end where it begins.
It begins with:
“Why have You forsaken me?”
But suffering does not get the final sentence.
Later the Psalm declares that God has heard the afflicted one's cry.
Then the horizon becomes enormous.
The nations are brought into view.
People yet unborn will hear what God has done.
The Psalm moves from abandonment and agony toward vindication, worship, proclamation, and worldwide hope.
In other words...
Jesus chose the opening words of a Psalm whose darkness does not win.
And neither would the darkness of Golgotha.
This is why we have to be careful when explaining the cry of Jesus.
Christians sometimes say that the Father simply stopped loving the Son, or that the Trinity somehow broke apart at Calvary.
Scripture does not require us to say that.
The eternal Father, Son, and Holy Spirit did not cease to be the triune God.
The divine nature of the Son did not suddenly dissolve.
The Trinity was not destroyed for three hours.
Yet neither should we empty Jesus' cry of its terrible weight.
The Son truly suffered.
He truly died.
He truly bore our sins.
He truly endured the judgment associated with our rebellion as our representative and substitute.
Galatians says:
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
Galatians 3:13.
Peter writes:
1 Peter 2:24.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful explanations comes from the same apostle:
“Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous...”
Why?
“...that he might bring us to God.”
1 Peter 3:18.
There it is.
To bring us to God.
That is the heart of the cross.
Jesus did not suffer so you could become slightly more religious.
He did not die so you could decorate your life with inspirational Christian quotations while remaining lord of your own heart.
He did not rise again merely to improve your mood.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
To forgive sinners.
To break the dominion of sin.
To give eternal life.
To make enemies children.
To bring the lost home.
And suddenly the scandal becomes grace.
The innocent One stands where the guilty belonged.
The King wears thorns.
The Creator is mocked by creatures.
The hands through whom creation came are stretched upon wood.
The One without sin bears the sins of others.
And the grave receives Someone it cannot keep.
That is Christianity.
Not humanity climbing toward God.
God coming for humanity in Jesus Christ.
Not good people earning heaven.
Sinners receiving mercy through a crucified and risen Savior.
Not pretending your past never happened.
Redemption.
This is why our message remains:
Maybe your story has scandal in it.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your worst chapter has your fingerprints all over it.
Maybe someone else's sin shattered you.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun what happened.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we wanted to admit.
But the cross also proves something else:
God's grace reaches farther than repentant sinners ever dared to hope.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending evil was good.
He rewrites everything through redemption.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed Paul into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Jesus could not climb down from his cross and rebuild his reputation.
He could not spend twenty years proving himself.
He could not repay everybody.
He had nothing left to offer except a desperate appeal to the King dying beside him.
And grace met him there.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs to understand.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to make Jesus willing to save you.
You come because you cannot save yourself.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender your excuses.
You stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
And you throw yourself upon the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Grace is free to us.
It was not cheap to Him.
Look again at the cross.
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
And then remember what comes afterward.
“It is finished.”
The cry of anguish was not the final word.
The tomb was not the final word.
Rome was not the final word.
The religious leaders were not the final word.
Your sin does not have to have the final word either.
Jesus does.
Three days later, the stone could not hold the Author of life.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
The crucified Messiah became the proclaimed risen Lord.
And because He lives, forgiveness is not wishful thinking.
Grace is not positive thinking.
Redemption is not religious poetry.
The Gospel announces that Christ died for sins, was buried, and was raised.
So now this article has to stop being merely about theology.
It has to become personal.
What are you hiding?
What have you refused to surrender?
What wound has become your identity?
What sin have you renamed so you can keep it?
What resentment are you feeding?
What secret would terrify you if everybody discovered it?
What happened to the person who once prayed with fire?
Where did you become cold?
Where did you stop trusting?
Where did following Jesus become merely looking Christian?
Nobody here can stop you.
But scrolling cannot silence the question forever:
What will you do with Jesus Christ?
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a spiritual performance.
Be honest before God.
Someone reading beneath this article may need the evidence of grace written in your story.
Don't underestimate what one honest testimony can do.
And don't keep this message trapped on this page.
There may be somebody on your Facebook friends list who would never walk into a church this week but would read something you shared at 1:17 in the morning.
Someone fighting addiction.
Someone contemplating giving up.
Someone angry with God.
Someone drowning in shame.
Someone who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to them.
Someone who desperately needs to hear that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
But if the Gospel has given you something worth proclaiming, using your influence to put Christ before another human being can become an act of witness.
There may come a night when you need to return to the truth that your feelings are not the final authority over whether God is faithful.
And invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelievers—to follow too.
Not to buy God's approval.
Not to earn salvation.
Not to prove you love Jesus.
Christ's finished work cannot be purchased.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the sin.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the secret chapter.
Bring Him the shattered pieces.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem a sinner's tomorrow.
At Calvary, the world saw scandal.
Heaven was accomplishing redemption.
The cross looked like defeat.
Sunday revealed victory.
The condemned thief saw a dying man and called Him King.
The centurion watched Him die and recognized something extraordinary.
The disciples thought everything had ended.
God was writing resurrection into the next chapter.
And perhaps that is why those terrifying words still echo across two thousand years:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Because Jesus entered the darkness sinners deserved so that those who belong to Him would never have to face judgment without a Savior.
Because Psalm 22 begins with anguish but moves toward proclamation.
Because Good Friday leads toward resurrection morning.
Because shame does not have to become your identity.
Because your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Because there is still blood-bought mercy for repentant sinners.
Still forgiveness.
Still a cross.
Still an empty tomb.
Still a risen King.
Still Jesus.
And comment something honest—not something impressive.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or simply tell us what Jesus has brought you through.
Because somewhere beneath your comment may be a stranger wondering whether grace could possibly reach someone like them.
Your story might whisper the answer.
The cry from the cross sounded like the end—but in the hands of Jesus, even the darkest sentence can become the doorway to resurrection.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: RIZPAH WAS SAUL’S CONCUBINE—THEN ANOTHER MAN WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH HER
paragraphs: RIZPAH WAS SAUL’S CONCUBINE—THEN ANOTHER MAN WAS ACCUSED OF SLEEPING WITH HER

She was introduced in Scripture in the middle of a sexual accusation between powerful men. Years later, she would be found beneath the bodies of her dead sons, fighting off birds and beasts. But if you read her story only for the scandal, you will miss the woman—and perhaps miss something painfully familiar about yourself.
Her name was Rizpah.
And the first time many people really notice her in the Bible, she is standing in the shadow of an accusation she did not make.
Not a love story.
Not a wedding.
Not a beautiful introduction.
An accusation.

The kingdom was fractured. Saul was dead. David was becoming stronger while the house of Saul was becoming weaker. Abner, commander of Saul’s army, had become enormously influential within the fading dynasty.
Then one sentence detonated inside Saul’s house.
The Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 3:7 says:
“וּלְשָׁאוּל פִּלֶגֶשׁ וּשְׁמָהּ רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה”
Ule-Sha’ul pilegesh, u-shemah Ritzpah bat-Ayyah.
In straightforward English:
“Now Saul had a concubine, and her name was Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.”
Then comes the accusation:
“מַדּוּעַ בָּאתָה אֶל־פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִי”
Maddua ba’ta el-pilegesh avi?
Literally, the language asks why Abner had “gone in to” his father’s concubine—a conventional biblical expression referring to sexual relations.
Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son and the king supported by Abner, was confronting the most powerful man holding his kingdom together.
Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?
And suddenly Rizpah’s body was at the center of a political explosion.
But there is something we must refuse to do if we want to handle Scripture faithfully.
We must not say more than God has said.
The Bible tells us that Ish-bosheth accused Abner.
It tells us Abner became furious.
It tells us the accusation contributed to a catastrophic break between Abner and Saul’s house.
But the narrative never pauses to give us a verdict saying, “Yes, Abner did it.”
Nor does it explicitly say, “No, the accusation was false.”
That silence matters.
Because sometimes careless Bible teaching turns an accusation into a conviction.
Scripture does not give us permission to do that.
And there is another silence that is even harder to ignore.
Rizpah does not speak.
Read the confrontation.
Ish-bosheth speaks.
Abner speaks.
Kingship is discussed.
Loyalty is discussed.
Betrayal is discussed.
Power is discussed.
But the woman whose body is at the center of the controversy?
No recorded words.
We are not told what Rizpah thought.
We are not told what Rizpah wanted.
We are not told whether she was consulted.
We are not told whether she wept.
We are not told whether she was terrified.
We are not even told, in this passage, what happened from her perspective.
And that should make us careful.
Because Rizpah is a real woman in the biblical narrative, not raw material for our imagination.
We should not invent conversations God did not record.
We should not manufacture motives the text does not reveal.
We should not transform biblical silence into fictional certainty.
But we can notice the silence.

And perhaps that is where her story begins reaching through the centuries and touching people who know exactly what it feels like to have everyone discussing what happened around them while almost nobody asks what happened inside them.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some people know what it is to become a sentence in somebody else’s argument.
Some know what it is to have their reputation discussed in rooms they never entered.
Some know what it is to become attached to a scandal they did not create.
Some know what it is to be remembered by what somebody else allegedly did.
Your name became connected to the divorce.
The betrayal.
The pregnancy.
The addiction.
The arrest.
The family breakdown.
The church controversy.
The affair.
The abuse.
The rumor.
The failure.
And suddenly people stopped seeing a human being.
They saw a story.
Rizpah’s story warns us how easily human beings can do that.
But there is more happening here than sexual scandal.

In the world of ancient monarchy, access to a deceased king’s concubines could carry political significance. Royal women could become entangled with questions of succession and claims to royal authority. That helps explain why Ish-bosheth’s accusation was not merely a private complaint about sexual morality. It could be heard as a challenge touching the throne itself.
That context makes Abner’s rage easier to understand.
He had been strengthening Saul’s house.
Now Ish-bosheth had accused him of wrongdoing involving Saul’s concubine.
Abner responded furiously and swore that he would help transfer the kingdom from Saul’s house to David.
One accusation.
One furious confrontation.
And political history moved.
Yet Rizpah remained Rizpah.
Not merely “Saul’s concubine.”
Not merely “the woman Abner was accused of sleeping with.”
A woman with a name.
A daughter.
“Rizpah, daughter of Aiah.”
And years later Scripture brings her back.
When it does, you may never forget her again.
There was famine during David’s reign.
The narrative connects the crisis with bloodguilt associated with Saul’s actions against the Gibeonites. After David consulted the Gibeonites, seven male descendants of Saul were handed over to them.
Among those seven were two sons of Rizpah.
Armoni.
Mephibosheth—the son of Saul and Rizpah, not Jonathan’s son of the same name whom David had earlier shown covenant kindness.
Imagine reading their names if you were their mother.
These were not statistics to her.
These were sons.
The men were killed and their bodies exposed.
Then the Bible gives us one of its most haunting pictures of maternal grief.
Rizpah took sackcloth.
She spread it upon a rock.
And she stayed.
From the beginning of the harvest until rain fell.
Day after day.
Night after night.
The birds came.
She drove them away.
The animals came.
She would not let them have the bodies.
The woman whose voice Scripture never records now performs an act so powerful that her actions reach the king.
Do not romanticize this scene.
It is horrifying.
A mother is beneath the exposed remains of her children.
There is no sentimental soundtrack.
No painless inspirational ending.
There is grief.
Heat.
Night.
Wild animals.
Birds.
Sackcloth.
Rock.
And a mother who refuses to abandon the dead.
How many nights did she stare into darkness?
Scripture does not tell us.
How many tears?
We do not know.
What prayers did she pray?
The Bible does not record them.
So we will not invent them.
But Scripture tells us what she did.
She stayed.
And eventually word reached David.
That detail is breathtaking.
Rizpah had almost no political power that the narrative tells us about.
She commanded no army.
Issued no decree.
Sat on no throne.
Yet her persistence became news powerful enough to reach the king.
David then acted.
He retrieved the bones of Saul and Jonathan and gathered the remains of those who had been exposed. They were buried in the tomb of Kish, Saul’s father.
The disgraced dead received burial.
And Rizpah’s vigil was remembered.
Do you see the strange arc of her biblical story?
She first appears while powerful men argue over her.
She reappears when powerful decisions have taken her sons.
In the first scene, men speak and Rizpah is silent.
In the later scene, Rizpah still has no recorded speech...
but everybody eventually hears what she is doing.
There are moments when faithfulness becomes a kind of testimony even before a sentence is spoken.
And maybe somebody reading this needs that.
Maybe you have spent years believing that because nobody heard your side, God did not see your side.
Those are not the same thing.
Human beings can overlook you.
God cannot lose sight of you.
Human beings can reduce you to your worst chapter.
God knows the whole book.
Human beings may remember the accusation.
God knows the truth.
And here we must go farther than Rizpah.
Because Rizpah can move us deeply, but Rizpah cannot save us.
Only Jesus Christ can.
The Bible is not ultimately a collection of inspirational survivors teaching us to become strong enough to rescue ourselves.
Scripture leads us to the Savior.
And when we reach Jesus, we meet Someone who knows what it means to be publicly accused, humiliated, condemned, exposed and treated as shameful.
But there is a crucial difference.
Jesus was sinless.
He did not merely become another tragic victim of human cruelty.
He willingly gave Himself according to the saving purpose of God.
At the cross, the innocent Son of God bore sin for sinners.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin...” says 2 Corinthians 5:21.
First Peter 2:24 says Christ “bore our sins in his body on the tree.”
That is where this story must ultimately take us.
Not merely to a grieving mother sitting beneath death.
To the cross where death itself met its Conqueror.
Rizpah guarded bodies she could not resurrect.
Jesus walked out of His tomb.
That changes everything.
Christian hope is not that we can somehow protect everything we love from death.
We cannot.
Christian hope is that Jesus Christ has entered death, defeated it through His resurrection, and promises eternal life to those who belong to Him.
Maybe your scandal is different from Rizpah’s.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
You have learned how to smile around it.
You go to work.
You answer messages.
You attend church.
You post pictures.
You tell people, “I’m okay.”
But there is a rock somewhere inside your soul where you have been sitting for years.
Guarding what was lost.
Fighting memories.
Fighting shame.
Fighting bitterness.
Fighting the voice that says your story ended when everything fell apart.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to make respectable people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
He came for the guilty who repent.
For the ashamed who come into the light.
For the broken who know they cannot repair themselves.
For the exhausted.
For the hidden.
For people with chapters they wish could be ripped from the book.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
It says your sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
Grace is not God pretending evil is harmless.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty people could never provide for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new life.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not cleaning yourself up so Jesus will tolerate you.
It is turning from sin and coming to the Savior because you finally understand that hiding cannot heal you.
Maybe you have spent years protecting your reputation while your soul was starving.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary but have never surrendered to Christ.
Maybe you can quote verses and still secretly love the sin that crucified your conscience.
Maybe you have confused being around Christianity with belonging to Jesus.
Come to Christ.
Confess what you have hidden.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Believe the Gospel.
There is mercy in Jesus that your worst night cannot exhaust.
There is cleansing in Christ deeper than the stain you thought would define you forever.
There is no scandal so powerful that the grace of Jesus becomes powerless.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean every relationship is automatically restored.
It does not mean repentance erases the temporal damage caused by sin.
It means something greater.
Your final identity does not have to be written by your rebellion, your shame, your suffering, somebody else’s accusation, or somebody else’s sin against you.
Jesus Christ can write redemption where you thought only ruins remained.
That is why our heartbeat is simple:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding from God, stop pretending He cannot see it.
He already sees.
Come into the light.
Somebody reading silently may need to discover that grace still reaches people in real life.
Not because clicking “Share” somehow earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
Someone may know Rizpah’s silence.
Someone may know scandal.
Someone may know grief.
Someone may desperately need to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.

Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's favor, prove your salvation, or make you more righteous before Him. Christ alone is our righteousness. But generous, willing support can help biblical teaching reach people who desperately need it.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
The Gospel does not need your money to become true.
Jesus is already Lord.

The question is whether His grace has taken hold of you so deeply that your time, your voice, your resources, your influence, your repentance, your generosity, and your entire life increasingly belong to Him.
It is surrender.
If you share, let it be mission rather than performance.
If you comment, let it be honest.
And whatever you do, do not leave Jesus outside the story.
Because Rizpah’s story eventually leaves us with a woman sitting beside death, unable to reverse it.
The Gospel takes us somewhere Rizpah could never take herself.
To an empty tomb.
To a risen King.
To Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry with you tonight is this:
The chapter that made people whisper your name does not have the authority to write the final sentence over a life surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PROVERBS LITERALLY TELLS A HUSBAND TO BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE
paragraphs: PROVERBS LITERALLY TELLS A HUSBAND TO BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE
Maybe the Bible’s answer to temptation is more beautiful—and more intimate—than many Christians were ever taught.
There is a sentence in Proverbs that sounds almost too passionate to be sitting inside the Bible.
Not because it is vulgar.
Because it is breathtakingly unashamed.
God does not merely tell a husband, “Do not commit adultery.”
He gives him something far more beautiful to pursue.
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
And then Scripture goes further.
Much further.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 5:19 ends with these words:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
A close rendering is:
“In her love, be intoxicated continually.”
Read that again.
Not intoxicated with another woman.
Not intoxicated with pornography.
Not intoxicated with fantasy.
Not intoxicated with the endless parade of carefully edited bodies glowing from a screen.
Not intoxicated with the attention of someone who is not your spouse.
With her.
Your wife.
The woman whose face you have seen exhausted.
The woman whose imperfections you know.
The woman who has seen yours.

The woman who may have stood beside you through bills, children, disappointment, arguments, sickness, aging, ordinary Tuesdays, unanswered prayers, and seasons when neither of you felt particularly romantic.
Scripture says something astonishing:
Keep finding your way back to her.

The Hebrew verb behind that startling statement is שָׁגָה — shagah. In this context it carries the imagery of being so captivated that one reels—as though intoxicated. That is why faithful English translations variously render the expression “intoxicated,” “captivated,” “exhilarated,” “enraptured,” or “lost” in her love.
This is not a mistranslation designed to make Scripture provocative.
The Hebrew really is that vivid.
And that matters.
Because some Christians were accidentally taught a version of holiness in which marriage is permitted but passion is suspicious.
Sexual desire became something Christians whispered about.
Bodies became embarrassing.
Romance became something tolerated before marriage and forgotten afterward.
And holiness somehow became synonymous with emotional coldness.
But Proverbs 5 will not allow that distortion.
God created marital intimacy.
And within the covenant of marriage, Scripture does not merely tolerate delight.
It celebrates it.
Proverbs 5:18–19 speaks of a blessed fountain, rejoicing in “the wife of your youth,” satisfaction within marriage, and continuing captivation by her love.
That is not pornography wearing religious clothing.
It is covenant poetry.
There is an enormous difference.
Pornography teaches you to consume bodies.
Covenant teaches you to cherish a person.
Lust says, “What can you give me?”
Love says, “How can I faithfully give myself to you?”
Pornography trains the eyes to wander.
Covenant calls the eyes home.
Adultery requires secrecy.
Biblical marriage invites nakedness without shame, faithfulness without divided loyalties, and intimacy without the terror that someone will disappear when pleasure stops being convenient.
And here is what makes Proverbs 5 even more powerful.
You cannot understand verse 19 if you rip it out of the chapter and turn it into a romantic slogan.
The chapter is a warning.

A father is teaching his son about sexual temptation. Forbidden desire initially tastes sweet, but the path eventually becomes bitter. The young man is warned not to surrender his strength, dignity, years, and life to sexual unfaithfulness.
Then, in the middle of that warning, Scripture does something beautiful.
It does not merely say:
Stay away.
It essentially says:
Come home.
Drink from your own well.
Rejoice in your wife.
Delight in her.
Remain captivated by her love.
That is a radically different picture of sexual holiness.
Holiness is not merely saying no to forbidden desire.
It is learning to say a wholehearted yes to what God has called good.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that before another marriage quietly freezes to death.
Your spouse should not have to compete with an imaginary woman who does not exist.
She should not have to compete with pornography.
She should not have to compete with your memories of somebody from twenty years ago.

She should not have to compete with filtered faces, curated bodies, private messages, flirtatious coworkers, secret accounts, or the fantasy that somewhere there is a person who would give you pleasure without ever requiring patience, sacrifice, forgiveness, responsibility, or covenant.
Fantasy is easy precisely because fantasy never asks you to love a real human being.
Marriage does.
Marriage eventually introduces you to morning breath and medical appointments.
Laundry.
Misunderstandings.
Financial pressure.
Stretch marks.
Scars.
Gray hair.
Children crying at 2:17 in the morning.
Seasons of grief.
Seasons of exhaustion.
Moments when affection feels effortless.
Moments when choosing love feels like carrying a cross.
And somewhere inside all of that ordinary humanity, God says:
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
That command becomes more beautiful the longer you sit with it.
Because the “wife of your youth” eventually stops being young.
So do you.
The hands change.
The face changes.
The body changes.
Life writes its history across both of you.
But covenant says:
I am still here.
I still see you.
I still choose you.
I will not train my heart to despise what time has touched.
I will not demand that the woman beside me compete with twenty-year-olds manufactured by algorithms for my attention.
I will remember the person beneath the changing body.
I will remember the promises.
I will remember the laughter.
I will remember the nights we almost broke.
I will remember the prayers nobody else heard.
I will remember the battles we survived.
And by the grace of God, I will keep learning how to delight in you.
That is far more powerful than lust.
Lust requires novelty.
Covenant discovers depth.
Lust becomes bored because it keeps asking for another body.
Love keeps discovering the mystery of the same person.
And perhaps this is where the verse stops being beautiful and starts becoming painful.
Because some husbands reading this know exactly where their affection has gone.
Some wives know exactly what it feels like to lie beside a man whose body is in the room but whose desire lives somewhere else.
Some husbands know what it is to have allowed resentment to turn tenderness into distance.
Some marriages have not experienced affection in months.
Some in years.
Some people reading these words have hidden browser histories.
Hidden conversations.
Hidden fantasies.
Hidden affairs.
Hidden wounds.
And Christianity does not heal us by teaching us to hide better.
Jesus brings hidden things into the light.
Not so sinners can be publicly humiliated.
So sinners can be redeemed.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had successfully made themselves spotless.
He came to save sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces that Christ died for sinners, rose again, calls us to repentance, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who come to Him.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
But look at the cross again.
You mattered enough for Him to bleed.
So if pornography has poisoned your marriage, bring it into the light.
If adultery has shattered trust, stop baptizing deception with excuses.
If flirtation has become emotional infidelity, stop calling it friendship simply because nobody has touched yet.
If bitterness has made you emotionally abandon your spouse, confess it.
If you have used Proverbs 5 as permission to demand intimacy while refusing tenderness, repentance belongs there too.
Because Proverbs 5:19 is not a divine authorization for husbands to treat wives as objects.
Quite the opposite.
The woman in the passage is not pornography with a wedding ring.
She is “the wife of your youth.”
A covenant partner.
A person to rejoice in.
A person whose love is treasured.
Biblical marital intimacy cannot be separated from the broader commands of Christlike love, faithfulness, honor, sacrifice, kindness, patience, forgiveness, and mutual care.
A husband following Jesus cannot demand that his wife become an instrument for his appetite while he ignores her heart.
Christ does not teach men to consume women.
He teaches His people sacrificial love.
Ephesians 5 points husbands toward the staggering standard of Christ’s love for the church—a love characterized by self-giving sacrifice.
That changes everything.
A Christian husband does not ask only:
“Does my wife satisfy me?”
He must also ask:
“Does she feel cherished by me?”
“Does she feel safe with me?”
“Have I listened to her?”
“Have I prayed for her?”
“Have I wounded her and refused to apologize?”
“Have I spent more energy pursuing strangers on a screen than pursuing the woman I promised before God to love?”
That last question may hurt.
Let it.
Sometimes conviction is mercy knocking before destruction kicks the door down.

And wives are not outside the call to covenant faithfulness either. Christian marriage calls both husband and wife away from contempt, manipulation, infidelity, cruelty, indifference, and selfishness and toward faithful, Christ-shaped love.
This is not about pretending every troubled marriage can be repaired with a romantic dinner.
Some marriages carry profound betrayal.

Some involve abuse, coercion, danger, or serious patterns requiring wise pastoral, professional, or legal help. Scripture's celebration of marital intimacy must never be weaponized to pressure someone into sexual activity or silence someone who is unsafe.
Biblical love never needs abuse to survive.
But where repentance is real, where safety is present, where two wounded people are willing to submit themselves to Christ, grace can begin doing what human pride said was impossible.
Slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Trust may return one honest conversation at a time.
Tenderness may return one gentle touch at a time.
Prayer may return awkwardly.
Forgiveness may involve tears.
A marriage may have to learn how to speak again before it learns how to laugh again.
And that is okay.
Restoration does not always look dramatic.
Sometimes resurrection begins with two people sitting at the kitchen table saying:
“We cannot keep living like this.”
Then one of them whispers:
“I'm sorry.”
And the other starts crying.
And somewhere unseen, grace enters the room.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful right now.
Protect it.
Maybe it is tired.
Nourish it.
Maybe it is wounded.
Seek help and bring the truth into the light.
Maybe you are single.

Then do not read Proverbs 5 as permission to awaken covenant privileges outside covenant. Let it teach you that biblical sexuality is not dirty, but neither is it casual. God's vision connects sexual delight with faithfulness rather than separating pleasure from responsibility.
Maybe you have already failed sexually.
Then hear this carefully:
Your failure does not outrun the blood of Jesus Christ.
Repentance is not pretending it never happened.
Grace is not permission to continue.
The Gospel gives something far better.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
A new direction.
A transformed heart.
You may carry consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Relationships may not instantly return to what they were.
But the cross means your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire life.
Peter had chapters he wished he could erase.
The woman at the well had chapters.
The woman caught in adultery had chapters.
David had horrifying chapters.
The church at Corinth was filled with people who had chapters.
And then Jesus entered the story.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners in the middle of it.
Maybe the greatest miracle your marriage needs is not for your spouse to become somebody different.
Maybe you need Jesus to change the way you see the person already beside you.
To give you eyes that stop wandering.
A heart that stops comparing.
Hands that learn tenderness again.
A mouth that speaks life instead of contempt.
Humility that knows how to apologize without adding, “but you…”
Courage to confess what has been hidden.
Strength to delete what needs deleting.
Wisdom to establish boundaries.
Grace to forgive.
Patience to rebuild.
And love that says:
After everything...
I want to learn you again.
Maybe tonight the holiest thing some married couple can do is put the phones down.
Sit beside each other.
Look at each other.
Not as roommates.
Not as coworkers managing children.
Not as two exhausted people sharing expenses.
As husband and wife.
And say:
“Where did we lose each other?”
Then listen.
Really listen.
And if the answer hurts, do not run immediately.
Bring Jesus into the wound.
Because the same Christ who forgives sinners can teach forgiven sinners how to love.
And perhaps now Proverbs 5:19 does not sound scandalous anymore.
Perhaps it sounds like rescue.
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
Be continually captivated by her love.
Come home.
Following Gospel Warrior keeps Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, and discipleship appearing in a feed designed to pull your attention in a thousand other directions.
Supporting Gospel work through sharing and voluntary financial support can be one way believers choose to steward resources for ministry; it should never be confused with earning God's favor.
Because Christianity's message is not that righteous people never become dirty.
It is that Jesus Christ still washes sinners who come to Him.
And maybe years from now, the greatest love story in your house will not be that two people never broke each other's hearts.
It will be that when everything seemed too broken to rewrite, Jesus picked up the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Mother Was Told Her Unborn Son Must Never Cut His Hair — But the Hair Was Never the Real Story
paragraphs: A Mother Was Told Her Unborn Son Must Never Cut His Hair — But the Hair Was Never the Real Story

Before Samson ever touched a lion, carried the gates of a city, loved the wrong woman, lost his eyes, or brought a Philistine temple crashing down around him, God spoke over his life while he was still hidden inside his mother’s womb.
There is something almost haunting about the beginning of Samson’s story.
Because before there was Delilah…
before there were scissors…
before there were Philistines celebrating over a blinded man…
there was a woman carrying an impossible child.
And there was a word from God.
Most people remember Samson because of his hair.
God remembered Samson before he had any.
That changes the story.
Judges introduces us to a man named Manoah from Zorah, from the tribe of Dan. Then Scripture quietly introduces the woman who would become Samson’s mother.
It does not even give us her name.
It gives us her pain.
She was barren.
She had borne no children.

In the ancient world, those words could carry years of grief behind them. Months becoming years. Expectations becoming disappointment. Perhaps watching other women hold babies while her own arms remained empty.
Scripture does not tell us every tear she cried.
It simply tells us what was impossible.
Then God walked directly into the impossible.
The angel of the LORD appeared to her and announced that although she had been barren, she would conceive and bear a son.
Then came the command that would mark the child's life:
“וּמוֹרָה֙ לֹא־יַעֲלֶ֣ה עַל־רֹאשׁ֔וֹ”
U-morah lo-ya'aleh al-rosho.
Literally, the idea is:
“No razor shall come upon his head.”
Then comes the reason:
“כִּֽי־נְזִ֧יר אֱלֹהִ֛ים יִֽהְיֶ֥ה הַנַּ֖עַר מִן־הַבָּ֑טֶן”
Ki-nezir Elohim yihyeh ha-na'ar min-ha-baten.
“For the boy shall be a Nazirite of God from the womb.”
And then something breathtaking:
“וְה֗וּא יָחֵ֛ל לְהוֹשִׁ֥יעַ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל”
Ve-hu yachel lehoshia et-Yisrael.
“He shall begin to save Israel.”
That wording matters.
He would begin.
Samson was never going to be the final Savior.
His strength would be extraordinary, but insufficient.
His victories would be real, but incomplete.
His calling would come from God, but Samson himself would remain a deeply flawed man in desperate need of the same grace every sinner needs.
And maybe that is why his story still feels uncomfortably familiar.
Because some of us know what it feels like to be called by God…
and still make terrible decisions.
To know Scripture…
and still flirt with temptation.
To experience God's mercy…
and still return to something that almost destroyed us.
To carry evidence of God's hand on our lives while secretly entertaining things that have no business being there.
Samson's story begins with consecration.
But it eventually becomes a story of compromise.
And somewhere between those two words may be your story too.
The Hebrew word translated “Nazirite” is נָזִיר — nazir, connected with the idea of being separated, dedicated, or consecrated.

Numbers 6 explains the ordinary Nazirite vow. The Nazirite was separated to the LORD, abstained from products of the vine, did not cut the hair during the period of consecration, and avoided ritual defilement associated with a dead body.
So Samson's hair was never supposed to be a magical battery.
There was no supernatural chemical inside his hair.
The hair was visible evidence of something deeper.
He belonged to God.
That is the part we often miss.
We stare at Samson's hair.
God's Word points us toward Samson's consecration.
And suddenly this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because we are very good at protecting the visible evidence of Christianity while neglecting the invisible reality of surrender.
We can carry a Bible and still carry bitterness.
Sing worship songs and secretly feed lust.
Post Scripture while refusing to forgive.
Know Christian language while living two different lives.
Look consecrated publicly while compromising privately.
Samson's greatest problem was never that eventually somebody cut his hair.
The tragedy had begun much earlier.
The scissors simply revealed where years of compromise had already taken him.
That is frightening because spiritual collapse rarely begins on the night everybody discovers it.
It usually begins quietly.
A boundary moves.
A conviction gets negotiated.
A temptation becomes entertainment.
Entertainment becomes permission.
Permission becomes habit.
Habit becomes bondage.
And bondage eventually asks for everything.
Samson kept getting closer to the edge.
And because judgment did not fall immediately, he could keep mistaking God's patience for God's approval.
Maybe somebody reading this understands that more than they want to admit.
You haven't abandoned Jesus.
Not exactly.
You still believe.
You still pray sometimes.
You still know the verses.
But something has been happening inside you.
The distance has been growing.
Something you once resisted no longer bothers you quite as much.
Something you once confessed you now explain.
Something you once ran from you now keep close enough to visit whenever you're lonely.
And perhaps nobody knows.
That is what makes Samson's story terrifying.
A person can possess a calling and still play with compromise.
A person can experience the power of God and still make foolish choices.
Past victories do not make present disobedience safe.
Eventually Samson meets Delilah.
Again and again she presses him to reveal the secret connected with his strength.
Again and again Samson plays dangerously close to the truth.
Until finally he tells her about his consecration and his uncut hair.
Then Samson sleeps.
The hair is removed.
He wakes believing he can escape as he had before.
But Judges records one of the saddest realities in his entire story:
he did not know that the LORD had departed from him.
Imagine being so accustomed to yesterday's strength that you do not recognize today's spiritual emptiness.
That sentence should frighten anyone who thinks outward Christian activity can substitute for inward fellowship with God.
The Philistines seize him.
They gouge out his eyes.
The mighty Samson becomes a prisoner.
The man who had terrified armies is reduced to grinding grain for his enemies.
Darkness.
Humiliation.
Consequences.
And perhaps that is where some people stop reading Samson.
But God doesn't.
There is a tiny sentence in Judges 16 that feels like grace whispering through prison walls:
the hair on Samson's head began to grow again.
Read that slowly.
It.
Began.
To grow.
Again.
The point is not that hair itself regenerated supernatural power.
The narrative is signaling that Samson's story is not finished.
The consequences are real.
His eyes do not magically return.
His imprisonment does not disappear.
Grace does not pretend sin never happened.
But neither does failure get the final word.
And this is where Samson's story begins pointing beyond Samson.
Because Israel needed more than a strong man.
They needed a Savior.
Samson could begin deliverance.
Jesus Christ would accomplish a far greater deliverance.
Samson was announced before his birth.
Christ's coming was announced before His birth.
Samson was set apart for God's purpose.
Jesus was perfectly obedient to the Father.
Samson repeatedly surrendered to temptation.
Jesus was tempted and remained without sin.
Samson's final victory involved his own death.
Jesus willingly laid down His life, and through His death defeated the powers of sin and death.
But the comparison eventually breaks apart because Samson was a sinner who needed grace.
Jesus is the sinless Savior who gives it.
Samson's arms stretched between the pillars of a pagan temple as his life ended.
Centuries later, outside Jerusalem, the arms of Jesus Christ were stretched upon a Roman cross.
But Jesus was not dying because His own compromise had finally caught Him.
He was bearing the sins of others.
Our sins.
Our compromises.
Our secret rooms.
Our shame.
Our rebellion.
Our self-righteousness.
Our lust.
Our lies.
Our addictions.
Our pride.
Our religious performances.
The Gospel is not that strong people finally learn how to behave.
The Gospel is that guilty people can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And because He lives, repentance is not a walk toward hopelessness.
It is a return to mercy.
Maybe your “hair” has already been cut.
Maybe what you thought nobody would discover has been exposed.
Maybe the relationship collapsed.
Maybe the addiction returned.
Maybe your children saw the hypocrisy.
Maybe your spouse found out.
Maybe you failed again after promising God that last time really was the last time.
Maybe you are living inside consequences you cannot undo.
Hear this carefully.
Biblical grace does not tell you that your sin does not matter.
Grace tells you that your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is greater than the sin you bring to Him in repentance and faith.
You do not need another hiding place.
You need Jesus.
You do not need to manufacture enough strength to become worthy of Him.
You need to come honestly.
Repent.
Confess.
Believe.
Return.
The same Bible that shows us Samson blind and humiliated also shows him crying out to the LORD again.
His final chapter is tragic. Scripture does not romanticize his choices.
Yet even there, Samson calls upon God.
And God hears him.
That does not make every decision Samson made acceptable.
It makes grace astonishing.
Because God has always been better at redeeming broken people than broken people are at hiding themselves.
Maybe that is what you needed tonight.
Not permission to continue compromising.
A reason to stop running.
There is a difference.
Grace is not Jesus standing beside your sin saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace is Jesus calling you out of darkness because you matter to Him, purchasing forgiveness at immeasurable cost, and giving His Spirit to transform those who belong to Him.
So ask yourself the question Samson's story forces us to confront:
What am I allowing into my life that is slowly cutting away at my consecration to God?
Don't answer publicly unless you should.
But answer God.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe emotional infidelity nobody has called adultery yet.
Maybe greed.
Maybe alcohol has become your hiding place.
Maybe approval is your addiction.
Maybe anger controls your home.
Maybe pride has convinced you that repentance is something other people need.
Maybe you have mastered the appearance of Christianity while your private relationship with Christ is starving.
Do not wait for your own Gaza.
Do not wait until compromise takes your sight before admitting you have been walking toward darkness.
Come home now.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can make one small confession of surrender.
Your comment may become the sentence another struggling believer reads at 2:00 in the morning and realizes, I'm not the only one fighting.
And please share this.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
They may simply read.
And God may use one sentence of Scripture to interrupt the direction of their life.
Because temptation has an irritating habit of returning after conviction fades.
Come back when you need to remember:
Samson's strength was never ultimately about hair.
It was about God.
And your hope is not ultimately your ability to hold yourself together.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling Christians, seekers, lukewarm believers, and even the unbeliever who has questions about Jesus to follow with you.
It doesn't.
Jesus purchased salvation; we cannot buy it.

But if this ministry genuinely serves Christ and faithfully helps people encounter His Word, financially supporting that work can be one practical way of participating in its mission. Give freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully—not from guilt or spiritual pressure.
And there is another reason to stay.
Not as advertising.
As a seed.
You may never know who reads it while sitting alone in a dark room.
You may never know whose secret compromise gets interrupted.
You may never know who whispers the name of Jesus again because something in this story reminded them that the Father still receives repentant sinners.
And perhaps that is the final thing Samson's mother could never have imagined while carrying that unborn boy.
She could protect his uncut hair while he was young.
She could obey what God commanded her.
She could raise a child marked by consecration.
But eventually Samson had to live before God himself.
So do you.
Your parents cannot surrender for you.
Your pastor cannot repent for you.
Your spouse cannot believe for you.
Your Christian posts cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
Your reputation cannot save you.
And your worst scandal does not have authority to write the final sentence either.
Jesus does.
No applause.
No flowing locks that made people stare.
No heroic image.
Just a broken man in darkness reaching toward God again.
Then look toward Calvary.
There is a better Deliverer there.
A Savior who did not merely begin to save.
A Savior who declared:
“It is finished.”
Run to Him.
Because maybe the most important thing about your story is not the chapter where everything fell apart.
Maybe it is what happens when, surrounded by the wreckage, you finally stop trusting your own strength…
and call upon Jesus.
The scissors may explain part of your scandal, but they do not get to write your ending—grace still has a pen, and Jesus Christ still saves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HANNAH’S RIVAL PROVOKED HER YEAR AFTER YEAR—BUT HEAVEN WAS WRITING A STORY HER RIVAL COULDN’T SEE
paragraphs: HANNAH’S RIVAL PROVOKED HER YEAR AFTER YEAR—BUT HEAVEN WAS WRITING A STORY HER RIVAL COULDN’T SEE

She went to worship God carrying the same unanswered prayer—and the same woman was waiting there to wound her with it. But what Hannah could not see through her tears was that her humiliation was not the final chapter.
There is a particular kind of pain that doesn't come from losing something.
It comes from never receiving it.
Watching other people hold what you have begged God for.
Watching somebody announce the pregnancy while you quietly delete another hopeful date from your calendar.
Watching someone celebrate the marriage while you go home alone.
Watching someone else's child come back to God while yours seems to be running farther away.
Watching doors open for people who barely prayed while you have worn grooves into the floor with your knees.
And perhaps the hardest part isn't even that they have it.
It's that somebody keeps reminding you that you don't.
That is where Hannah's story begins.
Not with Samuel.
Not with answered prayer.
Not with victory.
With an empty womb.
And a woman who would not let her forget it.
Scripture introduces Elkanah's household with almost unbearable simplicity: Peninnah had children, and Hannah did not.
Those few words contain an entire world of grief.
Then Scripture tells us something darker.
Hannah had a rival.
Peninnah.
And Peninnah knew exactly where Hannah hurt.
The ancient Hebrew of 1 Samuel 1:6 is painfully vivid:
וְכִעֲסַתָּה צָרָתָהּ גַּם־כַּעַס בַּעֲבוּר הַרְּעִמָהּ
Ve-khi'asattah tsaratah gam-ka'as...
The text describes Hannah's rival provoking, vexing, or irritating her severely.
She wasn't accidentally insensitive.
The biblical picture is of repeated provocation directed toward Hannah's deepest wound.
And then comes one of the most devastating expressions in the chapter:
שָׁנָה בְשָׁנָה
shanah v'shanah.
Year after year.
Not once.
Not one cruel afternoon.
Not one family argument everybody regretted afterward.
Year.
After.
Year.
Every annual journey to worship became another journey through the wound.
Think about that.
Hannah was going to the house of the LORD—and still getting hurt on the way.
Somebody needs to hear that.
Being wounded while trying to follow God does not mean you have stopped following God.
Crying on your way to worship does not make your worship fake.
Walking into church devastated does not make you faithless.
Sometimes the person lifting their hands during worship spent the entire drive there trying not to fall apart.
Sometimes the person sitting quietly in the back isn't cold toward God.
They're exhausted.
Sometimes somebody else's testimony is touching the exact place where your prayer still seems unanswered.
You smile.
You congratulate them.
You mean it.
And then you get into your car.
Close the door.
And cry.
Hannah knew that feeling.
Scripture says Peninnah's provocation became so painful that Hannah “wept, and did not eat.”
Her grief had reached her appetite.
Her body was carrying what her heart could no longer hide.
And perhaps you understand that more than you want anyone to know.
There are wounds we can explain.
Then there are wounds that change how we sleep.
How we eat.
How we enter rooms.
How we react to announcements.
How long we stare at somebody else's photograph before putting the phone down.
There are prayers we eventually become embarrassed to mention because we have prayed them for so long.
And somewhere along the way, the question changes.
At first you ask:
“God, when?”
Eventually you begin asking:
“God... have You forgotten me?”
That is where this story becomes dangerous to shallow Christianity.
Because the Bible does not pretend Hannah wasn't devastated.
It doesn't hand her a religious slogan.
It doesn't shame her tears.
It doesn't tell her that genuine believers never become emotionally exhausted.
Hannah was hurting.
Deeply.
Her husband loved her.
But even love could not erase the wound.
Elkanah asked why she was crying and why her heart was sad. He reminded her of his devotion to her.
He loved her.
But he could not completely enter the room inside Hannah's soul where this grief lived.
Have you ever had people who loved you but still couldn't understand you?
They meant well.
They said things meant to comfort you.
But somehow their words made the loneliness sharper.
Because some pain cannot be solved by another human being saying, “But look at everything else you have.”
Gratitude matters.
But gratitude does not require pretending grief isn't grief.
Hannah could be loved by Elkanah and still ache for a child.
You can recognize God's blessings and still bring Him the place that hurts.
And that is exactly what Hannah did.
She got up.
That may be one of the most overlooked moments in the entire story.
She got up.
Still hurting.
Still childless.
Still carrying years of humiliation.
Still without evidence that anything was about to change.
She got up...
and went toward God.
Not away from Him.
Scripture describes her condition with another striking Hebrew expression:
מָרַת נָפֶשׁ
marat nephesh.
Bitter, deeply distressed, anguished in soul.
And from that place she prayed.
Not polished.
Not impressive.
Not Instagram-ready Christianity.
A broken woman pouring herself before God.
She wept.
She prayed.
She surrendered.
And when Eli initially misunderstood her, Hannah explained that she was pouring out her soul before the LORD.
That may be where this story finds you.
Maybe you have been pouring yourself out in private while everybody assumes you're fine.
Maybe your Peninnah isn't a person.
Maybe it's the empty chair.
The doctor's report.
The rejection letter.
The bank balance.
The divorce papers.
The photograph of the family you thought you would still have.
The addiction you thought you would have defeated by now.
The child who stopped calling.
The ministry door that closed.
The dream that keeps looking more impossible every year.
Maybe your rival is simply comparison.
Every time you open your phone, somebody appears to be living inside your unanswered prayer.
And the enemy whispers:
“See?”
“They got theirs.”
“Where is your God?”
“Maybe He loves them more.”
That whisper is poison.
Hannah's story does not teach that God's love can be measured by how quickly we receive what we request.
And we must be careful here.
Hannah eventually received Samuel.
But Scripture does not give Christians permission to turn Hannah into a formula:
Pray hard enough and you will become pregnant.
Cry enough and you will get married.
Give enough and you will become wealthy.
Believe enough and the diagnosis will disappear.
That is not the Gospel.
Some faithful believers receive the thing they pleaded for.
Others remain faithful while carrying prayers whose answers look very different from what they hoped.
Our confidence is not that God owes us our preferred outcome.
Our confidence is that in Christ, God has not abandoned His people.
That distinction matters.
Because the greatest gift God ultimately gives us is not an answered circumstance.
It is Himself.
And the Bible's story does not climax with Hannah holding Samuel.
It climaxes generations later with another miraculous birth and another Son.
Jesus Christ.
Samuel would become a prophet.
Jesus is the promised Christ.
Samuel would speak God's word to Israel.
Jesus is the eternal Word who became flesh.
Samuel would serve before the LORD.
Jesus would give Himself for sinners.
At the cross, Jesus entered suffering deeper than anything we could carry alone.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Crucified.
And there, what looked like history's darkest scandal became the place where God's redeeming grace was displayed.
Sin met judgment.
Mercy flowed toward sinners.
The innocent Christ died for the guilty.
And on the third day, the grave discovered something every believer needs to remember:
God can write beyond the chapter that looks final.
That does not mean every earthly tragedy will reverse before our eyes.
It means suffering does not get the last word over those who belong to Jesus.
Death doesn't.
Shame doesn't.
Infertility doesn't.
Rejection doesn't.
Failure doesn't.
Your past doesn't.
Peninnah doesn't.
Jesus does.
Maybe this story isn't confronting your suffering.
Maybe it's confronting something much more uncomfortable.
Maybe...
you have been Peninnah.
Maybe you have used another person's weakness to feel stronger.
Maybe you've quietly enjoyed being ahead.
Maybe you posted something partly because you knew a certain person would see it.
Maybe you disguised cruelty as honesty.
Maybe you've compared children, marriages, ministries, careers, bodies, houses, accomplishments, or spiritual lives.
Maybe somebody's insecurity became your opportunity to feel important.
Scripture gives us no permission to romanticize cruelty.
Someone else's wound is not your pedestal.
Someone else's barrenness—whatever form that barrenness takes—is not evidence of your superiority.
And if that exposed something hidden in you, don't defend it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is coming into the light because Christ offers mercy to sinners who stop hiding.
Maybe you aren't Hannah in this story.
Maybe you're Peninnah.
Grace is available there too.
That is the scandal of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely comfort victims.
He transforms sinners.
He forgives the repentant.
He breaks pride.
He cleanses guilt.
He makes enemies into family.
He takes people whose stories should have ended in judgment and writes grace across them through His blood.
From scandal to grace... Jesus rewrites everything.
And Hannah?
Her prayer was heard.
In time she conceived and gave birth to Samuel.
The name Samuel is connected in the narrative with Hannah's testimony that she had asked for him from the LORD.
Imagine holding what you once cried over.
Imagine touching the answer to a prayer that once seemed to disappear into heaven.
But Hannah's greatest moment was not merely receiving Samuel.
It was remembering who Samuel belonged to.
She had prayed with open hands.
Then she had to live with open hands.
She brought Samuel to the LORD.
The gift did not replace the Giver.
That is mature faith.
Many of us want God to put something into our hands.
Hannah's story eventually asks whether we are willing to place everything back into His.
Your marriage.
Your children.
Your future.
Your reputation.
Your ministry.
Your money.
Your dream.
Your unanswered prayer.
Your answered prayer.
Everything.
Because Christianity isn't fundamentally about persuading Jesus to build the life we designed.
It is surrendering our lives to the King who purchased us with His blood.
And maybe that is why you needed to read this today.
You have spent so much time asking God to change the situation that perhaps tonight your prayer needs to become:
“Jesus, whatever You do with this story, don't let this pain pull me away from You.”
If you're exhausted, say it.
If you're angry, confess it.
If you're jealous, bring it into the light.
If you've been pretending, stop pretending.
If you've sinned, repent.
If you've wandered, come home.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, understand this clearly: Christianity is not about becoming impressive enough for God.
You cannot save yourself.
Christ came for sinners.
He died for sins and rose again.
Turn from sin and entrust yourself to Him.
Grace is not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
Grace cost blood.
And the hands that were pierced are still the safest hands for your broken story.
If this exposed a wound you've been hiding, you don't need to write your entire story publicly.
And if Christ has already carried you through a season you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may meet another Hannah in the middle of her “year after year.”
Don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, hope, and Jesus Christ, supporting and sharing Gospel Warrior is one practical way you can help put biblical encouragement in front of another person who may desperately need it.
If you want your online life to glorify God, use what He has placed in your hands—including your reach—to point people toward Christ.
Send it privately to the friend who keeps saying, “I'm okay,” when you know something underneath those words is breaking.
It is support for the work.
Your support helps Gospel-centered material continue being created, shared, and placed before people who may be scrolling through Facebook while privately fighting battles nobody sees.
Don't leave Hannah at the temple.
Take her story home.
Remember her the next time someone else's blessing makes your wound ache.
Remember her when another year passes.
Remember her when somebody misunderstands your tears.
Remember her when you cannot explain what is happening inside you.
And above all...
remember Jesus.
Because Hannah's story can encourage you.
But only Christ can save you.
Your Peninnah may keep talking.
Your circumstances may remain unresolved longer than you imagined.
People may misunderstand you.
There may still be nights when all you can bring God are tears.
Bring them.
Keep coming to Him.
Keep opening Scripture.
Keep praying.
Keep repenting.
Keep surrendering.
Keep your eyes on Christ.
Because the most important question is not whether God gives you everything you once asked for.
It is whether, in receiving Christ, you have discovered the Treasure no suffering, rival, disappointment, disease, rejection, failure, or grave can finally take away.
And perhaps the line you need to carry with you tonight is this:
Peninnah saw Hannah's empty arms—but she could not see what God was writing beyond her tears.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS DIDN’T SAY BEAUTY WAS SIN—So What Exactly Is “LUST”?
paragraphs: JESUS DIDN’T SAY BEAUTY WAS SIN—So What Exactly Is “LUST”?

Matthew 5:28 may be one of the most quoted teachings of Jesus about sexual purity—and one of the easiest to flatten into something Jesus was not actually saying. Because there is a difference between seeing someone beautiful…and choosing to turn that person into an object inside your heart.
Maybe nobody ever explained that difference to you.
Maybe you were taught that if your eyes noticed an attractive person, you had already sinned.
So you became afraid of your own eyes.
Afraid of attraction.
Afraid of beauty.
Afraid that one involuntary moment of noticing another human being meant you had already committed adultery before God.
And perhaps that fear created something even worse.
You began hiding.
You learned how to smile at church while carrying secret shame.
You learned how to worship with raised hands while wondering whether God was disgusted with what was happening inside your head.
Or maybe your story went in the opposite direction.
Maybe you stopped fighting altogether.
You told yourself everybody looks.
Everybody fantasizes.
Everybody scrolls.
Everybody secretly wants things they should not have.
And somewhere between shame and normalization, the words of Jesus became blurred.
But what if we actually listened to what Jesus said?
Not what pornography culture says.
Not what shame culture says.
Not what social media says.
Not what religious fear says.
Jesus.
Because His words are stronger than our excuses…
but they are also more precise than our shame.
Matthew 5:27–28 records Jesus saying:
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
And underneath that English translation sits something worth seeing.
The Greek reads:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial expression is:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai
It carries the idea of looking toward, or for the purpose of, desiring.
That matters.
Jesus does not say that the human eye becomes sinful simply because it recognizes beauty.
He is confronting something deeper.
The look that becomes intentional.
The gaze that is entertained.
The desire that is cultivated.
The moment another human being stops being someone made in the image of God and becomes material for private consumption.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because lust is not merely about what your eyes accidentally encounter.
It is about what your heart chooses to do with what your eyes have seen.
There is a difference between noticing and nurturing.
Between attraction and possession.
Between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside, giving it a chair, feeding it, replaying it, and asking it to stay.
And Jesus goes directly to that hidden room.
He does not merely ask, “What did your body do?”
He asks what your heart wanted to do.
That was devastating in a culture where a person could congratulate himself for technically avoiding physical adultery while privately cultivating adulterous desire.
Jesus takes the commandment deeper than external compliance.
“You shall not commit adultery” was already God’s command.
Jesus does not weaken it.
He exposes its roots.
Before adultery becomes a bed, it can become a fantasy.
Before betrayal reaches the hands, it can be welcomed by the heart.
Before certain sins become visible scandals, they have often been rehearsed privately where nobody but God can see them.
And that means some of the most dangerous spiritual battles of your life may happen in places nobody applauds you for winning.
Your bedroom.
Your phone.
Your browser.
Your imagination.
That second look.
That private message.
That profile you keep revisiting.
That fantasy you keep feeding.
That relationship you keep emotionally crossing boundaries with while insisting, “Nothing actually happened.”
Jesus cares about what happens there.
Not because beauty is evil.
God created beauty.
Not because sexuality itself is dirty.
God created human beings as embodied creatures and established marriage before humanity's fall into sin.
The problem is not that another human being can be beautiful.
The problem begins when desire refuses to honor the person.
Lust says:
I want your body without responsibility for your soul.
I want pleasure without covenant.
I want intimacy without faithfulness.
I want the image of God in you reduced to something that exists for me.
Love moves differently.
Love can recognize beauty without demanding ownership.
Love can experience attraction without making attraction its master.
Love asks what honors God and what protects the other person.
Lust asks what can satisfy me.
And suddenly Matthew 5:28 is no longer merely a verse about “looking.”
It is about worship.
Who gets to command your desires?
That is why Jesus’ next words are so severe.
He speaks about tearing out the right eye if it causes you to stumble and cutting off the right hand if it causes you to stumble.

Jesus is using shocking language to communicate the seriousness with which sin must be confronted. The point is not that physical mutilation can purify a sinful heart. Removing an eye cannot remove desire from the soul.
The point is that sin is not something to negotiate with.
There are things you may need to remove.
Not your literal eye.
Maybe the account.
Maybe the app.
Maybe the private conversation.
Maybe the secret folder.
Maybe the late-night scrolling.
Maybe the relationship whose boundaries you keep pretending are harmless.
Maybe the device should stop sleeping beside you.
Maybe accountability needs to become more than something Christians talk about.
Maybe repentance needs to cost you convenience.
Because we sometimes pray,
“Jesus, make me pure,”
while protecting the exact doorway through which impurity keeps entering.
And then we wonder why the battle never changes.
But there is another danger here.
Please don't miss this.
You can read Matthew 5:28 and become so obsessed with your failure that you forget who is speaking.
Jesus.
The One who exposes the heart is also the One who came to save sinners.
The Sermon on the Mount is not permission to minimize sin.
But neither is Christianity an invitation to spend the rest of your life drowning in self-hatred.
Jesus does something far greater.
He brings darkness into the light so darkness does not have to own you anymore.
Perhaps you have failed here.
Not once.
Hundreds of times.
Perhaps pornography became a secret refuge.
Perhaps fantasy became the place you escaped whenever loneliness became unbearable.
Perhaps you crossed emotional boundaries with somebody who was not your spouse.
Perhaps you have objectified people while publicly presenting yourself as spiritually mature.
Perhaps nobody knows.
And perhaps reading this has made your stomach tighten because you know exactly what God has been putting His finger on.
Don't run.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The same Bible that refuses to rename sin also refuses to tell repentant sinners that their sin is beyond the reach of Christ.
The answer to lust is not pretending it isn't serious.
The answer is not learning to hate yourself.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the cleaned-up version of you that you hope eventually exists.
Christ died for sinners.
Real sinners.
People with histories.
People with secret tabs.
People with memories they wish they could erase.
People who have betrayed.
People who have fantasized.
People who have been sexually broken.
People who have used others.
People who have themselves been used.
People whose hearts desperately need cleansing.
And Scripture gives us this astonishing promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not excuse.
Forgive.
Not redefine.
Cleanse.
Not pretend the wound never existed.
Redeem.
That is the difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God because of what you did.”
The Gospel calls:
“Bring what you did to Christ.”
Condemnation says:
“You are filthy, so stay away.”
Grace says:
“You cannot cleanse yourself. Come to the One who can.”
Repentance is therefore not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Biblical repentance turns.
It brings sin into the light.
It stops protecting what Jesus is asking us to surrender.
And sometimes repentance sounds less dramatic than we expect.
“Jesus, I have been feeding this.”
“I have been pretending this wasn't serious.”
“I have been blaming everybody except myself.”
“I have looked at people as bodies instead of souls.”
“I have entertained desires I should have surrendered.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
There is no performance required in that prayer.
No theatrical Christianity.
Just truth.
Because the most terrifying thing about hidden sin is not simply that somebody might eventually discover it.
It is that you can become comfortable hiding something from the God who already sees it.
But the most beautiful thing about grace is this:
God already knows the thing you are terrified to confess…
and still calls you to come.
Maybe this article is not really about somebody else's lust.
Maybe it is about yours.
Maybe this is the moment the excuses stop.
Maybe tonight you stop deleting history only from your browser and start bringing your history to Jesus.
Maybe you finally tell somebody trustworthy that you need help.
Maybe you install accountability.
Maybe you end the conversation.
Maybe you unfollow the account.
Maybe you confess to your spouse.
Maybe you stop calling bondage “just a weakness.”
Not because those actions purchase forgiveness.
Jesus already paid what you could never pay.
You take sin seriously because grace has made freedom possible.
And if you fall again?
Do not make peace with the fall.
Get up.
Confess.
Repent.
Run toward Christ again.
Fight again.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and surrendering yourself to it.
A wounded soldier is still a soldier.
So fight.
Not to convince Jesus to love you.
Fight because in Christ you have discovered a love worth becoming free for.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing that simply finding another person attractive made them filthy.
Hear this carefully.
Beauty is not the enemy.
Another person's body is not the enemy.
Women are not the enemy.
Men are not the enemy.
Your body is not the enemy.
The battle is over whether desire will remain under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
You can notice beauty and choose honor.
You can experience temptation and choose obedience.
You can feel desire without allowing desire to become your god.
And when you fail, you can repent instead of hiding.
That is freedom.
Not the absence of temptation.
The presence of a greater King.
Jesus.
So the next time your eyes notice somebody beautiful, perhaps the question should not merely be:
“Did I see?”
Ask:
“What am I choosing to do with what I saw?”
Am I honoring this person as somebody created in God's image?
Or am I mentally taking something that was never mine?
Am I letting attraction pass through open hands?
Or am I turning it into fantasy?
Am I looking…
or am I feeding?
That question may expose you.
Good.
Because whatever Jesus exposes, He calls us to bring into His light.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your private struggle.
But you also do not have to pretend.
There may be another believer reading the comments tonight who desperately needs to discover that they are not the only person fighting for purity.
And if you know somebody trapped between lust and shame, share this with them.
Not to expose them.
Not to embarrass them.
Send it because you love them enough to remind them that Jesus offers something stronger than secrecy.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially should never be treated as purchasing God's favor, forgiveness, blessing, or salvation. Giving in the New Testament is to be willing rather than coerced—“not reluctantly or under compulsion,” as Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But voluntary generosity can genuinely help Gospel work continue.

If you want to glorify God with your resources, supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one way—among many—to practice generosity and help put biblical teaching before people who desperately need Jesus.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help.
Because this was never supposed to end with an argument about what technically qualifies as lust.
It should end with a heart standing naked before Jesus and asking:
“Lord, what have I allowed myself to desire that I need to surrender to You?”
And maybe that is the question you have been avoiding.
The scandal may be what happened inside your heart where nobody could see it.
But Jesus sees deeper than the scandal.
He sees the sinner He came to redeem.
So stop hiding.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the years you cannot undo.
Bring Him the heart you cannot cleanse by yourself.
Repent.
Receive His grace.
Then get up and walk differently.
Because the final word over a repentant sinner does not belong to lust.
It does not belong to shame.
It does not belong to your browser history.
It does not belong to your worst night.
The sin you are terrified will become the final sentence of your story may become the very place where Jesus teaches you what redemption means.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MARTHA WAS SERVING JESUS—SO WHY WAS SHE BECOMING ANGRY?
paragraphs:
MARTHA WAS SERVING JESUS—SO WHY WAS SHE BECOMING ANGRY?
She welcomed Christ into her home, worked for Him, and tried to serve Him well. Yet somewhere between serving Jesus and resenting her sister, Martha lost sight of the very Person she was serving. Then Jesus said something every exhausted Christian needs to hear: “One thing is necessary.”
There is a frightening way to lose your peace without ever leaving the presence of Jesus.
You can still pray.
Still attend church.
Still serve.
Still give.
Still help people.
Still post Scripture.
Still carry responsibilities nobody else seems willing to carry.
Still genuinely love Jesus...
and slowly become angry at everyone who does not seem to be doing as much as you are.
