And being respected by strangers cannot compensate for being feared by your family.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully beautiful.
Christianity does not begin with good people proving how right they are.
It begins with sinners who need mercy.
Every Christian stands before the cross with empty hands.
We do not come saying, “Jesus, here are all the reasons my sin was understandable.”
We come confessing that we have sinned and need a Savior.
The cross destroys our ability to boast.
At Calvary, nobody gets to pretend he rescued himself.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose again.
Forgiveness is offered not because we successfully defended ourselves, but because Jesus gave Himself for us.
That means repentance is not the doorway to humiliation.
For the Christian, repentance is a doorway back into truth.
The Gospel gives a husband freedom to say, “I was wrong,” because his entire identity no longer depends on always appearing right.
Think about that.
If your worth depends upon being flawless, every correction becomes a threat.
Every disagreement becomes a courtroom.
Every mistake must be hidden, minimized, transferred, rationalized.
But if your identity rests in Christ, you can tell the truth.
You can be wrong without being destroyed.
You can confess sin without surrendering your dignity.
You can ask forgiveness without losing your identity.
Because Jesus already knows the worst thing about you, and He still calls sinners to come to Him.
Grace does not make sin insignificant.
Grace makes honest repentance possible.
But repentance is more than saying “sorry.”
Biblically, repentance involves a turning.
If a husband apologizes every Friday for the same cruelty and returns to it every Saturday without any desire to change, his wife eventually hears “I'm sorry” as punctuation rather than repentance.
Real repentance begins producing fruit.
Maybe that means learning to stop an argument before anger controls your tongue.
Maybe it means confessing patterns you have hidden.
Maybe it means seeking wise pastoral counsel.
Maybe it means asking trusted mature believers for accountability.
Maybe it means listening without preparing your rebuttal.
Maybe it means repairing what your actions damaged.

And where there has been abuse, threats, coercive control, or violence, an apology by itself is not sufficient. Safety, truthful accountability, outside help, and genuine change matter. Scripture should never be weaponized to force someone to remain silent about abuse.
But for many marriages, the beginning may still sound remarkably simple.
“I was wrong.”
“I sinned against you.”
“No excuses.”
“Please forgive me.”
“Help me understand how this hurt you.”
“What can I do differently?”
Men, your children may be listening too.
Your son is learning what strength looks like.
Your daughter is learning what love should feel like.
What if one of the greatest inheritances you could leave them is not the memory of a father who was never wrong, but the memory of a father who knew what to do when he was?
Imagine your son watching you walk across the room after losing your temper.
He expects another lecture.
Instead, you kneel.
“Son, Daddy was wrong.”
Imagine your daughter hearing:
“You didn't deserve the way I spoke to you. Will you forgive me?”
Something is being discipled in that moment.
They are learning that authority does not eliminate accountability.
They are learning that masculinity and tenderness are not enemies.
They are learning that Christians do not have to pretend.
They are learning that repentance belongs in ordinary homes, not merely at church altars.
Most importantly, they are learning something about grace.
Dad sins.
Dad confesses.
Dad asks forgiveness.
Dad gets back up.
Dad keeps following Jesus.
That is a legacy.
Maybe this article is hurting a little because there is already a name in your mind.
Maybe there is a conversation you have postponed for days.
Months.
Years.
Maybe she has stopped asking for an apology because she became tired of begging you to understand.
Maybe your child is grown now.
Maybe your father is old.
Maybe your friend no longer calls.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is putting His finger on a place you have spent years defending.
Do not turn conviction into shame.
Take it to Christ.
There is grace for repentant sinners.
First John 1:9 gives believers extraordinary hope: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
The answer to masculine pride is not masculine self-hatred.
It is the cross.
It is repentance.
It is grace.
It is becoming secure enough in Christ that you no longer need everybody else to believe you are always right.
So maybe tonight, before you sleep, there is something more important than another sermon.
More important than another Christian podcast.
More important than another debate online.
Maybe the most spiritual sentence you can speak tonight is the sentence your pride has been terrified to say:
“I was wrong.”
Not because a comment proves repentance.
It doesn't.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging the battle helps another believer realize he is not fighting alone.
And if a particular husband, father, brother, or friend came to mind while you were reading, do not use this article as a weapon against him.
Do not tag him to embarrass him.
Share it with grace.
Send it because you love him.
Because pride has a remarkable memory for other people's failures and a remarkably short memory for our own.
Come back to it when being right starts feeling more important than being Christlike.
Scripture itself guards us against spiritual pressure around money: “God loves a cheerful giver,” and giving is not to be done under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Because perhaps somebody reading your testimony tonight needs to discover that repentance is not the funeral of a man's strength.
In Christ, it can be the resurrection of it.
The strongest man in the room may not be the one who never bows.
He may be the one who finally lays down his pride, turns toward the person he wounded, and whispers through tears:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
And somewhere in that surrender, the scandal of human failure collides with the grace of Jesus Christ.
The marriage may have scars.
The man may have failed.
The story may contain chapters he wishes he could tear out.
But Jesus is still writing.
And grace can write something pride never could.
Sometimes the three words that feel most like losing are the very words through which Christ begins giving your home back its tenderness.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK AND SLEPT WITH HIM—WHY IS THIS HORRIFYING STORY IN THE BIBLE?
paragraphs:
LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK AND SLEPT WITH HIM—WHY IS THIS HORRIFYING STORY IN THE BIBLE?
Genesis 19:30–38 is not a story God gave us to excuse human depravity. It is a story He refused to hide—and buried inside its darkness is a trail that eventually leads somewhere almost unbelievable: toward Ruth, toward David, and ultimately toward Jesus Christ.
There are Bible stories people put on nursery walls.
Noah’s ark.
David and Goliath.
Daniel among the lions.
And then there are passages like Genesis 19:30–38.
The passages people read quietly.
The passages preachers may hesitate to touch.
The passages that make you stop, stare at the page, and wonder:
Why is this in the Bible?
A father.
Two daughters.
A cave.
Wine.
Two nights.
Two pregnancies.
Incest.
And somehow this is part of Holy Scripture.
But perhaps the first thing we need to understand is this:
The Bible is holy not because every human action it records is holy.
The Bible is holy because the God who speaks through it tells the truth—even when the truth about humanity is horrifying.
Scripture does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not sanitize dysfunctional families.
It does not pretend believers never collapse.
It does not delete the chapters that would embarrass the family.
And Genesis 19 is one of those chapters.
Lot had just escaped Sodom.
The city was gone.
His wife was gone.
His former life was gone.
The man who had once looked across the Jordan valley and chosen what appeared prosperous now found himself living with his daughters in a cave.
That image alone should stop us.
Lot had escaped the fire...
but escaping a city is not necessarily the same thing as escaping what the city has done to you.
The New Testament astonishingly calls Lot a righteous man who was deeply distressed by the lawlessness surrounding him.
That means we should resist the simplistic temptation to turn Lot into a cartoon villain.
But we should also resist the opposite mistake.
Being distressed by a corrupt culture does not mean that culture has had no influence on you.
You can hate what surrounds you and still carry wounds from living around it.
You can leave Sodom...
and discover that some of Sodom followed you into the cave.
Lot’s daughters looked at their circumstances and reached a terrifying conclusion.
Their father was old. They saw no available husbands. Their future appeared closed. Their family line appeared doomed.
So they decided to manufacture a future for themselves.

Genesis records their reasoning: they would intoxicate their father and use him to preserve offspring through him. The Hebrew idea behind their stated purpose is striking: וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע — unechayyeh me’avinu zeraʿ, essentially, “that we may preserve offspring/seed from our father.”
The word זֶרַע — zeraʿ means “seed” or “offspring.”
They wanted a future.
But instead of trusting God with the future, they attempted to produce one through sin.
And suddenly this ancient cave becomes frighteningly modern.
Because most of us will never do what Lot’s daughters did.
But many of us understand the temptation underneath it.
“What if God doesn’t come through?”
“What if I never get married?”
“What if I never have children?”
“What if this opportunity disappears?”
“What if I lose everything?”
“What if there is no other way?”
Fear starts talking.
Then fear starts reasoning.
Then fear starts calling compromise necessary.
And eventually a person can do something he once considered unthinkable while telling himself he had no other choice.
That is one of the terrifying lessons of this passage:
Fear can become a terrible theologian.
It can make God appear smaller than your circumstances.
It can convince you that obedience is impossible because the future looks impossible.
And once you believe that, sin begins offering itself as a survival strategy.
The daughters make Lot drunk.
The older daughter goes first.
The text says he was unaware of her lying down and getting up.
Then morning comes.
And perhaps this is one of the darkest details of all:
They do it again.
The following night the younger daughter does the same.
Genesis does not celebrate this.
It does not command this.
It does not present incest as acceptable.

In fact, when Israel later receives explicit covenant legislation concerning sexual relationships, sexual relations among close relatives are expressly prohibited. Leviticus 18 opens that section with the prohibition against approaching close kin for sexual relations.
So never confuse biblical description with biblical prescription.
When Scripture tells you Cain murdered Abel, it is not endorsing murder.
When Scripture tells you David committed adultery, it is not endorsing adultery.
When Scripture tells you Peter denied Jesus, it is not endorsing denial.
And when Genesis tells you what happened inside Lot’s cave, God is not calling evil good.
He is showing us something Christianity has never needed to hide:
Human beings desperately need redemption.
The Bible could have edited this family history.
God could have given us a polished book filled with polished people whose lives always made faith look respectable.
Instead, Scripture gives us Noah drunk.
Abraham afraid.
Jacob deceptive.
Judah compromised.
David adulterous and murderous.
Peter denying Christ.
Thomas doubting.
Disciples arguing about greatness.
And Lot’s family sitting in the wreckage of Sodom making catastrophic decisions.
Why?
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of impressive people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing, judging, rescuing, correcting, forgiving, transforming, and redeeming sinful people.
And now the story becomes even stranger.
Both daughters become pregnant.
The older daughter gives birth to a son.
She calls him מוֹאָב — Mo’av, Moab.

Genesis deliberately associates that name with his scandalous origin—“from [my] father.” The younger daughter names her son בֶּן־עַמִּי — Ben-ʿAmmi, commonly understood as “son of my people/kinsman.” Genesis identifies these sons as ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.
Imagine carrying a name connected to the circumstances of your conception.
Imagine having your beginning associated with a cave nobody wants to discuss.
Moab enters Scripture under a shadow.
And if Genesis 19 were the final chapter of the story, perhaps darkness would get the last word.
But keep reading your Bible.
Because generations later...
a woman walks out of Moab.
Her name is Ruth.
Yes.
A Moabite.
A descendant of the people whose biblical origin story reaches back to this horrifying cave.
Ruth loses her husband.
She could remain in Moab.
Instead she clings to Naomi and makes one of Scripture’s great declarations of covenant loyalty.
Naomi’s people will become her people.
Naomi’s God will become her God.
And Ruth eventually meets Boaz.
Boaz redeems.
Ruth becomes his wife.
A son is born.
His name is Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And then...
centuries later...
Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
And Ruth is there.
Matthew 1:5 names her.
“Boaz begat Obed of Ruth...”
The Moabite woman is inside the genealogy of the Messiah.
Do you see what just happened?
Genesis 19 gives us a cave filled with shame.
Ruth gives us a Moabite woman kneeling beneath the wings of Israel’s God.
Matthew gives us Jesus Christ.
The Bible does not say the incest became good.
It never did.
Grace does not rename evil as righteousness.
Grace does something infinitely more beautiful.
God can redeem people whose histories contain evil without approving the evil that shaped those histories.
That distinction matters.
Because somebody reading this has spent years believing your beginning disqualified your ending.
Maybe your family history is ugly.
Maybe your father failed you.
Maybe your mother wounded you.
Maybe addiction ran through your home.
Maybe adultery shattered it.
Maybe you were conceived in circumstances nobody talks about.
Maybe abuse left scars you still struggle to explain.
Maybe you made decisions you would give anything to undo.
Maybe there is a chapter in your life you hope nobody ever reads aloud.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not intimidated by your genealogy.
He is not frightened by your family history.
He is not standing outside your mess wondering whether His grace is powerful enough to enter.
The gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But grace is so powerful that the Son of God rose again.
Christianity does not say, “What happened doesn’t matter.”
Christianity says something far stronger:
What happened does not have to be your master anymore.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have the authority to become your god.
Your family may have handed you patterns.
You do not have to worship them.
Your parents may have given you brokenness.
Jesus can give you a new identity.
Your history may have written the opening paragraphs.
Jesus Christ still has authority over the ending.
That is why Genesis 19 belongs in the Bible.
Not because God wants us fascinated by scandal.
Because God wants us sober about sin.
Because He wants us to understand what fear can do when it stops trusting Him.
Because He wants us to see how compromise can travel through families.
Because He refuses to lie about human darkness.
And because when we finally understand how dark human darkness actually is, grace stops looking sentimental.
Grace becomes astonishing.
Maybe you have wondered why the Bible contains so many broken people.
Perhaps the better question is:
What kind of Bible would people like us need?
A Bible filled only with flawless humans would leave sinners with nowhere to stand.
But Scripture gives us people who lied.
People who failed.
People who ran.
People who lusted.
People who doubted.
People whose families were dysfunctional.
People whose histories were embarrassing.
And then Scripture points beyond all of them.
To Jesus.
He is not another broken patriarch needing rescue.
He is the Rescuer.
He is not another sinner hoping grace can cover Him.
He is the Lamb of God who bears sin.
He does not merely enter a broken human story.
He comes to redeem broken human beings.
This is where the story must become personal.
Because it is easy to stare into Lot’s cave and whisper, “How could they?”
It is harder to let Scripture turn the question around.
What have you done because you were afraid God would not provide?
What compromise did you justify because waiting hurt?
What relationship did you enter because loneliness became louder than obedience?
What habit do you keep feeding because pain convinced you that you need it?
What secret are you hiding because shame told you exposure would destroy you?
What have you called “necessary” that God calls sin?
Do not use Lot’s daughters as an excuse to feel morally superior.
Let their story become a warning.
Sin does not need you to become an atheist.
Sometimes it only needs you to become frightened enough to stop trusting God.
But if conviction is rising inside you right now, do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Run toward Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the cave.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the thing you are terrified somebody will discover.
You do not clean yourself before coming to the cross.
You come because you cannot clean yourself.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
Forgiveness is not pretending sin never mattered.
Forgiveness is possible because Christ paid for sin.
And when a sinner turns to Christ in repentance and faith, the deepest identity of that person no longer has to be the scandal behind them.
Grace can write what shame never could.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only person fighting.
Someone may pray because you were honest.
Someone may return to Christ because your testimony reminded them that grace still reaches people in caves.
Not because Genesis 19 is pleasant.
Come back and remember Ruth.
Come back and remember the genealogy.
Come back and remember the cross.
Not as religious decoration.
Send it to the believer who has disappeared.
Send it to the person who thinks Christianity is only for people who have their lives together.
Even send it to the skeptic who believes the Bible hides from the ugliness of real human life.
It doesn't.
Scripture walks straight into the cave.
And then it keeps walking until the story reaches Christ.
Supporting Gospel work should never replace giving faithfully, serving your local church, caring for your family, or helping people in need.
Because somewhere tonight there is still a person sitting emotionally in a cave.
Ashes behind them.
Fear around them.
Shame inside them.
Convinced the worst chapter has already determined the final sentence.
But Genesis 19 was not the end of the biblical story.
Moab was not the end.
The scandal was not the end.
Ruth came.
David came.
And in the fullness of time...
Jesus came.
And that is the truth shame desperately hopes you never understand:
The chapter you are most ashamed of may be part of your history—but when Jesus becomes Lord of your life, it does not get to be your final author.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT WAS PAUL’S THORN IN THE FLESH? THE ANSWER MAY BE MORE PERSONAL THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: WHAT WAS PAUL’S THORN IN THE FLESH? THE ANSWER MAY BE MORE PERSONAL THAN YOU THINK
Paul begged Jesus three times to take it away.
Jesus didn’t.
And perhaps the most unsettling part of the story is that Paul never tells us exactly what “it” was.
For nearly two thousand years, Christians have wondered about those mysterious words buried inside one of the most vulnerable passages the apostle Paul ever wrote.
Was it sickness?
Problems with his eyesight?
Persecution?
Temptation?
Depression?
A physical disability?
A demonic attack?
An enemy who continually opposed his ministry?
Something else entirely?
People have proposed all of these possibilities.
But Scripture does something fascinating.
It leaves the thorn unnamed.
And maybe before asking, “What exactly was Paul’s thorn?” we need to notice something even more important.
Paul tells us what the thorn did.
He tells us where it came against him.
He tells us how desperately he wanted it gone.
And then he tells us what Jesus said when the thorn stayed.
That is where this ancient mystery suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Because somewhere in your life, you may have something you have asked God to remove too.
Something you thought would be gone by now.
Something you prayed about when nobody was listening.
Something you have cried over.
Something you have rebuked.
Something you have surrendered.
Something you have asked God to heal, change, stop, restore, or take away.
And yet...
it remains.
So you started wondering whether God had forgotten you.
Paul knew that prayer.
Listen carefully to his own language.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7, the Greek text says:
“ἐδόθη μοι σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί, ἄγγελος Σατανᾶ, ἵνα με κολαφίζῃ”
Transliterated:
“edothē moi skolops tē sarki, angelos Satana, hina me kolaphizē.”
A close rendering is:
“There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, that it might buffet/strike me.”
The word translated “thorn” is σκόλοψ — skolops.
And this matters.
We often imagine a tiny rose thorn stuck beneath somebody’s skin.

Paul’s word can carry the sense of something pointed, sharp, even stake-like. Whatever Paul experienced, his imagery was not describing a cute inconvenience. It communicated something piercing and deeply distressing.
Then Paul uses another violent word.
κολαφίζῃ — kolaphizē.
It carries the idea of striking or buffeting, even striking with the fist.
Paul was not saying, “God gave me a mildly annoying problem.”
He was describing something that battered him.
Something humiliating.
Something persistent.
Something he desperately wanted gone.
And Scripture explicitly calls it “ἄγγελος Σατανᾶ” — angelos Satana — “a messenger of Satan.”
Yet here is where we must be careful.
Paul does not explicitly tell us what physical form or circumstance that messenger produced.
That silence matters.

Some interpreters throughout Christian history have suggested a physical illness. Others have connected the thorn with Paul’s bodily weakness or possible problems involving his eyes. Others have argued for persecution, hostile opponents, spiritual assault, or another form of suffering.
There are arguments for different possibilities.
But none of them should be preached as though Paul wrote, “My thorn was ______.”
He didn't.
The inspired text gives us boundaries.
It was a “thorn in the flesh.”
It was associated with a “messenger of Satan.”
It “buffeted” Paul.
It was severe enough that Paul repeatedly pleaded for its removal.
And it served, under God's sovereign providence, to keep Paul from becoming exalted because of the extraordinary revelations he had received.
Beyond that, certainty becomes speculation.
And perhaps that is exactly where many sermons go wrong.
We become obsessed with identifying Paul's thorn while overlooking the words Jesus actually wanted Paul to remember.
Because Paul prayed.
Once.
The thorn remained.
Paul prayed again.
Still there.
Then again.
Three times.
“Lord...
take this away.”
Imagine Paul praying that.
The apostle who saw Christ.
The missionary through whom churches were planted.
The man who preached Christ when preaching Christ could get him beaten, imprisoned, or killed.
Paul knew miracles.
Paul knew deliverance.
Paul knew supernatural power.
Paul had watched God do extraordinary things.
And still there was something in Paul's own life that would not leave when he asked.
That should destroy one dangerous idea immediately:
Unanswered prayer does not automatically mean you lack faith.
Sometimes enormous faith is found in the person who keeps trusting Jesus after the answer they wanted never arrives.
Paul says:
“ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν Κύριον παρεκάλεσα”
“Concerning this, three times I pleaded with the Lord...”
He wasn't casual.
He pleaded.
Take it away.
Take it away.
Please...
take it away.
And then Jesus answered.
But Jesus did not answer the way Paul requested.
He said:
“Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου.”
Arkei soi hē charis mou.
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Read that again.
Not:
“My explanation is sufficient for you.”
Not:
“Your strength is sufficient.”
Not:
“Try harder.”
Not:
“Pretend this doesn't hurt.”
Not even:
“I will remove it tomorrow.”
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Then comes the sentence that completely rewrites the meaning of weakness:
“For My power is perfected in weakness.”
This is Christianity in a sentence that human pride would never invent.
We want power without weakness.
Christ reveals power through weakness.
We want victory without scars.
Jesus conquered through a cross.
We want resurrection without death.
But the Gospel takes us straight through Calvary before it shows us the empty tomb.
And suddenly Paul's thorn begins pointing beyond Paul.
It points toward Christ.
Paul was learning that the Christian life is not ultimately the story of how impressive Paul could become.
It is the story of how sufficient Christ already is.
That changes everything.
Because perhaps you have been measuring God's love by what He removes.
Paul learned to recognize Christ's power even in what remained.
That does not mean suffering is good in itself.
It does not mean Satan becomes good.
It does not mean sickness, persecution, grief, temptation, trauma, or affliction should be romanticized.
And it certainly does not mean Christians should refuse medicine, counseling, protection, justice, wise help, or prayer for healing.
Paul himself asked for deliverance.
Three times.
There is nothing faithless about asking Jesus to remove the thorn.
Ask Him.
Cry before Him.
Seek help.
Pray boldly.
Call the elders.
Seek healing.
Seek wisdom.
Seek freedom.
But do not make this mistake:
Do not assume that because the thorn has not disappeared, Jesus has disappeared.
Paul discovered something astonishing.
The thorn could remain...
and Christ could remain closer.
The weakness could remain...
and Christ's power could remain greater.
The unanswered question could remain...
and grace could still be enough.
Maybe that is why Scripture never gives us Paul's medical chart.
Maybe God knew generations of wounded Christians would eventually read this passage.
The exhausted mother praying over a child.
The husband staring at a marriage he cannot repair by himself.
The believer fighting the same temptation again.
The pastor preaching while privately exhausted.
The Christian living with chronic pain.
The person carrying grief everybody assumes they should have “gotten over” already.
The believer asking God at 2:13 in the morning:
“Why hasn't this changed?”
You read Paul's story wanting the name of his thorn.
Then somewhere between verse seven and verse nine...
you realize you have been thinking about yours.
And that may be where this passage catches the soul.
Because some of us have secretly made God a bargain.
“Lord, once You fix this, I'll finally have peace.”
“Once You heal this, I'll trust You.”
“Once You restore this relationship, I'll worship again.”
“Once You remove this weakness, then You can use me.”
Paul's testimony destroys that bargain.
Christ can use you while you are weak.
Christ can sustain you while you are hurting.
Christ can humble you without abandoning you.
Christ can display His strength through places you desperately wish were stronger.
And sometimes the place you are most ashamed of becomes the place where you finally stop pretending you can save yourself.
That is Gospel territory.
Because the deepest thorn in humanity is not Paul's mysterious affliction.
It is sin.
And Jesus did not come merely to make uncomfortable people comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
Paul himself once stood on the scandalous side of that story.
Before Christians knew him as the apostle Paul, they feared him as Saul.
He approved Stephen's death.
He ravaged the church.
He dragged believers away.
He breathed threats against the disciples of Jesus.
Then Christ met him.
The persecutor became the preacher.
The enemy became the apostle.
The man who once tried to silence the name of Jesus eventually suffered to proclaim it.
That is scandal becoming grace.
Not because Paul's past became innocent.
Grace does not rewrite evil by pretending it never happened.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's future by forgiving, redeeming, transforming, and claiming those who come to Him.
Paul would never again be merely “the man who persecuted Christians.”
He became living evidence that the mercy of Christ can reach people whose histories look impossible to redeem.
And years later, that redeemed man was still weak.
Think about that.
Grace had transformed Paul.
Grace had not made Paul invulnerable.
He still needed Jesus.
Maybe you needed to hear that.
Spiritual maturity is not reaching the point where you no longer need grace.
Spiritual maturity is discovering how desperately you have always needed it.
Paul eventually says something almost shocking:
He will boast in his weaknesses so that the power of Christ may rest upon him.
Not because pain suddenly feels wonderful.
Because Christ has become more precious than the illusion of self-sufficiency.
That is the real revelation of the thorn.
The great mystery is not what was stabbing Paul.
The great revelation is what was sustaining him.
Jesus.
Jesus was enough.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you desperately wish God would remove, I will not insult your suffering by telling you it doesn't hurt.
Paul never did that.
Call the thorn a thorn.
Cry.
Pray.
Ask God for deliverance.
But while you wait...
do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Do not confuse weakness with uselessness.
Do not confuse suffering with rejection.
And do not allow the enemy to convince you that your unfinished battle disqualifies you from coming to Christ.
Come weak.
Come wounded.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with the prayer you have already prayed a hundred times.
Come with your sins exposed.
Come with nothing impressive left to offer.
Jesus did not die for a polished version of you.
Christ died for sinners.

He bore sin upon the cross, died, was buried, and rose again. Forgiveness is not earned through religious performance. Salvation is God's grace received through faith in Jesus Christ, producing a life turned toward Him in repentance and obedience.
Maybe your greatest need today is not discovering Paul's thorn.
Maybe it is finally admitting yours.
The hidden sin.
The pride.
The bitterness.
The secret addiction.
The resentment.
The exhaustion.
The fear.
The wound.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The thing behind the Christian smile nobody sees.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If something hidden has been exposed, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you cannot even explain what you're carrying anymore, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people in dark places.
No pretending.
No Christian masks.
Just people who need Jesus pointing one another toward Jesus.
And please don't let this article die on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor—it absolutely does not—but because someone connected to you may be quietly asking the same question Paul asked.
“Lord, why won't this leave?”
Your share could place Scripture in front of somebody at precisely the moment they need it.
Send this to the believer who thinks weakness means God cannot use them.
“Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου.”
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Supporting Christian ministry does not purchase God's blessing, prove salvation, or make someone more righteous before Him. Jesus cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased.
But generosity can help Gospel-centered resources continue being created, distributed, and placed before people who need them.
But before you leave, remember Paul.
He asked for the thorn to disappear.
Christ gave him something greater than an explanation.
Grace.
Perhaps one day God will remove the thing you have been begging Him to remove.
Perhaps He will answer differently than you imagined.
But either way, the Christian's final hope was never a thornless life.
Our hope is the crucified and risen Christ.
The Savior whose own body carried wounds.
The King who turns persecutors into apostles.
The Redeemer who turns shame into testimony.
The Lord who takes sinners headed toward judgment and clothes them in a righteousness they could never manufacture for themselves.
And the Christ who can look into the weakest place of your life and say:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
So what was Paul's thorn?
Scripture does not finally tell us.
And perhaps that unanswered question leaves us staring at the answer that matters most.
Paul's thorn had a mystery.
Paul's Savior did not.
His name is Jesus.
And sometimes Jesus does not remove the chapter you desperately wanted erased—He enters it, covers it with grace, and makes even your weakness tell the world who carried you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID A MAN FROM MARRYING HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—WHILE DEUTERONOMY SOMETIMES REQUIRED IT?
paragraphs: WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID A MAN FROM MARRYING HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—WHILE DEUTERONOMY SOMETIMES REQUIRED IT?

One verse calls it forbidden. Another tells a brother to do it. Critics call it a contradiction. But when you read the Hebrew carefully, something far more profound appears—and hidden inside this difficult law is a breathtaking picture of responsibility, redemption, and ultimately the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Imagine opening your Bible and discovering two commands that seem to collide.
Leviticus says:
“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife: it is thy brother's nakedness.” — Leviticus 18:16
Clear enough.
Your brother's wife is forbidden to you.
Then you turn several books forward and Moses appears to say almost the opposite.

“If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife...” — Deuteronomy 25:5
Wait.
What?
Leviticus says, “Do not.”
Deuteronomy says, under certain circumstances, “Do.”
Did Moses contradict Moses?
Did God's moral standard change somewhere between Leviticus and Deuteronomy?
Or have we missed something because we are reading two sentences while ignoring the circumstances surrounding them?
Stay with this, because the answer is much bigger than an obscure ancient marriage law.

And strangely enough, by the time we reach Jesus, this seemingly uncomfortable question about a widow and her brother-in-law will lead us straight into a conversation about resurrection, covenant faithfulness, and a God who refuses to abandon His people to death.
Start with the Hebrew.
Leviticus 18:16 reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָחִיךָ הִוא
‘Ervat eshet-achikha lo tegalleh; ‘ervat achikha hi.
The essential sense is:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; it is your brother's nakedness.”
The language belongs to the sexual-boundary laws of Leviticus 18.
The point is not mysterious.
A man's marriage creates a boundary his brother is not free to violate.
His brother's wife does not become sexually available merely because they are relatives, attracted to each other, living nearby, unhappy with their circumstances, or able to invent a justification.
She is his brother's wife.
There is a boundary.
Leviticus 20:21 reinforces the seriousness of that boundary:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִקַּח אֶת־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו נִדָּה הִוא
Ve'ish asher yiqqach et-eshet achiv, niddah hi...
“If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity/indecency...”
The ordinary rule is therefore unmistakable: a man does not take his brother's wife.
Then comes Deuteronomy 25.
But notice what has changed.
The brother is dead.
And the text specifies another crucial circumstance: he has died without offspring.
Now read the Hebrew:
כִּי־יֵשְׁבוּ אַחִים יַחְדָּו וּמֵת אַחַד מֵהֶם וּבֵן אֵין־לוֹ...
Ki-yeshevu achim yachdav, umet achad mehem, uven ein-lo...
“When brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no offspring...”
Then comes remarkable vocabulary:
יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וְיִבְּמָהּ
Yevamah yavo ‘aleha, uleqachah lo le'ishshah, veyibbemah.
Her husband's brother is to take her as his wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother toward her.
That final Hebrew word matters enormously.
וְיִבְּמָהּ — veyibbemah.
It comes from the same word-family associated with yavam, a husband's brother in this special relationship, and yevamah, the widow in the levirate relationship.
In other words, Deuteronomy is not casually overturning Leviticus.
It is describing a specifically defined covenantal circumstance.
The general boundary remains.
But God Himself legislates a particular exception for a particular tragedy.
The brother has died.
He has left no offspring.
His household faces extinction.
His widow faces a vulnerable future in the social world of ancient Israel.
His name and inheritance are in danger of disappearing from his family line.
And suddenly the surviving brother is no longer looking at another man's wife as an object of desire.
He is looking at his dead brother's widow as someone toward whom covenant responsibility may now be required.
That changes everything.
This is why reading isolated Bible verses can be dangerous.
Leviticus addresses a forbidden union.
Deuteronomy addresses a defined levirate obligation.
Same woman in terms of family relationship.
Radically different covenant circumstance.
One situation would violate the brother's marriage.
The other arises because death has ended that marriage and, in the specified childless situation, Israel's law places a responsibility upon the surviving family.
Deuteronomy then tells us why.
The firstborn resulting from the union was to continue the deceased brother's name so that, as the text says, “his name be not blotted out of Israel.”
Read that slowly.
This wasn't primarily a loophole for male desire.
It carried responsibility.
Legacy.
Family.
Inheritance.
Protection.
Name.
Continuity after death.
The surviving brother was being summoned to shoulder a cost for the sake of someone who could no longer repay him.
And that makes what happened with Onan in Genesis 38 much easier to understand.
Long before Deuteronomy formally codified Israel's levirate legislation, Judah told Onan to fulfill his duty toward Tamar after the death of his brother Er.
But Onan knew the offspring would not be reckoned as his brother's in the ordinary sense of family continuation, and he deliberately frustrated that responsibility.
His sin was not merely some isolated biological act ripped from its narrative.
The text emphasizes that he refused the responsibility attached to preserving his brother's line.
He wanted the sexual access while rejecting the costly obligation.
And suddenly an ancient story begins sounding painfully modern.
We want benefits without covenant.
Pleasure without responsibility.
Grace without repentance.
Christianity without surrender.
A Savior without a Lord.
Heaven without holiness.
Forgiveness without admitting there is anything from which we need to be forgiven.
We have become experts at wanting what God gives while quietly negotiating away what God asks.
And maybe that is why this strange passage reaches farther into the heart than we expected.
Because underneath the question, “Why could one brother marry another brother's widow?” lies another question:
What does covenant love do when obedience becomes costly?
It doesn't simply ask, “What can I get?”
It asks, “What faithfulness is required of me?”
There is another beautiful detail people sometimes miss.

Deuteronomy did not portray the brother as a mindless breeding instrument with absolutely no possibility of refusal. The verses immediately following describe what happened if he refused: the widow could go before the elders, and the public ceremony known later as chalitzah followed. His refusal carried shame because he would not “build up his brother's house,” but the text itself acknowledges the possibility of refusal.
So this wasn't Leviticus accidentally saying one thing and Deuteronomy accidentally saying another.

Later Jewish legal discussion wrestled explicitly with the relationship between the prohibition concerning a brother's wife and the exceptional command of levirate marriage. That very tension became a serious subject of interpretation rather than something ancient readers simply failed to notice.
And centuries later...
Jesus walked directly into this conversation.
The Sadducees came to Him with a scenario about seven brothers.
One brother dies childless.
His brother marries the widow.
Then that brother dies.
Then another.
And another.
Until their deliberately extreme scenario has the same woman married successively to seven brothers.
They were drawing upon the very law we have been discussing.
They asked Jesus whose wife she would be in the resurrection.
But they weren't sincerely trying to understand marriage.
They were attempting to make resurrection look absurd.
And Jesus refused to be trapped inside their assumptions.
“You are wrong,” He told them, because they did not understand the Scriptures or the power of God.
Then He explained that resurrection life cannot simply be reduced to an endless extension of present earthly marriage structures.
Think about that.
The law created to deal with the tragedy of death eventually became part of a debate in which Jesus proclaimed that death itself does not have the final word.
The Sadducees brought Jesus a puzzle about dead husbands.
Jesus answered them with the living God.
“He is not God of the dead, but of the living.”
And there...
right there...
the ancient law begins pointing our eyes toward something much greater than itself.
We should be careful here.
Deuteronomy 25 is not secretly a direct prophecy saying, “This is Jesus.” We should never force Christ into a passage by pretending its historical meaning does not matter.
Its immediate concern is Israelite family responsibility after a childless man's death.

But within the larger biblical story, themes of family redemption, preserving a name, protecting the vulnerable, costly faithfulness, and life confronting death belong to a trajectory that finds its ultimate hope in Christ.
Because humanity has a problem infinitely greater than a disappearing family name.
We have sin.
We have guilt.
We have death.
And no human relative can finally rescue us from the grave.
Then Jesus comes.
Not exploiting our helplessness.
Entering it.
Not owing us anything.
Giving Himself anyway.
Not preserving merely an earthly family name.
Bringing sinners into the family of God.
Not simply postponing death.
Defeating it.
The Gospel says that the eternal Son took on flesh, entered our broken human condition, bore sin at the cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
Our deepest scandal met God's astonishing grace.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years believing your scandal has already written the final chapter.
The affair.
The addiction.
The secret messages.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The abortion you still cry about.
The marriage you helped destroy.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The church wound you used as permission to walk away from God.
The double life.
The years of pretending.
The night you wish you could erase.
The prayers you stopped praying because you became convinced God was tired of hearing your voice.
Maybe people know your worst chapter.
Maybe nobody does.
But Jesus does.
And He walked toward the cross knowing exactly what kind of sinners He was dying to save.
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves sin is more serious than our culture wants to admit.
But the same cross proves grace is more powerful than our shame wants us to believe.
Repentance is not pretending your scandal never happened.
Repentance is finally bringing your rebellion into the light, turning from it, and running toward the Christ whose blood is sufficient for sinners.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is God rescuing guilty people who could never make themselves righteous.
You do not need a prettier past.
You need a Savior.
You do not need to rewrite your history until you look innocent.
You need Jesus to redeem the sinner standing inside that history.
Maybe this article started as a Bible question for you.
“How can Leviticus forbid what Deuteronomy commands?”
Interesting question.
But Scripture has a habit of turning the question around.
What if the deeper contradiction isn't sitting in the Bible?
What if it is sitting inside us?
We call Jesus Lord...
but keep certain rooms locked.
We sing about surrender...
while negotiating obedience.
We ask God for mercy...
while refusing to forgive.
We want Him to expose biblical contradictions...
while praying He never exposes ours.
And still Christ calls.
Come out of hiding.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Me.
No performance.
No religious costume.
No carefully edited Christian profile.
Just truth meeting grace at the feet of Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't write an essay defending yourself.
Maybe your first act of honesty can be painfully simple.
Sometimes a comment is not merely engagement.
Sometimes it is the moment somebody finally stops hiding.
One share may put this in front of the person who has been silently questioning Scripture.
One share may reach the believer who thought difficult questions meant weak faith.
One share may find someone awake at 2:00 a.m., carrying a scandal they believe Jesus could never forgive.
There will come a day when someone asks you about this supposed contradiction, and you may want the Hebrew and context in front of you rather than trying to remember a thirty-second explanation.
It doesn't.
Only Christ saves.
And not because supporting Gospel Warrior can replace the biblical responsibilities God has placed upon you toward your local church, your family, the poor, or other Gospel work.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel ministry continue.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should not be extracted through spiritual pressure: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And if you cannot financially support the ministry, do not believe for one second that you are less valuable here.
Pray.
Save biblical teaching.
The mission was never to create customers.
It is to point people toward Jesus.
Because eventually every one of us becomes the person standing helpless before something we cannot undo.
A death we cannot reverse.
A wound we cannot erase.
A sin we cannot make innocent.
A past we cannot rewrite.
And that is precisely where the Gospel becomes more than religious vocabulary.
We couldn't rewrite ourselves.
So Jesus entered the story.
The cross tells the truth about our scandal.
The empty tomb announces that the scandal doesn't have to get the final sentence.
And perhaps that is the line you need to carry with you tonight:
Your darkest chapter may explain how you arrived here—but when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ, it does not get to decide how your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN DOES ATTRACTION CROSS THE LINE INTO COVETING?
paragraphs: WHEN DOES ATTRACTION CROSS THE LINE INTO COVETING?
You noticed them. Something stirred. And now you’re wondering whether the feeling itself means you have already sinned—or whether the real battle begins with what you choose to do next.
There is a moment almost nobody talks about honestly.
You see someone.
They are beautiful. Attractive. Magnetic, even.
Something inside you notices before you have time to formulate a theological response.
And then comes the second feeling.
Guilt.
“Did I just lust?”
“Was noticing them already sinful?”
“Am I coveting someone just because I’m attracted to them?”

For some Christians, especially those who sincerely want to honor Jesus, that question can become exhausting. Every glance gets examined. Every physical reaction becomes evidence in an internal courtroom. Every moment of attraction feels suspicious.
But Scripture is more precise than that.
And its precision is both more merciful and more confronting than we sometimes realize.
Because the Bible does not teach that recognizing beauty is automatically the same thing as coveting.
But neither does Jesus allow us to hide behind the excuse, “I only looked.”
There is a line.
And sometimes the distance between noticing and crossing it is only a few seconds.
The tenth commandment says:
“Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife…”
The crucial Hebrew expression is:
לֹא תַחְמֹד — lōʾ taḥmōḏ
“Do not covet.”
The verb comes from חָמַד — ḥāmad, a word connected with desire, delight, or finding something desirable. Context matters enormously because desire itself is not automatically evil.
That is important.
Scripture is not teaching that the human capacity to desire is inherently corrupt.
God created human beings capable of affection, appreciation, longing, love, and marital desire.
The problem begins when desire turns toward something in a way that rebels against God.
Coveting says something more dangerous than:
“That person is attractive.”
Coveting begins whispering:
“I want what is not mine.”
“I deserve what God has not given me.”
“I want to possess this person in my imagination even though I have no righteous claim to them.”
And sometimes…
“I don't care what has to be violated to get what I want.”
That is why coveting is so dangerous.
It can commit rebellion internally before your hands ever do anything externally.
Jesus takes us directly into that hidden room.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He says:
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek phrase deserves careful attention:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
The key verb is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō.
It means to desire, long for, or strongly desire something.
And here is something Christians sometimes miss.
The Greek word itself does not automatically mean sinful lust every time it appears.
Jesus Himself uses the same verb in Luke 22:15 when He speaks of His earnest desire to eat the Passover with His disciples.
So the mere existence of strong desire is not the entire issue.
The object, direction, intention, and moral context of that desire matter.
In Matthew 5, Jesus is confronting a look directed toward another person for the purpose of cultivating wrongful sexual desire.
That is far deeper than simply realizing someone is physically attractive.
You can notice beauty without mentally undressing someone.
You can experience attraction without feeding fantasy.
You can recognize that someone is desirable without deciding, even secretly, to consume them in your imagination.
And this is where the uncomfortable question arrives.
Not:
“Did I notice?”
But:
“What did I do after I noticed?”
That question can expose us.
Because sometimes the first look encountered beauty.
The second look began negotiating with temptation.
Then came the third.
The replay.
The profile search.
The scrolling.
The fantasy.
The imagined conversation.
The private scenario.
The little world constructed in the mind where boundaries disappear and nobody except you and God knows what is happening.
You tell yourself you haven't touched anybody.
You haven't sent the message.
You haven't cheated.
You haven't crossed a physical boundary.
But Jesus goes deeper than appearances.
He goes into the heart.
Not because He delights in shaming you.
Because He came to rescue the whole person.
Jesus isn't interested merely in making your behavior look Christian while your imagination remains enslaved.
He wants your eyes.
Your thoughts.
Your desires.
Your sexuality.
Your loneliness.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your secret browser history.
Your midnight thoughts.
Your wounds.
Your hunger to be wanted.
Your need to feel desirable.
Even the parts of you that nobody else knows how to reach.
Maybe that is why this subject hurts.
Because sometimes what looks like lust on the surface is attached to something deeper underneath.
Loneliness.
Rejection.
A marriage that has grown painfully distant.
Years without affection.
Pornography that trained the brain to turn human beings into consumable images.
A desperate need for validation.
A breakup you never completely healed from.
The ache of being single longer than you expected.
Or the quiet addiction to imagining another life whenever your real one disappoints you.
None of those things makes sin righteous.
But understanding the wound can help expose where temptation keeps entering.
And Jesus does not merely say, “Stop.”
He calls us into freedom.
James describes the progression with frightening clarity:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.
Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin…”
Notice the movement.
Temptation.
Desire.
Enticement.
Conception.
Sin.
Death.
There is a process.
That means temptation itself should not automatically be confused with surrender.
Jesus Himself “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.”
That truth matters enormously to the believer tormented by unwanted temptation.
Being tempted is not identical to consenting to temptation.
Feeling attraction is not identical to committing adultery.
An unwanted thought entering your mind is not identical to deliberately entertaining it.
The question is what happens when desire knocks.
Do you send it away?
Or give it a room?
Because coveting does not merely notice.
Coveting begins to claim.
Lust does not merely recognize another person's body.
Lust reduces a person made in the image of God into material for personal gratification.
That beautiful woman is not scenery for your fantasy.
That handsome man is not an escape hatch from your marriage.
That married coworker is not “the person you should have met first.”
That person on your screen is not a collection of body parts created for your consumption.
They bear the image of God.
They have a story.
A soul.
Fears.
Wounds.
A future.
And they will stand before the same Creator you will.
When you begin seeing people that way, purity stops being merely a desperate attempt not to sin.
It becomes learning to love your neighbor again.
That changes everything.
The question becomes less:
“How much can I look before it counts as lust?”
And more:
“How can I see this person in a way that honors Christ?”
That is a much better question.
Because Christianity is not about discovering the closest possible distance to sin without technically crossing the line.
It is about becoming like Jesus.
Job spoke of making a covenant with his eyes.
Paul told Timothy to treat younger women “as sisters, with all purity.”
Jesus taught radical seriousness about whatever causes us to stumble.
And Paul wrote:
“Make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.”
That phrase is devastatingly practical.
Stop preparing the room for the temptation you keep praying God will remove.
Sometimes we pray:
“Lord, deliver me.”
Then preserve the messages.
“Lord, make me pure.”
Then follow the accounts.
“Lord, protect my marriage.”
Then keep feeding an emotional attachment our spouse knows nothing about.
“Lord, take away this lust.”
Then revisit the image.
We ask God to extinguish a fire while quietly carrying matches.
There comes a moment when repentance has to become practical.
Delete it.
Unfollow.
Stop returning.
Move the conversation out of secrecy.
Tell a mature believer you trust.
Put distance between yourself and the situation.
Stop romanticizing what God has told you to resist.
And if you fall?
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not the story of clean people congratulating themselves for never having dirty thoughts.
It is the story of sinners being washed by Christ.
David knew sexual sin.
The woman caught in adultery knew sexual shame.
The Corinthians came from lives containing serious sexual immorality, yet Paul could tell believers:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified…”
Were.
That word carries hope.
Your sin can describe your history without being allowed to define your identity.
Pornography does not get the final word.
Adultery does not get the final word.
Lust does not get the final word.
Your worst secret does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
This is why biblical conviction is different from hopeless condemnation.
Conviction says:
“Bring it into the light.”
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God until you're better.”
The Gospel says the opposite.
Come because you cannot make yourself clean.
Confess because hiding is killing you.
Repent because grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Run to Christ because His blood is greater than the thing you are ashamed to name.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
Maybe you have been asking the wrong question.
Maybe you came here wanting to know exactly when attraction becomes coveting so you could determine whether you technically crossed the line.
But perhaps the Holy Spirit is asking something more personal.
What desire have you been feeding?
Whose image do you keep returning to?
What conversation would make you nervous if your spouse saw it?
What fantasy have you renamed “harmless”?
What person have you secretly begun wishing belonged to you?
What appetite are you protecting while asking Jesus to transform you?
Don't answer publicly just to appear spiritual.
Answer God.
Because He already knows.
And strangely, that should comfort you.
The Jesus who knows the whole truth about you is still the Jesus calling you toward Himself.
Peter failed spectacularly.
Thomas doubted.
The Samaritan woman's relational history was already known to Christ before He spoke hope into her life.
Again and again, Scripture shows us people meeting God in places they would rather have hidden.
Their scandal wasn't stronger than His grace.
Neither is yours.
But grace does not say, “Stay there.”
Grace says, “Come out.”
Come into the light.
Come back to your covenant.
Come back to purity.
Come back to truth.
Come back to seeing people as souls instead of objects.
Come back to the Christ who was crucified for sinners and rose again so sinners would no longer have to remain slaves to what once mastered them.
Maybe attraction brought you to the edge.
You do not have to jump.
Maybe you already jumped.
There is still a Savior.
Repentance means turning.
Grace means you can turn without pretending you never wandered.
And redemption means Jesus can write something holy after chapters you wish had never existed.
Not because scandal doesn't matter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to describe your private sin to strangers. But you can make one small declaration that you are choosing the light.

And if Christ has already brought you out of a place you once thought would own you forever, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another person finally believes freedom is possible.
Send it privately to the believer who needs to remember that temptation does not have to become surrender.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you follow Jesus more seriously, stay close.
It doesn't.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
But generosity, when freely offered for the advance of Gospel-centered work, can itself be an act of worship.
Send it to someone fighting quietly.
Because sometimes glorifying God looks like giving.
Sometimes it looks like serving.
Sometimes it looks like praying.
And sometimes it looks like refusing to keep life-giving truth to yourself when someone you love desperately needs to hear it.
But before you leave, remember this:
You are not called to become a person who never recognizes beauty.
You are called to become a person whose heart has learned what to do with beauty.
Notice without possessing.
Appreciate without consuming.
Love without exploiting.
Turn away when desire becomes rebellion.
Repent when you fail.
Receive forgiveness when you confess.
And keep bringing your heart back to Jesus.
Because the goal was never merely cleaner eyes.
It was a surrendered heart.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing about coveting was never that your eyes saw something beautiful.
It was the moment your heart whispered, “I want this more than I want to obey God.”
That is the battlefield.
And that is exactly where Jesus still meets sinners.
The desire you surrender today may become the place where somebody sees Christ in you tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A POLYGAMIST BECOME A CHURCH LEADER?
paragraphs:
CAN A POLYGAMIST BECOME A CHURCH LEADER?
He May Be Forgiven. He May Be Transformed. He May Be Your Brother in Christ. But Does Grace Automatically Put a Man Behind the Pulpit?
There are questions Christians ask because they are curious.

Then there are questions that walk straight into somebody’s home, sit down at the dinner table, look at the faces of wives and children, open a Bible, and refuse to leave until somebody tells the truth.
This is one of those questions.
Can a polygamist become a church leader?
Imagine the man for a moment.
Perhaps he grew up in a culture where having multiple wives was normal. Perhaps nobody ever told him differently. Perhaps he married two or three women before he ever heard the Gospel clearly.
Then one day he hears about Jesus.
Not religion.
Not Western culture.
Not another set of rules imported from somewhere else.
Jesus.

He hears that the Son of God died for sinners. That Christ carried guilt to the cross. That the blood of Jesus cleanses those who repent and believe. That the grave could not hold Him. That sinners can be reconciled to God.
And the man believes.
He repents.
He is baptized.
His life begins changing.
He loves Scripture. He prays. He gives. He serves. People notice his spiritual hunger. Perhaps he can teach. Perhaps people respect him.
Then someone says:
“He should become an elder.”
And suddenly the room becomes quiet.
Because everybody knows what nobody wants to say.
He has more than one wife.
Now what?
If you answer too quickly, you can wound people Scripture commands you to love.
But if compassion becomes permission to rewrite Scripture, you have not loved them either.
So we have to do something increasingly rare.
We have to let the Bible speak even when the answer costs us something.
Paul wrote concerning an overseer:
“δεῖ οὖν τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίλημπτον εἶναι, μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα…”
The crucial words are:
“μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα”
mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, the expression carries the sense of a “one-woman man.”
Many English Bibles traditionally render it “the husband of one wife.” Others emphasize the idea of marital faithfulness.
And before someone dismisses this as one isolated phrase, Paul essentially repeats it while describing elders in Titus:
“μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ”
Again:
a one-woman man.
That matters.
Paul is describing the character required of someone entrusted with oversight of Christ’s church.
He begins with being above reproach and immediately addresses the man's relationship to a woman.
Not because marriage saves him.
Not because married men are spiritually superior to unmarried believers.
Paul himself demonstrates that singleness is no spiritual defect.
The point is character.
Fidelity.
Integrity.
A life whose private relationships do not contradict the truth he publicly teaches.
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
Because grace and qualification are not identical.
Read that again.
Grace and qualification are not identical.
A person may be completely forgiven by Christ and still not meet the biblical qualifications for a particular office.
The thief beside Jesus was promised paradise.
He was not promised a pastorate.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will receive you.”
The Gospel says sinners come to Christ because they desperately need the Savior they could never become for themselves.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
That includes the monogamous man.
That includes the polygamous man.
That includes the preacher.
That includes the person sitting silently in the back row hoping nobody discovers what happened last night.
Nobody enters the kingdom because his marriage history was impressive.
We enter through Christ.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (John 14:6).
So if a polygamous man genuinely repents and trusts Jesus Christ, we must never speak as though his family history places him beyond the reach of the cross.
It does not.
Jesus saves sinners.
But salvation does not erase every distinction concerning responsibility in the church.

Paul's requirements for overseers in 1 Timothy 3 include being above reproach, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not violent, not greedy, managing one's household well, spiritually mature, and having a good reputation with outsiders.
Then comes that piercing description:
a one-woman man.

Some interpreters understand Paul's expression primarily as a prohibition of polygamy. Others understand it more broadly as demanding complete marital and sexual faithfulness rather than merely counting how many marriages appear on someone's biography. The phrase has also generated debates concerning divorce, remarriage, and widowhood.
Christians should acknowledge those interpretive discussions instead of pretending they do not exist.
But none of those discussions provides a convincing basis for making active polygamy the model Paul describes.
Whatever additional situations “one-woman man” may address, an overseer simultaneously maintaining multiple marital relationships does not naturally fit the apostolic picture of a one-woman man.
That conclusion should not produce cruelty.
It should produce trembling.
Because there is another question hiding underneath this one.
What happens to the wives?
Suppose a man already has several wives when he comes to Christ.
Do Christians simply tell him:
“Keep the first one. Abandon the others.”
That may sound tidy in a theological argument.
It can become devastating in an actual village.
There may be women who have depended upon him for years.
There may be children.
There may be financial responsibilities.
There may be legal obligations.
There may be women who had no meaningful voice in creating the situation.
Repentance must never become an excuse for a man to baptize abandonment as obedience.

Scripture condemns faithlessness and commands believers to provide for those under their care. Churches facing existing polygamous households therefore need extraordinary biblical wisdom, pastoral patience, compassion, accountability, and careful attention to the responsibilities already created.
The Gospel does not authorize a man to manufacture new victims while claiming he is correcting an old sin.
But neither does the difficulty of untangling a broken situation mean the church should redefine leadership qualifications.
This is where grace becomes breathtaking.
A man can hear:
“No, you should not presently serve as an elder.”
And simultaneously hear:
“Yes, Jesus wants you.”
Those sentences are not enemies.
One concerns salvation.
The other concerns office.
He can pray.
He can worship.
He can learn.
He can love his family.
He can testify about Christ.
He can serve according to the opportunities and responsibilities Scripture permits.
He can become increasingly holy.
He can become a faithful brother.
He can spend the rest of his life demonstrating what repentance looks like inside circumstances that cannot simply be erased.
And perhaps that testimony will preach more loudly than a title ever could.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be about collecting titles.
It is about following Jesus.
Somewhere along the way, many Christians began treating “pastor,” “elder,” “bishop,” or “leader” as though these were trophies awarded to the most enthusiastic believers.
They are not trophies.
They are stewardship.
James warns that teachers will receive stricter judgment.
Jesus repeatedly shattered human obsession with status.
The kingdom is not asking:
“How important can I become?”
The kingdom asks:
“How faithfully can I obey?”
And sometimes obedience sounds like this:
“Lord, if You never give me the position I wanted, You are still enough.”
That may be the sentence someone reading this needs tonight.
Maybe polygamy is not your story.
But something else is.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove that because Jesus forgave you, God now owes you the platform you dreamed about.
He does not.
And this is where our pride gets exposed.
Would you still worship Jesus if nobody handed you a microphone?
Would you still serve Him if nobody printed your name on a church program?
Would you still love Him if your greatest ministry happened where nobody applauded?
Would Christ still be enough?
Because the greatest evidence of transformation is not that a man finally gets a title.
It is that Jesus becomes more precious than the title.
Look again at God's pattern for marriage.
Long before Paul wrote to Timothy, Genesis takes us back to creation.
God creates the man and the woman.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
The final words are unforgettable:
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
vehayu levasar echad.
“And they shall become one flesh.”
Jesus Himself reaches back to this creation text when teaching about marriage in Matthew 19.
He does not appeal to humanity's later complications as the standard.
He returns to “the beginning.”
That distinction matters because the Bible records polygamy without presenting every recorded practice as God's ideal.
Scripture tells the truth about human beings.
Abraham's household knew painful rivalry.
Jacob's family knew jealousy and competition.
David's household became a landscape of devastating sexual and familial disorder.
Solomon accumulated wives until Scripture explicitly tells us that his wives turned his heart away.
The presence of polygamy in biblical narrative does not automatically constitute divine endorsement.
The Bible also records murder, deception, adultery, idolatry, betrayal, and war.
Description is not necessarily prescription.
Jesus calls us back to God's design.
And when Paul describes the shepherd who will publicly represent mature Christian character before the flock, he speaks of the one-woman man.
So can a practicing polygamist be appointed elder or overseer?
The strongest reading of the New Testament qualifications is no.
But please do not stop reading there.
Because if all you heard was “no,” you missed the Gospel.
Can a polygamist come to Jesus?
Yes.
Can Christ forgive him?
Yes.
Can Christ transform him?
Yes.
Can he become your brother in Christ?
Yes.
Can the church love him instead of treating him like a theological problem with a face?
Absolutely.
Can God use his testimony?
Yes.
Can his life become a monument to mercy?
Yes.
Because Christianity does not announce that respectable people have finally found a respectable God.
Christianity announces that the Holy One came looking for sinners.
Jesus touched lepers.
Jesus ate with tax collectors.
Jesus received people whose reputations made religious crowds uncomfortable.
Jesus confronted sin without becoming indifferent to sinners.
Then He walked toward a cross carrying a burden none of us could carry.
Ours.
The scandal is not merely that human beings have complicated marriages.
The deeper scandal is that every one of us has betrayed the God who made us.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Hated.
Hidden.
Manipulated.
Coveted.
Worshiped ourselves.
Protected secret sins while criticizing visible ones.
And still Christ came.
The sinless One stood where sinners deserved to stand.
He was crucified.
Buried.
And He rose again.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters the darkness carrying resurrection.
That is why biblical qualification must never become spiritual superiority.
The monogamous pastor has nothing to boast about at the foot of the cross.
The elder who has been faithful to one woman for forty years still needs the blood of Jesus.
The missionary needs Jesus.
The theologian needs Jesus.
The broken polygamist kneeling in repentance needs Jesus.
You need Jesus.
I need Jesus.
There is only one Hero in this story.
Christ.
Maybe this article reached you because you are wrestling with leadership.
Maybe you know a church facing exactly this situation.
Maybe your family comes from a polygamous background.
Maybe somebody has used Scripture to humiliate you.
Maybe somebody else has used grace as permission to ignore Scripture.
Neither distortion will heal us.
We need truth with tears in its eyes.
We need conviction without cruelty.
We need grace without compromise.
We need Jesus.
And perhaps the question you came here asking was, “Can a polygamist become a church leader?”
But the question following you out of this article may be much more personal:
If Jesus asks me to surrender something I desperately want, will I still call Him Lord?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Because surrender becomes real when obedience costs something.
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God, comment, “Jesus, make me faithful.”
If your situation is complicated and you genuinely do not know what obedience should look like, comment, “Pray for me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed to survive tonight.
Not to embarrass them. Not to win an argument.
Questions like this rarely stay theoretical forever.
Supporting Gospel-centered ministry should never be treated as purchasing God's favor, proving your salvation, or forcing God's hand. We give freely, willingly, and cheerfully—not under compulsion.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot merchandise your way into forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
And when His Word contradicts your desires, trust Him enough to surrender those too.
Because maybe the most powerful church leader is not always the person standing behind the pulpit.

Maybe sometimes it is the man sitting quietly among the congregation who wanted the title, heard the Word of God, surrendered his ambition, cared faithfully for the people already entrusted to him, and whispered through tears:
“Jesus, I wanted the position. But I want You more.”
Remember that sentence when obedience becomes expensive.
Grace does not always give you the position you wanted; sometimes grace rewrites you until Jesus Himself becomes the treasure you wanted more.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON’S WEDDING GUESTS THREATENED TO BURN HIS BRIDE AND HER FATHER ALIVE
paragraphs:
SAMSON’S WEDDING GUESTS THREATENED TO BURN HIS BRIDE AND HER FATHER ALIVE
She betrayed Samson because she was terrified of dying. Then, in one of the darkest ironies in Scripture, the very death she tried to escape eventually found her anyway. But buried beneath this horrifying story is a warning about fear, compromise, revenge—and why only Jesus can finally break the cycle.

Imagine standing at your own wedding celebration and discovering that some of the men eating your food, sharing your table, and participating in your celebration have quietly decided that if they do not get what they want from you…
they will burn you alive.
Not embarrass you.
Not threaten your marriage.
Not ruin the celebration.
Burn you.
And your father.
With fire.
That is not an invented detail added to make Samson's story more dramatic.
It is in the Bible.
Judges 14 records Samson holding a feast connected with his marriage to a Philistine woman from Timnah. Thirty companions were assigned to him, and Samson presented them with a riddle.
The riddle came from something they could not possibly have known unless Samson revealed it.
Earlier, Samson had killed a lion. Later, he discovered bees and honey inside its carcass. From that strange experience came his riddle:
“Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet.”
Thirty men had seven days to solve it.
There were garments at stake. Pride was at stake. Honor was at stake.
And when they could not solve the riddle themselves, the celebration became something darker.
They went to Samson's bride.
The Hebrew text of Judges 14:15 preserves the brutality with terrifying simplicity:
“פַּתִּי אֶת־אִישֵׁךְ וְיַגֶּד־לָנוּ אֶת־הַחִידָה פֶּן־נִשְׂרֹף אוֹתָךְ וְאֶת־בֵּית אָבִיךְ בָּאֵשׁ”
The force of the threat is essentially:
“Entice your husband so that he tells us the riddle, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire.”
There is something chilling about those words.
בָּאֵשׁ — ba'esh.
“With fire.”
This woman was trapped between men using power in different ways.
The wedding guests wanted Samson's secret.
Samson would not give it.
And she knew something Samson apparently did not know:
there was a death threat hanging over the celebration.
So she cried.
She pressed him.
She accused him of not loving her.
“You hate me! You don't really love me!”
To Samson, perhaps it sounded like manipulation.
Behind her tears, however, stood a threat he apparently had not heard.
Fire.
Her father's house.
Death.
Suddenly the scene looks different.
This does not make every choice she made right.
It makes the tragedy human.
Because frightened people sometimes make terrible decisions while trying to survive.
Maybe you know something about that.
Maybe you have compromised because you were afraid of what would happen if you didn't.
Maybe you stayed silent because speaking truth might cost you a relationship.
Maybe you surrendered a conviction because you were terrified of losing someone's approval.
Maybe you returned to a relationship God was pulling you away from because loneliness frightened you more than compromise did.
Maybe you hid something.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you became someone you barely recognized because fear kept whispering:
Just survive this.
Just get through today.
Just give them what they want.
And everything will be okay.
That whisper has destroyed more lives than we realize.
Samson eventually told his wife the answer.
She told the men.
The men solved the riddle.
Samson knew something had happened.
Then the story exploded.
Anger.
Violence.
Humiliation.
Retaliation.
Separation.
Samson left.
His wife was eventually given to another man.
Then Samson returned.
