The thing in Rachel's hand was never the author of her miracle—and the thing you're desperately holding may be keeping your eyes from the One you actually need.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Eli’s Sons Were Priests—and Scripture Accuses Them of Sleeping With Women at the Tabernacle Entrance
paragraphs: Eli’s Sons Were Priests—and Scripture Accuses Them of Sleeping With Women at the Tabernacle Entrance

They wore the priesthood. They handled holy sacrifices. They stood near the presence of God. But Scripture says something terrifying about Hophni and Phinehas before it ever tells us about the women: “They did not know the LORD.” And that may be the most frightening sentence in their entire story.
Imagine walking toward the tabernacle at Shiloh.
You came carrying a sacrifice.

Maybe you were grieving. Maybe you had sinned. Maybe your family desperately needed God. Maybe you had traveled for miles because somewhere inside you was still the hope that when you came near the place associated with His presence, you would find mercy.
Smoke rises.
Animals are being prepared.
Prayers are being whispered.
The name of the LORD is being invoked.
And standing there are priests.
Hophni and Phinehas.
Sons of Eli.
Men born into a sacred family, serving around sacred things, occupying sacred positions.
From a distance, everything might have looked religious.
Then Scripture pulls back the curtain.
And what it reveals should frighten anyone who has ever confused being around God with actually knowing God.
“Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:12, KJV
The Hebrew is even more arresting:
וּבְנֵי עֵלִי בְּנֵי בְלִיָּעַל לֹא יָדְעוּ אֶת־יְהוָה
Uvenei ‘Eli benei veliyya‘al; lo yade‘u et-YHWH.
The crucial words are בְּנֵי בְלִיָּעַל — benei veliyya‘al: literally, “sons of worthlessness,” an expression describing thoroughly corrupt or worthless men.
Then comes the diagnosis beneath the scandal:
לֹא יָדְעוּ אֶת־יְהוָה — lo yade‘u et-YHWH.
“They did not know YHWH.”
Read that again.
They were priests.
And they did not know the LORD.
That is the horror of this story.
Their greatest problem was not merely sexual sin.
It was not merely greed.
It was not merely abuse of religious privilege.
Beneath everything was a catastrophic absence of genuine knowledge of God.
They knew religious procedure.
They knew sacrifices.
They knew priestly privilege.
They knew how the system worked.
They apparently knew enough about holy things to exploit them.
But Scripture says they did not know the One to whom all those holy things belonged.
And suddenly this ancient scandal becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to know Christian vocabulary and not know Christ.
Possible to raise your hands during worship while hiding what those hands touched last night.
Possible to post Bible verses while secretly feeding an addiction.
Possible to preach grace while refusing repentance.
Possible to carry a title that says “minister,” “pastor,” “leader,” “Christian,” or “believer” while living as though the eyes of God cannot penetrate a locked room.
Hophni and Phinehas are not preserved in Scripture merely so modern Christians can stare at two wicked men from thousands of years ago.
Their story is a mirror.
And mirrors become uncomfortable when we stop looking at everyone else.

The biblical account says these priests were already corrupting the sacrificial system. They took portions of offerings improperly and demanded meat before the fat had been offered to God. When worshipers resisted, their servants threatened force.
Think about what that means.
People were coming to worship God, and God's representatives were making obedience harder.
People brought sacrifices, and priests exploited them.
The sanctuary had become an opportunity for appetite.
Scripture therefore says:
“Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD: for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:17, KJV
That sentence is devastating.
Their behavior did not remain private.
Their corruption damaged other people's relationship with worship.
And this is why spiritual hypocrisy is never as private as the hypocrite imagines.
When someone uses the name of God to feed greed, lust, ego, control, or appetite, people can begin associating the ugliness of the representative with the character of the God supposedly represented.
Some people reading this know exactly what that feels like.
Perhaps someone who spoke about Jesus wounded you.
Perhaps someone carrying a Bible manipulated you.
Perhaps a church leader betrayed your trust.
Perhaps somebody used spiritual authority to get what they wanted and then expected everyone else to remain silent to “protect the ministry.”
Scripture does not protect Hophni and Phinehas by hiding what they did.
God had their corruption written down.
That matters.
Then comes 1 Samuel 2:22.

Eli was old, and the text reports that he heard what his sons were doing throughout Israel, including the accusation that they were lying with the women serving at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
The traditional Hebrew textual form underlying many familiar translations reads of the women:
הַנָּשִׁים הַצֹּבְאוֹת פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד
hannashim hatzove’ot petach ohel mo‘ed—
the women serving or assembling at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
And Scripture says Eli heard that his sons יִשְׁכְּבוּן — yishkevun, “were lying/sleeping,” with them.
This is why many translations straightforwardly render the accusation as Hophni and Phinehas sleeping with, lying with, or having sexual relations with these women.

There is, however, an important textual caution for careful Bible readers: the sexual accusation in this verse has a manuscript/textual-history complication, and some textual witnesses and modern translations do not include that clause. So we should not pretend there is no textual question here.
But neither should we soften the portrait Scripture unquestionably gives us.

Even apart from that disputed clause, Hophni and Phinehas are explicitly described as corrupt men who did not know the LORD, who abused the sacrificial system, treated the LORD's offering with contempt, ignored correction, and eventually came under divine judgment.
The Bible is not presenting misunderstood religious celebrities.
It is presenting corrupt priests.
And notice where the alleged sexual corruption occurs.
At the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
Near the place associated with worship.
Near sacrifice.
Near prayer.
Near holiness.
That juxtaposition is almost unbearable.
Holy place.
Unholy appetite.
Priestly clothing.
Corrupt hearts.
Religious proximity.
Spiritual estrangement.
And perhaps that is exactly where this story finds us.
Because sin rarely announces itself by saying, “I intend to destroy you.”
It whispers.
Just once.
Nobody knows.
You deserve this.
You can repent later.
You're still serving God.
You're still attending church.
You're still reading Scripture.
You're still posting Christian content.
You're still helping people.
Surely everything between you and God cannot be that bad.
Hophni and Phinehas stand forever in Scripture as evidence that proximity to holy things cannot substitute for holiness of heart.
You can stand near the altar and still be far from God.
You can know worship songs and not worship.
You can explain theology and refuse the Lordship of Christ.
You can fool a congregation.
You can fool followers.
You can fool your spouse.
You can fool your parents.
You can fool the person sitting beside you on Sunday.
But you cannot fool God.
And perhaps somebody reading this has grown exhausted from trying.
Exhausted from deleting evidence.
Exhausted from clearing browser histories.
Exhausted from pretending the marriage is fine.
Exhausted from preaching convictions you stopped practicing privately.
Exhausted from saying, “I'm okay.”
Exhausted from promising God, “This is the last time.”
Then falling again.
And again.
And again.
Listen carefully.
The lesson of Hophni and Phinehas is not that sinners are beyond mercy.
If that were the Gospel, none of us could stand.
The warning is what happens when sinners continually harden themselves against the God who confronts their sin.
Eli confronted his sons.
“Why do ye such things? for I hear of your evil dealings by all this people.” — 1 Samuel 2:23, KJV.
But they would not listen.
That detail changes everything.
God's confrontation was not an invitation to improve their image.
It was a summons to turn.
And they refused.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
Between falling and deciding the floor is home.
Between crying, “God, have mercy on me,” and saying, “God has no right to tell me what to do.”
Repentance does not mean you have never fallen.
Repentance means that when God exposes what is killing you, you stop defending it and turn toward Him.
This is where the story becomes more than scandal.
Because Hophni and Phinehas are not the final priests in the Bible.
Another Priest was coming.
Not corrupt.
Not predatory.
Not greedy.
Not exploiting worshipers.
Not taking sacrifices for Himself.
He would become the sacrifice.
Jesus Christ.

The New Testament presents Him as our great High Priest, holy and undefiled, the One who entered not through the blood of animals but through His own sacrificial work and who is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him.
Where corrupt religious men take from people, Jesus gives Himself for people.
Where corrupt priests use sacred office to satisfy appetite, Jesus lays down His life.
Where sinners dishonor God's holiness, Jesus fulfills righteousness.
Where guilty people deserve judgment, Christ bears sin at the cross.
And where scandal seems to have written the final chapter, grace picks up the pen.
That is the Gospel.
Not that your sin was insignificant.
Not that God shrugged at what happened.
Not that holiness stopped mattering.
Grace is infinitely more beautiful than that.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was cheap.
The cross declares how serious sin actually is.
And simultaneously, how astonishingly far divine love went to rescue sinners.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18, KJV.
The Just for the unjust.
The Holy for the unholy.
The innocent Christ for guilty sinners.
That means your secret does not have to become your identity.
Your pornography does not have to write your ending.
Your adultery does not have to write your ending.
Your hypocrisy does not have to write your ending.
Your greed does not have to write your ending.
Your pride does not have to write your ending.
Your years of pretending do not have to write your ending.
But grace is not permission to continue hiding.
Jesus does not rescue us so that we can decorate our chains with Christian language.
He calls us out of darkness.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring the hidden thing into the light before the hidden thing devours what remains.

If you have harmed someone, repentance may require more than tears. It may require confession, accountability, restitution where appropriate, surrendering authority, accepting consequences, and seeking help. Grace does not mean victims must pretend nothing happened, and forgiveness must never be weaponized to silence those who have been harmed.
Christ's grace is not camouflage for corruption.
It is rescue from corruption.
Maybe this article did not reach you because you needed another interesting Bible story.
Maybe you needed the frightening sentence:
“They did not know the LORD.”
You know church.
But do you know Him?
You know Christian content.
But do you know Him?
You know what to say when someone asks whether you're saved.
But when nobody is watching...
do you know Him?
Not merely facts about Jesus.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Son of God.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The Lord who refuses to leave His people enslaved to what He died to redeem them from.
But do not run from conviction either.
And if Christ has already pulled you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell enough of your testimony to give somebody else hope.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Not because anyone can purchase God's blessing.
And never because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
We support Gospel work because grace has already been freely given to us in Christ, and because we want biblical truth to continue reaching people who desperately need it.
Because somewhere tonight there is another person standing frighteningly close to holy things while drifting farther from the Holy One.
Maybe they still sing.
Maybe they still preach.
Maybe they still serve.
Maybe nobody suspects anything.
Maybe that person is reading these words.
Hophni and Phinehas teach us that a title cannot save you.
An altar cannot save you.
A religious family cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
So stop protecting the version of yourself that Christ is calling you to crucify.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the lust.
Bring the betrayal.
Bring the hypocrisy.
Bring the shame.
Bring the thing you swore nobody would ever know.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because the blood of Christ is the only reason your sin does not have to speak the final word.
The sons of Eli stood near an altar while their hearts wandered from God.
Jesus climbed onto a cross so wandering hearts could come home.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth you can carry away from this story is this:
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the cross—but it does not get to decide who walks away from it. Jesus does.
Because the goal was never merely to look religious.
The goal is to know Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Maybe God Isn’t Withholding a Better Life. Maybe You’ve Become Blind to the Life Already in Your Hands.
paragraphs: Maybe God Isn’t Withholding a Better Life. Maybe You’ve Become Blind to the Life Already in Your Hands.
Comparison keeps pointing at what is missing. Gratitude quietly opens your eyes to what grace has already placed within reach.
There is a frightening kind of poverty that can happen while your hands are still full.
You can have food on the table and feel deprived.
You can have people who love you and feel forgotten.
You can wake up breathing, walking, thinking, praying—and spend the entire morning grieving a life that belongs to somebody else.
That is what comparison can do.
It does not always steal the gift.
Sometimes it simply steals your ability to see the gift.
And perhaps that is why these words from Paul are more confronting than they first appear:
“Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:16–18
In Greek, the heart of the passage reads:
“Πάντοτε χαίρετε, ἀδιαλείπτως προσεύχεσθε, ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε…”
Pántote chaírete, adialeíptōs proseúchesthe, en pantì eucharisteîte…
“Always rejoice. Continually pray. In everything give thanks.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say everything that happens to you is good.
It does not tell a grieving mother to call death good.
It does not tell the betrayed spouse to call betrayal good.
It does not command the wounded to pretend they are not bleeding.
It does not require you to celebrate abuse, injustice, sickness, loss, loneliness, or sin.
Paul says, “ἐν παντὶ”—en panti—“in everything,” or “in every circumstance,” give thanks.
There is an enormous difference between thanking God for evil and remaining thankful in the presence of suffering.
Christian gratitude is not emotional dishonesty.
It is spiritual sight.
It is looking at a broken world without looking away from a faithful God.
And some of us have slowly lost that sight.
Not because God stopped giving.
Because comparison trained our eyes to notice everything except what He gave us.
Think about how easily it happens.
You once prayed for the job you now complain about every morning.
You once desperately wanted somebody to love you, and now the person beside you receives the exhausted leftovers of your attention.
You once prayed for children, and now the noise that proves they are alive sometimes feels like an interruption.
You once begged God to get you through a season you thought would destroy you.
He did.
But because another struggle arrived afterward, you barely remember that you survived.
You wanted a home.
Now you notice its imperfections.
You wanted transportation.
Now you notice what somebody else drives.
You wanted opportunity.
Now somebody else’s success makes yours feel embarrassingly small.
You wanted healing.
Then, once the pain faded, ordinary life became ordinary again.
And perhaps the saddest part is this:
Some of the things boring you today would have brought you to tears five years ago.
Read that again.
Somewhere in your past is a version of you who would look at something in your present life and whisper,
“God…You actually did it.”
But present-you barely notices anymore.
That is the tragedy of spiritual familiarity.
Mercies become furniture.
Miracles become routine.
People become background noise.
Daily bread becomes “just bread.”
And another person’s highlight reel becomes the measuring stick by which you declare your own life insufficient.
Comparison rarely walks into your heart announcing itself as idolatry.
It sounds much more reasonable.
“Why can’t my marriage look like theirs?”
“Why am I still struggling financially?”
“Why is her ministry growing faster?”
“Why did he get promoted?”
“Why does their family seem so happy?”
“Why does everybody else appear to be moving forward while I’m still here?”
And underneath all those questions, another question sometimes begins forming.
One we may be afraid to say aloud.
“God…why wasn’t what You gave me better?”
There it is.
Not always.
Not every desire for change is sinful. Scripture gives us room to lament, ask, seek, work, grow, and bring our needs honestly before God. Wanting improvement is not automatically ingratitude.
But comparison can corrupt a legitimate desire until desire becomes accusation.
Until someone else’s blessing starts looking like evidence that God has neglected you.
Until you cannot enjoy your portion because you are staring at theirs.
Until “I would like something different” becomes “What God has given me cannot possibly be enough.”
That is when comparison becomes dangerous.
Because eventually you are no longer merely comparing possessions.
You are questioning Providence.
You are quietly putting God on trial.
And social media can pour gasoline on that fire.
You wake up feeling reasonably content.
Then you scroll.
Somebody is getting married.
Somebody bought a house.
Somebody is traveling.
Somebody lost weight.
Somebody’s business exploded.
Somebody’s ministry reached thousands.
Somebody’s children look perfectly behaved.
Somebody is standing beside a new car holding an oversized ribbon.
Somebody posts the anniversary photograph with the caption about marrying their best friend.
Twenty minutes later, nothing in your physical life has changed.
Same room.
Same spouse.
Same income.
Same body.
Same calling.
Same breakfast.
Yet somehow you feel poorer.
What happened?
You consumed hundreds of fragments of other people’s lives and unconsciously assembled them into one imaginary person whose life seems better than yours in every category.
You compared your ordinary Tuesday to everybody else’s most photographable moments.
And your soul lost.
Because comparison is a game with no finish line.
There will always be someone with more.
More money.
More beauty.
More influence.
More opportunities.
More recognition.
A seemingly easier marriage.
A bigger platform.
A healthier body.
A more impressive testimony.
A nicer home.
Even if you somehow surpassed the person you envy today, comparison would simply introduce you to someone else tomorrow.
That is why comparison never finally says,
“Enough.”
But gratitude can.
Gratitude looks at daily bread and remembers that bread is mercy.
It looks at an imperfect spouse and remembers that covenant is sacred.
It hears children laughing—or crying, arguing, running through the house—and remembers that life itself is astonishing.
It wakes up with bills and remembers there is still a God to pray to.
It looks into an aging face and realizes those lines mean years were given.
It sits at a modest table and realizes Jesus never taught His disciples to pray for somebody else’s banquet.
He taught them:
“Give us this day our daily bread.”
Not tomorrow’s luxury.
Not our neighbor’s portion.
Daily bread.
Enough grace for today.
Enough mercy for today.
Enough Christ for today.
And this is where the Gospel exposes something even deeper.
Our greatest gift was never supposed to be the perfect circumstances.
Our greatest gift is Christ Himself.
If Christianity becomes merely a method for obtaining the lifestyle we envy, then we have missed Christianity entirely.
Jesus did not bleed on a cross so you could finally compete successfully with somebody on Facebook.
He came because our deepest poverty was not that somebody else had more than us.
Our deepest poverty was sin.
We needed reconciliation with God.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed a righteousness we could never manufacture.
We needed resurrection.
We needed grace.
And Christ came.
The sinless Son of God entered our brokenness, bore sin at the cross, died, and rose again.
The scandal of the Gospel is that guilty sinners are invited into grace not because we became impressive enough, but because Jesus was sufficient.
Repentance means turning from sin and returning to God.
Faith means trusting Christ rather than ourselves.
Grace means the story does not have to end where our failure says it should.
And suddenly gratitude becomes much bigger than saying, “Thank You for my house.”
It becomes:
“Jesus, thank You that I belong to You.”
“Thank You that my sins can be forgiven.”
“Thank You that shame does not get the final word.”
“Thank You that my failures do not outrank Your mercy.”
“Thank You that even when my circumstances are not what I hoped for, the cross has already proven that I am not abandoned.”
This is why biblical gratitude can coexist with tears.
You can grieve and give thanks.
You can be disappointed and give thanks.
You can want your circumstances to change and give thanks.
You can sit beside a hospital bed and still whisper the name of Jesus.
You can be uncertain about tomorrow while worshiping God today.
Paul’s command was never shallow positivity.
“Πάντοτε χαίρετε.”
Always rejoice.
“ἀδιαλείπτως προσεύχεσθε.”
Pray continually.
“ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε.”
In everything give thanks.
And then Paul anchors it:
“τοῦτο γὰρ θέλημα θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς.”
“For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.”
Notice where the Christian life is located.
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
En Christō Iēsou.
In Christ Jesus.
Not in perfect circumstances.
Not in somebody else’s lifestyle.
Not in finally possessing everything you thought would make you happy.
In Christ Jesus.
Maybe you need to put the phone down tonight.
Walk through your home slowly.
Look around.
Not at what needs upgrading.
At what remains.
Listen for the voices you have become accustomed to hearing.
Look at the face you have become accustomed to seeing.
Think about the prayers God answered so gradually that you forgot they were prayers.
Remember the doors He closed that later protected you.
Remember the nights you thought you would not survive.
Remember the sin He forgave.
Remember the people He sent.
Remember the strength that appeared when yours disappeared.
Remember Calvary.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember Jesus.
Maybe your life is not as empty as comparison has been telling you.
Maybe you have simply been staring through a window into everybody else’s house while forgetting to turn around and see what grace placed inside yours.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have been angry with your life lately.
Nothing seems enough.
You keep imagining that peace is waiting somewhere else—with another income, another body, another relationship, another city, another level of success.
But perhaps tonight the Holy Spirit is not merely asking what you want next.
Perhaps He is exposing what you stopped thanking God for.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we stop hiding what is happening inside us.
Someone else reading may desperately need to discover they are not the only believer struggling to remain grateful.
Then do something more difficult.
Before you sleep tonight, thank God specifically for five things you have stopped noticing.
Not impressive things.
Ordinary things.
A person.
A meal.
A conversation.
A place to rest.
Another morning.
The ability to pray.
Another opportunity to repent.
Another day in which the door of grace is still open.
We glorify God through faith, obedience, love, worship, truth, generosity, and lives surrendered to Christ.
But if this truth helped you see His goodness again, sharing it can become one simple act of witness.
Someone may need these words tonight.
Send this to the believer who keeps saying, “I’m behind.”
Send it to the friend whose heart has been exhausted by comparison.
The Gospel cannot be purchased, and God’s grace is not for sale.
Jesus is not merchandise.
Grace is not a transaction.
The forgiveness of sins is offered through Jesus Christ, and the proper response to the Gospel is repentance and faith.
So tonight, before you ask God why you do not have somebody else’s life, look again at the life already in your hands.
Maybe there is something there you stopped seeing.
Maybe there is someone there you stopped appreciating.
Maybe there is mercy there that became so familiar you started calling it ordinary.
Maybe God is still changing things you cannot see.
Maybe the chapter you resent is not the final chapter.
And maybe the God who met you in your scandal is still writing grace into places you thought were ruined beyond redemption.
Because comparison says:
“Look what you’re missing.”
But gratitude whispers:
“Look what God has carried you through.”
Comparison says:
“Their life is better.”
The Gospel says:
“Christ is yours.”
Comparison keeps your eyes moving sideways.
Grace lifts them toward Jesus.
So rejoice.
Pray.
Give thanks.
Not because everything is easy.
Not because everything is good.
Not because you must pretend the pain does not hurt.
But because even inside an unfinished life, Christ remains faithful.
And if you know someone whose eyes have become so fixed on what they lack that they can no longer recognize what God has already placed in their hands, share this with them.
Perhaps tonight you are not the only person God wants to remind.
Perhaps the article you almost scrolled past becomes the truth somebody else desperately needed you to pass along.
And when comparison returns tomorrow—and it probably will—come back and read this again.
Remember.
Give thanks.
Then look at your life one more time.
Not through the eyes of envy.
Through the eyes of grace.
Because one of the saddest ways to lose a blessing is never to lose it at all—but to become so accustomed to grace that you can no longer see what you are holding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Some Unanswered Prayers Don’t End With an Explanation. Faith Still Has to Live There.
paragraphs:
Some Unanswered Prayers Don’t End With an Explanation. Faith Still Has to Live There.
You prayed. You waited. You believed. Nothing changed. And perhaps the hardest part is that God never told you why.
There is a kind of pain Christians know how to talk about.
And then there is the kind we usually try to explain too quickly.
We know what to say when the prayer gets answered.
“The scans came back clear.”
“The marriage was restored.”
“The child came home.”
“The job finally opened.”
“The money arrived just in time.”
“The depression lifted.”
“The door opened.”
And we celebrate because we should.
We testify.
We tell everyone how faithful God has been.
But there is another testimony that rarely gets the microphone.
It belongs to the person who prayed just as sincerely...
and the scans did not come back clear.
The marriage still ended.
The child still has not come home.
The opportunity never arrived.
The pain became chronic.
The loneliness stayed.
The grave still had to be visited.
The door remained closed.
And after months—or years—of asking God for an answer, that person eventually discovered something frightening:
Sometimes the prayer remains unanswered in the way you desperately wanted...
and the explanation never comes either.
That is where shallow Christianity can become cruel.
Because someone will inevitably tell you that everything happened because “God has something better.”
Maybe.
But Scripture does not authorize us to invent God's hidden reasons.
Someone else may tell you that you simply did not have enough faith.
But the Bible will not allow that accusation either.
Someone may search your life for some secret sin that supposedly explains everything.

Someone may promise that if you pray harder, declare louder, fast longer, give more, believe more aggressively, or find the correct spiritual formula, God will finally do what you have been begging Him to do.
And perhaps beneath all those voices you have been carrying a question you are almost ashamed to say aloud:
What am I supposed to do with God when God does not explain Himself?
Stay here.
Because Paul once prayed for something to be taken away.
Not casually.
Not once.
Repeatedly.
And God said no.
Paul writes:
—2 Corinthians 12:8–9
Listen carefully to the Greek because one small phrase changes the emotional center of the passage:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου
Arkei soi hē charis mou.
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
The verb ἀρκεῖ (arkei) carries the sense of being sufficient, adequate, enough.
Enough.
Not because Paul's suffering was imaginary.
Not because weakness suddenly became pleasant.
Not because unanswered prayer stopped hurting.
Grace was enough because Christ Himself would remain present and powerful where Paul's weakness remained.
Paul asked for removal.
Christ answered with sustaining grace.
And those are not the same thing.
Paul identifies his suffering as a “thorn in the flesh”—Greek:
σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί
skolops tē sarki.
Scholars have debated exactly what Paul's “thorn” was, and Scripture does not settle the question for us.
That matters.
Because sometimes Christians become strangely confident about things God chose not to explain.
Paul tells us enough to know it tormented and humbled him, but not enough for us to identify it with certainty.
And perhaps that ambiguity is one reason generations of wounded believers have been able to recognize themselves inside this passage.
Because you have your thorn too.
Maybe nobody sees yours.
Maybe you worship while carrying it.
Maybe you serve while carrying it.
Maybe you post encouraging Scriptures while carrying it.
Maybe people think you are strong because they never see what happens when the room becomes quiet.
They do not know how many times you have whispered:
“Lord... please.”
They do not know how many nights you stared at the ceiling.
They do not know how many mornings you checked your phone hoping something had changed.
They do not know how many times you thought, “Surely this will be the week.”
They do not know how exhausting hope can become when disappointment keeps surviving it.
And maybe you have reached the place where you are no longer asking God for a miracle.
You are asking Him for an explanation.
“Why?”
Why this?
Why so long?
Why them?
Why me?
Why did You let me hope?
Why did You not intervene?
Why did You answer their prayer and seemingly not mine?
Why did You allow something You could have stopped?
Those questions do not automatically make you faithless.
The Bible is far too honest for that.
The Psalms contain cries of “How long?”
Habakkuk questioned what God was doing.
Job suffered while explanations remained painfully beyond his reach.
And Christianity reaches its emotional center not in a philosophical lecture about suffering...
but at a cross.
Jesus Christ Himself prayed in Gethsemane:
“Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me.”
Then came the words upon which human redemption would turn:
“Yet not what I will, but what you will.”
—Mark 14:36
Do not rush past that.
Jesus did not surrender because the Father lacked power.
“All things are possible for you.”
He knew exactly who His Father was.
And still He surrendered.
Christian faith is therefore not pretending God cannot do what you asked.
Sometimes faith is knowing He can...
asking Him to...
and trusting Him when His will remains different from yours.
That kind of faith bleeds.
Jesus understands that place.
Gethsemane destroys the idea that anguish itself is unbelief.
Christ was sorrowful.
Christ prayed earnestly.
Christ submitted perfectly.
And the cup was not removed.
He went to the cross.
There the sinless Son of God was crucified beneath human injustice, bearing our sins, accomplishing what none of us could accomplish for ourselves.
The apparent catastrophe became the place of redemption.
But be careful here.
The cross does not give Christians permission to look at every suffering person and announce, “I know exactly why God did this.”
We do not.
The cross gives us something better than speculation.
It gives us Jesus.
Christianity does not say you will eventually understand every chapter of your life before you die.
It says there is One you can trust when you do not understand the chapter.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because some wounds never receive tidy explanations.
Some graves remain graves until resurrection.
Some relationships are never restored in this lifetime.
Some bodies continue hurting.
Some dreams genuinely die.
Some questions accompany believers all the way home.
The Bible does not require us to rename those things “good.”
Death is called an enemy.
Grief is real.
Sin destroys.
Creation groans.
We groan.
But the Gospel declares that suffering, sin, death, disappointment, and unanswered questions do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why Paul's response is so astonishing.
After hearing Christ say, “My grace is sufficient for you,” Paul writes:
The phrase translated “may rest upon me” comes from ἐπισκηνώσῃ ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ (episkēnōsē ep’ eme), carrying the striking picture of dwelling or pitching a tent upon someone.
Paul discovered something he could not have learned merely by getting everything he requested.
There are places where weakness becomes the place in which the power of Christ rests upon a human life.
Not because weakness saves us.
Jesus saves us.
Not because suffering makes us righteous.
Christ's righteousness is our hope.
Not because pain is secretly wonderful.
Pain hurts precisely because something is wrong with this fallen world.
But because Jesus can meet His people inside what He has not removed.
Perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this has desperately needed:
Jesus can meet you inside what He has not removed.
You have been waiting for God to change the circumstances before you believed He was near.
But what if His presence has been holding you in the circumstances all along?
Think about what you have survived.
Not because you were invincible.
You were not.
There were days you nearly collapsed.
There were nights nobody knew how badly you were hurting.
There were prayers that barely qualified as sentences.
There were moments when all you had left was “Jesus.”
Maybe even that name came through tears.
Yet somehow...
you are still here.
Still reading.
Still reaching.
Still wondering whether faith can survive another disappointment.
It can.
But perhaps not the faith you once imagined.
Sometimes unanswered prayer burns away the transactional version of Christianity we did not realize we had constructed.
“I obey, therefore God gives me the outcome.”
“I pray correctly, therefore God fixes the problem.”
“I believe strongly enough, therefore tragedy stays away.”
Then life happens.
And suddenly you discover that Jesus never promised His disciples immunity from suffering.
He promised Himself.
“I am with you always.”
That is different.
And infinitely deeper.
Maybe you have been angry with God.
Tell Him.
He already knows.
Maybe you have felt betrayed.
Bring that wound into His presence.
Maybe your prayers have become embarrassingly small.
“Help me.”
“Hold me.”
“Don't let me leave You.”
Those are still prayers.
Maybe you stopped praying altogether because asking became too painful.
Come back.
Not because you have finally solved your suffering.
Come back because Christ is still Christ.
The Gospel does not begin with your ability to understand God.
It begins with God's mercy toward sinners.
Every one of us has sinned.
Every one of us has fallen short.
Our deepest problem is not that life failed to follow our plans. Our deepest problem is that sin separates humanity from the holy God who made us.
And no amount of religious performance can repair that breach.
So God came to us.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we could not live.
He died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
Christian hope therefore does not rest upon the promise that everything will become understandable tomorrow.
It rests upon a Person who walked out of a grave.
If Jesus Christ is risen, then your unanswered prayer is painful...
but it is not ultimate.
Your suffering is real...
but it is not sovereign.
Your disappointment may be enormous...
but it is not your god.
Your grave will not be permanent.
Your tears will not last forever.
Your unanswered questions will not have eternity to torment you.
Christ has risen.
And because He lives, mystery does not have to destroy faith.
Sometimes faith sounds less like:
“Now I finally understand.”
And more like:
“Jesus, I still don't understand...
but I am staying.”
Maybe that is where you are today.
Not victorious in the way people like to photograph.
Not standing on a mountaintop.
Not carrying an impressive testimony with a perfect ending.
Just staying.
And perhaps staying with Jesus while your heart is confused is one of the most honest forms of faith you have ever offered Him.
If something hidden broke open while you were reading this, you do not have to pretend.
You do not owe strangers the details.
Sometimes two words are enough for the Body of Christ to know that someone among us needs prayer.
And if you see someone write those words, do not interrogate them.
Pray for them.
There is probably someone on your Facebook friends list who has been quietly carrying disappointment for months.
Maybe years.
You are allowed to trust Christ without pretending you understand everything.
Because unanswered prayer rarely hurts only once.
There may be another night when the silence feels unbearable, and you will need to remember:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου.
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
It does not.
Grace cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
And supporting a Christian ministry is never a substitute for repentance, obedience, generosity to your local church, or faithful service to Christ.
But please remember why any of this exists.
Not to build a personality.
Not merely to sell products.
Not to turn someone's pain into engagement.
We want people to meet Jesus.
So share because someone needs Him.
Tag because someone is hurting.
Save because you may need these Scriptures again.
Follow because your soul needs truth more often than your feed will naturally give it to you.
But above everything else...
come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the grace you could never earn.
And when you cannot understand what God is doing, anchor yourself to what He has already revealed most clearly in Jesus Christ.
Paul asked three times.
The thorn remained.
But so did Christ.
Maybe your story currently has a sentence you would erase if God handed you the pen.
Maybe it contains a loss you never expected.
A prayer you cannot explain.
A chapter you never wanted.
A scandal.
A failure.
A wound.
A silence.
Do not confuse an unfinished chapter with a finished story.
The risen Jesus is still writing.
And sometimes grace does not look like God explaining everything.
Sometimes grace looks like waking tomorrow morning with the same unanswered question...
and discovering that Christ is still enough to take the next breath.
The prayer may still be unanswered. The mystery may still be unexplained. But the hands holding your story still bear the scars that prove how far Love was willing to go for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HEROD MARRIED HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—AND JOHN THE BAPTIST REFUSED TO KEEP QUIET
paragraphs: HEROD MARRIED HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—AND JOHN THE BAPTIST REFUSED TO KEEP QUIET

He could have saved his life with silence. Instead, John looked toward a ruler who could imprison him, destroy him, and eventually have his head carried into a banquet hall—and told him the one thing almost everyone else was too afraid to say.
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
That sentence would help put John the Baptist in a prison cell.
And eventually...
it would cost him his head.
But there is something even more disturbing in this story than the execution.
Herod actually liked listening to John.
Read that again.
The man who imprisoned the preacher was still fascinated by the preaching.
The man unwilling to surrender his sin still wanted to hear the truth.
And suddenly this ancient scandal stops feeling ancient.
Because some of us know exactly what that feels like.
We listen to sermons.
We underline verses.
We save Christian posts.
We whisper “Amen.”
We feel conviction.
We may even love hearing about Jesus.
But there can still be one locked room in the heart where we quietly tell God:
“You can have everything except this.”
And that is where Herod’s story becomes terrifyingly personal.

Mark tells us that Herod Antipas had John arrested because of Herodias, whom Herod had married even though she had been his brother’s wife. John did not massage the truth to preserve access to the palace. He did not rename sin so influential people would continue inviting him into the room. He kept confronting Herod.
The Greek of Mark 6:18 is brutally direct:
“Οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι ἔχειν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου.”
Ouκ exestin soi echein tēn gynaika tou adelphou sou.
In straightforward English:
“It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”
There is no flattering introduction.
No political maneuvering.
No attempt to make rebellion against God sound respectable.

John was confronting a relationship that violated God’s revealed moral law concerning a brother’s wife, reflected in Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21. The levirate provision involving a deceased, childless brother in Deuteronomy 25:5 was a different circumstance and does not turn Herod’s situation into an exception. Mark presents John’s judgment without ambiguity: this union was unlawful.

There is also a historical detail worth handling carefully. Mark 6:17 identifies Herodias as the wife of Herod’s brother Philip. The Herodian family reused names extensively, and ancient sources can be confusing at this point. The Jewish historian Josephus describes Herodias as first married to another son of Herod the Great—often identified as Herod or Herod Philip—and then marrying his half-brother Herod Antipas while her first husband was still alive. Josephus separately identifies Philip the tetrarch as the man who later married Herodias’s daughter Salome. Whatever complexities surround the names, the central historical point agrees remarkably well with the Gospel account: Herodias left one Herodian brother and became the wife of his brother Antipas.
John called it what it was.
Sin.
And that word can make modern people uncomfortable.
Not because sin has disappeared.
Because we have become extraordinarily talented at renaming it.
Pride becomes “knowing my worth.”
Greed becomes “ambition.”
Lust becomes “following my heart.”
Bitterness becomes “protecting my peace.”
Compromise becomes “being realistic.”
Disobedience becomes “my personal journey.”
And sometimes we desperately want a Jesus who comforts our wounds while never confronting our rebellion.
But the real Jesus does both.
Grace does not merely hold you while you remain chained.
Grace comes to break the chains.
John understood that repentance was not cruelty. His entire ministry had been preparing people for Christ. He preached repentance because the King was coming.
John was not trying to win an argument with Herod.
He was sounding an alarm.
Turn around.
Come back.
Repent.
There is still time.
And perhaps that is what makes Herod’s response so heartbreaking.
Mark tells us Herod feared John because he knew John was righteous and holy. Herod protected him for a time. When John spoke, Herod was deeply perplexed—and yet he continued listening gladly.
Imagine that.
Convicted...
but not surrendered.
Disturbed...
but not repentant.
Interested in truth...
but unwilling to obey it.
That may be one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions a person can enter.
Not hatred of God.
Familiarity with God without surrender to God.
You can enjoy Christian content and still resist Christ.
You can admire courageous preaching and still protect the very sin the preaching exposes.
You can know the preacher is right...
and still walk away unchanged.
Herod listened.
Herod felt something.
Herod knew John was different.
Herod apparently recognized something holy in him.
But conviction continually resisted can become another missed invitation.
Then came the banquet.

Herod celebrated his birthday surrounded by officials, military commanders, and influential men of Galilee. The room represented everything human beings are tempted to worship: status, recognition, appetite, power, approval.
Herodias’s daughter danced.
Herod was pleased.
His guests were pleased.
And Herod made a reckless promise before the room.
Ask me for whatever you want.
She consulted her mother.
Herodias had apparently never forgotten the preacher who refused to bless what God condemned.
Her answer was chilling.
John the Baptist’s head.
The girl returned and demanded it immediately, on a platter.
Then Scripture gives us one of the saddest glimpses into Herod’s soul.
He was deeply distressed.
He did not want to do it.
But because of his oaths...
and because of the people watching him...
he ordered John killed.
Think about that.
A man with enormous political authority became a prisoner of the opinions in his own dining room.
Herod could command soldiers.
But apparently he could not command his need to save face.
He could imprison John.
But he could not free himself from pride.
He had enough power to execute a prophet...
but not enough courage to admit:
“I was wrong.”
How many lives have been wrecked by those three missing words?
I was wrong.
How many marriages could have begun healing?
How many addictions could have been exposed?
How many secret relationships could have ended?
How many families could have started rebuilding?
How many people could have run toward Christ?
But someone was watching.
Someone might laugh.
Someone might find out.
Someone might judge.
Someone might say, “After everything you said, now you’re changing?”
So we protect the image while the soul bleeds behind it.
Herod chose the room over righteousness.
And John lost his head.
Yet John was not the greatest tragedy in that banquet hall.
John died faithful.
Herod continued living compromised.
We instinctively think the man holding the sword has the power.
The Gospel teaches us to look deeper.
The truly free man was the one in chains.
John’s body could be imprisoned, but his conscience could not be purchased.
Herod sat at the head of a banquet surrounded by powerful people, yet he was enslaved to appetite, reputation, fear, and sin.
One man had a prison cell and freedom.
The other had a palace and chains.
And now the story turns toward us.
Because eventually every one of us encounters a sentence from God that we wish had not been written.
Forgive them.
Flee sexual immorality.
Love your enemies.
Tell the truth.
Do not covet.
Put away bitterness.
Care for the poor.
Deny yourself.
Take up your cross.
Follow Christ.
And somewhere between what God says and what we want, the real battle begins.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe you have learned how to smile while hiding it.
Maybe you know exactly which conversation you keep avoiding with God.
Maybe you have been saying:
“Lord, anything but that.”
Anything but forgiving him.
Anything but confessing this.
Anything but ending that relationship.
Anything but admitting the addiction.
Anything but surrendering the bitterness.
Anything but giving up control.
Anything but repentance.
Herod’s story whispers across two thousand years:
Do not confuse hearing truth with surrendering to truth.
But there is something Herod’s story cannot fully show us by itself.
Someone greater than John was coming.
John himself knew it.
His entire life pointed beyond himself.
John was the voice preparing the way.
Jesus Christ was the One coming down that road.
And this is where scandal meets grace.
Jesus did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
He came because we could not save ourselves.
He came for adulterers.
Liars.
Hypocrites.
The proud.
The sexually broken.
The religiously self-righteous.
The secretly addicted.
The ashamed.
The people whose public image and private reality are two different worlds.
People like us.
But Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel comfortable while remaining enslaved.
He came calling sinners to repentance and offering something no amount of self-repair could produce:
forgiveness.
A new heart.
Reconciliation with God.
Life.
At the cross, Jesus did something infinitely greater than simply exposing our scandal.
He bore sin.
The sinless Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The One who had no sin stood where guilty people deserved to stand.
And then the tomb was opened.
Christ rose.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
Shame did not have the final word.
Your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire story.
That is why biblical repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you home.
Repentance says:
I will stop defending what nailed Christ to the cross.
Grace says:
Come anyway.
Repentance says:
I have sinned.
Grace says:
There is forgiveness in Christ.
Repentance brings the darkness into the light.
Grace announces that Jesus already knew how dark it was when He called you.
Maybe this article did not bring another person to your mind.
Maybe it brought you to your mind.
Good.
Do not waste that moment.
You do not need to pretend with Jesus.
He already knows.
The affair.
The pornography.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The greed.
The jealousy.
The pride.
The double life.
The wound you have turned into an excuse to wound others.
The thing you keep deleting from your phone but not surrendering from your heart.
He knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Come.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Christ is greater than your sin.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
Come without negotiating which rooms of your heart Jesus is permitted to enter.
Bring Him the whole ruined house.
He specializes in resurrection.
And if you are reading this while thinking, “I have gone too far,” remember who Jesus welcomed.
Remember the thief beside Him.
Remember Peter after his denial.
Remember Saul after persecuting Christians.
Remember the sinners who discovered that encountering Christ did not mean their past suddenly became good.
It meant their past no longer had to be their master.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because truth changes with culture.
But because Jesus Christ still transforms sinners.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe your next chapter begins with something painfully simple:
“No more excuses, Jesus. I surrender.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But do not run from conviction.
Somebody reading silently may need to discover that failure does not have to be final when a sinner turns to Christ.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person who has been drifting.
The friend smiling publicly while falling apart privately.
The believer who loves Jesus but has become trapped in compromise.
The person who believes Christianity has nothing left to say to someone with a scandalous past.
Better yet, send this article to them personally and say, “Read this when you have a quiet moment.”
John refused to keep quiet because truth mattered.
Christ went to the cross because sinners mattered.
If Gospel-centered messages like this help you grow closer to Christ, sharing them is one practical way you can help put biblical truth in front of people who might never walk into a church today.
There may come a night when you need to read it again.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of generosity when done freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully for the glory of God.
Do not become Herod.
Do not merely enjoy hearing truth.
Obey the truth you have heard.
Do not protect the secret room.
Open it to Christ.
Do not trade obedience for the approval of people sitting around your table.
Do not wait until conviction becomes yesterday’s memory.
Repent while your heart can still hear the knock.
Run to Jesus while grace is being offered.
And when you discover that Christ can forgive what you thought could never be forgiven, tell somebody.
John lost his head rather than make peace with a lie.
Jesus gave His life to rescue people trapped inside lies.
And now the question is not merely what Herod did with John’s words.
The question is what you will do with Christ’s.
Because sometimes the most dangerous prison has no bars—it is the life we refuse to surrender to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE TOLD PETER TO FORGIVE “SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN”
paragraphs: WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT WHEN HE TOLD PETER TO FORGIVE “SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN”
Peter wanted to know when forgiveness could finally stop. Jesus answered with a number—but He was really exposing something buried much deeper in the human heart.
There is probably a name you do not like remembering.
Maybe you have forgiven them.
At least, you said you did.
But then somebody mentions their name.
Your chest tightens.
The conversation starts replaying.
The betrayal comes back in color.
The words return with their original sharpness.
And suddenly you realize something uncomfortable:
The event happened years ago...
but part of you is still standing in the room where they hurt you.
That is why one question Peter asked Jesus nearly two thousand years ago still feels painfully modern.
Peter came to Jesus and asked:
“Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Then Jesus answered him.
The Greek of Matthew 18:22 reads:
“Οὐ λέγω σοι ἕως ἑπτάκις, ἀλλὰ ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά.”
Ou legō soi heōs heptakis, alla heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta.
In straightforward terms:
“I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

Some translations render the final expression “seventy-seven times.” The Greek phrase, ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά — hebdomēkontakis hepta, has generated discussion over precisely which numerical rendering is best.
But do not miss Jesus while arguing over the arithmetic.
Whether you understand the expression as seventy-seven or seventy times seven, Jesus was not handing Peter a forgiveness calculator.
He was destroying the calculator.
Peter wanted a number.
Jesus confronted the heart that wanted to count.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes ours.
Because we count too.
We remember the first lie.
The second betrayal.
The third apology that changed nothing.
The fourth promise they broke.
We remember what they posted.
What they whispered.
What they stole.
What they did to the marriage.
What they did to the family.
What they did to our reputation.
What they did when nobody else was watching.
We count because counting gives pain a structure.
And sometimes keeping the record makes us feel safer.
“If I remember exactly what you did, maybe you will never have the opportunity to destroy me again.”
That feeling is understandable.
But Jesus was showing Peter that there is a difference between wisdom and vengeance, between remembering what happened and making someone’s debt the center of your life.
Peter’s question was essentially:
“Jesus, when have I forgiven enough?”
And Jesus’ answer was essentially:
“Peter, you still think forgiveness is something you measure.”
Then Jesus told a story.
And this is where the passage becomes devastating.
A king decided to settle accounts with his servants.
One servant was brought before him owing an enormous debt.
The amount Jesus names is ten thousand talents.
It is difficult to translate that ancient amount neatly into modern money, and perhaps that is precisely why we should resist reducing it to a sensational dollar figure.
The point is simpler and more frightening.
The debt was impossibly large for the servant to repay.
He was finished.
There was no clever financial plan coming.
No second job.
No hidden savings account.
No way out.
He fell before the king and pleaded for patience.
And then something happened he had no right to expect.
The master had compassion on him.
He released him.
And forgave the debt.
Imagine walking into a room carrying a debt you could never repay...
and walking out owing nothing.
That is grace.
But Jesus was not finished.
The forgiven servant walked outside and found another servant who owed him a comparatively tiny amount.
And suddenly the man who had just received mercy became merciless.
He grabbed the other servant.
He demanded payment.
The other man pleaded with language strikingly similar to the plea he himself had just made.
But he refused.
Think about that.
The hands that had just received mercy were now wrapped around somebody else’s throat.
And before condemning him too quickly, look carefully into the mirror.
How many times have we walked out of worship celebrating the forgiveness of God...
and then gone home refusing to forgive someone else?
We sing about grace.
We post verses about grace.
We thank Jesus for grace.
We tell people we are saved by grace.
But then somebody actually needs grace from us.
Suddenly...
we become accountants.
That is the scandal Jesus exposes.
The servant had forgotten the size of the debt from which he had been released.
And perhaps unforgiveness often grows in the same soil.
We remember what they owe us while slowly forgetting what Christ forgave in us.
That does not mean what happened to you was insignificant.
Christian forgiveness does not require calling evil good.
It does not mean abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean betrayal did not matter.
It does not mean justice suddenly becomes sinful.
It does not mean you must immediately restore trust to an unrepentant person.
It does not mean reconciliation can always happen instantly—or even safely.
Forgiveness and trust are not identical.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Reconciliation ordinarily involves more than one heart. Forgiveness is the refusal to make personal vengeance, hatred, and endless debt-collection the throne of your own heart.
Jesus never commands you to pretend darkness is light.
He commands something far more supernatural.
Bring the debt to God.
Release your personal claim to vengeance.
Refuse to let another person’s sin turn you into a prisoner of hatred.
And keep doing it when the memory returns.
Sometimes forgiveness happens in a moment.
Sometimes the decision happens in a moment and the emotional healing takes much longer.
You may forgive someone today and wake tomorrow with the wound screaming again.
That does not necessarily mean yesterday’s forgiveness was fake.
It may mean the wound still needs healing.
And perhaps “seventy times seven” becomes painfully real there.
Not merely forgiving seventy different offenses...
but bringing the same wound back to Jesus whenever bitterness tries to resurrect it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
“Jesus, I gave this to You yesterday.”
Give it to Him again.
“Jesus, I thought I had forgiven them.”
Bring the pain back again.
“Jesus, why does remembering still hurt?”
Tell Him the truth again.
Forgiveness is not pretending you no longer bleed.
Sometimes forgiveness means refusing to use the blood as ink to write the rest of your life.
And there may be an even deeper biblical echo behind Jesus’ words.
Long before Peter asked his question, Genesis recorded the chilling boast of Lamech.
Lamech spoke of vengeance multiplied far beyond Cain’s.
Genesis 4:24 speaks of vengeance “seventy-sevenfold” in common modern renderings.
Then generations later, Jesus speaks about forgiveness using strikingly similar numerical language.
The contrast is breathtaking.
Humanity says:
Multiply revenge.
Jesus says:
Multiply mercy.
Lamech represents the ancient instinct of fallen humanity:
“You hurt me, so I will hurt you worse.”
Jesus announces the kingdom:
“You have received mercy you could never purchase, so do not build your life around making others pay.”
That is not weakness.
Look at the cross before calling forgiveness weak.
Jesus was mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Nailed to wood.
And while human beings were committing an unspeakable injustice against Him, Luke records Him praying:
“Father, forgive them.”
The cross is where Christianity destroys our illusion that forgiveness means sin does not matter.
If sin did not matter, there would be no cross.
At Calvary we discover both realities simultaneously:
Sin is more serious than we wanted to believe.
Grace is more magnificent than we dared to imagine.
God did not save us by pretending our debt did not exist.
Christ bore sin.
Jesus entered our judgment.
The innocent Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And because of His death and resurrection, forgiveness is offered not as a reward for people who finally become respectable, but as grace received through repentance and faith in Christ.
This is why the Gospel is scandalous.
The adulterer can be forgiven.
The liar can be forgiven.
The addict can be forgiven.
The hypocrite can be forgiven.
The religious fraud can be forgiven.
The person carrying secret shame can be forgiven.
The person everybody else has written off can be forgiven.
Even you.
Even me.
Not because our sins were small.
Because Jesus is enough.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this has been avoiding for years.
You have been asking God to forgive you while secretly believing your particular sin sits outside the reach of the cross.
You know the verse.
You know the sermon.
You know the theology.
But when the lights go out and the room becomes quiet, shame whispers:
“Not you.”
Listen carefully.
That voice is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say your sin was nothing.
The Gospel says Christ is greater.
Repentance is not pretending you never fell.
Repentance turns from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace changes what the scandal gets to become.
Peter himself would eventually understand this in a way he probably could not have imagined when he asked about forgiveness.
This was Peter.
The outspoken disciple.
The man who promised loyalty.
The man who insisted that even if others fell away, he would remain.
And then came the courtyard.
Questions.
Fear.
Denial.
Once.
Twice.
Three times.
Then the rooster.
Imagine that sound.
Imagine realizing that the mouth which had confessed Jesus as the Christ had just denied knowing Him.
Peter did not merely witness somebody else’s scandal.
Peter became the scandal.
Yet Jesus was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him.
The failure was real.
The denial was real.
The tears were real.
But failure did not receive the final sentence.
Grace did.
That is our theme because that is the Gospel:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing the need for repentance.
But by taking repentant sinners whose stories looked finished and making their lives testimonies of redeeming grace.
Peter asked how many times he needed to forgive someone else.
One day Peter would discover how desperately he himself needed forgiveness.
Maybe that is why this passage refuses to leave us comfortable.
Because eventually every one of us occupies both sides of the story.
We have been wounded.
And we have wounded others.
We have been lied to.
And we have lied.
We have needed mercy.
And we have withheld mercy.
We have been the person crying because somebody broke our heart.
And somewhere in our history, somebody may have cried because of us.
The Gospel leaves no room for superiority at the foot of the cross.
There are only sinners who need a Savior.
So think about that name again.
The person you thought of at the beginning.
Maybe forgiving them feels impossible.
Do not confuse forgiveness with pretending nothing happened.
Bring what happened into the light.
Seek wise help when necessary.
Maintain appropriate boundaries where necessary.
Pursue justice through rightful means where necessary.
But do not surrender your soul to bitterness.
You have already given that person enough.
Do not give them your future too.
And perhaps the person you cannot forgive is yourself.
You keep replaying the worst thing you ever did as though endless self-punishment could somehow improve upon the sacrifice of Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Confess honestly.
Turn away from sin.
But if you belong to Christ, stop treating shame like a second savior.
Shame cannot atone for you.
Jesus already shed the blood.
There is only one Savior.
His name is Jesus Christ.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may need proof that healing does not require hatred.
And think of one person who needs this tonight.
Not somebody you want to attack with an article.
Somebody who is tired.
Somebody whose heart has become heavy from carrying what another person did.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when an old wound knocks again.
You may need to remember that forgiveness is not saying, “What happened did not matter.”
It is saying, “What happened will not become my master. Jesus is my Lord.”
It does not. The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is the gift of God in Christ.
But generosity can be one practical way believers choose to help truthful, Christ-centered teaching reach more people.
But before you leave...
remember Peter’s question.
“How many times?”
We still ask it.
How many times must I forgive?
How many times must I surrender this memory?
How many times must I refuse bitterness?
How many times must I bring this wound back to Jesus?
And Christ keeps pulling our eyes away from the calculator...
and toward the cross.
Because forgiven people were never meant to spend their lives counting everybody else’s debts.
Maybe tonight the miracle is not that you finally forget what happened.
Maybe the miracle begins when what happened finally stops owning you.
The wound may explain part of your story—but because of Jesus, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN COMMUNION SAVE YOU?
paragraphs:
CAN COMMUNION SAVE YOU?
You Can Eat the Bread, Drink the Cup, Sit in Church for Years—and Still Miss the Savior Standing at the Center of It All
There is something almost frightening about how easy Communion can become.
The music softens.
The room grows quiet.
Someone holds up the bread.
Someone lifts the cup.
You bow your head.
You take a piece.
You drink.
And for a few sacred seconds, everything feels holy.
Then you go home.
Back to the secret addiction.
Back to the unforgiveness.
Back to the relationship nobody knows about.
Back to the pride.
Back to the bitterness.
Back to the hidden messages.
Back to the pornography.
Back to the compromise.
Back to the prayerless Christianity that has learned how to look alive in public while slowly suffocating in private.
And somewhere along the way, a dangerous thought can creep into the heart:
“I took Communion. I’m okay with God.”
But are you?
That question may make some people uncomfortable.
It should.
Because the Lord’s Supper was never given to us as religious anesthesia—a ceremony that numbs our conscience while leaving our rebellion untouched.
And this is where we have to ask the question many Christians have wondered about but few want to confront:
Can Communion save you?
The answer begins in an upper room.
Jesus knows Judas will betray Him.
He knows Peter will deny Him.
He knows His disciples will scatter.
He knows soldiers will soon seize Him.
He knows a whip is coming.
Nails are coming.
Mockery is coming.
Blood is coming.
A cross is coming.
And in those final hours before His crucifixion, Jesus takes bread.
Luke preserves His words in Greek:
“Τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ σῶμά μου τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν διδόμενον· τοῦτο ποιεῖτε εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν.”
“This is My body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”
That final expression matters:
“εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἀνάμνησιν.”
In remembrance of Me.
Not remembrance of your religious performance.
Not remembrance of your denomination.
Not remembrance of how many times you have received Communion.
Not remembrance of how respectable you appear.
Jesus puts Himself at the center.
The bread points to Christ.
The cup points to Christ.
The table points to Christ.
The broken body points to Christ.
The poured-out blood points to Christ.
Communion without Christ at the center has missed the very One the meal proclaims.
And yet Scripture refuses to let us treat Communion casually.
Paul's warning to the Corinthian church is almost shocking in its severity.

He tells believers to examine themselves before eating the bread and drinking the cup. He warns against participating “ἀναξίως”—unworthily, or in an unworthy manner—and says that failure to discern the body brings judgment.
Think about that.
Paul does not say:
“It’s only bread. Relax.”
He does not say:
“It’s only symbolism. Nothing matters.”
He treats the Lord’s Table with trembling seriousness.

Some Christians therefore emphasize the sacramental means by which Christ gives grace to His people in Communion. Others emphasize Communion as the covenant meal Christ commanded His redeemed people to observe in remembrance and proclamation of His death. Christian traditions differ significantly over Christ’s presence in the Eucharist and over precisely how the Supper relates to saving grace.
Those disagreements should not be erased.
But neither should the thing standing underneath them all.
Jesus Christ saves.
The ceremony is never a substitute for the Savior.
You cannot hide from Jesus behind something Jesus Himself commanded.
Paul writes:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith…”
Then comes the crushing blow to human pride:
“οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν, θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον.”
It is not from yourselves.
It is God’s gift.
And then:
“οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων…”
Not from works.
That means salvation is not a trophy placed into the hands of people who performed enough Christian activities.
You cannot say:
“I attended church.”
“I was baptized.”
“I gave money.”
“I served.”
“I prayed.”
“I took Communion every week.”
Therefore, God owes me heaven.
No.
Grace destroys boasting.
The Gospel leaves every sinner standing empty-handed before the cross.
And maybe that is what some of us hate.
We would rather bring Jesus a résumé.
He asks us to bring Him our sin.
We would rather show Him our attendance.
He exposes our heart.
We would rather tell Him how religious we have been.
He asks whether we know Him.
There is a devastating difference between receiving Communion and receiving Christ.
A person can learn Christian vocabulary without loving Christ.
A person can sing worship songs while cherishing secret sin.
A person can know when to stand, sit, kneel, pray, raise hands, close eyes, say “Amen,” receive bread and drink from the cup—and still possess a heart that has never truly surrendered to Jesus.
Judas should terrify every religious hypocrite.
He was close enough to Jesus to hear sermons from the mouth of God incarnate.
He witnessed miracles.
He traveled with the disciples.
He participated in ministry.
People looking from the outside apparently did not immediately identify him as the betrayer.
He looked like he belonged.
But proximity to Jesus is not the same thing as belonging to Jesus.
You can stand near holy things while your heart is far from God.
And perhaps the most dangerous place spiritually is not the gutter.
Perhaps it is the pew where someone has learned to feel safe without ever being transformed.
Imagine standing before Christ one day and discovering that the religious things you trusted were never supposed to replace Him.
The bread could not become your excuse.
The cup could not become your hiding place.
Your church membership could not carry your guilt.
Your parents’ faith could not save you.
Your pastor could not repent for you.
Your Christian Facebook posts could not regenerate you.
Your theology could not bleed for you.
Your good works could not erase your rebellion.
Only Christ went to the cross.
Only Christ bore sin.
Only Christ rose from the grave.
Only Christ is Savior.
This is why Communion is so breathtaking when understood rightly.
The table does not invite us to congratulate ourselves.
It confronts us with our helplessness.
Look at the bread.
Someone's body had to be given.
Look at the cup.
Blood had to be poured out.
Why?
Because sin is not a minor personality flaw.
Sin separates.
Sin corrupts.
Sin condemns.
Sin cannot simply be shrugged away by a holy God.
The cross tells us something terrifying about our sin:
It required death.
But the same cross tells us something astonishing about God's mercy:
Jesus willingly came.
That is the scandal.
The innocent One takes the place of the guilty.
The righteous One suffers for sinners.
The King receives the punishment rebels deserve.
And people with histories they would rather erase are invited into grace.
The adulterer.
The addict.
The liar.
The hypocrite.
The bitter church member.
The sexually broken.
The proud.
The greedy.
The person who walked away from God.
The person who has secretly wondered whether God could possibly want them anymore.
This is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Jesus did not wait for sinners to become impressive before going to the cross.
He went because sinners could not rescue themselves.
Maybe you have been carrying something nobody knows.
Maybe Communion has become one of the most painful moments of your week because while everyone else seems peaceful, you know what you did.
You remember the relapse.
You remember the lie.
You remember the person you hurt.
You remember what you watched.
You remember what you said.
You remember the promise you made to God—and broke again.
So you stare at the bread thinking:
“Surely Jesus is tired of me.”
Listen carefully.
The answer to your sin is not pretending it does not exist.
And the answer is not casually eating bread while refusing repentance.
The answer is Christ.
Confess.
Come into the light.
Turn from the sin you have been defending.
Stop negotiating with the thing that is destroying you.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back for grace.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can rescue you.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
And when Christians come to the Lord’s Table, we come remembering that our hope has never been our ability to keep ourselves spotless.
Our hope is the spotless Lamb of God.
So can Communion save you?
Do not reduce the answer to a slogan.
Communion is holy.
Christ commanded it.
Christians should not despise it.
Paul's warning proves that participation in the Lord's Supper is spiritually serious, demanding self-examination and discernment rather than casual ritual.
But never turn the sacred meal into a replacement for the One it proclaims.
Bread is not a religious lucky charm.
The cup is not permission to live in rebellion until next Sunday.
Taking Communion cannot be used as leverage against God, as though performing a ceremony puts heaven in our debt.
Salvation belongs to God.
Grace comes from God.
Christ accomplished redemption.
Faith receives God's gift.
And authentic faith does not leave us contentedly embracing the sin from which Christ came to redeem us.
That changes the question.
Instead of merely asking:
“Did I take Communion?”
Ask:
“Do I belong to Jesus?”
Instead of:
“Did I eat the bread?”
Ask:
“Am I trusting the Christ whose body was given for sinners?”
Instead of:
“Did I drink from the cup?”
Ask:
“Have I surrendered the life He purchased at such terrible cost?”
Instead of:
“Did I complete the ritual?”
Ask:
“Is Jesus changing me?”
Because someday there will be no church building to hide inside.
No religious vocabulary.
No carefully managed reputation.
No denomination printed beside your name.
No comparison with someone worse than you.
There will be you...
and Christ.
And on that day, the greatest question will not be whether people thought you were Christian.
It will be whether your hope was truly in Jesus Christ.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is needed.
Ask mature believers for help where you keep falling.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to Christ.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when someone finally stops pretending everything is fine.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle nobody sees.
Not because an algorithm matters more than a soul, but because there may come a Sunday when you need to remember why the bread and cup matter.
Not as a religious badge.
Send it privately to the person who stopped attending church because shame convinced them they were no longer welcome near Jesus.
Let an unbelieving friend read it.
Let the lukewarm believer read it.
Let the exhausted Christian read it.
Let the person drowning in secret sin read it.
It does not.
It does not.
And certainly not because giving money earns salvation.
It never could.
Support Christian ministry because you freely want Gospel truth to travel farther—not because anyone has manipulated your conscience by suggesting that God can be purchased.
If glorifying God is your desire, one practical way you can participate in spreading biblical truth is to voluntarily support and share faithful Gospel ministry.
Do not miss the center.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
The bread points to Him.
The cup points to Him.
Scripture points to Him.
Grace comes through Him.
Forgiveness is found in Him.
The cross belongs to Him.
The empty tomb belongs to Him.
And salvation is not about becoming religious enough to make God tolerate you.
It is about sinners being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
So the next time the bread reaches your hands...
look at it.
Remember.
The body given.
The Savior crucified.
The debt you could never pay.
The mercy you could never earn.
Then look at the cup.
Remember the blood.
Remember the covenant.
Remember the cross.
Remember that Christianity is not the story of good people climbing their way toward God.
