We wanted forgiveness without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We wanted the benefits of His kingdom while remaining rulers of our own.
Yet Christ died for sinners.
He rose again.
And now He does something far greater than merely canceling punishment.
He makes people new.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God liberating you from the exhausting delusion that you were ever meant to be king.
You can finally get off the throne.
You can stop pretending.
Stop hiding.
Stop protecting the secret.
Stop negotiating.
Stop telling Jesus, “Everything is Yours... except this.”
Maybe your Abishag has a name.
Maybe nobody knows it.
Maybe it is not sexual sin at all.
Maybe it is approval.
Money.
Control.
Resentment.
Jealousy.
Status.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A wound you have turned into an identity.
A private addiction.
A public image.
A dream you would rather possess without God than surrender to God.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit has been touching that exact place while you have been reading.
Do not run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers that there is no road home.
The Gospel announces that the road home has a name.
Jesus.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
This is why the cross is simultaneously devastating and beautiful.
At Calvary, God does not tell us our sin was insignificant.
He shows us how serious it was.
And then He shows us how enormous His mercy is.
Your scandal does not have to write your final chapter.
Peter’s denial did not.
Paul’s persecution of Christians did not.
The Samaritan woman’s broken history did not.
The thief’s criminal past did not.
And if you come to Christ in repentance and faith, yours does not have to either.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is exactly why you encountered this article.
Not merely to learn why an ancient prince wanted an ancient woman.
But to discover what your own heart has been reaching for.
Adonijah’s story forces an uncomfortable question:
After mercy spared you, what did you reach for next?
Do not answer that publicly unless you should.
But answer it before God.
Be honest.
Because the most dangerous throne may not be sitting inside a palace.
It may be sitting inside the human heart.
And there is only one King worthy of it.
Jesus Christ.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores broken people.
Not because every sentence is equally important, but because there may come a night when the thing you surrendered starts calling your name again.
Send it to the believer who looks strong publicly but may be exhausted privately. Share it with the skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely about respectable people behaving better.
Show them the scandal.
Then show them the grace.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and financially supporting a ministry is never a condition for glorifying God.
We glorify God through Christ-centered faith, obedience, worship, generosity, love, and faithful stewardship.
Your support helps us keep producing Christ-centered teaching, Scripture-based encouragement, discipleship material, and resources designed to point people back to Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is still reaching for the very thing God rescued them from.
Maybe they need this story.
Maybe you did too.
And remember this:
The throne you finally surrender may become the place where grace finally begins rebuilding you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS ASKED FOR THE CUP TO PASS—THEN HE CHOSE THE CROSS
paragraphs:
JESUS ASKED FOR THE CUP TO PASS—THEN HE CHOSE THE CROSS
Gethsemane reveals something terrifyingly beautiful: Jesus did not walk toward Calvary because suffering was easy. He walked toward Calvary because saving sinners was the Father’s will—and He surrendered completely.
There is a prayer Jesus prayed that becomes almost unbearable when you understand what He knew was coming.
It was not spoken before a cheering crowd.
There were no multitudes pressing around Him for healing.
No children running toward Him.
No astonished disciples celebrating another miracle.
It was dark.
The hour was late.
And somewhere beneath the ancient olive trees of Gethsemane, Jesus Christ fell on His face before His Father.
Within hours, Judas would arrive.
The arrest would begin.
The disciples would scatter.
Peter would deny Him.
False witnesses would speak.
Soldiers would mock Him.
His body would be scourged.
Thorns would be pressed upon His head.
Nails would tear through flesh.
And eventually the sinless Son of God would hang upon a Roman cross.
Jesus knew.
That changes everything about what He prayed next.
Matthew records His words:
“Πάτερ μου, εἰ δυνατόν ἐστιν, παρελθάτω ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο· πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω ἀλλ’ ὡς σύ.”
Pater mou, ei dynaton estin, parelthatō ap’ emou to potērion touto; plēn ouch hōs egō thelō all’ hōs sy.
“My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.”
—Matthew 26:39
Read it again.
Slowly.
Jesus asked for the cup to pass.
And then came the words upon which the road to Calvary continued:
“Not as I will, but as You will.”
That is Gethsemane.
Not pretending the suffering was painless.
Not denying the horror ahead.
Not performing some emotionless version of spirituality in which obedience means you never tremble.
Jesus brought the agony into the presence of His Father...
and surrendered.
Mark gives us another detail so intimate that the Gospel preserves the Aramaic word Jesus used:
Ἀββᾶ — Abba.
“Abba, Father.”
The Greek text reads:
“Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ, πάντα δυνατά σοι· παρένεγκε τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ· ἀλλ’ οὐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω ἀλλὰ τί σύ.”
“Abba, Father, all things are possible for You. Take this cup away from Me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what You will.”
—Mark 14:36
Abba is Aramaic for “father.”
Do not reduce it to sentimental baby talk.
The beauty is already powerful enough without exaggerating it.
Jesus is speaking to His Father in intimacy, trust, and obedience while facing an anguish almost beyond our comprehension.
And perhaps someone reading this understands a tiny shadow of that kind of prayer.
Maybe you have prayed:
“Father, please don't let this happen.”
“Please save my marriage.”
“Please heal her.”
“Please bring him home.”
“Please don't let me lose this.”
“Please open this door.”
“Please make the diagnosis different.”
“Please take this pain away.”
“Please change their heart.”
“Please change my circumstances.”
And sometimes Christians become ashamed of prayers like that.
We imagine mature faith means never admitting what we desperately want.
Then Gethsemane destroys that illusion.
Jesus asked.
He expressed His desire honestly.
There was no unbelief in His honesty.
There was no rebellion in His anguish.
The sinless Christ prayed, in essence, “If it is possible, let this cup pass.”
But He did not stop there.
That is where surrender begins.
“Nevertheless...”
Perhaps that is one of the most costly words ever prayed.
Father, this is what I want...
nevertheless.
Father, this hurts...
nevertheless.
Father, I do not desire this suffering...
nevertheless.
Father, if there is another way...
nevertheless.
Not my will above Yours.
Not my comfort above Your purpose.
Not escape at the price of obedience.
Your will.
That does not mean Christians should call every tragedy “God's will,” refuse medical treatment, remain in abuse, or passively accept evil.
Biblical surrender is not fatalism.
It is entrusting ourselves to the wisdom and authority of God while obeying what He has revealed.
And no one embodied that obedience more perfectly than Jesus Christ.
There is another reason the word cup matters.

Throughout Scripture, a cup can symbolize what God appoints someone to receive, and in sobering passages it becomes imagery associated with divine judgment. Isaiah speaks of “the cup of His fury” and “the cup of trembling.” Jeremiah describes the nations receiving the wine cup of God's wrath. The prophets repeatedly use this frightening picture.
So when Jesus speaks of τὸ ποτήριον — to potērion — “the cup,” we should not reduce Gethsemane merely to fear of physical pain.
Crucifixion would indeed be horrific.
But the Gospel takes us deeper.
At the cross, Christ would accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Scripture says:
“He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.”
—2 Corinthians 5:21
Peter writes that Christ “bore our sins in His own body on the tree.”
Paul says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, “having become a curse for us.”
Isaiah, centuries before Calvary, spoke prophetically of the Servant who would be “wounded for our transgressions” and “bruised for our iniquities.”
This is why Gethsemane cannot be separated from the Gospel.
Jesus was not an unfortunate victim trapped by circumstances.
He had repeatedly told His disciples what was coming.
He knew Jerusalem awaited Him.
He knew betrayal awaited Him.
He knew the cross awaited Him.
And still He went.
The cup did not pass.
Jesus drank it.
The cup that did not pass from Christ is connected to the mercy offered to sinners like us.
The judgment our sins deserve.
The condemnation we could never remove.
The debt we could never repay.
Christ went willingly toward the cross.
Not because humanity was innocent.
Because humanity was guilty.
Not because we had finally become lovable enough.
Because God loved sinners who could never rescue themselves.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
We prefer religions where respectable people climb upward toward God.
The Gospel announces something completely different.
God came down for sinners.
For adulterers.
For liars.
For hypocrites.
For addicts.
For the religiously proud.
For the sexually broken.
For people carrying secrets nobody knows.
For churchgoers who know exactly how to raise their hands during worship while quietly losing their souls.
For the person reading this who has deleted messages so nobody would discover the truth.
For the person who keeps promising God, “This is the last time.”
For the woman smiling in photographs while crying when nobody is watching.
For the man everyone thinks is strong who is spiritually exhausted.
For the believer wondering whether God could possibly forgive what happened again last night.
Gethsemane whispers something before Calvary shouts it:
Jesus knew exactly what saving sinners would cost Him...and He kept walking.
That does not make sin small.
It makes grace astonishing.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
Look at Gethsemane.
Look at Calvary.
Sin matters so profoundly that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And yet sinners matter so profoundly to God that the Son willingly gave Himself.
That is why the Gospel never says, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Jesus calls sinners to repent.
To turn.
To believe.
To leave darkness.
To come into the light.
Grace does not give sin permission to keep destroying you.
Grace breaks sin's claim over the person who belongs to Christ.
Maybe that is why this story makes us uncomfortable.
We want Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Heaven without surrender.
Grace without transformation.
Resurrection without a cross.
We want Christianity to fit around the life we have already decided to live.
Then Jesus falls upon His face in Gethsemane and prays:
“Not what I will, but what You will.”
Suddenly the question becomes personal.
What have you refused to surrender?
Not your neighbor.
Not your spouse.
Not that politician.
Not the hypocrite at church.
You.
What is the thing you keep protecting from the lordship of Jesus?
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Him?
The pornography nobody knows about?
The bitterness you have rehearsed so long that it feels like part of your identity?
The secret conversation?
The pride?
The addiction?
The money?
The unforgiveness?
The need to control everything?
The version of Christianity where Jesus may advise you but never command you?
We often pray, “Lord, change my circumstances.”
Gethsemane teaches us to add:
“Lord, even when You do not change my circumstances the way I want, make my heart obedient to You.”
That prayer is frightening.
Because surrender costs something.
Jesus never disguised that.
“If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me.”
Christianity was never supposed to be Jesus decorating the life of our choosing.
It is death and resurrection.
The old life surrendered.
A new life received.
And maybe tonight your Gethsemane is not a garden.
Maybe it is your bedroom floor.
Your parked car.
A hospital corridor.
A divorce lawyer's office.
An unanswered message.
An empty chair at the table.
A bank account you are afraid to open.
A temptation you are exhausted from fighting.
A prayer you have prayed for five years without seeing the answer you wanted.
Listen carefully.
Gethsemane does not promise that every cup you ask God to remove will be removed.
It gives us something deeper.
It shows us a Savior who understands anguish.
A Savior who prayed through sorrow.
A Savior who obeyed through suffering.
A Savior who can be trusted when obedience hurts.
And the story did not end in the garden.
Nor did it end at the cross.
Friday came.
The nails came.
The darkness came.
The tomb came.
But Sunday came too.
Jesus Christ rose.
The One who surrendered Himself unto death defeated death.
The crucified Christ became the risen Christ.
And because He lives, repentance is not the funeral of hope.
It is the doorway into life.
Your scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
Your worst night does not have to become your identity.
Your failure does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not from scandal to pretending it never happened.
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to religious image management.
From scandal...
through repentance...
into grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you arrived at this article thinking about Christ's surrender.
Maybe somewhere along the way you realized God was confronting yours.
If something hidden has been exposed in your heart, don't hide behind another scroll.
Be honest.
Or simply tell your story. Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person still fighting to follow Jesus.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them they are not walking alone.
Save this too.
There may come a night when “not my will, but Yours” becomes the prayer you need more than anything else.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow as well. We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Not because anyone can purchase God's favor.
You cannot.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It never will.
Salvation is God's gift of grace in Jesus Christ.
But Christians may freely support Gospel ministry from gratitude and a desire to help truth reach others.
Come to Christ.
Not to a page.
Not to a brand.
Not merely to a Christian community.
To Jesus.
If you have been running, repent and come home.
If you have been hiding, step into His light.
If you have been trying to clean yourself up before approaching Him, stop trying to become your own savior.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentant faith finds a Savior greater than their sin.
Gethsemane began with a cup Jesus asked to pass.
It continued with surrender.
It led to a cross.
The cross led to a tomb.
And the tomb became empty.
So when your own obedience becomes costly, remember the Savior beneath the olive trees.
Remember His face toward the ground.
Remember His prayer.
Remember His surrender.
Remember that He stood up afterward and kept walking toward those who had come to arrest Him.
And remember why.
He was going to the cross.
For sinners.
For redemption.
For grace.
For the glory of His Father.
The cup did not pass from Jesus—but because He drank it, sinners who deserve judgment can receive mercy through Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING OFFERED DANIEL FOOD FROM HIS OWN TABLE. DANIEL QUIETLY REFUSED.
paragraphs: THE KING OFFERED DANIEL FOOD FROM HIS OWN TABLE. DANIEL QUIETLY REFUSED.
Daniel’s first great test in Babylon did not look like persecution. It looked like privilege. And that may be why his quiet refusal still exposes us thousands of years later.
The table must have looked incredible.
This was not prison food.
This was not the ration of a forgotten captive thrown scraps beneath Babylon’s towers.
Daniel had been given something far more dangerous.
A seat close enough to power to taste what the king himself provided.
Imagine being young, displaced from home, surrounded by the language of your conquerors, carrying memories of Jerusalem while Babylon slowly begins rebuilding your life in its own image.
Then someone places the king’s food in front of you.
Rich food.
Royal wine.
A privilege other captives might have dreamed about.
And nobody at the table seems to be screaming, “Deny your God.”
That is what makes this moment so unsettling.
Because some of the most dangerous tests of faith do not arrive looking like lions.
Sometimes they arrive on beautiful plates.

Daniel 1 tells us that Nebuchadnezzar ordered selected young men from Judah to be educated in Babylonian literature and language. They were assigned daily provisions from the king’s own food and wine and were to be trained for three years before entering royal service.
Babylon was not merely changing Daniel’s address.
It was surrounding him with a new world.
A new language.
A new education.
Even a new name.
Daniel became Belteshazzar.
Hananiah became Shadrach.
Mishael became Meshach.
Azariah became Abednego.
Then came the table.
And suddenly Scripture slows down.
“But Daniel…”
Those two words change everything.
The Hebrew of Daniel 1:8 reads:
“וַיָּשֶׂם דָּנִיֵּאל עַל־לִבּוֹ”
Wayyāśem Dāniyyēl ‘al-libbô.
Literally, the wording carries the sense that Daniel “set” or “placed” it “upon his heart.”
Then comes his determination:
“אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יִתְגָּאַל”
That he would not defile himself.
Daniel did not accidentally remain faithful.
Before the public victory came an invisible decision in the heart.
That may be the sentence somebody reading this desperately needs.
You keep asking God to help you stand when temptation arrives.
But perhaps there are some things you need to settle before temptation gets there.
Daniel settled something in his heart.
Not loudly.
Not theatrically.
Not with a speech designed to humiliate everyone eating around him.
He simply knew there was a line he could not cross.

And this matters because Scripture does not explicitly tell us exactly why the royal food and wine would have defiled Daniel. Faithful interpreters have discussed possibilities involving Israel’s food laws, associations with pagan worship, and the deeper implications of dependence upon the king’s provision.
We should not pretend Scripture says more than it says.
What Scripture unquestionably tells us is enough:
Daniel believed accepting these provisions would defile him before God.
So he refused.
Think about that.
Babylon could change what people called him.
It could determine what language he studied.
It could decide where he lived.
It could place him inside the machinery of an empire he never chose.
But Babylon could not make Daniel surrender the part of himself that belonged to God.
And suddenly this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because Babylon still has tables.
Maybe yours does not contain royal delicacies.
Maybe it is the relationship you know keeps pulling you farther from Christ.
Maybe it is the private browser history nobody sees.
Maybe it is the money that requires you to compromise your integrity.
Maybe it is bitterness you have justified for so long that it now feels like part of your personality.
Maybe it is applause.
Maybe it is ambition.
Maybe it is a secret conversation with someone who is not your spouse.
Maybe it is the need to be accepted.
Maybe it is the version of Christianity that lets you sing about Jesus publicly while negotiating with sin privately.
And perhaps the frightening part is that what is destroying you does not look disgusting anymore.
It looks normal.
Comfortable.
Deserved.
Everyone else is eating.
Why shouldn't you?
That is the question Babylon whispers.
And Daniel quietly answers:
Because I belong to Someone else.
Notice something else beautiful in the text.
Daniel was courageous without becoming arrogant.
Daniel 1:8 says he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself.
He did not confuse holiness with hostility.
He did not become obnoxious in the name of conviction.
He did not insult the official.
He did not throw the food across the room.
Conviction gave Daniel a backbone without taking away his humility.
That is a word desperately needed in an age where some Christians mistake cruelty for courage and others mistake compromise for kindness.
Biblical conviction needs neither.
You can be gentle and immovable.
Respectful and uncompromising.
Humble and holy.
Daniel was.
And then something happened that Daniel could not manufacture.
God moved.
Scripture says:
“וַיִּתֵּן הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת־דָּנִיֵּאל לְחֶסֶד וּלְרַחֲמִים”
God gave Daniel favor and compassion before the chief official.
Do not miss who gets the credit.
Daniel resolved.
God gave.
Daniel obeyed.
God acted.
This story is not a motivational speech about becoming mentally tougher than everybody else.
It is a testimony about faithfulness under the sovereign hand of God.
Daniel then proposed a ten-day test: vegetables—or more literally, food from things sown or grown—and water instead of the king’s provisions.
After ten days Daniel and his companions appeared healthier than those eating the royal food.
But please do not reduce Daniel 1 into a miracle diet.
The point is not that vegetables are spiritually superior to steak.
Daniel 1 is not selling a meal plan.
It is showing us something far greater:
There are moments when obedience to God will require you to refuse what everyone around you considers desirable.
And obedience may initially feel costly.
Daniel could not see the end of his story from verse 8.
He did not yet see himself interpreting dreams.
He did not see kings recognizing the wisdom God had given him.
He did not see the lions’ den.
He did not see generations of believers reading his story.
He simply saw a table.
A decision.
A line.
God.
And sometimes that is all you get.
You do not always receive a preview of what obedience will produce.
Sometimes God gives you only enough light for the next “no.”
No, I will not go back.
No, I will not sleep with them.
No, I will not lie to protect myself.
No, I will not secretly feed the addiction.
No, I will not sell my conscience for acceptance.
No, I will not pretend that what Christ calls sin has suddenly become harmless because culture applauds it.
No.
Not because I am better than anybody.
Not because I have never fallen.
But because Jesus Christ bought me with a price.
And here Daniel’s story begins pointing beyond Daniel.
Because if this article ends with “Be more disciplined like Daniel,” we have missed the deepest need of the human heart.
You and I are not Daniel.
We have eaten from tables we should have refused.
We have crossed lines after promising God we never would.
We have known what was right and still chosen what was easy.
We have hidden things.
Wanted things.
Watched things.
Said things.
Done things.
Some of us have become experts at appearing spiritually healthy while quietly starving inside.
And if salvation depended upon maintaining Daniel-level faithfulness every day of our lives, who among us could stand?
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
There came another faithful Man.
Jesus Christ.
Where we compromised, He remained obedient.
Where humanity repeatedly surrendered to temptation, Christ resisted.
In the wilderness, Satan tempted Jesus with bread, spectacle, power, and kingdoms.
Jesus would not bow.
He remained faithful to His Father all the way to the cross.
Yet the sinless Christ was treated as though He were the defiled one.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The spotless Lamb bearing the sins of guilty people.
Your pornography.
Your adultery.
Your pride.
Your lies.
Your hatred.
Your hypocrisy.
Your greed.
Your secret addiction.
Your religious performance.
Your years running from God.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him receives forgiveness and new life by grace.
That is why repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Repentance is turning.
Coming home.
Dropping the excuse.
Leaving the table.
Running toward Christ.
Maybe your greatest Daniel moment is happening right now.
Nobody else can see it.
There is no lion.
No furnace.
No crowd.
Just you.
Your screen.
Your conscience.
And something the Holy Spirit has been pressing on your heart for months.
You know the table.
You know what keeps appearing on it.
You know what you keep telling yourself will be “the last time.”
And perhaps you have failed so many times that another Christian article telling you to “be strong” almost makes you want to close the page.
Then hear this instead:
Run to Jesus.
Not after you become Daniel.
Now.
Come guilty.
Come ashamed.
Come tired.
Come with the relapse.
Come with the wreckage.
Come telling the truth.
Christ did not come for people who could save themselves.
Grace is for sinners.
And grace does not merely forgive the person you were.
Grace begins transforming the person you are becoming.
This is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Your scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Your failure does not have authority to write the ending.
Your worst night does not outrank the blood of Jesus.
Your past does not sit on the throne.
Christ does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why Daniel’s quiet decision is so powerful.
Great spiritual victories often begin where nobody applauds.
A teenager closing a website.
A husband confessing what he has hidden.
A woman finally leaving the relationship that keeps dragging her from God.
A businessman refusing dishonest money.
A believer deleting the number.
Someone kneeling beside a bed at 2:13 in the morning whispering, “Jesus, I cannot keep living like this.”
Nobody posts it.
Nobody claps.
Heaven sees.
Before Daniel ever stood before lions, he stood before lunch.
Do not despise the small battlefield.
The compromise you refuse today may be preparing you for a faithfulness you cannot yet imagine tomorrow.
And if you already ate what Babylon offered?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is still for you.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Christ restored him.
Paul participated in the persecution of Christians.
Christ transformed him.
The cross is crowded with evidence that God knows how to take scandal and write grace over it.
So do not turn Daniel into another weapon for condemning yourself.
Let Daniel expose your compromise.
Then let Jesus lead you out of it.
Repent.
Believe.
Get back up.
Walk again.
And when tomorrow's table appears, remember whose you are.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending.
Sometimes one honest sentence beneath an article becomes the moment another struggling believer realizes, “I am not the only one fighting this.”
Not to purchase God's favor.
Not to prove that you love God.
Not because giving money earns spiritual merit—it never does.
We support Gospel work because grace has already been freely given to us, and because we want biblical truth to keep reaching people who desperately need Christ.
If you are ready to support the mission and go deeper:
But before you leave this page, return one last time to that room in Babylon.
Look at the table.
Look at the young exile.
Everything around Daniel is telling him that Babylon owns his future.
His homeland has fallen.
His name has been changed.
His environment has changed.
His education has changed.
The king controls the menu.
But the king does not own Daniel’s heart.
Daniel has already placed something there.
A decision.
I belong to God.
Centuries later, the true King would call sinners to another table—not a table where compromise makes us unclean, but one reminding His people that our cleansing was purchased at terrible cost.
The body given.
The blood poured out.
The Savior crucified.
The Savior risen.
The King who does not seduce you away from God...
but brings you home to God.
So when Babylon offers you something beautiful in exchange for something holy, remember Daniel.
And when you fail to be Daniel, remember Jesus.
Because your hope was never that you would become flawless enough to rescue yourself.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Babylon may keep setting the table, but grace can teach your heart whom it belongs to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY THREW JEZEBEL FROM THE WINDOW—AND JEHU DROVE HIS HORSES OVER HER
paragraphs: THEY THREW JEZEBEL FROM THE WINDOW—AND JEHU DROVE HIS HORSES OVER HER

She painted her eyes. Fixed her hair. Looked down from the window as though she were still untouchable. But the most terrifying thing about Jezebel’s final moments was not the fall, the horses, or even the dogs. It was discovering that the God she had spent years defying had never forgotten a single drop of innocent blood.
There is something almost unbearable about the final scene of Jezebel’s life.
Not because Scripture tries to make it dramatic.
It doesn’t have to.
The woman who had once moved through royal corridors with power, influence, servants, political protection, and the authority of the throne heard that Jehu was coming to Jezreel.
And she knew what was happening.
The dynasty was collapsing.
Judgment had reached the palace.
Her son Joram was already dead.
Jehu was coming.
And Jezebel?
She painted her eyes.
She arranged her hair.
Then she went to the window.
That detail has haunted readers for centuries.
Because there is something painfully human about it.
When everything is collapsing...
we still try to control how we look.
When the marriage is dying, we post the smiling photograph.
When our faith has become hollow, we learn how to sound spiritual.
When secret sin is eating us alive, we become experts at appearing fine.
When our hearts are far from God, we can still walk into church carrying a Bible.
We know how to fix the outside while something inside us is bleeding.
Jezebel knew something about appearances too.
Second Kings 9:30 records that when she heard Jehu had arrived in Jezreel, she put paint around her eyes, arranged her hair, and looked through the window.
Then Jehu entered the gate.
Jezebel looked down at him and essentially compared him to Zimri—the notorious royal assassin whose coup ended disastrously.
It was defiance to the end.
She still had a voice.
Still had a window.
Still had the posture of royalty.
Still looked down upon the man approaching below.
But having a high window does not mean you occupy high ground before God.
Jehu lifted his face toward that window and cried:
“Who is on my side? Who?”
Two or three eunuchs looked down.
Then came the command.
Throw her down.
And they did.
The Hebrew of 2 Kings 9:33 refuses to soften what happened:
וַיֹּאמֶר שִׁמְטוּהָ וַיִּשְׁמְטוּהָ
Vayyomer shimṭūhā, vayyishmeṭūhā.
“He said, ‘Throw her down,’ and they threw her down.”
Then Scripture continues:
וַיִּז מִדָּמָהּ אֶל־הַקִּיר וְאֶל־הַסּוּסִים וַיִּרְמְסֶנָּה
Her blood splattered against the wall and against the horses...
וַיִּרְמְסֶנָּה — wayyirmesenna.
“And he trampled her.”
Jezebel fell from the window.
The horses went over her.
And suddenly the woman whose name had inspired fear throughout Israel was lying beneath the feet of animals.
But if we stop there, we will misunderstand the story.
This is not biblical permission to celebrate when somebody you dislike gets destroyed.
It is not a Christian revenge fantasy.
It is certainly not permission to start calling difficult women “Jezebels.”
And it is not a promise that everyone who hurts you will eventually be publicly humiliated.
Something much larger had been unfolding.
Long before Jezebel fell from that window, another person had fallen beneath the machinery of royal power.
His name was Naboth.
And he had something King Ahab wanted.
A vineyard.
Naboth refused to surrender his ancestral inheritance to the king.
Ahab went home angry.
Jezebel stepped in.
Letters were written in Ahab’s name.
A false accusation was arranged.
Naboth was condemned.
And an innocent man was killed.
Then Ahab went down to take possession of the vineyard.
Imagine that.
A dead man.
A stolen vineyard.
A palace moving forward as though nothing had happened.
Perhaps everyone powerful enough to matter had agreed to forget.
But God had not forgotten.
That may be one of the most frightening and comforting truths in the entire story.
God remembers what powerful people bury.
He remembers the person nobody defended.
He remembers the lie everyone believed.
He remembers the tears nobody saw.
He remembers the blood somebody thought position, money, influence, intimidation, or reputation could conceal.
Through Elijah, God pronounced judgment upon Ahab's house and upon Jezebel.
Years passed.
That is important.
Years.
Because divine patience can be mistaken for divine indifference.
We do the same thing.
Nothing happened today.
Nothing happened last month.
Nothing happened last year.
So perhaps God doesn't care.
Perhaps that hidden sin isn't serious.
Perhaps repentance can wait.
Perhaps we can keep manipulating people.
Keep feeding the addiction.
Keep carrying bitterness.
Keep cheating privately.
Keep pretending publicly.
Keep returning to pornography.
Keep destroying people with gossip.
Keep worshiping money.
Keep using religion to hide pride.
Keep saying, “God understands,” when what we actually mean is, “I don't intend to surrender this.”
And because lightning does not strike us immediately, we begin confusing God's patience with God's approval.
That is dangerous.
Scripture says God's kindness is intended to lead us toward repentance.
Patience is not permission.
Mercy is not endorsement.
The fact that judgment has not arrived does not mean God has changed His mind about sin.
Jezebel had years.
Then one afternoon she heard horses.
And here is where this ancient story stops being safely ancient.
Because there is a window in every human heart.
A place from which we keep looking down while God keeps calling us to bow.
Maybe yours is pride.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you love Jesus publicly but there is something privately you keep protecting from Him.
Maybe you are exhausted from maintaining two versions of yourself.
The Christian everyone sees...
and the person only God sees.
Maybe you have learned how to paint the eyes.
Fix the hair.
Smile for the photograph.
Raise the hands during worship.
Say the right words.
But underneath all of it, your soul knows.
Something is wrong.
And perhaps that is why Jezebel's final scene feels so disturbing.
Because outward composure cannot reconcile an inward rebellion.
Eventually Jehu entered the palace and ate and drank.
Afterward he ordered that Jezebel be buried because, despite everything, she was a king's daughter.
But when the servants went outside...
there was almost nothing left to bury.
The dogs had consumed her.
Only portions of her body remained.
And Jehu recognized what had happened.
The word God had spoken through Elijah had been fulfilled.
The palace had not cancelled it.
The crown had not cancelled it.
Time had not cancelled it.
Her confidence had not cancelled it.
God had spoken.
And His word stood.
But now we have to ask the question that changes everything.
If God is truly this holy...
what hope is there for us?
Because it is easy to read about Jezebel and whisper:
“Good.”
Until Scripture turns the mirror around.
You may never have arranged someone's execution.
Neither have I.
But Jesus takes us deeper than external respectability.
He exposes hatred beneath murder.
Lust beneath adultery.
Pride beneath religion.
Greed beneath success.
Self-righteousness beneath morality.
And suddenly the distance between “wicked people” and “people like us” becomes uncomfortable.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
Not Jezebel and everyone else.
All.
Me.
You.
The preacher.
The skeptic.
The addict.
The church member.
The person reading this while hiding something.
The person writing Christian captions while quietly losing the battle inside.
The person who has spent years running from God while telling everyone else that everything is fine.
That is why Christianity cannot merely be a story about bad people receiving judgment.
If that were the whole Gospel...
none of us would survive it.
The Gospel is that the Judge did something almost incomprehensible.
He came for the guilty.
Jesus Christ entered our world.
Perfect.
Holy.
Sinless.
The One person who never deserved judgment willingly walked toward a cross carrying the sins of people who did.
And notice the staggering reversal.
Jezebel was thrown down.
Jesus willingly laid His life down.
Jezebel's blood marked the wall.
Christ's blood was poured out for sinners.
Jezebel encountered the consequence of persistent rebellion.
Christ bore judgment He did not deserve so rebellious people could receive mercy they could never earn.
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation required the blood of the Son of God.
But grace is so astonishing that God gave His Son anyway.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because God pretends rebellion never happened.
Not because holiness disappears.
Not because justice ceases to matter.
But because at Calvary justice and mercy meet in Jesus Christ.
The Greek New Testament uses a breathtaking word when speaking about repentance:
μετάνοια — metanoia.
Repentance.
Not cosmetic improvement.
Not religious makeup.
Not arranging the hair while the kingdom inside is collapsing.
A changed mind that turns toward God.
A surrender.
A coming home.
And maybe somebody reading this has been decorating a window God is asking you to leave.
You don't need better makeup for your rebellion.
You need Jesus.
You don't need to become impressive enough for God.
You need mercy.
You don't need another month of pretending.
You need repentance.
You don't need to clean yourself enough to approach Christ.
Come filthy.
Come ashamed.
Come tired.
Come exposed.
Come with the addiction.
Come with the secret.
Come with the bitterness.
Come with the failure you swore you would never repeat.
Come with the years you wasted.
Come with the damage you caused.
Come with the tears.
Come with nothing left except:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Because the wonder of the Gospel is not that Jesus saves people who successfully repaired themselves.
He saves sinners.
And He does more than improve them.
He gives new life.
There were people in Scripture with catastrophic histories whom grace transformed.
Paul participated in the persecution of Christians.
Then Christ met him.
Peter denied Jesus.
Then Christ restored him.
The thief beside Jesus reached the final hours of a ruined life with nothing to offer but faith...
and discovered that even there, mercy was still available.
That does not mean everyone automatically receives salvation regardless of response.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Grace is free.
But grace is not cheap.
It cost Christ everything.
And when grace truly reaches us, it does not merely excuse the old life.
It begins transforming it.
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment your soul is tired of pretending.
Then stop running.
You don't know how many tomorrows you have.
Neither do I.
Jezebel's story reminds us that judgment is real.
The cross reminds us that mercy is available.
And the empty tomb announces that Jesus Christ is alive.
This is not about being frightened into performing religion.
It is about waking up before another year disappears behind a mask.
Repent.
Believe.
Confess your sin to God.
Trust Jesus Christ.
Ask Him to break what you have been unable to break.
Ask Him to expose what needs exposing.
Ask Him to heal what needs healing.
And then walk with Him.
Not perfectly.
Honestly.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a spiritual answer for anybody.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting their way back toward Jesus.
And please don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that their faith is collapsing.
Supporting Gospel Warrior should never replace giving faithfully, serving your local church, caring for your family, helping the poor, or obeying Christ.
They are helping support the work.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the person struggling secretly.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the friend who does not yet believe.
Not so Gospel Warrior becomes famous.
So Jesus becomes impossible to ignore.
Because eventually every one of us discovers that appearances cannot save us.
Jezebel painted her eyes while judgment approached.
We paint our lives in different ways.
Success.
Religion.
Money.
Humor.
Busyness.
Relationships.
Church attendance.
Social media.
Anything that keeps us from looking directly at the condition of our souls.
But Jesus did not die to make your mask prettier.
He died and rose again to make you new.
So come down from the window willingly.
Lay down the pride.
Confess the sin.
Stop negotiating with the thing that is killing you.
Run toward the Savior whose hands still bear the testimony of how far love was willing to go to rescue sinners.
And remember this when everything else in this article fades:
You do not have to wait until your kingdom collapses to surrender your crown to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS SAY, “PEACE BE WITH YOU” AFTER APPEARING?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS SAY, “PEACE BE WITH YOU” AFTER APPEARING?
The first words the risen Christ spoke to frightened disciples were not “Where were you?” They were words that revealed what the Cross had accomplished.
Imagine being in that room.
The door is locked.
Not because the disciples are having a private worship service.
They are afraid.
Jesus has been crucified. Their Teacher has been publicly humiliated, tortured, and killed. The movement they thought would change everything appears to have collapsed in a matter of hours.
And they know something else.
When Jesus was arrested, they ran.
Peter had insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he never would.
Then the rooster crowed.
Three times Peter had denied even knowing Him.
Now Jesus is dead—or so they had thought—and the disciples are hiding behind locked doors.
Then something happens that changes human history.
Jesus stands among them.
Alive.
Try not to rush past this moment because you already know the ending.
Imagine you were Peter.
Imagine the last meaningful memory you carried of Jesus was the memory of failing Him.
Imagine looking into the face of the Man you abandoned and realizing that the grave could not hold Him.
What would you expect Him to say?
“Where were you?”
“Why did you leave Me?”
“Peter, I warned you.”
“You said you would die with Me.”
Maybe that is what some of us expect God to say when He finally reaches the rooms where we have been hiding.
We know what we did.
We know what nobody else knows.
We remember the prayer we stopped praying.
The temptation we entertained.
The compromise we justified.
The person we wounded.
The secret we buried.
The promise to God we broke.
The version of ourselves everybody sees—and the version only God sees.
So when Jesus walks into the locked room, something inside us expects judgment to be the first sound out of His mouth.
But John records something astonishing.
“Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.”
Eirēnē hymin.
“Peace to you.”

That is the Greek wording preserved in John 20:19: Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν. The noun eirēnē means peace, while hymin means “to you” or “for you.” The wording is therefore naturally rendered, “Peace be with you” or “Peace to you.”
But do not reduce this to Jesus simply saying hello.
Yes, peace was part of the world of Jewish greeting and blessing. But John has carefully prepared us to hear far more in these words.
Before the Cross, Jesus had already told His disciples:
“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” — John 14:27
And later:
“I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace.” — John 16:33
Then comes the Cross.
Then the tomb.
Then resurrection morning.
Then frightened disciples behind locked doors.
And the risen Jesus stands among them and says:
Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
Peace to you.
In other words, the peace He promised before Calvary is now spoken by the One who has passed through Calvary and conquered death.
And then Jesus does something that makes the moment even more powerful.
He shows them His wounds.
John places these events together: Jesus says, “Peace to you,” and then shows them His hands and His side. The disciples respond with joy when they recognize the Lord.
Think about that.
Jesus does not announce peace while hiding the scars.
He announces peace and shows them the wounds.
Because Christian peace is not pretending the wound never happened.
Christian peace comes through what Christ accomplished in His suffering, death, and resurrection.
The scars did not disappear when Jesus rose.
But their meaning had changed forever.
They were no longer evidence that death had defeated Him.
They had become the marks carried by the victorious Lamb.
And maybe somebody reading this has scars too.
Some are visible.
Most are not.
A childhood you rarely discuss.
A marriage that shattered.
A betrayal you still replay.
A child you worry about when everyone else is sleeping.
A sin you desperately wish you could undo.
Years wasted running from God.
An addiction nobody knows you are fighting.
A Bible collecting dust while your soul quietly starves.
A smile you have perfected so well that people think you are strong.
You have learned how to walk into church and say, “I’m blessed.”
You have learned how to post the photograph.
Answer the message.
Go to work.
Serve everyone.
Laugh at the right moment.
Then night comes.
The door closes.
And suddenly you are back inside that locked room.
But here is the Gospel:
Locked doors did not keep Jesus away from His frightened disciples.
John explicitly tells us that the doors were shut because the disciples were afraid, yet Jesus came and stood among them.
And perhaps the locked door is exactly where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because human beings still lock doors.
We just became better at hiding the locks.
Pride can be a lock.
Shame can be a lock.
Religion without repentance can be a lock.
Pornography can be a lock.
Bitterness can be a lock.
Success can be a lock.
Church activity can even become a lock when we use ministry to avoid confronting what is happening inside our own hearts.
We hide behind “I’m fine.”
We hide behind “God understands.”
We hide behind “Everybody does it.”
We hide behind “At least I’m not as bad as them.”
But the risen Christ does not merely come to make frightened sinners comfortable in locked rooms.
He comes bringing peace that cost Him blood.
This is where we must understand what biblical peace actually means.
Peace with God is not God deciding sin was never serious.
The Cross tells us precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God cannot be achieved by positive thinking, religious performance, moral comparison, or self-improvement.
Scripture says Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Paul says that because we have been justified by faith, “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1).
And Colossians describes Christ as making peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).
There is the heart of it.
The peace spoken in that locked room stands on the other side of a bloodstained Cross.
Jesus can stand before guilty, frightened, failed disciples and speak peace because He has accomplished what they could never accomplish for themselves.
He does not call evil good.
He bears sin.
He does not pretend rebellion does not matter.
He provides reconciliation.
He does not tell sinners to save themselves.
He saves.
This is grace.
And grace is far more scandalous than sentimental Christianity makes it sound.
Grace means Peter's failure was real...
but it would not have the final word.
Grace means the disciples really did run...
but Jesus came looking for them.
Grace means the Cross exposes the horror of sin while simultaneously revealing the staggering love of God.
Grace does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your sin mattered so much that Christ died—and His mercy is greater than everything you bring to Him in repentance and faith.”
That is why the Gospel is not a story about good people earning their way to God.
It is the announcement that God acted in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But the story becomes even more astonishing.
Jesus says it again.
“Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.”
“Peace to you.”
Then:
“καθὼς ἀπέσταλκέν με ὁ πατήρ, κἀγὼ πέμπω ὑμᾶς.”
“As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.”
The Greek text of John places Christ's repeated declaration of peace immediately alongside His sending of the disciples.
Do you see the movement?
Fear.
Jesus.
Peace.
Wounds.
Joy.
Peace again.
Mission.
The men hiding from the world are about to be sent into it.
The frightened become witnesses.
The scattered become sent.
The ashamed receive a mission.
Jesus does not merely restore their emotional stability.
He gives their lives direction.
That means resurrection peace is not permission to hide forever.
Jesus brings peace into the room...
and then sends His people out of it.
Some of us want the first “Peace be with you” without hearing what follows the second.
We want Jesus to calm us.
Heal us.
Forgive us.
Restore us.
Comfort us.
And He does.
But then He says, in effect:
Now go.
Tell them.
The Gospel was never meant to terminate with us.
Grace received becomes grace proclaimed.
Forgiven people become witnesses to forgiveness.
Those who have encountered the risen Christ carry the news of the risen Christ.
That is why sharing the Gospel matters.
Not because clicking “share” earns God's favor.
It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
But when grace has genuinely gripped your heart, you begin wanting somebody else to hear what rescued you.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list is sitting behind a locked emotional door tonight.
Maybe the friend who constantly jokes is quietly falling apart.
Maybe the relative who stopped going to church believes God would never take them back.
Maybe somebody who follows you is one night away from giving up on their faith.
Maybe an unbelieving friend has never actually heard Christianity explained as something more than “try to become a better person.”
Sharing one Christ-centered article cannot save anyone.
Jesus saves.
But God can use a shared testimony, a Scripture passage, a conversation, an invitation, or an article to put truth in front of someone who desperately needs to hear it.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to purchase a blessing.
Not to prove that you are a “real Christian.”
Jesus Christ still enters rooms filled with fear.
Send this to the believer who thinks their failure disqualified them forever.
Send it to the prodigal.
Send it to the skeptic willing to listen.
Send it to the Christian who is exhausted from pretending.
Because eventually, most of us find ourselves behind another locked door.
And when that day comes, you may need to remember what Jesus said when He entered the first one.
Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
Peace to you.
Maybe you need to become honest before God right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become more spiritual.
Now.
If you have been hiding something, you do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
Somebody reading your words may discover that they are not the only person who has cried behind a locked door.
This is what Christian community should look like.
Not perfect people performing perfection.
Redeemed sinners pointing one another toward a perfect Savior.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus paid the price.
Your response to that Gospel is repentance and faith in Him.
And perhaps that is why His first words in that room remain so breathtaking.
The disciples had failed Him.
Yet He came.
They were afraid.
Yet He came.
The doors were locked.
Yet He came.
They had nothing with which to impress Him.
Yet He came.
And He stood among them carrying wounds that testified both to the terrible cost of sin and the immeasurable depth of His love.
Then He spoke:
Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν.
Peace to you.
Maybe you thought peace would come when your circumstances finally changed.
When the anxiety disappeared.
When the family healed.
When the money arrived.
When the temptation vanished.
When everybody apologized.
When you finally forgave yourself.
But the disciples discovered something better.
Peace entered the room because Jesus entered the room.
The risen Christ Himself was their peace.
And the deepest Christian hope is not that Jesus promises us a life without wounds.
It is that the One who still bore His wounds walked out of His grave.
Your scars are not your Savior.
Your shame is not your master.
Your failure does not get to sit on the throne.
Death itself does not get the last sentence.
Jesus Christ does.
So unlock what you have been hiding.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent where you need to repent.
Receive the mercy Christ offers.
Return if you have wandered.
And when His grace has found you again, do not keep the news trapped behind a locked door.
And comment.
Tell us what Christ is healing.
Tell us what you are surrendering.
Tell us where you need prayer.
Because somebody else may be hiding in the same darkness you survived.
The disciples thought the locked room was where their story was ending.
Jesus walked in and turned it into the room from which they would be sent.
Never mistake the room where fear locked you in for the place where Jesus intends to leave you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY JESUS SEPARATES THE SHEEP FROM THE GOATS
paragraphs: THE DAY JESUS SEPARATES THE SHEEP FROM THE GOATS

Jesus described a final separation where religious appearance would no longer matter—and what He revealed about the sheep and the goats should make every Christian examine what grace has actually produced in their life.
There is a sentence you never want to hear from Jesus.
Not because it is shouted.
Not because it is cruel.
But because when He says it, every excuse is already dead.

Every reputation has become irrelevant. Every carefully maintained Christian appearance has lost its power. The church attendance, the Bible verses posted online, the worship songs played in the car, the Christian shirts, the arguments we won about theology, the people who thought we were spiritual…
None of those things can hide the heart anymore.
Jesus described such a day.
A day when the Son of Man comes in glory.
A day when the nations stand before Him.
A day when humanity is separated.
Sheep on one side.
Goats on the other.
Because the difference becomes visible in something painfully ordinary.
A hungry person.
A thirsty person.
A stranger.
Someone without enough clothing.
Someone sick.
Someone imprisoned.
Someone the world could easily overlook.
And Jesus says:
You met Me there.
Or…
You walked past Me.
That is the terrifying beauty of Matthew 25:31–46.
Jesus begins:
“Ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐν τῇ δόξῃ αὐτοῦ…”
Hotan de elthē ho huios tou anthrōpou en tē doxē autou…
“When the Son of Man comes in His glory…”
Matthew 25:31.
Notice who stands at the center of this scene.
Jesus Christ.
This passage is not ultimately a motivational speech about becoming nicer people.
It is about the King.
The returning Christ.
The Judge before whom every human life will finally be exposed.
Jesus continues that He will separate people from one another “as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.”
The Greek verb translated “separate” is ἀφορίζει — aphorizei, carrying the idea of separating, distinguishing, or setting apart.
The Shepherd knows the difference.
Humans can be fooled.
Congregations can be fooled.
Families can be fooled.
Social media can certainly be fooled.
Jesus cannot.
And perhaps the most sobering detail is that neither group appears to understand fully what their ordinary actions revealed.
The sheep ask:
“Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You, or thirsty and give You drink?”
They were not apparently keeping a spiritual scoreboard.
They were not feeding someone while whispering, “This should earn me heaven.”
They loved because something had happened inside them.
Then comes one of the most extraordinary statements Jesus ever made:
“Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν…”
Amēn legō hymin…
“Truly I say to you…”
“ἐφ’ ὅσον ἐποιήσατε ἑνὶ τούτων τῶν ἀδελφῶν μου τῶν ἐλαχίστων, ἐμοὶ ἐποιήσατε.”
“Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these My brothers, you did it to Me.”
Matthew 25:40.
The word translated “least” is ἐλαχίστων — elachistōn.
The insignificant.
The seemingly unimportant.
The easily forgotten.
And this is where Scripture refuses to let us remain comfortable.
Because Christianity can become strangely convenient when Jesus exists only inside church buildings.
We sing to Him there.
We praise Him there.
We lift our hands there.
We tell Him we love Him there.
Then Monday comes.
And someone becomes inconvenient.
Someone needs patience.
Someone cannot repay us.
Someone smells bad.
Someone has failed again.
Someone is lonely.
Someone needs food.
Someone needs forgiveness.
Someone needs to be heard.
Someone interrupts our schedule.
Someone has nothing to offer our reputation.
And suddenly love becomes expensive.
That is often where our theology walks out of the Bible and enters real life.
Maybe the person you struggle to notice is sitting at your own dinner table.
Maybe your spouse has been emotionally starving while everyone at church thinks your marriage is beautiful.
Maybe your child stopped telling you what hurts because every conversation became a lecture.
Maybe your aging parent keeps saying, “I’m fine,” because they hate feeling like a burden.
Maybe there is someone at church who stands alone after the service while everybody gravitates toward people they already know.
Maybe you know someone drowning financially and you keep saying, “I’ll pray for you,” even though God has given you enough to help.
Maybe someone wounded you years ago and you have secretly enjoyed watching their life fall apart.
Maybe the stranger is not across an ocean.
Maybe the stranger lives three houses away.
And maybe one of the hardest questions in Christianity is not merely:
“Do I believe in Jesus?”
But:
What has believing in Jesus done to the way I see people?
We must be very careful here.
Matthew 25 does not teach that sinners purchase salvation by accumulating charitable deeds.
The Gospel will not allow that interpretation.
Scripture says:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works…”
Ephesians 2:8–9.
But many people stop reading there.
The next verse says:
“For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works…”
Ephesians 2:10.
Grace is the root.
Good works are fruit.
We are not saved because we fed enough hungry people.
We feed hungry people because Christ has begun transforming the heart that once lived primarily for itself.
We do not earn the Father's love by loving others.
We learn to love because we have encountered the God who loved us when we had nothing with which to repay Him.
This is why James could say that faith without works is dead.
This is why John could ask how God's love can abide in someone who possesses material goods, sees a brother in need, and closes his heart against him.
And this is why Jesus said:
“By this all people will know that you are My disciples, if you have love for one another.”
Real grace leaves fingerprints.
Not perfect fingerprints.
Not sinless fingerprints.
But evidence.
A heart invaded by Christ slowly becomes incapable of remaining completely indifferent to suffering.
And that should confront us.
Because there is another group in Jesus' story.
The goats.
Jesus tells them:
“I was hungry and you gave Me no food, I was thirsty and you gave Me no drink, I was a stranger and you did not welcome Me…”
Then they ask essentially the same question.
When?
When did we ever see You like that?
If Jesus had physically appeared hungry at their doorway, perhaps they imagine they would have responded differently.
If the person asking for food had arrived glowing with heavenly glory…
Of course.
If the stranger had introduced Himself as the King of kings…
Come inside.
If Christ Himself had been lying in the hospital bed…
We would visit.
But that is precisely what makes the passage cut so deeply.
Jesus identifies Himself astonishingly closely with “the least of these.”
The test arrived disguised as inconvenience.
The opportunity wore ordinary clothes.
There was no trumpet.
No angel.
No spotlight.
Just somebody who needed mercy.
And they missed Him.
That should haunt comfortable Christianity.
We can become experts at loving humanity in theory while avoiding humans in practice.
We love “the poor.”
Until one asks something from us.
We love “broken people.”
Until their brokenness becomes exhausting.
We love “sinners.”
Until their particular sin disgusts us.
We love “the lost.”
Until they disagree with us.
We love “community.”
Until somebody needs us at an inconvenient hour.
We love “forgiveness.”
Until we are the one required to forgive.
Then suddenly the cross becomes decorative instead of transformational.
But look at Jesus.
Before we ever congratulate ourselves for helping “the least,” remember where Christ found us.
Spiritually hungry.
Thirsty.
Alienated.
Exposed.
Sick with sin.
Enslaved.
Unable to rescue ourselves.
And He did not walk past us.
The eternal Son of God entered our world.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable religion despised.
He welcomed children others considered interruptions.
He saw blind beggars whom crowds tried to silence.
He spoke with the Samaritan woman carrying the wreckage of her history.
He defended the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called sinners to repentance.
And then He went farther than charity could ever go.
He went to the cross.
Jesus did not merely give us bread.
He gave Himself.
He did not merely visit prisoners.
He came to liberate slaves to sin.
He did not merely cover nakedness.
He bore shame publicly.
He did not merely comfort dying people.
He entered death and conquered it.
At Calvary, the scandal of human sin collided with the grace of God.
The innocent Christ was crucified among criminals.
The righteous One bore sin.
The rejected Messiah became the refuge of the guilty.
And three days later, the tomb could not keep Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not “be kind enough and maybe God will accept you.”
The Gospel says:
You could never make yourself righteous enough, so Christ came to save sinners.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Jesus.
Receive mercy you could never purchase.
And then let that mercy destroy the selfishness that once ruled you.
Because people who have been forgiven much begin learning how to love much.
Perhaps this article is exposing something uncomfortable in you.
Good.
Do not run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
Maybe you have become spiritually cold.
Maybe you have been using Christianity to judge people instead of loving them.
Maybe you give generously when people can see it but become strangely unavailable when nobody will know.
Maybe you know Scripture better than you obey it.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to use you while repeatedly walking past the people He placed directly in front of you.
There is grace even here.
Peter failed spectacularly.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a scandalous history.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer.
Christ specializes in meeting sinners where their stories look ruined.
But grace never says, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Grace says:
“Come.”
Then grace begins rewriting everything.
That is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a turning involving a changed mind and direction.
You stop defending what Christ is confronting.
You stop hiding.
You stop pretending.
You bring the truth into His light.
And perhaps your repentance tonight begins with a name.
Someone you ignored.
Someone you refused to forgive.
Someone whose suffering you minimized.
Someone you could help.
Someone you have treated as an interruption rather than a person bearing God's image.
Do not merely feel emotional while reading this.
Ask Jesus what obedience looks like when you close Facebook.
Maybe it means making a phone call.
Buying groceries.
Visiting someone.
Listening without trying to fix everything.
Giving quietly.
Welcoming somebody.
Apologizing.
Forgiving.
Showing mercy.
Sitting beside someone everybody else avoids.
Or simply looking into another human being's eyes long enough to remember:
This person matters to God.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still transforms human hearts.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” proves someone is a Christian. It does not.
Because Matthew 25 is not merely something to read once.
It is something worth returning to whenever Christianity starts becoming comfortable enough to require nothing from us.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be confused with purchasing God's favor. Salvation cannot be bought. God is not indebted to anyone because they financially support Christian work.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, one biblical way to do that is to willingly support Gospel-centered work you believe is faithfully helping people encounter Christ—and then help that truth travel farther by sharing it with others.
Jesus is coming again.
The Shepherd knows His sheep.
And the Gospel does not merely change where we expect to spend eternity.
It changes what we do with the hungry person standing in front of us today.
One day every mask will fall.
Every platform will disappear.
Every title will become irrelevant.
Every bank account will belong to someone else.
Every applause will become silent.
And we will stand before Jesus.
Until then, there are people around us who are hungry.
Thirsty.
Lonely.
Rejected.
Sick.
Imprisoned.
Forgotten.
And somewhere inside the ordinary inconvenience of loving them, Jesus is teaching His people what His own heart looks like.
So when you encounter someone the world considers “the least,” remember this:
You may forget the face of the person you walked past—but Jesus never forgets the love you gave, or the mercy you withheld.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TORAH EVEN ADDRESSED SEX WITH A WIFE’S SISTER
paragraphs:
THE TORAH EVEN ADDRESSED SEX WITH A WIFE’S SISTER
You may open Leviticus 18 expecting an ancient list of forbidden relationships. But buried inside it is a command about two sisters, one husband, sexual intimacy, rivalry, and the kind of human devastation God refused to treat as insignificant.
There are verses in the Bible people hurry past.
Not because they are boring.
Because they are uncomfortable.
Leviticus 18 is one of those chapters.
Read it slowly and the comfortable distance between “ancient sinners” and modern human beings begins to disappear.
God speaks about incestuous relationships. Adultery. Sexual boundaries. Family relationships. Exploitation. Defilement.
Then comes a prohibition so specific that a modern reader might stop and ask:
Why did God even have to say that?
The Hebrew of Leviticus 18:18 reads:
וְאִשָּׁה אֶל־אֲחֹתָהּ לֹא תִקָּח לִצְרֹר לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ עָלֶיהָ בְּחַיֶּיהָ
Ve’ishah el-achotah lo tiqqach litzror legalot ervatah aleha bechayyeha.
A careful sense of the verse is:
You shall not take a woman in addition to her sister, making her a rival, to uncover her nakedness while her sister is alive.
That matters.
The Torah is not merely tossing out a bizarre sexual rule.
It is entering a household.
A marriage.
A bedroom.
A relationship between sisters.
And it is drawing a boundary around something capable of turning intimacy into rivalry and family into anguish.
The word לִצְרֹר — litzror carries the idea of creating hostility, rivalry, or distress.
And לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ — legalot ervatah, literally “to uncover her nakedness,” belongs to the sexual language running throughout Leviticus 18.
So the verse is considerably more specific than the sensational statement, “The Torah talked about sleeping with your wife’s sister.”
It did.
But context matters.
Leviticus 18:18 prohibits taking a woman’s sister as a rival wife and entering that sexual union while the first sister is still alive.
And suddenly an old story begins echoing in the background.
Rachel.
Leah.
Jacob.
Two sisters.
One husband.
And years of aching rivalry.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Leah knew she was not loved as Rachel was.
Children became entangled with longing.
Pregnancy became entangled with competition.
A family became a battlefield for affection.
You can almost hear one sister silently asking:
Am I enough now?
And the other wondering:
Why does she have what I cannot have?
This is where Leviticus stops feeling like an archaeological artifact.
Because perhaps you have never married two sisters.
But you know what comparison feels like.
You know what jealousy feels like.
You know what it means to look at somebody else and quietly wonder why they received what you desperately wanted.
Maybe you know what betrayal feels like.
Maybe you know what it is like when somebody who promised faithfulness made you feel replaceable.
Maybe the wound happened inside a marriage.
Maybe inside your family.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you learned to smile while bleeding.
And perhaps this is why passages like Leviticus 18 deserve something better than mockery.
Behind God's boundaries are real human beings.
Real bodies.
Real marriages.
Real families.
Real consequences.

God's commands concerning sexuality were never permission for Israel to imitate whatever surrounded them. At the beginning of the chapter, God tells Israel not to pattern itself after Egypt or Canaan.
Then comes the repeated declaration:
“I am the LORD.”
That is the center.
Not:
Do whatever feels right.
Not:
Whatever culture normalizes must therefore be holy.
Not even:
Follow these rules so God will finally love you.
The foundation is the identity and authority of God.
“I am the LORD your God.”
Before Israel gets to define holiness for itself, God speaks.
Before desire gets the final word, God speaks.
Before culture gets the final word, God speaks.
And that confronts something inside every generation.
Including ours.
We want a God who comforts our wounds.
We are less enthusiastic about a God who confronts our desires.
We want grace when we fall.
But sometimes we resist the boundaries designed to keep us from falling.
We love hearing that Jesus receives sinners.
And He does.
Gloriously.
But Jesus does not rescue sinners so sin can continue ruling them.
Grace is not God looking at destruction and calling it harmless.
Grace is God entering the wreckage to rescue the people inside it.
That is why the Bible's sexual boundaries cannot be understood properly if they are separated from the character of God.
Leviticus 18 is not saying sex is filthy.
Scripture never needs to despise sexuality in order to regulate it.
God created human bodies.
God created marriage.
God created sexual intimacy.
And precisely because sexuality possesses enormous power for covenant, intimacy, vulnerability, family, and human flourishing, Scripture refuses to treat it casually.
Fire in the fireplace can warm a home.
Fire unleashed across the floor can consume it.
The existence of a boundary does not prove hatred of the fire.
Sometimes the boundary exists because somebody understands its power.
And here is where this ancient command starts asking modern questions.
What are you doing with desire when nobody sees you?
What relationship have you been trying to justify because admitting the truth would cost too much?
What secret have you renamed so you no longer have to call it sin?
What betrayal are you hiding behind the sentence, “God understands”?
Yes.
God understands.
More completely than you imagine.
But God's understanding of our weakness never requires Him to lie about what destroys us.
And perhaps somebody reading this just felt exposed.
Not because you married your wife's sister.
Because your secret has another name.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Emotional infidelity.
Lust.
Deception.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A private message thread you keep deleting.
A browser history you would panic if somebody opened.
A fantasy you continually feed.
A compromise you once promised would happen only once.
And now you are reading an ancient law about somebody else's bedroom while the Holy Spirit is putting His finger on yours.
That is the moment when many people run.
Please understand where the Gospel tells you to run.
Not away from Jesus.
Toward Him.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that clean people can approach Christ.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners can.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity needed cosmetic improvement.
He came because sin had penetrated deeper than behavior.
We needed forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
We needed redemption.
We needed a Savior.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that God decided sin did not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that Christ bore judgment.
And grace is so astonishing that the One who knew no sin willingly gave Himself for sinners.
That means repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace finally makes hiding unnecessary.
You stop defending the darkness.
You bring it into the light.
You stop saying, “Everybody does it.”
You say:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
You stop negotiating.
You surrender.
And there is a world of difference between shame whispering, “Hide from God,” and conviction saying, “Come home.”
Remember the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Jesus did not join the crowd hungry to destroy her.
Neither did He redefine adultery so nobody had to repent.
Mercy and holiness stood together in Christ.
“No condemnation” was not transformed into “no transformation.”
Grace rescued her from the stones and then called her away from sin.
That is Jesus.
The Jesus who receives you is also the Jesus who changes you.
The Jesus who forgives your past refuses to surrender your future to the thing that nearly destroyed you.
And maybe that is why you needed to encounter Leviticus 18 today.
Not so you could stare at an unusual ancient prohibition and think:
Those people were messed up.
But so Scripture could turn the mirror around.
We are extraordinarily skilled at being horrified by sins we do not desire while becoming sophisticated theologians when explaining the sins we do.
Read that again.
It is easy to condemn what does not tempt you.
The deeper test is whether Jesus is Lord over what does.
Your sexuality.
Your imagination.
Your relationships.
Your loneliness.
Your body.
Your wounds.
Your secret browser.
Your phone after midnight.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your hunger to be wanted.
Your fear of being abandoned.
Even the part of your life you keep telling God He cannot touch.
“I am the LORD.”
Those words keep returning through Leviticus 18.
And beneath their authority is a question every disciple eventually has to answer:
Is Jesus merely my Savior when I need forgiveness, or is He also my Lord when obedience hurts?
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that question hurts.
You love Jesus.
But you are fighting something.
You fell again.
You prayed again.
You promised again.
Then failed again.
And now shame has convinced you that perhaps God has finally become tired of you.
Hear the Gospel.
Your hope was never the perfection of your record.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Do not turn that truth into permission to remain in sin.
Turn it into courage to confess it.
Bring the hidden thing into His light.
Seek accountability where necessary.
Break the pattern.
End what needs ending.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repair what can be repaired.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness must be asked.
And when you fall, do not build a house in the dirt.
Get up and return to Christ.
Again.
The cross is not an excuse to remain chained.
It is the announcement that your chains do not have to own the ending.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not scandal erased by pretending it never happened.
Scandal redeemed because Jesus stepped into the story.
Peter had denial in his story.
David had catastrophic sexual sin and bloodshed in his.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
Paul had persecution and violence against believers behind him.
None of their sins became virtues.
Grace did something infinitely more beautiful.
God refused to let sin have the final word.
And He can do that with your story too.
Maybe you have been betrayed sexually.
Jesus sees you.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Repent and come home.
Maybe sexual sin has held you captive for years.
Bring it into the light and seek Christ-centered help and accountability.
Maybe somebody used Scripture itself to manipulate or shame you.
Jesus is not honored by twisting His Word into a weapon for cruelty.
Maybe your marriage is carrying wounds nobody at church knows about.
Stop pretending healing is unnecessary simply because appearances still look respectable.
Maybe you are single and exhausted from being told your desires do not matter.
They matter.
But Jesus matters more.
And He is worthy of the parts of us that cost something to surrender.
That is discipleship.
Not merely posting Bible verses.
Not merely calling yourself Christian.
Not merely being offended by somebody else's sin.
Following Jesus means placing the keys of every locked room into His hands.
Even that room.
Especially that room.
So if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write your entire story publicly.
But you can take one small step out of hiding.

And if God has already brought you through a place you thought would destroy you, leave a testimony. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter when a sinner runs to Jesus.
