The terrifying connection between Numbers 25, Numbers 31, and Revelation 2 reveals something every Christian fighting temptation needs to understand: when the enemy cannot defeat you from the outside, he may try to seduce you into surrendering from within.
There is something deeply unsettling about the story of Balaam.
Not because a donkey spoke.
Not because a pagan diviner stood on a mountain and looked down upon the tents of Israel.
Not even because a frightened king desperately wanted God’s people cursed.
The most disturbing part comes later.
Because Balaam discovered something terrifying.
If Israel could not be cursed from the outside, perhaps Israel could be corrupted from the inside.
And suddenly this ancient story stops feeling ancient.
Because some of the most devastating spiritual defeats do not begin with persecution.
They begin with invitation.
A conversation.
A private message.
A glance that stays too long.
A relationship you already know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
A browser opened when nobody is watching.
A compromise you promised would happen only once.
A secret appetite you keep feeding while still singing worship songs on Sunday.
Nobody had to drag you away from God.
Something simply became attractive enough that you began walking away yourself.
That is why Balaam’s story should make every believer pay attention.
Balak, king of Moab, was terrified of Israel. He summoned Balaam because he wanted supernatural help against the people God had blessed.
But Balaam could not simply manufacture a curse against the will of God.
Again and again, blessing came from his mouth.
Israel appeared protected.
The enemy wanted them cursed.
God would not permit it.
And you might expect the story to end there.
It doesn’t.
Numbers 25 suddenly takes us somewhere darker.
Israel is staying at Shittim, and Scripture says the people began committing sexual immorality with the women of Moab. The women invited them to sacrifices offered to their gods. Israel ate.
Then Israel bowed.
Then came one of the most chilling sentences in the chapter:
Israel “joined himself unto Baalpeor.”
Notice the descent.
Sexual compromise.
Participation at the table.
Idolatry.
Bondage.
What looked like appetite became allegiance.
What began in the body reached the soul.
The Hebrew language of Numbers 31 later pulls back the curtain even further.
Moses says:
“הֵן הֵנָּה הָיוּ לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּדְבַר בִּלְעָם לִמְסׇר מַעַל בַּיהֹוָה עַל דְּבַר פְּעוֹר...”
Hen hennah hayu livnei Yisrael bidvar Bil'am...
The crucial phrase is בִּדְבַר בִּלְעָם — bidvar Bil'am.
It means, in context, “through the word/counsel of Balaam.”
Numbers 31:16 identifies Balaam as connected with the counsel by which Israel was led into unfaithfulness concerning Peor.
Now something that Numbers 25 did not initially explain has been exposed.
There was strategy behind the seduction.
And centuries later, Jesus Himself makes the connection unmistakable.
Speaking to the church in Pergamum in Revelation 2:14, Christ says that some among them held:
“τὴν διδαχὴν Βαλαάμ”
tēn didachēn Balaam—
“the teaching of Balaam.”
Then comes the explanation:
“βαλεῖν σκάνδαλον...”
balein skandalon—
to place a stumbling block before Israel.
And what did that stumbling block involve?
“φαγεῖν εἰδωλόθυτα καὶ πορνεῦσαι”
phagein eidōlothyta kai porneusai—
to eat things sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.
There it is.
Numbers 25 shows the fall.
Numbers 31 reveals Balaam’s involvement.
Revelation 2 explains the strategy.
Balaam could not successfully curse what God had blessed.
So the trap became compromise.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because Satan does not always need to convince you that God does not exist.
Sometimes he only needs to convince you that one hidden sin does not matter.
He does not always need you to renounce Jesus publicly.
Sometimes he is satisfied when you keep calling Jesus “Lord” while privately making peace with something Jesus died to free you from.
That is far more subtle.
And far more dangerous.
Still know worship songs.
Still quote Scripture.
Still tell people, “God is good.”
Still attend church.
Still own three Bibles.
Still know exactly when to say “Amen.”
And yet there can be one room inside your heart where you have quietly hung a sign:
Jesus, You can have everything except this.
That room may be pornography.
An affair.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Greed.
An ungodly relationship.
Secret conversations with someone who is not your spouse.
Alcohol controlling you.
The approval of people.
Money.
Pride.
An obsession.
An unforgiving heart.
Or some habit nobody knows exists because you have become extraordinarily good at appearing spiritually healthy.
That is why this story hurts.
Because Balaam’s strategy was not merely about getting people to break a sexual rule.
The sexual sin was tied to something deeper.
Worship.
Numbers 25 says they were invited to sacrifices, ate, bowed down, and attached themselves to Baal of Peor.
The real battle was ultimately over allegiance.
And that remains true today.
Sexual sin is never merely about sex.
Greed is never merely about money.
Pride is never merely about ego.
Addiction is never merely about appetite.
Every sin eventually asks the same ancient question:
Who will rule you?
And sometimes the most dangerous idols are not statues sitting inside temples.
They are desires sitting inside us.
That is why Jesus’ words in Revelation are so serious.
He was not speaking to pagans outside the church.
He was speaking to a church.
People who carried His name.
People living in a hostile environment.
People who had endured pressure.
Yet Christ still confronted compromise among them.
That should humble us.
Because surviving persecution does not automatically mean we have defeated temptation.
You can be courageous in public and compromised in private.
You can defend Christianity online and neglect Christ when the screen goes dark.
You can win an argument about morality while losing the battle for your own purity.
You can expose everybody else’s sin while carefully hiding yours.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is the one you already know:
God sees it.
Not the edited version.
Not the explanation.
Not the excuse.
Not the version your family believes.
Not the version your church friends see.
God sees what happens after midnight.
He sees the deleted conversation.
He sees the second account.
He sees what you search.
He sees what you fantasize about.
He sees what you keep returning to.
He sees the relationship you know you should leave.
He sees the bitterness you secretly enjoy rehearsing.
He sees the compromise you renamed “struggle” years ago because calling it sin would require repentance.
And yet...
He sees something else too.
He sees you.
Not merely your scandal.
Not merely your failure.
Not merely the worst thing you have ever done.
He sees the sinner Christ came to save.
This is where the Gospel changes everything.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people managed to keep themselves clean.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The same Bible that exposes sin announces a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to make immoral people behave better.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He lived the righteousness we could never produce perfectly.
He carried sin to the cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The answer to Balaam’s ancient trap is not merely stronger willpower.
It is Christ.
The answer to shame is Christ.
The answer to guilt is Christ.
The answer to slavery to sin is Christ.
The answer to the believer who has fallen and wonders whether there is any road home is still Christ.
But grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace calls us out.
Jesus does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
He offers something infinitely better:
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Freedom.
A new Master.
A new heart.
A new direction.
Repentance means we stop defending the thing that is destroying us and turn toward the One who can save us.
Maybe that is why you are reading this right now.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have begged God for forgiveness so many times that you are ashamed to pray the same prayer again.
Maybe you have promised, “Never again,” and then found yourself back in exactly the same place.
Maybe your greatest fear is not that somebody will discover your secret.
Maybe your greatest fear is that you will never change.
Hear the Gospel.
Your hope was never your ability to become your own savior.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Run to Him honestly.
Bring the ugly truth.
Confess it.
Stop protecting it.
Cut off what continually leads you toward it.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Open Scripture when your appetite tells you to open the door to temptation.
Pray before temptation becomes negotiation.
And when necessary, seek trustworthy pastoral or professional help rather than fighting alone in secrecy.
Because secrecy gives sin somewhere to breathe.
Confession drags it into the light.
Perhaps you have fallen badly.
Perhaps your story contains adultery.
Pornography.
Promiscuity.
An abortion.
Sexual brokenness.
Betrayal.
Years of secret addiction.
Or choices you would give almost anything to undo.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend those things never happened.
It declares that your past does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Christ.
There are consequences we may still have to face.
Relationships may require rebuilding.
Trust may take time.
Some scars remain.
Grace is not pretending damage never happened.
Grace means damage does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the cross is real.
The tomb is empty.
And Jesus Christ is still transforming sinners.
So be honest right now.
Not with me.
With God.
What is the thing you keep allowing near your soul because you are convinced you can control it?
What compromise keeps whispering, Just once more?
What relationship keeps weakening your obedience?
What secret would terrify you if somebody opened your phone tonight?
What appetite has slowly begun demanding your worship?
Balaam’s story is thousands of years old.
The trap is not.
Maybe your enemy cannot make you stop believing in Jesus.
So temptation tries something quieter.
It asks you to believe in Jesus while slowly learning to live without obeying Him.
Don't confuse God's patience with His approval.
Come home.
Someone reading beneath you may discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
One share may put the Gospel in front of someone who would never walk through the doors of your church.
There may come a night when temptation sounds more convincing than it does today, and you may need to remember again:
The enemy does not need to curse you if he can persuade you to compromise.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow in Scripture, conviction, repentance, healing, and faith in Jesus Christ, stay close by following this ministry and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow along for daily biblical truth and encouragement.
It does not.
And never because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
If your desire is to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, prayerfully consider whether supporting Gospel Warrior should be one expression of that stewardship.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.
Send this article to someone fighting quietly.
Jesus did not purchase you with a monthly payment.
He purchased His people with His blood.
And perhaps that is the final lesson Balaam never wanted Israel to remember.
The people of God did not need another curse to destroy them.
They needed only to forget whose they were.
So tonight, before you close this article, remember whose you are.
If you belong to Jesus, your secret temptation is not your lord.
Your appetite is not your lord.
Your past is not your lord.
Your shame is not your lord.
Jesus Christ is Lord.

And the same Christ who exposes what is killing you is the Christ who calls you out of darkness, receives the repentant sinner, cleanses the guilty, restores the broken, and teaches His people how to walk in the light.
Balaam may have understood how to build a stumbling block.
But he never possessed the final word over the people of God.
Neither does your scandal.
Neither does your failure.
Neither does the night you wish you could erase.
The enemy may remember the chapter where you fell. Jesus is still writing what comes after it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “YOUR BREASTS ARE LIKE CLUSTERS OF FRUIT”: The Song of Songs Passage Many Christians Never Hear Read Aloud
paragraphs: “YOUR BREASTS ARE LIKE CLUSTERS OF FRUIT”: The Song of Songs Passage Many Christians Never Hear Read Aloud
We are comfortable saying God created the human body—until the Bible starts talking about it.
There are verses Christians underline.
Verses we embroider on pillows.
Verses we print on coffee mugs, place over sunsets, memorize with our children, whisper beside hospital beds, and post when life falls apart.
And then there are verses like this.
Verses that make the room suddenly uncomfortable.
Verses a preacher may read faster than the others.
Verses that make some Christians wonder, for half a second, whether somebody accidentally slipped the wrong book into the Bible.
“Your breasts are like clusters of fruit.”
Yes.
That is in Scripture.
And the Hebrew is not embarrassed.
זֹאת קוֹמָתֵךְ דָּמְתָה לְתָמָר וְשָׁדַיִךְ לְאַשְׁכֹּלוֹת
Zot qomatekh damtah letamar, veshadayikh le’ashkolot.
Literally, the imagery says:
“Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts like clusters.”

The Hebrew word שָׁדַיִךְ (shadayikh) really does mean “your breasts.” The word אֶשְׁכּוֹלוֹת (eshkolot) means “clusters.” The comparison to the palm tree is right there in the Hebrew text. This is not an embarrassing mistranslation modern Christians need to rescue God from. It belongs to the poetry of Song of Songs itself.
And the next line becomes even more intimate:
אָמַרְתִּי אֶעֱלֶה בְתָמָר אֹחֲזָה בְּסַנְסִנָּיו וְיִהְיוּ־נָא שָׁדַיִךְ כְּאֶשְׁכְּלוֹת הַגֶּפֶן
Amarti e’eleh vetamar, ochazah besansinnav; veyihyu-na shadayikh ke’eshkelot hagefen...
“I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its branches. May your breasts be like clusters of the vine...’”
The Hebrew text really is that direct. The following imagery speaks of fragrance, apples, wine, desire, and the lovers belonging to one another.
And perhaps the first lesson is embarrassingly simple.
God is not embarrassed by what God created.
We are.
Somewhere along the way, many Christians learned a strange equation.
Holiness means pretending bodies do not exist.
Purity means never speaking about desire.
Spiritual maturity means becoming uncomfortable whenever Scripture becomes physical.
But then you open the Bible...
and discover a love poem.
Not pornography.
Not exploitation.
Not lust stripped of covenant, dignity, and personhood.
Poetry.
Beauty.
Longing.
A man beholding the woman he loves.
A woman speaking her own desire.
Two lovers celebrating one another with the vocabulary of gardens, vineyards, fruit, fragrance, wine, spices, flowers, gazelles, palms, and pomegranates.
And suddenly our embarrassment says more about us than it does about Scripture.
Maybe you were raised to believe that anything involving the human body was automatically dirty.
Maybe nobody actually said it.
Maybe you simply absorbed it.
You heard sermons warning you about lust—which Scripture rightly warns against—but almost never heard anyone explain that sexual desire itself was not invented by pornography.
God created humanity male and female before Genesis ever introduced the serpent.
Marriage existed before the fall.
The body existed before shame.
And Genesis says something astonishing about that original world: the man and woman were naked and were not ashamed.
Then sin entered.
And one of the first things humanity did was hide.
That matters.
Because shame has been whispering ever since.
Hide your body.
Hide your wounds.
Hide your desire.
Hide your failures.
Hide your history.
Hide what happened to you.
Hide what you did.
Hide what you secretly want.
Hide.
Hide.
Hide.
Then Jesus walks into human history looking for people hiding behind trees all over again.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it matters so much that He came to save sinners from it.
There is an enormous difference between biblical sexuality and the counterfeit sexuality sold by our culture.
Pornography takes a person and turns that person into a product.
Lust asks, “What can I take?”
Biblical love asks, “How can I cherish?”
Pornography disconnects the body from covenant, responsibility, sacrifice, and personhood.
The Song does the opposite.
The beloved is not merely anatomy.
She speaks.
She chooses.
She desires.
She belongs to her beloved, and her beloved belongs to her.
Just a few verses after this passage comes one of the Song’s most important declarations:
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve’alai teshuqato.
That sentence changes the atmosphere.
She is not presented as a disposable body.
She is the beloved.
She has a voice.
She answers desire with desire.
She is not merely being looked at.
She loves.
She speaks.
She chooses.
She belongs within a relationship of mutual delight.
And perhaps that is why Song of Songs makes both religious shame and modern sexual consumerism uncomfortable.
It refuses both lies.
It refuses to say the body is filthy.
And it refuses to say the body is merchandise.
It refuses prudish shame.
And it refuses exploitative lust.
It gives us something far more beautiful.
Love without dehumanization.
Desire without disposability.
Bodies without shame becoming bodies without boundaries.
Passion that still recognizes a person.
And that distinction desperately matters now.
Because some people reading this have spent years believing Christianity's answer to sexual brokenness was simply:
“Stop wanting.”
But Jesus came for something deeper than behavioral suppression.
He came for redemption.
There is a difference.
Christianity does not merely announce that certain desires must be resisted.
It announces that the entire human person can be redeemed.
Mind.
Body.
Memory.
Desire.
Identity.
Relationships.
Past.
Future.
Everything surrendered to Christ.
Maybe pornography has trained your eyes to consume instead of cherish.
Maybe sexual sin became the secret room of your life.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you clear the history.
Delete the conversation.
Close the app.
Promise God it was the last time.
Then return.
And afterward comes the familiar silence.
That horrible silence.
The moment when temptation has finished making promises and shame arrives to collect the bill.
Maybe your story is different.
Maybe someone used your body.
Maybe affection was weaponized against you.
Maybe the word “intimacy” does not make you smile.
It makes something inside you tighten.
Maybe religious people handed you shame for wounds somebody else caused.
Maybe you learned to hate the mirror.
Maybe you have spent years believing that what happened to your body somehow changed your worth.
And maybe you have wondered whether God could possibly look at all of it without turning away.
Look again at Jesus.
The Christ of Christianity is not a distant spirit floating safely above human suffering.
“The Word became flesh.”
God the Son entered human embodiment.
Jesus became hungry.
Tired.
Thirsty.
He wept.
He bled.
Human hands struck Him.
A Roman scourge tore His flesh.
Nails pierced Him.
His body was placed in a tomb.
And Christianity does not end with Jesus escaping His body.
It ends with resurrection.
The tomb was empty.
The body mattered.
And that changes everything.
Christian hope is not ultimately the liberation of good souls from disgusting bodies.
It is redemption so complete that Scripture points toward resurrection.
God does not save fragments.
Christ is making all things new.
That means your body is neither your god nor your garbage.
It is not something to worship.
It is not something to despise.
It belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And this is where Song of Songs becomes unexpectedly confrontational.
Because if your theology can only deal with souls and cannot deal with bodies, your theology is too small.
If your Christianity knows how to condemn lust but does not know how to describe holy love, something is missing.
If churches teach teenagers everything sex can destroy but never explain what covenant love was meant to protect, something is missing.
And if Christians are more embarrassed by biblical marital desire than the world is by pornography, something has gone terribly wrong.
Song of Songs will not let us pretend God is afraid of His own creation.
But neither will the rest of Scripture let us baptize every desire merely because we feel it.
That is the tension mature Christianity must be willing to hold.
The body is good.
Sin is real.
Desire is powerful.
Covenant matters.
Purity matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Repentance matters.
Grace matters.
And Jesus is Lord over all of it.
Not just Sunday morning.
Not just your theology.
Not just your worship playlist.
Your browser history.
Your private messages.
Your fantasies.
Your dating life.
Your marriage.
Your loneliness.
Your wounds.
Your sexuality.
Your body.
Your secret life.
Everything.
That may be the part that hurts.
Because sometimes we want Jesus as Savior while keeping locked rooms where He is not allowed to be Lord.
We say, “Jesus, forgive my sins.”
But quietly add:
“Please don't open that door.”
And Christ stands before the room we have spent years protecting.
Not because He wants to humiliate us.
Because He wants us free.
Repentance is not God screaming, “You are disgusting.”
Repentance is the terrifying mercy of God saying:
“You don't have to live here anymore.”
Come out.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the shame.
Bring the memories.
Bring the compromise.
Bring the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Bring the wounds you covered with pleasure.
Bring the hunger underneath the habit.
Bring the thing you promised yourself nobody would ever know.
Bring all of it into the light.
Because grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is Christ meeting sinners where they actually are and refusing to leave them there.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is offered not because we finally became clean enough to approach Him, but because His blood is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
The scandal is not that sinners need grace.
The scandal is how far Grace came to find us.
Maybe that is why this strange, beautiful, uncomfortable passage belongs in our Bibles.
It reminds us that Christianity is not frightened by reality.
Scripture can talk about breasts.
It can talk about desire.
It can talk about adultery.
Prostitution.
Infertility.
Betrayal.
Abuse.
Pregnancy.
Marriage.
Singleness.
Temptation.
Shame.
Blood.
Death.
And resurrection.
The Bible does not need us to sanitize humanity before God is allowed into the room.
God already entered the room.
His name is Jesus.
So maybe the question after reading Song of Songs 7 is not:
“Why would God allow language like this into Scripture?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
“Why did we become so uncomfortable with a God who refuses to abandon any part of human existence to darkness?”
Your sexuality does not need another counterfeit savior.
Your shame does not need another hiding place.
Your loneliness does not need another temporary anesthetic.
Your wounds do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
Not a sanitized Christ who only appears in church buildings.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Holy.
Merciful.
The Savior who tells sinners to repent and then gives repentant sinners something shame never could:
a new beginning.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make a simple declaration that refuses secrecy's power.

And if somebody came into your mind while reading this—someone carrying sexual shame, someone recovering from pornography, someone who thinks Christianity hates the human body, someone who has been wounded, someone trying to rebuild a marriage, someone who desperately needs to discover the difference between condemnation and conviction—send this to them.
Otherwise, send it quietly.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.

Scripture recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry—Paul writes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel. But Scripture is equally clear that Christian giving must never be manipulated: each person should give as he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.” Give first where conscience, Scripture, and faithful stewardship before God lead you.
And even if you cannot financially support the work, you can still help.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Pray for the people who will encounter it.
Because sometimes the post you almost did not share becomes the sentence someone reads at 2:13 in the morning while deciding whether they are too dirty to come home to God.
They are not beyond the reach of Christ.
Neither are you.
Because the final word over a surrendered life is not the browser history.
Not the affair.
Not the addiction.
Not what somebody did to you.
Not what you did.
Not the secret.
Not the scar.
Not even the shame.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
What shame tells you to bury, Jesus calls into the light—not to destroy you, but to begin writing what you thought could never be redeemed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE ONLY PICKED UP STICKS—THEN MOSES ORDERED HIS DEATH
paragraphs: HE ONLY PICKED UP STICKS—THEN MOSES ORDERED HIS DEATH
The terrifying story in Numbers 15:32–36 was never really about a handful of wood. And if you read it too quickly, you may miss the warning… and the grace… hiding in plain sight.
He was only gathering sticks.
That is what makes the story so disturbing.
Not murdering someone.
Not stealing gold.
Not bowing before an idol in the middle of the camp.
Sticks.
A man bent down on the Sabbath and gathered pieces of wood from the wilderness floor.
Someone saw him.
Then someone else.
Before long, they brought him before Moses, Aaron, and the congregation.
And the ending is difficult to read.
The man died.
If you have ever reached Numbers 15:32–36 and quietly wondered, Why was the punishment so severe? you are not irreverent for noticing how shocking the passage is.
You are supposed to feel its weight.
But before we accuse God of punishing a man for something as trivial as picking up firewood, we need to slow down and read what Scripture actually says.
Because the sticks were visible.
The deeper issue was rebellion.
And that changes everything.
Numbers 15:32 begins:
וַיִּהְיוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּמִּדְבָּר וַיִּמְצְאוּ אִישׁ מְקֹשֵׁשׁ עֵצִים בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת
Vayihyu v’nei-Yisra’el bamidbar, vayimtze’u ish meqoshesh etzim b’yom haShabbat.
In context: “While the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day.”
The Hebrew word מְקֹשֵׁשׁ — meqoshesh describes the man as gathering or collecting.
Nothing in that word, by itself, makes the act look dramatic.
And that is precisely why context matters.
This incident does not appear in isolation.
Immediately before it, God had distinguished between unintentional sin and something very different.
Numbers 15:30 describes the person who sins בְּיָד רָמָה — b’yad ramah.
Literally, the expression carries the picture of acting “with a high hand.”
Defiantly.
Presumptuously.
Openly setting oneself against the command of God.
Then comes the chilling explanation in verse 31:
כִּי דְבַר־יְהוָה בָּזָה וְאֶת־מִצְוָתוֹ הֵפַר
Ki devar-YHWH bazah, v’et-mitzvato hefar.
“For he has despised the word of the LORD and has broken His commandment.”
Then, immediately afterward, Scripture tells us about the man gathering wood on the Sabbath.
That placement matters.
The narrative invites us to read the incident against the distinction that has just been made between inadvertent wrongdoing and deliberate defiance.
This was not Israel accidentally discovering that God disliked firewood.
The Sabbath command had already been given.
Israel had already been told:
זָכוֹר אֶת־יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת לְקַדְּשׁוֹ
Zakhor et-yom haShabbat leqaddesho.
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.”
Exodus 20:8.
And Exodus 31:14–15 had already attached an extraordinarily serious covenant penalty to profaning the Sabbath.
So when Numbers says the man was found gathering wood on that day, the issue was not the market value of the sticks.
The issue was what his action represented within Israel’s covenant relationship with God.
Sometimes rebellion does not look dramatic.
Sometimes rebellion looks ordinary.
That may be the uncomfortable part of this story.
We tend to measure sin by appearance.
God sees the heart from which it comes.
We say:
“It was only one lie.”
“It was only one message.”
“It was only one night.”
“It was only bitterness.”
“It was only pornography.”
“It was only gossip.”
“It was only money.”
“It was only flirting.”
“It was only something nobody knows about.”
“It was only…”
Sticks.
And suddenly this ancient man in the wilderness does not feel quite so distant.
Because human beings have become extraordinarily skilled at shrinking what God has said so that disobedience feels manageable.
We rename greed “ambition.”
We rename lust “chemistry.”
We rename vengeance “closure.”
We rename pride “knowing my worth.”
We rename compromise “being realistic.”
We rename spiritual apathy “being busy.”
And sometimes we rename deliberate disobedience “a mistake” because mistake hurts less than rebellion.
But Numbers 15 will not allow us to hide forever behind softer vocabulary.
There is another detail people often miss.
Verse 34 says:
וַיַּנִּיחוּ אֹתוֹ בַּמִּשְׁמָר כִּי לֹא פֹרַשׁ מַה־יֵּעָשֶׂה לוֹ
They placed him in custody because it had not yet been made clear what should be done to him.
Think about that.
They did not simply become enraged and execute him on impulse.
They detained him.
They waited.
Then the LORD gave Moses the judgment recorded in the text.
Numbers 15:35–36 says that the man was to be put to death outside the camp, and the congregation carried out the sentence as the LORD had commanded Moses.
It is severe.
We should not sanitize it.
Neither should we detach it from its covenant setting and pretend the passage teaches Christians to execute Sabbath violators today.
It does not.
Ancient Israel existed under the Mosaic covenant as a covenant nation with civil, ceremonial, and moral dimensions intertwined in ways that do not simply transfer wholesale to the church.
Jesus’ apostles did not establish Christian congregations by reproducing Israel’s civil penalties.
But neither should we swing to the opposite extreme and conclude that the story has nothing to say to us.
Because the holiness of God has not disappeared.
And sin has not become harmless.
The Bible does something astonishing with that truth.
It takes us from a man condemned outside the camp…
to another Man who suffered outside the gate.
Hebrews 13:12 says:
“Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.”
Do not rush past that.
The guilty man of Numbers 15 was taken outside the camp and received judgment.
Then, centuries later, Jesus Christ—the sinless Son of God—went outside the gate bearing shame He did not deserve.
This does not mean Numbers 15 is a direct prophecy predicting the crucifixion.
We should not force Scripture to say something it does not say.
But when the whole biblical story is allowed to speak, the contrast is breathtaking.
We are the rebels.
Christ is the righteous One.
We broke God's commands.
Christ obeyed perfectly.
We deserved judgment.
Christ willingly bore judgment for sinners.
The gospel does not announce that sin was never serious.
The cross announces that sin was so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
That is why grace is not God shrugging His shoulders and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace says it mattered more than we could imagine…
and Jesus paid what we could never pay.
Isaiah had written of the suffering servant:
וַיהוָה הִפְגִּיעַ בּוֹ אֵת עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ
VaYHWH hifgia bo et avon kullanu.
“The LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Isaiah 53:6.
Then the New Testament brings the scandal of grace into terrifying clarity.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:21:
τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν
Ton mē gnonta hamartian hyper hēmōn hamartian epoiēsen.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin…”
So that in Christ we might become the righteousness of God.
That is Christianity.
Not good people proving that they deserve heaven.
Not religious people pretending they never gathered their own metaphorical sticks.
Not sinners hiding behind church attendance while secret rebellion consumes them.
Christianity begins with the devastating confession:
I have sinned.
And then comes the sentence Satan does not want the repentant sinner to believe:
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Maybe your “sticks” have a name.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you can sing on Sunday while carrying it.
Maybe you preach.
Maybe you lead.
Maybe you serve.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
God already sees behind the profile.
Behind the ministry.
Behind the smile.
Behind the excuses.
And yet the gospel invitation remains.
Repent.
Come home.
Not because your sin is small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
The Greek word so often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō: to repent, to change one's mind, to turn in response to the truth.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Peter wept bitterly.
But repentance is more than emotion.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And the good news is that you do not clean yourself up enough to become worthy of Jesus.
You come because you are not worthy.
You come because He is merciful.
You come because the crucified and risen Christ is the only Savior sinners have.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice the astonishing word.
Just.
How can a holy God forgive guilty people and remain just?
The answer stands on a hill outside Jerusalem.
The cross.
Jesus did not manipulate justice.
He satisfied it.
Romans 3:26 describes God as both “just” and the “justifier” of the one who has faith in Jesus.
The Judge Himself provided the rescue.
This is why the man gathering sticks should disturb us.
And this is why Jesus should overwhelm us.
We often want a God holy enough to punish everyone who has wounded us but lenient enough to overlook everything hidden inside us.
The Bible gives us something infinitely more frightening and infinitely more beautiful.
A God who is truly holy.
A humanity that is truly guilty.
A judgment that is truly deserved.
And a Savior who truly died and truly rose.
At Calvary, God did not pretend rebellion was harmless.
Christ bore sin's curse so that rebels who repent and believe could be reconciled to God.
That is scandalous grace.
Maybe you have spent years believing your history disqualified you.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Sexual sin.
Anger.
Abortion.
Adultery.
Pride.
A secret habit.
Years wasted running from God.
Words you cannot take back.
People you cannot unhurt.
Things you desperately wish you could erase.
Listen carefully.
The gospel does not give you a time machine.
It gives you a Redeemer.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending your sin never happened.
He rewrites what happens to the sinner who comes to Him.
Condemned becomes forgiven.
Far away becomes brought near.
Slave becomes free.
Enemy becomes reconciled.
Dead becomes alive.
Ashamed becomes clothed in Christ.
Not because the sinner became impressive.
Because Jesus is enough.
Maybe that is why you needed to find this article today.
Not to stare at a dead man holding sticks.
But to finally look at the living Christ with empty hands.
Stop negotiating.
Stop hiding.
Stop telling God, “It was only…”
He knows.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
And when you fall, do not turn grace into permission to remain in sin.
Run back to Jesus.
Grace is not a comfortable hiding place for rebellion.
Titus 2:11–12 says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Jesus did not die merely to make sinners feel less guilty while leaving them chained to what was destroying them.
He came to save.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Come back and remember.
God is holy.
Sin matters.
Jesus saves.
And grace is costly beyond imagination.
Not as a performance of righteousness and never as a way of earning God's favor.
Send it privately to the friend who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that repentance is still possible and Christ still receives sinners.
Supporting Gospel work should come from willing generosity, not spiritual pressure.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is still gathering sticks.
Somebody is still saying, “It is only this once.”
Somebody is still hiding.
Somebody believes the secret is too ugly to confess.
Somebody thinks judgment is the end of their story.
And somebody needs to hear that the same Bible that refuses to trivialize sin also announces a Savior whose grace reaches repentant sinners in places shame told them God would never enter.
The story in Numbers ends outside the camp with a sinner under judgment.
But the Bible does not end there.
Outside another city…
outside another gate…
stood a cross.
And on that cross hung the One who had never rebelled.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
And still calling sinners home.
So put down the sticks.
Stop hiding your hands.
Stop defending what is killing you.
Bring your sin into the light.
Come to Christ.
Because the most unforgettable thing about your story does not have to be the scandal of what you did.
It can be the grace of the One who saved you.
The sticks may reveal the rebellion—but the scars in His hands reveal how far grace was willing to go to bring the rebel home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Devil Doesn’t Need You to Deny Jesus If He Can Keep You Too Distracted to Follow Him
paragraphs: The Devil Doesn’t Need You to Deny Jesus If He Can Keep You Too Distracted to Follow Him

The frightening thing about spiritual drift is that you can still believe in Jesus, still call yourself a Christian, still open a Bible occasionally—and slowly build a life so crowded that you barely hear the One you say is Lord.
You didn’t deny Jesus today.
You just didn’t have time for Him.
That sounds less dangerous.
Maybe that is why it is so dangerous.
You woke up and reached for your phone before your heart reached for God.
One notification became another.
One message became ten minutes.
Ten minutes became thirty.

Then came work. Deadlines. Bills. Responsibilities. Videos playing in the background. Music filling the silence. News. Reels. Shopping. Messages. Another episode. Another scroll. Another notification demanding a tiny piece of your attention.
Nothing looked particularly evil.
That is the unsettling part.
There was no dramatic moment where you stood beneath a dark sky, shook your fist at heaven, and shouted, “I reject Jesus Christ.”
You still believe.
You may still pray.
You may still attend church.
You may still share Christian posts.
You may still know the songs.
But somewhere beneath all the movement, something quieter has been happening.
Jesus has been getting the leftovers.
And you hardly noticed.
Christ warned about something remarkably similar in the parable of the sower.

In Mark 4:18–19, Jesus describes people who hear the Word, but then something begins happening inside them. Mark preserves Christ’s warning in language that is painfully relevant to a world overflowing with things competing for our attention:
“καὶ αἱ μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ ἡ ἀπάτη τοῦ πλούτου καὶ αἱ περὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἐπιθυμίαι εἰσπορευόμεναι συμπνίγουσιν τὸν λόγον, καὶ ἄκαρπος γίνεται.”
A close rendering of that Greek is:
“And the cares of the age, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires for other things entering in choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.”
Read that again.
They choke the Word.
The Greek verb Mark uses is συμπνίγουσιν—sympnigousin, from sympnigō.
To choke.
To crowd.
To press around something until its life and fruitfulness are suffocated.
Jesus did not describe people who necessarily stopped hearing the Word.
They heard it.
The tragedy was what happened afterward.
Other things entered.
That may be one of the most uncomfortable descriptions of distracted discipleship ever spoken.
The Word enters.
Then something else enters.
Then something else.
Then something else.
Until what God planted is surrounded by so many competing desires, anxieties, pursuits, appetites, and concerns that there is little room left for fruit.
Notice what Jesus includes.
“Cares.”
“Riches.”
“Desires for other things.”
Not merely scandalous sins.
Ordinary things can become spiritually dangerous when they begin occupying a place in us that belongs to God.
That means your greatest spiritual danger may not always arrive looking like rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like being busy.
Sometimes it looks like entertainment.
Sometimes it looks like ambition.
Sometimes it looks like endless consumption.
Sometimes it looks like a calendar so full that prayer becomes whatever remains after everything “important” is finished.
Sometimes it looks like knowing everything happening on your feed while barely knowing what is happening in your own soul.
And no, this does not mean your phone is inherently evil.
It does not mean entertainment is automatically sinful.
It does not mean Christians cannot enjoy movies, hobbies, work, sports, technology, laughter, vacations, books, business, creativity, or rest.
Scripture does not require us to invent sins God has not called sins.
The issue is deeper.
What is discipling your attention?
What receives the clearest hours of your mind?
What gets immediate access to you?
What are you afraid to be without?
What occupies your thoughts when nothing else demands them?
And perhaps most painfully...
When was the last time you were alone with Jesus without simultaneously doing something else?
No television humming.
No notifications.
No scrolling between verses.
No hurry to finish.
No performance for anybody watching.
Just you.
Christ.
His Word.
And enough silence for your heart to stop pretending.
Maybe that question hurts because you remember when following Jesus felt different.
There was a season when you were hungry.
You opened Scripture because you wanted Him.
You prayed because speaking with God was not another item on your checklist.
You could hear a verse and carry it around all day.
Sin bothered you more quickly.
Grace astonished you more deeply.
Worship sometimes brought tears before you understood why.
You wanted Jesus.
Then life became louder.
Not necessarily darker.
Just louder.
Responsibilities multiplied.
Your attention fractured.
Your spiritual life became something squeezed between everything else.
Five minutes here.
A sermon clip there.
A verse while walking somewhere.
A hurried prayer while falling asleep.
And gradually you became accustomed to surviving on spiritual crumbs while feeding almost everything else in your life full meals.
You never officially walked away.
You drifted.
That distinction matters because Scripture repeatedly treats attentiveness to God as serious.
Jesus told Martha, who was “anxious and troubled about many things,” that “one thing is necessary,” while Mary sat at His feet and listened to His teaching in Luke 10:38–42.
Martha was not condemned for serving.
The warning concerned what her many concerns were doing inside her.
That sounds painfully modern.
We can be surrounded by many things that genuinely need attention and still neglect the One our souls need most.
We can even become busy doing things for Jesus while becoming too distracted to remain with Jesus.
And Jesus said something even more searching in John 15:5:
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
Not “less.”
Nothing.
Christian fruit does not grow from proximity to Christian content.
It grows through abiding in Christ.
That is why distraction deserves more spiritual seriousness than we often give it.
Because whatever repeatedly captures your attention eventually begins shaping your affection.
And whatever shapes your affection begins influencing your decisions.
Then one day you may discover that Jesus remained somewhere in your theology while becoming increasingly peripheral in your daily life.
You believe He is Lord.
But your schedule barely acknowledges Him.
You believe His Word is truth.
But algorithms receive more of your attention.
You believe eternity matters.
But the temporary repeatedly consumes you.
You believe prayer changes things.
But anxiety often gets the first conversation.
You believe Christ satisfies.
Yet whenever silence appears, your hand instinctively reaches for another screen.
This is not written to manufacture shame.
Shame by itself cannot restore you.
The Gospel offers something infinitely better.
Jesus.
The same Jesus who exposes what is choking the Word is the Savior who receives sinners who turn to Him.
The answer to distraction is not merely better productivity.

It is not simply deleting applications, buying a paper Bible, installing blockers, or constructing the perfect morning routine. Those things may sometimes help, but none of them can resurrect a cold heart.
The deepest answer is repentance and return.
“Repent” in the New Testament is connected with the Greek μετανοέω—metanoeō—the call to turn, to change one’s mind and direction in response to God.
Christian repentance is not self-hatred.
It is agreeing with God about our sin and turning toward the mercy He has provided in Christ.
And that mercy has a cross at its center.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make distracted people more disciplined.
He came to save sinners.

At Calvary, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners. He bore sin, died, and rose again. Forgiveness is not purchased by your ability to maintain a devotional streak. Reconciliation with God is not earned because you finally reduced your screen time.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith,” Ephesians 2:8 tells us.
Grace.
That changes everything.
Because when you realize you have wandered, Jesus is not telling you to clean yourself perfectly before coming home.
Come home.
Confess.
Turn.
Receive mercy.
Follow Him again.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need sophisticated language.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, I have made room for almost everything except You.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, show me what has been choking Your Word in me.”
“Jesus, teach me to want You again.”
“Jesus, take back the places in my heart I surrendered to noise.”
There are people reading this who are exhausted but cannot remember the last time they were truly still before God.
People whose minds are constantly stimulated but whose souls feel starved.
People who consume hours of content every day but struggle to remain in Scripture for fifteen uninterrupted minutes.
People who know they need prayer, yet feel an almost physical resistance to silence.
Maybe that person is you.
Then do not hide behind another scroll.
Bring that person to Christ.
The distracted person.
The spiritually tired person.
The person whose Bible has gathered dust.
The person who loves Jesus but has allowed lesser things to crowd Him toward the edges.
Bring the real you.
Because Jesus already knows who is coming.
And this is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Christ.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples scattered.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The Gospel is filled with people whose failures should have been the end of their stories if grace were not stronger than human failure.
Jesus rewrites stories.
Not by pretending the sin never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by making repentance unnecessary.
He rewrites them through forgiveness, redemption, restoration, and transformation.
The cross proves that God takes sin more seriously than we do.
The empty tomb proves that sin does not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
So perhaps tonight is not about promising God that you will never be distracted again.
Perhaps tonight begins with giving Him the next undistracted moment.
Put the phone down.
Open the Scriptures.
Stay there.
Not because fifteen minutes earns God's affection.
Not because a longer prayer makes you more worthy of salvation.
But because the Savior who purchased you is worthy of your attention.
Tomorrow, do it again.
And when you fail, return again.
When your mind wanders, return.
When your appetite for Scripture feels weak, return.
When prayer feels dry, return.
When the noise begins creeping back, return.
Christian maturity is not built by dramatic emotion alone.
Much of discipleship happens through thousands of quiet returns to Jesus.
A thousand small decisions saying:
You are worth listening to.
You are worth obeying.
You are worth following.
You are worth more than whatever is flashing on this screen.
And perhaps someone you love is drifting exactly this way.
They have not announced that they are abandoning Christianity.
They are simply becoming increasingly occupied.
Send this to them.
Not with superiority.
Not as an accusation.
Send it because you love them enough to say, “I needed this too.”
And if God has already been restoring your hunger for Him, tell somebody what He has been teaching you. Your testimony may become the encouragement another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Not because another saved post changes a life, but because tomorrow the noise will return, and you may need to remember what you recognized tonight.

The purpose is not to build an audience around ourselves. It is to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ where distracted people can encounter it.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him through Christ.
But before you click anything...
Before you share anything...
Before you comment anything...
Your attention.
Your repentance.
Your trust.
Your obedience.
Your heart.
Because perhaps the question was never merely whether you would deny Jesus with your lips.
Perhaps the quieter question is whether you have become so occupied with everything else that there is barely enough room left in your life to follow the Jesus you still say you believe in.
The good news is that this does not have to be the final page.
The notification does not get the final word.
The addiction to noise does not get the final word.
Your wandering does not get the final word.
Your wasted years do not get the final word.
Your spiritual numbness does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
So come back.
Not tomorrow.
Not when life becomes less busy.
Not when your emotions cooperate.
Come back while the screen is still glowing in your hand.
Come back while your heart still feels the conviction.
Come back because the Savior you crowded out is still worthy of everything.
And remember this when the world becomes loud again:
You can spend your whole life making room for everything—and suddenly discover that the One you were made for has been standing at the edge of your attention all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER—Then Gave Their Children Names That Sounded Like Judgment
paragraphs: HOSEA MARRIED GOMER—Then Gave Their Children Names That Sounded Like Judgment

One child was named after bloodshed. Another was called “No Mercy.” The last was called “Not My People.” But hidden inside one of Scripture’s most painful family stories is a message for everyone who has ever wondered whether they have wandered too far for God to call them home.
Imagine being a child and discovering that your name was a sermon.
Not a comforting sermon.
A warning.
Every time your mother called you home, the neighborhood heard it.
Every time your father introduced you, people remembered it.
Every time somebody spoke your name, judgment echoed through the room.
“Jezreel.”
“Lo-Ruhamah.”
“Lo-Ammi.”
Three children.
Three names.
Three living messages to a nation that had learned how to keep religion around while giving its heart somewhere else.
And perhaps that is why Hosea is so uncomfortable.
Because this book does not begin with a prophet standing safely behind a pulpit telling everybody else what is wrong with them.
God brings the message into Hosea’s house.
Into his marriage.
Into the names of his children.
Into the place where theology becomes painfully personal.

“The word of the LORD” came to Hosea, and the command that followed was staggering. Hosea was told to take a wife described by the Hebrew expression אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים — eshet zenunim, an expression associated with sexual unfaithfulness or prostitution, because Israel itself had been acting unfaithfully toward the LORD.
The marriage was going to become a prophetic sign.
Hosea married Gomer.
And then the children came.
The first was a boy.
God told Hosea:
קְרָא שְׁמוֹ יִזְרְעֶאל — qera shemo Yizre'el
“Call his name Jezreel.”

Jezreel—יִזְרְעֶאל, Yizre'el—carries the sense of “God sows” or “God scatters.” But in Hosea 1, the name immediately points toward judgment connected with the bloodshed at Jezreel and the coming end of Israel's kingdom.
Imagine Hosea holding that little boy.
Tiny fingers wrapped around his father's hand.
An innocent child carrying a name associated with national reckoning.
Every time Hosea whispered his son's name, prophecy entered the room.
Jezreel.
Something was coming.
Israel's military strength would not save her.
Her political arrangements would not save her.
Her outward prosperity would not save her.
God said He would “break the bow of Israel.”
Then Gomer conceived again.
A daughter was born.
And God gave her a name even harder to hear:
לֹא רֻחָמָה — Lo-Ruchamah.
The Hebrew word רָחַם — racham and its related forms speak of compassion, mercy, tender affection.
But place לֹא — lo, “not” before it...
and suddenly the name becomes terrifying.
Lo-Ruhamah.
“Not pitied.”
“Not shown compassion.”
Some translations render the idea “No Mercy.”
Imagine hearing that name shouted across a village.
“Lo-Ruhamah!”
People turn.
There she is.
A little girl carrying a warning far larger than herself.

The name was not teaching that this child personally had committed some terrible offense. The children function within Hosea's prophetic sign to Israel. The target of the warning was a covenant people persistently abandoning their God.
That distinction matters.
Because Scripture must never become permission for us to humiliate children, stigmatize people because of their parents, or weaponize Hosea against someone whose life has been scarred by sexual sin.
The scandal in Hosea is ultimately bigger than Gomer.
The scandal is Israel's spiritual adultery.
And if we read carefully enough...
the scandal eventually reaches us too.
Because idolatry does not always have a statue.
Sometimes your idol fits inside your hand.
Sometimes it has a screen.
Sometimes it looks like money.
Sometimes approval.
Sometimes pornography.
Sometimes romance.
Sometimes ministry.
Sometimes ambition.
Sometimes the desperate need for somebody—anybody—to tell you that you matter.
Anything we place where God belongs can become a rival for the heart.
You can sing worship songs while secretly worshiping people's opinions.
You can quote Scripture while nursing a private addiction.
You can post about Jesus while craving applause more than obedience.
You can know Christian language and still slowly give your heart to another master.
Israel's problem was not merely that people occasionally failed.
They had become persistently unfaithful to the God who had loved them.
And God loved them too much to call betrayal harmless.
That is something modern Christianity desperately needs to recover.
Grace does not require God to pretend sin is beautiful.
The cross proves the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the giving of the Son.
And God's love is so astonishing that the Son was willingly given.
Then another child was born.
And this time the name cuts even deeper.
לֹא עַמִּי — Lo-Ammi.
לֹא — lo: “not.”
עַמִּי — ammi: “my people.”
“Not My People.”
The covenant language itself appears shattered.
God explains the name with words Israel never should have wanted to hear:
כִּי אַתֶּם לֹא עַמִּי
ki attem lo ammi
“For you are not My people.”
Think about the progression.
Jezreel.
Judgment is coming.
Lo-Ruhamah.
Mercy is being withheld.
Lo-Ammi.
The covenant relationship has reached a terrifying rupture.
And maybe somewhere inside those names you recognize something about yourself.
Not because God has renamed you Lo-Ammi.
But because you know what distance from God feels like.
You remember when prayer felt natural.
Then something happened.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you fell back into the sin you promised God you would never touch again.
Maybe somebody wounded you inside a church and you quietly blamed God for what people did.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe grief hollowed you out.
Maybe success made you spiritually sleepy.
but privately you know.
Something has become cold.
And the most frightening thought comes late at night:
Have I gone too far?
That is where Hosea becomes breathtaking.
Because immediately after “Not My People,” something happens that judgment alone could never prepare you for.
God begins talking about restoration.
The Hebrew text moves from:
לֹא עַמִּי — Lo-Ammi — “Not My People”
toward the promise that in the very place where it had been said, “You are not My people,” they would be called children of the living God.
Then later Hosea gives us one of Scripture's great reversals.
God speaks of Lo-Ruhamah receiving compassion.
And concerning Lo-Ammi, God declares:
עַמִּי־אַתָּה — Ammi attah.
“You are My people.”
And the response comes:
אֱלֹהָי — Elohai.
“My God.”
Do you see it?
God takes the language of rejection and writes restoration across it.
Not because rebellion suddenly became acceptable.
Not because sin stopped mattering.
Not because judgment was imaginary.
Because mercy would have the final word for the repentant.
This is where Hosea begins pointing beyond Hosea.
Centuries later, the apostles reach back into this prophetic language.
Paul invokes Hosea in Romans 9:25–26 while explaining God's calling and mercy, including the calling of Gentiles.
Peter writes to believers:
Once you were not a people.
Now...
you are God's people.
Once you had not received mercy.
Now...
you have received mercy.
The ancient names begin sounding different beside the Gospel.
Not My People...
now God's people.
Without mercy...
now recipients of mercy.
Far away...
brought near.
Alienated...
reconciled.
Guilty...
forgiven.
Lost...
found.
Dead in sin...
made alive in Christ.
And this is where Hosea reaches straight through the centuries and finds the person reading these words while carrying a name God never gave them.
“Dirty.”
“Failure.”
“Addict.”
“Adulterer.”
“Unwanted.”
“Damaged.”
“Hypocrite.”
“Unforgivable.”
“Too far gone.”
Maybe somebody called you that.
Maybe Satan has whispered it.
Maybe you wrote it across yourself after your worst night.
But hear this carefully:
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
The Gospel says Jesus Christ is greater.
Your repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
Judgment matters.
The cross matters precisely because sin matters.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our self-esteem.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, justice and mercy are not enemies.
Christ bears judgment so guilty people can receive grace without God becoming unjust.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That means Christianity is not ultimately the story of people cleaning themselves enough to convince God to take them back.
It is the story of a holy God acting to redeem people who could never rescue themselves.
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Repentance is not negotiating with God.
It is turning from the idols that are killing us and returning to the One who gives life.
Maybe that is why this story bothers you.
Maybe you recognize Gomer more than you wanted to.
You know what it means to run toward something that promised satisfaction and eventually left you emptier.
You know what it means to betray your own convictions.
You know what it means to wake up after sin and wonder:
How did I become this person?
Then hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come looking for people with spotless histories.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He ate with sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed the repentant.
He confronted sin without surrendering compassion.
And at Calvary He carried what guilty people could never carry themselves.
So stop hiding.
Bring the secret into His light.
Confess.
Repent.
Return.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
You will never repent because you became worthy of grace.
You repent because Christ is worthy of your life.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can make one honest declaration:
Not as a magic phrase.
Not because a Facebook comment saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes an honest sentence is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.
That matters.
Someone running.
Someone smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Someone ashamed of what they did last night.
Someone convinced Christians would reject them if the truth came out.
Someone wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them anymore.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
Grace is grace.
But if Christ has given you truth worth hearing, there is nothing wrong with helping carry that truth farther.

Glorifying God is bigger than supporting any particular ministry, including ours. Yet one practical way believers can serve is by freely helping sound biblical teaching reach people who may never walk into a church.
Not out of guilt.
Not to buy a blessing.
Not to prove your Christianity.
Do it because the Gospel is worth spreading.
Send this to the believer who thinks relapse erased God's willingness to forgive the repentant.
Share it with the prodigal.
Share it with the skeptic.
Share it with the person who thinks Christianity is only for respectable people with respectable histories.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when the accusation returns:
“You've gone too far.”
And you may need to remember three strange names.
Jezreel.
Lo-Ruhamah.
Lo-Ammi.
And then remember what God did with them.
He turned the language of judgment toward restoration.
That does not mean everyone is automatically reconciled to God regardless of faith or repentance.
It means God's mercy has opened a way home.
And that Way has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling Christians, seekers, lukewarm believers—and even the person who does not yet believe—to follow with you.
But the greatest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
More Scripture.
More truth.
More reminders to repent when your heart wanders.
More encouragement when faith feels exhausted.
More biblical nourishment when the noise of this world becomes deafening.
And another opportunity to help carry the message of Jesus into somebody else's darkness.
but sin does not get the final word over the person who comes to Christ.
And if Hosea has made you realize you have been running from God while still looking religious on the outside...
“No more hiding.”
Because Hosea's story was never merely a scandalous marriage about an unfaithful woman.
It was a mirror held before an unfaithful people.
And eventually...
before us.
We wandered.
God remained holy.
Sin brought judgment.
Mercy opened a door.
And the New Testament takes Hosea's haunting language and places it in the blazing light of God's saving work.
Once not a people.
Now the people of God.
Once without mercy.
Now recipients of mercy.
That is why your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
Jesus does.
And perhaps the name you thought would follow you forever is about to become the place where people discover what His grace can do.
The place where your shame once introduced you may become the place where the mercy of Jesus introduces you again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF YOUR EYE CAUSES YOU TO SIN, TEAR IT OUT” — WAS JESUS BEING LITERAL?
paragraphs: “IF YOUR EYE CAUSES YOU TO SIN, TEAR IT OUT” — WAS JESUS BEING LITERAL?
The terrifying words of Jesus were never permission to destroy your body. They were a warning not to make peace with the sin destroying your soul.
There are verses people underline because they comfort them.
There are verses they put on coffee mugs.
And then there are the words of Jesus that make you stop reading.
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
What do you do with that?
Because Jesus did not whisper it.
He did not apologize for it.
And He did not soften it with, “But don’t take this too seriously.”
He said it in the middle of one of the most famous sermons ever preached.
And maybe the most disturbing thing about the sentence is not the image of losing an eye.
Maybe it is the possibility that Jesus knows how desperately we protect the things that are killing us.
Read His words in context.

In Matthew 5:27–30, Jesus turns from the outward act of adultery to the inward world of desire. He teaches that obedience to God cannot be reduced to maintaining a respectable exterior while secretly cultivating lust within.
Then comes the shocking language.
The Greek of Matthew 5:29 begins:
Εἰ δὲ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ὁ δεξιὸς σκανδαλίζει σε, ἔξελε αὐτὸν καὶ βάλε ἀπὸ σοῦ…
Ei de ho ophthalmos sou ho dexios skandalizei se, exele auton kai bale apo sou…
A close rendering is:
“And if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you…”
Then Jesus continues with the reason: it is better to lose one member than for the whole person to be thrown into Gehenna.
A few words matter enormously here.
The verb translated “causes you to sin” or “causes you to stumble” is σκανδαλίζει — skandalizei, from σκανδαλίζω — skandalizō.
It carries the idea of causing someone to stumble, fall, or be entrapped.
It is related to the word from which English eventually gets “scandal,” although reading the modern English meaning of “scandal” directly back into every New Testament occurrence would be misleading.
Jesus is talking about something that becomes an occasion for spiritual falling.
Something that keeps pulling you toward rebellion.
Something precious enough that you keep defending it even while it keeps dragging you away from God.
And then Jesus says:
ἔξελε αὐτόν — exele auton.
Take it out.
Remove it.
The language is deliberately violent.
But was Jesus commanding His followers to mutilate themselves?
The context strongly points in another direction.
Jesus had just relocated the moral battlefield from merely outward behavior to the heart.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’”
Then Jesus goes deeper.
The problem is not solved simply because your hands have remained technically innocent while your inner life has become a sanctuary for deliberate lust.
That matters because removing an eye would not remove lust from the human heart.
A blind person can lust.
Removing a hand would not remove greed.
A person without hands can covet.
Cutting flesh cannot perform surgery on the sinful desires of the heart.
And Jesus Himself later teaches that evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery and other sins proceed from within, out of the human heart (Mark 7:20–23).
So no, the point is not self-mutilation.
But do not breathe too easily yet.
Because once we recognize the forceful imagery, there is a temptation to domesticate it.
“Oh. It’s figurative.”
And then we move on.
As though “figurative” means “not serious.”
It does not.
Jesus uses shocking, hyperbolic imagery to communicate the deadly seriousness of sin and the radical response discipleship may require.
The command is not:
Destroy your body.
The command is closer to:
Stop negotiating with whatever repeatedly leads you into sin.
And suddenly the verse gets personal.
Because almost everyone has an “eye.”
Something you keep looking at.
Something you keep returning to.
Something you know awakens desires you should not feed.
Maybe it really is what your eyes consume.
The account you refuse to unfollow.
The conversation you keep reopening.
The private browser.
The messages you delete.
The relationship everyone thinks is innocent.
The fantasy you entertain because nobody else can see it.
The resentment you rehearse in bed.
The money you cannot stop worshiping.
The approval you need so badly that you will compromise your convictions to keep receiving it.
The bitterness you call discernment.
The pride you call confidence.
The gossip you disguise as concern.
The addiction you have renamed a coping mechanism.
The secret you have protected longer than you have protected your intimacy with Christ.
You keep saying:
“I can handle it.”
Jesus says:
“If it causes you to stumble…”
You say:
“I know when to stop.”
Jesus says:
“Throw it away.”
You say:
“But I need it.”
And Jesus forces the question you were hoping Christianity would never ask:
Do you need it more than you want holiness?
That hurts.
Because sometimes we want Jesus to forgive the sin we have no intention of abandoning.
We want grace without surrender.
Mercy without repentance.
A Savior who removes guilt without touching our idols.
But that is not the Jesus speaking in Matthew 5.
The Jesus who saves sinners is also the Jesus who calls sinners to repentance.
And repentance is not self-hatred.
Repentance is not paying God back.
Repentance is not punishing your body until God decides you have suffered enough.
The Greek New Testament commonly uses μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance: a turning of mind and orientation that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Grace does not teach us to become casual about sin.
Grace gives us somewhere to run when sin has exposed us.
And this is where the story changes.
Because perhaps you have already failed.
Maybe you are reading this after promising God for the hundredth time that you would never go back.
Then you went back.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your church does not know.
Your friends see the worship songs you share but not the war you fight when the room gets quiet.
You know how to say, “God is good.”
But inside you are wondering:
Would God still want me if people knew what I have become?
Look at Jesus.
Not at your record.
Not at your shame.
Look at Him.
The Gospel does not announce that good people finally learned how to behave.
The Gospel announces that sinners who could not rescue themselves were loved by a Savior who came to rescue them.
Christ did not come merely to make scandalous people more respectable.
He came to redeem sinners.
The cross is where the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God meet without either one being minimized.
Sin is so serious that Christians cannot shrug at Calvary.
Grace is so astonishing that Christians cannot look at Calvary and conclude that repentant sinners are beyond redemption.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
And forgiveness is not purchased by tearing out your eye.
It was purchased at immeasurable cost by Christ.
You do not mutilate yourself to become worthy of grace.
You come to Christ empty-handed.
Then, because His grace is real, you begin cutting away what keeps pulling you back toward the grave He rescued you from.
That may mean deleting something.
Blocking someone.
Confessing to someone trustworthy.
Ending an immoral relationship.
Moving the computer out of the bedroom.
Giving someone accountability.
Walking away from money you cannot receive honestly.
Leaving environments where your sobriety, fidelity, integrity, or obedience continually collapses.
Surrendering access.
Changing routines.
Admitting that what is “not technically sinful” for somebody else has become spiritually disastrous for you.
Not because those actions earn salvation.
They do not.
But sometimes repentance has fingerprints.
Sometimes freedom looks like a door that stays closed.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like deleting a number while your hands are shaking.
Sometimes obedience feels like grief before it feels like freedom.
That is part of the force of Jesus’ metaphor.
An eye is valuable.
A hand is useful.
Jesus deliberately chooses things a person would hate to lose.
Why?
Because following Christ may require surrendering something you genuinely value when keeping it continually leads you toward destruction.
There are things you can love and still need to leave.
There are people you can miss and still not call again.
There are environments you can enjoy and still never enter again.
There are habits that once comforted you that cannot accompany you where Christ is leading you.
Some doors need prayer.
Others need locks.
Some temptations need Scripture.
Others need Scripture and a blocked number.
Sometimes we pray, “Lord, deliver me from temptation,” while preserving five different ways for temptation to contact us.
Then we call the cycle mysterious.
Jesus is painfully practical.
If it repeatedly causes you to stumble, stop treating access to it as sacred.
But there is another danger here.
Someone carrying crushing shame can hear Matthew 5 and conclude:
“God must hate me.”
No.
The warning itself reveals that eternity matters.
Christ speaks urgently because sin matters, judgment matters, and people matter.
Biblical conviction says:
Come out of hiding and come to Christ.
Condemnation whispers:
Hide from Christ until you have repaired yourself.
Those are not the same message.
Think about Peter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
At the moment when loyalty became costly, the disciple who had spoken so confidently collapsed spectacularly.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine replaying the sound of your own voice:
“I do not know the man.”
But Peter's scandal was not the final chapter.
The risen Christ met him again.
Restored him.
Commissioned him.
Grace did not pretend the denial never happened.
Grace rewrote what happened next.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not because sin was imaginary.
Not because repentance became unnecessary.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
But because failure does not possess greater authority than Jesus Christ.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe it lives entirely behind your ribs.
Jesus sees that too.
And the same Christ who says, “Throw away what makes you stumble,” is the Christ who receives sinners who turn to Him.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“Was Jesus literally telling me to tear out my eye?”
Perhaps the question is:
What am I unwilling to tear out of my life even though I know it keeps tearing my life apart?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
What came to mind before you started making excuses?
A name?
An app?
A website?
A habit?
A relationship?
A hidden folder?
A bottle?
A conversation?
A place?
An ambition?
A grudge?
An image?
An identity built around being desired, admired, wealthy, powerful, noticed, or needed?
What did your heart immediately defend?
Maybe that is where the conversation with Jesus needs to begin.
Not with a knife against your body.
With honesty before God.
“Jesus, I have been protecting what is poisoning me.”
That confession can become the beginning of freedom.
And if you fall again, do not turn another failure into permission to surrender completely.
Run back to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get help.
Bring darkness into the light.
Take concrete steps.
Keep fighting.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the reason chains no longer have to define you.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who never struggled.
We are people who desperately need Christ.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because temptation has a way of making yesterday's convictions strangely difficult to remember.
Not as proof that you have everything together.
Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God's favor.
But supporting Christian ministry can be one practical way of helping biblical resources reach more people.
But before you leave this page, go back to the question.
Not somebody else's eye.
Not somebody else's hand.
Not somebody else's scandal.
Yours.
What are you protecting that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
You do not need to destroy your body.
Christ is calling you to stop making peace with the thing destroying you.
Bring it into the light.
Cut off its access.
Run toward Jesus.
And when shame tells you that your worst chapter has already written your ending, look toward the cross and the empty tomb.
Because the hands of Christ are still better authors than your failures.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived here, but when you surrender the pen to Jesus, it does not get to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?”
paragraphs:
“MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?”
The Cry From the Cross That Sounds Like Despair—Until You Discover What Jesus Was Really Saying
There are words in Scripture that comfort you.
There are words that correct you.
And then there are words that stop you cold.
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Jesus said them while hanging on a cross.
And perhaps the most unsettling thing about that sentence is not that it came from a dying man.
It came from the Son of God.
The One who said, “I and my Father are one” (John 10:30).
The One who prayed, “Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me” (John 11:41).
The One who told His disciples, “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (John 14:9).
Yet on Golgotha, beneath a darkened sky, with blood running from wounds made by nails, thorns, scourging, and human cruelty, Jesus cried:
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
Matthew preserves the cry this way in Greek:
“Ἠλί Ἠλί, λεμὰ σαβαχθανί;”
Then Matthew gives its meaning:
“θεέ μου θεέ μου, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες;”

“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
(Matthew 27:46)
Mark records the cry as:

“Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ, λαμὰ σαβαχθανί;”
(Mark 15:34)
The Gospel writers preserve an Aramaic form of Jesus’ agonized words because this cry mattered.
But what did He mean?
Had the Father stopped loving the Son?
Had the Trinity somehow broken apart?
Had Jesus ceased to be God?
Was the Father unable to look at Jesus?
