“I don’t know how to tell you how lonely I have become.”
“I’m afraid you don't desire me anymore.”
“I feel ashamed for even wanting you.”
These are not problems healed by throwing verses across the bed like grenades.
They need truth spoken in love.
They need patience.
They need repentance where sin exists.
They may need pastoral care, medical care, or qualified professional counseling.
Sometimes they need tears.
Sometimes forgiveness.
Sometimes difficult boundaries.
Sometimes protection.
Sometimes a long rebuilding of trust.
But they need Christ in the room.
Because marriage is not healed merely when two bodies occupy the same bed.
Marriage begins healing when two hearts stop hiding.
And for the person reading this who has been spiritually manipulated with this passage, hear the distinction clearly:
The Bible is not the abuser.
The misuse of the Bible is.
Jesus is not honored when Scripture is twisted to excuse cruelty.
Christ does not need distortion to defend holiness.
Truth can withstand context.
And perhaps someone reading this has carried secret shame for years because you were told that being a “godly spouse” meant never expressing pain, fear, exhaustion, or boundaries.
Maybe you thought God was angry every time your body froze.
Maybe someone quoted Paul while refusing to imitate Jesus.
Please read Paul again.
Read all the words.
ἀλλήλους.
One another.
ὁμοίως.
Likewise.
ἐκ συμφώνου.
By mutual agreement.
There is reciprocity running through this passage.
There is responsibility running both directions.
And there is something else we desperately need to recover.
Sexual intimacy in Christian marriage is not supposed to resemble a commercial transaction.
It is not “I performed my duty, now you owe me.”
It is covenantal self-giving.
That is precisely why selfishness can corrupt it from either side.
Marriage says:
I will not casually neglect you.
I will not manipulate you.
I will not punish you with my body.
I will not demand your body while ignoring your soul.
I will not reduce you to what you can give me.
I will learn you.
I will hear you.
I will bring my desires honestly before you.
I will care about your desires too.
I will seek your good.
And when sin enters this marriage—and it will, because two sinners live here—we will keep bringing our brokenness to Jesus.
That is the part pornography never teaches.
That is the part entitlement cannot understand.
That is the part selfishness hates.
Real intimacy requires vulnerability.
And vulnerability cannot flourish where fear rules the room.
Perhaps this article is exposing something uncomfortable in you.
Maybe you have quoted this passage selfishly.
Maybe you have pressured your spouse.
Maybe you have dismissed their pain.
Maybe you have used withdrawal deliberately to punish them.
Maybe resentment has been sleeping between you for years.
Maybe you have been pretending everything is fine because admitting the truth feels terrifying.
Then this is not an invitation to condemnation.
It is an invitation to repentance.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross merely to make guilty people feel worse.
He went to save sinners.
People like us.
Controlling sinners.
Selfish sinners.
Wounded sinners.
Sexually broken sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Religious sinners.
Secretly bitter sinners.
People who have hurt others.
People who have been hurt by others.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse sin.
He bore sin.
And because He rose again, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repentance can begin tonight.
An apology can begin tonight.
Truth can begin tonight.
“I was wrong.”
“I pressured you.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I used rejection to hurt you.”
“I have been hiding.”
“I need help.”
“Will you forgive me?”
“Can we pray?”
Those may not sound dramatic.
But sometimes resurrection begins with a sentence whispered through tears.
You do not have to tell strangers private details. Simply comment, “Jesus, teach me to love like You,” or “Christ is still healing me.”
Let believers pray instead of pretending believers never struggle.
Not because every person needs to know the private details of your marriage.
Someone may be living under religious guilt God never commanded.
Someone else may be neglecting their spouse and calling it spirituality.
Someone may desperately need to discover that biblical marriage is neither coercion nor manipulation but covenantal, mutual, Christ-shaped love.
Marriage has seasons, and you may need these words again when emotions are louder than wisdom.
It does not.
Not because money buys blessing.
It cannot.
We will not place that burden on Scripture.

The New Testament does teach that Gospel ministry may be materially supported, while also teaching that giving should come willingly rather than through compulsion. So if you have already purposed in your heart to financially support Christian teaching and discipleship, you may choose to make Gospel Warrior part of that voluntary giving.
And if financial support is not possible, please do not feel spiritually inferior.
Save these teachings.
Pray for the ministry.
There is more than one way to help truth travel.
Because ultimately this was never supposed to be about building an audience around us.
It is about pointing people toward Him.
Jesus Christ.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit His Bride but gave Himself for her.
The Savior who confronts sin without abandoning the sinner who comes to Him.
The King who enters our most embarrassing rooms and still offers redemption.

The One who can walk into a marriage scarred by selfishness, resentment, sexual brokenness, silence, manipulation, shame, or years of misunderstanding and begin writing something neither spouse believed was still possible.
Grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace meets us inside it, tells the truth about it, calls us to repent, and then places the pen into nail-scarred hands.
And maybe the most intimate question in your marriage tonight is not, “What does my spouse owe me?”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, what would it look like for me to love this person the way You have loved me?”
Because when Christ enters the places we were most ashamed to let Him see, the bedroom does not have to remain a battlefield.
It can become another place where grace begins rewriting the story.
The verse you thought was about what you could demand may actually be calling you to remember how deeply you were called to give.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE HAD EVERYTHING—AND STILL BETRAYED THE ONE WHO LOVED HER
paragraphs: SHE HAD EVERYTHING—AND STILL BETRAYED THE ONE WHO LOVED HER
Ezekiel 16 uses the shocking language of marriage, adultery, and prostitution to expose Jerusalem’s betrayal—but buried beneath the scandal is a truth about grace that may expose something in us too.
There are chapters of the Bible that comfort you.
There are chapters that strengthen you.
And then there are chapters that make you uncomfortable enough to wonder why God allowed them to remain in Scripture.
Ezekiel 16 is one of those chapters.
It is graphic.
Painful.
Deliberately humiliating.
It speaks of nakedness, marriage, adultery, prostitution, blood, lovers, betrayal, judgment, and shame.
Read quickly, and it can sound almost unbearably severe.
But read carefully…
and something devastating begins to emerge.
This chapter is not primarily a story about sex.
It is a story about covenant betrayal.
And before you distance yourself from Jerusalem and say, “I would never do what she did,” you may want to keep reading.
Because Ezekiel 16 eventually forces a much more frightening question:
What if spiritual adultery does not always look like leaving God?
What if sometimes it looks like keeping His name while quietly giving your heart to something else?
Jerusalem’s story begins in a place nobody would expect.
Not with prostitution.
Not with rebellion.
Not even with judgment.
It begins with abandonment.
God commands Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem with her abominations, and then He describes the city through the imagery of an unwanted newborn.
No one cared for her.
No one cleaned her.
No one wrapped her.
No one showed compassion.
She was pictured as discarded in a field.
Then God passed by.
And God said:
Live.
That is where the story begins.
Grace found her before beauty did.
Grace found her before status did.
Grace found her before she had anything with which to repay God.
Later, the imagery changes.
Jerusalem matures, and God describes entering into covenant with her.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:8 is striking:
וָאֶשָּׁבַע לָךְ וָאָבוֹא בִבְרִית אֹתָךְ
Va’eshava lakh, va’avo bivrit otakh.
In context: God swore an oath to her and entered into a בְּרִית — berit, a covenant, with her.
Then comes the breathtaking declaration:
וַתִּהְיִי לִי — vattihyi li
“You became Mine.”
Not because Jerusalem rescued herself.
God found her.
God gave her life.
God covered her.
God entered covenant with her.
God washed her.
God clothed her.
God adorned her.
God provided for her.
The abandoned became beloved.
The discarded became beautiful.
The one lying helpless became a bride.
And that is precisely what makes what happens next so horrifying.
Because the tragedy of Ezekiel 16 is not merely that Jerusalem sinned.
It is that she took the gifts of the One who loved her…
and used those gifts to betray Him.
God says Jerusalem became confident in her beauty.
Then Ezekiel uses a Hebrew verb that keeps haunting the chapter:
זנה — zanah.
It carries the idea of engaging in prostitution or harlotry.
Ezekiel 16 repeatedly employs sexual infidelity as a prophetic metaphor for Jerusalem’s covenant unfaithfulness.
This is not permission to demean women who have suffered exploitation, nor is Ezekiel giving human beings permission to weaponize sexual shame against sinners.
The target of the prophetic accusation is Jerusalem herself, personified as an unfaithful covenant partner.
The metaphor is intentionally shocking because covenant betrayal is serious.
Jerusalem had received gifts from God and redirected them toward idols.
She sought other “lovers.”
She pursued foreign powers.
She participated in idolatry.
And the chapter descends into something even darker: God accuses Jerusalem of sacrificing children.
This was not a harmless spiritual phase.
This was rebellion consuming human lives.
But there is something about the metaphor that becomes almost unbearable.
Ordinarily, Ezekiel observes, a prostitute receives payment.
Jerusalem’s behavior is portrayed as the reverse.
She gives gifts to her lovers.
She pays them.
Think about that.
She is not merely being tempted away.
She is financing her own betrayal.
She is spending what God gave her to pursue what cannot replace God.
And suddenly Ezekiel 16 stops feeling ancient.
Because we know something about doing that.
God gives us time…
and we can spend it avoiding Him.
God gives us influence…
and we can use it to glorify ourselves.
God gives us money…
and we can make money our master.
God gives us relationships…
and we can demand from people the security only God can ultimately provide.
God gives us bodies…
and we can turn desire into a ruler.
God gives us abilities…
and we can become addicted to applause.
God gives us technology…
and we can allow it to fill our minds with things that slowly deaden our hunger for holiness.
God gives us blessings…
and sometimes the blessing becomes more precious to us than the Blesser.
That is when Ezekiel 16 becomes personal.
Because an idol does not have to be a statue.
An idol can be anything we allow to occupy the place of trust, worship, identity, obedience, or ultimate devotion that belongs to God.
Success can become a lover.
Approval can become a lover.
Money can become a lover.
Pornography can become a lover.
Resentment can become a lover.
Attention can become a lover.
A relationship can become a lover.
Even ministry can become one if we begin loving the platform more than the Christ we claim to proclaim.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual affairs are the ones nobody sees.
You can still attend church.
Still quote Scripture.
Still post Christian content.
Still sing worship songs.
Still say “God is good.”
And somewhere beneath all of it, your heart can be whispering:
Jesus, You can have everything except this.
That sentence should frighten us.
Because Jesus is not looking for a religious arrangement in which we occasionally visit Him while our deepest allegiance belongs elsewhere.
He is Lord.
And Ezekiel 16 exposes the insanity of sin:
We abandon living water and then wonder why our souls remain thirsty.
We chase approval and remain insecure.
We chase pleasure and discover that appetite grows faster than satisfaction.
We chase control and become increasingly afraid.
We chase money and discover there is always another number.
We chase attention and discover applause cannot love us.
Jerusalem kept chasing lovers.
And she was not satisfied.
Neither are we.
Sin makes enormous promises.
Then sends an invoice.
Eventually the lovers Jerusalem pursued could not save her from judgment.
That is another truth we desperately need.
Whatever replaces God eventually fails under the weight of being God.
Your spouse cannot carry that weight.
Your children cannot carry it.
Your career cannot carry it.
Your pastor cannot carry it.
Your followers cannot carry it.
Money cannot carry it.
Pleasure cannot carry it.
You were created for God.
And there is another uncomfortable layer here.
Sometimes we think grace means God does not care very much about our betrayal.
Ezekiel 16 destroys that idea.
God's judgment in this chapter is severe precisely because covenant rebellion is not trivial.
Biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace becomes astonishing because sin does matter.
God is holy.
Evil matters.
Idolatry matters.
Injustice matters.
The shedding of innocent blood matters.
Our rebellion matters.
And yet Ezekiel 16 does not finish where you might expect.
After exposure…
after betrayal…
after judgment…
after shame…
God speaks about covenant again.
Near the end of the chapter, He promises to remember His covenant and speaks of establishing an everlasting covenant.
That does not erase the judgment.
It reveals something extraordinary about God.
Human unfaithfulness does not transform God into an unfaithful God.
And now the entire biblical story begins pulling us forward.
Because Jerusalem's problem was not merely political.
Humanity's deepest problem is not merely behavioral.
We need more than improved habits.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need cleansing.
We need a new heart.
We need a Savior.
And the Gospel announces His name.
Jesus Christ.
The New Testament brings covenant and bride imagery to its breathtaking fulfillment in Christ.
Jesus does not come searching for people who can prove they never betrayed God.
He comes to save sinners.
At the cross, He does not call evil good.
He bears judgment.
He deals with sin at immeasurable cost.
The scandal of grace is not that God shrugged at our rebellion.
The scandal is that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the One we betrayed becomes the only One capable of bringing us home.
That is why repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
Repentance is turning.
Coming out of hiding.
Dropping the idols.
Ending the affair with sin.
Returning to God through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been using God's gifts while ignoring God.
Maybe nobody knows what owns you when the room gets quiet.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your worship playlist.
Maybe bitterness has lived inside you so long that you stopped calling it bitterness.
Maybe success became your identity.
Maybe you love being seen as Christian more than you love Christ.
Maybe you have repeatedly promised God, “Never again,” only to find yourself crawling back to the same thing.
And perhaps shame has convinced you that after everything you have done, Jesus would never want you.
Then remember where Ezekiel 16 began.
In the field.
Abandoned.
Covered in blood.
Unable to rescue herself.
And God said:
Live.
Grace began before Jerusalem had anything impressive to offer.
And for the Christian, grace reaches its blazing center at a bloodstained cross.
You do not clean yourself enough to make Christ willing to save you.
You come to Christ because you cannot save yourself.
You confess.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender.
And Jesus does what our idols never could.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He gives life.
He begins transforming the very heart that wandered from Him.
This is why your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is mighty to save.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming rebellion as freedom.
Not by telling us we were secretly righteous all along.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's story through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and new life.
He takes what sin shattered and begins restoration.
He takes the guilty and justifies those who come to Him by faith.
He takes the spiritually dead and gives life.
He takes wanderers and brings them home.
He takes people hiding in shame and teaches them to walk in the light.
So do not finish this article by thinking only about Jerusalem.
Ask the harder question.
Who—or what—has been receiving the devotion that belongs to Jesus?
Do not answer publicly if doing so would expose something unsafe or deeply private.
But answer God.
Tell Him the truth.
No performance.
No religious language designed to impress anybody.
Just truth.
“Jesus, I have wandered.”
“Jesus, I have loved things more than You.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, teach me to want You again.”
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer reads at midnight and realizes they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to prove that you love God.
But because when believers freely support Gospel-centered work, they help that work continue reaching people with Scripture and the message of Jesus Christ.
And there is more waiting for those serious about going deeper.

If this ministry has been feeding your faith, sharpening your convictions, helping you understand Scripture, or pointing you back toward Jesus, consider becoming part of the community that helps keep this Gospel work moving.
Invite someone to follow with you.
And do not underestimate what God can do when biblical truth reaches one person at exactly the moment their heart is finally ready to hear it.
Because Ezekiel 16 leaves us with a truth far bigger than Jerusalem's scandal.
The God who exposes sin is also the God who calls sinners to return.
And when you finally stop running, you may discover that the story you thought ended in shame was standing at the doorway of grace.
The idol knows how to take your gifts. Jesus knows how to resurrect your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Joseph Ran. Samson Stayed. Their Stories Ended Very Differently.
paragraphs: Joseph Ran. Samson Stayed. Their Stories Ended Very Differently.

One man fled temptation and lost his coat. Another kept returning to temptation and eventually lost his strength, his freedom, and his sight. If you think you can keep standing where God is telling you to run, their stories deserve your full attention.
There are moments when victory does not look brave.
It looks like running.
No speech.
No dramatic prayer.
No attempt to prove how spiritually mature you are.
Just a door...
and your feet moving toward it.
Joseph understood this.
Samson learned it much later.
And somewhere between those two men is a warning for every person who has ever whispered:
“I can handle this.”
Joseph was a young Hebrew slave living in Egypt when temptation entered his life wearing opportunity.
Genesis 39 tells us that Joseph had risen in Potiphar’s household. God was with him. His master trusted him. Responsibility had been placed in his hands.
Then Potiphar’s wife noticed him.
Scripture says she repeatedly tried to seduce him.
Joseph refused.
But one day she caught him by his garment and said:
“Lie with me.”
The Hebrew text gives us Joseph’s response with breathtaking simplicity.
וַיָּנָס וַיֵּצֵא הַחוּצָה
Vayyanas vayyetse hachutzah.
“And he fled and went outside.”
Genesis 39:12.
He ran.
That was the sermon.
Joseph did not stay to demonstrate his self-control.
He did not negotiate.
He did not ask how close he could get without technically sinning.
He did not remain in the room because he believed his calling made him immune to temptation.
He ran.
And he left his garment behind.
Think about that.
Joseph was willing to lose something rather than lose himself.
His garment stayed in her hands, and she weaponized it against him. The innocent man who fled sexual sin was falsely accused because of the very evidence left behind when he escaped.
Joseph did the right thing...
and still went to prison.
That part matters.
Sometimes obedience costs before it rewards.
Sometimes fleeing temptation does not immediately make your circumstances better.
Sometimes purity costs a relationship.
Sometimes repentance costs access.
Sometimes obedience costs popularity.

Sometimes following Jesus means deleting the number, leaving the room, ending the secret conversation, refusing the invitation, installing the accountability, confessing what you have hidden, or walking away while part of you is still screaming to stay.
And sometimes after you obey...
life gets harder.
Joseph ran and landed in prison.
But he went into prison with something Potiphar’s wife could not steal.
His integrity.
Now look at Samson.
His story is different.

Samson was chosen by God for a particular purpose before his birth. Judges 13 describes his extraordinary calling. The Spirit of the LORD empowered him, and God used him against Israel’s Philistine oppressors.
Samson was strong.
Terrifyingly strong.
But physical strength can hide spiritual carelessness.
And giftedness can make a person believe he can survive environments his character is not prepared to withstand.
Then came Delilah.
Judges 16 says the Philistine rulers offered her money to discover the secret of Samson’s strength.
She questioned him.
He deceived her.
She tested his answers.
He saw what was happening.
And still...
he stayed.
Read that slowly.
He stayed.
The danger was no longer theoretical.
Every false explanation Samson gave her was followed by an attempt to exploit precisely what he had told her.
The trap was exposing itself in front of him.
And he stayed.
Eventually Scripture says Delilah pressed him continually until he was worn down.
Then Samson disclosed what had never been surrendered before.
His hair had never been cut because he had been a Nazirite to God from his mother’s womb.
While Samson slept, his hair was cut.
Then came one of the most frightening sentences in his story.
He woke and assumed he would escape as before.
But Judges 16:20 says:
וְהוּא לֹא יָדַע כִּי יְהוָה סָר מֵעָלָיו
Vehu lo yada ki YHWH sar me'alav.
“But he did not know that the LORD had departed from him.”
He did not know.
There is something horrifying about those words.
Samson had become so accustomed to escaping consequences that he apparently expected yesterday’s strength to rescue him from today’s compromise.
But this time...
it didn’t.
The Philistines seized him.
They gouged out his eyes.
They bound him.
The man who had once carried away the gates of Gaza was now grinding grain in captivity.
Joseph ran.
Samson stayed.
Joseph lost a garment.
Samson lost his freedom and his eyes.
Yet Scripture does not give us these stories so Christians can smugly divide humanity into “Josephs” and “Samsons.”
Because if we are truthful...
there is some Samson in all of us.
We stay too long.
We return to what weakened us.
We tell ourselves we are only looking.
Only talking.
Only curious.
Only checking.
Only friends.
Only having one drink.
Only sending one message.
Only watching one more video.
Only keeping the account because we “might need it.”
Only entertaining the fantasy.
Only carrying the bitterness.
Only revisiting the wound.
Only flirting with compromise.
We keep asking God for strength to resist something He may already be telling us to leave.
That is why the New Testament does not merely tell Christians to stand around proving how resistant they are to every temptation.
Sometimes its command is much more practical.
Φεύγε τὰς νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας
Pheuge tas neōterikas epithymias.
“Flee youthful passions.”
2 Timothy 2:22.
Φεύγε.
Pheuge.
Flee.
Run.
Paul uses the same basic command concerning sexual immorality in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
There are battles Scripture tells you to fight.
There are temptations Scripture tells you to flee.
Wisdom is knowing the difference.
Some of us keep praying:
“Lord, give me strength.”
And perhaps part of God’s answer is:
“Use the door.”
You do not need another supernatural feeling before blocking the number.
You do not need another prophetic word before leaving the compromising situation.
You do not need to prove that you can sit beside the fire without smelling like smoke.
You do not defeat every temptation by staring it down.
Sometimes holiness has footsteps.
Sometimes faithfulness sounds like a door closing behind you.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is run.
But there is another part of Samson’s story that cannot be ignored.
Because the Gospel is not merely for Josephs who ran.
The Gospel is also for Samsons who stayed.
Samson failed catastrophically.
He experienced devastating consequences.
But Judges 16 contains a quiet sentence filled with hope:
“But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.”
Hair was growing in the darkness.
Before Samson could see restoration...
something was already changing.
And eventually Samson prayed:
“O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once.”
God heard him.
Samson’s final act struck the Philistines with enormous force, and Hebrews 11:32 later includes Samson among figures remembered in the biblical record of faith.
His failure was real.
His consequences were real.
But failure did not make grace unreal.
And this is where Joseph and Samson eventually point beyond themselves.
Because neither man is our Savior.
Joseph cannot save you.
Samson cannot save you.
Your ability to run cannot save you.
Your record of resisting temptation cannot save you.
And your history of staying too long does not place you beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
The ultimate story is not:
“Become strong enough to save yourself.”
The Gospel says something far more beautiful.
Christ came for sinners.
Jesus entered our broken world without sin, lived the righteousness we could never perfectly achieve, went willingly to the cross, bore sin, died, and rose again.
The Christian message is not that good people climb their way toward God.
It is that God came down to rescue sinners.
Maybe you ran like Joseph.
Thank God.
Keep running.
But never worship your own discipline.
Maybe you stayed like Samson.
Maybe you stayed until something broke.
Maybe pornography became a prison.
Maybe lust became secrecy.
Maybe emotional infidelity became physical adultery.
Maybe resentment hardened into hatred.
Maybe alcohol became your hiding place.
Maybe approval became your idol.
Maybe greed slowly swallowed your contentment.
Maybe you kept returning to a person you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are doing well...
and you know they are looking at a version of you that does not exist when the door closes.
Listen carefully.
Shame says:
“Hide.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
Shame says:
“You have gone too far.”
Grace says:
“Repent and return.”
Shame says:
“Pretend nothing happened.”
The Gospel says:
Bring the truth into the light.
First John 1:9 promises that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning house.
Grace is not permission to remain inside.
Grace opens the door.
Run through it.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because you already know what your “Delilah” is.
Not necessarily a person.
Maybe it is a screen.
A conversation.
A secret account.
An appetite.
A fantasy.
An old relationship.
An addiction.
A grudge.
A place.
A habit.
A version of yourself you keep resurrecting even though Christ has called you into something new.
And you have been telling yourself:
“One more time.”
Samson probably thought he had one more escape too.
Do not build your theology around the fact that consequences have not arrived yet.
God’s patience is not permission.
Romans 2:4 teaches that His kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
So perhaps tonight is not about promising God that you will “try harder.”
Perhaps tonight is about finally running.
Delete it.
Confess it.
Leave it.
Call someone trustworthy.
Ask for prayer.
Put accountability around the weakness.
Stop arranging private meetings between yourself and the thing you keep asking God to defeat.
And if you already stayed...
if you already fell...
if the damage has already happened...
do not confuse consequences with abandonment.
Turn to Christ.
Repent honestly.
Receive His mercy.
Begin walking again.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul had persecuted Christians and became an apostle of Christ.
The thief crucified beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward Christ and heard a promise of paradise.
This is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending sin never mattered.
The cross proves how seriously sin matters.
Jesus rewrites everything because He bore what sinners could never remove themselves.
Grace is expensive.
Christ paid for it.
So stop hiding behind religious language.
Be honest.
What are you refusing to run from?
What compromise have you renamed because calling it what Scripture calls it would force you to make a decision?
What door has God already shown you?
And why are you still standing inside the room?
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
But because sometimes the first crack in secrecy is simply refusing to pretend anymore.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who have never struggled.
We are people whose hope is Jesus.
There are battles that become heavier when carried alone.
Not because you need another inspirational post sitting in a collection somewhere...
but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made painfully clear today.
Come back to these words when “just once” starts sounding reasonable again.

Supporting Gospel work should never replace giving faithfully where God calls you to give, serving your local church, caring for people in need, or obeying Christ personally. It cannot earn salvation. It does not make someone more spiritual.
And comment before you leave:
Because Joseph teaches us that sometimes obedience means leaving the coat behind.
Samson teaches us that staying near temptation can cost far more than we imagined.
And Jesus teaches us that even when we stayed too long, fell too hard, and finally woke up surrounded by the consequences...
repentance can still turn our face toward home.
Maybe you should have run yesterday.
Run today.
And if you already fell yesterday...
run to Jesus today.
You may have stayed long enough to lose something you loved, but you have not lived long enough to exhaust the mercy found in Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: NOCTURNAL EMISSIONS IN THE BIBLE: Yes, Scripture Actually Talks About Them
paragraphs: NOCTURNAL EMISSIONS IN THE BIBLE: Yes, Scripture Actually Talks About Them
The passage almost nobody talks about—and what it reveals about your body, shame, holiness, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
There are Bible questions people ask confidently in church.
Then there are Bible questions they type into a search bar at 2:17 in the morning.
This is one of those questions.
You wake up.
You realize what happened.
And depending on what you were taught about sexuality, purity, lust, and holiness, embarrassment can arrive before your feet even touch the floor.
Did I sin?
Was that because my mind is dirty?
Is God disappointed in me?
Do I need to repent for something my body apparently did while I was asleep?

Some Christians have carried this question silently for years because it feels too embarrassing to ask a pastor, too uncomfortable to discuss with parents, and far too awkward to bring up during Bible study.
But here is what may surprise you:
God was not too embarrassed to put it in Scripture.
Yes.
The Bible actually talks about nocturnal emissions.
And what Scripture says is far more careful—and far less shame-driven—than some believers have been led to believe.
Buried inside Deuteronomy is a law given to Israel concerning the holiness of the military camp. Then comes an extraordinarily specific situation:

“If any man among you becomes unclean because of a nocturnal emission, he must leave the camp and stay outside. When evening approaches, he must wash with water, and when the sun sets he may return to the camp.” — Deuteronomy 23:10–11
That is not a modern attempt to force sexuality into an ancient passage. The underlying Hebrew is remarkably direct.
The key expression is:
מִקְּרֵה־לָיְלָה
miqreh-laylah.

The expression refers to an occurrence or incident of the night—something happening during the night. In this context, major English translations appropriately render it as a “nocturnal emission.” The man becomes ceremonially unclean, washes, waits until sunset, and then returns to the camp.
Notice something extremely important.
The passage does not say the man committed adultery.
It does not say he committed sexual immorality.
It does not say he deliberately entertained lust.
It does not prescribe punishment for sexual wrongdoing.
It describes an occurrence during the night, gives instructions concerning ritual uncleanness, and then provides a straightforward path back into the camp.
That distinction matters.
A lot.
Because biblical uncleanness is not automatically identical to personal moral guilt.
If we confuse those categories, we can make the Bible say something it never actually said.
Leviticus makes the distinction even clearer.
“When a man has an emission of semen, he must bathe his whole body with water, and he will be unclean until evening.” — Leviticus 15:16
The Hebrew reads:
וְאִישׁ כִּי־תֵצֵא מִמֶּנּוּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע
Ve’ish ki-tetze mimennu shikhvat-zara…
Literally, the language describes semen going out from a man. The expression שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע (shikhvat-zera) refers to an emission of semen.
Then comes something that destroys the simplistic idea that “ceremonially unclean” must mean “sexually sinful.”

A few verses later, Leviticus describes sexual relations between a man and woman resulting in an emission, and both are to bathe and remain unclean until evening. The text itself therefore demonstrates that the ritual status associated with an emission cannot simply be equated with committing sexual immorality.
That changes the conversation.
Because maybe you have been confessing something Scripture never calls your sin.
Maybe you have awakened after an involuntary bodily event and immediately treated yourself as though you had consciously rebelled against God.
Maybe shame started preaching before Scripture had the opportunity to speak.
And shame is a terrible Bible teacher.
It takes one uncomfortable moment and whispers:
You are filthy.
God must be disgusted with you.
A real Christian wouldn't experience this.
Don't tell anyone.
Hide.
But when we actually open Scripture, we discover something different.
God already knew the human body.
He designed it.
Nothing about human biology surprised Him when Moses received the Law.
The God who created human beings did not suddenly discover reproductive physiology somewhere between Genesis and Deuteronomy.
And when Scripture addresses an involuntary nocturnal emission, the text does not treat the man as some uniquely depraved sexual offender.
It treats the matter within Israel's system of ceremonial cleanliness.
That does not mean sexual purity is irrelevant.
Far from it.
Jesus takes deliberate lust profoundly seriously.
He said:
“Everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” — Matthew 5:28.
Jesus reaches beneath outward behavior and exposes the intentional desires of the heart.
So there is another mistake we must avoid.

We should not use the involuntary nature of a nocturnal emission as an excuse for deliberate pornography, cultivated fantasies, habitual lust, or intentionally feeding the mind sexually explicit material while awake.
Those are different questions.

If someone deliberately feeds lust throughout the day and then experiences sexual dreams at night, wisdom calls that person to examine what he voluntarily places before his eyes and cultivates in his imagination.
But even then, the biblical target is the deliberate sin.
Not merely the involuntary biological event that occurred during sleep.
That distinction can liberate a Christian from two opposite errors at once.
One person says, “Everything sexual is dirty.”
Scripture does not teach that.
Another says, “Nothing happening in my sexual life matters spiritually.”
Scripture does not teach that either.
The Gospel gives us something better than repression on one side and indulgence on the other.
Truth.
Holiness without hysteria.
Conviction without invented guilt.
Repentance without shame-based religion.
Grace without permission to sin.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this desperately needed.
Because there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, Bring your sin into the light.
Condemnation says, Hide yourself from God.
Conviction leads you toward Christ.
Shame tells you to run away from Him.
And that old impulse to hide goes all the way back to Eden.
After Adam and Eve sinned, they hid themselves from the presence of God.
Sin still makes human beings hide.
We hide browser histories.
We hide addictions.
We hide fantasies.
We hide wounds.
We hide questions.
And sometimes we even hide things that were never sins in the first place because somebody taught us to be ashamed of having a human body.
Jesus did not come merely to make ashamed people behave better.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ dealt with something infinitely deeper than ceremonial uncleanness.
He dealt with guilt.
Real guilt.
Our rebellion.
Our lust.
Our pride.
Our deception.
Our secret sins.
Our outward sins.
The things nobody knows.
The things we desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
And this is where the subject becomes much bigger than nocturnal emissions.
Because eventually every honest conversation about purity reaches the same uncomfortable truth:
Our greatest problem is not what our bodies sometimes do involuntarily.
Our greatest problem is what our hearts willingly do against God.
And our greatest hope is not perfect control over every physiological process.
Our greatest hope is Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend you have never sinned.
It tells you that Christ died for sinners.
Scripture says of Jesus:
“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.” — 1 Peter 2:24.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One takes the place of the guilty.
The spotless Lamb carries the sins of stained people.
The One who deserved no judgment bears judgment so that people who could never cleanse themselves can be forgiven, reconciled, and transformed.
This is why Christians must learn the difference between an involuntary bodily function and willful sin.
Otherwise, we create commandments God did not create while sometimes ignoring the sins He actually commands us to confront.
A nocturnal emission itself is not identified in these passages as a moral transgression requiring repentance.
Under the Mosaic covenant, it produced temporary ceremonial uncleanness.
The man washed.
The sun went down.
He came back.
Read that again.
He came back.
There is something almost painfully beautiful about those words.
He came back.
The condition was temporary.
It did not become his identity.
He was not permanently expelled.
He was not branded as sexually corrupt.
He was not told that God could never use him again.
He washed.
Evening came.
And he returned.
Maybe somebody needs those words for something much bigger than the subject of this article.
You can come back.
Maybe you actually have sinned sexually.
Maybe pornography is not merely something you encountered; maybe it became something you pursued.
Maybe fantasy became a secret room inside your mind.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe you have repeatedly promised God, “Never again,” only to find yourself returning to the same darkness.
Then do not redefine sin.
Do not excuse it.
Do not baptize bondage with softer terminology.
Repent.
But understand what repentance means.
It means turning toward God, not running away from Him.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Confess your sin.
Seek accountability where needed.
Remove access to what repeatedly feeds temptation.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
And above everything else, run toward Christ.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9.
Notice who performs the cleansing.
He does.
Christianity is not the story of dirty people successfully pretending to be clean.
It is the story of sinners being washed by a Savior.
And perhaps that is why this strange, rarely discussed passage matters so much.
It reminds us to let Scripture define our categories.
Not embarrassment.
Not internet folklore.
Not exaggerated purity culture.
Not permissive culture.
Not fear.
Scripture.
When Scripture calls something sin, we should have enough reverence for God to call it sin.
When Scripture does not call something sin, we should have enough reverence for God not to manufacture guilt and place it on somebody else's conscience.
That is also part of honoring His Word.

So if you woke up after an involuntary nocturnal emission and wondered whether the physical event itself means you consciously sinned against God, Scripture gives you no basis for treating the emission itself as a deliberate moral offense.

If your conscience is troubled because of deliberate lust, pornography, fantasies you intentionally cultivated, or sexual behavior Scripture condemns, then deal honestly with those things before Christ.
But do not confuse involuntary biology with voluntary rebellion.
God knows the difference.
And perhaps the most healing realization is this:
You do not have to hide either one from Him.
You don't need to hide what wasn't sin.
And you don't need to hide the sin that really was.
Christ is sufficient for the truth about both.
For the innocent but ashamed, there is truth.
For the guilty and repentant, there is grace.
For the enslaved, there is freedom worth fighting for.
For the wounded, there is healing.
For the person convinced his secret history has written the final chapter of his life, there is Jesus.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this article exposed unnecessary shame you have carried, or confronted a real struggle you have been hiding, don't turn this moment into another secret.
You do not need to describe private sexual details publicly. Sometimes three honest words are enough to tell another struggling believer, You're not fighting alone.
And think about the person who will never search this question because he is too embarrassed.
The teenager terrified that God hates him.
The husband secretly drowning in shame.
The new believer who cannot distinguish temptation, bodily function, and deliberate sin.
The Christian carrying guilt God never commanded him to carry.
Sharing biblical truth can glorify God when our purpose is genuinely to help people see Christ rather than ourselves.
Grace cannot be bought. But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way to help biblical resources reach more people.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too.
Share it not because an algorithm needs another post.
Follow so we can keep opening Scripture together.
And remember this when shame tries to preach louder than Jesus:
What you keep trying to hide may become the very place where Christ teaches you the difference between shame that enslaves and grace that brings you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY THE GOSPEL BECAME BAD FOR BUSINESS
paragraphs: THE DAY THE GOSPEL BECAME BAD FOR BUSINESS
One silversmith looked at what Christianity was doing to Ephesus—and realized that if people truly believed Paul’s message, an entire business built around idols was in danger.
There is a moment in Acts that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Not because Paul was beaten.
Not because someone was imprisoned.
Not because a demon appeared.
Because somebody started losing business.
And suddenly, the Gospel became dangerous.
His name was Demetrius.
He was a silversmith in Ephesus, and according to Acts 19, his trade involved making silver shrines associated with Artemis. The business generated substantial work for the craftsmen.
Then people started listening to Paul.
And Demetrius realized something terrifying.
If these people actually believed the Gospel...
they might stop buying what his world was selling.
That is where this story stops being merely ancient history.
Because sooner or later, Jesus comes close enough to something we love, protect, excuse, monetize, hide, or depend upon—and we discover whether we want Christ Himself...
or merely a Christianity that never costs us anything.
Acts introduces the crisis with these words:
“Ἐγένετο δὲ κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος περὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ.”
The key expression is τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος—literally, “no small disturbance”—and it happened περὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ, “concerning the Way.”
The Way.
That was how the Christian movement could be described.
Not merely an opinion.
Not merely another religious accessory to place beside all the others.
A way.
A life reordered around the crucified and risen Jesus.
And Ephesus was about to discover what happens when the Way of Christ collides with a way of life built around idols.
Acts names the man at the center of the resistance:
“Δημήτριος γάρ τις ὀνόματι, ἀργυροκόπος...”
“A certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith...”
He made silver shrines connected with Artemis and provided considerable business for the craftsmen.
That matters.
Demetrius was not presented merely as an angry pagan shouting religious slogans for no reason.
There was money involved.
There were livelihoods involved.
There was an established religious culture involved.
There was social prestige involved.
There was an entire system that benefited from people continuing to believe what they had always believed.
And Paul had walked into that world proclaiming a truth devastatingly simple in its implications:
“οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοὶ οἱ διὰ χειρῶν γινόμενοι.”
Things made by human hands are not gods.
Read that again.
Paul did not need to smash every silver shrine.
He preached truth capable of making the shrine unnecessary.

That distinction is important because later, when the city official finally quieted the mob, he specifically observed that Paul’s companions were not temple robbers and had not blasphemed their goddess.
The Christian mission described here was not vandalism.
It was proclamation.
And proclamation was enough.
Because when the heart changes, the marketplace eventually notices.

Demetrius gathered the craftsmen and essentially told them what was at stake. Their prosperity came from this trade, yet Paul had persuaded many people in Ephesus and throughout much of the Roman province of Asia that handmade gods were not gods.
Demetrius could see where that road led.
If people stopped believing in the idol...
why would they keep paying for the shrine?
That may be one of the most economically disruptive sentences in Acts.
Not because Christianity taught people that earning money was evil.
Scripture does not teach that.
Not because craftsmanship was evil.
Scripture does not teach that either.
The problem was what the craftsmanship served.

Demetrius's own speech reveals that the controversy involved both livelihood and religious honor. He feared the trade would fall into disrepute and that the magnificent standing of Artemis and her temple would be diminished.
Then the crowd exploded.
“Μεγάλη ἡ Ἄρτεμις Ἐφεσίων!”
“Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
Again.
And again.
And again.
The city descended into confusion.
People rushed together.
Paul’s companions Gaius and Aristarchus were dragged into the theater.
Paul wanted to enter, but the disciples would not let him.
And then Luke gives us one of the most painfully human descriptions of mob behavior anywhere in Scripture.
Some people shouted one thing.
Others shouted something else.
And many did not even know why they had gathered.
Think about that.
People screaming for something they could not explain.
Defending something they had not examined.
Joining outrage they did not understand.
Two thousand years have passed.
Human nature has not changed nearly as much as our technology has.
We still have crowds.
We just carry them in our pockets now.
We still have slogans.
We still have outrage.
We still have identities built around things we are terrified to question.
And we still have idols.
They simply do not always look religious.
Your idol may never sit on an altar.
It may sit in your bank account.
Your bedroom.
Your browser history.
Your career.
Your reputation.
Your relationship.
Your politics.
Your ambitions.
Your need to be admired.
Your resentment.
Your secret habit.
Even your ministry.
An idol is not limited to a carved statue. Biblically, idolatry reaches into the heart. Paul would later tell the Colossians that covetousness is idolatry.
That means the frightening question raised by Acts 19 is not simply:
“What idols did the Ephesians worship?”
It is:
What becomes threatened when Jesus becomes Lord of me?
Because there is a version of Christianity that nearly everybody can tolerate.
Jesus can inspire you.
Comfort you.
Bless your plans.
Decorate your biography.
Appear in your captions.
Help when life hurts.
Just don't let Him touch the thing you refuse to surrender.
But biblical Christianity announces something far more radical.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And if Jesus is Lord, everything else must leave the throne.
That is why genuine repentance can become expensive.
Zacchaeus encountered Jesus and suddenly money looked different.
People practicing magic in Ephesus believed and publicly burned costly books associated with their former practices earlier in Acts 19.
The Gospel reached their hearts...
and eventually reached their possessions.
Not because salvation can be purchased through sacrifice.
Never.
We are saved by grace.
But grace that saves us also begins transforming us.
The order matters.
We do not destroy our idols so Jesus will finally love us.
We discover in Christ a love so overwhelming that our idols begin losing their claim upon us.
That is the difference between legalism and Gospel transformation.
Legalism says:
“Give this up so God might accept you.”
The Gospel says:
“In Christ, God has acted to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves. Now turn from your idols and come home.”
And perhaps that is why this story cuts so deeply.
Demetrius could recognize the economic consequences of conversion...
but apparently could not see the treasure standing behind it.
He could calculate what Artemis might lose.
He could calculate what the craftsmen might lose.
He could calculate what his trade might lose.
But Acts gives us no indication here that he stopped to ask:
What if Paul is right?
What if these objects really cannot save us?
What if the God Paul proclaims is actually God?
What if I have spent my life polishing silver while my soul was starving?
And now the story turns toward you.
Because perhaps there is something you are afraid Jesus will ask you to surrender.
Maybe nobody knows about it.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary well enough to keep it hidden.
You worship.
You pray.
You share verses.
You tell people God is good.
But there is one locked room inside you where you quietly whisper:
“Jesus, everything except this.”
And maybe this is exactly where the Gospel has found you today.
Not to humiliate you.
To free you.
The idol always promises something.
Security.
Pleasure.
Control.
Recognition.
Escape.
Love.
Power.
Money.
Approval.
And for a while, it may even appear to deliver.
That is why idols are seductive.
But eventually you discover the terrible bargain.
You thought you possessed it.
Then you discovered it possessed you.
Jesus does something radically different.
He exposes what enslaves us...
then offers Himself.
Not another shrine.
Not another transaction.
Not another religious product.
Himself.
The Son of God entered our broken world, lived without sin, went willingly to the cross, bore the judgment sinners deserve, died, was buried, and rose again.
Christianity does not announce that you can polish yourself until God finally accepts you.
It announces Christ crucified and risen.
Grace for the guilty.
Forgiveness for the repentant.
Life for the spiritually dead.
A King strong enough to destroy our idols without destroying the sinner who comes to Him for mercy.
That is why our theme will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the greedy.
He rewrites the sexually broken.
He rewrites the ashamed.
He rewrites the religious hypocrite.
He rewrites the addict.
He rewrites the proud.
He rewrites the person who wasted years worshiping something that could never love them back.
And maybe today He is confronting the little silver shrine hidden inside your own heart.
What are you terrified Christianity might cost you?
There.
Do not run from that question.
Sit with it.
Because sometimes the thing we are most afraid to surrender is the thing revealing where our deepest worship has gone.
If following Jesus never threatens anything in us except our Sunday schedule, we should examine what we mean by following Jesus.
The Gospel is free.
Discipleship is not weightless.
Jesus told His followers to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him.
But here is the beautiful paradox:
Whatever Christ calls us to surrender can never compare with Christ Himself.
Demetrius feared losing an industry built around representations of a goddess.
The Christian receives something no silversmith could manufacture:
reconciliation with the living God.
You cannot forge that.
You cannot purchase it.
You cannot mass-produce it.
You cannot earn it.
Grace must be received.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Maybe you have spent years protecting something Jesus has been exposing.
Maybe you are exhausted from maintaining two lives—the one everyone sees and the one only God knows.
Come into the light.
Repentance is not God standing over you waiting to crush you.
For the one who comes to Christ, repentance is turning away from the grave because Someone has opened the door toward life.
Jesus already knows what is behind your locked door.
And the cross proves He is not frightened by the ugliness of sinners.
He came for sinners.
So confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Ask for help where help is needed.
Turn toward Christ.
Let those words become more than engagement.
Let them become a line in the sand.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting through the night.
That matters.
Not because supporting a ministry proves that you glorify God—Scripture does not permit us to turn grace into a transaction. We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives shaped by obedient love.

More importantly, the purpose is deeper discipleship: continued biblical nourishment, spiritual sharpening, accountability, encouragement, and resources designed to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
Pray.
Pray that we never build another religious marketplace around Jesus while forgetting Jesus Himself.
Pray that truth matters more than reach.
Pray that Scripture matters more than applause.
Pray that souls matter more than numbers.
Pray that Christ remains at the center.
Because the deepest warning in Demetrius's story is not simply that a man loved money.
It is that the arrival of truth threatened a world he had learned to profit from.
And every one of us must eventually decide what happens when Jesus threatens the world we have learned to protect.
Maybe your Ephesus is not a city.
Maybe it is your heart.
Maybe your Artemis is not a statue.
Maybe it has a password.
A paycheck.
A person's name.
A secret folder.
A title.
A memory.
A craving.
Maybe nobody else can see the shrine.
Jesus can.
And He is not asking you to replace one handmade god with another.
He is calling you to Himself.
So when Christ puts His finger on your idol, do not start a riot inside your soul trying to protect what is killing you.
Open your hands.
Let the silver fall.
Come to Jesus.
Because the idol you are terrified to lose may be the very thing keeping you from discovering how completely Christ is enough.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MARY DIDN’T RECOGNIZE THE RISEN JESUS UNTIL HE SAID ONE WORD: “MARY.”
paragraphs: MARY DIDN’T RECOGNIZE THE RISEN JESUS UNTIL HE SAID ONE WORD: “MARY.”
She saw the empty tomb. She saw angels. She even saw Jesus standing in front of her—and still did not recognize Him. Then the risen Christ spoke her name.
There are moments when grief becomes so loud that even a miracle can stand directly in front of you and you cannot see it.
Mary Magdalene knew something about that kind of morning.
She came to a tomb looking for a dead Jesus.
Instead, she found an empty grave.

But before we rush to Easter celebration, before we imagine sunlight pouring across the garden and triumphant music swelling in the background, Scripture forces us to remain for a moment with a woman who is crying.
Mary stood outside the tomb weeping.
Not worshiping.
Not celebrating.
Weeping.
The resurrection had already happened, but Mary was still crying as though death had won.
Think about that.
Jesus was alive.
The stone had been moved.
The grave had been defeated.
History had already changed forever.
And Mary did not know it yet.
Maybe that is why this story reaches so deeply into the human heart.
Because sometimes God has already begun doing something we cannot yet see.
Sometimes we are crying beside an empty tomb.
Sometimes we are asking God why He allowed something while standing inches away from evidence that He has not abandoned us.
Sometimes our circumstances are saying one thing while heaven is doing another.
Mary looked into the tomb and saw two angels.
Even that did not stop her tears.
They asked why she was crying.
Her answer exposes the wound inside her:
“They have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have put him.”
She wasn't searching for a theological explanation.
She wanted Jesus.
Then she turned.
And there He was.
Jesus Christ.
Alive.
Breathing.
Standing in the garden.
The One whose hands had been pierced.
The One who had carried the cross.
The One whose body had been wrapped and placed inside the tomb.
The One death could not hold.
Mary was looking directly at Him.
And Scripture says something almost unbearable:
She did not know it was Jesus.
The Greek text of John 20:14 says:
“καὶ θεωρεῖ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἑστῶτα, καὶ οὐκ ᾔδει ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν.”
She sees Jesus standing there, yet she does not know that it is Jesus.
There is something painfully familiar about that sentence.
Have you ever wondered where God was while your heart was breaking?
Have you ever prayed until you ran out of words?
Have you ever opened your Bible and felt nothing?
Have you ever worshiped while secretly wondering whether God had forgotten your address?
Have you ever watched something you prayed desperately to save fall apart anyway?
A marriage.
A friendship.
A dream.
A ministry.
A future you thought God had promised.
Maybe you buried someone you loved.
Maybe someone walked away.
Maybe the diagnosis came.
Maybe the betrayal came from someone you trusted.
Maybe you are smiling publicly while privately trying to understand why Jesus seems so difficult to recognize in this chapter of your life.
Mary understands.
She knew what it was to love Jesus and still stand confused in front of what appeared to be unbearable loss.
Then Jesus spoke to her.
“Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?”
Mary thought He was the gardener.
The gardener.
There is almost a holy ache in the irony.
She is asking the risen Lord where someone has taken the body of the risen Lord.
She is talking to the answer while asking where the answer went.
“Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have put him…”
She was willing to carry away His body herself.
She still thought she needed to rescue what she believed death had taken.
But Jesus did not give her a theological lecture.
He did not shame her for failing to recognize Him.
He did not say, “Mary, how can you still not understand?”
He did not begin by explaining resurrection doctrine.
According to John, the turning point comes with her name.
The Greek text preserves the moment with stunning simplicity:
“λέγει αὐτῇ Ἰησοῦς· Μαριάμ.”
Jesus says to her:
“Μαριάμ.”
Mariam.
Mary.
That was it.
Her name.
And suddenly the Gardener was her Lord.
Suddenly the stranger was Jesus.
Suddenly the grave was not the end of the story.
One moment she was searching for a corpse.
The next moment she was standing before the risen Christ.
What changed?
Jesus called her by name.
And this becomes even more beautiful when you remember something Jesus had already said earlier in John's Gospel.
The Good Shepherd “calls his own sheep by name.”
By name.
Christianity is not merely the announcement that there is a God somewhere beyond the stars.
The Gospel announces that the holy God against whom we have sinned came near to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
He knows His sheep.
He calls them.
He saves them.
Mary was not merely another crying woman outside another grave.
Jesus knew her.
And He knows you.
Not the polished version of you.
Not your Facebook version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the person you pretend to be when somebody asks, “How are you?” and you automatically answer, “I'm fine.”
He knows the name attached to the wounds nobody sees.
He knows what happened.
He knows what you did.
He knows what they did to you.
He knows the temptation you keep fighting.
He knows the sin you keep trying to excuse.
He knows the prayer you stopped praying because disappointment became easier than hope.
He knows the secret that makes you wonder whether grace could possibly reach someone like you.
And this is where the Gospel refuses to become sentimental.
Being known by Jesus is not permission to remain unchanged.
The risen Christ does not merely comfort sinners.
He saves sinners.
He calls us out of darkness.
He calls us to repentance.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost blood.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin and judgment. The innocent Son of God gave Himself for the guilty. He died and was buried.
And on the morning Mary stood weeping beside that tomb, death discovered that it could not keep Him.
Jesus rose.
Not metaphorically.
Not merely as an inspiring memory inside the hearts of His followers.
The Christian proclamation is bodily resurrection.
The crucified Jesus was alive.
That is why Mary's tears matter.
She wasn't comforted because someone told her to “think positive.”
She was transformed because the One she thought was dead was standing in front of her.
And then Mary answered Him.
John preserves her response:
“Ραββουνι.”
Rabboni.
John explains the word for his readers as “Teacher.”
But imagine the emotion compressed inside that response.
Recognition.
Shock.
Love.
Relief.
Wonder.
The voice she thought she would never hear again had spoken her name.
Maybe you need to hear the truth behind that moment today.
Your worst chapter does not get the final sentence if Christ is writing your story.
Your scandal does not have more authority than His grace.
Your failure is real.
Your sin is serious.
Your wounds may be deep.
Your consequences may not disappear overnight.
But none of those things is stronger than the crucified and risen Jesus.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples scattered.
Mary wept outside a tomb because she could not understand what God had done.
Yet resurrection morning became a declaration that human failure, Satan, sin, shame, graves, and death itself do not get the last word over those who belong to Christ.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Not because scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because consequences never hurt.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes guilty people and offers forgiveness.
He takes rebels and makes them sons and daughters.
He takes people hiding in shame and clothes them in His righteousness.
He takes broken lives and makes them testimonies of mercy.
He takes people standing beside graves and sends them away carrying resurrection news.
And that is exactly what happened to Mary.
Jesus did not allow the encounter to terminate in private emotion.
He sent her.
“Go…”
And Mary went to the disciples carrying words that would echo across history:
“I have seen the Lord!”
Notice the movement.
She came grieving.
She encountered Jesus.
Jesus called her.
Then Jesus sent her.
That is discipleship.
We encounter Christ not merely so that we can privately feel better, but so that our lives can testify that He is Lord.
Maybe somebody in your world is standing beside their own tomb right now.
They still believe the story is over.
They still think their addiction has won.
They still believe their marriage is beyond prayer.
They still think their past disqualifies them.
They still think Christianity is nothing more than religious performance.
They still think Jesus wants nothing to do with people like them.
Maybe they would never walk into a church.
But they might read something you share because they trust you.
So if this article reminded you that Jesus Christ is alive, don't treat sharing it merely as an algorithmic favor to Gospel Warrior.
Think of a name.
One person.
That exhausted believer.
That prodigal son.
That daughter quietly falling apart.
That friend who stopped going to church.
That relative who says they no longer believe.
That person whose posts look happy while you know something underneath them is hurting.
Not to embarrass them.
Because sometimes love refuses to remain silent.
There may come a morning when you are the one crying beside an empty tomb, and you will need to remember that inability to see what Christ is doing does not mean Christ is absent.
Or tell your testimony.
Tell someone how Jesus met you in your own impossible chapter.
Your comment might become the sentence another hurting person needs to read tonight.
Supporting Gospel work is one practical way believers can participate in spreading biblical truth. But let's keep the order right: we do not purchase God's favor. We cannot buy His blessing.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
But grace creates generosity.
And there is another reason to stay close.
Then invite someone with you.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe at all.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is standing emotionally where Mary stood.
Crying.
Confused.
Searching.
Convinced something precious has been taken forever.
Maybe that someone is you.
And perhaps the most important truth you carry away from this garden is not simply that Mary eventually recognized Jesus.
It is that Jesus already knew Mary before Mary recognized Jesus.
He knew exactly where she was.
He knew why she was crying.
He knew what she was searching for.
And He knew her name.
The risen Christ was closer than her grief allowed her to understand.
So when heaven seems silent…
when prayers seem unanswered…
when the stone is already moved but you still cannot understand what God is doing…
when you find yourself asking where Jesus went…
remember the garden.
Remember the tears.
Remember the supposed gardener.
Remember the empty grave.
Remember the voice.
“Μαριάμ.”
Mary.
And remember what happened next.
She turned.
Maybe that is where your story begins again too.
Not with pretending you never failed.
Not with denying your wounds.
Not with cleaning yourself up enough to deserve another chance.
But with turning toward Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who conquered the grave.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who still turns graves into places from which testimonies walk away.
And if you belong to Him, your darkest chapter is not your identity.
Jesus is.
Your scandal may explain where you have been.
His grace declares whose you are.

The grave Mary thought had stolen Jesus became the place where she discovered that death had lost Him—and sometimes the place where you think your story ended is exactly where Christ begins teaching you what resurrection means.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Version of You Everyone Applauds May Be the Version of You God Is Asking You to Stop Performing
paragraphs: The Version of You Everyone Applauds May Be the Version of You God Is Asking You to Stop Performing
What if the most dangerous mask you wear is the one people call “godly”—and what if Jesus loves you too much to let you keep hiding behind it?
There is a version of you that people may love.
The strong version.
The faithful version.
The one who knows what verse to quote when somebody is hurting.
The one who posts Scripture.
The one who says, “God is good,” even when your heart feels like it is collapsing somewhere nobody can see.
The one who serves.
The one who gives.
The one who prays beautifully.
The one people message when their faith is falling apart.
And perhaps the frightening part is this:
Everybody thinks that version of you is doing fine.
Maybe they even admire you.
But God sees the room after everyone leaves.
He sees the phone placed facedown.
The smile disappearing.
The prayer that never gets prayed.
The temptation nobody knows about.
The resentment buried beneath Christian vocabulary.
The secret need to be noticed.
The exhaustion of maintaining an image you are terrified to disappoint.
The private compromises.
The hunger for approval.
The shame.
The loneliness.
The question you would never say at church:
“God… do You still want me when I am not impressive?”
And into that hidden room walks Jesus.
Not the Jesus we sometimes manufacture for public consumption.
Not a mascot for religious success.
Not Someone impressed by polished appearances.
Jesus Christ—the One before whom every mask becomes unnecessary.
And His words in Matthew 6 are uncomfortable precisely because they are spoken to people doing apparently righteous things.
Giving.
Praying.
Seeking God.
These are not obvious acts of rebellion.
That is what makes His warning terrifying.
Jesus says:
“Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them.”
Matthew 6:1
The Greek expression translated “to be seen by them” is πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς—pros to theathēnai autois.
That verb, θεαθῆναι (theathēnai), comes from θεάομαι (theaomai), carrying the idea of being seen, observed, or looked upon.
Jesus puts His finger on something painfully human.
It is possible to do something righteous while secretly craving an audience.
It is possible to speak about God while wanting people to notice us.
It is possible to serve Jesus while becoming addicted to the reputation that serving Jesus gives us.
It is possible to appear spiritually alive while slowly starving inside.
And before we turn this into an accusation against somebody else, perhaps we should sit with the question ourselves.
Who are you when nobody is watching?
Not who does Facebook think you are.
Not who your church thinks you are.
Not who your family thinks you are.
Not who your followers think you are.
Who are you before God?
Because religious reputation can become an idol when protecting the appearance of righteousness becomes more important than living truthfully before the God who sees the hidden person.
Jesus continues:
“Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do…”
Matthew 6:2
The Greek word translated “hypocrites” is ὑποκριταί—hypokritai.

Historically, the related Greek word could refer to an actor or performer. In the New Testament, however, the word carries the moral force of hypocrisy—someone whose outward presentation and inward reality do not agree.
That makes the warning disturbingly personal.
Because spiritual performance does not always look fake.
Sometimes it looks magnificent.
Sometimes people applaud it.
Sometimes people share it.
Sometimes people call it anointing.
Sometimes the performer himself eventually forgets he is performing.
You learn the vocabulary.
You learn when to raise your hands.
You learn what testimony is safe enough to tell.
You learn how much brokenness to reveal without damaging the image.
You learn how to say, “I’m trusting God,” when what you really want to say is:
“I’m exhausted.”
“I’m angry.”
“I’m jealous.”
“I’m struggling with lust.”
“I haven't forgiven them.”
“My prayer life is almost nonexistent.”
“I feel numb when I worship.”
“I keep returning to the same sin.”
“I am terrified people will discover that the person they admire is not the person I see when I am alone.”
So you keep performing.
Because applause is easier than exposure.
Reputation feels safer than repentance.
And being admired can become easier than being known.
But Jesus does something astonishing in this passage.
He repeatedly redirects our attention away from the audience and toward the Father.
When you give secretly, Jesus says:
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
Matthew 6:4
When you pray, He says:
“Go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret.”
Matthew 6:6
And again:
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
There is a beautiful phrase underneath those words:
ὁ πατήρ σου ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ
ho patēr sou ho blepōn en tō kryptō
“Your Father who sees in secret.”
Read that again.
Your Father sees.
Not merely your congregation.
Not your followers.
Not the people impressed by you.
Not the people disappointed in you.
Your Father sees.
He sees what nobody applauds.
He sees the prayer whispered through tears.
He sees you closing the browser.
He sees you choosing not to send the message.
He sees the money given quietly.
He sees the apology nobody online will ever know you made.
He sees you opening Scripture when your emotions tell you nothing is happening.
He sees the battle behind the testimony.
He sees the trembling repentance behind the smile.
He sees the Christian who is tired of pretending.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear something Christianity never gives us permission to forget:
God's answer to hypocrisy is not better acting.
It is truth and repentance.
The Gospel does not say, “Become convincing enough that nobody notices your sin.”
The Gospel says that sinners may come into the light because Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the story of impressive people finally becoming worthy of God.
It is the story of a holy God showing mercy to guilty people through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, your reputation cannot save you.
Your ministry cannot save you.
Your Bible knowledge cannot save you.
Your followers cannot save you.
Your charitable giving cannot save you.
Your Christian vocabulary cannot save you.
Your parents' faith cannot save you.
Your church attendance cannot save you.
Only Christ saves.
Jesus carried sin to the cross, died, and rose again.
The scandal of grace is that the person underneath your carefully managed image is precisely the person Christ commands to repent, believe, and come to Him.
You do not have to clean the mask.
You can put it down.
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps you have spent years building a version of yourself that everybody loves.
And now Jesus is asking for the person underneath it.
The frightened person.
The angry person.
The addicted person.
The insecure person.
The person who secretly loves human approval.
The person who has preached truths he has struggled to live.
The woman everyone calls strong who cries where nobody can hear her.
The father who prays over his children but privately wonders why his own heart feels so far from God.
The worship leader singing about surrender while protecting one locked room of the soul.
The pastor feeding everyone while quietly starving.
The young believer terrified that asking honest questions will make everyone think his faith is weak.
The Christian posting about peace while having panic-filled nights.
The person everyone assumes is spiritually successful.
You.
Not your brand.
Not your reputation.
You.
Jesus wants truth in the hidden place.
And this is where grace becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
The One who sees the secret place is also the One who went to the cross.
The God from whom nothing is hidden is the God who made a way for sinners to be forgiven.
So confession is not handing new information to God.
He already knows.
Confession is agreeing with God about what we have been hiding and bringing it into the light.
Repentance is not another performance.
It is surrender.
It says:
“Jesus, I am finished defending what You are asking me to forsake.”
Maybe nobody else knows what that sentence means for you.
God does.
Perhaps it means admitting that your public Christianity has become stronger than your private communion with Christ.
Perhaps it means confessing hidden sin.
Perhaps it means forgiving someone.
Perhaps it means seeking help.
Perhaps it means admitting that you enjoy being thought holy more than you enjoy actually being alone with God.
Perhaps your greatest spiritual danger right now is not that people think too little of you.
Maybe it is that they think so highly of you that you have become afraid to tell the truth.
But what if losing the performance is not losing yourself?
What if it is finally allowing Christ to deal with the real you?
There is freedom in no longer needing to convince everyone that you are okay.
There is freedom in praying when nobody knows.
Giving when nobody applauds.
Repenting without turning repentance into content.
Obeying without announcing it.
Serving without needing recognition.
Opening Scripture without photographing the Bible first.
Worshiping without wondering who noticed.
There is freedom when Jesus becomes enough of an audience.
And there is something profoundly healing about realizing that the Father who sees in secret is not fooled by your best day or surprised by your worst one.
The answer is not to become careless about holiness.
Quite the opposite.
Grace does not make sin insignificant.
Grace makes repentance possible.
The same Christ who forgives calls us to follow Him.
The same Gospel that removes condemnation begins transforming the person who believes.
Grace is not permission to keep the mask.
