Grace gives us somewhere safe to put it down.
No performance.
No Christian answer designed to impress anybody.
Just you before God.
What are you exhausted from pretending?
What part of your spiritual reputation have you become afraid to lose?
What would change if you cared more about being known by God than being admired by people?
And what is Jesus asking you to bring into the light?
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “no more hiding.”
Not because typing three words saves you.
Jesus saves.
But perhaps those words can become your public acknowledgment that you are finished pretending everything is fine.
If your spirit is exhausted and you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ has already begun dismantling an old version of you and rebuilding your life through grace, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And read the other comments.
Pray for someone.
Encourage someone.
Remind someone that repentance is not the end of their story.
Maybe somebody needs your testimony more than they need another polished Christian performance.
Not to expose them.
To remind them they do not have to carry the mask alone.
Not as proof that you are spiritual.
That would miss everything Jesus just taught us.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ—not through purchasing access to a page.
There may come a night when applause feels empty and the mask becomes unbearably heavy.
Come back and remember Matthew 6.
Your Father sees in secret.
Because somewhere tonight there may be a Christian surrounded by people who admire a version of them they can barely keep alive.
They do not need another lesson in pretending.
They need Jesus.
They need repentance.
They need grace.
They need to discover that being exposed before the mercy of Christ can be infinitely better than being applauded behind a mask.
The world may applaud the performance.
Jesus came for the person underneath it.
And perhaps the greatest scandal is this:
When the mask finally falls, grace does not run away.
Christ calls you into the light.
And when Jesus gets hold of the truth you were terrified to reveal, the collapse of your performance may become the beginning of your freedom.
You spent years protecting the version of you everyone applauded—while Jesus was waiting in the secret place for the person underneath.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE COULD MARRY WHOM SHE WANTED—BUT HER LAND COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING
paragraphs: SHE COULD MARRY WHOM SHE WANTED—BUT HER LAND COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING

Numbers 36 contains one of the Bible’s most easily misunderstood marriage laws. Behind it are five women, a dead father, inherited land, a threatened legacy—and a truth about grace that reaches all the way to Jesus Christ.
Imagine being told that you have received something generations before you prayed for.
Land.
Not merely property.
Not an investment.
Not a piece of real estate you could casually sell when the market improved.
This land carried your father’s name.
Your family’s history.
Your tribe’s inheritance.
It was connected to promises older than you were.
Then one day, people began asking a question that could change everything:
What happens when you fall in love?
That is where Numbers 36 takes us.
And if you have ever read this chapter quickly and thought, “So women in Israel were simply told whom they were allowed to marry,” stay with this story.
Because that is not quite what the text says.
The real situation is far more specific.
And far more fascinating.
Five women stand quietly behind Numbers 36: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah—the daughters of Zelophehad.
Their father had died without a son.

Earlier, in Numbers 27, these women had done something remarkable. They came before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders, and the congregation and asked why their father’s name should disappear simply because he had no son.
Their question was essentially:
Why should our father lose his inheritance because his children are daughters?
Moses did not dismiss them.
He brought their case before the LORD.
And God answered.
Their request was right.
They would receive their father’s inheritance.
Five daughters who might have been overlooked suddenly stood holding something extraordinarily significant: an ancestral inheritance in the Promised Land.
But then came the complication.
Numbers 36 opens with leaders from the clan of Manasseh approaching Moses.
They were not arguing that the daughters should lose the inheritance God had given them.
Their concern was what might happen to that inheritance afterward.
If one of these daughters married a man belonging to another Israelite tribe, her inherited land could become connected with the tribe into which she married.
Over time, land allotted to Manasseh could effectively pass into another tribe.
The concern was therefore bigger than one wedding.
It involved the preservation of Israel’s tribal allotments.
That is why the Hebrew word repeated throughout the chapter matters so much:
נַחֲלָה — naḥalah
Inheritance.
Possession.
Hereditary portion.
Numbers 36 is not primarily a chapter about controlling romance.
It is about protecting נַחֲלָה—an inheritance belonging within the covenant structure God had established for Israel.
Then comes the line that changes how the entire passage should be understood.
God says concerning Zelophehad’s daughters:
לַטּוֹב בְּעֵינֵיהֶם תִּהְיֶינָה לְנָשִׁים
La-tov be'eineihem tihyeynah le-nashim.
In context:
They may marry whom they consider good.
There is choice here.
But the sentence continues:
אַךְ לְמִשְׁפַּחַת מַטֵּה אֲבִיהֶם תִּהְיֶינָה לְנָשִׁים
Ach le-mishpaḥat matteh avihem tihyeynah le-nashim.
“Only/provided that they marry within the clan of their father’s tribe.”
That little Hebrew word אַךְ — ach matters.
It introduces the qualification.

They could choose whom they wished to marry—but because they were inheriting ancestral land, their choice had to remain within the boundary that would preserve that inheritance within their father’s tribe.
This was not a blanket declaration that every woman in Israel could marry only a man from her own tribe.
Numbers 36:8 identifies the particular situation:
וְכָל־בַּת יֹרֶשֶׁת נַחֲלָה
Ve-khol bat yoreshēt naḥalah...
“Every daughter who inherits an inheritance...”
That is the issue.
An heiress of tribal land.
Her marriage had consequences reaching beyond the household she was creating because the land she possessed represented a portion of Israel’s tribal inheritance.
And suddenly this obscure chapter begins breathing.
Because the question underneath Numbers 36 is not merely:
“Who are you going to marry?”
The deeper question is:
What will happen to what has been entrusted to you?
That question reaches farther than ancient Israel.
Some things in your hands did not begin with you.
Someone prayed before you knew how to pray.
Someone carried a Bible before you could read one.
Someone endured suffering that made your present possible.
Someone told you about Jesus.
Someone refused to abandon the faith.
Someone planted something whose fruit you are eating today.
And now something has reached your hands.
What will you do with it?

Numbers 36 should not be carelessly turned into a direct command that Christians today must reproduce Israel’s tribal land laws. Christians are not divided into Israel’s territorial tribal allotments, and the New Testament does not command Christian women who own property to marry within an ancestral tribe.
We must never force an Old Testament civil arrangement into a command God has not given the Church.
But the theological heartbeat underneath the story still confronts us:
God takes stewardship seriously.
What He entrusts to us matters.
And sometimes obedience means realizing that our decisions are bigger than the moment in which we make them.
That is uncomfortable.
Because our generation loves the sentence:
“It’s my life.”
Scripture repeatedly asks another question:
Who gave you that life?
“My money.”
Who gave you strength to earn?
“My time.”
Who numbered your days?
“My gifts.”
Who gave them?
“My platform.”
Who allowed your voice to reach anyone?
“My future.”
Who holds tomorrow?
And then comes the most devastating question of all:
“My soul?”
Who created it?
Who came looking for it when sin had dragged it into darkness?
This is where the road from Numbers 36 eventually forces the Christian heart to look beyond land.
Beyond Manasseh.
Beyond Zelophehad.
Beyond Moses.
Toward Christ.
Because the Bible’s story becomes the story of an inheritance far greater than acreage.
Peter describes believers as receiving an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for them (1 Peter 1:3–4).
Paul says that in Christ we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of His grace (Ephesians 1:7).
Do you see the movement?
Human beings were created for God.
Sin entered.
We rebelled.
We wandered.
We treated holy things cheaply.
We acted as though the life God gave us belonged exclusively to us.
And the inheritance we could never earn became ours only because Someone else paid the price.
Jesus Christ.
Not with silver.
Not with land.
Not with political power.
Not with religious performance.
With His blood.
At the cross, the Son of God took upon Himself the judgment sinners deserved.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The Holy One was mocked.
The King wore thorns.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by humanity.
And while sinners had spent their lives squandering what God had given them, Christ opened the way home.
That is the scandal.
And this is grace.
You may have wasted years.
Grace says Jesus can redeem what remains.
You may have destroyed trust.
Grace says repentance can begin today.
You may have carried secret sin so long that hiding feels normal.
Grace says come into the light.
You may know Scripture publicly while compromising privately.
Grace says stop performing and come back to Christ.
You may feel that you have already ruined your spiritual inheritance.
Look again at the cross.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to preserve themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Maybe that is why this ancient story about five women and inherited land can still make the heart uncomfortable.
Because sooner or later, every one of us must answer:
What am I doing with what God has placed in my hands?
Your children are watching.
Your friends are watching.
People who will never tell you they are struggling may be watching what you share.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be smiling in photographs while privately wondering whether God still wants them.
Someone may be addicted and hiding it.
Someone may have stopped praying.
Someone may be carrying shame from something nobody knows.
Someone may be one Gospel message away from finally asking, “Jesus, can You really forgive me?”
So do not underestimate something as simple as sharing truth.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
Send this to the believer who is struggling to remain faithful.

Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Scripture is nothing more than a collection of strange ancient rules. Let them see that context matters, that words matter, that truth deserves more than a screenshot and a slogan.
There will come a day when you need to remember that what God entrusts to us should not be treated casually.
What has God entrusted to you that you are afraid you have neglected?
Your family?
Your faith?
Your calling?
Your testimony?
Your time?
Your influence?
Your relationship with Christ?
If conviction is hitting somewhere you cannot explain publicly, simply write:
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer sees and realizes, “I am not the only one fighting this battle.”
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to produce content.
To keep putting Scripture in front of people.
To call sinners toward Jesus.
To strengthen tired believers.
To remind wounded Christians that conviction is not an invitation to run away from God but to run toward the mercy found in Christ.
To keep proclaiming repentance, forgiveness, redemption, restoration, and the Gospel in a world drowning in noise.
Scripture does not give us permission to make that claim.
It cannot.
Christ purchased our redemption. We do not.
But Christian generosity is biblical.
Supporting Gospel work is biblical.
Giving willingly, prayerfully, cheerfully, and according to what God has placed in your hands is biblical.

If you desire to glorify God through your resources, ask Him prayerfully where and how He wants you to give. And if Gospel Warrior is one of the ministries you believe is faithfully helping people encounter Scripture and Jesus Christ, we would be deeply grateful for your support.
More importantly, stay for the discipleship.
Stay for Scripture.
Stay because scrolling gives you thousands of voices every day, but your soul needs truth.
Give Christ your heart.
Because money can support a ministry.
A share can spread a message.
A comment can encourage another believer.
But none of those things can substitute for surrender.
Jesus does not merely want a transaction.
He calls us to Himself.
Mahlah.
Noah.
Hoglah.
Milcah.
Tirzah.
Five names near the end of Numbers.
Five women entrusted with an inheritance.
They obeyed the command given concerning that inheritance, marrying within the clans of Manasseh, and Scripture closes the matter with a quiet statement:
Their inheritance remained within the tribe of their father’s clan.
The inheritance remained.
Thousands of years later, perhaps that is the sentence we need haunting us in the best possible way.
What will remain after us?
Not our follower count.
Not our applause.
Not the image we carefully maintained.
Not the arguments we won online.
What will our children remember about our faith?
What will people who knew us say we loved?
Did we merely speak about Jesus?
Or did we belong to Him?
Did we preserve an appearance while privately surrendering our hearts to sin?
Or when we fell, did we repent, get back up, and run again toward Christ?
The daughters of Zelophehad had an inheritance worth protecting.
Christian, so do you.
Not a tribal field bordered by stones.

You have received the Gospel—the news that the crucified Christ rose from the dead, that sinners can be forgiven, that shame does not have to write the final chapter, that repentance is possible, that grace is real, and that Jesus still transforms lives.
Protect the truth.
Pass it on.
Live it.
And when you fail, do not rewrite the Gospel to make your sin comfortable.
Run back to the Savior who shed His blood to make sinners clean.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy is not that something precious was once broken.
Perhaps the greater tragedy would be standing before grace with broken pieces in your hands...
and refusing to let Jesus have them.
You may think your worst chapter has already determined the ending—but nail-scarred hands are still holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A CHRISTIAN MAN WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE—AND THE CHURCH WAS BOASTING
paragraphs: A CHRISTIAN MAN WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE—AND THE CHURCH WAS BOASTING
Paul was horrified by the sexual scandal. But what he said next reveals something even more frightening: the church had learned to live comfortably beside what should have broken its heart.
Imagine the letter being opened in church.
People gather.
Believers who know the songs. Believers who know the language. Believers who can talk about grace, spiritual gifts, wisdom, freedom, and the power of God.
Then Paul's words are read aloud.
And suddenly the room gets uncomfortable.
Because somewhere among them is a man openly involved with his father's wife.
Paul does not whisper about it.
He does not dress it up.
He does not rename it so everyone can remain comfortable.
He writes:
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia…
In plain sense:
“Sexual immorality is actually being reported among you…”
Then comes the detail:
“ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.”
…so that a man has his father’s wife.
—1 Corinthians 5:1
Notice the precision.

Paul says “his father’s wife.” Scripture does not explicitly tell us that she was the man's biological mother, so we should not claim more than the text gives us. But the relationship itself was unmistakably forbidden. The Old Testament had already declared, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife” (Leviticus 18:8).
This was not a gray area.
This was not two Christians disagreeing about a secondary doctrine.
This was blatant sexual immorality inside the professing church.
Yet here is what makes the passage terrifying.
The man’s sin was not the only scandal.
The church’s response was.
Paul continues:
“καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ…”
Kai hymeis pephysiōmenoi este…
“And you are arrogant!”
The word carries the idea of being puffed up.
Inflated.
Proud.
Paul looks at a church where serious sexual sin is being tolerated and essentially asks:
Why are you puffed up?
Why aren't you grieving?
He says they should have mourned.
That changes the temperature of the entire passage.
Because biblical holiness is not supposed to produce people who enjoy discovering someone else's sin.
It produces grief.
There is a difference between mourning sin and enjoying scandal.
There is a difference between confronting someone because you love Christ and exposing someone because you love attention.
There is a difference between holiness and self-righteousness.
Paul does not sound entertained.
He sounds heartbroken.
And perhaps this is where the ancient scandal in Corinth suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because we live in a world where scandal has become entertainment.
A marriage collapses.
People watch.
A pastor falls.
People share clips.
A Christian is exposed.
Someone confesses sexual sin.
Screenshots travel faster than prayers.
And sometimes the people shouting loudest about another person's darkness have carefully hidden rooms of their own.
But 1 Corinthians 5 will not let us hide behind someone else's scandal.
It turns the light around.
It asks:
What have you learned to tolerate?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe you still quote Scripture.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you raise your hands during worship while carrying something into God's presence that you have already decided you will not surrender.
Pornography.
An affair.
Secret messages.
Bitterness.
Dishonesty.
A relationship you know dishonors Christ.
A private addiction.
A double life.
A compromise you once resisted but now defend.
At first, your conscience screamed.
Then it whispered.
Then you learned how to worship over the noise.
That is one of sin's most frightening victories.
Not merely when you fall.
But when falling stops frightening you.
Not merely when you sin.
But when you become comfortable protecting what Jesus died to free you from.
Please understand what Paul is not teaching.
He is not telling Christians to become obsessed with policing unbelievers.

Later in this very chapter he makes the distinction clear. His immediate concern is someone who bears the name “brother” while persisting in serious, unrepentant sin. Paul explicitly distinguishes the church's responsibility toward those inside from God's judgment of those outside.
The church was never commissioned to stand outside the hospital screaming at sick people for being sick.
We were commissioned to proclaim the Physician.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the grave.
Calling sinners everywhere not to pretend, but to repent and believe.
And repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace finds us in the darkness and we finally stop arguing with the Light.
That is why Paul's severe instruction concerning the Corinthian man must not be reduced to revenge.
His words are shocking:
“παραδοῦναι τὸν τοιοῦτον τῷ Σατανᾷ…”
“To deliver such a one to Satan…”
But keep reading.
Paul gives a purpose:
“…ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ…”
“…so that the spirit may be saved…”
—1 Corinthians 5:5
Even discipline has redemption in view.
Even confrontation is supposed to look toward salvation.
The goal is not, “Destroy this disgusting sinner.”
The goal is that sin loses its hiding place, false security collapses, repentance becomes possible, and the sinner is driven back toward the mercy of Christ.
That is an enormous difference.
Biblical church discipline is not permission for cruelty.
It is not spiritual entertainment.
It is not gossip wearing a prayer-request costume.
It is not humiliation for clicks.
It is love refusing to call spiritual poison harmless.
Imagine a doctor discovering aggressive cancer and saying:
“I don't want to make you uncomfortable, so I'll call it a personality difference.”
That would not be compassion.
A love that refuses to tell the truth when someone's destruction is approaching is not the love Scripture describes.
But neither is truth without love.
Jesus gives us something infinitely better than both sentimental tolerance and merciless condemnation.
Grace and truth meet in Him.
And that brings us to the deepest wound in this story.
The Corinthian church had apparently become capable of boasting while corruption remained among them.
Paul answers with an image everybody who understood bread would recognize:
“μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ.”
A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
Sin rarely asks permission to destroy everything at once.
It begins smaller.
One compromise.
One hidden conversation.
One image.
One lie.
One rationalization.
One secret.
One sentence:
“It's not that serious.”
Then another:
“God understands.”
Then another:
“Everybody struggles.”
And yes—God understands.
Yes—Christians struggle.
Yes—grace is greater than our sin.
But none of those glorious truths means sin should become our protected roommate.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could make peace treaties with the chains He came to break.
Paul suddenly brings the entire discussion to Christ:
“καὶ γὰρ τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν ἐτύθη Χριστός.”
“For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”
There.
That is the center.
Not the scandalous man.
Not the embarrassed church.
Not even Paul.
Christ.
The Lamb.
The Cross.
The blood.
The sacrifice.
The possibility that guilty people can actually become clean.
Christianity does not say, “Clean yourself up so Jesus might love you.”
Christianity announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
But the grace that receives us in our filth does not celebrate leaving us there.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus breaks chains.
Jesus teaches forgiven sinners how to walk in the light.
Maybe that is why this chapter bothers us so deeply.
We would rather choose one of two comfortable lies.
Either:
“Sin doesn't really matter because God is gracious.”
Or:
“You sinned badly, so there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel destroys both.
At the Cross, God shows us that sin is so serious that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And at that same Cross, God shows us that His mercy is so astonishing that sinners who deserve judgment can be forgiven through Christ.
Your sin is more serious than your excuses tell you.
And Christ's grace is greater than your shame tells you.
Both are true.
Maybe you are reading this carrying something nobody knows.
Something happened last night.
Or five years ago.
Maybe you have begged God for forgiveness and still wake up remembering it.
Maybe you are not the person committing the scandal.
Maybe you are the person wounded by someone else's.
You were betrayed.
Cheated on.
Lied to.
Used.
Manipulated.
Humiliated.
And somebody used the language of “grace” to pressure you into pretending it didn't hurt.
That is not what this passage requires.
Grace does not call evil good.
Forgiveness does not require calling betrayal harmless.
Restoration does not mean abandoning wisdom, accountability, truth, or appropriate boundaries.
Jesus does not heal us by rewriting evil into something innocent.
He rewrites us.
That is what makes grace so breathtaking.
The Gospel does not need a sanitized past to create a redeemed future.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ was dying under criminal judgment.
Paul had persecuted the church.
Corinth was filled with people whose former lives included devastating sins, yet only one chapter later Paul could speak of their past and then say:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
There may be no more beautiful past-tense word in the Christian life.
Were.
Not because they became morally impressive enough to erase their histories.
Paul continues with what God had done:
They were washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for never becoming scandalous.
Dead people receiving life.
Dirty people being washed.
Guilty people being justified.
Captives being freed.
Prodigals coming home.
Sinners discovering that the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are stronger than the hands of their past.
So if this article exposed something hidden, do not run farther into darkness.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek trustworthy biblical accountability.
Make necessary changes.
Bring what is hidden into appropriate light.
If another person is endangered, abused, exploited, or victimized, seeking proper protection and lawful help is not a betrayal of grace.
And do not confuse repentance with merely feeling terrible.
Judas felt remorse.
Peter wept bitterly.
But Peter came back to Jesus.
Repentance turns.
It stops defending darkness and starts walking toward Christ.
You may stumble on that road.
You may need help.
You may have consequences to face.
Grace does not always remove consequences.
But consequences are not proof that Christ has abandoned the repentant sinner.
Sometimes the most painful chapter of your life becomes the place where pretending finally dies.
And when pretending dies, healing can begin.
Not because strangers need the details of your private sin.
They don't.
You do not owe the internet your confession.
But perhaps those three words can become your declaration:
No more hiding from Jesus.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the Light.
And if this made you think of someone who is quietly drifting from Christ, don't use this article as a weapon against them.
Send it with love.
One share can place the Gospel in front of a person you may never realize needed it that night.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions difficult to remember tomorrow.
Come back when compromise starts sounding reasonable.
Come back when shame tells you Jesus could never receive you.
Come back when somebody else's scandal tempts you to become proud.
And remember:
The appropriate Christian response to sin is neither applause nor self-righteous delight.
It is truth.
Grief.
Repentance.
Holiness.
Grace.
And Jesus.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But one practical way you can help Gospel-centered teaching reach more people is by supporting the work that produces and distributes it.

And comment—not to feed an algorithm with empty words, but to make the comment section a place where people see that Christians still believe repentance is possible, grace is real, and Jesus still restores sinners.
Because somewhere tonight, someone believes their scandal is the final sentence of their story.
It isn't.
The Cross stands between what you were and what Christ can make you.
And perhaps the line you need to carry away from Corinth is this:
Jesus does not expose darkness because He delights in your shame; He calls you into the light because He refuses to leave you buried where grace came to find you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A PASTOR HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES AND GIRLFRIENDS?
paragraphs:
CAN A PASTOR HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES AND GIRLFRIENDS?
The Biblical Answer May Cost Someone Their Pulpit—But It Could Save a Church From Calling Scandal “Grace”
There is a question Christians sometimes whisper because answering it publicly can become uncomfortable very quickly:
Can a pastor have multiple wives and girlfriends and still remain a pastor?
Imagine the scene.
Sunday morning.
The worship has ended. The lights soften. A man walks toward the pulpit carrying a Bible.
People trust him.

A struggling husband listens because he wants to become a better man. A young woman takes notes because she believes this pastor will teach her what godly love looks like. A teenager watches because he is still deciding whether Christianity is real. A wounded wife sits quietly in the congregation asking God to restore her faith after betrayal nearly destroyed her.
Then something comes to light.
The pastor has another woman.
Maybe more than one.
Maybe someone calls them “girlfriends.”
Maybe there are secret messages, hidden meetings, sexual relationships, another household, or even claims that Scripture permits him to have multiple wives.
And suddenly the question changes.
It is no longer merely:
“Is my pastor a gifted preacher?”
It becomes:
“Does the Bible permit the man teaching us holiness to live this way?”
That question deserves something better than gossip.
Better than denominational politics.
Better than cultural tradition.
Better than outrage on social media.
It deserves Scripture.
And Scripture speaks with uncomfortable clarity.
When Paul describes the qualifications of an overseer in 1 Timothy 3:2, the Greek text contains this striking expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra
Literally, the words are built around “one woman/wife” and “man/husband.”
Paul writes:
δεῖ οὖν τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίλημπτον εἶναι, μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα…
The sense is:
“Therefore, the overseer must be above reproach, a husband/man of one wife/woman…”
The Greek matters.
μιᾶς — mias — means “one.”
γυναικός — gynaikos — can mean “woman” or “wife,” depending upon context.
ἀνήρ / ἄνδρα — anēr / andra — can mean “man” or “husband.”
Paul repeats essentially the same requirement when instructing Titus about appointing elders:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ — mias gynaikos anēr.
Again:
A one-woman man.

This does not merely give us a mathematical formula for marital paperwork. The qualification sits inside a larger portrait of observable Christian character: above reproach, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not violent, not controlled by money, and capable of governing his household faithfully.
The pastor is not being asked merely:
“How many marriage certificates do you possess?”
Scripture is asking:
“What kind of man are you when nobody is applauding?”
That distinction matters.

Scholars and Christian traditions have debated some applications of “husband of one wife”—including questions involving widowers who remarry, divorce and remarriage, and whether Paul’s expression specifically prohibits polygamy or more broadly describes marital and sexual faithfulness.
But none of those debates provides a loophole for a married pastor maintaining girlfriends or sexual partners outside his marriage.
None.
Because Scripture does not leave sexual faithfulness hanging on one disputed phrase.
Paul gives another remarkably symmetrical command in 1 Corinthians 7:2:
ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω.
In context, Paul is addressing πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality.
Notice the symmetry.
Each man, his own wife.
Each woman, her own husband.
Not a pastor with a wife for church photographs and girlfriends for private pleasure.
Not holiness behind the microphone and secret sexuality behind a locked phone.
Not one covenant in daylight and another life after dark.

And before someone reaches into the Old Testament and says, “But David had multiple wives,” or, “Solomon had many wives,” we need to learn one of the most important principles of biblical interpretation:
The Bible recording something does not mean God is recommending it.
Scripture records murder.
That does not sanctify murder.
Scripture records deception.
That does not sanctify lying.
Scripture records adultery.
That does not turn adultery into discipleship.
And Scripture records polygamous households while repeatedly allowing us to see the jealousy, rivalry, fragmentation, favoritism, grief, and family disorder that so often followed.
If we want the clearest foundation for Christian marriage, we should not begin with fallen kings trying to satisfy fallen desires.
We should listen to Jesus.
Christ reaches behind human corruption and points back toward creation.
Genesis describes a man leaving father and mother, being joined to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
Jesus deliberately returns to that foundation when teaching about marriage.
Not:
“The powerful man accumulates women.”
But:
The two become one flesh.
This is where the issue becomes much deeper than denominational policy.
Marriage is covenant.
And Christian leadership is supposed to display a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
A pastor is not sinless.
Please hear that carefully.
If churches required sinless pastors, every pulpit on earth would be empty.
Pastors need grace too.
Pastors can be tempted.
Pastors can fall.
Pastors can confess.
Pastors can repent.
Pastors can be forgiven.
And yes—
Jesus can restore a fallen pastor as a brother even when restoration to pastoral office is a separate question.
Those two things must never be confused.
Forgiveness does not automatically mean qualification.
Grace does not require pretending consequences disappeared.
Repentance does not mean a congregation must immediately return someone to authority.

A man may be completely forgiven by Christ while still needing to step away from pastoral leadership because Scripture places serious character requirements upon those entrusted with shepherding Christ’s people.
That is not cruelty.
That is taking both grace and shepherding seriously.
This is where churches sometimes make devastating mistakes.
They become so frightened of appearing judgmental that they rename compromise “grace.”
Or they become so furious about scandal that they forget the Gospel entirely.
Neither response is Christian.
Truth without grace can become a weapon.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
Jesus gives us neither counterfeit.
Jesus gives grace that tells the truth and truth that leads sinners toward grace.

So if a married pastor is secretly maintaining girlfriends, committing adultery, engaging in sexual relationships outside his covenant marriage, deceiving his wife, deceiving the congregation, or using spiritual authority to obtain romantic or sexual access to women under his influence, the biblical question is not merely whether he can still preach a powerful sermon.
The question is whether his life presently satisfies the character required of an overseer.
“Above reproach.”
“One-woman man.”
“Self-controlled.”
“Respectable.”
Managing his household faithfully.
Those words become difficult to reconcile with an ongoing pattern of deception and sexual unfaithfulness.
And if spiritual authority has been used to manipulate women, silence victims, demand secrecy, or protect the leader’s reputation, the situation becomes even more serious.
A shepherd is entrusted with sheep.
He is not given sheep to consume.
But perhaps you are reading this and thinking about someone specific.
Maybe the pastor was someone you trusted.
Maybe you defended him.
Maybe you ignored warning signs because his preaching moved you.
Maybe you were told:
“Touch not God’s anointed.”
Maybe questioning leadership was treated as rebellion against God.
Maybe you were pressured to protect “the ministry.”
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not need sin hidden in order to protect His name.
Christ is not honored when darkness is covered with religious vocabulary.
The church belongs to Jesus.
Not to the pastor.
Not to the founder.
Not to the denomination.
Not to the charismatic personality whose face appears on every poster.
Jesus Christ purchased His people with His blood.
That means protecting a reputation can never become more sacred than protecting Christ’s flock.
And perhaps the person reading this is not the wounded church member.
Perhaps it is the pastor.
Brother…
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe there is a second phone.
A conversation you keep deleting.
A woman whose name you changed in your contacts.
A relationship you keep calling “emotional support” because admitting what it has become terrifies you.
Maybe nothing physical has happened yet.
But you know why you hide the messages.
You know why your wife cannot see them.
You know why you would panic if they appeared on the projector Sunday morning.
You preach repentance while negotiating with your own secret.
And every Sunday the microphone gets heavier.
There is still time to stop running.
Not because exposure is impossible.
Because grace is still available.
Jesus did not shed His blood only for respectable sinners.
He died for adulterers.
Liars.
Hypocrites.
Sexually broken people.
Religious people.
Secret sinners.
Public sinners.
People who destroyed things they once promised God they would protect.
The cross does not tell us sexual sin is insignificant.
The cross tells us sin was so serious that Christ died—and grace is so astonishing that sinners who repent and believe can be forgiven.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“Keep preaching until people forget.”
Not:
“Everybody makes mistakes.”
Not:
“God understands.”
Not:
“My calling excuses my conduct.”
The Gospel says:
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Stop manipulating.
Stop hiding.
Stop blaming your wife.
Stop blaming ministry pressure.
Stop blaming loneliness.
Stop using David’s failures to baptize your desires.
Stop using grace as camouflage.
Run to Christ.
There may be consequences.
There may need to be resignation.
There may need to be church discipline.
There may need to be professional counseling, accountability, disclosure to those legitimately affected, and years of rebuilding trust.

If coercion, abuse, exploitation, or criminal conduct is involved, church leaders should not treat the matter merely as an internal “spiritual problem”; appropriate safeguarding and civil authorities may also need to become involved.
Repentance is not controlling the consequences.
Repentance is surrendering the truth to God even when the truth costs you something.
And church, remember this:
The purpose is not humiliation.
The purpose is holiness.
The purpose is protection.
The purpose is repentance.
The purpose is restoration to Christ.
Because Christianity has never been the story of impressive people successfully hiding their scandals.
Christianity is the story of sinners meeting a Savior who refuses to leave them enslaved to what is destroying them.
Maybe that is why this question hurts so much.
Because somewhere underneath “Can a pastor have multiple wives and girlfriends?” is another question:
“Can someone fail terribly and still be loved by Jesus?”
Yes.
Absolutely yes.
But being loved by Jesus does not make rebellion holy.
Being forgiven does not make adultery permissible.
Being gifted does not make someone qualified.
Having thousands of followers does not overturn Scripture.
And having a powerful anointing story does not give anyone permission to build a private kingdom where biblical boundaries no longer apply.
Jesus forgave the woman caught in adultery, yet His mercy was never an endorsement of adultery.
Grace receives sinners.
Then grace begins changing them.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not:
“From scandal to excuses.”
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He can rewrite the betrayed wife’s story.
He can rewrite the confused congregation’s story.
He can rewrite the wounded child’s story.
He can rewrite the woman who was manipulated by someone she trusted spiritually.
He can even rewrite the fallen pastor’s story.
But rewriting begins when we stop lying about the page we are currently on.
If this exposed something hidden in your own life, you do not need to announce every private detail publicly. But you do need to stop hiding from God and seek wise, trustworthy Christian help.
Let those words become more than engagement beneath an article.
Let them become the beginning of honesty.
It cannot.
Not because giving money proves you love Jesus.
It does not.
Christ cannot be bought.
But voluntary support can become one practical act of stewardship that helps Gospel-centered teaching continue reaching people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and go deeper with us:
And above everything else, glorify God by obeying Christ—whether or not you ever give Gospel Warrior a cent.
Because the greatest support you can give the Gospel is not your money.
It is a life surrendered to Jesus.
And when the scandals of men make you wonder whether Christianity is still worth believing, remember the line that darkness desperately wants you to forget:
Never measure the faithfulness of Jesus by the unfaithfulness of the person holding the microphone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HEROD ACCEPTED THE CROWD’S WORSHIP—THEN AN ANGEL STRUCK HIM
paragraphs: HEROD ACCEPTED THE CROWD’S WORSHIP—THEN AN ANGEL STRUCK HIM
The crowd called him a god. Herod did not correct them. Heaven did.
There are moments in Scripture that make you uncomfortable because they refuse to let you keep God small.
Acts 12 contains one of them.
A king sits before a crowd dressed in royal splendor. People are watching him. Listening to him. Depending upon him.
Then the shouting begins.
“Θεοῦ φωνὴ καὶ οὐκ ἀνθρώπου.”
Theou phōnē kai ouk anthrōpou.
“The voice of a god and not of a man.”
And Herod lets them say it.
That may be the most frightening part of the entire story.
He does not interrupt them.
He does not tear his garments.
He does not say, “No. I am only a man.”
He receives what belongs to God.
And then heaven answers.
Acts 12:23 records:
“Παραχρῆμα δὲ ἐπάταξεν αὐτὸν ἄγγελος Κυρίου ἀνθ’ ὧν οὐκ ἔδωκεν τὴν δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ…”
Parachrēma de epataxen auton angelos Kyriou… ouk edōken tēn doxan tō Theō…
In context, the meaning is devastatingly clear:
Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him because he did not give the glory to God.
Then Luke tells us that Herod became skōlēkobrōtos—“eaten by worms”—and breathed his last.
A man was being praised as divine one moment.
Then dying the next.
But before we point at Herod, perhaps we should ask the question this passage quietly forces upon every human heart:
What praise have I been accepting that should have passed through me and gone to God?
Because Herod’s temptation did not die with Herod.
It simply changed clothes.
We may never sit upon a royal throne.
Nobody may ever shout that we are gods.
But we know what it feels like to crave recognition.
To refresh the post.
To check the reactions.
To notice who complimented us.
To feel strangely disappointed when something we did received less attention than we thought it deserved.
We know how easily “God used me” can slowly become “look what I did.”
We know how subtly ministry can become identity.
How service can become performance.
How gifting can become entitlement.
How applause can become oxygen.
How even something done in Jesus’ name can quietly become something we need people to admire us for.
That is why Herod’s story is not merely ancient history.
It is a mirror.
And mirrors are uncomfortable when the lights are bright enough.
The surrounding context makes the scene even more sobering.
This is Herod Agrippa I, the ruler who had James the brother of John killed and had Peter arrested. Earlier in the same chapter, Peter is sitting in prison while believers are praying.
Herod has guards.
Peter has chains.
Herod has political authority.
The church has prayer.
Herod appears powerful.
The Christians appear helpless.
Then God moves.
An angel enters Peter’s prison.
Chains fall.
Doors open.
Peter walks out.
And later in the same chapter, another angel appears.
But this time the angel does not come to release a prisoner.
The angel comes in judgment against a king.
Do not miss the contrast.
The same chapter shows heaven opening prison doors for one man and bringing down another man who refuses to give God glory.
Human power looked enormous.
God was never intimidated.
And there is an extraordinary historical detail outside the New Testament that makes the scene even more striking.

The first-century Jewish historian Josephus independently describes the death of Agrippa at Caesarea. His account is not identical to Luke’s, and we should not force it to be. Josephus describes Agrippa appearing at a festival wearing a magnificent garment made of silver. Morning sunlight struck it, creating a dazzling spectacle. Flatterers began addressing him as a god.
Josephus says Agrippa did not rebuke them.
Then severe pain struck him, and he died after several days.
Luke gives us the theological reality behind Herod’s downfall: Herod failed to give glory to God.
Josephus supplies historical details from another perspective.
Different writers.
Different purposes.
Yet both preserve the haunting picture of a ruler receiving divine honors shortly before his death.
The applause did not save him.
The robe did not save him.
The throne did not save him.
His influence did not save him.
His title did not save him.
And there is something painfully modern about that.
We spend so much of our lives constructing robes.
Not literal silver garments.
Other kinds.
The successful marriage everybody sees.
The ministry everybody admires.
The career that proves we mattered.
The body we want people to notice.
The platform.
The followers.
The house.
The achievements.
The reputation.
Sometimes even the appearance of being spiritually strong.
We polish the outside until the light hits it just right.
And people applaud.
But God sees beneath the robe.
He sees the exhausted man secretly addicted to approval.
The woman comparing herself with everyone on her screen.
The pastor beginning to love the platform more than the presence of Christ.
The Christian who knows how to say “all glory to God” while secretly becoming angry when someone else receives the recognition.
The person who serves everyone but inwardly resents anyone who fails to notice.
The believer whose public Christianity looks alive while private prayer is almost gone.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not on Herod’s throne.
But somewhere much quieter.
Maybe you have been starving for somebody to notice you.
Maybe rejection wounded you so deeply that admiration became medicine.
Maybe being overlooked made you promise yourself that one day everyone would see your worth.
Maybe you never wanted worship.
You just wanted to feel valuable.
And somewhere along the way, human approval became the place you started looking for what only God could give you.
This is where the Gospel changes the entire story.
Because Christianity does not merely tell you, “Stop being proud.”
Christianity gives you Someone infinitely greater than your pride.
Jesus Christ.
Think about the contrast.
Herod receives glory that does not belong to him.
Jesus possesses glory that actually does belong to Him.
Yet Christ humbled Himself.
Herod sits dressed as royalty while people exalt him.
Jesus, the true King, is stripped and mocked.
Herod receives the cry of people treating him like a god.
Jesus is God the Son, yet He allows sinful men to ridicule Him.
Herod clings to glory.
Jesus walks toward a cross.
Herod wants elevation.
Jesus embraces humiliation for sinners.
And at Calvary, the King who deserved every angelic song willingly endured human mockery so rebels like us could receive mercy.
This is why the answer to pride is not merely trying harder to think less of yourself.
The answer is seeing Christ more clearly.
When you see Him…
His holiness makes your self-exaltation ridiculous.
His cross makes your self-righteousness impossible.
His grace makes hiding unnecessary.
His resurrection makes earthly applause temporary.
His love makes the approval of crowds insufficient.
And His glory makes surrender beautiful.
The Gospel says you do not have to manufacture your significance.
You do not have to become your own god.
You do not have to convince everyone that you matter.
At the cross, Jesus Christ demonstrates both the horror of sin and the staggering depth of divine mercy.
The One who deserved glory took shame.
The guilty can receive grace.
The proud can repent.
The hidden can come into the light.
The spiritually exhausted can stop performing.
The sinner can come home.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But Acts does something brilliant after Herod dies.
Luke does not end the scene with worms.
He writes:
Ho de logos tou theou ēuxanen kai eplēthyneto.
“But the word of God continued to grow and multiply.”
Herod dies.
The Word keeps moving.
Read that again.
Herod dies.
The Word keeps moving.
Kings disappear.
The Word remains.
Empires collapse.
The Word remains.
Celebrities are forgotten.
The Word remains.
Platforms vanish.
The Word remains.
Algorithms change.
The Word remains.
Your name and mine will eventually disappear from human conversation.
Jesus Christ will still be King.
Perhaps freedom begins when that stops frightening us.
You do not need your name to last forever.
You need His Name to be glorified through the life you have been given.
John the Baptist understood it:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
That is not self-hatred.
That is freedom.
Freedom from having to be impressive.
Freedom from having to win every argument.
Freedom from needing everybody to recognize your sacrifice.
Freedom from pretending you are stronger than you are.
Freedom from building a throne inside your heart and begging people to sit beneath it.
And maybe right now the Holy Spirit is touching something you would rather keep hidden.
That craving for validation.
That jealousy.
That secret resentment.
That hunger to be seen.
That habit of comparing yourself.
That spiritual performance.
That quiet pride nobody around you knows exists.
Do not run from conviction.
Run to Jesus.
Conviction that drives you toward Christ is mercy.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for pleasure. Biblical repentance is turning from sin and returning to the God whose grace is greater than the identity you built without Him.
Tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, I have wanted glory that belongs to You.”
“Jesus, I have cared too much about what people think.”
“Jesus, forgive my pride.”
“Jesus, tear down every throne I have built for myself.”
“Jesus, teach me to live so people see You instead of me.”
And remember: we are not saved because we become humble enough.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
The same Gospel that exposes our pride offers forgiveness to the proud.
The cross says your sin is serious.
The cross also says mercy is available.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose again.
And the King who humbled Himself will one day be openly acknowledged as Lord.
So come down from the little throne before which you have been exhausting yourself.
You were never created to carry the weight of being your own god.
Let Jesus be King.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind a polished Christian answer.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending the battle is not there.

And if you are still fighting the need for approval, comment, “I’m still fighting.” Let another believer reading these words realize they are not the only person learning to surrender their pride to Christ.

Your support helps us keep creating and sharing Scripture-centered content that calls people toward Jesus, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformed lives. And sharing these articles costs nothing while helping biblical truth reach people who might never walk into a church but will stop for a story appearing in their feed.
And do not keep the invitation to yourself.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who has questions about Jesus.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the lesson of Acts 12.
Do not confuse applause with approval from God.
Do not confuse visibility with spiritual authority.
Do not confuse influence with holiness.
Do not mistake a shining robe for a surrendered heart.
Herod had a throne.
He had an audience.
He had authority.
He had applause.
For one terrifying moment, people even called him divine.
And none of it could give him another breath when God required an account.
Yet the chapter does not ultimately leave us staring at a dead king.
It leaves us staring at a living Word that keeps multiplying.
That is the choice hidden inside this story.
Build your life around a name that will disappear…
or surrender your life to the Name above every name.
Jesus does not need another competitor for His throne.
He is calling sinners to come down from theirs.
And perhaps the greatest thing that could happen to your reputation is that people eventually forget how impressive you were—but never forget the Jesus they saw changing you.
The crowd can give you a throne for a moment. Only Jesus can give you grace that survives the grave.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: AN ELDERLY DAVID SHARED HIS BED WITH ABISHAG—YET SCRIPTURE SAYS HE DID NOT HAVE SEX WITH HER
paragraphs: AN ELDERLY DAVID SHARED HIS BED WITH ABISHAG—YET SCRIPTURE SAYS HE DID NOT HAVE SEX WITH HER

She was young. She was beautiful. She lay beside Israel’s aging king to keep him warm. But then Scripture inserts one deliberate sentence that changes how we must read the entire scene: “the king knew her not.” Why did God make sure we knew that?
There are Bible stories people sanitize because they feel uncomfortable.
And then there are Bible stories people sensationalize because uncomfortable details attract attention.
The story of David and Abishag deserves neither.
It deserves to be read exactly as Scripture gives it to us.

Because the opening chapter of 1 Kings brings us into a room where Israel’s legendary warrior-king is no longer standing over Goliath, fleeing Saul through the wilderness, dancing before the ark, commanding armies, or ruling from the strength of his throne.
David is old.
Very old.
And cold.
“So King David was old and advanced in years. And although they covered him with clothes, he could not get warm.” — 1 Kings 1:1
Pause there.
This is David.
The shepherd boy who faced a giant.
The fugitive who survived caves and spears.
The warrior whose name made enemies tremble.
The king who had experienced extraordinary victories and devastating failures.
The man who had tasted worship, warfare, friendship, betrayal, lust, adultery, murder, repentance, discipline, forgiveness, grief, and mercy.
Now he cannot even keep himself warm.
Time has reduced the warrior to an elderly man beneath blankets.
There is something painfully human about that.
Age eventually reaches the body that once seemed unstoppable.
Strength fades.
Hands that once carried weapons begin to tremble.
Eyes dim.
Bodies weaken.
Titles cannot stop mortality.
Money cannot command youth to return.
And even kings eventually discover that the human body does not bow to human authority.
David's servants therefore proposed a solution that sounds startling to modern readers:
“Let a young woman be sought for my lord the king, and let her wait on the king and be in his service. Let her lie in your arms, that my lord the king may be warm.” — 1 Kings 1:2
They searched throughout Israel.
Then they found her.
Abishag.
A young woman from Shunem.
Scripture does not hide her attractiveness:
“The young woman was very beautiful…”
And then comes the sentence that makes this story so easily misunderstood.
She attended the king.
She served him.
She lay with him as part of the effort to keep the elderly David warm.
Yet Scripture immediately tells us:
“…but the king knew her not.” — 1 Kings 1:4
The Hebrew is striking:
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ
vehammelekh lo yeda‘ah
Literally, in context:
“And the king did not know her.”
The verb comes from יָדַע — yadaʿ, the ordinary Hebrew verb “to know.” But biblical Hebrew can also use “know” as a discreet expression for sexual relations.
Genesis gives us an unmistakable example:
“Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived…”
The connection between sexual union and conception makes the meaning clear.
So when 1 Kings deliberately tells us that David “did not know” Abishag, the narrator is telling us that despite their physical proximity, David did not have sexual relations with her.
That matters.
It means we should neither pretend the scene is less intimate than it is nor turn it into something Scripture explicitly says it was not.
Abishag was close enough to David to warm him.
She ministered to him.
She attended him.
She was beautiful.
She shared his bed.
And Scripture says:
He did not have sex with her.
Why does the Bible bother telling us?
The text itself does not stop and give us a theological essay explaining the narrator's reason, so we should be careful not to pretend God revealed motives that Scripture does not state.
But the detail becomes enormously important as the story continues.
Because David is dying.
And while an old king lies weak in bed, ambitious men are already thinking about the throne.
David's son Adonijah declares:
“I will be king.”
Suddenly 1 Kings 1 is no longer merely a story about an elderly man struggling to stay warm.
It is a succession crisis.
Power is moving.
Loyalties are being tested.
A throne is about to change hands.
Adonijah gathers supporters.
Nathan intervenes.
Bathsheba approaches David.
David reaffirms that Solomon is to succeed him.
Solomon is publicly anointed.
And the kingdom begins passing from David's hands into Solomon's.
Then David dies.
But Abishag's story is not over.
In 1 Kings 2, Adonijah approaches Bathsheba with a request.
He wants Abishag.
“Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.” — 1 Kings 2:17
Solomon reacts with extraordinary seriousness.
“Ask for him the kingdom also…”
Why?
Whatever every cultural and political nuance behind Adonijah's request may have been, Solomon clearly understood it as having implications for the throne.
That means Abishag was not simply an irrelevant young woman inserted into the opening verses of Kings.
Her position in David's household became entangled with royal succession.
But there is another reason this opening scene hits so hard.
Because anyone who knows David's history knows exactly why seeing a beautiful young woman beside his bed immediately creates tension.
We remember Bathsheba.
We remember the rooftop.
We remember desire.
We remember adultery.
We remember Uriah.
We remember the attempted cover-up.
We remember blood.
We remember Nathan walking into the palace and confronting the king:
“You are the man!”
David's sexual history was not spotless.
Not even close.
The Bible refuses to airbrush its heroes.
That is one reason Scripture feels so brutally human.
David could write psalms and still sin sexually.
David could worship deeply and still make catastrophic decisions.
David could defeat Goliath publicly while losing another battle privately.
And maybe that is already touching somewhere you do not like being touched.
Because some of us have learned how to look victorious while secretly bleeding.
We know how to sing.
We know how to quote Scripture.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know how to post the verse.
We know how to look faithful.
But there are rooms in the heart where Goliath was never the greatest enemy.
Lust was.
Pride was.
Bitterness was.
Pornography was.
Envy was.
Secret messages were.
An affair was.
An addiction was.
A hidden browser history was.
An unforgiving heart was.
A double life was.
Maybe everybody knows the version of you that killed the giant.
Very few know the version of you that stood on the rooftop.
That is why David's story is dangerous to reduce to either hero worship or scandal.
If all you see is the hero, you miss the warning.
If all you see is the scandal, you miss the grace.
David sinned terribly.
And when Nathan confronted him, David eventually stopped hiding behind royal power.
He said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13
Those are only a few words.
But confession often begins when excuses finally die.
David could not undo what he had done.
Repentance did not resurrect Uriah.
Forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence of David's actions.
Biblical grace is not God pretending sin did not matter.
Grace is costly precisely because sin does matter.
And this is where David's story begins pointing beyond David.
Because David was never the ultimate King.
Jesus is.
David needed mercy.
Jesus is the sinless Son of David who came bringing mercy.
David shed innocent blood.
Jesus willingly shed His own blood for sinners.
David's kingdom fractured.
Christ's kingdom will never end.
David failed.
Jesus did not.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus purchased forgiveness for those who repent and trust in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“Try harder so God will finally love you.”
Not:
“Hide your scandal so religious people will respect you.”
Not:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
And certainly not:
“You've sinned too badly, so there is no way home.”
The Gospel says that sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross—and grace is so astonishing that sinners can be forgiven through Him.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for imaginary sinners with respectable imaginary sins.
He died for real sinners.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People with regrets.
People who wish they could crawl backward through time and stop themselves from making that decision.
People who have cried afterward.
People who did it again afterward.
People ashamed to pray because they think heaven must be tired of hearing their apologies.
People who have wondered:
“After everything I've done, could Jesus possibly still want me?”
Listen carefully.
Your hope is not that your past becomes less sinful when enough years pass.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
Your hope is not your ability to rewrite yesterday.
Your hope is the One who can redeem a life you cannot rewind.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
That does not make repentance cheap.
It makes grace astonishing.
Real repentance does not say, “Jesus forgives me, so I'll keep feeding the sin that crucified Him.”
Grace teaches us to come into the light.
Grace calls us away from sin.
Grace restores us to God and begins changing us.
Maybe that is why this strange scene with an elderly David and Abishag is worth slowing down for.
We are seeing David near the end.
The body is weak.
The crown is about to pass to someone else.
His victories are behind him.
His failures are behind him too.
The giant is dead.
Uriah is dead.
Absalom is dead.
David's youth is dead.
And soon David himself will be dead.
But God's redemptive plan is not dead.
The story keeps moving.
David dies.
Solomon reigns.
Kings rise.
Kings fail.
The kingdom divides.
Prophets cry out.
Generations pass.
Empires rise and fall.
And eventually, in Bethlehem—the city of David—a Child is born.
Jesus.
The promised Son of David.
And suddenly we discover that the Bible was never ultimately asking us to place our hope in David.
David's life was always pointing beyond himself.
The warrior needed a greater Warrior.
The shepherd needed a greater Shepherd.
The king needed a greater King.
The sinner needed a Savior.
And so do we.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something nobody knows.
Maybe there is a chapter in your story you would erase instantly if God gave you the chance.
Maybe you are exhausted from performing Christianity while quietly wondering whether Jesus could still receive the real you.
Stop hiding from the One who already knows.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
You do not need a better mask.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes a small act of honesty becomes the moment someone finally stops pretending.
Your testimony might become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs to read tonight.
We do not buy God's favor. We do not purchase grace. We give because grace has already been freely given to us in Christ.
Save what you may need again.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
Pray that Jesus Christ—not Gospel Warrior, not a writer, not a platform—will be glorified through every person reached.
Because that is the point.
Not David.
Not Abishag.
Not scandal.
Not clicks.
Jesus.
The old king lying beside Abishag would eventually breathe his last.
But the King who came through David's line walked out of His tomb.
And that changes everything.
Your worst chapter does not need to become your final chapter.
Your hidden sin does not need to remain hidden.
Your shame does not need to become your identity.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Christ.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is a new life on the other side of surrender.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, the chapter you thought would bury you can become the place where grace begins writing something new.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE” — READ THE SENTENCE JESUS SAID BEFORE IT
paragraphs:
“THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE” — READ THE SENTENCE JESUS SAID BEFORE IT
We quote the promise. We print it on walls. We post it when we want freedom. But Jesus placed something immediately before those famous words—and once you see it, you may never read John 8:32 the same way again.
“The truth will set you free.”
You have probably heard those words even outside a church.
They appear in courtrooms, universities, movies, speeches, counseling rooms, social-media captions, and conversations about everything from politics to personal authenticity.
Sometimes they are used almost as though Jesus said:
“Discover whatever feels true to you, and you will finally be free.”
But He didn’t.
And this is where the verse becomes uncomfortable.
Because before Jesus spoke about freedom, He spoke about something many of us would rather skip.
Remaining.
Continuing.
Abiding.
Listen to the flow of His words:
“ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ…”
Ean hymeis meinēte en tō logō tō emō…
“If you continue—if you remain, if you abide—in My word…”
Then comes the sentence everybody remembers:
“καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν, καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.”
“And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”
Do you see it?
We love the freedom of verse 32.
Jesus connected it to the discipleship of verse 31.

The Greek verb translated “continue,” “remain,” or “abide” is μείνητε (meinēte), from μένω (menō). The idea is not a passing encounter with Jesus. It carries the sense of remaining, staying, continuing.
Jesus was speaking to people who had believed Him.
And He essentially told them that genuine discipleship would not be measured merely by a moment of enthusiasm.
It would be revealed by whether they remained in His word.
That changes everything.
Because maybe the greatest spiritual danger in your life is not that you have never heard truth.
Maybe it is that you have heard enough truth to recognize Christian language while quietly refusing to remain under the authority of Christ.
You can know worship songs and still be hiding.
You can repost Bible verses and still be feeding a secret sin.
You can say “God is good” while refusing to forgive.
You can attend church while privately living another life.
You can know how to raise your hands in worship while using those same hands later to open something you know is poisoning your soul.
You can look spiritually alive in public while something inside you is slowly suffocating.
And nobody knows.
Maybe that is why these words of Jesus can hurt before they heal.
“The truth will set you free.”
Yes.
But what happens when the truth first exposes you?
What happens when the Word of Christ reaches the room inside you that you keep locked?
What happens when Scripture stops being something you use to comfort yourself and becomes the mirror that confronts you?
That is where many people run.
Because we often want Jesus to remove our chains without touching the things to which those chains are attached.
We want freedom from consequences while protecting the sin.
Freedom from guilt without confession.
Freedom from shame without bringing the wound into the light.
Freedom from anxiety while insisting on controlling everything.
Freedom from bitterness while rehearsing the offense every night.
Freedom from lust while continuing to feed it.
Freedom from spiritual emptiness without actually abiding in Christ.
But Jesus loves us too much to offer counterfeit freedom.
And the conversation in John 8 gets even sharper.
The people answered Him by appealing to their heritage and insisting that they had never been enslaved.
Jesus answered by moving the conversation somewhere deeper than political captivity:
“Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin.”
John 8:34.
There it is.
The prison no human government can unlock.
Sin.
Not merely mistakes.
Not merely bad habits.
Sin.
The rebellion of the human heart against its Creator.
The terrible ability to desire what destroys us, defend what enslaves us, hide what shames us, and then convince ourselves that because nobody sees the chains, we must be free.
Sin can make slavery feel like independence.
That is one of its cruelest lies.
A person says, “Nobody tells me how to live.”
Yet appetite tells him how to live.
Pornography tells him how to live.
Money tells him how to live.
Approval tells him how to live.
Anger tells him how to live.
Pride tells him how to live.
Fear tells him how to live.
The opinions of strangers on a screen tell him how to live.
And all the while he calls it freedom.
Then Jesus enters the prison.
Not merely carrying better advice.
Not merely offering positive thinking.
Not merely telling broken people to try harder.
He comes as the Son.
And a few verses after “the truth will set you free,” Jesus gives the breathtaking conclusion:
“If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”
John 8:36.
Notice where the passage ultimately takes us.
Freedom is not merely found in possessing correct information.
Freedom is found in the Son.
That matters because later in John’s Gospel Jesus does not merely claim to teach truth.
He says:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
John 14:6.
Christian freedom, then, is not permission to become whatever our desires demand.
It is liberation from sin so that we can belong to the One for whom we were created.
And maybe you need to hear that today.
Because there may be something you have been calling “freedom” that has slowly become your master.
You said you could stop whenever you wanted.
But you haven’t.
You said it was only one drink.
One website.
One conversation.
One affair in your imagination.
One compromise at work.
One lie nobody would discover.
One grudge you deserved to keep.
One season away from God.
One Sunday you would skip.
One prayer life you would rebuild later.
Then weeks became months.
Months became years.
And somewhere along the way, the thing you thought you controlled began controlling you.
Perhaps people look at you and think you are doing fine.
You laugh.
You work.
You provide.
You serve.
You post.
You answer, “I’m good.”
But God knows about 2:13 in the morning.
God knows about the deleted messages.
God knows what happens after everyone goes to sleep.
God knows the memory you cannot silence.
God knows whose approval you are addicted to.
God knows the bitterness you keep feeding.
God knows the secret shame underneath your smile.
God knows how tired you are from trying to appear whole.
And here is the astonishing thing about the Gospel:
He knows…
and Christ still calls you toward the light.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because it matters so much that Jesus went to the cross.
The Gospel is not God looking at our rebellion and shrugging.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin at immeasurable cost.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, was crucified and rose again. He bore sin and conquered death so that forgiveness would not be wishful thinking but grace purchased at the cross.
That means repentance is not crawling toward a God eager to humiliate you.
Repentance is turning from the prison toward the Savior who opened the door.
Grace does not say your sin was insignificant.
Grace says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His mercy is so astonishing that sinners can be forgiven.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated history.
Zacchaeus had built wealth through corruption.
Paul once persecuted the church.
The thief beside Christ reached the final hours of a ruined life with nothing left to offer.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose stories look stained beyond repair.
Then Jesus enters the story.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does mean sin and shame do not receive the final word over everyone who comes to Christ.
Jesus does.
Maybe your scandal is not public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe yours has no newspaper headline.
Maybe your scandal is simply the version of yourself you are terrified somebody will discover.
The marriage that is quietly collapsing.
The addiction you promised God you would never return to.
The anger your children keep seeing.
The jealousy you disguise as discernment.
The pride you disguise as confidence.
The loneliness you disguise as independence.
The spiritual dryness you disguise with Christian vocabulary.
The secret thought:
If people really knew me, would they still love me?
Jesus already knows.
And the One who knows the whole truth is the One calling you out of hiding.
Not into denial.
Into repentance.
Not into self-hatred.
Into grace.
Not into pretending the chains do not exist.
Into freedom.
And perhaps this is the sentence somebody reading this needs to say for the first time without performing:
“Jesus, I cannot free myself.”
That may be where freedom begins.
Not with pretending you are stronger than the chain.
But with admitting that you need the Son.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the religious performance.
Bring Him the years you think you wasted.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish you could erase.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Abide in His Word.
Follow Christ.
And when you fall, do not turn your failure into permission to flee from Him. Confess your sin and return to the Savior.
Because the goal is not merely to feel better for five minutes after reading an emotional Christian article.
The goal is Jesus.
Knowing Him.
Following Him.
Remaining in His Word.
Being transformed by His grace.
Becoming the kind of person who no longer needs darkness to survive.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not perform for the comment section.
Or simply:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Someone reading beneath you may discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle nobody sees.
That matters.
Because testimony breaks isolation.
Honesty gives other wounded people permission to step toward the light.
And sometimes one surrendered sentence beneath an article becomes the moment another person realizes, Maybe I can come home too.
Not because every sentence here is equally important, but because the words of Christ are.
There may be a night when the old chain starts whispering again.
Come back to John 8.
Read verse 31 before verse 32.
Then keep reading until verse 36.
The truth does not merely expose the prison.
The Son opens it.
Not as a superstition. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
Jesus cannot be bought.

It is simply a practical way to help Gospel Warrior keep creating and distributing Christ-centered biblical content so more people can encounter Scripture, conviction, grace, repentance, hope, and the good news of Jesus Christ.
Christ Himself.
Because one day the shirts will fade.
The mugs will break.
The books will gather dust.
The algorithms will change.
Facebook itself will not last forever.
But Jesus Christ is Lord.
And the soul reading these words will stand before God.
So do not merely share an article about freedom while remaining chained.
Do not comment about Jesus while refusing Jesus.
Do not become so familiar with the sentence “the truth will set you free” that you miss the Savior who said it.
Go back and read what came before it.
“If you abide in My word…”
Stay.
Remain.
Listen.
Obey.
Repent when His Word exposes you.
Believe when the Gospel tells you grace is still available.
Follow when Christ calls you out of darkness.
And discover that biblical freedom was never God giving you permission to run farther away from Him.
It was the Son breaking the chains that kept you from coming home.
So be honest.
Did this hit harder than you expected?
Share it with the person whose battle nobody else can see.
Because perhaps the most dangerous prison is the one whose door Christ has opened while we are still afraid to walk out.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ISAIAH WALKED NAKED AND BAREFOOT FOR THREE YEARS: Why Would God Command That?
paragraphs:
ISAIAH WALKED NAKED AND BAREFOOT FOR THREE YEARS: Why Would God Command That?
One of the Bible’s strangest prophetic acts was not designed to entertain Israel. It was a living warning about the terrifying moment when everything you trusted instead of God is stripped away.
Imagine seeing him the first day.
You recognize the face.
Isaiah.
The prophet.
The man who had seen the Lord “high and lifted up.” The man whose lips had been touched by fire. The man who spoke words kings could not afford to ignore.
But something is wrong.
The sackcloth is gone.
His sandals are gone.
And Isaiah is walking through the land exposed and barefoot.
People stare.
Some whisper.
Some probably laugh.
Others look away.
Then tomorrow comes.
He is still walking.
Weeks pass.
Months.
Still walking.
A year.
Then another.
Then another.
Three years.
And perhaps the most disturbing part of the story is this:
God told him to do it.
Read the Hebrew carefully.
“הָלֹךְ עָרוֹם וְיָחֵף”
Hālōḵ ʿārôm we-yāḥēp̄.
Walking naked and barefoot.

Isaiah 20 does not soften the language for our comfort. The text says the LORD told Isaiah to remove the sackcloth from his waist and the sandal from his foot, and Isaiah obeyed, “walking naked and barefoot.”
Then God explained why.
“כַּאֲשֶׁר הָלַךְ עַבְדִּי יְשַׁעְיָהוּ עָרוֹם וְיָחֵף שָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים”
“As My servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot three years…”
And then come two Hebrew words that unlock the scene:
“אוֹת וּמוֹפֵת”
ʾôt ûmôp̄ēṯ.
A sign and a portent.
Isaiah had become a walking prophecy.
His body was carrying a sermon.
His bare feet were preaching.
His humiliation was announcing what words alone apparently had not made Judah understand.
And suddenly this bizarre chapter becomes frighteningly relevant.
Because Isaiah 20 is not primarily a strange story about nakedness.
It is a story about misplaced trust.
And that means it may be much closer to your life than you think.
The historical setting matters.
