That is the difference.
The Gospel does not merely forgive your scandal and leave you chained to it.
Christ calls you out.
Out of hiding.
Out of hypocrisy.
Out of secret compromise.
Out of self-righteousness.
Out of the exhausting theater of pretending you have everything together.
Perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you thought this article would give you ammunition against somebody else's doctrine.
Instead, somewhere along the way, Scripture turned the mirror around.
Good.
Let it.
Before asking, “Who is Paul condemning?”
ask:
“Lord, where have I allowed something other than Your Word to rule my conscience?”
Where have you called evil what God called good?
Where have you called good what God called evil?
Where have you trusted religious performance more than Christ?
Where are you hiding?
Where have you stopped receiving God's gifts with thanksgiving?
Where have you confused human tradition with divine command?
And where do you desperately need grace?
Sit with it.
Because eternity is too serious for performative Christianity.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing what has lived in darkness into honest confession is the moment somebody finally stops running.
Let believers who see it pray.
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
And if you are tired of pretending everything is fine while your soul is bleeding behind a Christian smile, simply write:
There may be another believer staring at the screen tonight who needs to discover that he or she is not the only person fighting.
Not because every sentence deserves remembering, but because the Scripture underneath it deserves returning to.
Go back to 1 Timothy 4.
Read the whole chapter.
Read 1 Corinthians 7 too.
Test what you have read here against Scripture.
Never outsource your discernment to a Facebook page, preacher, author, denomination, viral post—or even to us.
Open your Bible.
Search the Scriptures.
Follow Jesus.
One share may place the Gospel in front of the person who would never walk through a church door.
Your timeline can become more than a stream of photographs, arguments, advertisements, and memories.
It can carry Scripture.
It can carry testimony.
It can carry the name of Jesus.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow closer to Christ, you can also help us continue this work.
Supporting this ministry is not a purchase of God's favor. It is not a substitute for obedience, generosity to your local church, caring for your family, or helping people in need.
And we will never tell you that you must pay us in order to glorify God.
God is not for sale.
Grace is not behind a paywall.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from a willing heart and helps biblical ministry continue.

Your monthly support functions as a voluntary offering toward continuing and expanding this work—helping us create and distribute Christ-centered teaching, discipleship materials, Gospel messages, and resources designed to point people toward Jesus.
Send it privately to somebody struggling.
Send it to the married couple fighting for restoration.
Send it to the single Christian who has been made to feel spiritually inferior.
Send it to the believer drowning in shame.
Send it even to the person who does not yet believe.
Because somebody's scrolling may become somebody's searching.
And somebody's searching may lead them to Scripture.
And Scripture may lead them face-to-face with the truth about Jesus Christ.
And remember what Paul was really protecting Timothy's church from.
Not marriage.
Not singleness.
Not food.
Paul was guarding believers from a counterfeit holiness that placed human restrictions where God had given gifts.
The answer to counterfeit holiness is not rebellion.
It is not indulgence.
It is not “anything goes.”
The answer is Jesus Christ.
Christ above human pride.
Christ above religious performance.
Christ above our traditions.
Christ above our shame.
Christ above our scandals.
Christ crucified for sinners.
Christ risen from the grave.
Christ calling His people to repentance.
Christ forgiving those who come to Him.
Christ transforming lives that everyone else had already written off.
So maybe your story has chapters you wish had never been written.
Maybe there are pages stained by things you cannot undo.
Maybe somebody knows your worst chapter.
Maybe nobody does.
But your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His grace.
Walk in His truth.
And then spend the rest of your life becoming living evidence that the Gospel still does what religion alone never could:
it makes dead people alive.
And when shame whispers, “Your scandal is the end of your story,” remember the empty tomb—and answer:
“Jesus is still holding the pen.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: While Everyone Was Weeping Before God, Zimri Walked Into the Camp With His Sin
paragraphs: While Everyone Was Weeping Before God, Zimri Walked Into the Camp With His Sin

Israel was grieving at the entrance of the Tabernacle. Judgment had already begun. Moses was there. The congregation was crying. And then one man walked straight through the camp with a Midianite woman—as if the presence of God, the tears of his people, and the consequences of rebellion meant nothing.
There are moments in Scripture that are difficult to read because they happened thousands of years ago.
And then there are moments that are difficult to read because they sound frighteningly like us.
Numbers 25 is one of them.
Israel had survived Pharaoh.
They had survived the Red Sea.
They had survived hunger, thirst, wilderness, enemies, rebellion, and years of wandering.
But now another enemy had entered the story.
Not an army charging toward Israel with swords.
Seduction.

Numbers 25 opens with Israel staying at Shittim, where some of the Israelite men began engaging in sexual immorality with Moabite women. Those relationships became entangled with idolatrous worship. The people were invited to sacrifices offered to foreign gods, ate sacrificial meals, bowed before those gods, and became joined to Baal of Peor.
This was not merely sexual failure.
It was covenant rebellion.
The Hebrew of Numbers 25:3 is chilling:
וַיִּצָּמֶד יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַעַל פְּעוֹר
Vayyitzamed Yisra’el le-Va‘al Pe‘or.
“And Israel yoked/joined itself to Baal of Peor.”
The verb צָמַד (tsamad) carries the sense of being joined, attached, or bound.
Israel belonged to the LORD.
Yet Israel was attaching itself to another god.

That is what makes idolatry so devastating throughout Scripture. Sin is not merely breaking an abstract regulation. At its deepest level, it is the creature turning from the Creator and seeking somewhere else what can ultimately be found only in Him.
And judgment came.
But then Scripture gives us one of the most astonishing scenes in the chapter.
Numbers 25:6 says:
וְהִנֵּה אִישׁ מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּא וַיַּקְרֵב אֶל־אֶחָיו אֶת־הַמִּדְיָנִית לְעֵינֵי מֹשֶׁה וּלְעֵינֵי כָּל־עֲדַת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהֵמָּה בֹכִים פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד
The scene can be rendered:

“Behold, one of the children of Israel came and brought near to his brothers the Midianite woman, before the eyes of Moses and before the eyes of all the congregation of the children of Israel, while they were weeping at the entrance of the tent of meeting.”
Do not rush past that last phrase.
וְהֵמָּה בֹכִים
Vehemmah vokhim.
“They were weeping.”
The congregation was weeping before God.
And while they were weeping...
a man walked in with a Midianite woman.
Later the text identifies him.
His name was Zimri son of Salu, a leader from a Simeonite ancestral household.
The woman was Cozbi daughter of Zur, whose father was a Midianite tribal leader.
These were not nameless background characters.
Scripture deliberately identifies them.
And the contrast is almost unbearable.
People are crying.
Judgment is falling.
Israel's covenant unfaithfulness has been exposed.
God's holiness is not theoretical anymore.
And Zimri walks into the middle of it.
There is something terrifying about sin when it reaches the point where tears no longer disturb us.
Where warnings no longer disturb us.
Where consequences no longer disturb us.
Where the holiness of God no longer disturbs us.
Where other people are grieving over the very thing we have decided to parade.
And before we turn Zimri into a distant villain, we should allow the text to interrogate us.
Because there may be a little piece of Numbers 25 hiding inside many respectable lives.
Maybe nobody sees yours.
Maybe you would never walk publicly through a congregation carrying evidence of rebellion.
Maybe yours fits inside a phone.
A browser history.
A secret conversation.
A relationship you keep defending.
Money nobody knows about.
Bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
Pride disguised as strength.
Envy disguised as criticism.
A private addiction hidden underneath public worship.
Maybe people around you think everything is fine.
Maybe you still know exactly when to raise your hands.
Exactly when to say “Amen.”
Exactly which Bible verse to post.
Exactly how to sound spiritually alive.
And yet somewhere behind the Christian vocabulary is something you desperately hope nobody discovers.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because one of sin's most dangerous achievements is not merely getting us to fall.
It is getting us comfortable enough to stop grieving that we fell.
At first, conscience screams.
Eventually, conscience whispers.
Then one day we can carry openly what we once begged God to remove secretly.
That is frightening.
But Numbers 25 does not allow us to pretend that holiness does not matter.

Phinehas, son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, saw what was happening. He arose from among the congregation, took a spear, followed the Israelite man into the chamber, and killed both Zimri and Cozbi.
The plague was stopped.
Twenty-four thousand had died.
That part of the story must be handled carefully.

This passage is not permission for Christians to imitate Phinehas by committing violence against people caught in sexual sin, idolatry, or any other sin. Phinehas acted within a particular Old Covenant setting in ancient Israel, amid divine judgment on covenant rebellion. Christians are never commissioned to reproduce his act against sinners.
Jesus told Peter to put away his sword.
The apostles did not establish the church by executing the sexually immoral.
The New Testament calls the church to discipline, repentance, restoration, truth, holiness, and, when necessary, removal from church fellowship—not vigilante violence.
So if the application of Numbers 25 ends with “Go attack sinners,” we have profoundly misunderstood the Christian calling.
The spear is not yours.
But the warning is.
God is holy.
Sin is serious.
Idolatry destroys.
And we cannot casually embrace what nailed our Savior to a cross.
Yet this is exactly where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because if Numbers 25 were the final word, sinners like us would have very little hope.
The scandal is not merely that Zimri sinned.
The scandal is that humanity has.
Romans 3:23 says:
πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ
Pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou Theou.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
All.
That word destroys our favorite hiding place.
Comparison.
We look at Zimri and say, “I would never.”
Then Scripture looks at us and asks about lust.
Pride.
Greed.
Dishonesty.
Hatred.
Self-righteousness.
Secret compromise.
The things we deleted.
The things we concealed.
The things we justified because everybody else was doing them.
The things we promised God we would stop doing.
The things we did again anyway.
Suddenly, we are no longer standing safely outside Numbers 25 judging the scandal.
We are standing among sinners desperately needing grace.
And then comes Jesus.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not lowering God's holiness.
Not rewriting evil and calling it good.
Jesus comes precisely because sin is so serious that reconciliation with God required something we could never accomplish for ourselves.
At the cross, God's holiness and God's mercy are not enemies.
Christ bears judgment for His people.
The sinless One suffers for sinners.
The innocent One gives Himself for the guilty.
The Shepherd lays down His life for sheep who wandered away.
First Peter 2:24 says Christ Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree so that we might die to sins and live to righteousness.
Do you see the difference?
Grace does not say:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says:
“Your sin mattered so much that Christ bore it—and His mercy is so great that you do not have to remain enslaved to it.”
That is Gospel grace.
Not permission to remain Zimri.
Power to become someone new.

The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, related to the verb μετανοέω (metanoeō), describing a change of mind that, biblically, is inseparable from turning toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because you were exposed.
It is not crying because consequences arrived.
It is not deleting evidence.
It is not promising to “do better.”
It is turning.
Toward Christ.
Away from the sin you once defended.
Away from the idol you once protected.
Away from the darkness you once needed nobody to see.
And perhaps that is why you are reading this right now.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been carrying.
But God does.
And He is not calling you to hide it better.
He is calling you to come into the light.
The beautiful promise of 1 John 1:9 is that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice that Christianity does not offer salvation by pretending you were never guilty.
Christianity announces something infinitely better.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Reconciliation.
A new life.
Jesus does not merely improve the appearance of ruined people.
He redeems them.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting God's definition of sin.
By rewriting the sinner's future through His death and resurrection.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your marriage has wounds nobody sees.
Maybe your children think you are stronger than you are.
Maybe your church friends would be shocked.
Maybe you have spent years smiling while spiritually bleeding.
Hear this carefully:
You do not have to wait until your sin becomes public before you repent privately before God.
You do not have to wait for destruction.
You do not have to wait until the secret becomes a scandal.
Come to Christ now.
Confess.
Turn.
Ask for help.
Where another person has been harmed, seek wise, truthful, biblically appropriate steps toward accountability and repair.
Bring darkness into light.
And if you fall again, do not turn failure into an excuse to surrender yourself permanently to sin.
Run back to Christ.
Again.
And again.
Not because repentance is meaningless, but because His grace is greater than your ability to save yourself.
Someone reading this has been believing:
“After what I've done, God could never want me.”
Look at the cross.
The cross exists because sinners needed rescue.
Jesus did not die for imaginary people with imaginary sins.
Christ came into a world of real betrayal, real sexual brokenness, real idolatry, real greed, real violence, real shame, real hypocrisy, and real rebellion.
And sinners were saved.
Paul could write:
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we cleaned everything up.
Christ died for sinners.
And the risen Christ calls sinners to repent, believe, follow Him, and become His.
So be honest.
Did this expose something?
But if publicly responding would genuinely mark a moment of surrender for you, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but still fighting for your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you, comment, “pray for me.”

And if God has already brought you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell your testimony. Somebody hiding in the same darkness may need to know that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and Christ still restores people.
Then think of one person who needs this.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Not somebody you want to indirectly condemn.
Somebody you love.

Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership, but it should never be confused with earning God's favor. Those belong to the realm of God's grace, and salvation is received through Christ—not bought from a ministry.
But ministries do require people willing to help carry the work.
Think about Jesus.
Think about the cross.
Think about whatever you have been carrying into places where your heart should have been weeping.
Then bring it to Him.
Because the most tragic part of sin is not simply that we wandered.
It would be hearing the invitation to come home...
and choosing to keep walking away.
You may have walked into the camp carrying your scandal—but you can walk toward Christ carrying your surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ADAM “KNEW” EVE—AND SHE BECAME PREGNANT: THE STUNNING REASON THE BIBLE CALLS SEXUAL INTIMACY “KNOWING”
paragraphs: ADAM “KNEW” EVE—AND SHE BECAME PREGNANT: THE STUNNING REASON THE BIBLE CALLS SEXUAL INTIMACY “KNOWING”

Genesis 4:1 contains one Hebrew word that exposes what sex was meant to be, what sin has done to intimacy, and why some of the deepest wounds in the human heart come from being physically touched without ever feeling truly known.
There is something almost startling about the way the Bible describes the first recorded sexual union after humanity’s fall.
It does not say Adam “used” Eve.
It does not reduce the moment to anatomy.
It does not speak like pornography speaks, turning a human being into a body to consume.
It says:
“And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived…” — Genesis 4:1
But why “knew”?
Why would Scripture use a word associated with knowledge to describe something so physically intimate?
The answer becomes even more powerful when we look at the Hebrew text itself:
וְהָאָדָם יָדַע אֶת־חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ וַתַּהַר
Veha’adam yada et-Chavvah ishto, vattahar…
A close rendering is:
“And the man knew Eve his wife, and she conceived…”
The word that deserves our attention is יָדַע — yadaʿ.
It means “to know.”
But this is where we have to be careful.
It would be tempting to preach that yadaʿ always means some mystical, soul-level marital intimacy.
It does not.

The Hebrew word has a broad range of uses throughout the Old Testament. It can mean to know a fact, recognize something, understand, become acquainted with, experience, or know a person. Context determines its meaning.
Yet in Genesis 4:1, the context is unmistakable.
Adam “knew” his wife, and she conceived Cain.
Here, “knowing” functions as a modest biblical expression for sexual relations.
And that choice of language is worth sitting with.
Because sex, in the biblical vision, was never designed merely as two bodies colliding.
Before Genesis 4, there was Genesis 2.
A man and a woman were brought together in covenantal union, and Scripture declared:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” — Genesis 2:24
One flesh.
Not merely one bed.
Not merely one moment of pleasure.
Not merely one biological act.
One flesh.
There is something deeply personal about biblical sexuality because the person standing before you is not an object.
They bear the image of God.
They have a name.
A history.
Fears.
Memories.
Weaknesses.
Dreams.
A soul that cannot be reduced to skin.
And perhaps this is why Genesis 4:1 can sound painfully different to modern ears.
We live in a world where someone can know the shape of another person's body without knowing the weight that person carries in their heart.
People can sleep together and remain strangers.
They can exchange photographs without exchanging trust.
They can memorize each other's bodies while never learning how to carry each other's tears.
They can experience physical nakedness without emotional safety, covenant, faithfulness, or spiritual intimacy.
And suddenly that ancient word begins to sting.
Adam knew Eve.
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that hurts.
Because perhaps somebody touched you…
but never truly knew you.
Maybe somebody wanted access to your body but had no intention of carrying responsibility for your heart.
Maybe what you called love was actually loneliness wearing perfume.
Maybe you kept returning to someone's arms because, for a few hours, being desired felt almost like being valued.
Maybe pornography taught you to look at people without knowing them.
Maybe lust taught you to consume what love would have taught you to honor.
Maybe sexual sin promised intimacy but left you feeling more isolated afterward.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Maybe nobody knows.
You worship.
You smile.
You post Bible verses.
You say, “God is good.”
But there is a private history behind the screen.
Searches you delete.
Messages you hide.
Memories you cannot erase.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A secret habit that keeps whispering, Just one more time.
And perhaps the most frightening part is not that nobody else knows.
It is that God does.
But do not stop reading there.
Because that truth is not only terrifying.
For the person who comes to Christ, it becomes breathtakingly beautiful.
The God who knows the worst thing about you is the very God who invites you into the light.
David prayed:
“O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.” — Psalm 139:1
That is knowledge on another level entirely.
God knows.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows what you chose.
He knows what was done against you.
He knows what you regret.
He knows which memories still make your stomach tighten.
He knows the temptation you have never told another Christian about.
He knows where the wound ends and where your own sinful choices begin.
He knows what everyone else sees.
And He knows what you carefully make sure nobody sees.
Yet the Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.”
The Gospel says Christ came for sinners.
Jesus said:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” — Luke 5:32
Repentance matters.
Grace is not God pretending sin is harmless.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved to what Christ died to redeem us from.
The Gospel does not merely tell the sexually broken, sexually sinful, ashamed, addicted, wounded, compromised, or confused person, “Feel better about yourself.”
Jesus calls us out of darkness.
He calls us to repent.
He calls us to follow Him.
And then He offers something scandalous:
forgiveness.
John writes:
Read that again if shame has been discipling you longer than Scripture has.
To cleanse us.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction brings your sin into the light so you can run toward Christ.
Condemnation tells you to hide because you believe Christ could never want someone with your history.
But Scripture says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
Not because sin suddenly became insignificant.
Because Jesus bore judgment for His people.
At the cross, Christ did not excuse sin.
He paid for it.
That means your sexual past does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your pornography addiction does not have to be your master.
Your adultery does not have to write the final sentence.
Your fornication does not have to become your name.
Your hidden messages do not have to remain hidden forever.
Your worst night does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
And if someone sinned against you sexually, hear this carefully: another person's evil against you does not make you morally guilty for what they did.
Christ does not look at the wounded and call the wound their sin.
He knows the difference.
He knows.
There is that word again.
Known.
The Bible's language surrounding intimacy forces us to confront something our culture desperately needs to remember:
The body matters because the person matters.
This is why Christian sexual ethics cannot simply be reduced to a list of “don'ts.”
Biblical boundaries protect something sacred.
Jesus affirmed the Genesis vision of marriage when He said:
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh.” — Matthew 19:5
Sexual union was designed for the covenant of marriage between husband and wife—not because God despises sexuality, but because He created it and understands its meaning better than we do.
The world often says freedom means giving desire permission.
Jesus teaches a deeper freedom: desire does not have to be your god.
You can say no.
You can repent.
You can flee sexual immorality.
You can bring the phone into the light.
You can end the secret relationship.
You can confess to God.
You can seek wise pastoral help and accountable Christian community.
You can stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
And you can discover that holiness is not God stealing your joy.
Holiness is God refusing to leave you chained to counterfeits.
Paul wrote:
“Flee fornication.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18
And only a few verses later:
“For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.” — 1 Corinthians 6:20
Bought with a price.
There is the center of the entire story.
Not Adam.
Not Eve.
Not sex.
Not shame.
Jesus Christ.
Because Genesis does not end in Genesis 4.
Humanity falls deeper.
Sin multiplies.
Relationships fracture.
Desire becomes disordered.
People use people.
Bodies become commodities.
Covenants are betrayed.
Shame becomes hereditary human language.
And then Christ enters the story.
The Son of God takes flesh.
He walks among sinners without becoming corrupted by their sin.
He touches people others refuse to touch.
He speaks truth without surrendering compassion.
He exposes hypocrisy.
He calls sinners to repentance.
And eventually He allows His own body to be nailed to wood.
The hands that never committed sexual sin were pierced for sinners who had.
The eyes that never looked with lust watched His accusers mock Him.
The body of the sinless Christ was wounded publicly.
He carried shame He did not deserve.
And He died.
Then the tomb was sealed.
For a moment, it appeared sin had written the ending.
But Sunday came.
Jesus rose.
And resurrection means sin does not get the final word over those who belong to Him.
Your scandal does not have to be your conclusion.
Your shame does not have to become your biography.
Your failure does not have to be the last chapter.
Maybe this article was not really about an unusual Hebrew word for you.
Maybe God used one ancient sentence to uncover something modern inside your heart.
Maybe you came here curious about why Genesis says Adam “knew” Eve…
and somewhere along the way you realized there are places inside you that desperately need to be known by God, surrendered to Christ, confessed, healed, forgiven, or brought into the light.
Do not hide now.
Your comment might become the sentence another ashamed believer reads at 2:13 in the morning and realizes, I am not the only person fighting this battle.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
But let us keep the language biblical.
Scripture teaches generosity that is willing rather than coerced: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
He cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Send it privately to someone who is struggling.
Pray for the ministry.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Because the goal is not merely to build an audience.
The goal is to point people toward Christ.
And maybe that is where Genesis 4:1 finally brings us.
“Adam knew Eve…”
Human beings ache to know and to be known.
But beneath every human longing for intimacy is an even deeper reality:
You are already fully known by God.
Not the edited you.
Not the Sunday-morning you.
Not the version people applaud.
You.
And when the truth about you drives you to Jesus rather than away from Him, you discover one of the most astonishing truths of the Gospel:
You can be fully known…
deeply convicted…
called to repentance…
and still find mercy at the feet of Christ.
So be honest.
What did this expose in you?
Not for performance.
Not because typing certain words saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when hiding finally ends.
Because they may have spent years believing the worst thing they ever did—or the worst thing someone did to them—is the truest thing about them.
It isn't.

The wound may explain part of your story. The sin may mark part of your story. The scandal may have changed your story. But when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your story, none of them gets to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS FOLLOWING ADULT INFLUENCERS AFFECTING YOUR SOUL?
paragraphs:
IS FOLLOWING ADULT INFLUENCERS AFFECTING YOUR SOUL?
You Tell Yourself, “I’m Only Looking.” Jesus Asks a Much More Uncomfortable Question: What Is All That Looking Doing to Your Heart?
Nobody heard the click.
Nobody saw the follow.
Nobody knows what appears on your screen when the room gets quiet.
And maybe that is exactly why this conversation is so uncomfortable.
Because some battles do not leave receipts on the kitchen table. They leave fingerprints on the heart.
You can love Jesus and still be fighting something you are ashamed to admit.
You can worship on Sunday and scroll through temptation on Monday.
You can know Bible verses, love your family, serve at church, encourage other people, and still have a private digital world you desperately hope nobody ever sees.
Maybe it began innocently enough.
One suggested post.
One attractive person.
One profile.
One click.
Then another.
You told yourself you were curious.
Then you followed.
Then the algorithm learned you.
But Jesus does not merely ask what your thumb touched.
He asks what your heart wanted.
That changes everything.
The eyes can become a doorway to the heart.
Job said:
“בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי”
Berit karati le'einai.
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
That is Job 31:1.
Notice the language.
Not a suggestion.
Not a mood.
A covenant.
Job understood something our culture desperately wants us to forget: what you repeatedly permit your eyes to consume is not necessarily spiritually neutral.
And Jesus takes the issue deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Christ moves from the external command against adultery to the internal territory of desire.
The crucial Greek wording includes:
“πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν”
pros to epithymēsai autēn—
in context, looking at a woman with the purpose or movement of lustful desire toward her.
Jesus says that the person who looks in this way has already committed adultery “ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ”—en tē kardia autou—“in his heart.”
Jesus was not teaching that merely noticing that another human being is physically attractive is identical to adultery.
He was exposing something deeper.
The look that becomes lust.
The gaze that welcomes desire.
The deliberate inward possession of someone who does not belong to you.
Jesus moves the battlefield from merely what your body has done to what your heart is entertaining.
And suddenly the question is no longer:
“Did I physically sleep with somebody?”
The question becomes:
“What am I training my heart to desire?”
That question reaches directly into the phone in your hand.
Because you may never touch the influencer you follow.
You may never meet her.
You may never meet him.
You may never send a message.
You may never commit physical adultery.
But Christianity does not define purity merely as keeping your body out of somebody else's bed.
Jesus cares about the heart.
And that means your private scrolling matters.
Not because the internet is uniquely evil.
Not because every attractive photograph is pornography.
Not because Christians are commanded to become terrified of human beauty.
And not because sexual desire itself is inherently dirty.
God created sexuality.
God created marriage.
God created the human body.
The biblical problem is not that beauty exists.
The problem begins when another human being becomes material for lust.
When a person made in the image of God becomes a product in your imagination.
When following becomes feeding.
When looking becomes lingering.
When lingering becomes fantasizing.
When fantasizing becomes returning.
When returning becomes hiding.
And when hiding becomes a second life.
Maybe nobody knows about yours.
Your spouse may not know.
Your parents may not know.
Your pastor may not know.
Your friends may think you are doing wonderfully.
Your church may know the version of you carrying a Bible.
God knows the version of you holding the phone at 1:17 in the morning.
And here is where many Christian messages make a terrible mistake.
They make you feel filthy...
and then leave you filthy.
Jesus does not.
The Gospel does not expose you merely to humiliate you.
Jesus exposes darkness because He intends to bring people into light.
Perhaps you have whispered something like this before:
“God, this is the last time.”
You unfollowed.
Then followed again.
Deleted something.
Downloaded it again.
Repented.
Fell again.
Promised.
Failed.
Cried.
Repeated it.
Eventually, you stopped making promises because breaking them hurt too much.
Now there is a voice telling you:
Look at yourself.
You call yourself a Christian?
After everything God has done for you?
You will never change.
Listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation do not lead to the same destination.
Biblical conviction brings sin into the light and calls you toward repentance and Christ.
Condemnation tells you to hide from Him.
The Gospel says something astonishing to the person who has sinned sexually, mentally, digitally, secretly, repeatedly.
Come into the light.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Because Christ's grace is greater.
The same Bible that confronts sexual immorality also announces cleansing.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about people whose lives had been marked by serious sexual and other sins, and then gave three extraordinary words:
“But you were washed...”
“But you were sanctified...”
“But you were justified...”
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel is not God pretending sin never happened.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin at the cross.
Jesus Christ did not die for an imaginary, cleaned-up version of you.
He died for sinners.
At Calvary, sin was not excused.
It was judged.
And the Son of God bore the judgment.
Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something shame could never manufacture:
forgiveness.
You do not cleanse yourself enough to become worthy of Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to leave what is destroying us.
Jesus does not merely forgive us while encouraging us to keep feeding the chains from which He came to free us.
There are accounts you may need to unfollow.
There are apps you may need to remove.
There may be private browsing habits that need to become accountable.
There may be conversations with a spouse, pastor, mature Christian friend, counselor, or accountability partner that you have postponed because confession feels terrifying.
There may be a phone that needs to stop sleeping beside your bed.
There may be an algorithm you need to retrain.
There may be a screen you need to stop pretending has no influence over you.
That is not legalism.
It can simply be wisdom applied to weakness.
When Scripture says, “Flee sexual immorality,” the command is not “stand beside temptation and demonstrate how spiritually impressive you are.”
Flee.
Paul connects that command to an extraordinary reality in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20: the believer's body belongs to God, is associated with the indwelling Holy Spirit, and has been “bought with a price.”
Therefore:
glorify God in your body.
Think about that.
Your body is not garbage.
Your sexuality is not garbage.
Your eyes are not garbage.
Your story is not garbage.
Christ does not redeem people so they can learn to hate themselves.
He redeems people so their lives can increasingly belong to Him.
Maybe the question you need to ask tonight is not merely:
“Is following adult influencers technically sinful?”
Perhaps the more revealing questions are:
Why am I following them?
What am I seeking when I open their profiles?
Does this feed lust?
Would I comfortably invite Jesus into this habit?
Would I want my spouse doing exactly what I am doing?
Am I becoming more capable of seeing people as image-bearers of God—or increasingly accustomed to consuming their bodies?
Does this habit strengthen my walk with Christ, or does it repeatedly pull my imagination somewhere I know I should not live?
And perhaps the hardest question:
Why am I fighting so hard to keep something I keep asking God to forgive?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Maybe your finger has already hovered over the unfollow button while your mind began negotiating.
It's not that serious.
Everybody does it.
I'm not hurting anybody.
I can control it.
But freedom sometimes begins with one painfully ordinary act of obedience.
Unfollow.
Delete.
Confess.
Pray.
Walk away.
Then do it again tomorrow if necessary.
Not to purchase God's love.
Not to earn salvation.
Not because Jesus will love you more after you clean up your feed.
But because when grace captures the heart, we begin asking a different question.
Not:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
But:
“How freely can I belong to Jesus?”
And if you fail again?
Run back to Christ.
Do not use grace as permission to surrender to sin, but do not let failure persuade you that the cross has suddenly become unavailable.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Bring the secret into light.
Keep fighting.
Some victories happen instantly.
Others become long stories of sanctification in which Christ teaches us dependence, honesty, discipline, humility, and endurance.
You may have scars.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
You may have wasted years.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
You may have damaged trust and now need to patiently rebuild it.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
You may be reading this immediately after falling into the very thing you promised God you would never do again.
Jesus still writes redemption stories.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build an audience around shame.
To point broken people toward Jesus Christ.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you also do not have to pretend.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting in secret.
For a sensitive struggle, sending this privately may be wiser.
Not because an article can keep you pure.
It cannot.
There is probably someone in your circle fighting a battle they will never announce publicly. You do not need to know who they are before you put truth where they can find it.
Supporting Gospel ministry is one practical way believers may steward their resources for Kingdom work.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and continue walking with this community:
Invite your family.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the believer who is tired of pretending.
Invite the seeker who still has questions.
Invite the person who thinks their past has disqualified them.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is only about religious people pretending they never struggle.
Because the Gospel is not the story of impressive people rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy God saving sinners through Jesus Christ.
And maybe today the greatest act of courage is not pretending you never looked.
Maybe it is finally turning your eyes toward Someone better.
Toward the Christ who knows the search history.
The Christ who knows the fantasy.
The Christ who knows the relapse.
The Christ who knows the shame.
The Christ who knows every hidden room...
and still calls sinners to come into the light.
Repentance says:
I don't want darkness to own me anymore.
Faith says:
Jesus, I cannot save myself.
Grace says:
Come.
And transformation begins when the person who spent years asking, “How much can I hide?” finally begins asking:
“Jesus, how much of me can You have?”
Let Him have the screen.
Let Him have the eyes.
Let Him have the imagination.
Let Him have the sexuality.
Let Him have the secret.
Let Him have the shame.
Let Him have the future.
Because the most dangerous thing on your screen may not be the person you followed.
It may be the lie that whispered you were already too far gone to turn around.
Your secret may explain how you got into the darkness, but the scars in Jesus' hands tell you darkness does not get the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT DAVID REALLY MEANT BY “THE VALLEY OF THE SHADOW OF DEATH”
paragraphs: WHAT DAVID REALLY MEANT BY “THE VALLEY OF THE SHADOW OF DEATH”
Psalm 23 was never a promise that Christians would avoid dark valleys. It was the testimony of a man who discovered Who walks into them with us.
There is one sentence in Psalm 23 that almost everybody recognizes.
People whisper it beside hospital beds.
Pastors read it beside graves.
Families cling to it when the phone rings at an hour when good news rarely comes.
Soldiers have carried it into battle. Grieving mothers have cried through it. Frightened believers have repeated it when they could barely find enough faith to pray anything else.
“Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil…”
But what if those familiar words are even deeper than we have allowed ourselves to understand?
What if David was not merely talking about the moment when you die?
What if he was describing the terrifying places you sometimes have to walk through while you are still very much alive?
Because there are valleys where nobody dies physically…
but something inside you feels buried.
The marriage you thought would survive.
The child who stopped answering your calls.
The diagnosis you never expected.
The betrayal that came from somebody you trusted.
The secret sin you keep promising God you will never return to—and then somehow find yourself standing before it again.
The nights when everybody thinks you are sleeping, but you are staring into darkness asking questions you are almost afraid to say aloud:
“God… where are You?”
That is where Psalm 23 stops being decoration on a wall.
That is where it becomes survival.
David writes:
Gam ki-elekh b’gei tsalmavet, lo-ira ra, ki-attah immadi.
“Even though I walk through the valley of deep darkness, I will fear no evil, for You are with me.”
The famous Hebrew word is צַלְמָוֶת — tsalmavet.

For centuries it has famously been rendered “the shadow of death.” There is also strong linguistic reason, from the way the word appears elsewhere in Scripture, to understand it as intense darkness, deep gloom, or the darkest valley.
And that matters.
Because David’s words do not belong only to cemeteries.
They belong to anybody walking through a place where they cannot see what comes next.
Notice something else.
David does not say:
“Even though I sit in the valley…”
He says:
“Even though I walk…”
There is movement in the sentence.
The valley is real.
The darkness is real.
The danger is real.
But the valley is not presented as David’s permanent address.
He is walking through it.
Somebody reading this needs those two words:
through it.
You may be in it.
But by the grace of God, you do not have to build your identity there.
Your depression is not your name.
Your betrayal is not your name.
Your divorce is not your name.
Your addiction is not your name.
Your failure is not your name.
Your past is not your name.
Even the worst thing you have ever done does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ when a sinner comes to Him in repentance and faith.
David knew something about scandal.
This is the same David whose story contains courage and cowardice, worship and lust, faith and catastrophic moral failure.
He killed Goliath.
He wrote worship songs.
He became king.
And he also committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged circumstances that led to the death of her husband Uriah.
Scripture does not sanitize its heroes.
That is one reason you can trust its honesty.
The Bible does not airbrush David into somebody safe enough for religious merchandise.
It shows us the shepherd.
The warrior.
The worshiper.
The king.
The adulterer.
The schemer.
The broken man.
The repentant sinner.
And then it shows us grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that excuses rebellion.
Grace that exposes sin, calls the sinner to repentance, forgives the repentant, and begins rebuilding what sin tried to destroy.
David eventually prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
He knew valleys were not always places somebody else pushed you into.
Sometimes we dig them ourselves.
That may be the hardest sentence in this article.
Some of your darkness may have been done to you.
Some of it may have been done by you.
And sometimes both are true.
But the Gospel has good news for both.
Jesus Christ does not merely rescue innocent-looking people from unfortunate circumstances.
He saves sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with stains.
People carrying memories they wish they could erase.
People who have disappointed God, disappointed their families, and disappointed themselves.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of a holy God coming down to rescue people who could never save themselves.
And suddenly Psalm 23 becomes astonishingly personal.
David begins the psalm talking about God:
“The LORD is my shepherd…”
“He maketh me…”
“He leadeth me…”
“He restoreth my soul…”
“He leadeth me…”
Then the valley appears.
And something changes.
David stops merely speaking about the Shepherd.
He speaks to Him.
“For You are with me.”
Darkness turned theology into intimacy.
Before the valley: He.
Inside the valley: You.
There are things you can learn about God beside still waters.
There are other things you discover when you can barely see the next step.
You discover whether “God is faithful” is merely something you post…
or Someone you trust.
You discover whether Jesus is an accessory to your comfortable life…
or your life itself.
You discover whether prayer is religious vocabulary…
or the desperate breathing of your soul.
And David does not say, “I will fear no evil because there is no evil.”
That would be denial.
He says, in effect, “I will fear no evil because You are with me.”
Christian courage is not pretending darkness does not exist.
Christian courage is knowing darkness does not get the final word.
This becomes infinitely greater when we reach Jesus.
Because the Good Shepherd of the New Testament did something David could only anticipate from a distance.
Jesus said:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Think about that.
Psalm 23 gives us sheep walking through death-shadowed darkness with their shepherd.
The Gospel gives us the Shepherd willingly walking toward death for His sheep.
Jesus did not stand safely outside human suffering shouting instructions.
He entered our world.
He knew rejection.
He knew betrayal.
He knew grief.
He knew anguish.
He was mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And on the cross He bore sin, giving Himself as the sacrifice through whom guilty sinners could be reconciled to God.
Then came the silence of the tomb.
For His disciples, it must have looked like the valley had won.
Hope appeared buried.
The stone was sealed.
The Shepherd was dead.
Saturday must have felt endless.
But Christianity exists because Sunday came.
Jesus Christ rose.
Death did not write the final sentence.
Sin did not write the final sentence.
The grave did not write the final sentence.
Jesus did.
That is why a Christian can read “the valley of the shadow of death” differently.
Not because Christians never suffer.
We do.
Not because believers never grieve.
We do.
Not because faith guarantees that every disease disappears, every relationship returns, every financial crisis resolves immediately, or every prayer receives the answer we wanted.
Scripture never promises that.
Our confidence is deeper.
The risen Christ has already confronted the enemy we could never defeat ourselves.
The valley may still be dark.
But for those who belong to Christ, darkness is no longer sovereign.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe your valley has a name.
Maybe nobody knows it.
You smile in photographs.
You answer, “I’m fine.”
You go to church.
You quote Scripture.
You encourage everybody else.
And then you go home carrying something nobody sees.
Maybe you have even wondered whether God became tired of you.
Listen carefully.
Do not confuse God’s presence with comfortable circumstances.
David did not say, “You are with me, therefore there is no valley.”
He said there is a valley…
and You are with me there.
That changes everything.
The presence of the Shepherd does not always remove the valley immediately.
Sometimes His presence is what gets you through it.
And if the darkness in your life came through your own sin, do not turn Psalm 23 into permission to remain there.
The Shepherd leads.
Sheep follow.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly as you are forever.”
Grace says, “Come home.”
Repent.
Confess.
Turn.
Stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
Stop calling bondage your personality.
Stop making peace with the thing destroying your fellowship with God.
There is forgiveness in Christ, but biblical forgiveness is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive vocabulary.
Maybe it simply needs honesty.
“Jesus, I need You.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I cannot carry this anymore.”
“Jesus, lead me.”
Your testimony may become somebody else’s reason to survive tonight.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Not as religious decoration.
Send it to the believer who stopped coming to church.
Send it to the friend who is angry with God.
Send it to the person who does not even believe yet.
Sometimes glorifying God looks like refusing to keep life-giving biblical truth to ourselves.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation. It cannot.
Salvation is God’s gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
But believers can glorify God by willingly supporting faithful Gospel work and helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it.
If this ministry is helping you follow Jesus, help us carry that truth farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the friend who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Especially invite that person.
Because David’s story says otherwise.
Peter’s story says otherwise.
Paul’s story says otherwise.
The cross says otherwise.
The Gospel is filled with people whose darkest chapter looked final until grace entered the sentence.
And maybe that is what “the valley of the shadow of death” needs to mean to you tonight.
Not that nothing frightening will happen.
Not that Christians never break down.
Not that faithful people never walk through darkness.
But that if Jesus Christ is your Shepherd, you never enter the darkness alone.
You may cry there.
You may tremble there.
You may have questions there.
You may need other believers to hold you up there.
But keep following the Shepherd.
Because valleys are passages, not thrones.
Darkness is real, but it is not God.
Death is terrifying, but it is not Lord.
Your past is powerful, but it is not sovereign.
Your sin is serious, but for the repentant sinner, it is not stronger than Christ’s redeeming blood.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
It does not have the authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
So when you cannot see the road…
listen for the Shepherd.
When shame whispers, “Hide”…
listen for the Shepherd.
When fear says, “This is where your story ends”…
listen for the Shepherd.
When the valley becomes so dark that you cannot imagine morning…
remember the empty tomb.
The Shepherd who walked into death came out alive.
And everyone who belongs to Him can therefore say with David:
“I will fear no evil: for thou art with me.”
Perhaps the miracle is not that you never entered the valley.
Perhaps the testimony will be that the valley discovered it could not keep someone whose Shepherd is Jesus.
Because the darkest valley still does not get to write the last line.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOSIAH HEARD GOD’S WORD—AND TORE HIS CLOTHES
paragraphs:
JOSIAH HEARD GOD’S WORD—AND TORE HIS CLOTHES
What if the most frightening evidence of spiritual decline is not that we have rejected the Bible…but that we can hear it without being broken by it?
There is something deeply unsettling about 2 Kings 22.
Not because an enemy army was standing outside Jerusalem.
Not because the king had been assassinated.
Not because the Temple had burned.
Something had been lost.
And what had been lost was sitting inside the house of God.
The Book of the Law.
Think about that.
There was still a Temple.
There were still priests.
There were still religious activities.
There was still a nation that carried the name of the covenant God.
Yet somewhere inside the very place built for worship, the Word of God had become so neglected that its discovery became news.
Then somebody opened the book.
Somebody started reading.
And a king broke.
Second Kings 22:11 records the moment:
“וַֽיְהִי֙ כִּשְׁמֹ֣עַ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֶת־דִּבְרֵ֖י סֵ֣פֶר הַתּוֹרָ֑ה וַיִּקְרַ֖ע אֶת־בְּגָדָֽיו׃”
Vayehi kishmoa hammelekh et-divrei sefer hattorah, vayyiqra et-begadav.
“When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes.”
The Hebrew is painfully simple.
כִּשְׁמֹעַ — kishmoa — “when [he] heard.”
דִּבְרֵי סֵפֶר הַתּוֹרָה — divrei sefer hattorah — “the words of the scroll/book of the Torah.”
וַיִּקְרַע — vayyiqra — “and he tore.”
בְּגָדָיו — begadav — “his garments.”
He heard.
Then he tore.
Between those two actions lies one of the most uncomfortable questions a Christian can ask:
When was the last time the Word of God disturbed you?
Not entertained you.
Not inspired you.
Not gave you a caption to post.
Not supplied an argument for somebody you disagree with.
When was the last time Scripture exposed something inside you so clearly that defending yourself suddenly seemed ridiculous?
Because Josiah did not hear the Word and say, “That would make a great sermon.”
He did not say, “I know someone who needs to hear this.”
He did not immediately search for the sins of everybody else.
He heard God speaking...
and looked at himself.
That is where revival gets dangerous.
Josiah became king when he was only eight years old. He inherited a kingdom deeply scarred by generations of rebellion and idolatry. Yet Scripture says he did what was right in the sight of the LORD.
Then, in the eighteenth year of his reign, while repairs were being made to the Temple, Hilkiah the high priest made the discovery.
“I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD.”
Eventually the scroll reached Shaphan the secretary.
Shaphan brought it before Josiah.
Then he read it.
Imagine the room.
The king is seated in authority.
Servants nearby.
Officials watching.
The machinery of a kingdom surrounding him.
But suddenly there is an authority in the room greater than the throne.
God has spoken.
Josiah listens.
And the king tears his clothes.
In the biblical world, tearing garments could visibly express profound grief, horror, mourning, or distress.
Josiah understood something terrifying.
The problem was not that God's standard was unreasonable.
The problem was that God's people had departed from it.
He immediately commanded his officials to inquire of the LORD concerning what had been read, because he recognized that Judah had not obeyed what God had commanded.
Notice what genuine conviction does.
It does not merely say:
“That was powerful.”
It asks:
What must change?
And this is where Josiah's story stops being ancient history.
Because perhaps our generation has developed a strange spiritual ability.
We can hear terrifying truths without trembling.
We can read “love your enemies” while nurturing hatred.
We can read “forgive” while rehearsing what someone did to us five years ago.
We can read warnings about lust while protecting secret browsing histories.
We can read warnings about greed while allowing money to become our functional god.
We can sing about surrender while quietly keeping entire rooms of our lives locked away from Christ.
We can say “Jesus is Lord” while still insisting that we decide what He is permitted to command.
We know verses.
We own Bibles.
We download Bible apps.
We repost Christian videos.
We argue theology.
We listen to sermons while driving.
And still...
sometimes the Book is effectively buried in the Temple.
Close enough to religion to be honored.
Not close enough to our hearts to rule us.
That should frighten us.
Because the great question is not merely whether you possess a Bible.
The question is whether the Bible possesses your obedience.
Josiah heard God's Word and tore his clothes because Scripture did something that our pride desperately tries to prevent:
It told him the truth about where he stood before God.
And perhaps that is why some of us keep Scripture at a safe distance.
Because we know what might happen if we actually listened.
God might touch the relationship we know is pulling us away from Him.
He might confront the bitterness we renamed “boundaries.”
He might expose the pride we renamed “confidence.”
He might reveal the gossip we renamed “concern.”
He might confront the compromise we renamed “everybody does it.”
He might uncover the secret habit nobody at church knows exists.
He might put His finger on the thing we have spent years asking Him not to mention.
And suddenly the story of Josiah becomes personal.
What would you have to tear?
Maybe not your shirt.
Maybe the image you have carefully constructed.
Maybe your excuses.
Maybe your secret agreement with sin.
Maybe the version of Christianity that allows Jesus to comfort you without commanding you.
Because biblical repentance is not theater.
God was not impressed simply because fabric ripped.
The significance was what was happening in Josiah's heart.
Later, God's message through Huldah explains why Josiah received mercy:
His heart was tender.
He humbled himself before the LORD.
He heard God's judgment.
He tore his garments.
He wept before God.
God saw him.
That is breathtaking.
The king tears his clothes...
but God sees the heart underneath them.
And that distinction matters enormously.
You can cry without repenting.
You can feel guilty without surrendering.
You can be emotionally moved by a sermon and return to the same deliberate rebellion Monday morning.
Josiah's repentance moved.
He gathered the people.
He had the words of the covenant read publicly.
He committed himself before the LORD.
Then reform followed.
Idols came down.
False worship was confronted.
The Passover was restored.
The Word that broke him began rearranging the kingdom around him.
That is repentance.
Not perfection.
Not purchasing God's forgiveness with good behavior.
Not performing religious pain so God will love you.
Repentance is turning.
It is the heart that stops negotiating with the God who created it.
And here the story leads us somewhere even greater than Josiah.
Because Josiah could tear his garments...
but he could not tear away humanity's sin.
Josiah could restore neglected worship...
but he could not permanently restore sinners to God.
Josiah could renew a covenant...
but he could not carry the sins of the world.
We needed another King.
A greater King.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where scandal becomes grace.
We broke God's commands.
Christ bore judgment for sinners.
We wandered.
He came seeking the lost.
We deserved condemnation.
He stretched out His hands upon a cross.
The gospel is not that God looked at our rebellion and decided sin did not matter.
The gospel is infinitely more astonishing.
Sin mattered so much that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people slightly nicer.
He came to save.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He died for sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered through Him.
Grace does not tell you that your sin was harmless.
Grace tells you that your sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so magnificent that sinners who turn to Him can be forgiven.
That is why repentance and grace are not enemies.
Repentance runs toward grace.
The same Word that exposes the wound points us toward the Physician.
The same holiness that destroys our excuses makes the mercy of Jesus unimaginably beautiful.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying something nobody knows.
A secret.
An addiction.
A double life.
A resentment.
A failure.
A compromise that started small and slowly became a prison.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually strong.
Maybe you know exactly when to smile at church.
You know when to say “God is good.”
You know how to encourage everybody else.
But somewhere underneath the Christian vocabulary is an exhausted soul whispering:
“If they knew everything about me, would God still want me?”
Look at the cross.
Christianity does not require you to convince God that you were never guilty.
The gospel announces that guilty people can be forgiven because Jesus Christ saves sinners.
You do not need better hiding.
You need Christ.
You do not need another excuse.
You need repentance.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to become worthy of grace.
Come to the Savior who died and rose again.
Confess what God already knows.
Stop defending what His Word has exposed.
Turn from sin.
Trust Jesus Christ.
And discover something Josiah's torn garments still whisper across the centuries:
A heart broken before God is not a heart He despises.
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment your defenses were getting tired.
Be honest before God.
Your comment does not purchase grace. It does not save you. Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing what has lived in darkness into honest confession is the moment we stop pretending.
And somebody reading your words may finally realize they are not the only person struggling.
Do not keep this message trapped on this page either.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It absolutely does not.
Someone may have a Bible beside their bed and still feel a thousand miles from God.
Someone may be one honest encounter with Scripture away from repentance.
Someone may need to remember tonight that Jesus still receives sinners.

Supporting Gospel Warrior should never be confused with supporting God Himself, purchasing His blessing, proving your faith, or earning spiritual merit. Scripture gives us no right to make such a claim. The gospel cannot be bought.
But believers can freely choose to support Gospel-centered ministry so that biblical content and discipleship resources can continue reaching people.
Not for applause.
Not to prove how Christian you are.
Maybe somebody you love needs to hear it.
And before you leave, return one last time to that room in Jerusalem.
A king is sitting there.
A scroll is opened.
The Word is read.
Then...
rip.
Royal garments tear.
Pride loses its argument.
A heart becomes tender.
And history changes because one man refused to hear God's Word casually.
Now imagine the sound God desires from us.
Not necessarily fabric tearing.
Something deeper.
Excuses tearing.
Masks tearing.
Secret agreements with sin tearing.
The stubborn sentence “I will live my own way” finally tearing apart beneath the lordship and mercy of Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you have sinned.
The greatest tragedy would be hearing the truth that could lead you to Christ...
and walking away unchanged.
So open the Book.
Let it speak.
Let it expose you.
Let it wound your pride.
Let it lead you to repentance.
Then lift your eyes toward the cross.
Because when God's Word finally tears through everything you used to hide behind, you may discover that Jesus was never waiting on the other side to destroy a repentant sinner.
He was calling you out of hiding...
and into grace.
The garment Josiah tore could be replaced. The heart God awakened could never comfortably return to sleep.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LEAH ESSENTIALLY BARGAINED FOR A NIGHT WITH HER OWN HUSBAND
paragraphs:
LEAH ESSENTIALLY BARGAINED FOR A NIGHT WITH HER OWN HUSBAND
Genesis 30:14–16 is one of the strangest scenes in Scripture. But underneath the mandrakes, the bargaining, and the broken marriage is the cry of a woman who desperately wanted to be chosen—and the God who heard her when human love did not.
Imagine watching your husband come home from the field…
and knowing that before you can spend the night with him, there has been a negotiation.
Not with a stranger.
Not with another man.
With your own sister.
Over your own husband.
And the price?
A handful of plants your son found in a field.
It sounds almost too scandalous to belong in the Bible.
But Scripture does not airbrush broken families.
It tells the truth about them.
Reuben, Leah's eldest son, had gone into the fields during the wheat harvest and found what the Hebrew text calls דּוּדָאִים — dûdā’îm — traditionally translated “mandrakes.”
He brought them home to his mother.
Then Rachel asked Leah for some.
That request opened a wound much deeper than a plant.
Leah answered:
“Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also?” — Genesis 30:15
And Rachel answered with an astonishing proposition:
“Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes.”
Read that again.
Rachel effectively offered Leah a night with Jacob in exchange for Reuben's mandrakes.
Then Jacob came home.
Leah went out to meet him.
And what she said is even more startling in Hebrew:
כִּי שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ
ki sakhor sekhartikha
The wording intensifies the idea of hiring.
In plain sense:
“I have surely hired you.”
The text says she had hired him with her son's mandrakes.
And Jacob slept with Leah that night.
There is no need to sensationalize the Bible.
The Bible is already painfully human.
A wife had reached a place where intimacy with her own husband became something negotiated.
But if you only see the sexual bargain, you will miss the heartbreak.
Because Genesis 30 did not begin in that field.
This wound had been bleeding for years.
Leah had entered her marriage knowing something almost unbearable:
Jacob wanted Rachel.

Jacob had worked seven years to marry Rachel, only for Laban to deceive him and give him Leah instead. Jacob subsequently married Rachel too, and Genesis does not hide the emotional hierarchy inside that household.
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Think about what that could do to a heart.
To wake beside someone whose affection you desperately want…
while knowing his heart is somewhere else.
To cook.
To serve.
To bear his children.
To build his household.
To share his name.
And still wonder:
“Will he ever choose me?”
Leah's children became windows into that ache.
When she bore Reuben, she said, in effect, that the LORD had seen her affliction and hoped that now her husband would love her.
Then came Simeon.
Then Levi.
Again and again, you can hear a woman trying to turn motherhood into the love she could not command.
Maybe another son will make him love me.
Maybe this accomplishment will make me valuable.
Maybe if I give enough…
produce enough…
sacrifice enough…
become useful enough…
someone will finally choose me.
And suddenly Genesis 30 does not feel ancient anymore.
Because some people reading this have never traded mandrakes for affection…
but you have negotiated for love in other currencies.
You became quieter so somebody would stay.
Prettier so somebody would notice.
More successful so somebody would respect you.
More sexually available because you were afraid they would leave.
More useful because usefulness felt safer than vulnerability.
You kept saying yes while your heart was screaming no.
You tolerated what wounded you because loneliness frightened you more.
You gave people access to parts of you hoping access would become affection.
You performed.
You achieved.
You served.
You smiled.
You posted the picture.
You told everybody you were blessed.
And somewhere underneath all of it was one desperate sentence:
“Please choose me.”
That is what makes Leah's story so painful.
She was married…
and still knew rejection.
She had children…
and still knew loneliness.
She belonged to a household…
and still longed to belong in someone's heart.
Rachel had Jacob's affection but desperately wanted children.
Leah had children but desperately wanted Jacob's affection.
Each woman looked across the room and saw in her sister what she believed would finally make her whole.
That is what comparison does.
It makes you stare at somebody else's blessing until you become blind to your own.
Rachel wanted Leah's fertility.
Leah wanted Rachel's place in Jacob's heart.
And between them stood mandrakes.
The Hebrew דּוּדָאִים (dûdā’îm) refers to the plants traditionally identified as mandrakes. In the ancient world they were associated with sexuality and fertility.
But Scripture gives us a devastating irony.
Rachel obtained the mandrakes.
Leah got the night.
And the mandrakes are not credited with opening anybody's womb.
God is.
Genesis 30:17 says:
וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶל־לֵאָה
Vayyishma Elohim el-Le'ah.
“And God listened to Leah.”
Stop there.
Because that may be the most beautiful sentence in the entire scandal.
God listened to Leah.
The woman who felt unheard.
God heard her.
The woman who felt secondary.
God saw her.
The woman bargaining for one night of closeness with a husband whose heart she could never force.
Heaven had not forgotten her.
Scripture does not say:
“And the mandrakes worked.”
It says:
“And God listened to Leah.”
That distinction matters.
Genesis is not teaching Christians to use fertility charms.
It is not endorsing marital bargaining.
It is certainly not presenting Jacob's polygamous household as God's model for Christian marriage.
Scripture is showing us what human beings repeatedly do when desire becomes desperation.
We manipulate.
Compete.
Compare.
Scheme.
Trade.
Grasp.
We attempt to manufacture what only God can ultimately give.
Yet God remains sovereign even in families filled with astonishing dysfunction.
Leah conceived and bore another son.
She named him Issachar.
The name is connected in the narrative with שָׂכָר — sakhar — “wages,” “hire,” or “reward.”
The language deliberately echoes the strange transaction surrounding that night.
But Leah's deepest wound still had not disappeared.
Later, after another son was born, she said:
“Now will my husband dwell with me, because I have born him six sons.”
Six sons.
And she was still hoping.
Still waiting.
Still wondering whether this would finally be enough.
That sentence should break something inside us.
Because there are people who spend half their lives doing the same thing.
“Maybe after I lose the weight…”
“Maybe after I get married…”
“Maybe after I have children…”
“Maybe after the promotion…”
“Maybe after the ministry grows…”
“Maybe after people know my name…”
“Maybe after I become successful…”
“Maybe after I prove that I am worth loving…”
Then they will choose me.
Then I will matter.
Then I will finally be enough.
But there will always be another mandrake.
Another achievement.
Another person to impress.
Another number to reach.
Another relationship to secure.
Another version of yourself you think you must become before you are worthy of love.
And this is where Leah's story eventually reaches far beyond Leah.
Because God was writing something through this rejected woman that she could not possibly see.
Leah would become the mother of Judah.
Judah.
That name should make every Christian stop.
Because generations later, through the line of Judah, the Messiah would come.
Jesus Christ.
The rejected woman became part of the human ancestry of the Savior.
The woman desperately asking whether her husband would finally attach himself to her became woven into the story leading to the One who would call sinners to Himself.
That does not mean every action in Leah's household was good.
Grace does not rename sin as righteousness.
Grace means human brokenness does not have the final word.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not enter a sanitized human genealogy populated by people who had never failed.
He entered our actual history.
A history containing deception.
Sexual sin.
Family dysfunction.
Jealousy.
Prostitution.
Adultery.
Murder.
Outsiders.
Failures.
Scandals.
And sinners desperately needing mercy.
Then Christ came.
Holy.
Sinless.
The One person in the story who needed no redemption became the Redeemer of everyone who did.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He was wounded for sinners who had spent their lives searching for love in places that could never save them.
And He rose again.
This is why the Gospel is not:
“Fix your reputation and maybe God will accept you.”
It is:
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Stop trying to purchase what Jesus offers by grace.
You cannot bargain your way into God's love.
You cannot seduce your way into it.
Perform your way into it.
Donate your way into it.
Work your way into it.
Pretend your way into it.
Or religiously impress your way into it.
The price of redemption was not paid with mandrakes.
It was paid by Christ.
And that means there is something Christians must be extremely careful about.
Supporting a ministry does not purchase God's favor.
Sharing an article does not earn salvation.
Giving money cannot buy grace.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But when grace has truly gripped us, gratitude moves.
We begin asking a different question.
Not, “What can I give so God will love me?”
But:
“Because God has loved me in Christ, how can my life help somebody else hear about Him?”
Not to purchase God's blessing.
But because Gospel ministry worth spreading needs people willing to help carry it.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
Someone smiling publicly while privately wondering why they were never enough.
Someone begging for affection.
Someone comparing themselves with a sister, brother, friend, coworker, ex, spouse, influencer, or stranger.
Someone quietly trading pieces of themselves just to feel chosen.
Someone who needs to hear that Jesus Christ is not another person they must manipulate into loving them.
And comment.
Your honesty may give another wounded believer permission to stop pretending too.
Because Leah's story was never merely about a strange bargain involving mandrakes.
It was about the terrible things wounded hearts can do while begging to be loved.
And it was about a God whose purposes were larger than the dysfunction surrounding her.
Leah wanted Jacob to choose her.
God was already weaving her into a story that would eventually lead to Christ.
She could see one painful night.
God could see generations.
She could see a transaction.
God could see Judah.
She could see rejection.
God could see redemption coming.
And perhaps that is what somebody reading this needs tonight.
You are staring at the chapter that wounded you as though it must be the chapter that defines you.
It does not.
Bring your sin honestly to Jesus.
Bring the rejection.
Bring the jealousy.
Bring the shame.
Bring the compromises you made because you wanted somebody to stay.
Bring the nights you wish you could rewrite.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Seek healing where wounds remain.
Then stop asking broken human beings to become your savior.
There is already One.
His name is Jesus.
The cross proves that sin is more serious than we wanted to admit.
The empty tomb proves that grace is more powerful than we dared to imagine.
And the family line that ran through Leah and Judah reminds us of something breathtaking:
God can bring redemption through a history filled with chapters we would have preferred to hide.
So remember this when your past tries to introduce you by your worst moment:
The night Leah had to bargain for affection was not the end of her story—and the chapter that broke your heart does not have authority to finish yours when you surrender your life to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Can Be Faithful in Church and Unfaithful in Your Imagination
paragraphs: You Can Be Faithful in Church and Unfaithful in Your Imagination
You may never touch another person. You may never send the message. You may never cross the physical line. And still, Jesus loves you too much to leave the secret rooms of your imagination untouched.
There is a kind of unfaithfulness that leaves no lipstick on a collar.
No suspicious hotel receipt.
No hidden second phone.
No unfamiliar perfume.
No confession beginning with, “Something happened.”
Sometimes there is nothing for a spouse to discover because everything happened behind the eyes.
You went to church.
You sang the worship songs.
You opened your Bible.
You greeted people in the lobby.
You came home to the person you promised to love.
And nobody knew where your imagination had been.
That sentence may hurt.
But perhaps it needs to.
Because Jesus once spoke to people who knew how to measure sexual faithfulness by what the body had done, and then He moved the boundary deeper.
Into the heart.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
—Matthew 5:27–28
The Greek makes the force of His words difficult to escape.
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn.
The issue is not merely that the human eye noticed another human being.
Jesus was not teaching that recognizing beauty is adultery.
He was not saying that every involuntary temptation, unwanted thought, intrusive image, or momentary attraction means you have already committed adultery.
That distinction matters enormously, especially to believers tormented by unwanted thoughts.
The wording points toward looking with the purpose or direction of lusting—the gaze that does not merely encounter desire but welcomes it, feeds it, returns to it, and gives it somewhere to live.
There is a difference between temptation knocking at the door and pulling up a chair for it.
There is a difference between noticing and nurturing.
Between an unwanted thought and an entertained fantasy.
Between being tempted and deliberately turning another person into material for your private sexual imagination.
Jesus goes after that distinction because Jesus is not interested merely in producing people who appear sexually faithful.
He wants hearts that are becoming faithful.
And that is where this gets painfully personal.
You can remain physically faithful while secretly rehearsing betrayal.
You can sleep beside your spouse while fantasizing about somebody else.
