You can celebrate an anniversary while repeatedly visiting images you would panic to have projected onto the wall.
You can delete your browsing history and still carry the history in your imagination.
You can know exactly which accounts trigger you.
Exactly which scenes you replay.
Exactly which person you enjoy imagining.
Exactly when your spouse leaves the room.
Exactly when you reach for the phone.
And you can become frighteningly skilled at keeping all of it invisible.
No affair.
No physical touch.
No public scandal.
So you tell yourself:
“At least I never cheated.”
And Jesus asks a more penetrating question:
What is your heart learning to desire?
That is the hidden territory of faithfulness we rarely want to discuss.
Because physical boundaries are easier to measure.
The imagination has no witnesses.
Except God.
And perhaps that is why secret lust can survive for years inside outwardly respectable Christianity.
You can serve while hiding it.
Preach while hiding it.
Lead worship while hiding it.
Teach Bible study while hiding it.
Post Scripture while hiding it.
Hold your spouse’s hand in church while hiding it.
Nobody sees the private movie.
Nobody hears the internal dialogue.
Nobody knows how often you revisit the fantasy.
Nobody knows how much comparison has entered your marriage.
But Jesus does.
And remarkably, He still came for people like us.
That is where conviction must never be separated from the Gospel.
Because if all you hear in Matthew 5 is, “You are disgusting,” you have not yet heard the full voice of Christ.
Jesus exposes darkness because He came to rescue people from darkness.
He names sin because sin destroys what He loves.
The same Christ who says lust matters is the Christ who goes to the cross for lustful people.
The same Savior who exposes the heart offers to cleanse it.
Christianity is not the story of clean people standing far away from dirty people.
It is the story of sinners discovering that the Son of God came near.
Maybe your struggle has been pornography.
Maybe it has been someone at work.
Maybe it is an ex you keep resurrecting in your imagination.
Maybe it is a fictional person.
Maybe it is endless scrolling because you already know what kind of content the algorithm will eventually place before you.
Maybe you would never message the person whose pictures you repeatedly revisit.
Maybe your spouse has absolutely no idea.
Maybe you are single and have convinced yourself that faithfulness does not apply until marriage.
But sexual holiness is not merely loyalty to a present or future spouse.
It is first loyalty to Christ.
Paul wrote:
“Flee from sexual immorality.”
—1 Corinthians 6:18
Not negotiate with it.
Not domesticate it.
Not keep it close enough to enjoy while promising yourself you will never go “too far.”
Flee.
Why?
Because your body does not ultimately belong to your appetites.
“You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honor God with your bodies.”
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20
Bought.
At a price.
That changes the conversation.
Christian purity is not primarily about becoming impressive enough for God.
It is the response of someone who realizes:
Christ purchased me.
Christ loves me.
Christ died for me.
Christ rose for me.
I belong to Him.
So perhaps the question is no longer merely:
“How far can I go before this becomes sin?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“How completely can I belong to Jesus?”
That question reaches places religious performance never will.
It reaches the browser history.
The saved pictures.
The private messages.
The television choices.
The fantasies before sleep.
The person you deliberately look for across the room.
The comparison you keep making between your spouse and somebody else.
The memory you keep sexualizing.
The secret account.
The second glance.
The third glance.
The thought you could have released but chose instead to develop.
And suddenly holiness stops being a list of forbidden physical acts.
It becomes love.
Because if you are married, the person beside you deserves more than technical fidelity.
They deserve a heart continually being surrendered to Christ.
And whether married or single, the people you encounter are not bodies placed on earth for your consumption.
They bear the image of God.
They are somebody’s daughter.
Somebody’s son.
Somebody Christ calls you to regard with dignity rather than reduce to fantasy.
Lust asks:
“What can I take from this person in my imagination?”
Love asks:
“How can I see this person as God sees them?”
That battle may happen in seconds.
And sometimes you will lose.
That needs to be said too.
Because someone reading this has already failed so many times that another purity article feels like another stone being placed on your chest.
You promised God.
Failed.
Cried.
Deleted everything.
Returned.
Confessed.
Failed again.
Maybe you have wondered whether your repentance can possibly be real if the battle keeps returning.
Listen carefully.
Repeated temptation does not mean Christ has abandoned you.
But repeated surrender to sin should never be renamed harmless because you are tired of fighting it.
Grace does not tell you to make peace with the chains.
Grace opens the prison door.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Notice who is faithful when we have been unfaithful.
He is.
Jesus is.
Your hope is not that your record suddenly becomes flawless.
Your hope is that Christ’s mercy is greater than the record you bring Him—and that His grace does not merely pardon you but begins transforming you.
Repentance means you stop protecting what Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Maybe that means confessing to God without euphemisms.
Maybe it means removing an app.
Unfollowing someone.
Installing accountability.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Stopping the private conversation you keep pretending is innocent.
Talking to a mature believer.
Seeking pastoral counsel.
Having an appropriately honest conversation in your marriage.
Getting help when pornography or compulsive sexual behavior has become deeply entrenched.
Not because external safeguards can manufacture holiness.
They cannot.
But sometimes repentance looks remarkably practical.
Jesus did not die so you could become better at hiding.
He died to bring you into the light.
And the light may feel terrifying when you have lived in secrecy.
But secrecy has been charging you rent.
It takes peace.
Intimacy.
Confidence in prayer.
Tenderness toward your spouse.
Clarity of conscience.
Sometimes even your ability to look another human being in the eyes without internally turning them into something they were never meant to become.
Eventually the hidden room stops feeling like freedom.
It becomes a cell.
And Jesus stands at the door calling you out.
Not into humiliation.
Into freedom.
This is the scandal of grace.
Jesus already knows the version of you that you are desperately trying to keep everyone else from seeing.
And He still calls you to Himself.
Not so you can remain unchanged.
So He can remake you.
That is why the Gospel is infinitely better than image management.
Image management says:
“Make sure nobody finds out.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Image management says:
“Protect your reputation.”
The Gospel says:
“Confess and receive mercy.”
Image management says:
“Hide the scandal.”
Jesus says:
“Give Me the sinner.”
And at Calvary, the sinless Christ carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He was crucified.
Buried.
And He rose.
So the deepest message of this article is not:
“Try harder not to lust.”
It is:
Run to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the emotional affair.
Bring Him the wandering eyes.
Bring Him the imagination you cannot seem to control.
Bring Him your shame.
Bring Him your excuses.
Bring Him your failures.
And then keep bringing your mind under His lordship.
Not once.
Again tomorrow.
Again when temptation comes.
Again when you feel weak.
Again when the old images return.
Again when you realize holiness is not accomplished in one emotional night but formed through thousands of surrendered moments.
The goal is not merely to become someone who can say:
“I never physically cheated.”
The goal is to become someone whose secret life increasingly belongs to Jesus.
Maybe nobody else knows why you needed this article.
God does.
And perhaps your next act of worship is not another song.
Perhaps it is honesty.
Not because strangers need the details.
They do not.
You do not owe the internet your private confession.
But sometimes three simple words become a line in the sand:
No more hiding.
Your testimony may become the reason another believer realizes they are not the only person fighting in secret.
And please—do not merely read this and disappear.
Ask Jesus about you.
About your eyes.
Your thoughts.
Your habits.
Your imagination.
Your hidden rooms.
Because physical faithfulness is beautiful.
But Christ wants more than behavior that survives public inspection.
He wants the heart.
And when you finally hand Him the room you were most ashamed to open, you may discover that the place you expected Him to abandon you becomes the very place where His transforming grace meets you.
Jesus does not expose the hidden room to destroy you; He turns on the light because He intends to lead you out.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID HE IS WHERE HEAVEN TOUCHES EARTH—AND JACOB’S 2,000-YEAR-OLD DREAM EXPLAINS WHAT HE MEANT
paragraphs: JESUS SAID HE IS WHERE HEAVEN TOUCHES EARTH—AND JACOB’S 2,000-YEAR-OLD DREAM EXPLAINS WHAT HE MEANT

Jacob saw a stairway between heaven and earth. Centuries later, Jesus quietly placed Himself at the center of that ancient vision—and once you see the connection, John 1:51 becomes almost impossible to read casually again.
There are verses you can read for years and never realize there is an entire story hiding underneath them.
John 1:51 is one of those verses.
Jesus looks at Nathanael and says something astonishing:
“Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
That sounds beautiful.
Mystical, even.
But Jesus was not simply creating poetic imagery.
He was reaching backward into Genesis.
Back to a frightened man sleeping outdoors.
Back to a stone beneath his head.
Back to a family scandal.
Back to Jacob.
And once you understand what Jacob saw, the words of Jesus become breathtaking—because Christ was identifying Himself with the place where heaven and earth meet.
But there is something even more personal buried inside this story.
Jacob encountered that revelation while running from the consequences of his own brokenness.
And perhaps that is why you need this story too.
Because some people reading this are running.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still smile.
You still go to work.
You still post photographs.
You still say, “I’m okay.”
You might even still attend church.
But somewhere underneath the polished version of your life is a Jacob running through the darkness carrying things you wish you could rewrite.
Regret.
Failure.
Secret sin.
A fractured relationship.
A decision you cannot undo.
A version of yourself you are ashamed anyone ever met.
And then comes the question:
Can heaven still come near someone like that?
Genesis 28 answers from the darkness.
Jacob was not traveling because everything in his life had gone wonderfully.
He was fleeing.

The family of Isaac had become painfully fractured. Jacob had obtained Esau’s birthright and, later, through deception involving Rebekah, received Isaac’s blessing while pretending to be his brother. Esau became furious and intended to kill him after their father died, so Jacob was sent away.
This is important.
The Bible does not sanitize its heroes.
Scripture does not need Jacob to look impressive in order for God to look glorious.
Jacob arrives at a certain place after sunset, takes one of the stones there, puts it beneath his head, and sleeps.
No palace.
No altar prepared by human hands.
No cheering crowd.
Just a fugitive, a stone, darkness...
and God.
Then Jacob dreams.
Genesis 28:12 says:
“וְהִנֵּה סֻלָּם מֻצָּב אַרְצָה וְרֹאשׁוֹ מַגִּיעַ הַשָּׁמָיְמָה”
vehinneh sullam mutstsav artsah, verosho maggia hashshamaymah...
In context, Jacob sees what the Hebrew text calls a סֻלָּם — sullām.
It is traditionally translated “ladder,” though “stairway” is also used to communicate the image.
It is positioned upon the earth, with its top reaching toward heaven.
Then something happens upon it:
“וְהִנֵּה מַלְאֲכֵי אֱלֹהִים עֹלִים וְיֹרְדִים בּוֹ”
The angels of God are ascending and descending.
Do not miss those words.
Ascending.
Descending.
Earth.
Heaven.
Remember them.
Because centuries later, Jesus will use them again.
Jacob then receives the covenantal promise of God—the God of Abraham and Isaac reaffirming promises concerning land, descendants, blessing, divine presence, protection, and return.
Jacob wakes terrified and says:
“Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.”
Then:
“How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
The Hebrew expression is unforgettable:
שַׁעַר הַשָּׁמָיִם — shaʿar hashshamayim
“Gate of heaven.”
Jacob names the place Bethel—from beit/el, “house of God.”
Heaven and earth have suddenly collided in the experience of a runaway.
Hold that image.
Because now we move forward through Israel’s story until we meet another Israelite.
His name is Nathanael.
Philip tells Nathanael they have found the One written about by Moses and the prophets: Jesus of Nazareth.
Nathanael is skeptical.
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”
Philip gives him one of the simplest invitations to faith imaginable:
“Come and see.”
When Nathanael approaches, Jesus calls him an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.

That wording becomes especially interesting against the Jacob background, because Jacob—whose name later becomes Israel—is remembered in Genesis as a deeply complicated man whose story included deception.
Nathanael is stunned that Jesus knows him.
Jesus tells him that before Philip called him, He saw him under the fig tree.
Whatever Nathanael understood from that statement, his reaction is immediate:
“Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”
Then Jesus takes him somewhere much bigger.
John 1:51 preserves His words:
“ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὄψεσθε τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.”
Amēn amēn legō hymin...
“Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”
There they are.
The words from Jacob’s dream.
Heaven.
Opened.
Angels.
Ascending.
Descending.
But something has changed.
In Genesis, Jacob sees the sullām stretching between earth and heaven.
In John, the angels ascend and descend ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — epi ton huion tou anthrōpou:
upon the Son of Man.
Jesus has placed Himself at the center of Jacob’s imagery.
That is the shock.
Jesus does not merely tell Nathanael where the connection between heaven and earth can be found.
He points to Himself.
The ultimate meeting place between God and humanity is not geographical.
It is personal.
Jesus Christ.

This does not mean that Jesus is merely a “ladder,” as though that exhausts His identity. John’s Gospel has already said something vastly greater: the eternal Word was with God, the Word was God, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
The One standing before Nathanael is not simply showing humanity a route upward.
God has come down.
That changes Christianity completely.
Christianity is not fundamentally the story of human beings constructing a staircase high enough to reach God.
It is the Gospel announcement that God came near to sinners in Jesus Christ.
Religion says, “Climb.”
Grace announces, “Christ came.”
Pride says, “Make yourself worthy.”
The Gospel says that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Shame says, “Hide.”
Jesus calls, “Come.”
Humanity keeps trying to build Babel.
God gives us Bethel fulfilled in Christ.
And that is where this stops being merely an interesting Bible connection.
Because you are somewhere in this story.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to climb.
Trying to become good enough.
Trying to compensate for what you did.
Trying to prove to God that you deserve another chance.
Or perhaps you stopped climbing long ago.
You decided heaven probably did not want you anyway.
You know what you watched.
You know what you said.
You know whom you hurt.
You know what happened when nobody else was looking.
You know the promises you broke.
And somewhere inside you, shame whispered:
“Stay away from God until you fix yourself.”
But if sinners could repair themselves enough to reach heaven, why would the Son of God have come?
Jesus did not come merely to congratulate respectable people.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came for sinners.
He came calling people to repentance.
He came announcing the kingdom of God.
He came revealing the Father.
And ultimately, He walked toward a cross.
There the One who spoke of opened heaven would be lifted up before the world.
There the sinless Christ would give Himself for sinners.
There our rebellion would be confronted not with cheap excuses, but with costly grace.
Grace does not pretend sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin matters so profoundly that the Son of God gave Himself for us.
Yet grace also declares that your sin does not possess greater saving power than Christ's blood.
Repentance therefore is not decorating the prison cell.
It is turning toward the One who opens the door.
The Gospel does not say, “Your scandal never happened.”
It says something better.
Your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Jacob's story was not finished on the night he fled.
Peter's story was not finished when he denied Christ.
The thief's story was not finished when nails held him beside Jesus.
And if you belong to Christ, your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending either.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending evil was good.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by giving us religious slogans that allow us to continue comfortably in sin.
Jesus rewrites lives through forgiveness, repentance, reconciliation with God, and transforming grace.
And notice something else about Jacob's dream.
Jacob was asleep.
God initiated the encounter.
Jacob did not climb the stairway to persuade God to notice him.
He woke up astonished that God had already come near.
That pattern reaches its glorious fulfillment in the Gospel.
We did not engineer the Incarnation.
We did not send ourselves a Savior.
We did not create the cross.
We did not conquer death.
God acted.
Christ came.
Christ died for sins.
Christ rose.
And salvation is received by grace through faith, producing a life that increasingly belongs to Him.
So maybe the real question is not:
“How do I climb high enough for God to accept me?”
Maybe the question is:
“What will I do with Jesus Christ?”
Because the Gospel does not finally offer you a technique.
It offers you a Person.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
He does not merely know the way.
He is the way.
And the New Testament pushes this truth even further. First Timothy 2:5 says there is one God and one mediator between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, Himself human.
One mediator.
Not your achievements.
Not your reputation.
Not your religious résumé.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not a pastor.
Not a denomination.
Not money.
Jesus Christ alone.
That distinction matters enormously.
The glory belongs to Christ.
Always.
And if this article has helped you see Him more clearly, then you can turn that gratitude into mission.
Someone needs to know about Jesus.
Someone needs to know repentance is possible.
Someone needs to know forgiveness is real.
Someone needs to know their shame does not have to become their identity.
Send this to the believer who thinks failure has disqualified them forever.
And yes—even send it to the person who does not believe any of this yet.
Let them meet Christ in the Scriptures for themselves.
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not pretend it did not.
Someone else may recognize hope in your scars.
There will probably come a night when shame tries to preach to you again.
When that happens, return to Genesis 28.
Return to John 1.
Return to the cross.
Remember that Christianity is not the story of sinners successfully climbing into heaven.
It is the story of the Son of God coming for sinners and bringing those who trust Him to the Father.
Then invite someone with you.
Running.
Ashamed.
Tired.
Certain that heaven wants nothing to do with them.
And perhaps through one passage of Scripture, they will finally discover what Jacob discovered in the darkness:
God is nearer than they thought.
But we now know something Jacob could only see in shadow.
The gate is not merely a place.
The way to the Father has a name.
Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is the line you need to carry with you when this article is over:
You were never going to climb your way into heaven—so Heaven came down to rescue you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SEX DURING MENSTRUATION: The Biblical Command Most Christians Never Discuss
paragraphs:
SEX DURING MENSTRUATION: The Biblical Command Most Christians Never Discuss
There is a verse sitting quietly in Leviticus that almost nobody talks about in church—and once you actually read what God said, the question becomes impossible to ignore.
There are Bible verses Christians quote constantly.
John 3:16.
Philippians 4:13.
Psalm 23.
Jeremiah 29:11.
And then there are verses we seem to walk past very quickly.
Verses that make the room uncomfortable.
Verses that touch the bedroom.
Verses that force husbands and wives to ask whether surrender to God includes places in their marriage they assumed belonged entirely to them.
This is one of those passages.
And before going any further, something needs to be made unmistakably clear.
Menstruation is not shameful.
A menstruating woman is not disgusting, spiritually inferior, morally guilty, or somehow farther from God.
The Bible never teaches that menstruation itself is a sin.
Yet the same Bible does contain a remarkably direct command concerning sexual intercourse during menstruation.
And whatever conclusion a Christian eventually reaches about how that command relates to believers under the New Covenant, intellectual honesty requires us first to hear what the text actually says.
Because sometimes the most dangerous way to handle Scripture is not openly rejecting it.
Sometimes it is simply never talking about it.
Leviticus 18:19 reads in Hebrew:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el-ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ‘ervatah.
A close rendering is:
“And you shall not approach a woman in the menstrual condition of her impurity to uncover her nakedness.”
Those words deserve more than a nervous glance.
The Hebrew נִדָּה — niddah carries the idea of menstrual separation or the condition associated with menstruation.
לֹא תִקְרַב — lo tiqrav means “you shall not approach” or “come near.”
And לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ — legalot ‘ervatah, literally “to uncover her nakedness,” belongs to the sexual language of Leviticus 18.
In other words, this is not merely a vague ancient statement about hygiene.
The immediate context is sexual conduct.
Leviticus 18 speaks about forbidden sexual relationships, and verse 19 places intercourse during menstruation inside that discussion.
Then Scripture becomes even more explicit.

Leviticus 20:18 describes a man lying sexually with a menstruating woman and says that he has exposed “the source of her flow” while she has exposed “the source of her blood.” Under Israel’s covenant administration, the text attaches the severe sanction of both being “cut off” from their people.
That is uncomfortable.
But discomfort does not give us permission to pretend the passage does not exist.
Yet here is where careful Bible reading matters enormously.
Leviticus also contains an extensive system of ritual impurity, and ritual impurity is not identical to moral wickedness.
This distinction changes everything.

Leviticus 15 discusses menstruation alongside bodily discharges. The same chapter says that a man becomes ritually unclean after an emission of semen. Ordinary marital intercourse also made both husband and wife ritually unclean until evening.
So “unclean” cannot automatically mean “sinful.”
A bodily condition could make someone ceremonially unclean without making that person morally guilty.
That means a woman experiencing her monthly period was not committing a sin merely because she was menstruating.

She was experiencing a normal bodily process within a covenantal system where blood, bodily emissions, life, death, holiness, sanctuary access, cleansing, and separation carried profound symbolic meaning.
This is where careless preaching can deeply wound women.
God was not declaring women filthy.
Menstruation was not female guilt.
And no Christian husband should weaponize Leviticus to humiliate his wife, treat her body with disgust, or make her feel spiritually contaminated.
Jesus Christ never gives men permission to turn holiness into cruelty.
But another mistake lies on the opposite side.
Recognizing the ceremonial dimensions of Leviticus does not allow us simply to erase Leviticus 18:19.
Why?
Because the prohibition does not appear only in the ritual-purity regulations of Leviticus 15.
It appears in Leviticus 18 among sexual prohibitions.
It appears again with a penalty in Leviticus 20.
And generations later, Ezekiel uses strikingly similar language.
When Ezekiel 18 describes a righteous man, among the behaviors mentioned is that he does not defile his neighbor’s wife and does not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity.
Ezekiel 22:10 likewise includes violating women during menstrual impurity among Jerusalem’s covenant offenses.
So anyone claiming that the Bible treats the subject as completely insignificant has to wrestle honestly with more than one passage.
But Christians must wrestle with something else too.
The cross.
Jesus Christ fulfilled the Law.
The New Testament radically changes the believer’s relationship to the ceremonial structures of the Mosaic covenant.
We do not bring Levitical animal sacrifices to an altar.
We do not maintain Israel’s sanctuary purity system.
We do not assume that every regulation given to covenant Israel transfers unchanged into the church.
Christ has inaugurated the New Covenant, and Hebrews repeatedly points us toward the fulfillment found in Him.
This is why Christians must resist two opposite temptations.
One says:
“It is in Leviticus, therefore every detail applies to Christians exactly as it applied to ancient Israel.”
That is too simplistic.
The other says:
“It is in Leviticus, therefore Christians can ignore it.”
That is also too simplistic.
The real question is harder:

What does this command reveal about God’s holiness, sexuality, blood, covenant order, self-control, and the way His people should honor Him with their bodies—and to what extent does the specific prohibition continue as Christian moral obligation?
Faithful Christians have not all answered that final question identically.
The New Testament never gives Christians a sentence directly repeating, “Do not have intercourse during menstruation.”
That fact matters.
We should not manufacture a New Testament command that is not explicitly there.
At the same time, the Old Testament passages remain Scripture, and their repeated treatment of the practice means Christians should not mock, conceal, or casually dismiss the subject either.
Romans 15:4 reminds believers that what was written beforehand was written for our instruction.
Second Timothy 3:16 says that all Scripture is God-breathed and profitable.
So perhaps the mature Christian response is not:
“How quickly can I explain this verse away?”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, what are You teaching me here—and am I willing to obey You even when obedience reaches somewhere private?”
That question goes far beyond menstruation.
Because suddenly the bedroom becomes a mirror.
We live in a culture trained to believe that desire creates entitlement.
I want it.
Therefore I should have it.
I feel it.
Therefore it must be right.
We even carry that thinking into marriage.
But biblical marriage never means unlimited sexual entitlement.
First Corinthians 7 teaches profound mutuality between husband and wife, but the same passage assumes love, agreement, and consideration—not coercion.
Christian sexuality is never merely about what someone can obtain from another person's body.
It is supposed to become another place where Christ is Lord.
That changes how a husband looks at his wife when she is bleeding, hurting, exhausted, cramping, uncomfortable, or simply does not want sexual intercourse.
She is not an instrument for his appetite.
She is someone made in the image of God.
Someone he vowed to love.
Someone for whom Christ died.
And perhaps there is something deeply countercultural about a husband being capable of saying:
“My desire does not rule me.”
“I can wait.”
“I can hold you without demanding something from you.”
“I can love you when your body cannot give me what I want.”
“You are more valuable to me than sexual gratification.”
That kind of restraint does not weaken intimacy.
It can reveal love.
And wives need the same heart of surrender before Christ.
Marriage is not two people asking how close they can get to the boundary without technically crossing it.
Christian marriage is two redeemed sinners learning to ask:
“How can our bodies glorify Jesus?”
There is a deeper issue hiding underneath this entire conversation.
Who owns the locked rooms of your life?
We happily give Jesus Sunday morning.
We give Him worship songs.
We give Him Bible verses posted on Facebook.
We give Him Christian captions.
But what happens when Christ walks toward the bedroom door?
What happens when Scripture touches money?
Pornography?
Secret fantasies?
Resentment?
Sexual boundaries?
Forgiveness?
Pride?
The habits nobody at church knows about?
Suddenly theology becomes personal.
Because Jesus did not die merely to become a decoration hanging over your life.
He died and rose again as Lord.
And lordship means there is no room in the human heart with a sign saying:
“Jesus may not enter here.”
Maybe that is why this obscure passage feels heavier than expected.
The deepest question was never merely:
“Can Christians have sex during menstruation?”
The deeper question is:
When Scripture interrupts something I want, who gets the final word?
And that question exposes all of us.
Maybe your hidden issue has nothing to do with this particular subject.
Maybe yours is pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe lust.
Maybe an emotional affair nobody knows about.
Maybe you have learned to rename compromise so you no longer have to call it sin.
Maybe you know exactly what God has been confronting, and you have spent months constructing theological loopholes around something your conscience already knows needs to be surrendered.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to clean themselves up.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners could not save themselves, so Jesus came for them.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He shed His blood for our redemption.
He rose from the grave.
And now forgiveness is offered not because our record is spotless, but because His sacrifice is sufficient.
That means conviction is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come home.
Peter had scandal.
The woman caught in adultery had scandal.
The Samaritan woman had scandal.
The thief beside Jesus had scandal.
The Corinthians had scandal.
We have scandal.
But scandal does not get the final sentence when Jesus enters the story.
Grace does.
Not cheap grace that baptizes whatever we want.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives and then teaches us to walk differently.
Grace that reaches into the places we are ashamed to discuss.
Grace that tells the truth without crushing the sinner.
Grace that says repentance is not the end of your story.
It can be the doorway into a new one.
That is why our theme will never simply be “behave better.”
Be honest.

And if Jesus has already rescued you from sexual sin, secret compromise, shame, addiction, or a broken past, consider sharing a piece of your testimony. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance is possible and grace is real.
Let the conversation be gracious. Let it be biblical. Let it point people toward Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves somebody loves Jesus.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God's grace is a gift.
But Christians can freely choose to support Gospel work and discipleship resources because they want biblical truth to keep reaching people.
And whether you ever purchase anything or not, we want Scripture in your hands.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is drifting.
Invite the believer quietly struggling.
Invite the person who has stopped going to church.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing honest to say about real life.
Invite the person carrying a secret.
Because sometimes God begins rewriting a life when somebody finally has enough courage to open the page everyone else kept skipping.
And after all the Hebrew, all the difficult verses, all the theological questions, and all the uncomfortable discussion, remember what matters most:
Jesus is not afraid to enter the room you have been afraid to open.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ESAU MARRIED TWO WOMEN—AND HIS PARENTS WERE MISERABLE ABOUT IT
paragraphs: ESAU MARRIED TWO WOMEN—AND HIS PARENTS WERE MISERABLE ABOUT IT
Two verses. One marriage decision. A mother and father carrying grief inside their own home. And a warning about the choices we make when we want what we want more than we want the wisdom of God.
There are family wounds Scripture does not describe with shouting.
No slammed doors.
No dramatic confrontation.
No long explanation.
Just one devastating sentence.
Esau was forty years old when he married Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
Then Genesis tells us what those marriages did to Isaac and Rebekah:

“And they were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah.”
—Genesis 26:35, KJV
Read that again.
Not because Esau married.
Not simply because he married two women.
The text specifically identifies these women as Hittites, women from the peoples of Canaan.
And that detail matters.
The Hebrew of Genesis 26:35 says:
וַתִּהְיֶיןָ מֹרַת רוּחַ לְיִצְחָק וּלְרִבְקָה
Vattihyena morat ruach le-Yitzchaq ule-Rivqah.
The expression מֹרַת רוּחַ — morat ruach carries the sense of bitterness or grief of spirit.
Esau did not merely make a choice his parents happened to dislike.
Something about these marriages became bitterness to their spirits.
And if you have ever watched someone you love make a decision you could not make for them, you already understand something about this verse.
A parent can teach.
A parent can warn.
A parent can pray.
A parent can remember holding that child when he was small enough to sleep against their chest.
But eventually that child becomes an adult.
And adults make choices.
Sometimes choices that leave the people who love them wondering:
How did we get here?
Isaac knew something about marriage that Esau should have understood.
Years earlier, Abraham had been intensely concerned that Isaac not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. Abraham told his servant:

“Thou shalt not take a wife unto my son of the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell.”
—Genesis 24:3, KJV
This was not presented as ethnic superiority.
Genesis itself will not allow that interpretation.

The issue running through the patriarchal story is covenant faithfulness—God had called Abraham and his household into a particular covenant mission, while the surrounding Canaanite world represented religious allegiances and practices incompatible with that calling.
Abraham wanted Isaac's marriage to remain consistent with that covenant vocation.
Rebekah eventually expresses the same anguish even more dramatically.
After Esau's marriages, she tells Isaac:

“I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth: if Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me?”
—Genesis 27:46, KJV
That is not mild disappointment.
That is a mother saying, essentially:
I cannot bear watching this happen again.
Then Isaac calls Jacob and commands him not to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan.
The contrast is impossible to miss.
But something even sadder happens next.
Esau eventually realizes that the daughters of Canaan displease his father.
Genesis 28:8 says:
“And Esau seeing that the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father...”
So Esau goes and marries again—this time into Ishmael's family.
It is one of the most painfully human moments in his story.
He finally notices.
He finally sees the problem.
But his response appears to address the surface rather than undo the deeper pattern.
How many of us have done exactly that?
We experience the consequences of a decision, and instead of asking God to expose what is happening inside us, we try to rearrange the outside.
We change relationships without changing ourselves.
We change churches without confronting our pride.
We change jobs without confronting our dishonesty.
We delete the message without killing the lust.
We apologize because we were caught, but never ask why we wanted the sin.
We hide the bottle.
Erase the browser history.
Change the password.
Make another promise.
Post another Bible verse.
Smile in another church photograph.
And somewhere underneath all of it, the heart remains untouched.
That is why this ancient family story can become uncomfortable so quickly.
Because Esau is not merely somebody to observe.
There is something frighteningly familiar about wanting the blessing while resisting the God who gives it.
Earlier, Esau had come home exhausted and traded his birthright to Jacob for food.
Genesis says:

“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
—Genesis 25:34, KJV
The Hebrew verb is וַיִּבֶז — vayivez, from בָּזָה — bazah, meaning to despise, treat lightly, or regard as insignificant.
That sentence reaches far beyond lentil stew.
Esau treated something weighty as though it were light.
Something sacred as though it were expendable.
Something connected to his inheritance as though immediate appetite mattered more.
And that is still one of sin's oldest strategies.
Sin rarely walks into your life announcing:
I am here to destroy what God has given you.
It whispers:
You need this now.
One meal.
One affair.
One secret conversation.
One compromise.
One click.
One lie.
One night.
One decision made while angry.
One relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
One appetite you keep feeding because surrender feels too expensive.
And afterward you discover that the thing promising relief was quietly negotiating for something far more valuable.
Hebrews later uses Esau as a warning.
It calls him βέβηλος — bebēlos in Hebrews 12:16, commonly translated “profane” or “godless,” and reminds believers that for one meal he sold his birthright.
The New Testament does not tell Christians to laugh at Esau.
It tells Christians to learn from him.
Because you can become so dominated by what feels urgent that you lose sight of what is holy.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You love Jesus.
Or at least you say you do.
But there is one room you keep locked.
One relationship you refuse to surrender.
One resentment you polish every night.
One addiction you have renamed a “struggle” because calling it sin would require repentance.
One compromise everybody thinks you abandoned.
One version of yourself that appears at church...
and another version that comes alive when nobody is watching.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your children do not know.
Your Facebook friends certainly do not know.
But Christ knows.
And here is where the Gospel changes the direction of this article.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people managed to keep their families spotless.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The Bible contains fractured families because the Bible tells the truth about humanity.
Abraham's household was complicated.
Isaac's household was divided by favoritism.
Jacob's household would become painfully dysfunctional.
The family through which the promises moved was not a museum of flawless people.
It was filled with sinners who desperately needed grace.
And ultimately, the hope of Scripture does not rest on Isaac.
It does not rest on Jacob.
It certainly does not rest on Esau.
It rests on Jesus Christ.
When the angel announced His birth, Matthew explains His name:

“Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
—Matthew 1:21, KJV
The Greek says:
αὐτὸς γὰρ σώσει τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν
autos gar sōsei ton laon autou apo tōn hamartiōn autōn
“For He Himself will save His people from their sins.”
That is the center.
Not merely better decisions.
Not religious image management.
Not becoming respectable enough that your parents stop worrying.
Salvation from sin through Christ.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the reputation of broken people.
He came to save sinners.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And because He lives, repentance is not the funeral of your hope.
It can become the doorway home.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance: a genuine turning of mind and heart that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling terrible about consequences.
Esau's story warns us that sorrow and spiritual transformation are not automatically the same thing.
You can cry because something hurt without surrendering the thing that is destroying you.
You can regret what happened without turning toward God.
You can hate the consequences and still secretly love the sin.
The Gospel calls us deeper.
Jesus does not say, “Hide it better.”
He calls sinners to come into the light.
He does not say, “Repair your image.”
He offers forgiveness.
He does not say, “Pretend you were never dirty.”
He cleanses.
And Scripture gives this astonishing promise:

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Maybe this is where the article stopped being about Esau.
Maybe somewhere between his appetite, his marriages, his parents' grief, and his attempt to repair things, you saw your own reflection.
Then do not hide from it.
Run to Christ.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction drives the sinner toward the mercy of God.
The Gospel does not expose your darkness so Jesus can stand at a distance and mock you.
Christ calls sinners out of darkness because He is light.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing you could do after reading this is simply scroll to the next post.
Do not turn conviction into entertainment.
Stop for a moment.
Ask yourself:
What have I been treating as light that God calls weighty?
What appetite has been making decisions for me?
Whose heart has my rebellion been wounding?
What have I been trying to fix externally while refusing to surrender internally?
And most importantly:
Have I actually brought this to Jesus?
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you also do not have to keep pretending.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed tonight.

Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because there may come a night when appetite becomes louder than conviction, and you need to remember what Esau's story teaches: do not trade what is weighty for what is immediate.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach farther, but do not confuse supporting a ministry with glorifying God itself. We glorify God through Christ-centered faith, worship, obedience, love, generosity, witness, and lives surrendered to Him.
But before you leave, remember the two verses that began this entire journey.
Esau made his choices.
Isaac and Rebekah carried grief.
A family felt the consequences.
And yet the Bible continued moving toward something greater than their dysfunction.
Toward Bethlehem.
Toward Calvary.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward Jesus.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final identity.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
Your sin may have consequences.
Repentance may require painful honesty.
Reconciliation may take time.
Some earthly consequences may remain.
But for the sinner who comes to Christ, shame does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
So do not sell tomorrow's inheritance for tonight's appetite.
Do not keep decorating what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Do not spend another year trying to look healed when Jesus is inviting you to become honest.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His grace.
And follow Christ.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable truth hidden behind this painful family scene is this:
The choices that broke hearts do not have more power than the Savior who transforms hearts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Peter Was Sinking and Had Time for Only Three Words: “Lord, Save Me!”
paragraphs: Peter Was Sinking and Had Time for Only Three Words: “Lord, Save Me!”
He had enough faith to step out of the boat… but not enough strength to keep himself above the water. What Jesus did next is the Gospel in miniature.
There are prayers you pray when everything is peaceful.
And then there are prayers you pray when you are drowning.
No polished introduction.
No carefully arranged theology.
No beautiful Christian vocabulary.
No time to explain what went wrong.
Just desperation.
Just Jesus.
Just three words.
“Lord, save me!”
Peter was sinking.
Not metaphorically.
Not emotionally.
Not in the way we sometimes say, “I feel like I’m drowning.”
He was actually going down into the water.
And perhaps that is why this moment recorded in Matthew 14 is so painfully beautiful.
Because when everything unnecessary was stripped away, Peter discovered what desperate people have been discovering for centuries:
When you cannot save yourself, the name you need is Jesus.

Matthew tells us that after feeding the multitude, Jesus made His disciples get into a boat while He went away to pray. During the night, the boat was battered by the waves because the wind was against them.
Then, through the darkness, Someone came walking toward them.
On the water.
The disciples were terrified.
They thought they were seeing a ghost.
But Jesus spoke:
“Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.”
Peter answered Him with one of the boldest requests in Scripture:
“Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.”
Jesus did not give Peter a lecture.
He gave him one word:
“Come.”
And Peter came.
Think about that before remembering how the story ends.
Peter actually climbed out of the boat.
His feet touched something that should not have supported him.
For a moment, the impossible was beneath his feet because his attention was fixed upon Christ.
We often remember Peter as the disciple who sank.
Jesus also remembered him as the disciple who got out of the boat.
Then Peter noticed the wind.
Matthew 14:30 tells us that when Peter saw the strength of the wind, he became afraid.
And beginning to sink, he cried out.
The Greek preserves the raw simplicity of his prayer:
Κύριε, σῶσόν με.
Kyrie, sōson me.
“Lord, save me!”
Three words in Greek.
Κύριε — Lord.
σῶσόν — save, rescue, deliver.
με — me.
There is no performance left in that sentence.
Peter does not tell Jesus why he deserves another chance.
He does not remind Jesus that he was courageous enough to leave the boat.
He does not negotiate.
He does not promise that if Jesus rescues him, he will never doubt again.
He simply cries:
Lord. Save. Me.
Maybe that prayer feels more familiar than you would like to admit.
Maybe nobody knows how close you have been to sinking.
Your Facebook photos look fine.
You still answer, “I’m good.”
You still show up.
You still laugh.
You still know the worship songs.
You still know which Bible verses to quote when somebody else is hurting.
But somewhere beneath the version of yourself everybody sees, you are tired.
The marriage is hurting.
The temptation came back.
The secret became heavier.
The grief never really left.
Your prayers became shorter.
Your Bible stayed closed longer.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you did it again.
And again.
And somewhere along the way, shame whispered something poisonous:
“You cannot call Jesus now. Look at what you have become.”
But Peter's story destroys that lie.
Because Peter did not wait until he had climbed back into the boat before calling Jesus.
He called Jesus while he was sinking.
That matters.
Some people believe they must repair themselves before returning to Christ.
Get sober enough.
Get clean enough.
Become disciplined enough.
Stop lusting.
Stop lying.
Stop doubting.
Stop being angry.
Fix the marriage.
Fix the mind.
Fix the habits.
Fix everything…
then come back to Jesus.
But drowning people cannot perform surgery on themselves.
They need rescue.
And the Gospel begins with a devastating truth to human pride:
We cannot save ourselves.

Sin is not merely a collection of embarrassing mistakes requiring better habits. Scripture describes humanity apart from Christ as spiritually dead in trespasses and sins. We need more than inspiration.
We need resurrection.
We need mercy.
We need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
Notice what happens after Peter cries out.
Matthew 14:31 says:
“Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him.”
Immediately.
Peter's grip was failing.
Christ's was not.
Peter's courage had collapsed.
Christ's compassion had not.
Peter's circumstances exposed his weakness.
They did not exhaust Jesus' power.
And there is something here that wounded believers desperately need to understand.
Jesus did correct Peter.
He asked him why he doubted.
Grace does not pretend unbelief is harmless.
Grace does not rename sin so we can remain comfortable in it.
Jesus loves us too much to leave our hearts unchallenged.
But notice the order.
Jesus caught Peter before He corrected Peter.
The rebuke came from the One whose hand was already holding him.
That is extraordinarily important.
Biblical conviction is not Jesus standing safely in the boat shouting instructions to a drowning man.
Christ entered the storm.
Christ came across the water.
Christ reached toward the sinking disciple.
Christ brought him back.
And ultimately, what happened on that sea points us toward something infinitely greater.
Because Peter's deepest problem was never water.
Neither is yours.
Our deepest problem is sin and separation from a holy God.
And Jesus came for drowning sinners.
He did not merely stand at a distance and tell humanity to try harder.
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
Christ entered our broken world.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
There, the sinless Son of God bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The Gospel is not that good people managed to swim to God.
The Gospel is that God came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
That changes the way we read Peter's desperate prayer.
Κύριε, σῶσόν με.
Lord, save me.
Those words belong beside every hidden failure you thought disqualified you.
Lord, save me.
Beside the addiction nobody knows about.
Lord, save me.
Beside the bitterness you have been feeding for years.
Lord, save me.
Beside the pornography you promised yourself you would never watch again.
Lord, save me.
Beside the affair.
The lie.
The pride.
The envy.
The religious performance.
The secret resentment.
The cold marriage.
The exhausted faith.
The fear that you have wandered too far.
Lord, save me.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Jesus did not rescue Peter so Peter could remain underwater.
And Jesus does not save sinners so that we can make peace with the very sin from which He came to redeem us.
Grace calls us out.
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace transforms.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
The cross says the opposite.
Sin mattered enough that Christ died.
But the empty tomb announces something even greater:
Your sin does not have to have the final word.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back for mercy.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can give mercy.
Maybe you have spent years trying to make your scandal the final chapter.
Jesus specializes in rewriting endings.
Ask Peter.
This is the same Peter who would later swear that he did not know Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
He had walked with Christ.
He had seen miracles.
He had confessed Jesus as the Christ.
He had watched Him transfigured.
And when pressure came, Peter collapsed.
Again.
Only this time there was no sea beneath him.
There was simply the horrifying realization that he had denied the Lord he loved.
Then the rooster crowed.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
If Scripture ended Peter's story there, many of us would understand.
Failure.
Regret.
Shame.
The end.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, Christ restored Peter.
The man who denied Jesus became a public witness to Jesus.
The mouth that once said, in effect, “I do not know Him,” would boldly proclaim the crucified and risen Christ.
That is what grace does.
It does not pretend the scandal never happened.
It refuses to let the scandal become the final sentence.
From scandal to grace… because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe only God knows.
Maybe the person everyone thinks you are and the person you know yourself to be have become painfully different.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not hiding better.
The answer is not religious acting.
The answer is not another promise to become worthy of Jesus.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Call upon Christ.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
There is forgiveness in Him.
There is no sin made righteous by secrecy, and there is no repentant sinner beyond the sufficiency of Christ's grace.
You may be closer to Peter than you realized.
You started with confidence.
Then came the wind.
The diagnosis.
The betrayal.
The temptation.
The unanswered prayer.
The financial pressure.
The death.
The loneliness.
The disappointment.
The failure you thought you had conquered.
And suddenly the faith that once felt strong feels frighteningly small.
Perhaps your prayer tonight does not need to be impressive.
Perhaps it only needs to be honest.
Κύριε, σῶσόν με.
Lord, save me.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you also do not have to pretend you are invincible.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person still fighting to believe.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list may be sinking quietly right now.
You may never know it.
They may be smiling in their profile picture.
Working.
Parenting.
Posting memes.
Going to church.
Answering messages.
And privately wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” proves your Christianity. It does not.
Send it privately to the person who has gone quiet.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in spreading biblical truth, though our ultimate allegiance and glory belong to Christ alone.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is growth.
Scripture.
Accountability.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
A community continually being pointed away from itself and back toward Jesus Christ.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Salvation belongs to Him.
Grace is found in Him.
Forgiveness is found in Him.
Your hope is not in the strength of your grip on Jesus.
Your hope is in Jesus.
Peter discovered that while disappearing beneath the waves.
He did not have a sermon.
He had three words.
Κύριε, σῶσόν με.
Lord, save me.
And Jesus reached down.
Perhaps that is the picture you need to carry with you tonight.
Not Peter walking spectacularly across the water.
Peter failing.
Peter sinking.
Peter crying.
And the hand of Christ reaching toward him.
Because Christianity was never the story of people impressive enough to walk on water.
It is the story of sinners helpless enough to need a Savior…
and a Savior merciful enough to reach them.
So stop pretending you are not sinking.
Call His name.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Then tell somebody else where rescue is found.
The water may remember where Peter sank, but eternity remembers the hand that pulled him out.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Didn’t Wake Up Lukewarm. You Just Said “Tomorrow” to Jesus Too Many Times.
paragraphs: You Didn’t Wake Up Lukewarm. You Just Said “Tomorrow” to Jesus Too Many Times.
The frightening thing about spiritual drift is that it rarely feels like walking away from Jesus. Sometimes it just feels like telling Him, “Tomorrow.”
You probably never planned to become distant from God.
That may be the most unsettling part.
There probably wasn’t a morning when you opened your eyes, stared at the ceiling, and decided:
“I think I’ll become lukewarm today.”
You didn’t schedule spiritual numbness.
You didn’t write “neglect Jesus” into your calendar.
You didn’t necessarily stop believing the Gospel.
You didn’t wake up wanting a hardened heart.
It happened more quietly than that.
You were tired.
Busy.
Distracted.
Hurting.
Disappointed.
Maybe angry.
Maybe ashamed.
Maybe life simply became so loud that the voice you once listened for became easier to postpone.
You meant to pray.
Tomorrow.
You felt the conviction to forgive somebody.
Later.
You knew that habit was beginning to own you.
Soon.
You sensed God pressing on something hidden that needed to be confessed.
Not tonight.
You wanted to return to Scripture.
When life calms down.
You knew you needed to obey.
After one more compromise.
And somehow...
tomorrow kept becoming today.
Then today kept becoming another tomorrow.
Until one day, something that once would have broken your heart barely bothered you anymore.
That is what makes spiritual drift terrifying.
It does not always begin with hatred for Jesus.
Sometimes it begins with postponement.
And Hebrews gives us a warning that is far more personal than many of us realize:

“Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, in departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.”
— Hebrews 3:12–13, KJV
Read that last phrase again.
“...hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.”
The Greek is striking.
The word translated “hardened” is σκληρυνθῇ — sklērynthē, from σκληρύνω — sklērynō, meaning to become hard or to be hardened.
And the phrase translated “deceitfulness of sin” contains ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας — apatē tēs hamartias.
The deception of sin.
The deceitfulness of sin.
Sin does not always walk through the front door announcing what it intends to destroy.
It deceives.
It minimizes.
It whispers.
Not, “Abandon Christ forever.”
Just...
“Not today.”
That is often enough.
Because tomorrow can become one of the most spiritually dangerous words in your vocabulary when Jesus is calling you to obey today.
Tomorrow I’ll pray.
Tomorrow I’ll confess.
Tomorrow I’ll forgive.
Tomorrow I’ll stop.
Tomorrow I’ll surrender this relationship.
Tomorrow I’ll deal with the bitterness.
Tomorrow I’ll open my Bible again.
Tomorrow I’ll come back.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
Tomorrow.
And somewhere between all those tomorrows, the heart can begin learning how to live comfortably with what once disturbed it.
That is why Hebrews says:
“...while it is called To day...”
The Greek word is σήμερον — sēmeron.
Today.
Not someday.
Not when your emotions cooperate.
Not when temptation becomes easier.
Not when your schedule clears.
Not when you finally feel spiritual again.
Today.
There is an urgency in Hebrews because the human heart does not remain unaffected by repeated resistance.
Every time conviction is dismissed, resistance can become easier.
Every time obedience is postponed, postponement can begin feeling normal.
Every time sin is excused, the excuse can become more believable.
And eventually a person may still know Christian language...
still repost Christian content...
still say “God is good”...
still attend church...
still own a Bible...
still know worship songs...
and yet quietly become accustomed to living at a distance from the One whose name they confess.
That is what makes lukewarmness so frighteningly recognizable.
It does not always look like somebody shaking a fist at heaven.
Sometimes it looks like someone who still loves the idea of Jesus but keeps rescheduling surrender.
And maybe that sentence hurt.
Maybe because you recognize yourself in it.
There was a time when you prayed differently.
There was a time when Scripture could stop you in your tracks.
There was a time when conviction brought tears.
There was a time when you hated the thought of grieving God.
There was a time when worship was not background noise.
There was a time when you wanted Jesus more than you wanted comfort.
But something happened.
Maybe there wasn't even one dramatic scandal.
Maybe that is precisely the problem.
Nothing exploded.
Nothing looked catastrophic.
You just drifted.
A missed prayer became a prayerless week.
A prayerless week became normal.
One compromise became another.
One secret became a hiding place.
One excuse became a lifestyle.
One delayed act of obedience became another unfinished conversation with God.
And eventually you learned something dangerous:
how to postpone Jesus without feeling like you had rejected Him.
But Scripture never treats the condition of the heart casually.
Hebrews does not say, “Relax. You still have plenty of time.”
It says:
“Take heed...”
Watch yourself.
Pay attention.
Because hearts can harden.
Sin can deceive.
People can depart from the living God.
And we need one another urgently enough that Hebrews commands believers to encourage one another daily.
Daily.
Because Christianity was never meant to be a private arrangement between you and your preferences.
We need brothers and sisters who love us enough to interrupt our drift.
People who will remind us of Christ when our hearts become tired.
People who will not applaud what is destroying us.
People who will say, “Come back.”
Maybe this article is that interruption for somebody today.
Maybe for you.
And if you feel exposed right now, do not mistake conviction for rejection.
The Gospel is not the story of Jesus waiting for sufficiently clean people to approach Him.
The Gospel is the announcement that the Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus said:
“They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
— Luke 5:31–32, KJV
Do you see it?
The answer to spiritual drift is not pretending you never drifted.
It is returning to Christ.
The answer to sin is not better camouflage.
It is repentance.
The answer to shame is not hiding longer.
It is coming into the light and trusting the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
Because the same Bible that warns about hardened hearts also tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9, KJV
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are Gospel words.
Your sin is serious.
But Christ is not a weak Savior.
Your drift matters.
But you are not being told to repair yourself sufficiently before approaching Him.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Confess what you have been protecting.
Put down what you have been excusing.
Open the Scriptures you have been avoiding.
Pray the prayer you keep postponing.
Forgive the person whose name makes your chest tighten.
Ask forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Not because these actions purchase salvation.
They cannot.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
But grace does not make sin precious.
Grace teaches us to leave it.
Jesus did not endure the cross so we could become comfortable in the chains He came to break.
At Calvary, sin was not treated as a minor inconvenience.
Christ bore our sins.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The righteous for the unrighteous, that He might bring us to God.
And then the grave did not get the final word.
Jesus rose.
That means your story does not have to end where your compromise left you.
Your worst chapter does not have authority over the Author.
Your secret does not outrank His mercy.
Your shame does not have more power than His blood.
Your wandering does not make repentance meaningless.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples fled.
Paul once persecuted the church of Christ.
Scripture is filled with human wreckage interrupted by divine mercy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But notice what grace does not say.
Grace does not say:
“Keep sleeping.”
Grace says:
“Wake up.”
Grace does not whisper:
“Stay exactly where sin left you.”
Grace calls:
“Come.”
And maybe the word your soul needs most right now is the word Hebrews already gave you.
Today.
Today, pray.
Even if you feel nothing.
Today, confess.
Even if your pride screams.
Today, forgive.
Even if your emotions have not caught up.
Today, open your Bible.
Even if you only manage a few verses.
Today, turn away from what you know is pulling you from Christ.
Today, stop negotiating with the thing God has already convicted you about.
Today, tell another believer that you are struggling.
Today, come home.
Because nobody knows how many tomorrows they have.
And there is something else you need to hear.
Do not turn this article into another moment of conviction that disappears beneath your thumb.
If this exposed something hidden in you, be honest.
Not because typing words earns grace.
It doesn't.
But sometimes bringing what is hidden into the light begins with finally refusing to pretend.
And read the comments too.
Someone underneath this article may need to discover that they are not the only believer who has struggled.
Encourage them.
Pray for them.
Remind them of Christ.
Hebrews did not merely warn us against hardened hearts. It told us to exhort one another daily.
So do that.
And think of one person while you are reading this.
The friend who has slowly disappeared from church.
The son who says he still believes but wants nothing to do with God right now.
The daughter carrying shame nobody sees.
The husband silently drifting.
The wife spiritually exhausted.
The believer who still smiles on Sunday but has been losing the battle privately.
The skeptic who assumes Christianity has nothing to say to broken people.
The Christian whose faith has slowly become an accessory instead of a consuming allegiance to Christ.
Send this to them.
Let your timeline carry something eternal.
If the Gospel has given you life, use whatever reach God has placed in your hands to point people toward Jesus.
Sharing cannot save anyone.
Buying Christian products cannot save anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But believers can use their time, resources, voices, platforms, and generosity to help biblical truth travel farther.
Not to purchase God's favor.
Not to prove your Christianity.
Not because God needs your money.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him, and one expression of that surrender can be generously supporting faithful Gospel work when we are able.
And there is more available even without paying.
Not because every sentence is unforgettable.
And when it does, come back and remember Hebrews:
“...while it is called To day...”
And before you leave...
ask yourself the question you may have avoided through this entire article.
What have I been telling Jesus I will surrender tomorrow?
Name it.
Bring it into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Run toward Christ.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be that you openly screamed “No” at Jesus.
Perhaps it would be that you whispered “tomorrow” so many times that eventually your heart stopped trembling when He called.
But if you can still hear Him...
if His Word is still cutting through the noise...
if conviction is disturbing your comfortable distance...
do not waste that moment.
Today.
Come back today.
Because the heart that keeps saying “tomorrow” may one day forget why it ever wanted Jesus today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: God Drew a Line Through This Family: Why Scripture Forbade a Man From Taking Both a Woman and Her Mother
paragraphs: God Drew a Line Through This Family: Why Scripture Forbade a Man From Taking Both a Woman and Her Mother

There is something disturbing buried inside Israel’s sexual laws—and when you understand why God called it זִמָּה, “depravity,” you begin to see that this ancient command was never merely about an ancient household. It exposes what happens whenever human desire decides that another person's sacred boundaries no longer matter.
There are verses in the Bible people hurry past.
Not because they are boring.
Because they are uncomfortable.
Leviticus 18:17 is one of them.
And before we go any further, we need to correct something that is often repeated incorrectly.
The prohibition we are examining is not actually stated in Deuteronomy as the command forbidding a man from taking both a woman and her mother.
The explicit prohibition appears in Leviticus.
That matters.
Because if we are going to defend Scripture, preach Scripture, share Scripture, or build our lives upon Scripture, we must love God's Word enough to let it correct even our headlines.
The Hebrew text says:
“עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה ... שַׁאֲרָה הֵנָּה זִמָּה הִוא”
‘Ervat ishah u-vittah lo tegalleh ... she'erah hennah, zimmah hi.

In context, the command forbids uncovering the nakedness of a woman and her daughter and extends the boundary to close descendants. They are near kin. The text concludes with two chilling Hebrew words:
זִמָּה הִוא — zimmah hi.
“It is depravity.”
That final word matters.
Zimmah.
Not romance.
Not merely an unconventional family arrangement.
Not desire that somehow became inconvenient.
God names what human appetite would rather rename.
And that may be where this ancient passage suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because sin has always been talented at changing vocabulary.
What God calls greed, we can call ambition.
What God calls pride, we can call self-confidence.
What God calls lust, we can call chemistry.
What God calls adultery, a culture can call following your heart.
What God calls darkness, the human heart keeps searching for softer words to describe.
But Scripture refuses to flatter us into destruction.
Sometimes grace begins when God finally calls something what it really is.

Leviticus 18 places boundaries around sexual relationships inside the family and community. The prohibition concerning a woman and her daughter belongs to that larger collection of boundaries. Later, Leviticus 20:14 addresses the specific case of a man taking a woman and her mother and again uses the word zimmah.
That repetition is significant.
This was not merely about two women competing for one man's affection.
Something deeper was being violated.
Kinship itself was being violated.
The family was not supposed to become a hunting ground for appetite.
Think about the emotional reality behind the command.
A woman should not have to wonder whether the man joined to her is secretly looking at her daughter.
A daughter should not become her mother's sexual rival.
A mother should not become her daughter's rival.
Family affection should not be poisoned by predatory comparison.
The household should not become a place where everybody wonders who will become the next object of someone's desire.
God drew a boundary.
And boundaries are not always evidence that God wants to deprive human beings.
Sometimes boundaries are evidence that God sees exactly what human beings can do to one another when desire becomes sovereign.
That distinction matters.
Because our age frequently treats desire as though desire itself creates moral permission.
“I want this.”
“I feel this.”
“This makes me happy.”
“This feels authentic.”
And somewhere along the way, desire quietly moves from witness to judge.
But the Bible repeatedly asks a harder question.
Not merely, “What do I want?”
But:
“What does God call holy?”
That question reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
It reaches into bedrooms.
Phones.
Private messages.
Secret browser histories.
Workplace flirtations.
Emotional affairs.
Pornography.
Hidden relationships.
Relationships we know require somebody else's devastation before they can become ours.
It reaches the place where almost every serious temptation eventually takes us:
“I know where the boundary is...
but I want what is on the other side.”
That is why this strange Old Testament command can suddenly become a mirror.
Maybe you have never desired a woman and her mother.
Maybe the literal scenario feels impossibly distant from your life.
But perhaps you know what it means to negotiate with a boundary.
Perhaps you know what it is to keep a conversation alive because you enjoy being wanted.
Perhaps you deleted messages because you knew what they would look like in daylight.
Perhaps you kept telling yourself, “Nothing has happened.”
Yet.
Perhaps you have watched pornography while convincing everyone around you that your spiritual life was healthy.
Perhaps you have crossed boundaries nobody knows about.
Perhaps you became emotionally attached to somebody else's spouse.
Perhaps you are the spouse who discovered it.
Perhaps you were the child who watched adult desire rip a household apart.
Perhaps you are carrying shame from something you did years ago and still believe that if Christians knew the whole story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Now the passage is no longer ancient.
Now it has your heartbeat.
Because the deepest issue was never merely that one particular arrangement was prohibited.
The deeper issue is what happens when desire refuses to kneel.
Sin whispers:
Take.
God says:
Trust Me.
Sin says:
You deserve this.
God says:
Do not destroy what I have called you to protect.
Sin says:
Nobody will know.
God says:
I already do.
And perhaps that sentence hurts.
Because He knows.
The messages.
The fantasies.
The betrayal.
The affair.
The secret relationship.
The compromise.
The years you wasted.
The people you wounded.
The things you watched.
The person you used.
The marriage you damaged.
The promise you broke.
The version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
He knows.
And now we arrive at the moment where Christianity becomes either unbearably terrifying...
or unimaginably beautiful.
Because the God who knows is also the God who came looking for sinners.
The Bible does not end at Leviticus.
The story keeps moving.
Through sacrifice.
Through covenant.
Through failure.
Through prophets crying for repentance.
Through kings who fell.
Through adulterers.
Liars.
Cowards.
Religious hypocrites.
Broken families.
Scandal after scandal after scandal.
Until eventually...
Jesus Christ walks into the story.
And suddenly holiness has a face.
The One who never crossed God's boundaries walked among people who had shattered them.
He did not redefine sin to make sinners comfortable.
And He did not refuse sinners because their history was filthy.
That combination is the breathtaking scandal of grace.
Jesus could say, in effect:
What you did was sin.
And still say:
Come to Me.
The Gospel does not rescue us by pretending darkness is light.
Jesus rescues us by entering our darkness and bringing us into His light.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace finally makes us brave enough to stop running.
The New Testament word often associated with repentance is the Greek μετάνοια — metanoia.
It speaks of a profound turning—a changed mind and orientation that bears fruit in a changed life.
Not:
“I am sorry I got caught.”
Not:
“I will hide it better.”
Not:
“Everybody makes mistakes.”
But:
“Jesus, I was wrong.
You were right.
Have mercy on me.
Change me.”
And Christ receives repentant sinners.
That is not sentimental Christianity.
That is Christianity.
At the cross, Jesus does something astonishing with scandal.
He does not excuse it.
He bears sin's judgment.
He does not announce that holiness no longer matters.
He demonstrates how much it matters.
He does not tell humanity that rebellion was harmless.
The cross tells us precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption cost blood.
And God's love is so staggering that Christ willingly gave His.
This is why the Gospel is more powerful than shame.
Shame says:
“Hide.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
Shame says:
“You are only what you did.”
Jesus offers a new identity to those who belong to Him.
Shame says:
“Your story is finished.”
The risen Christ says otherwise.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not because scandal becomes acceptable.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes the sexually broken and teaches purity.
He takes adulterers and teaches faithfulness.
He takes liars and teaches truth.
He takes the proud and teaches surrender.
He takes the ashamed and clothes them with grace.
He takes people who thought their secret would be the final chapter...
and begins writing something new.
Maybe this article found you while you are still hiding.
Then stop reading for a moment.
Not because God is finished with you.
Because maybe you are finally ready to stop pretending.
You do not need better camouflage.
You need Christ.
You do not need to become skilled at appearing holy.
You need the Holy One.
You do not need another promise whispered to yourself at 2:00 in the morning that you will “never do it again.”
You need repentance.
Grace.
Accountability.
Truth.
The Spirit of God.
And the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Bring Him what you have been hiding.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from what you know is evil.
Where appropriate and safe, seek wise Christian accountability and make righteous amends for harm you have caused.
Do not use “grace” as permission to remain inside the thing Christ is calling you out of.
Grace is not Jesus helping you decorate your prison.
Grace opens the door.
Walk out.
And if this exposed something hidden inside you, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail.
But you can stop pretending.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle behind a smile.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally confess their own struggle because you were courageous enough to admit that you need Christ too.
Not to expose them.
Not to embarrass them.
Send it because sometimes love says:
Please don't disappear into the darkness. Jesus is still calling you home.
Because biblical truth should not merely be consumed.
It should transform us.
